profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-18T11:29:25.774+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.
Input text:

p.seg: Lǎozǐ
Lǎozi,
named Zhòng'ěr,
courtesy name Bóyáng,
was a native of Qǔrén Village in Kǔ County, the state of Chǔ.
His mother conceived after sensing a great shooting star.
Though he received his vital energy naturally,
and was seen in the Lǐ family,
he still took Lǐ as his surname.
Some say
Lǎozi existed before heaven and earth.
Some say
he was the refined essence of heaven,
belonging to the category of divine spirits.
Some say
his mother carried him for seventy-two years before giving birth;
at the time of birth,
he emerged by splitting open his mother's left armpit.
He was born with white hair,
hence he was called Lǎozi (Old Master).
Some say
his mother had no husband,
and Lǎozi was the surname of her family.
Some say
Lǎozi's mother
happened to be under a plum tree when she gave birth to Lǎozi;
he could speak at birth,
pointed at the plum tree and said:
"Take this as my surname."
Some say
during the time of the Upper Three Sovereigns, he was the Mystic Central Dharma Master;
during the time of the Lower Three Sovereigns, he was the Golden Tower Imperial Lord;
during Fúxī's time, he was Yùhuázi;
during Shénnóng's time, he was Jiǔlíng Lǎozi;
during Zhùróng's time, he was Guǎngshòuzi;
during Huángdì's time, he was Guǎngchéngzi;
during Zhuānxū's time, he was Chìjīngzi;
during Dìkù's time, he was Lùtúzi;
during Yáo's time, he was Wùchéngzi;
during Shùn's time, he was Yǐnshòuzi;
during Xià Yǔ's time, he was Zhēnxíngzi;
during Yīn Tāng's time, he was Xīzézi;
during King Wén's time, he was Wényì Xiānshēng.
Another account says
he was the Archivist.
Some say
in Yuè he was Fàn Lǐ,
in Qí he was Chīyízi,
in Wú he was Táozhū Gōng.
All these are found in various texts,
but not in the orthodox scriptures of the immortals.
They cannot be relied upon.
Gě Zhìchuān said:
"I, Hóng, believe that if Lǎozi were the essence-spirit of heaven,
he should appear in every age.
Stooping from the honorable to the humble,
abandoning ease for toil.
Turning his back on clarity and purity to enter foul turbidity,
forsaking celestial office to accept human ranks.
Where there is heaven and earth, there is the art of the Way;
those skilled in the art of the Way
are never lacking at any time.
Thus from Fúxī onward,
down to the Three Dynasties,
those renowned for the art of the Way
have existed in every generation;
why must it always be the same Lǎozi?
It is all due to later scholars,
fond of the strange and admiring the extraordinary,
who arbitrarily wish to exalt Lǎozi,
hence these claims.
In truth,
Lǎozi is one who attained the Way with exceptional refinement,
not a different kind of being."
According to the Records of the Grand Historian:
Lǎozi's son was named Zōng,
served
Míng Dynasty, Wújùn Shěn family, Yězhúzhāi manuscript;
Qīng Dynasty, Chén Zhì collated edition;
"served" written as "served as an official".
in Wèi as a general,
achieved merit,
and was enfeoffed at Duàn.
Down to Zōng's son Wāng, Wāng's son Yán, and Yán's great-great-grandson Xiá,
they served as officials in Hàn.
Xiá's son Jiě
was Grand Tutor to the Prince of Jiāoxī,
and his family settled in Qí.
Thus, Lǎozi was originally a divine
. Sòng Dynasty Jiǎ Xiáng's Preface to the Yóulóng Zhuàn states:
"Lǎozi was originally also a human spirit;
the character 'divine' is likely erroneous.
A spirit, that is all.
Shallow-minded Daoist priests,
wishing to make Lǎozi out as divine and extraordinary,
so that later scholars would follow him,
do not realize that this instead makes people disbelieve that longevity can be attained through cultivation.
Why?
If one says Lǎozi is one who attained the Way,
then people will surely strive and compete to emulate him;
if one says he is a divine spirit, a different kind of being,
then he cannot be emulated."
Some say:
Lǎozi wished to cross the pass westward,
and the Pass Official Yǐn Xǐ, knowing he was no ordinary man,
followed him to inquire about the Way.
Lǎozi, astonished,
stuck out his tongue, which was long and pendulous,
hence he acquired the appellation Lǎo Dān.
This is also not so.
Now, according to the Jiǔ Biàn and the Yuánshēng Shí'èr Huà Jīng,
before Lǎozi entered the pass,
he was already named Dān.
Lǎozi changed his name several times,
and Dān was not the only one.
The reason for this,
according to the Jiǔ Gōng, the Sānwǔ Jīng, and the Yuánchén Jīng, is:
in each person's life there are periods of calamity,
and when that time arrives,
if one changes one's name,
to follow the transformations of the primordial energy,
then one can prolong life and pass through the calamity.
In the present age, those who have attained the Way
also often do this.
Lǎozi was in Zhōu
for over three hundred years;
within these two hundred years,
there must have been not just one period of calamity,
hence his names gradually became numerous.
To correctly determine Lǎozi's origins and end,
one should primarily rely on the factual records of historical texts,
along with the Lǎo
Tàipíng Yùlǎn 659,
quoting the Shénxiān Zhuàn without the character 'Lǎo'.
secret texts of the immortal scriptures,
for mutual verification and examination.
Other accounts, like popular tales,
are mostly false and unreliable.
I, Hóng, consulted the Xī Shēng Zhōng Tāi, the Fùmìng Bāo, and the Zhū Tāo Yù Jī
Míng manuscript "jī" written as "jī",
Chūxué Jì 23, Yùlǎn 363,
quoting the Shénxiān Zhuàn as "zhá".
It should be that "zhá" was mistakenly written as "jī",
then transcribed as "jī".
and the Jīn Piān Nèi Jīng,
all say:
Lǎozi had a yellow-white
Yìwén Lèijù 78, Tàipíng Yùlǎn 363 quote without the character 'white'.
complexion,
beautiful eyebrows,
broad forehead and long ears,
large eyes and sparse teeth,
square mouth and thick lips;
his forehead had three to five clear lines,
sun-corner and moon-suspension;
his nose had pure bone and double pillars,
his ears had three leak-gates;
his feet trod the two fives,
his hands held the ten patterns.
During King Wén of Zhōu's time, he was the Archivist,
and by King Wǔ of Zhōu's time, he was the Pillar-Down Historian.
People of the time, seeing his longevity,
thus called him Lǎozi.
When a person receives the mandate,
there are those who inherently possess spiritual connection and far-sightedness;
their endowed energy differs from ordinary people's,
and they are fit to be masters of the Way,
thus they can be aided by heavenly spirits,
and followed by multitudes of immortals.
Therefore, the methods he promulgated for transcending the world—
the nine elixirs and eight minerals,
golden sweet wine and golden liquid;
next, preserving the mysterious and plain, guarding the One,
contemplating spirits and traversing the viscera,
circulating energy and refining the form,
dissolving disasters and warding off evil,
controlling ghosts and nurturing nature,
abstaining from grains and transforming,
subduing and teaching precepts,
methods for employing ghosts and spirits—
in all nine hundred and thirty scrolls,
with seventy scrolls of talismanic writings,
are all recorded in the middle chapter of Lǎozi's origins,
and have their own catalogue.
Those not included in this number
are all later additions by Daoist priests,
privately augmented,
and not the true texts.
Lǎozi was tranquil and without desires,
devoted solely to the pursuit of longevity;
thus, though he remained in Zhōu for long,
his name and position did not change,
for he wished to blend his light with the dust.
Internally, he was truly natural;
when his Way was accomplished, he departed—
indeed, he was an immortal.
Confucius once went to inquire about rites,
first sending Zǐgòng to observe.
When Zǐgòng arrived,
Lǎozi told him:
"Your teacher is named Qiū,
Mùgōng,
also known as Dōngwángfù,
also called Dōngwánggōng.
He is the primordial qi of Qīngyáng,
preceding all things.
He wears a crown of three dimensions,
and robes of nine-colored clouds and mists,
also titled Yùhuáng Jūn.
He resides among cloud chambers,
with purple clouds as his canopy,
and azure clouds as his walls.
Immortal youths stand in attendance,
and jade maidens scatter fragrance.
True officials and immortal officers,
numbering in the hundreds of millions,
each have their duties,
all receiving his commands,
and attending court to support and guard him.
Thus, men and women who attain the Dao
have their names registered under his jurisdiction.
In the early Han dynasty,
a child sang on the road:
"Wearing a blue skirt,
enter the heavenly gate,
bow to Jīnmǔ,
and pay homage to Mùgōng."
People at the time did not understand,
only Zhāng Zǐfáng knew.
He then bowed twice and said:
"This is the jade youth of Dōngwánggōng.
It means that when mortals ascend to immortality,
they all bow to Jīnmǔ and pay homage to Mùgōng."
Some say
he dwells in the eastern extremity's vast wilderness
"Wilderness" originally written as "reed,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
Within,
there is a mountain,
with rooms made of green jade,
several li deep and wide.
Officials and true immortals often visit to pay respects,
Jiǔlíng Jīnmǔ
"Mǔ" originally written as "dān,"
changed according to the entry on Líshān Mǔ in chapter 63 of this book.
visits his palace twice a year,
together they review and determine the ranks and merits of male and female true immortals,
promoting or demoting them,
overseeing their conduct records,
and reporting to Yuánshǐ,
while informing Yùchén,
to receive commands from Lǎojūn.
The kalpas of heaven and earth,
the alternation of yin and yang,
the rise and fall of fortunes,
the cycles of yang nine and hundred six,
the promotion of good and demotion of evil,
all are governed by him.
Sometimes with a jade maiden,
he plays a game of pitch-pot.
Each time he throws,
one throw yields ten
Shuōfú vol. 7 cites "ten" as "thousand."
two hundred xiao.
If there is an entry that does not come out,
heaven laughs
pronounced hū jiān qiè
with a chuckle
hū jiān means opening the mouth to laugh
If the xiao misses and fails to connect,
heaven scoffs at it.
Scholars record and detail this.
The term "wáng"
is an honorific title of supreme nobility,
not his clan name.
People take Wángfù and Wángmǔ as surnames,
which is also a mistake.
From Xiānzhuàn Shíyí.
Ming manuscript reads Shénxiān Zhuàn Shíyí.
Guǎngchéngzǐ
Guǎngchéngzǐ
is an immortal of ancient times.
He dwells in the mountains of Kōngtóng,
within a stone chamber.
Huángdì heard of him and visited,
saying:
"I dare ask about the essence of the supreme Dao."
Guǎngchéngzǐ replied:
"You govern the world,
birds fly without waiting for the season,
grass and trees wither before turning yellow,
how can you be worthy to speak of the supreme Dao?"
Huángdì withdrew and lived in seclusion for three months,
then went to see him again,
approaching on his knees.
Bowing twice, he inquired about the way to cultivate the body.
Guǎngchéngzǐ answered:
"The essence of the supreme Dao,
is profound and obscure,
with no sight, no hearing.
Embrace the spirit in stillness,
and the form will naturally be upright.
You must be pure and clear,
do not toil your body,
do not disturb your essence,
then you may attain longevity.
Guard the inner and close off the outer,
excessive knowledge brings ruin.
I hold fast to the One,
abiding in harmony,
thus for twelve hundred years,
my form has not decayed.
Those who attain my Dao become sovereigns above,
those who lose my Dao become dust below.
I shall leave you and enter the gate of infinity,
wandering in the fields of boundlessness,
sharing light with the sun and moon,
and enduring with heaven and earth.
All men will die,
but I alone remain."
From Shénxiān Zhuàn.
Huáng'ān,
a man of Dàijùn.
He served as a soldier in Dàijùn,
said to be lowly and unremarkable,
holding a whip among men.
Carrying thorns
Ming manuscript and Chén collated edition read "carry" as "embrace."
The character "yǐ" follows "thorns."
he read books,
drawing on the ground to keep count,
one night the ground became a pond.
People of the time said Ān plowed with his tongue.
Aged around eighty,
he appeared robust like a child.
He often consumed cinnabar,
his entire body red,
and wore no clothes in winter.
He sat on a turtle,
three chi wide and long.
When people asked how old this turtle was,
he said:
"When Fúxī first made nets,
he caught this turtle and gave it to me.
The turtle's back is already flat.
This creature fears the light of the sun and moon,
emerging once every two thousand years.
Since my birth,
this creature has emerged five times."
When walking, he carried the turtle and hurried along,
people called Ān 'Ten Thousand Years.'
From Dòngmíng Jì.
Mèng Qí,
a recluse of Qīnghé
"Qīng" originally written as "qīng."
Changed according to the Ming manuscript and Chén collated edition.
A recluse of Qīnghé,
aged around seven hundred.
When speaking of early Zhōu events,
he recalled them clearly as if before his eyes.
Qí once attended Zhōugōng ascending the altar,
Qí rubbed King Chéng's feet with his hand.
Zhōugōng gave him a jade tablet,
which Qí always treasured and held,
often wiping it with his sleeve.
The tablet was seven fen thick,
now worn thin and about to break.
He constantly consumed cassia leaves,
and hearing that Hàn Wǔdì favored immortals,
he parted the grasses
Ming manuscript reads "grasses" as "cover."
Same as in Dòngmíng Jì.
and came forth.
Wǔdì treated him generously.
Later, his whereabouts became unknown.
From Dòngmíng Jì.
Zhōu Mùwáng
King Mù of Zhōu, named Mǎn,
was born of Queen Fáng,
and was the son of King Zhāo.
King Zhāo went on an inspection tour to the south and never returned,
so King Mù ascended the throne,
at the age of fifty.
He reigned for fifty-four years,
living to the age of one hundred and four.
From a young age, the king was fond of the ways of immortals and divine beings,
and often wished to have the tracks of his chariots and horses
cover the entire world,
in emulation of the Yellow Emperor.
Thus, he rode in a chariot drawn by eight magnificent steeds,
traveled to the Róng region,
and had Zàofǔ serve as his charioteer.
He obtained a white fox and a black raccoon dog,
which he offered in sacrifice at the Hézōng.
Guiding his chariot across the Ruòshuǐ River,
fish, turtles, giant softshell turtles, and crocodiles formed a bridge for him.
He then ascended Chōng
"Chōng" originally written as "Chūn".
Corrected based on the Ming manuscript.
Mountain,
and again feasted with the Queen Mother of the West on the Yáochí Lake.
The Queen Mother sang a song:
"White clouds drift in the sky,
the road is long and far.
Mountains and rivers lie between us,
but if you do not die,
you may yet return."
The king replied:
"I shall return to the eastern lands,
bring harmony to all the Xià,
and when the myriad people are at peace,
I will come to see you again."
After three years,
he would return to these wilds.
He then reached Léishǒu and Tàiháng,
and finally entered the ancestral capital of Zhōu.
At that time, Yǐn Xǐ had already crossed the Liúshā Desert and dwelled in a thatched hut on the northern side of Zhōngnán Mountain.
The king traced his former tracks,
summoned the recluses Yǐn Zhé and Dù Chōng,
and settled them in the thatched hut,
hence naming it Lóuguàn.
He followed and visited them there.
The character "yān" was originally missing.
Added based on the Ming manuscript and the Chén collated edition.
Jì Fù came from Zhèng Pǔ to pay his respects,
and admonished the king regarding the rebellion of Xú Yǎn.
The king then returned to the capital,
and the ancestral temples were restored to peace.
When the king journeyed to Kūnlún,
he drank the stone marrow of Fēng Mountain,
ate the fruit of the jade tree,
and also ascended Qúnyù Mountain,
where the Queen Mother of the West resided,
and there he attained the way of soaring into the heavens with ethereal spirit.
Yet he left traces and assumed a physical form,
likely to show the people that there is an end.
Moreover, he drank the essence of wǎnyǎn jade,
partook of the flavor of sweet snow,
ate plain lotus and black dates,
green lotus roots and white tangerines,
all of which are things of immortals and divine beings.
How could he not prolong his life and attain longevity?
It is also said
that the Queen Mother of the West descended to King Mù's palace.
Together, they ascended on clouds and departed.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shí Yí"
King Zhāo of Yān
King Zhāo of Yān
was the son of King Kuài.
In the Ming edition by Xǔ Zìchāng, "King Kuài" is written as "Kuài, the King".
When he ascended the throne,
he was fond of the ways of immortals and divine beings.
The immortal Gān Xū served him as a minister,
and recounted to the king the matters of ascending to truth at Kūntái,
advising him to abandon desires,
cast aside music and beauty,
and be without thought or action,
so that he might attain the Way.
The king practiced this for a long time,
and Gǔ Jiāngzǐ descended from the void and gathered,
announcing to the king:
"The Queen Mother of the West is about to descend,
to observe your cultivation,
and show you the essentials of the mysterious and spiritual."
One year later,
the Queen Mother indeed arrived.
She wandered with the king beneath the Suì Forest,
expounding on the techniques of Yánhuáng's fire-drilling.
They lit green cassia oil to illuminate the night,
when suddenly a flying moth carrying fire
gathered at the king's palace.
They obtained round hill sand pearls,
"sand pearls" originally written as "cinnabar".
Corrected based on the Ming manuscript and the Chén collated edition.
and strung them together to wear as pendants.
The king ascended the Ài
In the Ming manuscript, "Ài" is written as "Jué".
In the "Shí Yí Jì" cited in scroll 402 of this book, it is written as "Wò".
Sun Terrace,
and obtained the Dòngguāng Pearl carried by a divine bird,
which dispelled the oppressive heat.
From then on, the Queen Mother descended to the Yān palace three times,
but King Zhāo became engrossed in military campaigns and conquests,
unable to adhere to Gān Xū's principle of clarity and tranquility,
and the Queen Mother never came again.
Gān Xū said:
"The feast set by the Queen Mother
is not of this mortal world;
jade wine and golden nectar,
even after ten thousand sacrifices,
since the king has tasted them,
he should naturally attain the Way.
Only he must remain in emptiness, doubt, purity, and simplicity,
preserving his longevity."
Gān Xū also ascended to heaven and departed.
In the thirty-third year,
the king passed away without illness,
his body and bones soft and pliant,
and a fragrant aroma filled the courtyard.
His son, King Huì, ascended the throne.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shí Yí"
Péng Zǔ
Péng Zǔ,
surnamed Jiān, personal name Kēng,
was the great-great-grandson of Emperor Zhuānxū.
By the end of the Yīn dynasty, he was already 767 years old,
yet showed no signs of aging or decline.
From youth, he preferred tranquility and quietude,
did not concern himself with worldly affairs,
did not seek fame or reputation,
did not adorn his carriages or clothing,
but solely devoted himself to nurturing life and cultivating his person.
The king, hearing of him,
appointed him as a senior official.
He often claimed illness and lived in seclusion,
not participating in government affairs.
He excelled in the arts of supplementation and guidance,
consuming powdered water-cinnamon, mica, and powdered deer antler,
and always maintained a youthful appearance.
However, his nature was deep and reserved,
and he never claimed to possess the Way,
nor did he perform deceptive, bewildering, transformative, or ghostly feats.
Serene and non-active,
he seldom traveled about,
occasionally returning to wander alone;
no one knew where he went,
and even those who waited and watched never managed to see him.
He possessed carriages and horses but often did not ride them;
sometimes for several hundred days,
or several tens of days,
he would travel without carrying provisions or supplies,
yet upon returning home, his clothing and food were no different from others'.
He often practiced breath retention and internal breathing,
from dawn until midday,
then would sit upright, wipe his eyes,
massage his body,
lick his lips and swallow saliva,
ingest breath several tens of times,
before rising to walk, speak, and laugh.
If his body felt thin, weary, or unsettled,
he would perform guiding exercises and breath retention
to attack the ailment.
Focusing his mind within his body,
his face
(Míng manuscript adds "head" before "face")
the nine orifices,
the five viscera and four limbs,
down to the hair and skin,
he would bring all to full awareness.
He would feel the breath like clouds moving within his body,
reaching from the nose and mouth to the tips of his ten fingers,
and soon his body would become harmonious.
The king personally went to inquire and visit,
but he did not divulge [his methods].
The king sent him precious curiosities,
amounting to tens of thousands in gold over time,
all of which he accepted,
but used to relieve the poor and lowly,
keeping nothing for himself.
There was also a woman named Cǎinǚ,
who had also attained the Way in her youth,
and knew the methods of nurturing life.
At 270 years old,
she looked like someone in her fifties or sixties.
She served in the palace women's quarters,
where a magnificent house with purple pavilions was built for her,
adorned with gold and jade.
The king then ordered Cǎinǚ to ride in a curtained carriage
to go and inquire of Péng Zǔ about the Way.
Upon arrival, she bowed twice,
and asked to be instructed in methods for prolonging life and increasing longevity.
Péng Zǔ said:
"If you wish to elevate your form and ascend to heaven,
to become an immortal official above,
you must use golden elixirs.
This is what the Nine Summons
(In Dù Guāngtíng's *Yōngchéng Collection of Immortals*, scroll 6,
the entry on Cǎinǚ has "Yuánjūn" instead of "Nine Summons")
is.
Tàiyī,
is the means by which one ascends to heaven in broad daylight.
This Way is supremely great,
and not something a ruler or king can accomplish.
Next, one should cherish and nurture the essence and spirit,
and ingest medicinal herbs;
this can lead to long life.
But it does not enable one to command ghosts and spirits,
or ride the void and fly.
If one does not understand the Way of interaction between yīn and yáng,
even ingesting medicines will be of no benefit.
If one can nurture the meaning of yīn and yáng,
it can be deduced and obtained,
but it is not something to be spoken of lightly;
why bother asking about it?
I was born posthumously,
lost my mother at three,
encountered the turmoil of the Quǎnróng invasion,
wandered displaced in the Western Regions,
for over a hundred years.
Added to this, I suffered early decline,
lost forty-nine wives,
lost fifty-four sons,
repeatedly met with sorrow and hardship,
and my harmonious vitality was damaged and broken.
Cold and heat
(Míng manuscript lacks the character for "heat")
(Chén collated edition has "lìng" instead of "cold and heat")
caused my skin and flesh to lose luster,
my nutritive and defensive energies to become parched and withered,
and I feared I would not pass through the world.
What I have learned is shallow and meager,
not worth disseminating.
On Dàwǎn Mountain, there is one called Master Qīngjīng,
said to be a thousand years old,
with complexion like a child's,
walking over five hundred lǐ a day,
able to go a whole year without eating,
and also able to eat nine times in a single day;
he is truly worth questioning."
Cǎinǚ said:
"May I ask, what kind of immortal is Master Qīngjīng?"
Péng Zǔ said:
"He is one who has attained the Way,
not an immortal.
Immortals are those who
either soar into the clouds,
flying without wings;
or ride dragons and mount clouds,
ascending to the heavenly steps;
or transform into birds and beasts,
roaming and floating in the azure clouds;
or move hidden through rivers and seas,
soaring over famous mountains;
some ingest primordial breath,
some consume magic mushrooms and herbs,
some come and go among humans unrecognized,
some conceal their forms unseen.
Their faces bear extraordinary bones,
their bodies have strange hairs;
generally, they prefer deep seclusion,
and do not associate with common folk.
However, although such beings possess deathless longevity,
they are removed from human feelings,
distant from glory and pleasure;
it is as if a sparrow transforms into a clam,
or a pheasant transforms into a giant clam,
losing their original true nature,
and instead guarding a different breath.
In my foolish heart,
I do not desire this.
Entering
(Míng manuscript and Chén collated edition have "rén" instead of "rù")
the Way should involve eating sweet delicacies,
wearing light and beautiful clothes,
harmonizing yīn and yáng,
and holding official rank.
Bones and joints firm and strong,
complexion harmonious and radiant,
aged yet not declining,
prolonging years and enduring vision.
Long dwelling in the world,
cold, warmth, wind, and dampness cannot harm,
ghosts, spirits, and myriad essences dare not offend,
the five weapons and hundred insects cannot approach,

Wèi Bóyáng
Wèi Bóyáng was a man of Wú,
originally the son of a noble family,
who had a natural affinity for Daoist arts.
Later, he entered the mountains with three disciples
to refine a divine elixir.
When the elixir was completed,
knowing that his disciples’ minds were not yet fully resolved,
he tested them, saying:
“Though the elixir is ready,
it should first be tested on a dog.
If the dog flies,
then humans may take it;
if the dog dies,
it must not be consumed.”
He then fed it to a dog,
and the dog died immediately.
Bóyáng said to his disciples:
“In refining the elixir, we only feared it would not succeed;
now that it is ready, the dog dies after eating it.
I fear it may not align with the will of the divine,
and taking it might lead to the same fate as the dog.
What should we do?”
A disciple asked:
“Will you, Master, take it?”
Bóyáng replied:
“I have turned my back on worldly pursuits,
abandoned my family to enter the mountains.
If I fail to attain the Dao, I would be ashamed to return.
Whether it brings death or life,
I shall take it.”
He then consumed the elixir
and died as soon as it entered his mouth.
The disciples looked at one another and said:
“We refined the elixir to seek immortality,
yet taking it brings instant death.
What should we do about this?”
Only one disciple said:
“Our master is no ordinary man.
His death after taking this
must hold some deeper meaning.”
He then took the elixir and consumed it,
and he too died.
The remaining two disciples said to each other:
“The purpose of obtaining the elixir
was to seek longevity.
Now that taking it leads to death,
what use is it?
By not taking this medicine,
we can still live for several more decades in this world.”
Thus, they did not take it
and left the mountain together
to seek coffins for Bóyáng and the deceased disciple.
After the two had departed,
Bóyáng immediately rose,
placed the elixir he had taken into the mouths of the dead disciple and the white dog,
and both revived.
The disciple’s surname was Yú,
and they all ascended as immortals.
On the way, they encountered woodcutters entering the mountain
and sent a handwritten letter to their village,
thanking the two disciples.
Only then did the two begin to feel regret.
Bóyáng composed the Cāntóngqì Wǔxíng Xiānglèi,
in three volumes altogether.
Its discourse is based on the Zhōuyì,
but in truth, it borrows the hexagrams and symbols
to discuss the principles of elixir refinement.
Yet Confucian scholars of the world,
unaware of the matters of divine elixirs,
often annotate it in terms of yīn and yáng,
greatly missing its true intent.

“the Purple Book of Longevity,” “the Three and Five in Accordance,” “the Inner Vision and Central Methods of the Purple Degree and Blazing Light of Yin, Shen, Si, and Hai.” Without these twelve matters,

The Emperor pleaded and kowtowed incessantly.
The Queen Mother again said to the Lady:

During the time of the Qín emperor,

Xiāo Shǐ
Xiāo Shǐ’s era of attaining the Way is unknown;
he appeared like a man in his twenties.
He excelled at playing the xiāo, producing sounds like those of the luan and phoenix.
With jade-like demeanor radiant and gleaming,
and bearing transcendent and lofty,
he was truly a celestial being.
Mingling in the world,
none at the time could recognize him.
Duke Mù of Qín had a daughter named Nòngyù,
skilled at playing the xiāo.
The duke gave Nòngyù to him as wife.
Thereupon he taught Nòngyù to produce phoenix cries.
After more than ten years dwelling together,
their xiāo playing resembled phoenix calls,
and phoenixes came to rest on their house.
The duke built a Phoenix Terrace for them.
Husband and wife dwelled upon it,
neither drinking nor eating,
for several years without descending.
One morning,
Nòngyù mounted a phoenix,
Xiāo Shǐ mounted a dragon,
and ascended to heaven and departed.
Qín built a Shrine to the Phoenix Maiden for them,
where the sound of the xiāo was occasionally heard.
Now at the summit of the Western Mountains in Hóngzhōu,
there remain Xiāo Shǐ’s stone immortal altar and stone chamber,
as well as cliff dwellings and true images.
Their age is unknown.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Xú Fú,
courtesy name Jūnfáng,
his origins unknown.
During the time of Qín Shǐhuáng,
in Dàwǎn there were many wronged dead lying across the roads.
Several times birds came carrying a herb,
covering the faces of the dead,
who all immediately revived.
Officials reported this to Shǐhuáng,
who sent an envoy bearing this herb
to inquire of Master Guǐgǔ of the Northern Outskirts.
He said it was the deathless herb from Zǔzhōu in the Eastern Sea,
growing in fields of jade,
also named the Spirit-Nourishing Fungus,
its leaves resembling wild rice stems,
growing not in clusters,
and a single plant could revive a thousand people.
Shǐhuáng then thought it could be sought and obtained,
and thus dispatched Fú along with three thousand boys and three thousand girls,
riding tower ships into the sea.
They sought Zǔzhōu and did not return;
later none knew where they went.
When Shěn Xī attained the Way,
Huáng-Lǎo sent Fú as an envoy,
riding a white tiger chariot,
Dùshì Jūn Sīmǎ Shēng riding a dragon chariot,
and Attendant Láng Bó Yánzhī riding a white deer chariot,
all coming to welcome Xī and depart.
From this, later people knew Fú had attained the Way.
Also, during the Táng Kāiyuán era,
a scholar suffered from half his body being withered and blackened.
Imperial physician Zhāng Shàngróng and others could not diagnose it.
The man gathered his clan and said:
"With my body like this,
how can I last long?
I hear there are immortals in the great sea;
I should seek an immortal prescription
to cure this illness."
His clan tried to detain him but could not,
so with an attendant,
he brought provisions to the seaside at Dēngzhōu.
Encountering an empty boat,
he loaded his belongings,
hoisted sail, and went with the wind.
After sailing over ten days,
he approached a solitary island.
On the island were several hundred people,
as if in court audience.
Soon he reached shore.
On the shore a woman was washing herbs,
so he asked who all those people were.
The woman pointed and said:
"The one sitting on the central dais,
with white beard and temples,
is Lord Xú."
He asked again who Lord Xú was.
The woman said:
"Do you know Xú Fú from the time of Qín Shǐhuáng?"
He said:
"I know of him."
"This is he."
After a moment,
the crowd dispersed.
He then went ashore to pay respects,
recounted the whole story,
and sought medical treatment.
Lord Xú said:
"Your illness,
meeting me means life."
First he fed him fine rice;
the vessels were all strangely small,
and the man thought them meager.
Lord Xú said:
"If you can finish this,
you may have another serving,
but I fear you cannot finish it."
The man ate continuously,
and felt full after several bowlfuls.
And for drink, a small vessel held wine;
he drank it and became drunk.
The next day,
he was given several black pills to eat.
After eating,
he excreted several sheng of black fluid,
and his illness was cured.
He begged to stay and serve.
Lord Xú said:
"You have official rank and fortune;
it is not yet suitable to stay.
I shall send you with an east wind;
do not worry about the long journey back."
He also gave him a bag of yellow medicine,
saying:
"This medicine excels at curing all illnesses.
When you return, if you encounter the sick,
you may give them a knife-point measure to drink."
He returned,
and after several days reached Dēngchuān.
He presented the medicine to the emperor.
At that time, Xuánzōng ordered the ill to take it,
and all were cured.
From "Xiānzhuàn Shíyí" and "Guǎngyì Jì"
The Messenger of the Queen Mother of the West
In the third year of the Tiānhàn era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
the emperor toured the Eastern Sea,
sacrificed at Héngshān,
and the Queen Mother dispatched an envoy to present four liǎng of divine glue
and a fur robe made from Jíguāng horse hair.
Emperor Wǔ handed them over to the outer treasury,
unaware of the wondrous properties of these two items,
thinking that although the Western Kingdom was distant,
its tribute was not extraordinary,
and he did not send the envoy away.
When the emperor visited the Huálín Garden,
he shot at tigers and rhinoceroses,
and his crossbow string snapped.
The envoy, who was accompanying the imperial carriage at the time,
stepped forward and said,
requesting to use a portion of the glue.
He moistened the glue with his mouth
and used it to mend the crossbow string.
The emperor exclaimed in astonishment:
"This is a remarkable object!"
He then ordered several warriors
to pull on it together,
but it did not come apart all day,
proving stronger than before it was mended.
The glue was bluish-green,
like jasper.
The Jíguāng fur robe was yellow-white,
likely from a divine horse species.
The robe would not sink even after a full day in water,
nor would it burn in fire.
The emperor, now enlightened,
generously rewarded the envoy and sent him away.
The "bowstring-rejoining glue" came from Fènglín Island,
located in the Western Sea.
The island's land was square,
each side measuring fifteen hundred lǐ,
surrounded on all sides by the Ruòshuǐ River.
It was home to many phoenixes and qílín,
gathering in flocks of tens of thousands.
By boiling phoenix beaks and qílín horns together
and refining them into glue,
it was named "bowstring-rejoining glue,"
also called "metal-joining paste."
For crossbow strings that had snapped
or swords and blades that had broken,
using this glue to join them
would ensure they never came apart again.
From "Xiānzhuàn Shíyí."
The Yuèzhī Envoy
In the spring of the third year of the Yánhé era of Hàn,
Emperor Wǔ visited Āndìng.
The king of the Western Hú Yuèzhī Kingdom
sent an envoy to present four liǎng of incense,
as large as sparrow eggs,
and black like mulberries.
The emperor, thinking incense was not scarce in the Middle Kingdom,
handed it over to the outer treasury.
They also presented a fierce beast,
shaped like a puppy fifty or sixty days old,
as big as a wildcat,
with yellowish fur.
When the kingdom's envoy brought it before the emperor,
the emperor saw the envoy carrying it in his arms.
It looked scruffy and unimpressive,
making the emperor even more suspicious of the tribute's worth.
He asked the envoy:
"This tiny creature—
how can it be called a fierce beast?"
The envoy replied:
"What overpowers all creatures
need not be judged by size.
Thus, the divine qílín is king of the giant elephant,
and the phoenix is sovereign of the great roc—
their status does not depend on size.
My kingdom is three hundred thousand lǐ from here.
We have long observed the east wind harmonizing with the pitch pipes,
lasting a hundred days without cease;
azure clouds aligning with the musical tones,
lingering for months without dispersing.
This signified that the Middle Kingdom would have a ruler devoted to the Way.
Our king, looking up to the Central Land and admiring its Daoist ethos,
valued spiritual treasures over gold and jade.
Thus, he sought rare wonders and searched for divine incense,
traversed celestial forests to request this fierce beast,
rode sturdy carriages to cross the Ruòshuǐ River,
and urged swift steeds to traverse the flying sands.
Through arduous paths
and rugged trails,
the journey has taken thirteen years to this day.
The divine incense wards off untimely deaths from plagues,
and the fierce beast repels all evil spirits and demons.
These two objects
are truly essential for saving the multitudes,
aiding supreme transformation and bringing peace.
How could we have imagined that Your Majesty
would fail to recognize their value!
This must be an error in our kingdom's wind divination.
Now, upon beholding Your Majesty's celestial countenance,
I see you are not a ruler devoted to the Way.
Eyes that look too much reveal greed and indulgence;
a mouth that speaks too much invites trouble and conflict;
a body that moves too much attracts bandits and calamity;
a heart with too many desires leads to extravagance and waste.
Never has one who embodied these 'four excesses'
achieved orderly rule over the realm."
The emperor fell silent, displeased.
He then ordered the envoy to command the beast to roar,
so he could hear it.
The envoy pointed at the beast
and ordered it to utter a cry.
The beast licked its lips for a long while,
then suddenly let out a sound like a thunderclap.
It roared again,
its eyes flashing like lightning,
and only after a long time did it stop.
The emperor was instantly thrown to the ground,
covering his ears, shaken,
unable
("able" originally written as "rán,"
emended based on the Ming manuscript and Chén's collated edition)
to stop himself.
Attendants and
("and" originally written as "nǎi,"
emended based on the Ming manuscript
and Chén's collated edition)
guards all dropped their staffs.
The emperor, resentful of this,
had the beast sent to the Shànglín Garden,

they all gathered and crouched in fear.
The emperor, angered by the envoy's disrespectful words,
wished to punish him.
The next day,
both the envoy and the fierce beast had vanished.
In the first year of the Shǐyuán era,
a great plague struck the capital,
killing more than half the population.
The emperor took the Yuèzhī divine incense and burned it within the city,
and all who had died within the past three days revived.
The fragrance lingered for three months without fading.
Convinced of the incense's divinity,
the emperor secretly recorded the remaining incense.
But one day, when he opened the case to inspect it,
the divine incense was gone.
This incense came from Rénniǎo Mountain on Jùkū Island.
The mountain was densely forested,
with trees resembling maples,
whose fragrance could be smelled for several lǐ.
They were called "soul-returning trees."
They could also produce sounds on their own,
like the bellowing of a herd of cattle,
terrifying to hear.
Chopping down their roots
and boiling the sap in a jade cauldron,
then simmering it over a gentle fire
until it formed black pellets,
which could be rolled into pills,
it was named "spirit-startling incense,"
or "soul-rousing pills,"
or "life-returning incense,"
or "sandalwood-rousing incense,"
or "death-repelling incense"—
one substance with six names.
Truly, it was a spiritual marvel.
From "Xiānzhuàn Shíyí."
Wèi Shūqīng
Wáng Cìzhòng was
an immortal of ancient times.
During the late Zhōu dynasty in the Warring States period,
amidst the alliances and strategies of the time,
he resided on Dàxià and Xiǎoxià mountains.
Considering the seal script of the world,
laborious yet of limited use,
difficult to produce quickly,
and with the four seas beset by troubles,
writing tools were of foremost importance.
He thus transformed the forms of seal and large seal script into clerical script.
After Qín Shǐhuáng had unified the world,
because its utility benefited people,
he summoned him to Qín,
but he did not come.
He again ordered an envoy to summon him,
commanding the envoy, saying:
"I have conquered the six directions,
unified the world under one rule,
who dares not submit!
Cìzhòng is but a scholar who defies the Son of Heaven's command;
if he does not rise,
you should kill him,
bring his head back,
to rectify customs,
and not let his insolence run rampant."
The imperial envoy arrived at the mountain to deliver the order,
Cìzhòng transformed into a great bird,
flapped its wings and flew away.
The envoy, astonished, bowed and said:
"I have nothing with which to report back,
and fear I will also be killed,
I beg the divine one to take pity."
The bird hovered in the air,
and deliberately dropped three flight feathers.
The envoy obtained them and presented them.
Shǐhuáng had always been fond of the ways of immortals,
hearing of this transformation,
he felt considerable regret.
Now it is called Luòhé Mountain,
located within Yōuzhōu's borders,
where the local villages offer continuous sacrifices.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Mòzǐ
Mòzǐ,
named Dí,
was a man of Sòng,
served Sòng as a senior official.
Externally he studied the classics,
internally he cultivated the arts of the Way,
authored ten books,
and was called Mòzǐ.
Many in the world studied under him,
forming a separate school from the Ruists,
advocating frugality and simplicity,
and often criticized Confucius.
There was a Gōngshū Bān,
who built cloud-ladder machines for Chǔ to attack Sòng.
Mòzǐ heard of this,
and went to Chǔ.
His feet were injured,
he tore his robes to wrap them,
and arrived after seven days and seven nights.
He met Gōngshū Bān and persuaded him, saying:
"You make cloud-ladders to attack Sòng,
what crime has Sòng committed?
To have excess land but insufficient people,
to kill what is insufficient to contend for what is in excess,
cannot be called wise;
to attack Sòng which is without crime,
cannot be called benevolent;
to know yet not contend,
cannot be called loyal;
to contend yet not succeed,
cannot be called strong."
Gōngshū Bān said:
"I cannot stop,
I have already spoken to the king."
Mòzǐ saw the king and said:
"Suppose now there is a man,
who abandons his ornate carriage,
and desires to steal his neighbor's broken cart;
abandons his brocade and embroidery,
and desires to steal his neighbor's short coarse cloth;
abandons his fine grain and meat,
and desires to steal his neighbor's dregs and husks,
what kind of man is this?"
The king said:
"If so,
he must be afflicted with madness."
Dí said:
"Chǔ has the deer of Yúnmèng,
the fish and turtles of Jiāng and Hàn,
being the wealth of the world,
while Sòng lacks pheasants, rabbits, and bream,
this is like fine grain and meat versus dregs and husks.
Chǔ has qǐ, zǐ, and yùzhāng trees,
Sòng lacks trees of several zhàng,
this is like brocade and embroidery versus short coarse cloth.
I have heard Your Majesty further deliberates attacking Sòng,
it is the same as this."
The king said:
"Well said,
however, Gōngshū Bān has already made the cloud-ladders,
and says we must take Sòng."
Thereupon he met Gōngshū Bān.
Mòzǐ loosened his belt to form a city wall,
used his headcloth as machines,
Gōngshū Bān then set up his siege mechanisms.
Nine changes and Mòzǐ repelled him nine times,
Gōngshū's siege machines were exhausted,
while Mòzǐ's defense still had surplus.
Gōngshū Bān said:
"I know how to attack you,
but I will not say."
Mòzǐ said:
"I know how you would attack me,
I also will not say."
The king asked the reason:
Mòzǐ said:
"Gōngshū's intention,
is merely to kill me,
thinking Sòng then cannot defend.
However, my disciples Qíngǔlí and three hundred others,
have long since taken up my defensive weapons,
and await the Chǔ invaders on Sòng's walls,
even if you kill me,
you cannot stop them."
Chǔ then desisted,
and did not attack Sòng again.
Mòzǐ, at eighty-two years of age,
sighed and said:
"The affairs of the world are already knowable,
glory and position cannot be kept forever,
I shall cast aside worldly customs,
to follow Chìsōngzǐ in wandering."
He then entered Zhōu Dí Mountain,
concentrated his thoughts on the methods of the Way,
and visualized the immortals.
Then he repeatedly heard from the surrounding mountain valleys,
the sound of someone reciting texts.
After Mòzǐ lay down,
someone came again,
and covered his feet with clothing.
Mòzǐ then lay in wait,
suddenly saw a person,
rose and asked him, saying:
"Are you not the numinous energy of the mountain,
or perhaps an immortal transcending the world?
I beg you to stay a while,
and instruct me in the essentials of the Way."
The divine person said:
"Knowing you have the will and love for the Way,
I have come to wait upon you.
What do you seek?"
Mòzǐ said:
"I wish to obtain long life,
lasting as long as heaven and earth."
Thereupon the divine person bestowed upon him a plain text,
the formula for Zhūyīng pills,
teachings and precepts of the Way's numinosity,
the transformations of the Five Phases,
altogether twenty-five chapters,
and told Mòzǐ:
"You have the bone structure for immortality,
and are intelligent,
obtaining this you will succeed,
no longer needing a teacher."
Mòzǐ bowed, received, compounded, and practiced,
and thereby obtained its efficacy,
then compiled and collected its essentials,
making the "Wǔxíng Jì".
He thus attained terrestrial immortality,
lived in seclusion to avoid the Warring States.
By the time of Hàn Wǔdì,
he dispatched envoy Yáng Wéi,
with bundles of silk and added jade discs,
to invite Mòzǐ,
but Mòzǐ did not emerge.
Observing his complexion,
it was often like that of a man around fifty.
He traveled around the Five Sacred Mountains,
not staying in one place.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn"
Liú Zhèng
Liú Zhèng was a man from
Pèi.
He possessed exceptional talent and extensive knowledge,
having studied all fields of learning.
He believed that worldly glory and wealth
were but fleeting moments,
and that it was better to study the Way,
through which one could attain longevity.
Thus, he abandoned the path of seeking advancement,
and pursued the arts of nurturing life.
He diligently sought out extraordinary knowledge,
traveling thousands of miles without regard for distance.
If he encountered anyone superior to himself,
he would treat them as a teacher, even if they were servants or retainers.
He also practiced the Five Elements Records of Mòzǐ,
and took the Zhūyīng pills,
living to over 180 years of age
with a complexion like that of a child.
He could transform and conceal his form,
dividing one person into a hundred,
a hundred into a thousand,
and a thousand into ten thousand.
He could also conceal an entire army,
turning them into a grove of trees,
or into birds and beasts.
He could take objects belonging to others,
move them to different places,
without anyone noticing.
He could also plant five types of fruit trees,
making them instantly blossom and bear edible fruit.
He could summon a traveling kitchen while seated,
providing meals for hundreds of people.
He could blow air to create wind,
lifting sand and stones into the air.
By pointing at buildings, mountains, or vessels,
he could cause them to crumble;
pointing again,
they would return to their original state.
He could also transform into the shape of a beautiful woman,
and create fire and water.
He could travel thousands of miles
in a single day.
He could exhale water to summon clouds,
raise his hands to create mist,
pile earth to form mountains,
and pierce the ground to create abysses.
He could suddenly age or rejuvenate,
grow large or shrink small.
He could enter water without getting wet,
walk on its surface,
and summon fish, turtles, flood dragons, and giant turtles from rivers and seas,
causing them to come ashore.
He could also exhale five-colored qi,
covering an area of ten square li,
rising straight up to connect with the sky,
and he could leap upward,
descending hundreds of zhang from the ground.
Later, he departed, and no one knew where he went.
From Biographies of the Divine Immortals.
Sūn Bó
Sūn Bó was a man from
Hédōng.
He possessed refined talent,
was skilled in writing,
and authored over a hundred books,
reciting hundreds of thousands of words of scriptures.
In his later years, he became fond of the Way,
practicing the arts of Mòzǐ.
He could make plants, trees, metals, and stones all turn into fire,
illuminating an area of several li;
he could also turn his own body into fire,
spitting flames from his mouth.
Pointing at a large tree or grass would cause it to wither and burn,
and pointing again would restore it to its original state.
Once, someone’s runaway servant
was hiding in an army camp,
and they could not capture him.
Sūn Bó said to the servant’s master:
"I will burn down the camp buildings for you,
and the servant will surely run out.
You just need to watch carefully and seize him."
Thereupon, Sūn Bó took a red pellet
and threw it at the camp gate.
In an instant, a fire broke out, illuminating the sky,
and the servant indeed ran out,
allowing him to be captured.
Sūn Bó then took a blue pellet and threw it,
and the fire immediately extinguished,
with the buildings and all objects
returning to their original state, undamaged.
Whenever Sūn Bó created a fire to burn something,
others would try to extinguish it with water,
but it could never be put out.
Only when he stopped it himself after a while
would the fire cease.
He could walk through fire and water without being burned or wet,
and could also lead hundreds or thousands of people to follow him through,
all remaining unharmed.
He could also go with others onto water,
spread a mat and sit,
eat, drink, and make merry,
and have crowds dance on the water.
Moreover, in the stone cliffs of the mountains
or the boulders on the ground,
Sūn Bó could enter them,
gradually revealing his back and both ears,
until after a long while, he completely disappeared.
He could also swallow thousands of swords,
and pass through walls
as if through holes.
He could turn a mirror into a knife,
or bend a knife into a mirror,
and it would remain unchanged for a long time.
Only when Sūn Bó pointed at it
would it return to its original form.
Later, he entered Línlǜ Mountain,
took the divine elixir, and ascended as an immortal.
From Biographies of the Divine Immortals.
Tiānménzǐ
Tiānménzǐ,
whose surname was Wáng and given name Gāng,
was particularly knowledgeable about the essentials of nourishment and cultivation.
Thus, his scripture states:
"Yang is born in Yín,
the essence of pure wood;
Yin is born in Shēn,
the essence of pure metal.
When heaven uses wood to strike metal,
it always causes harm;
thus, Yin can exhaust Yang.
The reason women apply powder and rouge
is to emulate the whiteness of metal.
Therefore, true persons and Daoist masters
must all pay close attention,
refine its subtleties,
and examine its waxing and waning.
I practice the Green Dragon,
they practice the White Tiger;
take their Vermilion Bird,
and refine my Black Tortoise—
this is the Way of immortality.
Moreover, the nature of women
is often eager to seek men,
yet outwardly they restrain
"restrain" originally written as "harm,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
and suppress themselves,
unwilling to invite men—
this illustrates that metal does not yield to wood.
The nature of men is firm and impatient,
with straightforward and simple aspirations.
Yet during social gatherings,
their speech is harmonious and gentle,
their words humble and deferential—
this illustrates wood’s fear of metal."
Tiānménzǐ practiced this Way,
living to 280 years of age
with a complexion still like that of a child.
He then consumed pearl liquor and attained immortality,
departing to Xuánzhōu Mountain.
From Biographies of the Divine Immortals.
Yùzǐ
Yùzǐ,
surnamed Wéi
(Míng chāo běn "Wéi" zuò "Zhāng")
named Zhèn,
was a man of Nánjùn.
In his youth, he loved to study the various classics,
but when King Yōu of Zhōu summoned him, he did not go.
He then sighed and said:
"In the human world,
each day passes and is lost,
one moves further from life,
and closer to death.
Yet people only covet wealth and honor,
not knowing to nurture their vital nature and life.
When life ends and breath ceases, they die.
Even if their rank is that of kings or marquises,
with gold and jade piled like mountains,
what benefit is that to dust and ashes?
Only by becoming a transcendent and transcending the world
can one attain the boundless."
He then took Chángsāngzǐ as his teacher
and received all his arts.
He then created his own school of methods,
composing over a hundred texts on the Way.
His arts focused primarily on Wùkuí,
and he was skilled in the principles of the Five Phases,
expounding their subtleties
to nurture life, cure illness,
and dispel calamities and misfortunes.
He could summon fierce winds,
tear off roofs and break trees,
and create thunder, rain, clouds, and mist.
He could instantly turn wood, tiles, or stones into the six domestic animals, dragons, or tigers.
He could divide his form into hundreds or thousands of people.
He could traverse rivers and seas.
Taking water in his mouth and spraying it out,
it would all become pearls and jade,
and would not change back.
Sometimes he would hold his breath without exhaling,
unable to be lifted when raised,
unable to be moved when pushed,
unable to be bent when forced,
unable to be straightened when extended.
Only after a hundred days or several tens of days would he rise again.
Whenever he traveled with his disciples,
he would roll mud into pellets to make horses for them,
instructing them all to close their eyes.
In a moment, they would become great horses,
and riding them, they could travel a thousand li in a day.
He could also exhale five-colored breath,
rising several zhang high.
Seeing a flying bird pass by,
he could point at it and it would immediately fall.
Facing a deep pool, he would cast a talisman,
summoning creatures such as fish and turtles,
all of which would come ashore.
He could enable his disciples to see things a thousand li away with their naked eyes,
though this could not last long.
When practicing Wùkuí,
he would fill a vessel with water,
place it between his two elbows,
and blow on it.
Immediately, a red light would appear on the water,
glowing and rising one zhang high.
Using this water to treat illness,
those with internal ailments would drink it,
while those with external ailments would wash with it,
and all would be instantly cured.
Later, he entered Kōngtóng Mountain to refine elixirs,
and in broad daylight, ascended to heaven and departed.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn"
Máo Méng,
courtesy name Chūchéng,
was a man of Nánguān, Xiányáng,
and the great-great-grandfather of Dōngqīng Sīmìng Jūn Yíng.
Méng was compassionate by nature,
fond of performing hidden virtues,
upright, tranquil, and widely learned.
Foreseeing that the Zhōu dynasty would decline,
he did not seek advancement among the feudal lords.
He often sighed that human life is like a flash of lightning,
and that one's actions should be timely.
Thus, he studied under Běiguō Guǐgǔ Xiānshēng,
receiving the arts of longevity
and the methods for divine elixirs.
Later, he entered Huà Mountain,
where he purified himself in stillness, cut off worldly dust,
cultivated the Way, and compounded medicines.
Riding a dragon and driving clouds,
he ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
Before this, a folk song in his hometown said:
"The transcendent attained by Máo Chūchéng,
rides a dragon ascending into the Grand Clarity.
At times descending to Xuánzhōu, sporting in Chìchéng,
succeeded in generations, and in my Yíng it continues.
If the emperor learns it, the year-end sacrifice becomes 'Jiāpíng.'"
When Qín Shǐhuáng heard this,
he changed the name of the year-end sacrifice to "Jiāpíng."
From "Dòngxiān Zhuàn"
Shěn Xī
Shěn Xī was a native of
Wújùn,
who studied the Dao in Shǔzhōng.
He could only dispel disasters and cure illnesses,
bringing relief to the common people,
and did not know how to consume elixirs.
His virtuous deeds moved Heaven,
and the celestial deities took notice of him.
Xī was traveling with his wife Jiǎ,
returning from a visit to their daughter-in-law Zhuó Kǒngníng's home,
when they encountered a carriage drawn by a white deer,
a carriage drawn by a green dragon,
and a carriage drawn by a white tiger.
Each had several dozen riders as attendants,
all dressed in crimson robes,
wielding spears and carrying swords,
their splendor filling the road.
They asked Xī:
"Are you Shěn Xī?"
Xī was startled,
not knowing who they were,
and replied:
"Yes, I am.
Why do you ask?"
The riders said:
"Xī has performed meritorious deeds for the people,
his heart never forgetting the Dao.
Since his youth,
his conduct has been without fault.
However, his lifespan is not long,
and his allotted years are about to end.
Huáng-Lǎo now sends immortal officials to descend and welcome him.
The Attendant Gentleman Bó Yánzhī
rides the white deer carriage;
the Lord of Transcending the World, Sīmǎ Shēng,
rides the green dragon carriage;
and the Welcoming Envoy, Xú Fú,
rides the white tiger carriage."
In a moment,
three immortal beings appeared,
clad in feathered robes and holding tallies,
presenting Xī with a white jade tablet, a green jade tablet, and a cinnabar-inscribed jade tablet,
which they bestowed upon Xī,
but Xī could not understand them.
They then carried Xī up to Heaven.
At the moment of his ascension,
all the farmers hoeing in the fields saw it,
but did not know what it was.
Soon, a great fog arose,
and when the fog cleared,
they had vanished without a trace,
leaving only the ox and cart Xī had been riding,
grazing on the seedlings in the field.
Some recognized it as Xī's ox and cart,
and informed Xī's family.
His disciples, fearing it was an evil spirit,
hid Xī in the mountains and valleys,
then searched for him across a hundred-mile radius,
but could not find him.
After more than four hundred years,
he suddenly returned to his hometown,
sought out and found a descendant several generations later,
named Huáixǐ.
Huáixǐ told him:
"I have heard from my ancestors that
a forefather of our family became an immortal,
and has long not returned."
Xī stayed for several dozen days,
and spoke of when he first ascended to Heaven,
saying he was not permitted to see the Emperor,
but only saw Lǎojūn sitting facing east.
Those beside him commanded Xī not to give thanks,
but only to sit silently.
The palace was lush and misty like clouds,
shimmering with five colors, dark and yellow,
indescribable in words.
There were several hundred attendants,
mostly women and few men.
In the courtyard were trees of pearls and jade,
clusters of divine mushrooms growing everywhere,
dragons and tigers gathered in groups,
frolicking among them,
and the sound of clanging like bronze or iron could be heard,
though it was unclear what it was.
The four walls glimmered,
inscribed with talismanic writings.
Lǎojūn's figure was slightly over ten feet tall,
with disheveled hair and patterned robes,
his body radiating light.
After a moment,
several jade maidens brought golden trays and jade cups,
and bestowed them upon Xī, saying:
"This is a divine elixir;
those who drink it will not die.
Husband and wife shall each have one cup,
and live for ten thousand years."
They then instructed:
after drinking it,
bow but do not give thanks.
After taking the medicine,
they bestowed two dates upon him,
as large as chicken eggs,
and a piece of dried meat five inches long,
telling Xī:
"Return temporarily to the mortal world
to cure the illnesses of the common people.
If you wish to ascend again,
write this talisman,
hang it from the tip of a pole,
and we shall welcome you."
They then gave Xī a talisman and a set of immortal prescriptions.
Xī suddenly felt as if he were in a deep sleep,
and found himself already on the ground.
Many have since verified the efficacy of his talismans.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn*.
Chén Ānshì was a native of Jīngzhào
and worked as a hired laborer in the household of Quán Shūběn.
He was naturally kind and compassionate.
Whenever he encountered birds or beasts on the road,
he would always step aside to avoid them,
not wishing to startle them.
He never trod on living insects
and had never killed any creature.
At the age of thirteen or fourteen,
since Shūběn was fond of the Dao and contemplated divine beings,
two immortals,
disguised as scholars,
came to accompany Shūběn in his travels
in order to observe and test him.
But Shūběn did not realize they were immortals,
and over time his attitude grew negligent.
Once, while Shūběn was inside
preparing fine delicacies,
the two immortals again came to his gate
and asked Ānshì:
"Is Shūběn here?"
He replied:
"Yes, he is."
Ānshì went in to inform Shūběn,
and Shūběn was about to go out,
but his wife pulled him back and stopped him, saying:
"Those hungry scholars
just want to come and fill their bellies again."
Thereupon, Shūběn sent Ānshì out to reply:
"Say I'm not here."
The two said:
"Earlier you said he was here,
but now you say he's not.
Why is that?"
He answered:
"My master instructed me to say so."
The two admired his honesty
and remarked, "Shūběn has toiled diligently for years,
and now that he happens to meet us two,
he has grown negligent.
This means he is not destined to encounter us—
almost succeeding, yet failing in the end."
They then asked Ānshì:
"Do you enjoy idle amusements?"
He replied:
"No, I do not."
They asked again:
"Are you fond of the Dao?"
He answered:
"Yes, I am,
but I have no way of learning about it."
The two said:
"If you truly are fond of the Dao,
meet us early tomorrow morning under the big tree north of the road."
Ānshì accepted their words
and went early to the appointed place.
He waited until the sun set in the west,
but did not see anyone.
He then rose to leave,
saying:
"The scholars must have deceived me."
But the two were already at his side,
calling out:
"Ānshì, why have you come so late?"
He replied:
"I came early,
but I did not see you, sirs."
The two said:
"We were sitting upright right beside you."
They tested him three times in this manner,
and each time Ānshì arrived early.
Seeing that he could be taught,
they gave Ānshì two pills of medicine
and instructed him:
"When you return,
do not eat or drink anything further,
but stay in a separate place."
Ānshì followed their instructions.
The two often came and went to his place.
Shūběn found this strange and said:
"Ānshì is in an empty room.
How can there be people talking?"
But whenever he went to look, he saw no one.
Shūběn said:
"Just now I heard the voices of many people,
but now I don't see a single person.
Why is that?"
Ānshì replied:
"I was just talking to myself."
Shūběn noticed that Ānshì no longer ate,
but only drank water,
and rested in a separate place.
Suspecting he was no ordinary person,
Shūběn realized he had missed the opportunity with the worthy ones.
He sighed and said:
"The Dao is revered and virtue is precious;
they do not depend on age.
My parents gave me life,
but without a teacher, none can enable me to attain longevity.
He who comprehends the Dao first
is the teacher."
Thereupon, he adopted the etiquette of a disciple,
serving and paying respects to Ānshì morning and evening,
and sweeping and cleaning for him.
Ānshì achieved the Dao.
He ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
Before departing,
he passed on the essential arts of the Dao to Shūběn.
Shūběn later also became an immortal and departed.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn* (Biographies of Immortals).
Zhāng Zǐfáng,
named Liáng,
was a man of the state of Hán.
He sought refuge in Nányáng,
then moved to and settled in Pèi,
later becoming a man of the state of Pèi.
In his childhood,
while crossing the Yí Bridge at Xiàpī,
the wind and snow were particularly severe.
He encountered an old man
wearing a black headscarf
and a yellow unlined garment.
The old man dropped his shoe under the bridge
and, looking at Zǐfáng, said:
"Young man, fetch it for me."
Zǐfáng showed no sign of weariness.
He went down the bridge, retrieved the shoe, and presented it.
The old man extended his foot to have it put on,
and Zǐfáng's demeanor grew even more respectful.
The old man smiled and said:
"You are a youth worth teaching.
Come here at dawn tomorrow,
and I shall have something to instruct you."
Zǐfáng arrived at daybreak,
but the old man was already there.
He said:
"You arrived after the appointed time;
you cannot be taught the Way."
This happened three times.
Zǐfáng arrived first,
yet showed no weariness or negligence.
The old man was pleased
and gave him a book, saying:
"Study this, and you shall become a teacher to emperors and kings.
If you seek me again,
I am the Yellow Stone at the foot of Gǔchéng Mountain."
Zǐfáng studied the book
and became capable of adapting to circumstances and exercising flexible strategies.
He assisted the founding ancestor of the Hàn in pacifying the realm.
Later generations called this book the "Yellow Stone Elder's Book."
Cultivating its teachings personally,
he could refine his vital energy, transcend physical strength,
lighten his body, and achieve feathered transformation.
Together with Qǐlǐ Jì, Dōngyuán Gōng, Lùlǐ Xiānshēng, and Xiàhuáng Gōng,
he formed a friendship as lofty as clouds and mist.
In the early Hàn dynasty,
he encountered four or five children playing together on the road.
One child said:
"Wearing a blue skirt,
enter the Gate of Heaven,
bow to the Golden Mother,
and pay homage to the Wooden Lord."
People of the time did not understand it,
but Zǐfáng understood.
He went and paid his respects, saying:
"This is the Jade Youth of the Eastern King.
The so-called Golden Mother
is the Queen Mother of the West;
the Wooden Lord
is the Eastern King.
These two primordial venerables
are the parents of yīn and yáng,
the origin of heaven and earth,
transforming and giving birth to all spirits,
nurturing and fostering all beings.
The Wooden Lord is the master of male immortals,
and the Golden Mother is the sovereign of female immortals.
Those who achieve longevity and feathered transformation,
upon ascending to heaven,
first pay respects to the Golden Mother,
then present themselves to the Wooden Lord,
after which they ascend to the Three Purities
and pay homage to the Supreme Elder.
This song is the Jade Youth teaching the world to bow to the Wooden Lord and pay respects to the Golden Mother."
Zǐfáng assisted the Hàn dynasty,
was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Liú,
and served as Grand Minister over the Masses.
He shed his physical form in this world
and was buried at Lóngshǒu Plain.
During the Red Eyebrows rebellion,
people opened his tomb
and saw only a yellow stone pillow,
which transformed and flew away
like a shooting star.
His corpse, clothing, and cap were not seen,
but they found a plain book and several chapters on military strategy.
Zǐfáng ascended to immortality,
holding the position of Tàixuán Tóngzǐ,
often accompanying Lǎojūn within the Tàiqīng realm.
His descendant, Dàolíng, attained the Way,
and on the evening he paid homage to Kūnlún,
Zǐfáng went to him.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí."
Dōngfāng Shuò,
childhood name Mànqiàn.
His father, surnamed Zhāng,
given name Yí,
courtesy name Shǎopíng;
his mother, surnamed Tián.
Yí lived to two hundred years old,
his face like that of a child.
Shuò was born for three days when Tián died,
the time of her death being the third year of Emperor Jǐng of Hàn.
A neighbor woman picked up Shuò and raised him.
At that time, the east had just brightened,
hence he took "Dōngfāng" (Eastern Brightness) as his surname.
At three years old,
he could memorize all the secret texts of the world,
reading them once and reciting them by heart.
He often pointed at the sky and talked to himself.
The neighbor woman suddenly lost Shuò;
after several months he briefly returned,
and she caned him.
Later he left again,
and returned only after a full year.
Seeing him, his mother was greatly startled and said:
"You travel for a full year and return just once,
how can this comfort me?"
Shuò said:
"I only briefly went to the Purple Mud Sea;
some purple water stained my clothes,
so I passed by Yúquán to wash them.
I left in the morning and returned by midday,
how can you say it was a full year?"
His mother asked again:
"Which countries did you pass through?"
Shuò said:
"After washing my clothes,
I rested briefly at the lofty terrace of Míngdū.
I fell asleep for a nap,
and a prince or duke fed me crimson chestnuts and rosy nectar.
I ate so much of it,
I was stuffed and nearly died of discomfort.
Then I drank half a measure of the dark sky's yellow dew.
I awoke immediately,
and on my return, encountered a gray tiger resting by the road.
At first, I rode the tiger back,
but I beat it too hard,
and the tiger bit my foot, injuring it."
His mother then lamented sorrowfully,
and tore her blue cloth skirt to bandage it.
Shuò again left home for ten thousand *li*,
and saw a withered tree.
He took off the cloth and hung it on the tree;
the cloth transformed into a dragon.
Hence, that place was named "Bùlóng Zé" (Cloth Dragon Marsh).
During the Yuánfēng era,
Shuò roamed the Hóngméng Marsh,
and suddenly encountered his mother picking mulberry leaves by the shore of the White Sea.
Soon after, a yellow-browed old man
pointed at his mother and said to Shuò:
"She was once my wife,
who took form as the essence of the Great White Star.
Now you are also the essence of this star.
I have abstained from food and swallowed *qi*,
for over ninety years now.
The pupils of my eyes
all have a blue light,
enabling me to see hidden and obscure things.
Once every three thousand years, I return my bones and wash my marrow;
once every two thousand years, I shed my skin and remove my hair.
Since I was born, I have already washed my marrow three times and removed my hair five times."
After Shuò grew up,
he served Emperor Wǔ of Hàn as Grand Master of the Palace.
In his later years,
Emperor Wǔ was fond of immortal arts,
and was intimate with Shuò.
One day, he said to Shuò:
"I wish to make my beloved favorites not grow old;
is this possible?"
Shuò said:
"Your servant can do it."
The Emperor said:
"What medicine must be taken?"
He said:
"In the northeast land, there is a mushroom herb;
in the southwest, there are fish that are born in spring."
The Emperor said:
"How do you know this?"
He said:
"The three-legged crow wanted to descend to earth and eat this herb,
but Xīhé covered the crow's eyes with her hand,
not allowing it to descend,
fearing it would eat this herb.
If birds or beasts eat this,
they immediately become pleasantly stupefied and unable to move."
He asked:
"How do you know this?"
Shuò said:
"When I was a child digging a well,
I fell into the well,
and for several decades had nothing to rely on.
Someone led me to go fetch this herb,
but we were separated by a Red Spring and could not cross.
That person gave me one shoe,
and I rode the shoe across the spring,
obtained it, and ate it.
The people of that country all weave pearls and jade into mats.
They invited me into a curtain of cloud-patterned knee-covers,
set out a dark jade-like carved pillow,
carved with patterns of sun, moon, clouds, and thunder.
It is also called the 'Hollow-Carved Pillow',
also called the 'Dark-Carved Pillow'.
They also offered a precious mattress of fine hair,
woven from a hundred kinds of hair into a mattress.
This hair mattress is cool,
often spread out in summer.
Hence it is named the 'Soft Hair and Waterweed Mattress'.
I raised my hand to wipe it,
fearing water had wet the mat,
but upon looking closely, it was light."
Afterwards, Emperor Wǔ was resting in the Língguāng Hall,
summoned Shuò beneath the window of blue patterned silk and the curtain of fine silk,
and asked Shuò:
"The Hàn dynasty's fate follows the virtue of Fire;
what essence or auspicious sign manifests as its omen?"
Shuò replied:
"Your servant once roamed the ruins of Hàorán,
east of Cháng'ān,
passing Fúsāng for seventy thousand *li*,
where there is a Cloud Mountain.
On the mountain peak is a well,
and clouds emerge from the well.
If it is the virtue of Earth, then yellow clouds;
if the virtue of Fire, then red clouds;
if the virtue of Metal, then white clouds;
if the virtue of Water, then black clouds."
The Emperor deeply believed him.
In the second year of the Tàichū era,
Shuò returned from the Xīnàxié country,
obtaining ten branches of Sounding Wind Wood,
which he presented to the Emperor.
They were nine feet long,
thick as a finger.
This wood comes from the waters of Yīnhuán,
which is what the *Tribute of Yǔ* calls 'Yīnhuán' arriving.
That is its source.
It emerges from Sweet Waves,
with purple swallows and yellow swans gathering upon it.
Its fruit is like fine pearls.
When the wind blows, the pearls sound like jade,
hence it is so named.
The Emperor bestowed the branches upon all his ministers,
granting them to those a hundred years old.
If such a person fell ill,
the branch would sweat;
if about to die, the branch would break.
In the past, Lǎo Dān in the Zhōu dynasty lived two thousand seven hundred years,
and this branch did not sweat;
Master Hóngyá,
in the time of Yáo, was already three thousand years old,
and this branch also never once broke.
The Emperor then bestowed it upon Shuò.
Shuò said:
"I have seen this branch wither and die three times,
dying and then reviving.
How could it merely sweat or break?
It is said:
'The year not yet a year,
the branch suddenly sweats.'
The Ming manuscript has 'not yet' for 'not',
and 'suddenly' for 'do not'.
The *Imperial Readings*, scroll 953, quoting the *Records of Penetrating the Obscure*, says: 'The year not yet half,
the branch does not sweat.'
This wood becomes wet once every five thousand years,
and withers once every ten thousand years."
The Emperor considered this correct.
Also, in the second year of the Tiānhàn era,
the Emperor ascended the Cānglóng Pavilion,
thinking of immortal arts.
He summoned various magicians
to speak of matters from distant lands and faraway regions.
Only Shuò left his mat, took up a brush, and wrote a memorial, saying:
"Your servant traveled to the North Pole,
reaching Mirror Volcano,
where the sun and moon do not shine.
There was a dragon holding fire in its mouth,
illuminating the four extremities of the mountain.
There were also gardens, parks, ponds, and parks,
all planted with exotic grasses and trees.
There was the Bright-Stem Grass.
Like a golden lamp,
broken to make a torch,
it illuminates the forms of ghostly creatures.
The immortal Níng Fēng
once used this grass to burn
'yú' originally written as 'wéi',
according to the Ming manuscript changed
at night.
In the morning, he saw light inside and outside his abdomen;
it is also called 'Belly-Penetrating Grass'.
The Emperor ground this grass into flakes,
Zhōu Yǐnyáo,
a Daoist priest from Dòngtíng Mountain,
claimed to be the grandson of Lùlǐ Xiānshēng.
On the mountain, there was a temple and village named after his ancestor Lùlǐ.
He said that for several generations, his family had attained the Dao.
He once resided on Jiāo Mountain,
studying the art of refining the form through the Great Yin.
He died in a cliff cave.
He instructed his disciples, saying:
"Examine my corpse,
and do not let it be harmed by any other creatures.
After six years,
if I revive,
you must clothe me with garments."
The disciples watched over it.
At first, it was foul and rotten, infested with worms,
only the five internal organs remained unchanged.
They followed his words and sealed it off for protection.
When they went to check after six years,
he had revived with his body fully intact.
The disciples prepared hot water for bathing
and dressed him in new clothes.
His hair was thick and black,
his beard coarse and straight,
like the mane of a beast.
After sixteen years, he died again as before,
and after another seven years, he revived once more.
This happened three times in total.
After more than forty years,
he was nearly eighty years old,
yet his appearance was like that of a man around thirty.
Emperor Suí Yáng heard of him
and summoned him to the Eastern Commandery,
bestowing lavish gifts upon him,
showing exceptional favor and courtesy.
Yet he earnestly begged to return to the mountains.
Soon after, he returned to his home commandery.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
he was summoned to Cháng'ān,
and accommodated in the inner palace,
where he was questioned about the path of cultivation.
He replied:
"What I cultivate
is the aspiration of an ordinary man,
its merit does not extend to others,
its benefit is only for oneself.
When an emperor cultivates the Dao,
the benefit of a single word
brings fortune to all nations.
The efficacy of attaining the Dao
is swifter than that of a minister.
The little I have learned
is not what the Son of Heaven in the ninefold palace should cultivate."
He earnestly requested to return to the mountains,
and soon after, he was allowed to go where he pleased.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Liú Shāng
Liú Shāng
was a descendant of the Prince of Zhōngshān Jìng.
He was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate
and served as the magistrate of Héféi.
Yet he deeply cherished the path of non-action, purity, and simplicity.
In the methods of alchemy and refinement,
the five metals and eight minerals,
those that were difficult to obtain
he would strive to acquire by all means.
If someone had a prescription
but lacked the means to refine and apply it effectively,
he would surely provide the medicinal stones,
supply the furnace and cauldron,
and assist in completing it,
never harboring any covetous intentions.
While boating on the Tiáo and Zhá rivers,
he chose to settle at the foot of Shàngqiáng Mountain in Wǔkāng.
Woodcutters and herb-gathering elders,
even if they brought common herbs,
if they came to his gate to sell,
he would also pay a good price.
One day,
a woodcutter came selling firewood,
and among it was a bundle of atractylodes,
which Liú Shāng also purchased at a high price.
In his courtyard and under the eaves,
within the fences and hedges,
various medicinal herbs
were already piled up.
Suddenly, while leisurely strolling with a staff,
sauntering beside the fields and paths,
simply enjoying himself,
he heard from within a dense grove
people conversing, saying:
"Liú Shāng of Zhōngshān,
today has been bestowed with the true art of atractylodes,
is it not due to the influence of his hidden merit and sincere devotion?"
Peering into the grove,
there was no trace of anyone.
He rushed back to fetch the atractylodes,
prepared it, and consumed it.
After over a month,
his teeth and hair grew even more luxuriant,
his appearance like that of an infant child;
his steps were light and swift,
able to keep pace with galloping horses;
climbing clouds and cliffs,
he no longer felt fatigue.
After another month or so,
he could sit and know affairs from all directions,
verifying them as if matching tallies,
then he entered the cave of Shàngqiáng.
At the beginning of the Xiántōng era,
a tavern keeper, noticing the woodcutter elder was somewhat extraordinary,
treated him with full courtesy.
After several months, he came again once,
and thus said to the tavern keeper:
"I am Liú Shāng from the mountains.
I have long practiced ink painting,
and I wish to leave a painting
to repay your generous treatment."
He asked them to prepare silk canvas,
and promised to return again.
One day, he indeed came to the tavern,
took up the brush and contemplated,
and in a moment painted thousands of mountains and rivers,
surpassing any craftsmanship of the mortal world.
As he was about to leave,
he said to the tavern keeper:
"My ancestor, the Prince of Huáinán,
