now serves as the Overseer of the Nine Seas,
holding a position among the ranks of perfected beings.
He has appointed me to the post of Commander of the Southern Seas' Waters.
In ten days, I will depart far away,
and will not return again."
Thus, after about ten days,
the sky cleared and brightened,
fragrant winds and auspicious clouds
filled the mountains and valleys,
and woodcutters saw riders in the sky,
soaring southward.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Báishí Xiānshēng
Báishí Xiānshēng
was a disciple of Zhōnghuáng Zhàngrén.
By the time of Péng Zǔ,
he was already over two thousand years old.
He was unwilling to cultivate the path of ascending to heaven,
only seeking immortality,
without losing the joys of the human world.
The methods he relied on
primarily focused on the arts of interaction,
with the elixir of golden fluid being the foremost.
Initially, due to poverty,
he could not obtain the medicine,
so he raised sheep and herded pigs.
Over ten-plus years,
he economized on clothing and expenses,
amassed wealth worth ten thousand gold,
and then purchased large amounts of medicine to consume.
He often cooked white stones as food,
and thus dwelt on Báishí Mountain,
so people of the time called him Báishí Xiānshēng.
He also ate dried meat and drank wine,
and consumed grains as well.
He could travel three to four hundred lǐ in a day,
and his complexion appeared like that of a man around forty.
He had a fondness for worshipping and serving deities,
and enjoyed reading esoteric scriptures and the "Tàisù Zhuàn."
Péng Zǔ asked him:
"Why do you not take the medicine to ascend to heaven?"
He replied:
"Can there be joy in heaven comparable to that in the human world?
I only wish to avoid aging and death.
In heaven, there are many supreme beings,
serving them
is even more toilsome than in the human world."
Thus, people of the time called Báishí Xiānshēng the Recluse Immortal,
because he was not eager to ascend to heaven and become an immortal official,
much like those who do not seek fame or prominence.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn"
Huáng Chūpíng
Huáng Chūpíng was
a man of Dānxī.
At the age of fifteen,
his family sent him to tend sheep.
A Daoist priest, seeing his goodness and diligence,
then took him to a stone chamber on Jīnhuá Mountain,
where he remained for over forty years
without ever thinking of home.
His elder brother, Chūqǐ,
traveled through the mountains searching for Chūpíng
but could not find him for many years.
Later, he saw a Daoist priest in the marketplace.
Chūqǐ called to him and asked,
"I have a younger brother named Chūpíng.
He was sent to tend sheep
and has been missing for over forty years.
No one knows whether he is alive or dead, or where he might be.
I beg you, Master, to divine his whereabouts."
The Daoist priest said,
"There is a shepherd boy in Jīnhuá Mountain,
surnamed Huáng,
styled Chūpíng.
He is undoubtedly your brother."
Upon hearing this,
Chūqǐ immediately followed the Daoist priest
and succeeded in finding his brother.
They met with both sorrow and joy.
After speaking,
Chūqǐ asked Chūpíng where the sheep were.
Chūpíng replied,
"They are nearby, east of the mountain."
Chūqǐ went to look,
but saw nothing,
only white stones, and returned.
He said to Chūpíng,
"There are no sheep east of the mountain."
Chūpíng said,
"The sheep are there;
it is just that you, brother, cannot see them."
Chūpíng and Chūqǐ went together to look.
Chūpíng then shouted,
"Sheep, arise!"
At that, all the white stones transformed into tens of thousands of sheep.
Chūqǐ said,
"Brother, you have attained such immortal arts.
Can I learn them too?"
Chūpíng said,
"If you truly devote yourself to the Dao,
you can attain it."
Chūqǐ then abandoned his wife and children and stayed,
studying under Chūpíng.
Together they consumed pine resin and poria,
and by the age of five hundred,
they could sit and vanish at will,
walk under the sun without casting a shadow,
and still retain the complexion of youths.
Later, they returned to their hometown,
but their relatives and clansmen had nearly all passed away,
so they departed once more.
Chūpíng changed his style name to Chìsōngzǐ,
and Chūqǐ changed his to Lǔ Bān.
Afterward, dozens of people attained immortality by taking this elixir.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn* (*Biographies of Immortals*).
Wáng Yuǎn,
whose courtesy name was Fāngpíng,
was a native of Dōnghǎi.
He was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate,
appointed as a Gentleman of the Palace,
and later promoted to Palace Attendant.
He was learned in the Five Classics,
and particularly well-versed in the essentials of astronomy, charts, prophecies, and the River Chart and Luo Writings.
He could foresee the periods of the world's prosperity and decline,
and the fortunes and misfortunes of the Nine Provinces
were as clear to him as if held in his palm.
Later, he abandoned his official post
and entered the mountains to cultivate the Way.
After attaining the Way,
Emperor Huán of Hàn heard of him
and repeatedly summoned him, but he did not emerge.
The commandery and kingdom were ordered to force him onto a carriage
to bring him to the capital.
Wáng Yuǎn lowered his head and kept his mouth shut,
not responding to the imperial edict.
Instead, he wrote over four hundred characters on the palace gate's wooden panels,
all discussing future events.
The emperor was displeased
and ordered them to be scraped off.
As soon as the outer characters were removed,
the inner characters reappeared,
with the ink having penetrated deep into the wood.
The more they scraped, the clearer the characters became.
Wáng Yuǎn had no descendants,
but the people of his hometown took turns supporting and making offerings to him for generations.
Chén Dān, the Grand Commandant of the same commandery,
built a Daoist chamber for Wáng Yuǎn
and paid respects to him morning and evening,
only seeking blessings,
not yet speaking of learning the Way.
Wáng Yuǎn stayed at the Chén family's home for over forty years,
during which the Chén family never suffered from illness or death,
and the same was true for their servants.
Their livestock multiplied and thrived,
and their fields and mulberry groves yielded double harvests.
Suddenly, Wáng Yuǎn said to Chén Dān:
"My destined time to depart has arrived;
I cannot stay much longer.
I will leave at noon tomorrow."
At that time, Wáng Yuǎn died,
but Chén Dān knew he had departed as an immortal.
Not daring to let his body touch the ground,
he only wept sorrowfully and sighed, saying:
"The master has abandoned me;
on whom shall I rely?"
He prepared a coffin and burned incense,
dressing the body on the bed.
On the third night,
the corpse suddenly disappeared,
with the clothes and cap left intact,
like a snake shedding its skin.
Over a hundred days after Wáng Yuǎn's departure,
Chén Dān also passed away.
Some say Chén Dān attained the Way through Wáng Yuǎn and transformed away;
others say
Wáng Yuǎn knew Chén Dān was nearing his end,
so he entrusted him and left.
Earlier, when Wáng Yuǎn intended to enter Kuòcāng Mountain in the east,
he passed through Wú
and stayed at the home of Cài Jīng at Xū Gate.
Cài Jīng
was merely a commoner,
but his bone structure indicated he was destined to become an immortal.
Wáng Yuǎn knew this,
so he stayed at his home.
He then said to Cài Jīng:
"Your fate is such that you should transcend the mortal world;
I intend to take you to fill an official post among the immortals.
However, you have lacked understanding of the Way from a young age,
and now you have little vital energy but much flesh,
so you cannot ascend directly.
You will have to undergo liberation by means of a corpse,
like passing through a dog hole."
He then imparted essential teachings to him
and entrusted Cài Jīng before departing.
Later, Cài Jīng suddenly felt his body burning like fire
and wanted cold water poured over him.
His whole family fetched water and poured it on him,
but it was like watering scorched stones.
After three days like this,
he became emaciated, reduced to skin and bones,
and entered his room,
covering himself with a quilt.
Suddenly, he disappeared.
Looking inside the quilt,
only skin remained,
with the head and feet intact, like a cicada shedding its shell.
Over ten years later,
he suddenly returned home,
looking youthful and vigorous.
His temples and hair were thick and black.
He said to his family:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month,
Lord Wáng will come.
On that day, prepare plenty of food and drink
to serve his attendants."
On that day,
the Cài family borrowed pots and utensils,
prepared over a hundred hú of food and drink,
and arranged them in the courtyard.
That day,
Lord Wáng indeed came.
Before his arrival,
the sounds of gongs, drums, flutes, pipes, and horses were heard first,
startling everyone nearby,
though no one knew where they came from.
When he arrived at Cài Jīng's house,
the whole family saw Wáng Yuǎn.
He wore a yuǎnyóu cap,
a crimson robe,
a tiger-headed pouch,
a multicolored sash,
and carried a sword.
He had a yellowish complexion and a sparse beard,
and was of medium height.
He rode in a feathered carriage,
drawn by five dragons,
each of a different color.
There were banners and insignia before and after him,
with flags guiding and following,
his majestic presence resplendent,
like that of a great general.
There were twelve attendants,
all with their mouths sealed with wax,
and musicians all riding dragons,
descending from the sky
and hovering to land in the courtyard.
The attendants were all over ten feet tall,
and they did not travel by ordinary roads.
Once they arrived,
the attendants all vanished,
and no one knew where they went,
only Wáng Yuǎn was seen sitting alone.
After a short while,
he summoned Cài Jīng's parents and brothers to meet him,
and then sent someone to summon Má Gū,
though no one knew who Má Gū was.
The message said:
"Wáng Fāngpíng respectfully reports:
It has been a long time since I visited the mortal world.
Now that I am here,
I wonder if you, Aunt, could come for a brief conversation?"
Shortly after, the messenger returned,
though the messenger was not seen,
only the message was heard, saying:
"Má Gū bows respectfully.
It has been over five hundred years since we last met.
There is a distinction between superior and inferior,
and I have no means to pay my respects.
I am troubled that you have sent a messenger to me there.
I will arrive shortly.
I first received orders to inspect Pénglái,
so I will make a brief stop there now.
After that, I will return,
and upon returning, I will come to pay my respects in person.
I hope you will not leave immediately."
After about two hours,
Má Gū was heard arriving.
Upon her arrival, the sounds of people and horses were also heard first.
Once she arrived,
her attendants numbered half of Wáng Yuǎn's.
When Má Gū arrived,
Cài Jīng and his whole family also saw her.
She was a beautiful woman,
appearing about eighteen or nineteen years old,
with her hair tied in a topknot,
and the rest flowing loosely down to her waist.
Her clothes were colorful and patterned,
yet not made of brocade or damask.
They shone brilliantly,
beyond description,
and were unlike anything in the mortal world.
She entered and bowed to Wáng Yuǎn,
and Wáng Yuǎn stood up for her.
After they were seated,
each presented their own feast,
all with unlimited golden plates and jade cups.
The dishes were mostly made of various flowers,
and their fragrance permeated inside and out.
They tore dried meat and ate it,
saying:
"This is kylin jerky."
Má Gū said of herself:
"Since I began attending to affairs,
I have already seen the Eastern Sea turn into mulberry fields three times.
Just now, when I went to Pénglái,
the water was shallower than during our previous meeting, about half as much.
Could it be that it will become hills and land again?"
Wáng Yuǎn sighed and said:
"Sages all say that the sea will one day turn to dust."
Má Gū wished to see Cài Jīng's mother and wife,
and at that time, Cài Jīng's sister-in-law had just given birth a few days earlier.
Má Gū saw her and knew this,
saying:
"Ah,
stand there and do not come forward,
quickly fetch a little rice."
Upon obtaining the rice, he threw it to the ground,
saying it was to use the rice to dispel the impurity.
Looking at the rice, it had all turned into cinnabar.
Fǎ Yuǎn laughed and said:
"The maiden is still young,
I am old,
and do not enjoy performing such clever transformations anymore."
Fǎ Yuǎn said to Cài Jīng's family members:
"I wish to bestow upon you fine wine,
this wine has just come from the heavenly kitchens,
its flavor is rich and mellow,
it is not suitable for ordinary people to drink,
drinking it might rot one's intestines,
now I shall dilute it with water,
do not find it strange."
Then with a dou of water,
he mixed a sheng of wine and stirred it,
and bestowed it upon Cài Jīng's family members,
each person drank about a sheng,
and all became drunk.
After a long while, the wine was finished,
Fǎ Yuǎn sent his attendants, saying:
"If it is not enough, go fetch more."
He gave a thousand coins to the old woman of Yúháng,
to buy wine.
In a moment, the messenger returned,
obtaining a leather bag of wine,
about five dou.
The messenger conveyed the old woman of Yúháng's reply:
"I fear the wine on earth may not be worthy for your honor to drink."
Má Gū's fingernails resembled those of a bird,
Cài Jīng saw them,
and thought in his heart:
"When my back itches terribly,
if I could use these claws to scratch my back,
it would surely be wonderful."
Fǎ Yuǎn already knew what Cài Jīng was thinking in his heart,
immediately had someone drag Cài Jīng and whip him,
saying:
"Má Gū is a divine being,
how dare you suddenly think her claws could scratch your back?"
They only saw the whip strike Cài Jīng's back,
but did not see anyone holding the whip.
Fǎ Yuǎn told Cài Jīng:
"My whip is not something one can receive lightly."
Next to Cài Jīng's house lived a man surnamed Chén,
whose given name is lost,
he had once been dismissed from his post as county captain,
hearing that there was a divine being at Cài Jīng's house,
he went to the door and kowtowed,
begging to have an audience.
Thereupon, Fǎ Yuǎn had him brought forward and spoke with him.
This man then wished to follow and serve,
comparing himself to Cài Jīng.
Fǎ Yuǎn said:
"Sir, please stand facing the sun."
Fǎ Yuǎn observed him from behind and said:
"Ah,
your heart is deviant and not upright,
ultimately you cannot be taught the way of immortality,
I shall confer upon you the office of an earthly overseer."
Before leaving,
he gave a talisman and a document,
placed in a small box,
to Captain Chén.
He told him, "This cannot enable you to transcend the world,
it can only preserve your original lifespan,
naturally extending beyond a hundred years.
It can be used to avert disasters and cure illnesses;
for those whose fate is not yet ended and who are without guilt,
if you take this talisman to their home,
they will recover.
If evil ghosts that feed on blood sacrifices cause calamities,
then carry this talisman,
and with the document command the officials,
to dispatch those ghosts.
You should also know the gravity of the matter in your heart,
and deal with it according to your judgment at the time."
Chén used this talisman to cure illnesses effectively,
and several hundred families served him.
He lived to be one hundred and ten years old and then died.
After his death, his disciples and sons used his talisman,
but it was no longer effective.
After Fǎ Yuǎn left,
the food and drink prepared by Cài Jīng's family,
amounting to several hundred hu, were all consumed,
yet no one was seen eating or drinking.
Cài Jīng's parents privately asked him:
"What kind of divine being is Lord Wáng,
and where does he reside?"
Cài Jīng said:
"He often stays at Kūnlún Mountain,
traveling to Luófú, Kuòcāng, and other mountains,
all of which have palaces upon them.
He presides over the affairs of the heavenly bureaucracy,
within a single day,
he goes back and forth between heaven and earth over ten times.
Matters of life and death from the five sacred mountains on earth,
all first come to report to Lord Wáng.
When Lord Wáng goes out,
sometimes
Yúnjí Qīqiān, scroll 109, citing Shénxiān Zhuàn, sometimes reads "sometimes"
he does not take all his officials along,
only riding a single yellow qilin,
with a dozen or so attendants.
Whenever he travels, he often sees forests and mountains below,
several hundred zhang above the ground,
wherever he arrives, the mountain and sea deities all come to welcome and pay homage to him."
Several decades later,
Cài Jīng briefly returned home again,
Fǎ Yuǎn had a letter for Captain Chén,
the letter was expansive,
large but not refined.
Previously, no one knew that Fǎng Píng's name was Yuǎn,
because of this they came to know it.
Captain Chén's family, to this day, generation after generation, preserves Lord Wáng's handwritten letter,
along with the talisman and document in a small box.
From Shénxiān Zhuàn
Bó Shānfǔ
Bó Shānfǔ was
a man of Yōngzhōu.
He entered Huàshān,
devoted himself to meditation and consuming elixirs,
from time to time returning to his hometown to visit relatives,
and thus for two hundred years did not age.
When visiting people's homes,
he would recount the good and evil, merits and faults of their ancestors,
as if seeing it before his eyes.
He also knew the future fortunes and misfortunes,
and his words never failed to come true.
His niece was old and afflicted with many illnesses,
so he gave her medicine.
The woman was already eighty years old at the time,
but she reverted to youth,
her complexion like peach blossoms.
Emperor Hàn Wǔ dispatched an envoy traveling through Hédōng,
when suddenly he saw a woman west of the city,
beating an old man with a rod,
who bowed his head and knelt receiving the blows.
The envoy found it strange and asked her,
the woman said:
"This old man is my son,
formerly my maternal uncle Bó Shānfǔ,
taught me divine medicine,
I taught my son to take it,
but he refused,
and now he has aged,
and cannot keep up with me,
therefore I beat him."
The envoy asked the woman and her son their ages,
she replied:
"I am already two hundred and thirty years old,
my son is eighty."
Later she entered Huàshān and left.
From Shénxiān Zhuàn
Mǎ Míngshēng
Mǎ Míngshēng was a native of Línzī.
His original surname was Hé,
and his courtesy name was Jūnxián.
In his youth, he served as a county clerk.
While capturing bandits,
he was wounded by them,
and momentarily died.
Suddenly, he encountered a divine being who saved him with medicine,
and he revived.
Míngshēng had no way to repay him,
so he abandoned his post to follow the divine being.
At first, he only wanted to learn a prescription for treating metal wounds,
but later he learned there was a way to achieve longevity,
so he followed him for a long time,
carrying his book satchel.
They went west to Nǚ'ér Mountain,
north to Xuánqiū,
and south to Lújiāng,
traveling throughout the world,
toiling diligently for many years,
until he received the three scrolls of the "Tàiyáng Shéndān Jīng" and returned.
He entered the mountains to compound the medicine and took it.
Not wishing to ascend to heaven,
he only took half a dose,
becoming an earthbound immortal,
constantly dwelling among humans.
He would change his residence every three years,
so people of the time did not know he was an immortal.
He built houses,
kept servants, carriages, and horses,
all just like ordinary people.
In this way, he moved from place to place,
traveling through the nine provinces.
After more than five hundred years,
many people recognized him,
and all marveled at his lack of aging.
Later, he ascended to heaven in broad daylight and departed.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn."
Lǐ Bābǎi was a native of Shǔ,
and no one knew his real name.
He was seen across generations,
and people of the time calculated his age to be eight hundred years,
hence he was given this epithet.
Sometimes he hid in the mountains and forests,
sometimes he appeared in the marketplaces.
Knowing that Táng Gōngfǎng of Hànzhōng had aspirations
but had not encountered an enlightened teacher,
he wanted to instruct him.
So he first went to test him,
working as a hired laborer,
which Gōngfǎng did not know.
Bābǎi drove and employed him with intent,
different from other laborers,
and Gōngfǎng grew fond of him for his uniqueness.
Bābǎi then feigned a severe illness,
on the verge of death.
Gōngfǎng immediately summoned doctors and compounded medicine for him,
spending hundreds of thousands of coins,
without considering it a loss.
His worry and concern
were evident on his face.
Bābǎi then developed a foul sore,
covering his entire body,
with pus, blood, and a foul stench,
making it unbearable to approach.
Gōngfǎng wept for him, saying:
"You have been a laborer in my household,
toiling diligently for years,
and now you have contracted this severe illness.
I sought doctors hoping to cure you,
sparing no expense.
Yet you still do not recover—
what should I do for you?"
Bābǎi said:
"My sore will not heal
unless someone licks it."
Gōngfǎng then ordered three maidservants
to lick it for him.
Bābǎi said again:
"The maidservants licking it will not cure it.
If you could lick it for me,
it would surely heal."
Gōngfǎng immediately licked it.
Bābǎi again said it was of no benefit,
and that if Gōngfǎng's wife licked it, it would be best.
So he also had his wife lick it.
Bābǎi then announced:
"My sore is about to heal.
I need thirty hú of fine wine
to bathe in, and then it will be cured."
Gōngfǎng immediately prepared the wine
and placed it in a large vessel.
Bābǎi then rose,
entered the wine to bathe,
and the sore was immediately healed.
His body became like congealed fat,
with no remaining scars.
He then told Gōngfǎng:
"I am an immortal.
You have aspirations,
so I tested you like this.
You are truly worthy of instruction,
and now I shall impart to you the secret of transcending the world."
He then had Gōngfǎng and his wife,
along with the three maidservants who licked the sore,
bathe in the wine he had used.
They all became youthful again,
with beautiful and joyful complexions.
He gave Gōngfǎng one scroll of a elixir scripture.
Gōngfǎng entered Yúntái Mountain to prepare the medicine.
When the medicine was completed,
he took it and ascended as an immortal.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn."
Lǐ Ā
Lǐ Ā was a native of Shǔ,
seen across generations without aging.
He often begged in the markets of Chéngdū,
and whatever he obtained, he distributed to the poor.
He left at night and returned in the morning,
and the market people did not know where he stayed.
Some went to ask him about matters,
but Ā said nothing.
They only observed Ā's expression:
if his expression was joyful,
then the matters were all auspicious;
if his countenance was sorrowful,
then the matters were all inauspicious;
if Ā smiled,
then there was great celebration;
if he sighed slightly,
then there was deep worry.
By observing him like this,
they were never mistaken.
There was a man named Gǔ Qiáng
who suspected Ā was an extraordinary person
and often attended to him personally.
He tried to follow Ā back,
and found that he stayed in Qīngchéng Mountain.
Later, Qiáng wanted to follow Ā again,
but as he did not know the way and feared tigers and wolves,
he secretly brought his father's large knife.
Ā saw it and angrily said to Qiáng:
"You are following me—
why fear tigers?"
He took Qiáng's knife and struck a rock with it,
and the knife broke.
Qiáng worried about the broken knife.
In the morning, as they left,
Ā asked Qiáng:
"Are you worried about the broken knife?"
Qiáng said he was truly afraid his father would be angry.
Ā then took the knife,
struck the ground with his left hand,
and the knife returned to its original state.
Qiáng followed Ā back to Chéngdū.
Before arriving,
they encountered a person driving a carriage on the road.
Ā placed his foot under the carriage,
and the wheel crushed his foot, breaking it.
Ā immediately died.
Qiáng was terrified
and kept watch over him.
After a short while, Ā rose,
rubbed his foot with his hand,
and it returned to normal.
When Qiáng was eighteen,
he saw Ā looking about fifty.
When Qiáng was over eighty,
Ā still looked unchanged.
Later, Ā told people he was summoned by Kūnlún Mountain
and had to leave.
He then never returned.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn."
Liú Ān
Liú Ān, the King of Huáinán of the Hàn Dynasty,
was the grandson of Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn.
His father, King Lì Cháng,
having offended the emperor, was exiled to Shǔ,
and died on the journey.
Emperor Wéndì pitied him,
and divided his territory,
bestowing it all upon Cháng's eldest son,
thus Ān was enfeoffed as the King of Huáinán.
At that time, the various princes' sons were noble and extravagant,
all devoting themselves to music, women, hunting, dogs, and horses,
but only Ān humbled himself to treat scholars with respect,
was deeply fond of Confucian learning,
and also practiced divination and occult arts.
He supported several thousand scholars,
all of whom were outstanding talents of the realm.
He composed the twenty-two chapters of the *Inner Book*,
and also eight chapters of a middle section,
which spoke of matters concerning immortals and alchemy,
titled *Hóngbǎo*,
and three chapters of *Wànbì*,
discussing the ways of transformation,
totaling one hundred thousand words.
Emperor Wǔdì, considering Ān eloquent, learned, and talented,
and being his uncle,
held him in great esteem and honor.
Special edicts and replies
were often drafted jointly by Sīmǎ Xiàngrú and others,
and then envoys were dispatched
to summon Ān to court.
He once commanded him to compose a commentary on the *Lísāo*,
and Ān received the edict at dawn,
completing it by mealtime,
and presented it.
Whenever Ān attended banquets and audiences,
he discussed gains and losses,
and presented various rhapsodies and eulogies,
entering at dawn and leaving at night.
Thus, scholars of the Way and practitioners of occult arts from across the realm,
not deterred by traveling a thousand *lǐ*,
came with humble words and generous gifts to seek an audience.
Then, eight elders arrived at his gate,
all with white hair and beards.
The gatekeeper secretly reported this to the king first,
and the king sent a gatekeeper
to question them according to his own judgment, saying:
"My king seeks, on the highest level, the Way of prolonging life and immortality;
on the middle level, great Confucian scholars who are broadly learned, grasp essential principles, and penetrate mysteries;
and on the lowest level, brave warriors and strong men who can lift tripods, subdue tigers, and act with force.
Now, you gentlemen are already advanced in years,
seemingly lacking the arts to halt decline,
and also lack the vigor of Mèng Bēn and Xià Yù.
How could you possibly delve into the *Sānfén*, *Wǔdiǎn*, *Bāsuǒ*, and *Jiǔqiū*,
plumb the depths and reach far,
exhaust principles and fully realize nature?
Since you lack all three,
I dare not admit you."
The eight elders laughed and said:
"We have heard that the king honors and respects worthy scholars,
tirelessly spitting out food and washing his hair to receive them.
If there is even a single good quality,
none fail to come.
The ancients valued even minor skills,
fostering the abilities of crowing and barking,
truly wishing to buy horse bones to attract thoroughbreds,
and learn from Master Guō to summon a host of talents.
Although we are aged and humble,
and do not meet your requirements,
we have come from afar to present ourselves,
and wish merely to see the king.
Even if we are of no benefit,
surely we would cause no harm.
Why should we be rejected and suspected because of our age?
If the king must see youth to deem one possessed of the Way,
and white hair to deem one a mediocre old man,
I fear this is not what is meant by splitting rocks to seek jade,
or probing deep pools to search for pearls.
If you despise us for being old,
then we shall be young."
Before the words were finished,
the eight elders all transformed into youths,
aged about fourteen or fifteen,
with hair tied in topknots of black silk,
and complexions like peach blossoms.
The gatekeeper was greatly astonished,
and ran to report to the king.
When the king heard this,
he did not even put on shoes,
but went barefoot to welcome them and ascended the Terrace of Longing for Immortals.
He spread brocade canopies and ivory beds,
burned hundred-blend incense,
presented gold and jade tables,
performed the rites of a disciple,
faced north, kowtowed, and said:
"I, Ān, with my ordinary talent,
have from youth been fond of the Way and its virtue.
Yet entangled in worldly affairs,
sunk in common customs,
I have been unable to cast off burdens,
and go forth from the forests bearing my satchel.
But day and night, with hunger and thirst,
I have longed for divine enlightenment.
Bathing in impurity and turbidity,
my essence and sincerity are shallow and weak.
My cherished feelings find no outlet,
distant as the Milky Way.
I never expected such great
"Great" originally read "original,"
emended according to *Yúnjí Qīqiān*, *juàn* 109, quoting *Shénxiān Zhuàn*.
fortune,
that the Lords of the Way would condescend to come.
This must be that my fate and fortune deserve such elevation.
Joy and fear overwhelm me,
and I know not what to do.
I only pray the Lords of the Way will pity and instruct me.
Then, like the caterpillar borrowing the wings of the swan,
I may soar to the heavens."
The eight youths then reverted to being old men,
and told the king:
"Although our knowledge is shallow,
we are fully versed in prior learning.
Hearing of the king's fondness for scholars,
we have come to follow you.
We do not know what the king desires in his heart?
One of us can summon wind and rain while seated,
raise clouds and mist while standing,
draw rivers on the ground,
and gather earth to form mountains;
one can collapse high mountains,
block deep springs,
restrain tigers and leopards,
summon flood dragons,
and command ghosts and spirits;
one can divide his form and change his appearance,
be present while sitting and vanish while standing,
conceal entire armies,
and turn day into darkness;
one can ride clouds and tread the void,
cross seas and tread waves,
enter and exit without hindrance,
and breathe across a thousand *lǐ*;
one can enter fire without being burned,
enter water without getting wet,
be unharmed by blades and arrows,
not feel cold in winter's freeze,
nor sweat under summer's sun;
one can undergo a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes,
doing as he pleases,
creating birds, beasts, plants, and trees,
instantly forming all things,
moving mountains and halting streams,
relocating palaces and changing dwellings;
one can cook mud into gold,
solidify lead into silver,
refine the eight minerals with water,
make flowing pearls fly and soar,
ride clouds and drive dragons,
floating above the Great Purity.
It is all as the king desires."
Ān then paid homage morning and evening,
offering wine and dried meat.
Each demonstrated what they had previously described,
with a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes,
all kinds of extraordinary arts,
none failing to prove effective.
They then bestowed the thirty-six scrolls of the *Jade Elixir Classic*.
When the elixir was completed,
he had not yet taken it.
Meanwhile, Crown Prince Qiān was fond of swordsmanship,
and believed no one could match him.
At that time, the court gentleman Léi Bèi
was summoned to spar with him,
and Bèi accidentally struck Qiān.
Qiān was greatly enraged,
and Bèi, terrified,
fearing Qiān would kill him,
requested to attack the Xiōngnú to redeem his offense.
Ān heard of this but did not grant permission.
Bèi, in great fear,
then submitted a memorial to the Son of Heaven, saying:
"By Hàn law,
if a feudal lord obstructs and prevents others from attacking the Xiōngnú,
the crime is punishable by death.
Ān should accordingly be executed."
Emperor Wǔdì had always esteemed the king highly.
He did not punish him,
but only stripped Ān of two counties.
Ān was angry with Bèi,
and Bèi feared for his life.
He was on close terms with Wǔ Bèi,
and Wǔ Bèi had previously offended Ān through deceit and private misconduct.
Ān's anger towards him had not yet been vented.
The two, fearing Ān would execute them,
joined in falsely accusing him,
claiming Ān was plotting rebellion.
The Son of Heaven sent the Minister of the Imperial Clan, bearing the imperial tally, to investigate.
The eight elders said to Ān:
"It is time to leave.
This is Heaven dispatching the king.
If the king had not committed these acts,
Day after day,
he was unable to leave the mortal world.
The Eight Lords had Liú Ān ascend the mountain to perform a grand sacrifice,
burying gold in the earth,
and he immediately ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
The stones on the mountain where the Eight Lords and Liú Ān stepped
all sank, leaving footprints,
and to this day, the traces of men and horses remain.
The Eight Lords told Liú Ān:
"Those who have a foundation
and are falsely accused by others—
the accusers shall perish immediately.
Wǔ Bèi and the others will now be executed."
Thereupon, the Minister of the Imperial Clan, unable to locate Liú Ān,
inquired and reported
that the King had departed to become an immortal.
The Emperor was disheartened,
and then secretly instructed the Commandant of Justice, Zhāng Tāng,
to impeach Wǔ Bèi,
claiming he had plotted treason.
Thus, the nine clans of the two Bèi were executed,
exactly as the Eight Lords had foretold.
The Han histories concealed this,
not stating that Liú Ān had attained the way of immortality,
fearing that later rulers of the world
would neglect all affairs of state
and compete in seeking Liú Ān's path.
Instead, they said Liú Ān committed suicide after being accused,
and did not become an immortal.
According to Zuǒ Wú's records,
before Liú Ān departed,
he wanted to execute the two Bèi,
but the Eight Lords advised:
"It cannot be done.
Those who depart as immortals do not wish to harm even crawling insects,
let alone humans."
Liú Ān then desisted.
He also asked the Eight Lords:
"May I bring along my close friends and relatives to that place,
and then send them back?"
The Lords said:
"Why not?
But no more than five people."
Liú Ān then took Zuǒ Wú, Wáng Juàn, Fù Shēng, and two others—five in total—
to Xuánzhōu,
and then sent them back.
Zuǒ Wú's records describe in detail:
Liú Ān had not yet ascended to heaven
when he encountered various immortal elders.
Liú Ān had been accustomed to nobility from a young age,
rarely showing humble courtesy.
His sitting and rising lacked reverence,
his speech was loud and clear,
and he mistakenly referred to himself as "guǎrén" (this humble one).
Thereupon, the presiding immortal elder reported Liú Ān, saying:
He shows disrespect
and should be expelled.
The Eight Lords apologized on his behalf,
and he was pardoned,
but demoted to guard the capital's latrines for three years.
Later, he became a wandering immortal,
unable to hold any position,
only achieving immortality without death.
Emperor Wǔ heard that Zuǒ Wú and others had followed the King to become immortals and then returned,
so he summoned them
and personally inquired about the details.
Zuǒ Wú answered fully.
The Emperor was greatly regretful and resentful,
and sighed, saying:
"If I could become the King of Huáinán,
I would regard the world as a cast-off sandal."
He then began recruiting worthy scholars,
also hoping to encounter the Eight Lords.
He could not succeed,
and was deceived by Gōngsūn Qīng, Luán Dà, and others.
Still not giving up his intent,
he hoped to obtain the true way.
Because Liú Ān's departure to become an immortal was clear,
he knew for certain that immortals truly existed in the world.
People at the time spread that when the Eight Lords and Liú Ān departed,
the remaining medicine vessels were left in the central courtyard.
Chickens and dogs licked and pecked at them,
and all ascended to heaven.
Thus, cocks crow in the heavens,
and dogs bark among the clouds.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn" (Biographies of Immortals).
Yīn Chángshēng
Yīn Chángshēng was
a native of Xīnyě,
a relative of the Han empress.
Though born into a wealthy and noble family from a young age,
he did not care for glory and status,
devoting himself solely to the arts of the Dao.
Hearing that Mǎ Míngshēng had attained the Way of transcending the world,
he sought him out,
and upon meeting him,
took on the duties of a servant,
personally performing menial tasks like carrying his shoes.
Míngshēng did not teach him the method for transcending the world,
but only engaged in lofty discussions with him day and night,
talking about contemporary affairs,
and managing agricultural work.
This continued for over ten years,
yet Chángshēng never slackened.
Of the twelve people who served Míngshēng alongside him,
all eventually left and returned home,
only Chángshēng remained, his reverence growing ever more solemn.
Míngshēng then told him:
"You are truly capable of attaining the Dao."
He then took him into the Qīngchéng Mountains,
where he boiled yellow earth into gold to show him.
Facing west, he erected an altar,
and bestowed upon him the "Tàiqīng Shéndān Jīng."
Míngshēng then departed.
Chángshēng returned home,
combined the ingredients and completed the elixir.
He consumed half a dose,
not finishing it
The Yúnjí Qīqiān, scroll 106, quoting the "Biography of Zhēnjūn Yīn," lacks the character "finish"
and immediately ascended to heaven.
He then produced over a hundred thousand catties of gold,
distributing it to benefit the impoverished throughout the world,
regardless of whether he knew them or not.
Traveling throughout the land,
he was accompanied by his wife and children,
and his entire family enjoyed longevity without aging.
He remained among the people for over three hundred years,
and later, east of Píngdū Mountain,
he ascended to heaven in broad daylight and departed.
He authored nine essays,
saying:
"There were many immortals in high antiquity,
too many to discuss fully.
But since the rise of the Han dynasty,
forty-five people have attained immortality,
making six including myself.
Twenty achieved liberation through simulated death,
while the rest all ascended to heaven in broad daylight."
The Bàopǔzǐ states:
"Hóng has heard a proverb in books saying:
'If you do not travel at night,
how can you know there are night travelers on the road?'
Now, those who have not attained immortality,
how can they know that among the mountains and forests of the world there are no students of the Dao who have attained immortality?"
Lord Yīn had already consumed the divine medicine,
and though he had not yet fully ascended to heaven,
as things of a kind gather together,
and like voices respond to each other,
he naturally assembled with the immortals.
Seeking and inquiring based on what he heard and saw,
he thus knew the number of these recent immortals.
Yet common people consider this untrue;
because they themselves have not heard of it,
they claim it does not exist.
Is this not lamentable?
As for scholars dwelling in the wilds,
who find fulfillment in reclusion,
amusing themselves with classical texts,
not displaying literary brilliance,
not spreading their fame,
not seeking advancement,
not striving for renown,
people still cannot recognize them.
How much less would immortals be in any hurry
to make their words known
to those who seek fame at the imperial court?
Lord Yīn himself recounted:
"In the first year of the Yánguāng era of the Han dynasty,
I, a son from north of the Xīnyě mountains,
received the essential formula for the divine elixir from an immortal lord.
Having achieved the Dao and departed the world,
I entrust it to the famous mountains.
If anyone obtains it,
they shall be ranked among the Perfected,
free to come and go.
Why bother with vulgar opinions?
The essential art of immortality
lies in the divine elixir.
Circulating breath and guiding energy,
bending and stretching,
consuming herbs and plants—
these may prolong life,
but cannot transcend the world,
much less lead to immortality.
If you wish to hear of the Dao,
these are the essential words.
Accumulated learning leads to it;
acting through non-action unites with the spirit.
Superior individuals undertake it,
striving diligently with added effort.
Inferior fools laugh loudly,
considering it untrue.
Only by knowing the divine elixir
can one gaze long upon eternal peace."
Thereupon, Lord Yīn tore a piece of yellow silk
and copied the "Elixir Classic" once,
sealing it in a stone box,
and placed it on Sōnggāo Mountain.
Another copy on yellow catalpa slips,
inscribed in lacquer,
sealed in a green jade box,
was placed on Tàihuà Mountain.
Another copy on golden slips,
engraved and inscribed,
sealed in a silver box,
was placed on Shǔ Suō Mountain.
One copy on silk,
combined into ten chapters,
was entrusted to disciples,
so that it might be passed down through generations.
He also composed three poems
to show to future generations.
The first says:
"My ancestors of old
assisted the rulers of Táng and Yú,
extending to the Han dynasty.
Adorned with purple and ai insignia.
I
The character 'I' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Ming manuscript
alone loved the Dao,
remaining a common man.
Noble and pure in aspiration,
I served no prince or marquis.
Coveting life, I gained life—
what more could I seek?
Transcending traces into the azure heavens,
riding dragons, driving on emptiness.
Qīngyāo
The character 'yāo' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Ming manuscript.
The Qing dynasty Huáng Shèng edition has 'qīngfēng' (green wind) for 'qīngyāo'
bears me on its wings,
becoming my companion.
Entering fire, I am not scorched;
treading waves, I am not wet.
Wandering freely in the Supreme Ultimate,
what cares, what worries?
Proudly sporting in the immortal capital,
I look down pitying the foolish masses.
The passing of years and fate
is like those river currents.
Suddenly, before long,
they become companions of mud and earth.
Rushing about seeking death,
unwilling to rest even briefly."
The second poem says:
"My
The character 'my' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Ming manuscript
holy teacher,
embodied the truth of the Dao.
Ascending and descending, transforming and changing,
he neighbored Qiáo and Sōng.
Only my fellow students,
twelve in number,
endured cold and hardship seeking the Dao,
for twenty years.
Most among them grew idle and negligent,
their will and conduct not steadfast.
Alas, these men—
fate comes from Heaven itself.
Heaven does not bestow recklessly;
the Dao must return to the worthy.
Their bodies buried in dark soil,
when can they return?
I sigh for you who come after:
diligently refine with utmost care.
Do not be led astray
by vulgar customs, wealth, and honor.
Once the divine Dao is achieved,
ascend to those nine heavens.
Longevity matching the three lights,
not merely billions and thousands."
The third poem says:
"Since I tied my hair as a youth,
I have loved the Dao and its virtue.
Abandoning home to follow my teacher,
east, west, south, and north,
I cast aside the five turbidities.
The Ming manuscript has 'completely' for 'cast aside,'
and 'classics' for 'turbidities'
Avoiding the world, hiding myself,
for over thirty years.
By the side of famous mountains,
in cold, no time for clothes,
Hungry, yet no time to eat;
yearning, yet not daring to return;
weary, yet not daring to rest.
Serving the holy master,
striving to please with joyful countenance,
face grimy, feet calloused—
only then was I praised and honored
(the characters "praised and honored" were originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript)
and thus received the essential teachings,
with grace profound beyond measure.
Wife and children extended in years,
all enjoying boundless longevity.
Gold and silver achieved,
wealth in thousands of millions,
commanding spirits and ghosts,
jade maidens attending by my side.
Now attaining transcendence of the world,
by the power of the divine elixir."
Yīn Jūn lived among the common people for one hundred and seventy years,
his complexion like that of a maiden,
ascending to heaven in broad daylight and departing.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn*
Zhāng Dàolíng
Zhāng Dàolíng was a native of
Pèiguó.
Originally a scholar at the Imperial Academy,
he was well-versed in the Five Classics.
Later in life, he sighed and said:
"This is of no benefit to one's lifespan."
Thereupon, he studied the Way of Longevity,
and obtained the Yellow Emperor's "Nine Cauldrons Elixir Method."
He wished to prepare it,
but the required medicines all cost a great deal of money and silk.
As Dàolíng's family was always poor,
he wanted to make a living,
but managing fields, herding, and raising livestock
were not his strengths,
so he did not succeed.
Hearing that the people of Shǔ were mostly simple and honest,
easy to teach and transform,
and that there were many famous mountains there,
he entered Shǔ with his disciples.
They resided at Húmíng Mountain,
where he composed twenty-four books on the Dao.
Then he concentrated his thoughts and refined his will.
Suddenly, celestial beings descended,
with thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of riders,
golden carriages and feathered canopies,
harnessing dragons and driving tigers—
too many to count.
Some called themselves the Pillar Scribe,
others called themselves the Youth of the Eastern Sea.
They then bestowed upon Dàolíng the newly revealed Way of "Zhèngyī Míngwēi."
Dàolíng received it,
and was able to cure illnesses.
Thereupon, the common people unanimously
served him as their master,
and the households of his disciples reached tens of thousands.
He then established Jìjiǔ positions,
to separately lead these households,
much like official chiefs.
He also established regulations and systems,
ordering his disciples
to take turns contributing rice, silk, utensils, paper, brushes, firewood, sundries, and the like according to circumstances,
and leading people to repair roads.
Those who did not repair them
were all made to fall ill.
Wherever in the county there were bridges and roads that needed repair,
the common people would then cut grass and clear filth,
doing everything necessary,
all according to his will.
But the foolish did not know this was created by Dàolíng,
and thought these writings had come down from heaven.
Dàolíng also wished to govern people through a sense of shame and integrity,
and disliked applying punishments.
So he established regulations:
Those who had illnesses
were to write down in detail the offenses they had committed since birth,
then write them by hand and cast them into water,
making a covenant with the spirits,
vowing not to break the law again,
and pledging with their very lives.
Thereupon, the people, mindful of this,
whenever they happened to fall ill,
would immediately confess their faults.
On one hand, they would be cured;
on the other, it made them feel ashamed,
daring not to offend again,
and moreover, they would reform out of fear of Heaven and Earth.
From then on,
those who had transgressed
all reformed and became good.
Dàolíng thus obtained much wealth and goods,
with which he purchased the medicines
to compound the elixir.
When the elixir was completed,
he took half a dose.
Not wishing to ascend to heaven immediately,
he was instead able to divide his form and become several tens of people.
In the pond in front of his dwelling,
Dàolíng often rode a boat and amused himself.
Meanwhile, the various Daoist priests and guests
came and went, filling the courtyard and lane.
The original text had "gài" for "lane";
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
On the seat there was always one Dàolíng
conversing with guests,
eating and drinking together,
while the true Dàolíng was still in the pond.
As for his methods of curing illnesses,
they all drew from Xuánsù techniques,
only altering their main outlines,
changing their beginning and end,
but the broad path still led to the same destination.
Circulating qì and consuming substances,
thus using immortal methods,
were also unchangeable.
Therefore, Dàolíng said to the people:
"You all still have many worldly habits not yet eliminated,
unable to abandon the world.
You may only obtain from me the practices of circulating qì, guiding and pulling, and chamber arts;
or perhaps obtain the recipes for consuming herbs to live for several hundred years."
As for the essential teachings of the Nine Cauldrons,
he entrusted them only to Wáng Cháng.
And later, there would be one person coming from the east
who should obtain them.
This person would certainly arrive at noon on the seventh day of the first month,
and he described his height and appearance.
When the time came, there indeed was a man named Zhào Shēng.
He did not come from the east.
The Ming manuscript lacks the character "not."
They had never
The original text had "yuán" for "never";
changed according to the Ming manuscript and the Chén collated edition.
met before,
yet his appearance was exactly as Dàolíng had described.
Dàolíng then tested Shēng seven times,
and he passed them all.
Only then did he impart the elixir scriptures to Shēng.
The seven tests were:
The first test:
When Shēng arrived at the gate, he was not admitted.
People were sent to curse and insult him.
For over forty days,
he slept outdoors and did not leave,
only then was he admitted.
The second test:
Shēng was sent to guard the millet in the grass and drive away beasts.
At dusk, an exceptionally beautiful woman was sent,
who claimed to be traveling far,
passing by and seeking lodging.
Her bed was placed next to Shēng's.
The next day, she again claimed her feet were sore and did not leave,
thus staying for several days.
She also flirted and teased,
but Shēng ultimately did not lose his integrity.
The third test:
While Shēng was walking on the road,
he suddenly saw thirty jars of abandoned gold.
Shēng walked past them and did not take them.
The fourth:
Shēng was ordered to go into the mountains to gather firewood.
Three tigers confronted him,
biting his clothes,
but did not injure his body.
Shēng was not afraid,
his expression did not change.
He said to the tigers:
"I am a Daoist priest.
Since youth, I have done no wrong.
Therefore, I have come a thousand miles without regard to the distance,
to serve the divine master,
seeking the Way of Longevity.
Why are you acting like this?
Is it not the mountain spirits who sent you to test me?"
After a short while,
the tigers then got up and left.
The fifth test:
Shēng bought over ten bolts of silk at the market.
After paying the price,
the silk seller falsely accused him,
saying he had not received payment.
Shēng then took off his own clothes,
sold them to buy silk and repay the man,
showing not the slightest sign of reluctance.
The sixth test:
Shēng was guarding the grain in the fields.
A man came, kowtowing and begging for food.
His clothes were torn and shabby,
his face dusty and grimy,
his body covered in sores and pus,
foul and disgusting.
Shēng was deeply moved,
his countenance stirred with compassion.
He took off his clothes and clothed the man,
prepared food with his own provisions,
and also gave him his own rice.
The seventh test:
Dàolíng led his disciples
to the top of a sheer cliff on Yúntái.
Below, there was a peach tree,
thick as a man's arm,
growing beside the stone cliff,
overlooking an unfathomable abyss.
The peach tree bore large fruit.
Dàolíng said to his disciples:
"Whoever can obtain the fruit of this peach tree,
I will tell him the essential teachings of the Dao."
At that time, over three hundred people lay down and peered over,
their thighs trembling and sweating,
none daring to look down for long.
All retreated and returned,
apologizing that they could not obtain it.
Shēng alone said:
"With divine protection,
what danger is there?
The sage master is here;
he will certainly not let me die in the valley.
Since the master has instructed thus,
it must be that this peach can indeed be obtained."
He then leaped down from above,
landing on the tree,
without stumbling or slipping.
He picked peaches until his arms were full.
But the stone cliff was steep and treacherous,
with nothing to hold onto,
so he could not return.
So he threw the peaches up one by one,
exactly two hundred and two in total.
Zhāng Líng received them and distributed one to each of his disciples,
ate one himself,
and kept one for Zhào Shēng.
Zhāng Líng then reached out his hand to pull Shēng up,
and everyone watched as
Zhāng Líng’s arm extended two or three zhang,
pulling Shēng up,
and Shēng suddenly returned.
He then gave Shēng the peach he had kept for him.
After Shēng finished eating the peach,
Zhāng Líng stood at the edge of the valley,
smiled playfully, and said:
"Zhào Shēng’s heart is upright,
so he could throw himself onto the tree
without stumbling.
Now I wish to test myself by jumping down,
and I should be able to obtain a great peach."
Everyone tried to dissuade him,
only Shēng and Wáng Cháng remained silent.
Zhāng Líng then leaped into the air,
but did not land on a peach,
and disappeared.
Everyone looked up in all directions,
above, the sky stretched endlessly,
below, there was no bottom,
and there was no path to follow,
leaving them all astonished and weeping in sorrow.
Only Shēng and Cháng,
after a long while, said to each other:
"Our master is like a father to us.
He has thrown himself into an unfathomable abyss—
how can we remain at ease?"
So they both leaped down,
and landed right in front of Zhāng Líng.
They saw Zhāng Líng sitting on a low-legged bed inside a tent,
and he smiled at Shēng and Cháng, saying:
"I knew you would come."
He then taught them the Dao,
and after three days, they returned.
They went back to their old dwelling,
where the other disciples were still astonished and grieving.
Later, Zhāng Líng, Shēng, and Cháng,
all ascended into the sky in broad daylight and departed.
The disciples looked up at them,
and after a long while, they disappeared into the clouds.
Earlier,
when Zhāng Líng entered the Shǔ Mountains,
he had refined half a dose of elixir,
and though he had not yet ascended,
he had already become an earthbound immortal.
Thus, he devised seven trials
to test Zhào Shēng,
in order to know
("zhī" originally written as "rú,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript and Chén’s revised edition)
his determination.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn"
Lǐ Shàojūn
Lǐ Shàojūn was
a man from Qí.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn recruited fangshi (masters of esoteric arts).
Shàojūn obtained from Master Ānqī the formula for the divine elixir and the furnace fire,
but his family was poor,
and he could not afford the ingredients.
He said to his disciples:
"Old age is approaching,
and my wealth is insufficient.
Even if I toil personally at farming,
it will not be enough to procure them.
Now the Son of Heaven is fond of the Way,
I wish to go and see him,
to seek to compound the medicine for him,
so I may do as I please."
He then presented the formula to the emperor,
saying:
"Cinnabar can be transformed into gold,
and when the gold is perfected, consuming it leads to ascension as an immortal.
Your subject once roamed the seas,
and saw Master Ānqī,
eating dates as large as melons."
The Son of Heaven held him in great esteem and respect,
bestowing upon him countless gifts.
Shàojūn once dined with Marquis Wǔ'ān,
among the guests was an old man,
over ninety years old.
Shàojūn asked his name,
and then said he had once roamed at night with the old man's grandfather
(Míng chāo běn notes 'night' as 'shooting'
and saw a child following his grandfather,
hence I recognize him.
At that, everyone present was astonished.
Also, Shàojūn saw that Emperor Wǔ had an old bronze vessel,
and recognizing it, said:
"Duke Huán of Qí often displayed this vessel by his resting seat."
The emperor checked and looked at its inscription,
and it was indeed an old vessel from Qí.
From this, he knew Shàojūn was a man of several hundred years.
He appeared to be around fifty,
his complexion and skin
were very lustrous,
and his mouth and teeth were like a child's.
Princes, dukes, and noblemen,
hearing he could make men immortal,
all admired him,
and the money and valuables given to him piled up like mountains.
Shàojūn then secretly concocted the divine elixir.
When the elixir was completed,
he said to the emperor:
"Your Majesty cannot cease arrogance and extravagance,
abandon music and beauty,
the killing and warfare do not stop,
your joy and anger are unrestrained.
Over ten thousand li, there are souls that do not return;
in the marketplaces and execution grounds, there are punishments that shed blood.
The great Way of the divine elixir
cannot be attained."
He then gave a small medicinal formula to the emperor,
and Shàojūn then claimed illness.
That night,
the emperor dreamed he and Shàojūn ascended Mount Sōnghāo together.
Halfway,
a messenger riding a dragon, holding a tally, came from amidst the clouds,
saying Tàiyǐ requested Shàojūn.
The emperor then awoke,
and immediately sent someone to inquire about Shàojūn's news,
and told his close ministers:
"Last night I dreamed Shàojūn abandoned me and left."
Shàojūn then became gravely ill.
The emperor went to see him,
and also sent someone to receive his formulas.
Before the matter was finished, he died.
The emperor said:
"Shàojūn did not die,
he merely transformed and left."
When they prepared the body for burial,
suddenly the corpse was missing from its place.
The inner and outer garments were all intact,
like a cicada shedding its skin.
The emperor sighed even more deeply,
regretting that he had not sought Shàojūn more diligently.
Initially, Shàojūn was close and affectionate with Court Discussion Lang Dǒng Zhònggōng.
Zhònggōng long had an illness,
his body withered and his qi was scant.
Shàojūn then gave him two doses of completed medicine,
along with its formula.
It used the herb of Wù-Sì,
Hòutǔ fat,
Huángjīng root,
beast sinking fat,
Xiānyǒu root,
fermented from a hundred flowers,
in the first ten days of the Hài month,
combined and decocted in a bronze vessel,
have a youth bathe and purify himself,
adjust the heat of the decoction,
to combine it into forms the size of chicken eggs,
three pieces constituting one course.
After finishing one dose,
the body becomes light;
after three doses,
teeth that fell out regrow;
after five doses,
one's lifespan lengthens and will not decline again.
Zhònggōng was a person of firm integrity,
learned in the Five Classics,
but he did not comprehend the arts of the Way.
He laughed at people in the world taking medicine and studying the Way,
and repeatedly submitted memorials admonishing Emperor Wǔ,
believing that human life is destined,
aging and decline follow a constant pattern,
and cannot be prolonged by arts of the Way.
Although he noticed Shàojūn was extraordinary,
he thought it was his innate nature,
not caused by arts.
He obtained the medicine but ultimately did not take it,
nor did he inquire about the formula.
Several months after Shàojūn left,
Zhònggōng became gravely ill.
He often heard Emperor Wǔ speak of the previous dream,
and regret missing Shàojūn.
Zhònggōng remembered the medicine Shàojūn had left him.
He tried taking it.
Before half was gone,
his body became light and strong,
and his illness suddenly vanished.
After finishing it,
his strength was like in his youth.
Only then did he believe there was a Way of long life and immortality.
He resigned from his post,
traveled seeking Daoist masters,
to ask about the formula,
but ultimately could not fully understand it.
Zhònggōng only achieved that his hair did not turn white,
his appearance was very robust,
and he died after reaching over eighty.
He instructed his son Dàoshēng:
"I obtained Shàojūn's medicinal formula in my youth.
Initially I did not believe,
only after the fact did I gain its benefit,
but was unable to comprehend it,
and will harbor regret in the Yellow Springs.
You should travel and seek matters of human arts and techniques,
understand the meaning of the formula,
long take this medicine,
and you will certainly transcend the world."
At that time, there was General Wénchéng,
who also obtained Shàojūn's arts.
He served Emperor Wǔ.
Later, the emperor sent an envoy to execute him.
Wénchéng said to the envoy:
"Convey my thanks to the emperor.
Could he not endure a short while and thus ruined a great affair?
May the emperor take good care of himself.
Thirty years from now,
seek me at Chéngshān.
Then we shall work together,
with no resentment between us."
The envoy returned,
and reported his words in detail.
The emperor ordered the coffin opened to look,
but there was nothing to be seen,
only a single bamboo tube.
The emperor suspected his disciples had stolen and hidden the corpse,
so he arrested them,
investigated and questioned for traces.
The emperor then greatly regretted executing Wénchéng.
Later, he again summoned various fangshi,
and again sacrificed to Tàiyǐ at Gānquán,
and separately set up an altar to sacrifice to Wénchéng,
with the emperor personally performing the rites.
Originally missing the source,
found to be from "Shénxiān Zhuàn" (Biographies of Divine Immortals).
Kǒng Yuánfāng was a native of Xǔchāng.
He regularly consumed medicines such as pine resin, poria cocos, and pine nuts,
and grew more youthful with age,
his appearance resembling that of a man around forty.
Xì Yuánjié and Zuǒ Yuánfàng were both his close friends;
they all abandoned the Confucian classics and the worldly affairs of their time
to devote themselves to cultivating the Daoist arts.
Yuánfāng was benevolent and kind,
wore coarse clothes and ate simple food,
and never drank more than one shēng of wine.
He was over seventy years old.
Sometimes Daoist practitioners would invite Yuánfāng to join them for a drinking gathering.
When it was Yuánfāng's turn,
he would propose a drinking game:
propping his staff on the ground,
he would then grip the staff with his hands and stand upside down,
head below and feet above,
holding a cup with one hand and drinking while inverted—
something no one else could do.
Yuánfāng had a wife and children
but did not accumulate surplus wealth,
cultivating the five grains to some extent.
Once, when a fire broke out,
many people came to help put it out,
carrying out clothing, grain, beds, and small tables from under the house.
Yuánfāng, however, did not assist at all,
merely sitting with his legs sprawled out by the fence, watching the fire.
His wife urged him to help gather their belongings,
but Yuánfāng laughed and said,
"Why bother clinging to these things?"
He also dug into the bank by the water
to create a cave chamber,
about ten feet square.
Yuánfāng would enter it to practice grain abstention,
sometimes for one or two months,
before returning.
His family members were also not allowed to come and go.
In front of the cave was a cypress tree,
growing among thorns and grass behind the path,
twisting and hidden from view.
If disciples had urgent matters
and wished to visit Yuánfāng's cave chamber,
none could find it.
Later, a youth from the east,
named Féng Yù,
who was fond of the Dao,
waited upon Yuánfāng
and eventually managed to find the cave chamber and see him.
Yuánfāng said,
"Many have come
but could not see me.
Since you have managed to see me,
it seems you can be taught."
He then gave him two volumes of plain-text books, saying,
"These contain the essential teachings of the Dao.
They can be transmitted to only one person every forty years.
If there is no suitable person in the world,
they must not be recklessly transmitted merely because the time limit is fulfilled.
If no one is transmitted to within forty years,
then after eighty years, if two people are worthy of transmission,
both may be transmitted to at once.
To be able to transmit but not transmit is called 'closing the Heavenly Dao';
to transmit to one who should not receive it is called 'leaking the Heavenly Dao'—
both bring calamity upon one's descendants.
I have now found someone to transmit to,
so I shall depart."
He then left his wife and children and entered the Western Peak.
More than fifty years later,
he briefly returned to his hometown,
and there were still people who recognized him.
From Biographies of the Divine Immortals.
Wáng Liè,
courtesy name Chángxiū,
was a native of Hándān.
He regularly consumed Solomon's Seal and lead,
and at the age of three hundred and thirty-eight,
he still retained a youthful appearance.
He climbed mountains and traversed perilous terrain,
walking as if flying.
In his youth, he was originally a scholar at the Imperial Academy,
having studied all texts without exception.
He often engaged in discussions with others on the sayings of the Five Classics and the Hundred Schools of Thought,
and his knowledge was comprehensive and extensive.
The Grand Master for Court Discussion, Jī Shūyè of Qiáoguó,
held him in great respect and affection,
frequently seeking his teachings.
They would enter the mountains together to roam and gather herbs.
Later, Liè went alone into the Tàiháng Mountains,
when suddenly he heard a rumbling from the east of the mountain like thunder.
Liè did not know what it was
and went to look.
He saw that the mountain had split open for several hundred zhàng,
with both sides composed of blue stone.
Within the stone was a cave opening,
about a foot in diameter,
from which a blue mud flowed out like marrow.
Liè took some of the mud and tried to form it into pellets;
in a short while, it turned into stone,
resembling the state of heated wax,
hardening and solidifying as he handled it.
Its aroma was like that of cooked non-glutinous rice,
and chewing it produced the same sensation.
Liè combined several pellets the size of peaches,
took a small amount back with him,
and said to Shūyè,
"I have obtained something extraordinary."
Shūyè was very pleased,
took it to examine,
but it had already turned into blue stone,
and when struck, it clanged like bronze.
Shūyè then went with Liè to see the site,
but the broken mountain had already returned to its original state.
Liè entered the Bàodú Mountains in Hédōng,
where he saw a stone chamber.
Inside the chamber was a white stone shelf,
on which lay two volumes of plain-text books.
Liè took them to read
but could not recognize the script,
so he did not dare take them away.
He placed them back on the shelf.
He secretly memorized several dozen characters from their forms
and showed them to Kāng.
Kāng recognized all the characters.
Delighted, Liè
went with Kāng to read them together.
When they reached the path,
it was clear and distinct,
but by the time they arrived,
the stone chamber had vanished.
Liè privately told his disciples,
"It is because Shūyè is not yet destined to attain the Dao."
Furthermore, according to the Scripture of Divine Immortals,
every five hundred years, a divine mountain opens,
and within it, stone marrow emerges.
If one obtains and consumes it,
one's lifespan equals that of Heaven.
What Liè obtained earlier must have been this.
In Hédōng, many people from Wénxǐ served Liè for generations.
During the Yǒngníng era of the Jìn dynasty,
he emerged in Luòxià,
traveled to various places,
and engaged in archery contests with others.
Liè drew a two-dàn bow,
shooting from a hundred paces,
with ten arrows shot,
nine hitting the target.
After a year, he departed again.
There was also a man named Zhāng Zǐdào,
over ninety years old,
who paid respects to Liè,
and Liè received his bow while sitting upright.
Those present found it strange,
but Zǐdào said,
"When I was eight or nine years old, I saw him,
and his appearance was no different from now.
Now I am old,
yet Liè still retains a youthful countenance."
Later, no one knew where he went.
From Biographies of the Divine Immortals.
Jiāo Xiān
Jiāo Xiān,
styled Xiàorán,
was a man from Hédōng.
He lived to be one hundred and seventy years old.
He often ate white stones,
which he shared with others,
boiling them until soft like taro before eating.
Every day, he went into the mountains to gather firewood to give to people.
Starting from the first house in the village,
he would go around in cycles.
He would carry the firewood and place it outside people’s doors.
When people saw him,
they would spread a mat and invite him to sit,
offering him food.
Jiāo Xiān would then sit.
He did not speak to anyone.
When he brought firewood,
if he did not see anyone,
he would secretly leave it at the door,
then depart.
He continued this for many years.
When the Wei dynasty received the abdication,
he lived by the riverbank,
building a thatched hut,
and dwelling there alone.
He did not set up a bed or mat,
using only a grass cushion to sit on.
His body was covered in filth,
as muddy as a swamp.
Sometimes he ate only once every few days,
walked without following paths,
and did not associate with women.
When his clothes wore out,
he would sell firewood to buy old clothes to wear,
wearing only a single layer in both winter and summer.
The prefect Dǒng Jīng
went to visit him,
but he still refused to speak.
Dǒng Jīng thus considered him even more virtuous.
Once, a wildfire burned his hut,
and people went to check on him.
They saw Jiāo Xiān sitting upright beneath the hut, unmoving.
After the fire passed and the hut was reduced to ashes,
Jiāo Xiān slowly rose,
his clothes completely unburned.
He then built another hut.
Suddenly, heavy snow fell,
and many people’s houses collapsed.
Jiāo Xiān’s hut also fell.
People went to look but could not find him,
fearing he had frozen to death.
They dismantled the hut to search for him,
and found Jiāo Xiān sleeping soundly beneath the snow,
his complexion radiant,
his breathing calm and steady,
as if sleeping off a drunken stupor on a hot summer day.
People realized he was extraordinary,
and many wished to follow him and learn the Way.
Jiāo Xiān said:
“I possess no Way.”
Sometimes he appeared old, sometimes young,
and lived like this for over two hundred years.
Later, he bid farewell to people and left,
and no one knew where he went.
Those who sought him never managed to get a single word from him.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn*
Sūn Dēng
Sūn Dēng
was a man of unknown origins.
He often dwelled in the mountains,
sitting in a cave,
playing the qin and reading the *Yìjīng*.
He wore only a single layer of clothing in both winter and summer.
When the weather was extremely cold,
people would see him
using his own hair to cover his body,
his hair being over ten feet long.
He also had an exceptionally refined appearance,
and across generations, people who saw him
noted that his complexion remained unchanged.
When he received money or goods from begging in the market,
he would give them to the poor,
keeping nothing for himself,
and he was never seen eating.
At the time, Yáng Jùn served as Grand Tutor,
and he sent messengers to invite Sūn Dēng,
but Sūn Dēng did not respond to their inquiries.
Yáng Jùn gave him a cloth robe,
which he accepted.
Upon leaving,
he borrowed a knife from someone,
cut the robe into two parts,
placed them at Yáng Jùn’s gate,
and then further chopped them into pieces.
People at the time thought him mad,
but later they realized that Yáng Jùn was destined to be executed,
so Sūn Dēng had created an omen of this.
Yáng Jùn detained him,
not allowing him to leave,
and Sūn Dēng eventually died.
Yáng Jùn provided a coffin
and buried him at Zhènqiáo.
A few days later,
someone saw Sūn Dēng at Dǒngmǎpō,
and he sent a letter to an old friend in Luòxià.
Jī Shūyè had ambitions transcending the mundane world,
and once visited Sūn Dēng,
but Sūn Dēng did not speak to him.
Jī Shūyè then posed challenging questions,
yet Sūn Dēng continued playing the qin calmly.
After a long while,
as Jī Shūyè was about to leave,
Sūn Dēng said:
“Young man, you are talented but lack wisdom,
and are poor at preserving yourself.
Can you avoid calamity?”
Soon after, Jī Shūyè was indeed executed.
Jī Shūyè was skilled at playing the qin,
so Sūn Dēng played a single-stringed qin,
producing a complete melody.
Jī Shūyè then sighed in admiration and gave up further thought.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn*
Lǚ Wénjìng
Lǚ Gōng,
courtesy name Wénjìng,
was fond of taking elixirs from a young age.
Taking one male servant and one maidservant,
he went to gather medicinal herbs in the Tàiháng Mountains.
Suddenly, he saw three people in a valley,
who asked Gōng:
"Do you seek immortality,
that you toil so arduously and dangerously like this?"
Gōng replied:
"I truly seek immortality,
but have not yet encountered a proper method.
Therefore, I gather and take these herbs,
hoping for some slight benefit."
One of them said:
"My surname is Lǚ, courtesy name Wénqǐ."
The next one said:
"My surname is Sūn, courtesy name Wényáng."
The next one said:
"My surname is Wáng, courtesy name Wénshàng."
These three were all immortals from the Tàiqīng Tàihé Prefecture.
"We have come to gather herbs for a time,
intending to complete the training of a new disciple.
Since you share our surname,
and your courtesy name contains half of mine,
this means your destiny is aligned with eternal life.
If you can follow us to gather herbs,
we will tell you the formula for immortality."
Gōng immediately bowed and said:
"I am fortunate to have encountered immortals,
but I fear I am dull and have many faults,
and am unworthy of instruction.
If you see fit to accept me,
it would fulfill my wish for rebirth."
He then followed the immortals for two days,
whereupon they bestowed upon Gōng a secret formula,
and sent him away, saying:
"You may return to see your hometown."
Gōng bowed in farewell,
and the three said to him:
"You have been here two days,
but in the mortal world, two hundred years have already passed."
Gōng returned home,
but saw only an empty house,
with not a single one of his descendants remaining.
He then met a man named Zhào Fǔ, a descendant of his fellow villagers several generations later,
and asked where all of Lǚ Gōng's family members had gone.
Fǔ said:
"Where have you come from,
that you ask about people from so long ago?
I once heard my ancestors say that
long ago, there was a Lǚ Gōng
who took his servants into the Tàiháng Mountains to gather herbs
and never returned.
It was thought he had been eaten by tigers or wolves,
and that was over two hundred years ago.
Lǚ Gōng has a descendant several generations later named Lǚ Xí,
who lives over ten lǐ east of the city,
practices as a Daoist priest,
and is revered by many of the common people.
He should be easy to find."
Following Fǔ's words,
Gōng went to Xí's home
and knocked on the gate to inquire.
A servant came out
and asked where the gentleman had come from.
Gōng said:
"This is my home.
I once followed immortals away,
and now over two hundred years have passed."
When Xí heard this, he was shocked and overjoyed.
Barefoot, he rushed out and bowed, saying:
"The immortal ancestor has returned!
I cannot contain my mingled grief and joy."
Gōng then bestowed the divine formula upon Xí and departed.
Xí was already eighty years old;
after taking the formula, he immediately regained youth and vigor.
He lived to two hundred years of age,
then entered the mountains.
His descendants for generations did not age or die.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn* (Biographies of Immortals).
Shěn Jiàn
was from Dānyáng.
His family for generations had been minor officials.
Jiàn alone was fond of the Dao,
refusing to serve in government.
He studied the arts of *dǎoyǐn* (guiding and pulling), taking elixirs,
and methods for restoring youth and repelling old age.
He could also cure illnesses;
regardless of severity,
he would heal them immediately.
Several hundred families revered and served him.
Once, Jiàn wished to travel far,
so he entrusted one maidservant, three male servants, one donkey, and ten sheep
to a host, giving each a single pill.
He told the host:
"They will only be a burden on your housing;
there is no need to trouble yourself with feeding them."
Then he left.
The host thought it very strange, saying:
"This guest has entrusted fifteen beings to me,
leaving not a single coin for their upkeep.
What am I to do?"
After Jiàn left,
the host offered food and drink to the servants,
but when the servants smelled the food,
they all retched and refused it.
When he tried to feed grass to the donkey and sheep,
they avoided it and would not eat;
some even tried to butt him.
The host was greatly astonished.
After over a hundred days,
the servants' bodies and complexions were radiant,
surpassing when they ate normally.
The donkey and sheep were all as plump as if fed.
Jiàn returned after being away for three years,
gave each servant, donkey, and sheep a pill,
and only then did they eat and drink as before.
Jiàn then abstained from grains, eating nothing,
and could travel lightly, flying through the air.
Sometimes he would leave, sometimes return.
He continued like this for over three hundred years,
then vanished without a trace, and none knew where he went.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn* (Biographies of Immortals).
Héshàng Gōng (The Old Man by the River)
Héshàng Gōng —
none knew his surname or given name.
During the time of Emperor Wén of Hàn,
he built a thatched hut by the riverside.
The Emperor was reading the *Lǎozǐ Jīng*,
and was quite fond of it.
He ordered all the princes and high officials to recite it.
There were several points he did not understand,
and no one at the time could explain them.
Hearing that people all said Héshàng Gōng could interpret the meaning and intent of the *Lǎozǐ Jīng*,
he sent someone with the unresolved issues to ask him.
Gōng said:
"The Dao is revered and virtue is precious;
they cannot be inquired about from afar."
The Emperor then visited his hut in person,
and asked him directly.
The Emperor said:
"Under the vast heavens,
there is no land that is not the king's land;
within the borders of the land,
there are none who are not the king's subjects.
Among the 'Four Greats' within the realm,
the king occupies one.
Although you possess the Dao,
you are still my subject.
You cannot humble yourself;
why do you hold yourself so high?"
Gōng immediately clapped his hands, sat up, and leaped,
floating gently into the empty air,
several *zhàng* above the ground.
Looking down and up, he replied:
"Above, I do not reach heaven;
in the middle, I do not burden men;
below, I do not dwell on earth.
How can I be considered a subject?"
The Emperor then descended from his carriage, kowtowed, and said:
"I, lacking in virtue,
have unworthily inherited the ancestral enterprise.
My talent is small, my responsibility great;
I worry I am unequal to the task.
Although I govern worldly affairs, my heart reveres the Dao.
Simply due to my ignorance,
there is much I do not comprehend.
I only wish the Lord of the Dao would instruct me."
Gōng then bestowed two scrolls of a plain-text book upon the Emperor, saying:
"Study them thoroughly.
All doubts regarding this scripture will be resolved.
There is no need for many words.
Since I annotated this scripture,
over seventeen hundred years have passed.
In total, it has been transmitted to three people;
with you, that makes four.
Do not show it to those unworthy."
When he finished speaking,
he vanished from his location.
A moment later,
clouds and mist darkened the sky,
and heaven and earth seemed to merge.
The Emperor held him in the highest esteem.
Commentators believe that because Emperor Wén was fond of the words of Lǎozǐ,
but the age could not fully comprehend them,
a divine person specifically descended to instruct him.
And fearing Emperor Wén's heart was not yet fully believing,
he manifested a divine transformation.
This is what is meant by 'The sage has no constant mind;
he takes the mind of the people as his mind.'
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn* (Biographies of Immortals).
Liú Gēn
nor can one become an immortal.
Among the superior medicines,
there are the Nine-Cycle Reverted Elixir and the Supreme Unity's Golden Liquor; consuming them enables one to immediately ascend to heaven,
without accumulating days and months.
Next,
there are substances like mica and realgar;
although they do not instantly allow one to ride clouds and drive dragons,
