they can still command ghosts and spirits,
transform and achieve longevity.
Next are the various herbal medicines,
which can cure all diseases,
replenish deficiencies and preserve youthful appearance,
abstain from grains and boost vital energy,
but cannot make a person immortal.
At best, they can extend life for several hundred years;
at worst, they merely preserve one's natural endowment.
They are insufficient to rely on for long.』
I bowed my head and said:
'Today, receiving this teaching,
is truly heaven-sent.'
The divine being said:
'If you truly desire longevity,
first rid yourself of the Three Corpses.
Once the Three Corpses are gone,
your will and intent will stabilize,
and your cravings and desires will be eliminated.'
He then presented me with five scrolls of divine formulas,
saying:
'The dormant corpses often ascend to heaven on the days of the full moon, new moon, and the last day of the lunar month,
to report a person's offenses and faults.
The Director of Fate then deducts from their allotted lifespan,
causing them not to live long.
The spirits within a person's body
desire the person to live,
while the corpses desire the person to die.
When a person dies, the spirits scatter,
becoming formless ghosts.
When sacrifices are made, they can enjoy the offerings,
hence they desire the person's death.
Dreams of struggling with evil people
are actually battles between the corpses and the spirits.'
I then followed his words,
prepared and consumed them,
and thus attained immortality."
Zhēn also often saw Gēn finish writing talismans,
and when he made summons,
it seemed as if people came to fetch them.
Sometimes, multiple times, he heard questioning,
with someone answering,
and even heard the sounds of whipping and beating,
yet he could not see any forms at all.
Occasionally, there was blood on the ground,
and no one could fathom the reason.
Gēn then taught Zhēn the methods of guarding the One, circulating qi, preserving the spirit,
sitting in observance of the Three Bonds and Six Principles,
and confessing faults to register one's name above.
Later, Gēn entered Jītóu Mountain and became an immortal.
From "Biographies of Immortals"
Lǐ Zhòngfǔ
Lǐ Zhòngfǔ
was a person from Yìlǐ, Fēngyì.
In his youth, he studied the Dao under Wáng Jūn,
consumed water elixirs with effect,
and also practiced Dùnjiǎ,
capable of stepping in sequences and becoming invisible.
Over a hundred years old,
he grew younger.
Initially, he hid for a hundred days,
reappeared after a year,
and later hid permanently,
only his voice could be heard,
conversing with people,
eating and drinking as usual,
but he could not be seen.
There was a scholar surnamed Zhāng,
who came to learn the art of invisibility.
Zhòngfǔ said, "Your temperament is narrow and impatient,
unsuitable for teaching."
However, the scholar persisted relentlessly,
spending hundreds of thousands
to provide wine and food,
yet gained nothing.
Zhāng grew resentful,
and went carrying a dagger.
First, he finished speaking with Zhòngfǔ,
then, following the direction of his voice,
leaped up,
drew the dagger,
and slashed left and right.
Zhòngfǔ was already on the bed,
laughing and saying:
"In the world, there are indeed foolish people like you,
who have not yet attained the Dao,
and seek to kill.
How could I possibly be killed?
I could truly cause your death.
But I pardon your stubborn foolishness,
it is not worth troubling over."
He had someone bring a dog,
placed it before the scholar, and said:
"See if I can kill the dog or not."
As soon as the dog arrived,
its head had already fallen to the ground,
and its belly was torn open.
He then scolded the scholar:
"I can make you end up like this dog."
The scholar knelt on the ground, kowtowed, and only then did it stop;
thus, he was pardoned.
Zhòngfǔ had an acquaintance
who lived over five hundred lǐ away,
and often made a living by setting nets.
One day, while setting nets,
he caught a bird,
and looking at it, it turned out to be Zhòngfǔ.
After speaking, they parted.
That same day,
Zhòngfǔ had already returned home.
He lived among the people for over three hundred years,
then later entered Xīyuè Mountain,
and never returned.
From "Biographies of Immortals"
Lǐ Yìqī
Lǐ Yìqī
was originally from Shǔ,
seen through generations,
a person from the time of Emperor Wén of Hàn.
He had no wife or children.
For those who wished to travel far and arrive quickly,
Yìqī would give them a talisman,
and write in cinnabar under both armpits;
then, even a thousand lǐ could be covered in less than a day and they would return.
Sometimes, when people spoke of the lands of the four directions,
palaces, temples, markets, and hamlets,
which they had never seen before,
the listeners could not grasp the meaning.
Yìqī would then take a pinch of earth and shape it,
only an inch in size,
yet everything within it was present,
vanishing in a moment.
Sometimes, he would go somewhere unknown,
and return after about a year.
Thus, when he begged for food and obtained things,
he would give them to the poor.
In a corner of Chéngdū,
he made an earthen cave to live in,
wearing single-layered clothes in both winter and summer.
He drank a little wine,
and ate dried meat, dates, and chestnuts.
When Liú Xuándé wished to attack Wú,
to avenge Guān Yǔ's death,
he sent for Yìqī.
When Yìqī arrived,
Xuándé treated him with great respect,
and asked about the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of attacking Wú.
Yìqī did not answer,
but asked for paper,
drew tens of thousands of soldiers, horses, and weapons,
then tore each one to pieces,
saying:
Alas.
He then drew a large figure,
dug a hole and buried it,
and went straight back.
Bèi was displeased,
and indeed was defeated by the Wú army,
with over a hundred thousand troops,
only a few hundred returning.
Armor, weapons, and military supplies were almost entirely lost.
Xuándé, filled with rage,
then died in the Yǒng'ān Palace.
Yìqī spoke little;
when people asked him questions,
he barely responded.
When people of Shǔ had worries and troubles,
they would go to ask him;
auspicious or inauspicious signs had their constant indicators,
one only needed to observe his expression.
If he appeared joyful, it was good;
if sorrowful, it was bad.
Later, he entered Lángyá Mountain,
and was never seen to emerge again.
From "Biographies of Immortals"
Wáng Xīng
Wáng Xīng was a man from Yángchéng,
living in Hú Valley,
an ordinary commoner.
He was illiterate and had no intention of studying the Dao.
When Emperor Wǔ of Hàn ascended Mount Sōng,
he climbed the Dàyú Stone Chamber,
built a Daoist palace,
and ordered Dǒng Zhòngshū, Dōngfāng Shuò, and others
to purify themselves and contemplate the spirits.
At night,
they suddenly saw an immortal,
twenty feet tall,
with ears extending from the top of his head
and hanging down to his shoulders.
Emperor Wǔ paid his respects and asked him,
and the immortal said:
"I am a deity from Jiǔyí.
I heard that on the rocks of the Central Peak,
the calamus grows one inch with nine nodes,
and consuming it can grant longevity.
That is why I have come to gather it."
Suddenly, the deity vanished.
The emperor turned to his attendants and said:
"He was not merely a cultivator seeking immortality through herbs;
he must have been a deity of the Central Peak, sent to enlighten me."
Thereupon, he gathered calamus and consumed it.
After two years,
the emperor felt discomfort and unease,
so he stopped.
Many of his officials also consumed it,
but none could persist for long.
Only Wáng Xīng, upon hearing that the immortal had taught Emperor Wǔ to consume calamus,
gathered and consumed it without cease,
and thus attained longevity.
Young and old in his neighborhood
all said they saw him generation after generation.
In the end, no one knew where he went.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn*.
Zhào Qú,
courtesy name Zǐróng,
was a man from Shàngdǎng.
He contracted leprosy,
which grew severe,
bringing him to the brink of death.
Someone advised his family:
"You should abandon him while he is still alive,
for if he dies at home,
your descendants for generations will be plagued by it."
His family prepared a year's worth of provisions for him,
sent him into the mountains,
and fearing harm from tigers and wolves,
barricaded him from the outside with wooden stakes.
Qú grieved and lamented his fate,
weeping day and night.
After more than a hundred days of this,
one night,
he suddenly saw three people in front of the stone chamber,
who asked who he was.
Qú reasoned that in such deep mountains and dense forests,
a place no ordinary person would tread,
they must be divine beings.
He then pleaded his case,
kowtowing and begging for mercy.
The figures moved through the barricade
as if through mist,
encountering no obstruction.
They asked Qú,
"If you truly wish to be cured of your illness,
you must take medicine.
Can you do it?"
Qú replied:
"I, a man of many faults and sins,
afflicted with this vile disease,
have been cast aside and abandoned.
Death is imminent.
If cutting off my feet or slicing my nose could let me live,
I would gladly do it.
How could I refuse to take medicine?"
The divine beings then bestowed upon him five *shēng* each of pine nuts and pine resin,
telling Qú:
"This will not only cure your illness
but also grant you longevity.
Consuming half will heal you,
but do not stop once you are cured."
Before Qú had finished taking it,
he was healed,
his body strong and healthy.
He returned home,
but his family thought he was a ghost.
After he explained what had happened,
they rejoiced.
He continued taking the medicine for two more years,
his complexion growing youthful,
his skin radiant,
and he could run like a flying bird.
In his seventies,
he ate pheasants and rabbits,
chewing even their bones,
and could carry heavy loads without tiring.
At one hundred and seventy,
while sleeping at night,
he suddenly saw a light in the room like a mirror.
When he asked those around him,
they said they saw nothing.
Later, one day,
the entire room grew bright,
and he could write at night.
He then saw two figures on his face,
three feet tall,
beautiful women,
exquisitely lovely,
though small,
playing on his nose.
Gradually, these two women grew
until they were human-sized,
no longer on his face
but appearing before him.
He often heard the sounds of zithers and lutes,
filling him with joy and delight.
He lived among mortals for over three hundred years,
his appearance always like that of a youth,
before entering the mountains,
and none knew where he went.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn*.
Wáng Yáo
Wáng Yáo,
styled Bó Liáo,
was a man from Póyáng.
He had a wife but no children.
He was quite capable of curing illnesses,
and there were none he could not heal.
He did not perform sacrifices,
nor did he use talismanic water, acupuncture, or medicine.
When he practiced healing,
he would only use an eight-foot cloth mat,
spread it on the ground to sit,
and without drinking or eating,
in a short while, the illness would be cured,
and he would then rise and leave.
For those afflicted by evil spirits causing harm,
Yáo would draw a prison on the ground,
then summon them.
Their forms would all become visible,
entering the prison.
Some were creatures like foxes, raccoon dogs, turtles, or snakes.
He would then behead and burn them,
and the patient would immediately recover.
Yáo had a bamboo box,
several inches long.
He had a disciple surnamed Qián,
who had followed Yáo for several decades,
yet had never seen Yáo open it.
One night,
during heavy rain and darkness,
Yáo had Qián carry this box on a nine-section staff,
and took Qián out,
braving the rain to travel.
Both Yáo and his disciple's clothes remained completely dry.
The path they took was not one they had traveled before,
and there were always two torchlights guiding them ahead.
After walking about thirty *li*,
they ascended a small hill,
entered a stone chamber,
where two people were inside.
After Yáo arrived,
he took the box his disciple was carrying and opened it.
Inside were three five-tongued bamboo mouth organs.
Yáo played one himself,
and gave the other two to the two people in the chamber.
They all sat and played them together.
After a long while,
Yáo bid farewell to leave.
He collected the three mouth organs,
and placed them all back into the box,
having Qián carry it.
The two people from the chamber came out to see them off,
and said to Yáo:
"You should come early;
why linger so long in the mundane world?"
Yáo replied:
"I will come when it is time."
Yáo returned home for a hundred days.
When it rained again,
Yáo suddenly began packing his belongings extensively at night.
Yáo previously had a single-layer hemp robe and a hemp cloth headscarf,
which he had not worn for over fifty years.
That night, he took them out and put them on.
His wife immediately asked:
"Are you planning to leave me?"
Yáo said:
"I am only going away for a short while."
His wife said:
"Will you take Qián with you?"
Yáo said:
"I go alone."
His wife then wept and said:
"Please stay a little longer."
Yáo said:
"I will return like this."
He then shouldered the box himself and left,
and never returned.
Over thirty years later,
his disciple saw Yáo at Mǎtí Mountain,
looking even younger,
likely an earthbound immortal.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn*.
According to the table of contents,
there should still be an entry for Chén Yǒngbó following this.
Now lost.
Tài Shān Lǎo Fù
Tài Shān Lǎo Fù,
no one knows his surname or given name.
When Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn dynasty was touring the east,
he saw an old man hoeing by the roadside,
with a white light several feet high above his head.
Finding it strange, the Emperor questioned him.
The old man appeared to be around fifty,
with the complexion of a youth on his face,
his skin radiant and smooth,
unlike ordinary people.
The Emperor asked what arts he practiced.
He replied:
"When I was eighty-five years old,
I was aged and near death,
with white hair and lost teeth.
I met a man of the Way,
who taught me to abstain from grains,
and only ingest *zhú* and drink water.
He also made a divine pillow for me,
inside which were thirty-two substances.
Among these thirty-two substances,
twenty-four corresponded to the twenty-four solar terms,
and eight poisonous ones corresponded to the eight winds.
I practiced this,
turning from old to young,
my black hair regrew,
my lost teeth reappeared,
and I could walk three hundred *li* a day.
I am now one hundred and eighty years old."
The Emperor received his formula,
and bestowed upon him jade and silk.
The old man later entered Dài Mountain.
Every ten or five years,
he would sometimes return to his hometown.
After over three hundred years,
he never returned again.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn*.
Wū Yán
Wū Yán, styled Zǐdū,
was a man from Běihǎi,
and served as the Commandant of the Imperial Escort during the Hàn dynasty.
When Emperor Wǔ was traveling,
he saw Zǐdū at the Wèi Bridge,
with a dense purple aura over a *zhàng* high above his head.
The Emperor summoned and questioned him,
"How old are you?
What art have you obtained,
that you possess such an extraordinary aura?"
He replied:
"I am already one hundred and thirty-eight years old,
but I have obtained nothing."
As they were about to depart,
the Emperor summoned Dōngfāng Shuò,
ordering him to discern what arts this gentleman possessed.
Shuò replied:
"This gentleman possesses the arts of the feminine principle."
Emperor Wǔ dismissed his attendants and questioned him.
Zǐdū replied:
"When I was sixty-five years old,
I suffered from back pain and cold feet,
unable to warm myself.
My mouth was dry and tongue bitter,
with watery discharge from my nose.
All my joints and limbs ached,
and I was numb, unable to stand for long.
Since obtaining this art,
for seventy-three years now,
I have had twenty-six children.
My body is robust
(Míng manuscript and Chén collated version have "robust" for "although")
and vigorous,
free from any illness or ailment.
My strength is like that of my prime,
with no worries or concerns."
The Emperor said:
"You are unkind;
possessing such an art and not informing me,
you are not a loyal minister."
Zǐdū replied:
"I truly know this art is genuine,
but matters of yīn and yáng,
the benefits within the palace,
are difficult for a minister to speak of.
Moreover, practicing it goes against human nature,
and few can do it.
Therefore, I dared not inform you."
The Emperor said:
"Do not apologize;
I was jesting with you."
He then received his method.
Zǐdū lived to two hundred years old,
ingested mercury,
and ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
Emperor Wǔ practiced his method to some extent,
but could not employ it fully.
Nevertheless, he achieved a longer lifespan than previous emperors.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn*.
Liú Píng
Luán Bā was
a native of Chéngdū in Shǔ Commandery.
From a young age, he was fond of the Way,
and did not engage in worldly affairs.
At that time, the Grand Administrator personally visited Bā,
and humbly requested him to serve as a Merit Officer.
He treated him with the courtesy due to a teacher and friend.
When Bā arrived
("Arrived" originally written as "Líng",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
the Grand Administrator said:
"I have heard that the Merit Officer possesses the Way;
might you demonstrate a marvel for me?"
Bā replied:
"Certainly."
He immediately sat upright,
then retreated into the wall,
fading away like a wisp of cloud.
After a short while,
Bā was nowhere to be seen.
Those outside the wall saw him transform into a tiger,
and everyone was startled.
The tiger went straight back to the Merit Officer's residence.
When people went to look at the tiger,
the tiger was Bā transformed.
Later, he was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt,
appointed as a Gentleman of the Palace,
and promoted to Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng.
At the Lúshān temple, there was a spirit
that could converse with people from within its curtain,
drink wine,
and toss cups in the air.
People went there to pray for blessings.
It could also command the winds on rivers and lakes,
parting them to raise sails,
so that boats traveling in opposite directions could meet.
When Bā arrived at the commandery,
he went to the temple,
and the spirit immediately vanished.
Bā said:
"The temple ghost has been fraudulently posing as a celestial official,
harming the common people for a long time.
Its crime deserves punishment.
I entrust the matter to the Merit Officer;
I will personally pursue and capture it.
If it is not dealt with promptly,
I fear it will later roam the world,
receiving blood sacrifices wherever it goes,
and unjustly afflicting good people."
He demanded heavy prayers,
then descended to its location,
questioning the mountains, rivers, and altars of the land,
seeking the ghost's traces.
The ghost then fled to Qí Commandery,
transforming into a scholar
skilled in discussing the Five Classics.
The Grand Administrator there married his daughter to him.
Bā learned of its whereabouts,
submitted a memorial requesting to be relieved of his commandery duties to go capture it,
but the ghost did not emerge.
Bā said to the Grand Administrator:
"Your honorable son-in-law is not human;
he is an old ghost fraudulently posing as the temple spirit.
It has fled here,
so I have come to apprehend it."
The Grand Administrator summoned him, but he did not come out.
Bā said:
"Making him emerge is very easy."
He requested the Grand Administrator's brush, inkstone, and a table,
and Bā then drew a talisman.
When the talisman was completed, he let out a long whistle.
Suddenly, someone in the air took the talisman away,
though no human form was seen,
startling everyone present.
When the talisman arrived,
the scholar said to his wife, weeping:
"If I go, I will surely die."
After a short while,
the scholar came to the courtyard carrying the talisman himself,
and upon seeing Bā, dared not approach.
Bā shouted:
"Old ghost, why don't you resume your true form?"
In response, it immediately turned into a wildcat,
kowtowing and begging for its life.
Bā ordered it killed,
and everyone saw a blade descend from the air,
the wildcat's head falling to the ground.
The Grand Administrator's daughter had already borne a son,
who also transformed into a wildcat,
and was likewise killed.
Bā left and returned to Yùzhāng.
The commandery had many ghosts,
and many one-legged ghosts,
that afflicted the common people.
After Bā arrived,
there were no more such troubles;
all demonic evils were eliminated at once.
Later, he was summoned to serve as a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat.
At the grand assembly on New Year's Day,
Bā arrived late,
appearing flushed as if from drink.
When wine was bestowed upon the officials,
he did not drink it but instead sprayed it toward the southwest.
The officials reported Bā for disrespect.
The emperor summoned Bā for questioning.
Bā said:
"In my hometown, because I could subdue ghosts and protect against illness,
the people built a temple for me while I was still alive.
This morning, some elders
all came to my temple to make offerings,
and I could not decline
(Ming manuscript copy and Chén's collated edition have "decline" instead of "drink"
) them early,
hence my flushed appearance.
Just now, I saw a fire in Chéngdū market,
so I rinsed my mouth with wine to help extinguish it.
I dared not be disrespectful;
I request an imperial inquiry,
and if it proves false, I will accept the punishment."
Then, a dispatch was sent to inquire in Chéngdū.
The reply stated:
"After the New Year's Day meal, a fire broke out.
After a short while,
three bouts of heavy rain came,
from the northeast,
and the fire was extinguished.
The rain that fell on people carried the scent of wine."
Later, one morning,
suddenly there was a great storm,
darkening heaven and earth,
so that people sitting opposite could not see each other,
and Bā was nowhere to be found.
Soon, it was heard that Bā had returned to Chéngdū,
bidding farewell to relatives and old friends,
saying he would not return again.
Old and young all saw him off at the temple.
It is said:
When he left, there was also wind, rain, and darkness.
No one knows where he went.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn"
Zuǒ Cí
Zuǒ Cí, styled Yuánfàng,
was a man of Lújiāng.
He was well-versed in the Five Classics,
and also proficient in astrology and qi observation.
Seeing that the Han dynasty's fortunes were about to decline,
and chaos was about to erupt across the land,
he sighed and said:
"In such times of decline and disorder,
those with high office are in danger,
and those with great wealth will die.
The glory and splendor of this world
are not worth coveting."
So he studied the Dao,
becoming especially skilled in the Liùjiǎ (Six Jia) arts,
able to command spirits and ghosts,
and summon a traveling kitchen at will.
He concentrated his thoughts and practiced in the Tiānzhù Mountains,
where in a stone chamber he obtained the *Scripture of the Nine Elixirs and Golden Liquor*,
enabling him to perform myriad transformations,
too numerous to record.
Duke Cáo of Wèi heard of him and summoned him.
He confined him in a stone chamber,
had people guard and watch him,
and cut off his grain for a full year.
When he was let out,
his complexion was as before.
Duke Cáo believed that among living people, none could survive without eating,
yet Cí was like this.
He must be practicing heterodox arts,
and he wanted to kill him.
Cí already knew this,
and requested to be dismissed (to retire his bones).
Duke Cáo said:
"Why so sudden?"
He replied:
"Because I am about to be killed,
therefore I ask to leave."
The Duke said:
"I have no such intention.
On the contrary, I admire your lofty aspirations,
and would not presumptuously detain you."
He then prepared wine for him,
and Cí said:
"Now that I am about to go far away,
I beg to share a cup of wine."
The Duke said:
"Good."
At that time it was cold weather,
and the warmed wine was still hot.
Cí took his Daoist hairpin and stirred the wine with it.
In a moment,
the hairpin had completely dissolved,
like someone grinding ink.
Initially,
when the Duke heard Cí request to share the cup of wine,
he thought he meant for the Duke to drink first,
and then give it to Cí.
But instead, Cí drew with his hairpin,
and the wine in the cup divided in two,
with a gap of several inches between them.
He then drank half,
and gave half to the Duke.
The Duke, displeased with this,
did not drink it immediately.
Cí begged to drink it all himself.
After drinking,
he threw the cup at the roof beam.
The cup hung there swaying,
like a bird dipping and rising,
seeming about to fall but not falling.
All those present could not help but watch the cup.
After a long while, it finally fell,
but by then Cí had already disappeared.
They searched for him,
and he had returned to his dwelling.
Duke Cáo then wanted even more to kill Cí,
to test if he could escape death.
He then ordered Cí's arrest.
Cí ran into a flock of sheep,
and the pursuers could not distinguish him.
They then counted the original sheep,
and indeed there was one extra,
so they knew Cí had transformed into a sheep.
The pursuers conveyed their master's intent,
saying they wished to see the master,
and asked him to return temporarily without fear.
Soon, a large sheep came forward, knelt down, and said:
"Is this really the case?"
The officers said to each other:
"This kneeling sheep
is Cí."
They wanted to seize it.
Then all the sheep in the flock turned toward the officers and said:
"Is this really the case?"
From this, the officers could no longer know where Cí was,
and they stopped.
Later, someone who knew Cí's whereabouts
informed the Duke.
The Duke again sent officers to arrest him,
and they captured Cí.
It was not that Cí was unable to hide,
but he deliberately displayed his divine transformations.
Thus he allowed himself to be taken to prison.
The jailers wanted to torture him,
but there was one Cí inside the cell,
and another Cí outside the cell,
and they did not know which was the real one.
The Duke heard of this and disliked him even more,
and ordered him taken to the marketplace to be killed.
In a moment,
they suddenly lost sight of Cí's whereabouts.
They then closed the market gates and searched.
For those who did not know Cí,
they asked his description.
They said he was blind in one eye,
wearing a blue hemp headscarf and a blue unlined garment.
Upon seeing such a person, they should arrest him.
As a result,
everyone in the marketplace was blind in one eye,
wearing hemp headscarves and blue garments,
so in the end they could not distinguish him.
The Duke ordered a widespread pursuit,
to kill him on sight.
Later, someone saw and recognized him,
beheaded him, and presented the head to the Duke.
The Duke was greatly pleased.
But when he went to look at it,
it was just a bundle of straw.
Examining the corpse,
it too had vanished without a trace.
Later, someone coming from Jīngzhōu
saw Cí.
The Inspector of Jīngzhōu, Liú Biǎo,
also considered Cí a deluder of the masses,
and planned to arrest and harm him.
When Biǎo went out to review his troops,
Cí, sensing he wanted to see his arts,
slowly went away,
but then went to see Biǎo and said:
"I have a meager gift,
which I wish to present to the army."
Biǎo said:
"You, a Daoist, are alone and traveling,
while my soldiers are many.
How could it possibly suffice?"
Cí repeated his offer.
Biǎo had someone look,
and there was one dǒu of wine,
in a vessel,
and a bundle of dried meat.
Yet ten men together could not lift it.
Cí then went out himself to fetch it.
Using a knife, he sliced the dried meat and threw it on the ground.
He asked a hundred men to serve the wine and meat,
to give to the soldiers.
Each had three cups of wine,
and one slice of meat.
It tasted like ordinary dried meat.
Altogether, over ten thousand men
were all fully supplied,
yet the wine in the vessel remained as before,
and the meat was also not exhausted.
Moreover, there were a thousand guests seated there,
and they all became thoroughly drunk.
Biǎo was then greatly astonished,
and no longer had any intention of harming Cí.
After several days,
Cí took his leave of Biǎo and departed,
entering Eastern Wú.
There was a man named Xú Duò,
who possessed Daoist arts,
and lived in Dāntú.
Cí passed by to visit him.
Duò had guests at his gate,
with six or seven ox-carts.
They deceived Cí, saying:
"Lord Xú is not here."
Cí knew the guests were deceiving him,
and left.
The guests then saw the oxen walking on the tops of poplar trees.
Just as they climbed the trees, they would disappear,
and upon descending, they would again be seen walking on the trees.
Also, the cart hubs all sprouted thorns,
a foot long,
which could not be cut through,
and the carts could not be pushed to move.
The guests were greatly frightened,
and immediately reported to Lord Xú,
saying: "There was an old man, blind in one eye.
We thought he was not an urgent visitor,
so we deceived him, saying:
'The master is not here.'
After he left, in a moment,
the oxen were all like this.
We don't know what he meant by it."
Lord Xú said:
"Alas!
This was Lord Zuǒ passing by to visit me.
How could you people deceive him?
Quickly pursue him, you might still catch up."
The various guests scattered to pursue him,
and when they caught up with Zào Cí,
Luó Bù kowtowed and apologized to him.
Zào Cí’s anger subsided,
and he immediately sent them back.
When they arrived,
the carts and oxen had all returned to their original state.
Zào Cí later met the Lord of Wú, Sūn Tǎojì,
who again wanted to kill him.
Later, when going out on an excursion,
he invited Zào Cí to accompany him,
ordering Zào Cí to walk in front of the horse,
intending to stab him from behind.
Zào Cí walked in front of the horse,
wearing wooden clogs,
holding a bamboo staff,
and proceeded slowly.
Sūn Tǎojì whipped his horse to gallop,
and brandishing his weapon, he chased after him,
but in the end, he could not catch up.
Sūn Tǎojì realized that Zào Cí possessed magical arts,
and so he stopped.
Later, Zào Cí informed Gě Xiāngōng of his intentions,
saying that he would enter Huòshān,
to refine the Nine-Cycle Elixir,
and thus he departed to become an immortal.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn*
Dà Máo Jūn
Dà Máo Jūn Máo Yíng.
He journeyed south to Jūqūzhīshān.
In the second year of the Yuánshòu era of the Hàn dynasty,
on the eighth month, jǐyǒu day,
the Southern Peak Perfected Person Chì Jūn, Western Citadel Lord Wáng Jūn, and various azure youths, along with Queen Mother of the West, descended upon Máo Yíng’s chamber.
Shortly after,
the Celestial August Great Emperor dispatched the embroidered-robed envoy Lěng Guǎng Zǐqī to bestow upon Máo Yíng the divine seal and jade insignia.
The Great Subtlety Emperor dispatched the Left Palace Censor of the Three Heavens, Guǎn Xiūtiáo, to bestow upon Máo Yíng the eight-dragon brocade and purple-feathered flowery robe.
The Supreme Great Dao Lord dispatched the Harmonious Dawn Grand Master Shūmén to bestow upon Máo Yíng the golden tiger true tally and flowing-gold bell.

The Golden Tower Sage Lord commanded the Great Ultimate Perfected Person Zhèngyī Zhǐxuán, Wáng Láng, Wáng Zhōng, Bào Qiū, and others to bestow upon Máo Yíng the four-season hidden embryo flowing-bright divine mushroom.
After the four envoys had presented their gifts,
they had Máo Yíng consume the mushroom, wear the seal,
don the robe and jade crown.
He stood girded with the tally and holding the bell,
and the four envoys declared to Máo Yíng:
“He who consumes the four-season hidden mushroom
shall attain the rank of True Minister;
he who consumes the golden tower jade mushroom
shall attain the rank of Director of Destinies;
he who consumes the flowing-bright golden blossom
shall attain the rank of Director of Emoluments;
he who consumes the long-shining paired-flight
shall attain the rank of Director of Destinies and True Earl;
he who consumes the nocturnal-luminous cavern herb
shall oversee the duties of the Left Censor.
You have consumed them all,
your lifespan shall equal heaven and earth,
your rank shall be Director of Destinies and Supreme Perfected,
Supreme Minister of the Eastern Peak,
commanding the immortals of Wú and Yuè,
and overseeing the mountain sources east of the river.”
When they had finished speaking,
the envoys all departed.
The Five Thearch Lords each descended to his courtyard with chariots and robes according to their directions,
conveying the command of the Great Thearch,
bestowing upon him the purple jade tablet,
and the golden inscribed text of the nine bestowals,
appointing Máo Yíng as Supreme Minister of the Eastern Peak, True Lord of Destinies, and Great Primordial Perfected Person.
When the matters were concluded, they all departed.
The Queen Mother and Máo Yíng’s teacher, Western Citadel Lord Wáng Jūn,
prepared a celestial feast and joyous banquet for Máo Yíng,
singing the Mysterious Numinous tune.
After the banquet,
the Queen Mother, taking Lord Wáng Jūn and Máo Yíng,
visited and cared for Máo Yíng’s two younger brothers,
imparting to each the essentials of the Dao.
The Queen Mother commanded the Supreme Primordial Lady
to impart to Máo Gù and Máo Zhōng the four precious scriptures, *The Hidden Book of the Great Empyrean* and *The Dao Essence of Cinnabar Radiance*.
The Queen Mother held *The Hidden Book of the Great Empyrean*,
and commanded the attendant maid Zhāng Língzǐ to hold the covenant of mutual trust,
to impart to Máo Yíng, Máo Gù, and Máo Zhōng.
When this was done,
the Queen Mother of the West ascended to heaven and departed.
Afterwards, the Purple Void Primordial Lady and Lady Wèi Huácún requested a fasting ceremony at the Hidden Primordial Terrace on Yángluòzhīshān,
and the Queen Mother of the West and the Golden Tower Sage Lord descended to the terrace,
riding in an eight-scenes carriage,
together proceeding to the Clear Void Upper Palace,
transmitting the four volumes of *The Jade Clarity Hidden Book*,
to impart to Huácún.

At that time, more than thirty Perfected Persons, including the Three Primes Lady Féng Shuāngzhū, the Purple Yang Left Immortal Lord Shí Lùchéng, the Great Ultimate High Immortal Earl, Yángài Gōngzǐ, the Western Citadel Perfected Person Wáng Fāngpíng, the Great Void Perfected Person, the Southern Peak Perfected Person Chìsōngzǐ, the Paulownia and Cypress Perfected Person Wáng Qiáo, and others,
each sang the tune of the Great Ultimate Yin Songs.
The Queen Mother sang for them, saying:
“Driving my eight-scenes carriage,
suddenly I enter Jade Clarity.
Dragon hosts brush the empyrean above,
tiger banners gather vermilion troops.
Wandering freely at the brink of the mysterious ford,
ten thousand streams never pause.
Lamenting this parting and meeting,
when kalpas end, heaven and earth will collapse.
One must seek the scenery within non-being,
neither dying nor being born.
Embodying that natural Dao,
in silent contemplation, merging with the great darkness.
The Southern Peak resembles a steadfast trunk,
jade blossoms shine with sharp essence.
Having a task, yet no affair to attend to,
with an empty heart, naturally receiving the numinous.
A joyous gathering descends at the river’s bend,
together we rejoice without end.”
After the Queen Mother finished singing,
the Three Primes Lady also finished her answering song.
The Queen Mother, along with the Three Primes Lady, the Purple Yang Left Lord, the Great Ultimate Immortal Earl, and the Clear Numinous Lord Wáng,
then took the Southern Peak’s Wèi Huácún with them and departed,
traveling southeast,
together proceeding to Tiāntāi and Huòshān,
passing by the golden altar at Jūqū,
feasting with the Great Primordial Perfected Person Máo Shēng
(Míng manuscript, Chén collated edition, Xǔ block-printed edition: “Shēng” written as “Shū”)
at the Huàyì Grotto-Heaven.
They left Huácún beneath the jade chambers of the Huòshān grotto-palace,
and all the Perfected Persons followed the Queen Mother ascending back to the Turtle Terrace.
From *Jíxiān Zhuàn*
Hú Gōng
Master Hú,
whose name is unknown.
All the talismans in existence today, such as the Summoning Army Talisman and the Jade Mansion Talisman for summoning ghosts and spirits to cure illnesses,
totaling over twenty scrolls,
all originated from him, hence they are collectively called the "Master Hú Talismans."
At that time, in Rǔnán, there was a man named Fèi Chángfáng,
who served as a market clerk.
Suddenly, he saw Master Hú arriving from afar,
entering the market to sell medicine.
No one recognized him,
but he sold medicine without haggling over prices,
and all illnesses he treated were cured.
He would tell the buyers:
"After taking this medicine, you will vomit a certain substance,
and you will recover on a certain day."
There was never a case where this did not prove effective.
He earned tens of thousands in coins daily,
which he then distributed among the poor, hungry, and freezing people in the market,
keeping only thirty to fifty for himself.
He often hung an empty gourd on the roof of his house,
and after sunset,
he would leap into the gourd.
No one else could see this,
but Chángfáng, from his upstairs vantage point, witnessed it,
and knew that Master Hú was no ordinary man.
Chángfáng then began sweeping the ground in front of Master Hú's seat every day,
and offering him food,
which Master Hú accepted without refusal.
This went on for a long time,
and Chángfáng never slackened,
nor did he dare to ask for anything.
Master Hú, recognizing Chángfáng's sincere devotion,
said to him:
"Come again when it is dark and there is no one around."
Chángfáng followed his words and went at the appointed time.
Master Hú said to him:
"When you see me leap into the gourd,
you should imitate my leap,
and you will naturally enter."
Chángfáng followed his instructions,
and indeed, without realizing it, he entered.
Once inside, it was no longer a gourd,
but a celestial palace world.
There were towers, gates, and elevated walkways,
and Master Hú was attended by dozens of servants.
Master Hú said to Chángfáng:
"I am an immortal.
In the past, I served in the celestial bureaucracy,
but I was reprimanded for neglecting my duties,
and thus was banished to the mortal world.
You are worthy of instruction,
which is why you have been able to see me."
Chángfáng stepped down from his seat, kowtowed, and said:
"I am but a mortal, ignorant and unworthy,
burdened with deep sins.
It is my great fortune that you have taken pity on me,
as if entering a coffin to bestow breath,
reviving the dead and restoring the decayed.
I only fear that my foul and stubborn nature
is unfit for your service.
If you show me compassion,
it would be the greatest fortune of my life."
Master Hú said:
"If you truly think so, that is excellent.
Do not speak of this to anyone."
Later, Master Hú visited Chángfáng upstairs and said:
"I have a little wine;
let us drink together."
The wine was downstairs,
and Chángfáng sent someone to fetch it,
but they could not lift the jar.
Even when dozens of people tried, they could not bring it up.
Chángfáng reported this to Master Hú,
who then went downstairs
and lifted it with a single finger.
He drank with Chángfáng,
and though the wine vessel was only about the size of a fist,
they drank until dusk without exhausting it.
Master Hú told Chángfáng:
"I will be leaving on a certain day;
can you come with me?"
Chángfáng said:
"My desire to leave
is beyond words,
but I wish for my family not to notice my departure.
What plan should I follow?"
Master Hú said:
"That is easy."
He then gave Chángfáng a green bamboo staff
and instructed him:
"Take this bamboo home,
pretend to be ill,
place this bamboo staff where you sleep,
and then come here silently."
Chángfáng did as Master Hú said.
After he left,
his family saw that Chángfáng had died,
with his corpse lying on the bed.
It was actually the bamboo staff,
but they wept and buried it.
Chángfáng went to Master Hú,
feeling dazed and unaware of where he was.
Master Hú then left Chángfáng among a pack of tigers,
who bared their teeth and opened their mouths, ready to devour him,
but Chángfáng showed no fear.
The next day,
he was placed inside a stone chamber,
with a square stone above his head,
several zhang wide,
suspended by a straw rope.
Then, several snakes came to gnaw at the rope,
and just as it was about to break,
Chángfáng remained calm.
When Master Hú arrived,
he patted Chángfáng and said:
"You are worthy of instruction."
He then ordered Chángfáng to eat feces,
along with maggots about an inch long,
which were exceptionally foul and disgusting.
Chángfáng hesitated,
and Master Hú sighed, dismissed him, and said:
"You cannot attain the Way of Immortality.
I grant you the position of an earthly ruler,
and you may live for several hundred years."
He gave him a scroll of talismans and seals,
saying:
"Carry this, and you can command all ghosts and spirits.
Always call yourself an envoy,
and you can cure illnesses and dispel calamities."
Chángfáng worried that he could not return home,
so Master Hú gave him a bamboo staff, saying:
"Just ride this,
and you will reach home."
Chángfáng mounted the bamboo staff, bid farewell, and left.
Suddenly, it felt as if he had awoken from a dream,
and he was already home.
His family thought he was a ghost,
but after he recounted everything that had happened,
they opened the coffin to look,
and found only a bamboo staff,
finally believing him.
The bamboo staff that Chángfáng had ridden
was discarded in Gěbēi Pond,
and when they looked at it, it had turned into a green dragon.
From the time he left until his return, it felt like a single day,
but when he asked his family,
he learned that a year had already passed.
Chángfáng then used the talismans,
capturing ghosts and curing illnesses,
with no case failing to heal.
Whenever he sat and talked with others,
he would often scold and get angry.
When asked why,
he said:
"I am scolding ghosts."
At that time, in Rǔnán, there was a ghostly creature
that would come to the commandery several times a year.
When it came, it rode with attendants like a governor,
entered the government office, beat drums,
and patrolled inside and out,
before finally leaving.
This caused great distress.
Chángfáng then went to the government hall,
just as the ghost arrived at the gate.
The governor hurried inside,
leaving Chángfáng alone.
The ghost knew of him,
and did not dare to approach.
Chángfáng shouted loudly,
and immediately seized the ghost.
The ghost then descended from its carriage, prostrated itself in the courtyard,
kowtowed, and begged for a chance to reform.
Chángfáng scolded it:
"You dead old ghost,
with no regard for gentleness and goodness,
you parade around without reason,
recklessly intruding upon the government office.
Do you know you deserve death?
Quickly return to your true form."
The ghost instantly transformed into a giant turtle,
as large as a cartwheel,
with a head over a zhang long.
Chángfáng then ordered it to resume human form.
He gave it a talisman on a slip of paper,
ordering it to deliver it to the Lord of Gěbēi.
The ghost kowtowed, weeping,
and took the slip away.
Someone was sent to follow and observe,
and they saw the talisman slip standing by the pond,
while the ghost, with its head
(Míng manuscript and Chén manuscript variant: "neck")
wrapped around a tree, had died.
Later, Chángfáng went to Dōnghǎi,
where a great drought had lasted for three years.
He said to those praying for rain:
"The Dōnghǎi Sea God came to seduce the Lady of Gěbēi,
and I detained him.
The circumstances were unpredictable,
and I carelessly forgot about it,
leading to this prolonged drought."
I shall now pardon him,
and command him to bring rain."
Immediately there was a great downpour.
Fáng possessed divine arts,
able to contract the veins of the earth;
though a thousand lǐ away,
they appeared right before one's eyes,
and when released, they stretched out again as before.
From Biographies of Divine Immortals.
Jì Zǐxùn
Jì Zǐxùn
was a man of Qí.
In his youth, he once served in the commanderies and prefectures,
was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt,
and appointed Gentleman of the Interior.
He also joined the army,
and was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Carriage.
No one knew he possessed the Way.
While in his hometown,
he only practiced trust and deference,
and engaged with others in affairs.
In this manner, over three hundred years passed,
yet his complexion did not age,
and people found it strange.
Those fond of such matters followed him,
but never saw what medicines he regularly took.
His nature favored purity and tranquility,
often dwelling in leisure to read the Book of Changes,
writing small compositions,
all of which had meaning.
Seeing a neighbor holding an infant,
Zǐxùn asked to hold it,
but his hand slipped and it fell to the ground,
and the child died immediately.
The neighboring family had always revered Zǐxùn,
and dared not show any sign of grief;
they simply buried it.
More than twenty days later,
Zǐxùn went and asked them:
"Do you still miss the child?"
The neighbor said:
"The child's fate,
was not destined to become an adult;
it has been dead for many days,
we can no longer miss it."
Zǐxùn then went outside,
and brought the child back to their home.
The family thought it was dead,
and dared not accept it.
Zǐxùn said:
"Just take it, there is no harm,
for this is indeed your original child."
The child recognized its mother,
saw her and smiled joyfully,
wanting its mother to take it.
She held it,
but still doubted and did not believe.
After Zǐxùn left,
the husband and wife together looked at the child they had buried;
in the coffin there was only a clay child,
six or seven inches long.
This child then grew up.
As for the elders whose beards and hair were completely white,
Zǐxùn would merely sit facing them and converse together;
overnight,
by the next morning, they had all turned black.
When the nobles in the capital heard of this,
none did not humbly seek an audience,
but had no means to bring him.
There was a young man who was Zǐxùn's neighbor,
and was a student of the Imperial Academy.
The nobles devised a plan,
and together called the student, saying to him:
"You toil diligently in study,
seeking to attain wealth and honor;
if you can summon Zǐxùn to come,
we will ensure you gain them without further toil."
The student agreed.
He then returned to serve Zǐxùn,
sweeping, cleaning, and attending upon him for several hundred days.
Zǐxùn understood his intent,
and said to the student:
"You are not studying the Way,
how could you be like this?"
The student still concealed it,
Zǐxùn said:
"Why do you not answer truthfully,
vainly pretending and embellishing?
I already fully understand your intent.
The nobles wish to see me;
how could I, for the sake of a single journey's effort,
cause you to miss attaining glory and position?
You may return to the capital,
I will go on such-and-such a day."
The student was very pleased,
took leave and went to the capital,
and fully informed the nobles.
On a certain day Zǐxùn was to arrive,
but when the time came, he had not set out;
the student's parents came to see Zǐxùn.
Zǐxùn said:
"Are you afraid I have forgotten,
causing your son to break his promise and not gain office?
I shall set out right after eating."
In half a day, he traveled two thousand lǐ.
Having arrived,
the student hurried to bow and welcome him.
Zǐxùn asked:
"Who wishes to see me?"
The student said:
"Many wish to see you, sir,
but dare not trouble you to come;
they only know that wherever you arrive,
they will come of their own accord."
Zǐxùn said:
"I have come a thousand lǐ without weariness,
would I begrudge a few steps?
Tell those who wish to see me
to each dismiss their guests;
tomorrow I shall visit each of their residences."
The student did as told and informed the nobles;
each dismissed their guests and swept clean,
and at the appointed time, Zǐxùn indeed came.
In all, twenty-three households,
each had one Zǐxùn.
The various court officials each thought Zǐxùn had come to their home first;
the next day at court,
each asked when Zǐxùn had arrived at their residence;
the twenty-three men all saw him at the same time,
his clothing, ornaments, and appearance were no different,
only his words,
answering according to the host's intent,
were not the same.
The capital was greatly astonished,
such were his divine transformations.
The nobles all wished to visit Zǐxùn;
Zǐxùn said to the student:
"The nobles say I have double pupils and eight-colored irises,
and thus wish to see me.
Now they have seen me;
I also have nothing to discuss about the Way,
I am leaving."
Just as he went out the door,
the nobles, with caps and canopies, came crowding the road.
The student fully explained that he had just left,
and that the one riding a mule on the eastern path was he.
Each galloped after him but could not catch up;
thus for half a day,
the distance between them remained about one lǐ,
and in the end they could not overtake him,
so each gave up and returned.
Zǐxùn went to Chén Gōng's home,
and said:
"Tomorrow at noon I shall depart."
Chén Gōng asked whether he was traveling far,
he said:
"I shall not return again."
Chén Gōng gave him a single robe of kudzu cloth as a farewell gift.
When the time came,
Zǐxùn then died;
his corpse stiffened,
his hands and feet crossed over his chest,
impossible to straighten,
like bent iron.
The corpse emitted a fragrant scent of five spices,
reaching the lanes and paths;
the scent was most extraordinary.
They then encoffined him.
Before they could take it out,
from within the coffin came a sudden sound like thunder,
light illuminating the house.
Those seated immediately prostrated for a long while;
looking at the coffin lid,
it had split and flown into the air,
within the coffin there was no one,
only a single shoe left behind.
In a moment,
they heard on the path the sound of people, horses, pipes, and drums,
heading directly east and away,
and then was seen no more.
After Zǐxùn left,
on the paths for several tens of lǐ,
the fragrance lingered for over a hundred days without fading.
From Biographies of Divine Immortals.
Dǒng Fèng
Dǒng Fèng,
courtesy name Jūnyì,
was a man of Hòuguān.
During the time of the first ruler of Wú,
a young man served as the county magistrate of Dǒng Fèng's home county.
Seeing Dǒng Fèng was over forty years old,
he did not know of his Way.
He left his official post and departed.
More than fifty years later,
he again held another position,
and happened to pass through Hòuguān.
All the former officials and people were old,
yet Dǒng Fèng's face and appearance were exactly as in the past.
He asked, saying, "Have you attained the Way, sir?
I saw you like this in the past,
and now I am already white-haired,
yet you have grown even younger.
Why is this?"
Dǒng Fèng said:
"It is merely by chance."
Also, Dù Xiè served as the Governor of Jiāozhōu,
and fell ill from a poisonous disease and died.
He had been dead for three days.
Dǒng Fèng was there at the time,
so he went,
and gave him three pills of medicine,
placing them inside his mouth,
pouring water to wash them down,
and had someone hold up his head,
shaking it to dissolve them.
In a short while,
his hands and feet seemed to move,
and his complexion gradually returned.
After half a day, he was able to sit up,
and after four more days, he was able to speak.
He said:
"When I died, it was suddenly like a dream.
I saw more than ten men in black clothes come,
took Dù Xiè and put him on a cart to leave,
entered a great red gate,
and went straight to be delivered into a prison.
Each prison cell had one door,
and the door could barely accommodate one person.
They put Dù Xiè inside one cell,
then sealed it from the outside with earth,
so he could no longer see the outside light.
Suddenly, he heard someone outside the door say:
'Tàiyǐ has sent an envoy to summon Dù Xiè.'
Then he heard the earth being removed from the door,
and after a long while, he was led out.
He saw a carriage and horses with a red canopy,
three people sitting together on the carriage,
one of them holding a tally,
who called for Dù Xiè to board the carriage.
Just as they were about to return to the gate, he awoke,
and Dù Xiè then revived."
Thereupon, he rose and thanked him, saying:
"I am greatly indebted to your great kindness.
How can I repay you?"
So he built a tower for Dǒng Fèng in the courtyard.
Dǒng Fèng did not eat other foods,
only consuming dried meat and dates,
and drinking a little wine.
Dù Xiè provided these three times a day.
Whenever Dǒng Fèng came to eat and drink,
he would sometimes be like a flying bird,
soaring through the air to sit down,
and when finished eating, he would fly away,
often without people noticing.
This went on for over a year,
then he bid farewell to Dù Xiè and left.
Dù Xiè wept and tried to keep him, but could not make him stay.
Dù Xiè asked where he wished to go,
and whether he needed a large boat.
Dǒng Fèng said:
"I do not need a boat,
only a coffin."
Dù Xiè immediately prepared one for him.
The next day at noon,
Dǒng Fèng died.
Dù Xiè encoffined and buried him with that coffin.
Seven days later,
someone came from Róngchāng,
and Dǒng Fèng appeared and instructed him, saying:
"Thank Dù Xiè for me,
and take good care of himself."
When Dù Xiè heard this,
he opened the burial and uncovered the coffin to look,
and found only a piece of silk remained.
On one side was painted a human figure,
and on the other side, a talisman was written in cinnabar.
Later, he returned to live at the foot of Lú Mountain in Yùzhāng.
There was a man who had a severe disease,
near death,
who was carried to see Dǒng Fèng,
kowtowing and begging for pity.
Dǒng Fèng had the sick man sit in a room,
covered him with a five-layered cloth towel,
and told him not to move.
The sick man said:
"At first, I heard something come and lick my body.
The pain was unbearable,
and it covered everywhere.
I estimate this tongue was about a foot wide,
its breath like an ox's,
and I do not know what creature it was.
After a long while, the creature left."
Dǒng Fèng then went to the pond
(Míngchāo edition: "removed the towel")
and bathed him with water,
sent him away,
and told him:
"You will recover soon,
do not expose yourself to the wind."
After more than ten days,
the sick man's body was red and skinless,
in great pain.
When he bathed in water,
the pain would immediately stop.
After twenty days,
his skin grew back and he recovered,
his body like congealed fat.
Later, there was suddenly a great drought.
The county magistrate, Dīng Shìyàn, deliberated, saying:
"I have heard that Master Dǒng possesses the Way,
he should be able to bring rain."
So he personally brought wine and dried meat to see Dǒng Fèng,
and explained the situation of the great drought.
Dǒng Fèng said:
"Rain is easy to obtain."
Then, looking at his house, he said:
"This poor Daoist's house is all open to the sky;
I fear when the rain comes, how will it withstand it?"
The magistrate understood his meaning,
and said:
"If you, sir, can bring rain,
I will certainly build you a fine house with a frame."
The next day,
Dīng Shìyàn personally led over a hundred officials and laborers,
transporting bamboo and wood,
and a house was built and completed immediately.
Just as they were gathering earth to make mud,
planning to fetch water from several miles away,
Dǒng Fèng said:
"That is not necessary;
by evening there will be heavy rain."
So they stopped.
By evening, heavy rain indeed fell,
leveling both high and low ground,
and the local people were greatly pleased.
Dǒng Fèng lived in the mountains and did not farm,
but daily treated people's illnesses,
and also did not take money.
For those who recovered from serious illnesses,
he had them plant five apricot trees;
for lighter cases, one tree.
After several years like this,
the total reached over one hundred thousand trees,
forming a lush forest.
He then had the hundred birds and various beasts of the mountains
play beneath them.
Weeds never grew there,
and it was always as if it had been weeded and tended.
Later, when the apricots ripened abundantly,
he built a thatched granary in the forest,
and announced to the people of the time:
"Those who wish to buy apricots
need not report to me,
but simply place a container of grain in the granary,
and then go themselves to take a container of apricots away."
Often, someone would place little grain
but take many apricots away.
Then, a group of tigers from the forest would roar and chase them out.
Terrified,
they would hurriedly grab the apricots and run,
but would stumble and overturn by the roadside.
When they measured the apricots at home,
they found them exactly matching the amount of grain they had brought.
If someone stole apricots,
a tiger would chase them to their home
and bite them to death.
Their family, knowing they had stolen apricots,
would then return them to Dǒng Fèng,
kowtowing to apologize for the fault,
and only then would he revive them.
Each year, Dǒng Fèng sold apricots to obtain grain,
and promptly used it to relieve the poor and needy,
and to supply travelers who were in want,
amounting to over twenty thousand hú annually.
The county magistrate had a daughter
who was bewitched by an evil spirit,
and medical treatment was ineffective.
So he turned to Dǒng Fèng to cure her,
saying that if the girl recovered,
he would offer her to serve him.
Dǒng Fèng agreed to this.
He then summoned a white alligator,
several zhàng long,
which came overland to the sick girl's door.
The attendant who served as envoy was beheaded,
and the woman's illness was immediately cured.
Fèng then took the woman as his wife,
but for a long time they had no children.
Whenever Fèng went out,
his wife could not stay alone,
so they begged for a girl to raise.
When she was over ten years old,
Fèng one day soared into the clouds and departed.
His wife and the girl remained in their house,
selling apricots for their livelihood.
If anyone cheated them,
a tiger would return to chase the offender.
Fèng remained in the human world for over three hundred years before leaving,
and his appearance was like that of a thirty-year-old man.
From Biographies of Immortals.
Lǐ Chángzài
Lǐ Chángzài
was a man from Shǔ Commandery.
From a young age, he practiced Daoist arts,
and generations of common people served him.
Estimating his age,
he was already four or five hundred years old but did not grow old,
always appearing around fifty years old.
When treating illnesses,
severe cases took three days
"day" originally written as "month,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
and mild cases were cured in one day.
At home, he had two sons and one daughter,
all of whom had married,
and then he left.
When leaving, he asked for a young boy from each of his disciples' families, the Zēng family and the Kǒng family,
each around
seventeen or eighteen years old.
The families did not know where Chángzài intended to go,
but they sent the boys with him.
Chángzài used a green bamboo staff to transport the two boys,
sending them back to the places where they slept in their homes.
He instructed them to go straight back
and not speak to their families.
The two boys followed his instructions,
returning home with the staff.
Their families did not see the boys leave at all.
Later, they each found them dead in their beds.
The two families mourned and wept,
burying them.
Over a hundred days later,
a disciple encountered Chángzài in Pí County,
traveling with these two boys.
The two boys wept and spoke with the disciple for a long time,
each entrusting him with letters to deliver.
The two families opened the coffins to look,
and found only green bamboo staffs inside.
Only then did they realize the boys were not dead.
Over thirty years later,
Chángzài lived at Dìfèi Mountain.
He remarried.
The son from Chángzài's previous wife went to seek him out.
Before ten days had passed,
Chángzài said to his later wife:
"My son is coming to find me.
I must leave.
You can give him a gold ingot."
When the son arrived,
he asked where his father was,
and the wife gave him the gold.
The son said:
"My father left me decades ago.
Day and night, I have missed and longed for him.
Hearing that my father is here,
I came from afar to visit him,
not seeking wealth."
He then stayed.
After thirty days, his father had not returned.
The son deceived his mother, saying:
"Since my father is not returning,
I will leave."
Once outside,
he hid in the grass.
Chángzài returned and told his wife:
"This son spoke deceitfully like this.
He will return.
Tell him,
'You are grown and no longer need me.
According to the Daoist law, I can no longer meet with you.'"
He then left.
A short while later, the son indeed returned.
The mother told him what Chángzài had said.
The son knew he would never see his father again,
so he wept and left.
Over seventy years later,
Chángzài suddenly departed.
Disciples saw him living at Hǔshòu Mountain,
where he remarried again.
He had sons and grandsons,
and generations saw him unchanged,
hence he was called "Chángzài" (Ever-Present).
From Biographies of Immortals.
Máo Jūn
Máo Jūn was a man from Yōuzhōu.
He studied the Way in Qí,
and after twenty years, having attained the Way, he returned home.
When his parents saw him, they were greatly angered and said:
"You are unfilial!
You did not personally provide for us,
but sought out strange and deluded things,
wandering to the four directions."
They wanted to flog him.
Máo Jūn knelt and apologized, saying:
"I have received a mandate from Heaven,
and am destined to attain the Way.
One cannot serve two purposes;
I have been far away and unable to provide for you.
Though I have been absent for many days, it was of no benefit,
but now I can bring peace to our household,
and ensure that my parents live long lives.
My Way is already complete;
you must not whip or humiliate me,
for I fear it will not be a trivial matter."
His father's anger did not cease,
and he took a staff to strike him.
Just as he was about to raise the staff,
it broke into several dozen pieces,
which flew about
like arrows shot from a bow.
Where they struck the wall, the wall was pierced;
where they struck a pillar, the pillar was dented.
Only then did his father stop.
Máo Jūn said:
"What I said earlier was precisely because I feared this—
lest by chance someone be injured."
His father said:
"You claim to have attained the Way.
Can you raise the dead?"
Máo Jūn said:
"The dead have heavy sins and accumulated evils;
they cannot be brought back to life.
But those who died untimely or prematurely—
they can be raised."
His father told him to demonstrate it, and it proved true.
Máo Jūn's younger brother held an official post with a salary of two thousand shí.
When he was about to take up his office,
several hundred people from the village came to see him off,
and Máo Jūn was also present.
He then said:
"Though I have not become an official of two thousand shí,
I am destined to hold a divine and spiritual office.
On such-and-such month and day, I will take up my post."
The guests all said:
"We would like to accompany you."
Máo Jūn said:
"If you are willing to see me off,
your kindness is indeed great.
But come empty-handed;
there is no need to spend anything.
I will have provisions to entertain you."
When the day arrived,
the guests all came,
and a great banquet was held.
There were dark green silk tents and canopies,
with thick white felt spread beneath.
Exquisite dishes and rare fruits
were arrayed in fragrant abundance.
Female musicians and music,
with metal and stone instruments all playing together,
their sound shook heaven and earth,
audible for several miles.
Over a thousand attendants
were all drunk and full.
When the officials came to welcome him,
there were several hundred civil officials in red robes with plain belts,
and military officials in armor with banners and flags,
their weapons gleaming in the sun,
encamped for miles around.
Máo Jūn bade farewell to his parents and relatives,
then mounted a feathered-canopy carriage and departed.
Banners and streamers flourished luxuriantly;
he was drawn by horned dragons and driven by tigers.
Flying birds and soaring beasts
leapt and covered above him;
flowing clouds and colored mists
drifted and swirled around him.
After traveling over ten miles from home,
he suddenly vanished from sight.
People far and near built temples to honor and serve him.
Máo Jūn, from within his tent,
spoke with people.
When he came out or went in,
he sometimes sent forth men and horses.
Sometimes he transformed into a white crane.
When people were ill,
they would go to seek blessings,
often boiling ten chicken eggs
and placing them inside the tent.
After a short while,
he would toss them out one by one and return them.
When taken home and cracked open,
if the yolk was intact,
the patient would recover.
If there was soil inside,
they would not recover.
This was often used as an omen.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn*.
Kǒng Ānguó
Kǒng Ānguó was a man from Lǔ.
He often practiced breath cultivation and ingested lead elixirs,
living to three hundred years of age,
with a complexion like a child's.
He lived in seclusion on Qián Mountain,
with several hundred disciples following him.
Whenever he abstained from grains and entered his chamber,
he would emerge after a year and a half,
looking even younger.
When he did not enter his chamber,
he ate and drank as usual,
no different from ordinary people.
Ānguó was a person of deep gravity,
and especially treasured and cherished the essentials of the Way.
He was unwilling to transmit them lightly.
Only after those who served him for five or six years
had been examined for their character and determination
would he transmit to them.
There was a man named Chén Bó,
from Ānlè,
who sought to serve Ānguó.
Ānguó accepted him as a disciple.
After staying for three years,
knowing his sincerity and trustworthiness,
he said to him:
"I too once endured hardship and toil,
seeking the arts of the Way,
going to every place,
yet I never obtained the method of the divine elixir and eight minerals to ascend to heaven.
I only received the method for becoming an earthbound immortal,
which merely allows one not to die.
Long ago, I served a fisherman by the seashore.
This fisherman
was none other than Fàn Lǐ, the former minister of Yuè.
He had changed his name and gone into hiding
to avoid the troubled times.
Taking pity on my determination,
he taught me secret methods of ingesting elixirs,
enabling me to transcend the world.
As for Dà Wǔ, Sī Chéng, Zǐ Qī, Jiāng Bó, and Túshān—
all of them, after a thousand years, became even more youthful and vigorous.
Since I received the Way,
I have been taking medicine for over three hundred years.
I once transmitted one formula to Cuī Zhòngqīng.
Qīng was eighty-four years old
and had been taking it for thirty-three years.
Looking at his body and energy, he is very robust,
his beard and hair not white,
his mouth and teeth intact and strong.
Go and meet him to see for yourself."
Chén Bó then went to serve him,
received his formula,
and also transcended the world without aging.
There was also the wife of Zhāng Hé,
fifty years old,
who after taking it looked instead like a woman in her twenties.
The whole county found it strange.
At eighty-six, she gave birth to a son.
He also taught several others,
all of whom lived to four hundred years.
Later, he entered the mountains and left.
There were also those who did not transcend the world,
due to the arts of the bedchamber.
From *Shénxiān Zhuàn*.
Yǐn Guǐ
Yǐn Guǐ,
styled Gōngdù,
was a man from Tàiyuán.
He was widely learned in the Five Classics,
and especially proficient in astronomy, celestial phenomena,
the River Chart and Luo Writing, and apocryphal texts—
all of which he mastered with profound subtlety.
Later in life, he took up the study of the Dao.
He regularly ingested the essence of huángjīng,
three ge per day,
and was said to be several hundred years old.
His predictions regarding the rise and fall of the realm,
its safety and peril, fortune and misfortune,
never failed to prove accurate.
At his waist, he wore over a dozen lacquered bamboo tubes,
each containing medicine,
which he said could ward off weapons and epidemics.
He often gave people a single pill,
instructing them to carry it.
When great chaos befell the age,
and many in his village suffered calamity,
only this household escaped disaster.
Also, during a major epidemic,
if one obtained a grain-sized amount to smear on the door,
the entire family would remain free of illness.
His disciple Huáng Lǐ
lived in the Lùhún Mountains.
He was troubled by fierce tigers.
Gōngdù had him cut wood into pillars,
and at a distance of five lǐ from his home,
bury one pillar in each of the four directions.
Gōngdù then stamped and sealed them,
and the tigers vanished without a trace,
turning back whenever they reached the five-lǐ boundary.
When a strange bird alighted on a house,
they informed Gōngdù.
Gōngdù wrote a talisman
and placed it where the bird was calling.
By evening,
the bird lay dead beneath the talisman.
Once, a man had a death in the family
and was due for burial but was impoverished,
anxiously unable to manage the arrangements.
Gōngdù passed by to check on him,
and the filial son recounted his orphaned hardship.
Gōngdù felt sorrow for him,
and told him to find a piece of lead.
Gōngdù entered Jīngshān,
set up a small hut,
and melted the lead in a furnace.
Taking a medicine he carried, the size of a grain of rice,
he tossed it into the lead and stirred,
whereupon it turned into fine silver.
He gave it to the man,
and told him:
"I sympathize with your poverty,
which prevents you from arranging the burial,
so I have come to your aid.
Be careful not to speak of this."
Another man owed a million in official money,
and was about to be seized and bound.
Gōngdù borrowed several thousand coins from a rich man and gave them to him,
instructing him to obtain tin.
He acquired a hundred liǎng.
Gōngdù melted it down again,
and threw in a square-inch spoonful of medicine,
turning it into gold,
which was used to repay the official debt.
Later, he went to Tàihé Mountain and ascended as an immortal.
From Biographies of Divine Immortals.
Jiè Xiàng
Jiè Xiàng,
styled Yuánzé,
was a man from Kuàijī.
He mastered the Five Classics through study,
and broadly perused the writings of the
(Míng manuscript and Chén collated edition have "hundred" for "one")
Hundred Schools,
being capable of literary composition.
Later, he studied the Dao and entered the Eastern Mountains.
He excelled in the arts of transcending the world and controlling breath.
He could light a fire on thatch to boil a chicken without scorching it;
he could cause all households within a lǐ to be unable to cook their food;
he could cause chickens and dogs within a lǐ to not crow or bark for three days;
he could cause all the people in a market to sit unable to rise;
he could conceal his form and transform into plants, trees, birds, or beasts.
Hearing of the Scripture of the Five Elixirs,
he traveled throughout the realm seeking it.
Failing to find its teacher,
he entered the mountains to concentrate his thoughts,
hoping to encounter a divine immortal.
Exhausted, he lay down on a rock.
A tiger came and licked Xiàng's forehead.
Xiàng awoke and saw the tiger,
then said to it:
"If Heaven sent you to guard me,
then stay;
if the mountain spirit sent you to test me,
then leave quickly."
The tiger then left.
Xiàng entered the mountains.
In a valley were stones,
purple in color,
with a very fine, glossy green sheen,
the size of chicken eggs,
too numerous to count.
He took two of them.
The valley was too deep to proceed,
so he turned back.
In the mountains, he saw a beautiful woman,
about fifteen or sixteen years old,
of extraordinary appearance,
clad in five-colored garments—
surely a divine immortal.
Xiàng begged her for a method of longevity.
The woman said:
"You must first return the objects in your hand to their original place,
then it may be possible.
You should not have taken these things;
that is why I have waited here for you."
Xiàng returned the stones,
and saw the woman at the former spot.
She said to Xiàng:
"Your aura of consuming blood and food is not yet exhausted.
Abstain from grains for three years and come again;
I will wait here."
Xiàng returned,
abstained from grains for three years, and went back,
finding this woman still at the former spot.
She then handed Xiàng a copy of the Scripture of the Reverted Elixir,
and told him:
"Obtaining this, you may attain immortality;
do not engage in other pursuits."
He then bid farewell and returned.
Xiàng often stayed at the residence of his disciple Luò Tíngyǎ,
behind the curtains of a screened bed.
Several students were debating the meaning of the Zuǒzhuàn,
and were at an impasse.
Xiàng, overhearing from the side, could not bear it,
and indignantly resolved the issue for them.
The scholars realized he was no ordinary man,
and secretly submitted a memorial recommending him to the ruler of Wú.
Xiàng learned of this and wished to leave,
saying:
"I fear official affairs will bind me."
Tíngyǎ firmly urged him to stay.
The King of Wú summoned him to Wǔchāng,
treated him with great respect,
and addressed him as "Lord Jiè."
He issued an edict to build him a residence;
the curtains and furnishings were all of brocade and embroidery,
and he presented him with a thousand yì of gold.
He studied the art of invisibility under Xiàng,
and when testing it by returning to the rear palace,
moving in and out of the women's quarters,
no one could see him.
Such magical arts,
and various transformations,
were too numerous to count.
Later, Xiàng reported that he was ill.
The emperor sent attendants and ladies-in-waiting,
and bestowed upon Xiàng a box of fine pears.
Xiàng ate them,
and shortly after died.
The emperor buried him.
He died at noon,
but by late afternoon he had already reached Jiànyè,
and gave the pears bestowed upon him to a garden official to plant.
The official later reported this by memorial.
The former ruler then opened the coffin to look,
and found only a talisman inside.
The emperor missed him,
and erected a temple for him,
often personally going to offer sacrifices.
White cranes often came to gather on the altar,
lingering awhile before departing again.
Later, disciples saw him in Gàizhú Mountain,
looking even younger.
From Biographies of Divine Immortals.
Sū Xiāngōng
The Immortal Lord Sū was a native of Guìyáng,
who attained the Way during the reign of Emperor Wén of the Hàn Dynasty.
He lost his father early in life,
and was known throughout his village for his benevolence and filial piety.
His home was located northeast of the commandery city.
Whether coming or going,
he paid no heed to dry or wet conditions.
As for food,
he did not mind whether it was fine or coarse.
His family was poor,
and he often herded cattle himself.
Together with the children of the village,
they took turns being the cowherd.
When he herded the cattle,
the cows would linger nearby
and return on their own without being driven.
When the other children herded the cattle,
the cows would scatter in all directions,
crossing hills and traversing dangerous terrain.
The children asked him,
"What technique do you use?"
He replied,
"This is not something you can understand."
He often rode a deer.
He often ate with his mother.
His mother said,
"We have no pickled fish for our meal.
Another day, you can go to the market to buy some."
Thereupon, he stuck his chopsticks into the rice,
took some money, and left.
In a short while, he returned with the pickled fish.
His mother had not yet finished eating
when she asked,
"Where did you buy this from?"
He replied,
"From the market in Biàn County."
His mother said,
"Biàn County is 120 lǐ from here.
The road is rugged and perilous.
For you to come and go so quickly—
you must be deceiving me!"
She intended to cane him.
He knelt and said,
"When I was buying the pickled fish,
I saw my uncle at the market.
He spoke to me, saying
he would come here tomorrow.
Please wait until my uncle arrives
to verify the truth of the matter."
His mother then relented.
The next morning,
his uncle indeed arrived.
He said that the previous day he had seen him buying pickled fish at the market in Biàn County.
His mother was then astonished
and realized he possessed divine powers.
He once carried a bamboo staff,
and people of the time said,
"Sū's bamboo staff
is truly a dragon."
Several years later,
he swept and cleaned his courtyard
and repaired the walls and buildings.
A friend asked,
"Are you expecting guests?"
He replied,
"Immortal companions are about to descend."
In a moment,
they saw from the northwestern corner of the sky
purple clouds swirling densely,
with several dozen white cranes
soaring within them,
gracefully descending to the gate of the Sū household.
They all transformed into youths,
with dignified and handsome appearances,
like people of seventeen or eighteen,
joyful and light-footed.
He composed himself to welcome them,
then knelt and said to his mother,
"I have received the mandate to become an immortal.
The summons has arrived at the appointed time.
The ceremonial escort is already here.
I must now part from your nurturing care."
He then bowed in farewell.
Mother and son wept.
His mother said,
"After you leave,
how will I survive?"
He replied,
"Next year, a plague will sweep the land.
The well water in the courtyard
and the orange tree by the eaves
can provide for you.
One shēng of well water
and one leaf from the orange tree
can cure one person.
I will also seal a chest and leave it for you.
If you lack anything,
you can knock on the chest and speak your need.
What you require will arrive.
Be careful not to open it."
After speaking, he went out the door,
lingered and looked back,
then leaped up into the clouds.
Purple clouds supported his feet,
and the flock of cranes soared,
ascending into the Milky Way and departing.
The following year,
a plague indeed occurred.
People from near and far all sought his mother for treatment.
Using the water and orange leaves,
everyone was cured without exception.
Whenever she lacked something,
she would knock on the chest,
and what she needed would arrive.
Three years later,
his mother grew suspicious
and opened the chest.
She saw a pair of white cranes fly away.
From then on, when she knocked on it,
there was no longer any response.
His mother lived to over a hundred years old
and one day passed away without illness.
The villagers buried her together
according to the customary rites of the world.
After the burial,
they suddenly saw over Niúpí Mountain northeast of the prefecture
a canopy of purple clouds,
and the sound of wailing was heard.
Everyone knew it was the spirit of Lord Sū.
The commandery governor and the villagers
all went to the mountain to offer condolences.
They only heard the sound of crying
but could not see his form.
The commandery governor and the villagers
earnestly requested to see him.
A voice from the air replied,
"I have been away from the mundane world for a long time,
and my appearance is far from ordinary.
If I were to reveal myself,
I fear it would truly startle and alarm you."
They insisted persistently,
so he showed half of his face
and one hand.
Both were covered in fine hair,
unlike an ordinary person.
He then said to the commandery governor and the villagers,
"You have troubled yourselves to come from afar to console me.
The road is treacherous and difficult.
You may return by a straight path.
Do not look back."
After speaking,
they saw a bridge spanning the ridge beside them,
extending all the way to the commandery city.
As they walked along it,
one official glanced back,
and the bridge immediately vanished.
He fell to the riverside,
where he saw a red dragon beneath his feet
coiling away.
At the place where he had wept,
two branches of cinnamon bamboo grew.
Without wind, they swept the ground on their own,
keeping the area perpetually clean.
Three years later,
the sound of crying was no longer heard.
Instead, a white horse was often seen on the ridge,
so Niúpí Mountain was renamed White Horse Ridge.
