Afterward, white cranes came to perch on the tower northeast of the commandery city.
Some people tried to shoot them with pellets.
A crane used its claws to scratch the tower's wooden boards,
as if writing with lacquer:
"The city walls remain,
but the people are not the same.
Once every three hundred jiǎzǐ cycles, I return.
I am Lord Sū—why shoot at me?"
To this day, those who cultivate the Way
burn incense and pay respects
at the former residence of the Immortal Lord on every jiǎzǐ day.
From "Biographies of the Immortals."
Another account says:
Sū Dān was a native of Guìyáng.
From a young age, he was renowned for his utmost filial piety.
His mother desired fish soup,
so Dān went to the lake.
He went to the market to buy some,
though it was 1,400 lǐ from home,
and returned in a short while.
His uncle was a clerk in the prefecture
and saw Dān at the market.
He wrote a letter home about it,
and the family was greatly astonished.
Dān later told his mother,
"I have received the mandate to become an immortal
and must soon leave to serve afar.
I leave two trays at home for you."
If one needed food,
they would tap the small plate;
if one desired money or silk,
they would tap the large plate,
and whatever was needed would immediately arrive.
The villagers all found this strange,
and reported it to the authorities.
Officials were sent to inspect the plates but found nothing,
yet Dān’s mother used them as if by divine power.
Earlier,
when Dān first departed, he had said:
"This year there will be a great plague,
and about half the people will die.
The water from the well at home,
if drunk, will keep one safe."
It indeed turned out as he said,
and the entire household remained safe and auspicious.
His mother lived to over a hundred years old before passing away.
People heard crying from the mountain,
which only ceased after the mourning period ended.
The common people built a shrine for her.
From "Dòngshén Zhuàn"
Immortal Lord Chéng
Immortal Lord Chéng,
courtesy name Wǔdīng,
was from Wūlǐ, Línwǔ, Guìyáng.
During the Later Hàn dynasty, at the age of thirteen,
he was seven feet tall.
He served as a minor clerk in the county,
possessing an extraordinary demeanor,
speaking little but with great magnanimity,
not flattering others,
so people called him foolish.
From a young age, he was well-versed in the classics,
though not taught by any master,
relying only on his innate nature.
Once, he was sent on an errand to the capital,
and on his way back, he passed through Chángshā Commandery.
Unable to reach the postal station in time,
he spent the night under a tree in the wilderness.
Suddenly, he heard voices from the tree saying:
"Let's go to the Chángshā market to buy medicine."
At dawn, he looked up
and saw two white cranes.
The Immortal Lord found this strange.
He then went to the market,
where he saw two men covered by white umbrellas,
walking together.
The gentleman called them over and offered them food.
After eating, they left immediately,
without even a glance of thanks.
The gentleman followed them for several miles,
until the two men turned and saw him.
They asked:
"What do you seek, following us without ceasing?"
The gentleman replied:
"I come from humble origins,
and I have heard that you possess the art of aiding life.
That is why I follow you."
The two men looked at each other and smiled,
then took out a jade case,
and examined a plain book.
Sure enough, Wǔdīng's name was written there.
They then gave him two pills,
instructing him to take them.
The two men said to the gentleman:
"You shall attain the status of an earthly immortal."
They then told him to return home.
He gained the ability to illuminate all things,
and could understand the sounds of beasts and the calls of birds.
After returning home,
the county sent him to deliver provisions to the Prefect.
The Prefect, Zhōu Xīn,
possessed the discernment to recognize talent.
Upon seeing the gentleman,
he called out:
"What is your name?"
He replied:
"My surname is Chéng, given name Wǔdīng,
a minor clerk in the county office."
The Prefect found him extraordinary
and kept him by his side.
After some time,
he appointed him as Literary Registrar.
Once, while sitting with others,
he heard sparrows chirping and laughed.
When asked the reason,
he replied:
"A cart has overturned in the eastern market, spilling rice,
and the sparrows are calling each other to go eat."
They sent someone to check,
and it was indeed true.
At that time, the officials and powerful families in the commandery
were puzzled why he had promoted a humble, lowly person, disrupting the established order.
The Prefect said:
"This is not something you all can understand."
After about ten days,
he had the gentleman stay in the pavilion for duty.
On the first day of the New Year's assembly,
with over three hundred people present,
he ordered the gentleman to serve wine.
After the wine had been served all around,
the gentleman suddenly sprayed a cup of wine toward the southeast.
The guests were astonished and found it strange.
The Prefect said:
"There must be a reason for this."
He then asked for an explanation.
The gentleman said:
"There is a fire in Línwǔ County,
and I am using this to extinguish it."
All the guests laughed.
The next day, the officials reported the matter,
accusing Wǔdīng of disrespect,
and immediately sent an envoy to Línwǔ County to verify it.
A man named Zhāng Jì from the county submitted a report,
stating: "On New Year's Day, during the celebration and drinking,
in the late afternoon, a fire suddenly spread to the main hall,
starting from the northwest.
The weather was clear at the time,
with a strong south wind.
We saw a cloud formation rise straight up from the northwest,
heading directly to the county,
bringing heavy rain.
The fire was immediately extinguished,
and the rain carried the smell of wine."
Everyone was amazed and puzzled,
and they realized that the gentleman was no ordinary person.
Later, the Prefect ordered the gentleman to move west of the commandery city,
where he established a residence to live,
with only his mother, a younger brother, and two young sons.
After about two years,
the gentleman reported being ill,
and passed away after four days.
The Prefect personally attended his funeral.
Two days later,
before the mourning garments were even prepared,
a friend of the gentleman came from Línwǔ
and met him on Wǔchāng Ridge,
riding a white mule westward.
The friend asked:
"The day is about to end;
where are you going?"
He replied:
"I am going to Míxī for a short while.
I will return shortly.
When I left,
I forgot my large knife by the door
and my shoes on the chicken roost.
Please tell my family to retrieve them."
The friend went to his home,
where he heard crying.
He exclaimed in surprise:
"I just met the gentleman on Wǔchāng Ridge,
and we spoke. He said he was going to Míxī for a short while
and would return soon.
He asked me to tell his family
to retrieve the knife and shoes.
How can this be?"
His family said:
"The knife and shoes have already been placed in the coffin.
How could they be outside?"
They immediately reported this matter to the Prefect.
The Prefect ordered the coffin to be opened for inspection.
Inside, they found no corpse,
only a green bamboo staff,
about seven feet long.
Only then did they realize that the gentleman had transformed and ascended as an immortal.
People of the time said that the gentleman rode a mule on Wǔchāng Ridge,
so it was renamed Mule Ridge,
located ten miles west of the commandery.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn"
Guō Pú
Guō Pú, styled Jǐngchún,
was a man of Hédōng.
He possessed extensive knowledge and broad learning,
with the insight of one who had transcended worldly ways.
In astronomy and geography,
turtle texts and dragon charts,
the hexagrams, images, prophecies, and apocrypha,
and the siting of tombs and dwellings,
there was nothing he did not probe to its subtlest depths.
He excelled at discerning the circumstances of both humans and spirits.
Lǐ Hóng and Fàn Lín's "Discourse on Illuminating the Way"
The Ming manuscript has the character "Hàn" above "Lín"
states that Jǐngchún was skilled in remote divination,
and scholars who composed writings
all revered him as their master.
During the revival of the Jìn dynasty,
Wáng Dǎo received his established principles
to build the state and its altars of soil and grain.
Pú fully established the rules, regulations, and systems,
looking up to model himself on the stars of the Tàiwēi constellation,
and looking down to follow the patterns of the Hé and Luò rivers and the Yellow River Chart.
Indeed, the founding acts of emperors and kings
must have the assistance of Heaven and men.
Wáng Dūn garrisoned Nánzhōu.
Wishing to plot a great rebellion,
he summoned Pú to assist him.
At that time, Emperor Míng was fifteen years old.
One evening, he gathered the court officials
and asked the Grand Astrologer:
"Will Wáng Dūn truly obtain the empire?"
The Historiographer-official replied:
"Wáng Dūn coerces the Son of Heaven,
he cannot obtain the empire."
Emperor Míng then rode alone in plain clothes,
and went straight into Gūshú City.
Dūn was just eating with Pú,
and for a long time, Pú did not inform Dūn.
Dūn said in alarm:
"We are now jointly discussing and deciding a great plan,
why do you not speak immediately?"
Pú said:
"Just now I saw the essence-spirits of the sun, moon, and stars,
and the deities of the Five Peaks and Four Seas,
all forming a retinue and providing escort.
Your humble official was so shaken and terrified that I lost my composure,
and could not immediately inform the General."
Dūn sent someone to inquire,
thinking it was a young servant playing with horses.
Upon investigation, it was determined this was not the case,
and he dispatched thirty horsemen in pursuit,
but they did not catch up.
Dūn said:
"Last night I dreamed I was in the river outside Shítóu City,
plowing with a plow.
Divine the meaning."
Pú said:
"Plowing with a plow in the great river,
means rebellion will not succeed,
and even if you rebel, you will achieve nothing."
Dūn angrily said to Pú:
"How much longer is your life-span?"
Pú said:
"Your humble official's life ends today."
Dūn executed Pú.
The river water suddenly rose in the market.
Pú's corpse
The Ming manuscript lacks the character "corpse"
emerged from a pit south of the city,
and it was seen that Pú's family had brought his coffin and burial implements,
which were already by the side of the pit.
Between two pine trees above was a magpie's nest,
just as Pú had foretold in a letter home.
He said to the executioner:
"When I was thirteen years old,
at Zhàtáng, I took off my robe and gave it to you.
My life is destined to end by your hand,
you may use my sword."
The executioner, moved by the past kindness and remembering the favor,
carried out the sentence with tears in his eyes.
Three days after the burial,
people in the southern market
saw Pú selling the clothes and ornaments he wore in life,
and conversing with acquaintances,
and not just with one person.
Dūn did not believe it,
and upon opening the coffin, there was no corpse.
Pú had attained the Way of liberation through violent death.
He is now the Elder of the Water Immortals,
and annotated the "Shānhǎi Jīng", "Xià Xiǎozhèng", "Ěryǎ", and "Fāngyán",
and authored "Yóuxiān Shī", "Jiāng Fù", "Bǔ Yáo", "Kè Ào", and "Dònglín Yún".
The "Jìn Shū" contains his biography.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn".
Yǐn Sī
Yǐn Sī,
styled Xiǎolóng,
was a man of Āndìng.
On the night of the fifteenth day of the first month in the fifth year of the Yuánkāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
he sat in his house
and sent his son to see if there was anything unusual in the moon.
His son said:
"This year there will be a great flood.
There is a person in the moon wearing a straw raincoat and carrying a sword."
Sī looked and said:
"There will be rebellious soldiers arriving."
His son said:
"How do you know?"
He said:
"The person in the moon is wearing armor and carrying a spear.
There will be great chaos for thirty years,
and then it will become slightly peaceful again."
Later events indeed turned out as he said.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn".
Liú Zǐnán
Liú Zǐnán
was the Champion General and Governor of Wǔwēi of the Hàn dynasty.
He studied under the Daoist priest Yǐn Gōng,
and received the Firefly Pill of Wùchéngzǐ,
which warded off epidemic diseases and miasmas, all ghosts, tigers, wolves, vipers, snakes, wasps, and scorpions, and all poisons,
as well as the five weapons, naked blades, bandits, thieves, and violent harm.
It used realgar
The Ming manuscript has "orpiment" below "realgar"
two liang of each;
fireflies and Tribulus terrestris (devil's thorn) one liang each;
the handle of an iron hammer, burned until charred black;
furnace ashes and goat horn, one and a half fēn each,
ground into a powder like flour.
Using egg yolk and the blood from the comb of a red rooster,
form pills the size of apricot kernels.
Place five pills in a triangular crimson silk bag,
always carry it on the left arm.
Those in the army should tie it at the waist,
those at home should hang it above the door,
to ward off thieves, bandits, and all poisonous creatures.
Zǐnán compounded it and wore it.
In the twelfth year of the Yǒngpíng era,
he encountered barbarians within the borders of Wǔwēi county,
engaged in a great battle and was defeated,
the remaining troops fled and scattered,
and he alone was surrounded by the enemy.
Arrows fell like rain,
but before reaching within several feet of Zǐnán's horse,
the arrows would fall to the ground,
and in the end, none could hit or injure him.
The barbarians thought he was a divine man,
and so lifted the siege and left.
Zǐnán taught it to his sons and brothers who served in the army,
and none were ever wounded,
so they were delighted at its efficacy,
treasured it, and passed it down through the generations.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
the Green Ox Daoist Fēng Jūndé obtained it,
and transmitted it to Huángfǔ Lóng of Āndìng.
Lóng taught it to Emperor Wǔ of Wèi,
and then it gradually spread among the people.
It was also called "Champion Pill",
and also called Wǔwēi Pill.
It is now recorded in the "Qiānjīn Yì".
From "Shénxiān Gǎnyù Zhuàn".
Guō Wén,
courtesy name Wénjǔ,
was from Luòyáng,
and has a biography in the Book of Jìn.
He lived in seclusion on Tiānzhù Mountain in Yúháng,
sometimes dwelling at Dàbì Cliff.
The Perfected Lord Tàihé once descended to his chamber,
imparting to him the Way of Transcendent Truth.
He concealed his traces and cultivated in secret,
unknown to the world.
A tiger once came with its mouth open to the front of his stone chamber,
as if to tell him something.
Wénjǔ reached his hand into the tiger's throat and retrieved a bone,
removing it.
The next day,
the tiger brought a dead deer and left it outside the stone chamber.
From then on, the tiger was often tame and lingered by his side,
and he could even pet and lead it by a rope.
When Wénjǔ left the mountain,
the tiger would always follow him.
Even amidst crowds in the city,
the tiger would lower its head and follow along,
not daring to act violently,
just like a dog or sheep.
Sometimes he would place books or scrolls on its back,
and it would carry them as it walked.
Wénjǔ once gathered tree fruits and bamboo leaves
to trade for salt and rice,
placing them in a basket
that the tiger carried on its back as it followed him.
When the Jìn Emperor heard of this,
he summoned him to the imperial court
and asked:
"Do you, sir, possess an art for taming tigers?"
He replied:
"It is simply natural.
If humans harbor no intent to harm beasts,
beasts will have no desire to injure humans.
What need is there for an art?
If you care for me, I will follow you—
a tiger is like the people;
if you oppress me, I become your enemy—
the people are like tigers.
Governing the people and taming tigers—
how are they different?"
The Emperor esteemed his words highly,
but when offered an official post, he declined
and returned to seclusion on Áotíng Mountain,
where he attained the Way and departed.
Later, people found beneath his sleeping mat
some ruò leaves,
inscribed with the "Gold Male Poem" and "Gold Female Record,"
the words of which were all prophecies of that time.
His shed skin was like that of a snake.
From "Shénxiān Shíyí."
The Old Man of Sōng Mountain
lived during the Jìn dynasty.
As the Shìshuō records,
north of Sōng Mountain there was a great cavern,
its depth immeasurable.
Commoners would visit and gaze into it each year.
The old man once accidentally fell into the cavern.
His companions, hoping he might still be alive,
threw food down into the cavern.
The fallen man obtained it and ate.
He then wandered through the cavern,
and after about ten days,
suddenly beheld a vast brightness
and a thatched cottage.
Inside, two immortals were playing chess opposite each other.
Beneath the chessboard were several cups of a white drink.
The fallen man told them of his hunger and thirst,
and the chess players gave him the drink.
After drinking it,
his strength increased tenfold.
The chess players asked:
"Do you wish to remain here?"
He answered that he did not wish to stay.
The chess players instructed him:
"Head west from here for several tens of paces,
and you will find a great well.
Within the well are many strange creatures;
take care not to fear them.
You must throw yourself into the well,
and you will naturally emerge.
If you are hungry,
you may take things from the well to eat."
Following their words, he entered the well.
Inside were many flood dragons,
but upon seeing the old man, they immediately cleared a path for him.
Thus, he proceeded along the well.
The substance in the well resembled blue mud but was fragrant and delicious;
eating it completely relieved his hunger.
After about half a year,
he emerged at Qīngchéng Mountain in Shǔ
and thus was able to return to Luòyáng.
He inquired of Zhāng Jǔ
(Míng manuscript and Chén collated edition have "Huà" for "Jǔ")
and Jǔ said:
"That is the abode of transcendent gentlemen.
What you drank was jade nectar,
and what you ate was the marrow of dragon-cave stone.
You, sir, must have attained transcendence!"
He then sought to return to the cavern,
but no one knows where he went.
As the Xuánzhōng Jì states,
in Qīngchéng Mountain of Shǔ Commandery, there is a cavern
that divides into three paths,
with the northwestern one connecting to Kūnlún.
The Biography of Lord Máo says
that Qīngchéng is the Heaven of the Fifth Cavern and Nine Immortals' Treasure Chamber,
with a circumference of two thousand lǐ,
one of the Ten Cavern Heavens.
Travel ten lǐ into the mountain to reach it.
From "Shénxiān Shíyí."
Xǔ Zhēnjūn
The True Lord Xǔ, named Xǔn,
styled Jìngzhī,
was originally from Rǔnán.
His grandfather was Yǎn,
and his father was Sù,
both of whom admired the ultimate Dao.
Mài, a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat of the Eastern Jìn,
and Mù, a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Chief Clerk of the Army Protector,
were both clansmen of the True Lord.
When the True Lord reached the age of twenty,
he became a disciple of the Great Cavern Lord Wú Měng,
from whom he received the "Essential Methods of the Three Purities."
He was recommended by his village as Filial and Incorrupt,
and appointed as Magistrate of Jīngyáng in Shǔ.
Soon, due to the chaos within the Jìn court,
he abandoned his post and returned east.
Thus, he traveled with Lord Wú to the region east of the river,
where they encountered Wáng Dūn's rebellion.
The True Lord then pretended to be a messenger with a tally,
seeking an audience with Dūn,
intending to stop Dūn's violence
and preserve the Jìn dynasty.
One day,
the True Lord and Guō Pú together waited upon Dūn.
Dūn, harboring anger, received them
and said to the True Lord:
"I had a dream last night,
and I wish to ask you, sir, to interpret it.
May I?"
The True Lord said:
"Please describe it in detail, Great General."
Dūn said:
"I dreamed of taking a piece of wood
and piercing the sky with it.
I abdicated the imperial throne.
Is this truly auspicious?"
Lord Xǔ said:
"This dream is certainly not auspicious."
Dūn said:
"May I ask for an explanation?"
The True Lord said:
"A piece of wood piercing the sky
forms the character 'wèi' (未).
Your Excellency should not act recklessly.
The fortune of Jìn is certainly not yet in decline."
Wáng Dūn grew angry
and ordered Guō Pú to perform a divination.
When the hexagram was completed,
Jǐngchún (Guō Pú) said:
"There will be no success."
Dūn also asked about his lifespan.
Pú said:
"If Your Excellency initiates action,
disaster will soon follow.
If you remain in Wǔchāng,
your lifespan will be immeasurable."
Dūn was greatly enraged
and asked further:
"How long will your own lifespan be?"
Pú said:
"My life ends today."
Dūn, furious,
ordered guards to seize Pú and take him out,
intending to execute him.
At that moment,
the two True Lords were drinking with Dūn.
Lord Xǔ threw his cup onto the beam,
where it flew and circled around it.
As Dūn and the others looked up at the cup,
Lord Xǔ vanished from his seat.
He then headed south, exiting the Jìn pass,
and reached the mouth of the Lújiāng River.
He summoned a boatman
to take him to Zhōnglíng.
At that time,
the boatman said:
"Although I have this boat,
I lack the manpower to row it;
I cannot take you."
The True Lord said:
"Just let me board the boat,
and I will make it move myself."
He then said to the boatman:
"You should go into the boat,
close the door and hide deeply.
If you hear the boat moving swiftly,
do not peek out."
Then the boat rose from the water,
soaring into the clouds.
The True Lord sat upright, conversing,
and in a moment,
they had already reached the summit of Zǐxiāo Peak, northwest of the Golden Gate Cavern on Lúshān.
The True Lord intended to pass through the cavern briefly,
but as the dragons descended lower,
the boat brushed against the trees,
creating a startling, crashing sound.
The noise was extraordinary,
and the boatman could not help but steal a glance.
The two dragons, realizing they had been seen,
left the boat atop the peak and departed.
The True Lord said to the boatman:
"You disobeyed my instruction,
startling and disturbing the two dragons,
causing them to abandon this boat atop a peak ten thousand ren high.
Because I am eager to join the other True Lords in eradicating evil,
I must leave this place for a time
and travel the rivers and lakes.
Since you have lost your boat,
you may return to the mortal world on foot.
You may dwell here on Zǐxiāo Peak,
and roam Kuānglú (Lúshān)."
He showed him the method of consuming spiritual herbs,
and pointed out the arts of becoming an earthbound immortal.
Thus, the bottom of the boatman's boat
left traces that remain to this day.
Later, in Yùzhāng, he encountered a youth,
handsome and well-groomed,
who called himself Shèn Láng.
Lord Xǔ spoke with him
and realized he was not human.
In the blink of an eye,
the youth bid farewell and left.
The True Lord said to his disciples:
"That youth just now
is actually the essence of a flood dragon or sea monster.
Considering that Jiāngxī has repeatedly suffered from floods,
if we do not eliminate him,
he is likely to escape."
The sea monster essence, knowing the True Lord had recognized him,
hid north of Lóngshā Islet,
transforming into a yellow ox.
The True Lord observed from afar with his Daoist vision
and said to his disciple Shī Dàwáng:
"That creature of essence
has transformed into a yellow ox.
I will now transform into a black ox,
and tie a handkerchief around my leg
to serve as identification.
When you see the oxen charging and fighting,
strike him with your sword."
"Him" originally read "later"
and was changed according to the Chén manuscript edition.
The True Lord then transformed and left.
Moments later,
indeed, a black ox was seen chasing a yellow ox.
Dàwáng swung his sword at the ox,
striking its left thigh.
It then plunged into a well west of the city.
The black ox transformed by Lord Xǔ
chased after it into the well.
The sea monster essence then fled from this well,
heading straight to Tánzhōu,
where it transformed back into human form.
Previously,
the sea monster essence had transformed into a handsome youth,
intelligent and elegant,
and also exceedingly wealthy.
Knowing that Jiǎ Yù, the Prefect of Tánzhōu,
had a beautiful daughter,
and wished to find a noble son-in-law to match her,
the sea monster essence lavishly used treasures
to bribe those close to Prefect Jiǎ,
and thus succeeded in becoming his son-in-law.
Afterward, he lived with his wife in the rear courtyard of the official residence.
Every spring and summer,
he often requested to travel the rivers and lakes,
returning each time with treasures and wealth
amounting to tens of thousands.
The relatives, in-laws, and servants of Prefect Jiǎ
all became wealthy by relying on him.
Now, however,
the sea monster essence returned empty-handed,
claiming
he had been injured by robbers.
While the whole family was sighing in regret,
the receptionist reported
that a Daoist named Xǔ, styled Jìngzhī,
requested to see the Prefect.
Prefect Jiǎ hastily received him.
The True Lord said to Prefect Jiǎ:
"I have heard you have a noble son-in-law.
May I briefly meet him?"
Prefect Jiǎ then ordered Shèn to come out and meet the Daoist.
Shèn Láng was terrified
and feigned illness to hide.
The True Lord said sternly:
"This is a creature that harms the rivers and lakes,
an old demon flood dragon and sea monster.
How dare you hide your form!"
Thereupon, the sea monster essence reverted to its original form,
writhing in the hall,
and was soon killed by the officers and soldiers.
The True Lord also ordered its two sons to be brought out.
He sprayed water on them,
and they immediately transformed into small sea monsters.
His wife, Lady Jiǎ,
was on the verge of transforming as well.
Her parents pleaded with the True Lord,
who then gave her a divine talisman to cure her.
Lǐ Quán, styled Dáguānzǐ,
dwelt on Shàoshì Mountain.
He was fond of the Way of divine transcendents,
often traveling to famous mountains,
and broadly gathering esoteric arts.
Upon reaching Tiger Mouth Cliff on Sōng Mountain,
he obtained a copy of the Yellow Emperor’s *Yīnfú Jīng*,
written on plain silk,
with a vermilion-lacquered scroll rod,
sealed in a jade casket,
and inscribed:
“On the seventh day of the seventh month of the second year of the True Lord of Great Wèi,
the Shàngqīng Daoist Kòu Qiānzhī
concealed this among the famous mountains,
to transmit it to those of shared devotion.”
The original was decayed,
and though Quán copied and read it thousands of times,
he ultimately could not comprehend its principles.
Thereupon, he entered Qín,
and arriving at the foot of Lí Mountain,
he encountered an old woman,
with a coiled chignon atop her head,
the remaining hair half hanging down,
clad in worn clothes and leaning on a staff,
her divine appearance most extraordinary.
By the roadside, seeing leftover fire burning a tree,
she spoke to herself:
“Fire is born from wood;
when calamity erupts, must it overcome?”
Startled, Quán asked her:
“This is from the opening passage of the Yellow Emperor’s *Yīnfú*;
how did you, mother, come to speak it?”
The mother said:
“I received this talisman
already three cycles and six sexagenary rounds of jiǎzǐ ago;
young man, how did you obtain it?”
Quán bowed deeply in prostration,
and fully recounted how he had obtained it.
The mother said:
“Young man, your cheekbones connect to the Gate of Life,
your destiny wheel aligns with the Sun Horn,
your blood vessels have not diminished
“diminished” originally read “extinguished”
emended according to the Ming manuscript and the Chén collated edition
your heart’s reflection is not askew,
your nature is worthy and fond of the Dharma,
your spirit is valiant and delights in the ultimate
the Ming manuscript reads “wisdom” for “ultimate”
truly you are my disciple.
However, at forty-five you will face a great calamity.”
Thereupon, she brought out a cinnabar-written talisman in one scroll,
threaded it onto the tip of her staff,
and ordered Quán to kneel and swallow it.
She said:
“Heaven and Earth will protect you.”
Then, sitting upon a stone,
she explained the meaning of the *Yīnfú* to Quán,
saying:
“This talisman consists of three hundred words in total:
one hundred words expound the Way,
one hundred words expound techniques,
one hundred words expound methods.
Above, it contains the Way of the divine transcendents ‘embracing the One’;
in the middle, methods for enriching the state and pacifying the people;
below, techniques for strengthening the military and achieving victory in battle.
All arise internally from the workings of the mind,
and externally accord with human affairs.
Observing its subtleties,
the *Huángtíng* and *Nèijǐng* cannot be considered profound;
perceiving its utmost essentials,
classics, commentaries, masters, and histories cannot be considered literary;
Sūn, Wú, Hán, and Bái cannot be considered extraordinary.
Unless one is a man of the Way,
they should not be allowed to hear it.
Thus, the ultimate person using it attains the Way,
the noble person using it attains the techniques,
the common person using it incurs disaster—
this is because their duties
the Ming manuscript reads “understanding” for “duties”
and stations differ.
If transmitting it to those of shared devotion,
you must purify yourself through fasting before bestowing it.
The one who possesses the original is the master;
the one who receives the writing is the disciple.
You must not regard the wealthy and noble as important,
nor the poor and lowly as insignificant.
Those who violate this will forfeit twenty years of lifespan.
On your birthdate, recite it seven times:
it will benefit the workings of your mind,
and increase your years of life.
Each year on the seventh day of the seventh month,
copy one volume and conceal it within the rocky cliffs of a famous mountain:
you will gain added years.”
After a while,
the mother said:
“It is already late afternoon;
I have some wheat porridge,
let us eat together.”
From her sleeve, she produced a gourd,
and ordered Quán to fetch water from the valley.
Once the water was full,
the gourd suddenly became heavy, over a hundred jīn,
and his strength could not control it,
so it sank into the spring.
By the time he returned,
the old mother had already vanished,
leaving only a few shēng of wheat porridge upon the stone.
Quán possessed strategic acumen,
and composed the *Tàibái Yīnfú* in ten volumes;
he had ministerial talent,
and authored the *Zhōngtái Zhì* in ten volumes.
At the time, he was sidelined by Lǐ Línfǔ,
and his position was not illustrious.
Ultimately, he entered the famous mountains to seek the Way,
and his whereabouts became unknown.
From *Shénxiān Gǎnyù Zhuàn*
Daoist Wáng Zuǎn
Dàoshi Wáng Zuǎn was a man of
Jīntán,
dwelling at Mǎjì Mountain.
He constantly used hidden merits to rescue creatures,
his benevolence reaching even the lowly.
It happened during the end of the Western Jìn dynasty,
when the Central Plains were in chaotic turmoil,
famine had already arrived,
and pestilence then arose.
At that time, there were poisonous miasmas,
and those who perished were many;
villages withered and lay desolate,
the dead lay piled upon each other.
Zuǎn, in his quiet chamber,
sent up a memorial to inform the Mysterious,
and for three nights,
he continued with weeping.
On the third night,
there was a light like daylight
illuminating his household.
Immediately, auspicious winds and numinous clouds
billowed densely in the sky.
Soon after, wondrous fragrances and celestial music
descended and gathered in the courtyard.
Over three thousand armored warriors bearing sharp weapons
stood arrayed as if awaiting something.
After a short while,
pearl banners and precious streamers,
rainbow pennants and feathered tallies,
and two each of red flags and embroidered banners
advanced facing each other as guides.
The banners were at the front,
the tallies were at the very rear.
Also, four azure youths held flowers and offered incense,
two maidservants held a table,
the ground spread with brocade mats.
A great screen was set up before them,
with Dragon and Tiger Generals on the left and right,
and attendant officers and commanders,
about twenty each,
standing on both sides of the screen,
as if providing guard.
Furthermore, there were twenty-six great generals in golden armor,
and fifty spirit beings.
After the two lords Dragon and Tiger,
the ranks were arrayed in solemn order.
In a moment,
the sound of pipes and reeds startled the sky,
coming from the north.
Five-colored wondrous light
shone dazzlingly brilliant and radiant.
One person, wearing a sword and holding a tablet, came forward
and announced to Zuǎn:
"The Supreme Dao Lord has arrived."
Thereupon,
a great seat of a hundred treasures
descended from the sky.
The Supreme Great Dao Lord,
attended by two Perfected Ones
and two Celestial Emperors.
Upon the seat,
the Dao Lord sat on a five-colored lotus flower,
with the two Perfected and two Emperors standing in attendance.
Zuǎn bowed with clasped hands to greet him,
kneeling and prostrating on the ground.
The Dao Lord said:
"You have compassion for the living people,
expressed in your true memorial,
cutting your heart and offering your blood,
deeply moving the hidden realms.
The terrestrial offices have reported your words,
and I have thus personally examined you."
After Zuǎn finished kowtowing in ritual thanks,
the Dao Lord informed him:
"Now, the one yīn and one yáng
transform and nurture the myriad things,
and the Five Phases are their function.
The Five Phases mutually
"mutually" originally read "and";
amended according to the Ming manuscript and the Chén collated edition
have mutual conquest,
each has its flourishing and decline,
succeeding and shifting,
without a moment's pause.
Therefore, generation follows generation without cease,
and breath follows breath in continuous succession
"succession" originally read "conquest";
amended according to the Ming manuscript and the Chén collated edition
Since countless kalpas past,
it has never ceased even briefly.
Those who attain life
merge with pure yáng,
ascend to heaven and become immortals;
those who attain death
sink into ultimate yīn,
reside on earth and become ghosts.
Among ghostly beings,
there naturally exist superior and inferior, strong and weak,
firm and yielding, good and evil,
no different from the human world.
The Jade Emperor Celestial Worthy,
concerned that ghosts and spirits might run rampant and harm people,
constantly commands the Five Emperors and Three Offices
to inspect, control, and govern them.
Laws, ordinances, and penal statutes
are all clearly and fully prepared.
However, the people of these latter days,
those who are shallow and deceitful are many.
The pure source having already scattered,
demonic fraudulence sprouts and grows.
They are not loyal to their sovereign,
not filial to their parents,
violate the teachings of the Three Bonds and Five Constants,
and cast themselves into the realm of death.
Due to the old ethers of the Six Heavens,
the followers of demonic ghosts,
together with those from past generations,
defeated generals and dead soldiers,
gather and form factions,
also slaughtering and harming the living people.
Riding the rain and driving the wind,
they take advantage of decline and watch for gaps,
causing all kinds of illnesses.
Those they wound and harm are extremely numerous;
there are also those who do not complete their natural lifespan,
meeting with untimely death and wrongful demise.
In the past, from the Dùyáng Palace, I issued the *Divine Incantation Scripture*,
bestowing it upon the Perfected Táng Píng,
so that he might spread it widely,
to rescue creatures,
and it exists among the people.
People of the world, seeing the names of Wáng Jiǎn and Bái Qǐ,
consider them false and baseless.
This is because these former commanders,
in life were leaders of troops,
in death become chiefs of ghosts.
Those with merit are transferred to become underworld officials.
Those who were cruel and harmful still belong to the demonic kind,
riding the defeated ethers of the Five Phases,
causing consumption and epidemics.
However, they fear the yang,
and submitting them with divine incantations,
they will naturally cease and desist.
Now, I bestow upon you again the two scriptures, *Divine Transformations* and *Divine Incantations*,
again bestowing them upon you,
to practice according to them,
in order to rescue and protect the myriad people."
He then commanded an attendant youth,
to open the nine-radiance case,
and bestowed upon Zuǎn the *Divine Transformations Scripture* and the oral instructions for the *Three-Five Great Purification*,
bestowing them upon Zuǎn,
saying:
"Strive and be diligent!
When your hidden merits are fully accomplished,
the true ranks can be hoped for!"
When he finished speaking,
a thousand chariots and ten thousand riders
rose toward the northwest,
ascending and returning to the Upper Clarity.
Zuǎn practiced the scriptural categories and purification rituals
in the region south of the Yangtze,
and the pestilential poison was suppressed and ceased.
Living beings became healthy again.
From the Jìn dynasty until now,
those who have received his blessings
cannot be fully recorded.
From *Biographies of Encounters with Immortals*
Zhēnbái Xiānshēng
The True White Master, Táo Hóngjǐng,
whose given name was Hóngjǐng,
courtesy name Tōngmíng,
was the seventh-generation descendant of Táo Jùn, the Governor of Jīng Province in the state of Wú,
and a native of Dānyáng.
When his mother was first pregnant with him,
she dreamed of a green dragon emerging from her bosom,
accompanied by two heavenly beings descending,
holding incense burners in their hands.
Upon waking, she told those around her,
saying she would give birth to a son,
no ordinary man,
and she feared greatly that she might have no heir.
When he was born,
he was extraordinary.
As a child, he was intelligent and perceptive;
as he grew, he became erudite and insightful.
After reading the *Biographies of Immortals*,
he developed the ambition to ride clouds and command dragons.
At the age of seventeen,
he, along with Jiāng Xiào, Chǔ Xuàn, and Liú Jùn,
became known as the "Four Friends of Shēngmíng" during the Sòng dynasty.
He served in the Qí dynasty,
holding the position of Tutor to various princes.
In his twenties,
he began to practice dietary and medicinal regimens.
Later, he sought instruction in the scriptures and methods from Master Sūn, the abbot of Xīngshì Temple,
and diligently practiced the essential teachings of the Way.
He attained profound and subtle understanding,
and was appointed
"Appointed" originally read "transmitted,"
changed according to *The Seven Bamboo Tablets of the Cloudy Satchel*, scroll 107, "Biography of Lǐ Bó's True White Master"
to the position of Attendant Gentleman,
but he submitted a memorial resigning from his post.
The imperial reply expressed admiration and regret,
and he was granted generous gifts.
High officials and nobles saw him off at Zhēnglǔ Pavilion,
with lavish provisions and tents,
and all said:
"Since the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
nothing like this has ever happened."
He then entered Máo Mountain,
and also obtained the true writings of Yáng Xī and Xǔ Mù.
He climbed the cliffs to declare his retirement into quietude,
calling himself "The Recluse of Huáyáng,"
and used this name in his correspondence instead of his given name.
During the reign of Emperor Míng
"Emperor" originally read "year,"
changed according to *The Seven Bamboo Tablets of the Cloudy Satchel*
of the Qí dynasty,
there was a proposal to invite him to Jiǎng Mountain,
but he earnestly declined and the matter was dropped.
Nevertheless, imperial edicts and gifts
were frequently sent to him in great abundance.
He then built a three-story tower to reside in,
living on the top floor himself,
with his disciples in the middle,
and receiving guests on the lower floor,
with only a young servant boy to relay messages.
He concealed his brilliance and hid his light,
cultivating secret practices internally,
with deep sincerity in his pursuits.
He was connected to spiritual beings from afar,
truly one who could be said to be moved and thus attained communion.
He was seven feet eight inches tall,
and his nature was accommodating, humble, and cautious.
His mind was like a bright mirror,
comprehending things as soon as he encountered them.
He deeply admired Zhāng Liáng's character,
and by nature, he was light and ethereal,
floating gracefully with the spirit of the clouds.
His understanding of things
all came from his own mind,
not something that could be matched by relying on others' knowledge.
He excelled at correcting errors and falsehoods.
In geography and calendrical calculations,
his writings were never empty,
and what he completed became authoritative works.
He constructed an armillary sphere,
and when rotated,
it matched the movements of the heavens.
He compiled the *True Declarations* and *Secret Instructions*,
annotated the *Lǎozǐ* and other texts,
totaling over two hundred scrolls.
In the third year of the Yǒngyuán era
"Yuán" originally read "píng,"
changed according to the Ming dynasty manuscript copy
he withdrew deeply into seclusion.
When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng overthrew the previous dynasty,
and the discussion of the new state's name was undecided,
the Master cited various prophetic records,
determining the signs that Liáng was destined to rise.
He also selected the auspicious day for the abdication ceremony,
and the spiritual efficacy was clearly manifested.
An imperial envoy was sent into the mountains,
to convey the emperor's gratitude.
The emperor had associated with him since early times,
and from then on, he reported all his activities to the Master.
Having obtained secret teachings and marvelous methods,
the Master believed that the divine elixir could be completed,
but he was constantly troubled by the lack of medicinal ingredients,
which the emperor supplied to him.
The emperor also sent handwritten edicts inquiring and inviting him,
so the Master painted two oxen:
one roaming freely in the water;
the other wearing a golden halter,
with a person holding a rope,
driving it with a stick.
The emperor laughed and said:
"This man will do anything;
he wishes to imitate the turtle dragging its tail in the mud,
how could he be summoned?"
At that time, whenever there were major affairs of state,
he had already presented memorials beforehand,
so people of the time called him the "Prime Minister in the Mountains."
In the early years of the Dàtóng era,
he presented two swords,
one named "Shànshèng,"
the other named "Chéngshèng,"
which were considered excellent treasures.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng initially did not understand Daoism,
but the Master gradually enlightened him.
Later, he visited the Celestial Master Zhāng Dàoyù,
and three hundred altars of mystery were established,
all funded by the Master.
Emperor
"Emperor" originally had the character "Wǔ" following it,
but since *The Master of the Golden Tower* was written by Emperor Yuán,
it is deleted according to *The Seven Bamboo Tablets of the Cloudy Satchel*
Yuán of Liáng wrote in *The Master of the Golden Tower*:
"Among recluses, I value Táo Zhēnbái;
among scholar-officials, I value Zhōu Hóngzhèng.
In terms of principles and reasoning,
they were profound and boundless,
truly renowned scholars of their time."
The Master once composed a poem:
"Yífǔ indulged in unrestrained freedom,
Píngshū sat discussing emptiness.
They did not believe the Zhāoyáng Palace
would become the Chányú's palace."
At that time, everyone discussed empty theories,
and neglected military affairs.
The rebellion of Hóu Jǐng
turned out just as he said.
The Master passed away on the twelfth day, Guǐchǒu, of the third month, the first day being Rényín, in the second year of the Dàtóng era, the year Bǐngchén,
at the age of eighty-one.
His complexion did not change,
and his limbs remained flexible as in life.
The fragrance in his room
lingered for days without dispersing.
On the fourteenth day of that month,
he was buried at Léipíng Mountain,
like Xuānyuán's burial of his robes and cap,
or like Zǐqiáo's concealment of his sword and shoes.
Comparing it to this day,
it matches the signs.
An imperial edict posthumously honored him as Grand Master of Palace Leisure,
and bestowed the posthumous title "True White Master,"
with an order for a palace attendant to oversee the funeral arrangements.
Mǎ Shū's *Biographies of Those Who Attained the Way* states:
"He received the position of Dūshuǐ Supervisor of Pénglái.
He had several hundred disciples.
Among those who attained the Way before him,
only Wáng Yuǎnzhī, Lù Yìchōng, and Huán Qīngyuǎn
carried on the Master's virtue."
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
he was posthumously honored as Grand Guardian with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon,
and Xiāo Lún, Prince of Liángjùn
the Xǔ printed edition reads "jùn" as "shào"
composed a stele inscription for him.
From *Biographies of Encounters with Immortals*,
the Ming dynasty manuscript copy states it is from *Collected Omissions on Immortals*
Huán Kǎi
Huán Kǎi was a man
whose origins are unknown.
He served the gentleman Táo Hóngjǐng,
as a menial laborer,
toiling diligently for over ten years.
His nature was consistently cautious, taciturn, and serene.
Beyond his assigned duties,
he engaged in no other pursuits.
One day,
two azure youths riding white cranes
descended from the sky
and alighted in the courtyard of the hermit's residence.
The hermit (Táo Hóngjǐng) joyfully went to the veranda to receive them.
The azure youths said:
"The Supreme Lord has commanded us to seek a certain Master Huán."
The hermit fell silent,
mentally reviewing his disciples and finding none surnamed Huán.
He ordered a search,
and it turned out to be the laborer, Master Huán.
Asked what practice he had cultivated to achieve this,
Master Huán replied:
"I have practiced the Way of Silent Audience for years,
and have personally attended the court of the Great Emperor for nine years;
hence today's summons."
As he was about to ascend to heaven,
Master Táo wished to take him as his teacher,
but Huán firmly maintained his humility,
and the request was not granted.
Master Táo then said:
"I have propagated the teaching and cultivated the Way,
and my diligence has been utmost.
Could it be that I have committed some fault,
causing my prolonged滞留 in this world?
I beg you to inquire on my behalf,
and inform me another day."
Thereupon, Master Huán donned celestial robes,
mounted the white crane,
and ascended to heaven and departed.
Three days later,
he secretly descended to Master Táo's chamber and said:
"Your merit in the hidden realm is significant.
However, in the *Materia Medica* you compiled,
you used creatures like horseflies and leeches as medicine.
While the benefit reaches people,
it harms living creatures.
Because of this, after one cycle of twelve years,
you shall shed your form and leave the world,
to take up the post of Controller of the Waters at Pénglái."
Having said this, he departed.
Master Táo subsequently compiled another three-volume *Materia Medica*
using plant and herbal medicines that could substitute for living creatures,
to redeem his transgression.
Later, he indeed shed his form and attained the Way.
From *Shénxiān Gǎnyù Zhuàn*; the Ming dynasty manuscript version cites *Shénxiān Shíyí*.
Lán Gōng
In Jiǔyuán Village, Gāopíng Township, Qūfù County, Yǎnzhōu,
there lived a supreme man named Lán Gōng.
His clan numbered over a hundred members,
all devotedly and exclusively practicing filial piety.
Their sincerity moved Heaven and Earth.
Suddenly, a Perfected Being from the Dipper
descended to Lán Gōng's dwelling,
declaring himself to be the King of Filial and Fraternal Piety.
He said, "I reside in the sun as the Immortal King,
in the moon as the Luminous King,
and in the Dipper as the King of Filial and Fraternal Piety.
When filial piety reaches Heaven,
the sun and moon shine brightly because of it;
when it reaches Earth,
the myriad things are born because of it;
when it reaches the people,
the Kingly Way is perfected because of it.
Moreover, when the Three Powers first divided,
they began with the Three Breaths.
The Three Breaths
are the Three Heavens of the Jade Clarity.
The Jade Clarity Realm is where the Primordial Beginning, the Great Sage, and the True King govern and transform.
The Grand Clarity Realm is where
the Mysterious Way circulates,
in emptiness, spontaneity, and naturalness,
governed by the Jade Emperor.
I, from the Upper Clarity downward,
have manifested in the human world
to demonstrate and propagate the teaching of filial and fraternal piety.
Later, in the Jìn dynasty, there will be a True Immortal, Xǔ Xùn,
who will transmit the essence of my Filial Way,
and he shall be the leader among the immortals."
Thereupon, he bestowed upon Lán Gōng the secret essentials of the supreme Way.
Having obtained this wondrous formula,
Lán Gōng's insight awakened to the true mechanism,
silently discerning past causes,
and clearly knowing former events.
Once, while out in the countryside with fellow villagers,
he suddenly beheld three ancient tombs.
He then said:
"These are the tombs where my three immortal selves shed their forms.
I request the people to report to the authorities
and have the path beside the tombs moved,
so that people and things do not tread upon them."
The officials then questioned Lán Gōng,
asking how these words could be verified.
Lán Gōng said:
"In the first tomb,
there once were the bones of a Perfected Being.
Now they have already regained form,
becoming an Earth Immortal,
long-lived and enduring.
In the second tomb, you will find a pair of immortal robes
and a case of Daoist scriptures.
There is also a person
who appears as if drunk and sleeping.
Upon waking him after a long while,
he will be able to speak.
This is due to refining the form through the Great Yin,
nurturing the true breath.
The third tomb contains Jade Liquid Elixir.
Whoever takes it
will soar into the sky in broad daylight."
At that time, the officials and Lán Gōng opened the three tombs together,
and the evidence revealed
was exactly as described in each case.
Lán Gōng then approached the tombs,
personally took the immortal robes and put them on,
and also took and swallowed the golden elixir.
He summoned the two Perfected Beings sleeping in the tombs,
and together they straightened their bodies and lightly ascended.
The officials repented and apologized,
bowing reverently and earnestly.
They inquired of Lán Gōng,
asking when he would descend again.
Lán Gōng said:
"From now on,
I will come here once every ten days.
After several more years,
it will be once every hundred days,
to implement the Filial Way,
in accordance with the Mysterious Statutes,
to aid those in cages,
and through talismans, reach the supreme Way."
From then on,
the fifteen youths of Wú Capital,
the three-year-old spiritual child of Dānyáng,
down to Lán Gōng himself,
were all manifestations of immortals.
The secret methods of the Filial Way he transmitted,
along with a precious scripture in one volume,
a box of golden elixir,
and bronze tallies with iron deeds,
were obtained only by the Eminent and Vast Envoy, the True Lord Xǔ.
From *Shí'èr Zhēnjūn Zhuàn*.
Ruǎn Jī
Ruǎn Jī was a man from Hénèi.
In the seventh year of the Jiàndé era under Emperor Wǔ of the Zhōu dynasty,
he entered the northeast of Wángwū Mountain while hunting a bear.
There he saw a Daoist priest sitting beneath a pine tree,
whose divine appearance was extraordinary.
Ruǎn Jī then laid down his bow and arrows,
and after bowing and greeting him,
the master instructed Ruǎn Jī, saying:
"You may go for a while to gaze upon the view from the temple."
Suddenly, a young boy appeared among the rocks,
leading Ruǎn Jī to the temple gate.
The terraces and halls were majestic and splendid,
all adorned with gold and jade;
the ground was pure and clean,
all made of deep blue and green glass;
the rows of trees were straight and upright,
with green leaves and red fruits;
a clear breeze arose from time to time,
producing a tinkling sound.
Ruǎn Jī stood at the gate and gazed upon it all,
his heart and spirit filled with awe and fear.
He bowed again and requested to leave.
When he returned to the master's location, the master smiled and said:
"Were you afraid to enter?"
Ruǎn Jī replied:
"I am but a mortal of flesh and blood,
unaware of the great Way.
Suddenly today,
I have beheld paradise,
and my feelings are truly joyful and delighted,
beyond my ability to contain.
I beseech the master, in his great compassion,
to save me from my deep delusion."
The master said:
"You are a person burdened with accumulated sins.
Due to slight karmic connections from a past life,
you have now encountered me.
Your life is about to end—
what can be done about it?"
Upon hearing this,
Ruǎn Jī was overwhelmed with fear and trembling.
He knocked his head on the ground a hundred times,
pleading for the elixir of life.
The master then instructed Ruǎn Jī
to abandon evil and follow goodness,
and to vow to discard his bow and arrows.
He then bestowed upon Ruǎn Jī the "Ten Precepts of Supreme Wisdom,"
and also provided him with a vegetarian meal.
After eating, he ordered him to leave.
Ruǎn Jī bowed deeply and took his leave.
The master said:
"When your life is about to end,
I will deliver you."
That winter,
Ruǎn Jī fell suddenly ill and died,
with only one finger on his left hand still warm.
His family did not bury him immediately.
After three days, he revived,
and after a long while, he was able to speak.
He said:
"At first, I saw two messengers in yellow robes
holding official documents,
leading me away.
Suddenly, I arrived at a place
that resembled a government office.
When we reached the screen gate,
the messengers led me inside.
In the great hall, I vaguely saw an official,
and before the steps were several dozen minor clerks,
all holding record books,
some green and some black.
One clerk held a black book
and said to me:
'Your accumulated sins are profound and deep;
you should enter hell.'
Upon hearing this,
I was suddenly terrified,
not knowing what to say.
After a long while of thinking,
I suddenly remembered the holy master,
and in my heart, I thought:
'At the time of parting,
he said, "When your life is about to end,
I will surely come to deliver you."
Today, in this perilous predicament,
I pray for your compassionate rescue.'
In a moment,
auspicious clouds suddenly rose in the northwest sky,
and a cloud carriage descended slowly
from the air,
coming directly before the steps
and stopping about ten feet above the ground.
Then I saw the holy master sitting in the carriage.
The underworld officials, upon seeing him,
all bowed and paid their respects.
The holy master said:
'I have a disciple here,
so I have come to deliver him.'
He then took a scripture scroll and gave it to me.
I bowed deeply and knelt to receive it.
Its title was 'The Supreme Scripture of Salvation from Suffering.'
He ordered me to read it once,
and the underworld officials all bowed and received the command, listening until I finished.
They said to me:
'You may go;
do not stay here.
Strive diligently and advance with vigor,
and we will meet you again later.'
After speaking,
the master disappeared from sight,
and I only felt a lingering fragrance in the air for a long time.
Then I saw a messenger in yellow robes
leading me home.
I only heard the sound of my family wailing and weeping,
and then I returned to life."
He sat in deep concentration for a long while,
recalling the scripture from his dream
without missing a single word.
He then carefully maintained his mindfulness of it,
copied it down, and transmitted it to the world.
He then bid farewell to his relatives and friends,
entered Wángwū Mountain,
and no one knew where he went.
From "The Biographies of Encounters with Immortals."
Dù Zǐchūn
Dù Zǐchūn was a man who lived during the transition between the Zhōu and Suí dynasties.
In his youth, he was carefree and unrestrained,
paying no attention to managing family property.
Instead, with a lofty and carefree spirit,
he indulged in drinking and leisurely wandering.
After squandering all his assets,
he turned to relatives and old friends for help,
but they all abandoned him because he refused to attend to practical matters.
In the midst of winter,
with tattered clothes and an empty stomach,
he wandered on foot through Cháng'ān.
As evening fell without having eaten,
he wandered aimlessly, unsure of where to go.
At the western gate of the East Market,
his appearance of hunger and cold was palpable.
He looked up to the sky and let out a long sigh.
An old man, leaning on a staff, appeared before him and asked,
"Why do you sigh, sir?"
Zǐchūn poured out his heart,
venting his frustration at the cold indifference of his relatives.
His emotions of indignation and gratitude
were vividly displayed on his face.
The old man asked,
"How many strings of cash would suffice for your needs?"
Zǐchūn replied,
"Thirty or fifty thousand would keep me alive."
The old man said,
"That's not enough."
Zǐchūn then said,
"One hundred thousand."
The old man replied,
"Still not enough."
Zǐchūn then said,
"One million."
Again, the old man said,
"Not enough."
Finally, Zǐchūn said,
"Three million."
Only then did the old man say,
"That will do."
He then took out a string of cash from his sleeve and said,
"This is for you tonight.
Tomorrow at noon,
wait for me at the Persian lodging in the West Market.
Be careful not to be late."
At the appointed time, Zǐchūn went,
and the old man indeed gave him three million cash.
Without revealing his name, the old man departed.
Once wealthy, Zǐchūn's unrestrained desires flared up again.
He believed he would never again face the hardships of a wandering life.
Riding fine horses and wearing light silks,
he gathered with fellow drinkers,
summoned musicians,
and indulged in song and dance at courtesan houses,
paying no heed to managing his livelihood.
Within a year or two,
he gradually exhausted his wealth.
His clothes, carriages, and horses
were exchanged for cheaper ones,
replacing horses with donkeys,
and donkeys with going on foot,
until he was back to his original state in the blink of an eye.
Once again without any plan,
he sighed at the market gate.
As soon as he uttered a sound, the old man appeared,
grasped his hand, and said,
"You are in such a state again—how strange!
I will assist you once more.
How many strings of cash would be sufficient?"
Zǐchūn, ashamed, did not respond.
The old man pressed him,
and Zǐchūn could only express his shame and gratitude.
The old man said,
"Tomorrow at noon,
come to the same place as before."
Swallowing his shame, Zǐchūn went
and received ten million cash.
Before accepting it,
he was filled with determination,
thinking that from then on, he would manage his life and livelihood,
and that even Shí Jìlún and Yī Dùn would seem like mere youngsters in comparison.
But once the money was in his hands,
his heart wavered again,
and his indulgent and carefree nature
returned as before.
Within a year or two,
he became even poorer than before.
He encountered the old man again at the same place,
and Zǐchūn, overwhelmed with shame,
covered his face and tried to flee.
The old man grabbed his sleeve to stop him and said again,
"Alas, what poor planning!"
He then gave him thirty million cash,
saying,
"If this does not cure you,
then your poverty is incurable."
Zǐchūn said,
"I have been carefree and unrestrained, indulging in frivolous wanderings,
until my livelihood was completely exhausted.
Not a single relative or wealthy clansman
cared to look after me.
Only this old man has aided me three times.
How can I possibly repay him?"
He then said to the old man,
"With this money,
I can establish myself in worldly affairs,
provide clothing and food for widows and orphans,
and fulfill my duties within the moral teachings.
Deeply moved by your profound kindness,
after I have accomplished these tasks,
I will be at your disposal."
The old man said,
"That is my wish as well!
After you have managed your livelihood,
come next year on the Ghost Festival
to see me under the twin junipers at Lǎojūn Temple."
Since many widows and orphans resided in Huáinán,
Zǐchūn transferred his funds to Yángzhōu,
where he purchased a hundred qǐng of fertile land,
built a grand mansion within the city walls,
and established over a hundred lodgings along major roads.
He gathered all the widows and orphans
and settled them in the mansions.
He arranged marriages for his nephews and nieces,
relocated and reburied deceased clan members,
showered kindness upon those who had been good to him,
and repaid those who had wronged him.
After completing these tasks,
he went at the appointed time.
The old man was whistling in the shade of the two junipers.
He then led Zǐchūn up to Yúntái Peak on Huàshān.
After traveling over forty lǐ,
they arrived at a place
with solemn and clean houses,
unlike ordinary dwellings.
Colorful clouds hovered in the distance,
and cranes soared above.
There was a main hall,
in the center of which stood a medicine furnace
over nine chǐ tall,
emitting purple flames
that illuminated the windows.
Nine jade maidens
stood encircling the furnace;
a green dragon and a white tiger
guarded the front and rear.
As the sun was about to set,
the old man
shed his ordinary clothes
and appeared as a Daoist priest in a yellow cap and patched robe.
He handed Zǐchūn three white stone pills
and a cup of wine,
instructing him to consume them quickly.
Then, he took a tiger skin,
spread it against the inner west wall,
and sat facing east.
He admonished Zǐchūn, saying,
"Be careful not to speak.
Even if noble gods, evil ghosts, yakshas,
ferocious beasts, or hell itself,
or even your own relatives
appear to torment you with endless suffering,
none of it will be real.
You must remain still and silent,
calm your mind and fear nothing,
and in the end, you will suffer no harm.
Focus your mind solely on my words."
After speaking, he departed.
Zǐchūn looked into the courtyard
and saw only a giant vat
filled with water.
As soon as the Daoist priest left,
banners, spears, and armor,
along with thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of cavalry,
filled the cliffs and valleys.
Shouts and roars
shook heaven and earth.
A man who called himself the Great General,
over ten chǐ tall,
with both man and horse clad in golden armor
that shone blindingly,
appeared with several hundred guards,
all wielding swords and drawing bows.
They marched straight into the hall
and shouted,
"Who are you?
How dare you not make way for the Great General!"
His attendants raised their swords and advanced,
demanding his name
and asking what he was doing there,
but Zǐchūn gave no response.
The questioner grew furious,
and the sounds of slashing, chopping, and shooting thundered like a storm,
yet Zǐchūn still did not respond.
The Great General, enraged to the extreme, departed.
Suddenly, fierce tigers and venomous dragons,
suānní lions and lions,
countless vipers and scorpions,
roaring and clawing, rushed forward to seize and devour him.
Some leaped over him,
but Zǐchūn’s expression remained unchanged.
After a while, they dispersed.
Then a torrential rain poured down,
with thunder, lightning, and darkness,
fiery wheels rolling around him,
lightning flashing before and behind,
so that he could not open his eyes.
In an instant,
the courtyard was flooded with water over ten feet deep,
with roaring thunder and flashing lightning,
as if mountains and rivers were splitting apart,
unstoppable.
In the blink of an eye,
the flood reached where he was sitting,
but Zǐchūn sat upright, paying no heed.
Soon, the general returned,
leading ox-headed jailers
and strange-looking ghosts and spirits.
They placed a large cauldron of boiling water before Zǐchūn,
with long spears and two-pronged forks,
surrounding him on all sides.
They announced:
"If you are willing to speak your name, we will release you.
If not,
we will pierce your heart with a fork and throw you into the cauldron."
He did not respond.
Then they brought his wife,
dragging her to the foot of the steps,
and said:
"Speak your name, and she will be spared."
Still, he did not respond.
They whipped her until she bled,
shot her, chopped her,
boiled her, and burned her,
causing unbearable suffering.
His wife wailed:
"I am indeed unworthy,
and have shamed you, sir.
Yet I have been fortunate to serve you
for over ten years.
Now I am seized by these fearsome ghosts,
suffering unbearable pain!
I dare not expect you to crawl and beg for me,
but if you would just say a word,
my life would be spared.
Who among humans is without emotion?
How can you bear to withhold a single word?"
Tears fell like rain in the courtyard,
as she cursed and reviled him,
but Zǐchūn paid no heed.
The general then said:
"Can I not torture your wife?"
He ordered a chopping block and pestle,
and had her chopped inch by inch from the feet upward.
His wife’s screams grew more desperate,
but still he paid no attention.
The general said:
"This villain’s sorcery is complete;
he cannot be allowed to remain in the world."
He ordered his attendants to behead him.
After the beheading,
his soul was led to see Yánluó Wáng.
Yánluó Wáng said:
"Is this the sorcerer from Yúntái Peak?
Seize him and throw him into prison."
Thus, he endured all manner of torments—molten copper and iron rods, pounding and grinding in mortars, fiery pits and boiling cauldrons, mountains of knives and forests of swords.
He experienced them all.
Yet, remembering the Daoist’s words,
he found them bearable,
and did not utter a single groan.
The jailers reported that his punishment was complete.
Yánluó Wáng said:
"This man is treacherous;
he does not deserve to be reborn as a man.
He shall be reborn as a woman."
He was assigned to be born into the family of Wáng Quàn, the county magistrate of Dānfù County in Sòngzhōu.
From birth, she was often ill,
with acupuncture and medicine
administered almost daily.
She also fell into fires and tumbled from beds,
suffering various pains,
yet never cried out.
As she grew older,
her beauty was peerless,
but she remained mute,
so her family regarded her as a mute girl.
Relatives and acquaintances
teased her in countless ways,
but she never responded.
A fellow villager, the jìnshì Lú Guī,
hearing of her beauty, admired her
and sought her hand through a matchmaker.
Her family declined, citing her muteness.
Lú said:
"If she is virtuous as a wife,
what need is there for words?
This will also serve as a warning to gossipy women."
Thus, they agreed.
Lú prepared the six rites
and married her.
After several years,
their affection grew deep,
and they had a son,
just two years old,
exceptionally intelligent.
Lú held the child and spoke to him,
but he did not respond;
he tried various ways to coax him,
but the child remained silent.
Lú grew furious and said:
"In ancient times, Minister Jiǎ’s wife despised her husband
and never smiled,
but when she saw him shoot pheasants,
she finally let go of her resentment.
Now, I may be less talented than Jiǎ,
but my literary skills are not limited to shooting pheasants.
Yet you remain silent!
A great man despised by his wife—
what use is this child?"
He grabbed the child by both feet
and dashed his head against a stone,
shattering it instantly,
blood splattering several paces away.
Zǐchūn’s love for her child stirred in her heart,
and she suddenly forgot her vow,
unconsciously crying out:
"Alas!" Before the cry faded,
she found herself sitting in her original place,
with the Daoist standing before her.
It was just before dawn.
They saw purple flames piercing the roof,
and a great fire rising from all sides,
consuming the house.
The Daoist sighed:
"Such a grave mistake you have made!"
He grabbed her by the hair
and threw her into a water jar.
Soon, the fire subsided.
The Daoist approached and said:
"Your heart had forgotten joy, anger, sorrow, fear, hatred, and desire.
The only thing left was love.
If you had not uttered that cry,
my elixir would have been complete,
and you would have ascended to immortality.
Alas,
how rare are those fit for immortality!
My elixir can be refined again,
but you must remain in this world.
Strive on!"
He pointed into the distance, showing her the way back.
Zǐchūn forced herself to climb the foundation to look,
and saw that the furnace was ruined,
with an iron pillar inside,
as thick as an arm
and several feet long.
The Daoist removed his robe
and began shaving it with a knife.
Zǐchūn returned home,
ashamed of having broken her vow,
and sought to atone for her failure.
She traveled to Yúntái Peak,
but found no trace of anyone.
Sighing with regret, she returned.
From "Xù Xuánguài Lù"
Zhāng Lǎo
Old Man Zhāng was a gardener from Liùhé County in Yángzhōu.
His neighbor was a man named Wéi Shù,
who had come from Yángzhōu after completing his term as a minor official during the Tiānjiàn era of the Liáng dynasty.
He had an eldest daughter who had reached marriageable age,
so he summoned a matchmaker from the neighborhood
and asked her to find a good husband.
Old Man Zhāng heard this and was delighted;
he waited for the matchmaker at Wéi’s gate.
When the matchmaker came out,
Old Man Zhāng insisted on inviting her in
and prepared wine and food for her.
After they had drunk for a while,
he said to the matchmaker:
"I heard that the Wéi family has a daughter about to marry,
and they are seeking a good match through you.
Is that true?"
She said:
"Yes."
He said:
"Although I am truly old and frail,
my work as a gardener
can still provide food and clothing.
I hope you will seek her hand for me.
If the matter succeeds, I will thank you generously."
The matchmaker scolded him loudly and left.
Another day, he invited the matchmaker again.
The matchmaker said:
"Old man, why don’t you consider your own position?
How could a child from a respectable family
be willing to marry a gardener?
This family is indeed poor,
but there are many among the scholar-official families who are their equals.
You, old man, are not a match.
How could I, for just a cup of your wine,
bring disgrace upon the Wéi family?"
The old man insisted:
"Please just mention it for me.
If they do not agree,
then it is my fate."
The matchmaker had no choice
and risked reproach to go in and speak of it.
Wéi Shù was furious and said:
"Do you think I am so poor
that you would slight me like this?
Moreover, how could the Wéi family have such a matter?
And what kind of person is this gardener,
that he dares to make such a proposal!
The old man is not worth blaming,
but how could you, matchmaker, be so indiscriminate?"
The matchmaker said:
"It was truly not appropriate to mention it,
but I was pressured by the old man
and had to convey his intention."
Wéi angrily said:
"Tell him for me:
if he can bring five hundred strings of cash today, then it can be done."
The matchmaker went out
and told Old Man Zhāng.
He said:
"Agreed."
Not long after,
he brought the money by cart and delivered it to the Wéi family.
The Wéi family was greatly astonished and said:
"What we said earlier was only a joke.
Moreover, this old man is a gardener.
How could he obtain such an amount?
We thought he certainly did not have it and so spoke.
Now, before much time has passed, the money has arrived.
What should we do?"
They then secretly sent someone to observe their daughter.
The daughter showed no resentment
and said:
"This must be fate."
So they consented.
After Old Man Zhāng married the Wéi daughter,
he did not abandon his gardening work.
He carried manure and hoed the ground,
selling vegetables without cease.
His wife personally tended the cooking and washing,
showing no sign of shame.
Their relatives despised them,
but they could not stop them.
After several years,
knowledgeable people among their relatives and friends reproached Wéi Shù, saying:
"Your family is indeed poor,
but are there no poor young men in the village?
Why did you give your daughter to a gardener?
Since you have cast her off,
why not make them go far away?"
Another day, Wéi Shù prepared wine
and summoned his daughter and Old Man Zhāng.
When they were drinking merrily,
he subtly revealed his intention.
Old Man Zhāng stood up and said:
"The reason we did not leave immediately
was for fear you might feel attached.
Now that you are displeased with us,
leaving is not difficult.
I have a small estate at the foot of Wángwū Mountain.
We will return there tomorrow morning."
As dawn approached,
he came to bid farewell to the Wéi family:
"In future years, if you miss us,
you can have your eldest son visit us south of Tiāntán Mountain."
He then had his wife ride a donkey wearing a bamboo hat,
while Old Man Zhāng walked with a staff, following her, and they departed.
There was no news of them at all.
Several years later,
Wéi Shù missed his daughter,
thinking she must be disheveled and dirty-faced,
unrecognizable.
He sent his son, Wéi Yìfāng, to visit her.
When he reached the south of Tiāntán,
he happened to meet a Kūnlún slave
plowing the fields with a yellow ox.
He asked:
"Is there a Zhāng family estate here?"
The Kūnlún slave dropped his staff and bowed, saying:
"Why has the eldest young master not come for so long?
The estate is very close from here.
I will lead the way."
So they went east together.
First they climbed a mountain;
below the mountain was water.
They crossed the water and passed through more than ten places in succession.
The scenery gradually became extraordinary,
unlike the human world.
Suddenly they descended a mountain,
and north of the water were vermilion gates and grand mansions,
with towers and pavilions rising and falling,
flowers and trees flourishing luxuriantly,
mist and clouds fresh and lovely.
Luan birds, cranes, and peacocks
soared and circled among them,
and the sound of songs and pipes was clear and bright to the ears.
The Kūnlún slave pointed and said:
"This is the Zhāng family estate."
Wéi Yìfāng was astonished and could not fathom it.
Soon they reached the gate.
There were clerks in purple clothing at the gate,
who bowed and led him into the hall.
The splendor of the furnishings
was something he had never seen before.
A rare fragrance filled the air,
pervading the cliffs and valleys.
Suddenly, the sound of pearl pendants drew near,
and two maidservants in green came out, saying:
"The master is here."
Then he saw over ten maidservants,
of peerless beauty,
walking in pairs,
as if guiding someone.
Soon he saw a person
wearing a yuǎnyóu crown,
dressed in red silk,
and trailing red shoes,
slowly coming out the door.
A maidservant in green led Wéi forward to bow.
His bearing was majestic,
and his complexion was delicate and youthful.
Looking closely,
it was Old Man Zhāng.
He said:
"The toils of the human world
are like being in a fire.
Before the body finds coolness,
the flames of worry blaze again,
with not a moment of peace.
Brother, you have been a guest here for a long time;
how have you amused yourself?
Your sister will finish combing her hair shortly,
and then she will come to see you."
He then bowed and invited him to sit.
Not long after,
a maidservant in green came and said:
"The lady has finished combing her hair."
She then led him in
to see his sister in the front hall.
The hall had beams of aloeswood,
doors inlaid with tortoiseshell,
windows of jadeite,
and curtains of pearls.
The steps were all cool, smooth, and bluish-green,
unidentifiable as to what material.
His sister’s attire and ornaments were magnificent,
unseen in the mortal world.
They briefly exchanged pleasantries,
inquiring only about their elders,
and her manner seemed rather abrupt.
After a while, food was served—
exquisite, fragrant, and indescribable.
After the meal,
they accommodated Wéi in the inner hall.
The next day, as dawn broke,
Old Man Zhāng and Wéi Yìfāng were sitting together
when suddenly a maidservant in green
came and whispered into his ear.
The elder laughed and said:
"There is a guest in the house.
How can I return in the evening?"
Then he said:
"My younger sister wishes to visit Pénglái Mountain for a while,
and your virtuous sister should also go,
but we will return before dusk.
Brother, please rest here."
Zhāng Lǎo bowed and entered.
Soon, five-colored clouds rose in the courtyard,
luan phoenixes soared,
and music from string and wind instruments played together.
Zhāng Lǎo and his sister,
each riding a phoenix,
with more than ten attendants riding cranes,
gradually ascended into the sky,
heading eastward,
until they disappeared from sight,
yet the faint sound of music could still be heard.
Wéi Jūn remained behind,
and the young maidservant served him with great care.
As dusk approached,
the sound of reed pipes and bamboo flutes was faintly heard,
and suddenly they returned.
When they descended into the courtyard,
Zhāng Lǎo and his wife met Wéi and said:
"Living alone is too lonely,
but this place is the abode of immortals,
not accessible to ordinary people.
Due to your past destiny,
you were fated to come here,
but you cannot stay long.
Tomorrow, we must bid farewell."
When the time came,
the sister came out again to bid farewell to her brother,
earnestly conveying her regards to their parents.
Zhāng Lǎo said:
"The mortal world is far away,
and there is no time to write a letter.
I offer you twenty yì of gold."
He also gave him an old straw hat, saying:
"Brother, if you ever lack money,
go to the medicine shop of Old Wáng in the northern quarter of Yángzhōu,
and take ten million coins,
using this as proof."
Then they parted,
and he again ordered the Kunlun slave to escort him out.
Returning to Tiāntán,
the Kunlun slave bowed and departed.
Wéi carried the gold back on his own,
and his family was astonished.
When asked about it,
some thought it was the work of immortals,
while others considered it sorcery or deception,
not knowing what to make of it.
Within five or six years, the gold was exhausted,
and he considered taking the money from Old Wáng,
but again doubted it was a trick.
Some said:
"To take such a large sum of money,
without even a single written word,
how can this hat be trusted?"
Eventually, in extreme hardship,
his family pressured him, saying:
"Even if you get no money,
what harm is there?"
So he went to Yángzhōu.
Entering the northern quarter,
he found Old Wáng arranging medicines in his shop.
Wéi stepped forward and asked:
"Old man, what is your surname?"
He replied:
"Wáng."
Wéi said:
"Zhāng Lǎo instructed me to take ten million coins,
using this hat as proof."
Wáng said:
"The money is indeed here,
but is this straw hat genuine?"
Wéi replied:
"Old man, you can examine it.
Do you not recognize it?"
Before Old Wáng could speak,
a young girl emerged from behind a blue cloth curtain and said:
"Zhāng Lǎo often visited,
and once asked me to sew the top of his hat.
At that time, I had no black thread,
so I used red thread instead.
The color of the thread and the stitching marks
can both be verified."
They took the hat to examine it,
and indeed it was the same.
Thus, he was able to take the money and return,
and finally believed it was truly the work of immortals.
His family again longed for their daughter,
and sent Yìfāng to search for her south of Tiāntán.
Upon arrival, he found only endless mountains and rivers,
with no path to follow.
Occasionally meeting woodcutters,
none knew of Zhāng Lǎo's estate.
Filled with sorrow and longing, he returned dejectedly.
The whole family concluded that the paths of immortals and mortals were separate,
and there was no hope of meeting again.
When they searched for Old Wáng again,
he too had disappeared.
Several years later,
Yìfāng happened to travel to Yángzhōu.
While wandering near the northern quarter
(the original text had "Máng" instead of "quarter,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript),
he suddenly saw Zhāng Lǎo's Kunlun slave approach and say:
"How is everything in the elder brother's household?
Although the young lady cannot return,
it is as if she serves by your side every day.
