No matter how big or small the affairs at home,
she knows them all."
Then he took out ten catties of gold from his bosom and offered it, saying:
"The young lady ordered me to give this to the elder brother.
The master and Old Wáng are drinking together at this tavern.
Elder brother, please sit here for a while,
and I will go in to inform them."
Yìfāng sat under the tavern's banner,
but as dusk fell, no one emerged.
He went inside to look,
and found the tavern full of drinkers,
but neither of the two elders nor the Kunlun slave was among them.
He took the gold to examine it,
and it was genuine gold.
Astonished, he returned home.
The gold supported the family for several more years,
and afterward, they never learned of Zhāng Lǎo's whereabouts again.
From "Xù Xuánguài Lù"
Péi Chén
Péi Chén, Wáng Jìngbó, and Liáng Fāng
pledged to be friends beyond worldly affairs.
During the Sui dynasty's Dàyè era,
they entered Báilù Mountain together to study the Dao.
They believed the arts of alchemy could be perfected,
and the elixir of immortality could be obtained.
Soaring through clouds and transforming with feathers—
all this was merely a matter of accumulated learning.
They toiled diligently, gathering and refining,
until their hands and feet grew calloused,
for over a decade.
Then, unexpectedly,
Liáng Fāng died.
Jìngbó said to Chén:
"The reason I left my country and forgot my family,
stopped my ears to music,
grew weary of rich meats,
turned my eyes from rare beauties,
abandoned splendid mansions to delight in a thatched hut,
and scorned pleasures to value solitude—
was it not in the hope of riding clouds and driving cranes,
frolicking in Pénglái and Húqiū?
Even if that failed,
I still hoped for longevity,
to live as long as heaven and earth.
Now, the sea of immortality is boundless,
longevity remains unattained;
after toiling beyond these cloudy peaks,
I cannot escape death.
What I, Jìngbó, find joyful now
is to descend the mountain, ride fat horses and wear light silks,
listen to songs and enjoy beauties,
and wander the capitals Luòyáng and Cháng'ān.
Once my desires are satisfied, I shall seek advancement,
achieve merits and establish deeds,
to bring glory to the mortal realm.
Even if I cannot rest on the three divine mountains,
drink from the Jade Pool,
ride dragons and wear rainbows,
sing with phoenixes and dance with simurghs,
or keep company with immortal officials,
at least I can wear gold at the waist and purple ribbons,
have my portrait displayed in the Língyān Pavilion,
and stand among the high ministers and nobles—
how would that be!
Why not return with me?
Do not die in vain in the deep mountains."
Chén said:
"I am one who has awakened from the dream;
I will not sink into delusion again."
Jìngbó then returned,
and Chén could not detain him.
It was the early years of the Táng dynasty's Zhēnguàn era.
By his former household registration, Jìngbó was appointed as Cavalry Officer in the Left Martial Guard.
General Zhào Fěi married his daughter to him.
Within a few years,
he was promoted to Court Reviewer of the Dàlǐ Temple,
wearing crimson robes.
Sent on a mission to Huáinán,
his boat passed by Gāoyóu.
As an imperial envoy traveled,
his shouts stirred the wind,
and other boats dared not move.
At the time, a light rain fell.
Suddenly, a fishing boat dashed past,
with an old man aboard,
wearing a straw raincoat and bamboo hat,
rowing away,
swift as the wind.
Jìngbó thought, "I am an imperial envoy,
my authority shakes far and wide;
how dare this fisherman dash past?"
He tried to look closely—
it was Chén.
He then ordered pursuit.
He requested to moor the boats,
invited him into the cabin,
clasped his hand, and consoled him:
"Brother, you have long dwelled in the deep mountains,
casting aside fame and office,
and have achieved nothing to this extreme.
The wind cannot be tied down,
shadows cannot be caught.
The ancients, weary of long nights,
still roamed with candles in hand;
how much more should we, in our youth, not waste the daylight?
Since leaving the mountain a few years ago,
I am now a Court Reviewer.
Recently, I judged cases with fairness,
and heaven bestowed upon me official robes.
There is a doubtful case in Huáinán;
now it is being reviewed by the authorities.
The emperor selected a clear-sighted official to reexamine it,
and I, Jìngbó, was chosen,
hence this journey.
Though I cannot yet claim high office,
compared to a mountain hermit,
I consider myself somewhat better off.
You, brother, willingly endure toil and hardship,
exactly as in the past—
how strange, how strange!
What do you need now?
I shall provide it for you."
Chén said:
"We are men of the wilds,
our hearts close to clouds and cranes;
do not try to scare us with a rotten rat.
I sink while you float;
fish and birds each follow their nature.
Why must you boast and show off?
As for what is needed in the human world,
I can provide it for you.
What will you give me in return?
I and my mountain friends
come to Guǎnglíng to buy medicine,
and we also have a place to rest.
East of Qīngyuán Bridge,
there is a cherry orchard spanning several miles.
North of the orchard is a carriage gate—
that is my home.
When your official duties leave you a little leisure,
you should seek me there."
Then he drifted away, carefree.
After Jìngbó arrived in Guǎnglíng for over ten days,
his duties eased somewhat.
Remembering Chén's words,
he went out to search for him.
Indeed, there was a carriage gate.
He inquired—
it was Péi's residence.
Someone led him inside.
At first, it seemed desolate,
but with each step, the scenery improved.
After walking several hundred paces,
he reached the main gate.
Towers and pavilions rose layer upon layer,
flowers and trees were fresh and elegant,
as if not of the human world.
Misty greenery flourished luxuriantly;
the scenery was enchanting and lovely,
beyond description.
A fragrant breeze swept by,
refreshing his spirit and clearing his mind.
He felt light, as if soaring above the clouds,
no longer valuing his status as an envoy,
seeing his own body as a rotten rat,
and his followers as ants.
Then, faint sounds of swords and pendants were heard.
Two maids in green emerged and said:
"Young Master Péi is coming."
Soon, a man appeared,
grandly dressed,
with extraordinary and handsome features.
Jìngbó stepped forward to bow—
looking closely, it was Chén.
Péi consoled him:
"In the dusty world of officialdom,
one long eats rank and greasy foods;
the fires of worry and desire
blaze in the heart.
Carrying such burdens while walking—
truly, it is exhausting."
Then he invited him in with a bow,
and they sat in the central hall.
The windows, doors, beams, and pillars
were adorned with rare treasures;
screens and curtains were all painted with clouds and cranes.
After a while,
four maids in green brought a jasper tray,
with vessels so rare and exquisite
they seemed not of this world;
fragrant wine and fine delicacies
were such as eyes had never beheld.
As dusk approached,
he ordered the mats drawn closer,
lit lamps of ninefold radiance,
filling the seats with brilliant light.
Twenty female musicians,
each of peerless beauty,
sat in a row before them.
Péi turned to a young attendant and said:
"Reviewer Wáng here
is my mountain friend.
His Daoist resolve was not firm;
he abandoned me and descended the mountain.
Nearly ten years have passed since we parted,
and he has only become a Court Reviewer.
Since his worldly heart is now settled,
he needs worldly courtesans to entertain him.
But the daughters of entertainers are not worth summoning.
We should summon the daughters of scholar-officials who are already married.
If there are no beauties nearby,
within five thousand li,
we may choose from there."
The young attendant assented and left.
The musicians tuned their jasper zithers.
Before the tuning was harmonized,
the attendant had already returned.
He led a courtesan up the western steps,
who bowed before Péi's seat.
Péi pointed and said:
"Cān Píngshì."
Jìngbó returned the greeting with a bow.
Looking closely,
it turned out to be Jìngbó's wife, Zhào shì.
Jìngbó was astonished and dared not speak,
and his wife was also greatly alarmed,
staring at him without pause.
Péi then had her sit beneath the jade steps,
and a servant girl presented her with a tortoiseshell zither.
Zhào had always been skilled at this,
so Péi ordered her to play together with the seated courtesans to accompany the drinking.
While Jìngbó was seated,
he picked up a deep red plum and tossed it to her.
Zhào glanced at Jìngbó,
and secretly tied it to her sash.
As for the tunes played by the courtesans,
Zhào was unable to follow along,
so Péi ordered them to adapt to what Zhào played,
pausing from time to time,
to present the melody.
Though the songs were not the music of the nine performances of Yúnsháo,
they were clear, bright, and melodious,
and the toasts and offerings were filled with joy.
As dawn approached,
Péi summoned the yellow-turbaned servant from earlier and said:
"Escort Lady Zhào."
And he said to her:
"This hall is a painted hall of the Nine Heavens,
where ordinary people cannot come.
In the past, I and the King were friends beyond the mundane world,
and I pitied him for being deluded by worldly affairs,
throwing himself into boiling water and fire,
burning himself with his own wisdom,
harming himself with his own clarity,
about to sink and float in the sea of life and death,
unable to find the shore.
Therefore, I arranged for him to be here,
to awaken him.
Today's gathering,
truly, is hard to come by again.
It is also due to your own destiny,
that you were able to visit briefly.
The clouds and mountains are myriad and layered,
and the journey back will be toilsome,
but do not decline."
Zhào bowed and departed.
Péi said to Jìngbó:
"Píngshì, your carriage has stayed here for one night,
surely it will alarm the commandery general,
so you should go to the guesthouse.
Before you go to the court,
you may visit me.
The dusty road is long and distant,
and myriad sorrows assail a person,
take care of yourself."
Jìngbó bowed in thanks and departed.
After five more days, when he was about to return,
he secretly went to bid farewell.
The gate no longer had a residence,
but was a desolate place,
with tobacco plants stretching as far as the eye could see,
and he returned feeling melancholy.
After he finished reporting matters in the capital,
and was about to return to his private residence,
the various members of the Zhào family angrily said:
"Our daughter may indeed be plain,
and not worthy of serving a gentleman,
but she has already been honored with generous rites,
and should also be respected.
Above, to continue the ancestral line,
below, to carry on future affairs,
how can it be done carelessly?
How could you use sorcery to bring her ten thousand miles away,
and entertain others' sight and hearing?
The red plum is still here,
her words are sufficient evidence,
why conceal it!"
Jìngbó told them everything,
and said:
"At that time,
I myself could not fathom it.
This must be because Péi has achieved the Way,
and used this to show off."
His wife also remembered Péi's words,
and so they did not blame him further.
Alas,
the transformations of immortals,
are they truly like this?
Or are they illusions created by sorcerers to cause confusion?
This is certainly beyond the understanding of ordinary wisdom.
Moreover, sparrows turn into clams,
pheasants into giant clams,
humans into tigers,
rotten grass into fireflies,
dung beetles into cicadas,
kūn fish into péng birds,
the transformations of the myriad things,
as recorded in books and traditions,
cannot be grasped by wisdom,
let alone what lies beyond sight and hearing?
From "Xù Xuánguài Lù"
Lú Lǐ Èr Shēng
Once there were two scholars, Lú and Lǐ,
who lived in seclusion on Tàibái Mountain to study,
while also practicing the arts of breath control and physical cultivation.
One day,
Lǐ announced his departure, saying:
"I cannot endure this harsh and bitter life any longer.
I shall wander the rivers and lakes,
and so I bid you farewell."
Later, Lǐ was put in charge of an orange orchard,
but his subordinates deceived and cheated him,
leaving him with a deficit of tens of thousands of strings of official funds.
He was detained and unable to return east,
and became extremely impoverished.
Once, while passing by the Āshǐ Bridge in Yángzhōu,
he encountered a man
wearing straw sandals and a cloth robe.
Looking closely, he saw it was Lú.
Lú had formerly been addressed as Second Uncle.
Lǐ spoke with him,
pitying his ragged appearance.
Lú scolded him harshly, saying:
"What do I have to fear in my poverty and lowliness?
You, sir, did not do good,
abandoning yourself to a place of vulgar corruption.
Moreover, you have incurred debts,
and are even imprisoned and confined.
Do you still have the face to meet me?"
Lǐ apologized profusely.
Second Uncle laughed and said:
"My dwelling is not far from here.
Tomorrow I shall come to fetch you."
At dawn,
sure enough, a servant arrived,
riding swiftly on a fine horse, and said:
"Second Uncle has sent me to welcome you, sir."
After they departed,
the horse sped like the wind.
Passing several tens of lǐ south of the city,
they saw a vermilion gate standing ajar by the roadside.
Second Uncle came out to greet them.
He wore a starry crown and rosy robes,
his countenance radiant and glowing,
attended by several dozen maidservants—
completely different from his appearance under the bridge.
He invited Lǐ to a banquet in the central hall.
Rare flowers and exotic trees surrounded them,
as if they were amidst the clouds.
He also repeatedly presented medicinal substances,
all of exceptional quality.
When night fell,
he led Lǐ to the north pavilion and ordered wine to be served,
saying:
"I have also found someone to accompany you in drinking,
who is quite skilled at playing the konghou."
In a moment,
red candles ushered in a young woman.
Her beauty was utterly dazzling,
and her new melodies were exquisite.
Lǐ looked at the konghou and saw
a line of vermilion characters that read:
"At the horizon, I recognize the returning boat;
amidst the clouds, I discern the riverside trees."
After the drinking ended,
Second Uncle said:
"Would you be willing to marry her?
She comes from a renowned family,
and her appearance and quality are as you see."
Lǐ said:
"How would I dare?"
Second Uncle promised to arrange it for him,
and then asked:
"How much official money do you owe?"
Lǐ replied:
"Twenty thousand strings."
So he gave him a walking staff and said:
"Take this to the Persian shop to collect the money.
You may follow this path to study the Dao;
do not defile yourself and sink into the salt and iron affairs."
Just as day broke,
the horse from before arrived,
and Second Uncle instructed Lǐ to leave.
He saw him out the gate
There is missing text after the character "gate."
The Yúnjí Qīqiān, scroll 113, has the following seventeen characters: "After returning,
he was quite suspicious and amazed, thinking it must be the work of immortals.
He then took the walking staff to the Persian shop."
When the Persian saw the staff,
he exclaimed in surprise:
"This is Second Uncle Lú's walking staff.
How did you obtain it?"
He complied and paid the money,
and thus Lǐ was freed from trouble.
That year,
he went to Biànzhōu,
where the military commander Lù Chángyuán married his daughter to him.
After the wedding,
she greatly resembled the woman he had seen in Second Uncle Lú's north pavilion.
Moreover, she could play the konghou,
and indeed there were vermilion characters inscribed on it.
Looking closely,
they were the two lines of the horizon poem.
Lǐ recounted in detail the banquet at Second Uncle Lú's pavilion south of Yángzhōu city.
His wife said:
"In my youth, my brothers playfully wrote this.
Last night I dreamed of an envoy who said:
'The immortal officials summon you,'
exactly as you described."
Lǐ sighed in amazement.
He went back to search for Second Uncle's dwelling,
but saw only wild grass,
and could no longer find the pavilions and terraces.
From Yì Shǐ.
Xuē Zhào,
it is not known from whence he hailed,
studied with the Jìnshì Cuī Yǔ
on Lúshān.
There were four companions in their studies,
two left before completing their studies,
Cuī Yǔ toiled diligently,
and soon passed the imperial examination.
Only Xuē Zhào devoted himself solely to cultivating the Way,
it is not known who his master was.
Within a few years,
he had attained the Way of the Immortals.
At the foot of Lúshān, there was a man suffering from a consumptive illness,
who after years of medical treatment showed no improvement,
and merely lay waiting for death.
Xuē Zhào passed by his door,
resting in the shade of a tree,
and upon hearing of the sick man,
wished to see him.
After seeing him, he said:
"This is very easy,
it can be cured."
He left a single pill of elixir,
smaller than a grain of rice,
and said to the sick man's relative:
"Tomorrow morning, break off half a pill,
swallow it with water,
and there will naturally be a response.
If not cured,
after three days, take the other half."
The family, having sought medical treatment for the long illness,
had spent vast sums of money,
yet still had not achieved a cure;
the sick man was emaciated,
barely clinging to life—
how could half a grain of this save him?
The next day, they tried giving it to him,
and the sick man rose,
by noon he could eat and drink,
and walked with a cane.
After three days like this,
he was robust and healthy.
He then took the other half pill,
and immediately his spirit and energy became transcendent,
his skin like jade,
his beard and hair dark and lustrous,
appearing to be about twenty years old.
Over a month later,
Xuē Zhào came again and said:
"You have the bone register,
encountering my medicine,
not only cured your illness,
but also allows you to attain the Way."
He then taught him the essentials of his cultivation,
and this man then ascended Wǔlǎofēng,
seeking the cavern abode and departed.
Cuī Yǔ, having passed the examination,
was soon appointed as an official in the eastern capital region,
and on his way to take up the post,
passing through Sānxiá Station,
he suddenly met Xuē Zhào.
Dismounting to reminisce,
he saw Xuē Zhào's appearance was travel-worn,
and felt quite pity and sorrow for him.
Cuī Yǔ, having passed the exam and received an official post,
was proud and self-satisfied.
They conversed for a long time,
and as the sun was setting,
Xuē said to Cuī:
"My humble dwelling is not far,
it is hard to meet,
come to my place for an evening chat,
is that acceptable?"
Cuī agreed.
He followed Xuē,
leaving his servants and carriage at the inn.
At first, they entered a small path,
very wild and overgrown,
walking for a li or two,
the fields, flowers, and trees
were all extraordinary, unlike the mortal realm.
After a long while, they arrived,
with tall buildings and large gates,
halls and pavilions towering and deep,
as if ruled by a king.
Cuī was startled and amazed in his heart.
Xuē entered first,
and was greeted by dozens of people who escorted him into the hall.
Then he summoned Cuī to ascend the steps,
and they sat and conversed intimately.
After a long time,
he said to Cuī:
"You have a good official post,
you cannot stay here,
but an evening of reminiscing is fine."
He urged them to summon musicians and set out a feast.
In an instant,
they were feasting and enjoying music in another hall.
There were no other guests,
only Cuī and Xuē.
Over forty female musicians,
bowed and sat to perform music.
Ten female entertainers were selected to drink with them.
One kōng hóu player,
was the most beautiful and outstanding,
Cuī sat with her.
Cuī saw on the kōng hóu ten characters written:
"Recognizing the returning boat at the horizon,
discerning the river trees amidst the clouds."
Cuī silently memorized them.
When the feast ended,
Xuē asked Cuī whom he fancied among those seated,
and Cuī answered it was the kōng hóu player.
Xuē said:
"Another day I will give her to you,
but for now it is not possible."
At dawn,
he bid farewell to Cuī,
presenting him with thirty catties of gold,
escorting him to the official road,
and they parted sorrowfully.
Cuī had been in office for over a month,
when he sought marriage and obtained a wife, Liǔ shì.
He often suspected he had seen her before but could not remember where.
One leisurely day,
he asked her to fetch the kōng hóu and play a tune,
and Cuī saw the ten characters written on it.
He asked her the reason,
and she said:
"At that time, I suffered from a fever illness,
and in a dream saw an envoy summoning me, saying:
'The Great Immortal of the Western City, Chénxī's Lord Xuē has a guest,
all maidens within five hundred li who understand music are to be summoned.'
There were over forty people,
so I followed.
I drank with Xuē and his guest, Assistant Magistrate Cuī, for one evening,
and upon waking, my illness was already cured.
Lord Xuē is an immortal,
Assistant Magistrate Cuī's appearance and demeanor
were no different from yours."
They each recounted their experiences,
and were greatly astonished,
only then realizing Xuē had attained the Way.
The Ming manuscript has here: "This is similar to the events with Messieurs Lú and Lǐ,
thus it is appended." Eleven characters.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Liǔ Guīshùn
Liǔ Guīshùn of Wúxīng,
in the twentieth year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era,
was traveling from Jiāngnán to Bālǐng
when a great wind blew him to the foot of Jūnshān.
He thus moored his boat and went ashore.
Following a small path,
he unwittingly walked four or five lǐ,
and, his spirits high,
he crossed ravines and streams,
not keeping to the path.
Suddenly, beside the road was a great rock,
transparent inside and out,
round and smooth as a whetstone,
some six or seven mǔ in circumference.
All around it grew emerald bamboo,
round and large like jars,
over a hundred chǐ tall.
Their leaves brushed against white clouds,
dense and luxuriant, reflecting the sky.
A clear breeze blew gently,
striking the bamboo to produce sounds like string and wind instruments.
In the center of the rock grew a tree,
a hundred chǐ tall,
its branches and trunk arching to form a canopy of five colors.
Its emerald leaves were like plates,
its flowers over a chǐ in diameter,
their color a deep green,
their stamens a deep red.
An extraordinary fragrance formed a mist,
drifting and settling on things.
There were several thousand parrots,
with vermilion beaks and emerald feathers,
their tails two or three chǐ long,
soaring among them.
They called to each other by name,
their voices clear and melodious.
There was one named Wǔ Yóuláng,
one named Ā Sū'ér,
one named Wǔ Xiānláng,
and one named Zìzài Xiānshēng.
There was one named Tà Liánlù,
one named Fèng Huātái,
one named Dài Chán'ér,
and one named Duō Huāzǐ.
One of them, singing a song, said:
"This tune of mine was often sung by Lady Gōuyì of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn.
The lyrics go:
'Dài Chán'ér,
clearly conveys the words to the sovereign lord.
In the Jiànzhāng Palace, not yet returned,
vermilion blinds and golden lamps, paired phoenixes dance.'" The one named Ā Sū'ér said:
"I recall Ājiāo weeping deep in the palace,
singing:
'In the past, I requested
[Note: The Míng manuscript lacks the character "requested."]
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú to compose the 'Rhapsody of the Chángmén Palace,'
only to waste a hundred catties of gold,
yet my lord never looked back.'"
Another, reciting
[Note: The original text has "lyrics" (cí), changed to "reciting" (sòng) per the Míng manuscript.]
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's "Rhapsody of the Great Man," said:
"When I first studied rhapsodies,
Zhāoyí of Zhào struck me with a seven-treasure hairpin as a whip.
The pain was unbearable,
but today I can recite it,
and it remains a lifelong skill."
The one named Wǔ Yóuláng said:
"I once saw Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
riding a golden boat,
floating on the Jícuì Pond,
playing a purple jade flute himself,
its tones clear and resonant.
The Emperor, pleased and content,
was accompanied by Lady Lǐ's song,
which went:
'Though lowly and base I gaze,
I receive your grace and favor.
I wish my lord,
ten thousand years of life.'" Then the one named Wǔ Xiānláng asked Guīshùn:
"What is your surname and personal name?"
Guīshùn said:
"My surname is Liǔ,
and I am the twelfth."
He said:
"Liǔ the Twelfth, where have you come from?"
Guīshùn said:
"I was heading to Bālǐng,
but encountered a wind that moored my boat.
In high spirits, I came here."
Wǔ Xiānláng said:
"Official Liǔ the Twelfth,
by chance encountering the wind,
you have reached this extraordinary realm.
This is what is called 'beauty arising from affliction.'
However, I, a lowly bird,
cannot exert effort for a living person.
I shall convey your presence to Lady Guì of the Thirtieth for you."
Then he called from afar:
"Ā Chūn,
there is a guest here."
Immediately, several patches of purple clouds
flew in from the southwest,
stopping about a zhàng above the ground.
The cloud vapor gradually dispersed,
revealing a pearl-adorned tower with emerald curtains,
multiple railings and soaring pillars,
encircling the edge of the rock.
A maidservant in green emerged from the door,
just thirteen or fourteen years old,
clad in pearls and jade,
her face exceptionally beautiful.
She said to Guīshùn:
"The Thirtieth Lady sends Ā Chūn to convey her words to you, sir.
Living in poor and remote quarters,
we trouble you to inspect this place.
I wonder if you have eaten this morning?
Please deign to sit briefly,
so we may prepare a vegetarian meal."
Immediately, someone brought out a crystal seat.
Guīshùn declined twice before sitting.
Ā Chūn then admonished the bird Fèng Huātái:
"Why aren't you attending to the guest?
The Thirtieth Lady, because Huángláng is not here,
dares not receive you, sir, directly.
If you are negligent,
you'll be beaten like last time."
A parrot immediately flew over and said:
"I am Fèng Huātái.
Recently I composed a poem.
Would you care to hear it?"
Guīshùn said:
"It is my lifelong delight,
truly matching my wishes."
Fèng Huātái then said:
"Yesterday I passed by the Jade Tower of Pénglái,
and thus composed a stanza:
Dew meets the morning sun, born anew,
Ocean waves churn like crystal.
The jade tower overlooks the vast expanse,
Heaven and Earth illuminate each other.
At this moment I descend to perch,
Leaving my traces on the old pillars.
Looking back, what shame have I?
Daily I walk in the company of immortals."
Guīshùn said:
"Beautiful it is, indeed beautiful.
But who, may I ask, is your teacher?"
Fèng Huātái said:
"I served at Wáng Dān's side
for over a thousand years.
Dù Lánxiāng taught me true talismans,
and Dōngfāng Shuò imparted secret formulas to me.
When Emperor Wǔ of Hàn sought a Grand Master of the Palace,
I saw Yáng Xióng and Wáng Bāo's rhapsodies and eulogies in the Shíqú Office,
and only then began to understand admonitions and discourses.
During the rebellion of Wáng Mǎng,
I finally returned to Wú.
Later, I was obtained by Zhū Rán,
who passed me on to Lù Xùn.
There I again saw the compositions of Jī and Yún,
and only then learned to compose poetry.
After Jī and Yún were executed,
I came here.
I truly do not know who is considered the master craftsman these days."
Guīshùn said:
"Xuē Dàohéng and Jiāng Zǒng."
He then recited several of their poems to show him.
Fèng Huātái said:
"Recent works are not without elegance,
but they greatly lack strength of character."
Soon after, Ā Chūn brought out a red jade tray
with ten thousand kinds of rare delicacies,
things never seen before,
their sweet fragrance assailing the nose.
After eating and drinking,
suddenly two Daoist priests flew down from the sky.
Seeing Guīshùn, they said:
"How rare to find you
conversing with parrots.
Are you not Liǔ the Twelfth?
The wind is favorable for your boat,
and they are searching for you urgently.
Why not hasten back?"
They then tossed down a chǐ of fine silk, saying:
"Cover your eyes with this,
and you will depart."
Guīshùn complied.
Suddenly, it was as if his body flew,
and he landed back in Bālǐng,
reaching his boat.
The boatmen were about to depart.
When asked,
they said Guīshùn had been missing for three days.
Later, he returned to this place,
moored his boat and searched,
but never saw it again.
From "Continued Records of the Mysterious and Strange."
Yuán Cángjī
The retired scholar Yuán Càngjī,
himself said
"himself said" originally read "said himself",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
was a descendant of Prince Xiàowáng of Qīnghé in the Later Wei dynasty.
During the reign of Emperor Yáng of Suí,
he held the official position of Fèngxìn Láng.
In the ninth year of the Dàyè era,
he served as an assistant to the envoy crossing the sea.
Not long after,
wind and waves wrecked the ship,
dark fog enveloped them from all sides,
all his fellow travelers perished,
but Càngjī alone was carried by a broken piece of wood,
for nearly half a month,
when he suddenly reached a shore among islands.
The islanders asked where he came from,
and he, dazed, told them everything that had happened.
The islanders said:
"This is Cāngzhōu,
tens of thousands of miles away from the Middle Kingdom."
They then brought out calamus flower and peach blossom wine for him to drink,
and his spirit and energy became clear and refreshed.
The island was a thousand li square,
its flowers and trees always like those of the second month,
the soil suitable for the five grains,
and the people mostly did not die.
It produced phoenixes, peacocks, divine oxen, spirit horses, and the like;
it also produced split-pedicel melons,
two feet long,
their color like mulberries,
two
In the lower part of "Dùyáng Zábiān" two is written as one
fruits with two pedicels;
there were green jujubes and red chestnuts,
all as large as pears.
The islanders mostly wore wide-sleeved robes,
and donned distant-travel caps,
when speaking with them about matters of the Middle Kingdom,
it was as clear and vivid as if before one's eyes.
Their dwellings were sometimes golden palaces and silver towers,
jade buildings and purple pavilions,
where they played the music of Xiāosháo,
and drank the fine wine of fragrant dew.
On the island was the Mountain of Long Gaze,
below the mountain flowed the Clear Water Spring,
the spring was a hundred paces wide,
also called the Flowing Channel,
even if metal or stone were thrown into it,
they would never sink,
so the islanders made boats and barges from earthenware and iron.
There was also a Golden Pond,
over ten li square,
its water, stones, sand, and mud,
were all like the color of gold.
In it were four-legged fish,
now the Vice Director Lú of the Ministry of Justice, Xún, said:
"On Jīnyì Ridge there is a pond like a basin,
in it are fish all with four legs."
There were also golden lotus flowers,
the islanders ground them into paste,
and used it to paint colors in between,
the brilliance dazzling and radiant,
no different from the real thing,
only they could not resist fire.
There were also golden-stem flowers,
like butterflies,
whenever a slight breeze arrived,
they would sway and flutter as if flying,
women vied to pick them to use as hair ornaments,
and there was a saying:
"If you don't wear the golden-stem flower,
you cannot dwell among the immortals."
They also used strong wood to build ships,
on them they adorned many pearls and jades,
for amusement.
Strong wood,
is wood that does not sink.
One square foot of it,
weighs eight hundred catties,
even if a huge stone is tied to it,
it ultimately will not sink.
Càngjī stayed for a long time,
when suddenly he longed for the Middle Kingdom,
the islanders then made a Wind-Soaring Boat to send him off.
It churned the water like an arrow,
in less than ten days it reached Dōnglái.
He asked about the state,
it was the Great Táng;
inquired about the reign era,
it was Zhēnyuán.
He sought his hometown,
it was overgrown with brambles;
traced his descendants,
they were distant relatives.
From the first year of the Suí Dàyè era to the end of the Zhēnyuán era,
was already two hundred years.
There were two birds,
greatly resembling orioles,
often soaring and flying in the air,
when Càngjī called them they would come,
sometimes he would order them to hold pearls in their beaks,
sometimes order them to receive human speech.
They were called message-relaying birds,
from Cāngzhōu.
Càngjī was skilled in poetry and fond of wine,
mixing with the common folk without restraint or formality,
for over ten years,
he traveled all over Jiāngbiǎo,
and no one knew of him.
But Zhào Guīzhēn once met Càngjī's disciple, the Jiǔhuá Daoist priest Yè Tōngwēi,
and sought to obtain the truth of the matter,
Guīzhēn then fully reported Càngjī's marvels to the emperor.
The emperor ordered a court usher to urgently summon him with a handwritten edict.
When they reached halfway on the road,
he suddenly vanished.
The court usher was terrified,
and immediately submitted a memorial detailing the reason,
the emperor read the memorial and sighed:
"I am not equal to Emperor Míng,
in summoning extraordinary men."
Later, someone saw Càngjī floating in a small boat on the sea.
To this day, among the Daoist followers in Jiāngbiǎo,
the story is widely transmitted.
From "Dùyáng Biān"
Wénguǎngtōng
Wén Guǎngtōng was a man from Téng Village in Chénxī County.
The county belonged to Chénzhōu.
Traveling one hundred lǐ upstream from the prefecture,
on the north bank was Téng Village,
where Guǎngtōng lived.
It was originally Hàn-dynasty Chénlíng County.
The "Wǔlíng Jì" records:
In the twenty-sixth year of the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty, Guǎngtōng
saw a wild boar eating his crops,
so he raised his crossbow and shot it.
It fled bleeding,
and following the blood trail,
he crossed over ten-odd lǐ,
entering a cave.
After walking about three hundred paces,
he suddenly emerged into bright daylight,
and abruptly saw several hundred households living there.
He could not fathom their origins.
Looking at the boar he had shot,
it had already returned to a villager's pen.
Soon an old man came out the door and said:
"Are you not the one who shot my boar?"
Wén replied:
"The boar came to violate my servant;
it was not I who violated the boar."
The old man said:
"If someone leads an ox to trample another's field,
indeed there is fault.
But to seize that person's ox—
the fault is even greater."
Wén then kowtowed and apologized for his transgression.
The old man said:
"To recognize a fault and correct it
is to have no fault.
This boar, due to past karma,
should receive this retribution.
Sir, there is no need to apologize."
The old man called Wéntōng to the main hall,
where he saw over ten scholars,
all wearing Zhāngfǔ caps
and garments with wide sleeves.
There was a learned scholar
sitting alone on a couch facing south, discussing the "Lǎozǐ."
He also saw in the western study ten people facing each other,
plucking a single-stringed qín,
yet the five notes harmonized naturally.
A youth poured wine
and was called to serve the guest.
Wén drank until half-intoxicated,
his four limbs feeling pleasant and at ease,
and then took his leave.
Observing the village paths and human affairs,
they were no different from the outside world,
yet he sensed a purity, emptiness, and unique remoteness—
truly a wondrous place.
He lingered, wishing to stay.
The old man then sent a youth to escort him out,
instructing him to firmly close the gate
and not allow outsiders to come again.
As Wén walked with the youth,
he asked about their origins and details.
The youth replied:
"Those worthies came here to escape the troubles of Xià Jié's reign,
and through studying the Way attained immortality.
The one sitting alone on the couch discussing the 'Lǎozǐ'
is the former Héshàng Gōng.
I am Wáng Fǔsì from Shānyáng in the Hàn dynasty.
I came here to inquire about
obscure meanings in the 'Lǎozǐ.'
Since I began sweeping the gate,
ten cycles have passed here,
and only now have I been summoned and advanced,
allowed to join the disciples.
Yet I have not deeply received the essential teachings;
I am only ordered to guard the gate."
Upon reaching the cave entrance,
they parted with earnest feelings,
saying they did not know when they would meet again.
Wéntōng, from the place he had entered,
saw that the crossbow he had used was already rotten and broken.
He had initially thought only a short while had passed,
but it had already been twelve years.
Wéntōng's family had already completed mourning for him.
Hearing of his return,
the entire village was shocked and doubtful.
The next day,
they went with villagers to search for the cave entrance,
but only saw a giant rock blocking it.
Burning and chiseling could not breach it.
From "Shénxiān Gǎnyù Zhuàn."
Yáng Bóchǒu was from Wǔxiāng, Féngyì.
He enjoyed reading the "Yìjīng"
and lived in seclusion on Huàshān.
In the early Suí dynasty, during the Kāihuáng era,
Emperor Wéndì sought out recluses and hermits.
Hearing that Yáng possessed the Way,
he summoned him to the capital.
Yáng showed no courtesy to dukes and ministers;
regardless of whether people were noble or base,
he addressed them all as "you,"
and others could not fathom him.
The emperor bestowed garments upon him,
but he wore them to the court hall,
then discarded them and left.
He often let his hair loose and feigned madness,
wandering through markets and alleys.
His body was filthy and unkempt,
and he never combed or washed.
He also opened a stall to tell fortunes,
and his divinations were never inaccurate.
Once, someone lost a horse
and went to Bóchǒu for a divination.
Bóchǒu was just then being summoned by the crown prince
and met him on the road.
He immediately performed a divination for him, saying:
"Go to the third shop south of the east wall in the western market
and buy fish to make sliced fish for me."
Following his words,
the man went to the indicated shop,
and sure enough, someone led the lost horse there,
so he captured him.
Hé Tuǒ once discussed the "Yìjīng" with him.
Hearing Hé Tuǒ's words,
he laughed and said:
"What use are the words of Zhèng Xuán and Wáng Bì?"
Thereupon, he separately
"Separately" originally read "divined";
emended according to the Míng manuscript copy.
reasoned, debated, and answered,
his thoughts and principles profoundly subtle,
greatly different from the tenets of earlier Confucian scholars.
Discussants said he possessed mysterious insight.
When asked about what he had studied,
he said:
"Beneath Tàihuà Mountain,
in the Jīntiān Cave,
I once received the 'Yìjīng' taught by Fúxī,
which is 'mysteriously identical' with the Great Way.
Its principles exhaust all subtleties.
How can the commonplace talk of worldly Confucians
fathom the tenets of divine immortals?"
After several years, he returned to Huàshān.
In later generations, people occasionally saw him.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí."
Liú Fǎshī
During the Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty,
at Yúntái Temple in Huàyīn, there was a certain Master Liú,
who practiced breath cultivation and abstained from grains,
for nearly twenty years.
Whenever he held the Triple Origin fasting ceremonies,
he would see a man,
wearing a patched robe,
with a dark and emaciated face,
come to sit at the very end,
and leave once the ceremony was over.
This went on for over ten years,
yet the man's clothing and complexion never changed.
Master Liú found this strange and asked him about it.
The man replied:
"My surname is Zhāng,
and my given name is Gōngbì.
I live in the eastern corner of Liánhuā Peak."
Master Liú thought this was an uninhabited place,
and asked to go with him.
Gōngbì cheerfully agreed, saying:
"It is very pleasant there.
If you, Master, can settle there,
you will surely not feel bored."
Master Liú then followed Gōngbì on his way.
After twenty or thirty lǐ,
they grasped vines and pulled at creepers,
until they found a narrow bird's path.
The cliffs and valleys were perilously steep,
so treacherous that even monkeys could not cross,
yet Gōngbì walked them as if they were level ground.
Master Liú followed along,
and encountered no difficulties either.
They then arrived at a stone cliff,
sheer as if cut by a knife,
towering over a thousand rèn high,
overlooking a bottomless valley below.
A path only a few inches wide
was where Master Liú and Gōngbì
stood sideways.
Gōngbì then knocked on the stone cliff with his finger,
and someone inside asked:
"Who is it?"
He replied:
"It's me."
Suddenly, a door opened with a scraping sound,
and inside the door were sky, earth, sun, and moon.
Gōngbì was about to enter,
and Master Liú followed him in.
The person inside then angrily said to Gōngbì:
"Why have you brought an outsider here?"
That person then closed the door,
and it turned back into a stone cliff.
Gōngbì said:
"This is no stranger,
but Master Liú of Yúntái Temple.
He and I have been friends for a long time,
so I invited him here.
Why do you refuse him so firmly?"
The door opened again,
and admitted Gōngbì and Master Liú.
Gōngbì said:
"Master Liú is very hungry from this journey.
You should provide him with a hearty meal."
That person then asked Master Liú if he would stay.
Master Liú requested to come at a later time.
That person then fetched a bowl of water,
mixed it with a spoonful of powder from a small blue pouch behind his elbow, and gave it to Master Liú to drink.
Its flavor was very sweet and fragrant,
and after drinking it, his feelings of hunger and thirst vanished instantly.
Gōngbì said:
"I mentioned yesterday that the mountains are very pleasant.
Why don't you put on a performance
for Master Liú to see?"
That person then sprayed water toward the eastern valley,
and suddenly, a blue dragon and a white elephant appeared,
dancing in pairs,
their dance exquisite;
a majestic phoenix and a colorful luan bird appeared,
singing in pairs,
their song clear and melodious.
After a short while,
Gōngbì escorted Master Liú back.
Master Liú looked back,
but saw only green cliffs and crimson ravines,
with no trace
of the earlier singing and dancing.
As they neared the temple,
Gōngbì took his leave.
Master Liú returned to the temple,
settled his affairs,
and went back to look for Gōngbì.
But every step was fraught with danger and obstacles,
and the path was utterly inaccessible.
Master Liú bitterly regretted not staying earlier,
crying out to heaven and earth in anguish,
and developed a back ailment.
Gōngbì never came again.
From "Xù Xuánguài Lù"
Mǎ Zhōu
Mǎ Zhōu was originally an immortal official of the Sùlíng Palace on Huàshān.
When the Táng dynasty was about to receive the Mandate of Heaven,
the Supreme Elder decreed that he descend to assist the state.
However, he became deeply addicted to wine,
sinking into the mundane world for twenty years,
wandering in hardship and hunger,
encountering obstacles wherever he went,
nearly stumbling and falling.
Hearing that Yuán Tiāngāng had entered Qín from Shǔ,
skilled in physiognomy,
he went to visit him
to determine his fortune.
Tiāngāng stared at him for a long time and said:
"Your five spirits have scattered;
you are but a walking corpse with days left to live.
What physiognomy is there to speak of!"
Zhōu was greatly alarmed
and asked for methods to avert disaster.
Tiāngāng said:
"From here, go straight east.
You will encounter an old man riding an ox.
Do not rush to speak with him;
simply follow him.
This disaster can then be averted."
Zhōu followed these instructions.
Before leaving the city gate,
he indeed saw an old man
riding an ox out of the city.
He silently followed behind.
Winding through village paths,
they ascended a great mountain.
Zhōu followed to the mountaintop.
The old man turned and saw him,
dismounted from the ox,
sat beneath a tree,
and spoke to him:
"The Supreme Elder commanded you to assist the holy descendant,
to establish a dynasty and save the world.
Why have you become lost in wine,
bringing hardship and hunger upon yourself?
Your five spirits have scattered;
your vital energy has withered.
You will die within days,
yet you do not cultivate and reflect?"
Zhōu remained dazed and uncomprehending.
The old man said:
"You were originally an immortal official of Sùlíng Palace.
Now, the Immortal King of Tàihuà has sent someone to summon you."
He then led him into the palace complex.
Passing through several palace gates,
they arrived before a great hall.
Feathered guards stood solemn and stern,
as if in an imperial residence.
Hurrying before the curtain,
a voice proclaimed and reprimanded him
for receiving the command disrespectfully,
neglecting his assigned duties,
ordering him to return to his former post
and reflect on his faults.
The old man and several envoys
escorted him to a separate courtyard outside the eastern wing.
The rooms were grand and splendid.
Looking at the door,
he saw his name inscribed there.
Unlocking and entering,
he saw stoves, cauldrons, vessels,
bed couches, and cushions,
exactly as if he had recently resided there.
He pondered deeply,
yet could not fully comprehend.
Suddenly, five figures appeared,
dressed in robes of the five directions,
tall and imposing,
standing before him, saying:
"We are the spirits of your five viscera.
Sir, your indulgence in wine and dissipation
has defiled your body.
We have long returned here.
Simply close your eyes,
and we shall return to the chamber of your spirit."
Zhōu closed his eyes for a moment.
Suddenly, he felt his mind clear and awaken,
and recalled past events.
Over twenty years
seemed but a span of ten days.
He locked his dwelling again,
left the Immortal King's court,
kowtowed to confess his faults,
and received his command anew.
Coming to Cháng'ān,
the next day he visited Tiāngāng again.
Tiāngāng exclaimed in surprise:
"What have you encountered?
You are already healed!
In sixty days, you will be promoted nine times in a single day;
in a hundred days, you will reach the position of Chancellor.
Strive to take care of yourself!"
Thus, during the Zhēnguàn era,
when an edict commanded civil and military officials to each submit strategies for governing the state,
Zhōu's submission
surpassed all others in insight.
That day, he was appointed Reminder, Investigating Censor, and Probationary Attendant.
From then on, he repeatedly held high offices,
eventually becoming Secretariat Director for several years.
One day, a host of immortals descended to his chamber, saying:
"Your merit in assisting the state is accomplished.
It is time to withdraw.
The Great Unity summons you;
you may no longer remain."
The next day, he passed away without illness.
He was posthumously titled Duke Zhōng.
His achievements and merits,
his support of state governance,
and the progression of his official ranks
are recorded in the state histories.
They are not fully detailed here.
From "Shénxiān Shíyí."
Lǐ Línfǔ
Lǐ Línfǔ, the Right Minister of the Táng dynasty,
at the age of twenty,
had not yet studied.
In the Eastern Capital,
he enjoyed hunting and playing polo,
galloping after hawks and hounds.
Every day at the locust tree altar beneath the city wall,
he would ride a donkey and strike the ball,
almost without rest.
When exhausted, he would abandon the donkey,
and rest with both hands braced on the ground.
One day,
a Daoist priest, very ugly,
saw Lord Lǐ squatting on the ground,
and slowly said:
"What pleasure is there in this,
that the young lord loves it so?"
Lǐ angrily looked back and said:
"What business is it of yours?"
The Daoist left,
and the next day repeated his words.
Lord Lǐ, clever and perceptive from a young age,
thought him an extraordinary man,
and so straightened his clothes, rose, and apologized.
The Daoist said:
"Although the young lord is skilled at this,
if you suddenly suffer a fall,
regret will be too late."
Lord Lǐ requested to cultivate caution from then on,
and no longer engage in it.
The Daoist smiled and said:
"Meet with the young lord here three days from now at the fifth watch."
He said:
"Agreed."
When he went,
the Daoist had already arrived first,
and said:
"Why are you late for our appointment?"
Lǐ then apologized to him.
He said:
"Come again in three more days."
Lord Lǐ went at midnight,
and after a long while, the Daoist arrived.
He was very pleased,
and their conversation and laughter were extremely harmonious.
Moreover, he said:
"I have wandered the world for five hundred years,
and have seen only one person like you, young lord.
You are already listed in the register of immortals,
and should ascend to heaven in broad daylight.
If you do not wish it,
then you may become prime minister for twenty years,
with great power in your own hands.
Young lord, return for now,
think it over carefully,
and meet here again in three days at the fifth watch."
Lord Lǐ returned and considered it, saying:
"I am of the imperial clan,
and have been a young gallant.
To be prime minister for twenty years,
with great power in my own hands—
how could I exchange that for ascending to heaven in broad daylight?"
His decision was already made,
and when the time came, he went to inform him.
The Daoist sighed and exclaimed in dismay,
as if unable to control himself,
and said:
"After five hundred years, I finally meet one person,
what a pity, what a pity."
Lord Lǐ regretted it,
and wanted to change his choice.
The Daoist said:
"It cannot be done,
the divine spirits already know."
He bid him farewell, saying:
"As prime minister for twenty years,
the power of life and death will be in your hands,
and your authority will shake the world.
However, be careful not to commit hidden evils;
instead, perform hidden virtues,
widely rescue and aid people,
and do not wrongfully kill anyone.
If you do so, then after three hundred years,
you will ascend to heaven in broad daylight.
Your official salary has already arrived;
you may proceed to the capital."
Lord Lǐ prostrated himself, weeping and bowing,
and the Daoist shook his hand and bid him farewell.
At that time, Lord Lǐ's paternal uncle served as a Vice Director in the Ministry of Treasury,
in the capital,
so he went to see him.
His uncle, considering him wild and unrestrained,
did not pay him much attention,
and was quite startled, saying:
"How did you get here?"
He said:
"I am aware of my past faults,
and now have come especially to pay my respects.
I ask to reform and study,
and am willing to accept whipping."
The Vice Director found this very strange,
but did not yet have him begin his studies.
Whenever there were guests,
he would send him to oversee the arrangement of cups and plates.
He did so with impeccable cleanliness.
Sometimes he was told,
"Do such-and-such for me,"
and even if the snow was deep enough to bury his ankles,
he would not leave.
The Vice Director grew increasingly fond and sympathetic toward him,
spoke of him among his colleagues,
and many came to know of him.
Afterward, through hereditary privilege,
he rose through the ranks to become a Grand Master of Remonstrance,
and within less than ten years,
he became prime minister.
Cunning, profound, and secretive,
he was able to discern the emperor's intentions,
and his favor and regard grew deep and harmonious.
He alone held the pivotal position,
and the awe he inspired among people
was no less than that of a ruler.
Several years later,
he became increasingly intent on securing his position,
instigating major trials,
and executing those who opposed him.
Wrongful deaths followed one after another,
and he completely forgot the Daoist's warning at the locust tree altar.
At that time, those who came to pay their respects at Lord Lǐ's gate
would, upon approaching,
inevitably dismount and proceed on foot,
not daring to ride on horseback.
Suddenly, one day around noon,
someone knocked at the gate.
The guards were startled and went to see,
and beheld a Daoist priest, very gaunt and emaciated,
who said:
"I wish to report to the Prime Minister."
The gatekeepers shouted at him and drove him away,
and the guards further bound him with ropes and sent him to the prefectural office.
The Daoist smiled slightly and left.
The next day at noon, he came again,
and the gatekeeper seized an opportunity to report it.
Lord Lǐ said:
"I do not recall him,
but try to let him in."
When the Daoist entered,
Lord Lǐ saw him,
and suddenly realized with clarity—
it was the man he had seen at the locust tree altar.
Overwhelmed with shame and fear,
he was at a loss.
Reflecting on the events of twenty years ago,
he realized they had now come to pass.
The teachings and warnings he had received
he had not followed even briefly.
His heart felt as if afflicted with illness,
and he bowed.
The Daoist stepped forward, smiling, and said:
"Is the Prime Minister well?
The request I made back then,
you did not follow at all.
I urged the Prime Minister to perform hidden virtues,
but now you have wrongfully killed people.
Heaven is very clear,
and its censure and punishment are fearsome.
What is to be done?"
Lord Lǐ could only knock his forehead on the ground.
The Daoist stayed overnight,
and Lord Lǐ dismissed all his servants.
They stayed in the central hall,
each occupying a couch.
The Daoist only ate a little tea and fruit,
and consumed nothing else.
Late at night,
Lord Lǐ said:
"In the past, I received your instruction,
and there was still the promise of ascending to heaven.
Can that still be achieved now?"
The Daoist said:
"Because of the Prime Minister's actions,
which did not accord with the Way,
there will be banishment and punishment,
and another three hundred years.
After six hundred more years,
it will be as promised."
Lord Lǐ said:
"My time in the human world is nearly fulfilled.
Since there is punishment for my crimes,
what will happen afterward?"
The Daoist said:
"Do you wish to know?
You may also make a journey."
Lord Lǐ descended from his couch and bowed in thanks.
He said:
"Let the Prime Minister calm his spirit and quiet his thoughts,
dispelling all distractions,
still as a withered tree."
"Then we can go together."
After a long while,
Lǐ Gōng said:
"I have no more thoughts or concerns."
He then descended and called out:
"We can go together."
Unconsciously,
Lǐ Gōng followed the Dàoshì away.
The main gate and the Chūnmíng Gate opened by themselves as they arrived,
and Lǐ Gōng, holding onto the Dàoshì's robe, passed through.
After walking for over ten lǐ,
Lǐ Gōng, being of noble status,
was particularly unaccustomed to walking,
and grew quite weary and distressed.
The Dàoshì also knew this,
and said:
"Would you like to rest?"
They then sat together by the roadside.
After a short while,
he handed Lǐ Gōng several sections of bamboo, saying:
"You can ride on this,
and stop when you reach the place.
Be careful not to open your eyes."
Lǐ Gōng then mounted it,
and soared into the sky.
He felt as if his body was floating over a vast sea,
hearing only the sounds of wind and water.
After the time it takes to eat a meal, it stopped,
and he saw a large city.
Hundreds of armored soldiers,
arrayed at the city gate,
upon the Dàoshì's arrival,
all greeted him with bows,
and also bowed to Lǐ Gōng.
After about one lǐ,
they arrived at a government office.
Entering another gate,
there were more armored soldiers,
and they ascended the steps to a great hall.
The curtains and couches were luxurious and extravagant.
Lǐ Gōng, exhausted,
wanted to lie down on the couch.
The Dàoshì, alarmed,
pulled him up and said:
"Not yet.
I fear you may not be able to return.
This is where you, Xiànggōng, will reside after your death."
Lǐ Gōng said:
"If this is truly the case,
I would have no regrets."
The Dàoshì laughed and said:
"These armored creatures,
"scaled" originally written as "armored",
amended according to the Ming manuscript copy
and the like,
among them, there are also many hardships."
He then led Lǐ Gōng back out of the main gate,
and again handed him the bamboo staff,
just as when they had come.
Entering his residence,
ascending the hall,
he saw his own body sitting with eyes closed on the bed.
The Dàoshì then called out:
"Xiànggōng, Xiànggōng."
Lǐ Gōng then awoke.
Tears and snivel streamed down,
and he kowtowed, expressing his gratitude.
The next day, as they parted,
Lǐ Gōng generously offered gold and silk as gifts,
but the Dàoshì accepted none of them,
merely waving his hand,
and said:
"Strive on.
Six hundred years from now,
I will see you again, Xiànggōng."
He then went out the door and vanished,
no one knew where.
Previously, Ān Lùshān often kept Dàoshù practitioners,
and once said to them:
"Even when facing the Son of Heaven,
I feel no fear,
but only when I see Lǐ Xiànggōng,
I feel as if there is no place to hide,
why is that?"
A Dàoshù practitioner said:
"You have five hundred yīn soldiers,
all with bronze heads and iron foreheads,
constantly by your side.
How can this be?
How can I see them?"
Ān Lùshān then requested that the Prime Minister be feasted at his residence,
and secretly sent the Dàoshù practitioner to spy from behind the curtain.
Upon returning, he said:
"It is strange.
When I first saw Lǐ Xiànggōng,
there was a young servant in blue,
carrying an incense burner, who entered.
The attendants and guards,
those with bronze heads and iron foreheads and the like,
all fled through walls and over roofs,
running away in panic.
I also do not know the reason.
He must be an immortal official temporarily exiled to the mortal world."
From "Yì Shǐ"
Guō Zǐyí
was from Huàzhōu.
Initially, he served in the army in the desert frontier,
and once went to the capital to expedite military provisions.
On his return, about ten lǐ from Yínzhōu,
as dusk fell,
suddenly a sandstorm darkened the sky,
making travel impossible,
so he entered an empty house by the roadside,
and prepared to rest on the ground.
After nightfall,
he suddenly saw red light on both sides,
and looking up into the sky,
he saw a curtained carriage with embroidered interiors,
inside which was a beautiful woman,
sitting on a couch with her feet dangling,
descending from the sky,
looking down.
Guō Zǐyí bowed and prayed, saying:
"Today is the seventh day of the seventh month,
it must be the Weaving Maiden descending.
I pray for longevity and wealth."
The woman laughed and said:
"Great wealth and honor,
and also long life."
Having spoken,
she slowly ascended back to the sky,
still looking directly at Guō Zǐyí.
After a long while, she vanished.
Later, Guō Zǐyí achieved great merit, attaining high rank and prominence,
his prestige resplendent and far-reaching.
In the early years of the Dàlì era,
while stationed in Hézhōng,
he fell gravely ill,
causing worry and fear among the three armies.
Guō Zǐyí summoned the imperial physician and his advisors Wáng Yánchāng, Sūn Sù, Zhào Huìbó, Yán Yǐng, and others, saying:
"I know myself that this illness has not yet reached the point of decline and death."
He then recounted the event he had encountered,
and all congratulated him joyfully.
Afterwards, he was appointed Grand Commandant, Shàngshū Lìng, and Shàngfù,
and passed away at the age of ninety.
From "Shénxiān Gǎnyù Zhuàn"
Hán Huàng
The Tang dynasty chancellor Hán Huǎng,
while serving as an inspector in Zhèxī,
was quite strong-willed and self-assured,
and often harbored ambitions beyond his station.
One day, a merchant named Lǐ Shùn
moored his boat beneath the Jīngkǒu weir.
Late at night, the anchor rope snapped,
and the boat drifted, with no idea where it would end up.
By dawn,
it had come to rest at the foot of a mountain.
The wind and waves gradually calmed,
so he went ashore to explore.
He found a faint, bird-like path
and walked five or six lǐ,
where he saw a man wearing a black headscarf.
With his cap pushed back and dressed in ancient attire,
he looked quite different from ordinary people.
The man led him up the mountain
to a palace complex,
with magnificent towers and pavilions,
far beyond anything in the mortal world.
They passed through several gates,
and the courtyard was vast.
From a distance, Lǐ Shùn bowed toward the hall,
and someone emerged from behind a curtain,
addressing him:
"I wish to send a letter to Lord Hán of Jīnlíng.
Do not be alarmed by the trouble I am causing you."
He then produced a letter
which Lǐ Shùn received with a bow.
An attendant escorted him out the gate
and back to his boat.
Lǐ Shùn then asked the attendant:
"What place is this?
I fear Lord Hán will question me,
and who is it that sent this letter?"
The attendant replied:
"This is Guǎngsāng Mountain in the Eastern Sea.
It is where Xuānfǔ Zhòngní of the State of Lǔ,
having attained the Way, serves as a true official,
governing this mountain.
Lord Hán is none other than Zhòng Yóu,
strong-willed and self-reliant by nature.
The Master fears he may fall into the net of punishment,
so he sends this letter to admonish him."
With these words, they parted.
Lǐ Shùn returned to his boat,
where a messenger warned everyone aboard:
"Sit quietly,
do not be alarmed,
and do not look outside the boat.
In a short while, you will return to your original place.
If you violate this warning,
the boat is sure to capsize."
Everyone on the boat followed his instructions,
not daring to look around.
The boat moved as if flying.
In no time,
they were back beneath the Jīngkǒu weir,
with no idea how many thousands of lǐ they had traveled.
Later, Lǐ Shùn went to the government office
to deliver the letter he had received.
Lord Hán opened the letter and examined it,
finding nine ancient characters
written in tadpole script,
completely illegible.
He questioned Lǐ Shùn about the origin,
finding it deeply strange,
and detained Lǐ Shùn,
suspecting him of sorcery and deceit,
intending to impose severe punishment.
He then sought out several individuals skilled in seal script,
but none could decipher it.
A guest with bushy eyebrows and dressed in ancient attire
came forward of his own accord,
claiming expertise in ancient script.
Lord Hán met with him
and showed him the letter.
The guest held the letter above his head,
bowed twice, and congratulated him:
"This is a letter from Kǒng Xuānfǔ,
written in the tadpole script of Xià Yǔ.
The text reads:
'To Hán Huǎng:
Be mindful of your duties as a subject,
and do not act recklessly.'"
Lord Hán treated him with exceptional respect and reverence.
The guest left through the gate,
and no one knew where he went.
Lord Hán sat in somber silence,
and after a long while, it became clear to him.
He recalled the events of Guǎngsāng Mountain,
realizing they were not far removed.
He sent Lǐ Shùn away with generous gifts and gratitude.
From then on, he became respectful, humble, and cautious,
and was able to maintain this to the end.
From "The Biographies of Divine Encounters"
Yīnyǐn Kè
In the first year of the Shénlóng era of the Táng dynasty,
a commoner named Yīn Yǐnkè from Zhúshān County, Fángzhōu,
was wealthy.
Behind his estate, he had been digging a well for two years,
having already excavated over a thousand chǐ without finding water.
Yet Yǐnkè’s determination to dig did not cease.
More than a month into the third year,
the workers suddenly heard the sounds of chickens, dogs, birds, and sparrows from underground.
Digging a few more chǐ,
they broke through to a stone cavern beside them.
The workers then entered the cavern to explore.
At first, after several dozen steps, they saw nothing,
only feeling their way along the wall as they walked.
Suddenly, they turned and saw a light like that of the sun and moon,
so they descended.
The cavern connected below to a mountain peak,
and the workers went down the mountain.
Standing upright and looking around,
they saw a completely different world of sky, earth, sun, and moon.
The mountain rose steeply for ten thousand rèn,
with a thousand cliffs and ten thousand ravines,
all of them wondrous sights.
The stones were all of a green lapis lazuli color.
In every cliff and ravine,
there were palaces and towers of gold and silver.
There were great trees,
their trunks jointed like bamboo,
their leaves like banana leaves,
and purple flowers as large as plates.
Five-colored butterflies,
with wings as large as fans,
fluttered and danced among the flowers.
Five-colored birds, as large as cranes,
soared and circled at the treetops.
In each cliff, there was a clear spring,
its color like a mirror;
and a white spring,
white as milk.
The workers gradually descended to where the palaces were,
intending to enter and inquire.
As they walked to the front of the palace,
they saw a plaque inscribed with the words:
"Tiānguì Shān Palace,"
written in silver characters.
Inside the two gate towers,
two people each rushed out in surprise.
Each was over five chǐ tall,
with youthful faces like jade,
clothes light and fine,
like white mist and green smoke,
vermilion lips and gleaming teeth,
beards and hair like black silk,
wearing golden crowns on their heads but barefoot.
They turned to the workers and said:
"Why have you come here?"
The workers explained everything from the beginning.
Before they had finished speaking,
several dozen people emerged from within the gate, saying:
"There is a strange, turbid aura."
They ordered the gatekeepers to be reprimanded.
The two gatekeepers said in fear and trepidation:
"There is a worker from the outer world
who arrived unexpectedly.
We were inquiring about his journey,
so we have not yet
"not yet" originally read "come,"
according to the Míng manuscript copy, changed to
reported."
After a moment,
a person in crimson clothes conveyed an order:
"Command the gate officers to treat him with courtesy and send him away."
The worker bowed in thanks, but before he finished,
the gatekeeper said:
"Since you have come this far,
why not ask to tour the place before returning?"
The worker said:
"I did not dare to ask earlier.
If you would grant me leisure,
I beg to take this opportunity to mention it."
The gatekeeper then sent in a jade tablet,
and shortly the jade tablet was returned.
The gatekeeper took it
and led the worker to the clear spring,
instructing him to bathe and wash his clothes.
Then they went to the white spring,
where he was told to rinse his mouth.
Its taste was like milk,
extremely sweet and delicious.
He drank several handfuls in succession,
feeling as if drunk and full.
Then the gatekeeper led him down the mountain.
Each time they reached a palace,
he was only allowed outside the gate,
and not permitted to enter.
Thus they traveled for half a day
until they reached the foot of the mountain,
where there was a city-state.
All its palaces and towers were made of gold, silver, jade, and marble,
with an inscription in jade characters that read:
"Ladder Immortal Kingdom."
The worker asked the gatekeeper:
"What kind of place is this kingdom?"
The gatekeeper said:
"These are all immortals who have just attained immortality.
They are sent to this kingdom
to cultivate for seven hundred thousand days,
after which they may ascend to the various heavens,
such as Yùjīng, Pénglái, Kūnlàng, or Gūyè.
Only then do they obtain positions in the immortal palaces,
holding registers and seals,
and flying freely at will."
The worker said:
"If this is an immortal kingdom,
why is it below our own country?"
The gatekeeper said:
"Our kingdom is the upper immortal kingdom of the lower realm.
Above your country,
there is also an immortal kingdom like ours,
also called 'Ladder Immortal Kingdom,'
no different at all."
After speaking,
he said to the worker:
"You may return now."
So they went back up the mountain,
searching for the original path.
He was again told to drink several handfuls from the white spring.
As they approached the mountaintop seeking the cavern,
the gatekeeper said:
"Though you have been here only a short while,
decades have passed in the human world.
Returning through the old cavern
is likely impossible.
Wait for me to request the key to the Heaven-Passing Pass to send you back."
The worker bowed in thanks.
After a moment,
the gatekeeper brought a golden seal and a jade tablet,
and led the worker up another path.
They arrived at a great gate,
as imposing as a tower,
with several people at the gate
bowing and waiting.
The gatekeeper showed the golden seal
and read the jade tablet,
and the gate swung open with a sound.
The gatekeeper led the worker upward.
As soon as they entered the gate,
he was swept away by wind and clouds,
and could see nothing.
He only heard the gatekeeper say:
"Go well,
and convey my regards to Chìchéng Zhēnbó."
In a moment, the clouds parted,
and he was already in a cave on the summit of Gūxīng Mountain, thirty lǐ north of Fángzhōu.
After emerging,
he inquired about Yīn Yǐnkè's household.
People of the time said:
"It has been three or four generations."
The reason for digging the well
was unknown to anyone.
The worker searched for the path himself,
but saw only a huge pit—
the collapsed remains of the well.
It was then the seventh year of the Zhēnyuán era.
The worker searched for his family,
but could find no trace of them.
After that, he took no pleasure in the human world,
and ceased eating the five grains,
wandering wherever his feet took him.
Several years later,
someone encountered him near Jīguān Mountain in Jiàngé.
After that, no one knew where he went.
From "Bóyì Zhì."
Tán Yí.
Tán Yí,
was the son of Shūpí, a commoner of Língzhōu,
born in the final years of the Kāiyuán era.
From birth, he was extraordinary;
he could speak as soon as he fell to the ground.
Within a few years,
his height exceeded six chǐ,
with beard, sideburns, and a bearing
unlike ordinary children.
He neither drank nor ate,
yet could run as fast as a galloping horse.
In his twenties,
he suddenly disappeared,
astonishing people far and near,
who considered him a divine being.
Thereafter, his parents longed for him,
and the villagers built a temple to worship him.
In the first year of the Dàlì era, bǐngwǔ,
he suddenly returned home,
wearing a rosy cloud crown and feathered robe—
a true immortal.
He told his parents:
"I have become an immortal official;
I should not remain in the mortal world for long.
Though my parents miss me,
it is also improper to have built this temple,
lest evil spirits take possession,
wielding power arbitrarily,
and harming people.
I ask that it be demolished.
Beneath the temple's foundation,
a great deal of gold was buried long ago.
After dismantling the temple,
dig into the ground to retrieve the gold,
which can be distributed to aid the poor,
and dispersed among the villagers."
After speaking,
he soared into the sky and departed.
Following his words,
they demolished the temple and dug into the ground,
and indeed found gold.
Where they dug,
a miraculous spring gushed forth,
exceptionally clear and pure,
not swelling with heavy rain,
nor diminishing during drought.
When the prefecture and towns prayed,
it would surely respond with divine efficacy.
Thus, it was named "Tánzǐ Pond,"
also called "Heavenly Pond."
Jìnshì Zhōu Guōfān
composed a poem to record the event, saying:
"Clear water spanning a hundred paces,
world-renowned as Tánzǐ Pond.
I asked the old man of Língyáng,
for whom was this pond named?
The elders told me the tale:
Shūpí of this prefecture, Tán.
In the final years of Kāiyuán,
he had a son named Āyí.
He could speak upon falling to the ground,
by nine, his beard and brows were full.
He neither drank nor ate,
never spoke of thirst or hunger.
At fifteen, he could walk so fast
that even swift horses could not catch him.
At twenty, he entered the mountain forests,
gone without a trace of return.
His parents deeply longed for him,
the village built a shrine for him.
In spring of Dàlì's first year,
this son suddenly came home.
On his head, a phoenix-adorned crown,
on his body, rainbow-feathered robes.
Universally saving the weary folk,
earnestly telling kin and friends:
'I am an immortal official now,
the mortal realm is not for prayers.
Fear evil spirits may take this guise,
better to level it early.'
'Here lies a hoard of gold,
guarded beneath this temple's base.
Dig it up, disperse to the living,
it can rescue the poor and weak.'
Gold emerged, followed by a divine spring,
clear as pure colored glaze.
Deep and pure, a sign of auspiciousness,
neither flood nor drought exhausts it.
Words finished, he bid farewell to emptiness,
vanishing into the distant, profound mystery.
Mortal sentiments could not keep him,
clinging and gazing, all cried in sorrow.
Following the immortal's command,
they tore down the temple, dug and peered.
Indeed, they obtained endless treasure,
shared equally, relieving distress and peril.
A great source flows from the ridge's peak,
gushing forth, rare in the world.
A wondrous site flows for a thousand ages,
blessing the four directions all year round."
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Wáng Kějiāo was a man of Kūnshān in Sūzhōu.
He made his living by farming and fishing,
and lived in Zhàotún Village south of the Sōng River.
Over thirty years old,
he knew nothing of the true Way.
He often caught large fish,
and delighted in clubbing them to death,
boiling them,
and pounding garlic and chives to eat with them,
believing there was no greater pleasure.
One day, rowing his fishing boat,
just as he was beating the oar and singing loudly into the river,
after traveling several li,
he suddenly saw a colorfully painted pleasure boat
drifting in midstream.
There were seven Daoist priests aboard,
all young,
wearing jade crowns and rosy capes,
their robes each of different colors.
They had over ten attendants,
with hair tied in topknots or coiled in clouds.
Also, four men in yellow robes
were aboard the boat.
One called Wáng Kějiāo by name,
and as he was still astonished,
he unconsciously found his fishing boat already beside the pleasure craft.
One Daoist ordered a topknotted attendant to lead Kějiāo aboard.
Before the seven men,
he saw each had blue jade plates, wine vessels, and fruits,
all luminous and translucent,
which Kějiāo did not recognize.
There were also over ten female musicians,
all holding instruments.
Kějiāo stood at a distance at the end of the banquet mat
and bowed all around.
The seven men looked at Kějiāo together,
and one said:
"Good bone structure,
fit for immortality,
but born among the lowly—
the space between his eyebrows has already been moxibusted."
Another said:
"Give him wine to drink."
An attendant poured wine,
but though he tried repeatedly, the wine in the vessel would not come out.
The attendant reported this in full.
The Daoist said:
"Wine is a spiritual substance;
it must enter the mouth
to transform his bones.
That it will not pour out
is also fate."
Another said:
"Give him chestnuts to eat."
Presently, one took two chestnuts from the banquet
and gave them to an attendant to hand to Kějiāo,
ordering him to eat them at once.
Looking at them,
the chestnuts were bluish-red,
shining like dates,
about two cun long.
Biting into them, they had skin,
unlike chestnuts of the mortal world;
the flesh was crisp and sweet as malt sugar.
After a long time, he finished eating them.
One said:
"Wáng Kějiāo has been seen;
he may be sent away."
He ordered a yellow-robed attendant to escort him ashore.
By the boat's side, he searched for his fishing boat but could not see it.
The yellow-robed man said:
"No need for the fishing boat;
just close your eyes and you will arrive."
So he closed his eyes,
and heard sounds like wind, water, trees, and forests rushing past.
Told to open his eyes,
he had arrived,
and the yellow-robed man was gone.
He saw only layered peaks,
pine and cypress reaching to the sky,
and sat on a stone in the grass.
Looking further, he saw a gate tower
with people coming and going.
Presently, over ten woodcutters and monks arrived,
asking Kějiāo who he was.
Kějiāo recounted the previous events in full.
They asked what day he had left home,
and Kějiāo said:
"I left home early today."
They asked what day it was today,
and he replied it was the third day of the third month.
The woodcutters and monks were astonished:
"Today is the ninth day of the ninth month;
it has been over half a year since the third day of the third month."
Kějiāo asked what place this was,
and a monk said:
"This is before the Pùbù Temple on Tiāntāi Mountain."
He asked how far it was from here to Huátíng,
and the monk said:
"Over a thousand li by land and water."
Kějiāo marveled endlessly.
Then the monks invited him back to the temple,
set out food,
but Kějiāo only said he was full,
disliked the smell of food,
and drank only water.
The monks questioned him carefully,
found it extremely strange,
and reported the circumstances to Tángxīng County,
which relayed it to Táizhōu,
and so it was made known.
The Surveillance Commissioner of Yuèzhōu, Wáng Fán, who long revered the Dao,
summoned him for an audience,
and considered it an extraordinary event,
the transformations of immortals being unfathomable.
Kějiāo was over seven chǐ tall,
with exceptional bearing and appearance,
and clear, refreshing speech.
Fán sighed:
"This is truly an immortal."
Also, as they shared the same surname,
he respected him even more,
and adorned him in Daoist robes.
He sent someone to Sūzhōu
to verify the facts.
It was fully stated that on the third day of the third month,
Kějiāo had taken his fishing boat into the river and not returned.
His family found the fishing boat,
thought he had fallen into the river and died,
dragged the river but found no trace,
and his wife and children held a soul-summoning burial.
Wáng Fán fully reported this to the court,
and the imperial decree expressed great wonder.
Later, Kějiāo returned to his hometown,
recounting everything clearly in detail.
With villagers, he went to the river,
pointing to where he had encountered the pleasure boat—it remained unchanged.
After eating the chestnuts,
Kějiāo had ceased eating grains,
and his movements seemed divinely aided.
He no longer farmed or fished,
but took his wife and children to Sìmíng Mountain.
After over twenty years,
he reappeared in Míngzhōu selling medicine,
had people buy wine,
and any money he received he simply gave to others.
He sometimes said the medicine was bestowed by Hú Gōng,
and the wine by the Ā Mǔ of Yúháng.
It was passed down that the medicine was extremely effective against illness,
and the wine very intoxicating.
In the lanes of Míngzhōu,
people all spoke of Immortal Wáng's medicine and wine,
unmatched in the mortal world.
Daoists and laypeople often made images of him,
and those suffering from malaria or evil spirits
would recover if an image was placed beside them.
After over thirty more years,
he reentered Sìmíng Mountain
and did not emerge again,
though people still sometimes see him.
From "Continued Biographies of Immortals."
Yáng Tōngyōu,
originally named Shíwǔ,
was a native of Shífāng in Guǎnghàn.
In his youth, he encountered a Daoist priest
who taught him the art of summoning through written proclamations.
He received the Three Sovereigns' celestial texts,
and could command ghosts and spirits,
with immediate response every time.
Expelling pestilence and epidemics,
eliminating baleful and evil vapors,
averting floods and droughts,
and summoning wind and rain—
he was capable of all these.
Yet he was simple, reticent, aloof, and proud,
unconstrained by common customs.
His arts involved numerous transformations and anomalies,
earning him renown far and wide.
When Emperor Xuánzōng fled to Shǔ,
after the events at Mǎwéi,
he was constantly preoccupied with thoughts of the Guìfēi,
often neglecting food and sleep.
His close attendant ministers
secretly ordered the search for and summoning of masters of esoteric arts,
hoping to slightly ease the emperor's troubled mind.
Someone said:
"Yáng Shíwǔ possesses the method of interrogation and summoning."
He was summoned to the traveling court.
The emperor inquired about his abilities,
and he replied:
"Even between heaven and earth,
within the dark and silent depths,
and among ghosts and spirits,
I can traverse and search for her."
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and set up an altar within the palace
for him to perform his arts.
That evening he reported:
"I have already searched extensively
within the Ninefold Earth below,
and among the ghosts and spirits,
but do not know her whereabouts."
The emperor said:
"The consort surely has not fallen among the ranks of ghosts and spirits."
On the second night,
he again reported:
"Between the Ninefold Heavens above,
among the stars, sun, and moon,
