and within the vast, distant void,
I have also searched everywhere but do not know her location."
The emperor, quiet and displeased, said:
"If she has not returned to heaven,
then where else has she gone?"
Incense was lit and candles offered in the darkness,
with even greater earnestness and sincerity.
On the third night,
he again reported:
"Within the human realm,
inside the mountain, river, and sacred peak temples,
and among the Ten Continents, Three Islands, rivers, and seas,
I have also searched everywhere,
with no knowledge of her whereabouts.
Later, above the Eastern Sea,
upon the summit of Pénglái,
in the southern palace's western wing,
where a host of immortals dwell,
there is a supreme female immortal named Tàizhēn—
she is the Guìfēi.
She said to Shíwǔ:
'I am a maidservant of the Supreme Elder,
attached to the Palace of Supreme Primacy.
The Sage Emperor is the Perfected One of the Vermilion Palace of the Solar Yang.
By chance, due to past karmic ties and worldly attachments,
his desires were rather heavy.
The Sage Emperor descended to dwell in the world,
and I was banished to the human realm
to serve as his guard.
After another cycle of twelve years,
we shall naturally meet again.
I wish for him to take good care of his sacred body,
and to harbor no further thoughts of longing.'
She then took half each of the gold hairpin and inlaid box bestowed during the Kāiyuán era,
and one jade turtle,
entrusting them as tokens,
saying:
'When the Sage Emperor sees these,
he will naturally awaken to remembrance.'
Having spoken, she wept and parted."
Shíwǔ presented these objects to the emperor,
who shed tears for a long while.
Then he said:
"Master, you ascend to heaven and enter the earth,
penetrating the hidden and reaching the dark,
truly a scholar who has attained the Dao and become an immortal."
He personally wrote and bestowed the name "Tōngyōu" (Penetrating the Hidden),
granted a thousand bolts of silk,
a thousand taels each of gold and silver,
five thousand mǔ of fine farmland,
a purple cloud cape and a white jade tablet,
showing him extraordinary ritual distinction.
During a leisure day, the emperor asked about the Dao he had received.
He replied:
"My master is the Perfected Lord Wáng of Xīchéng, the Qīngchéng Perfected One.
In the past, within the Hòuchéng Mountains,
he taught me the art of summoning and command, saying:
'You may assist and support a ruler of great peace,
and only then will you attain the Way of Ascension.'
He admonished me to guard my vital breath and speak sparingly,
not to gaze recklessly,
to renounce fame and profit,
and to distance myself from clamor and dust.
Then one can transcend the Three Realms
and ascend to the Grand Clarity."
The emperor also asked about ascending to heaven and entering the earth:
through which gate does one go,
and what are the obstructions?
He replied:
"A person who has attained the Dao
enters fire without being burned,
enters water without getting wet,
treads on emptiness as if on solid ground,
and touches the solid as if treading on emptiness.
Even with the thickness of the Ninefold Earth,
the vastness of the great seas,
the distance of the Eight Extremities,
and the immensity of the ten thousand directions,
in response to a thought, in an instant—
what could possibly hinder or detain him?
The phrase "the thickness of the Ninefold Earth" and the following twenty-five characters are supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy.
The reason it is so
is that form and the Dao are united.
The Dao is omnipresent;
in the fineness of a hair's tip,
and in the multitude of the ten thousand things,
the Dao resides in all."
The emperor praised his response.
After residing there for several years,
he ascended the Hòuchéng Mountain,
built a quiet chamber on its summit,
and occasionally returned to his home.
His disciples said that celestial beings repeatedly descended to the quiet chamber.
One morning, he departed together with a host of Perfected Ones.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí" (A Collection of Omitted Biographies of Immortals).
Sūn Sīmiǎo was a native of Huáyuán in Yōngzhōu.
At the age of seven, he began his studies and could recite over a thousand words daily.
By the time he reached adulthood, he was skilled in discussing the doctrines of Zhuāngzǐ, Lǎozǐ, and the various schools of thought, and also had a fondness for Buddhist scriptures.
Dúgū Xìn, the Governor of Luòzhōu, upon meeting him, sighed and said:
"This is a sage-like child, but it is a pity that his capacity is great while his discernment is small, making it difficult to employ him."
During the reign of Emperor Xuān of the Later Zhōu dynasty, Sūn Sīmiǎo, due to the many troubles in the royal court, retreated into seclusion in Tàibái Mountain.
When Suí Wéndì was assisting in governance, he summoned Sūn to serve as a Erudite of the National University, but Sūn pleaded illness and did not take up the post.
He often said to his close associates:
"In fifty years, a sage will emerge, and I will then assist him in saving people."
When Táng Tàizōng ascended the throne, he summoned Sūn to the capital and marveled at how youthful his appearance was.
He said to him:
"Now I know that those who possess the Way are truly worthy of respect. Xiànmén and Guǎngchéng—were they mere empty words?"
He intended to bestow upon him a noble rank, but Sūn firmly declined and did not accept.
In the fourth year of the Táng dynasty's Xiǎnqìng reign period
—the original text had "seventh," emended to "fourth" based on the Ming dynasty manuscript copy
—Emperor Gāozōng summoned him for an audience, appointed him as Grand Master of Remonstrance, but again he firmly declined and did not accept.
In the first year of the Shàngyuán reign period, citing illness, he requested to return home. He was specially granted fine horses and the estate of Princess Póyáng to reside in.
Eminent scholars of the time, such as Sòng Zhīwèn, Mèng Shēn, and Lú Zhàolín, all treated him with the rites of teacher and disciple.

Sūn Sīmiǎo once accompanied the emperor to the Jiǔchéng Palace. Zhàolín fell ill and stayed at Sūn's residence. At that time, there was a large pear tree in the courtyard, and Zhàolín composed a rhapsody about it.
Its preface says:

"In the year Guǐyǒu, I lay ill in the official residence at Guāngdé Ward in Cháng'ān. An elderly resident said it was the estate of Princess Póyáng. The princess died before marrying, so the estate fell into disuse. At that time, there was the retired scholar Sūn Sīmiǎo, whose understanding of the Way encompassed past and present, whose learning exhausted the arts of calculation and divination. In lofty discourse on the True Unity, he was like the ancient Master Zhuāng. In profound penetration of non-duality, he was like the present-day Vimalakīrti. As for calendrical calculations, astronomical measurements, and comprehending the cosmos, he was the equal of Luò Xiàhóng and Master Ānqī. He himself said he was born in the Xīn yǒu year of the Kāihuáng era and was ninety-three years old. Inquiry among the local villagers all said he was several hundred years old. Moreover, when conversing about affairs of the Zhōu and Qí periods, he recounted them vividly as if he had witnessed them himself. Considering this, he was no less than a centenarian. Yet his sight and hearing showed no decline, his spirit and demeanor were vigorous—truly one could call him an ancient, intelligent, broadly learned, and deathless man."

At that time, Zhàolín enjoyed great fame but was afflicted with a severe illness. Lamenting the differences in natural endowments and perplexed by the divergent outcomes of longevity and premature death, he thus asked Sūn Sīmiǎo:
"What is the principle by which a skilled physician cures diseases?"
Sūn replied:

"I have heard that those who are good at speaking about Heaven must seek verification in humans; those who are good at speaking about humans must base themselves on Heaven. Heaven has the four seasons and five phases, cold and heat alternating in succession. In their transformations, they harmonize to become rain, rage to become wind, congeal to become frost and snow, and expand to become rainbows and halos. These are the constant norms of Heaven and Earth. Humans have four limbs and five viscera, waking and sleeping, inhaling and exhaling, circulating to form comings and goings, flowing to become the nutritive and defensive energies, manifesting to become complexion and color, issuing forth to become sound and voice. These are the constant norms of humans. Yang employs the essence, Yin employs the form—this is what Heaven and humans share. When they go astray, blockage generates heat, obstruction generates cold, congealing forms warts and growths, sinking forms abscesses and ulcers, rushing causes panting and exhaustion, depletion causes withering and dryness. It is diagnosed on the face and manifests changes in the body. Extending this to Heaven and Earth, it is likewise. Thus, when the five planets wax and wane, stars lose their proper courses, sun and moon err in their paths, comets and shooting stars streak across—these are the dangerous ailments of Heaven and Earth. Untimely cold and heat—these are the blockages and obstructions of Heaven and Earth. Stones standing upright, earth heaving up—these are the warts and growths of Heaven and Earth. Mountains collapsing, earth sinking—these are the abscesses and ulcers of Heaven and Earth. Rushing winds and violent rains—these are the panting and exhaustion of Heaven and Earth. Untimely rains, rivers and springs drying up—these are the withering and dryness of Heaven and Earth. A skilled physician guides with medicines and minerals, rescues with acupuncture and decoctions; a sage harmonizes with virtue and the Way, assists with governance and administration. Therefore, the body has illnesses that can be cured, and Heaven and Earth have disasters that can be dispelled."
He also said:

"One's courage should be great, but one's mind should be cautious; one's wisdom should be round, but one's conduct should be square. The *Book of Songs* says: 'As if standing on the edge of an abyss, as if treading on thin ice'—this refers to caution. 'Valiant warriors, bulwark of the lords'—this refers to great courage. 'Not turning aside for profit, not feeling shame in the face of righteousness'—this is the squareness of conduct. 'Seize the opportunity and act, do not wait all day'—this is the roundness of wisdom."
His literary talent was outstanding as described. His mastery of the Way and arts was too numerous to record in full.

Initially, when Wèi Zhēng and others received the imperial order to compile the histories of the five dynasties—Qí, Liáng, Zhōu, Suí, etc.—fearing omissions, they repeatedly consulted Sūn Sīmiǎo, who transmitted information orally as if he had witnessed it himself.
Sūn Chùyuē, Vice Minister of the Eastern Bureau, once brought his five sons—Tǐng, Jǐng, Jùn, Yòu, and Quán—to visit Sūn Sīmiǎo. Sūn Sīmiǎo said:
"Jùn will achieve nobility first; Yòu will achieve success later; Quán will hold the most important position, but disaster lies in wielding military power." Later events all matched his words.
Lú Qíqīng, Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent, from his youth inquired of Sūn Sīmiǎo about matters of human relationships. Sūn Sīmiǎo said:

"Fifty years from now, you will attain the position of a Regional Governor. My grandson will be your subordinate official—you can protect him." Later, Qíqīng became the Prefect of Xúzhōu, and Sūn Sīmiǎo's grandson, Pǔ, indeed became the Assistant Magistrate of Xiāo County in Xúzhōu. When Sīmiǎo first spoke to Qíqīng, Pǔ had not yet been born, yet he foreknew this event.
All such extraordinary feats were mostly like this.
He died in the first year of the Yǒngchún reign period.

His will ordered simple burial, with no burial objects interred and no live sacrificial animals offered. After over a month, his facial appearance remained unchanged. When lifting the corpse into the coffin, there were only empty clothes—people of the time found this remarkable.
He personally annotated the Lǎo Zǐ and Zhuāng Zǐ.
He authored the Qiān Jīn Fāng in thirty scrolls, the Fú Lù Lùn in thirty scrolls, the Shè Shēng Zhēn Lù, the Zhěn Zhōng Sù Shū, and the Huì Sān Jiào Lùn,
each in one scroll.
During the Kāiyuán era,
someone again saw him living in seclusion on Zhōngnán Mountain,
where he associated with the Vinaya Master Xuān,
often visiting to inquire about essential doctrines.
At that time, there was a great drought.
A monk from the Western Regions requested to build an altar at Kūnmíng Pond to pray for rain.
An imperial edict ordered the relevant officials to prepare incense and lamps.
After seven days in total,
the water had receded several feet,
when suddenly an old man came at night to seek help from Vinaya Master Xuān, saying:
"I am the disciple, the dragon of Kūnmíng Pond.
It has been a long time without rain,
but it is not due to this disciple.
The foreign monk covets this disciple's brain to use as medicine.
He deceives the Son of Heaven by saying he prays for rain,
but my life is in imminent danger.
I beg the Reverend to use his dharma power to save me."
Master Xuān declined, saying:
"This humble monk merely upholds the precepts.
You should seek out Master Sūn."
The old man therefore came to him.
Sīmiǎo said to him:
"I know the dragon palace of Kūnmíng possesses thirty divine prescriptions.
If you can show them to me,
I will save you."
The old man said:
"These prescriptions are not permitted by the Supreme Emperor to be recklessly transmitted.
But now the situation is urgent,
so I certainly will not begrudge them."
After a short while,
he returned holding the prescriptions.
Sīmiǎo said:
"You may just return;
do not worry about the foreign monk."
From then on, the pond water suddenly rose,
overflowing the banks within a few days,
and the foreign monk died of shame and resentment.
Another time, a divine immortal descended
and said to Sīmiǎo:
"The Qiān Jīn Fāng you authored
has already greatly benefited people.
However, by using the lives of creatures as medicine,
you have also harmed many beings.
You will certainly become an immortal through liberation of the corpse,
but you will not be able to ascend lightly in broad daylight.
In the past, the Perfected Being Huán Kuǎi said the same to Táo Zhēnbái;
the matter was also like this,
as you surely know."
Afterwards, Sīmiǎo used herbs and plants as medicine
to replace the lives of gadflies and leeches,
and composed the Qiān Jīn Fāng Yì in thirty chapters.
Each chapter contained one prescription from the Dragon Palace,
which circulated in the world.
When Emperor Xuánzōng fled the rebellion of the Jié barbarians,
he traveled west to Shǔ.
After arriving in Shǔ,
he dreamed of an old man with completely white beard and temples,
wearing a yellow short jacket,
who bowed twice before him
and then addressed him, saying:
"Your subject is Sūn Sīmiǎo.
I have dwelt in a hut on Éméi Mountain for many years.
Now, hearing the imperial carriage has come to Chéngdū,
I have therefore come to pay my respects."
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"I have long been familiar with your name, Master.
Now that you have come from afar,
do you perhaps have some request?"
Sīmiǎo replied:
"Your subject lives in seclusion among clouds and springs,
and enjoys taking mineral medicines.
I have heard this region produces realgar.
I wish to be granted eighty liǎng of it.
If my request is granted,
I would be fortunate if an envoy could be sent to deliver it to Éméi Mountain."
Emperor Xuánzōng agreed,
and awoke with a start.
He immediately issued an edict ordering the court official Chén Zhōngshèng to take eighty liǎng of realgar
and go to Éméi to bestow it upon Sīmiǎo.
After receiving the edict,
Zhōngshèng entered Éméi
and reached Píngfēng Ridge,
where he saw an old man of exceptionally distinguished and ancient appearance,
wearing a yellow short jacket,
standing at the foot of the ridge.
He said to Zhōngshèng:
"Are you not the Son of Heaven's envoy?
I am Sūn Sīmiǎo."
Zhōngshèng said:
"His Majesty has ordered realgar to be bestowed upon you, Master."
The old man bowed and received it.
Then he said:
"I have received the Son of Heaven's gift of realgar.
Now I have a memorial of thanks,
but living in the mountains, I lack writing materials.
May the imperial envoy use his brush and paper to copy it for presentation?"
Zhōngshèng immediately summoned a clerk to hold the tablet and dip the brush.
The old man pointed to a rock and said:
"The original memorial is on that stone.
You may copy it from there."
Zhōngshèng looked at the rock;
indeed, there were over a hundred vermilion characters,
which were indeed the original memorial.
He then transcribed the characters.
When the copying was finished,
he looked for the old man and the rock,
but both had vanished without a trace.
He then fully reported the matter to Emperor Xuánzōng.
Emperor Xuánzōng asked Zhōngshèng,
and the old man's appearance indeed matched the one in his dream,
which made him regard Sīmiǎo as even more extraordinary.
From then on, he sometimes appeared and sometimes remained hidden.
At the end of the Xiántōng era,
in a household at the mountain's foot,
there was a boy over ten years old
who did not eat meat or blood.
His parents, considering him fond of goodness,
sent him to serve as an acolyte at the Báishuǐ Monastery.
Suddenly, a traveling visitor who called himself Recluse Sūn
toured the monastery grounds and, upon finishing,
took some medicinal powder from his sleeve and gave it to the acolyte,
saying:
"Prepare this for me according to the tea method."
The recluse sipped a little
and gave the remaining decoction to the boy.
The boy found the decoction extremely delicious
and asked to be granted a bowl.
The recluse said:
"This decoction was prepared for you."
He then gave him a square-inch spoonful of the powder
and had him prepare and drink it.
The boy went to tell his companions about it,
but when he went out the door,
the recluse had already left.
The acolyte also flew up into the sky,
to everyone's astonishment.
Looking back at the pot used to decoct the medicine,
they saw it had turned to gold.
Afterwards, people still occasionally saw Sīmiǎo.
From the Xiān Zhuàn Shí Yí and the Xuān Shì Zhì.
Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn,
courtesy name Zǐwēi.
He was erudite and skilled in writing,
excelling in seal script,
which was uniquely his own style,
known as the "Golden Scissors Calligraphy."
He lived in seclusion at Yùxiāo Peak of Tiāntāi Mountain,
calling himself Báiyúnzǐ.
He possessed techniques for taking elixirs,
and despite repeated summons by Empress Wǔ Zétiān, he did not respond.
Emperor Ruìzōng greatly revered Daoism,
and after repeatedly honoring him with distinctions,
Chéngzhēn finally accepted the summons.
Emperor Ruìzōng asked him about the arts of yīn-yáng and numerology.
Chéngzhēn replied:
"The Classic of Lǎozǐ says:
'Diminish it again and again,
until you reach non-action.'
Moreover, what the mind and eyes perceive and know,
even after repeated diminishment, cannot be fully eliminated;
how could one then engage in heterodox studies to increase intellectual worries?"
Emperor Ruìzōng said:
"Governing the self through non-action
leads to purity and loftiness;
but how about governing the state through non-action?"
How would that be?"
He replied:
"The state is like the body.
Lǎozǐ said:
'Focus the mind on tranquility,
blend the vital breath with stillness,
follow the natural course of things,
then there will be no selfishness,
and the world will be governed.'
The Yìjīng says:
'The sage aligns his virtue with heaven and earth.'
Thus, it is known that heaven does not speak yet is trusted,
and through non-action, accomplishments are achieved.
The essence of non-action
is the key to governing the state."
Emperor Ruìzōng deeply admired his exceptional views,
and wished to keep him and grant him a high position.
Chéngzhēn firmly declined.
Soon after, he requested to return to the mountains.
The emperor then bestowed upon him a precious qin and an embroidered cape as farewell gifts.
Many high officials composed poems to see him off.
The Regular Attendant Xú Yànbó,
selected over thirty of the finest poems,
composed a preface for them,
and titled the collection "Records of White Clouds,"
which has been passed down through the ages.
At that time, Lú Cángyòng had earlier lived in seclusion on Zhōngnán Mountain,
but later entered court service,
holding important official positions.
Seeing Chéngzhēn about to return to Tiāntāi,
Cángyòng pointed to Zhōngnán and said to him:
"There are many excellent places here;
why must you go to Tiāntāi?"
Chéngzhēn calmly replied:
"From what I observe,
this is merely a shortcut to an official career."
Cángyòng showed a look of shame.
When Emperor Xuánzōng ruled the empire,
he deeply favored Daoist arts,
and repeatedly summoned Chéngzhēn to the capital,
keeping him in the inner palace,
showing him great respect and courtesy,
and inquiring about methods for prolonging life and transcending the world.
Chéngzhēn spoke subtly and cryptically.
Emperor Xuánzōng also received and kept these teachings secret,
so no one else could learn of them.
Thus, Emperor Xuánzōng ruled the state for over forty years,
and even when Ān Lùshān breached the passes,
and the imperial carriage fled to Shǔ,
and after becoming the Retired Emperor,
he returned,
and lived another seven years,
before finally passing away.
This was truly due to heavenly fate,
but was it not also aided by the power of the Dao prolonging his life?!
Earlier, when Emperor Xuánzōng returned from performing the fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài,
he asked Chéngzhēn:
"What deities preside over the Five Sacred Mountains?"
Chéngzhēn replied:
"The Sacred Mountains are the greatest of mountains,
capable of producing clouds and rain,
and harboring hidden immortals and transcendents.
They are revered by the state;
however, they are spirits of the forests and mountains,
and there are also immortal officials who preside over them."
Thereupon, an edict was issued to establish temples for immortal officials atop the peaks of the Five Sacred Mountains,
beginning with Chéngzhēn's suggestion.
Also, a female Daoist from Shǔ, Xiè Zìrán, sailed across the sea,
intending to go to Pénglái to seek a teacher.
Her boat was blown off course by the wind,
and she arrived at a mountain,
where she saw a Daoist who pointed and said:
"Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn of Tiāntāi Mountain,
his name is recorded in the Cinnabar Terrace,
and he resides at Chìchéng;
he is a true and excellent teacher."
Pénglái is separated by three hundred thousand lǐ of the Ruò River,
which cannot be crossed by boat,
and none but flying immortals can reach it.
Zìrán then returned to seek Chéngzhēn to receive initiation.
Later, she ascended to heaven in broad daylight and departed.
Chéngzhēn lived in the mountains,
cultivating himself diligently and arduously.
Over a hundred years old,
he retained a youthful appearance and was agile and healthy,
like a man around thirty.
He had over seventy disciples.
One day, he told his disciples:
"Since I have lived on Yùxiāo Peak,
looking east toward Pénglái,
true spirits have often descended.
Now I am summoned by the Azure Lad Lord of the Eastern Sea and the Lord of Dōnghuá,
and I must depart from the human world."
Shortly after, his breath ceased,
as if he had shed his mortal form like a cicada and transformed.
His disciples buried only his clothes and cap.
Originally, the source was not noted.
It is found in "New Tales of the Great Táng."
When Li Gōng, the late Minister of the Táng dynasty, was stationed at the northern gate,
the character "shēn" was originally missing.
According to the Míng manuscript copy, it has been added.
there was a Dàoshi named Yǐn Jūn
who lived in seclusion on Jìn Mountain.
He did not eat grains,
often consuming cypress leaves instead.
Although his hair had turned completely white,
his appearance was like that of a youth.
He often wandered alone through the city markets.
Among the villagers was an old man over eighty years old,
who turned and said to others:
"When I was a child,
I once heard Elder Lǐ say—
Elder Lǐ was my maternal grandfather—
'When I was seven years old,
I already knew Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn.
Now, over seventy years later,
Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn's appearance remains unchanged.
Could he be an immortal?
I am growing old,
and I wonder how much longer I can remain among mortals.
You are still in your prime;
you should take note of Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn's appearance.'"
From then until now,
over seventy years have passed,
yet Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn has shown no signs of aging.
Could it be that for him, a thousand years is but an instant?"
Yán Gōngshòu of Féngyì, an official at the northern gate,
was an inquisitive man.
Admiring Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn's attainment of the Dào,
he would drive his carriage to visit him every ten days during his breaks.
Later, Yán Gōng
was originally followed by the character "wéi" here,

was promoted from military aide to commander of the northern gate.
He then invited Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn to his official residence,
housing him in the government quarters.
He spent all day sharing the same mat with him,
and a strange fragrance often emanated from Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn's skin.
Yán Gōng held him in even higher regard.
Yán Gōng had a younger sister who studied Buddhism.
She once said,
"Buddhism and the teachings of Huáng-Lǎo are fundamentally different."
She was also angry that her brother associated with a Dàoshi.
One day later,
she secretly added aconite juice to a broth
and asked Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn to drink it.
Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn drank it
and exclaimed in alarm, rising to his feet:
"Am I going to die?"
Soon after, he vomited something very hard,
from which a strange fragrance emanated.
Yán Gōng ordered it to be cut open and examined;
it was indeed a musk deer's navel.
From then on, Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn's appearance aged, and his teeth fell out.
That evening, he died in his quarters.
When Yán Gōng learned what his younger sister had done,
he was furious.
He immediately ordered his officers to arrange the funeral.
Two days later,
they buried Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn twenty lǐ west of the Fén River.
The following autumn,
a Dàoshi from Zhàoshèng Temple named Zhū Tàixū,
while performing the ritual of casting the dragon at Jìn Mountain,
suddenly encountered Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn in the mountains.
Tàixū asked in surprise,
"Master, why are you here?"
Dàoshi Yǐn Jūn laughed and said,
"Last year at the northern gate,
someone gave me aconite juice to drink.
I pretended to die because of it,
but how could aconite juice harm my true essence?"
After saying this,
he suddenly vanished from sight.
Tàixū secretly found this strange.
Upon returning,
he reported everything in detail to Yán Gōng.
Yán Gōng said,
"I have heard that immortals do not die.
If they appear to die,
it is only a liberation from the corpse.
Otherwise, how could such transformations occur?"
He considered opening the grave to verify this,
but fearing it would cause confusion among people,
he abandoned the idea.
From the "Xuānshì Zhì."
Luó Gōngyuǎn
was originally from Èzhōu.
During the spring banquet hosted by the prefectural governor,
spectators filled the entire commandery.
There was a man in white, over ten feet tall,
with a most unusual appearance,
who arrived following the crowd.
The gate guards all found him strange.
Shortly after, a young boy passed by nearby
and shouted at him:
"Why have you left your proper place,
frightening the officials?
Leave at once!"
The man then gathered his robes and fled.
The guards then seized the young boy and brought him to the banquet site,
reporting everything in detail to the governor.
The governor asked his name.
He replied:
"My surname is Luó,
my given name is Gōngyuǎn.
Since childhood, I have been fond of Daoist arts.
Just now, I saw the river-guarding dragon come ashore to watch,
and I hurriedly ordered it back."
The governor, not believing him, said:
"You must make me see its true form."
He said:
"Please wait until the day after tomorrow."
When the time came,
he dug a small pit by the water's edge,
only one foot deep,
and over ten feet from the bank.
He channeled water into it.
The governor and the commandery's people all watched.
After a short while,
a white fish,
five or six inches long,
came flowing with the current.
Leaping and growing gradually larger,
a thread of blue smoke
rose from the pit.
A moment later,
black qi filled the sky,
making it impossible to see even at close range.
Gōngyuǎn said:
"We can go up to the ferry

pavilion now."
Before they reached it,
lightning flashed and rain poured down like a waterfall,
but it ceased after a short while.
They saw a great white dragon in the middle of the river,
its head touching the clouds,
which vanished after the time it takes to eat a meal.
At that time, Emperor Xuánzōng was deeply fond of immortal arts.
The governor submitted a memorial detailing the event for the emperor.
At the time, Emperor Xuánzōng was playing chess with Zhāng Guǒ and Yè Fǎshàn.
The two men saw the memorial and laughed heartily, saying:
"What does a village boy understand of such matters?"
They then each grasped over a dozen chess pieces in their hands
and asked:
"What is in here?"
He replied:
"Empty hands."
When they opened their hands, indeed there was nothing;
all the pieces were with Gōngyuǎn.
Only then were they greatly astonished.
The emperor ordered him to sit as an equal with Zhāng and Yè.
When a fruit from Jiànnán was first presented,
called the "daily ripening fruit,"
Zhāng and Yè used their arts to fetch it,
and it would always arrive each day after noon.
That day,
even by night it still had not arrived.
They looked at each other and said:
"Could it be because of Master Luó?"
At the time, the weather was cold and they were gathered around a stove.
Gōngyuǎn smiled,
took a chopstick and planted it in the fire,
and when he removed it,
the fruit arrived.
Yè questioned the messenger.
He said that as they were about to reach the capital,
flames blazed across the sky,
blocking the road;
only when the fire subsided
were they able to pass.
From then on, everyone respected and submitted to him.
During the Kāiyuán era,
on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival,
Emperor Xuánzōng was enjoying the moon in the palace.
Gōngyuǎn addressed him, saying:
"Does Your Majesty wish to go to the moon to see it?"
He then took his walking staff
and threw it into the air,
where it transformed into a great bridge,
silver in color.
He invited Emperor Xuánzōng to ascend it with him.
After traveling several dozen lǐ,
a brilliant light dazzled the eyes,
and a cold aura assailed them.
They then arrived at a great city gate.
Gōngyuǎn said:
"This is the Moon Palace."
They saw several hundred fairy maidens,
all dressed in plain, wide-sleeved robes,
dancing in a vast courtyard.
Emperor Xuánzōng asked:
"What melody is this?"
He replied:
"The 'Rainbow and Feather Garments' dance."
Emperor Xuánzōng secretly memorized the tune,
and then they returned.
Looking back at the bridge,
it vanished step by step behind them.
He then summoned the court musicians
to compose the "Rainbow and Feather Garments" melody according to the tune he remembered.
At that time, Consort Wǔ Huì particularly believed in the Vajra Tripiṭaka Master.
When Emperor Xuánzōng visited the Merit Monastery,
he suddenly suffered from an unbearable itch on his back.
Gōngyuǎn broke off a bamboo branch,
transforming it into a Seven-Treasure Ruyi scepter to present to him.
Emperor Xuánzōng was greatly pleased
and, looking at the Tripiṭaka Master, said:
"Can the Venerable One produce something like this?"
He replied:
"This is mere illusion.
Your servant will fetch the real thing for Your Majesty."
He then took out a Seven-Treasure Ruyi scepter from his sleeve and presented it.
The one presented by Gōngyuǎn
immediately transformed back into a bamboo branch.
Later, when Emperor Xuánzōng traveled to the Eastern Capital Luòyáng,
Consort Wǔ accompanied him.
While at the Línzhǐ Hall of the Shàngyáng Palace,
just as they were about to renovate the hall,
there was a large square beam several zhàng long
and six or seven chǐ in diameter in the courtyard.
At the time, Gōngyuǎn, Master Yè, and the Vajra Tripiṭaka Master were all in attendance.
Emperor Xuánzōng said to Master Yè:
"I am feeling somewhat bored.
Could you demonstrate a minor art for amusement?
Master, please try to lift this square timber for me."
Yè received the command and performed his art.
One end of the timber rose several chǐ,
but the other end would not lift.
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"Master's divine power—
why has it failed?"
Yè said:
"The Tripiṭaka Master has commanded the Vajra Good Deity
to press down on one end,
so it cannot be lifted."
At that time, Emperor Xuánzōng revered Daoism,
while Consort Wǔ followed Buddhism.
Consort Wǔ showed considerable pleasure on her face,
and the Tripiṭaka Master also secretly felt pleased in his heart.
Only Gōngyuǎn lowered his head with a slight smile.
Emperor Xuánzōng said to the Tripiṭaka Master:
"Master's divine incantation is effective;
Yè cannot match it.
Can you chant an incantation for me to make Fǎshàn enter a water bottle?"
The Tripiṭaka Master received the command and set out a bottle.
He had Fǎshàn sit on a mat,
then chanted the Great Buddha's Crown True Words incantation.
Before he finished the first recitation,
Yè's body suddenly began moving toward the bottle;
before two or three recitations,
Yè was lifted to the bottle's mouth;
when the recitation was completed,
he vanished into the bottle.
Emperor Xuánzōng was displeased.
After a long while, he said to the Tripiṭaka Master:
"Master's power
should grant you free mastery.
Since you have made him enter,
can you make him come out?"
The Tripiṭaka Master said:
"This is the basic method of this monk."
He then chanted the incantation.
After reciting the Buddha's Crown True Words several times,
Yè still did not emerge.
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"My Dharma Master
has now been enchanted by the Tripiṭaka Master and has vanished;
I cannot see him anymore."
Consort Wǔ lost color in her face.
The Tripiṭaka Master was greatly frightened.
Emperor Xuánzōng said to Gōngyuǎn:
"What can be done to make Fǎshàn return?"
Gōngyuǎn smiled and said:
"Fǎshàn is not far away."
After a long while,
Gāo Lìshì reported:
"Master Yè has entered."
Emperor Xuánzōng exclaimed in great surprise:
"The bronze bottle is here—
from where did you come?"
He was brought in and questioned.
He replied:
"Prince Nìng invited me to dine,
and I was not allowed to decline in person.
I had just finished eating at Prince Nìng's house and came,
if not for a single incantation,
how could I have left?"
Emperor Xuánzōng laughed heartily,
and Consort Wǔ and Sānzàng both offered congratulations.
Soon after, he had Yè perform a magical ritual.
Thereupon, he took Sānzàng's gold-brocade kasaya and folded it,
covering it with a basin.
Yè performed the Yǔ steps, clicked his teeth,
circled it three times, and said:
"May the Supreme Lord Lǎo take it away."
The threads of the kasaya under the basin,
according to their colors, were all drawn away,
each forming a separate pile.
Sānzàng said:
"Alas, the gold-brocade,
to be destroyed like this!"
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"Can it be restored?"
Yè said:
"It can."
He covered it again,
and incanted:
"May the Supreme Lord Lǎo restore it."
When he opened it,
the kasaya was as before.
Yè then took Sānzàng's alms bowl,
heated it until glowing red,
and holding it in his hands, placed it on Sānzàng's head.
Sānzàng cried out and fled.
Emperor Xuánzōng laughed heartily.
Gōng Yuǎn said:
"Your Majesty finds this amusing,
but it is merely the lesser art of the Way.
Why must Master Yè show off like this?"
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"Can you not perform a single feat for me to bring me joy?"
Gōng Yuǎn said:
"May I ask instead how Sānzàng's magical arts compare?"
Sānzàng said:
"This humble monk requests to securely store the kasaya,
and have Luó Gōng try to take it.
If he cannot take it, then Luó Gōng loses;
if he can take it, then the monk loses."
Thereupon, they ordered it to be done in the ritual courtyard.
Sānzàng set up an altar, burned incense,
and sat cross-legged on the altar performing his method.
He took the kasaya and stored it in a silver box;
then placed it inside several layers of wooden cases,
all sealed and locked,
and set it on the altar.
Emperor Xuánzōng, Consort Wǔ, and Master Yè
all saw that inside there was one layer of Bodhisattvas,
outside them a layer of golden-armored deities,
and outside that a layer of Vajra beings surrounding them,
sages and worthies standing shoulder to shoulder,
forming a very strict encirclement.
Sānzàng watched over it,
not taking his eyes off it for a moment.
Gōng Yuǎn sat on a rope-bed,
talking and laughing as usual.
Emperor Xuánzōng and Master Yè both watched him.
After the time it takes to eat several meals,
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"Why is it taking so long?
Are you not exhausted?"
Gōng Yuǎn said:
"I am contending in power;
how dare I boast of my own ability?
It is only up to Your Majesty to have Sānzàng open it and look."
He ordered the cases opened to retrieve the kasaya.
Although the seals and locks remained intact,
the inside was already empty.
Emperor Xuánzōng laughed heartily.
Gōng Yuǎn reported:
"Please order someone to go to my courtyard,
and command my disciple
(the character 'zǐ' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy)
to open the cabinet and bring it."
He immediately ordered a palace envoy to fetch it,
and in a moment, the kasaya arrived.
Emperor Xuánzōng asked him about it.
Gōng Yuǎn said:
"The power of Bodhisattvas and divine warriors,
are among the holy ones;
armored soldiers and various deities,
are minor figures of the Way.
All can achieve merit in the upper realms;
but as for the supreme and true marvel of the Supreme Ultimate,
it is not something practitioners of arts can know.
I just had a Jade Purity goddess fetch it;
then the Bodhisattvas and Vajra beings did not see her form.
Taking it was like a smooth road;
what obstruction could there be?"
Emperor Xuánzōng was greatly pleased.
He bestowed countless rewards.
And only then did Master Yè and Sānzàng submit.
At that time, Emperor Xuánzōng wished to learn the art of concealment and withdrawal.
Gōng Yuǎn replied:
"Your Majesty's jade writings and golden records
are already recorded in the Nine Purities;
a true person has descended and transformed,
to protect the state and bring peace to the people.
Truly, you should practice the non-action of Táng and Yú,
and continue the frugality of Wén and Jǐng.
Set aside precious swords and do not wield them,
abandon famous horses and do not ride them.
How can the dignity of the Son of Heaven,
the nobility of the four seas,
the gravity of the ancestral temples,
the greatness of the altars of soil and grain,
be lightly pursued with minor arts,
as matters of play and amusement?
If I exhaust my arts for you,
you will certainly end up hiding the imperial seal in another's house,
trapped like a fish out of water."
Emperor Xuánzōng grew angry,
and cursed him.
Gōng Yuǎn then walked into a palace pillar,
and enumerated Emperor Xuánzōng's faults.
Emperor Xuánzōng grew even angrier,
had the pillar changed and broken,
but he entered again into a jade pedestal.
He changed the pedestal again.
Breaking it into several tens of pieces,
each piece bore Gōng Yuǎn's form.
Emperor Xuánzōng apologized to him,
and he returned to his original state.
Emperor Xuánzōng later insisted on learning the art of invisibility,
and pressed him relentlessly.
Thus, he taught him.
However, when concealing his body,
he often could not do it completely:
sometimes his robe or belt would be exposed,
or his shadow or traces would be seen.
Emperor Xuánzōng angrily beheaded him.
Several years later,
the palace envoy Fǔ Xiānyù,
on a mission to Shǔ,
saw Gōng Yuǎn on the road in Hēishuǐ,
wearing a cloud-and-mist patched robe and cape,
walking slowly with a staff.
Xiānyù urged his horse to chase him,
but he was always over ten paces away,
and ultimately could not catch up.
Xiānyù called out:
"Heavenly Master, you find contentment in clouds and waters,
but do you not remember our acquaintance in the inner palace?"
Gōng Yuǎn then stopped and looked back at him.
Xiānyù dismounted, bowed, and paid his respects,
then followed him for several miles.
By the official road, overlooking a long stream,
there was a large rock nearby.
They crossed the stream together and sat on the rock.
He said to Xiānyù:
"I dwell among forests and springs,
devoting myself to cultivating truth.
Since the Xiánhé era of the Jìn dynasty, I entered Shǔ,
seeking teachers among the various mountains,
long obscuring my name and traces.
Hearing that the Son of Heaven loved the Way and revered the Mysterious,
I left behind the joy of misty vistas and unfettered freedom,
braved the dusty world's foul and rank roads,
mingled among flocks of chickens and ducks,
and observed the realm of ephemeral mayflies,
not considering it wearisome,
all because I wished to use the nobility of the supreme Way
to condescend to instruct the ruler.
The sage emperor received me in a separate hall,
but hastily sought elixirs from me.
I told him that the organs of a mortal body,
filled with meat and blood,
the three fields not yet empty,
the six breaths not yet purified,
requested that he wait for another day to receive them,
setting a limit of ten years.
He could not keep this admonition and agreement,
and inflicted upon me the punishment of a cinnabar neck.
How hasty and rash!
However, one who has attained the Way,
merged with the breath of the Way,
how can worldly weapons, water, or fire harm me?
But I consider that the sovereign is listed in the register of cinnabar blossoms,
and has old ties of friendship in the Jade Capital.
I personally wish to deliver him,
this feeling of concern,
cannot be stopped."
Then he took out a letter from his sleeve,
and said to Xiānyù:
"You may present this to the emperor,
saying that my surname is Wéi,
my name is Mǒu Mǒu,
a disciple of Master Jìngzhēn.
The emperor will surely understand."
Having said this, he left,
and also entrusted some Shǔ dāngguī as a gift,
then vanished without a trace.
Xiānyù returned to the capital,
and presented the matter along with the sealed letter he had been entrusted with.
Emperor Xuánzōng read the letter,
and was filled with melancholy and displeasure.
As Xiānyù stepped out,
Gōngyuǎn had already arrived,
and was immediately ushered in for an audience.
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"Why did you change your name, sir?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty once removed my head,
so I changed it accordingly.
Removing the top of the character 'Luó'
leaves 'Wéi';
removing the top of the character 'Gōng'
leaves 'Sì';
removing the top of the character 'Yuǎn'
leaves 'Yuán'."
Emperor Xuánzōng bowed his head in apology,
hoping to be forgiven for his fault.
Gōngyuǎn cheerfully said:
"It was merely a jest.
Those who have attained the Way of Immortality,
even in times of calamitous cycles,
during the inauspicious yang-nine numbers,
when heaven and earth collapse and are destroyed,
cannot be harmed;
how much less could weapons
cause any harm?"
Another day,
Emperor Xuánzōng again inquired about attaining longevity.
He replied:
"The scriptures say,
'My life lies within me,
not dependent on others.'
One must first seek within before gaining from without.
To hollow out the heart and extinguish wisdom,
wear grass garments and eat plain food—
this is not something the Most Honored One can achieve."
Thereupon, he presented eight songs of the Three Peaks,
whose main themes were the practices of Xuánsù and Huángchì,
and the methods of returning to infancy and reversing the flow.
Emperor Xuánzōng practiced them for over a year,
and his spirit became transcendent, his energy flourished,
his years advanced,
yet his vitality did not wane.
A little over a year later,
Gōngyuǎn departed,
and none knew where he went.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
when Emperor Xuánzōng fled to Shǔ,
Gōngyuǎn again welcomed the imperial carriage at Jiànmén,
escorted it to Chéngdū,
then brushed off his sleeves and left.
It was only after Emperor Xuánzōng returned to the capital from Shǔ
that he understood the meaning of the "Shǔ Dāngguī" (Sichuan angelica) entrusted to him.
From the "Shénxiān Gǎnyù Zhuàn," "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí," "Yì Shǐ," and other texts.
Mr. Púpú,
it is unknown from whence he came.
He himself said his surname was Pú and his given name was Pú,
but no one knew his origins.
He lived at Huángtǔ Mountain in Lè'ān County, Guāngzhōu,
for over thirty years in total.
He devoted himself to refining and ingesting Apricot Elixir,
and his clothing, food, and drink were like those of ordinary people,
making his living by selling medicine.
In the third year of the Kāiyuán era,
the former magistrate of Wúdì County, Wáng Tāo, was residing at the foot of Huángtǔ Mountain,
when Mr. Púpú visited him.
Tāo ordered his son, Biàn, to act as host
and treat him well.
Mr. Púpú thus taught him the art of the Apricot Elixir.
At that time, Biàn's maternal uncle, Wú Míngguī, was the Deputy Prefect of Guāngzhōu,
and Biàn was staying at Guī's residence.
Shortly after,
Mr. Púpú rode a cloud and crossed over,
seen by tens of thousands of officials and commoners.
Biàn then looked up and pleaded:
"Sir, you have taught me the art of the elixir, but it is not yet complete.
How can you abandon me and leave?"
At that time, Mr. Púpú had already ridden the cloud and crossed over
fifteen times,
and no one could fathom it;
when Biàn spoke to him,
all the onlookers were astonished.
Someone reported this to Prefect Lǐ Xiūguāng.
Xiūguāng summoned Míngguī and interrogated him, saying:
"Your nephew has befriended a sorcerer;
you should arrest him."
His uncle thus ordered Biàn to go and summon him.
When Biàn arrived at the residence, Mr. Púpú appeared,
and Biàn fully reported the situation.
Mr. Púpú said:
"I am a man of the Way,
and I do not wish to meet with officials."
Biàn said:
"If they show proper courtesy,
you should then transform them;
if they act recklessly and lose propriety,
you should awe them,
making their hearts submit to the Way.
Would that not be acceptable?"
Mr. Púpú said:
"Good."
He then went to Xiūguāng's official residence.
Xiūguāng sat arrogantly to receive him
and berated him, saying:
"If you are an immortal, you should have gone away for good;
now you leave and return again—
you are a sorcerer."
Mr. Púpú said:
"Mágū, Cài Jīng, Wáng Fāngpíng, Kǒng Shēn, the two Máos, and others like them
inquired about the Way from me.
I had not finished explaining it to them,
so I stayed.
It is nothing else."
Xiūguāng grew even angrier
and shouted for his attendants to seize him.
Dragons and tigers appeared at his side,
and Mr. Púpú mounted them and departed,
rising more than ten feet above the ground.
Dark clouds gathered from all sides,
and in a moment, thunder and lightning arrived with great force,
shattering more than ten locust trees in the courtyard
and shaking the official residence until it collapsed.
All the onlookers fled in panic.
Xiūguāng, terrified, ran away,
losing his headscarf.
A clerk retrieved the headscarf.
Xiūguāng led his wife and children, barefoot, out of the residence
and subsequently moved his dwelling.
Xiūguāng reported the incident in a memorial.
Emperor Xuánzōng then issued an edict changing Lè'ān County to Xiānjū County,
establishing the Xiāntáng Abbey at the residence where Mr. Púpú had lived,
renaming Huángtǔ Village as Xiāntáng Village,
with County Lieutenant Yán Zhènghuì overseeing the construction.
Wáng Biàn was ordained as the abbot of the abbey,
concurrently appointed as Reminding Advisor,
and given the title Master Tōngzhēn.
Biàn, by ingesting the Apricot Elixir, reversed aging.
By the fourteenth year of the Dàlì era,
he was sixty-six years old in total,
yet his appearance was like that of a man just over forty,
and his physical strength matched it.
Later, a woman from Guǒzhōu, Xiè Zìrán,
ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
When Zìrán was studying the Way,
immortals frequently descended.
There was one surnamed Cuī,
who also said his name was Cuī;
there was one surnamed Dù,
who also said his name was Dù;
others with various surnames were the same.
This resembles the case of Mr. Púpú's name.
Could it be that when immortals descend to the human world,
they do not wish to have their names known among the customs of the time?
Later, a traveler was walking in the suburbs of Yìyáng.
As dusk fell, he could not reach the next village,
when he suddenly saw a thatched hut by the roadside
and went to seek lodging.
Inside the room was only an old man,
who asked the traveler his purpose.
The traveler replied:
"The sky is overcast, the day is short,
and by the time I reached here, it was dark.
I wish to ask for a night's lodging."
The old man said:
"Staying is no problem,
but there is no food."
After a long while,
the traveler suffered greatly from hunger.
The old man gave him several pills of medicine.
After eating them, he was full.
At dawn, he bid farewell and left.
On his return journey,
he suddenly saw the old man riding a five-colored cloud,
dozens of feet above the ground.
The traveler promptly bowed in reverence,
watching as he gradually went farther away.
The traveler arrived in Ānlù
and told many people about it.
The county officials considered it deluding the masses
and detained and interrogated him.
The traveler said:
"I truly saw an immortal."
Yet he had no way to exonerate himself,
so he prayed to the sky, saying:
"Immortal Lord, why did you appear to me,
that I now suffer this unforeseeable crime?"
As soon as he finished speaking,
a five-colored cloud came from the north.
The old man was sitting within the cloud.
Only then was the traveler released.
The county officials bowed repeatedly.
They asked the old man his surname and given name.
The old man said:
"I am a rustic man, Púpú.
What surname and given name do I have?"
The provincial authorities painted a portrait and reported it to the court.
An imperial order commanded that at the site of the thatched hut,
a temple to Mr. Púpú be established,
which still exists today.
From *Yìwén Jí* and *Guǎngyì Jì*.
Lán Cǎihé,
it is unknown where he was from.
He often wore a tattered blue robe,
with a black wooden belt of six plaques,
over three inches wide.
One foot was shod in a boot,
the other walked barefoot.
In summer, he would add cotton padding inside his robe,
and in winter, he would lie in the snow,
his breath steaming like vapor.
Whenever he wandered through the city singing and begging,
he carried a large clapper,
over three feet long,
and often, while drunk, performed a stepping dance and sang.
Old and young alike would follow and watch him.
Quick-witted and humorous,
when people asked him questions,
he would answer immediately,
causing everyone to laugh uproariously.
He seemed mad, yet not mad.
As he walked, he would shake his boot and sing
("sing" originally written as "speak"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy).
Stepping dance song:
"Stepping dance, Lán Cǎihé,
how long can the world last?
A rosy face is but a spring tree,
fleeting years are like a thrown shuttle.
The ancients, muddled, go and do not return,
today's people, in multitudes, come ever more.
At dawn, riding a phoenix to the azure heavens,
by dusk, seeing green fields turn to white waves.
Long light, bright radiance in the empty sky,
golden and silver palaces, towering high and steep."
His songs were extremely numerous,
mostly conveying immortal sentiments,
which people could not fathom.
He only accepted coins from people,
threading them onto a long rope,
and dragging it along the ground as he walked.
If some coins scattered and were lost,
he would not look back.
If he saw poor people,
he would give the coins to them,
or to taverns.
He roamed throughout the world,
and there were people who had seen him since childhood until their hair turned gray,
yet his appearance remained unchanged.
Later, while performing a stepping dance and singing at a tavern between the Háo River and the bridge,
riding on his drunkenness,
there came the sound of clouds, cranes, sheng pipes, and xiao flutes.
Suddenly, he lightly ascended into the clouds,
throwing down his boot, robe, belt, and clapper,
and drifted away, rising gradually.
From "Xù Shénxiān Zhuàn"
Wáng Yuǎnzhī
The Daoist priest Wáng Yuǎnzhī
was originally from Lángyá.
His father, Wáng Tánxuǎn,
was appointed as the Governor of Yángzhōu.
Wáng Yuǎnzhī's mother
was the daughter of Dīng Chāo, a Director of the Bureau of Equipment.
She often dreamed of colored clouds and divine phoenixes gathering upon her body,
and thus became pregnant.
She also heard sounds from within her womb.
The Buddhist monk Bǎo Gào said to Wáng Tánxuǎn:
"The child born will become a patriarch among immortals."
Wáng Yuǎnzhī was intelligent and keen from a young age,
widely versed in all kinds of books.
Initially, he entered Máo Mountain,
studying under Táo Hóngjǐng as his teacher,
and inherited his Daoist methods.
When Suí Emperor Yáng was the Prince of Jìn,
stationed in Yángzhōu,
he built the Yùqīng Xuántán altar
and invited Wáng Yuǎnzhī to preside over it,
sending Wáng Zǐxiāng and Liǔ Gùyán successively to summon him.
Wáng Yuǎnzhī then came for an audience,
and in a moment, his beard and hair turned white.
The Prince of Jìn, frightened, sent him away,
and shortly after, he returned to his original appearance.
During Táng Emperor Gāozǔ's period of obscurity before ascending the throne,
Wáng Yuǎnzhī secretly presented prophetic signs to him.
In the Wǔdé era,
Qín Prince Lǐ Shìmín and his staff member Fáng Xuánlíng, in plain clothes, went to visit Wáng Yuǎnzhī.
Wáng Yuǎnzhī greeted them and said:
"Among you is a sage;
could it be the Qín Prince?"
Tàizōng then told him the truth.
Wáng Yuǎnzhī said:
"You are about to become a peaceful Son of Heaven;
I hope you will take care of yourself."
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
he intended to confer a high position upon him,
but Wáng Yuǎnzhī firmly requested to return to the mountains.
In the ninth year of the Zhēnguān era,
the Tàipíng Temple was established at Máo Mountain in Rùnzhōu,
and twenty-seven people were ordained as priests,
with an imperial edict issued to console and encourage him.
Later, he said to his disciple Pān Shīzhèng:
"I have seen the register of immortals;
because in my youth I accidentally injured a child's mouth,
I cannot ascend to heaven in broad daylight.
Now I am summoned to become the Earl of Shàoshì Mountain,
and will depart shortly."
The next day,
he bathed, put on his cap and robes,
burned incense, and passed away,
at the age of one hundred and twenty-six.
He was posthumously titled Shēngxuán Xiānshēng.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
The Old Man of Yìzhōu
In the late years of Táng Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
there was an old man in Yìzhōu
who carried a medicine pot and sold medicine in the city.
Whenever he received money, he would immediately use it to aid the poor.
He himself often did not eat,
only drinking pure water from time to time.
This continued for over a year,
and the common people relied on him.
Those who were ill and received his medicine
were all cured without exception.
Sometimes he would wander by the riverbank alone,
gazing intently all day long;
other times he would climb to a high place and crane his neck,
remaining silent the entire day.
Whenever he met someone with understanding,
he would surely tell them:
"A person's body
is like a country.
A person's heart is the emperor,
with the organs arranged beside it
serving as the inner ministers.
The nine orifices opening outward
are the outer officials.
Therefore, if the heart is ill, neither the inner nor outer parts can be saved;
how is this different from a ruler above being in disorder,
and the ministers below being unable to rectify it?
If one wishes the body to be free from illness,
one must first rectify the heart,
not letting it seek chaotically,
not letting it indulge in wild thoughts,
not letting it succumb to cravings and desires,
not letting it be confused and deluded;
then the heart will first be free from illness.
When the heart is first free from illness,
then the inner ministerial organs,
even if ill, will not be difficult to treat;
and the outer nine orifices
will also have no way of falling ill.
Moreover, medicine also has its ruler and ministers,
its assistants and messengers.
If one intends to attack an illness,
the ruler medicine is used first, then the minister medicines,
after which assistants and messengers are employed,
naturally fitting appropriately.
If assistant medicines are used as messengers,
or messenger medicines are used as assistants,
even a slight mismatch in their use
will certainly cause internal disorder,
so how can they attack a person's illness?
This, again, resembles governing a country.
When I use medicine,
I often bear this in mind.
Whenever I encounter a person whose body
has a ruler that does not act as a ruler,
ministers that do not act as ministers,
causing the nine orifices to be filled with pathogenic influences
("pathogenic influences" originally written as "slanting"
changed according to "Shuō Fú" 33),
all harboring illness,
to the extent that even good physicians flee by themselves,
and famous medicines prove ineffective,
yet they still do not realize that treating the body's illness is already too late.
How lamentable!
Gentlemen and scholars, remember this."
Suddenly, one day, he went alone to Jǐnchuān,
removed his clothes, and bathed cleanly.
Reaching into his pot,
he selected only one pill of medicine,
swallowed it himself,
and said to the crowd:
"My sins are now full;
today I shall return to the island."
In a moment, he transformed into a white crane and flew away.
His clothes and medicine pot
both sank into the water,
never to be found again.
From "Xiāo Xiāng Lù"
Cuī Shēng
Jìnshì Cuī Wěi,
once traveled to Qīngchéng Mountain.
He dismounted from his donkey to rest,
but had no servant to tend it.
The donkey ran off,
and he could not catch up.
After traveling about twenty-some lǐ,
he reached a cave entrance.
It was already dark,
and the donkey ran inside.
Cuī Wěi, both frightened and exhausted,
lay down to sleep.
At dawn,
he noticed a faint light inside the cave,
so he entered.
After another ten lǐ,
he exited the cave mouth
and saw grasses, trees, cliffs, and valleys
completely unlike anything in the mortal world.
There was a golden city with crimson towers,
and several hundred armored guards.
Seeing him, they shouted questions.
He replied:
“I am a lowly scholar from the dusty world,
hoping to pay respects to the immortal elder.”
The guards hurried to report,
and after a long while, he was summoned for an audience.
A man sat in a jade hall,
wearing feather robes.
His body was perhaps over ten feet tall,
with hair and beard pure white.
Maidservants filled his sides,
each holding something.
He invited Cuī Wěi up into the hall,
and spoke with him very happily.
He had him stay overnight,
with wine and delicacies of the utmost rarity and abundance.
The next day, he said to Cuī Wěi:
“This is not the mortal world,
but an immortal’s abode.
Your donkey ran quite far,
so I invited you here.
I have only one daughter,
and I wish her to serve you, noble sir.
This too was predestined by fate,
and cannot be avoided.”
Cuī Wěi bowed in thanks.
The immortal looked to his attendants
and ordered them to bring the green case.
He took two pills of medicine
and gave them to Cuī Wěi to take.
Cuī Wěi felt his organs become clear and luminous.
Soon he began to itch and scratch,
and his skin shed like a cicada’s.
Looking in a mirror,
his face was like that of an infant.
That evening,
there were rainbow banners and feathered canopies,
immortal music and ethereal steps,
and he met his wife.
The Perfected Ones in the sky
all teased him as “Cuī-láng.”
Every new moon and full moon,
the immortal elders would ride cranes
to attend court at the Ruǐ Palace.
They said:
“My rank is still low and humble,
yet I am able to be among the ranks of the heavenly immortals.”
He would always bid farewell to Cuī Wěi,
then flutter away within the clouds and Milky Way.
After over a year,
enjoying pleasures and amusements beyond compare,
Cuī Wěi asked:
“I wish to bid farewell to my blood relatives once,
not out of lingering attachment,
but I beg to return briefly.”
The immortal elder said:
“You must not linger,
or the punishment will be severe.”
He gave him one talisman,
saying:
“If you fear encountering calamity,
this can conceal your form;
but be careful not to wander into the imperial palace.”
At parting,
he gave him another talisman, saying:
“Open it only in extreme urgency.”
Then he ordered the donkey he had ridden to be given to him.
Arriving in the capital,
he tried going into people’s houses,
and no one saw him.
So he entered the imperial gardens and the inner palace.
It happened that Jiànnán was presenting brocades for Tàizhēn Fēi’s birthday,
and he stole the finest ones to admire.
The Emperor said:
“In broad daylight, a thief could not possibly get here.”
So he summoned Luó Gōngyuǎn to perform magic.
Holding a vermilion inscription, he illuminated it outside the bedchamber doors.
Sure enough, they caught him,
and he told the whole story.
The Emperor did not believe it,
and ordered him beaten to death.
Suddenly remembering the talisman the immortal elder gave him at parting,
he hurriedly opened it.
Luó Gōngyuǎn and the captors all fell stiff.
After a long while, they could rise,
and Luó Gōngyuǎn immediately reported to Xuánzōng:
“He already belongs to the upper realm.
Killing him certainly will not succeed;
even if we managed it,
we officials would suffer calamity,
and it would not be a blessing for the state.”
Xuánzōng then released him,
personally summoning him to speak:
“Do not recklessly stay here.”
He then ordered a hundred men armed with weapons,
along with guards, to escort him,
and also to observe what happened.
Returning to the cave entrance,
they again saw the golden city with crimson towers.
The immortal elder, with stern attendants,
came out the gate and called:
“Cuī-láng, did you forget my words?
You nearly stumbled into disaster.”
Cuī Wěi bowed and was about to go forward.
The escorts also wanted to follow.
The immortal elder drew a line with his staff, creating a ravine,
several zhàng deep and wide.
He summoned Cuī Wěi’s wife to come,
tossed a scarf across,
and it became a five-colored rainbow bridge.
He sent Cuī Wěi to ascend it,
and as he stepped, it vanished behind him.
Once across,
Cuī Wěi looked back and said:
“Since it is so, you may return.”
In a moment, clouds and mist rose on all sides,
and even at arm’s length, nothing could be seen.
Only the sounds of phoenixes, cranes, reed pipes, and singing were heard,
for half the day before dispersing.
Gazing into the distance,
there was only an empty mountain,
and nothing more to be seen.
From “Yì Shǐ”
Féng Jùn
In the early years of the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man from Guǎnglíng named Féng Jùn,
who made his living as a hired laborer.
He was strong but simple and honest,
so he was easily employed.
He once met a Dàoshi
buying medicine in the market.
The Dàoshi had a bag
weighing over a hundred catties,
and he sought someone who could carry it alone,
promising to pay double the usual rate.
Jùn then offered to do it.
The destination was Liùhé,
and the agreed payment was one thousand coins,
to be collected upon arrival.
Jùn returned home to inform his wife before following the Dàoshi.
The Dàoshi said:
"Follow me,
but we don't have to go directly to Liùhé.
Now I intend to travel there by water.
If you can find a boat, just follow my boat,
and your payment won't be reduced."
Jùn agreed.
They then boarded a small boat,
with Jùn and the Dàoshi traveling together.
After leaving the river mouth for several miles,
the Dàoshi said:
"There's no wind,
we cannot proceed upstream.
I will perform a minor art."
He ordered the two others to lie down in the boat.
The Dàoshi remained alone on deck,
hoisting the sail and holding the oar.
The two in the boat
heard the sound of wind and waves,
and felt as if the boat was flying through the air.
Terrified, they dared not move.
After the time it takes to eat a few meals,
he finally ordered the boat to be opened.
Summoning them out,
they arrived at a place
with a vast, calm lake,
facing overlapping mountain ridges ahead.
Only after a long time did the boatman realize
this was Xīngzǐ Bay at the foot of Lú Mountain on Nán Lake.
The Dàoshi went ashore,
instructing Jùn to carry the medicine.
He then paid the boat fare to the boatman.
The boatman, awed and fearful, refused to accept it.
The Dàoshi said:
"I know you are from Xúnyáng.
I needed to arrive promptly,
so I borrowed your convenience.
How could I refuse payment?"
The boatman then bowed, accepted it, and left—
he was indeed a man from Jiāngzhōu.
The Dàoshi then led Jùn, carrying the medicine,
walking five or six miles among scattered rocks.
As they neared the mountain foot,
there was a large rock several zhang square.
The Dàoshi struck it dozens of times with a small stone,
and the large rock split into two.
A youth emerged from within the rock,
exclaiming joyfully:
"The Venerable Master has returned!"
The Dàoshi then led Jùn into the stone cave.
At first, it was very steep;
descending over ten zhang,
the path gradually widened and leveled;
after proceeding several dozen steps,
the interior became bright and cavernous.
There was a large stone hall,
with several dozen Dàoshi
playing chess and laughing merrily.
Seeing the Dàoshi, they all said:
"Why are you so late?"
They ordered Jùn to set down the medicine,
and instructed attendants to quickly send the visitor back.
The first Dàoshi ordered the attendants:
"The porter is very hungry,
give him some food."
They then served him sesame rice in a porcelain bowl,
and also gave him a bowl of a liquid,
sweet and smooth like milk,
though he did not know what it was.
The Dàoshi then escorted Jùn out,
saying to him:
"You have toiled, coming from afar.
I have a small gift for you."
He gave him one thousand coins,
instructing him to tie them under his waist.
"When you get home, untie and look at them—
you will surely find something extraordinary."
He also asked how many people were in his family.
Jùn replied:
"My wife and children, five in total."
He was given about a hundred pellets of elixir.
He said:
"Take one pellet per day.
It can sustain you for a hundred days without eating."
Jùn declined, saying:
"The journey back is long,
how will I know the way?"
The Dàoshi said:
"I will arrange it for you."
He then led him among the scattered rocks,
where they saw a rock lying like a tiger.
He told Jùn to mount it,
covered the rock's head with something,
and Jùn held its end,
as if holding reins.
He was admonished to close his eyes,
and to open them only when his feet touched the ground.
Jùn mounted the rock as instructed.
The Dàoshi whipped the rock with a whip,
and Jùn felt the rock rise into the air and fly.
By then, it was nearing evening.
After what seemed like the time to cook a meal,
he felt his feet touch the ground.
Opening his eyes,
he was already at the outer gate of Guǎnglíng.
People's homes were just beginning to light candles.
By the time he reached his house,
his wife and children were astonished at his speed.
He then untied what was under his waist—
it was all gold coins.
From then on, he no longer worked as a hired laborer,
but extensively acquired fields and gardens,
becoming a wealthy man.
The villagers all suspected he had become a thief.
Later, when a robbery occurred elsewhere,
the villagers thought Jùn was involved,
so they bound him and took him to the prefectural office.
At that time, the military governor Dù Yà valued alchemical arts highly
and was fond of extraordinary tales.
Hearing Jùn's account,
he ordered him to fetch his golden elixir.
When the elixir reached Yà's hand,
it fell to the ground as if dropped and vanished.
Jùn also mentioned that the rock he rode outside the city wall was still there,
so he was released.
From then on, Yà devoted himself earnestly to the Dào,
and became quite fond of alchemical practices.
However, he ultimately achieved nothing.
Jùn later died of old age.
His descendants remained very wealthy.
From "Records of Original Immortals."
The Ming manuscript copy states it is from "Records of Original Transformations."
Lǚ Shēng
The counties of Yǔxiāng and Yǒnglè are connected,
and those who follow the Way are often encountered there.
There was a certain Lǚ,
who lived between these two counties.
When he was a child,
he did not wish to smell the odor of cooked food.
Therefore, he went up the mountain, dug up huángjīng himself, boiled it, and consumed it.
After ten years,
he also ate it raw,
and did not partake of ordinary food at all.
Daily, he felt light and vigorous,
could endure wind and cold,
walked as if on a swift wind,
and whatever he read or heard from people, he never forgot.
His mother ordered him to study books,
so he then wished to take the míngjīng examination.
He recited several volumes daily,
but it was not really due to diligent effort;
he simply did not forget.
Later, his mother forced him to eat cooked rice,
but he refused.
His younger sisters urged and persuaded him morning and night,
but he would not comply at all.
So, his mother placed pork fat in wine,
and holding it herself, offered it to him to drink, saying:
"I am old.
Moreover, wine is not forbidden by Daoist practice."
Lǚ said:
"I have not known the taste of such things since childhood,
I truly cannot consume it."
She then forced it near his mouth and nose.
As he exhaled and inhaled,
an object fell from his mouth,
over two cùn long.
Everyone looked at it together;
it was a little golden man.
Lǚ then lay stiffly, unable to rise,
only saying he was exhausted.
His younger sister washed it with fragrant water,
tied it to Lǚ's belt,
and only after some time did he rise.
Previously, although Lǚ was nearly sixty years old,
his beard and hair were jet black.
But now, his head was white.
His mother then regretted it,
and tried to take back the golden man.
The place where it was tied remained as before,
but it was already gone.
Lǚ, filled with regret and sorrow, wept,
bowed twice to his mother, left through the gate,
saying he was going to Máo Shān,
and there was no further trace of him.
From *Yì Shǐ*
Messrs. Zhāng and Lǐ
During the Táng dynasty's Kāiyuán era,
there were two gentlemen, Zhāng and Lǐ,
who shared the same aspirations and were companions,
studying the Way on Tài Shān.
After a long time,
Lǐ, being of imperial lineage,
thought of pursuing an official career,
bade farewell, and returned.
Zhāng said:
"Each person has their own will;
to become an official is your will,
why be ashamed?"
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Lǐ had attained the post of Dàlǐ Chéng.
Due to Ān Lùshān's rebellion,
he took his family dependents,
exited through Wǔ Guān and went to reside in Xiāngyáng.
Soon, he was sent on a mission to Yángzhōu.
On the road, he encountered Zhāng,
whose clothes were glossy yet worn,
pretending to be lost.
Lǐ felt pity and concern for him,
and asked to lodge together.
Zhāng said:
"My host has considerable means for livelihood."
He invited Lǐ to go together.
When they arrived,
the gate and courtyard were grand and imposing,
the attendants were splendid,
appearing like nobility.
Lǐ was greatly astonished,
and said:
"How can it be like this!"
Zhāng warned him not to speak,
lest he be laughed at.
Afterwards, an extremely lavish feast was prepared.
After eating,
he ordered five female musicians skilled in various arts,
all holding their own instruments.
Among them was one holding a zhēng,
who looked exactly like Lǐ's wife.
Lǐ gazed at her especially intently,
and while drinking, stared fixedly at her several times.
Zhāng asked the reason.
Lǐ pointed to the zhēng player:
"She resembles my wife;
how can I not be concerned?"
Zhāng laughed and said:
"There are people who look alike in the world."
When they were about to disperse,
Zhāng called the zhēng-holding woman,
tied a crabapple to her skirt belt,
and then sent her back.
He said to Lǐ:
"How much money do you need to fulfill your wish?"
Lǐ said:
"If I get three hundred thousand coins,
I can manage my own affairs."
Zhāng had an old woven hat,
and said to Lǐ:
"Take this to the medicine shop,
ask for Old Wáng's house,
and say, 'Zhāng Sān ordered me to bring this to collect three hundred thousand strings of cash.'
He will give it to you."
Then they each went their separate ways.
The next day,
Lǐ went to that gate.
The pavilions and buildings were desolate and overgrown,
the locks had been closed for a long time,
and there were no traces of people at all.
So he inquired of the neighboring houses, seeking Zhāng Sān.
A neighbor said:
"This is the residence of Liú Dàoxuán;
no one has lived here for over ten years."
Lǐ sighed in amazement for a long time,
then took the hat to the Wáng family to ask for the money.
Old Wáng had the hat sent in to ask his family,
to verify whether it was indeed Zhāng's hat.
His daughter
(The characters "his daughter" were originally above the character "verify";
changed according to Lù Qìqīng's manuscript copy of *Guǎngyì Jì*)
said:
"The green thread sewn on it before is still there."
Lǐ asked who Zhāng was.
Wáng said:
"He was a customer who came for fúlíng fifty years ago.
Now there are over two thousand strings of cash in the medicine business."
Lǐ took the money and returned,
searched again,
but never saw him again.
Soon he returned to Xiāngyáng,
tried to check his wife's skirt belt,
and indeed found a crabapple there.
He asked her the reason.
She said:
"Last night I dreamed that five or six people pursued me,
saying it was Immortal Zhāng summoning me to play the zhēng.
When parting,
he tied a crabapple to my skirt belt.
Only then did I know that Zhāng had already attained immortality."
From *Guǎngyì Jì*
Xǔ Xuānpíng
was a native of Shè County in Xīn'ān.
During the Jǐngyún era of Emperor Ruìzōng of the Táng dynasty,
he lived in seclusion in the southern valley of Chéngyáng Mountain,
where he built a hut to dwell in.
No one knew what elixirs he consumed,
but he was observed not eating.
His complexion appeared as if he were around forty years old,
and he walked as swiftly as a galloping horse.
At times he would carry firewood to sell,
always hanging a gourd and a bamboo cane from his carrying pole.
Whenever he was drunk and staggering, he would lean on the cane to return home.
He would chant alone:
"Carrying firewood, I sell it at dawn;
buying wine, I return as the sun sets in the west.
Passersby, do not ask where I am headed;
I vanish into the white clouds, walking amidst the emerald hills."
For over thirty years since then,
he would sometimes rescue people from peril
or relieve them from suffering.
Many city dwellers sought to visit him,
but they could not find him.
They only saw a poem inscribed on the wall of his hut:
"In seclusion for thirty years,
in a stone chamber atop the southern peak.
On quiet nights, I admire the bright moon;
at dawn, I drink from the clear spring.
Woodcutters sing on the ridges,
valley birds play before the cliffs.
Joyful, I know not old age;
I have forgotten the passage of years."
Many enthusiasts recited his poem.
Sometimes, while traveling to Cháng'ān,
he would inscribe it at relay stations along the post road between Luòyáng and Tónghuà.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Lǐ Bái left the Hànlín Academy
and traveled east, passing by a relay station.
Reading the poem, he chanted it
and sighed in admiration:
"This is an immortal's poem!"
He then inquired among people
and learned the truth about Xuānpíng.
Lǐ Bái thus journeyed to Xīn'ān,
crossed streams and climbed mountains,
but despite repeated attempts, he could not find him.
So he inscribed a poem on the hut's wall:
"I chant the poem from the relay station,
and come to visit the abode of a true immortal.
Misty peaks obscure his lofty traces;
cloudy woods separate me from the great void.
Peering into the courtyard, I see only desolation;
leaning against a pillar, I stand in vain hesitation.
He must have transformed into a crane soaring to distant skies,
to return only after a thousand years or more."
That winter, a wildfire burned his hut,
and no one knew Xuānpíng's whereabouts.
Over a hundred years later,
in the seventh year of the Xiántōng era,
an old woman from the household of Xǔ Míngnú in the commandery
often went into the mountains with companions to gather firewood.
Alone in the southern mountains, she saw a man sitting on a rock,
eating a peach
that was very large.
He asked the old woman:
"Are you from Xǔ Míngnú's family?
I am Xuānpíng, Míngnú's ancestor."
The old woman said:
"I have often heard that you attained immortality!"
He replied:
"Go back
and tell Míngnú for me
that I am in these mountains.
I give you this peach to eat,
but you must not take it out.
There are many tigers and wolves in the mountains,
and the mountain spirits treasure this peach."
The old woman then ate the peach;
it was delicious,
and she finished it in a short while.
Xuānpíng sent the old woman home with the woodcutters to relay the message.
Míngnú's clan found this very strange,
and word spread among the commandery's people.
Afterward, the old woman abstained from food,
her face gradually becoming youthful,
and she grew more agile and vigorous than usual.
After the Zhōnghé era,
as wars and chaos ensued,
the residents lived in unrest.
Míngnú moved his family to escape the turmoil,
and the old woman entered the mountains and did not return.
Nowadays, when people gather firewood,
some occasionally see this old woman,
clad in vine leaves,
moving as swiftly as flying.
When pursued,
she ascends into the trees and departs.
From "The Continued Biographies of Immortals"
Liú Qīngzhēn
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Liú Qīngzhēn,
who, along with twenty of his followers, was producing tea in Shòuzhōu,
each man transporting one pack-load as goods.
Upon reaching Chénliú, they encountered bandits,
and someone guided them, instructing them to go to Wèijùn,
so Liú Qīngzhēn and the others proceeded there.
They then met an old monk,
who guided them toward Wǔtái.
Liú Qīngzhēn and the others, fearing the hardship and toil,
and as the Wǔtái temples were still far away,
the monk invited Liú Qīngzhēn and the others to return to his forest monastery to spend the night.
Liú Qīngzhēn and the others privately discussed,
suspecting the old monk was the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī,
and so they followed the monk back.
After traveling several lǐ,
they finally reached the forest monastery.
The halls and buildings were solemn and pure,
and they all felt reverence and awe,
as the monk expounded the Dharma for them,
greatly opening the gates of skillful means.
Liú Qīngzhēn and the others all resolved to leave the household life,
and followed him as their abbot.
After more than twenty years had accumulated,
the monk suddenly said to Liú Qīngzhēn and the others:
"A great demon is arising,
you all will certainly suffer from its harm,
it is best to take precautions beforehand;
if not,
then it will ruin our Dharma activities."
He then had Liú Qīngzhēn and the others kneel upright,
and the monk took water in his mouth and sprayed it all around,
reciting esoteric dhāraṇīs.
Liú Qīngzhēn and the others all transformed into stone,
their minds perfectly clear and awakened,
yet unable to move.
In a short while,
several dozen clerks and soldiers from Dàizhōu,
came to the mountain platform to make arrests,
arriving at the place where Liú Qīngzhēn and the others resided,
they only saw wild grass and stones,
and so each of them left and gave up.
When evening came,
the old monk returned,
and sprayed water on Liú Qīngzhēn and the others, turning them back into humans,
Liú Qīngzhēn and the others, realizing his divine power,
