knew they had encountered a Bodhisattva,
and all diligently devoted themselves to spiritual practice.
A little over a month later,
the monk said:
"Now demons will arise again,
they will certainly search extensively for you,
what is to be done about it?
I wish to send you far away,
will you all go?"
Liú Qīngzhēn and the others accepted his instruction,
the monk had them all close their eyes,
admonishing them:
"First, do not secretly peek,
or you will ruin this great matter.
Once you feel you have reached the ground,
then you may open your eyes.
If you arrive in a mountain,
and see a great tree,
you should all take shelter under it.
If medicine emerges from the tree,
you should also eat it."
He then gave each of them a pill of medicine, saying:
"After eating this, you will no longer feel hunger,
you should only contemplate the holy path,
as a bridge for transcending the world."
Having finished speaking, he performed a bow,
and after the bow, they closed their eyes,
and gently rose upward,
their bodies in empty space.
After about half a day,
their feet finally touched the ground.
Opening their eyes,
they saw a great mountain forest.
They encountered some woodcutters,
and asked the name of the place,
which turned out to be Lúshān.
After walking over ten lǐ,
they saw a great wisteria tree,
its circumference about five or six arm-spans around,
its emerald shade blocking the sun.
Liú Qīngzhēn and the others joyfully said:
"The wondrous tree the great master spoke of,
must be this one."
Each cleared the grass and sat down.
Several days later,
white fungi emerged from the tree,
fresh, beautiful, and glossy,
constantly fluttering and moving.
The group said to each other:
"This is the spiritual medicine the great master spoke of."
They picked and shared it to eat.
Among them was one person,
who deceitfully ate it all first.
His companions were all indignant and angry,
rebuking and blaming him, saying:
"You have disobeyed our great master's teaching."
But since it was already done,
they could not beat him.
After a long while,
he suddenly disappeared,
and looking up, they saw him sitting peacefully atop the treetop.
Liú Qīngzhēn and the others then said:
"You, because you swallowed the medicine, are able to ascend to such heights."
That person ultimately did not come down.
After seven days,
his entire body grew green hair.
Suddenly, a crane soared and circled above him.
He then said to the nineteen others:
"I have truly wronged you,
but now I have attained the Way,
and will leave you,
to pay homage to the Emperor in the palace of this heaven.
You should each strive diligently,
to achieve the ultimate truth."
Liú Qīngzhēn and the others urged him to come down from the tree to bid farewell.
The immortal paid no heed,
and then rode the clouds upward,
a long time before disappearing.
Liú Qīngzhēn and the others, having lost the medicine,
thus each dispersed and returned to the human world.
Zhāng Lún from Zhōngshān,
personally heard Liú Qīngzhēn and the others tell it thus.
From the "Guǎng Yì Jì".
Zhāng Zhí
was a native of Dǎojiāng in Péngzhōu.
He encountered the Daoist Jiāng Xuánbiàn,
who imparted to him the technique of commanding the Six Ding deities.
During the Dàlì era,
Cuī Níng, the military governor of Xīchuān,
once had an urgent matter and dispatched a messenger on horseback to deliver a memorial to the court.
Three days after the messenger had departed,
he suddenly discovered among the documents on his desk
that the clean, final copy of the memorial he had submitted was still there;
what had been sealed in the envelope
was merely the draft.
Considering the distance the messenger had already traveled,
it was impossible to catch up with him.
Cuī Níng was deeply worried and anxious,
unable to devise a plan.
Knowing of Zhāng Zhí's arts,
he summoned him and explained the situation.
Zhāng Zhí said:
"This is easy;
there is no need to worry."
He then lit an incense burner,
placed the clean, final copy of the memorial over the incense smoke,
and suddenly it flew away.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
the sealed draft fell before Zhāng Zhí.
When the messenger returned and was questioned,
he was completely unaware of the switch.
At the time he presented the memorial,
the seal and markings on the envelope were as before.
Lord Cuī was profoundly amazed by this
and treated Zhāng Zhí with extraordinary respect and courtesy.
He asked Zhāng Zhí about the origin of the Daoist arts he had received.
Zhāng Zhí said:
"My teacher, Jiāng Xuánbiàn,
during the Zhìdé era,
spent several years performing menial tasks and burning incense at the Jiǔlóng Temple.
There, he happened to pick up four or five tattered pages of a scripture,
which contained the Supreme Lord's method for commanding the Six Ding deities.
The incantations and techniques were complete.
He then selected a deep mountain valley, a place without any trace of people,
and, following the method, constructed an altar and recited the incantations,
devoting himself diligently day and night.
The original scripture stated
that it would take fourteen days,
but for Jiāng Xuánbiàn, the response came on the ninth day.
Suddenly, there were black winds and torrential rain,
terrifying to behold,
yet when he looked, although the rain fell,
the altar ground was not
wet.
There was also thunder and lightning,
but he was not frightened.
After a long while,
he saw ghosts and spirits of strange shapes and forms circling around him,
but he felt no fear.
After a short time,
thousands of armored soldiers in iron armor appeared,
and thousands of soldiers in golden armor,
descending with a clamor,
yet he remained unafraid.
After some time,
the divine troops formed ranks,
as if awaiting something.
Then a heavenly maiden appeared,
wearing embroidered shoes and robes,
a large crown, and standing with a sword at her waist.
She addressed Jiāng Xuánbiàn, saying:
'Since you have summoned us,
what do you seek?'
Jiāng Xuánbiàn requested the arts of divination and magic.
The Six Ding troops and weapons
vanished in an instant.
From then on, one Ding deity attended him each day.
Whatever he sought or commanded,
it was immediately fulfilled.
It was these arts that he imparted to me."
Jiāng Xuánbiàn said to me:
'Technique and the Dao
must proceed together.
Without technique, the Dao cannot be attained by oneself;
without the Dao, technique cannot be prolonged.
If one obtains technique but not the Dao,
it is like wishing to travel ten thousand li but being unable to walk.
Although techniques may manifest in myriad hidden ways,
they do not remove one's name from the register of death.
Therefore, one must settle the mind in the wondrous realm,
focus thoughts on the elixir's splendor,
perform meritorious deeds to aid the external self,
refine the soul to preserve the internal self.
When internal and external are unified as one,
then one may approach the Dao,
and may achieve long life.
In Mount Éméi,
there are over ten thousand immortals and divine beings.
Under the leadership of Huángrén,
they have established palaces and offices,
divided into departments and bureaus,
to guide and save people.
You and I have glimpsed but a fragment of the Dao;
we have not yet reached its profound subtleties.
At the time of the Dragon and Snake conjunction,
I will take you into the cavern mansions,
to pay homage to the true teachers,
so that we may discuss the principles of longevity.'
My teacher, Jiāng Xuánbiàn, withdrew from the world for over twenty years.
In this year, at the Dragon and Snake conjunction,
I am to follow my teacher to ascend Mount Éméi
and enter the cavern heavens.
I will be departing soon."
That year was the twelfth year of the Dàlì era, the year of Dīngsì.
Zhāng Zhí and Jiāng Xuánbiàn withdrew from the world
and were seen no more.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Xiāo Jìngzhī
Xiāo Jìngzhī of Lánlíng
failed the imperial examinations.
His nature inclined him strongly towards the Dao.
He set aside his books,
abstained from grains, and practiced breath cultivation,
building a hut by the Zhāng River.
After more than ten years, his face had become haggard and憔悴,
his teeth and hair had fallen out.
One day, looking into a mirror, he grew angry
and moved to Yèxià,
joining the market crowds to seek a merchant's profit.
After several years, his wealth and resources became ample,
and he purchased land to build a house.
While digging, he unearthed an object
resembling a human hand,
plump and moist,
with a slight reddish hue.
He sighed and said:
"Could this be the spirit of Tàisuì,
come to bring calamity?"
He then cooked and ate it.
It was delicious,
and he finished it all.
After a month, his teeth and hair grew back,
his strength returned, and his appearance became youthful,
though he did not know why.
By chance, while traveling in Yèdū,
he met a Daoist priest.
Looking at Jìngzhī in astonishment, the priest said:
"Your vital energy and spirit are like this;
you must have consumed an immortal's medicine."
He asked to examine his pulse,
then said:
"What you ate was a fleshly fungus,
born from the earth,
resembling a human hand,
plump, moist, and red.
One who eats it will enjoy a lifespan like that of the tortoise and crane.
However, you should now seclude yourself deep in the mountains and forests,
and further seek the ultimate Dao.
You must not allow yourself to be sullied again amidst the foul and turbid world."
Jìngzhī followed his advice,
left his family to wander like clouds and water,
and ultimately, no one knew where he went.
From "Shénxiān Gǎnyù Zhuàn"
Zhū Rúzǐ
was a native of Ānguó in Yǒngjiā.
From a young age, he served the Daoist priest Wáng Xuánzhēn,
residing at Dàruòyán.
He deeply admired the Daoist path to immortality,
often climbing the mountain peaks
to gather and consume huángjīng.
One day,
while washing vegetables by the stream,
he suddenly saw two small flower-patterned dogs chasing each other on the bank.
Rúzǐ found this strange,
and so he followed them into a cluster of gǒuqǐ shrubs.
Returning, he told Xuánzhēn about it,
who was also surprised.
Then, together with Rúzǐ, he went to watch for them,
and again saw the two dogs playfully leaping about.
As they approached,
the dogs once more vanished beneath the gǒuqǐ.
Xuánzhēn and Rúzǐ searched together and dug there,
unearthing two gǒuqǐ roots,
shaped like flower-patterned dogs,
and as hard as stone.
They washed them, carried them back, and boiled them.
Rúzǐ diligently added firewood and tended the fire,
for three days and nights,
never leaving the side of the stove.
He tasted the broth
and kept eating it.
When he saw the roots had softened,
he informed Xuánzhēn, and together they came to take them,
and began to eat.
Shortly after, Rúzǐ suddenly soared into the air and alighted on the peak ahead.
Xuánzhēn was astonished for a long time.
Rúzǐ bid farewell to Xuánzhēn,
and ascended on a cloud, departing.
To
(The original text had "bid farewell" instead of "to,"
emended based on the Ming manuscript copy.)
Nowadays, people commonly call that peak Tóngzǐfēng (Child Peak).
Later, Xuánzhēn consumed the remaining roots.
His lifespan is unknown,
but he too withdrew to Táoshān, west of the cliff.
Those gathering herbs or hunting
sometimes saw him.
From "Continued Biographies of Immortals"
The Herb-Gathering Commoner
During the Xiǎnqìng era of Emperor Gāozōng of Táng,
there was a commoner from Qīngchéng County in Shǔ Commandery,
whose name is unknown.
He once went to gather herbs at the foot of Qīngchéng Mountain,
where he encountered a large yam.
He dug it up to a depth of several zhàng,
and its root gradually grew as large as a vat.
This man kept digging without stopping,
reaching a depth of five or six zhàng,
and the ground continued to collapse,
until it was over ten zhàng deep.
This man fell into the hole,
with no way to get out.
Looking up at the opening of the hole,
it appeared as small as a star.
He thought he was surely going to die.
Suddenly, he noticed a side passage,
and upon entering it,
it gradually widened.
Crawling slowly forward,
after several tens of steps,
he looked ahead
and saw something like a light.
He followed it and walked,
for over a lǐ,
as the passage gradually rose.
Walking around the passage for about a lǐ,
he finally emerged at the mouth of a cave.
Above the cave was water,
spanning several tens of steps.
On the shore, he saw a village of several tens of households,
with mulberry trees, paper mulberries, flowers, plants, and trees,
as if it were the second or third month of the year.
There were people,
men and women in clothing
unlike that of modern people.
Farmers and fishing children
could be seen here and there.
One person, surprised, asked how he had come,
and he told them the reason.
They then ferried him across in a small boat.
The man told them:
"I haven't eaten for three days already."
So they fed him sesame rice, cypress seed soup, and various pickled vegetables.
After only a few days,
this man felt his body gradually becoming lighter.
He asked his host,
what place this was,
and also requested the way back to Shǔ.
The people there laughed together and said:
"You are a mortal,
unaware that this is an immortal realm.
Since you have managed to come here,
it must be that you are fated to have an immortal destiny.
You may stay here for now,
and I will take you to pay respects to the Jade Emperor."
Then among them, they called to each other:
"Tomorrow is the Shangsi Festival,
we can go to pay homage."
So they took this man along.
Some of the people there rode on clouds and mists,
others drove dragons or cranes.
This man also walked on foot among the clouds.
In a short while,
they arrived at a city,
all adorned with gold and jade.
The palaces within
were all made of gold and treasures.
Everyone entered in turn to pay homage.
Only this man was left outside the palace gate.
Beside the gate was a large ox,
red in color,
with a very unusual appearance,
its eyes closed, drooling foam.
The host instructed this man to bow to the ox
and seek the path to immortality.
If the ox spat out a treasure,
he should immediately swallow it.
The man did as told, bowing and begging.
After a short while,
the ox spat out a red pearl,
over an inch in diameter.
Just as the man was about to reach out and take it,
suddenly a red-clad child picked it up and left.
The man begged again,
and obtained a blue pearl,
which was also taken by a blue-clad child.
Then there were yellow and white ones,
all snatched away by children.
The man then hurriedly cupped his hands over the ox's mouth,
and after a short while, obtained a black pearl,
which he quickly swallowed himself.
A black-clad child arrived,
but finding nothing, left empty-handed.
The host then led him to pay homage to the Jade Emperor.
The Jade Emperor resided in a hall,
appearing like a king,
with seven attendants,
wearing crowns and swords, standing on either side.
There were several hundred jade maidens
guarding the hall courtyard.
Exotic flowers and fruits,
with fragrances not found in the mortal world.
The Jade Emperor then questioned the man.
He answered truthfully in full,
but the man greedily glanced at the jade maidens on either side.
The Jade Emperor said:
"Do you admire the beauty of these attendants?"
The man prostrated himself and begged for forgiveness.
The Jade Emperor said:
"If you diligently devote yourself to the wondrous path,
you will naturally have such things;
but your cultivation is not yet sufficient,
you must put in effort,
you cannot attain them lightly."
He ordered his attendants
to bring immortal fruits on a jade plate.
The fruits were dark red,
extremely large, the size of a fist,
resembling the quince of the mortal world but with unparalleled fragrance.
Showing them to the man, he said:
"You may freely use your hands to scoop them up."
From "the fruits were dark red"
to "you may freely use your hands to scoop them up."
The original text said: showing them to the man, he said:
"You may freely use your hands to clasp them,
the number you obtain."
The fruits were dark red,
extremely large, the size of a fist,
resembling the quince of the mortal world but with unparalleled fragrance,
clasp them with your hands.
Now amended according to the Ming manuscript copy.
The number you obtain
is the number of attendants.
He estimated that by clasping with all his might, he could get over ten.
So he used his hands to scoop them up,
but only obtained three.
The Jade Emperor said:
"This is your allotted share."
Since he had just arrived and had no rank,
he was temporarily sent back to his previous host.
He was ordered to have three maidens serve him,
and given a separate house to live in.
He was instructed to follow the various fellow cultivators
in guiding his practice.
This man then returned to the previous place,
where the various Daoist practitioners transmitted true scriptures to him,
teaching him to take medicine and circulate qì,
cleansing his worldly thoughts.
The three serving maidens also taught him Daoist techniques.
Later, during several audiences,
whenever he saw the Jade Emperor,
he was always encouraged to maintain his utmost sincerity.
The plants and trees in that place
were always as in the third month,
with no changes of flourishing and withering, cold and heat.
He estimated that in human terms,
about a year or more had passed.
The man thought that his immortal path was already achieved,
but suddenly, in the middle of the night, he sighed.
Those around him asked.
He said:
"Although I have now attained the Dao,
I originally came here by chance.
When I left, my wife had just given birth to a daughter,
only a few days old.
My family is poor,
I don't know how they are now,
I wish to go back and check on them."
The jade maiden said:
"You have been away from the mortal world for a long time,
your wife and others must have already passed away,
how can you seek them again?
It must be that your worldly thoughts are not yet dispelled,
leading to this mistaken idea."
The man said:
"It's only been about a year now,
my wife should still be fine,
I just want to clarify the matter."
The jade maiden then told the neighbors.
The neighbors all sighed in sympathy.
They also reported to the Jade Emperor.
The Jade Emperor ordered him to be sent back.
The various immortals held a farewell feast with music and singing on the water.
The three jade maidens also bid him farewell,
each giving him a gold ingot,
saying:
"We fear that when you return to the mortal world,
if you seek to return and cannot,
use this for expenses."
The middle maiden said:
"When you arrive there,
if you see nothing,
and wish to return,
I have medicine inside the gold ingot,
take it and swallow it,
and you can return."
The youngest maiden said:
"I fear that you will be invaded by worldly thoughts,
There are no more immortals,
but there is medicine in the cauldron.
I fear
(Míng manuscript has "not" instead of "is")
it is not secure.
I know there is nowhere left in your home to search,
except for a pounding stone east of the house that still remains.
I have already placed the medicine beneath it.
If there is none in the cauldron,
simply take this and consume it."
After speaking,
he saw a flock of swans
flying across the sky.
The crowd said to the man:
"Do you see them?
Just follow them and go."
The crowd lifted the man up,
and he also soared upward,
reaching the flock of swans.
The swans were not startled,
and he flew through the air with them.
Looking back,
he still saw the people on the shore waving their hands in farewell—
about a hundred of them.
Then he arrived at a city,
where there were many people.
When he asked about the place,
it turned out to be Línhǎi County,
already far from Shǔ.
He then sold his gold for provisions
and traveled for a year before reaching Shǔ.
It was the end of the Kāiyuán era.
When he inquired about his family,
no one knew of them.
There was a man over ninety years old
who said:
"My grandfather once went to gather herbs
and never returned.
It has been ninety years now."
This was the man's grandson.
They held each other and wept.
He said:
"Your sisters and brothers have all passed away.
The daughter born at that time married and has died,
and her son is already over fifty years old."
They searched for the old residence,
but it was all rubble and overgrown wilderness.
Only the old pounding stone remained.
The man then broke the cauldron to seek the medicine,
but just as he was about to swallow it,
he suddenly lost sight of the medicine.
So he lifted the stone
and found a jade box,
inside which was a golden elixir.
He swallowed it immediately,
and his mind became clear,
remembering the way back.
Although this man attained the Way in an immortal cave,
he was originally an ordinary person
and could not inquire in detail about the matters.
At that time, Master Luó Tiānshī was in Shǔ
and heard the man speak of where he had been.
He then said:
"That was the Heaven of the Ninth Chamber, the Treasure Immortal of the Fifth Grotto.
The Jade Emperor is the Celestial Emperor.
The great ox is a dragon-bearing beast.
As for the pearls it spat out:
if one swallows the red one,
their lifespan equals that of heaven and earth;
the green one grants fifty thousand years;
the yellow one, thirty thousand years;
the white one, ten thousand years;
the black one, five thousand years.
This man swallowed the black one,
so although he could not learn the Way,
he will still live five thousand years in the human world.
The seven figures standing before the Jade Emperor
are the seven stars of the Big Dipper."
The man obtained the medicine,
took it, and entered the mountains,
and no one knew where he went.
It seems he returned to the grotto-heaven.
From "Records of Primordial Immortals,"
(Míng manuscript says from "Records of Primordial Transformations")
Yuán and Liǔ, the two gentlemen.
In the early years of the Yuánhé era,
there were Yuán Chè and Liǔ Shí,
who resided in Héngshān.
Both gentlemen had paternal uncles serving as officials in Zhèyòu.
Due to involvement with the rebel Lǐ Shùrén,
each was exiled to Huānzhōu and Àizhōu respectively.
The two gentlemen packed their luggage together and went to visit them.
Arriving at Hépǔ County in Liánzhōu,
they boarded a boat intending to cross the sea,
planning to reach Jiāozhǐ.
They moored their boat at the Hépǔ shore.
At night, villagers were making offerings to the gods,
with flutes and drums creating a clamor.
The boatmen and the two gentlemen’s servants all went together to watch.
As midnight approached,
suddenly a hurricane abruptly arose,
snapping the mooring ropes and setting the boat adrift,
carrying it into the open sea,
with no one knowing where it was heading.
It tangled with the fins of a giant whale,
collided with the back of a colossal turtle,
waves floated like snowy peaks,
the sun surged like a wheel of fire.
It struck the dwelling of sea serpents, halting like a shuttle,
crashed into a mirage palace, shattering it to pieces.
Tossed and rocked repeatedly,
nearly capsizing and sinking,
they finally reached a solitary island where the wind ceased.
The two gentlemen, distressed and gloomy, ascended the island.
They saw a revered statue of the Heavenly King,
gleaming upon the ridge,
with a golden incense burner and spent ashes,
but nothing else besides.
As the two gentlemen were surveying the area,
they suddenly glimpsed a gigantic beast on the sea surface,
raising its head and looking all around,
as if observing and listening,
its teeth dense like swords and halberds,
its eyes flashing like lightning,
and after a long while, it vanished.
Moments later,
purple clouds again surged from the sea surface,
spreading out for several hundred paces,
within which was a large five-colored lotus,
over a hundred zhang tall,
each leaf unfurling,
inside were curtains and canopies,
as if embroidered silks interwoven,
dazzling to the eye.
They also saw a rainbow bridge suddenly extend,
reaching directly to the island.
Soon, a maidservant with double hair buns,
holding a jade box,
and carrying a golden incense burner,
came from the lotus leaves to the place of the Heavenly King,
replaced the spent ashes,
and lit an extraordinary incense.
Seeing this, the two gentlemen
stepped forward, kowtowed,
their words filled with sorrow and anguish,
begging to return to the human world.
The double-bunned maid did not answer.
The two gentlemen pleaded earnestly for a long time.
The maiden said:
"Who are you,
that you have come here so abruptly?"
The two gentlemen fully explained the truth to her.
The maiden said:
"Shortly, the Jade Void Venerable Master will descend upon this island,
to meet with the Lady of the Southern Seas.
You must firmly entreat him,
and you will achieve your wish."
Having spoken,
a Daoist priest riding a white deer,
driving colored clouds,
descended directly onto the island.
The two gentlemen together bowed and tearfully pleaded.
The Venerable Master, taking pity on them, said:
"You may follow this maiden to pay respects to the Lady of the Southern Seas,
there will be a time for your return,
you need not worry."
The Venerable Master said to the double-bunned maiden:
"I will come there shortly after finishing my cultivation."
The two gentlemen received his instruction,
and went before the canopy to perform the rites of bowing and paying respects.
They saw a maiden not yet of hair-pinning age,
clad in five-colored patterned splendor,
her skin like pure white jade,
her rosy glow rich and captivating,
her spirit clear as the vast ether,
her aura solemn as the deep sea.
The two gentlemen reported their names.
The Lady smiled and said:
"In former times, Tiāntāi had Liú Chén,
now there is Liǔ Shí;
in former times there was Ruǎn Zhào,
now there is Yuán Chè;
in former times there were Liú and Ruǎn,
now there are Yuán and Liǔ:
is this not Heaven’s will?"
She set out two couches for them to sit.
Soon the Venerable Master arrived,
the Lady welcomed him with a bow,
then returned to her seat.
There were several immortal maidens,
playing sheng, huang, flutes, and pipes.
Beside them, phoenixes performed songs and dances,
perfectly matching the rhythm.
The two gentlemen felt dazed,
as if dreaming of the heavenly music,
something rarely heard or seen in the human world.
Then she ordered wine cups to fly.
Suddenly, a black crane
carrying a colored note in its beak arrived from the sky, saying:
"Ānqīshēng, knowing the Venerable Master is attending the Southern Seas gathering,
humbly requests your honored presence."
The Venerable Master read it,
and said to the black crane:
"I shall go there shortly."
The Venerable Master said to the Lady:
"With Ānqīshēng, a thousand years have passed since we last met;
not having traveled south,
I had no chance to visit and converse."
The Lady then urged her maidens to serve the feast,
the jade vessels gleaming and pure.
The Lady partook of the meal,
but the two gentlemen were not given food.
The Venerable Master said:
"Although these two are not yet fit to partake of this food,
yet for their sake, fetch some human-world food to give them."
The Lady said:
"Indeed!"
Immediately separate dishes were brought,
which were of human-world flavor.
After the Venerable Master finished eating,
he took out from his bosom a scroll of cinnabar registers and presented it to the Lady.
The Lady bowed and received it,
then he announced his departure.
Turning back to look at the two gentlemen, he said:
"You possess the bone structure for the Dao,
returning will not be difficult;
however, meeting by chance,
it is fitting that I bestow upon you some spiritual medicine.
But according to your inherent destiny, you already have a master,
I should not be your master."
The two gentlemen bowed.
The Venerable Master then departed.
Soon, on the sea appeared a warrior,
tens of zhang tall,
clad in golden armor,
advancing with a sword in hand, saying:
"Having been sent by the celestial envoys to clear the way—
'way' originally written as 'advance'—
according to the Chén revised edition, changed—
was not diligent,
by law should be publicly executed,
now the punishment has been carried out."
He then hurried off and vanished.
The Lady commanded a maiden in purple robes and phoenix crown, saying:
"You may escort the guests away.
But what shall they ride?"
The maiden said:
"There is the Hundred Flowers Bridge that can carry the two gentlemen."
The two gentlemen expressed gratitude and bowed farewell.
The Lady gifted them a jade pot,
over a foot tall.
The Lady took up a brush and inscribed a poem on the jade pot as a gift, saying:
"You came from within a single-leaf boat,
you go upon the Hundred Flowers Bridge.
If you reach the human world and tap the jade pot,
mandarin ducks will themselves understand clear speech."
Suddenly, a bridge several hundred paces long appeared,
on its railings and balustrades,
all were extraordinary flowers.
The two gentlemen, peeking stealthily among the flowers,
saw thousands of dragons and tens of thousands of snakes,
swiftly intertwining to form the bridge’s pillars.
They also saw the beast from earlier on the sea,
now with body and head severed,
floating upon the waves.
The two gentlemen then questioned the envoy.
The envoy said:
"This beast was because it did not know of you two gentlemen."
The envoy said:
"It is not my duty to be the envoy and escort you,
but there is a profound intention I wish to entrust to you,
so I forced myself to make this journey."
Then from within her lapel, she untied an amber box,
inside was something faintly resembling a spider’s shape.
She said to the two gentlemen:
"We are water immortals.
Water immortals are yin,
and have no males.
I once met a youth from Pānyú,
and through deepest affection, had a child.
Before he was three years old,
it was fated that he be given up.
The Lady commanded that he become the son of the Southern Mountain God,
and it has been a long time since then."
I heard that the envoy from the Southern Peak's Returning Goose Peak
had business in the Water Palace.
Upon his return,
he was entrusted to bring back the jade ring that my son used to play with,
but the envoy concealed it,
which greatly vexed me.
I hope you two gentlemen can take this box to the foot of Returning Goose Peak,
visit the envoy's temple and cast it in,
and something extraordinary will surely occur.
If you retrieve the jade ring,
please deliver it to my son.
My son will certainly repay you in turn.
Be careful not to open it."
The two men accepted it
and asked the envoy:
"The lady's poem says:
'If you reach the mortal world and tap the jade pot,
mandarin ducks will understand and speak clearly.'
What does this mean?"
He replied:
"When you return and have matters to attend to,
simply tap the jade pot,
and mandarin ducks will respond,
ensuring that all affairs are carried out."
They also asked:
"The Venerable Master Yùxū said
that we have our own master.
Who is this master?"
He replied:
"It is the Great Ultimate Master of the Southern Peak.
You will naturally encounter him."
They then bid farewell to the envoy.
At the end of the bridge,
they reached the place where the boat had been moored in Hé Pǔ in the past.
Looking back, the bridge had already vanished.
When the two men inquired,
they found that twelve years had passed.
Their relatives in Huānzhōu and Àizhōu
had already passed away.
They planned to return to Héngshān,
but on the way, feeling hungry, they tapped the pot.
Mandarin ducks then spoke:
"If you desire food and drink,
continue forward, and you will naturally encounter it."
Soon, by the roadside, there was a lavish spread of food,
which the two men ate.
For several days afterward, they had no desire for other flavors.
They soon arrived home.
The children from the past
had already reached adulthood.
However, the wives of the two men had each passed away three days earlier.
Their families were overwhelmed with grief and joy,
saying:
"People said you had perished at sea,
and the mourning period has already passed nine autumns."
The two men, weary of the mortal world
and having attained a state of purity and emptiness,
saw their wives' deaths
without excessive sorrow.
Together, they went directly to Returning Goose Peak,
visited the envoy's temple,
and cast the box into it.
Suddenly, a black dragon several zhang long appeared,
stirring winds and spewing lightning,
uprooting trees and tearing apart houses.
With a thunderous crash, the temple was instantly shattered.
The two men trembled with fear,
not daring to look closely.
From the air, a jade ring was thrown down.
The two men retrieved it and delivered it to the Southern Peak Temple.
Upon returning,
a youth in yellow robes appeared,
holding two golden boxes.
He went to the homes of the two men and said:
"My master ordered me to bring this medicine,
called 'Soul-Returning Ointment,'
to repay you two gentlemen.
If anyone in your household has died,
even if it has been sixty years,
applying it to the crown of the head will revive them."
They accepted it, and the envoy vanished.
The two men then used it to revive their wives.
Later, they sought the way of clouds and waters together,
searching for the Great Ultimate Master,
but found no trace of him.
Disheartened, they returned.
During a heavy snowfall,
they saw an old man carrying firewood to sell.
Feeling pity for his frailty and age,
they offered him wine.
Noticing the characters "Great Ultimate" on his carrying pole,
they bowed to him as their master
and told him about the jade pot.
The old man said:
"The one who stored the jade liquid
has been gone for dozens of sixty-year cycles.
I am delighted to see it again."
The two men then followed him to Zhùróng Peak,
and from then on, they attained the Way,
never to be seen again.
From *Continued Biographies of Immortals*
Yè Fǎshàn
Yè Fǎshàn, styled Dàoyuán,
originally hailed from Yèyì in Nányáng,
and now resides in Sōngyáng County, Chùzhōu.
For four generations, his family cultivated the Dao,
all using hidden merits, secret practices, and the arts of exorcism and summoning to save and aid people.
His mother, née Liú,
while napping during the day,
dreamed of a shooting star entering her mouth;
she swallowed it and became pregnant,
giving birth after fifteen months.
At the age of seven,
he fell into a river
and did not return for three years.
When his parents asked him the reason,
he said:
"A blue-clad youth led me,
gave me cloud-nectar to drink,
so I stayed a short while."
He also said the blue-clad youth led him to pay homage to the Supreme Lord,
who nodded and kept him there.
Upon reaching adulthood, he stood nine feet tall,
with two 'wǔ' characters on his forehead.
His nature was pure, harmonious, and unsullied;
he did not consume pungent or meaty foods.
He often dwelled alone in secluded rooms,
or wandered through forests and marshes,
or visited cloudy springs.
After returning from the immortal realm,
he already possessed the art of command,
and thus entered to dwell in Mǎoyǒu Mountain.
Near the mountain gate,
a huge rock blocked the path,
and people always had to detour around it.
The Master cast a talisman and raised the rock;
in a moment, it flew away,
and the path became level.
All were astonished.
He once wandered to White Horse Mountain in Kuòcāng,
where in a stone chamber he encountered three divine beings,
all in brocade robes and jeweled crowns,
who said to the Master:
"We have received the Supreme Lord's command
to convey a secret decree to you.
You were originally the Left Immortal Minister of the Supreme Ultimate and Purple Tenuity,
but due to negligence in your duties of checking and recording,
you were banished to the human world.
You must quickly perform meritorious deeds to aid people;
when your service to the state is complete,
you shall resume your former post.
We are ordered to impart to you
the methods of the Orthodox Unity, Three and Five.
Also, diligently practice and assist in transformation.
Strive hard in this."
Having spoken, they departed.
From then on, he exterminated and cleansed spirits and monsters,
swept away and beheaded evil and calamitous beings;
wherever he traveled,
his aim was to save people.
His granduncle, Yè Jìngnéng,
possessed considerable divine arts.
During Emperor Gāozōng's reign,
he entered service in the Hànlín Academy,
serving as Chancellor of the National University.
When Empress Wǔ supervised the state,
he was exiled south and died there.
Initially, Emperor Gāozōng summoned the Master to the capital,
offering him the position of High Minister,
but he declined,
requesting instead to be ordained as a Daoist priest,
and he came and went within the palace.
When the emperor wished to announce the completion [of rituals] at Mount Zhōngyuè,
many of the retinue fell ill;
whenever he sprayed water and incanted,
the sick were all cured.
In the two capitals, those who received the Daoist registers from him
numbered over a thousand disciples, civil and military, Chinese and foreign, male and female.
The gold and silk he received
were all used to repair temples and monasteries,
and to relieve orphans and the poor,
without any stinginess.
After a long time,
he took leave and returned to Sōngyáng.
Along the places he passed through,
he saved countless people.
The wife of Commandant Zhāng in Shǔchuān
died and came back to life,
resuming marital relations.
The Master recognized it and said:
"This is the illness of corpse-seduction.
If not quickly eliminated,
Zhāng will die."
The Master cast a talisman, and she transformed into a black vapor.
The deceased daughter of Chancellor Yáo Chóng
was deeply missed;
he cast a talisman and raised her.
In the Qiántáng River, there was a giant clam-monster
that often harmed people,
causing boats to sink and capsize,
much to the distress of travelers.
He cast a talisman into the river,
commanding a divine being to slay it.
Eliminating harm and destroying evil,
his mysterious merits spread far and wide;
each is recorded in his biography.
Throughout the four seas and six directions,
famous mountains and celestial grottoes,
he traveled extensively.
At age fifteen,
he was poisoned and nearly died,
but saw a blue-clad youth who said:
"Miáo Jūn of Tiāntāi
has sent a flying seal to rescue you."
Thus he revived.
He also studied under Zhào Yuányáng on Qīngchéng Mountain,
receiving the art of Dunjiǎ.
With Wéi Shànjùn from Sōngyáng, he transmitted the Eight Histories;
going east into Méng Mountain,
a divine being bestowed a book.
Going to Sōng Mountain,
an immortal bestowed a sword.
Once while crossing a great body of water,
he suddenly sank beneath the waves;
thinking he had drowned,
he emerged after seven days,
his clothes and shoes not even wet,
saying:
"I briefly traveled to Pénglái with the Earl of the River."
Empress Wǔ summoned him to the Divine Capital,
requesting he cast dragon-tablets at various famous peaks.
When Emperor Zhōngzōng was restored to the throne,
Wǔ Sānsī still held state power.
The Master, having frequently detected ominous signs,
protected Emperor Zhōngzōng, the Prince of Xiāng, and Emperor Xuánzōng,
incurring Wǔ Sānsī's jealousy,
and was exiled to the Southern Sea.
The people of Guǎngzhōu,
long admiring his name,
awaited him facing north.
The Master rode a white deer,
arriving from across the sea,
and stopped at the newly built Lóngxīng Temple.
People from near and far paid respects and made offerings,
donations were plentiful,
and he used them all to repair the temple buildings.
After over a year,
he entered the Western Mountains of Hóngzhōu
to nurture his spirit and cultivate the Dao.
On the ninth day of the third month in the fourth year of Jǐnglóng, the xīnhài year,
the three divine beings of Kuòcāng descended again,
conveying the Supreme Lord's command:
"You shall assist my Ruìzōng and the Kāiyuán Sage Emperor.
You may not hide your traces in mountain cliffs,
neglecting the commission entrusted to you."
Having spoken, they departed.
At that time, the two emperors had not yet ascended,
yet their temple names and reign titles
were all known in advance.
In the eighth month of that year,
an edict indeed summoned him to the capital.
Later, after pacifying Empress Wěi,
establishing the Prince of Xiāng as Emperor Ruìzōng,
and Emperor Xuánzōng succeeding to the throne,
the Master, in the upper capital,
assisted the sage sovereign.
All matters of fortune and misfortune, action and stillness,
he would surely memorialize and report.
Once, Tibet sent an envoy presenting a sealed treasure box,
saying:
"We request Your Majesty open it yourself,
and not let others learn the secret."
The court was silent,
but Yè Fǎshàn said:
"This is a box of malice.
I beg Your Majesty not to open it;
instead, order the Tibetan envoy to open it himself."
Emperor Xuánzōng complied.
When the Tibetan envoy was ordered to open it himself,
a crossbow bolt shot from the box,
striking and killing the Tibetan envoy.
It indeed happened as Fǎshàn had said.
Soon he was appointed Silver青光禄大夫, Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial, Duke of Yuè, and Abbot of Jǐnglóng Temple.
His grandfather, Yè Zhòng,
excelled in numerological arts,
was skilled in investigation and summoning,
and performed meritorious deeds among the rivers and lakes;
he was posthumously titled "The Accomplished Daoist Gentleman,"
and has his own biography.
His father, Yè Huìmíng,
was posthumously granted the title of Prefect of Shèzhōu.
The Master requested that his residence in Sōngyáng be made into a temple,
bestowed with the name "Chúnhé,"
with the emperor personally composing the stele inscription and writing the plaque,
bringing honor to his hometown.
On the twenty-seventh day of the first month the following year,
suddenly several hundred companion clouds and cranes,
in formation from the north,
soared and gathered over his former mountain,
lingering for three days.
Auspicious clouds of five colors
covered the place where he dwelled.
In the year Gēngshēn, on the third day of the sixth month, which was Jiǎshēn,
he passed away at the Jǐnglóng Temple in the capital.
His disciples Jì Qíwù and Yǐn Yīn,
having witnessed the descent of the true immortal,
kept it secret and did not speak of it.
On the twenty-first day,
an imperial edict posthumously awarded him the titles of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (Golden Purple Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments) and Governor of Yuèzhōu.
He was one hundred and seven years old.
The courtyard where he resided was filled with an extraordinary, fragrant aroma,
and celestial music swirled about.
A column of blue smoke rose straight up, illuminating the sky,
and did not dissipate until the end of the day.
The Master had requested to be buried in his hometown.
An imperial decree ordained his nephew, Zhòng Róng, who was a Sima in Rùnzhōu, as a Daoist priest,
and together with a palace eunuch envoy to oversee the arrangements,
he was buried in Sōngyáng.
An edict ordered the prefectures of Qú, Wù, and Kuò to assist with the burial.
They supplied
"supplied" originally written as "ended",
changed according to the Ming dynasty manuscript copy
all that was needed.
On the day the funeral procession set out,
an imperial order commanded officials in plain white garments to bid farewell to the coffin outside the capital gates.
In the early Kāiyuán era,
on the night of the first full moon of the first month,
Emperor Xuánzōng moved his retinue to the Shàngyáng Palace to view the lanterns.
The imperial craftsman Máo Shùnxīn
constructed over thirty colorful towers,
adorned with gold, jade, pearls, and precious stones
interspersed within.
The towers were one hundred and fifty feet high,
and when touched by a gentle breeze,
they chimed melodiously.
The lanterns were shaped like dragons, phoenixes, hornless dragons, and leopards in lively postures,
seeming almost beyond human craftsmanship.
Emperor Xuánzōng was greatly pleased upon seeing them,
and urgently summoned the Master to view them from below the towers,
though no one else knew of this.
The Master said:
"The splendor of these lantern displays
is certainly unparalleled;
however, the lanterns in Xīliáng Prefecture tonight
are also nearly as magnificent."
Emperor Xuánzōng asked:
"Has the Master recently traveled there?"
He replied:
"I have just returned from there,
and upon my return, I received your urgent summons."
Emperor Xuánzōng, finding his words strange,
said:
"I wish to go there now.
Is it possible?"
The Master said:
"That is easy."
He then instructed Emperor Xuánzōng to close his eyes,
and stipulated:
"You must not look around recklessly.
If you mistakenly look at something,
you will certainly be greatly alarmed."
Following his instructions,
Emperor Xuánzōng closed his eyes and leaped,
and found himself already high in the heavens.
Soon after, his feet touched the ground.
The Master said:
"You may look now."
Upon seeing the lantern displays,
which stretched continuously for several tens of miles,
with carriages and horses crowded together,
and men and women gathered in great numbers,
Emperor Xuánzōng praised their magnificence for a long time,
and then requested to return.
Again closing his eyes, he soared upward through the air,
and in a moment, he was back below the towers,
with the song and dance performances not yet finished.
While in Liángzhōu,
Emperor Xuánzōng had pawned an iron-inlaid ruyi scepter for wine.
The next day, he dispatched a palace eunuch envoy,
under the pretext of other matters,
to go to Liángzhōu,
to retrieve the ruyi scepter and bring it back.
Upon examination, it was indeed the same, proving it was no falsehood.
On another occasion, during the full moon night of the eighth month,
the Master and Emperor Xuánzōng traveled to the moon palace,
where they listened to the celestial music of the moon.
When asked the name of the melody,
the reply was:
"The 'Zǐyún Melody'."
Emperor Xuánzōng, being well-versed in musical temperament,
silently memorized the tune,
and upon returning, transmitted its melody.
He named it "Nícháng Yǔyī".
On their way back from the moon palace,
passing over the city of Lùzhōu,
they looked down to see the city walls quiet and still,
with moonlight as bright as day.
The Master then requested Emperor Xuánzōng to play a tune on his jade flute.
At that time, the jade flute was in the sleeping palace,
but the Master had someone fetch it,
and it arrived in a moment.
After playing the tune,
he dropped a gold coin into the city before returning.
Ten days later,
Lùzhōu reported that on the full moon night of the eighth month,
celestial music had descended upon the city,
and they had also obtained a gold coin, which they presented.
Emperor Xuánzōng repeatedly tested the Master's Daoist arts with his close ministers,
which were too numerous to exhaustively recount,
but the verifications were clear,
and none were illusory or false,
so he specially accorded him increased respect and courtesy.
Other feats, such as summoning mountain deities,
commanding wind and rain,
cooking dragon meat,
and dispelling demons and falsehoods—
these miraculous efficacies
are all recorded in his main biography,
and are not fully listed here.
Furthermore, Zhāng Yuè, the Duke of Yān,
once visited the temple to pay his respects,
and the Master ordered wine.
Zhāng Yuè said:
"There are no other guests."
The Master said:
"There is a certain Recluse Qū here,
who has long lived secluded in the mountains and forests.
His nature is cautious and reticent,
but he is quite fond of wine—
a whole bell or stone measure would suit him."
Zhāng Yuè requested to summon him,
and he arrived in a moment.
His form was less than three feet tall,
yet his waist was girded by a belt several spans wide.
He was made to sit in a lower seat,
and his bowing and saluting manners
were also rather rustic and simple.
When the wine arrived,
he drained every cup and bowl,
yet his expression remained unchanged.
As the Duke of Yān was about to leave,
the Master suddenly brandished a sword and shouted at Recluse Qū:
"You have never engaged in lofty or extensive discourse,
only indulging in excessive drinking—
what use are you!"
With that, he struck him down,
and it turned out to be merely a large wine vessel.
He once said to his disciples:
"One hundred and sixty years from now,
there will be one whose arts surpass mine,
who will come to dwell on Mǎoyǒu Mountain.
Earlier,
when the Master resided below Sìmíng Mountain,
east of Tiāntāi Mountain,
for several years,
suddenly, on the first day of the fifth month,
an old man came to his gate,
wailing and pleading for rescue.
The disciples thought he was ill.
The Master led him in and asked him,
and he said:
"I am a dragon of the Eastern Sea.
By decree of the Heavenly Emperor,
I am in charge of the treasures of the eight seas.
Every one thousand years, the position is rotated,
and those without fault are elevated to immortal rank.
I have served for nine hundred and seventy years already,
and my modest achievements are nearly complete.
But a Brahmin is displaying his illusory arts,
dwelling on a sea peak,
chanting incantations day and night,
and has been doing so for thirty years already.
His method is about to succeed,
and the seawater is like clouds,
rolled up halfway to the sky.
By the fifth day of the fifth month,
the sea will run dry.
The treasures that govern heaven and pacify the seas,
the objects the Supreme Deity uses to control the spirits,
will certainly be taken by that illusory monk.
At noon on the fifth day,
I beg you to bestow a cinnabar talisman to deliver and save us."
When the time arrived,
the Master commanded a cinnabar talisman,
which flew to their rescue,
and the seawater returned to its former state.
The monk, ashamed and resentful,
threw himself into the sea and died.
The next day,
the dragon brought precious goods and rare treasures by carriage as repayment.
The Master refused, saying:
"In the wild forests and fields,
a place where the spirit dwells in seclusion
has no use for pearls, jade, or precious goods."
He accepted nothing at all,
but instead said to the dragon:
"On this cliff of stone,
far from the water,
if you could just provide a clear spring,
that would be a kindness."
That night,
the sound of wind and rain was heard,
By dawn,
around the four sides of the mountain's base,
a stone channel had formed,
with spring water flowing into it,
which did not run dry even through the winter.
To this day, it is called the Tiānshī Canal.
Another account says:
During the Xiǎnqìng era,
Fǎshàn was ordered to perform the Huánglù Zhāi ritual at Tiāntāi Mountain,
and his route passed through Guǎnglíng.
The next morning, he was to cross at Guāzhōu.
That day,
the ferrymen by the riverbank,
having moored their boats, were waiting.
It was late spring at the time,
the riverbank was clear and warm,
when suddenly two old men, one yellow and one white, said to each other:
"Let's take this chance to enjoy a game of Go."
They then called out into the air for Míng'ér.
In a moment, a young boy with hair tied in two tufts parted the waves and emerged,
his clothes completely dry.
One old man said:
"Bring the Go board and a mat along."
Shortly after,
the boy did as ordered,
and laid the mat on the sand.
Sitting opposite each other, they agreed:
"The winner shall eat the Daoist priest coming from the north tomorrow."
They then laughed loudly and began placing stones.
After a long while,
the white-clad old man said:
"You have lost!
I hope you won't encroach on something so delicious?"
Gazing into the distance and hesitating for a moment,
he slowly walked upon the waves,
and disappeared into the distance.
The boatmen, knowing they intended to harm Fǎshàn,
were filled with anxiety and unease.
At daybreak,
a palace eunuch arrived galloping on horseback ahead,
to oversee the preparation of boats.
The boatmen then reported in detail what they had seen the previous day.
The eunuch was shocked and displeased.
Fǎshàn soon arrived afterward,
and the eunuch again relayed the boatmen's account to Fǎshàn.
Fǎshàn smiled faintly and said:
"Is that so?
Please do not worry."
At that time, Fǎshàn's talismanic arts were divinely effective,
known to both the wise and the foolish,
yet the eunuch and the boatmen in the accompanying party
were so worried they had no peace.
Fǎshàn, aware of this, urged them to cast off,
and when they had left the shore just a short distance,
a violent storm with fierce waves arose,
darkening the sky and sun.
Everyone in the boat
looked at each other, their faces pale.
Fǎshàn calmly said to his attendant:
"Fetch my black talisman,
and throw it at the prow."
Once thrown, the waves and currents grew calm and still,
and shortly after, they crossed over.
Fǎshàn turned to the boatmen and said:
"You can gather your clansmen widely,
and along the river for ten lǐ,
on reed marshes or sedge islets,
there is a giant scaled creature.
You may take it,
and will surely gain great wealth from it."
The boatmen followed his instruction,
and before they had gone a few lǐ,
indeed there was a white fish about a hundred chǐ long,
over thirty arm-spans in girth,
lying stiff and exposed on the sand.
Approaching to look,
there was a hole in its head, sunken and oozing fluid.
The boatmen thus cut it into pieces, loaded it, and returned.
The nearby villages
ate fish for months on end.
From *Jí Yì Jì* and *Xiān Zhuàn Shí Yí*.
Xíng Hé Pú
Master Xíng, named Hé Pú.
He was skilled in esoteric arts,
often carrying bamboo counting rods,
each rod six cùn long.
When someone requested his services,
upon arrival he would lay out the rods to form hexagrams,
arranging them vertically and horizontally,
using several hundred rods in the process,
spreading them to fill the bed.
After laying out the numbers,
he would then tell the family their fortunes or misfortunes,
speaking of the person's lifespan and official prospects,
with divine accuracy.
Master Xíng had a frail and thin appearance,
practiced breath cultivation,
and occasionally took small doses of medicine.
People also did not know his origins.
In the twentieth year of the Táng dynasty's Kāiyuán era, he arrived in the capital,
where nobles and officials awaited him,
and his gate was as busy as a marketplace.
He could increase a person's allotted lifespan,
and could also revive the dead.
Master Xíng once went to beneath Báimǎ Bǎn,
and passed by
"Passed by" originally written as "encountered",
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
a friend.
The friend had already been dead for two nights,
and his mother wept and begged him.
Hé Pú then brought out the deceased and placed him on the bed,
pulled over the quilt,
took off his own clothes, and lay down to sleep together.
He ordered the door closed,
and fell into deep sleep.
After a long while, he got up,
prepared hot water,
but the friend was still dead.
Hé Pú sighed deeply and said:
"The Great One made an agreement with me but broke it—
why is this?"
He again ordered the door closed.
And slept once more.
Soon he rose and said:
"He lives!"
The mother entered to look,
and her son had already revived.
The mother asked him.
Her son said:
"I was taken and imprisoned in a cell,
being interrogated and tortured severely,
when suddenly I heard from outside:
'The King summons this
"This" originally written as "suffering",
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
person.'
The official refused, saying:
'The interrogation is not finished,
he cannot leave.'
A little later,
someone else rushed in anxiously and said:
'Immortal Xíng himself has come to summon this
"This" originally written as "suffering",
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
person.'
The officials went out to greet him,
bowing repeatedly in fear.
They then ordered me to follow the Immortal back,
hence I came back to life."
Another case involved a man who had taken a young concubine,
skilled in singing and dancing, who died suddenly.
He requested Hé Pú to revive her.
Hé Pú wrote a talisman in black ink,
and had it placed where the concubine lay.
Soon he said:
"The black ink talisman is useless."
He then wrote a talisman in vermilion ink,
and again ordered it placed on the bed.
Soon he said again:
"A mountain deity has taken her;
we must order her pursuit."
He then wrote a large talisman and burned it.
Soon the concubine revived.
She said:
"A foreign deity led several hundred followers to seize me,
closed the palace gates,
and was feasting and drinking merrily.
Suddenly someone pushed the door open and said:
'The Ambassador of the Five Paths summons the singer.'
The deity did not respond.
A moment later, it was said again:
'King Luó sends for the singer.'
Only then was he alarmed.
Still, he said:
'Wait a little longer.'
In a short while,
several hundred horsemen galloped into the palace,
shouting loudly:
'By the decree of the Heavenly Emperor,
how dare you arbitrarily take the singer!'
They ordered the deity dragged down,
given a hundred strokes,
and then released the singer to return.
Thus I came back to life."
Hé Pú had many such incidents.
Later, it was unknown where he went.
From *Jì Wén*.
Táng Ruòshān
was a native of Lǔjùn.
During the Xiāntiān era of the Táng dynasty,
he served successively as a Gentleman in the Imperial Secretariat,
and consecutively administered important commanderies.
In the Kāiyuán era,
he was appointed Governor of Rùnzhōu,
where he implemented many benevolent policies,
earning praise from near and far.
Ruòshān had always been fond of the Way of Longevity.
His younger brother, Ruòshuǐ,
was a Dàoshi at Héngyuè,
who had mastered the essentials of Embryonic Origin and Valley Spirit.
He was once summoned to the inner palace,
but soon earnestly requested to return to the mountains.
An edict permitted it.
Ruòshān had always been fond of esoteric arts.
Wherever he went,
he would invariably gather guests who practiced alchemy with furnaces and cauldrons.
Even if their techniques were of no practical use,
he would receive them all with courtesy.
His family wealth was nearly exhausted;
his salary income
never had any surplus.
The expenses for minerals and metals
were beyond measure.
In his later years, his dedication grew even stronger.
Even the government treasury funds of Rùnzhōu
were also used to purchase elixirs.
His advisors and close family members
often urgently admonished him,
but Ruòshān would not listen to any of them.
One day,
an old man,
emaciated in appearance,
with a withered and gaunt countenance,
came to pay his respects.
He claimed to possess the Way of Longevity.
Those who saw him all laughed at his decrepitude.
When Ruòshān saw him,
he treated him with utmost courtesy and respect,
and kept him as a guest for over a month.
The topics the old man discussed were never about the essentials of cinnabar and minerals.
Ruòshān had extensively collected secret formulas and methods,
chanting verses and studying diagrams and records,
leaving nothing unexamined.
When he asked about the old man's expertise,
it all seemed insignificant.
Moreover, the old man was fond of rich meats, fine wines,
and exquisite delicacies.
Though a thin, withered old man,
he ate enough for three or four people.
Ruòshān served him respectfully and attended to him,
never showing any sign of weariness.
One evening,
the old man calmly said to Ruòshān:
"Your household has a hundred mouths to feed,
and its provisions are often insufficient.
Though you are honored as a Regional Governor,
your resources are still greatly lacking;
once you retire from office,
how will you provide for them?
Moreover, you have embezzled
a considerable amount from the treasury's funds and silks.
I am truly concerned for you."
Ruòshān, startled, said:
"I have governed this place for a long time,
and will soon hand over my duties.
I have also often worried about this,
but could think of no solution.
If I am reprimanded for this,
I am certainly willing to accept it;
I only fear my family will suffer from cold and hunger."
The old man said:
"Do not worry too much."
He urged Ruòshān to order wine,
and drank several cups in succession.
Ruòshān usually drank very little,
but that day he also poured three or four cups,
yet felt no intoxication at all,
which greatly surprised him.
That night, the moon was very bright,
and the old man slowly paced in the courtyard.
After a long while, he said to Ruòshān:
"Have a servant
carry several items like cauldrons, pots, and ironware to the elixir chamber,
and have the servant lay out mats and stack the furnace."
He said:
"Gather the cauldrons and pots into two piles,
add blazing charcoal,
until they glow red-hot like a kiln,
too bright to look at directly."
The old man then untied a small gourd from his waist,
took out two elixir pills,
and threw one into each pile.
He closed the door and came out.
He said to Ruòshān:
"You possess the bone structure for the Way,
and by principle, you are destined to transcend this world.
Moreover, you sincerely uphold integrity and righteousness,
and your nature is free from anger and resentment.
Immortals particularly value such conduct.
I am a True Man of the Supreme Ultimate,
traveling and observing the human world,
to deliver those with sincere aspirations.
Moved by your diligent dedication,
I have come to deliver you.
The gold and silver I have transformed,
partly to leave for your descendants,
and partly to aid the poor and needy.
Another part to replenish the treasury,
so you leave no future worries.
You may now order a boat to travel on the river,
and make plans to leave this world.
Tomorrow, wait for me midstream."
Having said this,
he vanished without a trace.
At dawn, Ruòshān opened the door to inspect,
and the transformed substances
glittered brilliantly, illuminating the room.
He locked the door again,
and immediately, with three or five guests,
boarded a boat and floated on the river,
intending to visit Jīnshān Temple.
Once they reached midstream,
river fog darkened the sky,
making even a short distance indiscernible.
Ruòshān alone saw the old man,
rowing a fishing boat,
coming directly alongside his vessel.
He bowed to Ruòshān and invited him into the fishing boat,
then departed, transcending the ordinary.
After a long while,
the wind and waves gradually calmed,
and the dark fog cleared.
Ruòshān was already gone.
In the commandery office, on the desk,
they found Ruòshān's farewell letter, directing family matters;
they also found a memorial he left behind,
which was submitted to the emperor.
Its main message was:
"Worldly prosperity is fleeting,
this floating life is hard to preserve.
Only by attaining truth and casting off worldly ties
can one hope to outlast Heaven itself.
In the past, Chancellor Fàn sailed the Five Lakes,
knowing his ruler could not share his joy;
Marquis Liúhóu left to follow the Four Haos,
fearing his ruler could not long endure.
The departures of these two men
differ from your subject's.
Your subject's fortune coincided with a glorious reign,
and repeatedly received honors and titles.
I realized early the principles of rise and fall,
and deeply understood the rules of knowing when to stop.
My heart dwells in the mysterious gate,
and by chance, I obtained the secret of the elixir.
Gold can be made—
truly, as the King of Huáinán once said;
daylight can be extended—
observe the wondrous use of the true scriptures.
Having obtained this,
what more is there to seek?
Thus, I wave my hand to the red dust,
and soar my spirit to the azure sea.
Fúsāng is in sight,
Pénglái Island is not far.
Gazing from afar at the imperial gates,
I cannot express enough my dog-and-horse attachment to my lord."
Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng, reading the memorial, found it extraordinary,
and immediately ordered generous care for his family.
He urgently summoned Táng Ruòshuǐ,
and with a eunuch envoy bearing an edict,
searched along the river regions and seashores,
but found no trace or news.
Twenty years later,
an old subordinate of Ruòshān, on a mission from Zhèxī to Huáinán,
saw Ruòshān selling fish in a market,
blending in with ordinary people.
Ruòshān glanced at the subordinate and invited him into a narrow alley,
which wound for several hundred paces,
before reaching a splendid mansion.
He had the subordinate stay and eat,
pitying his long poverty,
and told him to buy twenty iron ingots.
The next day, when they met again,
the iron had already turned to gold,
which he gave entirely to the subordinate.
The subordinate's surname was Liú.
Today, Liú's descendants live in Jīnlíng,
and among them are also practitioners of the Way.
Also, Chancellor Lǐ Shēn,
courtesy name Gōngchuí,
often studied at Huàshān.
When provisions at the mountain retreat ran out,
he walked out of the valley on foot,
to seek grain from distant places.
He returned only as dusk fell,
when suddenly a heavy rain arrived,
He took shelter under a huge cliff,
where the rain had drenched everything as if washing it clean.
Upon reaching the base of the cliff,
he saw a Daoist priest,
who had moored his boat on a rock.
A village boy stood holding an oar.
The man greeted him with a bow.
The Daoist priest smiled and said:
"Is that you, Gōngchuí?"
His words were as if from a close friend,
though they had never met before.
He then asked Lǐ Shēn:
"Do you perhaps know of Táng Ruòshān?"
Lǐ Shēn replied:
"I have often read the dynastic histories,
and have seen the accounts of Ruòshān attaining the Dao.
I have always admired him."
The Daoist priest said:
"I am Ruòshān.
I was about to travel to Pénglái,
but chanced upon river fog,
so I tied my boat here.
Due to our connection from a past life,
we have met briefly.
Have you truly forgotten?"
He then took Lǐ Shēn aboard the boat.
The river fog had cleared,
the mountain peaks were as bright as day,
and the moonlight was brilliant.
The boat sailed through the air, floating along,
and in a moment, they had reached the island of Pénglái.
Golden towers and jade halls
stood in majestic rows against the sky.
Several immortals were there,
all old friends.
They wished for him to stay.
One among them said:
"Gōngchuí is still destined to assist the state in governing affairs.
Only after fulfilling that fate may he return."
Lǐ Shēn also held ambitions for managing worldly affairs,
and did not yet wish to dwell here.
The assembled immortals again instructed Ruòshān to escort him back to Huàshān.
Later, he indeed became a chancellor,
successively wielding military authority.
After his passing from this world,
he would also ascend again to the ranks of the immortals.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Sīmìng Jūn
Sīmìng Jūn
was often born among the common people.
In his childhood,
he studied together with Táng Yuánguī.
Yuánguī said:
His family had for generations served the Dao.
Morning and evening, with incense and candles,
they recited the "Gāoshàng Xiāozāi Jīng" and the "Lǎojūn Zhěnzhōng Jīng".
Repeatedly there were auspicious signs:
strange fragrances and auspicious clouds
arose within the courtyard.
His mother dreamed of heavenly beings filling the sky,
all over ten feet tall,
with banners, streamers, and canopies,
shading their dwelling.
A yellow light shone upon her body,
like the color of gold,
and she conceived and gave birth to him.
At birth, he opened his eyes and mouth,
with an expression as if smiling.
From a young age he was intelligent and perceptive,
reciting and studying the classics,
surpassing what Yuánguī could achieve.
At fifteen or sixteen,
he suddenly disappeared to an unknown place,
likely traveling the world seeking teachers and inquiring about the Dao.
It is unknown who his teacher was,
but he obtained the secrets of the immortals.
In the second year of the Bǎoyìng era.
Yuánguī served as a censor,
appointed as an investigative commissioner for the Hénán circuit.
Arriving at the outskirts of Zhèngzhōu,
he suddenly met Sīmìng Jūn.
Sīmìng Jūn's clothes were ragged,
and his appearance haggard.
Yuánguī deeply pitied him,
and spoke with him, reminiscing about old times.
He asked what he had been studying.
Sīmìng Jūn said:
"After we parted,
I have only been cultivating the truth."
He invited Yuánguī to his home,
asking his mounted attendants to wait at the inn.
Sīmìng Jūn went with Yuánguī,
leading him to the side of the market.
The gate and alley were low and small,
with only one or two followers.
As soon as they entered,
the outer gate closed,
and the attendants could not enter.
The second gate was somewhat more spacious.
Entering another gate,
the buildings were very large.
He bowed to Yuánguī at the gate.
First entering to prepare the mats,
after a long while he came out to welcome him.
Yuánguī saw that his appearance was majestic and radiant,
looking about twenty years old,
wearing a cloud-patterned cap and rainbow-colored robes.
Around him were jade boys and maidens, thirty or fifty in number,
none of whom seemed of this world.
Yuánguī could not fathom it.
He was led up to the hall.
The food set out was exquisite and delicious,
the vessels rare and extraordinary.
Even a feast bestowed by a king
could not compare.
After clearing the meal, wine was served.
Sīmìng Jūn sat together with his wife.
He then said:
"We cannot let the Attendant Censor sit alone."
He immediately summoned someone,
who sat beside Yuánguī.
Yuánguī looked at her—
it was his own wife.
Music was played, and they drank merrily.
Once drunk, each departed,
and in the end, no personal sentiments were asked or expressed.
At dawn they bid farewell,
and Sīmìng Jūn gifted Yuánguī a golden ruler and a jade whip.
After walking several *li* from the gate,
Yuánguī sent someone to find the place again,
but there was no trace left.
Upon returning to the capital,
he asked his wife, "Did anything unusual happen?"
She recounted in detail:
"On that day, I felt drowsy,
and a man in black clothes came,
saying Sīmìng Jūn summoned me,
so I followed him.
Upon reaching Sīmìng Jūn's palace,
I saw myself drinking with you."
What she described matched exactly,
with no discrepancy.
Ten years later,
Yuánguī was on a mission to the Jiānglíng region.
Mooring his boat again at Jiāngxī,
he saw Sīmìng Jūn on the shore.
He was invited into a thatched hall,
and again arrived at an immortal realm.
They lingered, eating and drinking,
but the music and attendants
were somewhat more numerous than before,
and all were unfamiliar faces.
When they parted,
Sīmìng Jūn gifted Yuánguī a drinking vessel.
It resembled jade but was not jade,
and he did not speak its name.
From then on they bid farewell,
and never met again.
It is also unknown what Sīmìng Jūn presided over,
what Dao he cultivated,
what his rank among the immortals was,
how high or low it was fixed,
or even what his surname and given name were.
One day,
a foreign merchant came to Yuánguī's residence in the Eastern Capital,
and said to Yuánguī:
"There is an aura of a rare treasure in your house.
I wish to see it."
Yuánguī showed him his family's possessions,
but none were it.
Then he brought out the drinking vessel gifted by Sīmìng Jūn and showed it to the merchant.
The merchant rose respectfully, then knelt to receive it.
Holding it, he kowtowed and said:
"This is the Flowing Splendor Precious Goblet of the Celestial Emperor.
Placed under the sun,
it emits a white vapor connecting to the heavens;
placed on a jade plate,
it shines with a red light illuminating the surroundings."
He and Yuánguī immediately tested it in the sunlight.
White vapor rose like clouds,
billowing directly upward,
connecting with the sky.
Sun
(Míng manuscript: "Sun" written as "Said")
Testing it again at night,
this was also true.
This treasure is one of the twenty-four treasures in the Supreme Northwest Treasury that guard the Central Plain.
In recent years, they have begun to descend in succession.
This is now the twenty-second treasure.
It will also not remain long in the human world.
It is about to fly away.
He who obtains this treasure
will receive blessings for seven generations.
Revere it!
Yuánguī placed it on a jade plate.
At night, he saw red light filling the room.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Xuánzhēnzǐ
Xuánzhēnzi's surname was Zhāng,
and his given name was Zhìhé.
He was from Shānyīn in Kuàijī.
He was widely learned and capable in writing,
and was selected as a jìnshì.
He was skilled in calligraphy
("Yúnjí Qīqiān" 113b has "calligraphy" as "painting").
He could drink three dǒu of wine without getting drunk.
He preserved his authenticity and nurtured his qì,
lying in the snow without feeling cold,
and entering water without getting wet.
He traveled to and visited
all the famous mountains and rivers under heaven.
Duke Lǔguó, Yán Zhēnqīng, was a close friend of his.
When Zhēnqīng served as the prefect of Húzhōu,
he gathered with his guests for a drinking party,
and they took turns composing "Fisherman's Songs" in response to each other.
The first one to sing was Zhìhé's song,
which went:
"By the banks of Xīsài Mountain, white birds fly;
peach blossoms on flowing water, mandarin fish grow plump.
A green bamboo hat,
a green straw raincoat—
slanting wind and fine rain, no need to return."
Zhēnqīng, along with Lù Hóngjiàn, Xú Shìhéng, and Lǐ Chéngjǔ, composed twenty-five songs in total,
each praising and admiring the others' work.
Zhìhé then ordered an artist to cut plain silk
and paint scenes according to the lyrics
("Yúnjí Qīqiān" 113b has "according to" as "matching").
In a short while,
five versions were completed.
The flowers, trees, birds, and fish,
the landscapes and scenery,
and the traces of wondrous and extraordinary sights
were unparalleled in both ancient and modern times.
Zhēnqīng and his guests passed them around to admire,
and they sighed in admiration without end.
Later, when Zhēnqīng traveled east to Píngwàng Station,
Zhìhé, in a state of tipsy exhilaration,
performed a water play:
he spread a mat on the water and sat alone on it,
drinking, laughing, and reciting poetry.
The mat moved back and forth, sometimes slow, sometimes fast,
as if propelled by the sound of oars.
Moreover, clouds and cranes followed and covered him from above.
Zhēnqīng, along with his relatives, guests, and attendants who were watching,
were all astonished.
Soon after, Zhìhé waved his hand on the water
to bid farewell to Zhēnqīng,
and ascended upward, departing.
To this day, his paintings are still treasured and passed down among mortals.
From "Xù Xiān Zhuàn"
Liú Báiyún
Liú Báiyún
was from Jiāngdū in Yángzhōu.
His family was wealthy and he was fond of righteousness;
he possessed much wealth and silk,
which he often used to aid others.
He was also unaware of the practices of accumulating hidden merit and self-cultivation.
Suddenly, while in Jiāngdū,
he encountered a Dàoshi,
who called himself Lè Zǐcháng
and said his home was in Hǎilíng.
He said:
"You possess the celestial bones of an immortal register,
yet you wander adrift in the dust of the mortal world—
why is that?"
He then took out two scrolls from his sleeve and gave them to him.
Báiyún received the books with both hands,
opened them, and looked at the chapter titles.
Just as he was about to express his thanks,
Zǐcháng sighed and said:
"You must first attain transformation
before receiving the Dào.
This was predetermined."
He then pointed out and taught him the methods in order.
After a long while,
Zǐcháng disappeared from sight.
Báiyún followed his teachings and practiced accordingly.
He became able to command wind and rain
and transform all things.
Then, on a small hill across the river in Xiāngzhōu, he transformed into several thousand soldiers,
among whom he erected a purple cloud tent,
with celestial beings serving as guards.
This lasted for months without dispersing.
The military governor, Yú Dí, suspected it was demonic illusion,
and ordered the military commander Lǐ Xīhuá to lead troops to attack it.
The tent and its guards gradually rose higher,
so that arrows could not reach them.
The administrative officer, Dòu Chǔyuē, said:
"This is illusionary magic;
defiling it will make it disperse."
They then took corpse filth and burned it beneath the tent,
and indeed, the soldiers and guards scattered.
Báiyún, riding a horse with over forty followers,
fled across the Hàn River,
treading on the waves and stirring up dust
as if walking on flat ground,
making it impossible to pursue him.
He said to his pursuers:
"I am Liú Báiyún."
Later, in Jiāngxī and Húnán,
many people saw him,
and he appeared even more youthful and fair-skinned.
At that time, the prefect of Húnán, Wáng Xùn, was fond of the Dào,
and Báiyún often came to the commandery.
Suddenly, one day, he bid farewell and left,
saying to Xùn:
"I am going to Hóngzhōu,
and we will meet again in Zhōnglíng."
With a single bow, he departed.
At first, Xùn did not understand his meaning.
Báiyún departed from Língchuān in the morning,
and by noon, he was already in Xiāngtán.
Many people recognized him,
and upon verifying his journey,
it was found he had traveled seven hundred lǐ in an instant.
Ten days later,
Wáng Xùn was indeed appointed to Hóngzhōu.
After assuming his post,
Báiyún also came to visit him.
He also encountered the Perfected Lè again in Jiāngdū.
The Perfected said:
"You have wandered the mortal world
for many years now.
The scripture of the Golden Liquid and Nine Elixirs,
commanded by the Supreme,
is to be bestowed upon you.
You may choose a famous mountain or blessed land to refine and ingest it.
After a thousand days,
you will be able to ascend to the clouds and heavens."
During the Qiánfú era,
he was still selling medicine in Cháng'ān market.
There were those who recognized him,
but they could not approach him closely,
and thus had no way to learn from him as a master.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Xī Jiàn
Zhèng Shǔ of Xíngyáng,
was the younger brother of Zhèng Qián, a court historian.
He was erudite and versatile,
fond of the extraordinary and devoted to chivalrous deeds.
Once, while hosting guests,
the conversation turned to strange occurrences in the world.
Zhèng Shǔ said:
"Have you gentlemen read the History of the Jìn Dynasty?
Did you see the account of Grand Marshal Xī Jiàn?
Although the History of the Jìn says that man died,
he is actually still alive today."
The seated guests exclaimed in surprise:
"We would like to hear your explanation."
Zhèng Shǔ said:
"I have a friend, Duàn Yáng of Wǔwēi,
who served as the magistrate of Dìngxiāng.
Duàn Yáng had a son named Duàn Jí,
who from a young age loved purity and emptiness, admired the Way,
and abstained from wine and meat.
At the age of sixteen,
he requested of his father:
'I wish to seek out famous mountains,
and visit extraordinary individuals to inquire about the Way.'
Duàn Yáng consented,
gave him a hundred thousand coins,
and allowed him to follow his aspiration.
In the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era, Duàn Jí,
while traveling through Wèi Commandery,
lodged at an inn.
At the inn, there was a guest
who drove a donkey himself,
and had purchased several dozen catties of medicinal herbs,
all substances for nourishing life and abstaining from grains.
Among these herbs, there were some difficult to obtain and not yet fully acquired,
so every day he would visit the market lodgings to seek out foreign merchants for them.
Duàn Jí observed this guest:
he was over seventy years old,
with snow-white eyebrows and frosty beard,
yet his complexion was like peach blossoms,
and he also did not eat grains.
Duàn Jí knew he was a Daoist practitioner,
and was overjoyed.
Waiting for a moment of leisure,
he bought rare fruits and fine delicacies,
medicinal foods and fine wine,
and offered them to the guest.
The guest was very surprised,
and said to Duàn Jí:
'I am a mountain elder,
who came here to purchase medicine,
and do not wish for the world to know of me.
How did you perceive me and come to this?'"
Duàn Jí said:
'Although I am young in years,
my nature delights in emptiness and tranquility.
Seeing your actions,
I knew you must be a Daoist practitioner,
and thus wished for a joyful meeting.'
The guest was pleased,
and they drank until evening,
then stayed together overnight.
After several days, when his affairs were concluded and he was about to depart,
he said to Duàn Jí:
'My surname is Mèng,
given name Qīsī,
and I reside on Héng Mountain,
ninety lǐ northwest of Xíngtáng County.
Now you know my name as such.
Duàn Jí then prepared a farewell feast for him,
kowtowed sincerely and pleaded,
