wishing to go to the mountains
to inquire and receive the essentials of the Way.
The elder said:
'If that is so,
I see your determination is firm,
and you may dwell with us;
however, dwelling in the mountains is very arduous,
one must endure hunger and cold,
thus many who study the Way
often give up their resolve;
moreover, there are venerable elders in the mountains,
whom I must inform.
Consider this carefully.'
Duàn Jí again firmly requested.
The elder, knowing he was determined,
then said to him:
'On the twentieth day of the eighth month,
I will go to Xíngtáng.
You may go thirty lǐ to the northwest,
where there is a solitary old woman's estate.
The old woman of this estate
is a most extraordinary person.
You should pay her a visit.
Explain your purpose and intent,
and wait there for me.'
Duàn Jí bowed twice and accepted the arrangement.
When the time came, he went,
and indeed found this solitary estate.
The old woman came out and asked him.
Duàn Jí told her everything.
The old woman patted his back and said:
'Such a young lad as you,
yet able to love the Way—
how splendid!'
She then stored his baggage in a cabinet,
and seated Duàn Jí in the hall's front chamber.
The old woman's household was very wealthy,
and provided Duàn Jí with all he needed in great abundance.
After twenty days, Mr. Mèng arrived.
Looking at Duàn Jí, he said:
'I originally thought it was just casual talk,
never expecting you would truly come;
however, I have business in Héng Prefecture,
you stay here for now,
and I shall return in a few days.'
As he said, he returned,
and again said to Duàn Jí:
'I have further informed the venerable elders,
and will go with you together,
returning again in a few days.'
He instructed the old woman to take charge of all Duàn Jí's belongings and baggage,
and had Duàn Jí bring only his personal clothes and bedding along.
Duàn Jí then followed Mr. Mèng into the mountains.
For the first thirty lǐ,
the path was extremely rugged and perilous,
yet he could still tread it;
for another thirty lǐ,
he had to grasp vines and creepers with his hands,
and tread on steep cliffs with his feet,
his spirit trembling and sweat pouring out,
barely able to reach the destination.
As for their dwelling place,
to the east and south,
there were towering mountains and massive rocks,
with dense, verdant forests.
The north side was somewhat level,
where various ridges and peaks stood.
The west side dropped precipitously,
with layered ravines a thousand rèn deep,
yet there were fertile fields,
which the mountain dwellers cultivated extensively.
Among these were six tiled houses,
with several structures in front and behind.
To their north,
the various masters resided.
The eastern wing had a kitchen stove,
with a flying spring cascading down between the eaves,
serving in place of drawing water from a well.
Inside the northern door,
the two western rooms formed one chamber,
its door closed.
The eastern and western rooms formed two chambers,
where six masters lived.
In the corridor in front of their chambers,
there were several shelves of books,
two or three thousand volumes in total.
There were a thousand dàn of grain,
medicinal substances in great abundance,
and fine wine always several dàn in quantity.
Duàn Jí paid his respects to the various masters.
The masters told him:
'Dwelling in the mountains differs from the human world,
and is also very arduous.
One must endure hunger and privation,
and consume medicinal preparations.
Only if you can accept this
may you dwell here.
Can you do it?'
Duàn Jí said:
'I can.'
Thus he stayed.
After five days in all,
Mr. Mèng said:
'Today, why not pay a visit to the Old Master.'
So they opened the western chamber,
within which was a stone hall.
The hall opened to the north,
looking directly down upon the river valley below.
And the Old Master sat upon a rope-bed,
facing north with a purified heart.
Duàn Jí respectfully paid homage to the Old Master.
After a long while, the Old Master opened his eyes,
and said to Elder Mèng:
'Is this the one you spoke of?
This youth is excellent.
Let him be your disciple.'
Then they took their leave and exited,
and closed the door again.
In front of the courtyard, facing the western ravine,
there were ten pine trees,
each several rèn tall.
Beneath them were massive rocks,
where a hundred people could sit.
On these rocks, a board was carved,
and during their leisure time, the various masters
would often play chess and drink wine there.
Duàn Jí served as an attendant,
and observing the masters' chess games,
found them all unskilled,
so he taught them the strategies and formations.
The various masters said:
'You also understand Go,
you may sit.'
Thereupon he played against the old men,
and none of the old men could match him.
Then the old master ordered the door to be opened and went out,
leaning on his staff as he stood facing the cliff.
Gazing westward for a long time,
he then turned and said the old man could play Go,
Mèng Qīsī said:
'None of us can match this young fellow.'
The old master smiled,
then sat down and summoned Jì.
'I will play against you.'
After a while, the master's Go skills were slightly inferior to Jì's.
He smiled again and said to Jì:
'What art would you like to learn?'
Jì was young,
and did not know to seek esoteric arts,
but merely said he wished to study the Book of Changes for now.
The old master instructed Old Man Mèng to teach it to him.
The old master then returned to his room,
and closed his door.
Jì studied the Book of Changes for over a year and gradually became proficient.
He practiced divination and laid out hexagrams,
and his predictions were as if divine.
Jì stayed on the mountain for four years,
and during that time, he saw the old master come out of his door
no more than five or six times.
He only sat upright on a rope-bed in his room,
focusing his mind in meditation,
and once he entered meditation, he would not emerge for two or three hundred days.
The old master often kept his eyes mostly closed,
his appearance was that of a child's face,
his body was extremely plump and full,
and he no longer ate at all.
Whenever he emerged from meditation,
he would sometimes drink a small amount of medicinal liquid,
but its name was unknown.
Later, the old master suddenly said:
'I made an appointment with the Zhūgé immortal family of Nányuè,
and now the time has come,
I must go.'
Jì had been on the mountain for a long time,
and suddenly missed home,
so he requested to return home to visit his family,
and then come back.
Master Mèng angrily said:
'If you're going home, then go home,
what do you mean by coming back!'
He then reported this to the old master.
The old master reproached Old Man Mèng, saying:
'Knowing that this person would not persist,
why did you bring him here?'
Thereupon, he sent him home.
One year after returning home,
he went back again to seek the various masters,
but when he arrived, the house was as before,
the doors and windows were sealed shut,
and there was no one there at all.
He went down the mountain and asked an old woman in a solitary village.
The old woman said:
'The various masters have not come,
it has been
Míng manuscript has "xiàng" for "shàng"
a year already.'
Jì then regretted it almost to death.
While on the mountain,
Jì often asked Old Man Mèng.
'What is the old master's name?'
The old man took the Book of Jin, Biography of Xī Jiàn, and had him read it,
saying:
'If you wish to know the old master,
he is Grand Marshal Xī.'
From Records Heard
Monk Qìxū
There was a monk named Qìxū,
originally the son of the Lǐ family from Gūzāng.
His father served as a Censor during Emperor Xuánzōng's reign.
From childhood, Qìxū was fond of the Buddhist dharma.
At the age of twenty,
he shaved his head, donned coarse robes,
and resided in a Buddhist temple in Cháng'ān.
When Ān Lùshān breached the Tóng Pass,
and Emperor Xuánzōng fled west to the Shu region,
Qìxū retreated into the Tàibái Mountains,
gathering cypress leaves to eat,
and from then on abstained from grains.
One day,
a Daoist priest named Qiáo Jūn,
with a gaunt and refined appearance,
his beard and temples completely white,
came to visit Qìxū.
He said to Qìxū:
"Master, your spirit and bone structure are remarkably solitary and outstanding;
in the future, you will surely roam the immortal capital."
Qìxū replied:
"I am a mundane person;
how could I possibly reach the immortal capital?"
Qiáo Jūn said:
"The immortal capital is very near;
Master, you can strive to go there."
Qìxū then asked Qiáo Jūn to guide him on the path.
Qiáo Jūn said:
"Master, you should prepare food at an inn in the Shāng Mountains.
When you encounter a porter
(pronounced fèng),
that is, one who carries a bamboo pack and trades,
then offer him provisions at the Shāng Mountains.
If anyone asks where you are going,
simply say you wish to visit Zhìchuān
(The original text had "用" for "川";
amended according to the Huáng block-printed edition.)
and a porter will guide you there."
Hearing these words,
Qìxū was overjoyed.
After Ān Lùshān's defeat,
when the Emperor returned from Shu to Cháng'ān,
and peace was restored under heaven,
Qìxū went to the Shāng Mountains,
staying at an inn.
He prepared fine and pure food,
waiting to offer it to a porter.
After several months,
he encountered over a hundred porters,
all of whom ate their fill and departed.
Qìxū's resolve began to waver,
and he thought Qiáo Jūn had deceived him.
He prepared to return to Cháng'ān,
and had already packed his belongings.
That evening,
a very young porter
said to Qìxū:
"Where does my master wish to go?"
Qìxū replied:
"For years, I have wished to visit Zhìchuān."
The porter exclaimed in surprise:
"Zhìchuān is an immortal palace;
how could my master possibly reach it?"
Qìxū responded:
"Since childhood, I have been fond of immortals.
I once met a transcendent being
who encouraged me to visit Zhìchuān.
How far is the journey?"
The porter said:
"Zhìchuān is very near.
Does Master truly wish to accompany me there?"
Qìxū said:
"If I can truly visit Zhìchuān,
I would not regret it even in death."
Thereupon, the porter and Qìxū went together to the highlands of Lántián,
to prepare their gear.
That evening, they ascended the Jade Mountain.
Traversing perilous paths,
climbing over cliffs and peaks,
for about eighty *lǐ*,
they reached a cave,
from which water flowed.
The porter and Qìxū together gathered stones to block the cave entrance,
damming the flow.
After three days,
the water in the cave finally ceased.
The two entered the cave together;
it was dark and obscure, impossible to see.
They saw a gate several tens of *lǐ* away,
and proceeded towards it.
Once outside the cave,
the breeze and sunlight were gentle and warm,
the mountains and waters clear and beautiful—
truly an immortal capital.
Traveling another hundred-plus *lǐ*,
they climbed a high mountain.
The mountain's peaks clustered together, towering and steep;
the stone path was perilous and precipitous.
Qìxū grew dizzy and hesitant, not daring to ascend.
The porter said:
"The immortal capital is nearly upon us;
why hesitate?"
He then took Qìxū by the hand and proceeded.
Upon reaching the mountaintop,
the surface was level and broad.
Looking down at the rivers and plains below,
they appeared distant and indistinct.
Traveling another hundred-plus *lǐ*,
they entered another cave.
Upon emerging,
they saw boundless accumulated water.
In the water was a stone path,
about a foot wide,
stretching over a hundred *lǐ* long.
The porter led Qìxū, treading the stone path forward.
Reaching the foot of a mountain,
before them stood a giant tree,
its dense foliage casting deep shadows,
towering several thousand *xún* high.
The porter climbed the tree and let out a long whistle.
After a while,
an autumn wind suddenly arose from the treetops.
Presently, they saw a giant rope tied to a traveling pack,
being lowered from the mountaintop.
The porter instructed Qìxū to close his eyes and sit in the pack.
After about half a day,
the porter said:
"Master, you may awaken and look now."
When Qìxū looked,
he was already atop the mountain.
He saw a city with palaces and towers,
where jade and pearls shone upon each other,
beyond the clouds and mist.
The porter pointed and said:
"This is Zhìchuān."
Thereupon, they went together to that place.
They saw hundreds of immortal youths,
arrayed in rows before and behind.
One immortal said to the porter:
"Who is this monk?
Is he not a man of the mortal world?"
The porter replied:
"This monk has long wished to visit Zhìchuān,
so I brought him here."
Soon they reached a hall,
where one wearing hairpins and a crown,
of exceedingly majestic appearance,
sat leaning on a jade table.
Guards stood in a circle around him,
their prohibitions and commands extremely strict.
The porter instructed Qìxū to bow in reverence,
and said:
"This is the True Lord of Zhìchuān."
Qìxū bowed.
The True Lord summoned Qìxū forward,
and inquired:
"Have you severed the enmity of the Three Péngs?"
Qìxū could not reply.
The True Lord said:
"You truly cannot remain here."
He then ordered the porter to ascend the Cuìxiá Pavilion.
This pavilion spanned the void,
its railings standing amidst towering clouds.
They saw a man with bared shoulders, his eyes closed,
his hair several tens of feet long,
glossy, dark, and black,
piercingly bright to the eye and mind.
The porter said to Qìxū:
"You may approach and bow to him."
Qìxū bowed.
He then asked, "Who is this person?
Why are his eyes closed?"
The porter said:
"This is Gentleman Yáng.
Gentleman Yáng was a member of the Suí imperial clan,
serving as a Gentleman in the Southern Palace.
At the end of the Suí dynasty,
when the empire was fragmented and torn,
and weapons and armor caused great turmoil,
he retreated to dwell in the mountains.
Now he has attained the Dao.
These are not closed eyes;
this is 'penetrating vision.'
One with penetrating vision
fixes his gaze upon the human world."
Qìxū said:
"May I ask him to open his eyes?
Would that be possible?"
The porter then addressed Gentleman Yáng directly.
Suddenly, he opened his eyes and looked around;
their light grew even more radiant,
like the shining of the sun and moon.
Qìxū trembled with fear, his back sweating,
every hair on his body standing on end.
They also saw a man lying beneath a stone cliff.
The porter said:
"This man's surname is Yǐ,
his given name is Zhīrùn.
He too was a man of the mortal world,
who attained the Dao and reached this state."
Afterwards, Bèngzǐ led Qìxū back,
and the path they traveled was the same as the one they had taken before.
Qìxū then asked Bèngzǐ:
"Earlier when I paid my respects to the True Lord,
he asked me about 'the enmity of the Three Péngs,'
but I could not answer.
He said:
"Péng is the surname of the Three Corpses,
which constantly reside within humans,
observing and noting their transgressions.
Every Gēngshēn day,
they report to the Supreme Emperor.
Therefore, those who study immortality must first eliminate their Three Corpses;
only then can they attain divinity.
Otherwise,
no matter how much they torment their minds, it will be of no avail."
Qìxū understood the matter,
and from then on he returned,
settling on Tàibái Mountain,
abstaining from grains and inhaling qi,
never speaking to anyone about the matter of Zhìchuān.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
he moved to live beneath Huà Mountain.
There were Zhèng Shēn from Xíngyáng and Shěn Yù from Wúxīng,
both traveling east from Cháng'ān through the pass,
and when they reached the foot of Huà Mountain,
it was dusk and a heavy rain fell,
so the two men stopped.
Because Qìxū abstained from grains,
he did not prepare meals.
Zhèng found it strange that he did not eat,
yet his bones were robust and his appearance elegant,
so he inquired about the truth.
Qìxū then told Zhèng about the matter of Zhìchuān.
Zhèng, being a curious person,
upon hearing the story,
was both amazed and astonished.
When he returned from east of the pass,
he revisited Qìxū's dwelling,
but Qìxū had already disappeared,
and no one knew where he had gone.
Zhèng often recounted the story,
calling it "The Record of Zhìchuān."
Taken from "Records of the Xuan Chamber"
The Nine Heavens Envoy
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Emperor Xuánzōng dreamed of divine beings with feathered guards,
thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of riders,
gathered in the sky.
One person in vermilion robes and a golden crown,
descended in a chariot,
and paid homage to the emperor, saying:
"I am an inspector of the Nine Heavens,
patrolling and correcting affairs in the mortal world.
I wish to establish a lower palace
northwest of Lú Mountain,
where there are already foundations of wood and stone,
but only labor is needed."
The emperor immediately dispatched a palace envoy
to the northwest of the mountain,
and indeed, the foundations were clearly visible.
After a couple of days,
thousands of large timbers
arrived naturally,
not transported by humans.
Halls, palaces, corridors, and chambers
were supplied with wood according to their needs,
all sufficiently provided.
Some say
these timbers were once felled by the Prince of Jiǔjiāng,
intended for building a palace,
but sank in the Pénpǔ River of Jiāngzhōu;
now, divine beings transported them
for use here.
West of the temple, a long corridor
had pillars and foundations suspended in the air,
over a great ravine.
Below, rushing waters roared,
deep and unfathomable,
yet over many years,
it never collapsed or sank.
When the temple was first built,
timbers arrived together,
countless in a single night,
all bearing water marks.
The foundations of the gates, halls, and corridors
naturally formed,
not built by human hands.
Often, divine light of five colors
illuminated the temple grounds,
bright as daylight.
Workers wielded axes and labored
without rest,
yet never grew weary,
and the temple was completed in ten days.
Upon completion,
the palace envoy dreamed of a divine being saying:
"Red clay, white chalk, cinnabar, and green pigments
are in the ground north of the temple;
search and you will find them,
no need to seek afar."
So they searched,
gathered them for use,
and lacked nothing.
Later, over five hundred spirit officials from Jiànchāng Crossing,
dressed like Daoist priests,
all said they were going to the Envoy's temple.
Their images are preserved to this day.
Initially, when Emperor Xuánzōng dreamed of the divine being,
he summoned the Tiāntái Daoist priest Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn
to inquire about the matter.
Chéngzhēn reported:
"Now, the gods of famous mountains and rivers who receive blood sacrifices
preside over worship and offerings.
The Supreme Elder, concerned they might abuse their power,
harming the common people,
has assigned superior true beings
to oversee mountains and rivers.
There are True Lords of the Five Sacred Mountains.
Moreover, the Elder of Qīngchéng is the chief of the Five Sacred Mountains,
the Nine Heavens Director of Lifespans of Qián Mountain establishes the registers of life for the Nine Heavens,
and the Nine Heavens Envoy of Lú Mountain holds the tallies of the Three Heavens,
impeaching myriad gods.
All are superiors of the Five Sacred Mountains.
Why not establish temples for each,
with vegetarian offerings for worship?"
Emperor Xuánzōng complied.
That year,
temples were established
at each of the Five Sacred Mountains and Three Divine Mountains.
Taken from "Records of the Extraordinary"
Ten Immortals
Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng once dreamed of over ten immortals,
riding auspicious clouds and descending to line up in the courtyard,
each holding musical instruments and playing them.
The melody was clear and transcendent,
truly the music of the immortal realm.
When the music ended,
one immortal stepped forward and said:
"Does Your Majesty know this music?
This is the immortal tune 'Purple Cloud Melody.'
Now I wish to impart it to Your Majesty,
to be the orthodox music of the Great Táng.
It is certainly different from the Xiánchí and Dàxià melodies."
Emperor Xuánzōng was overjoyed,
and immediately received the transmission.
Soon he awoke,
the lingering echoes still as if in his ears.
Emperor Xuánzōng hastily took a jade flute and practiced playing it,
mastering the rhythm completely;
yet he kept it secret and did not reveal it.
At dawn,
he held court at the Zǐchén Hall.
When ministers Yáo Chóng and Sòng Jǐng entered,
presenting matters before the throne,
Emperor Xuánzōng lowered his head as if not hearing.
The two ministers grew fearful
and presented their matters again.
Emperor Xuánzōng stood up,
still ignoring the two ministers.
The two ministers grew even more afraid
and hurried out.
At that time, Gāo Lìshì was attending Emperor Xuánzōng,
and he memorialized:
"The ministers are requesting decisions;
Your Majesty should decide face-to-face whether to approve or not.
Earlier, what Chóng and Jǐng said
were all important matters of state and military affairs,
yet Your Majesty ignored them completely.
Have the two ministers committed some offense?"
Emperor Xuánzōng smiled and said:
"Last night I dreamed of immortals playing music called 'Purple Cloud Melody,'
and they imparted it to me.
I lost the rhythm,
so I silently practiced it,
and thus had no time to listen to the two ministers' reports."
He then took out the jade flute from his robe
and showed it to Lìshì.
That day, Lìshì went to the Central Secretariat
and told the two ministers what had happened.
The two ministers' fear somewhat subsided.
Later, the tune was passed to the Music Bureau.
Taken from "Biographies of Encounters with Immortals,"
the Chén manuscript edition cites "Records of the Xuan Chamber"
Twenty-Seven Immortals
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Emperor Xuánzōng was resting during the day,
feeling drowsy and wanting to sleep.
He dreamed of twenty-seven immortals who said:
"We are the twenty-eight lunar mansions.
One of us is on duty,
remaining in heaven and not descending.
We have been residing in a place called 'Luódǐ' for three years,
guarding the nation's borders for Your Majesty,
preventing foreign tribes from invading the frontiers.
We immortals often change our forms and mingle incognito while traveling and dwelling."
After waking,
he ordered a search throughout the empire's mountains, rivers, commanderies, and counties
for any place with the characters 'Luódǐ'.
Ultimately, it could not be found.
Another evening, he dreamed again, and they said:
"Where there is music, that is the place."
He
"[He]" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Míng manuscript and Chén's collated edition.
again issued an edict to search.
About five lǐ southeast of Níngzhōu,
there was a place named Luóchuān,
and on the river was a county,
named after the river.
There was Mount Luózhōu,
and legend spoke of a cave there,
but it was overgrown and impassable.
Woodcutters and herdsmen heard the sound of music.
Imperial envoys were sent to search for it,
but for a long time, they could not find it.
Suddenly, a white rabbit emerged from the forest
and went straight under a cliff.
Following where it entered, they found a crevice in the rock.
Inside was a spacious stone chamber,
containing twenty-seven stone statues of true immortals.
They retrieved them and presented them to the emperor.
He then set up altars in the inner palace,
burning incense morning and evening,
personally paying homage.
He ordered artisans using the jiāzhù (lacquer-cloth) technique to make twenty-seven statues,
and sent them to the original cave.
He established the Tōngshèng Temple at that location,
and changed the county's name to Zhēnníng to commemorate it.
He bestowed precious incense and a censer,
and the censer remains there to this day.
Local villagers said:
"In the past, there was an old man named Dǐ,
no one knew where he came from.
He had thick eyebrows and white hair,
different from other old men.
Sometimes he would appear, sometimes he would stay hidden,
and the local customs all respected him.
He sold wine at the foot of the mountain,
and often had extraordinary people come to drink.
Sometimes medicine-gathering boys or woodcutting fathers
would come and go from his home.
One day, the crowd said to Old Man Dǐ:
'Increase your brewing,
and let us drink one more time,
for we will not come again.'"
As they said,
he increased the brewing and waited.
When the wine was ready,
the group of immortals indeed arrived.
After drinking merrily,
one of those seated below
said to the others:
'I propose we carve the forms of all the immortals
to leave for the world.'
He then took twenty-seven pieces of stone
and carved them into twenty-seven figures.
In a moment,
he had captured the true appearances of all the immortals,
placed them in the cave,
arranged as they were seated while drinking.
He inscribed the names and titles of the immortals on their backs.
After finishing the arrangements, they dispersed.
Old Man Dǐ also was never seen again.
People of the time all said they had ascended as immortals.
As for Old Man Dǐ,
it is suspected he was the Dǐ (Root) lunar mansion.
Later, Dōngmén Gào, a Gentleman of Writings,
composed a eulogy and preface to record this.
From "The Transmission of Divine Immortal Encounters"
Yáo Hóng
During the years of Táng Emperor Tàizōng,
there was a Chán master whose practice was exceptionally profound,
dwelling on Nányuè (Mount Heng).
Suddenly one day,
he saw a creature walking upright towards him,
coming directly before the monk.
Green fur covered its body.
The Chán master was afraid,
thinking it was some kind of owl-like creature;
but looking closely at its face,
it was like a human's.
The monk then asked:
"Patron, are you a mountain spirit?
Or a wild beast?
And for what reason have you specifically come here?
This humble monk dwells in meditation here,
disturbing no living creature.
If spirits have awareness,
do not trouble me."
After a long while,
the creature joined its palms and said:
"What era is it now?"
The monk said:
"The Great Táng."
It said again:
"Does the reverend know of the Jìn and Sòng dynasties?
How many years have passed from then until now?"
The monk said:
"From Jìn until now,
it has been nearly one hundred and four years."
The creature then said:
"The reverend is well-versed in antiquity and knows the present,
surely you know of Yáo Hóng?"
The monk said:
"I know of him."
The creature said:
"I am Hóng."
The monk said:
"I have read the 'History of Jìn',
which states that Yáo Hóng was captured by Liú Yù,
who relocated the Yáo clan south of the river,
and executed Hóng in the marketplace of Jiànkāng.
According to that record,
Hóng died then.
How is it that today you again call yourself Yáo Hóng?"
Hóng said:
"At that time,
my state was indeed destroyed by Yù,
and I was sent to the marketplace of Jiànkāng
to be made a public example;
however, before the execution could be carried out,
I managed to escape and go into hiding.
Since Yù could not find me,
he then used someone who resembled me and beheaded him instead,
to establish his authority,
and show the people what followed.
I am truly Hóng's original self."
The monk then invited him to sit,
and said to him:
"Can the histories' accounts be false words?"
Hóng laughed and said:
"Reverend, have you not heard of Liú Ān, the Prince of Huáinán of the Hàn?
He actually attained immortality and ascended,
yet Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù depicted him as a rebel who was executed.
The falsehoods of Hàn histories,
are they not surpassed by later histories?
This is proof that historians speak falsely.
Since I escaped to the mountains and wilds,
I have roamed freely at will,
exploring every blessed land and quiet hut.
I have investigated them all.
Having ceased cooked food,
I traveled far to this peak,
delighting in the Way and wandering free,
consuming only the leaves of pines and cypresses.
As years and ages passed,
green fur grew all over my body,
and I have attained the Way of long life and deathlessness."
The monk asked further:
"Eating pine and cypress leaves,
how could it lead to such fur growth?"
Hóng said:
"In the past, palace women of Qín, fleeing the chaos and withdrawing from the world,
entered the peaks of Tàihuà (Mount Hua),
and fed on its pines and cypresses.
As the years and sacrifices slowly passed,
their bodies grew bluish-green fur over a chǐ long.
If they encountered people of the world,
the people would be startled and amazed.
To this day, it is called Máonǚ Peak (Hairy Maiden Peak).
Moreover, you reverend seem to believe in antiquity quite a bit,
surely you know and believe this in detail?"
The monk then asked what sustenance he required.
Hóng said:
"I have not consumed the flavors of the world for a long time,
I only drink one bowl of tea."
He then recounted for the monk the events of the Jìn and Sòng dynasties through the ages,
as clearly as pointing to his own palm.
Furthermore, regarding matters historians omitted and did not record,
Hóng recounted them all in detail.
Afterwards, he bid farewell to the monk and departed,
and was never seen again.
From "Unofficial Histories"
Lǐ Wèigōng
In Sūzhōu's Chángshú County, there was a Dān Zūnshī of the Yuányáng Temple,
whose religious name was Yǐqīng.
During the Dàlì era,
he often traveled to Jiāxīng.
Once, while boarding a boat,
he noticed a rather strong fragrance,
and suspected there might be an extraordinary person aboard.
Looking around at the passengers on the boat,
they all appeared to be merchants and traders,
except for one person at the bow of the boat,
whose appearance was quite unusual,
and whose demeanor was serene and tranquil.
When Dān Jūn reached the middle of the journey,
he told the boatman
to change his seat to the bow,
so he could speak with that person.
After they sat together,
the fragrance became even stronger.
Dān Jūn then calmly inquired about it.
The man replied:
"I am originally from this area.
When I was young, I contracted leprosy,
and my eyebrows and hair all fell out.
Disgusted with myself,
I secretly fled into the deep mountains,
intending to let tigers and leopards devour me.
After several days,
the mountain path grew deeper,
and there were no traces of people anywhere.
Suddenly, I met an old man who asked:
'Who are you,
coming so far into the mountains?'
I explained my intentions in detail.
The old man took pity on me.
Looking at me, he said:
'Your illness has brought you to me,
and now it can be cured.
Follow me.'
So I followed the old man,
traveling over ten li into the mountains,
until we reached a stream.
Crossing the water for over ten paces,
the view suddenly opened up to a broad expanse,
with several thatched cottages.
The old man said:
'You cannot enter just yet.
Stay in this cottage for a month,
and I will come back to see you.'
He then gave me a packet of pills,
telling me to take them.
He also said:
'In this cottage, there are yellow essence, lily bulbs, poria, Chinese yam, dates, chestnuts, perilla, honey, and the like—
eat as much as you wish.'
I entered the cottage and stayed there,
and the old man left,
going even deeper into the mountains.
After taking the medicine,
I felt neither hunger nor thirst,
only a sense of lightness in my body.
After about two months had passed like this,
the old man finally returned.
Seeing me, he laughed and said:
'You are still here—
you truly have determination!
Your illness is already cured,
do you know?'
I replied:
'I do not know.'
The old man said:
'Look at your reflection in the water.'
My hair and eyebrows had all grown back,
and my complexion was much younger and healthier.
The old man said:
'You are not meant to stay here long.
Since you have taken my medicine,
not only is your illness cured,
but you can also live long in the human world.
Practice the Daoist arts diligently,
and I will meet you again in twenty years.'
He then instructed me to return to the human world.
At our parting,
I bowed and asked:
and hope you will graciously tell me?'
The old man said:
'Have you not heard of Lǐ Jìng, the Duke of Wèi from the early Táng dynasty?
That is me.'
So I bid farewell and left the mountains.
Now, I fear my cultivation may not yet meet the sage's expectations,
and as the twenty-year deadline approaches,
I am returning to the mountains to seek my teacher again."
Dān Jūn recorded this story
and told it to others.
From "Records of Original Immortals,"
the Ming manuscript version says "Records of Original Transformations."
Zhāng Guǒ
Zhāng Guǒ was a man who
lived in seclusion on Tiáo Mountain in Héngzhōu,
often traveling between Fén and Jìn.
People of the time spread word that he possessed secret arts for longevity.
Elders said:
"When we were children, we saw him,
and he himself claimed to be several hundred years old."
Táng Tàizōng and Gāozōng repeatedly summoned him,
but he did not respond.
When Zétiān summoned him to leave the mountains,
he feigned death in front of the Dùnǚ Temple.
At that time, the weather was extremely hot,
and in a short while, his body became foul, rotten, and infested with worms.
When Zétiān heard of this,
she believed he had truly died.
Later, someone saw him again in the mountains of Héngzhōu.
Guǒ often rode a white donkey,
which could travel tens of thousands of *lǐ* in a day.
When resting, he would fold it up,
as thin as paper,
and place it in a small box;
when he wanted to ride it, he would sprinkle water on it,
and it would transform back into a donkey.
In the twenty-third year of the Kāiyuán era,
Xuánzōng dispatched the Court Receptionist Péi Wù
to ride post-haste to Héngzhōu to welcome him.
Guǒ, in response to Wù, feigned death by holding his breath.
Wù then burned incense and made a respectful request,
conveying the emperor's intention of seeking the Way.
After a short while, Guǒ gradually revived.
Wù did not dare to pressure him further,
and hurried back to report.
The emperor then ordered the Secretariat Drafter Xú Qiáo
to follow with an imperial edict to welcome him.
Guǒ followed Qiáo to the Eastern Capital,
where he was settled in the Jíxián Academy.
He was carried into the palace in a sedan chair,
and treated with the utmost respect and courtesy.
Xuánzōng then casually said to him:
"You, sir, are one who has attained the Way.
Why are your teeth and hair so aged?"
Guǒ replied:
"In my decrepit years,
lacking any arts of the Way to rely upon,
they have naturally become like this.
It is truly shameful;
if I were to remove them all now,
would it not be better?"
Thereupon, in front of the emperor, he plucked out the hair from his temples
and knocked out his teeth,
causing blood to flow from his mouth.
Xuánzōng was greatly startled
and said to him:
"Sir, please retire to your quarters,
and we shall converse again shortly."
After a short while, he summoned him.
Guǒ now had dark hair at his temples and gleaming white teeth,
looking even more vigorous than in his prime.
One day,
the Director of the Palace Library Wáng Jiǒngzhì and the Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices Xiāo Huá once visited him together.
At that time, Xuánzōng intended to have him marry a princess,
but Guǒ was unaware of this.
Suddenly, he laughed and said to the two men:
"To take a princess as a wife
is a truly frightening prospect."
Jiǒngzhì and Huá looked at each other,
not understanding his words.
Shortly after, a palace eunuch arrived
and said to Guǒ:
"His Majesty, because the Princess Yùzhēn has been devoted to the Way since her youth,
wishes to bestow her upon you, sir."
Guǒ laughed heartily,
and in the end did not accept the decree.
Only then did the two men understand his earlier words.
At that time, many high officials went to pay their respects and visit him.
Some questioned him about matters beyond the mundane world,
but he always gave evasive answers.
He often said:
"I am a man from the Bǐngzǐ year of Yáo's time."
At the time, no one could fathom his meaning.
He also said:
"During Yáo's time, I served as a Palace Attendant."
He was skilled in embryonic breathing,
able to go for days without eating.
When he did eat, he only drank fine wine and took Sānhuáng pills.
Xuánzōng kept him in the inner palace
and offered him wine.
He declined, saying a mountain recluse could not drink more than two *shēng*.
He had a disciple, however,
who could drink about one *dǒu*.
Xuánzōng was pleased to hear this
and ordered the disciple summoned.
Shortly, a young Daoist priest,
flew down from the palace eaves.
He appeared to be about sixteen or seventeen years old,
of handsome appearance,
with refined and subtle demeanor.
When he paid his respects to the emperor,
his speech was clear and crisp,
and his manners were impeccable.
Xuánzōng ordered him to be seated.
Guǒ said:
"This disciple always stands in attendance at my side;
it is not fitting for him to be granted a seat."
Xuánzōng looked at him with even greater pleasure,
and then bestowed wine upon him.
The disciple drank up to one *dǒu*
without declining.
Guǒ then declined on his behalf, saying:
"He should not be given more.
If he exceeds his limit, something is sure to go amiss,
which will only cause Your Majesty to laugh."
Xuánzōng insisted and bestowed more wine upon him.
Suddenly, the wine gushed forth from the top of the disciple's head,
his hat fell to the ground,
and transformed into a wine vessel
(Míng Chāo edition has "vessel lid" after "vessel")
Xuánzōng and the palace ladies were all startled and laughed.
When they looked,
the Daoist priest had already vanished.
They only saw a golden vessel on the ground.
When they lifted the lid,
the vessel was found to contain exactly one *dǒu*.
Upon examination,
it was discovered to be a vessel from the Jíxián Academy.
He repeatedly demonstrated his immortal arts,
which were too numerous to record fully.
There was a master
(Original text has "guī" instead of "shī";
corrected according to the *New Book of Tang, Biographies of Technical Experts*.)
named Yè Guāng who was skilled at seeing ghosts.
Xuánzōng once summoned Guǒ to sit before him,
and ordered Yè Guāng to observe him.
Yè Guāng came before the emperor and reported:
"I do not know where Zhāng Guǒ is.
I wish to observe and investigate."
Yet Guǒ had been sitting before the emperor for a long time;
Yè Guāng ultimately could not see him.
There was also another man named Xíng Hépú,
who possessed skill in calculation.
Whenever he observed a person,
he would lay out counting rods before him.
In no time,
he could already determine in detail their name,
(Míng Chāo edition and Xǔ Kè edition have "dá" instead of "yuǎn".)
circumstances, good or evil deeds, and lifespan.
He had calculated for thousands of people before and after,
and never failed to analyze even the minutest details.
Xuánzōng had long marveled at him.
When he ordered him to calculate for Guǒ,
Hépú manipulated the rods for a long time,
until his mind was exhausted and his spirit dejected,
yet he ultimately could not determine Guǒ's birth year.
Xuánzōng said to the influential eunuch Gāo Lìshì:
"I have heard that for those who are divine immortals,
neither cold nor heat can harm their bodies,
and external things cannot stain their inner being.
Now, even a skilled calculator like Hépú cannot determine Zhāng Guǒ's age,
and a ghost-seer like Yè Guāng cannot perceive his form.
Such sudden, elusive movements of an immortal—
is this not proof of a true one?
However, I have often heard that drinking *zhènzhēn* wine causes death.
If he is not an immortal,
it will surely damage his substance.
We can test him by having him drink it."
It happened to be a heavy snowfall,
and the cold was severe.
Xuánzōng ordered *zhènzhēn* wine to be presented and bestowed upon Guǒ.
Guǒ then raised it and drank,
emptying three cups,
until he showed a flushed, drunken countenance.
He looked around at the attendants and said:
"This wine is not of good flavor."
He then lay down and slept.
After the time of a meal, he awoke.
Suddenly, he took up a mirror to look at his teeth:
they were all mottled and charred black.
He immediately ordered an attendant boy to fetch an iron *ruyi* scepter,
with which he knocked out all his teeth.
He then gathered them and placed them in his robe sash.
Slowly, he loosened his clothing,
took out a packet of medicine,
which was slightly red and glowing with a crystalline luster.
Guǒ applied it to the cavities of his teeth.
Having done so, he lay down to sleep again.
After a long while, he suddenly awoke.
Taking up the mirror again to look at himself,
his teeth had already regrown.
They were firm, gleaming white,
even better than before.
Only then did Xuánzōng truly believe in his supernatural abilities.
He said to Lìshì:
"Can he be anything but a true immortal?"
He then issued an edict, saying:
"The gentleman Zhāng Guǒ of Héngzhōu
is one who wanders beyond the mundane world.
His traces follow the lofty ancients;
his mind enters the profound and obscure.
For long he has mingled with the light and dust,
Summoned to the imperial court.
No one knows his age,
and he is said to be a man from before the time of Fúxī.
When asked about the essence of the Way,
he fully grasped its ultimate principles.
Now, as he is about to perform court rituals,
I hereby bestow this honor upon him:
he is granted the title of Silver-Green Light Grand Master,
and additionally bestowed the title of Master Tōngxuán."
Not long after,
Emperor Xuánzōng was hunting in Xiányáng,
and captured a large deer,
slightly different from ordinary ones.
As the cook was preparing it,
Guǒ saw it and said:
"This is an immortal deer,
already a thousand years old.
In the fifth year of the Yuánshòu era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
I once accompanied him,
hunting in the Shànglín Park.
At that time, this deer was captured alive,
and later released."
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"There are many deer;
with the passage of time and changes of eras,
how could it not have been captured by hunters?"
Guǒ said:
"When Emperor Wǔ released the deer,
he marked it with a bronze plaque under its left antler."
So he ordered it to be examined,
and indeed, a bronze plaque about two inches long was found,
though the inscription had faded and darkened.
Emperor Xuánzōng also asked Guǒ:
"What year in the sexagenary cycle was Yuánshòu?
How many years have passed since then?"
Guǒ said:
"That year was Guǐhài,
when Emperor Wǔ first excavated the Kūnmíng Pond;
now it is the year Jiǎxū,
eight hundred and fifty-two years later."
Emperor Xuánzōng ordered the court astrologer to verify this against the long calendar,
and there was no discrepancy.
Emperor Xuánzōng regarded him with even greater wonder.
At that time, there was also a Daoist priest named Yè Fǎshàn,
who was also skilled in many arts.
Emperor Xuánzōng asked him:
"Who is Guǒ?"
He replied:
"I know;
but if I speak, I will die immediately,
so I dare not say.
If Your Majesty removes your crown and goes barefoot to save me,
I may live."
Emperor Xuánzōng agreed.
Fǎshàn said:
"He is the essence of a white bat from the time of the division of chaos."
As soon as he finished speaking,
blood flowed from his seven orifices,
and he collapsed to the ground.
Emperor Xuánzōng hurried to Guǒ's residence,
removed his crown and went barefoot,
and confessed his fault.
Guǒ slowly said:
"This child talks too much;
if I do not punish him,
I fear he will ruin the affairs of heaven and earth."
Emperor Xuánzōng pleaded with him for a long time.
Guǒ sprayed water on his face,
and Fǎshàn immediately revived.
Afterward, Guǒ repeatedly pleaded old age and illness,
requesting to return to Héngzhōu.
An edict was issued to provide him with a relay escort to Héngzhōu.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
Emperor Xuánzōng again sent a summons for him.
Upon hearing this,
Guǒ suddenly died.
His disciples buried him.
Later, when the coffin was opened,
it was found to be empty.
From *Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng*, *Records of the Xuānshì*, and *Continued Biographies of Immortals*.
Zhái Qiányòu
was a man of Yún'ān.
He had thick eyebrows and a broad forehead,
large eyes and a square jaw.
He stood six chǐ tall,
with hands over a chǐ in length.
Whenever he bowed to others,
his hands would pass in front of his chest.
He once studied under Master Lái at Huánghè Mountain,
mastering all his teachings.
He could circulate his vital energy and write cinnabar talismans,
control tigers and leopards on land,
and subdue flood dragons in water.
When he slept, he often used an empty pillow.
He often spoke of future events,
and his words never failed to come true.
Once, when he entered Kuízhōu market,
he said to people:
"Tonight, eight men will pass by here.
You should treat them well."
That evening, a fire burned down over a hundred households.
Those who understood explained:
"The 'eight men' form the character for 'fire'."
Whenever he entered the mountains,
a pack of tigers would follow him.
He once admired the moon by the river with over ten people.
Someone asked:
"What exactly is there in the moon?"
Qiányòu laughed and said:
"You can look with my hand."
Then they saw the moon filling half the sky,
filled with jade towers and golden palaces.
After a long while, it vanished.
The Yún'ān well was located along a tributary branching off from the great river,
some thirty lǐ away.
For the fifteen lǐ near the well,
the water was clear as a mirror,
and boats faced no danger.
But for the fifteen lǐ near the river,
it was all treacherous rapids and rocks,
making navigation difficult.
Qiányòu, mindful of the hardships faced by merchants and travelers,
ascended Hànchéng Mountain
and set up an altar to summon and interrogate,
calling forth the dragons.
In all, from fourteen places,
they transformed into old men
and answered the summons.
Qiányòu explained the dangers of the rapids and waves,
how they harmed creatures and wearied people,
and ordered them to calm the waters.
In a single night,
amidst the rumble of wind and thunder,
fourteen lǐ
were all turned into calm pools.
Only one rapid remained as before,
and its dragon did not come.
Qiányòu again sternly ordered the divine officers to summon it.
After another three days,
a woman arrived.
He then reproached her for disobeying the summons.
The woman said:
"The reason I did not come
was that I wished to help the Celestial Master broaden his work of aiding all beings.
Moreover, wealthy merchants and great traders
all have ample resources,
while those who hire out their labor to carry loads
are all lacking in means.
Among the poor of Yún'ān,
many make their living by carrying goods from the river mouth to the pools near the well
to provide for their food and clothing.
Now, if light boats could travel easily
and the river were calm and safe,
then the poor of the city
would have no place to hire out their carrying labor,
cutting off their means of food and clothing.
Those who would suffer are many.
I would rather keep the rapids dangerous to provide for the hired carriers
than make boating easy to benefit the wealthy merchants.
The reason
"suǒ" originally written as "wú",
emended based on the Ming manuscript and Chén's collated edition.
I did not come
lies in this principle."
Qiányòu praised her words,
and thus ordered all the dragons to restore things as they were.
In a moment, with wind and thunder,
the long rapids returned to their former state.
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
he was summoned to the capital,
where he received generous favor and treatment.
After over a year, he returned to his old mountain,
and soon attained the Way and departed.
Earlier,
in Shǔ, there was a Daoist who feigned madness,
commonly known as "Huīdài" (Ash Bag),
who was Qiányòu's disciple in his later years.
Qiányòu often warned his disciples:
"Do not bully this man.
He surpasses even me."
Once during heavy snowfall,
he wore a cloth robe
and entered Qīngchéng Mountain.
At dusk, he sought lodging at a temple.
The monk said:
"This poor monk has only one robe.
The weather is cold,
I fear this may not sustain your life."
The Daoist merely said:
"Just allow me a bed, that is enough."
By midnight,
the snow was deep and the wind rose.
The monk, worried the Daoist had died,
went to check on him.
Several chǐ from the bed,
steam rose as if from a stove,
and he lay sweating, uncovered.
Only then did the monk realize he was an extraordinary man.
Before dawn,
he left without saying goodbye.
He often stayed in villages,
and wherever he stayed, people trusted him more.
Once he suffered from mouth sores,
and for several months ate nothing,
appearing as if near death.
The villagers, who had long revered him as divine,
held a Daoist fasting ceremony for him.
When the ceremony ended,
he suddenly rose and leaned on his pillow,
saying to the crowd:
"Try looking into my mouth.
What is there?"
He then opened his mouth wide like a winnowing basket,
revealing all his internal organs.
His companions were astonished,
bowed, and asked him about it.
He only said:
"This is disgusting enough!
This is disgusting enough!"
Later, no one knew what became of him.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ* and *Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí*.
Fán Bāxiōng
As for Fán Bāxiōng,
it is unknown what rank he held among the immortal registers.
He was the grandson of Suí Crown Prince Yǒng,
named Dézǔ,
and served in the Táng dynasty as the Director of the Imperial Carriages.
His nature inclined strongly toward the Dao,
devoting himself to the art of prolonging life through golden elixirs.
The expenses for furnaces and cauldrons
left his family without surplus wealth;
his official post was minor and his salary meager,
often leaving him short even for porridge.
Whenever he had a little money,
he would immediately spend it on charcoal and medicinal ingredients.
Suddenly, Fán Bāxiōng visited his home,
discussing mysteries and emptiness,
debating methods and arts.
He considered the preparation of golden elixirs
no great labor,
and transformations of yellow and white
could be achieved as easily as coughing or spitting.
Dézǔ grew even more respectful of him.
However, Fán was rigid, irritable, noisy, and disorderly,
fond of wine and gluttonous,
truly unbearable;
he went out by day and returned at night,
fearing no street curfews;
rich meats and strong wines
he demanded regardless of the hour.
Dézǔ, fully aware of his nature,
took pains to prepare in advance,
ensuring to meet his every request.
Thus he lingered for several months.
One day,
he ordered Dézǔ to fetch cauldrons, pots, pans, and the like and arrange them in the medicine room.
Fán himself smashed them,
piled up iron and added charcoal,
and forged them with a fierce fire.
He scattered ten spoonfuls of powdered medicine over them,
then locked the room from the outside,
turning his back to the lamp in a corner of the wall.
Then he walked with Dézǔ in the courtyard under the moonlight.
At midnight, he said to Dézǔ:
"I am an immortal of the Great Ultimate.
Because you devote your heart to the ultimate Dao,
and uphold your principles unwaveringly,
I have come to instruct you.
On this bright moonlit night,
can you journey far?"
Dézǔ agreed.
So they went out the door together,
and looking back,
the lock and key were as before.
They walked slowly for about twenty or thirty lǐ,
the road quite level,
and rested on a mountaintop,
where Dézǔ felt weary.
Bāxiōng said:
"We are now a thousand lǐ from Cháng'ān.
You must be very tired!"
Dézǔ was startled by the distance,
and indeed replied that he was tired from walking.
Bāxiōng let out a long laugh,
and in a moment,
a white beast arrived.
He ordered Dézǔ to mount it,
and it traveled with great speed,
gradually making the distance feel even farther.
He then asked about the distance to Cháng'ān.
Bāxiōng said:
"This is eighty thousand lǐ."
Dézǔ fell silent.
Suddenly he thought of not having bid farewell to his family.
The white beast halted firmly, refusing to go further.
Bāxiōng laughed and said:
"Indeed, you still have worldly thoughts;
leaving the mortal world cannot be achieved by such means."
He promptly ordered the white beast to take Dézǔ to the Cloud Palace,
to pay respects to Master Jiěkōng.
In a moment, they arrived.
The Master invited him to sit,
and had a blue lad serve him a golden elixir.
Dézǔ received it,
but saw it was a poisonous, stinging thing,
and could not bring himself to eat it;
then he was offered jade liquid to drink,
but again smelled its foul odor,
and could not drink it either.
The Master ordered the white beast to return Dézǔ to his home.
Fán Bāxiōng was never seen again.
Upon reaching his home,
the candles were still burning,
and the night was not yet over.
The next morning, he looked at what had been transformed:
gold and silver gleamed brilliantly.
Although his wealth was now abundant,
the immortal demeanor of Bāxiōng
was nowhere to be seen.
One day,
he suddenly saw the servant of Fán Bāxiōng
passing by his gate carrying baskets.
He asked where Master Fán resided.
"He is in the immortal abode.
He sent me briefly to the mortal realm.
If I see the Director,
he said you may come along as well."
From then on, Dézǔ followed the immortal servant of Master Fán and left,
never to return.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Lǐ Xiázhōu
Lǐ Xiázhōu
was quite skilled in Daoist arts.
During the Táng dynasty's Kāiyuán era,
he was once summoned into the imperial palace.
Later he requested to leave and reside at Xuándū Temple.
Táng Chancellor Lǐ Línfǔ once went to visit him.
Xiázhōu said to him:
"While you live, your household will be secure;
when you die, your household will perish."
Línfǔ bowed and wept,
begging him to rescue and resolve this.
He laughed without answering,
saying:
"I was only joking."
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
when Lùshān grew arrogant, domineering, and rebellious,
people near and far were worried;
yet the emperor remained unawakened to the situation.
One day, Xiázhōu vanished,
and no one knew where he went.
But on the wall of his dwelling,
he had inscribed several poems,
speaking of Lùshān's usurpation and the emperor's flight to Shǔ.
At the time, no one understood them,
but later events verified them.
The final piece said:
"All the men of Yān market have gone,
the horses at Hánguān never return.
If you meet the ghost beneath the mountain,
on the ring fasten a silk robe."
"All the men of Yān market have gone"
refers to Lùshān raising all the troops of Yōujì.
"The horses at Hánguān never return"
refers to Gēshū Hàn's defeat at Tóngguān,
where not a single horse returned.
"If you meet the ghost beneath the mountain"
refers to Mǎwéi, the name of a station in Shǔ.
"On the ring fasten a silk robe"
refers to the Guìfēi, whose childhood name was Yùhuán;
at Mǎwéi,
Gāo Lìshì strangled her with a silk scarf.
His foresight
was all of this kind.
From "Mínghuáng Zálù"
Xǔ Lǎowēng
The Elder Xǔ,
it is unknown from where he hailed.
He secluded himself on Mount Éméi,
his era unknown.
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
the wife of a certain Liǔ, a Registrar in Yìzhōu, named Lǐ,
possessed a beauty of unparalleled grace.
At that time, the Military Commissioner Zhāngchóu Jiānqióng,
having newly captured the Ānróng city from Tibet,
dispatched Liǔ to deliver goods to the city,
and for three years he did not return.
Lǐ remained in the official residence,
its heavy gates unopened,
when suddenly a Military Officer Péi arrived at the gate,
claiming to be a maternal uncle of Lǐ's.
Lǐ said:
"I have no relative from the Péi family."
She did not order the gate opened.
Péi then mentioned Lǐ's childhood name,
and also spoke of her maternal and paternal clans.
Only then did Lǐ order the gate opened to receive him with a bow,
and intended to offer him a meal.
Péi's demeanor was exceedingly refined,
and he asked how long Lǐ's husband had been gone.
She replied:
"Already three years!"
Péi said:
"After three years, the bond of righteousness is severed,"
as the ancients said,
what do you intend to do now?
Moreover, your uncle and you,
are destined by karma to become husband and wife,
I hope you do not refuse this.
And in the end, she was bewitched by Uncle Péi,
as if it were not a matter for human consent.
This Military Officer Péi,
was also already married.
When Commissioner Zhāngchóu heard of Lǐ's beauty,
he wished to catch a glimpse of her.
He then ordered his wife to specially arrange a banquet,
inviting the wives of the prefectural and county officials,
and none failed to gather.
Only Lǐ declined, citing her husband's absence on distant duty.
Zhāngchóu's wife insisted she must attend.
She said:
"Just come,
do not trouble yourself with refusal."
Fearing reprimand, Lǐ went.
She wore a yellow gauze skirt with silver-paste decoration,
a five-hued gauze blouse with silver-paste decoration,
and a single-thread gauze red-ground silver-paste cape,
which was indeed the finest attire of Yìdū.
Péi looked at her clothes and sighed, saying:
"The garments of this world,
their splendor ends here."
Turning to a young servant, he said:
"Go back and open the chest,
bring the third set of clothes."
Lǐ said:
"Why not give me the first, but the third?"
Péi replied:
"The third is already not something of this mortal world."
In a moment, the clothes arrived,
filling the room with an extraordinary fragrance.
Péi looked at them again,
smiled and said to the young servant:
"Should clothes really be like this?
What does Zhāngchóu know?
I only fear the Elder Xǔ might find out."
They then boarded the carriage and went to the Commissioner's residence.
Upon entering,
the lady of the house and all the seated guests
all descended the steps to pay their respects.
Having donned the heavenly garments,
Lǐ's appearance became even more extraordinary.
The onlookers adored her.
Once seated,
the lady ordered someone to inform Zhāngchóu:
"The Registrar's wife,
her beauty and attire are of unparalleled grace."
Zhāngchóu came directly into the courtyard,
instructing everyone not to rise.
Seeing Lǐ's attire,
he sighed repeatedly,
then borrowed the cape to examine it,
and realized it was not of this world.
Testing it with fire and water,
it neither burned nor became soiled.
He then detained and questioned her.
Lǐ recounted the whole story in detail.
Sending someone to Péi's dwelling,
he was nowhere to be found.
Jiānqióng then changed her clothes and presented her,
also reporting the matter of the Elder Xǔ.
An imperial edict ordered that a plan be devised to seek out the Elder Xǔ.
Zhāngchóu suspected that an immortal's comings and goings
must be at an apothecary.
He thus ordered an apothecary to watch for his whereabouts.
After four days, he was found.
Initially, a young boy came to the shop to buy medicine.
The apothecary, thinking he was the disciple,
gave him inferior medicine.
The boy left but returned again,
and said:
"My master is angry the medicine is no good,
and wants to beat me."
The apothecary asked:
"Who is your master?"
The boy said:
"The Elder Xǔ."
The apothecary was very pleased,
and led the boy to report to the prefecture.
Zhāngchóu ordered a hundred strong men
and fifty officers,
to follow the boy to the mountain,
and conveyed the official order.
The mountain peaks were precipitous and sheer,
the crowd could not ascend.
The boy then called out loudly from below.
In a moment, the old man appeared on the stone cliff,
asking why he had brought so many people.
The boy explained the matter in full.
The old man asked the boy why he did not come up,
the boy why he did not come up,
The four characters "the boy why he did not come up"
are not repeated in the Ming manuscript copy.
The boy then gracefully tread the void and ascended.
The officials kowtowed, begging for mercy, saying:
"The Governor's tyranny,
you, Elder, are aware of."
The old man then agreed to go,
and said to the officials:
"You just return to the prefecture,
I will follow."
The officials and soldiers had not long returned to the prefecture,
when the Elder also arrived.
Zhāngchóu saw him,
and bowed twice, prostrating himself.
The Elder showed no sign of respect.
Zhāngchóu then asked who it was that married Lǐ.
The Elder said:
"He is the official in charge of the wardrobe of the Lady of the First Origin,
whose worldly passions are not yet exhausted."
Zhāngchóu requested the Elder to go to the Emperor.
Xǔ said:
"Going is not difficult."
He then arranged with the memorial presenter to meet at Cháng'ān on a set date.
He arrived ahead of schedule.
An edict was issued to summon him for an audience.
Emperor Xuánzōng treated him with great courtesy.
Once seated,
the Emperor asked:
"Does Heaven know of the wardrobe official's crime?"
The Elder said:
"He has already been banished to become the ruler of a kingdom in the mortal world."
The Emperor asked again:
"What about the clothes, in the end?"
Xǔ said:
"Set up a mat and lay out the clothes in a pure place,
someone will come to take them."
The Emperor ordered it done as he said.
At first, no one was seen,
but a whirlwind swept the clothes into the clouds,
and in the blink of an eye,
the Elder Xǔ was also gone.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Another account says:
During the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a scholar surnamed Cuī,
who served as a County Lieutenant in Bāshǔ,
but died shortly after arriving in Chéngdū.
At that time, the Regional Commander Zhāngchóu Jiānqióng,
pitying his wife for being young and having nowhere to go,
set up a villa for her at the foot of Mount Qīngchéng.
Moreover, because of her beauty,
he had intentions of marrying her.
Unable to devise a plan,
he said to his wife:
"Noble as the wife of a feudal lord,
why not lavishly set out a feast,
and invite female guests?
Within five hundred lǐ,
all can be welcomed."
His wife was very pleased.
Jiānqióng then ordered his officers
to inform all the young ladies within five hundred lǐ,
to assemble in Chéngdū on a set date,
intending to detain the deceased Lieutenant's wife during the gathering.
Little did he know she had already been taken in by her clan uncle, Mr. Lú.
Uncle Lú secretly knew Jiānqióng's intention,
and had the Lieutenant's wife decline on grounds of illness.
Jiānqióng was furious,
and hastily dispatched a hundred horsemen to arrest her.
Uncle Lú was eating at the time,
and the soldiers had already surrounded his residence.
Lú conversed and laughed as usual,
utterly unperturbed.
After finishing his meal,
He said to his wife:
"Jiānqióng's intentions are clear,
you must go.
In a little while,
they will send plain-colored clothes,
you should put them on and go."
After speaking,
he rode a mule out the gate.
The soldiers and horsemen ahead could not stop him,
he departed slowly,
and they could not catch up.
Soon a young boy was sent carrying a box,
inside were an old blue skirt, a white blouse, a green cape, and crimson silk gauze and plain silk,
all not of this world.
The commandant's wife wore them to Chéngdū.
All the young ladies had arrived ahead of time.
Jiānqióng watched from behind the curtain,
and when the commandant's wife entered,
radiance surrounded her body,
her beauty shone from all sides,
one could not look directly at her.
Those seated all held their breath,
unconsciously rising to bow.
After the gathering ended and she returned,
she died three days later.
Jiānqióng was greatly alarmed,
and fully reported the matter.
Emperor Xuánzōng asked Zhāng Guǒ.
Guǒ said:
"I know,
but dare not speak.
Please ask Wáng Lǎo of Qīngchéng."
Emperor Xuánzōng then ordered Jiānqióng
to seek out Wáng Lǎo and bring him.
Jiānqióng searched the area around Qīngchéng Mountain,
but found no such person.
Only at the market herb shop did they say:
"Often two people,
come daily to sell herbs,
claiming to be sent by Wáng Lǎo."
When the two arrived,
Jiānqióng immediately ordered a yá official to follow them,
they entered the mountain for several li,
reaching a thatched cottage.
Wáng Lǎo had white hair at his temples,
leaning on a table, sitting upright.
The yá official followed in,
then announced the imperial decree,
and also conveyed Jiānqióng's intent.
Wáng Lǎo said:
"This must be that talkative little kid Zhāng Guǒ."
He then agreed with Jiānqióng on a date to reach the capital.
He ordered them to send the memorial first,
unwilling to ride the official post.
Jiānqióng complied.
The envoy had just reached Yíntái,
when Wáng Lǎo also arrived.
Emperor Xuánzōng immediately summoned and questioned him.
At that time Zhāng Guǒ was still at Emperor Xuánzōng's side,
seeing Wáng Lǎo,
he fearfully bowed repeatedly.
Wáng Lǎo scolded Guǒ:
"Little one, why didn't you speak?
And sent so far to fetch me."
Guǒ said, "This minor immortal dares not,
I was solely awaiting the words of the immortal elder."
Wáng Lǎo then reported:
"Second Uncle Lú is the storekeeper of Lady Tàiyuán.
Because he borrowed leave to descend and wander,
and as the deceased commandant's wife slightly possessed immortal bones,
he took her as a concubine.
Not long after,
he stole Lady Tàiyuán's clothes for her to wear,
and has already received a heavy punishment.
Now he is the Yùdān Heavenly Son.
The deceased commandant's wife, because she wore Lady Tàiyuán's clothes,
has fallen into the Avīci Hell."
After reporting,
he firmly wished not to stay.
Emperor Xuánzōng ordered him released to return,
and later no one knew where he was.
From "Xuánguài Lù"
Lǐ Jué
was from Jiāngyáng in Guǎnglíng.
His family had long resided in the city,
making their living by buying and selling grain.
Jué himself was upright and cautious in nature,
different from ordinary folk.
When he was fifteen years old,
his father happened to travel elsewhere,
and entrusted Jué with the grain business.
When customers came to buy grain,
he would sell it to them.
Jué would hand them the measuring vessels,
letting them measure it themselves.
Regardless of whether prices were high or low at the time,
he sought only two coins of profit per dou,
using it to support his parents.
As the years passed,
his clothing and food became abundant.
His father, finding this strange, asked him about it.
Jué truthfully explained everything.
His father said:
"In this trade of ours,
none among our peers fail to use different measures for buying and selling:
using a smaller measure when selling and a larger one when buying,
to seek greater profit.
Though the authorities inspect and regulate in spring and autumn,
they ultimately cannot eliminate this malpractice.
I have merely used the same measure for both buying and selling,
and long considered myself impartial.
But now you go further, letting customers measure it themselves as they please—
this is something I could not match.
Yet your clothing and food are abundant;
is this not perhaps divine assistance!"
Later, after his parents passed away,
and even when Jué was over eighty years old,
he did not change his trade.
It happened that another Lǐ Jué left his post as chancellor
to govern Huáinán as military commissioner.
Our Jué, because the new military commissioner shared his name,
became extremely alarmed,
and changed his name to Kuān.
A few months after Lǐ Jué (the commissioner) arrived at his post,
he was observing a period of purification and fasting.
One night, he dreamed of entering a grotto-heaven,
where he saw a scene of spring in full bloom,
with misty blossoms in radiant splendor,
soaring phoenixes and dancing cranes,
colorful clouds and auspicious mists,
and pavilions and towers stretching far and wide.
Jué walked alone beneath them
and saw a stone wall, smooth and gleaming,
inscribed with characters filled in gold,
listing people's names.
Among them appeared to be "Lǐ Jué,"
the characters over two feet tall.
Jué looked at it and was overjoyed,
thinking to himself that he had been born in an enlightened age,
had long served in high office,
and had even risen to the position of chief minister;
surely he had accumulated merit and virtue benefiting the realm.
Now that his name was recorded in the grotto-heaven,
he must be an immortal.
He rejoiced again and again.
Just as he was delighting in this,
two immortal youths emerged from the left and right of the stone wall.
Jué asked:
"What place is this?"
They replied:
"This is the Huáyáng Grotto-Heaven.
But this name is not yours, sir."
Jué was startled
and asked again:
"If not me, then who is this Jué?"
The immortal youths said:
"He is a commoner from Jiāngyáng under your jurisdiction, sir."
When Jué awoke at dawn,
he recalled the events of the dream in detail
and was even more astonished.
He inquired among Daoist priests,
but none knew of such a person.
He then considered summoning the officials of Jiāngyáng to question them.
They too knew nothing.
So he ordered a search within the prefectural city for anyone sharing the same name.
After several days,
through inquiries in military camps and neighborhoods,
they found Lǐ Kuān, whose former name was Jué.
This was reported to Commissioner Jué.
He then had Lǐ Kuán brought by carriage,
settled him in a quiet chamber,
purified himself, bathed, and paid him respects,
addressing him as "Daoist elder brother."
The entire household revered and served him,
paying homage morning and evening.
Lǐ Kuān's demeanor was serene and detached,
his Daoist appearance elegant and extraordinary,
with a beard over a foot long,
pure white and lovely.
At the age of sixty,
a Daoist priest had once taught him embryonic breathing,
and since then he had long abstained from eating.
Commissioner Jué revered him even more.
After over a month,
he finally asked:
"Elder brother, what Daoist arts have you attained in your life?
What elixirs have you refined and ingested?
I once dreamed of entering a grotto-heaven,
where I saw a name on a stone wall.
The immortal youths pointed it out,
which is why I invited you here to serve as my teacher.
I wish you would impart this to me."
Kuān declined, saying he knew nothing of Daoist arts or elixir refinement.
Jué again bowed reverently
and asked what practices Kuān cultivated.
Kuān declined, saying he was but an ignorant commoner who knew of no cultivation,
and then truthfully recounted his grain trade.
Jué questioned him repeatedly,
and finally sighed:
"This is something ordinary people find difficult to achieve—
such hidden merit is beyond reach."
He continued:
"Now I understand that every action and inaction, every breath and meal in this world,
brings retribution without exception.
If one accumulates virtue,
even in poverty and lowliness,
divine beings will protect and aid,
inscribing one's name in the register of immortals,
as a warning to the mundane world."
He also asked about the method of embryonic breathing and abstaining from food.
Kuān explained everything.
Jué learned embryonic breathing from him
and also stopped eating.
Kuān lived to over a hundred years old,
Suddenly he told his descendants:
"I have lingered in this world for many years;
though I have cultivated my vital energy,
it brings no benefit to you all."
He passed away one night.
Three days later, there was a sound of his coffin splitting open.
When they looked,
his clothes and sash were intact,
like a cicada shedding its shell—
he had already achieved liberation from the corpse.
From "Continued Biographies of Immortals"
Zhāng Quánsù
In Wújùn there was a scholar named Jiǎng,
who was fond of the ways of the immortals.
In his youth he abandoned his family,
and secluded himself at the foot of Sìmíng Mountain,
where he once studied alchemy with a Daoist priest.
Thus he built furnaces and cauldrons,
stoking the fire and working the bellows,
for a full ten years;
yet in the end he failed to produce the elixir.
Afterwards, while traveling and lodging in Jīngmén,
he saw a man begging in the marketplace,
whose skin was extremely withered,
naked and ill,
and shivering with cold, unable to speak.
Jiǎng took pity on his destitution,
took off his own fur robe to clothe him,
and then ordered him to serve at his side.
He inquired about his family.
The man replied:
"I am a son of the Zhāng family of Chǔ,
my name is Quánsù,
my home is in Nánchāng,
where we have several hundred acres of fertile fields.
Due to years of famine,
I wandered and drifted in the region of Jīngjiāng,
for almost ten years now.
The fields reverted to the government,
my body is ill and I cannot support myself,
I am fortunate that you, sir, take pity and shelter me."
Thereupon he returned with Jiǎng to the foot of Sìmíng Mountain.
But Quánsù was very lazy,
often sleeping late and indulging in ease.
Jiǎng scolded him harshly and beat him countless times.
Jiǎng had an inkstone on his desk,
when suddenly one day,
Quánsù said to Jiǎng:
"You, sir, are fond of the ways of the immortals,
and have studied alchemy for a long time.
If one consumes the elixir of immortality,
then the bones turn to gold,
how could one not attain long life in that case?
Now, sir, with your divine elixir,
can you transform this inkstone into gold?
If so,
I would consider you a Daoist adept with true arts."
Jiǎng, knowing in his heart he could not achieve it,
felt deeply ashamed;
and so refused him with other words, saying:
"You are a mere servant,
how could you understand the affairs of immortals!
If you speak recklessly,
you will only hasten the humiliation of beating and scolding."
Quánsù laughed and left.
Over a month later,
Quánsù took out from his clothes a very small gourd,
and turning to Jiǎng, said:
"Inside this gourd is an elixir of immortality,
capable of transforming stone into gold.
I wish to take your inkstone,
and apply a small amount of the powder onto it.
May I?"
Jiǎng was by nature impulsive and rash,
and moreover considered this absurd and false,
so he cursed and shouted:
"I have studied alchemy for ten years,
and still have not fully grasped its mysteries;
how dare a servant chatter and debate with me!"
Quánsù pretended to be afraid and did not reply.
The next day,
Jiǎng went alone to wander among the mountains and waters,
ordering Quánsù to guard the house,
and so he locked the door and left.
When he returned in the evening,
he saw that Quánsù had already died.
Jiǎng then used a mat to cover the corpse,
intending to order a coffin and bury it in the wilds.
But when he removed the mat,
Quánsù's corpse had already vanished,
only his hat, belt, clothes, and shoes remained.
Jiǎng was greatly astonished,
and thought he must have been an immortal who attained the Dao,
immediately looking at the inkstone on the desk,
it too had vanished.
Jiǎng grew even more amazed.
A day later,
Jiǎng saw a light beneath the medicine cauldron.
Jiǎng said:
"Could this be my elixir of immortality?"
He then searched among the ashes,
and found the inkstone,
on which over an inch
had transformed into purple gold,
its light exceedingly clear and bright.
It was the transformation wrought by Quánsù's elixir of immortality.
Only then did Jiǎng realize Quánsù was indeed an immortal,
regretting deeply that he had failed to recognize him,
he felt even more ashamed and resentful.
Afterwards, Jiǎng's study of alchemy ultimately failed,
and he eventually died on Sìmíng Mountain.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
Wáng Jiǎ
Wùzhōu Military Adviser Wáng Jiǎ,
originally from Tàiyuán,
moved his family to Tánhuái,
but his ancestors' graves
were in Línrǔ.
Jiǎ was intelligent and bright from a young age,
never having made any mistakes,
and was calm and reserved, speaking little.
At the age of fourteen,
he suddenly said to his elder brothers:
"Within three days,
there will be a fright in our household,
and a great funeral will occur."
After two days,
a fire broke out in the house,
spreading to the main hall,
and their elderly grandmother, shocked and frightened,
threw herself onto the bed and died.
His elder brother reported Jiǎ's words to their uncles,
and the uncles questioned Jiǎ.
Jiǎ said:
"I knew through divination."
Later, he also told his uncles:
"South of Tàiháng,
within a bend of the Bì River,
two dragons reside.
If you wish to see true dragons,
please come with me to observe them."
His uncles angrily said:
"This boy loves to speak strange and frightening nonsense;
he should be caned."
Jiǎ knelt and said:
"They truly exist."
Therefore, he requested they go see them.
His uncles angrily said:
"This boy is fond of the strange."
And they went with him.
Jiǎ requested they prepare raincoats.
Thus they reached a deep part of the Bì River's shore.
Jiǎ entered the water,
drew a line with his whip,
and the water parted for him.
Below was a large rock,
with two dragons coiled around it,
one white and one black,
each several zhang in length.
Upon seeing people, they soared into the sky.
His uncles were greatly astonished,
gazing for a long time.
Jiǎ said:
"Now that you have seen them,
they will return."
Then, waving his whip,
the water closed as before.
Immediately, clouds and mist darkened the day,
and thunder and lightning were about to arrive.
Jiǎ said:
"Uncles, ride away quickly."
They galloped off,
and before they had gone more than a li,
torrential rain poured down.
Only then did they realize he was no ordinary person.
At age seventeen,
Jiǎ went to the capital to take the Filial and Incorrupt examination,
and after passing,
he married a woman from the Cuī clan of Qīnghé.
Later, he was selected and appointed as Military Adviser of Wùzhōu,
and on his way back, he passed through the Eastern Capital.
A cousin of Jiǎ's mother
had died a year earlier,
but often spoke from within the spirit curtain,
managing household affairs.
The children and servants
dared not do anything wrong.
Whenever she demanded food, drink, or clothing,
if her requests were not met,
she would cane and scold them.
The relatives all found it strange.
Jiǎ said:
"This must be a demonic anomaly."
He then went to his aunt's house,
to offer condolences to her sons.
Earlier, the aunt had told her sons:
"Tomorrow, our Wáng family nephew will come;
you must not let him enter.
This young man is a great sinner."
When Jiǎ arrived at the gate,
he was not allowed to enter.
Jiǎ summoned an old servant and said to him:
"The one speaking inside the house
is not your mistress,
but a demonic spirit.
Just whisper to your masters
to let me in,
and I will remove it for them."
The family had long been troubled by this,
so they secretly told the young masters.
The young masters also realized,
and invited Jiǎ in.
Jiǎ paid his condolences and then addressed the spirit, saying:
"I heard that since my aunt's passing, she has become very divine,
speaking as she did in life.
Now I have come to visit my aunt;
why does she not speak with Jiǎ?"
There was no response.
Jiǎ pressed further, saying:
"I have come specifically to visit;
if my aunt does not speak,
I will never leave,
but will stay right here."
The spirit, knowing it could not avoid this,
then spoke from within the curtain:
"Nephew, are you well?
Who would have thought that after parting,
life and death would separate us.
That you have not forgotten me,
and could still visit,
fills me with unspeakable shame."
Then, weeping and speaking,
her voice was exactly that of the aunt in life.
Her sons, hearing this, wailed and wept.
The aunt ordered a meal prepared,
seated Jiǎ before her,
poured wine for them to face each other,
and was exceedingly attentive.
After becoming drunk,
Jiǎ then requested:
"Since my aunt is so divine,
why not let Jiǎ see your form?"
The aunt said:
"The paths of the hidden and the visible are different;
why insist on meeting?"
Jiǎ said:
"If my aunt cannot appear fully,
please reveal half your face.
If not,
show a hand or a foot,
so that Jiǎ may see it.
If you do not show yourself,
I will still never leave."
The spirit, hard-pressed by his insistence,
then revealed its left hand,
with fingers clearly visible,
exactly the hand of the aunt.
Her sons wailed again.
Jiǎ then stepped forward and seized the hand.
The aunt cried out to her sons:
"Your cousin is being rude;
why don't you raise a hand?"
Before her sons could approach,
Jiǎ pulled the hand,
threw it to the ground,
and it still cried out mournfully.
After beating it several times,
it died,
and was revealed to be an old fox.
Its form now visible,
its body was naked and hairless.
They ordered it burned with fire,
and the spirit's speech ceased.
Jiǎ arrived in Wùzhōu,
and on business went to Dōngyáng.
The magistrate there had a daughter
who had been afflicted by a demon for several years,
and doctors could not cure her.
The magistrate invited Jiǎ to his residence,
served tea and food but dared not speak of it.
Jiǎ, knowing of it,
said to the magistrate:
