"I heard your daughter is ill from a demon;
I will remove it for you."
He then made a peach-wood charm,
and had it placed before the bed where she slept.
The girl saw the charm, wept, and cursed.
Shortly after, she fell into a deep sleep.
A large wildcat, cut in half at the waist,
lay dead beneath the bed,
and her illness ceased.
At that time, Dù Xiān was also a Military Adviser in Wùzhōu,
and served alongside Jiǎ;
they got along very happily.
Together with Xiān, he was assigned to lead a mission
to Luòyáng.
Crossing the Qiántáng River,
they climbed Luó Chà Mountain,
to view the Zhèjiāng tide.
He said to Xiān:
"The Great Yǔ was truly a sage;
when regulating the waters,
he used golden caskets and jade tallies
to suppress rivers and waterways.
If this Hángzhōu city were not suppressed,
it would soon sink."
Xiān said:
"How do you know this?"
Jiǎ said:
"It is beneath this rock.
Let us go see it together."
He then told Xiān to close his eyes,
and took his hand,
He ordered Xū to jump down.
Xū suddenly closed his eyes,
and in an instant, he reached the bottom of the water.
The open space there was like a hall,
with a large stone cabinet,
over ten feet tall,
locked shut.
Jiǎ used his hand to open the lock,
removed its lid,
took Xū’s hand and helped him climb up,
then together they entered the cabinet.
Inside was another golden cabinet,
about three feet tall,
secured with a golden lock.
Jiǎ said:
"The jade tally is inside,
but mortals are not meant to see it."
After Xū had looked at it,
Jiǎ took his hand again,
and ordered him to leap out.
Xū sprang and reached the shore.
Once they had become close friends,
Jiǎ told Xū:
"You have the fortune to become a prime minister,
and should take care to protect it."
He then revealed the sequence of official posts Xū would hold,
as well as his lifespan,
explaining everything in detail.
Later, Xū was promoted and appointed to posts,
exactly as Jiǎ had said.
Later, when they stopped the boat in Wújùn,
Jiǎ’s daughter died young,
at the age of five.
Her mother mourned her with deep sorrow,
but Jiǎ did not weep.
Xū held Jiǎ in high regard,
and they each introduced their wives and children,
becoming like one family.
Then, facing his wife, Jiǎ said to Xū:
"I am a celestial being from the third heaven,
who committed a crime,
and was exiled to the mortal world for twenty-five years,
which is now complete.
I will depart the day after tomorrow.
This girl is also not my daughter,
which is why she died young.
My wife, Madame Cuī, is also not my wife—
she is actually the wife of Lǐ Yǐ, the Deputy Prefect of Jízhōu.
Because the time had not yet come,
Lǐ Yǐ was not yet meant to marry.
Since mortals must also have households,
the Director of Fate temporarily assigned her to be my wife.
Now that my term has ended,
she will return to Lǐ.
Lǐ Yǐ holds a third-rank salary and will serve in several posts,
and will have five sons.
Mortals do not know this—
why weep without cause?"
His wife had long known her husband was extraordinary,
so she stopped crying and pleaded:
"I am still in the prime of my life—
how can you bear to abandon me?
Moreover, the summer heat is on the road,
and I am so alone—
please escort me to Luò,
so I may settle there.
Even strangers on the road
deserve compassion;
how much more so the bond of husband and wife?
How can you suddenly cast me aside?"
Jiǎ smiled but did not answer.
He then ordered a coffin to be made,
placed his deceased daughter inside,
and set it beneath the boat.
He also entrusted Xū with his posthumous affairs, saying:
"After my death,
prepare a plain coffin,
seal its seams with lacquer,
and take it to my ancestral gravesite,
where both my daughter and I will be buried together.
After the burial, depart immediately,
and travel to Sòngzhōu.
Madame Cuī’s uncle serves as Deputy Prefect of Sòngzhōu—
he will surely keep his niece there.
Allow it.
By early winter,
Lǐ Yǐ will certainly travel to the capital for the census,
and will meet Madame Cuī’s uncle—
they are old acquaintances—
and will propose marriage.
Deputy Prefect Cuī will give his niece to him in marriage,
and the matter will be settled."
Xū agreed.
Jiǎ’s wife wept day and night,
begging him to stay a little longer.
He never answered.
On the day, he bathed,
put on new clothes,
and in the evening summoned Xū,
to converse face-to-face.
After a while, he lay down
and passed away.
Xū wept bitterly for him,
prepared mourning garments for a friend,
and buried him as instructed.
When they reached Sòngzhōu,
Deputy Prefect Cuī indeed kept his niece.
Xū traveled to Línrǔ,
where he gave Jiǎ and his daughter a lavish burial.
That winter,
Lǐ Yǐ arrived in Sòngzhōu
to seek a wife.
Deputy Prefect Cuī gave her to him in marriage.
Later, Xū became prime minister,
served both in the capital and the provinces,
exactly as predicted.
From "Jì Wén"
Yán Zhēnqīng
Yán Zhēnqīng, styled Qīngchén,
was a native of Línyí in Lángyá.
He was the fifth-generation descendant of Yán Zhītuī, a Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gate during the Northern Qí.
From a young age, he was diligent in his studies,
passed the imperial examinations,
and repeatedly achieved top honors.
When Yán Zhēnqīng was eighteen or nineteen years old,
he lay ill for over a hundred days,
and no physician could cure him.
A Daoist priest passed by his home,
claiming to be the Lord of the Northern Mountains,
and produced a grain-sized amount of cinnabar to save him.
He recovered instantly.
The Daoist said to him:
"You possess a reputation for purity and simplicity,
and your name is already recorded in the Golden Terrace.
You are fit to transcend the mortal world
and ascend to the celestial palace.
You should not sink yourself into the sea of fame and officialdom.
If you cannot free yourself from the dusty net,
on the day you depart this world,
you may refine your spirit in the shadowy realms with your form,
and thereafter attain the Way."
He then gave him another pellet of cinnabar,
admonishing him:
"Uphold integrity and assist your sovereign,
be diligent and frugal in cultivating yourself.
After a hundred years,
I will await you between the Yī and Luò Rivers."
Yán Zhēnqīng also prided himself on his talent and capability,
awaiting a great appointment.
Yet, in his leisure from reading and reciting,
he often turned his mind to the Daoist path of immortality.
After passing the imperial examinations,
he was appointed four times as Investigating Censor,
and served as the Military Inspector for the Héxī and Lǒngzuǒ garrisons.
In Wǔyuán, there was an unjust case
that had long remained unresolved.
When Yán Zhēnqīng arrived,
he adjudicated it.
The weather had been dry,
but rain fell after the case was decided.
The local people called it "the Censor's Rain."
In Hédōng, there was a man named Zhèng Yánzuò
whose mother had died twenty-nine years earlier
and was still interred in a plot of land by a monastery wall.
Yán Zhēnqīng impeached him.
The brothers were ostracized for thirty years,
causing a sensation throughout the land.
He was promoted to Palace Censor and Vice Director of the Ministry of War.
Yáng Guózhōng was angered by his refusal to align with him,
and had him appointed as the Grand Administrator of Píngyuán.
Ān Lùshān's rebellious intentions were becoming evident,
so Yán Zhēnqīng used heavy rain as a pretext
to repair the city walls and dredge the moats,
secretly mustering able-bodied men
and stockpiling supplies.
He pretended to order scholars to go boating,
drinking wine and composing poetry.
Ān Lùshān secretly spied on him,
thinking him a mere scholar,
not worth worrying about.
Not long after,
Ān Lùshān rebelled,
and the region north of the Yellow River fell entirely,
except for Píngyuán, which was prepared.
He then sent his Military Advisor to gallop and report.
Emperor Xuánzōng said joyfully:
"Of the twenty-four commanderies in Héběi,
only Yán Zhēnqīng stands firm.
I regret not yet knowing his appearance."
After Ān Lùshān captured Luòyáng,
he killed the留守 Lǐ Chéng
and used his head to summon surrender in Héběi.
Yán Zhēnqīng, fearing this would shake people's resolve,
killed the messenger
and told his generals:
"I knew Lǐ Chéng;
this head is not genuine."
Later, he used it as a cap ornament,
attached a grass body to it,
and buried it in a coffin.
Ān Lùshān stationed troops to guard Tǔmén.
Yán Zhēnqīng's elder brother, Yán Gǎoqīng,
was the Grand Administrator of Chángshān,
and together they breached Tǔmén.
Seventeen commanderies submitted on the same day,
electing Yán Zhēnqīng as their commander.
They gathered two hundred thousand troops,
dominating Yān and Zhào.
An edict added to his titles: Vice Minister of Revenue and Grand Administrator of Píngyuán.
At that time, a visitor from Qīnghé commandery, Lǐ È,
came to the army headquarters.
Yán Zhēnqīng consulted with him on strategy,
and together they defeated over twenty thousand of Ān Lùshān's followers at Tángyì.
When Emperor Sùzōng moved to Língwǔ,
an edict appointed him as Minister of Works and Censor-in-Chief.
Yán Zhēnqīng took a byway to court at Fèngxiáng,
was appointed Minister of Justice,
and soon additionally made Censor-in-Chief.
He impeached officials and oversaw promotions and demotions,
greatly upholding court discipline.
He successively administered Púzhōu and Tóngzhōu,
leaving behind affection wherever he served.
Framed by Censor Táng Shí
and resented by the chief ministers,
he was demoted to Prefect of Ráozhōu.
Later appointed Military Commissioner of Shēngzhōu and Zhèxī,
he was recalled as Minister of Justice.
Again slandered by Lǐ Fǔguó,
he was demoted to Assistant Prefect of Péngzhōu.
When Emperor Dàizōng succeeded,
he was appointed Prefect of Lìzhōu,
then recalled as Vice Minister of Revenue,
Military Commissioner of Jīngnán,
soon appointed Right Vice Director,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Lǔ Commandery.
The chancellor Yuán Zài,
privately forming factions,
feared court officials discussing his faults,
petitioned that all officials wishing to discuss affairs
must first inform their superiors,
who would inform the chancellor,
before reporting to the emperor.
Yán Zhēnqīng submitted a memorial vehemently opposing this, and it was stopped.
Later, while overseeing sacrifices at the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
he reported to the court that the sacrificial vessels were not maintained.
Yuán Zài considered this slander against the government,
and had him demoted to Assistant Prefect of Xiázhōu,
later appointed Prefect of Fǔzhōu and Húzhōu.
After Yuán Zài was executed,
he was appointed Minister of Justice.
Upon Emperor Dàizōng's death,
he served as Master of Ceremonies.
He also proposed that the posthumous titles for the seven emperors from Gāozǔ onward
were excessively numerous,
and suggested using the initial posthumous titles as definitive.
Resented by Chancellor Yáng Yán,
this was not implemented.
He was changed to Junior Tutor of the Heir Apparent,
secretly stripped of his authority.
Later changed to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
At that time, Lǐ Xīliè captured Rǔzhōu.
The chancellor Lú Qì,
who had long resented his integrity,
sought to harm him.
He petitioned that Yán Zhēnqīng, with his great virtue,
was respected everywhere.
Sending him to admonish Lǐ Xīliè
could subdue the great rebel without bloodshed.
The emperor agreed.
When this was carried out,
the court and the public were aghast.
Lǐ Miǎn, hearing of it,
thought losing a senior statesman
would bring shame to the court,
and secretly petitioned to retain him.
He also sent people to intercept him on the road,
but failed.
When Yán Zhēnqīng met Lǐ Xīliè,
just as he was proclaiming the imperial decree,
over a thousand of Lǐ Xīliè's adopted sons
rushed forward with drawn swords, wanting to kill him.
Surrounding and cursing him,
his expression remained unmoved.
Lǐ Xīliè shielded him with his body,
and he was taken to the guesthouse.
Lǐ Xīliè held a banquet for his followers,
summoning Yán Zhēnqīng to sit and watch.
He had performers mock court politics as entertainment.
Yán Zhēnqīng angrily said:
"You, sir, are a subject of the emperor.
How can you allow such lowly people to act like this?"
He then stood up and left.
Lǐ Xīliè sent someone to ask Yán Zhēnqīng about ceremonial regulations.
He replied:
"This old man is aged,
but I once oversaw state rituals.
What I remember are the rites for feudal lords paying homage."
Afterward,
Lǐ Xīliè had firewood piled in the courtyard
and doused it with oil.
He sent someone to say:
"If you will not submit,
you must burn yourself."
Yán Zhēnqīng threw himself into the fire.
His rebel followers rescued him.
Yán Zhēnqīng then wrote his own final memorial, epitaph, and sacrificial text,
showing his resolve to die.
The rebel faction had him strangled
on the third day of the eighth month in the first year of the Xīngyuán era.
He was seventy-seven years old.
When the court heard of it,
suspended audiences for five days,
and bestowed the posthumous title Wénzhōng Duke.
Yán Zhēnqīng served with great virtue under four reigns,
upright and daring to speak out,
growing more vigorous with age.
Slandered by Lú Qì,
he met his end at the hands of rebels.
The world considered him wronged.
The "Separate Biography" states:
When Yán Zhēnqīng was about to be hanged,
he untied his golden belt and gave it to the envoy, saying:
"I have practiced the Dao,
and regard the preservation of the body as foremost.
After my death,
only cut my limbs to draw blood,
and use the blood from my throat
to deceive them.
Then I will die without regret."
The executioner followed his words.
After his death,
they collected and buried him.
When the rebellion was quelled,
Yán Zhēnqīng's family moved his remains to the capital.
Upon opening the coffin to view him,
the coffin was decayed, yet the corpse remained intact,
the flesh as if alive,
the hands and feet soft and supple,
the beard and hair dark and black,
the fists clenched tight,
the fingernails piercing through the back of the hands.
People near and far were astonished.
As they journeyed midway,
the traveling coffin gradually lightened,
and upon reaching the burial site,
it was but an empty coffin.
The "Records of Messages from the Kaiyuan and Tianbao Eras" records this in detail.
The "Separate Biography" further states:
When Yán Zhēnqīng was about to go to Càizhōu,
he said to his son:
"Both Yuán Zǎi and I took the highest elixir,
but he was ruined by wine and lust,
so he did not attain what I have.
This journey to Càizhōu,
I will surely be killed by the rebel traitors.
Afterward, you may retrieve my remains from Huàyīn,
open the coffin and look,
and it will certainly be different from others."
When the coffin was opened,
indeed they witnessed the marvel.
The Dàoshi Xíng Hépú said:
"This is what is called a 'form immortal.'
Even if concealed within iron or stone,
once the refinement of the form is complete,
it will naturally split open and fly away."
More than ten years later,
a servant of the Yán family
was sent from Yōng to Zhèngzhōu
to collect rent from the estate.
Returning to Luòjīng,
this servant happened to visit Tóngdé Temple,
where he saw Lord Lǔ (Yán Zhēnqīng) wearing a long white gown,
holding a canopy,
sitting in the Buddha hall.
The servant hurried to approach and bow to him.
Lord Lǔ then turned and left.
Looking up at the Buddha wall,
he moved left and right, following it.
Ultimately, he did not let the servant see his face.
Then he descended from the Buddha hall,
and left the temple.
The servant also followed on foot,
directly to a desolate vegetable garden in the northeast corner of the city.
There were two dilapidated rooms,
with a curtain hanging on the door.
Lord Lǔ lifted the curtain and entered.
The servant then bowed from outside the curtain.
Lord Lǔ said:
"Who is it?"
The servant replied with his name.
Lord Lǔ said:
"Come in."
After the servant entered and bowed,
he was about to weep.
Lord Lǔ hastily stopped him.
Then he briefly asked about one or two of his sons and nephews.
Lord Lǔ reached into his bosom,
took out ten taels of gold, and gave it to the servant
to aid the family's expenses,
then urged him to leave quickly,
"Do not speak of this to anyone upon returning.
If the family is in need later,
come again."
The servant returned to Yōng,
and the family was greatly astonished.
They exchanged the gold for currency,
and it was indeed genuine gold.
The Yán family's son then bought a saddle and horse,
and with the former servant hurried to pay a visit.
Returning to the previous place,
they found only overgrown brambles and weeds,
with nothing at all.
People of the time all said that Lord Lǔ had achieved the Dao through liberation from the corpse.
From "Supplementary Records of Immortal Biographies," "Leisurely Talks from the Military Tent," and "Idle Conversations from the Jade Hall"
Wéi Yǎn
Wéi Yǎn, styled Jǐngzhào.
During the Kāiyuán era,
he sat for the imperial examination but failed to pass,
and traveled to Shǔ.
It was late spring at the time,
with many scenic spots still in their prime.
Together with his friends, he sought out flowers and visited unusual places,
spending his days on outings and banquets.
Suddenly, one morning, an inviter came and said:
"About ten miles south of the commandery,
there is a Lín Tíng belonging to the Zhèng family.
The flowers are in full bloom,
and the scenery is transcendent and splendid.
We would like to invite you to join us for a visit."
Yǎn was delighted
and went with them.
Indeed, ten miles to the south,
they found the Zhèng family pavilion.
The main hall was lofty and majestic,
standing imposingly on all four sides.
The mountain gate was adorned with flowers,
and winding paths were shrouded in mist.
Gazing at it,
he had no time to look elsewhere—
it was truly a scene beyond the mortal world.
Soon, Yǎn was invited to ascend a grand pavilion.
Winding corridors encircled the structure,
decorated with pearls and jade,
almost certainly not of this mortal realm.
He was then introduced to over a dozen immortals,
with attendants on both sides.
Their splendid robes and exquisite makeup
were also unlike anything seen in the mortal world.
One among them spoke to Yǎn,
and Yǎn bowed repeatedly and questioned her.
The beautiful woman said:
"We have heard that you, sir, traveled west to Shǔ's capital,
visiting fine scenery along the way.
Spring warmth is about to end,
and the flowers are fragrant and beautiful.
We wish to offer you a drink in passing,
so please do not doubt our hospitality."
Once seated,
music was played and wine served.
The arrangement of dishes and delicacies,
the exotic flavors and rare fruits,
were unlike anything tasted in the mortal world.
The music of metal, stone, silk, and bamboo,
with its elegant melodies and clear singing,
was also unheard of in the mortal world.
Yǎn seized the opportunity to ask:
"I have traveled from the capital through the two imperial cities,
and have seen the majesty of the imperial palace
and the prosperity of noble households.
There is nothing I have not witnessed.
But what I see today
cannot be compared to any of that.
May I ask why you, fair lady, are so noble?"
The beautiful woman replied:
"I am not of the mortal world;
this is the Jade Clarity Immortal Palace.
We wished to summon you,
so we borrowed the Zhèng family pavilion for the occasion.
I have a new melody,
called 'Purple Clouds.'
Now, the Son of Heaven reveres the way of immortals,
so I wish to entrust this music to you,
to present it to the sovereign of the Great Táng,
and to rely on you for this task.
Is that acceptable?"
Yǎn said:
"I am merely a scholar,
in Cháng'ān.
I toil in the bustling streets,
striving for a single name.
The gates of the Son of Heaven are beyond my sight;
nor am I a connoisseur of music.
If I were to present a new melody,
it would surely be impossible."
The beautiful woman said:
"Since you cannot,
I will convey it to the Son of Heaven through a dream.
However, since you have come here,
it is due to the workings of fate.
I wish to give you three treasures as gifts.
If you sell them,
you can enjoy wealth for the rest of your life."
After the drinking concluded,
she ordered an attendant to bring out a cup,
called the 'Jasper Jade Cup,'
which was luminous and translucent.
Then she brought out a pillow,
called the 'Red Ruí Pillow,'
resembling jade but with a chestnut hue,
its patterns slightly red,
and its luster bright and clear.
Next, she produced a purple jade case,
resembling cloth,
but with a brilliance surpassing jade.
All were given to Yǎn.
He bowed and expressed his gratitude,
then took his leave.
Before he had traveled a mile,
he looked back and found the pavilion gone,
with only wild brambles remaining.
He then took the treasures to Cháng'ān.
The following year, he again failed the examination,
and traveled east to Guǎnglíng.
A foreign merchant sought out Yǎn,
inquiring about his treasures.
Yǎn brought them out to show him.
The foreigner bowed and said:
"These are treasures of the Jade Clarity Perfected One.
For thousands of years, no one has seen them—
they are truly rare treasures of the world."
He offered hundreds of thousands in gold to exchange for them.
Yǎn became immensely wealthy,
built a house in Jiāngdū,
and never again sought fame or advancement,
with no one knowing his eventual fate.
Several years later,
Emperor Xuánzōng dreamed of over ten immortals
gathering in the courtyard with musical instruments,
playing a melody to impart to him.
They requested it be made the orthodox music of the Central Plains,
and the melody was named 'Purple Clouds.'
Upon waking in the morning,
he practiced it by playing it on a jade flute,
and it was passed down to the Music Bureau.
This corresponded to what Yǎn had encountered—
the melody they had wished for Yǎn to present.
From *The Biographies of Encounters with Immortals*.
Shēn Yuánzhī,
it is not known from where he hailed.
He traveled to famous mountains,
extensively collecting esoteric arts,
and harbored the aspiration of cultivating immortality to transcend the mortal world.
During the Kāiyuán era,
he was summoned to the court
and resided at the Kāiyuán Temple,
where the imperial favor he received grew ever more profound.
At that time, there were also Xíng Hépǔ, Luó Gōngyuǎn, Yè Fǎshàn, Wú Yún, Yǐn Yīn, Hé Sīdá,
Míngchāo edition writes "dá" as "yuǎn"
Shǐ Chóng, Yǐn Chóng, and Mì Xīyán,
who assisted in promoting the profound teachings of Daoism,
and supported the sage ruler.
The teachings of purity, tranquility, and non-action
shone brightly across the myriad realms.
Even the reverence for Daoism during the reigns of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn and the Northern Wèi
could not compare to this.
When the emperor traveled to the hot springs
and visited the eastern capital Luòyáng,
Yuánzhī often accompanied him.
At that time, he was skilled in discussing the principles of the mysterious and the void,
and sometimes lingered in discussions on the Dao,
with the passage of time unnoticed.
Only the Noble Consort and a few palace ladies, such as Zhào Yúnróng,
served alongside the emperor,
and were able to hear these matters.
Zhào Yúnróng was tasked with serving tea and medicine.
Yuánzhī took pity on her respectful and diligent demeanor.
Seizing an opportunity, she begged for medicine,
hoping to prolong her life.
Yuánzhī said:
"I have nothing to withhold,
but you will not remain in this world for long."
She earnestly bowed and begged incessantly,
saying:
"Hearing the Dao in the morning,
one may die content in the evening;
how much more so for one who serves a great immortal,
yet cannot transcend the mortal world?
It is like reaching into a treasure trove with empty hands.
I beg the Celestial Master to take pity on me."
Yuánzhī, moved by her sincere determination,
gave her a single Crimson Snow Elixir.
He said:
"If you take this elixir,
your body will not decay after death.
Enlarge your coffin,
widen your burial chamber,
place genuine jade in your mouth,
and ensure ventilation,
so that your soul does not scatter,
nor your spirit decay.
After a hundred years, you will be revived.
This is the method of refining the form through the Great Yin,
and you will become an earthbound immortal.
After another hundred years,
you will move to reside in a celestial grotto."
Yúnróng accompanied the emperor to the eastern capital,
but fell ill at the Lánchāng Palace.
The Noble Consort took pity on her,
and Yúnróng recounted this matter to the Noble Consort.
After her death,
the eunuch Xú Xuánzào buried her according to her requests.
By the end of the Yuánhé era, a hundred years had passed,
and Yúnróng indeed revived.
Yuánzhī still roamed among mortals,
calling himself Master Tián.
Those in the know said:
"Yuánzhī was a man from the Wèi era,
already several hundred years old."
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Mǎ Zìrán
Mǎ Xiāng, styled Zìrán,
was a native of Yánguān in Hángzhōu.
His family for generations had served as minor clerks in the county,
but Xiāng alone was fond of the classics and histories,
studied literature,
and cultivated the arts of the Way.
He traveled all over the world,
and later returned to Jiāngnán.
Once, while drunk in Húzhōu,
he fell into the Zhà River.
He only emerged after a full day,
his clothes not even damp,
and sat upon the water, saying:
"I was just summoned by Xiàng Yǔ to drink,
and wished to get thoroughly drunk
before returning."
Onlookers by the riverbank were packed like a wall.
The smell of alcohol still emanated from him,
and his manner was as if mad.
Many passersby followed and watched him.
At times, he would also thrust his fist into his nose,
and when he withdrew his fist,
his nose was as before.
He also pointed at the river water, making it flow backwards for the time it takes to eat a meal;
pointed at a willow tree, making it follow the river water back and forth;
and pointed at a bridge, making it break and then reconnect.
Later, while traveling in Chángzhōu,
he met the Táng dynasty chancellor Mǎ Zhí, who had been demoted
and transferred to serve as Prefect of Chángzhōu.
Having long heard of Xiāng's fame,
Zhí invited him for an audience,
and received him with exceptional courtesy, treating him as extraordinary.
Zhí asked:
"I am fortunate to share the same surname as you, Elder of the Way.
I wish to become sworn brothers,
hoping to learn your arts of the Way. Is that acceptable?"
Xiāng said:
"What is Your Excellency's ancestral home?"
Zhí said:
"Fúfēng."
Xiāng said:
"Your Excellency is from Fúfēng,
but Mǎ Xiāng is as unrelated as 'wind, horse, and ox.'
Let us simply know each other,
with no need to claim kinship based on shared surname."
This meant he and Zhí were completely unrelated.
Zhí kept him at the prefectural residence,
and respected him even more.
Once during a meal,
Zhí requested to see a minor feat of magic.
Thereupon, at the banquet table,
Xiāng used a porcelain vessel filled with soil to plant melon seeds.
In a moment, vines sprouted,
blossomed, and bore fruit.
He picked them for the guests to eat,
and all praised their fragrance and deliciousness,
different from ordinary melons.
He also rubbed coins from his entire body and socks;
the coins that came out were countless,
all cast as bronze coins.
He threw them into a well,
then called them, and they flew out one by one.
If someone picked them up,
they would disappear again shortly after.
Also, Zhí mentioned that rats in the city were extremely numerous.
Xiāng wrote a talisman,
and had someone post it beneath the southern wall.
He then struck a plate with chopsticks and let out a long whistle.
Rats came in droves,
ran to beneath the talisman, and prostrated themselves.
Xiāng then called the rats,
and one large one approached before the steps.
Xiāng said:
"You are tiny, hairy creatures.
Heaven grants you grain to eat.
How dare you bore through walls and tunnel under houses,
disturbing His Excellency day and night?
Moreover, with a heart of compassion,
I cannot kill you all.
You should now lead each other away from here."
The large rat then turned back,
and all the rats came forward,
as if kowtowing to apologize.
They then formed a line—no one knew how many—
and left through the city gate.
Afterwards, rats completely disappeared from the city.
Later, he traveled south to Yuèzhōu,
passing by the Dòngyán Chányuàn monastery.
Three hundred monks were just having their meal,
while Xiāng was traveling with Wáng Zhīwēi, a Dàoist from the Mùmǎyán in Yǒngkāng County, Wùzhōu, and his disciple Wáng Yánsōu.
The monks saw Xiāng sitting cross-legged alone and eating,
with hardly anyone greeting him.
They only provided him with rice,
which Xiāng did not eat.
He urged Zhīwēi and Yánsōu to eat quickly and leave.
Before the monks' meal was finished,
they went out the gate.
He again urged them to hurry.
They reached an inn south of Zhūjì County,
about over seventy lǐ from the monastery.
Late at night,
they heard voices seeking the Dàoists.
The innkeeper hastily responded
that there were three here.
Those outside were extremely pleased,
and asked the innkeeper
to allow them to see the Dàoists.
When they entered,
they were two monks, who merely bowed and pleaded mournfully:
"We Chán monks did not recognize you, Masters of the Way.
Yesterday we failed to welcome and receive you properly,
causing you to reprimand us.
Three hundred monks are now unable to get out of bed.
We two monks are in charge and were not sitting,
so we were able to come.
We earnestly beg you to forgive them."
Xiāng only slept and did not respond.
Zhīwēi and Yánsōu merely laughed at them.
The monks pleaded even more mournfully.
Xiāng then said:
"Henceforth, do not take matters lightly or be disrespectful.
Go back and enter the gate;
the sitting monks will then be able to get out of bed."
The monks returned, and it happened just as he said.
The next day, Xiāng again traveled south.
It was just spring,
and he saw a household with fine cabbage,
but his request for some was denied.
He even heard harsh words.
He ordered Yánsōu to fetch paper and brush.
Zhīwēi then said:
"Our request for cabbage was refused;
truly there is no reason to dispute it.
Moreover, as followers of the Dàoist path,
how could we resort to such measures?"
Xiāng laughed and said:
"I am not disputing anything,
just playing a little trick."
Thereupon, Yánsōu handed him the paper and brush.
Xiāng painted a white egret,
sprayed water on it,
and it flew into the vegetable patch to peck at the cabbage.
The owner chased it off,
but it flew down again and again.
Xiāng then painted a small dog,
which ran and chased the egret,
and together they trampled all the cabbage.
In a moment, it was all utterly destroyed.
The owner saw the Dàoist laughing playfully
and realized it was because he had requested cabbage.
Fearing further magical acts,
he came to plead mournfully.
Xiāng said:
"I did not originally seek cabbage,
but was just playing with you."
He then called the egret and the dog,
and both flew and ran to throw themselves into Xiāng's bosom.
Looking at the cabbage, it was as before,
completely undamaged.
He then traveled south to Huòtóng Mountain,
entering Chángxī County.
At night, he sought lodging at an inn.
The inn had few rooms, but many travelers were already there.
The innkeeper said jokingly, "There is no place to stay.
If the Dàoist master can sleep on the wall,
then we can accommodate you."
As dusk was already approaching,
Zhīwēi and Yánsōu were anxious to find lodging.
Xiāng said:
"You two just sleep among the ordinary travelers,
while I leap onto the beam."
He hung upside down from the beam by one foot to sleep.
It happened that the innkeeper got up at night
and saw him by candlelight.
He was greatly astonished.
Xiāng said:
"If I can do this on a beam,
what difficulty is a wall?"
Soon he entered the wall,
and did not emerge for a long time.
The innkeeper bowed and apologized.
He moved Zhīwēi and Yánsōu to a clean place inside the house to rest.
At dawn,
the innkeeper tried to detain them,
but suddenly Xiāng was nowhere to be found.
Zhīwēi and Yánsōu walked ahead several lǐ,
and found him already waiting by the roadside.
Returning from Huòtóng to Yǒngkāng County, he stayed at the Tiānbǎo Temple to the east.
In the temple grounds was a large withered pine tree.
Xiāng pointed at it and said:
"This pine is already over three thousand years old,
and will soon turn to stone."
Afterwards, the pine indeed turned to stone.
Suddenly, there was a great wind and thunderous quake;
the stone toppled by the mountainside,
breaking into several sections.
It happened that Yáng Fā, demoted from Military Governor of Guǎngzhōu to Wùzhōu,
was by nature fond of the strange and extraordinary.
He had two sections moved to the prefectural residence,
and two sections delivered to the Jiǔsōng Courtyard of the Lóngxīng Temple.
Each stood six or seven chǐ tall,
with a diameter of over three chǐ,
their stones resembling pine bark with scaly wrinkles,
and they remain to this day.
When someone came to him with an illness,
Hán Xiāng had no medicine,
but would strike the painful area with a bamboo staff;
for ailments in the abdomen or throughout the body,
he would point at them with the bamboo staff,
blow on the staff’s head, producing a sound like thunder,
and the illness would be cured.
There was a person suffering from a hunched back and bent legs,
who came leaning on a staff;
Hán Xiāng also struck him with the bamboo staff,
telling him to let go of his own staff,
and immediately the man’s body straightened.
Sometimes people offered him wealth or silk,
but he declined and would not accept it;
if they insisted on giving it to him,
he would then distribute it among the poor.
Wherever he traveled,
whether to palaces, temples, caves, or grottoes,
he often inscribed poems.
His poem on climbing Qínwàng Mountain in Hángzhōu reads:
"Where to seek the division of Tàiyǐ’s beginning?
Only the cycles of time remain, shifting human hearts.
The sun and moon of the nine heavens shift from dawn to dusk,
The rivers and mountains over ten thousand lǐ change from past to present.
Wind stirs the water’s glow, swallowing distant peaks,
Rain adds to the mountain mists, obscuring tall forests.
Qín Shǐhuáng vainly devised plans to drive away mountains,
The vast blue sea only grows deeper and more profound."
He returned to his hometown to visit his elder brother.
It happened that his brother was out,
and his sister-in-law and nephew were delighted at their uncle’s return.
Hán Xiāng said to them:
"I share this house with my brother.
Now that I have returned, I need to clarify the ownership of this place—
I only desire the eastern garden."
His sister-in-law was astonished and said:
"Younger uncle, you have been away from home for so long.
You’ve returned, yet you haven’t even met your brother face-to-face.
How can you speak of dividing the property?
The bond of flesh and blood
surely cannot bear such a thing."
He stayed for three days,
and his sister-in-law and nephew were surprised that he did not eat,
drinking only wine.
He waited, but his brother did not return,
and that night he suddenly passed away.
The next day, his brother returned
and asked what had happened.
His wife and son told him the truth. The elder brother was deeply moved and sorrowful,
and said:
"My younger brother studied the Dào for many years.
He did not return to divide the house—
he returned to entrust his transformation to me,
to sever my longing for him."
So they placed him in a coffin.
That evening, the coffin made a loud noise,
startling the whole family.
They then buried him in the garden.
This was in the tenth year of the Dàzhōng era.
The following year,
Dōngchuān reported that Dàoist Mǎ Zìrán of Zǐtóng County, Jiànzhōu,
had ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
Hán Xiāng, while in Dōngchuān, said to people:
"I am from Yánguān."
An imperial order was sent to Hángzhōu in the Zhèxī Circuit to investigate,
and when they opened the tomb and examined the coffin,
they found only a bamboo branch inside.
From "Continued Biographies of Immortals"
Zhāng Jùjūn
Zhāng Jùjūn—
it is unknown where he was from.
At that time, there was a man named Xǔ Jìshān
who fell ill and did not recover.
He purified himself through fasting and made offerings at Tài Shān, pleading for his life,
praying and lamenting day and night.
Suddenly, a divine being came and asked him:
"Who are you?
Why do you bitterly plead to the underworld?
Heaven has sent me to question you—
answer truthfully."
Jìshān said:
"I am Xǔ Jìshān from Píngyú in the southeast.
I have been ill for three years,
and I do not know where my offense lies.
Therefore, I came to this sacred mountain
to seek a judgment on life and death."
The divine being said:
"I am the immortal Zhāng Jùjūn.
I possess the Way of the Yìjīng,
and can discern the source of your misfortune."
Jìshān then bowed again and pleaded:
"I am fortunate that an immortal has deigned to descend.
I beg you to enlighten me."
Jùjūn performed a divination for him.
He obtained the hexagram Zhèn changing to Héng.
The first, second, and third lines
were all changing lines.
Jùjūn said:
"You are a man without virtue—
how can your illness be cured?"
Jìshān said:
"I beg you to reveal it."
Jùjūn said:
"You once traveled with a guest,
seeking to avenge your father.
Along the way, you killed the guest
and threw him into an empty well,
covering it with a large stone.
This man appealed to the celestial court,
and it is because of this that you are afflicted with this illness."
Jìshān said:
"I indeed committed this crime."
Jùjūn said:
"Why did you do it?"
Jìshān said:
"My father was once assaulted by someone,
and I felt the shame of this all my life.
At the time, I and the guest were unable to take revenge,
and the guest intended to inform the enemy,
so I killed him."
Jùjūn said:
"The principles of the underworld are difficult to deceive.
You must diligently cultivate yourself.
I will return to the mountain and plead for your life."
Jìshān gradually recovered.
Jùjūn taught Jìshān divination,
and Jìshān thus became skilled in the Yìjīng.
However, he did not seek from Jùjūn the method to transcend the world—
what a pity!
From "Biographies of Cave Immortals"
Péi Shìzǐ
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
in Cháng'ān, there was a man surnamed Péi,
who lived at a manor outside the Yánpíng Gate.
He and his two brothers were not yet officials,
but were known for their filial piety and righteousness.
Although poor, they were fond of bestowing kindness.
An old man once passed by and asked for a drink,
his clothing and appearance somewhat unusual.
The Péi son treated him with great respect
and asked what he did.
He said:
"I make my living by selling medicine."
When asked about his clan,
he said:
"There is no need to speak of it."
From then on, he would come and go, resting and lodging at the Péi residence,
and for several years showed no sign of weariness.
One day he said to Péi:
"I observe that you and your brothers are extremely poor,
yet you are always able to humble yourselves and remain tireless in hosting guests.
You are truly virtuous elders;
accumulating virtue like this,
you are certain to receive great fortune.
I too am grateful for your kindness,
and now I shall obtain a small amount of wealth for you
to serve as provisions for several years."
Péi respectfully thanked him.
The old man then asked for several catties of charcoal,
dug a pit in the ground to make a furnace,
and lit a blazing fire.
After a short while,
he instructed them to fetch several small bricks and tiles the size of fingers,
burned them,
and soon they all turned red.
He took a small amount of medicine from his bosom and threw it in,
whereupon purple smoke arose,
and after the time it takes to eat a meal, they transformed into gold,
weighing approximately one hundred taels.
He gave it to the Péi son,
saying to Péi:
"This is worth twice the usual amount,
enough to cover your household expenses for three years.
I will depart from here now,
and when your family's resources are exhausted,
I shall return."
The Péi brothers revered the old man even more
and bowed to him.
They then asked where he lived.
He said:
"I will show you later,"
and bid them farewell before leaving.
The Péi family then sold the gold and stored up grain.
The following year, when floods and droughts struck,
they alone were spared from the disaster.
Three years later,
the old man returned,
and again burned gold to give to them.
One of the Péi brothers expressed a desire to study under him.
The old man then took him westward,
and after several li, they arrived beneath the western cliffs of Tàibái Mountain.
There was a large flat stone,
with a stone wall to the left.
The old man tapped it with his staff,
and it opened after a moment.
It was a cave paradise.
Daoist priests and young attendants came to welcome them.
The old man led Péi into the cave.
At first it seemed dark,
but gradually it grew bright,
and they saw city walls and people,
within which were palaces, halls, and temples,
like the monasteries and temples of the mortal world.
Countless Daoist priests, jade attendants, and fairy maidens
welcomed them inside,
with abundant singing and music.
Some of the Daoist priests played the qin, played chess, recited texts, or engaged in discussion.
The old man led Péi to pay his respects,
and said to the others:
"This is the master of the city."
They then stayed for one night,
and were served sesame rice, unicorn jerky, and immortal wine.
Péi announced his intention to return.
They bid each other farewell.
The old man escorted him out of the cave again,
and gave him gold and treasures as a parting gift.
He said to Péi:
"It is not yet time for you to stay long;
return for now.
Twenty years from now,
the world will be in chaos.
This is the Zuǒyǎn Cave of Tàibái Mountain.
When that time comes,
you may return here,
and I will welcome you."
Péi bowed and took his leave.
By the time the Ān-Shǐ Rebellion broke out,
the Péi family went there together
and hid in the cave for several years.
Living in this immortal realm,
they all received Daoist arts.
After the rebellion was quelled, they emerged again.
Several of the brothers
all attained high official positions;
the entire household, noble and humble alike,
also enjoyed longevity.
From "Yuánhuà Jì"
Cuī Wěi
During the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a man named Cuī Wěi,
the son of the former Imperial Censor Cuī Xiàng.
Xiàng was renowned among the people for his poetry,
and ultimately served as an Assistant in Nánhǎi.
Wěi resided in Nánhǎi,
his disposition was carefree and open,
he did not manage family property,
and he greatly admired heroic and chivalrous deeds.
Within a few years,
his wealth and estate were completely exhausted,
and he often took shelter in Buddhist temples.
At the time of the Zhōngyuán festival,
the people of Pānyú would display rare and exotic items in Buddhist temples,
gathering various performances at Kāiyuán Temple.
Wěi went to observe,
and saw an old beggar woman
who stumbled and overturned someone's wine jar.
The tavern keeper beat her.
The cost was only a string of cash,
but Wěi pitied her,
and took off his own clothes to pay the debt for her.
The old woman left without thanking him.
Another day, she came again and told Wěi:
"I thank you for rescuing me from my difficulty.
I am skilled at moxibustion for warts.
Now I have a little moxa from Yuèjǐnggǎng to offer you.
Whenever you encounter a wart,
just one cone of moxa,
will not only cure the ailment,
but also bring about beautiful elegance."
Wěi smiled and accepted it.
The old woman vanished in an instant.
Several days later,
while visiting Hǎiguāng Temple,
he met an old monk with a wart on his ear.
Wěi took out the moxa and tried moxibustion on it,
and it worked as described.
The monk was deeply grateful,
and said to Wěi:
"This humble monk has nothing to offer in return.
I can only recite sutras to pray for blessings for you, sir.
At the foot of this mountain, there is a man named Rén Wēng,
who has stored away vast wealth,
and also suffers from this ailment.
If you, sir, can cure him,
you will surely receive a generous reward.
Please allow me to write a letter of introduction for you."
Wěi said:
"Very well."
Upon hearing this, Rén Wēng was overjoyed and excited,
and invited Wěi with great courtesy and respect.
Wěi then took out the moxa,
and with one application, he was cured.
Rén Wēng told Wěi:
"I thank you, sir, for curing my suffering.
I have no worthy reward to offer,
but I have one hundred thousand cash to present to you.
I hope you will stay at your leisure,
and not leave in haste."
Wěi thus remained there.
Wěi was skilled in the subtleties of string and wind instruments,
and hearing the sound of a zither from the front hall of his host's house,
he asked a servant.
The servant replied:
"It is our master's beloved daughter."
Wěi then requested the zither and played it.
The girl listened in secret and developed feelings for him.
At that time, Rén Wēng's family worshipped a ghost called the One-legged Spirit,
and every three years they had to kill a person as a sacrifice to it.
The time was already approaching,
and they had not found a suitable person.
Rén Wēng then turned treacherous,
and called his son to discuss it, saying:
"Our guest is not a relative,
(Note: Some versions omit 'not a relative'.)
he has no blood relations,
so he can be used as the sacrifice.
I have heard that great kindness need not be repaid,
let alone curing a minor ailment."
He then ordered the sacrificial offerings to be prepared.
As midnight approached,
they planned to kill Wěi,
having already secretly locked the room where Wěi was staying,
but Wěi was unaware.
The girl secretly learned of this,
and stealthily brought a knife to the window crack,
telling Wěi:
"My family worships a ghost,
and tonight they intend to kill you and sacrifice you.
You can use this to break the window and escape;
otherwise,
you will die shortly.
I hope you will also take this knife,
and not implicate me."
Wěi was terrified, sweating profusely,
took the knife and the moxa,
cut through the window lattice and leaped out,
broke the lock and fled.
Rén Wēng soon realized,
and led over ten servants,
armed with knives and torches, pursuing him for six or seven li,
nearly catching him.
Wěi lost his way,
stumbled, and fell into a large dry well.
The pursuers lost track and returned.
Although Wěi fell into the well,
he was cushioned by dry leaves and uninjured.
At dawn, he looked around,
and saw it was a huge cavern,
over a hundred zhang deep,
with no way to climb out.
The surrounding walls were hollowed out and winding,
capable of holding a thousand people.
In the center coiled a white snake,
several zhang long.
In front was a stone mortar,
and from the rock above, something dripped down,
like syrup or honey,
collecting in the mortar,
which the snake drank from.
Wěi observed that the snake was extraordinary,
so he kowtowed and prayed to it:
"Dragon King,
I am unfortunate,
having fallen here,
I beg Your Majesty to have pity on me,
and hopefully not harm me."
He then drank the remainder,
and felt neither hunger nor thirst.
Looking closely at the snake's lips,
he saw it also had a wart.
Wěi, grateful for the snake's compassion,
wanted to perform moxibustion for it,
but had no way to obtain fire.
After a long while,
a distant flame drifted into the cavern.
Wěi then lit the moxa,
opened the snake's mouth and applied moxibustion,
and the wart immediately fell off.
The wart had long hindered the snake's eating and drinking,
and once removed,
it found great convenience,
so it spat out a pearl about an inch in diameter to reward Wěi.
Wěi did not accept it and said to the snake:
"Dragon King, you can command clouds and rain,
the mysteries of yin and yang are unfathomable to you,
divine transformations are at your will,
your actions and concealments are within your control.
Surely you have the means
to rescue one who is sunk in despair.
If you would deign to lift me up,
allowing me to return to the human world,
then I would be eternally grateful,
engraving it upon my very flesh.
I only wish to return,
and do not desire to possess treasure."
The snake then swallowed the pearl,
and writhed as if preparing to go somewhere.
Wěi then bowed deeply,
mounted the snake, and departed.
They did not exit through the cavern's mouth,
but traveled only within the cave,
for several tens of li.
It was pitch dark inside,
but the snake's light illuminated both walls.
From time to time, he saw paintings of ancient gentlemen,
all wearing caps and belts.
Finally, they reached a stone door,
on which was a golden beast biting a ring,
and beyond it was suddenly bright and clear.
The snake lowered its head and did not advance,
but let Wěi dismount.
Wěi thought he had reached the human world.
Entering the door,
he saw only a single chamber,
vast and empty, about a hundred paces across.
The walls of the cavern
were all carved into rooms.
In the center were several brocade curtains and canopies,
hanging in golden and purple hues,
further adorned with pearls and jade,
glittering and dazzling like connected stars.
In front of the curtains was a golden incense burner,
on which were dragons, phoenixes, turtles, snakes, and other birds,
all with open mouths spewing fragrant smoke,
rich and luxuriant in aroma.
Beside it was a small pool,
lined with golden walls,
filled with mercury and floating ducks and gulls,
all carved from fine jade.
Along the four walls were beds,
all decorated with rhinoceros horn and ivory,
and upon them were zithers, pipes, drums, and other instruments,
too numerous to record.
Wěi examined them closely,
and saw that the handprints were still fresh.
Wěi was then bewildered,
unable to fathom what kind of cavern palace this was.
After a long while,
He took the qin and tried playing it.
All the doors and windows on the four walls opened,
and a young maidservant came out, smiling, and said:
"The Jade Capital Messenger has already delivered Sir Cuī here."
She then turned and went back inside.
After a short while,
four women appeared,
all wearing ancient coiled hairstyles,
draped in rainbow-hued garments.
They said to Cuī Wěi:
"Why has Sir Cuī presumptuously entered the Dark Palace of the Emperor?"
Cuī Wěi then set aside the qin and bowed twice.
The women returned the bow.
Cuī Wěi said:
"Since this is the Dark Palace of the Emperor,
where is the Emperor?"
They replied:
"He has temporarily gone to attend a banquet with Zhùróng."
They then invited Cuī Wěi to sit on the couch and play the qin.
Cuī Wěi then played "Hújiā."
The women asked:
"What piece is this?"
He said:
"It is 'Hújiā'."
They said:
"What is 'Hújiā'?
We do not understand."
Cuī Wěi said:
"Cài Wénjī of the Hàn dynasty,
the daughter of Court Gentleman Cài Yōng,
was captured by the northern tribes.
When she returned,
moved by the stories from her time among the tribes,
she composed this piece while playing the qin,
imitating the mournful, sobbing sound of the tribes' reed pipes."
The women all said delightedly:
"Truly a new piece."
They then ordered sweet wine to be poured and cups passed around.
Cuī Wěi kowtowed,
expressing his earnest desire to return home.
The women said:
"Since Sir Cuī has come,
it is all due to predestined fate.
Why must you hurry?
Please stay a while longer.
The Yángchéng Messenger will arrive shortly,
and you may follow him."
They said to Sir Cuī:
"The Emperor has already promised Lady Tián to serve you with broom and dustpan,
so you may meet her now."
Sir Cuī could not fathom the situation,
and dared not respond.
They then ordered a maidservant to summon Lady Tián.
Lady Tián refused to come,
saying:
"Without receiving the Emperor's edict,
I dare not meet Sir Cuī."
Summoned a second time, she still did not come.
They said to Cuī Wěi:
"Lady Tián is virtuous and beautiful,
peerless in the world.
We hope you will treat her well;
this too is due to past karma.
Lady Tián is the daughter of the King of Qí."
Sir Cuī asked:
"Who is the King of Qí?"
The women said:
"The King's taboo name is Héng,
the one who, after the fall of Qí in early Hàn times, lived on a sea island."
After a moment,
a ray of sunlight shone into the room.
Cuī Wěi looked up
and saw an opening above,
dimly revealing the human world and the Milky Way.
The four women said:
"The Yángchéng Messenger has arrived."
Then a white goat
descended slowly from the sky,
and in a moment reached the seat.
On its back was a man,
dressed in formal attire,
holding a large brush,
and also carrying a sealed green bamboo tube,
on which were seal script characters.
He presented it on the incense table.
The four women ordered a maidservant to read it:
"Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ Xú Shēn has died;
Ānnán Dūhù Zhào Chāng is appointed as his replacement."
The women poured sweet wine for the messenger and said:
"Sir Cuī wishes to return to Pānyú;
we hope you will take him along."
The messenger assented,
and said to Cuī Wěi:
"Another day, you must change clothes and repair my temple
to repay my labor."
Cuī Wěi merely assented.
The four women said:
"The Emperor has issued an edict,
commanding us to give the young master the national treasure, the Yángsuì Pearl.
When you go there,
a foreigner will surely offer a hundred thousand strings of cash to exchange for it."
They then ordered a maidservant to open a jade box,
take out the pearl, and give it to Cuī Wěi.
Cuī Wěi bowed deeply and received it with both hands.
He said to the four women:
"I have never paid homage to the Emperor,
nor am I a relative;
why am I so abruptly bestowed with such a gift?"
The women said:
"Your ancestor once wrote a poem on the Yuètái,
which moved Xú Shēn,
leading to its restoration.
The Emperor felt ashamed,
and also composed a poem in response.
The intent behind bestowing the pearl
is already revealed in the poem;
there is no need for us to explain.
Surely you understand, young master?"
Cuī Wěi said:
"I do not know what poem the Emperor wrote."
The women ordered a maidservant to inscribe the poem's title on the Yángchéng Messenger's brush holder:
"A thousand-year-old ruined terrace crumbles by the roadside;
Once troubled the Prefect to restore it with fragrant earth.
Moved by your care, how can I repay it enough?
I give you a beautiful lady and a bright pearl."
Cuī Wěi asked:
"What is the Emperor's original surname and name?"
The women said:
"You will know in due time."
The women said to Cuī Wěi:
"On the Zhōngyuán Festival,
you must prepare fine wine and a sumptuous feast in the quiet room of Guǎngzhōu's Pújiàn Temple.
We will send Lady Tián to you then."
Cuī Wěi then bowed again and took his leave,
intending to step onto the messenger's goat's back.
The women said:
"We know you have Bào Gū's mugwort;
please leave a little behind."
Cuī Wěi left some mugwort,
though he did not know who Bào Gū was,
and so he left it.
In an instant, he emerged from the cave
and stood on level ground.
The messenger and the goat had already vanished.
Looking at the stars and the Milky Way,
he saw it was already the fifth watch.
Soon he heard the bell of Pújiàn Temple,
and reached the temple.
The monks offered him morning porridge,
and then he returned to Guǎngzhōu.
Cuī Wěi had previously rented a house;
arriving that day, he went to inquire at the house.
They said:
"It has been three years."
The landlord said to Cuī Wěi:
"Where have you been,
that you have not returned for three autumns?"
Cuī Wěi did not tell the truth.
Opening his door,
he found the couch covered in dust.
He felt deeply sorrowful.
Inquiring about the Cìshǐ,
he learned that Xú Shēn had indeed died and Zhào Chāng had replaced him.
He then went to a Persian merchant's lodge,
and secretly tried to sell the pearl.
An old foreigner saw it at once,
prostrated himself, and said with clasped hands:
"Young master must have entered the tomb of Nányuè King Zhào Tuó;
otherwise,
you could not have obtained this treasure."
For Zhào Tuó had used the pearl as a burial object.
Cuī Wěi then told him the whole truth,
and only then realized the Emperor was Zhào Tuó,
who had also once proclaimed himself Emperor Wǔ of Nányuè.
The foreigner then offered a hundred thousand strings of cash to exchange for it.
Cuī Wěi asked the foreigner:
"How did you recognize it?"
He replied:
"This is the Yángsuì Pearl, a treasure of our Dàshíguó.
In early Hàn times,
Zhào Tuó sent an extraordinary person to cross mountains and seas,
and stole it back to Pānyú.
Now it has been nearly a thousand years.
In our country, there are those skilled in astrology
who said that next year the national treasure would return.
Therefore, our king summoned me,
provided a large ship and ample funds,
and sent me to Pānyú to search for it.
Today, I have indeed found it."
He then brought out jade liquid to wash it,
and its light illuminated the entire room.
The foreigner promptly boarded his ship and returned to Dàshíguó.
Cuī Wěi obtained the gold,
and thus secured his family's wealth.
However, when he sought the Yángchéng Messenger,
there was no trace of him.
Later, when he had business at the City God Temple,
he suddenly noticed that a statue resembled the messenger,
and saw fine writing on the deity's brush,
which was the inscription made by the maidservant.
Just as he had prepared wine and dried meat to make offerings,
he also applied heavy whitewash and painted decorations,
and expanded the building.
From this, it is known that Yángchéng is the city of Guǎngzhōu.
In the temple, there are five rams.
He also inquired about Rèn Wēng’s chamber,
and the village elder said:
"It is the tomb of Rèn Áo, the commandant of Nányuè."
He also climbed the terrace of the Yuèwáng Hall,
and saw a poem by a predecessor:
"On Yuèjǐngāng, the pines and cypresses grow old;
on the Yuèwáng Terrace, autumn grasses sprout.
For many years, the ancient tomb has had no descendants;
common folk tread upon it, turning it into an official road."
Together with the Yuèwáng’s matching poem,
the traces were quite unusual,
so he inquired with the caretaker.
The caretaker said:
"Grand Master Xú Shēn, upon climbing this terrace,
was moved by Attendant Censor Cuī’s poem,
so he heavily whitewashed and decorated the terrace hall,
making it resplendent and glorious."
Later, as the Zhōngyuán Festival approached,
he prepared abundant and pure incense, delicacies, and sweet wine,
and stayed in the monks’ quarters of Pújiàn Temple.
As midnight approached,
sure enough, four maidens accompanied Lady Tián,
her appearance radiant and graceful,
her words elegant and serene.
The four maidens and Cuī Shēng raised their cups in jest and banter,
and as dawn approached, they bid farewell.
Cuī Zǐ then bowed twice,
delivered a letter to the Yuèwáng,
with humble words and generous gifts,
expressing only reverence and gratitude.
Thereafter, he returned to his chamber with the lady.
Wěi asked the lady:
"Since you are the daughter of the King of Qí,
why were you matched with a man of Nányuè?"
The lady said:
"My kingdom was destroyed, my family lost,
and I was captured by the Yuèwáng to serve as a concubine.
When the king passed away,
I was consequently buried with him as a sacrificial offering.
I do not even know how much time has passed since then.
Watching Lì Shēng being boiled alive
feels like it was only yesterday.
Whenever I recall these past events,
tears cannot help but flow."
Wěi asked:
"Who are the four maidens?"
She said:
"Two were presented by King Yáo of Ōuyuè,
and two were offered by King Wúzhū of Mǐnyuè,
all buried as sacrificial offerings."
He asked further:
"Earlier, the four maidens mentioned Bào Gū—who is she?"
She said:
"She is the daughter of Bào Jìng,
and the wife of Gě Hóng.
She often practiced moxibustion in Nánhǎi."
Wěi was then astonished, realizing that the old woman from before was her.
He also asked:
"Why is the snake called Yùjīngzǐ?"
She said:
"In the past, Ānqīshēng often rode this dragon to pay homage at Yùjīng,
hence it is called Yùjīngzǐ."
Because Wěi had drunk the dragon’s leftover froth in the cave,
his skin became tender,
and his muscles and strength light and vigorous.
Later, he lived in Nánhǎi for over a decade,
then dispersed his gold and exhausted his wealth,
devoting his heart to the Daoist path.
He then took his family to Luófú,
to seek out Bào Gū.
Afterward, his whereabouts were ultimately unknown.
From "Chuánqí"
Perfected Person Chéng
Perfected Person Chéng,
his name is unknown,
and his origins are also unknown.
At the end of the Táng dynasty’s Kāiyuán era,
a palace envoy returned from beyond the southern mountains,
paid respects at the Jīntiān Temple,
and after completing the offerings and prayers,
playfully asked the shaman:
"Is the Great King present?"
The reply was:
"He is not."
The palace envoy was surprised by the answer,
so he inquired further:
"Where has the Great King gone that you say he is not present?"
The shaman said:
"He has gone thirty lǐ beyond the pass to welcome Perfected Person Chéng."
The palace envoy immediately sent someone to wait at the pass.
There was a Daoist priest,
wearing tattered clothes and carrying a cloth sack,
coming from beyond the pass.
When asked, his surname was Chéng.
He was invited to the relay station,
and questioned about his practices,
but he gave no response.
He was taken to the capital by post-horse,
lodged in a private residence,
and the matter was secretly reported to the emperor.
Emperor Xuánzōng found it highly unusual,
summoned him to the inner palace,
and lodged him in Pénglái Courtyard.
He was commanded to speak on Daoist arts and his cultivation practices,
but he only remained silent and did not respond,
appearing profoundly simple and unadorned.
After more than half a year,
he earnestly requested to return to the mountains.
Since nothing had been learned from him,
he was allowed to go wherever he wished.
Carrying his cloth sack, he slowly walked out from the inner palace.
Those who saw him all laughed.
The officials swept and cleaned his quarters,
changed the curtains and hangings,
and saw an inscription on the wall:
"On the Shǔ road heading south,
the Yān army arrives from the north.
Originally intending to ascend to heaven in broad daylight,
now watch the black dragon drink from the Wèi River."
The more the characters were scrubbed, the clearer they became.
The matter was reported to the emperor.
The emperor remained silent for a long while,
deeply reflecting on it.
Later, Lùshān rose in Yān,
and the imperial carriage fled to Shǔ,
all as foretold in the prophecy.
From "Xiānzhuàn Shíyí"
Bǎiyè Xiānrén
The Cypress Leaf Immortal, Tián Luán,
lived in Cháng'ān.
His family had held official positions for generations,
and by Luán's time, the household was wealthy.
He had five or six brothers,
but none lived past thirty.
When Luán was twenty-five,
his mother grew deeply worried,
and Luán himself became fearful.
He had often heard that those who practiced the Dao possessed arts of longevity,
so he entered Huà Shān,
seeking to inquire of true companions of the Way,
his heart's wish being most earnest.
When he was several tens of *li* from the mountain's base,
he saw a Daoist priest in a yellow cap emerging from the mountain.
Luán paid his respects and made obeisance,
praying and asking for secret formulas.
The Daoist priest raised his head, pointed to a cypress tree, and showed it to him, saying:
"This is the medicine of longevity.
Why seek far and wide?
It only depends on how steadfast your will is."
Luán then searched through and studied the immortals' recipes.
One said:
"If one takes lateral cypress leaves long and without cease,
one can attain longevity."
So he took cypress leaves, dried them in the sun,
ground them into powder, and ingested it.
He slightly moderated his consumption of rich flavors,
and with single-minded concentration,
he took it for perhaps sixty or seventy days.
There were no other benefits,
only that he constantly felt feverish and hot.
Yet he never stopped taking it.
After more than two years,
he fell ill with fever.
His head felt as if splitting,
and sores broke out all over his body.
His mother wept and said:
"It was originally to extend your years,
yet now you are instead being killed by the medicine."
But Luán's resolve never wavered;
he still took it.
After seven or eight years,
the febrile illness grew even worse.
His body was like fire,
so that people could not approach him.
All could smell the odor of cypress leaves.
The various sores ulcerated and festered,
and yellow fluid covered his body like glue.
His mother also thought he would die.
Suddenly he said of himself:
"My body now feels slightly better;
I need to bathe."
He then ordered a *hu* of warm water prepared in the room.
Several people carried him and laid him in the *hu*.
Since falling ill, he had not slept for over ten days.
Suddenly, as if thinking of sleep,
he ordered his attendants to close the door and not disturb him.
He then slept in the *hu*.
After three days he finally awoke.
He called for people to help him up.
All the sores on his body
had already been swept away.
His complexion was radiant and clear,
his eyebrows and beard a deep bluish-green.
He immediately felt his eyes and ears keen and bright.
He said of himself:
"When I first slept,
I dreamed of several Daoist priests in yellow caps,
holding banners and ceremonial staffs to guide me.
I paid homage at Shàngqīng [the Supreme Clarity heaven/palace].
I paid respects to all the immortals of ancient times.
They all said to each other:
'Has the Cypress Leaf Immortal come here?'
They then bestowed upon me the arts of immortality,
had my name inscribed on a jade tablet in golden characters,
and stored it in Shàngqīng.
They said to me:
'For now, remain in the human world to cultivate your practice.
Later, when a position becomes available,
we will summon you.'
Then they led me back."
From then on, Luán abstained from grains,
and moreover had no desire for food or drink.
He lived in seclusion at Sōngyáng.
By the Zhēnyuán era [785-805],
he was already one hundred and twenty-three years old,
yet he constantly had a youthful appearance.
Suddenly he informed his disciples,
and passed away without illness,
his complexion unchanged.
It was a case of liberation from the corpse.
At his death, a strange fragrance filled the room,
and music was heard in the air.
He had gone to create the Green Metropolis.
He went to keep his appointment with the immortals.
From *Huà Yuán Jì*.
The Ming manuscript says from *Yuán Huà Jì*.
Qí Yìng
Minister Qí Yìng,
when sitting for the imperial examinations,
went to the ministry to inquire about news.
He rested at the southern courtyard of the Ministry of Rites.
Caught in the rain and having not eaten,
he wandered aimlessly, not knowing where to go,
and slowly walked along the wall.
There was an old man,
dressed in white and leaning on a staff,
with two young servants following him.
He bowed to Lord Qí and said:
"The sun is already high,
surely you have not yet eaten.
My dwelling is not far;
could you come for a short while?"
Yìng thanked him, feeling embarrassed,
and followed him to outside the gate.
The old man said:
"I will go ahead;
I'll leave a servant to guide you, young master."
He leaped onto a white donkey and sped off like flight.
Lord Qí then walked to the north of the West Market,
entered a quiet ward and a new residence,
where the gate and winding paths were strict and clean.
After a long while,
the old man came out again.
More than ten maidservants attended him,
each holding something.
They went to sit in the central hall,
which was splendid, clean, and luxuriously appointed.
After a long while,
a feast was spread upstairs,
with wine and delicacies abundant and extraordinary.
After a short time,
someone reported that a hundred thousand coins had been delivered.
The old man said:
"This is income from the wine shop.
I use one pellet of medicine to make one urn of wine."
When evening came, [Yìng] asked to leave.
The old man said:
"Young master has an extraordinary appearance.
Do you wish to become a prime minister?
Or to ascend to heaven in broad daylight?"
Lord Qí pondered for a long time,
and said:
"Prime minister."
The old man laughed and said:
"Next year you will certainly pass the examinations,
and this official position is assured."
He presented him with several tens of bolts of silk,
and said:
"Be careful not to speak of this to anyone.
When you have leisure, come again."
Lord Qí bowed in thanks.
Afterwards, he went several times,
and each time received sympathy gifts.
When spring came, he indeed passed the examinations.
His fellow candidates, seeing his carriage and clothes neat and proper,
while drunk, questioned him about it.
Unconsciously, he told them everything.
Together with more than twenty others,
they arranged to go together to visit [the old man].
When the old man heard of it, he deeply regretted it.
When they arrived, he excused himself, claiming illness, and refused to see them.
He presented each with one bolt of fine silk,
but summoned only Lord Qí inside.
He reproached him, saying:
"How could you so lightly reveal this?
Previously, the matter of ascending to immortality was also possible,
but now it will not come to pass."
Lord Qí sorrowfully apologized and admitted his fault,
then left through the gate.
Ten days later he came again,
but the residence had already been sold,
and he did not know where [the old man] had gone.
From *Yì Shǐ*.
Wáng Sìláng
Wáng Jū, the Commandant of Luòyáng.
He had a nephew born of a concubine, whose childhood name was Fourth Lad.
When the boy was still in his infancy,
his mother went off to marry another man,
and he went along with her.
After that, he would come to Wáng Jū’s home every five or ten years,
but the Wáng family no longer kept track of him.
During the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
Wáng Jū, due to a regular transfer,
was traveling from Zhèngzhōu to the capital.
As he passed through the Eastern Capital,
just as he was crossing the Tiānjīn Bridge,
Fourth Lad suddenly knelt and bowed before his horse.
He wore plain clothes and straw sandals,
and his appearance was rustic and wild.
Wáng Jū did not recognize him.
So the lad stated his name himself.
Wáng Jū felt pity for him for a long while.
Then the lad said:
"Uncle, you are now going to the capital for your official appointment,
and your expenses must be considerable.
I have a little something to offer you,
to help with the costs."
He then took out some gold from his bosom,
about five liǎng or so,
its color like a rooster’s comb.
He then said:
"This cannot be valued at the ordinary price.
When you reach the capital,
just go to the gold market and seek out Zhāng Péngzǐ to give it to him,
and you should get two hundred thousand cash."
Wáng Jū found this strange,
and immediately said to him:
"Where have you been all this time?
And where are you going now?"
He replied:
"I used to live in a cave at the foot of Wángwū Mountain,
and now I am going to Éméi Mountain.
Knowing that you, Uncle, were passing through here,
I came specifically to pay my respects."
Wáng Jū asked further:
"Where are you staying now?"
He replied:
"At the inn of the Xí family at Middle Bridge."
At that time, a light rain had just begun,
and as Wáng Jū happened not to have brought a raincoat,
he hurried off, saying:
"I will come to your lodgings right away."
Fourth Lad bowed again and said:
"My journey is on a tight schedule,
I fear I may not be able to wait respectfully for you."
Wáng Jū went straight back,
changed his clothes, and went there,
but Fourth Lad had already left.
He then inquired of the Xí family.
They said:
"He had four or five wives and concubines,
all of exceptional beauty;
as for their clothes, saddles, and horses,
they were extraordinarily luxurious and splendid.
That Master Wáng rode in a sedan chair and left first,
saying he was going to Jiànnán."
Wáng Jū privately thought this remarkable,
but did not fully believe it.
When he reached the capital,
commodity prices at the time were soaring,
and his funds were rather tight.
He thus said to his family servant Jí’ér:
"Take what Fourth Lad left and go inquire about it."
Sure enough, there was a Zhāng Péngzǐ.
Jí’ér then showed him the gold.
Péngzǐ was pleasantly surprised,
and holding it, he kowtowed, saying:
"Where did you get this?
How much do you want for it?"
Jí’ér immediately said:
"Just two hundred thousand."
Péngzǐ then prepared wine and food,
feasted Jí’ér,
and paid the requested amount.
He also said:
"If you have more,
you can come again."
Jí’ér returned with the money.
Wáng Jū was greatly astonished.
The next day, he went personally to see Péngzǐ.
Péngzǐ said:
"This is transformed gold sold by Fourth Lad Wáng.
Western Region merchant Hu traders
specialize in waiting to buy this,
and there is no fixed price for it.
It simply depends on the original agreement with Fourth Lad regarding the amount;
if it exceeds that, one must not accept it."
Wáng Jū therefore did not take any more.
Afterwards, he made careful inquiries,
hoping to meet him once more.
But he never saw him again.
From the Jíyì Jì.
Wéi Dān
After Grand Master Wéi Dān passed the imperial examinations,
he successively held the post of Censor in the Western Terrace.
He had always been fond of the Dào,
but had never had an encounter.
In the capital, there was a Dàoist practitioner
who had been friends with Wéi Dān for many years.
Suddenly one day, he said to Wéi Dān:
"Your heart in pursuing the Dào is firm,
but generally speaking, your bone structure is not formed for it.
I cannot fully understand the matter;
you can go personally to Xúzhōu and ask Héilǎo."
Wéi Dān then requested leave and set out,
heading for Xúzhōu.
After several days,
he made inquiries.
Everyone said there was no Héilǎo.
He summoned a yámen clerk and asked him:
"In this prefectural city, there is a Héilǎo.
Where is his home?"
The clerk said:
"There is none within the city walls.
Five lǐ from here, in a melon garden,
there is a man surnamed Chén.
He is dark, skinny, poor, and cold,
working as a hired laborer for others,
renting half a thatched hut to live in.
People in this prefecture see that he is dark and skinny,
and everyone calls him Héilǎo."
Master Wéi said:
"Could you invite him here for me?"
The clerk went to the melon garden to summon him.
Héilǎo absolutely refused to come.
So he was driven and forced to come to the post station.
Master Wéi had already put on his official robes
and was respectfully waiting at the gate.
As soon as Master Wéi saw him,
he bowed twice.
Héilǎo said:
"I am a hired laborer seeking food.
I don’t know what crime I have committed
that I am now seized and brought here.
I wish only to return alive."
Moreover, he was terrified and frightened,
and wanted to run out the door,
but was blocked by the clerks and others who would not let him go.
From morning until evening,
Master Wéi’s courtesy became even more respectful.
Héilǎo grew increasingly alarmed and flustered.
He was briefly invited to go up to the hall,
but ultimately could not be persuaded.
Around the second watch of the night,
he finally stepped onto the stairs,
but refused to sit properly.
Master Wéi bowed twice and earnestly requested,
kowtowing and questioning without cease.
By the third watch,
Héilǎo suddenly lay down on the bed,
his snoring like thunder.
Master Wéi stood trembling respectfully before the bed.
After a long time,
due to extreme fatigue,
he unconsciously, still in his official robes, also lay down on the floor in front of the bed and fell asleep.
By the fifth watch,
Héilǎo got up
and, placing his hand on Master Wéi’s back, said:
"Get up, get up.
You seem fond of the Dào,
and I appreciate that.
But generally, your bone structure is not formed for it.
For now, you must pursue wealth and honor in the human world.
When the time is right for you to attain it,
I will come to welcome you.
Otherwise,
I fear you might lose your way.
On an early autumn day,
come back here again,
and I will speak with you fully."
Having said this,
he vanished in an instant.
Master Wéi then returned.
On the evening before the day of Lìqiū,
he reached Xúzhōu,
but Héilǎo had already died at the chén hour.
Master Wéi was deeply saddened;
he buried him and left.
After that, all contact ceased.
For twenty years, there was no news.
Master Wéi held the post of Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī.
Two years after arriving in the commandery,
suddenly one day,
an old man said to the gatekeeper:
"Report to the Master,
you can say that Héilǎo has come."
When the Master heard this,
he rushed out to welcome him, even putting his shoes on backwards in his haste.
The next day, Master Wéi, though not ill,
suddenly passed away.
Everyone said that Héilǎo had welcomed Master Wéi to become an immortal.
From the Huìchāng Jiěyí Lù.
Féng Dàliàng
Féng Dàliàng was
a man from Dǎojiāng.
His family was poor, but he loved the Dao,
though he did not practice any cultivation.
Whenever a Daoist priest or a practitioner of esoteric arts passed by his door,
he would always invite them in and entertain them.
He owned only one ox, which he used to turn a millstone to support himself.
One day, the ox died,
and he and his wife wept together.
Sighing, they said:
"Our clothing and food depended
entirely on this ox.
Now that the ox is dead,
how shall we feed ourselves?"
A Daoist priest from Címǔ Mountain
often passed by their home
and would rest there for several days.
At this time, the priest came again,
and the couple told him of their plight.
The priest asked:
"Do you still have the hide and horns?"
They replied:
"Yes."
He then took the hide, stitched it together into the shape of an ox,
carved wooden legs for it,
and tied its mouth with a rope.
When he drove it, it stood up,
as plump and strong as before.
He said:
"This ox will no longer eat or drink,
but you may use it day and night.
Be careful not to untie its mouth.
With this ox pulling the millstone,
its strength will be twice that of an ordinary ox."
The priest never came again.
Several years later, during the height of summer,
the ox was panting heavily.
A young cowherd took pity on it
and untied its mouth.
Immediately, it became nothing but hide and bones.
By then, however, the family had gradually grown wealthy
and had opened a wine shop.
Féng Dàliàng often practiced the Dao, praying to encounter an immortal,
and diligently performed acts of charity,
being fond of hosting guests.
There were three or five woodcutting elders
who would come to his home to drink wine.
He never spoke of money,
but treated them with courtesy,
and his respect for them only grew over time.
Suddenly, one of them said:
"There are eight of us,
and tomorrow we will all come
to enjoy a hearty drink together.
Do not be surprised at our number."
When the time came,
the eight woodcutting elders arrived together.
One of the guests took from his sleeve a nanmu branch,
only five or six inches long,
and planted it in the courtyard.
They then drank wine to their hearts' content and departed.
They said:
"We have troubled you to provide fine wine,
and have nothing with which to repay you.
When this tree reaches a foot in diameter,
your family wealth will amount to a million.
At that time, you may offer tribute to assist the Son of Heaven,
and your name will be recorded in the national history.
Ten years from now,
we will meet at the Giant's Palace on Mínlǐng,
where we shall impart to you the way of flying immortals."
Having said this, they left.
Within ten days, the tree had soared into the sky,
reaching over a hundred feet in height,
and its trunk was already a foot in diameter.
Gold and jade came to his family of their own accord,
treasures and goods accumulated by themselves,
and their wealth grew even more abundant.
Even the households of Wángsūn and Mí Zhú
could not compare.
Five years later,
when Emperor Xuánzōng fled to Shǔ,
Dàliàng contributed three hundred thousand strings of cash
to aid the state's needs.
From Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí
Xú Zuǒqīng
On the Double Ninth Festival in the thirteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era of Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng, he was hunting at Shāyuàn.
At that time, a lone crane circled and soared among the clouds.
Emperor Xuánzōng personally drew his bow and shot it.
The crane, carrying the arrow, slowly descended,
