and when it was about ten feet from the ground,
it suddenly straightened its wings
and flew southwest until it vanished.
The crowd gazed into the distance,
but it disappeared after a long while.
Fifteen lǐ west of Yìzhōu city,
there was a Daoist temple.
Nestled against mountains and facing water,
with deep, serene pines and osmanthus trees,
only Daoist practitioners of sincere and diligent cultivation were allowed to reside there.
The first courtyard in the eastern corridor of the temple
was especially secluded and quiet.
There was a man who called himself Xú Zuǒqīng, a Daoist priest from Qīngchéng Mountain.
He was pure, refined, and of noble antiquity,
and would come three or four times a year.
The elders of the temple
had thus kept the main hall of that courtyard vacant
to await his arrival.
Whenever Zuǒqīng came, he would lodge there,
sometimes for three to five days,
sometimes for ten days or a month,
before saying he was returning to Qīngchéng.
He was greatly admired by the Daoist community.
One day, he suddenly arrived from outside,
his spirit and appearance troubled,
and said to the people in the courtyard:
"While walking in the mountains,
I was accidentally struck by a flying arrow.
I am already fine now;
however, this arrow is not of the mortal world.
I will leave it on the wall here.
In the coming years, when the owner of this arrow arrives,
you must give it to him.
Be careful not to lose it."
He then took up a brush and wrote on the wall:
"The time I leave this arrow
is the ninth day of the ninth month of the thirteenth year."
Later, when Emperor Xuánzōng fled the turmoil and took refuge in Shǔ,
he took a leisurely day to travel and explore,
and by chance came to this temple.
Delighting in its beautiful surroundings,
he toured all the Daoist chambers.
Upon entering this hall,
he suddenly saw the arrow.
He ordered his attendant to take it and examine it,
and indeed, it was his own imperial arrow.
Deeply astonished,
he inquired of the temple's Daoist priests.
They told him the whole truth.
Looking at Zuǒqīng's inscription,
he realized it was the arrow he had used while hunting at Shāyuàn the previous year,
and that Zuǒqīng was actually the lone crane he had shot.
Reflecting on the inscription,
it seemed that after being shot at Shāyuàn and flying away,
it had arrived here that very day.
Emperor Xuánzōng found this utterly marvelous,
and so he kept the arrow as a treasure.
After this, no one in Shǔ ever encountered Zuǒqīng again.
From Guǎngdé Shényì Lù
Tuòbá Dàláng
During the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a magistrate of Fúfēng County.
His family was originally powerful and noble,
and he relied on his influence to look down on others.
Guests who were poor and humble had no means to approach and pay their respects.
Because of this, criticism and gossip filled the roads.
At that time, the Registrar Lǐ and the Deputy Péi
were fond of hosting guests.
Péi was quite fond of the Dao,
and had also often lived in seclusion among famous mountains.
He was also fond of giving alms,
and often made up for the magistrate's shortcomings.
Once, during a leisurely day,
a banquet was held in the town.
All the guests were influential and noble,
but Deputy Péi, claiming illness, did not attend.
Just as the guests had gathered,
suddenly there was a guest
with a broad forehead,
over seven feet tall,
leaning on a staff and carrying a hat.
His demeanor was lofty and ancient.
He said to the gatekeeper:
"Tuòbá Dàláng wishes to see the Prefect."
The gatekeeper said:
"The Chief is currently dining;
he cannot receive visitors.
Please wait until the banquet is over."
The guest angrily said:
"What kind of petty fellow is this,
to dare refuse a guest like this?
I will enter on my own."
The gatekeeper was frightened
and ran to report to the magistrate.
The magistrate, having no choice,
ordered him to be invited up the steps.
The magistrate was displeased,
and the guest was also indignant.
Once the banquet began,
he was generally not deferential.
By the end of the banquet,
no one was happy.
The guest left without a bow.
The magistrate merely gave a long bow in return.
The guest looked extremely angry,
and left muttering.
At the time, Registrar Lǐ suspected he was an extraordinary man.
Lǐ returned
and summoned Deputy Péi to tell him:
"The banquet was unhappy
because of this guest.
Judging by his appearance,
I fear he is a knight-errant,
and I worry he may cause harm.
I should summon him and apologize."
So he waited together with Péi,
ordered a clerk to invite the guest,
and the guest, without declining, arrived.
By then it was nearly night.
Lǐ received him with great respect.
When Deputy Péi saw him,
he suddenly hurriedly retreated to another room.
Lǐ bowed and invited the guest to sit,
then got up again to ask after Péi.
Péi looked extremely frightened and nervous.
He said to Lǐ:
"This is indeed an extraordinary man.
He is a man of Mount Éméi,
one of the highest masters of Daoist arts.
I once studied under him for several years,
but halfway through I abandoned him and fled.
Now I fear I cannot face him."
Lǐ therefore first made a plea on Péi's behalf.
Péi then put on his official robes and hurried in,
bowing deeply and repeatedly to apologize for his offense.
The guest looked at him for a long time.
Lǐ again spoke on his behalf.
Only then did he order him to sit.
Their conversation did not touch upon the matter.
Péi became even more reverent and solemn,
and Lǐ also increased his respect,
additionally mentioning the magistrate's fault.
Lǐ apologized repeatedly on his behalf.
The guest then stayed the night in Lǐ's hall.
Lǐ attended to him day and night,
but he had already disappeared,
yet the doors and windows were still locked as before.
This made him even more amazed.
At dawn,
clerks came running to report:
"The magistrate has suddenly been struck by an evil,
his breath is about to cease, though his heart is still slightly warm."
The various colleagues went together to check on him.
By mealtime, he revived.
The magistrate then summoned Registrar Lǐ to see him,
kowtowed, and thanked him, saying:
"I rely on you to have escaped death."
Lǐ asked the reason.
He said:
"Last night's guest
was surely a divine being.
Last night I was taken away.
I saw Tuòbá sitting on a folding chair,
reprimanding me for not receiving guests.
He then ordered mulberry branches broken to whip me.
The rods were small but the pain was severe.
I had no words to apologize,
and he whipped me several hundred times.
Then he said:
'Thanks to the Registrar speaking for you,
otherwise you would have died.'
He ordered his attendants to send me back,
and only then did I revive." He showed them, and the whip marks were still there.
They ordered a carriage to go north of the county to search.
After traveling thirty *li*,
they indeed saw a large mulberry grove.
Below were many footprints of people and horses,
on the ground were over ten broken mulberry branches,
and blood was still on the ground.
From then on, the magistrate knew fear.
And Tuòbá from then on was not known where he went.
He was likely an immortal.
From *Yuánhuà Jì*.
Wèi Fāngjìn's Younger Brother
Táng Dynasty Censor-in-Chief Wèi Fāngjìn
had a younger brother over fifteen years old
who could not speak,
with drool and snot covering his body.
His brothers and relatives all regarded him as an idiot,
and no one cared for or supported him.
Only one elder sister pitied him,
providing him with clothing and food,
ordering servants to wash and bathe him,
showing no sign of weariness.
One morning, he was outside the gate sunning himself and scratching an itch.
His neighbors saw a messenger in red robes
leading several dozen riders arrive.
They asked:
"Where is the Immortal Master?"
They then ran over and saw the one scratching the itch.
Bowing, they hurried forward,
prostrated themselves, and expressed their thanks.
After a long while,
he suddenly shouted in a loud voice:
"Why have you come so late!
Have you finished handling the matters?"
They said:
"They are in order."
He also said:
"Why not finish them quickly?
Now go!"
His spirit and appearance were penetratingly clear,
his voice and tone bright and fluent,
showing none of the signs of an idiot's affliction.
After the red-robed ones had left,
as before, drool flowed down to his mouth,
and he scratched his itch incessantly.
That night, he then died.
Lord Wèi and the others, though startled by the event,
did not treat him differently as a person,
and so buried him according to custom.
Only the elder sister was deeply sorrowful and grieving,
secretly preparing the funeral rites.
On the day of the minor encoffining,
she took a yellow embroidered padded jacket,
something he had cherished in daily life,
and secretly placed it in the coffin.
Later, Lord Wèi accompanied the imperial carriage to Mǎwéi,
and his elder sister also went along.
The imperial guard troops rioted,
executing Yáng Guózhōng.
Lord Wèi was a relative,
and he and his clan all met with disaster.
At that time, his elder sister happened to be outside the inn,
heard of the calamity and fled,
leaving behind her three children,
all five or six years old.
They had already been chopped into mincemeat.
By early morning when the army departed,
she tried going into the inn to search for them.
Stiff corpses lay one upon another.
On a bed slightly deeper in the northeast,
there seemed to be some clothing.
Approaching to look,
her three children
were all there within.
What covered them was precisely the yellow embroidered jacket used to bury her idiot brother.
She wept with sorrow and grief.
Mother and children went together into the mountains,
and all escaped the calamity.
From *Yìshǐ*.
Lǐ Qīng
was a man from Běihǎi.
His family had for generations been engaged in the dyeing trade.
Qīng studied the Dao from a young age,
and often invited Daoist adepts and practitioners from Qí and Lǔ,
receiving them with utmost sincerity and reverence,
yet in the end encountered nothing,
though his diligence in seeking grew ever more earnest.
His family was wealthy,
and had long been prominent gentry in the prefecture.
His children, grandchildren, and relatives by marriage, both paternal and maternal,
numbered nearly a hundred households,
all able to live idly and profit in Yìdū.
Every year on Qīng’s birthday,
they would vie to present gifts,
accumulating over a million in total.
Qīng was by nature benevolent and frugal;
he did not refuse what came,
but neither did he distribute what he received.
Thus, over time,
his storerooms became filled and piled high.
At the age of sixty-nine,
ten days before his birthday,
he suddenly summoned his relatives,
laid out a great feast of wine and food,
and then said to them:
"I have relied on your diligent efforts and faultless conduct,
each of you able to make a living,
and thus I have enjoyed ample support;
yet I have worn plain clothes and eaten simple food
for over thirty years now,
how could I still have any desire for extravagance!
You, considering me the elder of the family,
each year present me with birthday gifts of clothing, finery, and curios,
and the extravagance has reached its peak;
yet all that I have long received,
I have sealed away in a room,
never once looking at it,
only wasting what you could have used yourselves,
adding to my own dust and dirt—
what purpose does it ultimately serve!
Fortunately, Heaven has not yet taken my spirit and breath,
and soon it will be my birthday again;
I know well that you will again prepare gifts for prolonging my life,
so the reason I have gathered you ahead of time
is precisely to stop this habitual practice of yours."
His children and grandchildren all said:
"Prolonging life has been a custom since ancient times;
without this, how can we express our humble, filial devotion?
We beg you not to stop it,
lest your relatives feel uneasy."
Qīng said:
"If your determination cannot be swayed,
then follow what I desire and bring that—
is that acceptable?"
They all said:
"We wish to hear your esteemed intention."
Qīng said:
"Each of you can give me a hundred feet of hemp rope, thick or thin;
tallying it all together,
I would then obtain several thousand hundred feet.
Using this to continue and prolong my life,
would that not indeed extend it!"
They all said:
"We respectfully obey your instruction.
Yet your esteemed intention must have a reason;
we humbly dare to ask."
Qīng smiled and said to them:
"In the end, I must let you know.
I am a mundane man of the lower world,
who presumptuously sought the Dao;
my spirit, mind, and strength,
I devoted diligently day and night,
and now for sixty years,
yet without even a shadow or echo of success.
My age is already advanced,
decay and ruin are nearly complete;
I expect these bones and sinews will not last more than two or three years.
I wish to take advantage of my sight, hearing, and ability to walk while they still function,
to carry out my long-held ambition.
I hope you will not hinder me."
Before this,
ten li south of Qīngzhōu there was a high mountain,
overlooking the commandery city,
with its peak split down the middle,
forming a steep cliff pass.
The households of the prefecture all sat facing its misty peaks;
returning clouds and passing birds,
were clearly visible in detail.
According to maps and records, it was called Yúnmén Shān,
commonly also known as Pī Shān,
and Qīng had long contemplated it.
At this point, he said to his relatives:
"Yúnmén Shān is the abode of immortals;
I shall go there.
On my birthday, I will sit in a large bamboo basket,
and lower myself down with a windlass,
using the thin ropes as a tether;
if I cannot proceed forward,
I will quickly pull the tether,
and you can then pull me out by the end of the rope.
If I encounter something and can fulfill my ambition,
I may also return again."
His children, grandchildren, and relatives wept and pleaded:
"Dark, silent, deep, and far,
its limits cannot be fathomed;
moreover, mountain spirits, tree demons,
serpents, vipers, and strange creatures—
what kind is not stored there?
How can you bear to cast your precious body
into such a place?
Is this a step toward long life and eternal vision?"
Qīng said:
"This is my resolve.
If you insist on hindering me,
then I will go privately.
Then I will not have the safety of the bamboo basket and thick ropes."
Seeing they could not change his mind,
they all prepared the matters together.
When the day arrived, relatives and townspeople,
altogether nearly a thousand people,
vied to bring wine and food.
At dawn,
they gathered at the mountain ridge.
Qīng then waved his hand, bid farewell, and entered.
After a long while, he reached the ground;
it was extremely dark inside,
looking up, the sky was only the size of a palm.
Feeling the four walls,
they only allowed space for about two mats.
To the southeast was a cave,
one could stoop and enter.
So he abandoned the basket and ventured in.
At first it was very narrow,
but as he went forward, he could straighten his back.
After walking about thirty li like this,
a faint, bright light appeared.
Soon he reached the cave entrance;
the scenery of mountains and rivers,
clouds, mist, grass, and trees,
seemed utterly unlike the human world.
He gazed into the distance for a long time.
Only to the southeast, over ten li away,
something shimmered as if there were dwellings.
So he slowly walked toward it;
upon arriving, there was a steep, isolated terrace,
its foundation and steps extremely lofty,
but facing south, one could ascend.
So he climbed with devout sincerity,
feeling considerable fear.
When he reached the top,
he saw the hall was very solemn,
with four or five Daoist priests inside.
Qīng then knocked at the gate.
Soon a blue-robed youth answered the gate and asked.
He replied:
"Lǐ Qīng, a dyer from Qīngzhōu."
The blue-robed youth reported his words as told.
Qīng heard from the central hall:
"Lǐ Qīng has come?"
Then he was told to come forward.
Qīng, alarmed and fearful, hurried forward and bowed.
Someone by the window in the distance said:
"It is not yet time for you to come;
why have you arrived so hastily?"
Then he was told to bow to all the worthies.
At that time, it was already noon,
when suddenly a white-haired old man entered through the gate,
paid his respects,
and announced:
"Dīng Zūnshī of Pénglái's Xiámíng Guàn has newly arrived.
The multitude of sages order an invitation to all the Perfected to ascend to Shàngqīng to attend the gathering."
So the assembled Perfected departed together,
and said to Qīng:
"You stay here for now."
As they were leaving, they looked back and said:
"Be careful not to open the north door."
Qīng inspected the courtyard and buildings,
and also opened the east and west doors;
his spirits soared elatedly,
and he thought to himself he would dwell forever in this true realm.
Then he went to the north of the hall,
and saw the north door slightly ajar;
he happened to step out and look.
Below was Qīngzhōu,
clearly visible before his eyes;
thoughts of parting and a longing to return
lingered for a long time before subsiding.
Regretting and wishing to go back,
the Perfected had already returned.
Among them, they said to each other:
"We told him not to touch the north door,
yet he confused himself after all;
truly, one knows the realm of immortals cannot be rashly reached."
Then they gave him a bowl of wine from a bottle,
its color thick and white.
After a while, they said:
"You may return for now."
Qīng then kowtowed, begging for mercy,
It is also said:
"There is no way back."
The crowd said to Qīng:
"You are destined to arrive here,
but the time has not yet come.
Do not suffer over having no path;
just close your eyes,
and when your feet touch the ground, you will have reached your hometown."
Qīng had no choice,
and tearfully bid farewell to depart.
Someone among them remarked:
"Since we are sending him back,
we must ensure he has a means to make a living."
Qīng, relying in his heart on his great wealth,
was surprised by this remark, thinking they did not know him well.
One person turned to Qīng and said:
"Go to the pavilion within the hall,
take a scroll of books with you.
After Qīng obtained it,
he said to Qīng:
"If you return with nothing to rely on,
you can use this book to support yourself."
Qīng then closed his eyes,
feeling his body like a flying bird,
hearing only the sound of wind and water clashing.
In a moment, he stepped on the ground.
Opening his eyes, he was at the south gate of Qīngzhōu,
and it was only around the end of the Shēn hour.
The city walls and fields,
seemed as before,
but as for the houses and trees,
the people and their clothing,
all had completely changed.
Walking alone all day,
he did not meet a single person he knew.
He then went to his former residence,
but the grand mansion and wide gate from that morning
had changed, old and new,
with no resemblance at all.
To the left was a dyer's workshop,
so he approached and spoke with him.
The man said his surname was Lǐ.
He himself said:
"I was originally a wealthy family from Běihǎi."
He then pointed to the surrounding neighborhoods,
"These are all the former estates of my ancestors.
I have heard that my ancestor, on his birthday in the fourth year of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era, went to the southern mountains by rope and
was never seen again,
which led to the decline of our family's fortunes."
Qīng was melancholy for a long time.
He then changed his surname and name.
He traveled and lodged in cities and towns.
Taking out the book he had obtained, he read it,
and it turned out to be prescriptions for curing various children's illnesses.
That year, an epidemic struck the children of Qīngzhōu,
and those treated by Qīng
were all cured immediately.
Within less than a month,
his wealth was restored.
It was the first year of the Gāozōng emperor's Yǒnghuī era,
and the world was prosperous and populous.
In Běihǎi, there were often those who knew of Qīng,
and because of this, people from Qí and Lǔ who followed him to learn the Daoist arts numbered in the hundreds and thousands.
By the fifth year,
he bid farewell to his disciples, saying:
"I am going to Tàishān to observe the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices."
From then on, no one knew where he went.
From the "Collection of Marvelous Tales"
Wéi Xiānwēng
During the Dàlì era of Emperor Dàizōng of the Táng dynasty,
while napping during the day,
he often dreamed of a person who said to him:
"On the Tàihuà Mountain in the Western Peak,
there is an emperor's altar.
Why not send someone to seek it out,
perform the fēng ceremony and pay homage to it?
You will surely obtain great fortune."
That very day, he issued an edict dispatching the Investigating Censor Wéi Jūn,
who rode post-horses to the mountain to search for it.
Upon reaching the foot of the mountain,
the prefecture and county officials had prepared an inn,
set up a meal inside,
and ordered all travelers
to move elsewhere.
An old man said to the innkeeper:
"Attendant Censor Wéi will only have one meal and then pass through.
I am old and ill, unable to go far away.
May I just sit in the room?
Is that acceptable?"
The innkeeper agreed.
A short while later, Wéi Jūn arrived at the inn.
After a long time,
he suddenly heard a cough from the room.
Wéi asked, "Who is in there?"
and sent someone to look.
The person returned and said:
"There is an old man."
Wéi Jūn asked the old man his surname.
He replied:
"My surname is Wéi."
Wéi Jūn said:
"Since we share the same clan,
we should establish our generational connection."
He invited him to share the same mat.
The old man then inquired about Wéi Jūn's grandfather's official title and taboo name;
he also asked who his great-great-grandfather was.
Wéi Jūn said:
"My great-grandfather's taboo name was so-and-so,
and he served as such-and-such an official.
My great-great-grandfather devoted himself to the Dào and did not serve in office.
During the Suí dynasty, he entered this mountain,
and his whereabouts are unknown."
The old man sighed deeply and said:
"I am your great-great-grandfather.
My name is Jí.
I had two sons.
You are the great-grandson of my younger son.
Who would have thought I would meet you here?"
Wéi Jūn wept and bowed repeatedly.
The old man stopped him,
saying:
"Your grandmother is still alive.
You have two great-grandaunts,
who are also in the mountain.
Today, encountering the Cold Food Festival,
I entered the city walls
to seek a little rouge and powder for them.
I have a cloth bundle,
inside which are slices of poria cocos powder,
which I wish to sell to purchase these items."
He asked Wéi Jūn:
"Where are you heading now?"
Wéi Jūn said:
"I have received an imperial decree to seek the true altar in this mountain.
Neither the prefecture and county officials nor the people in the mountain
know of it.
I wonder if you, venerable sir, know of this place?"
The old man said:
"On the southwest side of the Lotus Flower Central Peak,
there is an ancient altar,
with traces of its remaining foundation.
That should be it;
but I am not entirely certain."
He then stayed overnight with Wéi Jūn.
The old man abstained from grain and did not eat,
only drinking a little wine and ginseng-poria cocos soup.
The next day,
Wéi Jūn was about to enter the mountain.
The old man said:
"I will go with you."
Wéi Jūn then offered him his horse to ride.
The old man said:
"You ride it yourself.
I will go ahead on foot with my staff."
Wéi Jūn galloped on horseback,
but ultimately could not catch up,
as the old man was always thirty steps ahead of the horse.
Upon reaching the mountain's base,
the path was steep and treacherous,
and the horse could not proceed.
Wéi Jūn then dismounted
and followed the old man into the valley.
After walking less than a lǐ,
they arrived at a dwelling,
where they saw three elderly women.
The old man said:
"These are your grandmother and your two great-grandaunts."
Wéi Jūn wept sorrowfully and bowed repeatedly.
The grandmother appeared to be around seventy or eighty years old,
the aunts each over forty,
all with hair hanging down,
and wearing leaves as clothing.
Wéi Jūn was almost unable to bear the sight.
The old man walked as if flying,
looking back at Wéi Jūn and laughing.
They went straight to the southwest corner of the central peak,
and indeed there was an altar.
Wéi Jūn swept it clean, paid homage,
set up a marker, and returned.
Returning to the old man's stone chamber,
he bid farewell to leave the valley.
Wéi Jūn said:
"After I return to the capital and report,
I will request leave to come back and pay my respects."
The old man said:
"Strive hard,
and serve your sovereign well."
Wéi Jūn then descended the mountain,
returned to the imperial court,
and reported everything in detail.
Emperor Dàizōng sighed in amazement,
and then sent Wéi Jūn with a handwritten edict into the mountain,
ordering the prefect to invite the old man with due ceremony.
Wéi Jūn went into the mountain to search,
but lost the old path.
After several days of searching, he could not find it.
He inquired among the elderly at the mountain's foot,
who all said:
"Since our youth,
we have seen this old man come to the city walls once every two or three years.
His appearance has remained unchanged,
and we do not know where he resides."
Wéi Jūn gazed at the mountain, wept bitterly, and returned.
Emperor Dàizōng was filled with regret and sorrow,
and ordered the events to be recorded and submitted to the Historiography Institute.
From the "Yì Wén Jí"
Younger Brother of Duke Yáng Yuè
In the early Jiànzhōng era of the Táng dynasty,
Yáng Jí, the Sīmǎ of Chǔzhōu,
traveled from the capital to his post
and lodged at Huàyīn.
At night, an old man,
wearing a large hat,
came to the inn.
He approached the stove to warm himself by the fire.
Seeing his advanced age, Yáng Jūn
offered him wine and food.
He asked his surname.
The old man said:
"My surname is Yáng."
Yáng Jūn further inquired about his ancestors.
The old man said:
"Duke Yuè is the closest."
Yáng Jūn was Duke Yuè's grandnephew,
so he asked again in detail.
The old man said:
"Pressed by you,
I will speak fully.
I am the youngest brother of Duke Yuè.
After my elder brother met his demise,
I encountered the true Dào."
Upon hearing his surname, Jí
bowed again and sat back down.
The old man said:
"I also knew you were passing through here,
so I came to see you.
Your grandmother and several aunts are all here.
Do you wish to see them?
I will go and inform them first."
A short while later, he returned.
The next morning,
he went into the mountain with Yáng Jūn.
After about a lǐ or so,
there was a large ravine,
several zhàng wide.
The old man leaped over it effortlessly.
Turning back, he said to Yáng Jūn:
"You should stop here.
I will go and call your grandmother for you."
After a short while,
an old woman, along with daughters and six or seven others,
came winding around the cliff.
Yáng Jūn gazed from afar and bowed,
speaking to them across the water.
They all sighed with emotion,
and some wept.
After a long while, they said:
"You should go now.
We must not hinder your official duties."
Yáng Jūn then bowed.
After retreating several tens of steps and looking back,
he could still see someone waving a sleeve.
The next day, he returned,
but there were only deep waters and high peaks.
He saw nothing at all.
From the "Yì Shǐ"
Yángpíng, the Banished Immortal,
did not speak of his surname or name.
In the beginning,
Zhāng Shǒuguī, a man of Jiǔlǒng,
had a tea plantation on Xiānjūn Mountain.
Each year he summoned over a hundred laborers to pick tea;
men and women hired for the work mingled together in the plantation.
There was one youth,
who said he had no relatives or clan,
and hired himself out to pick tea.
He was very diligent, sincere, and clever.
Shǒuguī took pity on him
and adopted him as a righteous son.
There was also a young woman,
twenty years of age,
who likewise said she had no relatives or clan,
and wished to become the wife of the righteous son.
She was filial, righteous, upright, and respectful.
Shǒuguī thought very highly of her.
One day, mountain waters flooded,
blocking the roads to the market town,
and salt and fermented dairy products became scarce.
Shǒuguī was very worried about this.
The new bride said:
"These can be bought."
Taking some coins, she went out the door a dozen or so steps,
placed the coins under a tree,
tapped the tree with her staff,
and obtained salt and fermented dairy to bring back.
Later, whenever something was needed,
she would simply have them tap the tree to obtain it,
and nothing was ever unobtainable.
Her husband could also perform this art.
Once, with over ten neighboring women,
they met at the market in Bèngkǒu.
He bought a bowl of wine for them
and gave it to the women to drink.
They all became greatly intoxicated,
yet the wine in the bowl did not diminish.
Far and near, the tale spread,
and people all found it strange.
Shǒuguī asked from whom they had learned this art.
The youth said:
"I am an immortal from the Yángpíng Cavern.
Because of a minor transgression,
I was banished to the human world.
I shall not remain here long."
Shǒuguī asked:
"Is the size of the cavern mansion similar to the city gates and palaces of the human world?"
He replied:
"There are twenty-four transformations,
each with a great cavern.
Some are a thousand li square, some five hundred li, some three hundred li.
Within them all are suns and moons, flying essences,
called the roots of the hidden dawn,
which shine down upon the caverns,
no different from the world.
Within them all are immortal kings, immortal officials, ministers, and assistants,
like the offices and duties of the world.
Those who have attained the Dao,
and those who have accumulated merit and transformed their spirits to return to life,
all dwell within,
forming the common people.
Each year, during the three great festivals of Yuán,
the various heavens each have superior perfected beings
who descend to roam the cavern heavens,
to observe the good and evil deeds done there.
Human life and death, rise and fall,
floods, droughts, wind, and rain,
are all preordained within the caverns.
Dragon-god shrines and temples,
and offices that receive blood sacrifices,
are all governed by the cavern mansions.
Beyond the twenty-four transformations,
Qīngchéng, Éméi, Yìdēng, Címǔ, Fányáng, Bōzhǒng
also have caverns,
but they are not counted among the ten great cavern heavens or the thirty-six minor cavern heavens.
The immortal departments within the caverns
are like the commanderies, counties, and settlements of the human world;
they cannot all be recorded in detail."
Within ten days,
the couple suddenly disappeared.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
The Medicine-Selling Elder,
no one knew his name.
If people questioned him,
he said that this alone was his true name.
Some who saw him as children,
upon reaching old age,
saw him again,
and his appearance had not changed.
He often carried a large gourd to sell medicine.
When people told him of illness and sought medicine,
whether they gave money or not,
he gave it to them without hindrance,
and the medicine was always said to be effective.
If someone without illness playfully sought medicine,
upon obtaining the medicine,
they would inevitably lose it soon after.
Thus, people did not dare to seek it frivolously,
and revered him like a deity.
He was often drunk in the city markets,
and any money he received he also gave to the poor.
Once, someone jokingly asked him:
"Do you sell the Great Return Elixir?"
He said:
"Yes,
one pellet for a thousand strings of cash."
People all laughed, thinking him mad.
Often in the city markets, he would laugh and scold people, saying:
"You have money but won't buy medicine to take,
you'll all end up as earthen steamed buns!"
No one understood his meaning,
and they laughed at him even more.
Later, while selling medicine in Cháng'ān,
just as many were buying medicine,
he shook his gourd—it was already empty.
Inside, only one pill came out,
extremely bright and luminous.
Placing it on his palm,
he said to the people:
"For over a hundred years I've sold medicine in the human world,
passing by hundreds of millions of people,
yet not a single one was willing to spend money to buy medicine to take.
How deeply lamentable!
Now I shall take it myself."
As soon as the medicine entered his mouth,
five-colored clouds arose beneath his feet,
the wind rose, swirling,
and he flew away, soaring aloft.
From "Xù Xiān Zhuàn"
Yán Shìzé
At the end of Emperor Wénzōng's reign in the Song dynasty,
("End of Wénzōng's reign" is recorded as "end of Dàzhōng" in the Jùtán Lù),
the Ming manuscript erroneously writes "end of Tàizōng's reign."
Yán Shìzé, the Prefect of Jiànzhōu,
originally served as the Imperial Wardrobe Attendant during Emperor Mùzōng's reign.
He was quite fond of the true Dao.
On the day of the Duanwu Festival,
he lost his way while gathering herbs in the Zhōngnán Mountains,
wandering among the cliffs and peaks.
After several days,
the provisions he had brought were exhausted,
(the character "exhausted" was originally missing,
and was supplemented based on the Ming manuscript).
Looking around, he saw no inhabitants,
and estimated that the distance
from the capital was no less than five or six hundred li.
However, the forested mountains were deep and secluded,
with bright and beautiful scenery.
Suddenly, several thatched huts appeared
beneath the pine and bamboo trees.
Mist and vines surrounded them on all sides,
with only a narrow path leading through.
Shìzé knocked repeatedly on the door,
but for a long time, no one came out.
Peering through a gap in the fence,
he saw a person
lying on a stone couch, reading a book.
Shìzé pushed the door open
and went straight up to him.
Only then did the person gather his clothes and rise.
After Shìzé bowed,
he explained his situation.
The hermit then invited him to sit on a large rock,
asked about recent events in the capital,
and inquired how many years it had been since the emperor ascended the throne.
He said:
"Since the Ān-Shì Rebellion reached the capital, I have lived here
until today."
Shìzé described his arduous journey in detail,
explaining that his provisions were exhausted
and he was starving,
so he begged for food and drink to save himself.
The hermit said:
"Since I have lived in these mountains and valleys,
I have not lit a fire for cooking.
However, there is one thing that can cure hunger.
Considering you have come from afar to visit,
I will get it from the rafters."
He took down a paper bag,
opened it,
and inside were over a hundred objects
shaped like flat beans.
He instructed Shìzé to fetch a pot from the medicine room,
gather firewood and draw water,
and boil one of the beans for a long time.
A faint aroma emerged,
and when he looked, the bean had grown as large as a palm.
The hermit said:
"You may eat it now.
If you are thirsty, drink the remaining water in the pot."
Shìzé had only eaten half
when he felt completely full.
The hermit continued:
"Your arrival here
must be due to a predestined connection.
From now on, for thirty years,
you will never again feel hunger or thirst.
Worldly concerns and mundane attachments
will gradually fade away.
In the future, you will rise to the position of a Regional Governor,
and will be near Luófú.
If you can cast off worldly glory,
you may also attain the way of longevity.
You have been away from home for a long time;
it is time to return."
As Shìzé prepared to take his leave,
he worried about losing his way again.
The hermit said:
"Do not worry.
About two or three li from here,
you will meet a woodcutter;
you may follow him.
From there, it is not far to the capital gates."
Once he left,
he indeed encountered a woodcutter by the roadside.
When he asked for the hermit's name,
the woodcutter simply returned to the mountains without answering.
After only two nights,
he had already reached the villages of Fánchuān.
Upon returning to the capital,
he no longer enjoyed tasting flavors,
and each day felt more vigorous in spirit and clearer in mind,
as if he could ride phoenixes and cranes.
Dressed in coarse cloth and leaning on a stick,
he often stayed among cliffs and peaks.
Jū□ Shǒulú, the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
was deeply devoted to mystical silence
and wished to meet extraordinary individuals.
A Daoist priest recounted Shìzé's story,
and so he was invited to his residence.
Upon hearing the prediction about becoming a Regional Governor,
Shǒulú recommended him as a Recluse-Scholar for an official post.
Starting as the Assistant Prefect of Zǐzhōu,
he later became the Prefect of Jiànxī,
by which time he was already ninety years old.
He served in the prefecture for only one year
before resigning and returning to Luófú.
When Prime Minister Wéi Zhòu was stationed south of the Yangtze River,
he sent someone to visit Shìzé,
and he was still living in the mountains and valleys.
In the fourteenth year of the Dàzhōng era,
on his way to take office in Jiàn'ān,
he passed through the region south of the Yangtze.
At that time, Prime Minister Xiāo was inspecting customs in Zhèyòu,
and invited him to a banquet at the Guìlóu.
Shìzé only drank a few cups of wine
and ate nothing else.
From the Jùtán Lù.
Lǐ Mì
Lǐ Mì, styled Chángyuán,
was a native of Zhōngshān in Zhàojùn.
His sixth-generation ancestor was Lǐ Bì,
Grand Preceptor of the Táng dynasty.
His father, Lǐ Chéngxiū,
served as Magistrate of Wúfáng in the Táng dynasty.
Chéngxiū married a woman of the Zhōu clan from Rǔnán.
Earlier,
when Lady Zhōu was still young,
an extraordinary monk named Sēngqié came from Sìshàng,
saw her, and found her remarkable.
He then said:
"This girl will later marry into the Lǐ family,
and give birth to three sons.
The youngest among them—
be careful not to dress him in purple robes,
for he will rise to wear gold and purple,
and become a teacher to emperors."
When Lady Zhōu was pregnant with Mì,
it lasted a full three years
before she awoke and gave birth.
Mì was born with hair reaching his eyebrows.
Previously, each time Lady Zhōu gave birth,
she would be exhausted for days,
but only when delivering Mì was she free from ailment;
hence his childhood name was Shùn.
Mì was intelligent and quick-witted from a young age;
he could recite any text after a single reading,
and began learning literary composition at six or seven.
In the sixteenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
Emperor Xuánzōng held a grand feast at the tower,
and that night, a high seat was set up below the tower
to summon scholars of the Three Teachings for debate.
Mì's maternal cousin Yuán Chù,
aged nine,
secretly asked his aunt to prepare Confucian robes for him,
ascended the high seat at night,
and his arguments flowed forth sharply,
overwhelming all the debaters.
Emperor Xuánzōng, amazed,
summoned him into the tower
and asked his name.
He then said:
"A grandson of Bànqiān—
no wonder he is like this."
He then asked if there were any other extraordinary children like him outside.
Chù replied:
"My maternal cousin Shùn,
aged seven,
is agile in composing poetry."
The emperor asked where his residence was,
ordered a eunuch to secretly wait at the gate,
carry him in,
and warned not to let his family know.
Emperor Xuánzōng was then watching a game of chess with Zhāng Yuè,
when the eunuch brought Mì in.
Chù and Liú Yàn
were both by the emperor's side.
When Emperor Xuánzōng saw Mì,
he said to Yuè:
"This later child is utterly different from the previous one;
his bearing truly marks him as a vessel of the state."
Yuè said:
"Indeed."
He then ordered Yuè to test him in poetry.
He immediately commanded him to compose a poem on square, round, movement, and stillness.
Mì said:
"I wish to hear the description."
Yuè responded:
"Square like a chessboard,
round like a chess piece,
movement like a piece coming to life,
stillness like a piece dead."
Considering his youth,
Yuè instructed him further:
"You may only compose abstractly based on the idea;
you must not mention chess again."
Mì said:
"That is very easy to do at will."
Emperor Xuánzōng laughed and said:
"His spirit is greater than his body."
Mì then spoke:
"Square like practicing righteousness,
round like employing wisdom,
movement like displaying talent,
stillness like fulfilling intent."
Yuè then congratulated him:
"This is an auspicious sign of a sage era."
Emperor Xuánzōng was greatly pleased;
he held him in his arms,
stroked his head,
and ordered fruits and sweets to be fed to him.
He was then sent to the Zhōngwáng residence,
returning only after two months.
He was also bestowed with clothing and several dozen bolts of colored silk.
The emperor instructed his family:
"He is young;
I fear an official post might harm him,
so I cannot grant him one yet.
Take good care of him,
for he is a vessel of the state."
From then on, Zhāng Yuè invited him to his residence,
ordering his sons Jūn and Jì
to treat him like a teacher and friend,
and their affection grew very close.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng, Hè Zhīzhāng, Zhāng Tíngguī, and Wéi Xūxīn
all admired and cherished him upon first meeting.
Hè Zhīzhāng once said:
"This child's eyes are like autumn water;
he will surely become a minister or chancellor."
Zhāng Yuè said:
"Recently, the emperor wanted to give him an official post.
I said it was not yet appropriate.
I cherished him,
waiting for him to mature into a vessel."
When he was a child,
his body was light,
able to stand on a screen
and walk on an incense burner cage.
A Daoist said:
"At fifteen, he will surely ascend to heaven in broad daylight."
His parents cherished and protected him,
and his relatives loved him dearly.
Hearing this,
they all felt as if a great calamity were impending.
One day, an extraordinary fragrance filled the air,
along with the sound of music.
Lǐ Mì's blood relatives
all came out to curse it.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month of that year,
flute songs echoed in the room,
and colored clouds hung over the courtyard trees.
Lǐ Mì's close relatives
pounded large amounts of garlic paste,
up to several hu,
and when the strange music and fragrance arrived,
they secretly had someone climb onto the roof
and use a large ladle to splash thick garlic paste,
whereupon the fragrance and music dispersed,
and never returned.
Two years later,
he composed a long song, saying:
"Heaven covers me,
earth bears me;
did heaven and earth intend my birth or not?
If not, let me abstain from grains and ascend the heavenly path,
or let me sound my jade ornaments and roam the imperial capital.
How can I neither be noble nor depart,
merely an imposing man in vain?
A man, oh a man—
his lifelong aspirations are his true plan.
I ask you to look at the affairs of a hundred years;
when achievements are made, a small boat will drift on the Five Lakes."
After the poem was completed,
all who copied and circulated it praised it.
When Zhāng Jiǔlíng saw it,
he alone admonished him:
"Gaining fame early
will surely bring setbacks.
You should conceal your brilliance;
this is the path of perfection.
Holding talent within oneself
is valued by the ancients—
how much more for a child!
You should only write poems appreciating scenery
or praising ancient sages;
it is best not to promote yourself."
Mì tearfully thanked him.
Thereafter, in his writings,
he no longer spoke of himself.
Jiǔlíng especially appreciated his thoughtfulness,
saying his future prospects were immeasurable.
He also once directly admonished Jiǔlíng with pointed words.
Jiǔlíng was moved by this.
He thus called him "young friend."
When Jiǔlíng was posted to Jīngzhōu,
he invited Mì to stay in the commandery for a year,
then sent him to study in the Eastern Capital.
Mì then traveled to Héng Shān and Sōng Shān.
There, he encountered the immortals Huán Zhēnrén, Xiànménzǐ, and Ānqī Xiānshēng descending to him.
Feathered carriages and banners,
flowing clouds and divine light
illumined the mountain valleys,
and they departed as dawn approached,
bestowing upon him the methods of immortality, feathery transformation, and elixir ingestion.
They also admonished him:
"The Supreme Sovereign has decreed
that, as the state's fortune faces peril
and the court endures many troubles,
you should use the ways of civil and martial arts
to assist the ruler,
bringing merit to the living beings,
and only then may you attain transcendence and cast off worldly ties."
From then on, he often abstained from grains and practiced breath control,
cultivating the essentials of the Yellow Light and Valley Spirit.
When he returned to the capital,
Prince Níng hosted him at his residence.
Princess Yùzhēn addressed him as younger brother,
showing him special respect and admiration.
He often composed poems,
His compositions were inevitably broadcast among the royal and ducal musical movements.
When his father passed away,
he abstained from food and became emaciated from grief.
After the mourning period ended,
he resumed his travels to Sōngshān, Huàshān, and Zhōngnán,
disregarding fame and official salary.
In the tenth year of Tiānbǎo,
Emperor Xuánzōng summoned him to the palace,
where he presented a discourse on the "Míngtáng and Nine Tripods."
In response to an imperial command, he composed the text "The Sacred Fortune of the Great Táng,"
often discussing the Dào and expounding on the classics.
When Sùzōng was the crown prince,
he was ordered to form commoner friendships with the crown prince and various princes,
which aroused the jealousy of Yáng Guózhōng.
Using the poems of reflection he had written,
which criticized current politics,
Yáng framed and slandered him,
resulting in an edict to place him under house arrest in Qíchūn Commandery.
In the twelfth year of Tiānbǎo,
his mother, Zhōu, passed away,
and he returned home.
The crown prince and various princes all sent envoys to offer condolences and sacrifices.
Soon after, Ān Lùshān captured Tóngguān,
and Emperors Xuánzōng and Sùzōng separately embarked on imperial tours.
Lǐ Mì secretly composed poems,
expressing intentions to restore the dynasty.
Prince Guó Jù served as the military governor of Héluò,
and sent people to seek Lǐ Mì in the Sōngshào region.
Coincidentally, a handwritten letter from Sùzōng arrived,
and Prince Guó prepared carriages and horses to escort him to Língwǔ.
Sùzōng received him in his private chambers,
consulting him on all matters of importance,
planning grand strategies,
which eventually led to the recovery of the two capitals.
Lǐ Mì shared a sleeping chamber with the emperor, facing his couch,
and when they went out, they rode side by side.
During the reign of Dàizōng, when he was still Prince Guǎngpíng,
he was appointed commander-in-chief of the empire's military forces,
and an edict appointed Lǐ Mì as Chief of Staff of the Commander-in-Chief's Office for Military Planning and National Affairs, overseeing military operations,
and he was still accommodated within the palace.
Cuī Yuán and Fáng Guǎn arrived from Shǔ,
proclaiming Sùzōng as emperor,
and also bestowed upon Lǐ Mì handwritten edicts, clothing, horses, pillows, and bedding.
After achieving great merit,
the favored minister Lǐ Fǔguó, jealous of his abilities,
sought to harm him.
Lǐ Mì thus submitted a petition requesting to travel to Héngyuè.
A gracious edict granted his request,
providing him with the salary of a third-rank official.
He lived in the mountains for many years,
and one night, he was attacked by bandits,
who threw him into a deep valley.
By dawn,
he managed to climb out using another path.
Cushioned by dry leaves,
he suffered almost no injuries.
Earlier,
when Sùzōng was in Língwǔ,
he often worried that generals like Lǐ and Guō,
who had already been appointed as dukes and chancellors,
having reached the pinnacle of honor and status,
would have no further rewards after the recovery of the capital.
Lǐ Mì replied:
"In previous dynasties, noble titles were used to reward merit,
and official positions were used to appoint the capable.
From Yáo and Shùn down to the Three Dynasties,
this principle never changed.
After the recovery now,
if they are rewarded with fiefdoms,
it would merely be a small prefecture of two to three hundred households—
how difficult would it be to control?"
Sùzōng said:
"Excellent."
Lǐ Mì then said:
"As for my own wishes,
they are particularly different from others."
Sùzōng asked:
"Why is that?"
Lǐ Mì replied:
"I abstain from grains and have no family;
official salaries and fiefdoms
are not what I desire.
For planning strategies in Your Majesty's tent,
after the recovery of the capital,
I only wish to rest my head on the emperor's knee for a nap,
so that the officials may report a guest star encroaching upon the imperial throne—
a single celestial phenomenon would suffice."
Sùzōng laughed heartily.
When they traveled south to Fúfēng,
at each stop,
Sùzōng always ordered Lǐ Mì to lead the vanguard of the army,
clear the traveling palace,
secure the keys,
and report back,
before Sùzōng arrived.
Upon reaching Bǎodìng Commandery,
Lǐ Mì grew somewhat weary
and fell asleep in his own courtyard first.
Sùzōng came to the courtyard
and ordered no one to disturb him.
He climbed onto the bed,
lifted Lǐ Mì's head, and placed it on his knee.
After a long while, Lǐ Mì awoke.
The emperor said:
"The emperor's knee has already been your pillow.
When will the day of recovery arrive?
You must hasten to fulfill your promise."
Lǐ Mì hastily rose to express his gratitude.
Sùzōng held him down and would not allow it.
Lǐ Mì then replied:
"On this journey,
from my perspective,
with the blessings of the ancestral temples
and the authority of Your Majesty,
it will surely be as the commandery's name suggests—
Bǎodìng (Securely Settled)."
After reaching Fúfēng,
within ten days, troops from the Western Regions, Héxī, and Lǒngyòu all assembled,
and taxes and supplies from Jiānghuái also arrived successively,
greatly pleasing Sùzōng.
On another occasion, Sùzōng sat late at night,
summoning his three younger brothers, Prince Yǐng and others,
to dine together on a felt rug by the floor stove.
Since Lǐ Mì often abstained from grains,
Sùzōng personally roasted two pears to give to him.
Prince Yǐng, relying on his favor, stubbornly requested one,
but Sùzōng refused,
saying:
"You are full from eating meat;
the Master abstains from grains—
why must you compete for this?"
Prince Yǐng said:
"We are testing Your Majesty's heart—
why show such favoritism?
If not,
let the three of us brothers share one pear."
Sùzōng still refused,
instead ordering other fruits to be given to them.
The princes said again:
"We requested it because Your Majesty roasted it personally—
what use are other fruits?"
They then said:
"The Master receives such abundant favor—
let us compose a linked verse
to serve as a tale for future years."
Prince Yǐng began:
"How many years has the Master lived,
yet his complexion resembles a child's?"
Next, Prince Xìn said:
"At night, he embraces the bones of the nine immortals;
by day, he dons the robes of the first rank."
Then, Prince Yì said:
"He consumes not a thousand measures of grain,
but only feasts on two pears."
Afterward, the three princes requested the completion of the verse.
Sùzōng thus added:
"Heaven sent this extraordinary talent
to aid me in transforming through non-action."
Lǐ Mì rose to express his thanks.
Sùzōng again stopped him, saying:
"When you dwelled in the mountains,
you secluded yourself in deep forests,
avoiding human affairs;
when you resided within the court,
you secretly planned to save and correct,
your actions aligning with profound mysteries—
you are a pillar of the state."
Lǐ Mì received such exceptional favor
that figures like Yuán Zǎi and Lǐ Fǔguó
envied him as if he were an enemy.
When Dàizōng ascended the throne,
he repeatedly bestowed rewards,
with palace envoys constantly traveling the roads.
He was given the additional title "Master of the Tiānzhù Peak in the Central Mountain"
and presented with a jade tablet for audience with the emperor.
Soon after, he was summoned to the Hànlín Academy.
Yuán Zǎi petitioned for him to be appointed as a Court Gentleman for Comprehensive Duty, Acting Vice Director of the Palace Library,
and serve as Judicial Officer for the Jiāngxī Observation Circuit.
After Yuán Zǎi was executed,
he was recalled to the capital,
but again faced jealousy from Cháng Gǔn,
who appointed him as Prefect of Chǔ Prefecture.
Before he could depart,
he was reassigned as Military Commissioner of Fēng and Lǎng Prefectures,
concurrently holding the title of Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and later transferred to Hángzhōu,
where he was praised for his governance wherever he served.
At the beginning of the Xīngyuán era,
he was summoned to the imperial headquarters,
promoted to Left Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and soon appointed as Chief Official of Shǎn Prefecture,
serving as
"serving as" originally read "first";
amended according to the Táng History, biography of Lǐ Mì, chapter 130.
Defense Commissioner of Shǎn-Guó.
Three thousand garrison soldiers from Chén-Xǔ
fled back from west of the capital
and reached the borders of Shǎn Prefecture.
Lǐ Mì secretly deployed troops at strategic narrow passes,
They were completely defeated.
He also opened three land transport routes spanning eighteen li,
eliminating the hazards of the Gongzhù Rapids for grain transport,
greatly benefiting the capital.
In the sixth month of the second year.
He was appointed concurrently as Vice Director of the Central Secretariat and Participating in Determining Governmental Matters,
with the additional title of Grand Academician of the Chóngwén Institute,
tasked with compiling the national history,
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yè.
At that time, the Crown Prince (later Emperor Shùnzōng) was in the Eastern Palace,
and the mother of his consort, Lady Xiāo, was Princess Gàoguó,
who had illicit communications with outsiders.
The Emperor suspected she harbored other intentions,
and several people were implicated and demoted or dismissed.
The Crown Prince was in peril and fear,
but Lǐ Mì mediated and presented memorials,
causing Emperor Dézōng's mind to be eased.
He displayed considerable forthrightness and rectitude.
In the spring of the fifth year,
Emperor Dézōng established the first day of the second month as the Zhōnghé Festival.
Lǐ Mì memorialized that the relevant officials should present agricultural texts,
offer seeds of early and late-ripening grains,
that imperial relatives and nobles should present spring garments,
and that officials and commoners should exchange greetings.
Lǐ Mì also created Zhōnghé wine,
performed sacrifices to the God of Agriculture, Gōumáng,
to pray for a good harvest.
This practice continues to this day.
Lǐ Mì was broad-minded, perceptive, and eloquent,
fond of grand statements.
Since entering and leaving the imperial palace,
he was repeatedly ostracized by powerful ministers,
yet always escaped by his wits.
Ultimately, through his persuasive and far-reaching discourse,
he enlightened the sagely sovereign,
and ascended to the position of chancellor.
In the third month of that year, he passed away,
and was posthumously awarded the title of Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
In that month, the palace envoy Lín Yuǎn,
encountered Lǐ Mì at an inn at Lánguān Pass.
He was riding alone in ordinary attire,
saying he was temporarily going to Héng Mountain,
and spoke of the significant encounters through four reigns.
After a long, sorrowful conversation, they parted.
When Lín Yuǎn reached Cháng'ān,
he then heard of Lǐ Mì's death.
When Emperor Dézōng heard this,
he was especially grief-stricken and astonished.
He said:
"The Master himself said,
that he would assist four sagely emperors and then cast off his sandals (i.e., leave the world).
These words have proven true."
After Lǐ Mì observed mourning for his parents,
he no longer harbored hopes for fame or officialdom.
He practiced breath cultivation and pursued the Dao,
traveling extensively to famous mountains,
and went to Master Zhāng in Nányuè to receive registers.
Emperor Dézōng posthumously honored Zhāng as Master Xuánhé.
He also associated with Chan Master Míngzàn,
and authored the "Míngxīn Lùn".
Among the Buddhist followers, Míngzàn was called Lǎncán (Lazy Remnant).
Lǐ Mì once studied at the Héngyuè Temple,
and found his behavior extraordinary.
He said:
"He is no ordinary man.
Listening to his midnight Sanskrit chanting,
the sound reverberated through the mountains and forests."
Lǐ Mì was quite knowledgeable in music,
able to discern joy and sorrow.
He said of Lǎncán's sutra chanting:
"First sorrowful, then joyful,
he must be a banished immortal,
whose time to depart is approaching."
Waiting until midnight,
he secretly went to pay his respects.
Lǎncán invited him to sit,
raked the fire, took out a taro, and gave it to him to eat.
He said to Lǐ Mì:
"Be careful not to speak much.
You will receive ten years as chancellor."
Lǐ Mì bowed and withdrew.
In the eighth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
while at the home of his maternal cousin Zhèng Shūzé,
he had already abstained from grains for many years.
His body was light,
able to rise from atop a screen.
Directing his fingers to circulate his breath,
he could blow out candles from a distance.
Whenever he practiced guiding and pulling exercises,
his joints would tinkle with a sound,
so people of the time called them 'lock-bones'.
While at the Zhèng household,
he suddenly fell into a deep coma for two days,
unaware of human affairs.
After awakening,
he saw his spirit emerge two or three inches from the top of his head.
Beside him were numinous immortals,
waving their hands and moving their eyes,
as if encouraging and assisting him.
It was as if from his feet to the crown of his head.
Then he thought to himself that his great task was not yet finished,
and he still had attachment to his family,
wishing to complete family affairs.
Then, those beside him all saw a person,
of very imposing appearance,
dressed in regal attire like an emperor.
Before him was a woman,
in ceremonial dress, kneeling.
The emperor-like figure reproached her:
"Since his affections are not yet severed,
why did you summon him here,
troubling the numinous immortals to come in person?"
The kneeling woman replied:
"Not so.
I am merely teaching him to draw near to the Son of Heaven."
Then he awoke.
Two years later,
he was summoned by Emperor Xuánzōng.
Later, there were often eight recluses,
with very unusual appearances and attire,
who came to visit the Zhèng household.
They repeatedly spoke of their strict and complete immortal methods,
claiming there was nothing they could not accomplish.
As they were leaving, they sighed:
"His worldly ties are ultimately not yet severed.
It is a pity for his heart and bones."
Lǐ Mì begged to follow them.
They said:
"It cannot be!
We shall merely let him serve as chancellor for a while."
They went out the gate and were seen no more.
Consequently, he composed the "Bā Gōng Shī" to narrate this.
There was another recluse,
who brought a boy of six or seven to visit,
saying:
"I have urgent business,
must travel south,
and will return in about a month.
Because this boy suffers from dysentery,
and since we are both followers of the Dao,
I wish to entrust him to you temporarily."
He also left a letter, saying:
"If his illness proves fatal,
I hope you will bury him with this."
After Lǐ Mì agreed,
he asked the boy:
"Will you be content to stay here without complaint?"
The boy said:
"Yes."
Then the man left.
Lǐ Mì sought medicine to treat him,
but he never recovered.
After eight or nine days, he died.
Lǐ Mì immediately placed him in the box,
and buried him under the rose trellis in the courtyard.
After several months,
the man still had not returned.
He tried opening the letter to look.
Inside was a black stone.
Naturally square in the center.
On it were characters as if carved with an awl, saying:
"The divine essence refining the form, the years not yet complete,
transformed into my son, the merit continues.
The Chancellor buries him, engraving the dark jade.
How long the immortal path, how swift death."
Lǐ Mì often sought out recluses and selected marvels,
gathering strange, coiled branches of trees,
which he used in seclusion,
calling them 'Nourishers of Harmony'.
People to this day imitate and make them,
and he composed the "Yǎnghé Piān",
which he presented to Emperor Sùzōng.
After Lǐ Mì left for three or four years,
the two emperors (Xuánzōng and Sùzōng) passed away,
and Emperor Dàizōng ascended the throne.
He then issued an edict summoning Lǐ Mì to the court,
lodging him in the Yánxǐ Pavilion of the Pénglái Hall.
Regarding appointments and demotions of officials above the rank of Jǐshì and regional military governors,
[The character 'demote' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Ming manuscript copy.]
Emperor Dàizōng would always consult him.
Military and state affairs of great importance
were also all decided with Lǐ Mì's participation.
When the conversation turned to Prince Jiànníng's achievements at Língwǔ,
he requested that he be posthumously honored as Crown Prince.
Emperor Dàizōng was moved and mourned for a long time,
saying:
"My younger brother's merit,
without you, Sir, the world would not know.
How could it be limited to posthumously honoring him as Crown Prince!"
He immediately ordered the retrieval of the remains from Péngyuán,
posthumously honored him as Emperor Chéngtiān,
and buried him at the Qí Mausoleum.
When the procession reached the city gate,
it was reported that the dragon hearse would not move.
Emperor Dàizōng, from the Pénglái Hall, said to him:
"My younger brother seems to wish to see you, Sir.
You should quickly go and offer libations and prayers,
and also convey my thoughts.
Moreover, my younger brother's great merit in determining the strategy..."
The Tang dynasty chancellor Liú Yàn,
was fond of Daoist arts from a young age,
diligently and tirelessly pursuing them,
yet without encountering any success.
He often heard that extraordinary individuals often frequented marketplaces,
as their bustling and chaotic nature
allowed them to blend in unnoticed.
Later, while traveling in Cháng'ān,
he came upon a medicine shop,
and casually inquired:
"There are often three or four elderly men,
wearing gauze caps and leaning on staffs, who come to buy wine,
drink it and then leave immediately.
Sometimes they also look for medicine,
but they never buy much.
They must be extraordinary individuals, not ordinary folk."
Liú Yàn asked:
"When will they come?"
The reply was:
"They are due to come tomorrow."
Liú Yàn went early the next morning,
and after a short while, three Daoist practitioners indeed arrived.
They filled their cups and drank wine,
chatting and joking with great delight,
as if no one else was around.
After a long while, one said:
"Are there still people in the world like us?"
Another replied:
"Wáng Shíbā."
Then they left.
From then on, Liú Yàn often thought of this,
but could not find them.
Later, when he became a prefectural governor,
he traveled to the southern regions.
Passing through Héngshān County,
it was early spring,
the weather was mild and warm,
and he ate a plate of cold noodles,
with fragrant herbs like yīnchén and such,
which were exceptionally aromatic and fresh.
Liú Yàn found this strange,
and asked the postal officer:
"Is there no scholar or official living nearby?
Where did these vegetables come from?"
The reply was:
"The county has an official gardener named Wáng Shíbā who can grow them,
so the guesthouse often has these vegetables."
Liú Yàn suddenly remembered with surprise what the Daoist practitioners he had encountered had said,
and said:
"Is the garden far or near?
Can we go there?"
The reply was:
"It's right behind the guesthouse."
So he went.
He saw Wáng Shíbā,
wearing a dúnbí kù and watering the vegetable beds,
his appearance rustic and wild.
Upon seeing Liú Yàn, he hurried over to bow, trembling with fear.
Gradually, Liú Yàn sat with him,
and asked about his hometown and family.
Wáng Shíbā said:
"I drift like duckweed and do not remember,
and I have no relatives or clan."
Liú Yàn found this strange and suspicious,
invited him to sit,
and called for wine to drink with him.
Wáng Shíbā firmly refused.
Upon returning,
Liú Yàn then went to the county office,
and personally requested to take Wáng Shíbā with him to the southern regions.
The county magistrate did not understand at all,
but sent him off at the time.
Wáng Shíbā did not strongly resist either,
wearing tattered clothes and straw sandals,
he boarded the boat and set off.
Liú Yàn gradually became familiar with him,
had his wife and children come to pay respects to him,
and sat together for tea and meals.
However, Wáng Shíbā's appearance and clothing
grew increasingly filthy and shabby day by day.
The family members all secretly despised him.
Liú Yàn's wife said:
"How could this person be extraordinary?
Why are you treating him like this?"
But Liú Yàn did not slacken in his care.
When they were several hundred lǐ from their destination,
Wáng Shíbā fell ill with dysentery,
growing weaker day and night,
and the boat was narrow and cramped,
so he stayed close to Liú Yàn's quarters.
Those around covered their noses and stopped eating,
unable to bear the hardship.
But Liú Yàn showed no sign of disgust or weariness,
only worry and sorrow.
He urged Wáng Shíbā to take broth and porridge,
but after a few days, Wáng Shíbā died.
Liú Yàn sighed, wept, and sobbed,
and the funeral rites
were all meticulously prepared.
He was then buried by the roadside.
A year later,
Liú Yàn's term ended and he returned to the court.
When he reached Héngshān County,
the magistrate came to greet him outside the city.
After sitting down, the magistrate said:
"The gardener you took with you,
left and then returned,
probably because he couldn't bear the hardship."
Liú Yàn asked in surprise when he had returned.
The magistrate said:
"He returned a little over a month later.
He said:
'I was ordered to be released and sent back.'" Liú Yàn was greatly astonished,
and immediately walked to the garden.
The thatched cottage still stood,
but there was no sign of anyone.
A neighbor said:
"Wáng Shíbā left yesterday evening."
Liú Yàn's regret and sorrow deepened,
he bowed twice toward the cottage,
and returned weeping.
Upon checking the date of Wáng Shíbā's return to the county,
it turned out to be the very day he had died on the journey.
Liú Yàn sent someone to open his grave,
but only his clothes remained.
Several months later, when he reached the capital,
and was serving as an official in the court,
he suddenly fell seriously ill,
and was on the verge of death.
His family, wife, and children
gathered around, watching and wailing.
Suddenly, there was a very urgent knocking at the door,
and the gatekeeper ran in shouting:
"Someone named Wáng Shíbā
is here and asks to report."
The whole family rejoiced and rushed to welcome him, bowing in respect.
Wáng Shíbā smiled slightly and entered the sickroom.
Liú Yàn had long been unconscious from his illness.
Wáng Shíbā had all the screens and such removed, as well as the medicine,
then took a gourd from his waist and opened it,
pouring out three pills of medicine,
as small as beans.
Using a reed tube to draw half a bowl of water,
he administered them and shook him.
After a short while, there was a sound like thunder in his abdomen,
and soon he opened his eyes,
suddenly sat up,
showing no sign of his previous illness.
His wife said:
"Wáng Shíbā is here."
Liú Yàn then wept profusely,
clutched his clothes, and bowed twice,
as if overwhelmed with emotion.
His wife, daughter, and servants all wept.
Wáng Shíbā said sadly:
"To repay our old friendship,
I have come to save you.
One of these pills
can extend your life by ten years.
When the time comes, I will return to retrieve it."
He drank a bowl of tea and left.
Liú Yàn earnestly asked him to stay a little longer.
He refused.
Liú Yàn also wanted to give him gold and silk.
Wáng Shíbā only laughed heartily again.
Later, Liú Yàn became chancellor,
and also oversaw the salt and iron monopolies.
He was implicated in an incident and demoted to Zhōngzhōu.
Thirty years had passed.
One day, he fell ill.
Wáng Shíbā came again and said:
"I wish to see the chancellor."
Liú Yàn was deeply moved and sighed,
invited him into his chamber,
and earnestly pleaded again.
Wáng Shíbā said:
"Your illness will be cured,
but I must take back the medicine."
He then took a liǎng of salt,
mixed it with water, and had him drink it.
After drinking, Liú Yàn vomited heavily,
and in the vomit were three pills,
their color no different from those he had taken thirty years earlier.
Wáng Shíbā asked for fragrant water to wash them.
Liú Yàn's nephew,
who was attending to him at his side,
snatched two of the pills and swallowed them.
Wáng Shíbā looked at him carefully and laughed:
"You have the aura of the Dao,
I knew you would take them."
He hurried out and left,
without saying goodbye.
Liú Yàn soon recovered.
Several months later, an imperial edict arrived,
and he passed away.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Cuī Xīzhēn
In the early years of the Dàlì era,
a guest in Zhōnglíng named Cuī Xīzhēn
lived west of the commandery.
He was skilled at playing the qin,
proficient in painting,
and fond of cultivation techniques.
On the first night of the tenth month in the second year, heavy snow fell.
At dawn, Xīzhēn went out the door
and saw an old man
wearing a straw raincoat and bamboo hat,
sheltering from the snow beneath his gate.
Cuī found this strange
and invited him inside.
After the old man removed his raincoat and hat,
Cuī observed his spirit, complexion, hair, and bones—
he was no ordinary person—
and grew even more respectful.
He asked:
"My household has some barley flour;
we can make a simple meal of it.
Can you, venerable elder, eat this?"
The old man replied:
"Barley receives the qi of the four seasons—
it is among the finest grains.
If you can moisten it with fermented bean juice,
it will be even better."
Cuī then ordered his family to prepare it.
He also offered pine flower wine.
The old man said:
"The flowers make it astringent and tasteless.
I am a man of the wilds
and can make it mellow and delicious."
He then took from his bosom a pill of medicine,
yellow in color and hard.
The old man crushed it with a stone,
placed it in the wine,
and it immediately became sweet and fine.
He also gave several pills to Xīzhēn.
When Xīzhēn inquired further,
the old man smiled without answering.
Cuī entered his residence
and peered through the window.
He saw the old man before the curtained bed, on the plain silk hanging there,
as if applying something,
and in a flash he was done.
A short while later, Cuī prepared a meal and offered it;
the old man accepted without declining.
Cuī later went inside,
and when he came out, the old man had already left.
He then followed the footprints in the snow,
for several li until he reached the river,
entering a reed marsh,
where he saw a large boat.
On the boat were several people
with extraordinary appearances,
and the woodcutter guest was among them.
One of them looked back and laughed, saying:
"Gě Sān was indeed pressured by that man."
Turning to Cuī, he said:
"The rites of honoring the Way and revering the master
need not be so rigid."
Cuī bowed and thanked him.
Returning home, he looked inside the bed curtain
and found a painting there.
It depicted three people, two trees, a white deer, and a medicine basket.
Two of the people appeared to be beyond the mundane world,
holding mysterious mushrooms as herb gatherers;
one was an immortal.
The trees resembled cypresses, both broken;
the basket was weathered by wind and rain.
Their withered appearance,
with roots interconnected,
was beyond ordinary comprehension.
Later, he took the painting and the pills
to Máoshān
to ask Celestial Master Lǐ Hánguāng.
The Celestial Master said:
"This was painted by the third son of the Perfected Person Gě Hóng."
Master Lǐ also said:
"Depicting the form of a spirit person beneath withered trees
suggests that those who attain the Way live longer than pines and cypresses.
The medicine is thousand-year pine resin."
From "Records of Original Transformations."
Venerable Wéi
Venerable Wéi, a Dàoshi of Sōngshān,
was by nature taciturn and spoke little.
It was unknown by what arts he attained immortality.
He often kept a dog,
shaggy and yellow,
and usually took it with him.
Sometimes he sat alone in the mountains and forests,
sometimes he slept in rain or snow,
and sometimes every three to five days he would go to the mountain temple
to seek leftover vegetarian food to eat.
No one could understand him.
In the final years of the Táng dynasty's Kāiyuán era,
he led his dog to the mountain temple to seek food.
The monks competed angrily,
asking why he had come again.
Venerable Wéi said:
"I seek food to give to my dog."
The monks grew angry and insulted him,
ordering a servant to fill a bowl with leftovers
and give it to the old beggar Dàoshi.
Venerable Wéi gave it all to his dog.
The stronger, braver monks
again insulted him
and wanted to beat him.
The dog watched the monks' angry expressions.
Venerable Wéi patted its head.
After a while,
the monks gradually withdrew.
Venerable Wéi then went out
and washed his dog in the pond before the hall.
Suddenly, five-colored clouds filled the valleys and streams.
The monks watched in astonishment
as the clouds gathered over the pond.
In an instant,
the dog grew several zhàng long
and became a great dragon.
Venerable Wéi also washed himself,
put on silk garments,
mounted the dragon and sat firmly,
with five-colored clouds supporting his feet,
and slowly ascended to heaven and departed.
The monks in the temple bowed in repentance,
but it was already too late.
From "Records of Astonishing Tales."
The Villager of Máyáng
A villager from Máyáng County in Chénzhōu
had a pig that ate his grain.
Angered,
he took a bow and arrows and lay in wait.
The next day, it appeared again.
The man shot the pig,
and the pig ran several li
into a large gate.
Inside the gate, he saw magnificent buildings,
and an old man
with snow-white beard, holding a staff,
followed by a servant boy in blue.
He asked the man how he had come here.
The man said, "The pig ate my grain,
so I shot it
and followed it here."
The old man said:
"If someone's ox tramples your field and you seize the ox,
isn't that excessive?"
He ordered a boy to give the man wine to drink.
Walking forward several dozen paces,
they reached a great hall,
where he saw a group of immortals
in feathered robes and black caps,
some playing liubo,
some playing chess,
some drinking wine.
The boy went to the drinking area.
He conveyed the order:
"The lord commands that this man be given a cup of wine."
After drinking it, the man felt no hunger.
They then went to another place,
where there were several dozen couches,
each with a person sitting on it,
holding books,
as if listening to a lecture.
After a long while, they returned to the lord's place.
The lord reprimanded the gatekeeping boy:
"Why did you open the gate,
allowing the pig to come and go without your knowledge?"
Then he said to the man:
"This is not a real pig.
You should leave now."
He ordered the previous boy to escort him out.
The man asked who the old man was.
The boy said:
"This is the so-called Héshàng Gōng,
sent by the Supreme Deity to lecture the immortals on the 'Yìjīng.'"
The man asked who the boy was.
The boy said:
"I am Wáng Fǔsì.
Since I received the 'Yìjīng,'
nearly five hundred years have passed,
yet I have not mastered its profound meaning.
Thus I am punished to guard the gate."
After the man left,
the boy kicked a large stone to block the gate,
and it was never seen again.
From "Extensive Records of the Strange."
The Compassionate Immortal
In the second year of the Guǎngdé era of the Táng dynasty,
Yuán Cháo, a rebel from Línhǎi County,
raided Yǒngjiā.
His ships encountered a storm,
drifting eastward for several thousand lǐ.
In the distance, they saw a mountain,
lush and verdant, dense with trees,
with city walls,
shimmering in five colors.
They turned the rudder and approached to moor,
seeing a temple,
with glazed tiles for its roof,
and tortoiseshell for its walls.
Once they entered the corridors,
it was silent, with no one in sight.
In the rooms, there were only over twenty foreign pug dogs,
and all the utensils were made of gold,
with no miscellaneous items.
There were also quilts and cushions,
exceptionally brilliant,
mostly made of rare and heavy brocade from Shǔ.
There was also a city made of gold,
with piles of broken gold scattered about,
too many to count.
The rebels, seeing no one,
competed to take the objects.
Suddenly, they saw a woman emerge from the golden city,
about six chǐ tall,
dressed in embroidered silk garments and a purple gauze skirt.
She said to the rebels:
"Are you not part of Yuán Cháo's gang?
How did you get here?
What business do you have with these objects,
that you dare to take them!
Earlier, you saw the pug dogs—
did you think they were dogs?
No,
they are dragons.
As for the things you have taken,
I truly do not begrudge them,
but I fear the dragons will harbor anger,
and lead your ship forward,
causing your death in an instant!
You should quickly return them."
The rebels lined up and bowed,
each returning the objects to their original places.
They then asked what place this was.
The woman said:
"This is the place where the Compassionate Heart Immortal of Jìnghú Mountain cultivates the Way.
You, for no reason, have become rebels with Yuán Cháo.
Within ten days,
you will face great calamity.
You should be deeply cautious."
The rebels then begged for a favorable wind
to return to the coast.
The woman turned her head and gave instructions.
Soon, the wind rose,
and the rebels bowed in farewell,
then raised their sails.
After several days, they reached Línhǎi.
Their ships ran aground on the sand and could not disembark,
and they were killed by government troops,
with only six or seven women surviving.
Xiè Quánzhī, a deputy commander in Zhèdōng, was assigned a maidservant,
named Qū Yè,
who personally recounted this event.
From the "Guǎngyì Jì."
A Person from Bāqióng
There was a person from Bāqióng,
whose name is unknown.
His family had an orange grove,
and after the frost,
all the oranges had been harvested.
Two large oranges remained,
as big as three- or four-dǒu jars.
The person from Bā found this strange,
and immediately had them picked.
Their weight was like that of ordinary oranges.
When cut open,
each orange contained two old men,
with white beards and eyebrows,
and ruddy, moist skin.
They were playing elephant chess facing each other,
their bodies only about a chǐ tall,
chatting and laughing as if nothing were amiss.
After being cut open,
they showed no fear,
but continued with their game.
After the game,
one old man said:
"You owe me ten liǎng of the hair of the seventh daughter of the Sea Dragon God,
twelve forehead ornaments of Zhìqióng,
a set of purple silk capes,
two yǔ of Xiáshí powder from Jiàngtái Mountain,
nine hú of Yíngzhōu jade dust,
four cups of Āmǔ's marrow-congealing medicinal wine,
and eight pairs of Āmǔ's daughter, Tàiyíng Niángzǐ's, ethereal dragon-patterned silk stockings.
You will return them to me later at Mr. Wáng's thatched cottage in Qīngchéng."
Another old man said:
"Mr. Wáng promised to come,
but we waited in vain.
The joy within the orange
is no less than that of Shāng Mountain;
but we cannot take deep root and secure our stems,
as we have been plucked."
Another old man said:
"I am hungry,
I must eat some dragon-root jerky."
He then pulled out a grass root from his sleeve,
about a cùn in diameter,
its shape twisting like a dragon,
with every detail perfectly rendered.
He began to slice and eat it,
and as he sliced, it grew back.
After eating,
he sprayed water on it,
and it transformed into a dragon.
The four old men mounted it together,
and clouds billowed beneath their feet.
In an instant, wind and rain darkened the sky,
and they were gone without a trace.
The people of Bā passed down the story:
"This has been happening for over a hundred and fifty years,
seemingly between the Suí and Táng dynasties,
but the exact era is unknown."
