From the "Xuánguài Lù."
Zhāngqiú Jiānqióng
Minister Zhāngqiú Jiānqióng was stationed in Xīchuān,
and often ordered his subordinates to search for Daoist adepts.
There was a wine seller
whose wine was superior to others',
and who was not eager for profit,
allowing many to buy on credit.
Four men wearing gauze hats and carrying goosefoot staffs often came to drink,
each consuming several dǒu,
accumulating debts of over ten shí,
which they would repay all at once.
They joked and laughed,
leaving in high spirits.
In their conversations, they often spoke of Sūn Sīmiǎo.
They also said:
"What does this youngster know?"
Someone reported this to Lord Zhāngqiú.
He then sent a close attendant to wait until they were half-drunk,
and approach them, saying:
"The Minister sends word:
'I have devoted myself to cultivation,
and know that an immortal official is here.
I wish to pay my respects;
I wonder if you would grant me this honor.'"
The four paid no attention,
continuing to drink merrily as before.
After a while,
they asked the wine seller:
"How much wine did we just drink?"
He replied:
"One shí."
They all clapped and laughed:
"Too much."
After saying this,
without leaving their seats,
they vanished.
The messenger reported this in detail to Lord Zhāngqiú,
who then ordered a dedicated search.
For over a month afterward, they did not return.
One day, they came again,
and Lord Zhāngqiú secretly went to visit them,
accompanied by three or four attendants.
In his official robes, he approached,
stepped forward, and bowed deeply.
He announced his name,
and they looked at each other and slowly rose.
Only four pieces of charcoal ash remained
in front of the seats.
They were never seen again.
At that time, Emperor Xuánzōng favored Daoism,
so Lord Zhāngqiú reported the matter,
and an edict summoned Sūn Sīmiǎo to inquire.
Sūn said:
"These are the stars of Tàibái, the god of wine.
Their immortal rank is extremely high.
They often roam the human world to drink,
going everywhere,
but they especially enjoy Shǔ."
Afterward, further searches were ordered,
but no trace was found.
From the "Yìshǐ."
Shí Jù
Shí Jù was a man of the Hu people
who resided in Yōuzhōu.
He had a penchant for consuming elixirs.
During the Dàlì era, he fell ill for over a hundred days.
His body became emaciated and frail,
yet his spirit and vitality remained undiminished.
Suddenly, he said to his son:
"At Héqiáo, there is a fortune-teller.
You should go and invite him here for a consultation."
The son returned and said:
"There is no fortune-teller at all,
only an old woman."
Shí Jù said:
"Precisely, she is the one to summon."
The son invited her to their home.
Shí Jù lay inside a paper screen in the main hall.
The old woman went straight to where Shí Jù was,
and they spoke in very hushed tones.
Shí Jù's son listened from outside,
but could not hear anything.
After a long while, the old woman left.
A few days later,
in the morning, a white crane descended from the sky,
pierced through Shí Jù's paper screen,
and entered his chamber.
It sang harmoniously for about the time it takes to eat a meal,
then suddenly rose into the air,
transformed into a white crane, and flew away.
Shí Jù's son went to look,
but could no longer see Shí Jù.
The son then followed the crane,
arriving at a large mound east of the city.
There, he saw several dozen large white cranes
following one another as they ascended to the heavens,
gradually fading away until they vanished.
The Chief Administrator Lǐ Huáixiān
summoned Shí Jù's son to inquire about the matter,
and the son provided a detailed account.
Lǐ Huáixiān did not believe it
and said to the son:
"This is a matter of demonic falsehood.
If your father has truly attained immortality,
then my jurisdiction is suffering from a severe drought.
He should bring us rain.
If it does not rain, I will have you killed."
The son returned home,
burned incense, and conveyed the message above.
Lǐ Huáixiān sent Adjutant Jīn to bring wine and dried meat
to Shí Jù's residence to offer sacrifices.
That day, heavy rain fell,
sufficient for both near and far.
Since his request had been miraculously fulfilled,
Lǐ Huáixiān erected a temple at Shí Jù's residence,
where sacrifices were offered annually.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
Lǐ Shānrén
Vice Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Wèn,
while serving at court,
was fond of occult practitioners.
At that time, a mountain hermit named Lǐ was staying at his residence as a guest,
and Lǐ Wèn respected him greatly.
Lǐ Wèn had several sons,
the eldest of whom was named Lǐ Yuányǔn.
He had previously arranged a marriage with the Wěi family of Xiāngyáng,
and so he traveled from the capital to Xiāngyáng
to attend the joyous wedding ceremony.
After his departure,
the mountain hermit said to Lǐ Wèn:
"Your esteemed son is facing a calamity,
and I can save him.
However, he must avoid human affairs for a short while
and seek a quiet place to stay."
Lǐ Wèn agreed.
The mountain hermit moved to a separate residence,
and after a long while, he emerged and said:
"Your esteemed son's calamity has already passed.
However, the horse he was riding has died,
and one of his attendants has perished.
He himself suffered a minor injury with a little bleeding,
but otherwise, he is largely unharmed."
Lǐ Wèn was half-convinced and half-doubtful,
so he sent someone to Xiāngzhōu
to investigate along the way.
The messenger returned with news:
"On the journey, they crossed a large bridge.
The bridge collapsed,
the horse died, and a servant perished.
Your son was struck by a horizontal beam, injuring the area between his chin and jaw,
with a little bleeding,
but he recovered shortly after."
Lǐ Wèn sighed in amazement.
Later, the mountain hermit suddenly bid farewell, saying:
"I have been a guest here for a long time,
and the time for my transformation and departure is approaching."
Lǐ Wèn felt increasingly sorrowful.
He asked:
"Why must it be so sudden?"
The hermit replied:
"Fate dictates it,
and one must submit to it."
Lǐ Wèn said:
"Can you stay a little longer?"
The hermit replied:
"I can."
Lǐ Wèn insisted on keeping him,
and after over a month, the hermit said again:
"I wish to proceed as planned earlier."
Lǐ Wèn kept him for another half month.
The hermit said:
"Now I must leave."
He then rose at dawn
and bid farewell to Lǐ Wèn.
Afterward, all the families who knew him
said:
"On the same day, Lǐ Shānrén came to bid us farewell.
When he first said goodbye, he remarked:
'I have a small matter
to mention regarding the third young master.'"
They asked what it was.
He said:
"Fifteen years from now,
by the edge of Kūnmíng Pond,
if you see a child in a household with a birthmark on the cheek,
that will be me."
Then he departed.
After that, no one knew where he went.
From "Yuán Huà Jì"
Táo and Yǐn, Two Gentlemen
In the early Dàzhōng era of the Táng dynasty,
there were two old men, Táo Tàibái and Yǐn Zǐxū,
who became close friends.
They often roamed the peaks of Sōngshān and Huàshān,
gathering pine resin and poria cocos for a living.
The two men brought along some brewed wine,
ascended Fúróng Peak,
seeking wondrous scenery,
and rested beneath a large pine forest.
As they poured wine and drank,
they heard the sound of two people clapping and laughing from atop the pine trees.
The two gentlemen rose and asked:
"Are you perhaps immortals?
Why not descend and share a cup of this wine!"
The laughers replied:
"We two are not mountain spirits or tree demons.
I am a laborer from the Qín dynasty,
and she is a palace maiden from Qín.
Hearing the fragrance of your wine,
we long for a taste of intoxication.
But our forms have altered,
our hair and appearance are strange and unusual.
We fear you might be startled and tremble,
so we cannot descend immediately.
Please set your minds at ease and wait patiently;
we shall return to our cave to change clothes and then come.
We hope you will not hastily abandon us and leave."
The two gentlemen said:
"We respectfully heed your command."
Thus they waited for a long time.
Suddenly, beneath the pine trees, they saw a man,
in ancient attire, solemn and elegant;
and a woman,
with coiled hair and colorful garments.
Both arrived.
The two gentlemen bowed in greeting,
and they cheerfully sat down together.
After a while,
Mr. Táo inquired of the immortals from which era they came,
and how they had arrived here?
"Since we have been granted the honor of meeting you,
we wish to dispel our confusion."
The ancient man said:
"I am a laborer from the Qín dynasty.
My family were originally people of Qín.
When I was just becoming a youth,
it happened that the First Emperor favored the arts of immortality,
seeking the elixir of eternal life.
Thus, deceived by Xú Fú,
he gathered a thousand boys and girls,
to take them to the islands of the sea.
I was a boy then,
and was among those chosen.
All I saw were whale-like waves crushing snow,
mirage pavilions towering in the sky,
the pillars of stone bridges leaning perilously,
the mist of Pénglái's peaks distant and faint.
Fearing to be buried in the bellies of fish,
yet still clinging to life like a sparrow.
Amidst this peril and hardship,
I devised a clever plan,
and thus escaped this disaster.
Returning, I changed my surname and took up the scholarly profession.
Within a few years,
I again encountered the First Emperor's burning of the classics and texts,
and the burying alive of scholars.
Officials wept tears of blood,
courtiers wailed in grief.
At that time,
I was again among their number.
In the midst of that danger and fear,
I again devised a clever plan,
and thus escaped this suffering.
Again I changed my surname and became a rammed-earth laborer.
Again I encountered the Qín emperor's sudden belief in demons and falsehoods,
and thus the Great Wall was built,
starting from Líntáo in the west,
reaching the coastal bend in the east.
Geese of Lǒng mourned by day,
frontier clouds choked the sky.
Thoughts of home caused souls to drift,
labor in the sandy desert exhausted one's strength.
Toes fell, bones were injured,
sinking in snow, striking ice.
I was a laborer,
again among their number.
Thus, amidst the toil and hardship,
I again devised a clever plan,
and escaped this calamity.
Again I changed my surname and took up the artisan's trade.
Then it came to pass that the Qín emperor died,
and they excavated Líshān,
building a grand burial ground on a vast scale:
jade steps and golden masonry,
pearl trees and jade branches,
ornate halls and brocade palaces,
cloud towers and rosy pavilions.
Workers and master craftsmen
were all sealed inside the dark tunnels.
Considering myself an artisan,
I was again among their number.
Again I devised a clever stratagem,
and escaped this suffering.
In all, I devised four ingenious plans,
and escaped great disasters each time.
Knowing I would not meet with fortune in the world,
I fled to this mountain,
eating pine resin and tree fruits,
and thus attained extended life.
This Máonǚ,
was a palace maiden of Qín,
also among those to be buried with the dead.
I together with her escaped the disaster at Líshān,
and we have hidden here together.
I do not know how many sixty-year cycles have passed until now?"
The two men said:
"From Qín to the present age,
nine dynasties have succeeded the legitimate line, over a thousand years.
The events of rise and fall,
cannot be recounted in full."
The two gentlemen then both bowed their heads to the ground and said:
"We two petty fellows,
are fortunate to encounter a great immortal.
Through many kalpas of causes and conditions,
we are enabled to meet harmoniously today.
Regarding the golden elixir and great medicine,
may we hear of it?
Our decaying bones and rotting flesh,
truly hope for your shelter and protection."
The ancient man said:
"I was originally an ordinary man.
Only by cutting off worldly thoughts,
and through eating tree fruits,
did I attain soaring in emptiness.
As years passed and days deepened,
my hair turned dark green,
and I no longer perceived distinction between life and death,
or between the mundane and the immortal.
Birds and beasts are my neighbors,
monkeys and gibbons share my joy.
Flying and soaring at will,
clouds and mists follow along.
Form lost, form gained;
no nature, no emotion.
I do not know what the golden elixir or great medicine might be."
The two gentlemen said:
"Great immortal, the method of eating tree fruits—
may we hear of it?"
He said:
"At first I consumed cypress seeds,
later I ate pine resin.
My whole body broke out in sores and ulcers,
and my intestines were wracked with pain.
But before a full month had passed,
my skin became lustrous and smooth,
my hair glossy and sleek.
After a few years had not yet passed,
soaring in emptiness felt as if there were a ladder,
treading perilous places as if walking on level ground.
Drifting lightly, I soared with the wind,
brightly white, I rose with the clouds.
Gradually merging with emptiness and nothingness,
silently in accord with creation and transformation.
That and I,
regard as not two separate things.
Concentrating the spirit, the spirit becomes refreshed;
nourishing the vital breath, the breath becomes clear.
Preserving the root of the embryo,
containing and storing the girdle of life.
Heaven and earth can still cover and support,
clouds and mists can still gather and steam,
sun and moon can still darken and brighten,
rivers and mountains can still melt and congeal.
Thus my body,
cannot be destroyed."
The two gentlemen bowed and said:
"We respectfully heed your command."
As the wine was nearly finished,
the ancient man broke off a pine branch,
tapped the jade pot and chanted:
"Consuming cypress, body light amidst layered peaks;
right and wrong hold no intent to reach the dusty world.
Robe and cap temporarily donned to discuss the floating life;
a moment's cloud-wandering in the azure heavens."
Máonǚ continued in harmony:
"Who knows what is ancient right and present wrong?
Leisurely treading azure mists, distant emerald hues.
Flute and pipe of Qín towers must be silent now;
colored clouds vainly cling to vine and fern garments."
The ancient man said:
"Meeting you by chance encounter,
how could there be no feeling of attachment?
I have a little of the pine resin of ten thousand years,
and cypress seeds of a thousand autumns.
You may each take a share and consume them;
you too should transcend the world."
The two gentlemen received them with bowed heads, grateful,
and swallowed them with wine.
The two immortals said:
"We must depart now!"
Take good care of yourself,
do not let the leakage of vitality harm your nature,
lest your divine energy be exposed within the cave dwelling."
The two gentlemen bowed and bid farewell,
only feeling as if they had transcended the mundane,
with no knowledge of where the figure had gone.
Soon they saw the clothes he had been wearing,
transformed by the wind into flower petals and butterfly wings, scattering into the air.
The two gentlemen, Táo and Yǐn,
now dwell atop Liánhuā Peak,
their faces slightly flushed,
their hair entirely green,
their speech filling the air with fragrance,
their steps leaving no dust upon their bodies.
Taoists from Yúntái Temple
often encounter them,
and occasionally hear in detail the story of how they attained the Way.
From "Chuánqí"
Xǔ Què
claimed to be from Gāoyáng.
In his youth, he was a jìnshì candidate,
but repeatedly failed the examinations.
Later, he studied the Way on Wángwū Mountain,
traveling extensively through the famous mountains and cave abodes of the Five Sacred Peaks.
Afterward, he passed through Èméi Mountain and the two capitals,
then from Xiāng and Biàn,
he arrived at Jiāng and Huái,
Máoshān, Tiāntāi,
Sìmíng, Xiāndū,
Wěiyǔ, Wǔyí,
Huòtóng, Luófú—
there was none he did not traverse.
Wherever he went,
he would inscribe on cliffs and steep rocks, in places inaccessible to others:
"Xǔ Què, from Èméi Mountain in search of Yǎnyuèzǐ, arrived here."
Those who saw his brushstrokes
could not help but marvel at their divine wonder,
yet none ever understood who Yǎnyuèzǐ was.
Later, he often wandered around Lújiāng,
frequently drunkenly reciting:
"Before the flowers of Làngyuàn lies the land of drunkenness,
overturning the Queen Mother's nine-glow cup.
The host of immortals clap their hands, disdainful of my frivolity,
banishing me to the mortal realm to be a wine-crazed madman."
Curious individuals sometimes questioned him.
He would say:
"I am a celestial immortal.
Just now, I was feasting on Kūnlún,
but due to a breach of etiquette, I was banished."
People all laughed at him,
considering him insane.
Later, during a spring scene,
he adorned his head full of flowers,
danced with blossoms in hand,
ascended to a tavern's upper floor, drunkenly singing,
then soared on clouds and flew away.
From "Xù Shénxiān Zhuàn"
Yáng Yúnwài
During the Qiánníng era of the Táng dynasty,
Yáng Yúnwài, a Taoist of the Hànchéng Temple in Yún'ān County,
often concealed himself through wine,
yet his actions and demeanor were extraordinary.
The former jìnshì Qián Ruòyú held him in great esteem.
One day, after purifying himself through fasting and bathing, he visited the mountain temple,
staying overnight in the Taoist quarters.
The next day, reverently straightening his robes, he addressed him:
"Venerable Master,
this humble youth is of common and lowly understanding.
Regarding matters of immortals and deities,
though I have heard tales of them,
do they truly exist?"
Yáng replied:
"They do exist,
and I am one of them.
If I were to demonstrate soaring through the sky, treading on emptiness,
walking on water or dancing through fire,
thousands would come to seek me daily,
would that not be troublesome and profane!"
Thereupon, he leaped and ascended,
floating gently in the air,
for a long while before descending.
Ruòyú kowtowed,
and from then on believed in the existence of immortals.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Dù Cóng
Dù Bīngōng Cóng,
when he was a child,
often went to Zhāoyìng Temple,
playing in the fields with other children.
Suddenly, a Taoist priest,
calling out to Cóng alone,
stroked his head with his hand and said:
"Young master, study diligently,
do not play with these other children."
Pointing to the temple, he said:
"I reside here.
Would you be able to visit me?"
After he left,
Cóng went to see him.
But all he saw was desolation,
with nothing else there.
Only a single hall stood majestically,
inside which was a statue of Lǎojūn.
Earlier, the Taoist's face had been half purple-black,
and now, examining the statue closely,
it somewhat resembled the Taoist he had seen.
It turned out that half of the statue's face had been stained by leaking rain.
From "Yùquánzǐ"
Nányuè Zhēnjūn
The Nányuè Taoist Qín Bǎoyán
was diligent in his devotions and practices.
Once he addressed the Zhēnjūn, saying:
"Why would an exalted immortal require paper money?
This is something I do not understand."
Later, he dreamed at night that the Zhēnjūn said:
"Paper money is what the underworld officials rely upon.
Why would I need such a thing?"
From then on, within Nányuè, he was even more trusted and respected.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Xuē Zūnshī
Xuē Zūnshī was born into a family of high status and renown.
Toward the end of Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
several of his brothers
all held official positions with salaries of two thousand shi.
He himself served as the magistrate of Yángzhái County.
However, within a few years,
his brothers had all passed away, one after another.
Consequently, he devoted his heart entirely to the Dao,
abandoned his official post, and entered the mountains,
leaving behind his wife and children.
He summoned like-minded companions,
but only a minor clerk from his county, named Táng Chén, was willing to follow him.
Carrying a staff and a bag on his back,
they headed toward the entrance of Sōng Shān.
Suddenly, they encountered a man
emerging from the mountains.
He introduced himself as a fellow seeker of the Dao,
surnamed Chén.
He mentioned that a celestial realm was nearby.
Xuē then asked him for directions.
Chén said:
"I have a small matter to attend to in the capital,
and I expect to return in three days.
Upon my return, I will guide you.
Please wait here for me."
Xuē and young Táng stopped at the mountain pass.
Chén returned as promised.
Chén said:
"Just wait here,
I will enter the mountains to seek it out.
Once I know the way,
I will come back to inform you."
They agreed on a period of five days,
but the deadline passed,
and even after ten days, Chén had not returned.
Xuē said:
"Could it be that Mr. Chén has deceived us?
I must go myself."
So he followed the stone steps into the valley for thirty or forty li.
Suddenly, by the side of the path, he saw a dead man,
half-eaten by a tiger—it was the mountain-dweller Chén.
Young Táng said to the Venerable Master:
"We entered the mountains seeking immortality,
yet here we are, becoming food for tigers and wolves.
If even Mr. Chén met such a fate,
who am I to escape it?
It would be better to return to the human world and live out my natural lifespan."
The Venerable Master replied:
"I have heard that Sōngyuè is originally a sacred land of immortals.
How could such harm occur here?
This must be Mr. Chén's way of testing our resolve.
You may return,
but I will press on to the end.
Even if I meet an unfortunate death,
I will have no regrets."
Having spoken, he proceeded straight ahead,
and Táng also resolved to follow him.
At night, they rested beneath rocky cliffs;
by day, they traveled along the stone steps.
After several days,
they suddenly saw beneath a cliff
hundreds of tall pine trees,
among which were six Daoist priests,
seemingly preparing medicines.
Xuē bowed deeply and sought their guidance.
The Daoist priests said:
"Although we have come here,
we only take medicines ourselves.
We have no arts to impart to you."
Shortly after, they noticed a meditation chamber
where an old monk resided.
Again, they bowed and sought instruction.
The monk also remained silent.
Suddenly, beneath the monk's bed, they saw vine tendrils winding along the wall and out the door.
The monk pointed to the vines and gestured.
Xuē then followed the vines out the door.
The vines extended continuously along the cliff face,
and after two days, they still had not reached the end.
Suddenly, they arrived at a flowing spring.
In a stone chamber were several Daoist priests,
playing weiqi and drinking wine.
The mountain-dweller Chén was also there.
Smiling, he said to Xuē:
"How did you suddenly arrive?
Your determination is worthy of instruction."
He then imparted the essential teachings of the Dao.
They also saw ordinary people there, ceaselessly gathering firewood and collecting herbs.
When asked about the location,
they replied, "Beneath the Zǐgé Peak of Zhōngnán Shān,
seventy li from Cháng'ān City."
After achieving mastery of the Dao, the Venerable Master entered the capital
and resided at the Hàotiān Temple,
where his profound influence grew even stronger.
At that time, Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng revered the Dao,
and frequently summoned him to the palace to pay respects.
Toward the end of the Kāiyuán era,
when he was already over a hundred years old,
he suddenly told his disciples:
"The Heavenly Emperor has summoned me to become the master of the Bāwēi Temple."
Without any illness, he sat and passed away,
his complexion unchanged.
A pagoda was then built for him within the temple grounds,
with its entrance left unsealed.
Every night,
he would summon his disciple Mr. Táng
to instruct him in the methods of cultivation.
Later, due to the disturbance caused by ordinary people coming to pay their respects,
an imperial decree ordered the pagoda entrance to be sealed.
Mr. Táng later also became a National Preceptor.
From "Yuán Huà Jì"
Wáng Lǎo
There was an old man named Wáng,
who often sold medicine in the Western Capital,
and had been seen for generations.
There was a man named Lǐ, a granary official,
whose home was in Shèngyè Lǐ.
Knowing that Wáng was a magician,
he always held him in respectful awe,
and treated him with extra courtesy.
Thus, Old Man Wáng came and went, relying on and staying with the Lǐ family,
for more than ten years.
Later, Lǐ requested to follow him into the mountains,
and Wáng also invited him.
So, with several servants and attendants,
they rode horses and went together.
After traveling over a hundred *li*,
the peaks and ridges were high and steep.
Climbing vines and scaling trees,
they went straight up for several *li*,
to a place where no human footprints reached.
Wáng said:
"Even traveling with you,
I still fear we may not reach the realm of the immortals;
this is not a place for servants and attendants to reach,
they should all be sent back."
Lǐ did as he said,
and went with Wáng to the peak's summit.
The fields were flat and even,
with medicinal herb plots and stone springs,
and beautiful scenery arranged in order.
In a moment,
they reached the forest entrance again,
where several Daoist priests
came to ask after Old Man Wáng.
Knowing he had invited a distinguished guest,
they had come to wait for them.
Lǐ followed them to their dwelling,
with thatched huts and bamboo pavilions,
elegant and pleasing to the eye.
Inside were several dozen students,
who, upon seeing Lǐ, each came to ask after their relatives.
Some did not speak.
Some, with melancholy, said:
"The Master is not here,
you should stay a while now.
We have prepared kitchen meals and vegetables,
no different from the human world."
They set out food for Lǐ.
After several days,
five-colored clouds and mists covered the ground,
and three white cranes descended with the clouds.
Then the scholars each came out,
as if to welcome and wait.
After a while, they said:
"The Master has arrived."
They saw an old man,
with crane-white beard and hair,
coming from the edge of the clouds.
Old Man Wáng led Lǐ to welcome and bow by the roadside.
The Master asked Old Man Wáng:
"Why have you brought another person here!
After the various students paid their respects,
each went to their rooms.
Lǐ also entered a room.
At the time, it was quite hot,
so Lǐ went out to find a spring,
intending to bathe.
After walking over a hundred steps,
he reached a stone spring,
and saw several dozen white cranes
descending from the rocky ridges,
coming onto the stones,
and lining up in rows.
Soon they began to play music,
with sounds clear and bright,
unlike anything in the human world.
Lǐ humbly crouched and listened to their wondrous music.
When the music ended, they flew away.
Lǐ returned and recounted the event.
The Master asked, "Did you perhaps offend the immortal officials?"
He replied:
"I did not dare."
The Master said to Mr. Lǐ:
"You have official rank and salary,
and are not yet fit to stay here;
wait until your official service is complete,
then you may come."
He then ordered Old Man Wáng to escort Lǐ out,
saying:
"We need two oxen in the mountains,
you can deliver them to the foot of the vines."
Lǐ bought oxen and delivered them,
and then could no longer see the path.
From *Guǎngyì Jì*
Hēi Sǒu
During the Bǎoyìng era of the Táng dynasty,
the wife of Huángfǔ Zhèng, the Military Commissioner of Yuèzhōu, was a Lady Lù,
who was beautiful in appearance but had no children.
In the prefecture, there was a temple named Bǎolín,
within which was a shrine to the Demon Mother deity.
For the gentry and women of Yuèzhōng who sought sons or daughters,
prayers there were always answered and proven effective.
On a day of leisure,
Zhèng led his wife and family into the temple.
Upon reaching the Demon Mother hall,
he took incense and prayed, saying:
"I beg for a son.
I vow to donate a million strings of cash from my salary to construct a hall."
Lady Lù also said:
"If my wish is granted,
I will also contribute a million in cosmetics money
to separately commission paintings of divine immortals."
Afterwards, they toured the temple,
and did not return until dusk.
After more than two months,
his wife became pregnant,
and indeed gave birth to a boy.
Zhèng was overjoyed.
He constructed a three-bay hall,
making it extremely luxurious and splendid.
Lady Lù piled up a million cash outside the temple gate,
to recruit painters.
From Biàn, Huá, Xú, Sì, Yáng, Rùn, Tán, Hóng, and painters from across the land,
some arrived daily.
However, because the promised reward was excessively large,
none dared to undertake the task.
Suddenly, a man who did not give his name,
claiming to be from Jiànnán,
and saying he was skilled in painting,
lodged in the temple for over a month.
One day, looking at the hall walls,
he nodded several times.
The monk in charge said:
"Why not quickly complete the task?"
The man laughed and said:
"Please prepare lamp oil,
for I will work on it through the night."
The monk followed his words.
By dawn,
it was brilliantly radiant and luminous,
a complete wall painting.
The painter had already vanished.
Zhèng held a grand vegetarian feast,
and wealthy merchants gathered.
Zhèng also selected a day,
leading military officers and the prefecture's people,
to put on a grand display of music and performances.
At noon,
a man appeared, ugly and dark in appearance,
eight feet tall,
wearing a bamboo hat and a sedge raincoat,
carrying a hoe, and arrived.
The gatekeeper tried to stop him,
but Zhèng ordered him admitted.
He went straight up to the Demon Mother hall,
raised his hoe and struck the painting on the wall.
The wall then crumbled.
The crowd of a million people
erupted in an uproar of shock and commotion.
The guards on both sides wanted to seize and kill him,
but the old man showed no fear.
Zhèng questioned him, saying:
"Are you insane?"
The old man said:
"No."
"Are you skilled at painting?"
The old man said:
"No."
Zhèng said:
"Then for what reason did you strike this?"
The old man said:
"I resent the painter's deception of his superiors.
The lady and her husband donated two million,
to depict divine immortals,
yet compared to living people,
they still fall short."
Zhèng angrily rebuked him.
The old man clapped his hands and laughed, saying:
"If you do not believe it,
my rustic old wife
is sufficient proof."
Zhèng asked:
"Where is your wife?"
The old man said:
"Her dwelling is a couple of miles south of the lake."
Zhèng ordered ten men to follow the old man to summon her.
The old man, from among some reed huts,
led out a woman,
aged fifteen or sixteen,
lightly adorned with powder and makeup,
her clothing not overly extravagant,
her charming appearance captivating,
her radiant beauty stirring the crowd.
In a moment,
they reached Bǎolín Temple.
The crowd of a million people,
craned their necks in astonished viewing,
all saying the painted divine mother
indeed could not compare.
Led to the steps before the hall,
Lady Lù paled in comparison.
Zhèng said:
"You, a lowly man,
keep such a woman?
She should be presented to the Son of Heaven."
The old man said:
"Allow me to return and bid farewell to my rustic family."
Zhèng dispatched fifty soldiers
and ten maidservants,
to go together to his home.
Reaching the river and about to cross,
the old man was alone in a small pleasure boat,
while the guards, maidservants, and the old man's wife were together on a large boat.
As they were about to cross the river,
without anyone noticing, the old man's wife, at a place of swift currents,
suddenly flew into the pleasure boat.
Everyone was terrified and alarmed.
They swiftly rowed to pursue them.
The husband and wife had already emerged,
walking hand in hand.
They pursued them further,
and the two both transformed into white cranes,
and soared into the sky, flying away.
From "Huìchāng Jiěyí" and "Hédōng Jì."
Liú Wúmíng
was a native of Chéngdū.
He was originally a descendant of the former ruler of Shǔ
and resided in Shǔ.
He was born intelligent and perceptive.
At eight or nine years old,
a Daoist priest passed by his home,
saw him, and sighed:
"If this child studies the Dao,
he will become a long-lived immortal."
From then on, he loved the Dao and explored its mysteries,
taking no pleasure in fame and profit.
Upon reaching adulthood,
he read Daoist scriptures,
learned breath-swallowing and morning worship,
and practiced techniques of preserving truth and inner cultivation.
He often observed the Three Corpses on Gēngshēn days,
preserved his spirit and silently chanted,
consumed huángjīng and báizhú,
aspiring to prolong life.
Sometimes he saw ancient prescriptions,
saying that herbal medicines
only cure illnesses with slight effects;
when exposed to fire, they turn to ashes,
unable to solidify themselves—
how could they have the power to prolong life?
Thus he traveled across mountains and rivers,
seeking teachers and inquiring about the Dao.
After several years, he entered Wùzhōng Mountain,
where he once met someone who taught him to take realgar as an elixir,
which he did for over thirty years.
One day, two men,
with red scarves and crimson robes,
came straight to his room.
Liú asked who they were
and how they had come here.
They replied:
"We are messengers from Tàishān,
sent to apprehend you.
We do not know what technique you use,
but there is a yellow light above your head.
For three days now,
our underworld deadline has been pressing,
yet we have no way to approach you.
We fear we will be reprimanded by the underworld authorities
and punished for delay,
so we have manifested to ask you."
Liú said:
"I have no other technique;
I only concentrate my mind on the supreme Dao,
pay no heed to sound and profit,
dwell quietly in secluded mountains,
and aspire to transcend this world."
The two messengers said:
"The yellow light above your head,
shining brightly,
extends several zhang high—
is it not the effect of realgar?
However, we have heard that the interaction of yin and yang is called the Dao,
and the combination of metal and stone is called the elixir.
You have only consumed the stone,
not ingested the metal;
you have obtained only the yang,
not yet understood the yin.
How then can you transcend the difficulty of life and death
and hope for the path of ascension?
Moreover, one must extensively perform hidden merits,
saving people and aiding beings,
be gentle, refined, and tranquil,
free from desire and non-action,
supremely filial and loyal,
cultivating inwardly with secret practices.
When merits fill three thousand,
then the black register will erase your name,
and the azure splendor will confirm your record.
You will control spirits and ghosts,
drive clouds and dragons,
ascend to supplement the ranks of immortals,
and forever be removed from the earth's registers.
Nine ancestors will be refined and transcend,
seven mysteries will ascend to heaven.
Only then will you not be pursued by underworld officials.
Now, although your Three Corpses have departed,
your accumulated merits are not yet evident;
your great lifespan is exhausted,
and death approaches.
How can you merely avoid it?"
Hearing their words,
Liú's heart and soul were shaken,
filled with anxiety, pressure, and fear,
not knowing what to do.
The two messengers slowly said to him:
"Mín-É and Qīngchéng
are abodes of immortals;
you may seek true teachers there,
and inquire about the essentials of the Dao.
We have heard that lead, mercury, and vermilion marrow
can lead to soaring to the heavens,
but unless one is a lofty true being or superior immortal,
one cannot obtain the essence of their cultivation.
We will find someone with the same name and surname as you,
whose lifespan is exhausted,
to substitute for you.
Strive and diligently cultivate,
do not slacken midway."
Liú thanked the two messengers.
The two messengers then vanished.
Liú followed their words,
entered Éméi and Mín Mountains,
climbed steep and perilous paths,
searched caves and grottoes,
but for years encountered nothing.
He then entered Qīngchéng Mountain,
and beneath the northern cliff found a cave.
After walking several li,
he suddenly felt a level expanse,
almost otherworldly.
He encountered an immortal residing there,
called the Qīngchéng Zhēnrén.
Liú pleaded and kowtowed incessantly,
fully recounting his encounter with the ghost messengers sent to apprehend him,
wishing to be shown the essentials of the Dao,
to save and uplift the sunken,
and be granted deliverance from the suffering of life and death.
The Zhēnrén pointed to a rocky chamber,
had him dwell there,
then instructed him to purify his heart for seven days,
after which he revealed the methods of the yang furnace and yin cauldron,
the techniques of softening metal and refining jade-like water,
and the secrets of subduing mercury and refining lead into vermilion marrow.
He said to him:
"Hú Gāngzǐ and Yīn Chángshēng
both attained this Dao."
It is also called the Scripture of the Golden Fluid and Nine Elixirs.
The elixir is divided into three grades.
Lead is the sovereign,
mercury is the minister,
the eight minerals are the envoys,
and yellow sprout is the seedling.
When sovereign and minister harmonize,
and the fire application is complete,
after seven days it becomes light mercury,
after fourteen days it transforms into purple edge,
after twenty-one days the five colors appear,
red inside and yellow outside,
resembling window dust.
After applying fire for another two years,
completing six hundred cycles,
and passing through the four seasons again,
reaching the winter solstice once more,
initially, after ten months it leaves its embryonic state,
becoming the initial grade.
It can then dry mercury into silver;
formed into pills and ingested,
it can cure illnesses.
Beyond three years,
those who take it prolong life and increase longevity,
their white hair turning black again.
After three years,
taking a tiny amount
allows roaming famous mountains,
traveling across the four seas.
The initial grade,
taken in half a dose by terrestrial immortals,
enables myriad transformations,
sitting here and appearing there, vanishing at will,
driving flying dragons,
and ascending to heaven in broad daylight.
Generally, this medicine,
after sixteen stages,
becomes the middle grade.
It can then make people long-lived.
On the day the medicine is completed,
the five metals and eight minerals,
yellow sprout and various substances,
along with the sovereign and minister medicines,
no longer intermix chaotically.
After a thousand days of effort,
it is named the superior-grade returned elixir.
Store it carefully,
do not show it to the unworthy;
if in the world there is a suitable person,
observe their form and qi,
if their merits and conduct align with the Dao,
transmit it according to the method."
Liú received the elixir secrets,
returned to Wùzhōng Mountain,
built a chamber and cultivated the refinement,
completing it in three years.
In the second year of the Kāichéng era,
he still resided in Shǔ,
personally wrote the Biography of Wúmíng,
to show later generations.
He then entered Qīngchéng
and his whereabouts were unknown.
From Xiānzhuàn Shíyí.
Hè Zhīzhāng had a residence in the Xuānpíng Ward of the Western Capital.
Across from his gate was a small wooden door,
and he often saw an old man riding a donkey going in and out there.
After five or six years had passed,
he observed that the old man’s complexion and clothing remained unchanged,
and he never saw any family members either.
Upon inquiring among the neighbors in the alley,
they all said he was Old Man Wáng, who sold strings of cash at the Western Market,
and had no other occupation.
Suspecting he was no ordinary person,
Hè often visited him on leisurely days.
The old man received him with great respect and courtesy,
with only a young boy serving him.
Hè then asked about his occupation.
The old man answered casually.
As they interacted,
Hè gradually treated him with more courtesy and respect,
and their conversations grew more intimate,
until the old man revealed he was skilled in the art of alchemy.
Hè, who had always believed in and valued such things,
wished to serve him.
Later, he and his wife brought a luminous pearl,
saying they had obtained it in their hometown,
had treasured it for a long time,
and were now specially presenting it to the old man,
seeking instruction in the Daoist arts.
The old man immediately gave the pearl to the boy,
instructing him to buy cakes with it.
The boy exchanged the pearl for over thirty foreign-style cakes,
and then invited Hè to stay.
Hè privately thought that such a precious pearl had been lightly used,
and felt quite displeased.
The old man said:
"The Dao can only be grasped with the heart;
how can it be attained through forceful striving?
If miserliness has not ceased,
the art cannot be accomplished.
One must go to deep mountains and remote valleys,
diligently seek it to attain it;
it is not something bestowed in the marketplace or court."
Hè then understood somewhat,
thanked him, and left.
A few days later, the old man had disappeared.
Hè then sought to retire from office,
embraced Daoism, and returned to his hometown.
From "Yuánhuà Jì."
Xiāo Yǐngshì,
a records officer,
once traveled incognito.
While staying at an inn in Chénliú,
he was just eating when
he suddenly saw an old man,
with white beard and hair,
and particularly striking eyebrows and eyes.
He came to the door,
gazed at Xiāo for a long time,
sighed softly,
and seemed to recognize him.
Xiāo, puzzled by his meaning,
stood up and bowed, asking.
The old man said:
"Looking at your appearance, young master,
you resemble someone,
and I couldn’t help feeling sorrowful."
Xiāo asked whom he resembled.
The old man said:
"You greatly resemble the Prince of Póyáng of Qí."
The prince was Xiāo’s eighth-generation ancestor.
Startled, Xiāo asked:
"The prince is indeed my eighth-generation ancestor;
how do you know him?"
The old man wept and said:
"My surname is Zuǒ.
In the past, I served as a clerk under the Prince of Póyáng,
and received his generous favor.
When Lǐ Míng’s calamity occurred,
I fled into exile,
barely escaping disaster.
I then entered the mountains to cultivate the Dao,
and thus attained transcendence.
Just now, I was startled by you, young master,
not knowing you were the prince’s descendant."
They then wept together.
Xiāo regarded him with awe and wonder,
asked his age,
and learned it was three hundred and twenty-seven years.
After a long while, they parted.
He now lives on Qián Shān,
and occasionally appears among humans.
Later, no one knew where he went.
From "Yuánhuà Jì."
Lǐ Xiānrén.
In Luòyáng, there was a woman named Gāo Wǔniáng,
renowned for her beauty,
who remarried Lǐ Xiānrén.
Lǐ Xiānrén was an immortal banished from heaven.
After forming a bond with Gāo,
he always lived in Luòyáng,
practicing alchemy as his livelihood.
Gāo was able to learn his methods.
By the end of the Kāiyuán era,
Gāo and Lǐ had been living harmoniously for five or six years.
One night, after the fifth watch,
they heard a voice from the sky calling Lǐ once.
He put on his clothes and went outside.
After speaking,
he returned and said to Gāo:
"I am a celestial immortal.
Some time ago, due to a minor offense,
I was banished to the human world.
Now my penalty is complete,
and the celestial authorities have come to summon me.
Since I cannot stay,
after years of deep affection,
how can I not feel sorrowful?
After I leave,
you should support yourself through alchemy,
but be careful not to teach others.
Do not extensively perform smelting for others,
not only because it will harm you,
but it may also bring misfortune to those before you."
With these words, he flew away.
Initially, Gāo followed his instructions.
Later, as she sold more and more silver,
she was reported by the ward authorities.
At the time, the Vice Governor of Hénán, Lǐ Qí, knew of the matter,
released her without questioning,
and secretly summoned her,
for whom she smelted over ten beds’ worth of silverware.
Lǐ then reported this to high officials at court.
Within a year,
both Lǐ and Gāo died.
People at the time believed it was heavenly punishment.
From "Guǎngyì Jì."
Hé Xuàn.
At the end of the Jiànzhōng era of the Táng dynasty,
a scholar named Hé Xuàn
once bought an ancient book on yellow paper.
While reading it,
he found a coiled hair inside the scroll,
four inches in circumference,
like a ring with no end.
Xuàn then broke it,
and from the broken ends, over a shēng of water dripped out.
When burned, it gave off the smell of hair.
Xuàn once mentioned this to a Daoist,
who said:
"Alas!
You are indeed of mortal bone;
encountering this yet unable to ascend as an immortal—
it is fate.
According to an immortal scripture:
'If a bookworm eats the characters for "immortal" three times,
it transforms into this object,
called Mài Wàng.
At night, if you hold its ring up to the central star in the sky,
the star envoy will immediately descend.
You can seek the reverted elixir,
take this water, mix it, and ingest it,
and instantly your bones will be transformed, and you will ascend.'"
He then took the ancient book to examine it,
and found several places with wormholes.
Reading according to the meaning,
the characters were all "immortal."
Xuàn then sighed in admiration.
From "Yuánhuà Jì."
Huáng Zūnshī.
Master Huáng Zūnshī resided on Máoshān Mountain,
his Daoist arts were exquisite and profound.
There was a firewood seller
who found over ten pages of ancient texts in a rocky cave,
believing them to be immortal scriptures.
Thus, he went to Master Huáng,
earnestly requesting to become his disciple.
Master Huáng accepted his texts
but said nothing,
instead ordering him daily to chop fifty bundles of firewood.
If he was slightly late or the number was insufficient,
Master Huáng would scold and even beat him with a cane,
yet the man showed no resentment.
One day,
he saw two Daoist priests playing chess on a mountain rock.
Watching them, he lost track of time until dusk,
and returned empty-handed.
Master Huáng flew into a rage, shouting and cursing,
caned him twenty strokes,
and asked for an explanation.
The man then recounted everything in detail.
Master Huáng said:
"In the deep mountains where no one lives,
how could there be chess-playing Daoist priests?
You are surely lying."
The man kowtowed and said:
"It is true,
tomorrow I will capture them and bring them here."
When he went again,
he saw them playing chess once more.
He pretended to approach and watch,
then tried to seize them.
The two Daoist priests, along with the chessboard,
soared into the air and up a tall tree.
He only managed to grab a few chess pieces.
The Daoist priests laughed and said to him:
"Take a message to the immortal master:
from now on, he may receive and transmit the ritual registers."
The man then returned with the chess pieces
and recounted the entire incident.
Master Huáng laughed heartily,
then had him bathe and purify himself,
and fully transmitted the ritual registers to him.
After receiving them, the man bid farewell and left,
and nothing more is known of his end.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Péi Lǎo
During the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a certain Wáng Yuánwài who was fond of Daoist arts.
Although he held a court position,
he associated with commoners and mountain recluses,
spending his days in their company.
One morning, several Daoist companions were in the main hall,
and Wáng was in high spirits, laughing and clapping,
when Péi Lǎo, the latrine cleaner,
arrived with his cleaning tools to serve Wáng.
Hearing the guests' conversation,
he secretly laughed at them.
Wáng's servants all found this strange.
Shortly after,
Péi Lǎo finished his cleaning duties.
As Wáng was about to use the latrine,
he encountered Péi Lǎo inside.
Péi Lǎo straightened his clothes,
as if he had something to say.
Wáng thus asked what the matter was.
Péi Lǎo gradually stepped forward and said:
"Yuánwài is truly fond of the Dao."
Wáng, startled, said, "I do indeed devote myself to this."
Péi Lǎo said:
"I know Yuánwài is deeply devoted,
but you have yet to encounter the true path.
The two guests in the hall just now
are utterly ordinary,
merely deceiving Yuánwài in hopes of food and drink."
Wáng was astonished and remained silent for a long while.
His wife shouted and scolded:
"You are a court official,
yet you associate with such a filthy man!
Have someone drive him away."
Wáng said:
"Those who follow the true Dao
do not discriminate based on status."
Péi Lǎo asked to leave.
Wáng earnestly invited him to stay and relax.
After a long while, Péi Lǎo agreed.
Wáng asked:
"Can you come tomorrow?"
Péi Lǎo said:
"No,
I will come the day after tomorrow."
When the day arrived,
Wáng prepared a clean separate room and waited.
His wife cried out:
"How can you be so intimate with a latrine cleaner!"
Wáng said:
"I still fear he may not deign to visit me."
Shortly after, Péi Lǎo arrived,
wearing a cloth robe and carrying a staff,
exuding the demeanor of a recluse.
Wáng sat and conversed with him,
serving tea and wine in turn.
Péi Lǎo occasionally offered profound remarks,
showing no trace of his former filthy appearance.
He said:
"Yuánwài is not truly devoted to the Dao,
but rather to alchemy.
I have some small skill in this.
Since I am here,
would you like to witness a demonstration of furnace fire?"
Wáng kowtowed and said:
"I am deeply fascinated,
but dare not make any request."
Péi Lǎo pointed to an iron box weighing about two catties,
and said:
"Yuánwài, please bring a fire,
split the box into two pieces,
place them inside,
and cover them with fire."
In a moment, the iron turned red.
Péi Lǎo untied a small pouch from the corner of his robe,
took out two pills of medicine,
each the size of a hemp seed,
removed some of the charcoal,
crushed and sprinkled them on the box,
then piled the fire back on to burn it.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
Péi Lǎo said:
"It is done."
He instructed Wáng's strongest servant
to use fire tongs to take it out
and throw it on the ground.
After a short while,
it had transformed into a box of the finest gold,
with a color like a rooster's comb.
Wáng descended the steps and bowed twice,
kowtowing to express his gratitude.
Péi Lǎo said:
"This gold, one tael of it
is worth three taels of ordinary gold.
However, Yuánwài should not keep it,
but rather use it for charity."
As he prepared to leave, he said:
"From now on, I will not come again."
Wáng bowed and begged:
"I am but an ignorant and vulgar man,
yet I wish to express my sincere devotion.
I must visit the immortal elder's mountain abode
to pay my respects."
Péi Lǎo said:
"There is no need for that."
But he agreed to meet again in three days,
at the large vegetable garden west of Lánlíng Ward.
Wáng went as scheduled,
and upon arrival, he indeed saw a small gate.
He knocked,
and a servant with yellow hair came out and asked:
"Are you perhaps Yuánwài Wáng?"
He then brought a folding chair,
and asked Wáng to sit outside the middle gate.
Shortly after, he was led inside,
where there was a small hall, very clean and serene.
Péi Lǎo, dressed in Daoist robes, descended the steps to greet him.
There were ten maidservants and attendants,
all of them beautiful.
Péi Lǎo invited him in and inquired after his well-being.
His demeanor and appearance
were entirely different from before,
as if he were a man in his forties.
The tea, wine, and fruits were exceptionally rare and exquisite,
the rooms were immaculate,
and the furnishings were refined and luxurious.
In the evening, when Wáng prepared to leave,
Péi Lǎo saw him out the gate.
Ten days later, Wáng returned,
but the residence had already been rented to others,
and Péi Lǎo had vanished without a trace.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Lǐ Yú
Lǐ Yú, an official from Xìnzhōu,
once traveled to Huàshān with the scholar Yáng Léng,
thoroughly exploring the cliffs and valleys.
At that time, Lǐ had not yet taken office,
and both he and Yáng aspired to a life of seclusion.
Whenever they encountered a serene and beautiful spot,
they would linger, composing poetry.
Soon they reached a small cave,
its entrance only a few feet high.
After just three or four steps inside,
the path became very high,
yet the footing was extremely level and easy.
Wishing to explore it to the end,
they walked about four or five *lǐ*,
but turning back seemed impossible,
so they encouraged each other to press on.
After another two or three *lǐ*,
it grew slightly brighter.
Shortly after, they reached the cave's exit.
It was around the time of Shēn and Yǒu (3-7 PM).
The streams, cliffs, grass, and trees
were unlike those of the mortal world;
there were even people farming.
A farmer, seeing the two men, appeared quite surprised
and said:
"How did you gentlemen get here?"
They explained everything in detail.
After another two *lǐ* or so,
there was a Buddhist hall,
where several people were just then drinking tea.
Lǐ and the others went to ask for lodging.
One person inside said:
"We must report to the cave master."
Shortly after, they saw a man in purple robes,
riding a small horse,
with four or five attendants,
clearing the way as he arrived.
His bow of greeting was very elegant.
He asked:
"How did you come to be here?"
One of them recounted the story fully.
The man said:
"This place is rather crude and remote. Please come to my residence."
So they went together on foot.
They arrived at a government office-like compound,
with many bamboo halls.
The rooms and seating were very clean,
and there were several dozen clerks and attendants.
The host then introduced himself:
"My surname is Dù,
given name Zǐhuá.
I fled the chaos of war to escape the world,
encountered immortal companions,
and have lived here for several hundred years now."
He then hosted them for the night.
The food and drink were all exquisite and abundant;
among the dishes was camel *mǐ*,
which looked like beef.
They conversed day and night,
and he inquired about affairs of the imperial court.
After being detained for several days,
he gave each of them several silver vessels
and sent a guide to lead them back.
He said:
"This is a suitable place for seclusion.
Would you be able to stay?"
The two men showed reluctance on their faces.
Zǐhuá smiled,
clasped their hands in farewell,
and requested they not reveal this to others.
Later, Yáng went again to search for the cave,
but it could not be found.
Yáng later changed his name to Jiǎn,
rose to the office of Censor,
but was exiled to Pānyú where he died.
Lǐ also ended up drifting and wandering.
Truly, for divine immortal realms,
unless one genuinely desires them,
one should not seek them out based on reputation alone.
Let later gentlemen take heed of this.
From *Yì Shǐ* (Unofficial Histories).
The Recluse Xiàhóu,
no one knows where he was from.
Toward the end of the Dàzhōng era (847-860),
he roamed between Máoshān and Tiāntāi,
carrying only a cloth sack and a bamboo staff.
He ate and drank like ordinary people,
but lived alone in a single room,
not mingling with the crowd.
Sometimes he would sleep in the open on altars,
in the grass, or under trees.
When people tried to spy on him,
they would only see dense, billowing clouds and mist,
and could not see his body.
Whenever he traveled thirty or fifty *lǐ*,
climbing mountains and crossing waters,
he would close his eyes and sleep soundly.
His companions would hear the sound of his snoring,
yet his steps never faltered or stumbled,
and his feet never tripped or met obstacles.
Upon reaching their destination, he would wake up.
He was nicknamed the "Sleeping Immortal."
Later, no one knew what became of him.
From *Shénxiān Shíyí Zhuàn* (Biographies of Gathered Immortals).
Quán Tóngxiū
The scholar Quán Tóngxiū,
having failed the imperial examinations during the Yuánhé era (806-820),
was traveling in the Sūzhōu-Húzhōu region.
He fell ill and was impoverished and destitute.
He had a servant from a village in his hometown,
who had been serving him for a year already.
During his illness, Quán craved sweet licorice and bean soup,
and sent the servant to buy licorice root.
The servant was gone for a long time,
but returned only with a pot and fire.
The scholar thought he was being negligent in his duties,
but then saw him break off a handful of tree branches,
rub them repeatedly in his hands,
and hold them slightly near the fire—
they suddenly turned into licorice root.
The scholar was greatly astonished,
and realized the man must be a Daoist adept.
After a long while,
the servant took several handfuls of coarse sand,
kneaded and rubbed it—and it became beans.
When the soup was ready,
it was no different from ordinary soup.
Quán's illness also gradually improved.
The scholar said to him:
"I am so impoverished and hard-pressed,
with no means to advance even an inch.
So I'll take off this dirty robe and give it to you.
You can use it to get a little wine and meat.
I plan to invite the village elders,
to beg for a small travel allowance."
The servant smiled and said:
"That's hardly enough to manage it.
I will provide for it."
He then chopped down a withered mulberry tree,
cut it into several bundles of sticks,
gathered them on a tray,
blew on them with a spray of breath—
and they turned into beef.
He then drew several bottles of water,
poured them out—
and it became fine wine.
The village elders all ate and drank their fill.
Quán received fifty bolts of fine silk as gifts.
Ashamed, the scholar thanked the servant and said:
"I was originally arrogant and ignorant,
failing to recognize you as a Daoist adept.
Now I ask instead to become *your* servant."
The servant said:
"I am indeed an extraordinary man,
but due to a minor transgression,
I was exiled to a lowly station,
destined to serve you, scholar.
If my term of service is not completed,
I would have to labor for others again.
I beg you, scholar, not to change our usual routine,
so that I may complete my task."
Although the scholar agreed,
every time he called for or directed him,
his face showed distress and unease.
The servant then took his leave, saying:
"If you are like this, scholar,
it truly hinders my task."
He then discussed the scholar's destined span of life, poverty, and success,
and mentioned that all things can be transformed,
except for vermilion-lacquered chopsticks and hair in muddy silt—
even medicinal power cannot transform them.
Then he disappeared, and no one knew where he went.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ* (Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang).
Perfected Person Yǐn
Over ten li east of Qiánwéi Commandery,
there is a Daoist temple located deep within a cliff.
Surrounded by stone walls on four sides,
a Daoist priest named Yán resides there.
In the temple hall, there is a stone casket,
over three chǐ in length.
On its surface are carved birds, beasts, flowers, and plants,
with patterns so delicate and exquisite,
they border on supernatural craftsmanship.
Its seals and locks are extremely secure,
seamless without the slightest gap.
The local people pass down a legend,
saying it is the stone casket of Yǐn Xǐ.
The deeds of this transcendent,
are clearly recorded in historical biographies in great detail.
When the transcendent was about to ascend to heaven,
he entrusted the stone casket to his disciples,
admonishing them:
"Inside this casket are talismanic registers.
Be careful not to open it,
or great calamity will surely follow."
Thus, all the people of the commandery revered it.
During the Dàlì era,
there was a gentleman named Cuī from Qīnghé,
who served as the governor of Qiánwéi.
Cuī had always
"always" originally read "had,"
amended according to the Ming manuscript copy.
relied on his own firmness and decisiveness.
Upon arriving at the commandery,
hearing of the transcendent Yǐn's casket,
he laughed and said to his subordinates:
"This is just like Xīn Yuánpíng's deception."
He immediately went to the temple,
and ordered the locks to be broken.
Daoist priest Yán said:
"This is the stone casket of transcendent Yǐn.
The transcendent left a teaching, saying:
'Whoever opens my casket will suffer great calamity.'
I beg you, my lord, not to violate the transcendent's injunction."
Cuī angrily replied:
"Transcendent Yǐn died a thousand years ago;
how could his stone casket alone remain?
I do not believe it."
Daoist priest Yán insisted on his words,
but Cuī stubbornly refused to listen.
He then ordered the locks to be broken.
For a long time, they remained immovable and unyielding.
Enraged, Cuī
tied a giant rope to the casket's nose,
using dozens of oxen to pull the rope,
whipping and driving them.
After nearly half a day,
the stone casket finally opened.
Inside were several dozen scrolls of talismanic registers,
with yellow silk as the backing,
inscribed in cinnabar writing,
all bright and fresh as if new.
After Cuī had finished examining them,
he turned to Daoist priest Yán and said:
"I had thought there would be rare treasures inside the casket,
hence I opened it to look;
now there are only these talismanic registers."
He then ordered it to be sealed and locked as before.
Upon returning to the commandery,
that very evening,
the governor suddenly died a violent death,
but revived after three days.
His officials, subordinates, generals, and clerks
all went to Cuī to inquire and question him.
Cuī said:
"I was very foolish,
having never heard of the affairs of transcendents.
Previously, I happened to open transcendent Yǐn's stone casket,
and indeed, I was summoned by the underworld officials.
At first, I saw a person
dressed in purple robes,
who came to my bedroom,
and said to me:
'I am an official of the underworld administration,
now ordered to summon you.
You must not refuse,
for refusal will only bring greater calamity.
You should come quickly.'
Upon hearing this, I was distressed,
and wanted to decline and avoid it.
But unconsciously, I went out of the commandery city with the messenger.
After traveling only fifty li,
we reached the underworld administration.
The official there was none other than the former chancellor, Lord Lǚ.
He said to me:
'Why did you open transcendent Yǐn's stone casket?
By the command of the Supreme Deity,
your official ranks and lifespan are to be reduced.
What do you say to that!'
Then he summoned a clerk,
ordering him to check the register of my ranks and lifespan."
The clerk reported to Lord Lǚ:
'Cuī is to hold five official appointments.
He has a lifespan of seventeen years.
Now, by the decree of the Supreme Deity,
all five official appointments are to be stripped,
and fifteen years of his lifespan are to be cut.
Now he has only two years of appointment left.'"
Thereupon, Cuī was allowed to return.
Two years later, he indeed passed away.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
Lú Shānrén
During the Bǎolì era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a recluse named Lú in Jīngzhōu,
who often traded in burnt lime,
traveling between Báifù and Náncǎoshì.
From time to time, he would subtly display miraculous abilities,
which others could not fathom.
A merchant named Zhào Yuánqīng, who was fond of extraordinary matters,
wished to befriend him.
He frequently purchased goods from Lú,
offered him fruit and tea,
and inquired about his methods for making profit.
Lú sensed this
and said to him:
"I see that your interest does not lie in the goods you purchase.
What is your true intention?"
Zhào then replied:
"I have secretly learned that you, venerable one, conceal your true form and virtue,
and possess insight surpassing divination.
I humbly ask for a word of guidance."
Lú smiled and said:
"Today, I shall give you a demonstration.
Your host will encounter an extraordinary calamity at noon.
If you trust my words,
he can avoid it.
You may inform him.
Approaching noon,
a craftsman carrying a bag will arrive.
In the bag, there will be over two taels of silver,
but his intentions will certainly not be benign.
He should close his doors,
and his wife and children should not lightly respond.
At noon,
the man will surely curse vehemently.
The entire family must then go near the water to avoid him.
If they do this,
they will only lose three thousand four hundred coins."
At that time, Zhào was staying at the home of a commoner named Zhāng,
so he hurried back to inform him.
Zhāng had always regarded Lú with awe,
so he closed his doors and waited.
As noon approached,
indeed, a man matching Lú's description arrived,
knocking on the door to buy grain.
Angered by the lack of response,
he kicked the door.
Zhāng reinforced it with a heavy barricade.
Soon, a crowd of several hundred gathered.
Zhāng then exited through the back door
and took refuge with his wife and children.
Just past noon,
the man left,
but after walking several hundred paces,
he suddenly stumbled, fell, and died.
His wife arrived,
and the crowd told her what had happened.
She wept bitterly,
then went to Zhāng's house,
falsely accusing him of causing her husband's death.
The officials could not determine the truth.
The crowd described how Zhāng had closed his doors and fled.
The magistrate said to Zhāng:
"You are indeed not guilty,
but you should arrange for his burial."
Zhāng gladly complied with the judgment,
and the wife was also satisfied.
When purchasing the coffin and hiring bearers,
the cost was exactly three thousand four hundred coins.
Because of this, people flocked to Lú as if to a market.
Lú found this troublesome,
so he secretly departed to the border of Fùzhōu,
and moored his boat at the estate gate of Scholar Lù Qí.
Someone told Lù:
"Recluse Lú is no ordinary man."
Lù then invited him.
Lù was planning to go to the capital to seek out acquaintances,
so he asked Lú to resolve his doubts.
Lú said:
"If you do not move this year,
I fear disaster will strike soon.
Behind the hall where you live,
there is a jar of coins,
covered with a plank.
They do not belong to you.
The owner of the coins is now only three years old.
You must not use a single coin,
for using them will certainly bring calamity.
Can you follow my warning?"
Lù was startled and thanked him.
After Lú left,
before the ripples on the water had settled,
Lù laughed and said to his wife:
"If what Lú says is true,
what more could I ask for?"
He then ordered a servant to dig the ground.
Before reaching a few feet deep,
they indeed encountered a plank,
which they removed.
There was a large urn
filled with scattered coins.
Lù was overjoyed,
and his wife also helped move them,
threading them with grass strings.
When they had gathered nearly ten thousand coins,
their children suddenly suffered unbearable headaches.
Lù said:
"Could it be that Lú's words are coming true?"
He then rode a horse to catch up with Lú,
apologizing for violating the warning.
Lú angrily said:
"If you use them,
it will certainly bring calamity upon your flesh and blood.
Consider the weight of your family's well-being against profit—
you must judge for yourself."
He rowed his boat away without looking back.
Lù hurried back,
performed a ritual and reburied the coins,
and the children recovered.
When Lú arrived in Fùzhōu,
he often strolled leisurely with several others.
On the road, they encountered six or seven men in fine attire,
all reeking of alcohol.
Lú suddenly scolded them:
"If you do not reform your ways,
your lives will not last long."
Those men all prostrated themselves in the dust and said:
"We dare not, we dare not."
His companions were astonished.
Lú said:
"These men are all robbers."
His extraordinary abilities were like this.
Yuánqīng said:
"Recluse Lú's appearance
varied between old and young, not constant.
Nor did people often see him eat or drink.
He once told Zhào:
'There are many assassins in the world who can conceal their forms.
If a Daoist master obtains the art of invisibility,
and refrains from using it,
after twenty years, he can transform his form,
which is called 'liberation.'
After another twenty years,
he will be registered among the earthly immortals.'
He also said,
'When an assassin dies, his corpse also disappears.'
His discussions were often strange and wondrous,
likely because he belonged to the lineage of immortals."
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
Xuē Xuánzhēn
Xuē Xuánzhēn was
the great-great-grandfather of Xuē Bógāo, who served as a Jǐshìzhōng in the Táng dynasty.
From a young age, he was fond of the Way,
and had no taste for fame or officialdom.
He roamed among the clouds and springs,
and attained the Way of longevity.
He often rested and dwelled among the Five Ridges,
and whenever he met people, he would say:
"The Jiǔyí Mountains and the Five Ridges
are the abodes of immortals and spirits,
where the mountains and waters are secluded and wondrous,
and the mists and rosy clouds are exceptionally beautiful.
For example, the peaks of Yángshuò stand tall and straight,
and the caverns of Bóluó are pure and ethereal—
these cannot be forgotten.
This is why Zhùróng dwelled as a spirit on Héng Mountain,
Yú Shùn ascended to immortality in Cāngwú,
Hèxū left his traces on Qián Peak,
and the Yellow Emperor flew his chariot to Dǐnghú.
As for the other lofty perfected beings and ranked immortals,
ministers and assisting chancellors,
those who soared and wandered freely—
there is no mountain without them.
What is the reason for this?
The mountains are secluded and numinous,
the waters are deep and clear,
pines and bamboos reflect each other,
clouds and vines stretch into the deep and dim—
these are certainly not what those with mundane bones and dusty hearts love.
Moreover, within the deep caverns,
another heaven and earth opens up,
with jade-like ointments and dripping stalactites,
numinous herbs and splendid ganoderma—
how could dusty eyes perceive them,
or ordinary footsteps tread there?
To attain the Way of prolonging life
and wander leisurely in such a place—
truly, it is a joy!"
At the end of the Zhēnyuán era,
Zhèng Yúqìng was demoted
(the character "demoted" was originally missing,
and was supplemented based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy)
to serve as the Chief Clerk of Chēnzhōu.
A subordinate official came from afar to visit Yúqìng.
Before reaching Chēnzhōu, about ten or so lǐ away,
he stopped to rest at an inn,
where he encountered Xuánzhēn.
Xuánzhēn’s appearance was like that of a twenty-three or twenty-four-year-old,
his spirit and demeanor were outstanding and vigorous,
and his words often drew upon antiquity.
When he spoke of events from the Kāiyuán and Líndé eras,
it was as if he had witnessed them himself.
He also said that in the second month of the following year,
Yúqìng would return to the court.
His other words were all wondrous and extraordinary.
When asked his surname and name,
he repeatedly refused to answer.
Pressed earnestly,
he said:
"I have set my heart on forests and springs,
and long ago abandoned my homeland.
I do not wish my kin to know of my whereabouts.
My surname is Xuē,
and my name is Xuánzhēn."
The subordinate official reported this to Yúqìng.
Yúqìng sent people to search for him,
but no further traces were found.
In the second month of the following year,
Yúqìng was summoned back.
When he arrived in Cháng'ān,
he spoke of this strange event.
Jǐshìzhōng Xuē Bógāo, with tears streaming down his face, replied:
"My great-great-grandfather
abandoned his official post as Left Attendant-in-Ordinary to follow the Way,
secluding himself in Zhōngnán,
and his fate remains unknown.
It must have been him."
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Yú Tāo
Regarding Yú Tāo.
He was the nephew of the Tang dynasty chancellor Cóng.
When Cóng was demoted and sent south,
they passed by the Píngwàng Courier Station.
While they had just moored the boat and were eating,
an old man entered through the gate,
went straight to the small side room of the hall,
and approached Tāo.
When the old man arrived,
the station officials suspected he was accompanying the chancellor,
so they did not question him;
the chancellor suspected he was someone from the station,
and likewise did not interrogate him.
Once he reached where Tāo was resting,
Tāo asked:
"Who are you, old man?"
He replied:
"Old Man Cáo."
Tāo asked where he came from.
He replied:
"You, young master, have an extremely good official position;
you need not worry about this journey."
Tāo was about to embark on a long and arduous journey,
and was deeply troubled,
but upon hearing his words,
he happily welcomed him,
invited him to take a seat with a bow.
Tāo, along with his cousin, former proofreader of the Imperial Library, Xuē, spoke with him,
asking about his abilities.
He said:
"This old man has no special skills,
but I see that you, young master, will later hold high and prominent official positions;
I cannot describe them all one by one,
so please moisten your brush, take up your pen,
and record them as I speak."
Thus, Tāo followed the old man’s words and wrote down several passages,
the language of which was mostly cryptic,
almost like prophetic folk songs;
it also described the chancellor’s restoration to favor.
Then he asked about Proofreader Xuē’s future.
The old man said:
"A thousand miles away,
meeting 'west' he will stop.
As for his official position,
though not a true prefect,
he will still be a false commandery governor."
Tāo then asked, "What about matters in my residence in the capital?
Can you know them?"
The old man bowed his head for a long time and said:
"The capital residence is very peaceful.
Today in the hall, there are such-and-such a lady, such-and-such a nun."
The names of the guests,
he recognized each one clearly.
"Under such-and-such a corridor, there is a young servant boy,
leading a bronze turtle, running and playing."
Tāo also verified that these details were accurate,
and wrote them all down in his book.
As time passed, what was recorded
already filled several pages.
They looked at each other, laughing and talking,
as dusk was about to fall.
Tāo then pointed to the concubine Xuē Yúnxiāng.
He said to the old man:
"What about this person?"
He replied:
"Extremely good;
even three thousand miles away, she will also obtain a good official position."
At first, Tāo had followed the words and recorded the matters,
his mind sharp and believing;
but upon hearing that this concubine would also have a good official position,
he was surprised at its absurdity,
and his attention began to wane.
At that time, Tāo’s cousin Dù Rúxiū, a supervising secretary,
was serving as prefect of Húzhōu.
He had sent a jug of Ruòxià wine,
about five pecks in capacity.
Tāo then asked the old man if he liked wine.
The old man gladly accepted the offer,
so Tāo gave him a silver bowl,
letting him pour and drink by himself.
In a short while, the wine was finished,
and it was already dark.
The old man then used the silver bowl as a pillow and fell asleep.
At the time, mosquitoes were abundant,
yet none approached the old man.
By dawn, the old man had disappeared,
only the silver bowl remained.
They were just starting to ask in surprise and search for him,
but no one knew where he had gone.
Some people said:
"This was none other than Doctor Cáo Xiū."
Cáo Xiū,
a member of the Wèi imperial clan,
served as a historian during the Jìn dynasty,
and during the Qí and Liáng periods, he occasionally held court positions.
He attained the Way of Immortality,
often wandering among rivers and lakes,
coming and going as a merchant,
constantly saving people,
benefiting others through hidden merits.
Many people had seen him,
and received his legacy.
Later, Tāo was appointed as defense commissioner of Sìzhōu and prefect of Shèzhōu,
assisting the Prince of Wú, Yáng Xíngmì of Huáinán, as deputy commissioner.
The chancellor also soon returned north.
Proofreader Xuē assisted in the guest bureau of Jiāngxī,
overseeing military affairs in Yuánzhōu.
During a time of military conflict,
he took his family to Mǐn,
arriving at a small town,
where the concubine soon fell ill and died.
In the mountains, there was no place to obtain a coffin,
so he entrusted a village elder.
The elder gave up his own prepared burial coffin and buried her.
This coffin was lacquered, gilded, and colored,
quite splendid and precious.
After she was buried,
they realized the truth of the words about "obtaining a good coffin."
As for the capital residence,
on that day, the guests and the young servant boy leading the bronze turtle at play—
all these things came true without exception.
From "Biographies of Divine Responses."
Tián Xiānshēng
Mr. Tián was a great immortal from the Jiǔhuá Cave.
During the Yuánhé era, he lived in seclusion at Pótíng Village in Ráozhōu,
running a small school to teach a dozen or so village children.
People did not know he was an immortal.
Qí Tuī, the prefect of Ráozhōu, married his daughter to a Jìnshì named Mr. Lǐ.
After several months, she became pregnant.
Mr. Lǐ went to Cháng'ān to take the imperial examinations.
His pregnant wife was about to give birth in the rear hall of the prefectural office
when she dreamed that ghosts and deities reproached her for the foulness of childbirth
and drove her away.
Qí Tuī usually did not believe in ghosts and deities, so she dared not speak of it.
Before she could move to another residence,
she gave birth and was harmed by malevolent ghosts,
dying with blood flowing from her ears and nose.
She was temporarily buried beside the official road,
awaiting the prefect's transfer from his post so she could be moved north for burial.
The following year,
Mr. Lǐ, having failed the examinations, returned to Ráozhōu.
As evening fell,
he saw his wife in the wilderness.
She told him about being harmed by ghosts and deities,
and then said:
"Go to the school in Pótíng Village,
seek out Mr. Tián,
and ask for his divine power.
Perhaps I can be revived."
Mr. Lǐ did as she said.
He went to the village school to see Mr. Tián,
approached on his knees,
prostrated himself on the ground,
and sorrowfully recounted the events,
begging the great immortal to take pity and save her.
At first, Mr. Tián firmly refused.
Mr. Lǐ kowtowed and pleaded incessantly,
tears streaming down his face.
From morning until night,
he never took a seat.
After the students had dispersed,
Mr. Tián said:
"Since you are so sincere,
what reason do I have to hide?
But you did not tell me earlier;
her physical form has already decayed.
I will truly make arrangements for this."
He then walked over a hundred steps from the house into a mulberry grove.
Night had already grown dark,
but suddenly it became as bright as day.
The place transformed into a grand mansion with towering gates,
guards and attendants arrayed solemnly.
Mr. Tián, wearing a jeweled crown and purple robe,
sat behind a desk,
resembling a king.
He then called out for the local deities.
Soon, over ten groups arrived,
each with over a hundred riders,
rushing forth.
They were all over ten feet tall.
The herald announced their names and ushered them in, saying:
"The deities of Lúshān, the riverbanks, and Pénglí have arrived."
Mr. Tián said:
"The prefect's daughter was killed by violent ghosts during childbirth.
Why did you not hear of this and bring it to justice?"
They replied:
"There was no one to bring the case,
so we could not proceed with punishment.
The culprit is Wú Ruì, the Prince of Póyáng.
The prefect's residence is where he dwells.
Angered by the foulness of childbirth,
he committed this violent act.
We have since captured Wú Ruì
and submitted a memorial to the heavenly court for his execution.
An investigation states:
'Mr. Lǐ's wife is destined to live thirty-two more years
and bear two sons and three daughters.'"
Mr. Tián said:
"What about her decayed physical form?"
An old official said:
"In the Eastern Jìn dynasty, in Yèxià,
there was a man who died by mistake.
His physical form had already decayed,
but he was destined to return to life.
This case is similar.
At that time, Immortal Gě Xiān judged that his soul should form a body,
which would be no different from the original,
except that on the day his lifespan ended, he would have no form.
If you permit it,
we can simply summon the soul of Mr. Lǐ's wife
and unite it into one body.
Apply divine glue to it,
and once the great king dispatches her back to life,
she will revive immediately."
They saw seven or eight women
who resembled Mr. Lǐ's wife.
An official led them forward
and pushed them together.
There was a medicine like thin porridge
that was applied to her body.
In a moment, the officials and attendants all dispersed.
Mr. Lǐ, his wife, and Mr. Tián were in the mulberry grove.
Mr. Lǐ and his wife earnestly thanked him.
Mr. Tián said:
"Just say you were revived on your own;
do not speak of this further."
