With that, Mr. Tián vanished.
Mr. Lǐ and his wife returned home.
In the years that followed, her lifespan and the children she bore
were all as foretold.
From "Xiānzhuàn Shíyí".
Mù Jiàngfú
Mù Jiàngfú was the nephew of Mù Rényù, a Jǐshìzhōng of the Táng dynasty.
From a young age, he loved learning,
did not crave fame or profit,
and did not seek worldly honors.
Instead, he delved deeply into the mysteries of the Dao,
indulging in freedom and unrestraint.
No one knew who his teacher was,
but he had already mastered the art of internal cultivation through breath control.
He enjoyed drinking,
was aloof and disdainful,
and no one could fathom him.
Yáo, a wine shop owner in the East Market of Cháng'ān,
was his friend.
Mù often visited his home,
where they would drink and discuss the Dao,
spending days and nights together.
Suddenly, Yáo died abruptly,
throwing his entire family into panic.
They sent someone to urgently fetch Jiàngfú.
He arrived late at night.
Yáo was already lifeless,
with no breath left.
Jiàngfú was drunk at the time.
Yáo's family wailed and told him what had happened.
He laughed and said:
"He can be saved;
do not worry or fear."
He then took off his clothes and lay under the same quilt as Yáo.
He instructed the family
to prepare ginseng soup and thin porridge and wait.
They were not to weep, wail, or cry out in alarm.
They should only respond when called,
and then extinguish the candles and rest.
In the quiet of midnight,
he called for candles to see.
Yáo had already sat up.
He slowly fed him ginseng soup,
and after a long while,
gave him porridge to aid recovery.
Yáo was then able to speak, saying:
"Just now, three or four yellow-clad envoys
took me away on horseback,
traveling westward very quickly.
The road was dim,
as if under a faint moon.
Suddenly,
a red light appeared,
like the rising sun,
illuminating the path."
The yellow-clad envoys urged their horses even more urgently,
when suddenly they heard a proclamation:
"By decree of Tàiyǐ,
heavenly soldiers are dispatched to send him back."
He then saw riders and banners
arrayed in solemn ranks.
The horse he was riding and the yellow-clad envoys
fled and vanished without a trace.
Another red-clad figure
led him back.
From then on, Yáo recovered fully as before.
Jiàngfú then left in seclusion,
and no one knew where he went.
Xuānyuán Xiānshēng of Luófú
was a man of the Dao.
During the Dàzhōng era,
he was summoned to the capital.
Upon arriving in the capital,
he immediately sent someone to seek out Jiàngfú,
but Jiàngfú had already left in seclusion.
Xuānyuán Xiānshēng said:
"Mù the Recluse is a hidden immortal;
his name and rank are among the highest in the Nine Heavens.
Do not fault him for his fondness for drink and drunken stupor;
he truly blends his light with the common world."
In the Huái and Zhè regions, his extraordinary deeds were quite renowned,
heard and seen by many,
like those of Zuǒ Yuánfàng and Gě Xiàoxiān.
From "Shénxiān Shíyí".
Fáng Jiàn
Duke of Qīnghé, Fáng Jiàn,
resided in Hánshān Commandery.
He was of an eccentric disposition
and fond of the teachings of Xuányuán.
He often followed Daoist priests to receive the Six Jia talismans and the Nine Chapters of True Registers,
accumulating twenty years of practice.
Later, he traveled south to Héngshān,
where he encountered a Daoist priest,
whose demeanor was bright and refined.
Speaking with Jiàn,
he recounted the wonders of the Shangqing Celestial Capital, Pénglái, and Fāngzhàng,
each account as if he had personally experienced them.
Jiàn found this extraordinary.
More than ten days later,
Jiàn traveled from Héngshān to the South Sea.
The Daoist priest said to Jiàn:
"I once sojourned in the South Sea,
and it has been ten years since then.
There will be a temple official, Lord Lǐ, who oversees the troops there.
Lord Lǐ gave me a jade hairpin.
I now bestow this hairpin upon you,
and you should treasure it."
Jiàn obtained the hairpin
and was overjoyed.
Thus, they parted ways.
That autumn,
Jiàn arrived at the South Sea.
One day, he visited Kāiyuán Temple alone.
In the northern pavilion of the temple,
there were two figures molded from brick in the likeness of Perfected Beings.
The one on the east was the Perfected Being Zuǒ Xuán.
Upon examining the appearance of Zuǒ Xuán,
it was indeed the Daoist priest he had encountered at Héngshān.
He marveled and sighed for a long while;
and upon observing the crown of Zuǒ Xuán,
he noticed the hairpin was already missing.
At the time, several resident Daoist priests of the temple were present.
Jiàn recounted the events in detail,
and produced the jade hairpin to show them.
The Daoist priests exclaimed in astonishment:
"In years past, there was a temple official, Lord Lǐ,
who oversaw troops in the South Sea.
He once adorned the two Perfected Beings with jade hairpins,
and it has been nearly ten years since then.
The hairpin of Zuǒ Xuán
has been missing for ten years,
and the one you have obtained now is indeed that very hairpin."
Jiàn found this extraordinary,
and thus returned the jade hairpin to the Daoist priests.
From "Records of the Xuānshì"
Xiāo Dòngxuán
The Daoist priest Xiāo Dòngxuán of the Língdū Temple on Mount Wángwū,
devoted his heart to learning the art of refining the divine elixir.
After several years,
he had ultimately achieved nothing.
Not long after,
he encountered a divine being who bestowed upon him the secret formula of the Great Return, saying:
"The method ends here;
however, you must also find a like-minded companion,
to work together as inner and outer,
only then can you succeed.
Why not seek one out?"
Dòngxuán then traveled throughout the land,
traversing the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers,
famous mountains and extraordinary realms,
capital cities and settlements,
wherever human footprints gathered,
there was nowhere he did not go.
After more than ten years,
he still had not found such a person.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Dòngxuán traveled from eastern Zhèjiāng to Yángzhōu,
arriving at Chěngtíng Dam.
He moored his boat at an innkeeper's place.
At that time, tens of thousands of ships,
were congested along the riverbank.
When the sluice gate opened, they vied for passage,
ships going up and down,
jostled against each other for some time,
the boatmen exerted all their strength to push through.
He saw a man whose boat suddenly halted,
his right arm was crushed and nearly broken.
Onlookers shuddered with fear for him,
yet the man's complexion did not change,
nor did he utter a single groan.
Calmly, he returned to his boat,
and ate and drank as usual.
Dòngxuán deeply sighed in amazement,
and secretly rejoiced, saying:
"Is this not Heaven's blessing upon me?"
He asked the man his name,
who replied he was Zhōng Wúwéi.
Thus, he befriended him,
and they conversed joyfully about the Dao,
becoming inseparable thereafter.
They immediately went together to Mount Wángwū.
Dòngxuán showed him the secret formula of the Return Elixir.
Wúwéi studied and pondered it with him.
After another two or three years,
their cultivation was fully perfected.
Dòngxuán said to Wúwéi:
"On the night we perform the ritual,
I will cast spells to protect and uphold it.
You must diligently guard the elixir furnace.
If you remain silent until the fifth watch,
then we will ascend hand in hand."
Wúwéi said:
"Although I possess no other arts,
as for enduring and refraining from speech,
this you know of me."
Thus, for ten days they prepared the altar,
lit the golden incense burner,
and adorned the elixir furnace.
Dòngxuán circled the altar, performing the ritual steps of the Void.
Wúwéi sat before the medicine furnace,
upright and solemn,
vowing in his heart to remain silent even unto death.
After the first watch,
suddenly two Daoist priests descended from the sky.
They said to Wúwéi:
"The Supreme Emperor sends us to ask you,
do you wish to attain the Dao?"
Wúwéi did not respond.
Shortly after,
he saw a host of immortals,
who called themselves Wáng Qiáo, Ānqī, and others.
They said:
"Just now the Supreme Emperor sent his attendants to ask you something,
why did you not answer?"
Wúwéi still did not speak.
After a while,
he saw a woman,
about sixteen years old,
with dignified and beautiful features,
her voice gentle and serene,
her silken garments fluttering,
her fragrance overwhelming the earth.
She lingered for a long time,
flirting and teasing Wúwéi.
Wúwéi paid her no heed.
Suddenly, there appeared over ten kinds of tigers, wolves, and fierce beasts,
roaring and leaping about,
opening their mouths toward Wúwéi.
Wúwéi remained unmoved.
After a while,
he saw his deceased ancestors, parents, and relatives,
all standing before him.
They said:
"You see us,
how can you not speak?"
Wúwéi's tears streamed down,
but he still did not speak.
Suddenly, he saw a yaksha,
three zhang tall,
with eyes like flashing red lightning,
a mouth as red as blood,
vermillion hair standing upright like poles,
saw-like teeth and hook-like claws.
It charged directly at Wúwéi.
Wúwéi did not move.
Then came a man in yellow,
leading two attendants.
He said to Wúwéi:
"The Great King summons you.
If you do not wish to go,
just speak the reason and you will be spared."
Wúwéi did not speak.
The man in yellow then ordered the two attendants to drag him away.
Wúwéi had no choice but to follow them.
Soon they arrived at a government office,
said to be that of King Pingděng.
Facing south, leaning on his desk,
his majesty was exceedingly stern.
He sternly said to Wúwéi:
"You are not yet due to come here.
If you can speak even one word in your defense,
I will release you back."
Wúwéi did not reply.
King Pingděng then ordered him taken to the prison,
to see all those suffering punishment.
The cruelty and agony,
were of countless kinds and names.
After returning,
he again said to him:
"If you do not speak,
you will be thrown in here."
Though Wúwéi's heart was filled with fear,
he still did not speak.
King Pingděng said:
"Now order him to receive a new birth,
and not be released back to his original place."
From then on, Wúwéi's mind became confused,
silent and unaware of anything.
Suddenly, he regained consciousness,
and found his body reborn into the household of the noble Wáng family in Cháng'ān.
While still in his mother's womb,
he remembered his past vow of silence;
after birth,
his features were complete and perfect,
only he did not know how to cry.
On the third day, the full-month celebration,
his family held a grand gathering of relatives and guests,
with extensive music and entertainment.
The wet nurse carried the child out.
Among the crowd, everyone took turns admiring and caressing him.
His parents said to each other:
"Our son will surely become a nobleman one day."
Thus, they named him Guìláng.
His intelligence grew daily,
only he still did not cry.
By the age of three, he could walk,
gentle and not fond of play.
By five or six years old,
though he could not speak,
his actions were elegant and of lofty character.
At ten, he could wield a brush,
and immediately compose essays.
Whether in motion or at rest, in play or leisure,
he would fill pages with ink.
Upon reaching adulthood,
his appearance was exceptionally handsome,
his demeanor graceful and dignified,
a model for others;
however, considering himself mute,
he refused to enter government service.
His family's wealth rivaled that of the royal house,
with gold and jade filling the halls.
Maids, concubines, songs, and bells,
reached the height of luxury.
At twenty-six,
his parents arranged a marriage for him.
His wife also came from a wealthy family,
with peerless beauty,
skilled in crafts and music,
excelling in all.
Guìláng's official name was Shènwēi.
Throughout his life, he prided himself on happiness.
A year after marriage,
they had a son,
handsome, clever, and witty,
unmatched by any.
Shènwēi loved and cherished him,
even more than ordinary affection.
One day, his wife and Shènwēi,
were playing together in the spring courtyard.
In the courtyard was a large stone,
which could seat ten people.
His wife held their child atop it,
and suddenly said to Shènwēi:
"Seeing your love for me,
so deep and profound,"
If you do not speak for me today,
I will dash your son to death."
Shènwēi struggled for his son but could not prevail,
and his wife raised her hand to smash the child against the stone.
Brains splattered out,
and Shènwēi, stricken with grief, clutched his chest,
unconsciously letting out a cry of shock and horror.
Suddenly he awoke
to find himself before the alchemical furnace.
The stone slab from before
was actually the alchemical furnace.
At that moment, the ritual on the Dòngxuán Altar had just concluded,
and dawn was about to break.
Soon, they heard Wúwéi sighing,
and suddenly the alchemical furnace vanished.
The two of them wept bitterly together
and thereafter redoubled their efforts in cultivating their minds and practicing the Way.
Later, no one knew what became of them.
From *Hédōng Jì*
Jiǎ Dān
Chancellor Jiǎ Dān of the Táng dynasty,
who served as military governor of Huázhōu,
once ordered the making of a set of deer-skin clothes.
After they were completed,
he selected a nimble and robust officer,
handed him a sealed letter, and said:
"Go to a certain mountain.
Wherever the thorns are thickest, press forward.
Find Master Zhāng and deliver this letter to him,
no matter how far you must go."
The messenger accepted the order,
took provisions, and set off,
though he was deeply perplexed.
After traveling about a hundred *lǐ* into the mountain,
he encountered deep and perilous thickets of thorns,
traversing them all.
He reached a peak,
where halfway up, a stone cliff rose steeply.
There, he saw two Daoist priests playing chess.
The messenger bowed to the Daoists and said:
"Chancellor Jiǎ has sent me."
They opened the letter and laughed heartily,
then wrote a reply, saying:
"Tell the Chancellor to return soon.
Why is he so attached to wealth and honor?"
The messenger took the letter and returned.
Chancellor Jiǎ was overjoyed
and rewarded him generously.
Yet he never knew the reason behind it all.
On another occasion, he ordered a sturdy soldier
to enter a dry well to retrieve some documents.
Sure enough, he found several scrolls,
all of which were Daoist texts.
Jiǎ then dispatched over ten people to copy them.
Just as they finished,
a Daoist priest burst in,
shouting Jiǎ's name and cursing:
"How dare you steal these books!"
Jiǎ humbly apologized.
The Daoist priest then took the books away.
East of the Púshè Slope in Zhèngzhōu stood a pagoda.
Jiǎ sent a messenger with an official dispatch to the prefecture,
ordering them to retrieve a white crow from within that pagoda
and then seal it up.
Sure enough, they found it,
sent it in a cage,
though again, no one knew why.
Jiǎ Dān was a banished immortal,
and there are many stories about him.
These three are particularly notable.
From *Yì Shǐ*
Dīng Yuē
During the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Wéi Xíngshì who served as the Investigation Commissioner of Xīzhōu.
He had a nephew named Zǐwēi,
who had just reached the age of twenty,
was intelligent and gentle,
deeply fond of Taoist texts,
and captivated by the practices of immortals and alchemical cultivation.
There was a foot soldier named Dīng Yuē,
who performed menial duties under his command,
diligent and conscientious in his service,
never showing the slightest negligence,
and Zǐwēi held him in high regard.
One day, Dīng spoke with a sorrowful and trembling voice,
saying he wished to go elsewhere.
Zǐwēi angrily replied:
"Your name is registered in the army,
how can you act on your own whim?"
Dīng said:
"My decision to leave is already firm,
and I cannot stay;
however, I have served you diligently,
for two years now,
and I cannot forget your kindness,
so I wish to repay you in some way.
I am not one who merely seeks sustenance through mediocrity,
but I am still entangled in the mundane world.
I have a single pill of medicine,
which I offer to you as a parting gift.
It cannot grant eternal life,
but it will ensure you remain free from illness within its limits."
He then loosened his clothing and retrieved from within
a pill resembling a grain of millet,
which he presented to Zǐwēi.
He further said:
"Young master, your devotion to the Tao is profound,
and you are honest even in the dark,
so you will eventually renounce the mundane world,
though two 'dusts' still separate you from it."
Zǐwēi asked:
"What do you mean by 'two dusts'?"
Dīng replied:
"Confucians call it a 'generation,'
Buddhists call it a 'kalpa,'
and Taoists call it a 'dust.'
If you steadfastly maintain this heart of yours,
you will also enjoy a long life.
In about fifty years, we will meet near the capital,
and when that time comes, do not be surprised."
Having said this, he departed.
Zǐwēi was astonished,
and immediately ordered someone to pursue him,
but it was already too late.
The commanding officer reported his desertion,
requesting the removal of his name from the military register.
Thereafter, Zǐwēi thought of him constantly,
keeping an eye out in search of him,
but ultimately found no trace.
Later, Zǐwēi passed the imperial examination in the Míngjīng category,
and was appointed to several
"Several" originally read "sù,"
but was changed according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.
county magistracies.
By the time he reached the age of seventy,
his hair had turned completely white,
which was in the thirteenth year of the Yuánhé era.
As he was about to return to the capital,
one evening at an inn on Líshān,
he heard a great commotion on the main road.
Inquiring about the cause,
he was told:
"Liú Wù has captured the rebel general Liǔ Shīdào and his officers and is bringing them to the capital."
Zǐwēi stepped out to look,
and saw a heavily guarded procession of soldiers,
with prisoners shackled in chains.
Among them was one person
who turned out to be Dīng Yuē.
His arms were bound behind his back,
and he was being driven westward,
yet his teeth and hair remained strong and vigorous,
no different from before.
Zǐwēi found this extremely strange.
Amidst the crowd of hundreds and thousands,
just as Zǐwēi recognized him in surprise,
Dīng had already seen him.
Smiling, he called out from afar:
"Do you still remember our parting in Línqióng?
Fifty years have passed in an instant,
and I am fortunate to see you now.
Please accompany me to the next post station."
Shortly after, they arrived at Zīshuǐ Station,
where the prisoners were dispersed and confined in the corridor quarters,
with a small opening provided for food.
Zǐwēi peeked inside,
and soon saw Dīng remove his shackles,
cover them with a mat,
and leap out through the opening.
He then took Zǐwēi by the hand and went up to a roadside tavern,
where they spoke of the regrets of their long separation,
and Dīng sighed at Zǐwēi's aged appearance.
Zǐwēi asked him:
"Since you, immortal brother, possess the foresight,
and the sacred dynasty rules over all under heaven,
why did you side with a rebel minister?"
Dīng replied:
"This has long been predetermined,
how could I escape it?
When we parted in Shǔ,
did I not say we would meet near the capital?
I urged you not to be overly surprised."
Zǐwēi asked further:
"Will you truly be executed?"
Dīng answered:
"In the Taoist path, there are methods of liberation through corpse, weapon, water, and fire,
and indeed there are many practitioners.
Jī Kāng and Guō Pú
both suffered violent deaths;
I am merely shedding my mortal shell.
This is different from Hán Xìn and Péng Yuè, who ended up as manure and dirt.
If I wished to avoid this,
I could escape from here,
and who could pursue me?"
He did not answer other questions,
only saying he needed a brush.
Zǐwēi searched his book bag and offered one.
Dīng accepted it with a nod of gratitude.
Zǐwēi said:
"Tomorrow morning, I will watch at the execution ground.
Will you shed your shell there?"
Dīng replied:
"Not yet.
This evening there will be heavy rain,
preventing the execution.
After two days, when the rain stops,
the state will have a minor incident.
The nineteenth day is the appointed time.
If you could,
please come to bid me farewell then."
Having said this, he returned to the station,
re-entered through the opening,
and sat down wearing the cangue.
Zǐwēi went back to the hot springs,
and as the sun was setting,
a sudden wind stirred up dust,
and that night, heavy rain indeed poured down.
At dawn,
the mud reached up to the shins,
and an edict postponed the execution.
After two days, when the skies cleared,
a princess passed away at an outer residence,
leading to three days without court sessions.
It was indeed on the nineteenth day
that the ancestral temple ceremonies and market inspections were conducted,
and only then was the mass execution carried out.
On that day, Zǐwēi fed his servant and groomed his horse,
and at daybreak went to the execution ground to wait.
Around noon,
as the orders were being carried out,
the spectators numbered in the hundreds of millions,
making it impossible to see faces or hear words clearly,
and even a step could separate people.
When the prisoners arrived,
Dīng had already noticed Zǐwēi,
and from afar, he looked at him,
smiling and nodding three or four times.
At the moment the blade fell,
Zǐwēi alone saw a broken brush.
In the flash of the cold blade,
Dīng leaped out,
and amidst the vast crowd,
he tiptoed forward,
then ascended a wine shop,
speaking as he had in Shǔ.
He removed his clothes to exchange for wine,
and drank with Zǐwēi.
He said:
"From now on, I will wander freely;
strive diligently in your devotion to the Tao,
though two 'dusts' still separate you.
I will await you in the stone chamber of Kūnlún."
Having said this,
he descended from the tavern,
and drifted slowly westward,
disappearing after a few steps.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
by the Taoist priest Qú.
Huáng Zūnshī cultivated the Way on Máoshān,
his mastery of talismanic registers was exceptionally high,
and his spiritual responses were manifold.
His disciple, Dàoist Qú,
was young
and not very diligent or earnest,
and was often caned by Master Huáng.
East of the thatched hall was a small cave,
eight feet high,
overgrown with wild vines,
as if snakes or serpents lurked within.
One day, Qúshēng was again lazy and negligent,
and was whipped by his master.
Hesitating to avoid the rod,
he entered this cave.
Huánggōng was astonished,
and sent people to search through the grass,
but they found nothing.
After the time of a meal, he came out,
holding a Go piece,
and said:
"Just now I watched a game of Go,
[Note: The character 'Go' was originally written as 'Qín',
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.]
and when it was time,
the people invited me to stay for a meal and gave me this;
this is a Go piece from the Qín people."
Huánggōng found this strange,
and still suspected he had been bewitched by a fox spirit,
so he did not quite believe it.
Máoshān has been traditionally passed down as an immortal abode,
with hundreds and thousands of people studying the Way there,
all revering Huánggōng,
and all believing that his virtue and practice, rank and grade,
would soon lead to ascension to immortality.
Whenever auspicious days arrived,
they would all gaze at the clouds and cranes.
On the night of the full moon in the eighth month of the following year,
the weather was clear and crisp,
the moonlight bright as day;
at midnight, clouds and mist rose greatly,
the clouds were of five colors,
gathering between the windows,
immortal music filled the courtyard,
and again there was the sound of pacing the void.
The disciples all thought the time for Huánggōng's ascension to immortality had arrived,
and hastily prepared incense and fire.
Huánggōng bathed and put on court robes,
awaiting his true companions.
As dawn approached,
the misty smoke gradually dispersed,
and they saw Qúshēng riding a five-colored cloud,
emerging from the east into the courtyard,
with divine music, phoenixes, and cranes,
filling the sky,
and from amidst the clouds he bowed twice to Huánggōng and said:
"The Venerable Master will come soon,
but you must continue to cultivate diligently,
for it will not be long."
He then bid farewell to the various disciples,
rode the wind and departed,
gradually going far until he was no longer seen,
but faintly the sound of the multitude of music could still be heard.
The elders of Jīnlíng
often pass down this story.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Wáng Qīng
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
in Yǐngzhōng there was a wine shop owner named Wáng Qīng,
whose shop was near the southern outer wall.
Whenever it was a festival day,
a Dàoist priest would often pass by,
drink his fill, and then leave through the outer wall.
This went on for several years.
Later, because the Dàoist priest came again,
Qīng then dressed and prepared to follow him secretly,
trailing him for several miles.
The Dàoist priest looked back and saw him,
greatly startled, and said:
"Why have you come?"
Qīng then bowed in respect,
wishing the divine man would allow him to serve as a servant.
The Dàoist priest firmly refused,
but Qīng firmly followed him.
Whenever they passed ravines and valleys,
some over ten feet high or wide,
the Dàoist priest would leap over them,
lightly lifting himself across.
Qīng lightly followed his steps,
and was also able to cross.
After walking several tens of miles,
they came to a cliff over a hundred zhang high.
The Dàoist priest soared up and rose.
Qīng could not climb it,
so he earnestly begged and bowed in respect.
The Dàoist priest from above said to him:
"Why do you insist on following me?
Go back quickly on your own;
if not,
you will sit and suffer hardship and stumbling."
Qīng said:
"The dangers and obstacles crossed earlier,
were all thanks to the Venerable Master's command;
now if I turn back, there is no path,
I will surely die.
I beg to be rescued and protected."
The Dàoist priest extended his hand down the cliff,
telling Qīng to raise his hands and close his eyes,
leap up and be drawn flying,
and he had already reached the top of the cliff.
Above was a flat, expansive, misty scene,
unlike the human world.
They walked another ten-plus miles,
until they reached the Dàoist priest's dwelling.
The gate and courtyard were neat and solemn,
and he made Qīng stay outside the dwelling in the grass.
He said to him:
"You stay here for now,
I will bring you food.
Wait for an opportunity, and I will let you see the Celestial Master."
Qīng hid in the grass.
For three days, the Dàoist priest brought food each time,
and it was always sufficient.
Later one day,
he suddenly saw the Celestial Master come out the door,
leaning on a staff,
with four or five Dàoist priests attending him.
The Celestial Master's appearance was majestic and grand,
with clear and distinct eyebrows and eyes.
The Dàoist priest secretly beckoned Qīng,
telling him to pay respects by the side of the path.
The Celestial Master was startled and said:
"How did you manage to come here?"
Qīng then explained.
The various Dàoist priests said:
"This person is cautious and honest,
perhaps he can be put to service,
we could let him guard the stove for now."
The Celestial Master ordered him to be taken in,
and then led Qīng into the courtyard,
to the kitchen area.
They saw a large stove,
with fire burning below,
and an iron cylinder on top,
sealed with several layers of lids.
The Dàoist priest ordered Qīng to guard the stove,
to watch it exclusively,
and not to peek recklessly,
lest he cause it to fail and fall.
The other four Dàoist priests,
some drew water and gathered herbs,
steamed, dried, and prepared food,
to supply the Celestial Master.
At night, they also made Qīng sleep under the kitchen to tend the fire.
After six or seven days,
no one came to check on the contents of the cauldron.
Later one day,
Qīng, for no reason, secretly opened it to peek at the medicine.
Suddenly he saw a white rabbit,
walk out from the iron cylinder,
with a sudden, sharp sound.
The Dàoist priest said:
"The medicine is already lost!"
They all rushed to look,
fearful and pale with fright.
In a moment,
the Celestial Master was greatly angered and said:
"Why did you suddenly bring a worldly person here,
causing the loss of the medicine."
Soon he summoned the previous Dàoist priest to reprimand and shame him,
intending to whip him.
The Dàoist priest kowtowed,
begging to go capture and search for it.
Several Dàoist priests,
in the courtyard, lit incense and performed Yǔ steps.
Two Dàoist priests,
transformed into white cranes,
and flew up to the sky.
After the time of a meal,
the cranes had already captured the white rabbit and brought it back,
and they ordered it thrown into the cauldron,
to be firmly sealed and refined.
The Celestial Master ordered them to quickly drive out the worldly person and send him back.
The Dàoist priest then led him out and said:
"You almost caused me trouble,
your heart is not yet firm,
you should go back for now."
He then led him to the foot of the high cliff,
held his hand and bid farewell.
"In twenty years,
we will meet again in the market of Fénzhōu."
Qīng then found his way back,
and after several days reached the outer wall,
already a year had passed.
He then became a Dàoist priest.
More than ten years later,
while traveling in Tàiyuán,
he ultimately did not know whether he would have any encounter.
From "Yuán Huà Jì"
The Hermit of Héngshān,
whose name is unknown.
Often because he sold medicine,
he would come and go, lodging at the mountain temple.
Sometimes he would go four or five days without eating,
which the monks found strange.
He returned to sell medicine at the monks' place.
Seeing that he did not eat,
the temple community realized he was an extraordinary man,
and treated him with great respect and hospitality.
It happened that a musician brought his daughter to the temple;
the girl was beautiful,
and many wished to marry her.
Her parents asked for five hundred thousand [cash],
and everyone withdrew.
The hermit heard the girl was to be married,
invited a monk to go see her,
was delighted and wished to take her [as his wife],
then brought two ingots of gold,
exactly two hundred liǎng,
and said to the girl's father:
"This gold is worth seven hundred strings [of cash],
but now let's not haggle over it."
After handing over the gold, he took her away.
The musician was then serving in an official capacity,
so they parted in haste.
The hermit showed them where he lived,
saying:
"It is over forty lǐ from here;
just reach the mountain and you will know."
After the girl's parents had finished their affairs, they missed their daughter,
and went to visit her.
They saw vermilion gates, lofty and splendid;
they knocked,
and the hermit and the girl both came out to welcome them.
Upon arriving, they ate one meal,
and afterward were no longer hungry.
Staying for five or six days,
they also did not think of eating.
When the parents were about to return,
the hermit, using a five-colored box,
filled it with five ingots of gold as a gift,
and said to the parents:
"This place is deep and secluded,
and is no longer fit for human habitation.
Henceforth, there is no need to seek it again."
Afterward, the parents went again,
but saw only mountain grass;
no longer was there any human dwelling.
Only then did they realize it was an abode of immortals.
From Guǎngyì Jì.
Méi Zhēnjūn
Cuī Jǐngtáng, a man of Rǔyīn,
had a very wealthy household.
Once there was a Daoist priest,
who said his surname was Méi,
who came to visit Cuī.
Cuī hosted him for several months.
Jǐngtáng had purchased a jade saddle,
and was going to Shòuchūn
to present it to the military commissioner Gāo Shěnsī.
He said to Méi:
"Sir, just stay here;
I am going to Shòuchūn,
and will return in ten days or a month.
I will have my sons and nephews serve you;
you have nothing to worry about."
Méi said:
"I am actually a man of Shòuchūn;
I came here to visit a relative or friend,
and am about to return.
You go ahead.
Having stayed here long,
I wish to have something to repay you.
Does your household have any mercury?"
He replied:
"Yes."
And immediately offered ten liǎng of it.
Méi then placed it in a cauldron,
and refined the mercury,
and after a short while it turned into silver.
Thereupon he said to Jǐngtáng:
"Take this as travel provisions.
When you reach Shòuchūn,
you may visit my home in the eastern part of the city."
Then he and Jǐngtáng parted ways and left.
Jǐngtáng reached Shòuchūn,
and went to the eastern part of the city,
to inquire after the Méi family.
For several days he could not find it.
The villagers all said:
"There is no Méi family here,
nor anyone who is a Daoist priest;
only in the Huáinán mountain temple,
there is an image of Méi Zhēnjūn.
Could it be this?"
Following their words, he went to visit it,
and indeed it was Méi Zhēnjūn.
Afterward, he never encountered him again.
From Jīshén Lù.
Bái Yōuqiú
In the eleventh year of the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the xiùcai Bái Yōuqiú,
had repeatedly failed the imperial examinations for years.
That year, disheartened by his lack of success,
he later followed a prince of Xīnlúo across the sea.
At Dàxiègōng Island,
they encountered a storm at night.
Bái Yōuqiú and several dozen companions were blown by the wind,
speeding south for two days and two nights,
not knowing how many thousands of miles they had traveled.
When the wind subsided somewhat,
they proceeded slowly
and saw mountains and forests.
They then straightened their oars and headed towards it.
Upon arriving in front,
the mountain was ten thousand rèn high.
On the southern face, halfway up the mountainside,
there was a city wall.
Its towers, pavilions, gates, and buildings were exceedingly magnificent.
They tied up their boat and ascended.
When they were about one or two lǐ from the city,
dragons and tigers were seated in rows on both sides of the path.
Seeing Yōuqiú,
they stared at him intently.
Yōuqiú proceeded along the path, filled with great fear,
wishing to find his companions.
Losing his voice, he wandered anxiously
and stopped beneath a large tree.
Its branches rubbed together in the wind,
sounding like a person reciting poetry.
Yōuqiú listened carefully,
and it said:
"Jade banners span the azure void,
This is where the Perfected Ones reside.
You linger, still not advancing,
Evil thoughts remain hard to dispel."
Yōuqiú hesitated, still not daring to go forward,
when suddenly a person in crimson robes emerged from the city gate,
proclaiming an edict:
"The Perfected Lord of the Western Peak has come to visit."
All the dragons and tigers prostrated themselves and said:
"He has not yet arrived."
Yōuqiú then hurried forward,
but saw the crimson-robed person enter without a glance back.
Yōuqiú could neither advance nor retreat.
The dragons and tigers on either side occasionally glanced at Yōuqiú,
as he lingered there.
Several dozen people emerged from the gate,
the dragons and tigers ran about,
and the people all mounted them and went down the mountain.
Yōuqiú also followed them,
reaching the place where their boat was moored.
All those riding dragons and tigers walked upon the surface of the sea.
In a moment, they vanished into the distant azure.
Yōuqiú did not know where to go.
Food was being prepared in the boat.
Suddenly, he saw a procession with banners and insignia approaching from the west,
numbering nearly a thousand people;
simurghs, cranes, and bluebirds
flew leading the way;
some rode dragons, others controlled tigers,
some rode tortoises, others rode fish.
There was a person riding a horse with a crimson mane,
wearing robes of purple clouds with suns and moons,
above him a green canopy was spread,
arriving as if borne by the wind.
Yōuqiú could only prostrate himself.
They then entered the city gate.
Yōuqiú again followed to observe them.
The dragons and tigers and others resumed their former positions in rows.
Along with the trees, flowers, herbs, birds, and sparrows,
they all moved in rhythm, swirling and circling as if dancing.
Yōuqiú himself also unconsciously began to move his feet in step.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
the crimson-robed person came out holding a document,
and said to the dragons and tigers:
"Summon the Perfected Lord of the Water Palace.
The dragons and tigers did not come forward.
The crimson-robed person then looked at Yōuqiú and handed him the document.
Yōuqiú did not know where to go.
The crimson-robed person said:
"To the Water Palace."
And pointed with his finger.
Yōuqiú followed the direction pointed,
and his body felt as if riding the wind,
descending the mountain and entering the sea's depths.
Although he entered the water, he did not perceive it as water,
hazy and dim, as if walking under the midday sun.
There were also trees and flowers,
when touched, they made a tinkling, jade-like sound.
In a short while, he reached a city,
its palaces were very grand.
The gatekeepers looked at him in surprise,
and prostrated themselves along the road.
Soon, several dozen people appeared,
all with dragon heads and scaly bodies,
holding banners and staffs,
and led Yōuqiú into the Water Palace.
The Perfected Lord, facing north from below the hall, bestowed upon him the talisman and document.
After bowing and rising,
he then went out the gate.
Already, dragons and tigers with riders were waiting.
Solemnly, they set off,
and in an instant, they arrived back at the former place.
Yōuqiú reached the gate,
but again did not dare enter.
Although he had not eaten,
he also did not feel hungry.
After a little while,
someone came looking for the Water Palace messenger.
Yōuqiú answered and entered,
bowed before the hall,
and was led to the western corridor,
where he joined the other messengers sitting below.
The food and drink were not of the flavor of the mortal world.
Slowly, he asked among the messengers:
"What place is this?"
They replied:
"This is the Spring Terrace where the various Perfected Lords roam.
The host is the Perfected Lord of the Eastern Peak.
Each of the four seasons has its assigned position,
each in its respective direction.
The host also changes according to the location and season."
In the eastern corridor of that hall,
several hundred jade maidens were arrayed,
playing music.
White cranes and peacocks
all raised their wings and moved their feet,
further harmonizing with the mystical songs.
When evening came, they left the hall.
On the eastern and western sides of the mountain was the Moon-Greeting Hall.
There was also a palace observatory for viewing the sun.
By the shēn hour (3-5 p.m.),
the bright moon had emerged.
Each Perfected Lord composed a poem welcoming the moon.
One Perfected Lord's poem said:
"The sun sets, misty waters grow dim,
How could the color of the Lízhū pearl be dulled?
Its cold light shoots for ten thousand lǐ,
Frost-white silk spreads over a thousand gates."
Another Perfected Lord's poem said:
"The jade soul opens in the east,
Cháng'é chases its shadow, coming near.
Cleansing the heart and washing the eyes,
Light and shadow roam the Spring Terrace."
Another Perfected Lord's poem said:
"Clear waves surge, azure grows dark,
The sky's vault lies somber and continuous.
Where the two principles cannot be distinguished,
Suddenly, a clear, round light is emitted."
Another Perfected Lord's poem said:
"The crow sinks by the western shore of the sea,
The toad spews forth from the eastern head of the sky."
He forgot the next line,
and the rest of the poems were also forgotten.
After composing the poems,
one Perfected Lord then commanded an evening performance.
In a short while,
over thirty child attendants and jade maidens,
some sitting in empty space,
some walking on the sea's surface,
with reed pipes, panpipes, and various instruments,
alternately sang and harmonized.
There were those who sang the Songs of Pacing the Void,
numbering several tens to a hundred.
Yōuqiú remembered one of them.
Its lyrics said:
"Thirty-six phoenixes,
The azure sky is high, the Great Purity vast.
The Primal Lord's Consort treads the clouds and speaks,
The cold wind soughs, blowing the goose-feather panpipes."
By the fourth watch (1-3 a.m.),
a person in deep red clothes walked in,
bowed, bent his knee, and announced:
"Dawn is about to break."
He acknowledged and hurried out.
The various lords ordered their carriages and each took their leave.
The next day,
the crimson-robed person from the previous day bent his knee and said:
"Bái Yōuqiú has already served as a Water Palace messenger,
and has performed meritorious service."
The various Perfected Lords deliberated and said:
"Let him then be assigned to sweep and clean the Spring Terrace."
Yōuqiú, distressed and anxious,
bowed and begged to be allowed to return to his hometown.
One Perfected Lord said:
"Where is your home?"
He replied:
"In Qínzhōng."
The lord also said:
"Why are you so attached to returning to your hometown?"
Yōuqiú did not answer.
The lord also said:
"Come, follow me."
The crimson-robed person indicated he should follow the Perfected Lord of the Western Peak.
The various Perfected Lords also each descended the mountain,
each having their own dragons, tigers, simurghs, phoenixes,
crimson-maned horses, tortoises, fish,
banners, insignia, feather streamers, and the like.
Each Perfected Lord had over a thousand attendants.
He walked upon the surface of the sea.
Yōuqiú also rowed a boat, following behind the True Lord of the Western Peak.
A favorable wind arose,
swift as lightning.
At dawn they reached an island.
He saw the True Lord ascend and fly away.
Yōuqiú's boat was limited,
so he left the boat and went ashore on the island.
Gazing after the True Lord,
he could still faintly see the banners and insignia gradually disappearing.
Yōuqiú, filled with regret and sorrow, wept bitterly.
Then he meandered up the island.
He saw signs of human habitation in the distance,
gradually approached and inquired,
and was told it was Míngzhōu.
He was overjoyed to have returned to his homeland.
From then on, Yōuqiú abstained from grains,
regularly consumed poria cocos,
loved to roam among mountains and waters,
often staying in the Five Sacred Mountains,
forever severed from official ambitions.
From "Bóyì Zhì".
Wáng Tàixū
The Perfected Being of the Eastern Extremity, Wáng Tàixū,
lived in seclusion in the Wángwū Mountains.
In the Rénchén year of the Xiántōng era,
the magistrate of Wángwū, Wáng Tú,
who had long been devoted to the Dao,
often recited the "Huángtíng Jīng".
He frequently wished to annotate it himself,
but had not yet grasped its profound mysteries.
He merely recited it five or six thousand times daily.
Hearing that Wángwū contained the Grotto-Heaven of Xiǎoyǒu,
a mansion of immortals,
he sought appointment as magistrate of Wángwū,
intending to build a hut within it,
hoping to occasionally visit and pay homage.
After leaving office,
he abstained from food and practiced breath circulation for several months,
gradually feeling his spirit vigorous and body light.
He entered the cave dwelling,
vowing never to return.
Initially traveling twenty or thirty *lǐ*,
sometimes through broad, bright spaces,
sometimes through dark, muddy blackness.
Feeling the walls, he stooped and walked,
for three or five days.
Suddenly, it opened into a level, expansive area,
with steep cliffs leaning against the sky,
soaring straight up ten thousand *ren*.
Below was a recessed chamber,
capable of seating several hundred people.
Stone beds and tables
appeared as if someone lived there.
On a table was an ancient scripture scroll.
Not daring to take it immediately,
he kowtowed and bowed, saying:
"I am a lowly minister from the mundane world,
with a turbid form and foul breath.
Yet I admire the Way of Longevity.
Fortunately entering this Grotto-Heaven,
I gaze up at this spiritual mansion—
a rare encounter across ten thousand kalpas.
Now I behold these traces left by celestial beings,
this jade table and mysterious scripture.
I dare not take it recklessly.
I pray the True Immortals witness and bless me,
allowing my dusty eyes to peruse its pages once.
Then I would receive boundless grace."
After kowtowing for a long time,
he begged for a sign in response.
Suddenly, a person sat beside the table and said:
"Have you forgotten?
You are a descendant of the immortals of Gōushì,
able to love the Dao.
Your name may be listed on the green tablets.
I am the Perfected Being of the Eastern Extremity,
of the same surname as you.
This precious scripture, the 'Huángtíng',
I have annotated it myself,
and now bestow it upon you."
He also gifted him peaches,
amounting to several *dou*.
He said:
"Eating these enables one to fly by daylight.
Grinding and consuming their pits
not only cures illnesses,
but also extends one's lifespan.
Although you have the will,
you cannot reside here yet.
In twenty years, we shall meet again on this mountain.
Strive and be diligent,
and you will attain the Dao."
Having spoken,
he vanished.
Tú also dared not stay long,
and returned carrying the peach pits and the scripture.
He ground and consumed the peach pits,
his body became healthy and free from illness,
his appearance grew even more youthful.
In the mortal world, copies of the "Huángtíng Jīng" annotated by the Perfected Being of the Eastern Extremity thus began to circulate.
From "Xiānzhuàn Shíyí".
Wáng Zǐzhī
Wáng Zǐzhī, styled Xiānmiáo,
is said to be from Gōushì in Hénán.
He often traveled between the capital and Luòyáng.
Elders said:
"For fifty years, we have seen him,
and his appearance has always been like that of a man around forty,
with no one knowing his true age.
He enjoyed cultivating his vital energy and was fond of wine.
In the first year when the military governor of Pú, Lángyá Gōng Chóng Yíng, took office,
Xiānmiáo resided at the Zǐjí Palace,
and the governor treated him with great hospitality.
Hearing of his fondness for wine,
he sent him three jars of wine daily.
One day, Xiānmiáo went out
and encountered a woodcutter
carrying a load at the palace gate.
His appearance was extraordinary,
and Xiānmiáo found him quite unusual.
He thus bought his firewood,
paying him generously.
The woodcutter took the money
and left without declining.
Zǐzhī secretly ordered someone to follow him
and observe him.
The woodcutter went straight to a tavern,
drank his fill, and returned.
Another day, he came again.
Zǐzhī said to him:
"I know you are fond of wine.
I have fine wine given to me by the governor.
I will give it to you in exchange for your firewood.
Is that acceptable?"
He replied:
"Yes."
He then drank several bowls
and said to Zǐzhī:
"This wine is excellent,
but it is far inferior to the brew of the Shí family in Xiè County.
I have just come from there,
but regret that I had no companion then,
so I could not fully enjoy the drink."
Zǐzhī then descended the steps, took his hand,
and sat with him by the stove.
He earnestly asked the woodcutter:
"Can the fine wine of the Shí family be obtained?"
The woodcutter nodded.
He then ordered a cinnabar brush,
wrote a talisman,
and placed it on the fire.
Before the smoke cleared,
a young servant appeared before them.
The woodcutter commanded him:
"You lead the master's servant,
take these two jars,
and go to the Shí family to fetch wine.
I will wait here to get drunk with the master."
It was already dark,
and the gates were closed and locked.
The young servant said to Zǐzhī's servant:
"Close your eyes."
He then touched his head,
and both the man and the wine jars passed through the crack of the gate.
They soon reached Xiè County,
brought back the wine,
and shared it with Zǐzhī.
Its sweetness, richness, and intensity
were unmatched in the mortal world.
In the middle of the night,
the woodcutter said to Zǐzhī:
"We are already drunk.
I will summon a guest to drink with you.
Is that acceptable?"
Zǐzhī said:
"Yes."
He wrote another red talisman
and placed it on the fire.
In an instant, a strange fragrance filled the room,
and a man arrived,
stately with beautiful beard and eyebrows,
dressed in purple and holding a tablet.
He bowed to the woodcutter and sat down.
After two rounds of drinking,
the two jars were nearly empty.
The woodcutter heated an iron chopstick
and scorched
"Scorched" originally written as "授" (shòu),
the Ming manuscript has "焌" (qū),
now corrected according to *Yúnjí Qīqiān* 112.
the purple-robed man,
saying:
"You may leave now,
for dawn is approaching in the east."
They then bid farewell.
The woodcutter said to Zǐzhī:
"Do you recognize the man who just came?
In a moment,
you can go to the Hé Dú Temple and see for yourself."
Zǐzhī saw off the woodcutter,
and after he left,
he went to the temple.
There, he saw the man who had drunk with them the previous night—
it was a deity,
and the mark from the iron chopstick was clearly visible.
Zhào Jūn
"Jūn" originally written as "君" (jūn),
corrected according to *Yúnjí Qīqiān*.
the Vice Director, who was then in the military headquarters,
witnessed this event.
Sū Yuè, a Proofreader of the Hóngwén Guǎn, was also residing in Zhōngtiáo
and was very familiar with the details.
Later, Zǐzhī met the woodcutter immortal again,
who imparted to him the secrets of cultivation,
and he thus became an earthbound immortal.
From *Shénxiān Gǎnyù Lù*.
Liú Shāng
was a native of Péngchéng
and resided in Cháng'ān.
From a young age, he was fond of learning and possessed a strong memory,
devoting deep thought to literary pursuits.
He composed the "Eighteen Stanzas of the Barbarian Reed Pipe,"
which became widely popular in the world,
with children and women alike
all reciting it.
He passed the imperial examination as a jìnshì
and served successively in the central government as a láng.
His nature inclined toward Daoist arts,
and whenever he encountered a Daoist priest, he would take him as a teacher,
practicing alchemy and breath cultivation
with utmost diligence and earnestness.
He often lamented how swiftly time passed,
how his body gradually weakened,
how he rushed about from dawn till dusk,
only to toil and labor,
and how the empty honors and worldly offices
were of no benefit to himself.
The ancient sages all abandoned their official posts to seek the Way,
and many attained transcendence.
Now that I have fortunately completed the marriages of my children,
and am no longer burdened by worldly concerns,
am I any inferior to Xǔ Yuǎnyóu?
Thus, he resigned from office due to illness
and, dressed in Daoist robes, journeyed eastward.
Entering Guǎnglíng,
he met a Daoist priest on the city street
who was selling medicine,
gathering an extremely large crowd.
The medicine he sold
was said by people to be quite efficacious.
Among the crowd, he saw
"saw" originally written as "between,"
emended according to the Ming manuscript.
Shāng
and looked at him with a gaze of recognition.
He then ceased selling medicine,
took Shāng by the hand, and ascended a tower,
offering wine to toast him.
The topics discussed by the Daoist priest,
from the Qín and Hàn dynasties through successive eras,
all seemed as if he had witnessed them firsthand.
Shāng was astonished
and revered him as a teacher.
The priest further said that immortality and Daoist arts were not easily attainable.
When evening came,
Shāng returned to his lodgings.
The Daoist priest descended the tower
and vanished in a flash.
Shāng grew even more amazed.
The next day,
Shāng again sought him on the city street.
The Daoist priest was still selling medicine,
and upon seeing Shāng, he was even more pleased.
Once more, he led him up to the wine tower,
engaged in lively conversation, and urged him to drink until intoxicated.
He then took out a small medicine pouch and presented it to Shāng,
playfully reciting a verse:
"With no affairs, I came to Yángzhōu;
hand in hand, we ascended the wine tower.
This medicine pouch I give as a parting gift;
what more could one seek for a thousand years?"
Shāng memorized the verse,
and at dusk, they parted ways.
Later, Shāng repeatedly searched for him
but never saw him again.
He then opened the pouch to look inside
and found, wrapped in layers of paper, a gourd seed
containing nine pills of medicine,
resembling hemp or millet grains.
Following the Daoist priest's oral instructions, he swallowed them
and immediately felt spiritually invigorated, free from hunger,
his body light and clear.
He crossed the river and traveled to Máo Mountain.
After a long time,
he went again to Zhānggōng Cave in Yíxīng.
During his travels,
he grew fond of the scenery of Yǎnhuà Creek
and thus built a dwelling at Húfùzhǔ,
secluding himself in the mountains.
Woodcutters nearby still saw him
and said:
The character "said" was originally missing,
supplemented according to *The Seven Slips of a Cloudy Satchel*, scroll 113.
"I am Gentleman Liú."
But none knew where he ultimately settled.
He had already become an earth immortal.
From *Continued Biographies of Immortals*
Emperor Táng Xiànzōng
Lǐ Qiú was
a man from Yān.
In the second year of the Bǎolì era,
he traveled with his friend Liú Shēng to Mount Wǔtái.
On the mountain was a wind cave;
if travelers made even slight noise
or threw objects to strike it,
a great wind would immediately erupt,
ripping off roofs and uprooting trees,
and they would inevitably suffer harm.
Therefore, when climbing the mountain,
people warned each other not to touch it.
When Qiú reached the cave entrance,
he playfully threw a huge rock into the cave.
After a long while,
the sound of the rock finally ceased,
and indeed a swift wind rushed forth,
carrying out a log like a pillar
that flew out with the wind.
Qiú was bold and reckless,
with no regard for caution,
so he forcefully grabbed the log,
but fell into the cave instead.
Carried by the log,
Qiú could not get out either.
After a long while, he reached the ground
and saw a creature shaped like a lion but speaking human language,
who led Qiú into a chamber within the cave,
where two Daoist priests were playing chess.
The priests were pleased to see Qiú
and asked him about the path of cultivation he practiced.
Qiú had never known anything about cultivation practices,
so he remained silent, unable to respond.
The two immortals reprimanded the guide, saying:
"The essence of our supreme Dao
should be imparted to those with the bone structure of a worthy,
to those who practice the Dao;
why have you recklessly brought an ordinary mortal
into our immortal abode?
Quickly lead him away."
They then gave him a cup of water to drink,
saying to him:
"Although you are a mortal,
you have glimpsed our cave abode
and tread upon our true realm;
this means you have some affinity with the Dao.
It is regrettable that you have never practiced the Dao,
so we cannot speak to you of the essentials of cultivation.
But go now;
if you harbor a heart that yearns for life
and a will to transcend the world,
you may return another day.
Drink this divine elixir,
and it will also extend your years and longevity."
Qiú drank the water and bowed in thanks.
The guide then took Qiú to the side of the cave from earlier
and showed him another path, saying:
"This mountain is the Daoist Zǐfǔ Cave.
Upon its five peaks,
rare treasures from the four seas are placed to stabilize the summits.
It is like the Máo Mountain Cave,
which is stabilized by treasures from the Golden Rampart City of Ānxī.
Spring mountains with variegated jade,
encircling waters with fragrant jade,
secure the dwellings of the highest perfected ones.
The eastern peak of this mountain has the Líyuè Fire Orb,
the western peak has the Lìnóng Jade Chamber,
the southern peak has the Dòngguāng Pearl Tree,
the northern peak has the Jade Ravine and Exquisite Fungus,
and the central peak has self-illuminating gold and the ring-light jade.
Whenever accumulated gloom is about to disperse,
or prolonged heat is about to bring rain,
the many treasures shine with intersecting lights,
illuminating the cliffs and ridges.
On spring dawns and autumn mornings,
nine-colored qi connects to the heavens,
its radiance shimmering beyond the clouds.
The Great Emperor commanded Hán Sī Shǎoqīng, Dōngfāng Jūn, and Master Zǐfǔ,
leading six thousand immortal officials, divine kings, and powerful warriors,
to guard this place;
thus it is called the abode of immortals.
The cave has three gates:
one path leads west to Kūnlún,
one path emerges beneath this cliff,
and one leads to the wind cave from earlier,
which is the main gate of the cave.
All are guarded by dragons and serpents.
The master decreed:
'If a huge rock is thrown into the cave gate
and strikes our pillar,
it means that in the mortal world, there will be one who attains the Dao,
and will receive duties here.'
Thus, I was to bring him in.
I, too, have long studied the Dao
and am destined to attain immortal rank;
but aside from accumulated merits,
I have not eliminated the karma of speech,
and due to merits from past lives,
I have been assigned to guard this cave entrance.
After three hundred years,
I too shall ascend.
Because of the karma of speech,
I have taken this form.
I followed the master's command:
when the gate was struck by a rock hitting the pillar,
I guided you according to the teaching,
truly unaware that you had playfully thrown the rock.
Yet for hundreds of years,
few have thrown rocks,
and none have ever struck the pillar.
The palace of immortals
is not easily reached;
you too shall gain something from the profound and mysterious ford.
Here is the path of the northern cliff,
which can allow you to quickly return to the human world."
He then untied three pills of medicine from his sash,
threaded them onto the end of a withered branch,
and said to Qiú:
"If you see strange creatures along the path,
point the medicine at them, and they will not harm you;
if you consume this medicine,
you can remain free from illness."
Qiú took the medicine
and walked through the dark parts of the cave;
the medicine glowed like fire.
Several times, giant serpents
opened their mouths toward Qiú,
but when he pointed the medicine at them,
they cowered and dared not move.
Thus, he exited the cave gate.
Outside the gate, an ancient tree was half-rotted,
and the cave was about to be blocked.
Qiú broke through the soil and the rotten tree,
and after a long while, finally emerged,
already outside the temple gate.
Earlier,
after Liú Shēng had lost Qiú,
Qiú's son had accused Liú Shēng,
suspecting he had harmed his father,
and intended to take him to court.
The temple was holding a grand feast,
so they could not leave immediately.
When they saw Qiú return,
everyone rejoiced.
Qiú recounted the wonders he had seen.
He then took the three pills of medicine
and gave one each to Liú and his son to consume.
During the Qiánfú era,
Jìnshì Sītú Tiě, who had parted with Qiú over thirty years earlier,
at which time Qiú was sixty years old
with a white beard hanging down,
met Qiú in Hédōng.
Qiú was now over ninety years old,
but his appearance was like that of a thirty-year-old.
Speaking of his encounter,
he said:
"Since taking the medicine,
I have grown old but regained youth,
and my nature is such that I do not eat."
His son also looked about thirty years old
and was determined to cultivate the Dao.
He and his son went into Mount Wángwū.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí."
Sòng Xuánbái
is of unknown origin
and was a Daoist priest.
He stood over seven feet tall,
with features as if painted,
handsome, plump, and fair,
and elegant,
so that everyone who saw him adored him.
He possessed Daoist arts
and often roamed famous mountains.
Starting from the Xīxuán Temple in Rùnzhōu on Máoshān,
he later traveled to Kuòcāng and Xiāndū.
He practiced grain avoidance and breath cultivation,
yet he was fond of wine
and sometimes ate five catties of pork.
With a bowl of garlic paste,
he would pick up the meat with his hands and finish it,
then drink two dou of wine,
accompanied by a single white plum.
Those who managed to obtain a piece of his garlic to eat
said it carried no garlic odor,
and its flavor was exceptionally fine,
with a fragrance that lingered in the mouth all day without fading.
Many people obtained and ate his garlic,
and they remained free of illness throughout their lives,
living to eighty or ninety years of age.
Wherever Xuánbái went,
he would use gold and silk to acquire two or three beautiful concubines to live with,
but when he departed, he would leave them behind.
People believed he possessed the art of replenishing the brain and restoring vitality, like Lǎo Péng.
He also traveled to Yuèzhōu,
where a great drought occurred.
The locals were exposing the crippled and praying to dragons for rain,
but after ten days,
the scorching sun grew even more intense.
Seeing this, Xuánbái
believed that all rainfall
must await the Mandate of Heaven,
and without a memorial to the heavens, it could not be summoned.
Thus, at the Xuánzhēn Temple where he was staying,
he burned incense and offered prayers upward.
Overnight, a heavy downpour came,
and the rain proved sufficient.
The people of Yuèzhōu regarded him as profoundly miraculous.
Traveling further south to Fǔzhōu,
he again encountered a drought and prayers for rain.
A Daoist priest there knew Xuánbái could summon rain,
and the people of the prefecture requested his help.
He promptly performed a technique, flying nails into both eyes of the City God.
The prefect, Wéi Délín,
found it strange that he kept women and also nailed the City God,
considering such acts madness,
and intended to reprimand and humiliate him.
When the strong attendants tried to approach him,
their hands and feet became immobile,
and they all fell down on their own,
with shackles and canes breaking by themselves.
Xuánbái laughed and said to Délín:
"Does the Prefect wish to offend Liú Gēn
and bring punishment upon your ancestors?"
Only then did Délín become frightened and beg for forgiveness.
Shortly after, rain was brought,
and he sent Xuánbái off with courtesy.
His miraculous arts were frequently displayed,
too many to record in full.
Later, in Nánchéng County,
he ascended to the heavens in broad daylight and departed.
From "Continued Biographies of Immortals."
Xǔ Qīyán
was a man from Qíyáng.
He had passed the imperial examination,
and studied at the Hàotiān Temple.
Every morning and evening,
he would always gaze upon the true images,
praying to the spiritual immortals,
hoping for the blessing of longevity.
At that time, the Grand Marshal Wéi Gāo of Nánkāng was governing Shǔ,
and he welcomed guests,
so many from near and far admired his righteousness,
and there were many who traveled to Shǔ.
Qīyán planned to go to Shǔ,
and wanted to buy a horse, but his funds were not abundant,
so he went to the West Market to look for one.
There was a foreigner leading a horse,
thin and not expensive,
so he bought it and returned.
Because he was about to travel a long distance,
he fed it extra fodder daily,
but its flesh grew even thinner,
and he doubted it could reach the destination.
He tried going to a divination shop to have a reading done,
and got the hexagram Qián, ninth line, fifth position.
The Daoist said:
"This is a dragon horse,
you should treasure it well."
When he ascended the dangerous plank road of the Shǔ route,
Qīyán and the horse
both fell off the cliff,
but a pile of leaves caught them,
fortunately without injury.
Looking up, he could not see the top,
and the paths on all four sides were cut off.
Having no plan,
he removed the saddle and bridle,
and let the horse go wherever it wanted.
In the dry leaves, he found chestnuts as big as fists,
Qīyán ate them,
and was no longer hungry.
Following along the base of the cliff,
he saw a cave opening,
and walked, riding the horse,
sometimes descending, sometimes ascending,
for about over ten lǐ,
and suddenly reached a flat plain.
The flowers and trees were beautiful and unusual,
and the ponds were clear and pure.
There was a Daoist lying on a stone,
with two female attendants serving him.
Qīyán approached and requested an audience,
asking the two jade maidens,
who said it was the True Lord Tàiyǐ.
Qīyán then told the jade maidens about his journey.
The jade maidens took pity on him.
They reported to the True Lord.
He said:
"You, in the human world,
do you also like the Dao?"
He replied:
"I have only read the Zhuāngzi, Lǎozǐ, and Huángtíng."
He said:
"Among the three classics,
what lines have you grasped?"
He answered:
Lǎozǐ says:
"Its essence is very true."
Zhuāngzi says:
"Breathe through the heels."
Huángtíng says:
"Just think to repel and have endless longevity."
He laughed and said:
"You are close to the Dao,
you can be taught."
He invited him to sit,
poured a small cup and gave it to him to drink, saying:
"This is stone marrow,
Jī Kāng could not get near it,
but you have obtained it."
Then he invited him into another room.
There was a Daoist,
who was said to be the Venerable Master of Yǐngyáng,
calculating for the True Lord,
saying that tonight he would travel east for a hundred thousand lǐ.
Qīyán looked at him carefully,
and it was the horse-divining Daoist.
That evening,
Qīyán and the Venerable Master of Yǐngyáng followed the True Lord Tàiyǐ up onto the stone bridge of the West Dragon Mountain in the Eastern Sea,
to attend the gathering of the assembled immortals.
Among the seated immortal guests was Dōnghuáng Jūn,
who saw Qīyán and happily said:
"He is the grandson of Magistrate Xǔ,
he has the appearance of an immortal."
When it was dawn,
he again followed the True Lord Tàiyǐ back to the Tàibái Cave,
stayed for half a month,
then thought of home and asked to return.
Tàiyǐ said:
"You have drunk the stone marrow,
and are already a thousand years old,
do not lose it,
do not be dissolute,
come back here again to meet."
He gave him the horse he rode to send him off.
As he was about to leave,
he said to him:
"This horse is a dragon from my cave,
because it got angry and damaged crops,
it was punished to bear burdens.
You have immortal bones,
so you encountered it;
otherwise,
this Tàibái Cave Heaven,
this Jade Flower Upper Palace,
how could you have come here?
When you reach the human world,
release it at the Wèi River bend,
let it go where it wishes,
do not keep it again."
After parting,
in a short while he had reached Guó County,
but there was no longer his old home.
He asked the villagers,
and it had been sixty years.
When he left the cave,
the two jade maidens had asked him to buy a needle from Granny Tián of Guó County.
So he bought it,
tied it to the horse's saddle with a staff,
removed the saddle and released it,
and it transformed into a dragon and left.
Qīyán had seen Granny Tián
when he was young in his hometown,
and here only Granny Tián's appearance was as before,
so she too was an immortal.
In the last years of the Dàzhōng era,
Qīyán again entered Tàibái Mountain and left.
From "Chuánqí"
Wéi Shànjùn
Wéi Shànjùn
was a man from Dùlíng, Jīngzhào.
He traveled around visiting the Dao,
searching all the famous mountains.
He encountered an immortal,
who taught him the texts of the Three Sovereigns for summoning,
and he obtained the way of divine transformation.
Sometimes he quietly dwelled in the forests and wilds,
sometimes he lay drunk on the road.
He often carried a dog,
calling it Wūlóng.
Wherever he went,
he would always share his own food to feed it.
The dog also had mange,
its fur all fell off,
and everyone disliked and despised it.
His elder brother was a monk,
who had long lived at the Sōng Temple,
and was the most senior elder.
Shànjùn was about to ascend to heaven,
when he suddenly said to people:
"I have a small debt not yet repaid."
So he entered the mountain to see his brother.
The monks, because he was the elder's brother,
who had returned after many years,
respected and served him even more.
Every time he went up to the hall for the meal,
he would lead the dog by his side,
and share his food with it.
The monks already disliked it,
and reported it to the elder.
The elder was angry,
summoned him and scolded him,
struck him a dozen times with the rod,
and expelled him from the temple.
Shànjùn bowed and thanked him, saying:
"My old debt is already repaid,
I will not come back again from now on."
He further requested a bath,
and then would leave.
He was allowed.
After bathing for a while,
he led the dog away.
The dog had already grown to six or seven chǐ,
and when they walked to the front of the hall,
the dog transformed into a dragon,
tens of zhàng long,
and Shànjùn rode the dragon and ascended to heaven.
It grasped the corner of the hall,
and the traces are still there.
From "Xiānzhuàn Shíyí"
Lǐ Jífǔ
Grand Mentor Lǐ Jífǔ,
while in Huáinán,
encountered a widespread epidemic within the prefecture.
Lord Lǐ did not drink wine,
nor did he listen to music.
It happened that an imperial envoy arrived,
and he had no choice but to host a banquet,
yet his face showed deep sorrow and distress.
When the banquet concluded,
he addressed the guests, saying:
"Within this humble territory, a severe epidemic rages,
with deaths following one after another.
What methods do you, esteemed gentlemen, have to offer rescue?"
A scholar seated below rose and responded:
"I recently left Chǔzhōu,
where there is a Master Wáng,
who claims to have come from Tàibái Mountain,
to aid and relieve the illnesses in Jiāng-Huái,
abstaining from grains and practicing breath cultivation,
his spirit and bones are exceptionally pure.
Many have already been healed by him."
Lord Lǐ was greatly pleased,
invited him to the seat of honor,
and questioned him further.
He then ordered a letter to be written,
along with a personal note.
He dispatched men and horses to fetch him.
After ten days, he arrived,
and was lodged in the prefectural residence,
where Lord Lǐ addressed him as a disciple to seek his help.
Master Wáng said:
"Your Excellency need only gather many large cauldrons and giant pots in the marketplace,
assemble all the sick,
and there is no doubt they will be cured."
Lord Lǐ immediately ordered these preparations.
Once they were ready,
Master Wáng went,
and had the concoction boiled thick.
Those severely ill drank it freely,
while the lightly ill drank slightly less,
and after sweating, all recovered.
Lord Lǐ was delighted,
and offered him gold and silk,
but he declined.
He did not eat,
and spoke little.
He only followed the former Shānnán Jiedushi and Chancellor Wáng Qǐ,
and whenever Wáng was seated,
he would sit and speak with a smile,
as if they were old acquaintances.
Lord Lǐ then had Wáng invite him to stay overnight at his residence,
and asked what he desired,
but he spoke only a word and then departed.
Late at night, he said calmly:
"The Judge possesses immortal bones,
and if you study the Dao, you will surely ascend to heaven in broad daylight.
What do you think?"
Wáng remained silent.
After a long while, he said:
"This is merely the entanglement of worldly attachments.
If you remain in the mortal world,
there is no official position you cannot attain."
Wáng asked to treat him as an elder brother.
He also said:
"My original master resides at Báilù,
and he is also of the same family as the Judge.
Could you accompany me to pay him a visit?"
Wáng again hesitated.
He asked:
"What is the immortal master's name?"
He replied:
"My master dares not speak it?"
He then took a brush and wrote the character for "crane."
From then on, Master Wáng's whereabouts were unknown.
Wáng indeed attained great wealth and honor.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Lǐ Shēn
Therefore, the former Huáihǎi military governor Lǐ Shēn,
when young, once stayed with two friends in a cottage on the Western Mountain of Huàyīn.
One evening,
an old man from the forest who was holding a ritual to repay the gods came to invite them.
As it happened, Lǐ Shēn had a headache ailment,
so he did not go,
but his two friends attended.
At midnight, the thunder and rain grew fierce.
Lǐ Shēn entered and settled in an inner room.
Suddenly, he heard the sound of someone earnestly praying in the front hall.
Slowly rising, he peeked through the curtain
and saw an old man
with white eyebrows and beard,
sitting on the eastern bed.
A young blue-clad attendant,
holding an incense burner,
stood respectfully behind him.
Lǐ Shēn was astonished,
and in his heart, he knew this was an extraordinary being.
He put on his robe and shoes and went out to bow to him.
The elder said:
"Young man, do you recognize me?"
He replied:
"This humble youth has never had the honor of meeting you."
The old man said:
"I am Táng Ruòshān.
Have you heard my name?"
He replied:
"I have seen it among the records of immortals."
The old man said:
"I have long resided in the Northern Sea.
Tonight, the immortals of the Southern Sea are gathering at Luófú Mountain,
and I am going there.
Passing this place,
I encountered dragons fighting over Huà Mountain,
scattering rain throughout the sky.
As one who takes elixirs,
I do not wish to let it soak my clothes,
so I am resting here.
Are you not Lǐ Shēn?"
He replied:
"My surname is Lǐ,
but my given name is not Shēn."
The old man said.
The characters "the old man said" were originally missing,
and are supplemented based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.
"You are destined to be named Shēn,
styled Gōngchuí,
and are already recorded in the register.
Can you accompany me on a journey to Luófú?"
Lǐ Shēn said:
"It is the wish of my lifetime."
The old man was pleased.
After a while,
the wind and rain cleared.
The blue-clad attendant announced they could depart.
The old man then drew from his sleeve a slip,
shaped like a tablet.
Pulling it lengthwise,
it stretched over ten feet long.
Pulling it widthwise,
it widened several feet.
Folding and curling its bottom into a hollow,
it took the form of a boat.
The elder boarded and sat at the front,
had Lǐ Shēn sit in the middle,
and the blue-clad attendant sat at the rear.
The elder warned Lǐ Shēn:
"Close your eyes quickly,
and be careful not to peek."
Lǐ Shēn then closed his eyes.
He only felt wind and waves surging violently,
as if sailing on rivers and seas.
In a short while, the boat stopped.
The elder said:
"You may open your eyes now."
They were already before a mountain,
with towers and palaces rising unevenly,
misty as if beyond the heavens.
The sound of pipes and flutes
resounded clearly amid the clouds.
Over ten dignified and elegant scholars
happily greeted the elder.
Pointing at Lǐ Shēn, they said:
"Who is this?"
The elder said:
"It is Lǐ Shēn."
The group of scholars said:
"How extraordinary!
Gōngchuí has indeed come.
The mortal world is ordinary and turbid,
the sea of suffering is not shallow.
Unless one's name is tied to the immortal records,
by what path could one come here?"
The elder had Lǐ Shēn bow to each of them in turn.
The group of scholars said:
"Can you follow us?"
Lǐ Shēn said:
"Shēn has not yet established a family,
and cannot decline.
But I fear I might, like Huáng Chūpíng, cause worry for my brothers."
Before he finished speaking,
the group of scholars already knew:
"You long to return;
you should not enter this dwelling.
Although your name is recorded among the immortals,
your worldly dust is still heavy.
In this life, you will still sink in the realm of illusions.
A fine reputation and high office—
externally, you will attain them all.
Maintain integrity and cultivate stillness.
In your next life, once you come of age,
you will then reside here.
Strive hard! Strive hard!"
Lǐ Shēn again bowed to each of them and prepared to return with the elder.
After bidding farewell,
he closed his eyes.
There was a creature resembling a donkey.
It approached, and he mounted it.
Again, he felt as if running atop wind and waves.
After a moment,
he felt extremely stifled and wished to see.
As soon as he opened his eyes,
he fell to the ground and lost his mount.
Looking up at the Milky Way,
it was nearly the fifth watch.
He seemed to be north of Huà Mountain.
Walking slowly for several li,
he came upon a travelers' lodge,
which was the Luófú Inn.
It was over twenty li from where he had stayed.
He returned at a leisurely pace.
The next day,
his two friends and servants were just rushing about searching for him
when they met, greatly rejoicing.
They asked where he had gone.
He falsely claimed:
"Alone at night,
I was momentarily beguiled by a fox demon,
and followed to its dwelling.
As dawn approached,
I came to my senses and returned."
From then on, he changed his name to Shēn,
styled Gōngchuí.
Indeed, he passed the highest imperial examination and entered the Hanlin Academy,
served successively as a prefectural governor,
and held the weighty positions of both general and minister.
From "Xù Xuánguài Lù"
Bái Lètiān
In the first year of the Huìcháng era of the Táng dynasty,
Lǐ Shījì, the Vice Censor-in-Chief, served as the Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèdōng.
A merchant encountered a storm while sailing,
and did not know where he had drifted.
After more than a month,
he reached a great mountain.
There were auspicious clouds and exotic flowers,
white cranes and unusual trees,
all unseen in the human world.
Someone by the mountain greeted him and asked:
"How did you manage to come here?"
He explained in detail.
They instructed him to moor his boat and come ashore.
Saying:
"You must pay respects to the Celestial Master."
They then led him to a place,
resembling a large temple or monastery,
and escorted him through a passage
(Míng manuscript adds "priest" after "passage")
to enter.
The Daoist priest's beard and eyebrows were completely white.
He had several dozen attendants.
Sitting in the great hall,
he spoke to him, saying:
"You are a man of the Middle Kingdom.
Only by having a karmic connection with this place could you arrive here once.
This is Pénglái Mountain.
Since you have come,
would you like to have a look?"
He ordered his attendants to guide him on a tour inside the palace.
Jade terraces and emerald trees,
their brilliance dazzling to the eyes.
There were several dozen courtyards and buildings,
each with a name.
Arriving at one courtyard,
its gate was tightly locked and secured.
He peeked inside.
Flowers filled the courtyard,
the hall had cushions and mats,
with incense burning below the steps.
The guest asked about it.
They replied:
"This is Bái Lètiān's courtyard.
Lètiān has not yet come from the Middle Kingdom."
He secretly memorized this,
then bid farewell and returned.
After ten days he reached Yuè,
and reported everything in detail to the Surveillance Commissioner.
Commissioner Lǐ recorded it all and reported it to Lord Bái.
Previously,
Lord Bái in his lifetime had only cultivated the practice of the higher stages (of Buddhist practice).
Upon reading Commissioner Lǐ's report,
he then composed two poems himself,
to record the event and reply to Lǐ of Zhèdōng, saying:
"Recently someone returned from the sea,
seeing towers deep within the sea mountains.
Among them, a celestial niche
(Míng manuscript has "niche" instead of "cage")
opens a chamber;
all say this awaits Lètiān's coming."
He also said:
"I study the Empty Gate, not the way of immortals;
I fear your words are but empty tales.
The sea mountains are not my place of return;
to return, I should return to the Tuṣita Heaven."
Yet Lord Bái cast off worldly dust like worn-out shoes,
abandoned carriage and official cap,
and certainly differed from those who are deluded and ignorant.
How do we know he was not an immortal banished to earth?
From "Yì Shǐ"
Master Xuānyuán
Master Xuānyuán Jí of Luófú,
though over several hundred years old,
his complexion showed no decline.
Standing before the bed,
his hair would hang down to the ground;
sitting in a dark room,
the light from his eyes could extend several feet.
Whenever he gathered herbs in deep cliffs and steep valleys,
poisonous dragons and fierce tigers would guard him.
If common households prepared vegetarian meals to invite him,
even to a hundred places in a single day,
he could divide his body and arrive at all.
If drinking with others,
he would take out a flask from his sleeve,
which could only hold two or three shēng,
yet even with a full gathering of guests,
pouring from it all day would not exhaust it.
If someone urged him to drink,
he could consume a hundred dǒu without becoming drunk.
At night, he would hang his hair into a basin,
and wine would drip out,
the aroma of the fermented grains
