never diminishing or dissipating.
Traveling with hunters,
if there were those not among his companions,
moments later a dozen or so would appear,
identical in appearance and manner without distinction.
Sometimes he would cast red talismans into the air,
and they could reach a thousand lǐ;
the sick would wipe themselves with a cloth towel,
and all would be cured instantly.
Emperor Xuānzōng of Táng summoned him to the inner court,
treating him with great favor.
He then asked:
"Can the way of longevity be attained?"
Jí said:
"Cease music and sensual pleasures,
abandon rich flavors,
make sorrow and joy as one,
spread virtue without bias,
naturally unite your virtue with heaven and earth,
match your brightness with the sun and moon,
attain the way of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng;
as for the arts of longevity and enduring vision,
how could they be difficult?"
He also asked how the Master's way compared to Zhāng Guǒ's.
He said:
"I do not know other aspects,
only that I am younger than Guǒ."
When he withdrew,
the Emperor sent palace ladies to fetch a golden basin, covering a white magpie to test him.
Jí was resting in his quarters,
when he suddenly said to the eunuch attendant:
"How can the Emperor again order this old man to divine what is covered?"
The eunuch did not understand his words.
At that time, Emperor Xuānzōng summoned him to come quickly.
As soon as he reached the jade steps,
he said:
"The white magpie under the basin,
you should release it early."
Emperor Xuānzōng laughed and said:
"The Master already knew long ago!"
He sat before the imperial couch.
Emperor Xuānzōng ordered palace attendants to serve hot tea.
One who laughed at Jí's ancient, plain appearance,
with glossy black hair and red lips,
aged just sixteen,
in a moment turned into an old woman,
with chicken-like skin and hunchback,
hair at her temples like silk threads,
weeping profusely before Emperor Xuānzōng.
Emperor Xuānzōng, knowing the palace woman's fault,
ordered her to apologize to the Master,
and her appearance returned to its former state.
Emperor Xuānzōng then remarked that the capital lacked cardamom and lychee flowers.
In a moment, both flowers appeared with leaves attached,
each nearly a hundred blossoms,
fresh, bright, fragrant, and clean,
as if just plucked.
He also tasted and bestowed mandarin oranges.
He said:
"The ones from my mountain,
have a flavor surpassing these."
Emperor Xuānzōng said:
"I cannot obtain them."
Jí then took a green jade bowl from before the Emperor,
and covered it with a precious tray.
Moments later he removed the tray,
and the mandarin oranges arrived,
filling the hall with fragrance,
their size very large.
Emperor Xuānzōng ate them,
marveling at their unparalleled sweetness and deliciousness.
He further asked:
"For how many years will I reign as Son of Heaven?"
He immediately took a brush and wrote:
"Forty years."
But the character for "ten" had a jumping stroke.
Emperor Xuānzōng laughed and said:
"How dare I hope for forty years?"
When he passed away,
it was fourteen
("Fourteen" originally "forty,"
corrected according to "Dù Yáng Xīn Biān")
years.
When he first took leave to return to the mountains,
from Cháng'ān to Jiānglíng,
from a cloth sack,
he took out copper coins to give to the poor,
amounting to several hundred thousand.
A palace envoy followed him,
not knowing the reason.
Suddenly he vanished from his location,
leaving the envoy frightened and uneasy.
Several days later,
Nánhǎi reported that the Master had returned to Luófú Mountain.
From "Dù Yáng Piān"
Lǐ Yuán
Lǐ Yuán, the Remonstrance Official,
once lived in seclusion in a thatched cottage on Mount Sōng.
During the cold winter,
he lit a fire facing the door.
An old man wearing a large hat
walked straight in to warm his feet.
After a long while, he asked Lǐ,
"Could you perhaps go with me?
I know you have the aspiration."
He then said of himself,
"I am a eunuch from the Qín dynasty,
who avoided calamity and attained the Way."
He then removed his hat,
revealing a magnificent beard and whiskers,
saying,
"These all grew while I was in the mountains."
Lǐ pondered for a long time,
then replied,
"My family affairs are not yet settled.
Could I go in a few days?"
The old man rose abruptly and said,
"So that is your intention!"
He then went out the door and left directly.
Lǐ tugged at his sleeve, ashamed and apologetic,
but could not detain him even briefly.
The next day, Lǐ searched for him,
but found no trace at all.
From Yì Shǐ (The Lost History)
Wéi Qīngcái
Lú Yuángōng revered the Way.
In his leisure time, when conversing with guests and friends,
he would always talk about matters of immortals.
He said,
"I have a cousin, Wéi Qīngcái.
During the Dàhé era,
he was selected and appointed as a county magistrate in Jiānghuái.
On the day he left the capital to take up his post,
relatives and friends saw him off.
When parting from Bà Chǎn,
it was already dusk.
After traveling ten or twenty lǐ,
he felt the road gradually becoming different,
not like the routes he usually passed.
Looking ahead into the distance,
he saw the appearance of bright lamps and candles,
with lush, verdant trees,
seemingly not of the mortal world.
After a short while,
someone approached in front of his horse,
like an attendant official of a prefecture or county,
and asked Wéi,
"How did you get here?
This is not the mundane world."
Moments later,
another person arrived,
and said to the one who had approached earlier,
"Since he has arrived,
we must quickly report to Shànggōng."
Wéi asked,
"What rank and position is Shànggōng?"
The attendant did not reply,
but turned and hurried away.
After a short delay,
suddenly a voice called out repeatedly,
"Shànggōng has arrived?"
Wéi dismounted from his horse
and hurried through the gate.
Inside were lofty buildings with carved walls,
layered corridors and multiple pavilions,
with stern and solemn guards,
comparable to those of princes and marquises.
He saw a man about forty years old,
wearing a flat-topped headscarf
and plain clothes,
who said to Wéi from a distance,
"Ascend the steps."
Wéi bowed and went up.
He was invited to sit,
and after being comforted and greeted for a long time,
there were still no offerings of food, wine, soup, or fruit.
The man slowly said to Wéi,
"Due to the chaos of the world,
with the hundred schools contending,
I fled and took refuge here.
The crowd pushed me to be their leader,
forcibly calling me Shànggōng.
Since then, several hundred years have passed,
with no commands or restraints issued,
but simply letting things follow their natural course.
For you to have reached this place
is a fortunate event from the mundane world.
You cannot stay long;
you should leave quickly."
He ordered ten bolts of silk to be given as a gift.
Wéi went out the door, mounted his horse,
and tried to find the old road.
Looking back, he saw nothing.
In the middle of the night, under the hazy moon,
he walked wherever his feet took him.
By dawn,
he was already on the official road.
He rested briefly at an inn.
When he inquired with people,
none knew of the place.
He took out the silk to look at it;
it was glossy, white, and reflective.
Wéi then wrapped it up and entered the capital,
visited relatives and friends,
and fully recounted the event.
He then divided the silk to give to his beloved ones.
Wéi said,
"Estimating the location,
it was between Mount Lí and Lántián,
likely an earthly immortal."
From Shàngshū Gùshí (Anecdotes of the Minister)
Pān Zūnshī
The Dàoshì Pān Zūnshī of Mount Sōng, named Fǎzhèng,
was a Dàoshì of high attainment.
During the Táng dynasty's Kāiyuán era,
he said to his disciple Sīmǎ Liànshī,
"Táo Hóngjǐng became the Earl of Mount Sōng,
and it has been a hundred years now.
Recently, he requested a replacement from the Supreme Emperor,
and the Emperor ordered him to recommend someone he knew as a successor.
Hóngjǐng recommended me.
The records have already been settled;
I cannot remain in the human world much longer."
Within a few days,
he departed by means of shījiě (corpse liberation).
Later, west of the Sōngyáng Temple in Dēngfēng County,
there was a dragon pool.
A resident named Zhāng Chān
was washing his private parts at the pool
when he was suddenly seized by someone.
After being taken for several lǐ,
he arrived at a grand mansion.
In front of the gate were many dragons.
Entering the gate and walking over ten paces,
there was a large hall,
where he saw Fǎzhèng sitting in the hall.
Holding a vermilion brush and managing documents,
he asked Chān,
"You are from beside the temple;
do you recognize me?"
Chān said,
"I do.
You are Pān Zūnshī."
Fǎzhèng asked Chān,
"Why did you defile the dragons' dwelling?"
Chān repeatedly bowed and apologized.
Fǎzhèng asked again,
"Do you know Dàoshì Sīmǎ?"
Chān said,
"I know him."
Fǎzhèng said,
"I will now release you to return."
He then took a white feather fan from the table
and said to Chān,
"Take this for me to Dàoshì Sīmǎ.
Why does he not come, clinging instead to the pleasures of the world?"
He had someone escort Chān out onto the water.
Chān saw his own corpse lying on the bank,
felt disgusted in his heart,
and suddenly, as if in a dream,
he revived.
When Dàoshì Sīmǎ saw the feather fan,
he wept sorrowfully and said,
"This is what my master always held;
when he passed, it was placed in his coffin.
Now that you have brought it,
it clearly shows my master's presence is not false."
He then went deep into the mountains
and passed away after several years.
From Guǎng Yì Jì (Extensive Records of the Extraordinary)
Lǐ Hè
Lǒngxī Lǐ Hè, styled Chángjí,
was the grandson of the Prince of Zhèng of the Táng dynasty.
From a young age, he was capable in literature,
and was especially skilled at composing yuèfǔ lyrics,
with novel ideas and beautiful language.
Among those proficient in lyrics at the time,
none dared to rank alongside Hè,
and thus his fame spread throughout the land.
Because his father's name was Jìnsù,
he was consequently unable to take the imperial examinations.
He died while serving as an official in the Tàicháng bureau,
at the age of twenty-four.
His late mother, née Zhèng,
had deeply missed her son.
After Hè's death,
the lady's grief was inconsolable.
One night, she dreamed that Hè came to her,
just as he had been in life,
and said to the lady:
"I was fortunate to be your son,
and you missed me so deeply.
Therefore, from childhood I followed my parents' instructions,
studied poetry and books,
and wrote essays.
The reason for doing so
was not merely to seek an official position and adorn myself;
rather, I wished to glorify our family clan
and repay your kindness, lady.
Who could have expected that I would die one day,
unable to serve you morning and evening?
Is this not Heaven's will!
However, although I have died,
it is not truly death,
but a command from the Supreme Emperor."
The lady inquired about the matter.
Hè said:
"The Supreme Emperor resides in the dwelling of immortals.
Recently, he moved his capital to the Moon Garden,
constructed a new palace,
and named it 'White Jade.'
Because I excelled in lyrics,
he summoned me and several other literary scholars
to jointly compose a record for the new palace.
The Emperor also built the Níngxū Hall,
and had us compile musical compositions.
Now I am among the immortals,
very happy.
I hope you, lady, will not worry about me."
After that, he bid farewell and left.
The lady awoke,
and found the dream most extraordinary.
From then on, her grief somewhat eased.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
Zhāng Jífǔ
During the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
in a county under Qīngzhōu,
Zhāng Jífǔ and Chén Yòuxiá lived together while studying.
One night, they both dreamed of going to a place,
where they saw several Daoist priests,
who ordered Jífǔ and the others to inscribe a stele.
The inscription read:
"The Master of the Cānglóng Stream, Ōuyáng Mǒu, composed the True Formula of the Supreme Sovereign."
The characters were in seal script,
slightly different from the usual.
Jífǔ and the others remembered four lines, which went:
"In the past, I rode a fish-drawn carriage;
now I tread on auspicious clouds.
Treading the void, I gaze upon the path;
intricate and magnificent, like coiled clouds."
The postscript read:
"Officials of the Five Clouds Library: Chén Yòuxiá, Zhāng Jífǔ."
At dawn,
the two spoke of it together,
and their accounts were entirely the same.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Zhèng Cè
Zhèng Cè, the Prefect of Wēnzhōu,
was fond of the arts of Huáng-Lǎo,
and often practiced them in secret.
Due to illness,
he personally saw over three hundred female immortals.
They said:
"We have come to welcome you, sir."
He then ordered a feast to be set,
burned incense, and performed obeisance.
He also invited his elder brother Rǎn
to join him in bowing toward the sky.
After a short while,
he ordered five torches to be lit to guide him.
His brother Rǎn and the attendants saw nothing.
The next day at dawn,
again, yáng
(The Míng manuscript has "yáng" as "yīn";
note: "yīn" is the character for "yīn.")
an official came to urge him, saying:
"Your Honor's official fortune has come to an end;
please now ascend the carriage quickly."
He again ordered wine and fruit to be offered in sacrifice,
saying:
"Your Honor has been appointed to a post;
you will assume duties on the first day of the sixth month,
and at noon we shall respectfully welcome you."
Previously,
he had been a friend beyond the mundane world with the Tiāntāi Daoist Jīn Róu.
On that day at mealtime,
Róu came to visit him.
He told Róu of the previous events.
Then, together with Róu, he entered the purification hall to perform obeisance.
He also said:
"I have received an official document."
He reached out into the air to receive it.
He then opened the seal himself,
dipped a brush in the air with his right hand and signed it,
writing six characters himself.
He said to the messenger:
"Since there is a prior agreement,
I will certainly not be late."
Then he said the time had come,
bowed to Jīn Róu and pressed him to sit,
not allowing the four doors to be closed.
He also urged his servant Ā Lù to serve the meal.
He had earlier ordered steamed cakes to be made.
They were still hot.
There were only six or seven plates of dried meat and wine.
He sent his brother Rǎn outside.
The family arranged seven beds.
He said:
"Six yāyá have come to welcome me."
He invited them to sit,
as if repeatedly declining out of courtesy.
He knelt and bowed repeatedly,
then lowered his head and did not rise again.
The family hurried to inform his brother Rǎn and his wife.
After a short while, he passed away,
his body supple,
and his complexion unchanged.
According to "Zhēn Gào,"
those who have performed hidden virtues and are fond of the Dao and believe in immortals
often belong to this category.
Observing the traces of Zhèng's hidden transformation,
the position of emptiness and nothingness
is indeed clear and evident.
From "Yuánhuà Jì"
Chén Huìxū
Chén Huìxū was a man from
Jiāngdōng.
He was a monk
residing at the Guóqīng Temple on Tiāntāi Mountain.
Once, while roaming the mountains with companions,
they playfully crossed a stone bridge.
The water was swift, the moss slippery,
the cascading stream plummeted ten thousand fathoms,
with no bottom in sight below.
All the others trembled with fear and dared not proceed,
but Huìxū alone crossed with transcendent ease.
He went straight up the stone cliff,
and by evening had not returned,
so his companions all left him behind.
Huìxū reached the area beyond the stone cliff,
where there was a faint small path.
Gradually it became level and broad.
He then arrived at palace towers.
Flowers and plants grew in myriads of clusters,
too numerous to identify by sight.
Pavilions and towers connected with the clouds for about ten lǐ.
He saw an inscribed plaque on its gate reading "Huìzhēn Fǔ,"
the plaque on the left gate reading "Jīntíng Gōng,"
and the one on the right reading "Tóngbǎi."
The three gates faced each other, standing like a tripod,
all with golden towers and jade windows,
a hundred zhàng high.
Entering the western side inside the right gate,
there was another tall tower,
with a yellow gate,
its plaque inscribed "Yòubì Gōng."
Looking around, there were several thousand chambers,
winding and interconnected.
Jade steps and stairways,
flowing channels and rushing water,
everywhere was splendid and magnificent.
He nearly forgot to return.
Yet there was not a trace of human presence.
Entering another courtyard,
he saw five or six azure-clad youths,
who glanced at each other, laughing and chatting as they departed.
He questioned them repeatedly.
They replied:
"Ask Zhāng Lǎo."
In a moment, looking back,
he saw an old man approaching, leaning on a staff and holding flowers.
The old man exclaimed in surprise:
"You are a mortal,
how did you suddenly come here?"
Huìxū said:
"I have often heard that beyond the stone bridge lies a Luóhàn temple,
and from the human world, the sound of its bell is sometimes heard.
Thus I came seeking it.
By fortunate encounter with a monk,
I have reached this realm.
I do not know where the Luóhàn are?"
Zhāng Lǎo said:
"This is the blessed courtyard of true immortals,
the lower palace of the Heavenly Emperor,
named the Land of Immortality of Jīntíng,
the numinous realm for nurturing the true self.
Its circumference is one hundred and sixty lǐ.
The Lord Wáng Jūn, the Superior True One of the Right Assistant from Tóngbǎi, governs it.
There are three thousand ranked immortals,
immortal kings and mighty warriors,
heavenly youths and jade maidens—
each ten thousand strong.
It is a place of minor metropolitan gatherings.
The Supreme Elder descends to this palace three times a year,
to examine and rank the merits and deeds of those in the world who study the Dao.
This is a capital of immortals,
not a place for Luóhàn.
Lord Wáng
is the son of King Líng of Zhōu,
a disciple of Master Yáoqiū.
His rank is that of Superior True One."
Huìxū asked:
"Can one learn to become an immortal?"
Zhāng Lǎo said:
"Accumulate merits and virtues,
and the physical body may ascend to heaven.
It lies in steadfast and enduring resolve.
That you have been able to see this blessed courtyard
indicates there is hope for you to learn."
Huìxū asked further:
"Through what gate does one enter to learn immortality?"
Zhāng Lǎo said:
"Internally, preserve the spirit and refine the qì;
externally, ingest elixirs and radiant essences.
Transformation into an immortal
relies on the power of the divine elixir.
You cannot stay here long.
The Superior True One has just gone roaming in the Eastern Sea;
if his mounted guards return,
I fear there may be inquiries and reprimands."
Thereupon, he led him out the gate.
After walking a dozen or so steps,
they were already at Guóqīng Temple.
From then on, Huìxū yearned for the Dao,
and favored cinnabar and minerals.
Though his clothes were worn and his shoes torn through,
he did not consider it shabby.
Hearing of masters of furnace techniques and esoteric arts,
he would go to visit them, no matter the distance.
The expenses for cinnabar and minerals
were certainly great.
In his later years, he resided at the Péngrì Temple on Zhōngnán Mountain.
As he gradually aged,
his desire grew more intense.
Confined to bed by illness for over a month,
he became extremely weak and exhausted.
One day after a heavy rain,
an old man carrying a medicine bag entered the temple,
shouting loudly:
"Selling Great Return Elixirs!"
He circled the corridors several times.
All the monks laughed at him,
then pointed to the door of the sick monk Huìxū,
saying to the old man:
"This old fellow is quite fond of Return Elixirs;
you can sell them to him."
The old man cheerfully went to him.
Huìxū said:
"I know the Return Elixir is a numinous medicine;
how much for one dose?"
The old man said:
"According to what your means allow."
Huìxū said:
"I am old and ill,
bedridden and gravely afflicted for over a month.
Recently, when my turn came in the monks' rotation,
I could not go myself,
so I entrusted a neighboring monk to perform the alms-round on my behalf.
I received a small amount of donation money;
can that suffice for the medicine?"
The old man took his money,
left several pills of medicine,
and taught him the method of taking them.
Huìxū then swallowed them.
The old man then departed.
The monks came together to inquire.
Huìxū said he had bought a Return Elixir
and had swallowed it.
In a short while,
his long illness was completely cured.
From a distance, he stopped the monks, saying:
"Do not come near;
I sense a foul odor.
My illness is cured,
I only need a couple of new garments."
He leaped up from the bed,
with a momentum like flight.
All were astonished and marveled.
Those who had new clothes gave them to him;
he took them and put them on.
Suddenly, he flew up to the hall's roof,
lingered there calmly for some time,
waved his hand in farewell,
and gracefully ascended to heaven and departed.
This was in the wǔyín year of the twelfth year of the Dàzhōng era.
That year, he returned to the Tóngbǎi Temple,
and spoke with fellow Daoists about how he attained the Dao.
He said:
"I am now in the Tóngbǎi Palace;
the old man selling medicine
must have been Zhāng Lǎo."
Having said this, he vanished.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí."
Wēn Jīngzhào
Wēn Zhāng,
served as the governor of Zhèngtiān Prefecture during the Rénchén year of the Xiántōng era in the Táng dynasty.
He was greedy for wealth,
and dared to kill.
People also feared his severity and cruelty, so they did not dare to offend him.
Thus, he gained a reputation for effective governance.
According to the old regulations,
when the governor of the capital went out,
the main roads were cleared,
and the gates of the residential lanes were closed.
Anyone who laughed in front of his procession
would be beaten to death on the spot.
That autumn,
Wēn Gōng came out from Tiānjiē,
heading south toward Wǔmén.
The shouts of his attendants stirred the wind.
There was a Daoist priest, old and hunched,
wearing ragged clothes and dragging a staff,
who was about to cross right through the procession.
The attendants shouted at him but could not stop him.
Wēn Gōng ordered him to be seized,
and he was given twenty lashes on the back.
The priest shook his sleeves and left,
as if feeling no pain.
Wēn found this strange,
so he called an old street official,
ordering him to secretly follow and observe,
to see what the priest would say.
He also instructed the official to question the Daoist priest,
and then track him.
By dusk, the priest passed through Lánlíng Lane,
entered a small alley to the south,
where there was a simple gate—
his dwelling place.
The official followed him inside.
Several Daoist priests came out to greet him with great reverence,
saying:
"Why is the True Lord so late?"
He replied:
"I was humiliated by a cruel man.
Prepare hot water."
The Daoist priests led the way,
and a young attendant with double buns followed him inside.
The official also followed.
After passing through several gates,
they reached a hall that was splendid and magnificent,
with tall bamboo lining the path,
resembling the grand mansion of a prince.
Before reaching the courtyard,
the True Lord turned and said:
"Why is there the aura of a mundane being?"
The Daoist priests rushed out to search.
The official had nowhere to hide,
so he was captured
and brought before the True Lord.
The official kowtowed and prostrated himself,
fully explaining Wēn's intentions.
The True Lord said angrily:
"This cruel official does not know that disaster will befall his entire clan.
Death is approaching him,
yet he dares to inflict harm on others.
His crime is unforgivable!"
He scolded the street official and ordered him to leave.
The official bowed in thanks,
and hurried out.
He then rushed to the prefectural office,
requesting to see Wēn.
It was already late at night.
When Wēn heard the official had arrived,
he rose in alarm,
and summoned him to a side room.
The official recounted everything he had seen.
Wēn sighed deeply in regret.
The next day, as evening approached,
he summoned the official to lead the way.
After the street drums had ceased,
Wēn disguised himself in plain clothes,
and went with the official to the Daoist priest's dwelling.
By dawn,
the official knocked on the door.
The gatekeeper asked who it was.
He replied:
"Governor Wēn Shàngshū of the capital has come to pay respects to the True Lord."
After the inner gates were opened,
the official entered first and bowed.
He then announced:
"Governor Wēn Zhāng of the capital."
Wēn hurried in and bowed.
The True Lord sat arrogantly in the hall,
wearing a yuǎnyóu guān,
and dressed in a robe of nine clouds,
his expression stern and imposing.
Wēn prostrated himself and explained:
"I am tasked with governing a vast and bustling region;
my authority must be awe-inspiring and strict.
If I show the slightest fear or weakness,
it would diminish my prestige.
Yesterday, I unwittingly offended the great immortal,
bringing guilt upon myself.
Thus, I have come to confess,
hoping for your compassion and mercy."
The True Lord rebuked him:
"You are ruthless in killing to establish your name,
and insatiable in pursuing profit.
Disaster is about to befall you,
yet you still flaunt your cruel authority."
Wēn kowtowed repeatedly, begging for mercy,
but the True Lord remained angry and unyielding.
After a short while,
a Daoist priest came from the eastern wing,
stood respectfully beside the True Lord,
and knelt to plead:
"Although the governor has committed an offense,
he is still a high-ranking official of the Son of Heaven.
Moreover, the True Lord understands the duties of his position.
It would be appropriate to show him some courtesy."
After he finished speaking,
the True Lord ordered the Daoist priest to invite Wēn into the hall,
set up a small seat separately,
and asked him to sit.
Wine was served several times,
but the True Lord's angry expression did not soften.
The Daoist priest again pleaded:
"Although the governor's offense
is difficult to forgive,
the True Lord changed his attire and wandered in the mortal world—
how could ordinary people recognize him?
When a white dragon takes the form of a fish,
it may be trapped by Yùjū.
Please consider this."
The True Lord fell silent.
After a long while, he said:
"I will spare your clan.
But this is not a place for you to linger."
Wēn then rose,
bowed in thanks in the courtyard and left.
He hurried back to the prefectural office with the street official,
just as the morning bell tolled.
Even when speaking with close associates,
he kept this secret and did not allow it to be mentioned.
The following year, Princess Tóngchāng passed away,
and Emperor Yìhuáng was deeply grieved and could not let go of his sorrow,
angry that medicine had failed to save her.
Physicians such as Hán Zōngshào and three others were ordered to be thoroughly investigated by the prefectural office,
and they were to be executed.
But Wēn delayed the trial and postponed the punishment,
accepting gold belts and other valuables from Zōngshào and the others,
amounting to tens of millions.
When the matter was discovered,
he drank poison and died.
From "Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú"
Sōngyuè Jià Nǚ
There was a man named Tián Qiú, well-versed in the Three Rites,
who possessed great literary talent,
was thoroughly familiar with a wide range of books,
and was similar in his broad learning to his friend Dèng Sháo.
Both were obscure among men,
unable to display their brilliance.
They lived in Luòyáng.
In the year Guǐsì of the Yuánhé era,
on the evening of the Mid-Autumn full moon,
they carried wine vessels and went out late through the Jiànchūn Gate,
hoping to view the moon at Sháo's country villa.
After traveling two or three lǐ,
they encountered Sháo,
who was also carrying wine vessels coming from the east.
They halted their horses by the roadside,
undecided on where to go.
Two scholars riding piebald horses
also came out of the Jiànchūn Gate.
They bowed to Qiú and Sháo, saying:
"You two gentlemen are carrying wine vessels;
could it be you are seeking a place to view tonight's moon?
My humble estate,
with its waters, bamboos, terraces, and pavilions,
is famous throughout Luòyáng.
It lies two or three lǐ southeast from here.
If you could divert your reins,
I hope we may express the friendship of a chance meeting."
Qiú and Sháo were very pleased with this prospect,
and so followed them.
When asked their surnames,
the scholars replied with other topics.
After traveling several lǐ,
the cassia-wheel moon had already risen.
They reached a carriage gate;
upon entering, it seemed very desolate,
but after proceeding several hundred paces more,
an extraordinary fragrance greeted them from ahead,
and then a truly wondrous realm opened up before them.
Springs and waterfalls intermingled in their flow,
pines and cassias lined the path;
exotic flowers and rare grasses
shone as brightly as daylight;
beautiful birds soared and danced,
harmonizing with the moon's melody.
Qiú and Sháo requested to gallop their horses and pass the wine cups swiftly.
One scholar said:
"The taste in your vessels,
how is it?"
Qiú and Sháo replied:
"It is Gānhé Wǔdòu wine;
even the finest clarified cream of the highest heavens
could not surpass this flavor, we reckon."
The scholar said:
"I have Ruìlù wine,
brewed amidst a hundred flowers,
though I know not whether it surpasses your Wǔdòu."
He said to a young attendant:
"Pluck a Zhúyè flower,
and pour some for these two gentlemen to taste."
The flower had four petals and was deep red,
round like a small vase,
over three cùn in diameter,
with leaves shaped like cups,
which, when touched, produced lingering echoes.
The young attendant brought the plucked flower,
and from within the bamboo leaves, he poured several rounds in flight;
its flavor was sweet and fragrant,
beyond compare.
After drinking,
they proceeded southeast again.
After several lǐ they reached a gate.
The scholars bowed and invited the two guests to dismount.
They gave the remaining wine from the Zhúyè flower
to their attendants as a reward;
after drinking one cup each,
all became greatly intoxicated,
and each stopped outside the doors.
Then they led the guests inside.
There were several dozen luan birds and cranes
soaring and dancing in welcome.
Walking forward,
the flowers grew even more abundant,
and the wine's flavor became especially exquisite.
All the hundred flowers were fragrant,
their branches bending low by the roadside.
Passing by ponds, halls, and pavilions,
they all were laid out with feasts and mats,
as if awaiting something,
but they did not invite Qiú and Sháo to sit.
Qiú and Sháo had drunk much and were also very tired from walking,
so they requested to rest briefly at the feasts.
The scholar said:
"Sitting is no difficulty;
but it would not be beneficial for you."
Qiú and Sháo asked the reason.
He said:
"Tonight, the host of immortals from the mid-heavens
are gathering at this mountain.
Your spirits and souls are registered
as untainted by foul odors.
We ask you, as men who know ritual, to guide the proceedings.
These are all the seats of the immortals;
they should not be sullied by mortal dust."
When he finished speaking,
they saw straight north, floral candles stretching to the sky,
pipes and music filling the air.
A pair of mica carriages halted upon a golden embankment,
and a crystal square tray was set within a jade tent.
The host of immortals were just performing the "Rainbow Skirts and Feathered Robes" melody.
The scholar stepped forward
and ordered Qiú and Sháo to bow to the Lady.
The Lady lifted the curtain and said with a smile:
"Men from the lower realm,
yet you know ritual.
However, the aura of your mortal sustenance
still emanates strongly,
and you cannot approach the other noble sons-in-law.
Let each be granted a cup of Xūnsuǐ wine."
After Qiú and Sháo drank it,
they felt their skin become warm and moist,
slightly different from ordinary people,
and their breath carried an extraordinary fragrance.
The Lady asked her attendants:
"Who summoned them here?"
They replied:
"Wèi Fúqīng and Lǐ Bābǎi."
The Lady said:
"Then have these two youths receive them."
Thereupon, the two youths led Qiú and Sháo to gaze freely from behind the immortals.
Qiú asked:
"Who is the one presiding?"
They replied:
"Liú Gāng."
"And who are the attendants?"
They said:
"Máo Yíng."
"Who are the women playing the zhēng and striking the zhù in the eastern neighborhood?"
They said:
"Má Gū and Xiè Zìrán."
"Who sits within the tent?"
They said:
"The Queen Mother of the West."
Soon, a person arrived riding a crane.
The Queen Mother said:
"I have long awaited you."
A jade maiden asked:
"Have the ritual masters arrived?"
Thereupon, they led Qiú and Sháo forward,
and had them stand to the left below the hall of green jade.
Lord Liú said with a laugh:
"Just now, due to a memorial submitted by the scholar of Liánhuā Peak,
matters required decisions and dispatches;
many guests have yet to arrive.
How can you speak of long waiting?"
The Queen Mother said:
"Regarding the memorial matter,
what was it about?"
He said:
"The magistrate of Fúliáng County sought an extension of his years.
Because this man obtained office through bribery,
governed with harsh cruelty,
showed bias in legal documents,
and never heard of the ways of loyalty and forbearance,
being solely focused on wealth and goods,
devising clever schemes and changing methods,
he brought ruin upon himself,
shortening his remaining lifespan.
However, because the old man of Liánhuā Peak
pleaded on his behalf,
and the memorial was very earnest,
we specially postponed his death limit,
extending it by five years."
Qiú asked:
"Who is Lord Liú?"
They said:
"The Son of Heaven of the Hàn dynasty."
Then another person arrived,
riding a yellow dragon,
wearing a yellow banner,
preceded by pipe and song,
followed by consorts and concubines,
and descended to the jade tent.
The Queen Mother asked again:
"Why are you so late, Lord Lǐ?"
He said:
"I was commanding the dragon gods to devise plans for flood and drought,
to spread them across Huáicài,
in order to exterminate the demonic rebels."
The Hàn ruler said:
"But what of the common people?"
He said:
"The Supreme Deity also asked this question;
I submitted a memorial to resolve his doubts."
He said:
"May we hear it?"
He said:
"I cannot remember it all,
but will roughly state its main points.
The memorial said:
'So-and-so of such-and-such county,
Establishing a magnificent foundation,
with virtue reaching the multitude of people,
treading on the edge of deep and perilous situations,
I dare not slacken or neglect,
without mobilizing armies and chariots.
I have pacified the rebellions in Zhōngxià and Bāshǔ,
without exhausting the imperial treasury.
I have swept away the malevolent forces in Dōngwú and Shàngdǎng,
the nine regions have already been cleared, yet one area still harbors ominous clouds.
I humbly submit that venomous creatures wreak havoc,
causing pain in Huáicài,
wolves and jackals still bare their fangs,
ants and insects stubbornly guard their territories.
If we wait for times of abundance and peace among the people,
it will only embolden the wicked.
But if we allow famine and calamities to arise,
it will surely shake the hearts of the people.
Thus, turning their weapons against themselves,
we can sweep them away completely.
To eliminate the rebellious factions in the three prefectures,
the loss will be minimal.
To pacify the suffering people across the land,
the benefits will be great.
I humbly request the divine dragon to unleash floods,
and fierce ghosts to bring disasters,
thereby executing Heaven’s punishment.
To aid our military strength.”
The Hàn ruler said:
“The memorial is excellent,
since my brother has already consented,
we may now congratulate ourselves on the eradication.”
The scholar said to Qiú and Sháo:
“This is the sovereign of the peaceful era of Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo.”
Not long after,
the sound of flutes and pipes was heard descending from the sky,
and one holding a crimson tally stepped forward and announced:
“King Mù of Zhōu has arrived,
play music!”
All the immortals rose,
the Queen Mother stepped aside and bowed in welcome,
the two rulers descended the steps,
entered the tent and sat in a circle to drink.
The Queen Mother said:
“Why not bring old Xuānyuán here?”
They replied:
“He is presiding over the feast in the Moon Palace tonight,
it is not that we did not earnestly invite him.”
The Queen Mother also said:
“Since parting at Yáochí,
mountains and valleys have shifted many times.
I recently looked at the eastern city of Luòyáng,
and it has already become ruins.
On the western road of Dìngdǐng Gate,
suddenly a new marketplace has appeared.
Fame and profit remain as before,
how lamentable!”
King Mù raised his wine cup,
and requested the Queen Mother to sing.
She struck a plate with a coral hook and sang:
“I urge you to drink,
and feel sorrow for you.”
Then she chanted:
“Since I have often seen the changes in the marketplace and court,
I no longer have the heart for feasting at Yáochí.”
The Queen Mother held her cup,
and King Mù of Zhōu sang:
“I offer you wine,
do not lament the changes in the marketplace and court.
Had I known there would be no more joy at Yáochí,
I would regret hastily driving my steed Huáliú back.”
After singing,
he spoke with the Queen Mother about old times at Yáochí.
Then he sang another stanza:
“The eight steeds ride back on the boundless wind,
still thinking of past events resting in Zhāo Palace.
The feast moved to the southern garden as emotions deepened,
the music of the heavenly court played, the melody unfinished.
The slanting Milky Way dew congeals, the waning moon cold,
flowing rosy clouds fill the cup, the dawn light red.
Looking back at Kūnlún, I know not where it is,
suspecting I am in a drunken dream.”
The Queen Mother responded to King Mù’s song:
“A song of pipes and strings by the shores of Yáoshui,
once detained the swift-footed and halted the traveling chariot.
A thousand years in the mortal world,
a single round of cups in the immortal realm.
The jade rabbit and silver river never know night,
exotic flowers and fine trees forever in spring.
Quietly knowing the green sea is rich with verses,
singing to the vulgar crowd may mislead people.”
When the wine reached Emperor Hàn Wǔ,
the Queen Mother sang again:
“Pearl-like dew and golden wind, autumn descends to the mortal world,
the Han imperial tombs and trees stand cold and desolate.
Had you not then received the power of the immortal peaches,
you would have turned to dust drifting over the mound.”
The Hàn ruler offered wine to the Queen Mother:
“For over fifty years, the four seas were clear,
I personally tended the alchemical furnace to attain longevity.
If you say it was all due to the power of the immortal peaches,
look at the names on the register of immortals.”
The Emperor held his cup and said:
“I have heard that Dīng Lìngwēi can sing.”
He ordered his attendants to summon him.
When Lìngwēi arrived,
the Emperor also commanded Zǐ Jìn to play the shēng in harmony.
He sang:
“The moon shines on Líshān, dew weeps on the flowers,
as if mourning the immortal emperor’s early ascent.
To this day, there are still long-lived deer,
often circling the hot springs, gazing at the emerald canopy.”
The Emperor held his cup for a long time.
The Queen Mother said:
“We should summon Yè Jìngnéng to come,
and sing a song of those times.”
Jìngnéng soon arrived,
knelt and offered wine to the Emperor,
then sang:
“The smoke and dust of Yōujì parted from the ninefold heavens,
the singing bells ceased in the Consort’s hot spring palace.
At midnight, the imperial escort lacked full regalia,
the grand carriage hastily set out with six dragons.
The cosmetic case still holds golden kingfisher feathers,
the warm pool still immerses jade lotuses.
Brambles and thorns block the path to Cháoyuán Temple,
only the mournful wind blows through the evening pines.”
After the song,
the Emperor was sorrowful for a long while.
The other immortals were also saddened.
Then the Yellow Dragon held a cup,
and again bowed before the carriage, offering a toast:
“The divine maiden of Shàngqīng,
the immortal youth of Yùjīng.
Rejoice on this night,
harmoniously singing like the phoenix.
The phoenix sings in harmony,
soaring and gliding.
May you share Heaven’s eternity,
with endless streams of celebration.”
The immortal youth then gave five thousand bolts of jiāoxiāo silk,
three thousand rolls of sea-people brocade,
one hundred sets of glass and amber vessels,
ten hú each of bright moon pearls and Lízhū pearls,
to the immortal maidens who performed the music.
Then four cranes stood before the carriage,
carrying the immortal youth along with his attendants and assistants,
and also a precious flower platform.
Soon, a divine feast was served,
with several dozen dishes in total,
which also reached Qiú and Sháo.
Qiú and Sháo drank.
An immortal maiden held a jade box,
carrying red paper, brush, and inkstone, and approached.
She requested a poem urging the bride to adorn herself.
Then Liú Gāng composed a poem:
“Jade as your substance, flowers as your face,
cicada-wing hair, clouds as your locks.
Why trouble to apply powder or rouge?
Already emerging graceful and ethereal.”
Then Máo Yíng composed a poem:
“The crystal curtain opens, silver candles bright,
the wind sways pearl pendants, connecting with clear clouds.
Do not even out rouge to adorn the flower’s charm,
early drive the paired phoenixes to Yùjīng.”
Cháo Fǔ composed a poem:
“Three stars in the sky, the Milky Way turns,
the dawn light of the mortal world comes from the east.
Jade sprouts and jade stamper are also suitable for the night,
do not let a single flower bloom at dawn.”
After the poems were presented,
the sound of jade pendants was heard inside.
Then several dozen jade maidens
led the immortal youth into the tent.
They summoned Qiú and Sháo to perform the rites.
After the rites,
the two scholars again led Qiú and Sháo to bid farewell to the Lady.
The Lady said:
“It is not that I lack treasures to give you,
but your strength cannot bear to carry them.”
She gave each a cup of longevity-extending wine,
saying:
“This can add half a jiǎzǐ cycle to your mortal lives.”
She then ordered Wèi Fúqīng and others to guide them back to the mortal world,
so that their return journey would not be lonely.
Then the two youths led Qiú and Sháo away,
picking flowers and pouring wine,
regretting each step of parting.
Wèi Jūn said to Qiú and Sháo:
“The Lady ascended to heaven in broad daylight,
riding phoenixes and cranes,
is merely the result of accumulated practice.
I have never believed
that one who accumulates virtue and benevolence,
possesses talent and learning,
would ultimately not enjoy rank and emolument.
If you can transcend the bonds of the mortal world,
and break free from worldly shackles,
fifteen years from now,
I will await you at the Thirty-Six Peaks.
Please treasure yourselves and take care.”
When they came out again through the carriage door,
they shook hands and bid farewell.
After parting,
they walked four or five steps,
and then vanished without a trace,
leaving only Mount Sōngshān.
Towering and leaning against the sky.
They found a woodcutter’s path and returned home.
By the time they reached home,
more than a year had already passed.
Their families had held a soul-summoning burial for them in the plains of Běimáng,
and the grass on their graves had long since grown.
Thereupon, Qiú and Sháo abandoned their homes and families,
and together entered Shàoshì Shān.
Today, it is unknown where they are.
From "Zuǎnyì Jì"
Péi Háng
During the Chángqìng era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a scholar named Péi Háng.
Having failed the imperial examinations, he traveled to Èzhǔ,
to visit an old friend, the former Chancellor Cuī.
The Chancellor happened to bestow upon him two hundred thousand coins,
and he decided to take them far away, back to the capital.
Therefore, he hired a large boat
to travel along the Xiāng and Hàn rivers.
On the same boat was a Lady Fán,
a woman of peerless beauty.
Though words were exchanged indirectly,
and the intimacy felt through the curtain was palpable,
Péi Háng, despite feeling close,
had no means to communicate directly and meet her.
So he bribed her maidservant, Niǎoyān,
asking her to deliver a poem, which read:
"Even if we were as far apart as Hú and Yuè, I would still yearn.
How much more so, encountering a heavenly fairy separated by brocade screens?
If you were to ascend to the Jade Capital for the morning audience,
I wish to follow the simurgh and crane into the azure clouds."
The poem was sent,
but after a long time, there was no reply.
Péi Háng questioned Niǎoyān several times,
and she said:
"My lady saw the poem but acted as if she hadn't heard it.
What can be done?"
Péi Háng was at a loss.
Then, along the journey, he sought out famous wines and rare fruits to present to her.
The Lady then had Niǎoyān summon Péi Háng to meet.
When the curtain was lifted,
her jade-like skin gleamed with a cool light,
her beauty shone like a radiant flower,
her cloud-like hair was piled low,
her slender brows were like a faint moon,
her demeanor was that of one beyond the mists and clouds,
unwilling to be paired with the mundane world.
Péi Háng bowed repeatedly,
for a long while.
The Lady said:
"I have a husband in Hànnán,
who is about to abandon his official post to live in seclusion among cliffs and valleys.
He has summoned me for a final farewell.
My heart is deeply troubled and unsettled,
fearing I may not arrive in time.
How could I have the heart to linger with thoughts for another?
It is truly not so.
I am merely pleased to share the same boat and cross the river with you, sir.
Please do not take my earlier banter to heart."
Péi Háng said:
"I dare not."
After drinking, he returned to his place.
Her conduct was as pure as ice and frost,
not to be trespassed upon.
Later, the Lady had Niǎoyān deliver another poem, which read:
"One drink of jade nectar stirs a hundred feelings,
When the Mystic Frost is pounded fully, Yúnyīng appears.
Lánqiáo itself is a grotto of immortals,
Why must one toil up the rugged path to the Jade Clarity?"
Péi Háng read it.
He felt only empty shame and admiration,
yet he could not fully grasp the poem's deeper meaning.
Afterwards, he did not see her again,
only having Niǎoyān convey polite greetings.
Then they reached the lower reaches of the Xiāng and Hàn rivers,
and the Lady, with her maidservant carrying her dressing case,
departed without bidding farewell.
No one knew where she had gone.
Péi Háng searched for her everywhere.
But her traces vanished, her form concealed,
and in the end, there was no sign or omen.
So he tidied himself and returned to the capital.
Passing near the Lánqiáo postal station,
as he was extremely thirsty,
he left the main road to seek some drink.
He saw three or four thatched huts,
low and cramped.
An old woman was spinning hemp.
Péi Háng bowed and asked for a drink.
The old woman called out:
"Yúnyīng, bring a bowl of drink.
This gentleman wishes to drink."
Péi Háng was startled,
remembering the line about Yúnyīng in Lady Fán's poem,
though he deeply did not understand the connection.
Soon, from beneath a reed curtain,
a pair of jade hands emerged holding a porcelain bowl.
Péi Háng took it and drank.
It was truly jade nectar.
He only felt an extraordinary fragrance, rich and pervasive,
wafting out the door.
As he returned the bowl,
he abruptly lifted the curtain.
He beheld a maiden,
like dewy jade blossoms,
her spring-like warmth melting snowy brilliance,
her face surpassing smooth jade,
her hair like dense clouds.
Shyly, she covered her face and hid her form.
Even hidden orchids in a secluded valley
could not compare to her fragrant beauty.
Péi Háng was astonished and captivated,
rooted to the spot, unable to leave.
So he said to the old woman:
"My servant and horse are very hungry.
I wish to rest here.
I will reward you handsomely.
I hope you will not refuse."
The old woman said:
"As you wish, sir."
And so he fed his servant and groomed his horse.
After a long while, he said to the old woman:
"Earlier, I saw the young lady.
Her stunning beauty startled me.
Her grace and appearance surpass the world.
That is why I hesitate and cannot bring myself to depart.
I wish to offer a rich betrothal gift and marry her.
Is it possible?"
The old woman said:
"She is already promised to someone,
but the time has not yet come.
I am now old and ill.
I only have this granddaughter.
Yesterday, an immortal
left a spiritual elixir, one 'knife-point' measure.
But it must be pounded with a jade mortar and pestle for a hundred days
before it can be swallowed.
Then one can attain longevity and avoid aging.
If you, sir, seek to marry this girl,
obtain the jade mortar and pestle,
and I will give her to you.
As for gold and silk,
I have no use for them."
Péi Háng bowed in thanks and said:
"I ask for a hundred days as the deadline.
I will surely bring the mortar and pestle.
Please do not promise her to anyone else."
The old woman said:
"Agreed."
Péi Háng left, filled with anxious longing.
Upon reaching the capital,
he paid no mind to the examination affairs at all.
Instead, in the city wards, bustling markets, and noisy streets,
he loudly inquired about the jade mortar and pestle,
but there was not even a trace of news.
When he met friends,
it was as if he did not know them.
Everyone said he was mad.
After several months,
he met an old man who dealt in jade, who said:
"I recently received a letter from Old Biàn of the medicine shop in Guózhōu,
saying he has a jade mortar and pestle for sale.
Since you, sir, seek it so earnestly,
I will write a letter of introduction for you."
Péi Háng felt deeply grateful and honored.
Indeed, he obtained the mortar and pestle.
Old Biàn said:
"It cannot be had for less than two hundred strings of cash."
Péi Háng then emptied his purse,
and also sold his servant and his horse,
before he could raise the amount.
Then he hurried alone, carrying the mortar and pestle, and reached Lánqiáo.
The old woman from before laughed heartily and said:
"Is there a man of such good faith?
How could I begrudge giving my girl
and not reward his labor?"
The girl also smiled and said:
"Even so,
you must pound the medicine for me for another hundred days,
before we discuss marriage."
The old woman took the medicine from her sash.
Péi Háng immediately began pounding it.
He worked by day and rested at night.
At night, the old woman would take the medicine and mortar into the inner room.
Péi Háng again heard the sound of pounding medicine.
Peeking in,
he saw a jade rabbit holding the pestle and mortar.
Its snowy light illuminated the room,
bright enough to see the finest hair.
From then on, Péi Háng's resolve grew even firmer.
When the full number of days was completed,
the old woman took the medicine and swallowed it, saying:
"I shall enter the grotto to inform the relatives
and prepare the bridal chamber for Péi Háng."
Then she took the girl into the mountains,
saying to Péi Háng:
"Just wait here a little while."
In a short while, carriages, horses, servants, and attendants
came to welcome Péi Háng.
He then saw a great mansion touching the clouds.
Pearl gates shimmered in the sunlight.
Inside were canopies, screens, and curtains,
pearls, jade, and rare treasures,
nothing was not of the utmost excellence,
even more splendid than a noble family's home.
Immortal boys and maidens
led Péi Háng into the bridal chamber to complete the rites.
Péi Háng bowed to the old woman,
weeping with emotion and gratitude.
The old woman said:
"Péi Háng is a descendant of the Perfected Being Péi Qīnglěng.
Since it was destined to emerge into the world,
there is no need to deeply shame an old woman!”
When he was introduced to meet the various guests,
many were among the immortals.
Later, there was a celestial maiden,
with coiled hair and rainbow garments,
who said she was his wife’s elder sister.
After Péi Háng bowed,
the maiden said:
“Does Sir Péi not recognize me?”
Péi Háng replied:
“In the past we were not related by marriage,
so I do not recall having paid my respects to you.”
The maiden said:
“Do you not remember sharing a boat back from Èzhǔ and arriving at Xiāng-Hàn?”
Péi Háng was deeply startled and dismayed,
and earnestly expressed his apologies.
Later he asked the attendants,
who said:
“This is the elder sister of the young lady, Lady Yúnqiāo.
She is the wife of Immortal Lord Liú Gāng,
already a lofty perfected one,
serving as an official under the Jade Emperor.”
The old woman then sent Péi Háng and his wife into the Jade Peak Cave,
where they dwelt in jade towers and extraordinary chambers.
They were fed elixirs of crimson snow and jade blossoms.
Their bodies and natures became pure and empty,
their hair turned dark green,
their spiritual transformations were effortless,
and they transcended to become superior immortals.
During the Tàihé era,
his friend Lú Hào
encountered him west of Lánqiáo Station,
and thus learned of his attainment of the Dao.
He then presented him with ten catties of fine Lántián jade
and one grain of Purple Mansion Cloud Elixir,
conversed with him all day long,
and asked him to deliver a letter to his beloved ones.
Lú Hào kowtowed and said:
“Elder brother, since you have attained the Dao,
how about granting me a word of instruction?”
Péi Háng said:
“Lǎozǐ said,
‘Empty the mind,
fill the belly.’
People nowadays,
their minds are ever more filled—
how can they grasp the principle of attaining the Dao?”
Lú Hào was bewildered,
and Péi Háng told him:
“When the mind is full of delusive thoughts,
and the belly leaks essence and overflows,
then emptiness and fullness can be known.
Mortals inherently possess the art of immortality
and the method of the cyclically transformed elixir,
but you are not yet ready to be taught.
Another day we shall speak of it.”
Lú Hào knew he could not press further,
and only after the banquet ended did he depart.
Later generations never encountered him again.
From “Chuánqí”
Hóu Dàohuá
At the Dàojìng Temple in Yǒnglè County, Hézhōng,
a scenic spot within Púzhōng,
where Daoist priests resided,
numbering over ten.
During the Táng dynasty under Emperor Wénzōng,
the Daoist priest Dèng Tàixuán refined an elixir in the medicine courtyard.
When the elixir was completed,
he suspected its efficacy was not yet perfected,
so he stored it within the temple,
and it was jointly guarded.
After Dèng Tàixuán died
(“died” originally written as “teacher.”
Changed according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.)
his disciple Zhōu Wùxiān took charge of the temple affairs.
At that time, there was a man from Pú named Hóu Dàohuá,
who served Wùxiān as a supply attendant.
All the Daoist priests treated him as a slave,
assigning him sweeping and menial tasks,
leaving nothing undone,
yet Dàohuá grew ever more content.
He also often enjoyed the classics of history,
never letting scrolls leave his hand,
and whatever he read once, he would recite aloud.
When others asked him,
what use was this,
he replied:
“In heaven there are no foolish or ignorant immortals.”
They all laughed heartily at him.
In Púzhōng there were many large dates,
and it was said throughout the land
that in a year no more than one or two would be seedless.
Dàohuá, for three consecutive years, managed to eat them.
One morning,
Dàohuá took an axe
and trimmed an ancient pine until its branches hung nearly bare,
as if shaved clean.
No one in the temple understood his intent.
The next day at dawn,
when everyone rose in the morning,
Dàohuá was nowhere to be seen in his room.
Beneath the ancient pine was placed a table,
on which stood a cup of water,
and before it, a pair of shoes were removed.
Dàohuá’s clothes hung on the pine tree.
The temple members looked and
found a poem left behind, which read:
“Within the packet, the great cyclically transformed elixir,
for many years its color unchanged.
Last night I stole and ate it,
today I soar through the azure sky.
Ashamed yet deeply treasuring it,
treasuring it, Dèng Tiānshī.
In another year, when the elixir is refined,
keep it for Nèizhī.
My teacher knows this art,
refine it swiftly, do not delay.
The Three Purities await specially,
the Great Loftiness has its appointed time.”
Below were written smaller characters,
stating that on the first day of the seventh month last year,
he was granted by Lord Hán the surname Lǐ and the name Nèizhī,
assigned to reside in the Shàngqīng Shànjìn Temple,
followed by a dozen or so more words.
It was the twenty-first day of the fifth month in the fifth year of the Táng Dàzhōng era,
when the temple members realized Dàohuá had stolen Dèng Tàixuán’s elixir and ascended as an immortal.
They then jointly reported to the military governor, Minister Zhèng Guāng,
who verified the traces and found them true,
and immediately memorialized the matter to the throne.
An imperial decree bestowed five hundred bolts of silk,
along with imperial robes,
to repair the corridors and halls,
and the temple was renamed Shēngxiān Temple.
From “Xuānshì Zhì”
Yíjūn Wáng Lǎo
Wáng Lǎo
was a native of Yíjūn County in Fāngzhōu.
He lived in a village cottage,
and was quite fond of the Dao and hospitable to guests,
devoting his efforts to performing secret virtuous deeds.
His wife was also of the same mind and tireless in this.
One day, a ragged Daoist priest arrived at his gate,
and Wáng Lǎo and his wife both welcomed and treated him with courtesy.
After staying for over a month,
the priest would occasionally chat and drink with Wáng Lǎo,
and they became quite intimate and friendly.
Suddenly, the priest suffered from malignant sores all over his body,
so Wáng Lǎo sought medicine and treatment for him,
attending to him even more diligently and earnestly,
yet the sores grew worse by the day.
When nearly a year had passed,
the Daoist priest said to Wáng Lǎo:
"These sores cannot be cured by ordinary medicine;
they will heal on their own if soaked in several hú of wine."
So Wáng Lǎo carefully brewed clean wine for him,
and when it was ready,
the Daoist priest said to put the wine in a large urn,
"I will add medicine and soak in it myself."
He then entered the urn,
and after three days emerged,
with his beard and hair all turned black,
his face restored to youth,
and his skin like congealed lard.
Wáng Lǎo's entire household looked on in astonishment.
The Daoist priest said to Wáng Lǎo:
"This wine can be drunk;
it can make people fly up to heaven."
Wáng Lǎo believed him.
Initially,
the urn contained over five hú of wine.
But when they looked,
only two or three dǒu remained,
exceptionally clear, cool, fragrant, and delicious.
At that time, they were threshing wheat,
so Wáng Lǎo, his wife and children, and the wheat threshers all drank it together,
and they all became heavily intoxicated.
The Daoist priest also drank,
and said:
"Shall we go up to heaven now?"
Wáng Lǎo was willing to follow wherever his master went.
Then, an auspicious wind suddenly arose,
and colorful clouds billowed like steam.
The house, grass, and trees,
along with the entire family, people, chickens, and dogs,
all flew away at once.
In the sky, the sound of wheat threshing could still be heard,
and several villagers watched in amazement and admiration.
Only the cat was abandoned and did not go.
When the wind settled,
the two hired wheat threshers
were left under a tree in another village.
Afterward, they also stopped eating,
and both attained longevity.
Thirty lǐ west of Yíjūn County,
the Shēngxiān Village remains to this day.
From "Xù Xiān Zhuàn."
Chén Shī
The Méi family, who ran an inn in Yùzhāng,
were quite charitable to travelers.
When monks or Daoist priests sought lodging,
they never asked for payment.
There was always one Daoist priest,
dressed in ragged clothes,
who came to stay at their home,
and Méi treated him generously.
One day, he said to Méi:
"Tomorrow I will hold a vegetarian feast,
and I ask you for twenty new porcelain bowls
and seven pairs of chopsticks.
You should also come to the gathering;
you can find me in front of the Tiānbǎo Cave, asking for Chén Shī."
Méi agreed,
and the Daoist priest took the bowls and crossed the river.
The next day, Méi went to the front of the cave,
and asked the villagers about it.
No one knew the place.
After a long while, as he was about to return,
he happened upon a small path,
very bright and clean.
He tried following it,
and indeed came upon a courtyard.
A young attendant answered the gate,
and upon inquiry,
it turned out to be Chén's residence.
Entering, he saw the Daoist priest,
now dressed in splendid attire,
who invited him to sit.
He ordered food to be prepared,
and shortly after, the food arrived.
It was a steamed infant,
and Méi, terrified, refused to eat.
After a long while, more food was served,
this time a steamed puppy,
and Méi again refused to eat.
The Daoist priest sighed,
and ordered the bowls he had obtained the previous day to be brought as a gift for the guest.
Looking at them,
they were golden bowls.
He said to Méi:
"You are a good man,
but you cannot attain immortality.
Millennium-old ginseng and wolfberries,
you were unwilling to eat them;
such is your fate."
He thanked him and sent him off.
After that, he was never seen again.
From "Jī Shén Lù."
Chén Jīn
Chén Jīn
was a soldier in his youth,
serving under Liú Xìn, the military governor of Jiāngxī.
During the siege of Qiánzhōu,
Chén Jīn privately went with five of his comrades
to excavate a large tomb.
Opening the coffin,
they saw an old man with a white beard.
His face looked as if alive,
and he was dressed entirely in white silk garments,
all as good as new.
As soon as the coffin was opened, a white vapor rushed skyward,
and an extraordinary fragrance filled the tomb.
Chén Jīn alone noticed something like powder on the coffin lid,
emitting a faint smell of sulfur.
Having heard before that sulfur from a coffin could be used as medicine,
he immediately scooped it up with the hem of his garment and carried it back with him.
There were no other treasures in the tomb,
so they resealed it and left.
When they returned to the camp,
the people in the camp were all surprised, saying:
"Where is this fragrance coming from today?"
Chén Jīn, aware of the sulfur's unusual properties,
would draw water every morning and take it with the sulfur,
until it was all consumed.
After the city was pacified
("Pacified" originally read "within.")
According to the Ming manuscript edition, corrected
he entered a Buddhist temple to stay,
and happened to mention this to a monk there.
The monk said:
"This was the distant ancestor of a wealthy family in the city.
The descendants passed down the story
that their ancestor was fond of the Dao,
and an extraordinary person taught him to take sulfur as an elixir.
He said that when his allotted lifespan ended, he would die,
and three hundred years after his death,
the tomb would open,
which would be the time of his liberation and transformation.
Now it has been exactly three hundred years."
They went together to look again,
and found the coffin empty,
with only the clothes remaining,
like the shed skin of a cicada.
From then on, Chén Jīn was free from illness.
Now he is a minor officer in the Qīnghǎi Army,
over seventy years old,
with a withered and thin physique,
but as light and vigorous as before.
From "Jī Shén Lù."
Chén Fùxiū
Chén Fùxiū,
also known as Chén Qīzǐ.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
he came to reside in Bāochéng,
engaging in farming and woodcutting,
no different from ordinary people.
He appeared to be around fifty years old
and possessed many transformative arts.
In Bāochéng, there were curious young men,
five or six in number,
who often prepared wine and food for him,
hoping to learn his arts,
and were tirelessly diligent in their efforts.
Fùxiū made an agreement with them, saying:
"I will go out to the western outskirts;
whoever can keep up with me,
I will teach them my arts."
Fùxiū walked slowly,
while the group of young men ran after him,
but ultimately could not catch up.
They stopped,
and none obtained his arts.
Later, when he went to the market,
the crowd again ceaselessly attended to him.
Fùxiū went with them to the outskirts,
and sat under a large tree.
Before he finished speaking about the Way,
he suddenly died a violent death,
and in a short while, his body decayed and became foul.
Everyone fled in shock,
not daring to look back.
From then on, the young men did not dare to bother him,
and he often wandered drunk in the market.
The commander of Bāochéng, Lǐ Dǎng,
angered, had him imprisoned,
intending to add to his crimes.
The shackles were very strict,
but suddenly he stopped eating and died.
Soon, his body became foul and rotten,
with maggots flowing out.
He was discarded
The characters "discarded" were originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript.
in the outskirts.
Shortly after, he returned home,
and was again in the market.
Dǎng then treated him with increased courtesy and respect,
building a house for him on the southern bank of the Bāochéng River,
and giving him many gifts,
but he accepted almost none.
Liǔ Gōng Zhòngyǐng of Hédōng, Chancellor Zhōu Chí, and Duke of Yān Guó Gāo Pián,
who held command over three provinces,
were all men of great prestige and authority,
and deeply honored him with courtesy,
sending letters and gifts continuously,
but Fùxiū accepted none of them.
Only a crane-feather cloak and cloth robe
he accepted and stored away,
but never wore.
Hú Fǎng, the magistrate of Chāngmíng,
often served him as a teacher.
When about to take up his post,
he left five thousand coins
for Fùxiū to buy wine.
Fùxiū laughed and did not take them, saying:
"I have plenty of gold and jade,
it's just a pity I cannot use them."
He handed a hoe to Fǎng,
telling him to dig the ground.
After digging no more than two or three inches,
gold, jade, coins, and goods
emerged with each dig.
He said:
"The things of the human world
are indeed like this.
But people's allotted shares are fixed,
and one should not take more.
If I were to use them,
would there be any limit?"
When Fǎng went to Chāngmíng,
Fùxiū saw him off at Xiānliú River,
pointed to the sand,
and told Fǎng to retrieve wine vessels.
Fǎng scooped a few inches of sand
and obtained five or six pieces of vessels.
After drinking wine,
they buried them back in the sand.
He also joked:
"I once hid fruits in the sand,
they should still be there now."
He again told him to retrieve them,
and they were all found.
The Shu Chancellor, Duke of Yān,
sent someone with a letter to his residence in Bāochéng to summon him.
Fùxiū left Bāochéng on the same day.
The messenger arrived after ten days,
but Fùxiū had already reached Chéngdū that very day.
Yet there was another Fùxiū traveling with the messenger,
never leaving his side.
The Duke of Yān questioned the messenger,
and treated him with even greater wonder.
Once, at a banquet hosted by the governor of Bā’nán,
he was insulted by a wine-serving courtesan.
Fùxiū smiled and looked at her face,
and in a moment, the courtesan grew a beard several feet long.
She wept and complained to the governor,
who pleaded for forgiveness on her behalf.
Fùxiū chanted over a cup of wine,
and had her drink it.
After a while, she returned to her original state.
He also had a pill of medicine,
which he threw into water.
It sank, floated, and spun around,
obeying people's pointing and calls,
changing between visibility and invisibility.
There were many such feats,
too numerous to record in full.
In the fifth year of Zhōnghé
The character "five" was originally missing.
Supplemented based on the Ming manuscript and the Xǔ block-printed edition.
The Huáng edition reads "the first year of Guāngqǐ."
year,
when the imperial carriage returned to the capital,
Fùxiū also arrived at the palace gates.
Tián Jìngōng, the military commissioner,
asked how many years of peace the capital would have,
and he said:
"Twenty."
Indeed, twenty days after the question,
the emperor again went to Chéncāng.
Later, on the road, he sent a poem to Tián Jìngōng, saying:
"Sitting at night in the empty courtyard, the moonlight faint,
a single cold plum tree sprouts two branches."
When the imperial carriage reached Liángyáng,
the commander of Bīn, Zhū Méi, established Prince Xiāng as regent.
The two branches of the cold plum tree were thus verified.
From then on, the imperial escort proceeded to the capital,
mostly stationed in Xīxiàn, Sānquán, and along the Bāoxié route.
Fùxiū's arts
had long been passed down among people.
Once, someone nailed his hand to a pillar,
but soon someone rescued him and pulled it out,
and he suffered no harm.
Over a year later,
he died at home,
and was buried at the foot of the mountain south of the river.
Several months later,
curious people dug up his grave,
but found nothing inside.
They saw Fùxiū in Cháng'ān.
When the imperial carriage was stationed in Huàzhōu,
Fùxiū had also arrived in Xīngdé Prefecture.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Yīn Tiānxiáng.
Yīn Qīqī,
named Tiānxiáng,
also named Dàoquán,
once called himself Qīqī,
and was commonly addressed as such,
though no one knows where he was from.
He traveled throughout the world,
and people said they had seen him for a long time,
unable to guess his age or lifespan.
His face was bright and fair,
as if he were around forty years old,
and he would change his name and surname unpredictably wherever he went.
He once sold medicine in Jīngzhōu,
when an epidemic was raging among both the Han and Tibetan people in Língtái,
and those who obtained his medicine were cured as soon as they took it,
so all regarded him as divine.
He would give away the money he earned to others.
He was also often seen drunk in the city streets.
Zhōu Bǎo had known him earlier in Cháng'ān.
Later, when Zhōu became the military governor of Jīngyuán,
he invited Yīn with great respect and ceremony,
admiring his Daoist arts and the arts of the bedchamber.
After Zhōu was transferred to govern Zhèxī,
several years later,
Qīqī suddenly arrived
and resumed selling medicine.
Zhōu was overjoyed to hear of it,
summoned him,
and treated him with even greater reverence as a teacher.
Every day, Qīqī would sing drunkenly:
"Plucking the jade-green melody on the zither,
refining cinnabar into white elixir.
Brewing wine in an instant,
making flowers bloom out of season."
Zhōu often tested him,
and all his feats proved effective.
He also sought to grow melons and fish,
like the immortal Gě Xiānwēng.
At Hèlín Temple, there was an azalea
over ten feet tall,
which bloomed luxuriantly every late spring.
The temple monks passed down a story
that during the Zhēnyuán era,
a foreign monk came from Tiāntāi,
carrying its roots nurtured with medicine in a bowl to plant it.
Since then, the temple had been adorned,
and the flower courtyard was kept locked.
Occasionally, people would catch glimpses of three women,
dressed in bright red and strikingly beautiful,
strolling together beneath the tree.
Anyone who dared to pick a branch
would surely be haunted by them.
It was commonly said they were the flower goddesses.
Thus, everyone treasured and protected the tree,
making it flourish more extraordinarily than ordinary flowers.
When the flowers were about to bloom,
reports would be sent in stages,
and the military governor, his guests, officials, and subordinates
would come day after day to admire and enjoy them.
Later, the entire city's men and women,
along with people from all directions,
would bring wine to revel and roam freely.
From spring into summer,
from dawn till dusk,
among the neighborhoods,
work was nearly abandoned.
One day, Zhōu said to Qīqī:
"The flowers of Hèlín Temple are uniquely marvelous in the world.
I have often heard you can make flowers bloom out of season—
can you make these bloom?"
Qīqī replied:
"It is possible."
Zhōu said:
"Now the Double Ninth Festival is approaching—
can you make them bloom on that day?"
So, two days before the festival, Qīqī went to stay overnight at Hèlín Temple.
At midnight,
a woman came and said to Qīqī:
"Do you, Daoist, wish to make these flowers bloom?"
Qīqī then asked who she was,
coming here so late at night.
The woman said:
"I am commanded by the highest heavens
to oversee these flowers below.
However, these flowers have been in the mortal world for over a hundred years,
and soon they will return to Làngyuàn.
Now, I will open them together with you, Daoist—
without you, I would not have been moved to appear."
With that, the woman vanished in an instant.
The next morning,
the temple monks were astonished to see the flower buds gradually opening.
By the ninth day,
they were in full bloom as if it were spring.
When this was reported,
Zhōu and the entire city's gentry and commoners were amazed,
and they came to admire them just as in springtime.
A few days later,
the flowers suddenly disappeared,
with no fallen petals on the ground.
Later, Qīqī happened to visit the home of an official,
just as a banquet was underway.
The host and guests hurried to welcome and attend to him.
Among the entertainers serving wine,
two particularly mocked and disrespected him.
Qīqī then said to the host:
"May I propose a drinking game with two chestnuts?"
Everyone was delighted,
thinking there must be some trick to add to the merriment.
He passed the chestnuts around,
and those who received them all marveled at their extraordinary fragrance.
Only the two entertainers who had laughed at Qīqī
found stones stuck to their noses,
which they could not pull off,
and they complained of an unbearable foul smell.
The two began to dance wildly together,
their hair ornaments falling to the ground,
weeping bitterly in turn,
their makeup streaming down.
Soon, all the entertainers started dancing chaotically,
and the drums and music began playing by themselves,
quite in rhythm.
Even when the music stopped, the dancing continued.
Everyone at the banquet
laughed until they were doubled over.
After a long while,
the host pleaded with Qīqī to forgive them.
Shortly after,
the stones fell from their noses,
turning back into chestnuts.
When smelled, they had an extraordinary fragrance.
Their hair ornaments and makeup were all restored as before,
completely undamaged.
From then on, everyone treated him with reverence.
Qīqī could also turn water into wine by ladling it,
carve wood into dried meat,
make people walk backward,
stop a boat with a pointed finger,
call birds to fall from the sky,
and revive dead fish with his spit.
He could scoop earth and draw on the ground,
depicting the shapes of mountains and rivers;
break off grass and gather ants,
transforming them into a city.
Those who had traveled to such places
saw it all vividly recreated,
only somewhat smaller.
All his arts were too numerous to record.
Twenty years later,
Xuē Lǎng and Liú Hào rebelled.
Zhōu fled south to Hángzhōu,
but as he took command of the garrison and governed,
he executed many innocent people.
The former prefect of Shàngráo, Chén Quányù, passed through his territory,
and Zhōu framed him,
exterminating his entire clan.
Zhōu was eighty-three,
still exceptionally strong and vigorous,
with hundreds of female entertainers,
having fully mastered Qīqī's arts.
Later, he was haunted by the vengeful spirits of the innocent and Quányù,
and one day suddenly died.
During the military revolt of Liú Hào,
Qīqī was pushed off the north bank at Gānlù Temple by the crowd,
and it was said he fell into the river and died.
Later, people saw him selling medicine in Jiāngxī for over ten years,
then entering Shǔ,
and no one knew where he went.
Hèlín Temple was burned down in the war.
The tree lost its roots and trunk,
truly having returned to Làngyuàn.
From "Continued Biographies of Immortals."
Lǘqiū Zǐ
There was Zhèng Yòuxuán from Xíngyáng,
a son of a distinguished family.
He resided in Cháng'ān,
and from childhood studied together with a boy from the neighboring Lǘqiū family
under a teacher.
Yòuxuán was arrogant by nature;
relying on his family's noble and prestigious lineage,
while the Lǘqiū family was poor and lowly,
he often teased and insulted him, saying:
"The Lǘqiū family is not of my kind,
yet we study together under the teacher.
Even if I do not speak,
are you not ashamed in your heart?"
The Lǘqiū boy fell silent with a look of shame.
Several years later,
the Lǘqiū boy died of illness.
After ten years,
Yòuxuán passed the imperial examination with distinction in the classics,
and was later appointed as a参军 (staff officer) in Táng'ān Commandery.
Upon assuming office,
the commandery governor ordered him to act as the deputy magistrate of Tángxīng County.
There was a fellow lodger named Qiú,
son of a great merchant,
just twenty years old,
whose family assets amounted to tens of thousands.
He met with Yòuxuán daily,
and Yòuxuán repeatedly accepted money and gifts from him,
often feasting and socializing together.
However, Qiú was not from a scholar-official family,
so Yòuxuán never treated him with courtesy.
One day,
Yòuxuán hosted a grand banquet,
but Qiú was not invited.
As the drinking neared its end,
someone said to Yòuxuán:
"Qiú shares lodgings with you and often feasts together,
yet he was not invited to this banquet.
Is this not an offense?"
Yòuxuán felt ashamed
and immediately summoned Qiú.
When Qiú arrived,
Yòuxuán offered him a cup of wine.
Qiú declined, unable to drink it all,
and firmly apologized.
Yòuxuán angrily scolded him:
"You are a commoner from the marketplace,
only knowing petty profits.
How dare you overstep your place among officials?
Moreover, associating with you
is truly your good fortune;
how dare you decline the wine?"
He then shook his robes and stood up.
Qiú felt deeply humiliated;
he bowed and withdrew,
then resigned from his post and shut himself at home,
avoiding contact with others.
After several months, he fell ill and died.
The following year,
Zhèng was dismissed from office
and took up temporary residence in a Buddhist temple in Méngyáng Commandery.
Zhèng had always been fond of the teachings of Huáng-Lǎo.
At that time, there was a Dàoshi Wú,
renowned for his mastery of the Way,
who lived as a hermit on Shǔmén Mountain.
Yòuxuán admired his lofty demeanor
and immediately went to visit him,
wishing to become his disciple.
Dàoshi Wú said:
"Since you admire immortals,
you should reside in the mountains and forests,
and not be so eager for worldly affairs."
Yòuxuán joyfully thanked him and said:
"You, sir, are truly a man of the Way.
I wish to serve by your side;
may I?"
The Dàoshi agreed and kept him there.
After fifteen years in total,
Yòuxuán's determination gradually slackened.
Dàoshi Wú said:
"You cannot solidify your heart;
merely dwelling in the mountains and forests
is of no benefit."
Yòuxuán then bid farewell and left.
He feasted and socialized in Méngyáng Commandery for a long time.
Later, he traveled east to Cháng'ān.
Stopping at Bāochéng,
he lodged at an inn,
where he met a boy over ten years old,
with a very handsome appearance.
Yòuxuán spoke with him,
and the boy's eloquent wisdom was endlessly transformative,
making Yòuxuán feel he could not match him.
After a while, the boy said to Yòuxuán:
"I have been your old friend for years;
do you remember me?"
Yòuxuán said:
"I have forgotten."
The boy said:
"I was once born into the Lǘqiū family,
living in Cháng'ān,
studying with you under the teacher.
You considered me poor and lowly,
and said I was not of your kind.
Later, I was reborn as the son of the Qiú family,
serving as deputy magistrate in Tángxīng,
sharing lodgings with you.
You accepted much money and many gifts from me,
yet you never treated me with courtesy,
insulting me as a commoner from the marketplace.
Why are you so exceedingly arrogant?"
Yòuxuán was shocked
and bowed repeatedly in apology, saying:
"It is truly my fault.
But unless you are a sage,
how could you know about three lifetimes?"
The boy said:
"I am the Tàiqīng Zhēnrén (Great Clarity True Man).
The Heavenly Emperor, seeing that you had the aura of the Way,
thus sent me to be born among humans,
to befriend you,
and to impart to you the secrets of becoming a true immortal.
