But you, with your arrogant nature,
ultimately could not attain the Way.
Alas,
how lamentable!"
Having spoken,
he suddenly vanished from sight.
After Yòuxuán realized what had happened,
he felt deeply ashamed and resentful,
and eventually died of sorrow.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
Zhāng Zhuó
Zhāng Zhuó was a man from Shǔ.
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
he passed the imperial examination in the “Míngjīng” category
and returned to Shǔ to visit his family.
He had only one donkey,
on which he carried his clothes and books,
so he had no time to ride it
and simply drove it along.
Taking a shortcut
through the Xiégǔ valley,
after several days
he was nearing Yángzhōu
when the donkey suddenly bolted into a deep bamboo thicket
and could not be found.
Dusk was approaching,
there were no houses around,
and though he wished to spend the night in the woods,
he feared wolves and tigers.
That night the moon was bright;
he walked about several tens of lǐ
until he reached a main road.
After another two or three lǐ,
he saw a large mansion
with a vermilion gate facing west.
When dawn broke,
a mountain boy came out from the mansion,
and Zhuó asked him for water.
The boy went back inside,
and soon a man appeared,
wearing a vermilion crown and tall shoes,
leaning on a staff as he walked out.
Zhuó hurried forward and bowed to him.
The great immortal said:
“You are a man of the dusty world—
why have you come here?”
Zhuó explained everything in detail.
The immortal said:
“It is fate.”
He then invited Zhuó to sit
and offered him a cup of water.
It was fragrant, smooth, clear, and cool,
and his body felt light and vigorous.
After serving a fine meal,
he had Zhuó bathe in the western courtyard
and gave him a chest of clothes to wear.
The immortal said:
“Your bones are not yet fully formed;
it is your destiny to stay here.
I have a daughter,
and I wish to betroth her to you.”
Zhuó rose and bowed in thanks,
and that evening the wedding was held.
After several days,
Zhuó suddenly thought of home.
The immortal gave Zhuó two red talismans and two black talismans:
“One black talisman can be placed on your head—
when you enter someone’s house, it will make you invisible;
one black talisman can be placed on your left arm—
within a thousand lǐ,
you can reach out and take what you desire;
one red talisman can be placed on your tongue—
if someone cannot be driven away,
open your mouth and show it to them;
one red talisman can be placed on your left foot—
it will allow you to tread upon the earth’s veins and resist extraordinary threats.
But do not rely on these spiritual talismans
to become reckless and arrogant.”
Zhuó arrived in the capital
and saw a large mansion
crowded with people and horses,
extremely luxurious and splendid.
Zhuó entered,
passed through several gates,
and reached the main hall,
where he saw lavish furnishings arranged
and guests filling the room.
Inside a curtained area, a girl was being adorned,
about fifteen or sixteen years old.
Zhuó took hold of her
and hid by the middle gate.
He heard anxious voices throughout the mansion saying:
“The Grand Councilor has lost his young lady.”
The matter was reported to the emperor,
who ordered Masters Luó and Yè to search the mansion.
Master Yè stamped his feet, clicked his teeth,
and spat water, transforming it into a black vapor
that went straight to Zhuó,
revealing a young man holding the girl’s sleeve.
The Grand Councilor on the right seat was furious
and ordered his men to seize him.
Zhuó raised his arm,
and it was like striking a wall—
they could not get near him.
They quickly splashed him with dog and horse blood
and attacked him with swords and blades,
so Zhuó opened his mouth,
and the blades broke and shattered.
Then an imperial envoy announced an edict,
ordering that his head be cut off and presented.
Zhuó heard this and grew afraid,
so he removed his left shoe
and stretched out his foot to push.
The Grand Councilor, Masters Luó and Yè, and the imperial envoy
all fell backward.
Master Yè said:
“When we first entered the gate,
I sensed an extraordinary aura,
and when he opened his mouth,
it indeed revealed the envoy of Tàiyǐ.
Grand Councilor, you have recovered your beloved daughter—
why must you harm him?”
Zhuó then released the girl,
and the emperor sent guards to escort him back to the old mountain.
The immortal, leaning on his staff, met him on the road and said:
“Young Zhāng, you did not heed my words
and were nearly caught in a net.”
The imperial guards were still following,
so the immortal used his staff to draw on the ground,
and it turned into a great river,
with vast, surging waves
stretching two or three lǐ wide.
His wife threw her rosy cape over the water,
and in an instant it transformed into a flying bridge
suspended in midair.
The immortal went first,
Zhuó followed,
and his wife came after,
the three of them crossing the bridge.
With each step, the bridge retracted,
and all that could be seen were green mountains encircling them
and sheer cliffs rising in countless layers.
The people all bowed from afar.
When this was reported to Emperor Xuánzōng,
he immediately sent envoys to the mountain to perform sacrificial rites.
Thus it was called Géxiān Shān,
located sixty lǐ west of Yángzhōu.
It remains there to this day.
From the *Huìchāng Jiěyílù*.
Qílín Kè
The Qílín Guest was
a hired servant of Zhāng Màoshí of Nányáng.
Màoshí lived at the foot of Huàshān.
In the early Dàzhōng era of the Táng dynasty,
he happened to travel to Luòzhōng,
and hired a servant at the Southern Market,
where he obtained one man.
His name was Wáng Xiòng,
around forty years old,
and his monthly wage for labor was five hundred coins.
He was diligent, capable, and selfless,
acting with deep sincerity.
If there was something to be done,
he did not wait to be ordered.
Màoshí valued him,
changed his name to Dàlì,
and intended to double his wage,
but the man firmly declined.
His family pitied him even more.
After residing there for five years,
he calculated that his wages were fully paid.
One morning, he bid farewell to Màoshí, saying:
"Xiòng originally lived in the mountains,
and my family estate was not meager.
I happened to encounter misfortune,
and needed to hire myself out to labor to dispel it.
I was certainly not one without means who sold his strength.
Now the misfortune has ended,
please allow me to take my leave from here."
Màoshí could not fathom his words,
and dared not detain him,
letting him go.
At dusk,
he came in and said to Màoshí:
"I am grateful for your kindness and tolerance,
and deeply wish to repay you.
Xiòng's home is very near here,
and the scenery and delights within
are also quite worth seeing.
Could you accompany me for a visit?"
Màoshí happily said:
"What fortune!
However, I do not wish my family to know.
Could we go secretly for a visit?"
Xiòng said:
"Very easy."
Thereupon, he cut a bamboo staff several feet long,
inscribed a talisman on its upper part,
and handed it to Màoshí, saying:
"Take this staff into your room,
and complain of a stomachache.
Have all the attendants fetch medicine.
After they leave,
secretly place the bamboo in your quilt,
and then slip away."
Màoshí followed his instructions.
Xiòng happily said:
"You truly are one who can visit my dwelling."
They traveled south together for over a li,
where a yellow-turbaned attendant held one azure qílín
and two red-striped tigers,
waiting by the roadside.
Màoshí, startled, wanted to retreat,
but Xiòng said:
"Do not worry,
just proceed forward."
When they reached the front,
Xiòng mounted the qílín,
and Màoshí and the yellow-turbaned attendant each mounted a tiger.
Màoshí, afraid, dared not approach,
saying:
"Xiòng accompanies you,
please do not fear.
Moreover, these creatures are among the most magnificent in the human world;
just try mounting them."
So he leaned on and mounted it,
finding it indescribably steady.
Thereupon, he followed him up to Xiānzhǎng Peak.
Crossing ravines and scaling mountains,
they passed as they wished,
utterly unaware of steepness or danger.
By around the third watch,
they had traveled several hundred li.
Descending a mountain,
they found myriad things fresh and lovely,
with pines and rocks delightful,
and towers, terraces, palaces, and observatories
unlike anything in the mortal world.
Approaching the gate,
the usher bowed and said:
"Young master, why
Míng manuscript lacks "why" character
have you come?"
Several hundred officials in purple robes
lined the path and bowed.
Once inside,
several dozen attendants in dark clothing,
each with exceptional beauty,
wearing bright, splendid garments
beyond description,
each holding musical instruments, led them in bowing.
Then, in the central hall, they feasted until finished,
and Xiòng had Màoshí sit.
Xiòng went to change clothes,
returned to sit,
his clothing, hat, and crown
so majestic in appearance and demeanor,
truly bearing the grace of an immortal.
The windows, doors, steps, and gates,
the abundance of screens, curtains, cushions, and mats
were certainly not of the mortal world.
Phoenixes singing and dancing,
and all the music
were things never heard before.
His spirit soared high and free,
no longer thinking of mortal affairs,
reaching the peak of joy.
The host said:
"This is an immortal dwelling,
not a place mortals can reach.
Due to your past karma,
you were fated to come here once,
hence this encounter of escaping misfortune.
The paths of immortals and mortals differ;
dust and purity are hard to mingle.
You should return to cultivate your mind.
After three or five kalpas,
we shall meet again.
Xiòng's worldly attachments are nearly exhausted;
my name is recorded in the upper realm.
I was fortunate to meet the Great Purity True Man,
summoned into the Lesser Existence Cavern,
shown the joys of the Nine Heavens,
and again commanded to descend and point to the waves of the sea of life and death."
And he said:
"Though joy is hard to seek,
suffering is also easily dispelled.
Like one building a mountain:
grasping soil increases its height;
not grasping, it stops;
digging, it collapses.
For
"For" originally "heaven".
According to Míng manuscript emended
those ascending high,
is it not difficult to go up and easy to come down?"
"From then on, I cultivated and practiced,
passing through six or seven kalpas,
before attaining this body.
Looking back at the discarded bones,
they piled up like mountains.
The waters of the four
"Four" originally "said".
According to Míng manuscript emended
great seas
are half the tears shed in parting by my parents, wife, and children from past lives.
Yet, with constant thought and cultivation,
a lifetime passes in an instant.
Though the physical form is distant,
if one does not forget to cultivate and attain,
the achievement is also not far.
There are also times when the mind is distant and the spirit clear,
and one awakens with a single word.
Strive on!"
He bestowed a hundred yì of gold,
as aid for sustaining the body,
and again mounted the qílín,
ordering the yellow-turbaned attendant to hold it.
Xiòng escorted him on foot back home,
where his family was just weeping around him.
Màoshí threw the gold into the well,
Xiòng removed the bamboo staff,
and had Màoshí secretly lie down in the quilt.
Xiòng said:
"I shall go to Pénglái to pay respects to the Great Immortal Elder.
Tomorrow morning on Liánhuā Peak,
there will be a multicolored cloud carriage departing—
that is my conveyance."
Thereupon, he bowed and left.
Màoshí suddenly groaned;
everyone, startled, asked him.
Màoshí deceived them, saying:
"When the stomachache first came,
suddenly it was as if someone summoned me,
and then I lost consciousness,
not knowing how much time passed."
His family said:
"After fetching the medicine and returning,
we called but got no response.
It has been seven days already,
only the warmth in your chest remained,
so we had not encoffined you."
The next day, looking out,
on Liánhuā Peak,
there indeed were colored clouds.
Thereupon, he abandoned his office to wander the famous mountains.
Later, he returned,
took the gold from the well and gave it to his family,
then went out again to wander the mountains,
and later, his whereabouts were unknown.
From "Xuán Guài Lù Xù"
Wáng Fǎjìn
Wáng Fǎjìn was a person from Línjīn, Jiànzhōu.
From a young age, he was fond of the Dao.
His home was near an ancient Daoist temple.
Although no Daoist priests resided there,
during his play, he never once showed disrespect to the statues and images.
When he was over ten years old,
a female Daoist priest, traveling from Jiànzhōu through the outer counties,
passed by his home.
His parents, seeing his admiration for the Dao,
entrusted him to the female Daoist for her protection.
She bestowed upon him the Zhèngyī Yánshēng Xiǎo Lù register,
and named him Fǎjìn.
He diligently attended to the incense and fire offerings,
observing fasts and maintaining the rituals.
He also consumed cypress and abstained from grains,
and from time to time experienced spiritual visitations.
At that time, the Sānchuān region suffered famine and scarcity.
The price of grain soared,
and six or seven out of ten people died.
Many gathered wild kudzu and mountain yams to stave off hunger.
Suddenly, three azure youths descended into his courtyard
and said to Fǎjìn:
"The Supreme Deity, seeing that you have long possessed an immortal's bone,
devoted your heart with purity and sincerity,
and never neglected the Dao,
has commanded us to welcome you to receive duties in the Upper Capital."
Unconsciously, he rose into the air.
Directly reaching the place of the Great Emperor,
he was ordered to be bestowed a jade cup of rosy nectar.
Slowly, the Emperor said to him:
"For a human to occupy the great position among the Three Powers,
embodying the harmony of Heaven and Earth,
obtaining human form,
and being born in the Central Land—this is exceedingly difficult.
Heaven circulates the qi of the four seasons,
Earth receives the excellence of the Five Phases,
producing the five grains and hundred fruits
to nourish humanity.
Yet humans do not know the grace of Heaven and Earth's nurturing,
lightly discarding the five grains,
disdaining and abandoning silk and hemp,
causing the farmers who till the land
and the women who spin and weave
to toil their bodies yet not get their fill,
exhaust their strength yet not ward off the cold,
vainly expending their labor.
There has never been any who cherished and treasured these things.
This is indeed what the divine spirits condemn,
and why Heaven and Earth do not protect them.
Recently, based on the reports from the Earth Offices and the Mountain and River Deities,
that the people of the world despise and cast away the five grains,
not valuing the foundation of clothing and food,
I have already commanded the Prefecture of Tàihuà
to gather the spirits of the five grains.
The crops planted will not succeed,
and the common people will starve,
thus demonstrating punishment and reproach
to chastise their hearts.
However, I soon received the compassionate decree of the Supreme Venerable,
that the Great Dao favors life,
and its priority is to save beings.
Although Heaven, Earth, and the divine spirits condemn them,
the ignorant people do not know the source of their transgressions,
and thus have no path for repentance, supplication, and seeking forgiveness.
You shall become an attendant youth in the Upper Palace,
entering to serve in the Celestial Prefecture.
For now, I order you to descend back to the world,
to instruct and enlighten the common people,
so they may repent their sins,
treasure and cherish agriculture and sericulture.
This will also be your hidden merit."
He ordered a maidservant to give him one scroll of the "Língbǎo Qīngzhāi Gàoxiè Tiāndì Yí" (Numinous Treasure Pure Fast Ritual for Thanking Heaven and Earth),
to be transmitted and practiced in the world.
He said:
"Have the people of the world gather in secluded mountains and places of high tranquility,
to perform the fast, repent, and give thanks.
If done twice a year,
then past sins can be eradicated,
and the spirits of the Grain Father and Silkworm Mother
will bring about abundance and plenty.
In the year of the Dragon and Tiger,
I shall summon you again."
This is the present-day method of the Pure Fast to Heaven's Duke for giving thanks.
Fǎjìn, in the rénchén year of the Tiānbǎo era's twelfth year,
then ascended to Heaven again.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí"
Wéi Yáng Shí Yǒu
The Ten Friends of Wéiyáng were
all moderately wealthy in family property,
content with their lot and knowing satisfaction,
not seeking official positions or salaries,
not coveting goods or wealth,
but admiring the mysterious and understanding the Way.
They made a pact to be friends,
like brothers.
At that time, the land was greatly peaceful,
and the people were all joyful.
Thus they took pleasure in wine and food,
enjoying themselves according to their aspirations.
Starting from one household,
they rotated among the ten homes,
making it a regular practice.
Suddenly, there was an old man,
his clothes filthy and worn,
his appearance frail and weak,
seeming like a scholar of impoverished and insufficient means.
He also wore hemp clothing,
joining the end of the ten men
"joining the end of the ten men" originally read "leading ten men here."
Changed according to the Ming manuscript
and came to their gathering.
Since everyone was in good spirits,
they all pitied him,
and did not drive him away.
He left on his own after getting drunk and full,
and no one knew where he went.
One day, he said to the group:
"I am a man of limited strength,
fortunate that you all allow me to accompany you at the end of the seat,
not blaming me for it.
Now that the ten of you have held banquets,
I have been able to attend them all.
Since the rounds are now complete,
I also wish to make an effort to host one gathering,
to repay your great kindness.
Let us set a date,
and I hope you will all come along."
When the time came,
the ten friends did as he said,
gathering together to wait.
At dawn,
the poor old man indeed arrived,
and led them slowly on foot,
to the outskirts of Dōngtáng.
They did not realize it was far.
In the wilderness were two or three thatched huts,
leaning and about to collapse.
He led them beneath them.
There were several beggars there,
all with disheveled hair and ragged clothes,
their appearances filthy and ugly.
When the old man arrived,
the beggars looked at each other and stood up,
standing against the wall to await his command.
The old man ordered them to sweep the place,
set out mats,
spread out reed mats,
and invited everyone to sit in a circle.
The day had already grown late,
and everyone looked hungry.
After a long time,
they each placed vinegar, salt, and bamboo chopsticks
before the guests.
After a while,
several of them together lifted a huge board like a table,
four or five feet long,
and set it in the middle of the mats,
covered with an oilcloth.
The ten friends looked at each other,
thinking it must be something to relieve their hunger,
and were very pleased.
When the oilcloth was removed,
steam rose so thickly it was still hard to make out,
but after looking for a long time,
they saw it was a steamed child.
Probably over ten years old,
already rotten and mushy,
with ears, eyes, hands, and feet
half fallen off.
The old man bowed and urged them,
encouraging everyone to eat.
The group deeply disliked it,
most excusing themselves by saying they were full,
some angrily ran away,
and none were willing to eat.
The old man freely ate his fill,
as if enjoying a delicious feast.
What was left uneaten,
he ordered the beggars to take away,
telling them to finish it.
Then he said to the others:
"What we ate here
is a thousand-year-old ginseng,
quite difficult to find,
not something one encounters easily.
I obtained this thing,
and feeling grateful for your kindness in allowing me to join you,
I wished to repay you briefly.
Moreover, those who eat it
ascend to heaven in broad daylight,
becoming high immortals.
Since you all did not eat it,
it must be fate."
Everyone was shocked and amazed,
but before they could regret and apologize,
the old man hurriedly asked the beggars,
telling them to come as soon as they finished eating.
Soon, the beggars transformed into azure boys and jade maidens,
with banners, canopies, and attendants leading the way,
and together with the old man, they ascended to heaven in an instant.
The ten friends, hearts torn with regret, tried to pursue them,
but could see them no more.
From "Biographies of Encounters with Immortals"
Jīn Kějì
was a man of Xīnluó,
a tribute scholar.
His nature was calm and he loved the Way,
not admiring extravagance or luxury.
Sometimes he practiced breath control and refined his form,
finding joy in it himself.
He was widely learned and had a strong memory,
and his literary compositions were elegant and beautiful.
He had handsome features,
and in his movements, speech, and demeanor,
he distinctly had the style of the Central Plains.
Soon he passed the imperial examination,
and built a dwelling in Zǐwǔ Valley of Zhōngnán Mountain,
cherishing the taste of reclusion and leisure.
He personally planted many exotic flowers and rare fruits,
often burning incense and sitting quietly,
as if deep in thought.
He also recited the "Dàodé Jīng" and various immortal scriptures without cease.
After three years,
he thought of returning to his homeland,
and left by sea.
He came back again,
wearing Daoist robes,
and reentered Zhōngnán.
He devoted himself to performing hidden virtues;
when people sought something from him,
he never refused at first.
He was diligent and earnest in his affairs,
and others could not keep up with him.
In the twelfth month of the eleventh year of the Táng Dàzhōng era,
he suddenly submitted a memorial saying:
"Your servant has received the Jade Emperor's edict
to become Vice Minister of the Yīngwén Terrace,
and will ascend on the twenty-fifth day of the second month next year."
At that time, Emperor Xuānzōng found it extremely strange,
and sent a palace envoy to summon him into the inner court,
but he firmly declined and did not go.
He also asked for the text of the Jade Emperor's edict,
but was told it was held by other immortals,
and not left in the human world.
Then he was bestowed four palace maids,
incense, medicine, gold, and silks,
and two more palace envoys were sent
specifically to attend to him.
Jīn Kějì lived alone in a quiet room,
and with the palace maids and envoys,
he mostly did not get close.
Every night,
the sound of guests talking and laughing was often heard in his room.
The envoys secretly peeked,
and saw immortal officials and immortal maidens,
each sitting on dragons and phoenixes,
solemnly facing each other,
with many guards as well.
But the palace maids and envoys
did not dare to disturb them rashly.
On the twenty-fifth day of the second month,
the spring scenery was beautiful and charming,
flowers blooming brilliantly.
Indeed, there were five-colored clouds, crying cranes,
soaring phoenixes and white swans,
sheng flutes, xiao flutes, metal, and stone chimes,
feathered canopies and jade wheels,
banners and streamers filling the sky.
The immortal entourage was extremely numerous,
and he ascended to heaven and left.
Officials and commoners of the court,
watchers filled the valleys, crowding them,
and none did not gaze in reverence, sighing in wonder.
From "Continued Biographies of Immortals"
Yáng Zhēnbó
Yáng Zhēnbó of Hóngnóng,
was gifted in literature from a young age,
and was so engrossed in books and histories
that he would forget to eat or sleep.
His parents could not stop him;
sometimes they would take away his candles
and hide his poetry and books.
Zhēnbó found this quite troublesome,
so he fled to the region between Hóng and Ráo,
where he studied in an empty courtyard of a temple
for over half a year.
On the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival,
while he was reading,
around the second watch,
someone suddenly knocked on his study window.
Zhēnbó, absorbed in his classics, did not notice.
Soon, someone pushed the door open and entered—
it was a young maidservant with double buns,
who said:
"My lady has long dwelled in seclusion,
nourishing herself on qi and consuming spiritual herbs,
often traveling between the clouds and waters of Dòngtíng.
Knowing that you, sir, have recently arrived here,
and that your spirit is pure and clear,
with steadfast and unsullied aspirations,
she wishes to share her heartfelt feelings with you."
Zhēnbó paid no attention at all,
and the maidservant left.
After the third watch,
he heard the sound of jade pendants and ornaments outside the door,
accompanied by an extraordinary, fragrant aroma.
Soon, the maidservant announced that the lady was about to arrive.
She appeared to be around sixteen years old,
wearing a crown of blue clouds and phoenix wings,
and dressed in a robe of purple clouds, sun, and moon,
radiating a brilliant light.
She approached and took a seat,
but Zhēnbó still did not look at her or utter a word.
After a long while,
she took an inkstone from Zhēnbó's desk,
and the maidservant presented paper.
The lady wrote a few lines of a letter,
then shyly departed.
Zhēnbó then rose
and looked at the poem she had left:
"You, sir, stubbornly resist,
leaving no way to convey my sincere feelings.
The bright moon over the sea and mountains,
the autumn wind—shall I return alone?"
Afterward, he never learned who the lady was.
Could she have been one of the immortals of Dòngtíng?
Judging by the sentiment of her poem,
could it have been the words of a mortal?
From *Bó Yì Zhì*.
Hán Yù's Nephew
The nephew of Hán Yù, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel in the Táng dynasty,
his name is forgotten.
From a young age, he was unruly
and did not study books,
but enjoyed drinking.
At the age of twenty,
he went to Luòyáng to visit relatives,
but became enamored with the clouds and waters and did not return.
For nearly twenty years,
there was no news of him.
During the Yuánhé era,
he suddenly returned to Cháng'ān,
looking disheveled and unkempt,
his clothes dirty and worn,
and his behavior eccentric.
The Minister, having not seen him for so long,
tolerated and forgave him.
After their first meeting,
he was told to converse with his cousins in the academy,
but he showed no interest in poetry or books,
appearing almost like a clay figurine,
and only gambled with the servants.
Sometimes he would lie drunk in the stable for three to five days,
or stay out overnight.
The Minister feared he would break the law,
and occasionally admonished him.
One day during leisure, the Minister happened to see him
and asked about his talents.
He replied:
"I am skilled at tossing coins through a hoop."
The Minister tested him:
he planted an iron rod over a foot tall,
and from a hundred paces away, tossed three hundred and sixty coins,
each passing through the hoop
without a single miss.
He also occasionally composed verses,
which amused everyone.
Moreover, from fifty paces away,
he could write the characters "天下太平" (peace under heaven) in double-lined cursive,
with extremely precise strokes.
He could also pile thirty catties of charcoal in a stove,
keeping the fire burning for three days,
the flames constantly vigorous,
only dying down after the time was up.
The Minister found this remarkable
and asked him about cultivating the Way.
He then spoke of profound mysteries and pure discourse,
covering profound truths,
and was thoroughly versed in matters of immortals.
He spoke of minor skills,
saying he could dye flowers:
he could turn red ones blue,
or make a single flower display five colors,
all achievable.
That autumn,
he dyed a cluster of white peonies in the Minister's backyard,
saying:
"Next spring, they will surely bloom with indigo hues,
some with golden edges and red halos,
and on each side, there will be one flower with five colors."
He dug up the roots, placed medicine beneath them,
and then replanted them,
waiting for spring to verify the results.
Soon after, he secretly left,
and no one knew where he went.
That year,
the emperor welcomed the Buddha's relic in Fèngxiáng,
viewing it from the tower.
The entire city's people
neglected their work and forgot to eat.
The Minister submitted a memorial to admonish directly,
offending the emperor,
and was demoted to Prefect of Cháozhōu.
On the way to Shāngshān,
the mud was slippery and the snow deep,
and he felt quite depressed.
Suddenly, he saw his nephew standing before his horse.
The nephew bowed and greeted him,
holding the stirrup and taking the reins,
showing great attentiveness.
The next day, when the snow cleared,
he escorted the Minister to Dèngzhōu,
then said to him:
"My master is here.
I cannot go farther.
I am about to enter Xuán Hù Yǐ Dì Peak."
The Minister was astonished by his words
and asked about his master.
It was Master Hóngyá.
Dōngyuán Gōng was then using soft gold and liquid jade
to refine the Jiǔhuá Elixir,
and the fire control was so precise
that he could not leave even briefly.
The Minister, with increased respect, asked:
"Can immortality be attained?
Can the supreme Way be sought?"
He replied:
"To gain it lies in the heart,
to lose it also lies in the heart.
Assessing merits and virtues,
the strictness of promotions and demotions
resembles the prohibitions of kings.
I will pay my respects another day;
please allow me to depart here."
The Minister composed a fifty-six-character poem to bid him farewell:
"At dawn, I presented a memorial to the ninefold heavens;
by dusk, I was banished to Cháoyáng, eight thousand li away.
I intended to rid the sacred court of malpractices;
how could I, in my declining years, cherish my remaining life?
Clouds shroud Qín Ridge—where is my home?
Snow blocks Lán Pass—my horse will not advance.
I know you have come from afar with purpose;
please gather my bones by the miasmic river's edge."
After presenting the poem,
he waved his tears and parted.
The nephew walked into the forested valley,
swift as flight.
The following spring,
the peonies bloomed,
and the colors of several flowers
were exactly as he had said.
Moreover, on each petal of the flowers,
there were fourteen characters in regular script:
"Clouds shroud Qín Ridge—where is my home?
Snow blocks Lán Pass—my horse will not advance."
The calligraphy was exquisite,
beyond human capability.
If not an immortal who had attained the Way,
able to foresee and know in advance,
how could this be achieved?
Some say
that the Minister later saw him again
and also learned the method of transcending the world through moonlight.
But this was not publicly known.
From *Xiān Zhuàn Shí Yí*.
Liú Qián
(pronounced Qián),
childhood name Yígē,
was the elder brother of the Tang dynasty chancellor Liú Zhān.
Qián’s family was poor, but he was fond of the Dao.
Once, a Daoist priest passed by his home,
saw Qián, and found him extraordinary.
He then asked, “Do you know the Dao?”
Qián replied:
“I know of it,
but my nature is full of worldly attachments,
my karmic burden is not yet purified,
how could I rashly force myself to study it?”
The Daoist said:
“Could you take me as your teacher?”
Qián said:
“How would I dare?”
Thereupon, he served him as his teacher.
The Daoist instructed Qián:
“To dwell in the mountains seeking the Dao,
you need not necessarily wrap your head in a scarf.”
Qián then wore his hair in twin buns and dressed in plain cloth,
following the Daoist into Luófú Mountain.
Earlier,
Qián and Zhān had both studied books and practiced writing,
but Qián’s nature inclined solely toward lofty ideals,
while Zhān’s heart yearned for glory and success.
Qián once said to Zhān:
“I will certainly not pass the imperial examinations,
and so will wander free in the mountains and wilds.
You will pass the examinations,
and so will toil in the dusty world of affairs,
ultimately not reaching my state.
Yet be cautious with wealth and honor,
forty years from now,
this will be proven.”
Zhān said:
“Immortals are distant and difficult to seek;
Qín Shǐhuáng and Hàn Wǔdì
were not without earnest effort.
The court is but a step away, easy to reach;
Mǎ Zhōu and Zhāng Jiāzhēn
can be followed in succession.”
After this, Qián grew ever more refined in the Dao,
and then hid himself in Luófú.
Zhān passed the imperial examinations as a jìnshì,
repeatedly held high and prestigious offices,
and when he rose to become a chief minister,
he gained considerable fame for harmonious governance.
Suddenly, he was demoted to Rìnán,
and while traveling, he stopped at Cháotái in Guǎngzhōu,
mooring his boat by the riverbank.
Suddenly, a youth with hair in twin buns and dressed in plain cloth
came rushing through a heavy rain,
his clothes and shoes not wet at all.
He said he wished to see Zhān.
Zhān’s attendants were all astonished,
and questioned him.
“Just say Yígē has come.”
They reported this,
and Zhān asked about his appearance,
which they described in full.
Zhān sighed in amazement,
and welcomed him in to see him.
Qián’s face and appearance seemed to be only about twenty years old,
while Zhān was white-haired and frail with age,
and now an exiled official.
Overwhelmed with sorrow and joy,
Qián further encouraged him, saying:
“We are brothers,
sharing the pain of flesh and blood.
The words of former days,
now forty years have passed.”
Zhān also sighed with emotion.
He said to Qián:
“Can I still cultivate it?”
Qián said:
“You have sought glory and favor,
held office harmonizing yīn and yáng,
your mind stirred by action and stillness—
could this be without harm?
Unless it were my elder brother of the Máo family,
who has already ascended as a celestial immortal,
who could save you?
Now I have only come to bid farewell,
not to save you.”
Thereupon, they traveled together in the boat,
speaking of all the events that had separated them in life,
and one night Qián disappeared from where he was.
Nowadays, in Luófú Mountain,
he is occasionally seen.
Zhān then proceeded south,
and died in the place of his exile.
From “Xù Xiān Zhuàn”
Lú Jūn
Chancellor Lú Gōngjūn of the Táng dynasty,
having passed the imperial examination and been appointed a secretary in the Ministry of Personnel,
was sent out to serve as the prefect of Jūnzhōu due to illness.
Upon arriving at the prefecture, his illness gradually worsened;
he became emaciated and frail,
unable to bear seeing people.
He often secluded himself in a mountain retreat behind the prefectural office to cultivate his nature in solitude.
Even his attendants and servants
were kept at a distance;
unless summoned by the chancellor,
none dared approach.
Suddenly, a man dressed in tattered clothing
climbed over the wall and entered,
saying
his surname was Wáng.
When asked where he came from,
he replied,
"From the mountains."
The chancellor smiled and said to him:
"So you are the mountain hermit Wáng.
What brings you here to instruct me?"
Wáng said:
"Your honor's status
has reached the pinnacle among officials,
yet your lifespan will not be long.
Misfortune is deepening,
and thus you suffer from this lingering illness.
That is why I have come to rescue you."
There was no water in the mountain retreat,
so the chancellor intended to summon someone to fetch hot water and tea,
but Wáng stopped him.
He dipped his waist sash into the well,
took out a bright red pill,
twisted the water from the sash to swallow the pill,
and made an agreement with him, saying:
"Five days from now,
your illness shall be cured,
and your health will be twice as robust as before.
Two years later,
you will face a great calamity.
Diligently accumulate hidden merits,
with the intent to save people and show compassion to all beings.
At that time, we shall meet again,
in early summer."
From then on, Chancellor Lú's illness was cured,
and within ten days, he fully recovered.
The following year, he resigned from his post and returned to the capital,
where he was appointed as a judge in the Salt and Iron Commission.
In the fourth month of summer,
on the left side of the road east of Wùběn Gate,
he suddenly saw the mountain hermit.
The hermit soon arrived at Lú's residence,
and joyfully said:
"This year marks the end of your second allotted span.
The calamity was extremely severe,
but because you served as a prefect
and last year exonerated an unjustly imprisoned case,
saving the lives of three people,
the calamity has already been dispelled.
Within this month,
you will only experience minor discomfort for three to five days,
so there is truly nothing to worry about."
The next day,
the mountain hermit had two servants take ten thousand coins
to distribute among the poor and sick at Gǒují Slope.
After this, he departed again,
saying:
"On the fifth day of the fifth month, at noon, in the twenty-third year,
have a Daoist priest await me atop Wàn Mountain.
By then, you will be governing the region of Hàn,
and I shall bestow upon you the essence of the moon.
Do not miss the appointed time."
From then on, Chancellor Lú's career flourished with prestigious and influential posts,
becoming increasingly prosperous and honored.
In the year after he was appointed to govern Hànnán,
which was the twenty-third year,
when the time arrived,
he ordered the Daoist priest Niú Zhīwēi
to ascend to the summit of Wàn Mountain at noon on the fifth day.
The mountain hermit was there,
and with two golden elixirs,
he had Niú Zhīwēi swallow them,
saying to him:
"You possess the aura of the Dao but lack hidden merits;
you have not yet attained the rank of the Dao.
You must cultivate yourself more diligently."
With ten golden elixirs,
he instructed him to deliver them to the chancellor.
He said:
"You shall enjoy a long life,
but do not forget to practice refinement.
Once your worldly span is complete,
you shall await your return to the Pénglái Palace!"
After bidding farewell to Niú Zhīwēi with a bow,
he suddenly vanished.
Afterwards, Niú Zhīwēi lived to over eighty years of age,
his appearance always like that of a thirty-year-old.
Chancellor Lú lived to ninety,
with keen hearing and clear vision,
and his strength never waned.
After he passed away,
a wondrous fragrance filled the room.
From "Biographies of Encounters with Immortals"
Xuē Féng
Xué Féng from Hédōng,
during the Xiántōng era, served as the prefect of Miánzhōu.
After more than a year,
he dreamed of entering a cave dwelling,
where there were many delicacies but no people to be seen.
He did not dare to partake of them,
and so he went out the door.
Someone said to him:
"This is the Heavenly Granary."
The next morning, he spoke of it to his guests and friends.
Someone said:
"Within the prefecture's borders lies Chāngmíng County,
where there is a Tiāncāng Cave.
Inside, food and drink appear naturally,
and often those who wander among the clouds and waters obtain and eat it."
He immediately sent the Daoist priest Sūn Língfèng and a trusted subordinate to investigate.
Entering the cave for about ten *li*,
they still needed to hold torches.
Beyond ten *li*, it gradually grew brighter.
After another three to five *li*,
it opened up, no different from the human world.
The cavern was extremely vast,
capable of holding a thousand people.
The ground below was level and even,
with stone beds arranged in rows.
Upon them were many famous varieties of food and drink,
all as if freshly prepared,
soft, delicious, sweet, and fragrant.
Língfèng bowed and ate them.
He also opened another three or five places,
intending to offer them to Lord Xué as proof.
But when he carried them out of the cave entrance,
their shapes remained exactly as they were,
yet they had all turned to stone.
To the left and right within the cave,
scattered flour and kneaded dough,
piles of salt and heaps of fermented beans,
were beyond measure.
Proceeding another one or two *li*,
they encountered a swiftly flowing stream,
both wide and deep.
Across the stream, they could clearly see mountains, rivers, and dwellings.
Not daring to cross, they stopped.
Near the bank in the sand,
there were footprints coming and going,
each two or three feet long,
only then did they realize it was a place where people walked.
Lord Xué, hearing of this,
marveled at its spiritual wonder,
yet could not fathom the reason for it.
I note that according to the *Yǔdìzhì*:
Shàoshì Mountain has naturally occurring grains, sweet fruits,
divine mushrooms, and immortal herbs.
Prince Jìn of the Zhōu dynasty, studying the Dao to become a transcendent,
left ninety years' worth of provisions
in the mountains.
Shàoshì is seventeen *li* west of Sōng Mountain.
Ascending forty *li* from the southeast,
one reaches Xiàdìngsī.
Another ten *li* up is Shàngdìngsī.
Within these ten *li* is a great stone gate,
which is Zhōngdìngsī.
Proceeding west from Zhōngdìngsī,
to the edge of the cliff,
below is a stone chamber,
inside which is water
and many white quartz crystals.
Within the chamber are natural scriptures and books,
and natural food and drink.
This is no different from the aforementioned.
Also, east of Tiāntāi Mountain there is a cave.
Entering over ten *li*,
there are dwellings and marketplaces,
where much food and drink is sold.
During the Qiánfú era,
a wandering monk entered the cave,
passed through the market,
and being very hungry,
he smelled the fragrance of food,
bought some steamed buns, and ate them.
A fellow monk traveling with him,
practicing breath cultivation, did not eat.
After traveling over ten *li*,
they exited the cave entrance,
and were already in Mùpíng County, Qīngzhōu.
But the monk who had eaten immediately turned to stone.
From this it is said:
Wáng Liè's stone marrow,
Zhāng Huá's dragon fat—
those who obtain and eat such things
must also have accumulated hidden merits
and been endowed by heaven with an immortal's bone,
only then can they ascend to the rank of immortals.
If an ordinary person eats them,
they will certainly transform into stone.
From *Shénxiān Gǎnyù Zhuàn*.
Fèi Guànqīng
was a man of Chízhōu.
Having passed the imperial examination as a jìnshì,
he was about to return to his hometown
and took leave of the Prime Minister, Lord Zhèng Yúqìng.
The lord had long been friends with Magistrate Liú of Qiūpǔ,
and was pleased with Fèi’s journey,
entrusting him to deliver a letter.
The handwritten letter filled the page,
and it was sealed and given to Fèi,
with the lord cautioning him:
"Magistrate Liú has long been in the arena of fame,
but the reason he has not ascended to the ranks of the top candidates
is due to his narrow-mindedness and straightforwardness,
not conforming to the times.
He abandoned the imperial examinations for a lowly official post,
so you should treat him well."
Fèi then requested the lord to briefly write a note of recommendation at the end of the letter,
hoping that through this consolation and recommendation,
he might receive some favor.
The lord agreed,
opened the letter and wrote a few lines,
then sealed it again as before.
When Fèi arrived at Qiūpǔ,
he first sent his name card to Liú.
Liú read the card,
tossed it onto the table,
and paid it no attention.
Fèi stood trembling, awaiting instructions,
but after a long time, there was no response.
Suspecting that it was not acceptable,
he then gave the Prime Minister’s letter to the gatekeeper.
Liú opened the seal and read it,
then cursed disdainfully:
"That old man Zhèng,
what use is this letter?"
He tore it up and discarded it.
Fèi grew even more fearful,
pushed the door open and entered,
hurriedly bowing before him.
Liú suddenly looked at him with pity,
greeted him and invited him to sit and talk.
As dusk fell,
Liú urged him to arrange for lodging at an inn.
Fèi said:
"It is already dark,
and even if I could find a traveler’s lodge,
it would be too late.
I beg to stay under the hall’s corridor,
spread a mat on the ground for one night,
and tomorrow I will slowly make my way to the inn."
He then unpacked his bag himself,
spread a felt mat on the ground,
and Liú immediately brushed his sleeves and went inside.
After a long while, he came out and said:
"This is no place to host a guest;
there is a small room inside."
Soon after, he closed the door,
and locked it very securely.
Fèi did not know why,
but he rested on the couch.
That night, the moon was bright,
and through a crack in the door, he peered outside,
where it was silent and still.
He saw Magistrate Liú holding a broom and dustpan himself,
sweeping and cleaning inside and outside the hall.
The courtyard, corridors, steps, and walls
were all meticulously attended to.
Fèi found this strange,
sat upright holding his breath,
and stayed awake, watching.
As the first watch approached,
suddenly there was an extraordinary fragrance,
exceptionally rich and intense,
unlike anything in the mortal world.
After a long while,
Liú stood respectfully in the courtyard holding a tablet,
as if waiting for something.
The fragrance grew even stronger,
and then he saw an immortal wearing a cloud-patterned crown and purple robes,
eight or nine feet tall,
accompanied by dozens of followers.
Liú bowed twice and kowtowed.
The immortal went straight into the hall,
and Liú stood waiting at his side.
Soon, a banquet was laid out,
with exquisite dishes and rare fruits,
their fragrance wafting to the room below.
Fèi smelled it
and already felt his spirit refreshed and invigorated.
Shortly after, music was played and wine was drunk.
The immortal ordered Liú to spread a mat on the ground,
and he also served and drank wine.
The melody of the music
was also not a tune of the mortal world.
The immortal suddenly asked Liú:
"Have you received a letter from Zhèng?"
Liú replied:
"I have received the letter and am well."
A moment later, he asked again:
"Have you received Zhèng’s letter?"
Liú replied:
"Senior Fèi Guànqīng came from Cháng'ān,
and I received the letter."
The immortal smiled and said:
"Fèi Guànqīng is to be congratulated on passing the examination;
is he here now?"
Liú replied:
"He is."
The immortal said:
"It is not yet time for me to meet him,
but give him a cup of wine.
Just tell him to cultivate the Way early,
and then we may meet."
He then ordered Liú to pour a cup of wine
and send it to the small room.
Fèi saw Liú take a sip of half the wine himself,
then add water from a basin on the steps to the cup,
and hesitated to drink it.
Suddenly, the immortal descended the steps,
and with his followers, rode the clouds away.
Liú bowed farewell, sobbing,
and the immortal cautioned him:
"When you see Zhèng,
just tell him to cultivate the Way,
and we will meet then."
After they left,
Liú went into the small room.
The wine was still there,
and he exclaimed in surprise:
"This wine is something one cannot encounter even in ten thousand kalpas;
why did you not drink it?"
He lifted it and drank it himself.
Fèi struggled to get some,
and managed to take a sip or two.
Liú then became a companion in cultivating the Way with Guànqīng,
and they chose to live on Jiǔhuá Mountain.
When Fèi was summoned to serve as Left Reminder,
he ultimately did not take up the post.
Prime Minister Zhèng soon also passed away.
Liú and Fèi kept the matter quite secret,
and it is unknown which true immortal descended that day.
From "Biographies of Encounters with Immortals"
Shěn Bīn
Shěn Bīn of Wúxīng
was fond of the Way from a young age.
After retiring and returning to Gāo'ān,
he constantly engaged in morning cultivation and elixir ingestion.
Once, while visiting the Yùmù Cave Temple,
he suddenly heard music in the air.
Looking up at the clouds,
he saw dozens of female immortals
slowly descending
and heading straight into the temple.
They went to each statue to burn incense,
and after a long while, they left.
Bīn hid in a room, not daring to come out.
After they left,
he entered the hall to pray,
and found leftover incense on the tables.
Bīn gathered it all and placed it in the incense burner.
Later, he regretted it, saying:
"All my life I have loved the Way,
yet today I saw immortals but could not pay my respects,
and obtained immortal incense but could not consume it.
Is this because I lack the destiny?"
Earlier,
Bīn had often warned his son:
"The hall where I live
is precisely an auspicious site;
bury me there."
When he died,
they followed his words.
Digging the ground, they found a naturally formed brick tomb,
exquisitely crafted,
with the characters "Wúxīng" inscribed on the bricks.
Bīn lived to be over eighty years old.
Later, in Yùzhāng, a fisherman threw raw rice into a pond to catch fish
and, without realizing it, went far.
Suddenly, he entered a stone gate,
where it was bright and clear.
After walking several hundred steps,
he saw an old man with a white beard.
Looking closely,
he resembled Bīn.
The old man said to the fisherman:
"This is no place for you to come;
leave quickly while you still can."
The fisherman hurried out and climbed ashore,
only to realize he had been in the water for three days.
The elders who knew said:
"That is the southern gate of the Western Immortal’s Tiānbǎo Cave."
From "Records of Divine Investigations"
Hánshānzǐ
Hánshānzi,
his name and surname are unknown.
During the Dàlì era,
he lived in seclusion on Cuìpíng Mountain in Tiāntāi.
The mountain is deep and remote,
and even in summer, there is snow,
so it is also called Hányán (Cold Cliff).
Thus, he took the name Hánshānzi.
He was fond of composing poetry,
and whenever he finished a piece or a line,
he would inscribe it on trees or rocks.
Those who took an interest
would follow and record them,
gathering over three hundred poems in total.
Many describe the joys of secluded life in the mountains and forests,
while others satirize the trends of the time,
serving to warn and inspire the common people.
The recluse Xú Língfǔ of Tóngbǎi
compiled and prefaced them,
dividing them into three volumes,
which circulated among the people.
More than ten years later, he suddenly disappeared.
In the twelfth year of the Xiántōng era,
the Dàolì priest Lǐ Hè of Pílíng,
who was narrow-minded and impatient,
enjoyed bullying and insulting others.
Suddenly, a poor scholar came to Hè begging for food.
Hè refused to give him any
and even scolded him harshly.
The poor man meekly left.
A few days later,
six or seven people dressed in white, riding white horses, came to see Hè,
who received them with courtesy.
They then asked Hè:
"Do you remember me?"
Hè looked at his appearance
and realized it was the poor scholar from before.
He hesitated, wanting to apologize,
but shame kept him from speaking.
Suddenly, the man said to Hè:
"You practice cultivation but do not know the proper path,
and you delight in bullying others and insulting customs.
What hope do you have of attaining the Way?
Do you know of Hánshānzi?"
Hè replied:
"Yes."
The man said:
"That is me.
I initially thought you could be taught,
but now I see you cannot.
The path to cultivating life
lies in eliminating desires and cravings,
cherishing the spirit and embracing harmony,
so that one is free from burdens;
restraining the heart within,
and examining the body without,
so that one is free from faults;
putting others before oneself,
knowing softness and maintaining humility,
so that one finds peace;
attributing goodness to others,
and taking blame upon oneself,
so that one accumulates virtue;
merit need not be great,
but one must establish it without slacking;
faults need not be great,
but one must eliminate them without repeating them,
so that one accumulates merit.
Only then will inner cultivation be fulfilled and the outer elixir arrive,
allowing one to glimpse the Way.
Your three poisons remain uncut,
and you adorn yourself with official caps and hairpins.
You are like a tiger or leopard's skin
wrapped around the substance of a dog or pig."
He then went out, mounted his horse, and left,
never to be seen again.
From "Xiānzhuàn Shíyí"
Xuānyuán Mímíng
Xuānyuán Mímíng,
no one knows where he was from.
He roamed between Héng and Xiāng for over ninety years,
excelling at capturing and expelling ghosts and spirits,
and capable of subduing flood dragons, serpents, tigers, and leopards.
No one knew his age.
Jìnshì Liú Shīfú
once encountered him in southern Xiāng.
On the fourth day of the twelfth month in the rénchén year of the seventh year of Yuánhé,
as Mímíng was about to travel from Héng Mountain to Tàibái,
returning
(the Míng manuscript has "passing through" instead of "returning").
to the capital,
he met Shīfú,
who invited him to stay overnight.
There was a collator, Hóu Xǐ,
who had recently gained fame for his poetry.
Sitting by the stove at night,
he discussed poetry with Liú.
Mímíng was beside them,
his appearance extremely ugly,
with white temples and a dark face,
a long neck and a prominent Adam's apple.
He also spoke in the Chǔ dialect.
Xǐ looked at him as if he were no one.
Suddenly, Mímíng lifted his robe, raised his eyebrows,
pointed to the ancient tripod in the stove, and said to Xǐ:
"You claim to be skilled in poetry.
Will you compose a poem with me about this?"
Shīfú, having known him from Héng and Xiāng,
seeing his aged appearance,
respected him greatly,
but did not know he was literate.
Hearing this proposal, he was delighted
and immediately took up a brush to write the first two lines:
"A skilled craftsman carved the mountain's bones,
hollowed its center for boiling and cooking."
He then passed it to Xǐ.
Xǐ eagerly added the next two lines:
"Outwardly wrapped in dried moss patterns,
within, hidden waves startle."
After writing, he recited it.
Mímíng laughed mockingly and said:
"Is your poetry only this much?"
He then tucked his hands into his sleeves, shrugged his shoulders,
leaned against the north wall, sat down,
and said to Liú:
"I do not understand worldly script.
You write it for me."
Thereupon, he chanted loudly:
"The dragon's head shrinks, dull and clumsy;
the pig's belly swells, bloated and puffed."
At first, it seemed unintentional,
but the poetic intent appeared to mock Xǐ.
The two looked at each other, ashamed and alarmed.
Yet, wishing to overwhelm him with quantity,
they composed two more lines and passed them to Xǐ:
"Large as a martyr's gall,
round like a horse's tasseled cap."
Xǐ added another two lines:
"In the cold, it finds its own peace;
when burned, its resolve grows firmer."
Mímíng again told Shīfú to write:
"Autumn melon falls from its stem;
frozen taro forcibly sprouts."
Shīfú then chanted:
"Grind away its angular edges,
polish it to a glossy sheen."
Finished,
he handed it to Xǐ.
Xǐ thought even harder,
determined to surpass Mímíng.
Each time he pondered and was about to speak,
his chanting grew more mournful.
He took up the brush to write,
but paused before putting it down,
and in the end could produce nothing remarkable.
He said:
"On the side, two pierced ears;
above, a solitary topknot supports."
After he finished chanting,
Mímíng said:
"At times, through earthworm holes,
faintly comes the buzz of flies."
His lack of effort was as before,
yet his words grew even more extraordinary,
beyond comparison,
and all his remarks targeted the two.
As the night drew to a close,
the two rose and apologized:
"Venerable Master, you are no ordinary man.
We submit.
We wish to become your disciples
and dare not compose more poetry."
Mímíng exclaimed:
"Not so.
This piece must be completed."
He said to Liú:
"Take up the brush, take up the brush!
I will finish it with you."
He then continued chanting in succession:
"When will it emerge from the ashes?
No way to escape the bottle and jar.
Wrongly placed among cauldrons and tripods,
constantly subjected to fire and water's strife.
Its shape mocked by women,
its capacity belittled by children.
In vain, its steadfast nature,
holds no more than a pint or two.
Rather cling to warmth and heat's decay,
than join with cold and chill.
Suddenly struck by the fault of tipping and spilling,
truly failing the trust of its duty.
Its crude form bears the pouring,
its narrow middle shames the lifting.
How could it boil immortal elixirs?
Yet it has not been tainted by mutton stew.
Petty efforts, vainly exerted;
trivial matters, hardly worth presenting.
Hardly fit for sacrificial use,
not to be handled by hand.
I beg you, do not mock or ridicule,
for this object is still in use."
After Shīfú finished writing,
Mímíng immediately had him read it aloud,
and when it was done,
he said to the two:
"These are not worth discussing.
Is this considered literature?
I merely composed according to what you are capable of,
not what I learned from my teacher and can do.
What I am capable of,
you are not fit to hear,
and not just literature alone.
I will now keep my mouth shut."
The two were greatly afraid.
They both stood up from their seats,
bowed, and said:
"We dare not ask anything else,
only one question:
You said, 'I do not understand worldly script.'
May we ask what script you do understand?
We only wish to hear this."
They asked repeatedly, but he did not respond.
The two, feeling uneasy,
withdrew and returned to their seats.
Mímíng leaned against the wall and slept,
his snoring like thunder.
The two, pale with fear,
dared not even breathe heavily.
After a while,
the dawn drum sounded dōng dōng.
The two were also exhausted,
so they sat and dozed off.
When they woke with a start and looked around,
Mímíng was already gone.
They asked the servant boy,
who said:
"As day was about to break,
the Daoist priest got up and went out the door,
as if to relieve himself.
He did not return for a long time,
and when we searched for him, he was nowhere to be found."
The two, astonished and regretful, blamed themselves.
They then took the poem to Hán Yù of Chānglí:
"May we ask who this man is?"
Yù said:
"I have heard of a recluse named Mímíng.
Could it be him?"
He then wrote a preface for the "Stone Tripod Linked Verse,"
which circulated in his time.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shíyí."
Cài Shàoxiá.
Cài Shàoxiá was a native of
Chénliú.
His temperament was serene and harmonious,
and from a young age he devoted himself to the Dao.
In his early years, he passed the imperial examination on the Confucian classics,
and was selected to serve as a military advisor in Qízhōu.
When his term of office was completed,
he drifted and sojourned in the region between the Jiāng and Zhè rivers.
After a long time,
he was again appointed as an assistant magistrate in Sìshuǐ County, Yǎnzhōu.
Thereupon, he purchased a mountain twenty *li* east of the county seat, built a dwelling,
and made plans to end his days there.
His residence was secluded and remote,
overlooking the Guīméng mountains.
The waters, rocks, clouds, and mists
created a scene of exceptional beauty.
Shàoxiá had severed worldly attachments early on,
and was especially in harmony with his long-held aspirations.
One day, while walking alone along a stream,
he suddenly came upon a lovely, shady spot.
He rested there,
his spirit and thoughts growing dim,
and unwittingly fell asleep.
There, a man in coarse clothing and a deer-skin cap summoned him in a dream.
He followed him on a distant journey,
until they reached a certain city wall.
The azure sky was vast and empty,
the auspicious sun hazy and bright.
The people and customs were pure and clean,
the plants and trees fresh and lush.
As Shàoxiá lifted his eyes and moved his feet,
he felt bewildered and uneasy.
Immediately, he was guided forward.
Passing through gates and halls,
their depth unfathomable,
he saw from afar a jade-like figure standing alone before a pavilion.
Shàoxiá hastily composed himself and paid his respects.
The jade figure said to him:
"I take pity on your sincere heart.
Now it is fitting for you to take charge of an affair."
Shàoxiá did not understand what was meant.
Again, the deer-capped man led him to the eastern corridor,
and stopped him beside a stone stele.
He said to Shàoxiá:
"We have summoned you to inscribe this.
Rejoice in encountering this excellent cause."
Shàoxiá had never been skilled at calligraphy,
and so firmly declined.
The deer-capped man said:
"Simply copy the text.
Why refuse and disobey?"
Soon, two youths
came from the north.
One held an ivory case
containing two scrolls of purple silk documents,
the other brought brushes and an inkstone.
These were given to Shàoxiá.
Focusing his spirit and grasping the brush,
he finished in a moment.
Then, as he read over it,
he had already committed it to memory.
The title read:
"Inscription for the New Palace at Cānglóng Stream,
composed by Mountain Mystic Lord Zǐyáng, the Perfected One.
On the western slopes of Liángcháng,
where the source's waters flow east.
The new palace stands grand and vast,
its lofty pavilions towering high.
Carved jade forms the coiled plinths,
engraved sandalwood the pillars and lintels.
Blue-green tiles lie like fish scales,
jasper thresholds shine, sharply cut.
Towers congeal with auspicious haze,
storeyed buildings span with lucky rainbows.
The *zouyu* patrols the bounds,
Chāngmíng holds the gate.
Pearl trees align in perfect circles,
jade springs stretch in measured lines.
Numinous breezes gather from afar,
the holy sun gazes down, clear and bright.
The Great One journeys here to visit,
the Limitless provides convenient access.
A hundred spirits guard and protect,
all the Perfected line up in ranks.
Immortal elders stand like cranes,
Daoist masters pure as water.
They drink jade transformed into nectar,
dine on jasper ground to powder.
Cassia banners hang unmoving,
orchid canopies are set in turn.
Marvelous music vies in performance,
flowing chimes sound intermittently.
Heavenly pipes play slow and spacious,
phoenix flutes clear and penetrating.
Phoenix songs harmonize with the pitch-pipes,
crane dances meet the rhythm.
Thrice transformed, the dark clouds;
ninefold perfected, the crimson snow.
What could Yìqiān's disciples tell of this?
What could Tóngchū's adepts possibly say?"
Just as he was about to look around further,
he was hurried along by the deer-capped man.
Suddenly hastening to return,
he awoke with a start.
He urgently called for paper and brush,
and immediately recorded it.
From then on, curious people from Yǎn and Yù
often went to Shàoxiá,
to inquire about the event.
There was one Zhèng Huángǔ
who wrote a biography for him.
Moreover, Shàoxiá was merely an old *xiàolián*,
so it was known for certain that he was not being untruthful.
From *Jíyì Jì* (A Record of Collected Marvels).
Zhèng Jūzhōng
The courtier Zhèng Jūzhōng
was a man of lofty elegance
who loved Daoist arts.
He often met with a certain Master Zhāng,
and they roamed about together frequently.
People simply called him 'Little Master Zhāng',
and did not know what he was capable of.
Jūzhōng lived in the region between Xiāng and Hàn.
He was appointed as a Secretary in the Central Secretariat,
but did not take up the post.
In the spring of the second year of the Kāichéng era (837 CE),
he went to the Sōngyuè mountains in eastern Luòyáng.
Taking three or four household servants,
he traveled with monks,
leaving no place unvisited,
and lingered for several months.
One day, as evening fell, they reached a place
with beautiful, pure woods and springs.
He loved it so much he forgot to return.
It happened that the monastery monks were absent.
Lighting a candle and kindling a fire, he prepared to stay the night.
He sent a servant to fetch something,
and also to fetch a brush,
as if intending to compose a poem.
As he took up the brush,
the lamp went out and the fire died completely.
A servant boy at his side
heard the sound of Lord Zhèng collapsing to the ground.
A rough breath came from his throat,
and a light like a chicken's egg
circled his neck and went out.
They hastily blew on the kindling to relight it,
but he was already beyond saving.
On the paper were four characters:
"The incense and fire vow is fulfilled."
The character for 'fulfilled' was barely incomplete.
Later, mountain dwellers and hunters sometimes saw him,
his clothing as if he were on a journey.
It must have been that Master Zhāng secretly foretold the day of his end,
and Lord Zhèng left his family to avoid it.
Is this not one who understood fate?
From *Yì Shǐ* (Forgotten History).
Yī Yòngchāng
Xiōng Jiǎo, the Supplemental Attendant, said:
In recent years,
there was a man named Yī Yòngchāng,
whose origins were unknown.
His wife was very young,
exceptionally beautiful,
and skilled in music and needlework,
mastering them all with perfection.
Though her husband suffered from hunger and cold, begging for food,
she never showed any shame.
When wealthy young men
tried to tease or flirt with her through words and laughter,
she always wore an expression that forbade any offense.
Her husband was a heavy drinker,
often wild and unrestrained,
so people of the time called him Yī Fēngzi.
He traveled extensively in regions such as Jiāngzuǒ, Lúlíng, and Yíchūn,
speaking carelessly and disrespectfully,
and was often beaten by crowds.
He loved composing lyrics to the tune "Wàng Jiāngnán,"
and he and his wife would sing them in harmony.
Sometimes they stayed in ancient temples or abandoned shrines,
and whenever they encountered something, they would compose verses about it,
all of which carried profound meaning.
Xiōng only remembered the lyrics about the drum, which went:
"The drum of Jiāngnán,
with its spindle-shaped belly and two curved ends.
Nailed without knowing it pierces to the marrow,
beaten without a heart or liver.
Hollow, it is toyed with by others."
The rest he could not recall.
In Jiāngnán, there was a type of rush grass,
which the poor gathered to weave into sandals.
Because the land was low and damp,
this grass was water-resistant,
and many poor people wore such sandals.
Yī Fēngzi once went to the gate of Chálíng County
and wrote in large characters:
"Chálíng has one fine long street,
with willows planted on both sides, not scholar trees.
After nightfall, no drum of the night watch is heard,
only the pounding of rushes to weave straw sandals."
The county officials and clerks were greatly displeased,
and he was beaten by a mob,
driven out of the county.
In Jiāngnán, frivolous and shallow verses were called "fùkē."
His wife admonished him, saying:
"It is often said that one should avoid frivolity in small matters,
yet you insist on being frivolous.
It is like riding a wild horse;
if you fall, your foot may get caught in the stirrup,
causing unnecessary injury.
There is no need for you to suffer so."
Thus, both husband and wife had a frivolous demeanor.
In the Guǐyǒu year of the Tiānyòu era,
the couple arrived at the Nánchéng County seat in Fǔzhōu,
where a villager had slaughtered a calf.
The couple begged for ten to twenty catties of beef,
which they roasted at the local school,
consuming it all in one night.
By dawn,
the couple had swollen from the meat,
and both died inside the school.
The county officials, clerks, and townspeople
wrapped their bodies in reed mats
and buried them about a hundred paces to the left of the southern road of the county.
The local garrison commander, surnamed Dīng,
A year later, when he was relieved of his post and returned to the prefecture,
Liú Gōng had already passed away.
Suddenly, one morning, under a market shed in the northern market,
he saw Yī Fēngzi and his wife,
singing "Wàng Jiāngnán" lyrics while begging for money.
Upon meeting, they were overjoyed
and reminisced about old times.
They took Dīng by the hand and went up to a tavern,
where the three of them drank several dǒu of wine.
Dīng became heavily intoxicated and fell asleep,
and Yī Fēngzi then asked for a brush and wrote on the tavern wall:
"This life was born before this life,
why follow the mysterious yet not return to mystery?
Already behind the chickens and dogs of Huáinán,
now I ascend before the Jade Emperor."
After writing this,
the couple linked arms, singing loudly as they left the city,
crossed the river, and arrived at Yóuwéi Temple.
They wrote on the back of the True Lord Hall,
with the inscription:
"The ruler of countless trillions of armies and nations, the Southern Red Dragon Deity King, Yī Yòngchāng."
The verses read:
"Daily auspicious clouds and radiant energy gather,
destined for our household to become great immortals.
The brush tip stirs the power of wind and thunder,
the sword's edge commands the forces of creation.
Further adding rites and music to the barbarians,
forever halting the beacon fires of the northern tribes.
The achievements of the immortals are just like this,
ascending directly to the first heaven of the Three Purities."
After writing this,
they linked arms and entered the Western Mountains.
People of the time saw them walking on air,
and from then on, they never reappeared.
As for Commander Dīng, when he awoke from his drunken stupor in the tavern,
he found ten taels of purple gold in his bosom.
The gold was later delivered to Nánchéng County in Huáihǎi.
Later, when people opened their grave,
they found only two reed mats
wrapped around over ten catties of rotten beef,
so foul-smelling it was unbearable to approach,
with nothing else inside.
Xiōng said that when he was six or seven years old,
he still remembered seeing Yī Fēngzi.
Sometimes he wore Daoist robes,
and was addressed as Venerable Master Yī.
Xiōng once suffered from a painful boil on his head,
the pain unbearable.
Venerable Master Yī took three mouthfuls of water,
sprayed it on the boil, causing it to burst,
and it never troubled him again.
To this day, the scar remains.
Xiōng said he witnessed these events firsthand,
and it was no false tale.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Xī Wángmǔ
The Queen Mother of the West,
is the Golden Mother of Turtle Mountain, the Nine Numinous and Supreme Marvel,
also known as the Primordial Sovereign, the Golden Mother of the Turtle Terrace of the Ninefold Radiance of the Great Void.
She is the utmost marvel of the Western Florescence,
the supreme honored one of the Cavernous Yin.
In ancient times, when the Dao's vital breath congealed in stillness,
and her profound substance was serene and non-active,
desiring to enlighten and initiate the mysterious workings,
and transform and generate the myriad things,
first, with the ultimate and true vital breath of the Eastern Florescence,
she transformed and generated the Lord of Wood.
The Lord of Wood was born above the Azure Sea,
upon the mound of Fragrant Numen,
to preside over the vital breath of yang harmony.
He governs in the East,
and is also called Lord Dōng Wánggōng.
Then, with the ultimate and marvelous vital breath of the Western Florescence,
she transformed and generated the Golden Mother.
The Golden Mother was born in Yīchuān of the Divine Land,
her surname being Hóu.
Born capable of flight,
she presides over the primordial,
nourishing the divine and the mysterious and profound.
Within the vast and boundless,
she divided the pure and essential vital breath of the Great Dao,
condensed the vital breath to take form.
Together with Lord Dōng Wánggōng, she jointly governs the two vital breaths,
nurturing and rearing Heaven and Earth,
molding and shaping the myriad things.
The foundation of gentleness and compliance,
she is the origin of the ultimate yin,
her position corresponds to the West,
mothering and nurturing all categories of beings.
In Heaven above and Earth below,
throughout the Three Realms and the Ten Directions,
all women who ascend to immortality and attain the Dao,
are under her jurisdiction.
The palace she resides in,
is located in the capital of Chūnshān in Turtle Mountain, in the Western Land,
in the garden of Kūnlún.
In the park of Lángfēng.
There is a city a thousand li wide, with twelve jade towers,
jade-flower watchtowers, radiant-jasper halls, nine-layered mysterious chambers, purple-jade and cinnabar rooms.
To the left is girded by the Jasper Pool, to the right encircled by the Emerald Waters.
Beneath that mountain,
lies the Weak Water, ninefold deep.
With surging waves ten thousand fathoms high.
Without a whirlwind chariot or feathered carriage,
one cannot reach it.
What is called the jade watchtowers reaching the heavens,
the green terraces supporting the firmament.
Halls of azure jade,
rooms of vermilion and purple,
connected jade screens and colored canopies,
the bright moon shining in all four directions.
She wears a flowery headdress,
adorns herself with a tiger emblem,
attended on the left by immortal maidens,
on the right by feathered youths.
Precious canopies layer upon layer,
feathered banners shade the courtyard.
Below the veranda steps,
are planted trees of white jade rings,
forests of cinnabar firmness,
ten thousand branches of empty azure,
jade trunks a thousand fathoms high,
without wind, divine pipes sound of their own accord,
ringing clearly, all are the music of the nine performances and eight harmonies.
The Divine Land lies southeast of Kūnlún,
therefore the *Erya* says:
"Beneath the eyes of the Queen Mother of the West is it."
It also says:
"The Queen Mother with disheveled hair,
wearing a flowery headdress.
With tiger teeth and skilled at roaring,
this is the Queen Mother's emissary,
the spirit of the White Tiger of the Metal Direction,
not the Queen Mother's true form.
The Primordial Heavenly King bestowed upon her the Register of the Square Heaven, Primordial Unity, Turtle Mountain, and Ninefold Radiance,
enabling her to command and summon the myriad numina,
oversee all true sages,
supervise covenants and verify trust,
and lead all the feathered insignia of the heavens.
When the Heavenly Venerables and superior sages,
hold morning and evening assemblies,
or places of examination and evaluation,
the Queen Mother is present to oversee them.
The precious scriptures of the Upper Clarity,
the jade texts of the Three Caverns,
whenever there is transmission and conferral,
she is invariably involved.
When the Yellow Emperor campaigned against the violence of Chīyóu,
his might was insufficient to restrain him,
and Chīyóu transformed and changed in many ways,
summoning winds and calling forth rain,
blowing smoke and spraying fog,
causing the army to be greatly confused.
The Emperor returned and rested at the slope of Mount Tài,
drowsy and worried, he fell asleep.
The Queen Mother dispatched an emissary,
clad in a black fox fur robe,
who presented a talisman to the Emperor, saying:
"Tàiyī is in front,
Tiānyī is behind,
he who obtains this will be victorious,
in battle he will overcome."
The talisman was three inches wide,
one foot long,
blue and lustrous like jade,
with cinnabar blood forming the patterns.
After the Emperor had donned the talisman,
the Queen Mother then commanded a woman,
with a human head and bird body,
who said to the Emperor:
"I am the Mysterious Maiden of the Nine Heavens."
She bestowed upon the Emperor the strategies of the three palaces and five intents of yin and yang,
the arts of Tàiyī's hidden stem, six rén, and pacing the Dipper,
the mechanisms of the hidden tallies,
and the texts of the numinous treasure five tallies and five conquests.
Thereupon he overcame Chīyóu at Zhōngjì,
cut down the descendants of Shénnóng,
executed Yúwǎng at Bǎnquán,
and the world was greatly settled,
establishing the capital at Zhuōlù in Shànggǔ.
Several years later,
the Queen Mother dispatched the emissary, the spirit of the White Tiger,
riding a white deer,
who gathered at the Emperor's court,
and bestowed upon him a map.
Later, when Yú Shùn assumed the regency,
the Queen Mother dispatched an emissary to bestow upon Shùn a white jade ring.
When Shùn ascended the throne,
she again bestowed an expanded map,
thus broadening the Yellow Emperor's nine provinces to twelve provinces.
The Queen Mother also dispatched an emissary to present Shùn with a white jade pitch-pipe,
which when blown harmonized the eight winds.
The *Shangshu Dì Yàn Qī* says:
"The land of the Queen Mother is in the western wilderness."
In the past, Máo Yíng, styled Shūshēn;
Wáng Bāo, styled Zǐdēng;
Zhāng Dàolíng, styled Fǔhàn,
and the Nine Sages and Seven Perfected,
all who attained the Dao and received texts,
paid homage to the Queen Mother at the watchtower of Kūnlíng.
At that time, Shūshēn and Dàolíng attended upon the Supreme Dao Lord,
riding in a carriage with nine canopies,
steering the tracks of flying dragons,
crossing the peaks of Jīshí,
ferrying across the ford of the Weak Stream,
floating on the White Water,
traversing the Black Waves,
looking around in an instant,
they arrived before the Queen Mother at the watchtower.
Zǐdēng purified and fasted for three months,
and the Queen Mother bestowed upon him the *Qiónghuá Bǎoyào Qī Chén Sù Jīng*.
Lord Máo, following Lord Wáng of the Western City, went to the White Jade Turtle Terrace,
to pay homage to the Queen Mother,
seeking the way of longevity.
He said:
"Yíng, with this unworthy body,
yearns for the years of dragons and phoenixes,
wishing with the fragility of the morning mushroom,
to seek the span of accumulated months."
The Queen Mother, taking pity on his diligent aspiration,
told him:
"I formerly studied under the Primordial Heavenly King and the Imperial Heaven Fúsāng Emperor Lord,
who bestowed upon me the Way of the Jade Pendant and Golden Earring, the Two Radiances' Refining and Twining,
ascending to the Supreme Ultimate,
descending to create the Ten Directions,
irrigating the moon and chewing the sun to enter the Heavenly Gate,
named the Scripture of Mysterious Perfection.
Now I bestow it upon you,
you should diligently cultivate it."
Thereupon she commanded Lord Wáng of the Western City,
to explain it point by point and bestow it upon him.
Also, during the time of King Mù of Zhōu,
he commanded the eight steeds and the seven-flowered knights,
with Zàofǔ as the charioteer,
ascended Kūnlún to the west,
and was a guest of the Queen Mother.
King Mù presented white jade tablets and heavy brocades,
as birthday gifts for the Queen Mother,
the events are detailed in the biography of King Mù of Zhōu.
In the seventh month, on the seventh night, of the first year of the Yuánfēng era of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
she descended at the Hàn palace.
The account is within the biography of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
and is not repeated here.
From the *Jí Xiān Lù*.
Yúnhuá Fūrén,
the twenty-third daughter of the Queen Mother,
is the younger sister of Tàizhēn Wáng Fūrén.
Her name is Yáojī,
and she has received the Way of the Whirling Wind, Blending Myriad Scenes, Refining Spirit, and Flying Transformation.
Once, while returning from a journey to the Eastern Sea,
she passed by a river,
where there was Mount Wū.
Its peaks and cliffs stood tall and straight,
its forests and ravines were secluded and beautiful,
and there was a massive rock like an altar.
She lingered there for a long time.
At that time, Dà Yǔ was regulating the waters
and had encamped at the foot of the mountain.
Suddenly, a great wind arose,
shaking the cliffs and collapsing valleys, uncontrollable.
Thus, he encountered the Lady,
bowed, and sought her assistance.
She immediately commanded her attendant maidens
to give Yǔ the book for summoning ghosts and deities,
and then ordered her deities Kuáng Zhāng, Yú Yú, Huáng Mó, Dà Yì, Gēng Chén, Tóng Lǜ, and others
to assist Yǔ in cutting through rocks and dispersing the waves,
breaking blockages and clearing obstacles,
to guide the flow of the waters.
Yǔ bowed and expressed his gratitude.
Yǔ once went to visit her,
and at the summit of a lofty peak,
in the moment he glanced around,
she transformed into stone;
or suddenly she would soar and fly,
scattering into light clouds,
then gently come to a halt,
gathering into evening rain;
or she would transform into a roaming dragon,
or a soaring crane,
in a thousand forms and myriad appearances,
impossible to approach closely.
Yǔ suspected she was deceitful and bizarre,
not a true immortal,
and asked Tóng Lǜ about it.
Lǜ said:
"The foundation of heaven and earth is the Dào,
and those who operate the function of the Dào are sages.
The ranks of sages
are the Zhēnrén and the immortals.
Those who receive the vital breath and become true,
attaining the Dào without cultivation,
are Mùgōng and Jīnmǔ.
They are the ancestors of the two breaths, the origin of yīn and yáng, the masters of the immortals and the true, the primordial light of creation.
Yúnhuá Fūrén
is the daughter of Jīnmǔ.
In the past, she studied under Sānyuán Dàojūn,
received the Shàngqīng precious scriptures,
