and received texts at the foot of the Zǐqīng palace,
becoming Yúnhuá Shànggōng Fūrén.
She presides over and guides the teachings for youths of truth,
managing affairs at the Yùyīng Terrace.
Hiding and appearing, transforming and changing,
are her normal state.
It is also because she condensed breath to become true,
uniting with the Dào as one body,
not a form born from a womb or transformed by endowment,
but the breath of Xīhuá Shàoyīn.
Moreover, breath permeates heaven and earth,
operates within animals and plants,
encompassing creation on a grand scale,
and entering into the finest hair.
In humans, it becomes human;
in things, it becomes things.
How could it be limited to clouds, rain, dragons, and cranes,
or flying swans and soaring phoenixes?"
Yǔ accepted this.
Later, when he went to visit her,
he suddenly saw cloud towers and jade terraces,
jade palaces and gemstone gateways, majestic and dense.
There were spirit officials and guards,
whose names could not be recognized.
Lions guarded the gates,
celestial horses cleared the path,
poisonous dragons and lightning beasts,
the eight awesome ones fully arrayed in chariots.
The Lady sat in repose upon the jade terrace.
Yǔ kowtowed and inquired about the Dào.
Summoning Yǔ, she bade him sit and said:
"When the sage craftsman first arose,
he split the one simplicity of the great chaos,
issuing forth as billions of bodies.
He opened the one bud of the great store,
scattering it into endless things.
Thus, he paced the three lights and established the sundial's shadow,
delimited the nine regions and instituted states and countries,
created clepsydras to divide day and night,
established cold and heat to complete the yearly cycle,
set Dui and Li to correct the positions,
used mountains and rivers to distinguish yīn and yáng,
built city walls to gather the people,
made tools and weapons to protect the masses,
established carriages and robes to distinguish noble and base,
and cultivated grains to prepare for famine.
All these institutions
receive their mandate from the stars and constellations above,
and take their model from the spirits and the true,
to nourish the corporeal things.
Therefore, the sun and moon have darkness and brightness,
life and death have cold and heat,
thunder has its times of emergence and withdrawal,
wind and rain have their regular patterns of movement and stillness.
The clear breath floats above,
while the turbid masses scatter below.
The numbers of decline and rise,
the cycles of order and chaos,
the substance of worthiness and foolishness,
the nature of good and evil,
the breath of hardness and softness,
the fate of longevity and premature death,
the positions of nobility and baseness,
the order of respect and humility,
the responses of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness,
the periods of obscurity and prominence—
all these are received from the Dào,
suspended by heaven,
and the sages establish their measures.
Nature issues from heaven, and destiny is completed in humans.
Heaven establishes it,
and the Dào operates it.
Where the Dào exists, there is being;
where the Dào departs, there is non-being.
There is nothing the Dào cannot preserve,
but without cultivation, it cannot be attained.
Xuánlǎo has said,
'Attain the utmost vacuity,
maintain steadfast stillness,
and the ten thousand things will return of themselves.'
Returning means returning to the Dào and enduring forever.
The function of the Dào
changes and transforms in ten thousand ways, yet not one is sufficient to encompass it.
Therefore, heaven participates in the mystery of mysteries,
earth participates in the chaos of yellow,
and humans participate in the Dào and virtue.
Beyond these,
there is no Dào.
The essential for long-lastingness
is for heaven to preserve its mystery,
for earth to guard its things,
and for humans to nurture their breath,
thereby achieving completeness.
Thus, my life is in my own hands;
it is not that heaven and earth kill me,
or that ghosts and spirits harm me,
but that I lose the Dào and perish by myself.
Be mindful!
Be diligent!
Your merit has reached things,
your diligence has extended to the people,
and your goodness has moved heaven,
yet you have not heard the essentials of the ultimate Dào.
I once received texts at the Zǐqīng palace,
treasured them, and diligently practiced them.
My teacher, Sānyuán Dàojūn, said:
'The Inner Classic of the Upper True,
treasured by the heavenly true ones,
is sealed in the golden terrace.
Wearing it, one enters Tàiwēi;
then cloud chariots ascend above,
divine warriors guard the gates,
one shakes out one's robes in the jade chamber,
roams and feasts in the rare forest,
summons the immortal lords on the left,
perches on the White Mountain on the right,
and gazes down upon the great void.
Floating upon the Celestial Ford,
one rides clouds and drives dragons;
traveling to these famous mountains,
the true ones come to one's chamber,
ten thousand people offer their protection,
and mountain spirits await and welcome.
In movement, there are the eight scenes and jade chariots;
in stillness, one feasts and resides in golden halls.'
This is also called the wondrous text of 'the Supreme Jade Pendant and Golden Earring.'
You wish to cross the vast sea without a whirlwind chariot,
traverse flying sands without a cloud carriage,
climb perilous paths without any conveyance,
wade through muddy waves without any vehicle,
on land you are distressed by distant isolation,
on water you fear drifting and sinking,
yet you wish to guide the hundred valleys and dredge the ten thousand streams.
Perilous and distant indeed!
The Supreme, taking pity on your utmost sincerity,
will also bestow upon you the Lingbǎo true texts,
to command tigers and leopards on land,
control flood dragons in water,
sever and behead a thousand evils,
restrain and drive away all malevolent beings,
to accomplish your task.
They are in the land of Yángmíng.
The precious texts I have received
can also enable one to enter water and fire,
summon and command the dark and hidden,
and subdue tigers and leopards.
He summoned the Six Dīng spirits,
hid and submerged in the eight directions of the earth,
reversed the five planets,
preserved his body through prolonged vision,
and leaned in harmony with Heaven."
Thereupon, she ordered her attendant maid Líng Rónghuá to bring forth the cinnabar-jade case,
opened the Precious Texts of Shàngqīng to bestow them,
and Yǔ bowed in acceptance before departing.
He also received the assistance of Gēng Chén and Yú Yú,
and thus was able to channel the waves and breach the rivers,
accomplishing his task,
securing the Five Sacred Mountains,
and demarcating the Nine Provinces.
Heaven then bestowed upon him a dark jade tablet,
recognizing him as a Perfected of the Purple Court.
Later, the Chǔ minister Sòng Yù
recounted these events to King Xiāng,
but the king failed to inquire into the essential principles of the Way to seek longevity.
Instead, he built a terrace at the Gāotáng Lodge,
erected the Yángtái Palace to offer sacrifices to her,
and Sòng Yù composed a "Rhapsody on the Divine Immortal" to convey his sentiments,
which was licentious and vulgar.
How could such a lofty and transcendent immortal
be slandered and summoned down?
There is a shrine at the foot of the mountain,
which the world calls the Great Immortal.
Across the river lies the Divine Maiden Stone,
which is what she transformed into.
There is also the Stone Celestial Venerable Divine Maiden Altar,
beside which grows bamboo
that hangs down like a broom.
When withered leaves or flying objects land on the altar,
the bamboo sways with the wind to sweep them away,
keeping it eternally pristine and unsoiled.
The people of Chǔ have offered sacrifices there for generations.
From the "Records of Assembled Immortals."
The Two Maidens of Xuántiān
In the second year of King Zhāo of Yān's reign,
the state of Guǎngyán sent two skilled dancers as tribute.
One was named Xuán Bō,
the other Tí Mó.
Both had jade-like complexions and smooth skin,
their bodies light and their aura fragrant.
Graceful and slender,
they were unparalleled since ancient times.
Sometimes they walked without leaving shadows or traces,
and for years they never felt hunger.
King Zhāo housed them in sheer silk canopies and splendid tents,
fed them with ointment of rǔmín jade,
and nourished them with grain from the Cinnabar Spring.
When the king ascended the Chóngxiá Terrace,
he summoned the two to his side.
Suddenly, a fragrant breeze arose,
and they whirled and danced as if soaring,
almost unable to support themselves.
The king brushed them with tasseled threads,
and both began to dance.
Their beauty was enchanting and alluring,
surpassing even soaring phoenixes,
and their singing voices were light and soaring.
He then had female musicians sing in their stead,
and the melody was clear and resonant, flowing with charm.
Even if it could stir dust from the rafters,
it could not surpass them.
One of their dances was called "Entwining Dust,"
referring to their lightness of body,
which mingled with the dust.
The next was called "Gathering Feathers,"
referring to their graceful turns,
like feathers following the wind.
The last was called "Whirling Embrace,"
referring to the suppleness of their limbs,
as if they could slip into one's sleeves.
He then laid out a mat with a qilin pattern,
and scattered Huāruò incense.
This incense came from the state of Bōyì.
When sprinkled on the ground, even the soil and stones became fragrant;
when applied to rotten wood or withered grass,
they would all flourish luxuriantly;
when used to fumigate dried bones,
flesh and muscle would regrow.
He spread its powdered form on the ground,
four or five feet thick,
and had the two dance upon it.
Even after a full day, there were no footprints,
due to their lightness of body.
At that time, a white luan bird soared alone,
carrying a thousand stalks of grain in its beak.
The grain hung in the air,
spontaneously producing flowers and fruit.
When they fell to the ground, they took root and sprouted leaves,
yielding a hundred harvests in a single year.
A single stalk could fill a cart,
hence it was called "Bountiful Cart Grain."
The qilin-patterned mat
was inlaid with various treasures,
all depicting clouds, mist, qilins, and phoenixes.
King Zhāo again waved his sleeve at them,
and the dancers all stopped.
Knowing they were divine and extraordinary,
he housed them in the Chóngxiá Terrace,
provided bedding and mats for them to rest and feast,
and dispatched guards to protect them.
The king was fond of the arts of immortality,
so the maidens of Xuántiān
assumed the forms of these two.
By the end of King Zhāo's reign,
no one knew where they had gone.
Sometimes they wandered along the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
or by the banks of the Yī and Luò rivers,
traveling throughout the world,
now near, now far.
From "Wáng Zǐnián's Records of Omissions."
Tàizhēn Fūrén
was the youngest daughter of the Queen Mother of the West.
She appeared to be about sixteen or seventeen years old,
her given name was Wǎn,
and her courtesy name was Luófū.
She later married Xuándū Tàizhēn Wáng.
She had a son who served as Sīzhí in the Supreme Prefecture of the Three Heavens,
in charge of overseeing and correcting violations and errors in the Celestial Ministry,
comparable to a high minister on earth.
Being young, he was fond of wandering and leisure,
neglecting his official duties and abandoning his work.
The authorities impeached him,
and for failing to personally oversee his responsibilities,
he was demoted to preside over affairs at Mount Dōngyuè,
removed from the roster of True Kings,
and made to oversee the masters of ghosts and spirits,
with the position changing every five hundred years.
Fūrén came to visit him,
exhorting him to cultivate and diligently attend to his administrative duties,
so as to make amends for his faults.
While passing through Línzī County,
a minor official named Hé Jūnxián
had been wounded by bandits
and was near death.
Fūrén took pity upon seeing him
and asked about his condition.
Jūnxián answered truthfully.
Fūrén said:
"Your wounds are from heavy blades that pierced your lungs and internal organs,
causing your five viscera to leak,
blood to congeal in the crimson chambers,
and vital energy to surge, injuring the exterior.
This is a fatal calamity;
you cannot be revived.
What is to be done?"
Jūnxián realized she was a divine being
and kowtowed, begging for mercy.
Fūrén took from a tube at her elbow
a single pill of medicine,
as large as a small bean,
and immediately instructed him to take it.
He was healed instantly,
the bleeding stopped and the wounds closed,
with no further pain.
Jūnxián bowed twice and knelt, saying:
"My family's wealth is insufficient;
I do not know how to repay your gracious kindness.
I can only exert my humble efforts
to repay what I have received."
Fūrén said:
"If you truly wish to thank me,
can you follow me?"
Jūnxián then changed his name
and called himself Mǎ Míngshēng,
following Fūrén to serve her.
Fūrén returned to a stone chamber on a steep cliff of Mount Dàizōng in the Dōngyuè range,
perilously high and isolated,
hidden deep among layered cliffs.
It was over a thousand zhang above the ground.
In the stone chamber were a golden bed and a jade table,
with rare and wondrous treasures,
a place no human could reach.
At first, Míngshēng only wished to learn the formula for treating metal wounds.
But after seeing immortals come and go
and learning of the Way of immortality,
he served morning and night, sweeping and cleaning,
not daring to slacken or grow weary.
Fūrén also tested him with ghosts, monsters, tigers, wolves, and various bewildering transformations,
but Míngshēng's spirit remained clear and upright,
and he never felt fear.
She also sent Míngshēng to other places to stay overnight,
using beautiful women to tease and approach him intimately,
but Míngshēng's heart remained firm, calm, and steadfast,
without any wicked thoughts.
When Fūrén went away on other journeys,
she would return every ten or five days,
or sometimes after a month or twenty days.
He often saw immortal guests
riding on dragon-unicorns
or driving tigers and leopards coming and going.
Sometimes there were those who came to pay respects,
and true immortals filled the seats all day long.
When guests arrived,
she would always have Míngshēng go out to another chamber.
Sometimes exquisite meals would instantly appear,
with delicacies, fruits, fragrant wine, and rare beverages,
indescribable in name.
Sometimes she would invite him to sit
and eat and drink with them.
He also heard the sound of zithers and lutes in the air,
with songs exquisitely beautiful.
Fūrén would also sometimes play the zither herself;
with a single string, she could produce all five notes,
clear, resonant, and stirring,
audible for several li.
All kinds of birds would gather in the caverns and chambers,
hovering and flying about,
unwilling to leave even when driven away.
It was nearly the music of celestial beings,
a wonder of nature itself.
When Fūrén rested,
she often shared the same stone chamber with Míngshēng but on separate beds.
In that secluded and silent place, only the two of them were present.
Sometimes when she went away,
she did not say where she was going,
but he always saw a white dragon come to greet her.
Fūrén would then put on a cloud-light embroidered robe,
mount the dragon, and depart.
Her robe was adorned with bright moon pearls on the collar,
and she wore a jade pendant
and a golden floral Tàixuán crown.
No attendants were seen.
Once she returned,
the dragon would leave on its own.
On the jade bed in the stone chamber where she resided,
there were purple brocade quilts and mattresses
and a purple gauze canopy.
Within the canopy were garments and playthings,
exquisite gold boxes and jade objects,
arranged in dark and yellow hues,
none of which existed in the mortal world,
and whose names could not all be known.
There were two scrolls of plain silk books,
inscribed with the title "The Supreme Dao Scripture of the Nine Heavens."
Míngshēng did not dare to open and read the text,
but only attended to sweeping and cleaning,
guarding the cliff chamber.
After five years like this,
he became even more diligent and respectful.
Fūrén sighed and said to him:
"You are truly teachable
and certainly capable of attaining the Dao.
Though you are a mortal,
you are neither licentious nor disrespectful,
reverently honoring the numinous energy,
and never abandoning it.
Even if you sought death,
how could you obtain it?"
She then told him her origins and background:
"I have long been in the human world,
but now, by the command of the Celestial Emperor
and following the summons of the Supreme One,
I can no longer stay.
Considering your dedication and earnestness,
I therefore tell you this,
wishing to teach you the method for longevity
and the art of extending life.
But what I have received,
the elixir of the Taihé Zìrán Lóngtāi that I ingest,
is suitable only for传授 to the True Humans of the Three Heavens.
It cannot be taught to a beginner;
it is certainly not something you can hear of.
Even if you were to hear of it,
you could not use it to sustain yourself.
There is Master Ānqī's method of refining the Golden Liquid Elixir;
its formula is secret and essential,
and it can be used immediately upon attainment.
It is the Dao of Yuánjūn Tàiyǐ,
enabling one to ascend to heaven in broad daylight.
Tomorrow, Ānqī will come,
and I will entrust you to him.
If you follow him for some time,
he will certainly transmit the art to you."
The next day, Master Ānqī indeed arrived,
riding a piebald unicorn,
wearing a vermilion robe and a distant journey cap,
with a jade pendant and a tiger-headed leather pouch.
He appeared to be around twenty years old,
fair-skinned and dignified.
He was accompanied by six or seven immortals,
all holding tallies and serving as guards.
Seeing Fūrén, he bowed with great respect,
addressing himself as "this humble official."
Soon, wine, fruits, and a feast were set out,
and they drank and feasted for about half a day.
Ānqī said of his own accord:
"In the past, when I traveled with Fūrén to the shores of the Western Sea in Ānxīguó,
we ate dates of exceptional beauty;
the dates here are far inferior.
Recalling this, it feels not long ago,
yet two thousand years have already passed."
Fūrén said:
"In the past, I shared a single date with you,
and it was not even finished.
The small dates here
how can they compare?"
Ānqī said:
"This humble official recently went to the Jiǔhé,
where I saw Sīyīn and the Western Hàn Fūrén traveling together.
They asked about the cycles of yángjiǔ and bǎiliù,
and the kalpas when a sage ruler receives the mandate.
This humble official replied that I was still young and ignorant,
unaware of the epochs of fortune and calamity,
and that I would have to consult Tàizhēn Wáng Fūrén separately.
Now that I have been granted a seat,
I wish to inquire about these numbers."
Fūrén said:
"The cycles of fate are vast and obscure,
not something you can fully comprehend in a short time."
Now, Heaven and Earth have the Great Yángjiǔ and Great Bǎiliù,
and the Lesser Yángjiǔ and Lesser Bǎiliù.
Heaven's calamity is called Yángjiǔ,
Earth's deficiency is called Bǎiliù.
These two disasters are the Heaven and Earth's alternation of obstruction and prosperity, yīn and yáng,
the eclipses of the Nine Earths.
The great cycle is nine thousand nine hundred years,
the small cycle is three thousand thirty years.
And when this fate converges,
even sages cannot avert it.
Now the great calamity is not yet,
but the Táng era is the beginning of the Lesser Yángjiǔ.
Calculating until the coming Jiǎshēn year,
the Bǎiliù will meet.
At that time, virtue and the Way will flourish,
while wickedness will suddenly run rampant.
The sage ruler will receive the Mandate,
which will be in the Rénchén year.
Not another thousand years,
it will soon arrive.
The Lady of the Western Hàn has already witnessed it all,
hence her questioning,
must be a test.
Yet it is also constrained by the Lord of the Dark.
Now, Yángjiǔ means
Heaven's drought, the seas recede, and the land withers of itself.
Bǎiliù means
the seas dry up and hills fill themselves,
the waters of the four seas diminish,
the vast ocean becomes mountains.
Whales spanning cities,
sharks of ten thousand zhàng,
unaware of the measure of the destined cycle,
only knock on Heaven begging for water.
Petitions and disputes,
fill the high offices.
The Three Heavens are troubled by the review,
the Director of Fate is also weary from handling them.
The mouth of the Nine Rivers,
is where the Red Waters rush,
its depth is unfathomable,
now it is gradually drying up.
Human qi steams from mountains and marshes,
flowing sand and dust fill the plain's mouth.
Then the four seas will gather,
groups of dragons will dance and drum,
and you will need the Jiǎshēn year,
when flying floods will reverse their flow.
Now the waters have not yet ascended the Heavenly Gate to announce the time,
the Accumulated Stones open myriad springs to clear the path,
flying yīn winds to disturb the common people,
pouring dark currents to spread far and near,
overflowing within a few years,
spreading and extending until the end of nine years.
Having attained the truth of the Way,
embodying the numinous and uniting with the wondrous,
when the time comes,
you should only soar into the void and gaze upon the mountains and slopes.
Wander the floating peaks and look upon the broad rivers,
ride the dark swan to gather at the prefectural city,
drive the dragon carriage and stride upon the radiant clouds.
In the blink of an eye,
suddenly you will be there,
you can soar and delight your eyes,
why trouble your mind over it?
Today, let us discuss matters of wine,
what use is this?"
Then, pointing to Míngshēng, she said to Ānqī:
"This youth has a heart of admiration and longing,
he can probably be taught.
In the past, encountering a karmic connection,
he came to follow and see.
Though his substance is still defiled and not yet numinous,
his lustful desires have already dissipated.
Now he is not yet ready to receive the Way of Mysterious Harmony and Great Truth,
but I wish to have him learn from you the formula of the Golden Elixir.
If you can obtain it,
it would be fitting to take him.
Now, common people of the vulgar world,
their heart and lungs are frail and perilous,
their meridians and stomachs thin internally,
their blood and fluids weary and weak,
their liver
(The original text had "yòng" for "liver".
According to the Míng manuscript copy, it is amended to "liver".)
and spine do not nourish their eyes,
their lips and mouth cannot discern the mechanism.
Because great compassion does not accord with
(The original text had "tiān" for "with".
According to the Míng manuscript copy, it is amended to "with".)
human desires,
they rush about but cannot reach the numinous flight.
It is appropriate to comfort and encourage them,
to fulfill their aspirations.
You must not test him with the Eight Powers of Immortal Transformation,
and by no means force him to lose his correctness."
Ānqī said:
"Yes.
But I fear my Way is shallow and my arts meager,
insufficient to instruct and impart.
This humble official formerly received this formula from the Elder of Hànchéng,
this is the accomplished method of my former teacher,
I truly dare not transmit it hastily.
The key is to ensure that within two thousand years,
he will certainly glimpse the Heavenly Path.
This humble official once met with the young lady at Xuánqiū,
viewed the layered ruggedness of the Nine Heavens,
gazed upon the Weak Waters flowing east,
were granted to drink the Mysterious Jade fragrant wine,
unaware of high or low, we chanted,
together we should have opened the precious case of numinous registers,
and by chance saw the formula of the Jade Embryo and Qióng Paste.
Taking a speck of it,
one immediately ascends to the cloudy heavens,
liberates the form through myriad transformations,
and becomes the True Sovereign above.
This art is direct and wondrous,
indeed more concise than the essence of the Golden Elixir,
and swifter than the edge of the Ninefold Frost and Snow.
Now I do not dare to criticize,
abandoning the near for the distant,
discarding the direct path to pursue the troublesome,
but I truly wish to hear the grades of the divine formulas,
and wish to know the lofty ranks of the true immortals.
If humble descent has its time,
it is not fitting to discuss,
but the formula of Qióng Paste,
is it perhaps that your attendant is not yet permitted to use it?"
The Lady said:
"Do you not know, sir?
This is the numinous formula of the Heavenly Sovereign,
suitable only for the Heavenly Perfected to use,
not something that the lower corpses of the vulgar stream can glimpse.
Immortal formulas altogether have nine grades.
The first is called the Ferment of the Great Harmony's Natural Dragon Embryo;
the second is called the Paste of the Jade Embryo and Qióng Liquid;
the third is called the Flying Cinnabar, Purple Blossom, Flowing Essence;
the fourth is called the Paste of Vermilion Light, Cloudy Jade;
the fifth is called the Divine Cinnabar of the Nine Kinds of Red Blossoms;
the sixth is called the Essence of the Great Purity's Golden Liquid;
the seventh is called the Cinnabar of Ninefold Frost and Snow;
the eighth is called the Nine Tripods' Cloudy Essence;
the ninth is called the Cloudy Light, Stone Flow, Flying Cinnabar.
These are the successive stages of the ninefold refinement.
Those who attain immortality also have nine grades.
The first is the Highest Immortal,
titled the Ninefold True King of Heaven;
the second is the Secondary Immortal,
titled the Three Heavens' True King;
the third is titled the Supreme Great Perfected;
the fourth is titled the Soaring Heaven Perfected;
the fifth is titled the Numinous Immortal;
the sixth is titled the Perfected;
the seventh is titled the Numinous Person;
the eighth is titled the Flying Immortal;
the ninth is titled the Immortal.
These are the graded ranks of the nine immortals.
Each has its distinctions and descent,
one cannot skip and learn.
His knowing of the Golden Elixir,
is already excessive.
As for what the Jade Emperor consumes,
it is not for the shallow learner to hear of.
Although you, sir, have attained the Way,
and have long been in the world,
clamor and turbidity have stained your upright qi,
dust and grime have stirred your Three-in-One,
you are still not ready to ascend to the Three Heavens and pay court to the Supreme Great,
or stride to Fúsāng and pay homage to the Great Truth.
The formula of the Jade Embryo,
is still not to be discussed,
how much less a person of lesser talent,
to let him hear its chapter titles?"
Ānqī had a ashamed expression,
withdrew from his mat and said:
"This humble official truly did not know the wondrousness of the numinous medicines,
that their grades and distinctions were such,
it is truly startling to hear."
Then he stated on his own:
"This humble official has heard that the young lady possesses the 'Scripture of the Way of the Nine Heavens' Great Truth'.
Clear, empty, mirror-like non-being,
illuminatingly bright, mysteriously dark,
truly not something a person of lesser talent can hope to look up to.
Yet having received your favor for so long,
each reception and guidance has been weighty.
Not examining my own capacity,
I beg for instruction.
Might I ask if that book can be seen?
If I could but glimpse the Great Truth for a moment,
then fish eyes could easily change their substance."
The Lady smiled with a slight laugh,
and after a long while said:
"The Way of the Supreme Great is extraordinary,
the mansion of truth is distant and remote,
it is not something a person of lesser talent can connect with.
You, sir, should only expand your present merits,
and not undertake labors beyond your portion.
I am just about to go north to Xuánzhōu for a while,
east to Fāngzhàng,
to rinse the Dragon Embryo in the palace of Xuándū,
The jade maiden was tested in the hall of the assembled immortals.
Heavenly affairs are not to be neglected,
and when matters allow for leisure,
I shall show you the Supreme True Scriptures.
If you can diligently cultivate the Correct Unity in the Great Clarity,
command the Heng and Huà mountains and order the four great rivers,
then seek me at the hill of the Three Heavens,
and search for me at Zhōngshān and Wángwū,
the true texts may be granted to you.
If not,
do not vainly bend a swift steed to tread the dark ford,
or damage a boat to cross the vast sea.
As for the previously discussed cycles of calamity,
they descend according to their time.
Safety and danger are not fixed,
adversity and prosperity are paired.
Transcendently gazing far,
one sighs with melancholy and emotion.
The disaster of extreme excess
can be avoided but not averted.
Clearly, what fate has ordained,
even a sage ruler cannot know.
Thus Bóyáng abandoned Zhōu,
and the Guardian of the Pass realized his state's decline.
The affairs of heaven and humanity
are manifest in all things.
Why do you linger so long as an earthbound immortal?
Would it not be better to awaken first and soar high,
transcending worldly dust to purify yourself,
avoiding the calamity in the dark path,
and join the true spirits as their equal?"
My words are fully spoken,
may you strive for this."
Ānqī knelt and said:
"Today I receive your instruction,
and shall diligently cultivate it."
The Lady said to Míngshēng:
"I cannot stay longer.
You go with this gentleman,
do not worry or long for me.
I will also visit you from time to time."
She then gave him two five-character poems as gifts,
to encourage each other.
Míngshēng tearfully bid farewell,
and followed Ānqī, carrying his books, into Nǚjī Mountain.
The Lady rode a dragon and departed.
Later, Míngshēng traveled with his teacher to Qīngchéng and Lúqián,
for twenty years in all.
He then received the formula for the golden elixir,
refined it, and ascended to heaven.
From *Biographies of the Immortals*.
È Lǜhuá
È Lǜhuá
is a female immortal.
She appears about twenty years old,
dressed entirely in green garments,
with an exceptionally refined appearance.
On the night of the tenth day of the eleventh month in the year jǐwèi, the third year of the Shēngpíng era of Emperor Mù of Jìn, she descended to Yáng Quán's home.
She said she was from the southern mountains,
but it is unknown which immortal she is.
From then on, she visited his home six times each month.
Quán's courtesy name was Dàoxué,
and he was the grandfather of Yáng Xīn, who served as Gentleman of the Yellow Gate under Emperor Jiǎnwén of Jìn.
Both Quán and Xīn
devotedly cultivated the essentials of the Way,
immersed in mystery and savoring truth.
Lǜhuá said:
"My original surname was Yáng."
She also said she was Luó Yù, who attained the Way in the Jiǔyí Mountains.
In a past life,
she had poisoned the wet nurse Xuánzhōu, who was her teacher's wife.
Because her former offense was not yet extinguished,
she was temporarily banished to this foul and turbid realm
to repay her transgression.
She gave Quán a poem,
along with a fire-washing cloth handkerchief,
and gold and jade bracelets, one each.
The bracelets were like finger rings but larger,
exceptionally exquisite.
She told Quán:
"Be careful not to reveal my descent;
if you do, both of us will incur guilt."
She then said:
"For those who cultivate the Way,
they view brocade and embroidery as worn cloth,
view rank and position as passing guests,
view gold and jade as gravel.
They have no thoughts, no worries,
no affairs, no deliberate actions.
They practice what others cannot practice,
learn what others cannot learn,
are diligent where others cannot be diligent,
and attain what others cannot attain.
Why?
Ordinary people pursue desires,
I practice austerity and solitude;
ordinary people engage in worldly affairs,
I learn tranquility and detachment;
ordinary people strive for fame and profit,
I strive for inner cultivation;
ordinary people attain old age and death,
I attain long life.
Thus, I have practiced this for nine hundred years."
She gave Quán the medicine for liberation from the corpse,
and then vanished, transforming her form,
and now resides in the mountains of Xiāngdōng.
From *Declarations of the Perfected*.
Lady Wèi
Lady Wèi,
was a native of Rènchéng.
She was the daughter of Wèi Shū, Duke Wénkāng of Jùyáng, who served as Minister over the Masses in the Jin dynasty.
Her given name was Huácún,
and her courtesy name was Xián'ān.
From a young age, she was fond of the Dao,
being tranquil, silent, respectful, and cautious.
She read the works of Zhuāngzi and Lǎozǐ,
the three commentaries, the Five Classics, and the writings of the hundred schools,
all of which she thoroughly studied.
Her aspiration was to admire divine transcendents,
savoring the genuine and immersing herself in the mysterious.
She wished to seek ascension to the heavens.
She often ingested Hemp Powder and Poria Pill,
practiced exhalation and inhalation of breath and fluids,
and nurtured her life in peace and tranquility.
When relatives came and went,
she paid them no attention at all.
She often wished to live separately in a quiet place,
but her parents would not permit it.
At the age of twenty-four,
she was compelled to marry Liú Wén of Nányáng, who served as an Assistant to the Grand Guardian,
whose courtesy name was Yòuyàn.
She bore two sons:
the elder named Pú,
and the younger named Xiá.
Later, Yòuyàn became the Magistrate of Xiūwǔ.
Lady Wèi's heart longed for the hidden and numinous,
and her sincerity and devotion grew ever more profound.
Once her two sons were somewhat established,
she separated from the household,
observing purification rituals in a separate chamber.
Just as she was about to pass three months,

suddenly, the Great Ultimate Perfected Ān Dùmíng, the Great Divinity of the Eastern Florescence, the Azure Lad of Fāngzhū, the Divine King of the Yang Valley of the Green A of the Fusang, the Perfected Jǐnglín, the Transcendent Maiden of the Small You, and the Perfected of Clarity and Emptiness, Wáng Póu, descended.
Póu said to the Lady:
"I have heard that you secretly weave the genuine breath,
focus your mind on the Three Clarities,
and have toiled diligently to the utmost.
The Great Thearch of the Fusang has commanded me to impart to you the Way of the Divine Perfected."
The Azure Lad Lord said:
"The King of Clarity and Emptiness,
is your teacher."
Dùmíng said:
"You have earnestly sought the Dao with a bitter heart,
and now the Dao has come to you."
The Perfected Jǐnglín said:
"The Emperor of Emptiness has observed your diligent devotion,
and the Great Ultimate has already inscribed your name as a transcendent on the jade tablets.
Strive diligently!"
The Azure Lad Lord also said:
"If you do not further hear the superior methods of the inner techniques
"techniques" character originally missing.
According to the Ming manuscript copy, supplemented.
of the 'Jade Scripture of the Morning Scenery,'
you will have no chance to achieve the transcendent Dao.
In the future, we shall meet at Mount Yángdí,
keep this secret."
Lord Wáng then commanded the attendant maidens Huá Sàntiáo, Lǐ Míngduì, and others,
to open the cloud-enshrouded cases,
unlock the jade caskets,

and bring forth scriptures such as the 'Supreme Treasure Writings,' the 'Hidden Writings of the Eight Simplicities,' the 'Perfect Scripture of the Great Cavern,' the 'Numinous Writings of the Eight Ways,' the 'Purple Measure's Flaming Light,' the 'Stone Essence and Golden Horse,' the 'Divine Perfected Tiger Script,' and the 'Transcendent's Feathery Mystery,'
thirty-one scrolls in total.
He then personally handed them to the Lady.
Lord Wáng then informed her, saying:
"I once studied the Dao here,
and encountered the Southern Pole Lady and the Lord Wáng of the Western City,
who bestowed upon me thirty-one scrolls of precious scriptures.
By practicing them, I became a Perfected,
and attained the rank of Transcendent King of the Small You Cavern-Heaven.
What is now bestowed upon you is the original text from the Southern Pole Primordial Lady and Lord Wáng of the Western City.
This mountain cavern terrace
is merely a detached palace of Clarity and Emptiness."
Thereupon, Lord Wáng stood up facing north,
held the scriptures, and offered an invocation, saying:
"The Supreme Triad, the Nine Stars' Lofty Perfected, the subtle entry into the Dao,
the Jade Dawn of the Upper Clarity,
Póu, by command of the Great Thearch,
is to instruct Wèi Huácún.
This month, Dānliáng,
on the auspicious day of Wùshēn,
I reverently handle the precious scriptures.
The 'Divine Golden Tiger Script,' the 'Perfect Scripture of the Great Cavern,' and the 'Jade Chapters of the Eight Simplicities,' totaling thirty-one scrolls,
are the scriptures that Póu once pondered with utmost concentration on the Western Mountain of Yángmíng,
and received from the Perfected Grand Master, the Purple Primordial Lady.
Huácún must reverently follow the clear methods,
to achieve the utmost perfection,
recite and cultivate the Dao of Emptiness,
and forever become a soaring transcendent.
Should anyone divulge my scriptures,
their entire clan will be implicated,
their bodies becoming lowly ghosts,
blocked at the sources of the rivers.
The Nine Heavens have decreed it;
I dare to inform Huácún."
After the invocation concluded,
Lord Wáng also said:
"I received secret instructions from the Purple Primordial Lady,
hearing the teachings from my master, saying,
this text should be transmitted to various Perfected ones,
not just that I obtained it.
Now that you have received it,
it is by the command of the Great Thearch.
This book, from me onward, should be obtained by seven individuals.
With white jade as the slips,
and green jade for the characters,
by the time it reaches Huácún, it will be the fourth."
Thereupon, Jǐnglín also bestowed upon the Lady the 'Scripture of the Inner Landscape of the Yellow Court,'
instructing her to concentrate on it day and night.
After reading it ten thousand times,
she would then be able to see through ghosts and spirits,
pacify and harmonize the six viscera,
regulate the three ethereal souls and the five solid organs,
master radiant complexion,
return to the state of an infant,
which is the Way of immortality.
Thereupon, the four Perfected ones chanted and sang,
each commanding jade maidens
to play the zither, strike bells, and blow panpipes,
keeping rhythm as they began to sing.
After the singing ended,
Lord Wáng then explained and extracted the regulated practices from the scriptures,
along with the essential meaning of the precious scriptures,
the oral formulas for conducting affairs, and all key points were fully conveyed.
Then, slowly, they departed separately.
At that time, the Great Ultimate Perfected commanded the Northern Cold Jade Maiden Sòng Liánjuān,
to play the nine-breaths stone chimes;
the Azure Lad commanded the Eastern Florescence Jade Maiden Yān Jǐngzhū,
to strike the Western Fullness Bell;
the Divine King of the Yang Valley commanded the Divine Forest Jade Maiden Jiǎ Qūtíng,
to blow the phoenix-cry panpipes;
the Perfected of Clarity and Emptiness commanded the Soaring Mystery Jade Maiden Xiānyú Xū,
to pat the nine-harmonies jade clappers.
The Great Ultimate Perfected initiated the song that parts the skies;
the Azure Lad chanted the tune of the great rosy clouds;
the Divine King recited the morning-opening verses;
the Clarity and Emptiness Perfected sang the lyrics of riding the whirlwind.
After they dispersed,
the various Perfected and Primordial Ladies
descended day and night.
Although Yòuyàn was next door,
he remained silent and unaware.
Later, Yòuyàn passed away.
It happened that the world was in chaos and famine,
and the Lady cared for both internal and external family,
extending aid to the impoverished and needy.
Also, the true transcendents silently showed her omens,
so she knew the Central Plains would fall into turmoil.
She took her two sons and crossed the river.
Pú served as Sīmǎ for Yǔ Liàng,
and also as Sīmǎ for Wēn Tàizhēn,
later becoming the Grand Administrator of Ānchéng.
Xiá served as Attendant Gentleman of the Household and General of the Center for the Grand Marshal Táo Kǎn.
The Lady, from Luòyì to the regions south of the Yangtze,
amidst bandits and rebels,
wherever she passed,
divine spirits protected and aided her,
and the outcomes were always greatly auspicious.
Once her two sons were established in their positions,
the Lady was thus able to immerse her mind in purification and tranquility,
repeatedly sensing the true numinous beings.
The benefits of cultivating perfection
advanced together with each passing day.
She remained in the world for eighty-three years in total.
In the ninth year of the Xiánhé era of Emperor Chéng of Jin,
the cyclical year being Jiǎwù,
Lord Wáng again descended with the Azure Lad and the Lord of the Eastern Florescence,
bestowing upon the Lady two doses of perfected medicine:
one called the Divine Powder of the White Rider for Transferring the Spirit,
and the other called the Numinous Pill of Stone Essence and Golden Light for Transforming the Form.
They instructed her to take them at once,
and she claimed illness and did not go out.
After seven days in total,
the Great Unity Mysterious Transcendent dispatched a whirlwind chariot to welcome her.
The Lady then entrusted her sword, transformed her form, and departed,
directly entering Mount Yángluò.
The next day,
the Azure Lad Lord, the Four Perfected of the Great Ultimate, and the Clarity and Emptiness Lord Wáng,
instructed the Lady to observe purification for five hundred days,
read the 'Perfect Scripture of the Great Cavern,'
and separately elucidate the essential secrets of the true scriptures.
The Celestial Master Dào Líng also bestowed the 'Brilliant and Awesome Memorials' and the oral formulas for 'Summoning and Commanding Clerk Soldiers and Talismanic Registers.'
The various Perfected each imparted their ultimate instructions,
and after three days, they departed.
The reason Dào Líng comprehensively entrusted her with detailed instructions
was because the Lady, while in the world, was to serve as a female official libationer,
overseeing duties and governing the people.
The Lady recited the scriptures ten thousand times,
accumulating sixteen years,
and her countenance remained like that of a young maiden.
Thereupon, the Golden Mother of the Nine Emptinesses of Turtle Mountain, the Sagely Lord of the Golden Portal, and the Primordial Lady of the Southern Pole,
together welcomed the Lady as she ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
She proceeded north to beneath the jade portals of the Palace of Upper Clarity.

The Thearch of the Great Tenuity, the Central Yellow Old Lord, the Lord of the Three Primes of High Origin, the Grand Dao Lord of the Supreme Jade Dawn, the Lord of the Three Primes of the Great Simplicity, the Great Thearch of the Fusang, and the Sagely Lord of the Later Golden Portal,
each dispatched envoys to convey their decrees,
bestowing the 'Jade Tablets and Golden Scripts of Heaven and Humanity,'
and conferring the rank of Primordial Lady of the Purple Emptiness,
appointed as the Lady of the Southern Peak, Director of the Fate of Upper Perfected,
with rank comparable to a Transcendent Duke,
to govern within the cavern terrace of the Great Huò Cavern-Heaven of Tiāntāi,
primarily responsible for instructing and serving the Dao below.
The professor should become an immortal.
Males are called Zhēnrén,
females are called Yuánjūn.
After Fūrén received the bestowal and the matters were completed,
Wángmǔ, Jīnquè Shèngjūn, and Nánjí Yuánjūn each departed.
They had Fūrén stay in the Xiǎoyǒutiān within Wángwū,
where she further observed purification and fasting for two months. After completion,
Jiǔwēi Yuánjūn, Guīshān Wángmǔ, Sānyuán Fūrén, and the multitude of various true immortals,
all descended to the Xiǎoyǒu Qīngxū Shàng
(Below the character "shàng" in the "Yúnjí Qīqiān" volume 96, there are twenty-two characters: "gōng jiàng fáng zhī zhōng shí fūrén yǔ wáng jūn wéi bīn zhǔ yān shè qióng sū yù jiǔ jīn shāng")
Four performances were played,
each commanding their attendant maidens to present melodies harmoniously completed,
the nine spirits in unison with the rhythm,
the eight tones reaching the numinous realm,
Wángmǔ beat the rhythm and sang,
Sānyuán Fūrén played the yún'áo and responded with a song,
the remaining true ones each sang,
in a short while, the deities of Sīmìng and various subordinates,
along with the welcoming officials from Nányuè, all arrived.
Tiger banners and dragon carriages,
radiance dazzling for a hundred li,
Wángmǔ and the various true ones,
then together with Fūrén traveled southeast,
all proceeding to Tiāntāi Huòshān Tái,
also passing by Jùyóu Jīntán Máo Shūshēn along the way,
feasting for two days and two nights,
together reaching Huòshān.
Fūrén safely halted her jade carriage,
then they each parted.
Initially,
Wáng Jūn informed Fūrén, saying:
"Those who study the Way should eliminate ailments and cure illnesses."
Thereupon he bestowed the Gāncǎo Gǔ Immortal Formula,
which Fūrén ingested.
Fūrén was capable of clerical script; Xiǎoyǒu Wáng Jūn transmitted it together,
the matters being very detailed and thorough.
She also composed the "Huángtíng Nèijǐng Zhù",
and described the formula for Qīngjīng rice.
Later, she frequently descended to Máoshān.
Her son Pú later attained the position of Shìzhōng,
Fūrén commanded Pú to transmit the methods to the Sītú Lángyé Wáng Shèrén Yáng Xī,
and Hùjūn Zhǎngshǐ Xǔ Mù.
Mù's son Yùfǔ,
both ascended to immortality.
The Nánzhēn referred to in Táo Zhēnbái's "Zhēngào",
is precisely Fūrén.
In the third year of Xīngníng of the Jìn dynasty, yǐchǒu,
she descended to the Yáng household,
and said to Yáng Jūn:
"Those who cultivate the Dao,
should not wish to see flesh and blood;
even if they see it and avoid it,
it is not as good as not seeing it at all."
She also said:
"Earlier, passing through the Eastern Sea,
the sound of the waves was like thunder."
She also said:
"In Péi Qīnglíng Zhēnrén's brocade pouch, there is the 'Bǎoshén Jīng',
which he received in the past from Zǐwēi Fūrén.
I also have this definitive version from the Western Palace,
which is precisely the upper terrace of Xuánpǔ's northern altar, Xīyáo,
where the celestial true precious texts are all stored within."
Thereupon she bestowed a text, saying:
"As for those who look up and cast the cloud wheel,
grasp the reins of the great void,
hands holding the night mist,
feet treading the royal court.
The body ascends to the imperial gate,
dons treasures and inhales the azure,
discusses the transcendent measures of the nine mysteries,
immerses in the eternal life of ten thousand springs,
true words mysteriously clear,
lofty discourse of Yùqīng.
Now, returning the numinous to the dust,
instructing my disciples,
looking all around at the five turbidities,
laboring the spirit amidst foul stench.
What you strive for is the Dao,
what you study and chant is the wondrous.
Having attained the Dao's wondrousness,
you, my son, add to it;
fear this scattering and dissipation,
be mindful and cautious of it."
She further said:
"To the west of Hédōng Tóngbóshān,
a collapse of over two hundred zhang just occurred.
Yesterday, I went with Máo Shūshēn to the Qīngxū Palace,
to confer the registers of true immortals,
matters of gain and loss.
Forty-seven persons were immediately stricken off,
only three were reinstated.
One must indeed cleanse the mind and advance in emptiness,
diligently focus until principle is exhausted,
heart weary and intention spent,
as if treading on ice and fire.
Persisting long in this manner,
the path to immortality will also not remain hidden.
But it lies in solemn reverence and sincere dedication,
and severing thoughts of licentiousness.
If one harbors a lustful mind,
yet practices the path of the higher true ones,
those stricken off by the pure palace,
are all such persons.
Not only will their names be removed from the living register,
they will moreover be examined by the Three Offices.
Strive diligently, be cautious.
Those who revere the Dao value freedom from evil,
those who dwell in truth find peace in tranquility and joy.
Ultimate stillness is not the master that guides compliance,
indifference is not the craftsman that imparts teaching.
Therefore, one must endure vexation to comprehend non-being.
For those practicing the Dao, essence is sufficient;
having essence but not diligence,
having ability but not dedication,
is of no benefit.
The key lies in dissolving a grudging heart,
swiftly opening up foul thoughts.
One may frequently gaze upon the Eastern Mountain,
diligently look upon the triple excellence,
which can somewhat further benefit.
Speech determines the complete success or failure of nature and life,
trust is the key to gain and loss.
Zhāng Liáng's three periods,
can be said to be sincere in the Dao and clear in mind."
She also said:
"Attaining the Dao and departing the world,
some manifest, some conceal.
Entrusting the body and leaving traces behind,
is the concealment of the Dao.
In the past, some drank jade nectar twice and knocked on their coffin;
some ingested a small amount of elixir and their corpse decayed.
Lùpí Gōng swallowed Yùhuá and flowing worms emerged from his door;
Jiǎ Jìzǐ swallowed golden liquor and a stench was heard for a hundred li;
Huángdì refined the nine tripods at Jīngshān,
yet still has a tomb at Qiáolǐng;
Lǐ Yù
(The Ming manuscript copy writes "Lǐ" as "Jì".)
("Yǒuyáng Zázǔ" "two" writes it as "Jì Zhǔ")
ingested cloud powder to ascend in concealment,
yet his head and feet were in different places;
Mò Dí drank rainbow elixir and submerged in water;
Nìng Shēng ingested stone marrow and went into fire;
Wù Guāng cut water chestnuts and entered the clear cold spring;
Bǎichéng absorbed qi and his intestines and stomach rotted three times.
Examples such as these,
are too numerous to record.
Subtle indeed is attaining the Dao;
the traces of advancing and withdrawing,
certainly have no constant pattern."
Bǎomìng Jūn said:
"What is called liberation from the corpse,
is borrowing a form to show death,
not true death."
Nánzhēn said:
"When a person dies, one must look at their form;
if like a living person,
it is liberation from the corpse.
Feet not blue, skin not wrinkled,
is also liberation from the corpse.
Eyes fallen and not bright,
(Ming manuscript copy writes: "eyes bright and not fallen")
no different from a living person,
is liberation from the corpse.
Hair all fallen and losing the form of bones,
is liberation from the corpse.
Liberation from the corpse in broad daylight,
is naturally becoming an immortal.
If not of the category of liberation from the corpse,
after death passes through Tàiyīn,
temporarily undergoing the Three Offices,
flesh sheds, pulses scatter,
blood sinks, ashes decay,
yet the five viscera regenerate themselves,
bones become like jade,
the seven pò attend and serve,
the three hún guard the dwelling,
perhaps after thirty years, twenty years, ten years, three years,
flesh and blood will regenerate,
substance will reform into shape,
certainly surpassing the appearance before death in former days.
This is called refining the form.
Tàiyīn transforms the appearance,
it is the immortal of the Three Offices."
The Heavenly Emperor said:
"Tàiyīn refines the body's form,
surpassing ingesting the nine-cycle elixir.
Appearance dignified and solemn,
countenance like numinous clouds,
ascending to the Tàijí gate,
receiving the writ to become a Zhēnrén."
This is it.
As for those who temporarily wander in Tàiyīn,
Tàiyī guards the corpse,
the three hún attend to the bones,
the seven pò serve the flesh,
the embryonic numinous records the qi,
all when the numbers are full, they regenerate and soar to heaven.
Those who use other medicines for liberation from the corpse,
not being the numinous pill,
If one cannot return to their hometown,
it is because the Three Officials have seized them.
Those who die and then revive,
whose corpses disappear before being encoffined,
whose skin and form remain but whose essence is gone,
whose clothes remain knotted and unfastened,
whose garments remain but whose form has departed,
whose hair falls out and whose form flies away,
whose heads are severed and who have died,
yet emerge from the side—
all these are cases of corpse liberation.
Liberation during daylight is superior;
liberation at midnight is inferior;
those who depart toward dusk or evening
become rulers of the underworld.
These are the varying grades of attaining the Dao.
When a person cultivates the Dao,
if disasters press and misfortunes arise,
their form decays and their vital breath perishes,
it seems to be due to speaking too much while guarding the One,
or pursuing many paths while hoping to avoid harm.
Thus, a layered nest collapses from a broken branch and falls,
a hundred victories are lost in a single defeat—
how regrettable!
How could a talent capable of transcending to immortality
be brought to death by two petty fellows?
Wisdom, when boundless, injures one's nature;
the mind, through desires and aversions, scatters one's authenticity.
How could this compare to guarding the root in stillness,
dwelling upon and refining the three spirits,
pervading and penetrating all things,
where the mysterious mirror is profoundly tranquil,
blending indistinguishably with the Mud Ball into one,
bringing inner and outer equally into bliss?
A Perfected Person returns the mind to the One,
entrusting it to eternal faith.
When the mind returns, it becomes upright;
when the spirit is harmonious and faith compliant,
these are auspicious signs of benefiting authenticity,
natural responses.
They do not depend on dualistic boundaries.
If outwardly there is an aura of scrutiny and observation,
and inwardly there is stifled resentment and suppressed anger,
for one with such traits,
I see their downfall,
but never see their establishment.
The rulers of the underworld
are the civil officials of the lower path.
The ghost commanders of the underworld
are the military officials of the lower path.
Civil liberation advances once every one hundred and four years;
military liberation takes twice that time.
People of the world diligently pursue their desires,
mixing flavors with purity and uprightness,
adorned eyes following worldly trends.
Those who fear death yet hope for immortality
mostly achieve military liberation,
the lowest form of corpse liberation."
The Lady then chanted a poem with the assembled Perfected:
"Mysterious resonance beyond wondrous forms,
Harmonious tones summon each other.
Numinous clouds gather at purple dawn,
Orchid winds fan the green carriage.
The Highest Perfected feast on Jasper Terrace,
Far removed, marking Earthbound Immortals.
What is aspired to is noble and far-reaching,
Thus enabling outstanding elegance to soar.
Savoring those eight-syllable verses,
The Dao's completion is not distant at its start.
How can human affairs be predetermined,
Causing your form and vital breath to dissipate?"
After the Lady traveled to the region south of the Yangtze,
she established a quiet chamber on Bìngshān in Fǔzhōu,
and also set up an altar complex west of the Línrǔ River.
Over the years, they became overgrown and blocked,
their traces nearly leveled.
There was a female Daoist named Huáng Línghuī,
over eighty years old,
whose appearance was like that of an infant.
She was called Flower Maiden,
and she specially restored and adorned the sites,
repeatedly receiving numinous responses.
The Lady also appeared to her in dreams to give instructions,
and later she too ascended to heaven.
Emperor Xuánzōng ordered the Daoist Cài Wěi to compile this into the Later Biographies of Immortals.
In the third year of the Dàlì era, wùshēn (768 CE),
Duke of Lǔguó, Yán Zhēnqīng, extensively renovated the sites again,
erecting a stele to record these events.
From Records of the Assembled Immortals and Her Basic Biography.
The Bright Star Jade Maiden
The Bright Star Jade Maiden
dwelled on Huàshān.
She drank jade nectar
and ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
On the mountain peak is a stone turtle,
several acres in breadth,
and three ren in height.
At its side are ladder-like stone steps,
visible from afar.
In front of the Jade Maiden's shrine are five stone mortars,
called the Jade Maiden's Hair-Washing Basins.
The water within them
is emerald green, clear and limpid;
rain does not cause them to overflow,
drought does not diminish them.
Inside the shrine is a jade stone horse.
From Records of the Assembled Immortals.
Chāngróng
Chāngróng
was a daughter of the King of Shāng.
She cultivated the Dao on Chángshān,
eating the roots of the péngléi plant for over two hundred years,
yet her face appeared as if she were around twenty.
She could procure purple herbs,
sell them to dyers,
and use the money to give to the poor and sick.
She came and went in the cities and markets,
and people saw her generation after generation.
People from near and far,
over a thousand households, served her,
yet none ever knew what Dao she cultivated.
She often walked under the midday sun,
but cast no shadow.
Some say:
"Chāngróng was one who could refine her form."
Suddenly she soared into the sky and departed.
From Biographies of Female Immortals.
Yuán Kè's wife
was a divine maiden.
Yuán Kè
was a man from Jìyīn.
He was handsome in appearance and virtuous,
and many in the district wished to give him their daughters in marriage,
but Kè never married.
He constantly planted five-colored fragrant herbs,
accumulating them for several decades,
and ate their fruit.
Suddenly, five-colored moths gathered on the fragrant herbs.
Kè collected them and laid them on cloth as a mat.
They produced magnificent silkworms.
When it was time for the silkworms to emerge,
a maiden came of her own accord to help Kè raise the silkworms,
also feeding them with the fragrant herbs.
The silkworms grew strong,
producing one hundred and thirty cocoons.
The cocoons were as large as jars;
for each cocoon,
it took six or seven days to fully reel the silk.
After the reeling was finished,
this maiden and Yuán Kè both departed.
In Jìyīn today, there is a shrine to the magnificent silkworms.
From Biographies of Female Immortals.
Tài Xuán Nǚ,
surnamed Zhuān,
named Hé,
lost her father in her youth.
Some physiognomists read the fortunes of her and her mother,
and all said they would not live long.
She was deeply saddened and considered it a worry.
She often said:
"When a person lives in this world,
once life is lost, it cannot be regained.
Moreover, hearing that the span of life is so brief,
only by cultivating the Dao can one prolong life."
She then traveled to seek out enlightened masters,
purified her heart to seek the Dao,
and obtained the arts of Wángzǐ.
Practicing them for many years,
she became able to enter water without getting wet.
In the severe cold of heavy snow,
wearing only a single layer of clothing on the ice,
her complexion would not change,
her body remained warm,
and this could last for days on end.
She could also move government offices, palaces, cities, towns, houses, and residences to other places;
looking at them, they appeared no different,
but pointing at them would cause them to vanish from their location.
Doors, windows, cabinets, and chests that were locked,
she could open by pointing at them.
Pointing at a mountain, the mountain would crumble;
pointing at a tree, the tree would split.
Pointing again,
they would immediately return to their original state.
Leading her disciples through the mountains,
at dusk,
she would tap a rock with her staff,
and a door would immediately open.
Entering inside,
there were houses, beds, bedding, curtains, and canopies,
with ample provisions of wine and food as usual.
Even if traveling ten thousand *lǐ*,
wherever she went, it was always like this.
She could make small objects suddenly become as large as a house,
and large objects suddenly become as small as a hair's tip.
Sometimes she would spew fire that filled the sky,
and with a puff, extinguish it.
She could also sit amidst blazing flames,
with her clothes and shoes not burning.
In an instant,
she could transform into an old man,
or become a young child,
or become a carriage and horse,
there was nothing she could not become.
She practiced thirty-six arts with great efficacy,
reviving the dead and bringing them back to life,
saving countless people.
No one knew what elixirs she ingested,
nor were there any who obtained her arts.
Her complexion grew increasingly youthful,
her hair dark as a crow's feathers.
Suddenly, in broad daylight, she ascended to heaven and departed.
From *Nǚ Xiān Zhuàn* (Biographies of Female Immortals).
Xīhé Shàonǚ (The Maiden of Xīhé)
The Maiden of Xīhé
was the niece of the immortal Bó Shānfǔ.
Shānfǔ was from Yōngzhōu,
he entered Huàshān to study the Dao,
diligently practiced meditation and ingested elixirs,
occasionally returning to his hometown to visit his relatives.
After more than two hundred years,
his appearance had grown even more youthful.
Entering people's homes,
he would immediately know the good and evil deeds, merits and faults of that family's ancestors,
as if he had witnessed them himself.
He also knew future fortunes and misfortunes,
and his words never failed to come true.
Seeing that his niece was young and often ill,
he gave her medicine.
When the girl took the medicine,
she was already seventy years old,
but gradually regained her youth,
her complexion becoming like that of an infant.
During the Hàn dynasty, an envoy was traveling through Xīhé,
and east of the city, he saw a woman
beating an old man with a rod.
The old man's hair was white as snow,
and he knelt receiving the blows.
The envoy, finding it strange, asked her about it,
the woman replied:
"This is my son.
In the past, my uncle Bó Shānfǔ,
having attained the way of the immortals,
lived in seclusion in Huàshān.
Taking pity on my many illnesses,
he gave me divine medicine,
and I gradually regained youth and vigor.
Now this son of mine,
I told him to take the medicine but he refused,
resulting in this old age and decline.
He cannot keep up with me when walking,
I am angry with him,
hence I am beating him with this rod."
The envoy asked the woman and her son their respective ages,
the woman replied:
"I am one hundred and thirty years old,
my son is seventy-one."
This woman also entered Huàshān and departed.
From *Nǚ Xiān Zhuàn* (Biographies of Female Immortals).
Liáng Yùqīng
*Dōngfāng Shuò Nèi Zhuàn* (The Inner Biography of Dōngfāng Shuò) says:
When Qín annexed the six states,
the Great White Star (Venus) secretly took the weaving maid's attendants Liáng Yùqīng and Wèi Chéngzhuāng,
and fled into the Shàoxiān Cave in Wèi City,
not emerging for forty-six days.
The Heavenly Emperor was angered,
and ordered the Five Sacred Mountains to search and capture them.
The Great White Star returned to his position,
Wèi Chéngzhuāng escaped.
Liáng Yùqīng had a son named Xiū,
and Yùqīng was exiled beneath the Northern Dipper.
It was often spring,
and her son was then assigned to Hé Bó (the River Earl),
serving as an outrider for the rain-making processions.
Whenever her son Xiū reached the Shàoxiān Cave,
ashamed that it was the place of his mother's illicit elopement,
he would turn his chariot around,
therefore this place often had little rain.
From *Dú Yì Zhì* (Records of Unique Marvels).
Jiāng Fēi
Zhèng Jiāofǔ often roamed the Hàn River,
and saw two women,
both dressed in beautiful, splendid attire,
wearing two bright pearls,
as large as chicken eggs.
Jiāofǔ saw them and was delighted,
not knowing they were divine beings.
He said to his servant:
"I wish to go down and request their pendants."
The servant said:
"The people of this region
are all skilled in speech,
if you fail, you may incur regret."
Jiāofǔ did not listen,
and went down to speak to them, saying:
"You two ladies must be tired."
The two women replied:
"The traveler is the one who is tired,
how could we be tired?"
Jiāofǔ said:
"The orange is a type of citrus,
I place it in a bamboo box,
set it adrift on the Hàn River,
letting it flow downstream.
I walk alongside it and pluck it,
knowing I am being presumptuous,
yet I wish to request your pendants."
The two women said:
"The orange is a type of citrus,
placed in a basket,
set adrift on the Hàn River,
letting it flow downstream.
We walk alongside it,
gather its *zhī* plant and consume it."
With their hands, they untied their pendants and gave them to Jiāofǔ.
Jiāofǔ received them and placed them in his bosom.
Once he hurried away,
after walking several tens of steps,
he looked in his bosom—it was empty, no pearls.
The two women had suddenly vanished.
*The Book of Songs* says:
"By the Hàn River are roaming maidens,
but one cannot seek them."
This speaks of how they guard themselves with propriety,
and none dare violate them,
how much more so with the transformations of immortals?
From *Liè Xiān Zhuàn* (Biographies of Exemplary Immortals).
Máo Nǚ (The Hairy Maiden)
Originally "Nǚ" (maiden) was written as "Shì" (clan).
Changed according to the Ming dynasty manuscript copy.
Her name was Yùjiāng,
and she was in the Huàyīn Mountains.
Mountain travelers and hunters
saw her generation after generation.
Her body had grown hair,
and she said of herself that she was a palace woman of Qín Shǐhuáng.
When Qín fell,
she fled into the mountains.
A Daoist taught her to eat pine needles,
and thus she was never hungry or cold,
her body became so light.
By the time of the Western Hàn dynasty,
she was already over one hundred and seventy years old.
From *Liè Xiān Zhuàn* (Biographies of Exemplary Immortals).
Qín Gōngrén (The Qín Palace Woman)
During the reign of Emperor Chéng of the Hàn,
hunters in the Zhōngnán Mountains saw a person
without clothes,
their body covered in black hair.
The hunters wanted to capture them,
but this person leaped over pits and crossed valleys,
as if flying,
and could not be caught up with.
So they secretly observed where this person stayed,
surrounded the area, and captured them.
When questioned;
they said:
"I was originally a palace maid of Qín,
and heard that bandits from Guāndōng had arrived,
the King of Qín surrendered,
the palaces were burned,
so in panic I fled into the mountains.
With no food to eat when hungry,
I was about to starve to death,
when an old man
taught me to eat pine needles and pine nuts.
At first they were bitter and astringent,
but later I gradually became accustomed to them,
and then felt neither hunger nor thirst,
not cold in winter,
nor hot in summer."
Considering this, the woman must have been a palace maid of Zǐyīng, the King of Qín.
By the time of Emperor Chéng,
she was about a hundred years old.
The hunters took her back,
and fed her grain.
At first she found the smell of grain foul,
vomited,
and only after several days did she adjust.
After about a year like this,
the hair on her body gradually fell out,
she aged and died.
Had she not been captured by people,
she would have become an immortal.
From Bàopǔzǐ.
Lady Gōuyì,
was from Qí,
surnamed Zhào,
and from a young age loved purity and tranquility.
She lay ill for six years,
with her right hand clenched,
eating and drinking little.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn,
those who observed the ethers said there was an aura of nobility in the northeast,
and through divination found her,
summoning her to court.
Her beauty was extraordinary,
Emperor Wǔ opened her hand and found a jade hook,
and her hand could then stretch out.
He favored her,
and she gave birth to Emperor Zhāo.
Emperor Wǔ later had her killed,
but her encoffined corpse did not grow cold and was fragrant.
A month later,
when Emperor Zhāo ascended the throne,
she was reburied,
but the coffin was empty,
containing only silk shoes.
Therefore, her palace was named Gōuyì,
later changed to Gōuyì to avoid a taboo.
From Lièxiān Zhuàn.
Princess Nányáng
Princess Nányáng of the Hàn,
was married to Wáng Xián.
During Wáng Mǎng's administration,
the princess had long admired emptiness,
and revered the supreme Dào.
Often recalling the peaceful reigns of Emperors Wén and Jǐng,
and knowing that during Emperor Wǔ's time,
immortals frequently descended,
she said to Xián:
"The state is in peril and the world in chaos,
not something a woman can support.
I should only preserve my own tranquility,
withdraw to cultivate the Dào,
gradually distancing myself from the clamor and strife,
surely I can prolong my life.
If I busily follow the times, advancing and retreating,
I fear I cannot avoid the suffering of fragmentation,
the calamity of being driven and pursued."
Xián said he would strive for worldly fortune,
and did not follow her words.
The princess then built a hut on Huàshān,
dwelling there for over a year.
Through intense contemplation and earnest practice,
the true numina responded,
and she abandoned her hut and left.
Some saw her,
slowly crossing a deep ravine,
riding the clouds and mist, drifting away.
Xián entered the mountains to pursue her,
crossed great ravines,
climbed layered peaks,
weeping and gazing after her,
but found only vast emptiness without a trace.
Suddenly, on a ridge, he saw a pair of red shoes left behind,
went forward to take them,
but they had already turned to stone.
Thus it was called Princess Peak.
Pān Ānrén wrote an account of it,
which circulated in the world.
From Jíxiān Lù.
Chéng Wěi's Wife
The wife of Chéng Wěi, a Qīmén Láng of the Hàn,
was one who had attained the Dào.
She could communicate with spirits and perform transformations,
but Wěi did not find it very remarkable.
Once, Wěi was to accompany the imperial carriage on an excursion,
but his attire was incomplete,
and he was greatly worried.
His wife said:
"It's only lacking clothes,
why worry so much?"
Immediately, two bolts of silk appeared,
suddenly arriving on their own.
Wěi also was fond of the arts of alchemy,
but when he tried to refine metals, he could not succeed.
His wife then took a small amount of medicine from a pouch,
placed mercury in a vessel,
added the medicine and heated it,
and in a moment it turned into silver.
Wěi wanted to learn the formula from her.
But in the end, he could not obtain it.
She said
that Wěi's bone structure indicated he should not attain it.
He pressed her incessantly,
and his wife suddenly collapsed and died.
Her corpse was liberated, and she departed.
From Jíxiān Lù.
Liáng Mǔ
Liáng Mǔ was a woman from Xūyí.
She lived as a widow with no children,
and ran an inn at the Píngyuán Lodge.
When travelers came to rest there,
they all felt as if they had returned home.
As for how much money the guests paid,
she never said a word.
Even if guests stayed for months,
she never grew weary of them.
Beyond her own clothing and food,
whatever she earned she gave to the poor and needy.
Once, a young man stayed for several days,
and his behavior was unusual.
As he was about to leave, he said:
"I am a youth from the Eastern Sea."
Liáng Mǔ did not know who this youth was.
In the fourth year of the Yuánhuī era of the Sòng dynasty, on the bǐngchén day,
the Dàoshì Xú Dàoshèng from Mǎ'ěr Mountain briefly arrived at Méngyīn.
West of Fēngchéng, he encountered a green ox-cart
that was moving on its own.
"Moving" — in the Yúnjí Qīqiān, it says "stopped."
He saw a youth calling for Dàoshì Xú to come forward.
Xú Dàoshèng advanced
and stopped about three steps away from the cart.
He then saw two other youths,
both around twelve or thirteen years old,
wearing yellow robes,
with crimson cloth wrapped around the buns on their heads.
Their appearance and attire were dignified and neat,
unlike anything in this world.
Someone inside the cart sent a youth to relay a message:
"I am Liáng Mǔ from the Píngyuán inn.
Now I have been summoned back by Tàishàng,
and I am to pass by Pénglái to seek Zǐqiáo.
After undergoing examination at Tàishān,
I wished to see you,
and indeed you have come.
The spiritual reins flutter,
the mountain paths are perilous" — originally "xuán gāng yīn,"
changed according to the Yúnjí Qīqiān —
"the ferry stations are limited,
the journey is three thousand days" — originally "three days, three characters,"
changed according to the Yúnjí Qīqiān.
The audience is near,
my heart is weary with worry.
I shall soon ride the mists to the Three Purities.
These three youths are escorting me to the Xuándū Kingdom.
Please convey my gratitude to all the devout men and women of the East.
Peace is near,
ten remain with one.
Strive well to guide and save others,
for beyond this lies peril and sorrow."
Raising her hand in farewell, she said:
"We shall meet in peace."
The cart sped away and vanished into the distance,
disappearing from sight.
Xú Dàoshèng returned to the inn to inquire,
and it was indeed the day Liáng Mǔ had transcended the mortal world when they met.
From the Jíxiān Lù.
Dǒng Yǒng's Wife
Dǒng Yǒng's father died,
and he had no means to bury him,
so he sold himself into slavery.
His master, knowing his virtue,
gave him ten million coins and sent him away.
After Dǒng Yǒng observed the three-year mourning period,
he wished to return to his master
to fulfill his duties as a slave.
On the way, he met a woman who said:
"I am willing to be your wife."
So she went with him.
The master said to Dǒng Yǒng:
"I gave you the money as a gift."
Dǒng Yǒng said:
"Thanks to your kindness,
my father was properly buried.
Though I am but a humble man,
I must work diligently
to repay your great virtue."
The master asked:
"What can your wife do?"
Dǒng Yǒng replied:
"She can weave."
The master said:
"If that is so,
then have your wife weave a hundred bolts of fine silk for me."
So Dǒng Yǒng's wife wove for the master's household,
and in ten days, the hundred bolts were completed.
From the Sōushén Jì.
Jiǔ Mǔ
Jiǔ Mǔ was a wine-seller woman from beneath the palace gates.
She met a master named Yú Lǎo,
though no one knew where he was from.
He appeared to be in his fifties,
but claimed to be several hundred years old.
The wine-seller woman found this strange
and always treated him with respect.
One day, he suddenly came and said to her:
"Prepare quickly,
I will take you to answer the summons of Zhōnglíng Wáng."
That night, a strange person indeed came,
holding two straw dogs.
He gave one to Yú Lǎo
and one to the wine-seller woman,
telling both to ride them —
and they turned out to be dragons.
They followed him up Huàyīn Mountain,
often shouting loudly:
"Yú Lǎo and Jiǔ Mǔ are here!"
From the Nǚxiān Zhuàn.
Nǚ Jǐ
Nǚ Jǐ was a wine-seller woman in the market of Chén,
and the wine she made was always excellent.
An immortal passed by her home to drink wine,
and used five volumes of plain-text books as collateral for the wine money.
Nǚ Jǐ opened and looked at them —
they were methods for nurturing life and achieving longevity.
Nǚ Jǐ secretly copied down the essential techniques
and practiced according to them.
After three years,
her complexion grew even younger,
like someone around twenty.
A few years later,
the immortal who had pawned the books for wine returned.
Smiling, he said to her:
"To steal the Way without a master —
you have wings but cannot fly."
Nǚ Jǐ followed the immortal away.
She lived on the mountain for many years,
and people often saw her.
Later, no one knew where she went.
The place where she lived is now called Nǚ Jǐ Mountain.
From the Nǚxiān Zhuàn.
Má Gū
During the reign of Emperor Huán of the Hàn dynasty,
the immortal Wáng Yuǎn,
courtesy name Fāngpíng,
descended upon the home of Cài Jīng.
Shortly before his arrival,
the sounds of bronze drums, panpipes, and men and horses were heard,
and the entire household saw
Wáng Fāngpíng wearing a yuǎnyóu cap,
clad in crimson robes,
a tiger-headed pouch at his waist,
a multicolored silk ribbon,
and a sword.
He had a sparse beard,
a yellowish complexion,
and was of average build.
He rode in a feathered carriage
drawn by five dragons,
each of a different color.
With command staffs, banners, and flags,
and attendants guiding the way before and following behind,
his majestic bearing was imposing,
like that of a great general.
The musicians all rode on qílín,
descending from the heavens.
They alighted and gathered in the courtyard,
his attendants all over ten feet tall,
not arriving by the road.
Once they had arrived,
the attendants all vanished,
their whereabouts unknown.
Only Fāngpíng was seen,
meeting with Cài Jīng's parents and brothers.
After sitting alone for a long while,
he immediately sent someone to inquire after
[Míng manuscript note: The characters "Mágū" appear below "inquire after" here]
The Cài family also did not know who Mágū was.
The message said:
"Wáng Fāngpíng respectfully informs the Lady:
I have long been absent from the mortal realm,
and am now gathered here.
I wonder if the Lady could come for a brief conversation?"
After a short while,
the messenger returned.
The messenger was not seen,
but only his words were heard, saying:
"Mágū bows twice.
It has been over five hundred years since we last met.
Though there is a distinction between noble and humble,
I have had no means to pay my respects.
A message has been sent,
and I have received word of your presence there.
I have been climbing the mountain, topsy-turvy
Note:
See the entry for Wáng Yuǎn in chapter seven of this book.
"Climbing the mountain, topsy-turvy" should read "I will arrive in the time it takes to eat a meal."
But I received your command earlier,
and am currently scheduled to inspect Pénglái.
I will now make a brief visit.
Once this is done, I shall return,
and upon returning, I will pay a personal visit.
I hope to come
[Míng manuscript note: "lái" (come) is written as "wèi" (not yet)]
and then depart immediately."
About the time it takes for two meals,
Mágū arrived.
Upon her arrival, the sounds of men, horses, panpipes, and drums were also heard first.
Once she arrived,
her attendants numbered half those of Fāngpíng.
When Mágū arrived,
Cài Jīng and his entire household also saw her.
She was a lovely maiden,
appearing about eighteen or nineteen years old.
Her hair was done in a topknot,
with the remaining locks hanging down to her waist.
Her garments were patterned,
though not of brocade or damask,
their brilliance dazzling to the eye,
beyond description.
She entered and bowed to Fāngpíng,
and Fāngpíng stood up for her.
Once seated,
he summoned the traveling kitchen,
all of gold plates and jade cups.
The dishes were mostly various flowers and fruits,
and their fragrance permeated inside and out.
The shredded dried meat served
was like bǎi líng
[The "Collection of Immortal Records" writes "sì líng" as "zhì" (roast).]
Note: "Bǎi" should be "Mò".
"Mò zhì" appears in Gān Bǎo's "In Search of the Supernatural"
and is said to be qílín jerky.
Mágū said of herself:
"Since I began attending and serving,
I have already seen the Eastern Sea turn into mulberry fields three times.
Just now when I went to Pénglái,
the water was again shallower than when we last met, by about half.
Could it be that it will once again become hills and dry land?"
Fāngpíng laughed and said:
"The sages all say that dust will again fly over the sea."
Mágū wished to see Cài Jīng's mother and his wife and nieces.
At the time, his sister-in-law had given birth just a few dozen days before.
Mágū saw her from a distance and knew,
saying:
"Ah!
Stop, do not come forward."
She then asked for a little rice.
Upon receiving the rice, she scattered it, throwing it to the ground.
Looking at the rice,
it had all turned into genuine pearls.
Fāngpíng laughed and said:
"The Lady is still young after all.
I am old,
and no longer enjoy performing such clever transformations."
Fāngpíng said to the Cài family:
"I wish to bestow wine upon you all.
This wine comes from the celestial kitchen,
its flavor rich and strong.
It is not suitable for mortals to drink;
drinking it might rot your intestines.
Now I shall dilute it with water.
Do not be surprised."
He then took one shēng of wine,
mixed it with one dǒu of water and stirred it,
