and gave the Cài family about one shēng to drink.
After a long while, the wine was finished.
Fāngpíng said to his attendants:
"It is not worth fetching from afar.
Take a thousand coins and send word to the old woman of Yúháng,
asking her to buy wine."
In a moment, the messenger returned,
obtaining an oilskin bag of wine,
about five dǒu.
The messenger relayed the old woman of Yúháng's reply:
"I fear the wine of the mortal world is not fit for your esteemed self to drink."
Also, Mágū had bird-like claws.
When Cài Jīng saw them,
he thought to himself:
"When my back itches terribly,
getting these claws to scratch my back
would surely be wonderful."
Fāngpíng already knew what Cài Jīng was thinking,
and immediately had someone seize Jīng and whip him.
He said to him:
"Mágū is a divine being.
How could you think her claws could be used to scratch your back?"
Only the whip striking Jīng's back was seen,
with no one seen holding the whip.
Fāngpíng told Jīng:
"My whip is not to be received lightly."
On that day,
he also bestowed a talisman upon Cài Jīng's neighbor, Captain Chén,
enabling him to summon demons and spirits with proclamations,
and to heal people and cure illnesses.
Cài Jīng also obtained the method of liberation through molting,
like a cicada shedding its skin.
Jīng often accompanied Lord Wáng on journeys through mountains and seas.
Sometimes he would briefly return home.
Lord Wáng also had letters for Captain Chén,
mostly in seal script,
or sometimes in regular script characters,
spacious and large.
Captain Chén treasured them for generations.
When the banquet concluded,
Fāngpíng and Mágū ordered their carriage and ascended to the heavens and departed,
with panpipes, drums, and attendants along the way as before.
From "Biographies of Immortals"
Xuánsú's Wife
The woman of the Héjiān King is
the wife of Xuánsú.
Xuánsú attained the Way of divine immortality,
and had resided in Héjiān for several hundred years.
The villagers said they often saw him,
and at midday he cast no shadow.
He only consumed bādòu and yúnmǔ,
and also sold them in the marketplaces.
Seven pills cost one coin,
and they could cure a hundred ailments.
The King of Héjiān fell ill,
bought and took the medicine,
and expelled over ten snake-like creatures.
When asked about the principle of his medicine,
he replied:
"The reason for Your Majesty's illness
is due to calamities remaining from six generations past,
and not something you brought upon yourself.
Your Majesty once released a nursing deer,
which was the mother of a qílín.
This benevolent heart moved Heaven,
and thus you were fated to encounter me."
An old retainer of the king's household said:
"I have heard my parents say
that Xuánsú casts no shadow at midday."
The king summoned him to see, and it was indeed true.
The king's daughter had abstained from meat and blood since childhood.
She was pure and fond of the Way.
The king gave this daughter to him in marriage.
After living there for several years,
he entered Chángshān Mountain with the woman.
There were those who saw them at times.
From "Biographies of Female Immortals".
Yángdū Woman
was the daughter of a tavern keeper in Yángdū City.
She was born with unusual features:
her eyebrows were joined,
and her ears were slender and long.
The crowd considered her strange,
and suspected she was a celestial being.
At that time, there was an immortal of Hēishān Mountain named Dúzi,
a native of Yè.
He often dwelt on Hēishān Mountain,
gathering and consuming pine seeds and fúlíng.
He had done so for several hundred years,
and no one knew his real name.
He often rode a calf,
so people of the time called him Dúzi (Calf).
At times he was robust, at times old;
at times ugly, at times beautiful.
He came and went to Yángdū.
The tavern keeper's daughter took a liking to him,
and so she attended upon him.
One day, the woman followed Dúzi out to pick peaches.
They returned after one night,
having obtained many peaches.
They were sweet and delicious, still attached to their leaves,
different from ordinary peaches.
The townspeople waited for them to leave.
Once they had gone out the gate,
the two together pulled the calf's ears and ran off.
Their speed was like flying,
and people could not catch up.
Thus they came and went.
They returned to the marketplace for several more decades,
and then husband and wife both departed.
Later, they were seen below Pānshān Mountain,
selling peaches and dates in winter.
From "Records of the Immortals of the Walled City".
Lady Sūn
was the wife of the Celestial Master of the Three Heavens, Zhāng Dàolíng.
They lived in seclusion together on Lónghǔ Mountain,
cultivating the Way of Silent Audience to the Three Primes for many years,
and repeatedly experienced spiritual responses.
At that time, the Celestial Master obtained the technique of the Yellow Emperor's Dragon-Tiger Inner Elixir.
When the elixir was completed and he ingested it,
he could divide his form and scatter his shadow,
sitting here while standing there, appearing and vanishing.
The Celestial Master entered Sōnggāo Mountain
("Pān" in the original text, corrected to "Sōng" according to "Records of the Immortals of the Walled City")
from Póyáng,
and obtained the esoteric text "Art of Controlling Fate",
enabling him to summon and command ghosts and spirits.
At that time, the land within the seas was in turmoil,
and those in positions of power were often in peril.
Moreover, the Great Way was in decline,
insufficient to save the endangered and assist the world.
He began cultivating the Dao only at the age of fifty.
By the time his elixir was completed,
over twenty more years had passed.
Once his arts and techniques were refined and wondrous,
he entered Shǔ,
traveled to various famous mountains,
and personally led by example in teaching the Way.
Lady Sūn cultivated her authenticity in the region south of the Yangtze,
and the transformation through the Dao flourished greatly.
In the first year of Yǒngjiā, yǐyǒu, of the Hàn Emperor Huán
(Note: "Emperor Huán" is suspected to be an error for "Emperor Chōng")
, she arrived in Shǔ,
dwelling at Yángpíng Sanctuary,
refining the Golden Liquid and Reverted Elixir.
Following the method of the Yellow Emperor bestowed by the Supreme Unity Lordless Sovereign,
after many years the elixir was completed,
enabling her to transform her form and soar in metamorphosis,
capable of all things.
In the second year of Yǒngshòu, bǐngshēn, of Emperor Huán,
on the ninth day of the ninth month,
she and the Celestial Master, at Làngzhōng Yúntái Sanctuary,
ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
Her rank became Supreme Perfected, Lady of the Eastern Peak.
Her son Héng,
courtesy name Língzhēn,
continued the aspiration, cultivating and refining,
and was known in the world as the Heir Master.
In the second year of Guānghé of Emperor Líng,
the year jǐwèi,
on the twenty-third day of the first month,
at Yángpíng Sanctuary,
he ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
Her grandson Lǔ,
courtesy name Gōngqī,
was known in the world as the Heir Master.
When the Hàn dynasty's fortune was declining,
and the Central Plains were in chaos,
he served as Governor of Liáng and Yì Provinces,
General Who Guards the South,
governing from Hànzhōng.
Emperor Wèi Tàizǔ carried out Emperor Líng's command,
and bestowed upon him additional ranks and emoluments.
Soon after, when Liú Zhāng lost Shǔ,
and the First Ruler of Shǔ raised troops,
Gōngqī transformed and returned to authenticity,
vanishing into hidden shadows and departing.
Initially,
when Lady Sūn resided in the sanctuary,
people from near and far revered and served her,
and those paying respects and visiting were as numerous as a market crowd.
She then transformed a spring at the mountain's foot,
so that those coming to pay respects
could wash and cleanse themselves with its water
before then approaching the Daoist quietude.
It was called the Water for Dispelling Defilement,
and it remains there to this day.
The mountain has three tiers,
symbolizing the Three Realms.
In front there is the Báiyáng Pool,
which is where the Supreme Venerable Sovereign Lǎojūn roamed and feasted.
Behind there is the Dēngzhēn Cave,
connected to the cave abodes of Qīngchéng, Éméi, Qīngyīshān, and Xīxuánshān Mountains,
thus making it the foremost of the twenty-four sanctuaries.
From "Biographies of Female Immortals".
Lady Fán
Lady Fán was
the wife of Liú Gāng.
Gāng served as the magistrate of Shàngyú,
possessed the Way's arts,
could summon ghosts and spirits with written proclamations,
and was skilled in the arts of prohibition and transformation.
He also practiced cultivation in secret,
so no one knew of it.
His governance emphasized purity, tranquility, simplicity, and ease,
yet his decrees and orders were widely implemented,
and the people benefited from them.
There were no disasters from floods, droughts, epidemics, poisons, or violent attacks,
and the harvests were bountiful year after year.
In his leisure time,
he often competed with his wife in the use of their arts.
Once, both sitting in the hall,
Gāng created a fire to burn a guest's mill house;
it started from the east,
but Lady Fán prohibited it, and it immediately extinguished.
In the courtyard were two peach trees;
husband and wife each chanted over one,
making them fight and strike each other.
After a long while,
the one Gāng chanted over was inferior
"如" originally written as "知".
Changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
and repeatedly walked out beyond the fence.
Gāng spat into a plate,
and it turned into a carp.
Lady Fán spat into a plate, and it turned into an otter,
which ate the fish.
When Gāng and Lady Fán entered Sìmíng Mountain,
their path was blocked by a tiger.
Gāng prohibited it,
and the tiger crouched, not daring to move.
Just as he was about to pass,
the tiger immediately killed him.
Lady Fán walked straight forward;
the tiger immediately faced the ground,
not daring to look up.
Lady Fán tied the tiger to the bedpost with a rope.
Whenever Gāng competed with her in arts,
he lost in every matter.
When they were about to ascend to heaven,
beside the county office was a large honey locust tree.
Gāng climbed the tree several zhang high,
before he could fly up.
Lady Fán sat upright,
and slowly rose like a cloud of qi,
ascending to heaven together with him.
Later, during the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
in Xiāngtán, there was an old woman.
She did not speak of her surname or given name,
but was called the Xiāngtán old woman.
She often stayed in people's houses
for over ten years.
She often used cinnabar seal script characters to cure illnesses among the villagers,
and none failed to respond.
The villagers revered her
and built
The character "搆" originally had the two characters "御名" below it.
Originally a note from the Sòng dynasty to avoid the personal name of Emperor Gāozōng.
Now deleted
several splendid rooms to serve the old woman.
The old woman said:
"Not so.
Just a simple house of earth and wood
is my wish."
The old woman's hair was dark as clouds,
her skin plump and pure as snow.
Leaning on a staff and dragging her shoes,
she could travel several hundred lǐ a day.
Suddenly, she met a village girl
named Xiāoyáo.
Sixteen years old,
beautiful and charming,
she carried a basket to gather chrysanthemums.
Meeting the old woman, she stared,
unable to move her feet.
The old woman looked at her and said:
"Do you love me?
Would you come with me to my dwelling?"
Xiāoyáo happily threw down her basket,
straightened her sleeves, called herself a disciple,
and followed the old woman to her room.
Her parents ran after her,
struck her with a staff,
and scolded her to return home.
Xiāoyáo's resolve grew firmer;
secretly, she sought to hang herself.
Relatives and friends urged her parents,
asking them to let her go.
Seeing they could not control her,
they finally let her be.
She went again to the old woman,
only sweeping dust, fetching water,
burning incense, and reading Daoist scriptures.
Over a month later,
the old woman told the villagers:
"I am indeed going to Luófú for a while.
Lock the door,
and be careful not to open it."
The villagers asked where Xiāoyáo was going.
She said:
"She has gone ahead."
Thus, for three years,
people only peeked from outside the door,
seeing small pines and sprouting bamboo shoots growing in clusters on the steps.
When the old woman returned,
she called the villagers to open the lock together.
They saw Xiāoyáo sitting dazed in the room,
her appearance as usual,
only her straw sandals were strung on bamboo tips between the beams.
The old woman then tapped the ground with her staff and said:
"I have arrived;
you may awaken."
Xiāoyáo awoke as if from sleep,
and just as she rose,
about to bow,
suddenly her left foot fell off,
as if severed onto the ground.
The old woman quickly told her not to move,
picked up the foot, aligned it with the knee,
sprayed water on it,
and it became as before.
The villagers were greatly astonished,
revered her as a deity,
and from several hundred lǐ around, they all submitted to her.
The old woman's appearance was very composed,
and she did not like many people recognizing her.
Suddenly, she told the villagers:
"I wish to go to Dòngtíng to save over a hundred lives.
Who is willing to prepare a boat for me?
In a day or two, you may watch together."
There was a villager named Zhāng Gǒng whose family was wealthy.
He requested to prepare a boat and oars,
and personally sailed to escort her.
The day before reaching Dòngtíng,
there was a great storm and waves,
which capsized a large boat,
sinking and shattering on Jūnshān Island.
It carried several dozen families,
nearly over a hundred people,
yet they were not injured.
No boats came to rescue them,
and they scattered to live on the island.
Suddenly, there was a white alligator,
over a zhang long,
swimming on the sand.
Several dozen people blocked and beat it to death,
dividing and eating its flesh.
The next day,
a city like snow
encircled the island,
and the people could not discern what it was.
The city gradually narrowed and tightened,
and the people on the island panicked, terrified, and screamed.
Their bags and sacks were all ground to powder,
and they were bundled together into a cluster.
Its width was no more than a few zhàng,
and they could not climb it,
the situation already critical.
The people of Yuèyáng
also saw the snow city from afar,
but could not understand it.
At that time, the old woman's boat had already reached the shore.
The old woman then ascended the island,
brandished her sword and paced the Dipper,
sprayed water, flew her sword, and stabbed it.
The white city made a sound like thunder,
and the city then collapsed.
It was a huge white alligator,
over ten zhàng long,
writhing and dying,
with the sword standing in its chest.
Thus, she saved the lives of over a hundred people.
Otherwise,
in a moment, they would have been bound into flesh and blood.
The people on the island
gratefully wept and bowed in thanks.
She ordered Gǒng's boat to return to Xiāngtán,
but Gǒng could not bear to leave immediately.
Suddenly, a Daoist priest met the old woman and said:
"Lady Fán, where have you been all this time?"
They were very pleased to see each other.
Gǒng questioned him,
and the Daoist priest said:
"She is Lady Fán,
the wife of Perfected Lord Liú Gāng."
Later, people realized the old woman was Lady Fán.
Gǒng then returned to Xiāngtán.
Later, the old woman and Xiāoyáo simultaneously returned to their true forms.
From "Biographies of Female Immortals."
Dōnglíng Shèngmǔ,
was a native of Hǎilíng in Guǎnglíng.
She married into the Dù family,
and studied the Dao under Master Liú Gāng.
She could alter her form and transform,
appearing and disappearing unpredictably.
Her husband Dù did not believe in the Dao,
and often grew angry with her.
When Shèngmǔ treated illnesses and saved people,
or went somewhere to do so,
Dù became even more resentful.
He brought a lawsuit against her to the authorities,
saying:
"Shèngmǔ is a wicked sorceress,
who neglects household duties."
The officials arrested Shèngmǔ and imprisoned her.
Shortly after,
she flew out from the prison window.
The crowd saw her,
ascending higher into the clouds,
leaving behind a pair of her shoes beneath the window.
Thereupon, people near and far established temples to make offerings to her.
When the people served and worshipped her,
their prayers were immediately answered.
There was often a blue bird at the place of sacrifice.
If someone lost something,
and begged to know its whereabouts,
the blue bird would immediately fly and alight upon the thief.
No one would pick up lost items on the road.
As time passed,
this also ceased to happen.
To this day, within Hǎilíng County, no one dares commit theft or wicked deeds.
For major offenses, they are drowned by wind and waves,
or killed by tigers and wolves;
for minor ones, they fall ill again.
From *Nǚxiān Zhuàn*.
Hǎo Gū
The Temple of Hǎo Gū is located forty-five *li* northwest of Mò County in Mò Prefecture.
Folklore says
that Hǎo Gū, styled Nǚjūn,
was originally from Tàiyuán,
but later lived in this district.
During the Qīnglóng era of the Wèi dynasty,
she and ten neighboring girls
were picking vegetables by the Ōutíxiè River.
Suddenly, three blue-clad youths
came before Nǚjūn and said:
"The Duke of the Eastern Sea wishes to take you as his wife."
Having spoken,
they spread a mat upon the water,
and walking and sitting upon it,
it was as if on dry land.
The blue-clad youths then attended at her side,
and they drifted downstream.
The neighboring girls ran to tell her family,
who went to look,
but could not find her.
Nǚjūn called from afar:
"I am fortunate to become a water immortal;
please do not worry or fear."
She also said that every fourth month,
she would send knife fish as a token.
From ancient times until now,
within the fourth month each year,
many knife fish come upstream.
The villagers always pray in the fourth month.
If prefectural or county officials visit this temple,
they must bow first before entering.
Before the temple, a piece of bluish-white stone suddenly appeared,
measuring over three feet in length and width,
and over two feet in height.
An old inscription says:
"This is Gū's husband's mounting stone." It remains there to this day.
From *Mòzhōu Tújīng*.
Zhāng Yùlán
Zhāng Yùlán
was the granddaughter of the Celestial Master
and the daughter of Língzhēn.
From childhood, she was pure and austere,
and did not eat meat or blood.
At the age of seventeen,
she dreamed of red light descending from the heavens.
Within the light were seal-script characters in gold,
coiling for several tens of feet,
and they entered her mouth with the light.
Upon waking, she felt uneasy,
and subsequently became pregnant.
Her mother reproached her,
but she never spoke of her dream,
only her maidservant knew.
One day, she said to the maidservant:
"I cannot bear this shame and live.
After I die, cut open my belly
to prove my heart."
That evening, she died without illness.
The maidservant reported the matter.
Her mother, not wishing to disobey,
hoped to clear her doubts.
Suddenly, something like a lotus flower
burst forth from her abdomen.
Opening it,
they found ten scrolls of the *Běnjì Jīng* in plain gold script,
on plain silk about two *zhang* long.
Each scroll was six or seven inches wide.
The writing was exquisite and marvelous,
surely not the work of human hands.
For ten months after Yùlán's death,
a strange fragrance often lingered.
They then copied the scripture and buried Yùlán.
Over a hundred days later,
there was a great storm with thunder and rain.
Heaven and earth grew dark,
and the scripture was lost.
The tomb where Yùlán lay opened by itself,
the coffin lid flew onto a large tree.
Looking inside,
it was an empty coffin.
Her tomb is now in Yìzhōu,
at the Nǚláng Temple in Wēnjiāng County.
The ninth day of the third month is the day Yùlán ascended to heaven.
To this day, the villagers often hold vegetarian feasts to sacrifice to her.
Língzhēn was the son of the Celestial Master,
named Héng,
styled the Successor Master.
On the twenty-third day of the first month in the second year of the Guānghé era of Emperor Líng of Hàn (179 CE),
he ascended to heaven in broad daylight at Yángpíng Abbey.
Yùlán produced the scripture and attained the Dao,
which should have been after Língzhēn's ascension,
during the turbulent era of the Three Kingdoms.
From *Chuánxiān Lù*.
Wáng Miàoxiǎng
was a female Daoist from Cāngwú.
She practiced grain avoidance and ingested qi,
dwelling by the water next to Huángtíng Abbey.
Morning and evening, with utmost sincerity,
she focused her thoughts on the cinnabar field,
thereby achieving spiritual communion.
Every month on the first day,
there were often extraordinary phenomena of light, clouds, and unusual sights;
the layered peaks and secluded valleys
were places people rarely reached.
Miàoxiǎng never spoke of this to anyone.
This continued for over a year.
Then, on the first day of a month, music suddenly appeared,
distant in mid-air,
lingering without descending,
and after a while, it dispersed.
Another year passed,
when suddenly an intense, fragrant spiritual aroma arose,
auspicious clouds filled the courtyard,
and the sound of celestial music
shook the forests and valleys.
Light illuminated the altar hall,
as bright as ten suns.
The sky took on hues of gold and jade,
dazzling and blinding,
making it impossible to look directly.
After a moment,
thousands upon thousands of chariots and riders
descended from the sky,
all mounted on qílín, phoenixes, dragons, cranes, and celestial steeds.
The entourage of figures and ceremonial guards numbered in the thousands;
each person was over ten feet tall,
holding halberds, spears, weapons, and staffs,
with banners, pennants, and canopies.
After a long while,
came a crane-canopied phoenix carriage,
leading a carriage drawn by nine dragons,
which descended before the altar.
There was one person in feathered robes and a jeweled crown,
wearing a sword and trailing his shoes,
who ascended the hall and sat down.
His body radiated a brilliant five-colored light,
and he was attended by several hundred immortals.
Miàoxiǎng immediately went forward to see and pay respects.
The Great Immortal said to Miàoxiǎng:
"I am none other than Emperor Shùn.
In the past, weary from governing the myriad states,
I cultivated the Way in this mountain.
I have always wished to guide and teach later generations,
to show the world that the Way can be taught to anyone.
Moreover, the great Way lies within,
not without;
the Way is in oneself,
not in others.
As the Xuán Jīng says: 'Cultivate it in yourself,
and your virtue will be complete.'
This means cultivation is your own affair;
achieving immortality and becoming a perfected being
cannot be accomplished by others.
I observed the report from the earthly administration
that you have been on this mountain for over thirty years,
consistent from beginning to end,
upholding the Way without deviation,
maintaining pure thoughts and spirit,
and adhering to the mysterious precepts.
You have reached the utmost.
If one achieves no realization,
it is because the Way has abandoned that person.
The Xuán Jīng states:
'Constantly excel at saving things,
and abandon nothing.'
The Way bestows its grace universally,
wishing for all things to achieve completion,
and all people to attain deliverance.
However, worldly people have meager blessings and fruits,
their Dao-qi is shallow and floating;
they cannot devote themselves wholeheartedly to the Way.
Even if they undertake some cultivation,
they are not diligent or persistent.
Before the Dao-qi responds,
they already grow weary and slack.
Thus, people abandon the Way themselves;
it is not the Way that abandons them.
Your sincerity and dedication are singular and utmost,
spanning a hundred lives, a thousand lives.
Hoping for that to which you are devoted,
without weariness or retreat,
is deeply pitiable and commendable.
In the past, I encountered Tàishàng Lǎojūn,
who showed me the Dàodé Zhēnjīng,
for governing the state and cultivating the self,
delivering people and spreading teachings.

This can also span heaven and earth, fill the cosmos, penetrate the nine heavens, permeate the myriad things, serving as the essence of transformative practice and the foundation of cultivation and realization,
beyond what can be fully expressed by analogy or words.
I have always engraved it in my heart,
disseminated it among beings,
broadly transforming and aiding customs,
not daring for a moment to be negligent or remiss.
To this day, I receive and follow my master's teachings,
a treasure for all kalpas.
But in the mundane world, many are frivolous, deceitful, deluded, and mistaken;
they ridicule those who embody humble light,
considering them cowardly;
they belittle the path of withdrawing from the world,
considering it impractical and inferior;
they laugh at the principle of rejecting sageliness and discarding wisdom,
considering it absurd;
they scorn the words of renouncing benevolence and righteousness,
considering them harsh and extreme.
This is because the deluded common people do not understand.
The intention of the mysterious sages
is to return to simplicity and purity, to honor the Way and reject falsehood.
Once crooked paths are removed,
the ultimate Way naturally manifests;
once simplicity and purity are established,
superficial competition naturally fades away.
Then, the need for restrictive measures becomes unnecessary,
the compassion of universal love finds no place to apply,
the brilliance of sagely wisdom finds no use,
and clever, deceptive strategies find no way to proceed.
All under heaven merges into one,
returning to great harmony.
This is the great intention of the mysterious sages.
Alas, the mundane world is frivolous and false;
people rush toward extravagance and cunning.
If rulers cannot govern with tranquility,
then myriad affairs become entangled and chaotic;
if the transformation of the Way cannot proceed smoothly,
then the hundred schools of thought contend and compete.
Thus it is said:
People have been deluding themselves
for a long time indeed.
If one can cleanse the heart and purify the self,
cultivate oneself alone,
able to take the ultimate Way as teacher and resource,
and longevity as the ultimate goal,
even such a person is hard to find.
Because of your diligent and earnest cultivation,
I have come briefly to visit you.
Your innate bone structure and inherent endowment—
what further doubt could there be?
You will certainly attain it.
In the past, when I was among the common people,
still young in years,
I suddenly felt Tàishàng Dàdàojūn descend into my secluded chamber,
teaching me the way of cultivating the self
and the essentials of governing the state.
He had me close my eyes and sit peacefully,
then gradually rise through the air,
reaching a southern land called Yángzhōu.
Above, it aligned with the Ox and Dipper constellations;
below, it overlooked the Huái marshes.
Entering the Gate of Ten Dragons,
floating on the Zhāohuí River,
at the ferry of the Gourd Melon,
I found a water source named Fāngshān,
each side spanning a thousand li.
Within were jade walls and jade-gemmed towers:
this is the Jiǔyí Mountains.
The mountain has nine peaks;
each peak has one river.
Nine rivers flow separately below,
pouring into the six directions,
cycling and returning to the beginning,
flowing upward here
to fill the Heavenly River.
Thus, the nine rivers originate from this mountain.
Flowing up and down,
circulating throughout the four seas,
I was made to guide the nine provinces and open the eight regions,
and credit was attributed to this mountain.
The mountain has three palaces:
first, the Palace of the Celestial Emperor;
second, the Zǐwēi Palace;
third, the Qīngyuán Palace.
As my allotted time in the world passed,
I returned to govern this mountain,
residing above in Zǐwēi,
and stabilizing below here.
Constantly using the way of long vision and non-action,
I appoint celestial officials
to teach below to people.
Now, the exalted sages of the various heavens,
the high perfected and great immortals,
pity that kalpas and eras are not constant,
that fortunes shift and flow,
that yin and yang alternate and hide,
that life and death push and change.
In a brief moment,
people encounter the meetings of yángjiǔ and bǎiliù calamities.
Diligently, they teach below,
to save people,
even more urgently than worldly people seek the Way.
Worldly people seek the Way
halfheartedly, sometimes earnest, sometimes neglectful;
tying their thoughts and focusing their minds,
not one in a million is diligent and persistent.
The celestial beings pity the common folk,
I often dwell among mortals,
concealing my form and transforming my appearance,
enlightening people according to their circumstances,
yet among thousands, not a single one is teachable.
As the ancient saying goes:
"If one cultivates the Way as diligently at the end as at the beginning,
the attainment of the Way will be abundant."
Most are diligent at first but become lazy midway,
abandoning all their previous efforts.
How could the Way ever fail people?
You must spread my teachings,
widely enlightening and awakening others.
Within this mountain, the nine peaks
all contain palaces and halls,
each governed by true officials.
Below them lie precious jades, the five metals, numinous mushrooms, divine herbs, medicines guarded by the Three Heavens, and scriptures preserved by the Supreme Elder.
Some are hidden in stone chambers, cave platforms, cloud-covered cliffs, or nestled valleys.
Thus, there are also spiritual overseers in charge,
with giant serpents and fierce beasts,
flying snakes and venomous dragons,
serving as guardians.
The first peak is called Cháng'ān Peak,
the second Wànnián Peak,
the third Zōngzhèng Peak,
the fourth Dàlǐ Peak,
the fifth Tiānbǎo Peak,
the sixth Guǎngdé Peak,
the seventh Yíchūn Peak,
the eighth Yíchéng Peak,
and the ninth Xínghuà Peak.
Below them are palaces and towers,
each serving as a governing center.
The nine waters are:
first, Yínhuā Water,
second, Fùshū Water,
third, Cháo Water,
fourth, Xǔ Spring,
fifth, Guī Water,
sixth, Shā Water,
seventh, Jīnhuā Water,
eighth, Yǒng'ān Water,
and ninth, Jìn Water.
These nine waters branch out to the four seas,
irrigating endlessly.
Within the mountain, there are rare beasts and precious birds,
with nothing lacking,
and no venomous, stinging, or predatory creatures.
Here, one can transcend the mundane world,
nourish life,
cultivate the Way,
and ascend to perfection.
Since you have resided in this mountain,
you have never wandered to its four borders,
brushed your garments beyond the dust,
gazed afar into the empty azure,
or looked down upon the layered peaks.
Naturally, you could not have known these things.
I shall guide you,
so you must strive and cultivate diligently,
until you can ride the light and command the void,
and then reflect upon the origins and ends."
Thereupon, he ordered an attendant
to bestow upon her the two scriptures of the Dàodéjīng and the Zhùjǐng Língwán pills before departing.
In this manner, he would descend upon Huángtíng Temple once every year or every three to five years.
Ten years later,
Miàoxiǎng ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
This mountain was where Shùn cultivated the Way,
hence it was called Dàozhōu Yíngdào County.
From the Jíxiān Lù
Chénggōng Zhìqióng
In the state of Wèi, there was a clerk named Xián Chāo from Jìběi Commandery,
whose courtesy name was Yìqǐ.
One evening during the Jiāpíng era, while sleeping alone,
he dreamed that a divine maiden came to him,
claiming to be the Jade Maiden from heaven,
a native of Dōngjùn,
with the surname Chénggōng,
and the courtesy name Zhìqióng.
She had lost her parents early.
The Lord of Heaven pitied her loneliness and hardship,
and allowed her to descend and marry.
While Xián Chāo was dreaming,
his spirit was keenly aware,
and he marveled at her extraordinary beauty,
waking with admiration and longing.
This happened for three or four nights.
One day, she appeared in person,
riding in a covered carriage,
accompanied by eight maidservants.
She wore robes of silk and gauze,
her appearance and countenance
were like that of a flying immortal.
She said she was seventy years old,
but looked like fifteen or sixteen.
In the carriage were jugs and vessels,
pure white and translucent like glass,
containing rare and exotic food and drink,
with sweet wine and delicacies,
which she shared with Xián Chāo.
She said to him:
"I am the Jade Maiden from heaven,
sent down to marry,
so I have come to be with you.
It is due to a connection from past lives and the workings of fate
that we should become husband and wife.
I cannot bring you great benefit,
nor can I cause you harm.
However, you will always be able to ride in light carriages and on fat horses,
and your meals will always include rare and exotic delicacies.
Silks and fine fabrics will be plentiful and never lacking.
But as I am a divine being,
I cannot bear you children,
nor do I possess a jealous nature,
so I will not hinder your marital obligations."
Thus they became husband and wife.
She presented him with a poem, which read:
"Drifting and floating, meeting by chance,
Soaring among clouds and rocks, nourished.
The orchid's essence needs no watering,
For supreme virtue aligns with the times.
How could the immortals descend in vain?
They come in response to fate to assist.
Accept me, and glorify your five clans;
Reject me, and bring disaster upon yourself."
This is the general meaning of the poem;
its text contained over two hundred characters,
which cannot be fully recorded here.
She also composed seven volumes on the *Yìjīng*,
containing hexagrams and images,
with commentaries attached to the judgments.
Thus, its written explanations
contained both moral principles
and could be used for divining fortune and misfortune,
much like Yáng Zǐ's *Tàixuán*
or the Xuē family's *Zhōngjīng*.
Xián Chāo was able to grasp their meaning fully
and used them for divination.
After seven or eight years,
when Xián Chāo's parents arranged a marriage for him,
she would share days for feasting
and nights for resting separately,
coming at night and leaving at dawn,
swift as flight.
Only Xián Chāo could see her;
others could not.
Whenever Xián Chāo had to travel
(the original text had "yǒng" for "lái,"
amended to "lái" based on the Ming manuscript copy
Zhìqióng would already have the carriage ready at the gate.
A hundred lǐ would take no more than two hours,
and a thousand lǐ no more than half a day.
Later, Xián Chāo served as a clerk under the Prince of Jìběi.
When Wén Qīn rebelled,
and Emperor Míng of Wèi marched east to suppress it,
the princes were relocated to the Yè palace,
and their officials followed the supervising prince westward.
The accommodations in Yè were cramped,
with four clerks sharing one small room.
Xián Chāo slept alone,
and Zhìqióng could still come and go.
His roommates
grew quite suspicious of the unusual occurrences.
Zhìqióng could conceal her form,
but not her voice;
moreover, her fragrant scent
permeated the room,
leading his companions to suspect him.
Later, Xián Chāo was once sent to the capital on an errand,
and he entered the market empty-handed.
Zhìqióng provided him with five bolts of delicate red silk and five lengths of fine hemp cloth.
Their colors were radiant and lustrous,
unlike anything available in the Yè market.
When his fellow clerks inquired about the situation,
Xián Chāo, being straightforward and ineloquent,
told them everything.
The clerks reported it to the supervising prince,
who questioned him in detail,
fearing that such supernatural phenomena might exist in the world.
However, he did not reprimand or blame him.
That evening, when Xián Chāo returned,
the Jade Maiden asked to leave,
saying:
"I am an immortal being.
Although I have associated with you,
I did not wish others to know.
But you are too open and careless,
and now my true nature has been exposed.
I can no longer associate with you.
After years of companionship,
our bond of affection is not light.
To part suddenly like this,
how can it not be sorrowful?
But circumstances compel me to do so.
Let us each strive on our own."
She called her attendants to bring wine and food,
opened a chest,
and took out a woven skirt, a robe, and a double-layered vest to give to Xián Chāo.
She also presented him with another poem,
clasped his arm to bid farewell,
tears streaming down her face,
then solemnly ascended her carriage
and departed like a swift current.
Xián Chāo grieved for many days,
nearly to the point of exhaustion.
Five years after her departure,
Xián Chāo was sent by his commandery to Luòyáng.
When he reached the foot of Yúshān in Jìběi,
walking westward along the path,
he saw in the distance at a bend in the road
a horse-drawn carriage
that resembled Zhìqióng's.
He hurried forward,
and upon looking, it was indeed her.
They drew aside the curtain and met,
overwhelmed with both sorrow and joy.
She handed him the carriage strap, and they rode together to Luòyáng,
restoring their former relationship.
They were still together during the Tàikāng era,
though they did not meet daily.
On the third day of the third month,
the fifth day of the fifth month,
the seventh day of the seventh month,
the ninth day of the ninth month,
and the first and fifteenth of each month,
she would come,
staying overnight before leaving.
Zhāng Màoxiān composed a rhapsody titled *Shénnǚ* about her.
Its preface reads:
"There are many tales of immortals in the world,
but few are ever verified.
As for the case of the Xián family,
it is one that is credible and supported by evidence."
During the Gānlù era,
those traveling between the Hé and Jì regions and the capital
often spoke of this matter,
though many dismissed it as ghostly or demonic sorcery.
When I traveled to the eastern regions,
the discussions were abundant,
with different people giving the same account.
Still, considering them as vulgar commoners
fond of spreading false and exaggerated tales,
I simply regarded it as rumor,
without taking the time to verify it.
Later, I met Chief Clerk Liú of Jìběi,
a man of clear judgment and honest faith.
He had personally seen Yìqǐ,
heard his account,
read his writings,
and seen the clothing and gifts given to him.
These were certainly beyond the ability of an ordinary and untalented man like Yìqǐ to fabricate.
Moreover, upon inquiring among those around him who knew of it,
they said:
"When the divine maiden came,
we all smelled the fragrant scent and heard the sound of her voice."
This clearly shows it was not a case of Yìqǐ being deluded by dreams or fantasies.
Additionally, people saw that Yìqǐ was exceptionally robust,
walking through heavy rain in the marshes without getting wet,
which further astonished them.
When ghosts or demons approach humans,
they invariably cause weakness, illness, and emaciation.
Yet Yìqǐ remained safe and unharmed,
and even feasted, rested, and indulged in passions
and desires with a divine being.
How could this not be extraordinary!
From *Jíxiān Lù*
Páng Nǚ
Páng Nǚ (also written as Páng) was a woman who,
from a young age, did not eat,
and always admired purity and emptiness.
She often said:
"I shall ascend to heaven;
I do not wish to remain in this world."
Her parents thought these were just playful words.
Once, while traveling past Mount Dōngwǔ,
she suddenly saw immortals flying through the air, approaching,
from south to north,
about to cross a thousand li.
The girl stood upright,
not daring to advance.
The immortals also arrived at the mountaintop and did not disperse.
Immediately, they manifested a golden city with jade towers, jade palaces and pearl halls,
filling the entire mountaintop.
One person descended from the mountain,
his body radiating light of five colors.
He came before the girl
and summoned her to ascend into the palace complex.
Numerous immortals stood in rows,
their ceremonial guards solemn and orderly.
He said to her:
"You have the bone register;
you are destined to become a superior transcendent.
The Supreme Elder commands me to bestow upon you the Lingbao Chishu, the Five Sections of True Script.
Practice according to it,
and the time for your ascension will be set.
In the past, Ā Qiū and Empress Huángfēi
both reverently practiced this,
attaining the status of lofty transcendents.
How can you not be diligent?"
After receiving the True Script,
the host of immortals also vanished.
Ten years later,
she ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
The place where she encountered the heavenly transcendents, Mount Dōngwǔ,
is what is now called the Gēngchú Transformation.
Later, the Daoist priest Zhāng Fāng
also dwelt on this mountain,
residing in a stone chamber.
A red tiger often came and went outside the chamber.
Fāng was not afraid of it,
and he too attained the Dao and ascended to heaven.
(Note: Páng is also written with the character Páng.)
From the *Collected Records of Immortals*.
Bāo Nǚ
Bāo Nǚ was
a person from Hànzhōng.
She was a descendant of Lord Bāo,
and thus took Bāo as her surname.
She lived between the Hàn and Miǎn rivers.
From a young age, she loved the Dao,
serene and tranquil, without worldly pursuits.
After reaching adulthood (hair-pinning age),
while washing silk by the Jìn River,
amidst clouds, rain, and darkness,
she seemed to have been affected and became pregnant.
Her parents reproached her,
and she became ill from worry and distress.
On the verge of death, she said to her mother:
"After I die, when you bury me,
I wish to be taken to the top of the Western Mountains by ox-cart."
Having spoken, she died.
Her parents placed her in the cart,
but before they could harness the ox,
the cart moved by itself.
It crossed the Miǎn and Hàn rivers,
flowing straight across,
and went directly up to the summit of Mount Píngyuán at the mouth of the Jìn River.
Píngyuán is the Jìnkǒu Transformation.
Her family pursued it,
and saw only five-colored clouds like a canopy,
heavenly music filling the sky,
with banners, ceremonial guards, and attendants leading the way.
They saw the girl ascend to heaven and depart.
When they looked inside the cart,
there was only an empty coffin.
The local people erected a shrine to worship her,
and prayers to her for rain or clear weather were all answered.
To this day, the traces of two cart tracks remain on the mountaintop at Jìnkǒu.
Later, Chén Shì'ān also attained the Dao on this mountain
and ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
From the *Collected Records of Immortals*.
Lǐ Zhēnduō
Lǐ Zhēnduō was the younger sister of the transcendent Lǐ Tuō.
Tuō cultivated the Dao at the foot of Lóngqiáo Peak on Mount Jīntáng in Shǔ,
and the people of Shǔ saw him through successive generations.
Estimating his comings and goings spanned over eight hundred years,
hence he was called Lǐ Bābǎi (Li the Eight-Hundred).
Initially, during the time of King Mù of Zhōu,
he resided on Mount Qīxuán in Láiguǎnghàn,
completed the fusion of the Nine Splendors Elixir,
and wandered among the Five Peaks and Ten Grottoes,
for over two hundred years.
On the sea, he encountered Fēiyáng Jūn,
who taught him the methods of Water and Wood.
He returned to this mountain
and succeeded in refining the medicine.
After several more centuries had passed,
sometimes hidden, sometimes visible,
he wandered in marketplaces and courts.
He also ascended Lóngqiáo Peak
to make the Nine Tripod Golden Elixir.
The elixir was completed eight hundred years ago.
He studied the Dao three times on this mountain,
so people of the world called this mountain Sānxué Shān (Three Studies Mountain),
also called Xián Shān (Worthy Mountain),
likely because of the name Bābǎi (Eight-Hundred).
When the elixir was completed, he tested it
by smearing it on a cliff rock.
The stubborn stone turned into jade,
lustrous and glossy.
The place where he tested the medicine still exists today.
If anyone tried to chisel the cliff to take it,
wind and thunder would arise and cause disturbances.
Zhēnduō followed her elder brother in cultivating the Dao,
residing in Miánzhú.
Traces of ancient sites related to Zhēnduō still exist there today.
Sometimes she came and went by the side of Fú Shān,
now called the Zhēnduō Transformation,
which is the ancient Fú Shān Transformation.
It is like the Dìfèi (Earth's Lung) floating upon obtaining water.
Zhēnduō, from a young age, possessed a transcendent bearing
and was deeply devoted to profound principles.
Bābǎi taught her the essentials of the Morning Primordiality and Silent Chastity method.
Practicing it for several centuries,
her appearance remained like that of a twenty-year-old.
Her spirit and energy were dignified and solemn,
her bearing heroic and imposing,
different from the demeanor of a delicate woman.
When people saw her,
they dared not look directly at her.
Afterwards, the Supreme Elder Lord (Lǎojūn) and the Three Masters of Primordial Antiquity descended and guided her to transcendence,
bestowing upon her the method of ascension.
She ascended to heaven in broad daylight before Bābǎi did.
Beside the transformation site is a pool,
whose water is often red,
being the spring where ancient transcendents refined cinnabar.
Fú Shān is also called Mount Wàn'ān,
on which are the Two Masters' Wells.
Drinking from them cures illnesses.
Now, because of Zhēnduō's name,
it is called the Zhēnduō Transformation.
Bābǎi also, on Mount Xiānjū in Shífāng,
ascended to heaven in broad daylight on the eighth day of the third month.
From the *Collected Records of Immortals*.
Bān Mèng
Bān Mèng —
it is not known from where she came.
Some say she was a woman.
She could fly through the air for days,
could sit in empty space and converse with people,
and could also enter the earth.
When first entering, she would sink up to her chest,
gradually going deeper,
until only her cap and headscarf remained visible,
and after a long while, she would completely disappear from sight.
By pointing her finger at the ground,
she could create a well from which one could draw water.
Blowing on the tiles of a house's roof,
the tiles would fly into people's homes.
She could gather several thousand mulberry and fruit trees,
pulling them together into one pile
that accumulated like a mountain.
After more than ten days like this,
she would blow on them, and each would return to its original place as before.
She could also hold a mouthful of ink,
spread paper before her,
chew the ink and spray it out,
and it would all form written characters,
filling the entire sheet of paper,
each with its own meaning.
She ingested wine and elixirs,
and at four hundred years old, she became even younger.
She entered Mount Dàyě.
From the *Biographies of Divine Transcendents*.
The Two Maidens of Tiāntāi
Liú Chén and Ruǎn Zhào
went into Tiāntāi to gather herbs,
but went too far and could not return.
After thirteen days, they were starving.
Looking into the distance, they saw a peach tree on the mountain with ripe fruit,
so they climbed the perilous slope, pulling themselves up by vines, and reached the tree.
They ate several peaches,
and their hunger ceased, their bodies feeling full.
When they wished to descend the mountain,
they used a cup to fetch water,
and saw leaves of turnip flowing downstream,
looking very fresh and beautiful.
Then another cup floated down,
containing sesame rice.
They then said to each other:
"This means people are nearby."
So they crossed the mountain.
They came upon a large stream,
and by the stream were two women,
extremely beautiful in appearance.
Seeing the two men holding cups,
they smiled and said:
"Liú and Ruǎn, you two gentlemen have brought back our cups."
Liú and Ruǎn were startled.
The two women then joyfully acted as if they were old acquaintances,
saying:
"Why have you come so late?"
They then invited them back to their home.
On the south and east walls
"South and east walls" originally read "rain walls, east wall,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
The Huang edition reads "west wall, east wall."
each had crimson silk curtains,
with bells hanging from the curtain corners,
and gold and silver interwoven above.
Each had several maidservants to attend them.
Their meal consisted of sesame rice, dried goat meat, and beef,
all very delicious.
After eating, they served wine.
Soon a group of women came holding peaches,
laughing and saying:
"Congratulations on your grooms' arrival."
They drank merrily and made music.
After nightfall, each retired to a curtained bed to sleep,
and their gentle grace was extraordinary.
After ten days, they asked to return home,
but were earnestly kept for half a year.
The climate and vegetation
were always like springtime,
with hundreds of birds singing,
making them miss their homeland even more.
Their longing to return was very bitter.
The women then escorted them,
pointing out the way back.
Their hometown had declined and scattered,
and ten generations had already passed.
From "Records of Immortals."
The Ming manuscript cites "In Search of the Supernatural."
Lǔ Miàodiǎn
Lǔ Miàodiǎn
was a female Daoist official of Jiǔyí Mountain.
From birth, she was intelligent, wise, lofty, and pure,
not eating meat or drinking wine.
At over ten years old,
she said to her mother:
"Morning and evening, I smell the foulness of food,
and it often causes pain in my nose and head.
I wish to stop eating."
Her whole family pitied her.
She also learned the methods of breath cultivation and taking medicinal herbs.
After ten years of dwelling thus,
she often felt melancholy and unhappy.
So she said to her mother:
"The highest human lifespan
does not exceed a hundred and twenty years.
Sorrow and joy daily harm each other;
moreover, as a woman's body,
how can I further bury and obscure my chaste nature,
mixing with the common and vulgar?"
A Daoist priest from Lùchuáng passed by her,
and bestowed upon her the great cave scripture "Huángtíng Jīng,"
saying:
"The 'Huángtíng Jīng'
is a golden text from the palace of the Great Emperor of Fúsāng.
One who recites it ten thousand times
can become an immortal;
it only requires diligence and tirelessness.
The scripture says:
'Recite it ten thousand times and ascend to the triple heavens,
a thousand calamities vanish, all illnesses cured.
Fear not the ferocity of tigers and wolves,
and also repel old age, extending life forever.'
Dwelling alone in the mountains,
reciting it once,
is like having ten companions,
and one will have no fear.
Why?
This scripture summons all the spirits within the body,
clarifying and rectifying the spirit and energy.
When spirit and energy are rectified, external evils cannot interfere;
when all spirits are gathered, fear cannot reach.
If the form is whole and spirits gathered,
energy rectified and mind clear,
then one can see clearly a thousand miles away,
with not the slightest hidden.
The trouble is that people cannot know it,
or knowing it cannot cultivate it,
or cultivating it cannot refine it,
or refining it cannot persist.
Losing it midway,
abandoning previous efforts,
not only incurs the responsibility of the mysterious laws,
but also leads to drifting through life and death,
with endless bitter retribution."
Miàodiǎn received the precepts and accepted the scripture,
entered Jiǔyí Mountain,
and dwelt in caves in stillness and silence.
Repeatedly, demons tested her,
but she remained chaste and steadfast, unyielding.
After more than ten years,
a divine person spoke to her:
"This mountain was governed by the great Shùn,
the general overseer of heaven and earth, the ancestral master of the nine provinces.
In ancient times, there were lofty Daoist adepts
who made three deer-bed places,
which could shelter from wind and rain,
and house the form while nurturing chastity.
As the years passed,
they gradually all decayed and perished.
Now I make them for you,
so you can follow your nature and rest peacefully."
After another ten years,
true immortals descended,
bestowed upon her spiritual medicine,
and she ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
Initially,
when Miàodiǎn dwelt in the mountain,
there was no water on the peak.
A divine person transformed a stone basin,
three feet wide,
four feet long.
The basin always naturally had water,
inexhaustible in use.
There was also a large iron mortar,
also sent by the divine person,
its purpose unknown.
Both remain there now.
On the immortal altar stone,
clearly visible are the footprints of an immortal;
and
