an ancient mirror,
three feet wide;
a bell,
shaped like a reclining moon.
All were sent by the divine person,
and are items left behind when Miàodiǎn ascended to heaven.
They are now at Wúwéi Temple.
From "Records of Assembled Immortals."
Chén Mǔ
Yīng Mǔ,
surname Shèn,
courtesy name Yīng,
her origins are unknown.
During the Western Jìn dynasty,
she resided at the Huángtáng Temple in Dānyáng Commandery,
devoting herself to the cultivation of the supreme Dào.
People who saw her from childhood until old age
observed that her appearance never changed.
The masses called her Yīng Mǔ (Infant Mother).
Once, while entering the Wú market,
she saw a youth,
around fourteen or fifteen years old.
He approached and bowed before the mother, saying:
"I should become your son."
The mother said:
"Young one, where have you come from?
To bow and call me mother,
since we are not of the same kind,
is not in accordance with the great Dào."
The youth then departed.
Over a month later,
again in the Wú market, she encountered a three-year-old child,
crying sorrowfully and calling out.
Suddenly meeting Shèn Mǔ,
he grasped the hem of her robe and said:
"Where has my mother come from?"
The mother, pitying him, took him in and raised him,
caring for him more than if he were her own.
When he grew up,
he was intelligent, filial, and respectful,
different from ordinary people.
From the age of capping (around twenty),
his demeanor and spirit were outstanding and transcendent.
Where he lived, there were often unusual clouds and vapors,
with shimmering light and shadows,
and he would occasionally speak of matters pertaining to Pénglái and Làngyuàn.
The mother found him extraordinary,
and said to him:
"You and I are temporarily connected here.
By what title should you be called?"
The son said:
"In the past, I received a covenant and spiritual texts from the Celestial Truth,
was bestowed with a name and rank,
designated as the Filial Dào Luminous King.
Now it is fitting to address me as such."
He then taught his mother the secrets of cultivating perfection, saying:
"You must always seek high, mysterious terraces,
withdraw from and sever ties with heterodox factions,
cultivate leisure amidst hills and mounds,
nourish yourself in harmony with the yang harmony,
calmly pacify the mysterious garden,
and reflect upon and discard past faults.

Then the teachings of the Wúyīng Gōngzǐ, the Yellow Emperor and Lǎozi's 'Jade Book', the 'Perfected Scripture' of the Great Cavern, the Seven Primes of Huòluò, and the Concealed Mystery of the Supreme Elder can be attained.
Rest peacefully within the barrier of flowing rosy clouds,
gaze upon the terrace of Wénchāng.
One who attains this Dào,
will have nine phoenixes singing in unison,
the celestial registers startling the void,
soaring bodily, controlling the nodes,
entering the light, floating in the air,
with dragon chariots and tiger banners,
roaming freely through all eight directions.
Mother, you should treasure this."
One day,
the Filial Dào Luminous King silently vanished.
The mother secretly cultivated the Dào methods,
accumulating practice over several decades,
unknown to others.
Afterwards, Wú Měng and Xǔ Xùn traveled south from Gāoyáng,
visited the mother,
and requested transmission of the Dào she had obtained.
She then covenanted with them and bestowed it upon them.
The methods of Filial Dào
subsequently spread throughout the region south of the Yangtze.
In her leisure, she often told the two men:
"It is said in the world that in the past, I was Xùn's teacher.
Now, within the Jade Emperor's Mystical Registers,
Měng is the Censor,
while Xùn is the Luminous Ambassador,
overseeing the promotion of the five ranks of the immortal registers.
Furthermore, each governs one of the twelve earthly branches,
corresponding to the celestial fields of the twelve ancient states.
Xùn oversees the field of Xuánxiāo,
which corresponds to the branch zǐ;
Měng governs the domain of Xīngjì,
which corresponds to the branch chǒu.
Xǔ should reside above Wú,
in accordance with the descending hierarchy of the immortal ranks."
Several more years later,
a carriage of clouds and dragons arrived,
with thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of riders to welcome her,
and Shèn Mǔ ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
Now, forty lǐ east of Gāo'ān County in Hóngzhōu,
there is the Huángtáng Altar and Quietude,
which is the place where Lord Xǔ established a shrine to worship the Holy Mother.
The site of her ascension to heaven
is within Dānyáng Commandery.
Later, to avoid the taboo of Emperor Xuānzong of Táng's temple name,
the shrine in Zhōnglíng was named the Shèn Mǔ Shrine.
The methods of Filial Dào
differ slightly from those of the Língbǎo tradition.
The people of Yùzhāng have practiced them generation after generation.
From the 'Records of the Gathered Immortals of Yōngchéng'.
Xū Mǔ
Xū Mǔ
was a person from Yùzhāng.
Outwardly, she blended with the mundane world,
while inwardly, she cultivated the essential truths.
She often said:
"A thousand years ago,
I once lived on the Western Mountain.
When worldly burdens lessen somewhat,
I should return to authenticity there."
Her son's name was Liè,
courtesy name Dàowēi.
He lost his father young,
and was renowned for serving his mother with filial piety.
The family was poor,
yet he managed to provide delicious food for her,
never lacking,
and was praised by the village.
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of the Western Jìn dynasty,
Wú Měng and Xǔ Xùn from the same commandery,
through refined cultivation, achieved communion and resonance,
and the transformation of the Dào was widely propagated.
They resided on Hóngyá Mountain,
building an altar and establishing a quiet retreat.
After Wú Měng passed away,
Xǔ Xùn then used precious talismans and true registers to save the common people and rescue them from calamity.
People from near and far revered him.
Xùn served as a record-keeper in ? Prefecture,
and afterwards, he would return home on the first and fifteenth of each month to pay respects.
Some people saw him riding a dragon,
traveling back and forth with great speed,
as if covering only a short distance.
Lord Xū was sincere, honest, and loyal,
and Xùn entrusted him with duties.
He then built a thatched hut with his mother about eighty paces northeast of Xùn's residence,
serving him morning and night,
with diligence, willingness, reverence, and solemnity,
never showing negligence.
His mother often gathered flowers and fruits from the mountain,
to present to Lord Xǔ.
Lord Xǔ valued their sincere devotion,
and often wished to save and elevate them.
In the second year of Yuánkāng
("Kāng" originally written as "Qìng",
changed according to the 'Records of the Gathered Immortals of Yōngchéng')
, on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, rénzǐ year,
the Supreme Elder commanded the Jade Perfected Senior Lord Cuī Wénzǐ and the Supreme Mystery Perfected Elder Xiáqiū Zhòng,
to issue a decree summoning and appointing Lord Xǔ as the Luminous Ambassador and Chief of the Nine Provinces, the Overseer of All Immortals,
and he ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
Xǔ said to Dàowēi and his mother:
"I have received the command of the Great Emperor,
and cannot remain long.
You may follow the immortal carriage later,
with the hope of meeting on another day."
Mother and son were overwhelmed with grief,
bowed repeatedly and pleaded,
wishing to serve by the cloud-borne chariot.
Lord Xǔ granted their request,
immediately bestowing spiritual medicine for them to ingest,
and personally transmitted the true secrets to them.
Thereupon, at noon, they ascended to heaven following Lord Xǔ.
The altar and well remain to this day.
The villagers did not dare to embellish or decorate them lavishly,
due to Lord Xū and his mother's frugal and modest nature.
The world calls it the Xū Mǔ Well.
From the 'Records of the Gathered Immortals'.
Dù Lánxiāng
Dù Lánxiāng was a figure
encountered by a fisherman on the banks of the Xiāng River at Dòngtíng Lake.
Hearing the sound of a child crying,
he looked around but saw no one,
only a three-year-old girl by the shore.
The fisherman took pity on her and raised her.
When she was over ten years old,
her heavenly beauty was extraordinary,
her spiritual countenance radiant and exquisite,
truly like a celestial being.
Suddenly, a blue-robed spiritual being
descended from the sky
and came to their home,
taking the girl away.
As she ascended to heaven,
she said to her father:
"I am the celestial maiden Dù Lánxiāng,
who was banished to the mortal world for a transgression.
My time here is limited,
and now I must depart."
Afterward, she occasionally returned home.
Later, she descended to the home of Zhāng Shuò at Bāo Mountain in Dòngtíng,
who was a cultivator of the Dao.
Lánxiāng descended to him for three years,
teaching him the methods of ascension and transformation,
and Shuò also attained immortality.
When she first descended,
she left behind a jade tablet, a jade spittoon, and a red fire-washed cloth,
as tokens of her celestial visit.
One evening,
she ordered her attendant to present Shuò with a yellow-feathered cloak, crimson shoes, a black hat, crane-feather robes, and a red jade pendant, along with a sword,
which she bestowed upon Shuò,
saying:
"These are the garments of a high immortal,
not found in the cave heavens."
It is unknown what rank Zhāng Shuò attained as an immortal official.
The fisherman also grew old,
but then became increasingly youthful,
often abstaining from food.
He too studied the Dao along the rivers and lakes,
and his whereabouts became unknown.
From the "Records of Assembled Immortals" of Yōngchéng.
Báishuǐ Sùnǚ
Xiè Duān
was a native of Hòuguān in Jìn'ān.
He lost his parents at a young age,
had no relatives,
and was raised by neighbors.
By the age of seventeen or eighteen,
he was respectful and cautious,
never engaging in wrongdoing,
and began to live independently.
He had no wife,
and the villagers pitied him,
planning to find him a bride,
but without success.
Duān slept late and rose early,
toiling diligently in the fields,
never resting day or night.
Later, in the village, he found a large snail,
as big as a three-liter pot.
Considering it unusual,
he took it home
and kept it in a jar.
After more than ten days,
whenever Duān went to the fields early in the morning
and returned,
he found meals, soup, and a fire prepared in his home,
as if someone had done it.
Duān thought it was a kindness from his neighbors.
After several days of this,
Duān went to thank his neighbors.
The neighbors all said:
"We never did such a thing;
why thank us?"
Duān thought the neighbors did not understand his meaning,
but the occurrences continued repeatedly.
Later, he inquired earnestly,
and the neighbors laughed, saying:
"You must have taken a wife yourself,
secretly keeping her at home to cook,
and now you say we prepared your meals!"
Duān fell silent,
puzzled and unsure of the reason.
Later, he left at the first crow of the rooster,
but secretly returned early in the morning,
peeking into his home from outside the fence.
He saw a young maiden emerge from the jar,
go to the stove, and light the fire.
Duān then entered the house,
went straight to the jar to look at the snail,
but saw only the shell.
"Shell" originally read "maiden,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript.
He then went to the stove and asked her:
"Where have you come from, new bride,
to cook for me?"
The woman was flustered,
wanting to return to the jar,
but could not.
She replied:
"I am Báishuǐ Sùnǚ from the Heavenly River.
The Heavenly Emperor pitied you for being orphaned young,
yet respectful and cautious,
so he sent me temporarily to guard your home and cook.
Within ten years,
you would have become wealthy and found a wife,
and I would have returned.
But you secretly spied on me without reason,
and my form has been revealed.
It is no longer fitting for me to stay;
I must leave you now.
Though things will be somewhat harder afterward,
if you work diligently in the fields,
fish, gather, and manage your livelihood,
and keep this shell to store grain,
you will never lack."
Duān begged her to stay,
but she refused.
Suddenly, wind and rain arose,
and she vanished in an instant.
Duān set up a shrine for her,
offering sacrifices seasonally.
He lived in ample comfort,
though not in great wealth.
Then the villagers gave him a wife.
Duān later rose to become a magistrate.
This is the Sùnǚ of the Dao today.
From "Records of Searching for the Divine."
Cài Nǚxiān
Cài Nǚxiān
was a native of Xiāngyáng.
From a young age, she was clever and skilled,
excelling at embroidery,
praised by her neighbors.
Suddenly, an old man came to her door,
asking her to embroider a phoenix.
He said that on the day it was completed,
he would point out the eyes.
When the embroidery was finished,
it glowed with five-colored brilliance.
The old man examined it
and pointed to where the eyes should be placed.
Soon the work was done,
and the two phoenixes leaped up, dancing and flying.
The old man and the celestial maiden each mounted a phoenix
and ascended to heaven.
They occasionally descended on the trees of Nán Mountain in Xiāngyáng,
which the people of the time named Fènglín Mountain.
Later, Fènglín Pass was established there,
and on the side of Nán Mountain, there is a Phoenix Terrace.
An imperial decree established the Jìngzhēn Temple at her residence,
where a true image of the celestial maiden is preserved.
It is said she lived during the Jìn Dynasty.
From "Supplementary Records of Immortal Biographies."
Péng Qiú
West of Bèiqiū lies the Jade Maiden Mountain.
Legend has it that
during the Tàishǐ era of the Jìn dynasty,
Péng Qiú from Běihǎi,
courtesy name Bójiān,
entered the mountain to gather wood.
Suddenly, he noticed an extraordinary fragrance,
and so he followed the wind to the northern mountain.
There, he found a vast palace complex, lush and winding,
with towering pavilions and spacious terraces.
Péng Qiú entered the gate and peered inside,
seeing five jade trees;
advancing a bit further,
he saw four women,
of peerless grace and beauty,
playing chess together in the hall.
Upon seeing Péng Qiú, they all rose in surprise,
and said to him:
"Why has Lord Péng come here?"
Péng Qiú replied:
"I followed the fragrance and arrived."
They then resumed their game.
The youngest of them went upstairs to play the qín,
and those remaining at the game called out to her:
"Yuánhuī, why have you gone upstairs alone?"
Péng Qiú stood beneath the tree,
feeling somewhat hungry,
so he licked the dew dripping from the leaves.
Suddenly, a woman arrived riding a crane,
and angrily
"angrily"
originally written as "kindly."
Changed according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.
said:
"Yùhuá,
why do you have such a mundane person here?
The Queen Mother of the West immediately orders Wáng Fāngpíng to inspect the various immortal chambers."
Péng Qiú, frightened, went out the door,
and looking back,
everything had suddenly vanished.
When he returned home, it was already the Jiànpíng era,
and his old home and neighborhood
had all become ruins.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
The Female Taoist Priest of Zǐyún Temple
In the spring, second month of the twenty-fourth year of the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the emperor was in the Eastern Capital,
and appointed Lǐ Shìzhī as Governor of Hénán.
On that day, there was a great wind,
and a female Taoist priest rode the wind to Yùzhēn Temple,
alighting on the bell tower.
Those who came to see her crowded like a wall.
This was reported to the Governor.
The Governor was a rough and hasty man,
angered by the gathering crowd,
so he stripped her and caned her.
After ten strokes,
the wind-rider neither begged for mercy
nor showed any injury or harm,
her complexion unchanged.
At this, Shìzhī was greatly alarmed,
and only then did he treat her with courtesy, requesting to report the matter to the emperor.
An imperial edict summoned her into the inner palace,
and upon inquiring about her origins,
it was learned she was a female Taoist priest from Zǐyún Temple in Púzhōu.
She had long practiced grain abstention,
making her body light,
and thus rode the wind to fly here.
Emperor Xuánzōng was greatly awed and respectful,
bestowed gold and silk upon her,
and sent her back to Púzhōu.
Several years later,
again during a great wind,
she flew away and never returned.
From "Jì Wén"
The Woman from the Qín Era
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the military governor of Dàizhōu, because there were many itinerant monks at Wǔtái Mountain,
feared the rise of demonic or false affairs,
decreed that those without a fixed residence
be all expelled.
The itinerant monks, fearing expulsion,
mostly fled temporarily into the mountains and valleys.
There was one named Fǎlǎng
who went deep into Yànmén Mountain.
Within a secluded ravine was a stone cave,
large enough for a person to enter and exit.
Lǎng had plenty of dried provisions,
and wishing to stay in this mountain,
he thus sought out the cave and entered.
After several hundred paces, it gradually widened,
reaching level ground.
He waded across a flowing stream,
reached the other bank,
where the sun and moon were very bright.
Proceeding another two lǐ,
he came to a thatched hut,
inside which was a woman,
dressed entirely in grass and leaves,
with a dignified and beautiful countenance.
Seeing the monk, she was frightened and startled,
asking:
"What manner of being are you?"
The monk said:
"I am a human."
The woman laughed and said:
"How could a human have a form like this?"
The monk said:
"I serve the Buddha.
The Buddha requires renouncing physical form,
hence it is so."
She then asked:
"What is the Buddha?"
The monk explained in detail.
They looked at each other and laughed, saying:
"Your words are quite reasonable."
She asked again:
"What is its essential doctrine?"
The monk proceeded to expound the "Diamond Sutra."
She praised it repeatedly.
The monk then asked:
"What world is this place?"
The woman said:
"I am originally from the Qín era,
following Méng Tián to build the Great Wall.
Tián employed many women,
and we could not endure the hardship,
so we fled and hid here.
At first, we ate grass roots,
which allowed us not to die.
Since coming here, we no longer know the years,
and have not returned to the human world."
She then kept the monk there,
feeding him grass roots,
but they were astringent and inedible.
The monk stayed there over forty days,
then took temporary leave,
to go to the human world to seek food.
When he reached Dàizhōu,
prepared provisions and went back again,
but became lost and could not find the place.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
Hé Èrniáng
In Guǎngzhōu, there was a woman named Hé Èrniáng,
who made a living weaving shoes,
aged twenty,
living with her mother.
She had never practiced any immortal arts,
but suddenly said to her mother:
"Living here is stifling,
I wish to travel."
The next day, she flew away,
ascending to a temple on Luófú Mountain.
The mountain monks asked her reason for coming,
and she replied:
"I wish to serve the reverend monks."
From then on, she constantly stayed and resided there.
At first, she did not eat or drink,
but often gathered mountain fruits for the temple community to supplement their vegetarian meals,
though none knew where she obtained them.
North of Luófú Mountain is Xúnzhōu,
four hundred lǐ from Nánhǎi.
In a Xúnzhōu mountain temple was a bayberry tree,
several dozen arm-spans in girth.
Hé Èrniáng would often pick its fruit,
and return by mealtime.
Later, monks from the Xúnzhōu mountain temple came to Luófú Mountain,
and said:
"On such-and-such month and day, an immortal maiden came to pick bayberries."
Checking the dates,
it indeed matched the day Hé Èrniáng had gathered them.
From this, near and far knew she had attained immortality.
Afterwards, she no longer resided at the temple,
but would come perhaps once every ten days or a month.
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
an imperial edict ordered a eunuch envoy to go to Guǎngzhōu,
to seek Hé Èrniáng.
They found her,
and she went to the capital with the envoy.
Along the way,
the eunuch envoy lusted after her beauty,
intending to proposition her but not yet speaking.
Suddenly she said:
"The palace envoy harbors such thoughts,
I cannot remain."
Having said this,
she leaped up and departed,
none knew where.
After that, she left no trace and did not come to the human world again.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
Jade Maiden
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
at the Yúntái Temple on Huàshān, there was a maidservant named Yùnǚ.
At the age of forty-five,
she contracted a severe illness,
causing her entire body to fester, emitting a foul stench.
Fearing contamination, the people at the temple
together sent her to a secluded spot in a mountain stream.
Yùnǚ groaned in pain and agony.
Suddenly, a Dàoshì passed by,
tossing three or four stalks of green grass from afar,
which resembled vegetables.
He said to her:
"Strive to eat these,
and you will soon recover."
Yùnǚ immediately consumed them.
From then on, her illness gradually healed,
and within ten days, she was restored to her former self.
At first, she forgot about eating and drinking,
indulging only in wandering and gazing,
her mind feeling as if floating,
disliking the human world,
and even unwilling to pass by the front, back, left, or right of the temple.
The people at the temple thought she had long since vanished,
and no one went to look for her again.
Yùnǚ roamed the mountains,
drinking from springs and eating wild fruits.
Later, beneath a cliff,
she suddenly encountered the previous
Dàoshì, who said to her:
"Since your illness is cured,
there is no need to remain in the human world.
Two lǐ west of Yúntái Temple, there is a stone pool.
Every day at the hour of Chén,
toss a small stone into it,
and a water lily will emerge.
You may pluck and eat it,
and over time, it will surely bring you benefit."
Yùnǚ followed his instructions,
and from then on, her sinews and bones became light and strong,
soaring freely as she pleased.
Although she was occasionally encountered by people from the temple,
they did not recognize her as Yùnǚ.
After several decades like this,
her hair grew six or seven chǐ long,
green hair sprouted all over her body,
and her face became as white as a flower.
Often, when people in the mountains passed by her,
they would only kowtow and bow from afar.
During the Dàlì era,
there was a scholar named Bān Xíngdá,
who was coarse and careless in temperament,
disparaging Buddhism and Daoism.
He was studying in the western wing of the temple.
Yùnǚ went to the stone pool daily,
and this became her routine.
Xíngdá observed and spied on her,
and became familiar with her routine of tossing stones and picking the lily,
which followed a precise schedule.
One day,
he arrived at the pool slightly earlier,
and when Yùnǚ tossed the small stone and the water lily emerged,
Xíngdá snatched it away.
Yùnǚ was far away on the mountain cliffs,
or perched on treetops,
and by the time she arrived, it had already been taken.
She could only sigh and return.
The next day,
Xíngdá did the same again.
After more than ten days,
Yùnǚ gradually began to compete with Xíngdá to arrive first,
their steps drawing closer.
Suddenly, he swiftly grabbed her hair,
and Yùnǚ could not escape.
Using his brute strength, he seized her body,
and pressed her further.
Yùnǚ cried out for help,
vowing to die rather than submit,
but her strength was exhausted,
and she was ultimately violated by Xíngdá.
He locked her in a room.
The next day, when Xíngdá went to the temple,
he saw a white-haired old woman,
extremely frail and sickly,
struggling to move,
with dim vision and hearing.
Xíngdá was shocked,
and immediately summoned the people from the temple.
After recounting the story in detail,
they went together to question Yùnǚ,
who recounted everything from beginning to end.
Some at the temple had heard of her story before,
and calculated that she was over a hundred years old.
Everyone pitied her,
and together they released her.
Within a month, she passed away.
From "Jíyì Jì"
Biān Dòngxuán
At the end of the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
in Zǎoqiáng County, Jìzhōu, there was a female Dàoshì named Biān Dòngxuán.
She had practiced Daoism and ingested elixirs for forty years,
and was eighty-four years old.
Suddenly, an old man appeared,
holding a bowl of soup noodles,
and came to Dòngxuán, saying:
"I am an immortal from the Three Mountains.
Because you have attained the Dào,
I have come to fetch you.
These soup noodles are made from jade essence powder,
treasured by immortals.
Many who have recently attained the Dào have consumed it.
You may eat it without doubt,
and in seven days, you will surely ascend to immortality."
After Dòngxuán finished eating,
the old man said:
"I will go ahead now,
and you will follow later."
After speaking, he vanished.
Two days later,
Dòngxuán suddenly felt her body lighten,
her teeth and hair completely renewed.
She said to her disciples:
"Shàngqīng has summoned me,
and I will soon depart.
I think of you all.
Can you bear the sorrow?
Devote yourselves to cultivating my Dào,
and do not indulge in worldly pleasures,
lest your souls scatter like dust in a coffin."
When the seven days were complete,
her disciples went in the morning to inquire about her condition,
and saw purple clouds densely gathering,
filling the courtyard and doors.
They also heard several voices in the air,
and dared not enter,
all stopping outside the gate.
After a moment, the gate opened,
and Dòngxuán rode on the purple clouds,
soaring into the air and standing upright,
over a hundred chǐ above the ground,
bidding farewell to her disciples and fellow practitioners.
At the time, the prefect Yuán Fù,
along with tens of thousands of officials, commoners, and others,
all watched and paid their respects from afar.
After a while, the sun rose,
and the purple aura transformed into five-colored clouds.
Dòngxuán ascended slowly and gracefully,
and after a long time, she vanished.
From "Guǎngyì Jì"
Cuī Shūshēng
During the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras of the Táng dynasty,
there was a scholar named Cuī.
He lived at the mouth of Luógǔ in Dōngzhōu
and was fond of cultivating famous flowers.
In the late spring,
the blossoms were fragrant and luxuriant,
their scent detectable from a hundred paces away.
Every morning at dawn,
the scholar would invariably wash
(The original text had "yǔ" for "wash";
emended based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.)
and rinse, then go to admire them.
Suddenly, a maiden appeared,
riding a horse from the west,
followed by several maidservants, young and old.
The maiden was of exceptional beauty,
and the steed she rode was superb.
Before Cuī Shēng could get a good look,
she had already passed by.
The next day she passed by again.
Cuī Shēng then, beneath the flowers,
first set out wine, tea, cups, and ladles,
spread out mats and cushions,
and then stepped forward to bow before her horse, saying:
"I have a fondness for flowers and trees;
every plant in this garden was planted by my own hand.
Now they are in full, fragrant bloom,
quite worthy of a lingering glance.
As you, young lady, pass by day after day,
I reckon your servants and steeds must grow weary.
I dare to offer some plain wine,
awaiting your rest."
The maiden passed by without a glance.
Afterwards, one of the maidservants said:
"Just prepare wine and food;
why worry she won't come?"
The maiden looked back and scolded:
"Why do you lightly speak with others!"
The next day, Cuī Shēng again arrived first,
whipped his horse to follow them,
arriving before a country villa,
dismounted again,
and bowed, pleading for a long time.
An elderly maidservant said to the maiden:
"The horse is very tired;
a brief rest would do no harm."
She then took the reins herself
and led the horse to the foot of the bed.
The elderly maidservant said to Cuī Shēng:
"Since you, sir, are not yet
(The original text had "qiú" for "not yet";
emended based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.)
married,
shall I act as matchmaker?"
Cuī Shēng was overjoyed,
bowing repeatedly and kneeling to beg.
The maidservant said:
"The matter is settled then.
In fifteen or sixteen days,
there is a most auspicious date.
At that time, you, sir,
need only prepare all that is required for the wedding ceremony,
and also prepare wine and food here.
Now, the young lady's elder sister is in Luógǔ,
suffering from a minor illness,
so we go daily to visit her.
After I leave,
I will immediately inform her,
and when the date arrives, everyone will come here."
So they all departed together,
with Cuī Shēng following behind.
He then prepared everything needed for the auspicious day as instructed.
When the day arrived,
the maiden and her sister both came.
Her sister was also exceptionally beautiful in appearance and bearing.
She sent the maiden to stay, returning with Cuī Shēng.
Cuī Shēng's mother was at their old home,
completely unaware that Cuī Shēng had taken a wife.
Because Cuī Shēng had married without informing her,
he only mentioned taking a concubine.
His mother saw that the new bride's beauty was extraordinary.
After more than a month,
suddenly someone sent food for the maiden,
sweet and fragrant, exceptionally delicious.
Later, Cuī Shēng noticed his mother's kindly face had grown haggard and sorrowful,
so he prostrated himself before her low table to inquire.
His mother said:
"I have only you, one son,
hoping you would be safe and whole.
Now, this new bride you have taken,
her bewitching beauty is peerless.
I have never seen her like,
even among clay statues or painted figures.
She must be a fox spirit or such creature,
who will bring you harm.
That is why I am worried."
Cuī Shēng entered the chamber
and saw the maiden, tears streaming down her face, saying:
"I intended to serve you with broom and dustpan,
hoping to stay with you until heaven's end.
I did not know your honored mother regards me as a fox spirit.
At dawn tomorrow, I must leave."
Cuī Shēng could also only weep, unable to speak.
The next morning,
the maiden's carriage and horses arrived again.
The maiden rode one horse,
and Cuī Shēng also rode a horse to accompany and see her off.
They entered Luógǔ for thirty lǐ,
where amidst the mountains was a river valley.
In the valley grew exotic flowers and rare fruits,
too many to describe;
the halls, buildings, and rooms
were more luxurious than a king's palace.
About a hundred maidservants came forth to bow and greet them, saying:
"You faithless Cuī Láng,
why have you brought her here?"
They then escorted the maiden inside,
leaving Cuī Shēng outside the gate.
Not long after,
a maidservant conveyed the elder sister's words:
"Regarding Cuī Láng's sending her away
(The original text had "qiǎn" for "sending away";
emended based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.)
on this journey,
your honored mother suspected and prevented it,
so this matter should now be severed.
It is not fitting for you to meet again;
however, my younger sister once attended upon you.
You should still be invited in."
Shortly after, Cuī Shēng was summoned inside.
The elder sister reproached and berated him repeatedly,
her words clear and gentle.
Cuī Shēng could only bow and prostrate himself, accepting the reprimand.
Afterwards, he was seated in the inner chamber to dine with them.
After the meal, wine was ordered,
and female musicians were summoned to perform in harmony,
the sounds clanging and changing myriad ways.
When the music ended,
the elder sister said to the maiden:
"We must have Cuī Láng return now.
What will you give him as a parting gift?"
The maiden then took a white jade box from her sleeve and gave it to Cuī Shēng.
Cuī Shēng also bid his farewells.
Then, sobbing, they each went out the door.
When he looked back from the mouth of Luógǔ,
there were only a thousand cliffs and ten thousand ravines,
with no distant path in sight.
He returned home weeping bitterly,
often holding the jade box,
depressed and unhappy.
Suddenly, a foreign monk knocked at his door begging for food, saying:
"You, sir, possess a most precious treasure.
I beg you to show it to me."
Cuī Shēng said:
"I am but a poor scholar;
how could I have such a thing as you request?"
The monk said:
"Did you not receive a gift from an extraordinary person?
I, a humble monk, know by observing the emanations."
Cuī Shēng tentatively took out the jade box to show the monk.
The monk stood up
and asked to buy it for a million coins,
then departed.
Cuī Shēng asked the monk:
"Who was that maiden?"
He replied:
"The wife you took
is the third daughter of the Queen Mother of the West,
Lady Yùzhī.
Her elder sister also enjoys a reputation for beauty in the immortal capital,
let alone in the mortal world!
It is a pity you could not keep her for long.
If she had stayed for one year,
your entire household would have attained immortality!"
From "Xuánguài Lù" (Records of the Mysterious and Strange).
Líshān Mǔ,
it is unknown from which era she hailed.
Lǐ Quán was fond of the ways of divine transcendents,
often traversing famous mountains,
extensively gathering esoteric arts.
Upon reaching the stone chamber at Hǔkǒu Cliff on Mount Sōng,
he obtained the original text of the Yellow Emperor's "Yīnfú",
written on plain silk,
sealed very securely.
An inscription read:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month in the second year of the Zhēnjūn era of Great Wèi,
the Daoist priest Kòu Qiānzhī concealed this among the famous mountains,
to transmit it to those of like mind."
As it was crumbling with decay,
Quán copied and read it several thousand times,
yet ultimately could not comprehend its principles.
Subsequently, he entered Qín,
arriving at the foot of Mount Lí,
where he encountered an old woman.
Her hair was coiled in a bun atop her head,
the remaining locks half-falling down,
clad in worn clothes and leaning on a staff,
her divine appearance most unusual.
By the roadside, she saw a leftover fire burning a tree,
and thus spoke to herself:
"Fire is born from wood,
when calamity erupts, it will surely overcome it."
Quán, hearing this, was startled,
stepped forward and asked:
"This is the secret text of the Yellow Emperor's 'Yīnfú',
how did you, mother, come to know it?"
The old woman said:
"I received this talisman,
already three yuán and six cycles of jiǎzǐ have passed.
One cycle of a yuán,
accounts for one hundred and eighty years,
six cycles total one thousand and eighty years."
"one thousand and eighty years" originally read "one thousand and eight years".

Young man, from where did you learn of it?"
Quán kowtowed and bowed deeply,
fully recounting where he obtained the talisman,
and then inquired about its profound meaning.
She had Quán stand upright,
facing the light, and looking at him said:
"One who receives this talisman,
must have their name listed among the registers of transcendents,
their bone structure corresponding to that of an immortal,
only then can one speak of the profound mysteries of the ultimate Way,
and unlock the key to the mysterious gate.
Otherwise,
one will instead incur misfortune.
Young man, your cheekbones connect to the Gate of Life,
your Destiny Wheel aligns with the Sun Horn,
your blood vessels are not diminished,
your heart's reflection is not askew,
your nature is virtuous and you delight in the Dharma,
your spirit is courageous and you rejoice in wisdom,
truly you are my disciple!
However, at forty-five years of age,
you will face a great calamity."
Thereupon, she produced a vermilion-written talisman,
threaded it onto the end of her staff,
and ordered Quán to kneel and swallow it.
Saying:
"May Heaven and Earth protect you."
Then she bade him sit,
and explained the meaning of the "Yīnfú", saying:
"The Yīnfú,
is a secret of the Supreme Clarity,
revered by the Mysterious Terrace.
In governing a state, it brings great peace;
in cultivating the self, it leads to attainment of the Way.
It is not merely for tactical advantage and securing victory,
but is the essential pivot of the ultimate Way.
How could it be a common text of the human world?
In antiquity, although there was

violence and tyranny,
the Yellow Emperor promoted the worthy and employed the capable,
punished the strong and quelled rebellion,
to assist Shénnóng's governance.
For three years and a hundred battles,

He purified his heart and prayed to Heaven,

The Nine-Spirited Golden Mother commanded the envoy of Méng Hú,

He ordered the Mysterious Maiden to instruct him in military strategy,

This book then circulated in the world.
In total, it contains over three hundred characters:
one hundred characters expound the Way,

Above, it contains the Way of the divine transcendents embracing the One;
in the middle, methods for enriching the state and pacifying the people;
below, arts for strengthening the military and achieving victory in battle.
All originate from the Heavenly Mechanism,
and accord with divine wisdom.
Observing its essence and subtleties,
then the Eight Scenes of the Huángtíng
cannot be considered profound;
examining its utmost essentials,
then the Classics, Commentaries, Masters, and Histories
cannot be considered literary;
comparing its clever wisdom,
then Sūn, Wú, Hán, Bái

It is also called the Yellow Emperor's Book of the Heavenly Mechanism.
It cannot be recklessly transmitted except to extraordinary individuals.
Those whose nine orifices and four limbs are incomplete, who are stingy, greedy, foolish, ignorant, arrogant, extravagant, licentious, or dissolute,
must certainly not be allowed to hear of it.
Whenever transmitting to those of like mind,
one must purify oneself and then transmit it.
The one possessing the original is the master,
the one receiving the book is the disciple.
One must not value the wealthy and noble while slighting the poor and lowly.
Those who violate this will have twenty years deducted from their lifespan.
On the seventh day of the seventh month each year, copy one volume,
and conceal it within the rocky cliffs of a famous mountain;
one will gain added years.
On one's birthdate, recite it seven times;
it benefits the mind's mechanism,
adds to one's lifespan,
expels the Three Corpses,
and dispels the Nine Worms.
Guard it secretly and value it highly,
and transmit it only to those of like mind.
For this book, the perfected person studying it attains the Way;
the worthy person studying it attains the methods;
the ordinary person studying it incurs calamity.

Those who reveal the Heavenly Mechanism sink for three kalpas.
Can one not be cautious?!"
When she finished speaking,
she said to Quán:
"The sun has already declined.
I have some wheat gruel,
let us share a meal."
From her sleeve, she produced a gourd,
and ordered Quán to fetch water from the valley.
Once it was full,
the gourd suddenly became heavy, over a hundred jīn,
his strength could not control it and it sank into the spring.
Returning to beneath the tree,
the old woman was nowhere to be found,
only several shēng of wheat gruel remained on a stone.
Gazing wistfully until evening,
he did not see the old woman again.
Quán ate the wheat gruel.
From then on, he did not eat,
thus abstaining from grains

and composed the "Zhōngtái Zhì Kǔnwài Chūnqiū".
These circulated in the world.
He served as Deputy Military Commissioner of Jīngnán and Prefect of Xiānzhōu.
From the "Collection of Biographies of Transcendents"
Huáng Guānfú
Huáng Guānfú was the daughter of a commoner in Bǎizhàng County, Yǎzhōu.
From childhood she did not eat meat or blood,
preferring purity and tranquility.
Her family was poor and had no incense,
so she burned cypress leaves and cypress seeds instead.
Often she would sit in deep, still meditation,
with no other pursuits,
and remain untired throughout the day.
Sometimes she ate cypress leaves
and drank water to sustain herself,
having no taste for the five grains.
Her parents pitied her
and generally let her follow her own inclinations.
When she reached the age of marriage and they wished to wed her off,
she suddenly said to her parents:
"There is something most unusual in the water before our gate."
The girl had often spoken to her parents of strange events and omens beforehand,
and they were often proven true.
Hearing this,
they therefore believed her,
and went with her to look.
The water indeed came surging forth,
and she threw herself into it,
remaining submerged for a long time without emerging.
When they dredged the water,
they retrieved an ancient wooden statue of a Celestial Worthy.
Its golden colors had already faded,
but its features and appearance were no different from the girl's.
The water then became clear and still.
They placed the wooden statue by the roadside
and returned home weeping and wailing.
Her mother would come from time to time to look at it,
unable to stop thinking of her.
Suddenly there appeared colored clouds and celestial music,
with a great many escorts and attendants,
along with three maidens,
who descended into their courtyard.
They said to the parents:
"Your daughter was originally an immortal of the Upper Clarity Heaven.
Having committed a minor transgression,
she was exiled to the mortal world.
Now that her allotted term has ended,
she has returned to the heavens.
Do not grieve or worry excessively.
The three who came with me:
one is a Jade Emperor's attendant maiden,
one is the Celestial Emperor's attendant of the hours,
and one is an Upper Clarity attendant scribe.
From now on she will not return.
Coming to this place now,
we see that many have died from plague.
We leave gold for you, parents,
so that you may move your household to Yìzhōu
to avoid this calamitous year."
They then left several ingots of gold
and ascended to heaven and departed.
The parents did as they were told
and moved their household to Shǔ Commandery.
That year the plague was virulent,
especially in Lízhōu and Yǎzhōu,
where three or four out of ten perished.
This was during the Líndé era of the Táng dynasty.
Nowadays she is commonly called Huáng Guānfó,
likely because people did not recognize the Daoist image of the Celestial Worthy,
and through oral transmission the name became corrupted,
changing Huáng Guānfú to Huáng Guānfó.
From the "Collection of Biographies of Immortals."
Yáng Zhèngjiàn
Yáng Zhèngjiàn was the daughter of a commoner named Yáng Chǒng in Tōngyì County, Méizhōu.
From childhood she was intelligent, perceptive, kind, and compassionate,
with an elegant fondness for purity and emptiness.
When she reached marriageable age,
her parents betrothed her to a certain Mr. Wáng from the same commandery.
The Wáng family was also very wealthy
and fond of entertaining guests.
One day,
her parents-in-law were gathering with relatives and old friends.
They had bought fish
and told Yáng Zhèngjiàn to prepare it as sliced raw fish.
The guests were gambling and playing games in the main hall,
and by late afternoon the food on the plates was still not ready.
Zhèngjiàn pitied the living fish;
playing with it in the basin,
she ultimately could not bear to kill it.
As dusk approached,
her parents-in-law pressed and scolded her for the delay with the meal.
Frightened,
Zhèngjiàn fled to the neighborhood,
and simply walked along wild paths.
After several tens of lǐ,
she felt no weariness.
She saw flowers and trees lining the path,
different from those of the human world.
She came to a mountain cottage
where a female Daoist adept resided.
Zhèngjiàn fully explained her circumstances to her.
The female adept said:
"You possess a compassionate, life-sparing heart;
you can be taught."
She therefore let her stay.
The mountain cottage was beside the Zhǔbù Shrine in Pújiāng County.
The dwelling had no water,
so she often had Zhèngjiàn fetch water from the stream.
The female adept normally did not eat,
but for Zhèngjiàn's sake,
she would sometimes go outside the mountain to seek provisions
to support her.
This went on for several years.
Zhèngjiàn was respectful, cautious, diligent, and conscientious,
upholding the etiquette of a disciple
without ever being remiss or negligent.
Suddenly, at the place where she drew water,
there appeared a small child,
fair and lovely,
just over a year old,
who smiled happily upon seeing people.
Zhèngjiàn held and comforted it, showing it affection,
and this became a regular occurrence.
Because of this, she returned late from fetching water several times.
The female adept grew suspicious and asked her about it,
and Zhèngjiàn told her what had happened.
The female adept said:
"If you see it again,
you must carry the child straight here;
I wish to see it once."
From then on, after over a month,
when Zhèngjiàn went to fetch water,
the child appeared again.
She therefore carried it back with her.
As they neared the cottage,
the child had already stiffened.
Looking at it closely, it resembled the root of a plant or tree,
weighing several jīn.
The female adept saw it and recognized it;
it was a piece of poria fungus.
She instructed her to clean a steamer and steam it.
It happened that the mountain provisions ran out,
so the female adept went out of the mountain to seek supplies.
She left Zhèngjiàn with one day's worth of food and three small bundles of firewood,
instructing her:
"The thing in the steamer—
once you have used up these three bundles of firewood,
you may stop the fire.
Do not look at it arbitrarily."
The female adept left the mountain,
expecting to return by that evening.
That evening there was a great storm,
mountain waters overflowed,
the road was blocked,
and she did not return for ten days.
Zhèngjiàn's food ran out and she grew very hungry.
Smelling the fragrance from the steamer,
she secretly ate its contents.
Within a few days she had eaten it all,
and only then did the female adept return.
Hearing what had happened, she sighed and said:
"Becoming an immortal is indeed a matter of predetermined fate!
Had it not been for the rain and flood that ruined the road,
how could you have eaten all the numinous medicine?
My master often said:
'On this mountain there is a human-shaped poria fungus;
whoever eats it will ascend to heaven in broad daylight.'
I have watched for it for twenty years.
Now you have encountered it and eaten it;
you are truly one who has attained the Dao."
From then on, Zhèngjiàn's appearance and demeanor became increasingly extraordinary,
her radiance dazzling to behold.
Often many immortals would descend to her chamber
and discuss with her matters of the true palaces and immortal abodes.
A little over a year later,
she ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
This was on the third day of the eleventh month of the rénshēn year, the twenty-first year of the Kāiyuán era.
She once said to her master:
"Having eaten the numinous medicine,
I should have ascended to immortality that very day.
The reason for my delay
was that in my youth,
I saw my parents selecting tax money to deliver to the authorities.
There were some bright, clean, round, and fine coins,
and I secretly hid two of them to play with.
Because of this offense of concealing government money,
I was punished to remain in the human world for one more year."
The place where she ascended to heaven
is the present-day Zhǔbù Shrine in Pújiāng County, Qiōngzhōu.
The place where she drew water still exists there.
Long ago, Wáng Xīng, a registrar of Guǎnghàn,
ascended from this spot.
From the "Records of Collected Immortals."
Dǒng Shàngxiān was a woman from Fāngyì in Suízhōu.
At the age of seventeen,
her divine beauty was radiant and alluring.
She ate and drank little,
preferring tranquility and harmony,
yet she did not withdraw from the world.
The villagers, admiring her appearance and virtue,
all regarded her as an immortal,
hence she was called "Shàngxiān."
Suddenly one day, purple clouds descended and spread,
and celestial music sounded in her courtyard.
Two azure youths
led her upward to heaven.
Her parents, being simple and ignorant,
wailed and called out to her incessantly.
When she was several dozen zhang above the ground,
she descended again and returned home.
The purple clouds and azure youths
soon vanished without a trace.
After several months,
she ascended to heaven again as before.
Her parents once more wept and wailed,
and after a long while, she descended again.
During the Táng dynasty's Kāiyuán era,
the emperor was fond of and revered immortals.
Hearing of this matter,
he issued an edict summoning her to Cháng'ān.
After more than a month,
she begged to return to her hometown,
and he permitted it.
A palace envoy escorted her back home.
After over a hundred days, she ascended to heaven again,
and her parents wept for her once more.
Thereupon, she shed her skin on the ground
and flew away.
The skin resembled her form,
with her clothing tied and unfastened,
like a cicada shedding its shell.
They then lacquered it and kept it.
An edict established the Shàngxiān and Tángxīng temples at her dwelling place.
Now they are located over ten lǐ north of the prefecture,
on the banks of the Fú River.
From the "Records of the Assembled Immortals."
Zhāng Liánqiào
The female Daoist Zhāng Liánqiào from Huángméi County
was eight or nine years old.
She often carried a jar to fetch water.
Suddenly, she saw a lotus flower in the well, like a small plate,
gradually emerging from the well's mouth.
When she went to take it, it shrank back;
when she did not take it, it emerged again.
This happened several times,
and she then entered the well.
Her family wondered why she had not returned for so long
and went to look.
They saw Liánqiào standing on the water in the well.
When she came out,
she suddenly developed a laughing ailment.
When asked the reason,
she said someone from behind had touched her armpits with their hands,
making her unbearably ticklish.
Her parents believed she was afflicted by ghosts or demons,
and secretly moved her to her maternal uncle's family in the middle of the night.
Only then did she stop laughing.
After a short while,
she returned home again,
saying she was hungry
and asking for food.
She ate several dǒu of rice daily,
and even at night, pickles and dishes were placed by her bed,
which she would eat upon waking.
After six or seven days like this,
she began to smell the food's odor,
and from then on, she ate no more.
Occasionally throughout the year, she would eat three or four dates.
Her parents then ordered her to leave home and become a Daoist.
At the age of eighteen,
she was sitting alone in the temple during the day
when she saw two coins fall from the sky.
Liánqiào got up and went to pick them up.
A neighboring woman pushed the fence down
and also scrambled to pick them up.
Liánqiào used her body to cover the coins.
She was also given three yellow pills,
and she quickly got up to take them.
The woman pried her hand open
and snatched one pill away.
Liánqiào then swallowed the other two pills,
and soon both fell dead.
Liánqiào awoke after a short while,
feeling strong and clear-minded,
twice as much as usual.
The woman who swallowed one pill
revived after a full day,
eating and drinking as before.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Liánqiào was in the temple
when she suddenly felt sorrowful longing for her parents,
as if she intended to go somewhere.
The common people and local officials
all saw a five-colored cloud embracing a precious carriage
descending from the sky.
People thought Liánqiào had already left
and rushed to see.
Liánqiào initially noticed nothing,
and the cloud also dispersed.
Those who discussed it said:
"Because of the crowd, she did not leave."
Liánqiào remains to this day,
her two armpits joined together,
her body withered and haggard,
and she eats nothing.
From the "Extensive Records of the Strange."
Zhāng Gǎo's Wife
Zhāng Gǎo was a man from Nányáng.
In his youth, he diligently pursued his studies,
secluding himself on Wángwū Mountain,
never letting go of his books.
At the foot of the mountain was a tavern.
Gǎo would take his books and go there,
drink two or three cups, and return.
One day,
he saw a beautiful woman at the tavern,
bowed to her, and spoke with her,
inviting her to drink together.
She cheerfully showed no refusal,
her words were clear and articulate,
and her appearance was lovely and beautiful.
When it grew late, she bid farewell and left.
Gǎo deeply missed her
and could not sleep all night.
Before dawn,
he went again to wait for her.
She was already at the tavern.
He invited her to drink again,
hinting with subtle words.
The woman said:
"You are no ordinary man.
I wish to entrust myself to you.
If you can be with me for life,
that is my desire."
Gǎo agreed,
took her home,
and they lived in the mountains for ten years.
But Gǎo was diligent in studying the ancient classics,
and his affection gradually waned,
sometimes becoming angry and resentful.
The woman said:
"If your feelings are like this,
I cannot stay long.
Just obtain one dǒu of carp fat for medicine,
and that will be enough."
Gǎo did not know what it was for
but diligently sought it and gave it to her.
The woman threw the carp fat into the well
and followed it down.
In a moment,
she rode a carp leaping out of the well,
soaring into the sky, about to depart.
She said to Gǎo:
"I had hoped to wait for you to achieve merit and accomplish deeds,
so we could ascend together to the Great Purity.
Now that it is like this,
it is truly your lack of fortune.
In the future, when you cannot maintain your position to the end,
what use will regret be!"
Gǎo bowed and apologized, repenting his faults.
Thereupon, she rode the fish and ascended to heaven, departing.
Gǎo later left the mountain,
served in office, and rose to the position of chief minister.
As the Dūtǒng of Hénán,
he often remembered the words about not ending well,
and each time blamed himself.
Later, he was demoted to Sīhù of Chénzhōu,
then recalled to office and died,
at just sixty years old.
Whenever he spoke with guests and friends,
he considered it a lifelong regret.
From the "Biographies of Encounters with Immortals."
Tàiyīn Fūrén
Lú Qǐ, in his youth,
lived in poverty in the Eastern Capital,
renting a room in an abandoned estate.
His neighbor was an old woman named Má, who lived alone.
Qǐ fell seriously ill,
and lay bedridden for over a month.
Má Pó came to make him congee and soup.
After he recovered,
he returned home late one evening
and saw a golden calf-drawn carriage outside Má Pó's door.
Lú was astonished.
Peering inside,
he saw a girl of about fourteen or fifteen,
truly a divine being!
The next day, he secretly visited Má Pó.
Má Pó said:
"Do you wish to marry her?
Let me try to discuss it."
Qǐ said:
"I am poor and lowly;
how dare I entertain such thoughts?"
Má said:
"What does it matter!"
When night fell,
Má Pó said:
"The matter is settled.
Please fast for three days,
then meet at the abandoned temple east of the city."
When he arrived,
he saw ancient trees and wild grass;
the place had long been uninhabited,
and he hesitated.
Suddenly, thunder, lightning, wind, and rain erupted violently,
transforming into towers and pavilions,
with golden halls and jade curtains—
the scenery was magnificent.
A curtained carriage descended from the sky;
it was the girl from before.
She met Qǐ and said:
"I am a celestial being,
sent by the command of the Heavenly Emperor
to the mortal world to seek a mate.
You possess the countenance of an immortal,
so I sent Má Pó to convey my intention.
Fast for another seven days,
and we shall meet again."
The girl called Má Pó
and gave her two pills of medicine.
In an instant, thunder, lightning, and dark clouds arose,
and the girl had vanished.
The ancient trees and wild grass were as before.
Má Pó returned with Qǐ.
After fasting for seven days,
they dug the ground and planted the medicine.
As soon as it was planted, it began to spread;
in no time,
two gourds grew on the vines,
gradually enlarging to the size of two-hú jars.
Má Pó carved out their interiors with a knife.
She and Qǐ each entered one,
and she instructed him to prepare three oiled cloaks.
Suddenly, wind and thunder arose,
lifting them into the azure sky.
Their ears were filled with the sound of waves.
After a long time, they felt cold,
so she told him to put on an oiled cloak.
It felt as if they were in ice and snow,
so she told him to put on all three layers,
and he became very warm.
Má Pó said:
"We are already eighty thousand lǐ from Luò."
After a long while,
the gourds came to a stop,
and they saw palaces, towers, and pavilions,
all with walls made of crystal.
Hundreds of armored guards stood with weapons at the ready.
Má Pó led Qǐ inside to meet the girl.
In a purple hall, about a hundred female attendants stood by.
The girl asked Qǐ to sit
and served him wine and food.
Má Pó stood discreetly among the guards below.
The girl said to Qǐ:
"You are entitled to three choices.
Choose one as you wish:
stay forever in this palace,
with a lifespan as long as heaven;
next, become an earthly immortal,
living in the mortal world,
but able to visit here from time to time;
last, become the prime minister of the Middle Kingdom."
Qǐ said:
"To stay here is truly my greatest wish."
The girl joyfully said:
"This is the Crystal Palace.
I am Tàiyīn Fūrén,
and my immortal rank is already high.
For you, this would mean ascending to heaven in broad daylight.
However, you must be certain,
and cannot change your mind,
lest you bring trouble upon us."
She then prepared a petition on blue paper,
and kneeling in the courtyard to present it,
said:
"We must inform the Heavenly Emperor."
After a short while,
a voice was heard from the northeast, saying:
"The Heavenly Emperor's envoy has arrived!"
Tàiyīn Fūrén and the other immortals hurried to welcome him.
Soon, banners, ceremonial staffs, and fragrant streamers appeared,
leading a youth in red robes who stood at the foot of the steps.
The red-robed youth proclaimed the Emperor's command:
"Lú Qǐ,
according to Tàiyīn Fūrén's petition,
wishes to reside in the Crystal Palace.
Is this so?"
Qǐ remained silent.
The lady urged him to answer quickly,
but still he said nothing.
The lady and her attendants grew greatly alarmed.
She rushed inside,
took five bolts of sharkskin silk,
and bribed the envoy,
hoping to delay him.
After about the time of a meal, he asked again:
"Lú Qǐ!
Do you wish to reside in the Crystal Palace,
become an earthly immortal,
or be the prime minister of the mortal world?
This time you must decide."
"Decide" originally read "quickly,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
Qǐ shouted loudly:
"The prime minister of the mortal world!"
The red-robed youth hurried away.
Tàiyīn Fūrén turned pale and said:
"This is Má Pó's fault.
Take him back quickly!"
She pushed him into the gourd.
Again, he heard the sounds of wind and water,
and returned to his former dwelling.
The dusty bed was just as before.
It was already midnight,
and the gourd and Má Pó were nowhere to be seen.
From "Yì Shǐ"
The Three Sons of the Yáo Family
Táng Dynasty Censor Yáo Shēng,
having left his official post,
resided in a village to the left of Púzhōu.
He had one son and two nephews,
each with a different surname,
all of whom had reached adulthood,
yet were stubborn, foolish, and unworthy.
Yáo's son was slightly older than the other two youths.
Yáo regretted their lack of learning,
daily instructing and reproaching them,
yet they remained idle and wandering, unrepentant.
So, on the southern side of Tiáo Mountain,
he built thatched huts for them to live in,
hoping to cut off outside affairs,
so they could focus on their studies.
The forested valleys were deep and layered,
far from the clamor and dust.
On the day he sent them off,
Yáo admonished them, saying:
"Every season I will test your abilities;
if your studies show no progress,
you will surely face the cane!
Strive hard."
Upon arriving in the mountains,
the two younger ones never opened a book.
They only busied themselves with chopping wood and plastering walls.
After several months,
the eldest said to the two:
"The test date is approaching,
yet you both haven't studied your books at all;
I fear for you."
The two paid no heed,
while the eldest studied diligently.
Suddenly, one night,
around midnight by candlelight,
as he leaned on his desk reading,
he felt the fur robe he was wearing
being tugged from behind by something,
the collar gradually slipping down.
He thought nothing strange of it,
slowly pulling it back on.
Soon it happened again,
and so it went several times.
Finally, he turned to look,
and saw a small piglet,
lying nestled in his robe,
its color very pure white,
glossy and smooth like jade.
So he struck it with the paperweight ruler he used for pressing books,
and the piglet fled with a startled cry.
He hastily called the other two to bring candles,
and they searched the hall.
The windows and doors were tightly shut,
and looking all around, there were no gaps,
yet they could not tell where the piglet had gone.
The next day,
an old servant arrived on horseback and knocked at the door,
entered with his tablet tucked at his waist,
and said to the three:
"My mistress sends her regards.
Last night, her young child, unknowing,
mistakenly entered your robe's hem;
she is deeply ashamed.
However, you struck him too severely.
Now he has recovered,
so please do not worry."
All three humbly apologized,
looking at each other, unable to guess the reason.
A short while later,
the same mounted youth returned,
carrying the injured child,
along with several wet nurses,
all dressed in fine silks,
exquisite and beautiful beyond ordinary sight.
Again, he conveyed the mistress's words:
"The child is unharmed,
so we have brought him to show you."
Drawing closer to look,
from his eyebrows to the tip of his nose,
there was a red line,
the mark left by the ruler's edge.
The three grew even more frightened.
The messenger and the wet nurses
all spoke sweetly to comfort and reassure them,
adding:
"Shortly, the mistress herself will come."
Having said this, they left.
The three all wanted to slip away and hide,
but hesitated, uncertain.
Dozens of old servants and purple-robed palace eunuchs came rushing,
setting up screens and curtains in front,
with mats and cushions resplendent,
and an extraordinary fragrance.
Soon, a lacquered carriage appeared,
with a black ox and red hubs,
swift as the wind,
accompanied by several hundred fine horses,
leading and following before and after,
and stopped at the gate.
It was the mistress.
The three hurried out to bow,
and the mistress smiled and said:
"I did not expect my child to come here.
The injury you inflicted yesterday
was not too severe,
but I feared you might worry,
so I have come to reassure you."
The mistress appeared to be over thirty,
her demeanor graceful and composed,
her movements divine,
yet they did not know who she was.
She asked the three:
"Do you have wives?"
"Not yet" originally read "come,"
amended according to the Huáng edition.
All three replied they did not.
She said:
"I have three daughters,
of exceptional beauty and virtuous character,
who may be matched with you three gentlemen."
The three bowed in thanks.
The mistress then stayed without leaving,
creating a separate courtyard for each of the three.
In the blink of an eye,
painted halls and extended pavilions
were instantly completed.
The next day,
curtained carriages arrived,
with attendants splendid and beautiful,
surpassing even imperial relatives.
The carriages and robes dazzled,
their radiance illuminating the ground,
fragrance filling the mountain valley.
The three daughters descended from the carriages,
all aged seventeen or eighteen.
The mistress led the three daughters into the hall,
and invited the three youths to take their seats.
The wine and delicacies were rare and exquisite,
the fruits abundant and plentiful,
unlike anything in the mortal world,
many of which they had never seen before.
The three were utterly beyond their expectations.
The mistress pointed to the three daughters and said:
"Each shall be matched with you."
The three rose from their seats and bowed in thanks.
There were also several dozen accompanying maidens,
like immortals.
That evening, the wedding ceremony was held.
The mistress said to the three:
"What people value most is life,
and what they desire is nobility.
If you do not reveal this to anyone for a hundred days,
I will grant you eternal life in this world,
and positions at the pinnacle of officialdom."
The three bowed in thanks again,
but worried about their own foolishness and obstinacy.
The mistress said:
"Do not worry,
this is easy."
She then commanded the local earth deity
to summon Kǒng Xuānfù.
In a moment,
Confucius arrived fully robed, with his cap and sword.
The mistress stood at the steps,
and Xuānfù bowed in reverence, very respectful.
The mistress stood upright,
slightly inquiring after his labors,
and said to him:
"My three sons-in-law wish to study;
please guide them."
Xuānfù then instructed the three youths,
pointing out the contents of the Six Classics to show them,
and they all understood clearly, grasping the main ideas thoroughly,
as if they had long been familiar with them.
Soon after, Xuānfù took his leave.
The mistress then commanded Zhōu Shàngfù,
showing them the secret formulas of Xuánnǚ's talismans and jade huáng pendants,
and the three again mastered them without omission.
Sitting and conversing again,
they were now men of both civil and martial talents,
their learning probing the realms of heaven and humanity.
The three looked at each other,
feeling their own bearing broad and serene,
their spirits clear and bright,
fully equipped to be generals and ministers.
Later, Yáo sent a household servant to deliver provisions,
who, upon arrival, was greatly startled and fled.
Yáo asked the reason,
and he reported in detail the splendor of the buildings and curtains, and the multitude of beautiful people.
Yáo exclaimed in alarm to his relatives:
"These must be mountain ghosts or mountain spirits!"
He urgently summoned the three youths.
As the three were about to leave,
the mistress admonished them:
"Take care not to reveal anything;
even if beaten with canes,
do not speak of it."
When the three arrived,
Yáo was also surprised by their radiant and refined spirits,
and their elegant and composed responses.
Yáo said:
"These three boys are acting strangely,
as if possessed by ghosts."
He pressed them for the reason,
but they would not speak,
so he had them whipped dozens of times.
Unable to bear the pain,
they told the whole story from beginning to end.
Yáo then confined them in a separate place.
Yáo had long been hosting a great scholar,
so he summoned him and spoke with him.
The scholar exclaimed in astonishment:
"How extraordinary! How extraordinary!
Why did you punish the three boys?
If they had not revealed the matter,
they would certainly have become dukes or ministers,
reaching the highest rank among officials.
Now that they have revealed it,
it is their fate!"
Yáo asked for the reason,
and he said:
"I observed that the stars of Zhīnǚ, Wùnǚ, and Xūnǚ have all lost their light.
These three female stars have descended to the human world
to bring fortune to the three boys.
Now that they have divulged the heavenly secret,
it is fortunate that the three boys escaped disaster."
That night,
the scholar led Yáo to observe the three stars,
and indeed the stars had no light.
Yáo then released the three boys
and sent them back to the mountain.
Upon arriving, the three women seemed distant, as if they did not recognize them.
The lady reproached them, saying:
"You did not heed my words.
Since you have divulged the heavenly secret,
we must part ways here."
She then gave the three boys a decoction to drink.
After drinking it,
they became dull and foolish as before,
knowing nothing at all.
The scholar said to Yáo:
"The three female stars are still in the human world,
and not far from this region."
He secretly told his confidants the location,
and some said it was the home of Zhāng Jiāzhēn in Hédōng.
Later, that family produced generals and ministers for three generations.
From "The Biographies of Encounters with Immortals."
Zhào Xù
Zhào Xù of Tiānshuǐ,
orphaned young and aloof by nature, was fond of study,
possessed handsome features,
excelled in refined conversation,
and practiced the Way of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi.
He resided in Guǎnglíng,
once living alone in a secluded dwelling he had repaired,
attended only by two servants.
He once dreamed of a maiden,
dressed in blue garments,
who smiled and teased him at the window.
Upon waking, he found it strange,
and thus prayed, saying:
"What divine wonder is this?
I wish to behold your immortal form,
and humbly pray you grant me a sacred bond."
At midnight,
he suddenly heard faint laughter outside the window.
Knowing it was a deity,
Zhào Xù prayed again.
Then a voice said:
"I am a celestial maiden from the upper realm.
Hearing of your accumulated virtue, purity, and simplicity,
I take advantage of your waking and dreaming,
wishing to entrust myself to your pure breeze."
Zhào Xù, startled and delighted,
straightened his clothes and rose, saying:
"The dream of King Xiāng at Wūshān,
the bond of the cave flute with the Qín maiden—
now I understand them."
As the divine mirror suddenly descended,
joy and happiness mingled together,
and he turned up the lamp, brushed off the mat to invite her in.
Suddenly a pure fragrance filled the room,
and a maiden appeared,
aged about fourteen or fifteen,
her beauty unparalleled in her time,
wearing a gown of six-zhu misty silk,
treading in shoes of five-colored interwoven patterns,
who parted the curtain and entered.
Zhào Xù bowed deeply.
The maiden smiled and said:
"I am the Green Maiden from heaven,
long dwelling in the pure forbidden precincts.
My secluded heart, constrained and lonely,
my rank being of the lowest grade,
often harbors worldly thoughts,
so the Emperor punished me to descend to the mortal world to be matched according to my feelings.
As your spirit is ethereal and bright,
your body attuned to profound silence,
I am fortunate to entrust myself to your pure resonance,
wishing to harmonize with your divine charm."
Zhào Xù said:
"With my ephemeral nature,
barely breathing by the water clock's measure,
I never expected a lofty immortal to stoop and save me;
how dare I rashly stir vulgar feelings?"
The maiden then smiled and said:
"You possessed the Way in a past life,
your bone structure destined for immortality,
and your name is already recorded in the golden registers.
You are fated to play the cave flute atop a red tower,
and strum the cloud zither amidst the azure heavens."
Then she invited him to sit,
and spoke of the inner scenes of the Jade Emperor's realm.
As the night drum sounded,
she bade him prepare bedding.
Zhào Xù, being poor, had nothing to offer.
The maiden smiled and said:
"Do not trouble yourself, immortal gentleman."
Then she ordered the bedchamber prepared.
In a moment, mist darkened the room,
and after the time of a meal, it cleared,
the chamber now furnished with rare treasures,
beyond all knowing.
Then hand in hand they went inside,
her radiant beauty shining forth,
rare in the world, seldom heard of.
Late at night,
suddenly a maiden's voice called from outside:
"Lady Green!"
Zhào Xù, startled, asked about it.
She replied:
"It is a maiden from the same palace seeking me,
do not answer."
Then the caller tapped the pillar and sang:
"Moonlight and dew drift, the Milky Way slants,
alone I walk, graceful, in a floating cloud chariot.
The immortal gentleman alone invites the Green Maiden,
weaving affection in silken curtains, hearts blooming as one."
The song was very long,
Zhào Xù only remembered two rhymes.
He said to the Green Maiden:
"May we invite her in?"
She replied:
"This maiden talks too much;
I fear she might leak our affair to the upper realm."
Zhào Xù said:
"Lutes and zithers are set,
tuned by human hands—
what is there to fear!"
Then he rose to welcome her.
He saw a goddess in mid-air,
about ten feet above the ground,
attended by six or seven maidens,
holding a canopy with nine bright coiling dragons,
wearing a golden essence dancing phoenix crown,
her long skirt trailing in the wind,
dazzling to the eyes and heart.
Zhào Xù bowed deeply and invited her;
she then descended, saying:
"I am the Cháng'é maiden.
Hearing of your gathering with Lady Green,
I have come to catch the fugitive."
Then she entered the room.
Lady Green smiled and said:
"How did you already know my whereabouts?"
She replied:
"A fine rendezvous, yet you did not tell me—
whose fault is that?"
They laughed and enjoyed themselves together.
Zhào Xù, overjoyed, did not know what to do;
once they shared in the merry harmony,
as dawn approached,
a maid announced:
"The rooster crows;
the patrol will check."
The maiden said:
"Prepare the chariots."
The reply came:
"They are ready."
They agreed on a later meeting;
she replied:
"Take care not to speak of this to the world;
I will not abandon you."
Upon going out the door,
there were two five-cloud chariots,
floating in the air.
Then each boarded a chariot and bid farewell;
a divine wind rustled,
lifting them into the void,
and they vanished from sight at the horizon.
Zhào Xù had never imagined such a thing;
filled with immense joy, he merely swept, sprinkled, burned fine incense, and cut off worldly affairs to await her.
After several nights, she came again;
each time she came, a pure breeze would first arise solemnly,
followed by an extraordinary fragrance,
and the celestial maidens accompanying her grew more numerous,
their joyous pastimes daily more harmonious.
For Zhào Xù, she brought forth rare delicacies from a traveling kitchen,
all unrecognizable,
exceptionally sweet and delicious.
Each time he ate,
he would not feel hunger for ten days,
only sensing his body's energy surging and refreshed.
Zhào Xù then sought the Way of long life and enduring vision,
secretly receiving esoteric formulas.
They largely resembled the practices in the Inner Chapters of Bàopǔzǐ,
and Zhào Xù, through sincere devotion, achieved resonance.
She also brought celestial music for Zhào Xù;
immortal musicians flew playing at the eaves and pillars but did not descend,
saying to Zhào Xù:
"You are not yet ranked among immortals,
not fit to receive the proper performance,
therefore we do not descend."
The music comprised only sheng, xiao, qin, and se,
somewhat similar to the mortal world,
the rest he could not recognize,
their tones pure and clanging.
When the performance ended, clouds and mist drifted densely,
and they were already gone.
She also brought Zhào Xù precious jewels and wondrously beautiful objects,
then said:
"These things should not be seen by the mortal world;
I give them because in a past life you were destined to become immortal,
and may indulge your desires.
Yet the immortal path is secret and subtle,
its ways different from the world;
if you reveal it,
I cannot come again."
Zhào Xù made repeated vows.
Over a year later,
Zhào Xù's servant stole a glass bead and sold it in the market,
where he happened upon a foreigner,
who cupped it reverently,
offering a price of a million.
The servant, shocked, refused to comply;
the foreigner pressed him, and they fought.
The authorities investigated,
and the servant confessed everything.
Zhào Xù knew nothing of it.
That night the maiden came,
sorrowful and without her usual countenance, saying:
"The servant has leaked our affair;
I must depart."
Only then did Zhào Xù realize the servant was missing,
and was overcome with grief.
The maiden said:
"I well know your heart,
yet it is also not fitting for me to associate with you long-term,
It is merely the workings of fate.
From this point, we part ways.
Strive diligently in your cultivation,
and we shall meet again soon.
The essential principle is that when the heart dies, the body can live;
preserving essence can lead to divinity."
She then left behind five chapters of the "Xiān Shū Lóng Xí Yǐn Jué,"
which contained many cryptic phrases,
but she also pointed out and verified them for Xù,
and Xù comprehended them thoroughly.
As dawn approached, she departed.
Xù, overcome with sorrow and choked with emotion, held her hand.
The woman said:
"From where does this sorrow arise?"
Xù replied:
"It is born from the attachments of the heart."
The woman said:
"When the body is bound by the heart's attachments,
the path of ghosts is near."
Having spoken,
she straightened her body and ascended,
suddenly vanishing from sight.
All the curtains, drapes, and utensils in the room disappeared as well.
Xù was left in a daze, feeling a sense of loss.
Thereafter, whether awake or asleep,
he seemed to still sense her presence, as if they continued to interact.
In the early years of the Dàlì era,
Xù was still in Huáisì.
Later, someone saw him in Yìzhōu—
short in stature, with a handsome appearance,
often trading goods in the marketplaces.
Thus, people of the time could not recognize him.
The five chapters of the "Xiān Shū,"
each followed by Xù's own records of events,
were described in great detail.
From the "Tōng Yōu Jì."
The Girl from Yúqīng
In the early Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
a girl from Yúqīng Village,
over ten years old,
was cleaning fish by a well.
A fish jumped and fell into the well,
and as she chased after it,
she also fell inside.
An old man caught and held her,
taking her into a hollow space about a hundred paces to the side,
where she saw a hall,
exceptionally beautiful, clean, bright, and spacious.
An old woman sat in the center,
with many attendants around her.
The old man said:
"You should bow and call her 'Auntie.'"
She lingered for several days,
enjoying delicacies and sweet fruits,
and had no desire to return home.
The old woman said:
"Your parents miss you;
you cannot stay."
The old man carried her back to the top of the well
and gave her two gold coins.
When her parents saw her,
they rushed over in shock to receive her.
The girl, however, closed her eyes and clenched her fists,
urgently calling for two plates.
When they were brought,
she found them foul-smelling,
ordered them washed with ash,
then poured a coin onto each plate,
after which she returned to her normal state.
From then on, she ate no food,
drinking only broth and tea.
After a few days,
finding her home foul and filthy,
she requested to practice cultivation in a temple.
Over a year later,
a traveler seeking shelter from the heat at the temple gate
fell into a deep sleep
and suddenly dreamed of a figure in golden armor with a vermilion spear shouting:
"A celestial official resides here;
how dare you cause a disturbance?"
Startled, he awoke sweating and fled.
Later, no one knew where she went.
From the "Yì Shǐ."
Wet Nurse of the Xiāo Family
She herself said that when she was born, she encountered famine and chaos.
Her parents, believing she would not survive,
took her to Nánshān,
wrapped her in a quilt,
and abandoned her on a rock,
a place rarely visited by people.
Soon, several refugees
saw her and took pity,
and together
[The character "yǔ" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy]
they took her to an earthen niche,
moistening her lips with spring water soaked in pine needles.
After several days,
she grew healthier and stronger.
By the age of one, she could speak,
and she no longer ate other foods,
consuming only pine and cypress.
Hair began to sprout from her nose and mouth.
By the age of five or six,
she felt her body light enough to soar into the air,
reaching heights of over ten feet.
There were strange children,
sometimes three, sometimes five,
who led her in play,
though it was unknown where they came from.
Green hair gradually grew from her elbows and armpits,
nearly a foot long,
and her body became slightly capable of flight.
She roamed the seas with the group of strange children,
reaching the palace of the Queen Mother of the West,
listening to celestial music,
and eating divine fruits.
However, once a month she would visit the home of the elderly couple who had raised her,
sometimes presenting them with rare flowers or medicinal herbs.
Ten years later,
when the bandits were pacified,
her birth parents came to the mountains,
intending to find her remains for burial.
