They met the couple who had raised her,
who recounted the whole story.
They wept bitterly.
For several nights, they waited,
hoping to see her once.
Soon, she arrived,
perching on the eaves,
unwilling to come down.
Her father gazed at her, weeping in sorrow.
The elderly woman who had raised her said:
"These are your true parents;
why not come down and see them?"
She shook her head without answering
and flew away into the sky.
Her parents returned home,
unable to forget her.
They bought fruits and chestnuts,
packed provisions, and went back,
waiting for her to come again.
After a few days, she returned.
The elderly woman who had raised her called out to her,
and she descended from the sky.
Her parents rushed forward to embrace her,
weeping for a long time,
and urged her to return home.
She said:
"I am very happy here;
I do not wish to return."
Her parents offered her the fruits they had brought.
After a moment,
over ten of the strange children arrived,
perching on the trees by the eaves,
and called out:
"Come play with us;
the celestial palace is making music right now."
She went out.
As she prepared to leap,
she fell back to the ground.
The children cried out in unison:
"She has eaten mundane food;
how unfortunate!"
They then dispersed.
Her parents took her home,
where she later married and became a wife,
bearing two children.
During another famine,
she became a wet nurse.
From the "Yì Shǐ."
Xiè Zìrán
Xiè Zìrán,
her ancestors were from Yǎnzhōu.
Her father, Huán,
lived in Nánchōng, Guǒzhōu,
was recommended as a Xiàolián,
and was highly esteemed by the local community.
In the early Jiànzhōng era,
the prefectural governor Lǐ Duān,
appointed him as an assistant based on his examination for the position of collator in the Imperial Library.
Her mother, of the Xū clan,
also came from a prominent family in the county.
Zìrán was exceptionally intelligent by nature,
and did not consume meat or blood.
At the age of seven,
her mother had her follow the nun Yuèhuì,
but she returned after a year due to illness.
She was then made to follow the nun Rìlǎng,
but sought to return after ten months.
Her words often concerned Daoist matters,
and her speech was lofty and extraordinary.
Her family lived at the foot of Dàfāng Mountain,
on whose summit stood an ancient statue of Lǎojūn.
Zìrán, having paid homage there,
was unwilling to descend.
Her mother complied,
and they moved to dwell on the mountaintop.
From then on, she often recited the *Dàodé Jīng* and the inner chapters of the *Huángtíng*.
At the age of fourteen,
in the ninth month of that year,
after eating newly harvested rice,
she said:
"It is all maggots."
From then on, she ceased eating grains.
She repeatedly took soapbean pods, boiled them into a decoction, and drank it,
which caused severe vomiting and diarrhea,
expelling all the parasites from her abdomen,
leaving her body light and her vision clear.
The parasites were of various sizes, red and white,
with many different forms.
After this, she still ate cypress leaves,
consuming one branch daily.
After seven years,
she ceased eating even cypress;
after nine years,
she still did not drink water.
In the third month of the third year of the Zhēnyuán era,
she went to the Kāiyuán Temple to visit the grain-abstaining Daoist Chéng Tàixū,
and received the five-thousand-character *Zǐ Língbǎo Lù*.
In the fourth month of the sixth year,
when the prefectural governor Hán Yì arrived in the commandery,
suspecting her claims to be false,
he had her confined in the eastern chamber of the northern hall of the prefecture,
locking her up for several months.
Only then did he lead his family, young and old,
to unlock and bring her out.
Her skin and body remained as before,
her voice clear and vigorous.
Yì then had his daughter Zìmíng take her as a teacher.
Previously,
her father Huán had traveled
"Traveled" originally written as "returned,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
for many years.
Upon his return,
seeing Zìrán cultivating the Dao and not eating,
he considered it demonic and false,
saying:
"Our family has for generations upheld Confucian ways;
beyond the Five Constants,
what does not accord with the laws of the ancient kings
should not be allowed—how can there be such demonic delusion?"
He then locked her in a hall for over forty days,
but she became even more radiant and elegant.
Only then was Huán shocked and awed.
In the ninth month of the seventh year,
Hán Yì had her carried to Dàfāng Mountain,
where an altar was set up,
and he requested Chéng Tàixū to prepare the *Sāndòng Lù*.
In the eleventh month,
Zìrán was moved to dwell within the prefectural city walls.
In the ninth year of Zhēnyuán,
when the prefectural governor Lǐ Jiān arrived,
Zìrán informed him, saying:
"Dwelling within the city walls is not suitable;
I wish to reside by springs and rocks."
Jiān then built a dwelling for her on Jīnquán Mountain,
and moved Zìrán to live there.
On the mountain was a stone crevice and cavity,
with water pouring into its opening,
where one could bathe and purify body and spirit,
dispelling foul vapors.
When Zìrán first settled on the mountain,
there was a man, about forty years old,
who called himself a *tóutuó*,
but his clothing and appearance
were unlike those of a Buddhist monk.
He said:
"I hasten to visit the Perfected One."
The entire household refused him,
saying:
"There is no Perfected One here."
The *tóutuó* only laughed.
The whole family bowed to him,
but he alone would not accept Zìrán's bow.
They offered him two hundred coins,
which he ultimately did not accept;
then they offered a hand towel,
which he accepted,
saying:
"On the day we meet again, I will show this to you."
In a moment, he went out the door,
and no one knew where he went.
After a long while,
at noon, there was a great snake,
three feet in girth,
over ten feet long,
with two small white horns,
that laid its head against the door of the room,
filling the chamber with its breath.
Soon, clouds and mist gathered from all sides,
and when the mist dispersed,
the snake was also gone.
The room where Zìrán lived
could only accommodate one bed,
with just enough space around it for a person to pass.
After the white snake left,
there were often over ten small snakes,
some as large as an arm,
some larger than a thigh,
present day and night around the bed.
Some were black, some white,
some emitted breath,
some made sounds,
each coiled up,
none harming or biting the others.
There were also two tigers,
which always accompanied her when she went out or in,
but when people approached, they would hide and disappear.
The family dog barked at the tigers for a full eight years.
After she moved to dwell within the city walls,
the dog remained on Fāng Mountain
"Mountain" originally written as "out,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
After her ascension,
the dog was nowhere to be found.
As for Zìrán's room,
even her parents dared not sit together with her on the bed.
If anyone went there without reason,
there would surely be strange occurrences.
From then on, it was called the Immortal Maiden's chamber.
She often dwelt alone day and night,
in deep mountains and remote valleys,
without any fear or terror.
She also said:
"I once accidentally stepped on a snake's back;
it was as cold as ice.
Tigers walked before and behind,
exceptionally rank and foul-smelling."
She also mentioned that there were often eight celestial envoys attending beside her.
Two youths in blue garments wearing caps,
and the eight envoys in yellow garments.
Additionally, two celestial deities guarded her door and screen.
They were like the various deities in wall paintings,
holding spears and halberds.
Whenever she moved or stopped,
these envoys and deities would drive away others and guard her.
She also said:
"The mountain deity of a certain mountain is named Chén Shòu,
a man from the Wèi-Jìn period."
She also explained that the Perfected Ones hold high rank,
while Immortals hold lower rank,
and said that she was about to be appointed to the position of Perfected One of the Eastern Extremity.
On the third day of the third month in the tenth year of Zhēnyuán,
she moved into the Jīnquán Dàochǎng.
That day, the clouds and scenery were radiantly beautiful,
unlike ordinary scenes.
Zìrán said:
"On this day, the heavenly Perfected Ones and all the Immortals are gathering."
In the Jīnquán woods, there were always deer,
which never avoided people.
Even with many men and women present,
they remained tame and undisturbed.
The next day,
a superior Immortal sent a white saddle,
inlaid with precious ornaments.
The superior Immortal said:
"Give this to her;
this place is suitable for her to dwell in peace."
On the eighth day of the fifth month,
the Golden Mother, Primordial Sovereign, sent Envoy Lú to descend to her,
staying from noon until late night;
on the twentieth day of the sixth month, Envoy Wén came,
staying from noon until evening;
on the first day of the seventh month,
Envoys Cuī and Zhāng,
stayed from dawn until noon.
They mostly spoke of matters concerning the immortal officials and their bureaus,
saying that in the upper realm they enjoy playing chess,
and there is much music.
In casual conversation, he often discussed the profound and mysterious principles of the supreme Way.
He also said:
"The thousands of snakes and insects on this mountain
have all been driven westward,
and the mountain is entirely suppressed by dragons."
In the ritual arena, there were always two tigers, five qílín, and two green luán birds,
sometimes in front, sometimes behind,
sometimes flying, sometimes calling.
The qílín resembled horses in shape,
with five-colored bodies and horns;
among the purple qílín,
the one with a white mane and tail often walked in front,
raising its tail like a whisk
(The character "whisk" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy
On the eleventh day of the seventh month,
the immortal messenger Dù descended upon the stone altar,
holding a talisman,
a pill resembling a medicinal pellet,
which he had Zìrán take naturally.
On the fifteenth day,
five incense burners should be lit on the altar,
and five inside the chamber,
for at that time, the Perfected One would come each time.
At the fifth watch on the fifteenth day,
seven figures in black attire arrived,
one among them named Zhōnghuá,
said:
"At mealtime, the Supreme Perfected One will arrive."
After a long while, the messenger Lú arrived,
saying:
"The Golden Mother is coming."
In a moment,
the Golden Mother descended into the courtyard,
and Zìrán bowed in reverence.
The Mother said:
"It has been two kalpas since I parted from you!"
She personally arranged tables and settings,
with rare treasures overflowing before the eyes.
She then invited Zìrán to sit.
Initially,
the messenger Lú stood in attendance,
but after a while,
he was also ordered to sit.
Lú said:
"I shall briefly visit the Zǐjí Palace."
To observe the Mid-Year Festival ritual arena,
where officials, scholars, and commoners were all gathered.
Shortly after, the messenger Lú returned and said:
"This occasion surpasses all previous vegetarian feasts."
When asked the reason,
he replied:
"This time, nipple incense was not burned,
as the heavenly beings detest nipple incense.
Only blended incense may be burned."
On the seventh day,
the two messengers Cuī and Zhāng arrived,
asking Zìrán:
"Can you reside in Chánglín?"
He replied:
"I cannot."
The two messengers appeared displeased.
On the twenty-second day before noon,
the Golden Mother descended again and said:
"For refusing to reside in Chánglín,
you have been demoted one rank."
Chánglín is a celestial palace.
At the hour of xū, the Golden Mother departed,
and only then did the messenger Cuī say:
"In the upper realm, the Golden Mother is the most revered."
She bestowed a vessel of medicine,
yellow and white in color,
with a sweet taste.
Zìrán did not finish consuming it,
and it was taken back.
She also presented a set of garments,
interwoven with vermilion, jade-green, and emerald colors,
plain on the outside,
but patterned within,
the garments were ethereal,
and when held, they did not seem to touch the hand.
They were also taken back for the time being,
"Later, we shall come to fetch you."
She also brought a branch of peaches,
larger than an arm,
with thirty peaches on it,
jade-green in color,
as large as bowls.
She said:
"These are still the smaller ones."
That day, the Golden Mother rode a luán bird,
while her attendants all rode dragons and cranes,
amidst five-colored clouds and mist,
floating beneath them.
The Golden Mother said:
"We shall now pass through the prefecture among the host of immortals."
After they departed,
looking from afar, they were all seen within the clouds.
That day, the prefecture's horse stables, kitchens, and halberd gates all reported:
"A long rainbow has entered the prefecture."
The next day, Lǐ Jiān inquired of Zìrán,
and only then was it verified.
The Zǐjí Palace also reported a rainbow entering,
witnessed by people far and near.
On the ninth, tenth, and eleventh days of the eighth month,
groups of immortals came daily,
conveying the Golden Mother's decree,
urgently ordering him to let his hair hang loose for forty days.
The Golden Mother would then come personally.
The descending messenger sometimes said his surname was Cuī, given name Mǒu
(The character "Mǒu" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Huáng manuscript copy
carrying a board,
two chǐ wide,
five chǐ long,
adorned with nine colors.
Whenever the host of immortals was about to arrive,
the walls would glow brightly like mirrors,
and each immortal also had their own tables and attendants.
Whenever Zìrán let his hair hang loose,
yellow clouds would swirl around his body.
There were also seven figures,
wearing yellow garments and caps,
attending to his left and right.
From the nineteenth day of the eighth month onward,
he recited the Huángtíng Jīng ten times daily.
While reciting, two young attendants stood by,
and after each recitation, it was transcribed;
upon reaching ten recitations,
one of the young attendants would take it up to the upper realm.
On the first day of the ninth month,
the host of immortals came again,
bringing a branch of peaches,
as large as a dou measure,
half red, half yellow, and half crimson,
saying
(The character "saying" was originally written as "cloud" [雲],
corrected based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy
"Your hometown is abundant with this fruit."
He cut a slice to eat,
and the rest was taken back by the attendants.
On the fifth day of the ninth month,
the Golden Mother came again,
holding three talismans,
ordering him to swallow them,
not allowing them to touch water;
after taking them, he felt his body and mind exceptionally uplifted.
The Golden Mother said:
"One more visit, and then I shall not come again."
She then pointed to an immortal beside her and said:
"This is of your same kind."
At dawn on the fifteenth day,
an immortal messenger arrived,
not stating his name,
bringing three talismans,
conveying the Golden Mother's decree,
ordering him to take them all.
He also brought six slices of peach for him to eat;
after eating three slices,
the rest was taken away.
The messenger did not return until dusk.
On the eleventh day of the tenth month,
while entering the meditation chamber,
an immortal came to summon him,
and he immediately mounted a qílín and ascended to heaven.
Celestial garments were brought to welcome him,
and the clothes Zìrán had been wearing were left on the rope bed;
upon returning,
he put on his old garments,
placing the celestial garments on a crane's back to be taken away.
It was said:
"When departing, he rode a qílín;
when returning, he rode a crane."
On the nineteenth day,
the immortal messenger Lú came,
staying from chén to wèi before departing.
Whenever the heavenly envoys descended,
thousands of luán birds and cranes would gather,
and hosts of immortals would assemble in full.
Those of higher rank rode luán birds,
the next rode qílín,
and the next rode dragons.
The wings of each luán bird and crane spanned over a zhàng in length.
Recently, a great bird descended upon Cháng'ān,
similar in size to a luán bird,
but its feathers and colors were different.
It was said that the one descending upon Cháng'ān was named the celestial què,
also called the divine què,
and whenever it descended, the state would receive great fortune.
On the twenty-fifth day,
blood seeped from all the pores of his body,
staining his clothes.
All formed patterns of flowing water and horizontal lines like a draped cloak.
When washed in the stream,
they became even more distinct;
viewed in sunlight, they appeared golden,
and when touched, they sounded like metal.
On the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh days,
the Lady of the Eastern Peak came together,
urging her to bathe,
using fragrant water,
but not allowing any frankincense.
She also said:
"In heaven there are gods,
not the spirits of ghosts.
In the upper realms, there are no shaven-headed people;
if one attains the Dao,
all wear caps,
and their merit is the same.
For all fasting meals,
one must avoid tasting them,
and especially maintain purity,
as with the utensils.
The various gods of heaven
descend to observe during each fast,
deeply detesting impurity,
not only bringing no blessings,
but also incurring guilt."
Lǐ Jiān often recited scriptures with the Lady at the table,
first reading the outer chapters,
then the inner chapters,
the inner ones being the original text from the Biography of Lady Wèi.
Generally, those who concentrate and study diligently gain blessings,
while those who act carelessly incur guilt, which is immediately evident.
She naturally abstained from grains,
for a total of thirteen years.
While sleeping day and night,
seal marks suddenly appeared on her two knees,
smaller than official seals in the human world,
with ancient seal script characters on all four sides,
shining like white jade.
This year in the first month,
the seals moved to the inner sides of her knees,
and when her knees were brought together, the two seals matched perfectly,
without the slightest discrepancy.
She also possessed divine power,
able to travel two thousand lǐ in a day,
or at times a thousand lǐ,
with no one knowing.
In the deep darkness of night,
she could perceive even the finest details.
She also did not wear silk or cotton,
did not approach fire in the cold,
and did not fan herself in the heat.
When people asked about good or bad fortune,
she knew everything.
Her nature was solemn, deep, and secretive;
she did not speak of matters,
not even to her parents.
Because Lǐ Jiān revered the supreme Dao,
she gradually spoke a little,
saying:
"Heaven also wishes to send those in the world who serve the Dao to harmonize with it,
so that they may honor and illuminate the Daoist teachings."
She also said:
"When paying respects to revered images,
four bows are considered weighty,
three bows are considered light."
She also resided at the Jīnquán Dàochǎng,
and whenever she sat in meditation, herds of deer would always come.
She also said:
"If a person can purify a single room,
burn incense, and recite the Huángtíng Jīng or the Dàodé Jīng,
whether once
or seven times,
it surpasses all acts of charity and fasting.
Reciting scriptures lies in focused intent,
not in the number of repetitions.
Those who undertake this
but give up midway
suffer even greater loss,
worse than never having started at all.
Be cautious, be cautious!
Human life is of utmost importance;
killing many people shortens one's years and cuts life short.
The retribution for such actions
never ceases."
Also, whenever she traveled, she often heard heavenly music,
always beginning with the Bùxū Cí,
mostly stopping at three pieces,
the first, fifth, and eighth.
After the Bùxū,
music was played,
starting with the yún'áo.
The yún'áo is round like a mirror,
with strings.
When transmitting the Daoist methods,
one must choose the most trustworthy people.
In the Biography of Lady Wèi,
it strictly prohibits spreading the teachings,
only allowing secrecy,
fearing it may deviate from moderation.
The power of medicine can only prolong life;
to ascend to heaven and ride the light,
one must cultivate the Dao and take medicine.
Cultivating the Dao differs somewhat;
eating cypress leaves can enable one to abstain from grains.
If side cypress is hard to find in the mountains,
ordinary cypress leaves will do,
as long as they are not near graves,
they can be consumed,
and those on rocks are especially good.
Sun-dried ones are hard to manage;
picking and eating them fresh,
while still moist,
is easier to clear and benefits people.
Generally, cypress leaves, poria cocos, wolfberries, and sesame
can all grant longevity and clear vision,
and can be tested.
Cultivating the Dao requires quiet dwelling in mountains and forests,
not close to villages.
Cities are unsuitable,
because of the meat and fish smells;
divine immortals will not descend,
contrary to the Dao.
For refining medicine and drinking water,
spring water should be used,
well water is especially disliked.
One must also stay away from home and blood relatives,
lest feelings of affection suddenly arise,
which is not the conduct of cultivation.
Generally, eating rice makes the body heavy,
eating wheat makes it light.
To abstain from grains and enter the mountains,
one must follow various methods,
to eliminate the three worms and hidden corpses.
For breath control,
first regulate the breath,
then hold it,
breathing not through the mouth or nose,
letting it fill the body freely,
then life and death cannot invade.
In the ninth month of that year,
the rain was heavy,
Zìrán went from Jīnquán to Nánshān to visit Chéng Jūn,
arriving at the mountain at dawn,
with clothes and shoes not wet.
When questioned,
she said:
"I just left Jīnquán."
Chéng Jūn found it very strange.
On the ninth day of the eleventh month,
she went to the prefecture to bid farewell to Lǐ Jiān,
saying:
"I will leave in the middle of the month."
She did not enter the meditation room again.
At the chén hour on the twentieth day,
she ascended to heaven in broad daylight at the Jīnquán Dàochǎng,
with thousands of men and women
all watching in admiration.
Her grandmother Zhōu shì, mother Xū shì, younger sister Zìróu, and disciple Lǐ shēng
heard her parting words:
"Diligently cultivate the supreme Dao."
Soon, five-colored clouds stretched across the river,
with heavenly music and rare fragrances,
lingering for a long time.
The clothes, cap, hairpins, and robe she wore—ten items in total—
were left on the small rope bed,
tied as before.
Prefect Lǐ Jiān reported to the court,
and an imperial edict praised her.
Lǐ Jiān composed the "Jīnquán Dàochǎng Stele,"
recording the whole story in a biography,
saying:
"In heaven there is a white jade hall,
where Lǎojūn resides.
On the hall walls are listed the names of true immortals,
like wall records in the human world.
At times, red writing notes below:
'Descended to the world as an emperor' or as a 'prime minister.'"
Also, when Zìrán was about to ascend to heaven,
there were fifty-two characters written on the east wall inside the hall,
saying:
"A message to the master and all family members:
Just preserve your whole selves,
do not give rise to sorrow,
you can diligently cultivate merit.
Together with all good hearts,
establish fields of blessing,
fast purely and contemplate the Dao.
After a hundred kalpas,
I hope there will be good karma,
and we will meet early in the land of clear origins,
then we shall see each other."
The writing remains.
From the Jíxiān Lù.
Lú Méiniáng.
Cuī Shàoxuán was the youngest daughter of Cuī Gōng, the Prefect of Fénzhōu during the Táng dynasty.
Her mother dreamed of a divine being,
clad in silk garments,
riding a red dragon,
holding a purple case,
and receiving it amidst the azure clouds.
She then became pregnant and gave birth to Shàoxuán after fourteen months.
Upon her birth, an extraordinary fragrance enveloped her.
She was dignified and exceptionally beautiful,
with dark blue hair covering her eyes
and earrings reaching her chin.
On her right hand was a mark reading "Wife of Lú Zìliè."
Eighteen years later, she married Lú Chuí,
whose childhood name was Zìliè.
A little over a year later,
Chuí was assigned to official duties in Mǐnzhōng.
While passing through Jiànxī,
he gazed into the distance at Wǔyí Mountain
and suddenly saw azure clouds approaching from the eastern peak.
Within them was a divine being,
wearing an emerald crown and crimson robes,
who addressed Chuí, saying:
"Has Yùhuá Jūn arrived?"
Chuí, puzzled by these words, asked:
"Who is Yùhuá Jūn?"
The being replied:
"Your wife is Yùhuá Jūn."
Chuí then relayed this to his wife.
She said:
"Fúsāng Fūrén and Zǐxiāo Yuánjūn have indeed come to welcome me!
The matter is now clear;
it can no longer be concealed."
She then straightened her attire and went out to meet the divine being.
They conversed for a long time,
but Chuí could not understand the language of Fūrén.
After a moment, she bowed and withdrew.
Chuí bowed and inquired further.
The being said:
"Although Shàoxuán was born of mortal womb,
she is not the product of earthly karma.
She once resided in the Heaven of Non-Desire,
serving as the Left Attendant Scribe to the Jade Emperor,
with the title Yùhuá Jūn,
overseeing the thirty-six grottoes of Daoist practitioners in the mortal realm.
Every year on the Autumn Equinox,
she would bring the register to visit those dedicated to the Dao.
Once, she was demoted
for an offense committed with four others from the same palace.
While retreating to a quiet chamber,
she lamented the matter,
and in a moment of distraction, entertained worldly desires.
The Supreme Elder reprimanded her
and exiled her to the mortal realm,
where she became your wife for twenty-three years.
Now, having encountered Zǐxiāo Yuánjūn, who arrived earlier,
she will no longer remain close to you."
Upon reaching Mǐnzhōng,
she spent her days alone in a quiet chamber.
Chuí, both astonished and fearful,
dared not enter her space.
Often, female transcendents,
sometimes two, sometimes four,
clad in long silk garments,
with ancient-style coiled hair,
and bodies radiating light
as bright as day,
would visit her chamber.
They would ascend to the hall, sit together on couches,
and converse and laugh throughout the night.
When Chuí went to observe them,
he found their speech to be that of celestial beings,
unintelligible to him.
When he tried to inquire,
they said:
"The secrets of the immortals
must not be divulged,
especially as the burden of karma is heavy.
It is necessary to remain concealed."
Chuí heeded their admonition
and often kept their affairs secret.
After Chuí left his official post,
and Cuī Gōng also resigned from his position,
the family settled in Luòyáng.
Bound by his wife's oath,
Chuí dared not reveal anything to Gōng.
Two years later,
she said to Chuí:
"Shàoxuán's father's lifespan
will end on the seventeenth day of the second month.
Although I am an immortal born into the mortal world,
I owe him the grace of upbringing.
If I do not save him,
I would fail in my duty of repayment."
She then addressed her father, saying:
"Your life, honored father,
will reach its end on the seventeenth day of the second month.
Shàoxuán, indebted to your toilsome care,
cannot but protect you."
She then opened a crimson case
and took out the golden texts of Fúsāng Dàdì,
the Huángtíng and Nèijǐng scriptures,
presenting them to her father, saying:
"Your lifespan, honored father,
has reached its natural limit.
Without these texts,
salvation would be impossible.
I now bestow them upon you.
Read them ten thousand times
to extend your life by twelve years."
She then instructed Gōng to bathe, face south, and kneel.
Shàoxuán stood before a small table,
prepared a merit petition,
wrote it on blue paper,
sealed it in a plain case,
and presented it to the Supreme Deity.
She also summoned the True Lord of the Southern Dipper,
who oversees life,
to submit the petition to the Supreme Deity.
Shortly after,
three figures in crimson robes descended from the sky,
knelt before Shàoxuán,
presented dried meat delicacies,
drank three cups of wine,
took the merit petition, and departed.
Gōng was greatly astonished
and privately questioned Chuí,
but Chuí kept it secret.
Over a month later,
she suddenly instructed Chuí, saying:
"The companions of the Jade Clarity
will soon exonerate me before the Supreme Elder.
I am now summoned again to serve as the Left Attendant Scribe Yùhuá Jūn to the Jade Emperor,
overseeing the transformation of primordial essence and energy
and distributing immortal ranks.
I am about to return my spirit
to the formless,
to serve the Jade Emperor once more
and return to the Jade Clarity.
Do not reveal these words,
lest my parents grieve.
Moreover, having disclosed the method of saving my father,
I have leaked immortal secrets
and cannot remain long.
My mortal affections end here."
Chuí knelt before her,
weeping and sobbing, saying:
"I, a lowly mortal like an ant or louse,
have defiled an immortal,
condemning myself to eternal filth and impurity,
unable to ascend.
I beg for your guidance
to save me from this deep affliction,
so I may never forget your grace."
Shàoxuán said:
"I will leave you a poem.
The writings of the celestial beings in the upper realm
are all in cloud-dragon seal script.
When viewed in the mortal realm,
they may be distorted or incomplete,
and none can comprehend them.
I shall take up the brush and record it."
The verses read:
"Attained from the One Origin,
not bestowed by heaven.
The truth of the Great Elder,
the supreme immortal.
Light contained, shadow concealed,
form manifest in nature.
True peace is not sought;
the spirit abides long.
Pure and beautiful is its essence,
its substance both firm and gentle.
In crimson skies and azure voids,
companions of the highest sages.
A hundred years hence,
only an empty mound remains."
Chuí bowed deeply and received the verses,
but found their meaning obscure.
He knelt and begged for an explanation
to illuminate their meaning.
Shàoxuán said:
"Your understanding of the Dao
is not yet mature.
The meaning of this celestial verse
will become clear in time.
In the year of Bǐngshēn,
you will meet a gentleman from Lángyá who can interpret it.
At that time, he will explain it to you,
and you will glimpse the celestial path.
Until then, guard it well."
With these words, she passed away.
Nine days later, during her burial,
the coffin felt weightless.
When opened for inspection,
only her clothes remained—she had shed her mortal form.
She had lived in the chamber for eighteen years.
He resided in Mǐn for three years,
returned to Luò for two,
and spent twenty-three years among mortals.
Later, both Chuí and Gōng preserved her poems,
showing them to those who were well-versed in Confucianism and Daoism,
yet none could comprehend them.
In the Jǐngshēn year,
the Jiǔyí Daoist priest Wáng Fānggǔ,
whose ancestors were from Lángyá,
was returning from a journey to Huàyuè
and stopped by Shǎnjiāo.
At that time, Chuí was also a guest in that commandery.
Over poetry and wine one night,
they discussed matters of immortals.
All present revered the Dao and esteemed virtue,
each recounting their own extraordinary experiences.
Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ Guō Gù, Zuǒ Shíyí Qí Tuī, Yòu Sīmǎ Wéi Zōngqīng, and Wáng Jiàn were all old acquaintances of Cuī Gōng,
and thus inquired of Chuí about Shào Xuán's story.
Chuí shed tears,
regretting that no one had ever understood the poems left by his wife.
Fānggǔ requested the verses,
and after reciting them for a moment,
he grasped their meaning.
He sighed and said:
"The transformations of the Great Void,
the Great Immortal of Jīnhuá,
have indeed been passed down to later learners!"
All the seated guests listened intently to his words,
as he explained each line,
flowing like strung pearls,
in several thousand words,
until he had fully conveyed their meaning.
He then instructed Chuí to take up the brush
and record the master's words in full,
titled *Shào Xuán Xuánzhū Xīn Jìng*.
Devotees of the Dao
often kept copies in their homes.
From *Shào Xuán Běn Zhuàn*.
Miàonǚ
In the first year of the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty, in the fifth month,
in Jīngdé County of Xuān Prefecture, there was a maid of the Cuī family,
named Miàonǚ,
who was about thirteen or fourteen years old.
One evening, while drawing water in the courtyard,
she suddenly saw a monk
who struck her three times in succession with his monk's staff.
Startled and terrified, she collapsed,
and then complained of heart pain.
In a moment, she became confused and disoriented;
acupuncture and moxibustion could not diagnose it.
After several days, she improved slightly,
but vomiting and diarrhea did not cease.
When she recovered,
she no longer ate;
if she ate, she would immediately vomit,
consuming only hollyhock flowers and salted tea.
Thereafter, she became thin and clear-spirited,
her complexion fresh and radiant.
Only then did she explain that during her initial period of unconsciousness,
she saw a person leading her, riding on white mist,
to a place
with very solemn palaces,
all resembling the Western Paradise of Buddhism.
Among the heavenly immortals there,
many were Miàonǚ's kin.
They said she was originally the youngest daughter of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King,
but for leaking matters from the heavenly gates,
she was banished to the mortal world,
and this was already her second lifetime.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra's surname was Wéi, his given name Kuān;
his younger brother was older,
and was titled Shàngzūn.
His wife's surname was Lǐ,
and she was titled Shànlún.
The Eastern King Duke was her youngest paternal uncle,
named Kuò,
the eighth [in the family].
Miàonǚ called herself Xiǎoniáng,
saying her father and relatives were traveling together in the world searching for her,
and now they had found her here.
The monk she had seen earlier struck her waist
to make her vomit and purge the filthy, mundane qi hidden within,
so that she could then ascend to heaven.
The dwellings in heaven were magnificent and splendid,
each having relatives and servants,
no different from the human world.
The servant she employed was named Qúnjiǎo,
the maids were named Jīnxiāo, Piāntiáo
(The character "tiáo" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy)
, and Fènglóu.
In her previous life, she had a son,
named Yáo,
and when she saw him now, she still recognized him.
On the day she came [to this world],
she parted from her son on the Golden Bridge,
and composed a poem,
of which she only remembered two lines:
"Hands grasping the bridge pillar, standing,
Tears dripping, filling the Heavenly River."
At times she would recite this herself,
overwhelmed with sorrow.
For five or six days she lay ill like this,
narrating past events.
One morning,
she suddenly said that Shàngzūn, her mother, and various heavenly immortals and servants
had all come to pay respects and give thanks,
and then, through spiritual possession, they spoke, saying:
"Our young daughter is foolish and ignorant,
fallen into the human world,
long favored by your care,
we are endlessly ashamed."
Her family was initially very alarmed,
but after a long while, they began to converse with them,
and the immortals all relied on her to narrate.
They also said:
"We are temporarily borrowing the young girl's residence
to speak with people of the world."
When Shàngzūn spoke,
it was a man's voice;
when Shànlún, her mother, spoke,
it was a woman's voice;
each changed their speech accordingly.
Thus, sometimes coming, sometimes going,
as days and months passed,
they talked, joked, and bantered
just like ordinary people.
Whenever they came, the room would fill with fragrance;
sometimes it was the scent of wine,
sometimes the fragrance of lotus flowers.
Later, Miàonǚ's original condition returned as before.
Suddenly one day,
Miàonǚ sang.
At that time, the weather was clear and bright,
when suddenly in the sky there appeared a cloud as large as a mat,
hovering above.
Soon, from within the cloud came the sound of a shēng,
its tone clear and resonant.
The whole family looked up and listened,
deeply moved in spirit.
Miàonǚ called for Dàláng to sing again,
and his voice became even more vigorous.
Miàonǚ sang,
her expression calm and natural,
her melody wondrous, clear, and smooth beyond words.
There was also a song titled "Sāng Liǔ Tiáo".
She also said her mother was just then in the clouds.
This went on all day before dispersing.
After about ten days,
she suddenly said:
"Two people in the family are about to suffer from swellings;
I will bear the affliction for them."
Several days later,
sure enough, on Miàonǚ's back and under her ribs,
two swellings appeared,
each as large as a cup,
causing extraordinary pain.
After a day,
seeing her in such agony, her mistress
ordered prayers for her relief.
Miàonǚ then fell into a deep, trance-like sleep.
Suddenly she spoke, instructing them to add incense,
and on the bell tower, she called to the heavenly immortals, chanting penitential prayers.
Her voice was clear and bright,
entirely in harmony with the Western [Paradise].
After about an hour,
she awoke, and the swellings subsided,
soon returning to normal.
Later, another maid suddenly fell seriously ill.
Miàonǚ said:
"I will ask Dàláng to send troops to rescue you."
The girl then appeared to be asleep.
After a short while, she awoke again,
saying the troops had arrived.
She urgently ordered the place to be swept and cleaned,
incense added to the quiet room,
then began to deploy the troops and horses,
assigning several to inspect certain places,
and several to bind the evil ghosts on the sick person's body.
The maid then recovered as before,
and said she saw the forms of the troops and horses,
like divine kings in wall paintings,
wearing barbarian hats on their heads,
all adorned with gold inlay.
The young girl of the family saw this,
and after a long while, it vanished.
The great general's surname was Xǔ, given name Guāng,
the lesser general was called Chén Wàn.
Whenever summoned to be dispatched,
the troops were very numerous,
their coming and going like the sound of wind and rain.
After another ten days or so,
she suddenly said the Weaving Maid was about to marry,
and she must go to watch.
Upon waking from sleep, she recounted:
"The wedding ceremony is exactly like that in the human world."
She said the girl's name was Chuílíngzi,
marrying into the Xuē family;
many details are not fully recorded.
Her family often had Miàonǚ do embroidery.
Suddenly she said she needed to leave temporarily,
and asked the maid Fènglóu to do the embroidery instead.
Thus, for a whole day,
she took on Fènglóu's appearance and demeanor.
Her spirit was different at times,
her embroidery skillfully exquisite,
and her speed doubled compared to usual,
but she did not speak with others,
only occasionally bowing her head and smiling.
After a long while, she said she had returned,
and immediately resumed her original state,
with no trace of Fènglóu's appearance.
She said Dàláng and the monk Sēngqié were coming to see the lady,
so they swept the room, added incense,
and brewed tea to await them.
Soon they arrived,
conveying greetings and inquiries.
Miàonǚ suddenly laughed and said:
"Why is Dàláng wrestling with the venerable monk?"
At that moment, the whole family heard the sound of vigorous stomping and tumbling on the bed,
which lasted a long time before they left.
Sometimes she said she went to the West to drink,
and upon returning, vomited wine,
lying drunk all day.
One evening,
she said she would take one soul of the lady and one soul of the young lady to go sightseeing,
to let them converse and laugh with Shànlún and friends.
That night,
the lady and others all dreamed of being in one place,
enjoying themselves with many people.
At dawn, Miàonǚ
asked the young lady about her dream,
and every detail matched.
For over a month like this, she abstained from food.
Suddenly one day, she said sorrowfully and tearfully:
"Dàláng and mother are calling me back."
It was very mournful.
She said painfully:
"Having been in the mortal world for a long time,
I am deeply attached to the lady,
unable to bear leaving her."
For several days like this, she wept.
She also said:
"It is not fitting for me to interact with worldly people,
but you insist on staying;
what can be done about it?"
Then she bid farewell into the air,
her words quite solemn,
and from then on gradually fell silent.
She told the lady:
"I am so attached that I cannot leave.
Since I am in the human world,
I still need food and drink.
Just give me a red robe to wear
and some laxative medicine."
As requested, these were given to her,
and she gradually began to eat and drink.
Although she occasionally spoke of future events,
none came to pass.
There were many detailed matters
that cannot all be recorded.
The family's account of the events ends here,
and it is unknown what later became of the maidservant.
From Tōng Yōu Jì
Wú Qīng's Wife
In the twelfth year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
Wú Qīng, a minor village head of Húchéng in Guózhōu,
had a wife named Yáng Shì,
also known as Jiānzhēn.
She lived in Chēgǔ Village, Tiānxiān Township.
Due to a headache,
she stopped eating.
From spring to summer,
she would often sit quietly in meditation,
each time for several days.
Villagers came to see her,
and on three occasions,
they saw her obtain a total of twenty-one pills of medicine,
which she swallowed with water;
two bowls of jade liquid broth,
which she brewed into tea and drank.
On the night of the fifteenth day of the fourth month,
she burned incense and sat upright,
when suddenly she disappeared.
On the seventeenth day,
the county magistrate personally burned incense and prayed.
That night, during the fourth watch,
the oxen and donkeys were startled,
and a robe was seen among the thorns on the wall;
moments later,
Yáng Shì was seen sitting naked on the ox shed roof,
with her clothes in front of her,
her body extremely cold.
They helped her down to the courtyard,
and with the villagers burning incense and striking the chime,
she finally awoke at chen hour.
She said that at noon on the fourteenth day,
she saw an immortal crane that spoke to her:
"Wash your head."
On the fifteenth day, she bathed,
and at the fifth watch,
two female Daoists, along with a crane
("Crane" originally written as "dragon,"
corrected according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy)
riding on five-colored clouds, arrived,
and she then mounted the crane and left.
She arrived at Xiānfāng Terrace,
where she saw a Daoist who said:
"On Huà Shān, there are five companions traveling together,
brewing tea and awaiting you."
From Biànzhōu, surnamed Lǚ,
named Dézhēn;
from Tóngzhōu, surnamed Zhāng,
named Xiānzhēn;
from Yìzhōu, surnamed Mǎ,
named Biànzhēn;
from Sòngzhōu, surnamed Wáng,
named Xìnzhēn.
They also went to the eastern sea, where there were many trees on the mountain,
and to the mountains on the Tibetan border,
with all five companions following along.
Returning to Xiānfāng Terrace,
she saw immortal bones,
and a revered master said:
"These are the immortal bones of three generations of the Yáng family."
He instructed her to pay her respects.
She then requested to return, saying:
"I have an elderly father at home."
Thus, she returned.
A female Daoist rode a crane to escort her back.
She said:
"I received one immortal poem,
and four more poems."
Written on chestnut bark, it said:
"The Dao awakens the sincere heart, clarity gradually grows,
Heaven commands fasting to test true devotion.
Beyond the clouds, immortal songs blend with pipes and flutes,
Amidst flowers, the wind leads the steps of the void's chant."
The second poem said:
"With a clear heart and tranquil surroundings, I hear wondrous fragrance,
recalling the past, I awaited
("With a clear heart" and nine other characters were originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng manuscript)
your dwelling in seclusion.
A single star, lotus flower, mountain-top meal,
immortal's palm scripture of Solomon's seal."
The third poem said:
"Birds cannot reach, people cannot climb,
in seclusion for ten years, never descending the mountain.
Who will deliver the short letter in my sleeve?
The Huà Shān Daoist returns from selling medicine."
The fourth poem said:
"As the sun sets, I burn incense and sit at the altar
("Altar" originally written as "awake,"
corrected according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy)
for the ceremony,
courtyard flowers damp with dew as the night deepens.
Pure water, immortal lad brewing jade liquid,
spring night, feathered guest refining golden elixir."
The fifth poem said:
"Gathering thoughts, deep contemplation draws colorful clouds,
burning incense in an empty room facing misty blossoms.
The Dao unites with the clouds, roaming the purple mansion,
serene true realm brings auspiciousness to the royal house."
From Yì Shǐ
Guō Hàn
Guǒ Hàn of Tàiyuán,
from youth was refined and noble,
possessing a pure and lofty character.
His appearance and bearing were handsome and elegant,
he was skilled in discourse,
and excelled at cursive and clerical script.
Orphaned early, he lived alone.
During the height of summer,
he lay in the courtyard under the moonlight.
A cool breeze arose at that moment,
and he gradually noticed a fragrance growing stronger.
Guǒ Hàn found this very strange.
Looking up into the sky,
he saw someone descending slowly and gracefully,
coming directly before Guǒ Hàn.
It was a young maiden.
Radiantly beautiful, peerless in her generation,
her brilliance dazzled the eyes.
She wore robes of dark silk gauze,
trailed a shawl of frost-like gossamer,
donned a phoenix crown adorned with kingfisher feathers,
and trod in slippers embroidered with jade-like patterns and the nine insignia.
Two maidservants accompanied her,
both of exceptional beauty,
stirring and captivating to the heart and spirit.
Guǒ Hàn straightened his clothes and cap,
rose from his couch and bowed in reverence, saying:
"I never imagined a noble spirit would descend from afar.
I pray you bestow your virtuous words."
The maiden smiled and said:
"I am the Weaving Maiden from heaven.
For long I have had no companion,
and my happy meetings have been obstructed and distant,
leaving my secluded heart full of longing.
The Lord on High has granted me leave to wander the mortal realm.
I admire your pure character,
and wish to entrust myself to this divine bond."
Guǒ Hàn said:
"I dare not hope for this,
yet my feelings are all the more deeply moved."
The maiden ordered her maids to sweep the room clean,
hung curtains of frosty mist and crimson silk,
spread a mat of crystal and jade splendor,
and fanned a breeze-summoning fan,
making it feel like clear autumn.
Then hand in hand they ascended to the chamber,
removed their garments and lay together.
Her undergarment of light crimson silk
was like a small perfume sachet,
its scent filling the entire room.
There was a dragon-brain pillow for two,
covered by a quilt embroidered with paired threads in a mandarin duck pattern.
Her soft flesh and smooth body,
deep affection and intimate manner,
were exquisitely beautiful beyond compare.
As dawn approached, she took her leave.
The powder on her face remained as before.
Guǒ Hàn tried wiping it,
and found it was her natural complexion.
Guǒ Hàn saw her out the door,
and she soared into the clouds and departed.
From then on, she came every night,
and their affection grew increasingly intense.
Guǒ Hàn teased her, saying:
"Where is the Herdboy?
How dare you travel alone?"
She replied:
"The changes of yīn and yáng,
what concern are they of his?
Moreover, the Milky Way separates us,
and he cannot know;
even if he did know,
it would be no cause for worry."
Then, stroking Guǒ Hàn's chest, she said:
"It is merely that people of the world lack clear perception."
Guǒ Hàn also asked:
"You, my lady, have entrusted your spirit to the celestial bodies.
Regarding the gateways of those celestial bodies,
may I hear of them?"
She replied:
"Viewed from the mortal world,
they are seen only as stars,
but within them naturally exist palaces and dwellings,
where hosts of immortals roam and observe.
The essence of all things
each has its image in heaven,
and takes form on earth.
Changes among those below
must manifest in the heavens above.
As I observe them now,
I recognize them all clearly and distinctly."
Thereupon, she pointed out for Guǒ Hàn the positions and divisions of the constellations,
detailing their movements and measures exhaustively.
What people of that time did not comprehend,
Guǒ Hàn thus came to understand thoroughly.
Later, as the Seventh Night approached,
she suddenly stopped coming.
After several nights, she finally arrived.
Guǒ Hàn asked:
"Was the meeting joyful?"
Smiling, she replied:
"How can heaven compare to the mortal world?
It is simply that the ordained cycle of feelings demanded it,
not for any other reason.
Do not be jealous, sir."
He asked:
"Why were you so late in coming?"
She answered:
"Five days among men
is but one evening there."
She also brought Guǒ Hàn celestial delicacies,
all things not of this world.
Looking carefully at her garment,
he saw it had no seams.
Guǒ Hàn asked her about it.
She said to Guǒ Hàn:
"Heavenly garments are not made with needle and thread."
Each time she left,
she would always take her clothes with her.
After a year had passed,
suddenly one evening,
her countenance was sorrowful and distressed,
tears streaming down her face.
Taking Guǒ Hàn's hand, she said:
"The Emperor's command sets a deadline;
now we must part forever."
Then she choked with sobs, unable to contain herself.
Guǒ Hàn, startled and dismayed, asked:
"How many days remain?"
She replied:
"Only this very night."
Then they wept in sorrow,
staying awake until dawn.
At daybreak,
they embraced and parted.
She left a seven-treasure bowl as a parting gift,
saying that on a certain day the following year,
she would send a letter with greetings.
Guǒ Hàn gave her a pair of jade rings in reply.
Then she stepped into the air and departed,
looking back and waving her hand,
a long time before finally vanishing.
Guǒ Hàn pined for her until he fell ill,
never forgetting her for a moment.
The next year, on the appointed day,
sure enough, the former maidservant came,
delivering a letter.
Guǒ Hàn then opened the seal.
The paper was of blue silk,
the characters written in red lead,
the language pure and lovely,
the feelings of longing layered deep.
At the end of the letter were two poems.
The poems said:
"Though the River of Stars is said to be wide,
the Seventh Night still holds a promised time.
But for us lovers, it is finally over;
when again shall we have a joyful meeting?"
And also:
"Vermilion towers overlook the clear Han,
jade palaces govern purple chambers.
Here lies the feeling of our happy meetings,
only it breaks one's heart."
Guǒ Hàn replied with a letter on perfumed paper,
his sentiments profoundly earnest.
He also included two poems in response and as a gift.
The poems said:
"The mortal world compared to the heavens above—
from the start, they could never be joined.
Who would have known that a single glance back
would weave mutual longing for us both?"
And also:
"The pillow you gave still holds your fragrant scent,
the clothes I weep on still bear tear stains.
Your jade-like face is within the Milky Way;
in vain, my soul travels back and forth."
After this, all contact ceased.
That year,
the Grand Astrologer reported that the Weaving Maiden star had lost its light.
Guǒ Hàn could not cease his longing.
All mortal beauties
no longer held any interest for him.
Later, due to the need for an heir,
and the great duty of marriage,
he reluctantly married a daughter of the Chéng family.
Finding her unsatisfactory,
and again having no heir,
they ended up quarreling and falling out.
Guǒ Hàn later attained the office of Attendant Censor and then died.
From *Líng Guài Jí* (Records of the Strange and Supernatural).
Yáng Jìngzhēn
was the daughter of a farming family from Tiānxiān Village, Chángshòu Township, Wénxiāng County, Guó Prefecture.
At the age of eighteen,
she married Wáng Qīng from the same village.
Her husband's family was poor and worked the land.
Yáng was very diligent in her wifely duties,
and her husband's clan regarded her as a hardworking new bride.
Her nature was calm and quiet;
she did not enjoy playful laughter.
Whenever she had leisure, she would always sweep and clean a quiet room,
shut the door, and live in seclusion.
Even if neighboring women tried to befriend her,
she ultimately did not interact with them.
She bore three sons and one daughter.
She was twenty-four years old.
On the night of the twelfth day of the fifth month in the twelfth year of the Yuánhé era,
she told her husband:
"My spirit and consciousness feel quite unsettled,
and I dislike hearing people speak.
I should calm myself in a quiet room.
You should temporarily stay in a different room with the children."
Her husband agreed.
Yáng then bathed,
put on new clothes,
burned incense, closed the door, and sat down.
By dawn,
surprised that she had not risen late,
he opened the door to look.
Her clothes lay on the floor by the bed,
as if she had shed them like a cicada's shell.
Her body was already gone,
but they noticed an extraordinary fragrance filling the room.
Her husband, alarmed, reported this to his parents,
and they all sighed in wonder.
Several people came and said:
"Last night around midnight,
heavenly music came from the west,
as if from within the clouds.
It descended upon your house,
played music for a long time,
then gradually rose back up.
The entire village heard it.
Did your household not hear it?"
Moreover, the extraordinary fragrance was intensely strong,
spreading for several tens of lǐ.
The village official reported it to the county magistrate Lǐ Hán,
who dispatched officials and people to search far and wide,
but no trace was found.
He therefore ordered that her clothes not be moved,
the door be closed,
and a thorn fence be placed around it,
hoping she might perhaps return.
On the night of the eighteenth, during the fifth watch,
villagers again heard heavenly music and an extraordinary fragrance in the clouds coming from the east.
It again descended upon the Wáng family residence,
played music for a long time, and then departed.
No one in the Wáng household heard it.
At dawn, they came to look.
The thorn-sealed door was as before,
but from the room came sounds as if someone were there.
They hurriedly
"Hurriedly" originally read "place";
emended according to the Ming manuscript copy
ran to report to Magistrate Lǐ Hán.
He personally led monks, Daoists, officials, and clerks,
and together they opened the door.
There the woman was, seemingly on the bed.
They only noticed her face glowing with light,
possessing an extraordinary appearance.
Hán asked:
"Where did you go before?
Where have you come from now?"
She replied:
"On the night of the fifteenth, at the beginning,
an immortal rider came and said:
'Madam is destined to ascend to immortality.
Clouds and cranes will arrive shortly.
You should await them in a quiet room.'
By the third watch,
there were sounds of immortal music and colorful insignia,
rainbow banners and crimson tablets,
a multitude of simurghs and cranes,
and five-colored clouds descended,
entering the room.
A messenger came forward and said
"Came forward and said" originally read "said forward";
emended according to the Ming manuscript copy
'Madam, according to the register, you are destined to become an immortal.
The Immortal Master has sent envoys to welcome you.
You will meet at Western Peak.'
Then two colorful attendants presented a jade box.
Inside the box were extraordinary garments,
neither damask nor gauze,
cut like a Daoist's robe,
precious, splendid, fragrant, and pure,
beyond description.
After I finished putting them on,
the music played three movements.
A blue-clad attendant led forward a white crane and said:
'You should ride this.'
At first I still feared it was dangerous,
but I tried riding it,
and it was indescribably steady.
It flew up, and the five-colored clouds lifted me out,
with the colorful insignia leading the way ahead,
until we reached Huàshān's Yúntái Peak.
On the peak was a flat stone,
where four women were already waiting.
One said her surname was Mǎ,
from Sòng Prefecture;
one's surname was Xú,
from Yōu Prefecture;
one's surname was Guō,
from Jīng Prefecture;
one's surname was Xià,
from Qīng Prefecture.
They had all become immortals that same night,
and gathered here together.
A young immortal nearby said:
'Having all renounced illusion,
and attained verification as true immortals,
you should now be given fixed names,
which should include the character "zhēn" (true).'
Thus, Mǎ was named Xìnzhēn,
Xú was named Zhànzhēn,
Guō was named Xiūzhēn,
and Xià was named Shǒuzhēn.
At that time, the five-colored clouds lay unevenly,
covering the cliffs and valleys everywhere.
Exquisite music was arrayed,
playing intermittently before them.
The five congratulated each other, saying:
'Born together in the turbid realm,
all of us mortal bodies,
suddenly, effortlessly,
we are separated from the dust.
What night is this night,
that we joyfully meet here?
We should each compose a poem
to express our thoughts.'
Xìnzhēn's poem said:
'Through kalpas I purified vexing thoughts,
and now this body is barely achieved.
I vow to hide beyond the clouds,
and not remain within the world.'
Zhànzhēn's poem said:
'Graceful, I leave the dusty world;
composed, I ascend to the Grand Clarity.
Cloud garments never fray;
the crane carriage vanishes on the distant journey.'
Xiūzhēn's poem said:
'Huà Peak is not three chǐ tall;
the Eastern Sea is but a cupful.
Riding a colorful phoenix into the clouds,
singing and dancing, I ascend to Pénglái.'
Shǒuzhēn's poem said:
'Together we become companions of cloud-clad mountains,
all bidding farewell to the world's dust.
Quietly I ponder events of days past,
cast off this body of several years.'
Jìngzhēn also composed a poem:
'The human world is but turmoil and disturbance;
this life resembles a dream's splendor.
Who would have thought that within this very night,
I would bow my head to gaze upon clouds and mist?'
Then came carved platters of rare fruits,
whose names were unknown.
Exquisite music clanged and chimed,
its echoes stirring the cliffs and valleys.
After a while, the one holding the tablet said:
'You should proceed to Pénglái
to pay respects to the Great Immortal Elder.'
The five zhēn asked:
'Who is the Great Immortal Elder?'
He replied:
'It is Lord Máo.'
Musicians, simurghs, and cranes
again led the way east.
In an instant, they had reached Pénglái.
Its palaces were all of gold and silver;
the flowers, trees, towers, and halls
were all creations not of the human world.
The Great Immortal Elder resided in a golden palace and jade hall,
with very strict guards.
Seeing the five zhēn, he said happily:
'Why have you come so late?'
He served them jade cups of drink
and bestowed upon them golden tablets, phoenix-patterned robes, and jade-flower crowns,
assigning them to reside in Pénglái's Splendid Courtyard.
The other four went out,
but Jìngzhēn alone stepped forward and said:
'My royal father is advanced in years
and has no one to serve and care for him.
I beg to return to serve him in his remaining years.
After my royal father passes from the world,
I will then follow your command.
I truly cannot bear to obtain joy and forget my royal father.
I beg the Immortal Elder to pity me.'
The Immortal Elder said:
During the Bǎolì era,
there was a Filial and Incorrupt candidate named Fēng Zhì,
who lived on Shǎoshì Mountain.
His appearance was pure and bright,
and his nature was quite chaste and upright.
His aspirations lay in the ancient classics,
and he secluded himself in the forests and marshes.
He would ponder their meanings until the stars returned to the rotting grass,
and pore over the texts until the moon sank beyond his secluded window.
Diligent and tireless,
he turned night into day,
doing nothing but searching for hidden profundities,
never once idly wasting his time.
By the side of his study,
the scenery was delightful to behold:
the springs and rocks were clear and cool,
the osmanthus and orchids elegantly subtle.
Playful monkeys often stole fruit from his courtyard,
and crying cranes frequently perched on the pines by the stream.
The empty breeze sighed from time to time,
and fine dust lay still in the daytime quiet.
Mist veiled the emerald joints of the bamboo,
dew nourished the red blossoms of the azaleas.
Creepers clothed the walls,
moss formed a velvety carpet on the steps.
As midnight approached,
a sudden, intensely rich, extraordinary fragrance wafted by,
gradually filling the courtyard.
Soon, a curtained carriage descended from the sky,
its painted wheels creaking,
coming right up to the eaves and pillars.
A celestial maiden appeared,
with splendid attendants.
Her jade pendants chimed like stone chimes,
her silk skirts trailed like clouds.
Her form surpassed the radiant whiteness of gleaming snow,
her face outshone the enchanting beauty of lotus blossoms.
Composing her expression and straightening her sleeves, she bowed to Zhì and said:
"My register originally belongs to the higher immortals;
I have been exiled to dwell in the mortal realm.
Sometimes I wander among the Five Sacred Peaks of the human world,
sometimes I reside upon the three peaks above the sea.
When the moon reaches my jade steps,
sorrow keeps me from listening to the phoenix pipes;
when insects chirp on my powdered walls,
regret prevents me from sleeping beneath the mandarin duck quilt.
Swallows' frivolous chatter makes me pace in hesitation;
the phoenix's empty songs drift faint and distant.
I have ceased to play the precious zither,
and lazily leave the horned goblet unfilled.
The blooming branches of red apricots,
stir hidden frowns within my ornate palace;
the fragrant buds of green peaches,
draw longing gazes from my jade tower.
Having grown weary of morning adornment,
spring thoughts gradually melt my heart.
I have observed, sir, that your earthly bearing is profound and pure,
your mind upright and bright.
Your learning gathers like fireflies,
your writing contains the hidden leopard.
Therefore, I admire your genuine simplicity,
and love your solitary distinction.
I have specially sought your radiant presence,
wishing to take up broom and dustpan in service.
Yet I do not know what your noble intention might be?"
Zhì adjusted his robes, lit a bright candle,
sat with a stern expression,
and said:
"My family has always been chaste and incorrupt,
my nature is solely solitary and aloof.
I covet the dregs of the ancients,
I probe the essential meanings of former sages.
I weave willow strips in hardship,
I burn chaff in darkness.
Coarse clothes and simple food,
burning mugwort and eating wild greens.
I only seek to remain steadfast in poverty,
and will never act recklessly.
I certainly dare not accept the descent of an immortal.
My resolve is fixed thus,
I beg you to turn your carriage back early."
The maiden said:
"I have just arrived at your gate,
and have not yet fully expressed my earnest plea.
Let me leave a poem for you,
and return again in seven days."
The poem said:
"Exiled from Jasper Pool, I left Penglai Isle;
spring's charm, mist and flowers, stir thoughts all the while.
For love of your heart, so pure and white,
I wish to serve with broom, by screen and drape's light."
Zhì read it as if he had not heard.
The cloud-carriage departed,
leaving fragrance at the window,
yet Zhì's heart remained unmoved.
Seven nights later,
the maiden came again,
with the same mounted retinue as before,
her beauty radiant, her robes pure,
charming and eloquent.
She entered and said to Zhì:
"I am entangled by karmic bonds,
demonic obstacles arise sharply.
On Penglai and Yingzhou isles,
in embroidered tents and brocade palaces,
regret sprouts on crimson mats,
sorrow grows in kingfisher quilts.
It is hard to glimpse dancing butterflies among fragrant grasses,
I often envy orioles flitting through ornate thickets,
for none fail to fly in pairs,
all able to stand facing each other.
Proud of my solitary rest,
I instead become confused in the empty chamber.
In autumn, putting out the silver lamp,
I only gaze fixedly at the sliver of moon;
in spring, seeking the jade garden,
I vainly express my thoughts to fading flowers.
Therefore, I was so fervent before,
laying bare my sincere devotion,
hoping you would deign to accept it,
not obstruct my genuine feelings.
Again, I do not know what your intention ultimately is?"
Zhì again spoke with a stern expression:
"I dwell among mountain thickets,
my will is already simple and ignorant.
I do not recognize cosmetics,
how would I know feminine charms?
I beg you to leave quickly,
do not blame me for this."
The maiden said:
"I hope you will not harbor deep doubts,
I beg you to accept my humble self.
Let me offer another poem,
and return again in seven days."
The poem said:
"Nòng Yù had a husband, both attained the Way;
Liú Gāng with his wife ascended, immortal they stay.
If you could carefully observe the morning dew,
you must follow the cloud-chariot to worship the grotto-heaven true."
Zhì read it and again did not change his mind.
Seven nights later,
the maiden came again,
her manner gentle, her beauty captivating,
adorned in fine clothes, with bright eyes.
She spoke again:
"The flowing waves are hard to halt,
the western sun easily declines.
Flowers and trees do not linger,
the dew on onions is not long-lasting.
Light bubbles floating on water,
last only a moment;
a tiny candle in the wind,
endures no more than an instant.
Vainly contending with spirit,
how long can it last?
Relying on a stubborn youthful face,
in a moment it becomes withered wood.
Thus, though you now boast of your complexion and hair,
not yet faded and fallen,
and firmly confine yourself to silks and satins,
greedily exhausting the classics.
When you reach old age and decline,
how will you sustain yourself?
I have the Cyclically Transformed Elixir,
quite able to halt fate.
If you consent to rely on me,
I will surely pour out my heart.
I can make your lifespan rival the three pines,
your pupils square like two eyes,
the immortal mountains and divine abodes,
you may roam at will.
Do not plant hibiscus flowers,
which display their beauty only at dawn;
cease striking flint for fire,
which still emits light in the dark of night."
Zhì then glared angrily and said:
"I dwell in my study,
I do not deceive the dark room.
Let Xià Huì be my witness,
let Shūzǐ be my teacher.
What manner of demon are you,
to harass and pressure me so bitterly?
My heart is like iron and stone,
speak no more.
If you tarry and linger,
I will surely subject you to distress and shame."
A guard admonished:
"Young lady, turn the carriage back.
This wooden puppet of a man,
is not worth speaking to;
moreover, a poor and humble fellow destined to be a lowly ghost,
how could he be a match for an immortal?"
The maiden sighed deeply and said:
"The reason for my earnestness
is that he is a descendant of the Green Ox Taoist;
besides, if this opportunity is lost now,
I must again dwell alone for six hundred years—
this is no trivial matter.
Alas, this man,
is truly a heartless one."
She also left a poem that said:
"Xiāo Láng pays no heed to the Phoenix Tower maiden,
Through misty paths she turns her carriage, tears fresh on her face.
Grieving, she thinks of the way back to Péngyíng,
Hard to glimpse the green peach blossoms of the old garden's spring."
Her carriage passed through the gate,
Pearls and jade chiming in the air,
The flutes and pipes sounded clear and cold,
Amidst the distant clouds and dew.
Yet Fēng Zhì remained unmoved.
Three years later,
Fēng Zhì fell ill and died,
Summoned by Mount Tài,
Bound with heavy chains,
The envoy drove him forward,
Heading toward the underworld.
Suddenly they encountered a procession of immortals on horseback,
Clearing the way with great solemnity.
The envoy bowed by the roadside and said:
"Lady Shàngyuán is touring Mount Tài."
Soon an immortal rider
Summoned the envoy and the prisoner to approach.
When Fēng Zhì arrived and looked up,
He saw it was the immortal maiden who had once sought his love,
But those around her clicked their tongues and sighed with pity.
The immortal maiden then asked for the warrant and said:
"I cannot be without feeling for this man."
She then requested a large brush and wrote her judgment:
"Though Fēng Zhì was stubborn in the past,
His integrity was pure and steadfast,
Truly due to his simple honesty,
It is hard to blame him for lacking romantic sentiment.
He should be granted an additional twelve years of life."
Those around ordered Fēng Zhì to kneel and give thanks,
And the envoy then removed the iron chains.
Once released by the immortal official,
The underworld dared not pursue him further.
The envoy led him back,
And after a long while, he revived.
Later, he regretted the events of the past,
Weeping bitterly and blaming himself alone.
From Chuánqí
The Female Immortal of the Yùruǐ Courtyard
At the Tángchāng Temple in Ānyè, Cháng'ān,
There were once jade pistil flowers.
Whenever these flowers bloomed,
They resembled forests of jade and trees of precious stone.
During the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
When spring scenery was at its peak,
Carriages and horses came in succession to admire them.
Suddenly one day,
A maiden of about seventeen or eighteen,
Dressed in green embroidered robes,
With her hair tied in two buns,
Without hairpins or earrings,
Her appearance gentle and graceful,
Stood out far above the crowd.
She was accompanied by two female Daoists and three young attendants,
All with hair tied in childlike buns and wearing yellow robes,
Exquisitely beautiful beyond compare.
Then she dismounted,
Shielding her face with a white horn fan,
And went straight to the flowers,
An extraordinary fragrance wafting from her,
Perceptible from dozens of steps away.
Onlookers suspected she came from the palace,
And none dared approach to look closely.
She stood there for a long while,
Then ordered her attendants to pluck a few branches of flowers and left.
As she was about to mount her horse,
She turned to the attendants in yellow and said:
"I have an appointment at Jade Peak,
Let us depart from here."
At that time, the onlookers crowded like a wall,
All sensing mists swirling and cranes calling,
The scenery glowing brilliantly.
She took the reins and rode about a hundred paces,
When a light wind gathered dust,
And followed her as she departed.
In a moment, the dust settled,
And looking up, she was already halfway in the sky,
Only then did they realize it was an immortal's visit.
The lingering fragrance did not dissipate for over a month.
At that time, Yán Xiūfù, Yuán Zhěn, Liú Yǔxī, and Bái Jūyì all wrote poems about the descent of the immortal at the Yùruǐ Courtyard.
Yán Xiūfù's poem said:
"All day I fasted and prayed to the Jade Emperor,
My soul dissolved, my eyes cold, yet I met no true immortal.
Better to face a tree of jade pistils,
Smiling at the flower-hiding maiden in the cave."
He also wrote:
"Her fragrant carriage secretly descended from Jade Tortoise Mountain,
How could the mortal world glimpse her youthful face?
Only the heartless snow on the branches,
Blown by the fair wind, adorns her green-cloud hair."
Yuán Zhěn's poem said:
"When Nòngyù secretly passed by the jade tree,
She did not let the bluebird emerge from the flowers.
Surely no one else noticed,
Only Yán Láng himself knew."
Liú Yǔxī's poem said:
"The jade maiden came to see the jade tree flowers,
An extraordinary fragrance led her seven-scented carriage.
Climbing the branches, playing with snow, she turned her head,
Surprised at how quickly the sun slants in the mortal world."
He also wrote:
"Snowy pistils, jade-like blossoms fill the courtyard with spring,
Feathered attendants tread lightly, raising no dust.
In vain the monarch asks beneath the curtain,
For another always accompanies the flute player."
Bái Jūyì's poem said:
"When the fairy maiden secretly rode the phoenix down,
She paused in the cave to play with jade branches.
If not for the chattering spring birds,
Could the green-locked immortal lad have known?"
From Jùtán Lù
Mǎ Shìliáng
In the early Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
in Wànnián County, there was
("有" in the text; the Ming manuscript reads "所由" instead)
a man named Mǎ Shìliáng
who had committed a crime.
At the time, the Presented Scholar Wáng Shuǎng was the Capital Prefect,
and he enforced the law with extreme severity.
He intended to execute him.
Shìliáng thus fled for his life into the Southern Mountains.
He reached the shore of the Tàn Gǔ Qiū pond,
and hid beneath a large willow tree.
Just at dawn,
he saw a celestial maiden descend in a five-colored cloud to the water's edge.
She had a golden mallet and a jade tablet.
After striking the water several times in succession,
blue lotuses emerged,
their buds
("蕋旋" in the original text;
emended to "葉施" based on the Ming manuscript)
gradually opened.
The celestial maiden picked and ate three or four of them,
then rode the clouds away.
Shìliáng saw that the golden mallet and jade tablet were still there,
so he leaped down and struck the water with them.
After a short while, lotuses emerged again.
Shìliáng ate over ten of them,
and immediately felt his body become light,
able to fly and rise up.
He then grasped the vines, searching for the place where the five-colored cloud had gone.
Soon he saw a grand palace with lofty halls.
The lotus-eating maiden was there among a group of immortals.
Seeing him, they were greatly startled.
They rushed down
and struck him repeatedly with their bamboo staffs,
causing him to fall by the edge of the Hóngyá ravine.
The ravine water was clear and pure.
Exhausted, he fell into a deep sleep.
When he awoke,
he saw a young maid with double hair buns sharpening a knife.
She said to him:
"You stole the spiritual medicine.
I have been ordered to take your life."
Shìliáng was terrified
and prostrated himself, begging for rescue and a solution.
She replied:
"This should be unavoidable.
Only divine liquid
can save you.
You must take me as your wife."
She then left.
After a short while, she returned holding a small green bowl,
inside which was white rice.
Shìliáng ate it all
and slept again.
After a short while he awoke.
The maid with double buns said:
"The medicine is now ready."
She showed it to him:
seven luminous, crystalline pills,
the color of azure.
Shìliáng was overjoyed and sighed in admiration.
Looking at his abdomen, he saw what appeared to be a red line—
it was the scar from the knife.
The girl rubbed the medicine on it,
and it vanished instantly.
She warned him:
"Just cultivate and study on your own.
Be careful not to tell anyone.
If you leak the secret,
the abdominal wound will surely split open."
They then lived together by the side of the pond.
She also said:
"I am the daughter of the Valley Spirit.
I guard the spiritual medicine of the high immortal,
and that is how I could save you."
By the early Huìchāng era,
people would often see them.
Fishermen
("漁者" two characters missing in original;
supplemented based on Ming manuscript)
who caught no fish in the Tàn Gǔ Qiū pond
would throw in a written request,
and would surely obtain fish according to the weight stated.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Zhāng Yúnróng
Xuē Zhāo was
a county lieutenant of Pínglù during the late Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty.
He prided himself on his righteous spirit,
and often admired the conduct of Guō Dàigōng and Lǐ Běihǎi.
While on night duty,
there was a prisoner who had killed someone to avenge his mother.
Xuē Zhāo gave him money and let him escape.
The county reported this to the surveillance commissioner,
who memorialized the throne,
and Xuē Zhāo was demoted to commoner status and exiled to the eastern coast.
On the day the imperial decree arrived,
he did not inquire about his family property,
but simply shouldered his cangue and departed.
There was a guest named Tián Shānsǒu,
who some said was several hundred years old.
He had always been on good terms with Xuē Zhāo,
and so brought wine to block the road and drink a farewell toast.
He said to Xuē Zhāo:
"You are a man of righteousness,
relieving another's calamity and taking it upon yourself—
truly a peer of Jīng Kē and Nì Zhèng!
I ask to follow you."
Xuē Zhāo refused,
but after Tián insisted, he agreed.
When they reached Sānxiāng at night,
Tián Shānsǒu took off his clothes to pawn for wine,
got very drunk,
dismissed the attendants and said to Xuē Zhāo:
"You can flee now."
Taking his hand, he led him out to the eastern outskirts,
and presented him with a pill of medicine, saying:
"This not only cures illness,
but also allows one to abstain from grain."
He also made an appointment:
"From here, whenever you encounter a place north of the road with dense, overgrown woods and thickets,
you may hide there temporarily.
Not only will you escape hardship,
but you will also obtain a beautiful maiden."
Xuē Zhāo bade farewell and set off.
Passing by Lánchāng Palace,
he saw ancient trees and tall bamboos
surrounding the place on all sides.
Xuē Zhāo climbed over the wall and entered.
The pursuers merely ran back and forth east and west,
unable to discover his traces.
Xuē Zhāo hid in the western chamber of an ancient hall.
When night came,
the breeze was clear and the moon bright.
He saw three beautiful women before the steps,
chatting and laughing as they arrived.
Bowing and yielding to each other, they ascended onto a floral mat,
and poured wine with rhinoceros-horn cups to offer.
The woman at the head made a libation, saying:
"Auspicious, auspicious,
good people meet,
evil people avoid."
The next one said:
"On this fine night's feast,
even if there are good people,
are they easily met?"
Xuē Zhāo, hearing this from a window crack,
and remembering Tián's words,
leapt out and said:
"I just heard the lady say,
'Are good people easily met?'
Though I am untalented,
I wish to be counted among the good people."
The three women were startled and silent for a long time,
then said:
"Who are you,
hiding here?"
Xuē Zhāo told them the whole truth.
They then set a seat for him south of the mat.
Xuē Zhāo asked their names.
The eldest was Yún Róng,
of the Zhāng family;
the next was Fèngtái,
of the Xiāo family;
the next was Lán Qiào,
of the Liú family.
As the drinking grew merry,
Lán Qiào called for dice,
and said to the three women:
"Tonight, with this fine guest gathered,
there must be pairing.
Let us cast dice;
whoever gets the strongest throw
shall share the pillow and mat."
They all cast in turn;
Yún Róng's throw was best.
Qiào then had Lord Xuē sit close to Sister Yún Róng,
and holding a pair of cups, presented them, saying:
"This is truly what is called the 'joining of the gourd cups'!"
Xuē Zhāo bowed in thanks.
He then asked:
"Where are you ladies from?
How did you come here?"
Róng said:
"I was a serving maid of Consort Yáng Guìfēi during the Kāiyuán era.
The Consort was very fond of me,
and often had me dance the 'Rainbow and Feather Garments' solo at Xiùlǐng Palace.
The Consort gave me a poem:
'Silken sleeves stir fragrance, fragrance unceasing;
Red lotus sways gently in autumn mist.
Light clouds on the ridge suddenly sway in the wind;
Tender willow by the pool first brushes the water.'
When the poem was finished,
Emperor Míng Huáng chanted it for a long time,
and also composed a matching verse,
but I do not remember it.
She then gave me a pair of golden armlets,
and thus I received favor surpassing the others.
At that time, I often encountered the Emperor discussing the Way with Master Shēn the Celestial Master,
and only I, with the Consort, could secretly listen.
I also several times served tea and medicine to the Celestial Master,
and he took some pity on me.
Seizing a private moment,
I kowtowed and begged for medicine.
The Master said:
'I do not begrudge it,
but you have no destiny for it,
