and will not remain in this world long.
What then?'
I said:
'If I hear the Way in the morning,
I may die in the evening without regret.'
The Celestial Master then gave me a crimson snow elixir pill, saying:
'Just take this.
Though you die, you will not decay.
Only make your coffin large, your burial spacious, place true jade in your mouth, and ensure ventilation,
so that your soul does not drift in emptiness,
nor your spirit sink into silence.
With something to restrain it,
molded by yīn and yáng,
after a hundred years,
if you encounter the vital energy from the union of a living person,
you may be reborn,
and become an earthbound immortal.'
When I was buried at Lánchāng,
I fully informed the Consort.
The Consort, pitying me,
ordered the eunuch Chén Xuánzào to handle the matter.
The burial implements
were all as agreed.
Now a hundred years have passed.
The Celestial Master's prophecy—
could it be this very night's fine meeting!
This is preordained destiny,
not mere chance."
Xuē Zhāo then inquired about Master Shēn the Celestial Master's appearance,
and it was Tián Shānsǒu's imposing stature.
Xuē Zhāo exclaimed in great surprise:
"Shānsǒu is clearly the Celestial Master!
Otherwise,
how could he have meticulously arranged for me to fulfill the events of the past?"
He also asked about Lán and Fèng.
Róng said:
"They were also palace ladies of beauty at that time,
envied by the Nine Immortal Maiden,
who poisoned them to death.
They were buried beside my tomb,
and we have kept company,
not just for a day or a night."
Fèngtái requested to beat the mat and sing,
offering wine to Xuē and Róng with a song:
"Flower-like face unbloomed, holding hidden sorrow;
This evening's sunny spring alone turns autumn.
I guard a lone lamp, no daylight seen;
Cold clouds on the mound add yet more grief."
Lán Qiào harmonized:
"In secluded valley, orioles cry, preening wings;
Rhinoceros sinks, jade chills, sighing long alone.
Moonlight cannot bear to lock the spring's door;
Dewdrops on pine branches chill the night."
Yún Róng harmonized:
"Splendid light unseen, divided into dust;
Once taking golden elixir, suddenly spirit gained.
Unexpectedly, Xuē brings the old measure;
Alone opens in secluded valley a branch of spring."
Xuē Zhāo also harmonized:
"By mistake entering palace walls, a man slipped through the net;
Moonlight silently washes dust from jade steps.
I suspect I've flown to Pénglái's peak;
Three branches of jade beauty, midnight spring."
When the poems were finished,
soon a rooster crowed.
The three said:
"We may return to the chamber."
Xuē Zhāo held her clothes,
and they soared away.
At first, the doorway seemed extremely narrow,
but passing the threshold,
there was no hindrance.
Lán and Fèng also bade farewell and went elsewhere.
Only candlelight flickered,
maidservants stood motionless,
bed curtains were brocaded and embroidered,
like a noble family's home.
Then they shared the bedchamber.
Zhāo was greatly comforted and delighted.
Several nights passed like this,
yet he did not know whether it was dawn or dusk.
Róng said:
"My body has already revived,
but my clothes are old and torn.
If I can get new clothes,
then I can rise.
Now I have a gold armlet,
you may take it to a nearby county to exchange for clothes."
Zhāo was afraid and dared not go,
saying:
"I fear being captured by the local authorities."
Róng said:
"Do not be afraid.
Just take my white silk with you.
If there is an emergency, cover your head with it,
and no one will be able to see you."
Zhāo agreed,
and went out to Sānxiāng to trade it.
He bought clothes,
and at night returned to the cave,
where Róng was already smiling at the entrance.
She led him in and said:
"Just open the coffin,
and I will rise by myself."
Zhāo did as she said,
and indeed saw that Róng's body had come back to life.
Looking back at the curtains and bed,
there was only a large cave,
filled with many funerary objects, clothes, playthings, gold, and jade.
He only took the precious vessels and left,
then returned with Róng to live in seclusion in Jīnlíng.
They are still alive to this day,
and Róng's hair and temples show no signs of aging.
Is this not because they both consumed the divine medicine of the Celestial Master?
The Celestial Master's name was Shēn Yuán.
From "Chuánqí"
Wéi Méng's Wife
Wéi Méng's wife, Madame Xǔ,
lived in Yìshàn Lane in the Eastern Capital.
She herself said:
"The Xǔ family has had immortals for generations,
all of whom have ascended to become high transcendents,
receiving important responsibilities from the Heavenly Emperor."
She was of a pure and clean nature,
well-versed in the two classics, the "Shī" and the "Lǐ",
and was known for her filial piety in serving her parents-in-law.
Méng was a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat,
and died young.
Madame Xǔ's parents-in-law also passed away,
leaving only one daughter,
twelve years old,
very intelligent and wise,
already able to memorize the "Yì" and the "Shī".
Suddenly, she died without any illness.
Madame Xǔ deeply pitied her,
and could not bear to bury her far away,
so she interred her beside the hall.
After several months,
she heard her daughter speaking from the burial chamber.
Madame Xǔ, along with her serving maid Zǒngjī,
opened the coffin to look,
and she had come back to life.
She described the state when she first died, saying:
"Suddenly I saw two blue-clad boy attendants,
about twelve or thirteen years old,
holding a red banner, coming into the courtyard.
They called my name, saying:
'Wéi Xiǎozhēn,
Heaven summons you.'
Then they led me to ascend to Heaven.
After about half a day, we reached Heaven,
and I saw palaces and towers lofty and magnificent.
The heavenly beings all wore brocade and feathered garments of five colors,
with golden crowns and jade tablets.
There were also many jade boys and jade girls,
all wearing garments of pearls and jade in five colors.
The flowers and trees were like shapes of glazed glass and precious jade.
When the wind blew,
they made sounds like musical tunes,
resonant, harmonious, and elegant.
After arriving at the palace,
I saw Lord Hán, the Director of Destinies, who said:
'Your ninth-generation ancestor rendered meritorious service to the state,
and bestowed kindness upon the people.
Recently, he has been promoted to be an underworld ruler,
and will soon be elevated to the rank of terrestrial immortal.
Your mother's heart is devoted to the supreme Dao,
and she is fit to ascend to the immortal ranks.
Therefore, we now summon you to the gates of Dānlíng.
Your ancestors for three generations
have all already been reborn in Heaven.'
Then he sent the two attendants to escort me back.
Mother should now purify herself through fasting and ablutions,
for the envoy of the Great Unity will arrive soon."
Madame Xǔ often recited the "Miàozhēn Jīng",
and often evoked strange fragrances.
And extraordinary lights and colors.
Everyone found it remarkable.
More than ten years had passed,
and three days after Xiǎozhēn returned,
indeed the sound of immortal music descended into their courtyard.
Madame Xǔ, along with Xiǎozhēn and Zǒngjī, ascended to Heaven at once,
with over thirty dragon and tiger soldiers and cavalry leading and following them as they left.
This was in the year Xīnchǒu, the first year of the Chángqìng era.
From "Xiānzhuàn Shíyí"
The Female Immortal of Cí'ēn Pagoda Monastery
In the second year of the Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty,
at the pagoda courtyard of Cí'ēn Temple in Wéiqǔ, south of Cháng'ān city,
on an evening with a moon,
suddenly a beautiful woman was seen,
coming with three or four blue-clad attendants,
circling the Buddha pagoda, talking and laughing,
with much charm and grace.
Turning to look at her serving maid, she said:
"Tell the monastery head,
to bring brush and inkstone."
Then on a pillar of the north corridor, she inscribed a poem, saying:
"At Huángzǐpī's head, the moonlight is fine,
Forgetting the splendid feast, I journey till dawn.
Mist clears, mountains low, dark green brows stretch wide,
I pluck a lotus flower to give to the distant one."
After inscribing it,
the monastery head took a candle to look at it,
and they all transformed into white cranes,
soaring into the sky and departing.
The writing remains to this day.
From "Hédōng Jì"
Xǔ Fēiqióng
In the early years of the Kāichéng era of the Táng dynasty,
the presented scholar Xǔ Chán was traveling in Hézhōng,
when he suddenly fell gravely ill,
losing consciousness,
with several relatives and friends
sitting around guarding him.
On the third day,
he abruptly rose up,
took a brush, and wrote largely on the wall:
"At dawn entering Jasper Terrace, the dew's air is clear,
Among those seated, only Xǔ Fēiqióng is there.
My worldly heart not yet ended, mundane ties remain,
Ten li down the mountain, the moon shines empty and bright."
After writing, he slept again.
The next day,
he startled awake again,
took a brush, and changed the second line to: "Heavenly wind descends, the sound of pacing the void."
After writing,
he sat dazed as if drunk,
and did not sleep again.
After a long while,
he gradually spoke, saying:
"Yesterday I dreamed of reaching the Jasper Terrace,
where there were over three hundred immortal maidens,
all dwelling in a great hall.
One among them said she was Xǔ Fēiqióng,
and she bade me compose a poem.
When it was done,
she again ordered me to change it, saying:
'I do not wish the people of the world to know of me.'
After finishing,
I was greatly praised and admired,
and she ordered all the immortals to harmonize with it,
saying:
'You will eventually come here,
but for now, return.'
As if someone was guiding me,
I thus managed to return."
From "Yìshǐ"
Péi Xuánjìng was the daughter of Péi Shēng, the magistrate of Gōushì County,
and the wife of Lǐ Yán, the county captain of Hù County.
From a young age, she was intelligent and clever.
Her mother taught her poetry and books,
and she memorized them all without forgetting.
Upon reaching the age of fifteen,
she adorned herself with the skills and demeanor befitting a woman.
However, she was fond of the Dao,
and requested her parents
to set up a quiet room for her to practice and wear Daoist attire.
Her parents were also fond of the Dao,
so they permitted it.
Daily, she offered incense and paid respects to Daoist statues.
When maidservants attended to her,
she would invariably drive them outside.
Living alone,
she nonetheless had female companions with whom she talked and laughed.
When her parents looked in,
they saw no one else,
and when questioned, she would not speak of it.
Pure in thought and serene in disposition,
even when frequently meeting her own flesh and blood,
she still observed proper etiquette,
never showing any disrespectful demeanor.
When she reached the age of twenty,
her parents wished to marry her to Lǐ Yán.
Upon hearing this,
she firmly refused,
desiring only to enter the Daoist path,
seeking transcendence from the mortal world.
Her parents restrained her, saying:
"For a woman, marriage is the proper rite.
The time for marriage must not be missed,
and the rites must not be neglected.
If entering the Daoist path does not succeed,
then you will have nowhere to belong.
Lady Wèi of Nányuè also followed the path of marriage and bearing children,
and later became a superior immortal."
Thus, she married Lǐ Yán,
and the rites of a wife were fully observed.
Within less than a month,
she informed Lǐ Yán:
"Because I have long cultivated the Dao,
the divine beings do not permit me to be your wife.
I request to end this."
Lǐ Yán also admired the Dao,
and thus consented.
She then lived alone in a quiet room, practicing with incense and cultivation.
At night, Lǐ Yán heard talking and laughter.
Slightly suspicious,
he did not dare disturb them,
but secretly peeked through a crack in the wall.
He saw the room filled with bright light
and an extraordinary, fragrant aroma.
There were two women,
about seventeen or eighteen years old,
with phoenix-shaped hair buns and rainbow-colored garments,
graceful and beautiful in appearance.
Several maidservants,
all with cloud-like hair buns and sheer garments,
stood elegantly by their side.
Péi Xuánjìng was conversing with the two women.
Astonished, Lǐ Yán withdrew.
The next morning, he questioned Péi Xuánjìng,
who replied:
"Yes, there were.
These were immortal companions from Kūnlún visiting me.
The superior immortal already knew you were peeking
and used magic to stop you,
though you were unaware.
When they come again, be careful not to peek,
lest you be reprimanded by the immortal officials.
However, my karmic connection with you is very shallow;
it is not the path for me to remain long in the mortal world.
Considering that you have no heir yet,
when the superior immortal comes again,
I will speak of this on your behalf."
Later, one evening,
a celestial maiden descended into Lǐ Yán's chamber.
After a year,
she descended again,
bringing a child to Lǐ Yán:
"This is your son.
Péi Xuánjìng will soon depart."
Three days later,
five-colored clouds swirled,
immortal maidens played music,
and a white phoenix carried Péi Xuánjìng up to heaven,
heading northwest.
This occurred on the eighteenth day of the eighth month of the eighth year of the Dàzhōng era,
at the Lǐ family's villa in Gòngdào Village, Wēn County.
From "Continued Biographies of Immortals."
Qì Xuánfú
Qì Xuánfú was the wife of a commoner in Jìzhōu.
At the age of three, she fell ill and died.
Her parents were wailing in extreme grief
when a Daoist priest passed by their door and said:
"This child can be saved."
He took her in his arms, showed her to them, and said:
"She is destined to become an immortal;
she has merely suffered a qi blockage."
He untied a black talisman from his robe belt to save her,
and after a long while, she revived.
Her parents expressed their gratitude,
and the Daoist priest said:
"I am the True Lord of Běiyuè.
This girl may be named Xuánfú,
for she will later attain the way to ascend to heaven."
Having spoken, he vanished.
Thus, she was given this name.
When she became the wife of a commoner,
her parents-in-law were harsh and cruel,
yet she served them with even greater diligence.
She often said to other women:
"I have obtained a human body,
was born in the Central Kingdom,
and yet I am a woman—this is also a deficiency.
My parents died early,
so only my parents-in-law are to be honored.
Even if beaten and whipped,
I bear no resentment."
At night, an immortal descended to her
and bestowed spiritual medicine.
It is unknown what path she cultivated,
but on the tenth day of the eighth month of the bǐngzǐ year in the tenth year of the Dàzhōng era, she ascended to heaven.
From "Records of the Assembled Immortals of Yōngchéng."
Xú Xiāngū
Xú Xiāngū was the daughter of Xú Zhīcái, the Deputy Chief of the Northern Qí dynasty.
Her teacher is unknown.
She was already several hundred years old,
yet her appearance remained constantly like that of a twenty-four or twenty-five-year-old.
Skilled in incantation and spell techniques,
she traveled alone throughout the land,
visiting all famous mountains and scenic places.
She often stayed in caves at the foot of cliffs or in forest grottoes,
and also occasionally lodged in Buddhist monasteries.
Once, she was provocatively teased by a group of ten arrogant monks.
Xiāngū scolded them.
The monks, enraged,
sought to subdue her by force,
their words and expressions growing increasingly insolent.
Xiāngū laughed and said:
"I am a woman,
yet I can abandon home to wander like clouds and water,
unafraid of flood dragons, tigers, and wolves.
How could I fear you rats?"
She then removed her clothes and lay down to sleep,
immediately extinguishing the candle.
The monks were delighted,
thinking they had achieved their aim.
At dawn,
Xiāngū gathered her things and left the mountain.
All the monks had remained stiffly standing or sitting like corpses throughout the night,
as if bound,
mouths shut and unable to speak.
Only after Xiāngū had gone several miles did the monks return to normal.
Traveling in the Jiāngnán region,
people of Wú saw her for over forty years,
yet her complexion remained unchanged.
She moved as if flying,
and wherever she went,
people revered and feared her as a divine being,
none daring to tease or insult her.
In the early years of the Xiántōng era,
she said to the Daoist priest Táo Kuìyún of the Báihè Temple in Shàn County:
"My late father served in the Northern Qí dynasty,
renowned for his esoteric arts,
and his hidden virtues benefited others.
Now he has also attained the Dao.
Therefore, blessed by his virtue,
I too have prolonged life and longevity."
From this, it can be inferred
that she is indeed the daughter of Xú Zhīcái.
From "Records of the Assembled Immortals of Yōngchéng."
Gōu Xiāngū
was a native of Chángshā.
She became a Daoist nun
and resided on Héng Mountain,
being over eighty years old,
yet her appearance was very youthful.
At the Immortal Altar of Lady Wèi, she diligently cultivated incense offerings
for more than ten years,
solitary and without companions.
There were many tigers beside the altar,
and visitors had to form groups and carry weapons to enter,
yet the nun concealed herself there
without ever feeling fear.
Several years later,
a blue bird,
shaped like a dove or pigeon,
with a red crown and long tail,
flew to her dwelling
and spoke on its own:
"I am a messenger of the Lady of the Southern Peak.
Because you, nun, cultivate the Dao with utmost diligence and austerity,
dwelling alone in this remote forest,
she has commanded me to be your companion."
Another day it said again:
"The Queen Mother of the West's surname is Gōu;
she is your ancestor.
Hearing that you cultivate the Dao with utmost diligence,
a true official will descend to impart the Dao to you,
but the time has not yet come.
You should strive diligently in your cultivation and self-discipline."
Whenever people came to tour the mountain,
the blue bird would always first announce their names.
It also said:
"Gōushì in Hénán
is the former mountain where the Queen Mother cultivated the Dao."
Another day,
the blue bird flew in and said:
"Tonight there will be violent intruders,
but they will cause no harm;
do not be afraid."
That evening,
sure enough, over ten monks came to destroy the Immortal Altar of Lady Wèi.
It was a large stone,
about ten feet square,
hollow underneath,
resting atop another rock.
When one person pushed it, it would sway;
with many people, it stood firm and shook.
That night,
the group of monks, holding torches and brandishing blades,
intended to harm the immortal nun.
Entering her room,
the nun was on the bed, but the monks could not see her.
Once the monks went out the door,
they immediately tried to demolish the immortal altar.
There was a thunderous sound,
shaking the mountains and splitting the valleys.
They thought it had already toppled,
but in the end, it could not be moved.
The monks then fled together.
By dawn,
someone from a distant village arrived and said:
"Nine of the ten monks were eaten by tigers;
the one who did not join in pushing
was thus spared."
Over a year later,
the blue bird told the nun to move and live elsewhere.
Thus she relocated to Húnán,
and the bird also followed her there.
No one ever heard it speak.
Zhèng Tián
("Tián" originally written as "lüè";
corrected according to the Ming manuscript copy.
Same below)
was demoted from the position of Academician Recipient of Edicts to Wúzhōu
and took the nun as his teacher.
The nun said to Tián:
"Hereafter, the world will face many difficulties;
the mortal realm is not a place to dwell for long.
I will withdraw to Jiǔyí Mountain."
One morning, she then departed.
From the *Collection of Immortals from the Walled City*.
Wáng Shì Nǚ
The woman of the Wáng clan
was the niece of Wáng Huī.
Her father followed his elder brother into Guānzhōng,
while Wáng Huī was then in the Hànlín Academy.
Wáng Shì, along with her birth mother Liú and her legal mother Péi, lived at Húfúzhǔ, Guìyán Mountain, in Yìxīng County, Chángzhōu,
close to the Dònglíng Temple.
From childhood, Wáng Shì abstained from wine and meat,
devoted herself to poetry and literature,
excelled at the qin,
and favored the Way of non-action, purity, and tranquility.
Upon reaching adulthood,
she vowed not to marry.
She often recited the thirty-nine chapters of the *Great Cavern* and passages from the *Classic of the Way and Its Virtue*;
within her room,
there was often an extraordinary fragrance.
Her parents regarded her with reverence and awe.
One morning, she fell slightly ill.
Péi and Liú went to Dònglíng Temple to perform fasting and pray for blessings.
That day, she felt somewhat better
and also went together to the front of the Dònglíng Buddha statue.
They burned incense and prayed.
Upon returning at dawn,
she sat on a flat stone to the right of the door
and inscribed a quatrain:
"Roaming waters, climbing mountains—never enough time;
Frequently, the immortals descend to listen to my chanted poems.
This heart does not cling to dwelling in the human world;
I only see a pair of cranes flying at the edge of the sky."
That evening, she peacefully passed away.
By dawn,
two cranes perched on the courtyard tree;
immortal music filled the room,
and an extraordinary fragrance was perceived.
People far and near were astonished
and rushed together to see.
Neighbors reported this to the officials of Húfú Town for detailed investigation.
The cranes had already flown away,
so they imprisoned those who had reported it.
Péi and Liú burned incense and prayed to her:
"If you have attained the Dao,
please send down the cranes again
to clear the neighbors,
so they do not wrongly incur guilt."
After a long while,
a pair of cranes descended into the courtyard.
Ten days later, they descended again.
She was buried beneath Guìyán Mountain.
Her coffin was light,
and only an extraordinary fragrance was noticed.
They opened the coffin to look.
There were only her clothes and shoes left.
Now, her dwelling at Guìyán is used as a Daoist chamber.
This was in the first year of the Qiánfú era.
From the *Collection of Immortals from the Walled City*.
Xuē Xuántóng
The woman of the Xuē clan,
was the wife of Féng Huī, the Junior Vice-Magistrate of Hézhōng.
She styled herself Xuántóng.
After marrying Féng Huī,
it was only twenty years later that she spoke of her lifelong aspiration.
Pleading illness, she lived in solitude,
burning incense and reciting the *Scripture of the Yellow Court*,
two or three times a day.
After another thirteen years,
two jade maidens in black garments descended into her chamber one night.
As they approached,
a light like moonlight
illuminated her courtyard and corridors,
and a fragrant breeze rustled softly.
It was early autumn at the time,
and the lingering summer heat was still intense,
yet the air became cool, clear, and refreshing,
as if floating within a cave.
The two maidens announced:
"The Primordial Lord of the Purple Void oversees the southern regions,
and is currently inspecting the registers below.
She has commanded all true and great immortals
that within the six directions,
in famous mountains and great rivers,
wherever there are those who aspire to the Way,
they must descend to instruct them.
Xuántóng's virtuous deeds
have been repeatedly reported by the earthly offices,
and her name is recorded in the registry of the Purple Void;
moreover, hearing of a woman who has set her will on the Way,
the Lord especially commends her,
and will personally descend here today."
This continued for five nights in total,
each time with incense burning solemnly and in abundance,
awaiting the Primordial Lord.
On the fourteenth day of the seventh month in the fifteenth year of the Xiántōng era,
the Primordial Lord descended into her chamber with a retinue of twenty-seven attendants and true immortals,
and Xuántóng bowed in welcome at the door.
The Primordial Lord rested and sat for a long while,
instructed her on the essential principles of clarifying the spirit and cultivating preservation as found in the *Scripture of the Yellow Court*,
and bestowed upon her a single Nine-Flower Elixir pellet,
instructing her to swallow it eight years later.
"Then I shall dispatch jade maidens with wind-borne chariots
to welcome you at Mount Sōng."
Having spoken, they dispersed.
From then on, Xuántóng immersed her mind in stillness and tranquility,
often abstaining from food.
Although true immortals descended to visit,
their radiant light illuminating the sky,
with numinous winds and extraordinary fragrances,
cloud-borne chimes and harmonious music
resounding in her chamber,
Féng Huī remained unaware of it all,
and often mocked and laughed at her.
When Huáng Cháo invaded the passes,
Féng and Xuántóng took refuge in Jìnlíng.
In the tenth month of the first year of the Zhōnghé era,
while traveling by boat to the mouth of the Dú River,
intending to reach their country villa,
they suddenly saw officials in vermilion and purple robes, along with armored warriors bearing spears and halberds,
standing in ranks and formation
as if awaiting and welcoming someone.
Bandits and robbers were rampant in the area,
and when the boatmen saw this,
they were shocked and halted, not daring to proceed.
Xuántóng said:
"Do not fear."
She then steered the boat toward them,
and the officials all bowed.
Xuántóng said:
"Not yet.
It is still mid-spring.
Just go now,
do not hurry."
Thereupon, they each dispersed.
Those aboard the same boat could not fathom what had happened.
In the second month of the following year,
Xuántóng bathed,
and ingested the elixir bestowed by the Purple Numen.
Two immortal maidens also secretly descended into her chamber.
On the fourteenth day,
she claimed illness and passed away.
Thirty-six immortal cranes
soared and gathered in the courtyard.
Her body was soft and supple,
appearing as if she were still alive,
with a point of white light on her forehead,
which after a long while transformed into purple vapor.
During the bathing,
her dark hair regrew,
instantly growing several inches long.
On the night of the fifteenth,
clouds and colors filled the sky,
and suddenly there was thunder and lightning.
The coffin lid flew into the courtyard,
and the corpse was nowhere to be found,
leaving only empty garments behind.
Extraordinary fragrances and flocks of cranes
continued unabated for ten days.
At that time, Emperor Xīzōng was in Shǔ,
and Zhèxī Military Governor Zhōu Bǎo memorialized the event,
whereupon an imperial edict ordered it recorded by the Historiographers.
From the *Collected Records of Immortals from the Rampart City*.
Qī Xiāoyáo
was a native of Nángōng in Jìzhōu.
Her father made his living as a teacher.
When Xiāoyáo was over ten years old,
she was fond of the Way and lived simply,
not engaging in childish play.
Her parents also favored the Way
and often performed hidden acts of virtue.
Her father taught Xiāoyáo the *Admonitions for Women*,
but Xiāoyáo said:
"These are matters for ordinary people."
She then took the immortal scriptures of Lǎozǐ to recite.
When she was over twenty years old,
she married Kuǎi Xún of the same district.
Her parents-in-law were harsh,
reproaching her for being lazy in sericulture and farming.
But Xiāoyáo devoted herself day and night to purification and spiritual practice,
giving no thought at all to livelihood matters,
and Kuǎi Xún also frequently reproached her.
Xiāoyáo addressed her parents-in-law,
requesting to return to her own parents.
But even at her parents' home, she was pressured,
and ultimately, as she could not engage in worldly affairs,
she wished to live alone in a small chamber to cultivate the Way,
and to provide for her parents-in-law from there.
Both Kuǎi Xún and her parents-in-law were suspicious,
and so they confined her to the chamber.
But Xiāoyáo sustained herself only with fragrant water,
abstaining from food and meditating in stillness.
She sang of her own accord:
"Laughing, I watch the azure sea about to turn to dust;
Before the Queen Mother's flowers, I bid farewell to all the true immortals.
A thousand years hence, I shall return to the heavens above,
but with a heart that still treasures the people of this world."
The Kuǎi family and the neighbors all considered her a demon.
At night, they heard voices speaking within her chamber,
and at dawn,
seeing Xiāoyáo sitting alone,
they were not alarmed.
Another three days later, at daybreak,
the entire household heard a thunderous sound as if the house were splitting.
They saw only the clothes and shoes she had worn left inside the chamber,
and looking up at the mid-sky,
they saw clouds, mist, phoenixes, and cranes,
along with immortal music and fragrant carriages,
colorful insignia arrayed in ranks,
with Xiāoyáo and a host of immortals together in the clouds,
clearly heard speaking words of farewell.
Kuǎi Xún rushed to report to Xiāoyáo's parents,
and when they arrived, they still beheld the sight.
The people of the town and district
all rushed to watch,
and none were not amazed and sighed in wonder.
From the *Continued Biographies of Immortals*.
The Tea Granny
The Tea Granny of Guǎnglíng,
her surname and native village are unknown.
She always appeared to be about seventy years old,
yet she was agile, vigorous, and strong,
with sharp hearing and clear vision,
and her hair and temples were lush and black.
The elders passed down stories saying:
After the Jin court's southern crossing,
she had been seen for several hundred years,
yet her appearance had not changed.
Every morning,
she would bring a vessel of tea to sell in the market,
and the market-goers would compete to buy it.
From morning till dusk,
the tea in her vessel remained as if freshly brewed,
never diminishing.
When officials arrested and imprisoned her,
the granny, holding the tea vessel she sold,
flew away through the window.
From the *Collected Records of Immortals from the Rampart City*.
Zhāng Jiànzhāng
Zhāng Jiànzhāng served as the military commander of Yōuzhōu.
He had always been fond of the classics and histories,
and had amassed a collection of books reaching ten thousand volumes.
His residence had a library tower,
and he devoted himself solely to reading and maintaining a pure, quiet life.
Once, the regional commander ordered him to go to Bóhǎi.
He encountered wind and waves and moored his boat.
Suddenly, a servant in black clothes arrived in a small leaf-like boat,
and said to Jiànzhāng:
"By the command of the Great Immortal, I invite the Grand Master."
Jiànzhāng agreed.
He arrived at a large island,
and saw towering towers and pavilions.
Inside, a female immortal resided,
attended by a grand retinue.
The utensils and food were all common flavors from Jiànzhāng's hometown.
After the meal, he bid farewell to leave.
The female immortal said to Jiànzhāng:
"You do not deceive in the dark chamber,
truly what is called a gentleman.
Do not worry about the hardship of wind and waves;
I will order this servant in black to come and go, guiding you."
When he returned,
the wind and waves were calm,
and he had nothing to fear on his journey back and forth.
When he returned to the western shore,
he passed by the stele commemorating Tàizōng's campaign against Liáo,
half-submerged in the water.
Jiànzhāng wrapped silk around dough
("dough" originally written as "face" [miàn],
changed according to the Ming dynasty edition).
He felt it and read it,
not missing a single character.
His dedication to learning was such,
that the people of Jìmén
could all tell of it.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Zhōu Bǎo
Zhōu Bǎo was the military governor of Zhèxī.
While repairing the city walls and moat,
upon reaching Hèlín Gate, they discovered an ancient tomb,
the coffin nearly decayed.
Opening it,
they found a woman whose face looked as if alive,
her lead powder makeup and clothing undecayed.
The overseer of the laborers reported it,
and Bǎo personally went to see.
Someone said:
"This person must have taken an elixir in her time,
awaiting the moment to awaken;
this awakening is the time of her liberation and transformation."
Bǎo then ordered her reburial,
providing a carriage with music for the procession.
Bǎo and his officials climbed the city wall to watch.
After traveling several *li*,
a purple cloud covered the hearse.
All present saw a woman
emerge from the carriage,
sit upon the purple cloud,
and rise gently upwards,
disappearing only after a long while.
When the coffin was opened again, it was empty.
From "Jī Shén Lù".
Zhào Gāo
Qín prince Zǐyīng
was once resting in Wàngyí Palace.
At night he dreamed of a person,
ten *zhàng* tall,
with exceptionally majestic hair and beard,
wearing jade shoes and riding in a red chariot,
drawn by vermilion horses,
who came to the palace gate and said:
"I wish to see Prince Yīng of Qín."
The gatekeeper allowed him entry.
Zǐyīng then spoke with him.
He said to Yīng:
"I am a messenger from Heaven,
come from Shāqiū.
The world is about to fall into chaos;
there will be those who wish to punish the violent.
They will rise tomorrow."
Zǐyīng, already suspicious of Zhào Gāo,
thereupon imprisoned Gāo in the Xiányáng jail.
They threw Gāo into a well,
but he did not die for seven days;
then they tried to boil him in a cauldron,
but it would not boil for seven days either.
They executed him.
Zǐyīng asked the jailer:
"Is Gāo a spirit?"
The jailer said:
"When we first imprisoned Gāo,
we saw he carried a blue pill in his bosom,
the size of a sparrow's egg.
A fangshi once explained:
'Zhào Gāo's ancestors received Hán Zhòng's method of the elixir.
One who receives this pill
can sit on ice in winter
and lie on a stove in summer,
feeling neither cold nor heat.'" After Gāo was executed,
Zǐyīng discarded his corpse at a crossroads of nine roads,
and a thousand households wept as they escorted it.
All saw a blue sparrow emerge from Gāo's corpse,
flying straight into the clouds.
The proof of the Nine Cycles [of the elixir]—
is it not credible here!
From Wáng Zǐnián's "Shí Yí Jì".
Dǒng Zhòngjūn
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn doted on Lady Lǐ.
After Lady Lǐ died,
the Emperor wished to see her again.
He summoned Dǒng Zhòngjūn
and spoke with him, saying:
"I long for Lady Lǐ;
can she be seen again?"
Zhòngjūn said:
"She can be seen from afar, but cannot share your mat and pillow."
The Emperor said:
"One glimpse is enough;
make it happen."
Zhòngjūn said:
"North of the Black River,
there is a city facing the wilderness.
It produces the Stone of Latent Splendor.
Its color is blue,
its substance light as down or feathers.
When cold is extreme, the stone is warm;
when summer heat is extreme, the stone is cold.
If carved into a human likeness,
its spirit and speech are no different from a real person.
Send this stone statue,
and the Lady will arrive.
This stone man can translate human speech;
it has sound but no breath,
hence we know it is divine and strange."
The Emperor said:
"Can this stone be obtained?"
Zhòngjūn said:
"I would need a hundred tower ships,
and a thousand men of great strength."
Those who could float on water and climb trees,
all must be versed in the arts of the Way,
and have the elixir of immortality.
They then reached the Dark Sea.
After ten years they returned.
Of the men who went before,
some ascended on clouds and did not return,
some feigned death by assuming other forms;
only four or five men returned,
and obtained this stone.
He then ordered craftsmen
to carve a likeness of Lady Lǐ according to a previous portrait.
Soon it was finished.
Placed behind a light gauze curtain,
she was graceful as in life.
The Emperor was greatly pleased
and asked Zhòngjūn:
"Can I approach her?"
Zhòngjūn said:
"It is like suddenly dreaming at midnight—
can you then be intimate with her by day?
This stone is toxic;
it is only suitable for viewing from a distance,
you cannot press close.
Do not, in your position as the Son of Heaven,
be deluded by this essence and phantom."
The Emperor then followed his advice.
After seeing the Lady,
Zhòngjūn had someone pound this stone man into nine pieces,
so [the Emperor] would no longer dream of her.
He then built the Terrace of Dream Souls,
and made seasonal sacrifices there.
From Wáng Zǐnián's "Shí Yí Jì".
Gě Xuán,
courtesy name Xiàoxiān,
received the "Nine Elixirs and Liquid Gold Immortal Scripture" from Zuǒ Yuánfàng,
but before he could compound the elixirs,
he regularly ingested atractylodes.
He was particularly skilled at curing illnesses;
ghosts and spirits would all manifest their forms before him,
and he would either dispatch or slay them.
He could abstain from grains,
remaining unfamished for years on end;
he could sit atop a pile of firewood set ablaze,
and when the wood was consumed, his clothes and hat remained unscorched.
After drinking a hú of wine,
he would enter deep mountain streams to lie down,
emerging only when the wine had dissipated,
his body not the least bit damp.
Gě Xuán had thoroughly studied the Five Classics,
and also enjoyed discourse and debate.
Several dozen enthusiastic young men
followed Xuán to travel and study.
Once, while traveling by boat,
he saw several dozen talismans and written charms stored in a container,
and thus asked:
"What efficacy do these talismans possess?
What feats can they perform?
Might we witness it?"
Xuán replied:
"What can a talisman possibly do?"
He then took one talisman and cast it into the river,
where it floated downstream.
Xuán said:
"How about that?"
A guest remarked:
"If I cast one, it could do the same."
Xuán took another talisman and cast it into the river
from "floated downstream" to "cast it into the river" this sentence,
was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy
and it floated upstream.
He said:
"How about that?"
The guest exclaimed:
"Extraordinary!"
He then took yet another talisman and cast it into the river,
where it stood still without moving.
After a moment, the lower talisman rose, and the upper talisman descended,
the three talismans converging in one place,
whereupon Xuán retrieved them.
Also, there was a laundry woman by the riverside,
and Xuán said to the young men:
"Shall I make this woman run for you all?
How about it?"
The guests said:
"Excellent."
So he cast a talisman into the water,
and the woman fled in alarm,
not stopping for several li.
Xuán said:
"We can make her stop now."
He cast another talisman into the water,
and the woman immediately stopped and returned.
Someone asked the woman:
"What frightened you so that you ran?"
She answered:
"I myself do not know the reason."
Xuán once visited a host,
whose host was ill,
and was making sacrifices to a daojing spirit.
The spirit
the character "jīng" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy
had Xuán drink wine,
and the spirit's speech was insolent.
Xuán grew furious and said:
"Treacherous ghost, how dare you!"
He ordered five bailiffs to drag the spirit out,
bind it to a pillar, and whip its back.
Immediately, it appeared as if someone was pulling the spirit out;
reaching the courtyard, it embraced a pillar,
removed its clothes and threw them to the ground.
Only the sound of whipping was heard,
blood flowed profusely,
and the spirit deliberately spoke in ghostly language, begging for its life.
Xuán said:
"I pardon you from the death penalty.
Can you cure the illness of the living person?"
The spirit said:
"I can."
Xuán said:
"I give you three days.
If the patient is not cured,
I shall deal with you."
The spirit was then released.
Xuán once passed by a temple,
whose deity often compelled passersby
to dismount from their horses or carriages
before reaching within a hundred paces.
Within the temple grounds were several dozen large trees,
populated with many birds,
and none dared offend them.
Xuán rode his carriage past
without dismounting.
Shortly after, a great wind arose, swirling around Xuán's carriage,
filling the sky with dust,
causing his attendants to retreat in alarm.
Xuán then grew furious and said:
"Petty evil, how dare you!"
He immediately raised his hand to halt the wind,
and the wind ceased.
Upon returning,
Xuán cast a talisman into the temple,
and all the birds in the trees fell to the ground and died.
Several days later,
the temple trees withered in the height of summer,
and soon after, a fire broke out in the temple building,
reducing everything to ashes.
Xuán once saw a fish vendor by the waterside,
and said to the fish owner:
"I wish to trouble this fish to go to Hé Bó's place.
Is that acceptable?"
The fish seller said:
"The fish is already dead.
What can it do?"
Xuán said:
"Do not worry."
So the fish was given to Xuán.
Xuán inscribed a cinnabar charm on paper and placed it inside the fish's belly,
then threw the fish into the water.
In a moment,
the fish returned, leaping onto the bank,
and spat out a black script that turned blue-green,
flying away like a large leaf.
Xuán often had guests who arrived later;
he would go out to welcome them,
yet there would be another Xuán in the seated company,
conversing with guests,
and both would similarly attend to welcoming and seeing off.
Once when the weather was cold,
Xuán said to a guest:
"Living in poverty,
I cannot provide a stove fire for everyone.
Allow me to make a fire,
so all may be warmed."
Xuán then opened his mouth and exhaled,
and a blazing fire issued forth,
filling the room in moments.
The guests all felt as if under the midday sun,
yet it was not overly hot.
Some scholars requested Xuán to perform some amusing tricks.
Xuán was suffering from the heat at the time,
lying on his back,
having someone powder his body,
and had not yet put on his clothes.
He replied:
"It is too hot;
I cannot rise to perform tricks."
Xuán then slowly rubbed his belly against the roof beam several dozen times,
returned to his bed,
and as he descended,
he floated down gently like mist.
The powder from his belly adhered to the roof beam,
and remained there for days.
Xuán was once dining with a guest;
after eating, he rinsed his mouth,
and the rice in his mouth transformed into several hundred large bees,
flying about and buzzing.
After a long while, he opened his mouth,
and the swarm of bees flew back into his mouth.
Xuán chewed them,
and they were again rice.
Xuán clapped his hands against the bed,
and frogs, various insects, flying birds, swallows, sparrows, fish, turtles, and the like
were made to dance,
all keeping rhythm as if human;
when Xuán stopped them, they ceased.
In winter, Xuán could produce fresh melons for guests;
in summer, he could summon ice and snow.
He could also take several dozen coins,
have people scatter and toss them into a well,
then slowly hold a vessel over it and call for the coins to emerge.
Thereupon, they flew out from the well one by one,
all entering the vessel.
When Xuán served wine to guests,
with no one passing the cups,
the cups would come before each person on their own.
If someone did not finish drinking,
the cup would not leave.
He would paint flowing water,
and it would immediately flow backward for over ten zhàng.
At that time, there was a Daoist priest
who was quite capable of curing illnesses.
He had come from the Central Plains,
deceiving people
by claiming to be several hundred years old.
Xuán knew he was lying.
Later, they met at a gathering.
Xuán said to an acquaintance:
"Would you like to know this gentleman's age?"
The close relative said:
"Good."
Suddenly, someone descended from the sky,
drawing the gaze of everyone present.
After a long while, he landed on the ground,
wearing a vermilion robe and a scholar's cap.
He approached the Daoist and said:
"The Heavenly Emperor commands me to ask: how old are you truly,
that you dare deceive the common people?"
The Daoist was greatly terrified,
descended from his seat and knelt down,
replying:
"I am guilty of misconduct;
I am actually seventy-three years old."
Gě Xuán then clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
Suddenly, the man in vermilion disappeared,
and the Daoist was greatly ashamed,
then vanished without a trace.
Emperor Wǔ of Wú summoned Gě Xuán for an audience,
intending to bestow upon him a position of honor,
but Xuán would not accept it.
When he sought to leave but was not permitted,
he was treated as a guest.
He often accompanied the emperor on outings and banquets.
Once, while seated, they saw people on the road praying for rain.
The emperor said:
"The people are praying for rain;
can it be obtained?"
Xuán said:
"Easily."
He then wrote a talisman and placed it in the village shrine.
In an instant,
heaven and earth grew dark,
and heavy rain poured down,
filling the courtyard with over a foot of water.
The emperor said:
"Can the water be made to contain fish?"
Xuán said:
"Yes."
He wrote another talisman and cast it into the water.
In a moment,
over a hundred large fish appeared,
each about one or two feet long,
swimming in the water.
The emperor said:
"Can they be eaten?"
Xuán said:
"Yes."
He then had them caught and prepared,
and they were genuine fish.
Once, while accompanying the emperor on a boat trip,
they encountered a great wind.
The boats of the officials, regardless of size, were mostly capsized or submerged,
and Xuán's boat also vanished beneath the waves.
The emperor sighed and said:
"Even Master Gě, with his Daoist powers,
could not avoid this fate!"
He then ascended Sìwàng Mountain,
and sent men to hook the sunken boat.
The boat had been submerged for a full day and night,
when suddenly Xuán was seen emerging from the water.
Upon arriving,
he still bore the flush of wine.
He apologized to the emperor, saying:
"Yesterday, while in your service,
Wǔ Zǐxū forcibly seized me and took me away,
so I was unable to part from him.
I have troubled Your Majesty,
exposing you to the elements by the water."
Whenever Xuán traveled,
if he suddenly encountered a close acquaintance,
he would invite them to a spot beneath a tree by the road,
pluck some grass, and prick the tree with it.
Using a cup or vessel to catch the flow,
sap would stream out like a spring,
stopping only when the cup was full.
Drinking it,
it tasted just like fine wine.
He would also take soil, stones, grass, or wood to accompany the wine,
and upon placing them in the mouth, they would become dried venison.
When he pricked the tree,
and held a cup beneath it,
the sap would flow as soon as the cup was placed there,
stopping only when the cup was full.
If others tried to take it,
it would never flow for them.
Sometimes, when someone invited Xuán,
if he did not wish to go,
and the host insisted,
he would reluctantly follow.
After walking several hundred paces,
Xuán would complain of a stomachache,
stop and lie on the ground,
and in a moment, appear to die.
If his head was lifted, it would detach;
if his limbs were lifted, they would detach.
Moreover, the body would become foul, rotten, and infested with maggots,
making it impossible to approach.
The person who had invited him would rush to inform Xuán's household,
only to find Xuán still at home in his hall.
That person would not dare speak of what had happened,
but upon returning to the place where Xuán had died,
the corpse would already have vanished.
When walking with others,
he could cause them to rise three or four feet above the ground,
yet they would still walk side by side.
Once, while Xuán was traveling in Kuàijī,
a merchant passed by a temple in the Central Plains.
The temple deity sent his clerk to instruct the merchant, saying:
"I wish to send a letter to Master Gě;
could you deliver it for me?"
The clerk then threw a sealed letter onto the bow of the merchant's boat,
where it stuck like a nail,
impossible to remove.
When the merchant reached Kuàijī,
he reported this to Xuán.
Xuán went to retrieve it himself,
and succeeded immediately.
He said to his disciple Zhāng Dàyán:
"I am being detained by the Son of Heaven,
and have no time to prepare the great elixir.
Now I shall undergo liberation by means of a simulated corpse.
I shall depart at noon on the thirteenth day of the eighth month."
When the time arrived,
Xuán, dressed in his robes and cap, entered his chamber,
lay down, and ceased breathing,
yet his complexion did not change.
His disciples burned incense and kept vigil for three days.
At midnight, a great wind suddenly arose,
tearing off roofs and breaking trees,
with a sound like thunder,
extinguishing the torches.
After a long while, the wind ceased,
and Xuán was suddenly nowhere to be found.
Only his clothes remained on the bed,
with the sash still tied and unfastened.
In the morning, they asked the neighbors,
who said there had been no great wind at all.
The wind had been confined to that one residence,
where the fences and trees
were all damaged and broken.
From "Shénxiān Zhuàn" (Biographies of Immortals).
Dòu Xuándé
was a man from Hénán.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
he served as the Commissioner of Waterways.
At that time, he was fifty-seven years old
and was dispatched on a mission to Jiāngxī.
As he set out on his journey and boarded a boat,
there was a man who joined as a fellow passenger.
Whenever Dòu finished his meal,
he would always share the leftovers with this fellow passenger.
This continued for several days.
As they were about to reach Yángzhōu,
the fellow passenger bid farewell and prepared to leave.
Dòu asked him:
"Why so soon?"
The man replied:
"I am a messenger of the Director of Fate.
Since Commissioner Dòu is traveling to Yángzhōu,
the Director of Fate has dispatched me to pursue him."
Dòu said:
"I am the Commissioner of Waterways.
Why didn't you say so earlier?"
The man replied:
"Although I was pursuing you,
your fate dictates that your life should end in this place.
Since we had not yet arrived here,
I could not reveal the secret.
That is why I was able to accompany you this far.
On the journey, I relied on your leftover food,
and I have felt deeply ashamed in my heart.
I wish to spare you from this calamity
to repay your profound kindness as a noble elder."
Dòu asked:
"Can it be averted?"
The man replied:
"Have you heard of the Daoist priest Wáng Zhīyuǎn?"
Dòu said:
"I have heard of him."
The messenger said:
"He now resides in Yángzhōu Prefecture.
Matters of the netherworld are highly confidential;
I hope you will not divulge this.
But during my days on the boat,
I constantly relied on your generosity for food,
and I feel deeply ashamed.
If I do not save
"save" originally written as "extreme,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript
you,
I would be failing in virtue.
Master Wáng's practice and conduct are revered in both the hidden and visible realms,
and he is widely respected.
His actions and deeds
are esteemed by both humans and celestial beings.
When he performs memorials and rituals for others,
those in peril and difficulty
are all rescued by the Celestial Ministry.
You should humble yourself and seek his counsel and assistance;
then you may overcome this calamity.
Tomorrow evening, I will report back on whether it has been averted."
After receiving the imperial decree,
Dòu had just arrived in Yángzhōu
when all the officials, from the Chief Administrator down, came to welcome him.
Before discussing official matters,
Dòu asked the assembled officials:
"Have you seen Master Wáng?"
At that moment, the officials
could not fathom his intention,
but they hurriedly sent someone to invite him.
Shortly after,
Master Wáng arrived.
Dòu dismissed the attendants and explained the situation in detail.
Master Wáng said:
"Lately, I have been cultivating the orthodox teachings internally,
and as for the practices of sacrificial rituals,
I no longer engage in them.
However, since your mission is of great importance,
I will exert myself to perform one for you.
As for the efficacy of the ritual,
I dare not predict it in advance."
Thereupon, he ordered an attendant to draft the memorial,
ascended the altar, and performed the ritual of submission.
The next evening,
the messenger came and reported to Dòu:
"It has not been averted."
Dòu pleaded even more earnestly.
The messenger said:
"Since things have come to this,
have him submit another memorial.
I will report back tomorrow evening.
Also, buy fine white paper to make spirit money,
and in a pure place, inform the clerks of the Celestial Ministry,
then burn it immediately;
if it is not burned,
it cannot be used.
Otherwise,
the Ministry's offices will delay,
and you will incur further offenses."
Dòu agreed to this
and informed Master Wáng,
who was very displeased.
Dòu said:
"I will follow your instructions,
and I beg for your compassionate rescue."
Master Wáng took pity on him
and performed another memorial.
The next evening, the messenger came
and reported again:
"It has not been averted."
Dòu pressed him intensely for the reason,
but at first, he refused to speak.
Finally, he bowed his head and replied:
"Daoist memorials and petitions
are like memorials submitted to the human sovereign.
In the first memorial submitted,
there were characters written incorrectly;
in the second memorial,
the characters 'réng qǐ' were written in cursive script.
When submitting memorials to the sovereign,
one must still be meticulous and proper,
how much more so when addressing the Celestial Venerable and the Great Dao?
How can they be treated carelessly?
The memorials that were submitted
were all discarded and thrown aside.
Since they were not heard clearly,
how could they be of any help?"
Dòu again earnestly requested that he seek assistance,
and he also informed Master Wáng of the matter in detail.
Master Wáng was very pleased and said:
"Is that so?
I have long privately suspected that memorials, petitions, and talismanic reports
were merely erroneous and false.
If what you say is true,
then their efficacy is indeed as such!"
He then took the submitted memorial from the altar
and saw that the characters were incorrectly written in cursive script,
exactly as Dòu had described.
Master Wáng said:
"For this memorial,
I will write it myself."
After repeatedly ensuring it complied with the standards,
he performed the ritual according to the proper method.
The next morning, the messenger reported to Dòu:
"The matter has been successfully resolved."
Master Wáng said:
"This extends your life by twelve more years."
Dòu said to his relatives:
"Previously, when I observed Daoist practices,
I never believed in them.
Now that I have been rescued and delivered,
their efficacy is truly as such.
From now on,
I vow to serve the Dao for the rest of my life."
He then received the Daoist register from Master Yǐn at the Qīngdū Temple
and led his entire household in revering the Dao.
He passed away at the age of sixty-nine.
From Xuánmén Língmiào Jì
Zhāng Shānrén
Táng Dynasty Prince Cáo was demoted to Héngzhōu.
At that time, there was a man named Zhāng Shānrén,
a practitioner of magical arts.
The prince often went hunting,
and once he had cornered over ten deer,
having encircled them,
he was certain to capture them,
but unexpectedly they disappeared,
and no one knew where they had gone.
He summoned Zhāng Shānrén to inquire.
Zhāng Shānrén said:
"This is the work of a sorcerer who has hidden them."
He then requested water,
and performed a spell with a knife over it.
After a short while,
in the water appeared a Daoist priest,
only about an inch tall,
carrying a bag and leaning on a staff,
walking with difficulty.
Everyone looked,
and all could see him.
Zhāng Shānrén then took a cloth needle,
and in the water, pierced the Daoist priest's left foot.
They then saw him walking with a limp.
He immediately announced:
"This man is easy to pursue,
he is only about ten miles away."
He then ordered them to run north and chase him.
After ten miles,
they indeed saw a Daoist priest walking with a limp,
his appearance identical to the one seen in the water.
They then invited him on the prince's orders.
The Daoist priest smiled and came.
Zhāng Shānrén said:
"Do not scold or anger him,
but request politely."
When the Daoist priest arrived,
the prince asked where the deer were.
He said:
"The deer are here.
Earlier, I saw these deer about to die for no reason,
so I pitied them,
and thus hid them with a spell;
I also did not dare release them,
they are now by the mountain."
The prince sent attendants to look,
and the deer were hidden on a small slope, unmoving.
The prince asked about the cause of his foot ailment,
and he said:
"After walking several miles,
it suddenly became painful."
The prince summoned Zhāng Shānrén,
and when they looked at each other,
they turned out to be old acquaintances.
The Daoist's foot soon recovered as well.
He was Hóu Shēng from Liánshān Temple in Chēnzhōu,
and the prince calmly sent him away.
Not long after,
a traveler passed through Chēnzhōu,
and stayed overnight at this temple.
He tied his horse at the temple gate,
and the manure was quite a mess.
The temple master saw it and reprimanded him.
The traveler became furious,
cursed the Daoist priest, and left.
Within ten days,
the traveler suddenly encountered Zhāng Shānrén.
Zhāng Shānrén said to him:
"You are about to face a great calamity,
likely because you have offended someone."
The traveler then recounted his recent argument with the Daoist priest.
Zhāng Shānrén said:
"This is an extraordinary man,
he has brought disaster upon you.
You must quickly go and apologize to him.
If you do not go immediately,
you cannot escape.
This is a thunder calamity.
Tonight, wherever you go,
cut a piece of cypress wood,
as long as your body,
and place it where you sleep,
covering it with clothes and bedding;
then move to another room,
make seven datewood nails,
nail them into the ground in the shape of the Big Dipper,
with the Chen position established,
and hide under the second star.
Then you may be spared."
The traveler was greatly alarmed,
immediately turned back,
obtained cypress wood,
came to Chēnzhōu,
and stayed at a mountain lodge,
setting up the method as instructed.
At midnight,
suddenly there was a great storm,
with thunder and lightning striking the front room.
In a moment, lightning flashed straight into his lodging.
The traveler hid under the star,
not daring to move.
The lightning entered the room several times,
as if searching for something,
but finding nothing, it stopped.
By dawn, when he looked,
the cypress wood had already been turned to powder.
The traveler became even more frightened,
rushed to apologize to the temple master,
and begged for his life.
Only after a long time was he forgiven.
The temple master said to the traveler:
"One must not look down on others.
Even venomous snakes
can harm people,
how can one be so disrespectful and offend others!
Now I have forgiven you."
The traveler confessed his fault and left,
then sought out Zhāng Shānrén,
and repaid him generously.
From "Yuán Huà Jì"
Wáng Mín
Master Tàihé, Wáng Mín,
is one who has attained the Way.
He often roamed the famous mountains and the Five Peaks,
and his appearance resembled that of someone just over thirty.
His father also achieved the Way,
and he had an aunt who likewise attained the Way,
whose mastery of the Way surpassed that of his father.
Mín often said:
"My aunt is already seven hundred years old."
There were those who knew his aunt;
she often stayed at Héngyuè,
or traveled to Tiāntāi and Luófú,
and her appearance was like that of a child or infant.
Her conduct was comparable to Chén Xiàjī,
relying solely on the arts of the bedchamber to achieve immortality,
and she had many husbands wherever she went.
In the early years of the Tiānbǎo era,
there was someone who recommended Mín,
and an imperial edict summoned him.
Upon arrival, he was settled in the inner Daoist sanctuary.
His learning encompassed both internal and external teachings,
and he excelled in Buddhism.
The emperor and his noble consort, Yáng shì, paid respects to him morning and evening,
bowing beneath his couch,
inquiring about Daoist arts,
and Mín instructed them according to the matters at hand.
However, his teachings largely centered on cultivating oneself with frugality and restraint,
taking compassion as the foundation.
Since the emperor was not fond of Buddhist scriptures,
Mín often used Buddhist teachings to guide him,
extensively elaborating on karmic retribution,
to broaden his aspirations.
The emperor also sincerely believed in him.
Although Mín was skilled in consuming elixirs,
he often drank wine without ceasing.
When he drank, he always used small cups,
taking a long time to finish a single cup.
Yet when conversing with others,
he responded appropriately to the situation,
demonstrating a divine-like quality.
After people left, they all gained something they had not possessed before.
His attire changed with the four seasons.
Sometimes he ate crucian carp,
and with each meal, he had rice,
but never in excess.
As for pungent foods like scallions, leeks, and other strong-flavored items, as well as salty and sour things that are not conducive to nurturing life,
he never consumed them.
He liked to encourage people to eat radish roots and leaves,
saying:
"Eating them over a long time yields great benefits and strength;
they are substances that nurture life."
There were people who claimed to have seen him generation after generation,
and his appearance remained unchanged,
suggesting he had reached a thousand years of age.
He stayed in the capital for many years.
In the sixth year of Tiānbǎo,
the Daoist Lǐ Xiázhōu from Nányuè,
fearing that Mín would cling to the capital and not leave,
declared:
"I will become the emperor's teacher,
and impart secret registers to him."
The emperor then ordered a search for him.
In the winter of the seventh year, Xiázhōu arrived,
met with Mín,
and urged him:
"Does Wáng shēng cling to worldly pleasures,
unable to leave?
It is time to depart."
Thus, he persuaded Mín to leave.
Mín then requested to jointly refine elixirs at Láoshān in Gāomì,
and Emperor Xuánzōng permitted it.
Consequently, Láoshān was renamed Fǔtángshān,
and Mín was allowed to reside there.
Mín once said:
"Zhāng Guǒ is a celestial immortal;
he has been in the human world for three thousand years.
Jiāng Fǔ is an earthly immortal;
he is ninety-three years old.
Fǔ enjoys killing living beings,
which diminishes his own lifespan—
this is something immortals abhor.
This man will ultimately never ascend to heaven in broad daylight."
From "Jì Wén"
Lù shēng
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man from Wú named Lù Shēng,
who had come to the capital to sit for the míngjīng examination.
Being poor and without servants,
he often rose early to visit acquaintances.
(The original text had "欲試" for "就識",
changed according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.)
He would ride his own donkey.
One day, the donkey suddenly startled and bolted,
breaking its halter and running off.
Shēng chased after it,
exiting through the Qǐxià Gate.
It went straight to the foot of the Zhōngnán Mountains,
where he saw a path.
He ascended the mountain,
finding it very familiar.
The donkey went straight up,
and Shēng followed it.
After five or six lǐ, they reached a place
that was very level and open,
with a household,
its gates and courtyard neat and orderly.
Shēng peeked inside
and saw a grapevine trellis in front of a thatched cottage,
with his donkey tethered under a tree.
Shēng then knocked on the gate.
After a long while,
an old man opened the door
and invited Shēng inside.
His countenance was most unusual,
and he treated Shēng with considerable respect.
He then bade Shēng,
"Sit."
Shēng requested his donkey so he could return.
The host said,
"Young sir, is it only for the donkey that you have come?
That you have managed to arrive here
is a fortunate meeting.
I deliberately took your donkey to summon you.
Please stay a little while,
and you will understand in due course."
He then invited his guest further into the residence,
where Shēng saw magnificent halls and deep chambers,
groves, pavilions, ponds, and marshes—
it was truly a fairyland.
He stayed for one night,
was feasted with delicacies,
and drank wine joyfully;
the music and performers were all of an immortal kind.
Shēng's heart was filled with astonishment,
unable to fathom the reason.
The next day, as he was about to take his leave,
the host said,
"This is in fact a grotto-heaven.
Because you possess the Way,
I therefore summoned you."
Pointing to several boy attendants on either side, he said,
"These men were originally butchers and wine-sellers from the city,
all taught by me.
Those who have mastered the Way can summon clouds and bring rain,
sit here and appear there instantly,
drifting through the mortal world
without others recognizing them.
You should stay here,
where your lifespan will be as enduring as heaven and earth.
How could that compare to the fleeting, mushroom-like glory of the human world!
Do you wish for this?"
Shēng bowed in thanks and said,
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
The old man said,
"For the ritual of accepting a teacher and receiving instruction,
it is proper to present a maiden.
I reckon you have no means to obtain one,
so I will now teach you a method to seek her."
He then had someone fetch a green bamboo pole,
measuring it to be as tall as a person.
Handing it to Shēng, he said,
"Take this into the city.
Among the court officials there,
in the households of those ranked fifth grade or higher, but below the third grade,
when you see a maiden,
throw the bamboo pole at her,
and you can take the maiden away.
Just keep my instructions in mind,
and have no worries;
however, be careful not to enter the homes of the powerful and noble,
for their influence might be able to subdue you."
Shēng then took the staff and entered the city.
Not knowing the mansions of the high ministers,
he had already entered several households
without finding a maiden,
and no one had seen his form either.
He mistakenly entered the residence of Vice Minister Wáng of the Ministry of Revenue,
and went further into the inner chambers,
where he saw a maiden doing her morning makeup before a mirror.
Shēng threw the staff onto the bed,
and took the maiden away.
As he reached the bottom of the stairs and looked back,
he saw the bamboo had transformed into the maiden's form,
lying stiff on the bed.
The whole household cried out in alarm,
"The young lady has suddenly died!"
As Shēng was taking the maiden away,
Vice Minister Wáng happened to be returning from court.
At that time, the street was filled with important officials coming to pay their respects,
and the mansion gates were deep and layered,
so Shēng could not get out.
He hid beside the middle gate.
When Wáng heard his daughter had died,
he entered the residence to see her,
with attendants running about incessantly.
Shortly after,
all the officials from the highest ministers down
had arrived at the gate.
At that time, Celestial Master Yè was at court,
and they urgently sent for him.
Shēng had been hiding by the door for half a day.
A little later,
Celestial Master Yè arrived.
After examining the situation, he said,
"This is not the work of ghosts or demons,
but rather someone using Daoist arts."
He then took water, chanted a spell, and sprayed it on the dead maiden,
who immediately turned into a bamboo pole.
He also said,
"The perpetrator is not far away;
a search will find him still here."
He then took a knife, performed an incantation,
and searched around the residence.
Sure enough, he found Shēng by the side of the gate.
Once captured,
Shēng was put in cangue and chains, beaten and interrogated,
questioned about his sorcery.
Shēng then recounted the whole story.
They went to the southern mountains together to apprehend the old man,
and had Shēng's neck locked in the cangue.
Leading their men to the mountain's foot,
they found the path from before
had completely vanished.
The officials in charge grew even more convinced it was illusory nonsense,
and prepared to take Shēng back.
Shēng faced the mountain and wailed,
"Old man, do you mean to kill me?!"
Raising his head, he saw a path appear.
He saw the old man descending, leaning on his staff.
When he reached the mountain's base,
the officials immediately tried to press forward.
The old man used his staff to draw a line on the ground,
which turned into a stream of water,
over ten feet wide.
Shēng kowtowed, pleading for help.
The old man said,
"When I left you, I told you
not to enter the homes of the powerful and noble.
You deliberately disobeyed my command,
so you brought this trouble upon yourself;
however, I cannot not save you."
While the attendants were staring in shock,
the old man took a mouthful of water and sprayed it.
Black fog spread for several lǐ,
turning bright day as dark as dusk,
so people could not see each other.
After about the time of a meal, it dispersed.
Lù Shēng was already gone,
with only the cangue and chains lying on the ground.
The mountain path and the stream of water
had also vanished.
From "Yuánhuà Jì".
Fǔ Shéntōng.
Master Huáng of Máo Mountain,
was highly accomplished in the Daoist registers and rituals.
At the side of Máo Mountain,
he built a Hall of the Celestial Worthy,
where he lectured and taught,
attracting several thousand people daily.
At the time, a lecture assembly had just begun,
when suddenly a man pushed open the door and shouted,
his appearance coarse and dark,
his speech vulgar and crude,
with a mule whip stuck at his waist,
like someone accompanying merchants with mule caravans.
He cursed, saying:
"Priest,
are you just sound asleep!
What are you gathering a crowd for?
Instead of learning to cultivate the Dao in the deep mountains,
you still dare to spout nonsense!"
Master Huáng, unable to fathom him,
descended from the lecture platform and spoke humbly.
Everyone was frightened,
not daring to contradict him.
After a long while,
the man's tone and expression softened slightly,
and he said:
"Isn't it that you are building a hall,
but how much money is needed?"
Master Huáng replied:
"It requires five thousand strings of cash."
The man said:
"Bring all the broken pots, cauldrons, and miscellaneous iron here."
They gathered about eight or nine hundred catties,
dug a pit to make a furnace,
and melted it with fire.
The man reached into his bosom, took out a gourd,
poured out two pills of medicine,
and stirred the mixture with something.
After a short while, he removed the fire,
and it had already become fine silver.
He said:
"This should be worth over ten thousand strings of cash,
more than enough for the expenses of building the temple.
Lecturing
(The original text had "stir" for "lecture,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
yields little gain,
so just stop it."
Master Huáng and his disciples all thanked him.
When asked what he desired,
he laughed and went out the door,
and no one knew where he went.
More than ten years later,
Master Huáng, having received an imperial summons, went to the capital.
Suddenly, on West Long Street,
he saw the man with the mule whip,
carrying a bundle on his shoulder,
following an old man riding a donkey,
with none of the aura of Máo Mountain about him.
Master Huáng wanted to hurry over and bow.
But the man shook his hand,
pointed at the donkey rider,
and then repeatedly kowtowed.
Master Huáng could only salute from afar.
The old man's hair was white as silk,
yet his face was like that of a fourteen- or fifteen-year-old girl.
From "Yì Shǐ" (Lost Histories).
Lord Xǔ
The immortal Lord Xǔ,
during his lifetime in the mortal world,
once, while repairing a temple,
after the construction was completed,
wished to inscribe a stone to record it.
He thus obtained an ancient stele,
but the text was worn and incomplete,
impossible to read again,
so he scraped off the old text,
and carved a new record.
From then on, he felt uneasy and unsettled.
One leisurely day, strolling slowly on the courtyard steps,
he heard a voice from the air say:
"Lord Xǔ, Lord Xǔ,
quickly go to the Water Official to seek help,
otherwise,
unforeseen calamity will befall you."
Lord Xǔ was startled and found it strange,
and when he inquired further about the matter,
there was only silence with no reply.
So he burned incense and worshipped devoutly,
hoping to be shown the reason for seeking help.
After a long while,
the voice spoke again, saying:
"Although the old text of the stele you carved has been ground away,
the person who wrote the text at that time
has gone to the Water Official to lodge a complaint,
saying:
'He took away my name,
to make his own name prominent.'
Because of this, the Water Official is about to issue a summons for a confrontation.
You should quickly seek to resolve it."
Lord Xǔ then, to his surprise, managed to recover the old text,
and erected a stone to inscribe and record it.
One night,
he dreamed of a deity thanking him:
"You have made my name prominent again.
Having nothing with which to repay you,
I ask that you perform a great Land and Water Offering,
widely announcing it to the myriad spirits of the mountains and waters.
By obtaining the recommendation of the Three Officials,
you can verify the Dao."
Lord Xǔ followed the teaching and performed it,
and thus achieved the fruit of the Dao.
From then on, the ritual method of the Land and Water Offering
was transmitted among mortals.
From "Lù Yì Jì" (Records of the Unusual).
Dù Wū
When Minister Dù Wū was young and not yet prominent,
he once met a Daoist on Chángbái Mountain,
who gave him a pill of elixir,
and immediately had him take it. After taking it,
he did not desire food,
his complexion was joyful and radiant,
and he was light, healthy, and free from illness.
Later, when he served as Prefect of Shāng Prefecture,
he thought to himself that since he had already become a prefect,
and his official rank was lofty,
yet he did not eat,
it would likely alarm the people.
So he wished to rid himself of the elixir,
and asked every guest he met about methods to do so.
After more than a year,
a Daoist arrived,
very young,
and Dù Wū inquired of him.
The Daoist taught him to eat pork,
and also to drink blood.
Dù Wū followed his instructions and ate.
The Daoist instructed him to massage his throat.
In a moment,
Dù Wū vomited a great deal of phlegm and saliva,
and there was a lump the size of a chestnut.
The Daoist took it;
it was very firm.
The Daoist cut it open;
inside it was like fresh glue not yet dry,
with the elixir in the middle.
The Daoist took it and washed it,
placed it in his hand;
its color was green and lustrous.
Dù Wū said:
"Give it to me,
I will keep it myself,
to take in my old age."
The Daoist did not give it to him, saying:
"My teacher on Chángbái Mountain said:
'Dù Wū regrets taking my elixir,
and now wishes to expel it.
You can teach him,
and retrieve the medicine to bring back.'
Now I follow my teacher's command,
wishing to remove this divine object.
Since it is already removed,
yet you plan to keep it until old age,
even if you could retrieve it,
you could not use it.
You should simply put your mind at rest."
He then swallowed it and left.
Dù Wū, more than fifty years later,
exhausted his wealth burning medicines,
but ultimately did not succeed.
From "Xuán Guài Lù" (Records of the Mysterious and Strange).
Zhōu the Worthy
During the reign of Empress Zétiān of the Táng dynasty,
the fourth younger brother of Chancellor Péi Yán served as the Registrar of Guózhōu.
In Guózhōu, there was a man named Zhōu Xiánzhě,
who lived deep in the mountains,
and his origins were unknown.
He was on good terms with the Registrar
and said to him:
"Your elder brother is a chancellor, which is excellent,
but within three years,
he will face execution and the ruin of his family,
with his entire clan exterminated.
Is this not something to fear?"
The Registrar was fully aware of his deeds,
knowing he was no ordinary man,
so he wept and begged for a way to save them.
Zhōu Xiánzhě said:
"The matter has not yet come to pass,
so there is still a chance to escape.
Hurry to the capital,
tell your brother what I said,
and ask him to prepare fifty yì of gold to bring here.
I will perform a ritual in the Hóngnóng mountains
to transfer the calamity away."
The Registrar then took urgent leave and returned to the capital,
where he visited his elder brother, Marquis Hé Dōng, Péi Yán.
Péi Yán was a man who cherished family ties,
and was extremely affectionate toward his brothers.
Whenever a brother came from afar,
he would share a bed and talk and laugh with him,
even if it lasted for ten days,
he would not retire to his inner chambers.
In the middle of the night,
the Registrar told him what Zhōu Xiánzhě had said,
and asked for the gold.
Péi Yán did not believe in gods or ghosts,
and often scolded and raged against superstitious practices.
Upon hearing his brother's words,
he grew furious and said:
"Why are you so ignorant of proper principles,
and follow vulgar delusions?
What do these foolish people understand,
that you would give them gold?
Moreover, witches and sorcerers in this world
often invoke ghosts and gods
to take people's wealth.
I have always gritted my teeth at the sight of them.
Why do you suddenly say such things now?
Think calmly about it—
it deeply angers me."
The Registrar wept and said:
"Zhōu Xiánzhě
is no ordinary deluded person.
Every time he speaks,
his words never fail to come true.
You are the chancellor,
and our family is well-off and comfortable.
Why begrudge a little gold?
Why not turn disaster into good fortune?"
Péi Yán grew even angrier and did not respond.
The Registrar realized his brother's resolve could not be changed,
so he sorrowfully bid farewell and returned to Hóngnóng.
At that time, Marquis Hé Dōng had just established Zétiān as empress,
and he monopolized court affairs and wielded power arbitrarily.
Believing himself as secure as Mount Tài,
he did not believe Zhōu's words
and instead grew angry and resentful.
A little over a year later,
Emperor Gāozōng passed away,
and Empress Zétiān gradually took control of court affairs.
She grew suspicious of and harmed high officials,
and conflicts arose repeatedly.
Péi Yán then remembered Zhōu Xiánzhě's words
and immediately sent someone to Hóngnóng
to summon the Registrar to the capital.
Péi Yán prepared gold
and ordered him to seek out Zhōu Xiánzhě in the mountains of Hóngnóng,
but he could not be found.
They searched in the mountains of Nányáng, Xiāngyáng, and Jiānglíng,
and finally found him,
informing him of his brother's words.
Zhōu Xiánzhě then returned with him to Hóngnóng
and said to the Registrar:
"In the past, the calamity had not yet taken shape,
so it was possible to set up an altar and make a plea.
Now disaster and fortune are already set,
and your family will soon be exterminated.
What is there to seek?
Moreover, last month I went to Luòyáng
and saw Chancellor Péi executed,
with his head tied to his right foot.
Since things have already come to this,
there is no way to avoid it.
Do not speak of this further.
However, I have known you, the Registrar, for a long time,
and I cannot let you share the same fate as your brother.
You may seek a hundred liǎng of gold,
and I will perform a ritual for you alone to plead with the Emperor,
so that you may be spared.
As for Chancellor Péi,
it will ultimately be of no use."
The Registrar immediately bought gold and gave it to Zhōu Xiánzhě,
who entered the Hóngnóng mountains to set up an altar
and performed a ritual to plead for his life.
After the ceremony,
he hid the gold in the mountains
and said to the Registrar:
"Your household will be spared from calamity.
However, resign from your post immediately
and move your family to Xiāngyáng."
The Registrar then moved his family to Xiāngyáng.
A little over a month later, he contracted a wind illness,
and in the tenth month, Chancellor Péi was imprisoned and executed,
with his brothers, sons, and nephews all sharing his fate.
As for the Registrar, who was afflicted with wind illness
and in Xiāngzhōu,
the officials petitioned for his execution.
Empress Zétiān said:
"Since he is afflicted with wind illness,
he will die soon.
There is no need to interrogate him.
This household shall be specially exempted from death."
Thus, he was spared.
On the night Marquis Hé Dōng was killed,
a dog bit his head and dragged it away.
By dawn,
the guards found it
