and tied his head to his left foot with his hair,
exactly as foretold.
From "Jì Wén"
Wáng Cháng
Wáng Cháng was a man of
Luòyáng.
He was proud and upheld righteousness.
When he saw injustice done to others,
he would surely slay them with his own hand;
when he saw people suffering from hunger and cold,
he would even take off his own clothes and push his own food toward them,
without the slightest reluctance.
In the second year of the Zhìdé era,
Cháng was wandering in the Zhōngnán Mountains
when he encountered wind and rain,
and took shelter in a mountain lodge.
As midnight approached,
the rain cleared and the clouds scattered,
the moon shone brightly and the wind grew calm.
Cháng, filled with emotion, gazed around in all directions and sighed, saying:
"I wish to pacify the disorder in the world,
but I have no authority over even a single person to assist me,
nor a foot of land enfeoffed to me to support me.
I wish to relieve the hunger and cold of the world,
yet I myself lack sufficient food and clothing.
The gods of heaven and earth bless the good—
this is truly not to be believed."
When he finished speaking,
a divine being descended from the sky
and said to Cháng:
"Why do you say this?"
Cháng, gripping his sword, pondered for a long while,
then replied:
"What I speak of
is my lifelong aspiration.
What divine being are you,
descending here?"
The divine being said:
"I possess an art—
gold can be created,
and mercury can be fixed.
Though it may not suffice to pacify calamities and disorder,
it can somewhat relieve people's hunger and cold.
Will you accept this art from me,
to save the world from hunger and cold?"
Cháng said:
"I have heard that this art is the art of immortals,
but it exists only in name—
I have never witnessed it.
Moreover, within the records,
it is fully recounted how Qín Shǐhuáng and Hàn Wǔdì were fond of this path,
yet ultimately achieved nothing,
only becoming the subject of ridicule for a thousand years."
The divine being said:
"Qín Shǐhuáng and Hàn Wǔdì
were emperors.
Emperors occupy positions to save people;
they inherently possess the means to save people but do not employ them,
instead seeking the art of immortals—this is wrong.
You do not hold a position to save people,
yet you wish to save the people of the world—
surely you may practice this art."
Cháng said:
"Gold can be created,
mercury can be fixed—
does this truly exist?"
The divine being said:
"Do not doubt—
it exists indeed.
Now, gold is born from mountain rocks;
at its origin, it is the essence of mountain rocks,
and after a thousand years becomes mercury.
Mercury receives the energy of the great yīn,
thus it flows and drifts without solidifying.
If it slightly encounters the energy of pure yáng and merges,
then it transforms into gold in an instant.
Now, if you wish to transform mercury into gold,
it must be done within the mountains to transform;
outside the mountains, it will not transform.
Only when encountering rocks of pure yīn,
and the energies merge, will it transform.
I have a book—
accept it without doubt."
Cháng then bowed twice to the divine being.
The divine being took a scroll from his sleeve and gave it to Cháng,
and Cháng knelt to receive it.
The divine being admonished him, saying:
"Read this book,
and you will fully comprehend the Way of Yellow and White.
On another day, you must pass it on to another person.
Do not bestow it lightly,
nor keep it secret forever;
do not bestow it upon the noble and powerful;
do not bestow it upon Daoist practitioners or Buddhist monks—
they already possess some arts to save people;
do not bestow it upon the unrighteous—
they surely will not take hunger and cold to heart.
When gold is created,
beyond relieving people,
do not indulge in luxury and ease.
Treasure my art,
treasure my words;
if you do not,
heaven will shorten your lifespan."
Cháng bowed twice again and said:
"The divine being now bestows upon me this sacred art—
I shall certainly never forget it for life.
But I beg to be told what divine being you are,
so that I may know the source of this great kindness."
The divine being said:
"I am a mountain god.
In the past, a Daoist hid this book in my mountain;
now I have encountered you, a righteous and ardent person,
and thus I entrust it to you."
Having spoken, he vanished.
Cháng obtained this book and read it,
and thus mastered the art.
Thereafter, he traveled extensively throughout the world,
using gold to relieve the destitute.
From "Records of Strange Events"
Yè Xūzhōng
In the early years of the Táng Zhēnyuán era,
Wáng Qióng, the magistrate of Dānyáng,
after three years of evaluations for reassignment,
was repeatedly rejected,
and felt deeply resentful.
He then fasted and stayed with the Dàoshì Yè Xūzhōng of Máo Mountain,
requesting a memorial to inquire about his fortune.
Xūzhōng was over ninety years old,
and reluctantly composed the memorial for him.
The memorial flew up with the incense smoke,
disappearing into the mist.
After the time of a meal, it fell back to the ground,
with vermilion writing commenting at the end:
"Accepted one hundred taels of gold,
deduct three years of official salary;
wrongfully killed two people,
to be dealt with after death."
One year later,
Qíong indeed died of a sudden illness.
From "Records of Unique Wonders"
Zhèng Jūn
In the late years of the Táng Zhēnyuán era,
Zhèng Jūn was in charge of the salt and iron bureau in Xìnzhōu.
There was often a stubborn man,
of unknown origin,
who would intimidate clerks and officials for tea and wine.
Zhèng Jūn captured him and caned his back;
at that time, in the courtyard, they were smelting ore,
calculating tens of thousands of taels of silver.
After the caning, he was dragged away,
but his expression remained defiant,
and he shouted:
"Just see if this thing can be completed or not!"
Indeed, it ultimately did not change.
Zhèng Jūn, enraged,
shackled him and sent him to Lǐ Gōng, the salt and iron commissioner of Jiāngxī,
who immediately beat him to death.
Ten days later, he appeared again,
and once more spoke at the furnace:
"See if it can be achieved again or not!"
It was as before.
Zhèng Gōng ordered him seized and pinned down,
first breaking his legs, then caning him to death,
dousing him with pig's blood,
and burying him in the prison grounds.
The next morning,
he swaggered back through the gate.
The officials were astonished,
and all went to receive him.
He said:
"I was only playing with you all along;
the ore merely needs to be refined again,
do not worry."
Then he left.
Zhèng Jūn went to inspect the burial site,
and it was completely empty;
the silver had all been successfully produced,
and he was never seen again.
From "Unofficial Histories"
Chéng Yìrén
In Shàngdǎng there was a man named Chéng Yìrén,
who possessed talismanic arts.
When Liú Wù was the military governor of Zé-Lù,
a commoner named Xiāo Jìpíng from Línzhǎo County,
whose family was very wealthy,
suddenly one day died abruptly without illness.
Yìrén had once received great kindness from Jìpíng,
and upon hearing of his death,
immediately rushed to see him.
He told Jìpíng's son:
"Your father should not have died;
he was likely summoned by the mountain god.
If treated, he can still be revived."
Thereupon, he wrote a talisman in vermilion ink,
and cast it into the air.
In barely the time of a meal,
Jìpíng indeed revived.
His son asked his father where he had gone.
Jìpíng said:
"I had just gotten up today,
when suddenly I saw a man in green clothes who said,
'The god of Huòshān summons you.'
Thus, I went with the messenger.
After about fifty-some *li*,
we happened to meet a man in vermilion clothes,
who wielded a sword and glared angrily,
arriving from the sky.
He said to me:
'Chéng Zhǎnxié summons you;
you may go now.'
Thereupon, the green-clad one fled,
as if in fear.
The vermilion-clad man led me back together,
and after a while,
I suddenly felt as if awakening."
His family was astonished,
and thus questioned Yìrén, saying:
"Who is this Chéng Zhǎnxié you speak of?"
Yìrén said:
"I studied the 'Dragon-Tiger Evil-Slaying Talismanic Registers' from Master Guīshì."
He then untied the register pouch he wore to show them,
and only then did people believe he was not lying.
Yìrén later traveled to Mǐnyuè,
and ultimately, his whereabouts were unknown.
From *Xuānshì Zhì*
Lǐ Chǔshì
Lǐ Wéngōng Áo,
having left the Wénchāng Palace, was appointed as prefect of Héféi Commandery.
The Duke was by nature narrow-minded, straightforward, and upright,
and had never believed in matters of shamans and sorcerers.
There was a guest in the commandery named Lǐ Chǔshì,
who claimed he could communicate the words of spirits and men,
and his predictions of events were quite accurate,
so the entire commandery revered him with solemn respect,
as if serving deities.
A little over a month after the Duke took office,
this man sent in his name card requesting an audience,
his demeanor exceedingly arrogant.
The Duke said to him:
"Confucius was a great sage,
yet he said, 'Not yet understanding life, how can one understand death?'
Are you more worthy than Xuānwén?"
The scholar said:
"Not so.
Have you not seen how Ruǎn Shēng wrote *The Treatise on No Ghosts*,
with precise arguments and grand breadth,
and no one could refute him,
yet in the end, did he not come to see ghosts?
Moreover, among your flesh and blood,
there will soon be one who falls gravely ill.
If you are content with complacent poison, then so be it;
or
"or" originally written as "become",
amended according to *Táng Quēshǐ*
if the five constants are roughly present,
soaked
"soaked" originally written as "request",
amended according to *Táng Quēshǐ*
by the seven emotions,
who could bear to watch someone drown and not rescue them?"
The Duke grew even angrier,
and immediately ordered him shackled and imprisoned.
The Lady developed a back carbuncle,
and the next day it ruptured internally,
indeed she fell unconscious without eating,
for a hundred watches without improvement.
He summoned physicians far and wide,
yet there was not the slightest recovery.
He had ten beloved daughters,
of age but not yet married,
who gathered around the bed wailing and weeping,
blaming themselves for Wéngōng's shackling of Scholar Lǐ.
The Duke, bound by the weight of conjugal duty,
and moved by affection for his descendants,
had no choice
but to release him from bonds and beg and entreat him.
Then he said:
"If you write a text by hand,
and wait until night to pray with it,
it is best to leave the ink seal and burn it together;
then you may be spared."
He further cautioned:
"Be careful not to alter it with brush and tablet;
nothing else is needed."
The Duke ultimately accepted his instruction.
He then drafted the prayer words himself,
and with cleansed hands, wrote them.
The Duke was narrow-minded and suspicious by nature,
and several sheets all had errors,
but unable to break the agreement,
he wrote again.
As the candle wick burned late into the night,
he grew weary from brush and inkstone.
With determined effort on one sheet,
the transcription was somewhat careful,
yet within the official titles,
he ultimately altered one character.
Having passed the appointed time,
he then burned it together with the talisman.
After the burning,
her moans immediately lessened,
and the whole household celebrated together.
At dawn,
Scholar Lǐ came to pay his respects.
The Duke deeply felt indebted to him.
The scholar said:
"The calamity is thus avoided,
yet I would say it was delayed.
I cautioned you not to omit or alter anything;
why then did you annotate one character?"
The Duke said:
"I did not."
The scholar said:
"The prayer text is here."
Thereupon, he reached into his bosom and produced it to show him:
it was the text burned the previous night.
The Duke was shocked, stunned, ashamed, and blushed,
left his seat and bowed,
and offered him generous gifts.
In the end, he accepted nothing,
and after ten days bid farewell,
his whereabouts unknown.
The illness also gradually subsided.
From *Táng Quēshǐ*
Luò Xuánsù
In Zhàozhōu, Zhāoqìng County, there was a commoner named Luò Xuánsù,
who served as a minor clerk.
He offended the county magistrate,
and thus fled to hide his tracks.
The magistrate was furious,
and the search for him was extremely urgent,
so he concealed himself in the mountain valleys.
Suddenly, he encountered an old man,
dressed in coarse clothing,
whose appearance was ordinary and unrefined,
leaning on a staff and standing beneath a tall pine tree.
He called Xuánsù over and questioned him, saying:
"How did you come to be here?"
Xuánsù replied:
"I offended the county magistrate,
and fled here to escape.
I am fortunate that you, venerable sir, would tolerate my presence."
The old man led Xuánsù deep into the mountains.
After traveling only a little over ten li,
they reached a cave opening.
There, they saw two thatched huts facing each other, east and west,
with accumulated water in front,
and rare trees and exotic flowers
arrayed on both sides.
There was one serving boy,
very young in age,
with hair tied in two topknots and wearing a short coarse garment,
a white robe, a silk belt, and leather shoes.
He resided in the western hut.
In the eastern hut, there was a medicine stove,
and Xuánsù was ordered to tend the fire.
The old man called himself Dōng Zhēnjūn,
and instructed Xuánsù to address him as such.
Dōng Zhēnjūn gave Xuánsù over ten pellets of medicine,
ordering him to take them,
and said:
"This can cure your hunger."
From then on, Xuánsù abstained from eating grains.
After only about a year,
he was taught talismanic arts and methods of breath absorption,
mastering all their subtleties.
One day,
Dōng Zhēnjūn again said to Xuánsù:
"You may return now."
Soon after, he escorted Xuánsù several dozen li south of the county,
clasped his hand, and bid him farewell.
From then on, Xuánsù practiced talismanic arts within his village.
There was once a pregnant woman
who had passed her due date without giving birth.
Xuánsù gave her a talisman,
instructing her to swallow it.
That very evening, she gave birth,
and the talisman she had swallowed was found in the baby's hand.
His other miraculous effects
cannot all be recounted.
Later, Xuánsù violated the law,
and the provincial governor had him beaten to death with a staff.
For over a month,
his corpse remained as if alive,
showing no signs of decay or deterioration,
which was likely due to having taken the spiritual medicine.
Therefore, the villagers collected and buried him.
This occurred in the summer month of the first year of the Bǎolì era.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
Zhào Cāo
Zhào Cāo
was the illegitimate son of Táng Dynasty Chancellor Zhào Jǐng.
His nature was unrestrained and careless.
The Chancellor repeatedly admonished and disciplined him,
but he never reformed or repented.
Having committed a fault and fearing punishment,
he stole a minor clerk's donkey,
took two strings of his own private coins,
and fled to the base of a flagpole pavilion.
Within days, his money ran out,
so he exited south through the Qìxià Gate,
letting the donkey go as it pleased,
following wherever it went.
Soon, he reached the southern mountains,
gradually entering deep and remote areas,
on a path frequented only by apes and birds,
untrodden by mounts or conveyances.
Cāo then tethered the donkey to a mountain tree,
and climbed alone.
After walking about twenty li,
he suddenly encountered a dwelling,
and thus knocked on the door.
Once inside,
two white-haired old men said to Cāo:
"Since you have arrived,
you may stay awhile."
Cāo looked around their home;
wives, concubines, and young children
were no different from the mundane world.
Cāo had no particular duties to attend to,
but simply wandered freely through the mountains and waters,
and felt very much at ease.
After over a month,
the two old men said to Cāo:
"We trouble you to go to the capital,
to purchase some things we need from the mountains."
Cāo then accepted the task.
The two old men said:
"The donkey you rode,
if sold, could fetch five thousand coins.
Use this money
to buy according to our agreement and return."
Cāo then said:
"My father is currently the State Chancellor.
If I go to the capital now,
I fear he will detain me.
Moreover, the donkey is not my own animal;
how can I simply sell it?
Besides, it has been tethered at the mountain entrance,
for a month now.
Whether it is alive or dead is unknown."
The two old men said:
"Just follow our instructions,
do not worry excessively."
Cāo then left the mountains,
and indeed saw his donkey still there.
He remounted it and galloped off;
its strength was very robust.
He sold it,
and indeed obtained five thousand coins.
Then, feeling inside his robe for the letter the two old men had given him,
it only instructed him to buy mercury.
Cāo immediately conducted the transaction,
and returned as dusk approached,
reaching the two old men's dwelling by nightfall.
The two old men then used various medicines to smelt and refine it,
and soon it transformed into gold.
They thus demonstrated this art to Cāo.
Half a year later,
the two old men slowly said to Cāo:
"You may return home for a visit.
Three years from now,
we shall meet you again at the thatched cottage."
Cāo wished to stay but could not,
and so bid them farewell.
Upon reaching home,
the Chancellor had passed away two nights prior.
After Cāo observed the minor mourning anniversary,
he again entered the mountains.
However, the forked paths, trees, and rocks,
the peaks, ridges, and forests,
were all different from what he had traversed before.
Cāo hurriedly returned.
After completing the mourning period,
he bid farewell to his brothers,
and wandered the rivers and lakes.
To this day, he remains unbound by worldly affairs.
Many followed him to learn the Dao,
but Cāo ultimately transmitted it to none.
From "Jíyì Jì"
Cuī Xuánliàng
During the Tàihé era of the Táng Dynasty,
Cuī Xuánliàng was governor of Húzhōu.
There was once a monk named Dàoxián,
skilled in medicinal arts.
Cuī once sought his skills.
The monk said:
"This art is not difficult to obtain,
but those who benefit from it
will inevitably incur hidden retribution.
I can only let you, my lord, see it once."
He then had Cuī purchase one jin of mercury,
placed it in an earthenware pot,
added a purple pellet,
covered it with a square tile,
piled ashes to bury the pot,
and fanned the flames until they rose.
He said to Cuī:
"If it merely becomes silver,
it would not be convincing.
You, sir, should devoutly concentrate on envisioning an object,
and then it will form by itself."
After the time of a meal,
the monk clamped the pot and placed it in a water basin,
and asked with a smile:
"What object did you envision, sir?"
Cuī said:
"I envisioned my own form."
The monk took it out to show him;
it was as if cast in metal,
with eyebrows, eyes, headcloth, and tablet
all fully formed.
This is indeed the art of immortals;
it should not be heavily discredited.
However, one rarely encounters its practitioners.
Those who claim it for themselves
are all fraudulent.
From "Táng Nián Bǔ Lù"
Yú Sǒu
When Minister Wáng Gōngqián served as military governor of Jīngnán,
there was a young man named Lǚ,
wearing tattered clothes and holding a walking stick,
with a look of hunger and cold,
who presented his name card seeking an audience.
The minister did not show him any courtesy.
Greatly discontented,
he consequently lodged at an inn.
After more than a month,
his poverty and destitution grew even more severe,
so he sold the donkey he rode at the marketplace of Jīngzhōu.
There was a market gatekeeper named Yú Sǒu.
He summoned Lǚ and spoke with him,
and inquired about his circumstances.
Lǚ said:
"My family is north of the Wèi River,
the household is poor and my parents are old,
I have no means to provide them with sweet delicacies for nourishment.
The military governor is my distant maternal uncle,
I have come from afar,
hoping he would pity my poverty and assist me.
I entered for an audience, yet he did not even glance at me once,
is this not fate?"
The old man said:
"Although I am poor,
and lack the resources to relieve your urgent needs,
yet earlier when I saw you had a look of hunger and cold,
I felt very indignant.
Tonight I shall prepare a meal for you,
I hope you will lodge under my roof."
Lǚ had no reason to decline.
Lǚ agreed.
Thereupon he led him into a room,
low, cramped, humble, and crude,
with broken eaves and crumbling walls,
and no bed, couch, mattress, or mat.
He laid a worn mat on the ground,
and sat with Lǚ,
after talking for a long time, he ordered food,
serving only coarse rice in earthenware vessels.
After eating,
when night had grown deep,
he said to Lǚ:
"In my early years I was fond of the Way,
often living in seclusion on Sìmíng Mountain,
studying the arts of warding off old age from Daoist priests,
though the aspiration was not fulfilled,
I have concealed my traces here,
for nearly ten years,
and no one in Jīngzhōu knows of me.
Seeing you stranded in travel,
how could I not be moved in my heart?
Tonight I shall perform a small art for you,
to obtain provisions for your journey home,
would that not be acceptable?"
Although Lǚ suspected it was deceitful nonsense,
he nonetheless felt it very strange.
The old man then took an earthen jar and covered it on the ground,
after only the time of a meal,
he lifted it and looked,
and saw a person about five inches tall,
wearing a purple sash and golden belt,
bowing with folded hands.
Yú Sǒu pointed and said:
"This is the soul of Minister Wáng."
Lǚ looked closely at its appearance,
and indeed it resembled Minister Wáng,
he silently marveled in his heart.
Thereupon he admonished:
"Lǚ is your maternal nephew,
his family suffers from poverty,
with no means to provide for daily sustenance,
therefore he has come from afar north of the Wèi.
You ought to generously provide lodging and provisions,
fulfilling the duty of kinship affection.
Why are you so arrogant,
that you did not even glance at him once,
is this human-heartedness?
Now I shall not punish you,
you should richly supply him,
and not let him remain a stranded guest."
The purple-clad figure bowed and saluted,
as if accepting instruction.
The old man also said:
"Lǚ has no servant or horse,
you should provide one horse and one servant,
and two hundred bolts of fine silk,
to give to him."
The purple-clad figure again bowed and saluted.
Thereupon he covered it again with the jar,
after a while he opened it once more,
and there was nothing to be seen.
The next morning,
as dawn was about to break,
the old man said to Lǚ:
"You should leave quickly,
Minister Wáng will summon you soon."
When he returned to the inn,
Minister Wáng indeed sent for him,
and upon meeting him, apologized saying:
"You came from afar to visit me,
but as military affairs were pressing,
I did not manage to converse with you for a single day,
I deeply feel ashamed,
I hope you will understand."
That day he began lodging Lǚ at a post station pavilion,
and feasted and traveled with him for several days.
When Lǚ announced his departure,
Minister Wáng gifted him a servant, a horse, and two hundred bolts of fine silk.
Lǚ found it even more marvelous,
yet dared not speak of it.
After returning north of the Wèi,
several years later,
while staying overnight with several friends,
they spoke of spirits and marvels,
and only then did he tell others of this matter.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
Chén Jìqīng
Chén Jìqīng
was from a family in the region south of the Yangtze River.
Having left home for ten years,
he sat for the imperial examinations,
but his ambition remained unfulfilled, and he could not return home.
He lingered in the capital,
making a living by selling his calligraphy and literary works to support himself.
He often visited a monk at Qīnglóng Temple.
Once, when he encountered the monk away on other business,
he rested in the warm chamber
to wait for the monk’s return.
There was an old man from Zhōngnán Mountain
who was also waiting for the monk to return.
He was sitting by the stove,
and he gestured for Jìqīng to come sit by the fire.
After sitting for a while,
he said to Jìqīng:
"The sun has already set.
Aren’t you hungry?"
Jìqīng replied:
"I am indeed hungry,
but the monk is not here yet.
What can I do?"
The old man then untied a small pouch from his sleeve,
took out a piece of medicine about an inch square,
and brewed only one cup of it.
He gave it to Jìqīng and said:
"This should somewhat relieve your hunger."
After Jìqīng drank it,
he felt completely satisfied and comfortable.
The pains of hunger and cold
were washed away and healed.
On the eastern wall was a "Map of the World."
Jìqīng searched for the route to the region south of the Yangtze River
and sighed deeply, saying:
"If I could travel from the Wèi River to the Yellow River,
visit Luòyáng,
swim in the Huái River,
cross the Yangtze River,
and reach home,
I would not regret returning without success."
The old man smiled and said:
"This is not difficult to achieve."
He then asked a young novice to pluck a bamboo leaf from the steps,
made it into a leaf boat,
and placed it on the map over the Wèi River.
He said:
"Just focus your gaze on this boat,
and it will fulfill your wish as you described.
However, once you reach home,
be careful not to stay too long."
Jìqīng stared at it intently for a long time.
Gradually, he felt the waves of the Wèi River,
and the single leaf grew larger.
The sail unfurled,
and it felt as if he had boarded a boat.
Starting from the Wèi River to the Yellow River,
he moored the boat at a temple called Chánkū Lánruò.
He inscribed a poem on the southern pillar:
"The frosty bell rings as the evening wind grows urgent,
A flock of crows gathers again in the cold woods.
At this moment, I cease rowing, grieving and chanting,
Standing alone facing the Lotus Peak."
The next day,
he reached Tóngguān Pass.
He disembarked
and inscribed verses on the gate of the Pǔtōng Temple east of the pass:
"Crossing the pass, I grieve over my lost ambitions,
Myriad thoughts disturb my mind.
Descending the slope, my horse has no strength,
Sweeping the gate, dust covers my clothes.
Many plans have come to naught,
My heart and words contradict each other.
I have already made the shameful decision to return,
Yet better to return in shame than not to return at all."
From east of Shǎnxi,
all the places he passed through
were exactly as he had wished.
After more than ten days, he arrived home.
His wife, children, and brothers
greeted him at the door.
In the evening
"Evening" originally written as "side,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
he wrote the poem "Evening View from the Riverside Pavilion,"
inscribed in his study:
"Standing at the riverside pavilion, my eyes filled with sorrow,
Events of ten years ago feel distant and vague.
Fields and gardens have scattered like floating clouds,
Half the village has drifted away with the flowing water.
On the riverbank, I meet no old fishermen,
By the shore, the familiar sandpipers are hard to find.
If not for my hair and teeth not yet showing age,
Facing the distant mountains, I could chant until my hair turns white."
That evening, he said to his wife:
"My examination date is near,
I cannot stay long.
I must set off again soon."
He then chanted a poem to bid farewell to his wife:
"The moon slants, cold dew turns white,
This evening, I leave with a heavy heart.
Wine arrives, adding sorrow as I drink,
Poetry finished, I chant with tears.
Parting songs linger on the phoenix pipes,
The farewell crane laments on the jade zither.
Tomorrow night, in my longing place,
The autumn wind will blow over half the quilt."
As he was about to board the boat,
he left another poem to bid farewell to his brothers:
"In seeking a future, I did not start late,
But fate has been slow to arrive.
Old friends have all reached the heavens,
While I still wander at the crossroads.
After the north wind and light snow,
The evening scene is veiled in clouds.
Melancholy on the clear river,
I hurry along for the examination date."
After the first watch of the night,
he boarded the leaf boat again
and sailed away on the river.
His brothers, wife, and family
wailed on the shore,
thinking he had become a ghost.
The leaf boat drifted gently,
following the old route back to the banks of the Wèi River.
He then hired a carriage
and returned to Qīnglóng Temple,
where he saw the old mountain man sitting wrapped in coarse cloth.
Jìqīng thanked him and said:
"I have returned, indeed,
but was it not a dream?"
The old man smiled and said:
"You will know in sixty days."
As the day grew late,
the monk still had not returned.
The old man left,
and Jìqīng returned to his lodgings.
Two months later,
Jìqīng’s wife and children,
along with money and silk,
came from the region south of the Yangtze River.
They thought Jìqīng had passed away,
so they came to visit him.
His wife said:
"On such-and-such month and day, he returned home.
That evening, he wrote a poem in the western study
and left two farewell poems."
Only then did he realize it was not a dream.
The following spring,
Jìqīng failed the examinations and returned east.
When he reached Chánkū Temple and the temple at the pass gate,
he saw the two poems he had inscribed.
The ink was still fresh.
The year after, Jìqīng achieved fame,
then gave up eating grains
and went into Zhōngnán Mountain.
From "Records of Admiring the Extraordinary"
Mr. Chén
There was a man named Chén Shēng from Màoshān,
who abstained from grains and practiced breath cultivation.
He lived in a few thatched cottages.
Once, he happened to go to Yánlíng
and arrived at a laborer's workshop,
seeking someone to carry his medicinal supplies
back to his mountain dwelling.
Because the pay was low
[Note: "low" originally written as "money"],
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
most were unwilling.
There was one man, strong and robust,
but with a dull spirit,
somewhat like a fool,
covered all over with scabies and sores.
He stepped forward and bowed, saying:
"I can go."
So he was ordered to carry the bag and follow along.
As for how much the pay was,
he did not even ask.
Once they arrived,
he expressed a wish to stay and gather firewood,
without even discussing the price.
He made an agreement with Chén Shēng:
five bundles per day.
Chén said:
"I abstain from grains;
I have no rice to give you to eat."
He replied:
"I am a poor man;
where would I get food?
I can just dig up grass roots to eat;
that will do." So every day he chopped ten bundles of firewood,
keeping five bundles in the room to burn himself,
and providing five bundles for Chén Shēng.
It happened that at the foot of the mountain, there was a family of officials whose wife suffered from a tooth ailment.
They came to Chén Shēng seeking medicine,
and the family asked for it daily.
They also had a young maid send things like pears, fruits, and pastries.
Chén Shēng abstained from grains,
and did not eat fruits or food either.
Each time they were sent,
the laborer would take them and eat them.
He would still laugh and say:
"Bring more tomorrow,
and I will have the medicine."
This happened several times.
One day,
the laborer also delivered ten bundles of firewood,
placing them at Chén Shēng's place
for two days' use.
After nightfall, he then locked the door, lit a blazing fire,
and brought in a small pot.
Chén Shēng secretly watched him
and saw him pour several measures of mercury from a gourd
and heat it.
He stirred it until it became like thin porridge,
then added a pill of medicine,
and it turned into gold.
The laborer pinched off two pills,
wrapped them in paper, and placed them in his bosom.
The rest he made into a gold cake,
and secretly left through the door.
The next day, when the sun was high and he rose,
the person seeking medicine had already arrived.
So he took the pills and gave them to him.
He instructed the one suffering from the tooth ailment to hold them in her mouth.
Before half of one pill was used,
she had already recovered,
the pain stopped,
and she expelled several dozen worms.
Chén Shēng waited for the laborer to go out,
then searched his room and looked around,
finding two volumes of books.
He did not understand their meaning,
so he hid them.
When the laborer returned,
he was greatly angered
and scolded Chén Shēng.
Chén did not dare to hide it
and returned them to him.
He said:
"I will leave now."
Then he went out the door,
entered the water to bathe,
and transformed into a handsome young man,
no longer covered with sores and scabies.
After bowing,
he leaped into a deep ravine
and was never seen again.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Zhāng Dìng
There was a man named Zhāng Dìng,
a native of Guǎnglíng.
He entered school as a young child.
One cold, moonlit dawn,
he rose early,
and the streets were empty.
Walking alone for over a hundred paces,
he encountered a Daoist priest walking very hurriedly.
The priest turned and saw him,
stopped, and said:
"This one can be taught."
He then asked:
"What do you desire?"
Zhāng Dìng replied:
"I desire long life."
The Daoist said:
"That is not difficult to attain.
You possess the bone structure for immortality;
seeking the Dao, you will surely succeed.
I shall now teach you the art of transformation,
but do not reveal it to others.
After ten years,
I myself will come to receive you."
He then taught him the oral formulas.
Zhāng Dìng was cautious, taciturn, and careful,
and very filial at home.
He also secretly practiced this art;
summoning spirits and ghosts, transforming people and objects—
there was nothing he could not do.
Once, he went with his parents to Liánshuǐ to visit relatives.
Upon reaching the county seat,
there was music and theatrical performances.
Everyone went to watch,
but Zhāng Dìng alone did not go.
His parents said:
"These performances are magnificent;
all our relatives have gone.
Why do you alone not go to watch?"
He replied:
"I fear that if my elders wish to watch,
I will be unable to go."
His parents wished to go,
but Zhāng Dìng said:
"Here there is
a grand entertainment from Qīngzhōu,
which you can also watch."
He then took a water jar,
which could hold about two dǒu,
empty and containing nothing.
Placing it in the courtyard,
he performed the Yǔ steps, circling it two or three times,
then poured it out within the courtyard.
Countless people appeared,
all six or seven cùn tall.
Officials, generals, soldiers, ladies, and spectators
filled the courtyard with clamor.
Immediately, an unparalleled performance hall and theater appeared,
with arranged banquets and processional guards,
music and various entertainments,
pavilions, towers, carriages, and sheds—
all exquisitely detailed.
Such a feast and entertainment lasted a full day,
and his parents watched it.
When evening came,
he again tilted the jar in the courtyard,
and the people, objects, carriages, and horses,
thousands upon thousands of groups and teams,
filed in succession into the jar.
His parents took the jar to look inside.
Again, there was not a single thing.
He could also use a sword or knife to cut off his own hands and feet,
hollow out and excise his five viscera,
and hang them separately on the four walls.
After a long while,
he would restore his body,
peaceful and without suffering.
Whenever he saw screens or painted barriers
depicting people or music,
he would point at them with his finger,
and they would all fly, walk, sing, and dance,
talking, laughing, hurrying, and moving,
no different from real ones.
His parents asked him from whom he had learned this.
He said:
"My teacher's surname is Yào,
an immortal from Hǎilíng Mountain.
He has already bestowed upon me the Way of Ascension to Heaven,
appointing a time in ten years.
Now it has been seven years."
He bid farewell to his family and entered Tiānzhù Qián Mountain.
Before leaving, he told his parents:
"If you have thoughts of me,
I will return on my own;
do not worry deeply."
Thus, whenever his parents thought of him,
he would immediately return home,
then soon fly away again.
One day, he said to his parents:
"After sixteen years,
Guǎnglíng will become rubble.
You should move the family to Hǎizhōu,
to dwell in a blessed land."
He left two elixir pills with his parents,
saying:
"Taking these, you will have no illness for over a hundred years."
From then on, he never returned.
His parents took the elixir,
and their spirits and energy became light and refreshed;
their appetite and enjoyment of food
doubled compared to when they were young and strong.
They then moved to live in Hǎizhōu.
During the Qiánfú era,
his parents were still alive.
From "Xiān Zhuàn Shí Yí"
Shí Mín
There was a man named Shí Mín,
whose origins are unknown.
He wandered between rivers and lakes
for many years.
His Daoist arts were profound and marvelous,
almost unfathomable.
During the Chángqìng era,
he was a guest in Wǎnlíng Commandery.
There was a son of the Léi family,
who often served as a general in Xuānchéng.
One day,
he gathered with several friends to drink at a villa south of the commandery,
and Shí Mín was also present.
A servant of the household netted a fish,
several chǐ long,
and brought it to the house.
That day,
Mr. Léi and his guests were deeply intoxicated.
All the guests departed,
and only Shí Mín stayed overnight at the Léi family villa.
At the time, summer heat was at its peak,
and by the next day, when they looked at the fish,
it had already spoiled and was inedible.
The servant was about to discard it,
when Shí Mín said to him:
"Although this fish has spoiled,
I have a good medicine
that can still revive it.
How can you discard it?"
Mr. Léi laughed and said:
"Sir, you are deluded!
Even if you truly had a good potion,
how could it revive this fish?"
Shí Mín said:
"I hope you will observe."
Thereupon, he took out a small pouch from his clothing,
containing several grains of medicine,
and tossed them onto the spoiled fish.
In barely the time of a meal,
the fish became fresh and moist as before,
and soon it waved its fins and shook its scales,
as if in a great flowing river.
Mr. Léi was astonished,
and bowing twice, he thanked him, saying:
"Sir, your art
can truly be called divine!
We worldly people are deaf and blind;
gazing upon your lofty traces,
we are like a well frog and a cloud bird—
how could we possibly be your companions?"
Previously, Mr. Léi had suffered from an abdominal mass illness for years.
Subsequently, he sought the elixir from Shí Mín's clothing,
hoping to cure his long-standing affliction.
Shí Mín refused,
and said:
"My elixir is of the utmost purity and integrity.
You worldly people
have unrestrained desires.
Within your viscera,
foul and greasy substances accumulate.
If you were to place my elixir within them,
the energy of your viscera would clash with the medicine,
like fire and water battling each other.
How could there be a whole person then?
Be careful not to take it."
Shí Mín also said:
"Immortality is not difficult to attain,
but worldly attachments are many burdens.
Like caged apes and birds,
they merely have the heart to soar and transcend—
how could they possibly achieve it?"
During the Huìchāng era,
he died in Wú Commandery.
From "Xuān Shì Zhì"
A Magician of Emperor Wǔzōng's Reign in the Táng Dynasty
Emperor Wǔzōng of the Táng dynasty
was fond of supernatural arts and extraordinary techniques.
Taoist practitioners and alchemists from across the land
flocked to the capital in great numbers.
Zhào Guīzhēn explored profound mysteries
and mastered the art of refining lead and mercury,
earning awe and respect from all who saw him.
He requested permission to build a Gazing-at-Immortals Terrace within the palace grounds,
one hundred feet high,
believing it would allow him to harness phoenixes and crane-riding immortals,
enabling him to ascend to the heavens on a set date.
He often said that refining elixirs required raw silver.
An imperial edict ordered mining operations at Lèpíng Mountain,
but despite mobilizing a massive workforce,
only worthless rocks and barren ore were extracted,
with no silver to be found.
Guīzhēn then performed several days of fasting and rituals,
placing an imperial prayer in the mountain caves.
Soon, an old man leaning on a staff arrived and said:
"Treasures of the mountains and rivers
emerge only for those who possess the Way.
Moreover, since our enlightened ruler is devoted to cultivating perfection,
what spiritual response would not be granted?
Venerable Master, trouble yourself no more—
tomorrow, your request shall be fulfilled."
Having spoken, he departed,
and none knew where he went.
That night, a sound like thunder was heard,
and the mountain split open for several dozen yards,
gushing forth a torrent of molten silver,
exactly matching the amount needed for the elixir-making.
Much alchemical refinement took place within the palace,
but outsiders seldom knew its methods.
There were also two men from Jīnlíng, Xǔ Yuáncháng and Wáng Qióng,
skilled in writing talismans and performing transformations,
nearly capable of commanding ghosts and spirits.
During the Huìchāng era,
they were summoned to the capital
and moved freely within the palace.
Emperor Wǔzōng said to them:
"I have heard that in a previous reign, there was Míng Chóngyǎn,
skilled in talismanic arts,
who could fetch mandarin oranges from Luófú Mountain
to supply the imperial fruit table,
traveling thousands of miles
in just ten days.
Can you, my masters, not match the arts of that former reign
and rival Chóngyǎn's excellence?"
("Match" is likely a scribal error for "equal.")
According to the Jùtán Lù, this line reads: "Although my virtue does not equal that of former reigns,
surely your arts are not inferior to Chóngyǎn's.")
Yuáncháng rose and apologized:
"The methods I have received
have not yet reached such profound mystery.
To traverse mountains and seas
might risk misleading Your Majesty's virtue;
but within a thousand miles,
I can arrive within a day."
Emperor Wǔzōng said:
"Luòyáng regularly presents pomegranates,
which should now be ripe.
You shall fetch ten of them tonight."
Yuáncháng received the order and left.
By dawn,
as the bedchamber doors opened,
a golden tray bearing pomegranates
was placed beside the imperial couch.
Soon, a palace envoy reported
that the exact number of missing pomegranates had been discovered.
Such miraculous responses and transformations
were common with them.
Wáng Qióng excelled at enchanting objects,
capable of almost anything.
In midwinter,
he sealed several peach and apricot trees with medicine,
and overnight they burst into full bloom,
fragrant and luxuriantly colorful,
lasting over a month before withering.
After Emperor Wǔzōng passed away,
Guīzhēn and Qióng were both exiled to Lǐngbiǎo,
while Yuáncháng vanished,
his whereabouts unknown.
From Lièxiān Tán Lù.
(Míng manuscript: From Lièxiān Zhuàn.)
Note: See Jùtán Lù, lower scroll.
In Hǎinán
(Míng manuscript: Hǎinán reads as Nánhǎi)
Commander, there was a certain Yáng Jūshì,
whose name is lost,
but who called himself a "Jūshì" (recluse),
often wandering the counties of Nánhǎi,
lodging and eating with others,
with no fixed abode.
He would tell people:
"I possess extraordinary arts,
but you ordinary folk
could never comprehend them."
Later, he came to the commandery seat,
where the governor, a lover of curiosities,
hearing of the Jūshì's arrival,
was greatly pleased
and treated him with generous courtesy,
inviting him to drink.
At every banquet or excursion,
the Jūshì was always invited first,
and he grew quite proud of this.
One day, drunk and unruly, he offended the governor,
who could no longer tolerate him.
Later, another banquet was held at the commandery hall,
with singing girls and music,
but the Jūshì was not included.
Several other guests
were also not invited by the governor,
and they said to the Jūshì:
"You, sir, have often boasted of extraordinary arts,
and we have long admired you.
To meet you here today
is truly fortunate.
However,
now we hear the governor is hosting a grand banquet at the commandery hall,
yet you, sir, are excluded.
Can you not perform some extraordinary art to impress him?
Or perhaps you truly have no such arts?"
The Jūshì laughed and said:
"This is but a minor trick.
Watch me, gentlemen.
I shall summon those singing girls for you
to accompany our wine."
They all said:
"We would be delighted."
The Jūshì then ordered wine prepared,
had the guests sit in a circle,
and told a young servant to close the empty room in the western wing.
After a long while, he opened it.
Three or four beauties descended from the wing,
exquisitely adorned,
carrying musical instruments.
The Jūshì said:
"How is my art?"
The guests were utterly astonished,
finding it nearly unfathomable.
He bade the women sit in order,
and they played music and sang.
When guests inquired about his method,
the Jūshì only smiled without answering.
Dusk deepened.
Around midnight,
the Jūshì said to the singing girls:
"You may return now."
They all rose
and entered the empty room in the western wing.
The guests exchanged stunned glances,
though some still suspected ghostly or demonic trickery.
The next day,
a commandery clerk reported:
"Last evening, the governor held a banquet in the commandery hall,
with singing girls seated in rows.
Suddenly, they all collapsed to the ground,
and in an instant, a fierce wind arose,
sweeping their instruments away.
Only at midnight
did the girls awaken,
and the instruments returned to their original places.
The governor questioned the girls,
but they all said they saw only darkness
and could not explain what happened."
The guests were greatly alarmed
and recounted the entire affair,
which was reported to the governor.
The governor marveled in amazement,
then apologized and sent the Jūshì away,
not daring to keep him in the commandery.
This occurred around the beginning of the Kāichéng era.
From Xuānshì Zhì.
Zhāng Shìpíng
In the Táng Dynasty, Shòuzhōu Governor Zhāng Shìpíng,
from middle age onward,
both he and his wife suffered from blindness.
They sought various medical treatments,
but none could cure them.
They then retired to a separate villa,
secluded themselves and blamed themselves.
They only prayed and made offerings to the stars,
hoping for divine protection.
As years passed,
their family wealth gradually dwindled,
yet their sincere devotion did not wane.
In the seventh year of Yuánhé, on the rénchén day,
the seventeenth day of the eighth month,
a scholar came to their gate seeking an audience.
The family servant said:
"My master and his wife are ill,
and have not received guests for a long time."
The scholar said:
"Although I am a scholar,
I also study medicine.
Hearing that the Governor is ill,
I have come here for this reason."
The servant went in to inform Shìpíng,
who joyfully said:
"Due to long illness, I have not received guests,
but if you have a remedy,
I hope you will bestow your aid."
The scholar said:
"Just let me see the Governor once,
and I will have a good medicine."
Hearing this, Shìpíng
supported his illness to meet him.
The scholar said to the Governor:
"This illness does not require medicine.
Tomorrow, hire ten laborers,
with tools like shovels and spades,
to dig a well.
Your eyes will naturally be cured immediately."
They prepared as he instructed.
The scholar then selected an auspicious spot,
and from morning they dug the well
until evening when they reached water.
Shìpíng's eye illness suddenly lightened.
Upon obtaining the fresh water to wash his eyes,
they instantly became clear and bright,
restored as before.
The illness of ten years
vanished in a single day.
The husband and wife, grateful, thanked him,
and generously offered gold and silk.
The scholar said:
"I am not a person of this world;
I am an official of the Tàibái Star.
Because you have been ill for years,
yet never forgot the Way,
and devotedly prayed and made offerings,
you moved the stars above.
The Five Emperor Star Lords sent me down to impart this method,
to dispel your severe illness,
in response to your heart of cultivation and devotion.
The gifts of gold and silk
are not what I desire.
Therefore, I leave this method,
so you may teach it to the world,
to relieve suffering and illness,
and thereby increase hidden virtue.
The essentials are: in zǐwǔ years, the fifth month on wùyǒu days, the eleventh month on mǎochén days are auspicious;
in chǒuwèi years, the sixth month on wùhài days, the eleventh month on chénsì days;
in yínshēn years, the seventh month on hàizǐ days, the first month on sìwǔ days;
in mǎoyǒu years, the eighth month on zǐchǒu days, the second month on wǔwèi days;
in chénxū years, the ninth month on shēnwèi days, the third month on yínchǒu days;
in sìhài years, the tenth month on shēnyǒu days, the fourth month on yínmǎo days.
Choose the方位, year, month, day, and time accordingly,
and it will be a blessed site.
Dredge the well to reach the spring,
and there will surely be good effect."
Shìpíng bowed twice and received it.
After speaking,
he ascended to heaven and departed.
From "Biographies of Divine Encounters."
Féng Jiàn
Féng Jiàn of Hédōng
was from a renowned family.
He entered official service through the míngjīng examination,
but his nature was at odds with the vulgar world.
Later, he abandoned his post and lived in seclusion by the Yī River.
There was a Dàoshi named Lǐ Jūn, known for his mastery of the Way,
especially skilled at seeing ghosts.
Court officials all admired his ability.
Later, Lǐ Jūn retired and returned to Rǔyǐng.
He happened to meet Jiàn in the Yīluò area,
and knowing Jiàn possessed extraordinary arts,
he greatly respected him.
During the Dàlì era,
there was a certain Cuī Gōng of Bólíng,
who was a colleague of Lǐ Jūn,
and they were very close.
Lǐ Jūn sent a letter to Cuī, saying:
"In controlling ghosts nowadays,
none surpass Jiàn."
At that time, court officials all knew Jiàn had divine arts and numerology,
and often spoke his name.
Afterward, people in Cháng'ān generally wrote the character "Jiàn" on their doors,
precisely for this purpose.
From "Records of the Xuānshì."
Old Man Pān
At the Shàolín Temple on Sōngshān,
during the Yuánhé era,
it once happened that due to wind stopping,
an old man, leaning on a staff, knocked at the gate seeking lodging.
The temple attendants, as the gate was already closed,
could not open it again,
so they pointed to two empty rooms outside the temple,
asking him to stay there himself.
There were no beds or mats either,
but the old man entered the room.
After the second watch,
a monk, having risen,
suddenly saw great brightness outside the temple gate.
Finding it strange, he looked,
and saw inside the room where the old man was staying,
cushions, mats, and emerald curtains were set up,
extraordinarily luxurious and splendid.
He also saw delicacies laid out,
the old man eating and drinking calmly,
with no attendants around him.
Astonished at this,
yet not daring to open the door to inquire,
they all waited and watched together.
After the fifth watch,
the old man woke from sleep,
finished washing himself,
took a gourd from his bosom,
as big as a fist,
then collected the bed, mats, curtains, and tent,
all items used,
and put them all inside it,
nothing left out.
After packing,
he placed the gourd back into his bosom,
and the room was empty as before.
The temple monks, amazed,
opened the gate and went together to pay respects and ask,
but the old man only declined with thanks.
The monks insisted he stay,
asking his name.
He said his surname was Pān,
traveling from Nányuè north to Tàiyuán.
Afterward, he was seen from time to time.
From "Records of Original Transformations."
Mr. Wáng
During the early years of the Xiántōng era,
there was a Presented Scholar named Zhāng Cí.
After failing the imperial examinations,
he traveled extensively in the region between the Huái and Hǎi rivers,
possessing considerable skill in the Daoist arts.
He often practiced breath cultivation and abstained from grains,
and was fond of wine and obsessed with the game of Go.
When he saw commoners occupied with alchemical furnace techniques and elixir arts,
one day, upon observing them,
he laughed heartily in derision,
took up a brush and inscribed on their wall:
"What can one do about the Golden Crow?
It flies ceaselessly overhead.
Vainly you burn the crimson furnace to refine elixirs,
how can jade-like beauty be preserved?
This year the flowers bloom on the branches,
next year leaves fall from the tree.
Better to just drink wine,
morning and dusk, again and again."
People all found this strange.
By nature, he disliked elaborate adornment,
and frequented many wine shops,
due to his fondness for wine.
If someone invited him to drink,
and it suited his fancy,
he would request paper and cut out twenty or thirty paper butterflies,
blow on them with his breath,
and they would form a row and fly away.
After a while of this,
he would point at them to gather them,
and in a moment they would all be in his hand.
Those who witnessed this would ask him for the trick,
but he would always use other matters as an excuse to refuse.
Once, while traveling in Jiànchéng,
he was often beset by drunkenness.
Some unsavory types, wishing to take advantage of his inebriation to test him,
competed with him in a contest of strength.
The county magistrate happened to see this,
and had him arrested.
After he sobered up,
he was tasked with composing two regulated verses—one praising virtue and one expressing his feelings—to present to the magistrate.
The magistrate then immediately released him.
One of the recorded poems reads:
"The family tradition ever carries the fragrance of huì and lán orchids,
A renowned clan of ministers passes down a name that once dominated states.
His countenance, serene, hangs with the splendor of the autumn moon;
His literary works soar high, like the roar of ocean waves.
In the hall of litigation, with no disputes, he tunes his qin's pegs;
In the commandery's pavilion, what hinders him from getting drunk with jade cups?
Today, the water under the bridge east of Jiàn
(pronounced *jiān*)
will henceforth remain forever clear and placid."
Afterwards, the county magistrate greatly admired Zhāng's talent,
and subsequently sought his Daoist methods,
receiving and hosting him day and night,
wishing to learn his arts.
Zhāng, considering the magistrate to be from a noble and illustrious family,
young yet governing a bustling district,
likely had many desires for music, women, dogs, and horses,
and had no leisure to devote his mind to profound mysteries.
Therefore, he presented him with a poem to enlighten his thoughts:
"Why seek outside with ladders and intermediaries?
Long life is only achieved through inner cultivation.
Do not say the Great Dao is hard for people to attain;
It is simply that one's practice of the mind does not reach the end."
Another day, when he was about to depart,
he wrote on the qin hall and took his leave.
Later, many said he ascended to immortality in the Jiāngnán region.
On the day he first left,
riding on a wine-induced haze,
he asked for a scrap of paper,
cut out two cranes in front of the hall,
sprayed water on them,
and shortly they soared and flew away.
He then said:
"You may go first,
I will follow shortly."
At that time, the county magistrate was also drunk,
and had no time to detain him,
so Zhāng was able to leave.
What he inscribed read:
"Zhāng Cí, Zhāng Cí, by himself understands nothing,
Yet all the classics of the world are within his belly.
His body drifts aimlessly within the mortal world,
His heart wanders carefree beyond the heavens."
To this day, this is recounted by enthusiasts in the Jiāng-Huái region.
From *Guìyuàn Cóngtán*.
Cuī Yán
Cuī Yán
served in the Left Personal Cavalry Army.
One day, he fell ill, his eyes grew dim,
unable to distinguish people or objects even at close distance.
His eyebrows and hair fell out,
the bridge of his nose collapsed,
and sores like scabies broke out on his skin.
Everyone regarded it as a vile disease,
seemingly incurable.
Because he was an envoy returning to the camp via the Zǐwǔ path through Luò Valley,
he encountered a Daoist practitioner
emerging from the valley.
The man did not give his name,
but bestowed upon him a prescription:
"Gather one or two shēng of Chinese honey locust thorns,
burn them to ash.
Take rhubarb, steam and sun-dry it nine times,
then pound it into a fine powder.
Before meals,
decoct a strong rhubarb decoction,
and take it mixed with seven qiàn of the powder."
Within ten days,
his beard and hair grew back,
his skin became full and moist again,
the disease was suddenly cured,
and his eyesight became twice as sharp as usual.
After transmitting this prescription,
the Daoist practitioner turned and went back into the mountains.
No one knew where he went.
From *Shénxiān Gǎnyù Zhuàn*.
Zǐ Wéi
was an astrologer to Duke Jǐng of Sòng.
During Duke Jǐng's reign,
there was a man skilled in the patterns of the stars.
The duke offered him the position of Senior Grand Master,
housed him in multi-storied towers and extended pavilions,
to observe celestial phenomena.
He was provided with rare delicacies to eat,
and clothed in precious garments.
For food, there were ducks from Qúcān,
fried with cassia-flavored wine;
quails from Cóngtíng,
served with honey sauce;
carp from the Qí and Zhāng rivers
(*Shíyí Jì* notes "three carp" as "lǐ")
dried with green eggplants.
Pearl-like rice from Jiǔjiāng,
cooked with orchid-scented suet,
and the clear splendor of summer from Huáqīng
venison served on fine white silk
(the clear essence of Huáqīng well water)
The cook would strike a bell to announce the time,
and ring a chime stone when food was ready
(meaning bells and chimes were struck for each meal)
Clothes for the four seasons were hung,
adorned with gold and jade in spring and summer,
and kept warm with kingfisher feathers in autumn and winter.
Rare incense was burned on the altar platform.
Suddenly, a rustic man clad in grass, carrying a bamboo case,
knocked at the gate and entered, saying:
"I have heard you cherish the secrets of yīn-yáng, the five phases, celestial images, and the warp and weft of the cosmos;
I request an audience."
Duke Jǐng received him in the lofty hall.
Their conversation touched upon omens of the future,
then moved to events of the past,
with not a single error in ten thousand.
At night, he observed the stars and watched the ethers;
by day, he wielded calculating rods and consulted charts.
He did not wear the precious robes,
nor did he savor the exotic foods.
Duke Jǐng apologized, saying:
"Now the state of Sòng is in turmoil and disorder;
without you, how can I be assisted?"
The rustic man said:
"When virtue is not evenly distributed,
disorder will soon arrive.
Cultivate virtue and act with benevolence,
then Heaven will respond with auspicious signs,
and the people will look up to your transformative influence."
Duke Jǐng was convinced by his words,
bestowed upon him the surname Zǐ,
and named him Wéi.
The record states:
Sòng's Zǐ Wéi served for generations in the Ministry of Heaven,
excelling in observing the stars and pitch-pipes.
He can also be considered among the likes of Zǐ Shèn and Pí Zào.
Duke Jǐng treated him as a deity,
honored him with the highest rank,
clothed him in peerless garments,
and fed him delicacies from distant lands.
Even compared to the delicacies of the Three Pure Heavens' kitchens,
or the dragon-embroidered robes adorned with floral pendants,
these would still seem crude.
In the Spring and Autumn period, he was granted a surname at birth,
also because his clan became prominent through his affairs,
and he was called the Master of the Stars.
Towards the end of the state,
he wrote books on yīn-yáng,
the details of which appear in Bān Gù's "Treatise on Literature."
From *Wángzǐ Nián Shíyí Jì*.
Zhào Kuò
Zhào Kuò of Wǔchāng
was a man of Qí.
He studied the Way under Wú Yǒngshí Gōng.
After three years,
Kuò requested to return home.
Gōng said:
"Your mastery of the Way is not yet complete,
how can you return?"
Nevertheless, he sent him off.
When he reached the border of Qí and was traveling at his limit,
he stopped to rest.
A fellow traveler, who was an official, thought he was a lawbreaker
and was about to arrest him.
Kuò ran over a hundred paces,
transforming into a blue deer.
The official pursued him.
He then ran into a winding alley.
Utterly exhausted,
he crouched down to rest.
The official saw him and chased him again,
so he transformed into a white tiger
and fled urgently.
Seeing a pile of dung,
he entered it
and turned into a rat.
The official realized and said:
"This man can transform;
this must be him."
He then seized the rat and bound it,
whereupon Kuò's original form returned.
He was then handed over to prison.
According to the law, he should be executed in the marketplace.
Wú Yǒngshí Gōng heard of this
and sighed, saying:
"This is my fault."
He then went to see the King of Qí and said:
"I have heard that in your great state there is a prisoner
who can change his form."
The king then summoned Kuò
and ordered soldiers to surround him.
Kuò, as before, transformed into a rat.
Gōng, rising from his seat, suddenly became an old hawk,
seized the rat, and flew away,
soaring into the clouds.
From "Lièxiān Zhuàn"
Fán Yīng
Fán Yīng of the Hàn
was skilled in charts and prognostication texts,
penetrating the obscure and subtle.
During the Yǒngtài era,
he had an audience with the emperor.
He then spat toward the southwest.
The emperor asked him the reason,
and he replied:
"There is a fire in Chéngdū today."
Later, the commandery of Shǔ reported a fire disaster,
exactly matching that day.
It is also said
that at the time, rain came from the northeast,
so the fire did not cause great harm.
Yīng once suddenly let down his hair, drew a knife,
and struck within his house.
His wife, finding it strange, asked him the reason.
Yīng said:
"Xī Shēng has encountered bandits."
Xī Shēng, named Xún,
was Yīng's disciple
and was traveling far away at the time.
When he later returned, he recounted
that on the road he had met bandits,
but was saved by an old man with disheveled hair,
thus escaping unharmed.
During the Yǒngjiàn era,
a bell in the palace rang by itself.
The emperor was deeply troubled by this,
and none of the ministers could explain it.
So he asked Yīng,
who said:
"Mount Mín in Shǔ has collapsed;
the mother mountain collapsed, so the son bell rang.
It is not a disaster for the sacred court."
Soon after, a report came that Mount Shǔ had collapsed.
From "Yīng Biézhuàn"
Yáng Yóu
Yáng Yóu of the Later Hàn
was skilled in divination by observing signs.
He served as a commandery literary assistant.
Once, he was drinking with others.
He instructed his carriage driver:
"When the wine has gone around three times,
you should prepare the carriage."
He then hurriedly left.
Later, at the host's residence,
a sudden fight broke out, resulting in killings.
Someone asked how he had known in advance,
and Yóu said:
"Earlier, doves were fighting on the community tree.
This was an omen of armed conflict."
Many of his statements were like this.
From "Hòu Hàn Shū"
Jiè Xiàng
Jiè Xiàng of Wú, courtesy name Yuánzé.
He was discussing with the King of Wú about minced fish,
asking which was the most delicious.
Xiàng said:
"The mullet from the sea is the best.
I request to make a square pit in front of the hall
and fill it with water."
Xiàng lowered a fishing line into the pit,
and within the time of a meal,
he caught a mullet
and made minced fish.
From "Jiànkāng Shílù"
Guō Pú
Chén Shù of Jìn, courtesy name Sìzǔ,
had a fine reputation
and served as an assistant to the Grand General,
being greatly loved and valued.
When he died,
Guō Pú went to mourn him,
deeply grieved,
and called out:
"Sìzǔ,
how do you know it is not a blessing?"
Soon after, the Grand General started a rebellion,
just as he had said.
From "Shì Shuō Xīn Yǔ"
Yǔ Shēn
Yǔ Shēn of Xīnyě in Qí
was orphaned young
and devoted himself to reading.
In celestial phenomena and mathematics,
he was exceptionally skilled.
When Wǔxiàn Gōng Xiāo Yǐngzhòu was critically ill,
he said to Shēn:
"According to the calculations of fate,
will I be without blame?"
Shēn replied:
"The star Zhènxīng is in Xiāngyáng;
Jīngzhōu itself has little fortune.
Your Excellency will meet his end in a chaotic era.
Your reputation equals Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng,
which is enough to bring honor to your descendants.
What regret is there?"
The Duke said:
"You have understood it.
But the foolish ruler is wildly cruel,
and the people long for Yáo and Shùn.
I regret not seeing the empire purified
and the horses resting at Huà Shān."
He sighed and passed away.
It indeed turned out as he said.
Yǐngzhòu
was the son of Chìfǔ.
From "Tán Sǒu"
Zhāng Zǐxìn
When Wáng Yǎn of Lángyá in Qí killed Hé Shìkāi,
the imperial guard Xī Yǒngluò was sitting opposite Zhāng Zǐxìn of Hénèi.
Suddenly, magpies cried
and fought in the courtyard, then fell.
Zǐxìn said:
"The magpies' cries are inauspicious.
If toward evening a wind comes from the southwest,
passes through the trees,
and brushes the corner of the hall,
there will surely be matters of dispute.
If someone summons you tonight,
be careful not to go."
After Zǐxìn left,
indeed a wind came.
Yǎn sent someone to summon Yǒngluò,
claiming it was an imperial summons.
Yǒngluò intended to go,
but his wife advised him not to leave.
He then claimed he had fallen from his horse and injured his back,
thus avoiding the disaster.
From "Sān Guó Diǎn Lüè"
Guǎn Lù
Guǎn Lù of Wèi once visited Guō Ēn's home.
Suddenly, a flying dove came and perched on the beam,
crying very mournfully.
Lù said:
"A guest will come from the east to visit,
bringing pork and wine,
but there will be a minor incident."
By evening,
it was exactly as he said.
Ēn urged moderation in drinking and caution with roasting.
Later, they shot a chicken for food,
but the arrow shot from within the hedge
accidentally hit a young girl of several years old,
causing bleeding and terror.
From "Wèi Zhì"
Monk Chóu
Emperor Yang of Sui held a banquet for Zhūgě Yǐng, the Junior Supervisor of the Imperial Library, in the Guānwén Hall.
The emperor shared his own cup and bestowed it upon Yǐng.
He then said:
"In the past, I had a monk named Chóu.
He prepared various medicines for me,
gathering them all into a bamboo tube.
He would take a hatpin and insert it into the medicine in the tube,
leaving it for seven days before removing it.
When entertaining guests and drinking,
as the cup arrived,
he would take the pin and draw a line through the wine,
splitting it in two.
One side would be drained completely,
while the other side remained full.
He would then offer it to the guests,
and all who witnessed it considered it a rare and miraculous feat of a great sage."
From "Dàyè Shíyí"
Lǐ Chúnfēng
Lǐ Chúnfēng, the Grand Astrologer of the Tang dynasty,
was revising the new calendar.
The sun and moon were in conjunction,
and a total eclipse was predicted,
which was considered inauspicious according to divination.
Emperor Tàizōng was displeased and said:
"If the sun does not eclipse,
how will you account for yourself?"
Lǐ replied:
"If there is no eclipse,
I beg to die for it."
When the time came,
the emperor waited in the courtyard
and said to Lǐ Chúnfēng:
"I will allow you to bid farewell to your wife and children."
Lǐ replied:
"It is still early."
He marked the shadow on the wall at the predicted time:
"The eclipse will occur here."
As he said, the eclipse occurred,
without the slightest error.
Once, Lǐ Chúnfēng and Zhāng Lǜ were both attending the emperor when
a sudden gust of wind blew from the south.
Lǐ predicted that there would be mourners five li to the south,
while Zhāng predicted there would be music.
Messengers were sent on horseback to investigate,
and they encountered a funeral procession.
There was ceremonial music.
On another occasion, Lǐ reported to the emperor:
"The seven stars of the Big Dipper will transform into humans,
and tomorrow they will go to the West Market to drink wine.
We should send someone to wait for them."
Emperor Tàizōng agreed
and sent men to wait.
Seven Brahmin monks
entered through the Jīnguāng Gate,
went to a tavern in the West Market,
ascended to the upper floor,
and ordered a shí of wine.
They drank it from bowls,
and in a moment, the wine was finished.
They ordered another shí.
The messenger went upstairs
and announced the imperial decree:
"We now invite the masters to the palace."
The foreign monks looked at each other and laughed, saying:
"It must be that little fellow Lǐ Chúnfēng speaking of us."
They then said:
"Wait until we finish this wine,
and we will go with you."
After drinking, they descended the stairs.
The messenger went down first,
but when he looked back, the foreign monks had disappeared.
He reported this to the emperor,
and Tàizōng was astonished.
Earlier, when the monks were drinking,
they had not paid for the wine.
When the tavern staff collected the utensils,
they found two thousand coins under the seats.
From "Guóshǐ Yìzuǎn" and "Jìwén"
Yuán Tiāngāng
When Wǔ Zétiān of the Tang dynasty was still in swaddling clothes,
a man from Yìzhōu named Yuán Tiāngāng was skilled in physiognomy.
Wǔ Shìyuè had him examine his wife, Lady Yáng.
Yuán Tiāngāng said:
"Madam will give birth to noble sons."
He then summoned all her sons to examine them.
Speaking to Yuánqìng and Yuánshuǎng, he said:
"They may reach the rank of provincial governor,
but their lives will ultimately be troubled."
When he saw Lady Hánguó, he said:
"This daughter will achieve great nobility,
but it will be unfavorable for her husband."
At that time, Wǔ Zétiān was still an infant,
dressed in boys' clothing,
and was carried in by her wet nurse.
Yuán Tiāngāng raised his eyes for a glance
and exclaimed in astonishment:
"Dragon eyes and phoenix neck—
this is the pinnacle of nobility.
If this is a girl,
she will become the ruler of the world."
From "Gǎndìng Lù"
Ān Lùshān's Sorcerer
Ān Lùshān of the Tang dynasty employed many practitioners of the magical arts.
He once said to a sorcerer:
"I feel no fear even in the presence of the Son of Heaven,
but whenever I see Minister Lǐ, my spirit trembles with dread—
that is, Lǐ Línfǔ."
The sorcerer said:
"You have five hundred yīn soldiers,
all with bronze heads and iron foreheads,
who are always by your side.
How could you fear Minister Lǐ?"
Ān Lùshān then said:
"How can I see them?"
Ān Lùshān then requested a banquet for the prime minister,
and had the sorcerer observe from behind a curtain.
The sorcerer exclaimed in shock:
"When I first saw the report of the prime minister's arrival,
there were two attendants with double buns and two maids in blue
holding incense burners who entered first.
Then, the attendants and guards with bronze heads and iron foreheads
all fled by breaking through roofs and leaping over walls.
I do not know the reason for this.
It must be that he is an immortal official temporarily banished to the mortal world."
From "Yìshǐ"
During the prosperous Tang dynasty, the official Lǐ Péngyù
(The original text had "通" for "遇";
corrected based on Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán)
visited Sāng Dàomào.
He said:
"Esteemed official,
(The original text had "安" for "官";
corrected based on the Ming dynasty manuscript copy)
you will only govern this one district, but
your two worthy sons,
the elder will reach the highest ministerial rank,
the younger will govern nearly several military districts,
and your descendants will flourish for a hundred generations."
Later events matched his words.
The eldest son, Lǐ Shí,
served as both general and minister,
and his descendants achieved the highest imperial examinations for two generations.
As for the younger son, Lǐ Fú,
he governed seven military districts
and ultimately held the title of Vice Military Commissioner.
In total, he had eight sons;
three passed the imperial examinations and rose to positions such as Minister, Imperial Advisor, and Prefectural Governor.
All his grandsons wore the crimson and purple robes of high officials.
In the first year of the Jiànzhōng era (780),
Sāng Dàomào requested that the city of Fèngtiān be fortified as a residence fit for a king.
He laid out the city plan like a turtle's shell,
dividing the interior into six main streets.
Emperor Dézōng had always held Sāng Dàomào's words in mystical regard,
so he ordered the Capital Prefect Yán Yǐng to mobilize several thousand laborers,
who worked alongside soldiers from the Six Armies to build the city walls.
At the time, it was the height of summer,
yet massive earthworks were suddenly undertaken,
and no one understood the reason.
Only when the emperor later fled and took refuge there
was the prophecy verified.
During the rebellion of Zhū Cǐ,
Emperor Dézōng took refuge in Fèngtiān.
At that time, the frontier military governors
had all raised troops to escort the emperor.
Zhū Cǐ personally led his vicious horde
straight to the city walls.
There was a monk from the Xīmíng Temple
who had fallen into rebel hands.
He was very cunning
and instructed them in building siege cloud ladders,
over ninety feet tall,
equipped with wooden shelters and watchtowers on top,
allowing them to look down into the city.
Hún Jiān and Lǐ Shèng memorialized:
"The rebel's momentum is strong,
and their cloud ladders are formidable.
If we allow them to approach the city walls,
we fear we will be unable to defend.
While they are still far off,
we request to blunt their advance with elite troops."
They then led five thousand imperial troops,
arrayed in formation and advanced.
At that time, they had bundles of kindling prepared in the rear,
planning to set them ablaze once the battle grew fierce.
However, the wind direction was unfavorable,
and the fire could not be lit.
The two generals poured a libation of wine and prayed:
"The rebel Zhū Cǐ harbors treacherous intent,
secretly wielding cruel power.
He dares, this mad rebel,
to assail the imperial carriage.
Now he masses troops to threaten our sovereign,
pressing close to our city walls.
We pledge to devote our loyal service,
determined to annihilate this baleful aura.
If the state is to be restored to peace,
and its majestic spirit remains unextinguished,
may these cloud ladders be consumed by fire,
and the rebel faction melt away like ice."
Their words were impassioned and righteous,
and their men found courage a hundredfold.
Soon, the wind direction suddenly shifted,
and with shouts and drumbeats they advanced.
The fire blazed fiercely, fanned by the strong wind,
smoke and dust blotted the sky,
the ladders burned to ashes and the rebels fled.
Emperor Dézōng watched from the city tower,
and cheers of "Long live the Emperor!" rose from within and without the city.
After the capital was recaptured,
these two men's achievements were foremost,
and they were generously enfeoffed with lands.
In supporting and upholding the state,
they remained consistent from start to finish.
Lǐ Xīpíng (Lǐ Shèng) had four sons,
all of whom governed military districts,
honored and illustrious in their loyalty.
Earlier,
when Lǐ Shèng served in the Left Imperial Guard,
he remained in that post for a long time without promotion.
Hearing that Sāng Dàomào was skilled in physiognomy,
he took a bolt of silk
and went early in the morning.
At that time, believers flocked to Sāng in great numbers,
and visitors often could not see him immediately.
Hearing that Lǐ was at the gate,
Sāng personally went to welcome him,
set out food and wine,
and treated him with great attentiveness.
After a while, he said to him:
"In days to come, you will achieve monumental feats,
attaining honors beyond compare.
Should you ever hold power in your hands,
I entrust my life to you."
Lǐ could not fathom his meaning.
He merely felt embarrassed and assented.
Sāng requested to return the gifted silk
and exchange it for the sweat-stained shirt Lǐ was wearing.
He further asked Lǐ to write his name on the collar,
saying, "When you see this in the future, remember me."
When Zhū Cǐ rebelled,
Sāng Dàomào fell into rebel territory.
After the capital was recaptured,
all those who had followed the rebellion were executed.
At that time, Lǐ was ordered to carry out the executions.
As Sāng Dàomào was about to be executed,
he requested to speak.
He then brought up the matter of the sweat-stained shirt.
Lǐ Shèng memorialized that Sāng was not guilty,
and he was specially pardoned.
The Minister Dù Yòu once served as an administrative assistant to Yáng Yán.
The former minister Lú Qì was jealous of him
and wanted to have him posted away.
Dù went to see Sāng Dàomào, who said:
"If you are posted away within the year,
your fortune and longevity will be boundless."
Later, from a certain post,
after over ninety days he was appointed to another post.
The official titles are forgotten,
but his fortune and longevity indeed turned out as predicted.
From "Jù Tán Lù"
The Old Man at the Village School
The Tang dynasty chancellor Dòu Yìzhí,
originally named Mì,
came from a poor family.
He attended a village school for his studies.
There was an old man at the school who possessed magical arts,
though people were unaware of it.
One day towards dusk,
a fierce wind and snowstorm suddenly arrived.
The students could not return home,
so they stayed overnight in a leaky building.
In the cold, they all crowded around the fire,
only Dòu slept to the side.
In the middle of the night,
the old man helped Dòu up and said:
"Dòu Mì,
in the future you will become a high minister.
The potential for honor and longevity is yours;
strive hard and take care of yourself."
When Emperor Dézōng took refuge in Fèngtiān,
Dòu, having just passed the imperial examination,
also followed the imperial carriage westward.
Riding a lame donkey, he reached Kāiyuǎn.
The crowd was dense and the road narrow.
The city gates were about to close,
and Dòu feared the situation would prevent him from entering.
Suddenly, someone shouted at his donkey
and also whipped it from behind,
enabling it to dash swiftly through.
Looking back, he saw two black-clad soldiers
calling out:
"Scholar, in the future, do not forget this kindness from the common folk."
After he rose to high office,
he sought out and found their sons
and promoted them within the officialdom, where they became quite successful.
From "Yīn Huà Lù"
The Bone Physiognomist
In the late Zhēnyuán era of the Tang dynasty (785-805),
there was a mountain-dwelling bone physiognomist
who was blind in both eyes.
When people sought a reading,
he would feel them with his hands
and could invariably discern their nobility or baseness.
Fáng Cìqīng was then vigorously seeking advancement
and was among the first to visit him.
When he emerged from the house,
a crowd of later visitors filled the lane.
Seeing Fáng had come out,
they greeted him and asked:
"How was it?"
He replied:
"Not worth mentioning,
not worth mentioning.
He just said that a certain tall, thin Scholar Dù would reach the highest ministerial rank.
What more need be said?"
Some thereupon withdrew.
Later, Dù Xún indeed bore the seal of a chancellor and governed Western Shǔ.
From "Jiā Yǔ Lù"
Tián Liángyì and Jiǎng Hánhóng
In the early Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
the Nányuè Daoist priests Tián Liángyì and Jiǎng Hánhóng,
both possessed supremely high cultivation in the Daoist arts,
and were revered and respected far and wide.
They were known at the time as Masters Tián and Jiǎng.
They centered their minds on emptiness and non-being,
and treated all things with gentle warmth.
They did not engage in superficial adornment,
yet their natural demeanor was pure and lofty;
those who saw them found their pettiness and stinginess completely dispelled.
The Vice Ministers Lǚ Wèi and Yáng Píng,
who successively served as investigating commissioners in Húnán,
both treated them as teachers, facing north to pay them respect.
When Tánzhōu suffered a great drought,
and prayers for rain proved unsuccessful,
someone suggested inviting them.
Yáng said:
"Is Master Tián someone who would pray for rain for others?"
Nevertheless, they had no choice but to invite him.
The master, with unkempt hair and worn-out clothes,
cheerfully got into the carriage.
Upon arriving in the commandery, he still said nothing at all.
