That very day, rain fell.
At the Yuèguàn where he resided,
a Huánglù altar was constructed.
The ritual implements had already been arranged, but the sky was overcast and gloomy.
His disciples requested that he pray for clear skies.
Tián again said nothing,
but sat with his headband pushed back and his hair hanging loose.
When it was time to perform the fasting ritual,
attendants on either side straightened his cap and shoes for him,
and supported him as he ascended the altar.
The sky immediately cleared.
There was once an old village woman
who presented him with a blue silk jacket.
In front of everyone, he immediately put it on.
Those sitting there secretly laughed,
but he did not mind it at all.
Yáng Píng once welcomed him to Tánzhōu.
Tián was barefoot at the time.
When the messenger arrived,
he immediately boarded a small boat and departed.
An attendant caught up with him at the yámén gate with his shoes and socks.
He then sat on the steps and put on his socks,
as if no one else was around.
Yáng bowed twice in greeting,
and he did not stop him.
He often enjoyed drinking wine,
yet his words never touched upon fortune, misfortune, right, or wrong.
Later, when Yáng was demoted from Capital Governor to Assistant Magistrate of Línhè,
he sent someone to inquire after Tián
and presented him with silver vessels.
Tián accepted them
and immediately gave them all to his disciples to use for a Dharma assembly.
He told the messenger upon his return:
"Report to your master,
tell him not to worry deeply.
Before long, he was transferred to serve as Chief Clerk of Hángzhōu."
He never sought anything from others,
nor did he refuse those who came to him.
By nature, he rarely remembered people's official positions or family ranks.
His bond with Lǚ Wèi was deepest.
Later, when Vice Director Lǚ Wēn was appointed Prefect of Héngzhōu,
he came to pay his respects.
Attendants first informed Tián that the Governor was Vice Minister Lǚ's son.
When Wēn entered,
Tián got off his couch, patted him on the back, and said:
"So you are Lǚ Wèi's son."
Wēn, moved to tears, descended the steps.
Tián did not stop him.
Such was his genuine simplicity.
His mother was a nun at the Xǐwáng Temple.
All the nuns there addressed the master as "Teacher."
Every day, he would carry two bundles of firewood to present to his mother.
If something prevented him from going,
his disciples would deliver them for him.
It was rumored that one morning, the temple nuns saw a tiger pacing outside Old Lady Tián's door.
They went and told the old lady.
She said:
"It must just be my little disciple sending firewood.
There's nothing to fear."
Master Jiǎng possessed the capacity of primordial chaos.
Although not equal to Tián,
his cultivation, conduct, and inclinations
were also similar.
He served Tián as an elder brother,
and they were known as inseparable friends.
Jiǎng was initially skilled in talismanic arts,
but he concealed his Way,
so no one knew of it.
Later, residing at the Jiǔzhēn Temple,
he once sent a disciple to the county market to buy items for the fasting ritual.
The disciple did not return on time.
When questioned about the reason,
he said that at the mountain pass he saw a huge beast blocking the road,
and it did not leave for a long time,
hence the delay.
Jiǎng said:
"I have been sheltering him here for a long time.
How dare it act like this?"
He then placed a talisman at the spot where it was seen.
The next day,
the beast was found dead beneath the talisman.
When Jiǎng heard of it, he said:
"I originally used the talisman to repel it,
to make it not come.
How could I know it could not escape itself?
Since it has harmed a living creature,
what use are such arts?"
He took the talisman manual and burned it,
and from then on never paid attention to such things again.
There was a man named Ōuyáng Píng.
His conduct and cultivation were also lofty.
He also served Jiǎng as an elder brother,
and regarding Master Tián, he was like a neighbor who had entered the inner chamber.
One evening, Píng dreamed of three golden censers descending from the sky,
as if summoning someone.
After waking,
he secretly told people:
"The two masters will not be here for long.
I will follow them."
Soon after, Tián shed his mortal form and departed.
Jiǎng followed next,
and Píng also passed away.
"Passed away" originally read "traveled";
changed according to *Yīnhuà Lù*, scroll 4.
Chén Guǎyán, Xú Língfǔ, and Féng Yúnyì of Tóngbó Mountain,
were all disciples of Tián.
Zhōu Hùndùn of Héng Mountain
was a disciple of Jiǎng.
Chén and Xú, in the southeast,
were ranked comparable to Tián and Jiǎng,
while Féng was in the same category as Ōuyáng.
Zhōu entered the Daoist path from childhood.
His
*Yīnhuà Lù*, scroll 4, has "disciplinary" for "benefit"
methods were pure and strict,
and he is now the foremost at Nányuè.
From *Yīnhuà Lù*.
Dù Shēng
In the Xiāntiān era of the Táng dynasty,
Dù Shēng of Xǔzhōu was skilled in divination by stalks and milfoil.
His predictions about lost property, official positions, and salaries
all proved accurate, as if divine.
There was a man who had lost a slave.
He went to Dù and asked him.
Dù said:
"Just return home along the post road.
On the way, if you meet a post messenger with a good whip,
kowtow and beg for it.
If he does not give it to you,
tell him the situation, saying
Dù Shēng taught you to beg.
If you do this, you will certainly obtain it."
The man did as told.
He indeed met a post messenger
and, using Dù Shēng's words, begged for the whip.
The messenger, finding it strange, said:
"I do not begrudge the whip,
but then I will have nothing to whip the horse with.
You can break off a branch from the side of the road to replace it,
and I will give you the whip."
The man then went to break a branch,
and saw the lost slave hiding under the tree.
He captured him.
When asked the reason,
the slave said:
"I was just walking along the road
when I saw my master from afar,
so I hid here."
There was another man who had lost a slave and went to see Dù Shēng.
Dù said:
"Go back and get five hundred coins,
then wait for him on the official road.
When you see a falconer passing by,
ask to buy one of his falcons.
You will certainly find your slave."
The man waited as instructed.
Soon, a falconer arrived.
The man explained the situation
and asked to buy one of the falcons.
The messenger, finding it strange,
gave him a secondary falcon.
Just as he was about to take it in hand,
the falcon suddenly flew off and perched in a thicket.
The man went to retrieve it,
and indeed, the slave was hiding underneath.
He thus seized him.
He predicted people's official positions and salaries in many cases,
which are too numerous to detail here.
From *Jì Wén*.
Hóng Shī
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān of the Táng dynasty, Zhāng Jìngzhī,
often longed for the virtue of the Táng house.
He said to his son Guànzōng:
"What I now wear with respect
is actually the court attire of the usurper's dynasty."
He rose through the ranks to become Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
When he was about to be promoted to the third rank,
his son was going to submit the documents through the Ministry of Personnel.
There was a monk named Hóng, skilled in yīn-yáng divination and calculations,
who was an old acquaintance of Jìngzhī.
He said to Jìngzhī:
"Vice Minister, there is no need to seek the third rank."
Jìngzhī replied:
"This disciple seeks nothing for himself;
it is merely my son's idea."
Jìngzhī's younger brother Nèzhī served as Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
At that time, he fell ill
and was in critical condition.
(Hóng) pointed at Nèzhī and said:
"The Eighth Gentleman will attain the third rank."
Jìngzhī said:
"I worry about the severity of his illness;
how could I hope for the third rank?"
(Hóng) said:
"The Eighth Gentleman today is like standing at the edge of a ten-thousand-ren abyss,
but he will certainly not fall."
Everything happened as he said.
Hóng also helped Duke Yànguó Zhāng Yuè purchase the first estate southeast of Yǒnglè.
When there were people seeking earth (for construction),
he warned them, saying:
"The northwest corner of this estate is the most royal ground;
be careful not to take earth from here."
After a month,
Hóng came again
and said to Duke Yàn:
"The vital energy of this estate has suddenly become extremely desolate;
I fear someone must have taken earth from the northwest corner."
The Duke went with Hóng,
and arriving at the northwest corner of the estate,
indeed found several pits where earth had been taken,
each over a zhàng deep.
Hóng was greatly alarmed and said:
"A calamity!
Your Lordship's wealth and honor will end with yourself alone.
Beyond twenty years from now,
none of your sons will live out their natural lifespans."
Duke Yàn was terrified and said:
"Can we fill them back in?"
Hóng said:
"The borrowed earth has no vitality;
it is not connected to the earth's veins.
Even if we fill them all now,
it is like a person with sores and wounds;
even if you patch it with other flesh,
it will ultimately be of no benefit."
Duke Yàn's sons, Jūn
and others, were all employed by Ān Lùshān,
who appointed them as high officials of the rebel regime.
After the recovery (of the capital),
the Three Judicial Offices determined their crimes.
During Emperor Sùzōng's reign, they were sentenced to a commutation of the death penalty.
The Retired Emperor summoned Emperor Sùzōng and said:
"The Zhāng Jūn brothers all held powerful and important offices for the rebel traitor.
Among them, Zhāng Jūn even joined the traitor in slandering and destroying our family affairs.
They are worse than dogs and pigs;
their crimes cannot be pardoned."
Emperor Sùzōng descended from the dais, kowtowed, and bowed twice, saying:
"When your servant was in the Eastern Palace (as Crown Prince),
I was falsely accused and slandered;
three times I faced death,
and each time it was Zhāng Yuè who protected me,
allowing me to keep my head,
and reach this day.
Now Zhāng Yuè's two sons face death once;
if your servant does not strenuously plead for them,
should the deceased have awareness,
what face would I have to see Zhāng Yuè in the underworld?"
He sobbed and prostrated himself.
The Retired Emperor ordered his attendants:
"Help the Emperor rise."
Then he said:
"For your sake, I will handle it.
Zhāng Jūn shall be exiled to a distant, harsh place."
He eventually died in Lǐngbiǎo.
Zhāng Jūn should be executed in the marketplace.
Do not further plead bitterly for this one."
Emperor Sùzōng covered his face and wept as he received the decree,
and thus Zhāng Jūn met his death.
Everything happened as predicted.
From *The New Account of the Great Táng* and *Leisurely Talks from the Military Tent*.
Luó Sīyuǎn
In the Táng dynasty, Luó Sīyuǎn possessed many secret and extraordinary arts,
and was most skilled in invisibility.
Emperor Mínghuáng delighted in the method of invisibility
and diligently sought to learn it from Sīyuǎn.
Although Sīyuǎn taught him,
he did not impart all the essentials.
Whenever the Emperor performed it together with Sīyuǎn,
then he would vanish completely and no one could detect him.
But if he tried it himself,
then sometimes a bit of his sash would remain,
or the corner of his headscarf would be exposed,
so the people in the palace often knew where the Emperor was.
The Emperor bestowed many gifts and rewards,
or threatened him with death,
and sought the art,
but he never fully transmitted it.
The Emperor grew angry
and ordered a strongman to wrap him in an oilcloth,
place him under an oil press,
crush him to death, and bury him.
Not ten days later,
a palace eunuch returning from the Shǔ road
encountered Sīyuǎn on the path.
Riding a donkey, he laughed and said to the envoy:
"His Majesty's jest
was rather cruel."
From *Records of the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo Eras*.
Zhāng Jǐngcáng
The Head of the Secretariat and Duke of Hédōng, Péi Guāngtíng,
served as Chancellor during the Kāiyuán era.
Zhāng Jǐngcáng could predict fortune and misfortune.
One day,
he suddenly visited the Duke
and handed him a large sheet of paper with the character "Tái" written on it.
The Duke said:
"I currently hold the office of the 'Tái' (Censorate/Imperial Secretariat);
what does this mean?"
A few days later,
he was demoted to Prefect of Táizhōu.
From *Anecdotes from the Department of State Affairs*.
Yè Fǎshàn
On the night of the Lantern Festival, Emperor Xuánzōng of the Táng dynasty
had shadow lanterns displayed on a grand scale at the Shàngyáng Palace,
set up courtyard torches,
and from the palace gates looking toward the main hall gates,
all were arranged with wax candles,
connected without interruption,
illuminating the palace chambers through and through,
brilliant and resplendent as if it were daytime.
At that time, the chief artisan of the Imperial Workshop, Máo Shùnxīn, was highly ingenious and inventive.
He constructed colored silks
to make a lantern tower of twenty bays,
one hundred and fifty feet high,
suspended with pearls, jade, gold, and silver.
Whenever a slight breeze arrived,
they would clink and chime, forming a melody.
Moreover, the lanterns were shaped like dragons, phoenixes, tigers, and leopards leaping and prancing,
as if not made by human hands.
There was a Dàoshi named Yè Fǎshàn at the Shèngzhēn Temple.
The Emperor urgently ordered him summoned.
Once he arrived,
the Emperor secretly led Fǎshàn to view it from below the tower,
with no one else knowing.
Fǎshàn said to the Emperor:
"The magnificence of these shadow lanterns
certainly has no match in the world,
only Liángzhōu can truly be considered a close second."
The Emperor said:
"Master, have you recently traveled there?"
Fǎshàn said:
"I have just come from there,
and was immediately summoned."
The Emperor found his words strange
and said:
"Now I wish to go there once.
Is it possible?"
Fǎshàn said:
"This is easy."
Thereupon, he instructed the Emperor to close his eyes,
stipulating:
"You absolutely must not look recklessly.
If you look at anything,
you will certainly be startled and terrified."
The Emperor followed his words,
closed his eyes and leaped,
finding himself amidst the clouds and heavens.
After a while, his feet touched ground.
Fǎshàn said:
"You may look around now."
Once he looked,
he saw lanterns and candles stretching continuously for over ten lǐ,
carriages and horses crowded together,
gentlemen and ladies mingling in great numbers.
The Emperor praised it as excellent.
After a long while,
Fǎshàn said:
"The viewing is finished.
We may return now."
Again closing his eyes,
he ascended into the void with Fǎshàn.
In a moment, they returned to the original place,
and the singing and music below the tower had not yet ended.
Fǎshàn went to Xīliángzhōu
and pawned an iron rúyì scepter at a wine shop.
Another day,
the Emperor ordered a palace eunuch to go to Liángzhōu on the pretext of other business
and thereby retrieve the rúyì and bring it back.
Fǎshàn also once led the Emperor on an excursion to the moon palace.
There, they listened to its heavenly music.
The Emperor himself understood music theory,
silently memorized the melody,
and upon returning transmitted it.
Thus it became the "Níshang Yǔyī Qǔ" melody.
Fǎshàn was born in the Bǐngzǐ year of the Suí dynasty's Dàyè era,
and died in the Rénshēn year of the Kāiyuán era,
altogether one hundred and seventy years.
In Níngzhōu, there was a person
who lay ill for years on end
and sought Fǎshàn to use flying talismans to control it.
He was told to dig about five feet deep, seven paces south of the well at his residence.
There, an ancient curved table was found.
On the table were eighteen characters in a song, saying:
"Years and ages, eternal sorrow,
wings and feathers, nearly returning.
Alas, suffering from calamity and hardship,
causing me unable to fly."
The sick person then recovered.
According to Kǒng Yà's "Record of Kuàijī,"
after Gě Xuán attained immortality,
the table transformed into a three-legged beast.
To this day, people of Shàngyú often see this table in the mountains.
It seems to be an omen of wanting to soar and ascend.
"Records of the Six Dynasties of Jīnlíng" states:
"On the seventeenth day of the eighth month in the seventh year of the Chìwū era of the Wú Emperor,
Gě Xuán attained the Dào on Fāngshān
and ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
To this day, there is a medicine-cauldron for boiling,
and on the mountain, a pool for washing medicine,
still present.
Also, Bái Zhòngdū,
a disciple of Gě Xuán,
also ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
To this day, the sacrificial altar is still present below Báidū Mountain.
Also, Yáo Guāng, also a disciple of Gě Xuán,
claimed to have attained becoming a fire-immortal.
The Great Emperor of Wú piled up firewood and burned him.
Guāng sat peacefully within the fire,
his hand reading a volume of plain-text book.
Fǎshàn fully transmitted talismans and registers,
especially excelling at subduing ghosts and spirits.
Previously, Emperor Gāozōng once examined and verified the methods for creating gold and silver among various occult masters.
Thereupon, over ninety individuals emerged.
Once, an altar ceremony was set up at the Língkōng Temple in the Eastern Capital.
Gentlemen and ladies went to observe it.
Suddenly, several dozen people threw themselves into the fire.
The people were greatly alarmed.
The Master said:
"They are all ghosts and demons.
My method has captured them."
Posthumously, he was given the title Duke of Yuèguó.
From "Guǎngdé Shényì Lù."
Qián Zhīwēi
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty.
The occult master Qián Zhīwēi once went to Luòyáng,
residing
Míng transcript: "residing" as "yáng"
at the Tiānjīn Bridge selling divinations,
saying
one divination costs ten bolts of silk.
After ten days,
no one came to him.
One day,
a noble young man, thinking he must be extraordinary,
ordered silk brought as payment for a divination.
Qián arranged the yarrow stalks and the hexagram was formed.
He said:
"My divination can foretell a lifetime.
Why are you jesting, sir?"
The man said:
"The matter for divination is very urgent.
Could the Master be mistaken?"
Qián requested to speak in rhyme, saying:
"Two ends touched with earth,
the center hangs empty.
People's feet tread upon it,
unwilling to pay money."
The man's original intention was to sell the Tiānjīn Bridge to deceive him.
Such was his precision.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ."
Hú Lú Shēng
After a long while,
as the day was drawing toward dusk,
he heard someone inside the gate say:
"Do not disgrace the scholar's robe."
It was the mistress of the house.
Then she asked his name,
and Zhèng answered fully.
As they recounted their clans,
it turned out she was his fifth cousin on his father's side.
Thus she invited him to stay overnight.
A message was relayed that there were no grown sons in the house,
so the aunt herself came out to see the young gentleman.
She ushered Zhèng into the main hall.
After a short while,
lamps and candles were arranged,
and wine and food were prepared.
The lady was over fifty years old.
Zhèng bowed in greeting,
they exchanged pleasantries about the weather,
and he also mentioned the donkey incident.
Apologetically, he thanked his aunt, saying:
"Your nephew has been distant and out of touch,
completely unaware of your whereabouts.
If not for today,
how would we have met?"
Then they conversed warmly and intimately.
She inquired about relatives both within and outside the clan,
and there was none he did not know.
Then she asked about his marriage.
Zhèng said
he was not yet married.
At first, his aunt seemed pleased,
but after a moment, her face turned sorrowful as she said:
"Your aunt married into the Wéi family,
but unfortunately,
the children are still young,
and they are fatherless.
I have one son, just over ten years old,
and a daughter who last year was betrothed to a young man named Zhèng.
He was selected and appointed as the sheriff of Jiāngyīn,
and as he was about to depart for his post,
he passed away here.
My daughter is now orphaned and helpless,
with no one else to rely on.
Since you, young sir, are not yet an official,
if you could enter into this marriage,
and then proceed to take up the official post,
it would indeed be my great fortune."
Zhèng was secretly delighted,
and also thought of the diviner's accuracy,
so he thanked her and agreed.
His aunt said:
"Assuming office must meet the deadline for the journey.
The wedding must take place within five days.
As for your luggage and preparations,
I will provide everything."
Indeed, within less than seven days,
he achieved both marriage and official appointment.
Zhèng thanked Lú Shēng generously,
and took his wife to his post.
From "Yuánhuà Jì".
Scholar Lǐ
In the Táng dynasty, Lù Shào, a Director in the Ministry of War,
during the Yuánhé era,
once visited his elder male cousin at Dìngshuǐ Temple.
The monk of that courtyard then prepared honeyed pastries and seasonal fruits.
A monk from the neighboring courtyard was also acquainted with Lù,
so he ordered his attendants to invite him over.
After a long while,
the monk arrived together with Scholar Lǐ.
They sat in a circle, laughing and talking quite boisterously.
The courtyard monk looked at his disciple to brew fresh tea.
When the tea was served around, it did not reach Scholar Lǐ.
Lù, feeling this was unfair, said:
"Why was the tea initially not served to Scholar Lǐ?"
The monk said with a laugh:
"A scholar like this,
what need has he to know the taste of tea?
Let him drink the leftover tea."
The monk from the neighboring courtyard said:
"This scholar is a practitioner of arts,
Abbot, you should not speak lightly."
That monk said further:
"A good-for-nothing young man,
what is there to fear!"
Scholar Lǐ suddenly became angry and said:
"I, with the reverend monk,
have never met before,
how do you know I am a good-for-nothing?"
The monk spoke even more arrogantly:
"One who gazes at wine banners and frequents entertainment grounds,
how could he be any good?"
Lǐ then addressed the seated guests:
"I cannot help but act rashly before such honorable guests."
Thereupon, he cupped his hands within his sleeves,
pressed on his knees,
and shouted at that monk:
"Coarse monk,
how dare you be so disrespectful!
Where is the staff?
Strike him!"
Behind the door of the monk's room, there was a bamboo staff.
It suddenly leaped out,
and struck the monk repeatedly.
Though the others tried to shield and protect him,
the staff sought gaps between people and struck swiftly,
as if held by some invisible being.
Lǐ shouted again:
"Seize this monk and push him against the wall."
The monk then backed against the wall, cupping his hands in submission,
his face pale and gasping for breath,
only begging for his life.
Lǐ said again:
"Monk, you may go down the steps."
The monk then hurried down,
throwing himself to the ground countless times,
until his nose bled and his forehead was bruised, ceaselessly.
The others pleaded for him.
Lǐ said slowly:
"Because I am in the presence of gentlemen,
I cannot kill this one and cause trouble."
He then bowed to the guests and left.
The monk was only able to speak after half a day,
as if he had suffered a malign attack.
In the end, they could not fathom what had happened.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ".
Mountain Man Wáng
In the Táng dynasty, the Grand Preceptor, Duke Wèi, Lǐ Déyù, served as an aide in Bìngzhōu.
Not even a full month after taking up his post,
a Mountain Man named Wáng came to his gate requesting an audience.
When they were seated,
he said:
"I am skilled in examining the numbers of the underworld."
At first, Lǐ did not find this remarkable.
The man then requested an empty main chamber,
prepared only with a desk, paper, brush, and fragrant water,
and had heavy curtains hung, waiting quietly.
Lǐ sat with him in the western wing.
After a short while,
Mr. Wáng said:
"You may verify it now."
On the paper were written eight large characters,
with smaller regular script annotations beside them,
saying:
"Position reaching the highest among subjects,
lifespan sixty-four."
Mr. Wáng promptly asked to leave,
and ultimately, no one knew where he went.
Later, during the Huìchāng reign,
Lǐ thrice rose in rank to the first grade,
and passed away in Hǎinán,
his age indeed matching what Mr. Wáng had examined.
From "Sōngchuāng Lù".
Wáng Qióng
In the Táng dynasty, during the Yuánhé era,
the Jiāng-Huái practitioner Wáng Qióng was once at Duàn Jūnxiù's home.
He asked a seated guest to take a tile fragment,
drew a tortoise shell pattern on it,
and kept it in his bosom for about the time of a meal.
When he took it out, it had become a tortoise.
He released it in the courtyard,
where it walked along the wall.
After one night, it turned back into a tile fragment.
He also took a flower bud,
silently sealed it in a closed vessel,
and by the next morning, it had bloomed.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ".
Wáng Gù
Yú Dí of the Táng dynasty was in Xiāngzhōu,
when a hermit named Wáng Gù once came to visit.
Dí was by nature impatient,
and seeing Wáng bow and prostrate himself slowly and clumsily,
he did not treat him with much courtesy.
On another day, when Yú was out on an excursion and feast,
Wáng was again not invited to participate.
Wáng was deeply discontented.
He then went to the commissioner's office,
and visited Administrative Assistant Zēng Shūzhèng.
Zēng received him with considerable courtesy,
and Wáng said to Zēng:
"I came here from afar
because I heard that the Grand Councilor was fond of the unusual,
but now I am truly disappointed.
I possess one skill,
unprecedented since ancient times.
Now I am about to leave,
and in gratitude for your great kindness,
I shall briefly perform it for you."
He then went to Zēng's residence,
took out from his bosom a section of bamboo and a small drum.
The diameter was barely over
(The Míng manuscript has "look" for "diameter" and
"pass" for "over")
an inch.
After a long while,
he removed the stopper from the bamboo,
and broke off a twig to beat the drum.
Several dozen jumping spiders came out of the tube,
lined up in rows,
and divided into two formations,
as if facing each other in battle array.
Whether he beat the drum three or five times,
they changed formations according to the drumbeats.
Heavenly Balance and Earthly Axis,
Fish Scale and Crane Wing formations—
all were complete.
Their advances, retreats, dispersals, and regroupings
were beyond human capability.
After changing formations several dozen times,
they reformed their ranks and re-entered the tube.
Zēng, witnessing this, was greatly astonished,
and reported it to Lord Yú
(The two characters "Lord Yú" were originally missing,
and are supplemented here based on *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*, Part 5)
But Wáng had already secretly departed.
Yú regretted and lamented,
ordering a search to find him,
but he was not found.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*
Fú Qìyuán
Fú Qìyuán, a Dàoshi of the Hàotiān Temple in the capital of the Táng dynasty,
was from Mǐn.
His moral conduct and magical arts
were highly regarded at the time.
In the early Chángqìng era,
in mid-summer,
he told his disciples in the morning:
"I shall meditate quietly for a short while;
be careful not to make noise or disturb me."
He then closed the door and took a daytime nap.
Soon, four fellow Dàoshi
invited and escorted him out the door.
Wherever his mind wished to go,
his body would immediately arrive.
Having left his hometown for over thirty years,
he thought of visiting it once,
and in a moment, he reached his old home.
The buildings were dilapidated,
the gardens overgrown and desolate.
Of his old acquaintances and friends,
hardly any remained.
The seasonal fruits were not yet ripe,
but some neighborhood children
were climbing the trees to pick them.
Qìyuán tried to protect and scold them,
but no one paid him any heed,
which made him even angrier.
A Dàoshi beside him stopped him, saying:
"Whether ripe or unripe,
they all end up being picked and taken.
Why trouble your mind over it?"
He had also once lived on Tiáo Mountain refining elixirs,
and now thought of visiting it again.
Suddenly, he was already there.
He freely toured and gazed around,
exploring every cliff and valley.
The Dàoshi said:
"The sun is setting;
it is time to return."
So they traveled together back to the capital.
On the road, they suddenly encountered a procession with ringing bells,
with a very impressive escort.
Qìyuán quickly moved to avoid the road,
but the Dàoshi said:
"A living official should not yield to a ghostly official;
just follow the road and proceed."
In a moment,
several of the advance guards,
upon seeing Qìyuán, fled in panic.
When the official arrived,
Qìyuán looked closely,
and it was actually Vice Director Mǎ Zǒng,
who was then serving as Minister of Justice.
He had always been on good terms with Qìyuán,
and Mǎ was also in good health.
When Mǎ met Qìyuán,
he alone felt it was strange.
The day was already evening.
At dawn the next day,
Qìyuán went to Kāihuà Ward to visit Mǎ,
who was playing chess with Vice Minister Hán of the Ministry of War.
Thus, Qìyuán stayed the entire day.
He secretly observed Mǎ's speech, demeanor, and expression,
but found not the slightest abnormality,
and privately wondered at the reason.
Not long after,
he heard that Mǎ had fallen ill at home,
and within ten days, he passed away.
Also, according to Lǐ Zhōngmǐn, a Supervising Secretary,
this was actually Táo Tiānhuó,
a man of Dàoist arts,
to whom many Dàoist devotees at court were drawn.
Tiānhuó was originally from Ānnán,
not from Mǐn.
He was able, on days of deep meditation,
to let his spirit travel to various mountains.
The affair concerning Lord Mǎ was known by many.
From *Jíyì*
Bái Jiǎo
Fàn Zōngrén, an official of Héyáng,
during the Chángqìng era,
was traveling as a guest in Èzhǔ,
and upon reaching Jiānglíng,
was repeatedly insulted by the boatman Wáng Shēng along the way.
Zōngrén was then preparing for the imperial examinations,
and lacked the strength to control him,
so he often tolerated it with forbearance.
Upon arriving in Jiānglíng,
he reported the matter in full to the local authorities,
who then had Wáng Shēng severely flogged.
Zōngrén boarded another boat to travel up the gorge,
and within ten days of departing from Jīngzhōu,
the boat he was on
suddenly lost its mooring rope,
and neither the pole nor the oar could control it.
The boatman said:
"This boat has already been cursed by an enemy.
Yesterday, while traveling on the water, did we perhaps offend someone?
Now there is no way to proceed.
Within less than five hundred lǐ,
we will encounter the rocky rapids,
treacherous and difficult,
the most dangerous part of the entire river.
Judging by his malicious intent,
he must have calculated that our boat would arrive precisely there,
and then it would surely be smashed and sink.
It would be better to prepare in advance."
Zōngrén then went ashore with his servants,
tied the boat with a thick rope,
and followed along the shore, pulling it.
The next day, they reached the rapids.
The boat indeed rushed wildly and collided violently,
tossed and submerged at will,
and within moments, it broke apart.
Fortunately, they had the rope,
so although no one was injured,
all their belongings were completely lost.
The gorge path was deep and remote,
spanning several hundred lǐ up and down,
with no inhabitants at all.
Zōngrén and his servants then took shelter under the forest,
with no provisions or utensils,
absolutely nothing at all.
Stranded and in peril, suffering hardships,
they were filled with worry and distress.
Although they sent someone to report to the local official,
two days passed with no return.
They were on the verge of starvation.
That night,
they gathered firewood and lit a fire,
and Zōngrén and his servants all slept around it.
Late at night, they suddenly awoke.
They saw five mountain dwellers sitting in a row,
their appearances strange and unusual,
all carrying sharp weapons,
looking around with fierce and arrogant eyes,
speaking in a threatening and rude manner.
If they were to wield their blades,
Zōngrén and his companions would have no choice but to submit and await death.
Seeing the imminent danger,
Zōngrén loudly declared:
"You people make your living
here in these mountains.
I have unfortunately had my boat shattered,
and all my belongings lost.
Stranded on this ancient shore,
I await becoming food for jackals and wolves.
You, with your round heads and horizontal eyes,
show no pity for my plight,
but instead watch with glee and mock me,
delighting in my misfortune and danger,
to such an extent!
I have now run out of food
for more than a day.
Those of you who live nearby,
can quickly return home to prepare food and drink,
to save me from impending death."
The mountain dwellers looked at each other,
then ordered two of them to go.
Before dawn,
they returned carrying rice, meat, salt, and cheese.
Zōngrén relied on this to await the return message.
He then explained the reason for the boat's destruction.
The mountain dwellers said:
"In the gorge, many practice such sorcery,
and many also suffer such misfortunes.
However, others might have ways to undo it,
but only Wáng Shēng's curse,
unless one drowns, it does not cease.
I wonder if it is indeed this fellow.
In the southern mountains, there is Bái Jiǎo,
whose magical arts reach the divine,
and he can be invited
to dispatch and break the curse.
I know where Jiǎo is,
let me try to request him for you."
Zōngrén earnestly pleaded with them,
and one of the mountain dwellers set off.
The next day,
Jiǎo indeed arrived,
wearing a yellow cap and rustic clothes,
carrying a staff and wearing straw sandals,
his appearance that of a mountain hermit.
He regarded birds and beasts as his ancestors.
Zōngrén then explained his plight of being stranded.
Jiǎo laughed and said:
"A trivial matter.
I will summon him for you and behead him."
He then cleared the grass and cut branches,
marked out a circular area for an altar,
and arranged knives and water,
while Jiǎo stood in the center.
Late at night, with the moon bright,
the water clear and the mountains green,
fir and cassia trees faintly visible,
the sound of the stream quiet,
from time to time, Jiǎo was heard inhaling and calling out to summon Wáng Shēng,
his voice clear and prolonged,
the sound stirring and far-reaching,
but by dawn, no one had arrived.
Zōngrén whispered to his servant:
"How could Wáng Shēng, seven hundred lǐ away, be summoned in an instant?"
Jiǎo again asked Zōngrén:
"The belongings sunk and the boat shattered,
exactly as you said.
Could it not have been caused by wind and water?"
Zōngrén and the boatman again truthfully reported.
Jiǎo said:
"If that is so,
how can Wáng Shēng escape detection?"
He then said to Zōngrén's servant:
"However, I request the three-generation names of the young master,
in order to examine his sorcery."
The servant told him.
Jiǎo then went deep into the distance,
built another altar,
and at night summoned him again,
his long cries
just like the previous evening.
After a long while,
someone in the mountains suddenly responded to Jiǎo,
the voice choked and faint,
carried by the wind before it was heard.
After a long time, it finally reached Jiǎo,
and it was the spirit of Wáng Shēng.
Jiǎo then reprimanded him for his treachery and harm,
enumerating his crimes.
Shēng pleaded for mercy, bowing in submission,
kowtowing until his forehead bled.
Jiǎo said to Zōngrén:
"He has already admitted his guilt.
He can be executed."
Zōngrén said:
"Considering his extreme treachery and malice,
it is truly hard to forgive,
but to execute him outright
is also not permissible.
He should be subjected to other suffering."
Jiǎo then rebuked Wáng Shēng:
"I will spare your life,
but you shall die of bloody dysentery in a hundred days."
Shēng wailed and wept as he left.
Jiǎo bid farewell,
and Zōngrén took off his clothes to gift to Jiǎo,
but Jiǎo laughed and did not accept.
After a while,
a boat arrived,
and Zōngrén was able to proceed to Jiānglíng.
He inquired about Wáng Shēng,
and it turned out that on the night Jiǎo summoned him,
he fell ill with bloody dysentery at home,
and died after a hundred days.
From "Yì Wén Jí"
Jiǎ Dān
The Tang dynasty chancellor Jiǎ Dān, while in charge of governance,
served his sovereign with upright principles.
If there were disasters yet to sprout,
he was always able to prevent and eliminate them.
As for yīn-yáng, seasonal phenomena, and celestial portents,
there was nothing he did not thoroughly understand.
Once, a villager lost his ox.
He went to Diviner Sāng Guóshī to have a divination performed.
After the hexagram was formed,
the diviner said to him:
"Your ox
was stolen by Chancellor Jiǎ and placed in his turban and hat box.
You just need to wait for the morning court session, rush forward, and accuse him."
The old man then did as he was told and made his plea.
The Duke questioned him,
and the man fully reported the diviner's words to the Duke.
The Duke laughed from atop his horse,
and opened his turban box.
He took out a cosmograph (shì pán),
and leaning on his saddle, rotated it to examine it.
After a long while,
he said to the man who lost the ox:
"This Chancellor did not steal your ox.
However, if you want the Chancellor to know where the ox has gone,
you can simply go to the rear of the three gates of Ān Guó Guàn and search the magpie nest atop the large pagoda tree."
The village elder went straight to the three gates.
Seeing there was indeed a magpie nest on the treetop of the pagoda tree,
but finding nothing there at all,
he climbed down the tree.
Lowering his head, he saw the lost ox at the base of the tree,
tethered and grazing on grass.
Nearby was the home of the ox thief.
From "The Zhītián Records"
Máo Āndào
Máo Āndào of the Táng dynasty,
a Dàoshì from Lúshān,
could write talismans and command ghosts,
his transformations were boundless.
Those who studied under him often numbered in the hundreds.
He once taught two disciples the arts of invisibility and clairvoyance.
After a while,
both disciples requested to return home to care for their parents.
Āndào sent them off.
Still, he told them:
"I have transmitted and shown you my arts,
fully providing for your use in learning the Dào.
However, you must not recklessly flaunt these arts.
If you disobey my teaching,
I can cause your arts
to fail when put to use."
The two disciples accepted his command and left.
At that time, Hán Jìngōng Huǎng was in Rùnzhōu,
and deeply despised such people.
The two disciples went directly to pay him a formal visit,
thinking that if Lord Jìn did not treat them with courtesy,
they would then use their invisibility to leave.
When summoned inside,
they showed no respect.
The two disciples therefore behaved with laxity, arrogance, and wildness,
hiking up their robes and ascending the steps.
Hán was greatly angered,
and immediately ordered officers and soldiers to bind them.
So the two disciples then performed their art,
but the method indeed proved ineffective,
and they were both captured and bound.
As they were about to be executed,
the two disciples said:
"We initially did not dare to act like this;
it was our master who misled us."
Hán, wishing to also eradicate the source,
then said to them:
"You just need to provide your master's name and residence,
and I might spare you from death."
Just as the two disciples were about to state them,
Āndào was already at the gate.
The soldiers reported to the Duke,
who was greatly pleased,
thinking he could now capture and execute them all.
He hastily ordered Āndào summoned inside.
Āndào had thick eyebrows and a fine beard,
his appearance lofty and ancient.
The Duke saw him from afar,
and unconsciously rose from his seat,
inviting him to sit opposite.
Āndào said:
"I heard my two disciples, foolish and stupid,
have offended your dignity.
Now, whether their lives are short or long
hangs upon your gesture.
However, I request to question and shame them first,
and then await your execution."
The Duke then had them brought under guard of soldiers with blades,
their shackles and bonds very secure,
and summoned to the foot of the steps.
The two disciples kowtowed, begging for mercy.
Āndào said to the Duke's attendants:
"Please bring a vessel of water."
The Duke, fearing he might use water for an escape art,
therefore did not give it to him.
Āndào, unperturbed,
promptly went to the Duke's inkstone, drank its water,
and sprayed it onto the two disciples.
They immediately transformed into a pair of black rats,
scurrying chaotically in front of the hall.
Āndào, swift and vigorous,
suddenly changed into a giant hawk,
each claw seizing a rat,
and soared away into the sky.
Lord Jìn was astonished for a long time,
but ultimately could do nothing about it.
From "Records of the Unusual"
Luò Shānrén
When Tián Hóngzhèng of the Táng dynasty governed Zhènzhōu,
the three armies killed him and established Wáng Tíngcòu.
He was a descendant of Wáng Wǔhóu.
"Běimèng Suǒyán" notes "hóu" as "jùn",
and there is a "zhī" character below "zhī"
meaning lineage.
Tíngcòu was born at a country villa.
There were often several dozen turtledoves
that gathered in the courtyard trees by day,
and under the eaves by night.
A local man named Luò Débō found this strange.
When he grew up, he had fused ribs,
enjoyed texts like the "Yīnfú" and "Guǐgǔ",
served in military posts,
and won the hearts of his soldiers.
Once, on a mission to Héyáng,
returning midway,
overcome by wine, he slept by the roadside.
Suddenly, a man carrying a staff passed by,
looked at him intently and said:
"Noble, destined to rule over land,
no ordinary man."
The attendant awoke
and told Tíngcòu.
He galloped several lǐ to catch up,
paid his respects and asked.
The man said he was Luò Shānrén from Jìyuán,
and explained that seeing the breath from his nostrils,
the left resembled a dragon and the right a tiger,
the two breaths intersecting and flourishing,
the response should come this autumn,
with descendants succeeding him
for a full hundred years.
He also said,
"In your home's courtyard, there should be a large tree;
when the tree reaches the hall,
that is the omen."
That year, he was indeed supported and established by the three armies.
Later, returning to his country villa,
the courtyard tree was luxuriant,
its shade already covering the house.
The villa had a Shén of Fēilóng Mountain.
Tíngcòu went to offer sacrifices to it.
When he was about a hundred paces from the shrine,
a man fully dressed in cap and robes
respectfully intercepted him on the road.
When Tíngcòu entered the temple,
the deity's statue was already sitting sideways.
It then faced east.
The temple building remains to this day.
Tíngcòu was pure, frugal, fair, and just,
diligent in service to the court,
and benevolent towards the army and people.
His descendants inherited the position of Zhèn commander for generations.
By the time of the Later Liáng dynasty,
Wáng Róng was enfeoffed as Prince of Zhào,
but was destroyed by his subordinate general Zhāng Wénlǐ.
From "Běimèng Suǒyán"
Shí Mín
Táng Shímín possessed extraordinary arts,
residing in Yángzhōu.
Duàn Chéngshì, for several years,
would meet with him without fail every ten days or so.
By the beginning of the Kāichéng era,
among relatives and old acquaintances in the city,
people often spoke of Shí Mín's arts as unfathomable.
It was widely told that during the Bǎolì era,
Shí accompanied Minister Qián Huī to the Húzhōu Academy.
The disciples were all present,
and it was the hot summer month.
A hunter presented a rabbit,
and Qián ordered soup to be made from it.
As they were about to eat together,
Mín laughed and said:
"We could keep the rabbit skin,
to casually mark an event."
He then nailed the skin to the ground,
piled up bricks and plastered them,
and wrote a vermilion charm on top,
murmuring alone:
"Regret the verification is late,
regret the verification is late."
The Qián brothers questioned him,
and Shí said:
"I wish to join you all in remembering the Mǎo year."
In the ninth year of Tàihé,
Qián Kěfù met his end in Fèngxiáng.
The year was Yǐmǎo.
From the "Jíyì Jì".
Note: Seen in "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ" five.
Cí'ēn Monk
In the Táng, Wáng Méng and Zhào Jǐng were old friends from their commoner days,
and Zhào knew of his administrative talent.
When Zhào became chancellor,
Wáng, from his previous post as magistrate of Xīngàn County in Jízhōu, came to pay his respects.
Zhào was greatly pleased,
and provided him with generous support.
At the time, the Censorate was rather short of officials,
and Emperor Dézōng often found it difficult to make appointments.
Yet Zhào intended
The character "intended" is added based on the Ming manuscript copy
to appoint him.
One day, Wáng happened to visit Cí'ēn Temple,
and a physiognomist monk divined his aura and said:
"Observing your complexion,
it shows no auspicious signs at all.
In another year, you will obtain a one-year post as a frontier censor."
Méng laughed heartily and returned.
The next day,
Zhào seized an opportunity to memorialize that the Censorate was severely understaffed,
among which the position of Investigating Censor was particularly urgent and important,
and he wished to select a few people.
Dézōng said:
"It is not that I do not wish to fill this post,
but it must be filled by someone solitary, upright, substantial, and accomplished.
I reckon you would only pick frivolous young scions from court families;
it would be better not to appoint anyone."
Zhào said:
"In my humble opinion,
it is exactly as Your Majesty considers.
I wish to seek candidates from among the Record Keepers, Army Advisors, and County Magistrates."
The Emperor was greatly pleased and said:
"If so, that matches my intention.
Do you have anyone in mind?"
He then recommended two men.
After leaving,
he encountered Péi Yánlíng,
who at the time was next in line for an audience regarding financial matters.
Péi said:
"What matter did the Grand Councillor memorialize about that was so agreeable,
your joyful expression overflows."
Zhào did not reply to him,
and Yánlíng left angrily, cursing:
"Let's see if what this old soldier does can succeed."
After the audience concluded,
the Emperor asked Zhào Jǐng what he had just discussed and requested.
The Emperor said:
"Zhào Jǐng is extremely public-spirited."
He then spoke of the censor matter.
Yánlíng said:
"This is absolutely unacceptable.
Why does Your Majesty believe him?
Moreover, Zhào Jǐng, as Chancellor,
how could he be familiar
"Familiar" originally written as "request";
corrected based on the Xǔ manuscript
with the achievements and performance of prefectural and county officials?
The two men he mentioned before are also
"Yīnhuà Lù" six has "also" followed by "not"
being praised by others.
How could Jǐng know of them himself?
It must be private favoritism.
Your Majesty need only question him about their origins,
and you will know."
Another day, the Emperor indeed asked:
"How do you know these two men?"
He said:
"One is an old friend,
one is a distant relative of mine.
I know them."
The Emperor said nothing.
Another day when Yánlíng entered,
the Emperor said:
"Regarding Zhào Jǐng's request,
it was indeed as you surmised."
The appointment was thus shelved.
Méng instead returned to his old woodland retreat,
and Zhào passed away while still in the post of Chancellor.
Several years later,
a frontier commander recommended Wáng as an aide,
where he obtained the brevet title of Censor.
From "Yīnhuà Lù".
Zhū Yuè
In the Táng, Chén Shìmíng, a commander of ten in Èzhōu,
was handsome and robust from youth,
and often engaged in cockfighting.
He kept many at home;
from the time they were chicks,
he could discern their future courage or timidity,
and upon hearing their crowing, could distinguish their plumage color.
In the locality, there was a Daoist named Old Man Zhū Yuè,
who had mastered the art of contracting the earth.
He resided in È.
He built a house and dug a pond,
planted fruit trees and medicinal herbs all around,
and personally planted pines and cassias,
which grew to ten arm-spans in girth.
Yet he never ventured into the city markets.
Being Shìmíng's close neighbor, he became his protector,
and thus associated with him.
But Shìmíng treated the old man with excessive familiarity and disrespect,
often lacking in reverence.
The old man said:
"You rascal, good-for-nothing,
taking me for the 'Eastern Hill' ignoramus?
Shall I playfully test you or not?"
Shìmíng's residence was two or three hundred paces away.
The old man gave him wine to drink,
and sent him home to fetch a fighting cock.
He set out in the morning,
but by evening had not reached home.
Estimating the distance he had walked,
it exceeded fifty *li*,
yet when he looked back,
he had not gone beyond a hundred paces.
Shìmíng hurried back,
bowed and begged for forgiveness.
The old man laughed and said:
"Will the rascal insult me again?"
Shìmíng said:
"Just now on the road I was already exhausted;
how would I dare to do so again?"
He then shed tears,
and the old man released him.
Afterwards, he served the old man with the respectful etiquette due to a child serving a grandfather.
In the Yuánhé era, Shìmíng
was garrisoned in Bāqiū,
and thus parted from Old Man Zhū.
From "Guǎngdé Shényì Jì".
Wáng Shēng
During the Táng dynasty, Hán Huàng, the Duke of Jìn, was stationed as military governor of Rùnzhōu.
Because rice in the capital was expensive,
he offered to send in one million dàn of grain,
and requested an imperial order for the observation and military commissioners along the land route to arrange its transport.
The chief ministers at the time believed that, as the Salt and Iron Commissioner offering tribute,
it was inappropriate to further burden the prefectures and counties along the route.
The Emperor also found it difficult to refuse Hán Huàng's request,
so he referred the matter for deliberation by the two departments.
Left Rectifier of Omissions Mù Zhì said:
"The Salt and Iron Commissioner has his own officials to manage tribute offerings;
it is inappropriate to further burden the prefectures and counties along the route.
If the military governor were to randomly kill two hundred thousand people, it might still be acceptable;
why begrudge assigning one tribute officer?"
Those seated nearby secretly heard this,
and Hán Huàng then ordered his military officer Lǐ Qīhuá to go to the Remonstrance Bureau to question Lord Mù.
Hán Huàng said he had never wronged him,
so why did he speak like this.
He would come to the capital to debate with him openly at court.
He then left his post,
passed through Biànzhōu,
took Liú Xuánzuǒ with him,
and his influence overwhelmed both the court and the provinces.
Mù, fearful and uneasy,
secretly put on plain white clothes,
went to Xìngzhào to consult the diviner Wáng Shēng,
and presented him with a bolt of plain silk.
Wáng declined, saying:
"You have troubled yourself to bring such a generous gift;
I will perform a yarrow stalk divination for you tonight."
Mù then left Hán's birth year and fate data along with his own.
The next day,
he sent his brother-in-law Péi to request the divination result.
Wáng said to Péi:
"One of these individuals
has a birth year and fate of immense potency;
his authority and power within surpass even that of a king.
Who is he?
The other person's fate
clashes severely with the former's,
and there seems to be an intent to harm.
However, the former person certainly will not live to see next March.
The divination is now already in the eleventh month;
even if harm is intended,
the matter will not succeed."
Hán entered the capital in the eleventh month.
Mù said:
"Hán's claws and talons are like this;
to provoke him is to be shattered.
How can I survive for several months?"
He again questioned Wáng Shēng,
who ultimately said there was nothing to fear.
When Hán reached the capital,
his power and influence grew even greater.
He daily killed people with a club of orange wood;
the case-reviewing officials, whenever they went to see him, would all flee;
ministers and high officials wishing to pay their respects
hesitated and dared not approach.
Mù grew even more fearful,
and went to visit each of Hán's sons—Gāo, Qún, and others—seeking a resolution,
but none dared to speak out for him.
At that time, Hán Huàng ordered the officials of the Three Departments to assemble at the Secretariat to conduct business;
people all said it was for the open court debate,
and some advised Mù to plead illness,
but Mù, gripped by fear, could not decide.
When all the officials had finally gathered,
Hán then said:
"The other day, Zhāng Yán was appointed Prefect of Chángzhōu;
yesterday, another was appointed Prefect of Chángzhōu.
Because Zhāng Yán had previously been guilty of corruption,
he was therefore replaced.
I feared you gentlemen might not understand,
so I am informing you."
Everyone congratulated Mù;
it was not the open court debate.
Not long after, Mù had business to see Hán Huàng,
but before he could be announced,
he heard a loud voice from within the chamber saying:
"How dare Mù Zhì act like this!"
The usher unconsciously ran out
and told Zhì,
who was terrified.
The next day,
at the fifth watch, Vice Director of the Bureau of Budgets Qí Kàng came galloping on horseback and said to Zhì:
"You have been demoted to Sheriff of Shàoyáng County in Shàozhōu.
Take care on your journey."
Without another word, he clasped his hand in farewell,
urged his horse on, and left.
Zhì again sent Péi to ask Wáng Shēng.
Shēng said:
"Hán's allotted fortune is already exhausted;
he will not live past the day after tomorrow.
Tomorrow, moreover, there will be a state mourning,
so you can be completely assured and without loss."
By that evening,
an imperial announcement was issued from within the palace:
the Prince had passed away, and court was suspended.
The next day, the edict of appointment was not issued.
The day after, Hán collapsed during the court assembly,
was carried out on a bed,
and died.
At that time, there were those in the court who disliked Hán and favored Mù,
so they did not release the edict demoting Mù,
and also gave Mù the Shàoyáng appointment document.
From *Yìwén Jí*.
Jiǎ Lóng
At the end of Emperor Xīzōng's reign in the Táng dynasty,
in Guǎnglíng, there was a poor man named Dù Kěyún, over forty years old,
who loved to drink but did not eat,
and many said he abstained from grains.
He would go from tavern to tavern, moving between seats to ask for drinks,
yet he was never seen drunk.
When people took pity and gave him wine,
he still never drank much,
stopping after just two or three cups.
There was a Mr. Lè whose flag pavilion tavern was on the west side of the street,
who often allowed that if it was rainy or cloudy and Dù couldn't reach other places,
he could come here by arrangement,
and this became the usual practice.
One day, during heavy snow,
Dù went to Lè to ask for a drink,
and it happened that the manager reported to Lè:
"Since it has already been gnawed and damaged,
we must compensate the previous owner based on the item."
Lè was displeased by this statement,
and Dù asked:
"What is the reason?"
Lè said:
"Someone exchanged clothes for wine,
but they were not stored carefully,
and as a result, they were gnawed by rats."
Dù said:
"How many rooms and courtyards are there here?"
He replied,
a certain number.
Dù said:
"In my youth, I once remembered a talisman,
very effective at repelling rats,
but I don't know if it would work now.
Please let me try it.
If there is any effect,
it should be able to clear all the rooms and buildings here,
and rats will never appear again."
Lè obtained the talisman,
burned it according to the method,
and from then on, rat traces completely disappeared.
During the heavy siege by Qín Yàn and Bì Shīduó,
Dù's appearance remained unchanged,
all because he abstained from food.
Later, when Sūn Rú crossed the river,
he then took up residence in Pílíng.
He violated the nighttime curfew,
and was killed by a blade,
and it was said that he achieved liberation through the sword.
From "Guìyuàn Cóngtán"
Xǔ Jiànzōng
Six lǐ northeast of Jìyīn Commandery in the Táng dynasty, in front of the ancient Lóngxīng Temple on Zuǒshān,
on the west side of the road, in the first courtyard, there was a well,
its water extremely deep,
unfit for people to drink,
very foul and putrid,
and colored like blood.
Zhèng Huángǔ

The Ming dynasty manuscript adds twenty-two characters below the three characters "Zhèng Huángǔ": "In the early Tàihé era, together with Xǔ Jiànzōng, he stayed at Zuǒshān for just over a month. Hearing about this well, Jiànzōng said to Huángǔ"
said:
"We can go together to see it."
When they peered into the well,
he said:
"How about I change the taste of this water?"
Huángǔ and the temple monks said:
"That would be most fortunate."
He then ordered a red bowl, paper, and brush,
wrote a talisman and placed it in the well,
with no other method used.
They then stayed overnight in this courtyard.
After the second watch,
the courtyard grew dark with wind and rain.
Huángǔ peered through the window,
and amid flashes of lightning,
he saw a strong laborer,
using a fishing line in the well by himself,
as if fishing for something.
Each time the lightning flashed three times,
by the fourth flash, he was gone.
At dawn,
Jiànzōng sealed the well.
Three days later,
the water became sweet and delicious, different from all other waters,
and remains so to this day.
Huángǔ believed Jiànzōng was a Daoist adept,
and so sought his teachings,
but he said:
"I am not a Daoist adept,
I merely happened to obtain talismanic arts."
Huángǔ sought them but never obtained them.
Later, Jiànzōng left for Tàishān,
and no one knew where he went.
From "Chuányì Jì"
Xiàng Yǐn
During the Tiānfù era of the Táng dynasty,
Chéng Ruì was stationed in Jiānglíng.
The supervising army commissioner Zhāng Tèjìn's personal attendant Wēn Kèxiū was in charge of the medicine storehouse
and resided in a rented house within the city walls.
Zhāng's disciple Xiàng Yǐn lived to the north as his neighbor.
Yǐn studied calendrical calculations
and was also skilled in divination through covering objects,
never failing to hit the mark.
One day,
he said to Zhāng:
"From the Vice Commissioner and the Assistant Supervisor down,
everyone bears the complexion of impending disaster.
Why is this?"
Zhāng replied:
"People's fortunes vary year by year;
how could they all suffer disaster at the same time?
I do not believe it."
At that time, many dogs barked in the city.
Yǐn said to Kèxiū:
"The Commander-in-Chief
will lose his position in a certain year,
and this place will turn into ruins.
Please remember this."
Another day, he again said to Kèxiū:
"This place will change further,
and will have no settled ruler.
After five years,
someone from the northeast,
vaguely a relative of the imperial family,
will govern this region,
remaining unmoved for twenty years.
Please remember this."
Yet another day, he said:
"Twenty years after the arrival of the one from the northeast,
there will be another person, unconstrained by the Five Phases,
whose journey will be even longer.
I ask only that you remember this."
Wēn considered this baseless
and paid it no mind.
Yǐn also said to Wēn:
"In your future marriage, you will have no sons,
only a host of daughters.
In your old age, you will become a physician."
Later, a secret edict indeed ordered the execution of the Northern Bureau officials.
Zhāng Tèjìn, the Vice Commissioner, and the Assistant Supervisor were all put to death on the same day,
thus verifying the event.
Chéng Ruì suffered a military defeat at Èzhǔ and did not return.
Jiānglíng was then occupied by Lǎng
("Lǎng" was originally written as "Láng".
Corrected based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.)
people under Léi Mǎn.
The Xiāngzhōu army
("army" was originally written as "lord".
Corrected based on the Xǔ edition.)
seized it,
appointing Zhào Kuāngmíng as the acting military governor.
Dàliáng attacked
("attacked" was originally written as "replaced".
Corrected based on the Xǔ edition.)
Xiāngzhōu.
Kuāngmíng abandoned the city to secure himself,
and it was occupied by the Liáng general Hè Huán.
However, his prestige was not established,
and the Lǎng
("Lǎng" was originally written as "Láng".
Corrected based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.)
barbarians encroached and harassed.
He dared not leave the city,
merely holding his ground.
The Liáng sovereign appointed Prince Wǔxìn, Gāo Jìchāng, from Yǐngzhōu prefect to be the acting military commissioner of Jīngnán.
On the day he took office,
he rode with a few horsemen to Shātóu,
and the Lǎng
("Lǎng" was originally written as "Láng".
Corrected based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.)
army was awed and fearful,
gradually retreating.
Previously, Prince Wǔxìn had been granted the surname Zhū,
but later resumed his original surname.
This indeed matched the prophecy about an imperial relative.
Kèxiū lost his patron
and drifted to Zhǔgōng.
He collected famous prescriptions,
excelled at compounding medicines,
sold drugs to support himself,
and also practiced medicine.
After marrying,
he fathered only several daughters.
Everything was as Xiàng had said.
In the second year, Dīnghài, of the Tiānchéng era under Táng Míngzōng,
the imperial army besieged Jiānglíng.
The military government was filled with anxiety.
Wēn Kèxiū went up the city wall and reported to Prince Wénxiàn,
relating all this in detail.
Prince Wénxiàn did not fully believe him.
Wēn, considering the previous events had been repeatedly verified,
felt he surely would not deceive him.
Soon after, the court withdrew the army.
The following year,
Prince Wǔxìn passed away,
having ruled for exactly twenty-one years.
Then Prince Wénxiàn succeeded to the position,
also for twenty-one years,
until the title of Prince Nánpíng.
This was the "even longer journey",
and indeed it came to pass here.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Master Zhào
Master Zhào
was originally from Suìzhōu.
He used flying talismans to cure people's illnesses,
and had been doing so in his hometown for many years.
He was also skilled at commanding mountain spirits,
ordering them to carry his book bag and bamboo hat.
Therefore, within a hundred *lǐ* around his residence,
there were absolutely no monsters, ghosts, or harmful beings troubling people.
There was a commoner, Ruǎn Qióng, whose daughter
was bewitched by an evil spirit.
Every evening she would dress up separately,
as if waiting for someone,
and would certainly welcome them with joy,
laughing and talking as usual.
When healers were summoned,
she would know their names in advance.
Qíong then rushed to request Master Zhào's help to save her.
Zhào said:
"No need for me to go personally.
Just paste my talisman on the door or window,
and the effect will manifest itself."
He then gave him a large talisman, written in vermilion on white silk.
Qíong pasted it on the door.
At the first watch,
they heard the sound of a huge object striking it,
like ice falling to the ground.
They then gathered candles to look,
and found a giant soft-shelled turtle,
writhing on the ground,
which soon died.
The talisman then vanished.
The girl suddenly came to her senses,
startled and weeping in fear.
Qíong then smashed the turtle's head
and discarded it in a ravine.
He returned to Master Zhào
and reported the event in detail.
Zhào consoled and praised him,
and gave him a small talisman,
ordering the girl to swallow it.
From then on, she was unharmed.
The large talisman had already returned to the table.
From *Yěrén Xiánhuà*.
Master Quán
In the mountains and wilderness of Chángdào County during the Táng dynasty,
there was a shaman named Quán Shī,
skilled in death divination.
Regarding evil spirits and ghosts,
those hidden in concealment or fleeing,
secrets buried in the earth or hidden in mountains,
the timing of life and death,
there was nothing he did not foreknow.
When someone requested his services,
he would burn incense and invoke the gods,
then collapse onto a cushion,
appearing to pass away,
and after a while would begin to breathe again,
opening his eyes to speak of the matter.
Quán Shī's relative was named Guō Jiǔjiù,
a bold and powerful man,
who had amassed great wealth.
His wife had been bedridden for several years,
on the verge of death.
He summoned Quán Shī to divine for her.
Closing his eyes, Quán Shī said:
"Behind the main hall of your house, there are corpses buried,
nine in number."
He then instructed them to dig,
and according to the dimensions he gave,
they retrieved exactly nine corpses, not a single one off,
and promptly had them removed.
His wife immediately recovered,
and he offered a million coins as a gift,
but Quán Shī refused,
and only after being pressed
did he accept ten or twenty thousand,
saying the gods did not permit him to take more.
Another day,
while lying at a commoner's home,
he closed his eyes and counted on his fingers, saying:
"I am calculating the death register of the world,
and the number of deaths in distant and nearby prefectures and counties is very high,
next, in this prefecture's villages and townships,
there are also over ten people destined to die together,
among them is the prominent scholar Zhāng Fūzǐ, named Xíngrú."
Someone urgently informed Xíngrú,
who, upon hearing this, became afraid,
and summoned Quán Shī to come.
He said to Zhāng:
"I can petition for you,
submitting a memorial to Yán Luó's mountain
Míngchāo edition has "Luó" instead of "zuì"
and the character "mountain" is suspected to be an error,
it should be the character "out"
to exempt you."
Then, closing his eyes,
he wrote on paper,
half in seal script,
prayed, and burned it.
After finishing,
Zhāng offered him a pregnant mare as a gift,
but the shaman said:
"The gods only permit the mother,
the foal must be returned."
To wait for another day,
the over ten people from this prefecture whose fate he said was exhausted,
all died as predicted,
only Zhāng Xíngrú was spared.
When the mare gave birth to a foal,
he returned it to its owner.
The mare was called "Monk,"
and he said:
"This horse was once a monk who failed in his duties,
hence this retribution."
Since then, many people have requested his calculations,
and he has also helped many dig up hidden things from the ground,
those whose fate he said was exhausted,
died without missing a moment.
As a result, his household became very wealthy,
taking cattle, horses, and wealth from commoners,
filling his mountains and rooms.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Zhōu Yǐnkè
The Táng dynasty Daoist priest Zhōu Yǐnkè,
possessed magical arts,
and high officials and generals revered him like a deity.
The chancellor Lǐ Zōngmǐn performed the rites of a disciple,
and all written communications stated so.
Former chancellor Duàn Wénchāng, stationed in Huáinán,
fell ill,
and said:
"The Venerable Master said last year that I would fall ill,
and need to rest for six days."
Duàn and his guests were playing games and drinking tea,
Zhōu Shēng drank several bowls in a row,
and Duàn got up and urinated incessantly.
After a long while,
he exclaimed to the Venerable Master:
"I beg you to stop,
I am utterly exhausted and cannot control myself."
He laughed and said:
"I was just playing a trick on the Chancellor,
because I was too lazy to get up from drinking tea,
I made Duke Duàn do it for me."
From "Yì Shǐ"
Zhāng Shìzhèng
During the Táng dynasty, Wáng Qián was in Jīngzhōu,
and a commoner named Zhāng Shìzhèng was skilled at treating injuries and fractures.
A soldier had injured his shin,
and sought Zhāng for treatment.
Zhāng gave him a medicinal wine to drink,
cut open the flesh,
and removed a piece of shattered bone,
as large as two fingers,
applied ointment, and sealed it.
After a few days, it was as good as new.
Over two years later,
the shin suddenly hurt,
and he asked Zhāng again.
Zhāng said:
"The bone I removed earlier gets cold and hurts,
you should quickly find it."
Sure enough, they found it under the bed,
he told him to wash it with hot water,
and store it in cotton wadding,
and the pain immediately subsided.
Wáng's sons and younger brothers were close to him,
and once asked him to perform a trick.
Zhāng took a handful of grass,
rubbed it repeatedly,
and it all turned into moths that flew away.
He also painted a woman on the wall,
poured a full cup of wine for her to drink,
and not a drop was left.
After a moment,
the painted woman's face flushed red for about half a day.
His arts were never passed on to anyone.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Chén Xiūfù
During the Táng dynasty, Lǐ Dāng governed Xīngyuán,
and a recluse from Bāochéng County named Chén Xiūfù, also known as Chén Qīzǐ,
associated with gamblers,
and his behavior was unusual.
Lǐ, considering him a sorcerer, had him shackled,
but there was another Xiūfù in the marketplace.
Soon after, he died in prison,
quickly decaying,
and the authorities collected and buried him.
Afterward, he appeared again in Bāochéng,
and Lǐ, astonished, dared not question further.
One day, his beloved daughter suddenly died,
and his wife, grieving, fell ill,
with no one able to cure her.
An advisor said:
"Chén the Recluse is a true man of the Way,
he must possess the arts of Shàojūn,
can we ask him?"
Lǐ agreed,
and respectfully summoned him.
Chén said:
"This is a small matter."
At nightfall,
he set up lamps behind a curtain,
painted a door,
and asked the lady to lower the screen and hold her breath.
At midnight,
the deceased entered the hall through the painted door,
walked around several times,
the lady, overwhelmed with emotion,
cried out,
and the spirit vanished instantly.
He then admonished and comforted her,
urging her to restrain her grief.
From then on, Lǐ revered him.
From "Běimèng Suǒyán"
Fèi Jīshī
In the Táng dynasty, there was a man in Shǔ named Fèi Jīshī.
His eyes were red without black pupils.
He was originally from the Pú people.
Duàn Chéngshì saw him at the beginning of the Chángqìng era,
when he was already over seventy years old.
Whenever he treated someone's illness,
he would always use a chicken,
setting up a sacrifice in the courtyard.
He would also take a river stone the size of a chicken egg,
have the sick person hold it,
then pace about, gathering his breath and shouting.
The chicken would spin around and die,
and the stone would also shatter into four pieces.
Duàn Chéngshì's former servant Yǒng'ān initially did not believe him.
Fèi once said to him:
"You have a great calamity."
He then rolled a talisman into a pill and forced him to swallow it.
He also removed the shoe and sock from his left foot,
and the talisman was found spread out on the sole of his foot.
He also said to the servant Cāng Hǎi:
"You are about to fall ill."
He had him bare his back and lean against a door,
and repeatedly drew on the outside with a brush,
loudly saying:
"Pass, pass."
The ink marks then penetrated through to his back.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
The Yuèlù Monk
In the Táng dynasty, there was a military officer under the jurisdiction of the military governor of Guǎngnán, a certain Zhōng Dàfū,
his name forgotten,
who in his later years fell into hardship
and lodged in Língzhōu,
often staying in Buddhist temples.
Ōuyáng Kàn, the registrar of Rénshòu County, took pity on his old age and frailty,
and often invited and treated him.
During the hottest days of summer, Zhōng suffered from an abdominal illness,
lying in Ōuyáng's house,
and went over a month without eating.
Fearing he might pass away at any moment,
Ōuyáng intended to submit a document to the prefectural office,
hoping to obtain a statement from Zhōng,
to clarify his circumstances.
Zhōng said:
"I am indeed ill,
but I am not yet dead.
Since you are troubled by this,
there is no harm in reporting it."
Thus, the officials were informed.
Later, he recovered from the illness.
Sūn Guāngxiàn was then serving as the deputy prefect.
Zhōng graciously came to visit,
and Sūn asked about the cause of his suffering.
Zhōng then said:
"I was once in Xiāngtán,
and due to warfare, could not proceed.
Along with several fellow traveling merchants, I went to Yuèlù Temple to hold a vegetarian feast.
A monk at the temple had newly prepared Zhīmìng Dān (Knowing Fate Pills),
and said:
'After taking this medicine,
if you wish to withdraw its effects,
drink seaweed soup.
Or if your great appointed time is approaching,
you will feel a slight pain under your ribs,
and this pill will descend by itself.
Then you must arrange your family affairs,
and await your end.'
We each gave him a string of cash,
and swallowed one pill.
Another day, when I entered Shǔ,
reaching Lèwēn County,
I met a merchant who had also taken the pill,
who was lodging in Lèwēn.
We were able to talk of old times,
and he spoke of the effects of the pill he took.
Not long after,
this gentleman came to report pain under his ribs,
and within days, the pill indeed descended.
He hurriedly settled his family affairs,
and died after a total of twenty days.
I, marveling at the efficacy of the medicine,
used seaweed soup to bring it down,
washed and bathed with fragrant water,
and then swallowed it again.
The suffering I experienced recently,
the pill had not yet descended,
so I knew I was not yet to die."
He also took out the pill to show him.
Moreover, Zhōng's complexion was ruddy,
and he ate and drank heartily,
as if benefiting from the medicine's power.
Another day, no one knew his final end.
Because his knowing fate was verified,
it is therefore recorded here.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Qiáng Shēn
In the Táng dynasty, in Dōnggǔ, Fèngzhōu, there was a mountain hermit named Qiáng Shēn,
skilled in the Three Prohibitions,
and especially proficient in cloud divination.
When the Wáng family first annexed Qín and Fèng,
and displayed yellow banners on the main roads,
Qiáng pointed and said to Sūn Guāngxiàn:
"In another ten years,
there will be several Sons of Heaven."
He also said:
"From Bīng and Fén comes the long road,
what will become of Liáng and Shǔ later?"
At that time, Shǔ troops had just attacked Qíshān,
and people said they would slaughter it in a day or two.
Qiáng said:
"The Prince of Qín has long contemplated reckless action;
he is not a lord for all under heaven.
Even so,
he will die by his window,
which is his lot.
The people of Shǔ will ultimately not be able to conquer Qín,
but the land of Qínchuān will also become ruins."
Later, the great rebel and Wáng Fèngxiáng were unrestrained,
the Prince of Qín met his end,
the Wáng lineage's mandate was cut off,
indeed matching Qiáng's words.
He possessed the art of the deer-ladder footwalking technique.
He said of himself, "This old man is aged;
there is no one to transmit it to."
His book was hidden in a deep, secure place within an ancient fir tree.
He thus went with Sūn Guāngxiàn,
opened the tree bark,
unsealed the wax wrapping,
and took out a silk book.
He selected an auspicious day to bestow it,
but was stopped by an old woman of the Qiáng family.
She said Sūn was too young,
fearing it would cause him to become frenzied,
and made him commit it to memory for three years
before discussing whether it was permissible.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Péng Dīng Jīn
In the Táng dynasty, in the area between Péng and Pú,
there was a physiognomist named Péng Kèmíng,
nicknamed Péng Dīng Jīn (Péng the Iron Sinew).
His predictions often came true.
Because people believed he would certainly hit the mark,
he thus had the name 'Iron Sinew'.
There was a son of the Táng family, a villager of Jiǔlǒng.
His family was rich in grain.
Péng said to him:
"Young Master Táng, when you depart this world,
you will not have a single thread on you."
The Táng man said:
"My family has a fair amount of farmland,
food and clothing are plentiful.
How could I possibly end up naked?"
Later, one day,
the river water flooded,
and on a deep pool there was a rabbit
in the middle of the water.
Táng thought he must catch it,
so he took off his clothes and swam out.
Before long, he was swept away by the waves and drowned.
This was the so-called 'not a single thread on him'.
Other cases were all like this.
Numerous and not recorded here.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Cuī Wúyì
During the time of the former ruler of the pseudo Shǔ of Wáng,
there was a Daoist priest named Lǐ Hào,
also a descendant of the Táng imperial clan,
born in Xúzhōu,
who traveled in the three Shǔ regions.
He was eloquent and quick-witted,
and had some literary talent.
He resided at Yángpíng Temple,
was supported by sorcerers,
and had purple qi above him.
He then gathered a crowd to start an uprising but failed.
The sorcerers scattered like stars,
but Lǐ Hào alone suffered the consequences.
Earlier, Lǐ Hào had sent a letter
summoning the Jade Bureau immortal Yáng Déhuī to a vegetarian feast.
There was an old Daoist priest named Cuī Wúyì who claimed to be deaf,
possessed the Way and relied on divination arts,
often foretelling good and bad fortune.
Yáng Déhuī asked him:
"I am about to travel north,
how will it be?"
He had Cuī write characters on the ground.
So he wrote the characters for 'north', 'thousand', 'two', and 'cut'.
Cuī inserted the 'thousand' into 'north' to form the character 'guāi' (perverse/awry).
He said:
"If you go, you will become aware of the perversity."
Yáng consequently did not go.
On the day of Lǐ Hào's feast, he was captured,
and many Daoist priests suffered the consequences.
Yáng's fortunate escape
was due to Cuī's power.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
The Shu Gentleman
In the false kingdom of Shu, there was a man named Wáng Chéngxié,
who from a young age inherited his family's official rank,
possessing both civil and military talents,
a clever nature,
and was well-versed in music and rhythm.
He often kept a strategist under his patronage,
who secretly taught him the methods of battle formations,
unknown to others.
The strategist wore tattered clothes
and also refused to accept Wáng Chéngxié's monetary gifts.
Later, when the ruler of Shu was conducting military exercises at the foot of Xīngxiù Mountain,
Wáng suddenly presented an iron spear before the ruler,
weighing over thirty jin,
and requested to demonstrate it.
Thus, armored and mounted, he twirled the spear,
like a shooting star and flashing lightning.
Ten thousand people watched,
all marveling at his divine skill.
Upon entering the city,
he further requested to twirl the iron bar of the city gate,
weighing over fifty jin,
which two men lifted onto his horse.
Galloping through the streets,
he moved like a flash of lightning.
Greatly rewarded,
he was promoted to commander of the Lóngjié army.
As for the various military strategies,
the three commands and five armors,
they were always on his lips.
Due to his young age,
he was never entrusted with major military authority.
Such extraordinary skills
are indeed credible and exist.
From "Wángshì Jiànwén Lù"
Chén Mín
When the Later Táng Zhuāngzōng's heir, Prince Wèi Jìjí, campaigned against Shu,
on his return march,
the rebellion at Yèdū occurred.
Zhuāngzōng and Empress Liú ordered the eunuch Zhāng Hànbīn to deliver an urgent edict,
urging Prince Wèi to return to the capital wherever he was.
Zhāng Hànbīn rode post-horses,
traveling day and night with great haste,
and met Prince Wèi at Xīngyuán's Xī Xiàn,
where he proclaimed the imperial decree.
The prince, as his army was then suppressing Hànzhōu,
and Kāng Yánxiào was following closely behind,
wished to wait until they emerged from the mountains
to present a victory song.
Zhāng Hànbīn urged him on.
There was a military strategist named Chén Mín,
who had previously served the Liáng dynasty
and was familiar with Zhāng Hànbīn.
He secretly asked Zhāng:
"The Son of Heaven has changed;
who is it now?"
Zhāng solemnly replied:
"I have personally received the decree to proclaim to Prince Wèi,
and with the army on the march,
such talk is hardly appropriate."
Chén Mín said:
"Having long been honored by your acquaintance,
I dare to inquire.
For the past two days, there has been a rumor
that a new ruler has already ascended the throne.
Why keep up appearances?"
Zhāng then said:
"When I left, I heard Lǐ Sìyuán had crossed the river,
but I know nothing of recent events."
Mín said:
"Prince Wèi should linger here
to observe the situation
and not advance further."
Zhāng, bound by Zhuāngzōng's strict orders,
dared not delay,
