and urged them to march on.
Prince Wèi was killed upon reaching Wèinán.
From "Wángshì Jiànwén Lù"
Zhèng Shāngǔ
During the time of the false Shu's founding ruler,
there was an army officer named Huáng Chéngzhēn who went to Guǎnghàn Miánzhú County for provisions.
He met an old man named Zhèng Shāngǔ,
who said to Huáng:
"This kingdom lacks the metal element in the Five Phases,
bearing the name of 'Peeling Metal,'
called the Metal Scorching Ghost.
This year, the Shu palace will suffer a great fire,
and by the years Jiǎshēn and Yǐyǒu,
countless people will be killed.
I impart to you a secret technique
to present at the court.
If my teachings are followed to exorcise and pacify,
perhaps the slaughter can be reduced.
The merit of saving lives
is highly valued in Daoism,
and extending life can be tested through me.
However, if this technique is presented three times
and not accepted,
then even stopping will not avoid calamity.
For it reveals hidden cosmic mechanisms.
Can you follow me?"
Huáng, also curious,
replied:
"If I receive these profound words,
I will follow them through life and death."
He then carried the secret text to Shu.
After three unsuccessful submissions,
he vomited blood and died.
The great fire and the slaughter upon the kingdom's fall in Yǐyǒu indeed came true.
Sūn Guāngxiàn knew Huáng Chéngzhēn
and secretly glimpsed the secret text,
titled "Huángdì Yīnfú,"
different from the current "Yīnfú,"
totaling five to six thousand characters.
Huáng said he received it from Old Man Zhèng,
with every stroke and dot
aligned with the Five Phases,
flowing smoothly and profoundly.
Truly a remarkable book.
Yet, several sages of the Hàn dynasty
"Sages" originally written as "words,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
were born in Miánzhú.
Skilled in the study of prophecies and records,
the mentioned Old Man Zhèng
might be of the same ilk as Huáng Fú.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Mǎ Chùqiān
In the false kingdom of Shu, Yè Féng
was clever and perceptive from a young age,
seeking recognition through literary talent.
He once went with Sūn Guāngxiàn to consult the fortune-teller Mǎ Chùqiān,
inquiring about his fate's obstacles and openings.
Mǎ said:
"Only after forty
can you seek it.
Before then,
if you obtain it prematurely,
your life will not be long."
At that time, various provincial and prefectural offices sought to recruit him,
but due to many complications,
he did not succeed.
Later, he served as a deputy official in Húnán.
Before receiving the official appointment,
he dreamed of sailing to his post,
with attendants on the river
arriving in great numbers,
welcoming him into a stone cave.
After waking,
he recounted this to Guǎngchéng Xiānshēng Dù Guāngtíng.
Suddenly, news of the imperial decree arrived,
appointing him as Inspectorate Vice Director of the Water Bureau.
Guǎngchéng said:
"Last night's dream
must refer to a small river, no?"
From then on, he set sail
and capsized at Qīngyī Beach in Qiánwéi Commandery, where he died.
This was Mǎ Chùqiān's innate knowledge.
Yè Féng's ominous dream
how remarkably it came true!
Sūn Guāngxiàn, traveling downstream from Shu,
one night dreamed of Yè Féng saying:
"You too cannot avoid Qīngyī."
Waking, he found it strange.
Upon departing Jiāzhōu,
he took the Yángshān road,
boarding a small boat to avoid the dangers of Qīngyī.
Unexpectedly, the punt-pole broke,
and the current swept him into Qīngyī,
but fortunately, he survived.
Could it be that ghosts and spirits still play tricks?
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Zhào Shèngrén
In the false Shu state, there was Zhào Wēnguī,
who excelled in the arts of Yuán and Xǔ,
predicting people's calamities and auspicious signs,
with none of his divinations failing to hit the mark miraculously.
In Shu, he was called Zhào the Sage.
The military general Wáng Huī served the first ruler of Shu,
accumulating numerous military achievements.
His nature was fierce and brutal.
By the time of the later ruler,
he was suppressed and marginalized by a couple of powerful nobles,
remaining stuck in low positions for a long time,
which Wáng deeply resented.
One day,
he encountered Lord Zhào at the court gate.
Seeing him, Zhào was startled and alarmed,
so he dismissed the attendants and told him:
"Today I see murderous aura on your face,
and you are carrying a weapon,
intending to carry out a covert plot.
However, in the future, you will serve as a prefect three times,
and once as a military commissioner.
Since you will achieve success later in life,
you should not harm others,
thereby bringing calamity upon yourself."
Wáng was greatly terrified.
He then pulled out a dagger from his bosom and threw it to the ground,
weeping as he said:
"Today I was just about to assassinate that fellow,
and then take my own life.
I did not expect to meet you, who enlightened and released me from this.
I beg to stop here and now."
He bowed repeatedly in gratitude and withdrew.
Wáng later became a prefect,
and was promoted to military commissioner of Qínzhōu.
After Shu perished,
he lived out his old age in Xiányáng.
Prime Minister Fàn Zhì personally met
(The character "met" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy)
Wáng
and spoke of this matter.
From "Jade Hall Casual Talk"
Huáng Wànhù
During the false Wáng Shu period,
there was a Daoist priest named Huáng Wànhù at the Gāotáng Temple on Wūshān Mountain.
Originally a villager from Wànhù Village in Bādōng,
he studied the art of the White Tiger's Seven Transformations,
and also said he learned the Liùdīng method from Daoist priest Zhāng Jūn.
He often used an iron whip to cure illnesses,
and did not care about wealth or goods.
However, he enjoyed disputing and litigating with fellow villagers,
and was not highly regarded by the prefecture and county authorities.
Wén Sīlù, the prefect of Róngzhōu, also possessed playful arts.
Once, he cut a paper fish and threw it into a basin, where it came to life.
Huáng Wànhù cast a talisman that transformed into an otter and ate it.
His iron whip was taken by Wén Sīlù.
On returning to Fúzhōu, Wén lost the whip,
and it returned to Huáng.
There was a Yáng Xīgǔ
who wished to learn his arts.
Before he could even sit comfortably,
Huáng suddenly said,
"Your family already has mourning and impurity."
Thus, the transmission did not happen.
Soon after, Yáng received news from home that his mother had died.
Also, the first ruler of Shu summoned him to the palace,
presented all his sons,
and asked him to identify the heir.
Huáng Wànhù then pointed to the later ruler.
His other arts were all similar to these.
He only had one daughter, who became the wife of a Wūshān villager.
He had a son to whom he transmitted secret formulas.
When about to die,
he instructed
(The character "instructed" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy)
his family not to encoffin him.
After seven or eight days, he revived,
but died again not long after.
In Qīngchéng County, there was formerly Monk Mǎ,
who sat in meditation for thirty-five years,
with very high virtue.
When Huáng Wànhù was about to die,
he told his family:
"Monk Mǎ from Qīngchéng is coming,
so I shall pass away forever."
That year,
Master Mǎ also passed away.
From "Beimeng Suoyan"
Hé Kuí
During the false Wáng Shu period,
there was a man from Làngzhōu named Hé Kuí.
It was unknown what arts he practiced,
but his predictions were very effective.
Since he was neither a diviner nor a physiognomist,
people called him Hé the Ghost-Seer.
The powerful nobles of Shu all regarded him as divine.
In a silver shop, there was a man suffering from white leprosy,
which had been passed down for two generations.
Hé saw him and said:
"Your affliction,
I know about it.
I am arranging a marriage,
and am short of items like bracelets, hairpins, and combs.
Can you provide some?
Then your affliction will be cured immediately."
The leper gladly agreed.
Hé then said to him:
"In your home, there must be old devotional objects from others,
or items used for offerings that remain there.
The soul of the deceased relies on them,
thus causing this affliction.
Simply remove them, and you will surely recover."
The patient returned and looked in the devotional hall.
Originally, there was nothing else there.
After pondering for a long time,
his old mother said:
"The gauze window in front of the Buddha statue
is something that belonged to others during the siege.
We took it and placed it there.
Could it be this?"
They immediately removed it,
and also performed fasting and repentance.
The illness was then cured.
Hé ultimately received the gift of bracelets.
Before Hé achieved success,
he was not anxious about official positions.
In his later years, he sought a high official post.
From being a commoner, he was appointed as a minor official in Xīngyuán,
with golden seal and purple ribbon,
and his wife was granted an honorary title.
His son was also bestowed crimson robes.
He did not take up the post,
but returned to Làngzhōu and died,
clearly knowing the time of his death.
Although his arts and calculations reached the divine,
his official titles exceeded his station.
Those with discernment knew that the later ruler's governance was all of this kind.
From "Beimeng Suoyan"
Sūn Xióng
Sūn Xióng, a man from Jiājiāng County in Jiāzhōu,
was called Sūn Mǎo Zhāi.
His predictions were also of the same kind as Hé Kuí.
When the false ruler of Shu submitted to the new dynasty,
several officials, including the eunuch Sòng Yùzhāo and generals,
who had long been on good terms with Sūn,
also regarded his arts as divine.
As they were about to depart for Luòdū,
they all asked about their future rise and fall.
Sūn bowed his head and said:
"Gentlemen, remember this:
On this journey, there will be neither disaster nor good fortune.
But when you reach the lodging place near Yěhúquán,
and say, 'Is Sūn Xióng not a sage?'
At that moment, both the old and new masters will no longer be seen."
All the officials were skeptical.
Later, estimating their travel,
they would be around the area of Xiánjīng.
The later ruler suffered the calamity of the false edict,
and Zhuāngzōng encountered the upheaval in Yèdū.
This was the verification that the so-called old and new masters both could not be seen.
From "Beimeng Suoyan"
Lǐ Hànxióng
Lǐ Hànxióng
once served as prefect of Qīnzhōu.
After leaving his prefecture,
he resided in Chízhōu.
He excelled in the extraordinary arts of wind angles and astrological calculations,
and claimed that he would die by violence.
In the bǐngzǐ year of Tiānyòu,
he traveled to western Zhè.
Upon entering the prefectural city, he sighed and said:
"The aura in this prefecture is very ominous.
There will be military turmoil,
and the time is not far off.
I must return quickly."
After meeting,
the prefect treated him generously,
detaining him for ten days,
so he could not leave abruptly.
One evening, leaving the inn,
he looked around and sighed:
"Disaster will come tomorrow.
I cannot stay."
The next morning,
he entered the prefecture to bid farewell.
Sitting in the guest seat,
after a long while, he said:
"Disaster is coming right now.
If I leave quickly, I might still make it."
He then went out to the prefectural gate,
where he encountered the military officer Zhōu Jiāo launching a rebellion.
He was thus killed at the gate.
From "Records of Divinities"
Hán Zhì
During the reign of Emperor Hui of the Hàn Dynasty,
the world was at peace,
weapons of war were laid to rest,
and from distant lands and foreign regions,
envoys arrived through multiple translations to offer tribute.
At that time, there was a Daoist named Hán Zhì,
a descendant of Zhōng,
who came across the sea,
claiming to be an envoy of the Divine Lord of the Eastern Sea.
He said he had heard that the Emperor's virtuous influence reached every corner of the realm,
and thus came joyfully to submit at court.
At that time, from beyond the easternmost reaches of Fúsāng,
there was a country called Nílí,
which also came to pay homage to Hàn.
Its people were four feet tall,
with two horn-like protrusions resembling cocoons,
teeth protruding beyond their lips,
and from the waist down, they had hanging hair that covered their bodies.
They lived in deep caves,
and their lifespan was immeasurable.
The Emperor said:
"The fangshi Hán Zhì understands the languages of remote lands.
Ask him how long people live
and how many generations of events he has witnessed."
He replied:
"The Five Phases succeed one another,
life and death alternate,
like flying dust and fine rain—
existence and demise cannot be calculated."
The Emperor asked if one could inquire about times before Nǚwā.
He answered:
"Before the serpent-bodied beings,
the eight winds were harmonious,
and the four seasons followed their order.
They did not use force to please,
nor disturb the essence of cosmic movement."
He was also asked about times before Suìrén.
He replied:
"Since the discovery of fire transformed raw meat,
fathers grew old with kindness,
and sons lived long with filial piety.
But from the times of Fúxī and Xuānyuán onward,
people busily schemed to destroy one another,
becoming frivolous, boastful, and shallow,
excessive in ritual,
disorderly in music,
worldly desires grew deceitful,
and pure customs declined."
Zhì reported all this in detail.
The Emperor said:
"Profound and obscure indeed—
it is difficult to speak of such matters with anyone but one who comprehends the divine and understands principle."
Zhì then withdrew because of this,
and nothing more was known of him.
From Wáng Zǐnián's Shíyí Jì.
Xìng Líng
Xìng Líng of the Jìn Dynasty
was a native of Jiànchāng, Yùzhāng.
By nature, he spoke little.
When living among others,
if he was insulted or wronged,
he showed no anger.
People in his village all called him a fool,
and even his father and brothers thought him foolish.
He was often tasked with guarding the rice fields.
Once, an ox came to eat the rice.
Líng saw it but did not drive it away.
He waited until the ox left,
then straightened the trampled and scattered plants.
His father saw this and became angry with him.
Líng said:
"All things between heaven and earth
live according to their own nature.
The ox was simply eating the grain—
why should I drive it away?"
His father grew even angrier and said:
"If that's the case as you say,
then why bother straightening the damaged plants?"
Líng replied:
"This way, the rice can also fulfill its nature."
At that time, Fán Chángbīn of Shùnyáng was the magistrate of Jiànchāng.
He conscripted the people to build official boats,
ordering each person to make a pair of oars.
Líng finished making his but had not yet submitted them
when they were suddenly stolen by someone.
The thief suffered heart pain so severe he felt he would die.
Líng said:
"Did you steal my oars?"
The thief did not answer,
and soon the pain intensified.
Líng said:
"If you do not confess truthfully, you will die."
The thief, in desperation,
finally admitted.
Líng then gave him water to drink,
and his illness was cured.
When the boats were completed,
dozens of men tried to pull one boat,
but it would not move.
Líng helped them,
and the boat then moved.
From then on, people all feared him,
and some called him divine.
There was a daughter of Gǒng Zhòngrú
who had been ill for years,
her breath barely sustained.
Líng sprayed water on her,
and she recovered immediately.
Also, the mother of Lǚ Yī, Huáng shì,
had been paralyzed for over ten years.
Líng sat a few feet away from Huáng shì,
closed his eyes in stillness,
and after a while,
said to Yī:
"Help your mother up."
Yī said:
"She has been ill for years—
she cannot get up suddenly."
Líng said:
"Just try to help her up."
So two people helped her to stand,
and then he told them to let go.
She was immediately able to walk on her own.
He then left a vessel of water for her to drink.
In Gāo Kuī's household, there were ghosts causing disturbances, speaking,
and objects moving by themselves.
They extensively used shamans and exorcists to suppress it,
but could not stop it.
When Líng arrived at the door,
he saw many talismans and said:
"Using evil to combat evil—
how could that ever end?"
He had them all burned,
and the ghostly disturbances ceased.
From then on,
common people flocked to him like clouds.
Those whom Líng cured
mostly did not dare
to offer explicit thanks or gifts.
His nature was extremely gentle;
upon seeing people, he would bow first
and always state his own name.
Whenever plants or trees in the mountains and forests were damaged, he would always bury them or set them upright;
if objects were overturned on the road, he would always set them right.
From Yùzhāng Jì.
Zhào Yì
In the Later Wei dynasty, in Chóngyì Ward, there was a residence belonging to Dù Zǐxiū.
The terrain was prominent and spacious,
and its gate faced the imperial road.
At that time, there was a hermit named Zhào Yì,
who claimed to be a man from the time of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
He recorded much
of the old affairs of the Jìn dynasty.
In the early years of the Zhèngguāng era,
he came to the capital.
Seeing Zǐxiū’s residence,
he sighed and said:
"This was the Tàikāng Temple of the Jìn dynasty."
People at the time did not believe him.
When asked for the reason,
he replied:
"After General Lóngxiāng Wáng Jùn pacified Wú,
he established this temple.
Originally, there was a three-story pagoda
built with bricks."
Pointing to Zǐxiū’s garden, he said:
"This is the original site."
Zǐxiū dug it up to verify,
and indeed found tens of thousands of bricks,
along with a stone inscription that read:
"In the sixth year of Tàikāng of Jìn,
corresponding to the year Yǐsì,
on the first day of the ninth month, Jiǎxū,
the eighth day, Xīnsì,
Yítóng Sānsī, Marquis of Xiāngyáng, Wáng Jùn, reverently constructed this."
At that time, the garden was lush with fruits and vegetables,
and the trees were dense and flourishing.
They then believed Zhào Yì’s words
and hailed him as a sage.
Zǐxiū subsequently donated his residence to become the Língyìng Temple,
and the bricks he obtained
were used to build a three-story pagoda.
Curious people asked how the capital of the Jìn dynasty compared to the present day.
Zhào Yì said:
"The population of the Jìn dynasty was smaller than today’s,
but the mansions of princes and emperors were similar to those of today."
He also said:
"Since the Yǒngjiā era,
over two hundred years,
those who established states and called themselves kings
numbered sixteen rulers.
I have traveled to all their capitals and outlying regions,
and witnessed their affairs with my own eyes.
After their states were destroyed,
when I read their historical records,
none were truthful accounts.
Without exception, they shifted blame onto others
and attributed goodness to themselves.
Although Fú Shēng was fond of bravery and addicted to wine,
he was also benevolent and did not kill indiscriminately.
Observing his governance and laws,
he was not tyrannical.
But when examining his history,
all the evils of the world were ascribed to him.
Fú Jiān was by nature a worthy ruler,
yet he usurped the throne and seized power.
His history falsely recorded him as evil.
All historians of that time
were of this kind.
People all value the distant and disdain the near,
believing such records to be true.
As for people of the present day,
they are considered foolish while alive but wise after death—
this delusion is extreme indeed."
When asked the reason,
Zhào Yì said:
"During their lifetimes, they were merely mediocre people.
But after their deaths,
their epitaphs and tomb inscriptions
invariably exhaust the great virtues of heaven and earth
and the utmost capabilities of humankind.
As rulers, they are equated with Yáo and Shùn;
as ministers, they are ranked alongside Yī Yǐn.
Officials who governed the people
are praised as tigers floating away, admiring their pure conduct;
law enforcement officers
are lauded for burying their chariot wheels, praised for their integrity.
This is what is called: alive they are like the bandit Zhí,
dead they become Bóyí and Shūqí.
False words harm truthfulness,
and flowery language damages reality."
The literary scholars of the time
felt ashamed upon hearing Zhào Yì’s words.
Infantry Commandant Lǐ Dēng asked:
"The brick pagoda in front of the Grand Commandant’s office
is of very ancient construction.
I wonder in what year it was built."
Zhào Yì said:
"It was built by the soldiers of Liú Yù’s army
in the twelfth year of Yìxī of Jìn, when he campaigned against Yáo Hóng."
The Prince of Rǔnán heard of this and found it remarkable.
He then asked what elixirs Zhào Yì took to achieve such longevity.
Zhào Yì said:
"I am not skilled in nurturing life;
my longevity is natural.
Guō Pú once divined for me, saying
I would live five hundred years.
Now, only half of that remains."
The emperor provided him with a hand-drawn carriage,
and he traveled through the markets and wards.
Wherever he passed,
he often spoke of old sites.
After three years, he disappeared,
and no one knew where he went.
From "Luòyáng Qiélán Jì"
Liáng Sì Gōng
During the Tiānjiàn era of the Liáng Dynasty,
there were four lords:
𦋅闖 (pronounced "shàng" as xié,
"xià" as chēn qù),
䨲杰 (pronounced "shàng" as wàn,
"xià" as jié),
䴰䵎 (pronounced "shàng" as shǔ,
"xià" as tuān),
and 仉𦛯 (pronounced "shàng" as zhǎng,
"xià" as dǔ).
They paid a visit to Emperor Wǔ.
The Emperor was very pleased to see them,
and thus ordered Shěn Yǐnhóu Yuē to prepare a covered object,
intending to have all the officials together guess what was inside.
At that time, the Grand Astrologer had just caught a mouse,
so Yuē placed it in a box, sealed it, and presented it.
The Emperor divined and obtained the hexagram Jiǎn (䷦)
(with Gèn below,
Kǎn above)
changing to Shìhé (䷔)
(with Zhèn below,
Lí above).
After the Emperor completed his divination,
eight ministers received the command to present their hexagram interpretations.
They were ordered to wait until all were finished before presenting together.
The Emperor made his divination judgment,
placed it on the green rush mat,
and further ordered Lord Chuǎng to manipulate the yarrow stalks.
He replied:
"The sage has laid out the hexagrams,
and their imagery is auspicious
(the Míng manuscript has 'auspicious' as 'announced')
Interpreting objects based on the imagery,
why seek anything different?
I request to follow the Emperor's command regarding the hexagram."
It was the eighth month, on the day Gēngzǐ at the hour of Sì.
Lord Chuǎng memorialized, requesting Shěn Yuē to take one yarrow stalk from the Emperor's hexagram and give it to him.
After completing his divination interpretation,
he placed it on the green rush mat and withdrew.
The Emperor's divination was read aloud:
"First Jiǎn, then Shìhé indicates the timing.
Inner Gèn, outer Kǎn indicates the imagery.
Kǎn represents theft,
thus it is a mouse.
In the time of Jiǎn,
movement leads to being 'bitten' (Shìhé),
indicating it is confined.
In the hexagram Shìhé, among the six lines,
four are without blame,
one is beneficial for perseverance in hardship,
these are not matters of theft.
The top nine: 'Carrying a cangue and losing one's ears: ominous.'
This is suffering punishment due to theft.
It must be a dead mouse."
The assembled ministers danced and cheered "Long live the Emperor!"
The Emperor, proud of his accuracy,
wore a rather pleased expression.
Next, the interpretations of the eight ministers were read.
Some reasoned based on appearance,
some deduced from vital energy,
some took from the imagery,
some elaborated on the lines,
some relied on birds, beasts, turtles, dragons,
yīn-yáng, flight and concealment.
Their texts, though profound and far-reaching,
none hit the mark.
Finally, Lord Chuǎng's interpretation was opened and read:
"The day and hour are in a phase of royal prosperity,
so it must be a live mouse.
Moreover, yīn-yáng shifts from obscurity into brightness and culture,
from stillness and rest into movement and vibration.
Losing its nature, it is bound to be captured.
The month when metal is at its peak,
controlling it must involve metal.
Zǐ corresponds to the rat,
Chén combines in substance with Gèn.
Kǎn represents theft,
and also hidden concealment.
Hidden concealment signifies theft,
so this must be a live mouse.
The number of metal is four,
so the mouse must number four.
Lí represents brightness and culture,
the hexagram of the south,
but the sun at its zenith begins to decline.
How much more so for yīn creatures?
The oracle of the Jìn hexagram says:
'Death and abandonment.'
This truly describes the affair.
As the sun wanes, it must die."
When a live mouse was revealed,
all the officials lost color in their faces,
and they reproached Lord Chuǎng, saying:
"Your interpretation said there were four,
but now there is only one.
Why is that?"
The lord said:
"Please dissect it."
The Emperor, by nature averse to killing,
regretted his own inaccuracy.
As the sun declined towards evening,
the mouse was about to die,
so he ordered it dissected.
Indeed, it was pregnant with three offspring.
On that day,
the Emperor moved the four lords to the western pavilion of the Wǔmíng Hall,
ostensibly to show greater closeness,
but in reality, he confined them there.
Only on the first and fifteenth days of the month and during the Fú and Là festivals,
could they meet with the various academicians in the Yìxián Hall.
However, regarding doubtful military and state matters,
none were decided without their participation.
During the Dàtóng era,
the states of Pánpán, Dāndān, Fúchāng, and Gāochāng sent envoys presenting local products.
The Emperor ordered the relevant officials to set up the full court ceremonial carriages,
perform the nine movements of elegant music,
and all officials wore full court dress as for the Yuánzhēng ceremony.
The Emperor asked the four lords:
"Foreign states have come to our court.
Regarding the noble rank to confer,
I intend to grant them the rank of Senior Duke."
Lord Tuān said:
"During King Chéng's time of peace,
with the Duke of Zhōu assisting governance,
the Yuècháng clan came to offer tribute through multiple translations,
yet we do not hear of noble ranks being conferred upon them.
In the Spring and Autumn period, the rulers of Zhū and Chǔ
were not granted ranks higher than Zǐ.
Even if their ruler came in person on a mission,
according to the classical rites,
their position would only be that of Zǐ or Nán.
If we grant them Senior Duke,
I fear it is not in accordance with antiquity."
The Emperor insisted that Lord Tuān reconsider and determine it more carefully.
Suddenly, a violent whirlwind arose,
tugging at the Emperor's robe and sash.
The Emperor again asked about the matter,
and the lord said:
"Tomorrow will also not yield results.
Let us discuss it another day."
The Emperor was displeased,
and the academicians all criticized him.
Towards evening,
the Emperor's daughter fell from a pavilion and died.
Thus, the ceremony was ultimately not performed.
Later, when questioned,
he replied:
"The whirlwind assailed your robes,
your beloved child met a sudden death.
What further doubt is there?"
The state of Gāochāng sent an envoy presenting two lumps of salt,
each as large as a big dou measure,
white in color like jade.
Also dried grapes, honey from thorns, frozen wine, and white wheat flour.
The princes, dukes, scholars, and commoners all did not recognize them.
The Emperor, considering they came from a distant land ten thousand miles away to present tribute,
taking several years to arrive,
and that their writing and language
were somewhat similar to those of the Liáng state,
after three days,
with no one at court able to respond appropriately,
ordered Lord Jié to receive them.
He said to their envoy:
"One lump of salt is from Nán Shāoyáng Shān, collected on the night of the full moon;
the other is from Běi Shāoyáng Shān, not collected on the night of the full moon.
Seven of the grapes are from Wūlín,
three are from Wúbàn.
The frozen wine is not from the Bāfēng Valley freeze;
moreover, it is blended with Gāoníng wine.
The honey from thorns grows where salt forms,
not from Nánpíng City.
The white wheat flour is from Dàngchāng,
not the genuine product from Chānglěi."
The envoy fully confessed the true situation:
the flour had spoiled over the years, losing its color,
so they traded for Dàngchāng flour to fill the amount.
That year, due to wind disasters,
the grapes and honey from thorns did not ripen well,
hence the mixture.
As for the salt and frozen wine,
due to the king's urgent command,
they were not collected in their proper season.
He then further asked about purple salt and medicinal amber,
saying they were lost en route,
seized by Běiliáng,
and they dared not speak of it.
The Emperor asked Lord Jié about the peculiarities of these various goods,
and he replied:
"The salt from Nán Shāoyáng Shān has coarse grain patterns,
while that from Běi Shāoyáng Shān has fine grain patterns.
That collected on the night of the full moon
is clear and transparent like ice;
boiling it in a felt bag can verify this.
Grapes from Wūlín have thin skin and delicious taste,
those from Wúbàn have thick skin and bitter taste."
The wine is made from frozen grapes of the Bāfēng Valley,
and it does not spoil all year round.
Nowadays, its smell is sour.
The wine from Wūlín is smooth and light in color,
hence it is described as such.
In Nánpíngchéng, the yángcì plant has no leaves,
and its honey is clear, white, and sweet in taste.
In Yánchéng, the yángcì plant has large leaves,
and its honey is bluish in color and mild in flavor.
The white wheat flour from Chānglěi, when cooked until almost done,
is as white as new,
but nowadays, the flour is like mud and mushy.
From this, we know that the honey and wheat are adulterated.
In the flat desert between Jiāohé,
if you dig several feet deep,
you will find mòyán salt,
which is red or purple in color,
bright and sweet in taste,
and eating it relieves pain.
Digging another ten feet deeper,
you will find hǔpò amber,
blacker than pure lacquer,
sometimes as large as a cartwheel.
Grind it and take it,
and it can cure women’s ailments such as intestinal masses and abdominal lumps.
Such rare treasures from that country
must have been presented as tribute,
which is how I know of them.
Master Jié once spoke with various scholars about distant lands, saying:
"To the east, as far as Fúsāng,
the silkworms there are seven feet long,
seven inches in girth,
golden in color,
and do not die throughout the four seasons.
On the eighth day of the fifth month, they vomit yellow silk,
spreading it on branches,
but they do not form cocoons.
The silk is as brittle as thread,
but when boiled in the ash water of the Fúsāng tree,
it becomes tough and resilient.
Four strands of this silk can form a cord
strong enough to bear thirty catties.
The silkworm eggs are as large as swallow or sparrow eggs
and are laid beneath the Fúsāng tree.
If the eggs are brought to Gōulìguó,
the silkworms become smaller,
like the silkworms of the Central Plains.
In the king’s palace, there is a crystal city,
about one li square,
which shines as bright as day before dawn,
but the city suddenly disappears,
and the moon then eclipses.
To the west, as far as the Western Sea,
there is an island in the sea,
two hundred li square,
on which there is a great forest,
and all the trees in the forest are treasure trees.
There are over ten thousand households on the island,
and the people are all skilled,
able to craft precious vessels.
This is the so-called Fúlínguó.
To the northwest of the island, there is a pit,
winding and over a thousand feet deep.
If meat is thrown into it,
birds will carry out treasures,
the largest weighing five catties.
They say it is the treasure trove of the Heaven King of the Form Realm.
To the northwest of the Four Seas,
about ten thousand li away,
there is a women’s kingdom,
where snakes serve as husbands,
the men being snakes,
which do not bite people but dwell in burrows.
The women serve as officials and nobles,
living in palaces.
They have no writing or contracts,
but trust in curses and oaths.
Those who are honest suffer no harm,
while those who are deceitful die instantly.
Divine principles govern their teachings,
and no one dares to violate them.
To the south, beyond the Fire Continent,
on the Yánkūn Mountain,
the natives eat crabs and bearded snakes to ward off heat and poison.
On the continent, there is a fire tree,
whose bark can be made into cloth.
On the fiery hills, there are fire rats,
whose fur can be made into coarse cloth.
Both are unburned by fire,
and can be cleansed by washing in fire.
To the north, beyond the Black Valley,
there is a mountain so steep it reaches the sky,
covered in ice and snow all year round,
likely the dwelling of the Torch Dragon.
There is no sun during the day,
but facing north, it becomes brighter.
At night, looking straight up, one can see the North Star.
To the west, there is a Wine Spring,
whose water tastes like wine,
and drinking it intoxicates people.
To the north, there is a Lacquer Sea,
where feathers and fur dyed in it turn black.
To the west, there is a Milk Sea,
whose water is white and smooth like milk.
Between these three seas lies an area seven hundred li square,
with fertile soil and water.
Large ducks give birth to fine horses,
and large birds give birth to humans.
The males die, while the females survive.
The birds carry their daughters in their beaks,
flying to feed them.
If they cannot carry them, they carry them on their backs.
Once the girls can take small steps,
they are raised by chieftains.
All the girls are exceptionally beautiful,
but they are short-lived,
serving as concubines,
and die before reaching thirty.
There are rabbits as large as horses,
with pure white fur,
over a foot long.
There are martens as large as wolves,
with pure black fur,
also over a foot long,
and wearing their fur wards off the cold."
When the court heard his words,
they clapped their hands and laughed mockingly,
thinking them deceitful and absurd,
saying:
"This is just like the tales of Zōu Yǎn’s Nine Provinces and Wáng Jiā’s Collected Oddities."
The Left Chief Clerk of the Minister of Education, Wáng Yún, challenged him, saying:
"According to written records,
to the east of the women’s kingdom,
west of Cányá,
south of the dog kingdom,
there is a branch of the Qiāng and Yí peoples,
where one woman serves as ruler,
but there is no mention of snakes as husbands.
This differs from your account.
Why is that?"
Master Jié replied:
"Based on what we know today,
there are six women’s kingdoms.
Which ones?
To the east of the North Sea,
north of Fāngyí,
there is a women’s kingdom,
where a heavenly maiden descended to become its ruler.
In this kingdom, there are both men and women,
as in other ordinary customs.
To the west of the Bǎn Dùn tribe of the southwestern barbarians,
there is a women’s kingdom,
where the women are fierce and the men submissive.
The women serve as rulers,
taking noble men as husbands,
and keeping men as concubines,
some having as many as a hundred,
others only one.
To the southeast of Kūnmíng,
beyond the remote borders,
there is a women’s kingdom,
where apes serve as husbands.
The sons resemble their fathers
and enter the mountains and valleys,
hiding by day and roaming by night.
The daughters dwell in nests or caves.
To the southeast of the South Sea, there is a women’s kingdom,
where the entire nation takes ghosts as husbands.
The husbands provide food, birds, and beasts to sustain them.
To the west of Bólǜ Mountain,
there is a women’s kingdom,
a hundred li square.
From the mountain flows the Táihuǐ River,
and women who bathe in it become pregnant.
In this kingdom, there are no husbands at all.
Together with the snake kingdom, that makes six.
In the past, south of the dog kingdom, there was a women’s kingdom.
During the reign of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
the king of that country died,
and his wife took over ruling the country.
For nearly a hundred years,
it was called a women’s kingdom,
but later, the descendants returned as rulers.
As for the kingdoms with dog husbands, ape husbands, ghost husbands, or water-induced pregnancy,
those knowledgeable already know of them,
so I will skip them and not discuss them."
Soon after, an envoy from Fúsāng arrived to present local products,
including three hundred catties of yellow silk,
which was indeed the silk produced by the Fúsāng silkworms
and boiled in Fúsāng tree ash water.
The emperor had a golden brazier,
weighing fifty catties,
suspended by six strands of this silk,
and the silk still had strength to spare.
They also presented a sun-viewing jade,
as large as a mirror,
over a foot in diameter,
transparent like glass.
When held against the sun to view, one can see the palaces within the sun,
clear and distinct.
The emperor ordered Jiégōng to discuss with the envoys their customs, lands, and products,
their cities, towns, mountains, and rivers,
and also to inquire about their past, survival, and decline.
He also recognized the envoys' grandfathers, uncles, brothers,
causing the envoys to weep and bow their heads,
and they told the full truth of the situation.
A year later,
a merchant from the Southern Sea brought three bolts of fire-washing cloth.
The emperor mixed it with other fabrics and piled it up.
He ordered Jiégōng to be summoned on some other pretext,
and brought to the marketplace.
From a distance, Jiégōng recognized it and said:
"This is fire-washing cloth.
Two bolts are made from the bark of the jīmù tree,
and one is made from the hair of the xùshǔ rodent."
When questioned, the merchant
confirmed exactly what Jiégōng had said.
When asked about the difference between the tree and the rodent,
Jiégōng said:
"The tree bark is hard, the rodent hair is soft—
that is the distinction.
If you ignite them with a yang-sui mirror under the shade of a volcano's tuòmù tree,
the tree bark will change its usual nature."
When tested, it indeed proved true.
The following winter,
a large ship from Fúnán arrived from the Western Tiānzhú country,
selling a blue glass mirror,
with a surface one chi five cun wide,
weighing forty jin,
clear and bright inside and out.
When colored objects were placed upon it
and viewed in bright light,
their substance could not be seen.
Asked its price,
it was roughly a million strings of cash.
The emperor ordered officials to calculate,
but even emptying the treasury was not enough to pay for it.
The merchant said:
"The Heavenly King of the Form Realm has fortunate and joyful affairs;
when heaven pours down great rain,
treasures pile up like mountains.
They are stored in mountain vaults,
but retrieving them is difficult.
If large pieces of beast meat are thrown into the vault,
the meat rots and sticks to the treasures,
then a bird carries it out—
and this treasure is thus obtained.
No one in our entire country recognizes it,
and none dare to match its price."
Shown to Jiégōng,
he said:
"It is indeed a treasure from the upper realms.
Long ago, the king of Bōluónísīguó had great fortune
and obtained two precious mirrors.
The light of these mirrors illuminated
thirty li for the larger,
ten li for the smaller.
By the time of his great-great-grandson, fortune exhausted,
heavenly fire burned the palace.
The larger mirror's radiance
could ward off the disaster of fire,
preventing it from burning.
The smaller mirror's light was faint,
harmed by the fire.
Though its brilliance dimmed,
it could still repel all poisonous creatures
within a hundred paces around.
This must be that mirror.
At that time, the king sold it for over two thousand jin of gold,
and it entered a merchant's hands.
Later, a king with scant fortune
lost the great treasure;
he seized this mirror,
and it returned to the royal palace.
The tenth-generation descendant of that king lost the Way,
and the people plotted to harm him.
This mirror emerged again—
it must have been obtained by a high minister,
and thus should enter the hands of merchants.
Its price is a thousand pieces of gold;
even exhausting the treasury would not suffice."
Then he ordered Jiégōng to discuss the mirror with them,
and they were convinced and submitted.
Further asked: "Since this is an auspicious treasure,
if the king ordered it sold,
it should have been taken by kings or high ministers of great states like Dàqín, Bōluónàiguó, or Shīluóguó.
How could you foreign merchants
obtain it?
You must have stolen it to bring it here."
The foreign merchant hesitated, unable to reply.
Soon after, his country sent envoys pursuing it to Liáng,
saying the mirror had been stolen by thieves—
exactly as predicted.
Later, Wèi envoys came frequently,
also speaking of black sables, white rabbits, duck-horses, and the Nǚguó,
often coming to the capital.
The ministers of the Liáng court
then began to believe that Jiégōng had traveled throughout the universe,
traversed a hundred generations,
his words never empty talk,
all becoming fine tales.
Thus, his vast knowledge and strong memory,
broad learning and ability to resolve doubts—
even Confucius' detailed discussion of large bones,
or Zǐchǎn's explanation of Táitái—
could not surpass him.
Later, in the Tiānpíng era of Wèi,
corresponding to the Dàtóng period,
both sides enjoyed prosperous customs and peaceful times,
with talents flourishing abundantly.
In court debates and responses,
they praised figures and scholars.
As for receiving and entertaining guests,
only Jīngōng was specially included for questions and answers,
always striking first.
Therefore, when sent on missions to foreign regions,
or hosting banquets for guests,
he made them fall into his strategies,
repeatedly blunting their verbal prowess,
his tactics never futile,
every move without miscalculation—
all due to Jīngōng's ability.
In the second year of Xīnghé of Wèi,
they sent Cuī Mǐn and Yáng Xiūzhī on a diplomatic mission.
Mǐn, styled Chángqiān,
was from Dōngwǔchéng in Qīnghé,
broadly learned and richly cultured,
foremost in the current court,
equally famous as Wáng Yányè of Tàiyuán.
Moreover, he excelled in astronomy, pitch standards and calendars, medical formulas, medicinal substances, and divination
(the character "shì" for divination was originally "lùn" [discuss],
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy)
Upon arrival,
the emperor selected ten eminent learned Buddhist monks to debate with him before all officials in the imperial presence.
Many were defeated by Mǐn,
so the emperor bestowed over five hundred scrolls of books upon Mǐn,
and other goods twice as much.
The Four Dukes came forward and said:
"Cuī Mǐn's learning is shallow and superficial;
he is not worth troubling Your Majesty's profound mind.
Order your servant to oppose him—
he will surely die."
The emperor agreed.
Initially, in Jiāngdōng scholarly debates,
there was the *Twelve Śramaṇa Treatise*,
which meticulously analyzed and verified points;
there was the *Madhyamaka Treatise*,
which conveyed profound detachment through its vehicle,
discussing names and principles.
Those who spoke of name and principle revered its methods.
In the Northern
(the character "běi" [north] was originally "bǐ" [compare],
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy, Xǔ copy, and Huáng copy)
court, there was the *Yúshí Treatise*,
which determined the essence of rituals;
there was the *Huízhèng Treatise*,
which borrowed opportunities to refute meanings.
Mǐn mastered both the Southern and Northern schools and was proficient in both,
and what the śramaṇas specialized in
was solely Buddhism.
As for Confucianism and Daoism,
they remained ignorant, having never heard of them.
Mǐn combined the three teachings and excelled in them,
showing considerable pride.
Jīngōng had once in the Five Tiānzhú countries used Sanskrit to deeply inquire into the principles of the *Fēnbié Treatise*, *Great Fearlessness Treatise*, and *Hetuvidyā Treatise*.
He exhausted their principles and reached their subtleties.
Jīngōng was ugly in appearance and form,
but his voice and energy were clear and fluent.
Mǐn, having repeatedly defeated the group of monks,
then became arrogant toward others.
That day,
the emperor in the Jìngjū Hall ordered Jīngōng to debate intensely with Mǐn,
covering the Three Luminaries and Four Qi,
the Five Phases and Twelve Earthly Branches,
the Ten Heavenly Stems and Eight Constellations,
winds, clouds, and climates,
golden elixirs and jade fluids,
medicinal properties and acupuncture methods,
the Six Natures and Five Aggregates,
yin-yang and calendrical calculations,
strategies and tactical opportunities,
flying and hidden, solitary and empty,
the conditions of ghosts and spirits,
starting from the Classics and Histories,
ending with Laozi and Buddhism—
for over ten days.
They debated and elucidated the Six Arts and the Hundred Schools,
with Mǐn and Jīngōng alternating as host and guest.
Their standing debate was utterly captivating,
spectators all filled to capacity, forgetting to return home.
However, Mǐn's words and energy were then
(the character "jì" [then] was originally "shì" [matter],
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy)
defeated.
Frustrated and dissatisfied,
he consequently fell ill,
was carried north in sickness to return,
and died before reaching halfway.
From *Records of the Four Dukes of Liáng*.
Lù Fǎhé
Lù Fǎhé lived in seclusion on Bǎilǐzhōu, a hundred li from Jiānglíng.
His clothing, food, and dwelling
were the same as those of Buddhist monks.
He called himself a lay Buddhist,
never entered the city walls,
and his countenance was always composed,
so people could not fathom him.
When Hóu Jǐng first surrendered to Liáng,
Fǎhé said to Nánjùn's Zhū Yuányīng:
"This humble monk should join the patron in attacking Hóu Jǐng,
to render service for the state."
Yuányīng asked why they should attack him.
Fǎhé said:
"It simply must be so."
When Hóu Jǐng crossed the Yangtze,
Fǎhé was at Qīngxī Mountain at the time.
Yuányīng went to ask him:
"Hóu Jǐng is now planning to attack the city.
What will happen?"
Fǎhé said:
"We should wait until the time is ripe.
It will fall without being plucked.
Patron, just wait until Hóu Jǐng ripens.
Why trouble to ask?"
He was then asked whether they would prevail.
He then said:
"They will prevail,
and they will not prevail."
Hóu Jǐng sent his general Rèn Yuē,
with a force said to number fifty thousand,
to attack Xiāngdōngwáng at Jiānglíng.
As the troops were about to press close,
Fǎhé then went out to see Xiāngdōngwáng, saying:
"I have my own troops and horses
"Horses" originally written as "books",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
I beg to campaign against Rèn Yuē."
He summoned eight hundred disciples from the various Mán tribes,
stationed at Jiāngjīn,
and set out in two days.
The Prince sent the foreign monk Yòu
The Xu edition has "Yòu" written as "Yòu"
to lead over a thousand men and march with him.
Fǎhé boarded the warship and laughed heartily, saying:
"Countless troops and horses."
Jiānglíng had many spirit shrines,
where people customarily prayed.
Ever since Fǎhé's army set out,
not a single prayer was answered.
People thought it was because all the spirits had followed along.
Reaching Chìzhōu Lake,
they faced Rèn Yuē.
Fǎhé rode a light boat,
wearing no armor,
and sailed down along the current,
stopping one li from Yuē's army.
He then said to his officers and men from afar:
"Observe their dragon, asleep and unmoving.
Our army's dragon is very lively.
Attack now."
They released fire boats ahead,
but an adverse wind hindered them.
Fǎhé took a white feather fan and waved it to command the wind.
The wind direction then reversed.
Yuē's men all saw the Liáng troops walking on water.
Thereupon, they collapsed in great defeat,
and all threw themselves into the water.
Yuē fled and disappeared, his whereabouts unknown.
Fǎhé said:
"He will be captured tomorrow at noon."
When the time came, he had not been captured.
People asked him.
Fǎhé said:
"I previously built a pagoda on this islet when the water was dry.
I built a pagoda,
and told the patrons,
'Though this is a pagoda,
it is actually a marker for the bandit.'
Why not now search for the bandit beneath the marker?"
As he said,
they indeed saw Rèn Yuē in the water,
clinging to the pagoda pillar's top,
with only his nose above water.
They then captured him.
Yuē asked to die before the master's eyes.
Fǎhé said:
"Patron, you have the physiognomy
and will certainly not die.
Moreover, you have a karmic connection with the Prince.
Have absolutely no other worries.
The Prince will later gain some small service from you."
He was indeed released
and appointed as a commandery governor.
When
"When" originally written as "again",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
the western army
The character "army" was originally "absent",
supplemented according to the Ming manuscript copy
besieged Jiānglíng,
Yuē led troops to rescue it,
fighting fiercely there.
After Fǎhé had pacified Rèn Yuē,
he returned and said to Xiāngdōngwáng:
"Hóu Jǐng will be pacified naturally.
There is nothing to worry about."
When bandits from Shǔ were about to arrive,
Fǎhé requested to guard Wūxiá and await them.
He then assembled the various armies and went.
First, he transported stones to fill the river.
After three days,
the water then divided its flow.
He blocked it crosswise with an iron chain.
Xiāo Jì indeed sent Shǔ generals to cross the gorge mouth.
Their situation became desperate,
unable to advance or retreat.
Wáng Lín and Fǎhé made plans,
and annihilated them in one battle.
The mountains had many poisonous insects and fierce beasts.
Fǎhé taught them prohibitive precepts,
and they no longer bit or stung.
Wherever he approached rivers and lakes,
he would certainly tie grass on the bank,
saying this place was for releasing life,
and fishermen all refrained.
When leading troops,
he still forbade the armies from fishing and hunting.
If anyone secretly did so,
fierce beasts would certainly come in the middle of the night wanting to bite them.
Once, a disciple playfully cut off a snake's head
and came to see Fǎhé.
Fǎhé said:
"Why did you kill the snake?"
He then pointed to show him.
The disciple then saw the snake's head biting his trouser crotch and not falling off.
Another person tested a knife on an ox,
cutting its head off with one stroke.
He came to see Fǎhé.
Fǎhé said:
"There is an ox with a severed head
urgently demanding your life.
If you do not perform meritorious deeds for it,
retribution will come within a month."
The man did not believe it.
After several days, he indeed died.
His words were often proven true.
Emperor Yuán appointed Fǎhé as Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
Fǎhé did not call himself a subject.
In his memorials, he stamped his name and called himself a lay Buddhist.
Later, he called himself Minister over the Masses.
The Emperor said to the Vice Director of the Left Wáng Bāo:
"I never intended to appoint Lù as one of the Three Dukes.
Why does he call himself that?"
Bāo said:
"Since he regards himself as a master of the Daoist arts,
perhaps he foreknows."
The Emperor said:
"Fǎhé's achievements are somewhat significant."
He then appointed him as Minister over the Masses.
Later, he gathered a large fleet of warships,
wanting to attack Xiāngyáng and enter Wǔguān.
The Emperor sent someone to stop him.
Fǎhé then sent all his troops away
and said to the envoy:
"Fǎhé is a seeker of the Way.
I do not even covet the position of Śakra or Brahmā,
let alone the ruler's throne.
I only have an incense and fire karmic connection with the ruler to aid him.
Now that I am doubted,
this karma is certainly unchangeable."
He then made offerings,
preparing large steamed buns and thin cakes.
When Western Wèi raised troops,
Fǎhé went to Jiānglíng.
The Emperor sent someone to meet him, saying:
"We can defeat the bandits ourselves.
Just guard Yǐngzhōu.
There is no need to move."
Fǎhé then returned to the province,
whitened the city gate with lime,
wore a coarse white cloth shirt and cloth trousers,
a diagonal headscarf,
a large rope tied around his waist,
and sat on a reed mat.
Only at the end of the day did he take them off.
When he heard Liáng was destroyed,
he again took the former mourning clothes
and wore them to receive condolences.
When people of Liáng entered Wèi in the west,
they indeed saw the steamed buns and cakes.
From "Old Stories from the Riverside Palace"
Wáng Fànzhì
was a man from Líyáng in Wèizhōu.
Fifteen lǐ east of Líyáng city,
there lived a man named Wáng Dézǔ.
During the reign of Emperor Wén of Suí,
in his household there was a crabapple tree
that grew a gall as large as a dou measure.
After three years, it rotted and decayed.
Dézǔ saw it
and cut open its bark,
whereupon he saw a child curled up in an embryonic position.
Dézǔ then took him in and raised him.
By the age of seven,
he could speak
and said:
"Who raised me,
and what is my name?"
Dézǔ told him the whole truth.
Thus he was named Línmù Fàntiān
(Míng manuscript: Thus he was named Línmù Fàntiān. The line reads: "Thus he said, 'Double wood is Fàn,' and named him Fàntiān.")
Later it was changed to Fànzhì.
He said, "The Wáng family raised me,
so I can take the surname Wáng."
Fànzhì then composed poems to show people,
which were very meaningful and profound.
From Shǐyí.
(Míng manuscript: From Yìshǐ.)
Wáng Shǒuyī
In the early Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a commoner in Luòchéng
who called himself a man of Zhōngnán Mountain,
named Wáng Shǒuyī.
He often carried a large pot and sold medicine.
If someone sought to buy it but could not obtain it,
they would surely die of illness.
If someone in a hurry gave it to a healthy person,
that person would inevitably contract a severe and chronic illness within ten days.
There was a man named Liǔ Xìn,
whose family had lived in Luòyáng for generations,
accumulating great wealth,
but he had only one son.
After the son reached adulthood,
a lump of flesh suddenly grew on his brow.
They sought treatment repeatedly,
but it could not be removed.
Upon hearing of this commoner,
Liǔ Xìn personally went to pray and request his help.
Upon arriving at his home,
he presented his son to show him.
The commoner first burned incense
and ordered wine and dried meat,
as if performing a sacrificial offering.
Then he took a pill of medicine from his pot,
chewed it, and applied it to the flesh lump.
He also requested a full set of sacrificial vessels.
In a short while,
the flesh lump burst open,
and a small snake emerged from it, landing on the ground.
It was about five cùn long,
radiant with five colors,
and gradually grew to about one zhàng in length.
The commoner then drank all the wine
and shouted at the snake once.
The snake soared upward,
and clouds and mist darkened the sky.
The commoner joyfully rode the snake and departed,
and no one knew where he went.
From Dà Táng Qí Shì.
Lǐ Zǐmóu
Lǐ Zǐmóu
was the seventh son of Prince Cài of the Táng dynasty.
His demeanor was elegant and handsome,
his talent refined and lofty.
He was naturally skilled in music
and excelled particularly in playing the flute,
with no one in the world matching his ability.
According to the old custom in Jiānglíng,
on the evening of the first full moon of early spring,
shadow lanterns were displayed.
At that time, men and women gathered along the river,
crowding together to watch.
Zǐmóu was traveling as a guest in Jīngmén
and happened to encounter the event.
He said to his companions:
"With one tune on my flute,
I can make the entire crowd fall silent without a sound."
His fellow travelers then encouraged him to do so.
Zǐmóu ascended a tower,
leaned against the railing, and turned
(Míng manuscript: "turned" is written as "alone")
to play.
As soon as the clear sound emerged,
all performances stopped,
pedestrians halted their steps
(Míng manuscript: "steps" is written as "feet")
and those sitting stood up to listen.
After the tune ended, for a long time,
the noise of the crowd resumed.
Zǐmóu, relying on his skill,
remained composed and confident.
Suddenly, an old man with white hair
arrived from a small boat below the tower, chanting as he came.
His appearance was ancient and rugged,
and his speech was clear and resonant.
Zǐmóu and the seated guests
rushed forward to pay their respects.
The old man said to Zǐmóu:
"The one who played the flute earlier,
was it not you, young master?
Your natural talent is exceptional,
but it is a pity the instrument is merely ordinary."
Zǐmóu replied:
"This flute of mine
was bestowed by the late emperor.
As for whether it is a supernatural or extraordinary object,
I do not know,
but among musical instruments,
this is a treasure.
In my lifetime, I have seen over ten thousand,
and among all I possess,
none can compare
(Míng manuscript: "can compare" is written as "match it")
Yet you, old sir, consider it ordinary.
Is there an explanation?"
The old man said:
"I have practiced since youth,
and even in old age, I have not grown weary.
As for what you possess,
it is not something I dare to claim knowledge of.
If you, young master, do not believe it,
I shall give it a try."
Zǐmóu handed it to him,
and the old man drew breath and produced a sound.
As the sound formed, the flute cracked.
The entire audience was shocked and alarmed,
unable to fathom who this man was.
Zǐmóu then kowtowed, pleading pitifully,
hoping to encounter something rare and extraordinary.
The old man replied:
"What I have stored away,
you cannot play."
He then ordered a young servant
to bring it from the boat.
Zǐmóu went to look
and saw it was made of white jade.
The old man gave it to Zǐmóu,
telling him to play a tune.
Zǐmóu exhausted all his strength,
but not even the faintest sound was heard.
Zǐmóu grew increasingly uneasy,
and with utmost reverence and humility,
he begged the old man to play a subtle melody.
The hearts and bones of the seated guests felt a chilling sensation.
The old man said:
"I take pity on your dedication,
so I shall try playing once."
The clear sound was vigorous and soaring,
its distant resonance overflowing.
The five notes and six pitches
could not harmonize with it.
Before the tune ended,
wind and waves surged and roared,
clouds and rain darkened the sky.
After a short while, it cleared,
and the old man was nowhere to be seen.
From Jíyì Jì.
Lǚ Wēng
In the nineteenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
a Daoist named Lǚ Wēng,
traveling along the road to Hándān, stopped at an inn,
where he set up a couch and spread a mat,
then
(Míng manuscript reads "解" for "擔")
unpacked his bag and sat down.
Soon, a young man from the town named Lú Shēng,
wearing a short fur coat,
riding a black colt,
and on his way to the fields,
also stopped at the inn
and took a seat next to the old man.
They chatted and laughed with great ease,
and after a while,
Lú Shēng looked at his own shabby and worn-out clothes
and sighed, saying:
"How unfortunate it is for a man to be born into this world
and suffer such hardship!"
The old man said:
"I see that your complexion is rosy and healthy,
your body is plump and free from illness,
and your conversation is pleasant and comfortable.
Why, then, do you sigh about hardship?"
Lú Shēng replied:
"This is merely a meager existence for me.
How can it be called comfort?"
The old man said:
"If this is not comfort,
then what is comfort?"
Lú Shēng said:
"One should achieve merit and establish a name,
serve as a general abroad and a minister at home,
dine with rows of cauldrons,
select the finest music to listen to,
cause one's clan to flourish and one's household to prosper,
and only then can one speak of comfort.
I devoted myself to study and immersed myself in the arts,
and in my youth,
I thought high office was within my grasp.
But now I am past the prime of life,
and still toiling in the fields.
Is this not hardship?"
With these words,
his eyes grew heavy and he felt drowsy.
At that time, the innkeeper was steaming millet for a meal.
The old man then took a pillow from his bag and handed it to him, saying:
"Rest your head on this,
and it will grant you the glory and comfort you desire."
The pillow was made of porcelain, with openings at both ends.
Lú Shēng bowed his head and leaned on it.
In his sleep,
he saw the openings grow large and bright, forming a space he could enter.
He stepped inside with his whole body
and soon arrived at his home.
He married a woman from the Cuī family of Qīnghé,
who was exceedingly beautiful and came with a generous dowry.
From then on, his clothes, furs, carriages, and attendants
grew increasingly luxurious day by day.
The following year,
he passed the imperial examination,
achieving the highest rank,
shed his commoner's clothes and was appointed a collator in the Imperial Library,
then took the special decree examination
and was appointed the magistrate of Wèinán County.
He was promoted to investigating censor and remonstrance official,
and drafted imperial edicts.
After three years, he was confirmed in his position.
He was sent out to govern Tóngzhōu,
and soon transferred to Shǎnzhōu.
Lú Shēng was fond of public works,
and from Shǎnzhōu westward, he opened an eighty-li canal to facilitate transportation where it had been blocked.
The people of the region benefited from it,
and erected a stele praising his virtue.
He was promoted to investigating commissioner of Biànzhōu and the Lǐngnán circuit,
then entered the capital to serve as the prefect of Jīngzhào.
At that time, the Divine Martial Emperor was engaged in conflicts with the barbarians.
The Tibetans, under Xīnnuòluó and Lóngmǎngbù, had captured Guāshā.
The military governor Wáng Jūncuò had recently been
(Míng manuscript reads "fought with them at Héhuáng and was defeated" for "recently been...")
The emperor, considering the need for a commander,
appointed Lú Shēng as vice censor-in-chief and military governor of Héxī and Lǒngyòu.
He inflicted a major defeat on the barbarian tribes, killing seven thousand,
expanding the territory by nine hundred li,
and constructing three large fortresses to guard strategic points.
The northern frontier relied on him for security,
and a stone monument was erected to record his achievements.
Returning to court, his merits were rewarded,
and the imperial favor and honors he received were of the highest order.
He was transferred to the posts of censor-in-chief and vice minister of personnel.
His reputation was pure and esteemed,
and he enjoyed widespread support.
This greatly aroused the jealousy of the chief ministers at the time,
who slandered him with rumors,
resulting in his demotion to prefect of Duānzhōu.
After three years, he was recalled to court
and appointed minister of revenue.
Not long after,
he was made vice director of the Secretariat and joint manager of affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery,
sharing governance of major affairs with Xiāo Lìngsōng and Péi Shìzhōng Guāngtíng.
For ten years,
he offered wise counsel and confidential advice,
meeting with the emperor three times a day.
He presented proposals and offered loyal admonitions,
and was known as a worthy minister.
His colleagues envied him,
and falsely accused him of colluding with frontier generals
to plot treason.
He was imprisoned,
and officers led soldiers to his gate,
pressing urgently for his arrest.
Lú Shēng was terrified, not knowing what to expect.
Weeping, he said to his wife and children:
"Our family originally came from Shāndōng,
with several qǐng of good farmland,
enough to ward off cold and hunger.
Why did I toil to seek an official salary,
only to come to this?
Now I long to wear my short fur coat again,
ride my black colt,
and travel the road to Hándān,
but that is no longer possible."
He drew a knife to take his own life,
but his wife saved him, and he was spared.
All those implicated with him were executed,
but Lú Shēng alone had protectors among the palace eunuchs,
and his sentence was reduced from death.
He was sent out to serve as prefect of Huānmù.
After several years,
the emperor learned of his injustice,
and reinstated him as director of the Secretariat,
enfeoffing him as Duke of Zhào.
The imperial favor and grace were exceptionally generous,
reaching the pinnacle of the age.
Lú Shēng had five sons:
Zǔn, Tì,
Jiǎn, Wèi, and Yǐ.
Zǔn served as vice director of the bureau of evaluations,
Jiǎn as investigating censor,
Wèi as a secretary of the court of imperial sacrifices,
and the youngest son, Yǐ, was the most talented.
At twenty-four,
he served as a right rectifier of omissions.
Their marriages were all with prominent and illustrious families of the realm.
They had more than ten grandsons.
Twice he was exiled to Lǐngbiǎo,
and twice he ascended to the highest ministerial posts,
serving both inside and outside the court.
He moved among the highest offices,
and for over thirty years,
his glory and prominence were resplendent,
unequaled in his time.
In his later years, he became rather extravagant and dissolute,
fond of ease and pleasure.
The singing girls and beauties in his rear courtyard were of the finest quality.
He was granted, time and again, fine fields and mansions,
beautiful women and prized horses,
too many to count.
As he grew older,
he repeatedly requested to retire due to old age,
but permission was not granted.
When he fell ill,
palace eunuchs came to inquire after his health,
crowding the road one after another,
and the finest physicians and medicines were all brought to him.
As he approached his end,
he submitted a memorial stating:
"Your subject was originally a scholar from Shāndōng,
who found pleasure in fields and gardens.
By chance, I encountered the sagely fortune of Your Majesty's reign,
and attained an official position.
I received excessive honors and rewards,
and was granted extraordinary imperial grace.
Abroad, I commanded armies with banners and axes;
at court, I rose to the position of a chief minister.
I served both inside and outside the court,
for many long years.
I have brought shame upon the imperial favor bestowed upon me,
and contributed nothing to the sagely transformation.
My inadequacy invited trouble,
and I trod on thin ice with fear and trembling,
day after day,
unaware that old age was approaching.
Now I am over eighty,
and have held the position of one of the Three Dukes.
The water clock and hourglass both cease;
my sinews and bones are all worn out.
Lingering in severe illness,
I am near the end.
Looking back, I have no sincere achievements
to repay Your Majesty's brilliant virtue,
and I have vainly borne your deep favor.
I now take eternal leave from this sagely era,
overwhelmed with boundless emotion and attachment.
I respectfully submit this memorial to express my gratitude for Your Majesty's notice."
An imperial edict stated:
"With your outstanding virtue,
you served as Our chief minister,
You have served as a bulwark beyond the capital,
and assisted in governance within the court.
For two decades of peace,
we have truly relied upon you.
Recently, due to illness,
we daily hoped for your recovery.
How could we have anticipated such a sudden and severe decline?
We are deeply grieved and silent in sorrow.
Now we dispatch the General of Agile Cavalry, Gāo Lìshì, to your residence to inquire after your health.
We urge you to diligently apply acupuncture and moxibustion,
and take good care of yourself for our sake.
We earnestly hope for the absence of misfortune,
expecting the joy of your recovery."
That evening, he passed away.
Lú Shēng stretched and awoke.
He found himself still lying in the inn,
with Lǚ Wēng beside him.
The innkeeper's millet was still cooking and not yet done.
Everything around him was as before.
Startled, he rose and said:
"Was it all just a dream?"
The old man smiled and replied:
"The affairs of human life
are also like this."
Shēng agreed with him.
(Míng manuscript: "agreed" written as "remained silent")
After a long while, he expressed his gratitude, saying:
"The laws of honor and disgrace,
the principles of gain and loss,
the nature of life and death—
I now understand them fully.
This is how you, sir, have stifled my desires.
How dare I not accept your instruction?"
He bowed twice and departed.
From *Yìwén Jí*
Guǎn Zǐwén
When Lǐ Línfǔ first became chancellor,
a commoner in plain clothes came to visit him.
The gatekeeper said:
"The court has newly appointed the Chancellor.
Even high officials have not yet dared to approach his gate.
How can a commoner so easily seek an audience?"
The commoner, holding his name card,
waited by the roadside,
and loudly announced himself:
"I am Guǎn Zǐwén, a scholar versed in the eight styles of calligraphy,
wishing to see the Chancellor to speak a word."
Línfǔ summoned him to the guesthouse.
When night grew quiet,
he greeted him under the moonlight.
The scholar said:
"I am indeed seasoned in the art of calligraphy,
and since youth have wandered the gardens of literature and records.
I have privately observed the rises and falls of antiquity,
the affairs of wise rulers and worthy ministers.
Therefore, I wished to visit you, sir,
to speak a word."
Línfǔ said:
"I have merely by chance assumed the position of assistant,
truly lacking in talent and capability.
I already fear I am unequal to the great responsibility,
that fortune may pass and calamity follow.
You have honored me by visiting.
I dare to receive instruction from you.
I beg you not to spare words of admonition,
to benefit this humble person."
The scholar said:
"The ancients did not speak lightly,
for they knew that speaking is easy but listening is difficult.
If one can give even slight regard to easily spoken words,
and listen without taking them lightly,
then even droplets of water and grains of dust can contribute to the sea and mountains.
Moreover, the sages have said:
'One word can raise a state to prosperity,
one word can cause a state to perish.'
If you, sir, upon hearing a word, immediately wish to uphold and act upon it,
or when facing a matter, indulge your own whims and desires,
then even if
you daily receive men offering counsel,
it will be of no benefit."
Línfǔ then, with a respectful and cautious demeanor, said:
"Please, sir, just speak one word to instruct me.
I shall inscribe it on my sash and forever keep it as an admonition."
The scholar said:
"When you hear pleasing words, you are sure to be pleased;
when you hear harsh words, you are sure to be angered.
If I use pleasing words to flatter you,
it will not benefit your affairs.
If I use harsh words to admonish you,
I will offend your countenance.
Since I will offend your countenance,
you will again be angry with me.
Then I would be unable to fully express the harsh words.
Pleasing words are accommodating but harmful;
harsh words are straightforward but beneficial.
You should examine this thoroughly.
Tolerate my words,
and do not become angry again."
Unconsciously, Línfǔ sat upright on his knees to listen.
The scholar said:
"You serve as Chancellor,
assisting the Son of Heaven.
To assist the Son of Heaven
is to secure the ancestral temple and protect the state.
When the ancestral temple is secure
and the myriad states are tranquil,
then the Son of Heaven has no troubles.
When the Son of Heaven has no troubles,
then you, sir, have no troubles.
But if even one person in the realm is displaced,
the fault lies with the Son of Heaven.
If the fault lies with the Son of Heaven,
what use is a Chancellor?
The way of being Chancellor
does not necessarily require personally managing all affairs under heaven.
You should promote civil officials to govern the people of the realm,
and promote military officials to quell the disorders of the realm.
Then let benevolent men comfort the weary and sick,
and use righteous men to harmonize conflicts and battles.
Cultivate frugality yourself,
to admonish those above
and transform those below.
Maintain loyalty and integrity yourself,
to serve your lord
and discipline others.
Thus, you will naturally have no leisure to personally attend to every administrative detail.
If the right people are found for various affairs, they will be well-governed.
If the right people are not found,
even with talents like Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Shàng,
they will not be well-governed.
Alas,
Chancellor, be cautious in this."
Línfǔ listened, astonished,
and hastily rose to bow and thank him.
The scholar continued:
"Do you know whether this era's course is open or blocked?"
Línfǔ said:
"Please, sir, teach me fully.
I shall never forget it for the rest of my life."
The scholar said:
"Order gives birth to chaos,
chaos gives birth to order.
This has never changed, past or present.
Our state, since reforming the chaos of Suí to achieve order,
up to the present day,
chaos is about to arise.
Remember this, sir."
Línfǔ again bowed in thanks.
At dawn,
wishing to report this to the Emperor,
and to offer him an official position and salary,
he ordered his attendants to secretly guard him.
The scholar firmly sought to leave, saying:
"I originally only wished to convey one word to you, sir.
Now that I have exhausted my foolish sincerity,
and you have not disdained to accept it,
why further hinder this rustic's return?"
Línfǔ could not detain him despite his insistence,
and so he departed.
Línfǔ sent someone to secretly follow him.
The scholar went to a stone cave in the southern mountains.
The follower also entered the stone cave,
but suddenly could not see the scholar.
There was only an old, large writing brush.
The man took it and reported to Línfǔ.
Línfǔ placed the brush in his study,
burned incense, bowed, and prayed.
That evening,
the brush suddenly transformed into a five-colored bird and flew away.
None knew where it went.
From *Dà Táng Qí Shì*
Yuán Jiāzuò
Yuán Jiāzuò, tutor to the Prince of Nìng in the Táng dynasty,
was an upright and unyielding man,
capable of upholding great integrity,
daring to admonish the ruler even at the risk of offending him,
and unafraid of death.
Later, he served as Prefect of Yánzhōu,
and his exceptional integrity and purity were reported to the court.
At that time, Cén Xī and Xiāo Zhìzhōng were chancellors,
and they appointed Jiāzuò as Prefect of Kāizhōu.
Jiāzuò resented this,
repeatedly complaining of the injustice.
The two chancellors were furious,
and they berated
("Berated" originally written as "deceived,"
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy)
Jiāzuò, saying:
"Fool!"
and shouted at him to leave.
Jiāzuò, feeling dejected,
went to water his horse at a public well.
There was a man sitting with his back to the well,
washing his hands in the water,
and intentionally splashing it.
He startled Jiāzuò's horse several times,
and Jiāzuò, angered,
scolded him:
"You foul soldier,
why are you frightening my horse?"
The man turned to Jiāzuò and said:
"You are about to be sent as an envoy to the Yēmiē country,
and you don't even know where you will die.
Why are you angry with me?"
Jiāzuò pondered his words but could not understand them,
and found it strange.
The next day, when he returned to court,
he was indeed summoned by the two chancellors,
who greeted him and said:
"We know your reputation has always been high,
and we need you to undertake a court mission as an envoy.
We now appoint you as Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
to go to the Yēmiē country on a diplomatic mission.
Is that acceptable?"
Jiāzuò declined, citing his lack of ability,
but the two chancellors issued the official documents that very day.
Jiāzuò was greatly alarmed.
As he passed by the public well,
he again encountered the man who had startled his horse the previous day.
The man said to Jiāzuò:
"Yesterday
("Yesterday" originally written as "look,"
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy)
the chancellors wanted to send you as an envoy to a distant country.
Is it true?"
Jiāzuò dismounted and bowed to him.
The extraordinary man said:
"Do not worry, sir.
Just stay where you are and do not go.
The heads of those two chancellors are already hanging on spear blades.
How can they still threaten you?"
Having said this, he disappeared without a trace.
A day later,
both chancellors were executed,
exactly as the extraordinary man had predicted.
The Yēmiē country is located several thousand lǐ west of the Great Qín (Roman Empire),
and since ancient times, there had been no contact.
After the two chancellors died,
Jiāzuò ultimately did not go.
Zhèng Xiàngrú
Zhèng Qián was skilled in poetry and fond of wine,
and his nature was carefree and unrestrained.
Emperor Xuánzōng admired his open-mindedness,
and wanted to appoint him to a court position,
but because he did not attend to official duties,
the emperor specially established the Guǎngwén Academy,
appointing Qián as an Erudite,
and his reputation became widely known.
His courtyard was filled with carriages and horses,
all belonging to talented individuals.
There was a man named Zhèng Xiàngrú,
from Cāngzhōu,
who came to the capital to take the imperial examinations.
Hearing of Qián's great reputation,
and sharing the same surname, he paid him a visit.
Qián, considering their shared lineage, treated him as an uncle and nephew.
Seeing that Xiàngrú appeared aged and downcast,
he did not show him much respect.
A few days later, when Xiàngrú visited again,
Qián sat alone with him
and asked about his scholarly pursuits.
Xiàngrú smiled and said to Qián:
"Uncle, you do not yet know Xiàngrú,
and treat me as an ordinary man.
But people are not easily understood.
Since you have asked,
how dare I not speak fully?
If Xiàngrú were among Confucius's disciples,
he would belong to the Four Disciplines,
and would even rank above Yóu and Xià.
If Uncle were among Confucius's disciples,
he would not be listed among the Four Disciplines.
Now, born in an untimely era and bound by ordinary appointments,
I can only conceal my fame and obscure my traces."
Qián was greatly astonished upon hearing this,
and asked him to explain further.
Xiàngrú said:
"Confucius said that even a hundred generations hence,
those who continue the Zhōu dynasty's ways can be known.
Now, Xiàngrú also knows such things.
Our state, by the thirtieth year of the Kāiyuán era,
will change its reign title.
Fifteen years after that,
a calamity will occur.
By that time,
war will break out across the land,
and treacherous ministers will usurp the throne.
At that time,
Uncle will be forced to accept a false official post,
serving in the court and ministries,
and will suffer because of it.
If you remain loyal to your duty as a subject,
you may avoid this.
After that, the common people will suffer greatly and without end.
Xiàngrú will pass the imperial examinations this year,
and after five selections, will be appointed as County Lieutenant of Xìn'ān in Qúzhōu.
After three evaluation periods,
he will die in Qúzhōu.
Such are official rank and fortune—
they cannot be forced."
That year, Xiàngrú indeed passed the imperial examinations,
bade farewell to Qián, and returned to his hometown.
When the time came for appointment,
he met Qián in the capital,
and the Ministry of Personnel assigned him as County Lieutenant of Xìn'ān.
Xiàngrú showed a pleased expression,
and then took leave of Qián to assume his post.
After his first evaluation period,
Qián asked an official from Qúzhōu:
"How is Zhèng Xiàngrú?"
The official replied:
"He is very well."
When asked about his governance,
he said:
"He is like the ancients."
After the second evaluation period, he inquired again,
and the official said,
he was fine.
After the third evaluation period, he asked once more,
and the official said:
"After Xiàngrú's evaluation,
he fell suddenly ill and did not recover."
Qián was deeply astonished and sighed,
and only then reflected on Xiàngrú's words.
Then, in the fifteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
Ān Lùshān rebelled,
sending troops into the capital,
and capturing officials to take them to Luòyáng.
Qián was then a Court Historian,
and was forced to accept the position of Director of the Water Bureau.
After the rebellion was suppressed,
he was demoted to Registrar of Qúzhōu,
and died upon assuming the post.
Everything happened exactly as Xiàngrú had predicted.
The original text lacked a source,
the Míng manuscript copy cites it from "Guǎng Yì Jì"
Xù Shēng
In Púyáng Commandery, there was a man named Xùshēng.
