No one knew where he came from.
He was seven or eight chǐ tall,
stout and dark-skinned, with cropped hair
only two or three cùn long.
He wore no trousers,
only a tattered robe that reached his knees.
If people gave him money or silk,
he would pass it on to the poor.
Every year on the eighth day of the fourth month,
wherever there were marketplaces or entertainment grounds,
Xùshēng would be there.
A man from the commandery named Zhāng Xiàogōng did not believe this,
so he went to one entertainment ground himself
and saw one Xùshēng there.
He then sent his servant to check other places,
and the servant returned to report
that Xùshēng was present at every single ground.
This astonished him.
During droughts,
Xùshēng would lie down in muddy puddles,
stretching out and rolling about for a long time,
and rain would surely follow.
The locals called him the "Pig-Dragon."
In the market, there was a large pit
where rainwater collected,
and herds of pigs often rested there.
Xùshēng would come in the evening to sleep there as well.
In winter, when frost settled on his body,
upon waking, steam would rise from him as if he were sweating.
Not long after,
someone saw at night that the stove in the northern market was glowing red-hot,
and went straight over to look.
There was a giant serpent,
its body inside the stove
and its head protruding outside,
larger than a pig’s head,
with two ears as well.
Waiting until dawn,
they saw it was actually Xùshēng,
who brushed off the ashes and emerged.
Later, no one knew where he went.
From Guǎng’s Records of the Five Phases Through the Ages.
Zhāng Zuǒ
During the Kāiyuán era,
the former jìnshì Zhāng Zuǒ once told his uncle a story.
When he was young, traveling south to Hùdù,
while walking in the countryside,
he saw an old man
riding a black donkey.
Its four hooves were white,
and he carried a deerskin pouch at his waist.
His expression was very cheerful,
and his demeanor was extraordinary.
They first met on a side path that joined the main road.
Zuǒ found him very strange.
He tried asking where he came from,
but the old man only smiled without answering.
After repeated inquiries,
the old man suddenly angrily scolded:
"How dare a young fellow press me like this!
Am I some thief or grave robber,
that you must know where I come from?"
Zuǒ apologized humbly:
"I admire your lofty bearing, sir,
and wish only to serve at your side.
Why do you rebuke me so harshly?"
The old man said:
"I have no arts to teach you.
As for longevity,
you would likely scoff at my wretched state."
He then mounted his donkey and hurried off.
Zuǒ also whipped his horse to catch up.
They both arrived at an inn.
The old man used his deerskin pouch as a pillow
but had not yet fallen asleep.
Zuǒ, feeling tired,
bought some white wine to drink.
He ventured to invite him, saying:
"I have a single gourd of wine and hope you will share it with me, sir."
The old man jumped up and said:
"This is exactly what I like!
How did you know my mind?"
After drinking,
Zuǒ saw the old man looked pleased,
and slowly requested:
"I am young and ignorant.
I beg you, sir, to bestow some words
to broaden my knowledge and understanding.
I dare not hope for anything else."
The old man said:
"What I have witnessed
spans the Liáng, Suí, Chén, and Táng dynasties.
The wise and foolish, order and chaos—
the official histories already record them.
However, let me tell you of the unusual things I personally experienced.
During the Northern Zhōu dynasty of the Yǔwén family, I lived in Qí,
a man of Fúfēng.
My surname was Shēn, given name Zōng.
Admiring Emperor Shénwǔ of Northern Qí,
I therefore changed my name from Zōng to Guān.
At eighteen,
I followed the Duke of Yàn, Yǔwén Tàizhōng (Yǔwén Hù), in the campaign against Emperor Yuán of Liáng at Jīngzhōu.
The province fell,
and the great general was about to return.
I dreamed of two figures in black clothes who said to me:
'Lǚ walks the heavenly years;
rén turns toward zhǔ;
longevity not a thousand.'
I then went to a dream interpreter in the Jiānglíng market.
The dream interpreter said to me:
'Lǚ walking forms the character huí (return).
Rén turning toward zhǔ forms the character zhù (dwell).
Perhaps if you dwell (zhù), you will attain longevity (shòu).'"
At that time, troops were left garrisoned in Jiānglíng.
I then presented my situation to Commandant Tuòbá Liè,
who granted permission.
I then went back to the dream interpreter and said:
"Dwelling is acceptable.
But is there an art for longevity?"
The interpreter said:
"Your previous life was Xuē Jūnzhòu of Zǐtóng.
He enjoyed taking zhúruǐ powder.
He often sought out unusual books.
Daily, he recited one hundred pages of Huáng-Lǎo texts.
He moved to live below Hèmíng Mountain.
There was a thatched cottage of three rooms,
with flowers and bamboos planted in pairs outside the door.
Clear springs wound around,
cliffs and peaks stretched into the distance.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month,
he let out a long whistle and drank alone,
becoming quite exhilarated.
He declared loudly:
'Xuē Jūnzhòu is so detached and serene like this—
surely an extraordinary person will descend to visit!'
(Original text had 'zhǐ' (旨);
changed according to the Ming manuscript.)
Suddenly, he felt the sound of chariots and horses in his ears.
Then, feeling weary, he thought of sleeping.
His head had just touched the mat
when a small carriage appeared,
with vermilion wheels and a blue canopy,
drawn by a red calf,
emerging from his ear.
Each was only two or three inches tall,
and he did not feel any difficulty of them exiting his ear.
The carriage had two boys,
with green headbands and blue capes,
also two or three inches tall.
Leaning on the carriage rail, they called to the driver,
stepped on the wheel, and were helped down.
They said to Jūnzhòu:
'We come from the land of Dōu Xuán.
Just now we heard your long whistle under the moon,
its tone very clear and stirring.
In our hearts, we admired you,
and wished to engage in refined conversation.'
Jūnzhòu was greatly alarmed and said:
'You just came out of my ear.
What do you mean, you come from Dōu Xuán?'
The two boys said:
'The land of Dōu Xuán is within our ears.
How could your ear contain us?'
Jūnzhòu said:
'You are only two or three inches tall.
How could there be a country within your ears?
Even if there were,
would its people not all be mere gnats?'
The two boys said:
'Why would it be so?
Our country is no different from yours.
If you don't believe it,
please
(Original text had 'jìn' (盡);
changed according to the Ming manuscript.)
travel with us.
Perhaps you can stay,
then you will leave the suffering of life and death.'
One boy then tilted his ear to show Jūnzhòu.
Jūnzhòu peered in
and saw a different world altogether:
flowers and plants lush and abundant,
rooftops and buildings connected.
Clear springs wound around,
cliffs and caverns deep and distant.
So he touched the ear and entered it.
He arrived at a metropolis.
Its walls, moats, towers, and battlements
were of the utmost grandeur and beauty.
Jūnzhòu wandered about,
not knowing where to go.
Looking back, he saw the two boys from before
already at his side.
They said to Jūnzhòu:
'This country is smaller than yours.
Since you are here,
why not follow us to pay respects to Méng Xuánzhēn Bó.
Méng Xuánzhēn Bó resides in a great hall.
Its walls, steps, and stairways
were all adorned with gold and jade,
hung with kingfisher-blue curtains and canopies.
He sat alone in the center.
Zhēn Bó wore robes of clouds, mist, sun, and moon,
and a crown reaching to heaven,
with hanging tassels
as long as his body.
Four jade boys
stood attending him left and right.
One held a white whisk,
one held a rhinoceros-horn rúyì scepter.
After the two entered,
they bowed with clasped hands, not daring to look up.
A person in a tall hat, long robes, and green-edged clothes
announced a decree on blue paper:
"Since the division of the primordial chaos,
nations have numbered in the hundreds of millions.
You sank to the lower world,
humble among the myriad beings.
That you have reached this state
is truly due to a dark accord.
Moreover, your purity stems from sincere devotion,
in harmony with the True Ruler.
High office and generous rank
you are fit to enjoy.
You are appointed Zhǔlù Dàfū."
Jūnzhòu bowed and danced for joy, then went out the door.
Immediately, three or four people in yellow capes
led him to an official bureau.
Among the documents there,
many he could not recognize.
Each month he also received no salary,
but whenever a thought formed in his mind,
his attendants would know beforehand
and promptly provide it.
During leisure, he climbed a tower to gaze into the distance.
Suddenly, thoughts of returning arose.
He composed a poem:
"The breeze is soft, the scene mild and warm,
Strange fragrances fill the woods and ponds.
Climbing high for a long gaze afar,
Truly lovely, but not my homeland."
He then showed the poem to the two boys.
The boys angrily said:
"I thought your nature was tranquil and detached,
so I brought you to my country,
but the lingering habits of vulgarity
indeed have not yet left you.
What is it that you miss from your hometown?"
Then he swiftly chased Jūnzhòu away,
as if falling through the ground.
Looking up,
he fell from the boy's ear,
and was already back at his old place.
Looking around for the boy,
he was nowhere to be seen.
So he asked the neighbors,
who said Jūnzhòu had been missing for seven or eight years.
Jūnzhòu had been there for what seemed like a few months,
and not long after, Jūnzhòu died.
He was reborn into your family,
which is your present self."
The diviner also said:
"My previous life was the boy from the ear.
Because in your previous life you were fond of the Way,
you were able to reach Dōuxuán Country.
However, your worldly habits were not yet exhausted,
so you could not attain longevity.
Nevertheless, from now on you will live a thousand years.
I have received your talisman,
and will now return."
Then he spat out over a foot of red silk,
had him swallow it,
and the diviner resumed the form of a boy and vanished.
From then on, he no longer fell ill,
traveling all over the famous mountains of the world,
and it has been nearly two hundred years up to now.
However, I
"I" originally written as "without,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript.
have seen many strange things,
all recorded in a deerskin."
Then he opened his bag,
took out two very large scrolls of writing,
the characters quite fine,
which Zuǒ could not read.
He asked the old man to explain,
and he briefly recounted over ten stories,
half of which were clearly memorable.
That night, Zuǒ dozed off briefly,
and upon waking, the old man was gone.
A few days later,
someone saw him at Huīgǔ Qiū.
The old man said:
"Convey my regards to Lord Zhāng."
Zuǒ hurriedly searched for him,
but he was nowhere to be seen.
From "Xuánguài Lù."
Lù Hóngjiàn
A monk in Jìnglíng found an infant by the water,
raised him as a disciple.
As he grew older,
he divined for himself and obtained the hexagram Jiǎn changing to Jiàn.
The oracle said:
"The wild goose gradually advances on the land,
its feathers can be used as ornaments."
Thus he took the surname Lù,
the courtesy name Hóngjiàn,
and the given name Yǔ.
Yǔ was literary and cultured,
full of ideas,
and when describing something,
he never failed to capture its essence perfectly.
His tea art was most renowned.
Potters in Gǒng County often made clay figurines,
called Lù Hóngjiàn.
For every ten vessels bought,
one would get a Hóngjiàn.
If tea merchants had poor sales,
they would pour tea over it.
Yǔ was known in the rivers and lakes as Jìnglíngzǐ,
and in Nányuè as Sāngzhù Gōng.
He died at the end of the Zhēnyuán era.
From "Guóshǐ Bǔ."
Jiǎ Dān
When Chancellor Jiǎ Dān was stationed in Huátái,
there was a wealthy local family,
and the father suddenly fell ill,
his body gradually wasting away.
He could not consume porridge,
only drinking half a shēng of fresh blood daily.
His family was worried and fearful,
so they offered much gold and silk to recruit skilled doctors.
Doctors from both capitals and various regions east of the mountains
all came,
but despite generous hospitality,
they all left without success.
Later, someone came from Jiànnán,
examined him for ten days,
but still could not diagnose his condition.
He then said to the son:
"My medical skills
have been passed down for three generations in my family.
Whenever I see someone's illness,
I always trace its source.
Now, looking at the old man, I am utterly perplexed.
Could it be that my skill is insufficient,
or is this a calamity sent by heaven upon the old man?
However, I have heard that the regional commander is learned and capable,
truly an extraordinary man.
As for divination and medicine,
there is nothing he is not proficient in.
Can you spare fifty thousand coins?"
The son asked:
"What for?"
He replied:
"To give to the officials,
so when the lord goes out,
we can place the old man in a carriage before his horse,
letting him see him.
If he says anything,
then I can apply my efforts."
The son did as told.
The lord indeed went out for incense-offering,
saw him and stared intently,
about to speak.
But the supervising army envoy reported a matter,
and before he knew it, his horse had passed by.
The doctor then took his leave.
The father later said to his son:
"My illness is surely a sign of impending death.
Now I am quite irritable,
and if I am bothered by people talking,
you can take me to a place with mountains and water outside the city and leave me there.
Come check on me once every three days.
If I die, bury me there."
The son had no choice,
and took him away.
Finding a flat rock near a pond,
he left him there,
weeping sorrowfully as he returned.
The old man suddenly saw a yellow dog come to the pond,
diving in and out several times,
as if bathing.
After it left,
the water became fragrant.
The old man, thirsty and wanting to drink,
but weak and breathless,
crawled forward on his elbows.
After drinking,
he felt his limbs slightly lighter.
He drank continuously,
and soon could sit up.
The son, surprised and delighted,
took him back home.
Then he could eat and drink,
and within ten days, he recovered.
Another day,
Commander Jiǎ went out again,
and upon reaching the place where the carriage had been stationed before,
asked:
"Is the sick man from before still here?"
The official reported that he had now recovered.
The lord said:
"Some human illnesses are indeed unrecognizable.
This man had a louse tumor,
for which there is no medicine in the world to cure.
One must obtain a thousand-year-old wooden comb, burn it to ashes, and take it.
Otherwise,
drink the bathwater of a yellow dragon.
Beyond that, there is no cure.
I don't know how he recovered."
He sent an official to ask,
and the old man told him everything.
The lord said:
"This man's illness was given by heaven,
and he found his own medicine.
Such is fate."
When people heard of this,
they all admired the lord's extensive knowledge,
and the doctor's claim of an extraordinary man was indeed credible.
From "Huìchāng Jiěyí."
The Needle-Treating Daoist
During the reign of Emperor Dézōng,
a court official fell from his horse and injured his leg.
The imperial physician treated him by needling the leg.
When the needle was withdrawn,
a puff of smoke-like qi emerged.
By evening, the patient grew increasingly weak and exhausted,
nearing the point of being beyond rescue,
which terrified the imperial physician.
A Daoist priest arrived at the gate and said:
"I believe I can cure him."
He examined the site of the needle puncture,
and reproached the imperial physician, saying:
"Sir, how could you be so careless?
The acupuncture points governing life and death
are separated by mere fractions of an inch.
Human blood vessels interconnect like rivers and streams,
and acupuncture requires careful consideration of the vital passages.
You are also a skilled practitioner,
but you mistakenly hit the wrong point."
He then had them carry the bed closer,
and inserted a needle at a spot on the left leg where the qi was full, saying:
"When this needle goes in,
the other needle will jump out,
and it should reach the ceiling plank."
As soon as he finished speaking,
he inserted the needle over an inch deep.
The old needle from the previous site suddenly sprang out and flew up to the ceiling plank.
The place from which the qi had been escaping
closed up seamlessly,
and the patient recovered immediately.
The court official and the imperial physician bowed in gratitude.
They offered gold and silk as gifts,
but the Daoist priest refused to accept them.
He drank a bowl of tea and then departed,
and no one ever knew where he went.
From Yì Shǐ.
A Commoner at the End of the Zhēnyuán Era
At the end of the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a commoner
who frequented taverns in Cháng'ān,
reciting poems in exchange for wine to drink.
By night,
he would often return thoroughly drunk,
and the people at the inn sometimes considered him mad.
He had been lodging there for half a year
when it was late autumn.
The wind was crisp and the air clear,
all trees shedding their leaves,
the vast sky stretching endlessly,
with the cries of migrating geese echoing continuously.
Suddenly, the commoner sighed with emotion and gazed around in all directions,
tears streaming down and soaking his lapels.
An old man, finding this strange, asked him about it.
The commoner said:
"I have lived in this world for one hundred and thirty springs and autumns.
Whenever I see the warm spring sun,
the gentle spring breeze,
the fragrant and blooming flowers,
the singing orioles and dancing butterflies,
I cannot help but feel joy and happiness.
But when it comes to this autumn,
I have never failed to feel sorrow and grief.
It is not that I grieve for autumn itself,
but rather I grieve for human life.
Youth is just like spring,
and old age is like autumn."
Thereupon, he recited clearly:
"In the season of bright spring, heaven and earth are harmonious;
all things flourish fragrantly—but what of man?
In the season of plain autumn, heaven and earth turn austere;
glory and beauty among the groves of trees swiftly decline.
It is just like in the human world during youth,
when ardent hearts and dignified appearances are all in their prime.
But once the body grows frail and hair turns white,
memories of past wanderings only bring endless tears."
Hearing this poem, the old man
also wept, his tears soaking his lapels.
The commoner then recited another poem:
"That all physical forms decay—who does not know?
Cease chanting of spring scenes and autumn times.
Better instead to get drunk on Cháng'ān's wine;
what use is glory and splendor, whether blooming or fading?"
The old man then laughed joyfully,
and hand in hand with the commoner, they got drunk together at the tavern.
A few days later,
the commoner was nowhere to be found.
Some said they saw him by the river in Western Shǔ.
From Xiāo Xiāng Lù.
Liǔ Chéng
At the end of the Zhēnyuán era,
Rǎn Cóngcháng, a military officer in Kāizhōu who valued talent over wealth and esteemed scholars,
had many Confucian scholars and Daoist practitioners relying on him.
There was a painter named Níng Cǎi
who painted a picture titled "Gathering in the Bamboo Grove,"
which was extremely skillful.
Among the seated guests were the two scholars Guō Xuān and Liǔ Chéng.
They often clashed in temperament.
Suddenly, Liǔ glanced at the painting
and said to the host:
"This painting is clever in composition and posture,
but lacks in spirit and charm.
Now I wish to perform a small skill for you:
without applying any colors,
I will make its essence far surpass this.
What do you think?"
Rǎn said in surprise:
"I never knew you possessed such an art, Scholar.
But without using colors,
how is that possible?"
Liǔ laughed and said:
"I shall enter the painting to work on it."
Guō clapped his hands and said:
"Do you intend to deceive a mere child?"
Liǔ then challenged him to a wager.
Guō offered five thousand coins as stakes,
and Rǎn acted as guarantor.
Liǔ then leaped toward the painting and vanished.
The seated guests were greatly astonished.
The painting hung on the wall,
and everyone groped around but could not find him.
After a long while,
Liǔ suddenly spoke:
"Does Guō believe me now?"
His voice seemed to come from within the painting.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
he suddenly fell out from the painting.
Pointing at the portrait of Ruǎn Jí, he said:
"My skill only reached this far."
Everyone looked at it
and
noticed that Ruǎn Jí's portrait alone appeared different:
his lips seemed as if he were about to whistle.
When Níng Cǎi saw it,
he could no longer recognize it as his own work.
Rǎn, thinking Liǔ had attained the Dao,
along with Guō, both thanked him.
A few days later, Liǔ eventually went elsewhere.
The retired scholar Sòng Cúnshòu, who was at Rǎn's house at the time,
witnessed this event.
From Yǒu Yáng Zá Zǔ.
The Righteous Master of Sūzhōu
In Sūzhōu during the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a righteous master who appeared mad.
A commoner had built a row of over ten shops,
when the righteous master suddenly took up an axe and began damaging their eaves.
He could not be stopped.
The owner, who had long known of his divine nature,
courteously said:
"Disciple's livelihood depends on these."
The master looked at him and said:
"So you cherish them?"
Then he threw the axe to the ground and left.
That night, a market fire broke out,
and only the few shops whose eaves the righteous master had damaged remained intact.
He often stayed in the halls of abandoned temples,
keeping a fire burning regardless of winter or summer,
and he burned
(Míng manuscript reads "damaged")
banners and wooden statues, reducing them all to ashes.
He enjoyed burning carp alive
and eating them without preparing them in broth.
His face was always dirty and unwashed;
whenever he washed it, it would rain,
so the locals regarded it as a sign of rain.
As he was nearing death,
he drank several hu of ash-water,
then sat chanting Buddha's name,
ceasing to eat or drink.
The commoners came daily to observe him.
He sat for seven days and then died.
It was the height of summer then,
yet his complexion did not change,
and his limbs did not decay.
From Yǒu Yáng Zá Zǔ.
Wú Kān
In Yìxīng County of Chángzhōu,
there was a widower named Wú Kān,
who was orphaned young and had no brothers.
He served as a county clerk,
and was by nature respectful and obedient.
His home faced the Jīngxī stream,
and he often at his doorway,
used objects to shield and protect the stream water,
never allowing it to be dirtied.
Whenever he returned from the county office,
he would go to the water to gaze and admire it,
revering and loving it.
After several years had passed,
he suddenly found a white snail by the water's edge,
so he picked it up and brought it home,
keeping it in water.
Upon returning from the county office,
he saw that food and drink were already prepared at home,
so he ate it,
and this continued for over ten days.
However, Kān thought it was the neighbor's mother pitying his solitary state,
who was thus cooking for him,
so he humbly thanked the neighbor's mother.
The mother said:
"Why must you decline?
You have recently obtained a beautiful lady to manage your affairs,
why thank this old woman?"
Kān said:
"No, I haven't."
He then questioned the mother,
The mother said:
"Every time you go to the county office,
I see a young woman,
about seventeen or eighteen years old,
with dignified and beautiful features,
wearing light and elegant clothes,
who prepares the meal,
and then retreats into the room."
Kān suspected it was the doing of the white snail,
so he secretly said to the mother:
"Tomorrow I will pretend to go to the county office,
and ask to peek from a crack in your house.
May I?"
The mother said:
"Yes."
The next morning he feigned leaving,
and then saw the woman come out of Kān's room,
enter the kitchen to cook.
Kān entered through the door,
and the woman could not return to the room,
so Kān bowed to her.
The woman said:
"Heaven knows that you revere and protect the spring's source,
diligently perform your humble duties,
and pities your solitary state as a widower,
commanding me to serve as your mate.
I hope you will accept this,
and not doubt or resist."
Kān respectfully thanked her.
From then on, their mutual respect and harmony grew.
The neighborhood spread the story,
and it caused quite a stir of amazement.
At that time, the county magistrate, a powerful man, heard of Kān's beautiful wife,
and thus plotted to seize her.
Kān, as a clerk, was respectful and cautious,
and never incurred any flogging or punishment.
The magistrate said to Kān:
"You have long been skilled in your clerical duties,
now I require the hair of a toad and the arm of a ghost,
to be submitted by the evening session.
If you fail to produce these items,
the punishment will not be light."
Kān assented and left,
reckoning that such things did not exist in the human world,
and seeking them would be impossible.
His face turned pale and despondent,
and upon returning home, he told his wife,
saying:
"I am doomed tonight."
His wife laughed and said:
"If you were worried about other things,
I might not dare to accept the task,
but as for these two items,
I can obtain them."
Upon hearing this,
Kān's worried expression eased slightly.
His wife said:
"I will take my leave to fetch them."
In a short while, she returned.
Kān was thus able to submit them to the magistrate.
The magistrate looked at the two items,
smiled and said:
"You may leave for now."
Yet he still intended to harm him.
Another day later,
he again summoned Kān and said:
"I want a 'snail-fighting beast,'
you should quickly find one.
If you fail to bring it,
disaster will befall you."
Kān received the order and rushed home,
again telling his wife.
His wife said:
"Our household has one,
fetching it is not difficult."
She then went to get it.
After a long while,
she led a beast to him,
as big as a dog,
and similar in appearance,
saying:
"This is the snail-fighting beast."
Kān asked:
"What can it do?"
His wife said:
"It can eat fire,
a strange
"Strange" originally read "its,"
according to the Ming manuscript edition, corrected.
beast it is.
Hurry and deliver it."
Kān took this beast to the magistrate.
The magistrate saw it and angrily said:
"I demanded a snail-fighting beast,
but this is just a dog."
He then said:
"What exactly can it do?"
Kān replied:
"It eats fire.
Its excrement is fire."
The magistrate then had charcoal brought and lit,
ordering the beast to eat it.
After it finished eating,
it excreted on the ground,
and all of it was fire.
The magistrate angrily said:
"What use is this thing?"
He ordered the fire to be extinguished and the excrement cleaned.
Just as he was about to harm Kān,
the clerks, using objects to handle the excrement,
found it instantly burning through,
and a violent blaze erupted,
setting the walls and buildings ablaze.
Smoke and flames rose on all sides,
spreading across the city gates.
The magistrate himself and his entire household,
were all reduced to ashes.
Wú Kān and his wife then disappeared.
The county seat was subsequently moved several paces to the west,
which is the present-day city.
From "Yuán Huà Jì."
Miáo Jìnqīng
Miáo Jìnqīng was struggling in the examination arena.
One year it seemed he would succeed,
but he failed again.
The spring scenery was warm and beautiful,
so he mounted a lame donkey and left the capital gate,
bought a pot of wine,
spread out grass to sit on,
drank until intoxicated and fell asleep.
After a long time, he awoke
to find an old man sitting beside him.
He then bowed and greeted him,
offering the old man the remaining wine.
The old man thanked him apologetically and said:
"Young sir, are you troubled and distressed?
Would you like to know about your future?"
Jìnqīng said:
"I have been taking the imperial examinations for a long time;
do I have any chance of passing?"
The old man said:
"There is much more.
Just ask further."
Miáo said:
"I am troubled by poverty,
but I would love to govern a commandery;
is that possible?"
The old man said:
"Higher still."
Miáo said:
"An investigation commissioner?"
The old man said:
"Higher still."
Miáo, emboldened by the wine,
asked boldly:
"A general or minister?"
The old man said:
"Higher still."
Miáo became angry,
completely disbelieving,
and thus spoke recklessly:
"Higher than general or minister—
could I become the Son of Heaven?"
The old man said:
"The true Son of Heaven you cannot become,
but a provisional one you can."
Miáo thought it all bizarre and absurd,
bowed to him, and left.
Later, he indeed became a general and minister.
When Emperor Dézōng passed away,
he acted as chief minister for three days.
From "Yōuxián Gǔchuī"
The Madwoman of Yìníng Ward
In the early Yuánhé era,
in the Yìníng Ward of the upper capital, there was a madwoman,
commonly called Fifth Lady.
She often stayed overnight beneath the wall of Yǒngmù.
At that time, a palace envoy, Rú Dàfū, was on a mission to Jīnlíng.
In Jīnlíng, there was a madman,
whom the people called Xìnfū.
Sometimes singing, sometimes weeping,
his words often foretold future events.
In the height of summer, he wrapped himself in cotton wadding,
yet never sweated;
in severe cold, he exposed his body,
with no chapping or cracks on his skin.
As the palace envoy was about to return,
Xìnfū suddenly stopped his horse and said:
"I have a younger sister, Fifth Lady, in the city;
now I have a small message,
you must deliver it for me."
The palace envoy, knowing of his strangeness,
gladly agreed.
Then Xìnfū took out a bundle from his bosom
and placed it in the envoy's boot.
He also said:
"Tell Fifth Lady,
'If there is nothing to do, return quickly.'"
When the palace envoy reached Chánglè Slope,
Fifth Lady was already there.
She stopped his horse, laughed, and said:
"My elder brother has a message;
sir, you may return it now."
The envoy quickly took out the message and gave it to her.
Fifth Lady then opened the bundle;
inside were three pieces of clothing.
She put them on and danced,
laughed heartily, and returned,
going back to beneath the wall.
One night she died,
and the ward collected money to bury her.
A year later,
someone came from the south of the river,
saying that Xìnfū and Fifth Lady had died on the same day.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Zhāng Yǎn
At the end of the Yuánhé era,
a courier from Yánchéng named Zhāng Yǎn was delivering documents to the capital.
When he reached Sòngzhōu,
he met a man
and asked to travel together.
This man planned to stay overnight in Zhèngzhōu,
and said to Zhāng:
"If you let me treat you,
you can travel several hundred lǐ faster."
He then dug two small pits,
five or six inches deep,
told Zhāng to stand with his back to them,
and let his heels hang over the pit openings.
He needled both of Zhāng's feet;
Zhāng felt no pain at first.
Then, from below the knees to the shins,
he repeatedly stroked them,
and black blood filled the pits.
Zhāng felt his feet become remarkably light and nimble,
and by noon they reached Biàn.
The man then wanted to stay overnight in Shǎnzhōu,
but Zhāng declined, saying he lacked the strength.
The man said:
"You could temporarily remove your kneecaps;
it won't hurt at all,
and you'll be able to travel eight hundred lǐ."
Zhāng, afraid, declined.
The man did not insist,
but said:
"I have matters to attend to;
I must reach Shǎn by dusk."
Then he left,
walking as if flying,
and vanished in an instant.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Xī Lèshān
At the Chángdiàn of Tōnghuà Gate in the upper capital,
many cartwrights lived.
They amply prepared materials
and hired people to assemble carts;
wheels, shafts, spokes, and hubs
all had fixed prices.
For each wheel rim processed,
with three holes drilled through,
a hundred copper coins were offered.
Even for those with nimble hands, strong strength, and sharp tools,
only one or two could be done per day.
There was a man named Xī Lèshān
who brought his axe and chisels
and went to the gate to offer his services.
Seeing that his handling of the ruler and ink line was quite precise,
he calmly said to the owner:
"Please separate the rim materials for me;
I will work with all my strength."
The owner was surprised by his eagerness for work,
smiled, pointed to a room, and said:
"There are six hundred pieces here;
you can
"can" originally read "willingly,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
do as you please."
Lèshān said:
"I may work through the night;
please prepare lamps and candles."
The owner thought that working overnight
would double the usual output,
but certainly not much more than that;
he agreed to all requests.
Lèshān then closed the door, kept people out,
and worked tirelessly with clinking sounds.
By dawn,
he opened the door and told the owner:
"All are finished;
I wish to receive sixty strings of coins and leave."
The owner and the neighbors were greatly astonished.
They inspected his work—exquisite and precise,
without the slightest error.
Everyone was shocked.
The owner paid him the money,
and Lèshān thanked him and left.
The owner secretly followed to see where he went.
At that time, heavy snow had fallen for days,
and firewood and rice in the capital were extremely expensive.
Lèshān then used what he had earned
to distribute among the cold, begging, poor, and destitute who could not support themselves.
In a moment, it was all gone.
He then went south out of the capital city,
and was never seen again.
From "Jíyì Jì"
Lay Buddhist Wáng
There was a lay Buddhist named Wáng Jūshì of Chánglè,
who in his advanced years had crane-like white hair,
yet his spirit and vigor remained undiminished.
He often held prayer beads and chanted Buddha’s name,
and distributed medicine in the alleys and lanes.
His household consisted of over ten members,
living in modest comfort.
One day he visited the Língyìng Terrace on Zhōngnán Mountain,
where there were foundations for a Guānyīn Hall.
He inquired of the monks there.
They said:
"The beams, pillars, brackets, and rafters
are all already prepared,
but because the mountain path is perilous and steep,
transporting them up and down
requires a great labor force;
without three hundred strings of cash, the project cannot be completed."
Layman Wáng promised,
setting a deadline of ten days to bring the money.
Upon entering the capital,
he entrusted someone to spread the word:
"If there is a wealthy family with a critically ill patient
whom medicine cannot save,
I can revive them.
If I obtain three hundred thousand cash,
I can complete the Buddhist hall on Nán Mountain."
Indeed, there was a gold, silver, pearl, and jade merchant in Yánshòu Ward,
whose fifteen-year-old daughter
had fallen gravely ill.
All the doctors had thrown up their hands, unable to do anything,
and they were willing to pay the price for her treatment.
Layman Wáng then made a written pledge,
guaranteeing its effectiveness.
And he said:
"The construction work has been delayed for a long time;
now I leave behind a divine elixir.
Do not worry excessively.
I will first hasten to deliver this money to the monk in charge.
I hope to achieve both goals."
The gold merchant also followed Buddhism,
so he agreed.
Wáng left the elixir in a small pot
and went off with the strings of cash.
After ten days passed without news,
the girl died.
Her family began preparing mourning items
when Layman Wáng returned, leaning on his staff.
They then cursed and berated him
and detained him to send him to the county authorities.
Layman Wáng
"Layman" originally written as "且";
emended according to the Ming manuscript copy
said:
"If I were truly a great fraud,
how would I dare to return?
Please let me enter the house to see her."
She had been stiff and lifeless for a long time.
He then ordered a secluded room to be prepared,
burned moistened locust and willow wood inside,
filling the room with thick smoke,
so that people could not approach.
In the middle, he placed a flat couch,
laid the corpse upon it,
took out several pellets of medicine,
and placed them mixed on her forehead and nose.
He also used a bronze vessel to hold warm water,
placing it on her chest,
then carefully closed the door, kept the crowd away, and waited.
By dawn, when the smoke had cleared,
the room was blackened by the soot.
Layman Wáng dipped his finger in the water and said:
"She can still be saved."
He urgently ordered milk to be fetched,
crushed several pellets of the elixir,
and dripped it onto her lips.
In a moment, it flowed into her mouth.
He joyfully said:
"No need to worry now."
He then covered her nose with fine silk floss,
and again placed warm water on her chest.
When night fell,
he held a candle and waited.
After several marks on the water clock had passed,
the silk floss over her nose moved slightly with breath.
After several more marks,
the water on her chest rippled faintly.
He then dripped the previous medicine into her nose again.
After a short while, she suddenly sneezed.
By daybreak, her breathing had resumed.
The whole family was astonished.
They felt ashamed and thanked Layman Wáng.
Wáng then left more medicine and departed,
perhaps saying he might return again,
but he never came back.
Later, he moved his family elsewhere.
No one knew where he went.
The girl married,
bore several children, and then passed away.
From "Quē Shǐ"
Yú Sǒu
Wáng Qián, the Governor of Jiānglíng, had administrative talent,
and brought order wherever he served,
but he was lacking in righteousness.
During his time in Jiānglíng,
there was a young man named Lǚ from Jīngzhào,
who, suffering from hunger and cold, traveled from afar to visit Qián,
but Qián showed him no courtesy.
After over a month at the inn,
he had not yet managed to return home.
There was a gatekeeper named Yú Sǒu
who noticed Lǚ Shēng coming and going with a dissatisfied expression,
so he called him over and asked.
Lǚ said:
"I live north of the Wèi River.
Impoverished and unsuccessful,
I have nothing to support my parents.
Governor Wáng
is a cousin of my father.
I came from afar because of our kinship and old ties,
yet even after visiting him,
he never once inquired about me.
Is this what fate has brought me?"
Yú Sǒu said:
"I am also in straitened circumstances,
and have nothing to relieve your urgent needs,
but tonight you may stay under my roof,
so I can offer the hospitality of lodging and food."
Lǚ agreed.
After being invited in,
he saw broken eaves and windows,
a mat laid on the ground,
and after sitting and talking for a long time,
the food served was only coarse grains in earthenware.
Yú Sǒu said:
"I once studied the Dao on Sìmíng Mountain,
and by chance am living in obscurity here.
Just now, hearing that Governor Wáng has forgotten old ties,
I was greatly surprised."
He then overturned a pottery jar on the ground.
After a short while,
he lifted it to look,
and there was a man in purple robes,
about five inches tall.
Yú Sǒu pointed at him and said to Lǚ:
"This is Governor Wáng."
Lǚ looked closely;
it bore a striking resemblance.
Yú Sǒu then admonished him:
"Lǚ Shēng is your cousin's nephew.
Lacking even daily sustenance for his parents,
he has come a thousand lǐ from the capital.
You should provide him generous lodging and provisions,
and give him gold and silk as gifts.
How can you be so arrogant as to forget old ties?"
The purple-robed figure bowed humbly,
as if accepting the instruction,
and then vanished.
The next morning,
Yú Sǒu urged Lǚ to return to his inn.
Wáng Qián summoned Lǚ and accommodated him,
feasting and conversing with him for several days.
When Lǚ was about to depart,
Qián provided him with servants, horses, and a generous supply of luggage and goods.
From "Bǔ Lù Jì Zhuàn"
Héngyuè Dàorén
On the western plains of Héngyuè Mountain,
near the Zhūlíng Cave,
the mountains are perilous and steep,
with many large trees and fierce beasts.
Those who go there often lose their way,
or encounter giant snakes and cannot proceed.
During the Chángqìng era (821-824 AD),
there was a mendicant monk named Wùkōng,
who often carried provisions and his monk's staff,
entering the mountain forests at night,
stepping over corpses and confronting tigers,
showing no fear at all.
When he reached the Zhūlíng plains,
he wandered for several days,
grasping vines and descending cliffs,
leaving no secluded place unexplored.
Because of this, his feet became cracked,
and he rested beneath a cliff,
sighing deeply:
"I am so hungry and thirsty,
yet I have not met a host."
Suddenly, he saw a Daoist priest sitting on a rope-bed on the cliff ahead.
The monk approached him,
but the priest did not move.
The monk then reproached him for lacking the manners of a host,
and also told him of his hunger and exhaustion.
The Daoist priest suddenly stood up.
Pointing to a rocky area, he said:
"There is rice and a pickaxe here."
He dug into the rock several inches deep,
and told the monk to feel inside,
where he found over a dou of old rice,
which he then placed in a pot.
Using waterfall water,
he struck a fire and cooked the rice.
After watching the monk eat less than a mouthful,
the monk declined, saying it was not yet cooked.
The Daoist priest laughed and said:
"If you eat only this much,
you can be said to eat sparingly.
I will finish it."
He then ate the hard rice.
He also said:
"I will perform a trick for my guest."
He then took a flexible branch,
tossed it like a cover onto a precarious rock,
swinging like an ape and perching like a bird,
truly agile and dazzling to the eye.
After a while,
he again circled around the rope-bed,
spinning like tumbleweed with great speed,
until only the color of his clothes formed a circle,
and suddenly he disappeared.
The monk found his way back to the temple,
and for several months he felt neither hunger nor thirst.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Lǐ Yè
Lǐ Yè sat for the imperial examinations,
but having failed,
he was passing through the Shǎn-Guó mountain road,
when he encountered a violent thunderstorm,
and sought shelter at a village house.
The neighboring houses were very far away,
and the village household had only a young boy looking after the place.
Lǐ Yè tied his donkey under the eaves.
Lǐ Shēng of the Left Army and the traveling official Yáng Zhèn also sought shelter in the same house,
with Lǐ having a horse.
They all entered and stayed inside the house.
When the weather cleared slightly,
it was already evening.
The young boy said:
"My grandfather will be returning soon,
and he does not like to see guests,
so you should leave."
Lǐ Yè said to him:
"The nearest houses are extremely far from here,
and it is already late in the day,
so we certainly cannot proceed."
Shortly after, the old man returned,
and upon seeing the guests, he was delighted.
He treated them with exceptional courtesy and hospitality.
He insisted they stay overnight.
The next morning, he earnestly urged them to stay longer.
He wanted to prepare a meal.
Lǐ Yè repeatedly declined with gratitude.
He then said:
"Your grandson said that you, sir, do not like guests,
and I was also worried that we could not travel at night,
so I was very anxious and perplexed.
I did not expect such courteous hospitality;
how can I deserve this?"
The old man said:
"My family is poor,
and I have nothing to entertain guests with,
so I am ashamed to receive visitors—
it is not that I do not like guests.
However, all three of you are military governors,
how dare I not respectfully serve you?"
Lǐ Yè said:
"Among the three of us,
one is merely a traveling official;
you speak too highly of us."
The old man said:
"A traveling official holds authority over military affairs above that of a military commander,
while a scholar's authority is below that of a military commander.
However, you, scholar, will hold authority over five military regions;
strive to take care of yourself."
After failing the examinations for several years,
Lǐ Yè joined the military staff.
The following year,
Yáng Zhèn was promoted and employed by Qiú Shìliáng when he established his administration,
rising through the ranks to become a military commissioner,
and was appointed military governor of Jīngzhōu.
Lǐ Shēng and Zhèn became military commissioners at the same time,
with Lǐ Shēng governing as military governor of Bīnzhōu.
Lǐ Yè, due to his achievements in suppressing the Dǎngxiàng rebellion, was appointed military governor of Zhènwǔ, Bīnzhōu, and Jīngzhōu,
holding authority over a total of five military regions.
This was exactly as the old man had predicted.
From "Lù Yì Jì"
Shí Mín
During the Huìchāng era (841-846 AD),
there was a man named Shí Mín,
who possessed profound arts.
Once, while traveling in Wǎnlíng,
he stayed overnight at the forest pavilion of a man named Léi.
At that time, Léi's servant had caught a huge fish in a net,
but because Léi was drunk from hosting a banquet and had fallen asleep,
the fish had not yet been prepared.
As the weather was hot and humid,
by the next day,
the fish had already spoiled,
and they were about to throw it away.
Shí Mín said:
"I have a medicine
that can bring it back to life;
why throw it away?"
Léi then requested it.
Shí Mín then took a single pill of medicine
and placed it in the fish's mouth.
In a moment, its scales and tail began to move.
It became fresh and moist as before.
Léi was greatly amazed by this,
and so he bowed and asked for an elixir to prolong life.
Shí Mín said:
"My medicine
is of the utmost purity and clarity.
You people indulge your desires without restraint,
and within your internal organs,
all kinds of impurities accumulate.
If you were to take it hastily,
it would be like fire and water attacking each other;
how could it preserve your life?
However, the path of immortality can be learned,
but people are burdened by many attachments.
Like caged birds or imprisoned apes,
they may have the ambition to soar and leap,
but how can they achieve it!"
From "Bǔ Lù Jì Zhuàn"
The Hermit of Guǎncén Mountain
Lǐ Déyù once said:
I encountered three extraordinary men,
none of whom were fortune-tellers or priests,
but all were recluses who had withdrawn from the world.
When I first took up my post as recorder at the Northern Gate,
a hermit from Guǎncén Mountain
said to Déyù:
"Next year, you will be by the ruler's side, holding a literary position.
However, you must serve a young sovereign."
Déyù was astonished upon hearing this,
and his countenance changed drastically.
The hermit seemed to regret his slip of the tongue,
and rose from his seat, asking to leave.
Déyù asked:
"Why must I serve a young sovereign?"
He replied:
"You and the young sovereign are bound by karma spanning generations,
which is why I mentioned it."
That autumn, Déyù entered court service.
By the following January,
Emperor Mùzōng ascended the throne,
and summoned Déyù into the imperial gardens.
When he became
Originally, the character "wéi" was missing,
added based on the Ming dynasty manuscript copy
Vice Censor-in-Chief,
a hermit from Mǐnzhōng knocked on his door, requesting an audience.
Déyù invited him to sit and spoke with him. The hermit said:
"The current situation will not last long.
If you do not leave early,
by winter, you will certainly become chancellor,
and disaster will befall you.
If you urgently request an assignment outside the capital,
the one who replaces you will suffer the calamity.
Ten years from now,
you will ultimately become chancellor,
entering from the west."
That autumn, Déyù was appointed to govern Wúmén.
After a year, he returned for an audience,
and soon after, he was granted military authority over Nányàn.
In late autumn,
a fellow townsman named Yú Shēng brought a Dàoyìst from Yèjùn.
As soon as he ascended the guest steps,
before he could be offered a seat,
he said to Déyù:
"You will receive authority over the southwestern region.
Before the full moon in early winter,
the tally and insignia will arrive."
All three predictions matched the events,
with no discrepancy in the timing.
From the time he served in the Imperial Secretariat, it took exactly ten years for him to become chancellor,
entering from Western Shǔ.
The one who replaced Déyù as Censor-in-Chief
was soon also exiled.
Only when he was transferred again to the southern regions,
there was no foreknowing scholar
who spoke of it to Déyù.
Could it be that disasters cannot be foretold in advance,
being secrets of the divine way,
not to be heard beforehand?
From "The Record of Poverty and Sorrow"
Sòng Shīrú
Sòng Shīrú
repeatedly held minor positions in the Salt and Iron Commission,
and could foretell auspicious and inauspicious events.
Wáng Fán, the Grand Commandant of Huáinán, held him in high regard.
At that time, in Huáinán, there was a monk named Cháng Jiān
who also accurately predicted events.
Once, Cháng Jiān was discussing the Dào in the Attendants' Office,
when Shīrú entered afterward.
Cháng Jiān looked down on him greatly,
showing him slight disrespect.
Shīrú, displeased, said:
"The reverend monk faces a great calamity,
which will occur at the year's end."
Cháng Jiān glared and said:
"What matter is this?
Do not try to frighten me.
I can still tell east from west."
Shīrú said:
"The reverend monk's calamity is imminent.
Just remember not to leave the city for several days at the end of the year,
and do not ride a fine horse."
Cháng Jiān left in a rage.
Several months later,
Attendant Censor Zhèng bought a new fine horse,
exceptionally strong and swift,
and went to fetch Cháng Jiān.
Cháng Jiān said:
"This is not the fine horse that Sòng Shīrú spoke of,
so I shall ride it."
Before they had traveled a few li,
while descending a bridge,
someone carrying a large bundle of bamboo
threw it to the ground,
right in front of the horse.
The horse bolted into a narrow alley.
Cháng Jiān was dragged along the ground,
with his foot caught in the stirrup.
After several li,
people finally rescued him.
His head was gashed,
and blood flowed all over his body.
For the time it takes to eat a meal, he was unconscious,
and was carried back to the temple on a bed.
The Grand Commandant and the attendants summoned Master Sòng, asking:
"Can he avoid further harm?"
He said:
"In the bamboo grove of that courtyard,
there is something that has not yet left.
He must be cautious of open, empty places."
Cháng Jiān drank medicinal wine
and consumed too much rehmannia root,
causing abdominal illness.
He got up at night to use the latrine.
His disciples were unaware,
and he was pushed by a black object,
falling into the latrine.
He cried out for a long time
before his disciples came.
From the neck down,
he was completely soiled.
As it was bitterly cold at the time,
he was washed with freezing water,
and soon lost consciousness again.
Grand Commandant Wáng and the attendants quickly summoned Master Sòng,
finding this extremely strange.
"Can he avoid harm now?"
He said:
"Only if a monk living nearby dies suddenly
will he be spared."
Lord Wáng specifically sent someone to watch for this.
An old monk in the western chamber fell ill and died.
Lord Wáng said:
"He is spared now."
Master Sòng said:
"It must be a strong and healthy person without illness.
This one does not count."
A few days later,
a young monk was shaving his head,
cut himself with the blade, caught wind,
fell ill, and died.
Master Sòng said:
"Now there will be no further trouble."
Lord Wáng treated him with even greater courtesy,
and Cháng Jiān became close friends with Master Sòng.
From "The Forgotten History"
The Mad Scholar of Huìchāng
During the Huìchāng and Kāichéng eras,
a pillar in the Hányuán Hall needed replacement.
The emperor ordered the Right Army to procure and craft it,
selecting timber that met the required dimensions.
The military office assigned the task to the Zhōuzhì mountain area,
but for a full year, no suitable timber was found.
A heavy reward was offered.
A worker, greedy for the reward,
ventured deep into the wilderness, scaling perilous cliffs,
where no human footprints reached,
and fierce beasts roamed in packs.
He encountered a giant tree,
with a diameter of nearly ten feet,
and a length of over a hundred feet,
perfectly meeting the selection criteria.
After felling it,
they waited until the summer floods receded,
and only then, reaching the valley mouth,
hundreds of laborers hauled and dragged it,
finally bringing it to a level ground.
Both armies celebrated and reported the success to the emperor.
While the clean timber awaited the officials to choose an auspicious day,
suddenly, a wild-looking scholar,
appearing like a mystic,
circled the timber, sighing and lamenting,
muttering loudly and fiercely.
The guards scolded him,
intending to tie him up.
The man showed no fear at all.
Shortly after,
the supervisor seized him
and reported to the
army commander,
astonishing everyone inside and out.
They listened to what he said:
"You must saw it in the middle,
and at two feet, you will see proof."
When they sawed to one foot eight inches,
they were shocked to see a deep red color,
and at two inches, blood flowed.
They urgently ordered hundreds of men to push and drag it into the Wèi River to drift downstream.
The man said:
"Deep mountains and vast marshes
truly give birth to dragons and snakes.
Inside this timber is a giant serpent.
In another ten years,
it would have emerged from the treetop and left.
I have never heard of one being nurtured within.
If used as a hall pillar,
ten years later,
it would certainly carry this hall away to another kingdom.
Alas, how terrifying!"
After speaking,
he vanished,
and the man was nowhere to be found.
From "Records of Zhītián."
Táng Qìng
Táng Qìng, the Vice Censor-in-Chief of Shòuzhōu, was staying in the capital.
By chance, he hired a monthly laborer
who was extremely diligent and conscientious,
and never spoke of money.
At the beginning of winter, he was exposed, lying in the snow.
Táng, returning from outside,
saw him lying in the snow,
called him to rise,
and though the snow was several inches thick,
he showed no sign of cold,
and conversed with Táng.
Táng found this deeply strange.
Later, Táng was appointed as the Salt Commissioner,
and while passing through Hézhōng,
the laborer bid farewell to return home.
Táng said:
"You have been extremely diligent.
I am about to receive a generous salary,
and I can repay you."
The laborer earnestly requested to leave,
but Táng firmly insisted he stay, refusing to let him go.
When they reached Pǔjīn,
the laborer got drunk,
and got into a fight with someone.
The military governor's orders were strict,
and he was sentenced to twenty lashes on the back.
Táng tried but failed to save him from punishment.
Feeling disheartened, he prepared to depart,
and generously provided wine and meat.
Just as he left the city, the laborer arrived.
Táng said:
"How did you manage to come?"
He replied:
"I came to bid farewell to the Vice Censor-in-Chief."
Táng asked him to bare his back to inspect it.
There were no wounds at all,
to Táng's great astonishment.
The laborer then spoke of the incident of lying in the snow.
Táng dismounted and said to him:
"The reason I did not want to pass through Hézhōng
was to avoid this retribution.
Now it has been repaid,
I bid farewell to the Vice Censor-in-Chief and leave."
He did not accept the money or silk offered,
placed them on the ground,
bowed twice, and vanished.
From "Unofficial Histories."
Lú Jūn
When Chancellor Lú Jūn first passed the imperial examination,
he was quite strapped for
daily expenses.
Suddenly, a servant appeared,
willing to work for monthly wages.
His clothing was clean and bright,
and he was diligent and capable, unlike ordinary servants.
Seeing Lú's poverty,
he often provided financial assistance.
As the time for the
banquet approached,
Lú had not yet gathered the funds,
and his distress showed on his face.
The servant then asked what was wrong,
and Lú told him the truth.
The servant replied:
"This is a trivial matter.
Young master, you may give the orders.
What should be arranged first?"
Lú initially doubted his words,
but decided to test him,
and deceitfully ordered:
"If you have the skill,
I will host the banquet.
First, I need a large mansion
as the venue for the banquet.
We can plan the rest later."
The servant assented and left,
returning in a moment.
He reported to Lú:
"I have already rented a mansion.
Please, young master, come and inspect it."
The next day,
Lú reluctantly went to see it,
and found vermilion gates and a grand mansion,
comparable to the imperial palace.
Lú could not help but feel delighted.
He added:
"The banquet venue must be grand and proper,
and this is especially difficult to arrange."
The servant replied:
"Just choose a day and announce it.
As for the arrangements,
I will take full charge."
Lú began to worry that this was improper,
and questioned him repeatedly,
but the servant only smiled without answering.
Lú suspected he might be an extraordinary person,
and did not press further with his suspicions.
On the day of the banquet,
Lú arrived at the mansion,
and saw curtains, canopies, cushions, and carpets,
unmatched in splendor and brilliance.
Additionally, the pine trees, bamboo, flowers, and plants were all exquisite.
All of Lú's gathered funds were spent,
and from then on, among the ministers and nobles, none failed to marvel and praise.
The next morning,
the servant requested leave to return all the borrowed items,
and with that, he left and never returned.
Ten days after he left,
Lú, curious about the matter,
hurried to the old site to visit.
The flowers and bamboo from before
were completely gone,
leaving only crumbling walls and ruined beams.
Commentators believed that Lú's benevolence moved the spirits,
who thus helped create a spring's splendor for him,
and achieved a lifelong honor.
From "Collected Sayings."
Zhào Zhīwēi
The Daoist priest Zhào Zhīwēi of Jiǔhuá Mountain was the teacher of Huángfǔ Xuánzhēn.
From a young age, he harbored lofty ambitions that reached the clouds.
He entered this mountain,
built a hut in front of Fènghuáng Ridge,
recited Daoist scriptures,
cultivated his will in secluded silence,
wore garments of orchids,
and sustained himself with pine and cypress.
After several decades,
Zhào attained the profound mystery of Xuánpìn.
Because of this, curious scholars
often followed him.
Xuánzhēn, having performed the rites of a disciple,
served diligently and respectfully
for fifteen years as well.
In the Xīnmǎo year of the Xiántōng era,
Zhīwēi, needing Western-region herbs for alchemical refinement in the mountains,
sent Xuánzhēn to the capital,
where he lodged in the Shàngqīng Hall of the Yùzhī Temple.
Huángfǔ Méi was then residing at his estate in Lánlíng Ward,
and they met daily.
Thus, he inquired about Master Zhào's endeavors.
Xuánzhēn said:
"Since my teacher attained the Way,
no one has seen a lazy expression on his face.
He often said:
'The arts of dividing cups and congealing mist,
the methods of transforming bamboo and fishing for bream—
I mastered them long ago,
but I consider it shameful to practice them.'
Last year during the Mid-Autumn Festival,
from the new moon, continuous rain poured down
until the night of the full moon.
Xuánzhēn said to his fellow disciples:
'What a pity that such a fine night is marred by bitter rain.'
As he spoke,
Master Zhào suddenly ordered an attendant boy:
'Prepare wine and fruits.'
He then summoned all the disciples and said:
'Can we ascend Tiānzhù Peak to enjoy the moon?'
The disciples, though they assented,
secretly discussed that with such dense clouds and pouring rain,
if they indeed went,
they would likely get their scarves soaked and their clogs broken.
A short while later,
Master Zhào, leaning on his staff, went out,
and the disciples followed in his steps.
Once they pushed open the bramble gate,
the vast sky was clear and bright,
the bright moon shone like day.
Grasping vines and pulling on slender bamboos,
they reached the peak's summit.
Master Zhào sat upon a leopard-skin mat,
while the disciples, seated on fragrant grass, arranged themselves in attendance.
Soon, he raised a cup of wine
and recited several of Guō Jǐngchún's "Roaming Immortal" poems.
Some disciples whistled pure notes, others paced in the void, and some played the zither,
until the cold toad (the moon) hid behind distant peaks,
and they returned to the mountain lodge.
After each had gone to his bed,
the mournful wind and flying rain returned just as before.
Only then did everyone admire his wondrous power.
Xuánzhēn was unmatched at the game of Go,
and he also grasped the essential mysteries of alchemy.
In the spring, third month of the Rénchén year, he returned to Jiǔhuá,
and afterwards never came again to the capital or Luòyáng.
From "Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú."
Jī Zhúzi
Jī Zhúzi did not speak his name,
nor was it known where he was from.
He appeared to be over thirty years old.
In the wine shops of Chéngdū,
he would hold two bamboo sections in his hands and strike them together,
producing a clanging, resonant sound
that was pleasant to hear.
He sang in response to it,
begging from people.
His lyrics and meaning all perfectly accorded with the intent of the Way.
When he obtained money, he mostly drank wine.
No one truly knew him.
He continued like this for over ten years.
One day,
he went himself to the house of the son of the Huáng family, who sold raw medicine at the East Market.
Calmly, he said:
"I have known for some time
that you, Elder, are fond of the Way
and moreover possess much righteous spirit.
Now I wish to entrust my sincere final wish to you.
May I?"
The son of the Huáng family said:
"If you have a matter,
please just speak of it."
Jī Zhúzi said:
"I am a beggar.
I dwell beneath the Qīlǐtíng Bridge outside the North Gate.
Now I am gravely ill,
and fear I may not recover.
If I pass away,
I dare hope you will specially cremate me.
Here I bring two strings of cash myself,
to cover the cost of firewood.
Take care not to touch my heart and liver.
This is my request.
Hidden virtue will surely be repaid."
He then left his money.
The Huáng son did not wish to take it,
but he firmly left it and departed.
The next day, the Huáng son went to the bridge.
Sure enough, he saw Jī Zhúzi lying upon reeds.
Seeing the Huáng son come,
he was pleased and grateful.
Slowly, he said:
"My illness is beyond recovery."
He also gave the Huáng son two catties of gold,
and said again:
"As I said yesterday, it would be fortunate if no one touches my heart and liver.
Take care, and now I bid farewell."
Having spoken, he passed away.
The Huáng son, also moved to pity, shed tears
and sighed for a long time.
He then had people change his clothes,
prepare a coffin for burial,
and take him out to the wilds.
They piled up firewood and charcoal,
made offerings, and burned him.
Immediately, they heard an extraordinary, rich fragrance
and forest birds calling.
By evening,
only his heart remained,
ultimately unburned to ashes.
Moreover, it had grown as large as a bushel measure.
The Huáng son collected it and returned to the city.
He quickly told people to poke it with a staff.
Suddenly, they heard a crackling explosion,
its sound like thunder,
startling both people and horses.
In a moment,
a figure over a foot tall
emerged from the smoke and flames—
it was Jī Zhúzi.
Striking his bamboo in hand,
he produced a clear, ringing sound.
He soared upward, disappearing into the distance.
The Huáng son repented, made obeisance,
and everyone marveled at the wonder.
Alas!
Was it not because his heart was not touched
that he returned to the human world?
If his heart had been touched,
could he have then ascended as a guest of heaven?
Or did he wish to manifest his metamorphosis to the Huáng son?
Only then did they realize that Chéngdū is a place where immortals gather.
As for those like Jī Zhúzi,
they are also many.
In general, one must not treat lightly those scholars who are poor, lowly, or beggars.
From "Yěrén Xiánhuà."
Zhāng Jùn
When Huáng Cháo invaded the capital,
Emperor Xīzong fled to Shǔ.
Zhāng Jùn was then an unknown commoner without rank,
living at his estate in Yǒnglè, Hézhōng.
In the village was a Daoist,
sometimes wearing hempen clothes,
sometimes a feathered cape,
and not one to be casually familiar with.
One day, as Zhāng was walking on a village path,
someone called from behind:
"Zhāng Thirty-Fourth Young Master,
before the imperial carriage awaits your defeat of the rebels."
Turning to look,
it was this Daoist.
Jùn said:
"I am but a commoner.
By what means could I defeat rebels?"
The Daoist urged him to go to Shǔ.
At the time, Jùn's mother was ill,
so he did not proceed south.
The Daoist then gave him two pellets of elixir, saying:
"Taking these will ensure ten years free from ailment."
Jùn obtained the medicine and offered it to his parent;
her illness was cured.
Later, he rose to become a chief minister.
The Daoist was never seen again.
The prophecy about defeating rebels—
how accurately it was fulfilled!
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Jīnzhōu Daoist
Jīntǒng Shuǐ is in Jīnzhōu.
In the year when the rebel Huáng Cháo invaded the capital,
there was a certain Cuī who served as the prefect of Ānkāng.
The imperial carriage had already fled to Mín'é.
Only Jīnzhōu, being remote,
remained peaceful and undisturbed.
Suddenly, a Daoist priest came to see Cuī and said:
"Now that the Central Plains are in turmoil,
the imperial carriage wanders in exile,
the ancestral temples lie in ruins,
overgrown with weeds,
does Your Excellency have no intention of exterminating the rebels?"
Cuī replied:
"When Mount Tài has already collapsed,
can a single piece of timber prop it up?"
The visitor said:
"Not so.
What I mean by extermination
does not necessarily require clashing swords and spears,
or battling fiercely across the plains."
Cuī asked:
"What, then, do you propose?"
The visitor said:
"Within Your Excellency's jurisdiction, there is a Huángcháo Gǔ and a Jīntǒng Shuǐ.
Are you aware of them?"
Cuī said:
"I am not.
Let me inquire among the people of the prefecture."
The local people said:
"They exist."
The visitor said:
"The rebel Huáng Cháo received his life-force from this place.
I ask Your Excellency to dispatch laborers,
carrying baskets and spades,
to go with me and dig there.
We are sure to find something."
They went several hundred *li* from the prefecture,
and deep in the mountains, there indeed was a place with that name.
The visitor then ordered them to trace the source and dig it up,
and also to cut through the mountain ridge,
exhausting the spring's source.
In the spring source, there was a cave,
and in the cave was a yellow-waisted man.
Once cornered,
he threw himself down,
cried out, and died.
From the cave, they also retrieved a precious sword.
The visitor then said:
"I have now broken the rebel's power for the empire."
Cuī then sent the sword and the yellow-waisted man westward to the court.
Before the sharpness of the sword could be fully demonstrated,
news arrived that the Huáng Cháo rebellion had been pacified,
and the imperial carriage had returned to the capital.
From *Wángshì Jiànwén Lù*.
Lǐ Shēng
At the end of the Zhōnghé era.
A *míngjīng* candidate named Lǐ Shēng went to Cháng'ān to take the imperial examinations.
On the way, he met a Daoist priest traveling with him, and they lodged together.
After several days,
they found their conversation and thoughts agreeable.
Upon entering the pass, they parted ways.
The topic of alchemy came up.
The Daoist priest said:
"The art of transmutation
is a shallow technique among immortals.
But people in the world are mostly greedy,
intending to use it to satisfy their extravagance,
so the Daoist path keeps it secret.
The supreme Dao is not complicated;
immortal recipes are simple and easy.
Nowadays, some people prize the ingredients too highly,
or make the process difficult—
these are all wrong.
I observe that your nature is calm and you have few desires,
and you seem teachable.
Now I will give you a recipe,
intended only to relieve poverty and destitution.
If you can subsequently avoid official service,
you will also not lack for food and clothing.
If you obtain an official salary,
then do not practice it again.
To practice it then would be greed,
which the immortal path does not permit."
He then wrote out the recipe by hand, gave it to him, and they parted.
The recipe used only a few common medicinal herbs.
Whenever he encountered poverty or destitution,
he would follow the recipe to make it,
and it never failed.
Later, he passed the examinations,
and served as an official in various prefectures and counties.
He occasionally practiced it,
but the yields became increasingly smaller.
When he became the magistrate of Nánchāng,
he tried again,
but it completely failed.
His nephew, Zhìxiū, became a Buddhist monk.
Lǐ gave him several pills.
Later, Zhìxiū traveled to Zhōnglí,
and stayed at the home of a medicine seller.
He transmuted silver, obtaining twenty taels,
and used it to buy clothes.
At that time, Liú Rénguǐ was the prefect,
and was fond of such arts.
Zhìxiū was reported by someone,
but he escaped and avoided capture.
From *Jīshén Lù*.
Magistrate Xú
There was a Magistrate Xú of Jīnxiāng,
a recluse who possessed Daoist arts,
unfathomable to others.
In Hénán, there was Liú Chóngyuǎn,
a younger cousin of Liú Chóngguī.
He had a sister who was a Buddhist nun,
residing in Chǔzhōu.
A visiting nun often stayed with her.
Suddenly, this visiting nun fell ill with consumption,
grew extremely emaciated, and was near death.
Her elder sister came to visit her.
Everyone saw a vapor like flying insects emerge from the sick nun's body,
enter the elder sister's clothing,
and then disappear.
The sick nun died,
and the elder sister also fell ill.
Soon, everyone in Liú's convent fell ill,
and the sick invariably died.
The Liú family then sent a letter to Chóngyuǎn, asking him to seek help from Magistrate Xú.
Xú said:
"You have another residence in Jīnlíng.
Obtain one bolt of Jīnlíng silk,
and I will cure it for you."
They did as told and sent the silk.
The next day,
Liú's sister dreamed of a Daoist priest holding a tablet who came to her,
and with the tablet, he stroked her entire body.
A white vapor rose from her body like steam from cooking.
When she awoke,
she felt light and refreshed and could eat,
unlike her usual condition.
Shortly after,
Xú sealed the silk and sent it back, saying:
"Place the silk beneath your mat,
and sleep on it, and you will recover."
She did as instructed and was cured.
Later, looking at the silk,
she saw painted on it a Daoist priest holding a tablet,
exactly like the one in her dream.
From *Jīshén Lù*.
The Old Woman of the Huàyīn Inn
Yáng Yànbó was a native of Xīngàn in Lúlíng.
He passed the imperial examinations as a child prodigy.
In the xīnyǒu year of the Tiānfù era (901 CE),
he traveled to the capital to participate in the official selection process.
Upon reaching Huàyīn,
he lodged at an inn.
At that time, the capital was beset by many troubles,
and he had no relatives or acquaintances in the court.
The selection process could not proceed as scheduled,
which left him feeling deeply worried and depressed.
It so happened that a clerk from the Yùzhāng administrative office, surnamed Yáng,
an old acquaintance from his hometown,
was staying at the same inn.
This clerk advised him, saying:
"All travelers who come here
invariably pray to the Golden Heaven deity.
They always receive a response in their dreams.
Even if one has no dream,
the old woman who runs this inn can also foretell future events.
If you can obtain a single word from her,
that would suffice."
Yànbó therefore stayed an extra day
and performed a sincere and focused ritual sacrifice.
That night, however, he ultimately had no dream.
At dawn,
the innkeeper woman was busy greeting and seeing off other guests,
and again said nothing to him.
Yànbó grew even more disheartened.
As he was about to depart,
he then lost the shoes he was wearing.
He scolded his servant boy quite loudly about it.
After he had set out on the road,
the old woman came running after him, calling out:
"Young man, why are you making such a commotion?"
Yànbó then explained the whole matter to her.
The old woman said:
"Ah!
This is precisely the deity's message to you.
To lose one's shoes just as one is about to journey
means that none of your affairs will go smoothly.
And it is not merely this.
The capital will experience turmoil,
and it will likely be beyond recovery.
You, sir, will experience a hundred hardships,
but have no worry.
Your official rank and emolument lie in the Jiānghuái region.
Your office will reach that of Vice Director of the Chancellery."
Yànbó pondered this,
thinking, "How could there be a Vice Director of the Chancellery in Jiānghuái?"
He then proceeded to Cháng'ān.
It happened that the imperial carriage had just fled west,
and he followed it to Qílǒng.
The Liáng rebels besieged the city for three years,
during which Yànbó endured extreme hardship and toil.
After the imperial carriage departed the city,
Yànbó escaped and returned to Jízhōu.
The prefect, Péng Zhēn, treated him generously,
and he successively served as acting magistrate of several districts.
After the pseudo-Wú state pacified Jiāngxī,
he was again selected for office.
He rose at court to the position of Vice Minister of Revenue.
It happened that an imperial ceremony was held to appoint the Prince of Qí,
and Yànbó acted as Vice Director of the Chancellery for the proceedings.
After receiving the appointment,
he recalled the old innkeeper woman's words
and became greatly displeased.
Within a few months, he died.
From "Records of Divinities Investigated".
Lǐ Kè
Lǐ Kè did not speak his name.
He often wore a straw rain cape and bamboo hat,
carrying a cloth bag.
He sold rat poison in the city,
using a wooden rat as his sign.
If someone came to buy poison,
he would say:
"This not only kills rats,
it can also cure many human illnesses.
Just take it with your food,
and you will be cured."
People disliked that it was rat poison,
so few ever took it as medicine.
There was a commoner named Zhāng Zàn,
who made his living selling books.
His father was over seventy years old
and had long suffered from a wind-stroke illness.
One day, rats gnawed several volumes of his texts,
which enraged Zàn.
He bought the poison intending to feed it to the rats.
Before Zàn went to sleep,
he saw several large rats emerge under the lamplight.
They fought over eating the poison,
and Zàn thought they would certainly be poisoned.
Suddenly, he saw them all grow wings
and fly out the door.
Zàn found this profoundly strange.
He then went to Lǐ Kè and told him about it.
Lǐ Kè said:
"They probably weren't rats.
Don't speak nonsense."
Zàn asked for more poison,
but Lǐ Kè said it was all gone.
From then on, Lǐ Kè disappeared.
Zàn's father took the leftover poison the rats had eaten
and immediately felt his limbs could bend and stretch again.
He got out of bed and walked as in the old days.
From "Idle Talk of a Rustic".
The Prince of Jiā of the Former Shǔ, formerly,
when he was a prince
(Míng manuscript copy reads "imperial kinsman and garrison commander")
and garrison commander,
while managing his official residence
("Shǔ" originally written as "zhì";
corrected according to the Míng manuscript copy),
obtained an iron mirror.
Below it were twelve seal-script characters
(According to the seal script, there are thirteen characters;
the "two" should be the character "three")
that no one could decipher.
He ordered a craftsman to polish it,
and its shine could reflect objects clearly.
He hung it on a terrace.
It was visible for a hundred lǐ around.
It also reflected someone in the marketplace wielding a sword and spear and selling medicine.
He then summoned and questioned this person.
The man said:
"I only sell medicine.
I originally do not wield swords or spears."
The Prince of Jiā said:
"I have an iron mirror,
and it reflected you."
The medicine seller then stopped concealing it
and asked to see the mirror.
He slit his own belly with his arm,
placed the mirror inside his belly,
and, without his feet touching the ground,
gracefully ascended into the sky and departed.
In the end, no one knew where he was from.
The seal script characters are listed as follows
(seal characters omitted).
From "Compiled Affairs of Yùxī".
Liú Chùshì
Zhāng Yì was in Luòyáng,
when he met a retired scholar named Liú,
who possessed rather extraordinary arts.
Yì often associated with him.
Liú had once sold silver to a man in the market,
who owed him the payment.
Liú took Yì along to demand it,
but the market man not only refused to pay,
he also cursed Liú vehemently.
Liú returned
and said to Yì:
"That foolish man is so unreasonable;
I must give him a small punishment.
Otherwise,
he will surely incur severe reprimand from the local earth spirits."
When night fell,
they extinguished the candle and went to bed.
Liú placed burning charcoal before his bed to heat some medicine.
Yì had not yet fallen deeply asleep
when he saw a man in the darkness
approach the brazier and blow on the fire.
In the firelight, he recognized his face—
it was the market man from earlier.
By dawn, he was gone.
Yì later inquired
and asked the market man,
who said:
"One night I dreamed someone summoned me away,
forcing me to blow on a fire.
I was almost out of breath;
when I awoke,
my lips were swollen and I was breathless.
It took ten days to recover."
Liú was always treated with respect by Zhāng Quányì, the Governor of Hénán.
Once, while dining with Emperor Tàizǔ of the Liáng dynasty,
the emperor craved sliced raw fish.
Quányì said:
"I have a guest
who can procure it instantly."
He immediately summoned Liú.
Liú had them dig a small pit,
filled it with water,
and fished for a long while,
soon catching several fish.
Emperor Tàizǔ flew into a rage, saying:
"This is extreme sorcery and deceit!"
He immediately ordered Liú beaten twenty strokes on the back,
shackled, and imprisoned.
The next day, he was to be executed,
but that night he escaped and vanished.
Liú had a friend who was the magistrate of Dēngfēng County.
That day, Liú arrived at the county
and said to the magistrate:
"I am in trouble
and must depart from here."
He then left,
and no one knew where he went.
From "Records of Spirits"
Zhāng Wǔ
Zhāng Wǔ
was initially a deputy commander of a garrison on the Lújiāng road.
He was quite dedicated to aiding travelers.
Once, an old monk passed by his post.
Wǔ said to him:
"Master, you are old,
and the next inn is still far.
Would you stay in my humble dwelling tonight?"
The monk gladly agreed.
The garrison commander heard of this and angrily said:
"Now that north and south are at war,
spies are as numerous as trees in a forest.
Who knows who this monk really is?
How dare you host him!"
The monk then asked to leave.
But Wǔ said:
"I have already invited you, Master.
It is getting late,
just stay without worry."
Wǔ had only one bed in his room,
which he offered to the monk,
while he himself slept on the floor.
He personally prepared
all washing necessities.
He rose several times during the night to check on him.
By the fifth watch,
the monk got up and sighed,
saying to Wǔ:
"For a young man to be like this!
I have some medicine;
I give you ten pills.
Take one each New Year's Day,
and it can extend your life by ten years.
Take good care of yourself."
He bid farewell and left,
vanishing suddenly outside the door.
Wǔ is now the deputy military training commissioner of Chángzhōu.
Those who know him calculate that he is already a hundred years old,
though he always claims to be seventy,
and remains as agile and healthy as ever.
From "Records of Spirits"
Máoshān Dàoshi
A Máoshān dàoshi named Chén,
in the year Rénzǐ, traveled to Hǎilíng
and lodged at an inn.
Snow was falling heavily,
and a fellow lodger,
wearing only thin hempen clothes,
wished to share a bed with him.
Chén, however, disliked his dirtiness and shabbiness,
so he said:
"With such cold and snow,
how will you pass the night?"
The man replied:
"Just go to sleep,
do not worry about me."
After both had retired,
Chén secretly watched him.
He saw the man take several triangular shards of broken tile from his bosom,
strung them on a chain,
and placed them over the lamp to heat.
