Soon they glowed red-hot,
warming the entire room,
so that Chén had to remove his clothes and blankets to sleep.
Before dawn, the man departed,
and was never seen again.
From "Records of Spirits"
The Lodger
At an inn in Dàliáng, there was a lodger
whose origins were unknown.
He regularly sold a hundred soap-pod stems in the market;
the pods were unusually large and plump,
different from ordinary ones.
Each day, after earning a hundred coins,
he would drink and then leave.
A curious man, sensing he was no ordinary person,
shared a room with him.
At night,
he peeped through a hole in the wall.
He saw the lodger carefully hoeing and tilling a patch of ground several feet in front of his bed,
then planting several soap-pod seeds.
They sprouted almost immediately.
Watching from time to time,
he saw them grow rapidly.
By dawn, they were already bearing ripe pods.
The lodger then harvested them himself,
cut down the plants,
chopped them up, and burned them.
At daybreak, he took the pods and left.
From then on, he never returned,
and no one knew where he went.
From "Records of Spirits"
The Musician's Son
A musician from the Imperial Music Bureau had a son over ten years old,
who was constantly ill,
especially sallow and emaciated.
One day, he met a dàoshi on the road,
who said to him:
"Your illness is a food-congealing disorder;
I can cure it."
He then took several pills from his sleeve and made the boy swallow them.
Afterward, looking into his sleeve, he said:
"Ah,
a mistake.
These are fasting pills.
From now on, you will not need to eat.
But your illness will also be cured.
If you must eat,
try taking a little wood ear mushroom.
Another day, I will bring you the medicine for your food-congealing disorder."
He then left.
Within a month or two, the boy recovered.
His illness was cured.
But his parents constantly worried about his not eating,
and eventually forced him to take wood ear mushrooms,
after which he resumed eating normally.
Later, he regretted it, saying:
"I took immortal medicine without realizing it.
The dàoshi promised to bring me more medicine;
will I ever see him again?"
He told his parents
and asked to travel to all famous mountains
to seek the dàoshi.
His mother refused,
but his father agreed, saying:
"If he had not recovered,
he would be dead by now.
Since his resolve is so firm,
perhaps he has a destiny."
So they let him go,
and now no one knows where he is.
From "Records of Spirits"
Jiǎng Shùnqīng
Jiǎng Shùnqīng, a land survey official of Guāngzhōu, was traveling through the mountains when
he saw a man picking one or two crabapples.
The man gave them to him to eat,
and after eating them, he no longer felt hungry.
His family believed he had eaten ghost food,
and if left untreated, he would fall ill.
They urgently sought medical treatment,
but he could not be cured.
Later, they heard of an old man in Shòuchūn who was skilled in medicine,
so they went to visit him.
After traveling for one day,
they stayed at an inn,
where an old man asked about his ailment,
and they told him everything.
The old man said:
"I can cure him,
there is no need to travel far."
He took out a dose of medicine, about a square inch in size, and gave it to him to take.
The two crabapples then appeared as if they were fresh.
The old man collected them and left,
and Shùnqīng's appetite returned to normal.
After returning home,
they went to visit him again another day.
However, the inn and the old man
were nowhere to be seen.
From "Jīshén Lù".
Huáng Wànyòu
Huáng Wànyòu cultivated the Way in the uninhabited regions of Qiánnán,
and had been there for generations.
Every twenty or thirty years, he would come out to Chéngdū to sell medicine,
and his predictions of people's misfortunes were always remarkably accurate.
The King of Shǔ, Wáng Jiàn, welcomed him into the palace
and treated him with the utmost respect.
When asked about his diet and practices,
he kept them secret and did not speak of them.
He said:
"I am not an immortal,
nor am I one who consumes elixirs.
I merely cultivate my spirit and nurture my vital energy,
act with benevolence,
and minimize my faults, that is all."
When asked about his age,
he replied:
"I only remember the year when the Marquis of Yèláng became King of Shǔ,
and the year when Cáncóng Shì established his capital at Pí,
at which time I was invited to come out.
As for the rest, the sun and moon raced across the sky,
flowers bloomed and trees shed their leaves,
and I truly cannot remember the cycles of years."
Suddenly one day,
he gazed south toward Jiāzhōu and said:
"The land of Qiánwéi,
how fiercely it burns!
Please send someone to go there."
Following his words,
an envoy was sent to Jiāzhōu,
only to find the markets and streets had already been reduced to rubble.
Later, he firmly insisted on returning to the mountains.
Wáng Jiàn tearfully tried to keep him but could not make him stay.
When asked about future events,
he said nothing.
After he left,
on the wall of his residence, an inscription was found that read:
"Do not let the green pig's foot be stirred,
for once stirred, the flames will rage uncontrollably.
The fierce beast does not want both ends yellow,
for when yellow comes, the world will weep."
Even the wise could not fully understand it.
In the year Yǐhài,
Wáng Jiàn raised an army and marched east to capture various prefectures such as Qín and Fèng.
Just as news of victory arrived,
a fire broke out in the palace,
and all the treasures and stored valuables
were reduced to ashes.
Only then did they realize that the year Yǐhài
corresponded to the green pig,
marking the time of the conflagration.
Three years later,
in the year Wùyín, which belongs to earth, Wáng Jiàn passed away.
They then understood that yín corresponds to the fierce beast,
and both the heavenly stem and the earthly branch's element were earth,
earth being yellow in color,
hence the phrase "the fierce beast both ends yellow."
These words were accurate to the slightest detail.
From "Lùyì Jì".
The Ming dynasty manuscript version attributes it to "Yěrén Xiánhuà".
Rén Sānláng
Wáng Zī, an official of Bīnyòu in Fèngzhōu,
at the time served as a strategist in the administration of the Chancellor Mǎn Cún,
and was on the closest terms among the advisors.
There was a guest named Rén Sānláng there,
whom all the officials in the administration knew,
but he was particularly close to Wáng.
Not long after,
he suddenly said to Wáng:
"If you encounter some minor disappointment,
it will actually be a blessing for you."
Another month passed,
and Wáng suddenly fell out of favor with his lord,
so he feigned illness for over a hundred days.
His lord paid him no mind,
and there was no news from him.
Rén still visited from time to time.
One day, he said to Wáng:
"This place is about to suffer a disaster.
The large trees on the official streets have withered on their own.
The matter is pressing.
When the leaves fall,
the event will occur.
Quickly seek medical treatment
to escape this calamity." Wáng, believing his lord's anger had not yet subsided,
deeply felt it was not possible.
Rén said:
"Just submit three memorials,
and there will surely be instructions."
Following his advice,
within a few days, Wáng submitted three memorials,
requesting to seek medical treatment in the Guānlǒng region.
Indeed, someone was sent to convey the lord's encouragement,
and he was promptly given funds and silks according to the custom for leaving the administration,
much more generous than usual.
Wáng then went to express his gratitude,
was invited to stay for a banquet,
and was also given colorful silks, brocades, and embroideries for his family.
Within ten days,
he was urged to depart northward.
Chancellor Mǎn held a farewell banquet for him outside the city.
At the moment of parting,
there were only about two hundred people.
After five or six days, he rented a residence in Wúshān County,
and after another ten days, he reached Fèngzhōu.
People said a military mutiny had already occurred,
and Lord Mǎn had returned to Bāozhōng.
All his colleagues in the administration had died in the disaster,
but Wáng alone escaped the calamity.
Later that year, in a wine shop at the northwest corner of Kāihuà Lane in Cháng'ān,
he saw Master Rén again.
He asked where he was staying,
and when he went to visit him again,
he was nowhere to be found.
From "Lùyì Jì".
Huáng Qí
Huáng Qí
was a minor officer in Shǔ.
He had long been fond of the Way,
and for years had performed secret virtuous deeds.
At Cháotiān Ridge, he encountered an old man
with pure white beard and hair,
a face like a child's,
and skin like jade.
The old man spoke to him, saying:
"Since you are fond of the Way,
five years from now,
you will face a great calamity,
and I will surely save you.
Strive to think of virtuous deeds,
and do not abandon your previous aspirations."
Later, Huáng Qí went down the gorges,
and his boat capsized and sank.
When he reached the rapids,
it was as if someone rescued him.
He managed to reach the shore,
and when he looked,
it was the old man he had met before.
Soon, the old man disappeared.
From then on, he often saw him.
Suddenly, they met again in the market of Shífāng County,
and the old man summoned Huáng Qí to his dwelling.
They went outside the northern city wall,
walked through an alder forest,
for about two or three miles,
and arrived at his home.
The mountains, rivers, and forests
created an atmosphere of secluded beauty.
Huáng Qí stayed for one night,
and at dawn,
the old man escorted him out the door.
He found himself inside Hòuchéng Mountain,
more than seventy miles from the county.
After returning,
he also spoke of this to others.
From "Lùyì Jì".
Wáng Chùhuí
The Palace Attendant Wáng Chùhuí often received common scholars at his private residence.
One day, a Daoist priest,
with thick eyebrows and a large nose,
wearing ragged cloth clothes,
followed by a mountain youth,
who merely carried a staff and a medicine bag,
came to visit Lord Wáng.
On a bamboo leaf, he wrote in large characters: "The Daoist priest Wáng Tiāozhàng pays his respects."
Lord Wáng had always valued scholars,
so he was able to meet him,
and thus leisurely offered him wine.
Observing his conversation,
it was as refreshing as a clear breeze.
Chùhuí said:
"Your disciple aspires to a life of purity and leisure,
and wishes to establish a small Daoist temple at the foot of Qīngchéng Mountain,
to suit my leisurely nature."
The Daoist priest said:
"Not yet."
Then, he took a sword from the mountain youth,
carefully marked the earth in front of the steps, an area over a foot wide,
took two flower seeds from his bag and planted them,
ordering them to be covered with a pot.
Shortly after removing the pot,
the flowers had already sprouted,
gradually growing taller,
reaching about five feet in height,
with layers of blossoms,
two plants brilliantly lovely.
The Venerable Master said:
"This is merely to please the eye and suit one's nature;
these are the Immortal's Banner-Flower."
When offered food, he did not eat,
only drank a few cups and withdrew.
He said:
"Take care,
and be well in preserving yourself."
Having said this, he left,
and upon going out the door, no one knew where he went.
Later, Lord Wáng indeed served as military commissioner of two circuits,
before retiring from office.
Afterwards, people often obtained seeds of this flower.
From "Yěrén Xiánhuà"
Tiān Zìzài
In the market of Lìzhōu city,
there was a man,
with disheveled hair and bare feet,
wearing a short cloth jacket.
When speaking with people,
he often talked about matters of heaven.
If he encountered paper and brush,
he would gladly paint towers, figures,
holding musical instruments,
or images of clouds, dragons, phoenixes.
At night, he would stay in a temple.
People called him Tiān Zìzài.
South of the prefecture was a market,
bustling with people.
One evening, a fire broke out,
flames and smoke reaching the sky.
Tiān Zìzài, alone in the temple, said:
"The people of this place have long been wicked,
Heaven will kill them."
Then he reached into a stone basin of water in front of the steps,
and sprinkled it towards the sky.
Soon, a strange vapor emerged from the temple gate,
turning into heavy rain,
completely extinguishing the fire.
The temple keeper often told people about this,
and Tiān Zìzài then secretly departed.
The remaining residents were indeed swept away by the great fire,
and only then did they believe his earlier words had proof.
From "Yěrén Xiánhuà"
The Ear-Covering Daoist Priest
Outside the south gate of Lìzhōu,
was a place where merchants gathered for trade.
One day, a Daoist priest,
in ragged feather robes,
came among the crowd,
selling gourd seeds.
He said:
"Within a year or two,
they will be very useful.
Each plant bears only one fruit,
spreading across the ground."
He also used white earth to draw a pattern on the ground to show people,
the model was very large.
After a while, there were no buyers,
everyone said:
"A madman is not worth listening to."
The Daoist priest then covered his ears with both hands and hurried away,
saying, "Why is the sound of wind and water so loud?"
Children in the alleys,
vied to follow and mock him,
calling him the Ear-Covering Daoist Priest.
By the autumn of the following year,
the Jiālíng River waters,
flooded overnight,
sweeping away several hundred households.
As the waters spread wide,
everyone saw from afar the Daoist priest on the water,
sitting on a large gourd,
raising his hands to cover his ears,
shouting, "Why are the sounds of water and wind so loud?"
Drifting away,
no one knew where he went.
From "Yěrén Xiánhuà"
The Dragon-Holding Daoist Priest
At Báishā in Guànkǒu, there was a temple of the Lord of Mount Tài.
Every year in the third month of spring,
many people from Shǔ would go there to hold vegetarian feasts,
and even physicians and diviners from various prefectures
would also gather.
At that time, there was a man,
in tattered clothes,
with a haggard face,
who also went to the temple.
Everyone looked down on him.
As they walked along the riverbank,
everyone rested under the shade of trees,
and the poor scholar also sat on a rock.
After a while, he said to the people:
"There is a sleeping dragon in this water."
No one responded.
An old man nearby said:
"How can you see it?"
The poor scholar said:
"I can see it."
Everyone said:
"How can we see it?"
The poor scholar said:
"It's not difficult."
Then he took off his clothes and entered the water,
brought out a sleeping dragon,
quite foul-smelling,
its eyes tightly closed,
with claws, teeth, scales, and horns all complete.
Clouds and mist quickly gathered,
wind rose and waters surged.
Everyone fled in fear, bowing from afar,
calling him a sage.
He then returned the dragon to the water's depths,
put on his tattered clothes, and left.
He said to everyone:
"You all make your living as physicians and diviners,
saving people from illness and urgency,
knowing their fortunes and misfortunes,
which is close to the Way.
You must not look down upon poor and humble scholars."
Everyone could only apologize in shame.
After walking together for another ten li,
he suddenly vanished.
From "Yěrén Xiánhuà"
Hé Zhāohàn, a Vice Director of the Ministry of Revenue in the pseudo-Shǔ regime,
originally, the character "昭" was followed by the character "曰",
which has been deleted according to the Ming manuscript.
Hàn,
once served as an aide in Qiánnán.
On a leisurely day,
while strolling along a country path,
he saw an angler by the water's edge,
who said to Hàn:
"Are you not
originally "何" was written as "可",
changed according to the Ming manuscript
an aide?"
Hàn replied:
"Indeed."
The angler said:
"I am the rustic Zhāng Shè.
I have long been acquainted with you,
but you have forgotten me now."
Hàn was bewildered and did not recall.
They then sat down on the grass.
Shè said to Hàn:
"You will hold several official posts,
but will ultimately become the magistrate of Qīngchéng County.
I reside on Qīngchéng Mountain.
When your term ends,
I will return to the mountains with you.
However, I cannot come to your official residence now."
With that, he bid farewell and left.
Hàn deeply remembered this.
Later, he served in various official positions,
and eventually was appointed magistrate of Qīngchéng County.
He wore a worried expression.
The angler often came and went,
and Hé held him in high regard.
One day, a large army arrived at the city,
and bandits rose up on all sides.
The angler and Hàn fled hand in hand into the mountains.
Hé's family remained in the city.
The bandits entered the county,
saying they would kill the magistrate,
cut him into pieces, and eat him.
The bandit leader's son called himself the Little General.
That day, they searched but could not find him.
Upon closer inspection of the magistrate's head,
it was actually the head of the Little General.
The bandits then turned on each other,
and no one knew where the magistrate had gone.
Later, someone entered the mountains
and saw Hé and Zhāng traveling together.
Hé then sent a message to his wife and children, saying:
"I am not dead,
but have returned to the old mountains.
You must make a good living for yourselves,
and do not long for me."
From then on, no one saw him again,
and his whereabouts remained unknown.
From "Yěrén Xiánhuà"
Lú Yánguì
Lú Yánguì
was an official at the Ānrén Field in Xuānzhōu.
While traveling to his post, he was delayed by wind
and moored by the great river for several days.
He went ashore for a stroll
and unknowingly wandered far,
spotting what seemed to be a hut under a distant large tree.
As he drew closer,
he saw a creature inside the hut,
resembling both a human and a beast.
Upon seeing him, it stood up and approached.
Yánguì, frightened, retreated.
The creature repeatedly called out:
"Do not fear,
I am human."
Yánguì then approached it.
Its appearance was extraordinarily tall and imposing,
naked and covered all over with hair,
several inches long.
It said it was a merchant
who, years ago, was sailing
when it encountered a storm here.
Its entire family drowned,
but it alone managed to reach the shore.
For several days, it ate grass roots
and drank stream water,
thus surviving.
After over a year,
hair grew all over its body.
Since then, it neither drank nor ate,
grieving over its loneliness,
and no longer had any worldly thoughts.
It built a hut here
and had lived for over ten years.
Yánguì asked, living alone here,
did it not suffer harm from tigers and leopards?
It replied:
"I can now soar up and down through the air,
so tigers and leopards cannot harm me."
Yánguì stayed for a long time,
then asked if it needed anything.
It replied:
"Indeed, there is something.
Whenever I bathe in the stream,
I am always troubled that my body does not dry quickly.
If I could have a few feet of cloth as a towel,
that would be excellent.
Also, a small knife
to dig for medicinal herbs
would be even better.
Can you provide these?"
Yánguì invited it to his boat,
but it firmly refused.
So he gave it the towel and knife before leaving.
After his term ended,
he tried to find it again,
but lost his way.
No one encountered it thereafter.
From "Jīshén Lù"
Dù Lǔbīn
Dù Lǔbīn, a native of Jiànkāng,
made his living selling medicine.
Once, a customer claiming to be from Yùzhāng
often came to buy medicine,
never paying,
yet Lǔbīn treated him well.
One day, the customer came again,
buying a large amount of medicine,
and said:
"I owe you much for medicine,
and now I ask for more from you.
I am returning west,
to the
Ming manuscript has "天" as "大"
large market for lumber.
By the time I come again,
Ming manuscript has "求" as "來"
I will have enough to repay you in full."
Dù agreed.
After the customer left,
a long time passed before he returned,
giving Dù ten pieces of mountain peach wood,
left them, and departed,
his whereabouts unknown.
Dù received them
but did not pay much attention,
giving them away to relatives and friends,
keeping only three pieces.
Once, he had a craftsman split them open,
and inside one, they found a small iron mortar and pestle set,
about five or six inches tall,
the mortar with eight legs,
decorated with animal heads in between,
exquisitely crafted,
unlike human workmanship.
Dù, being an ordinary man,
did not know its use,
and eventually it was taken by someone,
its current whereabouts lost.
Dù also once built a house,
and there was a man selling soil
who said he was from Jīntán County.
He came and went frequently,
and Dù also generously supported him.
After the house was completed,
the soil seller was about to leave
and left a square foot of soil, saying:
"Take this as a parting gift."
He then left and never returned.
The soil was firm and fine,
different from ordinary soil.
Dù placed it in his medicine shop,
not considering it valuable.
Several years later,
Dù's residence was burned down by fire,
the house collapsed and the soil cracked.
Looking inside,
there was a small red snake in the crevice.
Splitting it open,
the snake was coiled around a small white stone turtle,
about two or three inches in size.
The snake left, but the turtle remained,
and to this day, it is treasured by the Dù family.
From "Jīshén Lù"
The Mad Monk of Jiànzhōu
In Jiànzhōu there was a monk whose name was unknown,
and he often acted like a madman.
His words and actions
were often proven true.
Shàowǔ County faced a stream in front,
and there was a large flat rock,
still a hundred paces from the water.
One day, he suddenly drew a line in ink across half of the rock,
then sat upon it,
holding a rod as if fishing.
The next day, a great flood came,
rising exactly to the ink line before receding.
In the year Guǐmǎo,
he cut off all the branches of the trees along the road that faced south.
When people asked him why,
he said:
"To avoid obstructing the banners and flags."
He also said:
"They must go to one side."
When the Wú army entered,
they all marched beneath them.
Also, outside the city at a Buddhist temple,
he wrote large characters on the walls,
inscribing how many people should be stationed there.
When the army reached the city walls,
they divided and occupied the temples,
using them as encampments,
and the number of people placed there
matched exactly without error.
In the end, the monk was killed by the soldiers.
At the end of the Wáng family's reign,
Mǐn and Jiàn experienced many troubles,
and the people could hardly survive.
Someone asked the mad monk:
"When will the times become peaceful?"
He replied:
"When I am gone, there will be peace."
After his death,
the Mǐn region was pacified,
just as he had said.
From *Jīshén Lù*
Liú Shēn
There was a man surnamed Liú,
in Zhūfāng,
with whom people dared not converse.
If anyone spoke with him,
they would inevitably meet with misfortune,
either suffering fatal illness themselves.
Only one scholar said there was no such principle,
believing it was merely coincidental obstruction.
Liú heard this,
and joyfully went to him,
saying he had been slandered,
and was glad the scholar could see clearly.
The scholar replied:
"The world echoes each other thoughtlessly,
why worry about it?"
Shortly after, a fire broke out,
and the scholar's wealth, livestock, clothing, and treasures were utterly destroyed.
Thereafter, everyone called him the owl.
If they met him on the road,
they would hastily drive their carriages or ride away,
covering their eyes and fleeing in panic.
Liú also shut his doors and kept to himself.
Once a year when he went out,
people would scatter in alarm,
as if they had seen a ghost.
From *Yì Yuàn*
Lú Yīng
In Huáinán there was a resident named Lú Yīng,
whose temperament and literary talent
were unmatched in the commandery.
Everyone called him Lú Sānláng.
But he was extremely ill-fated,
for if he was among a gathering,
the host would surely meet with sudden disaster,
such as a child falling into a well,
or a young girl falling into fire.
As this was long proven true,
people all avoided him.
At that time, Yuán Bóhé was the commandery governor,
and upon his arrival,
he admired Lú's talent and spirit,
and specially opened the central hall to hold a banquet.
All the guests gathered,
and after the meal,
Bóhé jokingly asked his attendants:
"Has any child fallen into a well?"
They said:
"No."
"Has any young girl fallen into fire?"
They said:
"No."
Bóhé said to the seated guests:
"It seems all of you are not up to the task."
Soon they drank together,
and the guests exchanged uneasy glances.
That day,
military officers surrounded the residence,
seized Bóhé, and executed him in the market.
The military governor Chén Shǎoyóu at the time,
found this very strange,
and upon seeing Lú's talent and appearance again,
said to him:
"With one move, this man
will not exhaust his talent unless he reaches the heavens."
He then generously gave him gold and silk, favoring and recommending him.
As Lú traveled to Tóngguān,
looking west at the smoke and dust,
someone galloping eastward said:
"Zhǔ Cǐ has rebelled,
and the emperor has fled to Fèngtiān County."
From *Dúyì Zhì*
Zhào Yànnú
Zhào Yànnú
was from Shíjìng in Hézhōu,
and lived in the grounds of Dàyún Temple.
When his mother was first pregnant,
after several months she gave birth to a tiger,
which was abandoned in the river;
she became pregnant again,
and after several months gave birth to a giant turtle,
which was also abandoned;
she became pregnant once more,
and after several months gave birth to a yaksha,
over a foot long,
which was abandoned;
she became pregnant again,
and after several months gave birth to Yànnú,
with eyebrows, eyes, ears, nose, and mouth all fully formed,
but from the neck down,
his body was like a severed gourd.
He still had shoulders,
and two hands and feet each several inches long,
but without elbows, forearms, wrists, or palms,
on the round flesh of each grew six fingers,
just over an inch long,
with fingernails also present.
Below were two feet,
one or two inches long,
also each with six toes.
After his birth,
they could not bear to abandon him.
When he grew up,
he was only a little over two feet tall.
He was skilled in water,
could handle boats,
and was very cunning and clever,
eloquent and quick-tongued,
but quite fond of killing,
making his living by fishing and butchering pigs.
Whenever there were boat races or exorcism rituals,
or competitions in singing bamboo-branch songs,
he was always the champion.
In market transactions,
he always acted as a broker.
He often wore black robes with a shaved head,
and people called him Zhàoshī.
In his later years, he merely had a bald head and wore a white shirt.
Sometimes he would bow, kneel, or jump about,
falling to the ground,
his form exposed,
and many people laughed at him.
Sometimes he would travel far on a donkey,
only having someone carry him,
lying sideways on the saddle,
like a clothing sack.
He had two wives and a daughter,
and his clothing and food were abundant.
Sometimes he would beat his family,
and no one could restrain him.
In the early Qiándé era,
he was only sixty years old,
with a waist and belly several spans around,
but his face was no different from an ordinary person's.
His daughter's right-hand ring finger
was seven or eight inches long,
also different from others.
From *Lùyì Jì*
Shì Móténg.
Originally a man of Central India,
he was handsome in demeanor,
understood the scriptures of both the Greater and Lesser Vehicles,
and often traveled to teach, acting with abandon
(the Ming manuscript reads “ren” for “kuang”)
Once he went to a small vassal state of India
to lecture on the Sutra of Golden Light.
When an enemy state invaded its borders,
Móténg thought to himself:
“The sutra says:
‘One who can expound this Dharma
will be protected by the earth deities,
bringing peace and joy to the land.’
Now that the clash of arms has just begun,
can this truly be of benefit?”
He then vowed to risk his own life,
personally going to mediate and persuade,
and thus the two states made peace.
From this, his reputation spread.
By the time of the Hàn dynasty’s Yǒngpíng era,
Emperor Míng dreamed at night of a golden man flying through the air and arriving.
He then assembled his ministers to interpret the dream.
The interpreter
(the Ming manuscript reads “rén” for “shì”)
Fù Yì reported:
“Your servant has heard that in the Western Regions there is a deity
named Buddha.
Your Majesty’s dream
must surely be of him.” The emperor agreed.
He immediately dispatched the court gentleman Cài Yīn, the academic disciple Qín Jǐng, and others as envoys to India
to seek the Buddhist Dharma.
When Yīn and the others arrived there,
they met Móténg
and invited him back to the land of Hàn.
Móténg, committed to spreading the teachings widely,
did not fear hardship or fatigue.
Braving the shifting sands,
he reached Luòyì.
Emperor Míng received him with great honor
and built a vihāra outside the western gate of the city to house him.
This was the beginning of Buddhist monks in the land of Hàn.
However, as the great Dharma was newly transmitted,
people were not yet devoted believers,
so he kept his profound understanding hidden
and did not widely expound it.
A short time later,
he passed away in Luòyáng.
There is a record stating:
Móténg translated the Sutra in Forty-Two Sections in one scroll.
It was initially sealed in the fourteenth chamber of the Lántái Stone Chamber.
The place where Móténg resided
is now the White Horse Temple outside the Yōng Gate west of Luòyáng city.
It is traditionally said
that a foreign king once destroyed many temples,
but before the Zhāotí Temple could be destroyed,
a white horse circled the pagoda at night, neighing mournfully.
This was reported to the king,
who then halted the destruction of the temples.
Thus, Zhāotí was renamed White Horse,
and many temples thereafter
took this as a model for their names.
From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
Zhú Fǎlán
was also a man of Central India.
He claimed to have recited tens of thousands of chapters of sutras and treatises
and was a teacher of Indian scholars.
At that time, when Cài Yīn arrived in that country,
Fǎlán and Móténg shared a commitment to traveling and teaching,
so he followed along.
When his disciples there tried to detain him,
Fǎlán slipped away and arrived.
Upon reaching Luòyáng,
he stayed with Móténg.
In a short time
(“zhǐ shǎo” originally read “bù”;
changed according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*)
he became proficient in the Hàn language.
The scriptures that Yīn had obtained in the Western Regions
were then translated by him.
These were the so-called five works: *Shí Dì Duàn Jié*, *Fó Běnshēng*
(“shēng” originally read “sēng”;
changed according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*)
, *Fǎ Hǎi Zàng*, *Fó Běnxíng*, and the *Sìshí’èr Zhāng*.
Due to the capital’s relocation and turmoil from invasion,
four of these texts were lost
and not transmitted to Jiāngzuǒ.
Only the *Sutra in Forty-Two Sections* survives today,
containing about two thousand words.
Among the scriptures currently existing in the land of Hàn,
this is the earliest.
Yīn also obtained from the Western Regions a painting of a seated image of Śākyamuni,
which was the fourth work by the sandalwood image master of King Udayana.
After it arrived in Luòyáng,
Emperor Míng ordered painters to copy it and place it in the Qīngliáng Terrace
and at the Xiǎnjié Tomb
(“líng” originally read “lín”;
changed according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*)
. The original image no longer exists today.
Furthermore, long ago when Emperor Wǔ of Hàn dredged the bottom of the Kūnmíng Pond,
he found black ash.
He asked Dōngfāng Shuò about it,
and Shuò said:
“You may ask a Brahmin from the Western Regions.”
Later, after Fǎlán arrived,
people pressed him with the question.
Fǎlán said:
“When the world reaches its end,
the kalpa fire will burn everything completely.
This ash is from that.”
Shuò’s words were thus verified,
and many believed.
Fǎlán later passed away in Luòyáng,
at over sixty years of age.
From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
Kāng Sēnghuì,
his ancestors were from the state of Kāngjū,
and for generations they resided in Tiānzhú (India).
His father moved to Jiāozhǐ due to trade.
When Huì was over ten years old,
both his parents passed away,
and he served them with utmost filial piety.
After the mourning period ended, he left home to become a monk,
and his conduct was exceptionally rigorous.
He was a person of broad elegance and discerning judgment,
steadfast in his aspirations and fond of learning,
proficient in understanding the Tripiṭaka,
well-read in the Six Classics,
and extensively versed in astronomy, charts, and apocryphal texts.
He was skilled in debate and
eloquent in writing.
At that time, Sūn Quán had already established control over the region south of the Yangtze River,
but Buddhism had not yet spread there.
Earlier, there was an upāsaka named Zhī Qiān, styled Gōngmíng,
also known as Yuè,
originally a man from the Yuèzhī tribe,
who came to travel within the Hàn territory.
During the reigns of Emperors Huán and Líng of the Hàn dynasty,
there was Zhī Chèn who translated
"translated" originally written as "regret,"
amended according to the Ming manuscript copy
numerous scriptures.
There was also Zhī Liàng,
styled Juémíng,
who studied under Chèn.
Qiān, in turn, studied under Liàng.
He extensively read the classics and texts,
mastering them all,
and was skilled in many worldly arts,
studying various esoteric books
and mastering the languages of six states.
In appearance, he was tall, slender, dark, and thin,
with eyes that were mostly white and yellowish pupils.
People of the time said of him:
"Zhī Láng has yellow in his eyes;
though his body is slender, he is a treasury of wisdom."
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, encountering turmoil,
he sought refuge in Wú.
Sūn Quán, hearing of his talent and wisdom,
summoned him for an audience,
appointed him as a court academician,
and tasked him with assisting and instructing the crown prince.
Together with Wéi Yào and others, he exerted himself to provide guidance and benefit,
but as he was born in a foreign land,
he was not recorded in the Wúzhì.
Qiān believed that although the great teaching (Buddhism) was spreading,
many scriptures were still in Sanskrit,
not fully translated.
As he was exceptionally skilled in languages,
he intended to gather various versions
and translate them into Chinese.
From the first year of the Huángwǔ era of Wú to the middle of the Jiànxīng era,
he produced forty-nine scriptures, including the *Vimalakīrti*, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, *Nirvāṇa*, *Dhammapada*, *Ruìyìng*, and *Běnqǐ*.
These accurately captured the sacred forms,
with elegant and refined language.
He also based on the *Wúliàngshòu* and *Zhōngběnqǐ*
to compose three sections of Sanskrit hymns for Bodhisattvas,
and annotated scriptures such as the *Liǎoběnxiānsǐ Jīng*.
All of these circulated in the world.
At that time, the land of Wú was newly touched by the great Dharma,
and its influence was not yet complete.
Sēnghuì wished to make the Way flourish in Jiāngzuǒ (the region east of the Yangtze),
and to establish temples and monasteries,
so he journeyed eastward with his monk's staff.
In the tenth year of the Chìwū era of Wú,
he first arrived at Jiànyè,
built a thatched hut,
set up images, and practiced the Way.
At that time, the state of Wú had just seen the appearance and robes of Buddhist monks,
but not yet understood their teachings,
and suspected them of being deceptive and strange.
An official reported:
"There is a strange person who has entered our territory,
calling himself a Buddhist monk,
with unusual appearance and attire.
The matter should be investigated."
Quán said:
"In the past, Emperor Míng of Hàn dreamed of a spirit,
called Buddha.
Could what he venerates be a remnant of that tradition?"
He immediately summoned Huì for questioning:
"What spiritual proof do you have?"
Huì replied:
"The Tathāgata passed away,
suddenly over a thousand years ago,
but his relics (śarīra)
shine with divine light, boundless and unfathomable.
In the past, King Aśoka built stūpas,
up to eighty-four thousand in number.
The rise of stūpas and monasteries
is to manifest the legacy of his teachings."
Quán thought this was exaggerated and fanciful,
so he said to Huì:
"If you can obtain relics,
I will build a stūpa for you.
But if this is false,
the state has its regular punishments."
Huì requested a period of seven days.
He then said to his followers:
"The rise or fall of the Dharma
depends on this one effort.
If we are not utterly sincere now,
what will come of it later?"
Together, they purified themselves in a quiet room,
placed a copper vase on a small table,
burned incense, and reverently prayed.
When the seven days ended,
there was silence and no response.
He requested an extension of fourteen days,
but again it was the same.
Quán said:
"This is deceit,"
and intended to impose punishment.
Huì further requested twenty-one days,
and Quán exceptionally permitted it.
Huì addressed his Dharma companions:
"Confucius said:
'King Wén is gone;
does not the culture reside here with us?'
The Dharma-cloud should descend,
yet we have not moved it.
Why wait for the king's law?
We must vow to die for this purpose."
On the evening of the twenty-first day,
there was still nothing to be seen,
and all were trembling with fear.
When the fifth watch arrived,
suddenly a clanging sound was heard from the vase.
Huì went to look himself,
and indeed obtained relics.
The next morning,
Quán personally held the vase
and poured its contents onto a copper plate.
Where the relics struck,
the plate immediately shattered.
Quán, greatly awed, rose in astonishment
and said:
"A rare and auspicious sign!"
Huì stepped forward and said:
"The majestic power of the relics
is not limited to mere luminous appearances.
Even the fire of retreating flames cannot burn them,
nor can a vajra pestle crush them."
Quán ordered this to be tested.
Huì made another vow:
"The Dharma-cloud is about to spread,
and all living beings look up for its grace.
May you again bestow a divine marvel
to broadly display your majestic power."
He then placed the relics on an iron anvil
and had a strong man strike them.
The anvil and hammer both sank,
but the relics remained undamaged.
Quán sighed deeply in admiration
and immediately built a stūpa.
As this was the first Buddhist temple,
it was named Jiànchū Temple,
and the area was accordingly called Tuólǐ.
From then on, the great Dharma flourished in Jiāngzuǒ.
When Sūn Hào ascended the throne,
his laws were harsh and cruel.
He abolished licentious cults
and also intended to destroy Buddhist temples.
Hào said:
"For what reason did this arise?
If its teachings are upright and correct,
and correspond with the sacred classics,
then its Way should be preserved and revered.
But if it lacks substance,
it should all be burned."
The ministers all said:
"The power of the Buddha
is different from that of spirits.
Kāng Huì elicited auspicious signs,
and the great emperor (Sūn Quán) founded the temple.
If we lightly destroy it now,
we fear we may later regret it."
Hào sent Zhāng Yù to the temple to question Huì.
Yù was exceptionally talented in debate,
posing difficult questions from all directions.
Huì responded with ready wit and eloquent speech,
his arguments sharp and incisive.
From morning until evening,
Yù could not defeat him.
After Yù withdrew,
Huì saw him off at the gate.
At that time, there was a licentious shrine beside the temple.
Yù said:
"Since the profound transformation has been spread,
why have these people nearby not reformed?"
Huì said:
"A thunderclap that splits a mountain,
the deaf cannot hear it,
not because the sound is faint.
If the principle is understood,
then even from ten thousand li away there is a response;
if it is obstructed,
then even liver and gall are as far apart as Chǔ and Yuè."
Yù returned,
sighing that Huì's talent and wisdom
were beyond what he could fathom,
and wished Heaven would examine and observe it.
Hào gathered the court worthies in great assembly,
and welcomed Huì with carriages and horses.
After Huì was seated,
Hào asked:
"What Buddhism elucidates,
the retribution for good and evil,
what is that?"
Huì replied:
"When an enlightened ruler instructs the world with filial piety and compassion,
then red birds soar and old men appear;
when benevolent virtue nurtures all things,
then sweet springs gush forth and fine seedlings emerge.
Since good deeds have auspicious signs,
so too do evil deeds.
Therefore, if one does evil in secret,
ghosts will punish them;
if one does evil openly,
people will punish them.
The Yì Jīng says, 'Accumulating good deeds brings abundant blessings';
the Shī Jīng sings, 'Seeking blessings without turning away.'
Although these are maxims from Confucian classics,
they are also the clear teachings of Buddhism."
Hào said:
"If so,
then the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius have already clarified it,
what need is there for Buddhism?"
Huì said:
"What the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius spoke of
briefly indicates the near traces;
as for the Buddhist teachings,
they exhaustively reach the profound and subtle.
Therefore, committing evil leads to the long suffering of hell,
cultivating good leads to the eternal bliss of heavenly palaces.
Raising these to clarify encouragement and deterrence,
is that not great?"
Hào at the time had no way to refute his words.
Although Hào heard the true Dharma,
his nature of darkness and violence
could not overcome his cruelty.
Later, he sent palace guards into the rear palace to tend the garden,
and from the ground they obtained a golden statue,
several feet tall,
which they presented to Hào.
Hào had it placed in an unclean place,
poured foul liquid over it,
and together with his ministers,
laughed and made merry.
In a short while,
his whole body swelled greatly,
especially painful in the private parts,
and he cried out piercing the heavens.
The Grand Historian divined and said:
"It is due to offending a great deity."
Immediately they prayed at various temples seeking blessings,
ordered palace maidens to welcome the statue and place it in the hall,
washed it dozens of times with fragrant water,
burned incense and repented.
Hào kowtowed on the ground,
confessing his crimes.
After a while, the pain subsided.
He sent an envoy to the temple,
requesting Huì to expound the Dharma.
Huì immediately followed and entered,
and Hào inquired in detail about the causes of sin and blessing.
Huì explained and analyzed for him,
his words extremely concise and essential.
Hào, having prior understanding and talent,
was greatly delighted,
and thus requested to see the monastic precepts.
Huì, because the precept texts were secret and prohibited,
could not lightly reveal them,
so he took the one hundred thirty-five vows of the Běnyè,
divided them into two hundred fifty items,
such that walking, standing, sitting, and lying down,
all were for the sake of sentient beings.
Hào, seeing the broad and universal compassionate vows,
increased his good intentions even more,
and immediately received the Five Precepts from Huì,
and within ten days his illness was cured.
Then at the place where Huì resided,
he further made renovations,
proclaimed it to the imperial clan,
and none failed to fully uphold it.
Huì, in the Wú court,
repeatedly expounded the true Dharma,
but because Hào's nature was fierce and crude,
he could not grasp the profound meaning,
so he only recounted recent events of retribution,
to open his mind.
Huì at Jiànchū Temple translated many scriptures,
such as the Ānán Niàn Mítuó Jīng
(the characters "tuó jīng" were originally absent,
added according to the Gāosēng Zhuàn)
, Jìng'ér Wáng Cháwēi Wáng Fànhuáng Jīng, etc.,
and also translated the Xiǎopǐn and the Liùdù Jí Zá Pìyù, among other scriptures.
All excellently captured the essence of the scriptures,
with text and meaning accurate and correct.
He also transmitted the Nièpán chant melody,
pure, harmonious, sorrowful, and clear,
a model for a generation.
He also annotated the Ānbān Shǒuyì Fǎ Jìng Dàoshù, among three scriptures.
And composed scripture prefaces,
with elegant and refined language,
and subtle, profound meaning.
All circulated in the world.
In the fourth year of the Tiānjì era of Wú, in the fourth month,
Hào surrendered to Jìn
(the character "Jìn" was originally written as "zhǐ",
corrected according to the Míng transcript)
In the ninth month,
Huì fell ill and passed away.
This year was the first year of the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn.
By the Xiánhé era of Emperor Chéng of Jìn,
Sū Jùn rebelled,
burning the pagoda built by Huì,
and Minister Hé Chōng again restored it.
General Píngxī Zhào Yòu, who throughout his life did not uphold the Dharma,
arrogantly despised the Three Jewels,
entered this temple,
and said to the monks:
"I have long heard that this pagoda repeatedly emits light,
but it is absurd and unfounded.
What is called believable,
if one must see it with their own eyes,
that is impossible."
As soon as he finished speaking,
the pagoda emitted five-colored light,
illuminating the hall and spire.
Yòu was awed, his hair standing on end,
and from then on believed and revered.
East of the temple, he further erected a small pagoda.
From afar, it was due to the spiritual response of the great sage;
from near, it was also the power of Kāng Huì.
Therefore, his image was painted,
and transmitted to this day.
From the Gāosēng Zhuàn.
Zhī Dùn.
Zhī Dùn, styled Dàolín,
originally surnamed Guān,
was a person from Chénliú.
Some say
he was from Línlǜ, Hédōng.
From childhood, he possessed divine understanding,
being intelligent and exceptionally clear-minded.
During the Jìn dynasty, he first arrived at the capital.
Wáng Méng of Tàiyuán held him in high esteem,
saying:
"His achievements in probing the subtle
are no less than those of Fǔsì."
Yīn Róng of Chénjùn
("jùn" was originally written as "qún",
corrected according to the Biographies of Eminent Monks)
had once associated with Wèi Jiè,
and said of him that his spirit and demeanor were outstandingly clear,
and that no later scholar could match him.
When he saw Dùn, he sighed,
feeling as if he had seen that man again.
His family had long served the Buddha,
and he early on comprehended extraordinary principles.
He lived in seclusion on Yúháng Mountain,
deeply contemplating the categories of the Way's practice,
and thoroughly studying the scriptures of Huìyìn,
standing out uniquely,
gaining insight from the heavenly mind.
At the age of twenty-five, he left home to become a monk.
Whenever he gave lectures,
he excelled at highlighting the essential tenets,
but sometimes overlooked the detailed exegesis,
for which he was looked down upon by those who adhered strictly to the texts.
Xiè Ān heard of this and was pleased, saying:
"This is like the ancients judging horses,
overlooking their color and focusing on their excellence."
At that time, Xiè Ān, Yīn Hào, and others,
all renowned figures of their generation,
engaged in intimate associations beyond worldly concerns.
Dùn once was at Báimǎ Temple,
discussing Zhuāngzǐ's "Free and Easy Wandering" with Liú Xìzhī and others, saying,
"Each finds ease by following their nature."
(Eight characters below "yáo" supplemented from the Biographies of Eminent Monks)
Dùn said:
"Not so.
Jié and Zhí took cruelty and harm as their nature;
if following one's nature leads to attainment,
then they too would have found ease."
Because of this, he withdrew and annotated the "Free and Easy Wandering" chapter.
All the Confucian scholars and traditionalists
could not help but sigh in admiration.
Later, he returned to Wú,
residing at Zhīxíng Mountain Temple.
In his later years, he wished to go to Shàn.
Xiè Ān was in Wú at the time,
and wrote to Dùn, saying:
"My thoughts of you accumulate daily,
counting the hours with eager anticipation.
I know you wish to return to Shàn to tend to yourself,
which saddens me greatly.
Life is but a sojourn.
Recently, the delightful affairs of a free and easy life
have nearly all come to an end.
All day long, I am sorrowful,
and everything I encounter fills me with melancholy.
I only await your arrival,
to dispel it through conversation;
a single day would then be worth a thousand years.
Here there are many mountains and waters,
the mountain county is quiet and peaceful,
quite suitable for recuperating from illness.
The circumstances are no different from Shàn,
but the medical care is not the same.
You must consider this connection,
to fulfill my accumulated longing."
Wáng Xīzhī was in Kuàijī at the time,
and had long heard of Dùn's reputation,
but did not believe it.
He said to others:
"Just a mad monk,
not worth mentioning."
Later, after Dùn returned to Shàn,
he went directly to the commandery.
Wáng intentionally went to meet Dùn,
to observe his demeanor and strength.
After arriving,
Wáng said to Dùn:
"May I hear about the 'Free and Easy Wandering' chapter?"
Dùn then expounded several thousand words,
setting forth novel principles,
with exceptional talent and striking brilliance.
Wáng then loosened his collar and belt,
lingering, unable to leave.
He then requested Dùn to stay at Língjiā Temple,
wishing to keep him close.
Soon after, Dùn again went to Shàn Mountain,
and at Wòzhōu's small ridge,
he established a temple to practice the Way.
Over a hundred monks
often followed to receive instruction.
Sometimes there were those who followed him,
so Dùn composed a "Maxim for the Seat" to encourage them.
Contemporary opinion held that Dùn's talent was suited to expounding scriptures,
but by purifying himself and rising above the vulgar,
he went against the way of broadly aiding the world.
Dùn then composed the "Shì Méng Lùn."
In his later years, he passed by Shíchéng Mountain,
and again established Qīguāng Temple.
He sat peacefully at the mountain gate,
letting his mind wander in the meditation gardens,
eating from trees and drinking from streams,
devoting his will to the unborn.
He then annotated various scriptures such as the Ānāpānasati and the Four Dhyānas,
as well as the "Jísè Yóu Xuán Lùn."
Dùn lingered in Jiànyè,
for nearly three years.
He then returned to Dōng Mountain,
submitted a letter to take his leave,
and was graciously permitted by imperial decree.
Provisions were supplied for his departure,
everything being abundant.
All the renowned figures of the time
gathered to bid him farewell at Zhēnglǔ Pavilion.
At that time, Cài Zǐshū arrived first,
and sat close to Dùn.
Xiè Wànshí arrived later,
and happened to find Cài temporarily away from his seat,
so Xiè moved to take his place.
When Cài returned,
he wanted to reclaim Xiè's seat,
but Xiè did not mind.
Such was the admiration he commanded from the worthies of the time.
Afterward, he withdrew to Shàn Mountain,
ending his life amidst forests and marshes.
Someone once gave Dùn a horse as a gift,
and Dùn accepted it and cared for it.
Some at the time criticized him for this,
but Dùn said:
"I admire its divine excellence,
and simply keep it for that."
Later, someone offered him a crane,
and Dùn said:
"You are a creature that soars to the heavens;
how could you be a plaything for the eyes and ears?"
He then released it.
When Dùn was young,
he once debated with his teacher about living beings,
saying that using chicken eggs for food
did not constitute killing.
The teacher could not refute him.
The teacher soon died,
and suddenly appeared in form,
throwing an egg to the ground.
The shell broke, and a chick walked out,
then shortly after, both vanished.
Dùn then felt remorse and understood,
and from then on, he ate only vegetables for the rest of his life.
Dùn had previously lived in the mountains of Yúyáo Wù,
and in his later years,
he still returned to Wù.
When asked his intention,
he replied:
"Xiè Ānshí used to come see me often,
and would stay for ten days at a time.
Now, everything I see stirs my emotions,
and I cannot help but think of him."
Later, when he became seriously ill,
he moved back to Wù,
and on the fourth day of the intercalary fourth month in the first year of the Tàihé era of the Jìn dynasty, he passed away at his residence,
at the age of fifty-three.
He was buried in Wù,
and his tomb remains there.
Some say he died in Shàn,
but this is not certain.
Xī Qǐ composed a preface and biography for him,
Yuán Hóng wrote an inscription and eulogy,
and Zhōu Yúnbǎo composed a funeral oration.
From the Biographies of Eminent Monks.
Fótúchéng
Fótú Chéng was
a man from the Western Regions.
His original surname was Bó.
He left home to become a monk in his youth.
Pure and sincere, he studied diligently from a young age,
memorizing several million words of scripture.
In the fourth year of the Yǒngjiā era of Emperor Huái of Jìn, he came to Luòyáng,
intending to propagate the great Dharma.
He was skilled in reciting divine incantations,
and could command spirits and ghosts.
By mixing sesame oil with soot and smearing it on his palm,
events occurring a thousand *li* away
would all appear clearly in his palm,
as if face-to-face,
and he could also enable those who purified themselves through fasting to see them.
Furthermore, he could interpret the sounds of bells to foretell events,
and none of his predictions failed to come true.
He wished to establish a monastery in Luòyáng,
but it happened that Liú Yào invaded and pillaged Luòtái,
throwing the imperial capital into turmoil.
Thus, Chéng's ambition to build a monastery did not come to fruition.
He then concealed himself in the wilderness,
to observe the changes in the world.
At that time, Shí Lè was stationed with his troops at Gěbēi,
relying solely on slaughter to establish his authority;
many Buddhist monks met with harm.
Chéng, pitying the common people,
wished to use the Dao to transform Lè.
Thereupon, taking his staff, he went to the army's gate.
Lè's general Guō Hēilüè had long revered the Dharma,
so Chéng went and lodged at Lüè's home.
Lüè received from him the Five Precepts,
and honored him with the rites of a disciple.
Later, when Lüè followed Lè on campaigns,
he would often predict victory or defeat beforehand.
Lè, suspicious, asked him:
"I do not perceive that you possess outstanding intelligence or strategy,
yet you always know the auspicious or inauspicious outcomes of military movements.
Why is this?"
Lüè said:
"General, you are endowed by Heaven with divine martial prowess,
aided by unseen spirits.
There is a Buddhist monk
whose arts and wisdom are extraordinary.
He says the General is destined to rule over this region of Xià.
He himself should be your teacher.
All the reports I have made to you,
are his words."
Lè was pleased and said:
"A gift from Heaven!"
He summoned Chéng and asked him:
"What miraculous proofs does the Buddhist Way possess?"
Chéng knew that Lè did not comprehend profound principles,
and could only be taught through magical arts.
Therefore, he said:
"Although the ultimate Dao is distant,
it can also be evidenced by matters close at hand."
He then took a vessel, filled it with water,
burned incense, and chanted an incantation over it.
In a moment, a blue lotus flower grew,
its radiance and color dazzling the sun.
From this, Lè believed and submitted.
Chéng then admonished him, saying:
"When a king's virtuous influence permeates the world, the Four Auspicious Creatures manifest as omens;
when governance is corrupt and the Dao declines, comets appear in the heavens.
These constant celestial phenomena manifest clearly,
good and ill fortune follow accordingly.
This is the constant principle of past and present,
the clear warning from Heaven and man."
Lè was greatly pleased by this.
Of all those who should have been executed or mutilated, nearly
eight or nine out of ten
received benefit from him. Consequently, the Hú people in the Central Plains
all wished to revere the Buddha.
At that time, there were chronic illnesses
that the world could not understand;
Chéng would treat and heal them,
and they would recover and improve in due time.
Those who silently received his covert benefactions
were too numerous to record.
When Lè returned from Gěbēi to Héběi,
passing by Fāngtóu,
people planned to raid the camp at night.
Chéng said to Hēilüè:
"In a moment, bandits will arrive.
You should let the Duke know."
It happened just as he said;
because they were prepared, they were not defeated.
Lè wished to test Chéng.
At night, he put on his helmet and armor, took up his blade, and sat,
then sent a man to tell Chéng:
"Tonight we do not know where the Great General is."
As soon as the messenger arrived,
before he could speak,
Chéng anticipated him and asked:
"Living in peace without enemies,
why the strict night watch?"
Lè respected him even more.
Later, Lè, in a fit of anger,
wished to harm various Daoist priests,
and also intended to trouble Chéng.
Chéng then took refuge at Hēilüè's residence,
and told his disciples:
"If messengers from the General come
asking where I am,
reply that you do not know where I have gone."
Messengers soon arrived,
but could not find Chéng.
They returned and reported to Lè.
Lè was startled and said:
"I harbored malicious intent towards the Sage,
and the Sage has abandoned me and left."
He stayed awake all night,
longing to see Chéng.
Chéng knew Lè's mind had repented.
The next morning, he went to see Lè.
Lè said:
"Where did you go last night?"
Chéng said:
"You, Duke, had an angry heart,
so I temporarily avoided you last night.
Now that you have changed your mind,
I therefore dare to come."
Lè laughed heartily and said:
"You, Reverend, are mistaken."
The water source for the moat of Xiāngguó city
was located five *li* northwest of the city.
This water source suddenly dried up.
Lè asked Chéng:
"How can we get water?"
Chéng said:
"Now we should command the dragon to fetch water."
Lè's courtesy name was Shìlóng (World Dragon),
so he thought Chéng was mocking him.
He replied:
"It is precisely because the dragon cannot bring water
that I am asking you!"
Chéng said:
"These are sincere words,
not a jest.
At the source of a spring,
there must be a divine dragon residing.
If we go and inform it with a command,
water can certainly be obtained."
He then went with several disciples, including Fǎshǒu,
to the site of the old spring source.
The original location of the source
had long been dry,
cracked like a wagon rut.
His followers doubted that obtaining water would be difficult.
Chéng sat on a rope-seat chair,
burned benzoin incense,
and chanted incantations and vows for several hundred words.
After three days of this,
water began to trickle in a faint stream.
A small dragon,
about five or six inches long,
came out following the water.
The various Daoist priests vied to go and look at it.
Chéng said:
"The dragon is poisonous;
do not approach above it."
After a while,
water arrived in great quantity,
filling the moat completely.
Chéng, sitting at leisure, sighed and said:
"Two days from now,
a minor incident will startle and disturb this place."
Soon after, a man of Xiāngguó named Xuē Hé
had two sons.
They were young and arrogant,
and lightly insulted a Xiānbēi slave.
The slave, enraged,
drew a blade and stabbed the younger brother to death.
He then seized the elder brother in the house,
and pointed the knife at his heart,
saying that if anyone entered the room,
he would immediately act,
and said to Xuē Hé:
"Send me back to my country,
and I will spare your son's life.
If not,
we will all die here."
Everyone inside and outside was shocked and terrified,
and none dared go to see.
Lè then went personally to observe.
He said to Xuē Hé:
"Sending the slave away to save your son
is indeed a good deed.
But once this precedent is set,
it will become a future calamity.
Please set your mind at ease;
the state has constant laws."
He ordered men to seize the slave.
The slave then killed the boy and died himself.
The Xiānbēi Duàn Mòbō attacked Lè,
his forces were very numerous.
Lè, afraid, asked Chéng.
Chéng said:
"Yesterday, the monastery bell rang, saying..."
The next morning at mealtime,
Duàn Mòbō will be captured.”
He and Lè ascended the city wall to observe Bō’s army,
but seeing no front or rear,
he turned pale and said:
“How can he be captured?
This is merely the Duke’s words to reassure me.”
He then sent Kuí Ān to ask Chéng again,
and Chéng said:
“Bō has already been captured.”
At that moment, an ambush force emerged north of the city,
encountered Bō, and seized him.
Chéng advised Lè to spare Bō,
and send him back to his own country.
Lè followed this advice,
and ultimately gained his service.
At that time, Liú Zài had already died,
and Zài’s cousin Yào usurped the throne and falsely established himself,
proclaiming the era name Yuánguāng.
In the eighth year of Guāngchū,
Yào sent his cousin, the Prince of Zhōngshān, Yuè, to lead troops to attack Lè.
Lè sent Shí Hǔ to lead infantry and cavalry to resist him.
A great battle took place west of Luòyáng,
and Yuè was defeated,
retreating to hold Shíliáng Wù.
Hǔ fortified the position and defended it.
Chéng and his disciples went from Guānsì Temple to Zhōngsì Temple.
As soon as they entered the temple gate,
he sighed and said:
“Liú Yuè is pitiable!”
His disciple Fǎ Zuò asked the reason,
and Chéng said:
“Last night at the hài hour, Yuè was already captured.”
It turned out just as he said.
In the eleventh year of Guāngchū,
Yào personally led troops to attack Luòyáng.
Lè wanted to go personally to resist Yào,
but all his officials and advisors,
without exception, advised against it.
Lè consulted Chéng about it.
Chéng said:
“The sound of the bell on the temple spire says:
‘Xiùzhī tìlìgāng,
púgǔ qútūdāng.’
This is the Jié language.
‘Xiùzhī tìlìgāng’ means ‘to go out,’
‘púgǔ’ refers to Liú Yào’s position as a Hú ruler,
and ‘qútūdāng’ means ‘to capture.’
This means the army will go out and capture Yào.”
At that time, Xú Guāng, hearing Chéng’s words, earnestly urged action.
Lè then left his eldest son Shí Hóng,
together with Chéng, to guard Xiāngguó,
and personally led the central army’s infantry and cavalry straight toward Luòchéng.
As soon as the two armies clashed,
Yào’s forces were utterly routed.
Yào’s horse stumbled into water,
and Shí Kān captured him alive and delivered him to Lè.
At that time, Chéng applied something to his palm and observed it,
seeing a large crowd,
with one person bound in the middle,
his elbows tied with red silk.
He thus reported this to Hóng.
At that very moment,
Yào was indeed captured alive.
After peace was restored,
Lè arrogantly declared himself the Heavenly King of Zhào and performed the duties of emperor,
changing the era name to Jiànpíng.
This was the fifth year of the Xiánhé era of Emperor Chéng of Jìn.
After Lè ascended the throne,
he served Chéng even more devoutly.
At that time, Shí Cōng rebelled.
That year,
Chéng warned Lè, saying:
“This year, there are worms among the scallions;
eating them will certainly harm people.
You should order the people not to eat scallions.”
Lè issued a proclamation throughout his territory,
urging caution against eating scallions.
By the eighth month,
Shí Cōng indeed fled.
Lè respected him even more,
consulting him on all matters before acting,
and honored him as the Great Monk.
Shí Hǔ had a son named Bīn,
whom Lè later adopted as his own son,
and Lè loved and valued him greatly.
Suddenly, Bīn fell violently ill and died,
and two days had already passed.
Lè said:
“I have heard that when the crown prince of Guó died,
Biǎn Què was able to revive him.
The Great Monk is a divine man of the state;
we must quickly go and inform him—
he will surely be able to bring blessings.”
Chéng then took a willow branch and chanted over it,
and shortly after, Bīn was able to rise,
and after a while, he fully recovered.
From then on, many of Lè’s young children were raised in Buddhist temples.
Every year on the eighth day of the fourth month,
Lè would personally visit the temple,
gaze upon the Buddha statue and make vows.
In the fourth year of Jiànpíng, in the fourth month,
the sky was calm and windless,
yet a bell on the pagoda rang alone.
Chéng said to the crowd:
“The bell’s sound says:
‘The state will have a great mourning,
within this year.’” That year, in the seventh month, Lè died.
The crown prince Hóng succeeded to the throne.
Not long after,
Hǔ deposed Hóng and established himself,
moving the capital to Yè,
and changing the era name to Jiànwǔ.
He devotedly served Chéng,
and revered him even more than Lè had.
He then issued an edict, saying:
“The monk is a great treasure of the state.
High titles are not bestowed upon him,
nor does he accept generous emoluments.
If honors and emoluments are not conferred,
how can his virtue be recognized?
From now on,
he shall be clothed in brocade and silk,
and ride in a carved carriage.
On days of court assembly,
the monk shall ascend the hall.
Officials of the rank of Chángshì and below
shall all assist in carrying him,
while the crown prince and dukes
shall support the carriage as he ascends.
The master of ceremonies shall announce ‘Great Monk,’
and all present shall rise,
to manifest his尊.”
He also ordered the false Sikōng Lǐ Nóng to personally inquire morning and evening,
and the crown prince and dukes
to pay respects once every five days,
to express my reverence.
Chéng was then residing at Zhōngsì Temple within the city of Yè.
He sent his disciple Fǎ Cháng north to Xiāngguó,
while his disciple Fǎ Zuǒ was returning from Xiāngguó.
They met
and stayed together overnight at Liángsāichéng.
They talked by their carts at night,
and the conversation turned to the monk.
At dawn, they each went their separate ways.
When Fǎ Zuǒ arrived,
he went to see Chéng as soon as he entered.
Chéng greeted him with a smile and said:
“Last night, you and Fǎ Cháng met with your carts and talked about your teacher, didn’t you?
The ancients have said:
‘Is it not said to be reverent?
Even in seclusion, one does not change;
is it not said to be cautious?
Even alone, one does not slacken.’
Seclusion and solitude are the foundation of reverence and caution—
do you not recognize this?”
Zuǒ was startled and felt ashamed and remorseful.
From then on, the people of the state often said to each other:
“Do not harbor evil thoughts—
the monk knows you.”
Wherever Chéng was,
no one dared to spit, relieve themselves, or face his direction.
At that time, Crown Prince Shí Suì had two sons in Xiāngguó.
Chéng said to Suì:
“Little Āmí will soon fall ill;
you should go and fetch him.”
Suì immediately sent a messenger to check,
and indeed, he had already fallen ill.
The imperial physician Yīn Téng and a foreign Daoist claimed they could cure him,
but Chéng told his disciple Fǎ Cháng:
“Even if a sage were to reappear,
he could not cure this illness—
how much less these people?”
Three days later, the child indeed died.
Shí Suì indulged in excessive drinking
and plotted rebellion.
He said to his attendants:
“The monk has supernatural powers;
if he uncovers my plot,
when he comes tomorrow,
we must eliminate him first.”
On the full moon, Chéng was about to go see Hǔ,
and he said to his disciple Sēng Huì:
“Last night, a heavenly deity called to me and said:
‘If you go tomorrow,
do not pass by anyone on your return.’
If I happen to pass by someone,
you must stop me.”
Chéng usually passed by Suì
when he entered.
Knowing Chéng was coming,
Suì eagerly awaited him.
As Chéng was about to ascend the southern terrace,
Sēng Huì tugged at his robe,
but Chéng said:
“The matter cannot be avoided.”
Before he could sit down,
he rose again.
Suì insisted on him staying, but he would not remain,
and the plot was thus thwarted.
Returning to the temple, he sighed and said:
"The crown prince is plotting rebellion,
and his scheme is about to succeed."
He wished to speak but found it difficult,
wished to endure but found it unbearable,
so he took the opportunity to tactfully admonish Shí Hǔ,
but Hǔ remained unenlightened.
Soon the affair erupted,
and only then did he realize the truth of Fú Chéng's words.
Later, Guō Hēilüè led troops to campaign against the Qiāng in the northern mountains of Cháng'ān,
and fell into a Qiāng ambush.
At that time, Chéng was sitting in the hall,
with his disciple Fǎcháng at his side.
Chéng suddenly changed his expression to one of distress and said:
"Lord Guō has fallen among the barbarians."
He ordered the assembly to chant prayers,
and Chéng himself also chanted prayers.
After a short while, he announced again:
"If he escapes toward the southeast, he will live;
any other direction, and he will be trapped."
He resumed chanting prayers,
and after a while said:
"He has escaped."
Over a month later,
Hēilüè returned and recounted
that amidst the Qiāng encirclement, he fled eastward,
but his horse grew exhausted.
Just then, he encountered a subordinate who pushed his own horse toward him,
saying:
"My lord, take this horse.
I will ride yours.
Whether we survive or not
is fate's decree."
Hēilüè obtained the horse,
and thus escaped.
Checking the date and time,
it was precisely when Chéng was chanting prayers.
The false Grand Marshal, Duke Yān Shí Bīn,
was appointed by Hǔ as Governor of Yōuzhōu.
In the garrison, a crowd of villains gathered,
and he thus indulged in tyranny.
Chéng warned Hǔ, saying:
"The heavenly spirits said last night:
'Quickly bring the pastured horses back.
By autumn,
Qí will surely rot and fester.'" Hǔ did not understand these words,
but immediately ordered all pastured horses to be returned.
That autumn,
someone slandered Bīn to Hǔ.
Hǔ summoned Bīn,
whipped him three hundred times,
and killed his birth mother, Lady Qí.
Hǔ bent his bow and grasped an arrow,
personally overseeing Bīn's punishment.
Deeming the punishment too light,
Hǔ then personally killed five hundred men.
Chéng admonished him, saying:
"Desires of the heart must not be indulged;
the dead cannot be brought back to life.
According to ritual, one should not personally carry out killings,
for it harms benevolence.
How can the Son of Heaven personally administer punishment?"
Hǔ then desisted.
Later, when the Jìn army advanced to the Huái and Sì rivers,
and the tile-walled cities north of Lǒng were all invaded and threatened,
with three fronts reporting emergencies,
and the people anxious and disturbed,
Hǔ angrily exclaimed:
"I have served the Buddha,
yet this brings foreign invaders upon us.
The Buddha has no divine power!"
Chéng entered early the next morning,
and Hǔ questioned him about the matter.
Chéng then reproached Hǔ, saying:
"In a past life, Your Majesty was a great merchant,
who went to a temple in Jìbīn [Kashmir]
and once provided for a grand assembly.
Among them were sixty arhats;
this very body of mine also attended that assembly.
At that time, an enlightened one told me:
'This host's life is ending;
he will be reborn in another form,
later in the land of the Jìn king.'
Now Your Majesty is king—
is this not fortune?
Border conflicts and military invasions
are common occurrences for a state.
Why then harbor resentment and slander against the Three Jewels,
and nurture venomous thoughts at night?"
Hǔ then believed and understood,
kneeling to apologize.
Hǔ often asked Chéng:
"The Buddha's law prohibits killing.
I, as the ruler of all under heaven,
cannot pacify the realm without punishments and executions.
Since this violates the precept against killing,
even if I serve the Buddha,
who will obtain blessings?"
Chéng replied:
"For an emperor to serve the Buddha,
he should embody reverence and sincere compliance,
and glorify the Three Jewels.
He should not be tyrannical or cruel,
nor harm the innocent.
As for the violent and wicked,
whom transformation cannot change,
those guilty must be executed,
and those evil must be punished.
But only execute those who should be executed,
and punish those who should be punished.
If one acts with tyrannical cruelty and willful indulgence,
killing those not guilty,
even if one lightly administers punishments according to law,
it will not avert calamity and misfortune.
I hope Your Majesty will curb desires and foster compassion,
extending it widely to all,
so that the Buddha's teachings may flourish eternally,
and blessings and fortune may endure far into the future."
Although Hǔ could not fully comply,
he benefited considerably.
Hǔ's ministers Zhāng Lí and Zhāng Liáng,
wealthy and devoted to Buddhism,
each erected a great pagoda.
Chéng said to them:
"Serving the Buddha lies in purity, lack of desire,
and a heart of compassion and pity.
Although you patrons outwardly revere the great Dharma,
your greed and stinginess remain unchecked,
your hunting is without limit,
and your accumulation of wealth knows no bounds.
You are incurring the sin of worldly indulgence—
how can you hope for any karmic reward?"
Lí and others were later all executed and exterminated.
At that time, there was also a prolonged drought,
lasting from the first month to the sixth.
Hǔ sent the crown prince to pray for rain at the Fǔkǒu west of Línzhāng,
but after a long time, none fell.
Hǔ ordered Chéng to go himself.
Immediately, two white dragons descended at the sacrificial site,
and that day heavy rain fell
across several thousand lǐ,
resulting in a great harvest that year.
The Róng and Mò tribes,
who previously did not know the Dharma,
hearing of Chéng's divine efficacy,
all bowed in worship from afar,
and were transformed without a word being spoken.
Chéng once sent a disciple to the western city market to buy incense.
After he departed,
Chéng told the other disciples
that in his palm he saw the incense-buying disciple being robbed at a certain place,
near death.
He then burned incense and chanted prayers,
rescuing him from afar.
The disciple later returned,
saying that on a certain day of a certain month at a certain place,
he was robbed by bandits,
and was about to be killed
when he suddenly smelled a fragrance.
The bandits, for no reason, became alarmed and said:
"The rescue troops have arrived!"
They abandoned him and fled. Hǔ was repairing an old pagoda in Línzhāng,
but lacked a dew-collecting basin.
Chéng said:
"Within the walls of Línzī city, there is an ancient King Ashoka pagoda.
Underground are a dew-collecting basin and a Buddha image.
Above it, trees and vegetation are lush;
you may dig and retrieve them."
He then drew a picture and gave it to the envoy.
Following his words, they dug and retrieved them,
and indeed obtained the basin and image.
Whenever Hǔ wished to attack Yān,
Chéng admonished him, saying:
"The state of Yān's fortune is not yet exhausted;
it will be difficult to conquer in the end."
After repeated military defeats,
he finally believed Chéng's warning.
As Chéng's teachings and transformations spread,
many people devoted themselves to Buddhism,
all constructing pagodas and temples,
vying to renounce the household life.
The genuine and false became intermixed,
giving rise to many transgressions.
Hǔ issued a decree inquiring of the Secretariat:
"The Buddha is called the World-Honored One,
and is venerated by the state.
Should commoners of the villages without rank or office
be permitted to serve the Buddha or not?
Moreover, all Buddhist monks should be lofty, pure, upright, and chaste,
their conduct capable and diligent,
before they can become religious practitioners.
Now monks are very numerous;
some are wicked evaders of corvée labor,
many of whom are unfit.
You may deliberate together."
The false Secretariat Editorial Director Wáng Dù memorialized:
"Now the king sacrifices
"sacrifices" originally written as "observes"
emended according to the Ming edition
to Heaven and Earth in the suburbs,
The worship of the hundred deities
is recorded in the sacrificial codes,
and the rites have their regular offerings.
Buddhism emerged from the Western Regions;
it is a foreign deity,
whose merits do not extend to the people,
and it is not a deity that the Son of Heaven and the various Chinese states should worship.
In the past, Emperor Míng of Hàn was moved by a dream,
and initially transmitted this doctrine,
permitting only people from the Western Regions to establish temples in the capital and cities,
to worship their deity.
Chinese people were not allowed to renounce the householder's life.
The Wèi, inheriting the Hàn
The original text has "Hòu" after "Hàn".
According to the Gāosēng Zhuàn, deleted.
system,
also followed the previous regulations.
Now the great Zhào has received the Mandate,
and follows the old statutes.
The systems of Chinese and barbarians differ.
Men and deities are distinct in their currents;
the foreign is not the same as the internal;
the offerings and sacrifices have different rites.
Those in the remote regions who submit and follow the rites
should not mix and confuse them.
The state may decree that the people of Zhào
are all not permitted to go to temples to burn incense and pay homage,
in order to honor the canonical rites.
All the officials and ministers,
down to the multitude of subordinates,
are to be prohibited by example.
Those who violate this
shall be punished the same as for illicit sacrifices.
Zhào people who are śramaṇas
shall return to wearing the clothing of the four classes of people."
This was the memorial submitted by the false Zhōngshū Lìng Wáng Bōtóng Dù.
Hǔ issued an edict saying:
"Dù's proposal states:
'Buddha is a foreign deity,
not one that the Son of Heaven and the various Chinese states should worship.'
I was born in a border region,
and unworthily encountered the cyclical fortune,
to rule over the various Xià
"Xià" originally written as "xià".
According to the Ming edition, corrected.
As for sacrificial rites,
they should combine and follow the native customs.
Buddha is a barbarian deity,
precisely the one who should be worshipped.
Now, regulations are set by those above,
to serve as models for all ages.
If affairs can be managed without deficiency,
why be constrained by previous dynasties?
Let the various barbarians of Yí and Zhào,
those who abandon their licentious rites and delight in serving Buddha,
all be permitted to follow the Way."
Thereupon, those who were lax in precepts
took advantage of this to become severe.
In the Yellow River, soft-shelled turtles originally did not live;
suddenly one was caught and presented to Hǔ.
Chéng saw it and sighed, saying:
"Huán Wēn will not enter the river for long."
Wēn's courtesy name was Yuánzǐ.
Later it indeed turned out as he said.
At that time, in Wèi County there was a displaced person,
none knew his clan or surname,
constantly wearing hempen jackets and cloth skirts,
begging in the market of Wèi County.
People of the time called him Márú.
His speech was extraordinary,
his demeanor like that of a madman.
When he begged and obtained rice or grain, he did not eat it,
but would scatter it on the main road,
saying he was feeding heavenly horses.
The Grand Administrator of Zhàoxīng, Jí Bá, arrested him and sent him to Hǔ.
Earlier, Chéng had said to Hǔ:
"Two hundred lǐ east of the state, on a certain month and day, a most extraordinary person will be sent;
do not kill him."
He indeed arrived on schedule.
Hǔ spoke with him,
but he uttered nothing unusual,
only saying, "Your Majesty will end beneath a single pillar hall."
Hǔ did not understand these words,
and ordered him sent to Chéng.
Márú said to Chéng:
"In the past, we met in the Yuánhé era;
suddenly it has come to this day.
The Róng have received the dark mandate;
the severed calendar will have its end.
Gold disperses into the soil;
the border wastes cannot be honored.
Driving away the traces of the numinous period;
none can stop its own virtue.
Descendant branches flourish with leaves;
their coming will accumulate;
how is this a time of rest?
Forever sigh over it!"
Chéng said:
"Heaven's cycle reaches its extreme;
adversity will not be sustained.
Nine woods, water brings difficulty;
nothing can be done through arts and learning.
Dark sages, though they exist in the world,
cannot base what must decay
Gāosēng Zhuàn has "decay" for "fragrance".
Long wandering in Jambudvīpa,
troubled and disturbed by these afflictions.
Walking, ascending to the cloudy firmament,
we shall meet in the space of empty wandering."
Chéng and Márú
conversed all day long;
no one could understand them.
Someone eavesdropped,
and only caught these few words,
