inferring they seemed to be discussing matters of several hundred years.
Hǔ sent him back to his home county by horse relay;
once outside the city walls,
he said he could walk,
saying:
"I have somewhere to pass by;
I cannot depart directly.
At Hé Kǒu Bridge,
you may wait for me."
The messenger galloped off as told,
but before reaching Hé Kǒu,
Márú was already on the bridge.
Examining his walking pace,
it was as if he flew.
Chéng had a disciple, Dào Jìn,
learned in both internal and external teachings,
who was highly regarded by Hǔ.
Once they spoke of recluses;
Hǔ said to Jìn:
"There is one Yáng Kē,
a subject of mine.
I summoned him for over ten years,
yet he did not defer to the royal command,
so I went to visit him.
He lay there arrogantly.
Though I may not rule over ten thousand states,
wherever my carriage goes,
heaven boils and earth surges.
Though I cannot make wood and stone kneel,
how can a commoner be so arrogantly aloof?
In ancient times, when Tàigōng went to Qí,
he first executed Huá Shì.
Tàigōng was a worthy sage;
could he have been mistaken?"
Jìn replied:
"In the past, Shùn showed favor to Pú Yī,
Yǔ called upon Bó Chéng,
Wèi honored Gān Mù,
Hàn praised Zhōu Dǎng,
Guǎn Níng did not respond to the Cáo clan,
Huángfǔ did not yield to the Jìn age.
Two sage emperors and four lords,
all commended their integrity,
wishing to stimulate and encourage the greedy and competitive,
to strengthen the pure wind.
I hope Your Majesty will follow the virtue of Shùn and Yǔ,
and not emulate Tàigōng's use of punishment.
A ruler's actions are always recorded;
how can we let the history of Zhào then lack a biography of reclusion?"
Hǔ was pleased with his words,
and immediately sent Kē back to where he lived,
dispatching ten households to supply him.
Jìn returned,
and fully reported this to Chéng.
Chéng smiled broadly and said:
"Your words were good,
but Kē's fate is already suspended!"
Later, when Qín Province troops rebelled,
Kē's disciples carried him on an ox fleeing west.
The garrison troops pursued and captured them,
and they were all killed.
Hǔ once napped during the day,
and dreamed of a flock of sheep carrying fish,
coming from the northeast.
Upon waking, he visited Chéng.
Chéng said:
"It is inauspicious.
Will the Xiānbēi possess the Central Plains?"
The Mùróng clan later indeed made it their capital.
Chéng once stayed with Hǔ in the central hall;
Chéng suddenly exclaimed in alarm:
"Yōu Province will have a fire disaster."
He then took wine and sprinkled it;
after a while, he laughed and said:
"Rescue has already been obtained."
Hǔ sent someone to verify in Yōu Province;
they reported:
"That day, fire broke out from the four gates;
a black cloud came from the southwest,
and a sudden rain extinguished it;
the rain also had a strong smell of wine."
In the fourteenth year of Hǔ's Jiànwǔ reign, in the seventh month,
Shí Xuān and Shí Tāo were about to plot to kill each other.
Xuān came to the temple at that time,
and sat together with Chéng.
A single bell on a pagoda rang alone.
Fótú Chéng said to Shí Xuān:
"Do you understand the bell's sound?
The bell says:
'The bearded one
('子' was originally written as '于',
changed according to the Biographies of Eminent Monks)
has crossed the Luò.'" Xuān changed color and said:
"What kind of talk is this?"
Chéng said misleadingly:
"This old bearded man, in practicing the Way,
cannot dwell in the mountains in silence.
Layered cushions and fine garments—
is this not crossing the Luò?"
Later, Shí Tāo arrived.
Chéng stared at him intently for a long time.
Tāo, frightened, asked Chéng.
Chéng said:
"I find the stench of your blood strange,
hence I was looking."
By the eighth month,
Chéng had ten disciples fasting in a separate room.
Chéng himself temporarily entered the eastern pavilion.
Shí Hǔ and Empress Dù came to inquire.
Chéng said:
"There is a traitor under your arm.
Within ten days,
from west of the Buddha's shrine
to east of the northern hall,
there will be bloodshed.
Be careful not to walk eastward."
Empress Dù said:
"Venerable, are you senile?
Where is there a traitor?"
Chéng then changed his words, saying:
"All that is received by the six senses
is entirely traitorous.
Old age naturally brings senility,
but let the young not be confused."
Thus he spoke in parable,
not making it explicit.
Two days later,
Xuān indeed sent men to kill Tāo in the Buddhist temple,
intending to use Hǔ's attendance at the funeral
to carry out a great treasonous act.
Because Hǔ had Chéng's prior warning,
he escaped harm.
When Xuān's plot was discovered and he was arrested,
Chéng advised Hǔ:
"Since he is Your Majesty's son,
why bring severe calamity upon him?
If Your Majesty can restrain anger and show mercy,
you may yet live over sixty more years.
If you must execute him,
Xuān will become a comet
sweeping down upon the Yè palace."
Hǔ did not listen.
He pierced Xuān's neck with an iron chain,
dragged him onto a pile of firewood, and burned him.
He arrested over three hundred of Xuān's officials,
had them torn apart by chariots and dismembered,
and threw them into the Zhāng River.
Chéng then ordered his disciples to end the fast
('室' was originally written as '空',
changed according to the Ming edition)
in the separate room.
Over a month later,
a demonic horse,
with its mane and tail appearing scorched,
entered through the Zhōngyáng Gate,
exited through the Xiǎnyáng Gate,
turned its head east towards the Eastern Palace but could not enter,
then ran northeast
and suddenly vanished.
Chéng, hearing of this, sighed:
"Disaster is approaching."
By the eleventh month,
Hǔ held a grand feast for his officials in the Tàiwǔ Front Hall.
Chéng chanted:
"Hall, oh hall!
Thorn-bushes will form a forest,
and will tear people's clothes."
Hǔ ordered the floor stones lifted to look beneath,
and found thorns growing there.
Chéng returned to the temple,
gazed at the Buddha statue and said:
"Regrettably, I could not adorn it."
He muttered to himself:
"Can I have three years?"
He answered himself: "No, no."
He said again:
"Two years? One year? A hundred days? One month?"
Answering himself "No," he fell silent.
Returning to his room,
he said to his disciple Fǎ Zuò:
"In the wùshēn year, turmoil will begin to sprout.
In the jǐyǒu year, the Shí clan will perish.
Before the chaos arrives,
I shall depart first."
He then sent someone to bid farewell to Hǔ, saying:
"All physical things must change;
body and life are not preserved.
This illusory body of mine, a poor monk,
has reached its time of transformation.
Having received exceptional grace,
I venture to inform you."
Hǔ said sorrowfully:
"I did not hear the Venerable was ill;
how suddenly you announce your end."
He personally went to the temple to offer consolation.
Chéng said to Hǔ:
"Entering and leaving life and death
is the constant way of the Dao.
Length of life is predetermined;
it is not for one to decide.
The Dao values practice and completeness;
virtue prizes unwavering diligence.
If one's conduct and discipline remain unblemished,
though gone, one is as if present.
To prolong life by transgression
is not my wish.
What remains on my mind now
is that the state holds Buddhist principles in heart,
and spares nothing in upholding the Dharma.
Temples have been built and raised,
magnificent and majestic.
For such virtue,
one should enjoy auspicious blessings.
Yet governance is harsh and severe;
punishments are cruel and accusations
(the original text lacked the character '罪',
added according to the Ming manuscript copy)
are excessive.
Outwardly, this violates
('违' was originally written as '为',
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy)
the sacred scriptures;
inwardly, it betrays the precepts.
Without self-reform and correction,
in the end there will be no Buddha's protection.
If you can humble your heart and change your thoughts,
bestowing kindness upon the common people,
then the state's fortune will be prolonged,
and both clergy and laity will rejoice and rely upon it.
Then, as my life ends and I depart,
I shall have no regrets."
Hǔ wept mournfully,
knowing Chéng would surely pass away.
He immediately had a tomb pit dug and a grave prepared.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month,
Chéng passed away at the Yègōng Temple.
This was the fourth year of the Yǒnghé era of Emperor Mù of Jìn.
Officials and commoners grieved sorrowfully;
the whole nation mourned and flocked to pay respects.
He was one hundred and seventeen years old.
He was buried west of Línzhāng at Zǐmò,
at the tomb site Hǔ had constructed.
Soon after, Liáng Dú rebelled.
The next year, Hǔ died.
Rǎn Mǐn usurped power and massacred,
and the Shí clan was completely exterminated.
Mǐn's childhood name was Jí nú (Thorn Slave),
fulfilling Chéng's earlier words about "thorn-bushes forming a forest."
On the left side of Chéng's chest was an opening,
four or five inches around,
piercing through to his abdomen.
Sometimes light shone from it.
He would sometimes stuff the hole with cotton wadding.
At night, when he wished to read,
he would pull out the wadding,
and the whole room would become brightly lit.
Also, on fasting days, he would go to the water's edge,
draw out his intestines to wash them,
then return them inside.
Chéng was eight chǐ tall,
with exceptionally graceful demeanor and beauty.
He profoundly understood the deep scriptures
and was also versed in worldly discourses.
On days when he lectured,
he correctly indicated the essential meaning,
making the beginning and end of the text
(the Ming manuscript copy has '如來之' for these three characters '始末文')
clear and comprehensible.
Moreover, his compassion extended to all living beings;
he rescued them from danger and suffering.
The two Shís were violent and fierce,
brutal and unprincipled in their harm.
If not for sharing their time with Chéng,
who could speak of it?
Yet the common people received benefits,
using them daily without knowing.
Buddha Tiān
(the Biographies of Eminent Monks has '调' for '天')
and Xūpútí, along with several dozen other renowned monks,
came from Tiānzhú and Kāngjū,
traveling tens of thousands of lǐ,
crossing the flowing sands on foot,
to seek instruction from Chéng.
Fán Fēi, Shì Dào'ān, and Zhōngshān's Zhú Fǎyǎ,
all traversed mountains and rivers,
to listen to Chéng's lectures.
They all profoundly grasped the essential principles,
delving into the subtle and profound.
Chéng himself said that his birthplace was over ninety thousand li from Yè,
he had renounced his family and entered the monastic life for one hundred and nine years,
never allowing wine to pass his lips.
He did not eat after noon,
did not step where it was forbidden by precepts,
and was without desires or cravings.
Those who studied under and followed him
often numbered in the hundreds,
and throughout his life, his disciples
amounted to nearly ten thousand.
In the provinces and commanderies he passed through,
he established eight hundred and ninety-three Buddhist temples.
The flourishing of his propagation of the Dharma
was unmatched by any before him.
Initially, Hǔ buried Chéng with his staff and alms bowl placed inside the coffin.
Later, when Rǎn Mǐn usurped the throne,
upon opening the coffin, only the bowl and staff were found,
with no corpse in sight.
Some said that on the day Chéng died,
someone saw him in the Liúshā Desert.
Hǔ suspected that he had not died,
and thus had the tomb opened and the coffin examined.
Only a stone was found inside.
Hǔ said:
"The stone is me.
My master buried me and then departed."
Not long after, Hǔ died.
Later, when Mùróng Jùn made Yè his capital,
residing in Shí Hǔ's palace,
he often dreamed of Hǔ biting his arm,
and believed that Shí Hǔ's spirit was haunting him.
He then ordered a search for Hǔ's corpse,
which was excavated at the Dōngmíng Hall.
The corpse was stiff and undecayed.
Jùn stepped on it and cursed:
"How dare a dead barbarian frighten a living Son of Heaven!
You built your palaces,
only to be plotted against by your own son,
let alone others."
He then had it whipped, disfigured, and insulted,
before throwing it into the Zhāng River.
The corpse leaned against a bridge pillar and did not drift away,
until the Qín general Wáng Měng retrieved and buried it.
This was the "one-pillar hall" that Má Rú had spoken of.
Later, when Fú Jiān attacked Yè,
Jùn's son Wěi was captured by Jiān's general Guō Shénhǔ,
which indeed verified the earlier dream about Hǔ.
Tián Róng's Zhào
(The original text had "Qǐ" for "Zhào."
Corrected based on the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.)
records state:
"Several years before Chéng's death,
he prepared his own tomb."
Since Chéng
(The original text had "Jì" for "Jì."
Corrected based on the Ming manuscript.)
knew that the tomb would inevitably be opened,
and that his corpse would not be inside,
how could he have prepared it in advance?
This is likely an error in Róng's account.
Chéng is sometimes called Fótú Chéng,
or Fótú Chéng,
both variations arising from differences in the Sanskrit pronunciation.
From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
Shì Dào'ān
Shì Dào'ān's surname was Wèi,
and he was from Fúliǔ in Chángshān.
His family had been Confucian scholars for generations,
but he lost his father's protection early on
and was raised by his maternal cousin, the Kǒng family.
At the age of seven,
he could recite texts after reading them twice,
which amazed his neighbors.
By the age of twelve, he left home to become a monk.
Though his mind was sharp and intelligent,
his appearance was quite ugly,
so his teacher did not hold him in high regard.
After several years,
he finally asked his teacher for a scripture.
He was given a single scroll of the *Biànyì Jīng*,
containing about five thousand characters.
Dào'ān took the scripture into the fields
and read it during breaks.
In the evening, upon returning,
he gave the scripture back to his teacher
and asked for another.
His teacher said:
"You haven't finished reading yesterday's scripture,
and you're asking for another already?"
He replied:
"I have already memorized it."
Though the teacher found this strange,
he said nothing
and gave him another scroll, the *Chéngjù Guāngmíng Jīng*,
containing no less than ten thousand characters.
Dào'ān took it as before,
and returned it in the evening.
The teacher tested him by covering the text.
He did not miss a single character.
The teacher was greatly astonished
and regarded him with respect and awe.
Later, he was ordained with full precepts
Original text: "jiè jù"
Corrected according to the Ming manuscript
and was allowed to travel for study.
He reached Yè,
where he met Fótúchéng
and took him as his teacher.
When the Shí clan's rule was about to fall into chaos,
he crossed the Yellow River southward with over four hundred disciples, including Huìyuǎn.
Traveling by night, they encountered thunder and rain,
advancing by the light of lightning.
Ahead, they found a household,
and saw inside the gate a horse post,
with a horse feedbag hanging between the posts,
capable of holding about one hú.
Dào'ān had someone call out for Lín Bǎishēng,
and Bǎishēng, thinking him a divine being,
received him with great hospitality.
Later, his disciples asked how he knew the man's name,
and Dào'ān said:
"Two trees make 'Lín' (林),
and the feedbag holds 'bǎi shēng' (百升)."
Upon reaching Xiāngyáng,
he again propagated the Buddhist teachings.
At that time, Xí Zàochǐ of Xiāngyáng was a brilliant and eloquent debater,
dominating the intellectual scene.
Having previously heard of Dào'ān's high reputation,
upon learning of his arrival,
he immediately went to visit him.
After taking his seat,
he declared:
"From all four seas, Xí Zàochǐ."
Dào'ān replied:
"Under the vast heavens, Shì Dào'ān."
People of the time considered this a famous exchange.
At that time, Fú Jiān had long heard of Dào'ān's fame,
and often said:
"In Xiāngyáng, there is Shì Dào'ān,
a vessel of divine talent.
I wish to summon him
to assist my person."
Later, he sent Fú Píngnán to attack Xiāngyáng,
and Dào'ān, along with Zhū Xù,
were both captured by Fú Jiān.
Fú Jiān said to his Vice Director of the Right, Quán Yì:
"I took Xiāngyáng with an army of a hundred thousand,
and gained only one and a half men."
Yì asked:
"Who are they?"
Fú Jiān said:
"Lord Ān is one man,
and Xí Zàochǐ is half a man."
After arriving,
he resided at the Wǔchóng Temple in Cháng'ān.
Initially, Fú Jiān had inherited the chaos left by the Shí clan,
but by then, the households were prosperous,
and the four quarters were largely pacified.
Only the region of Jiànyè remained,
unable to be subdued.
Whenever he spoke with his courtiers,
he never failed to express his desire to pacify Jiāngzuǒ.
His younger brother, the Duke of Píngyáng, Fú Róng, along with court ministers Shí Yuè and Yuán Shào,
all earnestly remonstrated,
but ultimately could not sway him.
Since everyone knew Fú Jiān trusted and respected Dào'ān,
they jointly requested of him:
"The sovereign is planning a campaign to the southeast;
can you, sir, not speak a word for the sake of the common people?"
It happened that Fú Jiān was going out to the Eastern Park,
and ordered Dào'ān to ride in the imperial carriage with him.
Vice Director Quán Yì remonstrated:
"Your servant has heard that in the Son of Heaven's ritual carriage,
the Palace Attendant accompanies him.
Dào'ān has mutilated his body [by becoming a monk];
how can he share the carriage?"
Fú Jiān flushed with anger and said:
"Lord Ān's virtue and wisdom are worthy of honor.
I consider the whole realm insufficient [to match him];
the honor of sharing my carriage
does not match his virtue."
He immediately ordered the Vice Director to assist Dào'ān into the carriage.
Soon after, turning to Dào'ān, he said:
"I intend to travel south with you to Wú and Yuè,
marshaling the six armies for an imperial tour,
ascending Kuàijī to gaze upon the vast sea—
is that not delightful?"
Dào'ān replied:
"Your Majesty responds to Heaven and rules the age,
possessing the wealth of eight provinces.
Residing in the central lands, you govern all within the four seas.
You should settle your spirit in non-action
and rival the glory of Yáo and Shùn.
Now you wish to use a million troops
to seek that low-lying land.
Moreover, the southeastern corner
is low-lying and its climate harsh.
Yǔ traveled there and stopped;
Shùn toured there and died;
the King of Qín went there and did not return.
In this humble monk's view,
this is not something a foolish heart would agree with.
The Duke of Píngyáng is your esteemed relative,
Shí Yuè is a senior minister;
they both said it should not be done,
yet you still rejected their advice.
This humble monk is insignificant and shallow;
my words will certainly not be heeded.
But since I have received your generous treatment,
I must exhaust my sincere loyalty."
Fú Jiān said:
"It is not that my land is not vast,
nor that my people are insufficient to govern.
I wish to discern Heaven's will,
to clarify where the great destiny lies.
Touring according to the season
is also recorded in ancient classics.
If it is as you say, Master,
then did the former emperors and kings lack texts about inspecting the regions?"
Dào'ān said:
"If the imperial carriage must move,
you could first proceed to Luòyáng,
display your might and accumulate sharpness,
issue a proclamation to Jiāngnán.
If they do not submit,
it will not be too late to attack them."
Fú Jiān did not listen.
He sent the Duke of Píngyáng, Fú Róng, and others with a vanguard of 250,000 elite troops,
while he personally led 600,000 infantry and cavalry,
reaching Xūchéng.
Jìn sent General Zhēnglǔ Xiè Shí and Xúzhōu Governor Xiè Xuán to resist them.
Fú Jiān's forward army suffered a great defeat at Bāgōngshān,
and the Jìn army pursued them north for over thirty lǐ.
Fú Jiān fled alone on horseback,
just as had been advised.
Dào'ān annotated various scriptures,
but feared his interpretations might not accord with principle.
So he vowed:
"If what I have explained is not too far
Original text: "dào"
Corrected according to the Ming manuscript
from the principle,
may I see an auspicious sign."
Then he dreamed of a Daoist monk,
with white hair and long eyebrows,
who said to Dào'ān:
"The scriptures you have annotated
are very much in accord with the principle.
I cannot enter Nirvāṇa;
I dwell in the Western Regions,
and shall assist in their transmission.
You should regularly set out offerings of food."
Later, when the ten
Original text: "rì"
Corrected according to the *Gāosēng Zhuàn*
recitations of the Vinaya arrived,
Venerable Yuǎn then knew that the monk in the dream was Piṇḍola.
Later, in the twenty-first year of the Jiànyuán era of Qín, on the twenty-seventh day of the first month,
suddenly a strange monk,
of very ordinary and ugly appearance,
came to the temple seeking lodging.
Since the temple quarters were narrow,
he was placed in the lecture hall.
At that time, the *Weinuó* was on duty in the hall.
At night, they saw this monk
entering and exiting through the window,
and immediately reported it to Ān.
Ān, startled, rose to greet him with courtesy and inquired,
asking his purpose for coming?
He replied:
"I came specifically for you."
Ān said:
"I consider my sins deep,
how could I be liberated?"
He answered:
"It is very possible to be liberated."
Ān asked about the place of his next rebirth,
whereupon he gestured with his hand toward the northwest sky,
and immediately the clouds parted,
revealing in full view the supreme and wondrous bliss of Tuṣita Heaven.
In the second month, on the eighth day of that year, Ān suddenly announced to the assembly:
"I am about to depart."
That day, after the meal offering,
he passed away without illness,
and was buried within the city at the Wǔjí Temple.
This was in the first year of the Tàiyuán era of the Jìn dynasty.
From the "Biographies of Eminent Monks."
Shì Dào'ān's original surname was Wèi,
from Fúliǔ in Chángshān
(present-day Jìxiàn, Héběi),
and his family had been scholars for generations.
His parents passed away early,
and he was raised from a young age by his maternal cousin, the Kǒng family.
At seven years old, he began studying,
able to memorize texts after a single reading,
reciting them immediately,
which amazed and astonished his neighbors.
At twelve, he was tonsured and entered monastic life.
Although his nature was intelligent and sharp,
because his appearance was dark and ugly,
he was not highly regarded by his teacher.
Only after several years did he begin requesting sutras to study.
His teacher gave him a scroll of the "Biànyì Sūtra,"
about five thousand characters long.
Dào'ān took the sutra to work in the fields,
reading it during breaks.
In the evening, after finishing work,
he returned the sutra to his teacher
and borrowed another to read.
His teacher said:
"You haven't finished reading the sutra I gave you yesterday.
Why do you want another?"
Dào'ān replied:
"I have already memorized yesterday's sutra."
Although the teacher was astonished,
he said nothing
and gave him another scroll, the "Chéngjù Guāngmíng Jīng," no less than ten thousand characters.
After receiving it,
he read it just like the previous one.
The next evening, after finishing work, he returned it again.
The teacher held the sutra and asked him to recite it,
and he did so without a single error.
The teacher was greatly amazed,
respected his talent,
and changed his original attitude toward him.
Later, he ordained him with full precepts
and even specially allowed him to travel and study freely.
Dào'ān went to Yèdū,
where he met Fótúchéng
and became his disciple.
Later, when the Shí clan regime was about to fall into internal turmoil,
Dào'ān, along with his disciple Huìyuǎn and over four hundred others,
crossed the Yellow River and headed south.
One night, while traveling, they encountered a thunderstorm,
and they advanced by the light of lightning.
As they walked,
a household appeared before them,
with a hitching post inside the gate
and a feed bag hanging between two posts,
capable of holding one hú
(one hundred shēng equals one hú)
of grain.
Dào'ān had someone call for Lín Bǎishēng,
and Lín Bǎishēng said Dào'ān was a divine man,
so he received them with generous hospitality.
Later, his disciples asked how he knew that person's name,
and Dào'ān said:
"Because the two posts form the character 'Lín,'
and that feed bag can hold 'Bǎishēng.'"
Upon reaching Xiāngyáng,
Dào'ān began preaching the Dharma there.
At that time, there was a Xí Záochǐ in Xiāngyáng,
eloquent and skilled in debate,
whose fame spread far and wide.
Originally, he had gained fame because of Dào'ān,
and upon hearing that Dào'ān had arrived in Xiāngyáng,
he went to visit him.
After seating themselves,
Xí Záochǐ boasted:
"Sìhǎi Xí Záochǐ,"
meaning
his reputation spread throughout the four seas;
Dào'ān then said:
"Mítiān Shì Dào'ān," meaning
under the vast sky, no one does not know the name Shì Dào'ān.
This exchange was highly renowned at the time,
especially Dào'ān's reply,
which became a celebrated couplet of the era.
Fú Jiān had long heard of Shì Dào'ān's reputation
and often said to others:
"In Xiāngyáng, there is a Shì Dào'ān,
a man of divine talent.
I intend to summon him
to assist me."
Later, he sent Fú Píng south to attack Xiāngyáng,
and both Dào'ān and Zhǔ Xù were captured and sent to Fú Jiān.
Fú Jiān said to his minister Quán Yì:
"I used a hundred thousand troops to capture Xiāngyáng,
only to obtain one and a half men."
Quán Yì asked:
"Who are this one and a half men?"
Fú Jiān said:
"Dào'ān is one man,
and Xí Záochǐ is half a man."
After Dào'ān arrived in Cháng'ān,
he resided at the Wǔchóng Temple in Cháng'ān.
Fú Jiān had initially inherited the chaotic realm of the Shí clan.
By now, the population had flourished, and life was prosperous.
The surrounding states were largely pacified.
Only the region of Jiànyè
remained unconquered.
He often discussed with his ministers,
constantly desiring to pacify the area east of the Yangtze River.
Fú Jiān's younger brother, Píngyáng Gōng Fú Róng, along with court ministers Shí Yuè and Yuán Shào,
earnestly advised against it,
but he could not change his mind.
They believed Dào'ān was the person Fú Jiān trusted and respected most,
so they jointly requested him:
"Our lord intends to send troops to the southeast.
How can you not speak a word for the sake of the people!"
It happened that Fú Jiān was coming out of the Eastern Garden,
and he ordered Dào'ān to sit beside him in his carriage.
Quán Yì remonstrated:
"I have heard that the Son of Heaven's carriage
should only be accompanied by the Shìzhōng.
Dào'ān, with his shaved head and altered appearance,
should not sit beside you."
Fú Jiān sternly rebuked him:
"Dào'ān Gōng's virtue commands respect.
I would not trade the entire world for him.
The honor of sharing a carriage with me
still does not match his virtue."
He immediately ordered Quán Yì to assist Dào'ān into the carriage.
Shortly after,
Fú Jiān looked at Dào'ān and said to him:
"I am about to travel south with you to Wú and Yuè,
leading the six armies on a southern inspection tour,
ascending Kuàijī to gaze upon the vast sea.
Wouldn't that be a delightful thing?"
Dào'ān said:
"Your Majesty, in accordance with the Mandate of Heaven, governs the realm.
Now you possess the territory of eight provinces,
residing in the Central Plains and ruling the four directions.
You should rest your spirit, act without action, and nurture life,
competing in prosperity with the eras of Yáo and Shùn.
Now you wish to use a million troops
to contend for that barren land.
Moreover, the southeast is remote, with harsh climate,
making military movements extremely unfavorable.
In the past, Emperor Yǔ traveled there but could not advance;
Emperor Shùn died there during an inspection tour;
and the King of Qín went there but never returned.
In this humble monk's view,
I do not agree to sending troops to Wú and Yuè.
Píngyáng Gōng is your closest relative,
and Shí Yuè is a senior minister.
They unanimously said it should not be done,
yet you still refused.
This humble monk is of such lowly status,
my words will surely not be heeded.
However, since I have received Your Majesty's generous treatment,
it is only right that I exhaust my utmost sincerity."
Fú Jiān said:
"It is not because the land is not vast
or the population not large
that it is insufficient to govern.
It is to expand the influence of Heaven's will
and demonstrate that the Mandate of Heaven is omnipresent.
I, in accordance with the times, inspect the four directions,
which also aligns with the precedents of former kings.
If it were as you, Master, have said,
then wouldn't the earlier emperors have had no records of inspecting the four directions?"
Dào'ān said:
"If the imperial carriage must set out on an inspection tour,
you could first go to Luòyáng,
resist the threat of powerful enemies there,
accumulate your strength,
and issue a proclamation of conquest to the lands south of the Yangtze.
If they do not submit,
then raising troops to punish them would not be too late."
Fú Jiān did not listen.
He dispatched Píngyáng Gōng Fú Róng and others with a vanguard of two hundred fifty thousand elite troops,
while Fú Jiān personally led six hundred thousand infantry and cavalry.
Leading his army southward,
he arrived at Xūchéng.
The Eastern Jin dispatched General Zhenglu Xiè Shí and Xúzhōu Governor Xiè Xuán to command troops and engage in battle.
Fú Jiān's vanguard forces suffered a major defeat at Bāgōng Mountain,
and the Jin army advanced northward for over thirty li.
Fú Jiān fled alone on horseback,
just as Dào'ān had admonished him.
Dào'ān annotated many Buddhist scriptures,
fearing that his annotations might not align with the teachings,
so he made a vow:
"If what I have said does not deviate greatly from the Buddhist principles,
I pray that the Buddha will reveal an auspicious sign."
Then he dreamed of a Daoist monk,
with white hair covering his head,
and long eyebrows,
who told Dào'ān:
"The scriptures you have annotated
are very much in accordance with Buddhist principles.
I cannot enter the muddy secular world,
but residing in the Western Regions will help you attain understanding.
You should regularly make offerings."
Later, when the *Shísònglǜ* arrived,
Yuǎngōng then realized that the monk in the dream was the head of a guest.
In the twenty-first year of the Jiànyuán era of the Former Qin,
on the twenty-seventh day of the first lunar month,
suddenly an unusual monk,
with a very dirty and ugly appearance,
came to the temple seeking lodging.
Because the temple rooms were narrow,
he was placed in the lecture hall.
At that time, the *wéinà* was on duty guarding the hall,
and at night he saw this monk entering and exiting through the window.
He immediately reported it to Dào'ān.
Dào'ān hurriedly got up,
and inquired of him according to etiquette,
asking about his purpose.
The monk replied:
"I came specifically for you."
Dào'ān said:
"I feel deeply burdened by my sins,
how could I possibly be liberated?"
The monk replied:
"You can absolutely be saved."
Dào'ān asked where he would be reborn in the next life,
and the monk pointed toward the northwest in the air,
where the clouds and mist suddenly parted,
clearly revealing the wondrous and supreme Tuṣita Heaven.
On the eighth day of the second lunar month of that year, Dào'ān suddenly announced to everyone:
"I am about to depart!"
On that day, after completing the fasting rituals,
he passed away without any illness,
and was buried in the Wǔjí Temple within the city.
This year was the first year of the Tàiyuán era of Jin.
Jiūmóluóshí,
which translates as "Youthful Longevity,"
was a native of India.
He was well-versed in the sutras, vinaya, and treatises,
and his teachings spread throughout the Western Regions.
When he traveled east to Qiūcí,
the king of Qiūcí had a golden lion throne built for him to sit upon.
At that time, Fú Jiān had usurped the title of emperor in Guānzhōng,
and the king of the Qiánbù kingdom and the younger brother of the king of Qiūcí came to pay homage to Jiān.
Jiān granted them an audience,
and the two kings persuaded Jiān, saying:
"The Western Regions abound in rare treasures;
we request troops to pacify them,
so that they may submit and become attached to the interior."
In the thirteenth year of Jiān's Jiànyuán era, in the first month,
the Grand Astrologer reported:
"A star has appeared in the celestial division corresponding to foreign lands;
this indicates that a great and wise virtuous person will enter to assist the Middle Kingdom."
Jiān said, "I have heard that in the Western Rong there is Jiūmóluóshí,
and in Xiāngyáng there is the śramaṇa Dào'ān.
Could it not be one of them?"
He immediately dispatched envoys to seek them out.
By the seventeenth year, in the second month,
the king of Shànshàn and the king of Qiánbù again persuaded Jiān to request troops for a western campaign.
In the eighteenth year, in the ninth month,

Jiān sent his valiant general Lǚ Guāng and the Lingjiāng General Jiāng Fēi, leading the king of Qiánbù and the king of Chēshī, among others, with seventy thousand troops to campaign west against Qiūcí.
Before their departure,
Jiān held a farewell banquet for Guāng at Jiànzhāng,
and said to Guāng:
"A sovereign rules in accordance with Heaven,
taking the loving care of the common people as fundamental.
How could I covet their land and attack them?
It is precisely to win over those from afar.
I have heard that in the Western Regions there is Jiūmóluóshí,
who deeply understands the dharma characteristics,
is skilled in yīn and yáng,
and is a master for later learners.
I long for him greatly.
Wise and sagely men
are the great treasures of a state.
If you conquer Qiūcí,
immediately send Shí by relay post."
Before Guāng's army arrived,
Shí said to the king of Qiūcí, Bái Chún:
"The fortune of the state is declining.
Moreover, a formidable enemy approaches from the east.
You should respectfully submit to them;
do not resist their advance."
Chún did not heed this and fought,
so Guāng subsequently defeated Qiūcí,
killed Chún,
and established Chún's younger brother, Zhèn, as ruler.
After Guāng captured Shí,
he could not gauge his wisdom and capacity.
Seeing that he was still young,
he treated him as an ordinary man and made sport of him,
forcing him to marry the daughter of the king of Qiūcí.
Shí refused and would not accept,
pleading with utmost earnestness.
Guāng said:
"The conduct of a Daoist priest
does not surpass that of his late father.
What reason is there for refusal?"
He then made him drink strong wine
and confined them together in a secret chamber.
Shí, being pressed to the extreme,
ultimately compromised his integrity.
Sometimes they made him ride an ox or a vicious horse,
hoping to make him fall.
Shí always bore the humiliation with patience,
showing no change in expression,
and Guāng merely felt ashamed.
As Guāng was returning along the way,
he encamped the army at the foot of a mountain,
and the officers and soldiers had already rested.
Shí said:
"We cannot stay here;
we are sure to encounter difficulties.
We should move the army to the ridge."
Guāng did not accept this advice.
That night,
there was indeed heavy rain,
and flash floods suddenly arose,
with water several zhàng deep,
killing several thousand men.
Only then did Guāng begin to regard Shí with secrecy and wonder.
Shí said to Guāng:
"This is an inauspicious and perilous place;
it is not suitable to linger.
Considering the circumstances and divining the signs,
you should quickly speak of returning.
Along the way, there will surely be a fortunate land where you can dwell."
Guāng followed his advice.
When they reached Liángzhōu,
they heard that Fú Jiān had already been killed by Yáo Chàng.
Guāng's three armies donned mourning garments
and held a grand lament south of the city.
Thereupon, he usurped the title of emperor outside the passes,
calling his reign era Tài'ān.
In the second year of Tài'ān, in the first month,
there was a great wind in Gūzāng.
Shí said:
"This is an inauspicious wind;
it indicates there will be treachery and rebellion,
but it will subside of its own accord without effort."
Soon after, Liáng Qiān and Péng Huǎng rebelled one after the other,
but they were quickly annihilated.
By the second year of Guāng's Lóngfēi era,
the Hú people of Lúshuǐ in Línsōng, Zhāngyè, Jǔqú Nánchéng and his cousin Méngxùn rebelled,
pushing the Jiànkāng Grand Administrator Duàn Yè to be their leader.
Guāng dispatched his son by a concubine, the Qínzhōu Governor, Duke of Tàiyuán, Zuǎn,
to lead fifty thousand troops to suppress them.
Contemporary opinion held that Yè and his followers were a motley crew,
while Zuǎn had a formidable reputation,
so victory was assured.
Guāng consulted Shí about this,
and Shí said:
"Observing this campaign,
I do not see its advantage."
Subsequently, Zuǎn was defeated at Hélí.
Soon after, Guō □ stirred rebellion,
and Zuǎn abandoned his main army to return lightly,
only to be defeated by □,
barely escaping with his life.
Guāng's Secretariat Director Zhāng Zī
was elegant and refined in literary composition.
Guāng held him in high regard.
When Zī fell ill,
Guāng sought far and wide for treatment to save him.
There was a foreign monk, Luó Chā,
who claimed he could cure Zī's illness.
Guāng was pleased
and rewarded him lavishly.
Shí knew that Chā was deceitful
and told Zī:
"Chā cannot do it;
he will only cause trouble and expense.
Though the workings of fate are hidden,
they can be tested through events."
He then took a five-colored silk cord,
tied it into a knot,
burned it to ashes, and threw them into water,
saying that if the ashes emerged from the water and returned to the form of a cord,
the illness could not be cured.
In a moment,
the ashes gathered and floated to the surface,
resuming their original shape as a cord.
Since Chā's treatment proved ineffective,
Zī died a few days later.
Not long after,
Guāng also passed away,
and his son Shào succeeded him.
A few days later,
Guāng's son by a concubine, Zuǎn, killed Shào and proclaimed himself ruler,
calling his reign era Yuán Xiánníng.
In the second year of Xiánníng,
a pig gave birth to a piglet
with one body and three heads.
A dragon emerged from the well in the eastern wing,
came to the front of the hall and coiled up to rest,
but by dawn it had disappeared.
Zuǎn considered this an auspicious omen
and named the great hall "Dragon Soaring Hall."
Soon after, a black dragon ascended at the Dāngyáng Jiǔgōng Gate,
and Zuǎn renamed it "Dragon Rising Gate."
Shí memorialized, saying:
"Recently, a hidden dragon has emerged and roamed,
and a monstrous pig has brought anomaly.
The dragon belongs to the yīn category;
its appearances and disappearances should occur at proper times.
But now it appears repeatedly,
which constitutes a calamitous omen.
There will surely be a rebellion of inferiors plotting against their superior.
You should restrain yourself and cultivate virtue
to respond to Heaven's warning."
Zuǎn did not accept this
and played a board game with Shí.
While capturing a piece, he said:
"Chop off the head of the Hú slave!"
Shí said:
"You cannot chop off the Hú slave's head;
the Hú slave will chop off someone's head."
These words had meaning,
but Zuǎn never realized it.
Guāng's younger brother, Bǎo,
had a son named Chāo,
whose childhood nickname was Hú nú ("Hú slave").
Later, Chāo indeed killed Zuǎn and beheaded him,
establishing his elder brother Lóng as ruler.
Only then did people understand the meaning of Shí's words.
Shí stayed in Liáng for many years.
Since Lǚ Guāng and his sons did not promote the Buddhist teachings,
he kept his profound understanding concealed,
with no opportunity to propagate them.
Fú Jiān had already perished,
so they never met.
When Yáo Chàng usurped the throne in Guānzhōng,
he also admired Shí's lofty reputation
and sincerely extended an invitation to him.
Lü Guang, knowing that Kumārajīva was highly intelligent and resourceful,
feared he might offer counsel to Yao Chang,
and thus did not permit him to enter the east.
After Yao Chang passed away,
his son Yao Xing succeeded to the throne,
and once again sent envoys to respectfully invite him.
In the third year of Hóngshǐ, during the third month,
there were trees with intertwined branches,
growing in the temple courtyard of the Xiāoyáo Garden,
and scallions transformed into lotuses,
which were considered auspicious omens,
signifying that a wise man should enter.
By the fifth month,
Yao Xing dispatched Duke Lǒngxī, Shuòdé, to campaign west against Lü Long,
and Lü Long's army was utterly defeated.
By the ninth month,
Lü Long submitted a petition surrendering,
and only then was it possible to welcome Kumārajīva into the pass,
arriving in Cháng'ān on the twentieth day of the twelfth month of that year.
Yao Xing treated him with the rites due to a National Preceptor,
showing him great favor and honor.
Since the great Dharma had spread eastward,
beginning with Emperor Ming of Hàn,
passing through Wèi and Jìn,
the scriptural texts and treatises gradually increased,
but those translated by Zhi and Zhu,
often suffered from rigid wording and forced interpretations.
Yao Xing had revered the Three Jewels from a young age,
and was keenly devoted to lectures and assemblies.
Once Kumārajīva arrived,
he was invited into the Xīmíng Pavilion and the Xiāoyáo Garden to translate numerous scriptures.
Kumārajīva, being well-versed in recitation,
thoroughly comprehended everything,
and moreover could speak Chinese,
making his phonetic translations fluent and smooth.
Upon reviewing the old translations,
he found many errors and deviations in meaning,
all due to earlier translators missing the original intent,
and not corresponding with the Sanskrit texts.
Therefore, Yao Xing had over eight hundred monks including Sēngqì, Sēngqiān, Fǎqīn, Dàoliú, Dàohéng, Dàobiāo, Sēngruì, and Sēngzhào,
consult and receive Kumārajīva's guidance.
He further ordered the translation of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Kumārajīva held the Sanskrit text,
while Yao Xing held the old translation,
to compare and collate them.
Where the new text differed from the old,
the meanings were all perfectly coherent,
and everyone was satisfied and convinced,
all praising with delight.
Kumārajīva, as a person, had a clear and penetrating spirit and insight,
lofty and standing out from the crowd,
comprehending according to the situation,
with few who could match him.
Moreover, he was sincerely benevolent and kind-hearted,
with universal love as his core,
humble and skilled in guidance,
tirelessly working all day long.
Yao Xing often said to Kumārajīva:
"Great Master, your intelligence and transcendent understanding,
are unmatched in the world.
If one day you pass away,
how can we let the Dharma seed have no successor?"
Thus, he gave him ten courtesans,
forcing him to accept them.
From that time onward,
he no longer resided in the monks' quarters,
but had a separate residence established for him,
with abundant provisions supplied.
Whenever he gave lectures,
he would often first use a parable himself,
saying it was like a lotus flower growing from foul mud:
one should only pluck the lotus flower,
and not take the foul mud.
Earlier, while in Qiūcí,
Kumārajīva had received the Vinaya from the Vinaya master Bēimóluóchā.
Later, Bēimóluóchā came to Guānzhōng,
and when Kumārajīva heard of his arrival, he was delighted,
treating him with the utmost respect and courtesy as his teacher.
Bēimóluóchā did not know about the forced incident,
and thus asked Kumārajīva:
"In the land of Hàn,
you have great and weighty karmic connections;
how many disciples
have received the Dharma from you?"
Kumārajīva replied:
"In the Hàn realm, the sūtras and vinaya are not yet complete;
the new sūtras and various treatises, etc.,
are mostly what I have transmitted and translated.
Three thousand disciples
have all received the Dharma from me.
However, my karmic obstructions are deep,
and thus I do not receive the respect due a teacher."
Also, the bhikṣu Bēidù was in Péngchéng,
and upon hearing that Kumārajīva was in Cháng'ān,
sighed and said:
"I played with this fellow,
and we parted over three hundred years ago,
with no news or expectation of meeting again.
It will be delayed until we meet in a future life."
A few days before Kumārajīva's end,
he felt his four elements were not healing,
and recited three divine mantras,
instructing his foreign disciples to chant them to save him,
but before they could exert effort,
he felt his condition turning critical,
and so, with great effort despite his illness,
bid farewell to the assembly of monks, saying:
"We met because of the Dharma,
yet I have not fully devoted my heart.
Facing the afterlife,
what words can express my sorrow?
I, in my ignorance,
have presumptuously undertaken translation and exposition.
All the sūtras and treatises I have translated amount to over three hundred scrolls,
and only the Ten Recitations Vinaya,
I did not have time to edit and abridge.
Preserving its original intent,
there surely will be no errors.
I hope that all I have expounded,
will be transmitted to later generations,
and all together widely propagated.
Now, before the assembly,
I make a sincere and truthful vow:
If what I have transmitted is without error,
then after my body is cremated,
my tongue shall not be burnt to ashes."
He passed away in Cháng'ān on the twentieth day of the eighth month in the eleventh year of Hóngshǐ of the false Qín,
which was the fifth year of Yìxī of Jìn.
Following foreign custom, his body was cremated by fire in the Xiāoyáo Garden,
the firewood consumed and his form reduced to fragments,
yet only his tongue remained unburnt.
From the "Biographies of Eminent Monks."
Kumārajīva,
meaning "Youthful Longevity" in translation,
was a native of Tiānzhú,
proficient in the three baskets of Buddhist scriptures: Sūtra, Vinaya, and Śāstra.
He traveled and taught in the Western Regions,
and when he journeyed east to Qiūcí,
the King of Qiūcí built a golden lion throne to seat him.
At that time, Fú Jiān ruled Guānzhōng.
The King of the Former Region from a foreign land, along with the younger brother of the King of Qiūcí, came to pay homage to Fú Jiān.
Fú Jiān summoned them,
and the two kings said to Fú Jiān:
"The Western Regions have many rare treasures,
we request you send troops to campaign,
and make them submit."
In the thirteenth year of Jiànyuán,
during the first month,
the Grand Astrologer reported:
"A constellation has appeared in the foreign border regions,
indicating that a great virtuous and worthy person will come to assist the Middle Kingdom."
Fú Jiān said:
"I have heard that in the Western Regions there is a Kumārajīva,
and in Xiāngyáng there is the monk Dào'ān.
Could it be him?
Immediately send envoys to seek him."
By the seventeenth year of Jiànyuán, in the second month,
the former King of the Former Region from Shànshàn and others came again to persuade Fú Jiān,
requesting him to send troops to campaign west.
In the eighteenth year, in the ninth month,
Fú Jiān dispatched the valiant general Lü Guang and General Lingjiāng Jiāng Fēi,
accompanied by the King of the Former Region and the King of Chēshī,
leading seventy thousand troops to campaign west against Qiūcí.
Before departure,
Fú Jiān held a farewell banquet for Lü Guang at Jiànzhāng Palace,
and said to him:
"A sovereign rules the world in accordance with the Mandate of Heaven,
taking compassion for all living beings as fundamental.
How can one attack others merely to covet their land?
It is precisely because I cherish those distant mountain people.
I have heard that in the Western Regions there is a man named Kumārajīva,
who is deeply versed in Buddhist teachings,
skilled in the study of yīn and yáng,
and serves as a model for later learners.
I think of him very much.
Wise and virtuous men are treasures of the state.
If you conquer Qiūcí,
immediately send Kumārajīva back."
Before Lü Guang's army reached Qiūcí,
Kumārajīva said to the King of Qiūcí, Bái Chún:
"The fortune of the state has already declined,
and moreover, a powerful enemy approaches from the east.
You should submit obediently,
and not engage them in battle."
Bái Chún did not heed his advice,
and sent troops to engage Lü Guang in battle.
Lü Guang defeated Qiūcí,
killed Bái Chún,
and his younger brother Bái Zhèn became the King of Qiūcí.
After Lü Guang obtained Kumārajīva,
he did not know the extent of his learning,
and seeing that he was still young,
treated him as an ordinary person,
and moreover teased him,
forcing him to marry the daughter of the King of Qiūcí.
Kumārajīva strenuously refused,
pleading bitterly with Lü Guang,
but Lü Guang said:
"The conduct of a Daoist priest,
is no different from that of your father.
Why refuse?"
Lǚ Guāng made him drink fine wine,
and locked him in a room with his wife.
After being forced to consummate the marriage with his wife,
Shī lost his chastity.
Lǚ Guāng also made him ride oxen or untamed horses,
hoping he would fall and be humiliated.
Shī endured these humiliations,
showing no sign of resentment or anger,
so Lǚ Guāng could only feel ashamed.
On the way back to Guānzhōng,
Lǚ Guāng stationed the army at the foot of a mountain.
After the soldiers had rested,
Shī said:
"We should not stay in this place;
staying here is dangerous.
We should move the army to flat ground."
Lǚ Guāng did not heed his advice.
That night,
it indeed rained heavily,
causing a flash flood,
with water rising several zhang,
drowning thousands of people.
From then on,
Lǚ Guāng secretly admired him as an extraordinary man.
Shī said to Guāng:
"This perilous place
is not suitable for long stays.
Upon reflection,
we should hurry back.
On the way to Guānzhōng, there must be good places to stay."
Lǚ Guāng followed his advice.
When the troops reached Liángzhōu,
they heard that Fú Jiān had been killed by Yáo Cháng.
Lǚ Guāng's entire army donned mourning attire,
and the troops approached the southern city.
Lǚ Guāng then occupied Liángzhōu,
declaring himself the ruler of Liáng,
with the era name Tài'ān.
In the second year of Tài'ān, in the first month,
a fierce wind blew in Gūzāng.
Shī said:
"This is an ominous wind.
It foretells treacherous rebellion,
but there is no need to send troops, as the rebellion will subside on its own."
Not long after,
Liáng Qiān and Péng Huǎng successively plotted rebellion,
but they were quickly suppressed.
By the second year of Lǚ Liáng's Lóngfēi era,
the Hú people Qú Nánchéng and his cousin Jǔqú Méngxùn from Lín Sōng Lú Shuǐ in Zhāngyè rebelled,
and they elected Duàn Yè, the governor of Jiànkāng, as their ruler.
Lǚ Guāng dispatched his son Lǚ Zuǎn, the governor of Qínzhōu and Duke of Tàiyuán,
with fifty thousand troops to suppress the rebellion.
At the time, people commented that
Duàn Yè's forces were a motley crew,
and Lǚ Zuǎn had long been renowned for his prestige,
so this expedition
was sure to achieve complete victory.
Lǚ Guāng consulted Jiūmóluóshí about this matter,
and Shī said:
"In my view, this campaign
will not succeed."
Later, Lǚ Zuǎn was defeated at Hélí.
Soon after, Guō □ stirred up trouble,
and Lǚ Zuǎn rashly ordered the army to retreat.
As expected, he was defeated by Guō □,
and only he alone escaped back.
Lǚ Guāng's Zhōngshū Jiān, Zhāng Zī,
was highly talented in literature,
and was gentle and refined in character.
He was greatly valued by Lǚ Guāng.
When Zhāng Zī fell ill,
Lǚ Guāng spared no expense to save and treat him.
There was a foreigner named Luó Chā,
who claimed he could cure Zhāng Zī's illness.
Lǚ Guāng was overjoyed
and gave him many gifts.
Jiūmóluóshí knew that Luó Chā was lying and deceiving people,
so he told Zhāng Zī:
"Luó Chā cannot cure your illness at all;
it is just a waste.
Although the length of one's life cannot be discerned,
there is one way to test whether your illness can be cured."
He twisted five-colored silk threads into a rope,
tied it into a knot,
burned it into ashes, and threw them into water,
saying that if the ashes floated to the surface and reformed into the rope,
the illness could not be cured.
After a short while,
the ashes gathered together and floated to the surface,
reforming into the original shape of the rope.
Since Luó Chā's treatment was ineffective,
Zhāng Zī died within a few days.
Not long after,
Lǚ Guāng also died,
and his son Lǚ Shào succeeded him.
A few days later,
Lǚ Guāng's son Lǚ Zuǎn killed Lǚ Shào,
declaring himself king,
with the era name Xiánníng.
In the second year of Xiánníng,
a pig gave birth to a piglet with three heads on one body.
A dragon flew out from the eastern well,
flew to the front of the palace and coiled up there.
The next morning, it disappeared.
Lǚ Zuǎn considered this an auspicious sign,
and named the great hall "Lóngxiáng Hall."
Not long after,
a black dragon flew to the Dāngyáng Jiǔgōng Gate,
and Lǚ Zuǎn renamed it "Lóngxīng Gate."
Jiūmóluóshí memorialized:
"In recent days, hidden dragons have emerged,
and monstrous pigs have given birth to strange creatures.
Dragons belong to the yin category
and do not emerge lightly.
Now that they appear continuously,
it indicates that disaster is about to strike.
Surely, someone will rebel against the ruler.
You should restrain yourself
and widely practice benevolence and virtue,
to repay Heaven's warning."
Lǚ Zuǎn did not heed his advice.
He made a bet with Jiūmóluóshí,
with the wager being:
"I will cut off the head of the Hú slave."
Jiūmóluóshí said:
"You cannot cut off the head of the Hú slave;
instead, the Hú slave will cut off someone else's head."
This statement had a hidden meaning,
but Lǚ Zuǎn never understood it.
Lǚ Guāng's younger brother, Lǚ Bǎo,
had a son named Lǚ Chāo,
whose childhood name was Hú nú.
Hú nú later indeed killed Lǚ Zuǎn and cut off his head,
installing his elder brother Lǚ Lóng as the King of Liáng.
Only then did people verify the statement Jiūmóluóshí made during the bet.
Jiūmóluóshí lived in Liáng for many years.
Because Lǚ Guāng and his sons never promoted Buddhism,
he kept his profound insights into Buddhist teachings hidden,
with no opportunity to propagate them.
Although Fú Jiān deeply admired his reputation,
he died
without ever meeting him.
After Yáo Cháng declared himself emperor in Cháng'ān,
he also admired Jiūmóluóshí's great reputation
and once humbly invited him.
However, Lǚ Guāng and his sons, because of Luóshí's wisdom and abilities,
feared he would offer strategies to Yáo Cháng,
and did not allow him to travel east.
When Yáo Cháng passed away,
and his son Yáo Xìng succeeded him,
he again sent someone to urge an invitation.
In the third year of Yáo Xìng's Hóngshǐ era, in the third month,
a connected tree grew in the Xiāoyáo Garden within the palace grounds.
Scallions turned into rushes,
and people said this was an auspicious sign,
indicating that a talented person would be summoned to Guānzhōng.
In the fifth month,
Yáo Xìng dispatched Duke of Lǒngxī, Shuò Dé, to lead a western expedition against Lǚ Lóng.
Lǚ Lóng's army was defeated.
By the ninth month,
Lǚ Lóng submitted a petition surrendering,
and Luóshí was finally welcomed into Guānzhōng,
arriving in Cháng'ān on the twentieth day of the twelfth month.
Yáo Xìng treated him with the rites of a state teacher,
and Luóshí was greatly honored and favored.
Since Buddhism was introduced to the East,
starting from Emperor Míng of Hàn,
through the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
the number of scriptures circulating in China gradually increased.
However, these scriptures were written in Sanskrit,
and were difficult to understand.
Yáo Xìng had revered Buddhist scriptures since his youth,
and was determined to gather those proficient in the scriptures to explain them.
Since Luóshí had come to Cháng'ān and settled there,
he was invited to begin translating various scriptures at the Xīmíng Pavilion and Xiāoyáo Garden.
Luóshí had previously read most of these scriptures thoroughly,
studying their meanings deeply and comprehensively.
Later, he also mastered Chinese proficiently,
making his translations smooth and effortless.
He found that many of the earlier translations contained errors in meaning,
stemming from the translators' misunderstandings at the time,
and did not match the original Sanskrit texts.
Yáo Xìng then had over eight hundred Buddhist scholars, such as Sēng Qì, Sēng Qiān, Fǎ Qīn, Dào Liú, Dào Héng, Dào Biāo, Sēng Ruì, and Sēng Zhào,
all come to seek guidance,
accept Luóshí's insights,
and work together on translation.
They also had them retranslate the "Dàpǐn" scripture.
Luóshí held the original Sanskrit text,
while Yáo Xìng held the old translated scripture,
and they compared and collated them together.
Where the new translation differed from the old,
the meanings were more complete and comprehensible than the original translations.
Everyone who read them felt satisfied and greatly admired them.
Jiūmóluóshí was open-minded in demeanor
and straightforward by nature.
He could grasp Buddhist principles with adaptability,
possessing exceptional insight,
and few could match him.
He was sincere and warm towards others.
He was loyal, kind, and benevolent,
harboring a spirit of universal love.
He was humble and open-minded,
patiently guiding others,
and tirelessly dedicated all day long.
Yáo Xīng often said to Luóshí:
"Master, your wisdom and enlightenment
are unparalleled in the world.
Once you pass away a hundred years from now,
how can we ensure the Dharma lineage has no successors?"
He then gave him ten dancing girls,
forcing him to accept them.
From then on,
Luóshí no longer lived in the monks' quarters,
but had a separate residence,
with daily provisions in great abundance.
Whenever he expounded the teachings,
he often used himself as an analogy,
like a lotus blooming from foul mud:
one should admire the purity of the lotus,
but not take the filth of the mud.
When Luóshí was in Qiūcí earlier,
he studied phonology with the Vinaya master Bēimóluóchā.
Bēimó later also came to Cháng'ān,
and Luóshí was overjoyed to hear of it,
showing him the utmost respect as a teacher.
Bēimó did not know about the forced acceptance of the dancing girls,
and merely asked Luóshí:
"You are in the land of Hàn,
with great affinity.
How many disciples
have received the Dharma from you?"
Luóshí replied:
"The scriptures and Vinaya in the land of Hàn are not yet complete.
The newly translated scriptures and many treatises
are mostly my work.
Three thousand disciples
study the Buddha Dharma with me.
However, my efforts in upholding the precepts and serving the Buddha are often deeply hindered,
so I do not receive their respect as a teacher."
Furthermore,
the monk Bēidù lived in Péngchéng.
Hearing that Luóshí was in Cháng'ān,
he sighed and said:
"I want to play a joke on this fellow.
Even if I cannot see him for over three hundred years,
I will surely meet him in a future life."
A few days before his death,
Luóshí felt unwell,
so he recited three divine mantras,
asking his foreign disciples to chant them
to heal himself.
Before the mantras took effect,
he felt his life was in danger,
and thus fell seriously ill.
He bid farewell to the monks, saying:
"Through the affinity of the Buddha Dharma, I met all of you.
I deeply feel that our connection is not yet exhausted,
but now I must depart again.
My sorrow and grief are beyond words.
With my foolish ignorance,
I mistakenly undertook the task of translation.
The scriptures and treatises I have produced exceed three hundred volumes.
Only the *Shísòng*
has not yet been revised and edited.
Adhering to its original intent,
it surely contains no errors.
I hope that the teachings I have expounded in my lifetime
may circulate in the world,
and that we may together propagate and study the Buddha Dharma.
Now, before all of you,
I make a sincere vow:
If the meanings of the scriptures I have transmitted are without error,
may my tongue not be charred after my body is cremated."
On the twentieth day of the eighth month of the eleventh year of Hóngshǐ,
Jiūmóluóshí passed away in Cháng'ān.
This was the fifth year of Yìxī of the Eastern Jìn dynasty.
After his death, he was cremated in Xiāoyáo Garden according to Western Region customs.
When the firewood burned out, his body turned to ashes,
but only his tongue remained unburnt.
Fǎ Lǎng
The Jìn dynasty monk Kāng Fǎlǎng studied in Zhōngshān.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
he and another bhikṣu traveled west to India.
After crossing the desert for over a thousand *lǐ*,
they saw a ruined Buddhist temple by the roadside,
with no halls or chambers remaining,
overgrown with weeds taller than a person.
Fǎlǎng and the others dismounted to pay their respects.
They saw two monks,
each sitting to one side.
One was reading scriptures,
while the other suffered from dysentery,
filling the room with filth.
The one reading scriptures
paid no attention at all.
Fǎlǎng and the others, moved by compassion,
stayed to cook porridge for him,
clean, wash, and tidy up.
By the sixth day,
the sick man grew somewhat weaker,
and his dysentery flowed like a spring.
Fǎlǎng and the others tended to him together.
That night,
Fǎlǎng and the others all thought the sick man would not recover.
But when they went to see him the next morning,
his complexion was radiant and joyful,
and his illness had suddenly vanished.
Moreover, the filth in the room
had all turned into fragrant flowers.
Fǎlǎng and the others then realized that these were enlightened beings testing them.
The sick man said:
"The bhikṣu in the next room
is my master.
He attained enlightenment long ago.
You may go and pay your respects to him."
Fǎlǎng and the others had previously disliked the scripture-reading monk for lacking compassion.
Upon hearing this,
they bowed and repented of their fault.
The scripture-reading monk said:
"All of you
All of you
According to the Chén edition, corrected
have sincerely arrived together with a shared vow,
and all should attain the Way.
However, Fǎlǎng's past learning is shallow,
so he will not fulfill his wish in this lifetime."
To Fǎlǎng's companion, he said:
"If your wisdom is deeply rooted,
you will attain your wish in this present life."
Thus, he kept him there.
Fǎlǎng later returned to the mountains,
where he became a great Dharma master,
revered by both monastics and laypeople.
From *Míngxiáng Jì*
During the Jìn dynasty, there was a Buddhist monk named Kāng Fǎlǎng,
who studied the Buddha Way in Zhōngshān.
During the Yǒngjiā era,
he and another ordained monk traveled west to India.
After crossing the great desert for over a thousand *lǐ*,
they saw a dilapidated temple by the roadside,
with no halls remaining,
and weeds taller than a person.
Fǎlǎng and the others dismounted to pay their respects.
They saw two monks sitting separately to one side:
one was reading scriptures,
while the other suffered from dysentery,
filling the room with excrement.
The scripture-reading monk paid no attention at all.
Out of compassion,
Fǎlǎng and the others stayed to cook porridge for the sick man
and clean and wash for him.
By the sixth day,
the sick man grew somewhat weaker,
and his dysentery flowed incessantly.
Fǎlǎng and the others tended to him together.
That night,
Fǎlǎng and the others all thought the sick man would not recover.
But when they went to see him the next morning,
they found him radiant and joyful,
with his illness completely gone.
Moreover, the excrement in the room
had all turned into fragrant flowers.
Fǎlǎng and the others then realized
that this was an enlightened being testing them.
The sick man said:
"The monk in the next room
is my master.
He attained enlightenment long ago.
You may go and pay your respects to him."
Fǎlǎng and the others had previously disliked the scripture-reading monk for lacking compassion.
Upon hearing this,
they bowed and apologized to him.
The scripture-reading monk said:
"All of you have arrived here together with a shared vow,
and all should attain the Way.
However, Fǎlǎng's usual learning is still shallow,
so he will not fulfill his wish in this lifetime."
To Fǎlǎng's companion, he said:
"Your Buddha-mind is deeply rooted,
so you may attain your wish in this present life."
Thus, he kept him there.
Fǎlǎng later returned to the mountains,
where he became a great Dharma master,
revered by many Buddhists,
both monastics and laypeople,
as their patriarch.
Lǐ Héng, a monk
Jìn Lǐ Héng, styled Yuánwén,
was from Qiáoguó.
In his youth,
a Buddhist monk visited Héng and said to him:
"Your blessings and retributions are about to arrive,
and further retributions will follow them.
If you can remain in poverty, cultivate the Way,
and not pursue an official career,
your blessings will increase and retributions will diminish.
You should strive for this."
Héng was by nature impatient,
and his family was poor,
so he only asked about what official rank he could attain,
and did not at all inquire into the meaning of cultivating the Way.
The monk offered him a scroll of scripture,
but Héng refused to take it,
insisting on asking about the path to glory and the heights of honor.
The monk said:
"You will wear gold and purple,
reaching the peak of three commanderies.
If you can stop at one commandery,
it would also be a good path."
Héng said:
"I will take wealth and honor for now,
why worry about future troubles?"
He then invited the monk to stay overnight.
Héng rose during the night.
He saw the monk's body filling the entire bed,
and called his family to come and look.
The monk then transformed into a large bird perched on the roof beam,
and by dawn, his form had returned to normal.
Héng escorted him out the door,
when suddenly he vanished.
Realizing this was a divine being,
Héng began to serve the Buddha because of this incident,
but he was still unable to achieve deep devotion.
Later, he served as the governor of Xīyáng, Jiāngxià, and Lújiāng,
and was given the additional title of General of Soaring Dragons.
During the Tàixīng era,
he was involved in the rebellion of Qián Fèng,
and was executed.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín"
Bēidù
Cup Ferryman,
whose real name is unknown,
often crossed rivers riding on a wooden cup,
hence he was given this nickname.
Initially in Jìzhōu,
he did not cultivate minor virtues,
yet his divine powers were extraordinary,
and the world could not fathom their origin.
Once in the north,
he lodged at a household,
which possessed a golden statue.
Ferryman secretly took it and was about to leave.
The head of the household noticed and pursued him,
seeing Ferryman walking slowly,
yet even galloping on horseback, he could not catch up.
Arriving at the Mèngjīn River,
he floated a wooden cup on the water,
relied on it to cross the river,
without needing wind or oars,
light and swift as if flying.
In a moment, he reached the shore,
arriving at the capital.
At that time, he appeared to be around forty years old,
wearing a rope belt and tattered clothes,
barely covering his body.
His speech was unpredictable,
his joy and anger inconsistent.
Sometimes he would break ice and bathe in the freezing water,
sometimes he would wear shoes and climb mountains,
sometimes he would walk barefoot into the market.
He only carried one reed basket,
and had nothing else.
Once he went to the Yánxián Temple to visit the monk Fǎyì,
and Fǎyì accommodated him in a separate room.
Later, he wanted to go to Guābù,
and arrived
("arrived" originally written as "river,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript)
at the riverside,
approached a boatman to request passage,
but the boatman refused to carry him.
Again, he stepped into his cup,
looking around and chanting,
the cup naturally drifted,
straight across to the northern shore.
Heading toward Guǎnglíng,
he encountered a village household, the Lǐ family's Eight Precepts fasting ceremony,
though they had not known each other before.
He went straight into the fasting hall and sat down,
placing his basket in the central courtyard.
The crowd, due to his shabby appearance,
showed no respect for him.
Mr. Lǐ saw the reed basket blocking the path,
and wanted to move it to the side of the wall.
Several people tried to lift it but could not move it.
After Ferryman finished eating,
he picked it up and left,
laughing and saying:
"The Lǐ family of the Four Heavenly Kings."
At that time, there was a young servant,
who peeked into his basket,
and saw four small children,
each only a few inches tall,
with端正 features,
and clean, bright clothes.
Then they searched for him,
but did not know where he was.
Three days later,
they saw him sitting under a ménglóng tree in the western area.
Mr. Lǐ bowed and invited him back home,
providing daily offerings.
Ferryman did not strictly observe fasting,
drinking wine and eating meat,
even spicy and raw dishes,
no different from ordinary people.
When commoners made offerings to him,
he sometimes accepted, sometimes did not.
Liú Xīngbó of Pèiguó was the governor of Yǎnzhōu,
and sent an envoy to invite him.
He came carrying his basket.
Xīngbó had people lift it to look,
but over ten people could not manage it.
Xīngbó looked himself,
and only saw a worn-out robe and a wooden cup.
Later, the Lǐ family had him for over twenty more days,
when one clear morning he suddenly said:
"I want a kasaya robe,
have it ready by noon."
Mr. Lǐ immediately set about preparing it,
but by noon it was not yet finished.
Ferryman said he would go out for a while,
and by dusk he had not returned.
The entire area smelled an unusual fragrance,
and suspected it was something strange.
They searched everywhere for Ferryman,
and finally saw him under a northern cliff,
spreading a worn-out kasaya on the ground,
lying on it and dying.
His head in front and feet behind,
lotus flowers grew from his back,
extremely fresh and fragrant,
but they withered overnight.
The village buried him together.
Later, someone came from the north and said, "I saw Ferryman carrying his reed basket,
walking toward Péngchéng."
So they opened the coffin together,
and only saw worn-out clothes.
After arriving in Péngchéng,
he met a commoner named Huáng Xīn,
who deeply believed in the Buddha's teachings.
Upon seeing Ferryman, he bowed in respect,
and invited him home.
He was extremely poor,
having only coarse wheat food,
yet Ferryman ate it contentedly.
He stayed for half a year,
then suddenly said to Xīn:
"Find thirty-six reed baskets for me,
I need to use them."
Xīn replied:
"Here we only have ten,
I am too poor to buy more,
I'm afraid I cannot get all of them."
Ferryman said:
"Just search carefully,
there should be some in the house."
Xīn then searched thoroughly.
Indeed, he found thirty-six,
and arranged them in the courtyard.
Although the number was correct,
many were broken and worn.
Ferryman told Xīn to look at them one by one,
and they had all become new and intact.
Ferryman sealed them tightly,
then told Xīn to open them,
and inside were full of coins and silk,
worth about a million.
Those who understood said that Cup Ferryman had manifested in other places,
and the alms he received,
he transferred to give to Xīn.
Xīn accepted them,
and used them all for meritorious deeds.
After about a year,
Ferryman bid farewell and left,
and Xīn prepared provisions for him.
The next morning,
they saw the provisions still there,
and did not know where Ferryman had gone.
After about a month,
he returned to the capital.
At that time, in Cháogōu, there was a man named Zhū Wénshū,
who had practiced Buddhism since youth.
Ferryman often came to his home.
Wénshū said to Ferryman:
"If this disciple should die,
I hope you will save and aid me,
so that I may be reborn in a good place,
and become a companion in the Dharma."
Ferryman did not answer.
Wénshū was pleased,
thinking that in the silent way of Buddhism,
it was already an agreement.
Later, he traveled east into Wújùn,
and on the road saw a fisherman,
so he went to beg for fish.
The fisherman gave him a dead one.
Ferryman turned it over in his hands,
then threw it back into the water,
and it swam away alive.
He also saw a net
("net" originally written as "go,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript)
fisherman,
and again begged for fish.
The net fisherman angrily scolded him and refused to give any.
Ferryman then picked up two stones and threw them into the water.
Soon, two water buffaloes fought in his net,
the net was torn and destroyed,
and the buffaloes were no longer seen,
Ferryman had also disappeared.
Traveling to Sōngjiāng,
he then placed his hat on the water,
and rode it to the shore.
Passing through Kuàijī Shànxiàn,
he ascended Tiāntāi Mountain.
After several months, he returned to the capital.
For a short time,
he wandered without fixed abode,
sometimes going when invited, sometimes not.
At that time, in Nánzhōu, there was a Chén family,
quite well-off with food and clothing.
Ferryman went to their home,
and was warmly received.
Hearing that there was another Cup Ferryman in the capital,
the Chén father and his five sons,
all did not believe it,
so they went to the capital
("capital" originally written as "hometown,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript)
to see for themselves.
Indeed, at their home, the appearance of Bēidù was of one kind.
They set out a box of honeyed ginger,
and a knife, frankincense,
The "Biographies of Eminent Monks" has the character "薰" (fragrant) after "子" (here meaning "knife"),
and the characters "手巾" (handkerchief) after "香" (incense)
and so forth,
waiting for Bēidù.
Bēidù then ate all the honeyed ginger,
while the other items remained exactly as before in front of his knees.
The father and his five sons,
fearing it was the Bēidù of their household,
immediately left two younger brothers to stay in the capital to watch over him,
while the other three returned home.
They saw Bēidù as before,
with the incense, knife, and other items also in front of his knees,
only differing in that he did not eat the honeyed ginger.
He then said to Chén:
"The knife is dull,
you should sharpen it."
The two younger brothers returned to the capital,
and said:
"Bēidù has already moved to Língjiù Temple."
His household suddenly requested two sheets of yellow paper,
wrote characters that did not form words,
and joined them together on the back.
Chén asked the venerable monk what kind of document he was writing,
but Bēidù did not answer,
and in the end, no one could fathom what it meant.
At that time, Zhū Língqī, a commoner from the Wú region, was returning from an envoy mission to Gāolì,
when he encountered wind,
and his boat drifted for nine days,
until it reached the shore of an island.
On the island was a mountain,
which was very tall and large.
Entering the mountain to gather firewood,
they saw people on the road.
Língqī then led several men to follow the road and beg for alms.
After traveling over a thousand *li*,
they heard the sound of a chime and smelled incense smoke,
so together they chanted the Buddha's name and paid their respects.
After a short while,
they saw a temple, very splendid and beautiful,
mostly adorned with the seven treasures,
and also saw over ten stone men,
so they paid their respects together.
Turning back and walking a short distance,
they heard the sound of chanting,
and going back to look again,
they were still stone men.
Língqī and the others said to each other:
"These are holy monks,
we are sinners,
and cannot see them."
Thereupon, together they sincerely repented.
Going again,
they then saw real people,
who prepared food for Língqī and the others.
The flavor of the food was that of vegetables,
but fragrant and delicious, unlike any other.
After everyone had finished eating,
they all kowtowed and paid their respects,
begging to quickly return to their homeland.
One monk said:
"From here to the capital is over two hundred thousand *li*,
but if you are sincere,
do not worry about not being fast."
He then asked Língqī:
"Do you know the monk Bēidù?
He replied that he knew him very well.
Then pointing to the north wall,
there was a gourd,
hanging a monk's staff and an alms bowl,
and said:
"This is Bēidù's dwelling place,
now, through you, I will give him the bowl."
He also wrote a letter and placed it in a case,
and there was another green bamboo staff,
which he said to Língqī:
"Just throw this staff into the water in front of the boat,
close your eyes and sit quietly,
without needing to exert effort,
it will surely make you arrive quickly."
So they bid farewell,
and he had a novice monk escort them to the gate,
saying:
"From this path,
walk seven *li* to reach the boat,
there is no need to take the previous road."
As instructed, they turned west,
walked about seven *li*,
and reached the boat.
They then did exactly as instructed,
only hearing the boat passing over the treetops of the mountain,
without seeing any water at all.
After three days,
they stopped at the Huái River in Shítóu,
and could no longer see where the bamboo staff was.
The boat entered the Huái River,
reached Zhūquè,
and then saw Bēidù riding on a large boat's railing,
striking it with a whip and saying:
"Horse, why won't you go?"
There were many onlookers.
Língqī and the others on the boat,
paid their respects from afar.
Bēidù then came down from the boat himself,
took the letter and the bowl,
opened the letter and looked at it,
the characters were not recognizable to anyone.
Bēidù laughed heartily and said:
"They want me to return."
He took the bowl and threw it into the clouds,
then caught it again and said:
"I haven't seen this bowl,
for four thousand years."
Bēidù was often at Fǎyì's place in Yánxián Temple,
and at that time, people considered this bowl a strange object,
and competed to go see it.
Another account says:
Língqī's boat drifted to a desolate mountain,
where he met a monk coming,
who said he was a disciple of Bēidù,
who had previously held his master's bowl and died at Yěchéng Temple,
and now, through you, he would return the bowl to his master.
He only needed one person to hold the bowl in front of the boat,
and they would peacefully arrive.
Língqī did as instructed,
and indeed safely crossed.
When Bēidù arrived in Nánzhōu,
it was the day Língqī was riding the railing.
That day, he went out early,
and by evening had not returned.
The Chén family the next morning only saw six green characters written on the door panel, which said:
"The path of blessings,
a spiritual being descends."
The characters were forceful and recognizable,
and the Bēidù of their household then disappeared without a trace.
The Bēidù of the capital came and went among mountains and towns,
often performing divine incantations.
At that time, a maidservant of Yǔ Cháng stole something and fled,
and though pursued four times, she was not captured,
so they asked Bēidù,
who said:
"She is already dead,
in an empty tomb by the riverbank in the city."
Going to look, it was indeed as he said.
Kǒng Nìngzǐ, then serving as a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, was at home suffering from dysentery,
and sent a messenger to invite Bēidù.
After performing the incantation, Bēidù said:
"It is difficult to cure,
I see four ghosts,
all injured and mutilated."
Nìngzǐ wept and said:
"In the past, when Sūn Ēn rebelled,
our home was broken into by soldiers,
and both my parents and uncle,
were brutally tortured."
Nìngzǐ indeed died.
Also, the wife of Qí Xié, née Húmǔ, was ill,
and though many treated her, she did not recover,
so they invited monks to prepare a vegetarian feast.
Among the seated monks,
one advised inviting Bēidù.
When Bēidù arrived,
with one incantation,
the patient immediately recovered.
Qí Xié served him as a teacher,
and therefore wrote a biography,
recording all his divine wonders from the beginning,
which cannot be fully recorded.
In the ninth month of the third year of Yuánjiā,
he bid farewell to Xié and went east,
leaving ten thousand cash and items with Xié,
asking him to prepare a vegetarian feast,
and then departed.
Traveling to Chìshān Lake,
he fell ill with dysentery and died.
Xié then prepared the vegetarian feast,
and also retrieved the corpse and brought it back,
burying it on Fùzhōu Mountain in Jiànkāng.
In the fourth year,
there was a man from Wú
"Wú" originally written as "五" (five),
corrected according to the Ming manuscript copy
xīng named Shào Xìn,
