who was very devout in the Dharma,
contracted a cold injury illness,
and no one dared to see him,
so he wept sorrowfully and recited Guānyīn's name.
Suddenly, a monk came,
saying he was a disciple of Bēidù,
and said:
"Do not worry,
my master will soon come to see you."
He replied:
"Bēidù has long been dead,
how could he come?"
The monk said:
"What difficulty is there in coming?"
Then from his clothing belt, he took out about a boxful of powder,
He gave him the clothes to wear,
and the illness was immediately cured.
There was also a man named Dù Sēng'āi,
who lived at the foot of Nángāng.
He had once served Bēi Dù.
His son fell gravely ill,
and he thought to himself,
regretting that he could not have Bēi Dù recite a divine incantation.
The next day,
he suddenly saw Bēi Dù arrive.
Bēi Dù spoke as usual,
and immediately recited the incantation,
and the sick child recovered.
In the fifth year, during the third month,
Bēi Dù came again to Qí Xié’s home.
Lǚ Dàohuì, Wénrén
(The original text had "而" for "人,"
corrected to "人" based on the "Biographies of Eminent Monks")
Dànzhī, Dù Tiānqī, Shuǐqiū Xī, and others were all present,
and they were greatly astonished.
They immediately rose and paid their respects.
Bēi Dù addressed the crowd,
saying that the year would bring great calamity,
and they should diligently cultivate blessings and good deeds.
The monk Fǎyì was a man of great virtue,
and they could go to him.
They should repair and restore the old temple
to ward off disaster and misfortune.
A moment later,
a monk called from outside the door,
and Bēi Dù took his leave,
saying:
"This humble monk will now head to the region between Jiāozhōu and Guǎngzhōu,
and will not return."
Qí Xié and the others respectfully bowed and saw him off,
and after that, he vanished without a trace.
In recent times, it is also said that he was occasionally seen.
From "Biographies of Eminent Monks"
Shì Bǎozhì
Shì Bǎozhì's original surname was Zhū,
and he was from Jīnchéng.
He left home to become a monk in his youth,
residing at the Dàolín Temple on the eastern side of the river,
where he cultivated and practiced meditation.
By the beginning of the Dàshǐ era of the Sòng dynasty,
he suddenly became eccentric and unusual.
He had no fixed dwelling,
ate at irregular times,
let his hair grow several inches long,
and often walked barefoot through streets and alleys.
He carried a monk's staff,
with scissors and a mirror hanging from its head,
and sometimes one or two bolts of silk.
During the Jiànyuán era of the Qí dynasty,
he began to display unusual feats,
going without food for several days
yet showing no signs of hunger.
When speaking with people,
his words were initially difficult to understand,
but later they all proved true.
At times, he would compose poems,
and his words were like prophecies.
The scholars and commoners of the eastern side of the river all revered him.
Emperor Wǔ of Qí, believing he was deluding the masses,
had him arrested and imprisoned in Jiànkāng.
The next morning,
people saw him entering the market,
but upon checking the prison,
Bǎozhì was still there.
Bǎozhì said to the prison guard:
"Two carts of food are coming from outside the gate,
with rice in golden bowls.
You may take them."
Soon after, Crown Prince Wénhuì and Prince Zǐliáng of Jìnglíng both sent food to Bǎozhì,
exactly as he had said.
The magistrate of Jiànkāng, Lǚ Wénxiǎn, reported the matter,
and Emperor Wǔ immediately welcomed Bǎozhì into the palace,
housing him in the rear hall.
Once, when the inner banquet was cleared,
Bǎozhì also left with the crowd.
But soon after, on Jǐngyáng Mountain,
there was still a Bǎozhì,
along with seven monks.
The emperor was furious,
and sent someone to investigate his whereabouts.
The gate
In the Ming manuscript, "gate" is written as "pavilion."
official reported:
"Bǎozhì left long ago
Originally, "left" was written as "had,"
but it was changed according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
for the provincial capital,
and just now he smeared his body with ink."
At the time, the monastic overseer Fǎxiàn wanted to give Bǎozhì a robe,
so he sent messengers to search for him at the Lóngguāng and Jìbīn temples.
Both temples said he had stayed the night before and left in the morning.
They also went to the home of Hóu Bó, whom Bǎozhì often visited, to look for him.
Hóu Bó said:
"Bǎozhì was here yesterday practicing the Way,
and he is still sleeping in the morning, not yet awake."
The messenger returned and reported this,
and Fǎxiàn realized that Bǎozhì had divided his body to stay in three places at once.
Bǎozhì often walked bare-chested
Originally, "bare-chested" was written as "bundled ancestor,"
but it was changed according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
in the depths of winter.
The monk Bǎoliàng wanted to give him a patched robe,
but before he could speak,
Bǎozhì suddenly came and took the robe away.
Later, Bǎozhì borrowed the divine power of Emperor Wǔ of Qí
to let him see Emperor Gāo in the underworld,
where he was constantly suffering from the pain of awls and knives.
From then on, the emperor permanently abolished the use of awls and knives.
Emperor Wǔ once summoned Bǎozhì to the Huálín Garden,
and Bǎozhì suddenly appeared wearing a triple-layered cloth hat.
Soon after, Emperor Wǔ passed away,
and Crown Prince Wénhuì and Prince Yùzhāng died one after another.
During the Yǒngmíng era,
Bǎozhì often stayed in the rear hall of the Eastern Palace.
One day at dawn,
as he was entering and leaving through the gate,
he suddenly said:
"There is blood on the gate staining my clothes."
He lifted his robe and hurried past.
When Yùlín was assassinated,
his body was carried out through this gate,
and the emperor's neck blood flowed over the threshold.
When Hú Xié, the Commandant of the Guards of Qí, fell ill,
he invited Bǎozhì.
Bǎozhì wrote "tomorrow" in reply,
but in the end, he did not go.
That day, Hú Xié died,
and his body was carried back to his home.
Bǎozhì said:
"The body will be carried out tomorrow."
When Yīn Qízhī, the Grand Commandant's Marshal of Qí, followed Chén Xiǎndá to guard Jiāngzhōu,
he bid farewell to Bǎozhì.
Bǎozhì drew a tree on paper,
with a bird on the tree,
and said:
"In an emergency, you can climb this."
Later, when Chén Xiǎndá rebelled,
he left Yīn Qízhī to guard the province.
After the defeat,
Yīn Qízhī fled into Lú Mountain,
with pursuing cavalry about to catch up.
Yīn Qízhī saw a tree in the forest,
with a bird on it,
exactly as Bǎozhì had drawn.
Realizing the meaning, he climbed the tree,
and the bird did not fly away.
The pursuers saw the bird,
thought no one was there, and turned back.
Thus, Yīn Qízhī was spared.
When Sāng Yǎn, the Cavalry Commandant of Qí, was planning to rebel,
he went to visit
Originally, "visit" was missing,
but it was added according to the Ming manuscript.
Bǎozhì.
From afar, Bǎozhì ran away,
shouting loudly:
"Surrounding the palace city,
planning to rebel,
your head will be chopped and your belly split open."
More than ten days later, the matter came to light,
and Sāng Yǎn fled to Zhūfāng,
where he was captured,
and indeed, his head was chopped off and his belly split open.
Lièwáng of Póyáng of Liáng
once invited Bǎozhì to his residence.
Bǎozhì suddenly urgently asked for a jujube branch.
After obtaining it,
he placed it on the gate,
and no one could understand why.
A short while later, the prince was appointed as the Governor of Jīngzhōu.
His ability to foresee events with such clarity
was not limited to this one instance.
Bǎozhì often traveled between the Xīnghuáng and Jìngmíng temples.
When Emperor Wǔ of Liáng ascended the throne,
he issued an edict stating:
"Bǎozhì's traces are like dust and grime,
his spirit wanders in obscurity.
Fire and water cannot scorch or soak him,
snakes and tigers cannot invade or frighten him.
Speaking of Buddhist principles,
his understanding is unsurpassed;
discussing his reclusive life,
his practice of the Way is highly esteemed.
How can he be restrained by the ordinary sentiments of common people?
How vulgar and shallow
it is to the extreme.
From now on,
he may come and go as he pleases,
and must not be restricted again."
From then on, Bǎozhì often entered and left the palace,
staying in the palace city.
Once, while eating sliced fish with Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
with Crown Prince Zhāomíng and the other princes attending,
after finishing the meal,
Emperor Wǔ said:
"I have not tasted flavor for over twenty years.
Master, why is this?"
Bǎozhì then spat out a small fish,
with its scales and tail still intact.
Emperor Wǔ found this deeply strange.
To this day, in Mòlíng, there is still a fish called "leftover sliced fish."
In the winter of the fifth year of Tiānjiān, there was a drought.
Rainmaking rituals were performed exhaustively,
but no rain fell.
Bǎozhì suddenly submitted a petition stating:
"Bǎozhì is ill and not recovering.
I beg the officials for my life.
If I do not report to the officials,
I should be whipped and caned.
I wish to lecture on the *Śrīmālā Sutra* in the Huáguāng Hall to pray for rain."
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng immediately had the monk Fǎyún lecture on the *Śrīmālā Sutra*,
and that night, heavy rain fell.
Bǎozhì also said:
"A basin of water is needed,
with a knife placed on top."
Soon after, heavy rain poured down,
saturating both high and low ground.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng once asked Bǎozhì:
"Your disciple's afflictions and delusions are not yet eliminated.
How can they be cured?"
Bǎozhì replied:
"Twelve."
Those who understood
Originally, "understood" was written as "prophecy,"
but it was changed according to the Ming manuscript.
believed it referred to the twelve links of dependent origination,
which are the medicine to cure delusion.
He also asked about the meaning
Originally, "meaning" was written as "text,"
but it was changed according to the Ming manuscript.
of the twelve?
Bǎozhì replied:
"It lies in the moments and hours of writing characters."
Those who understood believed that the book was among the twelve hours.
They also asked the disciples when they could calm their minds to practice cultivation.
The answer was:
"Ānlè
(The character 'lè' was originally written as 'yào'
and was changed according to the Ming dynasty manuscript copy) is prohibited."
Those who understood believed that 'prohibited' meant to stop,
and that when one reaches Ānlè
(The character 'lè' was originally written as 'yào'
and was changed according to the Ming dynasty manuscript copy),
the time then stops
(Originally, there was no character 'zhǐ'
and it was supplemented based on the "Gāosēng Zhuàn")
indeed.
Later, Fǎyún lectured on the Lotus Sutra at Huálín,
and when he reached the passage "even if black winds,"
(The phrase "even if black winds" was originally written as "even if winds are black"
and was changed according to the Lotus Sutra)
Zhì suddenly asked whether it existed or not.
The answer was:
"In worldly truth
(The character 'dì' was originally written as 'dì'
and was changed according to the Ming dynasty manuscript copy), it exists,
but in the highest meaning, it does not."
Zhì went back and forth three or four times,
then laughed and said:
"If the substance is illusory existence,
this too is incomprehensible,
difficult to comprehend."
The meaning of his words was obscure,
and all were like this.
There was a man named Chén Zhēnglǔ,
whose entire family served Zhì with great devotion.
Zhì once manifested his true form for him,
with a radiant appearance like that of a bodhisattva.
Zhì was known for his remarkable and extraordinary qualities,
for over forty years,
and the men and women who served him
were countless.
However, he often used urine to wash his hair,
and some vulgar monks secretly mocked him for this.
Zhì also knew that many monks did not abstain from wine and meat.
One who mocked him drank wine and ate pig stomach,
and Zhì angrily said to him:
"You laugh at me for washing my head with urine,
but why do you eat a bag filled with excrement?"
The mocker was frightened and ashamed, submitting to him.
When Prince Xiāo Gāng of Jìn'ān was first born,
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng sent an envoy to ask Zhì,
and Zhì clasped his hands and said:
"It is fortunate that the prince has been born,
but his enemy has also been born."
Later, when they traced the calendar calculations,
it was found that Hóu Jǐng was born in the same year, month, and day.
There was a virtuous monk at Línhǎi Temple in Kuàijī,
who often heard that in the capital of Yángzhōu, there was a Zhìgōng,
whose speech was mad,
unrestrained and free.
The monk said:
"He must be a fox spirit.
I wish to go to the capital
and find hunting dogs to chase him away."
So he took a light boat into the sea,
heading toward Pǔkǒu.
He intended to go west,
but suddenly a great wind blew him off course,
and he thought he was heading southeast,
but after six or seven days, he arrived at an island.
He saw a golden pagoda,
towering into the clouds and standing out beautifully,
so he followed a path toward it.
He arrived at a temple,
where the courtyards and buildings were exquisite and beautiful,
with fragrant flowers blooming,
and five or six monks,
all around thirty years old,
with handsome appearances,
all wearing round crimson robes,
leaning on staffs and talking under a tree by the gate.
The monk said:
"I intended to go to the capital,
but was blown off course by the wind,
and I do not know what country or region this place of yours is.
Now, looking around, I see only the sea encircling us,
and I fear I may never see my homeland again."
They replied:
"If you wish to go to Yángzhōu,
you will arrive immediately.
Now, take this letter to the second room on the south side of the western wing of Zhōngshān Temple,
and find Huángtóu to deliver it."
The monk then closed his eyes and sat in the boat,
and when the sound of the wind ceased, he opened his eyes,
and as they said, he suddenly arrived at the western shore.
After traveling several dozen miles,
he reached the capital.
He went directly to Zhōngshān Temple to inquire,
but there was no one named Huángtóu.
The monk explained the details,
and they reported:
"The second room on the south side of the western wing
belongs to the mad monk Zhìgōng.
Although he is assigned to this temple,
he stays in the capital's gathering and pleasure
(The character 'lè' was originally written as 'yào'
and was changed according to the Ming dynasty manuscript copy) places,
and does not come even once in a hundred days.
The room is empty, with no one there."
During the conversation,
they did not notice that Zhìgōng was already in the temple kitchen,
drunk and demanding food.
The people said that the meal time had passed and it was late,
and before they could respond,
he angrily shouted curses.
The temple monks tried to send a novice to the side of the kitchen,
and casually called out "Huángtóu."
Zhìgōng suddenly said:
"Who is calling me?"
He then followed the novice to where the monk was.
He said to him:
"You promised to bring hunting dogs to catch me,
why have you come empty-handed?"
The monk realized he was no ordinary person,
bowed in reverence and repentance,
and handed him the letter.
Zhìgōng looked at the letter and said:
"The abbot is calling me,
and I will return soon on my own."
Zhìgōng then counted on his fingers and said:
"I will leave on such-and-such month and day."
After that, he did not speak to this monk again.
Everyone just noted the month and day.
In the winter of the thirteenth year of Tiānjiàn,
he said to someone in the rear hall of Táichéng:
"The bodhisattva is about to leave."
Before ten days had passed,
he passed away without illness.
His body remained fragrant and soft,
and his appearance was serene and joyful.
Before his death,
he lit a candle and gave it to the rear chamber attendant Wú Qìng.
Qìng immediately reported it,
and Emperor Wǔ of Liáng sighed and said:
"The great master will no longer stay.
As for the candle,
is he entrusting the aftermath to me?"
He then arranged a lavish funeral,
and buried him at Dúlóng Hill in Zhōngshān.
He also established Kāishàn Temple at the gravesite,
ordered Lù Chuí to compose an inscription for the tomb,
and Wáng Yún to engrave a stele at the temple gate.
His portrait was circulated,
and preserved everywhere.
When Zhì first began to reveal his traces,
he appeared to be around fifty or sixty years old,
but even at his death, he did not seem old,
so people truly could not guess his age.
There was a man named Yú Jiédào,
who lived north of Jiǔrì Terrace in the capital,
and claimed to be Zhì's brother-in-law,
four years younger than Zhì.
Calculating the time of Zhì's death,
he should have been ninety-seven years old.
Also, in the Later Wèi, there was a monk named Bǎogōng,
whose origins were unknown,
with an ugly appearance,
but a mind of great insight,
knowing the past and future,
foreseeing the three times.
His words seemed like prophecies,
incomprehensible at the time.
Only after events occurred
were his words verified.
Empress Dowager Hú asked him about worldly affairs,
and Bǎogōng held millet and called to the chickens,
calling "Zhūzhū,"
which no one understood at the time.
In the first year of Jiànyì,
when she was later killed by Ěrzhū Róng,
his words were verified.
At that time, there was a man from Luòyáng named Zhào Fǎhé,
who asked to divine when he would receive a noble rank.
Bǎogōng said:
"A large bamboo arrow,
needs no feathers.
The eastern wing room,
quickly build it."
No one understood his meaning at the time.
After more than a month,
Fǎhé's father died.
"A large bamboo arrow"
refers to the mourning staff;
"the eastern wing room"
refers to the mourning hut.
He first composed the song of the twelve earthly branches,
and these were his final words.
This Bǎogōng and the one in Jiāngnán
It is unclear whether this refers to one person or two.
From the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* and *Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luòyáng*
Yǒngnàbámó
Yǒngnàbámó was
a monk from the Western Regions.
During the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
he traveled east, crossed the river,
and resided at the Qíyuán Temple in Jīnlíng.
Emperor Wén of Sòng once said to him:
"Your disciple has always wished to maintain a vegetarian diet,
to not kill living beings,
to sacrifice himself for all creatures,
yet I have not achieved this aspiration.
You, Master, have come from ten thousand *li* away,
to teach and transform this country.
What instruction do you have for me?"
He replied:
"The Way lies in the heart,
not in external matters;
the Dharma arises from oneself,
not from others.
Moreover, the cultivation of an emperor and that of a commoner
also differ.
As for commoners,
their status is lowly and their name insignificant,
their virtue does not reach far,
their teachings do not extend beyond their own gate and courtyard,
their words are not heeded even by their servants and concubines.
If they do not discipline their bodies and restrain themselves,
practice good deeds and uphold precepts,
how else can they apply their hearts?
An emperor regards the four seas as his home,
and the myriad people as his children.
Uttering one good word,
then scholars and commoners all rejoice;
implementing one benevolent policy,
then humans and spirits are harmonized.
If punishments are clear, then lives are not cut short;
if corvée labor is simplified, then their strength is not exhausted.
Thereafter, distinguish the pitch pipes and musical tones,
rectify the seasons and ordinances.
When the pitch pipes and tones are distinguished, then wind and rain are regulated;
when commands are timely, then cold and heat are orderly.
In this way, maintaining a vegetarian diet is already great,
and not killing is already extensive.
Why must it depend on
missing a single meal
or sparing the life of a single bird,
to then be considered broad salvation?"
Emperor Wén stroked his armrest and sighed in admiration,
praising it for a long time.
Then he said:
"Worldly people are confused about distant principles,
while monks are attached to immediate teachings;
those confused about distant principles call them empty talk,
those attached to immediate teachings cling rigidly to texts and phrases.
As for you, Master,
you are truly what is called enlightened and discerning,
one who can speak of the relationship between Heaven and humanity."
Fǎdù
The monk Fǎdù
was from Huánglóng.
In the early years of the Southern Qí,
he traveled to Jīnlíng.
The eminent scholar Míng Sēngshào of Qí Commandery,
who lived in seclusion on Shè Mountain in Lángyá,
admired Fǎdù's purity and truthfulness,
and treated him as a teacher and friend.
When Sēngshào passed away,
he bequeathed his mountain residence to become the Qīxiá Temple.
Previously, there was a Daoist priest who wanted to turn the temple grounds into a monastery,
but those who lived there died one after another.
Later, when it became a temple,
there was still much fear.
After Fǎdù resided there,
all the demons and strange phenomena ceased.
After over a year,
he suddenly heard the sounds of men, horses, drums, and horns.
Soon he saw a person present a name card to Fǎdù, saying:
"Jìn Shàng."
Fǎdù ordered him to come forward.
Shàng's appearance was very composed and elegant,
and his feather-bannered guards were numerous.
After paying his respects,
he then said:
"Your disciple has been master of this mountain
for over seven hundred years.
The way of the spirits has its laws,
and creatures may not interfere.
Those who previously sought refuge here
were perhaps not genuine.
Therefore, death and illness followed them,
which was also their fate.
You, Dharma Master, are the embodiment of virtue and the Way.
I respectfully relinquish this place to offer it to you,
and also wish to receive the Five Precepts,
to forever establish a karmic connection for the future."
Fǎdù said:
"The ways of humans and spirits are different;
it is not appropriate to impose upon each other.
Moreover, as a patron, you receive blood sacrifices and worldly offerings,
which is most prohibited by the Five Precepts."
Shàng said:
"If I am to enter your gate,
I will first cease killing."
Thereupon he took his leave.
The next morning,
a person delivered ten thousand coins,
along with incense, candles, and other items,
with a note stating:
"Your disciple Jìn Shàng respectfully offers these."
On the fifteenth day of that month,
Fǎdù held a ceremony,
and Shàng came again.
Together with the assembly, he paid homage, practiced the Way,
received the precepts, and departed.
Afterwards, the shaman of the Shè Mountain temple dreamed that the spirit told him:
"I have already received the precepts from Dharma Master Fǎdù.
From now on, those making sacrificial offerings must not kill."
From then on, only vegetables and rice were offered in the temple.
From *Illustrated Gazetteer of Shè Prefecture*
Master Tōng
At the end of the Liáng dynasty, there was a Daoist named Master Tōng.
His surname and given name are unknown.
He had no fixed abode.
His speech was wild and bizarre,
yet it always proved true.
He drank wine and ate meat,
wandering among the common people.
Hóu Jǐng trusted him greatly.
Before Yángzhōu fell,
he gathered countless dead fish heads
and piled them outside the Xīmíng Gate.
He also uprooted green grass and thorny plants and planted them in the marketplaces.
When Hóu Jǐng crossed the river,
he first massacred the people of the Eastern
(Míng manuscript: "Eastern Prefecture" instead of "Eastern Gate")
and the entire city was slaughtered.
Their heads were placed outside the Xīmíng Gate,
forming a mound as a warning.
The marketplaces were ruined,
and everywhere was desolate.
Master Tōng spoke of gains and losses,
which was inconvenient for Jǐng.
Jǐng disliked him,
but also feared he was no ordinary man,
and dared not harm him.
He secretly sent a minor general, Yú Zǐyuè, with four warriors to observe him.
Jǐng said to Zǐyuè:
"If he knows about the killing,
then do not harm him;
if he does not know, then secretly seize him."
Zǐyuè stationed the four men outside the gate
and entered alone to see him.
Master Tōng took off his clothes and warmed himself by the fire.
Addressing Zǐyuè first, he said:
"You have come to kill me.
Who am I?
How dare you kill me."
Zǐyuè bowed and said:
"I dare not."
Then he hurried back to report to Jǐng.
Jǐng bowed in apology to him,
and ultimately dared not harm him.
Later, Jǐng summoned Monk Tōng to a banquet.
Monk Tōng took some meat, pinched salt onto it,
and offered it to Jǐng.
He asked:
"Is it good?"
Jǐng said:
"Too salty."
Monk Tōng said:
"If not salty, it will rot."
After Jǐng died a few days later,
the crowd placed five *dan* of salt in his abdomen
and sent the corpse to the market of Jiànkāng.
The people fought to butcher it, slice it, and make soup,
eating it all.
Afterwards, Master Tōng's whereabouts were ultimately unknown.
From *Extensive Records of Past and Present Five Phases*
Master Zhuān
When Hóu Jǐng was the governor of Dìng Prefecture,
there was a monk whose clan and surname were unknown,
named Master Āzhuān.
He was often in the city markets,
and whenever he heard of gatherings for community feasts, vegetarian offerings, weddings, funerals, or banquets,
or places where young men gathered for falconry, dog racing, or banquets,
he was always present.
In quarrels and noisy disputes,
he would also take sides and support his friends.
This went on for many years.
Later, on the night of the fifteenth day of the first lunar month,
he offended the elders and youths at a banquet,
and they gathered to curse him with harsh words.
The host wanted to beat him to death,
but people from the market and streets rescued him and took him away.
The next morning, the brothers of the host went to capture him,
and they saw Master Āzhuān sitting astride a broken wall,
laughing and saying to them:
"Why do you all despise me so much here?
I will leave you."
The captors raised their sticks to strike him,
but the people from before stopped them again.
Master Āzhuān then said:
"You must truly despise me.
I am leaving."
He struck the wall with his stick,
shouting "Chì chì!"
The section of wall he was riding on
suddenly rose into the air,
reaching several tens of rèn high.
He raised his hand and bid farewell to the villagers, saying:
"Farewell."
All who saw this
bowed in reverence and repented of their faults.
In a moment,
he vanished into the clouds.
About a year later,
it was heard that he was in Cháng'ān,
still behaving as before.
After that, his fate is unknown.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì".
Master Ātū
In the early years of the Northern Qí,
there was a Master Ātū in Bīng Prefecture,
whose hometown, surname, and origins were also unknown.
Before Èrzhū was defeated,
he was already in Jìnyáng,
traveling through various commanderies and towns,
not residing in temples,
but moving among the common people.
His cryptic words always proved true.
Whenever he walked through the markets and streets,
crowds would surround him,
and he would shout loudly,
pointing to his chest and saying:
"I pity you common people for knowing nothing,
for not recognizing Master Ātū of Bīng Prefecture."
Thus, people came to call him by this name.
After Emperor Shénwǔ of Qí moved the capital to Yè,
because Jìnyáng was a military stronghold
and the foundation of the royal enterprise,
he often stationed himself in Bīng Prefecture.
Whenever he came to Yè,
all major military and state affairs
that had not yet left the inner chambers
were first leaked by Master Tū among the crowds.
In his later years,
he was captured and confined within the city,
with guards assigned to watch him,
forbidding him from leaving without permission.
If he escaped,
the gatekeepers would be held accountable.
On that day, at the three gates of Bīng Prefecture,
a Master Tū appeared at each, swinging out,
and they could not capture or restrain him.
Not long after,
someone came from the northern prefectures and said:
"Master Tū passed away under the city wall of Yànmén Commandery on the eighth day of the fourth month.
The people sent him off with incense and flowers
and buried him outside the city."
The people of Bīng Prefecture found this strange and laughed,
saying to him:
"Master Tū crossed the Fén Bridge on the eighth day of the fourth month,
heading east,
with one foot wearing a shoe
and the other bare,
but we don’t know which alley or neighborhood he entered.
Everyone saw him.
How can you say he died in Yànmén?"
This person returned to the northern prefectures
and reported this to his hometown.
Everyone opened the grave to look,
and found only a single shoe.
Later, he returned to wander in Bīng Prefecture.
Emperor Shénwǔ of Qí, because he could not control him
and his unrestrained words would not cease,
feared he would stir up the people,
so he executed him for sorcery and deception.
As a monk had no hair,
they used a rope to hook his head.
On the day of his execution,
the entire prefecture’s populace
went to the temple to witness it.
Master Tū smiled,
but said nothing more.
Six or seven days after the execution,
someone came from the Héxī tribes and said:
"On the road, I met Master Tū,
looking just as before,
but with a rope tied around his back,
encircling Master Tū’s head."
"Head" originally written as "desire,"
corrected according to the Míng manuscript.
When spoken to, he did not respond,
but hurried westward.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì".
Chán Master Chóu
The Northern Qi Dynasty's Master Chánshī Dòu
was from Yè.
Initially, he shaved his head to become a śrāmaṇera,
and there were many of his peers at the time.
Whenever they rested,
they often wrestled and leaped about as a game,
and Master Chánshī, being weak and inferior, was bullied.
Those who deceived, insulted, and beat him came one after another.
Master Chánshī felt ashamed of this,
so he entered the hall, closed the door,
embraced the feet of the Vajrapāṇi statue, and vowed:
"Because I am frail and weak,
I am despised and bullied by my peers.
The humiliation is too much to bear;
I would rather die.
You are renowned for your strength—
you should protect me.
I will hold your feet for seven days.
If you do not grant me strength,
I will surely die here,
with no intention of turning back."
After making this vow,
he sincerely prayed to it.
For the first couple of nights, he persisted as usual,
and his resolve grew even firmer.
On the sixth day, as dawn approached,
the form of Vajrapāṇi appeared,
holding a large bowl in his hand,
filled to the brim with sinews.
He said to Dòu:
"Young man, do you desire strength?"
Dòu replied:
"I do."
"Is your resolve firm?"
He said:
"It is."
"Can you eat these sinews?"
He said:
"I cannot."
The deity said:
"Why not?"
Dòu said:
"Because those who have left home abstain from meat."
The deity then picked up the bowl and raised a spoon,
showing him the sinews.
Master Chánshī did not dare to eat them.
The deity then threatened him with a vajra pestle,
and Dòu, out of fear, ate them.
As soon as they entered his mouth,
the deity said:
"You now possess great strength.
However, uphold the teachings well,
and strive diligently."
The deity departed as daybreak arrived,
and Dòu returned to his quarters.
His fellow monks asked him:
"Where have you been lately?"
Dòu did not answer.
Shortly after,
they gathered in the hall for a meal.
After eating,
his peers again invited him to playfully fight.
Master Chánshī said:
"I have strength now,
but I fear you cannot withstand it."
His peers tried to pull his arm,
but his sinews and bones were strong and powerful,
almost inhuman.
As they were shocked and suspicious,
Master Chánshī said:
"Let me demonstrate for you."
He then entered the hall,
walked sideways along the wall,
from west to east,
for several hundred paces.
He also leaped up to the beam four times,
and lifted a weight of a thousand jun.
His fists were swift and fierce,
astonishing all who saw and heard.
Those who had previously bullied him
prostrated themselves, sweating profusely,
not daring to look up.
Master Chánshī later attained enlightenment
and resided on Línlǘ Mountain.
He entered the mountains for several thousand li,
constructing meditation huts and halls,
exhausting the resources of timber and earth.
The monks who followed him in meditation
often numbered in the thousands.
Emperor Wénxuān of Qi grew angry at his gathering of crowds,
so he led tens of thousands of brave cavalry
and personally went to subdue him,
intending to execute him.
On that day, Master Chánshī
led his disciples to the mouth of the valley to await him.
Emperor Wénxuān asked:
"Master, why have you come here so hastily?"
Dòu said:
"Your Majesty intends to kill this poor monk.
I fear that bloodshed in the mountains would defile the saṃghārāma.
Therefore, I have come to the mouth of the valley to receive my execution."
Emperor Wénxuān was greatly astonished.
He descended from his carriage, paid his respects,
and begged for forgiveness of his wrongdoing.
Master Chánshī said nothing.
Emperor Wénxuān ordered a feast to be prepared,
and after offering it, he requested:
"I have heard that the master prayed to Vajrapāṇi and gained strength.
Now, I wish to see the master demonstrate a little of his strength.
May I?"
Dòu said:
"The strength of the past
was merely human strength.
Now, for Your Majesty, I will show divine strength.
Do you wish to see it?"
Emperor Wénxuān said:
"Please, let us witness it together."
Earlier, when Master Chánshī was building the temple,
various places had donated several thousand logs,
which lay at the mouth of the valley.
Master Chánshī chanted an incantation over them,
and the logs rose into the air,
striking against each other,
with a sound like thunder,
colliding and breaking apart,
falling like rain.
Emperor Wénxuān was terrified,
and his officials scattered and fled.
Emperor Wénxuān kowtowed and begged him to stop,
and then issued an edict allowing Master Chánshī to ordain people and build temples,
with no prohibitions.
Later, while constructing a pillar in Bīngzhōu,
he fell ill before it was completed.
On his deathbed, he sighed:
"Life and death
are the great division for all people.
Even the Tathāgata could not avoid it.
However, my meritorious deeds remain unfinished,
and this is my regret.
After death, I wish to be reborn as a powerful elder,
to continue and complete this work."
With these words, he passed away.
Thirty years later,
Emperor Suí passed through Bīngzhōu,
saw this temple,
and suddenly remembered,
as if it were an old place of practice.
He paid homage with reverence,
doing everything respectfully.
He ordered Bīngzhōu
to extensively repair and expand it,
and the temple was thus completed.
People at the time said the emperor was the powerful elder.
From "Jì Wén" and "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi."
Shìzhī Yuàn
In the Tang Dynasty, there was a monk from Yōuzhōu named Zhī Yuàn,
who was refined and erudite.
During the Sui Dynasty’s Dàyè era,
he resolved to create a stone chamber to house the entire Buddhist canon,
as a safeguard for the Dharma.
Subsequently, he carved a cave into the cliffs of the Western Hills in Yōuzhōu to serve as the stone chamber,
smoothing the four walls to inscribe the scriptures.
He also obtained square stones,
separately polished and inscribed them,
and stored them within the chamber.
Whenever a chamber was filled,
he would seal the entrance with stone,
securing it with molten iron.
At that time, Emperor Suí Yáng was visiting Zhuōjùn,
and the Vice Director of the Palace Secretariat, Xiāo Yǔ,
who was the empress’s younger brother,
was deeply devoted to Buddhism.
He reported this matter to the empress,
and she donated a thousand bolts of silk,
while Yǔ donated five hundred bolts.
When the court and the public heard of this,
they vied to make donations,
enabling Yuàn to complete his work.
Yuàn often considered that, with many laborers involved
and both monastic and lay followers gathering,
he wished to build a wooden Buddha hall and a dining hall in front of the cave.
However, he worried in his sleep that timber and tiles would be difficult to procure,
fearing it would incur excessive expenses,
and thus could not commence construction.
Suddenly, one night, there was a violent thunderstorm with lightning,
and when dawn broke clear,
they saw tens of thousands of large pine and cypress trees at the foot of the mountain,
washed down by water,
piled up along the roadside.
Monastic and lay followers were astonished,
unaware of their origin.
Thereupon, people near and far sighed in admiration.
Yuàn then had craftsmen select and take the timber,
distributing the remainder among the local villages.
The villages, delighted, assisted in constructing the halls,
and shortly thereafter, the work was completed.
It fulfilled his aspiration.
The stone scriptures created by Yuàn
had already filled seven chambers.
He passed away in the thirteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era.
His disciples continued his work.
From “Míng Bào Lù.”
Fǎ Xǐ
During the reign of Emperor Suí Yáng,
Nánhǎi Jùn sent a monk,
named Fǎ Xǐ.
The emperor ordered him to be accommodated within the palace.
At that time, a new hall had just been built inside,
and the master suddenly went up to inspect it.
Startled, he hurried down the steps,
looked back, and said:
“It nearly crushed me to death.”
That very night,
heavy rain fell from the sky,
and the hall collapsed,
crushing dozens of people to death.
Later, he again ran around inside the palace,
demanding a sheep’s head.
The emperor, hearing of this, was displeased,
considering it mad talk,
and ordered him locked in a room.
After several days,
a palace guard saw the master in the market,
and returned to report:
“Fǎ Xǐ is strolling leisurely in the market.”
The emperor reprimanded the responsible officials,
who inspected the place of confinement.
The door lock remained as before.
The guards also said:
“The master is inside the room.”
Thereupon, they opened the door and entered the room,
finding a kasaya covering a pile of white bones,
with the lock fastened around the neck bone.
They reported the situation to the emperor.
The emperor dispatched Chief Clerk Wáng Héng to verify,
and it was indeed so.
From then on, the emperor began to believe he was no ordinary man,
and ordered that he not be disturbed.
By evening,
the master returned to the room,
sometimes talking, sometimes laughing.
The gatekeeper reported this,
and the emperor ordered the officials to remove the lock,
releasing the master to go outside,
allowing him to go wherever he pleased.
Sometimes, within a single day,
there would be dozens of places offering vegetarian feasts,
and the master attended them all,
seen at every location.
Among these, he also drank wine and ate meat.
Soon after, he appeared to fall ill,
often lying in bed,
having the mat removed,
and instructing others to spread charcoal fire beneath the bed,
which was extremely hot.
After several days, he passed away,
his lower body scorched by the fire,
all charred and rotten.
He was buried at Xiāngshān Temple.
In the fourth year of the Dàyè era,
Nánhǎi Jùn reported:
“Fǎ Xǐ has been seen back in the commandery.”
The emperor ordered the coffin opened for inspection,
but there was nothing inside.
From “Shí Yí Jì,”
the Ming manuscript edition cites “Dàyè Shí Yí Jì.”
Fǎ Lín
During the Wǔdé era of the Tang Dynasty,
the Vinaya master Xuān of Zhōngnán Shān cultivated and upheld the precepts,
causing celestial beings such as General Wéi and eleven others to descend from heaven,
providing protection alongside him.
Among them was the Southern Heaven Prince Zhāng Yú,
who often attended the Vinaya master.
At that time, the monk Fǎ Lín drank wine and ate meat,
was indiscriminate in his associations,
and even had a wife and children.
When the Vinaya master was in the city,
Fǎ Lín visited him,
but the Vinaya master did not treat him with respect.
The Heaven Prince said to the Vinaya master:
“What manner of person do you consider yourself to be?”
The Vinaya master replied:
“I consider myself quite saintly.”
The Prince said:
“Master, you are not yet a saint;
you are merely a person of the four fruits.
Monk Fǎ Lín is a saint.”
The Vinaya master said:
“He breaks the precepts to such an extent;
how can he be a saint?”
The Prince said:
“He has attained the stage of a bodhisattva,
which is beyond your understanding.
However, when he comes again,
you should treat him well.”
The Vinaya master then changed his view.
Later, Fǎ Lín, drunk,
suddenly visited the Vinaya master,
sat directly on his bed,
and vomited beside it.
Although the filth was extremely foul,
the Vinaya master dared not show disdain.
Fǎ Lín then grabbed money intended for meritorious deeds,
stuffed it into his sleeve, and left directly,
using it to buy wine and meat in the market.
When the money ran out, he would come to take more,
and the Vinaya master, upon seeing him, would give it to him.
Later, Emperor Táng Gāozǔ, influenced by Daoist advisors,
intended to abolish Buddhism.
Fǎ Lín debated with the Daoists,
and the Daoists were shamed into submission.
He also offended Emperor Gāozǔ’s dignity,
firmly contending for Buddhism.
The preservation of Buddhism
was due to Lín’s efforts.
As for the Dharma-protecting bodhisattva in the Buddhist scriptures,
could it be referring to Lín?
From “Gǎn Tōng Jì.”
Xú Jìngyè
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān of the Táng dynasty,
Xú Jìngyè rebelled in Yángzhōu.
Wǔ Zétiān sent forces to suppress him,
and his army was defeated, forcing him to flee.
Jìngyè had previously adopted a man
who closely resembled him in appearance,
and treated him with great favor.
After Jìngyè's defeat,
the adopted man was captured,
and his head was cut off, being mistaken for Jìngyè.
In reality, Jìngyè had hidden in Dàgū Mountain,
where he built a hut with several dozen companions and cut off contact with the outside world.
He then shaved his head and became a monk,
and many of his companions did the same.
During the early Tiānbǎo era,
an old monk named Zhùkuò,
over ninety years old,
traveled with his disciples to Héngshān Temple in Nányuè to visit the monks and reside there,
staying for over a month.
Suddenly, he gathered the monks
and confessed to the sin of killing.
The monks were astonished.
The old monk said:
"Have you heard of Xú Jìngyè?
I am he.
After my military defeat,
I entered Dàgū Mountain,
where I diligently practiced the Way.
Now that my life is nearing its end,
I came to this temple
to let the world know that I have attained the fourth fruit."
He then announced the date of his death.
Indeed, he passed away on that very day.
He was buried at Héngshān.
From "Jì Wén."
Luò Bīnwáng
Sòng Zhīwèn, a Táng dynasty examination official, was demoted due to certain matters,
and later released and allowed to return.
He journeyed to the region south of the Yangtze River,
visiting Língyǐn Temple.
The moonlight was exceptionally bright that night,
and as he walked along the long corridor, reciting poetry,
he composed a verse:
"The Vulture Peak towers steep and high,
the Dragon Palace lies locked in silence."
He pondered deeply over this first couplet,
but remained unsatisfied.
An old monk, tending the eternal lamp,
sat on a large meditation bed
and asked:
"Young man, why are you awake so late at night,
reciting poetry with such effort?
What troubles you?"
Zhīwèn replied:
"I am devoted to poetry,
and I wish to compose a poem about this temple,
but inspiration eludes me."
The monk said:
"Try reciting the first couplet."
Zhīwèn recited it to him,
and after repeating it several times,
the monk said:
"Why not say, 'The tower overlooks the sun over the sea,
the gate faces the tide of the Zhèjiāng River'?"
Zhīwèn was astonished,
marveling at the vigor and beauty of the lines.
He then completed the rest of the poem:
"Cassia seeds fall from the moon,
heavenly fragrance drifts beyond the clouds.
Clutching vines, I climb the distant pagoda,
hollowing wood to draw water from afar.
Frost is light, flowers bloom again,
ice is thin, leaves have yet to wither.
Awaiting the path to Tiāntāi,
watch me cross the stone bridge."
The lines given by the monk
became the highlight of the entire poem.
At dawn, when Zhīwèn went to visit him again,
the monk was nowhere to be found.
A monk who knew the truth said:
"That was Luò Bīnwáng."
Zhīwèn pressed for details,
and the monk replied:
"When Xú Jìngyè was defeated,
he and Bīnwáng both fled,
and they could not be captured.
The generals, fearing they would lose the main culprits
and incur severe punishment,
and since tens of thousands had died at the time,
sought two men who resembled them, beheaded them, and presented their heads.
Later, although it was known they were still alive,
no one dared to capture and deliver them.
Thus, Jìngyè became a monk at Héngshān,
living to over ninety before passing away.
Bīnwáng also shaved his head,
traveled extensively to famous mountains,
and came to Língyǐn,
where he died after about a year.
Although they were defeated at the time,
they had acted in the name of restoring the Táng dynasty,
so many people helped them escape."
From "Běnshì Shī."
Xuánzàng
The monk Xuánzàng's secular surname was Chén,
and he was from Yǎnshī County.
From a young age, he was intelligent and wise,
with upright conduct.
During the early Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty,
he journeyed to the Western Regions to retrieve scriptures.
When he reached the kingdom of Jìbīn,
he found the path treacherous,
blocked by tigers and leopards, making it impassable.
Xuánzàng, unsure of what to do,
locked himself in his room and sat in meditation.
At night, he opened the door
and saw an old monk,
his face covered in sores,
his body oozing pus and blood,
sitting alone on the bed,
with no known origin.
Xuánzàng bowed and earnestly sought his guidance.
The monk orally transmitted a volume of the Heart Sutra to him,
instructing him to recite it.
Thereafter, the mountains and rivers became level,
the roads opened up,
tigers and leopards hid their forms,
and demons vanished without a trace.
Thus, he reached the Buddhist land,
retrieved over six hundred volumes of scriptures, and returned.
The Heart Sutra is still recited to this day.
Before Xuánzàng departed for the Western Regions,
he saw a pine tree at Língyán Temple.
Standing in the courtyard,
he stroked its branches and said:
"I am going west to seek the Buddhist teachings.
May you grow westward;
if I return,
then turn back eastward,
so that my disciples will know."
After he left,
the branches pointed westward year after year,
growing several zhang in length.
One year, they suddenly turned eastward,
and his disciples said:
"Our master is returning!"
They went west to welcome him,
and indeed, Xuánzàng returned.
To this day, people call this pine the "Head-Stroking Pine."
From "Dú Yì Zhì" and "Táng Xīn Yǔ."
Wàn Huí
Master Wàn Huí was from Wénxiāng,
and his secular surname was Zhāng.
Initially, his mother prayed to an image of Guānyīn and thus conceived Huí.
Huí was born foolish,
and only began to speak at the age of eight or nine.
His parents also raised him like a pig or dog.
When he grew older,
his father ordered him to plow the fields.
Huí plowed straight ahead without looking back,
repeatedly chanting "equality" with his mouth.
Thus, he plowed one ridge
for tens of miles,
stopping only when he encountered a ditch or pit.
His father became angry and struck him,
but Huí said:
"Both sides are being plowed;
why must there be differences?"
His father then stopped hitting him and ceased plowing.
Huí's elder brother was serving in Ānxī,
and news of him was cut off.
His parents thought he had died,
and wept day and night, consumed with worry.
Seeing how deeply his parents were grieving,
Huí suddenly knelt and said:
"Are your tears not because you worry about my brother?"
His parents were both doubtful and hopeful,
and replied:
"Yes."
Huí said:
"Think carefully about what my brother needs—
clothes, furs, dried provisions, shoes, and such things.
Please prepare them all,
and I will go to him."
Suddenly, one day,
he set off in the morning with the prepared items
and returned home in the evening.
He told his parents:
"My brother is safe and well."
Looking at him,
they saw the traces of his brother's journey,
and the whole family was astonished.
From Hóngnóng to Ānxī
was about ten thousand *lǐ*.
Because he returned from ten thousand *lǐ*,
he was given the name Wàn Huí.
Earlier, when Master Xuánzàng went to the land of Buddha to fetch scriptures,
he saw an inscription on a pillar of a Buddhist niche:
"The Bodhisattva Wàn Huí
has been exiled to Wénxiāng to teach and transform."
Master Xuánzàng hastened by post to Wénxiāng County,
asked if there was a Master Wàn Huí here,
and had him summoned.
When Wàn Huí arrived,
Master Xuánzàng paid him respects
and bestowed upon him the three robes, bowl, and alms bowl before departing.
Later, Empress Wǔ Zétiān summoned him to the palace,
and his words about events were often proven true.
At that time, Zhāng Yìzhī was constructing a grand mansion,
and Wàn Huí often pointed at it, saying:
"It will become the Directorate for Palace Buildings."
No one understood what he meant.
After Yìzhī was executed,
his mansion was turned into the Directorate for Palace Buildings.
He often said to Empress Wéi and Princess Ānlè:
"Sānláng will chop off your heads."
Empress Wéi, because Emperor Zhōngzōng was the third son,
feared the emperor would cause trouble,
so she poisoned him,
not realizing she would be executed by Emperor Xuánzōng.
Also, when Emperor Ruìzōng was still a prince,
he sometimes traveled incognito among the people.
Wàn Huí would loudly proclaim in the streets and villages:
"The Son of Heaven is coming,"
or,
"The Sage is coming."
Within a day or two of his proclamation,
Emperor Ruìzōng would surely pass through and linger there.
Prince Huìzhuāng,
the second son of Emperor Ruìzōng,
was once shown to Wàn Huí by Empress Wǔ Zétiān.
Wàn Huí said:
"This child is the essence of a great tree from the Western Regions;
raising him will benefit his brothers."
Later, Shēnwáng was born,
with a majestic and imposing appearance,
and was fond of eating and drinking.
During the Jǐnglóng era,
Wàn Huí frequently came and went,
and people of all social ranks,
noble and common,
competed to pay him respects.
Wàn Huí wore a brocade robe,
sometimes laughing and cursing,
sometimes beating a drum,
and then events would unfold as he predicted.
Princess Tàipíng built a residence for him to the right of her own mansion.
During the Jǐngyún era,
he passed away in this residence.
Before his death, he cried out loudly,
asking for water from his hometown river.
His disciples searched but could not find it.
Wàn Huí said:
"The river water is in front of the hall."
The crowd dug a well under the steps,
and suddenly river water gushed forth.
He drank it and then passed away.
The well water in this ward
remains sweet and delicious to this day.
From *Tán Bīn Lù* and *Liǎng Jīng Jì*.
Yīxíng
Monk Yīxíng’s surname was Zhāng,
and he was a native of Jùlù.
His original name was Suì.
After Táng Xuánzōng summoned and received him,
he said to him:
"What are your abilities?"
Yīxíng replied:
"I am only good at remembering and reading."
Xuánzōng then ordered the palace women’s quarters
to bring the register of palace women to show him.
After Yīxíng had looked through it completely,
the original was covered up,
yet he remembered it with perfect familiarity,
as if he had long been accustomed to it.
After reading several pages,
Xuánzōng unconsciously descended from the imperial couch,
performed a ritual bow to him,
and called him a sage.
Previously, after Yīxíng had followed Buddhism,
he took Pǔ Jì as his teacher on Sōng Shān.
The master once arranged a meal at the temple,
gathering a large assembly of monks and religious practitioners.
Those who lived several hundred lǐ away
all arrived as scheduled,
gathering over a thousand people.
At that time, there was a man named Lú Hóng,
whose virtue was lofty and learning profound,
and who lived in seclusion on Sōng Shān.
They therefore invited Hóng to compose a text
praising the gathering.
On the day,
Hóng brought his text to the temple,
and the master received it,
placing it on the table.
After the bells and chanting had begun,
Hóng requested of Pǔ Jì:
"I have composed a text of several thousand words,
moreover with obscure characters and unusual language.
Why not select the most intelligent and perceptive among the assembly of monks,
and I will personally transmit it to him."
So they summoned Yīxíng.
When he arrived,
he unrolled the paper and smiled slightly,
stopping after a single reading,
and placed it back on the table.
Hóng thought him careless and secretly found it strange.
Shortly after, the assembly of monks gathered in the hall,
Yīxíng rolled up his sleeves and stepped forward,
raising his voice to begin reciting,
without omitting a single word.
Hóng was astonished for a long time,
and said to Jì:
"This is not someone you can teach;
you should let him travel and study freely."
Yīxíng thus exhaustively studied the Great Expansion,
and from then on sought out teachers and mentors,
traveling thousands of lǐ without regard for distance.
He once went to the Guóqīng Temple on Tiāntāi Mountain,
where he saw a courtyard
with ancient pines several tens of paces away,
and a stream flowing before the gate.
Yīxíng stood between the gate and screen,
and heard a monk in the courtyard laying out counting rods in the courtyard,
their sound rustling.
After a while, the monk said to his disciple:
"Today, a disciple will come seeking my calculation methods;
he should already be at the gate.
Is there no one to guide him in?"
After removing one counting rod,
he said again:
"The water before the gate should now flow westward;
the disciple will arrive."
Yīxíng, following these words, entered,
bowed and requested the teachings.
The monk then fully transmitted his methods to him.
And the water before the gate, which originally flowed east,
suddenly changed to flow westward.
Xíng Hépǔ once said to Yǐn Yīn:
"Is Yīxíng not a sage?
Hàn dynasty’s Luò Xiàhóng, when creating the calendar, said:
'After eight hundred years,
there will be a discrepancy of one day,
and then a sage will correct it.'
Now that period has ended,
and Yīxíng created the Great Expansion Calendar,
precisely correcting the error.
Thus Luò Xiàhóng’s words were true."
Yīxíng also once went to the Daoist priest Yǐn Chóng to borrow Yáng Xióng’s Tàixuán Jīng.
After several days,
he went again to Chóng to return the book.
Chóng said:
"This book’s meaning is profound and far-reaching;
I have sought to understand it for years,
and still cannot comprehend it.
You, sir, should try studying it further;
why return it so hastily?"
Yīxíng said:
"I have already fathomed its meaning."
He then brought out the Great Expansion Mystical Chart and a volume of explanatory formulas he had composed to show Chóng.
Chóng sighed deeply in admiration.
He said to others:
"This young man is a Yánzǐ."
Earlier, when Yīxíng was young, his family was poor.
A neighboring old woman named Wáng
had assisted him with a total of several hundred thousand cash,
and Yīxíng often thought of repaying her.
By the Kāiyuán era,
Yīxíng enjoyed Xuánzōng’s respect and favor,
and his words carried great weight.
Not long after,
it happened that Old Woman Wáng’s son committed murder,
and the case was not yet settled.
The old woman went to Yīxíng seeking help.
Yīxíng said:
"If you, old mother, want gold or silk,
I will repay you tenfold.
But the sovereign upholds the law;
it is difficult to plead on emotional grounds.
What can be done?"
Old Woman Wáng pointed her finger and cursed loudly:
"What use was knowing this monk!"
Yīxíng followed and apologized to her,
but she never looked back.
Yīxíng then devised a plan. In the Húntiān Temple there were several hundred laborers.
He ordered a room emptied,
and moved a large vat to the center.
Secretly selecting two resident servants,
he gave them cloth sacks,
and said:
"At such-and-such ward, at such-and-such corner, there is a deserted garden.
Go there and lie in wait;
from noon until dusk,
creatures will come in.
If their number is seven,
capture them all.
If you miss even one, you will be caned."
They went as instructed.
After yǒu hour (5–7 p.m.),
indeed a herd of pigs arrived,
and they captured them all and returned.
Yīxíng was greatly pleased,
and ordered them placed in the vat,
covered with a wooden lid,
sealed with Six-One mud,
and inscribed with several dozen Sanskrit characters in vermilion.
His disciples could not fathom his purpose.
The next morning,
a palace eunuch urgently knocked at the gate summoning him.
He went to a side hall.
Xuánzōng met him and asked:
"The Grand Astrologer reported
'Last night the Northern Dipper was not visible.'
What omen is this?
Master, do you have a way to avert it?"
Yīxíng said:
"In the Later Wèi, Mars was lost.
Now the Imperial Chariot (the Dipper) is not seen—
has such a thing ever happened in antiquity?
Heaven is about to issue a great warning to Your Majesty.
When common men and women
do not find their proper place,
then frost falls unseasonably and droughts scorch the land.
Only when moved by great virtue
can the celestial bodies retreat from their stations.
The most effective way to move them
lies in burying the unburied dead and releasing prisoners.
In Buddhism, a wrathful mind destroys all goodness,
[Editor’s note: ‘goodness’ in some editions reads ‘joy’]
while a compassionate mind subdues all demons.
In my humble opinion,
nothing would be better than a general amnesty for the empire?"
Xuánzōng followed his advice.
That very evening,
the Grand Astrologer reported one star of the Northern Dipper had reappeared.
After seven days in all, it fully returned.
Toward the end of the Kāiyuán era,
Péi Kuān served as Governor of Hénán,
deeply believed in Buddhism,
and took Chán Master Pǔ Jì as his teacher,
visiting him day and night.
One day,
when Kuān went to see Jì,
Jì said:
"I have a small matter to attend to just now,
and have no leisure for conversation;
please wait a while and rest."
Kuān then held his breath
and stayed in an empty room,
where he saw Jì purify and sweep the main hall,
burn incense, and sit upright.
He had not sat long
when suddenly knocking was heard at the gate,
and a voice called out repeatedly, "Heavenly Master, Monk Yīxíng has arrived!"
Yīxíng entered,
approached Jì and bowed,
and after bowing,
leaned close to his ear for a secret talk,
his demeanor extremely reverent.
Jì only nodded in acknowledgment.
There was nothing that was not permissible.
After speaking, he performed a ritual,
and after the ritual, he spoke again,
repeating this three times.
Jì only said:
"Yes, yes."
There was nothing that was not permissible.
Once Yīxíng finished speaking,
he descended the steps and entered the southern chamber,
closing the door behind him.
Jì then slowly instructed his disciples, saying:
"Ring the bell!
Venerable Yīxíng has attained parinirvāṇa."
His attendants hurried to look,
and it was exactly as he had said.
After his parinirvāṇa,
Kuān wore mourning garments and buried him,
personally
(Note: The Ming manuscript and Chén's revised edition have "rì" instead of "zì")
walking out of the city on foot to see him off.
From "Records of the Kaiyuan and Tianbao Eras" and "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Minghuáng," "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng"
Wúwèi
During the Táng dynasty, the Tripitaka Master Wúwèi first arrived from India,
and the officials led him to have an audience with Emperor Xuánzōng.
Emperor Xuánzōng saw him and revered and trusted him,
and thus said to the Tripitaka Master:
"Master, you have come from afar,
so you must be weary.
Where do you wish to rest?"
The Tripitaka Master replied:
"When I was in India,
I often heard that the Vinaya Master Xuān of the Western Brilliance Monastery in the Great Táng was foremost in upholding the precepts,
and I wish to go and rely on him."
Emperor Xuánzōng granted his request.
Vinaya Master Xuān observed the precepts with strict austerity,
and his cultivation through burning incense was pure and meticulous.
The Tripitaka Master drank wine and ate meat,
and his speech and conduct were coarse and unrestrained.
Often, while intoxicated, he would make a clamor and compete,
defiling the mats and bedding,
which Vinaya Master Xuān found quite unbearable.
Suddenly, in the middle of the night,
Vinaya Master Xuān caught a louse
and was about to throw it to the ground.
The Tripitaka Master, half-drunk,
repeatedly called out:
"Vinaya Master, Vinaya Master,
are you going to crush a child of the Buddha to death?"
Only then did Vinaya Master Xuān realize he was an extraordinary person,
and he straightened his robes, paid respects, and served him as his teacher.
Vinaya Master Xuān was extremely diligent and austere,
often walking in meditation late at night.
Once, as he was about to fall from the edge of a step, he suddenly felt someone supporting his feet.
Xuān looked back and saw
that it was a youth.
Xuān hastily asked:
"Who are you, disciple?
Why are you here in the middle of the night?"
The youth said:
"I am no ordinary person;
I am Prince Nǎzhā, son of Vaiśravaṇa Deva King.
For the sake of protecting the Dharma,
I have been guarding you, Venerable,
for a long time now."
Vinaya Master Xuān said:
"In my cultivation,
I have no need to trouble the Prince.
Since the Prince possesses divine power and freedom,
if there is anything in the Western Regions that can be used for Buddhist affairs,
I hope the Prince can bring it here."
The Prince said:
"I have a Buddha tooth,
which I have treasured for a long time.
However, since even one's head and eyes can be given up,
how dare I not offer it?"
Vinaya Master Xuān obtained it,
and it is the Buddha tooth now enshrined in Chóngshèng Monastery.
From "Records of the Kaiyuan and Tianbao Eras"
Master Míngdá
Master Míngdá
—no one knows where he came from—
lived at the old monastery of Wànhuí in Wénxiāng County.
Travelers passing by
would all visit Míngdá
to inquire about their fortunes.
Míngdá would not answer,
but only revealed his intent through his actions.
Once, someone visited Míngdá
and asked:
"I wish to go to the capital to visit my relative.
Is my relative safe?"
Míngdá handed him a bamboo staff.
When he reached the capital, his relative had passed away.
Another person visited Míngdá,
and Míngdá took a horse from the monastery,
had him mount it,
and made him gallop north and south before departing.
That person arrived in the capital
and was appointed as an investigating judge,
traveling by post horse everywhere.
Yet another person visited Míngdá,
and Míngdá used the staff he was holding
to draw a mound on the ground,
then poked and tamped the ground to make a pit.
That person did not understand,
but when he reached the capital,
a swelling broke out on his back,
and when it was lanced,
he nearly died from the bleeding.
When Lǐ Línfǔ was Vice Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
he escorted the emperor on a return journey west
and visited Míngdá,
who placed a steelyard on his shoulder.
When he reached the capital, he became Chancellor.
Lǐ Yōngmén was the magistrate of Húchéng,
and Míngdá suddenly asked for his small horse,
but Yōngmén refused to give it.
A day later,
as Yōngmén was about to go out on horseback,
the horse suddenly reared up like a man in the courtyard,
and Yōngmén fell from the horse and died.
There were many such instances.
Míngdá would often gaze north from the monastery gate,
saying:
"Why are there so many soldiers and horses in this plain?"
He also sighed deeply and said:
"Everywhere here is filled with armies."
Later, when Gēshū Hàn amassed troops at Tóng Pass
to resist the rebel barbarians,
the area below the pass in Wénxiāng
became entirely a battlefield.
From "Records of Things Heard"
Huìzhào
From then on, he ultimately did not know where he had gone.
However, according to Zhào himself, he was born in the seventh year of the Pǔtōng era of the Liáng dynasty.
Consulting the history of the Liáng dynasty,
the seventh year of the Pǔtōng era
corresponds to the year Bǐngwǔ.
Counting until the tenth year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty, which is the year Yǐwèi,
a total of two hundred and ninety years have passed.
This indeed matches what Zhào said.
I have often compared what he said with the histories of the Liáng and Chén dynasties,
and there are quite a few similarities.
Thus, I am even more convinced that his account is not false.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
Xuān Lǜshī
In the spring, second month of the second year of the Qiánfēng era of the Great Táng dynasty,
Vinaya Master Dào of the Xīmíng Temple was pursuing quietude and cultivating the Way at the old Jìngyè Temple south of the capital city.
The Vinaya Master's accumulated virtue was lofty and far-reaching,
and he had long embraced simplicity.
Suddenly, a person came to the Vinaya Master's place,
paid his respects, and presented his courtesies.
After exchanging pleasantries about the warmth and cold,
the Vinaya Master asked:
"Where is the donor from?
What is your surname and given name?"
He replied:
"Your disciple's surname is Wáng, given name Fán,
and I was a Lántái official of Great Wú.
When the Master first arrived at Jiànyè,
Lord Sūn did not immediately grant permission,
ordering that a rare auspicious sign be felt,
to establish an extraordinary temple.
At that time, the gods of heaven and earth
all bestowed their numinous protection.
Within twenty-one days,
they indeed felt the presence of śarīra relics.
The King of Wú personally held a bronze vase,
pouring it into a bronze basin.
Where the śarīra struck,
the basin immediately cracked.
Even when subjected to burning by fire and hammering tests,
they could not be damaged.
People like Kǎn Zé and Zhāng Yù
also received the protection and assistance of heavenly beings,
who entered their bodies,
making their spirits clear and keen, their comprehension sharp,
and their responses harmonious and fitting.
Now my karma is in heaven,
and my task is to broadly protect the Buddha-Dharma.
Your disciple is an envoy under General Wéi, the Heavenly King of the South.
General Wéi has extremely many affairs,
protecting the Buddha-Dharma of three continents.
Whenever there are matters of conflict, aggression, or peril,
he personally goes without fail,
mediating and persuading to bring resolution.
Now, accompanying him respectfully,
as heaven is about to arrive,
and previous affairs are pressing and clamorous,
he will arrive shortly.
He specifically ordered us disciples to speak with you, Master."
Not long after, another person came,
saying his surname was Luó,
and he was from Shǔ.
He spoke with a Shǔ accent,
extensively discussing the aspects of the Vinaya.
When first meeting,
his etiquette was like secular courtesy.
He narrated the circumstances and reasons,
with much sequence and order,
but then it was suddenly forgotten.
Next came another person,
saying his surname was Fèi,
paying respects as before.
He said:
"Your disciple, during the time of Buddha Kāśyapa,
was born in the first heaven,
under General Wéi.
The various heavens are intoxicated by greed and desire,
but your disciple, due to the power of past vows,
does not engage in heavenly desires,
maintaining pure Brahmacarya.
I particularly revere the Vinaya.
General Wéi practices the childlike-truth Brahmacarya,
and does not accept heavenly desires.
Under each king,
there are eight generals, four kings, and thirty-two commanders.
They circulate throughout the four continents,
coming and going, protecting and assisting all those who have left home.
Among the four continents,
the northern heavenly continent
has little Buddha-Dharma.
The other three continents
have the Buddha-Dharma greatly propagated.
However, those who have left home
often violate the prohibitive precepts,
and few are as the Dharma prescribes.
In the eastern and western continents,
people have little wisdom and intelligence,
their afflictions are difficult to transform.
In the southern continent,
although many commit offenses,
they can be transformed to follow goodness;
their minds are easy to tame and subdue.
When the Buddha was approaching Nirvāṇa,
he personally entrusted and enjoined them,
ordering them all to guard and protect,
not letting demons harass.
If they do not guard and protect,
with such violation of precepts,
who would practice my Dharma teachings?
Therefore, the Buddha bestowed his injunction,
and we dare not not act.
Although we see violations of prohibitions,
we pity and protect them.
Seeing the practice of one good deed,
ten thousand faults are not blamed,
the matter is like forgetting flaws,
not dwelling on past errors.
Moreover, the foul odor of humans
rises and permeates the empty realm for four hundred thousand lǐ,
and the various heavens, being pure,
are all repelled by it.
But because they received the Buddha's entrustment,
ordering them to protect the Buddha-Dharma,
they still dwell together with humans.
The various heavens dare not not come.
Among General Wéi's thirty-two commanders,
he is the most devoted to broad protection.
There are many demon sons and demon daughters
who lightly toy with bhikṣus.
Those whose power in the Way is slight
are all deluded and disturbed.
General Wéi, anxious and hurried, rushes to them,
responding to the opportunity to remove and cut them off.
Therefore, when matters arise
requiring him to go to the place of the Four Kings,
the kings all rise upon seeing him.
This is because General Wéi cultivates childlike-truth conduct and protects the True Dharma.
Your disciple's nature delights in the precepts and Vinaya.
All the Vinaya rules instituted by the Tathāgata in his lifetime,
I listened to and received in the assembly."
Thereupon, he asked about various obscure meanings in the Vinaya texts,
and there was nothing unresolved or stagnant.
However, in this Eastern Land, the Three Jewels,
inherently have mountains, seas, waters, and stones,
which often manifest in many places,
but people merely call them numinous and revere them.
Considering and inquiring about the lost origins,
none know where to turn.
Therefore, due to this connection,
I followed and consulted him.
Moreover, the appearance of deep obscurity,
if reasoned and encompassed,
has never been upheld and contemplated,
and cannot be spoken of.
Master Xuān also asked the heavenly being using the Gǎntōng Jì:
"The multi-jewel stone Buddha in Chéngdū, Yìzhōu—
from which era's image is it,
that emerged from the ground?"
He replied:
"The original foundation of Shǔ's capital is on Mount Qīngchéng.
Present-day Chéngdū
is a great sea region.
In the past, during the time of Buddha Kāśyapa,
someone made it at the Xī'ěr River,
intending it to be the full-body likeness of the Multi-Jewel Buddha.
It was at the Jiùshān Temple on the Xī'ěr River.
A person from Chéngdū went there for trade,
requested the image and brought it back.
Reaching the place of the present Duōbǎo Temple,
it was sunk by a sea spirit trampling the boat.
Initially, the person who took the image saw the sea spirit roaming on the shore,
thought it was a mountain ghost,
and immediately killed it.
Because of this, the spirit, angered, capsized and sank it,
both person and image drowned,
on the same boat.
That Multi-Jewel Buddha originally was at the Jiùtóushān Temple.
The ancient foundation still exists,
and there is still a stūpa,
often emitting light.
Now, heading to that land,
the route passes through Lángzhōu.
Regardless of major and minor [distances],
it is over three thousand lǐ,
before reaching the Xī'ěr River.
The river is very wide,
sometimes a hundred lǐ,
sometimes five hundred lǐ.
There are mountain islands in the middle,
and also ancient temples.
Sūtras and images still remain,
but no monks reside there.
The sūtras are the same as these texts.
At times, the sound of bells is heard.
The common people are prosperous,
and each year at two times,
they make offerings to the ancient stūpas.
The stūpas are like precept platforms,
triple-layered, built of stone,
with a covering bowl on top.
Their number is extremely many.
The people of that land
merely call them spirit mounds.
Whenever they emit light,
people offer vegetarian food sacrifices to them,
seeking blessings and fortune.
That place is over two thousand lǐ northwest from Xīzhōu.
It is asked, it is not far from India,
and there are often those who reach there.
From below, and so on, until the Jìn dynasty,
there was a monk in this place.
He saw earthen mounds appearing and being removed as they appeared,
strange and impossible to level.
Later, he saw them broken open,
I deeply wondered about this.
Then I dug deep over ten feet,
and found the statue and human bones in a boat.
The skull, elbow, and shin bones
were all several times larger and coarser
than those of people today.
These were from the time of Buddha Kāśyapa,
when people in Jambudvīpa lived for twenty thousand years.
Now in this kalpa of decline,
lifespans are short and people are small,
which is naturally so,
and nothing to wonder about.
When it first emerged,
it was difficult to pull and drag.
A disciple transformed into an old man,
pointing and guiding with skillful means,
and in a moment it reached Zhōu,
hiding temporarily when the Dharma was extinguished.
When it revived again in the Suí dynasty,
it was brought out once more.
People of Shǔ only knew it emerged spiritually from the ground,
but could not fathom its origins.
Seeing the flower pedestal had the characters "Duō Bǎo",
they thus named it accordingly,
also calling it Duō Bǎo Temple."
I asked further:
"The characters 'Duō Bǎo' are in clerical script,
which emerged in the perished Qín dynasty.
How could there already be Chinese writing
in the time of Buddha Kāśyapa?"
The answer was:
"The clerical script of Lǐ Sī from perished Qín
is actually a recent inheritance from ancient times.
The rise of clerical script
occurred in the era of ancient Buddhas.
See now the southern continent, surrounded by over a thousand isles,
adorning Jambudvīpa;
in one direction there are over a hundred countries,
their writing and speech
are the same as in the Táng state today.
But because the sea routes are vast and distant,
often spanning hundreds of thousands of miles,
and repeated translations fail to transmit them,
this region remains isolated and stagnant,
which is not surprising.
Have you not heard, Master?
Gu Yěwáng of Liáng,
a great erudite of the Imperial Academy,
extensively researched the origins of characters,
finding them appearing and disappearing unpredictably,
so the preface to the Yùpiān states:
'When Chūnshēn Jun's tomb was opened, its inscriptions were obtained,
all in clerical script.'
Checking, Chūnshēn was contemporaneous
(Míng manuscript lacks "Zhōu Wǔ")
with the Six States period;
thus clerical script existed before the day of annexation.
The various scripts of seal and clerical in this country
are still obscure and unclear,
how could one know of matters from Buddha Kāśyapa's time?
Certainly these are beyond what their ears and eyes have heard or seen."
I asked further:
"Now west of Xījīng city there is a high earthen platform,
commonly called
Cāngjié's character-creation platform.
How can you say clerical script existed in ancient times?"
The answer was:
"Cāngjié added earth to build this platform,
observing bird tracks here
—this is not without basis.
Moreover, the tradition of Cāngjié
is rarely known in its origins in this land.
Some say he was a minister of Huángdì,
others say an ancient emperor.
Bird-track script changed with time,
one path now completely lost.
Such unprofitable words
need not be elaborated."
There was also a heavenly being,
surname Lù, name Xuánchàng,
who came to visit the Vinaya Master, saying:
"Disciple was born in the early heavens
during King Mù of Zhōu's time,
originally a heaven from Buddha Kāśyapa's time,
manifesting temporarily in Zhōu
for the purpose of conversion.
Regarding the high earthen platform you asked about,
originally Buddha Kāśyapa held his third assembly here,
preaching the Dharma to liberate people.
By King Mù's time,
Mañjuśrī and Maudgalyāyana came to convert,
and King Mù followed them;
these are the so-called 'transformational beings' mentioned in Lièzǐ.
The transformational being revealed to King Mù:
'The high platform is where Buddha Kāśyapa preached the Dharma.'
Thus the three-assembly site was established.
By Duke Mù of Qín's time,
a stone Buddha was obtained in Fúfēng,
but Duke Mù did not recognize it,
discarding it in the horse stable,
defiling this image.
The protective deity of the image became angry,
causing the duke to fall ill.
The duke also dreamed of visiting the Supreme Deity,
where he was severely reprimanded.
Awakening, he asked his attendant Yóu Yú,
who replied:
'I have heard that in King Mù of Zhōu's time,
a transformational being came to this land,
said to be a Buddha-deity.
King Mù believed it,
building the Zhōngtiān Platform on Zhōngnán Mountain,
over a thousand feet high,
its foundation still visible.
He also built a temple at Cāngjié's platform,
named the Three-Assembly Site.
Could your current affliction
be due to Buddha?'
The duke heard this and was greatly terrified,
saying to Yóu Yú:
'I recently obtained a stone figure,
its clothing not of current fashion,
and discarded it in the horse stable.
Could this be the Buddha-deity?'
Yóu Yú heard this,
went to look,
and replied:
'This is truly the Buddha-deity.'
The duke retrieved the image, bathed it,
and placed it in a pure location,
whereupon the image emitted light.
The duke was terrified again,
thinking the deity was angry,
and slaughtered three animals to sacrifice.
The various good deities
lifted and discarded them far away.
The duke was greatly terrified again,
asking Yóu Yú.
He replied:
'I have heard Buddha is pure,
does not accept wine or meat,
and cherishes living beings' lives,
protecting them like an only child.
All offerings
are merely incense burning;
what can be sacrificed
are things like cakes and fruits.'
The duke was greatly pleased.
Wishing to make a Buddha image,
he lacked artisans.
Again he asked Yóu Yú,
who replied:
'By the temple King Mù built,
there should be artisans.'
Thus south of the high platform village,
they found an old man,
surname Wáng, name Ān,
aged one hundred eighty.
He said he had seen people make them at the three-assembly site,
but now he was old
and lacked strength to work.
North of his village lived four brothers
who had worked for various artisans at the site,
so he requested they be summoned to create it together.
Following his words, they made it,
completing a bronze image.
Its features were perfect and complete;
the duke was pleased
and greatly rewarded them.
Those people, obtaining wealth,
also created merit,
building a multi-story pavilion on the earthen platform,
three hundred feet high.
People of the time called it the High Platform,
or High Tower.
Those people's surname was Gāo,
the eldest named Sì;
some say
because four brothers established it together.
Some took the eldest brother's name to designate it,
hence the name Gāo Sì,
still called so today."
I asked further:
"Maudgalyāyana and Śāriputra
had already passed when Buddha was present;
how could they reappear?"
The answer was:
"There were six people with the same name;
this Maudgalyāyana was not the great Maudgalyāyana.
By the time of Yǔwén Zhōu,
Mañjuśrī transformed into a Brahmin monk,
coming to travel in this land,
saying he wished to pay respects at Buddha Kāśyapa's preaching site
and visit where Mañjuśrī dwells,
named Qīngliáng Mountain.
He asked all monks and laypeople,
but none knew.
At that time there was Dharma Master Zhì Měng,
He repeatedly dreamed of seeing the Buddha on this mountain,
seated within a brick pagoda.
The Buddha spoke to Yào, saying:
‘You should drink less wine,
do not indulge in sensual desires,
dismiss the wicked and deceitful,
and promote the loyal and virtuous.’
Yào was unable to follow this advice.
Later, in Luòyáng,
he fell from his horse while drunk
and was captured by Shí Lè.
Initially, Yào, enlightened by the dream,
sent people to search the mountains and seek it out.
They then saw this image,
seated in a small brick pagoda,
