exactly matching the dream.
He then demolished the small pagoda
and built a larger one in its place,
nineteen stories high,
also constructing temple buildings.
They were made extremely magnificent and grand.
The temple was named Fǎdēng,
and three hundred monks were ordained to reside there.
After Yào perished and the Zhào state fell,
forty-three people in the temple
attained the third fruit of sanctity.
The mountain deity later built another temple behind the pagoda,
to provide for the monks who had attained the third fruit.
The deity went to Tàibái Mountain,
gathered magical herbs,
and offered them to the holy monks,
all of whom attained extended lifespans.
The temple still exists today,
though ordinary people cannot see it.
The bell sounds that are heard
are precisely the bells of that temple.
The original foundation of that pagoda,
though initiated by Liú Yào,
is still the site where King Mù established the temple,
and it is also the ancient temple of Kāśyapa Tathāgata.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
on the mountain north of Yùhuá in Cíwūchuān,
herds of deer were often seen gathering at a certain spot,
dispersing when chased but returning again.
Someone found this strange.
At the place where the deer gathered,
they dug down one zhàng deep
and unearthed a stone statue,
about one zhàng tall,
which is now venerated and provided for. ”
He also asked:
“Regarding the sandalwood statue in the former Dàmíng Temple in Jīngzhōu,
it is said to have been made by King Udayana,
and according to tradition, a copy was brought from there
to the Liáng dynasty.
Now there is also one in the capital.
Which one is the original? ”
The answer was:
“The Dàmíng statue is the original.
After Emperor Wǔ of Liáng passed away,
the statue came to Jīngzhōu.
In the third year of Emperor Yuán’s Chéngshèng reign,
after the Northern Zhōu pacified Liáng,
they collected the state treasures,
all of which were taken to Northern Zhōu.
As for the sandalwood statue,
the monk Zhēnzàng hid it in his room
and gave many valuables to the envoys,
so the statue was able to remain.
In the ninth year of the Suí dynasty’s Kāihuáng era,
Emperor Wén sent the envoy Liǔ Gùyán to fetch it.
The temple monks again pleaded for the statue,
asking that it remain to protect Jīngchǔ.
As Gùyán was a native of the region,
he agreed.
He ordered another sandalwood statue to be carved
to be presented to the emperor.
At that time, they sought a craftsman
and found a Brahmin monk,
named Zhēndá,
who made it.
This is the statue now in the Dàxīngshàn Temple in the Western Capital,
which is also very spiritually potent.
The original statue remains in Jīngzhōu.
The monks covered it with lacquered cloth.
Its appearance is not as fine as the true one.
Dàmíng was originally an ancient dwelling place of the Buddha,
which is why the spiritual statue refused to move north.
Recently, the virtuous monk Yì from Chángshā,
with divine aid in the unseen realm,
gained enlightenment and insight.
He separately removed the lacquered cloth,
revealing the true countenance again,
greatly inspiring faith.
Upon beholding the sacred form,
it was seen that the sandalwood statue
originally had no repairs or joins,
its pedestal was exceptionally radiant,
carved from ivory,
certainly not something made by human hands.
The statue in Xīngshàn Temple,
in every detail, diverges from the original. ”
He also asked:
“Beside the Xiāngsī Temple in Fúzhōu,
there are many ancient traces,
with seal-script inscriptions carved,
but their origin is unknown.
What is the story behind this? ”
The answer was:
“During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha,
there was a mountain deity surnamed Luó,
named Zǐmíng,
a man of Shǔ.
Originally a bhikṣu who upheld the precepts,
he developed hatred for those who broke the precepts
and made various evil vows:
‘After I die,
may I become a great evil spirit
who devours those who break the precepts.’
Due to these vows, he was reborn
as this mountain deity.
He had many followers,
and the land under his dominion
stretched over five thousand lǐ east to west,
and over two thousand lǐ north to south.
He devoured over ten thousand people each year.
This deity was originally a monk, an elder brother of Kāśyapa Buddha,
later becoming his disciple.
That Buddha, out of compassion,
came to teach and transform him,
performing various miraculous transformations,
and only then was he subdued.
He was given the five precepts,
and upon remembering his past lives,
he ceased devouring people.
Fearing he might later change his mind,
the Buddha left a trace behind.
King Aśoka built a pagoda above it,
on the mountain peak.
The deity then hid within the rock.
The pagoda was made of white jade.
The deity still exists now.
The temple pagoda below the city walls
was established by King Aśoka.
This is recorded in the Entrustment Ritual. ”
He also asked:
“At the Língkān Temple in the Xīngníng County area, north of Xúnzhōu in the Southern Sea,
there are many spiritual traces.
Why is this? ”
The answer was:
“This was originally a disciple of the holy Mañjuśrī
who became the deity of this mountain
and committed many evil deeds.
Mañjuśrī, out of compassion,
came to teach and transform him.
He then remembered his past lives
and requested that a trace be left,
saying, ‘I will constantly worship it,
so I may be freed from all evils.’
Mañjuśrī manifested it for him,
which is what is seen now.
In the third year of the Zhēnguàn era,
the mountain deity passed away
and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
Another spirit
came to dwell in this place,
who was a relative by marriage of the former deity.
He committed many evils.
The former deity, now in heaven, pitied him
and descended to request Mañjuśrī
to manifest a small trace
to transform the later deity,
who then also followed the true Dharma.
Therefore, on this mountain today,
traces both large and small appear,
none without a cause.
This is recorded in the Entrustment Ritual. ”
He also asked:
“The stone cave Buddha in the northern mountains of Qìnzhōu
often emits light.
How long ago did this image appear? ”
The answer was:
“This cave existed in both the times of Kāśyapa Buddha and Śākyamuni Buddha.
In the past, a disciple of King Mù of Zhōu made the image of Kāśyapa Buddha. ”
He also asked:
“In the Wèinán and Zhōngnán mountains,
there are the Buddha Face Mountain and the Seven Buddha Ravine. ”
The answer was:
“This matter is the same as the previous ones.
The heavenly treasury in the Kù Valley of the southern mountains
is the treasury made by Kāśyapa Buddha with his own hands.
There are now thirteen pratyekabuddhas
dwelling within the valley. ”
He also asked, “In this land, it is often transmitted that there are Buddhas
made during the time of the Yīn dynasty, King Zhāo of Zhōu, King Zhuāng, etc.,
with conflicting accounts.
How can this be determined? ”
The answer was:
“There are reasons for all of them.
The disciple was born in heaven during the time of Xià Jié,
It is fully evident that the Buddha bestows his teachings.
Moreover, the Buddha has three bodies.
The Dharma Body and the Reward Body
are not visible to ordinary people,
and both transform those who have reached the stage of enlightenment and above.
Only the Transformation Body
pervades the three thousand worlds,
with a hundred billion Śākyamuni Buddhas
responding according to people's faith.
Their appearances are not fixed in time,
sometimes in the late Yīn dynasty,
sometimes in the time of Lǔ Zhuāng,
all within the great chiliocosm.
Throughout, they transmit the same teaching,
their manifestations responding to opportunities,
with no fixed sequence.
If we speak of the Dharma Body and the Reward Body,
they are eternally serene and unchanging,
and thus not a cause for marvel."
He further asked:
"Many of the auspicious images seen in the Hàn region
are said to have been made by King Aśoka's fourth daughter.
The matter is obscure and mysterious,
making it difficult to ascertain the truth.
What is the situation regarding this?"
The reply was:
"This is indeed true without doubt,
it was King Aśoka's fourth daughter.
Her appearance was not beautiful,
and she remained unmarried for a long time.
She constantly lamented her ugliness,
so she drew an image of the Buddha's form,
making it resemble her own appearance.
After completing it, she made a vow.
The Buddha's majestic and excellent features
are extraordinary and unlike humans—how could they be the same as my form?
Because of this earnest plea,
after many months and years,
she later moved the Buddha to appear,
suddenly transforming her original appearance.
Her father inquired in detail,
and she recounted her vow.
The images now at Yùhuá in the Northern Mountains, Chángshā in Jīngzhōu, Gāo Kuī in Yángdū, and the Chóngjìng Temple in the capital city,
were all made by King Aśoka's fourth daughter.
Some have inscriptions on their halos and pedestals,
written according to the original Sanskrit texts.
Among Hàn people who read them,
few can recognize the script.
King Aśoka then had these images
entrusted to various spirits and ghosts,
to spread according to karmic affinities,
circulating to awaken people.
Now, looking at the faces of the images,
they are none other than a female form.
The land where Chóngjìng Temple stands
was originally a battlefield.
Towards the end of the Western Jìn dynasty,
the Five Barbarians rose in great force,
and weapons clashed in mutual slaughter.
This place especially had many human bones underground,
and even now, digging still yields them.
Those killed were innocent,
the slaughter was cruel and excessive,
so various spirits and ghosts
brought the image to pacify the place.
This allowed the wronged souls
to develop wholesome thoughts.
When the Zhōu dynasty suppressed the Dharma,
the spirits also moved it.
When the Suí dynasty's founder restored
[In the Fǎyuàn Zhūlín, vol. 22, "restored" is written as "again"]
prosperity,
the Buddha image was re-erected."
He further asked:
"Manifestations from the unseen realms
are common among ordinary people.
When the spirit departs, the body decays;
how can it return again,
sometimes after seven days or many days,
appearing no different from when alive?"
The reply was:
"Humans are endowed with seven consciousnesses,
each having its own spirit
[Originally "spirit" was written as "person"]
according to the Fǎyuàn Zhūlín, vol. 22, corrected]
The mind-consciousness is the master.
Although the master departs first,
the remaining spirits guard and protect,
which is not strange.
For example, in the Five Precepts,
each precept has five spirits,
so the five precepts have twenty-five spirits.
If a precept is broken, five spirits depart,
but the others remain.
When a fully ordained monk receives the precepts,
each precept has two hundred and fifty spirits,
and likewise, within each precept,
two hundred and fifty are obtained,
protecting the bhikṣu.
If a major precept is violated,
only the two hundred and fifty spirits depart,
the rest always remain."
The Vinaya master further asked the celestial being:
"Regarding the empty lamp that constantly shines
[Originally "empty" was written as "orchid"]
according to Dàoxuān Vinaya Master's Gǎntōng Lù, corrected]
at the Sānxué Mountain Temple in Jiǎn Prefecture of Shǔ region,
what is the reason for its existence?"
The reply was:
"On the mountain, there is a Bodhisattva temple,
first established during the True Dharma age of Buddha Kāśyapa,
built by the Bodhisattva Joyful King.
The temple is named Dharma Lamp.
From that time until now,
it has constantly illuminated the temple's exterior.
There are three hundred minor bodhisattvas
who abstain from grains and enjoy long life,
permanently residing on this mountain.
This lamp is also provided by the mountain spirit Lǐ Tè,
who subsequently made offerings,
so that during the first month,
lamps are lit everywhere
to make offerings to the Buddha's temple, so it is said."
From the Fǎyuàn Zhūlín
Huáyán Monk
Monk Huáyán studied under Shénxiù.
The Chán school
(The character "宗" was originally written as "師"
and was changed according to Chén's collated edition)
referred to him as the Northern Patriarch.
He often resided at Tiāngōng Temple in Luòdū,
with over three hundred disciples.
During the daily communal meals in the hall,
the monk maintained strict discipline,
requiring that alms bowls must be gathered in an orderly manner.
There was one disciple,
whose seniority in monastic years and spiritual attainment
surpassed his peers,
but his temperament was rather narrow-minded and irritable.
At the time, due to lying ill,
he did not join the assembly for the meal.
A novice monk whose alms bowl was missing
came to visit this monk,
bowed respectfully and said:
"I wish to attend the meal in the hall,
but I have no bowl.
May I borrow yours temporarily?
I will acquire my own tomorrow."
The monk refused, saying:
"I have used this bowl for several decades,
and I fear you might damage it."
The novice pleaded earnestly:
"I will only use it for the duration of the meal and return it immediately;
how could it possibly be damaged?"
After repeated entreaties,
the monk finally lent it to him, saying:
"I cherish this bowl as my life.
If it is damaged,
it would be like killing me."
The novice received the bowl
and carried it with great trepidation.
After finishing the meal and preparing to return it,
the monk had already begun urging him.
As the novice carried the bowl down from the hall,
he accidentally stumbled on a broken brick and fell,
shattering the bowl.
Shortly after,
the monk urged him again.
Frightened,
the novice went to the monk's quarters,
bowed to acknowledge his fault,
performing hundreds of prostrations.
The monk cried out loudly:
"You have killed me!"
He raged and cursed vehemently,
and because of this, his illness worsened,
and he died that very night.
Some time later,
the monk was at Sōngshān Yuè Temple with over a hundred disciples,
expounding the Huáyán Sūtra,
and the novice was also among the listeners.
Suddenly, a sound like wind and rain
was heard from the valley outside the temple.
The monk then summoned this novice
and had him stand behind his back.
In a moment,
a huge serpent appeared,
eighty or ninety feet long,
four or five arm-spans in girth,
heading straight into the temple.
Its eyes were furious, and its mouth gaped open.
Those on both sides wanted to flee,
but the monk admonished them not to move.
The serpent gradually approached the lecture hall,
ascended the steps and looked around,
as if seeking something.
The monk stopped it with his staff,
saying:
"Halt."
The serpent intended to approach the seat.
It then lowered its head and closed its eyes.
The monk admonished it,
tapping its head with his staff, saying:
"Since you understand your karma,
you should now turn your mind towards the Three Jewels."
He ordered the monks to chant the Buddha's name in unison
and administered to it the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
The serpent then writhed and departed.
At that time, some disciples of the deceased monk were present at the assembly.
The monk summoned them and said:
"This serpent is your teacher.
After many years of spiritual practice,
he should have attained the fruit of enlightenment.
But at the moment of his death,
because he cherished a broken bowl
and raged against this novice,
he was reborn as a python.
He came here just now
intending to kill this novice.
Had he killed him,
he would have fallen into the great hells,
with no hope of escape.
Fortunately, I stopped him
and administered the prohibitions and precepts.
Now he is about to relinquish this body.
Go and search for him."
The disciples received the order and went out.
Where the serpent had passed,
the grass and trees were flattened,
as if by a cart track.
After traveling forty-five *li*,
they reached a deep valley,
where the serpent had dashed its head against a rock and died.
They returned and reported to the monk:
"The serpent has now been reborn
as a girl in the household of Attendant Péi.
She is very intelligent,
and will die at the age of eighteen.
She will then be reborn as a male,
after which he will leave home to cultivate the Path.
Attendant Péi is my disciple;
you may go into the city
to convey my regards to him.
The girl is about to be born now,
but the birth is very difficult;
you should save her."
At that time, Péi Kuān was an Attendant in the Ministry of War,
and indeed a disciple of the monk.
The disciple received the order and entered the city,
pointing directly to the Péi residence.
He encountered Péi, who was on leave at home,
and had someone announce:
"Monk Huáyán sends his regards."
The Attendant came out to meet him,
his expression very worried.
The monk asked the reason,
and was told that his wife was about to give birth,
but it had already been six or seven days,
with candles lit and people keeping vigil,
and the situation was extremely critical.
The monk said:
"I can save her."
He then had a clean bed prepared
outside the hall door.
The monk entered, lit incense, struck the chime,
and called out "Venerable Master" three times.
His wife then gave birth peacefully to a daughter.
Later, indeed, she died at the age of eighteen.
From *Yuánhuà Jì*.
The monastic disciple of Táng Xiūjǐng.
During the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng of the Táng dynasty,
Táng Gōng Xiūjǐng served as chancellor.
There was once a monk
whose words often proved accurate,
and who was skilled in the arts of exorcism and averting misfortune.
Xiūjǐng held him in great esteem.
One day,
the monk came and said to Xiūjǐng:
"The Chancellor is about to face a great calamity,
and it is not far off—within a few months.
However, it can be averted through ritual means."
Xiūjǐng was extremely frightened
and immediately bowed to him.
The monk said:
"I have no special technique,
but I do have one plan.
I hope you will listen."
Xiūjǐng said:
"I am fortunate to receive my master's instruction."
The monk said:
"Now, the commandery governors of the realm—
are they not appointed by the Chancellor?"
Xiūjǐng replied:
"Yes."
The monk said:
"The Chancellor should, from among the lowly and insignificant officials,
seek out one who is isolated, of humble origins, poor, and yet talented and capable.
Have him appointed as Governor of Cáozhōu.
He will be deeply grateful for the Chancellor's favor,
and then he can be directed as needed.
Once you have found him,
I hope you will inform me."
Xiūjǐng, both pleased and thankful,
then made inquiries among his relatives and friends.
There was a certain Gentleman Zhāng,
whose family was very poor,
and who held a lowly post in the capital.
That very day, he was appointed as Reminder of the Crown Prince,
and ten days later,
he was made Governor of Cáozhōu.
Xiūjǐng then summoned the monk and said:
"I have followed the master's plan,
and have found Gentleman Zhāng.
So, can you instruct me further?"
The monk said:
"When Gentleman Zhāng departs for his commandery,
you must have him procure two dogs,
ones that are several feet tall and of extraordinary spirit and vigor."
Xiūjǐng assented.
Gentleman Zhāng, bearing the exceptional favor of Lord Táng,
yet did not understand its purpose.
When he was about to depart for his commandery,
he went to bid farewell to Xiūjǐng.
After expressing his thanks, he said:
"My name is obscure,
and my talents and knowledge are shallow.
For the Chancellor to raise me from this stagnant position
to govern a great commandery—
from having barely enough grain to store,
to receiving the salary of a two-thousand-bushel official—
it is like going from a dried-up rut to sailing the eastern sea,
or emerging from a deep valley to ascend the layered heavens.
Your virtue is indeed profound.
However, beyond my gratitude,
what privately worries and alarms me
is not knowing the Chancellor's true intent in this."
Xiūjǐng said:
"It is because of your talent,
nothing else.
However, I have often heard that your esteemed commandery has many fine dogs.
I wish to obtain two of extraordinary spirit and vigor."
Gentleman Zhāng said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
Upon arriving at his commandery,
after a few days,
he summoned all the commandery officials
and told them:
"I have received the deep favor of Chancellor Lord Táng,
who promoted me beyond the usual order,
allowing me to govern this great commandery.
Now Lord Táng seeks two fine dogs.
Can you procure them?"
One official stepped forward and said:
"My family raises a dog
of exceptional quality and appearance.
I wish to offer it."
Zhāng was greatly pleased
and accepted it immediately.
When it arrived,
the dog was several feet tall and stout,
its chest over a foot broad,
of extraordinary spirit and vigor,
and yet also tame and gentle.
Gentleman Zhāng said:
"What the Chancellor seeks are two dogs.
What can be done?"
The official replied:
"Within the commandery, there is only this one;
all others are ordinary.
However, ten lǐ south of the commandery, in a certain village, at a certain commoner's house,
there is also one.
The commoner treasures it extremely.
Unless Your Lordship goes in person,
it cannot be obtained."
Gentleman Zhāng immediately ordered his carriage prepared,
took ample funds, and went to visit.
He indeed obtained it.
Its appearance was no different from the one offered by the official,
but its spirit and brilliance surpassed it.
Gentleman Zhāng was very pleased.
He then summoned a trusted subordinate
to present the two dogs to Xiūjǐng.
Xiūjǐng was greatly delighted,
and marveled at their appearance,
believing he had never seen their like before.
He then summoned the monk to look at them.
The monk said:
"Take good care of them.
It is these two dogs
that will deliver the Chancellor from calamity."
Ten days later,
the monk came again
and said to Xiūjǐng:
"The event will occur tonight.
I hope the Chancellor makes strict preparations."
Xiūjǐng then had the monk stay overnight.
That night,
Xiūjǐng sat in the front corridor of his hall,
ordering over ten attendants
to stand at the corners of the dais holding bows and arrows.
The monk and Xiūjǐng shared the same dais.
At midnight,
the monk said with a smile:
"The Chancellor's calamity has been averted.
You may retire to sleep."
Xiūjǐng was overjoyed
and thanked him.
He then dismissed the attendants
and slept alongside the monk.
At dawn,
the monk called to Xiūjǐng:
"You may rise now."
Xiūjǐng got up
and said to the monk:
"The calamity is indeed averted,
but what use were the two dogs?"
The monk said:
"Let us go together and see."
He then went with Xiūjǐng to search for traces,
arriving at the rear garden.
There they saw a man lying dead on the ground.
Looking at his neck, there was blood—
he appeared to have been bitten by some creature.
They also saw the two dogs under a large tree,
looking upward.
Looking up, they saw a man stripped to the waist hiding in the tree.
Xiūjǐng, startled, questioned him:
"Who are you?"
The man wept and, pointing at the dead man, said:
"He and I
are both thieves.
Last night we came together,
intending to harm the Chancellor.
But we encountered these two dogs,
which circled us and barked fiercely.
He was then bitten and died.
I was terrified
and hid myself here,
waiting for them to leave elsewhere,
so I could escape.
But by dawn they still had not left.
Now I am resigned to die here."
Xiūjǐng immediately summoned his attendants
and ordered them to bind the man.
The monk said:
"His crime certainly deserves death,
but it was not his own intention;
he was compelled by others.
I beg you to release him."
Xiūjǐng ordered him untied.
The thief bowed, weeping, and departed.
Xiūjǐng thanked the monk, saying:
"Thanks to my master,
otherwise,
I would have died at the hands of these two men."
The monk said:
"This is due to the Chancellor's own fortune.
How could it be my doing?"
Xiūjǐng had a cousin named Lú Zhěn,
who was in Jīngmén.
A diviner told him:
"You are about to encounter disaster and calamity.
You should seek out someone skilled in averting misfortunes,
then perhaps you will be alright."
Zhěn had long known of this monk,
so he sent a letter to Xiūjǐng,
requesting his help.
The monk then gave a letter to Xiūjǐng, saying:
"The matter is contained within."
When the letter reached Jīngzhōu,
And Zhěn had already passed away.
His family opened and looked at his book,
only to see a single sheet of paper,
with no written words at all.
Xiūjǐng found it even more extraordinary.
Several years later,
the monk departed in seclusion,
and ultimately no one knew where he went.
From "Xuānshì Jì"
Chán Master Yíguāng
The Chan Master Yíguāng of Cháng'ān's Qīnglóng Temple,
was originally a member of the Táng imperial clan.
His father, Prince Lángyá,
joined Prince Yuè in raising troops
to attack Empress Tiānhòu,
but they were unsuccessful and died.
Empress Tiānhòu exterminated their entire clan, leaving none behind.
Only the Chan Master, then still an infant in swaddling clothes,
was carried away by his wet nurse as she fled.
Several years later,
Empress Tiānhòu heard that Prince Lángyá had a son living among the people,
and the search for him grew increasingly urgent.
The wet nurse had reached the border of Qízhōu,
where she supported herself by selling her needlework.
By then, the Chan Master was already eight years old,
exceptionally intelligent,
and of extraordinary appearance.
Fearing that his striking looks would lead to discovery and ruin,
the wet nurse was deeply worried.
She then obtained money to have clothes made for him,
and also placed two hundred coins beneath his waistband,
before taking him to a mulberry field,
where she told him the whole story of his origins.
Weeping, she said to him:
"I have raised you for eight years now,
fleeing for our lives, going wherever we could.
Now you have grown,
and Empress Tiānhòu's search decrees have not ceased.
I fear that if the matter is exposed,
both you and I will die.
Now you are exceptionally bright and talented,
capable of standing on your own.
I too shall vanish from here."
The wet nurse then parted from him with tears,
and the Chan Master also wailed uncontrollably,
only then learning of his origins.
After the wet nurse left,
he did not know where she had gone.
He then walked to an inn,
and played with the other children there.
There was a prefectural governor's wife,
whose husband was serving at his post.
She was resting at the inn
when she saw the Chan Master playing with the children.
Noticing his extraordinary appearance,
she took pity on him.
Summoning him, she said:
"Young man, where is your home?
Why are you alone here?"
The Master falsely replied:
"My manor is nearby;
I sometimes come here to play."
The lady gave him food,
and also bestowed five hundred coins upon him.
Though young, the Master was perceptive.
Fearing someone might take his money,
he loosened his clothes
and placed the coins beneath his waistband.
As it was already late in the day,
he sought out a small path
intending to head toward the village fields.
He encountered an old monk walking alone,
who called out to the Master:
"Young boy,
you are now alone,
your family destroyed.
Where will you go?"
The Chan Master stood still in shock.
The old monk continued:
"Leaving the household life brings freedom and ease,
and you will have no worries or fears.
Young boy, do you wish for this?"
The Master said:
"That is my wish."
The old monk then took him by the hand,
led him under the shade of a mulberry tree,
and had him pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
He then shaved his head.
Next, he opened his bag,
took out a kāṣāya robe,
and had him put it on.
It fit his body perfectly,
and he taught him how to drape and wear it.
Once the Chan Master was clad in the Dharma robe,
he held and arranged it
just like a seasoned monk.
The old monk joyfully said:
"This is due to his innate disposition."
As the monk was about to leave,
he pointed to the northeast and said:
"Several li from here there is a monastery.
Go directly there
and pay respects to the temple abbot, saying
that I have sent you to be his disciple."
Having spoken,
the old monk vanished.
Only then did he realize it was a holy manifestation.
The Master followed the instructions and hurried to the temple.
The temple abbot was astonished by his story
and thus kept him.
After nearly ten years,
the Chan Master had thoroughly mastered the sūtras and vinaya,
and attained deep meditative stillness.
When the Táng dynasty was restored,
and they sought the descendants of Prince Lángyá,
the Master finally told the temple monks about his origins.
The temple monks were greatly astonished.
They then went to see the Regional Inspector Lǐ of Qízhōu,
the Master's paternal uncle,
who was both sorrowful and joyful upon seeing him.
He then took him into his home
and intended to report the matter to the court,
but the Master firmly pleaded against it.
The Inspector had a daughter,
about the same age as the Chan Master.
Upon seeing the Chan Master, she was attracted to him
and wished to express her affections,
but the Master would not consent.
After over a month,
when the Inspector's wife was out,
the daughter, dressed in fine attire and accompanied by many attendants, came to pressure him.
The Master firmly resisted in every way,
ultimately refusing.
The Master then deceived her, saying
that he was not clean
and needed to bathe first.
The daughter agreed,
and had hot water prepared for bathing.
The Master waited for the daughter to leave,
then locked the door.
When the daughter returned and pushed at the door,
she could not enter.
Peering through the window,
she saw the Master holding a razor.
Looking back, he said:
"Because I possess this root,
I am troubled by desire.
Now that I have removed it,
how can desire trouble me?"
The daughter was terrified
and tried to stop him, but could not.
He then severed his root,
cast it to the ground,
and fainted.
Since the door was locked,
it could not be opened,
and the daughter was panic-stricken, not knowing what to do.
Soon, the Inspector's wife returned,
and the daughter explained the situation.
The Inspector ordered the door broken down.
The Master had already regained consciousness.
He summoned skilled physicians,
who heated the ground until it was red-hot,
poured bitter wine over it,
had the Master sit on the scorched ground,
and applied ointment.
After several months, his injury healed.
The Inspector reported that the Chan Master was the son of Prince Lángyá.
An imperial decree was issued,
ordering him to be escorted by post stations to the capital.
He was granted an audience and received with consolation,
bestowed with generous rewards,
and restored as a prince.
The Chan Master said:
"My parents met untimely deaths,
and my body is now mutilated.
To return to lay life and become a prince
is not my wish."
Emperor Zhōngzōng issued a decree,
ordering the Chan Master to widely lead disciples,
establish forest monasteries in the mountains,
and act as he pleased.
The Chan Master had a fondness for the Zhōngnán Mountains,
and thus resided at Xīngfǎ Temple.
He also built meditation huts and forest monasteries
at several locations near the valley entrances,
some deep in the mountains for dozens of li.
His followers, both monastic and lay, often numbered in the thousands,
who greeted, awaited, and attended upon him
more diligently than they would ministers or chancellors.
Having attained the fruit of the Way,
he often foretold future events,
and thus people increasingly turned to him.
On the twenty-third day of the sixth month of the twenty-third year of the Kāiyuán era,
he passed away without illness.
He first instructed his disciples on matters of cultivating the body and upholding precepts,
his words earnest and sincere.
Then he lay down,
his head pointing north,
his feet pointing south,
his hands supporting his head,
with his right side downward,
and thus passed away.
He left instructions to be buried on the southern side of Shàolíng Plain,
with a chamber dug into the plain and sealed.
As the coffin was about to be moved,
a rare fragrance wafted forth,
and his appearance was just as in life.
When the carriage passed through the city gate,
suddenly, several hundred white cranes
It danced and sang in the sky,
with five-colored clouds
lingering and covering the carriage,
and traveled for several tens of li.
At the place where the seal was bestowed,
the Tiānbǎo Temple was subsequently built,
and his disciples remained to guard it.
From "Jì Wén"
Xuán Lǎn
In the late Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
the Chán master Xuán Lǎn resided at the Zhìqǐ Temple in Jīngzhōu.
His virtue was lofty and his demeanor elegant,
yet people could not become close to him.
Zhāng Zǎo once painted an ancient pine on the wall of his study,
Fú Zǎi composed a eulogy for it,
and Wèi Xiàng wrote a poem about it—
it was considered a rare trio of masterpieces at the time.
Xuán Lǎn had them all plastered over.
When asked the reason,
he said:
"They were merely blemishes on my wall."
Monk Nà, who was his nephew,
caused trouble in the temple—
removing tiles to search for fledglings,
breaking walls to smoke out rats.
Yet Xuán Lǎn never reprimanded him.
There was a disciple named Yì Quán,
who wore simple clothes and ate only one meal a day.
Xuán Lǎn also did not praise him.
Some found this strange,
so he inscribed a poem on bamboo, saying:
"If you wish to know how vast my path is,
it does not contradict the nature of things.
The great ocean lets fish leap freely,
the vast sky allows birds to soar."
Suddenly one evening,
a foreign monk
pushed open the door and entered, saying:
"Venerable one, quickly prepare a dharma assembly."
Xuán Lǎn replied:
"I have never engaged in such worldly affairs."
The monk gazed at him intently and left,
closing the door behind him,
with the latch as secure as before.
Xuán Lǎn smiled and said to those around him:
"I am about to depart."
He then promptly bathed,
leaned on his armrest, and passed away.
From "Yǒu Yáng Zá Zǔ"
Fǎ Jiàng
In Cháng'ān, there was a monk named Fǎ Jiàng who lectured on the Nirvana Sutra.
He was intelligent and knowledgeable,
and his reputation was widespread.
Wherever he lectured daily,
monks and disciples gathered around him like a bustling market.
Fǎ Jiàng traveled to Xiāngyáng.
In Xiāngyáng, there was a visiting monk
who did not adhere to monastic rules—
he drank wine and ate meat,
and his body was extremely plump.
He associated with anyone,
without discrimination.
The monks despised him.
When Fǎ Jiàng arrived,
the monks welcomed and honored him,
providing him with refined accommodations
and serving him with utmost care.
The visiting monk suddenly brought a dou of wine and a steamed suckling pig to visit Fǎ Jiàng.
Fǎ Jiàng was just then expounding the principles of the dharma to monks and laypeople,
who were all listening attentively.
The visiting monk directly brought the wine and meat,
saying to Fǎ Jiàng:
"Lecturing is exhausting.
Stop discussing the sutra for now
and share this wine and meat with me."
Fǎ Jiàng was startled and fearful,
but could only decline politely.
The visiting monk then sat by the door,
tore the pork with his hands and ate it,
and drank the wine in large gulps.
In a short while,
the wine and meat were all gone,
and he climbed onto the bed and fell asleep.
When evening came,
the lecturing monk was reciting the Nirvana Sutra.
The drunken monk rose and said:
"Excellent recitation,
but I have also recited it before."
He then took some straw,
spread it beneath the western wall,
sat exposed on the straw,
and began to expound the Nirvana Sutra.
His words were clear and comprehensible,
flowing smoothly and pleasing to the ear.
The lecturing monk stopped his recitation to listen.
Whenever he encountered profound and subtle principles
that he had never understood,
hearing the drunken monk expound the sutra
brought him sudden clarity.
By the time dawn broke,
he had completed all forty volumes of the Nirvana Sutra.
All the doubts Fǎ Jiàng had harbored throughout his life
were instantly resolved.
Fǎ Jiàng, overjoyed at this rare encounter,
prepared a seat and bowed to him.
But by the time he lifted his head,
the drunken monk had vanished.
They searched everywhere for him,
but no one knew where he had gone.
From "Jì Wén"
Chán Master Hóng Fǎng
Hóng Fǎng of Shǎnzhōu,
was originally from Jīngzhào.
He left home to become a monk in his youth,
and later attained enlightenment.
His aspiration lay in meditation and tranquility,
yet he also engaged in lecturing on scriptures,
with disciples often numbering in the hundreds.
One day,
as Fǎng sat alone at the beginning of the night,
four men came before him and said:
"The Ghost King is currently holding a vegetarian feast for his daughter's recovery from illness,
and invites the Master to attend."
Fǎng said:
"I am a human, you are ghosts,
how can I go there?"
The four men said:
"Venerable Sir, just go,
we disciples can take you there."
Fǎng followed them.
The four men mounted horses,
each holding one leg of a rope-seat,
and they headed north.
After traveling several hundred *li*,
they reached a mountain,
on its side was a small vermilion gate.
The four men asked Fǎng to close his eyes,
before a meal's time had passed,
someone said:
"Open them."
They had already arrived at the king's court.
Its palaces, towers, rooms, and buildings,
were extraordinarily lofty and majestic,
with strict and ornate guards,
quite comparable to those of a human sovereign.
The Ghost King, fully robed and crowned,
descended the steps to welcome and greet him.
The King said:
"My daughter has been ill for a long time,
and now, fortunately, she has recovered.
Wishing to create a small blessing,
I am preparing a vegetarian feast,
hence I have invited the Master to grace us with your presence.
After the feast,
I will naturally have you escorted back without worry."
Thereupon, he was invited into the palace.
The feast venue was exquisitely decorated and magnificent,
with monks numbering nearly ten thousand,
and Buddha statues extremely numerous,
just like affairs in the human world.
Fǎng looked up at the sky,
but could not see the sun,
resembling a heavily overcast day in the human world.
After a short while,
the King's wife and several hundred women from the rear palace,
all came out to bow and pay respects.
The King's daughter, aged fourteen or fifteen,
her appearance alone bore the look of illness,
Fǎng performed the ritual prayers and blessings for her.
He saw people bringing over a thousand ivory trays of food,
which were distributed in order before the monks.
Fǎng was seated on a large couch,
with special delicacies set separately for him,
the food was very fragrant and clean.
As Fǎng was about to eat it,
the Ghost King addressed him:
"If the Master were to reside here permanently,
then you could partake of ghost food;
I dare not keep the Master here,
please do not eat."
Fǎng, frightened, stopped.
After the feast,
leftover food still amounted to several hundred trays.
Fǎng saw nearly a thousand guards, ministers, and officials,
all with a desire to eat showing on their faces,
Fǎng requested the King to bestow the leftover food upon them.
The King said:
"Quickly take it away,
and give it to them."
The various officials bowed in thanks,
looking at each other with joyful laughter,
their mouths opening wide enough to reach both ears.
The King then knelt and said:
"Since the Master has graciously come,
and I have no other offerings,
I have five hundred bolts of silk to present to the Master,
please accept them and bestow upon me the Eight Precepts fast."
The Master said:
"Ghost silk is like paper,
I have no use for it."
The King said:
"I will have human silk presented to the Master."
Thereupon, Fǎng administered the Eight Precepts fast to him.
After the fast was completed,
the King again ordered the previous four men,
to escort him back as before.
Fǎng suddenly opened his eyes,
and had already returned to his dwelling,
and dawn had not yet broken.
His disciples merely thought he had entered meditation,
unaware of where he had gone.
Fǎng suddenly opened his eyes,
ordered a lamp to be brought to illuminate the area before his couch,
and there were the five hundred bolts of silk.
His disciples asked him about it,
and he then told them the reason.
Since Fǎng's meditative practice was inherently lofty,
his reputation and esteem grew daily,
and when he went to the ghost realm,
it was only his spirit that traveled,
his physical form remained unmoving.
Not long after, as he sat in meditation in the morning,
a heavenly being,
whose substance was exceptionally beautiful,
came to bow and request:
"The Heavenly King of the South, Dhr̥tarāṣṭra,
invites the Master to the heavens to receive offerings."
Fǎng agreed.
Thereupon, they spread a heavenly garment for Fǎng to sit on,
two beings held the garment,
lifted him and soared into the sky,
and in a moment they had arrived.
The Heavenly King of the South, leading his attendants,
bowed deeply and said:
"The Master's spiritual practice is lofty and far-reaching,
the various heavens wish to witness the Master's lectures and recitations,
hence I have presumptuously invited the Master."
Thereupon, he prepared a high seat for Fǎng to sit on.
The ceremonial site was lofty and magnificent,
almost beyond the human world,
surpassing it by hundreds and thousands of times.
The heavenly beings were all tall and large,
their bodies emitting light.
The halls and trees,
were all made of the seven treasures,
all radiant with brilliance,
dazzling to human eyes.
When Fǎng first arrived in heaven,
his form and substance were still like a human's,
but after seeing the Heavenly King,
his body spontaneously grew large,
equal to the heavenly beings.
Various rare delicacies were set out,
all naturally flavored,
exceptionally sweet and delicious.
After eating,
the King then invited him into the palace,
where more offerings were set out,
their conversation was warm and sincere,
and the attending heavenly officials along with ghosts and spirits were very numerous.
Later, the King suddenly said:
"I, your disciple, must go to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to discuss matters,
please, Master, stay a little while."
He also instructed his attendants:
"If the Master wishes to stroll about,
allow him to go wherever he desires,
but do not let him go to the rear garden."
He repeated this several times before leaving.
After he left,
Fǎng thought to himself:
"What benefit is there in the rear garden,
that he does not wish me to go there?"
Seizing a moment when no one was around,
he secretly went to the rear garden.
The garden was very large,
with flowing springs and ponds,
trees, forests, flowers, and herbs,
everywhere present,
unlike anything seen in the human world.
Gradually going deeper in,
he distantly heard loud groaning
"Groaning" originally read "shouting",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
and shouting,
unbearable to hear.
He then went to its side,
and saw a large copper pillar,
several hundred feet in diameter,
a thousand *zhang* high,
the pillar had pierced holes,
left and right, passing through.
Some had silver chains locking their necks,
or piercing their breastbones,
amounting to tens of thousands of heads,
all were yakṣas.
With saw-like teeth and hook-like claws,
their bodies were twice the size of heavenly beings.
Seeing the Chan Master arrive,
they kowtowed and said:
"Because we ate humans,
we were locked up by the Heavenly King.
Now we beg for our release.
If we gain freedom,
we will only seek other food in the human world,
and certainly dare not eat humans and cause harm."
Driven by hunger and thirst,
as they uttered these words,
fire came out of their mouths.
Asked how long they had been locked up,
some said since the time of Buddha Vipaśyin's appearance in the world,
easily amounting to tens of millions of years.
There were also three or five elderly ones,
sincere in their intentions.
The monk promised to release them from their bonds and quickly returned.
In a moment, the king arrived,
first asking:
"Master, have you perhaps wandered into the rear garden?"
Those on the left and right said:
"No."
The king then rejoiced,
and sat down.
Fǎng said:
"I just went to the rear garden,
and saw tens of thousands of beings locked up.
What wrong have they committed?"
The king said:
"Master, you did indeed wander into the rear garden.
However, small compassion is the enemy of great compassion.
Master, you need not ask."
Fǎng pressed the question firmly again,
and the king said:
"These are all evil ghosts,
who constantly harm people,
and only eat human flesh.
If not for the protection of the various devas,
the people of the world would already have been devoured by these ghosts.
These are all great evil ghosts,
who cannot be treated with courtesy,
hence they are locked up."
Fǎng said:
"Just now I saw three or five elderly ones,
whose words seemed quite sincere,
saying they only seek other food from the human world.
I beg you to spare them.
If these ones do not eat people,
the rest could also
"also" originally had a "not" character below it,
according to the Ming manuscript copy, deleted
be released, could they not?"
The king said:
"The words of these ghosts are not to be believed."
Fǎng firmly pleaded.
The king signaled to those on the left and right,
ordering them to bring three or five of the elderly ones.
Soon they were brought,
kowtowing and saying:
"We are grateful for your grace in releasing us;
we are already old.
Now that we can leave,
we certainly dare not disturb people."
The king said:
"For the Chan master's sake,
I release you to the human world.
If you eat people again,
when you are brought back this time,
I will have you killed."
They all said:
"We dare not."
Thereupon they were released and left.
Not long after,
suddenly a deity was seen arriving before the king's court,
claiming to be a god of mountains, rivers, and marshes.
Clad in armor,
with a golden face,
he rushed in and said:
"I do not know from where,
but suddenly four or five yakṣas have come to the human world,
killing and eating many people.
They cannot be controlled,
so I report this."
The king said to Fǎng:
"Disciple, what did I say?
I just told you, Master,
small compassion is the enemy of great compassion.
How can the words of such evil ghosts
be trusted?"
The king said to the various gods:
"Quickly capture them."
Soon the various gods brought the yakṣas in custody.
The king angrily said:
"Why did you violate what was requested?"
He ordered their hands and feet cut off,
had iron chains pierced through their brains,
and dragged them away to be locked up.
Fǎng then requested to return,
and again the king ordered the previous two men to escort him to the temple.
The temple had already lost Fǎng for fourteen days,
yet in heaven it was but a short while.
Fǎng, within Shǎnchéng,
selected an empty, open space to build Lóngguāng Temple,
and also established a sick ward,
constantly caring for several hundred patients.
The temple was extremely lofty and magnificent,
and devotees, both monastic and lay, from near and far,
gathered like clouds.
Then he was invited by Śakra Devānām Indra
Ming manuscript copy has "Héngyīn" for "Bǎiguó"
as requested.
Fǎng was just washing his face in the morning,
when a yakṣa appeared before him,
carrying a five-colored rug on his left shoulder and saying:
"Śakra
"Śakra" originally written as "Shìjiā"
according to the Xǔ manuscript, corrected
Deva King,
invites the Master to lecture on the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra."
Fǎng silently returned to his seat,
and the yakṣa then took the rope-seat,
placed it on his left shoulder, and said:
"Please close your eyes, Master."
Thereupon he raised his left hand,
and extended his right foot,
saying:
"Please open your eyes, Master."
Looking,
he had already arrived at the Hall of Good Dharma.
Once the Chan master arrived in heaven,
heavenly light dazzled his eyes,
and he could not open them.
The Deva King said:
"Master, recite the name of Maitreya Buddha."
Fǎng immediately recited it,
whereupon his eyes opened without being dazzled.
But his human body was small and lowly,
and looking up at the heavenly forms,
he could not see their limits.
The Deva King also said:
"Chan Master, recite the name of Maitreya Buddha again,
and your body will become large."
As instructed, he recited it,
and with three recitations, his body grew three times,
finally becoming equal to the devas.
The Deva King, together with the various devas, paid respects and said:
"Disciple has heard that the Master is skilled in lecturing on the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
for a long time now.
Now the various devas admire and respect you,
and have reverently prepared a daochang,
so we invite the Great Master to lecture on the sutra for us to listen and receive."
Fǎng said:
"This matter is truly not burdensome,
however, in the sick ward,
there are several hundred patients
who depend on Fǎng for their lives.
I constantly beg for alms to provide for them.
If I now linger to lecture on the sutra,
in the human world, much time would pass,
and I fear the patients would starve to death.
Therefore, I must firmly decline."
The Deva King said:
"The daochang is already prepared,
this wish has long been held,
I firmly request the Great Master not to decline."
Fǎng would not agree.
Suddenly, a great deva appeared in the air,
his body several times larger than Śakra's.
The Deva King respectfully rose to welcome him.
The great deva said:
"Mahābrahmā Deva King has issued a command."
The Deva King, disappointed, said:
"I originally wished to keep the Master to lecture on the sutra,
but now Brahmā has issued a command forbidding it.
However, since the Master has already come,
could he not briefly open the sutra scroll,
and give a small lecture on its meaning,
to let the devas believe and receive it?"
Fǎng agreed.
Thereupon food was set out,
the utensils were all of the seven treasures,
the food and drink fragrant and delicious,
exquisite and wonderful beyond the ordinary.
After the Chan master ate
"ate" originally written as "day"
according to the Chén collated version, corrected
finished,
all the pores of his body
emitted wondrous light,
and within the pores,
he could see all things.
Only then did he realize the sublimity of the heavenly body.
Having ascended the high seat,
spread with heavenly robes,
Fǎng then mounted the seat.
In that Hall of Good Dharma,
there were hundreds, thousands, and tens of thousands of devas,
along with the Four Deva Kings,
each leading their followers,
gathered together to listen to the Dharma.
To the left and right below the steps,
were dragon kings, yakṣas, various ghosts, spirits, and non-humans,
all listening with palms joined.
Fǎng then opened the beginning of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra,
and lectured on a little more than one sheet.
His words and phrases were elegant and fluent,
fully expounding the essential meaning.
The Deva King greatly praised the merit.
When the sutra lecture concluded,
he again ordered the previous yakṣa to escort him back to his original temple.
His disciples had lost Fǎng
for twenty-seven days already.
According to Buddhist sutras,
the Hall of Good Dharma is in the Garden of Joy.
The capital of the Heavenly Emperor.
It is the main hall of the Heavenly King.
The hall is made of the seven treasures,
and its four walls are all of silver.
Below the steps, springs and pools flow and converge,
with streams and channels reflecting each other.
Its fruit trees
(Míng manuscript,
Chén collated edition reads "stream water" for "fruit trees")
are all aligned in rows with the trees,
and the precious trees, flowers, and fruits
are all extraordinary.
All the things and creatures
are unrecognizable to ordinary people.
Fǎng briefly described the general outline:
below the steps, the precious trees
are always aligned in rows,
each pair forming a counterpart,
and there is always a spring.
Winding among the branches,
flowing down from the leaves,
the water is milky in color,
and its taste is better than milk.
It flows down to the tree roots,
and sprinkles into the channels.
The heavenly beings drink the spring water from the tree trunks,
while the water that trickles down
is drunk by the multitude of birds.
The ground is made of gold,
and soft grass grows on it,
as soft as cotton.
When the heavenly beings tread on it,
their feet sink in,
but when they lift their feet, the ground becomes level again.
There are hundreds and thousands of birds,
with colors and names that are not fixed.
When they enter the forest of the seven treasures,
they take on the color of the trees.
All things in the heavens are naturally produced,
and when one thinks of food,
vessels of the seven treasures filled with food immediately appear.
When one thinks of clothing,
precious garments also appear.
There is no sun or moonlight,
for the light from the body of a single heavenly being
surpasses that of the sun and moon.
When they need to go to distant places,
they fly through the air,
arriving as soon as they think of it.
Fǎng, having witnessed these wonders,
described everything he saw in detail,
and then requested that paintings be made as screens,
totaling twenty-four panels.
Those who saw them were astonished.
When Fǎng first arrived at the temple,
through the pores of his skin,
he could see everything.
Later, when his disciples brought him food,
after eating,
his pores closed up as before.
Only then did he realize that the difference between human food and heavenly food
lies in their refinement and coarseness.
After Fǎng had fully revealed the appearances of the heavens,
people considered him a sorcerer.
At that time, Zétiān was on the throne,
and someone reported him.
Zétiān ordered the screens to be taken,
and also summoned Fǎng.
After Fǎng arrived,
Zétiān questioned him but did not punish him,
instead keeping Fǎng in the palace.
Zétiān personally prepared food for him,
offering generous provisions.
He stayed for several months.
Zétiān said to Fǎng:
"Does the Chan master have no words of instruction for your disciple?"
Fǎng, having no choice,
said:
"This humble monk only wishes that Your Majesty would not engage in excessive killing,
which greatly damages karmic retribution.
These are my only words."
Zétiān believed and accepted this,
and thus bestowed an imperial edict:
"Wherever Fǎng goes,
for the construction of meritorious deeds,
no
(the original text reads "wú jì" two characters,
changed according to the Chén collated edition)
obstruction shall be allowed."
Fǎng lived beyond the age of sixty,
and as if entering meditation,
he passed away in Shǎnzhōng.
From "Jì Wén"
A Monk from Between Xiàng and Wèi
Between Xiàng and Wèi, there was a monk
who from a young age extensively studied sūtras and treatises,
and was skilled in preaching.
Whenever he held a lecture,
he considered himself outstanding,
yet his listeners were few,
and the offerings he received were meager.
This continued for years,
and the monk grew discontented.
So he took his sūtras and treatises,
traveled to all the famous mountains,
seeking those who understood,
and later arrived at Héngyuè Temple.
He rested there for over a month,
often sitting alone in the temple's quiet quarters,
pondering the sūtras and treatises.
He also reproached himself, saying:
"Could it be that the principles I understand
deviate from the sage's intent?"
While deep in thought,
he suddenly looked up and saw an old monk,
who entered with a staff and said:
"What sūtras and treatises does the master study?
What principles does he investigate?"
The monk suspected he was an extraordinary person,
so he explained his situation,
and again reproached himself, saying:
"If I were to meet someone who understands,
and could clarify this matter,
I would seal my lips and remain silent,
never lecturing again."
The old monk laughed and said:
"The master's knowledge is vast,
how could he not understand this principle:
'Even the great sage cannot save those without karmic connection.'
How much more so for one with initial resolve?"
The master simply has no karmic connection with the multitude of monks."
The monk said:
"If that is the case,
must I remain like this for the rest of my life?"
The old monk said:
"Let me try to create karmic connections for you."
He then asked how much provisions the monk had,
and the monk said:
"Since leaving Nánxiàn,
traveling ten thousand lǐ,
all the food and expenses
have been exhausted.
Now I only have seven great robes left."
The old monk said:
"This is enough.
Sell them,
and use the proceeds to make porridge cakes and oily foods."
The monk did as instructed,
preparing enough for several thousand people.
Then they carried the food together to an open field,
scattered it,
burned incense, knelt down,
and chanted:
"May those who eat my offering today,
in future lives,
become my disciples.
I will teach them,
so they may attain bodhi."
After speaking,
birds and sparrows flocked down to peck at the food,
and on the ground, ants
were too numerous to count.
The old monk said to him:
"After twenty years,
you may return to open a dharma seat.
For now, travel around,
and do not lecture."
After speaking, the monk followed his advice.
Twenty years later,
he returned to Héběi to give lectures.
His listeners numbered in the tens of thousands,
all under twenty years of age,
with scarcely one or two among the old and middle-aged.
From "Yuán Huà Jì"
Dàolín
During the Diàolù era of the Táng dynasty,
a man from Guìzhōu named Xuē Jiǎ often provided for a monk.
The monk's religious name was Dàolín,
and his virtue was very high,
so Xuē Jiǎ's reverence and respect for him were especially sincere.
He provided for him in this manner
for over ten years.
Suddenly one day, the monk bid farewell and departed,
saying:
"This humble monk has been troubling and imposing upon you for many years,
and I have nothing with which to repay you.
Now I have an old sutra case,
which I will leave here in your house.
If I do not return within one year,
you may open it."
After more than a year had passed,
he opened the lock,
and saw several thousand taels of gold inside.
Later, he sold half of it,
used the proceeds to buy land and build the Bodhi Temple,
and also erected a true-body statue of Dàolín.
It has been venerated up to the present day,
and the statue's form still exists.
Xuē Jiǎ now has a grandson named Yǔ Bīn,
who holds an official post in Guìlín.
From "Guìlín Fēngtǔ Jì" (Records of Guìlín's Local Conditions).
Jìngmǎn
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
the monk Jìngmǎn of Lùquán Temple in Héngzhōu possessed lofty conduct,
which aroused the jealousy of the other monks.
They secretly drew a picture of a woman in a tall building,
with Jìngmǎn drawing a bow to shoot her,
and hid it in a sutra box.
They then ordered his younger brother to go to the imperial court and accuse him.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān was greatly enraged,
and ordered the Censor Péi Huáigǔ to investigate the case,
with the intention of executing him.
Huáigǔ firmly held his ground and did not yield.
Lǐ Zhāodé then stepped forward and said:
"Huáigǔ's investigation of the matter is careless and negligent,
I request that he be ordered to reinvestigate."
Huáigǔ declared loudly:
"Your Majesty's law makes no distinction between close and distant;
it should be applied uniformly throughout the land.
How can you have your subject execute an innocent person,
merely to curry your sacred favor?
If Jìngmǎn truly had the appearance of disloyalty,
how could I, your subject, have the face to pardon him?
I uphold impartial laws,
hoping there will be no wrongful executions.
Even if I die, I will have no regrets!"
Empress Wǔ Zétiān's anger then subsided.
Later, Huáigǔ served as deputy to Yán Zhīwēi on a peace mission to the Turks.
The Turks
"The Turks" two characters originally missing.
Supplemented according to Chén's collation.
established Zhīwēi as the Southern Khagan,
and invaded Zhào and Dìng.
Huáigǔ thus managed to escape and return.
He was originally frail and weak,
unable to endure running,
so he earnestly prayed to Heaven,
wishing to die in the southern lands.
Exhausted, he fell asleep.
He dreamed of a monk resembling Jìngmǎn,
who guided him, saying:
"You can exit via this path."
He awoke and followed it,
and indeed managed to survive intact.
People considered this the reward for his loyalty and compassion.
From "Dà Táng Xīnyǔ" (New Accounts of the Great Táng).
Fǎtōng
The Yìdé Chán Temple in Cháng'ān
was renamed and refurbished by Emperor Zhōngzōng of Táng to accumulate blessings for the posthumous honor of Crown Prince Yìdé.
It was renamed and refurbished.
Within the Chán temple was a large stone mortar,
weighing five hundred catties.
At the end of the Suí dynasty,
the Śramaṇa Fǎtōng from Hù County transported it from the southern estate to this temple.
Fǎtōng had left home to become a monk from a young age,
and was initially extremely weak and frail,
so his companions looked down on him.
He then vowed with great determination to become strong and robust.
One day, while napping under a tree,
he suddenly had three shēng of saliva flow from his mouth.
His mother, startled and alarmed, called to wake him.
Fǎtōng said:
"I suddenly dreamed that someone gave me three loads of sinews,
and told me to eat them.
I had just eaten one load
when I abruptly awoke,
and then became strong and robust."
He tried lifting the large stone mortar,
and did not find it difficult.
There was a temple monk named Xíngkān,
who was originally reputed to be very strong.
Fǎtōng then secretly took the kasaya Xíngkān was wearing,
lifted a hall pillar, and pressed it down on top of it.
Xíngkān saw this and was astonished;
he tried with all his might but could not retrieve it.
Fǎtōng slowly lifted the pillar and retrieved it,
greatly astonishing everyone.
Fǎtōng's strength was equal to that of a hundred men,
and everyone at the time was in awe of him,
believing it to be divine assistance.
From "Xījīng Jì" (Records of the Western Capital).
Master Sēngqié
was a man from the Western Regions.
His lay surname was Hé.
In the early years of the Lóngshuò era of the Táng dynasty, he came traveling to the northern lands,
and registered at the Lóngxīng Temple in Chǔzhōu.
Later, in the Xìnyì ward of Línhuái County in Sìzhōu, he begged for land, set up markers,
and intended to build a temple.
Beneath the markers,
he excavated an old stele inscription from the Ancient Incense Accumulation Temple,
along with a golden statue,
upon which were the characters "Pǔzhào Wáng Fó" (Universal Illumination King Buddha).
He then built the temple there.
In the second year of the Jǐnglóng era of Táng,
Emperor Zhōngzōng dispatched an envoy to welcome the Master,
brought him into the inner palace chapel,
and honored him as National Preceptor.
Soon after, he moved out to reside at the Jiànfú Temple.
He often stayed alone in a single room.
On the top of his head was an opening,
which he usually plugged with cotton wadding.
At night, he would remove the wadding.
Fragrant incense would emerge from the opening on his head,
filling the room with smoke,
exceptionally aromatic and rich.
By dawn,
the incense would return into the opening on his head,
and he would again plug it with cotton wadding.
The Master often washed his feet,
and people would take the water he used to drink it,
and all chronic illnesses would be cured.
One day,
Emperor Zhōngzōng said to the Master within the inner palace:
"The capital region has had no rain
for several months now.
I beseech the Master, in your compassion,
to relieve my anxiety and distress."
The Master then sprinkled water from a bottle,
and in a moment, dark clouds suddenly gathered,
and sweet rain poured down heavily.
Emperor Zhōngzōng was greatly pleased,
and issued an edict bestowing a name upon the temple he had built,
naming it the Línhuái Temple.
The Master requested that the name "Pǔzhào Wáng"
Míng manuscript and Chén's collated edition have "temple" for "character".
be used as the name,
wishing to follow the characters on the golden statue.
Emperor Zhōngzōng, because the character "zhào" was part of Empress Wǔ Zétiān's temple name taboo,
changed it to Pǔguāng Wáng Temple,
and personally wrote the plaque in his own hand to bestow upon it.
On the second day of the third month in the fourth year of Jǐnglóng,
he passed away sitting upright at the Jiànfú Temple in Cháng'ān.
Emperor Zhōngzōng immediately ordered a pagoda to be built for him at the Jiànfú Temple,
and his body lacquered and venerated.
Suddenly, a great wind arose,
and a foul odor spread throughout Cháng'ān.
Emperor Zhōngzōng asked:
"What omen is this?"
A close minister reported:
"Master Sēngqié's karmic affinity for teaching lies in Línhuái.
I fear he wishes to return there,
hence this manifestation."
Emperor Zhōngzōng silently consented in his heart,
and the foul odor immediately ceased.
In an instant,
an extraordinary, rich, and intense fragrance arose.
In the fifth month of that same year,
he was escorted to Línhuái,
where a pagoda was built for his veneration.
This is the pagoda that exists today.
Later, Emperor Zhōngzōng asked Master Wànhuí:
"Who is Master Sēngqié?"
Wànhuí said:
"He is an incarnation of Guānyīn.
As stated in the 'Universal Gate' chapter of the Lotus Sutra:
'For those who should be saved in the form of a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, etc.,
he manifests accordingly and preaches the Dharma to them.'
This is precisely that."
Previously, when the Master first arrived in Cháng'ān,
Wànhuí paid his respects and visited him with great reverence.
The Master patted his head and said:
"Young man, why have you lingered so long?
It is time for you to go."
After the Master passed away,
within a few months,
Wànhuí also died.
The Master manifested many miraculous deeds throughout his life,
all recorded in his main biography.
This merely records his beginning and end.
From "Běn Zhuàn" (Main Biography) and "Jì Wén Lù" (Record of Things Heard).
The Mad Monk of Huíxiàng Temple
In the final years of the Táng Xuánzōng's Kāiyuán era, he dreamed of someone saying:
"Take five hundred hand towels
and five hundred monastic robes
to distribute as alms at Huíxiàng Temple."
Upon waking,
he asked his attendants,
but none knew of such a place.
He then summoned eminent and accomplished Buddhist monks
and ordered them to search for it.
There was a mad monk,
who had no fixed abode,
and no one knew where he came from.
He came forward to answer the call, saying:
"I know the location of Huíxiàng Temple."
When asked how many men he needed,
he said:
"Just let me take the items!
And one jīn of fine incense,
then I can go."
These were given to him.
The monk went straight into the Zhōngnán Mountains.
After two days of travel,
he reached an extremely deep and precipitous place,
but saw nothing at all.
Suddenly, he came upon a millstone.
Startled, he exclaimed:
"This place is inaccessible to humans;
how can this be here?"
Then upon it,
he burned the incense he had brought,
bowed, prayed, and earnestly entreated,
from noon until evening.
After a long while,
mist rose in the valley,
obscuring everything within arm's reach.
As it gradually dispersed,
on the halfway point of the cliff,
there appeared vermilion pillars and white walls,
exquisite as a painting.
Soon it became clearer,
and he saw a temple as if amidst the clouds.
The main gate bore a large plaque.
Looking closely,
it indeed read "Huíxiàng."
The monk was overjoyed.
Climbing, he finally reached it.
It was already dusk.
He heard the sounds of bells, chimes, and Buddhist prayers.
The gatekeeper questioned where he came from,
then led him inside.
He met an old monk who said:
"May the Táng emperor enjoy boundless blessings."
He instructed someone to accompany him
to distribute the hand towels and other items room by room.
Only one portion remained.
One room had only an empty bed,
with no person there.
The monk reported this in detail.
The old monk smiled and told him to sit.
Turning to an attendant, he said:
"Fetch the chǐbā from that room."
It was a jade chǐbā.
The old monk asked:
"Did you see that foreign monk?"
He replied:
"Yes."
The old monk said:
"He is temporarily acting in your lord's place.
The country will soon fall into turmoil,
and countless people will die.
He is called the King of Annihilation.
That empty room is your lord's chamber.
Your lord was in this temple,
but because he loved playing the chǐbā,
he was exiled to the mortal world.
This is the one he often played.
Now his term has ended,
and he is about to return."
The next day,
they invited him to sit for the monastic meal.
After the meal, the old monk said:
"You must return now.
Take this jade chǐbā and give it to your lord.
Also, have him keep the hand towels and robes himself."
The mad monk prostrated in reverence and departed.
A novice saw him out.
After only a few steps,
clouds and mist closed in from all sides again.
When they dispersed,
the temple was nowhere to be seen.
He took the hand towels and the chǐbā
and presented them to Xuánzōng.
Upon being summoned for an audience,
he recounted the entire story.
Xuánzōng was deeply moved and pleased.
Taking the chǐbā, he played it;
it was exactly like the one he used to play.
More than twenty years later,
the rebellion of Ān Lùshān indeed occurred.
The foreign monk the mad monk had seen
was Lùshān himself.
From Yì Shǐ
Lǎn Cán
Lǎn Cán
was a laborer monk at Héngyuè Temple during the early Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty.
After meals,
he would gather the leftovers to eat.
He was lazy by nature and ate scraps,
hence he was called Lǎn Cán (Lazy Leftovers).
By day, he did all the temple's work;
by night, he slept beneath the herd of oxen,
never showing weariness,
for twenty years.
At that time, the future Marquis of Yè, Lǐ Mì, was studying in the temple.
Observing Lǎn Cán's behavior, he said:
"This is no ordinary being."
Listening to his midnight Sanskrit chants,
which resonated through the mountains and forests,
Lǐ Mì, being quite knowledgeable in music,
could discern sorrow and joy.
He said Lǎn Cán's sutra chants were first mournful and then joyful,
indicating he must be an exiled immortal.
His time to leave was near.
Waiting until midnight,
Lǐ Mì secretly went to pay his respects.
He knelt outside the thatched door, announced his name, and bowed.
Lǎn Cán cursed loudly,
spat toward the sky, and said:
"This is going to harm me."
Lǐ Mì only grew more reverent and cautious,
merely bowing repeatedly.
Lǎn Cán was poking the ox-dung fire
and took out a taro to eat.
After a long while, he finally said:
"You may sit on the ground."
He gave Lǐ Mì half of the taro he was eating.
Lǐ Mì received it respectfully,
ate it all, and thanked him.
Lǎn Cán said to Lǐ Mì:
"Be careful not to speak much of this.
You shall serve as prime minister for ten years."
Lǐ Mì bowed again and withdrew.
A month later,
the prefect was preparing a sacrifice at the mountain,
repairing the road with great strictness.
Suddenly, in the middle of the night, there was wind and thunder,
and a peak collapsed.
The mountain path
was blocked by a huge rock.
They tried to pull it using ten oxen harnessed together,
and had several hundred men shout and push it,
but their strength was exhausted and it remained firmly stuck.
There was no other route
to prepare for the ceremony.
Lǎn Cán said:
"No need for human strength.
Let me try to remove it."
Everyone laughed loudly,
thinking him mad.
Lǎn Cán said:
"Why must you ridicule me?
Just let me try."
The temple monks laughed and agreed.
He then stepped on the rock and moved it.
Suddenly, it turned and rolled down,
with a sound like thunder.
With the mountain path now cleared,
all the monks bowed in reverence.
The entire commandery hailed him as a sage,
and the prefect revered him like a deity.
Lǎn Cán remained quiet and aloof,
and then intended to leave.
Outside the temple, tigers and leopards
suddenly appeared in packs,
causing injuries and deaths daily,
with no way to stop them.
Lǎn Cán said:
"Give me a whip,
and I will drive them all away for you."
Everyone said:
"If he could move a giant rock,
tigers and leopards should be easy to handle."
So they gave him a thorny club.
They all followed to watch.
As soon as he stepped out the gate,
a tiger seized him and carried him away.
After Lǎn Cán left,
the tigers and leopards also vanished without a trace.
Later, Lǐ Mì indeed served as prime minister for ten years.
From Gān Zé Yáo
Wéi Gāo

Wéi Gāo, the late Grand Commandant and concurrent Secretariat Director who served as the Military Commissioner of Jiànnán during the Táng dynasty, was one month old when his family invited a group of monks for a meal.
There was a foreign monk,
whose appearance was very ugly,
who arrived without being invited.
The servants of the Wéi family were all angry with him,
and made him sit on a worn-out mat in the courtyard.
After the meal,
the Wéi family ordered the wet nurse to bring out the infant,
and asked the group of monks to pray for his longevity.
The foreign monk suddenly ascended the steps by himself,
and said to the infant:
"Has it been long since we parted? Are you well?"
The infant seemed to show a joyful expression,
and everyone found it strange.
Wéi Gāo's late father said:
"This child has only been born for a month. Why does the master say it has been a long time since we parted?"
The foreign monk said:
"This is not something you, the benefactor, can understand."
The Wéi family insisted on asking,
and the foreign monk said:
"This child is the reincarnation of Zhūgě Wǔhóu.
Wǔhóu, during the late Eastern Hàn,
served as the Chancellor of Shǔ,
and the people of Shǔ benefited from his grace for a long time.
Now he has descended into this world,
and will become the commander of Shǔ's gates,
and will receive the blessings of the people of Shǔ.
In previous years, I was at Jiànmén,
and was friends with this child.
Now I heard he has descended into the Wéi family,
so I came from afar."
The Wéi family found his words strange,
and thus named him with Wǔhóu's style name.
Later, Wéi Gāo, from the position of Junior Imperial Guard, commanded the Jiànnán army,
and was successively promoted to Grand Commandant and concurrent Secretariat Director.
He served in Shǔ for eighteen years,
indeed fulfilling the foreign monk's words.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
Shì Dàoqīn
Shì Dàoqīn resided at Xíngshān.
When asked about the Way,
he responded casually,
yet all reached the ultimate principle.
Liú Yàn, the former governor of Zhōngzhōu, often requested a heart gāthā,
and was told to hold the incense burner and listen.
Dàoqīn repeatedly said, "Do no evil.
Practice all good deeds."
Liú Yàn said:
"Even a three-foot-tall child knows this."
Dàoqīn said:
"A three-foot-tall child may know it,
but a hundred-year-old man may not be able to practice it."
To this day, this is considered a famous principle.
Also, the miscellaneous biography of Emperor Yuán of Liáng states:
At the end of the Jìn Huìdì era,
there was a monk in Luòyáng named Qíyù,
who was an enlightened one.
People from Cháng'ān dined with Qíyù at Cháng'ān Temple,
and people from the Liúshā region dined with Qíyù in front of a stone statue,
seeing him on the same day across tens of thousands of miles.
The monk Zhú Fǎxíng once bowed and begged for words of wisdom,
and Qíyù ascended the high seat and said:
"Guard your speech, restrain your thoughts,
and do not violate the precepts in your heart."
Zhú said:
"An enlightened one should teach what has not been heard before.
Now even an eight-year-old novice monk can recite this."
Qíyù smiled and said:
"An eight-year-old may recite it, but a hundred-year-old may not be able to practice it."
The Míng manuscript copy writes "zhì" as "zhì,"
and "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ" continuation four writes: "An eight-year-old may recite it, but a hundred-year-old may not be able to practice it."
Alas!
People all revere the enlightened ones,
but do not know that practicing is how one attains enlightenment oneself.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Master Xīn Qī
Master Xīn Qī was from Shǎn,
and Xīn was his surname.
From childhood,
he was very cautious and solemn,
never engaging in frivolous play,
and his parents found him unusual and cherished him.
At ten years old, he became fond of Buddhist teachings,
reading Buddhist scriptures daily,
and was able to understand Sanskrit sounds on his own,
without being taught by a master.
Later, his father served as the governor of Shǎn Commandery.
Previously, there were seven tile kilns south of the commandery.
When his father passed away,
Xīn Qī was deeply grieved.
One day,
he went mad and ran away.
The family servants tracked where he went,
and when they reached the south of the commandery,
they saw Xīn Qī sitting upright in one of the tile kilns,
his body emitting a strange light,
shining brightly like refined gold.
The servants were astonished.
Going to the next kiln,
they saw another Xīn Qī there.
Passing through all seven kilns,
there was a Xīn Qī in each one.
From then on, he was called Master Xīn Qī.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
The Monk from Jiāzhōu
Lìzhōu's Guǎngfú Chán Monastery
was originally founded by the former military commander Zhāng Chùzhāo.
He invited the elder Líng Guì to preside over it,
to settle the community of monks,
and several years passed.
Líng Guì was fond of alchemy,
and one day,
he took the urine of the monks and refined it in a large cauldron into frost,
filling the roads with a foul and disgusting odor.
In the hall, there was a monk
who had originally come from Jiāzhōu,
seeming dissatisfied,
and muttering to himself.
Líng Guì noticed this,
and thus asked him to be in charge of purchasing food rice for the monks,
hoping he would spend less time in the monastery.
Within ten days,
the monk brought all the account books and money,
and presented them to the abbot's room,
saying:
"Due to a small matter,
I will temporarily go out to a nearby place."
He then wished to take his leave.
That night,
he sat in the lotus position in his original place in the hall,
and peacefully passed away.
All the monks were surprised that he had no illness,
and performed the usual funeral rites.
When a monk in the hall passed away,
it was customary to break fifty bundles of firewood,
and all monks were invited to each carry one piece,
escorting it to the outskirts,
where it was stacked into a pyre and burned.
Afterward, they returned to the monastery and gathered the community,
and all the clothing and alms bowl of the deceased monk were distributed for communal use,
as was customary.
On that day,
the day originally written as "míng yuē,"
according to the Chén revised edition, changed to
the deceased monk was seated on the pyre,
and the Karmadāna completed the ten recitations.
They were about to set the fire.
Suddenly, the monk startled and rose,
and said to the Karmadāna:
"There are two strings of cash for rice money
with the supervisor
the Míng manuscript copy writes "jiān" as "lán"
novice."
He then joined his palms and said to all the monks:
"Coming and going is the norm.
Thank you all for coming from afar to see me off."
He closed his eyes, folded his hands,
and sat upright, unmoving.
The fire ignited from his right side,
and he turned to ashes.
Everyone was astonished.
From this, it is known that the true nature of the perfect and bright mind,
does not perish even in death.
Coming and going,
attaining freedom in fire—
it is indeed believable that such things exist.
From "Yěrén Xiánhuà"
Jīngāng Xiān
During the Kaicheng era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a monk named Jīngāng Xiān,
a man from the Western Regions,
who resided at the Xiáshān Temple in Qīngyuǎn.
He was skilled in Sanskrit incantations,
flicking his tongue and shaking his monk's staff while chanting spells over objects,
and there was nothing that did not respond.
He excelled at capturing and restraining ghosts and spirits,
binding flood dragons and hornless dragons.
With a single shake of his staff,
he could summon thunder, which would immediately rumble.
On this day, at Xiáshān Temple, there was a man named Lǐ Pǔ,
who was wielding an axe to fell a giant tree,
hollowing it out to make a boat.
Suddenly, he climbed the mountain
and saw a large flat rock,
on which there was a hole.
He observed a large spider,
its legs spanning over a foot wide,
scurrying in all directions.
