[The character "驰" (scurrying) was originally written as "虵" (snake).
Changed according to the Míng manuscript copy and the Chén collated edition.]
It gnawed at the plants, blocking its hole, and then left.
Soon, he heard a sound from the forest,
a violent, fierce, and sudden roar.
The worker, frightened, climbed a tree to watch.
Indeed, he saw a double-
[The character "双" (double) was originally written as "枳".
Changed according to the text below.]
headed serpent,
several tens of *zhàng* in length,
coiling and writhing in fury.
It encircled the spider's hole.
Its heads faced east and west.
Suddenly, the head facing west leaped,
sucked up the clump of plants at the hole, and flew away.
The tips were all stripped clean.
Afterwards, the head facing east turned,
widely opened its eyes,
gaped its mouth wide,
and sucked at the spider.
The spider scurried out,
using its legs to seize the mouth of the hole,
raising its curled venom,
crimson like fire,
and scorched the serpent's throat,
blinding the serpent's eyes.
The serpent, stunned, then revived,
lifted its head and sucked again,
but the spider was gone.
It further poisoned the serpent,
and the serpent then collapsed onto the rock and died.
The spider leaped out,
climbed onto the serpent's belly,
bit inside, broke off the two heads with its teeth,
both spewing silk which it wrapped around them,
and leaped back into its hole.
Lǐ Pǔ was astonished by this,
returned to Xiáshān Temple,
and told Jīngāng Xiān.
Xiān then asked Pǔ to verify the hole.
He shook his ringed staff and chanted a spell over it,
and the spider immediately emerged before the monk,
solemnly as if divinely listening.
When he extended his staff to touch it,
the spider then died beside the hole.
That night,
Jīngāng Xiān dreamed of an old man,
holding a bolt of silk as he approached and said:
"I am that spider,
and I can also weave."
He bowed to Jīngāng Xiān and said:
"I wish to become a robe for the field of merit."
Having spoken, he then vanished.
When the monk awoke,
the cloth was already by his side.
Its exquisite and marvelous craftsmanship
was not something that could be made from the silk of worldly cocoons.
The monk then made it into a robe,
which dust and dirt did not touch.
Several years later,
the monk went to Pānyú,
to board a ship and return to India.
Then, by the Jīnsuǒ Pond at Xiáshān,
he shook his staff, shouted loudly, and chanted a spell over the water.
Soon, the water parted, revealing the bottom.
Using a washing bowl, he scooped it up,
and there was a loach fish,
about three *cun* long,
that leaped into the bowl.
He said to the assembled monks:
"This is a dragon.
I will take it to Hǎimén,
boil it with medicine into an ointment,
apply it to my feet,
and then crossing the sea will be like walking on level ground."
That night,
an old man in white clothes, carrying a revolving-joint wine vessel,
went to the temple attendant Fù Jīng and said:
"I know Jīngāng Xiān is fond of wine.
This vessel contains fine brew on one side,
and poisoned wine on the other.
This vessel is the one that Jìn Emperor once used to poison General Niú.
Now I offer you a hundred *liǎng* of gold.
For taking this wine
and poisoning that monk.
That monk for no reason captured my son,
intending to make him into ointment.
My hatred for him runs deep,
the pain penetrates to the marrow of my bones,
but I have no plan, and what can I do?"
Fù Jīng was pleased,
accepted the gold and the wine,
learned the method of operating the revolving joint,
and went to Jīngāng Xiān.
As Xiān raised the cup to his mouth,
suddenly, a several-year-
[The two characters "数岁" (several-year-old) were originally missing.
Added according to the Chén collated edition.]
old child leaped out,
approached his hand, covered it, and said:
"The wine was brought by the dragon to poison you, Master."
The monk was greatly alarmed,
and questioned Fù Jīng.
Fù Jīng then did not dare to conceal the truth.
The monk then asked the child:
"Who are you, that you come to rescue me?"
The child said:
"I am the spider of days past.
Now I have left that evil karma behind,
and have been reborn as a human,
for seven years already.
My soul is slightly more perceptive than an ordinary person's,
and knowing you were in danger,
I sent my soul flying to offer rescue."
Having spoken, he vanished.
The assembled monks pitied him,
and together bowed to Jīngāng Xiān,
begging him to release the dragon's son.
The monk had no choice but to set it free.
Later, Xiān indeed boarded a ship and returned to India.
From *Chuánqí* (The Legendary Tales).
The Sparrow-Hawk Pigeon Monk
In Dèngzhōu, there was an old monk who daily ate sparrow-hawks and pigeons.
Both monks and laypeople all criticized him for it,
but the old monk never avoided doing so.
When he was preparing his meal,
a poor scholar came begging for food,
and the monk shared two legs with him to eat.
After eating,
the monk rinsed his mouth,
and two pigeons came out from his mouth.
One could walk,
the other crawled on the ground.
The poor scholar, astonished,
also vomited his rice,
and the two legs of his pigeon also grew back.
Afterwards, the monk no longer ate this kind of food,
and it was all
[In *Yúnxī Yǒuyì*, "都" (all) is written as "覩" (witness).]
verified.
Everyone respected him all the more.
He was called the Nányáng Sparrow-Hawk Pigeon Monk.
From *Yúnxī Yǒuyì* (Discourses from Cloudy Brook Friends).
Monk Xiù
At the Tiāngōng Temple in Luòdū, there was a Chan master named Xiù,
whose secular surname was Lǐ,
and who was from Chénliú in Biànzhōu.
He practiced meditation with utmost diligence and austerity.
He first arrived in Jīngzhōu,
and later moved to this temple.
He was deeply respected and honored by Empress Dowager Wǔ.
His profound insight and silent understanding
were perfectly aligned within, like matching tallies.
During the Cháng'ān era, he entered the capital,
and resided at the Zīshèng Temple.
Suddenly, he instructed the disciples in the meditation hall to extinguish all lamps and candles.
The disciples had kept a perpetual lamp burning,
but he also ordered them to extinguish it.
He then explained:
"The calamity of fire is unpredictable,
and one must be prepared.
There was once a temple that was unprepared regarding fire and candles,
and its Buddha hall was consumed by disaster;
another temple had its bell tower struck by fire,
and yet another had its sutra repository burned to ashes,
which is truly grievous and lamentable."
The monastic community did not understand his meaning.
That night, a fire broke out,
and indeed, the Buddha hall and bell tower,
along with three sutra repositories, were burned.
When Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng was still a prince,
he often visited with the other princes to pay respects,
and left a flute as an offering.
After Xuánzōng departed,
Xiù summoned a disciple and said:
"Carefully keep this,
for there will be a crucial time later
when it should be presented to him."
When Xuánzōng ascended the throne,
Dámó and others then understood his words,
and they retrieved the flute to present it.
Master Xiù lived to be one hundred years old,
and passed away at this temple.
He was buried at Lóngmén Mountain.
Thousands of monastics and laypeople rushed to pay their respects,
and Duke Yānguó, Zhāng Yuè, composed the inscription for his stele.
From *The Record of the Western Capital*
Yìfú
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a monk named Yìfú,
who was from Shàngdǎng.
He diligently cultivated pure conduct,
and his appearance was dignified and pure.
Officials, gentry, and commoners alike
unanimously turned to him for refuge.
Once, he accompanied the imperial carriage to the Eastern Capital.
In every commandery and county he passed through,
people were drawn to him,
and they donated tens of thousands in alms,
all of which he entrusted to others and left behind.
Suddenly, one day,
he summoned his disciples
and announced that his end was near.
The Vice Minister of War, Zhāng Jūn; the Vice Director of the Secretariat, Yán Tǐngzhī; the Vice Minister of Justice, Fáng Guǎn; and the Vice Minister of Rites, Wéi Zhì,
who regularly paid him ceremonial visits,
also came together that day.
Yìfú then ascended the seat
and expounded the Dharma for his disciples.
He then said:
"I will pass away today,
and so I bid you farewell."
After a long while,
Zhāng said to Fáng:
"I have been taking golden elixirs for years,
and since then, I have never attended a funeral."
Having said this,
Zhāng secretly left.
Yìfú suddenly said to Fáng:
"I have associated with Lord Zhāng for several years.
He will face an extraordinary calamity,
and both his reputation and integrity will be compromised.
If he had remained until the end of this Dharma assembly just now,
it would have been enough to avert the disaster.
What a pity!"
Then, taking Fáng's hand, he said:
"You will certainly become a renowned minister of the restoration.
Strive for it, sir."
Having spoken, he passed away.
During the rebellion of Ān Lùshān,
Zhāng Jūn fell into the hands of the rebels
and accepted a false appointment.
Fáng Guǎn served two courts with distinction,
and ultimately established great moral integrity.
From *Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Minghuang*
Shéndǐng
During the Táng dynasty, Master Shéndǐng refused to shave his head
and consumed a *dǒu* of fermented paste.
Whenever he made his rounds begging for alms,
if he received coarse cloth or tattered garments, he would wear them;
if he received fine brocade or silk, he would also wear them.
Once, while listening before Master Lìzhēn's seat,
he asked Master Zhēn:
"Are all things fixed?"
Zhēn said:
"They are fixed."
Dǐng said:
"If you, *ācārya*, say they are fixed,
then why do high banks become valleys,
and deep valleys become hills?
Where there is death, there is life;
where there is life, there is death.
All things are entangled with one another,
and the six paths revolve in cycles.
How can they be considered fixed?"
Zhēn said:
"All things are not fixed."
Dǐng said:
"If they are not fixed,
then why not call heaven earth,
and earth heaven?
Why not call the moon a star,
and a star the moon?
How can they be considered not fixed?"
Zhēn had no response.
At that time, Zhāng Wénchéng saw this
and said to him:
"I observe that the Dharma master is a practitioner of the Bodhisattva path."
Dǐng said:
"A Bodhisattva does not rejoice in gain,
nor grieve at loss;
does not become angry when struck,
nor resentful when scolded.
This is the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
Now, when I beg, I rejoice if I receive,
and grieve if I do not;
I become angry when struck,
and resentful when scolded.
Judging by this,
I am far from being a Bodhisattva."
From *Records of Affairs from Court and Country*
Guǎnglíng Dàshī
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a monk who was a guest in Guǎnglíng.
His name was lost,
and he called himself Dàshī (Great Master).
The people of Guǎnglíng therefore addressed him as Dàshī.
Dàshī was of very ugly appearance,
fond of eating meat and drinking wine,
and often wore a coarse fur garment,
not taking it off even in the intense summer heat,
causing fleas and lice to gather upon it.
He resided as a guest at the Xiàogǎn Temple,
occupying a single room alone,
closing the door each evening to sleep,
which became his regular habit.
His nature was wild and perverse;
he enjoyed slaughtering dogs and pigs,
daily brawling with the young men of Guǎnglíng,
or lying drunk by the roadside.
The people of Guǎnglíng all
(The original text had "fear" (懼 jù);
amended based on the Míng manuscript copy and the Chén collated edition to "all" (俱 jù))
despised him for this.
There was a young man
renowned for his strength.
One day,
this young man was gambling with someone.
Dàshī became greatly enraged,
striking the gaming board with his hand and shattering it completely.
The young man said:
"You fool,
how dare you oppose a strong man?"
Dàshī cursed and spat in his face,
whereupon he fought with the young man,
with thousands watching.
The young man ultimately could not prevail,
and finally fled.
From then on, the people of Guǎnglíng said Dàshī possessed divine strength,
and Dàshī also prided himself on his power,
often plundering money and clothing from the market.
The market people all feared his ferocity,
and none dared resist.
Later, an old monk summoned Dàshī and said:
"A monk should devote his heart to observing the precepts.
How can you eat meat and drink wine,
kill dogs and pigs,
plunder the money and goods of market people,
and brawl with young men?
Is this the way of a monk?
If one day officials arrest you and report you to the authorities,
will you not bring shame upon heaven?"
Dàshī angrily retorted:
"Flies and gnats merely crave rank and foul things;
how can they comprehend the heart of dragons and cranes?
Thus, my Way is also not for you to understand.
Moreover, I purify my inner self while appearing mixed in the world;
how could I be like you, petty and lacking in magnanimity?"
The old monk ultimately could not refute his words.
One day later,
Dàshī returned from outside,
entered his room,
and closed the door.
Someone peeping through a crack in the door
saw Dàshī sitting on his mat,
with a strange light
emanating from between his eyebrows,
brightly illuminating the entire room.
The observer found this remarkable
and reported it fully to the other monks.
The monks came
and saw the luminous sign between Dàshī's eyebrows.
Pointing, they said:
"We have heard that between the Buddha's eyebrows is the mark of the white curl, emitting light.
Now Dàshī possesses it;
he is indeed a Buddha."
Thereupon they bowed to him in unison.
By the next morning at dawn,
all the monks had gathered in the courtyard,
awaiting an audience with Guǎnglíng Dàshī.
When they opened the door,
Guǎnglíng Dàshī had already vanished.
The monks grew even more amazed by this event,
and thus they called Dàshī 'Dàshī Buddha'.
From "Xuānshì Zhì" (Records from the Chamber of Dissemination).
Héhé
The Táng dynasty Princess of Guó married Zhèng Wànjūn of Xíngyáng,
but for several years had no children.
At that time, there was a monk named Héhé,
who seemed mad and foolish,
and the masses called him a saint.
His predictions of events were often accurate.
He resided at Dà'ān Temple,
engaged in constructing and repairing halls and pavilions.
Héhé often visited the princess's home.
Wànjūn requested of him:
"I have no heir;
I wish to have a son.
If you, Master, would bestow your grace,
could it be achieved?"
The Master said:
"Give me three thousand bolts of silk,
and the princess will give birth to two boys."
Wànjūn gave the silk as instructed.
Héhé took the silk and delivered it to the temple,
saying it was for cultivating merit.
Then he said to Wànjūn:
"The princess is pregnant.
I have commanded two heavenly beings to descend
to be the princess's sons."
He also said:
"The princess's belly is small;
can it carry two boys simultaneously?
I shall make them born in the same year, one after the other."
The princess then became pregnant,
and at the beginning and end of the year,
she gave birth to one son each.
The elder was named Qiányào,
the younger Huìmíng.
Both were handsome men,
erudite and knowledgeable.
From "Jìwén Lù" (Records of Things Heard).
Master Kōngrú
Master Kōngrú,
it is unknown where he was from.
In his youth, he yearned to cultivate the Way.
His parents pressured him to marry,
so he cut off his genitals with a knife,
and thus stopped them.
Later, upon reaching adulthood,
when conscripted for labor service,
he wrapped his arm with hemp and wax,
set it on fire,
and became permanently disabled.
He entered Lùhún Mountain,
and dwelt in a hermitage.
Tigers did not harm him.
Once in the mountains, he happened to see a wild boar fighting a tiger.
Waving his wooden staff, he said:
"Patrons, there is no need to fight."
They immediately dispersed.
People all revered him,
and none dared show disrespect.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi" (Comprehensive Records of Court and Country).
Monk Xiē
In the early Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
in Jīngzhōu, there was a mad monk
named Xiē.
He was skilled at singing the song "Hémǎnzi".
Once he encountered a bailiff who was drunk,
who insulted him on the road,
ordering him to sing.
The monk immediately began to sing,
and the lyrics all revealed the bailiff's former hidden misdeeds.
The bailiff was shocked and felt remorse.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ" (Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng).
Master Āzú
Master Ā Zú,
no one knew where he came from.
His appearance was dull and coarse,
his demeanor not intelligent,
yet whenever he spoke,
nothing escaped his foreknowledge.
Though he had no fixed dwelling,
he often stayed in Wénxiāng.
People came and went in streams,
vying to pay respects and seek an audience.
He never cared to look at
the mountain-sized offerings of alms.
If someone was troubled or ill,
and obtained his guidance,
the results were miraculously swift.
At that time in Shǎnzhōu, there was a wealthy man named Zhāng Zhēn,
whose wealth amounted to tens of thousands,
but he had only one son.
The boy was about seventeen,
born foolish and dull-witted,
with crippled hands and feet,
and unable to speak intelligibly.
He only craved food and drink,
his mouth like a ravine.
His parents doted on him,
exerting all their efforts to care for him,
seeking doctors and medicines
from as far as a thousand lǐ away.
After more than ten years,
the family fortune was nearly exhausted.
Someone then said to him:
"Ā Zú is a sage,
a living Buddha in this world.
Why not seek him out
and hope for a cure?"
Zhēn and his wife
came to Wénxiāng,
kowtowing and wiping away tears,
begging for salvation.
After a long while, Ā Zú said to Zhēn:
"Your grievance has not yet dissipated;
it will take another ten years.
But out of pity for your diligence and devotion,
I will remove it for you."
He then instructed them to choose a day,
hold a vegetarian feast by the river,
widely summon a crowd,
and together witness the deliverance.
He also told them to bring their son
to the ceremony.
At the time, the crowd spoke of his supernatural powers,
and spectators stood like a wall.
As they craned their necks and stood on tiptoe,
Ā Zú pointed to three or four strong men,
who lifted and dragged the boy
and threw him into the river.
Zhēn and all those gathered
could not fathom his actions.
Ā Zú turned to Zhēn and said:
"I have removed your calamity."
After a while,
the son suddenly appeared more than ten paces downstream,
standing on the water's surface.
Pointing a finger at his parents, he said:
"The enmity between you and me
was due to karmic ties from past lives.
Fortunately, I encountered a sage,
who thus resolved it.
Had it not been so,
there would have been no end."
He straightened his body and cried out,
no longer foolish or dull-witted.
In a moment, he sank into the water,
and no one knew where he went.
From "Jíyì Jì"
Master Jiàn
In the early Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Féng from Chánglè,
whose family was in Wú.
Having passed the imperial examination, he was selected for an official post by the Ministry of Personnel,
but that year he was rejected by the authorities,
so he took up temporary residence in Cháng'ān.
There was an old monk named Jiàn,
who one day came to visit Féng,
saying to him:
"You share my surname."
Thus, they began to associate with each other,
for nearly a year.
When Féng was appointed as a sheriff in Dōngyuè,
and was preparing for his journey,
Master Jiàn came carrying his satchel,
to bid farewell.
Féng asked:
"Master, where are you going?"
Master Jiàn said:
"I once lived in the western wing of Língyán Temple for a long time,
and later traveled to Cháng'ān,
where it has been ten years now.
I was fortunate to meet you.
Now I am returning to my old home,
so I came to say goodbye.
Since you are going to Dōngyuè as sheriff,
your route will pass by Língyán Temple.
You should visit me there."
Féng promised:
"I will respectfully follow your instruction."
Several months later,
Féng set out from Cháng'ān to take up his post.
When he reached the gate of Língyán Temple,
he reined in his horse and gazed, saying:
"Isn't this the temple where Master Jiàn lived?"
He then entered and went to seek him.
At that time, a monk was in the courtyard.
Féng asked:
"I do not know where Master Jiàn's dwelling is;
I wish to visit him."
The monk said:
"Among our group of monks,
none is named Jiàn."
Féng began to feel suspicious and strange,
silently thinking to himself:
"Master Jiàn is a trustworthy man;
how could he deceive me?"
So he wandered alone through the temple courtyard,
until he reached the western wing.
Suddenly, he saw a group of portraits of monks,
one of whom looked exactly like Master Jiàn.
Féng exclaimed in great surprise:
"Master Jiàn is indeed an extraordinary man!
And he was able to appear to me in spirit."
He then wept with emotion for a long time.
Looking at the inscription, it read:
"A son of the Féng family,
a man of Wújùn.
At the age of ten,
he studied Buddhist teachings,
and became renowned for his virtuous conduct.
He died at the age of seventy-eight."
Féng read the inscription
and found it even more extraordinary.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
Cóng Jiàn
The Great Virtuous Monk Cóngjiàn of the Northern Chán Monastery at the Jìng'ài Temple in the Eastern Capital,
surnamed Zhāng,
was a native of Nányáng.
He moved to Guǎnglíng,
where his family became a local surname.
He stood eight feet tall,
with imposing and remarkable features.
Upon reaching the age of a mature man,
he suddenly attained profound enlightenment to the true principle,
and thus abandoned his wife and children to take the tonsure and become a monk.
Thereafter, he delved deeply into Chán meditation and contemplation,
his mind and state becoming clear and bright.
In less than ten years,
he was revered by elder monks and venerable virtuous ones,
all of whom praised and admired him.
When he came to Luòyáng,
he settled at the Jìng'ài Temple.
With both age and virtue accomplished,
he was revered by both Buddhist monks and Daoist priests.
Whenever he attended alms-offerings,
he would dine facing the Venerable Piṇḍola,
such was the reverence he received from humans and devas.
When Emperor Wǔzōng of the Táng dynasty succeeded to the throne,
he changed the era name to Huìchāng.
Fond of the rituals of riding phoenixes and harnessing cranes,
he held in low esteem the teachings that rely on ink and subdue dragons,
and thus issued orders to the commanderies and principalities,
to destroy pagodas and temples,
and to command Buddhist monks to return to lay life.
Monk Jiàn then donned a black hat and hemp clothes,
and secretly went to the country villa of Huángfǔ Mèi at the hot springs.
On the hill behind, tall trees grew densely together,
and a massive rock lay flat and smooth.
In the summer,
Monk Jiàn would often enter meditative stillness there,
or mend his monastic robes.
Suddenly one day,
dark clouds gathered and rain poured down fiercely,
with thunder striking a large sandalwood tree beside the rock.
As the rain arrived,
his fellow monks ran into the woods,
but Monk Jiàn sat calmly in lotus posture,
as if hearing nothing.
When the monks asked him about it,
he slowly replied:
"It was merely a vile beast."
By the beginning of the Dàzhōng era,
when Emperor Xuānzong restored Buddhism,
Monk Jiàn returned to his former residence in the Eastern Capital.
His son came from Guǎnglíng to visit him,
and happened to meet him at the monastery gate.
His dignified and stern appearance
made him unrecognizable.
The son then bowed and asked where the Great Virtuous Monk Cóngjiàn resided.
Monk Jiàn pointed and said:
"Near the eastern end."
After his son left,
he closed the gate and did not emerge.
His severing of the net of affection
(The original text had "gāng" instead of "wǎng";
amended according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy)
was also like this.
In the summer, the fifth month of the bǐngxū year of the Xiántōng era,
he suddenly visited all the families who held faith in him,
saying to each:
"Devote yourselves well to meritorious deeds.
This humble monk will journey far at the beginning of autumn,
hence I bid you farewell."
On the first day of the seventh month in autumn,
at dawn,
he washed his hands, burned incense,
and contemplated Maitreya Tathāgata.
Then he lay down on his right side.
Calling his disciples Xuánzhāng and others, he admonished them:
"Human life is difficult to obtain,
and the evil paths are easy to fall into.
Only by taking refuge in the Buddha
and diligently cultivating pure practices
can we meet again
at the assembly of the Dragon Flower.
Life has its limits;
I shall part from you briefly."
That day, without illness, he peacefully passed away,
at over eighty years of age.
Xuánzhāng and others, following his last wishes,
carried his body to the corpse-forest outside the Jiànchūn Gate,
offering it to birds and beasts.
After three days, they went to check:
his flesh and appearance remained as if alive,
and no creature dared approach.
They then covered him with cakes and pastries.
After a night,
there were tracks of wolves and foxes,
but only the cakes and pastries had been eaten,
while his full flesh remained intact.
They then cremated him according to the Indian method,
collected the remaining ashes,
and erected a white pagoda by the roadside,
where incense and offerings are made in spring and autumn.
From "Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú".
Lǐ Déyù
The Táng dynasty Chancellor Lǐ Déyù, while serving as Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent with duties in the Eastern Capital,
once summoned a monk
to inquire about his own fortune and misfortune.
The monk said:
"This cannot be known immediately.
I wish to set up an altar and arrange Buddha images."
The monk stayed within it
for three full days.
Then he said to the Duke:
"Your calamities are not yet over;
you must go ten thousand lǐ to the south."
The Duke was greatly angered
and rebuked him.
The next day,
he again summoned the monk to inquire,
worrying that what he had seen was not precise,
and requested him to observe again.
The monk then set up the altar for another three days
and told the Duke:
"The time for your journey south
is within a month.
It cannot be avoided."
The Duke became even more displeased
and said:
"If so, how can you, Master, prove that this is not false?"
The monk said:
"I wish to present a matter right before us as proof,
to show that I am not lying."
The Duke said:
"Indeed, you have something to say."
The monk then pointed to the ground and said:
"Below here is a stone casket;
please excavate it."
The Duke ordered the ground dug up several feet deep,
and indeed a stone casket was found.
Opening it, there was nothing inside.
The Duke, astonished, began to believe him somewhat,
and asked:
"Is it truly unavoidable that I go south?
But will I then never return?"
The monk said:
"You will return."
The Duke inquired about the reason,
and the monk replied:
"In your lifetime, Chancellor, you are destined to eat ten thousand sheep.
Now you have eaten nine thousand five hundred.
The reason you will return
is that you have not yet finished the remaining five hundred sheep."
The Duke, distressed, sighed and said:
"Master, you are indeed a transcendent being.
Moreover, in the thirteenth year of the Yuánhé era,
when I served as an assistant to Chancellor Zhāng at the Northern Capital,
I once dreamed of walking in the Jìn mountains,
seeing the mountains covered entirely with sheep,
with over ten shepherds
who came forward and bowed to me.
I then asked the shepherds,
and they said:
'These are the sheep you will eat in your lifetime, Your Honor.'
I have always remembered this dream,
but never revealed it to anyone.
Now it indeed matches what you, Master, have said.
Thus I know that the workings of hidden virtue are truly not false."
Ten days later,
Mǐ Jì, the military governor of Zhènwǔ, sent an envoy with a letter to the Duke,
and also presented five hundred sheep.
The Duke was greatly startled
and immediately summoned the monk to tell him of this.
The monk sighed and said:
"The ten thousand sheep will soon be complete;
I fear you will not return, Duke!"
The Duke said:
"If I do not eat them,
can I still avoid it?"
The monk said:
"Now that the sheep have arrived here,
they are already considered yours, Chancellor."
The Duke was sorrowful.
Ten days later,
he was demoted to Military Advisor of Cháozhōu,
and further demoted to Registrar of Yázhōu.
In the end, he died in the remote borderlands.
From "Xuānshì Zhì".
Monk of Qízhōu
When Shǐ Lùn was in Qízhōu,
he went hunting and reached the boundary of a county.
Resting in a Buddhist temple,
he noticed an extraordinary fragrance of peaches.
He inquired with the monk there.
The monk could not hide it in time.
He said that recently someone
had donated two peaches,
so he took them out from under the sutra table
and offered them to Lùn.
They were as large as rice bowls.
Lùn was hungry at the time,
so he ate them both.
The pits were as big as chicken eggs.
Lùn then asked where they came from.
The monk laughed and said:
"I actually lied earlier.
These peaches are over ten lǐ from here,
and the path is dangerous.
This humble monk happened to see them while traveling on foot,
found them unusual,
and picked a few."
Lùn said:
"I wish to leave my attendants and horses behind
and go with the venerable monk."
The monk had no choice,
and led Lùn through the wild undergrowth.
After about five lǐ,
they reached a river.
The monk said:
"I fear the Vice Censor-in-Chief cannot cross this."
Lùn was determined to go,
so following the monk's example, he removed his clothes
and floated across carrying them.
Upon reaching the shore,
they traveled northwest again,
crossed two more rivers,
climbed mountains and traversed ravines,
and after several lǐ arrived at a place.
With marvelous springs and strange rocks,
it was no ordinary human realm.
There were several hundred peach trees,
their branches sweeping the ground,
standing only two or three chǐ tall,
their fragrance overwhelming the nose.
Lùn and the monk each ate one fruit,
and their stomachs were full.
Lùn removed his clothes,
intending to wrap up as many as he could.
The monk said:
"This is a spiritual realm;
one must not take too much.
This humble monk often heard the elders say:
'In the past, someone also came here,
tucked away five or six fruits,
and got lost, unable to find his way out!'" Lùn also suspected the monk
("Monk" originally written as "student,"
changed according to the Ming dynasty manuscript copy)
was no ordinary person,
so he took only two peaches and returned.
The monk sternly warned Lùn not to speak of it.
When Lùn reached the prefecture,
he sent for the monk,
but the monk had already vanished.
From Yǒuyáng Zázǔ.
Master Bào Yù
Master Bào Yù was renowned for his virtuous conduct.
Residing in Cháng'ān,
those who took him as master and served him numbered in the thousands.
Every evening he stayed alone in a room,
closing the door and extinguishing the candles.
Once a monk peeked through a crack in the door
and saw auspicious clouds emanating from his mouth.
Later, at the age of ninety, he passed away.
It was during the height of summer,
yet his corpse showed no signs of decay.
The Táng dynasty chancellor Dìwǔ Qí was on good terms with the master.
Upon his death,
Qí came to handle the funeral arrangements.
When he was about to pour fragrant milk into the master's mouth,
auspicious light suddenly shone forth from his mouth,
brilliantly illuminating all around.
Lord Qí found this most extraordinary.
Some said:
"The Buddha possesses auspicious light;
now Master Bào Yù has it too.
He is truly a Buddha."
From Xuānshì Zhì.
Master Shù Cǎo
At the Bodhi Temple in Píngkāng Ward of Cháng'ān,
there was formerly a monk
who did not reveal his name.
He often carried a bundle of straw,
sitting or lying under the western corridor of the temple.
He refused to stay in a monastic cell,
and this went on for several years.
The temple overseer once urged him to take a room.
He said:
"Do you dislike me?"
That evening,
he used the bundle of straw to burn himself.
By dawn,
only ashes remained,
with no smell of blood or fat.
Only then did everyone realize he was an extraordinary person.
They molded his ashes into the form of a monk and placed it in the Buddha hall.
The world called him Master Shù Cǎo.
From Yǒuyáng Zázǔ.
Huì Kuān
Huì Kuān, a monk of Jìnghuì Temple in Miánzhōu,
when he was six years old,
followed his father in setting up a Huánglù vegetarian feast.
Everyone bowed to the stone statue of the Heavenly Lord.
Huì Kuān was present
but refused to bow,
saying:
"If I bow, the stone statue will fall over,
and it will be unbearable."
After the bowing, the Heavenly Lord statue indeed fell,
its waist broken.
Later, he left home and became a monk at the temple.
The temple was near a pond,
and many people made their living by catching fish.
Huì Kuān administered precepts to them
and said:
"You should not rely on this for sustenance.
I can ensure your gains
remain no less than before."
He then pointed to the pond's edge,
where mushrooms sprouted abundantly.
The fishermen gathered them,
saving effort and gaining profit.
Later people called them "monk's mushrooms."
From Chéngdū Jì.
Monk Sù
In the courtyard of Monk Sù's cloister at Xìngshàn Temple in Cháng'ān,
there were several green paulownia trees, all planted by Sù himself.
During the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
many ministers and high officials frequented this cloister.
In summer, the paulownias exuded a sap
that stained people's clothes like grease,
and it could not be washed out.
Minister Zhèng of Zhāoguó,
once seeking refuge from the heat with several vice ministers,
disliked the sap
and said to Sù:
"Disciple will cut down these paulownias for the venerable monk
and plant pine trees instead."
By evening,
Sù playfully prayed to the trees, saying:
"I have planted you for over twenty years.
You are disliked for your sap.
If you still have sap next year,
I will surely use you as firewood."
From then on, there was no more sap.
Monk Sù never left the cloister
and recited the Lotus Sutra thirty-seven thousand times.
At night, wolf cubs often came to listen to the sutra chanting.
During meal offerings,
crows and magpies would approach the table
(In the continuation of Yǒuyáng Zázǔ, volume five, "table" is written as "palm")
to take food.
In the early Chángqìng era,
a monk named Xuán Yōu inscribed a poem on this cloister:
"Thirty thousand Lotus Sutras over thirty springs,
half a lifetime without treading the dust beyond the gate."
It was considered an excellent couplet at the time.
From Yǒuyáng Zázǔ.
Huái Xìn
The Western Spirit Pagoda in Yángzhōu
was among the most towering structures in the Central Plains.
Toward the end of Emperor Wǔzōng's reign in the Táng dynasty,
one year before the temples were dismantled,
a poet from Huáinán named Liú Yǐnzhī was traveling lightly in Míngzhōu.
In a dream, it was as if he was sailing on the sea
and saw the pagoda crossing the sea eastward.
At that moment, he saw the gate monk Huái Xìn residing on the third level of the pagoda,
leaning on the railing and speaking to Yǐnzhī:
"I am temporarily escorting the pagoda across the Eastern Sea;
I will return in ten days."
Several days later,
Yǐnzhī returned to Yángzhōu
and immediately went to visit Huái Xìn.
Huái Xìn said:
"Do you remember our meeting at sea?"
Yǐnzhī suddenly remembered clearly.
A few nights later,
heavenly fire burned the pagoda completely to ashes.
White rain poured down like a waterfall,
but a nearby thatched hut
remained entirely undamaged.
From Dúyì Zhì.
Fótuó Sà
There was a man named Fótuó Sà,
who was registered at Fǎmén Temple in Qíyáng.
He claimed the surname Fó,
with Tuó Sà being his given name.
He often traveled alone between Qízhōu and Lǒngzhōu,
wearing yellow robes and carrying a monk’s staff.
Though old in years,
he looked like a child or simpleton.
He liked to shout loudly in the streets,
and sometimes reviled and insulted the other monks.
The monks were all angry with him.
As for his food, clothing, and supplies,
he begged for everything from the villagers.
The villagers pitied his simplicity,
and generously gave him food and clothing.
Thus, his resources were actually more abundant than those of the other monks.
Tuó Sà, in turn, distributed them among the poor and hungry in the village,
so the villagers pitied his heart even more.
In the sixth month of summer, in the fifth year of the Kāichéng era,
Tuó Sà summoned the villagers and announced:
"I will die this evening.
You must build a stūpa and bury my corpse."
Indeed, he sat upright and passed away.
Thereupon, the people of the village
built a stūpa on the western ridge of Qíyáng,
lacquered his corpse, and buried it.
Over a month later,
someone looked at his head
and saw his hair had grown about an inch long.
His disciples immediately shaved it off.
But it grew back again.
The villagers found this extremely strange,
so they sealed the door,
and never opened it again.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
The Abbot of Xīngyuán
West of Xīngyuán County there was a temple.
The abbot often drank wine and ate meat,
and the others all followed his example.
One day, he made many large pancakes,
summoned the assembly of disciples,
and entered the charnel ground.
He wrapped putrid corpse flesh in the pancakes and ate it,
devouring it repeatedly without stopping.
The other monks covered their noses and fled.
The abbot said:
"Only if you can eat this meat
may you eat other meats."
From then on, the monks in black robes thus achieved diligence.
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì"
Zhào Fān
Zhào Fān, Chancellor of the National University in the Tang dynasty,
served as a Lang official in the Southern Palace in the seventh year of the Tàihé era.
Suddenly, one day,
a monk came begging for food at his gate and said
to his servant:
"I wish to see Lord Zhào.
Is that possible?"
The servant informed Zhào Fān,
who then ordered him to invite the monk in and seat him.
The monk then said:
"You are about to face misfortune,
but it can also be averted."
Zhào Fān immediately bowed and begged him.
The monk said:
"Give me fifteen hundred tailor's knives, and perhaps I can free you from this calamity.
Otherwise,
within ten days,
you will become a prefect in the southeast."
Zhào Fān agreed,
promising to deliver them the next day,
and inquired his name and residence.
The monk said:
"I reside at Qīnglóng Temple;
my name is Fǎ'ān."
Having spoken, he left.
The next day,
Zhào Fān prepared and sent the knives.
When the messenger arrived at the temple,
he searched among the monks by description,
but none resembled him.
He asked where Master Fǎ'ān stayed,
searched all the courtyards and buildings,
but found no trace or shadow of him.
A few days later,
Zhào Fān was sent out to serve as Prefect of Yuánzhōu.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
Huái Jùn
In Zǐguī Commandery, there was a monk skilled in cursive script named Huái Jùn.
No one knew where he was from.
He arrived there around the beginning of the Qiánníng era of the Tang dynasty.
He knew the future and remembered the past,
all with divine accuracy.
He loved cursive script;
whether Confucian classics, Buddhist sutras, Daoist texts,
or even vulgar songs and trivial words,
all flowed from his brush.
If you spoke to him,
he would only reply "Ah, yes,"
so the locals treated him as a holy being.
The Prefect Yú, considering him a public deluder,
had him arrested and interrogated.
He then presented a poem in lieu of a statement:
"My home lies west and west of Mǐnchuān's streams,
Where orioles sing year after year, or so it seems.
Now I am not where orioles sing their lay,
The orioles sing where they sang in yesterday."
Interrogated again,
he offered another poem:
"My home lies east and east of Mǐnchuān's shore,
Where red flowers bloom year after year, and more.
Now I am not where the red flowers grow,
The flowers bloom red where they reddened long ago."
The Commandery Governor, amazed, released him.
Considering the meaning of his poems,
it seemed he was from across the sea.
Could he be of the same ilk as Bēidù?
Travelers passing by
would always moor their boats to pay respects,
seeking omens of fortune or misfortune.
He would only write three or five lines,
never speaking plainly,
yet events later proved him true.
When the senior officer of Jīngnán, Zhōu Chóngbīn, visited him,
he wrote characters for him, saying:
"Submit to the capital for investigation."
Later, when Zhōu went to present tribute,
due to the imperial army's southern campaign,
he was detained in the southern prefecture
and was eventually executed.
When the sheriff Sūn Dàonéng visited him,
he wrote characters:
"Submit to Zhúlín Temple."
That year, Sūn died,
and when they prepared his burial, it was on the old foundation of Ancient Zhúlín Temple.
When Huángfǔ Xuán governed the prefecture,
the monk drew a picture of a man bearing a cangue,
with a woman beside him.
Later, Huángfǔ married a commoner's daughter, faced a lawsuit,
and was imprisoned in the prefectural office.
A Persian named Mù Zhāosì loved medicine and techniques from childhood.
He visited the monk with his father,
and the monk drew a Daoist riding clouds and holding a gourd,
writing:
"Commander-in-Chief's official dispatch appoints as yátuī."
Later, Mù excelled in medicine,
and the Prince of Nánpíng, Gāo Cónghuì, gave him a headscarf
and appointed him as a yátuī in the prefectural office.
When the imperial army attacked Jīngzhōu,
the master sent a poem to the Prince of Nánpíng:
"Horse heads gradually enter Yángzhōu's way.
Kinsmen should wash their eyes to see this day."
That year, they pledged allegiance to the Huáihǎi region,
and the heavy siege was lifted.
Other such instances are too numerous to record.
One day,
he wrote on a banana leaf in the courtyard:
"Today I repay my debt.
Fortunately, the prefecture and county will investigate no more."
The next day, he was killed by someone.
His corpse remained intact.
Prefect Gāo had him cremated.
From "Běimèng Suǒyán"
The Wise Chán Master
In Shānyīn County, Yuèzhōu, during the Tang dynasty, there was a wise Chán master.
Within the temple grounds was a pond,
where he would always redeem living creatures and release them.
There was an alligator,
three feet long,
that constantly ate the fish.
The Chán master was troubled by this,
so he caught the alligator and released it into the pond before Yǔwáng Temple.
By night, it returned.
The Chán master said to it:
"If you do not eat my fish,
then you may stay here."
The alligator then went outside and excreted,
all of it being blue mud.
Whenever the Chán master came to the pond,
he would call the alligator, and it would emerge,
lying prostrate before the master.
After several decades,
it gradually grew to seven or eight feet long.
After the Chán master passed away,
the alligator was never seen again.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Fǎ Běn
During the Tiānfú era of the Jìn dynasty,
Zhào Zhū, an Attendant Gentleman of the Bureau of Merit Evaluation, said:
"Recently, a monk came from Xiàngzhōu.
He said:
'This humble monk spent the summer retreat together with a monk named Fǎběn in a Chán monastery in Xiāngzhōu.
We were together morning and night,
and our minds were in harmony.
Fǎběn often said:
"This humble monk is the abbot of Zhúlín Temple in the western mountains of Xiàngzhōu.
There is a stone pillar in front of the temple.
If you have leisure another day,
I must request that you visit."'
That monk, recalling these words,
therefore went there to seek him out.
Upon reaching a village at the mountain's foot,
he sought lodging at a local temple.
He asked the village monks
how far it was from there to Zhúlín Temple.
A monk then pointed to the side of a solitary peak in the distance and said:
'That place is it.
According to ancient tradition,
it was a place where sages and worthies once dwelled.
Now, only the name remains;
therefore, there are no monastery buildings.'
The monk was skeptical.
At dawn the next day, he went there.
When he reached the bamboo grove,
there indeed was a stone pillar,
but he saw no trace of its boundaries.
He remembered that when Fǎběn was parting, he had said:
'Just knock on the pillar,
and you will see the person.'
The monk then tapped the pillar several times with a small staff.
Suddenly, wind and rain arose on all sides,
and he could not see even a foot in front of him.
In an instant, his eyes and ears cleared,
and he saw towers and pavilions standing opposite each other,
with his body beneath the monastery gate.
After a short while,
Fǎběn came out from within.
Seeing him, he was very pleased
and asked about old matters from the southern regions.
He then led the monk,
passing through heavy gates,
ascending to a secret hall,
to pay respects to his venerable elder.
The venerable elder asked the reason,
and Fǎběn said:
'In earlier years, we spent the summer together in Xiàngzhōu,
and he promised to visit here,
so he has reached our monastery gate.'
The venerable elder said:
'After the meal, please see him out;
there is no seat for him here.'
After eating, Fǎběn escorted him to the monastery gate to bid farewell.
Immediately, heaven and earth turned dark,
and he did not know which way to go.
After a moment,
he found himself back beside the stone pillar in the bamboo grove,
with everything else vanished without a trace.
From this, one knows that the presence of sages and worthies in the world,
their concealment and manifestation, is difficult to fathom.
How could it be that only a Buddha like Jīnsù Rúlái is capable of such transformative appearances?"
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà".
Monk Huìxiáng
In the beginning of the Yìxī era of the Eastern Jìn dynasty,
Huìxiáng, a monk of Chánggān Temple in Jīnlíng, lived in adjacent halls with Fǎxiàng.
In the fourth watch of the night,
Huìxiáng called out from a distance for Fǎxiàng to come briefly.
Fǎxiàng went to see Huìxiáng.
Huìxiáng was lying on his back,
with his hands crossed over his
"chest" (original text had "head",
changed according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy)
chest.
He said:
'Please untie the ropes on my hands and feet.'
Fǎxiàng said:
'There are no ropes at all.'
Huìxiáng was then able to move.
He said:
'Just now, a crowd of people bound my hands and feet
and whipped me repeatedly,
asking why I bite lice.
They also said to me:
"If you do not stop,
we will put you between two mountains to crush you."'
From then on, Huìxiáng refrained from biting lice."
From "Sānjiào Zhūyīng".
The Statue of King Aśoka
In Chángshā Temple, there was a statue of King Aśoka,
traditionally said to have been made by King Aśoka's daughter.
During the Tàiyuán era,
it floated at night to a river crossing.
Fishermen saw a strange light as bright as day,
and though monks from various temples came with a thousand men to welcome it,
it stood firm and unmoving.
There was a Dharma Master Yì of Chángshā Temple,
whose conduct was pure and austere.
He led ten monks
and prayed with utmost sincerity,
whereupon it immediately allowed itself to be placed on a carriage.
Towards the end of the Qí dynasty,
the statue often walked at night.
Those unaware would stab it with a lance,
and it would make a metallic sound and fall over.
Whenever major events or disasters occurred in the Southern Dynasties,
it would necessarily sweat profusely for several days beforehand.
Since the teaching of images began,
this was the most spiritually responsive."
From "Zhǔgōng Yíshì".
Wáng Huáizhī
Wáng Huáizhī of the Sòng dynasty, styled Yuánzēng,
was from Lángyá.
His family for generations esteemed Confucian learning
and did not believe in the Buddhist teachings.
He often said that both body and spirit perish;
how could there be three existences?
During the Yuánjiā era,
he served as Magistrate of Dānyáng.
In the tenth year,
he fell ill and stopped breathing,
but after a short while, he briefly revived.
At that time, Hè Dàolì, the Magistrate of Jiànkāng, came to inquire about his illness,
just as he was about to pass away.
Huáizhī said to Dàolì:
'Now I know the Buddhist teaching is not false.
When a person dies, the spirit remains;
there is indeed evidence for this.'
Dàolì said:
'Your Honor, throughout your life, your arguments were not like this;
what have you seen now that makes you change?'
Huáizhī, knitting his brows, replied:
'The spirit truly does not perish;
one cannot but believe in Buddhism.'
With these words, he died."
From "Míngxiáng Jì".
During the Northern Wei Dynasty,
at the Chóngzhēn Temple in Luòyáng, there was a monk named Huìníng who died and returned to life after seven days.
He said:
"King Yánluó examined the records,
and released me due to a mistaken name."
Huìníng recounted in detail the events he had witnessed,
involving five other monks who were examined together.
One monk was Zhìshèng from Bǎomíng Temple,
who, through seated meditation and ascetic practices,
ascended to heaven.
Another monk was Dàopǐn from Bōrě Temple,
who recited the Nirvana Sutra in forty scrolls
and also ascended to heaven.
One monk was Tánmózuì from Róngjué Temple,
who lectured on the Nirvana and Huáyán sutras,
leading an assembly of a thousand followers.
King Yánluó said:
"Those who lecture on sutras
harbor thoughts of self and others,
acting arrogantly and oppressing others.
This is the coarsest conduct among monks.
Now we only test seated meditation and sutra recitation;
we do not inquire about lecturing on sutras."
Tánmózuì replied:
"Since I devoted myself to the Way,
I have only enjoyed lecturing on sutras;
I truly am not skilled in recitation."
King Yánluó ordered him handed over to the officials.
Immediately, ten attendants in black
escorted Tánmózuì toward the northwest gate.
The buildings there were all dark,
seemingly not a good place.
One monk was Dàohóng from Chánlín Temple,
who said of himself:
"I have taught the four groups of lay devotees,
and commissioned ten statues of human figures for all the sutras."
King Yánluó said:
"The essence of a monk
must be to restrain the mind and uphold the Way,
focusing on meditation and recitation.
One should not interfere in worldly affairs
nor engage in purposeful actions.
Although you commissioned sutras and statues,
your true intention was to obtain others' wealth.
Once you obtained wealth,
greed arose in your heart
(Míng manuscript and Chén edition have "arose immediately" for "arose"),
and below there are also the four characters "since greed filled the heart"
Thus, the three poisons remain unextinguished,
and afflictions are fully present."
He too was handed over to the officials,
and entered the black gate together with Tánmózuì.
One monk was Bǎomíng from Língjué Temple,
who said of himself:
"Before leaving home,
I often
("often" originally written as "emperor,"
corrected according to the Míng manuscript and Chén edition
) served as the governor of Lǒngxī.
After completing the construction of Língjué Temple,
I abandoned my official post to enter the monastic life.
Although I do not meditate or recite sutras,
I never neglect worship."
King Yánluó said:
"When you served as governor,
you perverted justice and twisted the law,
plundering the people's wealth.
You used that to build this temple—
it was not by your own efforts,
so why bother mentioning it?"
He too was handed over to the attendants and sent into the black gate.
When Empress Dowager Wei heard of this,
she dispatched the Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Xú Hé, to visit Bǎomíng and other temples as described by Huìníng.
In the east of the city was Bǎomíng Temple; in the city center was Bōrě Temple; in the west were three temples: Róngjué, Chánlín, and Língjué.
Upon inquiry, Zhìshèng, Dàopǐn, Tánmózuì, Dàohóng, and Bǎomíng
all indeed existed.
She then invited one hundred meditation monks
to be constantly supported in the palace halls.
An edict was issued prohibiting the carrying of sutras and statues to beg on streets and roads.
However, those who used their own wealth to commission sutras and statues were free to do so.
Huìníng also entered Báilù Mountain,
living in seclusion to cultivate the Way.
From then on,
monks in the capital all devoted themselves to meditation and recitation,
no longer focusing on lecturing sutras.
From "Records of Luòyáng"
Língyǐn Temple
In the early years of the Northern Qí,
there was a monk named Bǎo Gōng,
a lofty recluse of Sōng Mountain.
Once, while traveling from Línlǜ toward Báilù Mountain,
he lost his way.
As the sun approached mid-morning,
he suddenly heard the sound of a bell.
Following the direction of the sound,
he passed through layers of rugged cliffs,
climbing and hurrying along,
until he saw a temple.
It stood alone amidst deep forests,
its mountain gate facing due south,
resplendent and radiant.
Approaching the gate,
he saw the plaque: Língyǐn Temple.
Outside the gate were five or six dogs,
each as large as an ox,
with white fur and black muzzles,
some leaping, some lying down,
their eyes fixed on Bǎo.
Terrified, Bǎo was about to turn back
when, moments later,
he saw a foreign monk arriving from outside.
Bǎo called out, but the monk did not respond,
nor did he glance at him,
proceeding directly inside the gate.
The dogs followed him.
After a long while,
Bǎo saw people gradually entering the gate.
The buildings surrounded the courtyard,
with doors and rooms all closed.
Proceeding to the lecture hall,
he saw only mats, couches, and a high seat arranged solemnly.
Bǎo entered and sat on a mat in the southwestern corner.
After a long time,
he suddenly heard sounds from the eastern chamber.
Looking up,
he saw an opening like a well appear.
Monks flew down through the opening one after another,
until there were fifty or sixty of them.
They took their seats and begged,
asking each other,
"For today's meal offering,
where have you come from to eat?"
Some mentioned Yùzhāng, Chéngdū, Cháng'ān, Lǒngyòu, Jìběi, Lǐngnán, the Five Regions of India, etc.,
leaving no place unvisited,
traveling tens of thousands of miles in an instant.
Finally, one monk descended from the sky.
The others eagerly asked:
"Why are you so late?"
He replied:
"Today, at the lecture assembly of Master Jiàn at Bǐ'àn Temple east of Xiàngzhōu City,
each presented their interpretations.
There was a young man, intelligent and talented,
whose challenging questions arose sharply like blades,
truly remarkable to behold.
Unconsciously, it grew late."
Bǎo had formerly taken Jiàn as his master,
and upon hearing this,
hoped to join the conversation.
So he straightened his robes and stood up,
addressing the monks:
"Jiàn is my master."
The monks stared directly at Bǎo.
Moments later,
Língyǐn Temple had vanished.
Bǎo found himself sitting alone on an oak tree,
seeing nothing at all,
only cliffs and valleys.
Birds gathered and flew about noisily.
Upon leaving the mountain,
he asked Master Shàngtǒng about it.
The master said:
"This temple was built by Master Fótúchéng during the Later Zhào dynasty.
It is ancient and distant in years;
sages and worthies dwell there—it is not a place for ordinary beings. It may sink or hide, shifting without fixed location.
Even now, travelers in the mountains
still hear the bell ringing."
From "Hóu Jūnsù's Records of Marvels"
Hóu Qìng
Hóu Qìng, a man from Nányáng during the Sòng dynasty, owned a bronze statue about a foot tall.
He had an ox
that he intended to sell to gild the statue.
But encountering urgent matters,
he used the ox for other purposes.
After two years,
his wife, Mǎ Shì, suddenly dreamed that the statue said to her:
"You and your husband owe me gilding,
long unpaid.
Now I take your son, Chǒuduō,
to compensate for the gilding."
Mǎ Shì awoke feeling uneasy.
By dawn,
Chǒuduō fell ill and died.
Hóu Qìng was over fifty years old
and had only this one son.
The sounds of his grief
moved passersby.
On the day Chǒuduō died,
the statue suddenly acquired gilding on its own,
radiating light in all four directions.
Within the neighborhood,
all smelled a fragrant aroma.
Monastics and laypeople, old and young,
all came to witness it.
From "Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma"
The Traveling Monk of the Daye Era
During the Dayè era of the Suí dynasty,
a traveling monk arrived at the Tài Shān temple and requested lodging.
The temple keeper said:
"There are no other quarters here,
only the corridor of the temple shrine can be used for lodging,
but those who come to lodge here always die."
The monk said:
"That is no hardship."
Having no choice, the keeper complied,
and prepared a bed for him in the corridor.
When night fell,
the monk sat upright and recited scriptures.
Around the first watch,
he heard the sound of jade pendants from within the room.
Shortly after, the deity emerged,
and bowed in reverence to the monk.
The monk said:
"I have heard that many who lodge here die;
could it be that you, the patron, harm them?
I hope you will protect me."
The deity said:
"When those destined to die arrive,
upon hearing your disciple's voice,
they die of fear themselves;
it is not that I kill them.
Please, Master, have no worries."
The monk then invited him to sit and converse.
After about the time it takes to eat a meal,
he asked the deity:
"I have heard people say in legends:
'Tài Shān governs the ghosts;
is this truly so?'" The deity said:
"Your disciple, due to meager blessings, does have this duty.
Do you perhaps wish to see the deceased?"
The monk said:
"There were two fellow student monks who died earlier;
I wish to see them."
The deity asked their names,
then said:
"One has already been reborn in the human world;
the other is in hell, his sins heavy,
and cannot be summoned here.
Master, you may go to see him."
The monk was very pleased to hear this,
and rose to go out.
Not far, they arrived at a place,
where they saw the flames of hell burning fiercely.
The deity led the monk into a courtyard,
and from afar they saw a person
crying out amidst the flames,
unable to speak,
his form altered beyond recognition,
his flesh and blood scorched and foul-smelling,
a sight that saddened the heart.
The master did not wish to look further,
and compassionately asked to leave.
Soon they returned to the temple,
and sat again with the deity.
He then asked:
"If I wish to save my fellow student,
is there a way to achieve it?"
The deity said:
"Yes,
if someone can copy the Lotus Sutra for him,
he should then be freed."
As dawn approached,
the deity bid farewell to the monk and entered the hall.
In the morning, the temple keeper saw the monk was not dead,
and found it strange.
The monk then explained what happened.
He immediately copied one volume of the Lotus Sutra.
When the sutra was completed,
and the adornments finished,
he again took the sutra to lodge at the temple.
That night, the deity emerged as before,
joyfully bowing in reverence,
and inquired about his purpose in coming.
The monk told him the matter.
The deity said:
"Your disciple knows of it.
When Master copied the sutra,
as soon as the title was written,
he was already freed,
and has now been reborn in the human world.
However, this place is unclean,
and not fit to house the sutra.
I ask Master to take it back and deliver it to the temple."
They conversed for a long time,
and as dawn neared,
the deity bid farewell and departed.
From "Records of Hidden Retribution."
Clam Image
The Suí emperor was fond of clams,
and his meals always included clam flavor,
consuming over tens of millions.
Suddenly, there was one clam
that, when struck open as usual,
the emperor found strange,
and placed it on a table.
During the second watch, it emitted light,
and by dawn,
the flesh had fallen away on its own,
revealing inside an image of one Buddha and two Bodhisattvas.
The emperor grieved and repented,
vowing never to eat clams again.
From "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng."
Another account says,
Emperor Wénzōng of the Táng dynasty enjoyed eating clams.
One day,
his attendants brought a full plate,
among which was one that would not split open
originally lacked the character "not,"
added according to Chén's collation
when pried.
Wénzōng, suspecting it was unusual,
immediately burned incense and prayed to it.
Shortly after,
the clam opened on its own,
revealing inside two figures,
with dignified and elegant appearances,
fully formed bodies,
coiled hair knots and jeweled necklaces,
feet treading on lotus flowers,
called Bodhisattvas.
Wénzōng then placed it in a sandalwood box with gold and millet,
covered it with jade dust,
bestowed it upon Xìngshàn Temple,
and ordered it to be reverenced.
By the Huìchāng era,
during the destruction of Buddhist images,
it was no longer known where it went.
From "Dūyáng Miscellany."
Guāngmíng Temple
In Luòyáng's Yíshòu Lane, there was the residence of Duàn Huī, magistrate of Bāoxìn County.
From underground, the sound of a bell was often heard,
and sometimes five-colored light was seen,
illuminating the hall.
Huī found this very strange,
so he dug the ground,
and unearthed a golden statue,
about three feet tall,
along with two Bodhisattvas.
On the pedestal was an inscription:
"Made by Xún Xù, Palace Attendant and Supervisor of the Secretariat, on the fifteenth day of the fifth month of the second year of Tàishǐ of Jìn."
Huī then donated his residence to establish Guāngmíng Temple.
It was widely said
this was the former residence of Xún Xù.
Later, thieves tried to steal this statue,
but the statue and the Bodhisattvas
together shouted "Thief!"
The thieves were terrified,
and immediately fell down dead.
The monks, hearing the statue's cry,
captured them.
From "Records of Luòyáng's Buddhist Temples."
Ten Lights Buddha
In the northwest corner of Xìngfú Temple was a Suí dynasty Buddha hall,
on whose wall was painted the Ten Lights Buddha,
the brushwork extremely exquisite,
considered the finest in the land.
Those with knowledge said
this was the work of the national master painter, Cài Shēng.
Cài Shēng was renowned in the Suí dynasty for his skill in painting.
When the hall was first completed,
a monk offered a hundred pieces of gold to recruit a skilled painter,
and obtained Cài Shēng.
After painting,
he said to people:
"I have painted many works in my life,
but only today, as I wielded the brush,
it was as if ghosts and spirits assisted in its completion."
Thus, his fame spread throughout Cháng'ān.
In the early Zhēnguàn era,
the temple monks, considering this hall somewhat old,
feared it might collapse one day,
so they summoned several craftsmen,
gathered materials and funds,
and intended to renew its construction.
Suddenly one day,
the monks were having a meal in the temple courtyard.
After they sat down,
ten monks appeared,
all fair-skinned and slender,
with very ancient appearances,
arriving one after another,
and took seats at the table.
After eating, they rose together,
entered the Buddha hall,
and the other monks followed behind them.
Shortly after, the ten suddenly vanished without a trace,
and the monks looked at each other in astonishment for a long time.
Then, looking at the Ten Lights Buddha on the north wall,
they saw its demeanor
indeed matched that of the ten men from before.
From then on, the monks dared not destroy the hall,
and used this to honor the manifestation of the Ten Lights.
From "Records of the Xuānshì Chamber."
Lǐ Dà'ān
During the Táng dynasty, there was a man named Lǐ Dà'ān from Lǒngxī.
He was the elder brother of the Minister of Works, Lǐ Dàliàng.
During the Wǔdé era,
Dàliàng served as the Commander-in-Chief of Yuèzhōu,
and Dà'ān traveled from the capital to visit him.
Dàliàng sent several servants and maids to accompany his brother on the return journey.
When they reached Lùqiáo in Gǔzhōu,
they lodged at an inn.
Among the servants was one who plotted to murder Dà'ān.
He waited until Dà'ān was sound asleep,
and in the middle of the night,
he stabbed Dà'ān in the neck with a small sword,
piercing it through.
The blade lodged in the bedhead.
The servant then fled without pulling out the sword.
Dà'ān awoke in shock,
calling for his servants.
The loyal servants and maids wanted to pull out the blade,
but Dà'ān said:
"If you pull it out, I will die immediately.
First, fetch me paper and brush to write a letter."
After finishing the letter,
the local officials also arrived.
They then pulled out the blade,
cleaned the wound, and applied medicine.
Dà'ān then lost consciousness.
Suddenly, it was as if he were dreaming,
and he saw an object over a foot long.
It was four or five inches wide and thick,
shaped like a piece of pork,
and floated about two feet above the ground.
It entered through the door,
came before the bedhead,
and a voice from within it said:
"Quickly return my pork."
Dà'ān replied:
"I do not eat pork.
Why would I owe you any?"
Then, a voice from outside the door said:
"Wrong."
The object immediately turned and exited through the door.
Dà'ān then saw a pond in the courtyard,
clear, shallow, and lovely.
On the western bank of the pond,
there was a golden statue,
about five inches tall.
In a moment, it gradually grew larger,
and soon transformed into a monk,
wearing a very new and clean kasaya.
He said to Dà'ān:
"You are wounded.
I will now take away your pain for you,
and you shall recover.
Return home and chant the Buddha's name and cultivate goodness."
He then stroked Dà'ān's neck wound with his hand and left.
Dà'ān observed his appearance
and saw that the monk's kasaya had a patch of red silk,
about an inch square,
very distinct.
Soon after, Dà'ān awoke
and regained consciousness.
His wound no longer hurt,
and he could sit up and eat.
After several tens of days,
he was welcomed home by the young men of his household in the capital.
Family members and old acquaintances came to see him,
and Dà'ān recounted the circumstances of his injury and what he had seen of the statue.
A maid who was listening nearby
then said that when Dà'ān first set out on his journey,
his wife had instructed her to hire a craftsman to make a Buddha statue.
When it was first completed,
they painted its robes with colors,
and a drop of cinnabar stained the back of the statue.
They had asked the craftsman to remove it,
but he refused,
so it remained there to this day,
exactly as the young master had described.
Dà'ān then went with his wife and family to look at the statue.
It was indeed identical to what he had seen.
The cinnabar dot on its back
was precisely where the patch had been.
They were all amazed and sighed in wonder,
believing truly that the holy teachings are not false,
and thus their reverence and faith increased.
From "Míngbào Jì".
Wéi Zhīshí
During the Yǒnghuī era of the Táng dynasty, Wéi Zhīshí, a Military Officer of the Right Imperial Guard from Jīngzhào, was boiling a sheep's foot.
Even after half a day, it remained raw.
Zhīshí was angry.
His family said:
"We used ten times the usual amount of firewood,
we don't know why it's like this."
Zhīshí ordered it to be boiled again,
but it remained the same as before.
He then ordered it to be cut open,
and inside they found a copper statue,
about an inch tall.
It shone brightly,
with perfect features and form.
From then on, his family refrained from killing and released captive animals,
and dared not consume alcohol or meat.
From "Míngbào Jì".
Wife of Liú Gōngxìn
In the third year of the Lóngshuò era of the Táng dynasty,
Chén shì, wife of the Imperial Guard Liú Gōngxìn from Tōngguǐ ward in Cháng'ān city,
whose mother had previously died,
suddenly fell ill and died.
She saw herself being taken into hell,
witnessed all kinds of sufferings,
too numerous to describe in detail.
Finally, she saw one particular hell
with a solid stone gate.
Two large demons,
imposing and strong in appearance,
guarded the gate on either side.
They glared angrily at Chén and shouted:
"Who are you to come here?"
Then she saw the stone gate suddenly open,
and her deceased mother was inside, suffering torments,
too terrible to describe in detail.
When her suffering briefly subsided,
mother and daughter approached the gate to see each other.
The mother said to her daughter:
"Go back and strive to copy a sutra for me."
The daughter asked:
"Mother, which sutra do you want copied?"
The mother said:
"Copy the Lotus Sutra for me."
As soon as she finished speaking,
the stone gate closed.
Chén then revived
and told her husband everything.
She then relied on her brother-in-law, Zhào Shīzi, wanting to have the Lotus Sutra copied.
This Shīzi was formerly skilled in copying sutras.
There was a sutra copyist
who had brought a newly copied, unbound Lotus Sutra to Zhào Shīzi's place to pawn for money,
saying the sutra's owner was surnamed Fàn.
Shīzi agreed.
He then said to his wife
"Wife" originally written as "father".
Corrected according to the meaning of the following text.
and brother:
"Since we now need
"Need" originally written as "obtain".
Corrected according to "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín" chapter 57.
a sutra,
fortunately we have this Lotus Sutra at home.
Brother, could you redeem this sutra?"
Chén's husband agreed.
After it was bound,
he gave it to his wife,
who kept it at home to make offerings for her mother.
Later, she dreamed that her mother came to her asking for the sutra,
saying:
"I previously asked you to copy a Lotus Sutra for me.
Why haven't I received it yet?"
The daughter replied to her mother:
"I have already
"Already" originally written as "obtained".
Corrected according to the Ming manuscript and Chén's collated edition.
redeemed a Lotus Sutra for you, mother.
It has been bound
and is being kept at home for offerings."
The mother said to her daughter:
"Precisely because of this sutra,
I am suffering even more.
The jailers in the underworld have beaten my back until it's broken.
Look at the sores on my body.
The prison official said:
'Why did you take the Fàn family's sutra and claim it as your own?
What merit do you have?
This is a great transgression.'" When the daughter heard her mother say this,
she arranged to have the Lotus Sutra copied for her mother again.
Before the copying was finished,
the daughter again dreamed of her mother coming to urge her about the sutra.
Then she saw a monk
holding a scroll of the Lotus Sutra,
who said to the mother:
"Your daughter has already copied the first volume of the sutra for you.
The merit is already achieved.
Why must you hurry so?"
Later, when the sutra copying was completed,
the mother came to tell her daughter:
"Because you copied the sutra for me,
I have now been able to leave the underworld path
and am being reborn in a good place.
Thanks to your kindness and effort,
I have come to tell you.
You must live well,
behave properly as a wife,
and take faith as your foundation."
After speaking,
they parted in sorrowful tears.
Later, they inquired about the former owner of the redeemed Lotus Sutra,
and it was indeed surnamed Yuàn.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín".
The Holy Monk of Chánglè Village
In the twenty-second year of the Kāiyuán era,
there was a household in Chánglè Village east of the capital,
which had long revered Buddhism
and often provided food for monks.
Suddenly, they found a monk’s sitting mat on the road,
and since it had no owner to return it to,
they took it home and treasured it.
Later, when hosting a vegetarian feast, they used it as the seat for the Holy Monk.
After the feast ended and the crowd dispersed,
suddenly a monk knocked at the door asking for a meal.
The host said:
"How did you, Master, know that your disciple had prepared a feast and come here?"
The monk replied:
"Just now, when I reached the Chǎn River,
I saw an elderly monk sitting by the water’s edge,
washing a sitting mat,
and angrily saying:
‘They invited me to the feast,
but gave me only half the alms offered to the other monks,
and stained my sitting mat,
forcing this old body to wash it myself.’
I stepped forward to pay my respects,
but the elderly monk did not stop.
So I asked him:
‘Where did you attend the feast, Elder Monk?
Why are you washing it yourself?’
The monk explained the whole story
and also pointed out the location of this household,
so I came here."
The host was greatly astonished
and invited the monk inside.
Earlier, on the Holy Monk’s seat,
there was a spot where soup had spilled and stained it.
The host then told the monk:
"My family is poor,
and we hastily prepared this feast.
The alms were meager,
so we gave thirty coins to each of the other monks,
but only half that amount to the Buddha and the Holy Monk.
I never expected the Holy Monk to come in person,
and moreover, to stain his sitting mat.
Foolish, ignorant, and blind,
my mind was biased,
and I was not careful in my actions.
All of this is my fault."
From Jì Wén
Qūtū Zhòngrèn
Tóngguān County Magistrate Yú Xián was quite well-known.
In the spring of the twenty-third year of the Kāiyuán era, he was traveling to Wēn County.
By the roadside, there was a small thatched hut.
A man lived inside it,
who pricked his arm, mixed the blood with cinnabar, and used it to copy the entire Buddhist canon.
This man was nearly sixty years old,
his complexion sallow and emaciated,
yet he had already copied several hundred scrolls of scriptures.
Whenever visitors came,
he would inevitably beg from them.
If someone asked about his background,
he would also receive assistance.
The man said:
"My surname is Qūtū,
and my given name is Zhòngrèn.
I am the brother of Zhòngjiāng and Jìjiāng.
My father also served as a prefectural administrator.
He had an estate in Wēn,
and I was his only son.
He doted on me for being young,
and indulged all my actions.
My nature was averse to study,
and I only cared for gambling, archery, and hunting.
When my father passed away,
the household had several dozen servants,
assets worth several million,
and many estates and residences.
But I, Zhòngrèn, indulged in lavish rewards and lust,
drank recklessly and gambled,
selling and trading until nearly everything was gone.
A few years later,
only the estate in Wēn County remained.
I then sold off the fields and farmlands,
dismantled and sold the buildings,
and when even that was exhausted,
only a single hall within the estate stood tall.
All the servants and concubines were gone,
and the family was impoverished with no plan.
So, inside the hall, I dug pits and buried several jars,
storing the meat of oxen, horses, and the like.
I, Zhòngrèn, possessed great strength,
and had a servant named Mòhèduō,
whose strength also matched that of ten men.
Every evening,
I would go with the servant to steal oxen and horses,
always traveling over fifty lǐ from the site of the theft.
When encountering an ox, I would seize its two horns,
flip it onto my back,
and when encountering horses or donkeys, I would rope their necks,
also flipping them onto my back.
Upon reaching home, I would throw them to the ground,
and they would die.
Then I would skin and butcher them,
discarding the hides and bones into a large pit behind the hall,
sometimes burning them,
while the meat was stored in the buried jars.
During the day,
I would have the servant sell it in the city markets,
exchanging it for rice to eat.
This continued for over ten more years.
Because the thefts occurred far away,
no one ever suspected.
I, Zhòngrèn, had a nature fond of killing;
my dwelling was filled with bows, arrows, nets, spears, and slingshots.
The flying and running creatures I killed
were beyond count.
Whatever my eyes fell upon,
nothing escaped intact.
Even when catching a hedgehog,
I would wrap it in mud and roast it over fire.
Once it was cooked,
I would remove the mud,
and the hedgehog's skin and spines
would come off with the mud,
then I would take the meat and eat it.
The cruelty I inflicted
was all of this kind.
Later, Mòhèduō fell ill and died.
Over a month later,
I, Zhòngrèn, suddenly died,
but my heart area remained warm.
My wet nurse, now old,
was still alive
and kept watch over me, not yet burying me.
Then I, Zhòngrèn, revived,
and said:
"At first, I was captured and taken away,
to face trial alongside my servant.
We arrived at a large courtyard,
with over ten halls for handling affairs.
There were six judges,
each occupying two rooms.
My trial was at the westernmost end.
The judge was not present,
so I stood below the hall.
After a while, the judge arrived,
and it was actually my uncle-by-marriage, Zhāng Ān, the Simā of Yùnzhōu.
Seeing me, he was startled,
and led me up the steps.
He said to me:
'Nephew, in the human world, your wickedness was unparalleled.
The beings you killed number in the thousands and tens of thousands.
Now you have suddenly arrived here.
How can I possibly save you?'
I, Zhòngrèn, was terrified,
and kowtowed, pleading pitifully.
The judge said:
'Wait until I discuss it with the other judges.'
Then he said to the other judges:
'My wife's nephew, Qūtū Zhòngrèn, has committed countless sins.
Now he has been summoned here for trial.
His allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted.
I wish to release him back,
but I fear those he killed will not consent.
If we could open a path to release him alive,
would that be permissible?'
The other officials said:
'Summon an expert in the law to ask?'
Then an expert in the law arrived,
dressed in blue-green robes, cautious and restrained.
The judge asked him:
'We wish to release a sinner.
Is there a way?'
And so he explained the situation in detail.
The legal expert said:
'There is only one way he can be released,
but it requires the consent of those he killed.
If they do not consent,
it will be of no use.'
The official asked:
'What is the method?'
The legal expert said:
'All these creatures
were killed by Zhòngrèn.
They must first repay their bodily debts,
and then they can be reborn.
We should summon them all here,
and try to persuade them, saying:
"Qūtū Zhòngrèn has now arrived.
Once you have consumed and devoured him,
you will then be reborn.
Sheep will become sheep again,
horses will also become horses.
Since your remaining karma is not yet exhausted,
you will again receive animal bodies.
If Zhòngrèn returns as a human,
he will, as before, eat you.
Your karmic retribution
will then be endless.
Now, if we temporarily send Zhòngrèn back,
and have him perform meritorious deeds on your behalf to accumulate blessings,
enabling each of you to shed your animal karma,
and all attain human bodies,
never again to be killed by humans,
wouldn't that be far better?"
When the animals hear they can attain human bodies, they will surely rejoice.
Only then can he be released.
If they do not consent,
there is no other way.'
So they locked me, Zhòngrèn, in a room in front of the hall,
and summoned all the living beings I had killed.
In the judge's courtyard,
the ground covered about a hundred mǔ.
The living beings I, Zhòngrèn, had killed
filled it completely.
Oxen, horses, donkeys, mules, pigs, sheep, deer, wild deer, pheasants, rabbits,
even hedgehogs and flying birds,
tens of thousands in total.
They all said:
'Why have you summoned us?'
The judge said:
'Zhòngrèn has arrived.'
The creatures all roared in great anger,
leaping, shaking, and stamping their feet, saying:
'Great thief! Why not repay our debt!'
Just as they were enraged,
the bodies of the pigs and sheep grew large,
comparable to oxen and horses,
and the oxen and horses also grew many times larger than usual.
The judge then had the legal expert enter to explain and persuade them.
When the animals heard they could attain human bodies,
they all rejoiced,
and their forms returned to normal.
After driving all the animals back in,
they brought me, Zhòngrèn, out.
Two jailers arrived,
holding leather bags and a wooden club.
They stuffed me, Zhòngrèn, into a bag,
and beat it with the club.
The blood from my body, Zhòngrèn's,
flowed out from the holes in the bag and spilled onto the ground.
The jailers beat the bag with the club and my, Zhòngrèn's, blood
then flowed all over the front of the hall.
In a moment,
the blood deepened to the steps,
reaching about three chǐ.
Then, along with the bag, they threw me, Zhòngrèn, into the room,
and locked it again.
Then they summoned all the animals, etc.,
who angrily said:
"The rebel killed me,
now I drink your blood."
Then, together with Fei Niǎo and others,
they all drank his blood.
Once the blood was exhausted,
they licked it all up,
stopping only when the soil in the courtyard became visible.
