While drinking the blood,
the beasts were filled with rage,
their bodies growing several times larger,
and they continued to curse without cease.
After they had finished eating,
Míng Fǎ again announced:
"You have now received your debt,
so I now release Qūtū Zhòngrèn to return,
and order him to perform meritorious deeds on your behalf,
so that you may be reborn as humans."
All the beasts rejoiced,
each returning to their original forms and departing.
The judge then ordered Zhòngrèn to be taken out of the bag,
and his body was as before.
The judge said to him:
"Having witnessed retribution,
strive diligently to cultivate blessings.
If you prick your blood to copy all the scriptures,
this sin will be completely eradicated.
Otherwise, if you come again,
there will never be hope of release."
Zhòngrèn revived,
and firmly carried out his resolve.
From "Jì Wén"
Wùzhōu Guardian Deities
At the gate of Wùzhōu's Kāiyuán Temple, there are two guardian deities,
renowned in the world as divine,
so that birds and sparrows dare not approach.
Those who pray for healing from illness have repeatedly experienced efficacy,
and people come and go to pay their respects.
During the Kāiyuán era,
a state judicial officer held a banquet in the temple gate tower,
and everyone said that the guardian deities were present,
so it was not permissible.
One person said:
"They are merely clay,
what can they do?"
He then put wine and meat into their mouths.
In a moment,
clouds darkened and lightning flashed in the tower,
with both wind and thunder,
wine and meat flew about,
and everyone was terrified.
Only the one who defiled the guardian deities
was dragged out of the tower several tens of zhàng and struck dead by lightning.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
The Pig of Pútí Temple
In the eighteenth year of the Táng Kāiyuán era.
At the capital's Pútí Temple, there was a long-lived pig,
with a soft, plump, and large body,
which had been at the temple for over ten years.
That year, the pig died.
The monks cremated it,
and after the fire had burned out,
over a hundred śarīra relics were found in the ashes.
From "Jì Wén"
Lǐ Sīyuán
In the fifth month of summer in the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
Lǐ Sīyuán, a clerk in the Left Clear Path Commandant’s Office, died suddenly.
After his death, his body remained warm,
so his family did not dare to hold a funeral.
After twenty-one days had passed,
he revived in the middle of the night.
He immediately said:
"Someone has escorted me back,
so prepare a meal for thirty people."
He also said:
"I need ten thousand strings of cash to give to those who escorted me."
Sīyuán’s father served as a bureau director,
and his family was rather wealthy.
Thus, he ordered a feast to be prepared,
and paper money to be cut out.
When the food was ready,
he had it arranged in the hall as an offering for thirty monks.
Sīyuán then addressed them, saying:
"I am grateful for your kindness in escorting me back.
This meager meal of simple vegetables
is hardly worthy of your great virtue."
After a short while, as if they had finished eating,
he ordered five thousand sheets of paper money to be burned in the courtyard.
He then ordered a meal for two to be prepared,
with wine and meat.
Sīyuán turned toward the seats and said:
"I am grateful for your release,
and I deeply appreciate your great kindness."
After ordering another five thousand sheets of paper money to be burned,
he then lay down to rest.
By daybreak,
he gradually grew calm.
He then recounted:
"I was captured and taken to a certain place.
The official was not there,
but two clerks were present:
one named Féng Jiāngjìng,
and the other named Lǐ Hǎicháo.
Along with me, three people had been summoned.
The two clerks said:
'If you can give us five million in cash,
we will let you go.'
The other two did not respond,
but I alone agreed,
which pleased the clerks.
Soon, the official arrived
and said to the three of us:
'Two attendants are needed,
choose among the three of you.'
The official then led Sīyuán and the others to the king’s palace.
The city gates were multiple layers deep,
and the defenses were extremely thorough.
I saw the king’s residence had ten tall buildings,
with the three where the king resided being especially lofty,
all with curtains hanging down.
When Sīyuán arrived,
before he could enter,
he saw a man
wearing a golden seal with a purple ribbon,
who appeared very noble.
He was instructed to present his name card and request an audience with the king.
The king summoned him for an audience,
and Sīyuán followed him into the building, stopping below the tower.
The king ordered the curtains to be drawn aside,
and summoned the nobleman to ascend the tower.
As the nobleman ascended the steps,
the king rose upon seeing him
and invited him beneath the curtains.
The nobleman bowed,
and the king returned the bow,
then said to the nobleman:
"Now that you have come here,
you must face judgment.
I wonder what good deeds you performed in life?"
The nobleman replied:
"None."
The king said:
"Having lived for decades,
you performed no good deeds,
nor were you loyal or filial.
What should be done with you now?"
He then frowned and said:
"Let the relevant authorities deal with him."
The nobleman took his leave and descended,
but before he had gone down many steps,
a great black wind suddenly swept before the curtains,
carrying the nobleman away.
From afar, I saw the nobleman within the black wind,
his body suddenly stretching to several zhàng in length,
his form disintegrating,
now large, now small,
gradually drifting farther away
until he vanished from sight.
The king stood watching for a moment,
then said to those below the steps:
"This is the wind of karma,
blowing this man into hell."
The official then reported Sīyuán and the others to the king.
The king said:
"Let them draw lots to decide."
Three bolts of silk were then thrown down from beneath the curtains,
and the three were ordered to open them.
When the other two opened their silk,
they both bore the characters 'assigned to serve,'
but only Sīyuán’s silk had nothing written on it.
The king said:
"Keep the two,
release Sīyuán."
Sīyuán exited the palace gate,
where, to the west of the gate, there was a wall with an east-facing door.
Outside the door were several hundred monks,
holding banners and flowers to welcome Sīyuán,
saying:
"The Bodhisattva wishes to see you."
Sīyuán entered the courtyard,
where the ground was all clear pools,
and the halls and pavilions within were adorned with the seven treasures.
Inside the hall was a monk,
wearing a kasaya woven with golden threads,
sitting on a jeweled seat.
As Sīyuán bowed in reverence,
those beside him said:
"This is the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha."
Sīyuán then knelt.
All the monks chanted praises,
and hearing them, Sīyuán shed tears.
The Bodhisattva addressed the assembly, saying:
"Do you see this man shedding tears?
He has not been gone long,
and hearing the ancient Brahmic sounds,
he is moved to tears."
He then said to Sīyuán:
"You have witnessed the affairs of this place.
When you return to the human world, speak of them one by one,
so that people in the world may hear of them
and change their hearts to cultivate goodness.
In this life of yours, you have engaged in no mixed practices,
and you have maintained right mindfulness.
You may return here again."
He then ordered the monks to escort him back.
When Sīyuán first revived,
he prepared a meal for thirty people,
and separately prepared a meat meal for two,
all as offerings of gratitude,
for this reason.
Sīyuán lived for seven more days,
and after holding a grand vegetarian feast,
he died again.
By dawn, he revived and said:
"I was summoned again by the Bodhisattva,
who rebuked me, saying:
'I ordered you to fully proclaim the matters of retribution.
Why have you not spoken of them?'
He was about to cane me,
but I pleaded sorrowfully, and he released me."
Sīyuán had never consumed wine or meat,
and after being reborn,
he maintained a pure and permanent vegetarian diet,
and his entire household abstained from eating after noon.
Whenever Sīyuán attended gatherings,
he would always recount in detail the affairs of the underworld,
and people were all transformed by his words.
From "Records of Hearsay"
by Monk Qízhī.
The monk Qí Zhī of Shèngyè Temple enjoyed socializing with noble figures,
was quite knowledgeable in medical arts,
but his conduct was often mixed.
In the fifth month of the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he fell ill and died,
but revived after two days.
He then moved to the Eastern Chándìng Temple,
where he built a hall in the courtyard,
extremely ornate and decorated,
with a long altar horizontally arranged with seven life-sized statues.
From then on, he ceased socializing
and diligently upheld the precepts.
He recounted:
"Upon first dying, I was summoned to the court of the King of Ghosts,
where I saw a piece of flesh,
rotting and foul on the ground.
The King then asked:
'You are a monastic—
why have you killed someone?'"
Qí Zhī did not know how to respond.
The King said:
"Why did you beat to death the temple's maidservant?"
Only then did Qí Zhī realize.
Previously, a young monk in the temple named Hé Mǎshī had an affair with a maidservant of the temple.
Later, the maidservant had other intentions,
and Mǎshī grew angry with her,
so he framed the maidservant before the temple abbot.
This maidservant
was not a virtuous person,
and the abbot had long held a grudge against her.
While the monks were still gathered for the meal in the hall and had not yet dispersed,
he summoned the maidservant before the assembly
and proceeded to beat her to death.
Qí Zhī admonished the abbot:
"Those who have left the household life
guard body, speech, and mind;
the regulations of the precepts
must not be violated even in haste,
how much less by killing before an assembly?"
Mǎshī supported the abbot.
The abbot grew furious,
did not heed Qí Zhī,
and so blows rained down until
she died beneath the hall.
Thus, when Qí Zhī understood the King's question,
he said:
"The killer was the abbot;
the one at fault was Mǎshī.
Why am I being questioned now?"
The foul flesh before the King
suddenly made a sound, saying:
"Qí Zhī killed me."
The King angrily said:
"Maidservant, why do you not rise but speak lying down?"
The foul flesh suddenly rose and became a person—
it was the slain maidservant.
After several rounds of debate with Qí Zhī,
she then said:
"At the moment of death,
in agony and confusion,
I only heard someone beside urging to kill me;
I suspected it was Qí Zhī,
so I accused him."
The King said:
"Summon the abbot."
The official on duty said:
"His merits are too many; he cannot be summoned."
The King said:
"Summon Mǎshī."
The official said:
"Mǎshī's lifespan is not yet exhausted."
The King said:
"First detain the maidservant,
and release Qí Zhī."
When Qí Zhī first entered,
he saw a monk and a horse beside the King's seat.
As he reached the gate,
the monk also came out,
and Qí Zhī bowed in reverence.
The monk said:
"I am the Bodhisattva Dìzàng.
Due to your scant merit,
your life was about to end.
That is why you alone were summoned.
Now you must firmly uphold the monastic precepts,
abandon your worldly affairs,
dwell in a secluded and quiet temple,
and create seven life-sized statues.
If you cannot obtain the funds,
painted images will also suffice."
After Qí Zhī revived,
he then followed these instructions.
From "Jì Wén."
Zhāng Wúshì
In the winter of the twelfth year of the Táng dynasty's Tiānbǎo era,
the official Sīgē Zhāng Wúshì resided in Bùzhèng Ward.
While walking in the streets one night,
the drumbeats ceased and the gates were closed,
so he hurried under a bridge and crouched there.
At midnight,
dozens of riders suddenly arrived at the bridge,
halted their horses, and said:
"Send so-and-so to Bùzhèng Ward,
take a horse and fetch over ten people."
Among them, two were—
one, Wúshì's wife,
the other, the wealthy old man Wáng Wēng from the same lane.
Wúshì heard this and was greatly alarmed.
Soon, the fetcher returned and said:
"All the others have been taken,
but Wúshì's wife recites the Diamond Sūtra,
and benevolent deities protect her,
so she could not be taken."
He then called out the names of those captured,
and each responded:
"Here."
Wúshì also recognized Wáng Wēng's name.
After the responses finished,
soon the drums sounded.
Wúshì returned home,
and saw his wife still sitting and reciting scriptures, waiting.
When Wúshì arrived,
his wife said:
"You seldom stay out overnight;
I feared you had violated the curfew,
so I recited scriptures without sleep, waiting for you."
At daybreak,
they heard crying from the southern neighbor,
and when Wúshì inquired,
it turned out Wáng Wēng had died.
Wúshì was terrified,
and so told his wife the whole story;
his wife was also greatly frightened.
They then moved out of their residence,
visited renowned monks,
made vows to observe a permanent vegetarian diet,
and recited scriptures forty-nine times daily.
Thus they were spared.
From "Jì Wén."
Zhāng Yìng
Zhāng Yìng of Lìyáng was originally a follower of demonic teachings,
and married a Buddhist woman as his wife.
When his wife fell gravely ill,
performing demonic rituals brought no improvement.
His wife said:
"I was originally a Buddhist woman,
I beg to have Buddhist rites performed."
Yìng then went to the monastery to see Zhú Tánkǎi,
Tánkǎi said:
"The Buddha universally aids all beings,
you need only wholeheartedly receive and uphold [the teachings].
Tánkǎi will go to your house tomorrow."
That night,
Yìng dreamed of a person,
over ten feet tall,
hurrying in from the south and entering the door,
saying:
'This household is so impure.'
In the dream, he saw Tánkǎi,
following behind this person and saying:
'This place wishes to develop the intention [for the Dharma],
you cannot blame them for one or two things.'
Yìng awoke from sleep,
and immediately lit a torch to build a high seat.
The next day at mealtime, Tánkǎi went to Yìng's house,
the high seat was already completed,
husband and wife received the precepts,
and the illness soon healed.
In the second year of Xiánkāng,
Yìng became very ill,
and sent someone to call for Tánkǎi,
but he was repeatedly unavailable.
Yìng died and then revived,
saying at the time
"saying at the time" originally read "at the time saying",
changed according to the Míng manuscript
there were several people,
using iron hooks to drag him north down to a plank shore,
below the shore he saw cauldrons of boiling water, mountains of knives, forests of swords, and instruments of cruel torture.
Yìng forgot Tánkǎi's name,
and only cried, "Venerable monk, save me!"
He said
originally lacked the character "said",
added according to the Míng manuscript
to the people dragging him away:
"I am a child of the Buddha."
The people said:
"What is your venerable monk's name?"
Yìng forgot his name,
and only called upon the Buddha.
Soon they drew near the boiling cauldrons,
there was a person over ten feet tall,
holding a golden pestle about to strike.
Yìng fled,
and the people, frightened, scattered.
The tall man led Yìng back, saying:
"Your lifespan is exhausted,
you cannot return to life.
I give you three days,
to recite three gāthās.
Retrieve your venerable monk's name and return.
Then I will let you live
in the original text volume 113, entry for Zhāng Yìng,
after "Then I will let you live" there are the ten characters: "three days later you will die again and then be reborn in heaven"
He then pushed Yìng inside the door,
and he revived.
Three days later he died again.
From "Shénguǐ Zhuàn"
Dào Yán
There was a monk named Yán,
who resided at Chéngdū's Shílì Temple
Míng manuscript reads "Bǎoyìng" for "Shílì"
On the twenty-first day of the fifth month in the fourteenth year of Táng Kāiyuán,
in front of the Buddha hall's porch,
while lighting the eternal lamp,
he suddenly saw a giant hand,
on the western porch of the hall.
Dào Yán was terrified and shaken,
bowing his head and not moving.
After a long time,
he suddenly heard a voice from the air say:
"Fear not, fear not,
I am a benevolent spirit,
and dare not harm even a hair of the master.
Why bow your head and not move?"
After Dào Yán heard this,
his fear lessened somewhat,
and he asked:
"Who is the benefactor
Míng manuscript reads "Buddha" for "person"?
Hiding your body and showing only your hand?"
Soon he heard a reply from the air:
"Heaven commanded me to protect the grounds of the Buddha temple.
Because worldly people like to spit on Buddha shrine grounds,
I use my back to catch it,
receiving their spit.
Thus my back has sores,
which fester deeply into my flesh,
I wish to apply ointment and oil to it.
May I?"
Dào Yán then placed pure oil in the giant hand,
and the hand withdrew.
Dào Yán then requested:
"I now wish to see the benefactor's form,
so that a painter may depict it on the temple walls,
and record the event to manifest it,
hoping that worldly people will dare not spit on Buddha shrine grounds."
The spirit said:
"My appearance is very ugly,
if the master sees it,
will you not tremble in fear?"
Dào Yán said:
"Benefactor, only show your body,
do not deter me."
He saw under the western porch a spirit,
whose substance was most unusual,
with a large head and huge nose,
stern eyes and gaping mouth,
body shape massive and stout,
several zhang tall.
At first sight,
Dào Yán's back sweat poured like water.
The spirit then vanished.
Thereupon he fully described the spirit's appearance to the painter,
and had it depicted on the wall of the western porch.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
Xíng Cáojìn
The late Táng-dynasty bestowed Minister of Works Xíng Cáojìn,
since the Zhìdé era,
was a valiant general of Héshuò.
He held office in Wèi Commandery,
and thus was subordinated by Tián Chéngsì.
Once, during a campaign against rebels,
a flying arrow struck his shoulder,
his attendants tried to pull the arrow out for him,
but the arrowhead remained in the bone,
with its tip slightly exposed.
They then used iron pliers,
sending strong men to pull it out,
but the arrowhead was firmly immovable.
Cáojìn was in agony,
with no plan to apply.
His wife and children could only extensively perform Buddhist services,
hoping for compassionate protection.
After a few days,
he had himself tied to the bed with ropes,
and again ordered it pulled out,
but it remained as firmly fixed as before.
Cáojìn groaned and endured,
awaiting death.
Suddenly, while napping during the day,
he dreamed of a foreign monk standing in the courtyard,
Cáojìn then told him of his suffering.
After a while, the foreign monk said:
"If you can pour rice juice into it,
it will heal on its own."
Upon waking,
he told the physician.
The physician said:
"Rice juice is just rice water,
how can it be used to soak a wound!"
He then ordered extensive inquiries among people,
but none understood.
The next day,
suddenly a foreign monk came to the door begging for food,
and was hastily summoned inside.
Cáojìn saw from the central hall from afar,
that it was the one from yesterday's dream,
immediately invited him closer,
and told him of the danger and suffering.
The foreign monk said:
"Why not pour cold food syrup into it?
You will know its miraculous effect."
Cáojìn then realized,
syrup is rice juice.
Moreover, the one he saw again resembled the one in the dream,
so he obtained it,
applied it as instructed,
and upon contact felt coolness,
immediately reducing the soreness and pain.
That night,
the wound itched slightly,
so he ordered it pulled out as before.
The pliers had just touched the eyelid,
when the arrowhead suddenly came out.
Later, medicine was applied,
and within ten days he recovered.
Alas,
the Western Sage,
his grace and protection so clearly manifested,
is this not such a clear sign?
From "Jíyì Jì"
Wéi Shìzǐ
There was a man of the Wéi family who served as a Confucian scholar-official during the Yuánhé reign of the Táng dynasty.
From childhood, he revered Confucianism,
and would speak of nothing but Confucian teachings.
Therefore, he considered Buddhism a barbarian doctrine,
unsuitable for promotion in the Central Kingdom.
He had two daughters.
The elder married into the Xiànglǐ family,
while the younger married into the Hú family.
The elder daughter's husband upheld his father-in-law's views,
but the younger daughter's husband opposed them.
He constantly revered the Buddha and followed his teachings,
diligently studying the Buddhist scriptures.
For characters that were untranslated and should be read with Sanskrit pronunciation,
he would curl his tongue to imitate them,
and over time, his devotion grew even more sincere.
When the Wéi family man fell gravely ill,
he instructed his son, saying:
"I am a man of the Confucian school,
and I follow no teachings other than those of the ancient sage-kings.
Now that I am about to die,
be careful not to follow vulgar customs,
such as casting Buddhist statues or feeding monks,
or praying for blessings from barbarian deities.
Do not betray the convictions I have held all my life."
His son obeyed him.
After the mourning period ended, the wife from the Hú family died.
When the news of her death reached the Xiànglǐ family,
because their own daughter-in-law was bedridden with illness,
they did not inform her of the death.
Soon, her condition became critical.
Her family gathered around her, weeping,
and prepared for her final moments.
Suddenly, as if supported by spirits,
she abruptly sat up.
Calling to her daughter-in-law, she said:
"My younger sister has been dead for several months.
Why was I not told?"
As she spoke, tears streamed down her face, and she sobbed.
Her husband tried to deceive her, saying:
"How could such a thing be true?
Your virtuous sister had a minor ailment,
and we recently heard she has recovered.
These are the delusions of a troubled mind,
not to be relied upon.
Do not grieve so hastily.
You are very ill now,
and must rest and recuperate."
She wept again and said:
"My sister is here.
She told me she died in the tenth month this year,
and she has seen many things.
She summoned my brothers to come,
so she could relay a message to them.
Yesterday, when I arrived at the Western Bureau of the underworld,
I heard, from behind a high wall,
the sounds of anguish, torment, and cries of regret,
which sounded like my late father's voice.
Looking above, I saw flames bursting forth,
blazing like wind and thunder.
I sought to enter and pay my respects,
but could not.
So I wept and called out to him from afar.
My late father cried out in response, saying:
'Because I slandered the Buddha in my lifetime,
I suffer excruciating torment.
There is no day or night,
not a moment of respite.
The names of the punishments here
are beyond description.
Only by having the entire family dedicate merits
and exhaustively
[Manuscript note: "冥" is written as "竭".]
provide resources to accumulate blessings
can there be the slightest hope of rescue.
To endure through kalpas of轮回,
it is difficult to hope for any reduction or mitigation.
But if, within a hundred moments,
I could have just one moment of temporary rest,
it would allow me to briefly catch my breath.'
Although my sister's past sins were not light,
because her husband's family accumulated good deeds,
she will not fall into hell.
Instead, she will ascend to the heavenly palace.
I fear that because your heart is like my late father's,
you too will face several hundred years of retribution.
However, after you shed this physical form,
you will transform into a crow.
On the day of the seventh seventh-day memorial feast for the monks,
you can come here.'"
Her husband wept and said:
"The transformations within the great furnace of creation—
such things indeed exist among beings.
Sparrows turn into clams,
snakes into pheasants,
pheasants into doves,
turtledoves into hawks,
field mice into quails,
rotting grass into fireflies,
humans into tigers, apes, fish, or turtles—
such accounts fill the historical records.
As for the claim of turning into a crow,
how could I deeply doubt it!
However, when crows come,
they usually arrive in flocks of several dozen.
How could we recognize your form among them and pay you special respect?"
She replied:
"The one with white feathers at the base of its tail—that will be me.
On my behalf, admonish the people of this world:
those who do evil,
in the open will face human punishment,
in secret will face punishment by ghosts.
Not the slightest discrepancy exists.
According to the delusions they cling to,
they will undergo transformations corresponding to those delusions.
Do you not see that people from the Tiānbǎo era were many, but people today are few?
It is because those who do good are few,
while those who do evil are many.
Therefore, within a single latrine,
insects and vermin number in the tens of thousands;
beneath a single brick,
ants and termites number in the tens of millions.
Yet the famed cities and great towns of old
stand empty and desolate, devoid of people;
beautiful lands and level plains
stretch before the eye as nothing but wild grasslands.
Is this not proof of it!
I earnestly entreat the people of this world
to strive diligently to plant seeds of good karma."
Having spoken, she lay back down,
and that evening she passed away.
As a wife,
she served her elders with respect,
attended to her husband with obedience,
was kind as an elder,
and humble with those below her.
Therefore, the entire household cherished her,
and lamented that one so young and fragrant should transform into a different creature.
Young and old alike,
they wept as they awaited the crow.
When the day arrived,
several dozen crows came.
Only one alighted on a low branch of the courtyard tree,
peering toward her mother-in-law's door,
and cried mournfully, its body bent in sorrow.
It seemed as if it had something to tell.
The family, young and old, watched it,
and all were moved to tears.
Slowly, they examined its tail,
and indeed found two feathers
as white as frost and snow.
The mother-in-law stretched out her hand and prayed, saying:
"When my daughter-in-law was about to die,
she said she would transform into a crow with a white tail.
If you are truly my daughter-in-law,
fly and alight upon my hand."
As soon as she finished speaking,
the crow flew over,
tame and familiar, and ate from her hand
as if it had been raised by her.
When it finished eating, it flew away.
From then on, it came daily to seek food,
and everyone knew of it.
After several months,
the crow no longer came.
From "Xù Xuánguài Lù"
Jiāng Sēng
In the thirteenth year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,

the Minister of Works and Military Commissioner of Zhèng-Huá, Duke Xuē Píng, and the Military Commissioner of Chén-Xǔ, Lǐ Guāngyán, both in accordance with an imperial edict, each led their own troops from their respective commands to join the campaign against Dōngpíng.
They reached a point seven lǐ south of Púyáng,
and encamped their army there.
The local inhabitants had all scattered.
Within a village there was a stūpa,
inside which was a mummified monk,
sitting with eyes wide open,
his Buddhist robes still upon him.
When touched with an object,
he immediately crumbled into dust.
The soldiers all rushed to gather and look,
causing a congestion that lasted for days.
A soldier named Hǎo Yì from the Xǔ army said:
"How can such a thing be?"
He therefore stabbed at its heart with his knife,
which felt like striking soft earth.
Hǎo Yì had not descended more than three or four steps from the pagoda
when he clutched his chest and cried out loudly,
and with one cry, died.
Commander Lǐ then ordered the event to be marked and recorded,
and had Hǎo Yì buried beneath the pagoda.
The next day,
a soldier named Máo Qīng from the Chén army said:
"How could this be?
What happened to Hǎo Yì yesterday was merely a coincidence."
He then used the hilt of his knife to knock out two of the mummy's teeth.
Máo Qīng had not descended more than three or four steps from the pagoda
when he clutched his jaw and cried out loudly,
and with one cry, died.
Commander Lǐ again ordered the event to be marked and recorded,
and had him buried beneath the pagoda.
From then on, no one dared to violate it.
Soldiers came to pray for blessings and seek divine aid,
and incense offerings greatly accumulated.
For three or four lǐ all around,
the crowd was so dense one could not enter.
The soldiers donated money, silk, clothing, and other alms,
filling the area for one or two lǐ around.
Minister of Works Duke Xuē therefore ordered that soldiers who were severely wounded in battle
were permitted to leave the military register and settle there.
Within ten days,
they then rejoined the army marching east,
and the wealth that had gathered
was carried off by thieves and bandits—
which is hardly surprising.
To this day, the knife wound and the missing teeth
remain clearly visible.
From the *Collection of Marvels*.
Chicken Eggs
During the reign of Emperor Jìngzōng of the Táng dynasty,
as all under heaven was peaceful,
in his spare time from attending to governance,
he widely promoted the Buddhist teachings.
Because of this, the number of Buddhist monks in Cháng'ān increased greatly.
When Emperor Wénzōng succeeded to the throne,
he personally attended to all affairs of state,
thinking to eliminate those things harmful to the people.
He once said to his attendants:
"Since I became Son of Heaven,
I have not yet been able to benefit the people.
Now, fortunately, there are no wars under heaven.
I will completely eliminate those things that harm living beings,
so that the millions of common people
may point to today as an age of Yáo and Shùn—that would be enough.
If there is anything that does not aid transformation and instead harms living beings,
just speak of it."
One of his attendants replied:
"Only the Buddhists not only fail to aid the great transformation,
but also greatly harm living beings.
They can be expelled."
Emperor Wénzōng was troubled by this.
He first ordered the relevant officials
to issue an edict, both within and outside the court, to stop Buddhist monks from expounding the meaning of Buddhist scriptures.
There were also requests to expel those who did not cultivate the teachings.
Just as the edict was about to be carried out,
it happened that a chef from the Imperial Kitchen was preparing the imperial meal,
cooking chicken eggs in a cauldron.
Just as he lit the fire beneath it,
he suddenly heard a very faint sound from within the cauldron, like human speech.
Drawing close to listen,
he discovered it was a chorus of eggs calling out "Guānshìyīn Bodhisattva!"
Their voices were extremely mournful and choked with sobs,
as if pleading for something.
The Imperial Kitchen chef found this strange
and reported the matter in full to the emperor.
Emperor Wénzōng ordered his attendants to verify it,
and it was as the Imperial Kitchen chef had reported.
Emperor Wénzōng sighed and said:
"I did not know the power of the Buddhists was like this!"
The next day,
he commanded the Imperial Kitchen officials not to use chicken eggs in meals.
He then issued an edict to the commanderies and principalities,
ordering each to erect a statue of Guānshìyīn Bodhisattva in their temples.
From the *Records of the Xuānshì Hall*.
Gāo
The character "Gāo" was originally written as "Qí";
changed according to the Ming dynasty manuscript copy.
Xǔ Wéndù of Gāoyáng
lodged in Qíyáng Commandery during the Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty.
Later, he fell ill with a fever
that lasted over a month.
One day, he lay on his bed as if in a deep stupor,
and awoke only after several days.
Initially, Wéndù dreamed that several figures wearing yellow robes were traveling with him through the fields.
Looking all around,
he found it utterly silent, with no sound of chickens or dogs,
and he had no idea how many hundred lǐ they had traveled.
The sky was dim and dusky,
and his heart was knotted with sorrow.
One of the yellow-robed figures said to Wéndù:
"Do not suffer so.
Long life and early death
naturally have their limits.
Even a sage cannot escape his allotted span."
Wéndù suddenly realized his body had already died,
and was terrified.
After traveling another ten-odd lǐ,
they reached a body of water.
As far as the eye could see, it was boundless,
the waves like black ink,
and unfathomably deep or shallow.
The yellow-robed people all walked upon the water and departed,
leaving Wéndù alone, too afraid to cross.
After a while, two golden figures appeared,
each just over five inches tall,
emitting a strange, brilliant light.
They came from upon the water.
When the yellow-robed figures saw the golden ones,
their faces fell with fear and they trembled,
immediately retreating and galloping away,
not daring to steal a glance.
The two golden figures said to Wéndù:
"Why have you come to the underworld?
We will now take you back to the path of the living.
Do not be afraid."
Wéndù's fear gradually subsided,
and he bowed repeatedly in thanks.
Thereupon, the golden figures traveled with Wéndù for several tens of lǐ.
Soon they saw the gate of his village,
and his joy was overwhelming.
Suddenly, he heard a harsh voice calling his name, "Wéndù!"
Startled, Wéndù awoke,
to see his wife and children weeping before him.
He was both amazed and sighed in relief,
but was so weak and exhausted he could not move his limbs,
so he had no chance to speak of the event.
After ten days,
his illness had somewhat abated,
and he walked with a cane in the courtyard.
Suddenly, he saw two golden figures, each just over five inches tall,
beneath the Buddhist shrine in his house—
exactly the ones he had seen in his dream.
Looking at their appearance and form,
there was not the slightest difference.
His heart grew even more amazed,
and he finally told his wife about the event.
His wife said:
"Recently, because your illness was so severe,
my worries knew no end.
However, I had often heard that Buddhism has the power to relieve suffering.
Therefore, I sold my jewelry and valuables
to cast statues of two golden figures.
Every morning at dawn,
I regularly prepared food offerings to them.
Since then, your suffering has also been cured and removed—
surely it was their power."
Wéndù, moved by the swift efficacy of the two golden figures' response,
ceased eating meat from living sacrifices,
often read Buddhist scriptures,
and thus exhaustively pursued their essential meaning.
From the *Records of the Xuānshì Hall*.
Xuánfǎ Temple
The Xuánfǎ Temple in the Ānyì Ward of Cháng'ān
was originally the residence of a local man named Zhāng Pín.
Zhāng had once provided for a monk
who made reciting the *Lotus Sutra* his vocation,
continuing for over ten years.
A member of Zhāng's household slandered the monk, accusing him of having an affair with a maidservant,
and Zhāng used another matter as a pretext to kill him.
After the monk's death,
the entire residence constantly heard the uninterrupted sound of sutra recitation.
Zhāng soon realized the monk's injustice,
but his remorse and regret were too late.
He therefore donated his residence to become a temple.
From the *Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng*.
Lay Buddhist Shāng
There was a lay Buddhist named Shàng,
a native of Sānhé County.
At the age of seven,
he was able to understand Buddhist texts,
which astonished the villagers.
Later, he built a hut in the western fields of Sānhé County,
where he had several hundred volumes of Buddhist scriptures.
He would hold and read them by hand,
never missing a single day.
Over a hundred people followed him as disciples.
He often wandered alone through towns and cities,
accompanied by those who traveled with him.
It was heard that whenever the lay Buddhist moved his limbs,
a crisp sound like jade being struck would ring out,
which amazed those who heard it.
Some said:
"The lay Buddhist's bones
are truly chain bones.
Chain bones are interconnected like vines,
so when the body moves,
a clear and melodious sound is produced.
This is indeed the reason.
I once heard it said in Buddhist texts
that the Buddha's body contains śarīra bones,
while a bodhisattva's body has chain bones.
Now, this lay Buddhist Shàng—
could he not be a bodhisattva?
However, ordinary worldly people
certainly cannot discern this."
The lay Buddhist later lived to over ninety years old.
One day,
he bathed, dressed in full attire, and wore his cap,
summoned all his disciples for a meal,
and then told them:
"I am ninety years old now,
and I will die any day.
You must cremate my body,
and be careful not to disobey my wish."
The disciples wept and said:
"We will respectfully obey your command."
That evening, he sat and passed away.
Three days later,
the disciples cremated the lay Buddhist in the wilderness.
When they looked at his bones,
they were indeed chain bones,
interconnected throughout the body,
as if sewn together.
When the wind brushed against them, a delicate melody slowly arose.
Thereupon, the villagers vied to donate money,
built a pagoda,
and buried the lay Buddhist's chain bones inside it.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
The Auspicious Image of Huángshān
In the wilderness of Huángshān in Rénchéng, Lǔjùn, there was an auspicious image
that grew from stone,
shaped like an embryo.
In the past, a gatherer of firewood
saw the image in the mountains,
went to pray to it,
and his wishes were always fulfilled.
As a result, thousands of people from near and far came to see it.
The local magistrate, fearing that trouble might arise,
ordered stonemasons to break the mountain rock,
transport the auspicious image,
and place it under the gate tower of the large temple in the city.
Thereupon, the townspeople held a grand vegetarian feast at the temple,
gathering several thousand people in total.
After the feast, the crowd dispersed.
It was just noon
when suddenly a great wind arose,
dark clouds covered the temple,
fire blazed within the clouds,
lightning struck the gate tower,
and rain poured down like a river.
The townspeople exclaimed in alarm:
"The gate tower is on fire!"
Previously, the monks had built the gate tower,
over a hundred feet tall,
but before it could be painted with vermilion,
the tower began leaning eastward,
so they propped it up with large timbers.
When the rain stopped,
the tower had already straightened.
It seems that ghosts and spirits, for the sake of the image,
jointly supported it.
From "Jì Wén"
Mǎ Zǐyún
Mǎ Zǐyún, the county captain of Jīngxiàn,
was an unlucky man.
As a xiàolián, he served three terms as county captain of Jīngxiàn,
but each time, within a few months, he had to leave due to mourning obligations.
During his tenure,
he was tasked with transporting the local tax grain to the capital.
While traveling along the Huái River,
his boat encountered a storm and sank,
drowning ten thousand hú of official grain.
As a result, he was severely imprisoned.
While in prison,
Zǐyún devoted himself to chanting Buddha's name,
continuing for five years.
Later, he was pardoned and released,
so he fled to a mountain temple in Nánlíng,
often eating only one vegetarian meal a day.
In the tenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
he died in Jīngxiàn.
He had previously told people:
"My life has been full of hardships,
so I diligently practiced Buddhism.
Now my karma for the Western Pure Land is complete,
and I shall be reborn in the Land of Bliss."
The next day, he bathed,
put on new clothes,
and sat upright with palms joined.
Soon, a wondrous fragrance filled the room.
Zǐyún joyfully said:
"The transformed Buddha has come
to welcome me on my journey."
With these words, he passed away.
From "Jì Wén"
Guānyīn of Yúnhuā Temple
In Cháng'ān's Yúnhuā Temple, there was a Guānyīn Hall,
located in the northwest corner of the temple.
At the end of the Dàzhōng era,
a commoner named Qū Yán suffered from sores and was near death.
He dreamed of a bodhisattva touching his sores and saying:
"I am at Yúnhuā Temple."
Yán awoke in shock, sweating profusely,
and recovered within a few days.
He then went to the temple to search,
and upon reaching the hall of sacred paintings,
he saw the bodhisattva,
exactly as he had seen in his dream.
The entire city's populace came to pay respects.
Yán then established a devotional society,
built a hall, and moved the image there.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Lǐ Zhōu
Táng dynasty Qiánzhōu prefect Lǐ Zhōu wrote to his sister:
"If Śākyamuni were born in China,
he would establish teachings like Zhōu Gōng and Confucius;
if Zhōu Gōng and Confucius were born in the West,
they would establish teachings like Śākyamuni.
If heaven does not exist, so be it;
if it does, noble persons will ascend there.
If hell does not exist, so be it;
if it does, petty persons will enter there."
Those with insight considered this wise speech.
From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ"
Huìyuán
The monk Huìyuán,
originally surnamed Chūn,
was from Yìyáng.
In his youth, he made a living as an archer.
Once, in the Wǔlíng Mountains,
he shot a pregnant deer.
As it lay dying, it spoke:
"In a past life, I only killed you once,
but now you have killed both me and my child.
Since this is karmic retribution,
I should die by your hand."
It then added:
"I will soon attain Buddhahood.
You should practice good deeds,
life after life, generation after generation,
and never create enmity again."
Huìyuán immediately understood his past karma,
so he shaved his head at the place where the deer died
and built a monastery there,
naming it Qíshé Kūshān Temple.
According to Wáng Róng's separate biography,
ten years after Huìyuán's death,
someone saw him at the foot of Wǔdāng Mountain.
From "Lǎngzhōu Tújīng"
The Woman of Yānzhōu
In the past, in Yánzhōu, there was a woman,
fair-skinned and quite beautiful,
around twenty-four or twenty-five years old.
She wandered alone in the city,
and young men
all associated with her.
They engaged in intimate relations and shared her bed,
yet she never refused anyone.
After several years, she passed away.
The people of the prefecture all mourned and pitied her,
pooling money for funeral arrangements to bury her.
Since she had no family,
she was interred by the roadside.
During the Dàlì era,
suddenly a foreign monk came from the Western Regions.
Seeing the grave,
he spread out
(Míng manuscript note: "spread out" is written as "敷".)
his sitting mat,
paid respects, burned incense,
and circled around it, praising and sighing in admiration.
After several days,
people saw him and said:
"This was a licentious and wanton woman,
who took all men as her husbands.
Because she had no relatives,
she was buried here.
Why do you, monk, show such respect?"
The monk said:
"This is not something you laypeople understand.
This is a great sage,
compassionate, joyful, and selfless.
Worldly desires—
she did not refuse any.
This is the Bodhisattva of Interlocking Bones.
Her earthly affinities have been exhausted,
so the sage has passed away.
If you do not believe, open the grave to verify it."
The crowd then opened the grave,
and upon examining the bones all over the body,
found them interlocked like links of a chain,
exactly as the monk had said.
The people of the prefecture found this extraordinary,
held a grand vegetarian feast in her honor,
and built a pagoda for her.
From "Xù Xuánguài Lù"
The Iron Pagoda of Zhènzhōu
During the Tiānyòu era of the Táng dynasty,
a monk from Tàiyuán named Huìzhào dreamed that an iron pagoda was buried in the ruins of the former Xiàngguó Temple, thirty lǐ south of Zhènzhōu.
He specifically went to search for it.
Upon reaching the border,
he was noticed by the regional commander Wáng Zhōnglìng Róng,
who invited him to stay and be supported at the official residence.
A military officer, Rén Yǒuyì, suspected he was a spy from a neighboring region,
and feared unforeseen trouble,
so he earnestly urged interrogation and expulsion.
The commander initially became suspicious,
and Huìzhào fully explained his search for the pagoda.
Immediately, he was sent to search thirty lǐ south of the prefectural seat,
and indeed found the ancient site of Xiàngguó Temple.
Digging in front of the temple's foundation,
they unearthed an iron pagoda,
on which were engraved the names of three thousand men,
all of whom were current officers and personal guards of Chángshān.
Only Rén Yǒuyì's name was missing,
revealing that fate had been predetermined.
Who engraved this pagoda—
how divine and wondrous!
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
The Angler by the Wèi River
By the clear Wèi River,
a commoner's son
was fond of angling.
He neither farmed nor traded,
but made his living with fragrant bait.
From youth to middle age,
he caught fish beyond count.
Moreover, he had mastered the technique of Rèn Gōngzǐ,
often placing oil-fried swallow meat on fine hooks.
Catching fresh fish was as easy as retrieving them from a pool or rapid.
His family of several mouths relied on clothing and food
provided by his fishing rod.
Suddenly one day,
while fishing at the great cliff gorge,
he caught nothing all day.
As dusk approached,
he suddenly felt a tug on his single-strand silk line,
quite surprised by its heaviness.
Pulling it in gradually,
he retrieved a bronze Buddha statue.
Greatly annoyed,
he threw it back into the deep pool,
then moved to fish at another inlet,
but again caught nothing.
After a while,
he pulled out another bronze Buddha.
Thereupon, he broke his rod,
cut his line,
and never practiced his trade again for the rest of his life.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Lú Jǐngyù
Lú Jǐngyù of the Later Wèi, styled Zhòngrú,
at the beginning of Jiémǐn's reign,
served as a National Academy erudite.
He believed in Buddhism,
and annotated the "Zhōuyì" and "Lúnyǔ".
His cousin Shénlǐ
relied on fellow villagers to rebel,
forcing him to join forces in responding to the Western Wèi,
and he was imprisoned in Jìnyáng.
With utmost sincerity, he recited the Diamond Sutra,
and his shackles fell off by themselves.
When Qí Shénwǔ became chancellor,
he was specially pardoned.
From "Bàoyìng Jì"
Zhào Wénruò
Zhào Wénruò of the Suí dynasty,
at the beginning of the Kāihuáng era, fell ill and died.
After seven days,
as his family was about to encoffin him,
he suddenly drew in one foot,
so they stopped.
Upon reviving, he said:
He had been pursued by a person,
and followed him,
entering a palace city.
He saw the King, who said:
"What virtuous deeds did you perform in life?"
He replied:
"Only upheld the Diamond Sutra."
The King said:
"This is the foremost.
Although your allotted lifespan is exhausted,
because you upheld the sutra,
it is extended further."
He also said:
"Among all sins,
killing living beings is extremely grave.
You filled your belly with pigs and sheep—
what of that?"
He then sent an envoy to lead Wénruò to the place of suffering.
Heading north for about two or three lǐ,
they reached a high wall,
with a hole
just large enough for a body.
Exiting through this hole,
they climbed a high mound,
looking out in all directions over a vast expanse.
They saw a city extremely lofty and steep,
with smoke and fire reaching the sky,
and black gas overflowing the ground.
They also heard agonized wails and cries unbearable to hear,
so he covered his ears and eyes,
kowtowing and begging to leave.
Still, he felt his heart break,
and blood came from his mouth.
The envoy led him back to see the King, who said:
"Since you have eaten meat,
you cannot return empty-handed."
He then demanded five long nails,
which were driven into his head, hands, and feet, causing excruciating pain.
From then on, he devotedly upheld the sutra,
and ate no more meat.
Later, due to official business, he arrived at a courier station,
and suddenly dreamed of a young woman in blue clothing pleading for mercy.
He tried asking the station officer:
"What food is there?"
The reply was:
"We have prepared a sheep,
very plump and tender."
He inquired further,
and was told:
"A blue female sheep."
Wénruò said:
"I do not eat meat."
He then redeemed it and set it free.
From "Bàoyìng Jì"
Zhào Wénchāng
In the eleventh year of the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
Zhào Wénchāng, an assistant in the Court of the Imperial Treasury, suddenly died a violent death.
Only his heart remained slightly warm,
so his family did not dare to encoffin him.
Later, he revived
and recounted:
"When I first died,
someone led me to the court of King Yánluó.
The king asked:
'Throughout your life,
what meritorious deeds have you performed?'
Wénchāng replied:
'My family is poor,
and I lacked the means to perform virtuous acts.
I only devoted myself wholeheartedly to reciting the Diamond Sūtra.'
Upon hearing this,
the king clasped his hands and bowed his head,
praising:
'Excellent!
Since you have upheld the Prajñāpāramitā,
your merit is very great.'
The king then had someone lead Wénchāng
to fetch the Diamond Sūtra from within the scripture repository.
Wénchāng walked westward for five or six lǐ,
and saw several dozen rooms,
extremely splendid and magnificent.
Inside, scriptures filled the space completely,
with golden rollers and precious cases,
exquisitely adorned.
Wénchāng clasped his hands, closed his eyes,
and randomly drew out one scroll to open and look at.
It was indeed the Diamond Sūtra.
Wénchāng held it and brought it to the king's place.
The king ordered one person to hold the scroll in the west,
while Wénchāng stood in the east,
facing the scripture and reciting it,
not missing a single character.
The king was greatly delighted
and immediately released Wénchāng to return home.
He ordered someone to lead Wénchāng out through the southern gate.
Upon reaching the gate's entrance,
he saw Emperor Wǔ of the Northern Zhōu dynasty in a room beside the gate,
bound with three layers of chains and shackles.
He called out to Wénchāng:
'You are a native of my former kingdom.
Since you have come here temporarily,
I wish to speak with you.'
Wénchāng immediately bowed to him.
The emperor said:
'Do you recognize me?'
Wénchāng replied:
'Your subject formerly served as a guard for Your Majesty.'
Emperor Wǔ said:
'Since you are my former minister,
now that you are returning home,
speak on my behalf to the Suí emperor.
I wish to account for all my sins,
but only the grave sin of destroying the Buddhist Dharma
cannot be pardoned.
I hope he will perform some meritorious deeds for me,
so that through this blessed aid,
I may escape hell.'
Wénchāng received his words and departed.
Upon exiting the southern gate,
he saw a large manure pit,
with someone's hair protruding from it.
Wénchāng asked about it,
and the guide replied:
'This is the Qín general Bái Qǐ,
confined here temporarily,
his sins not yet resolved.'
Wénchāng returned home and revived,
and subsequently reported the matter to the emperor.
The emperor ordered the people of the realm to contribute a per-capita tax to have the Diamond Sūtra recited for Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu,
and held a grand offering for three days.
He also recorded the events
into the Suí dynastic history.
From the Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
The Scholar of Xīnfán County
In Wáng Lǐ Village, forty lǐ west of Xīnfán County, Yìzhōu,
during the Suí dynasty, there was a scholar
surnamed Gǒu,
skilled in calligraphy but not revealing his traces,
so no one could know of him.
He once, in an empty space east of the village
("empty" originally written as "room,"
changed according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy),
wrote the Diamond Sūtra on all four sides.
He finished in several days,
saying:
"This scripture is intended for the devas to recite."
At first, people were unaware of it.
Later, during a thunderstorm,
a cowherd boy stood at the place where the scripture was written,
yet was not drenched.
The ground there was dry,
for about a zhang or more.
When it grew dark,
the villagers found it strange.
After that, whenever it rained,
children often gathered there,
and their clothes did not get wet.
During the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty,
an extraordinary monk told the villagers:
"In the air above this place is the Diamond Sūtra.
The devas have set up a jeweled canopy covering it above;
it must not be lightly violated."
From then on, railings were set up around it
to prevent people and livestock from treading upon it.
Every fasting day,
villagers from all around would come to make Buddhist offerings there.
They often heard heavenly music,
its sound shaking the vast emptiness,
rich and harmonious, filling their ears.
From the Sānbǎo Gǎntōng Jì.
Kuǎi Wǔ'ān
Kuǎi Wǔ'ān of the Suí dynasty,
a man of Càizhōu,
possessed great strength
and was skilled with bow and arrows,
often hunting tigers.
Once, on the southern side of Sōng Shān, a tiger was causing great havoc,
so he went to shoot it.
As he gradually entered deep into the mountains,
suddenly a strange creature resembling a wild man
tore open a tiger skin
and threw it over Wǔ'ān's body,
then pushed him off into a ravine.
When he got up,
he had already become a tiger.
Terrified and shocked,
he did not know what to do,
when suddenly he heard the sound of a bell,
realizing it was a monastic dwelling,
and went to seek help.
Indeed, he saw a monk reciting the Diamond Sūtra.
He immediately closed his eyes and prostrated himself.
The monk stroked his head with his hand,
and suddenly there was a loud explosive sound—
his head had split open.
Wǔ'ān then emerged from within,
and immediately recounted everything that had happened.
The monk also stroked his back,
which opened up at his touch.
Once he emerged,
all his clothes were still on his body,
with only a few tiger hairs,
likely stuck there from the previous cauterized wounds.
From then on, he renounced the household life
and devoted himself exclusively to upholding the Diamond Sūtra.
From the Bàoyìng Jì.
Mù Yàntōng
Mù Yàntōng was a man of the Suí dynasty
who diligently upheld the Diamond Sūtra,
reciting it ten times daily as his practice.
When Lǐ Mì raised a rebellion,
Yàntōng was serving as magistrate of Wǔláo.
The local people wanted to kill him
to respond to the righteous banner.
Yàntōng learned of this beforehand
and threw himself down from the city wall.
The rebels drew their swords and pursued him.
Ahead was a deep ravine.
Pressed urgently, he leaped into it,
and it was as if someone caught his right arm
and placed him on a flat rock,
completely unharmed.
A voice in the air said:
"This is due to your recitation of the scripture;
therefore, you may return home."
The arm that had been caught
had a wondrous fragrant aura,
which did not fade for several days.
Later, he attained the position of a regional governor,
and died at over ninety years of age.
From the Bàoyìng Jì.
Dù Zhīliàng
Du Zhīliàng of the Suí dynasty,
during the Rénshòu era, served as a military advisor in the retinue of Prince Hàn, Liàng.
Later, Liàng raised troops in Bīngzhōu to rebel,
but was defeated.
Zhīliàng and his fellow officials were all imprisoned.
Zhīliàng was terrified,
weeping day and night.
Suddenly, one night he dreamed of a monk who said:
"If you just recite the Diamond Sutra,
you can pass through this calamity."
At dawn,
he immediately took the sutra
and devotedly practiced reciting it.
When the officials in charge led them all out for execution,
Zhīliàng was among them.
As names were called out, all died,
but only Zhīliàng's name was not called.
The officials in charge were all punished for their errors.
Soon after, a general pardon was issued, and he was spared.
During the Xiǎnqìng era,
he died while serving as Governor of Huángzhōu.
From "Records of Retribution."
Mùróng Wéncè
Mùróng Wéncè was a man of the Suí dynasty.
He constantly upheld the Diamond Sutra
and did not consume alcohol or meat.
In the seventh year of the Dàyè era, he died suddenly,
but revived after three days,
saying:
"At first, I saw two ghosts
holding a document,
chasing me to a city gate,
which looked extremely stern and imposing.
After entering and walking four or five li,
I saw a palace with feathered guards.
A king was sitting in the main hall,
with monks, Daoists, and people from the four barbarian regions
too numerous to count.
The messengers entered for an audience.
Wéncè was at the very back.
One by one, they were asked what good or evil they had done in life,
and were ordered to stand to the east or west accordingly.
Then Wéncè's name was called,
and he was asked:
"What good deeds have you done?"
He replied:
"Since youth, I have upheld the Diamond Sutra."
Hearing this, the king
placed his palms together and sighed, saying:
"Your merit is very great.
We shall release you for now."
Suddenly, he saw two monks
holding torches to guide Wéncè.
He immediately grabbed the corner of their kasayas and asked them.
The monks said:
"Because you uphold the sutra,
we have come to protect you.
You may follow the torchlight."
They then exited the city gate.
The monks said:
"Do you know where the hells are?"
Pointing to a large city gate, they said:
"That is it."
Wéncè could not bear to look
and begged to leave quickly.
The two monks then led him to a path.
There was a horizontal wall blocking the way.
The monks tapped it with their staffs,
and it immediately opened.
They said:
"You may go from here."
He then revived.
From "Records of Retribution."
Liǔ Jiǎn
Liǔ Jiǎn, the Sīmǎ of Xíngzhōu in the Táng dynasty,
in the tenth year of the Suí Dàyè era, served as Supervisor of the Qíyáng Palace in Qízhōu.
In the first year of the Yìníng era,
he was imprisoned in the Dàlǐ Temple on false charges.
Jiǎn devotedly recited the Diamond Prajñā Sutra.
There were two pages he had not yet mastered,
and he unintentionally fell asleep.
He dreamed of a Brahmin monk who told him:
"Benefactor, you should recite the sutra until it is complete;
then you should be able to leave."
Jiǎn suddenly awoke
and diligently recited without ceasing. After two days,
an imperial edict suddenly summoned him,
and he was released at the court hall.
Another time, when Jiǎn was reciting the sutra late at night until the third watch,
he suddenly smelled an extraordinary fragrance
that filled his entire residence,
lasting until dawn without dissipating.
This was likely caused by a spiritual response.
By the end of his life,
Jiǎn had recited the sutra over five thousand times in total.
From "The Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma."
Xiāo Yǔ,
a descendant of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
was the son of King Kuī of Liáng.
After Liáng was destroyed, he entered Suí service,
rising to the position of Zhōngshū Lìng
and was enfeoffed as Duke of Sòng.
His daughter was the empress of Emperor Yáng.
He was a devout believer in Buddhism
and often upheld the Diamond Sutra.
When he opposed the plan to attack Gāolì,
it did not accord with the emperor's wishes,
and the emperor was greatly angered.
He was imprisoned together with Hé Ruòbì and Gāo Jiǒng,
with the intent to execute them according to law.
While in confinement,
Yǔ recited the Diamond Sutra seven hundred times over eight days.
The next day,
his shackles suddenly fell off by themselves.
The guards were alarmed,
and put them back on him.
When brought before the court,
Yǔ alone was pardoned,
while the other two were severely punished.
Consequently, he wrote "Eighteen Instances of Spiritual Efficacy of the Prajñā Sutra"
and built a precious pagoda to store the sutra.
It was made of sandalwood
and was three chǐ high.
He was moved by a brass statue
that suddenly appeared in the courtyard.
He enshrined it in the pagoda
and obtained one hundred śarīra relics.
In the eleventh year of the Zhēnguān era,
he saw the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra
gradually moving westward and departing.
From "Records of Retribution."
Zhào Wénxìn
Zhào Wénxìn, a man of Suízhōu in the Táng dynasty,
died suddenly in the first year of the Zhēnguān era,
but revived after three days.
He recounted himself, saying:
When he first died,
he was pushed and driven along by people.
There were ten companions in total,
and they followed one another to the court of King Yánluó.
Among them was a monk.
The king first asked him:
"Venerable, what merits did you cultivate in life?"
The monk replied:
"This humble monk
(Míng manuscript note: The three characters '道徒自' are written as '貧道從'.)
since birth,
has only recited the Diamond Prajñā Sutra."
Hearing this, the king
suddenly stood up in surprise,
placed his palms together, and praised:
"Excellent, excellent!
Venerable, if you truly recite the Prajñā,
you should ascend to heaven.
Why have you mistakenly come here?"
Before he finished speaking,
heavenly garments suddenly descended
and led the monk up to heaven.
The king then called the man from Suízhōu forward and said:
"What merits did you have in life?"
The man replied:
"Your subject, throughout life,
did not read Buddhist sutras,
but only enjoyed the collected writings of Yǔ Xìn."
The king said:
"Yǔ Xìn is a great sinner.
He is seen here suffering punishment.
Do you recognize Yǔ Xìn?"
He replied:
"Although I have read his writings,
I do not recognize the man himself."
The king then ordered Yǔ Xìn to be brought out.
He appeared in the body of a turtle.
The king ordered him taken away again.
After a short while, he returned in human form
and said:
"Because in life I enjoyed writing essays,
falsely citing Buddhist sutras,
mixing them with secular texts,
and also slandering the Buddhist Dharma,
claiming it was inferior to the teachings of Confucius and Lǎozi,
I now receive retribution in the body of a turtle.
It is suffering."
After this man revived,
he recounted the event in detail.
The people of Suízhōu were fond of hunting,
but upon hearing this account,
they took it as a warning to each other,
permanently ceasing the karma of killing.
Each developed a sincere heart,
accepted and upheld the Prajñā,
and this continues to this day.
From "The Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma."
Liú Bì
In the Táng dynasty, there was Liú Bì.
In the first year of the Zhēnguàn era, he served as the county captain of Jiāngnán County.
Suddenly one day,
a crow cawed on a tree in front of his room.
The local people said:
"Where this crow perches is inauspicious."
Upon hearing this, Bì became fearful
and thought of cultivating merit and virtue,
but did not know which practice would be most effective.
That night, he dreamed of a monk
who highly praised the Diamond Sūtra,
instructing him to recite it a hundred times.
Upon waking,
he followed the command and immediately recited it until he reached a hundred times.
Suddenly, a great wind
came from the northeast,
uprooted that tree,
and flung it far beyond the houses into an alley,
leaving a pit in the ground where it was uprooted,
measuring fifteen feet in length and width.
Observing the path from which the violent wind came,
the small branches and delicate leaves
all bent and swayed with the wind,
and when the wind stopped, they stood upright again as before.
Only then did he realize that the power of the sūtra is inconceivable.
From the Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Yuán Zhìtōng
In the Táng dynasty, there was Yuán Zhìtōng,
a native of Tiānshuǐ,
who often upheld the Diamond Sūtra.
At the age of twenty,
he was conscripted as a soldier.
Defeated, he fled to steep cliffs,
and for days he could not obtain food.
Then he perceived two youths
bringing him a bowl full of rice.
Zhìtōng bowed,
and they suddenly vanished.
After he finished eating,
he did not feel hungry for several days.
Later, he managed to return to his hometown.
In the eighth year of the Zhēnguàn era, he fell ill and died,
but revived after two days,
saying:
"I was led to see the King,
who asked about the good deeds I had done in life.
I replied:
'I often upheld the Diamond Sūtra.'
The King was very pleased and said:
'For now, have him escorted back.'
Thus I came back to life."
From the Bàoyìng Jì.
Wéi Kèqín
In the Táng dynasty, Wéi Kèqín upheld the Diamond Sūtra from a young age.
He served as a lieutenant general
and joined the army to campaign against Liáo,
but was captured in Gāolì.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
when Emperor Tàizōng campaigned against Liáo,
Kèqín, who had upheld the Diamond Sūtra since youth,
saw the imperial troops
and came out at night to surrender to them.
In the darkness, he did not know the way,
so he wholeheartedly recited the sūtra.
Suddenly, he saw a torchlight guiding the way ahead.
Kèqín followed the fire
and thus reached the Hàn army.
From the Bàoyìng Jì.
Shěn Jiāhuì
In the Táng dynasty, there was Shěn Jiāhuì.
During the Zhēnguàn era, he served as a proofreader
but was exiled to Lánzhōu due to some matter.
He longed deeply to return home,
and every morning and evening,
he would bow toward the east to Tàishān,
praying to be able to return alive.
This continued for over two hundred days.
On the night of the third day of the tenth month in the sixth year of the Yǒnghuī era,
he saw two youths
of elegant appearance and attire,
who said they were sons of the Lord of Tàishān.
The Lord was moved by your daily worship and reverence,
so he sent us to welcome you."
Jiāhuì said:
"Tàishān is over three thousand lǐ away;
how can I go there?"
The youths said:
"Close your eyes, sir,
and do not worry about the distance."
He followed their words,
and in an instant, he arrived.
The palace was grand and magnificent.
The youths led him in to pay his respects.
The Lord then invited him into an inner chamber,
where they sat facing each other, chatting and laughing.
There was nothing the Lord did not know.
He said to Jiāhuì:
"When people commit evil,
if they are not punished by others while alive,
after death, they will inevitably be seized and judged by ghosts,
with no chance of escaping punishment.
But if one recites the Diamond Sūtra once daily,
all sins will be eradicated,
and ghost officials will be unable to detain you."
He also said:
"The previous Lord committed an error,
so the celestial court dismissed him.
My surname is Liú."
Jiāhuì did not dare to ask about other matters.
The Lord once played backgammon with Jiāhuì
and also served wine and food.
Jiāhuì rose
and saw in the small hall to the east, the magistrate of Gūzāng, Mùróng Rénguǐ, holding a tablet and sitting upright.
He said:
"I was summoned here by the Lord's order,
and it has been sixty days,
yet I have not received any judgment."
Jiāhuì sat down and reported this to the Lord,
who then summoned Rénguǐ in.
He said to him:
"In your county, there was a woman named Ā Zhào
who was unjustly tortured to death by the county captain.
Ā Zhào came to lodge a complaint,
and as a result, you were mistakenly summoned."
In front of the courtyard, there was a basin of water.
The Lord instructed him to wash his face,
and then sent a youth to escort him back.
Jiāhuì also took his leave.
The Lord again sent two youths to escort him.
He spent a total of twenty-eight days in Tàishān.
His family only noticed that his spirit seemed dull and confused,
but after his return, he was as before.
Jiāhuì spoke of Rénguǐ's matter to others.
The senior official Zhào Chímǎn sent someone to verify it,
and everything matched.
From then on, Jiāhuì often upheld the Diamond Sūtra,
and he was pardoned and allowed to return home.
From the Bàoyìng Jì.
Lù Huáisù
In the Táng dynasty, Lù Huáisù of Wújùn
experienced a fire in the twentieth year of the Zhēnguàn era.
The buildings were burned,
and everything turned to ashes,
but only the Diamond Sūtra remained intact.
The case and the scroll rods were completely destroyed,
yet the characters of the sūtra remained as before.
Those who heard of this were all astonished.
Huáisù was the elder brother of the wife of Xǔ Rénzé of Gāoyáng.
Rénzé witnessed it at the time
and often spoke of it to others.
From the Míngbào Jì.
Sīmǎ Qiáoqīng
In the Táng dynasty, Sīmǎ Qiáoqīng of Hénèi, a judicial officer of the Dàlǐ Temple,
was by nature pure and cautious,
with lofty aspirations and conduct.
During the Yǒnghuī era,
he served as the household registrar of Yángzhōu.
When his mother passed away,
he observed mourning, becoming emaciated to the bone.
He pricked his blood to copy two scrolls of the Diamond Sūtra.
Not long after,
two stalks of auspicious fungus grew beside his mourning hut.
In nine days, they grew to one foot eight inches in length,
with green stems and red caps.
Each day, they exuded a sheng of juice, which he consumed;
it tasted as sweet as honey.
After he took it, it would grow again.
Several of Qiáoqīng's colleagues witnessed this event.
From the Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Sūn Shòu
During the Xiǎnqìng era of the Táng dynasty,
Sūn Shòu of Píngzhōu was hunting by the seaside
when he encountered a wildfire.
The grass and trees were all burned away.
Only one thick patch of lush grass
remained unburned.
Suspecting that some animal might be hiding in the grass,
he tried to ignite it with fire,
but it would not catch.
Shòu found this very strange.
He entered the grass to investigate
and found a case containing the Diamond Sūtra.
Beside it was also a dead monk,
whose complexion remained unchanged.
The fire did not spread and burn the area
because of this.
Only then did he realize that sūtras and images are beyond ordinary comprehension.
Sūn Shòu personally recounted this.
From the Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Lǐ Guān
Lǐ Guān of Lǒngxī in the Táng dynasty,
during the Xiǎnqìng era, resided in Xíngyáng.
When mourning his father's passing,
he pricked his finger to write in blood one scroll each of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Heart Sūtra and the Sutra of Rebirth According to One's Vows.
Afterwards, an extraordinary fragrance constantly filled his courtyard,
exceptionally rich and intense,
and neighbors nearby often smelled it as well,
all praising and marveling at it.
Zhōngshān's Láng Xú
(The Míng manuscript copies record "Xú" as "Yú").
While passing through Zhèngzhōu,
he met his relatives and friends there,
and recounted the matter in detail.
From the "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín".
Dòulú Fūrén
The wife of Duke Dòu of the Chén state during the Táng dynasty, née Dòulú,
was the elder sister of Duke Ruì, Kuān.
The lady believed in karma and retribution,
and often recited the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Once, when she had not yet finished about a sheet's worth of the scroll,
she suddenly had a headache,
which grew worse by night.
The lady thought to herself,
"If I die, I won't be able to finish the sutra,"
and wanted to get up to recite it.
She ordered a maid to light a candle,
but all the fire had already gone out.
The maid returned empty-handed,
and the lady sighed with deep regret.
Suddenly, she saw a candle torch in the kitchen,
gradually ascending the hall steps,
directly entering her bedroom,
hovering about three feet above the ground,
with no one holding it,
its light as bright as day.
The lady was pleasantly surprised,
took the sutra, and recited it.
After a while,
the household managed to drill for fire and obtain it,
and the candlelight immediately went out.
From then on, she recited the sutra five times daily,
making it her regular practice.
Later, when Duke Ruì was about to die,
the lady went to see him.
The duke said to the lady:
"My elder sister, due to the merit of reciting the sutra,
will live to be a hundred years old,
and be reborn in a good place."
The lady lived to the age of eighty,
and passed away without illness.
From the "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín".
Nun Xiūxíng
In the first year of the Lóngshuò era of the Táng dynasty,
in the room of Bhikṣuṇī Xiūxíng at Jǐngfú Temple in Luòzhōu,
there was a servant girl named Wǔ Wǔniáng.
After she died,
Xiūxíng set up a spirit seat for Wǔniáng.
Over a month later,
her elder sister and younger brother, in the middle of the night,
suddenly heard groaning from the spirit seat.
Her brother was initially very frightened,
but later asked about it.
She replied:
"When I was alive, I ate meat in the temple,
and because of this, I am suffering great pain.
I have sores on my body,
and I fear they will soil the bed matting.
You should spread plenty of ashes on the bed."
Her brother followed her words.
After placing the ashes,
he saw a great deal of pus and blood on the bed.
She also said to her brother:
"Your sister is unable to sew clothes due to her suffering.
You are too ragged.
You should bring some cloth,
and I will make a shirt and socks for you."
Her brother placed cloth on the spirit bed,
and by the next morning, it was already finished.
She also said to her elder sister:
"When I was young and had an illness,
I killed a crab,
took its juice to apply to the sore, and it healed.
Now I have fallen into the Knife-Forest Hell,
and in my flesh, I see seven broken knives.
I beg my sister, out of compassion,
to perform meritorious deeds to rescue me.
Sister, you are pressed for time,
and it is difficult to arrange things quickly,
but the clothes I wore in life,
are of no use to the dead.
They are still undamaged,
please use them for this purpose."
Before her sister could reply,
she said:
"I will take them myself."
After a long while, she said again:
"The clothes have been brought,
and are now on the bed."
Her sister went to look,
and indeed, they were the clothes she had been buried in.
She then sent them to Master Bǎo Xiàn at Jìngtǔ Temple,
to commission the copying of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Each time a scroll was finished,
she would report:
"One knife has been removed."
After all seven scrolls were finished,
she said:
"All seven knives have now been removed,
and I am now blessed by this meritorious deed.
I will now go to be reborn."
She bade farewell with tears to her sister and brother,
and departed.
Shěn Xuánfǎ of Wúxīng recounted this,
and Monk Zhì Zhěng of Jìngtǔ Temple told the same story.
From the "Míngbào Jì".
Chén Wéndá
Chén Wéndá of the Táng dynasty,
was a native of Qī County, Zǐzhōu.
He often upheld the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
and vowed to recite it 84,000 times for his deceased parents.
There were many auspicious signs.
When he recited the sutra on behalf of others,
their difficulties were all averted.
Chén Yuē of Tóngshān County was once summoned by the underworld officials.
He saw a platform being built underground,
and asked about it.
They said:
"This is the Prajñā Platform,
awaiting Chén Wéndá."
Such was the respect he commanded from the underworld officials.
From the "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín".
Gāo Zhǐ,
was the grandson of Suí Dynasty's Vice Director Yǐng.
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era of the Táng dynasty,
he exited Cháng'ān through the Shùnyì Gate,
when he suddenly encountered two men on horseback,
who said:
"The King summons you."
Zhǐ refused to go with them,
not knowing they were ghost messengers.
He whipped his horse to avoid them,
but was again driven and surrounded.
Zhǐ had an elder brother,
who was a monk at Huàdù Temple.
He wanted to go into the temple,
but upon reaching the temple gate,
the ghosts blocked him from entering.
Zhǐ then punched one of the ghosts.
The ghost, enraged,
immediately dragged him off his horse,
saying:
"This fellow is terribly fierce and rough!"
He then fell to the ground,
and lost consciousness.
The temple monks had him carried into his brother's courtyard.
The next morning, he revived,
and said:
Initially, he followed the two messengers to see the King.
The King said:
"It is not yet your time to come.
You once slandered the Buddha-Dharma,
so we shall now make you suffer the consequences while alive."
He ordered his attendants to pull out his tongue,
and plow it with a plowshare,
but it was completely unharmed.
The King asked the official in charge:
"What merit does he possess to be like this?"
He replied:
"He once recited the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra."
The King praised this,
and immediately ordered him released.
Later, while speaking with a guest,
in the middle of conversation, he suddenly collapsed in distress,
as if swallowing something.
A white streak appeared below his throat,
flowing into his abdomen.
This happened three times.
People asked him about it.
He said:
"In my youth, I stole and ate fruit from the temple.
The underworld officials are punishing me by making me swallow iron pellets."
Later, he served as an Imperial Guard,
and devoted himself entirely to reciting the sutra.
From the "Bàoyìng Jì".
Bái Rénxī
During the Táng dynasty, Bái Rénxī
in the Lóngshuò era served as the deputy magistrate of Zhūyáng in Guó Prefecture.
He was assigned to transport rice to Liáodōng.
While crossing the sea, he encountered a storm.
Looking around, all was dark.
Rénxī was worried and afraid,
so he urgently recited the Diamond Sutra,
reaching three hundred repetitions.
Suddenly, as if in a dream,
he saw a Buddhist monk
who said to him:
"Because you recited the true sutra,
I have come to save you."
In a moment, the wind calmed,
and over eighty people were all saved.
From "Records of Retribution."
Dòu Déxuán,
during the Líndé era, served as a minister
and was sent on a mission to Yángzhōu.
While crossing the Huái River,
after the boat had left the shore several dozen paces,
he saw a person on the bank
who looked haggard and worn,
holding a small bundle and sitting on the ground.
Déxuán said:
"Night is falling,
and there are no more boats to cross."
He then ordered the boat to carry him.
Midway, noticing the man looked hungry,
he also gave him food.
They then crossed.
When Déxuán mounted his horse to leave,
the man followed him,
already for several miles.
Déxuán found this strange
and asked:
"Where are you going now?"
The man replied:
"I am not human;
I am a ghost messenger.
I am now going to Yángzhōu
to pursue Ambassador Dòu."
Déxuán asked:
"What is the ambassador's name?"
The man said:
"His name is Déxuán."
Déxuán was shocked and afraid.
He dismounted, bowed, and said:
"I am that person."
Weeping, he begged for a plan.
The ghost said:
"I am very grateful for your kindness in giving me passage
and also for offering me food.
I will let you go for now.
Quickly recite the Diamond Sutra one thousand times,
and I will come to report back."
After over a month,
when the recitations were completed,
the ghost indeed returned
and said:
"The sutra recitations are sufficient.
You are assured no other worries,
but you must still eventually follow me to see the king."
Déxuán then lay on his pillow and died,
but revived after one night.
He said:
Initially, following the messenger, he entered a palace city.
The messenger said:
"Please wait here;
I will first inform the king."
The messenger then entered.
From behind a screen,
he heard the king speak from afar:
"You made plans with him
and leaked my affairs,
so you shall receive thirty strokes."
The messenger came back out,
bared his back to show Déxuán and said:
"I have been beaten."
Déxuán repeatedly expressed shame and gratitude.
He was then led inside.
He saw a person wearing purple robes
who came down the steps to greet him
and said:
"You have great merit and virtue.
It is not yet your time to come.
Please return."
He fell into a pit
and thus came back to life.
The messenger later arrived
and said:
"I am hungry and have not eaten,
and I also beg for money."
Déxuán gave him both.
He asked about his future official ranks,
and the messenger said:
"Remember carefully:
from this, you will change to Diànzhōng Jiān,
then Dà Sīxiàn,
then Tàizǐ Zhōngyǔn,
then Sīyuán Tàicháng Bó,
then Zuǒ Xiàng,
and your age will reach sixty-four."
After speaking, he bid farewell and left,
saying:
"I will not be able to come again."
Later, everything happened as he said.
From "Records of Retribution."
Sòng Yìlún
During the Táng dynasty, Sòng Yìlún
served as Diǎnqiān for the Prince of Guó during the Líndé era.
He died suddenly
and revived after three days,
saying:
He had been summoned to see the king.
The king said:
"You once killed dogs, rabbits, and pigeons.
Now you are being judged.
Your allotted lifespan should be exhausted.
However, I just saw your master say:
'You recite the Diamond Sutra.
Not only does it eliminate sins,
but it also extends your years.'
I now release you.
Can you abstain from wine and meat
and uphold and recite the revered sutra?"
Yìlún bowed in gratitude and said:
"I can."
He also saw inside the hall, on a bed,
a monk about fifty or sixty years old,
wearing a patched robe.
Yìlún immediately bowed in reverence.
The monk said:
"I am your teacher,
so I came to save you.
You must follow the king's words."
Yìlún said:
"Yes."
The king ordered him to follow a messenger to see the hells.
Entering the first place,
he saw large cauldrons arranged in rows,
with fires burning beneath them.
People were boiling in the cauldrons,
