their sounds of pain
all heart-wrenching.
Entering another place,
there were very wide iron beds.
People lay on them,
burned and charred black,
their appearances unrecognizable.
Looking west, he saw three people,
withered and black, standing still,
rather resembling women.
They kowtowed to Yìlún and said:
"We have not had food to eat
for several hundred years."
Yìlún replied:
"I myself have none;
how could I give you any?"
Entering another hell,
he said to the messenger:
"It is getting late;
I fear my family will see me being encoffined."
So they left.
Walking southwest several dozen paces,
he was called from behind:
"Without a document,
I fear the gatekeeper will not let you out."
He then received three lines written in red,
but he could not read the characters.
The gatekeeper indeed questioned him,
looked at it, and let him out.
He then revived.
From "Records of Retribution."
Lǐ Gāng
Lǐ Gāng, the Minister of War of the Tang dynasty, fell ill and died suddenly,
with only his heart remaining warm.
After three days, he revived,
and said
he saw a person who led him to see a great general,
who ordered him to be seated.
The general searched for the case file and looked at it,
then said:
"We have mistakenly pursued you, sir."
After a while,
a prison guard brought in a tray,
on which were placed several iron pellets.
They also carried a cauldron and placed it in the courtyard,
where a fire naturally ignited beneath it,
and molten copper bubbled and boiled inside.
The iron pellets were cooked,
turning red as fire,
and the prison guard presented the tray.
The general offered it to Lǐ Gāng,
but Lǐ Gāng, terrified, said he was full.
The general then swallowed them himself;
as soon as they entered his mouth,
his entire body became transparent;
he then drank the molten copper,
and his body burst into flames.
In the time it took to bow and rise,
he had consumed everything,
and after a long while, he returned to his original state.
Lǐ Gāng then stepped forward and asked him about it,
and he replied:
"In the underworld, there is no other food,
only this thing,
so I consume it.
If I do not eat it,
in an instant, I will be burned by fierce flames,
which is even more painful than this.
If only you would copy ten volumes of Buddhist sutras
and recite the Diamond Sutra a thousand times,
you would not have to come here,
and I could also leave this place."
After Lǐ Gāng revived,
he strictly followed the agreement,
and deeply revered and marveled at it.
From "Records of Retribution"
Wáng Tuó
Wáng Tuó of the Tang dynasty served as Guǒyì in the Yīngyáng Prefecture.
Due to illness, he abstained from meat,
and resolved to recite the Diamond Sutra,
five times a day.
Later, he contracted a miasmic disease,
and saw a group of ghosts approaching.
Wáng Tuó immediately recited the sutra urgently.
Upon hearing it, the ghosts retreated,
and from afar, they said:
"The King has ordered us to pursue you;
stop reciting the sutra for now."
Wáng Tuó then stopped,
and the ghosts all advanced,
causing Wáng Tuó to fall into a coma, nearly dying.
After a moment, another ghost arrived and said:
"Reciter of the sutra,
the King has ordered a temporary reprieve of six months for you."
After waking,
he devoted himself wholeheartedly to reciting the sutra,
without ceasing day or night.
Although the six months passed,
the ghosts did not return.
At night, he heard a voice from the sky calling out:
"Due to the merit of your recitation of the sutra,
you shall live to be ninety years old."
In the end, it happened as the voice said.
From "Records of Retribution"
Wáng Lìngwàng
Wáng Lìngwàng of the Tang dynasty recited the Diamond Sutra from a young age.
While returning to Línxī in Qióngzhōu,
the road was extremely treacherous,
when he suddenly encountered a fierce beast,
and was terrified beyond measure.
He urgently recited the true sutra,
and the fierce beast stared intently,
then dragged its tail and left,
leaving saliva all over the ground.
He once served as Pànsī in Ānzhōu,
and while crossing the Yángzǐ River,
a storm arose at night,
and several hundred rental boats,
connected to each other, all sank,
but only Wáng Lìngwàng's boat remained intact.
Later, he ended his life as the magistrate of Qiáo County in Bózhōu.
From "Records of Retribution"
Chén Huì's Wife
Wáng shì, the wife of Chén Huì of the Tang dynasty, before she was married,
her cousin Chǔ Jìng wanted to marry her,
but her parents did not allow it.
Chǔ Jìng cursed, saying:
"If you do not marry me,
I will become a ghost,
and I will surely come for you."
Later, she married Chén Huì.
Chén Huì served as Rénshòu Deputy in Língzhōu,
and Chǔ Jìng secretly resented him.
After Chǔ Jìng died,
Wáng shì dreamed of him,
and soon realized she was pregnant,
but after seventeen months, she had not given birth.
Wáng shì was worried and afraid,
so she resolved to recite the Diamond Sutra,
without ceasing day or night.
Chǔ Jìng then ceased all contact forever,
the ghostly fetus also dissolved,
and from then on, she recited it seven times a day.
From "Records of Retribution"
Hé Hùn
Hé Hùn of the Tang dynasty,
during the early Tiānshòu era, served as magistrate of Wǔdé in Huáizhōu,
and often recited the Diamond Sutra.
When he reached Héyáng,
the water had risen and the bridge had collapsed.
It was already evening,
and people were scrambling to board boats.
The shore was far, and before they could reach it,
they were about to sink.
Hé Hùn was terrified,
and urgently recited the sutra.
In a moment, they approached the shore,
encountered hanging reeds,
and climbed out to safety.
More than eighty others drowned.
From "Records of Retribution"
Zhāng Xuánsù
Zhāng Xuánsù of the Tang dynasty,
a native of Luòyáng,
recited the Diamond Sutra from a young age.
During the early Tiānshòu era,
he served as magistrate of Huángméi.
Whenever his family faced calamity,
it would dissipate upon his recitation.
At the age of seventy, he fell ill,
when suddenly a flowery canopy descended from the sky.
He then bathed,
bid farewell to his family,
and passed away peacefully.
From "Records of Retribution"
Lǐ Qiūyī
In the Táng dynasty, Lǐ Qiūyī was fond of falcons, hounds, and hunting.
In the first year of the Wànsuì Tōngtiān era,
he served as Assistant Magistrate of Gāoyóu in Yángzhōu.
Suddenly one morning, he died abruptly.
He saw two men coming to apprehend him,
one of whom said his surname was Duàn.
At that time, over a hundred others were also being apprehended,
the men all wearing cangues,
and the women bound with their hands behind their backs.
Qiūyī, locked in fetters, was driven forward.
After walking about ten-some *lǐ*,
they saw several dozen large locust trees,
under which were horse troughs.
Duàn said:
"The Great God of the Five Paths, whenever he inspects the sins and blessings in the human realm,
rests his horse here."
Only then did Qiūyī realize he was dead.
Arriving at the King's gate,
Duàn pointed to a clerk and said:
"This man's surname is Jiāo, given name Cè,
and he is your case officer."
Thereupon, Qiūyī was led in for an audience.
The King said:
"How could you be so cruel and heartless,
taking pleasure in killing other lives
for your own amusement?"
After a moment,
he saw all the birds and beasts he had killed speaking in human language:
"We beg for an early judgment."
Jiāo Cè stepped forward and said:
"Qiūyī should not yet die."
The King asked:
"What meritorious deeds has he performed?"
He replied:
"He only once copied one scroll of the *Diamond Sūtra*."
The King immediately joined his palms and said:
"In the underworld, the *Diamond Sūtra* is hailed as the supreme meritorious deed.
Since you were able to copy it,
the blessings are not small."
He then ordered Jiāo Cè to lead Qiūyī to the scripture repository
to verify it.
They arrived at a treasure hall,
filled with numerous scriptures.
Qiūyī tried pulling out one scroll,
and indeed it was the scripture he had copied.
After returning to see the King,
who knew the copying was genuine,
he summoned all the killed creatures
and ordered Qiūyī to earnestly apologize
and promise to perform meritorious deeds.
Following the King's command,
Qiūyī vowed to copy the *Diamond Sūtra* one hundred times.
The creatures, overjoyed, all dispersed.
The King said:
"Release him."
Jiāo Cè led him out of the city gate
and said:
"I have exerted myself so much for you;
surely you will repay me?"
Qiūyī offered three hundred thousand cash,
but he would not accept it,
saying:
"Copy twenty sets of the scripture for me."
They came to a pit,
Cè pushed him,
and he revived.
His body was in a coffin;
he only heard crying sounds.
Three days had already passed.
He cried out in alarm, and people came.
They broke open the coffin, and he rose.
After ten days,
he finished copying twenty scrolls of the scripture.
Jiāo Cè came to thank him,
expressed his gratitude, and left.
Soon, the hundred scrolls were also completed.
The Governor of Yángzhōu reported the matter,
and by imperial decree, Qiūyī was promoted to the fifth rank
and additionally appointed as Pacification Commissioner of Jiāzhōu.
From *Records of Retribution*.
Yú Chǎng
In the Táng dynasty, Yú Chǎng
served as Records Administrator of Bīngzhōu during Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign.
Every day after the first watch,
he would pant and sweat profusely,
and it would worsen after the second watch.
His wife, Liǔ shì, wanted to summon a physician,
but Chǎng secretly told her:
"I have no other ailment;
it is only because I handle official duties during the day
and judge cases in the underworld at night,
that my strength cannot bear it."
Whenever he knew of impending disasters or misfortunes,
he would secretly make preparations,
never speaking of it openly.
This continued for six years.
Later, during his mother's mourning period,
he upheld the *Diamond Sūtra*,
and no longer served as an underworld official.
Thereupon, he earnestly spoke of the power of this meritorious deed,
instructing his descendants to recite and circulate it.
Later, he served as Military Administrator of Qìngzhōu.
At age eighty-four,
as he was about to pass away,
he suddenly smelled an extraordinary fragrance,
unlike any in this world.
He said to those around him:
"A sage is welcoming me to the Western Paradise."
Having spoken, he passed away.
From *Records of Retribution*.
Péi Xuānlǐ
In the Táng dynasty, Péi Xuānlǐ
served as Vice Minister of Revenue during Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign.
He constantly upheld the *Diamond Sūtra*.
Implicated in a case, he was imprisoned.
Xuānlǐ, anxious and distressed,
only wholeheartedly recited the scripture.
Suddenly one day, his cangue and fetters fell off by themselves.
The investigating officer personally visited him,
and he was subsequently cleared and released.
Censor Rèn Zhí, imprisoned together with him,
also recited the scripture and was spared.
From *Records of Retribution*.
Wú Sīxuán
In the Táng dynasty, Wú Sīxuán
served as Erudite of the Grand Academy during Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign.
He believed in Buddhism.
He upheld the *Diamond Sūtra*, reciting it twice daily,
and experienced many spiritual responses.
Later, he became somewhat negligent,
reciting only once per day.
□□□ Sīxuán fell ill in the capital.
There was a shaman named Chǔ Xì'ér who spoke of matters as if divinely inspired,
and people prayed under the stars.
Sīxuán went to see him.
Xì'ér exclaimed in surprise:
"What art do you possess,
that ghosts flee at the sight of you?"
Sīxuán privately reflected
and knew it was the power of the scripture.
He redoubled his diligence,
reciting it five times daily.
When his elder brother fell ill,
and medicine proved ineffective,
Sīxuán wholeheartedly recited the scripture,
and in three days, he recovered.
Sīxuán once saw an old man on the Wèi Bridge,
over eighty years old,
wearing coarse mourning garments.
He asked him about it,
and the man replied:
"It is for my birth mother."
Sīxuán found it strange,
and the man answered:
"When my mother was forty-three,
an extraordinary monk taught her, saying:
'Do you wish for long life?
Just recite the *Diamond Sūtra*.'
My mother then resolved to do so,
reciting it twice daily,
and lived to one hundred and seven.
My aunt and a neighboring mother also recited it,
and both lived past one hundred.
Now I follow my mother's practice.
I am already ninety."
From *Records of Retribution*.
The Old Man of Yínshān
At Yínshān in Ráozhōu,
there were over ten thousand mining households,
all living in thatched huts.
During the Yánhé era, a fire broke out,
and ten thousand homes were completely destroyed.
Only one household in the center
was untouched by the fire.
At the time, Yáng Tǐjī of the prefecture personally questioned the old man of that household.
The old man replied:
"My family serves the Buddha and upholds the *Diamond Sūtra*."
From *Records of Retribution*.
Cuī Wénjiǎn
Cuī Wénjiǎn of the Táng dynasty,
during the Xiāntiān era, served as Sīmǎ of Fǎngzhōu.
When the Tibetans suddenly arrived at the prefectural city,
he was captured along with others,
and his shackles were extremely tight.
He wholeheartedly recited the sūtra,
and after three days,
the shackles suddenly opened by themselves.
The captors suspected trickery,
flogged him,
and he truthfully explained everything.
They asked:
"What magic do you possess?"
He replied:
"I recite the Diamond Sūtra."
They ordered him shackled again,
but before he finished reciting, they came loose once more.
Everyone marveled in astonishment,
and they subsequently sent him beyond the border.
From "Records of Retribution"
Yáo Dài
Yáo Dài of the Táng dynasty,
a native of Zǐzhōu,
often recited the Diamond Sūtra,
and also commissioned one hundred copies for his mother.
Suddenly, a deer approached tamely to play,
unafraid upon seeing people,
and dogs did not bark at it either.
It lingered awhile before leaving on its own.
Someone slaughtered a sheep,
invited Dài to eat together,
and after eating, he died.
An escort led him away,
and he saw a city gate with an inscribed plaque above.
He was then ordered to enter and see the King.
The King demanded to know why he had eaten meat,
and Dài said:
"Although I ate meat,
I originally recited the sūtra."
The King praised this,
saying:
"Since you can recite the sūtra,
why not abstain from meat?"
He was thus allowed to return to life,
and he copied sūtras for his mother.
A butcher named Lí Huínú requested one volume,
burned incense, and made offerings to it.
After Huínú died,
someone saw him in the underworld,
his shackles having fallen off by themselves,
and he was also reborn into a favorable path.
From "Records of Retribution"
Lǚ Wénzhǎn
Lǚ Wénzhǎn of the Táng dynasty,
in the third year of the Kāiyuán era, served as Deputy Magistrate of Làngzhōng County.
He was fond of Buddhist sūtras,
and especially devoted himself to reciting the Diamond Sūtra,
reaching over thirty thousand repetitions,
with miraculous and extraordinary spiritual responses.
In his old age,
three of his teeth fell out.
He earnestly prayed while reciting the sūtra,
and his teeth grew back as before.
While in Làngzhōng,
during a severe drought,
Prefect Liú Jùn ordered him to pray for rain.
After reciting just one repetition,
abundant rain poured down.
Also, during continuous heavy rains,
the Assistant Prefect ordered him to pray for clear skies,
and the skies cleared immediately.
There were many such verifications before and after,
too numerous to list entirely.
From "Records of Retribution"
A Prisoner in Cháng'ān County
A death-row prisoner in Cháng'ān County during the Táng dynasty,
after more than forty days in prison,
incessantly recited the Diamond Sūtra.
When about to be executed, his shackles were removed,
and light emanated from the shackles,
extending several dozen zhàng in length,
illuminating the entire county.
The County Magistrate reported this to the emperor,
and Emperor Xuánzōng subsequently pardoned his crime.
From "Extensive Records of the Extraordinary"
Lǐ Xū
In the fifteenth year of the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
an imperial decree ordered that all village shrines and Buddhist chapels;
the smaller ones were to be demolished,
and their merits transferred to nearby Buddhist temples;
the larger chapels
were all to be sealed shut.
Unbelievers across the land,
following the trend, destroyed and dismantled them;
even large buildings and large statues
were damaged and ruined.
When the decree reached Yùzhōu,
Lǐ Xū, the magistrate of Xīnxì County, who was fond of drink and stubbornly defiant,
acted in violation and opposition.
He was just drunk when the prefectural order arrived,
and it still demanded a report within three days.
Seeing this, Lǐ Xū became furious,
and immediately bound the clerks and officials,
decreeing that anyone within his jurisdiction who destroyed or dismantled [shrines] would be put to death.
Thus, the entire area under his jurisdiction was preserved intact.
Lǐ Xū, as a person,
was fond of killing, obstinate, and perverse;
his actions invariably went against the Way.
At the time, it was not out of pity for Buddhist buildings that he acted,
but merely out of anger at the deadline that he preserved them;
and having preserved them, he did not take it to heart either.
A little over a year later,
Lǐ Xū fell ill,
and died after a few days.
It was the height of summer then,
and he was encoffined the next day.
The following day, as they were about to hold the funeral,
his mother and son wept around the coffin.
Late into the night, the weeping ceased,
and they heard from within the coffin a sound like fingernails scratching against the wood.
At first they suspected rats,
and did not realize the truth.
Soon it grew more intense,
and his wife and son fled in alarm.
Only his mother did not leave;
she ordered the coffin opened.
Those around her said:
"In the summer heat, it might have decomposed."
The mother grew angry,
and urged them to open it,
and Lǐ Xū came back to life.
His body was quite ulcerated and festering,
so they bathed him and nursed him back to health;
in over a month, he recovered.
Lǐ Xū said:
Initially, two guards seized me and brought me before the King;
the King was not present,
but I saw a clerk in front of the steps,
who turned out to be a clerk from Xīnxì,
deceased for over a year.
Upon seeing Lǐ Xū, he bowed and asked:
"How did you come here, Magistrate?"
Lǐ Xū said:
"I was just arrested and brought here."
The clerk said:
"Throughout your life, Magistrate,
you have only harbored a heart for killing and harm,
knowing neither sin nor blessing;
now you must face retribution—
what will you do!"
Hearing this, Lǐ Xū became afraid,
and begged for rescue.
The clerk said:
"Last year, when Buddhist chapels were being demolished,
within your jurisdiction alone they were preserved intact;
this merit is immense.
Even though you have died, Magistrate,
you should not have been summoned here.
In a moment, when the King questions you,
do not say anything more;
simply respond with this."
Only then did Lǐ Xū remember.
Shortly after, the King took his seat.
The officer in charge led Lǐ Xū to see the King.
The King said:
"Fetch the register of good and evil deeds for Magistrate Lǐ."
Immediately someone brought a large case,
as big as a person could embrace,
and two blue-clad boys also followed with the document case.
The King ordered the scroll opened and the sins proclaimed.
The clerk on the steps read:
"He particularly enjoyed cutting off sheep's legs."
The clerk said:
"He should receive one hundred strokes,
and also have a hundred catties of flesh cut from his body."
The King said:
"Let his flesh be cut."
Lǐ Xū said:
"Last year, there was a decree to demolish Buddhist chapels
and destroy Buddha statues;
within my jurisdiction alone they were preserved—
can this merit offset the sins?"
The King said in surprise:
"Is this truly so?"
The clerk said:
"No."
The Xīnxì clerk stepped forward and said:
"The register of blessings is in the heavenly hall;
it can be checked."
The King said:
"Check quickly."
South of the front wall of the hall, there were several buildings;
the clerk went up to the building to check,
but had not yet returned.
Two monks arrived before the hall.
The King asked what each master possessed,
one replied:
"I constantly recite the Diamond Sutra."
The other said:
"I constantly read the Diamond Sutra."
The King rose, joined his palms, and said:
"Please, Dharma Masters, ascend the steps."
Behind the King's seat,
there were two high seats,
gold on the right and silver on the left.
The King invited the reciter to sit on the gold seat,
and the reader to sit on the silver seat.
Once seated, they opened the sutra,
and the King listened with palms joined.
As the recitation and reading were about to conclude,
suddenly a five-colored cloud descended before the gold seat,
and a purple cloud before the silver seat.
The two monks rode the clouds and flew away,
vanishing into the sky.
The King said to those below the steps:
"Did you see the two monks?
They have both been reborn in heaven!"
Then the clerk arrived with the register of good deeds,
which consisted of only one sheet.
He then read:
"Last year, when the decree ordered the demolition of Buddhist chapels,
Xīnxì County alone preserved them intact.
This should offset the sins of one lifetime,
extend his life by thirty years,
and ensure rebirth in a favorable path."
When he finished speaking,
flames burst forth from the scroll of sins,
burning it completely to ashes.
The King said:
"Release Magistrate Lǐ and send him back."
He then ordered two clerks to escort him out through the southern city gate.
Along the road, he saw tall buildings and large houses on both sides,
with men and women sitting mingled together,
enjoying music, drinking, and singing.
Lǐ Xū loved string and wind music;
seeing this, he was delighted.
The two clerks said to him:
"Hurry past here without looking back;
looking back will bring harm."
But Lǐ Xū saw the drinking place,
and could not bear to walk on;
he stood still and watched.
Someone from the tavern called out:
"Come!"
The clerks said:
"This is not a good place;
since you do not heed our advice,
you may go as you wish."
Lǐ Xū, not yet understanding,
went to the drinking place.
The people there all stood up,
and he joined them, sitting down.
String and wind music played;
wine was brought.
After toasting and exchanging cups,
as he was about to drink,
it turned out to be a cup of dung juice,
extremely foul and filthy.
Lǐ Xū refused to drink,
whereupon an ox-headed jailer
emerged from under the bed,
and stabbed him with a trident,
piercing his chest.
Lǐ Xū hastily drank several cups in succession,
and then left.
The clerks led Lǐ Xū south,
into a small path through wild fields.
In the distance, they saw a lamp shining brightly;
beside the lamp was a large pit,
dark and bottomless.
The two clerks pushed him in,
and he revived.
Lǐ Xū was by nature violent and stubborn,
knowing neither sin nor blessing;
yet, drunk and defiant,
he preserved the Buddhist chapels—
clearly, this was not his original intent.
Nevertheless, he still gained rebirth in heaven,
his sin register burned by fire,
and received such blessings—
is this not the reward for doing good?
Compared to those who diligently and earnestly
devote themselves day and night to doing good,
uphold monastic discipline,
and constantly follow the Buddha's teachings,
yet cannot escape the cycle of life and death,
This has never happened before.
From "Jì Wén"
The Lú Family
During the Táng Dynasty's Kāiyuán era,
there was a man named Lú,
who was staying in Huàzhōu.
One day, while sitting idly in the main hall,
he saw two men in yellow robes enter the gate.
Lú asked who they were,
and they replied:
"We are village heads,
sent with a summons to apprehend you."
Lú was greatly startled
and asked why they were apprehending him.
He then asked to see the summons.
Seeing the seal bore the characters for Wèi County,
he opened it.
The writing was erroneous and garbled,
no longer resembling human script.
Puzzled, he questioned them.
The clerks said they were following orders to apprehend him,
but did not know the reason.
Soon, he saw a horse already prepared at the steps.
Having no choice, he mounted and left.
Looking back, he saw his own corpse
sitting on the bed,
which greatly disgusted him.
In the haste of the moment,
he did not realize he was dead.
He also saw the horse exiting not through the gate,
but walking along the walls.
Only then, shocked and weeping,
did he realize he must be dead,
regretting deeply that he could not bid farewell to his mother and sisters.
After traveling several tens of lǐ,
they reached a city,
which was very grand and magnificent.
He asked what city this was.
The clerks said it was the King's domain,
the jurisdiction to which he had been summoned.
After entering the city,
the clerks intended to take Lú to see the King.
Passing by one compound,
he asked what compound this was.
The clerks said:
"This is the compound of the Grand Master of Censorship."
He then asked the name of the Grand Master of the compound.
They said:
"His surname is Lǐ, given name Mǒu."
Lú was pleasantly surprised
and told the clerks:
"This is my maternal cousin."
He asked the clerks to deliver his card.
Shortly after, his cousin came out.
They met with great joy,
recounting past times in detail,
and he was invited inside to sit and talk.
The Grand Master said to him:
"Your recitations, brother,
have accumulated much merit,
truly because the Diamond Sūtra is the marrow of the sacred teachings,
embodying profound and inconceivable merit."
When Lú first entered the compound,
he saw several tens of people,
all dressed in official robes and caps.
Later, more than half were trapped in nets,
some without clothes,
some bare-headed.
Lú asked:
"Who are all these people?"
They said they were officials from the mortal realm.
Those in the nets were there due to heavy sins.
"If you, brother, could expound the Dharma for them,
all who see it will attain rebirth in heaven."
So he ordered a high seat to be brought,
and had Lú ascend to recite the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Some in the nets had already begun to emerge.
Halfway through,
they had all risen to the ground,
some in broad-sleeved robes,
some riding chariots or clouds.
When the recitation ended,
all had been reborn.
When he went to have an audience,
the King addressed him as Dharma Master,
showing him great respect.
The King said:
"Your deeds are most inconceivable,
and your lifespan is not yet exhausted,
all due to the merit of your recitations."
Soon, he ordered the clerks to escort him back.
Upon reaching his home,
he saw his family weeping with disheveled hair,
his corpse lying on the ground,
which saddened him deeply.
Suddenly, a maidservant entered the hall from the courtyard.
The clerks told him to follow her up the steps.
As he approached,
his soul suddenly re-entered his body,
and thus he revived.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
Chén Lìbīn
Chén Lìbīn
was from Kuàijī.
In his youth, he passed the imperial examination in the míngjīng category.
He excelled at writing,
and his poems were included in the "Jīnmén Collection."
The four characters "included in the Jīnmén Collection" are supplemented based on the Ming manuscript.
He began his official career as the Captain of Chángchéng.
From a young age, he recited the Diamond Sūtra,
and whenever he faced peril,
he often received its aid.
During the Kāiyuán era,
Lìbīn traveled from the Kuàijī River
to Dōngyáng.
It had been raining for a long time,
and the river was overflowing.
Lìbīn and his companions set out in over twenty boats,
raising sails to catch the wind.
Shortly after,
the sky grew dark,
and the wind grew stronger.
When they reached the stone sluice at Jièshí,
the water surged
Originally, there was a blank space here.
The character "surged" is supplemented based on the Ming manuscript.
blocking the flow downstream.
Waves crashed and pounded,
making it impossible to moor.
The more than twenty boats ahead
all capsized at the mouth of the sluice.
The boatmen were terrified.
Lìbīn hurriedly recited the Diamond Sūtra.
When they reached the confluence of the currents,
suddenly, a creature,
resembling a red dragon,
appeared sideways and supported the boat,
allowing them to ascend.
Commentators attributed this to the merit of reciting the sūtra.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
Wáng Hóng
Wáng Hóng
in his youth made a living by fishing and hunting.
During the Táng Dynasty's Tiānbǎo era,
while flying his hawk to chase a hare,
it ran into a burrow.
Hóng followed and explored it,
finding a scroll of the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
From then on, he gave up hunting.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
The Tián Family
Tián, the military advisor of Yìzhōu,
had a fondness for hunting,
and always kept falcons and hounds for this purpose.
In the early years of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
while flying his falcon in Yìzhōu,
he saw a scroll of text on a thorny bush in the thicket.
He picked it up to look,
and it turned out to be the Diamond Sutra.
From then on, he resolved to recite it,
and after several years,
he had already recited it over two thousand times,
yet he did not cease his hunting.
Later, he fell ill,
and died suddenly for several days.
He was summoned to the underworld,
where he saw all kinds of birds and beasts,
surrounding him for several acres,
demanding his life.
After a while,
he was brought before the King,
who asked why his sins were so many.
Tián had no answer.
The King ordered the officials to take him away for interrogation.
There were ten men in his group.
When they reached the officials' bureau,
the officials ordered them to open their mouths.
They threw a pill into each mouth,
and it immediately turned into a blazing fire that spread all over their bodies.
In a moment, they were reduced to ashes,
but soon they were restored to human form.
This happened to six or seven of them.
When it was Tián's turn,
three pills were thrown in succession, but no fire appeared.
The officials found this strange.
They brought him back to see the King,
and reported the truth in full.
The King asked what meritorious deeds he had performed in life.
Tián said:
"At first, I was devoted to hunting.
The King pressed him further,
and he said:
"During my lifetime,
I found the Diamond Sutra on a thorn bush in Yìzhōu,
and have recited it over two thousand times."
The King said:
"This alone eradicates all sins."
He ordered his attendants to check Tián's record of merits,
and they reported back as he had said.
The King himself ordered Tián to recite the sutra.
After only three pages,
he looked back at the courtyard, and the birds and beasts
were nowhere to be seen.
When he finished reciting,
the King praised him,
saying:
"For reciting it two thousand times,
you shall have your life extended by fifteen years."
Thus, he was allowed to return to life.
From "Guǎngyì Jì"
Lǐ Wéiyàn
Lǐ Wéiyàn, the magistrate of Jiàndé County,
had recited the Diamond Sutra since his youth.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
Wéiyàn served as a military advisor in Yúyáo Commandery.
When his term ended, he headed north to return home.
Passing by Wǔzhàng Diàn,
he encountered a breach in the dike of the Shàngyú River,
and the water had dried up.
It was midnight, dark and gloomy,
with no one around for miles,
and this road was known for frequent robberies.
Wéiyàn had several hundred bolts of Wú silk in his boat,
and fearing they would be taken by thieves,
he took up a sword
and went to the front of the boat to recite the sutra.
After the third watch,
he saw two torchlights on the dike,
approaching from afar.
Wéiyàn suspected they were villagers coming to guard him,
but when the torches were about a hundred paces from the boat,
they turned back.
He found this quite strange.
He recited the sutra even more loudly,
and secretly thought to himself:
"Could it be that the torches' behavior
is due to the power of the Diamond Sutra?"
At that time, the water in the dike had dried up, but the water outside was full.
Wéiyàn then thought to himself:
"If the dike breaks, we should get water assistance."
Half the night later,
he suddenly heard the sound of flowing water at the bow of the boat.
Startled, he said:
"The dike is several zhàng wide;
how could it have broken?"
After a long while,
he gradually felt the boat floating,
and by dawn,
the river water had already filled up.
Opposite the boat was a hole,
several chǐ in size.
Only then did he realize it was due to the aid of reciting the Diamond Sutra.
Wéiyàn's younger brother, Wéiyù, served as the deputy prefect of Qiánzhōu.
Seeing his elder brother's success from reciting the sutra,
he imitated him.
Later, while sailing through a gorge,
the current was swift, and the oar broke.
The boat was about to capsize,
so he recited the sutra with all his might.
Suddenly, he saw an oar floating down with the current,
and thus was saved.
Another member of their clan also often recited the Diamond Sutra.
During the rebellion of Ān Lùshān,
he hid in the wild grass.
As the rebels approached,
he wished for a pair of shoes to run away.
Suddenly, something fell on his back.
Startled, he looked.
It was a new pair of shoes.
{From "Guǎngyì Jì"}
Sūn Míng
Sūn Míng of the Táng dynasty,
a native of Yángwǔ in Zhèngzhōu,
came from a poor and humble family for generations.
He worked as a tenant farmer for the Lǚ family estate.
He was skilled in reciting the Diamond Sutra,
reciting it twenty times a day
for twenty years.
From the time he began reciting the sutra,
he abstained from meat and blood.
Later, while in the midst of reciting,
he suddenly saw two officials come to summon him.
Míng thought they were county officials,
so he followed them.
After walking about five or six lǐ,
they arrived at the gate of a mansion.
The gatekeeper said:
"The King has gone out on an inspection tour."
The officials thus locked Míng in an empty room.
The room was about fifty or sixty jiān wide,
and its roof was like a canopy of clouds.
After seven days,
the King finally arrived.
The officials led Míng into the mansion.
The King asked:
"What merits do you have?"
He replied:
"I have recited the Diamond Sutra for twenty years."
The King said this was a great merit,
and turning to his attendants, said:
"Yesterday, I received a petition from the Jetavana Monastery,
stating that Míng recites diligently and earnestly,
and requesting an extension of twenty years for him.
Now I know that cultivation is truly inconceivable.
The twenty-year extension
is to reward his efforts."
He ordered the officials to escort him back home.
His family had already completed his funeral arrangements.
Although his spirit had returned to his body,
his family did not know it.
It happened that a hunter passed by the burial site
and heard cries for help.
He reported it to the family,
and thus Míng was revived.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Míng had been alive again for six or seven years,
and was in good health.
{From "Guǎngyì Jì"}
Sān Dāo Shī
Master Sāndāo Táng,
whose secular surname was Zhāng,
and given name Bóyīng,
during the Qiányuán era,
served as a soldier in Shòuzhōu.
He was extremely filial by nature.
Because his father was in Yǐngzhōu,
he stole an official horse to go and visit him.
Upon reaching Huáiyīn,
he was captured by the guards at the checkpoint.
The prefect Cuī Zhāo ordered him taken outside the city and beheaded at the waist.
At that time, the executioner was known as "Able with the Blade."
He struck twice,
but initially caused no injury;
so he switched to a sharp blade,
exerted all his strength to hack,
yet still caused no harm as before.
The executioner exclaimed in astonishment:
"When I use the blade to strike,
upon reaching his body my hand goes weak,
I don't know why?"
He hastily reported this.
Cuī Zhāo asked the reason,
and he replied:
"In the past, at fifteen years old,
I once abstained from meat and blood,
and recited the Diamond Sūtra for over ten years.
Since the chaos of the Hú rebellion began,
being in the army,
I no longer recited it.
Yesterday, because I was accused of an unforeseeable crime,
I only wholeheartedly recited the sūtra."
Cuī Zhāo sighed and released him.
Thereupon he shaved his head and left home to become a monk,
wore a large iron bell and begged for food,
prepared a vegetarian feast for a thousand people,
and accomplished it in a single day.
People of the time called him Master Sāndāo,
saying he was the Bodhisattva of Arousing Reverence.
{From "Guǎng Yì Jì"}
Military Adviser Sòng
In the Táng dynasty, Military Adviser Sòng of Fāngzhōu had recited the Diamond Sūtra since youth.
When he took up his post,
he temporarily resided in the residence of the former Registrar of Personnel.
He already knew the house was haunted,
so every evening he constantly recited the sūtra.
Suddenly he saw a woman standing outside the door.
After a long while,
Sòng asked:
"Are you not a ghost?"
She said:
"Yes."
He asked further:
"The principles of the hidden and manifest realms are different;
it should not be appropriate for us to meet.
Could it be that you have some grievance?"
The woman then wept sorrowfully and said:
"Yes."
She said she was the wife of the former Registrar.
When the Registrar was sent on a mission,
his younger brother tried to force himself on her.
She resisted and did not yield,
and because of this was killed.
Her body was wrapped in felt
and thrown into the latrine in the northwest corner of the hall,
unable to bear the filth and accumulation.
Many people have come, and she wished to state her grievance,
but ordinary people are timid and cowardly.
Seeing her form, they would surely be afraid,
so her hidden resentment could not be conveyed.
Hearing that you, sir, diligently recite the sūtra,
taking this practice as your duty,
you should also greatly protect sentient beings.
Considering my wrongful defilement,
would you not pity me?"
Sòng said:
"My official position is lowly at the start,
I cannot rescue you alone.
Tomorrow,
I will certainly report this to the Prefect on your behalf."
The ghost then departed.
At dawn, he fully reported it.
They dug the ground down to the latrine,
but did not find her corpse.
Sòng recited the sūtra,
and the woman came again.
He asked why it was not found.
She replied:
"To the northwest, it's off by just one foot.
Tomorrow you should search there,
to complete your kindness."
Following her words, they then found it.
Inside the felt, only bones remained.
They washed them again,
and moved them to another place.
That evening she came again to bow in thanks,
joyfully saying:
"Your protection is exceedingly deep,
difficult to repay.
Although in the dark realm,
I also have some insight.
You have two sons.
The elder will be difficult to raise,
the younger will certainly have descendants,
and moreover will have honor and position."
She also spoke of Sòng's future several changes of official positions and salaries,
and further said:
"I am greatly ashamed before the Prefect,
not knowing how to repay him."
Sòng saw the Prefect,
and fully recounted what was said.
The Prefect ordered him to ask
what further offices he himself would hold.
That evening,
the woman came again.
Sòng thus conveyed the Prefect's meaning.
She said:
"In one month he will change office,
but it will not be to his satisfaction.
He will be transferred to Assistant Prefect of Guìzhōu."
Sòng fully reported this.
All these matters proved true.
Initially,
Sòng asked: since she was killed by someone,
why did she not seek revenge?
She said:
"That person is still an official today,
his fate is not yet due to die,
so I have not yet taken revenge."
{From "Guǎng Yì Jì"}
Liú Hóngjiàn
Liú Hóngjiàn was
a nephew of Censor-in-Chief Zhǎn.
In the early Qiányuán era of the Táng dynasty,
he fled southward during the turmoil.
A monk instructed him to recite the Diamond Sūtra,
and Hóngjiàn recited the sūtra daily.
By the Shàngyuán era,
he was staying in Shòuchūn.
One day, as he went out,
he suddenly saw two officers who said:
"We have received an order from the Grand Commandant to apprehend you."
Hóngjiàn replied:
"I have never met the Grand Commandant;
why am I being summoned?"
He intended to resist.
The two officers suddenly rushed forward and seized him.
Hóngjiàn asked to put on his robe,
but the officers refused to release him.
They dragged him along, and before long,
they swiftly crossed the Huái River
and arrived at a village.
Shortly after,
they brought a large hemp robe and a waistband for Hóngjiàn to wear,
laughing and saying:
"Truly a robe for a pedant!"
They then proceeded northward,
and the road gradually became rough and difficult.
Ahead, they reached a large city.
Entering the city, there was a government office
that was very imposing and splendid.
Suddenly, Hóngjiàn saw the monk who had urged him to recite the sūtra emerge from the office.
The boy behind the monk recognized Hóngjiàn,
went straight to him,
and asked why Sixteenth Young Master had come here.
He then ran to inform the monk, saying:
"Sixteenth Young Master Liú has just been apprehended by officers.
Due to the merit of reciting the sūtra,
shouldn't you go and save him?"
Hóngjiàn soon arrived at the monk's place,
earnestly bowing and pleading for rescue.
The monk said:
"Disciple, you will not suffer."
Shortly after,
the officers led Hóngjiàn into the hall.
Behind the desk was a five-colored pagoda,
three or four feet tall,
spinning and revolving.
Before the interrogation could begin,
the monk had already entered the door.
The pagoda transformed into a handsome man,
around thirty years old,
who said he was the Vice Censor-in-Chief.
He descended the steps to greet the monk.
He asked why the monk had come again,
and the monk said:
"Liú Hóngjiàn is my disciple.
He recites the Diamond Sūtra
with utmost devotion and effort.
Moreover, his allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted.
He should be released."
The King said:
"If he recites the Diamond Sūtra,
I would like to hear it."
He then ordered Hóngjiàn to kneel and recite it.
Hóngjiàn recited two pages,
but suddenly forgot the rest.
A person in the western part of the hall,
holding a golden-hooked dragon-headed banner,
with green characters on the banner
inscribing the Diamond Sūtra,
spread it before Hóngjiàn,
enabling him to recite the sūtra clearly to the end.
Then, all the people vanished,
leaving only the empty, silent hall.
Thereupon, he went out the door,
and saw only the pursuing officers.
Suddenly, something shaped like two suns
came and struck Hóngjiàn.
Hóngjiàn fled in fear and panic.
Suddenly, he saw water by the roadside,
and Hóngjiàn wanted to stop and drink it.
The pursuing officer said:
"This is human fat,
which has clarified over time, with the clear part on top.
Below it is all leftover skin and rotten flesh.
If you drink it, you cannot return."
Shortly after, he reached his home,
and saw his skeletal body lying on the bed.
His heart felt deeply sorrowful.
A ghost pushed him from behind,
and he fell into darkness as if entering a room's door,
and then revived.
The ghost received money and then left.
{From "Guǎngyì Jì"}
Zhāng Jiāyóu
Zhāng Jiāyóu of Guǎnglíng,
in the early Bǎoyìng era of the Táng dynasty, served as the Sīmǎ of Míngzhōu.
He fell ill and died,
and his coffin was transported back home,
buried outside the southern gate of Guǎnglíng.
In the early Yǒngtài era,
an old acquaintance of his named Láo
was walking to the southern outskirts,
and sat under a pagoda.
Suddenly, he saw Jiāyóu riding a white horse coming from the south.
Seeing Láo, he dismounted,
and they comforted each other as in life,
but he did not remove his hat,
speaking with his head bowed.
Láo asked what sins and blessings there were in the underworld.
Jiāyóu said:
"Sins and blessings are clear and evident;
all receive according to their deeds.
But because I have always recited the Diamond Sūtra,
I now have no burdens,
and I am about to go elsewhere,
within ten days or a month.
When you return,
please tell my elder brother
to recite the Diamond Sūtra a thousand times on my behalf.
Why did he put foul things in my incense burner?
Your family also has two scrolls of the sūtra;
I hope you will recite them,
to increase your own blessings."
After speaking,
they parted and he left.
Láo fell into a daze,
and after a long time, he awoke.
{From "Guǎngyì Jì"}
Wèi Xún
Wèi Xún of the Táng dynasty,
son of Left Supervisor of the Heir Apparent Shàngdé,
recited the Diamond Sūtra.
In the early Shéngōng era,
he served as Great General of the Palace Guard.
At that time, in the capital, there was a man named Cài Cè
who died suddenly,
and revived after several days.
He said of himself:
"When I first arrived in the underworld,
the officials were angry that the person they sought could not be apprehended,
and were about to whip their messenger.
The messenger said:
'General Wèi Xún recites the Diamond Sūtra,
and benevolent deities protect him,
so we cannot apprehend him.'
They immediately sent another messenger to apprehend him again,
and shortly after, he returned with the same report.
The underworld official said:
'Let us cease the pursuit for now.'" When Xún heard this,
he practiced even more diligently.
{From "Guǎngyì Jì"}
Dù Sīnè
Dù Sīnè, a native of Tóngtí County, Lùzhōu in the Táng dynasty,
due to the power of reciting the Diamond Sūtra,
recovered from illness.
Every time the day came for reciting the sūtra,
he would surely see divine light.
{From "Guǎngyì Jì"}
The Abbot of Lóngxīng Temple
In the Táng dynasty, at the Lóngxīng Temple in Yuánzhōu,
during a grand vegetarian feast,
the abbot was gathering the monks.
His seniority in monastic years was high,
making him a venerable elder.
He sat beneath the honored guest's seat.
There was a young monk
who arrived late from outside.
Having no place to sit,
he saw only an empty seat below the abbot.
As the young monk tried to sit there,
the abbot repeatedly scolded him.
This happened several times.
Fearing he would miss the meal time,
the young monk finally came and took the seat.
The abbot was furious.
Leaning against a pillar to sit,
he raised his hand to slap him.
Just as he was about to raise his hand,
his large sleeve was pinned by the pillar,
and he could not bring it down.
He joined his palms in astonishment.
The young monk, ashamed and disheartened,
left without eating and returned to his room.
The assembly discussed, fearing this was due to the young monk's virtue.
The abbot then went with the temple community to pay him respects.
The young monk, alarmed and fearful,
said he initially had no spiritual practice
and dared not undeservedly receive the elder's courtesy.
Hesitating, he walked away.
They then asked what practice he had performed in his life.
He said:
"For twenty years, I have only upheld the Diamond Sutra."
All sighed in admiration,
saying it was the protective power of the Diamond Sutra.
They then burned incense and bowed in reverence at the pillar,
chanting:
"If it is the divine power of the Diamond,
may this robe be returned."
Thereupon, it came out with a wave of the hand.
{From "Guǎngyì Jì"}
Chén Zhé
In the Táng dynasty, there was a Chén Zhé from Lín'ān.
His family lived in Yúháng.
He practiced diligently and purely,
upholding the Diamond Sutra.
At the beginning of the Guǎngdé era,
when the rebel Zhū Tán from Wǔkāng raided Yúháng,
Chén Zhé, being wealthy,
planned to move his property to avoid them.
Soon the rebels arrived.
Chén Zhé, thinking they were government troops,
asked how near the rebels were.
The band of rebels angrily said:
"What old dog is this,
daring to insult us!"
They vied to stab him with swords.
Each time a sword came down,
a five-colored circular light, five or six feet in diameter, would shield Chén Zhé's body,
and the stabs could not hit him.
The rebels exclaimed in amazement,
calling him a sage.
All felt ashamed and remorseful,
released him, and left.
{From "Guǎngyì Jì"}
The Beacon Soldier from Fēngzhōu
At the beginning of the Yǒngtài era in the Táng dynasty,
a beacon soldier from Fēngzhōu went out at dusk
and was captured by the Dǎngxiàng tribe and taken into Tibet to tend horses.
The Tibetan king ordered a hole bored through his shoulder bone,
threaded with a leather rope,
and assigned him several hundred horses.
After half a year,
the horses had doubled in number.
The Tibetan king rewarded him with several hundred sheepskins.
He was then transferred near the royal tent.
The son of the Tsanpo, appreciating his competence,
had him hold the banner by his side,
giving him leftover meat and cheese.
After another half year,
when given cheese and meat,
he wept sadly and would not eat.
The Tsanpo asked him why.
He said he had an old mother
whom he frequently dreamed of at night.
The Tsanpo was rather benevolent.
Hearing this, he felt sorrowful.
That night, he summoned him to his tent and said:
"Tibetan law is strict;
there is no precedent for release.
I will give you two of my strongest horses.
Escape via a certain route.
Do not say it was I."
The beacon soldier rode the horses at full gallop.
Both horses exhausted and died.
He then traveled by night, hiding by day.
After several days,
he injured his foot on a thorn,
and collapsed in the desert.
Suddenly, the wind blew something rustling past him.
He grabbed it to wrap his foot.
After a while,
the pain ceased.
He tried to rise
and walked as before.
After a day and night, he reached the Fēngzhōu border.
Returning home,
he found his mother still alive.
Weeping with joy, she said:
"Since I lost you,
I have only recited the Diamond Sutra,
never neglecting it even while eating or sleeping,
praying to see you again.
Now my vow has indeed come true."
She then fetched the sutra.
The binding was broken,
and several pages were missing.
She did not know why.
Her son then told of injuring his foot in the desert.
His mother had him unwrap his foot to look.
The wound was wrapped with several pages of the sutra,
and the wound had also healed.
{From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"}
Zhāng Yì
The Táng dynasty chancellor Zhāng Yì's
father, Zhāng Qíqiū,
fervently believed in Buddhism.
Each morning he would don new clothes,
hold the sutra before an image,
and recite the Diamond Sutra fifteen times.
He persisted diligently for several decades.
At the beginning of the Yǒngtài era,
he served as Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng.
A minor officer in his yamen, guilty of an offense,
fearing exposure,
incited several hundred soldiers
to plot a rebellion.
Zhāng Qíqiū, having left the yamen,
was strolling in a small hall.
Suddenly, several dozen soldiers
rushed in with drawn blades.
Zhāng Qíqiū had only servants with him.
They hurried toward the residence gate.
After passing the small hall a few steps,
he looked back.
There was no one there.
He suspected it was a ghostly apparition.
As he neared the residence,
his wife, daughter, and maidservants came crying out the door,
saying:
"There are two armored warriors
emerging from the hall roof."
Meanwhile, the yamen guards, hearing of the trouble,
rushed in chaotically with weapons.
Reaching the front of the small hall,
they saw over ten men
standing rigidly in the courtyard,
hands hanging, mouths agape,
dropping their weapons on the ground.
The crowd then captured and bound them.
Five or six were mute, unable to speak.
The rest confessed fully, saying:
"As we were about to enter the hall,
we suddenly saw two armored warriors, several zhàng tall,
glaring and shouting at us.
At first, it was like being struck by evil."
Hearing this, Zhāng Qíqiū
then abstained from wine and meat.
{From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"}
Cuī Níng
In the Táng dynasty, Cuī Níng
garrisoned Western Shǔ in the early Dàlì era.
At that time, Yáng Lín rebelled.
A soldier named Zhāng Guóyīng fought him
and was shot in the abdomen.
The arrowhead lodged inside and would not come out.
The physician said:
"He will surely die by nightfall."
His family prepared burial items
and tearfully bid farewell to his comrades.
Zhāng Guóyīng often upheld the Diamond Sutra.
That night,
he dreamed of a foreign monk giving him a pill.
By dawn,
he passed the arrowhead out.
The wound then closed and healed.
{From "Bàoyìng Jì"}
The Filial Son from Tàiyuán
During the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
in Tàiyuán, a horse thief falsely accused a Xiàolián (a degree holder) of being an accomplice.
After being tortured for ten days,
suffering to the extreme, he was forced to confess.
The investigating official suspected his wrongful conviction,
and the case was not yet concluded.
The man only recited the Diamond Sutra,
his voice mournful and earnest,
ceaseless day and night.
One day,
two sections of bamboo fell into the prison,
rolling to a stop before him.
Other prisoners fought to take them.
The jailer suspected a hidden blade,
broke them open to look,
and inside were two lines of text:
"Even the Dharma should be relinquished,
how much more so that which is not the Dharma."
The calligraphy was very fine.
The thief's leader, grieving and remorseful,
fully confessed that he had falsely accused him due to an old grudge.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
Lǐ Tíngguāng
In the Táng dynasty, there was a man named Lǐ Tíngguāng
who served as Sīmǎ of Dézhōu.
He revered the Buddha
and did not consume meat or blood.
He often recited the Diamond Sutra.
Whenever he recited the sutra,
a circular halo of light would appear before him.
When his devotion was intense and sincere,
the light would gradually enlarge;
if his mind harbored the slightest slackness or laziness,
the light would gradually diminish and dim.
Because of this, he disciplined himself,
becoming increasingly diligent and vigorous.
From *Bàoyìng Jì*.
Lù Kāngchéng
In the Táng dynasty, Lù Kāngchéng once served as Fǎcáo Yuàn (Legal Officer) of the Jīngzhào Prefecture government,
and did not avoid confronting the powerful.
After retiring from official duties one day,
he suddenly saw a deceased former clerk holding several hundred documents, requesting his signature.
He asked:
"You have already passed away,
how can you be here?"
The clerk said:
"These are the registers of the underworld."
Kāngchéng looked at them;
they only contained people's names,
with virtually no other details.
The clerk said:
"These are all people who will die by weapons next year."
Kāngchéng asked:
"Could I possibly be among them?
If so, please check and show me."
The clerk said:
"You are."
Greatly alarmed, Kāngchéng said:
"Since you are my former subordinate,
surely you have some affection for me!"
The clerk replied:
"That is precisely why I have come to inform you, my lord.
Only the Diamond Sutra can be relied upon."
Kāngchéng immediately agreed.
He then recited the Diamond Sutra,
dozens of times a day.
The following year,
Zhū Cǐ indeed rebelled,
and appointed Kāngchéng as Censor.
Kāngchéng rebuked Cǐ, saying:
"How dare you, a traitorous minister, presume to command a loyal officer of the state!"
Cǐ was enraged,
and ordered several hundred cavalrymen to surround and shoot him.
Kāngchéng silently recited the Diamond Sutra,
and none of the arrows harmed him.
Cǐ said:
"It is said that scholars use loyalty and good faith as their armor;
indeed it is true."
He then let him go.
Kāngchéng subsequently went into seclusion in the Zhōngnán Mountains,
and never served in office again.
From *Bàoyìng Jì*.
Xuē Yán
In the Táng dynasty, Xuē Yán
was Sīmǎ of Zhōngzhōu.
He was vegetarian and observed long fasts,
reciting the Diamond Sutra thirty times daily.
When he was about to die at seventy-two,
he saw banners, canopies, and music coming to welcome him.
His wife, Madame Cuī,
who was the aunt of Censor Ān Yǎn,
at the moment of his passing,
saw Xuē Yán gradually ascending to heaven, following the banners and canopies,
and calling to him, he did not look back.
The entire household smelled an extraordinary fragrance.
From *Bàoyìng Jì*.
Rèn Zìxìn,
a man from Jiāzhōu,
in the fifteenth year of the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty
traveled to Húnán.
He constantly recited the Diamond Sutra,
maintaining pure conduct without fault.
On Dòngtíng Lake,
a strange object like a cloud enveloped the boat,
dispersing after a short while.
Zìxìn was then missing from the boat,
and no one knew where he was.
After a long time,
he emerged walking upon the waves.
He said he had gone to the dragon palace,
paid respects to the Dragon King,
and four or five people ordered him to ascend to the hall and recite the Diamond Sutra,
giving him several tens of pieces of pearls and jewels.
Two monks escorted him out of the palace.
One monk entrusted a message to Zìxìn,
to deliver to Shàozhēn, the master at the Guānyīn Terrace of Héngyuè,
saying it was sent by "your monk,"
instructing him to transmit the Diamond Sutra.
He went to Nányuè to seek the monk,
and indeed found him,
but was told the monk had passed away five or six years earlier.
From *Bàoyìng Jì*.
Duàn Wénchāng
In the seventeenth year of the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Duàn Wénchāng traveled from Qízhōu to Shǔ,
accepting an appointment under Nánkāng Prince Wéi Gāo.
By Wéi Gāo's later years,
due to the slanderous schemes of the rebel Liú Pì,
(The original text had "bì" (favorite),
changed according to *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*, continuation seven.)
Wénchāng was demoted to serve as acting Wèi (a county official) of Língchí County.
Wéi Gāo soon died,
and Liú Pì assumed the position of Liúhòu (military governor).
Wénchāng had previously been at odds with Pì,
and upon hearing the news, left the county overnight.
Upon reaching the east gate of the city,
Pì soon issued an order,
forbidding all county officials from leaving their posts.
That evening was dark and windy.
As he turned back,
after leaving the outer wall for two *lǐ*,
he saw two torches flanking the road,
guiding him from a hundred paces ahead.
At first, he thought county clerks had come to welcome him,
but found it strange they did not approach,
maintaining a constant distance, high and low, far and near,
only extinguishing as he was about to reach the county walls.
When he asked the county clerks,
they had not yet received the governor's order.
At that time, Wénchāng had been reciting the Diamond Sutra for five or six years,
never missing a day.
Truly, sincere devotion must elicit a response,
and where there is a response, there must be an effect.
The guiding lights to his left and right
were manifestations of the sutra's power.
Later, as Liú Pì's rebellious intentions gradually became apparent,
the court appointed Yuán Zī as military governor.
Wénchāng's younger cousin, who had long served in the army
and was in charge of affairs in the Left Camp,
fearing he would be implicated in disaster,
conspired with the army supervisor
to send a secret message to Yuán Zī via a wax-sealed pill containing a silk letter.
The plot was soon discovered,
and all involved were slaughtered.
The rebels believed Wénchāng knew of the plan at the time.
One night, after reciting the sutra for a long time, Wénchāng
unintentionally fell asleep,
with all doors and windows closed.
Suddenly, he heard the sound of the door opening and someone entering, saying "Don't be afraid" repeatedly,
followed by the sound of something being thrown onto the table
with a loud noise.
Startled awake,
the sound still seemed to ring in his ears.
Looking around,
his clerks and servants were all asleep.
He ordered them to light torches and search everywhere,
but initially found nothing.
However, the door that had been bolted
was now open.
Wénchāng had recited and upheld this sutra over a hundred thousand times,
and its miraculous responses were numerous and evident.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
Liú Yìhuái
During the Táng dynasty, when Liú Yìhuái was in Biàn,
Hán Hóng served as the Right Wing Yúhóu,
and a certain Wáng served as the Left Wing Yúhóu.
Hán Hóng and Wáng were close friends.
Someone claimed that the two men were gathering military intelligence,
intending to harm Liú.
Liú was furious,
summoned them both, and interrogated them.
Hán Hóng was actually Liú's nephew.
He prostrated himself on the ground, kowtowed, and spoke loudly,
causing Liú's anger to subside slightly.
Wáng was old and his legs trembled with fear,
unable to defend himself.
Liú shouted an order to have him dragged to a seat,
and he was beaten thirty times with a rod.
At that time, a new red rod had been made,
its head several inches in diameter,
reinforced with sinew and lacquer,
standing upright without falling over.
Five or six blows would have been fatal.
Hán Hóng thought Wáng must have died.
At dusk,
he went to Wáng's home,
surprised to hear no sounds of weeping.
He thought perhaps they dared not cry.
He inquired with the gate guard,
who immediately said:
"The Commissioner is unharmed."
Hán Hóng, being long acquainted with him,
went straight to his bedroom.
He asked him,
and Wáng said:
"I have recited the Diamond Sutra for forty years,
and now its power has manifested.
I remember when I was first made to sit for punishment,
I saw a huge hand like a winnowing basket.
It suddenly covered my back."
He then bared his back to show Hán,
and there were no whip marks at all.
Hán Hóng had previously not favored Buddhism,
but from this point, he began associating with monks,
personally copying ten pages of scripture daily.
By the time he attained high rank,
he had accumulated several hundred scrolls.
Later, while serving in the Secretariat,
during intense summer heat,
a Remonstrance Official came to see him on business.
Hán was sweating profusely as he copied scripture.
The Remonstrance Official, puzzled, asked him about it,
and Hán then recounted the entire story of Wáng.
From "Yīnhuà Lù"
Sūn Xián
During the Táng dynasty, when Liáng Chóngyì was in Xiāngzhōu,
before
(The original text had "mò" (末),
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy and Xǔ edition to "wèi" (未).)
he rebelled with his troops,
a minor officer named Sūn Xián suddenly died,
but revived after two nights.
He said he had gone to a place resembling a king's residence,
with very strict ceremonial guards.
An official led a monk in for questioning.
The monk's religious name was Huáixiù,
who had been dead for over a year.
During his life, he had greatly violated the precepts.
Upon entering the underworld,
no good deeds could be recorded for him.
So he deceitfully said:
"I often instructed Sūn Xián to copy the Lotus Sutra."
An order was issued to have Sūn Xián brought for confrontation.
At first, Sūn Xián had no recollection,
but the monk insisted stubbornly.
The matter dragged on without resolution.
Suddenly, a śramaṇa appeared and said:
"Kṣitigarbha says,
if the disciple confesses,
he himself will also receive protection."
Sūn Xián then complied with these words,
and thus was cleared of trouble.
He also said that during the cross-examination,
he saw a foreign king,
with several hundred guards,
coming from outside.
The King of the Underworld descended the steps,
and they ascended the hall together, step by step.
They had not been seated long
when a great wind swept him away.
He also saw another person,
being interrogated to verify his sins and merits.
This person had often recited the Diamond Sutra,
but also loved to eat meat.
On his left side were several thousand scrolls of sutras,
on his right side, meat piled up into a mountain.
Because the meat was so abundant,
he was about to be severely judged.
Suddenly, a single spark of fire flew from the pile of sutras,
towards the mountain of meat,
and in an instant, it was completely consumed.
This person then walked away into the sky.
Sūn Xián asked Kṣitigarbha:
"Where was that foreign king blown by the wind just now?"
King Kṣitigarbha said:
"That king is destined for Avīci Hell.
The wind just now was the wind of karma."
He then led Sūn Xián to see the hells.
Upon reaching the gate,
smoke and flames blazed fiercely,
the sound like wind and thunder.
Sūn Xián, terrified, dared not look.
As he looked down at a cauldron of boiling liquid,
a splashing drop fell on his left thigh,
the pain piercing to the heart and marrow.
Kṣitigarbha ordered an official to escort him back,
forbidding him to divulge underworld affairs.
Upon returning, it was like waking from a dream.
His wife and children surrounded him, weeping.
A full day had already passed.
He then exhausted his family's resources to copy sutras,
and subsequently requested to leave the household life.
The spot where the drop fell in his dream became a sore,
which never healed for the rest of his life.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Monk Zhì Dēng
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Monk Zhì Dēng of Tiānchóng Temple in Jīngzhōu,
often recited the Diamond Sutra.
He fell ill and died.
His disciples, finding his hands still warm upon touching them,
did not immediately place him in the coffin.
After seven days, he revived.
He said:
Initially, he saw someone in the underworld resembling a king.
Because of his sutra recitation,
the king joined his palms and descended the steps.
He then inquired, saying:
"We grant the venerable monk another ten years in the world.
Strive to transcend birth and death."
He also asked: Among the monks in the human world, some consume coix seeds and medicinal foods after the noon meal.
This greatly violates the fundamental teachings.
Zhì Dēng replied:
"How about the clauses of permission and prohibition in the Vinaya?"
He said:
"These were added by later people,
not the Buddha's original intent."
Nowadays, among the Jīngzhōu monastic community, after the noon meal,
(The original text lacked the character "hòu" (後),
added according to the Míng manuscript copy.)
none consume medicinal drinks.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Wáng Shì
Wáng Cóngguì, a commoner from Chánlíng Village in Gōng'ān, had an unmarried younger sister
who often recited the Diamond Sutra.
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
she suddenly fell violently ill and died.
She had been buried for three days
when her family went to cover the grave mound.
Hearing moans from within the tomb,
they dug it open to look,
and indeed, she showed signs of life.
They carried her back home.
After several days, she could speak.
She said:
"When I first arrived in the underworld,
the underworld officials, due to the merit of my sutra recitation, released me to return."
Wáng Cóngguì was skilled in carpentry.
He once worked on construction at Línghuà Temple in Gōng'ān.
Monk Shǔ Zhōng of that temple once heard Wáng Cóngguì tell this story.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Zuǒ Yíng Wǔbó
When Wéi Gāo, Prince of Nánkāng in the Táng dynasty, governed Shǔ,
there was a squad leader of the left battalion
who, while stationed at the Western Mountain camp,
learned to recite the Diamond Sutra together with his fellow soldiers.
He was stubborn by nature,
and on the first day, he only managed to memorize the title.
That night, while gathering firewood outside the fort,
he was captured by Tibetan cavalry.
They traveled over a hundred li before stopping.
Before dawn,
they threw him to the ground,
tied his hair to a stake,
and covered him with a felt blanket.
They slept
(The original text had "wù" (awake),
but it was changed to "qǐn" (sleep) according to the Míng dynasty manuscript.)
on top of him.
This man could only recall the sutra's title,
when suddenly he saw a gold ingot
emitting light and stopping before him.
He tried to lift his head and move his body,
and all his bonds came loose.
He then stealthily rose,
and followed the gold ingot as it moved.
He estimated he hadn’t traveled more than ten li
when, as dawn approached,
he unexpectedly found himself already home,
which was in the eastern market of the prefecture.
His wife and children initially suspected he was a ghost.
He explained everything that had happened.
Five or six days after he returned home,
the camp commander reported his desertion.
At first, Wéi did not believe it,
but when the day of his escape matched the day he arrived home,
he was finally pardoned.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Sòng Yǎn,
a native of Jiānghuái,
took the imperial examination for the míngjīng degree.
In the early years of the Yuánhé era,
he arrived at Héyīn County,
but due to illness, he abandoned his studies
and became a clerk at the Salt and Iron Bureau,
earning two thousand coins a month.
He married and settled down,
not considering any other occupation.
Over a year later,
someone transporting rice by boat passed through Sānmén,
and because he was illiterate,
he invited Yǎn to accompany him
to manage the account books,
offering eight thousand coins per month.
Yǎn said to his wife:
"Now I don’t earn eight thousand in several months;
if I can get that in just one month,
it would be extremely profitable."
His wife, Yáng Shì, was very wise
and urged him not to go,
saying:
"The water route at Sānmén
is quite treacherous;
if something dangerous happens to you,
what good will the profit do?"
Yǎn did not listen
and left.
When he reached the place,
they indeed encountered a violent storm,
and all the boats in the fleet sank.
Only Yǎn fell into the water,
grabbed a bundle of millet stalks,
and gradually drifted near the shore.
He floated on the stalks until he reached land,
thus surviving,
while dozens of others all perished.
He then held the stalks and thanked them, saying:
"My humble life
was granted by you;
I vow never to abandon you, whether in life or death."
He then carried the stalks and hurried several li,
until he came to a place where an old woman sold tea,
with two thatched huts.
He went there to stay overnight
and told her everything that had happened.
The old woman took pity on him
and prepared porridge for him.
The next morning,
while drying clothes south of the hut,
he untied the stalks to sun them,
and inside the bundle, he found a bamboo tube.
Opening it,
he discovered it was the Diamond Sutra.
He immediately asked the old woman about it,
but she did not know the details.
The old woman said:
"Since you left, your wife
has been praying with disheveled hair,
copying the sutra with utmost sincerity,
and that is why she could save you."
Yǎn wept with emotion and asked to return home.
The old woman pointed to a path in the southeast and said:
"Just follow this path;
it is about two hundred li,
and you can reach home the day after tomorrow."
She gave him two shēng of rice,
and after bowing in thanks, he set off.
Indeed, two days later, he reached Héyīn,
and upon seeing his wife, he shamefully thanked her.
Yáng Yuán asked in surprise:
"How did you know?"
He recounted everything in detail.
Yáng Shì found it strange,
so Yǎn took out the sutra.
Yáng Yuán wept,
bowed, and reverently placed it on her head.
Yǎn asked:
"How can we verify it?"
She said:
"When copying it,
the person holding the pen mistakenly wrote the character for 'luóhàn' (arhat)
without the four dots on top,
so I went to Chán Master Héshàng at Hùguó Temple to ask him to add them.
The master was old and his eyesight was poor,
so the ink dots were too thick,
and the characters all turned dark.
But for the past ten days,
I didn’t know where it had gone."
They examined it,
and it was exactly as she said.
Yǎn sobbed again and bowed to his wife.
Every day, he burned incense and paid respects to the sutra in a purified room.
He then said to Yáng Yuán:
"We must not forget the old woman by the river."
He sent an envoy with tea and silk as gifts for her.
When the envoy arrived,
neither her dwelling nor the person could be found.
He asked a shepherd boy,
who said:
"The river has risen without bounds;
how could there be anyone selling tea here?"
He added:
"There isn’t even a path here;
it must have been a divine transformation."
Several years later,
Prime Minister Zhèng Gōng Yīn, as the military governor of the Eastern Capital,
summoned Yǎn and Yáng Yuán
and asked them about the whole story.
He also ordered them to bring the sutra,
and gave their son a military post,
with a monthly salary of five thousand coins.
He then requested the sutra,
and to this day, it is revered by the Zhèng family.
Therefore, the Chancellor of Yuèzhōu, Prime Minister Hóngnóng Gōng, upon witnessing this event,
recorded it
and titled it "The Manifestation of Yáng Yuán."
From "Bàoyìng Jì"
Chén Zhāo
In the early Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
Chén Zhāo, a clerk in Hànzhōu,
fell ill.
He saw a person dressed in yellow clothes come to his bedside and say:
"Judge Zhào summons you."
Zhāo asked the reason,
and the person replied:
"I come from the underworld.
Liú Pì and Dòu Xuán are confronting each other in a case,
and they need to summon you as a witness."
Zhāo then invited him to sit.
After a short while, another person arrived holding something like a bladder.
The earlier official wondered why he was late,
and he answered:
"It was only because of this—
I had to wait for the butcher's shop to open."
He then smiled and said to Zhāo:
"Do not be afraid.
To take the vital breath of a living person,
we need a pig's bladder.
You should lie on your side facing east."
Zhāo followed his instructions,
and before he knew it, he was following the two officials on a journey.
The road was very smooth.
After about ten lǐ or more,
they reached a city,
as large as a prefectural seat,
with armored soldiers guarding the gate.
Upon entering,
he saw a person with a terrifying, angry countenance—
this was Judge Zhào.
He said:
"When Liú Pì was defeated in Dōngchuān,
Dòu Xuán seized forty-seven head of cattle
and sent them to Zǐzhōu,
claiming they were slaughtered under Liú Pì's order.
But Liú Pì says:
'There was no official document beforehand.'
You were the clerk;
you should know the facts."
Before Zhāo could respond,
from the next room he heard Dòu Xuán call out:
"Where is Chén Zhāo?"
He also asked about the survival of his brothers, wife, and children.
Zhāo wanted to go see him,
but the underworld official said:
"Governor Dòu's appearance is extremely fearsome;
he does not wish to meet you."
Zhāo then explained in detail that the slaughter of the cattle was indeed carried out according to Secretary Liú's written instructions,
though it was not an official document.
The paper was hemp,
and it is still on a shelf in a certain private room in Hànzhōu.
Judge Zhào immediately ordered an official to take Zhāo to Hànzhōu to retrieve it.
The gatehouse was locked,
so they entered and exited through a hole in the joint.
When the instructions arrived,
Liú Pì had nothing more to say.
Judge Zhào said to Zhāo:
"Do you know that you yourself have a transgression?
Of the cattle Dòu Xuán killed,
you took one cow's head."
Before Zhāo could answer,
Judge Zhào said:
"Here it is different from the human world;
nothing can be falsified."
In a moment,
a soldier appeared carrying a cow's head.
Zhāo, terrified, begged for rescue.
Judge Zhào ordered the regulations to be checked:
he deserved one hundred strokes
and fifty days of imprisonment.
He then asked Zhāo:
"What meritorious deeds do you have?"
Zhāo immediately stated:
"I have held a certain number of vegetarian feasts
and painted Buddha images."
Judge Zhào said:
"Those bring blessings in the next life."
Zhāo also said:
"I once read the Diamond Sūtra at my cousin's house."
Judge Zhào said:
"Then put your palms together and recite it."
Zhāo did as told.
After a while,
a sūtra in a yellow-wrapped case descended from the sky
and stopped before Zhāo.
Zhāo took it and looked—
it was exactly the copy he had borrowed from his cousin,
with the burn mark on the cover still there.
He put his palms together again,
and the sūtra vanished.
Judge Zhào said:
"This is enough to spare you."
He then released him to return.
He ordered Zhāo to go to another bureau,
called the Bureau of Life Span,
to check and determine the length of his life.
The official reported:
"Zhāo's original name was Jiān (釗),
with the metal radical and knife,
but in a certain year he changed it to Zhāo (昭),
gaining an additional eighteen years."
Hearing this, Zhāo felt sorrowful.
Judge Zhào laughed and said:
"Eighteen years is plenty of time to enjoy life's pleasures;
why are you not happy?"
He then ordered an official to escort Zhāo back.
Halfway there,
they saw a horse blocking the road.
The official said:
"This originally belonged to you;
you may ride it."
As soon as he mounted it, he revived,
having been dead for half a day.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ".
In the third year of the Táng Dà
("Dà" originally written as "Yuán";
according to the Old Táng History, the campaign against Lǐ Tóng took place during the Wénzōng era's Dàhé period,
so "Yuán" is likely an error for "Dà".)
hé era,
Lǐ Tóngjié raised troops in Cāng
The original text had "zhōu" after "Cāng";
deleted based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.
jǐng,
and the emperor ordered Lǐ Yòu to command the Qí-Dé army to campaign against him.
Initially, they besieged Dézhōu city,
but the city was strong and could not be taken.
The next day they attacked again,
from mǎo to wèi hours,
suffering eighty to ninety percent casualties,
yet still could not capture it.
At that time, there was a strong soldier named Wáng Zhōnggàn from the Qízhōu yámén, one of eight officers,
a native of Bóyě County,
who had long recited the Diamond Sūtra,
accumulating over twenty years
without missing a single day.
On that day,
Zhōnggàn climbed a scaling ladder,
and just as he reached the parapet,
he was hit by arrows like a porcupine
and struck down by a rolling log.
His comrades dragged him outside the sheep-and-horse wall
and placed him on the inner bank of the moat.
As night fell,
Lǐ Yòu ordered a withdrawal.
At that time, arrows rained down from the city wall,
and in the rush,
his comrades forgot to retrieve Zhōnggàn's body.
After Zhōnggàn died,
he felt as if in a dream,
arriving in a wild wasteland.
He encountered a great river
but had no means to cross,
so he looked up to the sky and wept.
Suddenly, he heard a human voice.
Zhōnggàn saw a person
over ten feet tall
and suspected he was a deity,
so he asked for directions back to camp.
The person said:
"Do not be afraid;
I will enable you to cross this river."
Zhōnggàn bowed to him.
As soon as he lowered his head and before raising it again,
the deity grabbed his waist
and threw him into the air,
and after a long time, he landed on the ground.
Suddenly, it was as if he awoke from a dream.
He heard the watch in the enemy city sound the second watch.
At first, he did not remember crossing the river,
nor did he know about his wounds.
He raised his hand to touch his face—
blood covered his eyebrows and eyelashes,
and only then did he realize he was injured.
He forced his body to move,
walked over a hundred steps, then collapsed again.
He saw the same person holding a knife shouting at him:
"Get up! Get up!"
Terrified, Zhōnggàn
ran for over a lǐ,
then sat down to rest.
Only then did he hear his own army's password calls,
and he reached his camp.
He inquired after his comrades,
and only then did he learn that his body had been left on the inner bank of the moat,
which was the river he had crossed in his dream.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ".
Wáng Chēng
Wáng Chēng lived in Jìnzhōu,
and was of a stubborn and vulgar nature.
In the fourth year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
his household was struck by a pestilence,
and eight or nine out of ten died,
only Chēng alone was spared.
While ill,
he ate dog meat,
and consequently became blind.
He did not seek medicine or treatment,
but only prayed to ghosts and spirits,
yet for years received no response.
Suddenly, a strange monk came begging for food,
and said to him:
"My teacher's writings
contain the *Diamond Sūtra*,
which can dispel all sufferings,
and its retribution is swift and divine.
Can you, lay devotee, accept it?"
Chēng declined, saying he was foolish,
and moreover had no sight,
so he certainly could not memorize it.
The monk urged him to copy it.
Chēng followed his advice,
obtained seven scrolls,
and requested the monk to recite them.
After several days,
he dreamed that the previous monk came holding a knife to cut open his eyes,
and he awoke in fright.
He felt he could see something,
and after a long while, his sight was fully restored.
Within a few months, it was as good as before.
Chēng recited the sūtra for the rest of his life without ceasing.
From *Records of Retribution*.
Lǐ Yuányī
served as Sīmǎ of Ráozhōu in the fifth year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty.
He had a daughter living in a separate courtyard.
