In the middle of the night, she suddenly saw a divine being,
was frightened and died,
yet her complexion remained unchanged.
Her husband, Yán Nè, came from Qín,
and upon reaching Cānghú,
he hazily saw his wife walking on the water towards him.
Nè asked in shock,
and his wife wept, saying:
"I have already died,
and am now a ghost."
Nè was astonished and found it strange.
She said:
"Nearby, in Yànpǔ Village,
there is a Master Yán,
who teaches many students.
He possesses extraordinary arts.
If you, sir, go and earnestly plead for his merciful rescue,
I might be able to return to life."
Nè later indeed met Master Yán,
bowed, paid his respects, wept, and told his story,
revealing all the details.
Master Yán was initially very angry:
"Young man, are you mad?
How dare you insult me like this!"
Nè bowed again, weeping sorrowfully,
and only after a long time did Master Yán finally agree,
saying:
"The one who killed your wife
is General Wáng.
He is buried under the northwestern pillar in this hall.
You should copy the *Diamond Sūtra*,
have monks recite it,
and make offerings at that spot.
Your young lady will surely return."
Nè bowed in thanks,
and hurried to the commandery city.
He arrived the next day,
fully reported everything to Yuányī,
copied the sūtra,
and quickly had it recited.
After seven recitations,
the girl opened her eyes,
and after a while could speak.
She shamefully thanked her husband, saying:
"Under a certain pillar in this hall,
lies the dried bones of General Wáng,
holding a short sword.
Please rebury him,
and I request that the sword be kept
to repay your virtue."
They excavated it and it was indeed as she said.
So they reburied him,
and kept the sword.
Yuányī consequently copied several hundred scrolls of the sūtra
to bestow upon the silent darkness.
From *Records of Retribution*.
Yú Wànyíng
was a crude and fierce man from the marketplaces of Jīngzhào.
In the seventh year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
a large venomous snake resided in his house,
and all his family members who saw it were terrified.
Wànyíng grew angry.
One morning, he took a huge club,
waited for it to emerge,
struck and killed it,
then cooked and ate it.
He consequently fell ill,
with agonizing pain in his internal organs,
and died,
though his heart was still slightly warm.
After seven days, he revived,
and said:
Initially, he saw three or four underworld messengers pursuing him.
They walked over ten *lǐ* in darkness,
when he saw a man walking alone,
with light surrounding his body,
illuminating several feet around him,
and reciting a sūtra.
Wànyíng hurried over to his light,
asked his name,
and the man said:
"My surname is Zhào, given name Mǒu,
and I am one who constantly recites the *Diamond Sūtra*.
Just stay close to me."
The messengers dared not advance,
and gradually vanished.
After a long time,
they reached Wànyíng's home.
Wànyíng bowed in thanks, saying:
"Had I not met you, exalted one,
I certainly would not have returned."
That man taught him the *Diamond Sūtra*,
and by reciting it, he was able to return.
Upon being reborn,
he took a copy and recited it again,
without any omissions or errors,
and his illness also vanished.
He consequently abstained from alcohol and meat,
ceased killing,
and recited the sūtra fifty times daily.
From *Records of Retribution*.
Yú Lǐ Huí
Yú Lǐ Huí sat for the imperial examinations.
In the eighth year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
he failed and was about to return home.
A monk advised him:
"If you, young man, wish to quickly pass the examinations,
why not recite the *Diamond Sūtra*?"
So he recited it dozens of times daily.
He lodged at Wángqiáo,
and while walking under the moonlight,
a beautiful woman spoke to him,
and he was consequently lured away.
After over ten *lǐ*, they reached a village house,
where there was much playful laughter and noise.
He was led inside and up into a hall,
where he saw five or six people, all young women.
Lǐ Huí suspected they were spirits,
so he secretly recited the sūtra.
Suddenly, a strange light issued from his mouth,
and the group of women fled in terror.
He only smelled a foul, putrid odor.
It was apparently a fox den,
with brambles and thorns everywhere.
Lǐ Huí was bewildered,
not knowing where to go.
Suddenly, a white dog appeared,
its color surpassing frost and snow,
seeming to guide Lǐ Huí forward.
Light shone from its mouth,
illuminating the path again,
and soon he reached his original place.
Later, he recited it tens of thousands of times.
From *Records of Retribution*.
Qiáng Bódá
Táng Qiáng Bódá,
in the ninth year of the Yuánhé era,
lived in Fángzhōu.
His family had passed down an evil disease for generations;
his descendants, from a young age,
suffered from the illness of wind-leprosy,
for two hundred years.
Bódá contracted the illness just after coming of age.
He entrusted his father and elder brother, saying:
"This illness will certainly be incurable;
I fear it will bring future harm.
Please send me into the mountains."
His father and elder brother wrapped up provisions and sent him beneath a cliff,
then left weeping.
Not long after he had stopped eating,
suddenly a monk passed by.
Pitying him, he said:
"You should recite a four-line verse from the Diamond Sūtra;
perhaps you can be freed from this suffering."
Bódá then recited it,
and did not cease for several days.
During the day,
a tiger came.
Bódá was extremely afraid,
but simply closed his eyes and recited the verse with utmost sincerity.
The tiger then licked all his sores,
and he only felt a cool sensation,
as if a salve had been applied.
There was no other suffering at all.
After a long while, he looked at himself:
all his sores had already dried and closed.
The next morning,
the monk came again.
Bódá told him everything.
The monk immediately picked up
a handful of green grass by the mountainside and gave it to him,
saying:
"You can use this to wash the sores.
Just return home
and boil this for bathing."
Bódá then choked back tears and bowed in thanks.
The monk patted his back and departed.
When he arrived home,
his parents were greatly astonished.
He then explained the whole story.
After bathing,
his body was fresh and white,
completely free of sores and illness.
From then on, the hereditary illness stopped being passed down,
and he recited the verse for the rest of his life.
From "Records of Retribution."
Monk Wéigōng
Monk Wéigōng of the Fǎxìng Temple in Jīngzhōu during the Táng dynasty,
recited the Diamond Sūtra for over thirty years,
fifty times a day.
He did not adhere to monastic decorum,
was fond of wine,
and often stirred up disputes,
so he was disliked by the other monks.
When he fell ill and was near death,
there was a monk in the same temple named Língkuī.
His conduct was similar to Wéigōng's,
making them the two banes of the temple.
Língkuī went out on some other business.
One li from the temple,
he encountered five or six people,
young and very handsome,
with fresh, clean clothes,
each holding musical instruments,
like a Qīucí troupe.
They asked Língkuī:
"Where is the Venerable Wéigōng?"
Língkuī immediately told them the location,
suspecting there was an offering ceremony at the temple.
When he returned in the evening,
entering the temple he heard the bell tolling:
Wéigōng had already died.
He then recounted what he had seen earlier.
That day,
the entire temple heard the sound of string and wind instruments,
but no musicians had entered the temple.
A renowned monk of the time said:
"Wéigōng, by the power of the sūtra,
has been reborn in the Land of Immovability.
"Land" originally written as "net,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript copy.
This was also to use his example to admonish Língkuī."
Língkuī was moved to realization,
and reformed himself within the monastic order.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ."
Wáng Miǎn
During the Yuánhé era of the Táng,
when Grand Councillor Yán Shòu was in Jiānglíng,
the garrison commander of Cényáng, Wáng Miǎn,
often upheld the Diamond Sūtra.
Once, sent to Guīzhōu to investigate a matter,
on his return at Zhà Tān,
his boat wrecked,
and five people drowned together.
When Miǎn first entered the water,
it was as if someone handed him a bamboo pole.
He drifted with the waves,
until at Xiàláo Town,
he reached the shore alive.
Looking at the object in his hand,
it was the Diamond Sūtra.
From Zhà Tān to Xiàláo Town is over three hundred li.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ."
Dǒng Jìncháo,
joined the army during the Yuánhé era of the Táng.
Once while on night duty at the eastern city tower,
one evening under a bright moon,
he suddenly saw four people in yellow coming from the east.
They gathered and stood below the city wall,
stating their own names,
their manner seeming like that of pursuers.
Then they said to each other:
"Dǒng Jìncháo often upholds the Diamond Sūtra,
dedicating a portion of the merit to bless and protect the underworld offices.
We have received his grace;
how can we kill him?
We must await a wrongful death.
If this man goes elsewhere,
we will have nothing to rely on."
One of them said:
"Across from Dǒng Jìncháo's door lives a man
of the same age and surname,
whose allotted lifespan is similar.
He can serve as a substitute."
Then they suddenly vanished.
Jìncháo was astonished by this.
When dawn came,
he heard crying from across the street.
Asking the reason,
the dead man's parents said:
"Our son died suddenly last night."
Jìncháo, moved to tears, recounted his experience.
He then arranged the funeral and burial,
and provided for the mother.
Later he left home to become a monk,
taking the dharma name Huìtōng,
and resided at Xīngyuán Temple.
From "Records of Retribution."
Kāng Zhòngqī
In the eleventh year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng, went east across the sea.
For several years he did not return.
His mother had only this one son,
and as time passed she missed him constantly.
A monk came begging for food,
and the mother told him everything.
The monk said:
"Just uphold the Diamond Sūtra,
and your son will quickly return."
The mother was illiterate,
so she had someone copy the sūtra for her.
She then hollowed out a pillar of her house to embed it,
applied lacquer over it,
and reverently paid respects morning and evening.
One night,
there was a great clap of thunder,
which uprooted and carried away this pillar.
Over a month later,
her son indeed returned,
bringing home a large piece of wood in a brocade bag.
He entered and knelt before his mother.
His mother asked him about it.
Zhòngqī said:
"I encountered a storm at sea;
the boat wrecked and I fell into the water.
Suddenly there was a clap of thunder,
and this wood was cast upon the waves.
I then clung to it to stay afloat,
and managed to reach shore.
My life was given by it;
how dare I not revere it!"
His mother exclaimed in surprise:
"It must be the pillar in which I hid the sūtra!"
She then broke open the pillar and retrieved the sūtra.
Mother and son often recited it together.
From "Records of Retribution."
Wú Kějiǔ,
a man from Yuè,
lived in Cháng'ān during the fifteenth year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
and followed Manichaeism.
His wife, née Wáng,
also followed it.
After over a year,
his wife died suddenly.
After three years had passed,
she appeared in a dream to her husband and said:
"Because of my heretical views, I have been reborn as a snake,
beneath the pagoda at Huángzǐbēi.
I will die tomorrow morning,
so I beg you to invite monks
to go there and recite the Diamond Sutra,
hoping to spare me from other sufferings."
Not believing it in the dream,
he scolded her.
His wife grew angry
and spat in his face.
He woke with a start,
his face swollen and painful beyond endurance.
His wife then appeared in a dream to his elder brother, saying:
"Fetch the dragon-tongue herb from the garden
and pound it to apply; he will recover immediately."
The brother awoke, ran to fetch it,
and gave it to his younger brother,
who soon recovered.
At dawn the next day,
the brothers went together
to invite monks to recite the Diamond Sutra.
Soon, a large snake emerged from the pagoda,
raised its head and looked all around,
and died when the recitation ended.
Kějiǔ converted to Buddhism
and often recited this sutra.
From "Records of Retribution"
Kāi Xínglì
In the Táng dynasty, Kāi Xínglì,
a man from Shǎnzhōu,
was illiterate.
At the beginning of the Chángqìng era,
he often carried a scroll of the Diamond Sutra with him,
burning incense and paying homage wherever he went.
Once, while transporting goods out of Tóngzhōu,
he encountered over ten bandits.
Xínglì abandoned the goods and fled.
The goods weighed no more than fifty or sixty catties,
but when the bandits tried to lift them,
they could not move them at all.
Astonished, they looked at each other,
chased after Xínglì,
and questioned him.
He replied:
"There is a Diamond Sutra inside;
I fear it is divine power."
The bandits opened the bag
and indeed found the sutra inside.
They then gave him over a hundred thousand cash,
asked him to leave,
vowed to stop being bandits,
and upheld the sutra for the rest of their lives.
From "Records of Retribution"
Monk Fǎzhèng
In the Táng dynasty, Monk Fǎzhèng of the Prajñā Hall at Kāiyuán Temple in Jiānglíng
recited the Diamond Sutra twenty-one times daily.
At the beginning of the Chángqìng era,
he fell ill and died.
Upon reaching the underworld,
he saw someone like a king
who asked what meritorious deeds he had performed in his life.
He replied:
"I often recited the Diamond Sutra."
The king then invited him up to the hall,
seated him on an embroidered throne,
and had him recite the sutra seven times.
All the attendants joined their palms in reverence,
and the interrogations and tortures below the steps
ceased as everyone listened.
After the recitation ended,
the king sent an officer to escort him back.
The king descended the steps to see him off, saying:
"Venerable one, you shall have thirty more years in the human world;
do not cease your recitations."
Following the officer, he walked several tens of miles
until they reached a large pit.
The officer approached the pit
and pushed him from behind,
as if he were falling through empty space.
He had been dead for seven days,
but only his face was not cold.
Monk Chángjìng of Jīngzhōu personally witnessed this event.
From "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng"
Novice Dàoyìn
In Shíshǒu County during the Táng dynasty,
there was a novice named Dàoyìn
who often recited the Diamond Sutra.
At the beginning of the Chángqìng era,
while returning late from an outing,
he suddenly encountered a tiger on the road.
It roared and lunged forward.
Knowing he could not escape,
the novice closed his eyes and sat down,
silently reciting the Diamond Sutra,
hoping for rescue and protection.
The tiger then crouched in the grass and watched over him.
At dawn,
when villagers came and went,
the tiger left.
Looking at the spot where it had crouched,
they saw saliva had flowed onto the ground.
From "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng"
Hé Lǎo,
a man from Èzhōu,
was often a merchant
and devotedly recited the Diamond Sutra. During the Chángqìng era of the Táng dynasty,
while resting on a mountain road at night with a hired porter carrying goods,
he suddenly fell into a deep sleep.
The porter cut off his head
and threw it into a ravine,
then took the goods and hurried to the market.
Just as he was selling them,
he saw Hé Lǎo approaching.
He was terrified.
Hé Lǎo said:
"I have survived due to the power of reciting the sutra,
and I vow not to tell anyone."
They then both became monks.
From "Records of Retribution"
Gōulóng Yì,
a commoner from Jiānzhōu
(The original text has "里" for "俚";
amended according to the Ming manuscript.
"间" is likely an error for "简").
During the Chángqìng era of the Táng dynasty,
he worked as a laborer in Qīxiàn to support himself.
Once, when a fellow villager was ill,
he went to visit him
and saw him copying the Diamond Sutra.
For no reason, Yì destroyed and discarded it, putting a stop to it.
Upon returning home, he became mute,
and no doctor could cure him.
Stubborn and ignorant,
he still did not repent.
After nearly five or six years,
he suddenly heard a neighbor reciting this sutra.
Startled, he reproached himself:
"I slandered the true sutra before,
and thus contracted this mute illness.
If I repent now
and devote myself to it for life,
might I regain my speech?"
From then on, whenever he heard the sutra being recited,
he would lean against the wall and listen intently.
After over a month,
it seemed as if he could recite it.
A few days later,
while walking into a temple by chance,
he met an old monk
and paid his respects.
The monk asked what was the matter,
so he pointed to his mute mouth.
The monk then cut under his tongue with a knife,
and he was able to speak.
He then recited the sutra with the monk.
His voice was exactly like the neighbor's.
Later, when he tried to find the monk,
he was nowhere to be seen.
Pointing to a mural of Subhūti,
he said:
"This is him."
He then copied the sutra
and painted an image of Subhūti,
paying homage to it for the rest of his life.
From "Records of Retribution"
Zhào Ān,
a native of Chéngdū,
in the fourth year of the Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty,
often recited the Diamond Sutra,
ten times a day.
When the barbarian invaders retreated and returned,
Ān found military weapons along the road,
and collected them to store at home,
for which he was reported by an enemy.
Officers came to his door to arrest him,
and he wept, bowed to the sutra, and left.
Tortured by the prison guards,
he falsely confessed,
and was about to be sentenced.
When brought before the military governor,
his cangue and shackles fell off by themselves.
The governor questioned him,
and Ān said:
"I am not a thief;
I found these items on the streets.
Whenever I recite the Diamond Sutra,
I suspect it is its power."
The governor scolded him and did not believe it.
When the case was processed,
the governor suddenly wrote the character 'release' beside Ān's name,
and then said the rest should be dealt with according to the law,
though no one knew what he meant.
After returning home,
Ān bathed and paid respects to the sutra.
Opening the box to look at it,
he found the sutra torn and its scroll rod broken,
as if pulled apart by a strong man.
His wife said:
"I suddenly heard sounds from the box,
as if someone were striking it."
This was exactly when Ān was being interrogated and tortured,
with no discrepancy.
From the "Records of Retribution"
Hé Zhěn
Hé Zhěn made his living as a merchant.
His wife, née Liú,
abstained from alcohol and meat from a young age,
and often recited the Diamond Sutra.
First, she would burn incense before the Buddha statue,
praying to live only until forty-five,
to remain clear-minded at the moment of death,
and to know the day of her death in advance.
In the winter of the fourth year of the Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty,
she turned forty-five.
She donated all her belongings to support monks,
and as the year was ending,
she bid farewell to all her relatives and friends.
Hé Zhěn thought she was possessed by an illness
and did not believe her.
On New Year's Eve,
she invited monks to perform the initiation ceremony,
bathed and changed clothes,
secluded herself in a room,
sat cross-legged and recited the sutra aloud.
By dawn, she had fallen silent.
Her children pushed open the door to look,
and she had already passed away,
with her head still warm to the touch.
Zhěn buried her with Buddhist rites in a pagoda,
located in the northern part of Jīngzhōu.
From "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng"
Wáng Yīn
Wáng Yīn, a soldier of the Left Battalion in Shǔ,
often recited the Diamond Sutra
and abstained from meat and alcohol.
He served as a storekeeper for rewards,
and repeatedly became implicated by others' mistakes,
facing death sentences four times,
but was unexpectedly spared each time.
In the fourth year of the Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty,
Guō Zhāo was stationed in Shǔ.
Guō was strict and harsh.
The slightest displeasure could lead to execution.
Wáng Yīn presented brocade fabrics,
but Guō disliked their poor quality,
ordered him to bare his back,
and intended to beat him to death.
Guō had a foreign dog,
which followed him everywhere,
and would bite anyone
who was not from his household.
Suddenly, the dog barked,
stood up and embraced Wáng Yīn's back,
refusing to leave.
Guō found this strange,
and his anger subsided.
From "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng"
Wáng Hàn
In the fifth year of the Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty,
Wáng Hàn, a commoner from Shífāng County, Hànzhōu,
often pursued small profits in the market.
He suddenly died,
but revived after three days,
saying:
"In the underworld, sixteen people were summoned together;
fifteen were assigned elsewhere,
while I alone was taken to an office.
I saw a youth in blue robes,
who claimed to be my nephew,
serving as an attendant in the underworld official's hall.
He led me to meet the investigating clerk,
who also claimed to be my elder brother,
though their appearances were unlike.
My elder brother said:
'There is an ox with a grievance,
accusing you of burning the fields,
wrongfully burning it to death.
You also once sold bamboo to a dog butcher to make a kōng hóu,
resulting in the killing of two dogs,
and the dogs also accuse you.
Your name is not yet registered in the death records,
so you can still be spared,
but you must perform meritorious deeds.'"
Hàn wanted to hold a vegetarian feast
and copy the "Lotus Sutra" and the "Golden Light Sutra,"
but his brother said:
"That won't do."
Hàn then requested:
"Recite the Diamond Sutra seven times for them."
His brother happily said:
"That is enough."
After reviving,
he abandoned his livelihood and became a monk.
From "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng"
Níng Miǎn
Níng Miǎn was a man from
Yúnzhōng.
In his youth, he possessed great courage,
excelled at horsemanship and archery,
and could subdue fierce beasts with his strength,
without using weapons.
The governor of the Northern Capital, admiring his bravery,
appointed him as a yájiàng (military officer).
Later, he led four thousand troops to garrison Fēihú City.
At that time, the commander of Jìmén was arrogant and unruly,
disregarding the emperor's laws,
and news of his rebellion reached the imperial court.
Emperor Wénzōng of the Táng dynasty
ordered the governor of the Northern Capital to attack him from the south.
Before the imperial decree arrived,
the Jìmén troops launched a night attack on Fēihú.
The sound of gongs and drums shook the earth,
and the people of Fēihú were in a state of panic and unrest.
They said to Níng Miǎn:
"The Jìmén soldiers are fierce and formidable, impossible to resist.
They are about to arrive now,
and the situation is extremely urgent.
We wish to evacuate the city and flee.
Otherwise,
they will capture our city by morning or evening,
and we cannot bear to see our fathers, sons, and brothers all slaughtered by the enemy's blades.
Regret would then be too late.
Even if the Son of Heaven is divine and mighty,
how could he possibly redress our grievances?
We implore you to consider this carefully."
Níng Miǎn reckoned that his troops were few
and certainly could not blunt the vanguard of the Jìmén army.
He was about to heed the townspeople's words,
but feared offending the Son of Heaven.
He considered fortifying the walls and defending,
but also worried that all the people of the city would be massacred by the enemy.
As his anxiety grew deep and his strategy remained undecided,
suddenly a scout reported:
"The enemy has completely collapsed!
They have abandoned their armor beneath the city walls.
We request permission to retrieve it."
Níng Miǎn immediately climbed the city wall to look.
The moon was bright and clear at that time,
and he saw the enemy soldiers fleeing in haste,
with countless stumbling and falling,
as if a great army were attacking them from behind.
Níng Miǎn was overjoyed.
He opened the city gates,
released his troops to pursue them,
captured several dozen alive,
and obtained a great deal of abandoned armor.
Previously, Níng Miǎn was fond of Buddhism,
and often read the Buddhist scripture, the Diamond Sutra.
After defeating the Jìmén army,
he interrogated the captives.
A captive said:
"Toward evening, we saw several giant figures on the city wall,
over twenty feet tall,
majestic and terrifying,
with glaring eyes and gaping mouths,
bare-chested and holding swords.
When the Jìmén men saw them,
they were stricken with fear, sweating and trembling,
and immediately fled to avoid them.
How could they have any will to fight!"
Níng Miǎn realized the giants were Vajra deities,
and found it even more extraordinary.
Níng Miǎn's official rank was Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and he later served as Deputy Commissioner of Qīngsāi.
From "Records of the Xuānshì Hall"
Ní Qín was from
Zǐzhōu.
In the fifth year of the Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty,
he was renowned for his military strategy.
He was in charge of the Xìngjiào Granary in Fúzhōu,
and had long upheld the Diamond Sutra.
The granary had a hall facing the river,
a place of exceptional scenery.
He set up a Buddha image there
and read the sutra inside.
On the ninth day of the sixth month,
the river water rose greatly,
yet it did not reach this hall.
Ní Qín read and recited the sutra with even greater diligence.
After the water receded,
looking around for several miles,
he saw houses all submerged,
but this hall was barely touched by the water,
and the granary was also undamaged.
People all paid him reverence.
From "Records of Retribution"
Gāo Shè
In the winter of the seventh year of the Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty,
Lǐ Shí, the Imperial Advisor, served as the Military Commander of Tàiyuán.
The clerk Gāo Shè was staying overnight at the official compound.
When the drum sounded dōng dōng,
he went to a neighboring room.
Suddenly, he encountered a man
over six feet tall,
who called out:
"The Military Commander summons you."
Gāo Shè then went.
As he walked somewhat slowly,
the man pushed him from behind.
Unaware, he headed north,
traveling several tens of miles,
until he reached the wilderness,
gradually entering a valley bottom,
then ascending a mountain.
Reaching the summit and looking around in all directions,
he saw the city's houses all below his gaze.
He arrived at a government office,
where the pursuer called out:
"Gāo Shè has been brought."
Most of the people inside wore red and green.
The one presiding seemed to be Vice Minister Cuī Xíngxìn,
who pronounced judgment:
"Hand him over to the department for interrogation."
He was then taken to another place,
where several hundred people sat in the open,
mingled with pigs and sheep.
He was led before one person,
who turned out to be his brother-in-law Dù Zé.
Dù Zé said to him in advance:
"When you first became a clerk,
for the new office setup,
you sent me to buy four sheep.
Do you remember?
Now I am being held accountable for it,
and the suffering is extremely bitter."
Gāo Shè quickly said:
"At that time, I only asked you to buy meat,
not sheep."
Dù Zé then fell silent.
Gāo Shè then saw a sheep standing on its hind legs biting Dù Zé,
and shortly after, Dù Zé was led away elsewhere.
In an instant, he saw another place,
with an exposed frame of square beams.
On the beams were nailed large iron rings.
There were several hundred people,
all holding knives,
tying ropes to people's heads,
pulling them into the rings,
and carving and cutting them.
Terrified, Gāo Shè ran out,
only reciting the Diamond Sutra in his mind.
Suddenly,
he met an old acquaintance, Yáng Yǎn, who said:
"During the time of Minister Lǐ Shuō,
the bandit Lǐ Yīngdào was beaten to death for robbery.
He has already been reborn in various places for thirty years.
Now he is appealing the previous case.
Do you still remember it?"
Gāo Shè declined, saying he was young at the time
and did not recall.
He also met an old clerk, Duàn Yí,
who had previously sworn brotherhood with Gāo Shè.
Meeting Gāo Shè, he said:
"Brother, you used to recite the Diamond Sutra.
Have you not neglected it?
What you have just seen
is not the most extreme place of suffering.
Strive to cultivate good karma.
That you can return now
is also due to the power of the sutra."
He then escorted him home.
It was like a dream.
He had been dead for a night,
and the place where he was pushed remained bruised and swollen for several days.
From "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng"
Zhāng Zhèng.
A native of Qióngzhōu.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the third year of the Kāichéng era of the Táng dynasty, he died suddenly.
At first, he saw four men coming to seize him.
They traveled for half a day,
reaching a great river,
which was very broad.
The depth they waded through was about three chǐ,
and upon closer inspection, it was entirely pus and blood.
He then softly recited the Diamond Sutra.
The messengers' expressions changed.
Entering the city,
he saw a foreign monk over eight chǐ tall.
The monk scolded the messengers, saying:
"Why did you not follow the warrant?
You have wrongly seized an innocent man."
They were all startled and bowed.
When they were led to see the King,
the monk sat facing him and said:
"Zhāng Zhèng is a disciple of my own sect,
and has been wrongly brought here."
The King said:
"Wait, I will conduct a brief interrogation."
The monk's expression turned angry,
and the King ruled to release him.
Zhāng Zhèng saw the four messengers,
all wearing large cangues.
The monk personally led Zhāng Zhèng out of the city,
and the water they had crossed was no longer visible.
The monk said:
"I am the monk you revere.
Do you recognize me?
I am Subhūti."
Only then did he realize it was the power of reciting the sutra,
and he bowed repeatedly in reverence.
The monk said:
"Disciple, close your eyes."
The monk struck once with his staff,
and without realizing it, he cried out
and came back to life.
He had been dead for three days,
with only warmth remaining over his heart.
From "Records of Retribution."
Lǐ Jū
Lǐ Jū of the Táng dynasty,
a native of Chéngdū.
On the sixteenth day of the fourth month in the ninth year of the Dàzhōng era, he suddenly fell ill with a pestilential disease.
In his delirium,
he saw a man who called himself the "King of Disease-Spreading Ghosts."
He scolded Lǐ Jū, saying:
"You have offended me many times,
but I have not yet taken you away.
"Away" originally read "said,"
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy.
Tomorrow I will come again with three women;
prepare food and wine quickly,
for they are all my wives."
Lǐ Jū also responded, saying:
"How can you have three wives?"
He only heard scolding and chattering sounds,
but saw no one.
They came four times,
and on the twenty-first day they bid farewell and left.
Lǐ Jū also bowed and saw them off.
Upon turning back,
he felt his body lighten.
He paid respects in the Buddha hall
and was about to eat porridge.
As he was walking back,
he was suddenly blown away by the wind,
unable to stop his feet,
until he reached a great mountain.
He saw a river and sea without shore,
with people and animals standing with him on the bank,
not knowing which way to go.
After a long while,
a man in a yellow robe asked:
"Who are you, sir?
Follow me."
After only four or five steps,
he saw the river and mountains already far away.
The man asked again:
"What good deeds have you done?
If none,
you would have already become a pig or sheep on the water.
Speak in detail, lest the King asks."
Lǐ Jū said:
"In Chéngdū Prefecture,
I once led over a hundred households to create a mural of Western Paradise merits at Jìngzhòng Temple,
and commissioned the copying of the Great Canon of Scriptures for Dàshèngcí Temple.
Over five hundred scrolls have been completed,
and the dedication ceremony has been held."
The messenger led him away.
After about fifty lǐ,
they saw a great city.
Entering the gate and walking several lǐ,
he saw a monk on a hall, six or seven chǐ tall,
who said to the King:
"This man sincerely performed good deeds,
without deceit or flattery."
The King questioned the man in yellow:
How did you get the warrant
to seize an innocent man?
He replied:
"I found him being led at the foot of the mountain;
there was no warrant for the seizure."
The King said:
"Send him back quickly."
Then he saw the merits he had performed displayed in the hall,
with inscriptions clearly recorded.
The stone wall for creating the "Guǎnglì Prescriptions" was behind.
The messenger led him away
and they entered another courtyard.
He was told to sit,
and they said to Lǐ Jū:
"Because the Governor Wéi of Hànzhōu has died,
they wish to appoint you as Governor."
Lǐ Jū did not understand at all.
After six or seven days, he was released to return.
He passed through twelve places in total,
all called the King's Courtyards,
each with guards.
They all said to copy one scroll of the Diamond Sutra for them.
Then he reached home.
As the messenger bid farewell, he grasped his hand
and also said:
"I beg for one scroll of the Diamond Sutra."
Then he felt a headache.
Reaching beneath a pagoda,
he heard someone say:
"I am the monk Dào'ān.
I knock my head twice in illness,
wishing your resolve in the Way to be firm."
Then he awoke,
seeing Guānyīn Bodhisattva standing by his head, smiling.
From then on, he suddenly became fully conscious.
His wife and children surrounded him, weeping, saying:
"You have been dead for seven days,
with only warmth remaining over your heart."
He copied the sutra for those who had requested it
and recited it himself without negligence.
From "Records of Retribution."
The Magistrate of Bānán
Magistrate Wéi of Bānán
often recited the Diamond Sutra.
During the Guānghuà era of the Táng dynasty,
he reached Níxī.
He encountered a woman
wearing crimson clothes,
leading two children, walking together.
They climbed the mountain ridge together.
Other travelers stopped and shouted,
seeing it was a red-furred tiger and her two cubs.
After a moment,
they parted ways with Wéi and left.
Wéi never realized it,
which was due to the power of reciting the sutra.
From "Records of the Strange."
The Míng manuscript copy states it is from "Remarks from the Northern Dream."
Yuán Chū
Yuán Chū of the Táng dynasty,
a native of Jiǔjiāng.
He sold firewood in the market.
At seventy years old,
he often recited the Diamond Sutra.
Returning north of the river in the evening,
midstream, great winds and waves arose.
All others crossing with him drowned,
but only Chū floated on the water
and drifted to the southern shore.
The moored boats nearby
all belonged to great merchants.
Seeing light several chǐ high on Chū's back,
they thought he was a nobleman.
After he was saved,
they vied to give him clothes,
and further summoned him to give him food.
As they talked and became more familiar,
they realized he was a village elder.
They then asked about the source of the light.
He said:
"I have recited the Diamond Sutra for fifty years.
What is on my back is the sutra."
In all previous dangers and difficulties,
he had never failed to be spared,
knowing it was the power of the sutra.
From "Records of Retribution."
The Military Officer of Yǎnzhōu
During the Qiánfú era,
the military governor of Yǎnzhōu, Minister Cuī,
enforced laws and decrees with extreme severity.
Once, a military officer failed to attend the morning assembly at the yamen.
Minister Cuī was furious
and ordered him to be executed right at the yamen gate.
After the officer was beheaded,
his complexion remained unchanged,
and everyone was terrified by this.
That night, during the third watch, he returned home.
His wife and children were shocked and frightened,
thinking he was a ghost.
The officer said:
"When I was first sentenced to beheading,
it felt just like being drunk or asleep,
with no pain whatsoever.
In the middle of the night,
I realized I was lying on the street,
so I came back home."
His wife and children had no idea how this could be.
The next morning, he went to offer his thanks.
Minister Cuī exclaimed in astonishment:
"What kind of magic do you possess to achieve this?"
The officer replied:
"I have no magic at all.
Since I was young, I have recited the Diamond Sūtra
three times daily.
Yesterday, because I was reciting the sūtra,
I was late."
Minister Cuī asked if he remembered the moment of his execution.
He said:
"When I was first led outside the halberd gate,
I felt as if heavily intoxicated,
and I don't remember the execution at all."
Minister Cuī then asked where the sūtra he recited was.
He replied:
"At home, inside a locked box."
When it was fetched,
the lock was still intact.
They broke the lock
and saw the sūtra had been cut into two pieces.
Minister Cuī was greatly astonished and regretted his actions.
He comforted the officer
and bestowed upon him a set of clothes,
ordering him to copy the Diamond Sūtra one hundred times for offerings.
Now, outside the Yánshòu Temple in Yǎnzhōu,
there is an image depicting the officer's execution at the yamen and the severed sūtra,
which has survived to this day.
From "Records of Retribution."
The Younger Brother of Yáng Fùgōng
In the Táng dynasty, there was a eunuch surnamed Yáng,
whose name is forgotten;
he was the younger brother of Yáng Fùgōng.
He was trapped among the rebels of Qín Zōngquán, Lù Yànhóng, and Liú Jùróng
for over twenty years,
yet he never ceased reciting the Diamond Sūtra.
Although he was within the rebel city,
he never neglected this practice.
Later, when Qín Zōngquán's son became the military governor of Xiāngyáng,
Yáng served as the army supervisor.
Taking advantage of the people's fear and unrest,
Yáng incited his subordinate general Zhào Déyán to attack and kill Qín Zōngquán's son,
and then submitted a memorial recommending Zhào Déyán as military governor.
Thus, the military government gradually stabilized,
and the people resumed their former livelihoods.
Yáng's diligence in reciting the sūtra
became even more fervent.
Once, while burning incense and reciting the sūtra under a willow tree outside the yamen gate,
suddenly, a scroll of the Diamond Sūtra in golden characters
flew down from the sky.
Yáng bowed, received it with both hands, and stood up,
his heart and eyes filled with awe:
"Is it not because of sincere faith and devotion
that I have received this good reward?"
Thus, though trapped among the rebels for twenty years,
he ultimately succeeded in beheading the great bandits,
achieving extraordinary merit,
and preserving his fortune and rank—
all due to the hidden protection of the Buddha.
From "Records of Retribution."
The Ascetic from Càizhōu
During the Táng dynasty, when Sòng Wèn governed Huángzhōu,
Qín Zōngquán rebelled and created chaos,
intending to plunder the surrounding regions extensively.
In Càizhōu, there was an ascetic who recited the Diamond Sūtra,
revered by all the locals.
Qín Zōngquán assigned him as a spy
and ordered him to infiltrate Huángzhōu to gather intelligence.
The ascetic arrived in Huángzhōu,
but before ten days had passed,
he was reported and captured.
Sòng Wèn was furious
and ordered him to be publicly executed at the army gate.
Suddenly, news arrived that an envoy bearing promotions was coming.
The officers and generals advised,
saying that since joyous news was imminent,
it was inappropriate to carry out an execution hastily.
Thus, he was only imprisoned.
After a month,
the envoy still had not arrived,
so the execution was ordered again.
As he was being led out of the prison,
news came that the envoy had entered the region,
so the execution was halted once more.
After the envoy had left,
he was brought out for execution.
Just then, a senior general entered the yamen,
saw him,
and hurriedly reported to Sòng Wèn:
"Huángzhōu's troops and horses are elite and strong,
its city walls and fortifications are formidable—
why fear the prying of treacherous bandits?
This spy is not inherently evil;
he was forced by others.
If the general spares his life,
it would sufficiently demonstrate leniency."
Sòng Wèn agreed
and ordered him to be tonsured, fitted with a cangue,
and sent to solicit donations
for building a new Kāiyuán Temple.
On the night before the temple was completed,
Sòng Wèn dreamed that eight Vajrapāṇis told him:
"The monk bearing the cangue has practiced asceticism so diligently.
Now that the construction is finished,
why not remove his cangue
to honor the virtuous?"
Sòng Wèn awoke, greatly amazed,
and ordered the cangue removed,
treating him with special respect.
Thereafter, the entire region called him the "Vajra Monk."
From "Records of Retribution."
The Overseas Merchant
In the Táng dynasty, there was a wealthy merchant
who constantly recited the Diamond Sūtra,
always carrying the sūtra scroll with him.
Once, while trading in foreign lands,
he stayed overnight on a sea island.
The other merchants coveted his wealth
and together killed him.
They placed his body in a large basket,
added heavy stones,
and sank it into the sea along with the sūtra.
At dawn,
the other merchants' ships departed.
But the island where they had stayed the previous night
was actually a monastery.
Every evening, the monks of this monastery
would hear the sound of someone reciting the Diamond Sūtra
deep under the sea.
The monks were greatly astonished
and ordered skilled divers to investigate underwater.
They found an old man inside a basket reciting the sūtra
and pulled him up.
The monks asked him how this happened,
and he said:
"I was killed
and sunk into the sea.
I didn't realize I was in a basket;
suddenly, I felt as if I were in a palace,
with people constantly bringing me food and drink,
living in peace and comfort."
Upon hearing this, all the monks
praised and marveled greatly,
attributing it to the miraculous power of the Diamond Sūtra.
He then took monastic vows under the monks,
becoming a monk at the island monastery.
From "Records of Retribution."
Monastery Head Jìngshēng
In the Western Jìn dynasty, Monastery Head Jìngshēng of Shǔ Commandery,
renowned for his ascetic practices after leaving home,
served as the abbot of the Sānxián Temple in Shǔ.
He recited the Lotus Sūtra.
Whenever he recited the sūtra,
a tiger would often come and crouch before him to listen,
leaving only after the recitation ended.
He also constantly saw four attendants by his side.
Although he grew old,
his diligence and fervor only increased,
and he thus completed his religious practice.
From "The Forest of Pearls in the Garden of the Dharma."
Shì Tánsuì
In the Jin Dynasty, there was a monk named Shì Tánsuì,
whose origins are unknown.
He left home to become a monk at a young age
and resided at the Héyīn White Horse Temple.
He ate simple food and wore plain clothes,
reciting the Lotus Sutra.
He also interpreted the sutra's profound meanings
and explained them to others.
One night,
he suddenly heard a knock at the door, saying:
"We wish to invite the Dharma Master to expound the Dharma for ninety days."
Suì initially refused.
After repeated earnest requests,
he finally agreed.
While still in a state of sleep,
he felt as if he had already arrived at the White Horse Island shrine,
along with a disciple.
They went there secretly every day,
with no one else aware.
Later, when monks from the temple passed by the shrine,
they saw two high seats,
with Suì in the north
and his disciple in the south,
as if they were giving a lecture.
They also smelled an extraordinary fragrance,
and thus, both monastics and laypeople spread word of this miraculous event.
When the summer retreat ended,
the gods presented him with a white horse,
five white sheep,
and ninety bolts of silk.
After the blessings were chanted,
the events ceased.
From *The Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma*.
Shì Huìqìng
During the Song Dynasty, the monk Huìqìng,
a native of Guǎnglíng,
left home and resided at Lúshān Temple.
He was well-versed in sutras and monastic rules,
pure in conduct and disciplined in practice.
He recited the Lotus Sutra, the Ten Stages Sutra, the Sutra of the Profound Meaning, and the Vimalakirti Sutra.
Whenever he chanted at night,
he often heard snapping fingers and sounds of praise from the air.
Once, while traveling on the Great Thunder River, he encountered a storm,
and the boat was about to capsize.
Qìng continued reciting the sutra without pause.
He felt as if the boat in the waves
was being pulled by someone,
and in an instant, it reached the shore.
From then on, he became even more diligent
and devoted himself with renewed vigor.
From *The Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma*.
Fèi Shì
During the Song Dynasty, the wife of Luó Yǔ, Fèi Shì,
was a native of Níngshǔ.
Her father, Fèi Yuè, served as the governor of Níngzhōu.
Fèi was devout and faithful from a young age,
reciting the Lotus Sutra for several years
with unwavering diligence.
Later, she fell ill
and suddenly suffered severe heart pain.
Her entire family was terrified,
preparing for her imminent death.
Fèi thought to herself:
"I have recited the sutra diligently and painstakingly,
so I should receive divine protection,
and hopefully not die like this."
Soon after, she fell asleep,
and after a short while, she awoke,
having dreamed that the Buddha reached out from the window
and touched her heart,
whereupon she was instantly healed.
All the men, women, and servants in the hall
saw a golden light
and also smelled a fragrance.
Yǔ's cousin, who was visiting her bedside at the time,
also witnessed and heard everything.
From then on, she developed deep faith and understanding,
maintaining devout discipline until the end of her life.
She often used this experience to inspire and guide her children and nephews.
From *Records of the Extraordinary*.
*The Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma*, vol. 95, cites *Records of Miraculous Manifestations*.
Zhào Tài
Zhào Tài, courtesy name Wénhé,
was a native of Bèiqiū in Qīnghé.
He declined official summons,
devoted himself to the classics,
and was renowned in his hometown.
At the age of thirty-five,
during the Sòng
(the Biànzhèng Lùn, chapter eight, notes that "Sòng" is written as "Jìn" in some versions).
On the night of the thirteenth day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Tàishǐ era,
he suddenly died from heart pain,
though his chest remained slightly warm.
His body could bend and stretch.
After his corpse had lain for ten days,
a sound like thunder rose from his throat,
his eyes opened,
he asked for water to drink,
and after drinking, he rose.
He recounted that when he first died,
two men riding yellow horses,
accompanied by two soldiers,
simply said they were taking him away.
The two men supported him under the arms and headed east,
not knowing how many miles they traveled,
until they saw a great city,
towering like tin and iron.
Entering through the city's west gate,
they saw official buildings,
with two heavy black gates,
and several dozen beam-and-tile houses.
There were about fifty or sixty men and women.
The chief clerk, wearing a black unlined robe,
placed Zhào Tài's name thirtieth on the list.
Shortly after, he was taken in.
The prefect sat facing west,
reviewing and verifying names.
He was then taken south through a black gate,
where a man in crimson robes,
seated in a large hall,
called names in order,
asking what each had done in life,
what crimes they had committed;
what meritorious deeds,
and what good acts they had performed.
The answers varied from person to person.
The presiding officer said:
"You are all permitted to speak.
We constantly dispatch the Six Masters' supervising and recording envoys,
who are always among humans,
documenting the good and evil deeds people perform,
to cross-check them.
Upon death, there are three evil paths,
with killing living beings and offering sacrifices being the gravest.
Those who serve the Buddha, uphold the five precepts and ten good deeds,
cultivate a compassionate heart and practice charity,
are reborn in the abode of blessings,
where they dwell in peace, free from turmoil."
Zhào Tài replied that he had done nothing,
and had not committed any evil.
After the interrogation concluded,
he was made an overseer of the water officials,
leading over a thousand people
to carry sand onto the bank.
They toiled day and night, weeping and wailing,
regretting that they had done no good in life,
and now had fallen to this place.
Later, he was promoted to superintendent of water officials,
overseeing all prison affairs.
Given a horse,
he traveled east to inspect the hells.
He then came to the Naraka hell,
where there were six thousand men.
There was a fire tree,
measuring over fifty paces across,
and a thousand zhàng high.
Its four sides were covered with swords,
and fire blazed on the tree.
Below, in groups of ten or five,
people fell onto the fire and swords,
which pierced their bodies.
It was said:
"These people cursed and reviled others,
seized others' property,
and falsely harmed the good."
Zhào Tài saw his parents and a younger brother
weeping in this hell.
He then saw two men bringing documents,
instructing the prison officers,
saying that three people,
whose families served the Buddha,
had banners hung in temples and incense burned,
recited the Fǎhuá Jīng and made vows,
to redeem the sins committed in life.
They were to be taken to the abode of blessings.
He saw them naturally clothed,
approaching a gate,
called the Kāiguāng Great Hall.
It had three heavy black gates,
all with white walls and red pillars.
These three people then entered the gate.
They saw a great hall,
with treasures shining like the sun.
In front of the hall, two lions lay side by side,
bearing
("bearing" was originally written as "elephant,"
corrected according to the Míng manuscript.)
a golden jade bed,
said to be called the Lion's Seat.
They saw a great being,
about ten feet tall,
with golden-hued features,
and a halo of light around his neck,
sitting on this bed.
Many monks stood in attendance.
The seated ones were called true men and bodhisattvas.
He saw the prefect of Tàishān coming to pay respects.
Zhào Tài asked an officer who this was,
and the officer said:
"This is called the Buddha,
the teacher who delivers beings in heaven and on earth."
Then he heard the Buddha say:
"Now I wish to deliver all those in the evil paths and the hells, and release them."
Immediately, it was said that nineteen thousand people
were released at once,
and the hells were emptied.
("Emptied" was originally written as "time,"
corrected according to the Míng manuscript.)
He saw ten people being called,
destined to be reborn in heaven.
There were carriages and horses to welcome them,
and they ascended into the sky and departed.
He then saw another city,
and it was said:
"Measuring over two hundred lǐ across,
it is called the City of Transformed Bodies."
It was said:
"Those who in life never heard the Dharma,
and have completed their punishment in hell,
shall come to this city
to receive retribution through transformation."
Entering the north gate,
he saw several hundred earthen houses,
with a large tile-roofed house in the center,
over fifty paces wide.
Below were over five hundred clerks,
recording people's names,
and the good and evil deeds they had done,
determining the path of their transformed bodies,
according to where they were headed.
Those who killed were to become mayflies,
born in the morning and dead by evening;
if reborn as humans,
they would often be short-lived.
Thieves were to become pigs or sheep,
their flesh butchered to repay others.
The licentious were to become swans, ducks, or snakes.
Those with evil tongues were to become owls or other birds of ill omen,
with harsh cries,
that people would curse to death upon hearing.
Those who owed debts were to become donkeys, horses, oxen, fish, or turtles.
Under the large house were underground rooms facing north,
with one door facing south.
Those called from the north door
and exiting through the south door
all transformed into birds or beasts.
He then saw another city,
measuring a hundred lǐ across,
with tile-roofed houses where people lived in peace and happiness.
It was said:
"Those who did no evil in life,
but also no good,
shall remain among ghosts for a thousand years,
before being reborn as humans."
He then saw another city,
over five thousand paces wide,
called the Underground.
Those being punished and exiled,
unable to bear the suffering,

(the Biànzhèng Lùn, chapter eight, notes that after "unable to bear the suffering," there are thirteen characters: "return home seeking substitutes, their families redeeming their exile, all are in this city.")
numbered fifty or sixty thousand men and women,
all naked and unclothed,
hungry and distressed, supporting one another.
Seeing Zhào Tài, they kowtowed, weeping.
After Zhào Tài finished his inspection and returned,
the presiding officer asked:
"Are the hells in order?
You have committed no sins,
so we appointed you as superintendent of water officials.
Otherwise,
you would be no different from those in the hells."
Zhào Tài asked what brings joy in human life,
and the presiding officer said:
"Only Buddhist disciples,
who diligently practice and do not violate the precepts, find joy."
He then asked:
"Before serving the Buddha,
sins piled up like mountains;
now, having taken refuge in the Buddha's teachings,
can those sins be eradicated?"
The reply was:
"They are all eradicated."
The presiding official then summoned the Chief Registrar Messenger,
and asked why Zhào Tài had come to die.
The messenger opened the sealed case to examine the register of lifespans,
and said:
"He had thirty years of allotted life remaining,
but was wrongly taken by a malevolent ghost.
He is now being sent back home."
Because of this, the entire family, young and old, resolved to devote themselves to Buddhism.
For their ancestors and younger brother,
they hung banners and canopies,
and recited the Lotus Sutra to generate merit.
From Records of the Hidden and Dark.
Shì Huìjìn
In the Yǒngmíng era of the former Qí dynasty,
there was Shì Huìjìn of Gāozuò Temple in Yángdū.
In his youth, he was heroic, brave, and a wandering knight.
At the age of forty,
he suddenly realized the impermanence of life,
and thus renounced the household life.
He ate vegetarian food and wore simple clothes,
and vowed to recite the Lotus Sutra.
His mental exertion was arduous and bitter,
and he would fall ill as soon as he took up the scroll.
He then made a vow to sponsor the creation of one hundred copies to repent for his past hindrances.
He initially gathered sixteen hundred coins.
Bandits came to demand goods,
and Huìjìn showed them the money for the sutras.
The bandits were ashamed and withdrew.
After that, he completed the one hundred copies,
and his old illness was also cured.
Having recited the sutra extensively,
and his vow being fulfilled,
he dedicated the merit of this recitation practice,
vowing to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Nourishment.
He heard a voice from the sky announce:
"Your vow regarding the Dharma is already fulfilled,
you will certainly attain rebirth there."
He passed away without illness,
at over eighty years of age.
From Records of Auspicious and Strange Events.
The Ming manuscript copy says from Records of the Hidden and Strange.
Note: Appears in Records of Hidden Auspicious Signs.
Shāmén Fǎshàng
During the time of Emperor Wǔ of Qí,
a man from Dōngshān, while digging
"Digging" is suspected to be "excavating".
in the earth, saw an object
shaped like two lips,
with a tongue inside,
a bright, vivid red color.
He reported the matter to the emperor.
The emperor inquired among the monastic and lay communities.
Shāmén Fǎshàng said:
"This is the sign of one who upheld the Lotus Sutra, whose remains have not decayed.
If those who recite it gather to recite a thousand times,
the verification will be evident."
He then assembled those who upheld the Lotus Sutra,
to surround it and recite the sutra.
As soon as they began to vocalize,
the lips and tongue immediately moved.
Those who saw it were terrified, their hair standing on end.
They reported the matter to the emperor.
An imperial decree ordered it to be sealed in a stone casket.
From the Liang dynasty Biographies of Eminent Monks.
The Forest of Pearls in the Garden of the Dharma, chapters 35 and 85, both citations say from Records of Extraordinary Signs.
This is a matter of the Northern Qí,
and should not appear in the Liang dynasty Biographies of Eminent Monks.
Shì Hóngmíng
Shì Hóngmíng of the Qí dynasty
was from Shānyīn in Kuàijī.
He renounced the household life in his youth,
was pure, austere, and maintained the precepts.
He resided at Yúnmén Temple in Shānyīn.
He recited the Lotus Sutra,
practiced meditation,
and diligently performed rituals of worship and repentance,
without ceasing throughout the six periods of the day and night.
Every morning, his water pitcher would fill by itself,
moved by the divine youths of the heavens,
who served him.
Whenever he sat in meditation at dawn,
a tiger would often lie down inside his room.
From The Forest of Pearls in the Garden of the Dharma.
Shì Zhìzhàn
At the end of the Later Wèi dynasty,
there was Shì Zhìzhàn of Qízhōu,
who resided at Xiáncǎo Temple in the deep valley north of Tàishān.
He was simple in affairs and spoke little,
and neither people nor birds disturbed him.
He constantly recited the Lotus Sutra.
When he was about to pass away,
the divine monk Bǎozhì said to Emperor Wǔ of Liáng:
"The holy monk of Xiáncǎo Temple in the north,
will attain parinirvana today."
Zhìzhàn passed away
without distress, transformed.
Each of his two hands extended a single finger.
A Brahmin monk said:
"This is a person who has attained the first fruit [of stream-entry]."
He was buried in the mountains.
Later, when his grave was opened to look,
only his tongue remained as before.
The community erected a pagoda to mark the spot.
From The Forest of Pearls in the Garden of the Dharma.
The Monk of Wǔhóu Temple
A monk of Wǔhóu Temple in Fànyáng during the Later Wèi dynasty,
his name is lost,
recited the Lotus Sutra as his constant practice.
When he first died,
he was temporarily interred beneath an embankment.
Later, when he was reburied,
his bones were all withered,
but only his tongue was not decayed.
In Yōngzhōu, there was a monk who recited the Lotus Sutra
and lived in seclusion on Báilù Mountain.
He was moved by a youth who served him.
When he died,
his corpse was placed beneath a cliff.
The rest of his bones withered,
but only his tongue did not decay.
From The Forest of Pearls in the Garden of the Dharma.
Shì Zhìcōng
Shì Zhìcōng of Qīxiá Temple on Shèshān in Rùnzhōu during the Táng dynasty,
once resided at Ānlè Temple in Yángzhōu.
During the rebellion of the Dàyè era,
he longed to return but had no means.
He hid among the river reeds,
reciting the Lotus Sutra,
and did not eat for seven days.
A tiger constantly circled him.
Zhìcōng said:
"My life will end soon,
you may eat me."
The tiger suddenly spoke, saying:
"Heaven and earth were established,
but there is no principle like this."
"Principle" originally written as "ritual",
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
Suddenly, an old man appeared,
rowing a boat to him.
The old man said:
"Master, if you wish to cross the river to Qīxiá Temple,
you may board the boat now."
The four tigers shed tears at once.
Zhìcōng said:
"Do you have a connection with me?"
Thereupon, he took the four tigers and crossed the river safely.
Once they reached the southern shore,
the boat and the old man
were nowhere to be found.
Zhìcōng led the four tigers to the west of the śarīra pagoda at Qīxiá,
where he practiced walking meditation and seated meditation.
His followers numbered eighty,
and none left the monastery compound.
If there was any matter to attend to,
a tiger would enter the temple and roar,
which became the regular procedure.
Zhìcōng passed away during the Zhēnguān era of Táng,
at the age of ninety-nine.
From the Táng dynasty Biographies of Eminent Monks.
Chán Master Tányùn
The Chan Master Tányùn of the Táng Dynasty,
was from Dìngzhōu.
During the chaos and turmoil at the end of the Suí Dynasty,
he secluded himself in the northern mountains of Líshí.
He often recited the Lotus Sutra,
and wished to copy the scripture,
but had no like-minded companion.
This continued for many years.
Suddenly, a scholar came to visit him,
and requested to copy the sutra.
The Chan Master was overjoyed.
At dawn, after eating,
he bathed,
put on clean clothes,
entered a purified chamber,
received the Eight Precepts,
placed sandalwood in his mouth,
burned incense and hung banners,
and copied in silence,
not emerging until dusk.
The next day, it was the same as before,
and he never complained of weariness.
When the copying was completed,
and it came to the binding and mounting,
everything was done according to the proper Dharma.
The scholar announced his departure,
and as he was escorted to the gate,
he suddenly vanished.
The Chan Master upheld and recited [the sutra],
never once neglecting it.
Later, he encountered Hu bandits,
and in his hasty escape,
he placed the sutra in a square box,
and set it upon a high cliff.
After a year, the bandits were defeated,
and he went to search for the sutra.
He found it at the base of the cliff.
The cloth wrapper had rotted away,
crumbling to dust at a touch,
but brushing aside the decay, he saw the sutra,
as fresh and pristine as before.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Lǐ Shānlóng
Lǐ Shānlóng of the Táng Dynasty,
was from Féngyì,
and served as a Captain of the Left Gate Guard.
During the Wǔdé era,
he died suddenly, but his heart remained warm,
so his family could not bear to encoffin him.
On the seventh day, he revived.
He himself recounted:
"When I died,
I saw that I had been apprehended
and taken to an official compound,
which was very vast.
In the courtyard were several thousand prisoners,
shackled and fettered,
all standing facing north.
An officer led me into the courtyard.
On the hall sat a high official upon a tall seat,
with attendants like a king's.
Soon, I was called to the steps.
The King asked, 'What meritorious deeds did you perform in your life?'
I replied,
'Whenever fellow villagers held vegetarian feasts,
I was always invited to contribute offerings.'
The King said,
'What good deeds did you yourself perform?'
I said,
'I recited the Lotus Sutra,
two scrolls daily.'
The King said,
'Excellent.
You may ascend the steps.'
To the north was a high seat.
The King said,
'You may ascend the seat and recite the sutra.'
The King then stood up.
After I sat down,
the King sat facing me.
I opened the sutra and said,
'The Lotus Sutra of the Wonderful Dharma, Chapter One: Introduction.'
The King said,
'Please, Dharma Master, descend.'
I stood again below the steps,
and looking at the prisoners in the courtyard,
they had all vanished.
The King said,
'The merit of your sutra recitation
not only benefits yourself;
because the multitude heard the sutra,
they have all been spared.
Is this not excellent!
I now release you to return.'
He told an officer,
'Take this man to tour the various hells.'
The officer then led me east for over a hundred paces,
where I saw an iron city,
extremely vast.
Beside the city were many small windows,
and I saw men and women
flying up from the ground into the windows,
and not coming out again.
I asked in surprise,
and the officer said,
'This is the great hell.
Inside are divisions,
and according to their respective karma, the offenders
go to the hell to receive their punishment.'
Hearing this, I felt sorrow and fear,
called out 'Námó Fó',
and begged the officer to leave the compound.
I saw a large cauldron,
with fierce fire and boiling liquid,
beside which two people were sitting and lying.
I asked them,
and they said,
'Our karmic retribution was to enter this cauldron of boiling liquid.
Thanks to your noble calling of 'Námó Fó',
all the offenders in this hell
have gained a day's rest and weary sleep.'
I again called out 'Námó Fó'.
The officer said to me,
'The official bureaus frequently change.
Now that the King is releasing you,
you should inform the King and request a document.
Otherwise,
I fear other officials may not know,
and pursue and apprehend you again.'
I then went to see the King and requested the document.
The King wrote a line of characters and gave it to the officer,
saying,
'Go and get the seals of the Five Paths, etc.'
The officer received the order,
and took me to two more bureaus.
The halls and attendants at each were similar,
and the officers all requested their officials to seal it,
each writing a line before
handing it to me.
Upon exiting the gate,
three men said to me,
'The King is releasing you.
We each hope you will leave us something.'
The officer said to me,
'Those three men
are the messengers who apprehended you before.
One is the one who bound you with a red rope,
one is the one who struck your head with a club,
one is the one who sucked your breath with a bag.
Now seeing you return,
they have come to beg.'
I was alarmed and fearful, and apologized, saying,
'I was foolish and did not recognize you, gentlemen.
I beg you to come to my home where I will prepare offerings,
but I do not know where to send them.'
The three said,
'Burn them by the water's edge under an old tree.'
I agreed.
The officer escorted me home.
I saw my relatives weeping sorrowfully,
preparing the funeral arrangements.
I approached the corpse and revived.
I said,
'Take paper money, bolts of silk, along with wine and food,
and burn them yourself by the water's edge.'
Suddenly, I saw the three men come to thank me, saying,
'We are ashamed; you did not break your promise,
and have generously given us gifts.'
Having spoken, they vanished.
From *Míngbào Jì*.
Sū Zhǎng,
during the Wǔdé era,
served as Prefect of Bāzhōu.
While traveling to take up his post,
upon reaching the Jiālíng River,
wind and waves capsized the boat,
drowning over sixty members of his household.
Only one concubine, who often read the Lotus Sutra,
when water entered the boat,
placed the sutra case on her head,
vowing to drown with it,
and drifted with the waves.
Shortly, she reached the shore.
Following the sutra case, she emerged.
Opening it to look at the sutra,
it was completely unsoiled and undampened.
She alone survived.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
The nun Fǎxìn
During the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty,
in Hédōng, there was a disciplined nun named Fǎxìn,
who often read the Lotus Sutra.
She sought out a skilled calligrapher,
paid him several times the usual rate,
specially prepared a pure chamber,
and had him copy this sutra.
For each session, he would bathe once,
burn incense and change clothes.
Furthermore, in the room for copying the sutra,
a hole was made through the wall,
with a bamboo tube added,
so that whenever the copyist needed to exhale,
he would directly place the bamboo tube in his mouth,
and expel his breath outside the wall.
Seven scrolls of the sutra were copied,
taking eight years to complete.
The offerings were solemn and reverent,
exhausting all forms of respect.
The monk Fǎduān of Lóngmén once gathered a large assembly to lecture on the Lotus Sutra.
Knowing that this nun's sutra copy was meticulously prepared,
he sent someone to request it.
The nun firmly declined and refused.
Fǎduān reproached and admonished her,
and the nun, having no alternative,
personally delivered it.
When Fǎduān and others opened it to read,
they saw only yellow paper,
completely devoid of characters.
Upon opening the remaining scrolls,
they were all the same.
Fǎduān and the others, ashamed and fearful,
immediately returned it to the nun.
The nun received it weeping with sorrow,
washed the sutra case with fragrant water,
bathed herself and placed it upon her head,
circumambulated the Buddha and practiced walking meditation,
for seven days and nights without rest.
Afterwards, when she opened it to look,
the characters were as before.
Thus it is known that copying requires deep purity and cleanliness.
Previous failures to achieve efficacy
were solely due to insufficient diligence and reverence.
From "Míng Bào Jì"
Lǐ Shì
In Fēngqiū County, Jìzhōu during the Táng dynasty,
there was an old woman surnamed Lǐ,
aged seventy,
childless and living alone in old age,
with only two servant girls.
The family
The original text lacks the character "jiā" (family).
Added based on citation from "Fǎ Yuàn Zhū Lín," chapter 94.
ran a shop selling wine,
adulterated with ash in small amounts,
managing every trifle meticulously.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
she fell ill and died.
After two days,
the funeral preparations were complete,
but because her heart still retained a little warmth,
she revived and recounted:
Initially, two men,
both dressed in red clothes,
summoned her outside the gate,
saying they had an official warrant to pursue her,
so she followed them.
They traveled to a city,
resembling a prefectural capital.
She was led to a side courtyard,
where she saw an official,
dressed in wide-sleeved robes and headgear,
seated leaning on a desk.
There were many attendants on his left and right.
Below the steps were many people wearing cangues and fetters,
guarded as if they were alive.
The official sent someone to question the old woman:
"Why did you adulterate and sell wine,
taking excessive profit from others?
You planned to sponsor a copy of the Lotus Sutra,
nearly ten years have passed,
why have you not had it made?"
The old woman explained in detail:
"The wine was made by the servant girl,
and the measurements were also taken by her.
For the sutra, I already gave one thousand coins to Master Yǐn."
They immediately sent for the servant girl.
In a moment, the servant girl arrived,
was flogged forty times and sent back.
They sent to question Master Yǐn,
who reported that it was true.
Then they said to the old woman:
"We release you for seven days.
When the sutra is completed, you must return.
You will be reborn in a good place."
Thus she was revived.
Upon verification, when the old woman first died,
the servant girl suffered a violent fit,
taking a long time to revive.
Her abdomen was all black and swollen,
likely the marks of the forty strokes.
Master Yǐn, the Chán monk,
was originally a visiting monk,
assigned to a temple in Dùnqiū.
He was nearly sixty or seventy years old.
Since leaving home to become a monk,
he practiced asceticism and begged for food,
often eating only one meal a day and maintaining a vegetarian diet,
never pausing even briefly.
Virtuous monks far and near
all respected and admired him.
On the night the old woman fell ill and died,
Master Yǐn dreamed of a man in red clothes coming to question him.
In the dream, he replied:
"Sponsoring the sutra copy is true."
The old woman then gathered relatives from her village and Master Yǐn to practice walking meditation.
She sought out various
The original text has a blank space.
The character "zhū" (various) added based on the Ming manuscript copy.
sutra copyists,
and with many hands copying the sutra, it was completed
exactly on the seventh day.
She then saw the two men from before come forward.
The mother said:
"The messengers have come.
May you all dwell well."
As her voice ceased, she died.
Master Yǐn was still alive,
revered by monastics and laypeople alike.
From "Míng Xiáng Jì"
Master Chè
During the Táng dynasty, the monk Chè, a Shāmen at Yǐnquán Temple on Nángū Mountain in Jiàngzhōu,
was once traveling
when he encountered a leper living in a cave.
Master Chè brought him out of the mountain,
dug a cave for him and provided food,
and recited the Lotus Sutra for him.
The leper was originally illiterate,
and moreover dull and ignorant.
Master Chè taught him sentence by sentence,
never tiring of it.
When the leper had recited about half the sutra,
he dreamed of someone teaching him.
Afterwards, he gradually became more intelligent and understanding,
and had already mastered five or six scrolls.
His sores gradually began to heal.
When he finished the entire sutra,
his beard and eyebrows had regrown normally,
and his complexion was as before.
The sutra says:
"It is the good medicine for illness."
These words have been verified.
From "Míng Bào Shí Yí"
Monk of Wùzhēn Temple
During the Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a monk from Wùzhēn Temple on Wángshùn Mountain.
One night, he went to Lánxī.
Suddenly, he heard someone reciting the Lotus Sutra.
The voice was faint and distant.
At the time, the stars and moon shone all around,
and looking out for several tens of miles,
it was utterly silent with nothing to be seen.
The monk felt distressed and fearful.
When he reached the temple,
he reported the matter to the assembly of monks.
The next evening,
they all went to Lánxī to listen,
and heard the sutra recitation emanating from within the ground.
They then marked the spot.
The next day, digging beneath the marker,
they found a skull
in the accumulated soil.
The bone was dried up,
but the lips and tongue alone
were fresh and moist.
They then brought it back to the temple
and placed it in a stone casket under the western corridor of the Thousand Buddha Hall.
From then on, every evening,
the sound of reciting the Lotus Sutra often came from within the stone casket.
Men and women of Cháng'ān
came to see it in numbers reaching a thousand.
Later, a Silla monk was a guest at the temple.
After about a year,
one day when all the temple monks had gone down the mountain,
only the Silla monk remained.
He then stole the stone casket and left.
The temple monks traced his whereabouts,
but he had already returned to the eastern sea.
This was at the end of the Kāiyuán era.
From "Xuān Shì Zhì"
Shì Dàosú
In the Tang dynasty, there was a monk named Dàosú,
whose origins are unknown.
He dwelled in the mountains and plains of Lǐquán,
devoting himself to reciting the Lotus Sutra as his practice,
eventually completing the recitation thousands of times.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
he fell ill and was nearing death.
He told his friend, the Chan master Huìkuò:
"Although I have recited the sutra,
I hope it will bear some proof.
After I die,
wait ten years as a trial period,
then open my grave to examine me.
If my tongue has decayed,
you will know that the recitation was without merit.
But if my tongue remains as it was in life,
then erect a stūpa for me,
so that faith may arise among the common people."
Having spoken these words, he passed away.
When the eleventh year arrived,
they opened the grave as instructed.
His body and flesh had all decayed,
but only his tongue remained incorrupt.
All the gentry and commoners of the county
marveled and praised this.
They then placed the tongue in a casket
and built a stūpa on the bank of Gāngǔ.
From the *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Shǐ Āshì
South of the Tang capital's suburbs, in the shade of Fúshuǐ, there was a village called Shǐcūn.
A man named Shǐ Āshì,
who recited the Lotus Sutra,
served as a clerk in the government.
Whenever he traveled back and forth,
he always went on foot,
never riding a horse or carriage,
because he followed the sutra's teaching
to "have compassion for all beings."
He died of illness in his hometown,
and a fragrant aroma filled the village.
Monks and laypeople were astonished,
but none could fathom the reason.
Ten years after his death,
his wife passed away,
and they opened his grave to bury them together.
They saw that his tongue root
remained as fresh as living flesh.
This truly demonstrates the spiritual efficacy of reciting the Lotus Sutra.
From the *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
The Monk of Shíbì Temple
In the Tang dynasty, at Shíbì Temple in Bīngzhōu,
there was an old monk
who devoted himself to meditation and sutra recitation as his practice,
diligent and disciplined in his cultivation.
Toward the end of the Zhēnguàn era,
a pair of magpies nested on the pillar of his room,
and they hatched and raised two chicks.
Whenever the Dharma master had leftover food,
he would always take it to the nest to feed them.
Later, although the chicks gradually grew,
their wings were not yet fully formed.
While learning to fly,
they both fell to the ground and died.
The monk collected and buried them.
After about ten days,
the monk dreamed at night of two small children who said:
"We, due to minor offenses in a past life,
were reborn as magpies.
Recently, we daily heard the Dharma master reciting the Lotus Sutra.
Having heard this wondrous Dharma,
we have obtained human rebirth.
We will now be reborn as boys
in a family of such-and-such name in a village about ten *li* from this temple.
Within ten months,
we will be born."
The monk then went to visit at the appointed time
and saw the woman of that household
had indeed given birth to two sons at the same time.
When he attended their full-moon celebration,
the monk called them "magpie boys,"
and they both responded,
"Yes."
From the *Míngbào Shíyí*.
Dòu Fù
In the Jin dynasty, there was a man named Dòu Fù,
a native of Hénèi.
During the Yǒnghé era,
the Governor of Bīngzhōu, Gāo Chāng, and the Governor of Jìzhōu, Lǚ Hù, each commanded their own troops
and were at odds with each other.
Dòu Fù served under Gāo Chāng
as an official.
Lǚ Hù dispatched cavalry to raid them,
and Dòu Fù was captured.
Along with six or seven companions,
they were imprisoned together in a single cell,
bound with very heavy shackles and fetters.
They were scheduled to be executed on a set day.
The monk Zhī Dùnshān was in Lǚ Hù's camp at the time.
He had previously been acquainted with Dòu Fù.
Hearing of his dire predicament—
"predicament" originally written as "nun,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript and the Xǔ edition—
Dùnshān went to the prison to visit him,
and they spoke through the door.
Dòu Fù said to Dùnshān:
"Now I am in dire straits,
my life hangs by a thread.
Is there any way you can save me?"
Dùnshān said:
"If you can sincerely turn to and beseech [Guanyin],
there will surely be a response."
Dòu Fù had also heard somewhat of Guānshìyīn before.
Upon hearing Dùnshān's words,
he focused his mind single-pointedly,
for three days and nights,
sincerely taking refuge.
Observing his shackles,
he felt as if they had loosened,
different from usual.
He tentatively tried shaking them,
and they suddenly fell away from his body.
Dòu Fù then again focused his mind and said:
"Now I have received compassionate aid,
and my shackles have been loosened.
But I still have many companions here.
I have no mind to leave alone.
The divine power of Guānshìyīn universally aids all.
May it cause all to be spared together."
After speaking these words,
he pulled and tugged at the others' bonds,
and they all came loose in turn,
as if cut away by a blade.
They then opened the door and walked out.
Amidst the patrols and guards,
no one noticed them.
They scaled the city wall and fled directly away.
After traveling four or five *li*,
day broke.
Not daring to go further,
they all hid together in a forest.
Shortly after,
Lǚ Hù realized the prisoners were missing.
Men and horses in continuous streams
went out in all directions to search and capture them,
burning grass and trampling through woods,
leaving no place unchecked.
Yet only the patch of land, about one *mu* in size, where Dòu Fù and his companions were hiding,
remained completely unvisited.
Thus they were able to escape and return home.
Their hometown revered and believed in this extraordinarily,
and all came to devoutly follow the Buddha-Dharma.
Later, Dùnshān crossed the river
and fully recounted this event to the layman Xiè Fū.
From the *Zhēn Fù Shíyí*.
The Ming manuscript cites the *Míngxiáng Jì*.
Zhōu Dāng
Jìn Zhōu Dāng was a man from Shàn County, Kuàijī.
His family had for generations upheld the Buddhist Dharma.
At the age of sixteen,
Dāng already abstained from meat and recited scriptures.
When the first month’s extended vegetarian fast concluded,
he invited monks to perform the Eight Precepts Retreat and also requested his teachers, Zhú Fómì and Zhī Fǎjiē.
Fómì instructed him to bring the Lesser Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra to recite during the retreat.
On the third day, when the monks came for the retreat,
they forgot to bring the Lesser Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra.
After the midday meal,
when they intended to recite the scripture,
they only then remembered,
and were greatly distressed.
