Dāng’s home was in Bǎnyí Village,
thirty lǐ from the temple,
and there was no one to send to fetch it.
After the evening incense offering,
the family regretted not having the scripture,
and Mì grew increasingly uneasy.
After a while,
they heard someone knocking at the door,
saying they had come to deliver the Lesser Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra.
Dāng was astonished and overjoyed.
Opening the door,
he saw a young man wearing a single-layered robe,
whom he had never met before and who did not appear to be from that time.
Suspecting this was a divine marvel,
he knelt down to receive the scripture.
He tried to invite the youth inside to sit,
but the youth refused to enter,
saying,
"I shall come tonight to listen to the scripture recitation."
By the time he went out, the youth was no longer to be seen,
yet the fragrance filled the house.
When they looked afterward,
it turned out to be Mì’s scripture.
Both monastics and laypeople were amazed and delighted.
Mì’s scripture had originally been in the kitchen,
securely locked away.
Upon checking the lock,
it remained perfectly intact as before.
Thereupon, more than ten households in the village all began to uphold Buddhism.
Dāng subsequently left home to become a monk,
taking the monastic name Tánní.
He recited and chanted various scriptures totaling two hundred thousand words.
From "Records of Miraculous Manifestations."
Zhú Fǎyì
During the Xīngníng era of the Jìn dynasty,
the monk Zhú Fǎyì,
who lived in the mountains and was devoted to goodness,
resided at Bǎoshān in Shǐníng.
Later, he fell ill for an extended period.
Despite exhaustive attempts at treatment,
there was no improvement,
and his condition grew increasingly critical day by day.
He then ceased seeking medical treatment for himself,
and instead devoted himself sincerely to Guānshìyīn,
continuing thus for several days.
While napping during the day,
he dreamed that a Daoist priest came to tend to his illness
and proceeded to treat him,
cutting open his abdomen to remove his intestines and stomach,
washing and cleansing his internal organs,
where he saw many accumulated impurities.
After the cleansing was complete,
he returned them inside and said to Yì,
"Your illness is now cured."
Upon waking from the dream,
all his ailments vanished completely,
and he soon recovered his normal health.
Therefore, the scripture says,
"Sometimes appearing in the form of a monk or a Brahmin."
Perhaps this is what Yìgong dreamed of!
Yì passed away in the seventh year of Tàiyuán.
Sòng Dynasty Minister Fù Liàng recorded his story.
Liàng himself said,
"My late father associated with Yì,
and whenever Yì recounted this event,
he would become solemn with awe."
From "Records of Marvels."
"The Forest of Pearls in the Garden of the Dharma" cites this twice (chapters 17 and 95) as from "Records of Miraculous Manifestations."
Wáng Mín’s Wife
Wáng Mín of Lángyá in the Jìn dynasty
had a wife who bore no children.
She once prayed to Guānshìyīn, asking for a son.
Later, Mín encountered a foreign monk on the road
and felt very pleased with him.
The monk said,
"After I die,
I shall become your son."
Soon after, the monk indeed passed away,
and Mín’s wife became pregnant.
When the child was born, he could speak,
immediately understanding the Sanskrit languages of the sixteen Western Regions.
He was highly intelligent and possessed great bearing—
this was none other than Wáng Hóngmíng, later a Minister of the Jìn dynasty.
Thus his childhood name was Āliàn.
When he recounted events from his previous life,
everything proved true.
From "Treatise on Discernment of the Correct."
Zhú Chángshū
In the Jìn dynasty, there was a man named Zhú Chángshū,
originally from India,
who devoted himself to reciting the Guānyīn Sūtra as his practice.
Later, he lived in Wúzhōng.
When a fire broke out in the city,
with rows of houses and connected rooftops,
the flames reached
"the flames reached" — these two characters were originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy.
and everything was burned.
Chángshū’s home was directly downwind,
and he fully expected it to be destroyed,
so he single-mindedly invoked Guānshìyīn.
Just as the fire was about to reach his house,
the wind shifted and the flames died out,
astonishing the entire county.
At that time, some mischievous youths,
skeptical of this divine response,
waited until late at night when the wind was strong,
and threw fire at his house,
but each attempt was extinguished.
The youths sighed in admiration,
and by dawn,
they came to kowtow and confess their fault.
Shū said,
"I possess no divine power.
I simply devote myself to reciting Guānshìyīn,
and whenever trouble arises,
I am always able to escape harm."
From "Treatise on Discernment of the Correct."
Pān Dàoxiù,
a man from Wújùn,
was in his twenties
when he once followed the army on a northern campaign.
After the army suffered a minor defeat,
Xiù fled but was captured
and enslaved in several places.
A captive in a foreign land,
he had no means to return home.
Having some faith in Buddhism,
he constantly and sincerely invoked Guānshìyīn.
Whenever he slept,
he would see the image.
Later, while fleeing southward,
he lost his way.
In a remote mountain,
he suddenly beheld the true form,
like a portable statue,
and paid respects with joy.
Without realizing it, he walked safely
and found the road back,
thus returning to his homeland.
Afterward, he practiced with even greater diligence and sincerity.
From "Records of Miraculous Manifestations."
Luán Xún
Luán Xún of the Jìn dynasty,
whose origins are unknown,
had upheld the Dharma since youth.
He once served as magistrate of Fùpíng.
Previously, while on campaign against Lú Xún,
they encountered a minor setback.
Their boats were nearly consumed by fire,
and the enemy pressed close.
Right in the middle of the river,
with terrifying wind and waves before their eyes,
Xún was utterly terrified,
and he fervently invoked Guānshìyīn.
Suddenly, he saw a person standing upright alone in the river,
with the water level at his waist.
Xún knew in his heart that this was a response to his recitation,
so he jumped into the water toward him.
His body floated and rose,
his feet as if treading on solid ground.
Soon after, the imperial army sent boats to rescue the defeated soldiers,
and thus he was saved.
From "Records of Miraculous Manifestations."
Zhāng Chóng
Jìn Dynasty's Zhāng Chóng was
a native of Dùlíng in Jīngzhào.
In his youth, he upheld the Dharma.
During the Tàiyuán era,
after Fú Jiān was defeated,
over a thousand households from Cháng'ān
fled south to return to Jìn,
but were detained by the garrison troops,
who accused them of being wandering bandits.
Chóng and five others like him
had their hands and feet shackled and were placed in pits,
buried and tamped down
(The original text had "forbidden";
amended according to the Míng Dynasty manuscript copy.)
up to their waists,
each spaced twenty paces apart,
and the next day they were to be trampled by horses and shot.
Chóng, seeing no hope left,
could only purify his mind and recite Guānshìyīn's name.
In the night, the shackles suddenly broke by themselves,
and thus he managed to escape.
Passing by a temple on the road,
he again invoked Guānshìyīn's name,
and with utmost sincerity paid his respects.
Placing a stone before him,
he made a vow, saying:
"Now I wish to cross the river east,
to plead my case before the Jìn Emperor,
to seek justice for these wronged souls,
and to rescue their wives and children.
If my wish is fulfilled,
may this stone split in two."
After Chóng bowed,
the stone immediately split.
Chóng arrived at the capital,
submitted a memorial at the White Tiger Vessel,
and detailed the injustice.
The Emperor then granted clemency.
Those who had been captured and sold
were all redeemed and registered as commoners.
Dàozhì Shēng, a monk, personally witnessed these events.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Shì Kāidá
Jìn Dynasty monk Shì Kāidá,
in the second year of Lóng'ān,
went up to the Long region to gather licorice,
and was captured by the Qiāng.
At that time, there was a great famine,
and the Qiāng and Hú were eating each other.
They placed Dá in a pen,
intending to eat him.
There were originally over ten people in the pen,
but the Qiāng cooked and ate them day and night,
leaving only Dá still alive.
From the time Dá was captured,
he secretly recited the Guānshìyīn Sūtra,
never slackening in his heart.
The next day,
when he was to be eaten,
at the break of dawn,
suddenly a great tiger
approached the group of Qiāng from afar,
roaring furiously.
The Qiāng, terrified, all fled in panic.
The tiger then came forward and bit the wooden bars of the pen,
creating a small gap,
just large enough for a person to pass through,
and then slowly left.
When Dá first saw the tiger biting the pen,
he thought he would surely be harmed.
But since the tiger did not enter after breaking through the pen,
he suspected something unusual,
believing it to be the power of Guānshìyīn.
Calculating that the Qiāng had not yet returned,
he immediately slipped through the gap in the pen and escaped,
traveling by night and hiding by day,
and thus managed to avoid capture.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Zhú Fǎchún
Jìn Dynasty monk Zhú Fǎchún
was the abbot of Xiǎnyì Temple in Shānyīn.
During the Yuánxīng era,
while traveling to purchase timber for building a temple,
he took a route across a lake.
The timber owner was a woman,
and they traveled together in the same boat.
After entering the lake,
at dusk, a violent storm arose,
with waves as high as mountains.
The boat was small and took on water,
and since he was traveling with a woman,
his life hung by a thread.
He then wholeheartedly recited the Guānshìyīn Sūtra.
As it was already night,
and other travelers had ceased,
suddenly a large boat drifted toward them.
Chún immediately boarded it and crossed over,
while the small boat sank immediately.
The large boat tossed and swayed with the waves,
but soon reached the shore.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Shì Dàotài
Jìn Dynasty monk Shì Dàotài
was a monk at the Héngtáng Retreat in Chángshān.
During the Yìxī era,
he once dreamed of someone saying:
"Your life will end at sixty or seventy."
When Tài reached the age of forty-two,
he fell seriously ill,
and fearing he would not recover,
he donated all his possessions from his robe and alms bowl,
making generous offerings for merit.
He also devotedly recited Guānshìyīn's name,
for four days and nights,
diligently and without ceasing.
At the time, a curtain hung before the bed where he sat.
Suddenly, from under the curtain, he saw someone stride over the threshold and enter,
with golden feet,
illuminating the room with light.
Tài then lifted the curtain to look quickly,
but the figure vanished abruptly.
Astonished and overjoyed,
he broke into a profuse sweat,
and his chest and body immediately felt lighter.
His illness was cured.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Guō Xuān
In the eleventh year of Yìxī in the Jìn Dynasty,
Tàiyuán's Guō Xuān and Shǔjùn's Wén Chùmào
were previously friends with Liángzhōu Governor Yáng Shōujìng.
Shōujìng committed a crime and was imprisoned,
and Xuān and Chùmào were also shackled together.
They recited Guānshìyīn's name.
Ten days later,
at night, they dreamed of a Bodhisattva comforting them,
telling them they had nothing to fear for their lives.
Soon after, their shackles fell off by themselves,
but by dawn they were back on.
This happened repeatedly,
and the two then made a vow:
if they were spared punishment,
each would donate one hundred thousand coins to Míngxī Temple for meritorious deeds.
A few days later, both were spared.
Xuān, keeping his vow, sent the money to the temple,
but Chùmào broke his vow and did not send it.
When Lú Xún raised an army,
Mào was hit by a stray arrow at Xiāngpǔ,
and before dying, he said:
"I have committed a great sin."
After speaking, he died.
From *Biànzhèng Lùn*.
Lǚ Sǒng
Jìn Dynasty's Lǚ Sǒng, courtesy name Màogāo,
was from Yǎnzhōu.
He resided in Shǐfēng County,
where the southern stream
flowed swiftly with steep banks,
winding and twisting like a coiled thread,
and with many large rocks.
Even those traveling by day
felt particularly fearful and uneasy.
Sǒng himself recounted:
his father once traveled along the stream,
more than ten lǐ from home,
as dusk approached,
a great storm arose,
dark as lacquer,
and he no longer knew east from west.
Resigning himself to drowning,
he turned his heart to Guānshìyīn,
reciting and invoking the name.
Shortly after,
a firelight appeared on the bank,
as if someone were holding a torch.
It illuminated the stream clearly,
and he was able to find his way home.
The fire remained before and behind him,
about ten paces from the boat.
Sǒng later associated with Xī Jiābīn,
and this was recounted by Xī.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Xú Róng
There was a man named Xú Róng in Jìn,
a native of Lángyá.
He once traveled to Dōngyáng,
and on his return journey passed Dìngshān.
The boatman was inexperienced,
and mistakenly entered a whirlpool,
on the verge of sinking.
Róng had no other plan,
so he wholeheartedly called upon the name of Guānshìyīn.
In a moment,
it was as if dozens of people were pulling the boat together,
lifting it out of the whirlpool,
and it drifted down the river.
Night had fallen,
the sky was dark and gloomy,
the wind and rain were fierce,
and they did not know which way to go,
while the surging waves grew stronger.
Róng continued reciting scriptures without pause,
when suddenly he saw flames blazing brightly on a mountaintop.
He turned the boat toward it,
and directly reached the shore.
Once he arrived,
the flames were no longer visible.
The next morning,
he asked the people by the shore:
"What fire was on the mountain last night?"
Everyone was astonished and said:
"With such wind and rain,
how could there be fire?"
Then he knew it was the hidden aid of Buddha's power.
Later, Róng became the Dūhù of Kuàijī Prefecture.
Xiè Fū once heard Róng tell this story.
At the time, a monk named Zhī Dàoyùn was on the same boat as Róng,
a sincere and earnest man,
who also knew the full story.
He told it to Fù Liàng,
and it matched what Róng had said.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín."
Liú Dù
was a native of Liáochéng in Píngyuán.
In his hometown, over a thousand households
all followed the Great Dharma,
creating statues,
and providing for monks and nuns.
During the time of the tribal leader Mùmò,
this county often had fugitives.
Mò was greatly angered,
and wanted to exterminate the entire city.
Everyone was terrified,
certain they would be utterly destroyed.
Dù then led the people with pure sincerity,
and entrusted themselves to Guānshìyīn.
After a short while,
Mò saw something descend from the sky,
circling around the pillar of his house.
He looked in astonishment,
and it was the Guānshìyīn Sūtra.
Mò was overjoyed,
and thus reduced punishments and killings,
so the city was spared harm.
From "Míngxiáng Jì."
Nángōng Zǐ'áo,
a native of Shǐpíng,
was garrisoned at Xīnpíng City.
When the city was captured by the tribal leader Chánglègōng of the Fúfú tribe,
several thousand people in the city were all slaughtered.
Though Zǐ'áo was certain to die,
he still wholeheartedly recited Guānshìyīn.
When it was his turn,
blades fell upon him from all sides,
some high, some low,
but the men holding the swords suddenly grew weary and slack,
their limbs unresponsive.
At that time, Chánglègōng personally oversaw the execution,
and asked in surprise.
Zǐ'áo casually replied:
"I can make saddles."
So he was pardoned and released.
Zǐ'áo himself did not know why he said this at the time.
Later, he managed to escape,
and made a small statue of Guānyīn,
keeping it in an incense box,
and carrying it on his head when he traveled.
From "Míngxiáng Jì."
Xú Yì
Xú Yì of Fú Qín,
a native of Gāolù,
served as a Shàngshū,
and had followed Buddhism since youth.
At that time, wars broke out like swarming bees,
and bandits captured Yì,
intending to harm him.
They buried his feet in the ground,
and tied his hair to a tree.
At night,
Yì focused his thoughts on Guānshìyīn.
After a while,
he suddenly dreamed of someone saying to him:
"The situation is urgent now,
how can you sleep!"
Yì awoke in alarm,
and saw that the guards
were all tired and asleep.
He tried to struggle free,
and his hands and hair came loose,
his feet also freed.
He fled over a hundred paces,
and hid in the grass.
Then he heard the pursuers galloping back and forth,
but with torches, they did not see him.
By dawn, the bandits dispersed,
and Yì returned to seek refuge in a temple in Yè,
thus escaping harm.
From "Míngxiáng Jì."
Bì Lǎn
Bì Lǎn of Fú Qín,
a native of Dōngpíng,
had followed the Dharma since youth.
He followed Mùróng Chuí on a northern campaign,
was captured by the enemy,
and escaped alone on horseback.
Enemy cavalry pursued and were about to catch him,
so Lǎn wholeheartedly recited Guānshìyīn,
and managed to escape.
He entered the mountains,
but lost his way in confusion.
Again, he focused on reciting.
In the middle of the night, he saw a monk,
in monastic robes holding a staff,
who showed him the way,
and he safely reached home.
From "Míngxiáng Jì."
Shì Fǎzhì
The monk Shì Fǎzhì,
when he was still a layman,
once traveled alone to a great marsh.
Suddenly, a fierce fire broke out,
surrounding him on all sides,
cutting off his escape.
He then wholeheartedly bowed and recited Guānshìyīn.
Soon, the fire passed,
and all the grass in the marsh
was burned without a single blade left,
except for the spot where Fǎzhì stood, which was untouched.
From then on, he revered and followed the Great Dharma.
Later, he served as a general under Yáo Xīng,
and followed the campaign against the Suǒ tribe.
During the army's retreat, he lost his horse,
and was left behind in enemy encirclement.
He hid by a ditch among thorny bushes,
covering his head,
and again recited Guānshìyīn,
with utmost sincerity.
Across the ditch, someone called out to the rear army,
ordering them to kill him,
but when the army searched,
they could not find him,
and he escaped.
Later, he became a monk.
From "Míngxiáng Jì."
Sūn Dàodé
Sūn Dàodé of Sòng,
a native of Yìzhōu,
was a Jìjiǔ of the Daoist faith.
Over fifty years old,
he still had no children,
and lived near a temple.
During the Jǐngpíng era,
a monk said to Dàodé:
"If you truly wish for a son,
you must wholeheartedly bow and recite the Guānshìyīn Sūtra,
and you may have hope."
Dé then ceased his Daoist practices,
and with sincere devotion,
turned to reciting Guānshìyīn.
Within a few days,
he received a dream response,
and his wife became pregnant,
giving birth to a son.
From "Míngxiáng Jì."
Zhāng Xīng
Zhāng Xìng of the Sòng Dynasty,
a native of Xīnxīng,
was a devout believer in Buddhism.
He often received the Eight Precepts from the monks Sēng Róng and Tán Yì.
In the early Yuánjiā era,
Xìng was implicated by bandits,
and he fled to escape.
His wife was imprisoned,
and she was tortured with flogging for many days.
At that time, a fire broke out in the county,
and the prisoners were taken out to the roadside.
It happened that Róng and Yì were passing by together,
and they accidentally walked past the prisoners.
Xìng's wife cried out in surprise:
"Venerable ones, why do you not save me?"
Róng said:
"I am but a humble monk with little power,
unable to rescue you. What can be done?
You should only fervently recite the name of Guānshìyīn,
and perhaps you may be spared."
His wife then prayed and recited day and night.
After about ten days,
she dreamed at night of a monk stepping on her with his foot and saying:
"Hey, hey,
get up."
His wife immediately woke up startled,
and the shackles, locks, and fetters all came loose.
However, the doors were closed and guarded,
and there was no way to get out.
Fearing she might be discovered,
she put the shackles back on herself.
She then dreamed of the same monk again, who said:
"The door is already open."
His wife woke up and rushed out,
and the guards were all asleep.
She walked calmly and escaped.
Walking in the dark for several miles,
she suddenly encountered a person.
His wife, terrified, fell to the ground.
After a while, they spoke to each other,
and it turned out to be her husband.
They met with both sorrow and joy.
At night, they sought refuge with the monk Yì,
and Yì hid them,
allowing them to escape.
From "Míngxiáng Jì"
Tán Wú Jié
In the early Yuánjiā era of the Sòng Dynasty,
there was a monk from Huánglóng named Tán Wú Jié,
who recited the Guānshìyīn Sūtra
and cultivated ascetic practices with purity.
Together with twenty-five disciples,
he went in search of the Buddha's land,
enduring many hardships and dangers.
After reaching Śrāvastī in India,
they encountered a herd of mountain elephants on the road.
Jié took out the sūtra and recited it,
invoking the name and "taking refuge."
A lion emerged from the forest,
and the elephants fled in panic.
Later, there was a herd of wild oxen,
roaring as they approached,
intending to harm them.
Jié again took refuge as before,
and a large vulture flew over.
The oxen then scattered in fear,
and they were spared.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín"
Chē Mǔ
Chē Mǔ
encountered the Qīngní calamity during the time of Prince Lúlíng of the Sòng Dynasty
and was captured by the enemy.
He was held in the enemy camp.
His mother had long been devoted to Buddhism,
so she lit seven lamps before the Buddha
and at night earnestly recited the name of Guānshìyīn,
praying for her son's escape.
After a year of this,
her son suddenly rebelled and returned.
For seven days and seven nights, he traveled alone,
heading south.
The sky was often overcast,
and he did not know east from west.
From afar, he saw seven segments of firelight,
and he walked toward the light.
It seemed like a village he could seek refuge in,
but he could never reach it.
After seven nights like this,
he unexpectedly arrived home.
He saw his mother still prostrating before the Buddha,
and he also saw the seven lamps.
He then realized the truth.
Mother and son talked together,
and they knew it was the power of the Buddha.
From then on, they prayed earnestly
and devoted themselves to compassion.
From "Xuānyàn Jì"
Shì Tán Yǐng
In the Sòng Dynasty, at Chánggàn Temple, there was a monk named Shì Tán Yǐng,
a native of Kuàijī.
He left home to become a monk at a young age,
was strict in observing the precepts,
and recited over a hundred thousand words of sūtras.
He resided at Chánggàn Temple.
He was skilled in preaching and chanting,
naturally unparalleled.
Yǐng often suffered from a skin disease,
which persisted despite repeated treatments.
In his room, he always enshrined an image of Guānshìyīn,
paying homage morning and evening,
praying for a cure for this illness.
One day,
he suddenly saw a snake
climbing up the wall to the roof.
After a moment,
a small mouse
fell from the roof to the ground,
covered in saliva,
appearing as if dead.
Yǐng waited for it to revive,
then took bamboo to scrape off the saliva.
He also heard that mice swallowed by snakes
could cure skin diseases,
so he took the saliva and applied it to his skin condition.
After applying it all over,
the mouse also came back to life.
Within two days,
the skin disease was completely cured.
Only then did he realize that the snake and the mouse
were all brought about by his prayers.
Thus, he was esteemed by the ruler,
and his fame spread far and wide.
He later passed away at his place of residence,
at the age of eighty-one.
From "Gāosēng Zhuàn"
Xíng Huáimíng
Xíng Huáimíng of the Sòng Dynasty,
a native of Héjiān,
served as a military advisor to the Grand General.
He once followed the Nánjùn Prefect Zhū Xúnzhī on a northern campaign,
and they were both captured together.
Waiting for an opportunity,
they both fled south to return.
They traveled by night and hid by day.
After three days,
still fearing pursuit,
they sent someone ahead to scout the enemy's movements.
The person did not return for several days.
One evening,
as rain approached and it grew dark,
the person they had sent suddenly arrived just before dawn.
He said in surprise:
"Earlier, I saw a very bright firelight from afar,
so I came toward it.
How did it become dark just as I arrived?"
Xún and the others were astonished.
Huáimíng had long been devoted to the Dharma.
Since going on the campaign,
he always carried the Guānshìyīn Sūtra on his head,
reciting it without cease.
That night, he also recited it silently.
They all suspected it was the divine power of the sūtra
that allowed them to escape.
After living in the capital,
a monk suddenly visited Huáimíng and said:
"This humble monk sees bloodshed in this alley and in your home.
You should move to avoid it."
After speaking, he left.
Huáimíng followed him with his eyes,
but the monk disappeared as soon as he went out the door.
Huáimíng felt very uneasy about this.
After twenty days,
his neighbor Zhāng Jǐngxiù
injured his father and killed his wife.
Huáimíng thought this was the sign of bloodshed,
and he hoped to avoid trouble.
At that time, he lived in the same alley as Liú Bīn and Liú Jìngwén.
That year, they were all implicated as part of Liú Zhàn's faction
and were executed.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín"
Wáng Qiú
Sòng Wáng Qiú, styled Shūdá,
was from Tàiyuán.
He served as the Prefect of Fúlíng.
In the first year of the Yuánjiā era,
he lost control of his commandery,
was imprisoned,
and kept under strict confinement with heavy shackles.
Qiú had previously been diligent and devoted,
applying his mind with particular earnestness.
Among the over one hundred prisoners,
many were starving.
Whenever Qiú ate,
he would share his food with them,
maintaining a vegetarian diet daily,
and wholeheartedly recited the name of Guānshìyīn.
One night he dreamed of ascending a high seat,
where he saw a monk
who gave him a scroll of scripture,
titled *The Chapter on the Radiant Practice*.
It also contained the names of various bodhisattvas.
Qiú received it and began reading,
forgetting the name of the first bodhisattva,
the second was Guānyīn,
and the third was Dàshìzhì.
He also saw a wheel,
and the monk said:
"This is the gate of the five destinies."
Upon awakening,
his shackles had all broken and fallen off.
Qiú knew in his heart it was divine power,
and his concentration increased even more.
He then repaired the shackles himself.
After three days, he was pardoned.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Zhú Huìqìng
The Sòng monk Zhú Huìqìng
was from Guǎnglíng,
and was cultivated and virtuous in his practice.
In the twelfth year of Yuánjiā,
great floods struck Jīng and Yáng.
Huìqìng was about to enter Lúshān.
When his boat reached the river, a sudden storm arose.
The others in his group had already managed to reach the shore,
but only Huìqìng's boat was tossed about in the middle of the river.
The wind was fierce and the waves surged,
and they awaited only capsizing.
Huìqìng focused his mind and intent,
and recited the Guānshìyīn Sūtra.
People on the shore
saw his boat
cutting through the current against the gale,
as if dozens of people were pulling it,
and it went straight to the bank,
saving everyone aboard.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Biàn Yuèzhī
The Sòng lay devotee Biàn Yuèzhī,
was from Jìyīn.
He held a court appointment,
and lived at Cháogōu.
He was fifty years old
and still had no offspring.
His wife took a concubine for him,
but even after years, she did not conceive.
Wishing to pray for an heir,
he vowed to recite the Guānshìyīn Sūtra a thousand times.
As the number neared completion,
the concubine became pregnant,
and subsequently gave birth to a son.
This was in the fourteenth year of Yuánjiā.
From *Míngxiáng Jì*.
Zhāng Chàng
Sòng's Zhāng Chàng
constantly upheld devotion to Guānyīn.
When Nánqiáo plotted rebellion,
Chàng did not follow,
so the Prince wanted to kill him.
That night, the Prince dreamed of Guānshìyīn saying:
"You must not kill Chàng!"
So he did not dare harm him.
After the Prince's defeat,
Chàng was imprisoned.
He recited the Guānshìyīn Sūtra a thousand times,
and his shackles broke inch by inch.
The jailers replaced them, but they broke again.
The clerk reported,
"The clerk reported" – the Ming manuscript reads "a few days later".
"Release him."
From *Tán Sǒu*.
Wáng Xuánmó
Sòng's Wáng Xuánmó from Tàiyuán,
was forthright and unmatched.
During a northern campaign, he failed in command,
and by military law deserved death.
He dreamed of someone telling him:
"If you recite Guānshìyīn's name a thousand times,
you can escape disaster."
Mó said:
"My life hangs by a thread;
how can I manage a thousand recitations?"
Then he was taught:
"Guānshìyīn,
Námó fó,
with the Buddha there is cause,
with the Buddha there is condition,
the Buddha's Dharma connects conditions,
eternal bliss is my essence,
morning I recite Guānshìyīn,
evening I recite Guānshìyīn,
each recitation arises from the heart,
reciting the Buddha never leaves the heart."
Thereupon he completed the thousand recitations.
As he was about to be executed,
General Shěn Qìngzhī interceded,
and he was spared.
He later served as President of the Department of State Affairs, General of the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon, and Governor of Yùzhōu.
Original source missing.
The Ming manuscript states: From *Tán Sǒu*.
Shì Dàojiǒng
The Later Qín monk Shì Dàojiǒng,
in the eighteenth year of Hóngshǐ,
was sent by his master Dào Yì to collect stalactites at Huòshān in Hénán,
traveling with fellow practitioners Dào Lǎng and three others.
Carrying torches into a deep cave,
they entered about three *lǐ*
and encountered a deep stream,
crossing by a horizontal log.
Jiǒng crossed first,
but those behind fell into the water and died.
Then the torches also went out,
plunging them into utter darkness.
Jiǒng felt his life was at an end,
and could only weep bitterly.
Yet he firmly focused his mind, calling upon Guānshìyīn,
vowing that if granted a way out,
he would sponsor a hundred-assembly feast
to manifest gratitude for the divine power.
After one night, he saw a small light glowing,
like a firefly,
and in an instant,
the entire cave became bright.
Then he saw the path
and emerged from under the cliff.
From this, his faith and understanding deepened profoundly,
and he frequently witnessed miraculous manifestations.
In the nineteenth year of Yuánjiā,
the Prince of Línchuān, stationed in Guǎnglíng,
invited Jiǒng to receive offerings.
That year in the ninth month,
he held a ten-day Guānshìyīn retreat in the western studio.
On the ninth day,
in the fourth watch of the night,
when all the monks were asleep,
Jiǒng rose to bow in gratitude,
intending to sit in meditation.
Suddenly he saw countless monks on the four walls,
all appearing from the waist up.
One Buddha with a spiral topknot
was clearly visible.
There was a tall man,
wearing a flat-topped headcloth,
cloth trousers and jacket,
holding a long knife,
with an extremely majestic appearance,
who offered incense to Dàojiǒng.
Dàojiǒng at first refused to accept it,
but the monks in the wall said:
"Venerable Jiǒng, you should accept the incense
to protect the host."
Suddenly,
everything vanished.
At that moment,
he could no longer see the assembly of monks,
but only a walking statue of Shìjiāwén that had been placed there.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Fú Wànshòu
was from Píngchāng.
In the nineteenth year of the Yuánjiā era of the Song dynasty, while serving as a military staff officer in the guard headquarters in Guǎnglíng,
he requested leave to return to his home province.
In the early fourth watch of the night,
he crossed the river.
The long waves flowed peacefully,
but midway, a wind arose swift as arrows.
It was also nighttime,
and he did not know which direction to go.
Wànshòu had long practiced the Dharma;
he single-mindedly took refuge in Guānshìyīn,
reciting without pause.
Suddenly, he and several others in the boat
together saw a light on the northern shore,
resembling a village fire.
Delighted, he said:
"This must be the light of a settlement."
They turned the boat and headed toward it,
arriving before dawn.
When they asked the people there,
they all said:
"Last night, no one lit a fire."
Only then did they realize it was the power of divine aid.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Péng Zǐqiáo
Péng Zǐqiáo of the Song dynasty
was from Yìyáng County.
He served as the registrar of his commandery,
working under the Grand Administrator Shěn Wénlóng.
In the first year of the Jiànyuán era,
he was imprisoned due to a crime.
Zǐqiáo had been a monk in his youth;
after returning to lay life,
he often recited the Guānshìyīn Sūtra.
At the time, Wénlóng was in a great rage,
the guards and shackles were tightened urgently,
and he was determined to have him killed.
Zǐqiáo was worried and fearful,
with no other plan left,
so he just recited the sūtra with utmost sincerity.
After over a hundred recitations,
he grew tired and dozed off during the day.
There were about ten others imprisoned with him,
and they were all asleep as well.
There was a clerk from Xiāngxī County, Dù Dàoróng,
also imprisoned in the jail,
who drifted in and out of sleep,
not deeply asleep.
Suddenly, a pair of white cranes alighted on Zǐqiáo's screen.
After a while,
one crane descended beside Zǐqiáo,
and at times it seemed to transform into a beautiful person.
Dàoróng got up
and saw that Zǐqiáo's double shackles had come off outside his feet,
yet the marks from the shackles were still there.
Dàoróng looked in astonishment;
Zǐqiáo also awoke.
Together they looked at the shackles and sighed.
Zǐqiáo asked Dàoróng:
"Did you dream anything?"
He replied:
"I did not dream."
Dàoróng described what he had seen.
Although Zǐqiáo knew it must have been due to his own devotion,
he still feared the jailers would suspect he intended to escape,
so he took the shackles and put them back on.
After four or five days, he was pardoned and released.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Shì Huìhé
The monk Huìhé of the Song dynasty
was a monk at the Zhòngzào Temple in the capital.
During the Yuán
(*Fǎyuàn Zhūlín* chapter 27 cites Yuán as Yì;
Yìjiā was the era name established when Prince Jìn'ān of Liú Sòng raised troops.
See *Sòng Shū, Biography of Dèng Wǎn*.)
jiā disaster,
Huìhé was still a layperson,
attached to the forces of Liú Hú.
Hú often sent several dozen officers and soldiers east as spies;
Huìhé was also among them.
When they reached Quèzhǔ,
they encountered the imperial army advancing west.
The spies scattered,
each fleeing into the marshes.
Huìhé managed to escape
and went down to Xīnlín,
where he saw an old villager wearing tattered clothes.
Huìhé then exchanged his neat-looking trousers and jacket for the old man's clothes,
carried a basket and a load,
resembling a farmer.
At the time, various patrol troops were capturing these scattered spies;
looking at Huìhé's appearance,
they grew suspicious and questioned him.
Huìhé's answers were evasive and vague.
Thus he was beaten and tortured,
and was about to be executed on the spot.
Ever since Huìhé had fled and scattered,
he had constantly recited the Guānshìyīn Sūtra.
When he was about to be beheaded,
his pleas became even more earnest.
Then the soldier swinging the blade repeatedly stumbled;
three times he raised it, and three times it broke.
Astonished, they released him.
Huìhé then renounced the world to become a monk,
and eventually achieved profound practice.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Prince Jiàn'ān of Qí
Prince Jiàn'ān of Qí suffered from sores.
He recited Guānyīn's name without cease.
At night he dreamed of Guānyīn,
who applied medicine with her hand.
The next morning, his sores were healed.
From *Gǎnyìng Zhuàn*.
Máo Dézǔ
Máo Dézǔ of Xíngyáng
initially fled to the region south of the Yangtze,
sneaking along the road.
On the way, he encountered pursuing enemy cavalry.
He hid by the roadside among the weeds,
but half his body was still exposed.
He resigned himself to death.
His whole family recited Guānshìyīn's name.
Suddenly, clouds gathered and rain poured down,
and he escaped death.
From *Biànzhèng Lùn*.
Lǐ Rújùn
The troop commander Lǐ Rújùn was defending Hǔláo
when he was besieged by the Wei invaders.
In dire straits, he considered surrendering.
One night, he climbed over the city wall to escape.
He saw enemy soldiers lying scattered everywhere.
Rújùn then single-mindedly recited Guānshìyīn's name.
He passed through the enemy area
and headed toward an empty marsh.
The enemy immediately followed him.
Rújùn entered the grass,
but before he could hide completely,
the enemy closed in.
Rújùn was terrified.
He focused his mind solely on reciting the Guānshìyīn Sūtra.
Suddenly, he found a horse and galloped away,
thus managing to escape.
From *Biànzhèng Lùn*.
Shěn Jiǎ
Shěn Jiǎ of Wú Commandery
was imprisoned and sentenced to death.
On the day of his execution in the market,
he recited the name of Guānyīn
incessantly, both in mind and speech.
The executioner's blade broke by itself,
and he was consequently released.
Another account says:
Lù Huī of Wú was imprisoned and sentenced to death.
He instructed his family to make an image of Guānyīn,
hoping to escape death.
At the execution, three blades
all broke.
The officials asked him the reason.
He replied:
"I suspect it is the compassionate power of Guānyīn."
When they looked at the neck of the image,
three blade marks appeared on it.
He was then reported to the authorities and pardoned.
From *Xuānyàn Jì*.
Zhāng Dá
Zhāng Dá was imprisoned for a crime
and sentenced to death.
He devotedly recited Guānshìyīn's name.
His shackles and fetters fell off by themselves,
and he was thus spared.
He observed vegetarian fasts and precepts for the rest of his life.
From *Zhāngshì Zhuàn*.
Sūn Jìngdé
Sūn Jìngdé of the Eastern Wèi dynasty,
during the Tiānpíng era,
was a recruited soldier in Dìngzhōu.
He followed Buddhism,
and once had a statue of Guānyīn made,
to which he paid reverence himself.
Later, he was implicated by bandits,
and unable to endure the torture,
he suddenly dreamed of a monk,
who told him to recite the lifesaving Guānshìyīn a thousand times.
When he was bound and about to be executed,
having completed the recitation,
the blade broke into three pieces by itself,
without injuring his skin or neck.
Three times they changed the blade,
but each time it broke as before.
The officials reported the matter to the emperor,
and Chancellor Gāo Huān petitioned for his death sentence to be pardoned.
Upon returning home,
he saw that on the Guānyīn statue in his house,
there were three marks from the blade on its neck.
An imperial decree ordered the scripture to be copied and distributed throughout the world,
which is now called the "Gāowáng Guānshìyīn Jīng."
From the states of Jìn, Sòng, Liáng, Chén, Qín, and Zhào,
those who invoked the names and recited the scriptures of Guānyīn, Dìzàng, Mílè, and Mítuó,
and were saved,
are too numerous to record.
From "Míngxiáng Jì."
Gāo Xún
Gāo Xún of Xíngyáng,
was already fifty years old.
He was arrested for killing someone,
locked in an underground prison,
and resigned to the thought that he would surely die.
A fellow prisoner said:
"Let us strive together to recite Guānyīn's name."
Gāo Xún said:
"My crime is grave,
and I am willing to accept punishment.
How could I possibly be spared?"
The other prisoners urged him,
and so
"因" originally written as "日".
Corrected according to the Míng dynasty manuscript.
he first resolved,
vowing to abandon evil and practice good,
and to recite Guānyīn's name exclusively,
without interruption even in haste.
If he could escape,
he vowed to build a five-story pagoda,
offer himself as a servant,
and provide for the monks.
After ten days of earnest effort,
his shackles and locks opened by themselves.
The prison officials were astonished and fearful,
and said to Gāo Xún:
"If the Buddha's deity pities you,
you should not die even if beheaded."
On the day of execution,
the blade lifted and broke,
and his pardon was reported and granted.
From "Xuānyàn Jì."
Shǐ Juàn
Shǐ Juàn was learned and knowledgeable,
but followed Dàoism and disdained Buddhism.
He often told people:
"The Buddha is a minor deity,
not worth serving."
Whenever he saw Buddhist statues,
he would always mock them lightly.
Later, he fell ill with a contracted foot,
and tried various methods to pray for blessings,
but none were effective.
His friend Zhào Wén said to him:
"Among the blessings of the scriptures, the foremost is to try making a Guānyīn statue."
Shǐ Juàn, due to his urgent illness,
followed the advice and cast a statue.
When the statue was completed,
he dreamed of Guānyīn.
And indeed, he recovered.
From "Xuānyàn Jì."
The Shānmí of Dōngshān
During the early Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
there was a monk from Yángzhōu,
whose original name is forgotten,
who had mastered the recitation of the Nirvana Sutra,
and prided himself on this as his vocation.
In a village at the foot of Dōngshān in Qízhōu, there was a shānmí [novice monk],
who recited the Guānshìyīn Sūtra.
Both died suddenly,
and arrived together before King Yánluó.
The shānmí was placed on a golden high seat,
and treated with great respect.
The Nirvana monk was placed on a silver high seat,
and treated with slightly less reverence.
The monk felt great resentment,
and asked the shānmí where he lived.
After reviving,
he traveled from the south to Qízhōu,
found the shānmí,
and asked him in detail about the reason.
The shānmí said:
"Whenever I recite Guānyīn,
I go to a separate place, put on clean clothes,
burn fine incense, make vows,
and only then recite.
This method I never neglect,
and there is no other technique."
The monk apologized, saying:
"My fault is deep indeed.
When reciting the Nirvana Sutra,
my demeanor was not proper,
and my body and speech were impure.
Now it is proven."
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín."
Xú Shàncái
During the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty,
Xú Shàncái of Lǐquán County,
often observed fasting and precepts,
and recited the Guānshìyīn Sūtra
over a thousand times.
He once went to Yánxīng Temple in the capital,
to cultivate merits.
On his way home,
he encountered barbarian bandits on the road.
The bandits had captured hundreds of Hàn people,
and were taking them to Hóngyá,
to kill them one by one.
Shàncái knew he could not avoid it,
so he wholeheartedly recited the Guānshìyīn Sūtra.
When it was time to kill him,
he was completely unaware,
and only at the beginning of the night did he realize
he was on a tree branch in a deep ravine,
over three hundred feet from the bank.
He touched his neck with his hand,
and felt a slight pain but no injury.
Gradually, he climbed down the tree.
Walking south along the ravine,
for about fifty or sixty lǐ,
as dawn gradually broke,
he was far from the bandits,
and reached the official road,
then returned home.
Venerable Wǎn once recounted this story.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín."
Dù Zhìkǎi,
a man from Líhú in Cáozhōu.
From a young age, he loved Buddhist scriptures,
did not pursue an official career or marry,
wore monk's robes,
and lived in seclusion on Tàishān,
devoting himself to reading and reciting.
In the twenty-first year of the Zhēnguān era of the Táng dynasty,
while returning from the mountains,
he suddenly fell gravely ill and was near death.
Covering his body with a kasaya,
he fell into a deep dream-like state.
He saw an old woman
Originally, there was no "woman" character.
Added according to the Míng dynasty manuscript.
and over ten beautiful women repeatedly coming to disturb him,
but Zhìkǎi remained unmoved.
Gradually, they pressed closer,
and all said:
"Let us carry Zhìkǎi and throw him into the northern ravine."
They then all approached,
and together seized him,
with some grabbing his kasaya.
Suddenly, they all chanted the Buddha's name in unison,
then repented afterward,
and asked him to create an Amitābha Buddha statue,
and recite Guānyīn Bodhisattva's name over thirty times.
After a short while,
he felt his body break into a heavy sweat,
and immediately recovered.
Líhú is now Jìyīn.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín."
Lady Zhāng
Lady Zhāng, wife of Chén Xuánfàn,
devoutly served the Buddha,
and always wished to make a golden statue herself,
to offer lifelong worship.
Though her wish was unfulfilled,
she remained focused for a long time.
Suddenly, a golden statue of Guānshìyīn,
with a halo five feet in diameter,
appeared on a high seat.
Everyone marveled that this was due to her sincere devotion.
From "Biànzhèng Lùn."
Xǔ Yǎn
During the Línghuà and Lìndé eras of the Táng dynasty,
in the Yǒngxīng ward of the capital, there was a man named Xǔ Yǎn,
who made his living by catching fish.
Later, he fell ill,
falling into a death-like stupor,
his body red as fire,
and in pain as if being scorched by flames.
He said of himself:
"I only see a fiery chariot coming to burn my body,
because the officials blame me for catching too many fish,
and have sent me to suffer this punishment."
This went on for several days,
with him alternating between life and death.
His relatives urged him to perform meritorious deeds,
so he had two statues of Guānyīn made,
and also ordered his entire household to abstain from wine and meat.
His illness then subsided.
From the *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Monk Dàoxiàn
The monk Dàoxiàn of the Táng dynasty's Shèngshàn Temple,
whose secular surname was Yuán.
During the Kāiyuán era,
he resided at Dàyún Temple in Jiāngzhōu,
and was esteemed by his fellow monks.
At that time, a Governor Yuán
wished to have seven paintings of Guānshìyīn made,
and because Dàoxiàn was of pure conduct,
he entrusted him with the task.
Dàoxiàn instructed the painters to maintain a vegetarian diet and purify themselves,
and for all the pigments, nipple incense was used instead of glue,
ensuring utmost purity.
Governor Yuán greatly praised this.
After the task was completed,
Dàoxiàn went to Yùnìng to cut timber
for the construction of a Mañjuśrī Hall.
When the timber was ready and he was about to return,
he suddenly fell into the water.
The river current was swift and turbulent,
and his companions had no means to rescue him.
As Dàoxiàn fell into the water,
he began to think of Guānshìyīn.
He saw a strange light at the bottom of the water,
and after gazing at it for a long time,
he saw the seven Bodhisattvas he had painted
standing to his left and right.
They said to Dàoxiàn:
"You need only recite 'Námó Púsà.'"
Dàoxiàn's movements were as if in broad daylight.
He still knew he was at the bottom of the water,
and feared he might not escape death,
so he thought to himself:
"I shall recite 'Āmítuófó.'"
As he recited "Āmítuófó,"
the seven Bodhisattvas came together to lift his feet,
bringing him to the surface of the water.
His clothes were not stained in the least,
and he followed along with the timber,
traveling over forty *lǐ* together.
Dàoxiàn passed away in the early Tiānbǎo era.
To this day, the seven Bodhisattvas are still present at Dàyún Temple in Jiāngzhōu,
and the incident of his fall into the water is also depicted.
From the *Guǎngyì Jì*.
Chéng Guī
Chéng Guī,
in the early Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
served as the Deputy Magistrate of Chángshā.
He was tasked with escorting timber for the Hénán Bridge,
but upon reaching Yángzhōu,
they encountered repeated storms and floods,
resulting in significant losses.
The authorities in Yángzhōu accused Chéng Guī of stealing and selling the timber,
and tortured the laborers,
who, unable to endure the pain,
falsely confessed to having squandered it.
Yángzhōu forwarded the case to Tán Prefecture,
where Bān Jǐngqiàn served as Prefect,
known as a strict and meticulous official.
The Assistant General of Chángshā Prefecture, Qián Táng
(the Míng manuscript writes "Táng" as "Táng").
Yáng Jìn, coveting the mission for personal gain,
colluded with Bān Jǐngqiàn's associates.
Jǐngqiàn sent Yáng Jìn to arrest Chéng Guī and others.
When Yáng Jìn arrived in Yángzhōu,
he placed a small cangue on Chéng Guī
and transported him overland.
Upon reaching Níngjiāng,
they boarded a boat,
where he fastened the cangue with chains,
attaching it to the ship's beam.
All sides were nailed shut,
leaving only a small opening
for food and other necessities to pass through.
Chéng Guī believed that if he reached Tán Prefecture, he would surely die.
Upon departing Yángzhōu,
he began to wholeheartedly recite the name of the Bodhisattva Guānshìyīn, the Savior from Suffering.
He often ate only once a day,
and sometimes not at all,
consuming only water and maintaining a pure vegetarian diet.
After more than ten days,
they reached Chúkǒu.
At dusk,
as he recited with utmost sincerity,
his cangue and chains
suddenly came loose and opened,
leaving his body free and unencumbered,
with nothing binding him.
Waiting until deep into the night,
when all the boatmen were asleep,
Chéng Guī pried off the nails,
removed them, and climbed out onto the deck.
He went to Yáng Jìn's cabin above
and called out:
"Yáng Jìn,
what can you do to me now!"
Yáng Jìn, startled awake,
asked how he had gotten there.
Chéng Guī replied:
"I would rather be buried in the bellies of river fish
than let you and your kind succeed!"
With that, he resolved to throw himself into the water.
Upon first sinking to the riverbed,
he soon encountered a floating log
with an upright branch.
Chéng Guī straddled the log and clung to it,
managing to reach the surface.
In the darkness of midnight,
he looked around in all directions, seeing nothing but vast emptiness.
The log sank to the riverbed again,
but then floated back up.
Chéng Guī focused his mind on reciting Guānshìyīn's name,
and he drifted along.
Suddenly, the log flipped over,
and he floated with it downstream.
Realizing he had reached the shore,
he hid among the reeds.
Although there were many fierce beasts along the riverbank,
coming and going, looking around,
none harmed him.
At dawn,
he sought refuge in a nearby village,
where the villagers provided him with clothing
and sent him to Chúzhōu.
The officials there marveled and praised him,
buying him a donkey, horse, provisions, and other supplies.
Chéng Guī then went to the capital,
to appeal his case at the Censorate.
Initially, after losing Chéng Guī,
Yáng Jìn and his men scattered in disarray,
and Yáng Jìn himself later renounced secular life to become a monk.
From the *Zhuōyì Jì*,
the Míng manuscript states it is from the *Guǎngyì Jì*.
Wáng Qí
Wáng Qí of the Táng dynasty was from Tàiyuán.
He lived in Xíngyáng,
and from childhood did not consume meat or blood.
In the early years of the Dàlì era,
he served as Registrar of Qúzhōu.
By nature, he enjoyed constantly reciting the Guānyīn Sūtra.
From youth to adulthood,
he suffered from severe illnesses multiple times,
but through his recitations,
he always recovered.
In the original text, after the character "愈" (recovered), there were six characters: "複念誦無不差愈" (again, through recitation, he always recovered).
These were deleted according to the Míng dynasty manuscript.
When he recited,
there would always be strange, deceptive apparitions
that came to disturb and provoke him,
but because Wáng Qí's mind was upright, they could not affect him.
When Wáng Qí was nine years old,
he fell ill for five or six days
and consequently lost the ability to speak.
Suddenly, he heard someone outside the door calling his name, saying:
"I have come to fetch you!"
He then followed along.
After traveling about fifty lǐ,
they arrived at an official residence.
The official inside was greatly startled and said:
"Why was this child mistakenly brought here?
He should be sent back immediately."
Someone nearby said:
"Whenever someone is summoned,
they should not be released;
they must be assigned a task
before they can leave."
The official said:
"There is a dog that is due to die."
He ordered Wáng Qí to fetch the dog.
Wáng Qí pleaded that he was young and small
and could not go alone.
The official ordered him to go with the messenger.
On the way,
the messenger gave Wáng Qí a pill,
shaped like a ball,
and told him to throw it at the dog's house gate.
When the dog came out,
he was to throw it,
and the dog swallowed the pill and died instantly.
The official said:
"Now that the task is done, you may return."
Later, Wáng Qí fell ill again.
Suddenly, he felt there were eighty-two beings inside his four limbs,
each with eyes, eyebrows, mouths, and noses,
occupying their respective positions.
Those inside his arms and legs
moved about, attacking his flesh and blood.
Whenever they reached his wrist or ankle joints,
they would inevitably clash,
causing unbearable pain and distress.
Wáng Qí asked:
"Do you all want to kill me?"
They replied:
"We are managing your illness;
how could we be killing you!"
Wáng Qí said:
"If you are managing my illness,
I will prepare a lavish feast to feed you."
The ghosts were overjoyed and cried out from within his flesh.
The next day, he prepared food for them.
After they finished eating, they all left,
and his illness was cured.
Wáng Qí had previously kept a pure knife,
over a chǐ long,
which he always held when reciting.
When he contracted a seasonal epidemic,
he constantly placed the knife by his bedside
to protect himself.
Later, when his illness became severe,
he mustered his strength in the darkness to rise
and recite the name of Guānshìyīn Bodhisattva.
Suddenly, the darkness became as bright as day.
He saw the knife blade pointing upward,
and a monk came
to sit facing him.
The monk asked Wáng Qí what kind of knife this was.
Wáng Qí said:
"It is a demon-slaying knife."
The monk then vanished.
Soon, an iron hammer descended from the air,
striking the knife.
It struck over two hundred times;
the hammer shattered completely,
but the knife remained undamaged.
He also saw a large iron cauldron,
capable of holding over two hundred shí of water,
turned upside down.
Two large men stood beside it holding pestles.
They asked Wáng Qí:
"Do you recognize this?"
Wáng Qí replied:
"I do not."
They said:
"This is the Iron Cauldron Hell."
Wáng Qí said:
"I precisely need this hell to imprison demons."
As soon as he finished speaking, they vanished.
He also saw beds carrying delicacies,
perhaps a hundred beds,
exiting through the door.
He also saw several hundred people,
all in dazzling attire,
lined up in the house.
Then he saw his deceased father,
holding a knife,
angrily saying:
"There is no place for you here!"
Those people immediately scattered,
and shortly after, his illness was cured.
During the Qiányuán era,
while in Jiānglíng,
he fell seriously ill again.
Once more, he wholeheartedly recited Guānshìyīn's name.
From afar, he saw several hundred ghosts
arriving by boat.
They had come from afar and were hungry,
so they approached Wáng Qí to ask for food.
He then ordered his family to prepare food
and set it out in the courtyard.
The ghosts sat in rows.
Two ghosts leaped out from Wáng Qí's mouth
and joined them to eat.
After finishing, they initially said it was not enough.
Wáng Qí said:
"Do you also need clothing?"
The ghosts said that was exactly it.
He then ordered his family to make several dozen pairs of paper clothes
and also red and green shirts,
which they burned in the courtyard.
The ghosts put them on and dispersed,
and his illness soon recovered.
During the Yǒngtài era,
he fell seriously ill again.
Then, by lamplight,
he focused his mind and recited the Heart Sūtra.
Suddenly, there was a sound like a bird flying,
rising from within the flesh of his seated body.
Consequently, his mouth gaped open and could not close.
Thinking that this must be a demonic disturbance,
he focused his mind even more firmly.
After a short while, it returned to normal.
He also saw a swollen corpse in front of his bed,
a snake as large as a vat,
and various ghosts,
most of whom were deceased people he had known before,
chaotically dazzling him.
Wáng Qí closed his eyes
and recited the sūtra wholeheartedly twenty-four times.
They vanished into silence.
After thirty-nine recitations,
he relaxed and fell asleep.
The next day, he recovered again.
Also, his wife, Lǐ shì,
once contracted a pestilential disease.
Wáng Qí wholeheartedly recited the Heart Sūtra for her by lamplight.
After reciting four or five lines,
he suddenly saw three heads under the lamp.
The middle head
was that of a maid of Lǐ shì who had recently died.
Then he heard a sighing sound from Lǐ shì's mouth.
She sat up by herself,
staring wide-eyed, unable to speak,
but pointing east, west, up, and down,
as if seeing something.
Wáng Qí ordered a servant to use a long knife
to slash at whatever Lǐ shì pointed to.
After a long time, she awoke and said:
"Is that Wáng Sānláng?"
She called Wáng Qí by his familial name as a younger brother.
Wáng Qí asked what she had been pointing at.
Lǐ shì said:
"I saw a person in the window
with a nose several chǐ long;
also saw two creatures in front of the bed,
shaped like camels;
and also saw the entire house covered with red curtains,
all of which were slashed and torn apart by the servant's knife,
vanishing in an instant."
Wáng Qí then recited the sūtra forty-nine times,
and Lǐ shì soon recovered.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì".
Shǐ Shìguāng
Shǐ Shìguāng of Jìn,
was a man of Xiāngyáng.
In the eighth year of the Xiánhé era,
he died in Wǔchāng.
Seven days later,
the monk Zhī Fǎshān was reciting the Lesser Perfection of Wisdom Sutra,
and, weary, he dozed off slightly.
He heard sounds as if someone were speaking from the spirit seat.
The Shǐ family had a maidservant named Zhāng Xìn,
who saw Shìguāng at the spirit seat,
dressed in his usual clothes just as in life.
He said to Xìn:
"I was originally destined to fall into hell,
but the monk Zhī recited scriptures for me,
and Tán Hù and Tán Jiān welcomed me to the seventh Brahma Heaven, a place of bliss."
Hù and Jiān were both novices under Zhī who had already passed away.
Later, when Zhī Fǎshān went again
to recite the Greater Perfection of Wisdom Sutra,
Shìguāng came again and was present at the seat.
During his lifetime, Shìguāng
had offered two banners in worship.
They were at the temple at the time,
so he called for Zhāng Xìn to take the banners and escort him.
Xìn said:
"Yes."
Then she suddenly died.
Leading Xìn, who held the banners,
they flew together northwest to a green mountain,
which was the color of lapis lazuli.
Upon reaching the mountaintop,
they saw the gate of heaven.
Shìguāng then took the banners himself
and sent Xìn back.
He gave her a green incense,
like a croton seed,
saying:
"Give this to the monk Zhī."
Before Xìn returned,
she saw from afar Shìguāng enter directly through the gate of heaven.
Xìn returned along the path,
and in an instant she revived,
but she no longer saw the incense in her hand.
The banners were also back at the old temple.
When Shìguāng and Xìn departed,
their family had a six-year-old child who saw it.
Pointing, he said to his grandmother:
"Father flew up to heaven,
did you see it, grandmother?"
Later, Shìguāng returned to his home with more than ten heavenly beings,
lingering before leaving.
Each time he came, he was seen wearing a hairpin and cap;
each time he left, his hair was uncovered.
Xìn asked him about this,
and he replied:
"In heaven there are crowns,
so I do not wear these."
Later, he then wore
"these later then wore" five characters added according to the *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*, volume five.
a heavenly crown and, with a group of heavenly beings, played the qin and sang songs,
going directly to his mother's hall.
Xìn asked why he came so often,
and he said:
"I come
to make you all understand sin and merit,
and also to bring some joy to my mother."
The sound of the qin was clear and exquisite,
unlike ordinary sounds.
The whole family heard it,
but the sound was as if from behind a wall,
so they could not observe it closely.
Only Xìn heard it clearly and distinctly.
After a while he left,
and Xìn escorted him.
She saw Shìguāng enter a black gate,
then come out shortly after,
and say to Xìn:
"My maternal uncle is here, daily seeing beatings and floggings,
the pain unbearable.
I came to visit and am returning now.
My uncle committed the crime of killing,
so he receives this retribution.
You can tell my aunt
to gather monks to recite scriptures;
then he may gradually be spared."
The uncle was Jīng
"Jīng" character added according to the Ming manuscript.
Chē Jiāngjūn.
From *Míngxiáng Jì*.
Dǒng Jí
was a man of Yúqián.
For three generations his family had upheld the Dharma,
and Jí was especially diligent,
constantly observing precepts and fasting while reciting the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
When someone in the village fell ill,
they would ask Jí to recite the sutra,
and many were saved and recovered.
In the same county, Hé Huǎng also upheld the Dharma.
He suddenly fell ill from a mountain toxin and was in distress.
"Distress" originally written as "cause,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
Huǎng's elder brother panicked
and hurried to invite Jí.
The houses of Dǒng and Hé
were sixty or seventy *lǐ* apart,
and moreover separated by a large stream.
In the fifth month, there was heavy rain.
When Huǎng's brother first crossed,
the water had not yet risen.
Jí agreed to meet him for the midday meal,
but when he went, mountain torrents had surged and it was no longer possible to cross.
Jí could not swim,
so he paced back and forth, sighing for a long time.
Since Jí was faithful and upright,
he was determined to keep his promise.
So he earnestly resolved,
vowing to himself:
"I am saving someone in urgent suffering,
regardless of my own life.
I pray that the Tathāgata and the great beings
will illuminate my sincerity."
Then he took off his clothes,
placed the sutra in a bag and put it on his head,
and went straight into the water.
Judging its depth,
he thought it would reach his neck,
but when he crossed,
it only reached his knees.
Once he reached the shore,
he found the sutra bag missing
and was deeply grieved and regretful.
He soon arrived at Huǎng's home,
made three prostrations in repentance,
and wept in self-reproach.
In the time it took to bow and rise,
he saw the sutra bag on a high seat.
Jí, overjoyed, took it and looked;
it was damp as if wet,
but when he opened the bag to look at the sutra,
it was still dry as before.
Thereupon, the villagers all began to uphold the Dharma.
To the northwest of Jí's home,
there was a high and perilous mountain
with many demons and spirits inside,
who harmed the residents.
Jí, using the power of the sutras and precepts,
wished to subdue them.
On four or five *mǔ* of land at the mountain's edge,
he personally cut down trees,
built a small hut,
and set up a high seat.
He recited the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* for over a hundred days;
it was peaceful with no demons,
and the harm to the people gradually ceased.
Later, several people came
and spoke with Jí for a long time.
Jí thought they were not from Yúqián;
the remote mountains were secluded and cut off,
so how could they have come?
Suspecting they were spirits,
he said to them:
"Are you gentlemen perhaps ghosts from here?"
They replied:
"Yes.
We heard of your virtuous and pure conduct,
so we came to observe,
and we also have a request,
which we hope you will hear.
We have inhabited this mountain for generations,
it is where we roam and dwell.
Since you have come to stay here,
we fear we might offend you,
and we are constantly uneasy.
Now we wish to establish new boundaries;
we will kill trees to mark the division."
Jí said:
"I cherish this quiet place
to read and recite scriptures.
If we do not interfere with each other,
I would be glad for this.
I hope you will assist me."
The ghosts replied:
"We also rely on you,
and will not encroach."
Having said this, they left.
After one night,
outside the cleared land on all four sides,
the trees all withered and died,
as if burned.
From *Míngxiáng Jì*.
Lì Guó of Sòng.
There was a state in Sòng,
which bordered the land of the Rākṣasas.
The Rākṣasas frequently crossed the border,
devouring people without restraint.
The king made an agreement with the Rākṣasas:
From now on,
each household in the state
would be responsible for one day,
sending a person in turn,
so that they would no longer kill indiscriminately.
There was a Buddhist household
that had only one son,
just ten years old,
whose turn it was to be sent.
At the moment of parting,
the parents wept in grief,
and with utmost sincerity, they recited the Buddha's name.
Due to the Buddha's majestic spiritual power,
the great demons could not approach.
The next day,
they saw their son still alive,
and joyfully returned home together.
From then on, [the raids] ceased,
and the people of the state were spared.
From Yōumíng Lù.
Zhāng Yuán
Zhāng Yuán of the Later Zhōu, styled Xiàoshǐ,
was from Wànchéng in Héběi.
At the age of sixteen,
his grandfather had been blind for three years.
Yuán, filled with worry, wept
and practiced walking meditation day and night,
praying for blessings and protection.
He also read in the Medicine Master Sūtra:
"There are words about the blind regaining their sight."
He then invited seven monks,
lit a seven-tiered lamp,
and for seven days and nights, they recited the Medicine Master Sūtra.
Each day, while practicing, he prayed:
"I, Yuán, am an unfilial grandson,
causing my grandfather to lose his sight.
Now, with this lamp light,
I dedicate it to the entire Dharma realm,
begging that my grandfather's eyes see light again,
and I, Yuán, ask to take on his darkness."
He persevered diligently like this
until the seventh day.
That night,
he dreamed of an old man
using a golden scalpel to treat his grandfather's eyes,
who said to Yuán:
"Do not worry or grieve.
In three days,
your grandfather's eyes will surely be healed."
Yuán, overjoyed in the dream, leaped up,
startled awake,
and told his entire family.
After three days,
his grandfather's eyes were indeed healed.
From Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Shì Zhìxīng
Shì Zhìxīng of the Dàzhuāngyán Temple in the capital of the Táng,
was from Luòzhōu.
He cultivated his conduct with steadfast clarity,
followed the Vinaya Master Shǒu,
recited sūtras and upheld the precepts,
ceaselessly from dawn till dusk.
In the midwinter of the fifth year of the Dàyè era,
it was his turn as the temple's weínà to strike the bell.
A monk in the same temple named Sānguǒ
had an elder brother who accompanied Emperor Yáng on his southern tour to Jiāngdū,
and died along the way.
Initially, there was no news of his death,
but he appeared in a dream to his wife, saying:
"I reached Péngchéng on my journey,
unfortunately fell ill and died.
Having done no good deeds in life,
I now fell into hell,
suffering all five torments.
But thanks to the bell struck by the monk Zhìxīng of the Chándìng Temple on the tenth of this month,
its sound
resonated through hell,
and all those suffering together
were instantly liberated,
and I was reborn in a place of happiness.
Wishing to repay his kindness,
you should offer him ten bolts of silk,
and convey my sincere gratitude."
When she awoke and told this,
no one believed her.
Soon, she had the same dream again.
More than ten days later,
the news of his death matched the dream exactly.
She then offered the silk to Zhìxīng.
All the great virtuous ones of the temple gathered,
and asked Zhìxīng:
"What was the reason for your bell-striking
that elicited such a response?"
Zhìxīng replied:
"I have no other method.
I saw in the Buddhist scriptures it is transmitted:
'King Jì Nì Zhā suffered torment,
which ceased due to bell-ringing;
and in the Ekottarika Āgama Sūtra,
it says bell-ringing creates merit.'
Reverently following this teaching,
I strive to practice it diligently.
In the harsh winter, I climb the tower;
the wind cuts my skin and flesh.
Baring my hands to strike the bell hammer,
my palms crack and split,
yet I do not consider it suffering.
When I begin to strike the bell,
I first generate a virtuous vow:
May all sages and worthies together enter the Dharma arena,
and together receive the Dharma feast.
May all beings in the evil destinies,
hearing this bell sound,
simultaneously leave suffering,
and quickly attain liberation.
Such vows and practices
I constantly uphold and cultivate with sincere intent,
hence leading to this spiritual resonance."
From Yì Yuàn,
the Ming manuscript copy cites it from Gāosēng Zhuàn.
Dǒng Xióng
Dǒng Xióng of the Táng,
was from Hénán.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
he served as a Tàilǐ chéng.
He had revered the Buddha's teachings since childhood,
and maintained a vegetarian diet for many years.
Due to false accusations, he was imprisoned along with his colleagues Lǐ Jìngxuán and Wáng Xīn.
Xióng single-mindedly recited the Universal Gate Chapter,
thirty times a day.
Suddenly, one night, his locks fell open.
Startled, Xióng told Xīn and Xuán.
Xīn examined the locks:
they lay completely intact on the ground,
yet the hooks remained unopened,
separated by several feet.
He immediately informed the guards.
The censor Zhāng Shǒuyī was on night duty;
he ordered clerks to inspect it by candlelight and found it very strange.
He had the locks replaced, sealed, and left.
Xióng merely continued reciting the sūtra without pause.
By the fifth watch,
the locks fell open again with a sound.
Xióng again informed Xīn, Xuán, and others.
By dawn,
Shǒuyī inspected it:
the seals were as before,
yet the locks had separated by themselves.
Jìngxuán had never believed in the Buddha's teachings.
His wife read sūtras,
and he often said to her:
"Why are you bewitched by barbarian deities to read this book?"
But after witnessing Xióng's experience,
he deeply realized the fault of his disbelief,
and understood that the Buddha is a great sage.
At that time, Xīn also recited the names of the eight bodhisattvas,
completing thirty thousand repetitions.
During the day, his locks fell open,
and upon inspection, it was no different from Xióng's case.
Not long after, they were all released.
From Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Mèng Zhījiǎn
Mèng Zhījiǎn of the Táng dynasty was from Bīngzhōu.
In his youth, he fell ill and suddenly died.
He found himself in a government office,
just as in his lifetime,
unaware that he had died.
He encountered an old acquaintance who was serving as an official there,
who asked him,
"How did you come here?"
Mèng explained everything,
and only then did he realize he was on the underworld path.
The official checked the records for him and said,
"You have done no deeds of merit in your lifetime;
how can you return?"
Mèng replied,
"Throughout my life, I have recited the Heart Sūtra and the Gāowáng Sūtra.
Though I have not kept count,
it must be thirty or forty thousand times."
The official rechecked and found it to be true,
so he allowed Mèng to return.
The official asked if he wished to know about his official career.
Mèng said,
"I very much do."
The official then showed him a register,
which stated,
"Mèng Zhījiǎn is destined to begin his career
as a Cānjūn in Cáozhōu,
and later transfer to become a Sīcāng in Dèngzhōu."
He then covered it and would not let Mèng see more.
Mèng then reached a desolate wilderness,
fell into a dark pit,
and revived.
He did not understand what "destiny" referred to.
Soon after, an imperial decree called for the recruitment of grain transporters,
and through this, he was selected
and appointed as Cānjūn of Cáozhōu.
He then realized,
"This is what I saw in the underworld—a minor official post."
After completing his term, he was appointed Sīcāng of Dèngzhōu.
After leaving that post, he was selected again,
nominated as a Pànsī in Jìnzhōu,
but he died before taking office.
From "Records of Court and Country."
Cuī Shànchōng initially served as Tóngshān Chéng in Zǐzhōu.
Lǐ Zhīgǔ, the Prefect of Xīzhōu, recommended him to serve as Pànguān.
When the various barbarian tribes rebelled,
they killed Lǐ Zhīgǔ.
Cuī Shànchōng and over twenty others fled,
intending to seek refuge in Kūnmíng.
At night, they lost their way,
and Cuī devotedly recited the revered sūtra.
Suddenly, they saw a torch ahead,
and the group followed it.
By dawn, the torch extinguished,
and they had reached Kūnmíng.
From "Records of Retribution."
Táng Yàn, a native of Zǐzhōu,
recited the sūtra seven times daily.
In the early Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
he fled to Ānyuè County in Jìnzhōu to avoid trouble.
He had a conflict with someone,
who slandered him to the Prefect Liú Gōng.
Liú Gōng ordered men to capture Táng Yàn.
That night, Táng dreamed of a foreign monk who said,
"Leave quickly."
Startled, he rose and fled,
reaching Fāngyì County in Suízhōu.
Liú Gōng's agents suddenly arrived,
and with no way to escape,
Táng wholeheartedly recited the sūtra.
Though the pursuers crisscrossed the area,
none of them saw him,
and thus he escaped.
From "Records of Retribution."
Imperial Censor Zhāng
A certain Zhāng,
during the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty, served as an Investigating Censor,
and was dispatched to Huáinán to conduct a review.
As he was about to cross the Huái River,
a man in a yellow robe came running from behind, seeking to cross,
claiming to have urgent business,
so the boat was specially halted.
When he arrived,
he merely said:
"I just wish to ride along to cross the Huái."
The boatman wanted to drive him off and strike him,
and also reproached him,
asking why he wanted to cross and had thus caused the Investigating Censor's boat to stop.
Zhāng said:
"Do not strike him."
Instead, he reprimanded his own attendants, saying:
"Carrying one commoner across the Huái,
what hardship is that?"
He personally fed him with leftover food,
and the man appeared very ashamed.
After crossing,
he parted ways with Zhāng.
A short while later,
when Zhāng reached the next relay station,
the man was already at the gate.
Zhāng thought he had come to make a request,
and felt very displeased,
saying to him:
"I just ferried you across,
why have you come again?
You may leave at once."
The man said:
"I am actually not human,
but wish to discuss a matter with you, the Investigating Censor,
which should not be heard by those around you."
So Zhāng dismissed his attendants, and the man said:
"I have been ordered to fetch you,
and you were fated to drown in the Huái River.
Just now, I received a meal from you,
and certainly will not forget it.
Having received your great kindness,
I can only grant you a one-day stay of execution!"
Zhāng begged to return home,
to leave some final instructions.
The ghost said:
"Beyond one day,
I dare not disobey.
Although I am a messenger,
in the underworld,
my rank is akin to that of a village head or ward officer in the human world."
Zhāng wished to plead for rescue,
but the ghost said:
"Humans and ghosts belong to different paths,
it is not fitting to press me,
I fear it would be unavoidable."
Zhāng bowed from a distance,
and the ghost said:
"If within one day,
you can recite the *Life-Extending Sutra* a thousand times,
you may gain an extension of life."
Having said this, he went out,
but at the door turned back,
saying:
"Do you know the *Life-Extending Sutra*?"
Zhāng initially did not fully understand.
The ghost said:
"It is the *Diamond Sutra* in the human world."
Zhāng said:
"Today is already late,
how can I recite a thousand scrolls of the sutra?"
The ghost said:
"As long as it is recited by humans, it will suffice."
Zhāng then loudly called out, and dozens of people from the relay station and other commoners recited together.
By the evening of the next day,
they finished a thousand recitations.
The ghost came again and said:
"You, the Investigating Censor, are now spared,
but you must temporarily visit the underworld."
Everyone saw the yellow-robed official accompanying Zhāng out the door.
When he appeared before the King,
he fully stated that a thousand recitations of the *Life-Extending Sutra* were completed,
and he should gain an extension of life.
They checked the records and said:
"It matches what was recited."
Then, joining his palms, the King said:
"If so,
you should gain an additional ten years of life."
He was then released to return to life.
At the gate,
the official who had pursued him said:
"Because I delayed in fetching you, the Investigating Censor,
I have now been beaten."
He then bared his back to show him,
and begged for a little money.
Zhāng said:
"I am a poor scholar,
and moreover am at an inn,
I fear I cannot manage much."
The ghost said:
"Only two hundred thousand."
Zhāng said:
"If it is spirit money,
I can offer five hundred strings."
The ghost said:
"I am grateful for your kind intention,
but my virtue is shallow,
how could I accept so much money from you?
Two hundred thousand is just right."
Zhāng said:
"Now I am also a ghost,
returning to the inn at night,
it is not easy to obtain it."
The ghost said:
"You, the Investigating Censor, need only think intently,
instructing your wife to repay me,
and I will naturally receive it."
Zhāng then concentrated his thoughts very intently.
The ghost said:
"It has already been received."
A moment later, he returned again,
saying:
"Your wife wishes to give it,
but the wet nurse refuses."
He then instructed Zhāng to concentrate his thoughts on the wet nurse,
and after a moment said:
"It is done."
Zhāng then felt as if falling into a deep pit,
and thereupon revived.
He requested leave to return home,
and fully recounted the events.
His wife said:
"That night, I dreamed you had died,
and requested two hundred thousand in spirit money,
so I wanted to go buy and make it.
But the wet nurse insisted:
'How can one trust matters from a dream?'
That night,
the wet nurse also dreamed."
Thus, he gained ten more years before passing away.
From *Guǎng Yì Jì*.
Lǐ Xīn
In the Táng dynasty, there was a man named Lǐ Xīn,
who was skilled in reciting the Thousand-Handed, Thousand-Eyed Dhāraṇī.
There was a person afflicted by a malaria ghost,
and Xīn chanted the spell for him.
The ghost appeared and said to the person:
"I originally intended to cause you great hardship and humiliation,
but fearing Lǐ Shísì Láng,
I dare not go again."
Shísì Láng was Xīn.
Xīn's home was in Dōngjùn,
and he was traveling as a guest in Hénán.
His younger sister fell ill and died.
After several days, she revived,
and said:
"At first, I was led by several people into a graveyard,
and then there were several dozen others,
who wanted to assault and humiliate me.
Suddenly, one among them said:
'This is Lǐ Shísì Láng's younger sister,
where do you all think you are taking her?
Now Lǐ Shísì Láng has already returned,
and will soon arrive home.
He is a good man,
and if he hears that we have taken his sister,
he will certainly use his divine spell to cause us hardship and humiliation.
It would be better to send her back early.'"
So together they escorted the girl home.
After the girl revived,
Xīn also arrived home.
From *Guǎng Yì Jì*.
Niú Téng
Táng Niú Téng, styled Sīyuǎn,
served as Gentleman of the Palace Gate and Magistrate of Jiáchéng in the Táng dynasty.
He abandoned his official post to follow his true inclinations,
devoting his heart to Buddhism.
He pursued his aspirations throughout his life,
and often admired Táo Qián's sobriquet "Master of the Five Willows."
Thus, he called himself the Commoner Gentleman.
He was the nephew of the Marquis of Hédōng, Péi Yán, who served as Palace Attendant and Head of the Secretariat-Chancellery.
The marquis's surname was Péi.
Before reaching the age of twenty,
Táng Niú Téng passed the imperial examination in the Classics.
He was subsequently appointed as Cavalry Officer of the Right Guard.
The gentleman was calm and taciturn,
and from a young age displayed exceptional conduct.
The Marquis of Hédōng esteemed his virtue,
and consulted him on all government affairs of the court.
The gentleman maintained a pure and frugal lifestyle,
and his moral character surpassed that of others.
Thus, Wáng Bó and three others
all studied under his guidance.
In his prime, the Marquis of Hédōng was killed,
and the gentleman was demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Zāngkē Jiàn'ān.
As he was about to depart,
the Vice Censor-in-Chief Cuī Chá was in power at the time.
All demoted officials had to bid him farewell.
Those with whom he had long-standing grudges
were sometimes detained,
and many were executed.
At the time, Empress Wǔ was employing cruel officials,
and Cuī Chá had previously been at odds with the Marquis of Hédōng,
and had framed him.
As the gentleman was about to meet Cuī Chá,
he was terrified and did not know what to do.
Suddenly, he encountered a man on the street,
