whose appearance was exceptionally majestic,
dressed in splendid yellow robes.
He asked the gentleman:
"Are you going to see the Vice Censor-in-Chief?
Are you not afraid of death?"
The gentleman replied in alarm:
"Indeed, I am."
The man then said:
"Do you have a rhinoceros-horn knife?"
The gentleman replied:
"Yes, I do."
The extraordinary man said:
"It is excellent that you have a knife.
I will teach you a divine incantation.
When you see the Vice Censor-in-Chief,
simply bow and make a hand gesture,
saying you carry a rhinoceros-horn knife,
and form the hand gesture.
Then you may recite the incantation.
The gesture is as follows:
on the third segment of the left middle finger,
press the horizontal line with the thumbnail.
Then silently recite the incantation seven times,
and you will see something,
which will keep you safe.
The incantation is:
'Jí zhōng jí,
Jiā shù lǜ,
Tí zhōng yǒu lǜ,
Tuó ā pó jiā hē.'" The gentleman bowed and recited it.
Once he had memorized it,
he looked up, and the extraordinary man had vanished.
He was greatly astonished.
When he went to see Cuī Chá,
there were over thirty others with him.
The gentleman's name was twentieth on the list.
The first nineteen
were each called by name to approach.
Those with whom Cuī Chá had long-standing enmity
were detained for execution by hanging or beheading,
amounting to nearly half.
When it was the gentleman's turn,
he followed the instructions and recited the incantation.
Cuī Chá remained silent for a long time.
The gentleman looked up
and saw a divine being,
over ten feet tall,
with an extraordinary appearance,
emerging from the western steps,
walking straight up to Cuī Chá,
grabbing his right shoulder,
and twisting his head to the left,
so that his face was turned toward his back.
The others only saw Cuī Chá bow his head in silence,
his hand fixed on the character "dìng."
Thus, the gentleman managed to escape.
As he reached the screen and looked back,
he saw the divine being release Cuī Chá and vanish.
The gentleman arrived in Zāngkē,
where he always upheld sincerity and trustworthiness,
and devoutly revered Buddhism.
Although he was married and held office,
he lived like a monk observing precepts.
He did not speak carelessly,
nor did he gaze recklessly.
His words were never false,
and his actions were never biased.
Thus, the local tribes gradually came under his influence,
and he widely spread Buddhism throughout Zāngkē.
He often acted as the prefectural chief official,
establishing several Buddhist altars.
After three years, the tribes of Zhuāngzhōu rebelled,
and the rebellion spread to Zāngkē.
The people of the prefecture turned against and killed the chief official to join the rebellion.
A powerful local leader in Jiàn'ān raised troops in response,
and they seized the gentleman and made him sit under a tree,
intending to kill him.
Suddenly, a tribesman
drew his knife and beheaded the guard,
then scolded them:
"The Assistant Magistrate is extremely benevolent.
How can you bear to harm such a man?"
He then placed the gentleman in a basket,
and ordered a strong man to carry him away.
Thus, his family was also spared.
After the incident was resolved,
the prefecture reported the matter to the court.
An imperial edict restored his official duties,
and permitted him to return.
Later, he served as magistrate of several counties,
and in each, he received his salary based on the number of days served.
His integrity was unsurpassed,
a reflection of his innate character.
Later, he abandoned his official post,
devoted himself to Buddhism,
and experienced profound spiritual realizations.
From "Jì Wén"
Lǐ Yuánpíng
Lǐ Yuánpíng of the Táng dynasty was the son of the former prefect of Mùzhōu, Bó Chéng.
In the fifth year of the Dàlì era,
he was staying as a guest at the Dōngyáng Temple.
After studying there for over a year,
one evening at dusk,
he saw a woman
wearing a red skirt and embroidered jacket,
with a beautiful appearance and charming demeanor,
leading several maidservants
into the monastery.
Yuánpíng was delighted by her
and, catching sight of one of the maidservants,
asked where she was going and her name.
The maidservant angrily said:
"Who is this young man,
pressing so urgently?
We are both from scholarly families;
it is improper to behave so indiscreetly."
Yuánpíng bowed and begged to see her,
but she refused.
After a short while,
the woman herself came out of the courtyard and looked around.
Suddenly seeing Yuánpíng,
she seemed to recognize him as an old acquaintance.
Yuánpíng, beyond his expectations,
invited her in
and asked about her journey.
The woman said:
"I also wished to see you
to discuss matters from the past.
Please do not doubt or suspect me."
Once they were mutually pleased,
after seven days,
the woman said:
"I am not human.
Some time ago, my father served as the prefect of Jiāngzhōu.
In your previous life, you were a gatekeeper on duty.
Although you were poor and lowly,
your appearance was pleasing.
I was a young girl,
living alone in a secluded room.
At times, without thinking,
I would flirt and tease with you.
Due to karmic connections,
we developed this secret affection.
Just over a hundred days later,
you passed away.
Although I did not weep,
I could hardly bear the emotions,
so I secretly marked your left thigh with red ink
as a token of remembrance.
I often recited the Thousand-Eyed, Thousand-Armed mantra,
and each time I burned incense, I made a vow
that we would both be reborn into wealthy and noble families,
longing for each other and wishing to become husband and wife.
Please verify this."
Yuánpíng then looked at himself
and indeed found it as she said.
At dawn, when they were about to part,
she said to Yuánpíng:
"The time for my rebirth is approaching;
I cannot stay long.
The father of my next life
is currently serving as a prefect.
When I am sixteen,
you will be a county magistrate.
At that time, we are destined to become husband and wife.
Until then, please keep me in your thoughts
and be careful not to marry.
However, fate is already determined;
even if you marry someone else,
it will not be possible."
She wept sorrowfully and left.
In later years, they indeed became husband and wife.
From *Yìwù Zhì*.
A man from Chángshā,
a man from Chángshā in the Táng dynasty surnamed Wú,
was a soldier sent to suppress the southern tribes.
In his daily life, he made a living by hunting, fishing, and trapping.
Once, he caught a white turtle,
made soup from it, and ate it.
Afterward, his entire body broke out in sores,
all of which festered and ulcerated.
He cried out in pain,
unable to endure it for even a moment.
His eyebrows, beard, fingers, and toes all fell off,
but he did not die immediately.
He then begged on the streets of Ānnán.
A monk saw him and took pity on him,
saying:
"If you turn your heart to reciting the Great Compassion mantra,
I will teach it to you orally.
If you can diligently practice it,
you will surely receive a good reward."
The soldier followed his words and received the teaching,
reciting it with single-minded devotion.
Later, his sores gradually healed,
and his fingers and toes all grew back,
until he fully recovered.
He then shaved his head and became a monk,
taking the name Zhì Yì.
He built a monastery on the former site of General Fúbō's residence
and served as abbot of the Kāiyuán Temple in Quánzhōu.
The great virtuous monk Tōng Huì Chǔ Tóng personally knew Zhì Yì
and often spoke of him.
From *Bàoyìng Lù*.
A monk in the Qiánfú era,
during the Táng dynasty's Qiánfú era,
there was a monk whose name is forgotten.
He always devoted himself to reciting scriptures,
never neglecting it even for a moment.
While traveling down the Gorges,
he moored his boat at Báidì Chéng.
Late at night, when all movement had ceased,
as he was reciting,
he suddenly sensed a foul, fishy smell
and saw a figure on the water
gradually approaching the boat.
The monk asked who it was,
and the figure replied:
"I am not human.
My surname is Xǔ, given name Dàokūn.
In the early Táng dynasty, I served as the governor of Kuízhōu.
Due to my greed, cruelty, and tyranny,
after death, I received karmic retribution
and was made the dragon king of Yànyù Duī for three thousand years.
Now, two hundred and forty years have passed.
Just now, I heard your recitation,
which brought great benefit,
so I came to express my gratitude."
The monk asked:
"The Gorges are treacherous,
with many capsizing and drowning incidents.
Could you command the dragons to restrain themselves?"
The figure replied:
"Such matters are indeed numerous,
all caused by karmic retribution.
They cannot be controlled by ordinary means."
The monk found this very strange
and was about to ask more
when the figure suddenly vanished.
From *Bàoyìng Lù*.
Zhāng Yìng
Zhāng Yìng of Jìn,
a man of Lìyáng,
originally served common deities,
engaging in excessive and improper sacrifices.
In the eighth year of the Xiánhé era,
he moved to Wúhú.
His wife fell ill,
and Yìng prayed and made offerings exhaustively,
nearly depleting his family wealth.
His wife was a disciple of the Buddhist Dharma family,
and said to him:
"Now my illness grows worse by the day,
seeking ghosts is of no benefit;
I beg you to perform Buddhist rites."
Yìng agreed,
and went to the monastery,
where he met Zhú Tánkǎi.
Tánkǎi said to him:
"The Buddha is like medicine that cures illness;
to see the medicine yet not take it,
even with rites, is of no benefit."
Yìng promised to serve the Buddha,
and Tánkǎi set the following day for his visit.
Yìng returned home,
and that night dreamed of a man over ten feet tall,
coming from the south,
who entered the door and said:
"Why is this household so impure?"
He saw Tánkǎi following behind, who said:
"He has just begun to form the intention;
he cannot yet be blamed."
Yìng awoke from sleep,
and immediately lit a torch to make a high seat and a seat for Hārītī.
Tánkǎi came the next day,
and Yìng told him his dream.
He then received the Five Precepts,
removed the idols of the deities,
and held a grand offering for blessings.
His wife's illness improved for a time,
and she soon recovered completely.
In the second year of the Xiánkāng era,
Yìng went to Mǎgōu to trade salt.
Returning, he moored at Wúhú,
stayed overnight,
and dreamed of three men
hooking him with a barb.
Yìng said:
"I am a disciple of the Buddha."
They pulled and would not let go,
saying:
"This slave has been evading judgment for a long time."
Yìng, afraid,
said to them:
"Release me,
and I will give you a shēng of wine."
The hookmen then released him,
and said to Yìng:
"Only fear that later others will come to take you again."
After he awoke,
he suffered diarrhea and dysentery,
and upon reaching home was greatly afflicted.
Yìng said:
The nineteen characters starting from "Only fear" are supplemented based on the Ming manuscript.
"It has been a long time since I last saw Tánkǎi."
His illness grew severe,
and he sent someone to invite him,
but it happened that Tánkǎi was not there.
Yìng soon ceased breathing,
but revived after several days.
He said there were several men
who hooked him and were taking him north.
Descending a slope to a shore,
they saw many cauldrons of boiling water, knives, swords, and instruments of cruel torture.
Yìng realized it was hell,
and wanted to call his teacher's name,
but forgot Tánkǎi's style name,
so he only cried, "Venerable monk, save me!"
and also called upon the Buddha at times.
After a while,
a man came from the west,
over ten feet tall,
holding a golden pestle as if to strike.
The hookmen all fled in terror.
The tall man led Yìng away,
and said to him:
"Your lifespan is exhausted,
you will not live much longer.
You may return home briefly,
recite three gāthās of praise,
and obtain the venerable monk's name.
In three days, you must return to your fate,
and then you will be reborn in heaven."
Yìng then revived.
Within the three days,
he kept a vegetarian diet and recited praises,
and sent someone with a letter to obtain Tánkǎi's name.
On the appointed day, after finishing his meal,
he paid homage to the Buddha, chanted praises,
bid farewell to his family,
bathed, dressed, and capped himself,
and passed away as if falling asleep.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín".
Shì Dào'ān
The Eastern Jìn monk Shì Dào'ān of Héngshān,
having experienced the turmoil of Shí Zhào's reign,
took refuge in Xiāngyáng.
He wrote commentaries on the Prajñāpāramitā, Daoxing, and other sūtras, analyzing them.
"Analyzing" originally written as "praying";
corrected based on the Ming manuscript.
He doubted his explanations of over twenty scrolls,
fearing they might not accord with principle.
So he made a vow:
"If what I have explained does not violate principle,
may I see an auspicious sign."
Then he dreamed of a Daoist,
with white hair and long eyebrows,
who said to Ān:
"The sūtras you have commented upon
are entirely in accord with the principle.
I, unable to enter Nirvāṇa,
dwell in the Western Regions,
and shall assist in propagating the Dharma.
You may set out food offerings at times."
Later, Yuǎngōng said:
"The one the venerable monk dreamed of in the past
was Piṇḍola."
Thereupon, they established a seat to make offerings to him,
which became a permanent practice.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín".
Zhōu Mǐn,
a native of Rǔnán,
served as Protector of the Army during the Jìn dynasty,
and his family had long upheld the Buddhist Dharma.
During the rebellion of Sū Jùn,
the people of his town all fled east and west,
and Mǐn’s family possessed a copy of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra,
written back and forth
on a piece of plain silk eight zhàng long and half a width wide.
They also had several other sūtras,
with the Mahāprajñāpāramitā mixed among them.
As they had to flee alone to avoid the disaster,
they could not take them all,
and they especially regretted leaving the Mahāprajñāpāramitā,
not knowing in which volume it was.
They departed in haste,
lingering and sighing in sorrow.
Suddenly, without their noticing, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā emerged on its own.
Mǐn, overjoyed and astonished, took it with him,
and the Zhōu family treasured it for generations.
It remains to this day.
Another account says
that Húmǔ Shì, the wife of Zhōu Sōng, possessed a plain-silk copy of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā,
the silk being five cùn wide,
yet containing the entire Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
Along with it were relics,
placed in a silver jar,
and both were sealed in a deep box.
During the chaos of the Yǒngjiā era,
Húmǔ Shì fled south to escape the soldiers.
The sūtra and relics emerged from the box on their own,
so she sought them and carried them with her,
crossing the river to the east.
Once, they also encountered a fire,
and she had no time to retrieve the sūtra.
After the house was completely burned and the fire extinguished,
she found it beneath the ashes,
intact as before.
Sīmǎ Dàozǐ, Prince of Kuàijī, requested it from Yún, the great-grandson of Sōng, for veneration,
and it was later often kept temporarily at Xīnzhǔ Temple.
Liú Jìngshū said:
"I personally saw this sūtra;
the characters were like sesame seeds,
with clear strokes.
Xīnzhǔ Temple is today’s Tiān’ān Temple.
This sūtra was likely copied by the enlightened monk Huìzé."
Some say:
"It was once at Jiǎnjìng Temple,
recited by the nun Dào."
From *Míngxiáng Jì*.
Wáng Yì, Jìn Wáng Yì, styled Zhòngdé,
was a native of Tàiyuán
and served as General of Chariots and Cavalry.
His family believed in the Buddhist Dharma.
His father, Huáng,
served as Governor of Zhōngshān
and was killed by Dīng Cén.
Yì and his elder brother returned south with their mother.
Climbing and wading, hungry and exhausted,
they ran out of food with no plan,
so they turned their hearts solely to the Three Jewels.
Suddenly, they saw a youth leading a black ox,
who gave each of them a meal
and then vanished.
At the time, heavy rain had caused a great flood,
and ahead of Yì lay a vast expanse of water,
with no way to gauge its depth.
Suddenly, a white wolf appeared, circling tamely before them,
crossed the water and returned,
as if wanting to guide them.
This happened three times.
They then followed the wolf,
and the water reached only to their knees.
They found the road and returned to the court.
Later, Yì rose from Minister of War to Governor of Xúzhōu.
Once, when preparing to hold a vegetarian feast,
he had the place swept and cleaned the night before,
and displayed incense, flowers, sūtras, and images.
Suddenly, he heard chanting from the Dharma hall,
clear, melodious, and flowing.
Yì hurried to look
and saw five monks before the Buddha’s seat,
their divine bearing majestic and extraordinary.
Yì felt deep reverence.
The monks glanced around calmly,
and before Yì could finish gazing and bowing,
they all soared into the sky and flew away.
Relatives and guests who witnessed this
doubled their faith and understanding.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Xiè Fū
Xiè Fū, styled Qìngxù,
was a native of Shānyīn in Kuàijī
and the nephew of General Zhènjūn, Yóu.
From youth, he held lofty principles
and lived in seclusion at Dōngshān.
He devoutly believed in the Great Dharma,
diligent and tireless.
He hand-copied the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*
and once placed it at White Horse Temple in the capital.
When a neighboring fire spread to the temple,
all other belongings and sūtras
were reduced to ashes,
but this sūtra only burned the edges of the paper outside the ruled lines,
leaving the text completely intact
and undamaged.
When Fū died,
his friends suspected he had attained the Way.
Upon hearing of this sūtra,
they were even more astonished.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Sēng Fǎhóng
During the Jìn dynasty, the monk Sēng Fǎhóng resided at Wǎguān Temple.
In the twentieth year of the Yìxī era,
when the state prohibited casting,
Fǎhóng had vowed to cast a golden statue sixteen feet tall.
He cast it privately,
and it was still in the mold
when the authorities found out
and arrested and imprisoned him.
Fǎhóng recited Guānyīn’s name,
a hundred times daily.
Suddenly, he dreamed that the golden statue he had cast came to the prison,
stroked his head, and said:
"Do not worry."
On the statue’s chest, an area about one chǐ square
turned the color of scorched, boiling copper.
On the day Fǎhóng was imprisoned,
the state’s oxen and horses refused to enter their pens,
which was considered strange at the time.
After ten days, an amnesty was issued,
and Fǎhóng was released.
The statue then broke free from its mold and appeared on its own.
From *Biànzhèng Lùn*.
Liú Shìzhī
Liú Shìzhī of Péngchéng
constantly venerated a golden statue,
which once vanished without reason,
and its whereabouts were unknown.
Shìzhī reflected day and night on his faults and blamed himself,
and his sincere thoughts reached the unseen.
After a hundred days,
the statue suddenly reappeared on its original seat,
its divine light illuminating the room.
The whole family was astonished and overjoyed,
and their devotion redoubled.
From *Biànzhèng Lùn*.
Liú Líng
Sòng Liú Líng,
whose origins are unknown,
lived in the Lùchéng Village east of Jìnlíng.
He was quite devoted to Buddhism,
having established a shrine in his residence,
where he regularly held vegetarian feasts.
On the twenty-seventh day of the third month in the ninth year of the Yuánjiā era,
his father died suddenly.
At the time, shamans and diviners all said:
"Three more people in this household will die."
A neighbor, Wèi Jù, served as a Jìjiǔ in the Way of the Celestial Masters,
and often deceived the villagers with talismans and charms.
He said to Líng:
"The misfortunes in your household are not yet over,
because you worship an unclear deity.
If you convert to the Great Way,
you will surely receive blessings and protection.
If you do not change your mind,
your entire family will be wiped out."
Líng then respectfully invited the Jìjiǔ
and ceased his devotion to Buddhism.
Jù said:
"You should burn the scriptures and images,
and only then will the calamities be eliminated."
They then set fire to the shrine,
and the flames blazed for a full day,
yet only the building was destroyed.
The scriptures, images, banners, and pedestals
remained intact as before.
In the middle of the night, the images
emitted a great red light.
At that time, there were about twenty Jìjiǔ present,
and some, fearing the spiritual efficacy, secretly left.
Jù and his disciples, however, were still not deterred.
With disheveled hair and performing Yǔ steps,
they held
"held" originally written as "reported,"
corrected according to the Míng manuscript.
knives and ropes,
saying:
"Expel the Buddha back to his homeland,
do not let him remain in Zhōngxià to harm the people."
Líng, at that place,
felt as if someone were beating him,
and he suddenly fell to the ground.
His family helped him up,
and he was barely breathing.
He then became paralyzed and unable to walk.
Wèi Jù developed ulcers inside his body,
bleeding three shēng of blood daily,
and died in agony within a month.
As for his other companions,
they all suffered from leprosy.
The neighbor, Shuǐ Lìhé, the Prefect of Dōng'ān,
spread the story in Dōngyáng,
and many witnessed it at the time.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín"
Chén Ānjū
Sòng Chén Ānjū was a native of Xiāngyáng County.
His paternal uncle had from youth practiced shamanistic customs,
drumming and dancing in sacrificial rites,
with divine images filling his house.
His father alone reverently believed in the Buddhist Dharma,
constantly observing fasting and precepts himself.
Since his uncle had no son,
he adopted Ānjū as his heir.
Although Ānjū resided in his uncle's household,
he cultivated his conduct with utmost sincerity,
abolishing and ceasing all improper sacrifices.
Suddenly he fell ill and became deranged,
then would sing songs to the spirits,
confused, dazed, and perverse.
After persisting in this state for a full year,
his resolve grew even firmer.
He often vowed, saying:
"If the aspiration I hold
should ever be diminished or taken away,
I will first cut my own four limbs into pieces
before submitting to such a fate."
His family all saw
"saw" character originally missing,
a space left blank,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy.
this,
but Ānjū would not listen.
After three years,
he fell ill and died,
but his heart region remained slightly warm,
so his family dared not encoffin him.
On the seventh night,
the watchers perceived a wind, as if from between the corpse's feet,
fluttering the clothes and coverings,
and he revived with a sound.
His family, initially fearing a corpse leaping up,
all fled to avoid it.
Soon he was able to move slightly,
and then asked for water and broth.
His family was overjoyed,
asking where he had come from.
Ānjū recounted in detail what he had experienced.
At first, he saw someone like a messenger
with several tens of attendants,
who called him to go.
The followers wanted to bind him,
but the messenger said:
"This man has merit;
he cannot be bound."
They traveled about a hundred-some *li*,
arriving at a walled administrative city,
its buildings very orderly.
The messenger took him to the government office,
a place like a bureau headquarters.
Presently, someone handed him paper and brush,
ordering Ānjū:
"Write down twenty-four death-register names."
Ānjū, as instructed, wrote the names, completing several entries.
A man came out from within,
shouting loudly:
"Ān
"Ān" character originally missing,
supplemented based on *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín* 62.
jū may enter.
"Enter" originally written as "person",
corrected based on *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín* 62.
After entering
"Enter" originally written as "righteousness".
Corrected based on Ming manuscript copy
it was announced
Originally, the character "ān" was under the character "announced",
being a misplacement of the character from the upper line's "jū" character,
now deleted.
that an order was issued to deliver him to the Interrogator of Wrongs.
Two prison officers,
one said:
"Give him the large shackles."
The other said:
"This man has considerable merit;
only the three-foot shackles are appropriate."
They debated without reaching a decision,
so together they examined the documents.
After a long while,
they finally gave him the three-foot shackles.
A short time later,
he saw a noble person
with winged attendants numbering several tens,
elegant in form and appearance,
who said to Ānjū:
"How did you get here?"
Ānjū fully recounted the reason.
The noble person said:
"Your uncle has committed offenses,
but he should only be registered for judgment.
Because he previously cultivated minor merit,
he now dares to lodge a complaint only after being beaten and dispersed.
I and your father were close friends from childhood;
seeing you now, it is as before.
You may accompany me on a
"now dares" and the following twenty-two characters supplemented based on Ming manuscript copy.
tour of observation."
The prison officers were unwilling to remove the shackles,
saying:
"The Prefect has given no order;
we dare not act on our own authority."
The noble person said:
"Just hand him over to me;
I will not let him escape."
Then they released him.
The noble person took Ānjū all around to the various hells,
where he fully witnessed the torments,
largely corresponding to the descriptions in the scriptures.
Before the tour was finished,
a messenger came proclaiming:
"The Prefect summons Ānjū."
Ānjū, terrified,
sought rescue from the noble person.
The noble person said:
"You yourself have committed no offense;
just answer truthfully,
and you will surely have no worries."
Ānjū arrived at the gate,
where he saw several hundred people in fetters and cangues,
all advancing together at once.
Ānjū was third in line.
Reaching below the steps,
a man wearing a crown and official headdress stood before the prisoners,
reading the register of offenses.
The first offender's conduct:
In the past, at the beginning of his marriage,
he and his wife made a vow
that whether they had children or not,
they would never abandon each other.
But this man was originally a libationer,
who had also once served the Dao and made offerings,
and among his disciples he obtained a female disciple,
with whom he then committed adultery.
Consequently, he abandoned his original wife,
and his wife had once lodged a grievance.
The Prefect said:
"You and your wife violated your vow,
not upholding the great righteousness to the end—this is the first offense.
The bond between master and disciple is clearly defined among the three relationships,
yet you committed adultery with her.
This is no different from father and son engaging in licentiousness.
Hand him over to the Legal Bureau for detailed sentencing."
Next, the second woman's written complaint was read;
her name was forgotten.
It stated:
Her home was in Huángshuǐ Village, Guànjūn County, Nányáng.
Her family placed cooking vessels at the mouth of the stove,
and this woman laid her infant on the stove.
The baby crawled about,
and feces soiled the cooking vessels.
When this woman returned and saw it,
she immediately apologized to the deities,
and washed and cleansed everything meticulously.
But her father-in-law often cursed this woman,
saying there was no Way of Heaven or ghosts and spirits,
which allowed this wicked woman
to commit such defilement.
The Director of Fate heard of this,
and therefore registered and sent her here.
The Prefect said:
"Laying a child on the stove is no transgression;
a small child has no understanding.
Moreover, she has already apologized to the spirits.
She is without offense.
The father-in-law's curses are without principle,
falsely slandering the hidden numinous.
Register him and bring him here."
In a moment, he arrived.
Next, it was Ānjū's turn.
The man below the steps fully read the clear complaint,
which was the accusation by his uncle.
The Prefect said:
"This man serves the Buddha;
he is a man of great virtue.
His uncle killed the innocent,
deceiving and deluding the common people.
His offenses deserve thorough punishment.
Because he possesses minor merit,
no penalty has yet been applied to him.
Now he further slanders and accuses the innocent.
Issue an order to hasten his registration and summon him here."
Then the Prefect sent Ānjū back:
"You may go.
If you can accomplish superior deeds,
your lifespan may reach ninety-three.
Strive diligently,
and do not come here again."
As he was about to leave the prefecture,
the Bureau Officer said:
"You may remove the death-register names."
Thereupon, Ānjū pulled out the names one by one, and when finished,
and arrived at the residence of the nobleman he had previously visited.
The nobleman also arrived and said:
"I know you have no other crimes and have been allowed to return,
which is very good.
Strive diligently to cultivate merit and virtue.
Your blessings in this life are meager,
so you cannot ascend to heaven.
You will receive your retribution here,
assisting the Prefect,
and you will also enjoy leisurely wealth and honor—
a splendid path for a spirit.
My family is in Wǎn,
surname so-and-so, given name so-and-so.
When you return, convey my regards to them,
urging them to honor and uphold the Dharma precepts,
and not to violate any partial prohibitions.
You may fully inform them of what you have seen and heard."
Then he sent Ānjū back with three strong men.
After walking several hundred steps out the gate,
they transmitted instructions and handed a talisman to Ānjū,
saying:
"You may take this talisman,
and when passing through checkpoints and garrisons along the way,
show it to them.
Do not attempt to sneak through,
for sneaking through will result in punishment and demotion.
If you encounter water obstacles,
you may cast this talisman into the water,
and you will be able to cross immediately."
Ānjū received the talisman and set off on his return.
After walking for a long time,
he was blocked by a great river and could not cross.
Ānjū followed the instructions and threw the talisman into the water.
Suddenly, he felt dizzy as if his vision blurred,
and then he found himself in the courtyard of his own home.
Just then, he heard wailing and lamentation from inside the house.
The three men who had escorted him
urged him to return to his body.
Ānjū smelled his own body's foul odor and
said:
"I cannot return."
These men then forcibly pushed him,
and he collapsed onto the feet of the corpse.
After Ānjū recovered,
he wanted to verify the story of the woman from Huángshuǐ,
so he specifically went to Guànjūn County to inquire.
Indeed, there was such a woman.
When they met, it felt as if
they had known each other before.
She said:
"I died and then came back to life,
and my uncle died on that very day."
What she recounted of what she had seen and heard
was entirely consistent with Ānjū's account.
Ānjū indeed lived to be ninety-three years old.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*
Mǎ Chǔbó
Sòng-era Mǎ Chǔbó
was from Làngzhōng in Bāxī.
From a young age, he believed in the Buddha-Dharma.
He once served as the magistrate of Xuānhàn County.
In the twelfth year of the Yuánjiā era,
on a night in the seventh month,
he dreamed of three men in the sky,
over two *zhàng* tall,
with stern and imposing appearances.
"Stern" is written as "beautiful" in the Míng manuscript copy.
They looked down from the clouds,
with celestial musicians and music
filling the sky.
They announced:
"Your calamity lies in Jīngchǔ,
in the year of Wùyín,
on the fourth day of the eighth month.
If you dwell in mountains and marshes,
the disaster can be averted.
If you maintain a vegetarian diet and uphold precepts among people,
you may also escape it.
If you pass this date,
you will awaken to the Way."
At that moment, looking down, he saw eight acquaintances, including Yáng Xiān,
all wearing shackles and fetters.
He also saw the Daoist priest Hú Liáo,
half of his body emerging into the air.
The men in the sky recorded the year and month of the deaths of the eight men,
but only said to Liáo:
"If you can cultivate merit and virtue,
you may still extend your lifespan."
Xiān and the others all died as scheduled.
Liáo grew even more fearful,
devoted himself to the Dharma and lived in the mountains,
diligently and earnestly applying himself to the utmost.
Later, Chǔbó served as the Western Bureau Officer of Liángzhōu,
under the provincial governor Xiāo Sīhuà.
When Xiāo was transferred to Nánmán,
he again appointed Chǔbó as a traveling military advisor.
Chǔbó, recalling the words about Jīngchǔ,
felt very fearful in his heart.
He requested Xiāo to release him from his duties,
intending to go to Héngshān,
but Xiāo adamantly refused.
The thirteenth year was the year of Wùyín.
At the end of the sixth month, he fell ill,
and by the eighth month, his condition was critical.
On that day, after dusk,
he suddenly had clear and penetrating vision,
and from afar, he saw three men walking in the west,
about two *zhàng* tall.
The man in front wore layered robes with draped sleeves,
and his neck emitted light.
The two behind had golden, radiant forms,
with dignified and complete appearances.
They stood arrayed in the air,
several *ren* above the ground.
Chǔbó observed them carefully and in detail,
and they were indeed the ones he had seen in his previous dream.
After a short while, they disappeared,
and the lingering fragrance lasted for some time before fading.
Everyone in the household, young and old,
smelled the fragrance,
and as a result, they broke into a sweat,
and his illness immediately slightly improved.
Chǔbó's residence was rather lowly and humble,
but at that time, he felt as if he were in a hall,
with corridors and walls shining brilliantly,
all made of precious treasures.
Soon after, his ailment was completely cured.
From *Míngxiáng Jì*
Fèi Chòngxiān
Sòng-era Fèi Chòngxiān
was from Wúxīng.
From a young age, he believed in the Buddha-Dharma,
and was diligent and devoted.
In the third year of the Tàishǐ era,
he received the Bodhisattva precepts,
and stayed for a vegetarian retreat at the home of Xiè Huìyuǎn.
On the twenty-fourth day,
he maintained vigilance day and night without slackening.
Whenever he listened to sutras,
he often placed a magpie-tailed incense burner in front of his knees.
On the third night of the retreat,
he saw a person
with extraordinary appearance and attire,
who came directly and took the burner away.
Chòngxiān looked in front of his knees,
and the burner was still there.
Only then did he realize it was a divine marvel.
Reflecting to himself, his clothes were newly washed,
and there was absolutely nothing unclean,
except for a spittoon beside his seat.
After removing the spittoon,
he immediately saw this person return the burner to the front.
Before it reached the mat,
he still saw two burners,
but once it arrived, they merged into one.
Thus, what the divine being had taken
was likely the shadow of the burner.
Chòngxiān had also once heard people say
that at Fúyuǎn Temple, there was a nun named Qīn
who, through diligence and devotion, had attained the Way.
He joyfully wished to see her,
but before he could go,
he thought of her intently and earnestly.
Once, while observing a vegetarian retreat at another's home,
in the middle of the night,
he suddenly saw a nun,
with a dignified and solemn appearance and demeanor,
wearing a reddish-brown kasaya,
standing upright in front of the vegetarian seat.
After the time of a meal, she vanished.
When Chòngxiān later saw this nun,
her appearance, form, and attire
were exactly what he had witnessed the previous night.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*
Wèi Shìzǐ
Sòng Wèi Shìzǐ,
a man of Liángjùn,
was devout in his Buddhist practice and diligent in cultivation.
His children also revered and practiced Buddhism,
but his wife alone was deluded and stubbornly refused to believe.
His daughter, aged fourteen,
fell ill and died.
After seven days, she revived
and said:
"Please set up a high seat
and prepare the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*."
Shìzǐ immediately arranged the scripture and seat.
Although the girl had observed vegetarian precepts,
she had never read scriptures before.
Now she ascended the seat
and recited with a clear, fluent voice.
She then addressed her father, saying:
"When I died, I went to the Land of Immeasurable Life.
I saw that for you, my brother, and myself—the three of us—
there are already large lotus flowers in the pond,
and we shall later be reborn within them.
Only mother alone has none.
Unable to bear this suffering,
I have returned to report this."
When she finished speaking,
she passed away again.
Her mother then came to reverently believe in the Buddhist teachings.
From *Míngxiáng Jì*.
Hé Tányuǎn,
a man of Lújiāng,
his father was Wànshòu,
who served as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Tányuǎn upheld the Dharma and observed the Bodhisattva precepts.
At age eighteen,
he mourned his father's passing.
Grief-stricken, he fell ill,
nearly to the point of endangering his life.
Apart from wailing and lamenting,
he turned his heart to the Pure Land,
hoping to receive a spiritual response.
At that time, he invited several monks.
Tányuǎn confessed his past karmic offenses to the monks,
but for a long time, there was no sign of a response.
The monks often encouraged him,
urging him not to slacken.
Afterward, one night when he finished chanting scriptures,
and the monks had already retired,
Tányuǎn suddenly began to sing and recite on his own.
The monks, startled, asked him about it.
Tányuǎn said:
"I saw the Buddha's body, golden in color,
with radiance extending over ten feet,
accompanied by banners and flowers,
filling the empty space.
The Buddha came from the west
and called me to go quickly."
Tányuǎn had always been frail and weak,
but that evening he was vigorous and joyful.
He then took incense from the box and held it in his hand,
and also scattered garden flowers into the air.
His mother said:
"If you go now,
will you not think of me?"
Tányuǎn said nothing and suddenly lay down.
Those in the household who had long held faith,
hearing of this miraculous event,
were all reverently pleased,
and not overly grieved or afraid.
Tányuǎn, by the fifth watch,
suddenly passed away.
Fragrance filled the residence for several days.
From *Míngxiáng Jì*.
Chén Xiùyuǎn
Sòng Chén Xiùyuǎn,
a man of Yǐngchuān,
once served as Xī Cáo of Xiāngzhōu,
and resided as a guest in Línxiāng County.
From youth he had faith in the Three Jewels,
and even after passing sixty,
his devout practice did not wane.
In the seventh month of the second year of Yuánhuī,
while resting but not yet asleep,
he sighed, contemplating the myriad beings in life and death,
circulating without fixed course,
wondering from where he himself had come.
With single-minded devotion, he prayed,
hoping to receive a response in a dream.
That evening was overcast,
and the room had no lamp or candle.
After a while,
he saw something like fireflies by his pillow,
glowing and flowing, flying about.
Soon the whole room became bright,
and the space outside was as bright as day.
Xiùyuǎn quickly rose
and joined his palms, breathing rapidly.
He saw in the courtyard, some forty or fifty feet above,
a bridge and pavilion,
with lofty railings and colorful balustrades,
standing in the air.
Xiùyuǎn, without realizing it, ascended
and sat by the side of the bridge.
He saw men and women coming and going on the bridge,
their clothing no different from people in the world.
At the end was an elderly woman,
about thirty years old,
wearing a blue jacket and white skirt,
who came and stood before Xiùyuǎn.
After a while,
another woman, dressed entirely in white cloth,
with her hair coiled in a bun,
came forward holding incense and flowers,
and said to Xiùyuǎn:
"Your previous life was me.
Because I offered these flowers to the Buddha,
I was reborn as you."
She then pointed to the woman in blue and white and said:
"This, in turn, was my previous life."
Having finished speaking, she left,
and the latter one she pointed to also gradually vanished.
Suddenly, Xiùyuǎn found himself back down below,
and the light also soon vanished.
From *Míngxiáng Jì*.
Gě Jìzhī,
a man of Jūróng,
was a descendant of Zhìchuān.
His wife, née Jì, was from the same commandery,
graceful and elegant in appearance,
and possessed wifely virtue.
Jìzhī's family had long served immortals,
but Jì admired and delighted in the Buddha-Dharma in her heart,
constantly maintaining sincere faith without cease.
Suddenly one day while weaving,
she soon felt the clouds and sun clear,
and the sky became pure and bright.
She then dropped her shuttle and looked up toward the four directions,
seeing in the west the true form of the Tathāgata, with jeweled canopies and banners reflecting in the sky.
In her heart she joyfully thought:
The sūtra speaks of Immeasurable Life
"Shòu" originally written as "shòu"
corrected according to the Xǔ edition.
could this be it?
She then bowed with her head and face to the ground,
and called Jìzhī,
who also immediately saw half of the figure and the various banners and canopies,
which soon vanished.
Thereupon, the clouds and sun became radiant,
shining brilliantly in five colors,
witnessed by the entire village,
and only after some time did it cease.
From *Míngxiáng Jì*.
Dǒng Qīngjiàn
Qí Dǒng Qīngjiàn,
it is not known from where he hailed.
His father’s courtesy name was Xiánmíng.
At the beginning of the Jiànyuán era,
he served as Commandant of the Yue Cavalry.
Initially, when Qīngjiàn’s mother, née Sòng,
was pregnant with him,
she dreamed that someone spoke to her, saying:
“You will certainly bear a son.
On his body there will be a green birthmark;
you may name him Qīngjiàn.”
When he was born, it was as foretold,
and so he was named accordingly.
He had a dignified bearing,
handsome speech and smile,
and a disposition that was broad and harmonious.
His family members never saw him wear an angry expression,
and all who met him found him extraordinary.
By the age of fourteen, the province had recruited him as Registrar.
At the beginning of the Jiànyuán era,
when the Crown Prince was stationed in Fánhàn,
he served as Military Consultant for Water Affairs.
On the sixteenth day of the seventh month in the second year, he fell ill and took to his bed,
saying of himself:
“I will not recover.”
By the eighteenth day,
nearing his end, he sat up
and said to his mother:
“My sins are exhausted, blessings have arrived;
the bonds of karma are forever severed.
I hope you, Mother, will take care of yourself.
There is no need for worry or longing.”
Then he lost his voice and wept bitterly;
when his voice gave out, he passed away.
As they were about to place the coffin for burial before the fasting chamber,
that night his spirit spoke, saying:
“The paths of life and death diverge;
do not place it before the fasting chamber.
A monk who creates images will come of his own accord to receive the deceased.”
The next day,
a monk indeed came,
named Tán Shùn.
They then followed the spirit’s words
and relayed them to Tán Shùn.
Tán Shùn said:
“This humble monk resides at Nánlín Temple.
The creation of a sixteen-foot image is nearly complete.
That your worthy son had such a spiritual response—
to the west of the temple there is a small empty plot of land;
it would be suitable for burial.”
So they buried him beside the temple.
Three days later,
his mother, along with about ten close relatives,
saw Qīngjiàn east of the tomb, looking as if alive.
He said:
“I hope you, Mother, will cut short your grief and return.
I, Jiàn, now reside at the temple.”
His mother then ceased weeping and returned,
and the whole household adopted a vegetarian diet and observed a long fast.
On the eleventh day of the intercalary month,
Xiánmíng dreamed that Qīngjiàn said:
“I wish Father would temporarily go to the eastern fasting chamber.”
Xiánmíng then bathed himself with fragrant water,
observed purification rites, and went to the eastern fasting chamber.
On the night of the fourteenth,
in the brightness, he heard Qīngjiàn’s calling voice.
Startled, he rose,
and saw Qīngjiàn before the fasting chamber, looking as in life.
His father asked, “Where do you reside?”
Qīngjiàn said:
“Since my death,
I have resided in the Palace of Refining the Spirit.
After a full hundred days,
I shall be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
I could not bear to see my parents and brothers weeping in sorrow and anguish,
so for twenty-one days I paid homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
and entreated the Four Heavenly Kings,
thus gaining a temporary return.
I hope that from now on,
you, Father and Mother, will no longer wail or offer sacrifices.
Mother has already made a vow seeking to see me;
before long she will pass away,
and then we shall be reborn together in the same place.
Father’s lifespan can reach seventy-three.
After your life ends,
you will undergo three years of retribution for sins,
but if you diligently practice the Path,
you can be spared.”
His father asked:
“You come in the night;
how is there this light?”
Qīngjiàn said:
“Now I descend together with Bodhisattvas and various devas;
this is the light of their bodies.”
He asked further:
“Whom do you recognize in heaven?”
Qīngjiàn said:
“I have seen Chējì Wáng, Zhāng Wúxīng, and my maternal grandfather, Sòng Xīhé.”
Qīngjiàn said:
“I was not only born into this one family.
For forty-seven years,
through seven deaths and seven births,
I have already attained the four fruits of the Path.
I first made seven vows,
vowing to be born in the human realm;
therefore I passed through life and death.
From now on it is forever concluded;
I have escaped the seven sufferings.
When I was nearing my end,
I saw the seven places of my births and deaths.
The reason I wept bitterly
was parting from those seven families.”
His father asked:
“Into which families were you born?”
Qīngjiàn said:
“I was born into the families of Jiāng Lìbù,
(The original text had “用” for “部”;
amended according to *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*, chapter 52.)
Yáng Guǎngzhōu, Zhāng Wúxīng, Wáng Chējì, Xiāo Wúxīng, Liáng Jǐshì, and Dǒng Yuèjì, etc.
Only in this life did I live seventeen years;
in the other places it was merely three to five years.
From now on,
epidemics and calamities will increase year by year.
You should diligently cultivate merit and virtue.
I have seen that when people in the world die,
most fall into the three wretched paths,
while few are reborn in heaven.
If you diligently strive with vigor,
you can escape and cross over.
If you vow to be reborn in heaven,
we may also meet again.
If your practice and liberation differ,
there will be no chance to encounter each other.”
His father asked further:
“Your mother grieves and longs for you, nearly to death;
can she be allowed to see you?”
Qīngjiàn said:
“There is no need to meet;
it would only increase her tormented suffering.
Just relay to her what I have said.
The various devas have already departed;
I cannot stay long.”
With a sorrowful, pained expression,
he suddenly vanished.
After he left, the bamboo grove to the left and right still held a fragrant aroma,
and the family members all also caught the lingering scent.
Qīngjiàn said the seven families into which he was born were:
Jiāng Gài, Yáng Xī, Zhāng Yǒng, Wáng Xuánsòng
(The character “宋” is suspected to be extraneous.)
Mó, Xiāo Huìmíng, and Liáng Jìwén.
Xiánmíng subsequently left home to become a monk,
taking the Dharma name Fǎzàng.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Qí Jìnglíng Wáng
devoutly believed in the Buddhist scriptures.
He contracted a feverish illness
and was near death in the night.
He dreamed of a golden image
pouring divine broth into his hand,
and thus he recovered.
From *Biànzhèng Lùn*.
Zhāng Yì
Zhāng Yì was condemned to death for a matter.
He had previously made a golden image,
praying for his life morning and evening.
At the execution,
the blade broke and his neck was unharmed.
The official asked the reason;
he replied:
“Only because I made revering the image my practice.”
On the neck of that image were two blade marks like blood,
and thus he was spared death.
From *Gǎnyìng Zhuàn*.
The monk Sēng Hù
During the Northern Qí dynasty,
there was a monk named Sēng Huàn,
who upheld the Way with an upright heart,
not seeking wisdom or learning,
but wishing to carve a stone statue sixteen feet tall.
Everyone found his words strange.
Later, in a valley north of the temple,
he saw a lying stone,
about sixteen feet long,
and so he hired craftsmen to carve it.
After about a week,
the face and torso were roughly finished,
but the back was against the ground,
so they used six levers to lift it.
At first, it did not move,
but from night until dawn,
it suddenly flipped over by itself.
They then proceeded with the carving
and moved it into the Buddha hall.
On the day Jìnzhōu fell,
the statue sweated, its perspiration flowing to the ground.
When the Zhōu troops invaded Qí,
burning all the Buddhist temples,
this statue alone did not change color.
They also tried to topple it,
but even sixty large oxen could not pull it down.
Suddenly, a strange monk appeared,
surrounding it with tiles, wood, and earthen bricks,
and then the monk disappeared.
Later, the statue appeared in a dream to a faithful believer, saying:
"My fingers hurt."
The person woke up and looked,
and indeed, two of its fingers were injured by wood.
They were then repaired.
In the tenth year of the Kāihuáng era,
a thief who stole the statue's banners and canopy
dreamed of a sixteen-foot-tall man entering his room to reprimand him.
The thief was terrified, repented, and apologized.
The statue still exists.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín."
Sēng Chéngkōng
During the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era,
a monk named Chéngkōng,
just twenty years old,
vowed to cast an iron statue west of the Fén River in Jìnyáng,
seventy feet tall.
He gathered funds and charcoal,
sought resources and expenses,
and after twenty years,
the materials were finally ready.
He then announced it far and wide,
gathering many people, wise and foolish,
and chose a day to cast the statue.
When the smoke and flames died down,
after opening the furnace,
the statue had not formed.
Chéngkōng deeply blamed himself,
bowed in repentance,
reaffirmed his earlier vow,
and planned to cast it again.
Diligent and enduring hardship,
after another thirty years,
the resources were prepared again,
and he cast the statue once more.
When the casting was opened,
the statue again had not formed.
Chéngkōng then cried out to heaven, pleading for mercy,
kowtowed to confess his faults,
severely criticized himself,
and deeply encouraged himself.
After another twenty years,
the resources were gathered again,
and he chose a day
to cast the statue once more.
When the time came,
Chéngkōng climbed to the top of the furnace,
a hundred feet high and perilously steep,
and loudly declared to the spectators:
"I made a vow in my youth
to cast a great Buddha statue.
Now, after years of wasted effort,
if it fails again,
I will have no face to see the public.
I now await the opening of the furnace,
intending to give my life in the molten metal,
both to atone for my faults before the Buddhas
and to show my sincerity to all the virtuous.
If the great statue is completed,
fifty years from now,
I shall build a multi-story pavilion for it."
At that time, the spectators, numbering in the tens of thousands,
wept and pleaded with him to stop,
but Chéngkōng would not listen.
Soon, the molten metal poured forth,
blazing and surging,
and Chéngkōng waved his hand in farewell,
leaping into it like a flying bird.
When the furnace was opened,
the iron statue was majestic, dignified, and exquisite,
with every detail complete.
From then on, the people of Bìngzhōu
built a pavilion to cover it.
The Buddha's body was immense,
and its function was vast,
so without extraordinary effort,
it could not have been achieved.
In the early Táng Kāiyuán era,
Lǐ Hào served as military governor of Tàiyuán.
While traveling,
he looked up at the statue and sighed:
"Such a fine likeness,
yet exposed to wind and sun—
how lamentable!"
He immediately donated a million strings of cash,
and within a year,
the multi-story pavilion was completed.
To this day, in the northern capital, it is called the Equality Pavilion.
Calculating from the day the monk died and the statue was completed to Lǐ Hào's time,
it was exactly fifty years.
Judging by Buddhist principles,
could Lǐ Hào be the reincarnation of Chéngkōng?
From "Jíyì Jì."
Shì Huìkǎn
During the Suí dynasty, at the Dàguīshàn Temple in Jiǎngzhōu, there was a monk named Huìkǎn,
a native of Qū'ā.
He had spiritual connections to both the hidden and manifest realms,
which the world did not understand.
He revered statues with deep respect,
treating them as true Buddhas.
Whenever he saw a standing statue,
he dared not sit casually,
and when advising others to make statues,
he only recommended seated ones.
Later, he went to Lǐngnán,
practiced meditation,
and achieved great enlightenment.
While residing at Qīxiá,
he once went to Yángdū to visit Master Sī,
who received him with exceptional courtesy.
When about to return to the mountain,
Sī asked him to display his supernatural powers.
Huìkǎn then extended his arm out of the window,
untied the plaque from the Buddha hall of Qíxī Temple,
and said to Sī:
"People in the world lack foresight,
and seeing such things often causes astonishment,
which is why I do not usually do them."
In the first year of the Dàyè era,
he passed away at Dàguīshàn Temple.
On the day of his death,
Huìkǎn returned his three robes to the monks, saying:
"I am now dying,
may the community live well."
He then returned to his room.
The assembly, startled, rose and followed him,
only to find a skeleton in the room,
seated cross-legged on the bed.
When they tried to shake it,
it remained firm and did not scatter.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín."
Shì Dàojī
The monk Dàojī of the Pǔjì Temple in Púzhōu during the Tang Dynasty,
was a native of Ānyì County in Hédōng.
He was widely learned in the scriptures and teachings,
profoundly understood the mysterious principles,
and among the outstanding talents of Hédōng,
none could match his style.
Previously, the monk Bǎochéng had initiated the construction of a hundred-zhang tall great statue at Pǔjì Temple,
but the work and vow were left unfinished when he passed away.
The elders invited Jī to continue it,
and Jī accepted the earnest requests of the multitude,
extensively seeking alms and support,
with sandalwood and other materials transported ten times,
until the great statue was completed.
Both monastic and lay communities celebrated and relied on it,
moving both humans and heavens.
When Jī first accepted the invitation,
he dreamed of two lions beside the great statue,
continuously spitting bright pearls,
one after another without end.
Upon waking, he sighed and said:
"The free and unrestrained nature of the king of beasts
signifies the unimpeded flow of the Dharma.
The spontaneous gushing of precious pearls
further symbolizes the inexhaustibility of almsgiving.
The hidden workings of the unseen
(The character "冥" was originally written as "宜"
and was changed according to the sixty-third chapter of the *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.)
are secretly in accord,
and the evidence of their efficacy is here."
He then ordered craftsmen
to depict what he had dreamed in front of the Maitreya great statue,
and it remains there to this day.
The temple is located on the sunny side of Púbǎn,
lofty, clear, magnificent, and spacious,
facing the prefecture and city to the east,
and overlooking the rivers and mountains to the south.
The statue is set within a three-story structure,
with rock corridors enclosing a courtyard on four sides,
upper halls and lower courtyards,
resplendent and facing each other,
gardens, mills, fields, and vegetables,
all arranged in a circle and easily accessible.
The Buddhist affairs flourished grandly,
all due to Jī's achievements.
From the *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Monk Fǎchéng
Monk Fǎchéng of the Wùzhēn Temple on Zhōngnán Mountain,
was a native of Wànnián County in Yōngzhōu.
He took the monk Sēnghé as his teacher.
Hé was also revered and supported by his local clan.
Once, someone intended to harm Hé,
and went to his door at night,
but saw a fierce fire inside the room,
with flames leaping up to the canopy,
and immediately repented.
Chéng respectfully followed the teachings and exhortations,
often reciting the *Lotus Sutra*,
earnestly practicing it with devotion,
diligently from morning till night without slackening.
He was inspired in a dream by Samantabhadra,
who urged him to transcribe the great teachings.
After awakening,
he entered a pure practice path.
He repeatedly hired craftsmen,
having them transcribe the eight divisions of the Prajñāpāramitā,
with incense burners and precious scroll rods,
achieving solemn and magnificent results.
Also, on the horizontal ridge south of the temple,
he built a Huáyán Hall,
cutting through mountains and filling ravines,
with aligned pillars and connected roof ridges,
facing layered peaks in front,
and overlooking a slanting valley to the right,
breathing in and out clouds and mist,
looking down upon misty rainbows below,
truly a wondrous sight.
There was a scholar of the Hóngwén Academy named Zhāng Xiàojìng,
skilled in calligraphy.
Chéng then invited Xiàojìng to transcribe the Buddhist canon,
with pure fasting and diligent sincerity.
Greatly moved and responded to,
spiritual birds and extraordinary beasts
became tame around the monastery.
In the fourteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
he suddenly said to his attendant:
"All conditioned things are impermanent,
the karmic conditions of the Dharma have their exhaustion,
rebirth in the nine grades [of the Pure Land],
these words are now verified.
I shall depart from this world now,
do not grieve or worry."
After speaking,
light shone from his mouth onto the pillars,
and he peacefully passed away.
From the *Gāosēng Zhuàn*.
Zhāng Fǎyì
Zhāng Fǎyì of the Táng dynasty was a native of Zhèng County, Huàzhōu.
In his youth, he was poor and rustic,
and did not cultivate proper manners.
In the eleventh year of the Zhēnguàn era,
he entered Huà Mountain to cut trees.
There he saw a monk sitting in a cave.
Fǎyì approached and spoke with him,
and as it grew dark, he did not return.
The monk then prepared pine and cypress powder
to serve as food,
and said to Fǎyì:
"This humble monk has long wished to avoid being known by outsiders.
When you leave, Benefactor,
be careful not to speak of our meeting."
He then explained that ordinary people often have many sins and burdens,
and after death, all fall into evil paths.
But with sincere repentance,
these can be eliminated.
He then had Fǎyì bathe and purify himself,
dressed him in monk's robes,
and performed repentance rites for him.
At dawn, they parted.
In the nineteenth year,
Fǎyì fell ill and died.
He was buried in the wilderness;
being poor, he had no coffin,
so he was interred with firewood.
But he revived and pushed the wood aside to return home.
His family was astonished.
Fǎyì himself recounted:
At first, two men came to fetch him.
They traveled through the air
until they reached an official compound.
Entering the gate,
they proceeded south along a lane for about ten lǐ.
On both sides were official bureaus,
with gates facing each other,
too many to count.
Fǎyì arrived at one such courtyard,
where an official from afar reprimanded the messengers:
"This is Zhāng Fǎyì of Huàzhōu.
The original limit was three days;
why have you delayed for seven?"
The messengers replied:
"Fǎyì's family dog is fierce,
and there is also a shaman.
The shaman was beaten severely,
his back bruised and swollen, his clothes torn."
The official said:
"The delay is excessive;
each shall receive twenty strokes of the rod."
When he finished speaking,
the beating was also completed,
blood flowing and splattering on the ground.
The official said:
"Take Fǎyì to the clerk."
The clerk issued a document,
ordering him sent to the judge.
Summoning the keeper of records,
he retrieved Fǎyì's previous file—
the ledger filled an entire bed.
The keeper examined it in front of Fǎyì, saying:
Most entries in the ledger had already been marked with red checks,
and those not yet checked were recorded.
He said:
"In the eleventh year of Zhēnguàn,
Fǎyì's father had him cut grain.
Fǎyì turned back, glaring,
and privately cursed his father—
an act of unfiliality,
deserving eighty strokes of the rod."
As soon as this first entry was recorded,
the monk from the cave in the past appeared.
The judge rose to greet him,
asking what the matter was.
The monk said:
"Zhāng Fǎyì is this humble monk's disciple.
His sins have all been repented and eliminated.
In the celestial ledger, they have already been checked off.
Now he has been wrongly summoned;
he should not die."
The keeper of records said:
"Those who have undergone repentance—
this case has been checked off.
But as for glaring and cursing his father,
although he received repentance,
the matter has not been checked off."
The monk said:
"If it is not so,
then take the ledger and examine it.
Any beneficial merits
should be considered by the judge."
He ordered the keeper to take Fǎyì to the king's palace.
The halls were grand and majestic,
with dozens of guards.
The monk also followed to where the king was.
The king rose to greet the monk.
The king said:
"Has the Master come on duty?"
He replied:
"It is not yet my turn to be on duty.
My disciple Zhāng Fǎyì has been summoned here.
This man's past sins
have all been checked off by this humble monk;
he should not die."
The keeper of records again brought up the matter of glaring at his father before the king.
The king said:
"Glaring—even with repentance—
this should not be exempted.
However, since the Master has come to plead,
he may be released for seven days."
Fǎyì said to the monk:
"Since the days are few,
I fear I will not see you again later.
I beg to follow you now."
The monk said:
"Seven days are seven years.
You may go early."
Fǎyì insisted on following.
The monk then asked the king for a brush,
wrote a character on Fǎyì's palm,
and asked for the king's seal to stamp it.
He said:
"Hurry home now.
Rely on this to perform meritorious deeds.
If later you do not see me,
present the palm imprint to the king,
and the king will release you himself."
Fǎyì then took his leave and departed.
The monk had him escorted out
to his home.
Inside, it was pitch black;
Fǎyì dared not enter.
The messengers left him,
and he revived.
He felt he was in the earth,
very light and thin,
and pushed with his hands to get out.
Thereupon, he entered the mountains
to perform meritorious deeds with the monk.
The place on Fǎyì's palm that was stamped
bore a character that could not be deciphered,
but it all became a sore
that never healed.
It remains to this day.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Wáng Hóngzhī
Wáng Hóngzhī of the Táng dynasty served as magistrate of Héchuān County, Qìnzhōu during the Zhēnguàn era.
He had a daughter who married Cuī Guǐ of Bólíng.
In Héchuān, she fell ill and died.
After several dozen days,
her family suddenly heard Cuī Guǐ speaking at night.
At first, the whole household was terrified,
but later it became commonplace.
He said:
"Guǐ is a son-in-law;
although it is not proper to set up a spirit tablet in the wife's family home,
yet I suffer from having nowhere to rely.
Please set one up for me."
His wife complied with his request,
offering food morning and evening.
He did not allow meat to be offered,
only vegetarian food.
He constantly urged them to worship the Buddha
and also described matters in hell in detail, saying:
"In a person's lifetime, one can hardly avoid killing and unfilial acts.
Other sins are relatively minor."
He also said:
"Although Guǐ has no sins,
greatly aiding with blessings is beneficial.
Hold vegetarian feasts for Guǐ several times,
and copy sūtras such as the *Fǎhuá*, *Jīngāng*, and *Guānyīn*
two or three copies each.
After this, I will not come again."
The Wáng family fully followed his words,
copying sūtras and making offerings.
Cuī Guǐ suddenly came again to express gratitude, saying:
"Now I take my leave."
The whole family wept as they saw him off.
Guǐ had a posthumous son,
already four, five, or six years old.
Guǐ said:
"This son will surely become a famous official.
I hope you will raise him well."
From then on, he never came again.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Cuī Yìqǐ's Wife
Táng Sīyuán Shǎochángbó Cuī Yìqǐ,
wife Xiāo shì,
father Wénkēng,
from a young age did not consume meat, vegetables, wine, or alcohol.
Xiāo shì died in the fifth month of the third year of the Lóngshuò era,
and her family performed the seventh-day memorial service for her.
While the monks were eating,
her maid Sùyù suddenly said:
"Madam came and told me:
'In life, I heard Buddhist scriptures speak of hell,
and now I am experiencing it myself,
the suffering is indescribable.
Fortunately, my children and others are performing meritorious deeds on my behalf,
and I have been granted a temporary release to return.'"
She then confessed and repented before the monks,
and as she was about to leave, she said again:
"I will return again on the twentieth day,
to take Sùyù to witness the punishment."
When the day arrived,
Sùyù fell into a faint,
and after three days, she revived,
saying:
"At first, I followed Madam to a large city,
where there was a separate courtyard,
where Madam resided.
There were also cauldrons of boiling water and iron beds brought forth,
and Madam was soon boiled and roasted,
the cruelty and agony were unspeakable.
Suddenly, Madam's father, Wénkēng, riding on clouds in the sky, called out:
'Release Sùyù and send her back quickly.'
He said to Sùyù:
'My daughter did not observe the precepts in life,
so she indulged in greed and jealousy.
When you return,
tell Cuī-láng to perform many meritorious deeds,
to rescue her from this suffering.'
Then I saw a Brahmin monk descend from the sky,
speaking in Sanskrit,
instructing Sùyù to recite the Diamond Sutra, Lotus Sutra, and Medicine Buddha Sutra once each,
and then told her to leave.
After reviving,
she remembered everything without forgetting."
A Brahmin monk heard this,
and said:
"What Sùyù transmitted,
is like the language of the Western Regions,
different from that of China."
From "Records of Retribution."
Xiāngyáng Old Woman
During the Shénlóng era of the Táng dynasty,
Xiāngyáng was about to cast a Buddha statue,
and there was an extremely poor old woman,
who sought help and donations,
but ultimately could not
(Originally "chéng," changed to "néng" according to the Ming manuscript.)
obtain any.
The old woman had one coin,
which her mother had given her when she was a girl,
and she had treasured it for over sixty years.
When the statue was being cast,
the old woman took all she had,
and with a solemn vow,
threw it into the furnace.
When the mold was broken and the statue emerged,
the coin the old woman had offered,
was embedded in the Buddha's chest,
and they tried to grind it off.
One night,
the coin returned as before,
astonishing the monks,
and the coin remains there to this day.
Thus it is known that sincere devotion and intention,
will surely receive a sincere response.
The old woman's heart was utterly sincere,
so the Buddhas were moved by her,
causing later generations to regard this as a rare event.
From "Records of Hearsay."
Pǔxián Association
In the early years of the Kāiyuán era,
within the boundaries of Tóngzhōu, there were several hundred households,
forming the Eastern and Western Pǔxián Associations,
creating a statue of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra,
and holding daily vegetarian feasts.
In the Eastern Association, a servant girl from one of the households,
gave birth to a child on the day of the vegetarian feast, right at the feast site,
and named him Pǔxián.
By the age of eighteen,
he was employed as a foolish servant,
performing menial tasks,
having experienced all kinds of hardships.
Later, on the day of a vegetarian feast,
this servant suddenly pushed aside the statue of Samantabhadra and sat in its place.
The elders of the association who saw this,
were all enraged,
they not only reviled him,
but also whipped him severely.
Pǔxián laughed and said:
"Because of your sincere devotion,
I was born among you.
You cannot show respect to the true Samantabhadra,
so what good is seeking this earthen statue?"
Then suddenly, his form transformed into the body of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra,
with a golden body,
riding a six-tusked elephant,
flying away into the sky,
emitting great radiance,
with celestial flowers and colorful clouds,
interwoven in five colors,
and then he vanished.
The elders then realized he was a sage,
and were greatly astonished and ashamed.
In the Western Association, where they held vegetarian feasts for Samantabhadra,
as the monks were gathering,
suddenly a woman appeared,
heavily pregnant and about to give birth,
saying:
"I am about to have a child."
She then entered the Bodhisattva hall,
and though people scolded and tried to stop her,
they could not prevent her.
She gave birth to a boy,
right in front of the seat,
and as it was just born,
it was very filthy,
and the people could not lift it out,
deeply insulting and reviling it.
Suddenly, the woman disappeared,
and the boy transformed into Bodhisattva Samantabhadra,
with light shining brightly,
his features dignified and beautiful,
and the filth
all turned into fragrant flowers.
Then, riding an elephant, he soared into the sky,
gradually vanishing.
The elders, regretting their foolish ignorance,
for not recognizing Samantabhadra,
over ten of them gouged out their own eyes.
From this it can be said,
the manifestations of Bodhisattvas,
how can ordinary people recognize them?
From "Records of Hearsay."
Lǐ Qià
The mountain recluse Lǐ Qià
was traveling from the capital to Jīngzhào.
When he reached Bàshàng,
he encountered an official holding a warrant
and saying:
"We are here to apprehend Qià."
Qià looked at the warrant;
its writing was disordered and chaotic,
impossible to read again.
He said to the official:
"The writing on this warrant is utterly illegible."
The official replied:
"This is a warrant from King Yánluó."
Upon hearing this, Qià wept bitterly.
He begged the official to allow him to return temporarily
to bid farewell to his family.
The official accompanied him through the market,
where they saw the food offerings in various shops.
The official gazed at them for a long time.
Qià asked:
"Do you wish to eat?"
He replied:
"Yes."
So Qià took out a thousand coins
and bought whatever the official desired.
They stopped.
"Stopped" originally read "corrected";
emended based on the Ming manuscript.
They obtained one dish
"Dish" originally read "bed";
emended based on the Ming manuscript.
and after the official finished eating,
he was very pleased.
He said to Qià:
"Now you should quickly copy the *Sutra of Golden Light*;
perhaps you may be spared."
Qià returned home and finished copying the sutra.
The character "finished" was originally absent;
added based on the Ming manuscript.
He bid farewell to his family
and
"And" originally read "finished";
emended based on the Ming manuscript.
left with the official.
After traveling several dozen *li*,
they reached a city.
Its walls and buildings were steep and imposing.
He then asked what city this was.
The official said:
"When Ān Lùshān rebelled,
the authorities feared the bandits would break through,
so they built this city to block them."
He asked again who the city lord was.
The reply was:
"It is Wū Yuánchāng."
Qià had long been acquainted with the city lord,
so he requested an introduction.
Yuánchāng summoned him in,
and they met with mixed sorrow and joy.
After a short while,
hundreds of thousands of troops and horses
passed by the city.
Yuánchāng had Qià remain seated
while he went out to greet them;
only after a long time did he return.
Qià asked what these troops were about.
He replied:
"King Yánluó is going to the Dà'ān Guó Temple in the Western Capital."
When he arrived at the temple,
he ascended a seat a hundred feet high.
The King took out the register and examined it, saying:
"This person has newly copied the *Sutra of Golden Light*,
thus gaining extended years.
Therefore, he is not yet fated to die."
Yuánchāng sighed in admiration for a long time,
then ordered someone to escort him back.
Thus, Qià returned to life.
From *Guǎngyì Jì*.
Wáng Yǐ
Wáng Yǐ
had since childhood constantly recited the Cakravarti mantra.
In the early years of the Kāiyuán era,
he and two companions
were about to go to the Northern River.
A boatman offered to ferry Yǐ and the others,
not haggling much over the fare.
He said:
"I am going that way myself anyway,
so I am not concerned about the price."
Yǐ initially did not want to go,
saying to his companions:
"He is setting the price too low;
this is to lure us.
Could it be that he harbors malicious intent?"
The boatman said:
"The payment I receive
is only enough to cover the cost of wine and meat.
It is only because of you, elders,
that I am not leaving my luggage behind."
His companions believed him,
so they crossed.
They then bought wine and drank together.
Repeatedly, they raised their cups to urge Yǐ to drink.
Yǐ repeatedly heard a voice in the air saying not to drink,
which made him even more alarmed.
Because of this, he grew suspicious.
Although the wine entered his mouth,
he secretly spat it out.
Thus, he alone remained sober.
When night fell and candles were lit,
his companions were already snoring loudly.
Yǐ, fearing something untoward,
sat silently reciting the mantra.
Suddenly, he saw the boatman
holding a large axe,
its blade five or six inches long,
enter from the water cabin.
He cut off the heads of two servants,
then beheaded the two companions.
Next, it was Yǐ's turn.
Yǐ prostrated himself, awaiting death.
Suddenly, the candle went out.
Yǐ was struck three times with the axe.
Behind him was a door
that had long been nailed shut.
Suddenly, two people
supported Yǐ through the door and threw him into the water.
The water under the bank was deep,
but he was thrown onto the shore.
Although his body was covered in blood,
he did not feel much pain.
After walking more than ten *li*,
he reached a thatched hut.
He cried out loudly:
"I have been robbed by bandits!"
The people in the hut took Yǐ inside
and secured the doors.
When they reported to the county,
officials led Yǐ to the scene of the robbery.
He saw that the bank was several dozen *zhàng* high,
and only then realized the power of the divine mantra.
Originally, the character "bright" followed "mantra";
deleted based on the Ming manuscript.
Five or six days later,
bandits were captured in Biànzhōu.
When questioned about the incident,
they said:
"The candlelight suddenly dimmed,
and then Wáng Yǐ disappeared,
we do not know where he went."
Although one wound had broken open,
it did not damage the bone.
Soon, it healed as before.
This was the merit of reciting the Cakravarti mantra.
From *Guǎngyì Jì*.
Qián'ěr Hánguāng
Zhúshān County Assistant Magistrate Qián'ěr Hánguāng's
wife, née Lù,
had been dead for half a year.
When Hánguāng's term of office ended,
he moved his family to live at Zhúshān Temple.
There was a large mound there,
and on a leisurely day, he climbed it to look around.
Suddenly, beside the mound, he saw his wife Lù.
They met with sorrow and joy,
and when he asked about the circumstances of her death,
she then looked north,
and he saw a large city.
She said:
"My dwelling is there."
She invited Hánguāng to go with her.
Entering the city,
the buildings within were grand and beautiful,
no different from those in the human world.
Nearby was a courtyard.
Walking west within the courtyard,
there were several dozen rooms.
Lady Lù resided in the third room.
The affection between husband and wife
was no different from usual,
and her clothes, ornaments, and furnishings were also the same.
After a long while, as dusk fell,
she said to Hánguāng:
"The underworld is strict and severe.
You should return for now.
The day after tomorrow, you can bring our sons and others here.
I have some instructions to give.
There is no need for you to come tomorrow."
The next day,
Hánguāng went again.
Lady Lù saw him and exclaimed in alarm:
"I warned you not to come,
why have you come again?"
Shortly after,
a clerk in crimson robes,
accompanied by several dozen attendants, entered the courtyard.
Lady Lù made Hánguāng hide under the bed,
letting a felt rug hang down to the ground to conceal him.
She warned him not to look,
fearing offense between host and guest.
Soon, he heard someone outside call for "Lù Sìniáng" (Fourth Lady Lù).
Lady Lù went out.
Hánguāng was initially very frightened,
but later he stole a glance.
In the courtyard, there were twenty-eight women in total.
The crimson-robed clerk ordered each to undo her hair bun and tie them in pairs,
then threw them into a cauldron.
The sounds of misery and pain
could be heard for several *li*.
Only when the fire went out did they leave.
Lady Lù hurried straight into the room.
When Hánguāng saw her enter,
he took her hand on the bed.
After a long while, she fainted.
When she regained consciousness,
Hánguāng asked:
"In your lifetime, you observed vegetarian fasts, recited sutras, and chanted the Buddha's name.
Why must you suffer this torment?"
She replied:
"When I was about to die,
a monk came to see me,
urging me to have the *Sutra of Golden Light* copied.
I agreed at the time,
but my illness was critical and hurried,
so I forgot this final instruction.
For this, I am suffering the retribution for false speech,
enduring this cruel punishment.
The reason I wished to see our sons
was precisely to have the *Sutra of Golden Light* copied.
Now that you have seen this,
there is no need to trouble our sons."
Hánguāng returned home,
and fully recounted the matter to his sons.
They wept sorrowfully all night.
At dawn, when they went to look,
it was no longer to be seen,
only wild grass remained.
So they sold their family property,
obtaining five hundred thousand cash.
The Regional Inspector and those below him
each contributed funds,
making a total of two thousand strings of cash.
They then ordered the eldest son to take it to Wǔtái to have the sutra copied.
Upon reaching the mountains,
he toured all the terraces,
but had not yet settled on a place.
Soon, he ascended a terrace again.
Halfway up the mountain path,
he met an old monk.
The monk said to him:
"To copy a sutra to save your mother,
why do you hesitate so?
Leave the money at the terrace,
and quickly return to copy the *Diamond Sutra*."
Having said this, he vanished.
The son knew it was Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva,
left the money, and returned.
Upon returning home, he finished copying the sutra.
He then ascended the mound,
and again saw the hell-realm.
Thereupon, he entered directly.
Encountering a closed gate,
he knocked on it.
Someone inside asked who it was.
Qián'ěr Zànfǔ (i.e., Hánguāng) immediately said, "It is I."
The Ming manuscript lacks the characters for "who" and "I",
instead using "ye".
After a long while,
a woman came out and said:
"My lady asks me to thank you.
Through the power of copying the sutra,
she has already been reborn in the human world.
Take utmost care."
Hánguāng then asked:
"Madam, why do you reside here?"
She replied:
"My offenses are rather similar,
hence I am also here."
From *Guǎng Yì Jì* (Records of the Vast and Strange).
Xí Yù
In the early Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Xí Yù, serving as Investigating Censor,
was reviewing cases in Héxī.
Two postal stations away from Héxī,
he stopped for a meal,
asked for sheep's liver but could not get it,
and flogged the station master.
Someone outside announced, "The liver has arrived."
He saw the liver on a plate, trembling incessantly.
Yù frowned and brooded for a long time,
then ordered it taken away,
and took a bolt of silk
to have a Buddha image cast for the sheep.
About half a day later,
Yù suddenly died.
Following a clerk, he saw
"saw" originally written as "asked".
Changed according to the Ming manuscript.
the King [of the Underworld].
The King said:
"Killing living beings has its proper way.
Why did you take its liver while it was still alive?
How could you bear it?"
Yù said:
"Although I initially asked for the liver,
when it arrived and I saw it moving,
I truly did not dare to eat it."
Having said this,
he saw a small Buddha descend from the clouds.
