The King rose and paid homage.
The Buddha spoke as Yù had stated.
The King said to the sheep:
"He did not eat your liver,
what do you wish to do now?"
Soon after, he released Yù to return.
From *Guǎng Yì Jì* (Records of the Vast and Strange).
Péi Xiū
In the first year of the Kāichéng era of the Táng dynasty,
Chancellor Péi Xiū
devoted his mind to Buddhism,
excelling in Chán and Vinaya.
He was a disciple of Guīfēng Mì Chánshī.
He attained Dámó's sudden enlightenment. Regarding Mì Chánshī's commentary on the *Dharma Realm Contemplation* and *Chán Expositions*,
the Chancellor composed the prefaces.
He often wore a coarse woolen robe,
and in the quarters of singing girls,
holding a begging bowl, he sought alms,
saying of himself:
"Not stained by worldly sentiments,
one can preach the Dharma for others."
He often made a vow,
wishing to be reborn as a king in every lifetime,
to widely protect the Buddhist Dharma.
Later, the king of Yútián (Khotan) had a son,
on whose palm were the two characters "Péi Xiū".
This news reached the central court.
His family members requested to welcome him back,
but that country did not permit it, so it was stopped.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán* (Idle Talk of Northern Dreams).
The Son of a Junior Officer
In the Great Sage Monastery of Eastern Shǔ during the Táng dynasty, there was a wooden statue,
extraordinarily crafted and magnificent.
According to the elders' oral tradition:
It had previously drifted upstream from Jīngxiāng,
passing through counties such as Guī and Xiá.
The local people prepared boats and oars to retrieve it,
and a thousand men pulled and hauled,
yet it would not come ashore.
When it reached Yú,
the people of the prefecture burned incense and prayed,
and it responded to their voices and went ashore.
The prefect and the common people
then constructed the Great Sage Monastery to house it.
In Dōngchuān, there was a military officer
whose son had long been mute.
Suddenly one day, the boy drew on the ground
and told his father:
"My past karmic obstacles are deep and heavy,
afflicted by this illness.
I have heard of the divine powers of the Great Sage Monastery.
I wish to renounce the world and become a monk,
to reside there and make offerings,
hoping to eradicate the roots of my sins."
His father consented.
From then on, the boy devoted himself with pure reverence to burning incense and cultivation,
diligent day and night without slacking.
After several years,
he suddenly became able to speak,
his voice clear and articulate in debate,
surpassing his peers.
There was also a lame boy
who, witnessing this marvel,
vowed to undertake lifelong ascetic practice at the Great Sage Monastery,
repenting and seeking blessings.
Before a year had passed,
he suddenly became able to stand and walk,
his sinews and bones stretching naturally,
his steps unimpeded.
These events are fully recorded on the stele at this monastery.
In the hall's eastern corridor,
one can still see two portraits preserved: one of the mute monk and one of the lame boy.
From "Records of Retribution."
Xiè Huì
Xiè Huì, a Shàngshū of the Sòng dynasty, served as Governor of Jīngzhōu.
He believed that pagodas and temples should not be among people
and should be moved outside the city walls.
He personally led his subordinates to the gate of a new temple
and dispatched eighty soldiers
armed with knives and axes
to destroy the stūpa.
Venerated images lay scattered about,
tiles and timbers collapsing.
Suddenly, clouds and mist darkened the sky,
and a fierce wind and dust arose.
Xiè Huì, terrified, fled immediately,
and his soldiers scattered in alarm,
not knowing what had happened.
Xiè Huì and others dreamed at night,
all seeing a Buddhist monk
soaring in the air,
radiant and glorious.
They also saw two figures,
each over ten feet tall,
of imposing appearance,
who sternly rebuked them:
"Your actions are contrary to the Way;
you will soon know the consequences."
Afterward,
the soldiers all
In the Ming manuscript, "all" is written as "Shǐ Shuāng" (two characters).
developed leprosy over their bodies,
and died after some time.
The others all met their end by violating the law.
Xiè Huì suffered from emaciation illness for years.
Later, due to plotting rebellion,
his entire family was executed,
all dying unnatural deaths.
From "Discourse on Discrimination and Correction."
Bhikṣuṇī Zhìtōng
The Sòng dynasty bhikṣuṇī Zhìtōng
was a nun at the Jiǎnjìng Nunnery in the capital.
She was young in age and appearance
and not firm in her faith.
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā,
after her teacher died, she renounced the monastic life,
married as a concubine to Liáng Fǔ of Wèijùn,
and bore a son.
When the boy was seven years old,
the family was very poor,
and they had nothing to make clothes with.
When Zhìtōng was a nun,
she had several scrolls of sūtras such as the "Infinite Life Sūtra" and the "Lotus Sūtra,"
all of which she pounded and processed
to make clothes for her son.
A year later, she fell ill:
disoriented and terrified,
her flesh and skin festered and rotted,
appearing like burn sores.
There were tiny white worms,
over a shēng in volume removed daily,
causing agonizing pain and torment.
She screamed day and night.
She often heard a voice in the air saying:
"You destroyed sūtras to make clothes;
this is your retribution."
She died after more than ten days.
From "Records of Miraculous Manifestations."
Wáng Xízhī
Wáng Xízhī of Lángyá, Governor of Wúxīng during the Sòng dynasty,
was learned,
loved Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzǐ, but did not believe in Buddhism,
and only engaged in slaughtering.
Initially, as a Lángzhōng in the Western Bureau of Jìn,
he was fond of entertaining guests.
In front of the Inner Bureau, he kept a pair of geese,
which he cherished and enjoyed.
One night, he suddenly dreamed that a goose, its beak
The original text has "yuē" (said);
according to the Ming manuscript, it is amended to "kǒu" (mouth).
holding a scroll of scripture in its beak,
about ten sheets or so.
He took it to look and saw it all discussed matters of sin and blessing.
The next morning, he indeed saw it;
it was a Buddhist sūtra.
Because of this, he dared not slaughter anymore
and became exceptionally devout in his faith.
From "Discourse on Discrimination and Correction."
Zhōu Zōng
Zhōu Zōng
was a man from Guǎnglíng Commandery.
In the seventh year of Yuánjiā of Sòng,
he followed Dào Yànzhī on the northern campaign.
The imperial army was defeated,
and he fled with six fellow townsmen.
Traveling stealthily north of Péngchéng,
they came upon an empty temple
with no monks or disciples.
Inside was a statue
with a crystal face.
They conspired to steal it,
then went to a village to trade it for food.
One of them was sickly and weak,
and the others all looked down on him,
so he alone did not get a share.
Afterward, they each returned home.
Within three or four years,
Zhōu Zōng and the other five
successively fell ill with leprosy and died.
The one who did not get a share alone escaped.
From "Records of Miraculous Manifestations."
Shěn Sēngfù
Shěn Sēngfù of Wúxīng during the Sòng dynasty,
toward the end of the Dàmíng era,
when his homeland was famine-stricken,
wandered for food to Shānyáng.
By day, he entered villages to beg for food;
by night, he returned to lodge near temple buildings.
At that time, there were many small bronze statues in Shānyáng.
Shěn Sēngfù, together with several fellow villagers,
gradually stole them,
until several bags and boxes were completely full.
They then took them back home
and melted them down to cast coins.
When the matter was discovered,
they were arrested and sent to the capital.
Once on the boat, Shěn Sēngfù began saying:
"I see people burning me with fire."
He screamed day and night,
claiming the agony was unbearable.
Before he could be sentenced and executed, he died.
His entire body split open,
as if burned by fire.
Zhū Hēng of Wújùn,
who knew Shěn Sēngfù well,
witnessed the entire event.
From "Records of Miraculous Manifestations."
Monk Dàozhì
In the Song dynasty, there was a monk named Sēng Dàozhì,
a monk from Běiduōbǎo Temple.
He was once appointed by the community of monks to oversee the halls and pagodas,
but he secretly stole precious ornaments such as banners and canopies.
The items he took were numerous.
Later, he even stole the pearl from between the eyebrows of a statue.
Afterward, he broke through walls,
making it appear as if an outsider had committed the theft,
so the monks could not detect him.
After more than ten days, he fell ill.
He then saw a strange being
stabbing him with a spear.
It came and went intermittently,
and each time he would scream in terror,
bleeding in response.
At first, this happened only once or twice a day,
but as his illness worsened,
the stabbings became more frequent.
Wounds and sores spread all over his body,
and he groaned, unable to speak.
The monks in the same temple
strongly suspected he had committed a crime
and wanted to perform repentance rituals for him.
When first questioned,
he still concealed the truth and did not speak.
Two or three days before his death,
he finally confessed everything in detail,
weeping and pleading for help:
"I was foolish and ignorant,
believing there was no underworld,
and I carelessly committed sins,
bringing upon myself this severe calamity.
In life, I suffer torture,
and after death, I will face the cauldrons and knives.
This ruined body of mine
only begs for your compassion and forgiveness.
Now I have no other possessions left,
only clothes, bedding, felt, and shoes,
which may suffice for one assembly."
He repeatedly pleaded
for them to perform repentance on his behalf.
There were two pearls from the statue's brow,
one had already been given to an old woman,
and could not be recovered;
the other had been pawned for money
at Chén Zhāo's house,
and he asked them to redeem it.
After Dàozhì died,
the monks gathered together,
redeemed the pearl,
and held a vegetarian feast and repentance ceremony.
When the craftsman first tried to reattach the pearl,
he turned it back and forth,
but it would not fit securely.
The monks again bowed in worship and burned incense,
and only then did it adhere.
Over a year later,
his fellow monks, in the darkness of night,
heard a voice in the air.
Listening carefully, it was Dàozhì's voice.
He said:
"Since my death,
I have endured all kinds of pain and torment.
It will take years and kalpas
before I can escape.
Thanks to the monks' compassion and rescue,
redeeming the statue's pearl,
amidst the intense suffering,
I occasionally get brief respite.
I am endlessly grateful,
so I came briefly to express my thanks."
After saying this,
when they heard his voice,
there was a foul, rotten stench,
and the pain was unbearable.
After he finished speaking, it lasted a long time
before gradually fading away.
From "Míngxiáng Jì"
Táng Wénbó
In the Song dynasty, Táng Wénbó
was from Gànyú, Dōnghǎi.
His younger brother was fond of gambling,
and the family's wealth was completely exhausted.
In the village, there was a temple.
Passersby would sometimes offer money to the Buddha,
and the younger brother repeatedly stole it.
Later, he contracted leprosy.
A diviner said:
"The affliction is due to stealing Buddha's money."
The father angrily said:
"What kind of god is Buddha,
that he would make my son suffer like this!
I will test this by stealing again.
If he falls ill once more,
then it may be so."
The former county magistrate Hé Xīnzhī's wife
had offered four woven precious canopy straps,
and he stole them to make a belt.
Within a hundred days,
he contracted a severe illness again.
When the sores first appeared,
they started at the belt's location.
From "Míngxiáng Jì"
Cuī Píngyè
In the Liang dynasty, there was a man named Cuī Píngyè,
skilled in archery and horsemanship,
serving as a military supervisor.
Throughout his life, he made a living by stealing and melting down bronze Buddha statues,
selling the bronze to buy wine and meat,
feeling no shame or fear.
At the age of fifty,
his wife, children, and brothers all died.
He suddenly developed an eye disease,
suffering from hunger and cold,
and eventually starved to death.
From "Biànzhèng Lùn"
A Liang Dynasty Man Named Jìn
Note in "Biànzhèng Lùn" Volume 8: "Jìn" should be "Dào"
Dàoshi Wáng Zhèn'è,
was knowledgeable but lacked a good heart.
His words often involved slander and criticism,
and he was disliked by people of his time.
He disdained and mocked the Buddhist teachings,
and whenever he saw monks, he would insult and ridicule them.
Later, he made a living by teaching.
At that time, a monk named Fǎmǎn from Lùxī Temple left a bronze bell at his school.
Before it could be retrieved,
Zhèn'è stole it and melted it down to cast coins.
Later, after making an oath with Monk Fǎmǎn,
he suffered from a severe illness for years.
His tongue curled and shrank,
and he could not speak.
Realizing he had broken his oath,
he used his wealth to cast a bell to atone for his sin.
Until his death,
he remained unable to speak.
From "Wángshì Jiè"
Guō Zǔshēn
In the Liang dynasty, Guō Zǔshēn
submitted eighteen matters to Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
requesting the abolition of small temples within the capital and the removal of idle monks and nuns.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng did not accept his proposal.
Later, he dreamed that a deity spat on him,
and he contracted leprosy.
Although he regretted it, he did not recover.
From "Biànzhèng Lùn"
Wèi Yuánzōng
After Wèi Yuánzōng destroyed the Buddhist teachings,
he suffered from a feverish wind disease,
became weak and exhausted, and died.
From "Biànzhèng Lùn"
Jiāng Shèngshēng
Jiāng Shèngshēng, a native of the former Guànchéng County in Jìzhōu,
during the last years of the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty,
suddenly contracted a severe illness.
He then went to Méngshān for medical treatment,
but after years, he did not recover.
Later, he finally returned home,
his body covered in festering sores,
and his fingers and toes fell off.
One night while sleeping,
he suddenly dreamed of a white stone statue,
about three feet tall,
which said to him:
"Just repair my hand,
and you will recover immediately."
In the morning,
he suddenly remembered that in the early years of Wǔdé,
while hunting sparrows in a millet field,
he went into an old village Buddha hall
and tore a copy of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra,
using it to tie to a stick to scare sparrows.
Someone who saw him said:
"Stealing and tearing a sutra is a grave sin."
Shèngshēng instead cursed angrily,
then entered the hall
and broke off the right hand of a white stone statue.
The statue he saw in his dream
was exactly the same as the old one.
He then went before the Buddha,
bowed his head to the ground,
and repented with all his heart.
He hired a craftsman to repair the statue's hand,
commissioned forty volumes of sutras,
and built a meditation hall.
Within a year,
his illness was cured.
The villagers called it the Sacred Statue.
From "Míngbào Jì",
the Ming manuscript edition says from "Míngbào Shíyí Jì"
Fù Yì
Táng Dynasty Grand Astrologer Fù Yì,
originally from Tàiyuán,
in the late Suí era,
moved to Fúfēng.
In his youth, he was fond of extensive learning,
excelled in astronomy and calendrical calculations,
was intelligent and eloquent,
and skilled in spirited conversation.
From the Wǔdé to Zhēnguàn periods,
he served as Grand Astrologer.
By nature, he did not believe in the Buddhist Dharma,
often looked down upon monks and nuns,
even going so far as to use stone statues for brick and tile purposes.
In the autumn of the fourteenth year of Zhēnguàn,
he died of a sudden illness.
Initially, Yì and his colleagues Fù Rénjūn and Xuē Yí,
all served as Grand Astrologers.
Yí had previously owed Rénjūn five thousand coins,
and before he could repay, Rénjūn died.
Later, Yí dreamt of Rénjūn,
speaking as usual.
Yí then asked:
"To whom should the money I owe be given?"
Rénjūn said:
"It can be given to the Niílí person."
Asked who that was,
he replied:
"It is Grand Astrologer Fù Yì."
Then he awoke.
That same night,
Féng Chángmìng, the Director of the Imperial Workshops, also dreamt he was in a place
where he saw many deceased people.
Chángmìng asked about the retribution for sins and blessings as described in the scriptures,
wondering if it was truly certain.
The reply was:
"It all certainly exists."
He then asked about someone like Fù Yì,
who in life did not believe,
what retribution would he receive after death?
The reply was:
"Retribution for sins and blessings is definite,
and Fù Yì has already been assigned to Yuèzhōu as a Niílí."
From "Records of the Sufferings of Hell"
A Person from Bìngzhōu
There was a person from Bìngzhōu skilled in painting,
who once was captured by northern barbarians.
The Turkic Khagan ordered him to paint a Buddha image.
This person at the time stole some colored pigments,
fearing they would be discovered in a search,
wrapped them in paper and stuffed them into his nose.
His nose bled several shēng of blood.
This person later became a monk.
During the Táng Zhēnguàn period,
he resided at a temple in Shāndōng,
and gradually developed a nose ailment.
After two or three years,
flesh grew in his nose,
very large like a peach,
with pus and blood in a mess,
and incessant soreness and pain.
Later, he requested the monk Líng Yǐ to perform repentance rites,
but the illness did not heal,
and he died after ten years.
Líng Yǐ once resided at Cí'ēn Temple
and recounted this matter.
From "Extended Records of the Five Phases Ancient and Modern"
Xuē Gūxùn
In the twentieth year of Táng Zhēnguàn,
there was a campaign against Qiūcí.
There was a man named Xuē Gūxùn,
who served as the Army Granary Clerk.
After the army slaughtered the people of Qiūcí,
he then stripped the gold from a Buddha's face in a vihāra.
Within ten days,
all his eyebrows fell out.
Upon returning to Yīzhōu,
he repented before the Buddha,
using all the gold he obtained to perform meritorious deeds.
Not long after,
his eyebrows grew back.
From "Records of Miraculous Manifestations"
The County Magistrate of Xīzhōu
During the Táng Zhēnguàn period,
there was a man who served as a county magistrate in Xīzhōu.
He went to Gāochāng,
and at a temple obtained a pearl statue.
Upon reaching the capital,
several major temples wanted to buy it for a thousand strings of cash,
but he refused.
He then broke it,
and sold it for thirteen hundred strings.
Over a month later, he suffered from swelling.
While asleep and awake,
he saw a monk who said:
"Why did you destroy a venerable image?"
He then sent someone to pull out his tongue,
over a chǐ long.
In bitter pain and moaning,
he died after several days.
Xuē Kuí, the magistrate of Dé'ān County, knew this story in detail.
From "Records of Miraculous Manifestations";
the Ming manuscript copy cites "Extended Records of the Five Phases Ancient and Modern".
Dīnglíng
In the city of Yè in Xiàngzhōu,
there was a standing bronze statue sixteen chǐ tall.
A bandit named Dīnglíng,
of a fierce and perverse nature,
having no faith,
drew his bow and shot at the statue.
The arrow hit the statue's face,
and blood flowed down in streams.
Although it was later polished and decorated,
the bloodstain remained.
He also selected five hundred strong men,
ordering them to pull it down to the ground,
to melt and cast it into bronze
intended for making utensils.
Then a great sound issued forth,
resounding like violent thunder.
The strong men lost their souls and courage,
all fell to the ground,
dazed and writhing,
terrified and unable to rise.
Because of this, the bandit gang felt ashamed and fearful,
and many turned to faith.
Dīnglíng later fell ill,
and died after being executed.
From "Records of Manifestations"
Emperor Wǔzōng of Táng
North of Cháng'ān city was an ancient tomb mound,
over ten zhàng high,
traditionally said to be the tomb of King Mù of Zhōu.
On the fifteenth day of the first month in the sixth year of Huìchāng of the Táng dynasty,
someone traveling at night reached the foot of the tomb mound
and heard people talking in the woods.
Thinking they were thieves,
he hid in the grass to observe.
Soon, someone descended from the sky,
wearing red robes and holding a tablet,
who proclaimed:
"Where is the Tomb Warden?"
Two officials emerged and said:
"Here."
He then said:
"The messenger from the Lord of the Western Sea is to be recorded;
when will he arrive?"
The officials said:
"Calculating the journey, he will come only on the eighteenth day."
The red-robed one said:
"Why the delay?"
They replied:
"Lǐ Mǒu
(Emperor Wǔzōng's personal name)
for destroying the holy teaching,
had twelve years deducted from his lifespan.
He is to have his soul recorded on the same day as the Lord of the Western Sea."
Suddenly, merchant bells sounded from the east,
and the red-robed figure and the two officials all vanished.
Several months later,
the Emperor indeed passed away.
The Emperor was heroic, resolute, and decisive,
diligent in all governmental affairs.
As for welcoming a noble princess to break the Qiāng tribe,
recovering the heartland and annihilating cunning strongholds,
his military achievements shook and shone,
second only to Sùzōng and Xiànzōng.
However, the teaching of the Golden Man (Buddhism)
cannot be greatly slandered.
Thus, just as after the Qín burning of books and burying of scholars,
there was in Huàshān someone who reported the death of the First Emperor,
the matter is not false.
From "Records of Transmitting Spirits";
the Ming manuscript copy cites "Supplementary Records of Biographies".
Wáng Yìyì
During the Huìchāng era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Wáng Yìyì,
who commanded the Fèngxiáng army.
It happened that Emperor Wǔzōng was suppressing and destroying Buddhist temples.
Yìyì used his family wealth to purchase the tiles and timber
from these temples, taking the finest materials.
He then extensively built market properties
and also renovated his own residence,
making it the finest in the Qí region.
After living there for three years,
one day a minor clerk entered to report
an inauspicious matter.
Weeping, he said:
"I had just retired to my room for a nap
when a man in purple robes summoned me into a vermilion gate.
It resembled the general's residence.
I saw silk, music, and splendid silks,
with guests seated in rows filling the hall,
but the general alone was absent.
The man in purple pointed to a small path below the steps and said:
'This path will lead you to see the master.'
So I hurried northward,
and saw thorns and brambles covering the ground.
The path was barely wide enough for a person.
I walked until I reached a low hut,
pushed the door open and entered,
and saw the general lying on a bed,
his hands and feet bound.
Someone arrived holding a torch,
and was just about to set his hair on fire.
He then spoke through his tears, saying:
'I am unfortunate.
In life, I enjoyed buying and selling the foundation stones and materials of Buddhist temples,
greedy for their profit.
Now I am imprisoned here,
and will die in three days.
When you return, tell my family for me:
they must quickly demolish the market properties and residence,
and return them to the Buddhist temple.
They must not keep them.'
Then the flames grew fierce,
and he could not finish speaking."
Yìyì became angry and shouted at him.
The next day,
he indeed developed a carbuncle on his head,
and died after three days.
From "Biographical Records Appendix".
The Míng dynasty manuscript edition states: from "Biographical Records Supplement".
Excess Flesh
Buddhist causality
sometimes brings retribution.
In recent years, there was a man
who was both poor and lowly.
Suddenly, a piece of excess flesh grew on his upper lip,
about the size of two spread hands,
hanging down to cover his mouth.
Its appearance was ugly and strange,
almost beyond description.
Whenever this man was hungry or thirsty,
he had to lift the excess flesh to eat or drink,
which caused him great suffering.
When someone asked him the reason,
he said:
"In my youth, I was a ne'er-do-well
and served in the army.
We were often stationed in Buddhist temples.
Once, my comrades and I butchered a sheep together,
and I got a small piece of meat.
Beside me was a Buddha statue,
and I placed it on the statue's upper lip.
Not many days later, I fell ill,
and then this excess flesh grew."
From "Jade Hall Casual Conversations".
Xīmíng Temple
The bell of the Xīmíng Temple in Cháng'ān city,
after the rebel disturbances,
with the monks scattered and displaced,
the temple stood silent for several years.
A poor man, coveting its copper,
took a hammer and chisel in his sleeve and went to secretly chisel it,
obtaining one or two catties a day,
which he sold in the marketplace.
He continued like this for a year.
Everyone knew about it,
but the officials did not prohibit it.
Later, his family suddenly disappeared,
and the copper buyers also wondered why he did not come.
Later, when the officials wanted to move the bell to another temple,
they saw the temple bell lying flat on the bell tower.
When they toppled it over,
they saw the bell thief clutching the hammer and chisel,
sitting rigidly inside it,
already dried up and withered.
From "Jade Hall Casual Conversations".
Míngxiàng Temple
South of Fèngzhōu city was the Míngxiàng Temple,
with several Buddha statues
all adorned with gold.
After the turmoil of war,
a poor man scraped off the gold
and sold it to support himself.
By the time peace was restored,
the golden color was completely gone.
Then, ringworm broke out all over his body,
itching unbearably.
He constantly had to scratch himself with objects,
until the skin was gone down to the flesh,
and the flesh gone down to the bone, and then he died.
The fault of damaging the Buddha
receives such clear retribution.
From "Records of Miraculous Signs".
Monk Yìfú,
a man from Qīngshè,
understood the qin.
He resided at the Lóngxīng Temple in Jiānglíng,
and his behavior was strange and deceitful.
The local governor tolerated him generously,
entrusting him with money and silk
to go to Xīchuān to copy the Buddhist canon.
Someone stole the canon produced by the temple community and sold it.
Yìfú redeemed it at a low price,
and the surplus funds thus became his own.
Once this was discovered,
the seller of the canon died under a withered tree.
Although this monk escaped punishment,
not long after he fell ill.
His two lips turned outward,
resembling a donkey's mouth.
The burning pain was unbearable.
People were all afraid to see him,
and he died after extreme suffering.
In the same temple, several others
who had been trafficking in scriptures and images,
fearing retribution, gave up their wealth
to perform meritorious deeds,
using Yìfú as a warning.
From "Records of Hidden Retribution".
The Míng dynasty manuscript edition states: from "Beimeng Suoyan".
Thieves of Kāizhào Temple
At the Kāizhào Temple on Sānxué Mountain in Jīntáng County during the pseudo-Shǔ state,
a band of thieves entered the temple at night
and completely plundered the monks.
The temple originally possessed a lotus-fiber kasaya of Shakyamuni,
a rare object of a thousand years.
and one thief gave his share to his wife, who unraveled it and remade it.
Immediately, the husband and wife
had their finger joints fall off one by one,
and their beard and hair all fell out.
Soon the affair was exposed,
and they were executed in the marketplace.
From "Records of Warnings".
Monk Shàomíng
During the pseudo-Shǔ state, the Great Compassion Temple's purple-robed Master Cízhao Shàomíng,
in charge of the Mañjuśrī Pavilion,
often solicited money and goods,
claiming it was for making offerings to the Bodhisattva statues.
After accumulating them for years,
he kept more than half for himself.
Later he fell ill,
constantly seeing fire burning from his head to his feet,
cyclically and repeatedly,
unable to bear the suffering.
He repented and confessed his faults,
and chanted to give away robes,
but ultimately did not escape.
From "Records of Warnings".
Tóngjiāng Army
During the pseudo-Shǔ state, the Tóngjiāng
raised an army to attack and capture Lángzhōu.
The fires of war burned and plundered,
leaving the neighborhoods utterly devastated.
In a Buddhist temple, there was a large bell on the ground.
A soldier used a large rock to strike the bell,
intending to break it and sell the pieces.
When the bell cracked and burst apart,
a piece struck the soldier's shin squarely,
breaking both bones and killing him.
From "Records of Warnings".
Sūn Shū'áo
When Sūnshū'áo of Chǔ was a child,
he returned from an outing,
worried and refusing to eat.
His mother asked him the reason,
and he wept, saying:
"I saw a two-headed snake,
and I fear I will die."
His mother said:
"Where is the snake now?"
He replied:
"I heard that whoever sees a two-headed snake will die.
Fearing that others might see it later,
I killed it and buried it."
His mother said:
"Do not worry!
I have heard that those who perform hidden acts of virtue
will be rewarded with blessings by Heaven."
From the Jiǎzǐ.
Cuī Jìngsì
During the Táng dynasty, Cuī Jìngsì served as the Prefect of Fángzhōu.
When Emperor Zhōngzōng was exiled to Fángzhōu,
most officials treated him with disrespect.
Only Jìngsì showed him courtesy and respect,
providing him with abundant supplies.
Zhōngzōng often felt grateful to him.
After ascending the throne,
there was a Cuī Jìngsì who served as the Senior Official of Yìzhōu.
Since they shared the same name,
every time officials were recommended for promotion,
the emperor personally appointed him several times.
Later, when summoned for an audience,
he realized the mistake.
Upon inquiry, he learned that Jìngsì had already passed away.
He then sent Ān Shí to appoint Jìngsì's son to an official post.
Later, the son rose to a prominent position,
and his grandson was none other than Guāngyuǎn.
From the Tánbīn Lù.
Péi Dù
Péi Dù, Duke of Jìn and Chief Minister of the Secretariat during the Táng dynasty,
was small and unimpressive in appearance,
lacking the bearing of nobility.
He repeatedly failed in the imperial examinations,
and this troubled him greatly.
At that time, there was a physiognomist in Luòyáng
who was highly revered by the officials.
Péi Dù went to visit him
to inquire about his fate.
The physiognomist said:
"Your appearance and spirit
are slightly different from others,
and you lack the signs of a noble fate.
If you do not attain high status,
you will surely starve to death.
At present, I see no signs of nobility in you.
You may visit another day,
and I will examine you more carefully."
Péi Dù agreed.
Another day, while visiting the Xiāngshān Temple,
he wandered through its corridors
and suddenly saw a woman in plain clothes
placing a silk bundle on the temple railing.
After praying for a long time,
she bowed and left.
A short while later,
Péi Dù noticed the bundle still in its place
and realized she had forgotten it.
Knowing it was too late to return it to her,
he took it
and waited for her to return.
By evening, she had not come,
so he brought it back to his lodging.
The next morning,
he carried it back to the temple.
As the temple gates opened,
he saw the woman from the previous day
hurrying toward him,
crying out in distress,
as if struck by misfortune.
Péi Dù approached and asked her,
and she said:
"My father has been imprisoned though innocent.
Yesterday, I borrowed a jade belt and two rhinoceros-horn belts
worth over a thousand strings of cash
to bribe influential officials.
Unfortunately, I lost them here.
Now my father faces an unpredictable disaster,
and there is no escape."
Péi Dù was moved with compassion.
After carefully verifying the items,
he returned them to her.
The woman bowed and wept,
asking him to keep one as a reward.
Péi Dù smiled and sent her away.
Later, he visited the physiognomist again.
The physiognomist examined him carefully,
and his expression and tone changed abruptly.
He exclaimed in amazement:
"You must have performed a hidden act of virtue that benefited others.
Your future is boundless,
beyond my understanding."
Péi Dù then told him what had happened.
Indeed, Péi Dù later rose to the highest position among officials.
From the Zhíyán.
Liú Kē
Liú Kē, a Palace Censor of the Táng dynasty,
was a native of Sháoyòu.
In his youth, he traveled to Luófú and Jiǔyí,
studying the texts of Huáng-Lǎo,
seeking the path of transcendence.
He also explored Buddhist precepts at Cáoxī,
and thus donned monastic robes,
taking the Buddhist name Hǎinà.
He traveled north to temples such as Jūnchuān and Fāngshān,
and later resided at the Dōnglín Temple on Lú Mountain,
studying the Nánshān Chāo and the Bǎifǎ Lùn,
mastering their essential teachings.
While living alone in a room,
he repeatedly dreamed of a man in a short coarse robe, who said:
"I was a scholar.
While traveling for study,
I died in this room.
As the temple monks did not report to the local authorities,
they buried me beneath the window,
and my corpse is cramped and confined.
The dead follow truth—
how can I rest in peace?
If you can relocate my burial,
I will surely repay you."
Liú inquired among the monks,
and it was indeed true.
Liú removed his own robe
to cover the skeletal remains.
He prepared a coffin and reburied them above Hǔxī.
That night, he dreamed of the scholar coming to thank him,
bringing three chicken eggs
and urging Liú to eat them immediately.
Liú chewed one and swallowed the other two.
Later, he became proficient in Confucian studies
and excelled in writing.
He passed the imperial examinations
and served in the Historiography Institute.
Wishing to record the events of his dream,
he could not write his own biography.
The Vice Minister of Personnel, Hán Yù, who knew him well,
said:
"When I have some leisure,
I will write a piece to commemorate it."
But Hán Yù was demoted,
and the piece was never completed.
From the Yúnxī Yǒuyì.
Liú Hóngjìng
In the Táng dynasty, there was a man from Péngchéng named Liú Hóngjìng,
whose courtesy name was Yuánpǔ.
His family had lived for generations in the region between the Huái and Féi rivers,
possessing wealth amounting to several million.
He constantly cultivated virtue without showing off,
so no one knew of it.
Although his family was wealthy,
he did not resent others for profiting from his wealth,
and when bestowing kindness upon others, he did not expect repayment.
In the early years of the Chángqìng era,
there was a skilled physiognomist
who met Yuánpǔ on the road in Shòuchūn and said:
"Ah,
sir, please stop for a moment.
I have something to tell you."
Yuánpǔ then invited him into his residence and inquired,
asking:
"Your wealth is quite abundant.
However, in another two or three years,
your appointed time will arrive.
What will you do?"
Yuánpǔ wept and said:
"Life span and early death are determined by Heaven.
What can you, sir, do about it for me?"
The physiognomist said: "Physiognomy is not as important as virtue,
and virtue is not as important as magnanimity.
Although you, sir, are not destined for longevity,
your virtue is profound,
and your magnanimity is especially broad.
I will tell you what comes after.
But during these two or three years,
diligently cultivate excellent virtue,
hoping perhaps to extend it.
For one act of virtue can dispel a hundred calamities,
enabling one to enjoy rank and emolument—
how much more so longevity?
Strive and plan for it.
I will return here in three years."
Having said this, he departed.
Yuánpǔ tearfully saw him off
and then made plans for after his death.
He had a daughter about to be married,
so he went to Wéiyáng
to seek maidservants for her dowry.
Spending eight hundred thousand coins,
he obtained four people.
Among them was one named Fāng Lánsūn,
who possessed exceptional beauty,
and whose bearing and demeanor
were entirely unlike those of a lowly person.
Yuánpǔ questioned her about her circumstances.
After a long time, she finally replied:
"Your humble maid deserves death for her crime;
I dare not speak further."
Since you, my master, are deeply astonished,
how dare I conceal anything?
My family for generations were distinguished,
originally from Héluò.
My late father held a minor official post in Huáixī.
Unfortunately, we encountered the rampant rebellion of the Wú bandits.
Because our surname coincided with that of the state—
"state" originally read "bandits,"
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy.
—the same,
they suspected we were close relatives.
He himself fell to the sword,
and our family was confiscated by the state.
Because of this, we sank into obscurity,
with nowhere to plead our case.
All my other relatives,
after the bandits were pacified,
were captured as prisoners by the government troops.
I can no longer know their whereabouts.
I, your humble maid, have twice changed masters,
and now have come to this."
Yuánpǔ sighed deeply for a long time,
then said:
"Though shoes are new, they are not worn on the head;
though a cap is old, it is not trodden underfoot.
Although your family has perished,
you are still a daughter of official gentry,
and moreover, you bear such injustice.
Even a child of three feet
would still be able to feel righteous indignation—
how much more a true man!
If I do not now vindicate and clear your冤,
may I be punished by the spirits."
He then asked about her relatives
and learned that her maternal clan was named Liú.
Thereupon, he burned her deed of servitude,
took her as a niece,
and with five hundred thousand from his family wealth,
married her off before his own daughter.
In the second year of Chángqìng,
on the xīnmǎo day of the third lunar month in spring,
after Lánsūn had been married off,
Yuánpǔ dreamed of a person
clad in dark robes and holding a tablet,
who bowed toward the dust
and approached him tearfully, saying:
"I am Lánsūn's father.
Moved by your kindness,
how can I repay you?
I have heard that hidden virtue can move Heaven and Earth.
Now your allotted lifespan is about to end.
I shall plead for you before the Supreme Emperor.
Therefore, I come to inform you."
Having said this, he departed.
Three days later,
Yuánpǔ again dreamed of Lánsūn's father standing in the courtyard,
now in purple robes and an ivory tablet,
with a very stern retinue.
He came forward to thank Yuánpǔ, saying:
"Though I am untalented,
I was fortunate to be able to plead for you before the Emperor.
The Emperor granted my request to extend your life by twenty-five years,
and that wealth will reach three generations,
with your descendants free from future calamities.
As for those who harmed my family,
they will all be brought to justice.
Those alive will suffer personal disaster,
and the descendants of those deceased will receive punishment.
The Emperor also took pity on my冤,
appointing me to an important post,
granting me authority over the mountains and rivers in the region between the Huái River and the sea."
Then, sobbing, he bowed twice and left.
The next morning,
Yuánpǔ was lost in thought,
not fully believing it.
Three years later,
sure enough, the physiognomist returned.
He greeted Yuánpǔ and congratulated him, saying:
"Your lifespan has been extended!
Moreover, look at yourself from your eyebrows to your hairline."
Yuánpǔ tilted his cap, exposing his forehead.
The physiognomist said:
"Ah!
There is hidden virtue that has moved Heaven above.
From now on, for twenty-five years,
blessings will reach three generations."
Yuánpǔ then told him about Lánsūn's father.
The physiognomist said:
"In the past, Hán Jué secretly preserved the Zhào clan.
Sīmǎ Qiān recorded that the Hán family for ten generations held positions up to kings and marquises
because they possessed hidden virtue.
Moreover, Lánsūn's family had no heirs,
and Lánsūn herself was a lowly servant.
Despite this, you could disregard great wealth and exceptional beauty
and show compassion for her orphaned state—
how can this not be called profound hidden virtue?"
From "The Biography of Hidden Virtue."
Xiāo Fǎng
The Táng dynasty Chancellor, Duke of Lánlíng, Xiāo Fǎng,
was known for his pure reputation and frugal virtue,
highly esteemed by his contemporaries.
He once commanded troops in Pānyú,
earning praise for drinking from pure springs and casting incense.
Because of this, foreign merchants gathered in crowds,
so that even in Cháng'ān's treasure shops and medicine stores,
goods from the south were all abundant,
and from this, people's sentiments praised him.
Emperor Xīzōng was born in the rénwǔ year [and]
ascended the throne in the guǐsì year.
The imperial reign had lasted twelve years.
Thinking to appoint a virtuous elder
to assist in the great transformation,
he summoned him from the position of Minister of Sacrifices to become Chief Minister.
At that time, he was eighty-three years old.
He served in the highest ministerial post for several years,
recommending talented individuals,
and guiding the spread of imperial benevolence.
His frugal virtue being manifest,
frivolous customs were somewhat reformed.
When he passed away in office,
the Emperor deeply mourned him,
and suspended regular court sessions for three days.
The posthumous conferral ceremonies
were conducted with added honors.
Commentators said:
"High position and heavy emolument—
if one truly has the share for it,
the hidden spirits will surely aid his longevity.
Otherwise,
how could there be one who, past the age of retiring from office,
became chief minister for a ruler who had just been born?
Tàigōng, in his later years at seventy, encountered King Wén.
Now he exceeded the age of fishing at the Wèi River by twelve years.
Thus we know that the distinction between honor and disgrace—
how could it be accidental?"
From "An Unofficial History of the Táng."
Sūn Tài
Sūn Tài of the Táng dynasty,
a man from Shānyáng,
in his youth studied under Huángfǔ Yǐng,
and upheld integrity, possessing the demeanor of ancient worthies.
Sūn Tài’s wife was the daughter of his maternal aunt.
Previously,
his aunt was elderly.
She entrusted her two daughters to him, saying:
"The elder one has a damaged eye;
you should marry the younger sister."
After his aunt passed away,
Sūn Tài married the elder sister.
("Sister" originally written as "dì" [younger sister],
corrected according to Táng Zhíyán.)
Some questioned him,
and Sūn Tài said:
"She has a disability;
if not me, who would she be suitable for?"
Everyone admired Sūn Tài’s righteousness.
Once in the marketplace,
he came across an iron lamp stand for sale,
had it polished and cleaned,
and it turned out to be silver.
Sūn Tài immediately returned it.
During the Zhōnghé era,
he planned to settle his family in Yìxīng,
purchasing a villa
for two hundred thousand strings of cash.
After paying half the amount,
Sūn Tài traveled to Wúxīng Commandery,
agreeing to visit the villa upon his return.
After two months,
Sūn Tài returned,
moored his boat in front of the villa,
and paid the remaining sum,
asking the owner to move elsewhere.
At that moment, he saw an old woman
wailing loudly several times.
Sūn Tài, startled,
summoned and questioned her.
The old woman said:
"I once served my parents-in-law here;
my descendants are unworthy,
and it has become someone else’s property,
hence my sorrow."
Sūn Tài was lost in thought for a long time,
then deceived her, saying:
"I have just received a letter from the capital;
I have been appointed to another post,
so I cannot stay here.
Let your son take charge of this residence."
After speaking,
he untied the mooring rope and departed,
never to return.
His son, Zhǎn,
passed the imperial examinations as a jìnshì,
and served in the Liáng dynasty as a ministry official.
From Zhíyán.
Lǐ Zhì
During the Xiántōng era of the Táng dynasty,
Lǐ Zhì, a military officer in Jízhōu,
fell gravely ill and, near death, suddenly dreamed of entering the underworld.
He saw an official who said:
"You once saved seven lives,
which should extend your life by fourteen years."
The official took the register
to seek approval from higher authorities.
After a long while,
he came out and said to Lǐ Zhì:
"The matter is settled."
He then ordered an envoy to escort him back home.
Upon reaching a high mountain,
he was pushed off and awoke.
Lǐ Zhì secretly remembered the incident.
From then on, his illness gradually subsided,
and he indeed passed away fourteen years later.
From Bàoyìng Lù.
Prefect Fàn
In the Táng dynasty, there was a Prefect Fàn,
whose name is forgotten,
but he was quite knowledgeable in divination.
He was appointed as a county magistrate in Jiāngnán,
and he calculated his own fate, saying:
"Next autumn,
both my official salary and lifespan will end."
Before leaving the capital,
he consulted a fortune-teller,
who said:
"Your time will be up in July next year;
why take a distant post?"
Fàn replied:
"I already know,
but I have an unmarried daughter,
and I wish to use my meager salary for her dowry."
Upon taking office,
he bought a maidservant,
and asked her surname.
The maidservant said, "My surname is Zhāng;
my father once served as a dam official.
During the turmoil of war and banditry,
I was abducted and sold here."
Fàn stood up in shock,
asked her father’s name,
and realized he was an old friend.
He said to his wife:
"Our daughter need not worry about marriage;
use all her dowry
to marry her to a careful and kind local."
When his term ended and he returned to the capital,
the fortune-teller exclaimed in astonishment:
"Why did you deceive me so before?
I calculated that your salary and lifespan would end,
yet now you are unharmed.
Unless the calculations were mistaken,
you must have performed a hidden virtuous deed for which you are being rewarded!"
Fàn said:
"Neither is the case."
The fortune-teller pressed him repeatedly,
and Fàn told him about marrying off the maidservant.
The fortune-teller said:
"This is it.
Your fortune and longevity
are now immeasurable."
He later served several official posts before passing away.
From Bàoyìng Lù.
Chéng Yànbīn
Chéng Yànbīn, the walled-city commander of the pseudo-Shǔ state,
was from Línzī.
During the capture of Suìníng,
he personally led a hundred men,
braving arrows and stones.
The city fell.
They captured three young maidens,
all of striking beauty.
Chéng Yànbīn housed them in a separate room.
Within ten days,
their parents brought gold to ransom them.
Chéng returned the gold and the maidens,
explaining he had kept them unharmed.
The parents wept and thanked him, saying:
"May you soon attain high rank."
Chéng Yànbīn smiled and replied:
"My wish is only to die of old age without illness."
Later, he lived past sixty,
and indeed passed away without illness.
From Jǐngjiè Lù.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn
The Kūnmíng Pond,
dug by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
was for naval training.
Within it was a spiritual marsh and divine pool,
and it is said:
During the floods of Emperor Yáo’s time,
a boat was moored in this pool.
The pool connected to Báilù Plain,
and people fishing on the plain
had their lines break and drift away.
A fish appeared in Emperor Wǔ’s dream,
asking to have its hook removed.
The next day,
while the Emperor was amusing himself by the pool,
he saw a large fish holding a fishing line in its mouth,
and said:
"Is this not the fish from yesterday’s dream?"
He removed the hook and released the fish,
and later received a luminous pearl.
From Sānqín Jì.
Dōngfāng Shuò
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn was feasting in the Wèiyāng Palace,
just as he was eating millet and meat stew,
when he suddenly heard a voice say:
"This old subject risks death to present his plea."
He could not see the speaker's form.
After searching for a long time,
he saw an old man on a roof beam,
eight or nine inches tall,
with a ruddy, wrinkled face,
white beard and hair,
walking hunched over with a cane,
the very picture of extreme old age.
The Emperor asked:
"Old man, what is your surname and name?
Where do you reside?
What hardship afflicts you,
that you come to plead with Us?"
The old man descended along the pillar,
set down his cane and kowtowed,
but remained silent.
Then he looked up at the roof,
looked down and pointed at the Emperor's feet,
and suddenly vanished.
The Emperor was startled and bewildered,
not knowing what this was about,
and said:
"Dōngfāng Shuò will surely know."
So he summoned Dōngfāng Shuò and told him.
Shuò said:
"His name is Zǎo,
the essence of water and wood.
In summer he nests in secluded forests,
in winter he hides in deep rivers.
Your Majesty recently
has frequently undertaken construction of palaces,
newly cutting down his dwelling,
hence he came to plead.
Looking up at the roof,
and then looking down to point at Your Majesty's feet—
'feet' means 'enough.'
He wishes Your Majesty's palace construction to be enough here."
The Emperor was moved by this,
and soon halted the labor.
He visited the Hùzǐ River,
and heard the sound of string music and singing from beneath the water.
The old man from the beam before and several youths,
in crimson robes with plain sashes,
their tassels and pendants very bright,
all eight or nine inches tall,
with one person over a foot tall,
emerged riding the waves,
their clothes not getting wet.
Some carried musical instruments.
The Emperor was just eating,
but stopped his meal for this,
and had them sit in rows before the dining table.
The Emperor asked:
"We heard music played beneath the water—
was it you?"
The old man replied:
"This old subject previously risked death to return and plead,
and fortunately received Your Majesty's heaven-and-earth-like grace,
immediately halting the axes,
allowing our dwelling to be preserved.
We are overjoyed,
hence privately celebrate with music."
The Emperor said:
"Could you play some music?"
He said:
"We purposely brought music;
how dare we not play?"
The tallest one then strummed the strings and sang,
the song saying:
"Heaven and earth's virtue bestows utmost benevolence,
pitying hidden spirits, halting the axes;
preserving our cave-home, sheltering our humble selves,
we wish the Son of Heaven a lifespan of ten thousand springs."
The size of the singing voice
was no different from a person's,
clear and penetrating, winding around the beams and pillars.
Two others blew pipes and kept time,
harmonizing in tune with the melody.
The Emperor was delighted,
raised his wine cup and urged them all:
"Our lacking virtue is unworthy of such elegant gifts."
The old man and others all rose, bowed, and received the cup,
each drinking several shēng without getting drunk.
They presented the Emperor with a purple conch shell,
inside which was something
resembling ox tallow.
The Emperor asked:
"We are ignorant and cannot recognize this object."
He said:
"Dōngfāng Xiānshēng knows it."
The Emperor said:
"Could you bestow something even more rare and precious?"
The old man turned and ordered them to fetch a treasure from the cave.
One person received the order,
descended and vanished into the depths,
returning in an instant,
obtaining a large pearl,
several inches across,
brilliant and dazzling, surpassing the world.
The Emperor greatly admired and enjoyed it.
The old man and others suddenly vanished.
The Emperor asked Shuò:
"What is the thing inside the purple conch shell?"
Shuò said:
"It is the marrow of a flood dragon.
Applied to the face,
it makes one's complexion lovely.
Also, if a woman is pregnant,
childbirth will certainly be easy."
It happened that a woman in the rear palace had a difficult labor;
they tried it,
and it had miraculous effect.
The Emperor applied the fat to his face,
and it became radiant and smooth.
He also asked:
"Why is this pearl called the Cave Pearl?"
Shuò said:
"At the river bottom there is a cave,
several hundred zhàng deep.
Inside is a red clam,
the clam produces pearls,
hence the name."
The Emperor deeply marveled at these events,
and also admired Shuò's extraordinary knowledge.
From Yōu Míng Lù.
Máo Bǎo
During the Xiánkāng era of Jìn,
Yùzhōu Regional Inspector Máo Bǎo was garrisoning Zhūchéng.
There was a soldier
who bought a white turtle at the Wǔchāng market,
four or five inches long,
and kept it in a jar to raise it.
It gradually grew larger,
and he released it into the river.
Later, Zhūchéng suffered defeat by the Shí clan,
and those who fled into the river all drowned.
The man who had raised it, wearing armor, entered the water,
and felt as if he had fallen onto a rock.
After a moment, he looked:
it was the white turtle he had previously released.
Once he reached the shore,
it looked back at him and left.
From Yōu Míng Lù.
Kǒng Yú
Kǒng Yú once went to the Yúbù Pavilion in Wúxīng,
and saw someone caging a turtle by the road.
Yú bought it and released it.
When it reached the water,
it turned back to look at Yú.
Later, when he was enfeoffed as Marquis of this pavilion and his seal was cast,
the turtle's head on the seal was bent back,
and after three castings it was not correct,
resembling the turtle's look back in the past.
Such was the response of its numinous virtue.
Yú realized,
and then took it and wore it.
From Huìjī Xiānxián Zhuàn.
Zōng Shūlín
Jìnyáng Administrator Zōng Shūlín
obtained ten turtles,
and told the cook:
"Use two each day to make stew."
That night he dreamed of ten men,
in black clothes and trousers,
kowtowing and begging for mercy.
The next night,
he again dreamed of eight people begging for their lives.
Only then did he realize,
and released them.
Later he dreamed of eight people coming to thank him.
From Mèng Juàn.
Huán Miǎo
Huán Miǎo was in Rǔnán,
when a commandery resident brought four black ducks as a gift.
His eldest son dreamed of four black-clothed people pleading for their lives.
Waking up,
he suddenly saw the ducks about to be killed,
so he saved them,
buying meat as a substitute.
Later he dreamed of four people coming to thank him and leaving.
From Mèng Juàn.
Liú Shū
In the spring of the third year of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of the Sòng dynasty,
Liú Shū from Péngchéng,
courtesy name Zhèngyī,
was returning from Jiānglíng to Èxià
and spent the night at Shàngmíng Isle.
The moonlight was faint that night,
and as he was feasting and reciting poetry,
suddenly two men knocked on his boat,
loudly calling for Zhèngyī,
saying:
"We have come from Èxià
and wish to see Zhèngyī."
Shū raised his head to look
and saw two men on the shore,
each over five feet tall,
with handsome features and splendid attire, both dressed in white.
He then went out to speak with them.
They said to Shū:
"We have long wished to pay you a visit,
and now we meet at this fine hour."
Shū said:
"You have come from Èxià;
what do you wish to say to me?"
One of them said:
"We heard you are a scholar,
so we came to pay our respects."
Thereupon, they feasted together.
Late into the night,
both men became drunk
and lay down to sleep right where they had been drinking.
Shū found this very strange,
and those around him
all exchanged glances but dared not speak.
He then covered them with a quilt.
By dawn, they were still asleep.
When he tried to wake them,
he lifted the quilt
and saw two fish, each five or six feet long.
Their eyes were moving, but they appeared very weak.
Not daring to kill them,
he carried them to the river and released them.
That evening,
Shū dreamed of two men dressed in white,
each holding a pearl,
who placed them before his bed
and left without a word.
When dawn came,
there were two pearls before his pillow, each about an inch in diameter—
they were the two white fish.
From "Records of the Three Wú Regions."
Cài Xǐfū
During the Jǐngpíng era of the Sòng dynasty,
there was a great flood in Dōngyáng.
Cài Xǐfū of Yǒngkāng
took refuge at Nánlǒng.
At night, a large rat
came floating on the water
and crouched at the corner of his servant's bed.
The servant took pity on it and did not harm it,
often giving it food.
After the floodwaters receded,
Xǐfū was able to return to his former home.
The rat, using its front paws, held up a blue pouch
containing a pearl about three inches in size,
which it left in front of the servant's bed,
chirping as if trying to speak.
From "Garden of Marvels."
Liú Zhǎo
Liú Zhǎo of Zhōngshān, Magistrate of Mòlíng,
in the third year of the Tiānjiān era of the Liáng dynasty,
served as Supervisor of Jiànkāng.
While preparing food with his disciples,
they found a turtle in the stove,
about a foot long,
lying in the ashes,
completely unharmed by the fire.
Liú held a vegetarian feast
and released it into Lóu Lake.
Liú was soon promoted to Magistrate of Mòlíng.
From "Sequel to Records of the Strange."
Liú Zhīhēng
Liú Zhīhēng of the Liáng dynasty served in Nánjùn.
He once dreamed of two men surnamed Lǐ
who came to him begging for their lives.
Zhīhēng did not understand the meaning.
When morning came,
someone sent him two live carp.
Zhīhēng said:
"This must be connected to my dream."
He then released them.
That night, he dreamed the two men came to thank him, saying:
"We will extend your lifespan by one count."
From "Old Tales of the Zhǔ Palace."
Yán Tài
During the reign of Emperor Xuān of the Chén dynasty,
Yán Tài of Yángzhōu
encountered a fishing boat while traveling on the river.
He asked about it,
and they said:
"We have fifty turtles."
Tài used five thousand coins to ransom and release them.
"Released them" originally written as "them released,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript.
After walking several dozen steps,
the fishing boat capsized.
That evening,
fifty men dressed in black
knocked on Tài's door
and said to his parents:
"Your worthy son entrusted five thousand coins to us;
you may take them,
though the strings are all wet."
Though his parents accepted the money,
they wondered how this had come about.
When Tài returned and they asked him,
he recounted the strange incident of ransoming the turtles.
Thereupon, they turned their residence into a temple,
and the villagers named it Yánfǎ Temple.
From "Records of Unique Marvels."
Chéng Língxiǎn
At Huángdūn Lake in Shè County, Shèzhōu,
there was a giant clam in the lake—
the kind known as a jiāo-shèn.
It was often fought by the giant clam of Lǚ Lake.
In a village near the lake lived Chéng Língxiǎn,
a man of extraordinary and unrestrained character,
brave and skilled in archery.
He dreamed the giant clam transformed into a Daoist priest,
who told him:
"I am greatly oppressed by the giant clam of Lǚ Lake.
Tomorrow it will come again.
If you can help me,
I will richly repay you."
Língxiǎn then asked:
"How will I recognize you?"
The Daoist said:
"The one bound with a white silk ribbon is me."
Finding this strange,
the next day he and the village youths
made a clamor by the lakeside.
Soon after,
waves surged violently,
sounding like thunder.
They saw two bulls charging at each other;
one was greatly exhausted,
and its belly was all white.
Língxiǎn drew his bow and shot,
striking the latter clam.
Instantly, the water turned to blood,
and the clam disappeared without a trace.
The wounded clam then returned to Lǚ Lake
but died before reaching it.
Later, people named the place of its death Shèn Beach.
Lǚ Lake also gradually silted up from then on,
and now it is only about ten feet wide.
Over a year later,
Língxiǎn happened to be away
when a Daoist priest came to his mother asking for food.
After eating, he said:
"I have troubled you, mother, for a meal,
and have nothing with which to repay you.
Now that I am in such poverty here,
I shall find a good burial site for you."
He had the mother follow him up the mountain
and marked the spot with a white stone, saying:
"Burying here will bring sudden wealth."
Soon after, Língxiǎn returned.
His mother told him,
and Língxiǎn hurried to search for the man,
but found nothing at all.
He then moved the burial to that spot.
Later, when Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
Língxiǎn led over ten thousand troops from his commandery and hometown
to defend Xīn'ān.
He then followed Emperor Wǔ of the Chén dynasty to quell the rebels,
achieving many extraordinary feats.
In the army, he was called Chéng the Tiger.
When Emperor Wǔ of Chén received the abdication from the Liáng,
Língxiǎn, as a meritorious minister who assisted in the founding,
along with Zhōu Wényù and Hóu Āndū, was considered one of the Three Heroes,
like Xiāo Hé and Zhāng Liáng of the Hàn dynasty.
He later served as Governor of Dānyáng.
Note: Língxiǎn's residence was two lǐ east of the lake.
South of the residence was a paper mulberry tree,
several dozen arm-spans in girth.
The tree had a spirit,
and even today villagers often pray to it,
calling it the "Thousand-Year Tree" in their invocations.
His tomb is at the foot of Huángláo Mountain, northwest of the lake.
Chéng Hào, former Vice Director of the Ministry of Justice,
was his descendant.
From "Illustrated Gazetteer of Shèzhōu."
Wéi Dān
Wéi Dān, during the Táng Dynasty, served as the Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī.
Approaching forty years of age,
he had not yet passed the imperial examination in the Five Classics.
Once, riding a lame donkey,
he arrived at the Middle Bridge in Luòyáng.
There he saw a fisherman who had caught a giant softshell turtle,
several feet long,
which was placed on the bridge.
It was gasping and breathing its last,
on the verge of death in a short while.
A crowd gathered to watch,
and all wanted to buy it to cook.
Only Wéi Dān felt pity.
He asked how much it cost.
The fisherman said:
"I'll sell it for two thousand coins."
At that time, the weather was bitterly cold,
and Wéi Dān wore only a coarse robe and trousers.
He had nothing to pawn,
so he traded the inferior donkey he was riding for it.
Once he obtained the turtle,
he immediately released it into the water
and went away on foot.
At that time, there was a Mr. Húlú,
no one knew where he came from.
His behavior was eccentric and strange,
but his divinations were as if guided by spirits.
Several days later,
Wéi Dān went to ask about his fate.
Mr. Húlú hurried out to welcome him at the door,
and said happily to Wéi:
"I have been eagerly awaiting you for days.
Why have you come so late?"
Wéi said:
"I have come to pay my respects."
Mr. Húlú said:
"My friend, Prefect Yuán.
He speaks of your virtues incessantly,
and sincerely entrusted me to seek your acquaintance.
Let us go together now."
Wéi Dān thought for a long while,
knowing he had never heard of such an official or family.
Thus he said:
"Sir, you are mistaken.
I only ask you to determine my path out of destitution."
Húlú said:
"How could I know?
Your fortune and longevity
are not for me to know.
Lord Yuán is my teacher.
Go, and you will understand for yourself."
They walked together with canes to Tōnglì Ward.
In a quiet, secluded lane,
they saw a small gate.
Mr. Húlú knocked on it.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
someone answered the door and invited them in.
After several dozen steps,
they entered another plank gate.
After another ten or so steps,
they saw a main gate,
magnificent and splendid in construction,
comparable to the residences of dukes and marquises.
Several maidservants appeared,
all exceptionally beautiful,
who came out first to greet the guests.
The furnishings were fresh and splendid,
and a rare fragrance filled the room.
Soon, an old man appeared,
with white beard and eyebrows,
standing seven feet tall.
He wore a coarse fur robe and a leather belt,
and came out accompanied by two attendants in black.
He introduced himself:
"Yuán Jùnzhī."
He bowed first to Wéi Dān with full courtesy.
Wéi was startled
and hurriedly bowed in return, saying:
"I am but a poor and lowly scholar.
I never expected you, venerable sir, to show me such regard.
I do not understand."
The old man said:
"This old man's life, which was about to end,
was saved by you.
Such kindness and virtue
how could it ever be repaid?
A benevolent person certainly does not keep this in mind,
but the one who received the kindness thinks of sacrificing his life to repay it."
Wéi Dān then suddenly realized,
knowing it was the turtle.
But he never explicitly said it.
The old man then prepared a sumptuous feast,
and they lingered together the entire day.
When evening came,
Wéi prepared to take his leave and return.
The old man then took out from his bosom a document
and handed it to Wéi, saying:
"I know you wish to ask about your fate,
so I went to the celestial records office
and copied down your entire official career, salary, and future movements.
I offer this as a token of repayment.
All that you will have or lack,
is already your destined fate.
What is valuable is to know it in advance."
He also said to Mr. Húlú:
"I would be grateful if you could lend fifty thousand coins
to provide Wéi Jūn with a carriage for his journey.
He should decide to travel west early.
That is my wish."
Wéi bowed twice and departed.
The next day,
Mr. Húlú brought fifty strings of coins to the inn where Wéi stayed,
which Wéi relied on for relief.
The document stated in detail:
Next year in the fifth month, you will pass the imperial examination;
in a certain year, you will pass the selection exam and enter officialdom,
receiving the post of Wèiyáng County Magistrate;
the following year, you will enter the court,
serving as a certain official.
Thus, it listed seventeen official posts in succession,
each with specific year, month, and day.
Finally, in a certain year, you will be promoted to Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī,
rising to the position of Censor-in-Chief.
Three years after assuming that post,
when the honey locust tree in front of the office hall blooms,
you will be transferred north and return.
After that, it said nothing more.
Wéi always treasured and kept this document.
From passing the examination in the Five Classics onward,
up to becoming Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī,
every official appointment he received
matched the dates without any discrepancy.
In front of the office hall in Hóngzhōu,
there was a honey locust tree.
It had been there for many years.
Local custom held
that if this tree bloomed,
the local governor would face great worry.
In the eighth year of the Yuánhé era,
while Wéi was in office,
the tree suddenly bloomed one day.
Wéi then left his post
and died on the journey.
Initially, when Wéi met Prefect Yuán,
he found it quite strange.
Later, whenever he passed by the eastern road,
he would search for the old residence but could never find it.
He asked Mr. Húlú about it.
Mr. Húlú said:
"He is a divine dragon.
His transformations have no constant form.
How could you possibly find him?"
Wéi said:
"If that is so,
why did he suffer such hardship at the Middle Bridge?"
Húlú said:
"Hardship and adversity,
for ordinary people and sages alike,
and for divine dragons and crawling insects alike,
are all unavoidable at times.
How could they be any different?"
From "Records of Hédōng."
Xióng Shèn
During the Táng Dynasty, among the people of Yùzhāng, there was one named Xióng Shèn.
His father made a living by selling fish.
Once, while transporting fish, he spent the night on the riverbank.
He heard the sounds of hundreds and thousands reciting Buddhist sutras from inside the boat.
Startled, he went to investigate
and found it was the many fish in the boat.
Amazed, he took them all and released them,
and never again engaged in fishing.
Later, he sold firewood in Shítóu,
living in extreme poverty and hardship.
Once, he spent the night on the riverbank.
Suddenly, he saw a glow over a foot high in the sand.
He went to dig there
and obtained several catties of gold.
The next day,
he went to the market to sell it.
The market people said:
"This is what is called purple polished gold."
He was paid several hundred thousand strings of coins.
The Xióng family thus acquired great wealth and property,
and their descendants survive to this day.
From "Records of Retribution."
Wáng Xíngsī
In the false Shu state, in Qúyáng County near the mountains,
there was a wealthy man named Wáng Xíngsī.
He once kept a horse,
which he loved dearly.
He fed it hay and grain
twice as much as his other horses.
One day, he rode it to the commandery seat.
Encountering a sudden summer flood surge,
the boatman first ferried the horse across,
then returned with the boat to fetch Wáng.
Midstream,
wind arose and capsized the boat.
The horse, from the shore, rushed into the terrifying waves
to rescue its master.
In the vast expanse,
he was swiftly saved from drowning.
From "Jǐngjiè Lù".
Chén Hóngtài
In the false Shu state, among the commoners of Guǎngdū County was one Chén Hóngtài,
whose family was wealthy.
Once, someone borrowed ten thousand coins from him.
Hóngtài pressed for repayment urgently.
The man said:
"Please do not worry.
I have raised over ten thousand frogs.
Selling them
will be enough to repay you."
Tài, hearing this, was moved with pity.
He forgave the debt,
and additionally gave him another ten thousand coins,
ordering him to release all the frogs into the river.
Over a month later,
Tài was returning home at night,
when his horse startled and refused to advance.
Ahead, something gleamed brightly.
Looking at it,
it was a golden frog.
From "Jǐngjiè Lù".
Dù Bó
Dù Bó, named Héng,
served as a senior official of the Zhōu court.
King Xuān's concubine, named Nǚ Jiū,
wished to have relations with him,
but Dù Bó refused.
Nǚ Jiū accused him to King Xuān, saying:
"He secretly sought relations with me."
King Xuān believed her,
imprisoned Dù Bó at Jiāo,
and ordered Xuē Fǔ and Minister of Works Qí to kill Dù Bó.
His friend Zuǒ Rú remonstrated nine times, but the king would not listen.
After Dù Bó died,
he appeared to the king in human form, saying:
"What crime did Héng commit?"
The king summoned the invocator,
and told him what Dù Bó had said.
The invocator said:
"When you first killed Dù Bó,
who plotted it with you?"
The king said:
"Minister of Works Qí."
The invocator said:
"Why not kill Qí to appease him?"
King Xuān then killed Qí,
and had the invocator offer apologies.
Bó still appeared in human form and came,
stating his innocence.
The Minister of Works also appeared in human form and came, saying:
"What crime have I committed?"
King Xuān told Huángfǔ:
"The invocator advised me to kill people,
and those I killed all appear in human form to accuse me.
What should I do?"
Huángfǔ said:
"Kill the invocator to appease them,
that will do."
King Xuān then killed the invocator to appease them both,
but it was of no use.
They all appeared in human form and came.
The invocator also said:
"How was I to know?
Why make this a crime and kill me?"
Three years later,
King Xuān was hunting at Pǔtián,
with followers filling the wilderness.
At midday,
he saw Dù Bó riding a white horse in a plain carriage,
with Minister of Works Qí on the left,
and the invocator on the right.
A red-capped figure arose by the roadside,
holding a vermilion bow and red arrows.
He shot the king in the heart,
broke his spine,
and the king fell over his bow case and died.
From "Huán Yuān Jì".
Gōngsūn Shèng
King Fūchāi of Wú
killed his minister Gōngsūn Shèng without due crime.
Later, Yuè attacked Wú.
The king fled in defeat.
He said to Grand Steward Pǐ:
"I previously killed Gōngsūn Shèng
and threw his body below Xū Mountain.
Now our path passes by it.
Above, I fear the azure heavens;
below, I am ashamed before the earth.
I lift my feet but cannot advance;
my heart cannot bear to go.
You try calling out ahead.
If Shèng's spirit still remains,
there should be an answering voice."
Pǐ then ascended Yúháng Mountain,
and called out:
"Gōngsūn Shèng!"
Shèng immediately answered from above:
"Here."
Three calls were met with three answers.
The King of Wú was greatly terrified.
He looked up to heaven and sighed:
"Heaven above,
how can I, the solitary one, ever return!"
The King of Wú then died and did not return.
From "Huán Yuān Jì".
Yān Minister Zhuāng Zǐyí
was killed by Duke Jiǎn without crime.
Zǐyí said:
"If the dead have no awareness, so be it.
But if they do have awareness,
within three years,
I will make you, my lord, see it."
The following year,
Duke Jiǎn was about to perform sacrifices at Zǔzé.
Yān had its Zǔzé,
just as Sòng had its Sānglín—
the great state sacrifice,
attended by men and women.
Zǐyí arose by the roadside,
shouldered a vermilion staff and struck the duke.
The duke died in his carriage.
From "Huán Yuān Jì".
Yóu Dūn
Yóu Dūn,
courtesy name Yòuqí,
served as General of the Feather Forest Gentlemen in the Hàn dynasty.
He previously had a grudge against the Colonel Director of Retainers Hú Zhěn.
Zhěn then falsely accused Dūn and had him killed.
A little over a month after Dūn's death,
Zhěn fell ill.
His eyeballs then
(Thirteen characters below the character "suì" are supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy.)
fell out.
He only said, "I confess my crime.
Yóu Yòuqí is bringing ghosts here."
Then he died.
From "Huán Yuān Jì".
Wáng Hóng
Hàn's Wáng Hóng,
courtesy name Chángwén,
served as Governor of Fúfēng.
He and Minister over the Masses Wáng Yǔn were both killed by Lǐ Jué and others.
Hóng had long been at odds with Colonel Director of Retainers Hú Shēn.
Shēn took advantage of the imprisonment to settle the matter.
Hóng, facing death, sighed:
"Hú Shēn, you petty man,
do not delight in others' misfortune,
for misfortune will surely reach you."
Shēn later fell ill.
His head could not be lifted,
his eyes as if asleep.
He saw Hóng coming,
striking him with a large staff.
He died after several days.
From "Huán Yuān Jì".
Empress Sòng
Empress Sòng, consort of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
though lacking favor, occupied the principal position.
The favored beauties of the rear palace
collectively slandered and vilified her.
Earlier,
the Regular Palace Attendant Wáng Fǔ had unjustly executed Bóhǎi King Kuī and his consort;
the consort was the empress's paternal aunt.
Fearing the empress's future wrath,
Fǔ conspired with the Grand Master of the Palace Dàzhōng Dàfū Chéng Hé
to falsely accuse the empress of practicing heterodox arts and casting curses.
Emperor Líng believed them,
and confiscated the empress's seal and ribbons.
The empress went to the Bàoshì (Punishment Quarters) herself
and died of grief.
Her father and brothers were all executed.
All the regular attendants and eunuchs, large and small, stationed in the palace offices
pitted the Sòng clan, who were without fault.
Later, the emperor dreamed of Emperor Huán saying:
"What crime did Empress Sòng commit?
You listened to and employed wicked sycophants,
causing her life to be cut short.
Previously, Bóhǎi King Kuī
had already demoted himself,
yet he was also executed.
Now Empress Sòng and Kuī
have both brought their plaints before Heaven.
The Supreme Deity is enraged;
the crime is difficult to remedy."
The dream was exceptionally clear.
Upon waking, the emperor was frightened
and questioned the Left Commander of the Yǔlín Guards Xǔ Yǒng about the matter:
"What omen is this?
Can it be averted?"
Yǒng responded by describing the innocence of Empress Sòng and the Bóhǎi King,
and requested their reburial
to pacify their wronged spirits,
the return of the exiled Sòng family members,
and the restoration of the Bóhǎi fiefdom
to dispel the calamitous retribution.
The emperor did not act on this.
Not long after, he also passed away.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice"
Xú Guāng
Xú Guāng, in Wú,
often practiced magic arts in the markets and neighborhoods.
He would plant pear, orange, date, and chestnut trees,
and immediately have fruit to eat,
while the goods sold by market vendors
would all be depleted.
His predictions of floods and droughts were always very accurate.
Once, passing by the gate of the Great General Sūn Chēn,
he lifted his robes and hurried away,
spitting and stamping left and right.
When asked the reason,
he replied:
"The stench of flowing blood is unbearable."
Chēn, hearing of this, had him killed.
When his head was cut off, no blood flowed.
Later, when Chēn deposed the young emperor
and set up Emperor Jǐng instead,
and was about to pay respects at the imperial tombs,
upon boarding his carriage,
the carriage tipped over.
Then, looking back, he saw Xú Guāng on a pine and cypress tree,
leaning against it, pointing and gesturing,
mocking and laughing at him.
Chēn asked his attendants,
but none had seen it.
Chēn was disturbed by this.
Soon after, Emperor Jǐng had Chēn executed.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice"
Wáng Líng
As Sīmǎ Xuānwáng's (Sīmǎ Yì) achievements and influence grew daily,
and he executed the Wèi Great General Cáo Shuǎng,
signs of his intent to usurp became gradually apparent.
Wáng Líng was then the Governor of Yángzhōu.
Believing the Wèi emperor was controlled by powerful ministers
and unfit to be sovereign,
and that King Chǔ (Sīmǎ) Biāo was older and talented,
he planned to welcome and install him.
The Governor of Yǎnzhōu, Dǒng Mào,
reported Líng's secret plot to Xuānwáng.
Xuānwáng personally led the central army to campaign against Líng.
When the troops arrived,
Líng knew his situation was hopeless.
He went out to meet them alone in a small boat.
Xuānwáng then sent Líng back to the capital.
Reaching Xiàngchéng,
and passing by the side of Jiǎ Kuí's temple,
Líng cried out:
"Jiǎ Liángdào (Jiǎ Kuí),
I truly devoted my heart to Wèi's altars of state.
Only you, possessing divine awareness, know this."
Líng then drank poisoned wine and died.
His three sets of relatives were all executed.
That year,
Xuānwáng fell ill.
In broad daylight, he saw Kuí arrive,
accompanied by Líng, haunting him.
He then called out Líng's courtesy name:
"Yànyún, spare me!"
Xuānwáng's body also bore marks of beating.
He died shortly after.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice"
Xiàhóu Xuán
Xiàhóu Xuán of Wèi,
courtesy name Tàichū,
due to his contemporary talent and reputation,
was envied and killed by Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng (Sīmǎ Shī).
Xuán's clan held a sacrificial offering for him.
They saw Xuán come to the spirit seat,
remove his head and place it beside him,
gather all the fruit, meat, and food offerings to put into his head,
then reattach it to his neck and say:
"I have brought my plaint before the Supreme Deity.
Sīmǎ Zǐyuán (Sīmǎ Shī) will have no heir."
Soon after, Jǐngwáng passed away,
indeed leaving no son.
Wénwáng (Sīmǎ Zhāo) enfeoffed his second son, Yōu, as King of Qí
to succeed Jǐngwáng.
Yōu died.
Yōu's son Jiǒng succeeded to the position,
but was also killed.
During the Yǒngjiā Disturbance,
a shaman saw Xuānwáng (Sīmǎ Yì) weeping and saying:
"The downfall of our state
is precisely due to Cáo Shuǎng and Xiàhóu Xuán,
whose grievances were redressed."
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice"
Jīn Xuán
Emperor Míng of Jìn executed the strongman Jīn Xuán.
He said to the executioner:
"My neck has many sinews.
When you chop, make sure it severs immediately,
and I will repay you."
The executioner failed to pay heed.
He thus hacked several wounds
before Jīn Xuán died.
Later, people saw Jīn Xuán wearing a crimson cap and vermilion robes,
with a red bow and vermilion arrows,
shooting the executioner
and crying out:
"Jīn Xuán, spare me!"
The executioner died shortly after.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice"
Jīng Kuàng
Zhāng Cū and Jīng Kuàng, soldiers of Héjiān Principality,
were on friendly terms with each other.
On the fifth day of the fifth month in the fourteenth year of the Tàiyuán era of Jìn,
they climbed Zhōng Ridge together
and sat on the mountain peak.
Cū, drunk and out of his senses,
drew his sword and killed Kuàng.
Kuàng appeared in a dream to his mother,
saying he had been killed by Cū,
his corpse was in a ravine,
with his outer garment removed to cover his abdomen.
When searching for him,
it would certainly be hard to find,
but he would make the garment fly up at that spot.
The next morning, during the pursuit and arrest,
everything was as he had said.
Cū, knowing the affair was exposed,
planned to flee and rebel.
Upon leaving his door,
he saw Kuàng holding two swords,
thrusting towards his face,
and thus could not leave.
The mother then reported to the authorities,
and Cū was punished for his crime.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice"
Wàn Mò
Shí Mì, Magistrate of Shānyīn County in Jìn,
had previously served as a Censor
and falsely accused and had Jùróng Magistrate Wàn Mò executed.
Soon after, Mì saw Mò come to him in broad daylight
and kill him.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice"
Qū Jiǎn
In the first year of Zhāng Tiānxí of Former Liáng,
the Western Regions Commandant Zhāng Qí killed Qū Jiǎn.
Before his death, Jiǎn
