explicitly stated he would claim vengeance.
Later, Qí saw a white dog
and tried to strike it with his sword,
but missed.
Qí then fell to the ground and could not rise.
Those around him saw Jiǎn standing beside him,
and Qí suddenly died.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice"
The Court Musician
During the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
Lǐ Lóng and others committed robbery while traveling at night.
At that time, Táo Jìzhī of Dānyáng was the magistrate of Mòlíng County.
He ordered people to secretly search for and capture them,
and they subsequently apprehended Lǐ Lóng and his accomplices,
implicating a court musician in the process.
On the night the robbery occurred,
this musician had gone with companions to stay at someone's house,
where they performed music together.
Táo did not conduct a thorough investigation,
but instead forced a confession,
and submitted the case according to procedure.
However, the host where they stayed and the guests
all provided clear testimony in his favor.
Táo knew the musician was wrongfully implicated,
but because the documents had already been processed,
he did not want to personally intervene to rectify the matter.
Along with the ten robbers,
he had the musician executed at the commandery gate.
This musician was renowned for his talent and artistry,
and was exceptionally eloquent and intelligent.
On the day of his execution, he said:
"Although I am of lowly status,
since youth I have aspired to goodness,
never committed any wrongdoing,
and truly did not take part in the robbery.
Magistrate Táo should have known this fully,
yet I am wrongfully killed.
If there are no ghosts, then so be it.
But if ghosts exist, I will certainly appeal for justice."
He then played the pipa,
sang several songs, and went to his death.
Everyone knew of his wrongful death,
and none could hold back their tears.
After more than a month,
Táo dreamed that the musician came before him and said:
"I was wrongfully killed before,
and truly could not accept it.
I appealed to heaven and obtained justice,
so now I have come to take you."
He then leaped into Táo's mouth
and fell into his stomach.
Táo awoke in fright,
and soon collapsed,
his condition like madness.
After a long time, he regained consciousness.
The episodes recurred intermittently,
and when they struck, his body would contort violently,
his head bending backward until it touched his back.
He died after four days.
After his death, his family fell into poverty and decline.
His two sons died early,
and he had one remaining grandson
who became destitute and homeless.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice."
Dèng Wǎn
In the first year of the Tàishǐ era of the Sòng dynasty,
Dèng Wǎn, the governor of Jiāngzhōu,
installed Prince Zǐxūn of Jìn'ān, the regional inspector, as emperor,
and rebelled.
Earlier, Zhāng Yuè, the governor of Nánjùn, had been found guilty of an offense
and was being escorted under guard back to Yángdū.
When they reached Pénkǒu,
Dèng Wǎn pardoned him
and appointed him as General of the Champion,
entrusting him with military affairs.
After Yuán Yǐ was defeated,
Zhāng Yuè, fearing execution,
feigned a sudden illness
and set up hidden soldiers to summon Dèng Wǎn.
When Dèng Wǎn arrived,
Zhāng Yuè said to him:
"You initiated this disaster,
and now the situation is critical.
What plan do you propose?"
Dèng Wǎn replied:
"Execute Prince of Jìn'ān and await the imperial army;
perhaps we can avoid punishment."
Zhāng Yuè angrily said:
"You started this disaster,
and now you wish to sell out the young emperor to absolve your guilt?"
He ordered Dèng Wǎn beheaded before his bed,
and also killed his son,
then surrendered with Dèng Wǎn's head.
By the fifth year,
Zhāng Yuè lay ill,
and saw Dèng Wǎn appear as a vengeful ghost.
He then died.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice."
Kǒng Jī
Kǒng Jī of Kuàijī was diligent in his studies and possessed strong principles.
His clansman Kǒng Chǎng sent his two sons to study under Kǒng Jī as their teacher.
However, Kǒng Chǎng's sons were both vicious and cruel,
inclined toward wrongdoing.
Kǒng Jī repeatedly spoke to Kǒng Chǎng about this,
and the sons often harbored resentment toward him.
Kǒng Chǎng soon passed away,
and after the mourning period ended,
Kǒng Jī, as an old acquaintance,
took sheep and wine to visit the two sons.
The two sons still held a grudge from the past,
and secretly sent a servant to kill Kǒng Jī by the roadside.
Before the servant could return,
they saw Kǒng Jī approaching,
his eyes wide and sleeves rolled up,
shouting angrily:
"Treacherous, vile little wretches,
human-faced but beast-hearted!
I, in consideration of our past ties,
and upholding old
The "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín" volume 91 writes "old" as "restrain,"
and the Dunhuáng manuscript of "Records of Retribution for Injustice" also writes "restrain."
relations all my life—
what grievance or hatred have I caused you,
that you would ambush me on the road to kill me?
You defy heaven and forget your father;
neither men nor spirits will tolerate you.
I will see to it that your family line is cut off."
From then on,
he appeared to the Kǒng family for several days.
Not long after,
the elder son went to the toilet
and suddenly collapsed.
When people rushed to check on him,
he was already dead on the ground.
The younger son soon also died of a malignant ulcer,
ultimately leaving the brothers without descendants.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice."
Dámó Chàn
During the time of Jǔqú Méngxùn,
there was a Buddhist monk named Dámó Chàn,
who was knowledgeable and well-informed.
He was trusted and respected by Jǔqú Méngxùn.
The Wèi state sent Lǐ Shùn to confer the title of King of Liáng on Jǔqú Méngxùn,
and then sought Dámó Chàn.
Jǔqú Méngxùn, fearing to lose him, refused to give him up.
Dámó Chàn wished to go to Wèi,
and repeatedly requested permission from Jǔqú Méngxùn to leave.
Jǔqú Méngxùn, in anger, had him killed.
Afterward, attendants saw in broad daylight
Dámó Chàn striking Jǔqú Méngxùn with a sword,
and Jǔqú Méngxùn subsequently fell ill and died.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice."
Zhī Fǎcún
Zhī Fǎcún
was originally from a foreign tribe,
but grew up in Guǎngzhōu.
He excelled in medical arts,
and thus became extremely wealthy.
He owned a felt carpet eight or nine feet in size,
decorated with a hundred kinds of patterns,
radiant and dazzling to the eye.
He also had an eight-foot sandalwood bed,
which was always fragrant.
Wáng Tán served as the governor of Guǎngzhōu.
His eldest son, Shào Zhī,
repeatedly sought these two items,
but Zhī Fǎcún refused to give them.
Wáng then accused Zhī Fǎcún of arrogance and extravagance,
had him killed, and confiscated his family's wealth.
After his death,
his form appeared within the governor's residence,
where he would beat the drum beneath the tower,
as if crying out injustice.
This continued for a month.
Wáng soon fell ill,
constantly seeing Zhī Fǎcún watching over him,
and died shortly after.
As for Shào Zhī, by the time he reached Yángdū,
he also died.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice."
Zhāng Chāo
Zhāng Chāo from Jīnxiāng County, Gāopíng,
had previously been at odds with Zhái Yuàn from the same county.
During the Yuánjiā era of the Song dynasty,
Zhái Yuàn served as the magistrate of Fāngyú.
Suddenly, he was killed by someone.
Everyone suspected it was Zhāng Chāo.
Later, Zhāng Chāo was appointed as the magistrate of Jīnxiāng County.
After leaving his post and returning home,
he went into the mountains to cut timber.
Zhái Yuàn’s nephew, Tóngwū,
carrying a bow and arrows,
and bringing wine and gifts,
went into the mountains to present them to him.
After they had finished drinking,
Tóngwū said:
“Your Honor killed my uncle in the past,
and there is no way we can coexist under the same sky.”
He then drew his bow and shot him,
and Zhāng Chāo died.
That night, Tóngwū saw Zhāng Chāo in a vision, saying:
“I did not kill your uncle,
yet I was wrongfully murdered.
I have now appealed to the heavens,
and have come to take revenge.”
He then drew a knife and stabbed him,
and Tóngwū vomited blood and died.
From “Records of Retribution.”
Yuán Càn’s Youngest Son
When Qí Gāozǔ intended to usurp the throne,
Yuán Càn, the Minister of Works of the Song dynasty, raised troops in opposition
and was killed.
His youngest son
was secretly taken by his wet nurse to Dí Lìngqìng, a disciple of Yuán Càn.
Lìngqìng killed the child.
A year later,
he suddenly saw the child riding a dog and playing as usual.
Later, another dog
entered Lìngqìng’s home.
Upon encountering Lìngqìng,
it bit him to death.
His wife and children also died at the jaws of the dog.
From “Records of Ancient and Modern Times.”
Yǔ Hóng’s Slave
Yǔ Hóng served as an aide to the Prince of Jìnglíng,
and his family lived in Jiānglíng.
Yǔ Hóng ordered his slave, Wúhuàn,
to transport rice to his family.
Before traveling three li,
he encountered robbers and was killed.
His body drifted and washed ashore at Chákǒu Village.
At that time, a man named Wén Xīn lived by the shore.
His mother was ill.
A doctor said:
“You must obtain powdered skull bone for her to take,
and she will recover.”
Xīn offered a heavy reward to seek it.
A neighboring woman, Yáng shì, saw Wúhuàn’s corpse,
and cut off the head to give to Xīn.
Xīn burned it,
intending to remove the flesh,
but after three days and nights, it still would not char,
and the corners of its eyes opened and turned.
Although Xīn found it strange,
he still could not bear to discard it.
He then scraped the bones of the ears and cheeks,
and gave them to his mother to take.
She immediately felt the bones stuck in her throat,
and died after seven days.
Soon after, Yáng shì fell ill,
her entire body swelling greatly,
her appearance resembling that of an ox or horse.
She saw Wúhuàn’s head come and curse her:
“Can you escape the retribution for good and evil?”
Yáng shì told her son about this,
and as soon as she finished speaking, she died.
From “Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds.”
Wèi Huījùn
Zhāng Shàn, the governor of Yángdí in the Northern Qí dynasty,
was harsh, cruel, greedy, and rapacious,
and his evil reputation spread far and wide.
The imperial censorate dispatched the censor Wèi Huījùn
to the commandery to investigate him.
The evidence of bribery and corruption was in disarray,
and the crime warranted the death penalty.
While in prison, Zhāng Shàn
had someone secretly appeal,
falsely accusing Huījùn of accepting bribes from the people,
and wrongfully being subjected to investigation and imprisonment.
Emperor Wénxuān was furious,
believing that the judicial authorities had acted unjustly,
and insisted on a thorough investigation.
He ordered the Minister of Works, Left Assistant Lú Fěi, to reexamine the case.
Fěi then followed the emperor’s implied wishes,
fabricated Huījùn’s guilt,
and reported it.
Huījùn was executed in the prefecture.
Before his death, Huījùn told the clerk:
“The truth of my situation,
you have witnessed.
Today’s events,
may they be repeated.
Prepare one hundred sheets of paper,
two brushes,
and one inkstick,
to accompany my corpse.
If there are divine spirits,
I will surely seek retribution against Lú.”
The clerk mourned him,
arranged his burial,
and prepared the paper and brushes.
Fifteen days later,
Zhāng Shàn fell ill,
repeatedly saying “I kowtow,”
and died within ten days.
Just two months later,
Lú Fěi was accused of mocking and refuting the Wèi envoy,
and was reported by Wèi Shōu.
Emperor Wénxuān had him poisoned to death.
From “Records of Retribution.”
Zhēn Zǐróng
During the Northern Qí dynasty, he once served as the tax collector of Jǐngxíng Pass,
and his corrupt gains were extensive,
leading to his exposure.
The Qí ruler intended to enforce the law,
aiming for a thorough investigation.
He entrusted the case to Cuī Fǎyuàn, the city garrison officer of Bìngzhōu,
and Cài Huī, the Secretariat Drafter,
to jointly interrogate him.
However, Zǐróng’s crimes were all committed before the amnesty,
but Fǎyuàn and others, observing the emperor’s intentions,
suppressed this and treated them as post-amnesty crimes.
At the moment of his execution,
Zǐróng voiced endless grievances.
Seeing that he could not obtain justice,
he said:
“If such people act with fairness and integrity,
then there is no heavenly justice.”
Fifteen days later,
Fǎyuàn died of a sudden illness.
About a year later,
Cài Huī fell ill,
his flesh rotting and falling off completely,
his suffering increasing daily,
until he finally died.
From “Records of Retribution.”
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, Xiāo Yǎn, killed the Southern Qí ruler, the Marquis of Dōnghūn,
to seize his throne,
and executed many people.
On the day the Marquis of Dōnghūn died,
Hóu Jǐng was born.
Later, Hóu Jǐng rebelled against the Liáng dynasty,
captured Jiànyè,
Emperor Wǔ was imprisoned and starved to death,
Emperor Jiǎnwén was imprisoned and crushed to death,
and the Liáng imperial clan was nearly exterminated,
leaving almost no survivors.
People at the time said that Hóu Jǐng was the reincarnation of the Marquis of Dōnghūn.
From “Records of Court and Country.”
Zhāng Bì
In Xiàpī, there was a man named Zhāng Bì,
who came from a distinguished family lineage,
though its later generations had declined.
He had a granddaughter
of exceptional beauty.
A neighbor wished to take her as a concubine,
but Bì, considering her the descendant of an old, noble family, refused.
The neighbor grew furious,
and set fire to Bì's house,
causing Bì to burn to death.
His son, Bāng,
was away traveling at the time.
When he returned later,
he learned the full circumstances,
but fearing the neighbor's power
and coveting his wealth, he remained silent
and even married his daughter to him.
A year later,
Bāng dreamed of Bì, who said:
"You, as a son,
have acted against Heaven, showing no filial piety.
You abandoned your kin and sided with your enemy,
secretly aligning with the wicked."
He then seized Bāng's head
and stabbed him with a peach-wood staff in his hand.
Bāng fell ill for two nights
and died vomiting blood.
On the day Bāng died,
the neighbor also saw Bì push open the door and stride straight in.
Widening his eyes and rolling up his sleeves, Bì said:
"You relied on your power to commit evil,
acting with extreme cruelty and tyranny,
and wrongfully caused my death.
I have already appealed to the higher authorities,
and the matter has been redressed.
In a few days,
you will know the outcome."
The neighbor fell ill
and soon died as well.
From "Records of Redressed Injustices"
Yáng Dàoshēng
Yáng Dàoshēng of Tàishān in Liáng
served as a Military Consultant for Prince Shàolíng.
His elder brother, Hǎizhēn,
was the Governor of Zhà Prefecture.
Dàoshēng requested leave to visit him.
At their parting,
his brother prepared a farewell feast by the roadside
to see Dàoshēng off.
Dàoshēng saw a man tied to a tree.
Approaching to look,
he recognized him as a former retainer from his own unit.
Seeing Dàoshēng, the man wept and pleaded pitifully, saying:
"The Governor of Zhà intends to have me executed.
I beg you to save me."
Dàoshēng asked:
"What is your crime?"
He replied:
"I was discontent and fled, becoming a deserter."
Dàoshēng then said:
"This is most infuriating."
He immediately dismounted,
used his dagger to gouge out the man's eyes, and swallowed them.
The retainer cried out to heaven and wailed bitterly.
Soon after, Hǎizhēn arrived.
Dàoshēng also urged his brother to execute the man by beheading.
After a long while,
Dàoshēng suddenly felt the eyes stuck in his throat,
unable to go down.
He called for wine to wash them down,
gulping down several cups in a row,
but they still would not go away.
He began to feel increasingly bloated and obstructed,
and thus, unable to swallow them, he bid farewell.
He died a few days later on the road.
At the time, everyone believed it was the work of Heaven's justice.
From "Records of Redressed Injustices"
Monastery Monk Yuè
Zhāng Gāo, Governor of Eastern Xú Prefecture in Liáng,
was the grandson of the Minister Yǒng.
He had once been defeated and fled north,
where a local commoner
made a pledge with Gāo
to help him return south.
The commoner subsequently left home to become a monk,
taking the Dharma name Sēng Yuè,
and Gāo provided for him.
When Gāo was in Eastern Xú,
Sēng Yuè followed him to his post.
Relying on his past merit and long association,
he often offended Gāo with his words.
Gāo grew angry
and sent two of his students
to go and kill him at night.
Afterward, Gāo suddenly dreamed of Sēng Yuè,
who said:
"I have come to seek vengeance."
Soon after, while out practicing archery,
the nock of an arrow injured his finger,
drawing just a little blood.
He did not consider it serious.
Later, while cutting a pear,
pear juice soaked the wound,
causing it to fester.
After about ten days,
a sore inexplicably appeared on his arm,
with pus and blood connecting to the finger.
He died a little over a month later.
From "Records of Redressed Injustices"
A Gentleman of Jiānglíng
When Jiānglíng fell,
there was a man from within the Pass named Liáng Yuánhuī
who captured a gentleman,
surnamed Liú.
This man had previously suffered the chaos of Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
losing all his family members.
Only his young son remained,
just a few years old.
He carried the child on his back himself.
They encountered snowy, muddy conditions,
and could not advance.
Liáng Yuánhuī, who was supervising the captives entering the Pass,
forced him to abandon the child.
Liú, who cherished the boy deeply,
pleaded desperately, willing to die instead.
Yuánhuī forcibly seized the child
and threw him into the snow.
Rods and whips fell upon Liú,
driving him onward.
Liú kept looking back step by step,
his cries and wails heart-rending.
Exhausted from hardship and suddenly collapsing,
coupled with profound grief,
he died a few days later.
After his death,
Yuánhuī began to see Liú daily, reaching out his hands, demanding his son back.
Because of this, he fell ill.
Though he repeatedly repented and apologized,
the apparition did not cease.
Yuánhuī, ill, managed to return home but then died.
From "Records of Redressed Injustices"
Xú Tiějiù
In Dōnghǎi, there was a man named Xú Jiǎ.
His former wife, Madame Xǔ,
bore him a son,
named Tiě Jiù.
After Madame Xǔ passed away,
Xú Jiǎ remarried a woman named Chén.
She was extremely cruel and vicious,
and wished to kill the son from the previous wife.
Chén gave birth to a son,
and upon his birth, she prayed over him, saying:
"If you do not eliminate Tiě Jiù,
you are not my son."
Therefore, she named him Tiě Chǔ,
intending for him to pound the mortar (Tiě Jiù).
From then on, she beat Tiě Jiù,
subjecting him to all kinds of cruel suffering.
When he was hungry, she gave him no food;
when he was cold, she added no padding to his clothes.
Xú Jiǎ was weak-witted and timid,
and often was not at home.
Thus, his wife was able to carry out her cruel abuse as she pleased.
Tiě Jiù eventually suffered so severely from cold and starvation
and was beaten to death,
at the age of sixteen.
More than ten days after his death,
his ghost suddenly returned home.
Climbing onto Chén's bed, he said:
"I am Tiě Jiù.
I was truly innocent,
yet I was unjustly and brutally killed.
My mother has appealed to Heaven for justice,
and I have received a mandate from the celestial court,
to avenge my wrongs.
I will cause Tiě Chǔ to fall ill,
suffering the same hardships I endured.
The time for him to be taken away is set.
I will stay here now and wait for it."
His voice was as it was in life.
The family could not see his form,
but they all heard his words.
He often resided on the roof beams of the house.
Chén knelt and begged for forgiveness,
frequently making offerings to appease him.
The ghost said:
"There is no need for this.
You starved me to death—
how could a single meal repay that?"
Chén secretly spoke ill of him at night,
and the ghost responded, saying:
"Why do you speak against me?
Now I will cut your roof beam."
Immediately, the sound of sawing was heard,
and wood chips fell.
There was a loud cracking noise,
as if the beam had truly collapsed.
The whole family rushed out,
lit candles to inspect it,
but found nothing amiss.
He also cursed Tiě Chǔ, saying:
"You killed me—
do you think you can sit comfortably in this house and enjoy yourself?
I will burn your house down."
Immediately, flames appeared,
smoke billowed, and the fire blazed fiercely,
leaving the inside and outside in disarray.
But after a short while, the fire extinguished itself,
and the thatched roof remained intact,
with no visible damage.
Day after day, he cursed and reviled them,
and sometimes he also sang.
The song went:
"Peach and plum blossoms,
how can they withstand the harsh frost?
Peach and plum fruits,
the harsh frost falls early and destroys them."
His voice was deeply sorrowful and mournful,
as if lamenting his own inability to grow to adulthood.
At that time, Tiě Chǔ was six years old.
When the ghost arrived,
he fell ill, with body pain and a swollen belly,
and difficulty breathing that hindered his eating.
The ghost repeatedly beat him,
leaving bruises where he struck.
After a little over a month, Tiě Chǔ died,
and the ghost then fell silent.
From "Records of Redressed Injustices"
Xiāo Xù
Liáng Lúlíng Prince Xiāo Xù
served as the Governor of Jīngzhōu.
At that time, there was a Wǔníng Commandery Administrator named Zhāng Yánkāng,
who was very skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and was widely admired.
When his term ended and he was about to return
, the Prince invited him to stay
(The characters "invited him to stay" are supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy.)
for an event.
Yánkāng, eager for advancement,
declined and refused to stay.
The Prince then sought out crimes Yánkāng had committed during his tenure as Administrator,
had him imprisoned,
and sent a messenger to report and petition,
hoping the court would authorize the execution to be carried out in the province.
The Liáng Emperor had long known Yánkāng,
and moreover suspected the Prince's report was untrue,
so he ordered Yánkāng sent to the capital.
The Prince, already harboring resentment,
and fearing Yánkāng would appeal and clear his name,
leading to himself being punished instead,
before the imperial order was announced,
had a jailer persuade Yánkāng, saying:
"I hear the Prince intends to have you killed.
Why don't you escape and return to the capital to plead your case?
If you can leave,
I will facilitate it for you."
Yánkāng agreed,
and fled that night.
The Prince dispatched patrol troops to set an ambush,
and assassinated Yánkāng beneath the city wall,
then reported that he had broken out of prison and died resisting arrest.
There was also a Zhījiāng County Magistrate, a certain Wú,
who was about to return to Yángzhōu,
was also invited by the Prince to stay,
and likewise refused.
The Prince then had him attacked and killed on the road,
along with his entire family of several dozen members,
all drowned.
Several years later, the Prince fell ill.
Day and night, he constantly saw the figures of Zhāng and Wú.
The Prince could only say:
"Spare me, spare me."
Shortly after, he died.
From "Records of Redressed Injustices"
Yuè Gàiqīng
When the Prince of Lúlíng was in Jīngzhōu,
he once dispatched officials to survey and register civilian land.
A man from Nányáng named Yuè Gàiqīng
was also assigned as one of these envoys.
The Prince's mansion attendant, Wéi Pòlǔ,
issued the instructions and orders,
but they deviated from the Prince's original intent.
When Gàiqīng returned,
he was charged with several errors and found guilty.
Pòlǔ was terrified and anxious,
and dared not admit his fault.
Instead, he deceived Gàiqīng, saying:
"I will personally clear your name,
there is no need for you to appeal."
Within a few days,
Gàiqīng was executed in the marketplace.
Gàiqīng cried out in protest,
but had no way to present his case.
He only asked people to place paper and brush in his coffin.
A few days after his death,
Pòlǔ was by the trough looking after the oxen,
when he suddenly saw Gàiqīng, carrying his own head, enter.
He held out a bowl of minced garlic paste and gave it to him.
Pòlǔ cried out in alarm and tried to flee,
but in the end had to consume it.
He then fell ill,
and died not long after.
From "Records of Redressed Injustices"
Kāng Jìsūn Kāng Jìsūn had a nature fond of killing.
Hunting and fishing for delicacies were his constant pursuits.
If slaves or servants committed faults,
he might also put them to death.
Once, he fell gravely ill.
He dreamed that a person said to him:
"If you can cease killing,
this illness will improve.
If not, you will certainly die."
Right there in the dream,
he vowed to kill no more.
He woke with a start, trembling with fear,
drenched in sweat,
and his illness gradually recovered.
Several years later,
three of his students secretly ran off with two of his concubines.
He pursued and caught them,
and immediately beat them all to death.
That night,
he again dreamed of the previous person coming to him, saying:
"Why have you broken your pledge?
Their crime did not warrant death.
A private individual has no right to kill arbitrarily.
Now, even if you repent, it is of no avail."
By dawn, he was vomiting blood,
and died a few days later.
From "Records of Redressed Injustices"
Zhāng Xuàn
Chén Bàxiān initially established the ninth son of Emperor Yuán of Liáng, Prince Jìn'ān, as ruler,
and supported and upheld him.
Yú Shè of Kuàijī, who had served as a Palace Secretary and Vice Director of the Right in the Department of State Affairs during the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
at that time dreamed that Emperor Wǔ of Liáng said to Shè:
"You are my former attendant;
you may tell Lord Chén
that usurpation and murder will bring him no benefit."
The matter was very clear,
but as Shè had not yet seen any signs of usurpation or murder,
he dared not speak of it.
After several days,
he had the same dream again,
and [the emperor] also said to Shè:
"If you do not convey my message,
you too will fare poorly."
Though Shè sighed in distress,
he absolutely had no reason to speak.
A short time later,
the Grand Astrologer reported:
"There are urgent troops in the palace."
Bàxiān said:
"The urgent troops are precisely me."
Hastily, he dispatched disorderly soldiers to harm the young ruler and established himself.
Afterward, Shè fell ill,
and again dreamed of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng saying:
"You did not speak for me,
causing disaster to befall;
you and Lord Chén
will soon know."
Only then did Shè seal a report explaining the reason for the dream.
Lord Chén, as a person,
greatly believed in ghosts and spirits;
hearing this, he was greatly alarmed,
sent a carriage to fetch Shè,
and personally inquired and visited him,
then reproached Shè, saying:
"Why did you not speak of this strange matter?"
Six or seven days later, Shè died,
and soon after, the affair of Wéi Dài occurred.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice"
Wéi Dài
After Emperor Wǔ of Chén, Bàxiān, had killed Wáng Sēngbiàn, the Grand Minister of Works of Liáng,
he proceeded to subdue the various generals.
Wéi Dài, the Grand Administrator of Yìxīng,
was the fourth son of Wéi Fàng, a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate,
and staunchly defended [the city] for Lord Wáng.
Lord Chén repeatedly sent troops to attack and besiege it,
but could not capture it.
Later, he heavily levied troops against it,
and persuaded Dài, saying:
"Lord Wáng's close partisans
have all been annihilated;
what hope does this solitary city have?
Why persist in resisting?
If you can surrender,
you will not lose wealth and honor."
Dài said:
"A gentleman feels gratitude to one who understands him;
I originally resisted the great army for Lord Wáng,
thus becoming your enemy.
Now I also acknowledge that you, Illustrious Lord, have fully pacified the region east of the Yangtze;
this impoverished city defending itself
surely has no path to survival.
But blades have clashed repeatedly,
and the killing and wounding have been excessive;
the soldiers are resentful and angry,
and I fear I will not be spared.
My aged mother is at home,
and I greatly fear disaster will reach her;
this is why I have prolonged my days,
and have not yet laid down my arms.
If there is a sworn covenant,
I dare not long trouble your divine might."
Then [Chén] sent someone to execute a white horse to swear an alliance,
and Dài opened the gates.
Lord Chén also showed leniency and trust, returning to Yángdū.
Later, when Lord Chén ascended the throne,
he sent Dài to follow on a campaign;
due to a slight delay,
he used an old grudge to behead him.
Soon after, while conducting affairs in the great hall,
he saw Dài coming,
and fled in alarm into the inner quarters.
Moving his seat to the Guāngyán Hall,
Dài again pursued him inside;
looking around and asking his attendants,
none of them saw anything.
Because of this, he fell ill and died.
From "Records of Retribution for Injustice"
Sui Commoner Yǒng
When Yuándé, the Crown Prince of Suí Emperor Yáng, lay ill in bed,
the emperor sent the ghost-seer Cuī Shànyǐng to check for hauntings.
Shànyǐng had been blind since childhood,
yet said he saw Commoner Yǒng,
glaring and rolling up his sleeves,
shouting loudly:
"I will not let you go!"
Shànyǐng described Yǒng's appearance in detail,
as if they were old acquaintances.
From "Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma"
Jīngzhào Prison Guard
During the Dàyè era of Suí Emperor Yáng,
a Jīngzhào prison guard, whose name is lost,
was cruel and brutal to the prisoners,
and the prisoners could not endure the suffering,
yet the guard took it as amusement.
Later, he fathered a son
whose chin and shoulders
seemed to have a fleshy cangue,
with no neck;
he could not walk for several years and then died.
From "Extended Records of the Five Phases Through the Ages"
A Man from Qióng
During the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty,
a man from Qióng surnamed Wéi
made a promise with a woman,
vowing not to betray each other.
After years, his favor waned,
and the woman harbored resentment and hatred.
Wéi, fearing she would turn against him,
strangled her to death.
Several days later,
Wéi felt itchy all over his body,
and subsequently developed leprous sores and died.
From "Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma"
Dù Tōngdá
Dù Tōngdá, a man from Gāoyuàn in Qízhōu during the Táng dynasty,
in the Zhēnguàn years,
received a county order to escort a monk northward.
(The phrase "received a county order" is recorded in the Ming manuscript as "often had a monk seeking lodging at night.")
Tōngdá saw the monk's sutra box,
and thinking it contained silk and satin inside,
plotted with his wife
to strike and kill the monk.
Before the monk died,
he recited two or three sentences of a mantra,
and then a fly flew into [Tōngdá's] nose,
remaining stuck inside for a long time without coming out.
Tōngdá's eyes and nose suddenly became distorted,
his eyebrows and hair fell out,
he became confused and lost his way,
and his spirit was dejected.
Not long after,
he contracted a severe illness,
and died within a year.
At the moment of his death,
the fly finally flew out
and entered his wife's nose;
his wife fell ill
and died a little over a year later.
From "Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma"
Xíng Wénzōng
During the Tang Dynasty, there was a man named Xíng Wénzōng from Héjiān,
whose home bordered Yōuyān.
He was by nature crude and ruthless.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
he suddenly contracted a severe wind illness.
Within ten days,
his eyebrows and sideburns all fell out.
Afterwards, he went to a temple to repent.
He confessed:
"Recently, while traveling towards Yōuzhōu,
I met a traveler on the road
carrying over ten bolts of silk.
The marshland was deserted,
so I robbed and killed him.
That man said:
'I am heading to Fángzhōu
to buy scripture paper.'"
But he could not escape death.
A short while later,
an old monk who also intended to travel south
encountered Wénzōng.
Fearing the matter would be exposed,
Wénzōng raised his knife to strike the monk.
The monk kowtowed and said:
"I beg you to spare my life.
I vow never to speak of this for the rest of my life."
Wénzōng killed him
and discarded his body in the grass.
More than twenty days later,
while returning from his journey,
Wénzōng passed the place where the monk had died.
It was the hot summer season,
and he suspected the corpse would have rotted.
He went to look,
but the body appeared as if still alive.
Wénzōng then used his horsewhip to prod the monk's mouth.
A fly emerged from the mouth,
buzzing clearly,
and flew straight into Wénzōng's nose.
It remained trapped inside for a long time,
causing him to fall gravely ill.
He died a little over a year later.
Zhǎngsūn Wújì
Duke Zhào of the Tang, Zhǎngsūn Wújì, memorialized that separate imperial decrees for permanent exile
should be established as a permanent precedent.
Later, when Duke Zhào himself committed an offense,
an imperial decree exiled him permanently to Lǐngnán.
He never returned until his death.
This illustrates the flaw in establishing such a law.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Lóu Shīdé
Lóu Shīdé served as Military Commissioner of Héyuán while holding the position of Diànzhōng.
During the Táng Yǒnghé era,
he defeated the Tǔbō at Báiyángjiàn,
achieving eight pursuits and seven victories.
An imperial decree praised and honored him,
appointing him as Left Xiāoqí
(Míngchāo edition notes "qí" as "wèi")
Gentleman-of-the-Household.
Emperor Gāozōng's handwritten edict stated:
"You possess both civil and military talents,
therefore I confer upon you a military post.
Do not decline."
He was repeatedly promoted until he became Nàyán.
Several days before his death,
he was restless, unable to sleep or rise peacefully.
For no reason, he cried out in alarm:
"Who is patting my back?"
His attendant said:
"I see nothing."
Then he spoke alone,
as if arguing with someone,
saying:
"My lifespan should be eighty years.
Why are you pursuing me now?"
He then confessed that as an official he had mistakenly killed two people,
reducing his life by ten years.
His tone seemed as if submitting to a judgment.
Soon after, he breathed his last.
Even with Lóu's clarity and forbearance,
he still could not avoid excess.
Should not those in governance be cautious!
From "Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ"
Wáng Tiàn
Wáng Tiàn, Governor of Jìzhōu in the Tang Dynasty,
was of a cruel and violent nature.
Once, an imperial envoy arrived in the prefecture.
While Tiàn was speaking with the envoy,
Lìn Jiǎng, the County Lieutenant of Wǔqiáng, said:
"The sun has passed.
Move to the shade."
Tiàn became enraged
and ordered the prison warden to beat him.
Jiǎng's neck bone broke and he died.
The next day,
the prison warden sat on the threshold of the prefectural gate with his legs dangling.
The gate leaves suddenly opened by themselves
and struck both his shins, breaking them.
Tiàn fell ill
and saw Jiǎng coming.
He rose
and offered him wine and food, begging for mercy,
but Jiǎng refused.
Tiàn, disgusted,
turned his face toward the beam.
Jiǎng was on the roof beam.
Tiàn died within ten days.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Jiāng Róng
Jiāng Róng, a Left Commissioner of the Tang,
was upright and honest.
When Xú Jìngyè rebelled in Yángzhōu,
Jiāng was falsely implicated.
The cruel official Zhōu Xīng and others wrongfully accused and had him executed,
beheaded in front of the Dūtíng Post Station in the Eastern Capital.
As Jiāng was about to be executed,
he requested an audience to present his case.
Xīng said:
"How can a prisoner present a case?"
Jiāng angrily rebuked him:
"I am innocent and being wrongfully killed.
I will not let you go even in death."
He was then beheaded.
His corpse suddenly leapt up,
staggered more than ten steps,
and was kicked down by the executioner.
It sat up again.
This happened three times
before it finally ceased.
Even though his head was severed,
he seemed unceasing in his wrath.
Not long after, Zhōu Xīng died.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Lǐ Zhāodé
Lǐ Zhāodé, Vice Minister of the Fènggé Pavilion in the Tang Dynasty,
wielded power and authority himself.
He promulgated an edict stating:
"From now on,
for public offenses, penal servitude;
for private offenses, exile.
If one does not confess within a hundred days of an amnesty,
punishment shall be meted out according to the law."
Zhāodé had previously accepted bribes from Sūn Wànróng
and recommended him for a third-rank position.
Later, Wànróng occupied Yíngzhōu and rebelled.
The bribery affair was exposed.
Although he repeatedly received amnesties,
because he did not confess within a hundred days,
he was sentenced to strangulation based on the value of the bribes.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Gōng Sìyè
Gōng Sìyè, the Simā of Luòzhōu in the Tang Dynasty, and Zhāng Sìmíng, the Magistrate of Luòyáng,
had a large cangue made,
six feet long,
four feet wide,
and five inches thick.
When placed in front,
no one dared to offend.
Later, Sìmíng and Sìyè
provided funds to send the rebel Xú Zhēn north to join the Tūjué.
When the plot failed,
Sìyè and others were made to wear this cangue themselves.
The common people rejoiced at this.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Zhōu Xīng
During the Tang Dynasty, the Vice Minister of Justice, Zhōu Xīng,
was jointly handling cases with Lái Jùnchén.
Jùnchén had separately received
(The original text has "奏" for "奉",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
an imperial order to interrogate Xīng,
but Xīng was unaware of this.
While dining together,
Jùnchén said to Xīng:
"Prisoners often refuse to confess,
what method should be used?"
Xīng replied:
"It's very easy.
Take a large vat,
surround it with burning charcoal on all sides,
and place the prisoner inside.
Is there anything they wouldn't confess?"
Jùnchén immediately called for a large vat,
surrounded it with fire,
stood up, and said to Xīng:
"There is an internal order to investigate you, elder brother.
Please step into this vat."
Xīng, terrified, kowtowed,
and immediately confessed fully.
He was sentenced to death,
but was exiled to Lǐngnán instead.
The families he had ruined,
many were exiled,
and he was eventually killed by his enemies.
As the saying goes:
"He who often acts without propriety will bring it upon himself,"
indeed true!
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Yú Sīxuǎn
During the Tang Dynasty, Yú Sīxuǎn was a deep thinker,
and extremely ingenious.
The Emperor wanted to create a petition box,
summoned craftsmen,
but none could make it.
Xuǎn undertook the task as commissioned,
and made one that perfectly met the specifications,
so it was adopted.
Not long after, someone submitted a petition in the box accusing Xuǎn,
saying:
"When Xú Jìngyè rebelled in Yángzhōu,
Xuǎn made blade wheels for Jìngyè to charge the battle formations,
killing and wounding many government troops."
Under interrogation, he fully confessed,
and was executed.
To be hoist with one's own petard
reached such an extent.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Suǒ Yuánlǐ
During the Tang Dynasty, Suǒ Yuánlǐ
made iron cage-head devices to interrogate prisoners.
Later, he was implicated in a bribery case,
and refused to confess.
The interrogator said:
"Fetch Sir's iron cage-head."
Yuánlǐ immediately confessed.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Zhāng Chǔjīn
During the Tang Dynasty, Zhāng Chǔjīn served as Vice Minister of Justice.
He memorialized that those guilty of rebellion who held
(The Ming manuscript copy has "特" for "持",
same below.)
an imperial pardon exempting them from death,
their family members should still be executed by hanging or beheading, and their property confiscated, with the women enslaved, etc.
This was incorporated into the law.
Later, Chǔjīn was falsely accused of rebellion,
and though he held an imperial pardon exempting him from death,
males aged fifteen and above were beheaded,
and his wife and children were enslaved.
Those who understood said:
To be hoist with one's own petard,
this is what is called retribution.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Cuī Rìzhī
During the Tang Dynasty, the Capital Prefect Cuī Rìzhī issued orders regarding demoted and exiled persons in Cháng'ān, Wànnián, and other counties,
forbidding them to stop even briefly.
If they violated this even for a moment,
the responsible officials would administer cane strokes.
Not long after,
Rìzhī was demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Shè County.
Pressed by the county authorities,
he could not even bid farewell to his wife and children.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Sū Tǐng
During the Tang Dynasty, Minister Sū Tǐng,
when young, had a physiognomist read his face, saying:
"You will reach the rank of Minister,
and your final position will be of the second rank."
Later, he became a Minister of the third rank.
When critically ill,
he summoned shamans to examine him.
The shaman said:
"Your life span is exhausted,
you cannot recover."
Tǐng then mentioned the physiognomist's words again.
The shaman said:
"Originally, it was indeed so,
but because you killed two people while serving in Guì Prefecture,
these two people are now accusing you in the underworld.
The authorities there reduced your lifespan by two years,
hence you did not reach the second rank."
Tǐng had previously governed Guìzhōu,
where two clerks accused a county magistrate.
Tǐng had the magistrate executed, and the clerks killed.
He then sighed deeply for a long time and died.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
Lǐ Zhī
During the Tang Dynasty, Wáng Yuè served as Magistrate of Tángchāng.
He unjustly killed the Registrar Lǐ Zhī.
After Zhī died,
his eldest son, speaking as if possessed by the spirit, said:
"Wáng Yuè is unprincipled,
he wrongfully killed me,
I will certainly take revenge."
His voice was very fierce.
After several days,
while Yuè was sitting in his office during the day,
a fist suddenly struck his waist.
The sound was heavy and solid,
but looking around in alarm, he saw no one.
By evening,
the struck place was slightly swollen,
and painful.
That day,
Lǐ Zhī's son spoke again, saying:
"I have already struck Wáng Yuè,
hitting the vital spot exactly.
He will soon die."
Yuè became gravely ill,
went to Shǔ Commandery to seek medical treatment,
but did not recover.
The day before his death,
Lǐ Zhī instructed his family to prepare a meal for several people,
and still said:
"I am going to Shǔ Commandery with three guests,
to fetch Wáng Yuè.
After we finish eating, we will depart."
The next day, Yuè died.
The festering swelling on Yuè
was precisely on his right kidney,
which was Lǐ Zhī's doing.
From "Jì Wén"
Empress Wáng of the Tang Dynasty
The Tang dynasty's Consort Huì, née Wǔ,
enjoyed exclusive favor in the imperial bedchamber
and plotted to usurp the position of the principal wife.
Empress Wáng was by nature jealous,
and could not bear this situation.
Emperor Xuánzōng then deposed the Empress, reducing her to commoner status.
Slanderous reports were heard daily,
and when it came to deposing the Crown Prince,
Emperor Xuánzōng consulted Zhāng Jiǔlíng.
He replied:
"The Crown Prince is the foundation of the empire;
to move him would shake the hearts of the people.
The Crown Prince
Originally, the text read 'Jiǔlíng' for 'Crown Prince',
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.
has resided in the Eastern Palace,
and no great faults have been heard of him.
Your servant has heard that the way between father and son
is innate nature.
If a son has faults,
a father should forgive and conceal them;
it is not fitting to depose and sever ties.
Moreover, the evidence of his wickedness is not yet clear.
I fear outsiders might spy upon this,
harming Your Majesty's way as a compassionate father."
Emperor Xuánzōng was displeased,
but suppressed his feelings for a long time.
Lǐ Línfǔ and others held power,
secretly scheming with Consort Wǔ,
planning to establish her son to secure their own positions.
Consort Wǔ also allied with them.
They first had Jiǔlíng dismissed and then deposed the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince's full brothers, Prince È Yáo and Prince Guāng Jū, were executed on the same day.
The whole realm grieved for them,
calling them the 'Three Commoners'.
After the Crown Prince was wronged,
Consort Wǔ and those around her repeatedly saw apparitions causing trouble.
The palace was filled with fear all night long;
sometimes ghostly cries and laughter were heard.
They summoned sorcerers and shamans to examine it,
and all said it was the vengeful spirits of the Three Commoners.
Previously, when Prince È and Prince Guāng were seized,
the executioners shot them with arrows and buried them.
They were then ordered to be reburied,
with prayers and libations offered.
When Consort Wǔ died,
the hauntings ceased.
Emperor Xuánzōng then established Sùzōng as Crown Prince.
Línfǔ's schemes came to nothing,
and he became fearful and apprehensive.
The Three Commoners died on the 22nd day of the 4th month of the 25th year,
and Consort Wǔ passed away in the 12th month.
Those with insight knew there was divine retribution at work.
From "Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ"
Yáng Shènjīn
Wáng Lún, a Tang dynasty Investigating Censor, served as a Military Judge for the Shuòfāng military governor.
Traveling by post-horse,
he suddenly died on the road.
However, his complexion did not change,
and he still had warmth,
so they were afraid to prepare him for burial.
After fifteen days, he revived,
saying:
"I went to the underworld court,
and spoke with an underworld official.
The official was pleased with me,
and had me stand inside a room.
When the official went out,
Lún tried to open his case documents.
They were Yáng Shènjīn's accusation to the Emperor against Lǐ Línfǔ and Wáng Hóng.
It had already been decided that Wáng Hóng's clan would be exterminated.
So I dared not open them further,
placed them back in their original spot, and went to see the King.
In front of the King's hall, curtains hung along the eastern and western corridors.
I was seated beneath a curtain.
The Shènjīn brothers entered
and appealed to the King, claiming injustice.
The King said:
"Wáng Hóng's clan has already been exterminated;
he will arrive shortly."
In a moment,
Hóng arrived in chains.
Along with several of his sons and younger brothers,
all were shackled and bound,
with blood flowing from their seven orifices.
The King ordered them sent to the interrogation place.
Then I exited together with Shènjīn,
and was led back, whereupon I revived.
Over a month later,
the incident involving Xíng Zé occurred,
and Wáng Hóng died because of it.
From "Jì Wén"
Shī Yèguāng
During the Tang, there was a man named Shī Yèguāng,
a native of Jìmén.
In his youth he was intelligent and fond of study,
and greatly admired the Buddhist teachings,
so he became a monk,
residing in his commandery.
For nearly ten years,
he thoroughly mastered the profound mysteries of the Buddhist canon.
There was also a śramaṇa named Huìdá,
whose family was very wealthy,
possessing vast sums of money.
Admiring Yèguāng's learning,
he thus became friends with him.
At that time, Emperor Xuánzōng favored Daoist immortals and Buddhism,
extensively seeking out famous monks and masters of esoteric arts.
Yèguāng, constrained by poverty,
could not travel west to the capital,
and was constantly discontented.
Huìdá knew of this,
and therefore provided him with 700,000 coins to fund his journey,
saying to Yèguāng:
"Your learning, skill, and talent,
I privately believe none surpass you.
The Sage Emperor selects the finest talents of the realm;
you, my friend, will surely stand out from the crowd,
and bathe in his generous favor.
From now on, leaving behind the traces of a black-robed disciple,
you will become a minister of the enlightened Son of Heaven.
This can be awaited on tiptoe.
However, when that time comes,
there will surely be those holding brooms at your gate,
I hope you will not forget
Originally, the text read '忌' for '忘',
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.
our old acquaintance, even if only half-faced."
Yèguāng thanked him, saying: [132"Fortunately, Master, your generous gift allows me to proceed west.
If I attain the fifth rank for you,
I will repay your kindness."
Yèguāng reached Cháng'ān,
and by bribing the attendants of the Ninth Princess,
gained an audience
Originally, the text had '以' for the two characters '召見',
changed according to the "Táng Shū Shī Yèguāng Zhuàn".
at the hot springs.
After the character '泉', the Ming manuscript copy leaves nine blank spaces,
indicating missing text.
He ordered the eunuchs to select ten eminent and learned monks
to debate with the masters of esoteric arts.
Yèguāng was among those chosen.
Expounding profound mysteries,
and elucidating doubtful points,
none of the other monks dared compare with him.
The Emperor marveled at his eloquence,
issued an edict bestowing a silver seal with vermilion cords,
appointed him Erudite of the Four Gates,
attending daily by the Emperor's side,
granted him a first-class mansion,
and bestowed money and silks counted in the thousands.
He was known as a favorite minister.
Huìdá then traveled from Jìmén to Cháng'ān to visit him.
When Yèguāng heard Huìdá had arrived,
he thought he had come to collect the debt from him,
and was very displeased.
Huìdá understood his meaning,
and thus announced his departure.
After returning north for over a month,
Yèguāng, worried he might come again,
secretly wrote to the Jìmén commander Zhāng Tíngguī:
"Recently, Master Huìdá came to the imperial carriage's vicinity,
falsely accusing you, Sir, of repairing weapons and armor,
plotting rebellion.
Quite a few people are aware of this.
Given your loyalty, Sir,
known throughout the realm,
yet accumulated slander can melt metal—
you must be on guard."
Tíngguī was shocked and enraged,
summoned Huìdá, and had him flogged to death.
Several days later,
Yèguāng suddenly saw Huìdá come into his courtyard,
cursing Yèguāng:
"I provided you with 700,000 coins to go west.
How could you suddenly slander and falsely accuse me,
causing me to die unjustly?
How deeply you have wronged me!"
Having said this,
he leapt up,
seized and dragged Yèguāng.
After a long time, he vanished from sight.
All the servants of the Shī family witnessed this.
Several days after that,
Yèguāng died.
From "Xuān Shì Zhì"
Cuī Wèi's Son
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man from the Cuī family of Qīnghé,
whose home was in Xíngyáng.
His mother, née Lú,
was skilled at managing the household,
and the family was quite wealthy.
Her son had passed the imperial examinations in the capital,
and was appointed as the Deputy Magistrate of Tàihé County in Jízhōu.
His mother was attached to their old property,
so she did not accompany him to his post.
She arranged for her son to marry a woman from the Wáng family of Tàiyuán,
providing them with several hundred thousand in wealth,
and several servants.
As they set off to take up his post,
they planned to hire a boat for the journey.
A servant said:
"There is currently a man from Jízhōu surnamed Sūn,
who says his empty boat is returning home,
and the hiring price is extremely cheap.
If we discuss it with him,
it would likely be safe and convenient."
So they chose a departure date,
Cuī, his wife Wáng, and the servants all bowed in the hall,
and tearfully bid farewell before boarding the boat.
Not many days into the journey,
as evening fell by a wild shore,
the boatman, having long coveted their belongings,
waited until Deputy Magistrate Cuī was off guard,
and suddenly pushed him into a deep pool,
pretending to make a rescue attempt.
He then stepped back and said:
"What a pity, my efforts to save him were not in time!"
His family wailed in grief,
and Sūn showed them his blade,
so they all became terrified.
They dared not even breathe heavily.
That night,
he forced himself upon Wáng.
Wáng was already pregnant,
so Sūn used the wealth to settle in Jiāngxià.
Later, Wáng gave birth to a son,
whom the boatman raised as his own,
and loved dearly.
His mother secretly taught him writing and literature,
but she never told him the truth of his origins.
Cuī's elderly mother was in Zhèngzhōu,
puzzled by the long lack of news.
She waited in hope for several years.
With the empire in turmoil and separation,
many people were displaced,
and Cuī's mother was forever parted from her son.
Twenty years later,
the Sūn family had grown extremely wealthy from Cuī's fortune.
The adopted son was now eighteen or nineteen,
and his studies and skills were complete,
so they sent him to the capital to take the imperial examinations.
This young man traveled west,
and his route passed through Zhèngzhōu.
About fifty lǐ from the prefectural city,
he lost his way at night,
but a light constantly led the way ahead,
though no person was seen.
He followed the light,
and after more than twenty lǐ,
reached the gate of a manor,
knocked, and asked for lodging.
The master allowed it,
and housed him in the main hall—
it was the Cuī family manor.
The servants secretly observed him,
and reported to his grandmother:
"The guest lodging at our gate
looks very much like our young master."
The servants also observed his speech and mannerisms,
finding not the slightest difference,
and reported this to his mother again.
The mother wanted to see for herself,
so she summoned him into the hall,
and spoke with him.
He was exactly like her son,
but upon asking, he said he was from the Sūn family.
His grandmother wept again,
and the young man did not know why.
His grandmother said:
"Young master, you have come from afar,
tomorrow please stay for a meal."
The young man dared not refuse an elder's wish,
so he agreed.
The next day,
as his grandmother saw him preparing to leave,
she burst into loud, mournful weeping,
and said to him:
"Young master, do not be alarmed by this weeping.
In the past, I had only one son,
who once left to take up an official post,
and then all news ceased.
It has been twenty years now.
Seeing your appearance, young master,
so strikingly resembles my son,
I could not help but feel this sorrow.
Young master, as you travel west,
on your return you must visit again.
This old heart is lonely,
and seeing you is like seeing my own son.
I also have something to give you,
so strive to return early."
That spring,
the young man failed the examinations,
and returned to Zhèngzhōu,
visiting the grandmother's manor again.
His grandmother saw him with joy,
and kept him to rest for several days.
As he was about to leave, she gave him provisions for the journey,
and also a set of clothes, saying:
"These are my deceased son's clothes.
I kept them when he left as a memento,
but now we are forever parted.
Since you, young master, resemble my son,
I offer them to you."
She wept bitterly as they parted,
asking him to visit again whenever he passed by.
The young man returned home,
but did not tell his parents about this.
Later, he happened to wear the clothes left by the old woman,
and on the lower hem was a burn hole from a fire.
His mother was shocked and asked:
"Where did you get these clothes?"
He then recounted the whole story.
His mother then sent others away,
and weeping, told her son the truth:
"These clothes were made by me and your father.
When first ironing them,
I accidentally let the fire burn them.
On the day your father departed,
your grandmother kept this as a keepsake.
Because you were still young,
I feared justice could not be properly sought,
but who could have expected divine justice would be so clear today."
Hearing this, her son wept bitterly,
and went to the prefectural office to plead his grievance.
Upon investigation, the truth was indeed confessed.
Sūn was executed,
and his wife, for not reporting the crime earlier,
was sentenced as an accomplice,
but her son pleaded sorrowfully on her behalf, and she was spared.
From "Records of Original Transformations."
Chén Yìláng,
his father Yí Shuǎng,
together with Zhōu Màofāng were both from Fúchāng in the Eastern Capital Luòyáng.
They studied together at Sānxiāng.
Yí Shuǎng passed the imperial examination,
returned home and married the daughter of Guō Yīn.
Màofāng ultimately did not achieve fame,
and only maintained a sworn friendship with Yí Shuǎng.
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
Yí Shuǎng was assigned to an official post,
and received the position of magistrate of Yílǒng in Péngzhōu.
His mother was attached to her old home,
and did not follow her son to his official post.
The day of departure was set,
Lady Guō, using a bolt of silk she had woven and dyed herself,
cut and made a garment to present to her mother-in-law.
By mistake, she injured her finger with scissors,
and blood stained the garment.
She said to her mother-in-law:
"For seven or eight years, this daughter-in-law has served you morning and evening,
and now I am about to follow my husband to his post,
leaving you far behind.
I cannot bear the sorrow of parting.
However, I made this garment with my own hands,
and on it there is a bloodstain from accidentally injuring myself with scissors,
which cannot be washed away.
When you, my elder, see it,
you will not forget this daughter-in-law."
Her mother-in-law also wept.
Yí Shuǎng firmly invited Màofāng to accompany them.
His son Yìláng
was only two years old.
When Màofāng saw him,
he treated him as more dear than his own flesh and blood.
When they were over five hundred lǐ from Yílǒng,
the path was rocky and perilous,
the Bā River vast and boundless.
As they climbed vines to enjoy the view,
Màofāng suddenly conceived a wicked idea.
He ordered the servants to go ahead,
saying, "Prepare a meal for me at the postal station."
The two of them walked slowly,
leading the horse themselves.
Suddenly, at a steep and precipitous spot on the mountain path,
he drew a golden hammer and struck Yí Shuǎng,
shattering his skull,
and pushed him into the rushing torrent.
Then he pretended to wail, crying out:
"I had to relieve myself,
and when I turned back north,
I saw the horse startled and trampled the magistrate to death.
What shall we do now?"
That night, they held a mourning gathering.
Yí Shuǎng's wife and the servants offered wine in grief and sorrow.
Màofāng said:
"Since things have come to this,
what can be done?
Moreover, no one in the world knows about this.
I will temporarily assume the magistrate's name and take up the post with you, madam,
and enjoy the salary of one term of office.
When it is time, we can return north."
They then began the mourning rites.
The servants were all promised generous rewards.
The wife, unaware of the truth,
followed his plan.
Upon taking up the post,
he placated the servants.
After a year had passed,
he said to Lady Guō:
"My plan has succeeded,
I swear I will not betray you."
Lady Guō concealed her hatred,
unable to act on it,
as Màofāng guarded against her very closely.
When his term of office ended,
he was transferred,
and settled in Chángjiāng, Suìzhōu.
After another assignment,
he was appointed as a clerk in Suìzhōu.
Not long after,
seventeen years had passed,
and his son was now nineteen years old.
Màofāng believed no one could possibly know the truth,
so he taught the boy the classics.
When the boy was nearly accomplished,
and Màofāng's term in Suìzhōu ended,
he took his son to take the imperial examination.
That year, the examinations were held in the Eastern Capital.
Màofāng took the northern route,
while ordering his son to take the southern route,
intending for him to observe the condition of their old hometown.
Along the way at Sānxiāng,
an old woman selling food invited him to eat,
and repeatedly gazed at him intently.
After he finished eating,
and was about to pay her,
the old woman said:
"No need.
I pity you because you resemble my grandson in appearance."
She then opened her clothes chest,
took out the bloodstained garment left by Lady Guō and gave it to him,
weeping as she saw him off.
The son secretly placed it in his bag,
not knowing the reason,
nor the truth about his father.
The following year, he failed the examination,
and returned to Chángjiāng.
When his mother suddenly saw the bloodstained garment,
she asked in shock how he had obtained it.
Her son told her everything the old woman at Sānxiāng had said.
When she asked about her age and appearance,
she realized it was her mother-in-law,
and wept bitterly.
She led her son to a quiet room,
and told him everything:
"This man is not your father.
Your father was murdered by this man.
I have long wanted to tell you,
but feared you were too young.
I am but a woman,
and if my plan were ill-conceived,
then your late father's injustice
would never be avenged.
It is not that I fear death.
Now, this bloodstained garment I made with my own hands has returned.
Is this not the will of Heaven?"
Her son secretly sharpened a frosty blade,
waited until Màofāng was asleep,
then cut his throat,
and took his head to the authorities.
The regional commander praised his righteousness,
exempted him from punishment,
and he immediately accompanied his mother back east.
His grandmother was still alive.
After recounting their long separation,
they took out the garment to examine it,
and wept together with sighs.
Lady Guō cared for her mother-in-law for three years before passing away.
Dáxī Xún
When Emperor Sùzōng of Táng recaptured the two capitals,
Cuī Qì served as the Commissioner of the Three Judicial Offices.
He was harsh and took pleasure in others' misfortunes,
cruel and lacking in kindness.
Catering to the emperor's wishes, he applied the law harshly,
and memorialized that officials who had served the rebels should all be executed.
Lǐ Xiàn objected, saying:
"In any matter, there are leaders and followers,
and circumstances vary in severity.
If all are executed indiscriminately,
I fear it does not align with the principle of magnanimity.
In ancient times, when wise kings applied punishments,
they exterminated the chief culprits,
while sparing the accomplices.
Moreover, the remaining bandits in Héběi
are still not pacified.
If we allow some to slip through the net,
it would open a path to self-renewal.
If we execute them all,
it would only strengthen their rebellious resolve."
The pedantic officials,
unaware of the greater situation,
only after several days followed Lǐ Xiàn's memorial,
and from Chén Xīliè downward,
determined six grades of punishment.
Lǚ Yīn repeatedly recommended Cuī Qì for the positions of Vice Minister of Personnel and Censor-in-Chief.
Cuī Qì suffered from swollen feet,
and after over a month, his condition gradually worsened.
Whenever he closed his eyes, he would see Dáxī Xún,
and would only say:
"I kowtow to the Governor,
I had no choice."
When those around him asked,
after a long while he would reply:
"Governor Dáxī is appealing his injustice,
and I am pleading for him like this."
After three months,
it did not stop until he died.
Huáyáng Lǐ Wèi
After the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Zhāng who served as the military governor of Jiànnán.
On the Ghost Festival,
he ordered all the temples in the city
to display their finest decorations
to allow men and women to visit and admire them.
There was a man named Lǐ Wèi from Huáyáng,
whose wife was exceptionally beautiful,
renowned among the people of Shǔ,
and Zhāng had also heard of her.
When the temples were lavishly decorated,
the entire city flocked to see them,
and whenever officials and their families came to view the displays,
the attendants would always report it to Zhāng.
Only Lǐ Wèi’s wife did not come,
which struck him as odd.
He secretly sent someone to inquire of her neighbors,
and indeed, it was because of her beauty that she did not go out.
Zhāng then ordered a large courtyard to be selected at Kāiyuán Temple,
and dispatched the most skilled artisans of Shǔ
to devise an ingenious plan.
They created a set of wooden figures capable of producing music,
with mechanisms hidden inside,
complete with all kinds of string and wind instruments.
He allowed the common people and officials
to view them freely for three days,
saying:
"After three days,
they will be presented to the inner palace."
Carriages and crowds filled the area for a hundred lǐ.
For two days,
Lǐ Wèi’s wife still did not come.
On the third day, as dusk fell and the crowd dispersed,
Lǐ Wèi’s wife arrived in a sedan chair accompanied by a single maid.
As she was about to leave her residence,
people had already rushed to inform Zhāng.
Zhāng then changed his clothes and went ahead,
seating himself inside a hollow statue of a Buddha in the courtyard,
to secretly observe her.
Shortly after, she arrived,
first ordering someone to check that there was no one in the room,
and then she descended.
When Zhāng saw her,
he thought she was a celestial being,
not of this world.
After returning,
he secretly sought out Buddhist nuns and female shamans who frequented Lǐ Wèi’s household,
to convey his intentions.
Lǐ Wèi’s wife was alarmed and refused him.
It happened that Lǐ Wèi was accused of accepting bribes in a legal case,
exposed by his own servant.
Zhāng then ordered capable officials to investigate the case with severity,
and Lǐ Wèi was sentenced to sixty strokes of the cane,
exiled to the remote borderlands,
and died on the way.
Zhāng then lavishly bribed Lǐ Wèi’s mother,
and forcibly took Lǐ Wèi’s wife.
As Lǐ Wèi had been foolish and unrefined,
his wife had always resented being married to a common man,
so she consented.
She was settled in the prefecture,
and Zhāng doted on and revered her like no other.
However, from then on,
he often seemed to see Lǐ Wèi by his side.
He summoned sorcerers to perform exorcisms,
but they could not stop it.
A little over a year later,
Lǐ Wèi’s wife also passed away.
Several years later,
Zhāng fell ill,
and the apparition of Lǐ Wèi
became even more distinct.
Suddenly one day,
he saw Lǐ Wèi’s wife,
looking just as she had in life.
Startled, Zhāng stepped forward to ask her,
and Lǐ Wèi’s wife said:
"I am deeply grateful for your kindness,
and kindness must be repaid.
Lǐ Wèi has already appealed to the Emperor of Heaven,
and the time is set for this year.
However, you also have someone to rescue you.
If you can just get through this year,
you will surely be safe.
He has already come to fetch you,
but if you do not go out,
he will not dare to enter your hall.
Be careful not to go down."
Having said this, she left.
At that time, there was a Huàshān Daoist priest whose talismans were extremely powerful.
He set up an altar in Zhāng’s residence,
and his words were roughly the same.
For several months, Zhāng did not dare to descend the steps.
Lǐ Wèi’s wife also came again,
both teaching him the way of strict caution.
Then one day at dusk,
in the eastern wing of the hall, there was a cluster of bamboo.
Zhāng saw a red sleeve
beckoning to him from beside the bamboo,
thinking it was Lǐ Wèi’s wife coming.
Forgetting all the previous warnings,
he descended the steps
and rushed toward it.
His attendants followed, shouting,
but could not stop him.
When he arrived, he saw Lǐ Wèi dressed in women’s clothes,
dragging Zhāng under the trees,
and beating him for a long time,
saying:
"If this villain had not been beckoned by a red sleeve,
would he have descended the steps?"
Then he seized him and took him out the gate.
His attendants were as if drunk,
and when they awoke,
they saw Zhāng lying under the trees,
blood flowing from his eyes and nose,
only his heart still warm.
They carried him to the hall, where he died.
Duàn Xiùshí
When Zhū Cǐ of the Táng dynasty was defeated,
he fled to Jīngzhōu.
Lǐ Shèng, the deputy marshal of the capital,
recaptured the palace.
After Zhū Cǐ was defeated and fled,
he gathered his remaining soldiers,
only a hundred or two hundred men left.
Suddenly, he became confused,
unable to distinguish north from south,
so he asked an old farmer for directions.
The old farmer said:
"Aren’t you Grand Commandant Zhū?"
The false chancellor Yuán Xiū stopped him, saying:
"The Hàn Emperor."
The old farmer said:
"Heaven and Earth do not tolerate the wicked for long,
snakes and rats do not become dragons and tigers.
The net of Heaven is vast,
where can you go?"
Zhū Cǐ grew angry,
intending to kill him,
but suddenly the old farmer vanished.
When they were about a hundred lǐ from Jīngzhōu,
Zhū Cǐ, on horseback,
suddenly began kowtowing repeatedly, crying "Spare my life!"
His hands and feet flailed wildly,
as if resisting something,
and he fell from his horse.
After a long while, he regained consciousness.
His attendants asked him what had happened,
and he said:
"I saw Minister of Agriculture Duàn."
Soon after, he was beheaded by Hán Mín.
Mǎ Fèngzhōng
The Tang dynasty Imperial Censor Dù Shìfāng,
serving as the Surveillance Commissioner of Guìzhōu,
encountered a rebellion by the mountain bandits of Xīyuán,
and was ordered by imperial decree to suppress them.
Subsequently, a certain Langzhōng named Péi
was commanded to undertake a mission of appeasement,
and upon passing through Guìzhōu,
Shìfāng dispatched a Yāyá named Lè,
along with two deputy generals, to serve on duty.
Upon reaching Bīnzhōu,
Péi ordered Lè Shēng and the two deputy generals
to go to the bandits to convey the imperial decree,
and also to deliver a letter to their bandit chieftain,
ordering them to submit and return.
Lè Shēng was originally a Confucian scholar,
and possessed a sense of righteousness.
After arriving,
the bandit chieftain Huáng Shàoqīng was greatly pleased,
and detained them for several days of feasting.
He admired the saber worn by Lè Shēng,
and earnestly requested it from him.
Shàoqīng compensated its value with two young maidservants.
After completing their mission and reporting back,
the deputy generals were on bad terms with Lè Shēng,
and thus reported to Péi, saying:
"Lè so-and-so revealed the strengths and weaknesses of the government troops to the bandit chieftain,
and became intimate with him,
hence he was given female captives."
Péi was greatly angered,
and sent people to search and inspect,
and indeed found them.
Lè Shēng explained the whole story in detail,
saying:
"This saber of mine is worth tens of thousands,
and I treasure it greatly.
As I was on an official mission,
the bandit chieftain requested it,
and I had no choice but to give it to him.
He returned its value,
but the price of these two persons
is not even half of its worth.
What fault have I committed!"
Lè Shēng, being a man of spirit,
spoke with a rather stern tone and expression.
Lord Péi grew even angrier,
and had him imprisoned in the jail of Bīnzhōu.
He sent a letter to Shìfāng,
and also submitted an official document falsely accusing him of a major offense,
requesting that he must be executed.
Shìfāng, being stationed in a distant garrison,
and with the imperial envoy stating that his subordinate had accepted bribes from the bandits,
and was about to be punished,
had no choice but to apply the law to him,
yet he also knew in his heart that he was wronged.
Lè Shēng also submitted a statement explaining in detail.
Shìfāng then ordered someone to deliver the official document to summon him,
and personally instructed the messenger, saying:
"If he wishes to escape,
you must not prevent him,
and also convey my meaning to him."
When the messenger arrived,
he conveyed Shìfāng's meaning.
Lè Shēng said:
"I am not guilty,
I would rather die;
if I flee,
then I would be guilty."
After arriving,
Shìfāng summoned him in,
and questioned him.
Lè Shēng recounted the entire matter from the beginning.
Shìfāng then showed him the letter and official document from the imperial envoy, saying:
"Regarding today's matter,
it is not that I do not know of your injustice,
but there is no way to save you.
What can be done?"
He then ordered an interrogation.
Lè Shēng asked the interrogator:
"What is the Censor's intention?"
He replied:
"The Censor, due to the imperial envoy's intention,
cannot spare the Yāyá."
Lè Shēng said:
"If the Censor's intention is such,
what can I appeal?"
He then requested a brush to write his confession,
stating the circumstances of receiving goods from the bandit chieftain.
Shìfāng felt great pity and sorrow.
Before the execution,
he had him brought in and said:
"I know you have been greatly wronged.
Is there anything you wish to entrust?"
Lè Shēng said:
"Nothing."
Shìfāng said:
"Do you have a son?"
He replied:
"One."
"What position would he like?"
He said:
"It would be enough to obtain the position of Yáqián Yúhòu."
Shìfāng then issued an official document,
and also gave him a hundred thousand coins,
to be used for funeral expenses.
He asked again if there was anything else he desired.
Lè Shēng said:
"I have falsely confessed to death,
and will certainly not flee.
I request to have the shackles removed,
bathe,
see my wife and children,
and entrust family matters."
The lord granted all of these.
When the time came,
Shìfāng ascended the south gate of the prefecture,
ordered him to be brought out,
and bid him farewell.
Lè Shēng bathed and combed his hair,
bowed before the tower and said:
"I am about to die now,
but even in death I will not cease."
Shìfāng said:
"Do you resent me?"
He replied:
"No,
the Censor was pressured by the imperial envoy."
Shìfāng shed tears,
then ordered him to be taken to the polo grounds,
and provided a lavish feast of wine and food.
After eating,
he summoned his wife and children to bid farewell,
and asked:
"Has a coffin been purchased?
Quickly buy one,
and also fetch a thousand sheets of paper,
ten brushes,
and place them in the coffin.
After I die,
I will appeal before the Emperor of the Underworld."
He asked the supervisor of the execution:
"What time is it now?"
He replied:
"Noon."
Lè Shēng said:
"I will die at noon,
and by dusk,
I will go to Bīnzhōu,
to take the deputy general so-and-so.
And next year in April,
I will kill the imperial envoy Langzhōng Péi."
Raising his head, he saw one of the executioners,
who was a subordinate of the Yúhòu.
Lè had once acted as Dū Yúhòu,
and said to him:
"You are my former subordinate.
I am now about to die.
Be careful not to break my neck.
If you do so,
after I die I will immediately kill you."
The subordinate, at this moment,
had no time to heed or believe,
and thus followed the usual method,
snapped his neck and killed him,
then flogged the corpse,
and after flogging,
dragged it outside.
The executioner suddenly collapsed in shock,
fell face down on the ground and died.
Several days later,
a report came from Bīnzhōu
that the deputy general, on that day at dusk,
suddenly suffered a violent heartache.
The imperial envoy Péi,
died in April of the following year.
In October of that year,
Shìfāng was at the polo grounds arranging for the reception of an imperial commissioner,
and was drinking merrily,
when suddenly he raised his head, stared wide-eyed, and said:
"Lè so-and-so,
why have you come now?
I am not at fault either."
He asked for wine to pour on the ground as an offering,
and after a long while, said again:
"I know you were wronged,
and yet I ultimately killed you,
this is also my crime."
He then fell silent, unable to speak,
was carried back to the prefecture,
and died by night.
To this day, at the south gate of Guìzhōu,
the place where Lè Shēng died,
an area of about ten square feet,
remains without any grass growing.
Later, an official serving in Guìzhōu
observed it and found it to be true.
Since ancient times, there have been many who died unjustly,
but how supernatural Lè Shēng's case was.
Sòng Shēnxī
Táng Chéngxiàng Sòng Shēnxī,
initially served as prime minister,
receiving deep imperial favor,
and Shēnxī also took it as his personal responsibility to bring about peace and prosperity.
At that time, Zhèng Zhù was associating freely and acting without restraint,
usurping power and authority,
and Shēnxī wished to eliminate him.
He therefore appointed his friend Wáng Fán as the Governor of the Capital District,
secretly making an agreement with him,
ordering him to investigate Zhù's unlawful acts,
intending to present the evidence of his crimes,
arrest him at the Capital District government office,
and have him beaten to death.
After the agreement was made,
Fán was a fickle and petty man.
Seeing that Zhù was currently favored by powerful eunuchs,
he therefore sought to cultivate a close relationship with him,
and told him all about Shēnxī's plot.
Zhù consequently reported it to the Right Army,
and within less than ten days,
they forged evidence of Shēnxī's crimes,
having someone accuse him, saying:
"He used writings to connect with the various princes,
plotting treason,
using clothing, gold, treasures, and rare jade as pledges."
Moreover, they had someone imitate his handwritten notes,
all achieving extreme likeness.
The case was concluded within the palace,
and all the high officials and common people knew of his injustice.
Officials of the Three Departments and below
repeatedly submitted memorials arguing on his behalf,
and only then was he demoted to the position of Military Administrator of Kāizhōu.
After serving for several months,
he could not bear his indignation and died.
The following year,
an imperial edict of grace
ordered his remains returned to the capital for burial.
In the spring of the first year of the Tàihé era,
his wife, dozing off at midday in front of the hall,
saw Shēnxī enter through the central gate,
and involuntarily startled awake.
Shēnxī beckoned to her with his hand,
so she descended the steps,
and he said:
"Come,
there is a small matter
I need you to see."
He then led her out of the city,
seemingly going several li north to the Chǎnshuǐ River,
arriving at a ruined site,
where she saw a large pit,
beside which were several small bamboo cages and small wooden boxes,
all bearing seals.
Shēnxī then lifted one to show his wife, saying:
"This is that villain."
Filled with anger, he shouted sternly,
and she asked:
"Who is it?"
He replied:
"It is Wáng Fán.
I have received permission from the Supreme Deity."
She further questioned him about the others,
and he said:
"You will know in time."
Having finished speaking,
she suddenly awoke with a start,
sweating all over,
and immediately told her family and relatives,
also recording it with a brush in her clothing chest.
In the eleventh month of that year,
Fán was indeed executed by waist-cutting in the marketplace for his crimes,
several others suffering execution with him,
all buried together in a pit outside the city.
Thus it was known that Lord Sòng's divine spirit had not lied.
Shǔ Camp Clerk
The Táng Shǔ general Yǐn Yǎn
had a soldier in his camp
who was several ke late for the evening roll call,
and Yǎn intended to punish him.
The soldier was drunk,
arguing loudly in his own defense,
and Yǎn, enraged,
had him beaten several dozen times,
nearly to death.
The soldier's younger brother was a camp clerk,
who was fraternal and affectionate,
and felt Yǎn was unjust.
He therefore used a knife to cut his own flesh,
forming the characters "kill Yǐn",
and tattooed them with ink.
Yǎn secretly learned of this,
and used another matter as pretext to have the clerk beaten to death.
During the Tàihé era,
the Southern Barbarians invaded,
and Yǎn led tens of thousands of troops,
defending the Qiōngyǎn Pass.
Yǎn possessed extraordinary physical strength,
often teasing his attendants
by striking their shins with a thorn-knobbed staff,
causing their muscles to swell and bulge with each strike.
Relying on his strength,
he led his entire force out of the pass,
pursuing the barbarians for several li.
The barbarians sprang an ambush,
attacking from both sides,
and he was badly defeated, his horse fell,
and he was struck by several dozen spears and died.
When he first exited the pass,
he suddenly saw the clerk he had killed,
holding a yellow document case,
as large as a wheel hub,
leading the way ahead.
He felt deeply disturbed by this,
and asked his attendants,
but none had seen it.
He ultimately died in battle.
Hú Jī
The Táng figure Hú Jī
was the son of the former Lǐngnán Military Governor Dàn
"Dàn" is written as "Zhèng" in the Ming manuscript copy.
The Prime Minister Jiǎ Sù oversaw the examinations,
and Jī passed the Jìnshì examination.
During the Tàihé era,
at the time of the Gānlù Incident,
the Northern Army was arresting Sù,
and a Forbidden Army officer,
coveting Jī's family wealth,
said to Qiú Shìliáng:
"I fear Sù is at Jī's residence."
