Soldiers were therefore dispatched to search his home,
and though Sù was not captured,
they seized Jī and brought him before Shìliáng.
Shìliáng ordered him executed outside the camp gate,
and all his property was confiscated.
At that time, Jī's younger brother, Xiāng,
was in Hédōng Commandery.
Suddenly one day,
a household servant saw a headless person,
wearing green clothes,
the upper body all covered in flowing blood,
and found it very strange.
When the news of the misfortune arrived,
and they inquired about the circumstances,
it was the day Jī died.
Later, when Shìliáng died,
his family was also ruined,
which was likely retribution.
From "Bǔ Lù Jì Zhuàn"
Qín Kuāngmóu
Táng Grand Tutor and Duke of Fénguó Dù Cóng
served as military governor of Jiānglíng.
In the fourteenth year of the Xiántōng era,
Qiánnán surveillance commissioner Qín Kuāngmóu, due to a massive invasion by barbarian forces
and being unable to withstand them with his troops, fled and came seeking refuge.
After paying his respects to the Duke,
the Duke was angered that he had not previously attended his court,
and after dismissing him, sent an official to reproach him, saying:
"You are a commoner from Fèngxiáng.
Cóng twice served as military governor of Fèngxiáng,
yet you now show no recognition of your hometown."
Kuāngmóu replied:
"Although my family hails from under Qí Mountain,
I left the central plains at a young age.
When the Grand Tutor held the military tally,
I had already undeservedly received my own command,
and truly never had the chance to attend your court.
Moreover, now we are in Jīngnán;
if we speak of hometowns,
I fear this is not appropriate."
Cóng grew angry,
had him bound and imprisoned,
and sent a letter to Chancellor Wéi Bǎohéng, stating:
"Qín Kuāngmóu arbitrarily abandoned his city walls,
failed to die in service to the king,
I request he be executed."
Wéi, considering Cóng a senior minister of the state
and also due to their longstanding personal favor,
then memorialized requesting to follow Cóng's disposition.
Once the imperial decree was issued,
Cóng personally went to the marketplace to oversee the execution.
As Kuāngmóu was about to face the law,
he said to his son:
"My death today
is truly an unjust and baseless wrong.
But alas, there is no time to appeal;
only burn plenty of paper and ink for me,
and I shall pursue justice in the underworld."
During the execution,
the spectators were packed shoulder to shoulder.
At the moment the blade fell,
Cóng was greatly startled,
suddenly fell ill,
and was carried back by carriage.
Soon a whirlwind arose violently,
swirling up dust and debris,
which blew straight into the government office before dispersing.
That evening,
the prison guard went mad,
calling out his own name and berating himself, saying:
"I have already given you plenty of money and silk,
why do you still hide the various goods I enjoy?"
He threw himself to the ground and died.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month of that year, Qín Kuāngmóu was killed.
On the thirteenth day of the seventh month,
Cóng then died.
When they were to return his body to Luòyáng for burial,
they prepared a narrow catalpa-wood coffin and set out on the road.
On the evening they intended to place him in the coffin,
the chief officer realized the coffin was too short,
and was deeply worried and afraid,
yet it was also difficult to change it.
So he heavily bribed a yīn-yáng master,
who deceived Dù's sons, saying:
"When the Grand Tutor died, it was very inauspicious.
At the moment of placing him in the coffin,
if anyone draws near,
great misfortune will surely occur."
The sons believed this to be true,
and so they led all the family members
to wait in a separate room.
When they lifted the corpse for placement into the coffin,
the catalpa coffin indeed was short,
so they forced it in, crushing the chest and breaking the neck bones,
with no one aware of it.
Upon reaching eastern Luòyáng,
the eldest son, Wúyì,
died one after another.
As the years passed,
the matter gradually became known to the world.
Commentators held that Cóng, relying on his power and status,
wrongfully executed someone,
and thus received this retribution.
From "Nán Chǔ Xīnwén"
Adjutant Wéi
Cuī Yīng of Bólíng served as magistrate of Fúgōu during the Táng dynasty.
One day at noon, while sitting alone,
an old man requested an audience with Cuī Yīng.
Cuī Yīng questioned him,
and the old man replied:
"I have connections with the spirit world.
Today, Wéi, a judge from the underworld, is coming to pay his respects.
I hope you will treat him with great courtesy.
Please prepare an incense table,
dismiss your attendants,
and I will usher him in."
Cuī Yīng complied with the request.
The old man then went out to welcome him.
Upon reaching the courtyard,
the judge's form was faintly visible,
and he introduced himself by name and title,
stating
(Note: In the Xǔ and Huáng editions, "啣" is written as "銜" and "穪" as "稱".)
that he was Sī Mù.
He bowed and waited
(Note: "俟" originally written as "時",
corrected according to the Míng manuscript.)
for a response.
Cuī Yīng returned the bow,
and after several exchanges of courtesies,
the judge said:
"I hold an important position in the underworld.
I have heard of your great talent and noble character,
which are unmatched in this era.
I have thus brought a matter of concern,
hoping to entrust it to you.
That is why I have come to pay my respects during the noon break,
hoping not to startle you."
Cuī Yīng replied:
"I have heard that spirits are not obscure,
and now I see it is true.
I am but a humble and insignificant man,
ignorant and unrefined in all matters.
How fortunate that a bright spirit has descended upon me.
Yet, considering my lowly status,
I fear my strength may not match my intentions.
But if there is anything within my limited power,
I dare not refuse your command.
I hope you will guide me,
and I am willing to exert my utmost effort."
The underworld envoy said:
"I departed from the human world several years ago
and now hold a position in the underworld.
Since abandoning my wife and children,
my family affairs have fallen into disarray.
My beloved son, Wénqīng,
suffered misfortune from a young age.
He is rustic and uneducated.
He holds a position in the Zhèng-Huá office,
and for nearly ten years,
when it was time to hand over the office's affairs,
the account books were unclear,
resulting in a deficit of tens of thousands in coins and silk.
This was not actually used by him.
I wish to boldly ask for your strict yet fair judgment,
and to kindly protect and shelter him."
Cuī Yīng bowed and said:
"Alas,
I am merely the magistrate of Fúgōu.
How would I have any authority over the Zhèng-Huá office?"
The envoy replied:
"Not so.
Given your talent, official rank, and fortune,
how could you be limited to just one office?
From now on,
you will hold high and prestigious positions,
govern important regions,
and reach the pinnacle of human officialdom.
However, in a few months,
you will take over the duties of the Zhèng-Huá office.
If you do not betray today's promise,
I, in the underworld,
will exert my modest strength
to protect your honor and wealth,
not only for your lifetime
but also to bring blessings to your descendants."
Cuī Yīng said:
"Though I am ignorant and unworthy,
how dare I not obey your command?"
The underworld envoy was moved to tears,
and after bidding farewell, he departed.
Cuī Yīng heard that Chancellor Dù Cóng of Huáinán was seeking capable administrators,
so he happened to prepare a letter,
along with a record of his county's achievements.
He sent a messenger to Yángzhōu,
intending, based on Sī Mù's words,
to test the matter.
At that time, the chancellor was overseeing Wéiyáng and
concurrently managing the salt and iron monopoly.
He recommended Cuī Yīng to take charge of the Zhèng-Huá office.
When it came to handing over the account books, money, and silk,
there was a deficit of tens of thousands in coins and silk.
After confiscating Wénqīng's family assets to compensate,
there was still a shortfall of thirty to forty thousand with no means to cover it.
Initially, while in Fúgōu,
Cuī Yīng had accepted Sī Mù's entrustment,
and the matter had been earnestly discussed.
But upon arriving at the Zhèng-Huá office,
he broke his earlier promise,
saying:
"The deficit is vast.
How can it be clarified?
Although Wénqīng claims the embezzlement was not for his own use,
he failed to report it for years.
He must face severe punishment
to deter negligence.
Since fate has determined his poverty and misfortune,
what can ghosts change?
If I abandon the law to follow spirits,
I would be flattering them to seek blessings."
He then detained Wénqīng and reported the matter to his superior.
Wénqīng, believing he would surely die,
secretly hid poison in his clothing.
When he was imprisoned,
he tried several times to take it,
but the medicine kept disappearing,
and he could not find it despite searching.
When Wénqīng was sentenced to death,
on that day,
Sī Mù appeared before Wénqīng and said:
"Alas,
an untrustworthy man
has brought ruin to your family.
I have appealed to the Emperor of Heaven on your behalf,
and he has granted me permission to strip Cuī Yīng of his official rank.
My clan will also be destroyed."
Wénqīng prostrated himself, weeping.
Suddenly, his father vanished,
and Wénqīng found the poison he had hidden.
He looked up and died.
Cuī Yīng, along with Inspector Lǐ Shàn, Investigator Zhū Chéng, and Military Officer Jiǎ Jūn, then carried out the execution in an unauthorized location.
After Wénqīng's death,
Cuī Yīng began to regret his actions.
He arranged a proper burial for Wénqīng,
dressed in mourning clothes, and personally escorted the funeral procession.
Cuī Yīng was later promoted to Diànzhōng.
At that time, someone from Hándān presented a beautiful woman named Jīn Guī to Cuī Yīng.
Cuī Yīng accepted her and became infatuated.
From then on, Cuī Yīng became obsessed with sensual pleasures,
and his dedication to governance waned.
Two years later,
he was promoted to Shìyùshǐ
and put in charge of the Yángzǐ office.
He traveled there with his wife, Lǚ Shì, and Jīn Guī.
Soon after, he was appointed to the Zhèxī office.
From the time he assumed this position,
Jīn Guī's favor grew daily.
Outside the inner gate,
a separate residence was built for her,
more luxurious than the main hall.
After finishing his official duties,
Cuī Yīng would spend days without entering the inner quarters.
All the treasures and goods from his previous posts
were placed in Jīn Guī's residence.
Not long after,
someone else presented a Wú beauty,
even more stunning than Jīn Guī.
Cuī Yīng accepted her,
and his infatuation grew even stronger.
Whenever he was delighted by her singing and dancing,
he would take treasures from Jīn Guī and give them to the new beauty.
Enraged by this,
Jīn Guī conspired with her younger brother, Chén Xíngzōng, to poison wine,
which she offered to Cuī Yīng at night.
He drank it
and died shortly after.
They secretly moved his body to the main hall.
The next morning,
the family discovered it,
but no one knew the truth.
Lǚ Shì, being kind-hearted,
did not investigate thoroughly.
Jīn Guī then took the treasures
and left with her entire household.
The other concubines scattered,
and the Cuī family's fortunes declined daily.
Later, Lǐ Jūn of Lǒngxī took charge of the Zhèxī office.
Hearing of Jīn Guī's beauty,
he sought her out and took her in.
While Lǐ Jūn and Jīn Guī were holding a daytime banquet,
Cuī Yīng's ghost appeared in the courtyard,
scolding Jīn Guī:
"You poisoned me,
and now you are with Lǐ Jūn.
If you become dissatisfied later,
will you bring disaster upon him as well?"
Terrified, Jīn Guī resigned and left.
Later, when Lǐ Jūn was about to arrest Jīn Guī
to investigate the old case
and clear Cuī Yīng's name,
Jīn Guī suddenly fled, and her whereabouts became unknown.
From "Yīndé Zhuàn"
Yáng Shōu
Chancellor Yáng Shōu of the Táng dynasty,
was demoted and died beyond the Lǐng mountains.
At that time, Minister Zhèng Yú was stationed in Nánhǎi.
Suddenly one day,
the guest reception official reported:
"Chancellor Yáng is in the guest quarters,
wishing to see the Minister."
Zhèng Yú was shocked and alarmed,
as Yáng Shōu had recently been given a posthumous decree,
so how could he come here?
Nevertheless, he received him.
Yáng said:
"I was slandered by the Army Surveillance Commissioner Yáng Xuánjiè,
and unfortunately met with harm.
Now I have obtained permission from the Supreme Deity,
who has granted me ghostly soldiers to seek revenge.
I wish to entrust you, Minister, with hosting a feast for them,
and also to borrow ten thousand strings of cash."
Zhèng Yú agreed,
but regarding the money, he pleaded that military affairs were numerous,
and offered half.
Chancellor Yáng said:
"It is not copper coins,
but when burning them, please be careful not to let them touch the ground."
Zhèng Yú said:
"If that is the case, then I can certainly comply."
Yáng bowed leisurely and vanished.
Zhèng Yú ordered wine, food, and paper money to be prepared in the northern suburbs for a sacrifice.
Yáng Shōu had a nephew serving as an official in Shòuyáng.
He saw Yáng Shōu riding a white horse,
with a vermilion bow and red arrows on his arm,
and a celestial official in red robes holding the reins.
Yáng Shōu said to him:
"Now the Supreme Deity has allowed me to take revenge and kill Yáng Xuánjiè.
I will shoot him,
and he will surely die."
Soon after, Yáng Xuánjiè was shot and suddenly fell ill and died.
Máo Wénxí of Shǔ,
whose ancestor served as the prefect of Cháozhōu,
once served under Zhèng Yú,
and was well acquainted with this matter.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Sòng Róu
When Emperor Xīzōng of Táng fled to Mín and Shǔ,
the Yellow Turbans still roamed the Three Capital Regions.
In the Xīnchǒu year of the Zhōnghé era,
an edict appointed Chancellor Jìnguó Gōng Wáng Duó
as the overall commander of the various military camps,
holding the banners and drums,
descending through the Three Gorges,
and establishing his headquarters in Nányàn,
to command the eastern feudal lords.
Another edict appointed Army Surveillance Commissioner Xīmén Jìxuán as the supervisor.
In the autumn, the seventh month,
Wáng Duó arrived in Huá,
while the supervisor stationed in Línrǔ.
The commandery lay on the military route,
and the postal stations were all burned,
so they lodged at the Lóngxīng Northern Chán Monastery.
In the small courtyard of the western corridor,
the supervisor's deputy commander Hé Qún resided.
Hé Qún was from Huá,
and his family had long held prominent military positions.
Hé Qún was fierce and treacherous from a young age,
and his relatives and in-laws looked down on him.
So he traveled west to the capital,
to seek favor with powerful eunuchs,
and Xīmén took him in.
By this time, he was promoted to the deputy commander of the personal guard,
and military affairs were entirely entrusted to him.
Hé Qún was arrogant and overbearing,
treating his subordinates with contempt.
One day,
the military supervisor of Rǔzhōu, Dǒng Hóngzhì,
ordered the clerk Sòng Róu
to deliver a message to the supervisor.
As he was about to leave after delivering the message,
he encountered Hé Qún sitting on a folding chair at the gate.
Angered that Sòng Róu had not paid respects first,
Hé Qún shouted for several soldiers to drag him in,
beat him with a horsewhip, and sent him away.
Dǒng Hóngzhì heard of this and was greatly frightened.
He flogged Sòng Róu several dozen times,
dismissed him,
and no longer employed him.
He sent a letter to apologize to Hé Qún,
but Hé Qún showed no remorse.
Several dozen days later,
as the sun was setting,
Sòng Róu was walking alone
past the monastery gate,
when he again encountered Hé Qún returning from outside.
Hé Qún caught sight of him and became enraged,
repeatedly shouting for his attendants,
seized him and brought him into the courtyard.
Waiting until dusk,
he killed him, dismembered his body,
and threw it into a latrine.
After lighting the lamps,
he suddenly saw Sòng Róu with disheveled hair and bare feet,
covered in blood, standing behind the lamp.
Hé Qún jumped up in fright,
grabbed a sword and struck at him.
The apparition vanished in an instant,
but from then on, it appeared every night.
In the late autumn month,
the supervisor moved to Xíngyáng Commandery,
lodging at the Kāiyuán Monastery,
in the southeastern corner of the inner city.
By this time, Hé Qún's spirit was disturbed,
and he gradually grew uneasy.
So he conspired with his deputy Dòu Sīlǐ and others to rebel,
intending to plunder the commandery
and flee to Jiāngdōng.
The supervisor had about three hundred troops under his command,
all of whom feared Hé Qún and obeyed him.
It happened that the prefect Dù Zhēn sent an invitation for the supervisor to attend a night banquet.
When the invitation arrived,
Hé Qún said to Dòu Sīlǐ and the others:
"Opportunity waits for no one,
time will not come again.
We must act tonight,
without regret."
Dòu Sīlǐ and the others secretly prepared their troops.
By late afternoon,
the supervisor went to the banquet.
Hé Qún ordered a dozen or so trusted men to follow him,
instructing them:
"At the third watch,
you will set fire to the gate of the Six Offices courtyard,
and the monastery will surely respond with fire."
That evening, at the first watch,
Hé Qún was resting in his tent when
he dreamed that Sòng Róu shouted at him:
"My vengeance is avenged."
Startled awake,
he summoned Dòu Sīlǐ and told him,
to which Dòu Sīlǐ replied:
"This is just a dream,
what can it do?"
As the second watch was halfway through,
Hé Qún ordered his men to don armor.
He sent one soldier to climb the large catalpa tree west of the Buddha Hall,
to spy on the inner city.
Before long,
the commandery's patrol commander arrived at the monastery,
opened the gate and entered,
reaching the corner of the hall.
Looking up at the treetop,
he grew suspicious,
and ordered torches to be lit below.
There he saw an armored man crouching among the branches.
As he was questioning him,
Hé Qún repeatedly shouted:
"A soldier had a malaria attack
and fled up there,
nothing more."
The patrol commander's expression changed,
and he rushed out to order an alert.
Hé Qún called Dòu Sīlǐ and the others, saying:
"The situation is urgent,
if we do not act quickly,
we will be destroyed by these fools."
So he gathered his men,
broke through the east gate, and fled.
After traveling about two stops,
Hé Qún's mind grew unsettled,
unsure where to go.
His men gradually began to desert.
Exhausted, they rested by the water,
when they heard the distant sound of urgent drums.
They were at the northeastern corner of Púshè Slope.
Dòu Sīlǐ realized
"realized" (in the Ming manuscript, it is written as "stepped back").
He stepped forward,
asking to speak in secret.
As Hé Qún leaned his ear close,
Dòu Sīlǐ drew his sword
and swiftly cut off Hé Qún's head, which fell to the ground.
The remaining troops scattered in chaos.
Dòu Sīlǐ took Hé Qún's head,
and at dawn,
returned to submit to the supervisor.
He was pardoned for his crime
and ordered to recruit the scattered soldiers.
From "Sān Shuǐ Xiǎo Lù."
Wáng Biǎo
Péi Guāngyuǎn from Hédōng,
in the year Jǐyǒu of the Táng dynasty's Lóngjì era,
was appointed as the Wèinán County Lieutenant in Huázhōu.
He was greedy by nature,
covetous of goods and bribes,
and enforced harsh laws with severe punishments,
so the officials and people feared and detested him.
He was especially fond of playing polo,
and even during the sweltering heat of midsummer,
he would not take a break.
He kept a white horse,
strong and swift, capable of galloping,
but it eventually succumbed to exhaustion in the scorching summer months,
and died on the open field.
There was a village head named Wáng Biǎo,
whose family was wealthy,
but he had lost his wife early.
He had only one son,
about seven or eight years old.
The boy was fair-skinned, handsome, and well-mannered,
and often accompanied his father to the county office.
Péi Guāngyuǎn saw him and took pity on him,
calling him into his residence,
and giving him clothes and toys.
From then on, this became a regular occurrence.
Péi Guāngyuǎn had a close associate tell Wáng Biǎo:
"I have no son.
If you can give this child to me,
I will treat you well,
and even if you commit a major offense,
I will not hold it against you."
Wáng Biǎo replied:
"I am indeed lowly and insignificant,
subject to the control of my superiors,
but when it comes to my own flesh and blood,
I cannot comply with your request.
Moreover, this child lost his mother in infancy,
how can he be separated from his father again?
Even if I incur your displeasure for this,
I am willing to accept it."
Péi Guāngyuǎn heard this and harbored resentment.
A few days later,
he sent Wáng Biǎo on a mission to Cáonán,
and had bandits lie in wait at the border,
where they killed him and took his son.
In the spring of the year Xīnhài during the Dàshùn era,
Péi Guāngyuǎn fell ill,
and after more than a month, he became weak and exhausted.
At times, as if possessed by ghosts,
he would speak alone, saying:
"Wáng Biǎo has come,
I must return your son."
Then he spoke as Wáng Biǎo:
"Although I was a minor official,
I was cautious and discreet, never having committed any offense,
yet I was met with brutal harm,
and my infant child was taken by force.
I have already appealed to Heaven,
and now I come to demand your life."
Then he spoke on his own behalf:
"Now I will return your son,
and perform grand meritorious deeds for you,
offering you abundant underworld money.
Will you spare me?"
The response was:
"No."
A moment later, he said:
"The white horse has come."
Then he spoke as the horse:
"Being ridden by humans
naturally has its limits.
As for carrying loads and galloping,
there are also normal limits.
The toil of physical strength
is something I dare not shirk.
But how could you, in the height of summer,
play polo without cease,
causing my humble life to perish?
It was truly because of you.
I have already appealed to Heaven,
and now I come to take you."
Again, he spoke on his own behalf,
pleading as he had with Wáng Biǎo,
but it was ultimately ignored.
A few days later,
Péi Guāngyuǎn died.
From "Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú"
The Gānníng Prime Minister
In the second year of Gānníng of the Táng dynasty,
Wáng Xíngyú from Bīnzhōu joined Lǐ Màozhēn and Hán Jiàn in an audience with the emperor,
determined to carry out a plan to depose and install a new ruler.
The emperor, seeing the three commanders arrive together,
knew there must be a sinister plot,
so he ascended the tower to meet them.
He said to them:
"You have come without being summoned.
What is your intention?"
Lǐ Màozhēn and the others were drenched in sweat and unable to reply,
only saying:
"The southern and northern offices are disrupting court affairs."
They then criticized Wéi Zhāodù for his failed strategy in the campaign against Xīchuān,
and Lǐ Xī, whose appointment edict
was wept over by Liú Chónglǔ,
saying, "Your Majesty should not have appointed him against public opinion."
They then ordered the eunuchs to issue an edict to harm Wéi Zhāodù and others,
after which the three commanders returned to their garrisons.
Both inside and outside the court, people felt this was unjust.
Earlier, when Wáng Xíngyú was acting arrogantly,
the court intended to confer upon him the title of Shàngshū Lìng.
Wéi Zhāodù strongly opposed it, saying:
"Tàizōng used this office to consolidate power and ascend the throne.
Later, Guō Zǐyí, despite his merits across six reigns,
though he held great fame,
remained modest and yielding throughout his life.
How can such a title be lightly bestowed upon Wáng Xíngyú?"
He instead proposed conferring the title of Shàngfù,
and for this, he incurred Wáng Xíngyú's resentment and was later killed.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàishī.
Lǐ Xī, whose courtesy name was Mínwàng,
had his appointment edict issued,
but Liú Chónglǔ embraced it and wept,
so he was reassigned as the Tàizǐ Shàofù.
He then submitted ten memorials
and five essays admonishing against slander,
seeking to clear his name.
Later, he eventually rose to a high position
and exposed Liú Chónglǔ's misdeeds.
At the time, his colleague Cuī Zhāowěi had long been at odds with Wéi Zhāodù and Lǐ Xī.
Wáng Xíngyú controlled the court,
and sent his assistant judge Cuī Chán to the capital to handle affairs.
Cuī Chán colluded with Cuī Zhāowěi,
and through him conveyed messages.
As a result, Wáng Xíngyú led the three garrisons to coerce the emperor,
and Lǐ Xī also met with disaster.
His son, Lǐ Miǎn,
a man of great talent,
was killed on the same day.
Lǐ Xī authored a hundred volumes of books,
which were called the "Lǐ Shūlóu,"
and he was posthumously granted the title of Sītú.
After Lǐ Kèyòng from Tàiyuán defeated Wáng Xíngyú,
Cuī Zhāowěi was demoted and ordered to commit suicide.
Emperor Zhāohuáng gnashed his teeth and issued an edict to arrest Cuī Chán,
which was also evidence of retribution for injustice.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Wáng Jiǎnyì
Wáng Jiǎnyì, a Simǎ of Hóngzhōu during the Táng dynasty,
once suddenly fell ill.
A lump-like growth formed in his abdomen,
moving up and down with his breath,
attacking his internal organs,
and he remained bedridden for over a month.
One night,
the lump surged upward and struck his heart,
and he sank into a deep, death-like state.
Only after several hours did he awaken.
He said to his relatives:
"At first, I dreamed of a ghostly messenger
who called himself Dīng Yìng.
He held a warrant in his hand and said:
'By order of the City God,
I have come to apprehend Wáng Jiǎnyì.'
I then followed the messenger,
and after about ten *lǐ* or so,
we arrived at the City God's temple.
People at the gate said to each other:
'Wáng Jūn in the mortal world
was quite known for his good deeds;
he should not yet have died.
How did he come here so suddenly?'
Soon I was brought before the City God.
I pleaded to him:
'My time to die has not yet come;
I beg you to release me and send me back.'
The City God ordered his attendants to bring the register.
After checking it,
he said to Jiǎnyì:
'You are still allotted five more years of life.
You may go back for now.'"
After five years,
the lump in his abdomen again surged upward and struck his heart.
After a short while, he revived and said:
"I just went to the underworld court,
where I was accused by a young servant boy.
His accusations were relentless and impossible to refute."
His wife asked who this young servant was.
Jiǎnyì said:
"He was a page boy I employed in the past.
He was in the prime of his youth,
but due to a chance incident of discipline,
he ended up dying.
The lump in my abdomen is that young servant haunting me.
I also saw Zhōng Chū, the former prefect of Jízhōu,
bearing a large iron cangue,
wearing a yellow cloth garment,
with his hands and feet shackled.
The underworld court is investigating a case of unjust killing,
and the interrogation is very urgent."
His wife then questioned:
"That servant boy was lowly and humble;
how dare he act like this?"
Jiǎnyì said:
"In the mortal world, there may be distinctions of noble and base,
but in the underworld, all are equal."
His wife asked what crime is most severe in the underworld.
Jiǎnyì said:
"Nothing surpasses killing a person."
Having said this, he died.
From *Bàoyìng Lù*.
Fán Guāng
Fán Guāng, a Xiāng Yúhòu of Jiāozhǐ Commandery,
was attending to official business in his government office
at midday
when suddenly wind and thunder arose.
Guāng, along with his son and a yellow dog they kept, were all struck dead by lightning.
During the thunder strike, his wife
suddenly saw a Daoist priest
who lifted her and placed her body elsewhere,
thus allowing her to escape.
People asked her the reason.
His wife said:
"Once, two commoners were involved in a lawsuit against each other
and were both imprisoned.
The one without merit bribed Guāng,
and Guāng immediately released him.
The one with merit was severely tortured,
and forced to confess.
The food and drink sent to him
were all seized by Guāng and given to his son and dog to eat.
As the prisoner was starving and near death,
he let down his hair in prison and appealed to Heaven.
Not many days later,
this retribution befell Guāng and the others."
From *Bàoyìng Lù*.
Lǐ Yànguāng
Lǐ Yànguāng was the Dū Zhǐhuīshǐ of Qín, both internal and external.
His commander, the Zhōngshū Lìng Lǐ Chóng, entrusted him with authority,
granting him sole power over life and death.
He was cruel and corrupt, amassing wealth through bribery,
and many suffered wrongful deaths at his hands.
There was a subordinate general, a certain Fán,
who owned a mule
that was exceptionally fine and swift.
Yànguāng sent someone to convey his desire to obtain it.
Fán was reluctant and refused to give it,
which caused Yànguāng to harbor resentment.
Using another matter as a pretext, he framed Fán and imprisoned him.
He fabricated a confession,
and when the commander was drunk, he presented it to him.
The commander, without further investigation,
approved, and Yànguāng, falsely claiming the order, had Fán executed.
As Fán faced execution, he said:
"If death brings no consciousness, then so be it.
But if there is consciousness after death,
I will surely seek retribution without delay."
Before ten days had passed after his death,
Yànguāng fell ill.
Fán's form appeared to him,
never leaving, day or night.
Sometimes he came from the roof,
sometimes he emerged from the walls.
Holding a staff, he approached,
personally administering whippings and beatings.
All the attendants, young and old, fled in terror.
Then, the sounds of judgment and punishment could be heard,
unbearable to endure.
Yànguāng could only cry out, "I deserve death!"
This continued for over a month before he finally died.
Since then, those in power have taken this as a warning.
From *Yùtáng Xiánhuà*.
Hóu Wēn
During the period when the Liáng dynasty and Héběi were locked in conflict,
there was a deputy general named Hóu Wēn,
renowned in the army for his bravery.
Hè Guī was the commander,
and being authoritarian and jealous of those surpassing him,
he found a pretext to have Hóu Wēn killed.
Afterwards, Guī fell seriously ill.
On his deathbed,
those around him heard him call out "Hóu Jiǔ" for several days,
uttering words of plea and supplication,
deeply condemning himself.
An attendant saw a man emerge from the wall,
drag Guī to the ground,
and as the attendant cried out in alarm
and others rushed in,
Guī was already dead.
In the past, during the Hàn dynasty, Dòu Yīng and Guàn Fū were framed and killed by Wǔ'ān Hóu Tián Fén.
When Fén later fell ill,
a shaman who could see ghosts
witnessed Dòu and Guàn flanking him and beating him.
Fén ultimately died.
These events are quite similar.
From *Yùtáng Xiánhuà*.
Shěn Shēn
Mǎ Xīshēng, the military governor of Húnán,
during his tenure, often acted arbitrarily and recklessly.
There was a merchant named Shěn Shēn
who frequently traveled between Fānyú.
The ruler of Guǎng treated him favorably.
He ordered him to go north to seek a precious belt.
Shěn purchased a jade belt in the Luò-Biàn region,
which was a rare treasure.
On his return journey, passing through Xiāngtán,
Xīshēng secretly learned of this.
He summoned Shěn to his yamen,
treated him to wine and food,
and late at night sent him back to his inn.
He had previously instructed the military patrol
to kill Shěn for violating the night curfew.
The people of Xiāng all heard of this,
and none did not sigh in pity.
Afterwards, this merchant was often seen haunting the place,
sometimes on the roof ridge,
sometimes leaning against the railings,
never staying in one place.
Not long after,
Xīshēng died suddenly.
His younger brother, Mǎ Xīfàn, succeeded him,
and returned the jade belt to the man from Guǎng.
From *Běimèng Suǒyán*.
Fǎcáo Lì
In Lúlíng, there was a law clerk
who once prosecuted a monk,
falsely leading to his death,
and submitted the completed case to the prefecture.
That day,
his wife and daughter were at home,
sewing by the west window,
when suddenly two attendants in black clothes,
holding documents in their hands,
emerged from the kitchen,
and sternly said to his wife:
"Tell your husband,
do not wrongfully kill the monk."
Then they went out the door and left.
The wife and daughter were both shocked and sweating,
and only after a long while did they venture out.
Looking at their door,
it was still locked as before.
When the clerk returned,
they told him everything in detail.
The clerk was very frightened.
The next day, he intended to secretly retrieve the case file,
but it was already too late.
In the end, the monk was executed.
On the day of the monk's death,
the clerk encountered him on the road.
Despite trying every possible means to offer sacrifices and apologize,
within a month or so, the clerk died.
From "Records of Spirits"
Liú Cún
Liú Cún served as the prefect of Shūzhōu.
He appointed a Confucian scholar, Huò Mǒu, as the drill and training judge,
and trusted him greatly.
Later, due to slander from those around him,
Huò was framed for a crime,
imprisoned,
and Liú Cún reported to the higher authorities requesting his execution.
The military governor of Wú knew Huò was innocent,
and ordered him to be sent to Yángdū,
but Liú Cún had him strangled in prison.
Afterward, Liú Cún was promoted to military commissioner of Èzhōu.
Huò's friend was in Shūzhōu,
and dreamed of Huò, dressed in plain white clothes, emerging from the Temple of the Director of Fate,
clapping his hands and laughing loudly, saying:
"I have already obtained vindication."
Soon after, Liú Cún led troops to campaign against Húnán.
Huò's cousin, Mǎ Yè,
was the prefect of Huángzhōu.
One night, someone knocked on the gate of Qí'ān City, saying:
"The drill and training judge from Shūzhōu, Huò, is going to the front lines.
His horse is sick,
and he requests to borrow a horse from the prefect."
The guards on the wall reported this.
Mǎ Yè sighed and said:
"Lord Liú wrongfully killed Huò.
Now this man is going there.
Could it be that disaster is imminent?"
He then drew several horses on paper,
and burned them by the water's edge.
A few days later, Liú Cún suffered a crushing defeat
and died in battle.
From "Records of Spirits"
Yuánzhōu Record Keeper
The record keeper of Yuánzhōu, a certain Wáng, once prosecuted a robber.
The case was concluded, but an amnesty was declared.
Wáng believed the robber's crime was unforgivable,
so he killed him first and then announced the amnesty.
After being dismissed, he returned to Xīnyù.
A local guest, a certain Féng,
prepared wine and invited Wáng.
He was to go the next day.
That evening, he stayed at a monastery,
where he saw the robber, who said:
"My crime indeed deserved death,
but an amnesty had already been declared.
How dare you conceal the imperial pardon and kill me?
I have now obtained permission from the authorities.
Are you going to the Féng family tomorrow?
You may choose not to go."
After speaking, he vanished.
The monks in the monastery only saw Wáng talking to someone but could not see the other person.
The next day, while drinking,
Wáng suddenly died.
From "Records of Spirits"
Liú Fán
Military officer Liú Fán was by nature strong-willed, upright, and brave.
He was convicted of a crime and exiled to Hǎilíng.
The prefect, Chǔ Rénguī, disliked him,
falsely accused him of plotting rebellion,
and an edict ordered his execution at the market in Hǎilíng.
Before his death, Liú Fán
said to the execution supervisor:
"Tell my sons for me
to place plenty of paper and brushes in my coffin.
I will certainly sue him."
Several years later,
Chǔ Rénguī went to the capital.
His boat was moored at the mouth of the Jìtān River.
In the middle of the night,
he heard continuous calls from the shore:
"Chǔ Rénguī,
do you know you deserve to die?"
Everyone on the boat was startled and got up.
Looking at the shore, they saw no one.
Chǔ Rénguī said to those around him:
"Do you recognize this voice?
It is Liú Fán."
He immediately ordered wine and food
to make offerings and apologize to him.
When Chǔ Rénguī arrived in the capital,
he was imprisoned for cruelty and tyranny.
One night, a prison guard dreamed of a man,
tall, large, and dark-faced,
accompanied by over twenty others,
coming to the prison,
seizing Chǔ Rénguī, and taking him away.
After waking up,
he told this to Chǔ Rénguī's relatives.
One of them beat his chest and sighed, saying:
"My lord is sure to die.
That man is Liú Fán."
That very noon, a palace envoy arrived,
and Chǔ Rénguī was strangled in prison.
From "Records of Spirits"
Wú Jǐng
There was a military officer in Zhèxī named Wú Jǐng.
In the year Dīngyǒu,
he held a vegetarian feast at a monastery in Shítóuchéng.
That evening, after everything was set up,
he suddenly heard the very sorrowful crying of a woman.
At first distant, it gradually drew near,
and soon it was right at the vegetarian feast.
Wú Jǐng then told the monastery monk:
"Years ago, when I followed the army to capture Yùzhāng,
I captured a woman.
She was exceptionally beautiful.
Not long after,
her husband came to ransom her.
The general's orders were strict,
and it was not permissible to allow it.
I killed her immediately.
I have deeply regretted it since.
Today's vegetarian feast
is precisely for her."
He then went with the monk,
and indeed saw the woman there.
The monk prayed and pleaded for her.
The woman said:
"I have come to demand Wú Jǐng's life.
I know nothing else."
She suddenly rushed forward to chase him.
Wú Jǐng ran up to the Buddha hall,
shouting loudly:
"I return your life to you."
Then he collapsed and died.
From "Records of Spirits"
The Child from Gāo'ān Village
In Gāo'ān Village, there was a child working in the fields
who was killed by someone,
and the murderer was not caught.
On the anniversary of his death the following year,
his family held a vegetarian feast for him.
That day,
a child from the same village saw the deceased child, who said to him:
"I am the child from such-and-such family who died.
Today my family is holding a vegetarian feast.
Shall we go together to eat?"
The village child followed him,
and they went to his home.
They sat together on the spirit bed.
When food was offered, they ate,
but the family could not see them.
After a while,
the child's maternal uncle arrived later.
Looking at the spirit bed, he wept.
The child immediately pointed directly at him and said:
"This is the person who killed me.
I loathe seeing him."
Then he left.
After the child left,
the family saw the village child sitting on the spirit bed
and were greatly shocked.
They asked him why he was there.
The child told them everything in detail,
and also said that the child's maternal uncle had killed him.
They then seized the uncle and sent him to the authorities.
He then confessed to the crime.
From "Records of Spirits"
Chén Xūn
Chényì County Clerk Chén Xūn,
whose temperament was rigid and intolerant of others,
was falsely accused of crimes by ten county clerks together,
and was ultimately executed in the marketplace.
When the anniversary of his death arrived the following year,
his family held a vegetarian feast in his honor.
After his wife finished weeping,
she sighed alone before his spirit tablet, saying:
"In life, you were known for your integrity and uprightness.
Now, having been wrongfully dead for over a year,
why is your spirit so silent?"
That evening,
she dreamed of Chén Xūn, who said:
"I was completely unaware of my death.
Only upon hearing your words
did I suddenly realize it.
If that is the case,
I must seek revenge.
However, I cannot rashly enter the government office.
Tomorrow, you must go to the county to appeal the injustice on my behalf,
and I will follow you."
The next day,
his wife went as instructed.
As soon as she left the house,
she saw Chén Xūn following her with a sword in hand.
When they reached the county office,
they encountered one of the clerks who had wronged him on a bridge.
Chén Xūn struck the clerk's head with his sword,
and the clerk immediately fell over and died.
After entering the gate,
Chén Xūn went straight to the clerks' office
and struck them down one by one.
All those hit died.
Of the ten clerks, eight were killed.
The remaining two fled to Línchuān
and thus escaped.
Chén Xūn's home was in Gàizhú,
and the local people often saw his spirit.
They therefore built a shrine for him,
named the Temple of Lord Chén,
and tales of his spiritual power have been passed down to this day.
From *Jìshén Lù*
Zhōng Zūn
Zhōng Zūn, a Dàlǐ Píngshì in Jiāngnán, was the grandson of the Tutor to the Prince of Nánpíng.
Throughout his official posts, he was corrupt and greedy.
Sūn Yuè, a Yuánwàiláng in the Ministry of Waterworks,
had long been aware of his deeds
and secretly reported them to those in power.
Zhōng Zūn was ultimately imprisoned.
When a general pardon was issued, he was stripped of his official status.
Since Zhōng Zūn's crimes occurred before the pardon
and his grandfather had been granted an iron certificate
that pardoned his descendants from death twice,
he went to the capital to plead his case.
The matter was referred to the relevant authorities,
and the Dàlǐ Court reported that the evidence of his corruption was clear.
He was then executed in the marketplace.
Before the execution,
someone offered him wine,
but Zhōng Zūn refused to drink, saying:
"I must lodge a complaint in the underworld;
I cannot allow myself to become drunk."
About a month after Zhōng Zūn's death,
while Sūn Yuè was sitting with guests,
a small green snake emerged from between the roof beams.
When Sūn Yuè saw it,
he stood up in alarm, exclaiming:
"Píngshì Zhōng,
Píngshì Zhōng!"
He turned pale, went inside,
fell ill,
and died the next day.
From *Jìshén Lù*
Wéi Chǔshì
Wéi Chénggāo
was a military officer during the伪-Shǔ period.
There was a monk named Xíngzhēn, who held the title of Dàizhào,
and resided on Chángpíng Mountain in Shǔzhōu.
He once built a wooden pagoda at the local Lóngxīng Temple,
with a total of thirteen stories,
costing tens of thousands in coins and silver.
It was soon burned down by a heavenly fire.
It was only on the third attempt at construction
that he succeeded.
People believed he possessed alchemical arts.
When Wéi Chénggāo was appointed to administer Méizhōu,
he summoned Xíngzhēn to the commandery.
In the commandery, there was a Sīmǎ named Lú Jìngzhī,
who made his living through trade.
Wéi Chénggāo once said to him:
"When I was in the army,
I served alongside Xíngzhēn.
We met a certain Wéi Chǔshì,
who taught us the method for making gold.
Now that I have grown old and humble,
I have summoned Xíngzhēn
to refine the old formula together.
Once the elixir is completed,
I will share the benefits with you.
How about you give up your life as a merchant?"
Lú Jìngzhī agreed.
Just as the elixir was nearing completion,
Prefect Wéi was convicted of a crime and demoted to Cānjūn of Màozhōu.
As he was about to depart,
Lú escorted him to Máyílǜ.
Prefect Wéi sank the elixir cauldron into the river
and said to Lú:
"I am guilty!
Earlier, the Wéi Chǔshì who taught us the method—
I killed him to silence him.
Now, with this matter,
the elixir was about to succeed, yet disaster struck.
Is this not divine retribution?"
When the Shǔ state underwent changes
and resisted the army of the Prince of Wèi,
he was executed.
From *Běimèng Suǒyán*
Zhāng Jìn
Wáng Yǔnguāng, a Jǐshìzhōng in the伪-Shǔ period, had a harsh and severe temperament.
When clerks or commoners committed offenses,
he showed no leniency.
When he presided over the Penal Court,
the court's Zhàngzhíguān, Zhāng Jìn,
recited a quatrain by Jiāng Yígōng, the magistrate of Huǒjǐng County, titled *Ode to Jǐshìzhōng Wáng*, to a young servant in his residence:
"His father was no slave of Dàojùn;
Why is Yǔnguāng such a dwarf?
If given a pair of leather trousers,
Could he lift the Heavenly King's left foot?"
The servant remembered two lines
and often recited them.
When Wáng Yǔnguāng asked who taught him,
he replied:
"Zhàngzhíguān Zhāng Jìn."
Wáng Yǔnguāng was furious.
He soon reported that Zhāng Jìn had accepted bribes from criminals,
and Zhāng Jìn was executed under the severest punishment.
Later, Wáng Yǔnguāng fell ill with chills and fever.
He saw Zhāng Jìn holding a torch, burning his limbs,
and loudly shouting, "I demand your life!"
Wáng Yǔnguāng repeatedly shouted at him to leave, but to no avail.
He suffered extreme pain
and died after several days.
From *Jǐngjiè Lù*
Hǎo Pǔ
Hǎo Pǔ, a clerk of Huáyáng County in the伪-Shǔ period, was daily pursuing households in arrears on taxes.
Jiē Pànsī Gōu Lǐ sent his maidservant Ā Yí to the county office,
and instructed Hǎo Pǔ, saying:
"Do not detain her;
allow the remaining tax to be paid at a later date."
Hǎo Pǔ did not agree.
He sentenced Ā Yí to five strokes
and released her only after the tax was paid.
The following year,
the county office divided the property of commoner Zhāng Qióng's family.
Hǎo Pǔ took twenty thousand coins.
Zhāng Qióng filed a formal complaint.
The Jiēsī investigated the matter.
When Gōu Lǐ saw Hǎo Pǔ,
he laughed heartily and said:
"So you've come today!
Do not hope to live;
death is certain."
He ordered the clerk Rǔ Xūn to fabricate charges against him,
and Hǎo Pǔ was executed.
A few days later,
Rǔ Xūn saw Hǎo Pǔ coming to demand his life
and died suddenly the next day.
When Gōu Lǐ rose in the morning,
he suddenly saw Hǎo Pǔ entering the hall,
grabbing and beating him.
He subsequently developed a back sore and died.
From *Jǐngjiè Lù*
Péi Yuán
On the birthday of Wáng Zōng'àn, the military governor of Níngjiāng in the伪-Shǔ period,
the subordinate counties under his jurisdiction
all pooled money and goods
as congratulatory gifts.
Péi Yuán, the magistrate of Wūshān, citing the poverty of the registered households,
alone offered no tribute.
Wáng Zōng'àn was greatly angered.
He summoned Péi Yuán
and falsely accused him of other matters.
He had Péi Yuán thrown alive into the waters of Yànyù Duī.
For three days, the corpse did not drift away.
Wáng Zōng'àn sent men to pull it downstream,
but by the next day, it had floated back upstream against the current,
standing upright on the waves,
gazing directly at the government office.
Wáng Zōng'àn felt deeply uneasy,
his spirit troubled and disturbed.
He ultimately fell ill and died suddenly.
From *Běimèng Suǒyán*
Sū Duó
Wáng Zōngxìn, a prince of the false Shu state,
was stationed in Fèngzhōu.
There was a wrestler named Sū Duó,
to whom he entrusted patrol duties.
Sū Duó often clashed with Sūn Yányīng, one of Zōngxìn's attendants.
One day during his leisure, Zōngxìn ascended a tower,
and from there he saw Sū Duó
dressed in a brocade robe with a belt,
looking as if he were about to embark on a long journey.
Zōngxìn was surprised.
Duó was originally from Qí,
so Yányīng took the opportunity to slander him, saying:
"Although Sū Duó has been supported by Your Lordship,
he harbors treacherous intentions
and has long wanted to flee."
Zōngxìn was furious
and immediately ordered Duó seized.
First, his tongue was cut out and his flesh sliced,
and then he was beheaded.
Later, when Yányīng rebelled,
he was executed in exactly the same manner
as Duó had been.
From *Jǐngjiè Lù*.
Zhào Ān
In Shu, there was a wealthy man named Guō Jǐngzhāng.
While drunk,
he struck a poor man named Zhào Ān
with a wine pot,
and the spout pierced Ān's brain, killing him.
Ān had a son,
so Jǐngzhāng gave him a large sum of gold and silk
to conceal the matter,
and no one knew about it.
Later, a sore suddenly appeared on Jǐngzhāng's head,
about three to four fen deep,
exposing the bone.
Pus and blood flowed incessantly,
and at times he seemed to see Zhào Ān.
The sore penetrated his throat,
and he died.
From *Jǐngjiè Lù*.
Kētóu Shī
During the Liang dynasty, there was a monk named Kētóu Shī
who was extremely diligent in his practice.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng held him in great respect and trust.
One day, the emperor sent a messenger to summon Kētóu Shī.
At the time, the emperor was playing chess with someone
and was about to capture a group of stones.
He responded without thinking,
"Kill it."
The messenger immediately went out and beheaded the monk.
After the emperor finished his game,
he said,
"Summon the master."
The messenger replied,
"Earlier, Your Majesty ordered him killed,
and I have already carried it out."
The emperor sighed and said,
"What did the master say
before he died?"
The messenger said,
"The master said:
'This poor monk is not guilty.
In a previous life, when I was a novice,
I was digging with a spade
and accidentally cut an earthworm in two.
Your Majesty was that earthworm at the time,
and this is my retribution.'"
The emperor wept with regret and remorse,
but it was too late.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Táng Shào
Táng Shào was exceptionally intelligent from a young age
and remembered his previous life in detail,
but he never spoke of it to anyone,
not even to his wife or children.
Later, he served as a *jǐshìzhōng*.
Living across the street from him in the same neighborhood
was a gentleman named Lǐ Miǎo.
On his days off,
Shào often invited Miǎo over to chat and laugh with him,
and their friendship grew very close.
Sometimes Shào would prepare a meal,
and the two would dine together in the main hall,
but Miǎo never knew the reason for their closeness.
Shào's wife questioned him, saying,
"You have a great reputation
and hold a high and prestigious office.
You should be careful about whom you associate with.
Lǐ Miǎo is not your social equal,
yet you constantly socialize with him.
I secretly think this is unwise."
Shào remained silent for a while,
then said,
"This is something you cannot understand.
My bond with Lǐ Miǎo is deeper than you know."
In the early Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
a military exercise was held at Líshān.
Shào was then acting as Minister of Rites.
Emperor Xuánzōng took up the drumstick to beat the drum,
but before three rounds had been completed,
Guō Yuánzhèn, the Minister of War, abruptly ordered the ceremony to be declared finished.
The emperor was furious,
and had Yuánzhèn dragged down and seated beneath the army banner.
Zhāng Yuè knelt before the emperor's horse and pleaded,
saying that Yuánzhèn had rendered great service in protecting the state
and deserved to be spared the death penalty.
Yuánzhèn was thus released,
but the emperor's anger remained, and he ordered Shào beheaded.
The day before this,
Shào said to his wife and children,
"I have been close to Lǐ Miǎo,
and I must speak of this before I die.
The time has come."
He then briefly explained:
"Since childhood, I have remembered my previous life.
Tomorrow, during the military exercise,
I will not escape death.
In my previous life, I was the daughter of a certain family.
When I came of age,
I married the son of the Wáng family of Bàlíng.
My mother-in-law treated me very strictly.
When I was seventeen,
on the day before the winter solstice,
my mother-in-law ordered me to personally prepare the offerings.
After finishing,
I was extremely tired and weary.
But my mother-in-law then ordered me to sew a silk skirt,
to be worn at dawn
to receive guests.
I worked by the lamp,
worried I wouldn't finish in time,
and did not rest even late into the night.
Suddenly, a dog burst through the door into the room,
bumped into the lamp,
and knocked it over.
The oil spilled all over the skirt.
I was both frightened and angry,
so I scolded the dog.
The dog ran and dashed against the door,
causing it to swing shut.
The dog, flustered, retreated and hid under the bed.
I lit another candle
and tried to clean the stain on the skirt,
but it was a complete mess.
Fearing my mother-in-law's severe reprimand
and resentful of the dog for knocking over the lamp,
I lifted the bed
and stabbed the dog with scissors.
I happened to hit its neck,
and one blade of the scissors broke.
I used the other blade to stab it again,
and soon the dog died.
The next morning, I took the skirt to explain to my mother-in-law.
Just as she was scolding me,
my husband happened to return from outside.
Upon hearing what happened,
he pulled the dead dog from under the bed
and presented it to my mother-in-law,
which somewhat eased the situation.
I died at the age of nineteen
and was reborn into this body.
The dog I killed back then
is today's Lǐ Miǎo.
My death tomorrow
is due to retribution.
The one who executes me will surely be Lǐ Miǎo.
Retribution is a constant principle of the universe.
Do not be alarmed."
The next day, during the military exercise,
Shào was executed due to a mistake.
Indeed, it was Lǐ Miǎo who wielded the sword.
The first strike did not kill him, and the sword broke.
Miǎo took another sword and struck again,
and only then did Shào die.
The retribution of life and death
is indeed like shadow and echo.
Even the breaking of the sword was no different from before.
Clearly, the spirits do not deceive.
The *Tángshū* records that Emperor Míng later regretted killing Shào
and, because Lǐ Miǎo carried out the execution too hastily,
he never employed him again.
From *Yìzá Piān*.
Lǐ Shēng
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Lǐ.
His home was in the Héshuò region.
In his youth, he possessed great physical strength,
was arrogant and fond of chivalrous exploits,
paid no heed to minor rules of conduct,
and often associated with frivolous and dissolute youths.
Only after he was over twenty years old
did he change his ways and apply himself to studying,
composing songs and poems,
for which people praised him quite a bit.
He served repeatedly as an official in Héshuò,
eventually rising to the position of Registrar and Military Advisor of Shēnzhōu.
Lǐ was handsome and dignified in appearance,
skilled in conversation and wit,
thoroughly versed in official affairs,
honest, cautious, intelligent, and capable.
As for polo and drinking,
he was also known to be proficient,
and he was greatly appreciated by the Prefect.
At that time, Wáng Wǔjùn commanded the Chéngdé army.
Relying on his achievements and the support of the masses,
he disregarded laws and regulations,
and the prefects of the subordinate commanderies feared him and viewed him with apprehension.
Once, he sent his son, Wáng Shìzhēn, to tour the subordinate districts.
When he arrived at Shēnzhōu,
the Prefect prepared a grand feast with oxen and wine,
arranged musical entertainment at his residence,
and held a banquet for Shìzhēn.
The Prefect feared Wǔjùn,
and therefore served Shìzhēn with extreme deference,
and furthermore, worried that someone might offend Shìzhēn through drink,
for this reason, among his subordinate officials and guests,
he dared not summon a single one.
Shìzhēn was greatly pleased,
thinking that no other commandery could match this.
They drank until nightfall,
when Shìzhēn then said:
"I am fortunate that Your Excellency treats me so generously,
and I wish to enjoy myself fully tonight.
Surely there are no distinguished guests?
I would like you to summon them."
The Prefect said:
"This remote commandery has no notable figures.
I fear the authority of the Vice-Commander-in-Chief"
(Shìzhēn was then the Vice-Commander-in-Chief under Wǔjùn's military governorship.)
"and dare not invite any other guests to attend the banquet.
Only the Registrar and Military Advisor, a certain Lǐ,
is sufficiently qualified to accompany us in conversation and laughter."
Shìzhēn said:
"Just summon him."
Thereupon, Lǐ was summoned to enter,
and he hurried forward and bowed.
Shìzhēn looked at him,
his expression turning very angry,
yet then he ordered him to be seated.
Lǐ's demeanor grew even more respectful,
but Shìzhēn became increasingly displeased,
glaring, looking around, and rolling up his sleeves,
showing none of the earlier cheer.
The Prefect was terrified,
not knowing what this meant.
He glanced at Lǐ,
who looked ashamed and was sweating,
unable to hold his cup.
Everyone present was astonished.
After a while,
Shìzhēn shouted to his attendants,
"Bind this Lǐ and imprison him!"
The attendants immediately seized Lǐ by the sleeve and hurried him away,
shackled him, and threw him in prison.
Shortly after, Shìzhēn resumed drinking merrily as before.
When dawn approached and the banquet ended,
the Prefect, both alarmed and fearful,
secretly sent someone to the prison to question Lǐ, saying:
"Your demeanor was extremely respectful,
and you never spoke.
Clearly, you did not offend Lord Wáng.
Do you yourself know the reason?"
Lǐ wept sorrowfully for a long time,
then said:
"I have often heard Buddhists speak of retribution in the present life.
Now I understand it.
In my youth, I was poor,
with no means to support myself,
and therefore I enjoyed associating with knights-errant,
often plundering the wealth and silks of the villagers.
I would often gallop on horseback with a bow at my waist,
traveling back and forth on the main roads,
covering over a hundred lǐ in a day.
One day, I encountered a young man
whipping a fine mule,
carrying two large sacks.
Coveting his possessions,
and seeing that the surroundings were sheer cliffs thousands of rèn high,
with the sun gradually setting and darkness falling,
I forcefully pushed him,
and he fell down the cliff.
I immediately drove his mule swiftly to an inn,
opened his sacks,
and obtained over a hundred bolts of fine silk.
From then on, my family's circumstances gradually improved.
I then broke my bow and arrows,
shut my door and studied,
eventually becoming an official and reaching my present position.
To this day, it has been exactly twenty-seven years.
Last evening, when Your Excellency ordered me to attend Lord Wáng's banquet,
upon entering and seeing Lord Wáng's face,
I realized he was the young man I killed long ago.
After that single bow,
my heart was filled with shame and terror.
I knew my death was imminent,
and now I merely stretch my neck awaiting the blade.
What more is there to say?
Please convey my thanks to Your Excellency.
Fortunately, you know me well.
I dare to entrust my affairs after death to you."
After a while,
Shìzhēn, sobering from his drunkenness,
suddenly summoned his attendants,
ordering them to go to Lǐ and fetch his head.
("Go to Lǐ and fetch his head." The Ming manuscript reads: "Go and bring Lǐ's head here.")
The attendants immediately beheaded Lǐ in prison and presented the head.
Shìzhēn examined it closely and laughed.
Afterwards, he again drank heavily with the Prefect in the commandery office.
When he was drunk,
the Prefect, seizing the moment of cheer,
rose and said:
"I, lacking talent,
am fortunate to govern this commandery.
That the Vice-Commander-in-Chief has condescended to inspect our flawed administration,
and with leniency has not imposed punishment,
is a profound kindness.
Yesterday, the Vice-Commander-in-Chief ordered me to summon other guests.
This subordinate commandery is remote and small, without distinguished guests,
insufficient to provide worthy company for the joyous banquet.
I privately thought that Lǐ was a good drinker,
so I requested to summon him.
Yet Lǐ was foolish and stupid,
unfamiliar with ritual and law,
greatly offending Your Excellency.
This is truly my crime.
Now that Your Excellency has already executed him,
it is fitting.
However, there is something I still do not understand.
I dare to ask, what was Lǐ's crime?
I wish to hear it clearly enumerated,
so that it may serve as a warning for the future."
Shìzhēn laughed and said: "Lǐ committed no crime.
It is just that the moment I saw him,
I felt an intense anger stirring in my heart,
and already had the intention to kill him.
Now that he is killed,
I myself do not know the reason why.
Say no more about it."
After the banquet ended,
the Prefect secretly inquired about Shìzhēn's age.
He was twenty-seven years old.
It was exactly the year Lǐ killed the young man
that Shìzhēn was born into the Wáng family.
The Prefect sighed in wonder for a long time,
and then used his own family wealth to give Lǐ a lavish burial.
From the "Xuānshì Zhì."
The Daughter of Lú Shūlún
South of Cháng'ān,
there was once a monk who went to beg for food at noon.
By chance, he saw a young woman picking mulberry leaves in a tree.
He asked her:
"Nearby here, where are there any pious households
where I might beg for a meal?"
The young woman said:
"Three or four lǐ from here,
there is the Wáng family.
They are currently preparing a vegetarian feast.
They will surely be pleased to see a monk arrive.
You should go quickly."
The monk went in the direction she pointed.
Indeed, there was a group of monks
just about to take their seats.
They were very pleased.
They invited him in.
After the meal,
the mistress of the house was surprised that he had arrived so timely.
She asked him about it.
The monk told her everything truthfully.
The husband and wife were both astonished and said:
"Please come with us
to visit this young woman."
So they all went together.
She was still in the mulberry tree.
She was the daughter of a villager named Lú Shūlún.
Seeing the old man and woman,
she hurriedly climbed down,
abandoned her leaf basket, and ran home.
The two followed, chasing after her.
When they reached her home,
her parents already knew them.
The young woman entered her room,
barred the door with her bed,
making it firmly impossible to open.
Her mother, startled, asked her,
saying:
"Today at our home we prepared a vegetarian feast.
A monk said a young lady sent him.
We performed this act of merit,
but we never told anyone.
It's strange that the young lady knew.
That's why we came to see,
it's nothing else."
Her mother pushed the door, telling her to come out.
The girl firmly refused to come out.
Her mother then scolded her.
The girl said:
"I don't wish to see these old soldier and old crone.
Is that even a crime?"
Her mother said:
"The old man and woman from the neighborhood have come to see you.
For what reason won't you come out?"
The two became even more perplexed.
"異" originally written as "厚",
corrected according to the Míng manuscript.
They entreated her.
The girl suddenly cried out loudly:
"On such-and-such year, month, and day,
where are the father and two sons who sold Hu sheep now?"
The two then hurried out,
not daring to look back.
After they left,
her mother asked her.
She answered:
"In my previous life, I once sold sheep.
I came from Xiàzhōu,
and stayed overnight at this old man's estate.
My father and my two brothers were all killed by them,
and our goods were plundered.
In my previous life, I was then reborn as their son.
I was clever and sharp-witted beyond others,
and they doted on me greatly.
At fifteen I fell ill,
and at twenty I finally died.
The medical expenses they spent on me,
already exceeded several times what they had stolen.
They also held a vegetarian feast for me every year on the anniversary of my death,
husband and wife weeping bitterly.
I reckon their tears amount to over three or two dàn.
It happened that a monk asked where to beg for food,
so I directed him there.
This too was the debt being repaid."
From then on, the old man and woman never again held vegetarian feasts.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Cuī Wúyǐn
During the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
Cuī Wúyǐn of Bólíng told of a relative and friend:
"There was a certain Dù of the southern city,
who once, at the Zhāotí Temple in Biànzhōu,
was sitting and talking with the guest-master monk.
Suddenly, a visiting monk appeared,
and between his face, nose, and forehead,
there was an old knife scar,
running horizontally across his face.
He was then questioned about its origin.
After a long while, the monk, with a pained frown, said:
'My family is in Liáng,
where my parents and elder brother and sister-in-law live.
My elder brother made his living by trading goods from the rivers and lakes.
In the first year,
he returned to Dàliáng from Jiāngnán,
having doubled his profit.
In the second year, he went and did not return.
In the third year,
a fellow traveler said:
"Your elder brother drowned in wind and waves."
My parents and sister-in-law had not yet completed their mourning period
when suddenly a merchant from Hànnán arrived in Liáng,
seeking and calling for someone by my father's name.
I, at the Xiàngguó Temple,
answered, "Yes."
The merchant said:
"I have news from your elder brother."
I was both shocked and overjoyed, speechless for a moment,
then invited him to my home,
informed my parents,
and he said:
"Your son's elder brother suffered losses trading in Jiāngxī,
and so drifted to Hànnán.
A junior officer took pity on him,
reported to the commanding general,
and he is now in Hànnán.
Although his funds are nearly exhausted,
his clothing and bedding seem sufficient.
Due to his humble and impoverished circumstances,
he has not yet been able to return for a visit.
Therefore, he entrusted me to deliver this message."
My parents and sister-in-law wept uncontrollably, overcome by grief and joy.
The next day,
my parents sent me to Hànnán
to visit my elder brother.
I had traveled for about seven or eight days,
entering the Nányáng region,
when evening fell.
I passed through a great marsh,
where the east-west road ended,
and no human dwellings were in sight.
Dark clouds gathered from all sides.
As dusk deepened,
I encountered two or three scattered households
and wished to seek lodging.
The family said:
"Why has the Master come here?
Just two nights ago, there was a murderer ahead,
still being pursued and not yet caught.
The search is very urgent.
Lodging here is certainly not possible.
Three to five lǐ south from here,
there is a Zhāotí temple.
The Master can stay there."
I therefore
"I therefore" – these two characters were originally missing,
added based on the Míng dynasty manuscript.
spoke and went on my way.
The gloomy wind grew stronger,
and a pattering rain began to fall.
After about four or five lǐ,
I turned into a desolate marsh,
not knowing what to do,
and simply walked on.
After a short while,
a candlelight appeared ahead.
At first it seemed close,
but it took nearly ten lǐ to reach it.
The wind and rain intensified,
and without waiting to knock, I entered,
arriving at the hall and courtyard.
It was silent, with no living person,
but the room was full of corpses.
While I was looking around,
a clap of thunder sounded,
and I was chased by a woman's corpse.
I fled outside again.
Running for seven or eight lǐ,
I reached a house.
The rain had stopped,
and the moon shone faintly.
So I entered that house.
Outside the central gate was a small hall,
and in the hall was a bed.
Before I could settle down to rest,
suddenly a man,
over seven chǐ tall,
holding a white blade,
entered through the door.
Terrified, I
stood in a corner against the wall.
The man with the white blade sat on the bed for a long time,
as if waiting for something.
Soon, the man went east from the hall.
Earlier, there had been a pile of manure,
from which one could climb to spy into the house.
Soon, I heard three or four women in the house,
whispering by the wall.
Shortly after,
the man with the white blade brought a cloth bundle into the hall,
followed by a woman.
They were planning to escape together.
The man with the white blade then said:
"Is there no one in this room?"
He swept his blade along the wall.
I pressed myself firmly against the wall.
The blade passed over my face,
but the man did not notice me.
Then, carrying the bundle and leading the fleeing woman, he left.
I thought I could not stay there,
so I left and walked on.
After about one or two lǐ,
I fell into an old well.
There was already a dead person in the old well.
The body was warm.
I remained there in panic until nearly the fifth watch.
The master of the house discovered the missing woman,
searched and pursued to the old well,
shone a light,
and found both the corpse and me there.
I was seized and reported to the county authorities.
The county magistrate was discerning.
I provided a full account of the blade sweeping the wall and the whispers from the wall,
leading to the arrest of the criminals from among the aunts and such in the house.
Thus, my innocence was cleared.
Continuing southward, I was about to reach the Hànnán border
when I encountered a large juniper tree on the road.
An old man sat beneath it,
asked where I came from,
and I told him everything.
The old man said:
"I am skilled in the Yì,
let me try to divine for you."
I blew on the yarrow stalks,
the old man laid out the hexagrams and, sighing, said:
"In your previous life, you had two wives,
both of whom you wronged.
The running corpse that chased you earlier
was your principal wife.
The one killed by someone and placed with you in the well
was your concubine.
The county magistrate who discerned your innocence
was your mother from your previous life.
I am your father from your previous life.
"was your mother" – the following seven characters added based on the Míng dynasty manuscript.
father.
Your elder brother in Hànnán has already
"already" originally read "both."
Changed based on the Míng dynasty manuscript.
ceased to exist."
Having said this,
I shed tears.
While wiping my tears,
the old man vanished.
When I reached Hànnán,
I searched for my elder brother,
but found no trace.
The knife scar was inflicted by the man with the white blade.
Alas,
such are the workings of past enmities,
and the intricate signs and responses are thus.
So said Wúyǐn.
Mr. Dù has his own biography;
this is a brief record of it.
From "Bó Yì Jì"
Chéng Pǔ,
styled Jiāmóu,
was a general under Sūn Quán of Wú,
serving as the Administrator of Jiāngxià and General Who Smashes Bandits.
He once executed several hundred rebels,
ordering them all to be thrown into fire.
That very day, Chéng Pǔ fell ill with fever,
and died after over a hundred days.
The source was originally missing;
now seen in the "Sānguózhì: Wúzhì: Pǔ Zhuàn," Péi Sōngzhī's commentary quoting "Wú Shū."
Cui Jǐnsī, a Military Advisor of Qiánzhōu in the Táng Dynasty,
relying on the influence of Vice-Director Sūn Shàngróng,
was appointed to lead a transport convoy to the capital.
He delivered five thousand strings of cash,
taking three hundred coins from each string as a wrapping fee,
causing the people to lament with resentment,
crying out to heaven and earth.
When he reached the Guābù River,
his boat capsized in a storm,
leaving nothing behind.
His family assets and fields
were all sold off,
he was dismissed from his post and stripped of his rank,
and had nowhere to turn for survival.
This is what is called the resentment caused by extortion.
Qí Wànshòu
Qí Wànshòu, a Clerk of Qiánfēng County in the Táng Dynasty,
had a nature fond of killing people.
Whenever the county officials sentenced someone to punishment,
he would demand money from them.
If they did not give it to him in time,
he would take a thick rod and beat them.
Those who died in this manner
were too numerous to count.
Prisoners who saw him
would all lose their spirits in terror.
If he was even slightly displeased,
he would go to the prison and beat them,
tormenting them to the brink of death.
His wife gave birth to children
who either had fleshy cangues,
or fleshy shackles,
or lacked mouths and noses,
or had no hands or feet,
and all died at birth.
Guō Bà
Guō Bà, an Attendant Censor of the Táng Dynasty,
submitted a report leading to the execution of three hundred people in Sòngzhōu,
and suddenly obtained the fifth rank.
After a month, he fell gravely ill.
When officials from the Censorate came to inquire about his illness,
they saw an old shaman who said:
"Lord Guō cannot be saved.
There are several hundred ghosts,
covered in flowing blood,
rolling up their sleeves and gnashing their teeth,
all saying they will not let him go.
One person in a blue robe shouted at a person in crimson clothes:
'You should have left long ago,
why have you stayed so long?'
The reply was:
'It was because I had not yet obtained the fifth rank,
so I could not leave.'" Soon after, Guō Bà took a knife and stabbed himself below the breast,
stirring it around,
and said:
"How satisfying!"
His family rushed in and asked him about it,
and he said:
"Attendant Censor Sūn Róngshī stabbed me."
His son appealed to Attendant Censor Gù Cóng against Róngshī,
but Cóng dismissed it as delirious nonsense.
That night, Guō Bà died.
Róngshī died on the same date in the sixth month of the following year, the anniversary of Guō Bà's death,
though no one knew why.
Director Yuánzhāng of the Bureau of Honors, Zhāng Yuànyī, said:
"There has been a great drought since spring,
but when Guō Bà died, the rain became plentiful.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān asked what had happened outside the court,
and Yuànyī replied:
'There are three celebrations outside:
the drought has been broken by rain—
the first celebration;
the new Zhōng Bridge has been completed—
a benefit for ten thousand generations—
the second celebration;
Guō Bà has died—
and all the people rejoice—
the third celebration.'"
The Empress laughed and said:
"Is Guō Bà so detested!"
Cáo Wéisī
Cáo Wéisī, a Legal Officer of the Shǔ Commandery during the Táng Dynasty,
during the time of Zhāngchóu Jiānqióng,
served as the Transport Commissioner for the Western Mountains,
and was greatly trusted.
Wéisī reported matters to Jiānqióng,
and after Jiānqióng finished speaking with him,
ordered him to return to his transport duties.
Wéisī's wife had given birth to a son who was ill,
so he informed Jiānqióng of the situation,
requesting to stay for a few days.
Jiānqióng became furious,
shouted at him to leave,
and assembled a crowd to execute him.
His wife heard of this,
and rode a carriage with their two sons to bid him farewell.
Wéisī was already bound with his hair tied up,
and Jiānqióng came out to oversee the execution.
Wéisī's two sons kowtowed, begging for his life,
and came to cling to the horse's legs,
causing the horse to halt.
Jiānqióng shed tears for them and said:
"The execution has already been carried out."
Yet he had not yet been released.
In the commandery, there was a Chán monk,
whose spiritual practice was of the highest order,
and Jiānqióng's mother regarded him as her teacher.
The Chán monk then went to see Jiānqióng and said:
"Legal Officer Cáo's life is about to end,
I ask that you do not kill him,
spare him."
Jiānqióng then pardoned Wéisī.
The next day,
he appointed Wéisī to act as the Assistant Prefect of Lú Prefecture,
bestowed upon him the crimson fish-bag,
and put him in sole charge of the Transport Commissioner for the Western Mountains,
also allowing him to go with his wife.
Wéisī arrived at Lúzhōu,
and due to illness,
dreamed that a monk told him:
"In Cáo Wéisī's lifetime,
he has betrayed trust and killed many people,
with not a shred of good deeds.
Now his creditors from past wrongs are about to arrive,
what is to be done?"
Wéisī pleaded most sorrowfully,
and the monk said:
"If you can have your two sons ordained as monks,
and use all the money, goods, and clothing in your household
to donate to the temple,
and have the whole family eat vegetarian meals,
set up a dàochǎng in the main hall,
invite renowned monks,
and day and night chant scriptures and perform repentance rituals,
you may extend your life by a hundred days.
If you cannot do this,
you will die immediately."
Wéisī said:
"All these things are easy.
But the hardship of not eating meat,
what can be done about that!"
The monk said:
"Take sheep liver, soak it in water,
add pepper sauce and eat it,
then you will be able to eat."
After waking,
he told his wife everything,
and his wife agreed.
They immediately ordained their two sons as monks,
and as instructed, set up a dàochǎng and chanted scriptures,
and also ate sheep liver,
and were then able to eat,
continuing like this for over a month.
One morning as he sat,
his deceased mother and deceased elder sister both came to see him.
Wéisī was greatly startled,
and hurried to greet them.
There was a ghostly child,
holding a crimson banner leading the way,
who ascended from the western steps,
and planted the crimson banner there.
His deceased elder sister did not speak,
but only danced beneath the banner,
swaying unceasingly.
His mother wept and said:
"Wéisī, in life you were unaware of your sins,
having killed countless people.
Now your creditors are about to come,
I cannot bear to see you suffer,
so I have come to see you."
Wéisī ordered offerings to be set for his mother,
and his mother ate them.
His elder sister danced even more incessantly,
without exchanging a single word.
After his mother finished eating,
she left with his elder sister.
Wéisī's illness grew worse,
and then he could no longer eat sheep liver,
often lying in the dàochǎng,
sleeping and waking during the day.
There were two blue-clad youths,
their height like that of pygmies,
one sitting on his head,
one sitting on his feet.
Wéisī asked them,
but the youths did not speak to him.
Yet the youths' appearance was very leisurely,
their mouths had four teeth,
protruding beyond their lips.
The next day at mealtime,
Wéisī saw the people he had killed,
some with disheveled hair and burst intestines,
severed hands and feet,
or beheaded and bleeding,
who came in great anger to curse Wéisī, saying:
"Treacherous villain, you worked with us,
then hastily turned and killed us to silence us.
We have now appealed to the Emperor,
so we have come to take you."
After speaking, they ascended the steps,
but the two youths pushed them,
so they could not advance,
and only cursed, saying:
"You must go eventually."
Wéisī knew he could not escape,
and recounted everything that had happened.
Like this, they came daily,
but were always pushed back by the youths,
unable to reach Wéisī.
After over a month,
the two youths suddenly disappeared.
Wéisī was greatly afraid,
and bid farewell to his wife and sons.
Then the dead arrived in great numbers,
and everyone saw Wéisī as if being dragged.
He fell at the foot of the hall,
and then died.
Wéisī was not a good man;
from a Palace Guard he rose to be a Judicial Officer in Zézhōu and Xiàngzhōu,
often keeping several dozen bandits,
ordering them to commit robberies wherever they were and sheltering them.
When matters were exposed,
he would kill them to silence them,
killing over a hundred people in total,
hence this calamity befell him.
Xíng
During the Táng Dynasty, Xíng was an envoy to Xīnlúo,
and upon returning,
moored at Tànshān.
He encountered over a hundred merchants,
carrying several boatloads of goods,
all precious items like kingfisher feathers, agarwood, ivory, and rhinoceros horn,
worth tens of millions.
Taking advantage of their unpreparedness,
he killed them all,
threw them into the sea, and took their goods.
Upon reaching the capital,
fearing others would find out,
he presented them as tribute,
and by imperial decree they were returned and bestowed upon him,
which he used freely.
Later, his son Zǎi plotted rebellion with a prince,
and the Xíng clan was then destroyed,
which was also his retribution.
Wàn Guójùn
Wàn Guójùn, a Palace Censor of the Táng Dynasty,
rose from the position of Clerk,
and was cruel by nature,
devoted to inflicting torture.
He petitioned to become an envoy to the six circuits,
executing and beheading exiles,
killing countless people.
Later, as he left the Censorate,
and reached the south of Tiānjīn Bridge,
ghosts filled the road,
blocking his horse's legs,
so he could not advance.
They said:
"Kowtow and spare us."
He cried out in pain repeatedly,
and soon, leaning on his saddle,
his tongue grew several feet long,
and his whole body turned blue and swollen.
He was carried to his residence,
and died at midnight.
Wáng Yáo
During the Huìchāng era.
There was a man named Wáng Yáo,
who claimed:
"My distant ancestor was originally from Qīngzhōu,
and served under the military commissioner of Pínglú.
At that time, my lord's surname was Lǐ,
though I don't recall his given name.
He often suffered from a back ulcer,
which no physician could cure.
My ancestor requested to offer livestock and silk to pray at Dàizōng,
and was moved to appear in form,
lingering and looking back to inquire.
My ancestor then kowtowed until he wept blood,
hoping for pity and compassion.
The mountain god said:
'Your commander,
