holding the position of a regional lord,
has the duty of nurturing the people,
yet he cruelly harms living beings,
widely acts without virtue,
excessively uses punishment and indiscriminate penalties,
causing wronged souls to appeal above.
The back sore he suffers from,
is indeed the evidence of his whippings,
and certainly cannot be cured.
Heaven's law applies to him,
and none can pardon him.'"
My ancestor then bowed and begged to see his lord once,
but upon returning to Qīngqiū,
his lord had already passed away.
My ancestor fully recounted what he had witnessed at Tàishān,
to his lord's wife,
who said:
"What proof is there?"
My ancestor replied:
"I, while in the underworld,
also worried that upon returning I would not be believed,
so I requested to see my lord,
and fully observed his bonds.
My lord then tore a piece from the sleeve of his inner garment,
about an inch square,
and gave it to me, saying:
'When you return,
show this to my family.'
The piece of sleeve is still here."
The wife obtained it,
and then examined the clothes worn at the time of death,
and indeed there was a torn place,
with the sore's blood still on it,
thus knowing his words were not false.
From "Ěrmù Jì".
Chén Xiàn
When Wáng Shěnzhī first entered Jìn'ān in Mǐn,
he established his administration with many affairs,
and the funds were insufficient.
The clerk Chén Xiàn offered a plan,
suggesting to appoint wealthy men as market regulation officials,
allowing them to levy as they wished,
with minimal compensation.
The wealthy men suffered from this,
and Xiàn thus gained favor,
and was promoted to financial officer.
Several years later,
two officials holding documents came to Xiàn's village,
asking where Financial Officer Chén's home was.
People asked the reason,
and they replied:
"He offered the plan to establish market regulation officials,
causing many families to be ruined because of this.
All the ancestors of those ruined families
have appealed to the Water West Great King,
and the king has sent us to pursue you."
Xiàn was then in a position of power,
and people feared to speak.
The next day,
Xiàn hurried home from the administration,
urgently summoned his family,
set up a vegetarian feast and made offerings,
his expression anxious and frightened.
That day,
the village again saw the two officials enter Xiàn's home,
and he suddenly died.
Initially, when Shěnzhī started his enterprise,
his elder brother Cháo first advocated it,
and when Shěnzhī occupied central Mǐn,
he built a temple for Cháo west of the water,
hence it was commonly called the Water West Great King.
Xiāo Huáiwǔ
In the false Shǔ, there was a Search and Affairs Corps,
also called the Central Corps,
headed by the minor court commissioner Xiāo Huáiwǔ,
which was essentially a military patrol duty.
Huáiwǔ had captured thieves and bandits for many years through his corps,
his official rank was very high,
he accumulated tens of thousands in gold,
his mansion was second only to those of princes and marquises,
and his music, women, and entertainers
were the best of the time.
The Central Corps he managed had over a hundred people,
each of whom privately supported more than ten followers,
sometimes gathering, sometimes dispersing,
so that people could not distinguish them,
and called them dogs.
Even in deep alleys and remote lanes,
horse doctors, tavern keepers,
beggars, hired laborers,
and child peddlers,
were all his dogs.
If commoners spoke privately,
the authorities would invariably know.
There were also those scattered in the prefectures and counties and in the homes of the noble and powerful,
serving as cooks, stable keepers,
carriage drivers, and musicians,
all were his dogs.
Both public and private movements,
were all immediately reported to Huáiwǔ,
so people lived in fear,
often suspecting that those at their elbows, arms, hearts, and minds,
were all his dogs.
Huáiwǔ killed people beyond count,
and at the beginning of Shǔ's fall,
those who had not cooperated with him,
and those who had accumulated gold and hidden wealth,
he pursued day and night into the corps,
and killed them all.
Cries of injustice
were heard in the streets and alleys.
Later, when Guō Chóngtāo entered Shǔ,
someone reported that Huáiwǔ intended to plot a rebellion,
and his entire family of over a hundred people,
young and old, were executed in the market.
From "Wángshì Jiànwén".
Lǐ Guīzhēn
During the Qiándé era,
the false Shǔ censor Lǐ Guīzhēn long held his judicial post.
One day, he went out to Sānjǐng Bridge,
and suddenly saw over ten people,
with broken heads and disheveled hair,
shouting grievances and claiming injustice,
gradually pressing closer.
Guīzhēn was terrified,
turned his horse and went straight home,
and told his wife and children.
He then admonished his sons, saying:
"When you grow up and take office,
be careful not to become penal or judicial officials.
Even with my purity, caution, and fear,
there were still injustices.
Now, how can I regret it in time?"
From then on, he fell ill and died.
Chén Jié
The false Shǔ censor Chén Jié,
was by nature cruel and vicious,
in judging penalties and deciding cases,
he always aimed for severity.
Within ten years,
he sentenced a thousand people to death.
While avoiding the heat in a traveling pavilion,
he saw a spider hanging silk before him.
He reached out to catch it,
and it became a large spider,
bit his middle finger,
and was brushed off to the steps below,
transforming into a fierce ghost,
saying it came to claim his life.
He was extremely shocked,
his finger gradually developed a sore,
and after ten days of pain, he died.
Sū É
During the Hàn dynasty, Hé Chǎng served as the Inspector of Jiāozhǐ.
While touring his jurisdiction, he arrived at Gāoyào County in Cāngwú Commandery.
As evening fell, he lodged at Quèbēn Pavilion.
Before midnight had arrived,
a woman emerged from beneath the building.
She said of herself:
"This humble woman's surname is Sū, given name É,
courtesy name Shǐzhū.
I was originally a resident of Guǎngxìn County."
("Guǎngxìn" was originally written as "Xìnguǎng",
corrected based on the text below and the Ming dynasty manuscript copy.)
("Lǐ" is written as "lǐ" in the Ming manuscript copy.)
I
lost my parents early,
and had no brothers either.
My husband had also passed away long ago.
I possessed one hundred and twenty bolts of assorted silk fabrics,
and one maidservant,
named Zhìfù.
Being alone, destitute, and frail,
I was unable to support myself,
so I intended to go to a neighboring county to sell the silk.
I rented a cart and ox from a fellow county man named Wáng Bó,
for the price of twelve thousand coins.
It carried me and the silk,
with Zhìfù holding the reins.
On the tenth day of the fourth month, the year before last,
we arrived outside this pavilion.
By then it was already dusk,
and travelers had ceased,
so I dared not proceed further.
Therefore, we stopped and stayed here.
Zhìfù was suddenly seized by abdominal pain.
I went to the pavilion chief's house to beg for some water and to fetch fire.
The pavilion chief, Gōng Shòu, grasping a knife and holding a halberd,
came to the side of the cart.
He asked me:
'Madam, where have you come from?
What is loaded on your cart?
Where is your husband?
Why are you traveling alone?'
I replied to him:
'Why trouble yourself with such questions?'
Shòu then grabbed my arm, intending to violate me.
I did not submit.
Shòu immediately stabbed my side with the knife,
and I died on the spot.
He also killed Zhìfù.
Shòu dug beneath the building,
buried me and the maidservant,
and took the belongings away.
He killed the ox and burned the cart,
then threw the cart pole and the ox bones
into an empty well east of the pavilion.
My death was agonizingly cruel,
with no one to whom I could appeal.
Therefore, I have come to report this to Your Honor, the enlightened envoy."
Chǎng said:
"If I now wish to exhume your remains,
what shall serve as proof?"
The woman said:
"I am dressed entirely in white garments,
with black silk shoes.
They are not yet decayed."
They excavated the spot and indeed it was so.
Chǎng then dispatched officers to arrest Shòu.
Under interrogation, he confessed fully.
Chǎng sent down to Guǎngxìn County to investigate and question,
and the findings matched É's account.
Shòu's parents and brothers were all arrested and imprisoned.
Chǎng submitted a memorial stating that Shòu's crime of murder,
according to the regular statutes, did not warrant the extermination of his clan.
However, Shòu committed this evil deed,
concealed it for years,
and the king's law was unable to apprehend him.
That a ghost or spirit would personally bring a complaint—
this is an event not seen in a thousand years.
I request that they all be beheaded,
to aid the punishments of the netherworld."
The emperor approved his request.
From *Records of Retribution for Injustice*.
The Wife of the Magistrate of Fú
During the Hàn dynasty, Wáng Tún,
courtesy name Shàolín,
served as the Magistrate of Méi County.
He arrived at Tái Pavilion.
The pavilion had long been haunted by a ghost.
Tún lodged upstairs.
At night, a woman appeared,
claiming she wished to appeal an injustice,
but had no clothes and could not come forward.
Tún gave her some clothes.
She came forward and said:
"I was originally the wife of the Magistrate of Fú.
While traveling to my husband's post,
I stopped to lodge at this pavilion.
The pavilion chief killed my entire family of ten, young and old,
and buried us beneath this building,
taking our clothes and belongings.
That pavilion chief now serves as the Patrol Officer under the county gate."
Tún said:
"I will certainly bring him to justice for you.
Do not recklessly kill innocent people again."
The ghost dropped the clothes and left.
The next morning, Tún summoned the Patrol Officer for questioning,
and he immediately confessed.
Tún arrested over ten people involved at the time,
and executed them all.
He exhumed the several corpses,
and had them returned to their home for burial.
The pavilion was forever peaceful and clear thereafter.
The source was originally missing;
now found in *Records of Retribution for Injustice*.
Zhūgě Yuánchóng
Zhūgě Fù of Lángyá
served as the Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn during the Yǒngjiā era of the Sòng dynasty.
His family remained in Yángdū,
and he only brought his eldest son, Yuánchóng, to his post.
Fù fell ill and died in the commandery.
Yuánchóng was just nineteen years old at the time,
and was escorting the coffin back home.
Fù's disciple, Hé Fǎsēng, coveting their wealth,
together with a companion, pushed Yuánchóng into the water, where he drowned,
and then divided his possessions.
Yuánchóng's mother, Madame Chén, dreamed that Yuánchóng had returned.
He recounted in detail his father's death and the circumstances of his own murder,
how his corpse drifted in the water,
and the unparalleled bitterness of his grievance.
"Having been separated for many years,
I must now take my leave forever.
Harboring sorrow and swallowing hatred—
how can it be expressed?"
He sobbed and sighed, unable to control himself.
He also said:
"I traveled swiftly and am utterly exhausted.
Therefore, I lay down on the bed beneath the window,
resting my head against the window ledge.
Tomorrow, look at the place where your son slept,
and you will know this was not a dream."
Madame Chén, grief-stricken and startled, arose.
Taking a torch, she illuminated the place where her son had slept.
The spot was damp, exactly in the shape of a human figure.
Thereupon, the entire household wailed and wept,
and the matter was reported as discovered.
At that time, Xú Sēnzhī had just been appointed Governor of Jiāozhōu,
and Xú Dàolì served as his Chief Clerk.
Dàolì was Madame Chén's maternal cousin.
She wrote a detailed account of the dream,
and entrusted the two Xú officials to investigate it.
Xú Dàolì encountered the funeral boat carrying Zhūgě's remains.
Upon verifying the dates of death of father and son,
they completely matched the ghost's words.
He then arrested the two murderers,
who immediately confessed fully.
They were executed according to the law,
and men were dispatched to escort the coffin back to Yángdū.
From *Records of Retribution for Injustice*.
Lǚ Qìngzǔ
Lǚ Qìngzǔ of Yǒngkāng in the Sòng dynasty,
came from a very wealthy family.
He often had a servant named Jiàozi guard his country villa.
One day, Qìngzǔ went there to inspect the estate,
when he was suddenly killed by someone.
His younger clan brother, Wúqī,
had previously borrowed money from Qìngzǔ,
so everyone suspected him of the murder.
Wúqī then brought wine and dried meat to the coffin and prayed:
"You suffered such a cruel death,
and they say it was me.
If your soul has awareness,
make known the true culprit."
After he returned,
around the third watch of the night,
he saw Qìngzǔ appear and say:
"Recently while inspecting,
I saw the servant Jiàozi neglecting the fields.
I threatened to punish him severely.
The servant then struck my back with an axe,
stuffed my cap into my mouth,
but I managed to bite three of his fingers,
all of which are broken and bruised.
He then took a knife and stabbed my neck,
dragging me to the back door.
When I was first killed,
my attendant was also present,
but he did not intervene,
which was a failure in enforcing punishment.
The servant now wishes to flee,
but I have already nailed his head to the wall."
After saying this, he vanished.
Wúqī reported everything to Qìngzǔ's parents.
They secretly checked the wall where the servant stayed,
and indeed found a clump of hair,
nailed with a bamboo peg.
Looking at his fingers,
they also saw the injuries.
The servant was arrested and interrogated,
and he confessed.
When asked, "Since you rebelled,
why didn't you flee?"
he replied:
"My head felt as if tied down,
making escape impossible."
All witnesses confirmed the events matched.
Jiàozi was then burned to death,
along with his two sons.
From "Records of Repaying Injustice"
Yuánhuī
During the Yǒng'ān era of Emperor Zhuāng of the Later Wèi,
Prince Yuán Yǎn of Běihǎi entered Luòyáng.
Emperor Zhuāng traveled north,
and Prince Chéngyáng, Yuán Huī, donated his residence to establish Xuānzhōng Temple.
Ěrzhū Zhào captured Emperor Zhuāng,
and Huī sought refuge with the former Luòyáng magistrate, Kòu Zǔrén.
Zǔrén heard that Ěrzhū Zhào was offering a reward for Huī,
so he beheaded Huī and sent his head to Zhào.
Zhào dreamed of Huī saying:
"I have two hundred catties of gold
and one hundred horses
at Zǔrén's house.
You may take them."
Zhào then hung Zǔrén's head from a tall tree,
tied a large stone to his feet,
and whipped him,
demanding the gold and horses.
Zǔrén died,
and it was seen as retribution for his betrayal.
From "Extended Records of the Five Elements Through the Ages,"
the Ming manuscript cites "Records of Buddhist Temples" and "Records of Repaying Injustice."
Lǐ Yìyǎn
Lǐ Yìyǎn of Lǒngxī in the Táng dynasty,
during the Zhēnguàn era,
served as county captain of Huàzhōu.
A person suddenly went missing in this county,
with no one knowing his whereabouts.
His father and brother suspected a rival family of murder,
and appealed to the county with their grievance.
Yìyǎn investigated the case,
but could not reach a conclusion.
At night, holding a candle,
he meticulously pursued inquiries.
Late at night,
as Yìyǎn leaned over the desk with bowed head,
he suddenly realized the deceased was present,
still bearing the appearance of his injuries.
He said:
"So-and-so beat me to death
and placed me in a well at such-and-such location.
You must inspect it early,
otherwise,
I fear the body will be moved elsewhere,
and become impossible to find."
Yìyǎn immediately went in person,
and indeed found it as described.
The rival family then confessed in detail.
Those who heard and witnessed this
were all astonished and sighed.
From "Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma"
Abbot of Qízhōu Temple
In the thirteenth year of Zhēnguàn in the Táng dynasty,
there was an abbot in Qízhōu city
who had a feud with the temple's overseer, the Karmadāna.
He killed the Karmadāna,
dismembered him into twelve pieces,
and hid them in a latrine.
The temple monks, not seeing the Karmadāna for a long time,
reported to Assistant Inspector Yáng Ān for a joint inspection,
but found no trace.
As the Assistant Inspector was about to leave,
the monks escorted him out,
when they noticed fresh blood
on the abbot's left sleeve of his kasaya.
The Assistant Inspector interrogated him,
and he said:
"On the night of the murder,
I was not wearing the kasaya.
If there is fresh blood on it,
it must be the doing of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
He was eventually executed.
From "Extended Records of the Five Elements Through the Ages"
Registrar of Guǎntáo
A registrar of Guǎntáo County in Jìzhōu during the Táng dynasty, surnamed Zhōu,
his given name forgotten.
During the Xiǎnqìng era,
he was sent on a mission to the Yámǎ market at Línyú Pass.
When it was time to depart,
two assistants accompanied him.
Zhōu was carrying a considerable amount of money and silk,
so the two men killed him by pressing a soil sack over him.
All the money and silk
were stolen by them,
leaving only his personal clothes for burial.
At the end of the year,
his wife had a dream
in which he described the circumstances of his murder
and revealed where the stolen goods were hidden.
His wife then reported this to the authorities based on the dream.
The officials investigated and verified,
obtaining the full truth of the matter.
The money and silk were recovered,
and both men were sentenced to death.
Monk Huìyǒng of the Zhìlì Temple in Xiàngzhōu said
he personally heard this from Liú Rénkuān, a Taoist priest of the Míngtíng Temple.
From "Forest of Gems in the Garden of the Dharma"
Monk Tánchàng
During the Qiánfēng era of the Táng dynasty,
monk Tánchàng of Jīngxī Temple in the capital
took a servant and two mules to listen to lectures at Master Léng's place in Qízhōu.
On the way, he met a man
wearing a patched hat and ragged clothes,
counting prayer beads,
who called himself a virtuous observer of the Five Precepts,
and was also going to the lecture.
At night, they lodged at the Mǎwéi inn.
The Five Precepts observer paid homage to the Buddha and recited sutras,
not stopping until midnight,
which Chàng took as diligent practice.
By the fourth watch,
they set off together.
About ten li from the inn,
he suddenly drew two knives from his sleeve
and stabbed Chàng to death.
The servant dismounted and fled into the grass,
while the Five Precepts observer rode off on a mule with the baggage.
Before dawn,
the innkeeper dreamed of Chàng telling him:
"Last night, the Five Precepts observer killed this humble monk."
Shortly after, the servant arrived
and reported the same as in the dream.
A fellow lodger, a guardsman,
took his bow and arrows,
mounted a horse, and chased for over forty li.
Aiming his bow and arrows at him,
the observer dismounted and begged for death.
He was bound and sent to the county,
where he was executed.
From "Records of Affairs Within and Outside the Court"
Commoner of Wǔqiáo
Dù Mǒu, the Sima of Wèizhōu during the Táng dynasty, once served as the Wèi of Luòyáng,
in charge of apprehending bandits.
At that time, at Wǔqiáo in the south of Luòyáng city,
a household caught fire,
and seven people were burned to death.
Dù Mǒu was sitting in the official hall,
when suddenly a man was seized by the gatekeeper,
and brought before him in a disheveled state.
He asked the reason,
and the gatekeeper said:
"This man just came,
appearing greatly frightened,
first rushed into the county gate,
then rushed out again,
so I seized him."
The man said:
"I am the bandit who killed the people of the Wǔqiáo household,
so I have come to surrender.
I had five companions,
together we robbed that household,
obtaining hundreds of thousands in valuables.
Fearing the affair would be exposed,
we killed the people,
burned their house,
making it appear as if they died in a fire,
so no one would suspect.
We brought the valuables to the city,
stayed in Dàodélǐ,
and when my companions and I tried to leave,
we repeatedly encountered obstacles and could not depart.
Today, heading south from Dàodé Fāng,
I suddenly saw six or seven balls of fire in the air,
the largest like a gourd,
the smallest like a cup,
blocking my way forward,
preventing me from going south.
So I ran north,
and a small fire entered straight into my heart,
scorching my heart and organs,
causing burning pain and driving me mad.
Then, surrounded by these fires,
they drove me to enter the county gate.
Once inside, the fires disappeared,
and the fire in my heart also vanished.
Then when I went out the gate,
the fires reappeared in the air,
blocking me from leaving.
Knowing I could not escape,
I have confessed everything in detail.
Thereupon, orders were given to seize all his accomplices and the valuables,
and they were executed at the prefectural office.
From "Jì Wén"
Lú Shūmǐn
During the Táng dynasty, Lú Shūmǐn
resided in Gōushì County.
He was the maternal cousin of the late Grand Tutor, Duke Wénzhēn, Cuī Yòufǔ.
At that time, Yòufǔ had just been appointed Chancellor,
and sent a letter to Lú,
instructing him to take the míngjīng examination.
Lú then set out from Gōushì for the capital,
his travel provisions meager and poor.
He had a donkey,
two saddlebags,
and only one servant boy of just over ten years old.
When he first departed the county,
a man in purple clothes,
carrying a small bundle,
traveled alongside Lú,
saying:
"I am delivering letters to the city."
His speech and manner were very respectful.
Lú, because his servant was young,
found it very convenient to have him as a companion,
helping with the saddle and mounting.
Whenever they reached an inn,
Lú would always share tea and wine with him,
and the purple-clad man also showed much gratitude.
When they reached È Lǐng,
they set off early for over ten lǐ,
and dawn had just broken,
when the purple-clad man and the young servant were driving the donkey behind.
Suddenly, Lú heard the servant's cries,
saying:
"I'm being beaten by the purple-clad man!"
Lú said:
"If the servant has done wrong, just say so,
I will certainly punish him.
How can you just beat him yourself?"
As soon as he finished speaking,
he saw the purple-clad man draw a knife from his bosom,
and stab the servant, piercing his intestines and causing blood to flow.
Lú was shocked and fled.
At first, he was still riding the donkey,
but after traveling several dozen paces,
he saw the purple-clad man catching up from behind,
so he abandoned the donkey and his boots,
and ran for over ten paces.
The purple-clad man caught up,
stabbed him with the knife and felled him,
and he died on the ridge alongside the servant.
At that time, the Wèi of Gōushì, Zhèng Chǔxiāng,
was Lú's maternal cousin.
One morning, rising early,
he suddenly felt drowsy in the hall
and dreamed of Lú with disheveled hair,
his face stained with blood,
who said to the Wèi:
"I have been killed by a bandit."
Zhèng then asked the details,
and he said:
"I died unjustly,
but this bandit has not yet been captured."
Then he led forward a white ox,
limping on its left front leg,
and said:
"Brother, just remember this ox.
Next year, on the first day of the eighth month, at dawn,
the bandit will come from Hézhōng Fǔ,
having bought oxen with his accomplices.
They will pass here,
entering the western outer gate.
The one driving this ox last will be him."
Zhèng awoke with a start,
and told his colleagues.
The next day,
a prefectural order arrived to capture the bandit,
and only then did they learn that Lú had been killed by bandits.
Among his books and papers, they found Chancellor Cuī's handwritten letter.
The Governor of Hénán pursued the capture urgently,
but found no trace at all.
By the end of the seventh month the following year,
Zhèng discussed plans with the County Magistrate.
On that day, before the fifth watch,
they secretly deployed archers and constables outside the western outer gate.
Zhèng led his men personally,
and lay in ambush by the roadside.
When the sun first rose,
sure enough, someone came driving oxen from the west.
Behind, a white ox with a lame leg,
walked slowly,
unable to keep up with the herd.
A man was driving it.
This ox was precisely the one Lú had led in Zhèng's dream.
So they seized and captured him,
and also apprehended all six or seven of his accomplices.
The one driving the lame ox
was indeed the bandit who killed Lú.
Questioned, he confessed fully,
saying:
"This young master had been kind to me.
I saw the documents in his bag,
thinking they were silk and satin,
so I robbed and killed him.
When I opened it,
I realized it was not,
and only obtained two bolts of plain silk.
Ever since then,
I have often vaguely seen this young master by my side.
If the crime had not been exposed,
I might still have surrendered to die.
Now that I am captured,
how dare I conceal it!"
He then recounted the whole story from beginning to end,
and he and his accomplices were all executed in the marketplace.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Zhèng Shēng
In the Táng dynasty, there was a man named Zhèng from Xíngyáng,
skilled in riding and archery,
known for his bravery, fierceness, and agility.
He lived in the outskirts of Gǒngluò.
One day, while riding drunk,
with bow in hand and arrows at his waist,
he galloped on a swift horse,
riding alone through the fields,
traveling dozens of lǐ from his home.
As dusk fell,
a great storm arose,
and he took shelter under a large tree.
After a long while,
the rain cleared,
but it was already evening,
and he had lost his way.
Letting his horse wander,
he saw a gate and buildings by the roadside—
it was a temple.
He tied his horse outside the gate
and prepared to rest inside the building,
when suddenly, with a shudder, his heart stirred.
He hid himself under the eastern corridor,
hearing rustling sounds from an empty room to the left of the temple.
Suspecting it was a ghost,
he drew his bow and tensed the string, lying in wait.
Soon, he saw a man,
tall in stature and wearing short clothes,
carrying a bag on his back and holding a sword, emerging from the empty room.
Then, leaning on his sword, the man declared loudly:
“I am a thief.
Are you not a thief as well?”
Zhèng replied:
“I live in the outskirts of Gǒngluò.
Earlier, I was riding alone through the fields
when I encountered a great storm,
lost my way,
and thus hid myself here.”
The sword-wielding man said:
“Since you are not a thief,
surely you have no intention of harming me?
Moreover, if I flee,
my path must pass under the eastern corridor.
I ask you to remove the bowstring and hand it to me,
so that I may leave.
Otherwise,
I will die at your hands.”
Earlier, Zhèng had always kept an extra string in his sleeve.
After removing the string,
he threw it before the swordsman,
secretly attaching the spare string from his sleeve to his bow.
Once the thief obtained the string,
he proceeded to the eastern corridor
intending to kill Zhèng to silence him.
Zhèng quickly fitted an arrow to the string,
and the thief fled,
saying:
“You truly are a wise man.
I deserve to die.”
Zhèng said:
“I meant no harm.
Why did you suspect me?”
The thief bowed twice in apology.
Zhèng then moved to the western corridor to avoid the thief.
After the thief left,
Zhèng feared he might return with accomplices,
so he climbed a tree to hide.
After a long while,
the stars and moon began to shine brightly.
Suddenly, he saw a woman,
exceedingly beautiful in appearance,
emerge from the empty room
and weep in the courtyard.
When questioned,
the woman said:
“I live in a village.
A thief lured me here,
coveted my clothing and belongings,
and killed me in the empty room,
abandoning my corpse before leaving.
I beg you, noble sir, to avenge this injustice.”
She added:
“Tonight, he will hide at Tián Héng’s tomb.
I urge you to pursue him quickly,
do not miss this chance.”
Zhèng agreed,
and the woman thanked him before departing.
At dawn,
Zhèng went to look,
and indeed found a corpse.
He immediately rode to Luò,
and reported everything to the Governor of Hénán, Zhèng Shūzé.
The Governor ordered officials to arrest the thief,
and he was indeed captured at Tián Héng’s tomb.
From Xuānshì Zhì.
Gōngsūn Chuò
In the Táng dynasty, Gōngsūn Chuò, the Registrar of Wángwū,
had only been in office for a few months
when he suddenly fell ill and died.
Before he was buried,
the County Magistrate was alone in the hall
when he saw Gōngsūn, dressed in official robes,
enter through the gate.
Startled, he rose and said:
“You and I belong to different realms—the living and the dead.
Why have you come to disturb me?”
Gōngsūn said:
“I have suffered an injustice
and wish to see the Magistrate to seek redress.
I once served as your subordinate—
surely you cannot be without compassion!
My time was not yet meant to end.
I was cursed by my servants
for the sake of theft and profit.
My residence is in Héyīn County.
If you are willing,
secretly select capable officials
to take a warrant and arrest them—
they will not escape the net.
Under the seventh tile ridge from the east on the eaves of the main hall,
there is an effigy of me,
made of paulownia wood,
with nails driven into it.
It has already transformed.”
With these words, he vanished.
The Magistrate was greatly astonished.
He selected strong soldiers who had been close to Chuò,
gave them the warrant and a letter for the Magistrate of Héyīn,
and all the servants were arrested.
They searched under the eaves of the hall,
and indeed found a human-shaped figure,
over a chǐ in length,
with nails driven all around its body.
The wood had gradually turned into flesh,
and when struck, it made a dull sound.
The grain and wheat that Chuò had stored
for his leisure expenses
had all been stolen.
The county then reported to the prefecture,
and the several servants
were executed with dried wood.
From Yì Shǐ.
Wáng Ānguó
In the northern outskirts of Jīng Prefecture, there was a farmer named Wáng Ānguó,
who worked diligently at farming,
and was self-sufficient in food and clothing.
In the winter of the third year of the Bǎolì era of the Táng dynasty,
two thieves climbed over the wall at night and entered,
both holding sharp blades.
Ānguó dared not resist,
and all the clothing and furs inside the house
were taken away without a single item left.
Ānguó had one son,
named Hé Qī,
who was just six or seven years old.
Startled from sleep,
he cried out that there were thieves,
and was immediately shot by the thieves,
falling dead as the bowstring twanged.
Outside Ānguó’s gate, there were two purple donkeys,
which were also stolen.
At dawn,
the villagers gathered,
and together discussed plans to pursue and capture them.
Suddenly, Hé Qī’s spirit climbed onto the door and wailed:
“My death was fated,
and I no longer feel much pain.
What pains me
is the eternal parting from my father and mother.”
Then he wept grievously for a long time.
The neighbors who gathered, fifty or sixty in number,
all shed tears of sorrow.
He then said:
“Do not plan to pursue them.
Next year in the fifth month,
they will bring death upon themselves.”
He then called Ānguó,
whispered the names in his ear,
and urged him not to
(the character “leak” is likely missing after “not”).
When the wheat harvest came,
Ānguó had half a qǐng of wheat.
Just as he was gathering it,
two oxen came in the morning,
trampling and scattering it in disarray.
Ānguó led them back,
and told everyone in the village:
“Whose oxen have damaged my crops?
I have tied them up.
The owners should bring compensation to redeem them;
otherwise,
I will take this to the authorities.”
The villagers all went together,
and said:
“These are not oxen usually kept by anyone nearby.”
They gathered and looked for a long time,
when suddenly two travelers arrived and said:
“These are our oxen.
Last evening they were startled and ran away,
unexpectedly ending up here.
For the damage to the fields,
we ask to compensate double the value and return our livestock to us.”
The villagers questioned where they came from,
and upon checking the deed,
one of them had traded with a purple donkey.
Ānguó immediately recalled what Hé Qī had said,
and upon asking their names, they matched exactly.
So he bound them,
and said:
“You are the ones who shot my son and took all my wealth last winter.”
The two thieves looked at each other,
and no longer concealed the truth,
saying:
“It is heaven’s will, fate’s decree,
death cannot be avoided.”
They then recounted the story,
saying:
“After we committed the robbery and killing,
we fled north to the outskirts of Níngqìng,
thinking the matter had long passed.
So we bought oxen and planned to return to the Qí region.
Yesterday, when the oxen reached twenty lǐ north of the village,
they hesitated and would not advance.
We waited for nightfall,
intending to pass through here.
After falling asleep,
we dreamed of a child about five years old,
naked and dancing wildly,
confusing and bewildering us,
and only woke at daybreak.
When we awoke,
the ropes tying the two oxen were not broken,
yet they seemed to have been untied,
and the oxen had already run off.
We followed their tracks,
and came here by a small path.
As for last winter’s crime,
how could we dare escape it?”
The villagers sent them to the county authorities,
and they were dealt with according to the law.
From “Jíyì Jì.”
Niào Miàojì,
whose surname was Yè,
was a native of Xúnyáng in Jiāngzhōu.
She was first married to Rén Huá,
a merchant from Xúnyáng.
Her father, Yè Shēng,
traveled back and forth between Chángshā and Guǎnglíng with Huá.
In the spring of the eleventh year of the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
they went to Tánzhōu and never returned.
After several months had passed,
Miàojì suddenly dreamed of her father,
disheveled and naked,
covered in blood,
weeping and saying:
"Your husband and I
encountered bandits on the lake,
and both have already died.
Because your heart seems to be one of determination,
Heaven permits you to seek revenge,
but the intent of the netherworld
does not wish to speak plainly,
so I will report to you in cryptic words.
If you can truly ponder them and avenge us,
what regret would I have!"
Miàojì said:
"What are the cryptic words?"
Shēng said:
"The one who killed me is
'monkey in a carriage,'
'grass at the east gate.'"
Soon after, she saw her husband,
appearing like her father,
weeping and saying:
"The one who killed me is
'walking through the grain,'
'one day husband.'"
Miàojì clutched her chest and wept,
and was then awakened by her younger sister's call.
Weeping, she told her mother,
and the whole household was greatly alarmed.
They pondered the cryptic words,
but they were utterly incomprehensible.
They inquired with elderly neighbors and knowledgeable people in the village,
but none could decipher them.
In autumn, she went to Shàngyuán County,
a place where boats and oars converge,
where scholars and officials from all directions often rested.
Moreover, the county had the Wǎguān Temple,
and atop the temple was a pavilion,
leaning against the mountain and overlooking the river,
with a view stretching ten thousand *lǐ* before the eyes.
It was also an ultimate scenic spot of rivers and lakes,
where travelers would moor their boats
and invariably ascend to gaze afar.
"I will don monastic robes there,
and wait for someone I can ask.
Surely there will be someone who can clear my confusion."
Thus, wearing coarse clothes, she went to Shàngyuán,
offering her labor at Wǎguān Temple,
daily holding broom and dustpan,
sweeping and cleaning below the pavilion.
In her spare time, she would linger by the railings,
awaiting someone who might understand.
Whenever she saw someone with a tall hat and broad sash,
chanting and whistling as they approached,
she would bow and inquire.
After several years of residing there,
no one was able to decipher it.
In the seventeenth year,
the year being Xīnsì,
there was a certain Lǐ Gōngzuǒ,
who, having left his post as an assistant in Lǐngnán, arrived there.
He lifted his robes and ascended the pavilion,
his demeanor elegant and extraordinary,
quite unlike ordinary people.
Miàojì stepped forward, bowed, and wept,
and asked him about the previous matter.
Gōngzuǒ said:
"I have always enjoyed resolving doubts for others in my life.
Moreover, your grievance is so earnest,
and the spirits have revealed it thus.
I should ponder it for you."
He walked silently a few steps,
then happily beckoned Miàojì and said:
"I have it.
The one who killed your father is Shēn Lán,
and the one who killed your husband is Shēn Chūn."
Miàojì, both sorrowful and joyful, sobbed,
bowed, and asked for his explanation.
Gōngzuǒ said:
"Now, 'monkey' refers to the earthly branch *shēn*.
Remove the two ends of the character for 'carriage' (*chē*) and you get 'monkey' (*hóu*),
hence the character *shēn*.
'Grass' with 'gate,'
and 'gate' with 'east,'
is that not the character *lán*!
'Walking through the grain'
means passing through fields,
which also yields the character *shēn*.
'One day' added to 'husband'
forms the character *chūn*.
The ghosts and spirits wished to confuse people,
hence they interwove their words."
Miàojì, both sorrowful and joyful,
as if unable to contain herself,
after a long while, wiped her tears, bowed, and thanked him, saying:
"Since the bandits' names are now clear,
the path to clearing my grievance is open.
If I am able to resolve this confusion,
I vow to repay your profound kindness.
As a woman, I have nothing else,
only pure sincerity in serving the Buddha,
praying to increase the sea of blessings."
Earlier,
at the Fànshì Ordination Platform of Pǔguāngwáng Temple in Sìzhōu,
all who became monks had to pass through it.
People converged from all directions,
monks and nuns gathered in great numbers,
and spectators were as numerous as in a marketplace.
Gōngzuǒ, traveling from Chǔ to Qín,
moored his boat and went to see it.
There was a nun,
with clear, elegant brows and eyes,
as if an old acquaintance.
Each time she passed by, she would gaze intently at Gōngzuǒ,
as if intending to speak but not doing so.
After a long while,
as Gōngzuǒ was about to leave,
the nun suddenly called out:
"Did you not serve as an assistant in Nánhǎi during the Zhēnyuán era, Attendant Censor?"
Gōngzuǒ said:
"Indeed."
"Then do you remember this little master?"
Gōngzuǒ said:
"I do not remember."
Miàojì said:
"I am the one from the Wǎguān Temple pavilion who sought to decipher 'monkey in a carriage.'"
Gōngzuǒ, realizing, said:
"Did you eventually capture the bandits?"
She replied:
"After understanding the dream's words,
I dressed in male clothing,
changed my name to Shìjì,
and wandered, hiring myself out along the rivers and lakes.
After several years,
I heard that between Qízhōu and Huángzhōu there was a Shēn Village,
so I went there.
Wandering for a full year,
I then heard that in the northwest corner of the village there was one named Lán.
I quietly went to seek employment,
always lowering my price,
and Lán happily hired me.
I also heard that his paternal cousin was named Chūn.
Thereupon, I diligently and respectfully performed my duties,
never leaving day or night.
Whenever I saw something that needed doing,
regardless of its difficulty, I would do it,
never waiting for orders.
The Lán family valued me,
and though I toiled hard with the other hired hands by day,
I slept on a separate mat at night,
and no one knew I was not a man.
After more than a year,
I became even more diligent and capable,
and Lán grew increasingly respectful and fond of me,
regarding Shìjì
as even better than his own son.
Lán was sometimes a farmer, sometimes a merchant,
or sometimes stored goods in Wǔchāng,
entrusting all keys and locks, opening and closing, to me.
Thus, I examined the contents of his cabinets,
half of which were my family's belongings,
and I also saw the clothes my father and husband often wore,
weeping as I noted them.
However, Lán and Chūn, uncle and nephew,
never went out together,
so I feared that capturing one would alert the other to flee.
I harbored this for several years.
On the Double Ninth Festival during the Yǒngzhēn era,
the two bandits drank until drunk.
Shìjì rushed to report to the prefecture,
and they were captured while intoxicated.
Upon interrogation, they confessed and were executed according to the law.
I recovered what had been lost and returned home,
fully supported my mother, and requested to follow Buddhism.
I became a disciple of the nun Dòngwēi at Tiāngōng Temple in Hóngzhōu,
who was the one from whom I had received teachings in the past.
I, Miàojì, am but a woman,
yet with heartfelt sincerity I sought revenge,
and Heaven did not thwart it.
Thus, through the words of a dream,
I gained understanding from a gentleman.
As for those who were my enemies,
could I share the same sky with them?
Even shattering this humble body
could not repay a wise man.
In the monastery, there is nothing else,
only devout reverence for the Dharma and its images,
to repay and serve."
Gōng Zuǒ was greatly astonished by this,
and thus composed a biography for it.
In the year Gēngxū of the Tàihé era,
Lǐ Fùyán of Lǒngxī traveled to Bā Nán,
where he met the presented scholar Shěn Tián in Péngzhōu.
Tián then spoke of strange events,
and showed it to him.
After reading it once, he returned it.
On the day I recorded this strange tale,
I compiled it here.
From "Xù Yōuguài Lù".
Lǐ Wénmǐn
In the Táng dynasty, there was a man named Lǐ Wénmǐn,
who was appointed as the Recorder and Military Advisor of Guǎngzhōu.
Just before reaching the prefecture,
he encountered bandits who killed him,
sinking his body into the river,
and capturing his wife, Madame Cuī.
They had a five-year-old son,
who followed his mother and was taken away.
The bandit turned out to be the Capital Patrol Commander of Guǎngzhōu.
As the son grew older,
he was made to study the classics,
and he was very intelligent and handsome.
He went to the capital to take the imperial examination but failed,
and so he went to Huàzhōu.
When he reached the east of Wèinán County,
his horse bolted uncontrollably,
and by nightfall,
it entered a manor.
He then sought lodging at the manor.
He was wearing a half-sleeved, sky-blue gauze sweat shirt,
and the matron of the manor, upon seeing it, said:
"This garment resembles the one Madame gave to Lángjūn as a farewell gift years ago.
You, sir, resemble Lángjūn,
and also resemble the young lady."
She took the garment to examine it,
and it turned out that when it was made years ago,
it had been burned by lamp soot and torn,
and the half-sleeve belt was still in her home.
She then told him about Lǐ Wénmǐn's encounter with the bandits.
The son abandoned the examination,
and went straight home to question his mother.
She told him everything in detail,
and he reported it to the authorities.
The authorities then captured the Capital Patrol Commander,
bound him, and interrogated him.
Every word of his confession matched,
and he was executed.
They provided him with resources,
and ordered him to return to Wèinán.
From "Wén Qí Lù".
Fán Zōngliàng
In the Táng dynasty, Fán Zōngliàng served as the Prefect of Mìzhōu.
At that time, in one of the subordinate counties, there was a band of robbers
who led troops into the home of a commoner named Yīn,
plundered gold and silk,
and killed the father and sons,
resulting in three deaths.
The Prefect pursued them urgently,
but for over a month, they were not captured.
There was a man named Wèi Nánhuá from Jùlù,
who resided between Qí and Lǔ,
and his family was very poor.
Zōngliàng appointed him as Acting Judicial Clerk.
One evening,
Nánhuá dreamed of several people with disheveled hair,
lined up to plead with him, saying:
"We are of the Yīn family,
father and two sons,
all died innocent.
We beg Your Honor to clear our injustice."
Nánhuá asked:
"Who killed you?"
They replied:
"Ten lǐ east of where we lived,
there is a man surnamed Yáo,
who is the leader of the bandits."
Nánhuá promised,
and woke up startled.
A few days later,
"A few days later" (the Ming manuscript says "that same day").
Zōngliàng said to Nánhuá:
"The bandits killed our commoner,
and it has been almost a month,
yet we have not traced their whereabouts.
Could it be that the officials are not fulfilling their duties?
You are the Judicial Officer,
go and investigate immediately."
Nánhuá hurried there,
but before arriving,
he suddenly saw a fox emerge from the deep grass by the roadside,
and dash into the residence of a local man named Yáo.
Dozens of people shouted and chased it,
and the fox entered a burrow.
Nánhuá ordered it to be dug up with shovels,
and they found a great deal of gold and silk,
which turned out to be the wealth the bandits had robbed from the Yīn family.
He immediately summoned Yáo's son,
and questioned him about its origin.
His eyes shifted and his words faltered,
so he arrested and interrogated him.
Indeed, he was the leader of the bandits.
From then on, all his accomplices were captured,
about ten of them.
Although the fox had hidden in the burrow,
when they searched thoroughly, they found nothing.
Could it not have been an apparition of the wronged souls?
This happened during the middle of the Tàihé era.
From "Xuān Shì Zhì".
Xíngyáng Shì
Táng Yíngzhōu Lìng was about to assume his post when,
one night, he stopped at an old temple in a subordinate county.
Just as he was falling asleep,
he saw an old woman
covering her head with a paulownia leaf,
hunched over as she approached.
The magistrate used his walking stick to brush away the leaf,
and the old woman bent down to pick it up before leaving,
but soon she returned again.
This happened three times,
and after a long while, she did not come back.
Shortly after, someone in mourning clothes
ascended the steps from the northern door,
lifted the curtain, and came forward, saying:
"I have something to report to you, sir,
please do not be afraid."
The magistrate asked:
"What kind of monster are you?"
The figure replied:
"I am indeed a ghost,
not a monster.
Because my appearance is haggard and emaciated,
I dared not approach you directly.
Earlier, I secretly sent Granny Zhāng to convey my hidden feelings,
but she was insulted three times by your walking stick.
Granny firmly refused to go again,
ashamed to approach once more,
so I have come myself to plead sorrowfully,
hoping not to incur your anger.
I am the son of the Xíngyáng family.
My father governed this prefecture,
but before a year had passed,
a great family misfortune struck.
I then escorted the funeral procession back to Luòyáng,
and one night, we stopped at this temple.
My stepmother gave me and my younger sister poisoned Gěhuā soup,
and we both died that same night.
Granny Zhāng was about to cry out,
but her head was smashed by an iron hammer,
and we were all buried together in the bamboo shade by the northern wall.
My late mother from Lǒngxī appealed to the Supreme Deity that very day,
and the Deity decreed:
'As a wife,
she already cruelly killed servants and concubines;
as a mother,
she further poisoned and murdered orphaned children.
Though she dwells in darkness,
and such matters are hard to bring to light,
under Heaven's watchful gaze,
it is only right that she be executed.
Let her death repay death,
to atone to the orphans.'
He ordered the Director of Fate to carry out the punishment and report back.
On that day,
my late father also appealed to the Supreme Deity, saying:
'My wandering soul is not perceptive,
and I failed in vigilance,
allowing my wicked wife
to harm the orphaned children,
exposing this family scandal,
and defiling Heaven's hearing.
How can death alone
atone for such crimes?
I served three terms as a county magistrate,
twice received official tallies,
and truly had capable achievements,
bringing peace to the common people.
How could I have foreseen that my accumulated blessings would not flow on,
leading to such a wretched state?
My soul banner flutters aimlessly,
unable to pass beyond the subordinate city.
My eldest son has already died innocent,
and my widow is also made to repay with death.
Thinking of my coffin stranded here,
difficult to bury properly,
I humbly beg to extend her life,
so that I may return to Luòyáng for burial,
and be laid to rest in the ancestral tomb.
Then I would have no regrets.'
The following year, my stepmother arrived in Luòyáng,
and died from a carbuncle on her back.
The Supreme Deity's wrath
has already reached this extent,
so now I bear no resentment.
What pains me is
that the monks have built a latrine over our bones,
and the filth and foulness
are unbearable.
Moreover, my sister serves as a maid to the toilet goddess,
and I myself am a laborer for the toilet goddess.
For generations, our family wore official caps and tassels,
yet in one day, we fell into such degradation.
The gates of Heaven are blocked and distant,
and there is no way to appeal above.
Relying on your benevolence and virtue,
I have come to inform you."
The magistrate asked:
"What should I do?"
The ghost replied:
"If you could unearth our decaying bones,
bathe them with fragrant orchid water,
cover them with clothing and quilts,
and move them to higher ground,
and if you could further bestow a wooden coffin
and offerings of duckweed and algae,
that would be beyond our hopes."
The magistrate said:
"Agreed.
This is as easy for me as turning over my hand."
The ghost sobbed and bowed twice.
He then asked Granny Zhāng to secretly summon Lady Luán to also thank the illustrious lord.
Granny Zhāng hurriedly arrived,
urgently calling out:
"Lord Guō is angry that the screens in the hall are in disarray from the evening,
and has already summoned you three times."
At this, the one in mourning clothes hastily departed.
The next morning,
the magistrate summoned the monks
and told them everything he had been told.
He then ordered laborers
to dig up the latrine in search of the bones.
At a depth of three or four feet,
they found the skeletons
and reburied them elsewhere.
Wáng Jì's Maidservant
A servant of Jìn's Wáng Jì
often went into the inner chambers to fetch Wáng Jì's clothing from a maidservant.
The maidservant then tried to seduce him.
The man said:
"I dare not."
The maidservant said that if he did not comply,
she would scream.
The man still refused.
The maidservant then cried out:
"So-and-so tried to rape me."
Wáng Jì immediately ordered the man killed.
The man explained everything in detail,
but Wáng Jì did not believe him,
so he was dragged away.
Looking back at Wáng Jì, he said:
"I cannot accept this injustice;
I must appeal to the Lord of Heaven."
Wáng Jì then fell ill,
and suddenly saw this man, who said to him:
"I explained the truth earlier,
but since you did not heed it,
it is time for you to go."
Wáng Jì died a few days later.
From "Records of Repaying Injustice"
Wáng Fàn's Concubine
In the Jin Dynasty, Wáng Fàn, the magistrate of Fùyáng County, had a concubine named Táo Yīng,
who was exceptionally beautiful.
She engaged in illicit affairs with two men under his administration, Dīng Fēng and Shǐ Huáqī.
Once, when Wáng Fàn was away on a trip and had not yet returned,
his household supervisor Sūn Yuánbì heard the sound of jade pendants from Dīng Fēng’s room.
He peeked inside
and saw Táo Yīng lying under the same blanket with him.
Yuánbì knocked on the door and shouted at them.
Táo Yīng immediately got up,
gathered her skirt and tidied her hair,
then slipped on her shoes and went back inside.
Yuánbì also saw Huáqī wearing Táo Yīng’s musk-scented pouch.
The two, fearing Yuánbì would report them,
jointly slandered Yuánbì, claiming he had an affair with Táo Yīng.
Wáng Fàn, without investigating carefully,
had Yuánbì killed.
There was a man named Chén Chāo
who was present at the time
and helped secure Yuánbì’s conviction.
Later, when Wáng Fàn’s term ended and he returned
, Chāo also went out of the capital to see Wáng Fàn off.
As they reached the foot of Chìtíng Mountain,
they encountered thunder, rain, and dusk.
Suddenly, someone grabbed Chāo under the arms
and dragged him away
into a desolate marsh.
The lightning illuminated a ghost,
its face very dark and bluish,
with eyes lacking pupils.
It said:
“I am Sūn Yuánbì.
I appealed my grievance to the August Heaven,
and it was soon adjudicated.
I have long awaited you,
and now we meet.”
Chāo kowtowed until blood flowed.
The ghost said:
“Since Wáng Fàn is the mastermind,
he shall be killed first.
Jiǎ Jǐngbó and Sūn Wéndù are at the Xuán Hall beneath Tàishān,
jointly determining the registry of life and death.
Táo Yīng’s soul
has also been taken to the Nǚqīng Pavilion.”
By daybreak,
the ghost had vanished.
Chāo went to Yángdū to visit Wáng Fàn,
not daring to confess,
when he saw the ghost enter from outside,
heading straight into Wáng Fàn’s tent.
That night,
when Wáng Fàn had just fallen asleep,
he suddenly suffered a severe nightmare,
repeatedly calling out without waking.
His family led a black ox to stand over Wáng Fàn
and added a peach-wood figurine with a left-twisted rope.
Toward dawn, he briefly revived,
but died after ten-some days.
The concubine also died suddenly.
Chāo then fled to Chánggān Temple,
changing his name to Hé Guī.
Five years later, on the third day of the second month,
while drinking by the waterside,
Chāo said:
“Now I should no longer fear this ghost.”
As he lowered his head,
he saw the ghost’s shadow already in the water.
It struck Chāo with its hand,
causing his nose to bleed profusely,
about a liter’s worth.
He died a few days later.
From “Míng Bào Zhì.”
The Ming manuscript says from “Huán Yuān Jì.”
Sòng Palace Woman
Sòng Shàodì Zǐyè often made women run naked chasing each other.
One woman refused,
and he ordered her beheaded.
That night,
he dreamed of a woman cursing him:
“You are perverse and rebellious;
next year you will not live to see the harvest.”
The emperor, enraged,
found someone in the palace who resembled the woman in his dream
and had her beheaded.
That evening,
he again dreamed of the slain woman saying:
“You wrongfully killed me.
I have already appealed to the Supreme God.
He will gather all the shamans and the six palaces to capture the ghost.”
The emperor was soon assassinated.
From “Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì.”
Jīn Jīng
In the late Northern Wèi period,
Dù Chāng of Sōngyáng had a wife, Liǔ Shì, who was extremely jealous.
There was a maidservant named Jīn Jīng.
When Chāng bathed,
he had her comb his hair.
Liǔ Shì cut off both of her fingers.
Not long after, Liǔ was stung by a fox,
and both her fingers fell off.
There was another maidservant,
named Yù Lián,
who could sing well.
Chāng admired her and praised her skill.
Liǔ Shì then cut out her tongue.
Later, Liǔ Shì developed festering sores on her tongue.
In desperation,
she went to Chán Master Chóu to confess and repent.
The master already knew beforehand
and said to Liǔ Shì:
“Madam, due to your jealousy,
you first cut off the maid’s fingers,
and have already lost your own fingers.
Then you cut out the maid’s tongue;
now you too should have your tongue severed.
If you repent wholeheartedly,
you may yet be spared.”
Liǔ Shì bowed deeply and pleaded for mercy.
After seven days,
the master opened his mouth wide and chanted over her.
Two snakes, over a foot long, emerged from his mouth.
He urgently chanted,
and they fell to the ground.
Her tongue then healed completely.
From then on, she was no longer jealous.
From “Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.”
Dù Yì’s Concubine
In Liáng, Dù Yì of Xiāngyáng had newly taken a concubine,
who was both young and beautiful,
and he doted on her especially.
The concubine received a letter from her father
and was reading it leaning against the curtain.
Yì returned from outside,
and the concubine, being new to the household,
felt ashamed to let Yì know about this matter,
so she chewed and swallowed the letter.
Yì thought it was a letter from a lover,
and ordered her belly cut open to retrieve the letter.
The concubine was still breathing,
but the letter had already been taken out.
Yì read it through,
sighed, and said:
“I never imagined
I would act so rashly.
Having harmed the harmony of the world,
how can I last long?”
That night, he saw the concubine appeal her grievance.
Yì died within ten days.
From “Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì.”
Later Zhōu Woman
When Emperor Xuān of the Later Zhōu was still the Crown Prince,
Emperor Wǔ supervised and disciplined him very strictly,
always having the eunuch Chéng Shèn oversee and inspect him.
If there were even the slightest fault or error that was not reported,
Shèn would be put to death.
Thus, Shèn often reported the Crown Prince’s unlawful actions,
and Emperor Wǔ had him beaten over a hundred times with a rod.
After the Crown Prince ascended the throne,
he looked at the scar from the rod on his thigh
and asked where Shèn was.
Shèn had by then been sent out to serve in a commandery,
so an edict was issued to summon him back.
Upon his arrival, he was ordered to be executed.
Shèn cried out indignantly:
"This was done by your father—
what crime did Chéng Shèn commit?
In the aftermath of your rebellion,
I am unjustly implicated.
If ghosts have awareness,
they will never let you go."
At that time, the palace was under strict prohibitions:
people could only exchange glances when they met,
and were not allowed to speak or laugh together.
Supervisors were appointed
to record faults and offenses.
A woman under the Left Empress yawned and shed tears,
and was consequently impeached,
accused of having thoughts
and ordered to be interrogated under torture.
When they first struck her head,
the Emperor immediately felt a headache.
When they struck her again,
the same thing happened.
He then flew into a rage and said:
"This is my nemesis!"
He then ordered her waist to be broken,
and the Emperor again felt pain in his waist.
That night, he went to the Southern Palace,
and his illness gradually worsened.
The next morning, upon returning,
he was unable to ride a horse due to the pain in his waist.
He returned by carriage.
At the place where the woman was killed,
there was a black mark resembling a human shape.
At the time, it was thought to be blood,
but even after scrubbing it,
it reappeared as before,
and this happened repeatedly.
The authorities dug up the old ground
and filled it with new soil,
but overnight it returned to its previous state.
After about seven or eight days of this,
he developed sores all over his body and died.
When his body was initially laid out,
all the beds with curved legs
were firmly stuck and could not be removed,
except for the bed that this woman had used
(the Ming manuscript has "used" as "slept on").
This bed alone had straight legs,
so it was used for the purpose,
likely also due to the will of ghosts and spirits.
The Emperor died about
only twenty days after Chéng Shèn's death.
From "Records of Retribution."
Concubine of Zhāng Gōngjǐn
In the Táng dynasty, Mǎ Jiāyùn of Wèijùn,
in the sixth year of the Zhēnguàn era, was at home in the first month.
One evening, as he stepped out of the main gate,
he suddenly saw two men, each holding a horse,
standing under a tree outside the gate.
Jiāyùn asked who they were,
and they replied:
"Lord of the Eastern Sea has sent us to welcome Master Mǎ."
Jiāyùn had long been known for his learning and knowledge,
and was renowned throughout the prefecture.
Envoys from the court and distinguished guests from all directions often requested to meet him.
Thus, he was not particularly surprised by this.
He said to the messengers:
"I have no horse."
The messengers offered him a horse,
and Jiāyùn mounted it under the tree and rode away,
while his body lay collapsed under the tree.
Soon, he arrived at an official compound.
As he was about to enter the main gate,
he saw several dozen men and women
outside the gate, as if engaged in a lawsuit.
Among them was a woman
whom Jiāyùn had known before—
she was the concubine of Zhāng Gōngjǐn from the same commandery,
surnamed Yuán.
Holding a written document in her hand,
she approached Jiāyùn and said:
"Master Mǎ, do you still recognize me?
In the past, Commander Zhāng often had me meet with you.
The Commander acted without reason
and killed me unjustly.
I appealed to the Heavenly Court,
and for three years now,
the Heavenly Lord Wáng has been protecting Gōngjǐn,
so my case has been suppressed.
Now it has finally been heard,
and the authorities have summoned him.
He will arrive soon.
I thought I was the only one wrongfully harmed—
why has Master Mǎ also come?"
Jiāyùn had already known that Yuán had been killed,
and upon seeing her, he realized he was dead.
The messengers led him inside the gate,
and the gatekeeper said:
"The Lord is still asleep and cannot be visited.
You should go see Minister of Justice Huò instead."
This was Huò Zhāng, a secretary of the Yìzhōu regional administration.
He received Jiāyùn and invited him to sit,
saying:
"The position of record-keeper in this office is vacant.
The Lord of the Eastern Sea has heard of your talent and learning
and wishes to invite you to take this post."
Jiāyùn replied:
"I am content with my humble life, caring for my wife and children,
and have no desire to serve as an official.
It would be fortunate if I could be excused."
Huò said:
"If you cannot do it,
you may decline on the grounds of lacking the necessary learning.
You must have acquaintances—
you can recommend someone else to take the position."
Soon, someone came and said:
"The Lord has awakened."
Jiāyùn was led in
and saw a man sitting in the hall—
short, stout, and dark-skinned.
He called Jiāyùn forward
and said:
"I have heard of your talent and learning
and wish to invite you to serve as record-keeper.
Can you do it?"
Jiāyùn bowed and replied:
"It is an honor!
But I am but a rustic from the countryside,
who merely teaches classical studies to young students.
I am not fit for the role of record-keeper."
The Lord asked:
"Do you know Huò Zhāng?"
Jiāyùn replied:
"I do."
The Lord then summoned Huò Zhāng
and asked about Jiāyùn's abilities.
Huò said:
"I have always known him for his classical learning,
but I have never seen him write essays."
The Lord asked:
"Who is skilled in writing essays?"
Jiāyùn said:
"There is a man named Chén Zǐliáng
who is proficient in writing."
The Lord said:
"Release Master Mǎ and let him return."
He then ordered Chén Zǐliáng to be summoned.
Jiāyùn took his leave,
and Huò Zhāng bid him farewell.
Jiāyùn asked:
"Earlier, I saw the concubine of Zhāng Gōngjǐn.
Who is the Heavenly Lord she mentioned?"
Huò replied:
"He is Wáng Wǔjiè, a fellow villager of Gōngjǐn.
After his death, he became a Heavenly Lord
and often protected Gōngjǐn,
which is why he survived until now.
But now, even he cannot escape."
After speaking, they parted.
The messengers escorted Jiāyùn to a narrow path
and instructed him to return via this route.
In the seventh month of that year,
a man from Miánzhōu named Chén Zǐliáng suddenly died
but revived after one night.
He claimed to have met the Lord of the Eastern Sea,
who wanted to appoint him as record-keeper,
but he declined, saying he was illiterate.
Another man named Chén Zǐliáng died,
and Gōngjǐn also passed away.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
when the imperial carriage was at the Jiǔchéng Palace,
the Emperor heard of this
and sent the Vice Director of the Secretariat, Cén Wénběn, to inquire about the matter.
Wénběn recorded it and submitted a report.
Jiāyùn later became a National Academy Erudite
and died in office.
From "Records of Hidden Retribution."
Fàn Lüè's Maid
During the Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty,
Fàn Lüè of Púyáng had a wife named Rén.
Lüè had previously favored a maidservant,
and Rén, using a knife, cut off the servant's ears and nose.
Lüè was unable to stop her.
After some time,
Rén became pregnant,
and gave birth to a daughter,
who had no ears or nose.
As the girl grew older,
the maidservant was still present.
The girl asked the maidservant,
who told her the whole story.
The girl wept bitterly,
and resented her mother.
Her mother felt deeply ashamed,
but her remorse was too late.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Hú Liàng's Concubine
In the Táng dynasty, Hú Liàng, the County Magistrate of Huàméng County in Guǎngzhōu, followed Commander Zhōu Rénguǐ to suppress the Liáo people.
He obtained a chieftain's concubine,
favored her,
and was bringing her to the county.
Liàng was away at the prefectural office,
and his wife, Hé,
heated nails and branded the concubine's eyes,
after which the concubine hanged herself.
Later, Hé became pregnant,
and gave birth to a snake,
with no pupils in its eyes.
She asked a Chan master about it,
and the master said:
"Madam once branded a woman's eyes with hot nails.
Because of your poisonous nature,
this is the snake's retribution.
This is the woman you branded.
Madam, you should raise this snake well,
and you may avoid calamity.
If not,
disaster will befall you."
Hé raised the snake.
After a year or two, it gradually grew larger,
could not see,
and stayed only within the bedding.
Liàng was unaware of it.
Uncovering the bedding, he saw the snake,
was greatly alarmed,
and killed it with a knife.
Hé's eyes both dried up,
and she could no longer see.
Her remorse was too late.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Liáng Rényù's Maidservant
In the Táng dynasty, Liáng Rényù served as General of the Xiāo Wèi.
He had previously favored a maidservant.
His wife, Lǐ,
was extremely jealous and cruel,
tied up the maidservant, and struck her head.
The maidservant cried out:
"I am lowly and humble,
with no control over my fate.
Mistress, you bind my neck,
how bitterly cruel!"
Over a month after the maidservant died,
Lǐ fell ill,
and often saw the maidservant coming to summon her.
Four carbuncles grew on Lǐ's head,
her brain festered,
and she cried out day and night,
unable to bear the pain,
dying after several months.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Zhāng Jǐngxiān's Maidservant
In the Táng dynasty, Xià Róng, the Registrar of Zhījiāng County in Jīngzhōu, judged cases in the underworld.
The County Magistrate Zhāng Jǐngxiān favored a maidservant,
and his wife, Yáng, was jealous of her.
Jǐng was away on an official mission,
and his wife killed the maidservant,
throwing her into the latrine.
When Jǐng returned,
she deceived him, saying:
"The maidservant ran away."
Jǐng, knowing his wife was cruel,
did not inquire further.
The maidservant brought a complaint against her to Róng,
and Róng summoned her for questioning.
He asked Jǐng:
"Your wife is gravely ill."
He described her condition,
and Jǐng suspected he had an illicit affair,
and became angry.
Róng said:
"Your wife wrongfully killed a maidservant,
and threw her into the latrine.
She is now being investigated.
You should question her."
Jǐng understood,
and questioned his wife.
His wife was very ill,
and confessed the whole affair.
Róng ordered the bones to be retrieved from the latrine,
bathed them in fragrant water,
and gave them a lavish burial.
The maidservant would not relent,
and over a month later, she died.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Lǐ Xùn's Concubine
In the Táng dynasty, the daughter of Left Vice Director Wéi Ānshí
was married to Lǐ Xùn, a Registrar in the Court of the Imperial Treasury.
Before Xùn was married,
he had a concubine.
After he married,
he sent her away,
and she had already changed masters twice.
His wife suffered from consumption,
and suspected the concubine had cursed her.
Ānshí ordered Qín Shǒuyī, the Magistrate of Hénán, to arrest her.
She was tortured severely,
and finally confessed falsely,
receiving over three hundred strokes in total,
and was thrown into a well to die.
Within three days,
his daughter died,
and people of the time all believed it was caused by the wronged spirit.
Ānshí was demoted to Púzhōu,
and died in the eighth month of the first year of the Tàijí era.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Huā Yán
In the Táng dynasty, Wáng Hóng,
a native of Héngshuǐ in Jìzhōu,
was a rogue in his youth,
informing and framing good people.
He once traveled to Zhàodìng in Héběi,
"Dìng" originally written as "Jù".
Changed according to the Ming manuscript.
He saw an old man holding annual village feasts,
and reported him for killing two hundred people,
and was appointed as a Guerrilla General,
and soon promoted to Investigating Censor.
When someone reported Wáng Ānrén, the Military Governor of Shèngzhōu,
Hóng was secretly sent to investigate.
He demanded a large cangue to clamp Ānrén's neck,
but Ānrén would not confess.
Hóng then beheaded Ānrén while he was still in the cangue,
and immediately removed it.
Ānrén's son, who was in the army,
was also captured and beheaded.
Arriving in Fēnzhōu,
he was dining with Sima Máo,
when suddenly he shouted for him to be taken down,
beheaded him,
and the people were terrified.
Later, he was convicted of false accusations,
and exiled to Léizhōu,
taking along his young concubine Huā Yán,
whom he had always favored.
On the boat,
Hóng forged an imperial edict summoning him back.
Huā Yán advised him:
"Given the situation,
how can you bear to commit further wrongdoing?"
Hóng angrily said:
"This old woman wants to ruin my plans!"
He bound her hands and feet,
and threw her into the river.
The boatmen rescued her,
but Hóng flogged her two hundred times until she died,
and buried her by the river.
Soon, the forged edict was discovered,
and Investigating Censor Hú Yuánlǐ investigated the case.
Hóng was imprisoned and escorted back.
When they reached the place where Huā Yán died,
he suddenly said:
"Huā Yán has come to summon me for judgment."
Those around him saw nothing,
but Hóng alone cried out, kowtowing and admitting his crime,
as if hearing the sounds of cangues and clubs,
and died by midnight.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
The Concubine of the Man from Jìnyáng
When my maternal uncle Niú Sù served as a county lieutenant in Jìnyáng,
a man in the county killed his concubine.
As she was dying, she said:
"I am innocent,
yet you have killed me.
I will surely take revenge!"
Several years later,
the man who killed the concubine rose in the middle of the night
and went to his mother's bedroom door, calling out.
His mother asked him what was wrong.
The man said:
"I just dreamed that I was bitten by a tiger,
and the injury was so severe
that I died.
Upon waking, my heart was pounding,
and I felt deeply frightened and disturbed,
so I came to tell you."
His mother said:
"People say that dreaming of death actually means life—
it's because dreams are often inverted.
Why worry!
But you haven't fed the ox yet tonight,
go feed it quickly."
The man said:
"Yes."
In the darkness, he saw something
that looked like an ox that had broken loose.
He went forward to grab it,
but it turned out to be a tiger.
He was then bitten by it,
and he screamed until he died.
After the tiger killed the man,
it entered the courtyard,
went to his room, and lay on his bed,
as if sleeping.
His family waited until it was asleep,
then locked the door and reported it to the prefectural office.
Jì Xiūguāng was the military governor,
and he ordered it to be captured.
The captors climbed up,
broke through the roof,
and thrust spears at it,
until it died.
My uncle was then serving as an assistant to the military governor,
and he obtained the tiger's head,
lacquering it to make a pillow.
To this day, people believe the tiger was the concubine who had been killed.
From "Jì Wén"
Dòu Níng's Concubine
In the twenty-fifth year of the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the granddaughter of Liǔ Huàn, the governor of Jìnzhōu, a woman of the Cuī clan from Bólíng,
resided in Biànzhōu.
There was a man from Fúfēng named Dòu Níng,
who intended to marry her,
and sent a matchmaker to arrange the formalities.
However, Níng’s former concubine was pregnant,
so the Cuī woman stipulated that the concubine must be sent away before the wedding could take place.
Níng agreed,
and then traveled with the concubine to Sòngzhōu.
Sailing downstream, they stopped for the night at Chēdàokǒu.
That evening, the concubine gave birth to two daughters.
Taking advantage of her exhaustion and weakness, Níng killed her,
stuffed sand into her abdomen,
and sank her body along with the two infants into the river.
Afterward, he returned to Biànzhōu,
and deceived the Cuī woman, saying:
“The concubine has already been sent away.”
He then selected an auspicious day to hold the wedding.
Fifteen years later,
the Cuī woman had given birth to several children:
the sons did not survive,
but two daughters
each grew to adulthood.
In the fourth month of the second year of the Yǒngtài era,
unexpectedly,
a letter appeared on the table.
Upon opening and reading it,
they found it was a missive from Níng’s deceased father.
It stated that the matter of his wrongful killing of a soul had come to light,
and retribution was imminent within a month.
He should quickly put his household affairs in order;
his elder daughter could be married to Cuī Yán, a military officer in Biànzhōu,
and the younger daughter to Lǐ Rì, the former sheriff of Kāifēng.
Both were suitable matches.
Níng did not believe it,
and said to his wife:
“This is the work of a fox spirit,
not to be taken as evidence.”
After another ten days,
another letter appeared inside the room:
“I have already shown you the signs of impending disaster,
why are you still so deluded?”
Níng remained hesitant.
The next day,
yet another letter was found in the courtyard,
its words mournful and urgent,
saying:
“Calamity will strike at any moment.”
Only then did Níng become alarmed.
His wife said:
“You should reflect on what you have done.
You ought to perform rites to avert disaster.”
Although Níng kept it secret,
in his heart he truly feared the matter of the concubine.
At noon on the sixteenth day of the fifth month,
while everyone was resting,
suddenly there came a frantic knocking at the door.
Níng’s heart stirred with fear;
he went out to see who it was,
and it was the concubine he had killed,
dressed in splendid attire,
who stepped forward and bowed to Níng, saying:
“It has been a long time since we parted; have you been well?”
Níng was terrified,
and rushed inside to hide.
The ghost followed closely behind into the courtyard,
where she saw the Cuī woman.
Startled, the Cuī woman asked who she was.
The ghost then composed herself and recounted her story:
“I am the concubine of Dòu Shíwǔláng.
When Níng wished to marry you, madam,
he killed me at Chēdàokǒu,
along with my two daughters—all three of us lost our lives.
I had done no wrong to Níng,
yet he wrongfully killed me.
If Níng wanted to take a wife,
I would have withdrawn quietly on my own.
How could he bear to harm my life
to such an extent?
Though I am of lowly status,
for over fifteen years,
I have pleaded my case before the sacred mountains and rivers,
and my grievance has ascended
to reach the heavenly court.
The Supreme Emperor looked down with discernment,
and permitted me to seek vengeance.
Now I have come to take Níng.
This does not concern you, madam;
do not be afraid.”
The Cuī woman, grief-stricken and terrified, begged and apologized:
“Could we perhaps redeem his crime
through meritorious deeds?”
The ghost sternly replied:
“Níng repaying a life with a life is sufficient.
What meritorious deeds could equal a life?
If he had killed you, madam,
could meritorious deeds ever compensate for that?”
Her words were unyielding.
Then she cursed Níng, saying:
“The net of heaven is vast and lets nothing through;
what use is there in hiding like a fox or scurrying like a rat?”
She then entered the main hall, seized Níng,
and began biting, gnawing, pinching, and twisting him,
causing him to writhe in agony,
before departing at the end of the day,
saying:
“You need not consider dying just yet;
first you may experience what I am capable of.”
From then on, she came every day,
gnawing and chewing on his limbs.
Sometimes the ghost appeared in strange and monstrous forms,
transforming in extraordinary ways,
throwing the entire household into terror and dread.
They could devise no plan to deal with it,
and the ghost also attacked the two daughters,
who could not endure the torment.
At that time, there was a monk named Tán Liàng,
quite skilled in incantations,
whom Níng summoned for help.
They set up an altar in the inner chamber.
Shortly after, the ghost arrived
but did not dare ascend the steps.
The monk rebuked her, saying:
“The way of ghosts should not interfere with the human realm;
how dare you come here!
If I summon the Vajra deities,
you will be crushed to pieces in an instant.”
The ghost replied:
“Venerable monk, you serve the Buddha;
your heart should uphold impartiality.
Why do you shield injustice and conceal a criminal?
Moreover, Níng killed me without just cause;
how then am I interfering with the human realm?
The heavenly command shines upon me,
permitting me to take vengeance on Níng.
Would the Vajra deities unjustly slay one who has been wronged?”
Having spoken, she ascended the steps
and seized Níng as before.
The Cuī woman instructed the monk to secretly arrange marriages for the two daughters.
The ghost learned of this and angrily said:
“A monk acting as a matchmaker for others—
are you not ashamed?”
The monk left in shame.
Later, when the Cuī and Lǐ families came to betroth the daughters and they fled,
the ghost did not pursue them,
but instead declared:
“I have long bound your feet;
how could you go far?”
After a few years,
both daughters died.
Níng, poisoned by the ghost’s malice,
went mad,
began eating his own limbs,
threw himself into fire and water,
consumed filth and excrement,
until his skin became scorched and ulcerated.
Several years later, he finally died.
The Cuī woman took monastic vows in Dōngjīng,
as many people knew.
From Tōng Yōu Jì.
Táng
“Táng” originally written as “Guǎng,”
amended according to the Ming manuscript and Xǔ’s edition.
Yán Wǔ, the military governor of Xīchuān,
was in his youth reckless and chivalrous.
Once in the capital city,
he lived next to a military commissioner.
The military commissioner had an unmarried daughter,
whose appearance was exceptionally beautiful.
Lord Yán happened to catch sight of her
and bribed her attendants,
luring her to his residence.
After over a month,
he secretly fled with her,
heading east through the pass,
intending to hide in the region between Huái and Sì.
When the military commissioner discovered this,
he exhaustively tracked their trail
and questioned his family members.
He then reported it to the authorities,
and also submitted a memorial to the emperor.
An imperial edict ordered the thief-capturing official of Wànnián County to go specially to apprehend them.
The thief-capturing official traveled by relay,
covering several postal stations a day,
and along the way had already found their tracks.
Yán Wǔ, from Gǒng County,
had just hired a boat to go downstream
when he heard that the imperial commissioner was about to arrive.
Fearing he could not escape punishment,
he gave wine to the military commissioner’s daughter to drink.
In the middle of the night, taking advantage of her drunkenness,
he removed a string from a pipa and strangled her with it,
then sank her body in the river.
The next day, when the imperial commissioner arrived,
he searched Lord Yán’s boat,
but finding no trace, he gave up.
Later, Lord Yán became the military governor of Jiànnán.
When he was gravely ill,
his nature being inherently stubborn,
he especially disbelieved in shamans and sorcerers.
If anyone spoke of such things,
he would certainly punish them.
Suddenly one day at noon,
a Daoist priest arrived at the yamen gate,
claiming he had come from Mount Éméi
and wished to see Wǔ.
The gatekeeper initially did not dare to report it,
but the Daoist priest raised his voice sternly,
and having no choice,
he went in to announce him.
Wǔ also found it strange,
so he had him brought in.
He saw the Daoist priest reach the steps and begin shouting reproaches,
as if debating with someone.
Only after a long while did he stop.
After exchanging greetings,
he said to Wǔ:
“You are ill,
and calamity is extremely grave.
Your enemy is by your side.
Why do you not repent of your faults
and offer incense in atonement?
How can you instead remain so stubborn?”
Wǔ angrily did not reply.
The Daoist priest continued:
