“Please think carefully:
have you ever betrayed someone’s trust or killed anyone?”
Wǔ pondered silently for a long time
and said:
“No.”
The Daoist priest said:
“Just now, when I reached the steps,
the wrongfully killed one appeared to me to state her grievance.
At first I thought it was a mountain spirit or tree demon
causing trouble for you,
so I reproached it.
But she said
that the Heavenly Emperor had issued a decree:
because she was wrongfully killed by you,
her plea has already been granted.
How can you say there is none?”
Wǔ, unable to fathom this,
asked again:
“What does she look like?”
He said:
“A woman, only sixteen or seventeen years old,
with something around her neck like a cord,
resembling the string of a musical instrument.”
Wǔ suddenly understood.
He kowtowed to the Daoist priest and said:
“Heavenly Master, you are truly a sage.
It is so.
What can be done about it?”
The Daoist priest said:
“She wishes to see you face to face.
You must seek her yourself.”
He then had the hall swept and cleaned,
removed all other objects,
and burned incense inside.
He had Wǔ carried to the doorway of the hall,
told him to clear his mind,
put on his official robe and tablet,
and left only one young servant to attend by his side.
In the eastern section outside the broad hall,
there was a small chamber.
He also had it swept clean and hung a curtain.
The Daoist priest sat outside the hall,
took water in his mouth and sprayed it,
then used a willow branch to sprinkle the ground, sat back down,
closed his eyes, and clicked his teeth.
After a short while,
a sighing sound came from the chamber.
The Daoist priest said:
“Madam, you may come out.”
After a long time,
a woman appeared with disheveled hair,
a pipa string around her neck,
knotted below her throat.
She lifted the curtain and came forward.
When she reached the hall door,
she tied her hair behind her
and bowed to Wǔ.
Wǔ, upon seeing her, was greatly shocked and ashamed,
and covered his face.
The woman said:
“You were too cruel.
My following you
was my own moral failing;
toward you, I owed nothing.
If you feared punishment,
you could have simply abandoned me elsewhere.
How could you bear to kill me?”
Wǔ repented and apologized for a long time,
and also wished to offer generous amounts of Buddhist scriptures, paper money, and silk to pray for exemption.
The Daoist priest also earnestly pleaded on his behalf.
The woman said:
“It cannot be.
I was killed by your own hand.
I appealed to the Heavenly Emperor,
“Emperor” originally written as “this,”
amended according to the Ming manuscript.
for nearly thirty years.
Now it is impossible.
The time is set for tomorrow evening.”
Having said this, she turned and left.
When she reached the chamber door,
she vanished in an instant.
The Daoist priest then took his leave and departed.
Lord Yán then settled his family affairs,
and at dusk on that day, he died.
From “Yì Shǐ”
Yuán Qiào
Yú Xuánjī, a female Daoist priest at the Xiányí Temple in the Western Capital of the Táng dynasty,
styled Yòuwēi,
was a daughter of a common family in Cháng'ān.
Her beauty could topple cities,
and her thoughts were divinely inspired.
She delighted in reading and composing writings,
and paid particular attention to every line of poetry she chanted or recited.
At the age of sixteen,
she aspired to the purity and emptiness of Daoist practice.
In the early years of the Xiántōng era,
she thus donned the Daoist cap and stole at the Xiányí Temple,
yet her exquisite verses on the pleasures of wind and moon
were often circulated among the literati.
However, her delicate orchid-like constitution
could not maintain self-restraint,
and she was again teased by gallant men,
so she followed them in their wanderings and dalliances.
Thus, men of romantic disposition
vied to adorn themselves in order to seek intimacy with her.
Those who came with wine to visit her
would invariably play the qin and compose poetry,
interspersed with playful banter,
making the dull scholars feel inadequate in comparison.
Among her poems are lines such as: "On the splendid road, gazing far in spring,
With jade zither, autumn inspirations abound";
also: "Eager yet unable to speak,
A pair of crimson tears stream down";
also: "Burning incense, ascending the jade altar,
Holding the tablet upright, paying respects at the golden gate";
also: "Cloud-like emotions, brooding, vie to share the same dream,
Immortal beauty, ever fragrant, surpasses even flowers."
These couplets are among her finest.
She had a maidservant named Yuánqiào,
who was also intelligent and beautiful.
One day,
Xuánjī was invited by a neighboring courtyard,
and as she was about to leave,
she admonished Qiào, saying:
"Do not go out.
If any guests come,
just say I am at such-and-such place."
Xuánjī was detained by her female companions,
and did not return to the temple until dusk.
Yuánqiào met her at the gate and said:
"Just now a certain guest came,
and upon learning that the priestess was not in,
left without even dismounting from his horse."
This guest was someone with whom Xuánjī had long been intimate,
and she suspected that Qiào had a secret affair with him.
When night fell,
she lit a lamp and bolted the door,
then summoned Qiào into her bedroom to interrogate her.
Qiào said:
"For years since I began serving you,
I have truly guarded myself,
never allowing any semblance of fault,
lest I offend your honor.
Moreover, when that guest came and knocked on the door,
I answered from behind the door:
'The priestess is not in.'
The guest said nothing and rode away on his horse.
As for romantic love,
I have not harbored it in my heart for years;
I beg the priestess not to doubt me."
Xuánjī grew even angrier,
stripped her naked, and flogged her over a hundred times,
but Qiào only insisted there was nothing.
When she was utterly exhausted,
she asked for a cup of water to pour on the ground as a libation, saying:
"The priestess seeks the Way of the Three Purities and eternal life,
yet cannot forget the joys of removing girdle pendants and sharing a pillow.
Instead, with deep suspicion,
you falsely accuse one chaste and upright.
Qiào will surely die by your cruel hands today.
If there is no Heaven, I have nowhere to appeal;
if there is,
who can restrain my fierce spirit?
I vow not to remain ignorant in the darkness,
allowing you to indulge in wantonness."
Having said this,
she collapsed to the ground and died.
Xuánjī, terrified,
dug a pit in the backyard and buried her there,
thinking no one would know.
This was in the spring, the first month of the Wùzǐ year of the Xiántōng era.
When people asked about Qiào,
she would say:
"She ran away after the spring rain cleared."
Once, a guest was feasting in Xuánjī's room
and went to relieve himself in the backyard.
Right over the burial spot,
he saw dozens of blue flies gathering on the ground.
He shooed them away, but they returned.
Upon closer inspection,
it seemed there were bloodstains and a foul smell.
After leaving,
he secretly told his servant.
The servant returned home
and told his elder brother.
This elder brother was a patrolman in the prefectural streets,
who had once asked Xuánjī for money,
but she ignored him,
so the patrolman deeply resented her.
Hearing this,
he hurried to the temple gate to watch and spy.
He overheard people chatting
and was surprised that no one had seen Yuánqiào coming or going.
The patrolman then called several other patrolmen,
brought shovels and tools,
burst into Xuánjī's courtyard, and dug up the spot,
finding Yuánqiào's corpse looking as if she were alive.
The patrolmen then reported Xuánjī to the Jīngzhào authorities.
When questioned by the prefectural officials, she confessed.
However, many court officials spoke in her defense.
The prefecture then submitted a memorial to the throne,
and by autumn, she was executed.
While in prison, she also wrote a poem:
"Easy to find a priceless treasure,
Hard to find a man with a true heart.
The bright moon shines into dark crevices,
The clear breeze opens the short lapels."
This is among her beautiful lines.
From "Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú".
Mǎ Quánjié's Maidservant
Mǎ Quánjié, the Attendant-in-Chief and military governor of Wèi,
once had a maidservant
who displeased him momentarily,
so he beat her to death himself.
Several years later,
he contracted a severe illness,
and suddenly saw the maidservant standing before him.
His family only marveled that Quánjié was talking to himself,
as if in conversation.
At first he said:
"What do you want by coming here?"
Then he said:
"I'll give you money and valuables."
And again:
"I'll have a statue made for you and scriptures copied."
He pleaded pitifully for a long time,
but the deceased maidservant would not accept,
only demanding his life.
Within ten days, he died.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà".
Lǔ Sīyān's Daughter
The daughter of the eunuch Lǔ Sīyān,
was seventeen years old.
One day, as she faced the mirror to apply makeup,
she suddenly saw a woman in the mirror,
with disheveled hair and bare feet,
holding an infant.
Turning around, she found the woman behind her.
Terrified, she immediately collapsed,
and after a long time, regained consciousness.
From then on, she saw the apparition every day.
As time passed,
her family members also saw it.
Sīyān personally asked the ghost the reason,
and it replied:
"I am the daughter of a commoner in Yángzǐ County.
Years ago, a certain clerk from Jiànchāng County came to Yángzǐ on business,
and took me as his concubine.
Your daughter was his principal wife.
Over a year later,
I gave birth to this child.
Later, when the clerk went to a neighboring county,
your daughter threw me into a well,
along with this child,
and filled it with stones,
deceiving her husband by saying I had run away.
I was just bringing a lawsuit to the authorities
when your daughter happened to die.
Now, though she has been reborn,
she must still repay with her life."
Sīyān sent someone galloping to Jiànchāng to verify the matter.
The old clerk was still alive,
and as described, they excavated the well,
and indeed found skeletons.
The family tried various methods to exorcise the ghost,
but none worked.
The daughter later married into the Chǔ family,
but the haunting grew even more severe.
She was frightened day and night,
until she eventually died.
From "Jīshén Lù".
The Junior Officer of Èzhōu
There was a certain junior officer in Èzhōu,
originally the son of a farming family.
After taking office,
he wished to marry into a powerful clan,
and plotted against his former wife.
He thus accompanied her on a visit to her parents,
killed her on the road,
and abandoned her corpse by the riverbank,
also killing the maid who had accompanied them.
He then rushed to inform her family,
wailing and crying:
"She was killed by bandits."
No one suspected him.
Several years later,
he was sent on a mission to Guǎnglíng,
and lodged at an inn.
He saw a woman selling flowers,
who looked exactly like the maid he had killed.
As he drew closer,
it truly was the maid,
who, upon seeing him, also bowed twice.
He then asked whether she was human or a ghost,
to which she replied:
"I am human.
Back then, I was struck by the villain,
but fortunately did not die.
After regaining consciousness,
I found a merchant's boat,
and traveled eastward on it.
Now I am here,
merely selling flowers with my lady to earn a living."
He asked again where his wife was,
and she said:
"Nearby.
Would you like to see her?"
He replied:
"Yes."
He immediately followed her.
In a small alley,
she pointed to a poor dwelling and said:
"This is it."
The maid entered first,
and after a short while,
his wife came out.
They met, weeping sorrowfully,
and she recounted all her hardships in detail.
He was also bewildered,
unable to comprehend it.
Soon, food and wine were set out,
and he was further invited into the inner chamber.
Food and drink were also provided for his attendants,
who all became drunk.
As evening fell, he did not emerge.
His attendants gradually approached to peek inside,
but it was silent as if no one was there.
They thus went straight into the room,
only to see a set of white bones,
with clothes torn and tattered,
and blood flowing all over the ground.
When they asked the neighbors,
they said:
"This empty house has had no occupants for a long time."
Jīnzhī
Dīng Shì, wife of Chén Hóngyù, the garrison commander of Shǔqīngshízhèn,
out of jealousy,
beat to death her maid Jīnzhī,
secretly buried her in her own family's grounds,
and posted a notice on the main road stating:
"The maid Jīnzhī has run away."
After a year,
they moved to Jiājiāng.
Due to summer floods that eroded the embankment of their old residence,
the dead maid's body was revealed, her appearance unchanged.
The garrison commander submitted a report to the prefecture,
and upon investigation, she confessed.
The maid's corpse decayed overnight,
and Dīng Shì was thus punished according to the law.
From the "Jǐngjiè Lù"
Tián Cāng
In the Later Hàn, the Xīyí chieftain Tián Qiáng
sent his son Lǔ
to reside in Upper City;
his second son Yù
resided in Middle City,
and his youngest son Cāng
resided in Lower City.
The three fortifications were arranged in succession
to resist Wáng Mǎng.
In the 24th year of Emperor Guāngwǔ's reign,
he dispatched General Wǔwēi Liú Shàng to campaign against them,
but Liú Shàng had not yet arrived.
Cāng caught a white turtle and made it into soup,
lit a beacon to invite his two elder brothers,
but when they arrived, nothing was amiss.
When Liú Shàng's army came,
Cāng lit the beacon again,
but Lǔ and the others thought it was not genuine,
and Cāng thus died in battle.
From the "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
The Man from Línhǎi
At the end of the Wú period,
a man from Línhǎi went into the mountains to hunt.
In the night,
there was a person ten feet tall,
wearing yellow clothes with a white belt,
who came and said to the hunter:
"I have an enemy,
and tomorrow we will fight.
If you can assist me,
I will surely repay you."
The hunter said:
"I can certainly help you.
What need is there for thanks?"
He replied:
"At mealtime tomorrow,
you can go out to the streamside.
The enemy will come from the north,
and I will go south to meet him.
The one with the white belt is me,
and the one with the yellow belt is him."
The hunter agreed.
The next day, he went out
and indeed heard sounds from the north bank,
like wind and rain,
with grass and trees flattened in all directions.
Looking south, it was the same.
He only saw two giant snakes,
over a hundred feet long,
meeting in the stream,
and immediately coiling around each other.
The one with white scales was at a disadvantage.
The hunter thus drew his crossbow and shot,
and the one with yellow scales died immediately.
As dusk approached,
he again saw the person from the previous night come to bid farewell,
saying:
"Stay here and hunt for one year,
but leave next year.
Be careful not to come again,
for if you do, disaster will surely befall you."
The hunter said:
"Very well."
And so he stopped hunting.
Several years later,
he suddenly forgot the earlier warning
and went hunting again.
He again saw the man with the white belt, who said:
"I told you, but you did not heed my words.
My enemy's offspring is now extremely powerful,
and they are certain to seek revenge on you.
This is beyond my control."
The hunter heard this and was terrified.
He wanted to flee,
but then saw three people in black clothes,
all opening their mouths toward him,
and the hunter immediately died.
From the "Xù Sōushén Jì"
Chén Jiǎ
In Běixiāngtíng Village, Hǎiyán County, Wújùn,
there was a scholar named Chén Jiǎ,
originally from Xiàpī.
During the reign of Emperor Yuán of Jìn,
he was residing in Huátíng
and went hunting in the great marshes of the eastern wilds.
Suddenly, he saw a great snake, sixty or seventy feet long,
shaped like a hundred-hú ship,
with dark yellow and multicolored patterns,
lying beneath a ridge.
The scholar immediately shot and killed it,
but dared not speak of it.
Three years later,
he went hunting with fellow villagers
and came to the place where he had previously seen the snake.
He told his companions:
"I once killed a great snake here."
That night, he dreamed of a person,
dressed in black clothes with a black headscarf,
who came to his home
and asked:
"I was once unconscious and drunk,
and you shamelessly killed me.
I was drunk at the time,
and did not recognize your face,
so for three years I did not know who you were.
Now you have come to me of your own accord to die."
The man immediately awoke in fright,
and the next morning, he died of abdominal pain.
From the "Sōushén Jì"
Mágū
Sòng Yuán Zhìzōng was
a person from Hédōng.
In the sixteenth year of the Yuánjiā era,
he followed Ruǎn Yīn, the Prefect of Zhōnglí, to the commandery.
Yīn sent Zhìzōng on an errand to a distant village,
accompanied by the commandery clerks Gài Gǒu and Biān Dìng.
Upon arriving at a commoner's house,
he felt dazed as if falling asleep,
and then did not wake up again.
The commoners thought he was dead,
carried him outside the gate,
and were just preparing the burial implements
when, after a night had passed, he was able to speak.
He recounted that initially, about a hundred people
bound Zhìzōng and took him away.
After several tens of *li*, they reached a Buddhist pagoda,
where the monastic community made offerings,
no different from in the world.
One monk said:
"You are fond of hunting,
and now you should receive retribution."
He then took Zhìzōng,
skinned him, sliced and cut him into pieces,
exactly following the methods used for treating various animals.
He then placed him in washing water,
hooked him out by the mouth,
split, broke, and minced him,
as if making minced meat.
He also boiled him in a cauldron and roasted him over a furnace;
at first, he completely disintegrated,
but then immediately restored to his original form.
The pain, agony, and bitter torment
only ceased after three cycles.
He was asked if he wished to live,
and Zhìzōng immediately kowtowed, begging for his life.
The monk had him squat on the ground
and poured water over him,
saying:
"One pouring removes five hundred offenses."
Zhìzōng earnestly begged for more pourings,
but the monk said:
"Three is sufficient."
Seeing several ants,
the monk said:
"Although these are tiny creatures,
they too must not be killed,
let alone creatures larger than these.
From now on, you must abstain from fish and meat."
"Abstain" originally read "eat."
Changed according to the Ming manuscript.
On days of vegetarian feasts,
all wear new clothes;
if you have no new ones, you may wash your old ones."
Zhìzōng then asked:
"There were three of us on the journey,
yet I alone suffered this torment;
why is that?"
The monk said:
"Those two know their own offenses and blessings;
knowing, they do not transgress.
Only you are foolish and reckless,
unaware of karmic retribution,
hence this was used to admonish you."
Thereupon, he revived,
and after several days was able to rise.
From then on, he ceased fishing and hunting.
From *Xiángyì Jì*
Wáng Tánlüè
Wáng Tánlüè of Chéngfù in the state of Qiáo during the Sòng dynasty
often made his living by curing beef to make dried meat.
Once, about to kill an ox,
the ox saw the knife
and immediately jumped and stamped, trying to flee.
Tánlüè grew angry,
and first stabbed the ox in the eye with the knife.
A short time later,
his own eyes began bleeding for no reason.
From *Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì*
The Guǎngzhōu Man
During the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
three men from Guǎngzhōu
went together into the mountains to cut wood.
Suddenly, they saw three eggs in a stone nest,
as large as a *shēng* measure,
and took them to boil.
Just as the water began to heat,
they heard a sound like wind and rain in the forest.
In a moment,
a snake, ten arm-spans thick,
forty or fifty *zhǎng* long,
came straight to the boiling water,
took the eggs in its mouth, and left.
Not long after, all three men died.
From *Sōushén Jì*
The Dōngxīng Man
In Dōngxīng of Línchuān,
a man entered the mountains,
captured a baby gibbon,
and brought it home.
The mother gibbon followed from behind, chasing him to his house.
This man tied the baby gibbon to a tree in the courtyard
to show her.
The mother then slapped her own cheeks toward the man,
as if
"As if" originally read "wishing to."
Changed according to the Ming manuscript.
begging pitifully,
it was simply
"Simply" originally read "called."
Changed according to the Ming manuscript.
that she could not speak.
Since this man would not release it,
he eventually struck and killed it.
The mother gibbon cried out mournfully,
and throwing herself down, died.
This man cut open her belly to look,
and found her intestines all broken.
Within half a year,
his household was struck by plague,
and all died at once, extinguishing the family.
From *Sōushén Hòujì*
Chén Mǎng
Chén Mǎng of Línchuān
in his youth made hunting his profession.
Once, chasing a deer with others into the mountains,
there was a large tree,
about thirty arm-spans around,
and Mǎng rested beneath it.
Suddenly, a white vapor appeared,
about ten *zhàng* off the ground.
Mǎng shot an arrow at it,
as if hitting something,
and blood sprinkled across the ground.
A voice from the air was heard saying:
"It hit the Great King right on target."
Soon, a large snake was seen hanging from the tree,
with an arrow in its body.
In an instant,
a multitude of snakes converged toward Mǎng like spokes to a hub.
Although Mǎng tried to drive them off and strike them,
the coming snakes were numerous,
coiling around Mǎng's body,
making sucking sounds,
and shortly dispersed.
Looking at Mǎng,
only a pile of white bones remained.
From *Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì*
The Man from the State of Pèi
In the state of Pèi, there was a scholar
who had three sons born together.
As they approached capping age,
they could all make sounds but not speak.
Suddenly, a man passed by his gate,
and asked:
"What sounds are these?"
He replied:
"They are my sons,
all unable to speak."
The guest said:
"You should reflect inwardly;
what caused this?"
The host found his words strange,
pondered for a long while,
and then said to the guest:
"When I was a child,
there was a swallow's nest above my bed,
containing three chicks.
Their mother would bring food from outside,
and the three chicks would open their mouths to receive it—
this went on for many days.
I tried putting my finger into the nest,
and the swallow chicks also opened their mouths to receive it.
So I fed them three thorns,
and soon they all died.
This happened in the past,
and now I truly regret it."
The guest said:
"That is it."
As soon as he finished speaking,
the speech of his three sons
suddenly became fluent and steady—
likely because he was able to recognize his fault.
From *Xù Sōushén Jì*
Court Gentleman of the Qí Dynasty
In the early years of the Suí dynasty’s Kāihuáng era,
in a village outside Jìzhōu,
there was a boy
aged thirteen
who often stole eggs from his neighbors
and roasted them to eat.
The next morning at dawn,
someone knocked at the door,
calling for this boy.
His father told the boy to go out and answer.
He saw a man who said:
"An official summons you."
The boy said:
"If you’re calling me for labor service,
I’ll go inside to get clothes and provisions."
The messenger said:
"That’s not necessary."
He then led the boy away.
South of the village was an old mulberry field
that had been plowed but not yet sown.
Suddenly the boy saw a small city on the right side of the path,
with gate towers on all four sides,
painted in red and white, very imposing.
The boy wondered aloud:
"When did this city appear?"
The messenger scolded him to be silent,
and they proceeded to the city’s north gate,
where he ordered the boy to enter first.
When the boy stepped inside the threshold,
the city gate suddenly closed,
and he saw not a single person—
only an empty city.
The ground was all hot ashes and scattered embers,
deep enough to just cover his ankles.
The boy suddenly cried out
and ran toward the south gate,
but just as he was about to reach it, it closed.
He then ran toward the east and west gates,
and the same thing happened each time:
the gates would open before he arrived,
but as soon as he reached them, they would shut.
At that time, villagers had gone out to the fields to pick mulberry leaves;
there were many men and women,
and they all saw the boy weeping in the plowed field,
running frantically in all directions.
They said to one another:
"Is this boy mad?
Since morning he has been like this,
playing without rest."
By mealtime,
all the pickers had returned home.
The boy’s father asked:
"Have you seen my son?"
The mulberry-pickers replied:
"Your son is running and playing south of the village;
we called him, but he wouldn’t come."
The father went out of the village
and saw his son running in the distance.
He shouted his son’s name loudly,
and with that one call, the boy stopped.
The city and ashes suddenly vanished.
The boy collapsed before his father
and, weeping, told what had happened.
Looking at his feet,
they saw that from the middle of his shins upward,
the flesh was scorched and withered,
while from the knees downward,
it was red and blistered as if burned.
They carried him home to nurse and treat him.
The flesh above his thighs remained as before,
but from the knees down, it turned into dry bone.
When the neighbors heard of this,
they went to look at the places where he had run:
the footprints were clear and smooth,
with no trace of ashes or fire at all.
Truly, because of real karma,
he encountered a hell-realm wherever he went.
There was a Dharma Master Dàohuì,
originally from Jìzhōu,
who lived in a neighboring village of the boy
and personally witnessed this event.
From "Records of Miraculous Retribution."
General Wáng
There was a certain General Wáng, a Xiāoqí General,
a man from Dàijùn.
In the last years of the Suí dynasty’s Kāihuáng era,
he was stationed to guard Púzhōu.
He was fond of hunting
and killed countless animals.
He had five sons
and no daughters.
Later, a daughter was born to him,
graceful and beautiful;
all who saw her loved and pitied her,
and her parents doted on her especially.
After he returned to his hometown,
when the girl was seven years old,
she suddenly disappeared one morning.
Everyone suspected the neighbors had hidden her in play,
but inquiries yielded no trace.
Her brothers rode far in search,
and more than thirty lǐ from home,
they found her in the wilderness,
unconscious and unaware of anything,
only making rabbit-like cries from her mouth,
with a handful of thorns stuck in her feet.
After more than a month,
she died without eating.
Her parents were deeply grieved,
believing it was retribution for his hunting and killing.
Afterward, the whole family observed vegetarian fasts
and no longer ate meat.
Cài Xuānmíng, an official of the Dàlǐ Temple,
once served as a legal officer in the Dàifǔ
and personally related this story.
From "Records of Miraculous Retribution."
Jiāng Lüè
In the Suí dynasty, Jiāng Lüè, an Yīngyáng Lángjiàng from Tiānshuǐ,
was fond of hunting from youth
and skilled at flying falcons and setting hounds.
Later, he fell ill
and saw a flock of thousands of birds,
all headless,
encircling his bed,
crying out:
"Quickly, give us back our heads!"
Each time, Jiāng Lüè would suffer a headache and lose consciousness.
After a long while, he would revive.
He then invited many monks
to urgently perform merit-transferring services for the birds.
They promised to do so, and the birds all left.
Thereafter, he recovered.
For the rest of his life, he abstained from wine and meat
and did not kill living creatures.
Jiāng Lüè himself often told of this event.
From "Records of Miraculous Retribution."
Hè Yuè
In the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty,
Hè Yuè, a man from Dàníng in Xízhōu,
because a neighbor’s ox damaged his crops,
used a rope to cut off the ox’s tongue.
Later, he had three sons,
all of whom were mute,
unable to speak.
From "Forest of Pearls from the Garden of the Dharma."
Lǐ Shòu
In the Táng dynasty, Lǐ Shòu, Duke of Suì’ān and Governor of Jiāozhōu,
in the early Zhēnguān era,
left his post and returned to his residence in the capital.
He was fond of hunting
and often kept several falcons in cages,
killing neighboring dogs to feed them.
Later, the Duke fell ill
and saw five dogs come to demand his life.
The Duke said to them:
"It was my servant Tōngdá’s fault that you were killed,
not my crime."
The dogs said:
"How could Tōngdá act on his own?
Moreover, we did not steal your food;
we were merely passing by your gate
when you wrongfully killed us.
We must have our revenge;
this will never cease."
The Duke apologized
and asked to perform merit-transferring services for them.
Four dogs agreed.
One white dog refused,
saying:
"You killed me though I was guiltless.
While I was not yet dead,
you also cut flesh from me alive,
piece by piece, in agony.
When I think of this cruelty,
how could I let you go?"
Suddenly, a man appeared
and pleaded with the dog on his behalf:
"Killing him would do you no good.
Letting him go to perform merit-transferring services for you—
wouldn’t that be better?"
The dog then agreed.
After a while, the Duke revived,
but he suffered from hemiplegia,
with his limbs paralyzed.
He then performed merit-transferring services for the dogs,
yet his illness never improved.
From "Records of Miraculous Retribution."
Fāng Shānkāi
Fāng Shānkāi was a man from Wǔchéng in Cáozhōu during the Táng dynasty.
From a young age, he excelled with bow and arrows,
and was especially fond of traveling and hunting,
making it his profession,
and the number of creatures he killed was countless.
In the eleventh year of the Zhēnguàn era, he died,
but after one night, he revived,
and said:
"When I first died,
I was led away by twenty men.
After traveling about ten or more lǐ,
we came upon a mountain.
Three ghosts together pulled Shānkāi along,
climbing a ladder to ascend,
and were about to reach the summit.
Suddenly, a large white eagle,
with a beak and claws of iron,
flew over,
seized Shānkāi's left cheek, and flew away.
Then there was a black eagle,
also with an iron beak and claws,
that seized his right shoulder and flew away.
When they reached the mountaintop,
they led him to a hall,
where he saw an official,
dressed in crimson robes,
wearing a black headcloth,
who said to Shānkāi:
'In your lifetime, what virtuous deeds did you perform?
You may speak of them in detail.'
He replied:
'Since establishing myself in life,
I have not cultivated any virtuous deeds.'
The official said:
'You should be taken to the southern courtyard to observe.'
Two men then led him southward,
until they came to a city,
which was extraordinarily steep and formidable.
The two men knocked several times on the northern gate of the city,
and the gate then opened,
revealing that inside the city was blazing brightly,
entirely filled with fierce flames.
Beside the gate were several venomous snakes,
each over ten zhàng long,
with heads as large as five-dǒu hú measures,
spitting fire from their mouths,
as if about to shoot at people.
Shānkāi was terrified,
not knowing how to escape,
and could only kowtow and recite the Buddha's name.
The gate then opened by itself,
and he returned to see the official,
who intended to send him to receive punishment.
An attendant remonstrated, saying:
'Shānkāi is not yet due to die immediately.
But I fear that once he enters this city,
he will not be able to come out.
It would be better to release him for now,
and have him cultivate virtuous deeds.'
The official said:
'Good.'
He ordered the two men from before to escort him back,
descending along the original path.
Again, there were eagles wanting to seize him,
but thanks to these two men's assistance and protection, he was spared.
When they descended the mountain,
they saw a large pit,
extremely foul and vile.
Suddenly, he was pushed into it by the two men,
and in a moment, he revived.
On his face and right arm,
the claw marks remained clearly visible,
and never faded for the rest of his life.
He then left his wife and children,
turned his residence into a Buddhist monastery,
and constantly made reciting scriptures his occupation.
From the Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Wáng Zūn
Wáng Zūn of the Táng dynasty
was a man from Hénèi.
He had two brothers,
and all three fell seriously ill at the same time.
There was a magpie's nest at their house,
and the magpies flew about and chirped morning and night,
which angered them with the noise,
and the brothers all detested them.
After recovering from their illness,
they set up nets for the magpies,
cut off their tongues, and released them.
Afterward, the brothers all suffered from diseases of the mouth and teeth,
their family gradually became impoverished,
until they ended up begging.
From the Xuānyàn Zhì.
The Míng manuscript copy cites it as from the Xuānshì Zhì.
Note: The Imperial Readings (Yùlǎn) 744 cites it as from the Língyàn Jì.
Lǐ Zhīlǐ
Lǐ Zhīlǐ of Lǒngxī in the Táng dynasty,
was agile and nimble from a young age,
excelling at archery,
skilled in riding,
and also proficient at slingshot shooting,
having killed many creatures.
Sometimes he would catch fish,
countless in number.
In the nineteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
he fell ill and died after a few days.
Then he saw a ghost,
leading a horse,
larger than the horses commonly ridden in the mortal world,
who said to Zhīlǐ:
"King Yánluó is summoning you."
He then ordered Zhīlǐ to mount the horse,
and in an instant,
they suddenly arrived before the king.
The king commanded him:
"I am sending you to fight the enemy;
you must not be defeated.
If you are defeated, I will kill you."
There were twenty-four companions with him,
and looking toward the northeast,
they saw the enemy stretching as far as the eye could see,
the sky and earth completely darkened,
and dust falling like rain.
Zhīlǐ and the others were defeated,
and Zhīlǐ said to his companions:
"The king's orders are strict;
it is better to die advancing forward
than to return defeated."
Zhīlǐ turned his horse around,
and after shooting three arrows,
the enemy began to retreat slightly.
After five volleys of arrows,
the enemy was completely routed.
After the battle, he went to see the king,
who rebuked Zhīlǐ, saying:
"Said" originally read "you."
Changed according to the Míng manuscript.
"Although the enemy retreated,
why did you lose at the beginning of the battle?"
"At the beginning" in the Fǎyuàn Zhūlín, vol. 42, reads "immediately defeated."
He then bound his hair with hemp rope,
tied his hands and feet,
laid him on a stone,
and crushed and ground him with a large stone.
Four people before him
had all been crushed to a pulp.
When it was Zhīlǐ's turn,
he cried out loudly:
"Earlier, when the enemy retreated,
originally there was no 'retreated' character,
added according to the Míng manuscript.
it was entirely due to my efforts.
If I am still killed by the king,
there will be no way to encourage others in the future."
The king then released him and did not punish him.
After three days in total,
he suddenly walked toward the northwest,
entering a walled courtyard.
He saw birds and beasts,
filling about three or four acres,
all coming to demand his life,
gradually closing in on him.
He had once shot and killed a female dog,
and this dog went straight for his face, biting it,
then his body,
leaving no part unharmed.
Then he saw three large ghosts,
each over ten feet tall,
who stripped Zhīlǐ of his skin and flesh,
leaving nothing in an instant,
only his face and
the Míng manuscript has "only" before "face."
There is no "and" character.
his eyes, bones,
and internal organs remained.
They then divided this flesh among the birds and beasts,
but the flesh would regenerate after being stripped,
only to be stripped again,
and this continued for three days.
The suffering and torment were extreme,
beyond description.
After this was over,
the large ghosts and the birds and beasts
suddenly all disappeared.
Zhīlǐ looked around,
but saw nothing,
so he climbed over the wall and fled south,
not knowing where he was going.
It felt as if he could leap a thousand miles in a single bound,
but another ghost caught up with Zhīlǐ,
and trapped him in an iron cage.
Countless fish came to nibble at him,
and when they were done,
the ghost turned back,
and the fish also disappeared.
His family had long supported a monk,
who had died earlier,
and he came to remove the cage from Zhīlǐ,
saying to him:
"The patron is extremely hungry."
He gave Zhīlǐ three white pills,
like dates,
and told him to eat them,
and Zhīlǐ was immediately full.
Then he said:
"The patron should return home."
The monk then left.
To the north of Zhīlǐ's residence,
he saw a large pit,
filled with spears and halberds planted densely,
making it impossible to cross.
He saw his niece and a maidservant carrying a box,
inside which were coins and silk,
and another container with food and drink,
placed northeast of the pit.
In Zhīlǐ's mind,
he thought the maidservant and his niece were playing a game,
and found it very strange.
Turning his head to look north,
he immediately saw a ghost,
charging straight at him with a sword.
Terrified,
Zhīlǐ threw himself into the pit,
and immediately revived.
From the time he first died
until his rebirth,
six days had passed in total.
Later, he asked his family,
and learned that his niece had brought paper money, silk, and food as offerings.
What he had seen at the time
were actually copper coins and silk.
From the Míngbào Jì.
Lù Xiàozhèng
Lù Xiàozhèng of Yōngzhōu in the Táng dynasty,
during the Zhēnguàn era, served as Left Guǒyì of the Xíchuān Garrison of the Right Guard.
Xiàozhèng had a hot-tempered and impatient nature,
and often committed cruel acts.
In the garrison, there was originally a hive of bees,
which had split and gathered on a tree south of his residence.
Xiàozhèng sent someone to move them to another hive.
Before the bees had left,
Xiàozhèng became enraged,
and poured boiling water over the tree, killing them,
leaving almost none alive.
The following year in May,
Xiàozhèng was taking a nap in the hall during the day,
when suddenly a bee stung him on the tongue.
His tongue immediately swelled, blocking his mouth,
and he died a few days later.
From the Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Guǒyì
During the Zhēnguàn and Yǒnghuī eras of the Táng dynasty,
in the Zhōuzhì and Hù counties, there was a Guǒyì.
Whenever guests came,
he would always buy piglets to prepare a feast.
A guard's family had ten piglets,
and he bought them all.
The last one he bought
was still being cooked when it was not yet fully done.
The Guǒyì was sitting with his guest
when he suddenly heard the sound of a woman crying.
Suspecting it was his wife,
he went to check on her at home,
but she was not crying.
Returning to the hall,
he heard the crying again,
and when he checked on his wife, she was still not crying.
This happened several times.
Later, when he went home again,
he heard the crying outside the door;
if he went outside,
he heard the crying inside the house.
His guest was greatly alarmed,
unable to stay seated,
and seemed to hear the crying say:
"I gave birth to ten children,
and they were all eaten by the Guǒyì."
The guest listened carefully several times,
clearly hearing this,
and, moved by pity, immediately left.
The Guǒyì was terrified,
and fell ill because of this,
dying after several weeks.
In Cháng'ān
"'ān" originally read "kè."
Changed according to the Míng manuscript.
this story was widely circulated.
From the Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Liú Mó'ér
Liú Mó'ér was a man from Quán Village in Xiàoyì County, Fén Prefecture during the Táng Dynasty.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of the Xiǎnqìng era,
he fell ill and died.
His son, Shī Bǎo,
died the next day.
Throughout their lives,
father and son had both acted treacherously and deceitfully.
A neighbor named Qí Lǒngwēi,
while gathering firewood,
was run over by a cart and died,
but revived after several days.
He then saw Liú Mó'ér's son, Shī Bǎo,
in a cauldron of boiling water.
In a short while,
his skin and flesh were completely gone,
leaving no human form,
only white bones visible.
After a long time like this,
he returned to his original form.
Lǒngwēi asked him the reason,
and he replied:
"Because I hunted with bow and arrow,
I suffer this punishment."
Lǒngwēi also asked Bǎo:
"Where is your father now?"
He replied:
"My father's sins are grave,
you cannot see him immediately.
Since you are about to return,
I beg you to inform my family,
to perform vegetarian feasts and accumulate merit for me."
After he finished speaking,
he was urged by an attendant,
and proceeded to an official mansion,
where he saw lofty and imposing halls.
Over twenty people holding staffs stood there.
An official asked him:
"What meritorious deeds have you performed recently?"
He replied:
"Last year in the first month, Lǒngwēi
went to Dúcūn to listen to the recitation of the entire Buddhist canon,
donated a garment as alms,
and also received the Five Precepts,
which he has not broken to this day."
The official then said:
"If it is as you say,
with immeasurable merit,
why should you need to come here!"
He then ordered the register to be checked.
Upon seeing the register,
he said:
"This man's death is indeed fitting and not false.
A side note states:
'The merit from receiving precepts and giving alms aids him,
and he should have his lifespan extended.'"
He then had someone escort him back,
and he revived at that moment.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
The Shopkeeper's Wife
During the Xiǎnqìng era of the Táng Dynasty,
by the roadside on the western route of Cháng'ān City, a shopkeeper's wife gave birth to a baby boy.
On the full-month day,
relatives gathered for celebration,
intending to slaughter a sheep.
The sheep repeatedly knelt and bowed to the butcher.
The butcher reported this to the household,
but none of the family members, young or old, considered it an omen.
They then slaughtered it,
and placed the meat in a pot to boil.
Others were busy preparing scallions, garlic, pancakes, and food,
and had the new mother hold her child and watch the meat boil.
She held the child before the fire.
Suddenly, the pot broke on its own,
the boiling liquid splashed onto the ashes and fire,
directly striking the mother and child,
and both mother and child died.
Those among the shop people who saw or heard of this
mostly refrained from killing living beings thereafter.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
The Butcher
During the Zǒngzhāng and Xiánhēng eras of the Táng Dynasty,
in the capital, there was a butcher
whose family had practiced the trade for generations.
He fell ill and died,
but was then seized by a flock of sheep and suspended,
exactly in the manner of slaughtering a sheep.
Two sheep held his hands,
the other sheep held his feet,
and one sheep held a knife and stabbed his neck,
causing several *dou* of blood to flow,
and he died.
After a short while, he revived.
Before this man came back to life,
his family saw fresh blood around his neck.
Startled, they examined it together
and found a stab wound on his neck,
exactly like that of a slaughtered sheep,
with one side of the knife hole small
and the other side large.
It took several years for the wound to finally heal.
From *Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì*.
Liú Zhīyuán
Liú Zhīyuán, a Registrar of虔州 during the Táng Dynasty, was acting as Controller of the Granaries.
During a great feast,
the Military Administrator Yáng Shùnchén said to him:
"When buying meat, you must choose meat containing a fetus;
it is plump and tender, good to eat,
the rest, being lean, is not suitable."
Zhīyuán then selected and slaughtered pregnant calves, pigs, sheep, donkeys, and others.
Their fetuses still moved,
and only after a long time did they cease.
Not long after,
one of Shùnchén's slaves
died without illness,
but his heart area remained warm.
After seven days, he revived,
and said:
"I saw a white-faced calf,
followed by its young,
appearing before the King to complain, saying:
'I was five months pregnant,
and you wrongfully killed both mother and child.'
Shortly after,
pigs, sheep, donkeys, and others were also seen,
all leading their young to complain.
I saw Registrar Liú answering the charges,
implicating Military Administrator Yáng as having given such instructions."
Three days later, Zhīyuán died,
and another five days later, Shùnchén died.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Jì Quánwén
In the early years of Empress Wǔ Zétiān of the Táng Dynasty,
there was a man from the capital region named Jì Quánwén, whose family was wealthy,
but he had a fondness for killing.
Pigs, sheep, donkeys, and calves
were all cooked and slaughtered before him.
He often kept several dozen falcons and hawks,
catching fish and turtles in spring and summer,
and hunting foxes and hares in autumn and winter.
He often took his sons to catch birds,
cut off their heads evenly with a knife,
and then released them,
watching how far they could fly.
Those that flew farther were considered winners,
those that flew nearer were losers,
and they amused themselves in this way.
At home, he was extremely cruel and harsh.
If maids, concubines, or servants
committed a minor offense,
he would sometimes hang them and cut open their hearts,
or gouge out their eyes.
His wife gave birth to their first son,
who had skin hanging down from his upper eyelid
all the way to his nose.
From behind his forehead,
there was another piece of skin
hanging down to the back of his neck,
as if wearing a human hat.
Later, she gave birth to another son,
whose teeth and claws were like a tiger's,
and whose mouth resembled an eagle's beak.
She gave birth to yet another son,
who had a seam from his neck to his waist.
When opened and looked at,
his heart, lungs, and five internal organs were visible,
and he died at birth.
This man had an elder brother,
who also enjoyed falconry, dog hunting, and archery,
and whose nature was similarly cruel, harsh, and vicious.
His wife gave birth to sons
with fleshy collars on their necks,
sometimes shaped like birds, beasts, fish, or turtles,
and several were born without eyes or noses.
From *Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì*.
A Commoner from Dāngtú
In the customs of Wú,
fresh fish are all kept alive,
and when one wishes to eat them, they are thrown into boiling water,
where they writhe and turn for a while before dying.
In the eighth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
in Dāngtú there was a man who made his living catching eels.
That spring he caught three eels.
His son skinned the eels,
cut off their heads,
lit a fire, and was about to stew them.
Then the eels transformed into snakes,
with crimson patterns mottled and bright,
several feet long.
They slithered toward the door and outside.
The son ran away, looking back,
and saw the remaining two eels had already half turned into snakes.
In a moment, the transformation was complete,
and they all left.
The son then fell ill,
and died the next day.
Thereupon, the seven members of the family
all died one after another,
and within a little over ten days, they were all gone.
The magistrate of Dāngtú, Wáng Xiūyīn,
because there were no survivors,
ordered them buried.
From Jì Wén.
Zhāng Zòng
In the Táng dynasty, Zhāng Zòng, the county lieutenant of Jìnjiāng County in Quánzhōu,
was fond of eating minced fish.
Suddenly he fell ill and died,
but his heart remained warm.
After seven days, he revived.
He said:
Initially, a yellow-robed clerk informed him:
"The King summons you."
Zòng followed him,
and soon saw the King.
The King asked the clerk:
"I summoned Zhāng Zòng.
Why have you brought Zhāng Zòng?
You should quickly send him back."
Beside him, another clerk said to the King:
"This man is fond of eating minced fish.
He may be temporarily punished by being made a fish."
The King ordered Zòng to go and become a fish.
He also said:
"You shall return to your original body."
Then he was led by the clerk who had spoken to a riverbank,
pushed Zòng into the water,
where he transformed into a small fish,
about an inch long.
Day and night it grew,
until the seventh day,
when it was over two feet long.
Suddenly he saw a fisherman come to the river and cast his net.
In his mind he was very afraid,
but before he knew it, he had entered the net,
and was caught by the fisherman,
who placed him under the grass in the boat.
Soon he heard that the assistant magistrate of Jìnjiāng, Wáng, had sent someone to seek fish for minced fish.
The fisherman at first gave him the small fish,
but was beaten with a rod.
He returned to the netting place to search again,
and then found the carp under the grass,
took it back to the Wáng household.
Arriving at the front hall,
he saw the assistant magistrate's wife facing a mirror doing her makeup,
with one shoulder bared.
He was taken to the kitchen,
where the fish-slicer took a knife to scrape off the scales.
At first he did not feel pain,
only the coldness of the iron.
Soon his head was cut off,
and his original body then revived.
At that time, the palace censor Lǐ È had been demoted to lieutenant of Jìnjiāng,
and was just at the Wáng household eating minced fish.
Hearing that Zòng had revived,
he hurried to see him.
Once inside,
Zòng took his hand,
and said to È:
"Have you eaten your fill of minced fish?"
È then asked how he knew,
and Zòng recounted the whole story from beginning to end.
Only then did he realize that the fish he had eaten
was Zòng's own body.
From Guǎng Yì Jì.
Zhū Huà
There was a man from Luòyáng named Zhū Huà,
who made his living trading sheep.
In the early years of the Táng Zhēnyuán era,
he traveled west to Bīnníng,
to exchange for sheep.
A man saw Huà and said to him:
"You trade sheep for profit,
you should seek abundant gain.
You see small sheep
and think they are not worth exchanging for.
You simply do not realize that small ones will not be long before they grow large.
Exchange for them while they are small,
and by the time you sell them, they will be large.
Wouldn't the profit be great then?
If you exchange for large ones,
the number of sheep will certainly be few.
If you exchange for small ones,
the number of sheep will certainly be many.
Many sheep means thick profit,
few sheep means meager profit."
Huà agreed with him,
and told the man:
"If you know where there are small sheep,
I will exchange for all of them."
A few days later, the man led a sheep owner to him.
Huà then exchanged for over a hundred small sheep,
large and small sheep mixed together in a flock,
and returned to Luòyáng.
When they reached the pass,
one night all the small sheep he had exchanged for
transformed into ghosts and ran away.
Huà was greatly alarmed,
and could not fathom the reason.
The following year he went again to Bīnníng,
and saw the man who had earlier spoken of small sheep.
Huà was very angry,
and was about to seize him and take him to the authorities.
The man said:
"What crime have I committed?"
Huà said:
"You exchanged small sheep with me,
I drove them to the pass,
and they all turned into ghosts.
Was it not you using sorcery?"
The man said:
"You trade flocks of sheep,
seeking great profit,
killing living creatures,
without knowing any limit.
Your crime has already filled the heavens.
You yourself never realize it,
and instead are angry with me.
I am a ghost,
and shall join the flock of sheep to seize you and kill you."
Having said this, he vanished.
Huà was greatly shocked and terrified,
and soon died in Bīnníng.
From Qí Shì.
Lǐ Zhān
In the Táng dynasty, Lǐ Zhān
passed the imperial examination in the seventh year of Dàzhōng under Cuī Yáo.
All his life he widely sought flavors,
and whenever he ate turtle,
he would always bind its feet,
and expose it to the blazing sun.
The turtle, being thirsty,
would then drink wine, and he would cook it.
The turtle, just as it became drunk,
was already cooked.
Again, he would tether a donkey in the courtyard,
surround it with fire,
and the donkey, being thirsty, would drink lime water,
cleansing its intestines and stomach.
Then he would take wine,
mixed with various pungent flavors,
and give it to drink again.
Before the donkey died, it was scorched by the fire,
and the outside was already cooked.
One day, Zhān
was just putting on his headscarf,
when he lost strength, fell to the ground, and died.
Soon after,
Zhān's cook also died.
One night,
the cook revived and said:
"I saw Zhān,
being reproached in the underworld for his excessive harming of living creatures.
Zhān answered that it was all my doing,
and I said that Zhān's orders could not be disobeyed.
Thus I replied.
Zhān also said:
'I originally did not know,
it was all passed on by Dí Shènsī.'
Therefore I was able to return."
Not long after,
Shènsī also died.
Shènsī had also passed the imperial examination,
and at that time was a minor remonstrance official.
From Yùquánzǐ.
Wáng Gōngzhí
In the gēngyín year of the Xiántōng era of the Táng dynasty,
Luòyáng suffered a great famine.
The price of grain soared,
and there were people who starved to death in ditches and fields.
By the silkworm-rearing month,
most mulberry leaves had been eaten by insects,
and a pound of leaves was worth a huán.
Wáng Gōngzhí, a villager north of Cíjiàn Inn in Xīn'ān County,
owned several dozen mulberry trees,
which were exceptionally lush and shady.
Gōngzhí discussed with his wife, saying:
"With such scarcity and hardship,
our household has no visible grain stores.
Even if we exhaust our efforts on these silkworms,
we still do not know whether we will gain or lose.
In my estimation,
it would be better to abandon the silkworms,
take advantage of the high price to sell the leaves,
and obtain a hundred thousand coins.
We could then store a month's worth of provisions
and last until the wheat harvest.
Wouldn't that be better than starving to death?"
His wife said:
"Good."
So they took a shovel and dug a pit,
rolled up several trays of silkworms, and buried them there.
The next morning at dawn,
he carried the mulberry leaves to the city market to sell them,
earning three thousand coins.
He bought a pig's shoulder and some cakes to bring home.
When he reached Huī'ān Gate,
the gate guards saw fresh blood dripping from his bag
and continuously spilling onto the ground,
so they stopped and questioned him.
Gōngzhí said:
"I just sold the leaves for money,
bought pork and cakes, and stored them in my bag—
nothing else."
He invited the guards to search it.
Once the bag was opened,
they found only a human left arm,
as if freshly dismembered.
The guards then escorted him back to the military governor,
who ordered him handed over to the prefect of Hénán Prefecture, the upright Wáng Níng of Lángyá,
and commanded the judicial officer to interrogate him.
His statement indicated:
He had buried the silkworms, sold the mulberry leaves,
and bought meat to return home—
he truly had not killed anyone,
and specifically requested an investigation.
The prefect ordered the assigned officer to supervise and lead
an inspection at the village site where the silkworms were buried.
The officer led Gōngzhí to the village,
first gathered the neighbors and guarantors,
demanded written statements,
and all testified that they indeed knew Wáng Gōngzhí had buried the silkworms,
with no other evil deeds.
Then, together with the villagers and Gōngzhí,
they opened the silkworm pit.
Inside, there was only a dead person wrapped in a tray corner,
missing its left arm.
They retrieved the arm and attached it,
and it matched perfectly.
They then escorted Gōngzhí back to the prefecture
and reported to the prefect.
The prefect said:
"Although Wáng Gōngzhí did not commit murder,
he is guilty of burying silkworms alive.
The law might pardon him,
but sentiment cannot tolerate it.
Silkworms are spiritual creatures of heaven and earth,
the foundation of silk and cloth.
Thus, to exterminate them
is no different from killing a person.
He should be subjected to severe punishment
to eradicate such wickedness."
He then ordered Gōngzhí to be beaten to death in the market.
When they went to examine the dead body,
it had turned back into rotten silkworms.
From "Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú."
Huáng Mǐn
Huáng Mǐn, a military commander in Jiāngxī,
fell from his horse while resisting bandits,
breaking his left thigh.
His subordinates quickly crushed a live turtle with stones
and applied it to the wound.
After over a month, he recovered.
But the turtle's head was still alive,
and its abdomen had grown connected to the flesh of his thigh.
Mǐn then detested it,
and one day decided to cut it off.
As he was about to apply the blade,
the pain felt no different from cutting his own flesh,
so he stopped, unable to proceed.
What the turtle's eyes saw
was also the same as what he himself saw.
From "Wén Qí Lù."
Chén Jūnléng
On the western border between Cáo and Sòng prefectures was a large crane pond.
Chén Jūnléng, a villager to the left of the pond,
had been a fisherman since childhood.
Later, he contracted an illness
where he was constantly being eaten by numerous fish,
suffering pain he could not endure.
If a fishing net was placed over him,
the pain would stop.
Later, a villager stole the net away,
and within a few days,
he could not bear the pain and died.
Dèng, the prefect of Dé Prefecture, had once served as magistrate of Kǎochéng
and knew of this matter.
From "Qí Wén Lù."
Wáng Dòngwēi
Wáng Dòngwēi, a Dàoshi of Jǐngyún Temple in Fén Prefecture during the Táng dynasty,
lived in Xiàoyì County.
Initially a minor clerk,
he had a fondness for killing,
often fishing, hunting, and trapping.
From his youth to adulthood,
he killed wolves, foxes, pheasants, rabbits,
as well as fish, turtles, and birds,
totaling tens of thousands.
Later, as a village head,
he fell ill with a fever for over a month.
Suddenly, he felt tens of thousands of birds, beasts, fish, and turtles in his room
circling his bed and biting him,
covering his body with sores and wounds,
leaving almost no intact skin.
After midnight,
his parents and brothers
all heard from within Dòngwēi's bedroom
the chirping of flocks of birds,
clearly distinguishable.
After several years,
his illness grew worse.
Someone said to Dòngwēi's father:
"Your son is critically ill;
he should move to Jǐngyún Temple."
So they chose a day and relocated.
Over a month later,
during a gathering of Dàoshi for fasting and receiving registers,
Dòngwēi recovered that evening.
Ten years later,
he eventually died from illness.
From "Xuān Shì Zhì."
Sūn Jìzhēn
Táng Sūn Jìzhēn,
a man from Chénzhōu,
was fond of catching birds and animals in his youth,
and especially loved eating chicken eggs.
Whenever he wanted to eat them,
he would burn and cook them.
He had been dead for nearly three years.
A neighbor named Zhāng Shēng
had also died of illness three days earlier.
Suddenly, he sat up,
and after walking,
he went straight to Sūn’s house,
claiming to be Jìzhēn.
Listening
("Listening" originally written as "said,"
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy.)
to his words,
he was indeed Jìzhēn,
though his appearance was still that of Zhāng Shēng.
The Zhāng clan
immediately went to the authorities to lodge a complaint.
Sūn said:
"Previously, I should not have died,
but because I harmed many living creatures in my lifetime,
I was accused by those seeking vengeance for grievances.
Due to my excessive consumption of chicken eggs,
I was driven into an empty city.
As soon as I entered, the gates closed.
I saw only a city full of fiery ashes,
and as I was being scorched by the flames,
I did not know what to do.
Looking east,
I saw the city gates open wide,
so I rushed toward them,
but by the time I reached them, they closed again.
Looking west,
the same thing happened.
Looking south and north,
it was the same.
I suffered all kinds of torment.
One day,
the King said to Jìzhēn:
'Your lifespan is not yet exhausted,
but you have been dead for nearly three years.
How can you return?'
The official in charge said:
'A neighbor named Zhāng Mǒu
has been dead for only three days.
You may borrow his body to house your spirit.'
The King agreed,
so now I am truly Jìzhēn."
The authorities could not decide the case.
The prefect, Minister Liú Yì,
personally summoned and questioned him,
saying:
"You should mention something from your life
that no one else knows as proof."
Jìzhēn said:
"Before I died,
I once hid two volumes of Buddhist scriptures under the roof tiles of my house.
No one truly knows about this."
They were ordered to search,
and they were indeed found.
Thus, he was judged to belong to the Sūn family.
From "Yùquánzǐ"
Cuī Dàojì
Cuī Dàojì, a Jìnshì of the Táng dynasty,
after passing the imperial examination,
traveled in the Jiāng-Huái region.
Once, he became heavily intoxicated
and lay down in an inn.
His servant went to draw water from a well,
and a fish came up with the bucket.
The servant caught it
and reported it to Dàojì.
Dàojì happily said:
"Fish soup can sober one up very well.
Quickly cook it."
After eating it for a while,
a yellow-robed messenger
descended from the sky,
stood in the courtyard,
and repeatedly called Dàojì’s name.
He ordered people to seize him
and proclaimed an edict:
"Cuī Dàojì,
a lowly commoner of the mortal world,
dared to kill a dragon’s offspring.
Your official rank was destined to reach that of prime minister,
and your lifespan was to be seventy years.
Both shall now be revoked."
After speaking,
he ascended to the sky and departed.
That night, Dàojì died suddenly,
at the age of thirty-five.
From "Lù Yì Jì"
Hé Zé
Hé Zé of the Táng dynasty
was a man from Róngzhōu.
He once served as acting magistrate of Sìhuì County in Guǎngzhōu.
He was tyrannical by nature,
caring only for eating and drinking,
and was especially fond of geese and ducks.
Village officials and local heads
were constantly ordered to supply them,
and he often kept tens of thousands of geese and ducks,
slaughtering them daily.
Hé Zé had only one son,
whom he loved dearly.
One day, he was cooking two chickens,
boiling water in a pot,
when his son seemed to be seized by a ghostly force and placed into the cauldron.
The whole family was horrified
and rushed to pull him out,
but he had already been boiled to a pulp along with the two chickens.
From "Bàoyìng Lù"
A Man from Yuèzhōu
During the Xiántōng era of the Táng dynasty,
a villager from Yuèzhōu
drained a lake to catch fish
and obtained an especially large number of turtles.
He stripped all their flesh
and carried the turtle shells to Jiānglíng to sell,
earning a great deal of gold and silk.
After returning home,
he suddenly developed sores all over his body,
crying out in agony,
so much so that his neighbors could not bear to hear it.
He needed a large basin filled with water,
and he would plunge his whole body into it,
gradually transforming into the shape of a turtle.
After more than a year,
his flesh rotted and fell off, and he died.
From "Bàoyìng Jì"
Xú Kěfàn
Xú Kěfàn, a eunuch of the Táng dynasty,
was fond of hunting by nature
and killed a great many creatures.
He would take live turtles,
bore holes in their shells,
and pour hot oil into them,
calling it "turtle dumplings."
He also had a craving for donkey meat,
tying donkeys in a room,
placing a basin of seasoned broth in front of them,
and lighting fierce fires all around.
After the donkeys drank all the broth out of thirst,
he would take their intestines and stomachs to make dishes.
The number of creatures he slaughtered
was beyond count.
Later, while accompanying Emperor Xīzōng to Shǔ,
he fell ill.
Whenever he slept,
he would see flocks of beasts and birds pecking at his flesh,
causing him immense suffering.
He also needed to spread fire under his bed
and pour oil and vinegar over his body,
then cover himself with a fishing net
before he could sleep briefly.
Day and night,
he constantly required this,
and by the time his life was about to end,
he was nothing but a bundle of black bones.
From "Bàoyìng Jì"
A Woman from Jiànyè
In recent years, a woman in Jiànyè
had a tumor on her back,
as large as a sack holding several pecks.
Inside were many things like silkworm cocoons,
and they made sounds when she walked.
She often begged in the market,
saying she was a village woman
who used to raise silkworms with her sisters-in-law.
She alone suffered losses year after year,
so she stole a sack of cocoons from her sister-in-law and burned them.
Soon after,
she developed a sore on her back,
which gradually grew into this tumor.
If she covered it with clothing,
she would feel suffocated and breathless,
so she had to leave it exposed,
but it was as heavy as carrying a sack.
From "Sōushén Jì"
A Man from Guǎnglíng
In Guǎnglíng, there was a man who begged on the streets.
Whenever he saw horse dung,
he would pick it up and eat it.
He explained himself, saying:
"I once worked for someone feeding horses.
Being lazy, I couldn’t get up at night.
My master would often inspect the stables himself.
Seeing no hay in the trough,
he would reprimand me.
So I took black plums and fed them to the horses instead.
The horses’ teeth ached from the sourness,
and they couldn’t eat.
In the end, they died because of this.
Later, I fell ill,
and whenever I saw horse dung,
I would drool and crave to eat it.
When I ate it,
its taste was exactly like that of black plums,
with no foul odor at all."
From Jīshén Lù.
Hé Mǎzi
Hé Mǎzi, a man from Suízhōu, loved eating bee larvae.
He was convicted of a crime
and sentenced to public execution in the market.
Suddenly, several large bees appeared,
stinging his face,
causing him to cry out in pain.
The guards drove them away, but they returned,
and it wasn’t until dusk that they finally stopped.
This went on for about ten days until he died.
From Jǐngjiè Lù.
Zhāng Shào
There was a man named Zhāng Shào,
who often engaged in trade
and amassed great wealth,
yet he never abandoned his greedy and unscrupulous ways,
constantly exploiting others.
Once, he encountered a deer
that fled from people,
and its fawn was caught by Zhāng Shào.
Shào then beat it to death
and discarded it in the woods.
The mother deer saw this from afar and wailed mournfully,
her cries unceasing.
That same day,
Shào intended to travel at night,
plotting something.
Shào had only one son,
just coming of age.
The son went ahead of his father by a stretch of the journey,
and when he grew tired,
he rested under a large tree,
waiting for his father.
Before long,
he fell asleep in the shade of the tree.
Shào did not realize it was his son;
he only saw clothing and a bundle beside him,
and a person sleeping soundly.
So he drew his waist knife,
stabbed the person in the throat,
took the clothing and bundle, and continued on his way.
As dawn gradually broke,
he saw the clothing and bundle
and realized the person he had killed was his own son.
Alas,
with Zhāng Shào’s cruelty and recklessness being so extreme,
such retribution was only fitting.
From Yěrén Xiánhuà.
Hán Lìshàn
At the Jīnyàn Bridge in Shǔ,
there was a man named Hán Lìshàn
who made fishing hooks
for many years.
Once, while eating fish,
a bone got stuck in his throat, forming an ulcer,
and his jaw became dislocated, leading to his death.
From Jǐngjiè Lù.
Monk Xiūzhǔn
In Shǔjùn, at the Dàcí Temple, there was a Vinaya master named Xiūzhǔn.
Although he claimed to uphold the precepts,
his temperament was very narrow-minded and irritable.
In front of his hall, he had planted bamboo,
and many ants crawled along the railings.
Enraged,
Xiūzhǔn had the bamboo cut down,
gathered all the ants,
and threw them into a fire of ashes.
Later, Xiūzhǔn suddenly developed sores,
which spread all over his head and face.
Physicians said it was an "ant-leakage sore,"
incurable,
and he eventually died.
From Jǐngjiè Lù.
The Yǔwén Family
The Yǔwén family were wealthy in the pseudo-Shǔ state.
A widow of the family lived in the eastern gate of the city.
Once, she heard someone walking on the roof of her bedroom.
She ordered her servants to climb up and investigate,
and they captured three wildcat kittens along with their mother.
The Yǔwén widow killed the mother cat but kept the kittens.
Within a year,
the widow married the military commander Wáng Chéngpī.
Chéngpī killed the family of the judge Guō Yánjūn,
and the Yǔwén widow, along with one son and two daughters from her previous marriage,
were imprisoned and sentenced.
The children were pardoned,
but the Yǔwén widow was beheaded.
Alas,
was this not retribution for killing the mother cat?
From Jǐngjiè Lù.
Lǐ Zhēn
In the Jǐnpǔ neighborhood of Shǔ, there was a commoner named Lǐ Zhēn.
He kept a dog named Hēi’er.
Once, while drunk,
Lǐ Zhēn took an axe and killed the dog.
In his old age,
Lǐ Zhēn got into a dispute with a neighborhood troublemaker named Bái Chāngzuò.
Chāngzuò, taking advantage of his drunkenness,
struck Lǐ Zhēn with an axe, killing him.
At that time, Chāngzuò was nineteen years old,
the same age Lǐ Zhēn was when he killed the dog.
Chāngzuò’s childhood nickname was also Hēi’er.
The retribution was clear,
without the slightest discrepancy.
From Jǐngjiè Lù.
Monk Xiùróng
In Shǔjùn, at the Jīnhuá Temple, there was a Dharma master named Xiùróng.
His courtyard had many pine and cypress trees,
which were infested with hairy caterpillars,
yellow in color,
about two or three inches long.
Their numbers were beyond count.
Xiùróng had people sweep them up and bury them,
or discard them in piles of firewood.
A monk named Rénxiù took firewood to boil ingredients,
drying it under the scorching sun,
causing countless caterpillars to die.
About a month later,
Xiùróng died suddenly.
A monk from Jīnhuá Temple entered the underworld in a vision,
where he saw Xiùróng carrying an iron cangue,
sitting in an open space under the blazing sun,
with countless insects biting and gnawing at him.
When the monk returned to consciousness,
he recounted everything to Rénxiù,
who was greatly horrified.
Rénxiù then developed a sore on his back,
and died a few days later.
From Jǐngjiè Lù.
Wú Qiánzhāo
A man from Shǔ named Wú Qiánzhāo had an estate in Shèhóng County.
While he was there harvesting crops,
a deer, fleeing from hunters,
panicked and ran toward Qiánzhāo.
Qiánzhāo confined it in an empty room
and told the neighboring monk Fǎhuì about it.
Fǎhuì laughed and said:
"Heaven has delivered food to you;
how could you lightly let it go?"
So they killed the deer,
bought wine and roasted the deer meat,
and shared the meal with the monk.
After eating a piece,
the monk suddenly cried out:
"A knife is cutting my heart!"
He vomited blood
and died by evening.
From Jǐngjiè Lù.
Lǐ Shào
A commoner from Shǔ named Lǐ Shào loved eating dog meat,
having killed hundreds or even thousands of dogs over the years.
Once, he obtained a black dog,
and Shào took pity on it,
caring for it very well.
One night, Shào returned home drunk,
and the dog met him at the gate, barking.
Enraged,
Shào took an axe and struck the dog.
At that moment, his son ran out from inside,
and the axe struck the boy squarely on the head,
killing him instantly.
The whole family was thrown into panic and grief.
They tried to catch the dog,
but it ran away,
and no one knew where it went.
Later, Shào fell ill,
howling like a dog until he died.
From Jǐngjiè Lù.
Zhú Yǒngtōng
In the Sui dynasty, Zhú Yǒngtōng of Yù County, Bìng Province,
once borrowed sixty dan of grain from a temple.
After many years, he still had not repaid it.
When the temple demanded it,
he said:
"I have already repaid it."
He then swore an oath in the Buddha hall, saying:
"If I have truly not repaid it,
may I become an ox for the temple."
After this man died,
the temple gave birth to a yellow calf.
On its hooves were white markings,
which gradually became clear,
revealing the characters "Zhú Yǒngtōng."
The villagers gradually learned of this,
and thousands came to see it daily.
When his family found out,
they used one hundred dan of grain
to redeem the ox from the temple,
built a separate hut for it,
and served it as if it were alive.
They also had Buddha images made and sutras copied.
After a little over a month, it died.
From Yì Lù.
A Commoner of Yíchéng
In the eighth year of the Dàyè era of the Sui dynasty,
in the village southeast of Yí Province city, there was a commoner surnamed Huángfǔ.
His family had four brothers.
The eldest and the youngest brothers
were both diligent in their work and livelihood.
The second brother, named Qiān,
associated with bad friends
and did not engage in productive work.
His mother once took some money,
intending to have him go to the market to buy things,
and placed it on the bed.
When the mother went to the back of the house,
Qiān came in from outside.
Entering the hall and seeing no one,
he stole the money and left.
When the mother returned,
she could not find the money.
She then questioned everyone in the household, high and low,
but all said they did not know.
The mother was angry
and beat them all with a whip.
Everyone, young and old, resented it.
The following year, Qiān died.
His family's pig gave birth to a piglet.
When the eighth-month village festival arrived,
it was sold to a family in a distant village for the festival.
Then he appeared in a dream to his wife, saying:
"I am your husband.
Because I stole mother's money,
I wrongfully implicated the whole family,
causing them to suffer beatings for no reason.
Now I have been reborn as a pig to repay this debt.
I am about to be sold to the festival family,
and they will tie me up to kill me.
You are my wife.
How can you bear not to tell our children to redeem me?"
When the wife first dreamed this,
she suddenly woke up
but still did not believe it.
She slept again,
and the dream was the same as before.
She then got up and reported it to her mother-in-law.
The mother-in-law said:
"I had the same dream."
At dawn,
she sent the elder brother with money to the village festival official
to redeem it.
It died two years later.
Master Jìnglín of the Hóngfǎ Temple in Cháng'ān
was a neighbor of Qiān.
He personally saw the pig
and often spoke of this incident.
From Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Wéi Qìngzhí
During the Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty,
Wéi Qìngzhí, the Chief Clerk of the Prince of Wèi's mansion, had a daughter who died earlier.
Wéi and his wife deeply mourned her.
Two years later,
Qìngzhí was about to gather relatives and guests
and prepared food.
The servants had bought a sheep
but had not yet killed it.
At night,
Qìngzhí's wife dreamed of her deceased daughter,
wearing a dark green skirt and a white blouse,
with a pair of jade hairpins in her hair—
the clothes she usually wore in life—
coming to see her mother.
Weeping, she said:
"In the past, I often took things
without telling my parents.
Because of this karma,
I am now reborn as a sheep,
coming to repay my debt to my parents with my life.
Tomorrow morning I will be killed.
I am the green sheep with a white head.
I especially beg for your mercy,
to spare my life."
The mother woke in alarm.
In the morning, she went to see for herself.
Sure enough, there was a green sheep
with a white neck and shoulders,
and two white stripes on the side of its head,
resembling the shape of jade hairpins.
The mother wept sorrowfully at the sight
and told the servants not to kill it,
waiting for Qìngzhí to arrive
so she could release it.
Soon, Qìngzhí arrived and urged them to prepare the meal.
The cook reported:
"The mistress does not allow the killing of the green sheep."
Qìngzhí was angry
and immediately ordered it killed.
The butcher hung the sheep to kill it.
Several guests had already arrived
and saw hanging there a young woman,
with proper and端正 features,
pleading with the guests:
"I am Chief Clerk Wéi's daughter.
I beg you to save my life."
The guests were shocked,
and stopped the butcher.
The butcher, fearing Qìngzhí's anger,
only saw the sheep bleating,
and so killed it.
Afterward, the guests sat down but did not eat.
Qìngzhí, finding this strange, asked them,
and the guests told him everything.
Qìngzhí, grief-stricken, fell ill
and did not recover.
Many scholars in the capital knew of this matter.
From Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Zhào Tài
According to the customs in the markets of Cháng'ān during the Táng dynasty,
every year after New Year's Day,
people would take turns inviting each other for meals,
called "passing the seat."
Zhào Tài, a brush-maker in the East Market,
was next in turn to host.
A guest arrived early
and went to the back,
where he saw on the mortar a young girl,
thirteen or fourteen years old,
wearing a blue shirt and a white hat,
with a tight rope tied around her neck,
attached to the mortar pillar.
Weeping, she said to the guest:
"I am my master's daughter.
In a previous year, before I died,
I stole my parents' money
to buy cosmetics,
but died before I could use it.
The money is now in the northwest corner of the kitchen wall.
However, I did not use it.
Since I stole it,
I am guilty of this offense,
and now I must repay my parents with my life."
After speaking,
she transformed into a green sheep with a white head.
The guest, alarmed, told the master.
The master asked about her appearance,
and it was his young daughter,
who had died two years earlier.
They retrieved the money from the kitchen wall,
which seemed to have been placed there long ago.
They then sent the sheep to a temple,
and the whole family stopped eating meat thereafter.
From Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Lǐ Xìn
Lay Buddhist Lǐ Xìn of the Táng Dynasty was a native of Tàipíng Village in Wénshuǐ County, Bīngzhōu.
He served as a guard in the Longzhèng Prefecture.
In the winter of the Xiǎnqìng era,
he traveled to Shuòzhōu for his duty rotation as per regulation.
He rode a chestnut-colored horse and also brought along a foal.
At that time, it was the end of the year, with overcast skies and heavy snowstorms.
After traveling a dozen or so lǐ, the horse refused to go any further.
As Xìn was pressed for time, he whipped it several dozen times.
The horse then spoke in human language, saying to Xìn:
"I am your mother.
In my lifetime, I secretly gave over a shí of rice to my daughter behind your father's back,
and so I have received this retribution.
This foal is your sister.
I have already repaid the debt through labor.
Why must you press me so harshly?"
Upon hearing this, Xìn was shocked and wept, unable to control himself.
He then bowed in apology, personally removed the saddle and bridle, and said:
"If you are indeed my mother, please return home on your own."
The horse then proceeded forward, while Xìn carried the saddle and bridle, following it home.
When Xìn's brothers and others saw this, they faced each other in sorrow.
They built a separate stable to care for and feed it, serving it as they would their mother.
They invited monks to perform vegetarian feasts, and the entire household devoted themselves to spiritual practice.
The villagers, both lay and monastic, all marveled at this.
At the time, the Vice Minister of Works Sūn Wúyǐn and the Judicial Officer of Qízhōu, Zhāng Jīntíng, were at home observing mourning.
Hearing of this strange event, they visited Xìn's home to inquire.
They saw the horse was still there and asked about the details, which matched what had been told.
From "Supplementary Records of Retribution in the Underworld."
Xiè Shì
In Yán Village of Wànnián County, Yōngzhōu during the Táng Dynasty, located between the Bà and Wèi Rivers,
there was a woman named Xiè, married to Yuán Shì of the same county.
Her daughter was married to Lái Āzhào of Huílóng Village.
Xiè Shì passed away at the end of the Yǒnghuī era.
In the eighth month of the first year of the Lóngshuò era, she appeared in a dream to her daughter, the Lái family wife, saying:
"In my lifetime, I sold wine using a slightly smaller shēng measure, charging too high a price and giving less wine.
Now I am punished for this crime, reborn as an ox in a household north of the mountain.
Recently, I was sold to Monk Xiàhóu of Fǎjiè Temple,
and now I am taken to plow rice fields south of the city, enduring extreme hardship."
Upon waking, her daughter wept and told Āzhào about it.
By the second year, in the first month, a nun from Fǎjiè Temple came to Āzhào's village.
The daughter asked the nun, who confirmed:
"There is indeed a Monk Xiàhóu."
The daughter then went to the temple to inquire.
It was said:
