"Recently, an ox was bought from north of the mountain and is now plowing fields south of the city."
The daughter wept and pleaded.
The temple nun then sent someone to accompany the daughter to see it.
This ox was usually only controllable by one person; if it encountered others, it would certainly buck and butt.
But when it saw the daughter, it licked her all over and shed tears.
The daughter then paid Monk Xiàhóu to redeem it, and it followed her home.
It is now kept and cared for in Āzhào's household.
The daughter constantly serves it as she would her mother, without fail.
Noble consorts and ladies of the capital often summoned to see it, competing to donate money and goods.
From "Records of Retribution in the Underworld."
Wáng Zhēn
Wáng Zhēn of Ānjiā County, Dìngzhōu during the Táng Dynasty was skilled in gold and silver craftsmanship.
Once, he worked on a temple's merit project and received five hundred bolts of silk.
A fellow worker secretly used ten bolts, which Wáng Zhēn did not know about.
After this person died,
later
"Later" originally read "followed,"
emended according to the Ming manuscript.
When the Wáng family held a ceremony and bought a sheep, before it was slaughtered, the sheep repeatedly knelt countless times, which already struck Zhēn as strange.
That night, tied to a pillar, as Zhēn was about to sleep, someone knocked urgently on his door.
Looking, he saw nothing.
Zhēn lay down again, then heard it once more.
Getting up to look, he still saw nothing, finding it strange.
He then opened the door and lay down.
Before falling asleep, he saw a person who said:
"In the past, I worked with you on the merit project and stole ten bolts of silk for personal use.
You never knew.
Now I have been reborn as a sheep, and you are about to kill me.
I kowtow, begging for my life."
After pleading bitterly again and again, the person finished speaking, left the room, and immediately transformed into a sheep.
Wáng Zhēn's sister, in another place, also saw this person kowtowing, exactly as Zhēn had seen.
They then released the sheep to live out its life.
Both Zhēn and his sister's households abstained from eating meat thereafter.
In the fifth year of the Xiánhēng era, Zhēn went on a sea voyage.
With no vegetables on the ship, everyone ate meat, but Zhēn did not, only eating plain rice.
From "Extended Records of the Five Elements Through the Ages."
Wáng Huìshī
In the northern shop of the West Market in the capital during the Táng Dynasty, there was a man named Wáng Huìshī.
After his mother passed away and the mourning period ended, his household gave birth to a greenish-yellow female dog.
Huìshī's wife, thinking it had stolen food, struck it several times with a stick.
The dog then spoke in human language:
"I am your mother-in-law.
Daughter-in-law, you were terribly wrong to beat me.
In my life, I was too harsh with the family, hence this retribution.
Now that I have been beaten, I am ashamed to stay in your home."
It then immediately ran away.
Upon hearing this, Huìshī wept, carried it back home, but it left again.
This happened four or five times in total.
Seeing its resolve was firm
"Firm" in the Ming manuscript reads "resolute."
Huìshī then built a small hut behind the large wall of his shop in the northern market to house it, delivering food daily.
Market-goers and travelers came in great numbers to see it, and those who tossed it cakes were countless.
This dog never left the hut and would not eat during fasting periods.
After one or two years, it disappeared, and no one knew where it went.
From "The Forest of Pearls from the Garden of the Dharma."
Xiè Fèngxiān
The Luòyáng painter Xiè Fèngxiān was painting a mural for Prince Sìjiāng's household but fled before finishing.
When captured, he falsely claimed:
"The payment already matches the work done."
He then swore before the image:
"If I am disloyal, may I die and be reborn as an ox in your household."
Over a year later, Fèngxiān died.
After his death, a red calf was born to an ox in the prince's household, with white hair on its back spelling "Xiè Fèngxiān."
Crowds of onlookers gathered day and night.
From "Compilation of Strange Events from National History."
Tóng Ānyú
In the late Dàzhōng era of the Táng dynasty,
in Rǔkǒu Town, Guìxī County, Xìnzhōu, there was a man named Tóng Ānyú,
a wealthy man in his village.
Initially, he was extremely poor,
and he was on good terms with a fellow villager named Guō Gǒng.
Guō Gǒng once lent him sixty or seventy thousand coins,
which Tóng Ānyú used for trading.
Ānyú later became rich.
When Guō Gǒng demanded repayment of the loan,
Ānyú refused and denied it.
Guō Gǒng burned incense and prayed to Heaven, saying:
"Tóng Ānyu has betrayed kindness and forgotten righteousness,
borrowing money and not repaying it.
If divine principle is not to be deceived,
I pray that after Ānyú dies, he becomes an ox
to repay me."
His words were very earnest and bitter.
Ānyú also deceitfully said:
"If I truly owe Guō Gǒng money,
may I die and become a white ox
to repay Gǒng's debt."
Within a month,
Ānyú died.
Half a year after his death,
a cow at Guō Gǒng's home
gave birth to a white bull calf,
with black hair on its left flank
forming the characters "Tóng Ānyú",
clearly visible.
People near and far heard of it,
and spectators gathered like clouds.
Guō Gǒng sent someone to inform Ānyú's wife,
and Ānyú's wife, children, and relatives went to see it.
They felt greatly ashamed,
and offered a large sum of gold and silk,
requesting to redeem it.
Guō Gǒng, angered by their deception,
ultimately refused to allow it.
He kept the mother cow and calf
in a separate pen to feed them.
Ānyú's family led servants
armed with white clubs to seize them by force.
Guō Gǒng stationed many people to guard them,
and they ultimately could not be taken.
From "Records of Retribution"
Liú Zìrán
During the Tiānyòu era of the Táng dynasty,
in Qínzhōu, there was a man named Liú Zìrán,
who was in charge of the volunteer army records.
Because the regional commander Lǐ Jìzōng was conscripting local troops to defend against Shǔ,
a commoner from Chéngjì County named Huáng Zhīgǎn
had a wife with beautiful hair.
Zìrán desired it,
and said to Zhīgǎn:
"If you can obtain your wife's hair,
I will exempt you from this campaign."
Zhīgǎn's wife said:
"I, with my frail body, have entrusted myself to you.
Hair can grow back,
but when a person dies, it is an eternal parting.
If you go on the southern campaign and do not return,
what use would my beautiful hair be to me?"
Having said this,
she gathered her hair and cut it off.
Zhīgǎn was deeply pained and grieved,
but being pressured by the conscription,
he presented it to Liú.
Zhīgǎn was ultimately not exempted from garrison duty,
and soon died in the battle at Jīnshā.
Huáng's wife prayed to Heaven day and night, wailing and pleading.
That year,
Zìrán also died.
Later, a female donkey at the Huáng family
suddenly gave birth to a foal,
with characters on its left flank,
saying "Liú Zìrán".
The townspeople spread the news,
and it reached the commandery governor.
The commandery governor summoned Zìrán's wife and children to identify it.
Liú Zìrán's eldest son said:
"My father in life enjoyed drinking wine and eating meat.
If it can drink and eat,
then it is my father."
The donkey then drank several shēng of wine,
ate several pieces of meat.
After finishing,
it reared up and neighed loudly,
shedding streams of tears.
Liú's son offered a hundred thousand coins to redeem it,
but Huáng's wife refused to accept it.
She daily increased the whipping and beating,
saying:
"This is still enough to avenge my husband."
Later, after going through turmoil and chaos,
its whereabouts became unknown.
Liú's son ultimately died of shame and regret.
From "Records of Admonition"
Former Huǒjǐng County Magistrate of the Táng
The character "Magistrate" was originally missing,
and has been supplemented based on the Míng manuscript copy and the Huáng edition.
Magistrate Lǐ,
while passing through his own county,
was lodged at the private residence of the Yāsī Lùshì.
The host was about to prepare a feast,
and intended to slaughter a white sheep,
which was pregnant.
That night, Magistrate Lǐ dreamed of a woman in plain white clothes bringing two children to bow to him and beg for their lives.
Her words were very sorrowful and urgent.
Lǐ could not fathom the reason,
and said:
"I have never killed anyone."
The woman pleaded sorrowfully without cease.
Lǐ woke from sleep,
pondered but found no clue,
and slept again.
He again dreamed of the previous woman begging for her life,
saying, "My life is in imminent danger;
can you bear not to save me?"
Lǐ still did not understand her meaning,
but was only alarmed and distressed.
Sleeping again,
he once more dreamed of the previous woman saying:
"Your Honor ultimately cannot save me.
I am already dead,
but I have also repaid my debt.
In my previous life, I was the wife of the Yāsī Lùshì.
There was a maidservant who was pregnant,
carrying two children in her womb.
At that time, out of jealousy,
I beat her to death,
and deceived my husband, saying:
'The maidservant stole a gold hairpin and a box,
and died under torture during interrogation.'
Now I have received this retribution,
but I have already repaid my debt of injustice.
That gold hairpin and box
are inside the bracket arm west of the hall.
On my behalf, inform the master,
and ask him not to eat its flesh,
but to perform meritorious deeds for me."
Lǐ awoke in alarm,
summoned the host, and questioned him:
"Are you slaughtering a white sheep?
Are there twin lambs?"
He replied:
"Yes."
Lǐ recounted the dream from the night,
and they sighed in even greater wonder.
Upon searching inside the bracket arm,
they indeed found the two objects.
They then took the sheep and buried it,
performing meritorious deeds to offer prayers for it.
From "Records of Retribution"
Liú Yàoshi
In Shuǐmén Village, Lǒngyòu, there was an innkeeper named Liú Yàoshi,
his actual name not recorded.
He made his living by lending money at interest,
amassing a fortune of a thousand gold,
skilled in scheming and seeking profit,
adept at hoarding hard-to-obtain goods.
Taking the people's wealth and assets
was like holding a key,
opening people's chests, boxes, and treasuries,
no different from stealing their pearls and treasures.
Hence, he had the nickname "Yàoshi" (Key).
A neighbor had a wealthy family,
enticed by Yàoshi,
lent him money,
and for years did not inquire about it.
Suddenly one day,
Yàoshi took out the contract and calculated the debt,
and the amount had multiplied extremely.
Before the repayment was even completed,
he immediately added the year's interest to the principal,
with virtually no time limit,
until eventually the wealth, goods, and property
all went to "Yàoshi".
The debtor resented him endlessly.
After "Yàoshi" died,
that family's cow gave birth to a calf,
with the name "Yàoshi"
on the flesh between its ribs,
as if written with fine ink.
It was then whipped and put to work by the creditor's family,
leaving no patch of skin intact.
"Yàoshi"'s wife and son, Guǎng,
used valuable goods to purchase and redeem it,
placed it in the main hall,
and served it as if it were alive.
When it died,
they placed it in a coffin and buried it in the wild.
This is indeed similar to the case of Liú Zìrán.
This shows that the principle of retribution
is not false.
From "Jade Hall Anecdotes"
Shànggōng
In Dōng'ānrén Town of Yíchūn Commandery,
there was a temple called Qíjué Temple.
In the temple lived an old monk,
over ninety years of age,
whose disciples and students spanned one or two generations.
The local people all simply called him "Shànggōng,"
and no one remembered his Dharma name.
The temple's permanent estate had many fields
and a great number of livestock.
One night, Shànggōng
dreamed of an old woman
dressed in dark blue cloth clothes,
who bowed in farewell and left,
saying:
"I only owe the temple eight hundred coins."
Shànggōng woke up and found it strange,
so he took a brush and wrote it on the wall of his bedroom.
None of the monks living with him knew about it.
Within three to five days,
an old cow from the temple's permanent estate
died without cause.
The monk in charge of affairs sold it in the market,
but only received eight hundred coins in payment.
At several places like this,
the price did not exceed the previous offer.
The monk in charge reported to Shànggōng in detail, saying:
"The temple's cow died,
and we wanted to sell it.
Several butchers
all offered eight hundred coins."
Shànggōng sighed and said:
"The debt has been repaid in full."
He then had the monk in charge enter his bedroom
and read what was written on the wall.
Everyone sighed in amazement.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Shī Biàn
Shī Biàn, a military farm official in Lúzhōu,
once relied on his power to seize several dozen qǐng of land from the people.
The original owner was reduced to being his farm laborer
and could not seek justice for himself.
Several years later,
Biàn died.
The original owner's family gave birth to a calf,
with white hair on its belly
spanning several cùn.
As it grew,
the markings gradually became mottled,
and within a year,
formed the characters "Shī Biàn,"
with every stroke complete.
The Daoist priest Shào Xiūmò
personally witnessed this.
From "Jīshén Lù"
Gōngchéng Tōng
In Zhǔgōng, there was a commoner named Gōngchéng Tōng.
Throughout his life, he harbored hidden vices,
which others found difficult to know.
After his death,
a black donkey foal was born in a household in Húnán,
with white hair forming the characters "Jīngnán Gōngchéng Tōng."
His descendants, hearing of this, felt ashamed,
but in the end, they could not seek to redeem it.
Everyone in Jiānglíng knew of this.
From "Běimèng Suǒyán"
Monk Shěnyán
Yúndǐng Mountain's Cíyún Temple
attracted people from all directions,
and the offerings of food were abundant.
The temple's head monk, Shěnyán,
was greedy and despicable by nature.
He embezzled the temple's donated wealth,
drank wine, ate meat,
kept a wife and children,
and engaged in all manner of misconduct.
Monks who were even slightly solitary and pure
were inevitably subjected to humiliation and abuse.
One day, he fell gravely ill
and claimed to see a stone mortar hanging in the air by a rope,
with a rat gnawing at it.
The rope broke,
and the mortar struck him right in the heart.
He let out a loud cry and stopped breathing.
After a long while, he revived,
and this happened several dozen times
before he finally died.
A year later,
a calf was born in a village below the temple,
with the characters "Shěnyán" clearly visible on its belly.
From "Jǐngjiè Lù"
Emperor Yáo
During the time of Qín Shǐhuáng,
people from the country of Wǎnqú
arrived in snail-shaped boats,
saying:
"Our country is one hundred thousand lǐ from Xuānyuán Hill.
Our country's ancient sages
saw a black wind over Jìzhōu,
which indicated the emergence of a sage.
Indeed, Qìngdū gave birth to Yáo."
From Wáng Zǐnián's "Shíyí Jì"
King Wǔ of Zhōu
During Zhòu's reign of chaos and disorder,
he sought to kill the feudal lords,
sending Fēilián and Èlái to slaughter the virtuous and capable,
taking their precious vessels
and burying them beneath the Qióng Terrace.
He ordered Fēilián and others to set up
within the domains of the tributary states,
a continuous chain of beacon fires.
Zhòu would ascend the terrace to observe where the fires were lit,
then raise an army to attack that country,
kill its ruler,
imprison its people,
and seize its female musicians,
indulging in his depravity and cruelty.
The spirits and people were filled with indignation and resentment.
At that time, a vermilion bird appeared, carrying fire
that shone like stars,
disrupting the light of the beacon fires.
Zhòu became confused
and ordered the various states to extinguish their beacon fires.
When King Wǔ of Zhōu attacked Zhòu,
woodcutters and shepherd boys,
while searching for high bird nests,
found a red jade seal
inscribed with the words:
"The virtue of wood is about to perish,
the fortune of water is now flourishing."
The script was all in large seal characters,
recording that the era of Yīn had come to an end,
and the sagely virtue of Jī was now ascendant.
Thus, of the three parts under heaven,
two parts returned to Zhōu.
Then, the common people
lamented that Yīn's downfall came too late
and regretted that Zhōu's arrival was delayed.
From "Shíyí Lù"
King of Yuè
When the King of Yuè entered the state of Wú,
a vermilion bird flew alongside the king.
Thus, when Gōu Jiàn achieved hegemony,
he built the Wàngniǎo Terrace
to commemorate the auspicious sign of the vermilion bird.
From Wáng Zǐnián's "Shíyí Jì"
Líntáo Giants
During the time of Qín Shǐhuáng,
twelve giants appeared in Líntáo,
all dressed in foreign attire.
Thereupon, twelve bronze statues were cast
to depict them.
This was an auspicious sign for the twelve emperors of Hàn.
From "Xiǎoshuō"
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn
On the southern plains of Xíngyáng, there was a perilous well.
The elders said:
"Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn once hid from Xiàng Yǔ in this well
and was saved by a pair of turtledoves."
Thus, a common saying goes:
Hàn's founder, avoiding perilous times,
hid within the perilous well.
A pair of turtledoves gathered above him—
who knew someone was below?
Every New Year's Day during the Hàn dynasty,
a pair of turtledoves would be released,
originating from this event.
From "Xiǎoshuō"
General Fán Kuài asked Lù Jiǎ:
"Since ancient times, rulers
have all claimed to receive the mandate from Heaven,
saying there are auspicious omens.
Is there really such a thing?"
Lù Jiǎ replied:
"Yes.
If the eyelid twitches, one gains wine and food;
if the lamp sparks, one gains wealth;
if magpies chatter at noon, travelers arrive;
if spiders gather, all affairs bring joy.
Since small things have signs,
great ones should also be so.
Therefore it is said:
'If the eyelid twitches, chant over it;
if the lamp sparks, bow to it;
if magpies chatter at noon, feed them;
if spiders gather, release them.'
How much more so for the great treasure of the realm,
the weighty position of a ruler—
if not by the mandate of Heaven, how could one obtain it?
Auspicious treasures are signs of trust;
Heaven uses treasures as tokens of trust,
responding to human virtue,
hence they are called auspicious responses.
The mandate of Heaven is not without signs;
it cannot be seized by force."
From Xiǎoshuō.
Empress Yuán of Hàn
When Empress Yuán was at home,
once a white swallow carried a stone,
as large as a finger,
which fell into her spinning basket.
She picked it up,
and the stone split into two by itself.
Inside was an inscription saying:
"Mother of Heaven, Queen of Earth."
She then joined them together,
and they reunited,
becoming a treasured record.
When she became empress,
she often kept it in her seal box,
calling it the Heavenly Seal.
From Xījīng Zájì.
Emperor Zhāng of Later Hàn
In the fifth year of the Yǒngníng era of Emperor Zhāng of Later Hàn,
the country of Tiáozhī presented a strange bird,
named the zhīquè.
It was seven feet tall,
understood human speech,
and when the state was peaceful, it would flock and sing.
From Wáng Zǐnián Shíyí Jì.
Emperor Dà of Wú
Sūn Quán of Wú was hunting at Fánshān in Wǔchāng,
when he saw an old woman.
She asked Quán what he had caught,
and he said:
"Only a leopard."
She said:
"Why not raise its tail?"
Then she suddenly vanished.
When Quán assumed the imperial title,
he built a temple at the foot of the mountain.
From Wǔchāng Jì.
Emperor Míng of Wèi
During the time of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
patterned stones joined like intertwined branches appeared at the foot of Tàishān.
They were twelve zhang tall,
shaped like cypress trees,
their patterns vibrant and striking,
as if carved by humans,
joined from top to bottom yet split in the middle,
five feet wide.
Elders said:
"At the end of Qín,
the two stones were over a hundred paces apart,
overgrown and without paths."
By the beginning of Emperor Míng's reign,
they gradually seemed closer,
like a pair of gate towers.
Earth governs the yin category;
Wèi corresponded to the virtue of Earth,
and this was a spiritual sign.
Also, in Pèi State there was land corresponding to the wùjǐ position,
an auspicious sign of Earth's virtue.
So they built the Wùjǐ Altar,
and a yellow star shone brightly at night.
They also erected the Bì Áng Terrace to offer sacrifices,
saying it corresponded to Wèi's celestial division.
Sacrifices were performed there annually.
From Wáng Zǐnián Shíyí Jì.
The Sīmǎ Clan of Jìn
The essence of the planet Mercury
fell into Liǔgǔ in Zhāngyè Commandery,
transforming into a black stone,
over one zhang wide,
and three feet tall.
By the end of Later Hàn,
patterns gradually appeared on it,
though not very distinct.
In the Qīnglóng era of Wèi,
it suddenly shook as if by thunder,
the sound heard over a hundred lǐ away.
The stone stood upright by itself,
turned white,
and bore images of oxen, horses, immortals, jade rings, and inscriptions.
Later, the Sīmǎ clan received the mandate,
matching the virtue of Metal.
From Lùyì Jì.
White Swallow
In the year Wèi yielded to Jìn,
a white swallow appeared below the northern palace gate,
regarded as a divine creature.
It was placed in a golden cage
and kept in the palace,
but after ten days, it vanished without a trace.
Commentators considered it an auspicious sign of Jìn's Metal virtue.
In the past, during Shī Kuàng's time,
white swallows came to nest,
seen as an auspicious response,
and Shī Kuàng served Jìn.
Thus, ancient and modern interpretations correspond.
From Wáng Zǐnián Shíyí Jì.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn
When Emperor Wǔ of Jìn served as Fǔjūn,
in the rear hall of his office,
three stalks of grass suddenly grew.
Their stems were yellow, leaves green,
as if woven gold and drawn emerald,
with delicate, drooping flowers resembling golden dīng.
A Qiāng man named Yáo Fù,
courtesy name Shìfēn,
who tended horses in the stables
and understood the arts of yīnyáng,
said:
"This grass is an auspicious sign corresponding to the virtue of Metal."
The emperor gave the grass to Zhāng Huá,
who composed the "Golden Dīng Rhapsody," saying:
"Admiring the nine stalks in the Hàn court,
praising the three pearls in this hall;
precious, manifesting auspice for Metal's virtue,
comparing names and categories, yet easily confused."
From Wáng Zǐnián Shíyí Jì.
Emperor Huì of Jìn
Gāo Tánglóng once inscribed on a pillar of the Yè palace:
"After a certain number of years,
an emperor shall reside here."
When Emperor Huì of Jìn visited Yè,
the years matched exactly.
From Yìyuàn.
Emperor Yuán of Jìn
When the Jìn Middle Ancestor (Emperor Yuán) served as chancellor,
a chick had sparrows flying to perch on its back;
driven away, they returned again,
repeating this several times.
Diviners said:
"The chicken corresponds to yǒu;
yǒu corresponds to Metal.
Sparrows transforming and coming to join it
is an omen of the king ascending the throne."
It was also said:
"During Emperor Yuán's time,
three sparrows together climbed onto a rooster's back,
and three entered the Āndōng Hall."
Diviners believed this meant he would advance three ranks to become emperor.
From Dònglín Jì.
Lǐ Xióng of Shǔ
Elders in Shǔ said:
"Dàngqú was the ancient Sài country;
now there are Sài City and Lú City."
During Qín Shǐhuáng's time,
a man twenty-five zhàng tall
appeared in Dàngqú.
The Qín historian Húwú Jìng said:
"Five hundred years from now,
there will surely be an extraordinary person who becomes a great leader."
When Lǐ Xióng became king,
his ancestors hailed from Dàngqú,
and those with insight all saw it as a fulfillment.
From Huáyáng Guózhì.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Sòng
Emperor Yáng of Suí
In the late Suí dynasty, an observer of celestial omens reported:
"At the Qián Gate, there is an imperial aura,
stretching continuously to Tàiyuán, and it is very strong."
Therefore, Emperor Yáng built a detached palace
and frequently visited Fényáng to suppress it.
Later, Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng raised his righteous army in Fényáng,
and subsequently gained the empire.
From "Records of Portents and Confirmations"
Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng
In the third year of the Wǔdé era of Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng,
Lǎo Jūn appeared at Yángjiǎo Mountain.
The Prince of Qín ordered Jí Shànxíng to report this to the court.
Shànxíng told Lǎo Jūn:
"Entering the capital is very difficult;
I have no object to serve as proof."
Lǎo Jūn said:
"On the day you reach the capital,
someone will present a stone resembling a turtle;
that can serve as proof."
Upon arriving at the palace gate,
indeed, someone from Shào Prefecture presented a stone resembling a turtle.
Beneath it were six characters,
which read:
"The empire is at peace,
for ten million days."
From "Records of the Extraordinary"
Emperor Tàizōng of Táng
On the third day after Tàizōng's birth,
a scholar visited Gāozǔ and said:
"You, sir, are a noble man,
and you have a noble son."
Then, looking at Tàizōng, he said:
"He has the bearing of a dragon and phoenix,
the appearance of heaven and sun.
Your nobility will come because of this child;
by twenty, he will surely be able to bring peace to the people."
From "Records of Portents and Confirmations"
Prince Qí of Táng, Yuánjí
Prince Qí of Táng, Lǐ Yuánjí, obtained a green stone in the Jìnyáng Palace,
shaped like a turtle.
On it were four characters in vermilion script,
which read:
"Lǐ Yuān, ten thousand auspiciousnesses."
Yuánjí sent an envoy to present it.
The characters were clear and translucent,
as if naturally forming the shape of a turtle.
All who saw it found it extraordinary.
Gāozǔ said:
"This is not credible."
He then ordered it to be soaked in water and polished to test it.
After several days of soaking and polishing overnight,
the characters became even brighter.
Thereupon, congratulations came from both inside and outside the court.
Gāozǔ said:
"Heaven has issued a clear mandate,
bestowing ten thousand auspiciousnesses.
I am uncultured and of shallow virtue;
how can I presume to partake in this?
It is fitting to sacrifice to the stone turtle with a shǎoláo offering and then respectfully send it off with a libation."
From "Records of the Vast and Virtuous and the Divine and Extraordinary"
Emperor Zhōngzōng of Táng
Emperor Zhōngzōng of Táng was deposed by Empress Tiānhòu and exiled to Fánglíng.
He looked up to the sky and sighed,
making a silent wish in his heart.
He then threw a stone into the air, saying:
"If I am to be emperor again,
this stone will not fall."
The stone was then caught and hung on a tree branch,
and it remains there to this day.
Also, someone crossing a river
found an ancient mirror
and presented it to him.
The Emperor looked at his reflection in the mirror.
The reflection in the mirror spoke, saying:
"You will become the Son of Heaven."
Within ten days,
he was restored to the imperial throne.
From "Records of Unique Extraordinary Events"
Prince Xiāng of Táng
Dù Péngjǔ, the military governor of Ān Prefecture in the Táng dynasty,
was famous, as was his father.
During the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng,
when Empress Wéi was at the height of her power,
Péngjǔ suddenly died.
In the underworld court,
before his interrogation was concluded,
he was brought before the King's hall.
Suddenly, he heard an official say:
"The King now must establish Prince Xiāng as emperor."
The King rose and descended the steps.
Péngjǔ saw people, each over two zhàng tall,
a hundred in total, supporting a carriage.
Prince Xiāng, dressed in imperial robes and crown,
was inside the carriage.
The King of Ghosts saw him and welcomed him with a bow.
Prince Xiāng descended from the carriage and returned the bow.
After such rituals were completed, they departed.
After Péngjǔ revived, he spoke of this.
At that time, Prince Xiāng was serving as Chancellor.
A little over a year later,
Empress Wéi was about to endanger the Lǐ family.
Prince Xiāng's son, the Prince of Línzī,
raised an army and destroyed her faction,
and honored Prince Xiāng as emperor.
He then summoned Péngjǔ
and promoted him in office.
From "Records of Things Heard"
The Assistant Prefect of Lù Prefecture
When Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng was the Assistant Prefect of Lù Prefecture,
about to enter the court,
there was a man named Hán Nǐnglǐ from the military prefecture
who claimed to understand the Five Omens divination.
He used chopsticks to test it for him.
After laying out the hexagram,
one chopstick spontaneously stood up without reason.
It fell and rose three times in total.
Those watching considered it a great auspicious sign.
Subsequently, he exterminated the Wéi clan
and secured the heavenly throne.
(The original text had "bǎo" for "throne,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
This was due to this journey.
Nǐnglǐ was appointed to an official post, rising to the fifth rank.
From "Compilation of Anecdotes from National History"
The Golden Snail
When Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng was still a prince in his mansion,
snails formed the characters for "Son of Heaven"
on the wall of his bedchamber.
The Emperor, fearful of this,
covered them with mud to remove them.
After a few days, they reappeared as before.
This happened three times.
After he ascended the throne,
he had several hundred golden and silver snails cast
and offered them before the merit and virtue hall.
There were also ones carved from jade.
People of later times occasionally obtained them.
From "Records of the Extraordinary"
Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng
When Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng was still the Crown Prince,
he was resented by Princess Tàipíng.
She kept him under constant surveillance,
and even the slightest details were reported to the Emperor.
Moreover, those within the palace
secretly maintained ambiguous loyalties,
aligning themselves with Princess Tàipíng's influence.
At that time, Empress Yuánxiàn was pregnant.
Xuánzōng, fearing Princess Tàipíng,
wished to have her take medicine to terminate the pregnancy,
but had no one he could speak to about it.
Zhāng Yuè, through his position as a tutor, gained access to the Crown Prince's palace.
Xuánzōng, in a moment of leisure, consulted Yuè about the matter,
and Yuè also secretly supported the plan.
On another day,
when Yuè entered again to attend upon him,
he brought with him three doses of an abortifacient medicine and presented them.
Xuánzōng was pleased to receive the medicine.
He dismissed all his attendants,
and alone, he lit a fire in the hall,
and began to boil the medicine. Before it was fully cooked,
he grew weary and dozed off briefly.
In that hazy state between sleep and wakefulness,
he saw a divine being over ten feet tall,
with horse trappings and ornaments,
clad in golden armor,
holding a halberd.
It circled the medicine cauldron three times,
and the boiling medicine was completely overturned, leaving none behind.
Xuánzōng rose and saw this marvel.
He added more fuel to the fire,
put in another dose,
and boiled it in the cauldron.
Then he went to his couch,
waiting intently for a moment.
The divine being appeared again,
and overturned the brew as before.
Altogether, he boiled it three times,
and each time it was overturned,
so he stopped.
The next day, when Yuè came again,
Xuánzōng told him what had happened.
Yuè descended the steps and bowed solemnly,
congratulating him, saying:
"This is the Mandate of Heaven,
it cannot be removed."
Later, when Empress Yuánxiàn craved sour food,
Xuánzōng also told Yuè about it.
Yuè would often, during his lectures,
secretly bring quinces in his sleeve to present to her.
Therefore, during the Kāiyuán era,
no one received favor and grace comparable to Yuè's.
Emperor Sùzōng treated Yuè's sons, Jūn and Jì,
as if they were his own relatives and brothers.
From "Liǔ Shì Shǐ" (Liu's History).
The Golden Statue That Was Shouted At
In the early Táng, there was a divine statue
made of gold.
It was said
that between the Zhōu and Suí dynasties, a sorcerer cast and molded it.
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
it was ordered to be placed in the palace,
and the hall housing it was kept strictly locked.
Emperor Xuánzōng once visited that hall,
opened it, and viewed the statue.
At that time, Sùzōng was the Crown Prince,
and Dàizōng was still young;
both were attending the Emperor.
The Emperor asked the eunuch Gāo Lìshì:
"What is unusual about this divine statue?
Is there any story about it?"
Lìshì said:
"This was made in a previous dynasty.
It can be used to divine how many years a ruler will reign.
The method is to shout at it sternly.
If the reign is to be very long,
then the statue will shake and tremble for a long time.
Otherwise,
it will shake only once and stop."
The Emperor immediately shouted at it sternly.
The statue seemed afraid,
shaking and trembling for a long while,
then fell to the ground.
The Emperor laughed with joy and said:
"Just as you said,
how long will I be the Son of Heaven?"
Lìshì then bowed again to congratulate him.
The Emperor then ordered the Crown Prince to shout at it.
The statue shook slightly.
He then ordered his imperial grandson to shout at it,
and it also swayed for a long time.
The Emperor said:
"My grandson is like me."
Later, Emperor Xuánzōng reigned for fifty years,
Emperor Sùzōng reigned for six years in total,
and Emperor Dàizōng reigned for nineteen years,
fully matching the divination.
From "Xuān Shì Zhì" (Records from the Xuān Room).
The Tiānbǎo Talisman
In the late Kāiyuán era of the Táng,
a precious talisman was obtained at the ancient Hángǔ Pass in Hóngnóng.
It was a white stone with red markings,
forming the character 'wèi' (未).
Those who understood interpreted it, saying:
"'Wèi' signifies 'forty-eight',
thus indicating the number of years the Sage will reign."
In the following year when the Emperor fled to Shǔ,
it was exactly the forty-eighth year.
When the precious talisman was obtained,
songs spread throughout the land:
"Obtained the treasure, oh,
Hóngnóng, oh;
Hóngnóng, oh,
obtained the treasure, oh."
In the year the treasure was obtained,
the era name was changed to Tiānbǎo.
From "Kāi Tiān Chuán Xìn Jì" (Records of Trustworthy Tales from the Kaiyuan and Tianbao Eras).
Shǔ Dāngguī (Sichuan Angelica)
When the monk Yīxíng was about to die,
he left a package
for his disciples to present to the Emperor.
The Emperor opened and looked at it;
it was Shǔ dāngguī (Szechuan angelica root).
The Emperor did not understand at first,
but after he returned from his flight to Shǔ,
he realized its subtle meaning,
and deeply sighed in wonder.
From "Kāi Tiān Chuán Xìn Jì".
Wànlǐ Bridge
Emperor Xuánzōng visited the Eastern Capital.
It happened to be a clear autumn day.
He ascended the tower of Tiāngōng Temple together with Master Yīxíng.
Gazing into the distance for a long time,
the Emperor looked far away with a sorrowful expression,
heaving several sighs.
He said to Yīxíng:
"Will I be able to live out my years without calamity?"
Yīxíng stepped forward and said:
"Your Majesty will travel ten thousand lǐ,
and your sacred reign will be boundless."
When he first arrived in Chéngdū during his western journey,
looking ahead at a great bridge,
the Emperor raised his whip and asked his attendants:
"What is the name of this bridge?"
Military Governor Cuī Yuán spurred his horse forward and said:
"Wànlǐ Bridge (Ten-Thousand-Lǐ Bridge)."
The Emperor then sighed with recollection and said:
"Yīxíng's words
have now indeed come true.
I have no more worries."
From "Sōng Chuāng Lù" (Records from the Pine Window).
Emperor Sùzōng of Táng
While Sùzōng was in the Eastern Capital,
he was framed by Lǐ Línfǔ,
and several times his situation was nearly perilous.
Before long,
his temples turned gray.
Once during an early morning court session,
the Emperor saw him and said with a sorrowful expression:
"You should return to your residence quickly,
I will visit you."
When the Emperor arrived,
he looked around and saw that the courtyards and halls of the palace were not swept,
musical instruments and screens
were covered with dust,
and among the attendants and servants,
there were no female entertainers.
The Emperor was moved,
and turning to Lìshì, he said:
"The Crown Prince lives in such conditions,
General, why did you not let me know?"
When the Emperor was in the palace,
he often called Lìshì "General."
Original note: "often called" was written as "did not know,"
and there is a "call" above "as,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.
Lìshì replied:
"I once intended to report to Your Majesty,
but the Crown Prince would not allow it.
He said:
'Do not disturb the Emperor's thoughts.'"
The Emperor immediately ordered Lìshì
to instruct the Governor of the Capital,
to urgently select five tall and fair daughters from common families,
to be bestowed upon the Crown Prince.
Lìshì hurried away,
but soon returned and reported:
"On previous occasions when I conveyed Your Majesty's decree to the Capital Governor
to select and present daughters,
the common people became restless,
and those in the court who like to discuss affairs
took it as a pretext for criticism.
I believe that within the palace,
there are women from former official families who were confiscated into service,
who would be suitable for selection."
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and sent Lìshì to order the Director of the Palace,
to examine the registers and select,
obtaining three women,
who were then bestowed upon the Crown Prince,
and among them was Empress Wú of Zhāngjìng.
Shortly after,
when the Empress was attending in bed,
she fell into a deep sleep and did not wake,
moaning as if in pain,
and her breathing seemed unsteady.
Sùzōng called her but she did not respond,
and he secretly thought to himself:
"The Emperor bestowed her upon me,
yet she suddenly appears unwell and does not wake.
How would the Emperor know it is not due to my careless care?"
He quickly took a candle to look at her,
and after a long while, she awoke.
Sùzōng asked her,
and the Empress covered her left side with her hand and said:
"Just now in my dream,
there was a divine being over ten feet tall,
clad in golden armor and holding a sword,
who looked at me and said:
'The Emperor commands me to become your son.'
He then pierced through my left side with his sword and entered,
the pain was almost unbearable."
"Unbearable" was originally written as "painful,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.
"And it has not subsided even now."
Sùzōng examined her under the candlelight,
and there seemed to be a red mark like a thread remaining.
He immediately reported the situation,
and later Dàizōng was born.
On the third day after Dàizōng's birth,
the Emperor visited the Eastern Palace,
bestowed a golden basin,
and ordered it to be used for bathing.
Empress Wú was young,
and the imperial grandson's noble body was not yet fully developed,
so the nurse was anxious and confused,
and presented another prince born on the same day who was plump and robust.
The Emperor looked at him and was displeased,
saying:
"This child is not my grandson."
The nurse kowtowed and confessed.
The Emperor glanced at her and said:
"This is not something you understand,
bring my grandson here!"
Then the Crown Prince presented the child.
The Emperor was greatly delighted,
placed him in his palms,
and looked at him under the sun,
laughing and saying:
"This child's fortune and blessings will far surpass his father's."
The Emperor returned to the palace,
leaving all the palace musicians behind,
and said to Lìshì:
"In this one hall, there are three Sons of Heaven,
how joyful!
Let us drink with the Crown Prince."
From "Liǔshì History"
Emperor Wǔzōng of Táng
In the last years of the Táng Huìcháng era,
Emperor Wǔzōng suddenly changed his imperial name to "fire below fire."
When Emperor Xuānzōng ascended the throne as the Prince of Guāng,
in ancient script,
the character for "guāng" (光) is actually composed of "fire above fire" (火上火).
Alas,
the clarity of the omen was like this.
From "True Mausoleum Seventeen Histories"
Emperor Xuānzōng of Táng
When Emperor Xuānzōng of Táng was still a feudal prince,
he once followed the imperial carriage on its return,
but accidentally fell from his horse,
and no one noticed.
By the second watch,
he was finally able to get up.
At that time, heavy snow was falling,
and looking around, all was silent with no human sound.
The Emperor was extremely cold,
when a patrol guard arrived,
and was greatly startled.
The Emperor said:
"I am the Prince of Guāng,
unexpectedly ending up here.
I am exhausted and thirsty,
please fetch water for me."
The guard immediately found water nearby and presented it,
then left hastily.
The Emperor rose after a long while,
lifted the bowl to drink,
but looking at the water in the bowl,
it had all turned into fragrant wine.
The Emperor was delighted,
and feeling self-assured,
he drank the entire bowl.
Soon his body grew slightly warm and gained strength,
and he walked back to his princely residence.
Later, he ascended the imperial throne.
From "True Mausoleum Seventeen Histories"
Welcoming the Prince of Guāng
Lú Zhēn, the Crown Prince's Guest,
had a nephew
who once was a Buddhist monk.
During the Huìcháng era,
when monks were purged and returned to secular life,
he was appointed by hereditary privilege as a Military Advisor in the residence of the Prince of Guāng.
One day,
he dreamed that his former master came to his home to inquire about his well-being.
Lú then told him of his lowly
"Lowly" was originally written as "finished,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.
official position, which was trivial,
and not what he desired.
He often thought of shaving his head again
and donning the black robes of a monk.
The master said:
"If you truly have this aspiration,
the revival of the Buddhist teachings
is not far off."
Before he finished speaking,
suddenly on all sides appeared sun and moon banners and flags,
with thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of cavalry,
loudly proclaiming the welcoming of the Prince of Guāng to ascend the imperial throne.
Not long after,
Emperor Wǔzōng passed away,
and the Prince of Guāng indeed ascended the imperial throne.
Thus, it ultimately corresponded to the event.
From "Records of the Xuānshì"
Emperor Yìzōng of Táng
Emperor Yìzōng of Táng was profound in bearing and dignified in appearance.
While still a prince in his residence,
he fell gravely ill with a rash.
Imperial Consort Guō saw a yellow dragon emerge from his bedroom.
As the emperor’s illness gradually subsided,
the consort reported what she had seen.
The emperor said:
“Do not divulge these words;
if I become noble, I will not forget you.”
Another time, after a heavy snowfall of over a foot,
not an inch of snow was found on the roof of his bedroom.
All the princes who saw this were astonished.
In the late Dàzhōng era,
children in the capital would fold cloth, dip it in water,
and hold it up to the sun,
calling it “twisting the halo.”
When the emperor ascended the throne from the title of Prince of Yùn,
the words “twisting the halo” were fulfilled.
Emperor Xuānzōng composed the melody “Tàibiān Chuí Qǔ,”
with the lyrics:
“The seas and mountains are tranquil in Xiántōng.”
Thus, upon his accession, the emperor adopted the era name Xiántōng.
The emperor’s benevolence and filial piety were innate.
When Empress Dowager Zhèng passed away,
he observed a vegetarian diet and mourned with such grief and emaciation
that it matched the rites of common scholars.
All the ministers who offered condolences were deeply moved.
From “Dùyáng Zábiān.”
Emperor Xīzōng of Táng
When Chancellor Lǐ Wèi, Duke of Lǒngxī of Táng, raised his grand banner in Guǎnglíng,
it was the twelfth year of Xiántōng.
A report from Sìzhōu stated:
Two nuns arrived at Pǔguāng Temple to pray and pay respects.
They gazed around wildly, as if afflicted by madness,
saying:
“In two years, the state will face turmoil,
and the Great Sage Monk of this temple will ascend the precious throne.”
They ran along the corridors shouting,
gathering a large crowd,
with no trace of their origin.
The monks were greatly alarmed and were about to detain them
when the two suddenly climbed a high pagoda and threw themselves down.
One died instantly,
while the other was injured from the fall,
raving in pain and unconscious,
yielding no answers under questioning.
The chancellor immediately ordered the report burned
and commanded the prefecture to execute them by caning.
By the fourteenth year,
Emperor Yì indeed passed away.
In the eighth month,
Emperor Xīzōng ascended the throne—he was the Prince of Pǔ.
From “Táng Shǐ.”
Lǐ Hé
Lǐ Hé of Táng served as Prefect of Hèzhōu.
While traveling by river with courtesan Yè Màolián,
he composed “Tóuzi Xuǎn,”
called “yèzi” (leaf).
Since the Xiántōng era,
it became popular throughout the land,
yet no one realized it corresponded to the dynasty’s reign.
The character “yè” (葉) in its standard form
is composed of “twenty” (廿) over “world” (世) and “wood” (木) over “son” (子).
From the Wǔdé to Tiānyòu eras,
it was exactly twenty reigns.
From “Gǎndìng Lù.”
Tàizǔ of Later Táng
Tàizǔ of Later Táng was born after thirteen months in the womb.
On the night of his birth,
his mother was in critical condition,
so the clan sent someone to buy medicine in Yànmén.
They encountered a deity
who instructed them to gather tribesmen,
don armor, hold banners,
beat gongs and drums,
gallop on horses while shouting loudly,
and circle the residence three times before stopping.
They followed the instructions, and the birth proceeded smoothly.
At that time, rainbow light illuminated the room,
white vapor filled the courtyard,
and well water suddenly overflowed.
When he could speak,
he delighted in discussing military affairs.
At twelve or thirteen,
he excelled in horseback riding and archery.
Once, north of Xīnchéng,
he offered wine to the statue of Vaiśravaṇa Heavenly King,
requesting to converse with him.
The king, clad in armor and holding a spear,
faintly emerged from the wall.
In his tent,
clusters of fire often appeared,
sometimes taking the shape of a dragon,
astonishing all who saw it.
He once followed the army to suppress Páng Xūn,
appearing and disappearing on the battlefield like a deity,
earning the nickname “Dragon-Tiger Son.”
From “Běimèng Suǒyán.”
Míngzōng of Later Táng
Before ascending the throne, Emperor Míngzōng of Later Táng
accompanied general Lǐ Cúnxìn on a border patrol
and lodged at an inn in Yànmén.
The innkeeper’s wife was pregnant,
and when the emperor arrived,
she did not promptly prepare food.
The child in her womb spoke to the mother:
“The Son of Heaven has arrived;
quickly prepare food.”
The voice was audible outside.
The woman, astonished,
hurriedly rose to personally cook,
serving him with utmost respect.
The emperor, noting her change from arrogance to deference,
questioned her.
She said:
“Your nobility is beyond words.”
Asked for the reason,
she recounted the incident of the child speaking in her womb.
The emperor said:
“The old woman speaks humbly,
fearing I might take offense.”
Later, it indeed came true as she said.
From “Běimèng Suǒyán.”
Prince of Lù
When Qīngtài was in Qíyáng,
there was a cavalry and infantry administrator named Hé,
over eighty years old,
who suddenly died violently.
He said there was an envoy who detained and recorded him,
led him out,
and in the underworld he saw the Lord of the Underworld, who said:
"You have no other faults,
so now I release you to return.
Tell the Prince of Lù for me:
'Next year in the third month,
he shall become emperor of the realm.'
Hurry back quickly,
and convey my decree."
When he finished speaking, he was led out,
and the envoy sent him back.
Upon reviving,
he then secretly reported the matter to the Prince's attendants,
but all considered it demonic nonsense and did not believe it,
so it never reached the Prince's ears.
Over a month later,
he again died violently and entered the underworld,
once more seeing the Lord of the Underworld.
The Lord of the Underworld angrily rebuked him, saying:
"Why did you receive my instruction yet ultimately fail to convey it?"
Then slowly said:
"I release you to go,
quickly convey my words,
and also request the Prince to paint my likeness and an image of the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha."
Hé, terrified, withdrew.
He saw in the courtyard and corridors below,
documents and records in disarray,
clerks and officials bustling about.
Hé asked about it,
and the envoy said:
"This is because the dynasty is about to change,
these are the promotions, demotions, departures, and retentions—
the official ranks and titles of the future."
When he revived again,
he sought an audience with the Prince under the pretext of a legal dispute.
When he saw him,
he said:
"I have a secret matter to report to Your Highness."
The Prince then dismissed his attendants and asked him,
and Hé recounted in detail what he had seen,
but the Prince did not believe him.
Hé said:
"I am over eighty years old,
death is imminent,
how would I dare to speak falsely?"
The Prince silently dismissed him.
The following spring,
the Prince indeed issued an edict to attack Qíyáng,
and only Old Man Hé alone was pleased,
knowing it would certainly come true.
When the time came,
Old Man Hé's words
were not the slightest bit off.
When Qīngtài ascended the throne,
he promoted Old Man Hé to Magistrate of Tiānxīng County.
Thus it is known that underworld fates are predetermined,
how can human power stop them?
From "Wángshì Jiànwén Lù"
Jìn Gāozǔ
During the Qīngtài era,
Jìn Gāozǔ was still a hidden dragon in Bìngbù.
One day he casually said to his advisors:
"Recently, while napping during the day,
I suddenly dreamed as if in years past when I was in Luòjīng,
riding side by side with the Son of Heaven on the road.
Passing by my old residence,
the Son of Heaven invited me to enter his residence.
I declined repeatedly,
but unable to refuse,
I urged my horse forward and entered.
At the main hall I dismounted,
ascended the eastern steps,
and sat facing west.
The Son of Heaven had already driven his carriage away."
Such was his dream,
and none of the assembled officials dared to respond.
That winter,
there indeed occurred the event of dynastic change.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
The Uncle of the False Shǔ Ruler
The uncle of the false Shǔ ruler,
whose family had been wealthy and prominent for generations,
built a mansion at Xìngyì Gate.
Within the mansion were over twenty courtyards,
all with carved walls and lofty buildings,
high terraces and deep pools,
rare flowers and exotic plants,
clustered osmanthus and miniature mountains,
precious objects from mountains and rivers,
there was nothing not possessed.
In the courtyard of Dǒngchéng Village in Qínzhōu,
there was a red peony plant,
planted since ancient times.
He sent someone to fetch it,
dug up a square zhang of earth,
placed it in a wooden crate,
and from Qínzhōu to Chéngdū,
over three thousand lǐ,
passing through Jiǔzhé, Qīpán, Wàngyún, Jiǔjǐng, and the great and small Màntiān,
narrow, perilous, and precipitous roads,
only then was it delivered.
It was then planted in the new mansion,
and he invited the young ruler to visit.
The young ruler marveled at the splendid construction of the foundation,
rivaling the palace itself,
and playfully took up a brush,
writing a large character "Mèng" on a pillar,
as the custom of the time considered "Mèng" to mean 'unbearable.'
The next year, Shǔ was conquered,
and the Mèng clan entered Chéngdū,
occupying that mansion.
Suddenly, he noticed a red silk lantern between the pillars,
and upon closer inspection,
it was a character "Mèng."
Mèng said:
"This is auspicious,
I shall not change this residence."
That Mèng possessed Shǔ
was indeed a prior omen.
From "Wángshì Jiànwén Lù"
Lǚ Wàng
Lǚ Wàng was fishing by the Wèi River,
and caught a carp.
Cutting open its belly, he found a text that said:
Lǚ Wàng will be enfeoffed in Qí.
From "Shuō Yuàn"
Zhòngní
In the twenty-first year of King Líng of Zhōu,
Confucius was born in the era of Duke Xiāng of Lǔ.
At night, two divine maidens
held fragrant dew
and bathed Zhēngzài.
The Heavenly Emperor sent down the music of the钧天,
and a voice in the air said:
"Heaven is moved to birth a sage son,
therefore it sends down harmonious music."
There were five elders
arrayed in Zhēngzài's courtyard.
These five elders
were the essences of the five stars.
Before the Master was born,
a qilin spat out a jade book at a household in Quèlǐ,
the text said:
"Son of the Water Essence,
succeeding the declining Zhōu to become the Unadorned King."
Zhēngzài tied an embroidered ribbon to the qilin's horn,
and a physiognomist said:
"The Master is a descendant of Shāng Tāng,
possessing the virtue of water and becoming the Unadorned King."
In the twenty-fourth year of Duke Dìng,
Chú Shāng was hunting in the great marsh,
and caught a qilin.
He showed it to the Master,
and the tied ribbon was still there.
When the Master saw it,
he embraced it and untied the ribbon,
tears streaming down to wet his lapels.
From "Wángzǐnián Shíyí Jì"
Wén Wēng
Hàn dynasty Wén Wēng, when starting a field,
cut firewood to make a pond.
At night, over a hundred wild boars
carried earth in their snouts and placed it among the firewood,
and by dawn the pond was completed.
Rice always had a good harvest.
Once he wanted to cut down a large tree,
at the point he wished to cut,
which was eighteen feet from the ground,
Wén Wēng first chanted:
"If I am to become a two-thousand-shí official,
the axe shall strike exactly here."
Then he threw it,
and it struck precisely where he desired.
Later, he indeed became the Governor of Shǔ Commandery.
From "Xiǎoshuō"
Dǒng Zhòngshū
Hàn dynasty Dǒng Zhòngshū once dreamed of a flood dragon entering his bosom,
and then composed the "Chūnqiū Fánlù."
From "Xiǎoshuō"
Hé Bǐgàn
In the Hàn dynasty, Hé Bǐgān dreamed of distinguished guests,
with carriages and horses filling his gate.
Upon waking, he told his wife and children.
Before long,
an old woman appeared at his door,
around eighty years old,
seeking shelter from the rain.
The rain was heavy, yet her clothes were not wet.
Bǐgān invited her in
and treated her with courtesy.
She then said:
"Your ancestors descend from Hòujì,
and from assisting Yáo to the Jìn dynasty, they have accumulated hidden merit.
Now Heaven bestows upon you these tablets."
They were like slips,
nine inches long,
nine hundred and ninety in total.
She presented them to him, saying:
"Descendants who can wear these will attain wealth and nobility."
Having spoken, she went out the door
and was seen no more.
From "Yōu Míng Lù"
Wǔlù Chōngzōng
In the Hàn dynasty, Wǔlù Chōngzōng studied under Hóng Chéngzǐ.
When Chéngzǐ was young,
someone once visited him
and gave him a patterned stone,
as large as a swallow's egg.
Chéngzǐ swallowed it,
and thereafter became greatly enlightened,
becoming a universally learned scholar.
Later, when Chéngzǐ fell ill,
he vomited up this stone
and gave it to Chōngzōng,
who also became renowned for his learning.
From "Xī Jīng Zá Jì"
Wáng Pǔ
In the third year of the Yǒngchū era of the Later Hàn dynasty,
the state's resources were insufficient,
so it was ordered that commoners and officials could obtain office by contributing money.
Wáng Pǔ of Lángyá
had an ancestor named Jí,
who served as Commandant of Chāngyì.
Over generations, Pǔ's family declined,
and by the time of Emperor Ān,
his household was poor and without funds,
so he could not take office.
So he carried bamboo slips
and wielded his brush, working as a scribe in the Luòyáng market.
He was handsome in appearance,
and also highly literate,
so those who hired him for writing
— men would gift him clothes and caps,
women would give him gold and jade.
In a single day,
he would return with a cart full of fine clothes and treasures.
He accumulated grain filling ten granaries,
and his nine clans and relatives
all relied on him for clothing and food.
In Luòyáng, he was called good and wealthy.
Earlier, when Pǔ's family was poor,
they dug a well and obtained an iron seal,
inscribed with:
"Through labor, wealth reaches a hundred million measures;
one earth, three fields, master of the army gate."
Pǔ contributed a hundred million coins to the government,
and obtained the position of Commandant of the Central Barracks.
"Three fields and one earth" forms the character "lěi" (壘, barracks).
The Commandant of the Barracks was in charge of the northern army's barrack gates,
hence "master of the army gate."
From "Shí Yí Lù"
Yìng Shū
In the Later Hàn, Yìng Shū of Rǔnán had four sons.
He saw a divine light shining upon the village altar.
Shū saw the light
and asked a diviner about it.
The diviner said:
"This is a heavenly sign.
Your descendants shall flourish."
Then they discovered gold.
From then on, all his sons pursued official careers and studies,
and all gained reputations for talent.
Down to Yáng,
for seven generations they were prominent and illustrious.
From "Xiào Zǐ Zhuàn"
Yuán Ān
In the Hàn dynasty, Yuán Ān's father died.
His mother sent Ān with a chicken and wine to a diviner
to ask about a burial site.
On the way, he met three scholars.
They asked Ān where he was going,
and he told them everything.
The scholars said:
"We know a favorable burial site."
Ān offered them the chicken and wine as a courtesy.
After finishing,
they told Ān the location,
saying:
"Buried here, in this generation you shall become a high noble."
Then they parted.
After a few steps, Ān looked back,
but they had all vanished.
Ān suspected they were divine beings,
so he buried his father there.
He later rose to become Minister over the Masses,
and his descendants flourished,
producing five high nobles over four generations.
From "Yōu Míng Lù"
Chén Zhòngjǔ
When Chén Zhòngjǔ was still obscure,
he once traveled and lodged at the home of a host named Huáng Shēn.
That night, Shēn's household had a childbirth,
but Zhòngjǔ did not know.
At the third watch of the night,
there was a knock at the door.
After a long while,
he heard a response from inside:
"There is a noble person inside the gate,
you cannot approach from here.
You should go around to the back door."
Soon he heard the one who went returning.
The one inside the gate asked him:
"What child did you see?
What is its name?
How many years will it live?"
The returning one said:
"It is a boy,
named Ānú,
destined to live fifteen years."
He asked again:
"How will he die later?"
The answer was:
"While helping someone build a house,
he will fall to his death."
Zhòngjǔ heard this
and silently remembered it.
Fifteen years later,
when he was Governor of Yùzhāng,
he sent a clerk to inquire
about the boy Ānú from back then.
The family said:
"He was helping the eastern neighbor build a house,
fell from a beam, and died."
Zhòngjǔ later indeed achieved great nobility.
From "Yōu Míng Lù"
Zhāng Chéng
When the Sūn family was pregnant with Zhāng Chéng,
she was riding a light boat on the riverbank,
when suddenly she saw a white snake, three zhàng long,
leap into the boat.
She chanted:
"If this is auspicious,
do not poison or bite me."
She coiled it up and brought it back,
placing it in her room.
By the next morning, it had vanished,
and her mother sighed in regret.
The neighbors said to each other:
"Yesterday, the Zhāng household had a white swan
that soared on its wings into the clouds."
They told Chéng's mother.
His mother had a divination performed.
The diviner said:
"Auspicious.
The swan is a symbol of longevity.
From the room into the clouds
is an image of rising from low to high.
In the past, Wú Héliǘ buried his sister,
with beautiful women, precious swords, and treasures as sacrifices,
exhausting the wealth of Jiāngnán.
Before a thousand years had passed,
carved clouds covered her valley,
beautiful women roamed atop the mound,
white swans soared in the woods,
and white tigers roared on the mountainside —
all were the essences of that past era.
Now appearing in the world,
it portends that your descendants shall reach the highest ministerial positions,
and their fame shall dominate Jiāngbiǎo.
If a son is born,
you may name him Báihú (White Swan)."
Later, Chéng gave birth to Zhāo,
who attained the position of General Assisting Wú,
and lived to ninety years old —
the auspicious signs of the snake and swan.
From "Wáng Zǐ Nián Shí Yí Jì"
Zhāng Shì
In Cháng'ān of Jìn, there was a man named Zhāng.
One day while alone in his room,
a turtledove flew in from outside.
It perched on his bed.
Zhāng found this ominous,
so he opened his robe and chanted:
"Turtledove,
if you come as my misfortune,
fly up to the ceiling.
If you come as my fortune,
fly into my bosom."
The turtledove flew into his bosom,
and then transformed into a bronze hook.
From then on, his assets grew to tens of thousands.
From "Compiled Pearls from the Dharma Garden".
The Ming manuscript states it is from "The Forest of Pearls from the Dharma Garden".
Sīmǎ Xiūzhī
Sīmǎ Xiūzhī of Jìn,
a clansman of Emperor Ān,
fled when encountering disaster.
The piebald horse he rode
was often kept before his bed.
Suddenly, it neighed continuously and refused to eat,
staring fixedly at the saddle.
Xiūzhī then tried to mount it,
but it would not move.
When Xiūzhī returned to sit down,
the horse became agitated again.
So he mounted the horse,
and it swiftly galloped out.
After traveling over ten lǐ,
Mùróng Chāo's arresting officers had already arrived.
Galloping away,
he barely managed to return to Jìn.
From "Extensive Records of the Five Phases, Ancient and Modern".
Dù Cí
During Fú Shēng's Shòuguāng era in Qín,
at every banquet gathering,
those who arrived late were all executed.
The Secretariat Gentleman Dù Cí, exhausted from galloping,
dozed off in the ministry office.
He dreamed of a man riding a black donkey who said:
"Would you rather stay and die together,
or leave and live alone?"
Startled awake upon hearing this,
Dù Cí took his horse and fled,
thus escaping.
All the others were executed.
From "Extensive Records of the Five Phases, Ancient and Modern".
Wǔ Shìhuà
Wǔ Shìhuà of Táng,
was a man from Wénshuǐ County, Tàiyuán.
In his humble days,
he and a fellow townsman, Xǔ Wénbǎo,
made their living selling timber.
They once gathered tens of thousands of timber logs,
which one day transformed into a dense, flourishing forest,
thereby bringing them great wealth.
Shìhuà and Wénbǎo studied beneath the forest trees,
with Shìhuà calling himself "thick timber"
and Wénbǎo calling himself "withered wood",
privately stating they were destined for great nobility.
When Gāozǔ raised the righteous army,
Shìhuà followed into the pass wearing armor and helmet.
Thus his fellow villagers said:
"Because Shìhuà sold timber,
he indeed encountered the autumn of constructing the Xià."
When Shìhuà achieved high rank,
Wénbǎo relied on him
and reached the position of Provincial Governor.
From "Records of Tàiyuán Affairs".
Zhāng Wénchéng
The Táng Director of the Palace Timekeeping Bureau, Zhāng Wénchéng,
had an owl crow at dawn in a tree in his courtyard.
His wife considered this inauspicious
and repeatedly spat at it.
Wénchéng said:
"Quickly sweep and clean,
for I am about to receive a promotion."
Before he finished speaking,
congratulatory guests were already at the gate.
From "Compilation of Unusual Histories".
Another account says,
in the second year of Jǐngyún, Wénchéng
served as Assistant Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
His hat ribbon and green robe
were both gnawed by rats.
A spider as large as a chestnut
hung its silk across his bedroom door.
After several days,
a great amnesty was declared,
he was promoted in rank,
and appointed to the fifth grade.
His son, Bùzǎi,
also had his belt nearly gnawed through by rats.
Shortly after, he was selected and appointed as the Captain of Bóyě.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country".
Shàngguān Zhāoróng
Shàngguān Zhāoróng of Táng
was the granddaughter of Vice Director Shàngguān Yí.
Yí's son committed a crime,
and his wife, Lady Zhèng, was conscripted into palace service.
She gave birth to Zhāoróng posthumously.
On the night before her delivery,
she dreamed someone gave her a steelyard, saying:
"Use this to weigh the literary talents of the world."
Lady Zhèng hoped for a son,
but when Zhāoróng was born,
her mother looked at her and said:
"To weigh the world's talents—
could this be you?"
The baby made murmuring sounds,
as if responding "Yes."
From "Record of Refined Conversations".
Cuī Xínggōng
The Táng Deputy Director of the Palace Library, Cuī Xínggōng,
before attaining the fifth rank,
suddenly had a myna bird
carry an object into his room,
place it on his desk, and fly away.
It was the metal hook of a fish-bag insignia.
Within a few days,
he was promoted to Grand Master.
From "Compilation of Unusual Histories".
Lǐ Zhèngjǐ
Lǐ Zhèngjǐ of Táng, originally named Huáiyù,
was the younger brother-in-law of Hóu Xīyì.
When Hóu governed Zīqīng,
he appointed Huáiyù as Cavalry Commander.
Soon, slanderous rumors were fabricated,
and Hóu, angered, imprisoned him,
intending to execute him.
Huáiyù, harboring injustice with no one to appeal to,
stacked stones in his cell to form a Buddha image,
silently praying for hidden aid.
As it was near the twelfth lunar month,
he longed for his comrades,
sighed, and fell asleep.
He felt someone speak above his head:
"Lǐ Huáiyù,
your time of wealth and nobility has come."
Startled awake,
he looked around but saw no one.
It was still dark,
and he found it very strange.
He slept again,
and again heard someone say:
"When you see blue birds chirping on the wall,
that will be the time of your wealth and nobility."
Startled awake again,
he again saw no one.
Shortly after, day broke.
Suddenly, several dozen blue birds,
as large as sparrows,
gathered on the wall.
Soon, he heard the three armies shouting,
driving out Xīyì,
breaking the locks,
and fetching Huáiyù
to temporarily act as Military Commissioner.
From "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yóuyáng".
Emperor Dàizōng of the Táng dynasty was about to
(The original text had "emperor" for "about to,"
emended according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.)
ascend the palace hall to send off the commandery governors presenting their annual reports.
All officials were assembled outside,
and the imperial carriage had reached the horizontal gate of the hall.
The emperor suddenly halted the carriage,
summoned the officials of the northern bureau, and said:
"I often recall that in the previous reign, whenever the reporting officials were sent off,
there were always edicts of virtuous words,
to express exhortation and encouragement.
Now there is none.
Is this acceptable?"
The chancellor, in haste, had no time to respond.
The emperor said:
"Let us adjourn the court and draft the words,
to await another day."
The Secretariat Drafter Lǐ Kuí stepped out of rank, prostrated, and memorialized:
"Your Majesty sending off the reporting officials
— the decree has been issued for a long time,
and all near and far know of it.
If we suddenly change it now at court,
I fear that the four quarters, upon hearing of it,
may groundlessly become suspicious.
Now we only need the decree's wording.
I beg to take up the brush immediately,
and I implore Your Majesty to halt the imperial carriage briefly."
The emperor consented.
He then ordered paper and brush,
and commanded him to draft it right before the throne.
A scribe was immediately dispatched to transcribe it,
and it was completed in a moment.
When the edict was proclaimed,
at every crucial point,
the emperor would glance at Kuí among the ranks.
The court and the provinces daily awaited Kuí's new appointment.
At the time, it was the height of summer.
Kuí slept at night in the front corridor of the hall,
leaving the main central hall empty
as a place to avoid the heat during the day.
One night,
suddenly a huge fox cried noisily in the courtyard,
then stood up like a human and leaped about,
its eyes shooting out light.
After a long while,
it vaulted over the wall and left.
Kuí was greatly disturbed by this.
That night, before dawn,
he suddenly heard a commotion and clamor in the central hall,
as if there were some strange creature.
He immediately ordered a candle to be lit and the door opened to look.
The servants, terrified, turned and fled,
all saying:
"There is a very strange creature."
Kuí then went to peek,
and there was a toad,
as large as a three-dǒu cauldron,
its two eyes crimson,
squatting and chewing froth.
Kuí did not allow it to be harmed.
In front of the steps, there had long been a large bronze basin for soaking melons and fruits,
which could hold one hú.
He then ordered his family to cover it with the basin and trap it.
He then locked the door,
and there were no further changes.
As dawn approached,
Kuí went to court.
That day, he was appointed chancellor.
Upon returning,
his relatives lined up to congratulate him.
As they spoke of the various strange occurrences,
he immediately sent someone to open the door,
lift the basin, and look.
The creature was already gone.
From Yì Yuàn ("Garden of Marvels").
Jiǎ Yǐnlín
Emperor Dézōng of the Táng dynasty intended to travel west.
An astrologer memorialized:
"When you encounter a forest, stop there."
The emperor said:
"How dare you suggest that I stop among trees?"
Jiāng Gōngfǔ said:
"Not so.
It must also correspond to a place."
Then, the Fèngtiān county captain Jiǎ Yǐnlín paid his respects to the emperor at the temporary imperial quarters.
The emperor observed that Yǐnlín's bearing was heroic and outstanding,
and moreover, he came from a loyal and righteous family,
while his name matched the astrologer's statement.
Yǐnlín was the nephew of Jiǎ Xiūzhī from the late Tiānbǎo era.
The emperor then summoned him into the inner chamber
to probe the depth of his strategies.
Yǐnlín, before the imperial couch,
used his hand tablet to draw on the ground,
laying out plans for attack and defense.
The emperor found him most extraordinary.
Yǐnlín memorialized:
"Last night, I dreamed that the sun fell to the ground,
and I lifted the sun back to the sky with my head."
The emperor said:
"My coming here
was indeed predetermined."
He then appointed Yǐnlín as Investigating Censor,
to impeach and censure at the temporary quarters.
Soon, he was promoted to Left Regular Attendant.
From Shén Yì Lù ("Record of Divine Marvels").
Zhāng Zǐliáng
In the second year of the Yǒngzhēn era of the Táng dynasty,
in the third month of spring,
a rainbow entered the residence of the Rùnzhōu general Zhāng Zǐliáng.
First, it entered the fermented beverage
(The character for "fermented beverage" was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.)
jar,
and the water was exhausted.
Then it entered the well and drank from it.
On the ninth day of that month,
the military governor Lǐ Qí,
having been summoned by decree but not proceeding to the capital,
intended to rebel.
He ordered Zǐliáng to lead troops to capture Xuānzhōu and Shèzhōu.
Zǐliáng suddenly turned his troops around and besieged the city.
Lǐ Qí was captured,
and Zǐliáng was appointed General of the Imperial Guard.
Soon, he was appointed military governor.
From Xiáng Yì Jí Yàn ("Collection of Auspicious and Marvelous Verifications").
Zhèng Yīn
The residence of Táng chancellor Zhèng Yīn
was at the south gate of the Zhāoguó ward.
Suddenly, something came and threw tiles and stones,
continuing for five or six nights without cease.
When he moved to a residence at the west gate of Ānrén ward to avoid it,
the tiles and stones followed him there.
After a long time,
he moved back to Zhāoguó.
Minister Zhèng devoted his heart to Buddhism.
He often rested and dwelled in the meditation room.
When he returned to Zhāoguó
and entered the abbot's chamber,
the room was full of daddy longlegs spiders hanging threads,
one or two chǐ above the ground,
too many to count.
That night, the tiles and stones also ceased.
The next day, he was appointed chancellor.
From Xiáng Yì Jí Yàn ("Collection of Auspicious and Marvelous Verifications").
Péi Dù
Táng Wáng Zhìxīng, when he was still in humble circumstances,
once served as a gatekeeper in Xúzhōu.
There was a Dàoshi residing next to the gate,
and every morning when Zhìxīng rose to take up his broom,
sweeping away the filth from the path,
he would always sweep in front of the Dàoshi's door.
The Dàoshi was deeply moved by this.
Later, when Zhìxīng's mother passed away,
he went to bid farewell to the Dàoshi.
The Dàoshi said to Zhìxīng:
"I am skilled in examining burial grounds.
If you are planning a burial,
I should select a site for you."
On another day, Zhìxīng led the Dàoshi out to view the land.
The Dàoshi used the bamboo staff that Zhìxīng was holding
to mark a spot,
and said:
"You must bury her here.
You will enjoy longevity,
and for two generations, your family will hold the position of Fāngbó."
When Zhìxīng went again to dig the grave,
he found that the bamboo staff had sprouted branches and leaves.
He thought it very strange,
and so he buried her there.
Zhìxīng also once traveled from the commandery on official business to the capital,
and stayed overnight at an inn in Yǎnchéng.
He encountered the innkeeper's wife, who was about to give birth.
He saw two men enter the room where he was sleeping,
and they exclaimed in surprise:
"Wáng Dàizhōng of Xúzhōu is here!"
They also said:
"The child to be born
will die from a metal wound when he is five years old."
Zhìxīng took note of this.
When the time came,
he passed by the inn again,
and asked about the child the woman had borne.
She replied:
"Recently, he was injured by an axe
and has already died."
From "Táng Nián Bǔ Lù Jì Zhuàn".
Niú Shī
During the Chángqìng era of the Táng dynasty,
among the people in the lanes and alleys of Èzhōu,
everyone would use the word "niú" (ox) in their speech.
There was also a monk
who called himself Niú Shī (Ox Master).
Sometimes he acted foolishly, sometimes wisely.
If anyone offended him,
he would always say:
"My elder brother will arrive soon,
what can you do to me then!"
Not long after,
the former chancellor Niú Sēngrú, with the title Qízhānggōng, was appointed military governor of the Wǔchāng army.
Then the use of the word ceased,
but Niú Shī still remained.
Only then did people realize that the appointment of generals and ministers—
was it really by chance?
Earlier, at the beginning of the Yuánhé era,
Shàngshū Hán Gāo
garrisoned Xiàkǒu,
and was subsequently appointed military governor.
Afterwards, he again served as observation commissioner.
In the third year of Chángqìng,
Chancellor Cuī Zhí,
from the position of Minister of Justice, was appointed observation commissioner.
The following winter,
Sēngrú actually arrived.
For a grand councilor to establish a military governorship at Xiàkǒu
began with Sēngrú.
From "Yīn Huà Lù".
Dù Zhōnglì
In the Táng dynasty, Dù Gāo,
courtesy name Zhōnglì,
in his youth,
was wealthy in property,
but had no other accomplishments.
Those who associated with him
did so for the sake of wine and roasted meat,
but in truth they looked down on him.
One day,
they were together seeing off and welcoming guests outside the city walls.
There was a guest skilled in physiognomy
who looked over all the companions,
and pointing solely at Zhōnglì, said:
"This young man will one day become a general."
The entire company burst into laughter.
Later, Zhōnglì married Princess Zhēnyuán,
and ultimately became military governor of Cāngzhōu.
Initially, when Lǐ Zhuàn went out to take up his garrison command,
the flagpole broke along the way,
so he had the flag-bearer hacked to death.
Zhōnglì, on his journey, experienced the same,
and caned the bearer twenty strokes.
Zhuàn ultimately suffered no calamity,
but Zhōnglì died.
Could it be that killing him could avert the disaster?
From "Yù Quán Zǐ".
Lǐ Pín
In the Táng dynasty, the Minister of Works Lǐ Pín,
was originally named Qiú.
In the autumn when he went to take the examinations,
he happened to write his name on the wall of his room.
Overnight,
he suddenly saw that someone had added a stroke to his name,
turning it into the character for "louse" (shī).
Pín said:
"Shī becomes Pín,"
and so he changed his name to Pín.
The following year, he indeed passed the examinations.
From "Nán Chǔ Xīn Wén".
Mǎ Zhí
The Táng chancellor Mǎ Zhí
was dismissed from the position of Protector-General of Ānnán.
He had no connections with the current chief ministers,
and was further appointed to Qiánnán,
which greatly displeased him.
He moored his boat at an ancient temple in the gorge.
In front of the temple was a long embankment,
and beside the embankment were woods.
The moonlight that night was very bright.
He saw a man in white
strolling slowly on the embankment,
reciting:
"Cutting bamboo to make a flute to play,
on the Fènghuáng Pond, the phoenixes fly.
Toil on, sir, further to Qiánnán you go,
that is the time when all things are shaped on the potter's wheel."
It was clearly audible,
and he recited it several times.
Mǎ Zhí sent someone to invite him for questioning,
but he had already vanished.
Later, he went from Qiánnán to the capital to become Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
was promoted to Vice Minister of Justice,
put in charge of the Salt and Iron Monopoly,
and then became chancellor.
From "Běn Shì Shī".
Gāo Pián
In the Táng dynasty, Duke Yàn Gāo Pián, when he was still obscure,
served as Sima under Zhū Shūmíng,
commanding troops on inspection tours.
He saw a pair of eagles,
and said to the crowd:
"If I am to become noble,
my arrow should pierce both."
Then he watched as they flew up and down,
and indeed, one arrow pierced both eagles.
The crowd was greatly astonished,
and thus he was called the "Lord Who Shoots Down Eagles."
From "Gǎn Dìng Lù".
Kǒng Wēnyù
In the Táng dynasty, the Governor of Hénán, Kǒng Wēnyù,
while serving as a Bǔquē,
remonstrated against the campaign against the Dǎngxiàng,
and was demoted to Sima of Chēnzhōu.
After a long time,
he received a letter from his elder cousin, Minister Wēn Yè,
reporting:
"The Censorate wants you to serve as Attendant Censor,
and we await the imperial decree daily."
Suddenly, he received another letter saying:
"The chancellor has decided to appoint you as Right Historian."
But there was no further news.
One day,
a magpie appeared joyfully in his courtyard,
chirping as if speaking.
The children bowed and prayed, saying:
"We wish for an official post soon."
After the magpie flew away,
it dropped a small piece of paper,
on which were written the characters "Bǔquē."
He found it extremely strange.
Not long after,
he was reappointed to that very post.
From "Yīn Huà Lù".
Sūn Wò
In Cháng'ān City, there was a mansion belonging to the Sūn family,
which they had inhabited for several generations,
and its halls were very ancient.
In front of one of the pillars in the main hall,
a locust tree branch suddenly sprouted.
Initially, the Sūn family concealed it,
not wishing others to see it.
After a year,
it gradually grew lush and vigorous,
until the entire pillar transformed,
breaking through the roof,
making it impossible to keep hidden.
Officials, scholars, and commoners came to view it,
filling the streets with carriages and horses.
Not long after,
Sūn Wò served in the imperial court,
and Sūn Chǔ held a military governorship.
People believed this was an omen corresponding to the "Three Locusts" prophecy,
and considered it very extraordinary.
Recently, Sūn Wěi,
a descendant of Sūn Wò,
provided a detailed account of the event.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Lǐ Quánzhōng
At the end of the Qiánfú era of the Táng dynasty,
Lǐ Quánzhōng of Fànyáng,
was well-versed in the "Spring and Autumn Annals" from a young age,
and admired the teachings of Guǐgǔzi.
He once served as Simǎ of Dìzhōu,
when suddenly a reed,
sprouted in his residence,
growing to over a foot with three nodes.
Finding this strange,
he reported it to Deputy Inspector Zhāng Jiànzhāng.
Zhāng Jiànzhāng was a scholar well-versed in antiquity,
and said:
"In the past, Pú Hóng considered a nine-node reed growing in a pond as an auspicious sign,
and thus took the surname Pú,
and his descendants later flourished.
Reeds are grasses,
which should grow in marshes and wetlands,
yet this one sprouted indoors,
which is unusual.
You will surely attain noble status with fiefs in the future.
