The three nodes signify
that three generations will wield military authority.
You should remember this."
Later, Lǐ Quánzhōng served under Lǐ Kějǔ,
as a military officer.
The generals expelled Lǐ Kějǔ and established Lǐ Quánzhōng in his place.
He was repeatedly promoted to Acting Grand Commandant,
and was very authoritative in military affairs.
After Lǐ Quánzhōng's death,
his son Lǐ Kuāngwēi
was expelled by the army.
His younger brother Lǐ Kuāngchóu
led the family to the capital,
but upon reaching Jǐngchéng in Cāngzhōu,
was killed by Lú Yànshèng.
Earlier, Lǐ Kuāngwēi, in his youth, was fond of bravery,
unrestrained by minor proprieties,
and devoted himself to drinking and gambling.
One day, while fishing with some companions by the Chìlán Bridge over the Sānggān River,
he poured a libation of wine and said:
"If I am destined to govern Yōuzhōu,
then may I catch a large fish."
Indeed, he caught a fish three feet long,
which people found very strange.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Hóu Hóngshí
was originally from Púbǎn.
His family was poor in his childhood,
and he grew up as an outsider among military families,
around thirteen or fourteen years old.
He often slept under the eaves.
Once, as heavy rain was about to fall,
a rainbow descended from the river to drink water,
and suddenly passed into Hóu Hóngshí's mouth.
His mother saw this,
but dared not startle him.
After a long while,
the rainbow vanished from the sky into Hóu Hóngshí's mouth,
and did not reappear.
When he awoke,
his mother asked if he had dreamed anything.
He replied:
"I just dreamed of entering a river to drink water,
and returned fully satisfied."
His mother silently rejoiced upon hearing this,
knowing he would surely achieve greatness.
Several months later,
a Shǔ monk suddenly came to their door seeking alms.
Before leaving,
he said to Hóu's mother:
"You, disciple, will have future blessings,
and will rely on your son's strength."
Hóu's mother called Hóu Hóngshí out,
and asked the monk to read his physiognomy.
The monk looked at him and said:
"This is a hornless dragon.
But he must leave his hometown,
and serve near rivers or seas as an official,
then he will attain glory."
He added:
"This child has a cruel and vicious nature,
and will surely bring calamity upon living beings.
If he reverently believes in the Three Jewels,
he may have a peaceful end."
Having said this, he departed.
Hóu Hóngshí later indeed rose from the ranks,
to become a general.
In the third year of Tóngguāng,
he followed Prince Xìngshèng to conquer Shǔ.
After Shǔ was pacified,
not long after,
he rebelled with Kāng Yánxiào, the military governor of Shǎnfǔ, and others.
After Kāng Yánxiào was executed,
Hóu Hóngshí was pardoned,
and soon became Prefect of Méizhōu,
and military governor of Kuízhōu.
Later, from Níngjiāng,
he moved to Qiánfǔ,
governing one prefecture and two military districts,
all near great rivers,
and his official career was lofty.
He reverently served the Three Jewels,
with unwavering faith.
However, in military command and governance,
enforcing laws and controlling subordinates,
he was excessively harsh and cruel,
proving the Shǔ monk's words were not mistaken.
From "Jiànjiè Lù"
Dài Sīyuǎn
Dài Sīyuǎn, a general of the Liáng dynasty,
while stationed in Fúyáng,
had a subordinate named Máo Zhāng,
who was reckless and fierce by nature.
Once, while pursuing bandits with several dozen soldiers,
they lodged at an inn on their return,
and Máo Zhāng slept with his sword as a pillow.
At midnight,
his sword suddenly roared loudly,
and leaped out of its scabbard.
The soldiers who heard it
were astonished and amazed.
Máo Zhāng also found it miraculous,
and holding the sword, he chanted:
"If I am to possess these lands and rivers someday,
you shall roar and leap again;
otherwise, cease."
As Máo Zhāng slept again, not yet deeply,
the sword roared and leaped as before,
and he became deeply confident in his destiny.
Later, when Dài left the garrison,
Máo Zhāng requested to stay,
and Dài agreed.
Not long after,
Máo Zhāng surrendered the prefecture to Táng Zhuāngzōng,
who appointed him Prefect of Qízhōu.
He later even commanded Cānghǎi.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Zhāng Jiān
In his youth, Zhāng Jiān, Governor of Mìzhōu,
once had a flying bird,
resembling a wren,
carrying a bronze coin in its beak,
drop it into his sleeve.
Zhāng found this strange,
and often tied the coin to his clothing.
Thereafter, he amassed immense wealth,
and his resources never declined until his death.
The bird dropping the coin
was an omen of impending wealth.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
A commoner of Qízhōu
In Qízhōu, there was a wealthy old man,
whom the locals called Liú Shíláng,
who made his living selling vinegar and oil.
He himself said:
"In my prime,
I was extremely poor and lowly,
working with my wife as hired rice-pounders to support ourselves.
Suddenly one night,
before we finished pounding,
our pestle suddenly made a sound,
and when we looked at it,
it had broken in the middle.
Husband and wife looked at each other, worried and sighing,
and only after a long time did they fall asleep.
At dawn, when they awoke,
a new pestle was beside the mortar,
and they did not know where it had come from.
The couple approached to look,
both startled and delighted.
From then on, while digging the ground,
they obtained quite a few hidden treasures.
Believing the pestle was a gift from gods or ghosts,
(The original text had "wound" instead of "gift,"
amended according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
they treasured and stored it away.
They then abandoned the rice-pounding trade,
gradually learning to do business.
Within a few years,
their profits multiplied a hundredfold,
and their household accumulated a thousand gold pieces.
The couple deified the pestle,
covering it with embroidered silk,
placing it in a box,
and offering sacrifices to it throughout the four seasons."
Afterward, the couple grew wealthy and old,
and upon their death,
the family's fortunes gradually declined,
and now their children and grandchildren are impoverished.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Zhū Qìngyuán
Zhū Qìngyuán, the deputy of Wùyuán,
had just left his post and was awaiting reassignment,
his home being in Fēngchéng, Yùzhāng.
The courtyard ground was very dry and elevated,
when suddenly a lotus plant sprouted.
His family was terrified,
and tried various methods to exorcise it.
The lotus kept growing,
so they built a dike and drew water to encircle it,
which eventually formed a large pond,
with water caltrops and lotuses growing luxuriantly.
That year,
Qìngyuán was appointed magistrate of Nánfēng.
Three years later,
he entered the capital as a Dàlǐ Píngshì.
From "Jīshén Lù"
The Dwarves of Chíyáng
In the third year of Wáng Mǎng's Jiànguó era,
there were dwarves in Chíyáng,
about a foot tall,
some riding horses,
some walking,
handling various objects,
and the dwarves all referred to each other.
This lasted for three days before ceasing.
Wáng Mǎng found it very ominous.
Afterward, warfare and banditry grew daily,
and he was eventually killed.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì"
The Bèimíng Bird
In the first year of the Huánglóng era,
Wú first established its capital at Wǔchāng.
At that time, from south of Yuèxī, a Bèimíng bird was presented as tribute,
shaped like a crane,
it would not face the light when perching,
its nest always facing north,
with much flesh and little feathers,
its voice capable of a hundred changes,
and when it heard the sounds of bells, chimes, sheng, or yu, it would flap its wings and shake its head.
People of the time considered it an auspicious omen.
That year, the capital was moved to Jiànyè,
and distant lands presented many rare treasures.
The Wú people, through a slip of the tongue,
called it the Bèiwáng bird.
Within the state, it was considered a great portent of disaster,
predicting that within a hundred years,
there would be events of mourning, chaos, betrayal, and exile,
with people scattering and fleeing,
leaving ruins without smoke from hearths.
It indeed turned out as predicted.
Later, this bird was nowhere to be found.
From "Wáng Zǐnián Shíyí Jì"
Wáng Wǎn
In the seventh year of the Tàikāng era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
there was a white dog below the suburban altar,
three feet tall,
bright and shiny in color,
constantly lying beside the altar.
When it noticed someone approaching, it would leave.
The cavalry commander Wáng Wǎn,
chased it on a fine horse.
The dog walked slowly,
yet the horse could not catch up,
and when shot at, it escaped again,
with Wǎn leaving and it returning.
The suburban altar was not a place for dogs to guard,
and afterward, great chaos ensued.
Also, during Emperor Wǔ's time,
in Yōuzhōu, there was a dog
that walked on its nose for over three hundred paces.
The emperor did not heed Hé Qiào's advice and installed Emperor Huì,
leading to decline and chaos.
From "Guō Sòng's Shìyǔ,"
(the Ming manuscript copy has "Bān" instead of "Sòng")
Zhāng Pìn
During the Tài'ān era of Emperor Huì of Jìn,
the ox ridden by Zhāng Pìn of Jiāngxià said:
"The world is in chaos,
ride me."
Pìn, frightened, returned.
The dog also said:
"Why return so early?"
Soon, the ox stood up and walked like a human.
Pìn □□□□ said:
"The world is about to fall into chaos,
and it won't be limited to just one family."
That year, Zhāng Chāng rebelled,
first
(the Ming manuscript copy has "about to" instead of "first")
raiding Jiāngxià,
and the masses pushed him as
(the five characters "the masses of Jiāngxià pushed as" were originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng manuscript copy.)
commander.
Thus, five provinces were devastated by chaos,
and Pìn's clan was exterminated.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì"
Zhāng Lín
During the Yǒngjiā era of Emperor Huái of Jìn,
Zhāng Lín of Jiāxīng had a dog named Ā Yǒng.
At that time, famine plagued the land,
and the dog could barely walk.
Lín said:
"Ā Yǒng, you said you'd get meat
(the Ming manuscript copy has "before" instead of "said,"
and "food" instead of "meat")
That's why you were strong,
but now you're starving and can't walk anymore, huh?
Suddenly, the dog spoke:
"I say the people of the world are starving to death!"
The dog kept talking,
terrifying those who heard it into fleeing.
At that time, the land was plagued by famine and chaos,
and the emperor perished among the Hú people.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì"
The Duke of Dōngyíng
Sīmā Téng, the Duke of Dōngyíng of Jìn,
courtesy name Yuánmài,
was stationed in Yè in the first year of Yǒngjiā.
There was heavy snow at the time,
but in front of his gate, for over ten paces,
the ground alone was slushy without accumulation.
Téng, finding it strange, dug there,
and found a jade horse,
about a foot tall,
with all its teeth missing.
Téng thought that since "horse" was the state's surname,
it was an auspicious sign.
Some said a horse without teeth cannot eat.
Not long after,
great chaos befell Jìn.
From "Yì Yuàn"
The Man of Chángguǎng
At the end of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
a man from Chángguǎng recovered from an illness,
and could eat but could not lie down,
growing taller with each meal.
After several days like this,
his head protruded through the roof.
Duàn Jiū was the regional inspector,
and measured him at three zhàng tall,
then he gradually shrank back to his original size,
and died after a day.
Soon after, Emperor Wén was killed by Yuánxiōng.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì"
Huángqiū Village
On the first day of the ninth month in the second year of the Cháng'ān era of the Tang dynasty,
a total solar eclipse occurred.
The bandit Mòchuò arrived at Bìngzhōu.
By the fifteenth day,
a total lunar eclipse occurred at night,
and the bandits all retreated completely.
A common proverb says:
"Jujubes plug the nostrils,
hanging towers and pavilions are planted instead."
Another says:
"When cicadas and katydids call,
millet seeds and cake porridge are cut off."
Another proverb says:
"Spring rain on a Jiǎzǐ day,
barren land for a thousand miles;
summer rain on a Jiǎzǐ day,
enter the market by boat;
autumn rain on a Jiǎzǐ day,
ears grow on grain heads."
When magpie nests are built close to the ground,
that year brings great floods.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi".
Zhāng Yìzhī
In the tenth month of the fourth year of the Cháng'ān era of the Tang dynasty,
there was overcast rain and snow
for more than a hundred days, with no stars visible.
In the first month, the rebel bandits Zhāng Yìzhī, Zhāng Chāngzōng, and others were executed,
and Wǔ Zétiān was deposed.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi".
Sūn Jiǎn
When the Tang dynasty's Yōuzhōu military governor Sūn Jiǎn was about to enter bandit territory,
Xuē Nè sent him a letter saying:
"It is inauspicious to enter bandit territory in the last month of a season;
it is greatly ominous."
Jiǎn said:
"King Xuān of Zhou launched a northern expedition in the sixth month;
what does Xuē know?
Anyone who dares to say the army will not return will be beheaded."
On the day the army set out,
a white rainbow hung its head over the army gate.
That night,
a large star fell within the camp.
None of the soldiers or officers dared to speak of it.
After the army departed,
all the crows, magpies, kites, and other birds within the Yōuzhōu region disappeared,
having followed the army.
After twenty days, the army was annihilated,
and the kites ate their flesh.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi".
Venus Appears During the Day
On the seventh day of the first month of the Yánhé era of the Tang dynasty,
according to "Comprehensive Mirror" volume 210:
"In the autumn seventh month of Yánhé, a comet appeared in the west,"
the character "rì" (day) is suspected to be "yuè" (month).
Venus appeared during the day, crossing the sky.
That month,
the Retired Emperor abdicated the throne.
This was an omen of the change of ruler.
By the eighth and ninth months,
Venus again appeared during the day,
and the era name was changed to Xiāntiān.
Until the seventh day of the second month.
According to the "Tang History: Annals of Xuánzōng":
"On the Jiǎzǐ day of the seventh month in the second year of Xiāntiān, Tàipíng Gōngzhǔ, Xiāo Zhìzhōng, Cén Xī, and others were executed,"
"the seventh day of the second month" is suspected to be "the seventh month of the second year."
The Retired Emperor was deposed,
the Secretariat Director Xiāo Zhìzhōng and the Palace Attendant Cén Xī were executed,
Cuī Shí was exiled,
and soon executed.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi".
Large Star
On the night of the twenty-ninth day of the fifth month in the second year of the Kāiyuán era of the Tang dynasty,
a large meteor like a jar,
or as big as a basin,
pierced through the Big Dipper
and fell to the northwest.
Countless smaller ones followed it.
The stars in the sky all shook,
and did not stop until dawn.
"Stop" originally written as "up."
Changed according to the Ming manuscript and the Huáng edition.
In the seventh month,
Prince Xiāng died,
posthumously titled Emperor Shāng.
In the tenth month,
the Tibetans entered Lǒngyòu,
plundered sheep and horses,
and killed and wounded countless people.
That year in the sixth month,
a great wind uprooted trees and tore off roofs.
Of the trees on the streets of Cháng'ān,
seventeen or eighteen out of ten were uprooted.
The pagoda trees planted
by the Sui dynasty's Director of the Palace Buildings, Gāo Jiǒng,
when Cháng'ān city was first built, nearly three hundred years earlier,
were uprooted at this time.
Bamboo in the Zhōngnán Mountains
blossomed and bore seeds,
stretching across the mountain valleys,
the size of wheat grains.
That year there was a great famine,
and all that bamboo withered and died.
It was the same in Lǐngnán.
People gathered and ate them.
In Lǐquán, flour rained down
like grains of rice,
which people could eat.
Later, Hàn dynasty Xiāng Kǎi said:
"If bamboo and cypress wither within a state,
within three years,
the ruler will suffer for it.
If bamboo in a household bears fruit and withers,
the head of the household will suffer for it."
The bamboo in Zhōngnán blossomed and withered,
and in the fourth year of Kāiyuán, the Retired Emperor died.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi".
Fire Disaster
In the fifth year of Kāiyuán,
Hóngzhōu and Tánzhōu
again suffered fire disasters.
During the day,
people saw a fiery essence, glowing red,
and wherever it went, a fire would start.
During the Eastern Jìn dynasty,
when Wáng Hóng was the governor of Wújùn,
there was also such a disaster.
Hóng caned his subordinates,
thinking they had been careless.
Later, while sitting in his office hall,
he saw a red object like a signal banner
fly toward a family's house,
and shortly after, a fire started.
Only then did he realize the calamity was not caused by people,
and those whose homes were burned
were subsequently exempted from flogging.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi".
Flood Disaster
In the eighth year of the Kāiyuán era of the Tang dynasty,
the Qìdān rebelled.
Troops from Guānzhōng went to rescue the camp headquarters.
When they reached Quēmén at Miǎnchí,
they camped beside the Gǔshuǐ river.
At midnight, the water rose,
sweeping away more than twenty thousand people.
Only Xíng Gāng, who was gambling all night without sleep,
climbed to high ground and survived.
Village shops were all submerged.
Water overflowed in the Shàngyáng Palace,
and seventeen or eighteen out of ten palace women died.
That year,
the Xīngdào ward in the capital sank into a pool overnight,
submerging five hundred households.
Initially, at the Sānyākǒu in Dèngzhōu, two children were seen splashing water at each other;
shortly after,
a large snake more than ten arm-spans thick appeared,
opening its mouth toward the sky.
Some people tried to hack or shoot it,
but soon clouds and rain darkened the sky,
and floodwaters swept away two hundred households.
The children and the snake
were nowhere to be found.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi".
Monk Yīxíng
In the fifteenth year of the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the Chán master Yīxíng, on the verge of passing into Nirvana,
left a final memorial stating:
"In the future, be careful not to appoint a member of the imperial clan as chancellor,
nor a foreign vassal as general."
Later, Lǐ Línfǔ monopolized power within the court,
while Ān Lùshān stirred up military trouble beyond the borders,
and the Eastern Capital fell to the rebels.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
musicians and common folk in the alleys enjoyed singing the foreign song "Wèizhōu,"
which depicted the Huíhé people as being defeated.
Later, the rebel foreign troops
were indeed crushed by the Huíhé.
The rise and fall of the nation's customs
were subtly reflected in its music.
At that time, children in the two capitals
often took
("took" originally written as "small,"
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy.)
coins and scattered them on the ground,
competing for victory by tossing them into holes,
a game called "tóu hú" (tossing at the foreigners).
Later, officials and commoners indeed threw themselves into the service of the foreign courts.
A children's rhyme in the two capitals went:
"We fear not the Lándān official,
but dread the difficulty of defense.
With no money to seek a case officer,
life and death are left to the Dūguān."
After the recovery
of the capitals, the former officials and courtiers
were imprisoned in the Sānsī prison,
interrogated for their crimes,
their family properties exhausted,
their kin scattered,
with no way to appeal for justice—
this was the omen foretold.
From the "Guǎngdé Shényì Lù."
Wāng Fèng
In the Táng dynasty, a commoner named Wāng Fèng from Wú County, Sūzhōu,
had a residence at Tōngjīn,
where strange occurrences often arose.
Within less than a dozen years,
Fèng's wife, children, and servants
had nearly all died.
Fèng could no longer live there in peace,
so he sold it to a fellow townsman named Shèng Zhōng.
Zhōng had not lived there for five or six years
before his relatives began to perish,
and again, few remained.
Greatly worried and fearful,
he reduced the price and put it up for sale.
The people of Wú all knew the reason,
so for a long time, it could not be sold.
There was a county clerk named Zhāng Lì,
whose family was wealthy,
with a powerful clan,
and who acted as a pestilent bully in the county,
living in the same neighborhood as Zhōng.
Every morning on his way to the yamen,
passing by Zhōng's gate,
he would see from afar two bluish vapors,
thick as arrow shafts,
piercing sharply into the sky.
Lì thought there must be a treasure of jade buried below,
with its essence rising upward.
Without telling anyone,
he watched it daily.
He then went to Zhōng,
offering a hundred strings of cash to complete the transaction.
Soon after moving in,
he looked again at dawn,
and the vapors remained undiminished.
So he prepared shovels and spades in great quantity
to dig at the source of the vapors.
Digging less than six or seven feet down,
he encountered a slab of rock.
Removing the rock,
he found a stone chest,
carved and crafted
with exquisite workmanship,
bound all around with iron chains,
the seams sealed with molten iron,
and further secured with lime.
On each side were seven vermilion seals,
the script resembling twisted seal characters,
twisting and interlinking,
impossible to decipher.
Lì then applied pincers and hammers,
exerting all his strength to pry it open.
Once the stone chest was opened,
there was a bronze cauldron,
capable of holding about ten pecks,
with a bronze plate covering its mouth,
sealed with lead and tin.
Again, there were nine purple seals,
stamped in a circular pattern,
but the seal script differed from the earlier style,
resembling ancient seal script entirely.
No one could interpret it.
Lì removed the bronze plate,
to find the mouth of the cauldron covered with three layers of crimson silk.
As soon as Lì lifted it,
a large monkey suddenly leaped out.
Everyone was startled and terrified,
none daring to approach.
After a long while,
it bounded away and no one knew where it went.
Lì then looked inside the cauldron,
where there was a stone inscription stating:
"In the first year of the Zhēnmíng era,
on the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
the Mǎoshān Dàoshi Bào Zhīyuǎn
imprisoned the monkey spirit here.
Should anyone unearth it,
twelve years after the unearthing,
foreign troops will cause great turmoil,
smoke and dust will fill the six directions,
and the unearther will soon be exterminated along with his clan."
Zhēnmíng was the era name of Chén Hòuzhǔ Shūbǎo.
Lì unearthed it in the tenth month of the second year of Tiānbǎo,
and by the winter of the fourteenth year,
Lùshān raised his army.
Exactly a year later,
Lì's family was exterminated.
From the "Jíyì Jì."
Monk Pǔmǎn
During the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
in Zélù, there was a monk
named Pǔmǎn,
who acted as he pleased,
unconstrained by monastic decorum,
sometimes singing, sometimes laughing,
with no one understanding his intent.
As his predictions often came true,
people of the time regarded him as Wànhuí.
At the beginning of the Jiànzhōng era,
he wrote several poems on the walls of a Buddhist temple in Lùzhōu and then passed away.
One that was recorded reads:
"This water connects to Jīngshuǐ.
Twin pearls, blood fills the river.
The green ox leads the red tiger,
then peace returns to the year."
After the poem was written,
no one could understand it.
Only when the rebel Cǐ raised arms
did the masses begin to comprehend.
"This water" refers to the character Cǐ (泚),
and "Jīngshuǐ"
refers to the military rebellion starting from Jīngzhōu.
"Twin pearls"
refers to Cǐ and Tāo.
"Green ox"
refers to the yǐchǒu year of the second year of Xīngyuán,
where yǐ corresponds to wood,
and chǒu to ox.
The following year, the era name changed to Zhēnyuán,
which was the bǐngyín year.
Bǐng corresponds to fire,
and yín to tiger.
By then, the rebels had been pacified,
hence "the green ox leads the red tiger,
then peace returns to the year."
From the "Guǎngdé Shényì Lù."
The Banana Plant of Qínchéng
The land of Tiānshuǐ,
being near the frontier,
has cold soil
and does not produce plantains.
A Róng commander sent someone to Xìngyuán to seek them,
and planted two specimens in a pavilion garden.
Whenever winter approached,
they would dig them up with the soil attached,
and bury them in an underground cellar.
When warm spring arrived,
they would replant them.
Between the years Gēngwǔ and Xīnwèi,
there was a children's rhyme that said:
"Flowers bloom wrapped up,
flowers wither bundled up."
Moreover, the seasonal weather changed and became less cold,
with winters turning warm and mild.
Summers became intensely hot,
even more so than in the southern regions,
and the plantains then bloomed.
The people of Qín did not recognize them,
and men and women from near and far came to look,
crowding the streets and roads.
Soon after, the people of Shǔ invaded our borders,
and from then on, they came every year,
never missing the time when the plantains bloomed and withered.
In the year Yǐhài,
reinforcements from Qí and Lǒng did not arrive,
and from west of Lǒng,
the land was eventually taken by the people of Shǔ.
The climate of heat and humidity
became exactly like that of Bā and Qióng.
It seems the seasonal weather beyond the Jiàn Pass
first manifested in the city of Qín.
The words of the children's rhyme
cannot be ignored.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
The Monk of Ruìlíng
Beside Ruìlíng,
there lived a poor monk.
He wore grass clothing and straw sandals,
and did not interact with people.
He would burn wood to collect and store the ashes,
and there were also those who gave him money,
which he would hide in the ashes as soon as he received it,
never using it.
Whenever he went out or came in, he would pull a drag-cart,
saying to people:
"This is a carriage drawn by four horses,
do you know?
One day,
there will surely be imperial dragon and phoenix carriages
gathering in this place."
The local people could not fathom the reason.
When Emperor Hàn Gāozǔ,
built his tomb mound here,
for the pottery of the mausoleum,
ash was needed.
The monk had stored a great amount of ash,
and until the work was completed,
the supply was never lacking.
Moreover, from the accumulated ashes, a considerable amount of money was obtained.
The prophecy of the carriages
was not off by the slightest.
After the tomb mound was completed,
the monk also passed away.
The officials in charge of ceremonies at Ruìlíng
all knew of this.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Xìngshèng Temple
The old city of Shǔ once had Xìngshèng Temple,
which was abandoned and turned into a military camp,
its courtyards and buildings buried and ruined,
for several decades.
Those born in the army
for generations wore armor,
completely unaware that this was the foundation of a temple.
In the year Jiǎshēn,
for the birthday of the young ruler of Shǔ,
his subordinates planned to pool their salaries to hold a vegetarian feast.
Suddenly an order was issued,
directing the funds for the feast
to urgently repair Xìngshèng Temple.
The officials in charge of the work,
rushed as if by fire,
completed the temple in no time.
Before the red paint had even dried,
the Xìngshèng army entered Shǔ.
Alas,
the rise and fall of a state,
is predetermined by fate,
how can it be artificially prolonged?
From "Wángshì Jiànwén Lù"
Camel Staff
In the land of Shǔ, there were no camels,
and people did not recognize them.
When Shǔ was about to fall,
the nobles, high officials, and those favored with power who entered and left the palace
all vied to hold camel staffs as a ritual,
and from then on, both inside and outside, everyone imitated them.
The staff was about three feet long,
with one end curved.
It was covered with birch bark.
Those who understood saw it as an ill omen.
The following year,
the northern army arrived,
camels crowded the Jiànzhàn road as they came,
carrying and transporting treasures,
filling the cities and towns,
and only then was the omen verified.
From "Wángshì Jiànwén Lù"
Confucius
Confucius said to Zǐxià:
"In the month the unicorn is obtained,
there will be a blood-written text at the Lu end gate in the sky."
After Confucius passed away,
the Zhōu dynasty fell.
Zǐxià went to look,
and met a young man who said:
"At the gate there is blood,
which flew and became a red bird,
transforming into a written text."
From "Shuōtící"
Xiāo Shìyì
Xiāo Shìyì, a Huángmén Láng of the Later Hàn,
was executed in the second year of the Yǒngyuán era of Emperor Hé.
Several days before,
a dog that was usually kept in his household
came before his wife and spoke:
"You have extremely little fortune,
your family will soon be ruined,
what will you do about it?"
His wife remained silent,
and was not frightened either.
The dog left after a short while.
When Shìyì returned inside,
his wife recounted what the dog had said.
Before she finished,
the arresters arrived.
From "Xù Yì Jì"
Wáng Dǎo
The Jìn chancellor Wáng Dǎo dreamed that someone wanted to buy Chángyù for a million coins.
Dǎo was very disturbed by this,
and secretly made thorough preparations for prayers.
Later, when building a house,
they suddenly dug up a cellar of coins,
estimated to be ten billion.
He was greatly displeased,
and had them all hidden and sealed away.
Soon after, Chángyù died.
Chángyù's name was Yuè,
the second son of Dǎo.
From "Shìshuō Xīnshū"
Xiè Ān
During the Eastern Jìn, Xiè Ān was receiving guests at the rear residence.
His wife, Lady Liú,
saw a dog carrying Ān's head coming.
After a long time,
it disappeared.
That same month, Ān passed away.
From "Yì Yuàn"
Yǔ Liàng
When Yǔ Liàng of Jìn first garrisoned Wǔchāng,
departing from Shítóu,
the common people watching
sang from the shore:
"Lord Yǔ goes up to Wǔchāng,
fluttering like a flying bird;
Lord Yǔ returns to Yángzhōu,
a white horse pulls the flowing funeral banner."
They also sang:
"When Lord Yǔ first went up,
fluttering like a flying crow;
Lord Yǔ returns to Yángzhōu,
a white horse pulls the funeral carriage."
Later, he was repeatedly summoned but did not enter court,
and soon passed away,
returning to the capital for burial.
From "Shìshuō Xīnshū"
Wáng Zhòngwén
The Grand Commandant of the Song, Shěn Qìngzhī, requested to retire from office,
but the emperor did not permit it.
Qìngzhī said:
"Zhāng Liáng was a renowned worthy,
yet even Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn allowed him to retire.
What use am I,
that I should be needed by this sagely court?"
Then he kowtowed and wept.
The emperor issued an edict,
appointing him to the office of Kāifǔ,
and he went to the Court of Judicial Review to await punishment.
Qìngzhī could not recognize written characters,
nor did his hand know how to write,
yet his intelligence and understanding surpassed others.
Once, in the emperor's presence, he composed a poem,
ordering the Vice Director of the Left, Yán Shībó, to hold the brush,
while Qìngzhī dictated:
"This humble life has encountered much fortune.
I have met with a time of prosperous fate.
Now aged and frail, my sinews and bones are spent,
I walk on foot back to the southern ridge.
I resign from glory in this sage generation,
how could I be ashamed before Zhāng Zǐfáng?"
All marveled at the beauty of its phrasing and meaning.
Once, on New Year's Day, Qìngzhī dreamed that someone presented him with two bolts of silk,
saying:
"This silk is just enough!"
Upon waking, he sighed and said:
"Two bolts are eighty feet,
just enough with no surplus.
This old man will not escape death this year."
That year,
he was indeed executed by Yuán
According to the History of the Song:
"The deposed emperor's reign title was Yuánjǐnghé,
" so "Yuán" is likely an error for "Jǐng."
Hé.
From Tán Sǒu.
Liú Déyuàn
During the Tàishǐ era of the Song,
Liú Déyuàn, Inspector of Yùzhōu and a native of Péngchéng, was stationed in Shòuyáng.
While staying in an inner room,
with the door not fully closed,
suddenly a human head entered through the door,
peeping inside.
It was a man,
with hair exposed and a round face.
The people inside were alarmed and reported it,
they took torches and searched,
but found no one at all.
The following year, Liú was executed.
From Yì Yuàn.
Lǐ Zhèn
More than ten li south of Lúshān,
there is Jīshān (Rooster Mountain).
On the mountain, there is a stone rooster,
its comb and spurs as if alive.
The Daoist priest Lǐ Zhèn lived below here,
and often treasured and admired it.
One day, the rooster suddenly crumbled and was destroyed.
Zhèn told others:
"The rooster has suddenly become like this,
my end must be near!"
Thereupon, he bid farewell to his acquaintances and old friends.
A little over a month later, he indeed passed away.
From Yōu Míng Lù.
Liǔ Yuánjǐng
Liǔ Yuánjǐng of Hédōng, Grand General of Cavalry of the Song,
in the eighth year of Dàmíng,
when the young emperor ascended the throne,
Yuánjǐng was returning by carriage.
He had someone wash the carriage in the central courtyard,
and removed the shafts to dry them.
A whirlwind entered through the middle gate,
and came straight to charge at the carriage.
The following year, his entire household was executed.
From Shén Guǐ Zhuàn.
Xiàng Xuánjì
Xiàng Xuánjì of Hénán in the Song served as Governor of Nánjùn.
His wife was boiling silk,
when suddenly it rotted like porridge,
its liquid red like blood.
At night, someone knocked at the gate and called out:
"The Governor may now depart!"
Soon after, the Inspector, the Prince of Nánjùn, Liú Yìxuān, rebelled.
Xuánjì, being weak in strength,
could not secure himself,
and so attached himself to the rebels.
Both father and son were executed according to the law.
From Zhǔ Gōng Gùshì.
Téng Jǐngzhí
Téng Jǐngzhí of the Song had his home in Guǎngzhōu.
During the Yuánhuī era,
he ordered a maidservant to cook,
when a sound like thunder came from the cauldron.
The maid, alarmed, reported it.
Jǐngzhí and his family rushed to look,
and the sound from the cauldron grew even louder.
Dozens of blossoms appeared on the cauldron,
gradually growing like lotus flowers, but larger,
and red in color.
In a moment, they withered and vanished.
Ten days later,
Jǐngzhí fell ill and died.
From Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì.
Wáng Yàn
Wáng Yàn of the Qí, styled Xiūmò,
held a position of extreme power and prestige,
yet he became arrogant, full of himself, and resentful,
and was executed.
Just before disaster befell him,
he saw that all the rafters of his house were large snakes.
When he went to look closely, they vanished.
Yàn was disgusted by this,
so he ordered the rafters to be wrapped in paper.
Yet within the paper, they still moved and shook,
rustling with sound.
From Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì.
Liú Chǒng
Liú Chǒng of Dōngyáng, styled Dàohóng,
resided in Húshú.
Every night,
several sheng of blood would appear in his courtyard,
with no known source,
and this happened three or four times.
Later, Chǒng became General of the Breaking Charge,
and received orders to campaign north.
As he was about to depart, the cooked rice all turned into insects.
His family steamed wheat flour,
and it also turned into insects.
The fiercer the fire,
the stronger the insects grew.
Chǒng then marched north,
but his army was defeated at Tánqiū,
and he was killed by Xú Lóng.
From Fǎ Yuàn Zhū Lín.
Ěrzhū Shìlóng
Ěrzhū Shìlóng, Vice Director of the Later Wèi,
was napping during the day.
His wife, Xī shì,
suddenly saw a person
carrying Shìlóng's head out.
Xī shì hurriedly went to look,
but Shìlóng was sleeping as before.
When Shìlóng awoke,
he said to his wife:
"Just now I dreamed that someone
cut off my head and took it away."
A few days later, he was executed.
From Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì.
Liú Mǐn
During the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng of the Liáng.
Liú Mǐn of Zhījiāng retrieved a piece of Yùzhāng wood from the river,
several dozen arm-spans in circumference.
Mǐn sought to donate it to a temple.
Lù Fǎhé said:
"This wood is just right for your own family's use."
Mǐn did not understand the meaning of these words.
More than ten days later,
Mǐn's wife died,
and they immediately cut and used this wood to make a coffin.
Fǎhé said:
"It is still not finished."
Another month later,
Mǐn's younger brother died,
and using this wood was just enough.
From Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì.
Lǐ Guǎng
During the Tiānbǎo era of Emperor Wénxuān of the Northern Qí,
the Censor Lǐ Guǎng was diligent in study and knowledgeable about many things,
and was appointed Attendant Censor.
One night he dreamed of a person
emerging from within his own body,
who said to Guǎng:
"You exert your mind too bitterly,
it is more than your spirit can bear."
"Now I take my leave of you,"
and then he became dazed and confused.
A few days later, he fell ill,
and after a prolonged illness, he passed away.
From Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì.
Wáng shì
In the early years of the Wǔpíng era of the Later Lord of the Northern Qí,
the Wáng family of Píngyì formed a marriage alliance with the Lǐ family of the same town.
Carrying sheep and wine,
they intended to go to the in-laws' home for a feast.
After traveling no more than three lǐ,
the sun set and it gradually grew dark.
They saw fifty paces to the southeast,
a red object as large as a shēng,
like a shooting star trailing light,
came straight and attached itself to the cart wheel.
The ox immediately stopped moving,
and all who saw it were terrified.
His wife then got down from the cart,
bowed twice toward it,
and spread her skirt to draw it in.
It then entered beneath her skirt,
and she boarded the cart and returned home.
Upon inspection, it turned out to be genuine gold,
so they stored it in a chest.
Every auspicious morning,
they would always burn incense and pray for grace.
Later, rare goods from all directions
gathered at their home,
and their fields and silkworms yielded a hundredfold each year.
In the spring,
a mulberry tree grew in their courtyard,
its branches and leaves different from ordinary trees.
Within a few years,
it filled the entire courtyard.
Rare birds and exotic fowl
all came to roost and gather there.
Their family became immensely wealthy,
for nearly thirty years.
Wáng's wife eventually died of old age and illness.
Later, at dawn, a white bird resembling an egret
flew to the side of the mulberry tree,
vomited blood for a long time,
then fell to the ground and died.
In the afternoon,
a great whirlwind from the northwest,
rising to the heavens, came
and swirled around this tree,
lifting its branches upward,
taking the shape of a broom.
Within ten days,
the slaves and maidservants fled,
one after another,
and the family's wealth was nearly exhausted.
When they opened the chest to take out the gold,
they only saw fireflies, centipedes, and the remnants of rotten grass.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì."
Zhāng Diāohǔ
At the end of the Northern Qí,
the supervising clerk awaiting appointment, Zhāng Diāohǔ,
one day before his death,
was riding a horse on the road.
Someone looked at him
and could not see his head.
Soon after, he was killed.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì."
Qiáng Liàn
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of the Later Zhōu,
there was a man named Qiáng Liàn,
from Qíshān,
who feigned madness,
and was called Qiáng Liàn.
Before the downfall of the Chief Minister, Duke Jìn of the State, Yǔwén Hù,
Qiáng Liàn took a gourd,
went to his gate,
smashed it,
and said:
"The gourd is broken,
I pity your sons' suffering."
Hù was killed,
and all of Hù's sons died in agony.
At that time, the brothers Gāo Gōng Hóu Lóngsī were favored and treated well by the Chief Minister,
and their influence was overwhelming at the time.
Qiáng Liàn passed by their gate,
and Lóngsī's wife and other women sent a maidservant to call him in,
prepared food and drink for him,
and observed his words.
Liàn said to Lóngsī and the others:
"Become my maidservants."
All the women laughed heartily.
Liàn also said:
"Even as maidservants, you will not escape.
Others will take you away,
how can you surpass me?"
Not long after, the Chief Minister was executed,
and Lóngsī and his brothers were also killed together.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì."
Lǐ Mì
During the Suí dynasty, after Lǐ Mì had gathered his forces,
encamped at Luòkǒu,
and set up an altar,
displaying many banners and flags,
he announced to heaven and assumed the position of Duke.
That night,
foxes cried beside the altar.
The next day,
as he was about to conduct the ceremony,
a great wind arose from all directions,
lifting sand and uprooting trees,
and some of the flagpoles broke.
Later, he indeed met with defeat.
From "Gǎn Dìng Lù."
Zhāng Zhuó
During the Yǒnghuī era of the Táng dynasty,
Zhāng Zhuó was building a stable for horse troughs,
and dug a pit over a zhàng deep directly north of his residence.
At that time, a book of geomancy stated:
"If a hole is dug in the zǐ direction,
someone will inevitably fall into a well and die."
Zhāng had a slave named Yǒngjìn,
who was cleaning a well when the earth collapsed,
and he was crushed to death.
Also, at Zhāng's former residence,
there was a mulberry tree,
forty or fifty feet tall,
that withered and died for no reason.
Soon after, his grandfather passed away.
After his death,
someone knowledgeable in geomancy said:
"If a tall tree withers first,
all the sons will surely be orphaned."
This was its verification.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi."
Táng Wàngzhī
In the fourth year of the Xiánhēng era of the Táng dynasty,
the Registrar of Luòzhōu, Táng Wàngzhī,
was selected in the winter for the fifth-rank examination,
and his appointment had not yet been issued.
He heard that a monk had come looking for him.
At first, they did not know each other,
but he invited him in to sit together.
After a short while, the monk said:
"I am a poor monk, an ascetic,
and I also eat very little.
Because you are a famous man,
I secretly entrust myself to you.
Could you prepare a meal of sliced fish?"
The Registrar happily agreed,
and immediately arranged to buy fish.
This monk asked:
"See if there is any garlic?"
The Registrar's family said:
"The garlic is all gone."
This monk said:
"Since the garlic is gone,
I must leave."
And he stood up.
The Registrar tried to keep him,
saying:
"If the garlic is gone,
I can send someone to buy some right away."
The monk said:
"If the garlic is gone, I cannot stay any longer.
I cannot be kept."
The Registrar was not ill,
but that night, he suddenly died.
Garlic (suàn) signifies calculation (suàn),
and when the years are exhausted,
that is why the extraordinary monk informed him.
Xú Qìng
During the reign of Emperor Gāozōng of the Táng dynasty,
Xú Qìng served as an assistant commander on the campaign against Liáodōng.
There was a clerk,
whose name is unknown.
While Xú Qìng was with the army,
he suddenly dreamed that he had transformed into a sheep,
and was slaughtered by the clerk.
Upon waking, he was terrified and sweating profusely.
By dawn,
this clerk came to see Xú Qìng.
Xú Qìng asked if he had dreamed anything the previous night.
The clerk said:
"I dreamed that you, sir, became a sheep,
and I personally butchered you.
I was very unwilling in my heart,
but I was compelled by official duty and had no freedom of choice."
The phrase "was compelled by official duty and had no freedom of choice" appears as "then resolved the confusion of being compelled" in the Ming dynasty manuscript copy.
From then on, Xú Qìng ceased eating mutton.
The phrase "From then on, Xú Qìng ceased eating mutton" appears as "Xú Qìng comforted and retained him, and thereafter did not eat meat" in the Ming dynasty manuscript copy.
By the time of Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
Xú Qìng had been promoted successively to the positions of Vice Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries and Military Commander of Yōngzhōu.
By then, the clerk had already become a prison official in the Court of Judicial Review.
Later, Xú Qìng was falsely accused of conspiring with the Palace Secretary Líng Péi Yán,
in response to
(The Ming manuscript copy has "接" instead of "節")
the rebellion of Duke Yīng, Xú Jìngyè, in Yángzhōu.
He was arrested and sent to the Court of Judicial Review.
Suddenly, he saw this prison official in charge of the jail.
Xú Qìng then wept and said to him:
"The dream from the Liáodōng campaign,
is now about to come true."
On the day he was executed,
it was indeed this official who led him out.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì"
Zhōu Rénguǐ
Zhōu Rénguǐ of the Táng dynasty,
was from Wànnián, Jīngzhào.
He was a maternal relative of Empress Wéi, consort of Emperor Zhōngzōng (Xiàohé),
and was promoted successively to the position of General of the Imperial Guards,
and appointed as the Chief Administrator of Bīngzhōu.
He was cruel and fond of killing.
While in the province,
he suddenly saw a human arm under the hall steps,
as if freshly severed,
with blood dripping profusely.
Zhōu Rénguǐ ordered people to take it away to a place over twenty lǐ outside the provincial city.
After several days, he ordered someone to check,
and the arm was still there.
It was the height of summer heat,
yet the flesh showed no change in color.
Everyone found it strange.
That same month,
Emperor Zhōngzōng (Xiàohé) passed away,
and Zhōu Rénguǐ, as a member of the Wéi faction, was executed.
When the guards drew their swords to strike him,
Zhōu Rénguǐ raised his arm,
and where the blade struck,
his arm fell to the ground,
no different from the one seen earlier.
They then sent a fast rider to check the place where it had been taken earlier,
but upon arrival, nothing was seen.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì"
Xú Jìngyè
When Xú Jìngyè of the Táng dynasty raised an army,
a large star, vast like a basket,
passed through three constellations and then vanished.
Soon after, Xú Jìngyè was defeated.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Dù Jǐngquán
Dù Jǐngquán, Minister of Justice of the Táng dynasty, was appointed Chief Administrator of Bīngzhōu,
and traveled by post relay to assume his post.
That night,
a large star like a dipper
fell in front of the courtyard,
reaching the ground and then disappearing.
Dù Jǐngquán died at the border of Qí County in Bīngzhōu.
The assembled officials came to offer sacrifices,
and the food they brought was used as sacrificial offerings.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Hēichǐ Chángzhī
General Hēichǐ Chángzhī of the Táng dynasty was stationed at the Héyuán Army garrison.
The city walls were extremely formidable.
Three wolves entered the camp,
circling the official quarters,
and no one knew from where they came.
The soldiers shot and killed them.
Hēichǐ found this ominous,
and had them removed outside.
He petitioned to campaign against the Dǎngxiàng tribes of Sānqǔ,
and received an imperial edict granting permission.
He then appointed General Lǐ Jǐnxíng to replace him.
When Lǐ Jǐnxíng arrived at the army garrison,
he fell ill and died within ten days.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Gù Cóng
Gù Cóng, Vice Minister of Personnel of the Táng dynasty, had newly attained the third rank.
His son-in-law came to visit.
At the time, the main gate had just been completed.
Gù Cóng rode his horse to the gate,
but it snorted and stamped the ground, refusing to go forward.
He whipped it,
and it jumped and leaped inside,
and the horses of his attendants did the same.
After a while,
the gate collapsed without reason.
Gù Cóng was displeased,
and subsequently fell ill.
Officials, including directors and vice directors, came to inquire about his illness.
Gù Cóng said:
"I was not fit to enter the third rank,
but you gentlemen helped me achieve this.
I know I will not recover."
He died within ten days.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Lù Jìngchún
During the Rúyì era of Empress Wǔ Zétiān of the Táng dynasty,
the estate of Lù Jìngchún, a Court Historian, was in Jìyuán.
There was a water-powered mill,
and the mill's pillar stood five or six feet above the water.
One pillar was about to break,
and had been replaced.
The family took the old one for firewood.
Inside the pillar was a catfish over a foot long,
still alive.
Several years later,
Lù Jìngchún was convicted of a crime and executed.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì"
Zhāng Yìzhī
Zhāng Yìzhī of the Táng dynasty initially built a great hall,
very magnificent,
costing several million.
The walls were plastered with red powder,
the pillars were faced with patterned cypress,
and decorated with glass and eaglewood.
At night, a ghost wrote on the wall:
"How long can this last?"
Zhāng Yìzhī ordered it scraped off,
but the next day it was written again.
This happened six or seven times.
Zhāng Yìzhī then wrote beneath it:
"One month is enough."
After that, it was not written again.
Half a year later,
Zhāng Yìzhī's property was confiscated,
and taken by the government.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Zhèng Shǔbīn
During the Chángshòu era of the Táng dynasty,
there was Zhèng Shǔbīn from Xíngyáng, quite skilled in five-character verse,
yet he never gained fame or success.
In his old age,
he was finally appointed as a minor official in Jiāngzuǒ.
Relatives and friends bid him farewell at the Shàngdōng Gate.
Zhèng Shǔbīn composed a poem for the parting:
"Perilous roads stretch ten thousand miles,
my life nears a hundred years;
not knowing where my white head will go,
into which place of the Yellow Springs."
Drunk with wine, he recited it himself,
his tone mournful and moving,
moving all present to tears.
He ultimately died in office.
From "Dà Táng Xīnyǔ"
Liú Xīyí
In the Tang Dynasty, Liú Xīyí, also known as Tíngzhī,
was a native of Rǔzhōu.
From a young age, he displayed literary talent
and was fond of composing palace-style poetry.
His verses were sorrowful and bitter in theme,
and thus were not highly regarded by his contemporaries.
He was skilled at playing the pipa.
Once, he composed a poem titled "The Old Man with White Hair," which included the lines:
"This year, as the flowers fall, my complexion fades;
next year, when the flowers bloom again, who will still be here?"
Later, he regretted it, saying:
"This poem of mine is an ominous prophecy.
How is it different from Shí Chóng's line 'we shall return together with white heads'?"
So he composed another couplet:
"Year after year, the flowers remain alike;
year after year, the people are no longer the same."
Then he sighed and said:
"This line again seems like an ominous prophecy.
However, life and death are determined by fate;
how could they be caused by this?"
Thus, he kept both versions.
Less than a year after the poem was completed,
he was killed by a treacherous person.
Some say:
"Sòng Zhīwèn was responsible for his death."
Later, Sǔn Yù compiled the "Zhèngshēng Collection,"
and included Liú Xīyí's poems as the finest in the collection.
From then on, his works were highly praised by his contemporaries.
From "Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ."
Cuī Xuánwěi
In the Tang Dynasty, Cuī Xuánwěi was initially enfeoffed as the Prince of Bólíng.
He served as the Chief Administrator of the Yì Prefecture.
Upon receiving his enfeoffment,
he ordered the relevant authorities to construct a carriage. When it was first completed,
a strong wind blew and caused its canopy to collapse and break.
Those who understood omens considered this inauspicious.
Not long after,
his younger brother, Cuī Yùn, served as the magistrate of Yúnyáng County.
He was killed by a subordinate within the Yōngzhōu government office.
Cuī Xuánwěi, along with his relatives three degrees of kinship and above,
was exiled to Lǐngnán.
This was also a foreshadowing of misfortune.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi."
Sòng Shànwēi
In the Tang Dynasty, Sòng Shànwēi, a native of Ráoyáng in Yíngzhōu, once served as a county captain.
One day, while sitting during the daytime,
he suddenly took his boots, robe, and official tablet,
walked out the door to welcome someone,
bowed, and invited the guest inside.
Others could not see anyone,
but only heard voices.
Sòng Shànwēi ordered wine and food, and they drank joyfully with music.
He then composed a poem, which said:
"The moon sets over three trees,
the sun shines upon the ninefold heavens;
after a joyful feast on this fine night,
I bid temporary farewell to the year of Gēngshēn."
Later, Sòng Shànwēi indeed passed away in a Shēn year.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi."
Lǐ Chùjiàn
In the third year of the Kāiyuán era of the Tang Dynasty,
a bear entered the city of Guǎngfǔ during the daytime.
It passed in front of the Governor's gate.
Soldiers chased it for over ten miles
and shot it dead.
A little over a month later,
Governor Lǐ Chùjiàn died.
After that, Chief Administrator Zhū Sīxián was accused of rebellion,
imprisoned for half a year,
and died shortly after his release.
Sīmǎ Sòng Qìngbīn and Chief Administrator Dòu Chóngjiā also died one after another.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi."
Qū Xiānchōng
In the fourth year of the Kāiyuán era of the Tang Dynasty,
a pair of paulownia trees in front of the hall of the Bureau of Evaluation suddenly withered and died.
Ten days later,
Assistant Minister of Evaluation Shào died.
Soon after, Qū Xiānchōng was appointed as a Director
and took over Shào's old cases.
A little over a month later,
the tree on the west side withered and died again.
The officials in the bureau were worried,
and before long, Qū Xiānchōng also died.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi."
Lǚ Chóngcuì
During the Kāiyuán era of the Tang Dynasty,
Remonstrance Official Lǚ Chóngcuì,
a native of Dōngpíng,
was handsome, tall, and well-built,
with some literary talent.
His residence was in the Yǒngchóng Ward of the capital.
At home, he suddenly saw several children's legs,
from below the knees to above the ankles,
dripping with blood,
as if freshly severed.
Ten days later,
Lǚ Chóngcuì fell ill and died.
From "Guǎng Gǔjīn Wǔxíng Jì."
Yuán Qiányào
In the Tang Dynasty, Yuán Qiányào served as Chancellor.
He moved the official desk.
At that time, Yáo Yuánchóng was on leave.
When his leave ended and he returned,
he saw that the desk had been moved
and was furious.
Yuán Qiányào, frightened, bowed in apology.
Emperor Xuánzōng heard of this
and dismissed Yuán Qiányào.
It was taboo for a Chancellor to move the desk,
as moving it signified change.
After Yuán Qiányào was dismissed,
Yáo Yuánchóng was also removed from his post.
This was the consequence.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi."
Wú Mín
In the Tang Dynasty, Wú Mín served as Right Rectifier of Omissions.
He was erudite and possessed literary talent.
He submitted a memorial requesting the compilation of ancient histories
and first presented a catalog to the emperor.
Emperor Xuánzōng praised him
and awarded him one hundred bolts of silk.
He did not drink tea by nature
and wrote a "Preface to Substitutes for Tea."
It roughly stated:
"To relieve stagnation and dissipate blockages,
the temporary benefits of a single day may seem good;
but to weaken the qi and harm the essence,
the lifelong burden is truly great.
When benefits are gained, they are attributed to the power of tea;
when harm is incurred, it is not considered a disaster caused by tea.
Is it not that blessings near at hand are easily recognized,
while calamities far off are difficult to foresee?"
Later, he served in the Jíxiàn Academy.
Not long after, he suddenly died of a feverish illness.
Earlier, he had dreamed of wearing official robes and a hat while ascending Běimáng Mountain,
with relatives and friends seeing him off.
When he reached the mountaintop,
he looked back and saw no one.
He felt deeply troubled by this.
When he died,
his colleagues and friends escorted his funeral to Běimáng Mountain,
exactly as in his initial dream.
Emperor Xuánzōng heard of this and mourned him,
posthumously awarding him the title of Court Gentleman for Comprehensive Duty.
From "Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ."
Yáng Shèngjīn
Yáng Shènjīn of the Táng dynasty was
a descendant of the Suí imperial house.
His father, Chónglǐ,
served as Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury.
When he was buried at Shǎolíngyuán,
within the burial grounds,
the plants and trees all bled.
The caretakers reported this,
and Shènjīn was greatly frightened.
He consulted Shǐ Jìngzhōng.
Jìngzhōng possessed magical arts
and told Shènjīn
that he could perform an exorcism to avert the disaster.
So, a grand ritual was arranged in Shènjīn's rear garden.
After returning from court,
Shènjīn would strip naked, wear shackles,
and sit among thorny bushes.
This went on for several decades,
and the bleeding also stopped.
Jìngzhōng said:
"The disaster can now be averted."
Shènjīn felt indebted to him.
He sent his maidservant Míngzhū,
who was very beautiful,
to pass by the gate of the Eighth Aunt.
She was a younger sister of the Imperial Consort.
The aunt was just then ascending the tower.
Overlooking the main road,
the aunt was acquainted with Jìngzhōng.
She sent someone to ask:
"Why are you following the carriage?"
Jìngzhōng did not reply.
She had someone lift the curtain to look,
and the aunt then firmly detained him.
Inviting Jìngzhōng to sit in the tower,
she then said:
"The beauty in the carriage behind,
I ask that you give her to me."
Thereupon, she drove that carriage inside.
Jìngzhōng did not dare refuse.
The next day, the aunt entered the palace,
attended by the maidservant.
The Emperor saw her and found her remarkable,
asking where she came from.
Míngzhū said:
"I am from Yáng Shènjīn's household,
recently given to Shǐ Jìngzhōng."
The Emperor said:
"Who is Jìngzhōng,
that Shènjīn would casually give him his maidservant?"
Míngzhū then fully explained the matter of the exorcism.
The Emperor was furious,
and informed Línfǔ.
Línfǔ had long been jealous of Shènjīn's talent,
believing he would certainly become chancellor.
He used Jí Wēn to secretly harm him.
Wēn held a grudge against Shènjīn,
so they fabricated the case,
and handed it to Wēn for investigation.
Wēn found and arrested Jìngzhōng in Rǔzhōu,
falsely accusing Shènjīn of claiming to be a descendant of the fallen Suí,
secretly plotting rebellion,
and intending to restore his ancestral enterprise.
Thereupon, he was ordered to commit suicide,
and his entire clan was not spared.
From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Mínghuáng"
Wáng Biāo
Wáng Biāo, Assistant Director of the Household of the Heir Apparent and Messaging Attendant of the Táng dynasty,
was demoted after Emperor Sùzōng's restoration.
He was accused by someone,
and imprisoned in the Censorate.
In the ninth month of the year before his imprisonment,
Biāo was sitting in the hall at night with his favorite concubine
when a meteor as large as a jar,
bright and shining,
fell into the well.
It remained luminous in the well for a long time.
He sent someone to retrieve it,
but nothing was found.
Biāo, frightened, left his residence,
and was eventually exiled to Bōzhōu.
Biāo had not expected this at all.
On the journey, when he reached Fèngzhōu,
he died from a burst carbuncle on his back.
From "Jì Wén"
Cuī Shǔ
Cuī Shǔ of the Táng dynasty sat for the imperial examinations.
He composed a poem on the "Fire Pearl of the Bright Hall" for the supplementary test.
It said:
"Last night, the twin moons were full;
after dawn, a single star remains alone."
It was considered a striking couplet at the time.
The following year, Shǔ died.
He left only one daughter named Xīngxīng (Star).
People then realized it was a prophecy of his own fate.
From "Běnshì Shī"
Yuán Zǎi
When Yuán Zǎi was chancellor of the Táng dynasty,
a scholar visited him one day.
After meeting,
he bowed and said:
"I have heard of your high righteousness and fondness for scholars."
He then presented a poem,
to convey his meaning.
The words were:
"On the southern road, long with no place to lodge;
reed catkins flutter like willow down;
a sea swallow carries mud to build its nest,
but finding the empty house unmanned, flies away."
Zǎi did not understand its meaning either.
Once the scholar left the gate, he vanished.
Over a year later,
Zǎi was executed by law.
From "Tōng Yōu Lù"
Péng Yǎn
During the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
before Péng Yǎn had taken office,
someone once told him:
"You will obtain a pearl and become noble,
but later there will be calamity."
Soon after becoming an official, he offended and
was demoted to Military Administrator of Lǐzhōu.
After arriving,
since the river had many
"many" originally read "famous,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
clams,
Yǎn was pleased,
thinking he could obtain pearls.
He immediately ordered people to gather them,
and they collected many clams.
But in the end, none yielded pearls.
When Zhū Cǐ rebelled,
he summoned Yǎn to serve as false Secretariat Drafter.
Yǎn then realized that "obtaining the pearl" referred to Zhū Cǐ.
Later, he was executed.
From "Xuān Shì Zhì"
Liǔ Miǎn
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
military campaigns were underway in Huáixī.
At that time, Liǔ Miǎn was a minor officer.
Whenever captives were taken or ambushes laid,
Miǎn was always among them.
He suffered serious wounds repeatedly,
and nearly died several times.
Later, on a moonless night with strong winds,
he was again ordered to capture enemies.
Miǎn, stirred by indignation, advanced deep,
expecting certain death.
After traveling over ten *lǐ*,
he sat down, about to fall asleep.
Suddenly, someone woke him,
handed him a pair of candles, and said:
"You are destined for great nobility.
As long as you keep these candles in mind,
you will have no worries."
Miǎn later became a general,
and often saw the candlelight's shadow upon his twin banners.
Later, when he no longer saw the candles,
he returned to the capital in a carriage due to illness and died.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Hán Huàng
Chancellor Hán Huàng of the Táng dynasty traveled from Jīnlíng to the court.
Over a year later,
in the Yángzǐ River,
turtles and soft-shelled turtles filled the river floating downstream,
all headless.
At that very time,
Huàng died in the city.
No one knew the reason.
From "Róngmù Xiántán"
Yán Zhèn
Minister of Works Yán Zhèn of the Táng dynasty
was from Yántíng County, Zǐzhōu.
His residence lay against Fǔdài Mountain.
Whenever deer cried,
one person from the Yán family would inevitably perish.
One day,
a cousin was sitting opposite him
when they heard a deer cry.
The cousin said:
"At Fǔdài Mountain, the deer cries again."
Yán replied:
"This time, it should likely be my cousin."
The cousin immediately responded:
"Cousin is not a son of the Yán family;
it should be Third Brother or Fourth Brother."
Not many days later,
one of Yán's sons indeed died.
How strange this was.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
In the spring of the second year of the Bǎolì era of the Táng dynasty,
Zhū Kèróng, the military governor of Fànyáng, went hunting for deer.
Inside a deer's gallbladder, he found a pearl,
the size of a pellet,
black in color,
soft at first but later hardening,
shining like stone.
Someone asked Má Ānshí:
"What omen is this?"
Ānshí replied:
"Such an event has never occurred since ancient times.
Allow me to deduce its meaning."
Finding a pearl in a deer's gallbladder,
Kèróng considered it an auspicious sign for himself.
The deer (lù) symbolizes official salary (lù),
the death of the deer signifies the exhaustion of that salary.
The pearl being soft at first and later hardening
indicates a transformation of the pearl.
The exhaustion of salary and the transformation of the pearl
must foretell a change of events.
It is an omen of decline and ruin."
From then on, Kèróng's words and actions became rash and frivolous.
In the fifth month of that year,
indeed, a mutiny broke out among his troops,
and his entire family was killed.
From *Xiángyàn Jí*.
Wáng Yá
Wáng Yá, Chancellor of the Táng dynasty,
in the ninth year of the Dàhé era was in charge of state revenues,
and also supervised the salt and iron monopolies.
His son, Zhòngxiáng, once sought refuge from the heat in a mountain pavilion one day,
when suddenly he saw several dozen household servants, all headless,
covered in blood, approaching Zhòngxiáng.
After only about the time it takes to eat a meal,
they vanished.
Zhòngxiáng was extremely shocked and alarmed,
and immediately reported the matter in full,
wishing to resign from his powerful position.
Yá did not listen.
In the winter, the eleventh month of that year,
indeed, the calamity involving Zhèng Zhù occurred.
From *Xuānshì Zhì*.
Wēn Zào
At the residence of Minister Wēn Zào in Xīnchāng Lane,
Sāng Dàomào had once lived.
In the courtyard were two very tall cypress trees.
Master Sāng said:
"For a person's dwelling place,
if ancient trees grow lush and dense,
they should all be removed.
Moreover, when trees flourish, the earth weakens,
causing the residents to fall ill,
which is due to the weakening of the earth."
Therefore, he used several tens of *jūn* of iron,
and buried it beneath the cypress trees.
Afterwards, he told people:
"If later inhabitants
dig up the place where I buried the iron,
the head of that household will surely die."
In the ninth year of the Dàhé era of the Táng dynasty,
Wēn Zào resided in that house.
While constructing halls and buildings,
they dug up the ground,
and unearthed the iron that Master Sāng had buried.
Several days later,
Zào indeed died.
From *Xuānshì Zhì*.
Lǐ Zōngmǐn
Lǐ Zōngmǐn, Chancellor of the Táng dynasty,
in the summer of the seventh year of the Dàhé era, was appointed to govern Hànzhōng.
The following winter,
he returned to serve as Chancellor again.
In the summer of the year after that,
he once returned from court to his residence in Jìng'ān Lane.
In front of his couch, an iron suddenly
began jumping and tossing about for a long time.
Zōngmǐn found it strange and ominous.
At that time, Lǐ Xùn and Zhèng Zhù,
through deceit and trickery, had gained the emperor's favor.
They frequently spoke to the emperor.
Xùn learned of this,
and then submitted a memorial accusing him of a crime.
Ten days later,
an edict demoted him to Prefect of Míngzhōu,
and he was further demoted to Registrar of Cháozhōu.
This was the omen of it.
From *Xuānshì Zhì*.
Liǔ Gōngjì
Minister Liǔ Gōngjì,
in the Dàhé era of the Táng dynasty, was ordered by imperial decree to suppress Lǐ Tóngjiān.
After setting out with the army,
not long after,
the command flagpole suddenly broke.
A guest who witnessed it sighed and said:
"When a great general leads an army out,
if the gate banner or command flagpole breaks,
the army will surely be defeated.
If not,
the commanding general will die."
Several months later,
Gōngjì indeed passed away.
Whenever an army goes on an expedition,
if crows and kites follow behind it,
it is an omen of defeat and destruction.
There was a man named Zēng Jìng,
who once served as a deputy general in the Northern Capital.
When Lǐ Shīdào rebelled,
Zēng led several thousand soldiers from the marching camp.
Every time he led the army out,
crows and kites would follow behind,
and the army would surely be defeated,
which became a regular occurrence.
Later, he left his family to become a monk,
residing at the Níngdìng Temple in Tàiyuán.
In the ninth year of the Dàhé era,
Luó Lìyán served as Governor of the Capital District.
Once, while preparing for court attendance,
after donning his official cap and belt,
he looked at himself in a mirror,
but could not see his own head.
He then spoke of this to his younger brother, Yuēyán.
Later, he was indeed implicated in the case of Lǐ Xùn,
and executed.
From *Xuānshì Zhì*.
Táng
"Táng" originally written as "Sòng",
corrected according to the Míng manuscript and the Chén collated edition.
Three strange occurrences concerning Chancellor Wáng Yá of Yǒngníng.
Sū Guī, a rice washer,
originally a cook in the Wáng household,
only learned of it when he reached Jīngzhōu.
He was asked about the ominous signs in the Wáng household.
He said there was a well south of the residence,
which every night would often boil and surge with noise.
Looking into it during the day,
one might see a copper wine vessel,
or a silver iron,
and the water was foul and undrinkable.
Also, in Chancellor Wáng's inner study, there was a meditation couch,
made of mulberry wood and silk cords,
exquisitely crafted.
For no reason, it came apart,
each piece gathering in a separate place.
Wáng found it very ominous,
and ordered it burned in the kitchen stove.
Also, his eldest son, Mèngbó, rising in the morning,
saw several drops of clotted blood on the hall floor,
the trail of which extended all the way to the main gate before ending.
Mèngbó hastily ordered it scraped away.
Chancellor Wáng did not know of it at first.
Within a few months, disaster struck.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
Wáng Qián
During the Dàhé era of the Táng dynasty,
Wáng Qián served as military governor of Jīngnán.
For no reason, a white horse galloped into the gate of his headquarters and died,
lying stiff and blocking the path.
That year, Qián died,
which is akin to a horse calamity.
From *Yīnhuà Lù*.
Hán Yuē
Hán Yuē, during the Dàhé era of the Táng dynasty, served as Protector-General of Ānnán.
At that time, a local product was jade dragon ointment,
which southerners used
to transform silver into liquid.
According to elders' traditions,
this ointment must not be taken away,
for those who violate this will meet with disaster.
Yuē did not believe it,
and when his term ended and he returned to the capital,
he stored some to bring back.
At that time, he served as Commandant of the Capital Guards,
and indeed was the first to suffer in the Gānlù calamity,
all due to his greed for profit and coveting of goods.
From *Bǔlù Jì Zhuàn*.
The Wáng Family
At the estate of commoner Wáng in the southern part of Héyáng during the Táng dynasty,
there was a small pond,
with several large willow trees planted by its side.
At the end of the Kāichéng era,
leaves fell into the pond,
and soon transformed into fish,
as large as leaves,
tasteless when eaten.
By winter,
that household encountered legal troubles.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
Wáng Zhé
Wáng Zhé, the Prefect of Qiánzhōu during the Táng Dynasty, was building a residence in the western part of Píngkāng Ward.
While digging the ground,
his family members unearthed a stone.
On it was written in vermilion ink:
"Building here is inauspicious."
The family members wiped it,
but the characters became even clearer.
They then presented it to Wáng Zhé.
Suspecting his family was lazy with the shovels,
he ground it himself,
but the vermilion color penetrated deep like the stone's veins.
Wáng Zhé was greatly disturbed by this.
That same month, he died.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
Dù Mù
Dù Mù of the Táng Dynasty, having received an official appointment in the capital after serving in the Xuānchéng administration,
wrote a farewell poem which said:
"We came together but cannot return together;
encountering spring in my homeland, I am utterly desolate."
More than twenty years later,
he served successively as prefect of four commanderies.
Later, he was appointed Zhōngshū Shèrén from the post of Prefect of Húzhōu.
He wrote a poem on the Biàn River:
"Pitying my own exile, I hasten westward to return,
unable to see the spring breeze in the second month."
From commandery governor to becoming a Shèrén
could not be considered exile,
yet upon reaching the capital, he indeed died.
From *Gǎndìng Lù*.
Lú Xiànqīng
Lú Xiànqīng of Fànyáng,
during the Dàzhōng era of the Táng Dynasty, sat for the imperial examinations.
His literary talent was highly praised by his peers.
He composed the *Mǐn Zhēng Fù*, thousands of characters long,
which contemporaries considered second only to Yǔ Xìn's *Āi Jiāngnán*.
For years he failed to pass the examinations,
and wandered through Héng and Xiāng.
Arriving at Chēnzhōu, he fell ill.
He dreamed someone presented him a poem:
"I divine a dwelling on ancient suburban plains,
green hills are the only neighbors all around;
luxuriant trees wind around the house,
a solitary soul returns in loneliness."
Lú Xiànqīng died within ten days.
The Prefect of Chēn buried him in the nearby suburbs.
It was indeed early summer,
all matching what he dreamed.
From *Běnshì Shī*.
Lú Pián
Lú Pián, a Vice Director during the Táng Dynasty,
was a man of brilliant talent.
Suddenly one day, he arrived late at the Qīnglóng Temple,
rested in the monastic quarters,
his words and demeanor mournful and distressed,
as if harboring deep sorrow.
He sighed back and forth between the railings.
When the monks asked, he did not answer.
As night approached and he prepared to mount his horse to leave,
he paced about, looking around,
hurriedly called for brush and inkstone,
and wrote on the southern lintel:
"Though life's length is said to be fate,
prosperity and decay are also too biased;
I wonder where the Léi family's sword
will once again pierce the sky."
After writing the poem,
he departed in haste.
Within ten days he took up an official post,
and died within a month.
His poem remains in the temple to this day.
Whenever monks meet someone,
they often speak of this strange event.
From *Táng Quēshǐ*.
Fēng Wàngqīng
Fēng Wàngqīng of the Táng Dynasty
was the son of the Grand Councilor Fēng Áo.
When Dù Xīngōng Cóng governed Qíxià,
he requested him from the Department of State Affairs to serve as his administrative assistant.
On the wall of his usual residence,
there were ink splatters and traces.
One day, Wàngqīng
suddenly used his fingernails to scrape them all off,
his countenance as if in mourning.
When his attendants later asked the reason,
Wàngqīng remained silent and did not answer.
Not long after, he fell gravely ill.
He said to his attendants:
"Remember how I scraped off the ink marks with my fingernails the other day?
I was repulsed by them at the time,
but could not tell you.
Each spot was the character for 'ghost'."
He died a few days later.
From *Yùquánzǐ*.
Cuī Yànzēng
West of the city of Xíngyáng Commandery was Yǒngfú Lake,
fed by the Zhèng River to maintain its water level.
Normally, its banks were lined with pavilions, terraces, flowers, and trees,
serving as the place where the Grand Administrator held farewell and welcoming banquets.
To the southwest, on the flat land, were many tall bamboos and lofty trees;
this was the country estate of the late Military Governor of Xú, the Regular Attendant Cuī Yànzēng.
During the Xiántōng era of the Táng Dynasty,
Páng Xūn rebelled.
Yànzēng was captured by the rebels,
and the lake water turned as red as clotted blood for three days.
Soon after, news of his death arrived.
Long ago, when Prince Héjiān was campaigning against Fǔ Gōngshí,
traveling by river,
he held a banquet for his generals on the boat,
and ordered his attendants to dip river water with a golden bowl.
As he was about to drink it,
the water suddenly transformed into blood,
startling everyone present.
The Prince calmly said:
"The blood in this bowl
is an omen of Gōngshí's imminent beheading."
He indeed defeated him.
Thus, the difficulty of discerning fortune and misfortune is like this.
From *Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú*.
Cuī Yōng
Cuī Yōng, a Diarist,
was renowned for his pure and refined reputation,
and was especially fond of ancient books and paintings.
Thus, works by masters like Zhōng Yáo, Wáng Xīzhī, Hán Gàn, and Zhǎn Zǐqián
were gathered in his household.
He particularly treasured a scroll painting titled *Tàizhēn Mounting a Horse*,
considering it a top-grade artwork.
In the wùzǐ year of the Xiántōng era of the Táng Dynasty,
he was appointed Prefect of Hézhōu with a salary of two thousand shí.
At that time, Páng Xūn was staging a rebellion.
Between Fēng and Pèi, rebel forces were plundering everywhere.
Lìyáng was a small
"small" originally written as "Lì",
corrected according to the Ming manuscript copy.
commanderie.
As a historian and scholar,
he was incapable of armed resistance.
So he ordered a junior officer to take cattle and wine to appease the rebel leader,
requesting the preservation of the city walls and the lives of the common people.
Thus, the region was spared the calamity of slaughter and pillage.
Although he feigned negotiation,
he secretly submitted a memorial explaining himself.
However, a high minister who bore him ill will
used this to have him condemned by law.
Gentlemen and scholars mourned him.
Later, someone obtained the painting Cuī Yōng had treasured.
At the end of the scroll was inscribed:
"The dog of Shàngcài is lamentable—
life has come to this;
the crane of Huátíng cries in vain—
what can be done about Heaven's decree?"
The calligraphy was authentic,
but no date was written.
Those who understood said:
after receiving the death sentence,
he had no time for this.
Did he foresee it?
Or was it merely coincidence?
From *Táng Quēshǐ*.
Páng Cóng
In the bǐngchén year of the Qiánníng era under Emperor Zhāozōng of the Táng dynasty,
Zhū Liáng Tàizǔ executed those who did not submit to him.
Zhū Jǐn, the military governor of Yǎnzhōu, fled to the Huái-Hǎi region,
and Liáng Tàizǔ ordered Páng Cóng, the military governor of Xúzhōu,
whose former name was "Shīgǔ,"
to assemble an army of fifty thousand at Qīngkǒu.
During the Eastern Jìn dynasty, Xiè Ān was ordered to attack Qīngzhōu,
where he dammed the Lǚliáng waters,
erected palisades,
and built seven weirs to create channels,
harnessing the flow to facilitate water transport,
hence the name "Qīngzhōu Channel,"
though it was actually the Sìshuǐ River.
Floating chime stones were found in Xiàpī.
The place where they encamped
was what military texts call "desperate terrain."
People could not walk shoulder to shoulder,
and only after traveling thirty lǐ
did they reach level ground.
At that time, Liáng Tàizǔ sent trusted aides to oversee the operation,
but the commanding general was unable to control it.
(Míng manuscript notes: "dared not act independently.")
Within a couple of days,
Zhū Jǐn indeed arrived in person with tens of thousands of troops.
When Cóng heard that Jǐn had come personally,
the entire army lost its spirit.
When battle commenced,
no one dared to show any fighting will;
some drowned, some floated away,
and only one or two managed to escape.
Before Jǐn's army arrived,
the troops had experienced false alarms,
with many strange occurrences,
such as watch-stands moving on their own in front of the military tents.
Cóng's family in Xúzhōu
also witnessed frequent ominous events.
Behind the official residence,
there had long been a den of demonic foxes,
which would appear whenever the prefect faced disaster.
At that time, monks were ordered to hold a Buddhist ceremony in the Diāo Hall.
Because there were many fox demons,
eagles were painted inside as a deterrent.
Before Cóng perished,
his family saw a woman in red
on the Swallow Tower,
leaning against the railing in broad daylight.
When she noticed someone watching her,
she gradually moved backward and vanished.
At the time, the doors to the tower
were all locked.
A few days later,
news of the disaster arrived.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Lǐ Jūn
When Lǐ Jūn of the Táng dynasty arrived in Línrǔ,
the commandery had just experienced the massive troops of Wáng Xiānzhī.
The populace was frequently alarmed.
Lǐ Jūn, due to his limited military strength,
submitted a memorial to the emperor.
An imperial decree ordered 3,500 soldiers from the Zhāoyì Army to garrison there.
This was in the wùxū year of the Qiánfú era.
When the troops arrived,
they encamped west of the commandery's outer wall.
The following spring,
upon receiving mixed reports about Jūn's appointment to govern Shàngdǎng,
the garrison commanders
lined up on the main thoroughfare in front of the prefecture,
leading their subordinates into the yamen,
to perform the rituals between ruler and subject.
Suddenly, a fierce wind raised dust,
starting from the army gate and moving south,
coiling through the ranks,
and uprooting over a dozen large banners into the sky.
The townspeople stared in astonishment,
as the banners vanished into the horizon.
The next day,
villagers from Dàniúgǔ, twenty lǐ north of the prefecture,
found the banners and presented them;
the fabric was torn to shreds,
and the poles were all broken.
When Jūn reached Shàngdǎng,
he led his troops out through Yànmén,
but the soldiers, unrestrained,
brutally oppressed the local residents,
and he was eventually killed by the Měnghǔ Army.
From "Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú"
Gāo Pián
In the third year of the Guāngqǐ era of the Táng dynasty,
Grand Councilor Gāo Pián
was stationed in Huáihǎi.
Locusts appeared, crawling but not flying,
floating from the western moat,
climbing the city wall into the inner city,
gathering in the Daoist temple,
and could not be driven away.
Pine and bamboo trees, among others,
were stripped bare overnight as if cut.
Banners and painted images
all had their heads gnawed off.
A few days later,
they began to cannibalize each other.
In the ninth month,
after a heavy rain had just cleared,
small fish suddenly appeared in the ditches,
as large as a finger,
