known as "rain fish."
Diviners interpreted this as an omen of military conflict and mourning.
By the tenth month,
a large star fell at night in front of the Yánhé Pavilion,
with a sound like rolling thunder,
scattering light and shattering echoes,
illuminating the entire courtyard.
From the eleventh month to the following February,
a dense fog persisted without clearing.
Some said:
"This is an omen of subordinates plotting against their superiors."
At that time, the price of grain soared,
nearly tenfold higher.
People froze or collapsed in the rain,
with thousands of bodies daily
discarded outside the city walls.
When the fog cleared, the streets and alleys
were completely empty.
At that time, a mutiny occurred in the Zhèxī Army,
and Zhōu Bǎo fled to Pílíng.
Upon hearing this, Pián was greatly pleased,
and immediately sent an envoy with a letter to Zhōu, saying:
"I have learned that your swift horse
has already reached Bēnniú.
(Bēnniú is the name of a weir,
located west of Chángzhōu.)
Now I send you a jar of pickles
and ten catties of kudzu powder,
to meet your needs on the journey."
This was a veiled mockery, implying he would be minced to powder.
In the third month,
the administrative office held a flower-viewing banquet,
and Pián composed a poem for his subordinates.
The final lines read:
"In this world, sorrows are without end;
not a single branch can be plucked before the wine cup."
This was an omen of his impending downfall.
Later, when he was imprisoned and humiliated by Qín Yàn,
rations were distributed by headcount.
From the fifth to the eighth month,
the siege grew increasingly urgent,
and he met his demise.
From "Yāoluàn Zhì"
The Prefect of Jùlù
In the wùshēn year of the Wéndé era of the Táng dynasty,
north of the street in Nánhé County, Jùlù Commandery, there was a paper mill,
with long walls entirely covered in drying paper.
Suddenly, a whirlwind came from the west,
sweeping almost all the paper off the walls,
soaring straight up into the clouds,
looking like flying snow.
This was a major taboo in military affairs.
In the fifth month of summer,
the commandery prefect died.
From "Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú"
The Shǎnxi Military Governor
At the end of the Qiánníng era of the Táng dynasty,
in Shǎnxi, a snake and a rat fought inside the south gate,
with onlookers packed like a wall.
The snake died, and the rat fled.
Within ten days, the Shǎnxi military governor met with disaster.
This recalls the ancient case where the inner snake died and Duke Lì of Zhèng entered,
and when the rats fled, Púshān perished.
Omens arise from human affairs,
and should serve as a warning.
From "Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú"
Yán Zūnměi
Yán Zūnměi, the Left Army Supervisor of the Tang dynasty,
was a benevolent man among the eunuchs.
He once said that the Northern Bureau, serving as the Office of Attendants,
with officials wearing informal robes and attending to affairs,
lacked the ceremonial dignity of holding tablets.
He also said:
"The office of the Privy Council
is merely a three-room building with bookcases,
and it also lacks a hall for conducting official business.
After the memorials were submitted, yellow labels were attached,
and directives on public affairs
were handled by Yáng Fùtài.
(Note: In the Ming manuscript, "Tài" is written as "Gōng.")
This usurped the authority of the prime minister.
Zūnměi once went mad,
dancing and flailing his limbs.
Beside him were a cat and a dog.
The cat said to the dog:
"The Army Supervisor has changed his usual behavior."
The dog replied:
"Why bother about it?"
Shortly after, the dancing stopped,
and he was astonished by the words of the cat and the dog.
When Emperor Zhāozōng was forced to flee to Fèngxiáng,
Zūnměi requested to retire in Hànzhōng.
Soon after, he moved to the foot of Qīngchéng Mountain in Jiànnán,
where he chose a villa to live in.
He lived past eighty before passing away.
His loyalty, integrity, humility, and frugality
were comparable to those of Lǐ Xuán of Xīmén.
At that time, when eunuchs were being purged,
only Xīchuān did not comply with the imperial decree,
and thus he escaped disaster.
His family possessed an eight-volume record titled *The Rise and Fall of the Northern Bureau*,
which detailed the loyalty, treachery, virtues, and vices of the eunuchs.
These were akin to the palace attendants of old,
not all of whom were necessarily wicked or depraved.
It was largely due to the excessive contempt and jealousy of the Southern Court officials
that resentment and anger arose,
which was indeed a misfortune for the state.
Earlier, when Lù Yán was transferred from Chéngdū to Zhǔgōng,
the horse he was riding suddenly spoke in human language,
saying:
"Reed flowers,
after these flowers bloom, Lù will have no home."
Not long after, disaster befell him.
However, could the speech of animals
be attributed to some supernatural possession?
The stones speaking in Jìn
is a comparable case.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Chéng Ruì
Chéng Ruì of Jīngzhōu,
during the Tiānfù era of the Tang dynasty, followed an imperial decree to lead troops to rescue Jiāngxià.
His army encamped at Gōng'ān County.
There was a temple with two guardian deities,
whom the locals called the Two Saints,
and they were believed to be quite efficacious.
He moored his boat and went to pay homage to them,
praying for victory or defeat.
The omens for Ruì were all inauspicious.
Ruì was troubled by this,
but the clerk Yáng Shīhòu said:
"Your Lordship has already set out;
how can you hesitate or doubt?"
Thus, he had no choice but to advance.
In the end, his army suffered a crushing defeat,
and he died, his family perishing.
This was no accident.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Liú Zhījùn
When Liú Zhījùn, Prince of Péngchéng of the Liáng dynasty, was stationed in Tóngzhōu,
while constructing a camp wall,
they unearthed an object
weighing over eighty catties,
shaped like an oil sack.
He summoned his advisors, staff, and officers to inquire about it.
Some called it an "earth sack,"
others called it a "flying creature,"
and still others called it the "golden deity of seven killings."
Only Liú Yuán said:
"This is formed from accumulated grievances.
Since ancient times, such things have been found in places of imprisonment.
In the past, when Wáng Chōng occupied Luòyáng,
while repairing the prison of Hénán Prefecture,
they also discovered such an object,
and my distant ancestor recorded it.
It is formed from the spirits of wrongfully executed prisoners,
whose essence sinks into the earth,
gathering to form this object.
Over hundreds or thousands of years,
it congeals and does not disperse.
I have heard that wine can make one forget sorrow;
I suggest offering fine wine as a libation,
which may perhaps dissolve it.
However, the emergence of this object
is also an inauspicious sign."
Zhījùn ordered wine and food to be prepared for the offering,
and then reburied it.
Soon after, there was an incident of betraying the city and defecting to Qín,
which verified the omen.
From *Jiàn Jiè Lù*.
Tián Yūn
Tián Yūn, the military governor of Xuānzhōu,
was about to stage a rebellion.
One day toward dusk,
a red bird,
resembling a pheasant but larger,
with a tail emitting sparks of light,
like scattered stars,
flew in from outside
and disappeared after landing at the gate of the halberd-bearing guards.
The next day,
a great fire broke out in the government offices,
destroying all the administrative bureaus,
leaving only the armor and weapons intact.
Yūn used these to launch his rebellion,
but he was defeated the following year.
From *Jī Shén Lù*.
Sāng Wéihàn
Lord Sāng Wéihàn,
served as the prefect of Kāifēng.
One day,
while sitting alone in his main chamber late at night,
he was suddenly seized with great terror,
as if he had seen something,
and shouted fiercely into the air:
"How dare you come here!"
This happened several times.
For ten days, he remained agitated and resentful,
and even when his wife
(Note: In the Ming manuscript, "qí" is written as "tiē.")
was present, he dared not ask anything.
Not long after,
he dreamed that he was dressing in formal attire,
preparing his carriage and horses,
and about to go somewhere.
Just as he was about to mount,
the horse he was to ride suddenly vanished,
and he could not find it no matter how hard he searched.
After waking,
he felt deeply troubled by this,
and within a few days, disaster befell him.
From *Yù Táng Xián Huà*.
Zhōng Fù
Zhōng Fù, Prince of Nánpíng,
was in Jiāngxī.
There was a government clerk named Kǒng Zhīràng,
who had just built a new residence.
One day, a star fell into his courtyard.
Zhīràng found this very ominous,
so he requested a post outside the capital,
to leave the place empty.
Over a year later,
Xuē Shàowěi, the Vice Censor-in-Chief,
was demoted and sent to Yùzhāng.
Fù took this residence for him to live in,
and he eventually died there.
From *Jī Shén Lù*.
Dùn Jīn
Dùn Jīn, the prefect of Yuánzhōu,
left his post and returned to the capital.
Someone brought a purple-wrapped package
to his gate and left it for him.
When he opened it,
it contained a white, tattered robe.
He hurriedly went after the person,
but they had already vanished.
That same year, Jīn passed away.
From *Jī Shén Lù*.
The Mǎ clan of Húnán
The Prince Wǔmù of Húnán was inspecting the border when,
on his return journey, his boat reached the mouth of the Yíchūn River at Dòngtíng Lake.
Suddenly, a fierce storm arose,
with waves like continuous mountains.
Then, amidst the waves,
strange and bizarre sights appeared:
flood dragons and hornless dragons emerged and vanished,
clouds and mist grew dark and hazy.
There were figures resembling warriors holding spears and halberds,
civil officials with tablets and writing slips,
and others as if holding trays and vessels.
Some wore crimson, others green,
flashing and flickering, glaring and staring—
no one knew what they were.
The attendants were terrified,
and threw clothes and utensils into the water.
The boatmen wanted to offer up the concubines as a plea,
but the prince refused.
After some time, the wind calmed,
and they barely survived.
Several years later,
Prince Wǔmù passed away in office.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Wáng Shèncí
Wáng Shèncí, a Court Usher of Jiāngnán,
had a country villa west of Guǎnglíng City.
Shèncí often went there with relatives and friends.
One day,
he suddenly grew fond of the hill's topography and sighed:
"When I die, I must be buried here."
That night,
the village heard dogs barking.
Some rose to look and
saw Shèncí riding alone, lingering there.
When approached,
he vanished.
From then on, he came every night.
Over a month later,
Shèncí died
and was indeed buried there.
From *Jī Shén Lù*.
Ān Shǒufàn
Ān Sīqiān, the Military Governor of Péng Prefecture of the False Shǔ,
had a son named Shǒufàn.
Once, Shǒufàn visited the Tiāntāi Temple with guests
and composed a linked-verse poem.
Shǒufàn wrote:
"By chance I came to Tiāntāi's hall,
and met a monk beyond this world's thrall."
Yáng Dǐngfū, Assistant Judge of the Dìngróng Army, wrote:
"Forgetting schemes, we share one patriarch's line;
his words transcend the Three Vehicles' design."
Zhōu Shù, former Inspector of the Huáiyuǎn Army, wrote:
"Ancient trees in the courtyard, a stillness profound;
empty windows, the outer world clear and unbound."
Lǐ Rénzhào, former Administrative Assistant of Méi Prefecture, wrote:
"A moment beneath pines and cypress trees,
linked verses like a thousand lamps, if you please."
They recorded it on the temple wall and left.
The next day,
a poor beggar saw it while seeking alms
and declared loudly:
"People say things have a start but no end;
this has an end but no start.
Five years from now,
heads and necks will be shattered—
not as good as the final lines."
He clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
The temple monks drove him away.
The beggar ran off, shouting:
"After this, the master here
will come from afar,
not minding a thousand *lǐ*."
Everyone thought him mad,
unable to fathom his meaning.
Several years later,
Shǒufàn was executed,
and Dǐngfū died suddenly—
this was the meaning of "heads and necks shattered."
Zhōu and Lǐ
repeatedly received official promotions—
this was the meaning of "not as good as the final lines."
The temple abbot also soon died.
The succeeding abbot
came from Xīngyuán—
thus, "the master comes from afar, not minding a thousand *lǐ*."
The beggar's words
were not mistaken in the least.
From *Yěrén Xiánhuà*.
Bǎo Zhì
When Prince Jiǎnwén of Liáng was born,
Master Zhì told Emperor Wǔ:
"This child shares his birth year with his enemy."
That year, Hóu Jǐng was born in Yànmén.
He later brought chaos to Liáng,
exterminating nearly all of the Xiāo clan.
From *Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi*.
Shǐ Pǔ
Before Chén Bàxiān rose to prominence,
there was a Palace Guard named Shǐ Pǔ
who dreamed of a man in crimson robes holding a jade tablet,
descending from heaven.
On the tablet were golden characters:
"The Chén clan, five generations,
thirty-four years."
When the Later Ruler surrendered to Suí,
Shǐ Pǔ was still alive.
From *Dú Yì Zhì*.
Gěng Xún
During the Dàyè era of Suí,
Gěng Xún completed an armillary sphere and presented it.
The Emperor summoned the Grand Astrologer Yuán Kè
and the Director of the Imperial Workshops Hé Chóu to inspect it.
The measurements of the three celestial bodies
and their day-and-night movement—
"movement" originally read "not";
emended per the Ming manuscript.
—were accurate to the slightest degree.
The Emperor greatly praised it,
bestowing one hundred bolts of silk,
and intended to appoint him as Grand Astrologer.
Upon hearing this—
"hearing" originally read "asking";
emended per the Ming manuscript.
—Xún laughed and said:
"I have not yet obtained this post,
but at sixty-four or sixty-five,
it matters not.
However, if I become Grand Astrologer, my life will end."
Later, Yǔwén Huàjí usurped the throne,
and Xún was made Grand Astrologer.
Knowing Huàjí was doomed,
Xún plotted to defect to Táng,
but the plot was discovered, and he was killed,
aged sixty-five.
Judging by Xún's skill in arts and numerology,
he was likely of the same caliber as Zhāng Héng and Guō Pú.
From *Dàyè Shí Yí Jì*.
Yùchí Jìngdé
In the late Suí Dynasty,
there was a scholar living in Tàiyuán,
who suffered from family poverty
and made his living by teaching.
His residence was adjacent to the government treasury,
so he entered through a hole.
Inside, there were tens of thousands of strings of coins,
and he intended to take them away.
A golden-armored man holding a spear said:
"If you want money,
you must obtain a note from Yùchí Gōng.
This is Yùchí Jìngdé's money."
The scholar searched but could not find him,
until he reached an iron-smelting site,
where there was a blacksmith named Yùchí Jìngdé,
who was bare-chested and disheveled.
While he was forging,
the scholar waited for him to rest,
then stepped forward and bowed to him.
Yùchí Gōng asked:
"What is the matter?"
He said:
"I am impoverished,
while you, sir, are wealthy and noble.
I wish to beg for five hundred strings of coins.
Is it possible?"
Yùchí Gōng angrily said:
"I am a blacksmith;
how could I be wealthy and noble?
You are mocking me!"
The scholar said:
"If you can show compassion,
just grant me a note,
and you will understand in the future."
Yùchí had no choice,
so he told the scholar to take up a brush,
and said:
"Pay so-and-so five hundred strings of coins."
He added the date,
and signed his name at the end.
The scholar bowed in thanks and took it away.
Yùchí Gōng and his companions
clapped their hands and laughed heartily,
thinking it absurd.
After obtaining the note,
the scholar returned to the treasury,
and again presented it to the golden-armored man.
The man smiled and said:
"This is it."
He ordered it to be tied high on a beam.
He then allowed the scholar to take the money,
but only up to five hundred strings.
Later, Jìngdé assisted Shén Yáo,
achieved outstanding merits,
and requested to return to his hometown.
An imperial decree granted him money,
along with an unopened treasury,
and he thus obtained this money.
When checking the ledger,
he found a shortage of five hundred strings,
and was about to punish the keeper,
when he suddenly found the note on the beam.
Jìngdé looked at it
and realized it was the note he wrote while blacksmithing.
For several days he marveled in astonishment,
then sent someone to secretly seek out the scholar.
He found him,
and the scholar recounted everything he had seen.
Yùchí Gōng richly rewarded him,
and also distributed the treasury goods to benefit old friends.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Wèi Zhēng
In the Táng Dynasty, Wèi Zhēng served as Púyè.
He had two clerks serving him.
During a long audience,
Zhēng was sleeping.
The two men were discussing under the window,
one said:
"Our official positions
are entirely determined by this old man."
The other said:
"They are entirely determined by heaven."
Zhēng heard this,
so he wrote a letter,
and sent the one who said "by this old man"
to deliver it to the Shìláng.
It said:
"Give this man a good official position."
The man did not know,
but upon leaving, he developed a heartache.
He entrusted the one who said "by heaven" to deliver the letter.
The next day, during the appointment review,
the one who said "by the old man" was dismissed,
while the one who said "by heaven" was retained.
Zhēng found it strange,
so he inquired,
and they truthfully reported everything.
He then sighed and said:
"Official positions and salaries determined by heaven—
it seems this is not false."
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Lóu Shīdé
In the Táng Dynasty, Lóu Shīdé served as the county lieutenant of Jiāngdū in Yángzhōu.
Féng Yuáncháng also served as a lieutenant,
and together they visited Zhāng Jiǒngcáng.
Jiǒngcáng said:
"Both of you gentlemen will attain high status,
but Féng's rank will not match Lóu's.
Féng will only take much money,
and his official position will advance.
If Lóu takes even one coin,
his official career will be ruined."
Later, Féng served as the lieutenant of Jùnyí,
and frequently engaged in cruel and brutal acts.
The inspector considered him capable,
and recommended him for the position of lieutenant of Yúnyáng.
Later, due to a money-taking incident being cleared,
he was appointed as a capable inspector.
Lóu, however, never dared to take a single coin,
and his rank reached that of a high minister,
but his family remained extremely poor.
Féng's rank reached Shàngshū Zuǒchéng,
but later he committed an offense,
and was ordered to take his own life.
Lóu reached the position of Nàyán and died.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Wáng Xiǎn
In the Táng Dynasty, Wáng Xiǎn
had an old friendship with Emperor Wénwǔ, like that of Yán Zǐlíng.
They often played games of pulling trousers
and making merry with hats.
When the emperor was still obscure,
he often joked:
"Wáng Xiǎn, even in old age, will not spin a cocoon."
When the emperor ascended the throne and Wáng paid his respects,
he thus addressed the emperor:
"May I now spin a cocoon?"
The emperor laughed and said:
"That remains to be seen."
He summoned his three sons
and granted them all the fifth rank,
but Wáng alone was not granted anything.
The emperor said to him:
"You lack the appearance of nobility;
it is not that I begrudge you!"
Wáng said:
"To be noble in the morning and die in the evening would suffice."
At that time, Púyè Fáng Xuánlíng said:
"Since Your Majesty has an old friendship from before your rise,
why not try granting it to him?"
The emperor granted him the third rank,
bestowing upon him a purple robe and a golden belt.
That very night, he died.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Zhāng Bǎozàng
During the Zhēnguàn era,
Zhāng Bǎozàng served as a Chief Clerk of the Imperial Guards.
The original text lacked the character "史" (clerk).
It has been added based on the Ming Dynasty manuscript copy.
Once, after finishing his duty,
he was returning to Yuèyáng.
On the road, he encountered a young man hunting.
The hunter was cutting fresh game and eating in the wild.
Leaning against a tree, Zhāng sighed:
"I, Zhāng Bǎozàng, am seventy years old,
yet I have never once enjoyed food and wine like this.
How lamentable!"
A monk nearby pointed at him and said:
"Within sixty days,
you will attain an official rank of the third grade.
What is there to sigh about!"
Having spoken, he vanished.
Bǎozàng found this strange
and immediately returned to the capital.
At that time, Emperor Tàizōng was suffering from dysentery with gas pains,
and none of the many physicians could cure him.
He then issued an edict asking those in the palace court,
if anyone could cure this illness,
they would be heavily rewarded.
Bǎozàng had once been afflicted by this illness,
so he submitted a detailed prescription for milk decocted with bì bá (long pepper).
The Emperor took it and was immediately cured.
He announced to his chief ministers
that Bǎozàng was to be given a fifth-grade official post.
Wèi Zhēng raised difficulties,
and for over a month no appointment was proposed.
The Emperor's illness recurred.
He asked his attendants:
"The milk decocted with bì bá I took before was effective.
Have it prepared again."
After one sip, he recovered again.
He then reflected, saying:
"I previously ordered that the person who presented the prescription be given a fifth-grade post.
I have not seen the appointment made.
Why is this?"
Wèi Zhēng, afraid, said:
"When I received the decree,
it was unclear whether it was for a civil or military official."
The Emperor angrily said:
"If he could cure a chief minister,
he should already have been given a third-grade post.
I am the Son of Heaven.
Am I not superior to you?"
He then said sternly:
"Give him a third-grade civil official post.
Appoint him as Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglú Qīng)."
This was exactly sixty days later.
From *Dú Yì Zhì* (Records of Unique and Extraordinary Events).
Appointing an Official Who Judges the Underworld
Emperor Táng Tàizōng was in extremely good health.
The Grand Astrologer Lǐ Chúnfēng had an audience with the Emperor
and shed tears without speaking.
The Emperor asked him why.
He replied:
"Your Majesty will pass away this evening."
Tàizōng said:
"Life and death are fated.
What is there to worry about?"
He kept Chúnfēng to stay overnight.
In the middle of the night,
Tàizōng suddenly fell into a trance.
He saw a person who said:
"Your Majesty must come temporarily,
and will return shortly."
The Emperor asked:
"Who are you, sir?"
He replied:
"Your servant is a living man who judges matters of the underworld."
Tàizōng entered and saw
the judge questioning him about the events of the fourth day of the sixth month.
He was then ordered to return.
The person he had seen earlier again escorted and guided him out.
Chúnfēng observed the celestial signs
and forbade anyone to weep.
After a short while, Tàizōng awoke.
At dawn,
he sought the man he had seen the previous night
and ordered the relevant office to give him an official post.
They thus appointed him as a Deputy Official on the Shǔ circuit.
The Emperor found this strange and inquired.
The Board of Appointments reported:
"We acted upon an imperial directive to give him this post."
The Emperor did not remember this.
Those around him all heard
and thus realized that official appointments are all determined by Heaven.
From *Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi* (Comprehensive Records of Court and Country).
Wáng Wú'ài
In the Táng dynasty, there was a man named Wáng Wú'ài
who loved gambling games
and was skilled with falcons and hawks.
Before the Civil and Martial Sage Emperor (Táng Tàizōng) ascended the throne,
he once gambled with Wú'ài, competing for stakes,
and bore an old grudge from Lǐ Yángzhī.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
Wú'ài went into hiding and did not appear.
The Emperor ordered an attendant
to take a young falcon to the market to sell,
asking for twenty thousand coins.
Wú'ài, unaware of the situation,
offered eighteen thousand coins.
The attendant reported this.
The Emperor said:
"It must be Wáng Wú'ài."
He was then summoned
and, terrified, pleaded for mercy.
The Emperor laughed and rewarded him,
ordering him to wait at the Chūnmíng Gate
for three days for the tax carts from various prefectures,
and he could have them all.
Wú'ài sat for three days.
It happened that the Bà Bridge was damaged,
so he only obtained three carts of hemp
and nothing else.
The Emperor knew his fate was meager
and did not reward him further.
Wú'ài repeatedly requested a fifth-grade post.
The Emperor said:
"It is not that I won't give it to you,
but I fear you cannot bear it."
He insisted on requesting it,
so the Emperor finally agreed.
That very night, he died.
From *Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi*.
Yǔwén Róng
Liú Yǔxī said:
"If official posts are not predetermined,
how can it be called the true arbiter of fate?"
During the Yǒnghuī era,
Lú Qíqīng died temporarily.
Upon reviving,
he said he saw his maternal uncle, a certain Lǐ,
who served as a judge in the underworld court.
A clerk presented a document, saying:
"Yǔwén Róng is to become Chief Minister."
The uncle said:
"How can Yǔwén Róng be worthy of being Chief Minister?"
The clerk said:
"The decree from the Heavenly Ministry has already been issued,
stating the number of days."
It was then up to the judge.
The uncle thus decreed one hundred days.
Later, Yǔwén Róng was appointed Chief Minister,
and indeed was dismissed after one hundred days.
From *Jiāhuà Lù* (Record of Refined Conversations).
Lù Qián
Lù Jìngqián, the Recorded Affairs Adjutant of Huáizhōu, was implicated in the Qí Lián Huī affair.
He was interrogated at Xīnkāi
but escaped death and was exiled.
Later, his case was reviewed and cleared,
and he was appointed Magistrate of Suì'ān County in Mùzhōu.
All previous magistrates of that county had died in office.
Jìngqián wanted to decline the post.
His wife said:
"If you were fated to die,
during the Xīnkāi calamity,
you would have already lost your life.
Now you have obtained this county magistracy.
Is this not fate?"
He thus proceeded to the prefecture.
The county was several hundred *lǐ* upstream by water route.
In the western chamber of the residence's sleeping quarters,
there were three burial pits,
all containing former magistrates.
Jìngqián ordered laborers to fill them in.
An owl hooted on the screen,
and then hooted again on the ceiling.
He paid no attention to these things.
Whenever he ate with his wife,
dozens of rats,
some yellow, some white,
some blue, some black, would appear.
When he drove them away with a stick,
they would cling to the stick and squeak.
Other strange occurrences
are too numerous to detail.
After serving one full term of assessment,
he suffered no harm whatsoever.
He was selected and appointed as Wèi County Magistrate,
then promoted to Sima of Wèizhōu,
entered the capital as a Department Director,
and rose to the position of Secretariat Drafter.
From *Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi*.
Gān Zǐbù
Zhōu Gānzǐbù,
was erudite and talented.
At the age of seventeen,
he served as the Left Guard Chief Clerk,
but never reached the fifth rank.
During the Dēngfēng era, he fell ill.
He was forcibly carried to the foot of Mount Sōng in a donkey litter,
and by imperial grace was promoted two grades,
which should have placed him in the fifth rank.
Yet, in the end, he could not rise from his bed.
When fellow villagers and relatives came to congratulate him,
he was unable to don the official robes and cap.
So they covered him with a crimson robe,
and he passed away peacefully.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi".
Lǐ Jiǒngxiù
Lǐ Jiǒngxiù served as Minister of War.
When he fell ill,
court officials went to inquire after him.
Jiǒngxiù said:
"I know myself that I am destined to become a Shìzhōng,
so having this fate, I am certainly not worried."
After the court officials withdrew,
before they had even left the lane, he passed away.
The relevant office submitted a report,
and an imperial edict was issued posthumously granting him the title of Shìzhōng.
From "Dìngmìng Lù".
Dí Rénjié
When Táng's Dí Rénjié was demoted,
he passed through Biànzhōu,
wishing to stay half a day to seek medical treatment for an illness.
The magistrate of Kāifēng County, Huò Xiànkě, pursued him and insisted he cross the county boundary that very day.
Lord Dí harbored deep resentment towards him for this.
Later, when Dí returned to serve as Prime Minister,
Huò had already become a department director.
Dí wished to harm him but had not yet succeeded.
When Empress Zétiān ordered him to select a Deputy Censor-in-Chief,
on two separate occasions when he received the imperial command,
he forgot about it each time.
Later, when Empress Zétiān asked him again,
Lord Dí finally responded,
but having nothing to propose,
he could only remember Huò Xiànkě.
Thus, he recommended him.
An imperial decree appointed him Deputy Censor-in-Chief.
Later, Lord Dí said to Huò:
"I initially hated you,
but now I have recommended you.
Now I know it is fate,
how could it be due to man?"
From "Dìngmìng Lù".
Cuī Yuánzōng,
during Empress Zétiān's reign, served as Prime Minister.
A clerk named Xī Sān'ér said:
"Within sixty days from now, sir,
you will be exiled to the Southern Sea.
Within six years, you will face death three times,
yet ultimately you will not die.
After this, starting anew,
you will again hold official positions.
Later, you will return to sit in your former place.
Your lifespan will approach a hundred years.
In the end, you will die of starvation."
After sixty days,
he indeed incurred offense,
and was exiled to the far south of the Southern Sea.
After several years,
he suffered from bloody dysentery for a hundred days,
brought to extreme hardship, yet did not die.
When an amnesty allowed him to return,
he boarded a ship to cross the sea.
They encountered waves, the ship capsized and sank,
and all others on board perished.
Lord Cuī alone clung to a plank,
rising and falling with the waves.
Drifting to a small island in the sea,
he entered a thicket of reeds.
A long nail on the plank
pierced his back,
sinking in several inches deep,
with the nailed plank pressing down on him.
In the mud and water,
he could only endure the pain day and night, groaning.
Suddenly, some boatmen came to this island,
hearing his groans,
took pity and rescued him,
helping him onto their boat.
They stepped on him to draw blood and pulled out the nail,
after a long while he revived.
Asked his name,
he said he was a former Prime Minister.
The men pitied him,
aided him with provisions,
and he begged along the way.
Lying on the boat,
he saw an official dressed in blue-green,
who was a clerk from his time as Prime Minister.
He called to him and spoke,
and the man also gave him provisions,
enabling him to reach the capital.
Six years later,
he was reinstated and returned.
Having been recommended to the throne as a former Prime Minister,
Empress Zétiān ordered him given a post surpassing his qualifications.
On the day he went to give thanks,
he was led into the palace courtyard for an audience.
Lord Cuī was dressed in blue-green,
and Empress Zétiān saw and recognized him.
Asked what post he had received,
he reported the situation in full.
She then issued an edict to the Ministry of Personnel,
ordering him given a county captaincy with red robes.
On the day he was led to give thanks again,
she further decreed he be made a Censor.
From Censor he attained a directorship,
and by successive promotions reached Vice Director of the Secretariat.
At ninety-nine years old,
his sons and nephews had all died,
leaving him utterly alone,
ill and bedridden.
He ordered the servants to bring him rice porridge,
but the servants deceived him,
all laughing and not moving.
Since Lord Cuī could not reprimand or punish them,
and the servants would not accept any discipline,
he felt such indignation that he refused to eat,
and after several days, died.
From "Dìngmìng Lù".
Sū Wèidào
Sū Wèidào was three times due to receive the third rank,
and each time declined it.
Empress Zétiān asked the reason,
and he replied:
"Your servant knows himself that he is not fated to attain the third rank."
Empress Zétiān had him walk about,
observed him and said:
"You truly, the path now obtains
"the path now obtains" (Note: The Ming manuscript reads "obtains not fitting").
the third rank."
Thirteen years as Vice Director of the Secretariat and participating in policy-making,
yet he never reached the third rank.
Later, he was sent out as Prefect of Méizhōu,
then changed to Senior Administrator of Yìzhōu,
and by imperial decree was granted the purple sash.
On the day he arrived at the province,
after donning the purple robes,
that very night he died suddenly.
From "Dìngmìng Lù".
Lú Chóngdào
Táng's Minister of Sacrifices Lú Chóngdào,
implicated in the rebellion of his son-in-law, the Secretariat Director Cuī Shí,
and the Imperial Guard General Zhāng Xiān, implicated for verbally stating rebellious intentions to Xuē Jièrán,
were both exiled to Lǐngnán.
After a year,
there was not a day they did not wail in sorrow,
their eyes both swollen,
unable to bear the misery and longing,
so they both fled back.
Chóngdào hid in a residence in the capital.
He arranged for his son to marry a daughter of the Cuī family,
but the marriage was not yet completed.
A palace supply officer came,
to select a woman for the noble consort.
Chóngdào then bribed the officer,
who took a different Cuī family girl away instead.
When the matter within the palace was exposed,
the officer confessed fully,
and Chóngdào was apprehended.
Along with his three sons,
they were also seized.
By imperial decree, each was sentenced to a hundred strokes of the cane,
and all met their deaths.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi".
Liú Rénguǐ
Liú Rénguǐ, the Governor of Qīng Prefecture in the Táng Dynasty,
was in charge of maritime transport,
but lost an extremely large number of ships.
He was dismissed from his post and made a commoner,
and subsequently went to serve in Liáodōng.
There, he fell ill
and lay beneath the walls of Píngxiāng City.
Lifting the tent flap, he watched the soldiers attack the city.
One soldier came straight to the front and sat with his back to him.
Liú scolded him, but he would not leave.
Instead, the soldier cursed him viciously, saying:
"You want to watch,
and I also want to watch.
What business is it of yours?"
He refused to leave.
After a short while,
arrows were shot from the city wall,
and one struck him right in the heart, killing him.
If not for this soldier,
Liú Rénguǐ would have nearly been hit by a stray arrow.
From "Records of Court and Country"
Rén Zhīxuǎn
In the Táng Dynasty, Rén Zhīxuǎn
took the imperial examinations at the same time as Zhāng Yuè.
Later, Zhāng became the Head of the Secretariat,
while Rén ultimately failed the examinations.
He went to visit Zhāng,
who gave him a bolt of silk
to cover his living expenses.
Rén was about to return home,
but within a day or two,
he fell seriously ill.
He used the silk to buy medicine,
and when the silk was exhausted,
his illness naturally subsided.
Not only this time,
but other instances were also like this.
How extremely unfortunate his fate was.
From "Records of Court and Country"
Tián Yù
Tián Yù, an Imperial Physician of the Táng Dynasty,
said of himself:
"When I was young, I saw Xī Sān'ér suffering from a respiratory illness,
unable to sleep or eat peacefully.
I then offered to examine him,
and prescribed a decoction that cured him."
Sān'ér was greatly pleased and said:
"Since you have wholeheartedly treated my illness,
I will also wholeheartedly
determine your future rank and fortune for you."
He invited Tián to stay overnight.
At dawn,
he had paper brought to record Tián's official career and emoluments for his entire life.
Reaching the fourth appointment,
he said:
"You will become the Assistant Magistrate of Qiáolíng."
At that time, such a position did not exist,
so Tián questioned him.
He replied:
"Just wait until the time comes,
and this position will naturally appear."
He also said:
"You will serve as Imperial Physician for twenty-four years."
When the Great Emperor passed away,
Tián indeed became the Assistant Magistrate of Qiáolíng,
and later served as Imperial Physician.
After twenty-four years, he was transferred.
From "Records of Fixed Destiny"
Wáng Jùn
Wáng Jùn had served as the Magistrate of Wèinán for several years.
He said of himself:
"I have long grown weary of this county;
if only I could become the Military Advisor of Pú Prefecture."
At that time, Xī Sān'ér came from the north
and saw a ghost who said:
"I am delivering a document to Wèinán
to report that the Magistrate will change his post."
He asked what post,
and was told it was to become the Military Advisor of Pú Prefecture.
He then followed the ghost to Wèinán
and said to Wáng Jùn:
"You are about to be transferred to become the Military Advisor of Pú Prefecture."
At that moment, the ghost was standing bowed at the foot of the hall steps.
After Sān'ér finished speaking,
he left.
Indeed, after three or four days, Wáng was transferred to become the Military Advisor of Pú Prefecture.
More than twenty days after the transfer,
the official decree had not arrived.
He asked Sān'ér,
who later saw the same ghost
and inquired about the reason.
The ghost said:
"Because Wáng, while in office, embezzled government funds,
his merits were deducted.
Now the deduction is almost complete,
and by a certain time,
he will receive the appointment."
Later events confirmed his words.
From "Records of Fixed Destiny"
Gāo Zhìzhōu
was from Yìxīng.
In his youth, he lived together with Hǎo Chǔjùn from Ānlù, Lái Jì from Guǎnglíng, and Sūn Chǔyuē from Fùyáng at the home of Shí Zhònglǎn.
Zhònglǎn was from Xuānchéng
but had settled in Guǎnglíng.
He exhausted his family fortune to host these four men,
treating them with great generosity.
Once, while lying down at night,
they each spoke of their ambitions.
Chǔjùn spoke first, saying:
"I wish to hold the reins of power for just one day, and that would be enough."
Zhìzhōu and Lái Jì expressed similar wishes.
Chǔyuē suddenly rose from under his quilt and said:
"A great man may not dare hope for the reins of power,
but I wish to be an Usher of the Secretariat,
circulating in the palace halls and conveying memorials—that would be enough."
Zhònglǎn had always held these four in high esteem.
He once brought a physiognomist to examine them,
who said they would all reach the highest ministerial ranks.
Turning to look at Zhònglǎn, he said:
"You will achieve prominence through these four men."
Later, they each took up posts in various prefectures and counties.
Lái Jì had already become the Head of the Ministry of Personnel,
while Chǔyuē was a Clerk in Yíng Prefecture.
During the selection process,
he followed the procedure for assignment.
When Jì saw Yuē,
he immediately took up his brush and said:
"As you wished, as you wished."
He then appointed him as Usher of the Secretariat.
After the appointment was made, they descended the steps,
recounted their past conversation,
which was a fine story of the time.
Zhìzhōu had once left home to become a Buddhist monk,
but his fellow villagers regretted his talent and learning,
and urged him to take the imperial examinations.
He passed with distinction,
was appointed Military Advisor to the Prince of Yuè's household,
and was successively promoted to Magistrate of Fèi County,
where he shared his salary equally with his subordinate officials.
He was then promoted to Archivist in the Imperial Library,
and successively rose to Vice Director of the Secretariat,
participating in government affairs,
and was granted the title of Silver Seal and Blue Ribbon Grand Master for Splendid Happiness.
Zhìzhōu was intelligent and wise,
unmatched in the entire court.
He could recite tens of thousands of words daily
and memorize inscriptions and reconstruct chess games from memory.
He was indifferent to official rank and honors;
each time he resigned, he was promoted.
He was posthumously granted the title of Governor of Yuè Prefecture,
with the posthumous name Dìng.
From "Records of the Censorate"
Wáng Biāo
Wáng Biāo, an Usher of the Secretariat in the Táng Dynasty's heir apparent's household, said:
"A person's experiences are all tied to fate.
Destiny is predetermined,
and good or bad fortune follows accordingly.
How can one necessarily avoid it through caution?
In the past, the Empress Wǔ Zétiān executed members of the imperial clan.
One imperial clansman was imprisoned in the Dàlǐ Temple, sentenced to death.
The clansman sighed and said:
'Since I cannot avoid execution,
why should I dirty the blade and saw?'
That night,
he hanged himself with his collar.
At dawn, he revived,
and then talked, laughed, and ate and drank
no differently than when at home.
A few days later, he was executed,
his expression unchanged.
When he first revived, he said:
'When I first died,
an underworld official angrily said to me:
"You are supposed to be executed,
why have you come on your own?
Return quickly to receive your punishment!"'
The clansman asked the reason,
and the official showed him the underworld register,
which recorded that he had killed someone in a previous life,
and now the retribution was due.
Once the clansman understood,
he faced his execution without difficulty or change of expression.
From "Records of Hearsay"
Péi Zhòuxiān
The Minister of Works, Péi Zhòuxiān,
at the age of seventeen,
served as a secretary in the Court of the Imperial Stud.
His uncle, the Chancellor Péi Yán, was executed.
Zhòuxiān was dismissed and made a commoner,
and banished beyond the southern mountain ranges.
Zhòuxiān had always been forthright;
grieving over his uncle's innocence,
he submitted a sealed memorial to the court requesting an audience,
to personally present his views on right and wrong.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān was greatly enraged,
summoned him for an audience,
and received him with an imposing demeanor,
saying to Zhòuxiān:
"Your uncle rebelled,
violated the laws of the state,
and brought calamity upon himself—
what do you have to say?"
Zhòuxiān replied:
"Your servant now wishes to offer counsel for Your Majesty—
how dare I merely complain of injustice?
Moreover, Your Majesty was the empress of the late emperor,
a daughter-in-law of the Lǐ family.
After the late emperor passed away,
Your Majesty assumed the regency.
As a woman,
it was proper to entrust affairs to the great ministers,
to safeguard the ancestral temples and altars of state.
The crown prince is of age;
restoring him to the throne
would fulfill the hopes of heaven and men.
Now, not long after the late emperor's demise,
you hastily exalted your own family,
enfeoffed the various Wǔs as kings,
purged and expelled the Lǐ clan,
and proclaimed yourself emperor.
All within the seas are indignant and resentful;
the common people are disappointed.
My uncle was utterly loyal to the Lǐ family,
yet you falsely accused him of crimes,
and executed even his descendants.
If this is Your Majesty's plan,
I deeply lament it.
I hope Your Majesty will restore the Lǐ family's altars of state,
and welcome back the crown prince.
Then Your Majesty may rest easy,
and the various Wǔs will be preserved.
If you do not heed my words,
once the realm stirs,
the great cause will be lost.
The warning of Lǚ Chǎn and Lǚ Lù—
should it not be feared?
It is not too late for Your Majesty to adopt my counsel now."
Empress Wǔ angrily said:
"What insolent youth
dares to utter such words!"
She ordered him dragged out.
Zhòuxiān still turned back and said:
"It is truly not too late for Your Majesty to heed my words."
He did this three times.
Empress Wǔ ordered the court officials assembled in the audience hall,
had Zhòuxiān beaten with a staff one hundred times,
and banished him to Lǎng Prefecture as a convict laborer.
Zhòuxiān removed his clothes to receive the beating;
after ten strokes he appeared dead,
but revived at the ninety-eighth stroke,
and endured two more strokes to complete the count.
Zhòuxiān's wounds were severe;
he lay in a donkey cart,
and upon reaching the place of exile,
he ultimately did not die.
After several years in the southern regions,
he married a fellow exile, a woman of the Lú family,
and they had a son named Yuàn.
When Madame Lú died,
Zhòuxiān took Yuàn
and secretly returned to his hometown.
Over a year later, the matter was discovered;
he was again beaten one hundred strokes
and banished to Běitíng.
Engaging in trade for five years,
he amassed wealth amounting to tens of millions.
Zhòuxiān, being the nephew of a worthy chancellor,
traveled throughout Héxī,
associating with officials of two-thousand-dàn rank wherever he went.
Below the walls of the Běitíng Protectorate headquarters,
there was a barbarian settlement of ten thousand tents—
these were surrendered Hú tribes.
Their khan treated Zhòuxiān with respect
and gave him his daughter in marriage.
The khan had only this one daughter,
and doted on her greatly,
bestowing upon Zhòuxiān a great many gold, horses, cattle, and sheep.
Zhòuxiān thus gathered retainers and guests,
often numbering several thousand.
From Běitíng to the Eastern Capital,
he stationed guests along the routes,
to gather news and information from the Eastern Capital.
Movements in the imperial court
would invariably be known to Zhòuxiān within a few days.
At that time, the Reminder Lǐ Qínshòu was on duty in the Secretariat;
he submitted a sealed memorial stating:
"Since Your Majesty ascended the throne,
you have executed and expelled members of the Lǐ family and various great ministers.
Their family members and clansmen
living in exile abroad—
by my estimation—
number tens of thousands.
If one day they unite and gather to rebel,
taking Your Majesty by surprise,
I fear the state will certainly be endangered.
A prophecy says:
'The one to replace Wǔ is Liú.'
Now, Liú means 'to flow' (exile).
If Your Majesty does not kill these people,
I fear the calamity will be profound."
Empress Wǔ accepted this counsel,
summoning him in the night.
She said to him:
"Your name is Qínshòu (bestowed by Heaven)—
Heaven has bestowed you upon me."
To enlighten my mind—
she immediately appointed him Vice Director of the Bureau of Evaluations,
and still in charge of drafting edicts,
bestowing upon him crimson insignia,
ten female entertainers,
and gold and silk accordingly.
She plotted with him to dispatch ten imperial envoys to the ten circuits,
ostensibly to console the exiles."
In reality, they were given secret edicts for the governors and prefects:
to kill those who were exiled.
Once the edict was issued,
Zhòuxiān learned of it.
He gathered his guests to deliberate;
all urged Zhòuxiān to flee to the Hú territories.
Zhòuxiān followed their advice.
As evening fell,
they lodged outside the city walls,
and prepared their baggage.
At that time, there were two Guǒyì officers of the armored cavalry,
brave and strong,
who had been exiled for crimes.
Zhòuxiān had treated them well;
when they departed,
he had them lead eighty camels loaded with baggage,
all filled with gold and silk,
with over three hundred guests and household servants following.
They were equipped with armor and weapons,
half of them capable of leaping into chariots in full armor.
There were two swift horses capable of covering a thousand lǐ,
which Zhòuxiān and his wife rode.
Once packed, they set off hastily,
reckoning that by dawn when people realized,
they would already have entered barbarian territory.
However, they lost their way;
as dawn approached,
they had advanced only thirty lǐ,
so they galloped onward.
When it was fully light,
scouts reported that Zhòuxiān had fled.
The Protector-General ordered eight hundred cavalry to pursue him,
and his wife's father, the khan, also sent five hundred cavalry in pursuit,
instructing the pursuers:
"Spare Zhòuxiān and his wife;
kill all who accompany them.
Their goods and wealth shall be your reward."
The pursuers caught up with Zhòuxiān at the frontier,
who marshaled his troops and fought them,
his followers fighting desperately.
As dusk fell,
the two generals were killed in battle,
and eight hundred pursuing cavalry were slain,
but Zhòuxiān was defeated.
They bound Zhòuxiān and his wife onto camels,
and brought them to the Protector-General's headquarters.
Upon arrival,
they were shackled and imprisoned in a pit,
and a full report was submitted.
While awaiting a response, the envoy arrived,
summoned several hundred exiles,
and had them all killed.
Zhòuxiān was spared because the report had not yet been answered.
Empress Wǔ, assuming the exiles were already dead,
again sent envoys to console the exiles, saying:
"I previously dispatched ten circuit envoys to comfort the exiles;
why did the envoys not understand my intent,
but arbitrarily carried out killings,
acting with extreme cruelty?"
The envoys who had presumptuously killed the exiles
were arrested wherever they were,
taken to the places where they had killed the exiles, and beheaded,
to appease the souls of the dead.
Those exiles who had not died,
or were imprisoned for other reasons,
along with their families, were released and allowed to return home.
Thus, Zhòuxiān was spared,
and he returned to his hometown.
When the Táng dynasty was restored,
Péi Yán was posthumously pardoned,
and granted the posthumous title of Grand Governor of Yìzhōu.
Seeking his descendants,
his grandson Xiān Nǎi emerged,
and was appointed as Assistant Director of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
Within a year, he was promoted four times,
eventually reaching the position of Commander of Qínzhōu,
and later served as Military Governor of Guìzhōu and Guǎngzhōu.
He once served as Commander of Yōuzhōu,
four times as Commandant of the Capital Guards,
once concurrently as Censor-in-Chief,
and as Governor of Tàiyuán, Governor of Jīngzhào, and Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury,
holding third-rank official positions for nearly forty terms in total.
He achieved fame and accomplishments wherever he served,
and was hailed as a loyal minister of the Táng dynasty.
Later, he served as Minister of Works and remained in the Eastern Capital as its guardian until his death,
at the age of eighty-six.
From "Jì Wén"
Zhāng Wénguàn
When Zhāng Wénguàn was young,
someone once read his physiognomy and said:
"You will become a chancellor,
but you will not be able to eat meals in the hall."
After he attained this position,
every time he ascended to the hall intending to eat,
he would immediately suffer from abdominal distension, pain, and cholera-like symptoms,
so he could only eat one bowl of fermented rice water porridge each day.
Several years later,
he once violated the rule and ate a meal in the hall,
and that very night he passed away.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Yuán Jiāzuò
Yuán Jiāzuò served as Assistant Prefect of Huázhōu.
During his tenure, he maintained a clean and upright reputation,
but after leaving office, he had not been promoted.
The phrase "had not been promoted" was originally missing,
and was added based on the Ming dynasty manuscript.
He approached Chancellors Xiāo and Cén to state his case,
but the two chancellors rebuked him, saying:
"We know you have a good track record,
why are you so impatient in seeking promotion!"
Yuán retreated in shame,
and while resting under a tree by the roadside,
two men in yellow robes saw him and laughed.
Yuán asked why they were laughing,
and the two said:
"We are not laughing at you, but at those two chancellors!
Within two or three months, both will face family ruin,
and you will be the one to judge their crimes."
Yuán was startled and asked for details,
but they suddenly vanished.
A few days later,
an imperial decree appointed Yuán as Director of the Ministry of Justice.
Within a month,
the two chancellors were arrested,
and indeed, it was Yuán who judged their cases.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Qí Hàn
A fortune-telling monk in the Eastern Capital
associated with Vice Minister Qí Hàn.
Qí was demoted from Vice Minister of Personnel to County Defender of Gāo'ān County in Duānzhōu.
The monk said:
"From now on, in ten years,
you will return,
and will also hold significant power."
Later, as predicted,
he was appointed as Investigating Commissioner of Chénliú.
The monk once said:
"In your previous life, Vice Minister, you killed two people,
and now you are being punished for this crime,
hence the ten-year demotion."
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Zhāng Shǒuguī
Someone once recorded Zhāng Shǒuguī's official positions and salaries for eighteen terms,
and all turned out as predicted.
When he served as Prefect of Kuòzhōu,
he fell seriously ill,
but still told people:
"I am supposed to become Commander of Liángzhōu,
so I must not die yet."
Later, an abscess developed on his brain,
and the sore worsened.
He then said:
"My brothers all died from such sores,
so I must be posthumously granted the title of Commander of Liángzhōu."
He then bid farewell to the officials with a banquet,
and wrote his will,
passing away after five or six days of illness.
Later, he was indeed posthumously granted the title of Commander of Liángzhōu.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Péi Yǒuchǎng
When Péi Yǒuchǎng, Prefect of Hángzhōu in the Táng dynasty, fell seriously ill,
he ordered Xià Róng, Registrar of Qiántáng County, to examine him.
Róng said:
"Your Excellency has nothing to worry about,
but your wife must quickly perform blessings to ward off misfortune."
Lady Cuī, his wife, asked:
"What is needed for the ritual?"
Róng said:
"Your Excellency should take two concubines to counteract the misfortune,
and after three years, the danger will pass."
The wife angrily said:
"This barbarian is speaking nonsense!
My son is healthy and without illness."
Róng retreated and said:
"Since you do not believe me,
I dare not say more.
Your Excellency is destined to have three wives,
and if he does not take another,
it will be inauspicious for you."
The wife said:
"I would rather die
than agree to such a thing."
That year, the wife died suddenly,
and Péi took two concubines.
Róng's words proved true.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi".
Wáng Chāo
Wáng Chāo
once served as Magistrate of Sìshuǐ County.
Yán Sǔnzhī said to him:
"From now on, you will serve as a capital official,
and then become a prefect in Héběi twice."
Later, he indeed became a Court Gentleman for Editorial Service,
then Prefect of Zhēndìng,
and later changed to Governor of the Capital.
Wáng also said to Yán Jiǒng, Magistrate of Sìshuǐ County:
"You should cultivate blessings."
Yán did not believe him.
Later, he was indeed accused,
dismissed from office and stripped of his rank,
exiled, and died.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Zhāng Qíqiū
When Zhāng Qíqiū's wife was pregnant,
she went several months past her due date without giving birth.
Thinking it was an illness,
they were about to prepare medicine to treat her.
Nun Bǎozhū from Wújùn saw her and said:
"Do not take medicine,
for she will surely give birth to a future palace guard."
Later, she indeed gave birth to a boy.
After Zhāng Qíqiū rose to high rank,
an imperial decree granted him the privilege of appointing one son as an Attendant Official.
Zhāng Qíqiū petitioned:
"My two nephews were orphaned early,
and I wish to grant the position to them."
The emperor praised him,
and ordered that his two nephews be given sixth-rank or lower positions.
Zhāng Qíqiū's son
was still appointed as a palace guard,
at the age of only ten.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Féng Qī's Predictions
In Chénliú Commandery, there was a man named Féng Qī
who could drink alcohol,
consuming five dǒu at a time,
and whose predictions never failed.
Not long after,
he told the commandery officials:
"There is white qi in the city,
and the commandery governor will die."
Governor Péi Dūn
("Dūn" was originally written as "Guō",
corrected based on the Ming dynasty manuscript)
heard this and summoned him for questioning.
Féng Qī said:
"The qi is not yet fully formed,
but it should manifest within half a year."
Péi immediately sought to transfer.
After his transfer, Wéi Héng became governor,
but died before taking office.
People asked if the prediction had come true,
and he said:
"Not yet!"
Soon after, Zhāng Lìzhēn took charge of the commandery,
and died within the city.
Dù Huá once heard Monk Fǎhuàng of Chénliú say:
"Magistrate Shěn Xiáng of Kāifēng County should be promoted to a capital county magistrate,
and in fifteen months become Vice Censor-in-Chief."
Dù Huá believed this,
and also asked Féng Qī about it.
Féng Qī said:
"Shěn will not live more than ten days."
No one believed him.
After a few days,
Shěn reported being ill,
and Dù Huá went to visit him.
Shěn said:
"I am suffering from a headache,
and can hardly bear it."
He died a few days later.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Huán Chénfàn
Huán Chénfàn, the Prefect of Rǔzhōu, himself recounted:
"When I was going to the capital for my official evaluation during my previous term as prefect,
I reached Chángzhōu.
There was a certain Jí-shēng,
skilled in divination.
On the third day,
I had him drink wine,
and he became drunk.
By the fourth day,
he brought husked rice and a burning incense stick.
Jí-shēng held the incense stick in his mouth,
and suddenly seemed like a spirit
(The original text had 'yǐ shēn' [以伸],
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
and spoke.
At that time, I had an estate in Gōushì, near the Eastern Capital.
Some servants had just arrived there,
so I asked about any matters concerning the estate.
Jí-shēng said:
'This estate belongs to someone surnamed Lú,
not surnamed Huán.'
Seeing one male servant,
he also said:
'This servant will run away,
and will also steal two strings of cash.'
Seeing one maidservant,
he further said:
'This maidservant will have her head beaten until it bleeds.'
I asked what official post I would get after this transfer.
Jí-shēng said:
'You will become a prefect one thousand li to the northeast.
You must beware of a horse-related calamity.'
When I reached Yáng Prefecture,
that servant indeed stole two thousand cash and fled.
At the boundary of Xúzhōu,
that maidservant fought with her husband,
and her head was beaten until it bled.
Upon reaching the Eastern Capital,
I was reassigned as Prefect of Yíngzhōu.
Only then did I begin to believe him.
I constantly guarded against the horse calamity.
When I arrived at the commandery,
while bowing and kneeling in ceremony,
my left foot suddenly hurt,
and I became unable to walk.
There was a man who claimed to understand acupuncture.
After the needling,
the swelling worsened dramatically,
with burning pain extending to the knee.
I therefore requested leave,
and after one hundred days, I was relieved of my post.
That acupuncturist's surname was Mǎ (horse).
I had my assistant arrest and interrogate him.
The 'horse calamity'
referred to this very man.
Upon returning to the Eastern Capital,
while residing at Yīquē,
I sold that Gōushì estate to Lú Cóngyuàn.
Only then did I realize that none of the predictions had failed to come true.
Lord Huán from then on believed in fate,
and no longer sought advancement.
From *Dìngmìng Lù* (Records of Fixed Destinies).
Zhāng Jiāzhēn
Before Zhāng Jiāzhēn achieved prominence,
while he was still impoverished,
he once saw an old man selling divinations
on the road east of the city.
Jiāzhēn consulted him.
The old man then pasted together two scrolls of paper,
fully recording official posts and salaries,
from beginning to end,
and sealed them, instructing him not to open them.
Whenever he completed a term in an office,
he would open and look at one,
and indeed each matched.
Later, he rose to Chief Minister and Prefect of a certain prefecture,
and then to Prefect of Dìngzhōu.
When he was gravely ill and near death,
he said:
'I still have one scroll of official posts unopened.
How can I die now?
Since I am now in dire straits,
let me try opening it to look.'
Upon opening, the entire scroll was written with empty characters.
Zhāng indeed died.
From *Dìngmìng Lù* (Records of Fixed Destinies).
Monk Jīnshī
In Suīyáng, there was a Silla monk,
named Jīnshī,
who said to the Recorded Affairs Adjutant Fáng Guǎn:
'Grand Administrator Péi Kuān is about to be transferred.'
Guǎn asked when,
and he said,
'Tomorrow at noon,
the imperial edict will certainly arrive.
I will meet you at the southwestern corner of the commandery.'
Guǎn waited specially for him.
Before noon, a courier arrived,
but the sealed dispatch was not the relevant one.
Guǎn thought the monk was mistaken.
At noon,
another courier arrived delivering a dispatch,
saying:
'Lord Péi has been transferred to be Assistant Prefect of Ānlù.'
Fáng hastily ordered a carriage to fetch the monk,
and also went himself.
Sure enough, they met at the southwestern corner of the commandery.
Péi summoned and questioned him.
The monk said:
'Although your office is changed,
your official robes will not change.
However, your nephews and nieces will each disperse.'
Later, when the edict arrived,
appointing him Assistant Prefect,
his purple silk insignia was still retained.
As for his nephews and nieces,
they each dispersed.
From *Dìngmìng Lù* (Records of Fixed Destinies).
The Wéi Clan
During the Táng, Prince Píng suppressed the rebellious Wéi clan.
Cuī Rìyòng led troops to Dùqū,
and nearly exterminated the various Wéi clansmen.
Even infants in swaddling clothes
were pinched to death.
Many of the Dù clan were also wrongfully implicated.
Fúxiūzǐ commented:
'This was the crime of the rebellious Wéi clan.
What fault had their distant relatives?
It is like Rǎn Mǐn killing the Hú people;
those with high noses died unjustly.
Like Dǒng Zhuó executing the eunuchs;
those without beards were slaughtered indiscriminately.
Life and death are matters of fate.'
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi* (Abundant Records from Court and Country).
Zhāng Jiāfú
During the Táng rebellion of the Wéi clan,
Zhāng Jiāfú, the Minister of Personnel, was Pacification Commissioner for the Héběi Circuit.
When he reached the Wǔzhì post station in Huáizhōu,
an edict arrived ordering his execution at that very place.
Shortly after, another edict arrived pardoning him.
The messenger fell into a deep sleep on his horse,
delaying his journey by one post station.
By the time he arrived,
Zhāng had already been executed.
Is fate not Heaven's will?
Is Heaven's will not fate?
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi* (Abundant Records from Court and Country).
Sòng Yùn
When Emperor Míng of Táng was still a Prince,
he was acquainted with Sòng Yùn, the elder brother of Sòng Xuānyuǎn, Prefect of Jiàngzhōu.
After ascending the throne,
he often remembered him,
and wanted to appoint him to office.
Yùn, knowing his own fate was meager,
hid away in an outer prefecture.
Due to his parents' old age, he returned to attend to them.
Upon reaching the Dìngdǐng Gate outside the capital,
he met a close courtier.
That person entered and reported:
'I have just seen Sòng Yùn.'
The Emperor was pleased,
and summoned him in.
Over more than ten years,
whenever the Emperor wished to give him an official post,
Yùn would himself know he had no official fortune,
and would memorialize:
'If you give Yùn an office,
you will hasten my humble life.'
Later, when Dù Yòuqí of the Directorate of Education was appointed Left Advisor of the Heir Apparent,
an edict ordered that Yùn be given a fifth-rank official post as per precedent,
and he was thus appointed Right Advisor of the Heir Apparent.
That very night, he died.
From *Dìngmìng Lù* (Records of Fixed Destinies).
Fáng Guǎn
During the Kāiyuán era,
Fáng Guǎn was serving as the magistrate of Lúshì.
Xíng Zhēnrén Hé Pú came from Tàishān.
Fáng Guǎn received him with sincere respect and courtesy,
and they strolled together hand in hand,
unaware that they had walked several tens of lǐ.
They arrived at Xiàgǔ Village,
where they encountered a dilapidated Buddhist hall,
shaded densely by pines and bamboos.
Hé Pú sat beneath a pine tree,
tapped the ground with his staff,
and ordered his attendant to dig several chǐ deep.
They found a vase,
and inside the vase were letters from Lóu Shīdé to Yǒng Gōng.
Hé Pú smiled and said to him:
"Do you remember this?"
Fáng then suddenly became clear-minded,
and just then remembered that when he was a monk,
Yǒng Gōng was Fáng's previous life.
Hé Pú said to Fáng:
"When you die,
it will surely be because of eating sliced raw fish.
After your death,
you should be buried in a coffin made of catalpa wood.
However, you will not die in your private residence,
nor in an official guesthouse,
nor in a Daoist altar or Buddhist temple,
nor in the home of a relative or friend."
Later, when he was demoted to Lángzhōu,
he lodged in the prefecture's Zǐjí Palace.
After lying ill for several days,
the prefect suddenly prepared sliced raw fish,
and invited Fáng to the commandery study.
Fáng also happily ordered his carriage.
After eating, he returned,
and died suddenly.
The prefect ordered a temporary coffin placed in the palace,
and the coffin was indeed made of catalpa wood.
From "Mínghuáng Zálù"
Sūn Shēng
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
in Hángzhōu, there was a man named Sūn Shēng,
who was skilled at physiognomy.
When he arrived at Mùzhōu,
the commandery governor ordered him to read the faces of all the officials.
At that time, Fáng Guǎn was the Registrar,
and Cuī Huàn had been demoted from Wànnián County Captain to Assistant Magistrate of Tónglú.
Sūn Shēng said:
"Both of you gentlemen will reach the positions of Chief Minister.
However, Fáng will hold the great treasure of imperial authority,
fittingly in the palm of his hand;
Cuī will later fittingly become the Governor of Hángzhōu.
Although I will not see it,
I should also receive your kindness."
Later, Fáng, as a Chief Minister, carried the imperial edict from Shǔ to Língwǔ to confer it upon Sùzōng,
and Cuī indeed later became the Governor of Hángzhōu.
Upon taking office, he inquired after Sūn Shēng,
but he had already been dead for ten days.
He appointed Sūn's son as a Yájiàng officer,
and provided grain and silk to relieve his family.
From "Mínghuáng Zálù"
Zhāng Jiāzhēn
During the Kāiyuán era,
the Emperor was eager to govern well,
and paid particular attention to the Chief Ministers.
He often wished to appoint Zhāng Jiāzhēn as Chief Minister,
but had forgotten his name.
At night, he ordered a eunuch to hold a candle,
and went to the Department of State Affairs to ask who was on duty that night.
"Who" originally written as "various,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.
He returned and reported it was Vice Director of the Secretariat Wéi Kàng.
The Emperor immediately ordered him summoned to the bedchamber,
and the Emperor said:
"I wish to appoint a Chief Minister.
I often remember his demeanor as an important minister of the time,
surnamed Zhāng with a two-character name,
now serving as a northern regional commander.
I do not wish to ask those around me.
For ten days I have thought of it,
but ultimately forgot his name.
You, try to say it."
Kàng reported:
"Zhāng Qíqiū is now the Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng."
The Emperor immediately ordered him to draft the edict.
He also ordered a palace attendant to hold a candle,
and Kàng knelt before the Emperor,
taking up the brush and completing it.
The Emperor greatly praised his speed and elegant composition,
and thus urged him to finish writing the edict.
He ordered Kàng to return to stay in the Department of State Affairs,
and the Emperor did not undress, waiting for dawn.
Just as he was about to issue the edict,
before half the night had passed,
suddenly a palace attendant again urged Kàng to enter for an audience.
The Emperor greeted him and said:
"It is not Zhāng Qíqiū,
but the Tàiyuán Military Commissioner Zhāng Jiāzhēn."
He ordered a separate draft of the edict,
and the Emperor said to Kàng:
"My intention was already decided,
so I can speak of the appointment.
Just now, as I was reading recent memorials from high ministers,
the first one I picked up,
was a memorial from Jiāzhēn.
Because of this, I suddenly became clear-minded,
and just then remembered his name.
This is also Heaven's revelation,
not a matter of human effort."
The Emperor was pleased to have found the right man,
and sighed again that appointments and dismissals seemed as if guided by someone.
From "Mínghuáng Zálù"
Dù Xiān
When Dù Xiān was young,
he once crossed the river from Pǔjīn.
The river's current was swift and turbulent.
At that time, many people were boarding the boat,
and the boatman had already untied the mooring rope.
On the shore, there was an old man
calling, "Scholar Dù, could you come down for a moment?"
His words were extremely earnest.
Xiān had no choice but to go see him,
and they talked for a long time.
The boatman, waiting for Xiān who did not arrive,
left his bundle on the shore and set off.
Xiān and the old man had not finished their conversation,
when he looked back and saw the boat leaving,
feeling very regretful.
That day, the wind was strong and the waves rough,
when suddenly they saw dozens of hands in the water clutching the boat, sinking it.
All the passengers died,
only Xiān survived.
The old man said to Xiān:
"Your future, sir, is extremely noble,
therefore I came to save you."
After speaking, he disappeared.
Xiān later repeatedly advanced to become a high minister.
From "Guǎngyì Jì"
Zhèng Quán
In the twenty-fifth year of the Kāiyuán era,
Zhèng Qián served as a Doctor of the Guǎngwén Academy.
There was a man named Zhèng Xiàngrú,
over fifty years old,
who came from Lǒngyòu to take the míngjīng examination.
He visited Qián as a nephew.
Qián treated him without any special courtesy.
Another day, he visited again,
and the courtesy remained the same.
Xiàngrú then said to Qián:
"Does Uncle know whether I am capable or not?
The Master said:
'If there should arise one who would continue the work of the Zhōu,
even after a hundred generations, his principles could be known.'
I am perhaps close to this.
If placed within the school of Confucius,
I would not dare to rank near Yánzǐ,
but compared to disciples like Yányǎn and Zǐxià,
I certainly have nothing to yield."
Qián was greatly astonished by this,
and so questioned him to test his knowledge,
to which his responses were like echoes.
Qián then shut his door,
and for several days conversed intimately with him.
He then said to him:
"If so,
why did you not strive for advancement earlier,
and instead delay until such late years?"
Xiàngrú said:
"I am destined to achieve fame only next year;
the reason I did not come earlier
is that the time had not yet arrived."
Qián said:
"What office will you hold?"
He said:
"After seven years,
I will be appointed as the County Lieutenant of Xìn'ān County in Qúzhōu.
When my term ends, I will die."
Qián said:
"Can I hear about my own future affairs?"
He said:
"From now, after five years,
the state will change its era name.
After another fifteen years,
a great rebel will rise in Yōujì,
and at that time, Uncle will be implicated.
If you can remain utterly loyal to the state,
you may only be demoted;
if not,
the outcome is beyond prediction."
The following spring,
Xiàngrú indeed passed the míngjīng examination.
After seven years,
he was transferred and appointed as the Lieutenant of Xìn'ān in Qúzhōu.
As he was about to take up his post,
he bid farewell as a permanent parting,
weeping as they said goodbye.
After three years,
an investigating envoy came,
and Qián asked whether Xiàngrú was still alive.
He said:
"A few months after his replacement,
he died suddenly in a Buddhist temple."
In the twenty-ninth year,
the era name was changed to Tiānbǎo.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānbǎo,
Ān Lùshān rebelled and captured the Eastern Capital.
He sent the puppet-appointed Western Capital留守 Zhāng Tōngrú to Cháng'ān,
forcing court officials to go to the Eastern Capital Luòyáng.
Qián arrived at the Eastern Capital,
and was appointed as a puppet Director of the Water Department.
Recalling Xiàngrú's words,
he feigned a stroke,
and sought the position of Market Supervisor to tarnish himself,
while secretly submitting memorials to the throne.
When Sùzōng ascended the throne at Língwǔ,
that year the Eastern Capital was pacified,
and the Three Judicial Offices were ordered to investigate and punish those who had accepted rebel appointments.
Because Qián's heart had not sided with the rebels,
he was demoted to Registrar of Wēnzhōu, where he later died.
From "Qián Dìng Lù"
Cuī Yuán
Chancellor Cuī Yuán
was poor and落魄 in his youth,
living in the region between the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
His maternal uncle Lǐ Yànyǔn served as Minister of Justice.
Cuī traveled from the south to the capital,
paid a visit,
and sought a minor official position.
Lǐ placed him in the academy,
where he studied alongside the younger generations,
but treated him with disdain.
One night,
Lǐ dreamed that he was shackled,
along with two or three hundred others,
driven by soldiers with weapons,
into a large government office.
Upon reaching the hall,
they were called in by name.
He saw a man in purple robes seated behind a desk,
and when Yànyǔn looked at him,
it was Cuī.
He then cried out pitifully from below the steps, begging for mercy.
The purple-robed man laughed and said:
"Take him into custody for now."
He woke up in great alarm and astonishment,
and told his wife about it.
His wife said:
Originally, there was no "said" character,
added according to the Míng抄本.
"You should treat him generously;
who knows if the dream might not come true!"
From then on, his courtesy increased daily,
placing Cuī in a separate courtyard,
and dining together in the main hall.
After several months,
Cuī requested to leave,
intending to seek a position in Jiāngnán.
Lǐ and his wife prepared a lavish feast,
with all their children present.
After the meal,
Cuī bowed in thanks and said:
"Such kindness and affection—
I do not know how to repay it.
I have often felt I have received excessive favor,
without understanding the reason.
I beg Uncle to enlighten me."
Lǐ laughed and did not answer.
His wife said:
"A close nephew is no different from one's own son;
we only worry it is insufficient,
how could there be any special kindness?"
Lǐ stood up,
and his wife then said:
"Your honorable uncle had an unusual dream last night;
you, sir, are destined for greatness.
In the future, when Uncle faces calamity,
the matter will rest with you, sir.
Can you specially intervene to spare him?"
Cuī said:
"How could such a thing be?"
When Lǐ returned,
he repeated the matter seriously.
Cuī merely felt uneasy,
and did not respond further.
Lǐ said:
"Jiāngnán is a distant place,
not suitable for seeking advancement.
I am well acquainted with Minister Yáng,
and will entrust you to him."
At that time, Yáng Guózhōng served as Chancellor and concurrently as Military Commissioner of Xīchuān.
After Cuī paid his respects,
he was treated with great courtesy by Yáng,
who then recommended Cuī as a巡官 of the military commission,
in charge of留守 affairs.
On the day of departure,
Lǐ generously gifted him with gold and silk.
Upon reaching Xīchuān,
within less than a year,
the rebellion of Ān Lùshān occurred.
Emperor Xuánzōng fled the capital,
and Cuī was appointed Military Commissioner,
and within ten days, he was made Chancellor.
At that time, the capital had just been recaptured,
and those who had been coerced into serving as puppet officials, such as Chén Xīliè, were all executed.
Yànyǔn was among them,
and after the charges were discussed,
Cuī, as Chief Minister of the Secretariat,
presided over the detailed judgment.
Indeed, they were all surrounded by soldiers with weapons and brought in,
their names called out one by one,
and the judgment pronounced according to the law.
When it came to Lǐ,
he cried out:
"Does the Chancellor remember the dream from years past?"
Cuī nodded,
and then pronounced the judgment to take him into custody.
After the session ended,
he submitted a detailed memorial about the matter,
and requested to use his official position to redeem Yànyǔn's crime.
Emperor Sùzōng approved,
issuing a special decree to spare his life,
and exiled him to beyond the mountains.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Qū Sīmíng
Zhào Dōngxī served as Minister of Personnel.
Regarding the procedures for selection in the Ministry of Personnel,
each year, the officials and clerks of the selection department,
according to old custom, were each entitled to one additional post.
When it came to recommending relatives and clansmen,
everyone would make their requests.
There was one clerk named Qū Sīmíng,
who, within two years,
had never spoken up.
Dōngxī said to him:
"According to past practice in the selection department,
each is entitled to one official post,
or one may also recommend others."
Sīmíng still did not speak,
but merely assented and withdrew.
Dōngxī grew even more puzzled by this.
One day, he summoned him again and said:
"With the authority I hold today,
over three thousand candidates for selection—
with a stroke of my pen,
I can turn poverty into wealth,
raise the lowly to nobility,
satisfy hunger,
all from my pen.
Everyone has made their requests,
yet you alone remain silent. Why is that?"
Sīmíng replied:
"A person's life and death are fated,
wealth and honor are determined by Heaven.
Official positions are predetermined portions;
if one has not yet encountered them, why be troubled?
For these three thousand people,
each official title and name
is already fixed by fate;
it merely borrows the Minister's pen.
Sīmíng knows that his own fate has not yet flourished,
and dares not trouble the Minister with trivial matters."
Dōngxī said:
"If what you say is true,
you must be a worthy man,
and moreover, able to know your own fortune and misfortune?"
Sīmíng said:
"I dare not claim to be worthy.
Next year, Sīmíng
will first be entitled to receive an official post under the Minister,
which is why I have not yet made a request."
Dōngxī said:
"What post will you receive next year?"
Sīmíng said:
"I have forgotten that!"
Dōngxī said:
"How so?"
Sīmíng said:
"I now request to write down at the foot of the steps the month and day next year when I will receive an official post under the Minister,
as well as the salary and allowances I request,
and also ask the Minister to seal and record it together.
I ask to break a wall in the hall,
place the written record inside,
then seal it with plaster.
If, on the day I receive the post next year,
there is the slightest discrepancy,
I am willing to die at the foot of the steps."
Then he bowed twice and left.
Although Dōngxī said nothing,
in his heart he often thought it absurd and fantastic,
and often considered assigning him a different post.
Suddenly, one day,
the Emperor visited the hot springs,
saw a white deer ascending to heaven,
and thus changed the name of Huìchāng County to Zhāoyìng.
An edict was issued to the Ministry of Personnel,
ordering the assignment of officials there.
Dōngxī then assigned Sīmíng to that county.
After the matter was completed,
he summoned him and asked:
"Yesterday, the Emperor visited the hot springs,
a white deer ascended to heaven,
and the county was renamed Zhāoyìng.
This county is no different from Cháng'ān and Wànnián;
now I have assigned you a post there.
You spoke recklessly earlier—
could you have known this in advance?"
Sīmíng bowed and replied:
"I ask the Minister to break the wall and verify it."
So they dismantled the wall and opened the seal,
and saw the inscription, which read:
On such-and-such month and day next year,
the Emperor will visit the hot springs,
change the county's name to Zhāoyìng,
and I will be assigned a post there,
along with the salary and allowances I requested.
Not a single error.
Dōngxī was greatly astonished.
Thereafter, whenever anything happened,
he would send messengers to ask Sīmíng,
and there was never a prediction that did not prove miraculously accurate.
When Dōngxī left the Ministry of Personnel,
he sent someone to ask Sīmíng
what post he would next receive.
Sīmíng replied:
"You will receive a large commandery to the west."
And indeed, after about ten days,
the Emperor summoned Dōngxī,
asking about the customs and conditions of Jiāngxī.
Dōngxī's reply pleased the Emperor,
who then said:
"Dōngxī is truly a parent to Yùzhāng."
He was then appointed as Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngnán.
After arriving at the commandery,
whenever anything happened, he would send messengers to ask Sīmíng,
