and there was never a response that did not come true.
Two years later,
Dōngxī fell gravely ill.
He sent someone to ask Sīmíng,
who replied:
"You may arrange your family affairs."
Dōngxī knew he could not escape death,
and his illness grew critical until he passed away.
From "Huìchāng Jiěyí."
Mǎ Yóuqín
The clerk Mǎ Yóuqín of the Ministry of Personnel,
during the Kāiyuán era,
was due for reassignment upon completing his term.
At the time, Vice Minister Péi Guāngtíng,
considering him a long-serving clerk in the selection department,
asked what he desired.
Yóuqín did not reply.
When pressed,
he said:
"I already know what post I will receive,
and dare not make any further request."
Guāngtíng said:
"The decision lies with me—
how could you know?"
Yóuqín did not answer,
nor did he show any fear.
Guāngtíng angrily said:
"Since you know, you may as well speak."
Yóuqín said:
"This can be recorded,
but not spoken."
So he was ordered to write down the details,
which were hidden between the pillars and beams,
to be opened after the official appointments were announced.
Later, Lǎojūn appeared at Líshān,
and the imperial carriage personally visited the place,
so Huìchāng County was renamed Zhāoyìng County.
Guāngtíng, thinking there had never been a Zhāoyìng before,
believed Yóuqín could not have known,
and thus appointed him as the county's record keeper.
On the day the appointments were announced,
they opened the recorded document hidden between the beams,
and it was exactly as he had said.
From "Qiándìng Lù."
Although Xiāo Huá had fallen among the rebels
(The original text had "city" instead of "rebels,"
amended according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
Lǐ Mì had once recommended him.
Later, when Mì returned to the mountains,
Emperor Sùzōng eventually made Xiāo Huá his chancellor.
He only recommended Xuē Shèng to draft imperial edicts,
but this never came to pass.
Someone asked Mì about it,
and Mì said:
"Shèng's rank is too low,
making it difficult to initiate."
So he placed Shèng's "Tug-of-War Rhapsody" on his desk,
hoping Emperor Sùzōng would read it,
and then recommended him again.
When Emperor Sùzōng arrived,
he indeed read it,
but was not pleased,
saying:
"The Son of Heaven is the sovereign father.
How can the Son of Heaven's jade teeth be compared to glittering gold coins?"
On another day, he recommended him again,
but it never succeeded.
Truly, it was fate.
From "Gǎndìng Lù."
Yīxíng
The monk Yīxíng,
during the Kāiyuán era,
once memorialized to Emperor Xuánzōng:
"Your Majesty will travel ten thousand lǐ,
and the imperial fortune will be boundless."
Therefore, during the Tiānbǎo era,
when the Emperor visited the Eastern Capital,
it nearly reached ten thousand.
And when the Emperor traveled to Shǔ,
upon reaching the Ten Thousand Lǐ Bridge,
he finally understood.
From "Chuánzǎi."
Diviners
During the Xuánzōng era,
there was a magician
who claimed:
"I can judge what a person will eat,
knowing each item in advance."
High officials vied to invite him.
Only Grand Master Lǐ Qīyún did not believe him.
He summoned the magician and said:
"Carefully see what I will eat tomorrow."
After a long while, the magician said:
"You will eat two plates of rice paste cakes
and twenty bowls of tangerine peel soup."
Lǐ laughed,
then ordered the kitchen to prepare a feast,
intending to host court guests the next day.
At dawn,
an imperial order
"order" (Míng manuscript,
Chén collated edition reads "edict")
summoned him for an audience.
The Emperor said to him:
"Today the Capital Governor presented fresh glutinous rice,
original text has "cake" after "rice",
deleted per Míng manuscript.
We obtained rice paste cakes.
You, sir, shall only
"only" (Míng manuscript,
Chén collated edition reads "stay")
eat."
After a long while,
they were brought in a golden plate.
Lǐ bowed and ate them,
forcing himself to consume them before the Emperor.
The Emperor said happily:
"You eat with such relish,
I grant you another plate."
He finished that too.
After returning from court,
a severe stomach ailment struck,
he could not eat anything,
only drinking tangerine peel soup,
until midnight when he recovered.
Suddenly remembering the magician's words,
he asked his attendants:
"How much tangerine peel soup did I drink?"
They replied:
"Twenty bowls."
He sighed for a long time,
then immediately invited the magician,
and richly rewarded him with money and silk.
From "Lost Histories"
Dù Péngjǔ
Chancellor Dù Hóngjiàn's father was named Péngjǔ.
Father and son having names resembling brothers
has a reason.
Péngjǔ's father
original text lacks "father",
added per Míng manuscript.
once dreamed of going somewhere,
where he saw a large stele
said to be the Chancellor's Stele.
Names already appointed were filled with gold characters,
while future ones were inscribed on the pillars.
He asked: "Is there a Dù family son?"
The reply was:
"Yes."
"Look for yourself."
Looking,
he remembered the surname had a bird radical with a trailing stroke,
but forgot the character,
so he named his son Péngjǔ.
And told him:
"If you do not become chancellor,
then for generations your names
shall have bird radicals with trailing strokes."
Péngjǔ begot Hóngjiàn,
showing names are predetermined,
let alone one's office and lifespan?
From "Collected Tales"
Lǐ Qīyún
When Grand Master Lǐ Qīyún was still obscure,
he was about to take the selection exams.
At that time, there was a recluse named Tián in Yángzhōu,
a man of mist and clouds,
quite prescient.
Lǐ went to see him,
asking what office he would obtain.
The reply:
"Lìyáng County Lieutenant in Xuānzhōu."
Lǐ said:
"Among the court officials,
I also have relatives and friends.
The office I hope for
is certainly not this low."
After a long while, Tián said:
"Better is impossible.
I am also uncertain.
Take a letter to Master Zhāng at White Crane Temple in Chǔzhōu,
he will know."
Lǐ arrived,
found the temple,
overgrown with weeds blocking the path,
as if uninhabited.
Knocking for a long time,
someone finally answered,
led him in,
and he saw Master Zhāng, very ancient.
The old man said:
"That Tián fellow is reckless,
rashly telling you, young master.
Do you not wish to know your office?
What did he say?"
Lǐ said:
"Lìyáng County Lieutenant in Xuānzhōu."
He said:
"No.
GuǎnTáo Registrar in Wèizhōu.
But later you will hold high office,
your fame resplendent and illustrious,
do not mind this."
Upon reaching the capital,
he was appointed Lìyáng Lieutenant.
Lǐ was astonished,
thinking Master Zhāng's words incorrect.
A few days later,
an edict overrode the appointment,
changing it to GuǎnTáo Registrar.
Then he realized Tián and Zhāng had elucidated it for him.
Later, both men disappeared without trace.
Tián's younger brother became Sīmǎ of Jiāngzhōu,
named Shìyóng.
From "Lost Histories"
Dù Sīwēn
In the early years of the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a student of the Imperial Academy named Dù Sīwēn,
who was skilled at playing the qin.
He often visited the mansions of nobles and high officials,
and whenever there were banquets or outings,
he was often invited to attend.
Once, he accompanied some guests and spent the night at Chénggǒu Jiāzuǐ.
In the middle of the night, the mountain moon shone as bright as day,
and all the other travelers were drunk,
but Sīwēn alone took his qin and leisurely drifted on the water.
Suddenly, an old man appeared, resting his chin on his hand, and came to listen.
Sīwēn assumed he was one of the guests,
and did not turn to look at him.
Only after he finished playing the piece
did he realize this was not one of the companions he had traveled with,
and he hastily set down his qin and stood up.
The old man said:
"Young man, do not be afraid.
I am Liáng Zhì, the governor of Hénán during the Qín dynasty.
I met with disaster,
and my body perished here.
In life, I loved playing the qin.
Just now, I heard you playing,
the strings and tuning were clear and transcendent,
so I came to listen.
It is rare to meet one who understands music.
Do not refuse, but play another piece for me."
Sīwēn played "Chén Xiāng" for him.
The old man said:
"When this piece was first composed,
I once sought it out.
The fingering and notes are slightly different from this."
Sīwēn then asked about the differences.
Following the old man's corrections,
the melody and rhythm became imbued with antiquity,
and carried much sorrow and poignancy—
something no one of that time had ever heard.
The old man then said to Sīwēn:
"Are you not a student of the Imperial Academy?"
He replied:
"I am."
The old man said:
"Why do you not seek fame and reputation,
but instead often act as an entertainer in the homes of princes?"
Sīwēn, startled and respectful, said:
"I accept your instruction.
May I also ask about matters of poverty and success?"
The old man said:
"My youngest son
is in charge of the registers of official salaries in the human world.
I shall ask him on your behalf."
Two days from now,
we shall meet again here.
When the time came, Sīwēn went to see him,
and the old man also arrived.
He then informed him:
"Alas,
you will ultimately not achieve fame,
nor will you hold a proper official post.
However, you will have an acting salary in Bāshǔ,
for nineteen years,
with a continuous income.
But be careful not to take a military post,
for there will be a great disaster,
not to be averted by any prayers.
Remember this, remember this."
Having spoken,
he vanished.
The following year, Sīwēn again failed the imperial examinations,
so he gave up pursuing them,
traveled west, and reached Chéngdū,
where he sought an audience with Commandant Wéi using his artistic skills.
The Commandant held him in high regard,
repeatedly appointing him to important positions,
and for seventeen or eighteen years he served with the army,
the various salaries he received
amounting to no less than twenty thousand coins per month.
He also married the daughter of a great general,
and his carriages, horses, and residences were extremely grand.
Once, his father-in-law wanted Sīwēn to serve at the military headquarters,
but Sīwēn, remembering the old man's words,
repeatedly declined and did not take the post.
Two days later,
he secretly petitioned Commandant Wéi,
who then appointed him as a Pursuit and Attack Officer.
Only after the official document was issued was he informed,
and he dared not refuse again.
He constantly feared the coming of disaster,
and requested a distant assignment,
but in the end, it did not happen.
When Liú Pì rebelled,
Sīwēn was in Lùtóu City.
The city fell,
and he was killed by government troops.
His family's whereabouts were unknown.
From "Qián Dìng Lù"
Liǔ Jí,
a native of Hénán,
was the son of Liǔ Shū, who passed the imperial examination and earned the jìnshì degree during the Zhēnyuán era.
His family resided in Lǐyáng.
Once, while traveling as a guest, he reached Nánhǎi.
The military governor, because his father was renowned among the gentry and scholarly circles,
arranged for him to serve as an acting clerk in Guǎngzhōu.
Not long after,
he married the daughter of a local chieftain, Madame Cén.
They had a son,
named Zèngzèng.
As his parents were elderly and his hometown distant,
he was unable to bring them to live with him,
so he took his wife and son to visit his family in Lǐyáng.
Less than two years later,
finding his household insufficiently provided for,
he traveled alone again to the southern regions,
and upon arrival, secured an official post in Méng County,
where he remarried, taking Madame Shěn as his wife in Wǔxiān.
Once, when he went to the commandery on official business,
only Madame Shěn and her mother, Madame Sūn, remained in the county office.
It was autumn at the time,
and after midnight,
the sky was clear and the moon bright.
Suddenly, through the window, they saw a small child,
who beckoned to Madame Shěn with his hand and said:
"Do not fear, do not fear,
I am the son of a certain gentleman."
He recounted the circumstances,
clearly and audibly.
Madame Shěn told her mother about it.
Her mother then asked who he was,
and what request he had.
He replied:
"I am Zèngzèng,
who died in body last July,
and have come to bid farewell."
"When ordinary people die young,
before reaching seven years of age,
because they have committed no sins during their lifetime,
they do not undergo karmic retribution.
Even if they are not immediately reborn,
they are mostly employed as messengers by the celestial offices.
I am currently assigned to such duties,
merely delivering documents back and forth to the underworld.
The celestial offices record people's good and evil deeds,
and send them monthly to the underworld;
during the intervals,
I am also able to stroll about leisurely."
Madame Shěn then told him:
"Your father has gone to the commandery on official business,
but he should be returning soon."
Shortly after, Liǔ Jí returned,
and Madame Shěn told him everything.
Liǔ Jí firmly refused to believe it,
saying:
"In these remote borderlands,
there must be monsters and spirits,
pretending to be human affairs;
is this not likely the work of mountain sprites or tree demons?"
That evening,
the child again beckoned to Liǔ Jí through the window.
Liǔ Jí was initially suspicious,
and sternly questioned him,
but upon hearing the full story,
realized it was no other ghost,
and then wept and sobbed with grief.
He then inquired about the cause of his untimely death.
The child replied:
"In the middle of last July,
while playing, I contracted dysentery,
and medicine could not save me,
leading to this end;
such is fate.
Now I am employed by the celestial offices,
and there is still no time set for my rebirth."
Liǔ Jí said:
"Since you belong to the underworld administration,
you must know the predetermined affairs of human life.
Try to check my fate regarding poverty or prosperity, and my lifespan,
and come tell me."
The child replied:
"Yes."
He came again two evenings later,
and said:
"The underworld officials have a great city,
where the noble and the humble, each rank,
all have their fixed positions,
like pieces arranged on a chessboard.
When people in the world are about to die,
sometimes half a year,
sometimes several months beforehand,
their names are called in this city.
I have already heard your name, Father, being called,
and I deceitfully answered."
Afterwards, he privately said to Madame Shěn:
"Father's name
has already been called;
he will not remain in the human world much longer.
In the future, if someone seeks to marry you, Madame Shěn,
be careful not to consent.
If there is someone named Zhōu,
who holds a military post,
then you may consent to him,
for you will certainly grow old together,
with abundant clothing and food."
The other recent events he described
all proved true without exception.
Another evening, he came again and said:
"Because my term of service is limited,
I can no longer come to the human world.
From now on, we part forever."
His words were sorrowful and mournful,
and he left, weeping.
Four months later,
Liǔ Jí indeed died.
Madame Shěn soon also drifted like duckweed to Nánhǎi.
Whenever someone sought to marry her,
she consistently refused.
Later, there was a junior officer from Chángshā named Zhōu,
who was in charge of the commandery's funds and silk,
and engaged in trade in Guǎngzhōu;
he sought to marry Madame Shěn.
She consented as soon as he asked.
She remains there to this day.
Mèng Hóngwēi of Píngchāng, who was acquainted with Liǔ Jí,
fully recorded these events.
From "Qián Dìng Lù"
Wéi Fàn
Wéi Fàn was a man
whose origins are unknown.
In the early years of the Dàlì era,
he resigned from his post as the sheriff of Jīntán County in Rùn Prefecture.
Traveling as a guest in Wúxīng,
he moored his boat by the water's edge at the Xīngguó Buddhist Temple.
It was the night of the full moon in the first month,
and men and women had gathered in great numbers.
Just as Fàn was gazing around,
he suddenly died a sudden death.
The county officials came to investigate and detain the body,
but before the matter was concluded,
after two nights, he revived.
He said:
"I saw an officer holding a summons come,
saying:
'The prefectural office summons you.'
So I went with him.
After traveling some tens of li,
we suddenly arrived at a city,
heavily guarded by soldiers.
Upon entering, I saw many old friends and acquaintances coming and going.
Fàn asked the officer in surprise:
'What place is this?'
The officer said:
'This is not the human world.'
Only then did Fàn realize he was dead.
Soon I saw several riders clearing the way as they approached,
and among them was one person,
dressed in bright, splendid clothes,
with a very imposing appearance.
Fàn stepped forward to look at him,
and it turned out to be an old friend.
He said in surprise:
'Why have you come here?'
He replied:
'I was summoned by an officer.'
That person said:
'My duty is to summon souls,
but I don't recall summoning you.'
Then, after thinking for a moment, he said:
'Ah,
a mistake!
The one summoned is not you,
but Wéi Fàn, the sheriff of Jīnxiāng County in Yǎn Prefecture!'
He immediately scolded the officer and sent me back.
Fàn, overjoyed at being able to return,
and relying on their old friendship,
then asked about his official salary and lifespan.
That person had no choice,
so he secretly told an officer
to lead Fàn to a separate courtyard,
and had Fàn stand at the gate.
The officer went inside,
brought out a red brush,
and wrote on his left hand:
'First Yáng, then Yáng again,
the later Yáng grows stronger year by year.
When the seventh month's festival arrives, return to the dark realm.'
After Fàn came out,
the officer who had originally summoned him also escorted him back."
After waking up,
he recounted the entire incident in detail.
The Buddhist monk Fǎbǎo, who loved unusual tales,
learned all the facts,
and thus passed them on.
Six years later,
Fàn was transferred and appointed as the registrar of Yángqū County in Tàiyuán.
After his term ended, he went to the capital.
By chance, he met a relative who was acquainted with the Salt and Iron Commissioner,
and thus was recommended to be the patrol officer of Yángzǐ County.
He held this post for five years.
In the first year of the Jiànzhōng era,
on the twenty-eighth day of the sixth month,
as he was about to go for his selection appointment,
he died suddenly from a violent illness at an inn in Guǎnglíng.
That day was the Beginning of Autumn.
From "Records of Predestined Events"
Xuánzōng
On the third day after Táng Dézōng's birth,
Xuánzōng came to see him.
Sùzōng and Dàizōng stood in order

The nurse brought Dézōng, still in swaddling clothes, to present him.
Dézōng's complexion was not fair,
and he stumbled forward,
which displeased both Sùzōng and Dàizōng.
The two emperors passed him up by hand,
presenting him to Xuánzōng above.
Xuánzōng took one look at him and said:
"Truly, he is my son."
He said to Sùzōng:
"You are not as good as him."
He also said to Dàizōng:

Dézōng
The two characters "Dézōng" originally read "ér ér" (and the child),
corrected according to the Ming Dynasty manuscript
reigned for twenty-seven years,
and died at sixty-three.
Sùzōng reigned for five years,
Dàizōng reigned for fifteen years,
so indeed they did not match him.
Later, when Emperor Mínghuáng (i.e., Xuánzōng) fled to Shǔ,
on the way he said:
"Tiáo Láng (i.e., Dézōng) will also come here once."
When Dézōng later fled to Liáng,
this proved true.
Thus we know that when a sage responds to Heaven and receives the Mandate,
enjoying the state for many years,
it is certainly not without reason.
From "Records of Refined Conversations"
Qiáo Lín
In the winter of the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, Qiáo Lín
traveled from Tàiyuán to take the imperial examinations.
Arriving at Dàliáng,
he lodged at an inn.
At that time, the weather was bitterly cold with heavy snow,
Lín's horse died,
and his hired servants all left.
Hearing that the sheriff of Jùnyí, Liú Yànzhuāng, enjoyed hosting guests,
he went to seek his help.
Among Yànzhuāng's guests was a man named Shēntú,
skilled in judging people,
who claimed to be over eighty years old.
He was quite arrogant and sat with legs sprawled, holding others in contempt.
Even when guests of renown came,
he never exchanged formal greetings with them.
But when Lín arrived,
he spoke with him in a very familiar and intimate manner,
which surprised Yànzhuāng.
After Lín left,
Yànzhuāng said to Shēntú:
"Whether other guests were worthy or not,
I have never seen you, sir, say a single word.
Yet this Qiáo Lín is merely a commoner in plain clothes;
why were your words so close?"
Shēntú laughed and said:
"This man is certainly no ordinary person.
Moreover, he will become your superior official;
you should treat him well,
and you will surely receive his repayment.
My speaking with him earlier
was actually to help you forge a friendly connection.
However, it is a pity that his temperament contradicts his vital energy,
and his heart does not match his substance.
If he attains the highest position,
he will not last a hundred days.
After passing seventy years of age,
he will die a violent death.
You should remember this."
Yànzhuāng then hosted him for several days,
generously providing him with a carriage and horses,
and so he reached Cháng'ān.
Shēntú also bid farewell,
saying:
"I have received your kindness,
and now I have a way to repay it.
I shall take my leave from here."
No one ever knew where he went.
Lín later passed the imperial examination and earned the jìnshì degree,
and successively served in high offices.
During the Dàlì era,
he was appointed as the prefect of Huái Prefecture.
At that time, Yànzhuāng was serving as the magistrate of Xiūwǔ,
and had mistakenly adjudicated a case resulting in a death.
The family filed a lawsuit protesting the injustice,
and an imperial edict ordered the censors to investigate the matter.
When Lín arrived,
Yànzhuāng was ultimately spared.
In the early years of the Jiànzhōng era,
Lín was summoned to the capital and appointed as Vice Director of the Secretariat and participating in policymaking.
He held this position for eighty-seven days,
then resigned due to illness.
Later, when Zhū Cǐ rebelled,
Lín had just shaved his head to become a monk.
When Cǐ learned of this,
he forced him to accept the rebel appointment.
After the recovery of the capital,
Lín also explained his situation.
Grand Marshal Lǐ Shèng
wished to spare his life,
but the emperor would not permit it,
and so he was executed.
He was seventy-one years old at the time.
From "Records of Predestined Events"
Zhāng Qùyì
Empress Zhāng, wife of Emperor Sùzōng, had a grandmother named Dòu,
who was the maternal aunt of Emperor Xuánzōng.
Emperor Xuánzōng’s mother passed away early,
and Dòu had the kindness of raising him.
During the Jǐngyún era,
she was enfeoffed as Lady of the Dèng State,
and the emperor held her in high regard.
Her sons, Qùhuò, Qùyíng, Qùshē, and Qùyì,
relying on imperial favor,
lived in extreme luxury.
One day,
the brothers went hunting together at the Wèi River bend.
Suddenly, a huge serpent, twenty feet long,
leaped upon the grass,
swift as if flying.
Qùyì, reining in his horse and bending his bow,
shot and hit it with a single arrow,
then ordered his attendants to hang it up and carry it along.
Soon, fog rose over the Wèi River,
and within a foot’s distance, all turned dark and obscure.
A sudden downpour and terrifying lightning
left them nowhere to hide.
By chance, they found a wilderness temple,
and Qùyì abandoned his horse,
heading straight for the Buddhist shrine.
Fierce flames and thunderbolts
followed and gathered heavily.
Just as the thunder and fire were descending together,
a voice was heard from the sky saying:
“Do not alarm the Vice Director!”
The thunder and fire abruptly scattered,
but soon gathered again.
Again, a voice was heard from the sky saying:
“Do not alarm the Minister of Works!”
The thunder and fire immediately ceased.
Soon they gathered once more,
and again a voice was heard from the sky saying:
“Do not alarm the Grand Commandant!”
After that, the darkness cleared away completely,
and they ultimately suffered no harm.
However, the dead serpent and the horses
were already lost.
Qùyì, confident that he was destined for wealth and honor,
within a few years,
fell ill and died,
having reached the office of Minister of the Imperial Stud.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
his daughter was selected for the Eastern Palace,
serving as a Fine Lady.
When Emperor Sùzōng recovered the two capitals,
the Fine Lady contributed considerable assistance,
and in the second year of the Zhìdé era,
she was invested as Virtuous Consort.
In the first year of the Qiányuán era,
an edict ordered the Secretariat Director Cuī Yuán to bear the tally and invest her as Empress.
And Qùyì, as the Empress’s father,
was posthumously granted official titles three times,
exactly as announced from the sky.
From *Jì Wén*.
Lǐ Mì
In the fourteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
on the third day of the third month, Lǐ Mì
rode a donkey from Luòyáng back to his country villa.
His attendants had not yet arrived,
when by the roadside there was a carriage gate,
and the donkey went straight in,
uncontrollable.
He encountered the household servants,
each leading out donkeys and horses in a group.
Mì then asked them,
and they all entered the residence together.
They invited Mì inside.
After he sat down,
he saw the wife and children come out and bow in a circle.
Mì could not fathom it,
suspecting they were demons.
He asked their surname and was told Dòu,
then secretly ordered a servant to ask the neighbors,
and learned they were indeed surnamed Dòu.
Mì asked the reason,
and they replied:
“I am Dòu Tíngfēn.
Please stay the night.”
Continuing to speak,
the situation made it unavoidable,
so Mì stayed,
though he was very afraid.
Tíngfēn then said:
“At the Middle Bridge, there is a diviner named Húlúshēng,
renowned for his supernatural abilities.
Yesterday, through divination, he told me
that within three years,
I would face a calamity of clan extermination,
and must find Huángzhōngjūn to avoid it.
I asked how to find Huángzhōngjūn?
He said,
‘Ask Guǐgǔzǐ.’
I asked again, how to find Guǐgǔzǐ?
He said, ‘Your name, sir, is the one.’
I should, on the third day of the third month,
take my whole family out of the city to search.
If I did not find you,
I would undoubtedly be registered for death;
if I did find you,
then with my whole family earnestly praying,
I would certainly be spared.’
Just now, my whole family went out to search,
and by chance encountered you, sir.
This is Heaven sparing the lives of my entire clan.”
They provided the utmost hospitality.
The next day, Mì asked to leave,
saying he would return to his estate in Yǐngyáng.
Tíngfēn firmly detained him,
sent someone to Yǐngyáng,
to convey urgent matters,
and bring back a reply from his uncle.
In this way, he stayed over ten days
before he could return.
From then on, Tíngfēn sent gifts without cease.
When Ān Lùshān rebelled,
and Emperor Sùzōng recovered the Western Capital,
as he was about to return to Qín,
he captured Shǎn Prefecture,
and seized the prefect Dòu Tíngfēn.
Emperor Sùzōng ordered his execution and the confiscation of his family property.
Moreover, as a relative of Emperor Xuánzōng’s maternal family who had served the rebels,
he was firmly imprisoned for execution.
Mì then presented the whole story,
and requested to send someone to question him,
having him write a statement to verify it.
Emperor Sùzōng then dispatched an envoy.
When the envoy returned,
the details were exactly as Mì had said.
Emperor Sùzōng was greatly astonished,
and immediately ordered his pardon.
He then asked what Huángzhōngjūn and Guǐgǔzǐ meant.
Tíngfēn also said he did not know,
and Húlúshēng had already died.
Emperor Sùzōng deeply pondered the matter.
He then said:
“All affairs under Heaven
are predetermined.”

Zhāng Rénhuī
In the Táng dynasty, Shěn Jūnliàng
could perceive matters of the underworld.
During the Shàngyuán era,
Vice Director of the Bureau of Appointments Zhāng Rénhuī invited him to sit and asked:
"Esteemed sir, when do you think Huī will be promoted?"
Liàng said:
"A gentleman of the ministry does not even warm his seat,
why worry about not being promoted?"

and Liàng said to the others:

From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Péi Xū
In the second year of the Bǎoyìng era (763 CE),
Péi Xǔ, the Director of the Bureau of Revenue, was appointed as the Prefect of Lúzhōu.
In the commandery, there were two exiled officials:
one named Wǔ Chè,
who had been demoted from Palace Censor to Chief Clerk;
the other named Yú Zhòngqīng,
who had been demoted from Vice Director of the Ministry of Justice to Assistant Prefect.
Three days after Péi Xǔ arrived in the commandery,
the two came to pay their respects.
Péi Xǔ was just sitting with them
when a clerk came in holding a name card, saying:
"Fáng Guān, former Registrar of Cháoxiàn County and now a guest resident, requests an audience."
Péi Xǔ was in the middle of reminiscing with the two guests,
and did not wish to see Fáng Guān.
He told the clerk:
"Thank Registrar Fáng for his visit.
I am currently with two guests;
please ask him to come another day."
The clerk relayed this to Fáng Guān,
who said:
"I have an old connection with the Prefect;
it is proper for me to pay my respects today.
I will not accept this refusal."
The clerk went back in to report to Péi Xǔ,
who said:
"I have no old acquaintances among the Fáng clan, either on my father's or mother's side."
He then ordered the clerk to ask for the names and official titles of Fáng Guān's father and grandfather.
Fáng Guān provided them in detail.
He also took from his bosom an old letter
and handed it to the clerk.
After reading it, Péi Xǔ looked deeply moved.
He immediately ordered plain mourning garments,
led Fáng Guān to the eastern wing, and offered condolences,
expressing great sorrow.
After Fáng Guān left,
before Péi Xǔ had even changed out of his mourning clothes,
he turned to his attendants and asked:
"Is there a government post here with a monthly salary of seven or eight thousand cash?"
The attendants replied:
"The one called 'Míng Zhúyào' is such a post."
Péi Xǔ immediately ordered the clerk to issue an official document appointing Fáng Guān to it.
At this, the two guests looked at each other,
greatly astonished,
but dared not ask any questions.
Péi Xǔ then sat on his couch, sighed,
and said to the two guests:
"Do not worry any further about your demotions and exiles.
Such matters were predetermined long ago.
I

In the seventh year of the Kāiyuán era (719 CE),
I was dismissed from my post as Instructor of Hénán Prefecture.
At that time, I went to Dàliáng,
where Lù Shìjiā served as the Warden of Jùnyí.
I went to visit him.
Among Lù Shìjiā's guests were Lǐ Kuí, Warden of Chénliú, and Cuī Qì, Registrar of Kāifēng, who were just dining.
Fáng Ānyǔ, former Assistant to the Military Administrator of Xiāngzhōu, arrived later.
The seated guests, hearing that he was skilled in physiognomy,
all requested readings.
Fáng Ānyǔ did not decline.
First, he said to Lù Shìjiā:
"Your official position will change twice more;
you will pass away thirteen years later."
Next, he said to Cuī Qì:
"From now, in twenty years,
you will become the head of a ministry or court bureau,
holding power and rank but without direct involvement in its daily affairs;
you will also enjoy longevity."
Next, he said to Lǐ Kuí:
"This year, your name will reach the Emperor's ears.
Within thirteen years,
you will reach the highest position among officials.
Twelve years after that,
you will be dismissed and lose your standing,
though the reason will remain unclear."
Finally, he said to me:
"After this, you will successively hold pure and important posts,
but you will not become a general or chancellor.
You will live to eighty."
After finishing, as he was about to leave,
he privately said to me:
"In a little while, I have something to entrust to you.
I hope you can come to my inn."
After Fáng Ānyǔ returned,
I followed him there.
When I arrived, his words were very earnest and confidential.
He said:
"Twenty-eight years from now,
you will go from being a regular Director to become a Prefect of a commandery in Jiāngnán.
I will have a son next year,
who is destined to serve as an official in the commandery you will govern.
On the third day after your arrival,
I will have him come to pay his respects.
However, this son's fate is meager;
he cannot bear great wealth.
I ask that you grant him a salary of less than ten thousand cash."
This man (Fáng Guān) is Fáng Ānyǔ's son.
Wǔ Chè and the others were all amazed by this affair.
Lù Shìjiā later was reappointed as Investigating Censor and then died.
Cuī Qì later became Assistant Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries.
When Emperor Sùzōng was at Língwǔ,
Cuī Qì submitted a memorial that pleased the Emperor,
and he was swiftly promoted to Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries.
After returning to Cháng'ān,
he was repeatedly sent on missions.
For more than ten years afterward,
he never actually attended to the affairs of his own bureau.
Lǐ Kuí that year was appointed Right Rectifier of Omissions,
and eventually rose to become Chancellor.
Later, he fell out of favor with the times,
and was exiled to the southern regions for twenty years.
He was appointed Chancellor of the National University
and sent as an envoy to swear a covenant with Tibet.
He died just as he was about to depart.
All these events were as predicted.
Fáng Ānyǔ passed the imperial examination as a Presented Scholar in the twenty-first year of the Kāiyuán era (733 CE),
and his official career ended at Magistrate of Nányáng.
From "The Records of Predestination"
Lǐ Kuí
Chancellor Lǐ Kuí, having passed the imperial examination, was awaiting assignment in the capital.
He heard that a certain Mr. Wáng in Xuānpíng Ward was skilled in divination using the Book of Changes,
and went to consult him.
Mr. Wáng would decide a hexagram for five hundred coins per consultation,
and those who came were as numerous as gathering clouds.
From morning until evening,
there was no order, and some returned without being seen.
Kuí, holding a bolt of silk, went early in the morning.
Wáng opened the hexagram for him and said:
"Are you not a candidate selected for your literary talent?
You are destined to become a county lieutenant in Hénán Circuit."
Kuí, proud of his talent and brilliance,
felt this position was unsuitable for him.
His expression became gloomy and angry, and he left.
Mr. Wáng said:
"Do not be resentful.
Within a few months from now,
you will become a Left Reminder.
What I said before certainly has its limits."
Kuí's anger had not yet subsided.
Wáng said:
"If it indeed comes true,
I hope you will honor me with a visit."
Because Kuí did not pass the examination in calligraphy and judgment,
he was appointed as the lieutenant of Chénliú County in Biànzhōu.
He then began to realize that Mr. Wáng's words had some evidence.
Later, he visited him again.
Wáng took a sealed letter from under his table,
about a dozen pages long,
and handed it to him, saying:
"When you are appointed as Reminder,
you may open this seal.
Otherwise, there will be great misfortune."
Kuí kept it.
After arriving in Chénliú,
the investigative commissioner Ní Ruòbīng, considering Kuí's talent, brilliance, and family prestige,
retained him to temporarily serve in the prefectural office.
It happened that the commandery had a matter requiring a report to the court.
They sought someone with connections in the central court,
and none was better than Kuí,
so they requested he go.
During the Kāiyuán era,
when commandery and prefecture officials surnamed Lǐ submitted memorials to the court,
they first had to pay respects to the Director of the Imperial Clan.
At that time, Lǐ Qiú was the clan elder.
It happened that the emperor was being honored with a title.
After Kuí paid his respects to Qiú,
Qiú, having long heard of his talent,
requested he draft three memorials,
to be submitted in sequence.
The emperor summoned Qiú and said:
"Among the memorials submitted by the hundred officials,
none compare to yours.
I greatly commend you."
Qiú kowtowed and declined, saying:
"These were not written by me,
but by my nephew Lǐ Kuí, lieutenant of Chénliú."
An edict was then issued summoning Kuí.
At that time, Kuí was lodging at the residence of his paternal aunt, the Madame Lú, in Huáiyuǎn Ward.
His family members heard of the summons,
and he did not dare to go out immediately.
When he learned the emperor's intention was to select him for promotion,
he then went out.
After the audience,
an order was announced for the chief ministers to test his literary skill.
At that time, Vice-Director of the Secretariat Chén set three topics:
The first was "Rhapsody on the Purple Silk Dew-Gathering Pouch",
the second was "Letter in Reply to Tibet",
and the third was "Memorial Submitting the White Peacock on Behalf of Nányuè".
Kuí worked from noon until evening to complete them.
After sealing them,
he requested:
"The first two pieces have no omissions or limits,
but the last one may have some doubts.
I wish to review it in detail."
When permitted to open the seal,
he crossed out eight characters,
and added two phrases in the margin.
After they were submitted,
he was appointed Left Reminder the next day.
More than ten days later,
he opened Mr. Wáng's sealed letter to look at it.
All three compositions were inside,
with the crossed-out and added parts exactly the same.
He immediately ordered his carriage to visit Mr. Wáng in Xuānpíng Ward,
but in the end, he never saw him again.
From "Records of Predestination"
Dàozhāo
During the Yǒngtài era,
there was a monk named Dàozhāo,
who said he was from Lánzhōu,
and whose secular surname was Kāng.
When he was young, he fell ill and was beyond cure.
Suddenly he awoke and said:
"I saw the retribution for good and evil in the underworld,"
and subsequently left home to become a monk.
He lived on Tàiháng Mountain for forty years,
his monastic discipline rigorous and austere.
He often spoke of people's future affairs.
At first, they seemed obscure,
but later they all became clearly verified.
Once, two guests came.
One was named Yáo Miǎo,
who had passed the Mingjīng examination.
The other was named Zhāng,
who had official rank through inheritance,
but his given name is not recorded.
The monk said to Zhāng:
"You will hold office four times.
Be careful not to receive salary from Fànyáng.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, you will fall ill,
and it will be incurable."
Then he said to Miǎo:
"Official rank is not favorable for you.
If you can join the army,
you will also have no lack for thirty years.
If you fall ill, do not let a foreigner treat you."
That year,
Zhāng received an official post in the Xiāng-Dèng region.
Later, through successive selections,
he always sought posts in southern prefectures,
and also obtained them.
Later, he again went for selection,
and indeed was appointed magistrate of Lúshì County in Guózhōu.
He died two days after taking up his post.
The day of his death
was indeed the eighth day of the fourth month.
Only later did he realize that Fànyáng was the ancestral home of the Lú clan.
Miǎo later failed the examinations
and followed an acquaintance to Róngzhōu.
Assuming a nominal military guard position,
he was promoted through various right-side military posts over thirty years.
Later, because he took another wife and sought to serve as an assistant,
he fell ill.
He took medicine from an old woman named Huáng and died.
Later, when they inquired into Huáng's background,
she turned out to be a maid released by a tribal chieftain,
and was a foreign woman.
From "Records of Predestination"
Lǐ Léng
The former Palace Censor Lǐ Léng
passed the imperial examination in the second year of the Zhēnyuán era.
He had a separate estate in Jiāngníng,
where his family resided.
That year, Grand Marshal Hún Jiān was garrisoning Pǔjīn
and invited Léng to serve as his administrative assistant.
Léng then said:
"What you desire of me, sir,
but I am unfortunately not accustomed to discipline and restraint.
I have long loved the landscape of Lántián.
According to my official rank, I should be eligible for a county lieutenant position in the capital region.
Although my service record is shallow,
given your high merit and prestige,
if you specially petition for me,
it will certainly be granted.
If I obtain this post,
I can welcome my elderly parents from Jiāngnán,
and with a modest salary,
my wishes will be fulfilled."
Hún then submitted a memorial recommending him.
Emperor Dézōng ordered the Secretariat to deliberate.
They should have followed Hún's memorial.
Léng heard that Master Sāng Dàomào's predictions were divinely accurate,
so he went to visit him.
He asked about the success or failure of his request.
Dàomào said:
"What official post are you seeking?"
Léng explained the whole matter in detail.
He replied:
"From now, it will be twenty years
before you are suited for this post.
You cannot obtain it now."
Léng did not entirely believe him.
After more than a month,
Léng visited the chief minister,
who said to him:
"Your qualifications and experience are shallow,
and you are not yet suited for a capital region county lieutenant.
How can you rely on Hún's high merit
to seek an undeserved advantage?"
He then checked the regulations of the Ministry of Personnel and submitted them.
At that time, the emperor was personally attending to myriad affairs,
and the memorial was shelved.
Léng returned to Jiāngnán,
and indeed encountered the mourning period for his parent's death.
Nearly seven or eight years passed,
and then he suddenly contracted a lameness disease,
lasting almost twelve years.
In the winter of the first year of the Yuánhé era,
he finally entered the selection process again.
The Ministry of Personnel indeed registered him for the post of Lántián County Lieutenant.
When announced,
he joyfully accepted it.
He then recounted the whole story to his friends.
From "Continued Records of Destiny"
Dòu Lú Shǔ,
originally named Fǔzhēn.
In the sixth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
he took the imperial examination but failed.
He planned to travel to Xìn'ān,
and presented his writings to the prefect Zhèng Wǔ
(Qiándìng Lù records Wǔ as Shì)
Zhān.
Zhān treated him with great courtesy,
providing him lodging and support for several days.
As they grew more familiar,
Zhān said to Shǔ:
"You have a compound surname,
so it is unsuitable to have a two-character given name.
I intend to change it for you;
what do you think?"
Shǔ rose to express his gratitude,
and requested the new name.
Wǔ Zhān wrote several characters,
such as Zhù, Zhù, and Shǔ,
saying:
"I am concerned that someone among your clan might share the same name,
so I have written several characters;
you should choose one yourself."
That night, while staying at the lodging,
Shǔ dreamed of an old man who said to him:
"I have heard that the Prefect is changing your name.
You will achieve fame after four attempts at the examination;
the character 'four' is very auspicious.
Twenty years from now,
you will become the prefect of this commandery.
He then pointed to an empty plot within the commandery and said,
'This is where you can build a pavilion.'"
After waking, he pondered this:
"Four" refers to the character Shǔ (署),
so he adopted it as his name.
Two years later,
he failed the examination again.
He thought the dream had not come true.
Those who knew of it sometimes mocked him.
Another two years later,
he indeed passed the examination.
This was precisely the fourth attempt after changing his name.
In the ninth year of the Tàihé era,
Shǔ was appointed Prefect of Qúzhōu from the position of Junior Supervisor of the Palace Library.
Upon arrival,
he toured the entire commandery
and found the empty plot indicated in his dream.
He then constructed a pavilion there
and named it "Zhēng Mèng Tíng" (Dream Verification Pavilion).
From Qiándìng Lù.
Mèng Jūn
During the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a certain Vice Director Mèng.
In his youth, he took the imperial examination,
but repeatedly failed for a long time.
He was about to give up,
yet had nowhere to return.
He sought refuge at the residence of his father-in-law, Vice Director Yīn,
but was treated with contempt by the Yīn family,
to the point of near expulsion.
He suffered from increasingly severe malaria.
He then said to his father-in-law:
"I am poor and humble,
and my illness is certainly incurable.
I fear I will defile your splendid residence;
I resign myself to fate
and beg to await my end elsewhere."
The Yīn family did not even speak to him,
merely giving him three hundred copper coins.
He left, not knowing where to go.
West of the street was a skilled diviner
who performed divinations every morning,
closing his shop and lowering the curtain afterward.
Mèng Jūn went to consult him,
fully recounting his hardships and wanderings,
and his impending death in a ditch,
offering all three coins he had received as payment for the divination.
The diviner then let him stay overnight
and performed a divination at the appropriate time.
After completing the hexagram, he exclaimed in surprise:
"Young master, in ten days,
you will hold an important position,
with a salary of seventy thousand coins.
How can you speak of poverty and lowliness?"
The diviner then provided him with generous support.
When nine days had passed,
there was still no news.
He returned to the Yīn residence,
where the Yīn family treated him with great disdain
and did not detain him;
he lodged in the stable.
The next morning,
an imperial decree appointed a commander of the imperial guards as Surveillance Commissioner of the rebel border region.
This man was a friend of Yīn
and hurriedly knocked on the Yīn family's gate.
Being a military man, he was illiterate
and said:
"I urgently need a memorial of gratitude,
and also to pacify the bandits and rebels.
There are many matters to handle;
do you have any relatives or friends who are literary scholars
who could assist me?"
Yīn thought for a long time
but could think of no one to recommend.
Suddenly, he remembered that Mèng Jūn had long taken the examinations
and could handle the task.
He hastily summoned him
and had him draft a memorial.
The wording was exceptionally refined and sharp.
The commander then requested to appoint him to a military staff position,
overseeing memorials and reports.
A few days later, he was granted an official post,
with a monthly salary of exactly seventy thousand coins.
This was precisely ten days after the divination.
From Yì Shǐ.
Lú Chángshī
Lú Chángshī, Junior Supervisor of the Palace Library,
had passed the imperial examination.
He was of a detached and indifferent nature,
disliking official carriages and caps.
He showed no interest in worldly gains
and resigned his post to go to Luòyáng.
He said to his relatives:
"I am an old acquaintance of Minister Yú from Zhèxī;
I will visit him in about ten days."
He also said:
"In my previous life, I was a monk.
The place where I meditated is still in Kuàijī;
I also intend to visit the remains myself."
His family found it strange that he planned such a long journey without preparing a boat.
Within ten days, he passed away.
From Yì Shǐ.
Hán Huàng
When Duke Hán of Jìn, Huàng, served in the Secretariat,
he once summoned a clerk.
The clerk did not arrive promptly,
so the Duke, angered, intended to have him flogged.
The clerk said:
"I have another affiliation,
so I could not come immediately;
I beg for leniency."
Duke Jìn said:
"A clerk of the Chief Minister
—to whom else could you be affiliated?"
The clerk replied:
"Unfortunately, I am also affiliated with the underworld administration."
Duke Jìn thought he was being deceitful
and said:
"Since you are affiliated with the underworld administration,
what do you oversee?"
The clerk said:
"I oversee the food provisions for officials of the third rank and above."
Duke Jìn said:
"If so,
what will I eat tomorrow?"
The clerk said:
"This is no trivial matter;
it cannot be revealed openly.
Allow me to write it on paper,
and verify it afterward."
The Duke then pardoned him but detained the clerk.
The next morning,
an imperial summons arrived abruptly.
After the audience,
it happened that the imperial chef presented food:
there was a bowl of sweet rice porridge,
and the Emperor gave half to Duke Jìn.
Finding it delicious,
he was given another portion.
After leaving, he felt bloated.
Returning to his private residence,
he summoned a physician, who examined him and said:
"Something is obstructing you;
you should take a small dose of tangerine peel decoction.
By evening,
you may consume fermented rice water porridge.
By tomorrow morning, you will recover."
Recalling the clerk's words from the previous night,
he summoned him
and looked at his writing:
everything was exactly as described.
He then asked further:
"Are all human meals
recorded in registers?"
The clerk replied:
"Officials of the third rank and above receive daily provisions;
those of the fifth rank and above who hold influential positions receive provisions every ten days;
all officials from the sixth to the ninth rank receive provisions quarterly;
those who do not receive official salaries receive provisions annually."
From Qiándìng Lù.
Lǐ Fǔ
During the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a candidate named Lǐ Duǐ,
who was preparing for the imperial examination
and whose reputation was extremely high.
Suddenly, he dreamed of a man in purple robes saying:
"You will pass the examination under the supervision of Vice Minister of the Rites Ministry, Gù Shǎolián."
Upon waking,
he reflected that among the court officials, there was no one surnamed Gù.
Shortly after,
someone sent in a calling card,
claiming to be Jìnshì Gù Shǎolián requesting an audience.
Lǐ Duǐ, startled, received him
and fully recounted that he was destined to be his student.
Gù said:
"I have just arrived at the examination grounds;
this matter is certainly impossible.
The following year,
Lǐ Duǐ indeed failed the examination.
From then on, he did not take the examinations,
but withdrew and returned home.
By the ninth year of Zhēnyuán,
Gù Shǎolián, from his post as Vice Minister of Revenue, temporarily took charge of the examinations.
Lǐ Duǐ had still not passed,
so he secretly went to visit him.
Just before the results were posted,
the current Prime Minister specifically recommended another candidate,
and Lǐ Duǐ failed again,
merely weeping in despair.
In the autumn of the following year,
Gù Shǎolián was appointed Vice Minister of Rites,
and Lǐ Duǐ then passed the examination.
From "Gǎn Dìng Lù".
Cuī Zào
Chancellor Cuī Zào,
when he was still a commoner,
was known among scholars of Jiāngzuǒ as the "White-robed Kuí".
At that time, there were four individuals,
one was Lú Dōngměi,
the surnames and given names of the others are lost.
Cuī was demoted and posted to Hóngzhōu,
where the regional commander, Prince Cáo, intended to appoint him as deputy.
At that time, Emperor Dézōng was in Xīngyuán,
and since Prince Cáo was both meritorious and a relative,
his memorials were always approved.
There was a hermit named Zhào whose predictions were often accurate.
Cuī asked him:
"The local governor has memorialized to appoint me as deputy commissioner;
will it be approved?"
He replied:
"It will not."
Cuī pressed him:
"Given the timing and circumstances,
it should certainly be approved."
The hermit said:
"Instead, you will receive a prefectural governorship;
the imperial decree will arrive soon,
to a place even farther than this."
Cuī did not believe him,
and asked again:
"It is certain;
I even know the name of the prefecture,
but I cannot say it in advance."
He added:
"On such-and-such day of this month, the decree will arrive;
you will first be condoled, then congratulated."
Cuī felt fearful for a long time,
because the day mentioned
was actually Cuī's personal day of mourning.
He then summoned Zhào and said to him:
"If the hermit's words prove true,
I will offer you a hundred thousand cash;
if not, you will receive five light strokes of the cane.
Is that acceptable?"
The hermit smiled and said:
"I am not fated to receive a hundred thousand cash from Attendant Cuī,
only to have Attendant Cuī build me a single bamboo hut."
His words grew even more extraordinary.
Cuī then asked him:
"And do I have the destiny to become Chancellor?"
He said:
"Yes."
Cuī asked how soon,
and he said:
"Only one or two official posts away,
no more than three."
On the day of his personal mourning,
all his colleagues knew of the prediction.
As evening approached that day,
they all gathered at the river pavilion,
intending to console Cuī for his mourning.
Everyone looked north, awaiting news.
By the Yǒu hour,
they saw a man from the north bank boarding a boat,
stripped to the waist and urgently hailing the boat.
They sent someone to ask from afar,
and he replied:
"I am a courier from the prefecture."
As he neared the shore,
they asked:
"What new appointments are there?
And was Attendant Cuī's appointment as deputy commissioner approved?"
He said:
"It was not."
"Instead, here is the decree appointing him Prefect of Qiánzhōu."
The gentlemen were astonished and laughed.
That evening, they indeed first offered condolences, then congratulations.
The next day, Cuī reported this to Prince Cáo,
and Prince Cáo offered the hermit Zhào a hundred thousand cash,
which he declined.
Cuī built him a bamboo hut,
and he happily moved into it.
He also said to Cuī:
"After you go to Qiánzhōu,
you will experience great alarm and fear,
but then you will certainly enter the capital."
Later, Cuī's maternal uncle Yuán Xiū became Chancellor under Zhū Cǐ,
causing Cuī anxiety and distress.
An official summons arrived for him to enter the capital,
and he was deeply worried.
At that time, his old acquaintance Dòu Cān was Chancellor,
and Cuī was appointed Vice Minister of War,
soon promoted to Jǐshìzhōng and given the additional title of Pingzhāngshì (equivalent to Chancellor),
receiving the appointment simultaneously with Chancellor Qí Yìng.
From "Jiāhuà Lù".
Xuē Yōng
Vice Minister Xuē Yōng
was seen as having the potential to become Chancellor.
At that time, there was a hermit named Zhāng who was skilled in physiognomy.
Cuī Zào was then Vice Minister of War,
and former Jìnshì Jiāng Gōngfǔ was together with him in Vice Minister Xuē's reception room.
Xuē asked Her mit Zhāng:
"Among those seated here, is there a future Chancellor?"
His thoughts were mostly on himself.
Zhāng replied:
"Yes."
Xuē asked:
"How many?"
He said:
"Two."
Xuē assumed one of them was himself.
He asked:
"Who are they?"
He said:
"Masters Cuī and Jiāng will certainly become Chancellors,
and at the same time."
Xuē was surprised and resentful,
falling silent and displeased.
Later, Vice Minister Cuī calmly asked Zhāng:
"Why 'at the same time'?"
He thought that Jiāng was still in commoner's clothes,
while he was already a Vice Minister,
so their situations were not comparable.
Zhāng said:
"Their destinies are thus;
they must become so simultaneously,
and moreover, Vice Minister Cuī will follow after Jiāng."
Later, Jiāng served as Gōngcáo of the Capital Prefecture,
and was appointed to the Hànlín Academy.
When everyone learned that the Jīngyuán general Yáo Lìngyán had entered the city to fetch Zhū Cǐ—
Zhū Cǐ had once commanded Jīngyuán
and won the army's hearts—
Jiāng submitted a memorial urging vigilance against him.
Ten days after the memorial was submitted,
Emperor Dézōng fled to Fèngtiān,
regretting not heeding Jiāng's advice,
and at the temporary court, promoted Jiāng to Jǐshìzhōng with the additional title of Pingzhāngshì.
Cuī became Chancellor half a year after Jiāng,
appointed from the position of Vice Director of the Chancellery.
Indeed, they became Chancellors simultaneously, with Cuī following Jiāng.
Xuē ultimately only reached the level of a ministry director.
Thus it is known that seniors should not underestimate juniors.
From "Jiāhuà Lù".
Zhèng Dé Lín
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Zhèng Dé Lín, a county lieutenant of Xiāngtán,
had his home in Chángshā.
He had a relative living in Jiāngxià,
and each year he would make one trip to visit them.
Along the way, he would cross Dòngtíng Lake,
pass through Xiāngtán,
and often encountered an old man rowing a boat and selling water caltrops and foxnuts.
Though white-haired, he had a youthful appearance.
Dé Lín would converse with him,
often touching upon profound mysteries.
Once he asked:
"Your boat has no provisions;
what do you eat?"
The old man said:
"Water caltrops and foxnuts."
Dé Lín was fond of wine,
and often carried Sōngláochūn wine when crossing to Jiāngxià.
Whenever he met the old man, he would always share a drink with him;
the old man would drink without showing much gratitude.
Dé Lín reached Jiāngxià,
and was about to return to Chángshā.
He moored his boat beneath the Huánghè Tower,
next to which was a salt merchant named Wéi,
who traveled on a large vessel.
He was also heading to Xiāngtán.
That night, Wéi held a farewell drinking party with a neighboring boat.
Merchant Wéi had a daughter,
who resided in the stern cabin of the boat.
A girl from the neighboring boat also came to bid farewell.
The two girls stayed together, chatting and laughing.
As midnight approached,
they heard a scholar reciting a poem from the river:
"The boat lightly touched, my heart knows well,
The wind is calm, waves still, the moonlight faint.
Deep in the night on the river, sorrows dispel,
Picking a red lotus, its fragrance clings to my clothes."
The girl from the neighboring boat was skilled in calligraphy.
Noticing in Miss Wéi's dressing case
a sheet of red stationery,
she took it and wrote down the lines she had heard.
She also recited them for a long while,
yet could not discern who had composed them.
At dawn,
they parted ways, going east and west.
Dé Lín's boat and Wéi's boat
left Èzhǔ together and traveled for two nights.
By evening, they moored together again.
When they reached the shore of Dòngtíng Lake,
Dé Lín's boat and Wéi's boat
drew quite close to each other.
Miss Wéi was beautiful and radiant,
like delicate jade blossoms, smooth as clouds,
lotus stamens gleaming on waves,
her hibiscus-like grace washed by dew,
her pearl-like luster brightened by the moon.
She was fishing from the water-side window.
Dé Lín caught a glimpse of her
and was greatly pleased.
He then took a foot of red silk
and inscribed a poem on it:
"Slender hands hold the fishing line by the water window,
Red lotus in autumn hues adorns the long river.
If you can, like the maiden who untied her pendant for Jiāo Fǔ,
Bestow upon me a pair of bright pearls."
He forcefully attached the red silk to her hook,
and the girl retrieved it.
She recited and pondered it for a long time,
but though she could read it aloud,
she could not grasp its meaning.
The girl was not skilled in writing,
and ashamed to have nothing to offer in return,
she used her fishing line to send over the red paper inscribed the previous night by the girl from the neighboring boat.
Dé Lín thought she had composed it herself,
and, lost in thought,
"Lost in thought" originally read "doubtful";
emended according to the Ming manuscript copy.
he was quite pleased,
his joy evident.
Yet he could not understand the poem's meaning,
nor find a way to express his feelings.
Thereafter, the girl tied the red silk she received around her arm,
cherishing it dearly.
Under the bright moon and clear breeze,
Wéi's boat suddenly hoisted sail and departed.
The wind grew stronger,
the waves fearsome.
Dé Lín's small boat
dared not follow.
He felt deeply regretful.
As evening approached,
a fisherman told Dé Lín:
"That merchant's large boat
has already perished with all aboard in Dòngtíng Lake."
Dé Lín was greatly shocked.
His spirit wandered,
and he grieved for a long time,
unable to suppress his sorrow.
As night fell,
he composed two poems mourning the river maiden:
"O wild wind on the lake, blow not so fierce,
Where waves first break, the moonlight faint appears.
In silent depths, I think of her brimming tears,
Would that I might weep with the mermaid here."
And another:
"On Dòngtíng Lake, the breeze is soft, the reeds autumn-hued,
The newly lost dark moth stirs fine waves of sorrow.
Tears fall on duckweed, unseen by you,
Under the bright moon, light gulls on the river fly."
When the poems were finished,
he poured a libation and cast them into the water.
His essence reached the deities,
his utmost sincerity evoked a response,
and thus he moved the water god,
who took the poems to the underwater palace.
The palace lord read them
and summoned several of the drowned, saying:
"Who among you is beloved by Zhèng Shēng?"
But Miss Wéi could not understand the reason for this.
An attendant searched her arm,
saw the red silk, and reported to the palace lord,
saying:
"Dé Lín will one day be a wise magistrate of our district.
Moreover, he once showed me kindness;
I cannot but spare your life."
He then summoned the attendant,
ordering him to escort Miss Wéi to Zhèng Shēng.
Miss Wéi looked at the palace lord
and saw he was an old man.
Following the attendant, she hurried along unobstructed.
As the path neared its end,
she beheld a large pond,
its waters deep and azure.
The attendant then pushed her into it.
She sank and floated,
suffering greatly.
It was already the third watch of the night.
Dé Lín had not yet slept,
but was reciting the poem on the red paper,
his grief growing ever more bitter.
Suddenly, he felt something bump against the boat.
The boatmen were already asleep,
so Dé Lín took a torch to look.
He saw embroidered clothing that seemed to belong to a person.
Startled, he rescued her,
and it was Miss Wéi,
the red silk still tied around her arm.
Dé Lín was overjoyed.
After a long while,
the girl revived.
By dawn,
she could speak.
She explained that the palace lord, moved by him, had spared her life.
Dé Lín asked:
"Who is the palace lord?"
But he never came to understand.
He then took her as his wife,
marveling at this strange event,
and prepared to return to Chángshā.
Three years later,
Dé Lín was due for a regular transfer
and sought appointment as magistrate of Lǐlíng.
Miss Wéi said:
"You will not get that, but will become magistrate of Bālíng instead."
Dé Lín asked:
"How do you know?"
Miss Wéi replied:
"The water palace lord said you would be a wise magistrate of our district.
Dòngtíng Lake belongs to Bālíng,
so this can be verified."
Dé Lín kept this in mind.
When the appointment came, he indeed became magistrate of Bālíng.
Upon arriving at Bālíng County,
he sent someone to fetch Miss Wéi.
When the boat reached the shore of Dòngtíng Lake,
it encountered a headwind and could not advance.
Dé Lín sent five hired oarsmen to meet her,
among whom was an old man
who rowed as if without care.
Miss Wéi grew angry and spat at him.
The old man looked back and said:
"I once saved your life in the water palace.
Not only are you ungrateful,
now you show anger instead."
Only then did Miss Wéi realize who he was.
Terrified,
she invited the old man aboard the boat,
bowed, and offered him wine and fruit,
kowtowing, saying:
"My parents
must be in the water palace.
May I visit them?"
He said:
"You may."
In a moment,
the boat seemed to sink beneath the waves,
yet nothing was amiss.
Soon they reached the former water palace,
where all aboard wailed and wept.
She inquired after her parents.
The parents' dwelling was solemn and orderly,
their residence no different from those in the human world.
Wéi Shì asked what they needed,
and her parents said:
"All things that drown
can reach this place.
However, there is no fire for cooking,
so we eat only water caltrops and foxnuts."
They took several silver vessels and gave them to their daughter, saying:
"We have no use for these here,
so we can give them to you.
You cannot stay long."
They urged her to bid farewell.
Wéi Shì then sorrowfully parted from her parents.
The old man wrote in large characters on Wéi Shì's headscarf:
"Once by the river, the man of caltrops and nuts,
favored by your repeated drinks of pine-brewed spring.
Reviving your family as repayment,
cherish this, Zhèng Dé Lín of Chángshā."
After writing,
the old man then had several hundred servants
welcome her back to the mansion from the boat.
In a moment,
the boat emerged again by the lakeside.
Everyone on the boat
witnessed this.
Dé Lín examined the poem's meaning,
and only then realized that the old man of the water palace
was the former seller of water caltrops and foxnuts.
Over a year later,
a scholar named Cuī Xī Zhōu submitted a volume of poems to Dé Lín,
which included a poem about picking up lotus blossoms on the river at night—
precisely the poem on red paper that Wéi Shì had thrown to Dé Lín.
Dé Lín doubted the poem,
so he questioned Xī Zhōu.
He replied:
"Several years ago,
I moored a light boat at È Zhǔ.
The moon was bright over the river,
and as I had not yet slept,
a small object touched the boat,
its fragrance assailing my nose.
I picked it up to look,
and it was a bunch of lotus blossoms.
Thus I composed a poem,
and after reciting it for a long time,
I dare to answer truthfully."
Dé Lín sighed and said:
"It is fate."
Afterward, he dared not cross Dòngtíng Lake again.
Dé Lín rose to the office of prefectural governor.
From "The Tale of Dé Lín,"
"Classified Stories" 32 cites it as "Legends."
Zhào Jǐng and Lú Mài
Chancellors Zhào Jǐng and Lú Mài were both from Jízhōu,
and the traveling crowd called them Zhào the Seventh and Lú the Third.
Chancellor Zhào rose from obscurity to prominence,
largely because he was the son-in-law of Yáo Kuàng.
Yáo was on good terms with Dúgū Wèn Sú,
so he entrusted him,
and obtained the post of assistant in Húnán.
Through successive recommendations, he rose to the post of investigating censor.
When Chancellor Xiāo succeeded Wèn Sú as governor of Tánzhōu,
someone again recommended him to Xiāo,
who retained him as assistant,
and he rose to attendant censor.
When Xiāo entered court,
he was left in charge of affairs,
and his fine reputation
reached Emperor Dézōng,
so he was additionally appointed vice censor-in-chief,
becoming Húnán's surveillance commissioner
(original text had "commissioner" as "historian,"
amended according to the Xǔ edition)
When Lǐ Mì became chancellor,
he was unaware of him.
Soon after, Lǐ Yuán Sù was appointed to oversee Jǐng's Húnán affairs,
and Jǐng was summoned back to the capital.
Jǐng lived in the capital,
preferring quiet,
staying behind closed doors in a deep alley, not going out.
Yuán Sù visited him frequently.
Yuán Sù was Chancellor Mì's cousin.
Jǐng then went to bid farewell to Yuán Sù at Qīnglóng Temple,
saying to him:
"Zhào Jǐng should also have an official post,
and I swear I dare not resent others.
Truly, it is not accidental,
for I learned it from a fortune-teller."
He then secretly asked Yuán Sù about his own fate and lifespan.
Yuán Sù said:
"According to this fate,
you are also destined to be a man of wealth and honor."
Yuán Sù thus became self-assured,
and did not mention that Chancellor Mì was his elder brother.
Shortly after,
Emperor Dézōng suddenly remembered Jǐng,
granted him an audience,
and appointed him as a supervising secretary.
Chancellor Mì could not fathom the reason.
When there was a mission to make peace with the barbarians,
the newly appointed chancellor Guān Bō was made chief envoy,
with Zhāng Jiàn and Zhāng Huò as assistants.
Mì then submitted a memorial appointing Jǐng as deputy envoy.
Before reaching the barbarian lands,
a vacancy arose for vice director of the right,
and the chancellors submitted names.
Emperor Dézōng said:
"Zhào Jǐng is fit for this post."
He was summoned back and appointed vice director of the right.
Within a few months,
he was promoted to vice director of the left of the Department of State Affairs and became chancellor.
He served as chancellor for five years,
and died in office.
From "Records of Refined Conversation."
Zhào Jǐng
When Chancellor Zhào Jǐng was deputy envoy to the barbarians,
he said to the two assistant officials, Zhāng:
"A few miles ahead, there should be a river,
by the river there is a willow tree,
and under the tree there should be an official,
standing in mourning clothes."
Soon it was exactly so,
and the official was the quartering officer.
The two Zhāng asked him about it,
and Zhào said:
"Before I turned thirty,
I had already dreamed of this journey,
so I do not resent the chancellor of that time."
When Chancellor Zhào was about to die,
the households of the imperial guards at the various city gates of Cháng'ān
saw a small boy,
wearing a leopard-patterned apron,
carrying a five-colored rope,
looking for Chancellor Zhào.
Those who saw him knew it was strange.
Not many days later,
Zhào died.
From "Records of Refined Conversation."
Bāo Yì
Táng Bāo Yì was a man from
Jiāngdōng,
endowed with literary talent.
Initially, he traveled with the examination candidates
to the capital,
but arrived too late for the examination period.
A clansman, the Sacrificial Wine Jí, took pity on him
and lodged him in his private residence.
Yì often frequented Buddhist temples.
Before long,
he offended the Secretariat Drafter Liú Tàizhēn.
Tàizhēn, observing his appearance and status,
recognized him as a provincial graduate.
He ordered a servant to inquire about him,
but Yì retorted angrily:
"Provincial graduate Bāo Yì,
we have never met,
why trouble yourself to ask?"
Tàizhēn bore a deep grudge against him for this.
He even went specially to Jí to inquire about the man.
Upon hearing what Yì had done,
Jí was furious,
and after questioning and reprimanding him,
sent him to move to another lodging.
Yì showed no sign of shame.
The following year,
Tàizhēn presided over the examinations,
intent on ensuring Yì's permanent failure.
Therefore, he deliberately failed him in the miscellaneous essays,
intending to dismiss him clearly after the final session.
But then he regretted it, thinking to himself:
"Since this fellow has offended me,
to retaliate against him for it
would make me a petty man.
If I can ensure his permanent ruin,
why must it be done here?"
Thus, he passed him in the policy essays.
When Tàizhēn was about to post the list of successful candidates,
he first presented it to the Chief Minister.
On the list was a candidate with the surname Zhū who had passed.
The Chief Minister at the time, because the rebel Cǐ had recently committed great treason,
did not wish for this
"this" character originally absent,
added according to the *Zhìyán*
surname to pass,
and urgently ordered it changed.
Tàizhēn, startled and flustered, hurried out,
and could not recall any other candidate,
remembering only Yì.
When Yì
"when Yì" two characters originally absent,
added according to the *Zhìyán*
came to express his gratitude,
Tàizhēn then realized it was the man he detested.
He thus spoke frankly about it.
And thus it was understood that gain and loss are not within human power,
but are merely manipulated by unseen hands.
From *Zhìyán*
Xuē Shàoyīn
Xuē Shàoyīn from Hédōng sat for the imperial examination.
Suddenly one day,
he died abruptly in Chóngyì Ward of Cháng'ān.
An envoy holding a document appeared,
saying:
"The Grand Commissioner summons you."
He led him through the gate of a government office.
Once inside,
he saw an official,
who turned out to be Xiānyú Shūmíng.
Shàoyīn wanted to lodge a complaint.
Shūmíng said:
"The Cold Food Festival is approaching;
why are you carving eggs to eat?"
To the east, there was a monk,
holding a jeweled pagoda.
When the fan opened,
Shàoyīn was already inside it.
Shūmíng said:
"I was just about to report this matter;
why has the reverend saved this man?"
Then he was forced out,
and ordered to be taken to see the Judge.
Upon reaching the western courtyard outside the gate,
the gatekeeper went in to announce them.
After a short while,
they heard the order to enter only after changing into plain clothes.
The person he saw was his deceased elder brother.
After weeping and conversing for a long time,
his brother said:
"Because you have not yet achieved fame,
I wanted to recommend you here,
to share in handling official duties.
That is why I had you summoned;
it was for no other reason."
Shàoyīn had just recently married,
and earnestly wished not to stay.
His brother said:
"In the same office, there is Judge Wáng,
who holds a position in the Western Bureau.
Since you have come here,
you may pay him a visit before leaving."
He then instructed Shàoyīn to see him in the western courtyard,
where he was received with great hospitality.
Soon, a feast was prepared,
with delicacies from land and sea all laid out.
Before he could eat,
Judge Wáng suddenly stood up,
and saw the monk holding the pagoda from earlier.
The monk said:
"You must not eat;
if you eat, there will be no way to return."
Shàoyīn said:
"I am very hungry;
what should I do?"
The monk said:
"Only candied ginger may be eaten."
So he took some and ate it.
But Judge Wáng never returned.
The monk said:
"You may leave now."
Shàoyīn went out again,
approached his brother in tears,
and asked to depart.
His brother, knowing he could not be kept,
went in to inform the official,
who granted permission.
Shàoyīn said:
"Since I am to return to the human world,
I wish to know what office I will hold."
His brother said:
"This is very difficult to say;
and what use is it to know?"
Upon his earnest request,
his brother summoned a clerk,
who fetched the register and searched through it,
not allowing Shàoyīn to see it.
He said:
"You will achieve fame only in the year after next.
Your first appointment will be obtained in the far west;
next, you will serve as a registrar and assistant magistrate in the capital region;
then another post in the far south.
Beyond that, I do not know."
At parting,
his brother said:
"I used to have a servant named Lǐ Jùn;
I will have him accompany you.
In times of danger or urgency,
you may call upon him."
After leaving,
whenever he encountered danger,
he would see the monk leading the way ahead.
Shàoyīn said:
"Disciple, I have never met you before;
why does the reverend protect me like this?"
The monk said:
"Because you recite the Diamond Sūtra,
I protect you."
Upon waking,
he recounted the entire event.
In the spring of the following year,
he indeed passed the examination.
Not long after,
he was appointed Editorial Director in the Imperial Library,
and served as a Judge accompanying an envoy to the border tribes.
Upon returning,
he was reassigned as Registrar of Tóngguān County.
When his term ended,
he encountered Zhào Chāng, who was appointed Military Commissioner of Ānnán.
Shàoyīn had an old acquaintance with him,
and requested to serve as his aide,
hoping to fulfill the prediction of a post in the far south.
Zhào Chāng agreed.
He said:
"I am traveling by relay to assume my post;
there is no time to submit a memorial.
Upon reaching Jiānglíng,
I will submit a memorial to request it."
When the memorial arrived,
Shàoyīn soon went into mourning for his mother's passing.
After the mourning period ended,
he was selected and appointed as Assistant Magistrate of Wànnián County.
At that time, soldiers from Qīngzhōu and Zīzhōu fought with the household servants of the imperial son-in-law, resulting in deaths;
the Jīngzhào Prefecture did not report it promptly.
Emperor Dézōng was furious.
At that time, Shàoyīn was in charge of the banditry section
(original text: "jiè táng";
amended according to the Ming manuscript)
one day,
he was demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Léizé County in Gāozhōu.
For over ten years, he endured hardships,
and Lǐ Jùn often provided protection.
When Emperor Shùnzōng succeeded to the throne,
an edict was issued to reinstate demoted officials.
Shàoyīn was transferred to Guì
(original text: "guī";
amended according to the Ming manuscript and Chén's collation)
yáng,
traveling together with the demoted official Lǐ Dìng.
While crossing a river and reining in his horse,
he spoke with an attendant,
who turned out to be Lǐ Jùn.
He said:
"My term is now complete as of such-and-such day;
I bid you farewell and depart."
Shàoyīn said:
"My brother said my official career would end here;
now Lǐ Jùn is leaving too,
so my time must be short."
Lǐ Dìng was shocked and saddened by this event,
and upon asking,
Shàoyīn told him everything.
A few days later, he passed away.
From "Qián Dìng Lù"
Yuán Xiàoshū.
Yuán Xiàoshū was a man from
Chénjùn.
He lost his father young,
and was known for his filial piety in serving his mother.
His mother once fell ill and became delirious,
and did not recover for many days.
Xiàoshū suddenly dreamed of an old man who said to him:
"Your mother's illness can be cured."
Xiàoshū asked his name and residence,
but he did not tell,
saying:
"Tomorrow morning, meet me atop the stone altar,
and I will have medicine to give you."
Upon waking,
he then surveyed the surrounding area,
and within ten lǐ of his residence,
there was an abandoned temple with an ancient stone altar,
and he saw the old man there.
Xiàoshū was delighted,
and bowed in greeting, inviting him to his home.
The old man then took from his bag a pill of Jiǔlíng Dān,
and had her take it with freshly drawn water.
That very day, she recovered.
Xiàoshū was grateful to him,
and wished to offer something in return,
but the old man would not accept anything.
Sometimes he would come once every few months,
but it was unclear where he stayed.
Xiàoshū suspected he could predict fate, rank, and emolument,
and often wanted to ask,
but did not dare speak.
Later, one day he came and said to Xiàoshū:
"I will be going elsewhere,
and must bid you farewell."
From his bosom, he took out a volume of writings and gave it to him.
Saying:
"Your lifespan and official positions
are all recorded here.
These matters are predetermined,
and not within the reach of human intellect or effort.
Those who anxiously seek them now
merely toil in vain.
Keep this book of mine,
and be careful not to look ahead.
Only upon receiving an official appointment,
should you open one section.
If not,
there will be harm."
Xiàoshū knelt, received it, and they parted.
Later, Xiàoshū fell seriously ill,
nearly beyond saving.
His family asked about his final affairs.
Xiàoshū said:
"I have a book given by a divine being,
and have not yet opened it.
Why ask about final affairs so hastily?"
After over ten days,
his illness indeed improved.
Later, Xiàoshū, by virtue of family privilege, was appointed Wèichéng County Lieutenant of Mìzhōu,
and after five transfers became Línjìn County Magistrate of Púzhōu.
Each time he took up a post,
he would look at the divine being's book,
and the timing was never mistaken.
Later, when his term ended,
he returned to his country villa in Wénxiāng.
One morning as he rose,
and was about to comb his hair,
suddenly something fell into the mirror,
resembling a snake but with four legs.
Xiàoshū was startled and fell to the ground,
and then could not speak.
After a few days, he died.
Over a month later,
his wife, while going through his chest,
found the book left by the old man,
with still half a scroll remaining.
She then sighed and said:
"The words of the divine being
were also false.
The book is not yet finished,
yet the man has already died."
She then opened it to look,
and afterward there were only several blank sheets of paper,
with a picture of a snake coiled in a mirror.
From "Qián Dìng Lù"
Lǐ Gōng
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Lǐ Gōng, an arrest officer of Wànnián County,
in spring, with acquaintances, prepared sliced fish at an official pavilion west of the street.
A guest happened to arrive,
lingering without leaving,
his demeanor very arrogant.
Everyone asked what he could do,
and he said:
"I am skilled at knowing people's portions of food."
Lǐ Gōng said:
"Then look at today's sliced fish—
is there anyone among us who will not get to eat?"
The guest smiled and said:
"Only you, sir, will not get to eat."
Lǐ Gōng angrily said:
"I am the host,
and specifically prepared this sliced fish.
How could there be any reason I would not eat?
If this proves true,
I will offer five thousand coins.
If it is false speech,
you shall face hardship.
