Let those present be witnesses."
He then urged everyone to eat.
As they were about to start,
a man came galloping on horseback and said:
"The Capital Governor summons you."
Lǐ Gōng galloped off on horseback.
It happened there was official business,
and Lǐ Gōng feared it would be late,
so he sent word for the guests to go ahead and eat,
worried the sliced fish could not be kept waiting.
He told the cook:
"Just keep two plates for me."
Wanting to disprove the magician's words.
The guests were very surprised.
After a long while,
he came galloping back.
Everyone had already finished eating,
with only the reserved sliced fish remaining.
Lǐ Gōng took off his outer robe and sat down,
picking up his chopsticks and cursing.
The magician's expression did not change,
saying:
"What I saw was not wrong,
but I do not know why?"
Lǐ Gōng said:
"The sliced fish is right here.
How dare you still boast.
The earlier agreement stands.
How do you know I cannot hastily socialize?" Before he finished speaking,
the ceiling mud of the official pavilion collapsed,
an area several feet across,
falling down,
shattering the eating utensils,
and the sliced fish was mixed with dirt and filth.
Lǐ Gōng was shocked and amazed,
and asked the cook if there was more sliced fish.
He said:
"It is all gone."
He then richly rewarded the magician,
giving him five thousand coins.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Lǐ Zōnghuí
Lǐ Zōnghuí,
who was skilled in literary composition,
took the imperial examination.
Once he traveled with a companion from Luòyáng to the Guānzhōng region.
The companion said:
"I can predict in advance what people will eat and drink,
without the slightest error."
On the eve of New Year's Day,
they planned to go to Huàyīn County the next day.
The county magistrate was an old acquaintance of Lǐ,
and had sent a letter in advance.
Lǐ said to his companion:
"During the New Year festival, every household prepares special dishes,
especially since the county magistrate is my old friend.
Let's see what we'll be served
when we arrive tomorrow."
The companion clapped his hands and said:
"Brother,
[Note: "Brother" may be a miswriting of "strange"]
you and I will each drink a cup of pepper-and-scallion wine,
eat five kinds of wontons,
but get no rice to eat."
Lǐ did not quite believe him.
When they arrived at Huàyīn County,
the county magistrate sent word,
providing horses for them to ride,
settled them at an inn,
and invited both men to the county office.
Meeting them joyfully, he said:
"You two gentlemen have braved the cold,
so quickly bring two large cups of warm wine,
with pepper and scallions."
After a while, a tray arrived,
and a young servant whispered to the magistrate.
The magistrate said:
"Cook them all."
Then he said to the two guests:
"I have a daughter,
seven or eight years old,
who often says, 'Why don't you let me manage household affairs?'
Yesterday I was annoyed with her,
so I put her in charge of preparing the New Year's meal.
Just now she came to report
that there were five kinds of wontons,
and asked which kind to cook.
I said,
'Cook them all.'"
Shortly after,
the wontons were served in a large bowl,
and the two guests finished them.
Suddenly, an assistant official rushed in from outside and said,
"An imperial envoy has arrived."
According to custom, he had to be welcomed.
The county magistrate was startled,
hurriedly bowed to the two guests,
whipped his horse and left,
so the guests also departed.
They intended to finish their meal at the inn,
but their servants had already returned,
packed up and set off first,
having traveled several miles already.
The two men laughed heartily,
and together they continued their journey,
ultimately getting nothing more to eat or drink.
How strange—
such are the allotments of food and drink.
From Yì Shǐ
Cuī Pǔ
Chancellor Lǐ Pān
once resided in the Eastern Capital.
Approaching thirty years of age,
he had yet to gain any official reputation.
His wife was the daughter of Cuī Gòu
(The character "gòu" was originally missing;
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy)
the Vice Director.
Chancellor Lǐ was living with the Cuī family,
but they did not treat him very generously.
At that time, there was a fortune-teller named Hú Lúshēng at Zhōngqiáo
who, upon hearing
(The original text had the character "nǚ" below "wén";
deleted based on the Ming manuscript copy)
a person's voice,
could immediately discern their status, whether noble or lowly.
Chancellor Lǐ was suffering from a brain sore,
and also wanted to move his family to Yángzhōu,
which made him very worried and distressed.
He went with the Cuī brothers to visit Hú Lúshēng.
Lúshēng was fond of drinking wine,
and whenever people visited him,
he would always carry a gourd,
hence he was called Hú Lúshēng (Gourd Sheng).
Chancellor Lǐ and the Cuī brothers each brought three hundred coins.
Lúshēng was leaning against a rush cushion,
already half-drunk.
The Cuī brothers arrived first,
but Hú Lúshēng did not rise for them;
he merely extended his hand, inviting them to sit.
Chancellor Lǐ, due to his illness, arrived later.
Hú Lúshēng said:
"A noble person is coming."
He then ordered his attendant to sweep the floor.
Once finished,
Chancellor Lǐ had arrived.
Before he even dismounted from his donkey,
Hú Lúshēng smiled, greeted him, and took his hand, saying:
"Young master, you are a noble person."
Chancellor Lǐ said:
"I am poor and ill,
and moreover, I wish to move my family thousands of miles away.
How can there be any nobility in that?"
Lúshēng said:
"A person destined for the gauze lantern,
why fear hardship and adversity?"
Chancellor Lǐ asked about the matter of the gauze lantern,
but he never explained it.
Subsequently, he went to Yángzhōu.
He lived at Cānzuǒ Bridge.
In the administrative office, there was a senior official named Gāo
who interacted frequently with Pān and was very familiar with him.
One morning, he came to visit Pān.
After leaving,
he returned again in the evening,
which greatly surprised Chancellor Lǐ.
Once they met,
Gāo said:
"I came to pay my respects this morning,
but upon returning, I felt extremely tired.
During a daytime nap,
I dreamed of a person
who summoned me outside the city.
We walked through thorns and brambles,
and I saw an old estate tenant of mine,
who had been dead for ten years.
He said to me,
'Sir, you should not have come here.
You were lured by something.
You must return immediately,
and I will escort you back.'
He then led me to the city gate.
I asked him,
'How can you be here?'
He said,
'I serve as a minor clerk,
assigned to be on duty for Lǐ Sānláng.'
I asked,
'Which Lǐ Sānláng?'
He said,
'The one living at Cānzuǒ Bridge,
(Ming manuscript copy and Chén's collation note: "zhī" should be "zhī" (knowing) or "zhī" (of))
sir.'
'Since you interact with Lǐ Sānláng,
I am here to attend to you.'
I said,
'How can Sānláng be like this?'
He said,
'He is a person destined for the gauze lantern.'
I pressed him, but he refused to say more.
Then he said,
'I am hungry.
Could you, sir, give me some money for wine and food?'
'I dare not enter the inner city,
so please arrange it for me outside the city.'
I said to him,
'Can I get it from Sānláng's residence?'
He said,
'If you do that,
it would be killing me.'
Then I woke up.
I have already arranged for wine and food to be provided outside the city for him,
and I am here to report this good news to you."
Chancellor Lǐ smiled faintly.
Several years later,
when Vice Director Zhāng Jiànfēng was stationed in Yángzhōu,
he recommended Chancellor Lǐ for the positions of Patrol Officer and Editorial Director.
It happened that there was a monk from Xīnlúo
who could read people's fortunes,
and he said that Zhāng would not become chancellor.
Zhāng was very displeased,
so he ordered the monk to check in the administrative office
to see if any of the officials there could become chancellor.
The monk looked around for a long time
and said:
"None."
Zhāng was even more unhappy.
He said:
"Is there any official who has not yet entered the office?"
Someone reported:
"Patrol Officer Lǐ has not entered."
Zhāng immediately ordered him to be summoned urgently.
After a short while, he arrived.
The monk descended the steps to greet him
and said to Zhāng:
"This Patrol Officer is a person destined for the gauze lantern.
Even you, Vice Director, cannot compare."
Zhāng was overjoyed
and asked about the matter of the gauze lantern.
The monk said:
"For a chancellor, the underworld administration must secretly protect him with a gauze lantern,
fearing that he might be disturbed by malevolent beings.
Other officials do not receive this."
Only then did he understand what Hú Lúshēng and Gāo had said.
Chancellor Lǐ eventually became chancellor.
Truly,
a person's nobility or lowliness is predetermined.
From "Yì Shǐ" (The Lost History)
Wéi Zhíyì
Wéi Zhíyì was demoted from the position of chancellor to Senior Advisor to the Heir Apparent,
and further demoted to Military Advisor of Yázhōu.
Previously, when Zhíyì served as Vice Director of the Bureau of Operations,
the office presented maps of the various provinces.
Whenever maps of provinces south of the Five Ridges were presented,
he would always quickly order them taken away,
never examining them.
Later, when he became chancellor,
there was a map on the north wall.
After several days,
he tried to look at it,
and it turned out to be a map of Yázhōu.
He felt very disturbed by this.
When the time came,
he was indeed demoted to Yázhōu.
Two years later, he died at sea.
From "Gǎn Dìng Lù" (Records of Predetermined Feelings)
Yuán Zī
Fán Yángyuán, the Southern Section Judge and Palace Censor of Tángshān,
in the Yuánhé era,
went to the capital to present a memorial.
The various gentlemen at Qíxià brought musicians
and held a farewell feast for him at the Qīfāng Pavilion in the outskirts of Qí.
Among the staff were Supervising Censor Chén Shù and Dúgū Qiánlǐ, who had both been in the administration for six or seven years,
each lamenting their prolonged stagnation.
Yángyuán then said:
"A person's advancement or withdrawal
is nothing but fate.
I was originally named Yuányáng.
In the year I passed the imperial examination,
someone said I should go to the Western Prefecture to take up an appointment.
At that time, I was living idly in Luòxià.
I planned to go around the eighth month.
But in the seventh month of that year,
a cousin of mine who served as the magistrate of Mì County
sent someone to summon me urgently to Mì County.
I had no choice but to set out.
I stayed overnight at Yǒngtōng Gate.
That night, I dreamed of a tall burial mound,
on top of which was a person wearing hemp clothes,
as if preparing for a village drinking ceremony.
Looking around,
there were four other people.
The person on the mound
then beckoned to Yángyuán with his hand.
Yángyuán was unwilling to go.
Next, one person went up from in front of Yángyuán,
and another followed closely behind and ascended,
while the four people on the left and right all went up.
Suddenly, Yángyuán also wished to go,
so he followed and climbed up.
When the five of them reached the top,
they saw a document on the mound,
which was the list of recommended candidates sent by Hénán Prefecture.
The sixth name was Fán Yángyuán.
At that time, there was no Fán Yuányáng anymore.
When I woke up,
I found it very strange.
A few days later, I arrived at Mì County,
but then fell ill with dysentery.
It lasted for a full month,
and I was extremely exhausted.
When I recovered slightly,
I went straight back to Luòzhōng.
I said to my cousin:
"For the two prefectures to select candidates,
the old rule requires prior notification.
I am afraid I may not be selected by the Western Prefecture.
You, brother, should recommend me first to the magistrate of Mì County."
He said:
"That cannot be arranged."
He only instructed Mì County to recommend me,
insisting it was not a matter of entrustment.
By the time I returned to Luòzhōng,
it was already mid-September.
Friends in Luòzhōng advised me,
saying it would be better to seek recommendation from the Eastern Prefecture instead.
I had already missed the appointment with the Western Prefecture.
("Missed" is written as "connected" in the Ming manuscript copy.)
Yángyuán was initially undecided.
Suddenly, he saw the recommendation list submitted by Mì County to the prefecture,
with Yángyuán listed as the sixth person,
not Yuányáng.
The recluse Shí Hóng said:
"Yángyuán is indeed better than Yuányáng."
Yángyuán then recounted his dream to Hóng.
Hóng said:
"This dream involves going to a burial mound, which is a hill.
Could it not mean ascending the mound to become a disciple of the hill?
From this, great success may come,
though it is not certain.
Moreover, the ranking in the county's recommendation
matches the dream exactly.
This may well be an auspicious sign."
That year, Xǔ Mèngróng was the governor of the prefecture.
He also teased Yángyuán,
saying that as the sixth person from Mì County,
he had instructed the examination officials to promote him by two or three places.
However, when the prefectural list was released,
Yángyuán remained the sixth person as recommended by the county.
Mèngróng was angry
and reprimanded the examination officials.
Yángyuán then told him the whole story of his dream.
The following year,
he failed the imperial examination under Vice Minister Quán.
From "Continued Records of Destiny."
Wú Shàochéng,
when he was poor and lowly, served as a government soldier.
He deserted
and went to Shàngcài.
There, he suffered from cold and hunger
and begged among his peers.
Several hunters from Shàngcài County
caught a deer in the central mountains.
According to custom, when a large animal is captured,
its internal organs must first be offered as a sacrifice to the mountain god.
After the sacrifice,
the hunters were about to gather and eat.
Suddenly, they heard a voice from the sky saying:
"Wait for Minister Wú."
Everyone was shocked and frightened,
so they stopped.
After a long while, they were about to eat again,
when they heard the voice once more:
"The Minister is about to arrive.
Why not wait a little longer?"
Hesitating,
a messenger arrived,
carrying a small bundle.
Seeing the hunters,
he greeted them and sat down.
When asked, he said his surname was Wú.
Everyone was astonished.
After eating,
the hunters stood up and congratulated him, saying:
"You, sir, are destined for greatness.
Please remember our names."
They recounted the whole incident.
Shàochéng said:
"I am just a lowly soldier.
If I can avoid capture
and serve as a mere soldier, that is enough.
How could I ever achieve wealth and honor?"
He laughed heartily, bid them farewell, and left.
Several years later, he became a military governor
and concurrently held the title of Minister of Works.
He sent people to find the hunters
and rewarded them generously with money and silk.
From "Continued Records of Destiny."
Chén Yànbó
Chén Yànbó and Xiè Chǔ were both students at the Imperial Academy's Guǎngwén School.
When Yànbó was about to seek recommendation for the imperial examination,
he suddenly dreamed that he arrived at the capital hall.
He saw it lavishly decorated,
as if for a grand ceremony.
In the courtyard, there were curtains and canopies
adorned with brocade and embroidery.
In the center was a couch,
with a table arranged on it.
On the table was a document,
which shone like golden characters when viewed from afar.
Yànbó quietly asked an official in charge:
"What ceremony is this?"
The official replied:
"These are the names of next year's jìnshì candidates,
which will be sent to the celestial officials for review."
Yànbó was overjoyed
and asked to take a look.
The official led him to the table with the list.
There was a person in purple robes
holding an ivory tablet.
When Yànbó saw him,
he straightened his clothes and stepped back.
The person in purple said:
"Your name is here.
You may look."
Yànbó stepped forward
and saw thirty-two names,
with his own among them.
The two names above his were both surnamed Lǐ,
but Xiè Chǔ's name was not there.
After waking up, he was secretly pleased
but did not tell anyone.
When he and Chǔ took the examination together,
someone who had seen the list at the Secretariat
secretly informed Chǔ,
but did not mention Yànbó.
When Yànbó heard this,
he wept and could not eat.
Chǔ then comforted him, saying:
"Your ability is no less than mine.
Even if you do not succeed this year,
why be so upset?"
Yànbó then told him about his dream.
He added:
"If this dream does not come true,
I fear I will never succeed."
The students at the Imperial Academy said:
"If what you say is true,
the outcome is still uncertain."
The next morning, when they looked at the list,
it was exactly as in the dream.
Yànbó passed the jìnshì examination in the fifth year of Yuánhé under Vice Minister Cuī Shū.
The two above him were Lǐ Gùxíng and Lǐ Réngshū.
Xiè Chǔ passed the examination the following year under Yǐn Gōng.
From "Records of Predestination."
Lù Bīnyú
Lù Bīnyú was taking the imperial examinations,
residing in the capital.
There was a monk named Wéi Yīng,
skilled in music and physiognomy,
and also knowledgeable in divination.
Bīnyú associated with him.
Whenever he spoke of minor matters,
they invariably came true.
By the spring of the second year of the Bǎolì era,
Bīnyú wished to abandon the examinations and return to Wú,
and informed Wéi Yīng of his travel plans.
Yīng urged him to stay for one night.
The next morning,
he said to Bīnyú:
"If you achieve fame next year,
there is no need to return.
Just secure a recommendation from the Jīngzhào Prefecture,
and you will certainly rank high."
Bīnyú said:
"I have attempted three times with the Jīngzhào Prefecture,
but never succeeded.
This year's matter,
feels especially difficult."
Yīng said:
"Not so.
For your fame to be achieved,
if not through a Jīngzhào recommendation,
it cannot be attained elsewhere.
By the sixth day of the seventh month,
if you eat aquatic creatures,
then a distinguished rank and passing the examination are assured."
Bīnyú then wrote this on the window of his residence in Jìnchāng Lane,
and reviewed it daily.
Several months later,
while at the north gate of Jìnggōng,
waiting for a certain official,
he happened to encounter court visitors,
so he turned back to rest at the home of his grandnephew Wénlǐ.
Upon entering,
Wénlǐ joyfully greeted him, saying:
"Someone just gifted a pair of carp,
and I was about to wait for you, sir, to cook them."
Bīnyú had always been fond of fish,
so he ordered them made into soup,
and ate them all upon arrival.
Later, when he looked at the words written on his window,
it was the sixth day of the seventh month.
He immediately ordered his carriage to visit Wéi Yīng,
and deceived him, saying:
"I am about to travel to Pú Pass,
so I came to bid farewell."
Yīng laughed and said:
"You have already eaten the aquatic creatures,
why travel to Pú Pass?"
Bīnyú deeply believed him,
and thus sought a recommendation from the Jīngzhào Prefecture,
and indeed obtained a distinguished rank.
The following year, after completing the provincial examination,
he visited Wéi Yīng again.
Yīng said:
"You have already passed the examination,
but your ranking is not very high,
likely outside the top fifteen.
The top candidate's surname is Lǐ,
and his given name has a trailing stroke."
At that time, there was a student of the Guǎngwén School named Zhū Qiú,
whom contemporary opinion expected to pass.
The list submitted by the supervisory office did not include his name.
Bīnyú then asked if it wasn't the surname Zhū?
Yīng said:
"Among the thirty-three, none have the surname Zhū."
On the twenty-fourth day of the first month,
Bīnyú spoke of this to his cousin
Originally, the character "dì" was missing,
added based on the Ming manuscript copy
Fú,
Fú wrote it on the wall
Originally, "shū" was written as "yù",
changed based on the Ming manuscript copy
of the wall.
Over a month later, the results were posted,
the top candidate was Lǐ Hé,
Bīnyú's name was sixteenth,
making thirty in total.
Wéi Yīng also said to Bīnyú:
"After you achieve fame,
you will receive an official salary in the region of Wú-Yuè,
but one matter will be very swift."
Bīnyú later served in Yuè,
and after half a year, he died suddenly.
From "Qián Dìng Lù"
Wáng Fán
Wáng Fán passed the examinations in the fifth year of the Yuánhé era,
and dreamed that he became the Governor of Hénán.
In the morning, as he was attending to official duties,
two guests came to visit,
one dressed in purple sitting to the east,
and one dressed in crimson sitting to the west.
The crimson-clad one said to the purple-clad one:
"How should Lún Bāng be dealt with?"
He replied:
"Already sentenced to twenty strokes,
and expelled from the jurisdiction."
Upon waking,
he wrote this on a separate sheet behind his official document.
Twenty years later,
he was indeed appointed Governor of Hénán.
After taking office,
the Magistrate of Luòyáng and a郎官 in the branch department were both old acquaintances,
and they conversed leisurely over a banquet.
The郎官 said to the Magistrate:
"How should Lún Bāng be dealt with?"
The Magistrate replied:
"Already sentenced to twenty strokes,
and expelled from the jurisdiction."
Upon hearing this, Fán
immediately rose and went inside,
and did not emerge for a long time.
The two guests were very surprised, saying:
"Our earlier conversation was rather casual,
could Governor Wáng be angry?"
After a while,
Fán brought out the record he had written on the official document,
and showed it to the two guests.
Upon slowly inquiring about the person,
it turned out to be the郎官's household servant,
who had stolen property and fled,
was captured and sent to the county,
and the county had sentenced him thus.
From "Xù Dìngmìng Lù"
Cuī Xuánliàng
In the eleventh year of the Yuánhé era,
the Investigating Censor Duàn Wénchāng,
and Cuī Zhí entered the Censorate together.
Previously, the Investigating Censor Cuī Xuánliàng,
was the head of the Investigation Bureau.
Often, because the two censors had arrived later,
and not through the examination path,
he treated them with much neglect in his接待.
Duàn and Cuī deeply resented this.
In the spring of the fifteenth year of Yuánhé,
Emperor Mùzong ascended the throne,
and appointed the two gentlemen as chancellors.
Duàn was appointed from the position of Academician and Secretariat Drafter,
and Zhí was appointed from the position of Vice Censor-in-Chief.
They served together in the Secretariat.
At that time, Xuánliàng had been relieved of his post as Prefect of Mìzhōu,
and went to pay respects to the chancellors.
The two chancellors looked at each other,
and wrote Xuánliàng's name, saying:
"This man will soon be assigned elsewhere,
yet he seeks an official post with ambition."
At that time, the Vice Director of the Chancellery Xiāo Fǔ was also in Cháng'ān,
and inquired of the two chancellors.
The two chancellors fully related the matter.
Chancellor Xiāo said:
"If so,
then let this fellow idle for three to five years."
Not many days later,
Xuānzhōu reported a vacancy for the Prefect of Shèzhōu.
That day, the seal was at Chancellor Duàn's residence,
and he immediately appointed him Prefect of Shèzhōu.
The next day,
Duàn went to court,
completely forgetting the previous matter,
and upon arriving at the Secretariat, became furious,
rebuking the chief clerk of the personnel department, Yáng Shù, saying:
"Authority lies with you,
yet you still need to refer to the chancellor.
This must be that scoundrel bribing to obtain an appointment;
if it weren't for the clerks taking money,
how could Cuī Xuánliàng become Prefect of Shèzhōu?"
Shù, terrified, apologized, saying:
"The documents never reached our department;
yesterday, it was Your Excellency who personally wrote the draft name and submitted it to the Emperor."
Upon checking and verifying,
he then remembered and realized he had forgotten,
and indeed it was his own handwriting.
Zhí wanted to change the draft and report again.
Duàn said:
"How do we know it is not Heaven borrowing my hand?"
So he let the edict be issued.
From "Xù Dìngmìng Lù"
Wéi Guànzhī
Chancellor Yáng Shōu of the Táng state
was a person from Jiāngzhōu.
His grandfather served as the capital commander of this prefecture,
and his father, Wéizhí,
was the registrar of Lánxī County.
He fathered four sons:
Fā, Gǔ, Shōu, and Yán,
all of whom passed the imperial examinations.
Shōu eventually rose to the highest ministerial rank.
Fā and those below him all reached the positions of vice ministers.
Fā’s name was associated with spring,
and his sons were named Zhù and Chéng;
Gǔ’s name was associated with summer,
and his son was named Zhào;
Shōu’s name was associated with autumn,
and his sons were named Jù, Lín, and Jiàn;
Yán’s name was associated with winter,
and his sons were named Zhù, Shè, and Dòng.
They all possessed literary talent,
passed the highest examinations,
and were known as the Cultivated Yáng Family.
They were compared to the Jìnggōng branch of the Yáng clan
in terms of flourishing prosperity.
In his youth,
Shōu pursued studies on Lúshān.
One day,
while seeking seclusion in a deeply hidden place,
he encountered a Daoist who said to him:
“If you study the Dao,
you will attain immortality;
but if you insist on becoming an official,
you will reach the rank of the Three Dukes,
yet ultimately meet with disaster.
Will you follow me and study the Dao?”
Shōu hesitated,
firmly holding to his ambition for advancement,
and disregarded the Daoist’s words.
In later days, although he ascended to the highest court positions,
he ultimately met his end in the southern wilderness.
From “Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán.”
Zhèng Lǎng
during the Chángqìng era,
a monk at Qīnglóng Temple was skilled in the art of reading people.
Well-known scholars
all visited him.
Jìnshì Zhèng Lǎng paid a special visit,
but the monk did not speak to him at all.
When the results were posted,
Lǎng placed first on the list.
Lǎng did not believe it.
After several days,
a re-examination was ordered internally,
and Lǎng indeed failed.
Later, he visited the Qīnglóng monk again,
who received him cordially,
with even greater courtesy than before.
Lǎng questioned him:
the monk said:
“Previously, because you, sir, had no fame,
if you had passed,
it would not have been auspicious.
From now on, you will reach the highest ministerial rank.”
Later, he indeed served as a chief minister.
From “Gǎn Dìng Lù.”
Duàn Wénchāng
The former military governor of Xīchuān, Duàn Wénchāng,
styled Jǐngchū.
His father, È,
served as magistrate of Zhījiāng,
and later as magistrate of Jiānglíng.
Wénchāng was fond of Shǔ literature from a young age.
He grew up in Zhǔgōng,
but was constrained by mundane affairs,
and traveled as a guest to Chéngdū,
where he paid his respects to Wéi Nánkāng Gāo.
Gāo petitioned for his official appointment.
His path was not very smooth,
and he often prided himself on his ambitions.
Those he associated with were all men of high reputation
originally, “reputation” was placed before “men,”
according to the Ming manuscript edition.
It is suspected that it should read “men of high reputation.”
He then left Nánkāng’s office.
When General Jīnwú Péi Bīn was stationed in Liángchuān,
he recruited Wénchāng as an assistant,
and later appointed him as acting court reviewer.
After Péi’s office was dissolved,
Wénchāng arrived at a post station forty lǐ west of Xīngyuán,
named Gǔmíng,
situated by the Hàn River,
with Bā Mountain in front.
There was a monk named Qīng living in its vicinity,
no one knew where he came from,
and he often remained silent.
But when he did speak,
his words never failed to come true.
Wénchāng, while traveling from his office,
heard of Monk Qīng’s extraordinary abilities,
went directly to Monk Qīng to seek lodging,
hoping to learn about his future.
From evening until dawn,
the monk said nothing.
Suddenly, he asked, “Who in Shǔ is arriving with the most magnificent banners and flags?”
Wénchāng said:
“Could it be Gāo Chóngwén?”
The monk replied:
“No,
try again.”
Wénchāng said:
“The one replacing Chóngwén
is Military Attendant Huángmén.”
Qīng said:
“The nineteenth gentleman will soon become this person,
even more magnificent, even more magnificent.”
Wénchāng then questioned him,
and the monk said:
“A madman’s wild talk,
the master knows nothing.”
And he merely laughed heartily.
From then on, Wénchāng also became quite self-assured.
Vice Minister of Revenue Wéi Chǔhòu
was appointed prefect of Kāizhōu.
Duàn was then serving as vice minister of personnel,
handling salt and iron cases.
Wénchāng saw him off at the capital gate,
and Chǔhòu, who was deeply versed in Buddhism,
upon arriving at Gǔmíng,
first visited Monk Qīng.
Qīng welcomed Chǔhòu with joy.
Chǔhòu then asked about his return date,
and the monk said:
“A year and a half,
a year and a half.”
He also asked what his final official position would be?
The monk replied:
“Chancellor,
but you must obtain it by the river.”
He then asked where he would end up?
The monk did not answer.
He also asked about Duàn, the nineteenth gentleman?
The monk answered:
“It has already been said,
soon, soon.”
When Chǔhòu returned to the court,
it was exactly three years later,
fulfilling the prediction of “a year and a half.”
In the early Chángqìng era,
Duàn, from the position of chancellor, was appointed military governor of Xīchuān,
indeed fulfilling Monk Qīng’s words.
Chǔhòu only did not understand “obtain it by the river” for the chancellorship,
and sought widely for wise men to interpret it.
Some interpreted it by analogy,
saying that Chǔhòu would surely be appointed to Xiàkǒu in Zhèxī,
and from there enter court as chancellor.
But when Emperor Wénzong ascended the throne from his river residence,
he first appointed Chǔhòu as chancellor.
Only then was the prediction fulfilled.
Together with Duke Zōupíng, he led the repair of Monk Qīng’s pagoda,
and had a stone inscription made to record the events.
Also, when Zhào Zōngrú was military governor of Xīngyuán,
he asked about his transfer.
The monk then took paper and wrote two lines of poetry:
“When pear blossoms first bloom and apricot blossoms first appear,
from the southern suburbs, blessings abound.”
Zōngrú then examined it.
Monk Qīng only said:
“A mad monk’s casual words.”
The following February,
he was appointed Acting Right
originally, “Right” was written as “Empress Dowager,”
according to “Biography of Zhèng Yúqìng” in the “New Book of Táng,” volume 158.
In the ninth year of Yuánhé, he was appointed Acting Right Vice Director
Vice Director.
Zhèng Yúqìng replaced his position.
From “Dìng Mìng Lù.”
Cuī Cóng
In the second year of the Bǎolì era,
Cuī Cóng was stationed in Huáinán.
On the third day of the fifth month,
the Guābù garrison reported that ten racing boats from the region east of the Zhè River
had capsized and sunk beneath Jīnshān,
drowning all one hundred and fifty people aboard.
Cuī Cóng sighed in sorrow and indignation upon reading the report.
At that time, the military advisor Huángfǔ Shǔ came in to discuss official matters,
and they shared their astonishment over the incident.
Present at the gathering was a man named Sòng Guīrú, who remarked:
"That disaster is not so strange.
Something similar happened here as well,
with a comparable number of people,
though the manner of their deaths was different."
Ten days later,
a grand banquet was held,
set up in a large square,
with all kinds of performances on display.
Suddenly, a violent storm arose,
and several hundred horses belonging to the performers in the courtyard,
tethered under the long gallery,
were startled by a clap of thunder.
The horses all bolted in panic,
causing dozens of sections of the great gallery to collapse flat,
crushing to death everyone who was beneath it.
The Duke ordered a count of the victims,
and the number matched exactly that of the Zhejiang incident, not a single person more or less.
From *Dú Yì Zhì*
Guō Bāláng
Zhèng Fùlǐ, who later became Deputy Governor of Hézhōng, first sat for the imperial examinations
but failed ten times in a row,
falling into dire straits.
There was a monk named Hóngdào at Qiānfú Temple,
who, it was said, slept during the day behind closed doors
and attended to affairs in the underworld at night.
Of every ten who sought his counsel,
he would refuse eight or nine.
Frustrated and resentful in his plight,
Zhèng Fùlǐ chose an auspicious day, purified himself, and went to wait upon him.
Hóngdào received him quite warmly and said:
"I have never recklessly divulged secrets to anyone.
But now, seeing you, a talented scholar, long lamenting your piled-up firewood of misfortune,
I cannot bear to remain silent.
Strive onward in your pursuit,
and you will ultimately achieve a fine reputation.
However, the circumstances are rather unusual
and cannot be spoken of."
Zhèng bowed and asked about the timing.
Hóngdào said:
"It depends entirely on you.
Four conditions must converge,
and then your ambition will be fulfilled.
If even one is missing,
you will again suffer injustice.
In this manner, three generations of your close kin will successively pass the examinations.
Before these three rounds,
the difficulty will be like climbing a ladder to heaven.
After the three rounds,
it will become as easy as turning over one's hand."
Zhèng stared in astonishment, unable to comprehend,
and bowed again, asking to know the four conditions.
Hóngdào hesitated for a long while,
then said:
"Be careful not to tell anyone.
For you to achieve fame,
four things are required,
which can indeed be considered extraordinary.
First,
it must be the second year after the state changes its reign title;
second,
the Vice Minister of Rites must be serving as chief examiner for the second time;
third,
the second-place candidate must have the surname Zhāng;
fourth,
among the candidates of the same year, there must be a Guō Bāláng.
If any one of the four is lacking,
then your efforts will fall short at the final step.
For your worthy younger brother and nephew in the subsequent three rounds,
they must all conform to this pattern."
Although Zhèng greatly doubted his words,
he felt depressed and unhappy,
thinking there was no longer any hope.
He respectfully thanked the monk and withdrew.
In the second year of the Chángqìng era,
someone recommended his name to the chief examiner.
Zhèng, considering that this was not the examiner's second term,
felt very suspicious about it,
and indeed he did not pass.
It was not until the second year after the reign title was changed to Bǎolì,
when Lord Yáng Xīncháng again presided over the examinations,
that he privately rejoiced over the matter,
not daring to speak of it openly.
The following spring, he indeed passed the examination.
The second-place candidate had the surname Zhāng,
named Zhīshí,
and among the candidates of the same year was Guō Bāláng,
named Yányáng.
Zhèng marveled at this for a long time
and recorded it in a small notebook.
He said to himself privately:
"Hóngdào said that for three rounds it must be like this.
Once is already strange—
can it happen a second time?
Or even a third?"
Next, the former Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, Hán
(Hán, in the Ming manuscript, is written as a taboo character)
Xiàn sat for the examination.
In the second year of the Tàihé era,
he enjoyed a rather widespread reputation.
Because the chief examiner was not serving for the second time,
he indeed encountered obstacles on the day of the examination.
Afterward, he sat for the examination
(Originally written as 'sat afterward.'
Corrected according to *Quē Shǐ*)
in the ninth year of the Tàihé era,
but failed on the verge of success.
It was not until the second year after the reign title was changed to Kāichéng,
when Gāo Kǎi again presided over the examinations,
that the Right Assistant privately considered the matter extraordinary.
The following year, he indeed achieved a high rank.
The second-place candidate had the surname Zhāng,
named Táng;
and among the candidates of the same year was Guō Bāláng,
named Zhí.
He then also appended this to the end of his small notebook.
Although one of the three rounds was still missing,
the two rounds so far showed no discrepancy.
Within his household,
they said to each other privately:
"Could it really be so?"
By then, Monk Hóngdào had already disappeared, and no one knew where he had gone.
Next, the former Commandant-escort, Hào, sat for the examination.
His reputation grew even more favorable.
In the second year after the reign title was changed to Huìchāng,
Vice Minister of Rites Liǔ Jǐng again presided over the examinations,
and the Commandant-escort passed as the top candidate.
The second-place candidate had the surname Zhāng,
named Qián;
and among the candidates of the same year was Guō Bāláng,
named Jīng.
Everything Hóngdào had said proved accurate without error.
From *Yě Shǐ*
Zhāng Xuān
Zhāng Xuān, the magistrate of Lín'ān County in Hángzhōu,
during the Bǎolì era,
was transferred from the position of household clerk in Yuè Prefecture to his current official post.
Since his family was in eastern Zhèjiāng,
he wished to become the magistrate of Xiāoshān.
Three days before the official announcement of appointments,
he suddenly dreamed of a woman in her twenties,
who came to visit with a name card.
Xuān was always upright and reserved,
and in the dream, he refused to see the woman.
The woman said:
"I am a guest in your county next year,
how can you not meet me?"
Xuān then saw her.
Her demeanor was very respectful.
She said:
"I have eleven mouths,
residing in your honorable jurisdiction,
for many years now.
Now I hear that Your Excellency is about to arrive,
so I have come to pay my respects."
Xuān then asked the name of the county,
but she did not answer.
Xuān told his clansmen:
"Take note of this."
Later, when he was appointed magistrate of Ānjí County in Húzhōu,
Xuān felt it inconvenient for family matters,
and intended to decline the post.
His clansmen said:
"Not so,
the woman from the dream the other night,
does she not represent the character 'Ān'?
Eleven mouths—is that not the character 'Jí'?
This is predetermined by fate,
what good would declining do?"
Xuān understood and laughed, saying:
"If so,
it must indeed be predetermined."
He then accepted the post.
After his term ended,
several years later, he was about to be reassigned.
At that time, the Huái River region suffered from floods and poor harvests,
so Xuān moved his family to Hénán,
and firmly sought an official post in Sòng or Bó,
intending to take his family there.
He again dreamed of the same woman,
her appearance unchanged,
who said:
"Your Excellency will again govern a county,
which is my county."
Xuān said:
"I have already governed your county before,
how could I be appointed there again?"
The woman said:
"Since Your Excellency left office,
I have moved my residence.
Where I now reside,
is not the old place.
However, my former family members
have mostly passed away,
and now only three mouths remain as a burden.
A few months after Your Excellency arrives,
you will also leave."
After speaking,
she seemed sorrowful,
but Xuān did not understand.
When the official appointments were announced,
he was made magistrate of Lín'ān County in Hángzhōu.
Xuān sighed and said:
"Three mouths—that is the character 'Lín'.
Leaving after a few months—
am I to face misfortune?"
He died half a year after taking office.
From "Qián Dìng Lù"
Hán Jiǒng
Hán Jiǒng of Chānglí,
a descendant of the late Duke Jìn, Hán Huàng.
He was well-versed in the classics and history.
In the fifth year of Tàihé,
he was transferred from the position of Dàlǐ Chéng and selected for promotion,
passing the evaluation and entering the roster.
His ranking was neither exceptionally high,
nor achieved through fierce competition,
so he was mocked by younger colleagues.
At that time, Féng Yuán, the Tàicháng Chéng, was appointed Prefect of Yuèzhōu,
and spoke of how human affairs are predetermined.
At the end of Dézōng's reign,
Yuán served as Fènglǐ in the Tàicháng Temple.
At that time, he and Jiǒng were colleagues.
That year, the newly advanced scholar Shí Yuánzuǒ
served as Xiélǜ Láng.
The three agreed to perform the Shìdiàn ceremony at the Temple of Wǔchéng Wáng on the first Dīng day.
Yuán lived in Chánglè,
Jiǒng in Qīnrén,
and Yuánzuǒ in Ānyì.
Yuán, feeling enthusiastic,
pulled the two officials to the southwest corner of Tàipíng Xìngdào.
Yuánzuǒ suddenly said:
"I just had a good dream on horseback about you two gentlemen,
both of you will pass the evaluation and enter the roster,
how about that?
Please record it."
Yuán indeed wrote it down,
keeping it in his box.
In the sixth year of Xiànzōng,
Yuán passed the evaluation and entered the roster,
and was appointed Wèi of Xìngpíng County.
Jiǒng truly had no expectations for the imperial examinations,
but twenty-seven or twenty-eight years later,
Jiǒng also passed the evaluation and entered the roster,
all without error.
Before Yuán departed for Yuèyáng,
he summoned Jiǒng,
specifically recounting the events of that time,
and took out the record from his box to show him,
saying:
"Why should the gentlemen mock you?
It was fate that made it so."
Jiǒng also said
"The character 'qù' is suspected to be 'yún'"
"I have never forgotten this,
so how is it that you and I
differ so greatly in our fortunes?"
That year, Jiǒng was appointed Dàlǐ Zhèng.
From "Xù Dìngmìng Lù"
Páng Yán
Táng Dynasty Jīngzhào Yǐn Páng Yán served as Prefect of Qúzhōu.
A few months after arriving in the prefecture,
he suddenly dreamed of two monks entering his bedroom door.
Yán did not believe in Buddhism,
and in the dream, he scolded them.
The monks said:
"Do not be angry, Governor,
we have foreknowledge,
and thus have come to inform you."
Yán was pleased to hear this,
and asked:
"Will I become Chancellor?"
They said:
"No."
"Will I have military command?"
They said:
"No."
"Then what office will I hold?"
They said:
"Similar to a Liánchá but without military authority,
with land but not beyond the capital region.
Beyond this,
we do not know."
Yán asked:
"Then how long will I live?"
They said:
"Alas,
what you lack is longevity.
If you had longevity,
what could you not achieve?"
Yán asked:
"When will I leave this place?"
They said:
"On the twenty-second day of the fifth month next year, and next spring, you will be replaced.
First submit a petition to the Liánshǐ,
hoping to be allowed to wait under his command."
At that time, the Liánshǐ
"The nine characters 'yuàn dé shǐ xià xiāng dài' were originally missing,
added based on the Míng Dynasty manuscript copy"
Yuán Zhěn had always been on good terms with Yán,
and Yán believed his request would be granted.
The departure date was set.
On the last day of that month,
during a banquet,
Yuán sent a letter saying:
"Please wait for the handover."
Yán opened the letter and said:
"I already knew I could not leave yet."
He recounted his dream to those present.
He eventually departed on the twenty-second day of the fifth month.
Later, he became Jīngzhào Yǐn and died.
From "Qián Dìng Lù"
Zhāng Zhèngjǔ
Secretary Supervisor Liǔ Yǔxī,
whose son Xián Yǔn,
had long been in the examination circuit without success.
Yǔxī was resentful and regretful about his official career,
and loved Xián Yǔn very deeply.
Upon returning to the capital,
he pleaded his case to the worthy officials at court.
In the fourth year of the Tàihé era,
the former Minister of Personnel Cuī Qún had a deep friendship with Yǔxī from old times.
Seeing Yǔxī so frustrated,
he especially wanted to promote and support Xián Yǔn.
That autumn,
Qún’s protégé Zhāng Zhèngmó served as an examiner for the Jīngzhào Prefecture examinations.
Qún specially summoned Zhèngmó for Yǔxī,
personally entrusting Xián Yǔn to him,
hoping he would be ranked first.
When the results were posted,
Xián Yǔn’s name was placed very low.
Qún was angry about this,
and warned his gatekeeper:
"When Zhāng Zhèngmó comes,
do not admit him anymore."
Zhèngmó’s elder brother Zhèngjǔ,
formerly a参军 in Hézhōng,
participated in the selection for outstanding literary and judgment skills.
At that time, Qún was overseeing the candidates for the special examinations.
After the examiners had sealed the names and finished grading,
Qún read Zhèngjǔ’s judgment essay,
and secretly admired it in his heart.
Also thinking he was the younger brother of the late Minister of Works Zhèngfǔ,
he decisively recommended him for presentation to the throne.
When the imperial decree was issued,
Zhèngjǔ went with the other successful candidates to thank the chief examiner.
Only Zhèngjǔ stepped forward to address him,
and first spoke these words:
"I have no place to sacrifice my life to repay Your Excellency’s profound kindness.
Within one household,
two brothers,
both have received examination honors and promotion.
Even if our bones were ground and flesh sliced,
we could not repay you adequately."
Just as his tears were falling,
before his words were finished,
Qún suddenly realized this was Zhèngmó’s brother.
He flared up and said:
"You are Zhāng Zhèngmó’s elder brother.
Your worthy younger brother is utterly without conscience.
He used my name for his own gain.
How could such a thing happen?
What difference is there from a thief?
Your passing the examination was fate,
not my original intention.
Why thank me further?"
From "Xù Dìngmìng Lù".
Liú Zūngǔ
The late Minister of Justice Liú Zūngǔ of the Peì State,
in the fourth year of the Tàihé era,
was military governor of Eastern Shǔ.
Previously, a man in Shǔ had amassed a large collection of books.
After Liú arrived,
he once borrowed several hundred volumes from him,
but had not yet examined them in detail.
The following summer,
the Fú River flooded greatly,
breaching the walls,
and inundating the houses in the settlement.
After several days,
the water finally receded.
Liú’s books, utensils, and curios
were all soaked and soiled by the floodwaters.
Liú then ordered them laid out in the courtyard to dry.
A few days later,
Liú, among the pile of books,
found one scroll of the "Zhōuyì Zhèngyì",
with wonderfully skillful brushwork,
and somewhat ancient script,
clearly not a recent book.
At the end of the scroll was an inscription:
"On the eleventh day of the third month of the second year of the Shàngyuán era,
while reading the Zhōuyì,
I wrote this commentary.
From this point, after the era name changes twelve or thirteen times,
until the year reaching 'one person, eight thousand mouths',
there will be a great flood causing drowning,
whereby it will be unfolded and dried in the sun.
Héngyáng Daoist priest Lǐ Déchū."
Liú read this inscription,
and sighed for a long time,
trying to trace its origin.
It turned out to be a book from the Shǔ man’s collection.
He then summoned his assistants to show them.
The so-called "era name changes twelve or thirteen times",
"until the year reaching 'one person, eight thousand mouths'":
"one person, eight thousand mouths"
refers to the characters for "Tàihé".
From Shàngyuán, through Bǎoyìng, Guǎngdé, Yǒngtài, Dàlì, Jiànzhōng, Xīngyuán, Zhēnyuán, Yǒngzhēn, Yuánhé, Chángqìng, Bǎolì, to Tàihé.
In total, the era name changed thirteen times.
This indeed matched the record.
However, it was unknown who Lǐ Déchū was.
Perhaps he borrowed that name to show this to later generations?
From "Xuānshì Zhì".
Shū Yuányú
When Grand Commandant Lǐ was in the Secretariat,
Shū Yuányú, from the position of Attendant Censor,
asked to return to the Eastern Capital to move his family’s graves for reburial
(The character "奉" was originally missing in the text,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy
The Grand Commandant said:
"Recently a monk came from the east,
saying there is a plot of land.
If buried there, one will certainly reach the highest position.
Why not take this?"
Yuányú declined, citing family poverty,
and being unable to arrange for another site.
He then returned to oversee the reburial.
Another day,
the monk passed by again,
and again said to the Grand Commandant:
"The land mentioned before,
has already been used by someone."
Upon inquiry,
it turned out to be Yuányú.
Yuányú later rose from Vice Minister of Justice to become Chancellor.
From "Gǎndìng Lù".
Lǐ Déyù
Lǐ Déyù, from Rùnzhōu,
at age fifty-four was appointed to Yángzhōu,
and at fifty-eight entered the Chancellorship again.
Both ages matched those of his father, Lǐ Jífǔ.
The officials considered it an honor.
From "Gǎndìng Lù".
When Déyù was Junior Tutor to the Heir Apparent,
serving in the Eastern Capital branch administration,
he once heard of a monk
skilled at knowing people’s fortune and misfortune.
He thus summoned him.
The monk said:
"Your disaster is not over yet.
You must travel ten thousand lǐ to the south."
Déyù was very displeased.
The next day,
he summoned him again.
The monk said:
"Concerned my words were not precise,
I request to set up an altar for three days."
He then said:
"The time for your southern journey is set."
Déyù asked:
"Master, what proof is there?"
The monk immediately pointed to the ground,
saying there was a stone box below.
Déyù ordered it dug up,
and indeed found it.
However, upon opening it, there was nothing to see inside.
Déyù valued him highly.
He further asked, "Will I return from the southern journey?"
The monk said:
"You will consume ten thousand sheep.
Five hundred are still unmet.
You will certainly return."
Déyù sighed:
"Master, you are truly a transcendent person.
In the Yuánhé era,
when I served in the northern administration,
I once dreamed of traveling to Jìn Mountain.
As far as the eye could see, there were sheep.
There were several dozen herders,
who said to me,
'These are the sheep for the Attendant Censor to eat.'
I always remembered this dream,
and never revealed it to anyone.
Now I know the hidden fate
is indeed not false."
Over ten days later,
the military governor of Língwǔ sent
(The text in this book, volume 98, quoting the "Xuānshì Zhì" entry on Lǐ Déyù, lacks the character "送"
)Mǐ Jì, who presented five hundred sheep.
Greatly startled,
Déyù summoned the monk and told him of the matter,
and wanted to return them.
The monk said:
"The sheep have come here,
meaning they are already the Chancellor’s.
Returning them is of no benefit.
Will the southern journey not bring you back?"
Soon after, he was successively demoted,
down to a minor official in Yázhōu,
and ultimately died in the place of exile,
at the age of sixty-three.
From "Bǔlù Jì Zhuàn".
Lǐ Yán
There was a Presented Scholar named Lǐ Yuè,
who repeatedly took the imperial examinations but did not pass.
One night, he dreamed of someone saying to him:
"With a mountain on your head,
how can you achieve a high rank?"
When he awoke,
he realized he could not bear the name "Yuè" (which contains the character for "mountain").
Thus, he changed his name to "Yán."
Indeed, he then passed the examination.
From the Gǎndìng Lù.
Wáng Mù
Wáng Mù
was a second cousin of Wáng Yá.
He lived south of the Yangtze River,
old and impoverished.
Because Wáng Yá held the authority of Chief Minister,
Wáng Mù rode a lame donkey to the capital,
seeking provisions and renting a dwelling.
After staying for thirty days,
he finally managed to see Wáng Yá once at the gate screen.
His hopes were merely for a minor official post.
But Wáng Yá, seeing Mù's wretched state,
showed no fraternal affection.
In the autumn of the ninth year of the Tàihé era,
Mù managed to persuade a favored servant of Wáng Yá
to convey his desires.
Only then did Wáng Yá summon him once,
intending to grant him a lowly official position.
From then on, Mù visited Wáng Yá's gate morning and evening,
awaiting his command.
When Wáng Yá was executed,
and Qiú Shìliáng arrested his family members,
Mù happened to be at Wáng Yá's private residence.
Deeming him a member of the Wáng faction,
they did not spare him from execution.
From the Dùyáng Zábiān.
Shū Yuánqiān
was a clansman of Shū Yuányú.
Intelligent and perceptive,
in the prime of youth,
he was treated with considerable courtesy by Yuányú.
For ten years,
Yuányú treated him as a nephew,
recommended him to pass the Mingjīng examination,
and he served as a Collator.
When Yuányú
("chí" originally written as "shí,"
corrected based on the Dùyáng Zábiān)
held the seal of Chief Minister,
he promised to appoint him as a Departmental Director.
Not long after,
he suddenly became angry with Yuánqiān for no apparent fault,
so that even when Yuánqiān paid his respects on the first day of the month,
he was abruptly refused an audience.
From then on, reproaches increased daily,
and he was treated lightly even by servants.
Yuánqiān, feeling uneasy,
then left a letter at the gate,
bidding farewell to go south of the Yangtze,
and Yuányú did not inquire further.
The next day,
he packed and left Cháng'ān,
sighing over his ill fate,
disheartened and lost,
he halted his horse to look back,
tears streaming down.
Upon reaching Zhāoyìng,
he heard of Yuányú's calamity,
and only then felt relieved.
At that time, family members were arrested at the Chief Minister's residence.
Regardless of closeness or distance,
all were executed.
Contemporary commentators
regarded the differing fortunes of Wáng and Shū
as determined by fate.
From the Dùyáng Zábiān.
Dù Cóng's Nephew
Dù Cóng and Lǐ Déyù both served in the Secretariat.
One day,
Déyù said to Cóng:
"There is an extraordinary person in your household,
why not send him to visit me?"
Cóng said:
"There is none."
Déyù said:
"Try to think."
He said:
"There is only a nephew,
who came from afar seeking an official post."
Déyù said:
"That is the one."
Upon returning home,
Cóng sent him to visit Déyù.
Déyù questioned him,
and he replied:
"Grand Commandant, your position is at the pinnacle of human officials,
what need is there to ask?
Even trivial matters for ordinary people are predetermined,
how much more so for achievements, titles, and emoluments?
Moreover, tomorrow at noon,
a white beast will come from the south, leaping over the roof,
a young boy with hair in twin tufts, wearing purple,
aged seven,
holding a bamboo pole,
five feet long with nine nodes,
will drive the beast away,
and the beast will return south.
The boy is not from within the residence;
try to watch for him."
The next day at noon,
sure enough, a white cat
came from the south, leaping over the roof,
and a young boy with hair in twin tufts, wearing purple,
chased it,
and the cat went back south.
Déyù then summoned and questioned the boy,
who said:
"I am seven years old."
Measuring the bamboo pole he held,
it was five feet long with nine nodes.
The boy was the son of an outer retainer of the residence."
There was not the slightest error.
Matters great and small
are all predetermined.
From the Wén Qí Lù.
Shí Xióng
Shí Xióng initially served alongside Kāng Shēn as chief officers under the military governor of Xúzhōu, Wáng Zhìxīng.
Lord Wáng was wary of the two men's valor and prowess,
so he memorialized the court to have them remain in their current posts,
with Shí Xióng being appointed as Simǎ of Xǔzhōu.
Soon after, he was appointed Prefect of Shízhōu.
There was a man named Lǐ Hóngyuē,
who, from the time Shǐjūn Shí was in Xǔzhōu,
had been owed money and goods by him,
and had repeatedly pressed for repayment to his own distress.
Later, he went to Shízhōu
to demand what was owed to him.
Once he entered the borders of Shízhōu,
Hóngyuē hesitated,
fearing Shí's anger.
He came upon a village temple,
where all who prayed and made offerings claimed it was efficacious.
Hóngyuē then devoutly made his plea to the deity.
The temple priest and his son both claimed to be possessed by the deity,
asked for paper and brush,
and instructed Hóngyuē to write.
But he was illiterate,
so he found a village boy
and dictated to him:
"Shǐjūn Shí, from this point onward,
will be promoted by a high minister,
and will achieve military merit.
He is destined to become military governor of Héyáng and Fèngxiáng.
Yet there will be one official appointment that disappoints him.
Therefore, this matter must be kept secret,
and must not be heard by other ears."
Hóngyuē, based on the words of the shaman-priest,
first reported them to Shǐjūn Shí.
Shǐjūn Shí was very pleased when they met.
Soon, due to the rebellion of Liú Cóngjiàn in Lùzhōu,
the court deliberated on launching a campaign.
Lǐ Déyù was serving as chancellor,
and urgently employed Shí Xióng.
Shí Xióng exerted his military strength,
and seized Tiānjǐng Pass.
Later, together with Liú Zhèn, he also defeated various barbarian tribes at Hēishān,
routed the Southern Chányú,
and escorted the princess back to the state—
all these were Shí Xióng's achievements.
Yet these were the accomplishments of a hawk or hound;
without a good master, they could not have been driven to such feats.
When Lord Lǐ was appointed Tàizǐ Shàobǎo and assigned to Luòyáng,
Púyè Shí went to the Secretariat to discuss his official position, saying:
"For my merits in capturing Tiānjǐng Pass and at Hēishān,
and for my labors in two regions,
I further hope for one military governorship to support me in my old age."
The Secretariat replied:
"For your merits in Lùzhōu, Púyè,
the state has already rewarded you with the military governorship of Héyáng;
for your achievements on the western frontier,
you were further appointed to Fèngxiáng.
With the weight of two governorships,
is that not sufficient reward?"
Shí was then reappointed as Left and Right Commander of the Imperial Army,
which did not satisfy his hopes.
All of this was exactly as the shaman had foretold.
When Déyù was demoted to Cháozhōu,
a guest again mentioned the divine verification regarding Shí Xióng,
clarifying that his rise and decline were predestined,
which somewhat alleviated his depression.
From *Yúnxī Yǒuyì*.
Also, in the fourth year of the Huìchāng era,
Liú Zhěn was defeated.
Back when Cóngjiàn was alive,
there was a man who claimed
that Shí Xióng would arrive with seven thousand men;
Cóngjiàn had him executed.
By this time, Shí Xióng indeed entered Lùzhōu with seven thousand men.
From *Gǎndìng Lù*.
Jiǎ Dǎo
Jiǎ Dǎo, styled Làngxiān,
during the Yuánhé era,
when Yuán Zhěn and Bái Jūyì still favored lightness and simplicity,
Dǎo alone altered the style toward the obscure,
to correct excessive ornamentation.
Even while walking, sitting, sleeping, or eating,
he never ceased chanting verses.
Once, riding a donkey with a canopy,
he crossed the main thoroughfare.
At that time, the autumn wind was fierce,
and yellow leaves could be swept away.
Dǎo suddenly chanted:
"Fallen leaves fill Cháng'ān."
He sought a matching couplet but could not find one.
Consequently, he offended the Grand Capital Prefect Liú Qīchǔ,
was detained overnight, and then released.
Another time, he encountered Emperor Wǔzōng at the Dìngshuǐ Monastery,
and Dǎo was particularly unrestrained and disrespectful,
which surprised the emperor.
Some days later, an imperial decree was issued,
ordering him to be given a post and sent away,
specifically appointing him as County Lieutenant of Chángjiāng,
and he was later promoted to Registrar of Pǔzhōu, where he eventually died.
From *Zhíyán*.
Cuī Jié
The Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, Cuī Gōng, named Jié, was in Cháng'ān,
and went with the presented scholar Chén Tóng to the western part of the city to visit relatives and old friends.
Chén Jūn had other foresight,
which Cuī Gōng did not believe.
As they were about to leave,
Chén Jūn said:
"I will dine on sliced fish with you at Péi Lìnggōng's Pavilion."
Cuī Gōng did not believe him,
and laughed without responding.
Passing through Tiānmén Street,
they happened upon someone selling very fresh fish.
Cuī Gōng completely forgot Chén Jūn's words,
and said:
"Going there is also a leisurely affair;
how about eating some sliced fish?"
He then ordered his attendants to take money and buy fish,
obtaining ten catties.
He said:
"Where can we go?"
His attendants said:
"Péi Lìnggōng's Pavilion is very close."
So he first sent someone to arrange it,
and when they arrived at the pavilion and dismounted,
he suddenly realized Chén Jūn's prediction.
Cuī Gōng exclaimed in great surprise:
"Where can we find someone to slice the fish?"
Chén Jūn said:
"Just borrow a knife and cutting board.
A musician from the First Section will come."
In a moment,
three or four people in purple robes
arrived at the pavilion to stroll and look around.
One of them, seeing the fish, said:
"Extremely fresh and precious.
Do you two gentlemen wish to have it sliced?
I am skilled in this art,
and will prepare it for you."
When questioned,
he turned out to be a musician from the First Section of the Pear Garden.
The others all left,
and this person then removed his outer garment, took up the knife,
and demonstrated extreme skill and dexterity.
Just as the slicing was about to be completed,
Chén Jūn said:
"This sliced fish is for Brother Cuī to eat;
the one in purple shall not have any."
When it was finished,
suddenly a messenger called out:
"His Majesty is visiting Lóngshǒu Pond,
and summons the First Section musicians."
The slicer grabbed his robe and belt,
and ran toward the gate,
without even time to say farewell.
Cuī Gōng was greatly amazed by this.
After the two had eaten,
Chén Jūn said again:
"Shortly,
a ninth-rank official from three thousand *lǐ* to the southeast will come here,
and get to eat half a bowl of clear broth."
Before he finished speaking,
the County Lieutenant of Yánlíng, Lǐ Gěng, arrived.
He was about to take up his post,
and being a relative and old friend of Cuī Gōng's,
he learned that Cuī was at Péi Lìnggōng's Pavilion,
so he came to bid farewell.
While they were eating the broth,
Cuī Gōng said:
"Is there any sliced fish left?"
His attendants reported it was all gone,
only a little clear broth remained.
Cuī Gōng laughed heartily and said:
"Bring it here,
for the Lieutenant to sip."
So he ate half a bowl of clear broth and left.
The Lieutenant of Yánlíng was indeed a ninth-rank official.
Even in trivial matters like food,
the unseen path is already determined—
how much more so in greater affairs?
From *Yìshǐ*.
Lǐ Jǐngràng
When Táng Emperor Xuānzōng was about to appoint a chancellor,
he would always gather two or three names of individuals from both inside and outside the court who were suitable for the chancellorship,
roll them into pellets, and place them on his desk,
covering them with a bowl.
When a chancellorship was vacant,
he would always add incense and devoutly pray,
then draw a pellet to determine the drafting of the edict,
so earnest was he about the appointment.
Thus, Lord Lǐ Xiàogōng, Jǐngràng,
in the end, did not have his name drawn,
which shows the role of fate in this.
From *Lúshì Zájì*.
Lǐ Mǐnqiú
Lǐ Mǐnqiú sat for the imperial examinations,
over ten times in all,
but never passed.
He had no home in the world,
and in the end had few brothers or relatives by marriage.
Restlessly begging for food,
he almost lost the will to live.
In the early years of the Dàhé era,
in a guesthouse in Cháng'ān,
as night fell,
he sat in sorrow and lament.
Suddenly he felt his form and soul separate,
his body drifting lightly,
like a cloud, wandering.
Gradually he came to a wilderness of mounds,
beyond the desolate wilds,
with mountains, rivers, plants, and trees
no different from the human world.
Only he did not know where it was.
After a long while,
he saw a city wall,
and hurried toward it.
Again he saw many people,
calling out and coming and going,
with bustling carriages and horses.
Suddenly a man in white came running over
and bowed to Mǐnqiú.
Mǐnqiú said:
"Aren't you my old servant?"
The man said:
"This humble one is precisely Zhāng Àn, whom Second Young Master employed ten years ago.
At that time I followed Second Young Master to the Jīngzhōu bank,
and unfortunately died before you, like a dog or horse."
Mǐnqiú asked further:
"What do you do here?"
Àn replied:
"Since arriving here,
I have served Eighteenth Young Master Liǔ,
and have been much employed.
Eighteenth Young Master Liǔ now serves as a judge under the Lord of Mount Tài,
and is extremely noble and powerful.
Every day he handles many judgments,
and in his busyness cannot easily be seen.
Second Young Master, since you and Eighteenth Young Master Liǔ are old acquaintances from past and present affairs, you must see him."
Àn requested to enter first and announce him.
In a moment,
Zhāng Àn came out again,
and led Mǐnqiú into a large government office.
Directly north was a great hall,
with vermilion pillars and whitewashed walls,
magnificent to the extreme.
They passed through a side gate under the western corridor,
outside of which were many people wearing yellow or dark green robes.
He also saw those in crimson or purple official robes holding tablets and standing guard;
those in white robes with hair exposed, leaning against the wall;
some wearing cangues and shackles,
being led by others and awaiting orders;
some holding official documents,
peeking through the door and about to enter.
They were gathered like a thicket, numbering several hundred.
As Mǐnqiú was about to enter the door,
Zhāng Àn waved his hand to the crowd and said:
"An official guest has come."
Those people all at once bowed their heads and cleared a path.
Suddenly an usher bowed and invited Mǐnqiú in to meet,
an official in purple wearing full court robes,
standing below the steps.
Mǐnqiú hurried forward and bowed,
then looked up at him—
it was precisely the former scholar Liǔ Xiè.
Xiè looked closely at Mǐnqiú,
greatly surprised,
and said, "I never expected to meet you here."
Then he bowed and invited him to take a seat,
and they conversed intimately,
no different from when they were alive.
Xiè said:
"The realms of the dark and the light are separate paths.
Today, for you to come here,
is a most unexpected matter.
Could it be that someone has wrongly summoned you?
I am fortunate to hold a position here,
and should handle this matter for you."
Mǐnqiú said:
"The reason I have come here
is not because anyone called me."
Xiè pondered for a long while and said:
"This is certainly predetermined.
However, you should return quickly."
Mǐnqiú said:
"In life I suffer from poverty and hardship;
since you, my old friend, are in a position of power,
can you not help me?"
Xiè said:
"Even if you held an official post in the world of the living,
how could you handle public affairs
according to your private desires?
If you harbor such intentions,
demotion and punishment would be inescapable.
However, if you wish to know your official salary and fate,
per
"per" originally read "not";
amended according to the Ming manuscript copy
haps some effort can be made."
Thereupon he ordered a yellow-robed clerk among his attendants:
"Take Second Young Master to the bureau,
and briefly show him the events of the next few years."
Mǐnqiú immediately followed the clerk back out.
Passing east of the great hall,
they entered another courtyard.
The courtyard had a large quadrangular building,
about six or seven rooms wide,
with all windows open,
and the entire house filled only with large bookshelves,
holding yellow and white paper registers,
each labeled with tags,
arranged in rows beyond measure.
The clerk stopped at one shelf,
pulled out a volume of documents,
and with
"with" originally read "like";
amended according to the Ming manuscript copy
his hand flipped through several dozen pages,
then turned back over ten-some lines,
and told Mǐnqiú to read it.
The text said:
"Lǐ Mǐnqiú, until the second year of Dàhé, ceases examination attempts.
In the fifth month of that year,
obtains two hundred and forty strings of cash.
A side note in red characters states:
This money is supplied from the sale of a manor by Yī Zǎi.
Further, in the third year he obtains an official post,
and receives a salary under Zhāng Píngzǐ."
Having read to this point,
the clerk covered it again.
Mǐnqiú earnestly requested to see the rest,
but the clerk firmly refused,
and immediately led him out.
Passing through another gate,
whose door was slightly ajar,
Mǐnqiú tilted his head to peek inside,
and saw a large quadrangular room,
inside which were entirely beds and couches,
on each of which lay several hundred bronze seals,
mixed with red-spotted snakes,
large and small, numbering over a hundred.
There was nothing else.
Mǐnqiú asked the clerk:
"What are these used for?"
The clerk smiled but did not answer.
Then they returned to Judge Liǔ's place.
Liǔ said to Mǐnqiú:
"No one but an old friend could come here.
I would like to keep you longer,
but fear it would delay your return."
They clasped hands and bid farewell.
Liǔ also said to Mǐnqiú:
"Here it is very hard to obtain Yángzhōu felt hats;
someday, please send one."
Then he turned to Zhāng Àn and said:
"Take one or two capable attendants,
along with the saddle horse you rode,
and escort Second Young Master back.
Do not recklessly lead him through other places,
lest you disturb other living people."
Mǐnqiú went out beyond the government office,
and immediately mounted the borrowed horse.
The horse sped like the wind,
with two men leading the way,
and Zhāng Àn holding the reins.
In a moment they reached a place
where heaven and earth were pitch black.
Zhāng Àn said:
"Second Young Master, take care."
It was as if he were pushed into a large pit,
and then he awoke as if from a dream.
By then dawn was approaching,
and he was in the place where he had sat sorrowfully the previous night.
From then on, Mǐnqiú no longer had the heart to sit for the examinations.
Several months later,
his poverty and hunger became even more unbearable.
Several years earlier,
Mǐnqiú had been half-requested by the sons of Yī Shèn to marry their younger sister,
but at that time, taking the pursuit of advancement as his duty,
he did not consent to accept her.
Now, someone again spoke to Mǐnqiú about it,
and Mǐnqiú gladly desired it.
In less than ten days,
the marriage was completed.
The Yī family had five daughters,
four of whom were already married;
Mǐnqiú married the youngest.
Her elder brother, Zǎi,
was just then selling a manor south of the city,
obtaining one thousand strings of cash,
all of which he distributed among his five sisters as dowry.
After Mǐnqiú was married,
he immediately received two hundred strings.
His four sisters-in-law said:
"Our youngest sister,
Lǐ Láng is poor again;
why don't we each contribute ten thousand to help him?"
Thus, Mǐnqiú obtained two hundred and forty strings of cash without discrepancy.
Mǐnqiú had previously held a different official rank and name,
and for a long time had not been reassigned.
That year,
he used this money to participate in the selection process.
In the spring of the third year,
he was appointed as the Deputy of Xiàngchéng in Dèngzhōu.
After serving in office for several months,
he took a walk outside the county town
and, amidst broken walls and overgrown weeds,
saw an ancient stele.
The text was worn away and illegible.
Mǐnqiú happened to have the moss scrubbed off
and carefully examined the seal script title,
which read:
"Stele of Zhāng Héng of the Jìn Dynasty."
He then realized that the official salary was from Zhāng Píngzǐ—
how remarkably clear it was!
From "Hédōng Jì."
Another account says:
Lǐ Mǐnqiú suddenly died,
and saw two men in yellow clothes pursuing him.
Arriving at a grand government office,
he peeked inside
and saw Mǎ Zhí there,
wearing a short coarse garment,
sitting on the ground eating a meal,
with all four corners filled with document shelves.
Lord Mǎ had achieved success in the imperial examinations early on
and was on good terms with Mǐnqiú.
Mǐnqiú hurried in and said:
"How is it that you are here?"
Lord Mǎ was greatly startled,
and moreover did not wish to meet him,
turning his face toward the wall.
Mǐnqiú said:
"Surely there is no issue."
Then he sat down calmly.
Mǐnqiú asked:
"What is your responsibility here?"
Lord Mǎ replied:
"The money and goods people receive,
I allocate annually to meet their needs."
Mǐnqiú said:
"Now that I have met you,
it must be heaven's will;
I urgently wish to know what my annual allocation is."
Lord Mǎ then checked a large-leaf ledger for him,
with yellow paper tags,
and it read:
"Lú Hóngxuān's annual allocation: two thousand strings."
After turning several pages,
he came to Mǐnqiú's entry,
written in vermilion ink:
"Annual allocation: three hundred strings,
to be covered by the money from Yī Zǎi's house sale."
Mǐnqiú said:
"My own money ledger is already substantial,
but fortunately meeting you, sir,
I secretly wish to seek a little extra."
Lord Mǎ said:
"Twenty or thirty thousand would be acceptable,
but no more than that."
He then added a note with his brush:
"An additional thirty thousand,
to be covered by the money from four individuals including so-and-so."
He also saw an old woman over sixty years old,
who was the wet nurse of Mǐnqiú's aunt,
and whose home was in Jiānghuái.
Seeing Mǐnqiú, she joyfully said:
"I too have returned;
knowing that you, young master, are an old acquaintance of the judge,
please check my annual allocation for me, Wet Nurse Lǐ."
When Mǐnqiú was an infant,
he was nursed by Wet Nurse Lǐ,
so he had no choice but to go back in
and relay the matter to Lord Mǎ.
Lord Mǎ ordered his attendants:
"Quickly, check it."
A large document stated:
"Wet Nurse Lǐ's annual allocation: seven hundred."
Mǐnqiú hurried out
and told the old wet nurse,
who sighed with regret and shed tears.
The escorts urged Lord Lǐ to leave;
after traveling several tens of lǐ,
they returned to the city moat,
where he saw a deep, dark pit.
The escorts pushed him from behind,
and he then awoke.
His wife, children, and family
were gathered around weeping,
saying he had been dead for two days.
After a short while, he spoke
and requested paper and brush to record the details.
Mǐnqiú was the son-in-law of Yī Shèn.
His wife's elder brother, Yī Zǎi, was a military commissioner
and sold Lord Yī's house,
obtaining two hundred thousand cash.
By the end of the year,
he hoped to gain an additional thirty thousand.
But there was no hope for it.
By chance, on the street,
he met his father-in-law, who was traveling to the capital for the selection process,
having come from Jiāngnán.
They met with great joy.
He invited him to a meal.
Along with three fellow villagers,
all of whom had deep affection for Mǐnqiú,
they together gifted him thirty thousand cash,
exactly matching the amount in the ledger.
As for Lú Hóngxuān in the city,
someone who knew about this
told Lord Lú,
and Lord Lú calculated his official salary
along with the money he received as a military governor's deputy,
and it totaled exactly two thousand strings, with nothing left over.
Wet Nurse Lǐ had already fallen into destitution,
no longer living in her mistress's home,
and was begging for food on the road.
The amount of seven hundred
would have to be gathered bit by bit
before it could be obtained.
From "Yì Shǐ."
Lǐ Jūn
Deputy Envoy of Jiānglíng, Lǐ Jūn, once traveled from Luòyáng to take the imperial examination for the jìnshì degree.
Arriving at Huàyīn,
he saw a man dressed in white at an inn.
Lǐ Jūn spoke with him,
and they drank together by the stove, becoming very congenial.
Traveling together to Zhāoyìng,
the man said:
"I am a recluse,
residing at West Peak.
I am deeply grateful for your kind regard.
I have some business,
and must go ahead into the city early tomorrow morning,
so I cannot accompany you further.
Would you like to know about your future?"
Lǐ Jūn bowed repeatedly and earnestly requested.
The man then ordered paper and brush,
and under the moonlight wrote three letters in total.
He sealed and addressed them in order.
"Open them only in great urgency."
Then he left.
After failing the examination five or six times,
Lǐ Jūn wished to return home but had no provisions.
He intended to stay,
but could find no place to lodge.
He said:
"This is dire poverty.
It is time to open the immortal brother's letter."
So he bathed,
and at dawn the next day, burned incense and opened it.
It said:
"On such-and-such year, month, and day,
due to hardship and lack of resources,
open one letter.
Go sit in front of the Qīnglóng Temple gate."
After reading it, he went there.
By the time he arrived, it was already late.
He waited until dusk,
not daring to leave.
He laughed to himself, thinking:
"Sitting here,
can I obtain money?"
After a short while,
the temple's head monk arrived with an acolyte,
about to close the gate.
Seeing Lǐ Jūn, he said:
"Who are you?"
Lǐ Jūn replied:
"My donkey is weak and I live far away,
I cannot proceed further,
and wish to lodge here for the night."
The monk said:
"It is too windy and cold outside, that won't do.
Come inside the courtyard."
He then invited him in,
leading the donkey behind.
He prepared a meal and brewed tea.
Late into the night,
the monk looked intently at Lǐ Jūn,
bowing his head and remaining silent for a long time.
Then he said:
"What is your surname, young master?"
Lǐ Jūn replied:
"My surname is Lǐ."
The monk exclaimed in surprise:
"Do you know Official Lǐ of Sōngzī?"
Lǐ Jūn stood up with a pained expression and said:
"He was my late father."
The monk shed tears and said:
"I was an old friend of his for a long time.
Just now I noticed you bear a striking resemblance to the Official.
I have been seeking you for many days,
and now we finally meet."
Tears streamed down Lǐ Jūn's face.
The monk then said:
"You, young master, are very poor.
Your father had brought money and goods here to seek an official post.
He encountered difficulties here.
He left two thousand strings of cash,
deposited in a certain place.
Ever since then,
it has felt like a heavy burden.
Now that I can hand it over to you,
this old monk can live out the rest of his days without worries.
Tomorrow I will leave you a document,
and you can take it away."
Lǐ Jūn was both sorrowful and joyful.
At dawn,
he loaded the silver and left.
He bought a house and settled down,
quickly becoming a wealthy man.
After another three or four years without passing the examination,
worn down by hardship and distress,
he considered giving up.
He thought:
"This concerns my entire life's endeavor.
It is time to open the immortal brother's second letter."
He bathed again,
and at dawn opened it.
It said:
On such-and-such year, month, and day,
as you are about to abandon the examinations,
you may open the second letter.
"Go sit at the head of the Qiūpèi Row in the West Market."
After reading it, he went there again.
Upon arrival, he went upstairs to drink wine.
He heard people talking downstairs,
saying: "Have that young master come here at daybreak tomorrow.
If he has no money,
just say,
originally it was not about money to pass the exam."
Lǐ Jūn, startled, asked them about it.
A guest said:
"The Vice-Director's son has an urgent matter.
He needs one thousand strings of cash,
to secure passing the exam.
Yesterday someone had an appointment with him but didn't show up,
so now he is about to leave."
Lǐ Jūn asked:
"Is this matter true?"
The guest said:
"The young master is right now in the room upstairs."
Lǐ Jūn said:
"I am an examination candidate,
and I also have money.
May I pay a visit to the young master?"
The guest said:
"Since it is truly so,
why not?"
So he went back upstairs,
and indeed met him.
They talked and drank together.
The young master said:
"I am the Vice-Director's son.
He said
the chief examiner is my paternal uncle."
Then they made an agreement face-to-face.
The following year, Lǐ Jūn indeed passed the examination.
Later, he attained the office of Deputy Envoy of Jiānglíng in the Palace Administration.
He suffered from heart pain,
fainting several times in a short while,
his condition extremely critical.
He said to his wife:
"It is time to open the immortal master's third letter."
His wife then washed her hands,
opened and read it. It said:
"On such-and-such year, month, and day,
the Deputy Envoy of Jiānglíng suddenly suffers from heart pain.
You may arrange the family affairs."
Two days later, he died.
From "Yì Shǐ"
Mǎ Jǔ
Mǎ Jǔ, Military Governor of Huáinán, campaigned against Páng Xūn,
serving as the Capital Patrol Commissioner of the various circuit field headquarters.
During a major battle,
