there was a general under the black banner
who, observed from a distance, was not engaging the enemy.
Mǎ Jǔ sent two cavalrymen to behead him.
The riders returned and reported:
"It is your eldest son."
Mǎ Jǔ said:
"Just behead the negligent general.
How can I consider my own son?"
He sent them again to behead him.
The head was displayed on the battlefront,
and not long after, the enemy was defeated.
Later, during a minor setback for the main army,
Mǎ Jǔ fell from his horse,
tumbled off a bridge, and died.
Late at night, he revived.
He saw over a hundred people arriving,
saying:
"Vice Director Mǎ is here."
One person said:
"The Vice Director has a broken bone in his left side."
Another said:
"Quickly replace it."
Another said:
"There is nothing to replace it with."
Then they ordered to fetch willow wood for replacement,
and so they replaced it.
Shortly after, it was dawn,
his injury was healed,
and he felt no pain at all.
When he later governed Yángzhōu,
he held the additional title of Vice Director of the Left.
From "Wén Qí Lù"
Zhèng Yánjì
The food in the Prime Minister's hall,
ordinary people often dared not eat it.
When Zhèng Yánchāng was in the position of Prime Minister,
one day,
he was about to eat in his own hall,
when his younger brother Yánjì arrived,
so he ate together with him.
Yánjì was holding a bowl of noodles,
and after taking a few bites,
the bowl fell from his hand to the ground.
He then suffered a stroke,
and died overnight.
From "Stories from the Central Court"
Lǐ Shēng
Master Qìzhēn, Lǐ Yìfàn,
lived at Xuányuán Temple on Běimáng Mountain.
By the end of the Xiántōng era,
it had already been several years,
and every time he entered Luòchéng through the Huī'ān Gate,
he would change his clothes and rest his horse.
There was a certain Lǐ Shēng,
no one knew where he was from,
his age and appearance seemed to be over fifty,
and he addressed Master Yìfàn with the courtesy of a clan relative,
bowing and inviting him to his residence.
There were over ten schoolchildren,
and Shēng had one daughter and one son.
His dwelling was very poor,
and he struggled to make ends meet each day.
From then on, whenever Master Yìfàn passed by,
he often stayed at his school,
and they became exceptionally close.
Suddenly one evening,
Shēng went to Běimáng Mountain,
to bid farewell to Master Yìfàn.
They sat by the stove talking through the night,
and Master Yìfàn asked where he was going.
Shēng said:
"This farewell of mine is to depart from this world,
not to travel far.
I have received orders from the underworld,
to be in charge of supplying the daily water used by the households within a city.
Now that my monthly term has ended,
I cannot stay long.
In three days, I will die.
On the fifth day,
my wife and son will bury me at the foot of this mountain,
but what is lacking is someone to handle the funeral arrangements.
I am short by a thousand coins,
and I entrust you, Brother of the Way, to lend it to me,
hence this earnest request,
and also to bid farewell."
He then said:
"In the human world, water usage
should not exceed three to five shēng per day;
exceeding this will certainly reduce one's blessings and be accounted for,
so you must be very cautious."
Master Yìfàn asked about his family's livelihood after his death,
and Shēng said:
"My wife will hire a funeral laborer surnamed Wáng,
and my son will later become a monk.
However, that monk is in Jiāngnán,
and will not arrive until two years from now,
his name is Xíngchéng.
Before he arrives,
my son will temporarily stay and eat at your temple."
Master Yìfàn
("Shēng" below likely omits the character "yuē" [said])
asked, "Can he be made to enter the Daoist path?"
Shēng said:
"He is material for a monk,
not fit for the Dao.
This is not something human effort can change.
All this is predetermined by the underworld's records."
After speaking,
at dawn, he bid farewell and left.
From then on, due to repeated hindrances from cold and snow,
Master Yìfàn did not enter Luòchéng.
After about five days,
when the weather first cleared,
Lǐ Shēng's wife and several others came to see Master Yìfàn,
saying:
"Lǐ Shēng has passed away,
and was buried at the foot of the mountain this morning.
We are short a thousand coins,
and he said he had entrusted you to assist with it,
so we have come to collect it.
We also entrust our son to stay at your temple."
Later, the Jiāngnán monk Xíngchéng indeed arrived,
staying at Master Yìfàn's room,
so Master Yìfàn entrusted Lǐ Shēng's son to him,
and Xíngchéng gladly took him away.
He said:
"Since I have made a promise,
I will teach him a vocation,
and ordain him as a monk."
After over two years,
Xíngchéng came again,
and the boy had already become a monk.
He could recite the Lotus Sutra with great proficiency.
Initially, Master Yìfàn had taught him Daoist scriptures,
but even after a year, he could not memorize a single page.
The predetermined fate of a person
truly exists.
From "Records of the Extraordinary"
Chéng Ruì
During the Tiānyòu era of the Táng dynasty,
the Huái army besieged Wǔchāng,
and Commander Dù Hóng sought troops from King Liáng.
As Liáng and Jīng were on friendly terms at the time,
he persuaded Commander Chéng Ruì to lead troops to aid him.
Ruì intended to personally campaign,
so he vigorously built a huge warship,
which took three years to complete,
named the Hézhōu Carrier.
On the ship, halls and offices were arranged,
resembling the structure of a government office.
It also had names like "Leveling Mountains and Cutting Through Seas."
Its other magnificent and sturdy features
can thus be imagined.
He covered up his faults and rejected advice,
deciding solely based on his own will.
His staff members merely complied,
not offering a single word of counsel.
Only the clerk Yáng Hòu supported him.
When the ship anchored at Pòjūn Mountain,
it was set ablaze by the Wú army,
and Ruì ultimately drowned,
while his soldiers scattered.
Earlier, he had changed his name to Ruì,
the character meaning "inside water."
His death inside water
was perhaps a foreboding.
When the Húnán and Lǎngzhōu armies entered Jiānglíng,
they captured military and civilian officials, craftsmen, monks, Daoists, and entertainers,
and took them all back to Chángshā,
changing Ruì's name.
The name Hézhōu
was predetermined.
From "Idle Talk from North of Meng"
Yáng Wèi
In the Táng dynasty, Prefect Yáng Wèi governed Yángyuán.
Whenever the Daoist Chén Xiūfù came to the prefecture,
he often stayed at Zǐjí Palace.
Yáng (whose ancestral home was Hóngnóng) very much wished to meet him once,
but Chén (whose ancestral home was Yǐngchuān) would always go elsewhere.
So Yáng said to the Daoist priests:
"Next time he comes,
you must report it."
One day, when Chén came again,
they immediately reported it.
Soon, the prefect arrived with his entourage,
and they exchanged bows.
Yáng said:
"I have long admired you,
and am fortunate to finally meet you.
I dare to ask about my future official salary and lifespan,
please do not be surprised by my abruptness."
Chén addressed people as "qīng,"
and said to the prefect:
"You will serve as prefect three times,
and that is all."
Yáng was displeased,
as he had already governed two prefectures,
and this would be the third.
From then on, he often regarded his current post as his final place.
Later, when his term ended without incident,
he did not understand the meaning of those words.
Not long after, he was appointed to this prefecture again,
and also completed his term.
After leaving, he was again assigned to this commandery.
In total, he served three terms.
He eventually died in this region.
The prediction of serving as prefect three times
indeed came true here.
Yáng's youngest brother, Pín,
told me this story.
From "Idle Talk from North of Meng"
Ōuyáng Xiè
Ōuyáng Xiè was
the grandson of Sìmén.
He was somewhat skilled in poetry and rhapsodies,
and had been active in the examination halls
for nearly twenty years.
When the kind and amiable Wéi Zhōnglìng was in the cabinet,
Xiè would submit his examination papers at his gate.
For over ten years,
they never once met face to face,
yet Xiè never failed in his ceremonial congratulations and condolences.
Although Duke Wéi never spoke of it,
he felt great pity for him in his heart.
At the beginning of the Zhōnghé era,
the Duke accompanied the imperial carriage to Xīchuān,
where he was appointed chancellor.
At that time, Xiè was residing in Hànnán,
and the Duke, having learned of his whereabouts,
sent a private letter to the provincial commander Liú Jùróng of Xiāng,
instructing him to have Xiè accompany the tribute scholars to the capital.
Jùróng was overjoyed upon receiving the letter,
treated Xiè with great courtesy,
and besides recommending him as the top candidate,
provided him with over a thousand strings of cash,
and further held a grand banquet in the government office.
Soon after, a date was chosen for the journey.
Unexpectedly,
one night he died of a sudden heart ailment.
Jùróng then registered Xiè’s reply letter
and presented it to the Duke.
The Duke read it and sighed with sorrow.
He then said:
“Ten years without meeting,
yet clearly, he was not mistaken.”
From *Zhíyán*.
Yī Fán
When Huáng Cháo defiled and trampled the palace gates,
it was unlike the rebellions of Ān and Zhū.
Among the many extraordinary events,
each became a tale passed down by those fond of stories.
Officials, farmers, and merchants,
taking their wives and children to flee in secret,
were too numerous to record.
There were even those who, after months of being trapped among the rebels and fleeing all day long,
never once saw the enemy’s blades.
Only the former magistrate of Jīngyáng, Yī Fán,
was captured by the rebels,
yet repeatedly escaped death by the sword.
Later, he became separated from his blood relatives,
dressed in peasant clothes and traveling in obscurity.
When he reached Lánguān,
he was seized and devoured by a fierce beast.
When calamity strikes,
can one truly escape it by chance?
From *Táng Quēshǐ*.
Gù Yànlǎng
Gù Yànlǎng of Dōngchuān
appointed Cài Shūxiàng as his deputy.
Grateful for the kindness shown to him in his humble days,
Shūxiàng, though serving as a military deputy, was always treated with respect.
When Yànlǎng’s younger brother Yànhuī succeeded him,
he was extremely fond of cleanliness,
often finding others foul-smelling,
so his attendants had to perfume themselves before serving him.
The staff in his office were all sons of central court officials,
and also tended to be frivolous.
When Grand Commandant Wéi Zhāodù
recaptured the city of Shǔ,
he appointed Yànhuī as deputy commander of the punitive expedition.
While in the army,
Yànhuī would lead his staff officers each morning to pay respects to Zhāodù,
and the future ruler of Shǔ was also present,
but they all looked down on Yànhuī.
Even Zhāodù found him disrespectful.
Yànhuī had succeeded his elder brother’s position.
Later, he was defeated by the ruler of Shǔ,
who personally slaughtered his entire family,
and officials like Wēn Shù perished as well.
Earlier, Cài Shūxiàng
(the character “xiàng” was originally missing,
added based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy)
held the highest position among the staff,
and was the trusted confidant of the Gù family.
Together with the court officials he had recruited,
he enjoyed leisurely banquets,
which was quite different from the others.
The younger Gù, now in a position of honor,
grew resentful of his constraints.
A certain Mr. Wáng seized this opportunity,
spreading rumors to drive a wedge between them.
He even said:
“If we remove Vice Censor-in-Chief Cài,
let’s see if you can manage!”
As a result, Shūxiàng resigned and lived in seclusion,
and Wáng then raised an army to attack.
In Shǔ,
there was an occultist named Zhū Qià,
who often said to people:
“Although the two Gùs held the esteemed positions of regional commanders,
they had no mansions in life,
and no graves in death.”
No one understood what he meant.
Some said:
The two Gùs started as minor officers in the Tiāndé Army,
seized the opportunity to achieve merit,
and were then appointed to Dōngchuān,
with the brothers taking turns in control.
When the elder Gù passed away,
his will ordered his body to be cremated
and his ashes returned to Fēngzhōu for burial,
but due to the many troubles, this was not accomplished.
By the time the younger Gù met his desperate end,
the funeral rites were also lacking.
Thus, Mr. Zhū’s words
were proven true.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒyán*.
Lǐ Jiǎ
In the early years of the Tiānyòu era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Lǐ Jiǎ,
originally from Chángshān.
Due to a year of famine,
he moved his family to the mountain valley southwest of Xíngtái.
He gathered firewood and sold it
to support his daily life.
Once, he arrived at the foot of Dàmíng Mountain at night,
when a sudden storm arose,
so he entered a temple to take shelter.
Soon it was midnight,
and the thunderstorm had just subsided.
Lǐ Jiǎ then slept within the temple,
under a pine and cypress tree.
Shortly after, the sounds of attendants clearing the way
approached from afar.
He saw banners shimmering,
carriages and horses bustling,
some wearing armor and helmets,
some holding spears and halberds,
some wearing tall hats and large shoes,
some in court robes holding tablets,
bowing and yielding as they ascended the steps,
and over a dozen of them seated in rows in the hall,
just then ordering wine and food.
They conversed cheerfully for a long time.
The elder on the eastern couch
was the god of Dàmíng Mountain,
with a tall and sturdy build,
and an imposing, lofty demeanor.
The leader on the western couch
was the god of Huángzé,
whose appearance was sparse and thin,
and whose voice was clear and bright.
Next in rank
was said to be the Earl of the Zhānghé River.
The names of the others were unknown.
They sat and discussed,
deliberating on matters of the hidden and the manifest.
One of them said:
"By the command of the Jade Emperor,
and receiving the tally at the Golden Palace,
on the face of Tàiháng Mountain,
by the shores of the Qīngzhāng River,
across several hundred lǐ,
I am fortunate to be the ruler of men,
daring not to indulge in ease or idleness,
daring not to bend the law for personal gain,
daring not to abuse my authority to harm those below.
With caution and vigilance,
I serve the Supreme Emperor,
governing this region.
Thus, the year brings a bountiful harvest,
and the people are free from plague and disease.
Such is the state of my governance
this year."
Another said:
"In the realm of clear and cold waters,
the vast and expansive region,
where great peaks gather in the west,
and immense waters stretch to the east,
with connected marshes and converging lakes,
extending for a thousand lǐ and beyond.
I, by the decree of the Emperor,
reside here among the people,
though the occurrence of thunder and lightning is within my power,
and the rise of wind and waves is within my control,
to stir up fury and gallop freely,
none among men can restrain me.
Yet, unless by imperial decree,
I dare not act arbitrarily;
unless the time is opportune,
I dare not navigate recklessly.
Uprightly I govern,
calmly I guard,
thus causing plants and trees to flourish,
fish and turtles to multiply,
salt and minerals to accumulate and thrive,
reeds and rushes to grow lush and abundant.
Heaven looks down upon us,
and fortunately, there have been no calamities."
Yet another said:
"In the land of lofty peaks,
the capital of jagged cliffs,
occupying a corner of the vast expanse,
overseeing all the swift and flying creatures.
Bears, brown bears, tigers, and leopards,
crows, magpies, eagles, and owls.
All act in accordance,
daring not to harm the people.
This is simply my duty,
what need is there to elaborate?"
All those seated said in unison:
"Indeed, indeed."
The god of Dàmíng,
suddenly raising his eyes and scanning the horizon,
heaved a deep sigh and said to the assembled:
"You, gentlemen, govern your respective regions,
administering justly across the wilds,
whether over water or land,
each with your own strengths.
However, regarding the cycles of heaven and earth's operation,
the periods of calamity for living beings,
a great bandit is about to arise,
a great disaster is about to unfold.
Even with your skillful governance,
what can be done about it?"
All asked:
"What do you mean?"
Dàmíng said:
"Yesterday, I went to the court of the Emperor,
and secretly overheard the discussions of the sages about future events.
Within thirty years,
great warfare will erupt.
North of the Yellow River,
to the right of the Cāng Sea,
a total of over six hundred thousand people will be slaughtered.
At that time,
unless one has accumulated goodness and benevolence,
and is utterly loyal, filial, and pure,
none will be able to escape.
Moreover, to the northwest, there are the two countries of Huáxū and Zhēpí,
awaiting these multitudes of people,
to populate their lands.
Is it that these people have little divine protection,
that they should face such slaughter?"
All frowned and looked at each other, saying:
"This is beyond our knowledge."
After the meal concluded,
and dawn was about to break,
the guests each boarded their carriages and departed.
The god of Dàmíng,
also vanished to an unknown place.
By daybreak,
Lǐ Jiǎ's mind was in a daze,
as if he had encountered all this in a dream.
After returning home,
he recorded the entire event in writing.
He spoke of it to the virtuous elders of his neighborhood.
More than thirty years later,
when Emperor Zhuāngzōng confronted the Liáng dynasty across the riverbanks,
battles ensued one after another.
By the time of the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
when northern tribes brought chaos to Huáxià,
conflict never ceased,
and those who suffered devastation
numbered no less than six hundred thousand.
Now, considering what Mr. Lǐ recounted,
was it perhaps the will of Heaven?
Or was it not a matter of human affairs?
From "Liú Shì Ěrmù Jì"
Fáng Zhīwēn
The late military governor of Qīngzhōu, Lord Fáng Zhīwēn,
in his youth, along with his cousin Xú Yīn
The character "Yīn" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy
robbed in the region of Yǎn and Yùn,
hiding in ancient tombs during the day.
One evening, caught in the rain before they could leave,
two ghosts arrived.
One ghost said:
"Here lies a future
The Míng manuscript copy has "tǔ" instead of "shàng"
military governor,
we should go easy on him."
Both he and his cousin heard this.
The two asked each other:
"Did you hear what was said outside just now?"
Xú said:
"Yes."
Fáng said:
"You and I don't know which of us it refers to.
Tomorrow night, you should stay elsewhere,
and I will remain here alone to verify it."
When night came,
the two ghosts returned.
One ghost said again:
"The nobleman was still here last night."
Fáng heard this and was delighted.
Later, he indeed became military governor of several regions,
rising to the positions of Grand Preceptor, Secretariat Director, and Prince of Dōngpíng.
Thus, we know that the Jìnshū's account of Wèi Yángyuán being addressed by ghosts as one of the Three Dukes
is not unfounded.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Dòu Mèngzhēng
During the Later Liang dynasty, Academician Dòu Mèngzhēng of the Hanlin Academy
was renowned throughout the world for his literary talent.
At that time, Marshal Qián of the Two Zhe regions received an imperial appointment.
Dòu believed that Lord Qián had rendered no service to the imperial court,
being secluded in a remote corner,
yet he sat idly and received such generous favor,
which made him unworthy of this appointment.
So, he held the hemp mourning cloth and wept at court.
The next day,
Dòu was demoted to a minor official post in the eastern region.
After losing favor and being reprimanded,
he often felt depressed and unhappy.
Once, he dreamed that someone said to him:
"Do not torment yourself,
for you will soon be restored to your former position.
However, in the future, be careful not to become the Chancellor.
If such an appointment is offered,
you must avoid it by all means."
Later, Dòu indeed returned to serve in the imperial court.
After a while,
he was promoted to Vice Minister of the Ministry of Works.
Dòu suddenly recalled the words from his dream,
and deeply dreaded the matter.
However, having already accepted the appointment,
he could not decline or avoid it.
Not long after, he indeed passed away.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Xǔ Shēng
In the household of Zhū Rénzhōng, the Chief Military Officer of Biànzhōu, there was a retainer named Xǔ Shēng.
He died suddenly
and followed an envoy into the underworld.
The places they passed through
were all like prefectural cities.
Suddenly, he saw a pile of a thousand dan of grain on the ground,
with a plaque planted in the middle that read:
"Food provisions for General of the Imperial Guards, Zhū Rénzhōng."
Xǔ Shēng was extremely surprised by this.
When they arrived at the official office,
the envoy led him into a bureau.
The chief clerk checked his register and said:
"This person was mistakenly summoned."
He said to Xǔ Shēng:
"You may wait here,
I will report to the Lord of the Underworld.
But be careful not to peek at my register."
After the clerk left,
Xǔ Shēng secretly glanced at a labeled plaque on the shelf that read:
"Register of Human Food Provisions."
Xǔ Shēng secretly recalled that his master, Zhū Rénzhōng, did not eat soy sauce,
and wondered about the reason.
So, he opened the register to search for it,
but could not understand most of the text.
After a while,
the chief clerk returned in great anger.
Already knowing that Xǔ Shēng had been careless,
he glared at him and reprimanded him.
Xǔ Shēng, terrified, apologized for his mistake
and told the clerk:
"I have received great kindness from Zhū Rénzhōng in my life,
and I know that he does not eat soy sauce by nature.
That is why I dared to secretly check the food register to verify it.
I beg you to forgive my offense."
The clerk's anger gradually subsided,
and he took the food register himself.
Under Zhū Rénzhōng's name,
he added three ge of soybeans.
The clerk then sent the previous envoy to lead Xǔ Shēng out and release him back.
The path was narrow and winding,
and he followed the envoy as they walked.
Suddenly, he saw a woman,
with a haggard appearance,
wearing tattered clothes,
holding a child,
and bowing by the roadside.
She said to Xǔ Shēng:
"I am the deceased wife of Zhū Rénzhōng.
I died years ago due to childbirth,
and have not yet been reborn.
I suffer greatly from hunger and cold,
and I hope you can provide me with several thousand strings of cash."
Xǔ Shēng declined, saying he had no money.
The woman said:
"What I ask for is paper money.
After you return to life,
you can obtain it and burn it for me.
I also hope that Rénzhōng will copy the Golden Light Sutra for me as repentance,
so that I may find the path to rebirth."
Afterward, Xǔ Shēng continued on his way,
directly reaching the Xiàngguó Temple.
Just as he was about to cross the threshold,
he was pushed by the envoy,
fell to the ground, and woke up.
Zhū Rénzhōng was both sorrowful and joyful
and asked about the affairs of the underworld.
Xǔ Shēng said:
"You will not be long
before you are appointed General of the Imperial Guards."
He recounted the matter of the plaque and the grain,
and also mentioned seeing Zhū's deceased wife,
describing her appearance accurately without error.
Later, when dining with Zhū Rénzhōng,
he mentioned that after his wife's death,
he suddenly began to enjoy the aroma of soy sauce,
and now he craved it greatly.
This was the effect of the three ge of soybeans added to the register.
Afterward, when Zhū finished copying the sutra,
and Xǔ Shēng burned several thousand sheets of paper money,
the woman appeared in a dream to thank him and departed.
Zhū indeed became General of the Imperial Guards.
The affairs of the visible and invisible worlds
were not off by the slightest.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Yáng Dǐngfū
Jìnshì Yáng Dǐngfū was rich in literary talent,
and was praised by his contemporaries.
Some years ago,
he traveled to Qīngchéng Mountain.
Crossing the Zào River,
there were about fifty people on the same boat.
When they reached the middle of the river,
they encountered a violent storm and were tossed about.
The boat struck a large rock
and capsized in the raging waves.
All those traveling together
sank to the bottom.
Only Yáng Dǐngfū seemed to have something supporting him.
After reaching the shore,
he was also exhausted.
Suddenly, an old man extended a staff to pull him up,
and said with a laugh:
"Originally a man of salt,
not a creature of water."
Before Yáng Dǐngfū could thank him,
the old man disappeared.
He then composed a poem to record the event.
Later, when he returned to Chéngdū,
he spoke of it with close friends.
But no one could understand the meaning of "man of salt."
Later, he served as a clerk under the powerful minister Ān Sīqiān,
overseeing the salt monopoly office.
He fell ill and died suddenly.
His son, Wénzé,
used over a hundred catties of salt allocated by his department to wrap the body
and took it to the outskirts of Shǔ for burial.
Only then did the phrase "man of salt" become clear.
Yáng Dǐngfū's original poem reads:
"Qīngchéng Mountain steep, Zào River cold,
Once crossing it seemed so ordinary.
Oars against fierce winds drew near the shore,
The boat met strange rocks, shattered at the front bay.
Clutching a weak staff in desperate plight,
Life spared from raging waves in an instant's light.
Today, such deep grace I cannot repay,
Only shamefully recall the sparrow with the ring in its sway."
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Niú Xījì
Niú Xījì, Vice Censor-in-Chief of Shǔ,
was prolific in literature,
surpassing his contemporaries.
He himself said:
In his early years, before leaving the academy,
he thought the literary examinations could be easily passed.
Once, he dreamed of a person in golden armor saying:
"Young master, you are not destined for examination success.
Only after the age of forty-five
will you have an official salary."
He woke up and found it strange.
Soon after, he encountered turmoil and chaos,
and drifted to Shǔ,
relying on his paternal uncle.
His elder uncle was the Imperial Advisor, Niú Qiáo.
Due to his straightforward nature and love for wine,
he was reprimanded by his uncle.
He wandered in the southern region of Bā,
and soon heard of the founding of the state,
but did not participate in urging the ruler to ascend the throne.
He was also ostracized by his contemporaries,
and remained without promotion for ten years.
He was recognized by the founding emperor,
summoned for an audience,
and appointed as Chronicler,
eventually rising to the position of Vice Censor-in-Chief.
This shows how prophetic the earlier dream was,
how truly divine.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Text of the Lord of the Underworld
In recent years, there was a scholar who,
while asleep, felt as if he had been summoned by an official court.
He thus followed the messenger and departed.
They passed through a city,
which was said to be Zhènzhōu,
where the population was sparse.
They then passed through another city,
said to be Yōuzhōu,
where the population was dense and bustling.
The scholar then inquired of the messenger:
"Zhènzhōu is desolate,
while Yōuzhōu is prosperous.
Why is there such a difference?"
The messenger replied:
"Although Zhènzhōu has few people now,
before long it will likely resemble Yōuzhōu."
After a while, they arrived at a place
resembling a government office.
Inside was a high official
who, upon seeing the scholar approach,
immediately said:
"This person was mistakenly summoned.
He should be released at once."
The scholar realized this was the underworld court,
so he stepped forward and addressed the underworld official:
"Although I have been granted release,
I wish to know the highest official rank I will attain in my lifetime."
The underworld official ordered a sheet of paper to be brought,
then took a brush and ink to draw on the paper,
making nine circles.
He then took a blue brush
and, within the first circle,
placed a single dot before handing it to him.
The scholar tucked it into his sleeve,
bowed in thanks, and withdrew.
Upon waking,
the document bestowed by the underworld lord
was indeed still in his sleeve.
The scholar kept it very secret.
Later, soldiers in Zhènzhōu
successively killed and wounded many people.
Thus it was understood that the underworld's Zhènzhōu
would soon have a large population,
which was not mistaken.
The scholar eventually rose to the rank of Registrar of Jìzhōu,
and died in poverty.
The nine circles drawn by the underworld official
represented the Nine Provinces,
with Jìzhōu being the first among them,
hence the dot;
the blue dot
indicated that the scholar would only reach the rank of Registrar,
as green robes were worn by officials of that rank.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
The Poor Woman
A proverb says:
"Every sip and every bite
is bound by fate."
Though these words are simple,
they are not without reason.
I once heard the former guest official Zhāng Chéng say
that when he served as an assistant in Zhènzhōu,
there was a commoner's wife in his jurisdiction
who was poor and old,
and had never in her life owned a complete set of clothes.
Someone, pitying her poverty and lowly state
and her exposed body,
gave her a single garment.
When the woman received it,
just as she was unfolding it
and before it could touch her body,
it felt as if someone snatched it from behind.
Raising her hands, she found the garment already gone.
This was likely taken by a ghost.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Zhī Jiǎn
In the Jiangzuǒ region, there was a man named Zhī Jiǎn,
from Yúgān,
whose family had for generations been minor clerks.
By Jiǎn's time,
he alone loved learning and writing.
He privately called himself a xiùcai.
Once, on the night of the first full moon,
following the local custom of taking a winnowing basket,
dressing it in clothes,
inserting chopsticks as a mouth,
and using it to draw patterns in flour for divination,
Jiǎn saw his family performing this and
playfully prayed:
"Please divine what official rank Xiùcai Zhī will attain in the future."
The flour was then drawn into the characters for "Sīkōng" (Minister of Works).
Jiǎn also once dreamed of going to the underworld,
where he perused the register of names.
When he reached his own entry, it read:
"Will become Sīkōng,
living past fifty."
The entries of others he could not recall,
except for that of his friend Zhèng Yuánshū:
"Poor and lowly, without official rank,
will die at forty-eight."
Yuánshū later lived in Zhèxī,
where the Surveillance Commissioner Xú Zhījiàn treated him with respect as a guest,
intending to recommend him to the authorities.
Just as the day for departure approached,
he suddenly fell ill and died.
He was indeed forty-eight.
Jiǎn later became Observation Judge in Jīnlíng,
with the honorary title of Acting Sīkōng.
He often spoke of this matter to relatives and friends,
and eventually died in office,
at the age of fifty-one.
From "Jīshén Lù"
The Matchmaking Shop
Wéi Gù of Dùlíng,
orphaned young,
wished to marry early,
but with many obstacles,
his marriage proposals were unsuccessful.
In the second year of the Zhēnguàn era,
he was about to travel to Qīnghé,
and stayed at the Southern Inn of Sòngchéng.
A guest proposed a match with the daughter of Pān Fǎng, former Sima of Qīnghé,
and they agreed to meet the next morning at the gate of the Lóngxīng Temple west of the inn.
As Wéi Gù was eager to secure a marriage,
he went there at dawn.
The slanting moon was still bright,
and an old man leaned against a cloth bag,
sitting on the steps,
examining a book by the moonlight.
Wéi Gù peered at it,
but could not recognize the characters.
Wéi Gù asked:
"What book are you searching through, venerable elder?
I studied diligently from a young age,
and there is no character I do not recognize.
Even Sanskrit characters from the Western Regions
I can read.
Only this book contains characters I have never seen before.
How can this be?"
The old man laughed and said:
"This is not a book of the mortal world,
so it is natural that you have never seen it."
Wéi Gù said:
"Then what book is it?"
He replied:
"A book of the underworld."
Wéi Gù said:
"If you are from the underworld,
how did you come here?"
He replied:
"You are out early yourself;
it is not that I should not have come.
All underworld officials are in charge of human affairs,
in charge
"in charge" originally read "life",
amended according to the Ming manuscript
of human affairs; how could humans not be involved in them?
On the roads today,
humans and ghosts are equally present,
but you simply cannot distinguish them."
Wéi Gù said:
"Then what are you in charge of?"
He replied:
"The marriage registers of the world."
Wéi Gù said happily:
"I was orphaned young,
and have long wished to marry early,
to continue my family line.
For the past ten years,
I have sought a match in many ways,
but have never succeeded.
Today, I have an appointment here
to discuss marriage with the daughter of Sima Pān.
Will it succeed?"
He replied:
"No,
your wife is just three years old now.
At seventeen,
she will enter your household."
Wéi Gù then asked what was in his bag.
He replied:
"Just red strings,
used to tie the feet of husband and wife.
When they are seated, I secretly tie them together.
Even if they are from feuding families,
or separated by great differences in status,
or serving in distant posts,
or living in different lands like Wú and Chǔ,
once tied by this string,
they can never escape each other.
Your foot is already tied to hers;
what use is seeking elsewhere?"
Wéi Gù said:
"Where is my wife then?
What does her family do?"
He replied:
"She is the daughter of an old woman who sells vegetables north of this inn."
Wéi Gù said:
"Can I see her?"
He replied:
"Chén often carries her here
to sell vegetables.
If you can follow me,
I will show her to you."
When dawn came,
the person he was waiting for did not arrive,
and the old man rolled up his book, shouldered his bag, and left.
Wéi Gù followed him into the vegetable
"vegetable" originally read "rice",
amended according to the Ming manuscript
market.
There was a one-eyed old woman
carrying a three-year-old girl,
who was extremely plain and unkempt.
The old man pointed and said:
"This is your wife."
Wéi Gù said angrily:
"Can I kill her?"
The old man said:
"This girl is destined to enjoy great fortune;
she will gain a fief through her son.
How could she be killed?"
The old man then vanished.
Wéi Gù sharpened a small knife
and gave it to his servant, saying:
"You have always been capable;
if you can kill that girl for me,
I will reward you with ten thousand coins."
The servant said:
"Yes."
The next day,
he hid the knife in his sleeve and entered the vegetable market,
stabbed her in the crowd, and fled.
The market was thrown into chaos,
and he managed to escape.
Wéi Gù asked the servant:
"Did you strike her?"
He replied:
"I aimed for her heart,
but unfortunately only struck between her eyebrows."
After that, Wéi Gù continued seeking marriage,
but never succeeded.
Another fourteen years later,
through his father's influence, he joined the army in Xiàngzhōu
"army" originally read "lord",
amended according to the Ming manuscript
The prefect Wáng Tài appointed him as acting Registrar,
specializing in trying cases.
Impressed by his ability,
Wáng Tài gave him his daughter in marriage.
She was about sixteen or seventeen,
with a beautiful and radiant appearance.
Wéi Gù was extremely pleased.
However, she always wore a floral ornament between her eyebrows,
and even when bathing or at leisure,
she never removed it.
Over a year later,
Wéi Gù pressed her for an explanation,
and his wife said tearfully:
"I am the niece of the prefect,
not his daughter.
In the past, my father served as magistrate of Sòngchéng
and died in office.
At that time, I was still in swaddling clothes,
and my mother and elder brother died one after another.
We only had one estate south of Sòngchéng,
where I lived with my wet nurse, Chén.
It was near the inn,
and we sold vegetables to make ends meet.
Chén pitied me for being young
and could not bear to leave me even briefly.
When I was three years old,
she carried me to the market,
where I was stabbed by a madman.
The scar is still there,
so I cover it with this floral ornament.
Seven or eight years later,
my uncle took up a post in Lúlóng,
and I was able to stay by his side,
so he treated me as his daughter and married me to you."
Wéi Gù said:
"Was Chén one-eyed?"
She replied:
"Yes,
how did you know?"
Wéi Gù said:
"The one who ordered the stabbing was me."
They marveled at the strangeness of it.
He then told her the whole story,
and they respected each other even more deeply.
Later, they had a son named Wéi Kūn,
who became the governor of Yànmén,
and she was enfeoffed as the Grand Lady of Tàiyuán Commandery.
This shows that the arrangements of fate
cannot be changed.
The magistrate of Sòngchéng heard of this
and named the inn "The Matchmaking Inn".
From "Continued Tales of the Mysterious and Strange"
Cuī Yuánzōng
When Cuī Yuánzōng served as a military advisor in Yìzhōu,
he intended to take a wife,
and an auspicious day had already been set.
Suddenly, while dozing off,
he saw someone say:
"The woman from this family is not your wife;
your wife is only being born today."
Then, in the dream, he followed along,
heading toward a house located north of the west road at the crossroads of Lǚxìn Ward in Dōngjīng.
Entering the residence and walking east under the eaves,
he saw a woman giving birth to a girl,
and the person said:
"This is your wife."
Cuī awoke in alarm,
but did not believe it at all.
Soon after, the woman he had arranged to marry
suddenly died unexpectedly.
From then on, he rose to an official rank of the fourth grade,
and at the age of fifty-eight,
he married the cousin of Vice Minister Wéi Zhì,
who was only nineteen years old.
Although she disliked Cuī's age,
she ultimately married him.
The wedding took place at the Wéi family residence in Lǚxìn Ward,
and indeed, they lived in the eastern wing under the eaves.
Upon checking the dates,
it turned out to be exactly the day of his dream,
when his wife had just been born.
Cuī later rose to the third grade,
and lived to the age of ninety.
Madam Wéi grew old together with him,
for nearly forty years,
enjoying his noble status and emoluments.
From "Dìngmìng Lù"
Lú Chéngyè's Daughter
Lú Chéngqìng, Minister of Revenue from Fànyáng,
had a nephew,
and when his daughter was about to come of age and be married,
he said to his younger brother, Left Vice Minister of Revenue Lú Chéngyè:
"For this daughter of mine,
I have chosen a son-in-law named Péi Jūdào.
He will reach the highest ministerial position.
However, I fear he may meet an untimely death and bring ruin to his family,
so she should not be married to him."
Chéngyè replied:
"I wonder if this girl's fate
will ultimately lead to wealth and honor?"
He then called his niece out,
and the brothers examined her closely.
Chéngyè added:
"Péi will rise to the position of a senior official,
and his wife will pass away early.
Even if he later encounters trouble,
it will not affect her.
In the end, she was married to him.
Jūdào rose to the position of a department director,
and his wife indeed passed away.
Later, Jūdào was appointed as Chief Minister of the Secretariat,
but was executed and his family property confiscated,
and it took a long time before his name was cleared."
From "Dìngmìng Lù"
Qíntáizǐ
Lǐ Xīzhòng from Zhàojùn,
in the early Tiānbǎo era,
served as magistrate of Yǎnshī.
He had a daughter named Xiányí,
who at the age of nine
was playing in the flower garden of the official residence.
Suddenly, someone urgently called to Xiányí, saying:
"I have a sincere request,
and wish to entrust it to your virtuous nature.
I hope you will hear me out,
and do not be too alarmed."
Then she said:
"I was the wife of a Cuī,
and had two sons and a daughter.
One son was named Qíntáizǐ,
whom I cherished deeply.
When he was sixty days old,
I passed away.
You, Madam, will become Cuī's second wife,
and I dare to entrust my son to your care.
I truly beg for your compassion."
She then wept bitterly with sorrow and resentment,
and soon disappeared.
Xiányí also fell into a daze and lost consciousness.
Her family took good care of her,
and after ten days, she was unharmed.
When Xīzhòng's term of office ended,
he moved his family to Luòjīng.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
war broke out in Yōujì,
so Xīzhòng took his family eastward
to escape the turmoil of war.
When they reached Línhuái,
he paid a visit to the county magistrate Cuī Qí.
After meeting,
they felt an immediate bond.
They each recounted their ancestral
"祖" originally written as "相",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
connections.
It turned out that Cuī was a third cousin on both his father's and mother's side.
At that time, Cuī had been widowed for half a year,
with no one to manage the household,
and his young children were left helpless.
He thus asked to marry Xīzhòng's daughter.
Xīzhòng's family was poor, and times were dangerous,
as they were preparing to travel far away.
Moreover, his daughter was of marriageable age,
so he agreed to the marriage.
With his daughter settled,
he planned to continue south.
The incident in Yǎnshī
had long been forgotten.
One day,
he suddenly heard loud, sorrowful crying
from Cuī's central hall.
He immediately sent someone to inquire,
and it turned out to be Xiányí.
Xīzhòng personally went to ask her,
and she brought out a one-year-old orphaned child, saying:
"This is the one called Qíntáizǐ from the flower garden."
From then on, they cared for him with extra affection,
naming him Língyù.
When he grew up,
he rose to the position of prefect of Chénjùn.
From "Xù Xuánguài Lù"
Wǔ Yīn
Wǔ Yīn was
a man of Yèjùn.
He once wished
(Originally, the character "wished" was not present;
added based on the Qiándìng Lù)
to marry a woman of the same commandery, Zhèng Shì,
who was the daughter of his maternal aunt.
Her beauty was unparalleled in the world,
and she possessed noble virtue.
Yīn admired her greatly,
and the woman was also willing to follow him.
He thus sought to become her husband,
and a sincere agreement was made.
Not long after,
pressured by a recommendation from a close friend,
he was about to take the imperial examination.
They agreed on a three-year period,
and his maternal aunt consented.
When he arrived in Luòyáng,
he heard that Gōulóng Shēng was skilled in physiognomy
and also fond of drinking.
At the time, he paid him a special visit.
Shēng was extremely pleased
and spent the evening with him.
He then said to Yīn:
"Your official rank and longevity are considerable,
but you will encounter them late.
Before reaching seventy, you will face a minor misfortune."
Yīn said:
"My current concerns
do not extend to such matters.
Please speak of more immediate affairs."
Shēng said:
"When you speak of immediate affairs,
are you not referring to fame and marriage?"
Yīn said:
"Indeed."
Shēng said:
"In three years from now,
you will certainly achieve great fame.
As for marriage,
there is no sign of it at all."
Yīn said:
"I have an agreement to marry someone.
How can you say there is no sign?"
Shēng laughed and said:
"Are you to marry Zhèng Shì?"
Yīn said:
"Yes."
Shēng said:
"She is certainly not your wife.
You are destined to marry Wéi Shì.
She will be born two years from now,
and you will marry her when she is seventeen."
At that time, she will hold an official position,
but she will die within a year.
Yīn found his words strange
and insisted on asking about Zhèng Shì's husband.
Shēng said:
"It is Guō Zǐyuán of the same commandery.
Zǐyuán will die five years after marrying her.
However, on the eve of her wedding,
you will dream of her."
After two years,
Yīn failed the examination.
There was a man from Nèihuáng named Guō Shào,
whose family was wealthy.
Hearing of Zhèng Shì's beauty,
he offered bribes to seek her hand in marriage.
Zhèng Shì's mother gathered the clan to discuss, saying:
"My daughter has already reached marriageable age,
but Yīn has not yet achieved success.
I am old,
and I wish to see her settled.
Now, Guō Shào seeks to marry her.
I intend to consent.
What do you think?"
The family members said:
"We obey your command."
When Zhèng Shì heard this, she wept in anger
and repeatedly attempted to cut off her hair to become a nun.
On the eve of her wedding,
she suddenly fell ill, becoming dizzy and faint,
as if she would not survive.
At that time, Yīn was in the capital.
That evening, he dreamed of a woman
sobbing and weeping,
as if she had something to tell him.
Looking closely, he saw it was Zhèng Shì.
Startled, he asked her,
and after a long while, she said:
"I have long admired your virtue,
and I also knew your intentions,
and once promised to serve you.
Now, unfortunately, I am forced by my elders
to marry another.
What more can I say
about the regret of a lifetime?"
After speaking,
they faced each other and wept.
Yīn awoke in alarm, filled with sorrow and regret,
and found the matter strange.
He then sent a messenger to verify it,
and indeed, she had married someone.
When he asked for the surname,
it was Guō Shào.
After several days,
Yīn reflected that Gōulóng Shēng's words were quite accurate,
though he was puzzled by the discrepancy in the name.
Later, when Emperor Sùzōng was crown prince, his personal name was Shào,
so it was changed to Zǐyuán.
The following year, Yīn passed the examination.
Two years later, Zǐyuán died.
More than ten years later,
Yīn held various high-ranking positions.
Whenever he sought to marry,
it never came to fruition.
Later, he was demoted from the position of Imperial Secretary to serve in Shàoyáng,
where the commandery governor, Wéi Ānzhēn, insisted on giving his daughter to him in marriage.
Remembering Gōulóng Shēng's words,
Yīn earnestly declined but could not avoid it.
A few months after marrying, Wéi Shì died.
Afterward, everything came to pass
as Gōulóng Shēng had said.
From the Qiándìng Lù.
Lú Shēng
The daughter of the Hóngnóng County Magistrate had reached the age of capping,
and was betrothed to a man named Lú.
On the day chosen for the auspicious ceremony,
a sorceress came to visit.
The girl’s mother, Madame Lǐ, asked her:
“My daughter is to be married this evening.
Since Mr. Lú often comes here,
you must have seen him many times.
What are his prospects for official rank and emolument?”
The sorceress replied:
“The Mr. Lú you speak of—
is he not the one with the long beard?”
The mother said:
“Yes.”
“Then he is not your daughter’s husband-to-be.
Your daughter’s husband
is of medium build and fair-skinned,
and moreover, he has no beard.”
The mother was startled and said:
“My daughter is to be married this very evening—
will it happen?”
The sorceress said:
“It will.”
The mother said:
“Since she is to be married,
why then do you say it is not to Mr. Lú?”
The sorceress replied:
“I do not know the reason,
but in the end, Mr. Lú is not your daughter’s husband-to-be.”
Shortly after, Mr. Lú arrived with the betrothal gifts.
The mother angrily confronted the sorceress and showed her.
The sorceress said:
“The event is to take place this evening;
how dare I speak falsely?”
The family grew furious,
and together they spat at her and drove her away.
When Mr. Lú arrived in a carriage
to perform the ceremony of personally welcoming the bride,
the rituals between host and guest were completed.
As they were exchanging jade pendants and binding flowers,
Mr. Lú suddenly cried out in alarm and fled outside,
mounted his horse, and galloped away.
The guests pursued him, but he did not return.
The host, who was by nature proud and hot-tempered,
could not bear the humiliation.
Confident in his daughter’s beauty,
he invited all the guests to come inside,
and called his daughter out to greet them.
Her appearance was so lovely
that few in the world could rival her.
Pointing at her, he said:
“Is this girl one who could frighten anyone?
If he does not appear now,
people will think she has the form of a beast!”
None of the guests failed to feel indignation and sigh.
The host then declared:
“My daughter has been presented before you.
If among the guests there is one willing to marry her,
I hope he will do so this very evening.”
At that time, a certain official named Zhèng,
who had served as Mr. Lú’s attendant,
rose from his seat, bowed, and said:
“I am willing to serve in your household.”
Thereupon, betrothal documents were presented, a matchmaker was chosen,
and they boarded the carriage to complete the ceremony.
The appearance described by the sorceress matched exactly.
Only then did they realize that the sorceress had true knowledge.
Several years later,
when Zhèng was serving in the capital,
he met Mr. Lú and asked him about the incident.
Mr. Lú said:
“Her two eyes were red,
and as large as vermilion cups;
her teeth were several inches long,
protruding from the corners of her mouth.
How could I not have fled in terror?”
Zhèng had always been on good terms with Mr. Lú,
so he immediately brought out his wife to show him.
Mr. Lú was greatly ashamed and withdrew.
Thus it is known that the bond of marriage
is truly predetermined by fate,
and cannot be sought through careless means.
From “Xù Xuánguài Lù.”
Zhèng Huángǔ
Tàixué Bóshì Zhèng Huángǔ
was engaged to the daughter of Minister of Justice Liú.
After the betrothal rites were completed,
he stayed overnight in Zhàoyìng County with the Dàoshi Kòu Zhāng.
That night, he dreamed of riding in a carriage across three small bridges,
arriving at a house behind a temple,
where he went to be married.
The master of the house was surnamed Fáng.
Startled awake,
he told Kòu in detail,
and recorded the event with brush and paper.
Kòu said:
“It is not strange for a bridegroom to have such a dream occasionally.”
Not long after, Liú’s daughter passed away.
Several years later,
while traveling east to Luòyáng,
he remarried, this time to a woman of the Lǐ family.
On the day of the wedding banquet, held in a borrowed residence behind the Zhāochéng Temple,
it turned out to be exactly at the location of the three bridges,
and the owner of the house was surnamed Hán.
At that time, Fáng Zhíwēn was serving as Deputy Governor of Eastern Luòyáng,
and being an old acquaintance of the bride’s family,
the wedding feast and all arrangements
were overseen by Lord Fáng.
Only then did Huángǔ realize the meaning of his dream from years before.
He spoke of it to the guests,
and all who heard could not help but marvel.
From “Yì Shǐ.”
Record of Xiù Shī’s Words
In the Táng dynasty, Cuī Wù and Lǐ Rénjūn were cousins on their mothers' side,
Cuī being the elder of the two.
Towards the end of the Jiànzhōng era,
they came together to the capital for official assignment.
At that time, at the Jiànfú Temple, there was a monk named Shénxiù,
who was versed in the arts of yīn-yáng divination,
and had been appointed to serve within the palace.
One day,
Cuī and Lǐ together went to visit Master Xiù.
The master only exchanged general pleasantries,
and did not utter another word.
As they were leaving, he separately bowed to Lǐ behind the door panel and said:
"Could the Ninth Gentleman kindly grant me the favor of staying alone for one night?
This humble monk has a personal matter he wishes to confide to you."
Lǐ said:
"Certainly, certainly."
Later, Lǐ specially went to fulfill the overnight appointment.
The meal was lavish and clean,
and the courtesy shown was extremely respectful.
When midnight arrived,
the master said:
"The Ninth Gentleman is now destined to be selected as a district magistrate in Jiāngnán,
which will be very much to your satisfaction.
Six years from now,
you will be acting as the Investigating Censor of that prefecture.
That will be the day this humble monk faces execution,
and the supervising official will be none other than you, Ninth Gentleman.
This humble monk is a man of Wú,
and I am extremely fond of a particular plot of land behind the Wǎguān Temple, within the pine forest,
the highest and most open spot.
The finest scenery of Shàngyuán
is all encompassed there.
After my death, I beg the Ninth Gentleman to build a stūpa
(in Sanskrit, a 'stūpa')
there,
to serve as a place to inter this humble monk's remains."
Lǐ slowly replied:
"If these words prove true,
I will not violate this promise even under the bright sun."
Xiù shed tears sorrowfully for a long while.
He then said to Lǐ:
"Please convey my thanks to Gentleman Cuī on my behalf.
Moreover, Cuī will only hold this one official post,
his family affairs will decline,
and he will drift and dwell by the Jiāngnán border.
Cuī's orphaned child
will ultimately receive the Ninth Gentleman's exceptional assistance.
The Ninth Gentleman will in the end become Cuī's son-in-law.
Keep this secret, keep it secret."
Lǐ returned to the inn at dawn,
saw Cuī,
and only mentioned that Master Xiù said
he would eventually become his elder brother's son-in-law.
Cuī said:
"Even if my daughter's fate is meager and she dies early,
how could she possibly marry an old country bumpkin as his wife?"
Lǐ said:
"Compared to Zhāojūn leaving to marry the Chányú,
this would still be a life."
The two looked at each other and laughed heartily.
Later, Lǐ was appointed to fill the post of magistrate of Nánchāng,
and in office gained a reputation for capability.
Upon concluding his acting term as Investigating Censor of that prefecture,
an exiled convict arrived at the prefecture via post relay,
charged with leaking secrets of the inner palace.
At dawn, the imperial edict was proclaimed:
he was to be handed over to the prefecture for execution by flogging.
As the convict removed his clothes and prepared for the punishment,
he looked intently at the supervising official,
who was indeed Investigating Censor Lǐ.
The convict was none other than Shénxiù.
He cried out loudly:
"My request regarding the Wǎguān pine forest—
do not break your word."
After Xiù died,
Lǐ, concealing his tears, requested leave,
donated his salary to hire a small boat,
selected a capable minor official,
and sent the coffin to Shàngyuán District.
He purchased the land in the pine forest of Wǎguān Temple,
and built a stūpa to bury him there.
By that time, Magistrate Cuī had already passed away for several years.
Cuī's younger half-brother, Cuī Yè,
brought the orphaned young girl to Gāo'ān.
Yè was a carefree drifter,
fond of distant travels.
Only his concubine, Madame Yīn, remained behind.
Madame Yīn was also known as Tàichéng,
and also called the Immortal of the Nine Heavens.
She studied the Qín zhēng under Cháng Shǒujiān,
and fully mastered its subtleties.
She took in and provided for the orphaned girl,
treating her with great kindness.
It happened that an army musician from Nánchāng who could play the zhēng,
came to Gāo'ān seeking alms.
He was also a disciple of Cháng Shǒujiān,
so Madame Yīn was able to meet him.
She said to the army musician:
"The young lady of the Cuī family
is peerless in appearance and virtue.
She has already reached marriageable age.
When you serve
(The original text had 'bǎ' for 'him',
amended according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy)
and obtain her family register details,
upon your arrival at the prefectural seat,
could you seek a marriage match for her?"
The army musician agreed to her request.
Upon reaching the prefectural seat,
he took the family register and visited the gates of various gentlemen,
but received no response whatsoever.
Later, when paying a visit to the Salt and Iron Commissioner, Attendant Censor Lǐ
(who was Lǐ Rénjūn)
he took out the family register from his sleeve,
and spread it on the table.
Lǐ, moved with pity, said:
"I have lost my wife,
and it has already been a full year.
Those who attend to my hunger, fullness, cold, and warmth
are only a stubborn boy and an old maidservant.
This merely adds to my regret of living a lonely, half-dead existence,
which troubles my heart day and night.
Moreover, Cuī's orphaned daughter
is in fact my maternal cousin's daughter.
I regard her
as equal to my own younger sister.
She also regards me as an elder brother.
Recalling Master Xiù's words of old,
they prove true like matching tallies.
To take her as my second wife
would indeed fulfill my long-standing affection for Elder Brother Cuī."
Thus, he became engaged to the Cuī family.
From "Records of Strange Hearsay"
Lǐ Xíngxiū.
Therefore, the late Remonstrance Official Lǐ Xíngxiū married the daughter of the Jiangxi Surveillance Commissioner Wáng Zhòngshū.
She was chaste, virtuous, and wise,
and Xíngxiū respected her as an honored guest.
Madam Wáng had a younger sister,
whom she often took along with her.
Xíngxiū also deeply cherished and loved her,
as if she were his own sibling.
During the Yuánhé era,
a certain prominent gentleman was discussing a marriage alliance with the Huáinán Military Governor Lǐ Gōng Hōng,
and various clan members were in Luòyáng.
At that time, Xíngxiū had left his post as an assistant in Xuān Prefecture,
and was residing in East Luò.
The Lǐ family had set an auspicious date for the wedding,
and firmly requested Xíngxiū to be the escort.
That night, after the ceremony concluded,
Xíngxiū fell into a deep sleep.
He dreamed that he had remarried,
and his wife was Madam Wáng's younger sister.
Xíngxiū awoke in alarm,
and was greatly disturbed by it.
He immediately ordered his carriage and returned home.
Upon entering the door,
he saw Madam Wáng had risen early,
hugging her knees and weeping.
In Xíngxiū's household, there was an old servant,
whose nature was rather fierce and unruly,
and he often offended Madam Wáng's wishes.
At that moment, Xíngxiū thought Madam Wáng was upset because of the servant,
so he scolded:
"It must be this old slave again."
He intended to cane him,
but upon investigating the reason,
the household members all said:
"The old slave was talking in the kitchen himself,
saying he had a dream during the fifth watch.
He dreamed that the master remarried the Wáng family's young lady."
Xíngxiū, because this matched his own dream,
was even more disturbed by the matter,
so he forcefully comforted Madam Wáng, saying:
"This is just an old slave's dream,
how can it be believed?"
Not long after,
Madam Wáng indeed passed away due to illness.
At that time, Zhòngshū had gone out to govern Wúxīng,
and when the news of her death arrived,
Lord Wáng was overcome with extreme grief.
He then sent a letter,
intending to entrust Xíngxiū with continuing the family ties through marriage.
Xíngxiū's sorrow and mourning had not yet faded,
so he firmly declined Lord Wáng's request.
There was a Secretary named Wèi Suí,
who was the son of the former Governor of Jiānglíng, Bóyù,
and possessed the discernment to understand people,
his predictions about events were often accurate.
He suddenly said to Xíngxiū:
"Why does the Attendant Censor cherish the memory of his deceased wife so deeply?
If the Attendant Censor wishes to see his wife,
why not ask Old Wáng of Chóusāng?"
Two or three years later,
Lord Wáng repeatedly hinted to Xíngxiū,
entrusting him with his younger daughter,
but Xíngxiū steadfastly refused to accept.
When Xíngxiū was appointed as an Eastern Censorate Investigating Censor,
that year,
a man from Biàn named Lǐ Jiè drove out his military governor,
and an edict was issued to summon troops from Xú and Sì to suppress him.
Messengers on the roads galloped like shooting stars,
and there was also widespread requisitioning of horses.
Xíngxiū rode leisurely out of the pass,
and his journey stopped at the Chóusāng Relay Station.
He had already heard that several imperial envoys had arrived first,
so he went to stay at the Chóusāng Inn.
By that day, as dusk approached,
he went to the inn,
and saw an old man passing by from the east.
People from the north and south of the inn
vied to tug at his clothes, asking him to stay.
Xíngxiū inquired about the reason,
and the innkeeper said:
"Old Wáng is skilled at interpreting fate through writing,
and is respected by the local community."
Xíngxiū suddenly remembered Secretary Wèi's words,
secretly ordered him to be summoned,
and then told him of the matter on his mind.
The old man said:
"If the Eleventh Gentleman wishes to see his deceased wife,
he may do so tonight."
He then led Xíngxiū,
telling him to dismiss his attendants.
Slipping on his shoes,
they entered a earthen hill along a path.
They climbed a slope,
nearly several ren high,
and beside the slope, a grove of trees was faintly visible.
The old man stopped at the side of the road.
He said to Xíngxiū:
"The Eleventh Gentleman should just call out 'Miàozǐ' under the trees,
someone is sure to respond.
When they respond, reply saying,
'Pass on the message to the Ninth Lady,
tonight I am temporarily taking Miàozǐ to see my deceased wife.'"
Xíngxiū did as Old Wáng instructed,
calling out amidst the woods.
Sure enough, someone responded,
and he relayed the old man's words to them.
After a short while,
a young woman emerged,
about fifteen years of age,
and said:
"The Ninth Lady has sent me to accompany the Eleventh Gentleman."
After the young woman finished speaking,
she broke off a bamboo branch and straddled it.
Xíngxiū watched her,
and she was as swift as a horse.
In a moment,
she broke off a bamboo branch for Xíngxiū,
and also told Xíngxiū to straddle it,
riding alongside the young woman,
closely following as if attached.
Traveling southwest for about several tens of lǐ,
they suddenly arrived at a place.
The city walls and towers were majestic and splendid,
and ahead they passed a large palace,
which had a gate.
She then said:
"Just follow the western corridor straight north,
the second courtyard from the south,
is where your virtuous wife resides.
If you see anything inside,
you must hurry past it,
and be careful not to find it strange."
Xíngxiū kept this in mind.
Following the western corridor,
he saw under a crimson-lined, orange-red curtain a bright light,
and inside were hundreds of horizontal eyes over an inch long.
Xíngxiū did exactly as the young woman had said,
hurrying to the northern corridor.
Upon reaching the courtyard,
he indeed saw a maidservant who had died over ten years ago emerge,
who came forward to bow to Xíngxiū,
and then presented a couch, saying:
"Please sit for a while, Eleventh Gentleman,
the lady will be out shortly."
Xíngxiū had long suffered from a lung ailment,
and Madam Wáng had often prepared Gleditsia seed soup to treat his illness.
Since Madam Wáng's death,
he had rarely obtained this soup.
At this moment, the maidservant brought the soup,
and told Xíngxiū to sip it.
It was exactly the flavor of the soup Madam Wáng had personally brewed.
Before he could finish speaking,
his wife hurried out,
and they met, weeping.
Just as Xíngxiū was about to express how long he had missed her,
Madam Wáng firmly stopped him, saying:
"Now you and I are separated by the realms of the living and the dead,
I deeply do not wish for things to be like this,
causing trouble for me.
If you have not forgotten our lifelong bond,
just take in my younger sister and care for her,
that will fulfill my path completely.
The reason I wanted to see you,
was to entrust you with this."
Having said this,
they already heard the young woman outside the door calling:
"Lǐ the Eleventh Gentleman, come out quickly!"
Her voice was very urgent,
and Xíngxiū hastily finished eating and went out.
The young woman was both angry and reproachful:
"You pedant, lacking discernment,
you should return quickly."
As before, they straddled the bamboo branches and traveled together.
After a short while,
they returned to the original place,
where the old man was sleeping with his head on a clod of earth.
Hearing Xíngxiū arrive,
he quickly rose and said:
"Was it not as you wished?"
Xíngxiū replied:
"It was."
The old man said:
"You must thank the Ninth Lady,
for sending someone to escort you."
Xíngxiū also did as he instructed.
Xíngxiū was extremely exhausted,
so he asked the old man:
"What place is this?"
The old man said:
"This is the site of the Numinous Responsive Nine-Sons Mother Shrine on the plain."
The old man then walked,
leading Xíngxiū back to the inn.
The wall lamp flickered dimly,
and the stabled horses were munching fodder as before.
The servants and others were in a deep, exhausted sleep.
The old man then bid farewell and left.
Xíngxiū felt a sudden nausea and retched,
and the Gleditsia seed soup he had drunk came out.
At that time, Lord Wáng had passed away,
and had been transferred to govern Jiangxi.
From then on, Xíngxiū married into the Wáng family again.
Later, he rose to the position of Imperial Advisor.
From "Xù Dìngmìng Lù"
The Gardener's Infant Daughter
Once there was a xiùcai,
who had just reached the age of twenty,
and was eager to marry.
He had tried many places,
entrusting matchmakers to seek opportunities,
but had not yet found a suitable match.
So he went to a skilled diviner to resolve the matter.
The diviner said:
"The path of marriage
is also tied to predestined fate.
Your future wife
is only two years old now."
He then asked in which prefecture and county she would be found,
and what her surname was.
The diviner said:
"South of the city wall of Huázhōu,
with such-and-such a surname.
Her parents are gardeners by trade,
and they have only one daughter,
who will be your fine match."
The xiùcai, considering his own family status and scholarly reputation,
had been seeking a match from an illustrious clan.
Upon hearing the diviner's words,
he felt depressed and discontent.
Yet, not fully believing it,
he went to Huázhōu to verify the matter.
Upon arrival, he searched south of the city wall of Huázhōu,
and indeed found a vegetable garden.
He asked the old gardener his surname,
and it matched what the diviner had said.
He then asked if he had any children.
The gardener replied:
"I have a daughter,
just two years old."
The xiùcai grew even more displeased.
One day,
waiting until the infant girl's parents had gone out,
he went to their home,
lured the infant girl forward,
and inserted a fine needle into the crown of her head before leaving.
Soon after, he left Huátái,
believing the infant girl was dead.
At that time,
though the infant girl suffered this cruelty,
she ultimately came to no harm.
When she was five or six years old,
both her parents passed away.
The local county, seeing the orphaned girl had no one to care for her,
reported the matter to the Liánshǐ.
The Liánshǐ then took her in and raised her.
Within a year or two,
the Liánshǐ, moved by her cleverness and intelligence,
adopted her as his own daughter,
showering her with love and affection.
When the Liánshǐ was transferred to govern another prefecture,
the girl had grown up.
The xiùcai who had consulted the diviner,
had by then passed the imperial examinations,
and also served in various clerical posts.
Having never had any prior connection with the Liánshǐ,
while traveling on official business,
he presented his name card and requested an audience with the Liánshǐ.
Upon meeting him, the Liánshǐ admired his demeanor and bearing,
and treated him with great courtesy.
When asked about marriage,
he replied he was unmarried.
The Liánshǐ, knowing he was from a scholarly family,
and admiring his character,
decided to give his youngest daughter to him in marriage.
Secretly conveying his intention,
the xiùcai joyfully agreed.
Not long after, they were married.
The Liánshǐ provided a lavish dowry,
and his daughter was also exceptionally beautiful.
The xiùcai was deeply satisfied beyond his expectations,
and recalling the diviner's words,
he privately blamed them as absurd and false.
Afterwards, whenever the weather was overcast,
his wife would suffer from headaches,
which persisted for several years.
They sought out famous physicians.
One doctor said:
"The illness lies at the top of the skull."
He then applied medicine to seal the area on her head.
After a while,
a needle emerged from the festering spot,
and her illness was cured.
He then secretly inquired among the Liánshǐ's relatives and old acquaintances,
asking about the origins of the woman,
and only then learned she was the gardener's daughter.
Thus, he believed the diviner had not been mistaken.
Lù Xiàn, an official in Xiāngzhōu, once recounted this story.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Zhū Xiǎn
Zhū Xiǎn, a clerk in Shèhóng,
once wished to marry the daughter of Dù Jí, the magistrate of Píxiàn.
After the engagement was settled,
it happened that during the Former Shǔ period, she was selected to enter the palace.
Later, during the Xiánkāng era when the state submitted to the new dynasty,
Zhū Xiǎn served as a subordinate official in Péngzhōu.
He sought a marriage alliance again,
and found a granddaughter of the Wáng family,
who was also a former palace lady.
Zhū Xiǎn, while conversing with her,
mentioned his past wish to marry a woman from the Dù family,
and recalled that there had been an engagement letter which said:
"Only ashamed of the poverty of the southern Ruǎn,
how can I match the excellence of the eastern bed?"
The Wáng granddaughter then sighed deeply and said:
"I am that Dù woman.
The name Wáng is an assumed one.
After leaving the palace,
I had no one to rely on,
and was then taken in by the Wáng family."
Zhū Xiǎn was both sorrowful and joyful,
and the affection between husband and wife grew even deeper.
From "Yùxī Biānshì"
Hóu Jìtú
Minister Hóu Jìtú came from a scholarly Confucian family.
His hand never left a book,
and his mouth never ceased reciting.
When the autumn winds rose on all sides,
he was leaning against the railing of the Dàcí Temple tower.
Suddenly, a leaf drifted down and fell.
On it was a poem that read:
"Wiping green, I gather my twin moth-eyebrows,
for the sorrowful matters in my heart.
Grasping the brush, I descend the courtyard steps,
writing characters of longing.
These words are not written on stone,
nor are these words written on paper.
Written upon an autumn leaf,
I wish they would follow the autumn wind and rise.
All the faithless people under heaven,
may they understand longing and die."
He later stored it in a handkerchief box,
for about five or six years.
Soon after, he married a woman named Rén.
He often thought of this poem.
Lady Rén said:
"This is the 'Leaf Poem.'
I wrote it at the time in Zuǒmián.
How did it get here?"
Hóu compared her present handwriting for verification,
and it was identical to that on the leaf.
From "Yùxī Biānshì"
Zhāng Kuān
Zhāng Kuān, courtesy name Shūwén,
served as Palace Attendant during the Hàn dynasty.
He accompanied the emperor to offer sacrifices at Gānquán.
Upon reaching the Wèi Bridge,
they saw a woman bathing in the Wèi River,
with breasts seven chǐ long.
The emperor, finding this strange,
sent someone to question her.
The woman said:
"The person in the seventh carriage behind the emperor
knows where I come from."
At that time, Zhāng Kuān was in the seventh carriage.
He replied:
"The celestial star governing sacrifices—
if the fasting and purification are not strictly observed,
then the Female Star appears."
From "Hànwǔ Gùshì"
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn once traveled incognito to a host's home.
In the household, there was a maidservant of exceptional beauty.
The emperor was pleased with her,
and thus stayed overnight.
At night, he slept with the host's maidservant.
There was a scholar,
who was also lodging there.
He was skilled in astronomy.
Suddenly, he saw a guest star about to obscure the Imperial Throne constellation,
approaching very closely.
The scholar was greatly alarmed and frightened.
He repeatedly exclaimed "Duōduō!"
unconsciously raising his voice.
Then he saw another man,
holding a knife and about to enter the door.
Hearing the scholar's urgent cries,
he thought it was because of himself,
and thus retreated and fled.
The guest star then receded accordingly.
Such occurrences happened several times.
The emperor heard his voice,
found it strange, and questioned him.
The scholar recounted everything he had seen.
The emperor then realized and said,
"This must be that person's husband,
intending to commit violence against me."
He then summoned the Qīmén and Yǔlín guards,
and said to the host:
"I am the Son of Heaven."
Thereupon, they captured the servant,
interrogated him, and he confessed,
so he was executed.
The emperor sighed and said:
"This was surely Heaven enlightening the scholar's mind,
to assist and protect my person."
He then richly rewarded the scholar.
Originally missing the source;
Chén's collated edition attributes it to *Yōumíng Lù*.
Lǐquán
East of Tàiháng Mountain, there is a sweet spring,
its shape like a well,
its body originally stone.
Those wishing to draw water to drink
must all cleanse their hearts, kneel, and ladle it,
then the spring flows like a stream,
the amount sufficient for use.
If anyone is impure or disrespectful,
the spring recedes.
This is the constant will of the spirits.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
Huáinánzǐ
Huáinánzǐ said:
"When the east wind arrives, wine overflows."
Xǔ Shèn explained:
"The east wind is the direction of Zhèn.
Wine overflow refers to clear wine.
Wood's flavor is sour;
it is due to mutual resonance."
Gāo Yòu explained:
"Wine overflow refers to the fermenting of rice, flour, and yeast;
when the wind arrives, it bubbles and moves."
Lǐ Chúnfēng further noted:
When wine is newly mature,
and clarifying in the jar,
it constantly follows the sun's movement.
At dawn, the clear part is on the east side;
at noon, in the south;
at sunset, in the west;
at midnight, at the north (zǐ).
The clear part always follows where the sun is.
Also, in spring and summer,
for spring wine stored in shaded places on the ground,
the foam (like ants) on the jar
all moves following the wind.
Even if stored deep and secluded,
where no wind reaches,
it is still stirred and summoned.
From *Gǎnyìng Jīng*.
Yáng Xióng
Yáng Xióng was reading,
when someone spoke to him:
"Do not torment yourself in vain;
the Mysterious (Xuán) is hard to transmit."
Suddenly, the person vanished.
When Yáng Xióng was writing the *Xuán*,
he dreamed of spitting out a white phoenix that gathered upon it,
and after a moment, it disappeared.
From *Xījīng Zájì*.
Liú Xiàng
Hàn dynasty Liú Xiàng,
during the era of Emperor Chéng and Emperor Āi,
was collating texts at the Tiānlù Pavilion,
wholly absorbed in deep thought.
At night, an old man,
wearing yellow clothes,
tapped the pavilion with a lí-staff and entered.
Seeing Liú Xiàng sitting alone in the dark reciting texts,
the old man blew on the tip of his staff,
and it blazed brightly with light,
which he then used to illuminate Liú Xiàng.
He spoke of matters before the creation of the world,
and then bestowed the text of the "Hóng Fàn Wǔ Xíng".
Liú Xiàng tore his clothes and sash,
to record his words.
At dawn, the old man departed.
When asked his name,
he said:
"I am the essence of Tàiyǐ.
Hearing that the Jīnmǎo surname [i.e., Liú]
had a profoundly learned scholar,
I descended to observe him."
He then took out a bamboo tablet from his bosom,
containing matters related to astronomy and geography.
His son, Liú Xīn,
received this art from Liú Xiàng.
From Wáng Zǐnián's *Shíyí Jì*.
Yuán Ān
Yuán Ān was the magistrate of Yīnpíng,
and had benevolent governance.
The county previously had a hail abyss,
which never melted, winter or summer.
Every year, hail would emerge from it,
flying and spreading over ten-some lǐ,
greatly harming the people.
Yuán Ān then sincerely fasted and purified himself,
acknowledging faults and blaming himself.
His utmost sincerity moved the spirits.
The hail then sank down for him,
subsiding and not rising,
and there was no more bitter rain or mournful wind.
From *Xiǎoshuō*.
Fán Yīng Hàn dynasty Fán Yīng was skilled in charts and prognostication texts,
penetrating the obscure and subtle.
During the Yǒngtài era
(The character "tài" is suspected to be an error;
according to *Hànshū* vol. 112a, "Biography of Fán Yīng".
Fán Yīng lived during the times of Emperor Ān and Emperor Shùn of Hàn,
yet neither reign era used the character "tài".
It is suspected that "níng" is closer
he saw the Son of Heaven,
and facing west, spat southward.
An edict asked the reason.
He replied:
"Chéngdū has a fire today."
Later, the Shǔ commandery reported a fire disaster,
just as Fán Yīng had said.
It was said
that at the time, rain came from the northeast,
so the fire did not cause great harm.
Fán Yīng once suddenly let down his hair, drew a knife,
and struck within his house.
His wife, finding it strange, asked the reason.
Fán Yīng said:
"Student Xī has encountered bandits."
Student Xī, named Xún,
was Fán Yīng's disciple,
traveling far at the time.
Later, upon returning, he recounted
that on the road he had met bandits,
but was saved by an old man with disheveled hair who came to his aid,
thus escaping harm.
During the Yǒngjiàn era,
a bell in the palace rang by itself.
The emperor was troubled by this,
and the ministers could not explain it.
So he asked Fán Yīng.
Fán Yīng said:
"Mount Mín in Shǔ has collapsed.
When the mother collapses, the child therefore rings;
it is not a disaster for the sacred court."
Soon after, reports came of the mountain collapse in Shǔ.
From *Yīng Lièzhuàn*.
The Essence of the Five Minerals
The *Lùnhéng* states:
The yang-sui obtains fire,
the fāngzhū obtains water;
both objects must rely on their form and configuration to achieve this.
The yang-sui is shaped like a crescent moon,
the fāngzhū is shaped like a cup.
If both vessels were like flat boards,
how could they obtain fire and water?
To cast a yang-sui,
use the noon hour on the bǐngwǔ day of the fifth month,
smelt five-colored stones to make it,
its shape is like a round mirror,
facing the sun, it immediately obtains fire.
The fāngzhū,
use the midnight hour on the rénzǐ day of the eleventh month,
smelt five-colored stones to make it,
its shape is like a cup,
facing the moon, it immediately obtains liquid water.
Nowadays, taking a large clam or mussel and facing it towards the moon,
there is also moisture.
The *Huáinánzǐ* says:
The yang-sui sees the sun,
and dries to become fire.
The fāngzhū sees the moon,
and moistens to become water.
The commentary states,
both are the essence of the five minerals.
The yang-sui is round and faces upward to the sun,
obtaining fire;
the fāngzhū is concave and faces the moon,
obtaining water.
It also says,
the yang-sui's drawing of fire from the sun,
the fāngzhū's drawing of dew from the moon,
within heaven and earth,
mysterious, subtle, and elusive,
even the most skillful calendarist cannot calculate their numbers.
Yet, within the grasp of one's hand,
drawing analogy from the Supreme Ultimate above,
fire and water can be instantly obtained,
this is due to the mutual stimulation of yīn and yáng.
From the *Gǎnyìng Jīng*.
Pitch Pipes
The *Wùlǐ Lùn* states:
The twelve pitch pipes await the ethers;
first, on level ground, build a chamber with three layers,
each layer has three walls,
this is what Yángzǐ called the "nine enclosures within."
The outer chamber has a southern door,
with cloth as a curtain;
the middle chamber has a northern door;
the inner chamber has a southern door,
also with cloth as a curtain.
All are round above and square below,
sealed tightly without wind.
A person stays inside,
observing for three days.
For each of the twelve pitch pipes, use wood to make a stand,
each stand is lower inside and higher outside,
place the pitch pipe on top of it,
arranging them according to their positions.
Fill the ends with reed membrane ash from Hénèi.
If the ether arrives,
it blows the ash off the pipe's mouth;
a slight movement indicates harmony,
a large movement indicates ministers' strength.
Lǐ Chúnfēng said:
Since ancient times, those discussing musical tones and pitch pipes,
all base it on the twelve pipes,
using the response of ether causing ash to fly as proof.
At the end of the Later Wèi,
Sūn Sēnghuà created the Liùjiǎ Yīzhōu calendar,
its preface states,
using pipe pitch to await the response of the monthly and hourly pitch ethers for verification and comparison.
