Five or six instances before and after,
all did not match the calculations and methods of calendar specialists.
Besides this, in various books,
none mention the awaited ethers producing verifiable results.
Reasoning and searching,
I fear there is no true record.
Xìndū Fāng of Later Wèi,
himself said,
he created a wind fan to await the twenty-four solar terms,
whenever a solar term arrived,
the fan would lift.
This is also verification.
From the *Gǎnyìng Jīng*.
Chén Yè
Chén Yè, styled Wénlǐ.
Chén Yè's elder brother perished at sea.
At that time, those who had relied on him numbered fifty or sixty,
their flesh and bones decayed and mingled,
making them indistinguishable.
Chén Yè looked up to the August Heaven and swore to the Sovereign Earth, saying:
"I have heard that for blood relatives,
there must be a difference."
Thereupon, he cut his arm and let the blood flow,
sprinkling it on the bones.
Immediately, the blood soaked in where it belonged,
while the rest flowed away.
From the *Huìjī Xiānxián Zhuàn*.
Chén Shí
Chén Shí of Yǐngchuān had a son named Yuánfāng,
the younger named Zhòngfāng,
both renowned for their virtue and reputation.
The brothers were filial and supportive,
their household harmonious and respectful,
all within the realm admired their conduct.
The Four Offices all summoned them,
yet they did not yield to serve.
The brothers once visited their fellow commandery member Xún Shuǎng,
meeting for a night banquet.
The Grand Astrologer reported:
"Virtuous stars have gathered."
From the *Rǔnán Xiānxián Zhuàn*.
The Man from Three Provinces
A man from Three Provinces in Jìn,
made a pact to become father and sons.
The father ordered the two to build a house in the great marsh,
when it was nearly completed,
the father said:
"It would be better by the river."
So they moved.
When it was again nearly completed,
the father said:
"It would be better in the river."
The two then carried earth to fill the river,
for thirty days without success.
A scholar passing by,
made two earthen piglets and threw them into the river.
The father then stopped the two, saying:
"Have you ever seen a river or sea filled?
I was just observing your actions."
The next day, returning to the riverside,
the earth in the river had formed a mound over ten feet high,
extending over ten lǐ in length and breadth,
so they dwelt upon it.
From the *Xiàozǐ Zhuàn*.
Wèi Rénchéng King
When Wèi Rénchéng King Zhāng died,
he was buried with rites like those of Hàn's Dōngpíng King.
As the funeral procession departed,
the sound of hundreds weeping was heard in the air.
Those escorting said,
in the past, those killed or wounded by rebel armies had no coffins,
the King, in his benevolence and kindness,
collected their decayed bones.
The dead rejoice in the underworld,
their spirits are thus moved and grateful.
From Wáng Zǐnián's *Shíyí Jì*.
Lǚ Qián
In Wèi, Chángshā Commandery had prolonged rain.
Grand Administrator Lǚ Qián ordered the Household Registrar to fast and purify,
staying at the altar for three days and three nights,
praying for clear weather.
He dreamt of a white-haired old man who said:
"You have come late,
tomorrow it will clear."
And so it was.
From the *Chángshā Zhuàn*.
Guǎn Níng
Guǎn Níng died in Liáodōng; thirty-seven years later,
when his coffin was to return, it was hindered by sea winds.
Dozens of ships traveling together all sank,
only Guǎn Níng's ship saw a light,
and heading towards it reached an island.
Upon going ashore,
there was neither fire nor people.
Xuányàn Xiānshēng considered this the response of accumulated goodness.
From the *Dúyì Zhì*.
The Man from Héjiān
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
in Héjiān Commandery, there was a man and woman who were in love,
and they promised to marry each other.
Later, the man joined the army for many years,
and his parents arranged for the woman to marry someone else.
Not long after, she died of grief.
When the man returned, he was heartbroken.
He went to her grave,
and just as he was about to weep,
he could not contain his emotions.
So he opened the grave and the coffin,
and she immediately revived.
He then carried her back home,
and after nursing her for several days, she fully recovered.
Her husband then went to demand her back.
The man refused to return her,
saying:
"Your wife is already dead.
Who in the world has ever heard of a dead person coming back to life?
This is a gift from Heaven to me,
she is not your wife."
Thus, they took the matter to court,
but the commandery and county authorities could not decide the case.
It was submitted to the Commandant of Justice for judgment.
The Commandant memorialized that due to the utmost sincerity,
which moved Heaven and Earth,
she died and was revived.
This lies beyond ordinary principles,
and is not something that reason can adjudicate,
nor that punishment can decide.
He ruled that she should be given to the one who opened the grave.
From *Fǎyuàn Zhūlín*.
The Woman of Yíyáng
During the turmoil of the Yǒngjiā era of Jìn,
commandery and county administrations lacked stable governance,
and the strong preyed upon the weak.
In Yíyáng County, there was a woman,
whose surname was Péng and given name was É.
Her parents and over ten siblings
were killed by bandits from Chángshā.
At the time, É had gone out with a vessel to fetch water from a stream.
When the bandits arrived, she ran back,
only to see the walls of her home already broken.
Overwhelmed by grief,
she fought with the bandits.
The bandits bound É,
drove her to the stream's edge,
and were about to kill her.
By the stream stood a great mountain,
with cliffs tens of *zhàng* high.
Looking up, she cried out:
"Does the August Heaven have any divine power?
What crime have I committed,
that I should suffer this?"
Then she ran toward the mountain,
and the mountain suddenly opened wide for several *zhàng*,
forming a level road like a whetstone.
The bandits also chased É into the mountain,
and the mountain then closed up,
seamlessly as before.
The bandits were all crushed to death,
and É vanished, never to reappear.
The water vessel É had set down
turned into stone,
shaped like a chicken.
The local people thus named it Stone Chicken Mountain and Woman É Pool.
From *Yōumíng Lù*.
Zhāng Yìng
In Lìyáng Commandery of Jìn, there was a man named Zhāng Yìng,
who initially worshipped demons,
and married a woman from a Buddhist family.
In the eighth year of the Xiánhé era,
they moved to Wúhú.
His wife fell ill,
and because he performed demonic rituals,
the family wealth was nearly exhausted,
yet her illness did not improve.
His wife said:
"I am originally from a Buddhist family;
perform Buddhist rites for me."
Yìng then went to a monastery,
and met Zhú Tánjìng.
Jìng said:
"To universally aid all beings,
you must simply wholeheartedly uphold the faith."
Tánjìng set a time for the next day,
to go to their home.
That evening, Yìng dreamed of a person,
five or six *chǐ* tall,
who hurried through the door, saying:
"This household is quiet,
yet it is so impure."
He saw Jìng following behind this person,
explaining:
"This family is just beginning to awaken their intention;
they cannot be blamed."
When Yìng awoke from sleep,
he immediately lit a fire and prepared a high seat and a seat for Hārītī.
When Jìng arrived at mealtime,
the high seat and such
were already fully prepared.
Yìng recounted the dream in detail,
and then both husband and wife received the Five Precepts.
The illness was also cured.
From *Biànzhèng Lùn*.
The Clerk of Nánjùn
In Jìn, there was a clerk in the deliberation bureau of Nánjùn Commandery, surnamed Ōu,
who had been ill for a year.
His bones wasted away and his flesh diminished,
and though shamans and doctors were all consulted,
there was no further remedy.
His son, Yèrú, managed to sleep one night,
and dreamed of several Buddhist monks coming to see his father.
The next morning,
he went to the Buddhist temple.
He saw the monks,
and asked what kind of deity the Buddha was.
The monks explained the circumstances.
He then brought the monks
"rén" originally written as "hé",
corrected according to the Míng manuscript copy
back home,
and requested them to chant scriptures.
After two nights,
the patient himself felt his illness lighten.
During the day, he managed to doze lightly,
and as he raised his head,
he saw several dozen small children at the door,
all wearing colorful clothes.
Some held banners and staffs in their hands,
others held knives and spears.
They entered through the door.
Two small children were in front,
and went straight to the curtain.
Suddenly, they turned back,
and said to the crowd of little ones behind:
"The people living here are all monks."
Then they did not come forward again.
From then on, the illness gradually improved.
From *Língguǐ Zhì*.
The Monastery of Púbǎn
In the eighth year of the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
a great fire broke out in Púbǎn City, Hé dōng,
and it could not be extinguished.
Only the monastery, large and small, remained intact,
along with the scriptures and images in lay households,
none of which were damaged or lost.
The common people were astonished,
and redoubled their faith.
From *Biànzhèng Lùn*.
The Scripture Hall of Wúxīng
During the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
a fire once broke out in Wúxīng Commandery,
burning several hundred households to utter destruction.
Only the thatched scripture hall
remained intact and unburned.
At the time, it was regarded as divine.
From *Xuānyàn Jì*.
The Scholar of Nánxú
During the reign of Emperor Shào of the Sòng dynasty,
in Nánxú there was a scholar.
While traveling from Huàshān to Yúnyáng,
he saw a young woman at an inn,
about eighteen or nineteen years old.
He fell for her without any reason,
and it turned into a lovesickness illness.
His mother asked him the cause,
and he told her everything.
His mother went to Huàshān Yúnyáng,
found the young woman,
and explained everything to her.
The young woman, moved upon hearing this,
then took off her apron,
and told the mother to secretly hide it under his mat,
saying that lying on it would cure him.
After a few days, he indeed recovered.
Suddenly lifting the mat,
he saw the apron,
grasped it and wept,
almost fainting from grief.
He said to his mother:
"When I am buried, pass by Huàshān."
His mother followed his wish.
As they reached the young woman's door,
the ox stopped and refused to go further,
so they waited a moment.
The young woman finished dressing and bathing and came out,
singing:
"At the foot of Huàshān,
since you have died for me,
for whom should I live alone?
If you pity me,
let the coffin open for me."
As soon as she finished speaking,
the coffin opened,
and the young woman entered the coffin.
They were then buried together,
and called the tomb 'The Tomb of the Divine Scholar'.
From Xì Méng.
Xú Zǔ
Xú Zǔ of Jiāxīng,
orphaned young,
was raised by his uncle Wěi as his own son.
When Wěi fell ill,
Zǔ cared for him diligently.
That night,
he dreamed a deity told him:
"Your uncle is fated to die."
Zǔ kowtowed and begged for mercy.
Two deities said:
"Considering your devotion,
we will spare him for you."
Zǔ awoke,
and his uncle recovered.
From Sōu Shén Jì.
Liú Jīng
Liú Jīng, a commoner of Línjiāng commandery,
was respected in his village for his filial piety.
When the river suddenly flooded,
the residents were all swept away and drowned.
Jīng carried his mother, weeping and wailing.
Suddenly, a large turtle came before him,
and his entire family of seven
climbed onto the turtle's back.
After traveling about ten li,
they reached a high bank,
and the turtle then disappeared.
From Jiǔjiāng Jì.
Hé Jìngshū
Hé Jìngshū had followed Buddhism since youth.
He wanted to make a sandalwood statue,
but lacked the wood.
He first dreamed of a monk,
in patched robes, carrying a staff, who came and said:
"The Hè family behind the county office has a paulownia tree they cherish greatly;
if you plead earnestly, you may obtain it."
He sought it as in the dream,
and indeed obtained it.
From Mèng Juàn.
Xiāo Zǐmào
Xiāo Zǐmào, Prince Jìn'ān of Qí,
courtesy name Yúnchāng,
was a son of Emperor Wǔ.
When he was just seven years old,
Ruǎn Shūyuán once fell critically ill,
and monks were invited to perform rituals.
Someone offered lotus flowers for Buddha,
and the monks placed them in a bronze jar filled with water.
After three days like this, the flowers did not wither.
Zǐmào wept and paid respects to Buddha.
He vowed:
"If my aunt, through this blessed connection,
receives divine protection and recovers,
may the flowers remain fresh until the end of the fast."
When the seven-day fast ended,
the flowers were even more vibrant and red.
Looking into the jar,
they saw small roots had grown.
Shūyuán's illness soon recovered,
and contemporaries praised it as a filial miracle.
From Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Xiāo Ruìmíng
Xiāo Ruìmíng of Lánlíng, magistrate of Sōngzī in Qí,
had a mother who suffered from a chronic illness.
Ruìmíng prayed day and night.
It was cold and freezing,
and Ruìmíng's tears
froze like chopsticks.
Blood from kowtowing on his forehead
turned to ice without flowing.
Suddenly, a person
handed him a stone case, saying:
"This can cure your mother's illness."
Ruìmíng knelt and received it,
and the person suddenly vanished.
He presented the case to his mother;
inside was only a three-inch silk cloth,
with red characters forming the characters for 'sun' and 'moon'.
His mother's illness immediately healed.
From Tán Sǒu.
Xiè Shūqiān
Xiè Shūqiān of Yànmén in Qí
was summoned to court as an attendant,
but did not go.
His mother fell ill,
and Shūqiān, at night in the courtyard,
kowtowed and prayed for blessings.
He heard a voice from the air say:
"Obtain Dīnggōngténg to make wine, and she will recover."
He consulted doctors and herbal texts,
but none knew of it.
So he journeyed arduously in search,
reaching the area of Yídū,
where he saw from afar an old man in the mountains cutting wood.
He asked its use,
and the old man replied:
"This is Dīnggōngténg,
especially effective for treating wind ailments."
Shūqiān bowed again, weeping,
and explained in detail his purpose in seeking it.
The old man, moved with pity,
gave him the vine,
and also showed him the method for steeping it in wine.
Shūqiān received it,
and the man was never seen again.
He made the wine according to the method,
and his mother's illness was cured.
From Tán Sǒu.
Zōng Yuánqīng
Zōng Yuánqīng of Nányáng in Qí was exceptionally virtuous.
Orphaned early,
he was raised by his mother.
When his mother was ill,
Yuánqīng, even when far away,
would feel heartache:
"A serious illness caused great pain,
a minor illness caused slight pain.
This became the norm.
The village respected him,
and he was generally called 'Zōng Zēngzǐ'.
From Tán Sǒu.
Kuāng Xīn
Kuāng Xīn of Qí Lúlǐng lived in seclusion on Jīnhuá Mountain,
practicing dietary regimens and not associating with ordinary people.
His mother had already been dead for several days,
but when Xīn rushed back wailing,
his mother revived.
It was due to the power of filial devotion.
From Tán Sǒu.
Zēng Kāngzǔ
Zēng Kāngzǔ of Fúfēng in Qí
had a mother suffering from breast abscesses,
which no doctor could cure.
Kāngzǔ then knelt,
cupped her breasts with both hands,
and wept bitterly.
His mother's abscesses then healed.
From Tán Sǒu.
Cuī Shù
In Qiáojùn, there was a merit officer named Jiàn.
During the Tiāntǒng era,
Lái Fǔjūn of Jǐnán
was appointed as the governor of Qiáojùn.
The merit officer, Cuī Shù of Qīnghé,
was a young man of virtuous reputation.
At that time, there was a prolonged drought in spring and summer.
Over a thousand people came to bid farewell.
When they reached this stream,
the crowd was extremely thirsty,
and Lord Lái showed signs of longing for water.
Shù alone saw a blue bird
flying up and down in the stream.
Finding it strange, he approached.
The bird flew away,
revealing a stone,
about five or six inches square.
He poked it with his whip,
and clear spring water gushed forth.
They collected it in a silver bottle.
Once the bottle was full,
the water immediately ceased.
Only Lord Lái and Shù were able to drink from it.
Commentators believed this was due to the power of virtue.
People of the time found it extraordinary,
hence it was recorded as such.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Hé Hú
Liáng's Hé Hú, styled Zhòngbǎo,
served as a consultant for the northern campaign.
He was widely learned and studious,
and renowned from a young age.
His nature was pure and profound,
and he served his parents with reverence and respect.
When his mother fell ill and needed a doctor,
he did not ride in a carriage or on horseback.
Suddenly, he encountered a holy monk,
whose appearance was extraordinary.
Holding an incense burner,
he came seeking alms food,
arriving at any time, early or late.
Thus, Hé Hú suspected he was no ordinary person.
This continued for over ten days,
and his mother's illness began to improve.
The monk then bid farewell and left,
leaving behind a volume of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra in plain script.
Taking Hé Hú's hand, he said:
"This humble monk is one of the twenty-seven sages,
not one to avoid people
(The 'Biànzhèng Lùn' version eight writes 'avoid' as 'retreat')
Moved by your sincerity,
I came to visit.
The patient is now recovered,
and I should return."
After speaking, he walked forward
and suddenly vanished.
The smoke from the incense burner and its fragrance
lingered for ten days before dissipating.
Moved by such sincerity,
both the court and the common people sighed in admiration.
Hé Hú then donated his separate residence to establish
(the Ming manuscript writes 'establish' as 'because')
the Ài Temple.
From "Biànzhèng Lùn"
Chén Yí
Chén Yí, a man from Wú, served as a minor official in the commandery in his youth.
His mother enjoyed eating scorched rice.
While on duty,
Chén Yí always carried a bag.
Whenever he cooked food,
he would collect the scorched rice and offer it to his mother.
When Sūn Ēn rebelled,
Chén Yí fled like others.
His mother missed him,
crying day and night,
until she lost her eyesight.
When Chén Yí escaped danger and returned home,
he entered and saw his mother.
Bowing twice, he wept loudly.
Suddenly, his mother's eyes regained their sight.
From "Xiàozǐ Zhuàn"
Wáng Xūzhī,
a man from Xīchāng, Lúlíng.
At the age of thirteen,
he lost both parents.
For twenty years, he did not consume salt or vinegar.
Later, he fell seriously ill.
Suddenly, a person came to visit him,
saying:
"Your illness will soon be cured."
In an instant, the person vanished.
Moreover, the room where he lived
emitted a strange light at night,
and the tangerine tree in the courtyard
bore three fruits in the depths of winter.
His illness indeed soon recovered.
All believed this was due to his extreme filial piety.
From "Xiàozǐ Zhuàn"
The Woman from Hénán
During the Suí dynasty's Dàyè era,
a woman from Hénán did not serve her mother-in-law filially.
The mother-in-law was blind in both eyes,
and the woman fed her a soup made of earthworms.
The mother-in-law found the taste strange,
secretly kept a piece,
and saved it to show her son.
When the son saw it, he wept bitterly
and prepared to report the woman to the county authorities.
Suddenly, a violent storm of thunder and rain arose,
and the woman disappeared.
Soon, she was seen falling from the sky to the ground.
Her body and clothing remained as before,
but her head had transformed into that of a white dog,
though she could still speak as usual.
She said:
"For being unfilial to my mother-in-law,
I have been punished by the heavenly gods."
Her husband then drove her away.
Later, she begged for food on the roads,
and her whereabouts became unknown.
From "Míngbào Jì"
Cén Wénběn
Táng dynasty Secretariat Director Cén Wénběn,
a man from Jiānglíng.
From a young age, he believed in Buddhism
and often recited the Universal Gate chapter of the Lotus Sutra.
Once, while traveling by boat on a great river,
the boat wrecked,
and all aboard perished.
Wénběn sank into the water,
but heard a voice saying:
"Just recite the Buddha's name,
and you will not die."
This was repeated three times.
Soon, he was carried by the waves to the surface
and reached the northern shore,
thus escaping death.
Later, he held a vegetarian feast in Jiānglíng,
and monks gathered at his home.
One visiting monk lingered after the others left,
and said to Wénběn:
"The world is about to fall into chaos,
but fortunately, you will avoid its disasters.
Eventually, you will encounter peace
and attain wealth and honor."
After speaking,
he hurried out and vanished.
Then, as Wénběn partook in the feast,
he found two relics in his own bowl.
Later events indeed turned out as predicted.
From "Fǎyuàn Zhūlín"
Zhèng Xiān
Táng dynasty's Zhèng Xiān, styled Dàozǐ,
was skilled in physiognomy.
Knowing his own life would be short,
he thought of no way to extend it.
He dreamed of a monk asking him:
"Do you wish to extend your life?
On major fasting days,
release living creatures and cultivate goodness,
observe fasting and uphold precepts.
This can prolong your life and bring fortune."
Xiān thus followed the Dharma,
and indeed gained longevity.
From "Xuānyàn Jì"
Zhāng Chǔjīn
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign in the Táng dynasty,
Minister of Justice Zhāng Chǔjīn was framed by the cruel official Zhōu Xìng.
As he was about to be executed,
he looked up and sighed:
"Heaven and Earth,
do you not see loyalty and filial piety?
Why must an innocent man be condemned?"
Tears streamed down his face,
and the people in the market all sighed in sympathy.
Moments later,
dark clouds gathered from all directions,
as if moved by his plight.
Soon, an imperial pardon was issued, sparing his life.
After the proclamation,
the sky cleared,
and auspicious clouds swirled.
Contemporaries believed this was due to his loyalty and integrity.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì"
Luó Dàocōng
Táng Dynasty Sīzhúyuán's Luó Dàocóng submitted a memorial that offended the emperor,
and was exiled.
At the time, a fellow exile fell ill and died on the journey,
weeping and saying:
"My regret is to leave my bones in a foreign land."
Dàocóng said in response:
"If I return alive,
I will take you back with me."
He then buried him and departed.
Upon his return,
due to a great flood,
the grave's location was lost.
Dàocóng wept and prayed to him,
asking to be shown his spirit.
Soon after, the water's edge began to boil and surge,
and he chanted again:
"If you are truly beneath here,
please make it boil once more."
It did so again,
and thus he recovered the bones,
the epitaph still legible for verification,
and carried them back to their hometown.
From "Guǎngdé Shényì Lù"
Língkōng Guàn
In the fourth year of the Jǐnglóng era of the Táng Dynasty,
Língkōng Guàn in Luòzhōu caught fire,
and everything was consumed.
Only one zhēnrén statue,
towering and alone, remained intact,
though it was made of clay.
It was then renamed Shèngzhēn Guàn.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Huángfǔ Shì
Táng Dynasty Púyè Péi Zūnqìng's
mother, née Huángfǔ,
in her youth often chanted scriptures.
Inside the scripture box was a small coral tree.
On another occasion,
a small dragon skeleton suddenly appeared,
standing beside the tree.
People of the time considered it an auspicious sign for the Péi family.
During the Shàngyuán era,
Zūnqìng indeed rose to the position of chief minister.
From "Guǎngyì Jì"
Tián Rénhuì
Táng Dynasty Tián Rénhuì served as governor of Yǐngzhōu.
He exposed himself under the sun to pray for rain, and rain came.
People sang:
"Our parents raised us, but Governor Tián nourishes us;
His sincere devotion reaches the heavens above.
Rain falls in the fields, clouds emerge from the hills;
May he remain always, so we need not fear poverty."
From "Guǎngdé Shényì Lù"
Xúzhōu Soldier
When Wáng Zhìxīng was in Xúzhōu during the Táng Dynasty,
his laws and commands were extremely strict.
A frontier defense soldier returning from duty rotation
was being celebrated with a feast at home by his brother-in-law,
who was in the kitchen sharpening a knife,
intending to take his seat
(Míng manuscript note: the characters for 'take his seat' are written as '生' [to live/grow])
and slice a lamb shank.
After sharpening it,
he hurriedly walked with it.
His wife's brother walked from the hall into the kitchen,
and they abruptly collided,
the blade striking the wife's brother's heart directly,
killing him instantly.
The authorities arrested him and reported it.
Zhìxīng interrogated him,
but he claimed it was an accident,
with no malicious intent.
Zhìxīng did not believe him,
and ordered his execution.
The executioner's sword kept leaping from his hand,
and plunging straight into the ground.
Three different executioners tried, all with the same result.
Zhìxīng found this strange,
and thus did not kill him.
From "Yīnhuà Lù"
Táng Emperor Xuānzōng
In the early Dàzhōng era of the Táng Dynasty,
the capital experienced continuous rain for a month,
threatening the grain harvest.
Prayers were ordered in all directions,
but none were answered.
One day, Emperor Xuānzōng was in the inner palace,
and said to his attendants:
"In ancient times, Tāng took six faults upon himself,
offering his own body in place of a sacrifice.
Though the drought was severe,
it ultimately did not become a disaster.
I am now the lord of millions,
yet far inferior in virtue to Tāng.
With such a disaster occurring,
what will the people think of me?"
He then took an incense burner,
descended the steps into the mud,
burned incense and looked up to heaven,
as if blaming himself.
After a long time,
his imperial robes were soaked through,
moving all those around him.
In a moment, the heavy rain ceased;
the next day, the overcast skies cleared,
and by autumn there was a great harvest.
From "Zhēnlíng Shíqī Shǐ"
Lǐ Yànzuǒ
Lǐ Yànzuǒ was in Cāngjǐng.
In the ninth year of the Tàihé era of the Táng Dynasty,
an imperial edict ordered the Fúyáng troops to cross the Huáng Hé northward.
It was winter, the twelfth month.
Upon reaching Jǐ'nán,
the commandery ordered the ice to be broken to advance the boats.
The ice struck a boat,
capsizing it and causing the loss of the edict.
Yànzuǒ was shocked and fearful,
unable to sleep or eat for six days,
his hair turning white,
his appearance haggard and skin drawn,
so much so that his subordinates barely recognized him.
He then ordered the ferry officer
that if the edict was not found, all would die.
The officer, terrified,
requested to offer a prayer to the river,
relying on Yànzuǒ's sincere clarity,
to search for it at the risk of death.
Yànzuǒ then ordered ceremonial wine to be prepared,
and a prayer to be conveyed, questioning the river.
Its essence was:
The enlightened Son of Heaven reigns above,
rivers, streams, mountains, and peaks,
all receive their proper sacrifices from prayer officers.
Within my jurisdiction,
sacrifices have never been lacking,
yet
("yet" originally written as "two" [兩],
corrected per Míng manuscript)
the River Earl and leaders of the scaly and shelled creatures
should be guarding the Son of Heaven's edict;
why instead have you drowned it?
If it is not recovered,
I will fast and report to Heaven,
and Heaven will punish you.
After the officer finished the libation and prayer on the ice,
a sound like thunder was suddenly heard,
and the river ice split open,
for about thirty zhàng.
The officer knew Yànzuǒ's utmost sincerity had reached [the spirits],
and sank a hook to search and retrieve it.
The sealed envelope was as before,
only the seal imprint was slightly damp.
Wherever Yànzuǒ served,
his orders were strict yet affairs simple,
extending sincerity to all things,
earning a fine reputation as an official.
The Huáng Hé's waters are turbid and swift-flowing;
large logs and tiny specks
are carried a thousand lǐ in an instant.
How could it be that a boat capsized for six days,
yet one libation caused solid ice to crack,
one hook retrieved a sunken edict?
Was this not the ultimate sincerity?
From "Quē Shǐ"
Hú Shēng
Lièzǐ died in Zhèng,
and his tomb is now in the suburban wilderness.
It is said that the traces of the virtuous
sometimes prohibit woodcutting and gathering there.
In the village, there was a man named Hú Shēng,
whose family was poor.
From a young age, he worked as a mirror polisher and nail mender.
Whenever he encountered sweet fruits, famous teas, or fine wines,
he would offer them at Liè Yùkòu's grave mound,
as if seeking wisdom and aspiring to learn the Way.
After many years,
he suddenly dreamed of a person
who sliced open his abdomen with a knife,
placed a scroll of writings
into his heart and organs.
Upon waking,
the poetic inspiration
was all elegant and beautiful verse,
acquired without the aid of teachers or friends.
Even after completing his literary works,
he still did not abandon his humble trade,
truly embodying the demeanor of a recluse.
Far and near, he was called Hú Dīngjiǎo.
Prefects and renowned scholars
all looked up to him,
and his home often hosted esteemed elders.
If someone tried to offer bribes,
he would certainly refuse them.
But if someone brought tea or wine,
he would gladly accept and entertain them.
A few examples of his writings:
Delighted by the visit of Hán Shàofǔ from Pútián, he wrote:
"Suddenly hearing Méi Fú came to visit,
Smiling, I don my lotus robe and leave the thatched hall.
The children, unaccustomed to seeing carriages and horses,
Compete to hide deep within the reed flowers."
Also, viewing the embroidery patterns of the courtesans of Cuī Lángzhōng in Zhèngzhōu, he wrote:
"At dusk, the flower buds before the hall are delicate,
Competing to take small brushes and climb onto beds to trace.
Once embroidered, placed in the spring garden,
They lure orioles down from the willow branches."
On a child fishing by the river:
"A tousle-haired youngster learns to cast his line,
Sitting sideways on green moss, grass reflecting his form.
A passerby asks from afar; he waves his hand in reply,
Fearing the fish might be startled, he does not answer the man."
From *Yúnxī Yǒuyì*.
Liú Xíngzhě
In the marketplace of Lúlíng during the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Liú Xíngzhě.
He made a living as a nail mender.
He was extremely filial.
His mother had suffered from an eye ailment for over twenty years,
and Xíngzhě earnestly sought remedies and treatments.
One day,
suddenly a mendicant monk
carrying a clean water copper bottle
sought out Xíngzhě to polish and wash it,
offering a hundred pieces of gold as payment,
but Xíngzhě refused.
He explained:
"At home, my mother has suffered from eye disease for many years.
Venerable monk, do you perhaps have medicine to cure it?"
The monk said:
"Wait until I finish polishing and washing the bottle,
then I will treat her."
After the polishing and washing were done,
the monk went out the door,
and Xíngzhě followed, asking him.
The monk said:
"Just return home,
I have already treated her."
Having said this,
the monk disappeared.
Xíngzhě rushed back home,
and saw his mother suddenly fall from her bed to the ground,
her eyes wide open.
The whole family was shocked and overjoyed,
realizing then that the monk earlier was an arhat.
So they painted his image and made offerings to it.
It remains to this day.
From *Bàoyìng Lù*.
Wáng Fǎlǎng
Wáng Fǎlǎng, a Dàoshi of Kuízhōu during the Táng dynasty,
had a large and long tongue,
and his pronunciation of written characters was not very accurate or clear,
which he often regretted.
Thus, he made a vow to read the *Dàodé Jīng*.
He dreamed that Lǎojūn cut his tongue.
Upon waking, his speech was clear and fluent,
and he could recite the five thousand characters of the *Dàodé Jīng* with precision,
showing remarkable evidence of efficacy.
From *Lùyì Jì*.
Xī Fǎzūn
The Táng dynasty Dàoshi Xī Fǎzūn resided at the Jiǎnjì Guàn on Lúshān,
his practice of the Way was precise and earnest.
He managed the temple's affairs single-handedly,
for several years already,
with no disciples at all.
Suddenly, he dreamed that Fǎshī Xuánzhōng said to him:
"You lack manpower,
and your diligence is evident.
Now there are two children,
only regret they are too young."
After waking,
he told the others.
Going out of the mountain, he passed by the home of a commoner named Wáng,
where there was a child
just one year old.
Upon seeing Fǎzūn,
the child hugged his legs and refused to let go.
When Fǎzūn left,
the child cried day and night without cease.
When Fǎzūn returned, the child was joyful.
Several years later,
the parents relinquished the child to become an acolyte.
Another child, surnamed Liú,
had eyes that emitted five-colored light.
His parents suspected it was strange,
so they cauterized the area around his eyes,
and the light then ceased.
By the time he was four or five years old,
he too was given to the temple,
and they successively entered the Way.
This indeed matched the words imparted by Xuánzhōng in the dream.
From *Lùyì Jì*.
Wáng Huī
Wáng Huī, a general of Western Shǔ, once served as Prefect of Jízhōu.
Within the walls of Jízhōu city, there were no springs or water sources,
and the people all fetched water from the wilds.
When Qí troops urgently attacked the city,
and cut off its water route,
the city suffered from extreme thirst.
Within ten days,
quite a few had died.
Lord Wáng then made supplications in the middle of the night,
mournfully appealing to the deities.
Upon falling asleep,
he dreamed an old man told him:
"Beneath the prefectural prison,
there should be a fine spring."
Having said this, he left,
and Wáng also awoke startled.
At dawn,
he ordered baskets and spades,
and at the indicated spot dug several zhàng deep,
whereupon a spring flowed forth.
The residents drank from it,
and many were saved.
The Qí troops, knowing the city had no water,
intended to simply wait for them to perish.
Lord Wáng ordered dozens of jars of the spring water to be drawn,
and displayed them by pouring them out on the city walls,
whereupon the enemy withdrew.
That day, the miraculous spring also dried up.
Was this not moved by Lord Wáng's utmost sincerity?
The event of Shūlè worshipping the well
certainly was not unfounded.
Wáng later retired from office,
and settled in Yōngzhōu.
He once spoke of this,
hence it is recorded.
From *Yùtáng Xiánhuà*.
Lǐ Mèngqí
Lǐ Mèngqí, a soldier of the Báshān army of the false Shǔ, was captured by the enemy and taken to Qíyáng.
His elderly mother wept in sorrow,
and consequently became blind in both eyes.
Mèngqí, in Qíyáng,
prayed devoutly and earnestly,
wishing to see his compassionate mother again.
After three years, he finally returned.
Mèngqí pricked his thigh and used his blood to anoint his mother's eyes,
and they immediately returned to their former state.
Thus it is known that the resonance of filial piety
is clearly manifest.
From *Jǐngjiè Lù*.
Mèng Xī
In Shǔ, Mèng Xī
sold fruits to support his parents.
He catered to their expressions and complied with their wishes,
ensuring their warmth in winter and coolness in summer, and inquiring after their well-being morning and evening.
He would inform them when going out and report back upon returning,
never shirking hardship or toil.
His father often said:
"Though I am poor,
I have raised a Zēng Shēn."
When his father passed away,
he abstained from food and drink, wailing in grief,
nearly to the point of endangering his life.
He spread straw mats on the ground
and slept upon them.
For three years, he consumed no salt or dairy products.
People far and near sighed in admiration.
Once, he saw a rat digging in the ground
and uncovered several thousand taels of gold.
From then on, he became immensely wealthy.
From "Jǐng Jiè Lù".
The Old Woman of Lìyáng
In Lìyáng County, there was an old woman
who often performed good deeds.
Suddenly, a young man came to her door seeking food,
and the old woman treated him with great respect.
Before leaving, he said to the old woman:
"Go to the county gate from time to time.
If you see blood on the threshold, climb the mountain to avoid disaster."
From then on, the old woman went there daily.
The gatekeeper asked her why,
and she truthfully answered with what the young man had taught her.
The gatekeeper then playfully used chicken blood
to smear the threshold.
The next day,
when the old woman saw the blood,
she took her chicken coop and fled up the mountain.
That evening,
the county sank and became a lake—
now known as the Lìyáng Lake in Hézhōu.
From "Dú Yì Jì".
Sūn Quán
Péngkǒu City
was built by Guàn Yīng in the sixth year of Emperor Gaozu of Hàn.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
Sūn Quán once stayed in this city.
He personally marked a spot for digging a well,
and thus found an old well.
Inside the well was an inscribed stone that read:
"In the sixth year of Hàn,
Yǐngyīn Hóu opened this well.
It was divined that
after three hundred years it would be blocked,
and within a hundred years of being blocked,
it would be reopened by one responding to destiny."
When Sūn Quán saw the inscription, he was delighted,
considering it an auspicious sign for himself.
Everyone found it extraordinary.
From "Zhāng Sēngjiàn Xúnyáng Jì".
Gāo Jiǒng
At the northern end of the court in the Western Capital, there was a large locust tree.
In the Suí dynasty, it stood at the entrance of Tángxīng Village.
When Emperor Wén moved the capital to Cháng'ān,
the Director of the Imperial Buildings
(Míng Chāo Běn notes: "木" is written as "大")
Gāo Jiǒng often sat under this tree to oversee the work.
Later, when the trees were planted in an uneven row,
it was proposed to remove this tree.
The Emperor said:
"Gāo Jiǒng sat under this tree;
there is no need to cut it down."
Up to the present, one hundred and thirty years into the Xiāntiān era,
the tree still stands.
Its branches and leaves are lush and towering,
its roots and trunk spread like a massive rock,
different from all other trees.
Chéngtiān Gate directly faces the entrance of Tángxīng Village,
where the Táng family now resides.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi".
Shén Yáo
Emperor Yáng of Suí and Shén Yáo (Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng) were both grandsons of the Dúgū family on their mother's side.
Thus, Shén Yáo and Emperor Yáng often
(Míng Chāo Běn notes: "然則" is written as "因是",
"悔恡" is written as "侮狎")
teased each other.
After each court audience,
Emperor Yáng would
(Míng Chāo Běn notes: "背" is written as "皆",
"然" is written as "謔")
mutter mockingly.
Later, during a banquet,
Emperor Yáng, in front of everyone,
teased Shén Yáo.
Shén Yáo had a high forehead and wrinkled face,
so the Emperor called him "Grandma Face."
Shén Yáo was angry and unhappy.
Upon returning home,
he remained dejected and discontent.
Seeing his sons, including Emperor Wén,
he told Emperor Wén but said nothing
(Míng Chāo Běn notes: the six characters "告文皇皆無言" are written as "但流涕而不言")
Then he told Empress Dòu:
"My life is pitiable.
Today, I was further publicly insulted by the Emperor, called 'Grandma Face.'
I fear my descendants will not escape hunger and cold."
Empress Dòu joyfully exclaimed:
"These words are cause for the family to celebrate!"
Shén Yáo did not understand,
thinking she was trying to console him.
The Empress said:
"Your fief is Táng,
and 'Grandma' is the mistress of the hall (堂主),
and 'hall' (堂) sounds like 'Táng' (唐)."
Shén Yáo's worries melted away like ice.
He was delighted
and privately celebrated with the Princes of Qín, Qí, and others.
From "Zhī Tián Lù".
Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng
In Táng, at the Shòu Ruì Altar in Běijīng,
in the thirteenth year of the Suí Dàyè era,
Emperor Gāozǔ ordered Prince Qí, Yuánjí, to remain there.
On the Xīnchǒu day,
a bluish stone was found,
shaped like a dragon,
with four characters in vermilion script:
"Lǐ Yuān, Ten Thousand Auspiciousness."
Prince Qí presented it.
The characters were clear and luminous,
resembling the shape of a turtle.
The Emperor then ordered it to be soaked and polished to verify it.
After several days,
the characters became even clearer.
Everyone inside and outside the court congratulated him.
The Emperor said:
"Heaven has decreed a clear mandate,
bestowing ten thousand auspiciousness.
We should offer a Shàoláo sacrifice to the stone turtle
and ennoble the man who found the turtle."
Thus, the Shòu Ruì Altar was established.
From "Tàiyuán Shìjì Zá Jì".
Tàiháng Mountain
In the early Wǔdé era of Táng,
a great voice came from Tàiháng Mountain, saying:
"The Táng state will prosper,
ruling for ten thousand years."
From "Tàiyuán Shìjì Zá Jì".
The Mulberry Twig Song
After the Yǒnghuī era of Táng,
people sang the Mulberry Twig Song, saying:
45 Mulberry twigs, Wéi the woman is joyful.
By the Shénlóng era,
the rebellious Wéi responded to it.
The flatterer Zhèng Yīn
composed over ten verses of the Mulberry Twig Song and presented them.
The rebellious Wéi was greatly pleased,
promoted him to Vice Minister of Personnel,
and rewarded him with a hundred bolts of fine silk.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi".
Turkic Salt
Since the Lóngshuò era of Táng,
people sang a song called "Turkic Salt."
During the Shènglì era of Later Zhōu,
Yán Zhīwēi was sent to make peace with the Xiōngnú.
He was appointed Minister of Rites of the third rank,
and escorted Wǔ Yánxiù to marry Chéng Mòchuò's daughter.
Gold, silver, utensils, brocades, and clothing were sent as betrothal gifts,
too numerous to record.
The Turks rebelled,
and the Hàn envoys were all lost,
with Yán Zhīwēi being installed as Khan.
This was the fulfillment of "Turkic Salt."
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi".
Feng Zhōngyuè
During the Tiáolù era of Táng,
the Great Emperor intended to perform the Fēng sacrifice at Mount Zhōngyuè,
but it was halted due to the Turkic rebellion.
Later, he intended to perform it again,
but it was stopped again due to the Tǔbō invasion.
By the Yǒngchún era,
the imperial carriage finally reached Sōngyuè.
A ballad said:
"Mount Sōng has many layers;
it is not that one fears being unable to climb,
but only that one may not get the chance to climb.
Three times troops were mustered,
bustling along the roadside."
At the foot of the mountain, an epidemic broke out,
and he did not recover.
He returned to the palace and passed away.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi".
The Willow Ballad
After the Yǒngchún era of the Táng dynasty,
the song "Willow, willow, carrying a load on its head" was sung everywhere under heaven.
Later, Xú Jìngyé committed an offense,
was demoted to Military Administrator of Liǔzhōu,
then forged an imperial edict,
appointing himself Military Administrator of Yángzhōu,
killed Senior Secretary Chén Jìngzhī,
and rebelled, seizing the Jiāng-Huái region.
Lǐ Xiàoyì was sent to suppress him,
and Jìngyé was beheaded.
His head was carried by post horse into Luòyáng.
"Willow, willow, carrying a load on its head"
was fulfilled by this event.
From "Records from Court and Country"
The Yellow Munţjac Song
Since the Rúyì era of the Zhōu dynasty,
people began singing the Yellow Munţjac Song.
Its lyrics said:
"Yellow munţjac, yellow munţjac, hiding in the grass,
I bend my bow and shoot to wound you."
Soon after, the Qìdān rebelled,
killing Military Governor Zhào Huì,
and the camps and prefectures fell.
Commanders Cáo Rénshī, Zhāng Xuányù, Má Rénjié, and Wáng Xiàojié were successively sent with a million troops,
but they were defeated by the bandits at Yellow Munţjac Valley.
All the armies were lost,
with not a single survivor.
The Yellow Munţjac Song
was thus verified.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Bìqié Child
Since the Chuígǒng era of the Zhōu dynasty,
the capital sang the Bìqié Child song lyrics,
all of which were depraved tunes.
Later, it was known that Zhāng Yìzhī's childhood name was Bìqié.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Ānlè Temple
In the Jǐnglóng era of the Táng dynasty,
Princess Ānlè
("yú" character originally absent,
added based on the Ming dynasty manuscript copy)
built Ānlè Temple in the Dàoguāng ward of Luòzhōu,
spending millions in cash.
A children's ballad said:
"Pitiful Ānlè Temple,
clearly hanging from the treetop."
Later, when the rebellious Wěi clan was executed,
Ānlè was also killed,
her head severed and hung from a pole,
and she was posthumously renamed the Rebellious Commoner.
From "Records from Court and Country"
The Magpie's Nest
After the Shénlóng era of the Táng dynasty,
a ballad said:
"Magpie's nest on the southern hill,
golden camel on the northern hill.
The sickle's handle has no hole,
the axe's head has no handle."
This was the omen of the Turks' growing powerful,
and the common people being unable to cut mulberry, raise silkworms, plant grain, or harvest crops.
From "Records from Court and Country"
The Carp Child
A ballad from the Jǐnglóng era of the Táng dynasty said:
"Pitiful Shèngshàn Temple,
clad in green feathery robe.
Led to the river to drink,
it tramples the carp child to death."
By the Jǐngyún era,
Prince Qiáo entered the capital from Jūnzhōu to stage a rebellion,
was defeated and fled,
and drowned in the Luò River.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Pulling Down the Celestial Pivot
A ballad from the Jǐngyún era of the Táng dynasty said:
"A single hemp thread pulls down the Celestial Pivot,
it's gone for good."
When Emperor Shénwǔ ascended the throne,
he ordered the Celestial Pivot to be toppled,
and the copper collected and sent to the Imperial Workshops.
This fulfilled the omen.
From "Records from Court and Country"
The Yellow Calf
A ballad from the Jǐnglóng era of the Táng dynasty said:
"The yellow calf breaks the tow rope,
its two feet stamp the ground, breaking its shoes."
In the sixth month, Prince Píng executed the rebellious Wěi clan.
"Breaking the tow rope"
meant that Wěi wanted to rebel,
"breaking its shoes"
meant the affair would not succeed.
Lady Wěi was a descendant of the Yellow Calf.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Luò Bīnwáng
Luò Bīnwáng, Registrar of the Bright Hall during the Táng dynasty,
wrote in his "Ode to the Imperial Capital":
"Suddenly, borne by the wind, he grows wings;
in an instant, losing the waves, he sinks into the mud."
Later, Bīnwáng raised troops in Yángzhōu with Xú Jìngyé,
suffered a great defeat,
and threw himself into the river to die.
This was the prophecy fulfilled.
From "Records from Court and Country"
The Empress
During Táng Tàizōng's reign,
there was a secret record stating:
"After three generations of the Táng,
a female ruler, Sovereign Wǔ, will replace and possess the realm."
Tàizōng secretly summoned Lǐ Chúnfēng to inquire about this matter.
Chúnfēng replied:
"Based on my astrological calculations,
the omen has already formed.
Moreover, this person is already born within Your Majesty's palace.
From now, in no more than forty years,
she will possess the realm,
exterminating the descendants of the Táng house,
nearly wiping them out completely."
The Emperor said:
"What if we seek her out and kill her?"
Chúnfēng said:
"Heaven's mandate
cannot be averted.
A true sovereign does not die;
even if sought, I fear she cannot be obtained.
Moreover, according to the divination, she has already grown up,
and is again within the palace,
already a member of Your Majesty's household.
In another forty years,
she will then be aged.
When aged, she will be benevolent,
and towards Your Majesty's descendants,
the harm may not be too severe.
If you kill her now,
she will simply be reborn,
and after another forty years,
will again be fit to rule the realm.
In her youth and prime, she is severe and cruel;
killing her would create a blood feud,
and then Your Majesty's descendants would be left with none to carry on."
From "Records of Conversing Guests",
(Ming manuscript copy states: from "Records from Court and Country")
Yán Zhīwēi
Since the Líndé era of the Táng dynasty,
when commoners drank wine and sang songs,
if they sang from start to finish without stopping,
it was called "clan salt."
Later, Yán Zhīwēi followed the Turks and led bandits to defeat Zhào and Dìng.
When Zhīwēi later returned,
Empress Zétiān was furious,
had him dismembered at the Western Market,
and ordered all officials to shoot at him.
Prince Wǔ Yìzōng of Hénèi stood seven paces away,
shot three arrows,
and missed every time
—such was his cowardice.
Zhīwēi's body became like a hedgehog with arrows,
his bones and flesh were chopped up,
and his nine clans were exterminated.
Distant relatives who previously did not know each other
were all beheaded.
Children seven or eight years old
were driven and carried to the Western Market.
The commoners pitied them,
and those who threw cakes and fruit to them
still fought over them,
treating it as a game.
The supervising censor could not bear to harm them,
and petitioned to spare them.
The words "clan salt"
were thus fulfilled.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Zhǎngsūn Wújì
Zhǎngsūn Wújì, Duke of Zhào in the Táng dynasty,
made felt hats from black sheep wool,
and everyone under heaven admired them,
calling the hat the "Duke of Zhào's Felt Hat."
Later, he was implicated in an affair and exiled to Lǐngnán.
The words "felt hat"
thus proved prophetic.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Prince of Wèi
Liú Yǔxī said:
"Before the rebellious Hu barbarians would bring chaos to the Central Plains,
the great master Zhìgōng of the Liáng dynasty had already presented a verse, saying,
'A two-horned maiden in green attire,
turns her back to Tàiháng to entice the king;
in the month of one-stop, she is sure to perish.'
The two-horned maiden is the character 'Ān';
green (lǜ) signifies fortune (lù);
one-stop (yī zhǐ) is the first month (zhēngyuè).
Indeed, in the first month, she was defeated and perished.
How profound was the allegory of Master Zhìgōng!"
From "Liú Gōng Jiāhuà Lù"
Lǐ Huáiguāng
Mǎ Suì led a campaign against Lǐ Huáiguāng,
marching troops from Tàiyuán,
and encamped at
Bǎo
Dǐng.
Upon inquiring about the name of the place,
it was called Máihuái Village.
He was greatly pleased and said:
"We are sure to capture the rebel."
From "Guóshǐ Bǔ"
Wáng Duó
During the Qiánfú era of the Táng dynasty,
Jīngzhōu military commissioner Duke Jìn, Wáng Duó,
later became the overall commander of various circuits.
At that time, Jupiter entered the Southern Dipper,
and remained there for several nights without receding.
Duó observed this
and asked the astrologers:
"What are the auspicious or inauspicious omens?"
They all said:
"If Metal, Fire, or Earth trespass the Dipper,
it would be a calamity;
only Wood would bring fortune."
Some agreed.
At that time, there was a diviner named Biān Gāng,
deeply knowledgeable in astronomy,
and proficient in calendrical calculations.
He said to Duke Jìn:
"The Dipper is the constellation of the imperial palace,
and Wood is the god of fortune;
it should be interpreted in terms of the emperor.
Thus, if it does not bring fortune now,
it will surely manifest later;
I dare not speak further."
Another day,
Duke Jìn dismissed his attendants and asked in secret,
Gāng said:
"Jupiter entering the Dipper
is an omen of kingship.
Wood within the Dipper
forms the character 'Zhū'.
Those in the know say that during the Táng dynasty, there was a prophecy about crimson robes,
some saying it foretold a change in destiny,
either with the surname Péi,
or the surname Niú.
For Péi, the character resembles crimson robes;
for Niú, adding a person
makes Zhū.
That is why Duke Jìn Péi Dù,
and Chancellor Niú Sēngrú,
were often slandered by this.
When Duke Wèi Lǐ denounced 'Zhōu Qín Xíng Jì',
it was about this matter.
Who knew it would be fulfilled by Zhū of Dàngshān?"
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Wood Forms a Character
In the second year of the Kāipíng era of the Liáng dynasty,
they sent their general Lǐ Sī'ān to attack Lùzhōu,
encamping at Húkǒu Pass,
and felling trees to build a palisade.
When splitting a large tree,
they found six characters in clerical script written in vermilion inside the wood,
saying:
"Heaven fourteen year, Shí advances."
Sī'ān submitted a memorial reporting this.
All the ministers congratulated,
thinking that in the fourteenth year, distant barbarians would surely offer treasures.
The Deputy Director of the Astrological Bureau, Xú Hóng,
said to his confidants:
"Since ancient times, no single character has been used as a reign title;
if it is a heavenly mandate,
how could it be missing characters?
I believe in the bǐngshēn year,
there will be someone with the surname Shí ruling this land.
Move the two vertical strokes from the character 'four'
and place them on the left and right of the character 'heaven',
forming the character 'bǐng';
take the outer frame of 'four',
and pierce it with the character 'ten',
forming the character 'shēn'."
Later, in the bǐngshēn year,
the Later Jìn founder, with the surname Shí, rose from Bīngzhōu,
just as Hóng had said.
From "Jīshén Lù"
Grass Reborn
Before Dǒng Chāng was defeated,
a madman in Yuèzhōng at a flagpole inn and guesthouse
often wrote a four-line poem:
"Day by day, grass is reborn,
endlessly leaning against the plain city.
The feudal lords chase the white rabbit,
when summer fills, Mirror Lake is calm."
At first, no one understood the verses,
but after Chāng's defeat, it became clear:
'Grass reborn' is the character 'Dǒng';
'day by day' is the character 'Chāng';
'plain city' is Yuè City,
built by Suí dynasty Duke of Yuè, Yáng Sù;
'feudal lords' refers to
the monkey, which is Qián Liú,
born in the shēn year;
'white rabbit' is Chāng,
born in the mǎo year;
'summer fills'
is the sixth month;
'Mirror Lake'
is in Yuèzhōng.
From "Kuàijī Lù"
Táng Dynasty Intercalary Month
The Later Shǔ ruler Wáng Yǎn,
built the Shàngqīng Palace on the site of the Táng family residence.
In the hall of the statue of Lǎojūn,
he enshrined portraits of the eighteen emperors of the Táng dynasty.
Then, with full ceremonial procession, he paid homage to them.
Those who understood saw this as bowing to the Táng,
an omen of submission to its mandate.
Earlier, the Director of the Astrological Bureau, Hú Xiùlín, presented a calendar,
placing the intercalary month in the first month of the bǐngxū year.
Another recluse named Xiàng also presented a calendar,
using the Xuānmíng method,
placing the intercalary month in the twelfth month of the yǐyǒu year.
Since there was disagreement,
both sides argued,
and they fetched the Táng dynasty calendar from the border.
A close minister said:
"We should use the Táng dynasty intercalary month."
Thus, they changed to an intercalary twelfth month.
Calendar sellers in the streets said:
"There is only one month left."
That year, on the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month, the state fell.
Hú Xiùlín was the Deputy Director of the Astrological Bureau of the Táng dynasty,
serving in Shǔ,
where he created the Yǒngchāng Zhèngxiàng Calendar.
His calculations were so exquisite
that he was unmatched in the realm.
Yet, the matter of shifting the intercalary month was not mistaken;
calendar deliberations are not something ordinary people can lightly understand.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Bamboo [missing text]
The bamboo rat is
a rodent that feeds on bamboo.
It inhabits the deep mountains, stream valleys, and bamboo groves of uninhabited wilderness,
eating nothing but bamboo.
As large as a wildcat,
its flesh is plump and crisp.
Mountain dwellers prize it,
though digging it out from the ground is extremely arduous.
In the year of the Qí Liáng conflict,
throughout the lands of Qín and Lǒng,
from near to far, among cliffs and valleys,
these creatures emerged in swarms,
flooding into city moats and the homes of local people.
Some breached walls and damaged fortifications,
others entered through doorways and thresholds.
Dogs could not finish eating them all,
so they even invaded people's inner rooms,
glutting the bellies of the Qín populace.
Suddenly, a children's rhyme appeared:
"The rat leads the black ox,
heaven's will leaves no choice.
Just wait for the Wùyín year,
Yáng will be at the Shǔ River's head."
The wise could not decipher its meaning.
In the Gēngwǔ year,
Liú Zhījùn, the military commissioner of Tóngzhōu under the Great Liáng, rebelled against Liáng and joined Qín,
settling in Tiānshuǐ.
After Tiānshuǐ fell,
he fled to Shǔ.
A few years later,
the people of Shǔ sang another rhyme:
"The black ox has no tether,
the palm-fiber rope snaps at once."
The founding ruler of the pseudo-Shǔ state heard this
and feared, saying:
"The black ox
is Liú's childhood name;
the palm-fiber rope
refers to my descendants' names.
For the elder generation uses the character 'Zōng' in their names,
and the younger generation uses 'Chéng'—
'zōng chéng' is homophonous with 'palm-fiber rope.'
I am old;
must this not become a calamity for my descendants?"
Thereupon, he had Lord Liú killed to avert the omen.
The following year,
which was the Wùyín year,
the founding ruler fell ill.
Whenever he closed his eyes, he saw Lord Liú before him.
The people of Shǔ, terrified,
ground Liú's bones to powder
and scattered them into the Shǔ River.
Soon after, the founding ruler passed away.
Commentators then realized that the rat referred to Liú,
the black ox was Liú's childhood name,
and the scattering of bones into the Shǔ River in the Wùyín year was the fulfillment.
From "Wángshì Jiànwén."
Guō Línzōng
Guō Línzōng traveled to the capital,
and when he was about to return to his hometown,
over a thousand chariots came to see him off,
with Lǐ Yīng among them.
The crowd all gathered at the large locust tree inn to bid farewell,
but only Lǐ Yīng rode together with Línzōng,
in a simple, crude cart,
ascending the slope by the large locust tree.
Hundreds of onlookers
craned their necks to watch them,
their figures distant, like Sōng and Qiáo amid the heavens.
From "Shāng Yún Xiǎoshuō."
Lǐ Yīng
Lǐ Yīng often excused himself from greeting or seeing off guests due to illness,
receiving visitors only once every twenty days.
Only when Chén Zhònggōng came
would he ride out in a carriage to welcome him.
From Lǐ Yīng's "Family Records,"
the Ming manuscript copy writes "records" as "carriage."
Lǐ Yuánlǐ was imposing, like the wind through sturdy pines.
When Yīng resided in Yángchéng,
the disciples at his gate
always numbered four to five hundred.
Whenever Yīng produced a piece of writing,
his disciples would vie for it,
never letting it fall to the ground.
When Chén Zhònggōng first sent his eldest son Yuánfāng to visit,
Yīng spoke with him and then
had food sent from the kitchen.
Yuánfāng was delighted,
thinking he had made a favorable impression
and would surely be received again.
From "Shāng Yún Xiǎoshuō."
Niè Jìbǎo, from the same county as Yīng,
was of humble background
and dared not seek an audience with Yīng.
Dù Zhōufǔ, who knew Jìbǎo
but could not assess his worth,
spoke of him to Yīng.
Yīng summoned him for an audience,
seating him on a straw raincoat by the steps.
After just one conversation,
he concluded decisively:
"This man shall become a paragon of the state."
It ultimately turned out as he said.
From "Shāng Yún Xiǎoshuō."
Yīng served as Imperial Censor.
Across the six commanderies of Qīngzhōu,
only Chén Zhòngjǔ in Lè'ān
assumed his post;
the others all feigned illness.
Seventy counties all abandoned their offices and departed.
Such was his awe-inspiring authority.
From "Shāng Yún Xiǎoshuō."
Yīng was implicated in the factional purge
and imprisoned in Xīnjì County jail alongside Dù Mì and Xún Yǔ.
On New Year's Day,
Yǔ raised his cup and said:
"The new year begins with a modest start."
Yīng asked him:
"Death is what people naturally detest;
why do you show no regret?"
Yǔ replied:
"To seek benevolence and attain it—
what room is there for resentment?"
Yīng then sighed:
"Hàn is doomed,
Hàn is doomed!
The virtuous are the guiding principles of heaven and earth,
yet so many are harmed—
how can the state endure?"
From Lǐ Yīng's "Family Records,"
the Ming manuscript copy writes "records" as "carriage."
Xú Rúzǐ
Chén Zhòngjǔ deeply esteemed Xú Rúzǐ.
When appointed as the Grand Administrator of Yùzhāng,
upon arrival,
he immediately wished to visit him first.
His registrar said:
"The general sentiment is that you, Prefect, should first enter to pay respects."
Chén replied:
"King Wǔ bowed at the lane of Shāng Róng
without even warming his mat;
how could it be improper for me to honor the worthy?"
From "Shāng Yún Xiǎoshuō."
Xú Rúzǐ, at nine years old,
once played under the moonlight.
Someone said to him:
"If the moon had nothing in it,
would it be even brighter?"
Xú replied:
"Not so.
It is like the pupil in a person's eye—
without it, how could it not be dark?"
From "Shì Shuō."
Zhèng Xuán
When Zhèng Xuán was in Xúzhōu,
Kǒng Wénjǔ, then Chancellor of Běihǎi,
wished for his return to the commandery,
urging him with earnest sincerity,
sending messengers one after another.
He also instructed:
"Lord Zhèng has long traveled in the southern regions;
now that hardships have somewhat eased,
should he harbor thoughts of returning,
let no one occupy his house.
If fences, walls, or trees are damaged,
repair the walls and buildings to await his return."
When Xuán returned,
Róng informed his subordinates:
"In the past, the Zhōu people revered their teacher,
calling him 'Shàngfù.'
Now, all may address him as 'Lord Zhèng,'
and must not use his personal name."
When Yuán Shào first met Xuán,
he sighed and said:
"I originally thought Lord Zhèng was a renowned Confucian of the eastern regions,
but now I see he is a venerable elder of the realm.
To achieve eminence in the world as a commoner—
how could this be without reason?"
When Xuán departed,
Shào held a farewell feast for him east of the city,
determined to make him drunk.
Three hundred attendees
were all made to leave their seats and offer toasts.
From morning till dusk,
it was estimated Xuán drank over three hundred cups,
yet his composed demeanor
remained unflagging throughout the day.
From "Shāng Yún Xiǎoshuō."
Cài Yōng
In the month when Zhāng Héng died,
Cài Yōng's mother first became pregnant.
These two men's talent and appearance were very similar.
People of the time said:
"Yōng is Héng's reincarnation."
Earlier, Minister of Education Wáng Yǔn,
often held meetings with Yōng,
and Yǔn's arguments were frequently defeated,
so he bore a grudge against Yōng.
When Yǔn executed Dǒng Zhuó,
he also arrested Yōng.
Many people pleaded for him but could not save him.
Grand Commandant Mǎ Mìdī said to Yǔn:
"Bójiē (Cài Yōng) is loyal and upright,
and has always been filial.
Moreover, he is a rare talent of his generation,
well-versed in Hàn affairs,
and should compile the Ten Treatises.
If you kill him now,
the whole realm will be disappointed."
Yǔn said:
"Without Cài Yōng alone,
what harm is there in lacking the Ten Treatises?"
So he killed him.
From "Shāng Yún's Stories"
The eastern states revered Yōng,
not calling him by name,
but all referring to him as Lord Cài.
In Chénliú, Yǎnzhōu,
they painted portraits of Cài Yōng and praised him, saying:
"His literary talent equals that of Sānlǘ (Qū Yuán),
his filial piety matches that of Shēn and Qiān."
From "Biography of Yōng"
Cuī Rénshī
In the Táng dynasty, Cuī Rénshī served as Director of the Bureau of Revenue.
He reported on financial matters in thousands of words,
without holding the document in hand.
Emperor Tàizōng found it strange,
and ordered Dù Zhènglún to bring the document and read it aloud for comparison.
Not a single error was found.
From "Records of the Divine and Strange"
Zhāng Wénguàn
The ministers thought the meals provided at the Administrative Hall were too lavish,
and proposed reducing them.
Zhāng Wénguàn said:
"This food is valued by the Son of Heaven
to handle state affairs and treat talented individuals.
If we are not fit for our posts,
we should resign ourselves,
to make way for the worthy.
We should not reduce the public meals
to seek fame and reputation.
The state's expenses
are not in this area.
If it benefits public affairs,
this is not excessive."
From "Records of Conversing Guests"
Yú Shìnán
Emperor Tàizōng once went on a trip,
and officials requested to bring reference books along.
The Emperor said:
"No need."
With Yú Shìnán present,
he is the walking library for this trip.
Emperor Tàizōng praised Shìnán for
his broad knowledge, virtuous conduct, calligraphy, literary talent, and loyalty—
one person possessing these five virtues.
When Tàizōng heard of Shìnán's death,
he wept bitterly, saying:
"In the Shíqú and Dōngguàn libraries,
there is no one like him anymore."
When Shìnán served as a librarian,
he gathered in the back hall of the department
all useful materials from various books for literary purposes,
compiling them into "Běitáng Shūchāo."
This hall still exists today,
and the book remains widely circulated.
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Dynasty"
Mǎ Zhōu
Mǎ Zhōu traveled west to Cháng'ān,
reaching Xīnfēng,
where he stayed at an inn.
The host only attended to merchants and ignored Zhōu,
so he ordered wine and drank leisurely alone.
The innkeeper found this very unusual.
Later, he drafted over twenty proposals for Cháng Hé,
and Emperor Tàizōng was amazed by his ability.
He asked Hé,
and Hé replied:
"These are not my ideas,
but come from my guest, Mǎ Zhōu."
Tàizōng summoned him that same day.
Before he arrived,
the emperor sent messengers to urge him four times.
When they met,
their conversation was very pleasant,
and Zhōu was appointed Investigating Censor.
He proposed abolishing the practice of shouting announcements
and instead installing drums,
beating them to alert the public—
a method people found convenient at the time.
He was later promoted to Secretariat Director.
Zhōu suffered from diabetes,
which did not heal for years.
When the emperor visited Cuìwēi Palace,
he ordered a search for a favorable site
to build a residence for Zhōu.
Imperial physicians and envoys
were sent continuously.
He often had imperial meals provided for Zhōu's daily consumption,
and Tàizōng personally prepared medicine for him,
while the crown prince paid visits.
From "Records of Conversing Guests"
Yuán Bànqiān
Yuán Bànqiān's original name was Yúqìng.
He was close to Wáng Yìfāng,
who said to him:
"Once every five hundred years, a worthy appears—
you are that one."
So he changed his name to Bànqiān (Half-Thousand).
Emperor Gāozōng held court at Wǔchéng Hall,
summoned candidates,
and asked about heavenly formations, earthly formations, and human formations.
Bànqiān replied:
"An army acting with righteousness,
like timely rain,
is a heavenly formation;
troops having ample food,
farming while fighting,
is an earthly formation;
soldiers and chariots being agile and efficient,
with generals and commanders in harmony,
is a human formation."
The emperor was impressed,
and appointed him as envoy to Tibet.
When Empress Wǔ Zétiān ascended the throne,
she retained him, saying:
"The frontier is not worth troubling you with."
He compiled the new rites for the Mingtáng Hall and presented them.
He also wrote twelve inscriptions for the Fēngshàn altar.
He was promoted to Grand Master of Remonstrance,
concurrently serving as Kònghè Attendant.
Bànqiān believed there was no such title in ancient times,
and those appointed were frivolous individuals,
so he requested its abolition.
This offended the emperor.
From "Guǎngdé Records of the Divine and Strange"
Yán Ānzhī
Emperor Xuánzōng hosted a feast at Qínzhèng Tower,
with a grand celebration,
allowing officials and commoners to watch.
Various performances competed,
and the crowd was packed and noisy.
The imperial guards struck with white staffs like rain,
but could not control the chaos.
The emperor was troubled,
and said to Gāo Lìshì:
"I thought the realm was prosperous,
and all regions were peaceful,
so I held this grand feast
to share joy with the people.
I did not expect such disorder below.
Do you have any way to stop it?"
Lìshì replied:
"I cannot.
Your Majesty, try summoning Yán Ānzhī
to manage the grounds.
In my opinion,
he will surely handle it impressively."
The emperor agreed.
When Ānzhī arrived,
he walked around the square,
using his hand tablet to draw a line on the ground,
showing the crowd,
and declared:
"Those who cross this line will die."
Thus, the five-day feast concluded
with everyone pointing to his line, saying:
"Lord Yán's boundary"—
and no one dared to violate it.
From "Records of the Kāitiān Era"
Xiāo Yǐngshì
His literary works and scholarship
both led the literary world.
Despite his great reputation, he remained obscure and unrecognized.
Once, an envoy from Silla arrived,
saying:
"Scholars and commoners in the eastern barbarian lands
wish to invite Master Xiāo to serve as national tutor."
Although this did not materialize,
it shows how far his fame spread.
From "Grand Affairs of the Hànlín Academy"
(Míng dynasty manuscript version: "Hàn" replaced with "Rú")
In the Later Wei dynasty, Gāo Yǔn, styled Bógōng,
was the son of Gāo Tāo, who served as a Gentleman of the Palace Guard in Yān.
From an early age, he displayed extraordinary character,
and was thoroughly versed in the classics and histories.
During the Shénjiā
("Jiā" originally written as "Jiā",
corrected based on the Ming manuscript copy)
era,
together with Lú Xuán of Fànyáng, Lǐ Líng of Zhàojùn, Cuī Jiàn of Bólíng, and others,
all descendants of worthy and talented families,
they were summoned by imperial decree together,
and he was appointed as Vice Director of the Central Secretariat and concurrently Director of the Palace Library,
collaborating with Cuī Hào to compile historical records.
When Cuī Hào encountered persecution,
because Gāo Yǔn was loyal and upright, not given to flattery,
he was specially pardoned.
His nature was pure and frugal;
although he repeatedly held prominent and noble positions,
his aspirations remained aligned with those of the poor and humble.
Emperor Gāozōng visited his residence,
finding only a few thatched huts,
with cotton quilts and coarse padded robes,
and in the kitchen, nothing but salted vegetables.
The emperor sighed and said:
"Even among the ancients known for purity and poverty,
was there ever anything like this?"
He bestowed upon him grain and silk.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Cuī Guāng
After the Later Wei dynasty moved its capital to Luòyáng during the Tàihé period,
the state became prosperous and wealthy,
with overflowing storehouses and treasuries.
Coins and silk were piled in the open corridors and side rooms,
beyond counting.
The Empress Dowager granted commoners silk,
allowing them to take as much as they could carry.
All court officials took away as much as their strength allowed.
Only Zhāngwǔ King Yuán Róng and Chénliú Marquis Lǐ Chóng carried more silk than they could manage,
stumbled, and injured their ankles.
The Empress Dowager then denied them the silk,
making them leave empty-handed.
People of the time laughed at them.
Palace Attendant Cuī Guāng took only two bolts.
The Empress Dowager asked him:
"Attendant, why so little?"
He replied:
"Your servant has only two hands,
which can only manage two bolts.
What I have received is already plenty."
The court nobility admired his integrity and frugality.
From "Luòyáng Qiélán Jì".
Zhǎngsūn Dàoshēng
Minister of Works, Prince of Shàngdǎng, Zhǎngsūn Dàoshēng,
a native of Dàirén,
was by nature loyal, cautious, frugal, and simple.
Although he held the position of one of the Three Dukes,
his dwelling was lowly and crude.
After he left to assume a regional command,
his son somewhat repaired and improved the house.
Upon his return, he sighed and said:
"I serve as Chancellor,
yet have done nothing to repay the state,
and I fear the burden of my position.
In the past, Huò Qùbìng said that while the Xiōngnú remained undefeated,
there was no use for a house.
Now, powerful enemies still roam beyond the northern deserts.
How can I sit comfortably in a splendid and beautiful house?"
He then ordered it to be demolished.
People of his time compared him to Yàn Yīng.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng
When Emperor Sùzōng was still Crown Prince,
he often attended meals with his father.
The Imperial Kitchen served cooked meat on a stand,
including a piece of lamb shoulder.
The Emperor looked at it and had the Crown Prince carve it.
After Emperor Sùzōng carved it,
grease stained his hand.
He used a pancake to wipe it clean.
The Emperor watched intently and appeared displeased.
Emperor Sùzōng then raised the pancake and ate it.
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
He said to the Crown Prince:
"Blessings should be cherished in this manner."
From "Liǔshì Shǐ".
Emperor Sùzōng
Hán Zémù submitted a memorial praising Emperor Sùzōng's frugality,
noting that his entertainments lacked extravagant silk adornments,
and his meals lacked rare delicacies.
The Emperor then showed the sleeve of his garment and said:
"This garment of mine
has been washed three times."
From "Tánshì Shǐ".
Lú Huáishèn
Lú Huáishèn of the Táng dynasty
was pure, cautious, upright, and simple,
and did not amass property or assets.
His utensils and house
were extremely frugal and crude.
Even after becoming prominent,
his wife and children did not escape hunger and cold.
Yet towards old friends and relatives,
he distributed alms very generously.
While serving as Vice Director of the Chancellery,
overseeing selection affairs in the Eastern Capital,
his personal belongings
were contained in just one cloth bag.
Later, he became Director of the Chancellery,
concurrently serving as Minister of Personnel.
After lying ill for a long time,
Sòng Jǐng and Lú Cóngyuàn often visited him together.
Lú Huáishèn lay on a worn-out mat and a single bamboo sleeping mat,
with no curtain or screen at the door.
Whenever wind and rain came,
he would use the mat to cover himself.
He had always held Sòng Jǐng and Lú Cóngyuàn in high esteem.
Seeing them, he was very pleased,
kept them for the entire day,
and ordered food to be served.
There were only two bowls of steamed beans
and a few stalks of vegetables.
Beyond that, there was simply nothing else prepared.
Holding their hands, he said to them:
"You two gentlemen will surely serve as pillars of the state.
His Majesty seeks good governance with great urgency,
but having reigned for many years,
he has recently grown somewhat weary of diligent effort.
Petty men will surely seize this opportunity to advance.
Please remember this."
A few days later, he passed away.
When his illness became critical,
he personally wrote a memorial recommending Sòng Jǐng, Lú Cóngyuàn, Lǐ Jié, and Lǐ Cháoyǐn.
The Emperor read his memorial,
and felt even greater sorrow and regret.
After his death,
his family had no stored provisions,
and only an old servant sold himself
to provide for the funeral arrangements.
The Emperor was hunting in the southern suburbs,
and looking towards the village,
he saw a humble, low-walled dwelling.
It seemed something was happening at that household,
so he sent a rider to inquire.
The messenger returned and reported:
"It is the second anniversary of Lú Huáishèn's death,
and they are holding a vegetarian feast."
The Emperor therefore ceased the hunt.
Taking pity on their poverty and want,
he immediately bestowed fine silk upon them.
From "Mínghuáng Zálù".
Another account states:
Lú Huáishèn died suddenly without any illness.
His wife, Madame Cuī,
stopped their children from wailing.
She said:
"Your father's allotted lifespan is not yet finished.
I know this."
He was pure, frugal, and incorruptible,
cautious in advancement and humble in retreat.
Bribes and gifts from all quarters,
he did not keep a single thread.
He served as Chancellor concurrently with Zhāng Yuè.
Now, Zhāng Yuè has amassed bribes like a mountain,
and that man is still alive.
The retribution for extravagance and frugality—
how could it be false?"
At midnight,
Lú Huáishèn revived.
His attendants reported what his wife had said.
Lú Huáishèn said:
"The principle is naturally different.
In the underworld, there are thirty furnaces
that day and night forge ill-gotten wealth for Zhāng Yuè.
I have not a single one.
How can we be compared?"
Having spoken, he died again.
From "Dú Yì Zhì".
Lǐ Miǎn
During the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a scholar traveling and lodging in Sòngzhōu.
At that time, Lǐ Miǎn was young and impoverished,
and shared an inn with a scholar.
Within less than ten days,
the scholar fell seriously ill,
and it reached the point where he could not be saved
(The characters "不救" were originally absent,
added based on the Ming manuscript copy
On his deathbed, he said to Lǐ Miǎn:
"My family lives in Hóngzhōu,
and I was heading to the Northern Capital to seek an official post.
Falling ill and dying here,
such is my fate."
He then took out a hundred taels of gold from his bag and gave them to Lǐ Miǎn.
Saying:
"My servants
are unaware of this gold.
Please, sir, handle my funeral affairs for me,
and keep the remaining gold."
Lǐ Miǎn agreed to handle the matters,
but secretly placed the remaining gold in the coffin and buried it together with the scholar.
Several years later,
Lǐ Miǎn served as a county captain in Kāifēng.
The scholar's brothers arrived with official documents from Hóngzhōu,
having searched all along the way for traces of the scholar.
Upon reaching Sòngzhōu,
they learned that Lǐ had overseen the funeral,
so they specifically went to Kāifēng
to inquire about the gold.
Lǐ Miǎn requested leave and went to the gravesite,
retrieved the gold, and handed it over to them.
From "Shàngshū Tán Lù"
Dù Huángshang
Lǐ Shīgǔ was arrogant and domineering,
but he feared Dù Huángshang as chancellor,
and did not dare to be disrespectful.
He then ordered a capable clerk
to send several thousand strings of cash,
along with a felt-covered carriage,
also worth nearly a thousand strings.
The messenger did not dare to deliver it immediately.
Instead, he waited at the gate of Dù's residence for several days.
One day, a simple green carriage came out from the residence,
followed by two maidservants,
both dressed in plain, tattered blue clothes.
He asked who it was,
and was told:
"It is the chancellor's wife."
The messenger hurried back
and reported this to Lǐ Shīgǔ.
Lǐ Shīgǔ then abandoned his plan,
and never again dared to act improperly.
From "Yōuxián Gǔchuī"
Yáng Chéng
Yáng Chéng of Yángdàozhōu
never accumulated possessions,
keeping only what was essential for daily use.
If a guest praised something as fine or lovely,
Yáng would be pleased
and immediately give it to them.
There was a man named Chén Cháng
who would wait until Yáng received his monthly salary
(The Ming manuscript copy lacks the character "始";
Hán Yù's "Shùnzōng Shílù, Vol. 4" lacks the character "出"
and would often go to praise the beauty of the money and silk,
thus receiving a share each month.
From "Chuánzǎi"
When Yáng Chéng served as a court official,
his family suffered from poverty,
so he often pawned his wooden pillow and cloth quilt
for tens of thousands in cash,
and people eagerly sought to acquire them.
From "Chuánzǎi"
Zhèng Yúqìng
was known for his purity, frugality, and great virtue.
One day,
he suddenly invited several relatives, friends, and officials to a meal,
surprising everyone.
The court officials, respecting him as a former chancellor of high repute,
all arrived early in the morning.
By the time the sun was high,
Zhèng Yúqìng finally appeared.
After chatting for a while,
everyone grew restless.
Zhèng Yúqìng called to his attendants:
"Instruct the kitchen
to steam it thoroughly and remove the feathers,
but do not break the neck."
Everyone looked at each other,
thinking it must be something like steamed goose or duck.
After a short while,
a tray was brought out,
along with exceptionally fragrant and fresh soy sauce and vinegar.
After a long wait, the meal was served:
before each person was placed a bowl of millet rice
and one steamed gourd.
The chancellor ate with relish,
while the others forced themselves to eat a little before leaving.
From "Lúshì Záshuō"
Zhèng Huàn
Zhèng Huàn prided himself on frugality and simplicity.
While serving as governor of Hénán,
a grandson of his paternal cousin came from Tánhuái to visit him.
This man made a living through farming,
and had never sought favors through connections.
His bow was rustic,
and his attire was old-fashioned.
Zhèng Huàn's sons and servants
all laughed at his coarse manners,
but Zhèng Huàn alone felt sympathy for him.
He asked him what he desired.
The man replied:
"I have long served as a commoner in my hometown,
and I wish to fill a vacancy as a county captain,
so that I may return to my village in glory."
Zhèng Huàn agreed to this.
