Zhèng Huàn's reputation for integrity and virtue
was highly regarded by his contemporaries.
When he wrote to the commandery governor,
it was as effective as moving a finger with the arm.
On the day before the man's departure,
Zhèng Huàn invited his nephews to a meal.
There were steamed buns,
and the man removed the skin before eating.
Zhèng Huàn was greatly angered and sighed.
He said to him:
"What difference is there between the skin and the inside?
I have long been troubled by the frivolous and corrupt customs,
the arrogance and extravagance in personal indulgence,
and have wished to restore simplicity and honesty,
and foster sincere customs.
That is why I took pity on you, a hardworking farmer in worn clothes,
thinking you must understand the hardships of farming.
How can you be more frivolous and wasteful than the pampered, milky-smelling children of the noble families?"
He then reached out his hand, asking for the discarded skins.
The man was flustered and at a loss,
but gathered them and presented them.
Zhèng Huàn ate them all,
then bowed and sent the guests back to their quarters,
gifting the man five rolls of silk before sending him off.
From "Quēshǐ"
Emperor Wénzōng
Emperor Wénzōng ordered the palace eunuchs to announce to the commanders of the two armies, the various bureau commissioners, and the inner officials
that they were not permitted to wear gauze, crepe, or silk scarves.
Later, when the imperial son-in-law Wěi Chǔrén had an audience,
he wore a double-layered silk scarf.
The Emperor said:
"I originally admired your family for its purity and simplicity,
and thus condescended to select you as son-in-law.
Such scarves and attire
may be worn by other relatives,
but you need not follow them."
From "Lúshì Záshuō"
Xiàhóu Zī
When Xiàhóu Zī served as Left Reminder,
he once wore a coarse Guìguǎn cloth robe to court.
During the Kāichéng era,
Emperor Wénzōng was open-minded and
fond of literature.
He asked Xiàhóu Zī why his robe was so coarse,
and Xiàhóu Zī explained it was made of Guì cloth.
This cloth was thick
and could ward off the cold.
Another day,
the Emperor asked his ministers:
"I observe that Reminder Xiàhóu Zī
must be a man of integrity and principle."
The ministers detailed his discreet conduct,
comparing him to the ancient worthies Yán Huí and Rǎn Qiú.
The Emperor sighed in admiration for a long time
and also began wearing Guìguǎn cloth.
The entire court followed suit,
and the price of this cloth rose.
From "Zhītián Lù"
Péi Tǎn
Yáng Shōu and Duàn Wénchāng both rose from humble origins to become honored prime ministers,
yet both were fond of extravagance.
Yáng Shōu's daughter married the eldest son of Péi Tǎn,
and her dowry was exceedingly rich,
with many utensils made of gold and silver.
However, Péi Tǎn valued frugality,
and upon hearing this, he was displeased.
One day,
while feasting with his wife and children,
a tray was used on the table to hold fruits.
Péi Tǎn was initially pleased,
but upon looking inside the vessel,
he noticed it was adorned with rhinoceros horn.
In a fit of rage,
he immediately overturned the tea table,
shook his sleeves, and stormed out.
He then said:
"This will ruin my family."
Later,
Yáng Shōu indeed met his downfall due to accepting bribes,
ultimately meeting an unfortunate end.
It serves him right!
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Wēn Liǎn
Wēn Liǎn, an official in Yōuzhōu,
was a native of Yān,
renowned for his Confucian scholarship,
and had been close friends with Féng Dào, the Prince of Yíng, since childhood.
During a period of military turmoil,
someone was selling a lacquered lamp stand in the market.
Liǎn thought it was made of iron,
so he paid the price and bought it.
After several days,
his family used it to hold an oil lamp,
and while wiping it,
they realized it was actually silver.
Everyone, young and old, looked at it,
and all were overjoyed.
Only Liǎn sighed sorrowfully and said:
"Something obtained unjustly,
how can we treasure it?"
He then sought out the seller and returned it.
The seller said:
"I myself did not recognize its value,
and sold it in the market.
You, sir, paid a fair price,
it was not a forced purchase,
I dare not take it back."
Liǎn insisted on returning it,
and the seller finally bowed, accepted it, and left.
Later, the seller sold it for forty or fifty thousand coins,
and took half to thank Liǎn.
Liǎn steadfastly refused to accept it,
so the seller donated it to a Buddhist temple,
to adorn a statue of the Buddha,
hoping to pray for Liǎn's longevity.
At that time, people near and far all praised him sincerely,
for his benevolent conduct.
Later, he rose to the position of Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel before passing away.
From "Liú Shì Ěr Mù Jì"
Zhòng Tíngyù
In former Shǔ, Prince Jiā summoned Zhòng Tíngyù, a filial and incorrupt scholar well-versed in the classics,
to teach his sons.
Although Tíngyù was knowledgeable in ancient texts,
he often suffered from hunger and cold.
Upon arriving at the prince's residence,
he was not treated with much respect.
At the time, it was bitterly cold,
and an old brazier was sent to the academy.
Tíngyù was sitting alone, sighing,
poking the ashes with a pair of tongs.
Suddenly, he found a pair of golden fire tongs in the ashes,
and immediately requested an audience with the prince.
The prince said:
"A poor scholar seeking an audience with me
must have some request."
He ordered someone to tell Tíngyù:
"I will have clothes made for you."
Tíngyù explained:
"That is not my intention."
Prince Jiā had always been fond of immortals and the supernatural,
and dabbled in various esoteric arts,
fearing Tíngyù might have some special talent,
he reluctantly agreed to see him.
Tíngyù promptly produced the golden fire tongs
and explained the whole story.
The prince said:
"Our family lost this item ten years ago,
and you, sir, found it,
returning it to show us,
truly possesses the demeanor of the ancients."
He gifted him a hundred thousand coins,
a set of clothes,
and thirty dan of rice and wheat.
Ultimately, he treated him as an honored guest,
with great courtesy and respect,
and recommended him for the position of Record-Keeper and Military Advisor in Róngzhōu.
From "Yù Xī Biān Shì"
The Old Man of the Hàn Era
During the Hàn era, there was a man
who was old and childless,
wealthy,
but miserly and stingy by nature.
He wore shabby clothes and ate plain food,
rose at dawn,
and rested at night,
managing his estate,
accumulating wealth insatiably,
yet never daring to spend it on himself.
If someone came to him begging,
he would reluctantly go inside,
take ten coins,
and walk from the hall,
reducing the amount with each step.
By the time he reached the outside,
only half remained.
He would close his eyes and hand it to the beggar.
Soon after, he would add:
"I am giving you my family's entire fortune,
be careful not to tell others,
lest they imitate you and come."
The old man soon died,
his fields and houses were confiscated by the state,
and his wealth filled the imperial treasury.
From "Xiào Lín"
Shěn Jùn
Shěn Jùn of Wú,
courtesy name Shūshān,
was reputable but stingy and miserly by nature.
When Zhāng Wēn was sent as an envoy to Shǔ,
he bid farewell to Jùn.
Jùn went inside for a long time,
then came out and said to Wēn:
"I was just selecting a bolt of cloth
to give to you,
but none were coarse enough."
Wēn praised him for his honesty.
Another time, while passing by the shore of Tài Lake,
he had his attendant fetch some salt water.
Afterwards, he regretted taking too much,
and ordered him to pour some back.
Soon after, he said with self-reproach:
"This is my inborn nature."
It is also said that
Yáo Biāo and Zhāng Wēn both went to Wǔchāng,
where they met Shěn Héng of Wúxīng.
Stranded by the wind and running out of provisions,
Shěn Héng sent someone to borrow a hundred hú of salt from Biāo.
Biāo was stern and upright by nature,
and upon receiving the letter, did not reply.
He was in the midst of conversing with Wēn.
After a long while,
he called to his attendants:
"Pour a hundred hú of salt into the river."
He then said to Wēn:
"I want to make clear that it's not that I am unwilling to give,
but that I regret whom I would be giving it to."
Shěn Héng's younger brother, Jùn,
was reputable but stingy and miserly by nature.
From "Xiào Lín"
Lǐ Chóng
Gāoyáng Prince Yōng of the Later Wèi,
was extravagant and lavish by nature,
fond of fine food,
and indulged himself greatly.
A single meal of his cost tens of thousands of coins,
with delicacies from land and sea
spread out before him.
Marquis Chénliú, Lǐ Chóng, said to others:
"A single meal of Gāoyáng's
equals a thousand days of mine."
Chóng served as President of the Department of State Affairs and held the rank of Yìtóng Sānsī,
and was also immensely wealthy, with a thousand servants,
yet he was extremely frugal and stingy by nature.
He wore shabby clothes and ate coarse food,
often without meat in his meals,
having only leek greens and pickled leeks.
Lǐ Chóng's guest, Lǐ Yuányòu, told people:
"Minister Lǐ eats eighteen different dishes in one meal."
People asked him why.
Yuányòu said:
"Two leeks (二韭) make eighteen (二九)."
Those who heard this burst into laughter.
From "Luòyáng Qiélán Jì"
A Man from Nányáng
In Nányáng, there was a man
who was wealthy and well-resourced,
but exceptionally stingy and miserly.
On the winter solstice,
his son-in-law came to visit him.
He then set out a single bronze jar of wine
and a few slices of roe deer meat.
The son-in-law resented the meagerness of the offering,
and drank and ate it all in one go.
The host was astonished,
but, after some hesitation, ordered more to be brought.
This happened twice.
Afterwards, he scolded his daughter, saying:
"That husband of yours is fond of wine,
which is why you are always poor."
After his death,
his sons fought over the property,
and they drove out and killed their elder brother.
From Yánshì Jiāxùn
Xiàhóu Chǔxìn
In the Táng dynasty, Xiàhóu Chǔxìn served as Chief Clerk of Jīngzhōu.
A guest came to visit him.
Chǔxìn ordered a servant to prepare a meal.
The servant whispered in his ear:
"How much flour should I knead?"
Chǔxìn said:
"Two shēng for the two of us will suffice."
The servant went in
and did not come out for a long time.
The guest excused himself on account of some business.
Chǔxìn hastily called for the servant.
The servant said:
"I have already kneaded it."
Chǔxìn clicked his tongue and said:
"What an extraordinary thing
The Míng manuscript copy has "fèi" instead of "yì",
and after "shì" there is the character "yě"
After a long while, he then said:
"You can bake it all into cakes,
and I will eat them after returning from official duties."
Chǔxìn also once stored a shēng of vinegar in a small bottle
for his own consumption;
his family members did not get to taste a single drop.
The servant said:
"The vinegar is finished."
Chǔxìn took the bottle and held it upside down in his palm;
a few drops remained,
so he sucked them up with his mouth.
Whenever making purchases at the market,
he would always handle the goods himself before handing over payment.
Those who knew of this despised him.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi
Liǔ Qìng
Liǔ Qìng, the Registrar of Guǎngzhōu,
lived alone in a single room.
All utensils and food
were kept in his bedroom.
A servant once privately took a pinch of salt;
Qìng whipped him until he bled.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi
Xiàhóu Biāo
In summer, when food and drink bred maggots,
he would not let those below him have a taste.
Once, after seeing off a guest at the door,
he discovered that a servant had stolen and eaten a slice of meat.
Biāo returned and realized it,
and was greatly enraged.
He then caught a fly and made the servant eat it,
ordering him to vomit out the meat.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi
Zhèng Rénkǎi
Zhèng Rénkǎi served as Prefect of Mìzhōu.
A young servant informed him that his shoes were worn through.
Rénkǎi said:
"Old man will arrange shoes for you."
After a short while,
a gatekeeper wearing new shoes arrived.
There was a woodpecker
啄木也
nest in a tree in front of Rénkǎi's hall.
He sent the gatekeeper up the tree to fetch its young.
The gatekeeper took off his shoes and climbed the tree.
Rénkǎi then ordered the servant to put on the shoes and leave.
The gatekeeper ended up barefoot.
Rénkǎi wore a self-satisfied expression.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi
Dèng Yòu
Dèng Yòu, Protector-General of Ānnán,
was a native of Sháozhōu
and came from an extremely wealthy family.
He had a thousand servants and maids,
yet he always required them to provide their own food and drink,
and never entertained guests.
A grandson once privately used a duck,
and Yòu, for arbitrarily depleting the family assets,
whipped him twenty times.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi
Wéi Zhuāng
Wéi Zhuāng was quite well-read,
but he would count grains of rice to cook
and weigh firewood to burn.
If a single slice was missing from a roast, he would notice.
When his eight-year-old son died,
his wife dressed the body in ordinary clothes for burial.
Zhuāng stripped them off
and wrapped the corpse in an old mat.
After the burial,
he carried the mat back home.
When he remembered his son,
he would sob uncontrollably,
yet he remained miserly.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi
Old Man Wáng
During the Tiānbǎo era,
there was an old man named Wáng in Xiàngzhōu.
His home was in Yèchéng.
He was wealthy and possessed much property,
but there were only husband and wife,
with no children.
His accumulated grain reached nearly ten thousand hú,
yet the couple was exceedingly frugal and stingy.
They often ate stale food,
just enough to fill their stomachs,
never seeking richness or abundance.
His estate was particularly vast,
with over two hundred tenant households.
Once, while inspecting the tenant quarters,
he suddenly saw a tenant eating.
The meal on his plate was lavish and abundant.
The old man asked about his occupation.
The tenant said:
"I merely sell assorted powders and fragrant medicines."
The old man suspected he was a thief,
and asked, "With how much wealth do you live so lavishly?"
This person said:
"I only have a capital of five thousand coins.
Each day I live off the interest,
preserving only the principal,
and not hoping for anything beyond that.
Therefore, my clothing and food are always sufficient."
The old man was then greatly enlightened.
Returning home, he said to his wife:
"That man, with just a small profit,
uses it to sustain himself.
He can be called one who understands principle.
Now I have accumulated wealth amounting to tens of thousands,
yet my clothing and food are stale and spoiled,
and I have no descendants.
For whom am I saving it?"
Thereupon, he opened his storehouses
and widely purchased delicacies and fine things,
indulging in flavors as he pleased.
Within a few days,
both husband and wife dreamed that they were arrested by people,
shackled, imprisoned, and bound.
They were whipped and beaten,
and told:
"These people recklessly squandered military provisions."
Several years after this dream,
both husband and wife died.
When government troops besieged Ān Qìngxù in Xiàngzhōu,
they fully opened his granaries
to supply the army.
From Yuánhuà Jì
Wáng È
Wáng È served successively in major garrison towns,
and wealth and goods piled up.
An old acquaintance
admonished him about the principle of accumulating wealth and then being able to disperse it.
A few days later,
he saw È again.
È said:
"Regarding the admonition I received the other day,
indeed, as you said,
I have already dispersed it greatly."
The guest asked to be told the details.
È said:
"I gave ten thousand strings of cash to each of my sons,
and a thousand strings to each of my sons-in-law."
From Guóshǐ Bǔ
Péi Qú
Minister of Education Péi Qú
was by nature stingy.
When he was serving as an inspector in Jiāngxī,
all the utensils and decorative screens
were made anew to his specifications,
stored in an empty room,
and never actually used.
Whenever there was a banquet,
he would borrow them from the homes of court officials.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Guī Dēng
Minister Guī Dēng
was extremely miserly.
He once cooked a sheep's thigh,
cutting and eating it piece by piece,
and then sealing up the leftovers.
One day,
his wife mistakenly cut and ate from the sealed portion.
When Guī Dēng saw the original seal was gone,
he was furious with his wife.
From then on, he never ate meat again for the rest of his life.
Whenever Guī Dēng bathed,
he would always dismiss his attendants.
Someone once peeked at him from outside,
and saw he was a giant turtle.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Bào Zǐdū
Bào Zǐdū of the Wèi state
was traveling in the wilderness one evening
when he saw a scholar
suddenly suffer a heart attack.
Zǐdū dismounted
and massaged his heart.
After a short while,
the scholar died.
Zǐdū looked in his bag
and found a scroll of plain silk
and ten gold ingots.
He then sold one ingot
to arrange the scholar's burial,
placed the remaining nine under the head of the deceased,
and put the silk scroll beside the abdomen.
Several years later,
while Zǐdū was on the road,
a man on a piebald horse pursued him.
Upon catching up,
he accused Zǐdū of being a thief
and insisted on asking where his son's body was.
Zǐdū explained everything in detail,
and they went together to the site.
They opened the tomb
to retrieve the son's body for the return journey,
and saw the nine gold ingots under the head
and the silk scroll beside the abdomen.
The entire family was moved by Zǐdū's virtue and righteousness.
From then on, his reputation spread far and wide.
From *Dú Yì Zhì*.
Yáng Sù
The wife of Xú Déyán, a Gentleman of the Household of the Heir Apparent of the Chén dynasty,
was the younger sister of the last ruler, Shūbǎo,
and was enfeoffed as Princess Lèchāng.
Her talent and beauty were unparalleled.
Déyán, serving as a Gentleman of the Household of the Heir Apparent,
was facing a time of turmoil,
and feared they might not be able to stay together.
He said to his wife:
"With your talent and appearance,
if the state falls, you will surely enter the household of a powerful noble,
and we will be separated forever.
If our bond of affection is not yet severed,
and we still hope to see each other,
we should have a token of faith."
He then broke a mirror in two,
each keeping one half.
They agreed:
"In the future, you must sell your half in the capital market on the fifteenth day of the first month,
and I will be there.
I will search for you on that very day."
When the Chén dynasty fell,
his wife indeed entered the household of Duke Yuè, Yáng Sù,
where she received exceptional favor and affection.
Déyán, wandering and suffering hardships,
barely managed to reach the capital.
He then went to the capital market on the fifteenth day of the first month to search.
There was an old servant selling half a mirror,
asking an exorbitantly high price,
and everyone laughed at him.
Déyán immediately led him to his lodging,
gave him food,
explained the whole story,
and produced his half of the mirror to match it.
He then inscribed a poem:
"The mirror and the person both departed;
the mirror returns
"歸" originally written as "各"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript copy, Chén's collation, and Xǔ's edition
but the person does not return.
No longer the shadow of Cháng'é,
only the radiance of the bright moon remains."
When Madame Chén received the poem,
she wept and refused to eat.
Yáng Sù learned of this
and was deeply moved, his expression changing.
He immediately summoned Déyán,
returned his wife to him,
and additionally bestowed generous gifts upon them.
All who heard of it were deeply moved and sighed.
He then drank with Déyán and Madame Chén,
and asked Madame Chén to compose a poem:
"What a predicament today brings,
the new official facing the old official.
Daring neither to laugh nor to cry,
truly realizing how difficult it is to be human."
She then returned to Jiāngnán with Déyán,
and they lived together until old age.
From *Běnshì Shī*.
Guō Yuánzhèn,
at the age of sixteen,
entered the National University.
Xuē Jì and Zhào Yǎnzhāo were his friends.
Once, a letter from home arrived,
sending four hundred thousand coins
for his examination expenses.
Suddenly, a man in mourning clothes knocked on the door and said:
"Five generations of my family remain unburied,
each in a different place.
Now I wish to move and bury them all together,
but I lack the funds.
I heard your family letter has arrived—
could you possibly assist me?"
Guō immediately ordered the money to be loaded onto a cart and taken away all at once,
leaving nothing behind,
and he did not even ask the man's name.
He was deeply ridiculed for this by Xuē and Zhào.
Yuánzhèn said calmly:
"Helping him with such an important matter—
what is there to ridicule?"
That year, his funds ran out,
and he ultimately did not sit for the examinations.
From *Zhíyán*.
Dí Rénjié,
a native of Tàiyuán,
served as a Legal Advisor in the prefectural government.
At that time, his colleague Zhèng Chóngzī
had an elderly and ill mother,
yet he was assigned to serve as an envoy to a remote frontier region.
Dí Rénjié said to him:
"Your honored mother is critically ill,
and you are being sent on a distant mission.
How can you cause your parent to weep for you from ten thousand *lǐ* away?"
He then requested to replace Chóngzī.
From *Tán Bīn Lù*.
Jìng Zhāodào
Jìng Zhāodào served as a Dàlǐ Píngshì.
During the Yánhé era,
there were rebels in Yí,
and over four hundred people were implicated.
They were to be assigned to the Sīnóng office
(the Míng manuscript records "office" as "temple")
but before they could set out,
they were detained in the prefectural prison.
Zhāodào pardoned them based on the amnesty decree.
The chancellor at the time sternly reprimanded the Dàlǐ officials,
asking how they could pardon the families of rebels.
The Dàlǐ Qīng and other officials turned pale with fear,
and summoned Zhāodào.
The chancellor angrily rebuked him.
Zhāodào said:
"The amnesty decree states 'currently imprisoned prisoners,'
and the rebels are detained in the prefectural prison,
so they are indeed currently imprisoned."
After repeated questioning and debate,
five or six rounds in total,
the chancellor had no way to refute him,
and all those implicated were pardoned.
Zhāodào was promoted to Jiānchá Yùshǐ.
Previously, ten conscripts from Kuízhōu, including Shū Wànfú,
were passing through Bālíng,
and drowned while crossing a rapid.
Zhāodào was on a mission to Bāyú,
and when he reached Wànnián Station,
he dreamed that these ten men pleaded for mercy,
repeating their plea over and over.
He then summoned the station officer to inquire,
and the officer's account matched his dream.
Zhāodào immediately hired skilled swimmers,
retrieved their bodies,
and prepared wine and food to offer in libation.
All who witnessed this were moved to tears.
He then sent official notices to nearby counties,
prepared coffins,
and returned the bodies to their hometowns.
When the conscripts heard of this,
they were all deeply moved and filled with admiration.
From "Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ."
Wú Bǎo'ān,
courtesy name Yǒnggù,
was a man from Héběi,
serving as Fāngyì County Captain in Suízhōu.
His fellow villager Guō Zhòngxiáng,
was the grandnephew of Guō Yuánzhèn.
Zhòngxiáng possessed talent and learning,
and Yuánzhèn intended to help him establish a name and official career.
At that time, the southern barbarians rebelled,
and Lǐ Méng was appointed Military Governor of Yáozhōu,
leading troops to suppress them.
Before Méng's departure,
he took leave of Yuánzhèn.
Yuánzhèn then introduced Zhòngxiáng to him,
saying to Méng:
"This orphaned son of my younger brother,
has yet to gain fame or office.
You should take him along.
If you defeat the bandits and achieve merit,
I, being in charge of government affairs,
will surely recommend him,
enabling him to receive a modest official salary."
Méng agreed.
Zhòngxiáng was quite capable,
so he was appointed as his administrative assistant,
entrusted with military affairs.
When they reached Shǔ,
Bǎo'ān sent a letter to Zhòngxiáng, saying:
"Fortunate to share the same hometown,
I have long admired your reputation and virtue.
Although we have long been separated and I have not paid my respects,
my heart has always held you in admiration.
You, sir, are the nephew of the State Minister,
a man of great talent in the military headquarters.
Indeed, due to your fine abilities,
you have been entrusted with important duties.
General Lǐ combines civil and military talents,
has received the command to lead a campaign,
personally commands a great army,
and will soon pacify these petty bandits.
With the General's bravery and prowess,
combined with your own abilities,
the army's complete victory,
and the achievement of merit, are but a matter of days.
I, Bǎo'ān, loved learning from childhood,
and devoted myself to the classics as I grew.
My talent falls short of surpassing others,
and my official post is merely that of a county captain.
Remotely stationed beyond Jiàn,
the land is close to barbarian borders.
My homeland is thousands of miles away,
separated by mountain passes and rivers.
Moreover, this term of office has already ended,
and a future appointment is difficult to expect.
With my lack of talent,
I am hindered by the selection board's strict limitations.
To hope for even a meager salary again,
how could there be any chance?
I shall return to grow old in my village gardens,
and eventually perish in a ditch or ravine.
I have heard, sir,
that you are eager to relieve others' troubles,
and do not neglect the sentiments of fellow villagers.
I suddenly dare to hope for your exceptional favor.
If you could enable Bǎo'ān to take up the whip and bow,
to serve and follow you.
If you would record even my insignificant self,
allowing me to minimally share in the achievements.
Upon the triumphant return,
to be included among the lowest ranks.
This would be a kindness from you as weighty as a mountain,
a day I, Bǎo'ān, would engrave upon my heart.
I dare not presume it,
but I wish you would consider it.
I only hope you will perceive my sincerity,
and forgive my abruptness.
I earnestly await your guidance for my clumsy self,
hoping you will summon me to join you."
Zhòngxiáng received the letter,
and was deeply moved by it.
He immediately spoke to General Lǐ,
who summoned Bǎo'ān to serve as a secretary.
Before Bǎo'ān arrived, the barbarian bandits pressed closer.
General Lǐ reached Yáozhōu,
engaged them in battle, and defeated them.
Pressing the advantage, he advanced deep into enemy territory,
where the barbarians ambushed and defeated him.
Lǐ died in battle, and his army was annihilated.
Zhòngxiáng was taken captive.
The barbarians coveted Hàn wealth and goods.
Regarding those who were captured,
they all allowed messages to be sent,
instructing their families to ransom them,
at thirty bolts of silk per person.
When Bǎo'ān arrived at Yáozhōu,
he happened upon the army's defeat,
and lingered there, not returning.
Meanwhile, Zhòngxiáng, among the barbarians,
managed with great difficulty to send a letter to Bǎo'ān, saying:
"Yǒnggù, I hope you are well. [Note: Bǎo'ān's courtesy name. The original text had 'zǐ' (子), corrected to 'zì' (字) based on the Ming manuscript copy.]
I was previously honored by your letter but did not reply,
as the great army had already set out.
We advanced deep into the bandits' territory,
and indeed met with defeat.
Lord Lǐ died in battle,
and I became a captive.
I barely cling to life,
at the ends of the earth.
Looking at my life, it is over;
thinking of my homeland, it is distant and obscure.
My talent is inferior to Zhōng Yí's,
yet I am similarly bound in captivity.
I am not like Jīzǐ,
yet [Note: The original had 'shān' (山), corrected to 'qiě' (且) based on the Ming manuscript copy.]
I am seen as a slave.
Herding sheep by the seaside,
somewhat akin to Sū Wǔ;
shooting geese within palace walls—
how could I expect a Lǐ Líng?
Since I fell among these barbarians,
I have fully tasted hardship and bitterness.
My skin and flesh have been lacerated and cut,
blood and tears cover the ground.
The utmost sufferings of a living person,
I have endured them all.
A scion of a distinguished Zhōngyuá family,
now a destitute prisoner in a remote land.
Days pass, months go by,
heat retreats, cold assaults.
I long for my aged parents in my old country,
gaze toward the pines and catalpas at my ancestral graves.
Distraught, I nearly go mad,
my heart bursts with sorrow, tears flow in anguish,
I know not whence these tears come.
Even passersby who see me
are moved to pity.
You and I, Yǒnggù,
though we have not shared deep confidences,
are fellow villagers, and you are my senior and predecessor;
our temperaments and tastes are congenial.
I long to see your esteemed countenance,
you are never absent from my dreams.
Previously, I was honored by your inquiry,
and took the opportunity to speak on your behalf.
Lord Lǐ had long known of your talent and reputation,
so I requested he appoint you as secretary.
The great army had gone far,
and you arrived late.
Thus, you fell behind the military column yourself,
it was not that I neglected a fellow villager.
Your family transmits accumulated blessings,
Heaven rewards accumulated goodness.
Indeed, you did not join the campaign in time,
thus preserving both life and reputation.
Had you earlier served under his command,
participated in the headquarters alongside me,
then you, a man in this remote land,
how would you differ from me?
I am now in dire straits,
my strength exhausted, my plans at an end.
According to barbarian custom, captives are detained,
and relatives are permitted to come and ransom them.
Because I am the nephew of the State Minister,
unlike ordinary people,
they persistently press me hard,
demanding a thousand bolts of silk.
When this message reaches you,
they will further demand a hundred rolls of fine silk.
I hope you will quickly send a plain letter,
to inform my uncle.
He must ensure it arrives in time,
so I can be ransomed and return.
To make my wandering soul return home,
to put flesh back on my dead bones—
I place my hope entirely in you.
Regarding this matter today,
I beg you not to decline the toil.
If my uncle has already left the court,
and it is difficult to petition him,
then I wish you would,
personally redeem Shífù,
unhitch Yíwú's side horse like that,
go and ransom Huá Yuán,
imitating the affair of the Sòng people.
The way of aiding others,
even the ancients found difficult.
Because your moral integrity has always been lofty,
your reputation and integrity particularly outstanding,
therefore I make this request,
without harboring doubt.
If you, sir, do not take pity,
but degrade yourself to be like the common crowd,
then in life I shall remain a captive slave,
If I die, I will be a ghost among the barbarians.
What more can I hope for?
It's over, Wú Jūn,
do not ruin my affairs."
Bǎo'ān received the letter,
and was deeply saddened by it.
At that time, Yuánzhèn had already passed away,
so Bǎo'ān sent a reply,
promising to ransom Zhòngxiáng.
He then exhausted his family's resources,
obtaining two hundred bolts of silk to take with him.
He stayed in Xīzhōu,
not returning for ten years.
Managing his finances,
he accumulated seven hundred bolts of silk in total,
but the amount was still insufficient.
Bǎo'ān had always been poor,
and his wife and children were still in Suízhōu.
He was so focused on ransoming Zhòngxiáng
that he cut off contact with his family.
Whenever he obtained anything from others,
even if it was just a foot of cloth or a liter of grain,
he gradually saved it all.
Later, his wife and children suffered from hunger and cold,
unable to support themselves.
His wife then led their frail son,
riding a donkey,
and went south to Lú,
seeking Bǎo'ān's whereabouts.
On the way, their provisions ran out,
and they were still hundreds of miles from Yáozhōu.
His wife had no plan,
so she wept by the roadside,
her sorrow moving passersby.
At that time, Yáng Ānjū, the military governor of Yáozhōu, was traveling by post to the commandery,
and upon seeing Bǎo'ān's wife crying,
he found it strange and inquired about it.
The wife said:
"My husband is Wú Bǎo'ān, a local guard in Suízhōu's Fāngyì.
Because his friend was captured by the barbarians,
he begged to go and ransom him,
and thus stayed in Yáozhōu.
He abandoned me and our child,
and for ten years, there has been no news from him.
I am now impoverished and suffering,
and I am going to search for Bǎo'ān.
With no provisions and a long road ahead,
this is why I weep."
Ānjū found this extraordinary.
He said to her:
"I will go ahead to the post station,
and there I will await you, madam,
to provide for your needs."
When they arrived at the post station,
Ānjū gave Bǎo'ān's wife several thousand coins,
and provided her with a carriage to continue her journey.
Ānjū hurried to the commandery,
first seeking out Bǎo'ān to meet him,
and taking his hand, ascended the hall.
He said to Bǎo'ān:
"I have often read the books of the ancients,
and seen the deeds of the ancients,
but I never thought I would witness such a thing in person today with you.
How is it that your sense of duty and friendship runs so deep,
while your care for your wife and children is so shallow,
that you would abandon your family,
to ransom a friend,
and go to such lengths?
I have seen your wife come,
and thinking of your righteousness,
my heart was eagerly waiting,
hoping to see your face.
I have just arrived,
and have nothing to assist you with.
But I will lend you four hundred bolts of official silk from the treasury,
to aid you in this matter.
After your friend arrives,
I will slowly repay it."
Bǎo'ān was overjoyed,
took the silk,
and had a messenger among the barbarians take it
"take" originally written as "special,"
according to the Ming manuscript copy, corrected
and go.
After two hundred days, Zhòngxiáng arrived in Yáozhōu,
his appearance haggard,
hardly resembling a human.
When he and Bǎo'ān recognized each other,
they spoke and wept together.
Ānjū had once served under Minister Guō,
so he had Zhòngxiáng bathed and groomed,
gave him clothes,
invited him to sit together,
and feasted and entertained him.
Ānjū deeply respected Bǎo'ān's actions,
and treated him with great favor.
He then appointed Zhòngxiáng as a temporary guard under his jurisdiction.
Zhòngxiáng had been among the barbarians for a long time,
and knew their customs well,
so he sent people to the barbarian caves to purchase ten female slaves,
all of whom were beautiful.
After they arrived,
he bid farewell to Ānjū to return north,
and offered the barbarian women to him as a gift.
Ānjū declined, saying:
"I am not a merchant,
how could I expect repayment?
I admire Wú Shēng's sense of duty,
and thus helped bring this matter to completion.
You have elderly parents here,
let this serve as funds for their sustenance."
Zhòngxiáng thanked him, saying:
"That I, a humble man, was able to return,
is due to your grace.
That my insignificant life was preserved,
is your gift.
Even if I were to close my eyes in death,
I would not dare forget this great favor.
But these barbarian women,
were specifically sought for you.
If you refuse them now,
I will plead with my life."
Ānjū found it difficult to refuse,
so he pointed to his youngest daughter and said:
"Since you have insisted so earnestly,
I dare not go against your noble intentions.
This daughter is the youngest,
and I have always doted on her.
For her sake,
I will accept one of these women from you."
Thus, he declined the other nine.
Bǎo'ān, too, was generously treated by Ānjū,
and left with ample provisions and supplies.
Zhòngxiáng returned home,
having been away from his family for fifteen years.
He then went to the capital,
where he was appointed as a records officer in Yùzhōu for his merits,
and brought his parents to his post.
After two years,
he was again promoted to household registrar in Dàizhōu for his excellence,
and when his term ended, his mother passed away.
After the burial,
he observed mourning at the graveside,
and said:
"I relied on Wú Gōng to ransom me,
so I could take office and support my parents.
Now that my parents have passed and the mourning period is over,
I can fulfill my wish."
He then set out to find Bǎo'ān.
Bǎo'ān had been promoted from local guard in Fāngyì to assistant magistrate in Péngshān, Méizhōu.
Zhòngxiáng thus went to Shǔ to visit him.
Bǎo'ān's term had ended,
but he was unable to return home,
and both he and his wife had died there,
temporarily buried in a temple.
When Zhòngxiáng heard this,
he wept bitterly.
He then donned mourning garments of coarse hemp,
wore a mourning band and carried a staff,
and walked barefoot from Shǔ commandery,
weeping without cease.
When he reached Péngshān,
he performed sacrifices and libations,
then exhumed the bones,
marking each joint with ink
marking the bone joints with ink,
writing their order,
fearing they might be misplaced during burial
and placed them in a silk bag.
He also exhumed his wife's bones,
marked them with ink and stored them in a bamboo basket.
Then, barefoot, he personally carried them on his back,
walking thousands of miles,
to Wèi commandery.
Bǎo'ān had a son,
whom Zhòngxiáng loved like a younger brother.
He then used all of his family wealth, two hundred thousand coins,
to give Bǎo'ān a grand burial.
He also erected a stone stele praising his virtues.
Zhòngxiáng personally built a hut beside the grave,
and observed mourning for three years.
Later, he became a senior clerk in Lánzhōu,
and was further promoted to court gentleman for court service.
He took Bǎo'ān's son with him to his post,
arranged a marriage for him,
and cared for him with great kindness.
Zhòngxiáng never ceased to feel indebted to Bǎo'ān.
In the twelfth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
he went to the imperial court,
and yielded his official rank and position to Bǎo'ān's son as repayment.
People of the time held him in high esteem.
Initially,
when Zhòngxiáng was captured,
he was given as a slave to a barbarian chieftain.
His master favored him,
and he ate and drank the same as his master.
After a year,
Zhòngxiáng longed to return north,
and thus escaped to return.
They pursued and caught him,
and sold him off to the Southern Cave.
The cave master was harsh and cruel,
and upon obtaining Zhòngxiáng,
forced him into hard labor,
even whipping him severely.
Zhòngxiáng fled in escape,
but was chased down and caught again,
and sold to another Southern Cave.
This cave was called Púsàmán,
and Zhòngxiáng stayed there for a year.
In dire straits, he fled again,
but the Mán people pursued and caught him once more,
and sold him to yet another cave.
The cave master, upon obtaining Zhòngxiáng,
angrily said:
"This slave loves to run away—
is it so hard to stop him?"
He then took two planks,
each several feet long,
and made Zhòngxiáng stand on them.
He nailed
("zì" originally written as "qí,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript)
through the tops of his feet,
the nails penetrating into the wood.
Whenever he was put to work,
he often had to carry these two planks with him.
At night, he was placed in an underground cell,
and personally locked inside.
Zhòngxiáng's two feet
took several years for the wounds to finally heal.
Locked in the underground cell with the planks,
he endured this for seven years.
At first, Zhòngxiáng could not bear the sorrow.
When Bǎo'ān sent someone to ransom him,
they first found Zhòngxiáng's original master.
Through辗转曲折 efforts, they managed to retrieve him,
and thus Zhòngxiáng was able to return.
From "Jì Wén"
Péi Miǎn
Péi Miǎn served as Wang Hóng's administrative assistant.
Wang Hóng was convicted and executed.
Lǐ Línfǔ wielded power arbitrarily,
and everyone feared him.
Several of Wang Hóng's former aides
did not dare to even glance at Wang Hóng's gate.
Only Péi Miǎn collected Wang Hóng's corpse,
personally oversaw the funeral,
and buried him in the outskirts.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Lǐ Yīdé
was originally a lowly person
who fled from his master.
When Xuánzōng initiated the uprising,
he, along with Wáng Máozhòng and others, made contributions.
Yīdé rose to the rank of General of the Martial Guard.
His former master encountered him on the road
and hurried to avoid him,
not daring to look up.
Yīdé ordered his attendants to summon him,
and the master was extremely fearful.
Upon arriving at Yīdé's residence,
he was invited to take the seat of honor,
and Yīdé personally served him food and wine.
The former master, sweating profusely, declined,
but stayed for several days.
Yīdé then petitioned the emperor, saying:
"Your subject has received the nation's grace,
and my honors and emoluments are excessive.
My former
("jiù" originally written as "cáo,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript)
master is humble and insignificant,
and has never received the slightest official salary.
I request to halve my own salary, resign from my post, and bestow this honor upon him.
I hope Your Majesty will grant my sincere request."
The emperor praised his intent,
promoted the master to the rank of Lieutenant General,
and restored Yīdé to his original position.
The court esteemed him greatly for this.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi"
Mù Níng
Mù Níng's origins are unknown.
Yán Zhēnqīng recommended him as the Assistant Commissioner of the Hebei Circuit.
Níng entrusted his eldest son to his younger brother, saying:
"Wherever you go,
as long as our lineage does not lack heirs,
I will have no burdens."
He then went to Píngyuán,
and said to Zhēnqīng:
"My ancestors now have descendants.
As the ancients said, 'There are deaths lighter than a goose feather'—
I, Níng, am such a case.
I wish to fully assist you, sir,
in resolving this crisis."
Later, when Níng's plans sometimes failed,
Zhēnqīng abandoned Píngyuán
and crossed the river by night.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Zhào Huá
Zhào Huá was forced to remain among the rebels,
where he saw a woman.
Upon asking,
he learned she was a clan daughter of Wéi Huán, the Surveillance Commissioner of Jiangxi.
Her husband was a local official
who was killed for not joining the rebel army.
Lady Wéi was confiscated and made a slave.
Huá pitied her unjust suffering,
and ransomed her with money.
He had his wife settle her in a separate courtyard,
and Huá himself never met her again.
The following year,
when the Eastern Capital was recaptured,
Huá used his family wealth to provide for her
and sought out her relatives to return her to them.
Commentators all esteemed him for this.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Cáo Wénqià
was a deputy general under Zhèng Huá.
At the time, Yáo Nánzhōng served as Military Commissioner,
but was harassed by the eunuch supervisor Xuē Yíngzhēn, who relied on his power to interfere with military affairs.
Nánzhōng did not comply,
and Yíngzhēn repeatedly slandered him to the emperor.
The emperor grew quite suspicious.
Later, Yíngzhēn sent a minor envoy, Chéng Wùyíng, to deliver a memorial accusing Nánzhōng,
with severe slanders.
Wénqià was then on his way to the capital to report on affairs,
and secretly learned the contents of Yíngzhēn's memorial.
Wénqià was enraged,
and immediately traveled day and night to catch up with Wùyíng.
He reached Chánglè Station,
caught up with him,
and shared lodging with him.
In the middle of the night,
he killed Wùyíng,
threw Yíngzhēn's memorial into a latrine,
and then took his own life.
By late morning,
the station officials opened the door
and saw blood and injuries all over the floor.
Beside them, they found two letters from Wénqià:
one was an accusation against Yíngzhēn,
and the other was a memorial pleading Nánzhōng's innocence,
along with an apology for killing Wùyíng.
When Dézōng heard of the matter,
he was quite suspicious.
Nánzhōng, fearing the conflict would deepen,
went to court.
Upon his arrival,
the emperor said:
"Did Yíngzhēn harass you severely?"
Nánzhōng replied:
"Yíngzhēn did not harass me—
he merely undermined Your Majesty's laws.
Wherever men like Yíngzhēn are present,
even if Yáng Hù and Dù Yù were reborn,
they could not govern the people,
command the three armies,
achieve benevolent and parental governance,
or establish disciplined and well-ordered military systems."
Dézōng remained silent for a long time.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Yáng Chéng,
during the Zhēnyuán era,
lived in seclusion with his three younger brothers in the mountains of Xiàyáng, Shǎnzhōu,
vowing never to marry.
They subsisted on beans and water,
with rush mats and coarse quilts,
yet were joyful and harmonious,
sharing
one room.
Later, when famine struck,
they withdrew from sight and ceased interactions with fellow villagers,
fearing they might seek help.
Sometimes they gathered bark from mulberry or elm trees,
ground it into powder to make porridge.
They continued discussing the Book of Songs and Book of Documents,
never pausing.
They had an elderly servant named Dū’er,
who shared their convictions,
comparable to Guǎn Níng.
The villagers respected them and pitied them,
offering slightly better food,
but they would shut their door and refuse it,
scattering it for hungry birds.
Later, the villagers secretly had a middle household send over a dozen cups of chaff and husks,
which they then ate on the spot.
Another day,
a feudal lord from Shāndōng, hearing of their noble integrity,
sent an envoy with five hundred rolls of fine silk.
Yáng Chéng firmly refused,
but the envoy had orders not to return,
so Yáng Chéng placed it in a corner of the room,
never opening the package.
Not long after,
a man of principle named Zhèng Chù,
pressured by funeral arrangements,
sought help from others but received none,
and passing by his door,
went to visit him.
Zhèng Chù looked sorrowful and emaciated.
Yáng Chéng kept him for ten days, feeding him,
and asked where he was going,
and the reason for his distress.
Zhèng Chù told him everything.
Yáng Chéng said:
"I am moved by your integrity.
I have these gifts from a feudal lord,
which are of no use to me.
Let me assist you in fulfilling your duty as a son."
Zhèng Chù firmly declined.
Yáng Chéng said:
"If you are not being deceitful,
why decline?"
Zhèng Chù replied:
"Since you, sir, have bestowed such extraordinary kindness,
I wish to serve as your slave after completing my duty,
to repay you."
He then left.
After Zhèng Chù finished the burial matters in Luòyáng,
he returned on foot to Yáng Chéng,
to fulfill his earlier promise.
Yáng Chéng said:
"Why do this?
If you have no other ties,
we can study together as comrades.
Why speak of enslaving yourself to depend on me?"
Zhèng Chù wept and said:
"If so,
how fortunate this humble body is."
Zhèng Chù struggled with memorization and reading,
and after over a month,
Yáng Chéng had him recite the Book of Songs,
though he kept reading diligently.
When discussing it with him,
it was like water thrown on stone.
Zhèng Chù was deeply ashamed.
Yáng Chéng said:
"In your studies,
you are too close to my brothers and cannot part,
is that why this is so?
To the north of where we live,
there is a tall, conspicuous thatched study.
You can go there to study on your own."
Zhèng Chù was very pleased,
and immediately moved there.
After another month or so,
Yáng Chéng visited him,
and discussed the Guófēng with him.
Though Zhèng Chù had worked harder,
he still could not exchange a single phrase.
As Yáng Chéng had just left,
not twenty or thirty steps away,
Zhèng Chù hanged himself from a beam.
A serving boy peeped in,
and shocked, reported it to Yáng Chéng.
Yáng Chéng wailed as if his limbs were torn apart.
He ordered Dū’er to bring wine for an offering,
and personally wrote a eulogy for the sacrifice,
blaming himself for his lack of discernment.
"Though I did not kill Zhèng Chù,
he died because of me."
He removed his own clothes,
and had a servant carry them.
Dū’er administered fifteen strokes with a cane,
and they wore mourning garments of sīmá,
burying him with great care.
From then on, he was highly esteemed by the gentry.
Later, when serving as Reminding Counselor,
he vehemently advised that Péi Yánlíng was unfit to be Chancellor,
his words extremely earnest,
recorded in the Tang histories.
When he served as prefect of Jiānghuá Prefecture,
he cooked two hú of rice daily,
and a large pot of fish soup.
From imperial envoys to common villagers in coarse clothes,
all ate freely.
He also set out earthen bowls and ladles,
like a wine vessel at a crossroads.
From "Gàn Zǐzi."
Wáng Yì
was a servant of Péi Dù.
When Péi Dù was Vice Censor-in-chief,
on the day Wǔ Yuánhéng was assassinated,
Péi Dù was also attacked,
and Wáng Yì shielded him from the blade and died.
Thus Péi Dù escaped harm,
and he personally wrote a eulogy for him.
He generously provided for his wife and children.
That year,
among the jìnshì candidates who wrote biographies of Wáng Yì,
ten or twenty out of a hundred did so.
From "Guóshǐbǔ."
Péi Dù
During the Yuánhé era,
there was a newly appointed Registrar of Húzhōu,
who had not yet taken up his post,
when he encountered bandits.
He was robbed of nearly everything,
and the official documents of his appointment and his career records
were all lost without a trace.
He then begged for old clothes in a nearby town,
wandered about borrowing money,
and returned to the inn.
The inn was located close to the residence of Duke Pei Jìngōng.
At that time, Duke Jìn was on leave,
so he went out in plain clothes to visit the nearby inns,
and arrived at the inn where the Registrar was staying.
They exchanged bows and sat down,
conversed and interacted,
and the Duke asked about his circumstances.
The Registrar said:
"My bitter story
is unbearable for others to hear."
As he spoke, tears fell.
Duke Jìn took pity on him
and inquired in detail about the matter.
The Registrar replied:
"I served in the capital for several years,
was appointed to a post in the provinces,
encountered bandits who plundered everything,
and only my frail life remains—
this is but a minor matter.
However, I was about to marry but had not yet fetched my bride,
when the local governor forcibly took her
and presented her to the Prime Minister, Duke Pei,
whose rank is second only to the ruler of the state."
Duke Pei asked:
"What is the surname of your betrothed?"
He replied:
"Her surname is such-and-such, and her given name is Huáng'é."
Duke Pei was wearing purple trousers and a robe at the time,
and said to him:
"I am a close aide of Duke Jìn,
and will try to investigate for you."
He then asked for his name and left.
The Registrar later regretted it,
thinking that this person might be a close associate of the Prime Minister,
and if he went in and reported it,
it would surely bring disaster upon him.
He could not sleep peacefully.
At dawn,
he went to the side of Duke Pei's residence to investigate,
and saw that Duke Pei had already entered the palace.
By evening,
an official in crimson clothes came to the inn,
looking rather hurried,
and announced that the Prime Minister was summoning him.
Upon hearing this, the Registrar was terrified,
and hastily went with the official.
Upon arriving at the residence shortly after,
he was led into a small hall,
where he prostrated himself, sweating profusely,
not daring to look up.
He was then invited to sit.
Stealing a glance,
he saw that it was the man in purple from the previous day.
He repeatedly bowed and apologized.
The Prime Minister said:
"What I heard yesterday
truly moved my heart with pity.
Now, let this serve to comfort your distress."
He then ordered the official documents from a chest to be given to him,
and he was reappointed as Registrar of Húzhōu.
While he was still overjoyed,
the Duke added:
"Huáng'é may accompany you to your post."
He specially ordered her to be sent to his inn,
along with travel provisions worth a thousand strings of cash,
so they could go together to his post.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Liào Yǒufāng,
in the yǐwèi year of the Yuánhé era,
failed the imperial examination and traveled to Shǔ.
When he reached west of Bǎojī,
he stopped at a government hostel.
Suddenly, he heard groaning sounds.
Listening carefully, he detected faint gasps.
In a side room,
he saw a poor and sick young man.
He asked about his illness and circumstances,
and the man replied with effort:
"I have toiled through several examinations,
but never met a kindred spirit.
Gazing and bowing,
he spoke again after a long pause:
'I entrust my remains to you.'"
He could say no more.
Liào intended to seek medical help for him,
but the man suddenly passed away.
Liào then sold his saddle and horse cheaply to a village magnate,
prepared a coffin, and buried him,
regretting that he did not know his name.
As fellow scholars,
he felt deep sorrow at the parting.
He also composed an epitaph:
"Alas, you departed this world with an empty purse,
having toiled many times in the literary arena.
Though we met but briefly, I mourn for you with a cry,
not knowing where your hometown lies."
Later, when Liào returned from western Shǔ,
he took the eastern Chuān road
and arrived at Língkān Station.
The station master welcomed him to his private residence.
When he saw the station master's wife,
dressed in plain white clothes,
she bowed twice, sobbing,
overwhelmed with emotion,
lingering and speaking kindly,
as if they were close relatives.
He stayed for half a month,
and both his servants and horses were well-fed.
He was served rare delicacies like bear and tiger meat,
and treated with the utmost hospitality.
Liào could not fathom the reason for this,
and felt increasingly uneasy.
Upon parting,
the wife wept sorrowfully again,
and presented him with a load of silk and brocade as a farewell gift,
worth several hundred thousand cash.
The station master said:
"The Hú Wǎn scholar you buried this spring
was my wife's youngest brother."
Only then did Liào learn the deceased's name.
He recounted his condolences for the deceased,
but firmly declined the gifts.
The young wife and her husband
insisted on presenting them.
Liào said again:
"As a man,
I have some understanding of past and present principles.
I merely buried a fellow scholar by chance,
and cannot accept such generous gifts."
He then urged his horse forward,
while the station master rode after him to see him off.
After passing another station,
they still had not parted.
Liào paid no heed to the gifts,
and the station master held his sleeve.
Each regretted parting ways,
and the gifts were eventually abandoned in the wilderness.
The local elders reported this righteous deed to the prefecture.
The prefect submitted a memorial to the court.
Civil and military officials
all wished to meet Liào Yǒufāng,
and vied to recommend him.
The following year,
when Lǐ Féngjí oversaw the examinations,
Liào passed the imperial examination,
changed his name to Yóuqīng,
and his reputation spread throughout the land—
he was a righteous man of the Great Táng.
The station master, Dài Kèqín,
received an official dispatch from the provincial military commissioner,
and was promoted to the highest position.
The fame and righteousness of Kèqín
spread as far as that of Liào.
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì"
Xíong Zhíyì
Xíong Zhíyì was traveling to take the imperial examination
and stopped at Tóngguān.
Autumn rains had lasted for over a month,
and he was stranded at an inn.
Suddenly, he heard a scholar in the neighboring inn
sighing repeatedly.
Xíong secretly inquired about him,
and was told:
"Former Magistrate of Yáoshān, Fán Zé,
is traveling to take the special examination,
but upon arriving here,
his horse died and his funds ran out,
so he cannot proceed."
Xíong went to see him,
immediately gave up his own horse,
and emptied his purse to help him.
Xíong gave up the examination that year,
while Fán passed the following year.
From "Zhíyán"
Lǐ Yuē
Lǐ Yuē served as a Military Ministry Vice Director;
he was the son of Duke Qiān.
His insight and bearing were pure and expansive,
far transcending worldly concerns.
He served alongside Vice Director Zhāng Shěn of the Bureau of Receptions.
Together with the Recluse Wéi Kuàng,
they withdrew from the world behind their eastern walls,
neither marrying
nor managing any livelihood.
Lǐ was especially close to Zhāng.
Often, he would sit with Zhāng on a square couch, speaking quietly,
staying awake until dawn,
with no one else knowing what was said.
He once presented a poem to Zhāng, which read:
"I have matters in my heart,
not told to Wéi the Second.
On an autumn night in Luòyáng city,
the bright moon shines upon Zhāng the Eighth."
Once, Lǐ Yuē was traveling by river,
and his boat was next to that of a foreign merchant.
The merchant fell ill
and insisted on meeting him.
He entrusted his two daughters to Lǐ,
both of them being women of exceptional beauty.
He also bequeathed a pearl.
Lǐ Yuē simply assented to everything.
After the merchant died,
the wealth and treasures amounted to tens of thousands,
but Lǐ fully registered the inventory and sent it to the authorities.
As for the two daughters, he sought suitable marriages for them.
Initially,
when preparing the merchant's body for burial,
Lǐ Yuē had personally placed a night-shining pearl in his mouth,
with no one else knowing.
Later,
when relatives of the deceased merchant came to claim the assets,
Lǐ requested the officials to exhume the body for inspection.
Upon examination,
the night-shining pearl was indeed found inside.
His secret acts of integrity were all of this kind.
From "Shàngshū Gùshí".
Zhèng Huángǔ
was living leisurely in the Eastern Capital.
He became very familiar with a certain General Liǔ Dāng.
General Liǔ's residence was on East Lǚxìn Street,
renowned for its splendid towers, terraces, ponds, and trees.
His family was very wealthy,
with a great many singing girls and musicians.
Zhèng frequented their banquets and drinking parties.
Having grown familiar with the various singing girls through laughter and conversation,
he began to jest and banter with them.
The girls reported this to Liǔ.
Liǔ, admiring Zhèng's literary talent
and considering his poverty,
did not blame him for it.
When Zhèng was about to go to the capital to seek an official post,
Liǔ held a farewell feast for him.
When the wine was in full flow,
Zhèng presented a poem to one of the singing girls, which read:
"Your dazzling beauty emerges like an immortal,
your singing surpasses pipes and strings.
Watching the 'White Ramie' song performed,
I wish to ascend the azure-clouded sky.
Not yet planning to give birth to a Péi Xiù,
how could one beg for a Zhèng Xuán?
Do not let the waters of Golden Valley
flow past before the tower from which one fell."
Liǔ was very pleased upon seeing the poem.
He said:
"I do not begrudge this singing girl,
but you, my friend, are just seeking an official post.
Your resources are currently strained and scarce;
taking her away would certainly be difficult to manage.
I will wait specifically until I see your glorious appointment,
and then I will send her to the capital
as a congratulatory gift."
After Zhèng entered the capital,
within less than half a year,
he was appointed Erudite of the National University.
When Liǔ saw the appointment list,
he made arrangements to send her to the capital.
When the singing girl reached Jiāxiáng Station,
Zhèng had already passed away.
His coffin in transit soon arrived at the prefectural border.
Upon hearing this, Liǔ sighed endlessly with grief
and subsequently released the singing girl to go elsewhere.
From "Lúshì Záshuō".
A Scholar from Jiānglíng
There was a scholar residing in Jiānglíng;
his name has been forgotten.
He had a beautiful concubine,
but was very poor.
He sought official correspondence to travel between Jiāozhōu and Guǎngzhōu,
journeying to seek funds,
planning to secure five years' worth of provisions.
Before leaving, he instructed his concubine, saying:
"If I do not return within five years,
you may remarry as you wish."
After the scholar departed,
five years passed without his return.
The concubine was then taken in by the former Regional Inspector,
residing at the foot of Gāolì Slope.
The following year,
her husband returned,
only to find his concubine was no longer there.
He sought out and learned her whereabouts.
He then composed a poem,
requesting a matchmaker to deliver it to her.
The poem read:
"Dark clouds descend dimly from the Sunny Terrace,
having captivated King Xiāng, she does not return.
Five times viewing flowers, only tears in vain;
my heart, knotted as one, has never opened.
Delicate vines naturally cling to fragrant trees;
spilled water—who thinks of returning to the old cup?
Melancholy for the dwelling at Gāolì Slope's base,
spring light no longer descends the mountain."
When the Regional Inspector saw the poem,
he provided one hundred thousand cash along with travel supplies,
and sent her back to the scholar.
From "Lúshì Záshuō".
Zhèng Tián
Duke Wén, Zhèng Tián,
styled Táiwén.
His father, Zhèng Yà,
once served as Surveillance Commissioner of Guìguǎn.
Tián was born in Guì Prefecture,
and his childhood name was Guì'er.
At that time, Xīmén Sīgōng was the Army Supervisor,
and an imperial edict summoned him to the capital.
Yà held a farewell banquet for him in the northern suburbs.
Considering his own advanced age,
he entrusted Tián to Sīgōng's care,
saying:
"In days to come, I hope you will keep Guì'er in mind.
Even beneath the Nine Springs,
I shall not dare forget this."
Having spoken,
tears streamed down his face.
Sīgōng remembered this.
By the time Sīgōng became Commander of the Divine Strategy Army,
Yà had already passed away.
Sīgōng sent someone to summon Tián
and housed him in his own residence.
Tián was not yet capped (under twenty),
but Sīgōng loved him dearly,
treating him like a nephew.
He therefore selected teachers and friends to instruct him.
Tián later rose to the ranks of general and minister.
When Huáng Cháo entered Cháng'ān,
Minister Xīmén fled to take refuge in the Zhōngnán Mountains.
Tián used his family wealth to generously recruit brave men,
searched for and found him,
and brought him back to the Qí region.
He attended to his warmth and coolness and served his meals
as if he were his own father.
Sīgōng eventually passed away in Tián's care.
Tián buried him on the western ridge of Fèngxiáng.
The pines and cypresses there were all planted by Tián's own hand.
Not long after,
Tián also passed away.
He was buried near Xīmén's grave.
All the officials visited the two mounds to pay their respects,
and none could hold back their tears,
all deeply moved by his righteousness.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Xiào the Filial Son Zhāng
The Filial Son Zhāng, named Quányì,
was a man of Fúchéng in Eastern Shǔ.
He was orphaned young,
and was raised by his elder brother Quánqǐ.
When their mother fell ill,
Quánqǐ cut a piece of flesh from his own thigh to feed her,
and her illness indeed recovered.
Another day,
Quánqǐ went out traveling.
He died at an inn.
Quányì, moved by the kindness of their natural bond,
donned the coarse mourning garments of a son.
Further, because Quánqǐ had cut his flesh to feed their mother,
he then burned his fingers with fire,
to express his utmost grief.
He also copied out one volume of the Lotus Sutra in silver characters,
reciting it day and night,
and thoroughly comprehended its profound meaning.
Later, in Lóu Alley of Chéngdū Prefecture,
he took up residence there.
Beside it was a cinnabar furnace.
He kept no servants or pages,
alone in a single room.
He sold elixirs for money,
and whenever the amount reached two taels of gold,
he would immediately carve one statue.
The present Huátíng Chán Monastery
is the site of the layman's tall building,
and people spoke of it as the art of alchemy.
He once said to a fellow Daoist:
"Refining one tael of mercury
yields only one tael's worth of silver.
But if you make it into three hundred pills,
and each pill sells for a hundred coins,
that becomes thirty thousand coins.
The profit is vast indeed.
Yet the elixirs he sold were also miraculous."
After the layman arrived in Shǔ,
he made a clay figure beside the cinnabar furnace,
to serve in place of handling hot objects.
He cherished and protected it, never destroying it,
for nearly forty years.
He passed away during the Dàshùn era,
at the age of ninety-eight.
The temple monks painted his portrait on the wall,
and the Military Commissioner's Judge, former Prefect of Méizhōu Féng Juān, composed a eulogy to praise him.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
The Grave Robber
During the period between Guāngqǐ and Dàshùn,
in Bāozhōng, there was a robber who excavated graves.
A prolonged search failed to capture him.
The senior officials pressed the investigation very strictly.
Suddenly one day he was captured,
and placed in custody.
A year dragged by,
but they could not obtain his confession.
They tortured him severely,
employing every method.
Once a confession was finally obtained,
several others were implicated,
and all believed the case was solved without error.
At the moment of execution,
a man nearby pushed up his sleeves and shouted loudly:
"How can the king's law tolerate the wrongful killing of an innocent person!
I am the grave robber.
I move daily among the crowds,
and was not captured,
so what crime has this man committed,
that you wish to kill him?
Release him immediately."
He then produced the loot obtained from the tomb,
and upon examination,
it showed no discrepancy.
The one who had confessed under torture also produced his loot,
and upon examination, it also matched.
When the regional commander personally questioned the falsely accused man,
he said:
"Although I knew myself to be innocent,
I could not endure the flogging and torture,
so I had my family secretly fabricate this loot,
hoping to escape death."
The regional commander was greatly alarmed,
and reported the full details to the court.
The prison officials were punished,
the wrongly accused man was exonerated,
and the one who confessed voluntarily was given a yamen post and rewarded.
From "Yù Táng Xián Huà".
Zhèng Yōng
Before Academician Zhèng Yōng had passed the examinations,
he sought marriage with the daughter of Minister Cuī Yuǎn of Báizhōu.
He had just received consent,
when something happened in Bólíng,
and the girl, following the usual practice, was entered into the palace.
By the time before the Kāipíng era of the Later Liáng,
Lady Cuī, inside the palace, feigned illness.
An imperial decree ordered her release from the palace,
and she returned to her own family.
Zhèng then again sent matchmakers to convey his intentions,
and selected a day for the wedding procession.
For the wedding ceremonies of scholar-official families,
depending on their wealth or frugality,
nothing was lacking.
Soon after, she experienced the grief of losing her mother,
and he observed the full mourning period with staff,
all in accordance with ritual.
The scholarly community praised him greatly for this,
and his fine reputation was widespread.
In the examination halls, they stood on tiptoe hoping for him,
and in one attempt he passed
("passed" originally written as "him";
emended according to the Ming manuscript)
the top grade
and was listed on the roster of those granted the title of Secretary.
He doffed his plain clothes,
received appointment as a Secretary in the Imperial Library,
concurrently as an Academician of the Inner Court,
entering by the same decree as the Qiū family.
He died after only a few years.
From "Yù Táng Xián Huà".
Yáng Shèng
initially served under Lǐ Chāngfú, Military Commissioner of Fèngxiáng.
He repeatedly achieved military merits,
which caused Lǐ to become suspicious of him,
and secretly sought to harm him.
Lǐ Chāngfú's beloved concubine, Zhōu shì,
pitying his innocence,
secretly warned him,
enabling him to flee and escape.
Later, he became Commander of the Fifty-fourth Army in the Imperial Escort,
and was appointed Military Commissioner of Wēishèng Army.
He established his command at Péngzhōu.
He pacified and comforted the soldiers and people,
extended respect to guests and visitors,
including Buddhist monks and Daoist priests,
each finding their proper place.
He was generous in courtesy and respect,
and people held him in great affection.
After Lǐ Chāngfú's defeat,
he ordered a search for Zhōu shì.
When she arrived,
he served her as an adoptive mother.
Zhōu shì, considering herself still young
and possessing beauty,
earnestly expressed a desire for a conjugal relationship.
Yáng Shèng swore an oath to Heaven and Earth,
that he would never be improperly joined with her.
Every morning,
before attending to official business,
he would unfailingly perform the ritual of inquiring after her peace.
Even when trapped in a tight siege,
he never neglected this.
The newly administered commandery
had incomplete military strength,
and was suddenly besieged by the founding emperor of the Former Shǔ.
Defending an isolated fortress,
with relief forces not arriving,
for a thousand days in all,
he was defeated by Xīchuān and killed.
There was a Cavalry and Infantry Commander named Ān Shījiàn,
a trusted confidant of the Yáng family.
When the city fell, he was captured.
The founding emperor of Shǔ, knowing his loyalty and steadfastness,
hoped to employ him,
and wished to spare him.
Shījiàn said:
"I received
("received" originally written as "granted";
emended according to the Ming manuscript)
promotion from Minister Yáng,
and dare not cling to life."
The founding emperor sighed in admiration and had him executed,
then held a sacrificial ceremony and buried him.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Wáng Yīn
was the nephew of Wáng Zàn, Governor of Kāifēng under the Liáng.
During the Qiánhuà era,
he was the Military Governor of Xúzhōu.
His troops mutinied and defied his orders,
killing imperial envoys,
and mustering the townsfolk to issue armor.
A personal attendant named Miáo Wēn, along with several others,
judging that the rebellion would certainly not succeed,
secretly plotted a mutiny.
The affair
(Ming manuscript has "affair" for "official")
was leaked and they were captured,
and died by having their hearts cut out.
Miáo Wēn's wife was assigned as a conscript to a different army unit.
Utterly unwilling,
she took a short blade,
cut off her breasts, and perished.
Those who heard of it all sighed in admiration.
From "Yù Táng Xián Huà".
Chén Shí
Chén Shí once sighed and said:
"As for Zhōu Zǐjū,
he is truly a pillar of the state.
Compared to a precious sword,
he is the world's Lóngquán."
A guest once asked Chén Jìfāng:
"What merits and virtues does your esteemed father possess,
that he bears such a great reputation throughout the land?"
Jìfāng said:
"My father,
is like a cassia tree
that grows in the recesses of Mount Tài,
above it are heights of ten thousand ren,
below it are unfathomable depths;
above, it is moistened by sweet dew,
below, it is nourished by deep springs.
At such a time,
how could the cassia tree know the height of Mount Tài,
or the depth of the springs?
It does not know whether it has merit and virtue or not."
From Shì Shuō
Huáng Shūdù
Guō Tài went to Rǔnán,
visited Yuán Fènggāo,
his carriage did not stop its wheels,
the bells did not cease their ringing;
but when he called upon Huáng Shūdù,
he stayed for days on end.
Someone asked him the reason,
Línzōng said:
"Shūdù is vast like the waves of a thousand qǐng,
when clarified, they do not become clear,
when stirred, they do not become turbid,
his capacity is deep and broad, difficult to fathom."
From Shì Shuō
Guō Tài
Guō Tài stood tall and lofty,
serene and profound like a deep pool.
The scholars of the nine provinces,
all revered and looked up to him with awe,
regarding him as a sheltering cover.
Cài Bójiē told Lú Zǐgàn and Mǎ Rìdī:
"I have written many stele inscriptions for the world,
and never have I not felt ashamed.
Only when composing the stele eulogy for Master Guō did I feel no shame."
From Shì Shuō
Mǎ Róng
Zhèng Xuán was a disciple under Mǎ Róng.
Róng once could not resolve seven matters concerning the splitting of texts,
and Xuán pondered five of them,
while separately ordering Lú Zǐgàn to ponder the other two.
Róng told Gàn:
"Confucius said to Zǐgòng,
'Yán Huí hears one and knows ten,
I and you are not as good as him.'
Now, I and you,
can be said to be like this."
From Shì Shuō
Cài Yōng
Cài Yōng evaluated Chén Fān and Lǐ Yīng in order,
saying:
Chén Zhòngjǔ was strong in offending superiors;
Lǐ Yuánlǐ was strict in managing subordinates.
Yì
The Ming manuscript has the five characters "fàn shàng nán shè xià" above "Yì"
Zhòngjǔ is below the Three Lords
Xiè Shěn's Hàn Jì says:
The Three Lords,
were those esteemed in their time,
Dòu Wǔ, Liú Shū, Chén Fān
Yuánlǐ is above the Eight Paragons
"Above" originally read "esteemed,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript and Chén's collated edition.
Xuē Yíng's Hàn Shū says:
Lǐ Yīng, Wáng Chàng, Xún Kūn, Zhū Yǔ, Wèi Míng, Liú Yòu, Dù Kǎi, Zhào Diǎn were the Eight Paragons
From Shì Shuō
Gù Shào
Gù Shào once said to Páng Shìyuán alone:
"I have heard that you are a man of discernment,
who is better, you or I?"
Shìyuán said:
"In molding and transforming worldly customs,
and adapting to the times with subtle strategies,
I am not as good as you;
but in discussing the remaining strategies of hegemons and kings,
and observing the crucial points of rise and fall,
I also have some slight superiority.
Can Shào also do this?"
From Shì Shuō
The Zhūgé Jǐn Brothers
Zhūgé Jǐn,
his younger brother Liàng,
and his cousin Dàn,
all had great reputations,
each serving a different state.
At the time, it was said that Shǔ got the dragon,
Wú got the tiger,
and Wèi got the dog.
From Shì Shuō
Páng Shìyuán
Páng Shìyuán went to Wú,
and the people of Wú all befriended him.
Upon seeing Lù Jì, Gù Shào, and Quán Cóng, he evaluated them, saying:
"Master Lù is what is called a nag that has the use of swift
The character "yì" was originally missing,
supplemented according to Shì Shuō
feet,
Master Gù is what is called a nag ox that can bear heavy loads over long distances.
Someone asked,
is the evaluation of Lù as superior?
He said:
"Although a nag horse is fast and precise,
it can only carry one person.
A nag ox travels a hundred li in a day,
how can it carry only one person!"
The people of Wú had no way to refute him.
Master Quán is fond of fame,
like Fán
"Fán" originally read "Chǔ,"
changed according to Shì Shuō
Zǐzhāo of Rǔnán.
From Shì Shuō
Wǔ Gāi
Sīmǎ Wénwáng asked Wǔ Gāi:
"How does Chén Tài compare to his father, the Minister of Works?"
Gāi said:
"In broad learning and elegant fluency,
and in taking the world's teachings and culture as his own responsibility,
he is not as good;
but in clarity, practice, simplicity, and thoroughness,
in achieving merit and accomplishing tasks,
he surpasses him."
From Shì Shuō
Péi Wěi
The two sons of Jìzhōu Governor Yáng Huái,
Qiáo and Máo,
both showed promise from a young age.
Huái was friendly with Péi Wěi and Yuè Guǎng,
and sent them to see them.
Wěi was by nature broad-minded and unrestrained,
and loved Qiáo for his graceful bearing.
He said to Huái:
"Qiáo will surely equal you,
Máo is slightly inferior."
Guǎng was by nature pure and honest,
and loved Máo for his divine restraint.
He said to Huái:
"Qiáo naturally equals you,
but Máo is especially outstanding."
Huái laughed and said:
"The strengths and weaknesses of my two sons,
are the strengths and weaknesses of Péi and Yuè."
Commentators evaluated this,
believing that although Qiáo had lofty grace, he lacked restraint,
so Yuè's words were correct.
However, both later became outstanding pairs.
From Shì Shuō
The Xiongnu Envoy
Wèi Wǔ was about to meet the Xiongnu envoy,
but thought his own appearance was too humble,
insufficient to impress a distant state,
so he had Cuì Jìguī substitute for him,
while he himself held a sword and stood by the bed.
After the matter was concluded,
he ordered a spy to ask:
"What was the King of Wèi like?"
The envoy said:
"The King of Wèi had an exceptionally elegant demeanor,
but the man holding the sword by the bed,
he is a true hero."
When the king heard this,
he had the envoy chased down and killed.
From Shāng Yún's Xiǎo Shuō
Héng Wēn
After Jìn's Yīn Hào was dismissed from office,
Huán Wēn said to everyone:
"When we were young and rode bamboo horses together,
I would abandon mine and leave,
and Hào would always pick it up,
so naturally he is beneath me."
From Shì Shuō Xīn Shū
Xiè Kūn
Emperor Míng asked Xiè Kūn:
"How would you compare yourself to Yǔ Liàng?"
He replied:
"In governing the court with proper decorum,
and setting a standard for all officials,
I am not as good as Liàng.
But in finding contentment in hills and valleys,
I consider myself superior."
From Shì Shuō Xīn Shū.
In the fifth year of the Zhēnguàn era of Táng Tàizōng.
The Emperor said to Zhǎngsūn Wújì and others:
"I have heard that when the ruler is wise, his ministers are forthright.
It is hard for a man to know his own faults.
You gentlemen should discuss my merits and shortcomings."
Wújì said:
"Your Majesty's military achievements and civil virtues
surpass all, past and present.
Your decrees and commands
all benefit the people.
I can hardly keep up with following them;
truly I see no faults in Your Majesty."
The Emperor said:
"I wished to hear my own faults,
but you have instead flattered me with empty praise.
Now I shall discuss each of your strengths and weaknesses face to face,
to serve as a mirror and warning.
Those who speak of them can avoid error,
and those who hear can correct themselves.
Thereupon he said:
Wújì is skilled in planning and calculation,
and quick in response.
Even among the ancients,
he would have no equal.
But in military strategy and statecraft,
I fear these may not be his strengths.
Gāo Shìlián is well-read in past and present affairs,
clever and perceptive in mind,
unchanging in integrity when facing hardship,
and forms no factions as an official.
What he lacks is the bone to remonstrate frankly.
Táng Jiǎn is eloquent and sharp-tongued,
good at reconciling people,
and when the wine cup circulates,
he is quick to speak and open his mouth.
But in three years of serving me,
he has not once discussed the merits and faults of the state.
Yáng Shīdào is by nature pure and good,
and naturally without fault,
but in truth he is timid and weak,
not very experienced in affairs,
and unreliable in urgent matters.
Cén Wénběn is by nature honest and sincere,
excelling in literary composition,
his arguments always based on classical principles and far-sighted,
and he never contradicts reason.
Liú Jì is by nature most firm and steadfast,
his words often beneficial,
and moreover in his intentions and conduct,
he keeps promises to friends,
and can rectify his own shortcomings.
What more could one ask for?
Mǎ Zhōu perceives affairs quickly,
and his nature is very upright and correct.
As for evaluating people,
he speaks with straightforward honesty.
Since I appointed and employed him,
he has often satisfied my expectations.
Chǔ Suìliáng's learning is somewhat extensive,
and his nature is also firm and upright.
Since he has shown loyalty,
and become very close and attached to me,
like a bird relying on a person,
I naturally feel fondness and affection for him."
From Táng Huì Yào.
Lǐ Jì
In the early Wǔdé era,
Lǐ Jì captured the Líyáng granary,
and those who came for food numbered several hundred thousand.
Wèi Zhēng, Gāo Jìfǔ, Dù Zhènglún, and Guō Xiàokè were all traveling guests at his place.
At first sight among the crowd,
he treated them with courtesy and respect.
After pacifying Wǔláo and capturing Zhèngzhou's Chief Clerk Dài Zhòu,
he released and recommended him.
At the time, he was considered to have the insight to recognize talent.
From Táng Huì Yào.
Also, in the first year of Zhēnguàn,
Jì was the military governor of Bìngzhōu.
At that time, the Palace Attendant Zhāng Wénguàn served as a military advisor.
Jì once sighed and said:
"Zhāng Zhìguī will later be a Guǎn Zhòng or Xiāo Hé;
I am not his equal."
He treated him with exceptional courtesy.
At that time, there were two other officials
who also received courteous treatment.
When Jì was about to depart for the court,
he gave one a girdle knife,
and the other a jade belt,
but Wénguàn alone received nothing.
Wénguàn then accompanied him for over twenty lǐ.
Jì said:
"As the proverb says,
