'Seeing off for a thousand lǐ,
ends in a single parting.'
Zhìguī, why have you come so far?
You may turn back now."
Wénguàn said:
"We all received your honor and praise,
they both received gifts and returned,
but I alone was left out,
and so I feel melancholy."
Jì said:
"Do not be troubled, my friend;
this old man has an explanation.
That one is hesitant and indecisive,
so I gave him a knife,
admonishing him to be resolute;
that one is unrestrained and lacks restraint,
so I gave him a belt,
admonishing him to be disciplined and restrained.
But you, my friend, have great talent and exceptional understanding,
there is nothing you cannot accomplish;
what use would a gift be?"
Thereupon he strongly recommended and promoted him.
Later, Wénguàn was repeatedly promoted and became Palace Attendant.
From Guǎng Rénwù Zhì.
Xuē Shōu
In the Táng, Xuē Shōu, his paternal cousin's son Yuánjìng, and his clan elder's son Déyīn were equally famous,
people at the time called them the Three Phoenixes of Hédōng.
Shōu and Yuánjìng both served as academicians of the Literary Institute.
At that time, Fáng (Xuánlíng) and Dù (Rǔhuì) and others held positions of intimate trust,
and deeply befriended and relied on them.
Yuánjìng, wary of power and influence,
ultimately did not become intimate.
Rǔhuì often said:
"The junior recorder cannot be made close,
nor can he be made distant."
From Tán Bīn Lù.
Wáng Guī
In the sixth year of Zhēnguàn,
the Emperor feasted his attending ministers.
He said to Wáng Guī:
"Your discernment and judgment are refined and penetrating,
and you are especially skilled in discussion.
Starting with Fáng Xuánlíng and the others,
you should evaluate them all.
Also, assess yourself:
compared to these gentlemen, who is more worthy?"
Guī replied:
"In diligently serving the state,
knowing what must be done and doing it,
I am not as good as Xuánlíng.
In talent combining civil and military abilities,
capable of commanding armies and governing as minister,
I am not as good as Lǐ Jìng.
In presenting memorials with thorough clarity,
and handling affairs with fairness and trustworthiness,
I am not as good as (Wēn) Yànbó.
In managing complex and difficult tasks,
ensuring all duties are accomplished,
I am not as good as Dài Zhòu.
In having a heart for remonstrance;
ashamed if his ruler does not equal Yáo and Shùn;
I am not as good as Wèi Zhēng.
As for stirring the muddy and raising the clear,
hating evil and loving good,
compared to these several gentlemen,
I do have a slight strength."
Tàizōng deeply agreed with his words,
and the assembled lords also each considered it a true assessment of their own abilities,
calling it an accurate judgment.
From Táng Huì Yào.
Wáng Shīdàn
In the nineteenth year of Zhēnguàn,
the Vice Director of the Bureau of Evaluations Wáng Shīdàn oversaw the examinations.
He failed the policy essays of Zhāng Chānglíng and Wáng Gōngjǐn.
Tàizōng sighed and said:
"Both men possess literary talent."
He replied:
"Their character is frivolous and shallow,
their writing excessively ornate and flashy;
they will certainly not become fine vessels.
The reason I did not promote them
is for fear they would corrupt Your Majesty's elegant standards."
The Emperor considered this a wise saying.
Later events proved him right.
From Tán Bīn Lù.
Yáng Sù
When Féng Déyí was young,
the Minister of the Left Yáng Sù saw him and considered him extraordinary,
so he gave his niece to him in marriage.
He often patted his own seat and said:
"Lord Féng will surely occupy this seat."
Later, during the campaign against Liáodōng,
Lord Féng's ship sank,
and everyone thought he had died.
Yáng Sù said:
"Lord Féng is destined to become Minister of the Left,
so he must not be dead."
He sent someone to search for him.
Lord Féng had grabbed onto a plank,
adrift in the vast sea.
When his strength was exhausted and he was about to let go,
he suddenly remembered Yáng Sù's words,
and mustered his strength to hold on again.
His chest was rubbed and battered by the plank,
until the flesh was torn down to the bone.
The crowd rescued him.
Later, he indeed rose to the office of Minister of the Left.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Wáng Yìfāng
Yuán Bànqiān's original name was Yúqìng.
He studied under Wáng Yìfāng.
Yìfāng held him in high regard.
He once said to him:
"One sage appears every five hundred years—
you are that one."
Thus, he changed his name to Bànqiān.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Selecting Generals
Whenever Lǐ Jì selected generals before battle,
he would always choose those with an appearance of fortune and prosperity before dispatching them.
When asked the reason,
he replied:
"Those with ill-fated lives
are not worthy of achieving merit and fame."
Gentlemen considered this a wise saying.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Duke Yīng
During the reign of Emperor Gāozōng,
barbarian tribes gathered to raid.
Military campaigns against them repeatedly failed,
so Xú Jìngyè was appointed as the regional inspector.
The prefecture dispatched troops to greet him at the outskirts,
but Jìngyè dismissed them all and ordered them to return,
proceeding alone on horseback to the government office.
When the bandits heard that the new inspector had arrived,
they all prepared and waited on guard.
Jìngyè asked nothing about them.
Only after handling other matters did he finally say:
"Where are the bandits?"
The reply was:
"On the southern bank."
He then went there with only one or two assistants.
Onlookers were all shocked and astonished.
The bandits initially held weapons and watched cautiously,
but upon seeing that there was nothing in the boat,
they closed their camp and hid.
Jìngyè went straight into their camp
and announced:
"The state knows that you have suffered under corrupt officials.
You have committed no other evil.
You may all return to your fields.
Those who remain will be considered bandits."
He only summoned their leaders,
reprimanded them for not surrendering earlier,
had each beaten several dozen strokes, and then sent them away.
The entire region was pacified.
His grandfather, Duke Yīng, heard of this
and admired his courage and strategy.
He said:
"I could not have accomplished this.
However, the one who will ruin the family
must be this boy."
From "Guó Shǐ Yì Zuǎn"
Liú Qí
During the Zhèngshèng era of the Táng dynasty,
Liú Qí served as Vice Minister.
He appointed Zhāng Wénchéng and Sīmǎ Xuán as censors.
The two expressed their gratitude through Shéntú Yáng.
Liú Qí sternly said:
"Recommending the worthy is done without selfish motives—
why thank me?"
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
He styled himself Fúxiūzǐ.
Lóu Shīdé of the Táng dynasty,
was a native of Xíngyáng.
He served as Nàyán.
A guest asked Fúxiūzǐ:
"What is Lóu Nàyán like?"
He replied:
"Nàyán is upright yet gentle,
broad-minded yet stern,
outwardly simple but inwardly sharp,
superficially obscure but inwardly bright.
Like waves across ten thousand qǐng,
turbid yet not muddy;
like material tempered a hundred times,
polished yet not worn thin.
He may be called a virtuous gentleman,
a renowned lord of recent times."
The guest said:
"Dí Rénjié served as Nàyán;
what was he like?"
Fúxiūzǐ said:
"He had a cursory knowledge of classics and histories,
and was slightly skilled in writing.
In offering admonitions and frank remonstrance,
he possessed the manner of the ancients.
In cutting down excessive shrines,
he had the integrity of a determined scholar.
His mind and spirit were upright and honest.
Stained yet not blackened.
His courage and resolve were firm and strong.
Clear-sighted and capable of decision.
In his later years, he developed a craving for money—
was he a follower of Hé Qiáo?"
The guest said:
"The Fènggé Shìláng Lǐ Zhāodé,
can he be called a famous minister?"
He replied:
"Lǐ Zhāodé had great ambition but small capacity,
high spirit but shallow wisdom.
He borrowed authority to control things,
seized strategic points to oppress others.
He had more than enough stubbornness,
but insufficient respect and magnanimity.
This is not the way to preserve oneself."
Soon he was executed.
He also asked about the Luòyáng Magistrate Lái Jùnchén,
graceful and handsome in appearance—
was he a loyal and sincere man?
He replied:
"Jùnchén had a gentle face but a cruel heart.
His actions were risky and his virtue shallow.
His clever arguments resembled wisdom;
his skillful flattery resembled loyalty.
He overturned states and families,
and falsely accused good people.
Was he not a follower of Wāng Chōng?
Like wasps and scorpions harming others,
he was ultimately harmed by others."
Not long after,
he became Tàipú Qīng,
and was executed at the Western Market.
He also asked: Can Wǔ Sānsī be called a famous prince?
He replied:
"Sānsī relied on his imperial kinship,
and his position surpassed that of high ministers.
His appearance seemed respectful,
but his heart was extremely cruel.
Outwardly he showed fairness and uprightness,
but inwardly he wove dark plots.
He manipulated royal law to take revenge,
and borrowed court authority to harm others.
Later he was enfeoffed as Déjìng Prince,
but he was a traitor at heart,
and could not die a natural death."
In the end, he was killed by Crown Prince Jiémǐn.
He also asked about the Zhōngshū Lìng Wèi Yuánzhōng,
steadfast and upright—
a famous minister of recent times.
He replied:
"Yuánzhōng lacked both civil and military talents,
empty in both name and substance.
Outwardly he showed firmness and integrity,
but inwardly he harbored sycophancy.
In rebuking the faction of Zhāng Shíqí to his face,
he was as brave as a bear;
in flattering the likes of Wǔ Shìkāi,
he was as timid as a cur.
A man of two minds,
wavering between advance and retreat.
A creature like a lizard,
truly without a single steadfast will.
In bringing chaos to the court and ruining governance,
none were worse than this man.
He attached himself to the followers of Sānsī,
and denounced the clans of the Five Princes.
From my careful observation,
he would not meet a natural death."
Indeed, he was implicated in a case and exiled to Sīzhōu,
where he died of worry and resentment.
He also asked: What about the Zhōngshū Lìng Lǐ Qiáo?
He replied:
"Lord Lǐ had three perversities:
He loved promotion for himself,
but hated others' advancement;
he loved literary works,
but hated literary talent and writing;
he loved greed and corruption,
but hated others accepting bribes.
It is like the ancient female ruler
who loved rich and fresh food,
but forbade others to eat meat;
who loved fine silks,
but prohibited others from wearing brocade;
who loved licentious indulgence,
but hated others keeping singers and beauties.
Such was also the type of Lord Lǐ."
He also asked: What about the Sīxíng Qīng Xú Yǒugōng?
He replied:
"Yǒugōng was a man of integrity and uprightness.
Clear-sighted and courageous,
firm and decisive.
Amidst a declining fate,
he did not flatter to gain favor;
in a chaotic and turbulent court,
he did not use evasive words to avoid danger.
Those ensnared by Lái Jùnchén's fabrications
were released by Yǒugōng;
those tortured by Yuán Zhìhóng
were pardoned by Yǒugōng.
He trod on a tiger's tail without alarm,
and touched a dragon's scales without fear.
Like a phoenix standing among owls,
he remained upright to preserve himself;
like a leopard changing among jackals and wolves,
he stayed loyal to avoid harm.
If he had lived in a peaceful era,
could even Zhāng Shìzhī and Yú Dìngguó be mentioned in the same breath?"
He also asked: What about the Sīnóng Qīng Zhào Lǚwēn?
He replied:
"Lǚwēn's mind did not touch upon learning,
his eyes did not recognize writing.
His appearance was respectful but his nature cruel,
his wisdom small but his ambitions great.
He hesitated like a dog thief,
and darted about like a greedy pig.
A morning sheep lured outside,
unaware of its death;
a night moth covering a candle,
unaware of its doom.
With his head perched on his neck,
could it last long?"
Later, he joined Wéi's rebellion,
and his three clans were exterminated.
He also asked: Zhèng Yīn served as Xuǎnbù Shìláng;
what was he like?
He replied:
"Yīn was a reckless youngster,
a cunning mediocrity.
Shallow in learning and superficial in speech,
light in talent and thin in virtue.
He crouched like a fox among nobles,
and hid like a pheasant at the powerful.
Earlier he relied on Jùnchén,
later he attached himself to Zhāng Yì.
He broke branches at Déjìng's house,
and licked hemorrhoids at Ānlè's court.
Like a wren nesting on reed flowers,
or a minnow swimming in a boiling cauldron;
having no elegance or capacity,
he was ultimately ordinary material.
Seeking glory in this way,
death would be a fortunate outcome."
Later, he indeed plotted rebellion and was executed.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Lǐ Qiáo
When Imperial Censor Péi Zhōu was on a mission to Yōuzhōu,
he saw an advisor surnamed Hú,
who said he was from Yìzhōu,
though he could not recall his given name.
He had a knife scar on the back of his neck.
When asked about it,
he replied:
"I once served as a foreign official,
and attended upon the Special Advanced Lǐ Qiáo.
Qiáo praised my intelligence,
and whenever he composed poems,
he would have me collect and keep them.
He often looked at me intently and said:
'You are very intelligent,
but your fate is meager.
You will have little official salary,
and only after reaching the age of sixty
will you hold two official posts.
At thirty, you will face a grave calamity—
I do not know if you will survive it.
After that, you will face hardships,
unable to attain fame or position.'
When Hú reached thirty,
he suddenly encountered Sūn
("Sūn" originally written as "Zhāng,"
amended according to the entry on Sūn Quán in juan 163 of this book)
Quán's northern campaign,
and followed him into the army.
When the army was defeated,
the enemy's blade struck his neck but did not sever it.
He lay among the piled corpses,
and after one night,
he came back to life.
From then on,
whenever he recalled Lǐ's words,
he dared not seek office again.
He swept and cleaned in temples,
wandering until he reached sixty.
Then he came to Yánzhōu,
and became a guest in the home of Prefect Guō.
A fortune-teller saw him
and said to the prefect:
'This man has official fortune;
you should now recommend him.
By the tenth month, he will obtain an official post.'
The prefect said:
'This is a remote and lowly prefecture;
I have no public reputation—
how dare I rashly recommend someone?'
Soon, an imperial amnesty was issued,
ordering all prefects under heaven to each recommend one person.
In the fifth month of that year,
Guō recommended this man for his military strategy.
By the tenth month,
he passed the examination
and obtained a post as a guard officer in the Eastern Palace,
and also served as a military advisor in Fànyáng.
From Dìngmìng Lù.
Zhèng Gǎo
During the Shènglì era of the Táng,
Vice Minister Zhèng Gǎo appointed Hán Sīfù as Court Gentleman for Revenues and Yuán Xīshēng as Registrar of the Capital Prefecture.
He once said to others:
"This year's selection
has yielded these two men, Hán and Yuán—
this shows the Ministry of Personnel has not failed the court."
From Tánbīn Lù.
Lú Cóngyuàn
During the Jǐngyún era of the Táng,
Lú Cóngyuàn served as Vice Minister.
Dù Xiān was appointed from Wù
("Wù" originally written as "Guó,"
amended according to the entry on Dù Xiān in juan 186 of this book)
zhōu as an Army Consultant to the position of Defender of Zhèng County,
and later became Minister of Revenue.
When Lú entered the court from his post as Senior Administrator of Yìzhōu,
Dù stood above him
and said:
"How do you assess the selected candidates?"
Lú replied:
"It is due to my humble discernment
that Your Excellency has been able to stretch your legs for a thousand lǐ."
From Tánbīn Lù.
Péi Kuān
When Minister Péi Kuān left his commandery and returned west,
he sailed upstream and paused at noon,
tying up his boat for a brief stop.
He saw a man sitting under a tree,
worn and tattered in clothing,
so he called him over to speak.
Finding him extraordinary,
he considered him a kindred spirit
and said:
"With your talent and insight,
you are bound to attain wealth and honor—
why are you so poor?"
He offered him a boatload of money, silk, and servants.
The guest did not decline the gift.
After speaking, he boarded the boat,
and the lazy ones were whipped.
Péi found him even more extraordinary;
the man turned out to be from Xúzhōu, surnamed Zhāng
("zhōu" originally followed by the character "rén,"
deleted according to Yōuxián Gǔchuī)
From Yōuxián Gǔchuī.
Wéi Shēn
Wéi Shēn, Prefect of Rùnzhōu,
prided himself on his family's illustrious lineage.
When seeking a son-in-law,
even those from noble and powerful families
with great fame and reputation
were all deemed unsuitable by Shēn.
On New Year's Eve,
with nothing to do,
he took his wife and children to climb the city wall for a view.
They saw several people burying something in a garden.
Shēn found this strange
and summoned an officer, pointing to the spot
and ordering him to investigate.
The officer returned and reported:
"The place is where Army Consultant Péi Kuān lives.
I have brought Kuān with me."
Shēn questioned him about the reason,
and Kuān said:
"I have always admonished myself
not to taint my family with bribes.
Today, someone left a deer
and placed it before leaving.
Since I could not deceive myself,
I had my servant bury it in the backyard
to uphold my principles.
I did not expect the prefect to see it."
Shēn then descended the steps and said:
"I have a daughter
whom I wish to betroth to you, sir."
Péi bowed in thanks and left.
Returning home, Shēn said to his wife:
"We have long sought a good son-in-law,
and now we have truly found one."
His wife asked who it was,
and he said it was the man they saw burying something on the city wall.
The next day, he summoned him again.
The entire Wéi family watched from behind the curtains.
Kuān wore a blue robe
and was thin, tall,
and lanky
(according to old regulations,
those below the eighth rank wore blue).
When he entered,
the family burst into laughter,
calling him a "stork."
Shēn's wife wept behind the curtain.
After he left,
Shēn said to his wife:
"If you love your daughter,
you should let her become the wife of a worthy duke or marquis.
Why settle for someone as pale as a gourd, fit only to be a servant?"
Shēn ultimately married his daughter to him,
and Wéi's daughter grew old with Kuān.
Their fortune, longevity, and honor
were unmatched by any of their relatives.
Thus, during the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras,
when discussing renowned families of old prestige,
Kuān was ranked first.
From Mínghuáng Zálù.
Péi Tán
When Sū Tǐng was five years old,
Péi Tán visited his father.
Tǐng was present,
so he was tested by reciting Yǔ Xìn's "Ode to the Withered Tree."
As he approached the end,
he avoided the character "tán,"
and changed the rhyme instead:
"In years past, the willows were transplanted,
lingering by the Hàn's shade.
Now I see them sway and fall,
desolate by the river's edge.
If trees are thus,
how can men endure?"
Tán was astonished and sighed for a long time,
knowing that the boy would surely master literature in the future.
From Guǎng Rénwù Zhì.
Yáo Yuánchóng
Yáo Yuánchóng and Zhāng Yuè served together as chief ministers,
harboring considerable suspicion and discord between them.
They frequently encroached upon each other's affairs,
and Zhāng bore a deep grudge.
When Yáo fell ill,
he admonished his sons, saying:
"Chancellor Zhāng and I are not in harmony;
the rift between us is very deep.
However, that man has long cherished extravagance
and is especially fond of fine clothing and curios.
After my death,
since we once served as colleagues,
he will surely come to offer condolences.
You must then lavishly display all the fine clothing and curios I possessed in my lifetime,
the precious belts and valuable vessels,
arraying them before the curtain.
If he pays them no heed,
you must swiftly settle the family affairs,
for our entire clan will be wiped out.
If he looks at them,
then our people will have nothing to fear.
You should then record these curios and items
and present them to Lord Zhāng,
while also requesting from him a tomb inscription.
Once you obtain his text,
copy it immediately for presentation,
and having already prepared the stone slab in advance,
have it engraved at once.
Chancellor Zhāng is more deliberate than I am;
a few days later,
he is certain to regret it.
If he then seeks to retrieve the inscription text,
using the pretext of wanting to revise and edit it,
you should lead his messenger to see the engraved stone,
and inform him that it has already been reported to the Emperor."
After Yáo died,
Zhāng indeed came,
and glanced at the curios and fine clothing three or four times.
Yáo's orphaned sons all followed their father's instructions.
Within a few days, the text was completed,
its narrative comprehensive and detailed,
considered a masterpiece of the time.
It read in part:
"The eight pillars uphold the heavens,
establishing the positions of brilliance and height;
the four seasons complete the year,
preserving the work of nurturing and transformation."
Several days later,
Zhāng indeed sent a messenger to retrieve the text,
claiming the wording was not sufficiently thorough,
and wishing to make further deletions and revisions.
Yáo's sons then led the messenger to see the stele,
and informed him it had already been presented to the Emperor.
The messenger returned and reported,
whereupon Zhāng, beating his chest in regret and resentment, said:
"A dead Yáo Chóng can still outmaneuver a living Zhāng Yuè.
Only today do I realize how far my talent falls short."
From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Minghuang"
Lú Qíqīng
Lú Qíqīng, at the beginning of the Kāiyuán era, served as Governor of Yōuzhōu.
At that time, Zhāng Shǒuguī was a Guǒyì officer,
yet Qíqīng treated him with particular courtesy and attention.
He said to him:
"Within ten years, you will become a Military Commissioner."
It turned out exactly as he said.
From "Tán Bīn's Records"
Xuē Jìchǎng
When Left Chancellor Chén Xīliè first passed the imperial examinations,
he once composed a tomb inscription for someone.
That person's family was ruined during Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
and when their household assets were searched,
this text was discovered.
It was believed he had connections with rebels,
so the authorities sent Chén to the prefectural office in cangue and under guard.
When he met Hénán's Governor Xuē Jìchǎng,
Chén's expression showed no fear,
and he defended himself in over a hundred words.
Governor Xuē, observing him, found him remarkable,
and led him up to the main hall.
He said to him:
"You, sir, shall reach the highest ministerial position,
and this old man entrusts his descendants to you."
Later, Chén indeed rose to the position of Chancellor.
From "Records of Determined Fate"
Yuán Huáijǐng
When Lord Yàn, Yuè, was young,
Yuán Huáijǐng knew he would certainly achieve high status,
and married his daughter to him.
Later, Zhāng rose to become Chancellor,
and his several sons and daughters all formed illustrious marriages:
his sons married imperial princesses,
and his daughters became Ladies of the Third Rank.
From "Records of Determined Fate"
Zhāng Jiǔlíng
In the twenty-first year of Kāiyuán,
Ān Lùshān came from Fànyáng to report to the court.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng said to his colleagues:
"The one who will bring chaos to Yōuzhōu
is this barbarian."
Later, after Ān followed Zhāng Shǒuguī and suffered a defeat,
Jiǔlíng rendered judgment, saying:
"When Rángjū led the army,
he necessarily executed Zhuāng Jiǎ.
When Sūn Wǔ enforced his orders,
he still put palace maidens to death.
If Shǒuguī's military orders are to be upheld,
Lùshān should not escape death.
I request he be executed."
Emperor Xuánzōng valued his bravery,
and ordered him to serve as a commoner to atone.
Jiǔlíng firmly petitioned, requesting his execution.
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"Surely you are not suggesting I possess Wáng Yífǔ's insight regarding Shílè?"
Later, when he reached Shǔ,
regretting deeply that he had not followed Jiǔlíng's advice,
he ordered an envoy to offer a libation at his tomb.
From "Records of Stirred Convictions"
Wáng Qiū
In the eighth year of Kāiyuán,
Vice-Minister Wáng Qiū promoted Shānyīn County Captain Sūn Tì
and Jìnshì Wáng Lěngrán.
Within a few years, both were drafting imperial edicts.
Vice-Minister Cuī Lín selected the remaining candidates Péi Dūnfù, Yú Tèqīng, Lú Kǎi, and over ten others,
all of whom entered the central ministries.
The public considered them perceptive judges of character.
From "Tán Bīn's Records"
The Yáng and Mù Brothers
During the Zhēnyuán era,
the brothers of the Yáng and Mù families,
in terms of character and bearing,
were evenly matched.
Some said:
"The Yáng brothers'
guests are all alike;
the Mù brothers'
guests are all different.
This determines their superiority."
The Mù family had four brothers:
Zàn, Zhì, Yún, and Shǎng.
People of the time said Zàn was vulgar yet principled, like lào cheese;
Zhì was handsome and benevolent, like sū curds;
Yún was like tíhú refined butter;
Shǎng was like rǔfǔ fermented milk curd.
From "Supplements to the National History"
Lǐ Dān
The Gentleman of the Palace Li Dǎn was governing Háozhōu.
The Recluse Xiāo Fù had his family residing in Báitián, Chǔzhōu.
Hearing of Dǎn's righteousness,
he came to pay him a visit.
Having no servants,
he rowed a small boat,
accompanied only by a young girl servant of about ten years old.
The weather was cold at the time,
and his clothes were thin and worn,
the girl servant even more so.
Sitting in the guest quarters,
the girl servant went outside the door to seek fire to warm her hands,
and also took his boots away.
A clerk suddenly announced:
"The Gentleman of the Palace invites the Recluse."
Fù immediately entered wearing straw sandals,
Dǎn greeted him and invited him to sit,
and they briefly spoke of ordinary matters.
Fù suddenly realized the breach of etiquette regarding his feet,
and was startled.
He then addressed
"啟" originally written as "起",
changed according to the Chén collated edition
Dǎn, saying:
"I was driven by hunger and cold,
and by the instructions of my kind mother in the main hall,
ordered to enter the pass to seek out relatives and friends.
Having no servants,
there was a young girl servant,
so I had her accompany me to pay my respects.
Arriving here this morning,
the girl, being foolish and fearful of the official compound,
got lost.
The clerk has already announced me,
and I cannot retrieve my boots,
my coming and going is thus careless and improper,
leaving me only with fear and trepidation."
Dǎn said:
"Boots and shoes,
are both matters of momentary ritual.
In ancient times, removing one's socks to ascend the mat,
meant going barefoot as a form of ritual.
Boots,
are barbarian attire,
originating from King Wǔlíng of Zhào,
what canonical basis do they have?
This is not enough to trouble a gentleman's mind,
please just state your purpose in coming."
He then had him stay at ease,
and Fù followed his intentions.
He then said:
"Your talent, sir,
will surely one day hold important responsibilities."
Thereupon, he sent an envoy to Báitián,
and presented very generous gifts to Fù's mother.
He also saw Fù off with a horse and a bundle of silk.
Fù later indeed became Chancellor.
From "The Master of Gàn'èzi"
Zhèng Yīn
The ancestor of Liú Zhān was
a poor scholar.
Around ten years old,
he served by Zhèng Yīn's side, managing the writing brush and inkstone.
At eighteen or nineteen,
when Yīn was a Censor,
he was inspecting the Shāng Mountains in the Jīng region,
at the Xiēmǎ Pavilion,
overlooking the mountains and waters.
The rain had just cleared then,
the cliffs and peaks were strangely beautiful,
the springs and rocks were most excellent.
Yīn sat for a long time,
then got up and walked five or six *li*.
He said:
"Such a splendid view,
if I cannot compose a poem about it,
what harm is there in staying late?"
He returned to the pavilion,
intending to inscribe a poem.
Looking, he saw a quatrain,
the ink still wet on the paper.
Yīn was greatly astonished at its exquisite perfection.
At that time, there were no travelers north or south.
His attendants said:
"Only Liú Jǐng was following behind two or three *li* back."
Yīn teased him, saying:
"It wasn't you, was it?"
Jǐng bowed and said:
"I truly saw the Attendant Censor composing and admiring, which inspired me,
so I ventured to write a topical poem."
He acknowledged his fault and bowed again.
Yīn sighed with admiration for a long time before leaving.
Upon returning to the capital,
he instructed his disciples Hán, Hàn, and those below, saying:
"Liú Jǐng will one day possess extraordinary talent,
his literary learning is sure to be surpassing and exceptional.
From now on, you may have him stay with you in the academy,
his lodging and meals in all matters,
should be no different from yours.
I also will not order him about anymore."
After three or several years,
the essays he produced,
were all excellent in diction and reasoning, robust and strong.
After succeeding twice in the examinations and gaining fame,
Yīn summoned and appointed him to a pure rank in the legal temple's school directorate.
He then fathered Zhān,
who passed the imperial examinations and became Chancellor.
From "Records of Zhītián"
Lady Miáo
Zhāng Yánshǎng came from a line of generations who had held the highest ministerial positions.
His mother hosted banquets for guests,
selecting a son-in-law,
but none met her expectations.
His wife, Lady Miáo,
was the daughter of Grand Steward Miáo Jìnqīng.
The lady possessed discernment,
and was particularly adept at distinguishing outstanding talent.
She specifically chose the scholar Wéi Gāo, saying:
"This man's future nobility
is beyond compare."
She then married her daughter to him.
Not two or three years later,
because Wéi Láng's temperament was lofty and expansive,
and he did not bother with minor formalities,
Zhāng Gōng gradually regretted it,
to the point of not treating him with proper respect.
All the maids and servants in the household
gradually began to treat him with contempt and neglect.
Only Lady Miáo consistently treated him generously.
As for the others,
most regarded him
(Míng manuscript: "The rest regarded him as lowly")
and he felt depressed and resentful but could not restrain it.
Lady Zhāng (Wéi's wife) wept and said:
"Wéi Láng, with your seven-foot stature,
learned in both civil and military arts,
how can you remain stagnant in my family home,
being ridiculed by both superiors and inferiors?
With such fine times and splendid prospects,
how can you bear to waste them idly?"
Wéi then announced
("announced" originally written as "military"
, corrected according to the Míng manuscript)
his departure to travel east.
His wife emptied her dowry chest to give him gifts for the journey.
Yánshǎng was pleased he was leaving,
and gave him provisions
("provisions" originally written as "exhausted"
, corrected according to the Míng manuscript)
consisting of seven pack-loads of goods.
Each time he reached a postal station,
he would send back one pack-load via the postal relay.
After passing through seven stations,
all the goods given to him
had been returned.
All he had left
were the dowry items given by Lady Qīnghé (his wife) and his cloth bag of books.
Yánshǎng could not fathom his actions.
Later, Wéi temporarily took charge of military affairs in Lǒngyòu,
and it happened that Emperor Dézōng made an imperial progress to Fèngtiān.
Regarding the merit for securing the western front,
he alone stood at the top.
On the day the imperial carriage returned,
he was appointed, from the position of Commander of the Imperial Guards, to bear the imperial tally and go to Xīchuān,
to replace Yánshǎng.
He then changed his name,
altering the character for his surname Wéi to Hán,
and his given name Gāo to Áo,
and no one dared speak of it.
When he reached Tiānhuí Station,
thirty lǐ from the prefectural city
(where the Retired Emperor's carriage had turned back,
hence it was given this name),
someone specially reported to Yánshǎng:
"The one replacing you, Excellency,
is General Wéi Gāo of the Imperial Guards,
not Hán Áo."
Lady Miáo said:
"If it is Wéi Gāo,
it must be our Wéi Láng."
Yánshǎng laughed and said:
"How many people in the world share the same name?
That Wéi student should by now have been discarded in some ditch,
how could he ascend to my position?"
The words of women
are not worth mentioning.
Earlier,
there was a shamaness, Madame Zǎn,
who would often tell of fortunes and misfortunes,
and her words frequently proved true.
She often said:
"The guardian spirits attending the Excellency are gradually diminishing,
while the guardian spirits surrounding Wéi Láng are increasing daily."
They all considered these words demonic and absurd,
and did not summon her again
Lady Miáo also said:
"Although Wéi Láng was poor and lowly then,
his spirit soared to the heavens.
Whenever he heard your discussions, Excellency,
he never once spoke with subservience or flattery,
and was thus resented.
To accomplish great deeds and achieve merit,
it must be this man."
The next morning when he entered the prefecture,
they realized it was not mistaken.
Yánshǎng was worried and fearful,
not daring to look directly at him,
and said:
"I failed to recognize the man."
He left through the west gate.
All the former maids and servants
who had ever been disrespectful
were all beaten to death by Lord Wéi.
Their bodies were thrown into the Shǔ River.
Only Lady Miáo felt no shame before Wéi Láng.
How virtuous she was!
How virtuous she was!
Lord Wéi served his mother-in-law
even more attentively than in his plain-cloth days.
Since then, noble families throughout the land
have not dared to neglect a poor and lowly son-in-law.
Therefore, Guō Yuán wrote a poem saying:
"Even Confucius followed Zhōu and then went to Qín,
Which worthy of old did not emerge from the dusty world?
How astonishing it was that Zhāng Yánshǎng of that time
Failed to recognize Wéi Gāo as a man of noble destiny."
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì"
Dù Hóngjiàn
Chancellor Dù Hóngjiàn
was known in his time as a judge of character.
Upon seeing Mǎ Suì, Lǐ Bàozhēn, the new prefect of Lú, Qǐ, Chancellor Lù Zhì, Chancellor Zhāng Hóngjìng, and Chancellor Lǐ Fān,
he said they would all become generals and chancellors.
This later proved entirely true.
Even figures like Xǔ Shào and Guō Tài
could not surpass him in this.
From "Jiāhuà Lù"
Dù Yòu
Grand Minister over the Masses Dù Gōng (Dù Yòu),
upon seeing Chancellor Zhāng Hóngjìng, said:
"He will certainly become Chancellor."
Thus, men of high status often possessed such knowledge of people.
From "Jiāhuà Lù"
Liáng Sù
In the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng,
Lǐ Yuánbīn, Hán Yù, Lǐ Jiàng, and Cuī Qún passed the imperial examination in the same year.
Prior to this,
the four gentlemen had established their friendship long ago,
and together visited the home of Reminder Liáng Sù.
After two years,
Sù had still not met them,
yet the four worthies visited Sù frequently,
always going together.
Sù found this unusual.
One day he received them,
and praised Guān (likely referring to one of them, perhaps a textual variant or error) and the others for their literary talent,
further encouraging them in the ways of friendship.
Now, Sù had always possessed the discernment to judge people.
After Guān and the others had left,
he stopped Jiàng and Qún, saying:
"You gentlemen are well-matched in literary talent and conduct,
and in days to come you will both achieve great fame.
Moreover, you two gentlemen will reach the pinnacle of ministerial rank.
Strive hard,
strive hard."
Later, the two worthies indeed turned out as he said.
From "Zhíyán"
Lǚ Wēn
Earlier,
when Lǐ Shēn went to seek recommendation,
he often used ancient-style poems to seek recognition from Lǚ Wēn.
Wēn said to Vice Director Qí Zhào and his younger brother Gōng:
"From reading the writings of Scholar Lǐ Èrshí (Lǐ Shēn),
I see this man will certainly become a high minister or chancellor."
It indeed turned out as he said.
The poem says:
"In spring, a single grain is sown;
In autumn, ten thousand kernels are grown.
Across the four seas, no field lies fallow,
Yet farmers still starve and die."
"Hoeing the grain under the noon sun,
Sweat drips down upon the soil.
Who knows that on the plate each meal,
Every single grain comes hard?"
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì"
Gù Hé
Zhāng Xuánzhī and Gù Fū were the maternal and paternal grandsons of Gù Hé, respectively.
Both were intelligent and clever from a young age.
Gù Hé knew this well,
but he often said that Gù Fū was superior,
showing him particular affection and favoritism,
which left Zhāng Xuánzhī somewhat dissatisfied.
At that time, Zhāng Xuánzhī was nine years old,
and Gù Fū was seven.
Gù Hé took both of them to a temple,
where they saw a statue of the Buddha entering Nirvana,
with some disciples weeping
and others not weeping.
Gù Hé asked his two grandsons about this.
Zhāng Xuánzhī said:
"Those who were close to him wept,
while those who were not close did not weep."
Gù Fū said:
"That is not so.
It is because they were free from attachment that they did not weep,
and because they could not free themselves from attachment that they wept."
From Shìshuō Xīnshū.
Liú Yǔxī
Liú Yǔxī said:
Jìlóng shot people with a pellet bow,
and his father was angry with him.
His mother said:
"A strong calf must
"Must" originally written as "although,"
changed according to the Chén edition.
pull a cart until the shafts break,
and a fine horse must gallop freely and break free from the reins,
before it can bear heavy burdens and travel far.
As for children who speak boldly,
if they are not extraordinary or intelligent,
they will certainly not become exceptional talents."
From Jiāhuà Lù.
Hán Yù
Lǐ Hè presented his poems to Hán Yù of the Ministry of Personnel.
At that time, Hán Yù was a National Academy erudite on detached duty.
He had just seen off a guest and returned,
feeling extremely tired.
His attendant presented the scroll,
and he untied his belt and began reading it immediately.
The first poem, "The Governor of Yànmén," read:
"Black clouds press down on the city, the city about to crumble,
armor glints in the sunlight like golden scales opening."
He then fastened his belt again,
and urgently ordered that Lǐ Hè be invited in.
From Yúnxī Yǒuyì,
the Ming manuscript edition cites Yōuxián Gǔchuī.
Gù Kuàng
Minister Bái Jūyì, when taking the imperial examinations,
first arrived in the capital
and presented his poems to the court writer Gù Kuàng.
Gù Kuàng saw his name,
stared at Bái Jūyì and said:
"The price of rice is high now,
and living here is not easy."
He then opened the scroll,
and the first poem read:
"Lush grass on the plains,
withering and flourishing year after year.
Wildfires cannot burn it all,
with the spring breeze it grows again."
He then sighed in admiration and said:
"With words like these,
living here will be easy."
He thus praised him widely,
and Bái Jūyì's reputation grew greatly.
From Yōuxián Gǔchuī.
Yú Shào
Yú Shào was filial and fraternal by nature,
cultivating inner virtue and purity,
which grew even stronger in his old age.
Earlier,
Fán Zé had once been recommended as virtuous and upright,
and when Yú Shào first met him in the capital,
he said:
"This is a talent for generals and ministers."
Within five years,
Fán Zé became a military governor.
Cuī Yuánhàn was nearly fifty
when he first took the imperial examinations.
Yú Shào found his essays extraordinary,
and placed him first in the top rank.
He further said:
"Within ten years, he will be drafting imperial edicts."
This indeed came true.
Dúgū Shòu took the "erudite and eloquent" examination,
and the Ministry of Personnel ranked him first.
In the Secretariat,
he was promoted to the top rank,
and people praised the decision as fair.
From Tánbīn Lù.
Lǐ Déyù
Secretary Bái Mǐnzhōng was then serving in a minor official post,
and few knew of him.
Only Chancellor Lǐ Déyù of Zhūyá Commandery, who particularly valued him as a pillar of the state,
spoke highly of him among the gentry.
However, his financial resources were insufficient,
and he had no means to entertain his colleagues and friends.
One day,
the Chancellor sent him one hundred thousand coins,
enabling him to prepare wine and food.
He invited several renowned scholars from the central government,
scheduling a day for them to visit his residence together.
At that time, it was late autumn, with overcast skies,
and rain had been falling continuously for over ten days.
Hè Bá Rèn
In the Jùtán Lù, "Rèn" is written as "Jì"
had just finished his duties as a Vice Director,
and having failed to secure an official position,
he was about to leave the capital to wander about.
He had passed the imperial examination in the same year as Bái,
and he rode his thin horse to Bái's gate to bid farewell.
The gatekeeper, who was waiting for the morning guests,
told him that Bái had gone elsewhere.
Hè Bá stopped his carriage and left a letter,
fully expressing his intention to wander far from home.
Bái read the letter and said:
"A man's rise and fall in life
depends on fate and timing.
If a man without talent
relies on luck to gain favor,
that is not the proper way to advance oneself.
How can I store food and drink at home
only to invite powerful and influential nobles?
If I close my door to a poor friend from my examination days,
even if I later achieve glory and prominence,
how could I not feel ashamed in my heart?"
He immediately ordered his servant to have Hè Bá turn his carriage around,
and they shared the wine and food together.
Soon after, the invited morning guests
arrived on horseback one after another.
The gatekeeper
"Gatekeeper" originally written as "between,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript
explained that Bái was leisurely engaged with Hè Bá,
and they all left in disappointment and surprise
"Left" originally written as "not,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript and the Xu printed edition
The next day,
Bái went to the Chancellor's private residence to pay a visit.
The Chancellor asked which officials had come.
Bái replied that the guests had not yet arrived,
but that a fellow examinee had come to bid farewell before leaving the capital.
Pitying his friend's weary and distressed state,
he could not bear to abandon him,
so he kept him for a few cups of wine,
and thus missed the opportunity to receive the guests.
Having failed to fulfill the Chancellor's intention to promote him,
he was willing to accept the punishment of demotion.
The Chancellor praised him for a long time, saying:
"This truly embodies the way of the ancients.
Through this, one may achieve honor and prominence,
and it can inspire and encourage those who are shallow and fickle."
Within ten days,
Hè Bá was appointed from a low-ranking official
to a prestigious position first.
Bái was promoted from Director of the Treasury Department
to become a Hanlin Academician.
In less than three years,
he held the highest ministerial authority.
Later, he governed five frontier regions
and served twice in the central court.
He upheld righteousness and cherished benevolence,
remaining consistent from beginning to end.
His virtuous reputation spread far and wide,
and he was praised by the scholarly community.
During the Dàchū period
In the Ming manuscript, "chūzhōng" is written as "zhōngchū"
the border regions were unstable,
and the Tibetans were particularly arrogant and aggressive.
Emperor Xuānzōng decided to launch a punitive expedition,
and first consulted his ministers in the Yányīng Hall.
Bái was the first to propose sending troops,
and he was appointed commander.
Leading tens of thousands of soldiers from the frontier garrisons,
he advanced with drums beating.
At that time, the Tibetan army was arrayed on the
In the Ming manuscript, "yú" is written as "píng"
plain,
with several thousand untamed horses
hidden in the valleys.
After learning of this from spies,
he set up an ambush to await them.
There was a Tibetan chieftain
wearing a crimson fur robe
and a belt adorned with jewels.
He rode a white horse
of extraordinary excellence.
Before the battle began,
he rode out in front of the formation four times,
repeatedly challenging Han generals to single combat.
Bái ordered his soldiers not to respond.
Soon after, the chieftain halted his horse and gestured,
turning his back
"Back" originally written as "all,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript and the Xu edition
to our army, standing about a hundred paces away.
A young officer from Lùzhōu, brave and skilled in archery,
galloped out on horseback, drawing his bow.
He fired two arrows in succession,
both hitting the chieftain in the neck.
He then spurred his horse forward,
drew a short sword,
and knocked the chieftain onto his saddle.
Supporting him with his hand,
as if in a wrestling match,
the Tibetan army could only shout and cheer.
On the saddle, he stripped off the crimson robe,
removed the golden belt,
and seized the horse before returning.
The troops
"Troops" originally written as "return,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript
were all inspired to bravery.
Then, a great battle ensued in the desert,
and the enemy formation collapsed.
Pursuing the fleeing enemy in victory,
they nearly reached the foot of the Black Mountains.
The camels, horses, and supplies captured
were too numerous to count.
Thirty to forty thousand surrendered with their hands tied.
Previously, the territories of Héhuáng Commandery that had been under Tibetan control
were all restored to Táng territory from then on.
When Emperor Xuānzōng first read the victory report, he said:
"I knew Mǐnzhōng would surely annihilate the vicious enemy."
When Bái returned victorious,
he and his fellow ministers
"Minister" originally left blank,
supplemented according to the Ming manuscript
presented poems. His poem read:
"An imperial decree proclaimed throughout the four seas,
countless vile barbarians return bound.
No more war, flutes sound from watchtowers,
horses graze freely, neighing in the pastoral winds.
The winding Yellow River gathers its many bends,
the Long Mountains stretch a thousand miles, locking the passes.
Now peace reigns in the western and northern borders,
spreading word to the southern and eastern tribes."
Chancellor Mǎ Zhí's poem read:
"Shùn's virtue and Yáo's benevolence transform the Tibetan tribes,
allowing Héhuáng to submit to imperial grace.
Commanding civil and military affairs with divine strategy,
expanding the realm is the sage's achievement.
Four commanders campaign without shedding sweat from horses,
seven passes are guarded, bows already sheathed.
Heaven leaves this deed for the heroic ruler,
not in other years, but in Dàzhōng."
Chancellor Wèi Fú's poem read:
"Xiāoguān Pass restores the old mountains and rivers,
ancient garrisons on Qín plains, scenes fresh and clear.
Barbarians beg to surrender, returning to benevolent rule,
imperial might gradually overawes the stench of mutton.
Distant garrisons in felt tents, smoke and dust extinguished,
divine martial glory shines in historical records.
All in left-lapelled robes sing of the emperor's grace,
henceforth no need to guard the three frontiers."
Chancellor Cuī Xuàn's poem read:
"Imperial grace flows ten thousand miles to the border,
all under heaven join in victory songs.
Barbarian kings vie to untie their braids,
distant fortresses lay down their weapons.
Smoke and dust cease, autumn garrisons rest,
auspicious air clears the winding Jiǔzhé River.
Together we encounter the sage ruler's fortune of a thousand years,
watching customs flourish and times harmonize."
From the Jùtán Lù
Wéi Xiù
Chancellor Lú Xié of the Táng Dynasty,
in the early years of the Dàzhōng era,
passed the imperial examinations.
His appearance was unimpressive,
and his speech was also not clear,
pronouncing "Xié" as "Huì."
This was due to a short tongue.
The Wéi brothers all looked down upon and insulted him,
but only Minister Wéi Xiù treated him with respect,
saying to his brothers:
"Although Lú is rather unremarkable in appearance,
his writings show coherence and structure.
This man,
judging by this,
will surely achieve great things in the future."
Later, Lú indeed made a name for himself,
eventually rising to high office,
and he promoted Wéi Xiù to the position of Military Commissioner of Fújiàn.
As for those brothers who had once scorned him,
none achieved distinction.
Is this not an example of judging people by their appearance,
as seen with the Wéi brothers?"
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
The Monk Who Knew People
Dùnqiū Lǐ Chóng of the Northern Qí Dynasty,
was the son of Duke Chénliú, Lǐ Dàn.
During the reign of Emperor Gāozǔ,
he served as the Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
Yǎnzhōu had been plagued by frequent robberies,
so Lǐ Chóng had a tower built in every village,
each with a drum suspended from it.
Wherever a robbery occurred,
the drum would be struck wildly.
In the surrounding villages,
the first to hear it would beat their drum once,
and those who heard it next would beat theirs in response, creating a rhythm.
In a short time,
the sound would spread across a hundred *lǐ*.
By setting up ambushes at strategic points,
the robbers were invariably captured.
The practice of placing drums in various prefectures
began from this.
During the reign of Emperor Shìzōng,
he was appointed Governor of Yángzhōu.
Lǐ Chóng was astute and meticulous,
and evildoers feared him,
calling him the "Crouching Tiger."
From "Tán Sǒu."
Mr. Wèi
Mr. Wèi was born in the Zhōu region,
and his family resided in Sòng.
Beyond Confucian classics,
he thoroughly studied musical compositions.
In the early Suí dynasty,
he traveled west of Hánguān.
At that time, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices was examining music,
and the debaters had not reached a consensus.
Upon hearing of Mr. Wèi's arrival,
they vied to visit and consult him.
Mr. Wèi then took the musical instruments captured from the conquest of Chén,
and together with music officials such as Sū
(Míng manuscript note: "Sū" is written as "Lín" in some versions)
Kuí and Cài Zǐyuán,
examined their pitch standards in detail.
Thereafter, the bells, chimes, strings, and flutes
all found their proper places,
and the Qīngshāng Office was established within the court.
The Grand Music Officer collected two hundred bolts of silk to reward him.
Mr. Wèi did not enter government service again
and returned to Liáng and Sòng,
finding amusement in the qin and wine.
When warfare arose at the end of the Suí dynasty,
and Yáng Xuángǎn was defeated in battle,
his strategist Lǐ Mì fled to Yànmén,
changing his name to become a teacher.
Mr. Wèi, being from the same locality,
thus began associating with him.
They often discussed bells and pitch standards,
which Lǐ Mì was quite knowledgeable about.
Mr. Wèi thus teased him, saying:
"Observing you, your spirit is dejected and your eyes are unsettled,
your mind is agitated and your speech evasive.
A dejected spirit indicates recent defeat;
unsettled eyes show lack of focus;
an agitated mind means your spirit is not yet calm;
evasive speech suggests you are planning something with others.
Now they are arresting members of the Púshān faction—
could it be that you are the leader?"
Lǐ Mì started in alarm,
grabbed Mr. Wèi's hand, and said:
"Since you can recognize me,
surely you can also save me?"
Mr. Wèi said:
"You lack the bearing of an emperor,
nor the talent and strategy of a general—
you are merely a hero of troubled times."
Lǐ Mì said:
"Please analyze for me whether to advance or withdraw—
I will then decide whether to step back."
Mr. Wèi said:
"As for those who become emperors,
they embrace heaven and earth,
setting examples for past and present.
Externally, people benefit daily without realizing it;
internally, they achieve yearly accomplishments through self-reliance.
Yáo consulted the Four Peaks,
appointed Gǔn and later executed him at Yǔshān—
this arose from selflessness;
the Hàn employed the Three Heroes,
adopting good plans to besiege Gāixià—
this also arose from selflessness.
Thus, the phoenix has claws and beak but does not use them,
the qilin has hooves and charges but forever refrains—
able to entrust themselves to the Way,
and forever gather in their own time—
this is the bearing of an emperor.
As for those who become generals,
they raise the banner of Tàiyī,
lead armies that do not need to fight,
and punish crimes against the people.
Once the carved spears are bestowed,
and the jade crossbows drawn,
truly, as the saying about the bridle goes,
how could Jìliáng still be present?
Therefore, they focus on feasts and rewards,
seeking ease while awaiting fatigue,
and cultivate military farms.
They watch for cracks
(The character "xìn" was originally missing,
supplemented from the Míng manuscript)
and act accordingly.
Thus, they make the wind rise and the tiger roar—
none can resist their might;
clouds gather and the dragon soars—
none can thwart their momentum.
Zhòngní said:
'When I fight, I conquer.'
Mèng Kē said:
'Who then can oppose me?'
This is the talent of a general.
As for those who harbor their wisdom and ability,
acting with secret strategies,
publicly toward the state they are commanding ministers,
privately for themselves they are called rebels and bandits.
Those who act for themselves
inevitably plunder wealth and women,
slaughtering city inhabitants.
Zhū Hài becomes a guest of honor,
Fán Kuài a visitor welcomed into the hall.
Hearing in the morning and dying by evening—
Gōngsūn ultimately failed within the city;
'Rather I betray others'—
how could Cáo Cāo unite all under heaven?
Thus, they forget the gift of a thousand gold carried in a carriage,
and the gratitude for a single meal—
there are people who feel thankful,
but no masses who long to return.
Moreover, the warning in the Lǔ history says 'assess virtue,'
the text of the Liánshān says 'await the time.'
If you still seek to plot with others,
you cannot bring benefit to yourself.
Heaven and mankind detest chaos,
the celestial order has its destination.
Seasonal rain falls and baleful vapors disperse,
the sun rises and layers of ice melt.
Pulling a rope to bind a tiger—
hardly hoping for the gate of the flying hare;
entering water holding a bottle—
how could that be a place of safety?
I have observed the aura over Fén and Jìn—
a sage has been born there.
If you can go and serve him,
wealth and honor can be attained."
Lǐ Mì flicked his sleeves and said:
"The Suí house seized the world through regicide,
while my family stands above others due to merit and virtue.
If I raise my arm and call,
the masses will surely respond.
Leading troops in timely campaigns,
nowhere I go will not submit.
If the Way prevails, I can take all within the Four Seas;
if not, I am still sufficient to rule one region.
To submit myself to the times—
truly, I cannot bear it.
You are merely a petty Confucian,
unfit to discuss great matters."
Thus, he broke with Mr. Wèi.
Later, he expressed his feelings in a poem,
which was discovered by a local clerk.
Lǐ Mì escaped westward,
recruiting soldiers wherever he went.
He relied on Líyáng in the north,
and occupied Luòkǒu in the south,
linking camps numbering a million,
contending with Wáng Shìchōng.
For three years from start to finish,
he ultimately faced defeat and collapse.
Recalling Mr. Wèi's words,
he that very day submitted to the Táng.
He was then appointed as an official in the Department of Agriculture.
Later, he again rebelled at Táolín.
Mr. Wèi was a man who had attained the Way;
his name is not recorded,
but he was likely a clansman of Wénzhēn.
From "Gān Zé Yáo"
Lǐ Yìchēn
During Tàizōng's reign,
Princess Wénchéng, returning from Tibet, was bringing several hundred jin of gold as tribute
when she encountered bandits at Qízhōu.
Envoys were dispatched repeatedly to investigate,
but none captured the thieves.
Tàizōng summoned all the censors and looked them over,
specifically commanding Lǐ Yìchēn to step forward, saying:
"Your bearing is clear and outstanding;
I shall trouble you briefly to pursue them—
you will surely capture the thieves."
Chēn accepted the command,
employed secret strategies,
and within a few days captured all the thieves.
Tàizōng was pleased,
specially promoting him seven ranks,
and bestowing twenty liang of gold.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì"
Jiǎng Héng
During the Zhēnguàn era,
the wife of Zhāng Dí, the owner of the Bǎnqiáo Inn in Wèizhōu, returned to her parents' home.
Three guards from Wèizhōu, including Yáng Zhēn, sought lodging at the inn.
They departed early in the fifth watch.
During the night, someone took Yáng Zhēn's sword and killed Zhāng Dí,
then returned the sword to its scabbard.
Yáng Zhēn and the others were unaware of this.
By dawn,
the inn's staff pursued Yáng Zhēn and his companions.
Upon inspection, bloodstains were found on the sword,
so they were imprisoned and interrogated under torture.
Suffering from the severe torture,
they falsely confessed.
The Emperor was suspicious of the case,
and dispatched Investigating Censor Jiǎng Héng to re-investigate.
Upon arrival,
he summoned all the inn's staff aged fifteen and above to assemble.
As not everyone was present,
he dismissed them for the time being.
Only an old woman over eighty was kept behind,
and released late in the day.
He ordered a prison clerk to secretly observe her,
saying:
"When the old woman leaves,
note the name of anyone who speaks with her,
and ensure the information does not leak."
Indeed, someone spoke with her,
and his name was recorded.
The same happened the next day,
with that person asking the old woman:
"What is the envoy investigating?"
This occurred for three days,
and it was the same person each time.
Jiǎng Héng then summoned over three hundred men and women to assemble.
From among them, he called out the one who had spoken with the old woman,
and dismissed all the others.
When questioned, he confessed fully.
He said:
"It is true that I committed adultery with Zhāng Dí's wife and killed him."
This was reported to the Emperor,
who bestowed two hundred bolts of silk upon Jiǎng Héng,
and promoted him to Attendant Censor.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*
Wáng Jìn
During the Zhēnguàn era,
Left Assistant Lǐ Xínglián
had a younger brother named Lǐ Xíngquán,
whose son from a previous marriage, Lǐ Zhōng,
had an illicit relationship with his stepmother.
They then secretly fled together.
It was claimed that an imperial decree had summoned them to the palace.
Lǐ Xínglián, unaware of the truth,
submitted a memorial [reporting their disappearance].
An imperial order was issued for a rigorous investigation.
The stepmother then feigned being strangled with a scarf,
and lay in the street.
When questioned by the Cháng'ān County authorities,
she said:
"Someone falsely proclaimed an imperial decree summoning me.
A man in purple robes detained me for several nights.
I do not know his name.
He strangled me and left me in the street."
Lǐ Zhōng, in fear,
secretly sought a divination.
He was suspected by constables,
arrested, and sent to the county office.
County Captain Wáng Jìn took him into a room
for interrogation, but he did not confess.
Wáng Jìn first had a man hide under the bed mat to listen,
then had another man report:
"The Senior Official summons you."
Wáng Jìn then locked the door and left.
The mother and son said to each other:
"We must not confess."
They also exchanged other secret words.
When Wáng Jìn returned and opened the door,
the man under the mat also stood up.
Mother and son were greatly shocked.
They both confessed fully
and were executed.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*
Lǐ Jié
Lǐ Jié served as Governor of Hénán.
A widow accused her son of being unfilial.
Her son could not defend himself,
and only said:
"I have offended my mother.
I am willing to accept death."
Lǐ Jié, observing the circumstances,
judged that he was not an unfilial son.
He said to the widow:
"You are widowed,
with only this one son.
Now that you have accused him,
the crime carries the death penalty.
Will you not regret it?"
The widow said:
"The son is worthless,
and does not obey his mother.
Why should I cherish him?"
Lǐ Jié said:
"If it is truly so,
you may buy a coffin
to collect your son's corpse."
He then sent someone to follow her secretly.
After the widow left,
she said to a Daoist priest:
"The matter is settled."
Soon, she returned with a coffin.
Lǐ Jié, still hoping she might repent,
admonished her repeatedly,
but the widow remained as determined as before.
The Daoist priest was standing outside the gate.
Lǐ Jié secretly ordered his arrest.
After one interrogation, he confessed,
admitting to an affair with the widow.
They were often restrained by her son,
so they wished to eliminate him.
Lǐ Jié released the son,
had the Daoist priest and the widow beaten to death,
and placed them together in the same coffin.
From *Guóshǐ Yìzuǎn*
Péi Zǐyún
Péi Zǐyún, the Magistrate of Xīnxiāng County in Wèizhōu, was skilled in ingenious strategies.
A man under his jurisdiction, Wáng Jìng, was conscripted for border duty,
and left six female cows with his maternal uncle, Lǐ Jìn.
After five years of rearing,
they had produced thirty calves.
According to custom, [the value of the calves] exceeded one hundred strings of cash.
When Wáng Jìng returned and demanded the cows,
two had died.
Lǐ Jìn returned only the four old cows,
claiming the others were not born from Wáng Jìng's cows,
and refused to return them.
Wáng Jìng, angered,
submitted a petition to the county office.
Péi Zǐyún ordered Wáng Jìng taken into custody,
and summoned the alleged cow thief, Lǐ Jìn.
Lǐ Jìn, frightened, came to the county office.
Péi Zǐyún rebuked him, saying:
"The thief has implicated you in jointly stealing thirty cows,
which you have hidden at your home."
He then called for the thief to confront him.
Wáng Jìng's head was covered with a cloth garment,
and he stood against the south wall.
Lǐ Jìn, in a panic,
then confessed, saying:
"The thirty cows
were all born from my nephew's female cows.
They were not actually stolen."
Péi Zǐyún had the cloth garment removed.
When Lǐ Jìn saw it was Wáng Jìng, he said,
"This is my nephew."
Péi Zǐyún said:
"If so,
return his cows to him."
Lǐ Jìn fell silent.
Péi Zǐyún said:
"For your five years of labor in rearing the cows,
you may keep a few.
Return the rest to Wáng Jìng."
The entire county admired his astute judgment.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*
Guō Zhèngyī
The Secretariat Drafter Guō Zhèngyī, having captured P'yŏngyang,
obtained a Koguryŏ maidservant,
named Yùsù,
who was extremely beautiful and charming.
He put her in charge of the treasury.
One night, Zhèngyī needed some congee,
and only Yùsù could cook it for him.
Yùsù then poisoned it and served it.
Zhèngyī urgently said:
"This maid has poisoned me!"
He sought clay water and licorice to take,
and after a long while, he recovered.
Searching for the maid, she could not be found,
and more than ten pieces of gold, silver, and utensils were also missing.
A report was recorded and submitted,
and an imperial order commanded Cháng'ān and Wànnián to apprehend her.
The constables were beaten until their backs were raw,
the search for the thief was in an uproar,
but for three days, she was not captured.
The constable commander Wèi Chǎng had a strategy:
he took household slaves from the Drafter's residence,
selected three young and handsome ones,
dressed them in cloth shirts and covered their heads, then took them to the street.
He arrested four guards,
and asked who, in the past ten days,
had come looking for the Drafter's residence.
The guards said:
"There was a surrendered Koguryŏ man who left a letter,
and sent it to the Drafter's horse groom.
The letter is still here."
Upon examination, it said:
"In the Jīnchéng ward, there is an empty house,"
and nothing more.
The constables went to the empty house in the Jīnchéng ward,
and searched it thoroughly.
Arriving at one house,
it was tightly locked and sealed.
They broke the lock and opened it,
and the maid and the Koguryŏ man were both inside.
After interrogation,
it turned out that the surrendered Koguryŏ man and the horse groom had hidden her together.
By imperial order, they were beheaded in the Eastern Market.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Zhāng Chǔjīn
During the Chuígōng period,
when Empress Wǔ Zétiān supervised the state,
false accusations and entrapment arose.
The assistant official of Húzhōu, Jiāng Chēn, took the judgment documents of Prefect Péi Guāng,
cut out characters and pieced them together to form coherent text,
and fraudulently presented it as a rebellious letter from Xú Jìngyè to report.
An envoy was dispatched to interrogate Guāng,
who acknowledged that the writing was his,
but suspected the words were not his.
Three envoys were sent successively to interrogate,
but they could not reach a decision.
An imperial order commanded to dispatch someone capable of handling the case,
to investigate and ascertain the truth.
Everyone said:
Zhāng Chǔjīn is suitable,
so he was sent.
Chǔjīn was worried and depressed,
lying on his back by the west window.
When sunlight came,
he looked toward it,
and the characters seemed [to be pieced together].
When viewed flatly, it was not noticeable,
but when facing the sun, it became visible.
He ordered the prefectural officials to be summoned and assembled,
fetched a jar of water,
and commanded Chēn to throw the letter into the water,
where the characters dispersed one by one.
Chēn kowtowed and confessed his crime.
An imperial order commanded to administer one hundred blows,
and then behead him.
Chǔjīn was rewarded with one hundred bolts of silk.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Dǒng Xíngchéng
Dǒng Xíngchéng of Hénèi County in Huáizhōu was capable of deducing thieves.
There was a man who, from the Chángdiàn in Héyáng,
stole a traveler's donkey along with a leather bag.
As dawn was about to break,
he reached Huáizhōu.
Xíngchéng saw him in the street,
shouted:
"You thief, stop!
Get off the donkey immediately,"
and he then confessed.
People asked how he knew?
Xíngchéng said:
"This donkey is walking hurriedly and sweating,
meaning it hasn't traveled long;
upon seeing people, it pulls the reins to pass far away,
showing fear;
thus I knew."
He arrested him and sent him to the county office.
After a short while,
the donkey owner followed the tracks and arrived,
and everything was as he had said.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Zhāng Zhuó
When Zhāng Zhuó was the deputy magistrate of Héyáng County,
there was a schemer named Lǚ Yuán who forged a document in the name of the granary supervisor Féng Chén,
to steal and sell granary grain.
Chén did not acknowledge the document,
but Yuán firmly insisted,
and it could not be determined.
Zhuó took Lǚ Yuán's complaint document,
covered both ends,
leaving only one character visible,
and asked:
"If this is your writing,
then mark 'yes,'
if not,
then mark 'no.'"
Yuán then marked "no."
Removing the cover,
it was indeed Yuán's document,
and he was sentenced to five blows.
Then he covered one character on the forged Féng Chén document,
and asked about it,
and Yuán marked "yes."
Removing the cover,
it was the forged document.
Yuán's neck turned red,
and he kowtowed and confessed his crime.
There was also a traveler
whose donkey's reins broke,
and the saddle was also lost.
After three days of searching without finding it,
he reported to the county.
Zhuó urgently investigated.
At night, he released the donkey,
but hid its saddle,
which was worth five thousand coins.
Zhuó said:
"This can be figured out."
He ordered the halter to be removed and the donkey let go,
and the donkey headed toward its old feeding place.
Zhuó ordered a search of that household,
and the saddle was found under a pile of grass.
People admired his ability.
Originally missing the source,
now seen in "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Zhāng Sōngshòu
Zhāng Sōngshòu served as the magistrate of Cháng'ān.
At that time, there was a robbery and murder by the side of Kūnmíng Pond.
By imperial order,
the thief had to be captured within the day,
and if violated,
those responsible would be punished.
Sōngshòu went to the robbery site,
searching for clues.
He saw an old woman selling food under a tree.
He approached,
had her brought to the county office on horseback,
and provided her with wine and food.
After three days,
he sent her back by horse to her original spot.
He ordered a trusted person to watch,
and if anyone spoke with the old woman,
they were to be apprehended immediately.
Shortly after,
a man came and asked:
"How is the magistrate pursuing the case?"
He was immediately covered with a cloth shirt over his head,
and sent to the county office.
Upon interrogation, he fully confessed,
and the stolen goods were also recovered.
People at the time considered this divine insight.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Sū Wúmíng
During the reign of Empress Tiānhòu,
she bestowed upon Princess Tàipíng two food boxes filled with fine utensils and treasures,
worth a thousand yì of gold.
The princess stored them in her treasury,
but over a year later when she retrieved them,
they had all been taken by thieves.
When the princess reported this,
Empress Tiānhòu was furious.
She summoned the Chief Administrator of Luòzhōu and said:
"If you do not capture the thieves within three days,
you will be punished."
The Chief Administrator, terrified,
said to the officials in charge of apprehending thieves in the two counties:
"If you do not catch the thieves within two days,
you will die."
The Commandant then said to the constables and patrol officers:
"You must capture them within one day.
If you fail to capture them,
you will die first."
The constables and patrol officers were terrified,
but had no plan.
On the street, they encountered Sū Wúmíng, the Assistant Prefect of Húzhōu,
and together they invited him to the county office.
The patrol officers reported to the Commandant:
"Someone who can recover the stolen goods has arrived."
Wúmíng quickly advanced to the steps,
and the Commandant greeted him and asked the reason.
Wúmíng said:
"I am the Assistant Prefect of Húzhōu.
I am here for an official assessment."
The Commandant shouted at the constables,
"How dare you falsely accuse and insult the Assistant Prefect?"
Wúmíng smiled and said:
"Do not be angry with the constables,
for there is a reason.
Wherever I have served as an official,
I have been renowned for apprehending the cunning and exposing hidden crimes.
Whenever thieves
come before me,
none can escape.
These men must have heard of this beforehand,
so they brought me here,
hoping I could resolve their predicament."
The Commandant was pleased,
and asked for his method.
Wúmíng said:
"Let us go to the prefectural office,
and you may enter first to report."
The Commandant reported the situation,
and the Chief Administrator was overjoyed.
He descended the steps, took Wúmíng's hand, and said:
"Meeting you today
has spared my life.
Please explain your plan."
Wúmíng said:
"I request to see Her Majesty face-to-face on the jade steps,
and then I will speak."
So Empress Tiānhòu summoned him,
and asked:
"Have you captured the thieves?"
Wúmíng replied:
"If you entrust me with capturing the thieves,
do not set a time limit,
and also relax the pressure on the prefecture and counties,
ordering them not to pursue the matter urgently.
Furthermore, assign all the constables and patrol officers from the two counties responsible for apprehending thieves
to me,
and I will capture them for Your Majesty,
and it will not take more than a few dozen days."
Empress Tiānhòu agreed.
Wúmíng instructed the constables:
"If you proceed slowly, keep me informed."
Over a month later,
it was the Cold Food Festival.
Wúmíng summoned all the constables,
and instructed them:
"Form groups of ten or five,
and keep watch at the east and north gates.
If you see a group of more than ten foreigners,
all dressed in mourning clothes,
heading toward Běimáng,
follow them and report back."
The constables kept watch,
and indeed spotted them.
They rushed to report to Wúmíng.
He went to observe,
and asked the watchers:
"What are the foreigners doing?"
The watchers said:
"The foreigners arrived at a new grave,
set up offerings,
and cried without sorrow.
They then removed the offerings,
walked around the grave,
and looked at each other and laughed."
Wúmíng happily said:
"I have found them."
He then ordered the constables
to arrest all the foreigners
and excavate the grave.
When the grave was opened,
they cut open the coffin and looked inside,
and the coffin was filled with treasures.
This was reported to the Empress,
who asked Wúmíng:
"How did you, with such exceptional wisdom and talent,
manage to capture these thieves?"
He replied:
"I have no special strategy,
but I simply recognize thieves.
On the day I arrived in the capital,
it was the day these foreigners were holding a funeral.
As soon as I saw them, I knew they were thieves,
but I did not know where they had hidden the stolen goods.
Now, during the Cold Food Festival, when people visit graves,
I reckoned they would surely leave the city,
so I followed their whereabouts,
and thus located their grave.
Since the thieves set up offerings but cried without sorrow,
it was clear that the person buried was not a real deceased.
After finishing the offerings and crying,
they walked around the grave, looked at each other, and laughed,
rejoicing that the grave had not been damaged.
If Your Majesty had pressured the prefecture and counties,
this
this character was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy
thief's plan would have been urgent.
They would surely have taken the goods and fled.
But now, with no urgent pursuit,
they naturally relaxed,
so they had not yet retrieved the goods."
Empress Tiānhòu said:
"Excellent."
She rewarded him with gold and silk,
and promoted him two ranks.
From "Jì Wén"
Zhào Juān
In the early years of Yǒngtài,
a fire broke out in the palace,
burning several dozen rooms,
and it came dangerously close to the Eastern Palace,
deeply alarming and suspicious Emperor Dàizōng.
Zhào Juān was the patrol commissioner,
and was ordered to investigate immediately.
Juān conducted a thorough investigation and examination,
and determined that the fire was caused by a eunuch on duty.
The interrogation was clear and thorough,
fully uncovering the facts of the matter,
and Emperor Dàizōng greatly praised and rewarded him.
When Emperor Dézōng was still in the Eastern Palace,
he often admired Juān's detailed and thorough investigations.
Later, when Juān was serving as prefect of Qúzhōu,
he was old,
and Hán Huàng petitioned to have him removed from office.
When Emperor Dézōng saw his name,
he said to the prime minister:
"Is this not Zhào Juān, the censor from the early years of Yǒngtài?"
The reply was:
"Yes."
That same day, he was appointed Left Deputy Director of the Department of State Affairs.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Yuán Zī
When Duke Li Qiān (Li Mian) was governing Fèngxiáng,
a farmer from a subordinate county, while hoeing his fields,
found a jar of horse-hoof gold.
The History of the Han records Emperor Wu's edict:
"Gold has appeared at the Eastern Peak,
with auspicious signs of white unicorns and divine horses.
It is fitting to cast gold into unicorn-hoof and horse-hoof shapes,
to correspond with the auspicious omens."
This refers to casting gold in the shape of horse hooves.
Afterwards, many among the common people imitated this.
The villagers sent it to the county office.
An official document was to place it in the prefectural court.
The county magistrate was delighted to have obtained this treasure,
and wished to claim it as his own extraordinary achievement.
Fearing that the official treasury's custodians were not strict,
he therefore had it placed in his private residence.
After two nights,
when he reopened it with his officials to look,
it had all turned into lumps of earth.
When the jar of gold was first unearthed,
the entire village had come to witness and verify it;
its sudden transformation
caused universal astonishment.
The situation was reported to the prefect.
Those discussing it all said:
"It was swapped through deceitful scheming."
So he dispatched the judicial officer and several military officials
to investigate the case on the spot.
Consequently, the villagers who had obtained the gold
all testified together.
The county magistrate was pressured by the crowd,
overwhelmed and unable to act freely.
Soon the interrogation and humiliation intensified,
and he thus confessed to the crime of exchanging the gold.
His confession was fully recorded,
but the hidden location of its use was not yet uncovered.
They then detained his servants and slaves,
threatening them with punishment.
Some said it was hidden in the manure pile,
others said it was thrown into the water.
Confusion and wrongful coercion ensued.
Once the case was concluded,
the officials prepared the legal documents
and submitted the case report upwards.
Duke Qiān, upon reading it, was also angry.
Soon after, during a banquet,
he set down his cup and spoke of this matter.
The seated guests
all joined in the talk and banter.
Some spoke of imitating the plundering of the men of Qí,
others spoke of having Yáng Zhèn's flaw.
After talking and laughing for some time,
they considered it mere burglary or tunneling theft,
nothing to be surprised about.
At the time, Chancellor Yuán Zī was also present in the assembly,
but he bowed his head, offering almost no response.
Duke Li looked at him several times and said:
"Is the county magistrate not a close relative of the judge?"
Chancellor Yuán said:
"I have no prior acquaintance with him."
Duke Li said:
"Hearing of his crime,
why are you not very pleased?"
Chancellor Yuán said:
"I strongly suspect this matter is not yet resolved;
I beg the Chancellor
[The character 'xiàng' (Chancellor) was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Ming manuscript copy]
to examine it carefully."
Duke Qiān said:
"The evidence for the gold swap is extremely clear.
If you say it is not resolved,
you must have some other insight;
no one but the judge can probe the truth or falsehood."
Chancellor Yuán said:
"Agreed."
He thus had the case transferred to the prefecture for interrogation.
He then ordered an examination of the jar,
finding over two hundred and fifty lumps.
Questioning the original finders,
he confirmed the original substance remained.
He then sought gold from the market shops,
melted and cast it into shapes equal to the lumps.
Once completed,
he began weighing half of it,
and it already reached three hundred jīn.
Inquiring about the carrying manpower,
it was two farmers
who had carried it to the county border on a bamboo pole.
Calculating the approximate weight of the gold,
it was impossible for two men to lift with a bamboo pole;
thus it was clear that when they set out on the road,
the gold had already turned to earth.
Thereupon, all doubts were greatly dispelled.
The county magistrate was thus cleared and exonerated.
Duke Qiān sighed in admiration endlessly,
often saying his wisdom and ability were inferior.
Afterwards, [Yuán Zī] advanced through distinguished posts,
and by the reign of Emperor Dézōng, he became Chancellor.
I have often heard that gold and treasures hidden in the earth
may sometimes change their substance when accidentally discovered.
In the Dūnhuà ward of the Eastern Capital, there was the abandoned Lìndé Temple,
its halls all in ruins.
During the Xiántōng era,
Chancellor Bì Xián,
ordered separate construction;
while laying the foundations,
they found a large jar
filled with white silver.
The carters and craftsmen, thirty or forty in total,
during the day,
fearing it would be taken by the authorities,
covered it with timber
to wait for darkness.
At night,
each wrapped some in clothing and took it home.
The next morning when they opened it,
it was like hard earth carved into silver ingots.
This account is exactly the same as the previous one.
