Hán Huàng
When Hán Huàng was in Rùnzhōu,
he went up to the Wànsuì Tower at night with his assistants,
just as they were merry,
he set down his cup, displeased.
He said to his attendants:
"Do you hear a woman weeping?
Whereabouts is it?"
Someone replied it was at a certain bridge, a certain street.
The next morning,
he ordered an officer to arrest the weeping woman and interrogate her.
After two nights,
the case was not yet complete.
The officer, fearing punishment,
kept watch by the corpse.
Suddenly, a large blue fly settled on its head.
Upon loosening the hair bun to examine it,
it was indeed that the woman had an affair with a neighbor,
got her husband drunk, and killed him by driving nails into him.
The officer considered him divine.
When asked,
Duke Jìn (Hán Huàng) said:
"I observed her weeping:
urgent but not sorrowful,

Wáng Chōng's Lùn Héng states:
When Zhèng Zǐchǎn went out in the morning,
he heard a woman weeping.
He placed his hand on his servant's hand and listened.
After a while,
he had an officer seize and question her;
she had personally killed her husband.
Another day,
his servant asked:
"How did you, Master, know?"
Zǐchǎn said:
"When one dies by the hand of a loved one,
one knows the illness and worries,
faces death with fear,

thus I knew of her treachery."

Lǐ Jǐnglüè,

and

the wealthy man confessed everything.
The completed case file was submitted

Ten strokes of the cane.

Péi Xiū
Péi Xiū admired antiquity and had a fondness for curiosities.
While serving as a drafter of imperial edicts,
he had a relative who was appointed as the magistrate of Qūfù.
While the locals were cultivating the land,
they unearthed an ancient vessel called an "àng,"
with a capacity of three dǒu,
a shallow neck, short legs,
a round mouth, and square ears,
plain and archaic in appearance,
seemingly about to decay in the soil.
After it was washed,
and polished,
nine ancient seal characters faintly appeared around its waist.
The magistrate of Qūfù could not decipher them.
In Yǎnzhōu, there was a scholar surnamed Lǔ,
who was skilled in the eight styles of calligraphy.
He was summoned to the county,
and the vessel was shown to him.
He said:
"This is ancient seal script.
It is not in use today,
though I have studied it to some extent.
These nine characters read:
'Cast in the year of Duke Huán of Qí's meeting at Kuíqiū.'"
The magistrate was greatly astonished by this interpretation.
When compared with the seal script,
the character forms matched.
The vessel was then transported to Péi Xiū's residence.
Péi Xiū believed it to be an artifact from the time of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
and thus a testament to antiquity.
He treasured it as highly as the Zhōngjué and Gàodǐng vessels.
During breaks from drafting edicts,
he would show it to close friends and relatives.
Thus, in the capital, it became renowned as a priceless treasure.
Later, when Péi Xiū served as the vice minister of rites overseeing the imperial examinations,
some of his students requested to see the treasured vessel.
One day, Péi Xiū hosted a banquet
and gathered his disciples.
He brought out the vessel in the courtyard,
and they stood around it in a circle, observing it closely,
taking turns to ask questions.
Only Liu Tuì, a secretary in the imperial secretariat, believed it was not an artifact from that era
but a modern forgery.
Péi Xiū was displeased and said:
"Do you really have
have (originally written as 'not',
corrected according to the Ming manuscript, Xǔ刻本, and Huáng刻本)
an explanation?"
Liu Tuì replied:
"In my youth, I specialized in the writings of Zuǒ Qiūmíng,
which record in detail how Duke Huán of Qí (Xiǎo Bái) convened the feudal lords nine times,
establishing his authority and hegemony.
The meeting at Kuíqiū was the eighth alliance.
Moreover, according to the Classic of Rites,
feudal lords were buried five months after their death,
and allies would attend the funeral.
After the burial,
the 'yú' sacrifice was performed,
followed by the '卒哭' (final wailing) ceremony,
after which the posthumous title was determined.
Thus, the event at Kuíqiū
occurred during his lifetime,
so the posthumous title 'Huán' could not have been used.
This is undoubtedly a modern forgery."
Péi Xiū suddenly realized the truth
and ordered the vessel to be smashed.
He then raised his cup, drank it dry, and ended the gathering.
From Táng Quēshǐ
Cuī Jié
Cuī Jié served as Governor of Hénán,
punishing evildoers and eliminating tyrants,
becoming a model for officials across the land.
Previously, there was a merchant named Wáng Kějiǔ,
from a wealthy family.
Each year he sold tea between the Jiāng and Hú regions,
often returning with substantial profits.
That year,
he again packed his goods and went to Chǔ,
and was just returning by boat to Péngmén,
when he encountered Páng Xūn's rebellion.
Trapped in the bandit-controlled territory,
he did not return by the expected time.
He had a beautiful young wife,
and no brothers, sons, or other relatives.
The wife often offered high rewards to hire people
to search the four borders of the rebel region,
but ultimately no one could trace his whereabouts.
Some said:
"He has already been killed by bandits,
and his goods plundered."
In Luòchéng, there was a man named Yáng Gānfū, renowned for his skill in divination.
One morning, the wife took a bolt of silk
to seek answers from him.
Yáng had long been familiar with the matter,
and coveting her wealth,
plotted to ensnare her with a scheme.
He then solemnly arranged the yarrow stalks and prayed,
and once the hexagram lines were revealed,
he said:
"Your concern is surely for your husband, is it not?
That man has long since perished.
The signs show a grave.
He encountered robbery and murder together."
As the wife wailed and prepared to leave,
he immediately urged her further, saying:
"The sun is already setting;
please choose an auspicious morning,
come again at dawn to inquire,
and I shall divine for you once more."
The wife believed him sincerely.
On another day,
she went again for a divination,
and he obtained exactly the same hexagram as before.
He then said:
"The spirits are extraordinary;
there is no more hope."
He further said that wailing and grief were not the way to complete the rites;
she should instead select a day to hold the mourning ceremony,
commission Buddhist images and offer food to monks,
to accumulate blessings for the afterlife.
The wife, both grieving and ashamed,
took his words as truthful,
and entrusted all matters, great and small,
entirely to him.
Yáng took charge of the arrangements,
diligently fulfilling her wishes.
He then said to her:
"A woman living alone,
and in possession of wealth,
while banditry is rampant,
invites disaster upon herself.
You should relinquish your attachment and plan for safety and comfort."
The wife initially would not consent,
but at night, he had stones thrown to frighten her,
by day, he spread rumors of bandits to make her fear,
and then sent matchmakers to tempt her.
The wife, moved by Yáng's apparent righteousness,
finally agreed to marry him.
Having achieved his aim,
Yáng then registered all her property under his name,
firmly taking possession of the substantial assets.
After another month,
he sold off the old properties,
and taking his wife, chose a residence north of the Lè
(Míng manuscript note: Lè is written as Luò)
Canal.
The following year,
Xúzhōu was pacified,
the armies of the land were disbanded,
and an edict stated that except for the chief culprits who were captured,
those coerced into joining them
were to be pardoned and not questioned,
given official documents as proof,

Kějiǔ, shorn and naked, returned,
emaciated, sickly, and covered in sores and filth,

Upon arrival, he sought his former house,

He inquired everywhere about his wife,

Wandering through hunger and cold,

He saw his wife and Yáng

His wife stared in shock and confusion,

Unable to bear this injustice,

When the judicial officers investigated and pressed charges,

and when testimony was taken from the wife,

The magistrate at the time was upright and lenient but unable to discern the deceit,
and instead charged Kějiǔ with false accusation.
He was severely beaten on the back,
and driven out of the district, supported by the shoulders.
Kějiǔ, entangled in冤屈 and pain,

But before his thread of life snapped,

Swallowing his blood and bearing his冤屈, he appealed to the new administration,

The previously investigating clerk,

"To bring litigation concerning a previous administration's case—

So they again tore open his wounds,
exiled him to a distant town,
and consigned him to hard labor.
Kějiǔ's eyes streamed with blood,

At that time, Duke Bólíng (Cuī Jié) was residing in retirement,

Heaven provided a favorable opportunity:
he was again appointed to oversee the Three Rivers region.
The prison officers held their breath in fear,

On the third day of his inspection tour,

He then commanded officers to arrest Yáng Gānfū's entire household,
along with the former investigating clerk,

He also ordered Kějiǔ to secretly list the clothing and curiosities in the household;

And the clerk's bribery
was clearly revealed by the丑恶 evidence.
After beating their ribs,
and making their backs bleed,
he then tore out their hair and broke their legs,

At that time, the sky was overcast and cold,

On the day the case was decided,
the sun wheel shone brightly through,

(From the Táng Quē Shǐ)
Zhào Hé
In the early years of the Xiántōng era,
there was a man named Zhào Hé from Tiānshuǐ who served as the magistrate of Jiāngyīn.
He was renowned for resolving lawsuits with just a few words.
Thus, he repeatedly governed important counties,
and in each case, his success in redressing injustices earned him excellent evaluations.
Even in cases involving ambiguous or deceptive matters,
he was always able to handle them with reason and judgment.
At that time, there was a farmer from Huáiyīn in Chǔzhōu,
whose neighboring estates had all prospered through trade in years of good harvests.
His eastern neighbor had acquired several hundred acres of fertile land.
However, he had not yet paid the full price for it,
so he mortgaged the deed to his estate to his western neighbor,
borrowing one million strings of cash.
The contract was clearly documented and verified.
He also stated that he would repay the principal and interest the following year to redeem it.
When the time came,
he indeed made substantial profits from the fertile land,
gathered the funds to redeem the contract,
and first paid eight hundred strings of cash.
He only asked to inspect and retrieve the deed.
He planned to exchange the remaining funds for the deed the next day.
Since it was only a matter of two nights,
and they were on friendly terms,
he did not demand a receipt for the payment.
The next day,
he brought the remaining cash,
but the western neighbor refused to acknowledge the transaction.
Moreover, since there was no guarantee,
nor any written record,
he was ultimately rejected.
The eastern neighbor filed a grievance at the county office.
The county investigated the matter,
but there was no way to prove it.
The county magistrate said to him:
"I truly suspect you have been wronged,
but the official procedure relies on the contract.
Without this as evidence,
how can the case be resolved?"
He then appealed to the prefecture.
The prefecture was unable to resolve it either.
The eastern neighbor, overwhelmed with indignation,
hearing from afar of a skilled adjudicator in Jiāngyīn,
crossed the river south to appeal to Magistrate Zhào.
Magistrate Zhào said to him:
"The county's jurisdiction is limited,
and this matter crosses administrative boundaries.
How can I help you seek redress?"
The eastern neighbor wept bitterly and said:
"If justice cannot be obtained here,
I have no way to clear my name."
Zhào said:
"Just stay at my residence,
and let me think of a plan."
After a night, he summoned him and said:
"I have a plan.
Are you truly not lying?"
The man replied:
"How dare I deceive you?"
Zhào said:
"If what you say is true,
I will enforce the law for you.
He then summoned several capable officers tasked with capturing bandits,
and sent them with an official document to the Huái River region,
stating:

There are bandits who have gathered and are plundering the river.

living at a certain place,
with a specific name and appearance,
all pointing to the western neighbor.
Request that he be shackled and sent here.
According to the laws of the neighboring prefecture,
anyone who robs with weapons on the river
must not be hidden or sheltered.
When the official document arrived there,
they indeed captured him and brought him back.
However, relying on the fact that there was no evidence,
he was not very afraid.
Upon arrival, he was detained in the courtyard.
Zhào sternly said to him:
"You are fortunate to make a living by farming and weaving.
Why did you become a river bandit?"
The prisoner loudly cried, tears streaming down, and said:
"I am a farmer,
and have never even been on a boat."
Zhào continued:
"The evidence is complete,
and the name matches.
If you persist in lying stubbornly,
then we will resort to torture to extract the truth."
The prisoner became terrified,
kowtowing until his head bled,
as if he were suffering a great injustice.
Zhào then said:
"Fortunately, the stolen goods include much gold, treasures, and fine silks,
which are not things a farming household would keep.
You should list the assets in your house to prove your innocence."
The prisoner felt slightly relieved.
He then detailed his stored possessions,
not suspecting that his eastern neighbor had crossed the river to file a lawsuit.
He mentioned a certain amount of grain,
paid by tenants such as so-and-so;
a certain amount of silk,
produced by his household's loom;
a certain amount of cash,
redeemed by his eastern neighbor for the contract;
and a certain number of silver vessels,
forged by a craftsman named so-and-so.
Magistrate Zhào was greatly pleased.
He then re-examined the matter.
He said to the prisoner:
"If you are truly not a river bandit,
why did you conceal the eight hundred strings of cash redeemed by your eastern neighbor?"
He then summoned the plaintiff neighbor,
and had him confront the prisoner as evidence.
At this, the prisoner turned pale with shame and fear,
begging for death in front of the hall.
Zhào ordered him to be shackled and taken back to his hometown,
to retrieve and hand over the contract deed,
and then punished him according to the law.
From "Táng Quēshǐ"
by Liú Chóngguī
In the year when Liú Chóngguī governed Nánhǎi,
there was a young son of a wealthy merchant, fair-skinned and handsome,
somewhat different from the common peddlers.
He moored his boat by the river.
On the shore stood a gatehouse,
inside which he saw a woman in her twenties,
with enchanting beauty and alluring charm,
unlike anything he had ever seen.
She did not avoid people,
allowing him to gaze at her freely.
Seizing the opportunity, he spoke again,
saying, "I will come to your residence at dusk."
She showed no sign of difficulty,
merely nodding with a faint smile.
When dusk fell,
she indeed opened the door and waited for him.
Before he could arrive for the rendezvous,
a thief entered directly to commit theft.
Seeing a room without a candle,
he rushed inside.
The woman joyfully approached him.
The thief, thinking he was being captured,
stabbed her with a kitchen knife,
dropped the knife, and fled.
Her family remained unaware of this.
The merchant's son arrived shortly after,
and as he entered the door,
he stepped in blood,
slipped, and fell to the ground.
At first, he thought it was water,
but when he touched it with his hand,
he smelled the strong scent of fresh blood.
Feeling further, he found someone lying there,
so he ran out.
He went straight to his boat,
and set sail overnight.
By dawn,
he had already traveled over a hundred miles.
Her family traced the blood to the riverbank,
and reported the case.
The authorities interrogated the residents along the shore,
who said:
"On that night,
a certain merchant's boat set sail overnight."
Officers were immediately dispatched to pursue and capture him,
and he was imprisoned,
subjected to severe torture,
and confessed everything truthfully.
Only he did not admit to murder.
Her family presented the kitchen knife to the prefect.
The prefect then issued an order:
"On a certain day, a grand feast will be held,
and all the butchers in the jurisdiction
must gather at the polo ground,
to await slaughtering duties."
When the butchers had assembled,
he announced:
"Today's tasks are done,
you may return tomorrow.
But leave your knives in the kitchen before leaving."
The prefect then ordered the collection of all their knives,
and replaced the murder weapon
with another knife.
The next morning,
he instructed each to come to the yamen to claim their knives,
and everyone recognized their own and left.
Only one butcher remained last,
unwilling to take the knife away.
The prefect questioned him,
and he replied:
"This is not my knife."
When asked whose knife it was,
he said:
"This should belong to so-and-so."
Upon inquiring about his residence,
he ordered his arrest,
but the man had already fled.
So, he used another prisoner who was due for execution
to substitute for the merchant's son.
Late at night, he was executed in the market.
The fugitive's family,
day and night, secretly sent people to watch,
and after the false prisoner was executed,
within a day or two,
he indeed returned home,
and was captured.
He confessed fully to the crime of murder,
and was punished according to the law.
The merchant's son,
for entering someone's house at night,
was only punished with caning on the back for the crime of illicit intercourse.
Lord Péngchéng's investigation of the case
can be said to be astute.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
The Wife Killer
I heard from the elders:
Long ago, a man returned from a trip
to find his wife killed by an adulterer and thief.
But her head was missing,
though her limbs were intact.
Grief-stricken and terrified,
he reported it to his wife's family.
Upon hearing this,
the wife's family seized the husband and brought him to the officials.
They falsely accused him, saying:
"You killed our beloved daughter."
The jailers tortured him severely with whips and clubs,
and he could not prove his innocence.
Unable to endure the suffering,
he falsely confessed to the murder,
resigning himself to death.
Once the confession was recorded,
everyone believed it was correct.
The prefect entrusted the case to his assistant,
who doubted
the confession
(the original text had "kuǎn," amended according to the Ming manuscript)
and hesitated to decide.
He said to the prefect:
"I, though unworthy, hold this position,
and should indeed serve with utmost dedication.
When dealing with human life,
death cannot be reversed.
If we mistakenly apply the law,
how could we ever regret it enough?
I must ask to delay and investigate thoroughly.
Moreover, as a husband,
who could bear to kill his wife?
Especially since they were a loving couple,
how could he sever her neck?
Even if there were grievances and he harmed her,
why not devise a plan to escape blame?
He could have claimed she died of illness,
or pretended she died suddenly.
Why keep the body but discard the head?
The logic is very clear."
The prefect approved his reasoning,
so the assistant arranged a separate residence,
temporarily used as a prison.
He carefully selected custodians,
moved the prisoner there,
and interrogated him in detail,
providing him with food, drink, and bathing facilities,
treating him as an ordinary person.
He locked the doors and fortified the walls,
preventing any external contact.
Then he thoroughly investigated all the undertakers in the city,
ordering each to provide statements
on recent burials and grave locations they had handled.
Afterward, he questioned them:
"In your work for families,
was there anything suspicious?"
One person said:
"I handled a burial for a wealthy family,
who claimed they had killed a wet nurse.
They carried the coffin over the wall,
and the coffin seemed unusually light,
as if empty. It is now in such-and-such ward."
They opened it,
and indeed found a woman's head.
They then matched the head with the body,
and asked the accuser to identify it.
He said:
"This is not her."
They arrested the wealthy family and interrogated them,
and they confessed and provided a detailed account.
It turned out they had killed a wet nurse,
buried her head separately,
and used her body to replace this good family's wife,
keeping the latter hidden in their private quarters.
The wealthy man and his entire family were executed in the market.
Alas!
Investigating cases through careful examination of testimonies,
should we not be cautious?
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Xǔ Zōngyì
Among the military commanders of Shǔ,
few were not fond of wealth.
There was one Xǔ Zōngyì,
who, despite holding authority and military power,
alone maintained integrity.
He once governed Jiànzhōu.
A citizen had been robbed by bandits.
Under lamplight, he recognized the violent intruder,
and at dawn reported to the patrol.
The thief could not withstand the torture,
and from afar confessed his crime.
He was imprisoned and sent to the prefecture.
Zōngyì conducted the investigation.
The bound prisoner repeatedly appealed,
saying that the silk and fine silk fabric were actually his family's property,
and he and the robbery victim exchanged arguments.
Zōngyì quickly ordered two silk reeling machines,
and asked what each had used as the spindle core when reeling the silk and fine silk fabric?
What was used again?
One said an apricot kernel,
the other said a tile shard.
He then ordered them to unwind the silk thread,
and found the apricot kernel,
matching the prisoner's statement.
He also placed the silk skein on the machine,
measured its weight and size,
and it too was the prisoner's family's original property.
Thus, the robbery victim had the fault of falsely claiming,
and the patrol officers bore the guilt of wrongful torture.
In the blink of an eye,
he cleared the wrongful accusation.
He was indeed a good official.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Liú Fāngyù
Liú Fāngyù, a scholar from Zhènzhōu, had family wealth amounting to several hundred thousand.
Fāngyù's wife Tián shì died early,
and Tián's younger sister became a nun,
often visiting Fāngyù's home.
Fāngyù had the nun grow her hair long,
and made her his second wife.
There was a Tián Lìngzūn,
Fāngyù's brother-in-law.
Skilled in trade,
Fāngyù entrusted him with his accumulated wealth,
asking Lìngzūn to manage and grow it.
Fāngyù had a young son,
and two daughters who were both married.
Fāngyù fell ill and died.
His son was young,
unable to oversee the family business.
Fāngyù's wife and two daughters,
since the family wealth had long been managed by Lìngzūn,
plotted together as a clan,
requesting that Lìngzūn take the surname Liú,
to become Fāngyù's heir.
They then had the deed writer Ān Měi,
draft the adoption deed for the relatives.
Once settled,
they had Lìngzūn wear mourning clothes and observe the mourning period.
But when the two daughters first established Lìngzūn,
they first demanded a monthly provision of thirty thousand in wealth.
Later, their demands became insatiable,
and their husbands, Shí and Lǐ,
urged the two daughters to sue at the prefectural office, saying:
"Lìngzūn falsely took the surname,
seizing our father's family wealth."
Lìngzūn was imprisoned.
The clans of the Shí and Lǐ husbands colluded with key
key originally written as "ān",
according to the Ming manuscript copy changed
officials and relatives in the prefectural office—the prefectural commander's judge, the行军司马,
the随使都押衙,
each accepted bribes of several thousand strings of cash from Fāngyù's two daughters,
and thus claimed that Lìngzūn, his sister, and the deed writer Ān Měi conspired in theft,
and all were executed in the market.
People knew they were wronged.
The prefectural commander Lǐ Cóngmǐn,
had his wife come to court,
fearing the matter would be exposed,
he ordered his brother-in-law to cover it up.
The imperial censor Zhào Dū, detesting the evil, submitted a memorial.
Emperor Míngzōng was shocked and angry,
and sent to Zhènzhōu,
entrusting the deputy envoy Fú Méng to investigate.
Indeed, the facts were uncovered.
From the close official Gāo Zhīróu,
to the judge and行军司马,
along with the bribed monks and women,
all were executed in the market.
Only Cóngmǐn was initially demoted and suspended from duty,
but the empress interceded for mercy,
and he was ultimately fined three months' salary.
Commentators believed that accepting bribes, perverting the law, and killing people,
yet not being subject to the Eight Deliberations,
was a failure of justice.
After Ān Zhònghuì was executed,
it was due to the influence of Consort Wáng.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Dōngfāng Shuò
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn saw a painting of Bóyí and Shūqí,
and asked Dōngfāng Shuò,
"Who are these people?"
Shuò said:
"Ancient fools."
The Emperor said:
"Bóyí and Shūqí,
are the most upright men in the world.
Why call them fools?"
Shuò replied:
"I have heard that the wise in this world,
adapt to changes,
and are not rigidly attached to things.
Why did they not ascend the hall and drink the broth,
floating freely like ducks in water,
and go along with the current?
Under the Son of Heaven's chariot wheels,
one can live in seclusion.
Why torment themselves at Shǒuyáng?"
The Emperor sighed deeply.
Again, Emperor Wǔ was touring Shànglín Park,
and saw a beautiful tree.
He asked Dōngfāng Shuò,
and Shuò said:
"Its name is 'Shànzāi' (Excellent)."
The Emperor secretly had someone mark the tree.
Several years later,
he again asked Shuò,
and Shuò said:
"Its name is 'Qúsuǒ'."
The Emperor said:
"Shuò, you have deceived me for long.
Why is the name different from before?"
Shuò said:
"A horse is large,
a foal is small;
a chicken is grown,
a chick is small;
an ox is large,
a calf is small;
a person is born a child,
and grows old;
and formerly it was 'Shànzāi',
now it is 'Qúsuǒ';
growth, youth, death, life,
the decay and completion of all things,
how can they be fixed!"
The Emperor then laughed heartily.
From "Xiǎoshuō"
Kuāng Héng
Kuāng Héng, styled Zhìguī,
studied diligently but had no candle.
His neighbor had candles but would not share,
so Héng bored a hole in the wall to let in the light,
and read by reflecting the book in it.
A wealthy local, Wén Bùshí,
was rich and had many books.
Héng worked as his laborer,
without asking for payment.
The master found it strange and asked him,
and Héng said:
"I only wish to read all of your books."
"I wish to read all of your books."
The master was moved and sighed,
and provided him with books.
Thus, he became a great scholar.
He was skilled at explaining the "Book of Songs".
People of the time said of him:
"Do not discuss the Songs,
for Kuāng Dǐng comes;
when Kuāng discusses the Songs,
he brings smiles to faces."
Dǐng
was Héng's childhood name.
People of the time held him in such awe and admiration,
that hearing him would bring smiles and laughter.
A fellow villager who discussed the Songs,
Héng followed him,
and questioned him with doubts.
The villager was defeated and convinced,
and left in such haste he put his shoes on backwards.
Héng chased after him, saying:
"Sir, stay and listen,
let us further discuss the previous argument."
The villager said:
"I am exhausted."
And left without looking back.
From "Xījīng Zájì"
Biān Wénlǐ
Biān Wénlǐ met Yuán Fènggāo,
and became flustered and disordered.
Fènggāo therefore teased him, saying:
"In ancient times, when Yáo sought to employ Xǔ Yóu,
his face showed no sign of shame.
Why is it, sir, that your robe and gown are all topsy-turvy?"
Wénlǐ replied:
"As Your Excellency has just arrived,
the virtue of Yáo is not yet manifest.
That is why this humble subject's robe and gown are topsy-turvy."
From *Shì Shuō*.
Xún Címíng
Xún Címíng met with Yuán Shǎolǎng of Rǔnán.
When asked about the scholars of Yǐngchuān,
Címíng first mentioned his elder brothers.
Shǎolǎng sighed and said:
"One may only show favor to one's own kin."
Címíng replied:
"On what classic, sir, do you base your objection?"
Shǎolǎng said:
"I asked about the state's eminent scholars,
yet you began with your brothers.
That is why I criticize it."
Címíng said:
"In ancient times, Qí Xī recommended within his family without overlooking his own son,
and recommended outside without overlooking his enemy,
and this was considered the utmost impartiality.
The Duke of Zhōu was the son of King Wén of Zhōu.
Why is it that the *Shī* does not discuss the virtue of Yáo and Shùn,
but praises Wén and Wǔ?
It is the principle of honoring one's kin first.
The principle of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
is to treat the central states as internal and the various Xià states as external.
Moreover, if one cannot love one's own kin but loves others,
should that not be considered contrary to virtue?"
From *Shì Shuō*.
Cáo Zhí
Emperor Wén of Wèi once went on an outing in the same carriage with his brother, Prince Sī of Chén, Cáo Zhí.
They came upon two oxen fighting between walls.
One ox was inferior,
fell into a well, and died.
The emperor ordered Zhí to compose a poem on the dead ox,
but he must not mention it was an ox,
nor that it was a well,
nor speak of their fighting,
nor speak of its death.
He was to ride his horse for a hundred paces,
and compose forty characters within that distance.
If he failed to finish by the end of the ride,
he would be executed.
Zǐjiàn (Cáo Zhí) urged his horse to gallop,
then took up his brush and composed:
"Two lumps of flesh proceed side by side on the road,
wearing horizontal bones upon their heads.
Arriving at the fierce warrior's head,
they rise up in a clash to confront each other.
Two foes cannot both be strong;
one lump of flesh lies in an earthen cave.
Not that its strength was lacking,
but its great will could not be vented."
The poem finished,
his ride was not yet complete.
He then composed another thirty-character poem lamenting himself:
"They boil beans to make a broth,
filter the fermented beans to extract the juice.
The beanstalk burns beneath the cauldron,
the beans in the cauldron weep.
Born of the same root originally,
why press each other so urgently?"
From *Shì Shuō*.
Zhūgé Kè
Sūn Quán was temporarily touring Wǔchāng.
He said to his ministers:
"In the future, you must all diligently assist and instruct the Crown Prince.
If the Crown Prince improves,
you all shall receive generous rewards.
If he does not improve,
you will certainly face severe punishment."
Zhāng Zhāo and Xuē Zǒng
were both unable to reply.
Zhūgé Kè said:
"Now the Crown Prince is refined and exceptionally perceptive.
By the time the blue canopy returns,
the Crown Prince, with his sagely and wise nature,
will surely understand ten things upon hearing one.
How could we ministers vainly expect to receive rewards?"
Sūn Quán once asked Kè,
"How do you compare to the Chancellor (Zhūgé Jǐn)?"
Kè said:
"Your subject surpasses him."
Quán said:
"The Chancellor received the late emperor's testament to assist in governance.
The state grew prosperous and punishments were clear.
Even Yī Yǐn, who matched Heaven's will,
and the Duke of Zhōu, whose brilliance reached the four corners,
could not surpass him by far.
Moreover, he is your uncle.
How can you say you surpass him?"
Kè replied:
"It is indeed as Your Majesty's wise edict states.
However, when it comes to serving a corrupt ruler,
willingly submitting to a false sovereign,
and being ignorant of the Mandate of Heaven,
then he is not as good as your subject, who serves in a peaceful and prosperous court,
praising a ruler who commands the world."
Quán asked Kè again:
"How do you compare to Bù Zhì?"
Kè replied:
"Your subject is not as good as him."
He asked again, how about Zhū Rán?
He also said:
"Not as good."
He asked again, how about Lù Xùn?
He also said:
"Not as good."
Quán said:
"You are not as good as these three men,
yet you claim to surpass your uncle. Why?"
Kè said:
"I dare not deceive Your Majesty.
A small state having a ruler
is not as good as the great states lacking one.
That is why I surpass him."
From *Liú Shì Xiǎoshuō*.
Chē Jùn
Lù Xùn, hearing of Chē Jùn's fine reputation,
requested to meet him.
He said to him:
"I have long admired your graceful demeanor.
Why do you coil like a dragon and stand like a phoenix,
unwilling to condescend to visit?"
Jùn replied:
"I truly know that you, my lord,
emulate the Duke of Zhōu's broad acceptance
and match Confucius's skillful guidance.
However, a lizard cannot borrow thick clouds to ascend,
and a sparrow cannot ride a fierce wind to soar.
That is why there is no opportunity."
Among the guests present at the time,
many were from Wú.
They looked at each other and said:
"Wǔlíng is a barbarian commandery,
yet it has produced such an extraordinary man!"
Jùn said:
"Tàibó of Wú, with his dignified robes and caps, transformed
the custom of wearing hair loose and tattooing the body.
Now, above, we have an outstanding sage ruler;
below, we have produced worthy ministers.
What is so unusual about that?"
Xùn sighed and said:
"The state will surely prosper,
for it has such a man."
From *Liú Shì Xiǎoshuō*.
Zhūgé Jìng
Zhūgé Jìng was in Wú,
attending a grand assembly at the court.
Sūn Hào asked him:
"Your courtesy name is Zhòng Sī (Second Thought).
What do you think about?"
He replied:
"At home, I think of filial piety;
serving the ruler, I think of loyalty;
with friends, I think of trustworthiness.
That is all."
From *Shì Shuō Xīnyǔ*.
Cài Hóng
Jìn Cài Hóng went to Luòzhōng.
Someone asked him:
"The new government has just been established,
and all the lords are recruiting talents.
They seek outstanding individuals from humble backgrounds,
and select worthy and talented men from remote caves and mountains.
You are a man from Wú and Chǔ,
a remnant of a fallen state.
What exceptional talent do you possess
to respond to this recruitment?"
He replied:
"The pearl that shines at night
need not necessarily come from the Mèngjīn River;
a jade disc measuring a full foot
need not necessarily be mined from the Kūnlún Mountains.
Great Yǔ was born among the Eastern Barbarians,
and King Wén came from the Western Qiāng.
Where sages and worthies emerge,
why must it always be from the same place?
In the past, King Wǔ attacked Zhòu.
He relocated the stubborn people to Luòyì.
Could it be that you gentlemen are their descendants?"
They again asked Hóng,
"What are the old prominent families of Wú like?"
He replied:
"Lord Wú Fǔjūn is a great assistant to our sagely court,
an outstanding talent in this enlightened era.
Zhū Yǒngcháng possesses the great virtue of governing affairs,
and the high reputation of being selected through pure evaluation.
Yán Zhòngbì is like the great swan of the nine marshes,
the white colt in the empty valley.
Gù Yànxiān is like the qín and sè among the eight tones,
the dragon's emblem among the five colors.
Zhāng Wēibó is like the luxuriant pine in the winter cold,
the escaping light in the deep night.
Lù Shìlóng is like the swan hovering in flight,
the suspended drum awaiting the mallet.
All these gentlemen
take their mighty brushes as plows and hoes,
take paper and slips as fertile fields,
take dark ink as crops,
take righteousness and propriety as bountiful harvests,
take discourse and debate as flowers and splendor,
take loyalty and forgiveness as precious treasures,
compose writings as brocade and embroidery,
contain the Five Classics as silk and cloth,
sit upon humility as mats and cushions,
spread their ideas and intentions as curtains and canopies,
practice benevolence and righteousness as their house and rooms,
and follow the Way and virtue as their walls and dwelling."
From "Liú Shì Xiǎoshuō."
Fàn Bǎinián
Sòng Liángzhōu's Fàn Bǎinián, due to official matters, had an audience with Emperor Míng.
During the conversation, the emperor
mentioned Guǎngzhōu's Greedy Spring,
and then asked him:
"Does your province also have such a spring?"
Bǎinián replied:
"Liángzhōu only has the Civil Stream and Martial Township,
the Spring of Integrity and the Stream of Humility."
The emperor then asked, "And where is your residence located?"
He said:
"Your servant lives between Integrity and Humility."
The emperor praised him.
Later, he was appointed as Governor of Liángzhōu.
From "Tán Sǒu."
Zhāng Róng
Zhāng Róng of Wújùn, styled Sīguāng,
was the son of Chief Clerk Chàng,
and grandson of Court Gentleman Wěi.
Róng was divinely intelligent and outstanding,
quick-witted and eloquent as a flowing stream.
He once had an audience with Emperor Tàizǔ at the Western Hall of Tàijí.
It took him a long time to ascend.
The emperor smiled and said:
"Why are you so late?"
He replied:
"Ascending from earth to heaven,
it stands to reason one cannot be fast."
Róng served as a Gentleman of the Central Secretariat.
He once sighed and said:
"I do not regret that I cannot see the ancients;
I regret that the ancients cannot see me."
Róng excelled at cursive and clerical script.
Emperor Tàizǔ once said to him:
"Your calligraphy has remarkable bone strength,
but it is a pity it lacks the method of the Two Wángs."
He replied:
"It is not a pity that your servant lacks the Two Wángs' method,
but also a pity that the Two Wángs lack your servant's method."
From "Tán Sǒu."
Yǔ Gǎozhī
Emperor Wǔ of Qí once said to his ministers:
"What posthumous title will I receive after my death?"
No one answered.
Wáng Jiǎn then signaled with his eyes for Yǔ Gǎozhī to reply.
Gǎozhī said:
"Your Majesty's longevity compares to the Southern Mountain,
your brilliance equals the sun and moon.
A thousand years hence,
how could it be something your servants lightly presume to measure?"
People of the time praised his eloquent reply.
From "Tán Sǒu."
Wáng Jiǎn
Wáng Jiǎn of Qí, styled Zhòngbǎo,
was the son of the Golden and Purple official Sēngchuò,
and grandson of Palace Attendant Tánshǒu.
He was orphaned young,
and even as a child possessed the quality of a jade tablet.
At four or five years old,
he was already different from ordinary children.
He once composed a five-character poem:
"Jì and Xiè aided Yú and Xià,
Yī and Lǚ assisted Shāng and Zhōu.
Examining myself, I am ashamed before the sages of old;
I shall straighten my robes and retire to the hills."
Therefore, commentators considered him destined to be a chancellor.
Later, he became Minister of Personnel.
A guest surnamed Tán came to Jiǎn seeking an official post.
Jiǎn said:
"Duke Huán of Qí destroyed Tán;
how could there still be you?"
The guest replied:
"The son of Tán fled to Jǔ,
hence there is your servant."
Jiǎn appreciated him.
The emperor once visited the Lèyóu Garden for a feast,
and the ministers offered music.
The emperor said:
"Who shares my love for fine music?"
Jiǎn replied:
"Bathing in the imperial breeze,
all are moistened, house by house.
Being already in Qí,
one forgets the taste of meat."
The emperor praised him.
Jiǎn once gathered scholars of talent and learning,
compiling objects and making them beautiful,
calling it "beautifying things."
The practice of "beautifying things" began from this.
All the guests were stumped,
only Hé Xiàn of Lújiāng excelled,
and was rewarded with a five-colored patterned bamboo mat and a white round fan.
Xiàn sat on the mat holding the fan,
looking immensely pleased with himself.
Wáng Chī, Magistrate of Mòlíng, arrived later.
He took up the brush and completed it immediately.
The content was splendid and beautiful,
and the diction was also华丽.
Chī then ordered his attendants to take the mat and snatch the fan,
got into his carriage and left.
Jiǎn laughed and said:
"This is what is called 'a great strength carries it away swiftly.'"
From "Tán Sǒu."
Zhōu Yóng
Zhōu Yóng of Rǔnán lived in seclusion on Zhōng Mountain,
maintaining a long-term vegetarian diet.
Wáng Jiǎn said to him:
"While living in the mountains,
what do you eat?"
He replied:
"Red rice and white salt,
green mallows and purple knotweed."
Jiǎn also asked:
"Which vegetable is the most delicious?"
Yóng said:
"Early chives in early spring,
late cabbage in late autumn."
Yóng later served as Vice Director of the Central Secretariat.
From "Tán Sǒu."
Wáng Róng
The Wei envoy Sòng Biàn arrived,
and the emperor ordered Wáng Róng to concurrently serve as the Director of the Reception Bureau.
Róng asked Biàn:
"West of Qín and north of Jì
are truly abundant in fine steeds,
yet those you present
are not even as good as inferior nags.
Seeking reputation while examining affairs,
this is particularly puzzling.
Moreover, oaths of faith may sometimes be broken,
and the herds of sturdy horses
may perhaps fail to continue."
Biàn replied:
"We would not tolerate empty, false reputations;
it must be that they are unaccustomed to the water and soil."
Róng said:
"King Mù of Zhōu's horse tracks
covered all under heaven.
If the nature of fine steeds
changes according to the land,
then even Zàofǔ's whip
would sometimes stumble."
Biàn said:
"Why are you so earnest about thousand-lǐ horses?"
Róng replied:
"Since your state has proclaimed their superiority or inferiority,
and you have come to inquire,
if the thousand-lǐ horses must arrive,
our sage ruler will harness them to drum carriages."
Biàn could not reply.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Lǐ Yīng
Liáng's Lǐ Yīng was talented in debate.
Emperor Wǔ said to him:
"How does the present Lǐ Yīng
compare to the Lǐ Yīng of old?"
He replied:
"Your servant believes the present one is superior.
The Lǐ Yīng of old
served under the reigns of Huán and Líng;
the present Lǐ Yīng
serves a ruler like Táng and Yú."
All were pleased and convinced.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Shāng Kēng
Shāng Kēng of Dōngjùn named his son Wàichén (Outer Minister).
Wàichén took office as a Court Justice Reviewer.
Kēng entered to give thanks for the imperial grace.
Emperor Wǔ asked:
"You named your son 'Outer Minister',
why then did you have him enter government service?"
Kēng replied:
"Wàichén was born in the late Qí period,
so people longed to conceal their traces;
now, fortunately encountering this sage age,
there are no more people left hidden in the marshes."
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Xiāo Chēn
Emperor Wǔ once threw a date at Xiāo Chēn of Lánlíng.
Chēn then took a chestnut and threw it at the Emperor,
hitting him squarely in the face.
He said:
"Your Majesty casts your 'red heart' (date) at your servant,
how dare your servant not 'tremble' (chestnut) before Your Majesty?"
Chēn once, at the imperial seat,
drank with the Northern envoy, Vice Director of the Palace Secretariat Lǐ Dàogù.
Dàogù declined,
saying:
"In the public court, there is no private etiquette;
I cannot accept your urging."
All present changed countenance,
fearing there was no way to respond.
Chēn slowly said:
As the Odes say:
"Rain falls on our public fields,
and then reaches our private plots."
Dàogù then reluctantly accepted the wine.
Chēn served as Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Zhū Yān
When the Grand Empress Dowager Féng of Later Wèi passed away,
Qí sent the Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary Péi Zhāomíng to offer condolences.
He wished to perform the rites in court attire.
The Director of Receptions questioned him.
Zhāomíng said:
"Not allowing court attire for performing the rites,
from which classic does this principle derive?"
The Assistant Editorial Director Zhū Yān received and replied to him,
saying:
"Auspicious and inauspicious occasions differ;
ritual has established norms.
Not to mourn in black caps
is known even by children.
In the past, when Jìsūn was about to travel,
he inquired about the rites for encountering mourning.
A thousand years later,
he is still praised together.
You, coming from the distant Jiāngnán to offer condolences,
cannot follow established practices,
and instead ask from which classic the principle derives.
The envoy's propriety or impropriety—
how exceedingly strange is this!"
Zhāomíng said:
"When the Qí emperor previously passed away,
Lǐ Biāo conveyed condolences.
At that time, he did not wear plain garments from the start.
The Qí court did not consider it remiss.
Why must we now endure such harsh insistence?"
Yān said:
"That court did not follow Gāozōng's longing remembrance of the distant past,
but instead ended mourning after just over a month.
When Lǐ Biāo came to offer condolences,
the Qí ruler and ministers
all had jade pendants chiming in the court,
vermilion and purple robes shining like the sun.
Since Biāo had not received his host's instruction,
how could he alone, in plain garments, insert himself among those in caps and gowns?
Your reproach, though lofty,
I dare not accept.
Our emperor's nature of benevolence and filial piety
equals that of Yú Shùn.
Since the mourning period began,
all officials have obeyed the Prime Minister.
How can you compare that situation with this?"
Zhāomíng then waved his hand and said:
"The Three Sovereigns had different rites;
I also know where propriety and impropriety lie."
Yān said:
"If it is as you say,
do you consider Yú Shùn and Gāozōng wrong?"
Zhāomíng replied:
"Lacking filial piety means having no regard for parents.
I request a decision on mourning attire.
Now, being pressured by the Wèi court,
I will surely incur blame in my own state."
Yān said:
"If there are gentlemen there,
and you uphold your mission with firmness,
you should receive high reward;
if there are no gentlemen,
simply let there be the glory of honoring your state.
Even if you unreasonably incur offense,
what does it matter?
The southern historians and Dǒng Hú would naturally record it truthfully."
Emperor Gāozǔ rewarded him,
and transferred him to Editorial Director.
Qí also sent Vice Director Hé Xiàn and Director of Receptions Xíng Zōngqìng to the court.
They sent Yān to receive and reply to them.
Zōngqìng said to Yān:
"The alliance between north and south has lasted long,
yet recently you abandoned trust and severed friendly relations,
acting for profit's sake.
Is this the principle of a great state being a good neighbor?"
Yān said:
"Those who act as kings
are not bound by minor scruples.
In the central plains there are beans;
the skilled gatherer obtains more.
How can one cling steadfastly to Wěishēng's trust?
Moreover, Qí's former king served the Sòng dynasty through successive reigns,
accumulating a debt of gratitude over generations.
How could he then simply usurp the throne?"
Qìng and the others looked at each other, their countenances changing.
Hé Xiàn knew Yān had formerly come from the south to the north,
and said to Yān:
"Why did you not become a Yú Jìn, but became a Lǔ Sù instead?"
Yān replied:
"I abandoned danger for security,
wishing to follow in the footsteps of Chén Píng and Hán Xìn.
What has Yú Jìn to do with it?"
Xiàn could not reply.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Cuī Guāng
Later Wèi's Emperor Gāozǔ named his sons Xún, Yú, Yuè, Yì.
Cuī Guāng named his sons Lì, Xù, Miǎn.
Emperor Gāozǔ said to Guāng:
"My sons' names all have the 'heart' radical.
Your sons' names all have the 'strength' radical."
He replied:
"This is what is called 'the gentleman labors with his heart,
the small man labors with his strength'."
The Emperor sighed deeply with pleasure.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Chén Yuánkāng
Chén Yuánkāng of Héyáng in the Northern Qí,
was a clerk skilled in writing,
and excelled at writing in the dark.
Once on a snowy night,
the Grand Ancestor ordered him to draft military documents.
In a short while, he produced several dozen pages,
and his brush did not even have time to freeze.
The Grand Ancestor joyfully said:
"How does this man compare to Confucius?"
From then on, he was trusted and employed.
Thus, people of the time had a saying:
"Three Cuīs and two Zhāngs,
are not equal to one Chén Yuánkāng."
The three Cuīs:
were Cuī Xiān, Cuī Jìshū, and Cuī Áng.
The two Zhāngs:
were Zhāng Déwēi and Zhāng Zuǎn.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Lǐ Xié
Lǐ Xié of Dùnqiū in the Northern Qí,
was the grandson of Prince Péngchéng, Lǐ Yí,
and the son of the Minister of Personnel, Lǐ Píng.
In his youth, he was handsome and forthright,
and possessed talent and eloquence.
He served as a Gentleman Attendant at the Palace Gate,
but was removed from office,
and composed the "Rhapsody on Expressing Myself."
It roughly said:
Alone, I am carefree and follow my own will,
like an empty boat that is not moored.
Since I do not know whence I came,
how can I know whither I shall go?
Thus, gain and loss are both dismissed,
and forgetting worldly concerns comes naturally.
Wherever I encounter things, I rest;
wherever I tread, it becomes a mountain forest.
Although similar to the traces of floating westward,
how does it differ from the heart of the eastern capital?
He was appointed as a Regular Attendant,
and served as an envoy to the Liáng dynasty.
Upon arriving in Liáng,
the host official Fàn Xū was sent to greet him.
Xū asked:
"It is still warm here now;
the north must be somewhat colder than here."
Lǐ Xié replied:
"Our land lies in the proper position of yīn and yáng,
where cold and heat are timely,
so I do not know how much colder it is."
Xū said:
"I have heard that your capital is located
in a place where the sun's shadow is slanted."
Lǐ Xié said:
"It is the imperial capital,
not far from here;
can we not speak of it in general terms?"
Xū said:
"Since Luòyáng is praised as magnificent,
why did you move the capital to Yè?"
Lǐ Xié said:
"It is not fixed in one city;
we have moved the capital five times.
For a king, there is no 'outside';
wherever he is, there are passes and rivers—
what is so strange about that?"
Xū said:
"The Shāng people faced calamities,
so they moved to Xiàng and Gěng;
why did your court move?"
Lǐ Xié said:
"The sage conceals the past and knows the future,
acting according to the times;
why must one wait for rise and fall?"
Xū said:
"The royal aura of Jīnlíng
began in former generations;
the yellow banners and purple canopies,
originally come from the southeast.
To rule over all states,
it is fitting to be here."
Lǐ Xié said:
"The imperial mandate and signs,
how can they compare with the Central Plains in grandeur?
Purple canopies and yellow banners
ultimately entered Luòyáng."
Xū fell silent and had no reply.
The scholars of Jiāngnán
all sighed in admiration.
After the matter was concluded,
he composed a poem by the river:
The emperor's offering unites the two realms,
yellow blossoms clear for a thousand miles.
Border pipes sound atop the walls,
the cold moon brightens the riverbank.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Lú Kǎi
The Minister of Rites, Lú Kǎi of Fànyáng, concurrently oversaw personnel selection for the Ministry of Personnel.
He appointed Dáyě Kèshī as the Commander of Lánzhōu.
Kèshī declined, saying:
"What crime have I committed,
to be sent to live next door to the Türks?"
Lú Kǎi said:
"Where do the Türks have a wall?"
Kèshī said:
"Meat is their cheese,
ice is their broth,
their yurts are tents and felt is their wall."
Lú Kǎi
was the son of Zǐgāng, the Director of the Secretariat.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Lú Sīdào
Lú Sīdào, the Grand Administrator of Wǔyáng,
was often drunk at dawn.
At the gate of the department,
he saw his nephew Lú Bēn.
Bēn said:
"Uncle, where have you been drinking?
So unsteady this early in the morning."
Lú Sīdào said:
"Cháng'ān wine,
costs two hundred coins;
if I'm not unsteady,
then what's the point of being unsteady?"
Lú Bēn
was the son of the Duke of Yān Commandery, Lú Jǐngrén,
and the nephew of the Vice Director of the Secretariat, Lú Jǐngyù.
He held the position of Minister of Ceremonies.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Wáng Yuánjǐng
Wáng Yuánjǐng was once heavily drunk.
Yáng Zūnyàn said to him:
"Why so unsteady?"
Wáng Yuánjǐng said:
"When millet ripens, its head bows low;
when wheat ripens, its head stands tall.
Since I have both millet and wheat,
that's why I'm unsteady."
From "Tán Sǒu".
Yáng Jiè
Dù Gōngzhān of Jīngzhào in the Suí dynasty,
was the nephew of Táiqīng, the Commandant of the Guards.
He once invited Yáng Jiè to his home.
When they were merry with wine,
they began to banter and jest.
Gōngzhān said:
"Since you, elder brother, bear the surname Yáng,
Yáng Huǒ once insulted Confucius."
Jiè said:
"Since you, younger brother, bear the surname Dù,
Dù Bó once shot King Xuān."
Niú Zǐchōng of Lǒngxī, a General of the Palace Guard,
was praised by his colleagues for his wit and eloquence.
He once said to Jiè:
"You, Yáng, have a 'jiè' (a cooking vessel),
but I fear it cannot handle the kitchen."
Jiè said:
"You, Niú, are already 'chōng' (full),
so you are just right for slaughtering and cooking."
Seeing Jiè eat pickled mustard greens,
he said:
"Your name is Jiè,
how can you still eat jiè cài (mustard greens)?"
Jiè replied:
"Since you are surnamed Niú,
how can you not abstain from niú ròu (beef)?"
There was a Granary Director named Zhāng Cè,
who debated with Jiè at Yúnlóng Gate and was defeated in argument.
He said to Jiè:
"You originally lack virtue and measure,
yet suddenly share the same name as Shūbǎo."
Jiè retorted loudly:
"You are no hero,
yet dare to share a taboo character with Bófú."
Xiāo Xǔ of Lánlíng, a Tutor of the Crown Prince, was handsome, talented, and eloquent.
He once said to Jiè:
"When Gònggōng was exiled to Yōuzhōu,
the north of Yì was hardly a land of joy."
Jiè said:
"When Huāndōu's clan was banished to Chóngshān,
was Jiāngnán a land of victory?"
Táng Yǒng, the Prince of Jìnchāng and Recorder of the Department of State Affairs, said to the various provincial officials:
"You should each speak of the treasures of your own province."
The people of Dìngzhōu considered fine silks and damasks as treasures;
the people of Cāngzhōu considered fish and salt as treasures.
When it came to Jiè,
Táng Yǒng said:
"You are from Yōuzhōu;
what do you consider as treasures?"
Jiè replied:
"A clear and strict provincial governor,
civil and military officials upholding the law—
these are the treasures of Yōuzhōu."
Táng Yǒng showed a look of shame.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Xuē Dàohéng
Xuē Dàohéng, the Vice Minister of Personnel of the Suí dynasty, once visited the Kāishàn Temple on Zhōng Mountain.
He asked a young monk:
"Why does the Vajra deity glare with bulging eyes?
Why does the Bodhisattva lower her gaze with gentle brows?"
The young monk replied:
"The Vajra glares with bulging eyes
to subdue the four demons;
the Bodhisattva lowers her gaze with gentle brows
to show compassion to the six realms of existence."
Dàohéng was taken aback and could not reply.
From "Tán Sǒu"
Xuē Shōu
In the Táng dynasty, Xuē Shōu served in the Prince of Qín's residence.
Proclamations and public announcements
were mostly drafted by Shōu.
His compositions were swift and clever,
as if prepared overnight,
completed on horseback,
without a single revision.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Zhāng Hòuyì
Zhāng Hòuyì was in Bīngzhōu
when Tàizōng studied the Zuǒzhuàn commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals under him.
Later, Hòuyì was summoned to an imperial banquet,
where past events were discussed.
Tàizōng leisurely asked him:
"How does your disciple compare today
如 originally written as 知,
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy
Hòuyì replied:
"In the past, Confucius led three thousand disciples,
yet none attained the rank of a noble.
I have assisted but one person,
who became the ruler of ten thousand chariots.
Judging by my achievement,
I surpass the ancient sage."
Tàizōng was greatly pleased
and immediately bestowed upon him five horses.
Later, Hòuyì became Minister of Rites.
He was buried in the Xianling Mausoleum.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Cuī Rénshī
Cuī Rénshī served as Director of the Bureau of Revenue.
Once, he reported to the throne on revenue and goods, speaking thousands of words
without holding a script.
Tàizōng found this strange
and ordered Dù Zhènglún to bring the script.
Rénshī recited from memory,
without a single discrepancy.
The Ministry of Justice proposed that for crimes of rebellion,
confiscating brothers as government slaves was too light,
changing it
輕改 originally written as 改輕,
changed according to Sòng Kǒng Píngzhòng's "Xù Shì Shuō 1"
to execution.
Rénshī argued,
believing that father and son are bound by nature,
and brothers share the same breath.
Executing a father and son
is enough to weigh on one's conscience;
if one disregards this,
why would they care for brothers?
If the law is to be changed,
please deliberate carefully.
In the end, Rénshī's argument was adopted.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Lú Zhuāngdào,
a man of Fànyáng,
was renowned throughout the land as a distinguished scholar.
His intelligence and quick wit
surpassed both ancient and modern times.
His father, Lú Yàn, was an old acquaintance of Gāo Shìlián.
Zhuāngdào was orphaned young;
at age twelve,
he visited Shìlián.
Shìlián, treating him as the son of an old friend,
invited him to sit.
Just then, a memorial was presented.
Zhuāngdào secretly glanced at it
and said to Shìlián:
"This document was written by me, Zhuāngdào."
Shìlián, surprised, said to him:
"Young man, do not speak recklessly
or engage in frivolous behavior.
Recite it, then."
He indeed recited it flawlessly.
Shìlián then asked him to recite it backwards,
and again he succeeded.
Shìlián praised him for a long time.
Zhuāngdào then knelt and apologized:
"This document was not actually written by me;
I merely glanced at it from the side and memorized it."
Shìlián took other documents and official papers,
ordered him to read them,
and at a single glance, he could recite them backwards.
He also presented his own writings.
Shìlián reported all this to the throne.
Tàizōng summoned him for an audience,
tested him, and he passed with high marks.
At age sixteen, he was appointed as the sheriff of Héchí.
After two years in office,
he passed the special imperial examination with the highest grade.
Summoned for an audience,
Tàizōng said:
"Is this my clever little boy?"
He was specially appointed as the sheriff of Cháng'ān.
When Tàizōng was to review prisoners,
Zhuāngdào was only twenty years old.
The county magistrate, considering his youth,
feared he would not manage
and intended to replace him with another sheriff.
Zhuāngdào refused.
At that time, over four hundred prisoners were detained,
all with written records prepared in advance.
Zhuāngdào, however, remained at leisure,
paying no attention to them.
The magistrate and his deputies grew anxious and fearful,
repeatedly urging him,
but Zhuāngdào remained calm and composed.
The next day,
Tàizōng summoned the prisoners.
Zhuāngdào then slowly wrote the records and presented them,
leading the prisoners in.
Before the emperor, he assessed the severity of their crimes,
their detention periods,
responding as if divinely inspired.
Tàizōng was astonished and impressed.
That very day, he was promoted to Investigating Censor.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì"
Xǔ Jìngzōng
When Emperor Gāozōng journeyed east to perform the fēng sacrifice,
Dòu Déxuán rode alongside.
The emperor asked Déxuán:
"Púyáng was anciently called Dìqiū;
why is that?"
Déxuán could not answer.
Xǔ Jìngzōng urged his horse forward and answered the question,
earning the emperor's approval.
Jìngzōng later told others:
"A high minister must not be unlearned.
When I saw Déxuán unable to answer,
I felt truly ashamed for him."
Déxuán, upon hearing this, said:
"Each person has strengths and weaknesses;
it is good to acknowledge one's limitations
and not pretend to know what one does not."
Lǐ Jì said:
"Jìngzōng is widely learned,
which is indeed admirable,
but Déxuán's words
are also wise."
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Hú Chǔbīn
Hú Chǔbīn composed texts with remarkable speed,
often writing only after drinking to mild intoxication.
Whenever Emperor Gāozōng ordered him to write,
he would have wine served in a golden cup,
ordering him to drink,
and then bestow the cup upon him.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Péi Yǎnzhī
When Péi Yǎnzhī served as Household Registrar of Tóngzhōu,
he was just twenty years old,
and concerned himself only with pleasure-seeking,
paying little attention to official documents.
The Regional Inspector, Duke Li Chóngyì of Qiáoguó, found this strange and questioned the assistant registrar.
The assistant said:
"The Registrar is the son of a high official;
I fear he is not skilled in writing judgments."
After several days,
Chóngyì said to Yǎnzhī:
"The affairs of Tóngzhōu are inherently
(Míng manuscript: 'inherently' as 'burdensome')
numerous,
and the Household Registrar's duties are especially so.
Why don't you seek another capital post,
rather than stagnate in this office?"
Yǎnzhī merely assented.
After a few more days,
official documents piled up,
and people secretly discussed that Yǎnzhī was illiterate,
only fond of wandering about.
Another day,
Chóngyì summoned him,
with stern expression and harsh words,
intending to petition for his dismissal.
Yǎnzhī went out
and said to his assistant:
"How many documents are there?"
The reply was:
"Over two hundred urgent ones."
Yǎnzhī said:
"What's so many about that,
to press someone like this?"
He ordered ten sheets of paper attached to the back of each case,
and had five or six men prepare ink and moisten brushes.
His attendants reluctantly assented.
Yǎnzhī paid them no heed,
asked the chief clerk to briefly explain the matters,
leaned against a pillar and decided them,
with reasoning flowing freely,
language brilliant and radiant,
his hand never ceasing,
covering the paper like flying.
All the officials of the prefecture,
spectators like a wall,
could not cease their exclamations of amazement.
The documents reached Chóngyì,
who at first said:
"Did the Registrar understand how to judge?"
The assistant registrar said:
"The Registrar's writing is of superb skill;
yet we still did not find it extraordinary.
By the fortieth or fiftieth case,
the literary elegance grew even more refined."
Chóngyì, startled and ashamed,
summoned Yǎnzhī,
descended the steps and apologized, saying:
"With literary talent such as yours,
how could you bear to conceal your edge,
allowing this lowly fellow's fault?"
That day, his fame shook the entire prefecture.
After several days,
it was heard in the capital.
Soon he was promoted and appointed Household Registrar of
(Míng manuscript: 'Xióng' as 'Yōng')
Prefecture.
From "Records of the Censorate"
Sū Tǐng
Sū Tǐng was exceptionally intelligent and perceptive,
reciting several thousand words daily.
Although his memory and reading were godlike,
his father Sū Guī instructed and urged him with extreme strictness,
often making him wear a blue cloth jacket,
kneel beneath the bed,
and extend his shins to receive cane strokes.
Upon reaching adulthood, his literary learning was broad and comprehensive,
unsurpassed in his time.
By nature carefree and handsome, he was fond of drink.
When Emperor Xuánzōng had pacified the internal troubles,
and wished to draft an edict,
finding a suitable person was very difficult.
He turned to Guī and said:
"Who can compose the decree?
Try to think of someone."
Guī said:
"I know of no other,
but my son Tǐng is very quick-witted,
and can serve your command.
However, he is fond of drink;
if he can avoid being dead drunk,
he should be able to manage the task."
Xuánzōng promptly ordered him summoned.
When he arrived, his hangover from the previous night had not yet cleared;
he roughly performed the bows and dance,
then, still drunk, vomited at the foot of the hall.
The emperor ordered a palace attendant to support him to lie down before the throne,
and Xuánzōng personally lifted a quilt to cover him.
Once sober,
he was given writing materials,
and completed it instantly.
His talent and literary grace flowed freely,
the reasoning and language elegant and ample,
greatly pleasing Xuánzōng.
Patting his back, he said:
"No one knows a son like his father.
Is it truly so?"
From then on, he was highly regarded,
and the emperor already intended to give him important employment.
When Wěi Sìlì was appointed Secretariat Director,
Guī drafted the official announcement,
Tǐng composed the text,
Xuē Jì calligraphed it,
and contemporaries called it the "Three Perfections."
When Tǐng could just speak,
a Capital District Governor visited Guī,
who asked Tǐng to compose a verse on the character "Yǐn" (尹).
He then said:
"Chǒu (丑) has feet though misshapen,
Jiǎ (甲) is not whole in body,
seeing you, it lacks a mouth,
knowing Yī (伊), it misses a man."
Guī had long been acquainted with Zhōu Yànyún, a Daoist priest of the Dōngmíng Temple.
Zhōu at the time wished to erect a stele for his master,
and said to Guī:
"To fulfill this wish of mine,
it would only trouble several of your sons:
the fifth young master for the text,
the sixth young master for the calligraphy,
the seventh young master to obtain the stone."
Guī laughed heartily,
saying nothing but inwardly admiring his fairness.
Guī's sons: Tǐng was the fifth,
Shēn the sixth,
Bīng the seventh.
Shēn excelled at clerical script.
From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng"
Wáng Jù,
a man of Jiàngzhōu,
served as Secretariat Drafter during the Kāiyuán era.
Previously, when the Five Princes left the palace,
they were to receive their patents on the same day,
but the officials had forgotten to prepare the patent texts.
With all officials assembled,
they realized the ritual lacked this element.
Jù summoned five minor clerks,
each holding a brush,
dictated to them separately,
and all were completed simultaneously.
From "Collected Sayings"
Lǐ Bái
During the Kāiyuán era,
Hanlin Academician Lǐ Bái received an imperial command to draft a preface on white lotus blossoms opening and ten palace poems.
At the time he was heavily drunk;
a palace eunuch splashed cold water on him,
and he sobered slightly.
Before the emperor,
Lǐ asked for a brush and with one sweep,
wrote without corrections.
From "Collected Sayings"
Liǔ Fāng
There was a man named Lǐ Yòuqí,
who during the Kāiyuán era,
sought patronage from Liǔ Fāng with his literary skill.
Once, reciting to Fāng a hundred-couplet poem,
Fāng had already memorized it secretly,
then wrote it on the wall,
without missing a single character.
He said to Yòuqí:
"This is my poem."
Yòuqí was greatly astonished,
showing an indignant expression.
After a while, Fāng slowly said:
"Just teasing you;
this is what you recited."
He then asked Yòuqí to recite other writings of his,
and could write them all down after one hearing.
From "True Stories from the Department of State Affairs"
Wáng Zǎo
Wáng Zǎo and Wáng Sù,
during the early Zhēnyuán era, took the examinations,
equally famed as the fourteenth.
Whenever they visited each other's families,
they were called the Fourteenth Young Master

(Míng manuscript: 'Whenever they visited each other's families, they were called the Fourteenth Young Master' as 'Whenever they went to visit each other's families, they addressed each other as Wáng the Twenty-fourth Young Master'),
if asked,
they said:
"Zǎo and Sù."
From "Transmitted Records"
Hán Yù
When Chancellor Líng Hú Táo of the Táng dynasty,
was stationed in Huáihǎi, his secretary Bān Méng and other staff members visited the western corridor of Dàmíng Temple.
Suddenly, they saw an inscription on the front wall that read:
"One person, grand and imposing,
two luminaries shining together,
a spring deep, one foot and one inch,
remove the dot beside ice,
two persons connected,
not missing a side,
three beams and four pillars ablaze with fire,
remove the double hooks, two suns complete."
All the guests and staff gazed at it,
pausing for a long while,
but none could decipher it.
Only Bān Méng said:
"Does 'one person' not mean the character '大' (dà)?
'Two luminaries' refers to the sun and moon,
which is the character '明' (míng), is it not?
'One foot and one inch' is eleven inches,
which is the character '寺' (sì), is it not?
'Remove the dot beside ice'—
the character '水' (shuǐ);
'two persons connected'—
the character '天' (tiān);
'not missing a side'—
the character '下' (xià);
'three beams and four pillars ablaze with fire'—
the character '無' (wú);
'remove the double hooks, two suns complete'—
the character '比' (bǐ).
Does it not read: 'The water of Dàmíng Temple
is unparalleled under heaven'?"
Everyone was enlightened and said:
"Such extraordinary wit
is no different from the legendary 'yellow silk' riddle!"
They praised him all day long.
Upon inquiring with an elderly monk, he said:
"Some years ago, a visitor came alone,
inscribed this, and left,
without revealing his name."
From "Guìyuàn Cóngjì"
Chén Yuánfāng
In the late Hàn dynasty,
Chén Tàiqiū Shí made an appointment to travel with a friend,
but when the time passed and the friend did not arrive,
Chén Tàiqiū left without him.
After he left, the friend finally arrived.
His son Yuánfāng,
seven years old at the time,
was playing outside the gate.
The guest asked Yuánfāng:
"Is your esteemed father at home?"
He replied:
"He waited for you, but you did not come,
so he has already left."
The friend angrily said:
"What an inhuman act!
To make an appointment to travel together
and then abandon someone and leave."
Yuánfāng said:
"You and my father agreed to meet at noon.
When the time passed
(Míng manuscript note: 'shēn' is written as 'zhōng')
and you did not come,
that is a lack of trustworthiness.
To scold the father in front of the son
is a lack of propriety."
The friend felt ashamed,
got down from his carriage to approach him,
but Yuánfāng turned and entered the gate without looking back.
From "Shāng Yún Xiǎoshuō"
Sūn Cè
Sūn Cè of Wú was fourteen years old
when he visited Yuán Shù in Shòuyáng.
Shortly after his arrival,
Liú Yùzhōu Bèi arrived,
and Sūn Cè immediately asked to leave.
Yuán asked:
"What does Liú Yùzhōu have to do with you?"
He replied:
"If not,
heroes are wary of each other."
He then left,
descending the eastern steps,
while Liú Bèi ascended the western steps.
Liú Bèi only turned to watch Sūn Cè's departing steps,
almost unable to move forward.
From "Yǔlín"
Zhōng Yù
Zhōng Yù and Zhōng Huì
were renowned from a young age.
At the age of thirteen,
Emperor Wén of Wèi heard of them
and said to their father Zhōng Yáo:
"Have your two sons come to see me."
Thus, they were summoned for an audience.
Zhōng Yù's face was sweaty.
The Emperor asked:
"Why is your face sweaty?"
Zhōng Yù replied:
"Trembling with fear and anxiety,
sweat pours like thick soup."
He then asked Zhōng Huì:
"Why are you not sweating?"
Zhōng Huì replied:
"Trembling with fear and dread,
sweat cannot come out."
On another occasion, while their father was napping during the day,
they secretly drank the medicinal wine.
Their father woke at the time
and pretended to sleep to observe them:
Zhōng Yù bowed before drinking,
while Zhōng Huì drank without bowing.
When questioned afterward,
Zhōng Yù said:
"Wine is for completing rituals,
so I dared not omit the bow."
When Zhōng Huì was asked
why he did not bow,
he said:
"Stealing is inherently against ritual,
so I did not bow."
From "Xiǎoshuō"
(Míng manuscript note: from "Shìshuō")
Sūn Qíyóu
Sūn Qíyóu and Sūn Qízhuāng, when young, visited Duke Yǔ.
Duke Yǔ asked Qíyóu what his courtesy name meant,
and he said:
"Qíyóu."
Duke Yǔ asked:
"Whom do you aspire to equal?"
He replied:
"To equal Xǔ Yóu."
He then asked Qízhuāng what his courtesy name meant,
and he answered:
"Qízhuāng."
Duke Yǔ asked:
"Whom do you aspire to equal?"
He said:
"To equal Zhuāng Zhōu."
Duke Yǔ said:
"Why not admire Zhòngní (Confucius) but admire Zhuāng Zhōu?"
He replied:
"Sages are born with knowledge,
so they are difficult to emulate."
Duke Yǔ was greatly pleased with the children's responses.
From "Shìshuō Xīnyǔ"
Lù Xiù
Lù Sì, Prince of Dōngpíng of the Later Wèi,
was from the Dài people
and was intelligent and resourceful.
His son Lù Fù inherited his father's demeanor.
Gāo Chóng saw him and admired him,
saying to the court officials:
"I have often marveled that his father's wisdom surpassed his stature,
but this son surpasses his father."
He served as Governor of Xiàngzhōu
and later as Grand Coachman.
Lù Fù's son, Lù Xiù,
was nine years old.
Lù Fù said to him:
"Your grandfather, the Prince of Dōngpíng, had twelve sons.
I am the eldest legitimate son
and inherited the family estate.
Now I am old,
and you are still a young child.
How can you possibly become the head of the Lù clan?"
Lù Xiù replied:
"If it does not depend on physical strength,
why worry about youth?"
Lù Fù found him extraordinary
and designated him as the legitimate heir.
From "Tán Sǒu"
Wáng Xuàn
Sòng Wáng Jǐng,
the son of Sēng Lǎng,
was handsome in appearance
and skilled in profound discourse.
Together with Xiè Zhuāng, Zhāng Chàng, and Hé Yǎn,
he enjoyed great renown.
At that time, Jǐngwén’s original given name was Yù.
As it was the same as Emperor Míng’s name,
he was referred to by his courtesy name.
His eldest son, Xuàn, at the age of five or six,
was exceptionally alert and perceptive.
His maternal grandfather, Hé Shàngzhī, admired and regarded him as extraordinary.
Once, while teaching him to read the *Analects*,
upon reaching the line “How resplendent is its culture!”
he playfully said to him:
“You could change it to ‘How crooked, crooked is its culture!’”
Xuàn immediately replied:
“The name of an elder,
how can it be made a subject of jest?
Then one could also say, ‘When the wind blows upon the grass, it bends.’”
The *Analects* says:
“When the wind blows upon the grass, it bends.”
Yǎn was the son of Shàngzhī.
Xuàn died while serving as Assistant Director of the Palace Library.
From *Tán Sǒu*.
Xiāo Yáoxīn
Xiāo Yáoxīn, Duke of Qǔjiāng of the Southern Qí dynasty, displayed remarkable spirit and capability from a young age.
When he was a child,
there was a boy nearby shooting down flying birds with a slingshot,
never failing to bring them down with each shot.
Yáoxīn said to him:
“There are many kinds of games;
why must you shoot these in such haste?
The birds soar freely among the clouds—
what concern is it of human affairs?”
The boy was moved by his words
and never again took up a slingshot for the rest of his life.
At that time, Yáoxīn was eleven years old.
Many among the gentry and commoners competed in this pastime,
but after Yáoxīn’s single remark,
within ten days to a month, word spread,
and those who heard of it near and far
ceased engaging in it.
From *Tán Sǒu*.
The Son of the Fáng Family
During the Táng dynasty, Wéi Zhì fell ill,
and Minister of Revenue Fáng Guǎn sent his sons and nephews to inquire after him.
They were led into the inner chamber,
where every step was cushioned by carpets.
The son of the Fáng family, still wearing his socks, stepped onto the stairs,
causing the maidservants to laugh at him.
The entire court regarded the Wéi family as noble and prosperous,
while the Fáng family was seen as pure and frugal.
Both were considered admirable topics of conversation.
From *Guó Shǐ Bǔ*.
Zhāng Xiù
The youth named Zhāng Xiù
was the son of Zhāng Shěnsù.
In the twenty-second year of the Kāiyuán era,
Xiù killed Palace Censor Yáng Wànqǐng at the palace gate,
avenging his father.
Earlier, Shěnsù had been implicated in a bribery case,
and an edict ordered Wànqǐng to investigate.
Wànqǐng’s investigation unjustly implicated Shěnsù,
leading to his execution
and the banishment of his family to the frontier.
Xiù was able to return under an amnesty,
still not yet capped as an adult.
He then pursued his long-held grievance
and, together with his younger brother Zhāng Huáng, personally slew Wànqǐng in the capital.
Those who heard of it were shocked.
The emperor, admiring his filial piety,
intended to pardon him.
However, the officials argued firmly against private killing,
and Xiù was sentenced to death.
People of the time mourned him
and buried him at Mount Máng,
constructing false tombs for him—
likely fearing that the Yáng clan might desecrate his grave.
Thus, Vice Director Gù Yún of the Ministry of Works eulogized him, saying:
“Breaking the law to avenge a wrong,
he indeed could not escape punishment;
yet sacrificing himself for filial piety
truly aligns with the principles of ritual and classics.
Moreover, since ancient times,
who has avoided death?
If one meets death in such a cause,
what regret can there be?”
From *The Collected Works of Gù Yún*.
Hún Jiān
Grand Tutor Hún Jiān, at the age of eleven,
accompanied his father, Hún Shìzhī, on winter garrison duty.
The Shuòfāng Military Commissioner Zhāng Qíqiū jokingly asked:
“Did you bring your wet nurse along?”
That same year, Jiān distinguished himself in battle with exceptional bravery.
Two years later,
he captured the Shíbǎo Fortress
and seized the Lóngjū Island,
achieving extraordinary feats in both campaigns.
From *Guó Shǐ Bǔ*.
Jiǎ Kuí
During the Hàn dynasty, Jiǎ Kuí, at the age of five,
displayed intelligence surpassing ordinary people.
His elder sister was the wife of Hán Yáo.
Yáo had no heirs,
and his wife was also praised for her virtue and wisdom.
Hearing the scholars in the neighborhood reciting texts,
she would daily carry Kuí to listen by the fence.
Jiǎ Kuí would listen quietly without uttering a word,
which delighted his sister.
By the age of ten,
he could recite the Six Classics from memory.
His sister asked Kuí:
“Our family is impoverished;
we have never had scholars enter our home.
How do you know of the world’s ancient texts like the *Sānfén* and *Wǔdiǎn*,
and recite them without missing a single line?”
Kuí replied:
“I recall how you used to carry me to the fence
to listen to the neighbors reading;
now I remember it all without error.”
He then stripped bark from the mulberry tree in the courtyard to use as writing tablets,
or wrote on doors and screens.
He recited while memorizing.
After a year,
he had thoroughly mastered the classics and histories.
Disciples came to study under him,
traveling from afar, even thousands of miles.
Some carried their children on their backs,
lodging by his gate,
and he would orally impart the classical texts to them.
Gifts and offerings piled up, filling his granaries.
Some said:
“Jiǎ Kuí did not gain his livelihood by tilling the land;
reciting classics until his mouth grew weary,
he plowed with his tongue for generations.”
From *Wáng Zǐnián’s Shíyí Jì*.
Lǐ Bǎiyào
During the Táng dynasty, Lǐ Bǎiyào could compose literary works by the age of seven.
Lù Yì, a Secretariat Drafter of the Qí dynasty,
once attended a banquet hosted by Bǎiyào’s father, Lǐ Délín.
Someone discussing the writings of Xú Líng mentioned:
“Cutting the rice of Lángyá.”
All the guests present claimed there was no such event.
Bǎiyào stepped forward and said:
“The *Zuǒzhuàn* records that the people of Yǔ gathered rice,
and the commentary states:
‘The state of Yǔ was located in Kāiyáng County of Lángyá.’”
Everyone was astonished and delighted, saying:
“This child is truly a prodigy.”
Bǎiyào suffered from many illnesses in his youth,
so his grandmother named him Bǎiyào, meaning “hundred medicines.”
As the son of a renowned minister,
his talent and conduct carried on the family legacy.
Eminent scholars from across the land
all revered and looked up to him.
His literary thoughts were profound and rich,
and he excelled particularly in five-character verse.
Even woodcutters and shepherd boys
would recite his poems.
Upon retiring from office in old age,
he lived contentedly and at ease,
digging ponds and building hills in his garden,
hosting guests for literary discussions and wine,
fulfilling the aspirations of his lifetime.
He lived to the age of eighty-five.
Earlier, he had composed a matching poem to Tàizōng’s “Ode to the Imperial Capital,”
and an imperial rescript praised him:
“How is it that your body is old, yet your talent remains vigorous?
How is it that your years are advanced, yet your ideas are ever fresh?”
His son, Lǐ Ānqī,
was promoted to Secretariat Drafter in the late Yǒnghuī era,
making three generations in charge of drafting imperial edicts.
Ānqī’s grandson, Lǐ Yìzhòng, also served in the Secretariat.
From *Tán Bīn Lù*.
Wáng Bó
Wáng Bó, courtesy name Zǐ'ān,
was able to compose literary works at the age of six.
His pure talent flowed forth profoundly,
and his conceptualization was without obstruction.
At the age of thirteen,
he visited his father in Jiāngxī.
It happened that the provincial governor was hosting a banquet at the Téngwáng Gé.
