At that time, the governor's son-in-law was skilled at writing essays.
The governor wished to boast of him to his guests and friends,
so he had secretly composed a preface for the Téngwáng Gé beforehand,
intending to present it when the guests gathered,
making it appear as if it were composed impromptu at the banquet.
After the gathering,
the governor indeed presented writing paper to the guests,
and the guests all declined.
When it came to Bó's turn,
Bó immediately accepted it.
The governor, already displeased that his plan was disrupted,
was angered by Bó's lack of deference,
so he sent someone to watch Bó as he began to write.
The first report came:
"Nánchāng, the old commandery,
Hóngdū, the new prefecture."
The governor said:
"This is merely a platitude."
The next report said:
"The stars divide at Yì and Zhěn,
the land connects Héng and Lú."
The governor pondered silently for a long while.
Then came the report:
"The sunset clouds fly together with a solitary duck,
the autumn river shares the same color with the vast sky."
The governor said:
"This is immortal."
From "Zhíyán"
Yuán Jiā
Yuán Jiā was exceptionally bright and talented from a young age.
He could draw a circle with his right hand,
and a square with his left hand,
while reciting classics and histories aloud,
counting a flock of sheep with his eyes,
composing a forty-character poem simultaneously,
all completed at once,
and writing a five-character quatrain with his foot:
six tasks performed simultaneously.
He was called the Divine Child by his generation.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Máo Jùnnán
Máo Jùn of Bīngzhōu gave birth to a son,
who, at the age of four,
was summoned by Wǔ Zétiān to the palace to test his writing.
He was able to write the entire Thousand Character Classic from memory.
He was bestowed with clothing and sent home.
People all believed he was possessed by a spirit.
Afterward, his whereabouts became unknown.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Sū Tǐng
Sū Guī initially did not recognize Tǐng's talent.
He often kept Tǐng in the stables,
working alongside the hired laborers.
One day,
a guest visited Guī,
waiting in the reception hall.
Tǐng, holding a broom, hurried across the courtyard,
and dropped some written documents.
The guest picked them up to look,
and they turned out to be poems about Kūnlún slaves.
The verses read:
"Ten blots of ink on the fingertips,
two spoons on the ears."
The guest found this strange.
After a while, Guī came out,
and lingered with the guest.
Amidst the guest's laughter and conversation,
he recited the poem,
and described Tǐng's appearance,
asking Guī who he was,
and if he was not an illegitimate child of Guī's clan.
Guī explained the whole story in detail.
The guest was astonished and congratulated him,
urging Guī to treat Tǐng with respect and nurture him,
asserting that he would surely become an outstanding son of the Sū family.
From then on, Guī gradually grew closer to him.
It happened that someone presented Guī with a rabbit,
which was hung under the corridor eaves.
Guī then summoned Tǐng to compose a poem about it.
Tǐng immediately presented a poem, saying:
"The rabbit lies dead and limp,
brought here and hung on a bamboo pole.
Try holding a bright mirror to it,
how different is it from gazing at the moon?"
Guī was greatly amazed,
and suddenly began to treat him with regard and courtesy.
From then on, his learning renewed daily,
and his literary compositions became unparalleled in his generation.
From "Kāitiān Chuánxìn Jì"
Liú Yàn
Emperor Xuánzong presided at the Qínzhèng Lóu,
where grand music was performed,
and a hundred courtesans were arrayed.
At that time, in the Imperial Music Academy, there was a woman named Wáng Dàniáng
who was skilled at balancing a hundred-foot pole,
on which a wooden mountain was placed,
resembling the mythical islands of Yíngzhōu and Fāngzhàng.
She had a child hold a crimson banner,
moving in and out among them,
singing and dancing without cease.
At that time, Liú Yàn, a child prodigy, served as a proofreader in the Imperial Library,
just ten years old,
and of rather ugly appearance.
Yet he was exceptionally intelligent and perceptive.
Emperor Xuánzong summoned him beneath the curtains in the tower,
and Consort Yáng placed him on her lap,
applied powder and makeup for him,
and combed his hair.
Emperor Xuánzong asked Yàn:
"You serve as a proofreader;
how many characters have you corrected?"
He replied:
"All characters under heaven are correct,
only the character 'péng' (friend) has not yet been corrected."
Consort Yáng then ordered him to compose a poem about Wáng Dàniáng's pole-balancing.
Yàn responded immediately:
"Before the tower, a hundred acts compete in novelty,
only the long pole is divinely marvelous.
Who would have thought
(Míng Dynasty manuscript copy has 'wèi' instead of 'dé')
that silken robes could turn so strong,
still嫌 it too light and adding a person."
Emperor Xuánzong, Consort Yáng, and the various palace ladies laughed joyfully for a long time,
their voices heard outside,
and thus he commanded an ivory tablet and a yellow-patterned robe to be bestowed upon him.
From "Mínghuáng Zálù"
Lín Jié
Cuī Xuàn
Duke Wèi, Chancellor Cuī Xuàn,
was the son of Cuī Yuánlüè.
When he was a child,
he accompanied his father on a visit to Duke Hán Huàng.
Huàng saw him and took a liking to him.
His father said:
"This child has recently made considerable progress in the art of poetry."
Huàng then pointed to a falcon on its perch and ordered him to compose a poem about it.
He then had paper and brush brought,
and without the slightest hesitation,
he presented his verse:
"A heart and nature from the edge of heaven, a body perched upon the stand,
Wishing to soar and fly, yet lacking the means.
One day it will go off into the vast blue skies,
But who will be the one to untie its leash?"
Huàng was even more amazed by him.
He sighed and said:
"This child can truly be said to have a future of ten thousand miles ahead."
In the third year of the Dàlì era,
he passed the imperial examination under Vice-Minister Cuī Yǎn,
and indeed, he long served at court,
three times holding the authority of a military governor.
During the Dàzhōng and Xiántōng eras,
he was praised by his time as a man of pure reputation and great virtue.
Emperor Xuānzōng, after a regular court session,
said to his attending ministers:
"Cuī Xuàn is truly a noble man,
while Péi Xiū is truly a poor scholar."
Earlier, when Lǐ Shí was governing Jiānglíng,
he recruited Cuī as a military aide,
but one day Cuī brushed his sleeves and left.
After entering the capital,
he achieved top honors in the examination,
and soon rose to the Hanlin Academy.
Before Lǐ had even left Jīngzhǔ,
Cuī was already wielding the power of the state.
Lǐ then sent a letter to congratulate him, saying:
"I long ago paid my respects to your illustrious presence,
and was honored to receive your favor and regard,
deeply granted exceptional treatment,
and frequently engaged in refined conversation.
Fortunate to have once been looked upon with great kindness,
I humbly see that you still follow our old bond.
Last year, I took command in the southern Chǔ region,
and received my commission in the western Qín.
While longing for worthies, I sang of the 'Fine Fish,'
but dwelling here, I am truly ashamed before the majestic phoenix.
When the guest banquet first began,
I once shared in the joy of cups and dishes.
Before the general's tent had moved,
I was already under your nurturing care.
Light shines upon the neighboring region,
joy overflows at the headquarters gate.
Not only will the nine regions gain peace,
this is also a great fortune for this one area."
These were the words composed by the secretary Lǐ Zhì,
and they are still widely circulated today.
From "Nán Chǔ Xīnwén"
Lǐ Qí
Lǐ Qí was from a renowned clan.
His father, Lǐ Jìng,
served in Wáng Duó's staff in Huàzhōu during the Guǎngmíng era of the Táng.
Qí was born intelligent and exceptional,
mastering the Six Classics by age ten.
He then broadly studied literature and history,
as if recalling past learning.
At thirteen,
his cí, fù, poems, and odes
were greatly admired and appreciated by the eminent scholars of the time.
The regional commander Wáng Duó heard of him and found him remarkable.
However, whenever he saw Qí's compositions,
he also had some doubts.
Duó once invited Qí's father, Jìng, and the staff officers to a drink,
and secretly sent someone to test Qí with the topic "The Three Heroes of Hàn Gāozǔ,"
waiting for him to finish before taking it away.
At the end of the fù, it said:
"With scholars, one prospers;
without worthies, there is no support.
The friends of the dragon's head are precious;
the ministers forming the tripod's legs are to be valued.
How fitting, then, the reason for Xiàng's downfall—
he could not even employ one Fàn Zēng."
Duó exclaimed in amazement:
"This child is a vessel of great capacity!"
Wishing to promote the value of his writings,
he showed the fù to the seated guests,
and the entire gathering praised it.
Another day, Qí, with his hair in tufts, paid a visit to Duó.
Duó looked at him and said:
"An edict from Shǔ has just arrived,
appointing Tuòbá Sīgōng of Xiàzhōu as Capital-North Recovery Commander-in-Chief.
Can you compose a poem on this?"
He immediately took up the brush and composed on the spot:
"Swift riders pass through Bā's plank roads,
Imperial grace reaches Xià's terrace.
He will go forth from the heavens above,
A man coming from beside the sun.
Here, the Golden Gate is far;
When will the jade carriage return?
Soon pacify the bandits west of the pass,
Do not wait for the edict to urge you on."
Duó was even more amazed by him,
and taking Qí's hand, said:
"This is truly a phoenix feather!"
He was fourteen years old at the time.
The following year, he observed mourning for his mother,
and thus drifted and resided between Qīng and Qí.
Burning chaff for light, using firewood as a lamp,
making night into day,
he read several thousand volumes of books,
and occasionally wrote poems and fù.
When Táng Emperor Xīzōng fled to Liángyáng a second time,
he secretly composed a fù that said:
"In grief and pain, he issues no edict;
Who will present a memorial to ascend and seal the mountain?"
By the time of Emperor Zhāozōng's reign,
he successively passed the imperial examinations.
Yet he was suddenly unhappy,
regretting that he had not been able to master the four styles
and write in the language of edicts and proclamations.
When Liáng Tàizǔ accepted the abdication,
Qí, starting from his former position as Palace Censor,
was promoted to Hanlin Academician.
From "Preface to the Collected Works of Lǐ Qí"
Child Prodigy Liú
Child Prodigy Liú
in the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng, was elevated through provincial recommendation and passed the examination,
at the age of only six.
The Emperor summoned him to a side hall to test him again,
and the child prodigy recited the classics clearly,
without the slightest error from start to finish.
The Emperor greatly praised him,
and accordingly took fruits from the imperial tray to bestow upon him.
The attending ministers on both sides
all showed expressions of envy.
Therefore, the former official Zhèng Gǔ presented him with a poem, saying:
"Study and reading from a past life,
Monks' discussions suffice to make clear.
Returning home, though understanding the bitterness
(Míng manuscript copy has 'bitterness' as 'joy')
Passing the exam, yet unaware of the glory.
Seasonal fruits once received as gifts,
The spring gate cannot restrain his feelings.
Before the lamp, he still dislikes lying down to sleep,
Muttering in sleep, the sound of reciting books."
From "The Poetry Collection of Zhèng Gǔ"
Lù Déyán
was the nephew of Yán Xiàng, the chancellor of Dānzhōu.
He was able to compose poetry at a young age.
While residing in the school dormitory,
he once wrote a poem about the banana plant:
"A kind of wondrous sprout, unique in nature,
Its innate form and character are delicate.
Its leaves resemble slanted ruled paper,
Its heart seems like an upside-down book being pulled out."
After the poem was completed,
it spread throughout the capital the next day.
It happened that the chancellor of Dānzhōu was executed for a crime,
so Déyán was unable to advance for a long time.
During the early Guānghuà era,
he finally took the imperial examination and passed,
and his poetry gained great value.
He also wrote a poem titled "Reflecting on the Past":
"First riding a bamboo horse, I chanted of banana leaves,
Once honored, my name recited throughout the court by esteemed ministers.
With five characters, I was allowed past the crimson tent,
A single branch, I sought to pluck from the crimson sky.
Who would have known I'd drift like duckweed, far and adrift,
Unaware of the passing of distant years.
The nation's borders are ever peaceful, yet I've not established myself,
To this day, I dwell in Yán's humble lane, guarding my simple bowl and gourd."
During the Tiānyòu era,
he was appointed Left Reminder.
It happened that the military governor of Hézhōng, Zhū Yǒuqiān, took command of the region,
and recruited Déyán to serve as his secretary.
Yǒuqiān initially treated him with considerable respect.
However, Déyán's nature was frivolous, arrogant, and disrespectful,
and his actions often offended others.
Yǒuqiān gradually became alienated.
Déyán then composed a fifty-verse poem titled "The Child" to satirize Yǒuqiān.
When Yǒuqiān heard of it, he was furious,
and there was cause for incurring disaster.
Thus, taking advantage of Déyán's drunkenness, he drowned him in the Yellow River.
The poem was indeed an excellent work.
Although there were later imitations,
none could match Déyán's.
The poem reads:
"Emotions and demeanor follow nature's course,
Peach-red glow on both cheeks, fresh and bright.
First steps taken, all gaze in unison,
First words spoken, guests show much affection.
Arms and shoulders plump like gourds,
Skin and flesh softer than silk.
Long hair just covering the forehead,
Parted locks gradually draping the shoulders.
Unrestrained, free from worldly cares,
Carefree, occupying the realm of immortals.
Lining up in the red pavilion,
Shouting clear the way before the painted hall.
Harmonizing in songs of willow,
Unison in stepping to gather lotus.
Running on dikes, dashing through fine rain,
Dashing through lanes, chasing light mist.
Tender bamboo ridden as horses,
Fresh cattails snapped as whips.
Young orioles tied with golden threads,
Puppies led by colored silk.
Holding cranes, returning to sunny isles,
Driving geese into warm springs.
Willow catkins vie to play with snow,
Elm leaves together gather coins.
Tin mirror hung upon the chest,
Silver pearls dangling by the ears.
Head wrapped in dark falcon style,
Sleeves learning Tuòzhī dance gestures.
Wine lingering, cinnabar warm,
Tea催促小玉煎。
Frequently invited to insert longevity flowers,
Often begging for embroidery needles to thread.
Treasure box holding red beans,
Dressing case collecting kingfisher hairpins.
Short robe draped like a desk mat,
Poor hat worn like boot felt.
Unrolling paintings, hastening to the Three Sages,
Opening screens, laughing at the Seven Worthies.
Pocketing green apricots, small and tender,
Forehead adorned with round green lotus.
Tears of surprise staining silk gauze,
Delicate drool soiling brocade.
Tired of books, full of charming play,
Loathing medicine, cleverly delaying.
Playing with bed curtains, phoenix silk shimmering,
Hiding under quilts, phoenix knots tangled.
Fingers tapping to welcome drumbeats,
Chopsticks plucking strings for deity competitions.
Curtains brushing, fishhooks swaying,
Zither pushed, goose bridges slanting.
Chessboard adding path drawings,
Flute pipes lacking engraved tones.
Annoying guests just falling asleep,
Startling monks half-entering meditation.
Seeking spiders across roof tiles,
Probing for fledglings along rafters.
Tossing fruit, busily opening mouths,
Hiding hooks, randomly throwing punches.
At midnight, gathering around firewood,
At dawn, assembling to swing.
Breaking bamboo to fashion clay swallows,
Adding string to fly paper kites.
Mutually boasting of waterwheel turns,
Imitating each other, spinning pinwheels.
Banners small, cut from red silk,
Letters secret,截取碧牋。
Spreading nets for pigeons afar,
Aiming low, shooting fly strings.
Auspicious words spoken from time to time,
Folk songs流传 everywhere.
Hiding by windows, shoulders slightly bent,
Blocking paths, arms linked together.
Playing grass competition on spring paths,
Vying for balls from evening fields.
By willows, lazily sitting alone,
Under flowers,困倦 lying across.
Waiting for magpies hidden by fences,
Listening to crickets crouched by steps.
By branches, catching dancing butterflies,
Near trees, seizing chirping cicadas.
Flat isles crossed on stilts,
Layered cliffs scaled showing agility.
Tender moss bearing small cart tracks,
Deep snow preserving完整的 footprints.
Pointing together at clouds rising from peaks,
Shouting in unison at the moon climbing the sky.
Ant nests sought along paths to dig,
Beehives around steps filled in.
Woodcutter's songs echoing from deep ridges,
Flute songs descending to distant rivers.
Stacking wood to build house frames,
Mixing earth to make盘筵。
Dangerously piling high terrace stones,
Precariously挑着峻塔 bricks.
Suddenly climbing neighbor's trees,
Leaping onto backyard pond boats.
Xiàng Tuó acclaimed as teacher's day,
Gān Luó becoming chancellor's year.
In enlightened times, virtue should prevail,
I urge you to reduce your wild frenzy."
Wéi Zhuāng
When Wéi Zhuāng was young,
he often lived in Xiàguī County, Huázhōu,
and frequently played with children from neighboring lanes.
After the Guǎngmíng rebellion,
he passed through his old neighborhood again,
recalling past events,
only traces remained.
Thus, he composed a poem to record this.
Also, while traveling, he encountered the Lǐ family brothers,
and also wrote a poem reflecting on the past.
The poem about Xiàguī reads:
"In childhood,
childhood originally had a repeated character,
deleted according to the Ming manuscript and Xǔ edition
ignorant of sorrow,
I idly rode bamboo horses around the county.
Once sneaked out of the city to view flowers,
also skipped school to briefly climb towers.
Inviting townsfolk to come and get drunk,
only when the teacher left would I rest.
Today, old friends are nowhere to be found,
only setting sun and withered grass over desolate mounds."
The poem on encountering the Lǐ brothers reads:
"West of the imperial canal, a vermilion-gated estate,
I remember the good brothers of that time.
At dawn, by willow shade, riding bamboo horses,
at night, by lamplight, teasing the teacher.
Patrolling streets chasing butterflies, clothes torn,
climbing roofs探雛手脚轻。
Today we meet, all grown old,
worrying over family and country, all are now ministers."
Yuè Guǎng
In Jin, Yuè Lìng Guǎng's daughter married the great general, Prince of Chéngdū, Sīmǎ Yǐng.
The prince's elder brother, Prince of Chángshā, Sīmǎ Yì,
held power in Luòyáng,
and thus raised armies against each other.
The Prince of Chángshā was close to petty men,
and distanced himself from noble men.
All those at court
lived in fear and apprehension.
Yuè Lìng, being esteemed at court,
and additionally connected by marriage,
was slandered by petty men to the Prince of Chángshā.
The prince once questioned
questioned originally was heard,
corrected according to the Ming manuscript
Yuè Lìng,
who remained calm and composed,
and slowly replied:
"Would Guǎng trade five sons for one daughter?"
From then on, the prince was relieved,
and harbored no further suspicions.
From *A New Account of the Tales of the World*
Liú Rénguǐ
During the Tang Dynasty, Liú Rénguǐ served as Left Vice Director,
and Dài Zhìdé served as Right Vice Director.
People generally praised Liú and looked down upon Dài.
Once, an old woman came to submit a petition.
Just as Dài Zhìdé was about to write a response,
the old woman looked around and asked:
"Is this Vice Director Liú?
Or Vice Director Dài?"
Those around her answered that it was Vice Director Dài.
She hurried forward and said:
"This is the Vice Director who doesn't understand matters.
Give me back my petition."
Dài Zhìdé laughed,
and ordered it be returned to her.
Vice Director Dài left no remarkable achievements during his tenure,
and at court, he seemed incapable of speech.
After his death,
Emperor Gāozōng sighed:
"Since I lost Zhìdé,
I hear nothing further.
When he was alive,
if there was anything improper,
he never let me get away with it."
He then brought out the memorials Dài had submitted,
filling a whole chest.
Reading them, he shed tears,
and the court began to honor Dài's memory.
From "Guó Shǐ Yì Zuǎn" (Anecdotes from the National History).
Lóu Shīdé
Nàyán Lóu Shīdé,
a native of Zhèngzhōu,
served as Minister of War.
On a mission to Bīngzhōu,
the county magistrates from the bordering areas followed him.
When they reached a post station late in the day,
fearing they would trouble the station staff,
he ordered everyone to eat together in the main hall.
The Minister's rice was white and fine,
while the others' rice was black and coarse.
He summoned the station master and reprimanded him:
"Why are you treating guests with two different standards?"
The station master was terrified
and replied:
"We happened to run out of polished rice unexpectedly.
I deserve death for this."
The Minister said:
"A guest may arrive suddenly, but a host cannot prepare suddenly.
What harm is there?"
He then exchanged his fine rice for the coarse rice and ate it.
While inspecting military farms,
he went to Liángzhōu.
A fellow townsman surnamed Lóu, who served as a garrison officer,
had committed corruption.
The Regional Commander Xǔ Qīnmíng intended to execute him as a warning to others.
The townsman appealed to the Minister,
hoping to be saved.
The Minister said:
"When one violates the national law,
even if it were my own son,
I could not spare him,
let alone him."
The next day, at a banquet,
the Commander and the Minister
sat together discussing the violation of national law.
The Minister
(The original text had the character 'wèi' before 'Minister'.
Deleted according to Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi, vol. 5.)
said:
"I heard someone violated the national law,
and it's said he is from my hometown.
I truly do not recognize him,
I only herded cattle with his father when we were children.
Commander, please do not relax the national law on my account."
The Commander immediately ordered the man brought in without shackles.
The Minister sternly rebuked him:
"You left your parents
to seek an official post.
You failed to remain honest and clean.
What more can be said?"
He handed him a plate of dumplings, saying:
"Eat up,
and go be a well-fed ghost!"
The Commander then spared him.
Later, he served as Nàyán and participated in state affairs.
Again
(Míng manuscript has 'yòu' instead of 'fù'.)
while inspecting military farms,
he was about to depart on a journey.
He advised his attendants to set out early.
Lóu had a foot ailment,
and while waiting for his horse to arrive,
he sat on a horizontal beam outside the Guāngzhèng Gate.
Shortly after,
a county magistrate,
unaware he was the Nàyán,
upon introducing himself,
sat down beside him.
The magistrate had a servant
who observed from afar,
ran over and reported:
"It's the Nàyán."
The magistrate was greatly alarmed,
stood up and said:
"I deserve death."
The Nàyán said:
"People may not know each other.
By what law is this a capital offense?"
The magistrate then complained:
There was a Zuǒ Yì,
who, due to his old age and poor eyesight, petitioned for dismissal.
I can write memorials at night as well,
my eyes are truly not dim.
The Nàyán said:
"You claim you can write memorials at night,
so why can't you recognize the Prime Minister in broad daylight?"
The magistrate, greatly ashamed, said:
"I beg the Nàyán not to mention this to the Prime Minister.
The Nàyán said, 'Námófó, I will not speak of it.'"
His attendants all laughed.
On a mission to Língzhōu,
after finishing a meal at a post station,
he called for his horse.
The administrative assistant reported
that even plain water could not be obtained from the station household,
and they were completely uncooperative.
The Nàyán said:
"Shīdé has already mounted his horse,
I will handle this for you."
He went and summoned the station master, reprimanding him:
"What difference is there between the administrative assistant and the Nàyán?
Why do you not provide supplies?
Bring the rod."
The station master, terrified, prostrated himself.
The Nàyán said:
"I want to give you a beating,
but a high official beating a station officer
is a trivial matter,
and would only tarnish my reputation.
If I report this to your prefecture or county,
you would not keep your life.
I will let it go for now."
The station officer knelt, kowtowed, sweating profusely,
and fled in disarray.
Lóu watched him go,
and said to the administrative assistant:
"I have straightened things out for you."
Everyone marveled and sighed.
His conduct was often like this.
Fúxiūzǐ commented:
Sīmǎ Huī and Liú Kuān
could not surpass him.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi" (Records from Court and Country).
Lǐ Zhāodé served as Nèishǐ,
and Shīdé served as Nàyán.
They entered court together.
Lóu, being portly, walked slowly.
Lǐ repeatedly looked back and waited,
but he did not catch up.
Lǐ finally became angry and said:
How
(Míng manuscript has 'pǒ'.)
intolerable is this bumpkin!
Lóu heard this,
and laughed, saying:
"If Shīdé is not a bumpkin,
then who is?"
When Shīdé's brother was appointed Prefect of Dàizhōu,
and was about to depart,
Shīdé said to him:
"I, despite my lack of talent,
hold the position of Prime Minister.
Now you have also obtained a governorship.
This excessive favor
will incur others' jealousy.
How will you preserve the body and skin inherited from our ancestors?"
His brother knelt upright and said:
"From now on,
even if someone spits in my face,
I will not dare to speak,
I will merely wipe it off.
By disciplining myself thus,
I hope not to cause you worry."
Shīdé said:
"That is precisely what worries me.
When someone spits on you,
it is because they are angry.
If you wipe it off now,
you show you dislike the spit.
Disliking it and wiping it off
goes against their anger.
If you do not wipe the spit,
it will dry by itself.
How about that?"
His brother laughed and accepted the advice.
During Empress Wǔ's reign,
he ultimately maintained favor and position.
From "Guó Shǐ Yì Zuǎn" (Anecdotes from the National History).
Lǐ Jì
Duke Yīng of the Táng, Lǐ Jì, served as Minister of Works
and participated in government affairs.
A foreign official who had been rejected in the selection process
came to bid farewell to Duke Yīng.
The Duke said:
"Come see me early tomorrow morning
at the court hall."
At the appointed time, he arrived,
with the Directors and Vice Directors present nearby.
The foreign official came to take his leave,
and Duke Yīng, frowning, said to him:
"You have long been ignorant of how to serve the Ministers and Vice Ministers;
I, an old man, am illiterate,
and have nothing to teach you.
How could you possibly stay?
I am deeply ashamed before you.
Strive hard and go well."
The Vice Ministers and others were alarmed and fearful,
and hastily asked for his name.
They ordered him to check the list at the Southern Bureau,
and shortly after, he was brought in
and assigned to a clerk position in the Ministry of Personnel.
When Duke Yīng was serving as Chancellor,
a fellow villager once visited his residence.
He prepared a meal for the guest,
who tore off the edge of a pancake.
Duke Yīng said:
"You are too young.
This pancake—
the land was plowed twice until fertile,
seeds were sown, weeded, and hoed,
harvested, threshed, and winnowed,
ground and sifted into flour,
and only then made into a pancake.
For a young man to tear off its edge—
what kind of behavior is this?
Here it may still be tolerable,
but if before His Majesty,
you were to act like this,
you might very well lose your head."
The guest was greatly ashamed and frightened.
Fúxiūzǐ said:
During the Yǔwén dynasty,
Huàzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Pí
had a guest who tore off the edge of a pancake.
Pí said:
"This pancake required great effort
before it could enter your mouth.
Since you tore it,
you must not be hungry yet,
so please put it down."
The guest was stunned.
Also, when an imperial envoy brought food to Pí,
the attendant cut the melon skin too thickly
and threw it on the ground.
Pí picked it up from the ground
and ate it,
leaving the attendant utterly terrified and breathless.
Nowadays, frivolous young men tear pancake edges
or cut melons too deep into the flesh,
thinking themselves sons of high officials,
but this is something sensible people never do.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Lǐ Rìzhī
Lǐ Rìzhī, Minister of Justice in the Táng, from his time as a local official in the capital region,
never administered corporal punishment,
and his affairs were successfully accomplished.
When he became Minister of Justice,
there was a clerk who, three days after receiving an imperial decree,
forgot to carry it out.
The Minister called for a rod and had the clerk stripped,
summoned all the clerks together,
and intended to punish him.
He reprimanded him, saying:
"I want to give you a beating,
but I fear people everywhere will say of you,
'He provoked Lǐ Rìzhī's anger,
and suffered Lǐ Rìzhī's rod.'
You would no longer be a man,
and even your wife and children would not respect you."
So he released him.
From then on, no clerk dared to offend.
If there were delays or mistakes,
everyone would collectively reprimand the offender.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Lú Chéngqìng
Minister Lú Chéngqìng,
in the early years of the Zǒngzhāng era, evaluated all officials, both internal and external.
There was an official in charge of grain transport
who lost rice due to a storm.
Rice (original text said "water," corrected according to the Míng dynasty manuscript)
Lú evaluated him, saying:
"Supervising transport and losing grain—
evaluation: middle-low."
The man's demeanor remained composed,
and he withdrew without a word.
Lú, impressed by his composure,
changed the evaluation to "beyond his control,"
rating him middle-middle.
He showed neither joy
nor words of shame.
Lú changed it again, saying:
"Undaunted by favor or disgrace,
he may be rated middle-high."
From "Guóshǐ Yìzuǎn"
Péi Miǎn
Lǐ Qíwù,
in the early Tiānbǎo era, served as Cìshǐ of Shǎnzhōu.
He cleared the dangerous Dǐzhù rocks,
and an iron plowshare found in the stone bore the characters "píng lù,"
so he changed the name of Héběi County to Pínglù County.
Qíwù was narrow-minded and impatient,
and once publicly humiliated Shǎnxiàn Wèi Péi Miǎn on the main road of the city,
earning the disdain of the scholarly elite.
Later, when Miǎn became Chancellor,
he appointed Qíwù as a Crown Prince's Advisor.
People at the time praised Miǎn for not seeking personal revenge.
From "Tánbīn Lù"
Guō Zǐyí
Guō Zǐyí served as Zhōngshū Lìng (Head of the Secretariat).
The Army Supervisor Yú Cháo'ēn invited him to visit the Zhāngjìng Temple,
and Zǐyí agreed.
The Chancellor, concerned that they were not on good terms,
sent an official to hint,
urging him not to go.
An official from Bīn hurriedly informed Lord Guō,
saying that the Army Supervisor intended to harm him,
and also informed the various generals.
Shortly after,
Cháo'ēn's messenger arrived.
As Zǐyí was about to depart,
three hundred soldiers, wearing concealed armor, requested to accompany him.
Zǐyí angrily said:
"I am a high minister.
Unless he has a secret imperial decree,
how dare he harm me!
If it is by the Son of Heaven's command,
what could you all do?
He went alone with only a dozen or so servants.
Cháo'ēn awaited him and,
surprised, said:
"Why is your entourage so small?"
Zǐyí replied with what he had heard.
And said:
"I feared troubling your concern."
Cháo'ēn clasped his chest and hands,
sobbing and shedding tears, saying:
"If not for your magnanimity,
would there not have been suspicion?"
From the "Tán Bīn Lù."
Zǐyí feared that his high merit would go unrewarded.
Palace eunuchs, jealous of his achievements,
had thieves in Huàzhōu
dig up the graves of his ancestors.
His subordinate general Lǐ Huáiguāng and others were furious,
wanting to seek out and capture the culprits.
When Zǐyí entered to report to the emperor,
during the audience,
he only wept and blamed himself.
He then memorialized:
"I lead troops
on campaigns abroad,
often lasting years.
I have caused the deaths of many people's brothers,
killed many people's fathers.
There are many righteous men
who wish to stab me in the belly.
Now that this disgrace has occurred,
it is fitting retribution.
(The original text had 'xìng' for 'gū';
amended according to the Ming manuscript.)
But my heart is for the state,
and even in death I have no regrets."
From then on, both inside and outside the court, all were in awe and could not fathom him.
His son Guō Hóngguǎng often had the family mansion in Qīnrén Lǐ widely opened.
People from the alleys, petty traders,
up to sons of nobles and officials,
could come and go without question.
It was said:
Lady Wáng and her beloved daughter Zhào shì,
while making up and facing the mirror,
often when generals and officers under his command went out to garrison,
or when officials,
were summoned,
they were ordered to fetch water and hold towels,
treated no differently from servants.
One day,
his sons and nephews anxiously advised him,
but he did not respond three times.
Then they continued with tears, saying:
"Your achievements are already accomplished,
yet you do not exalt yourself.
Both the noble and the lowly
roam your private chambers.
We think even Yī Yǐn and Huò Guāng would not have acted thus."
He smiled and said to them:
"You all truly do not understand.
I receive official provisions for five hundred horses,
and rations for a thousand men.
Advancing, I have nowhere to go;
retreating, I have no base.
If I were to build high walls and lock the gates,
cutting off inside from outside,
resentment would arise.
They would frame me for disloyalty,
and those greedy for merit and envious of ability
would accomplish their schemes.
Then my entire clan would be ground to dust,
and regret would be too late.
Now, with openness and no barriers,
the four gates wide open,
even if slander arises,
it cannot add anything.
This is why I act thus."
All his sons bowed in acceptance.
According to the Guō family's old history:
Xīn Yúnjǐng once served as an official under the young master.
Later, he was appointed Dūdū of Tánzhōu.
When about to take leave,
for several days he could not get an audience.
Lady Wáng and her beloved daughter Zhào shì said to Yúnjǐng:
"You are leaving,
I will speak for you to the Lìnggōng."
Yúnjǐng bowed in the courtyard.
Lady Wáng, applying powder inside,
said:
"I am very pleased,
and glad you have a place to earn your keep."
Zhào shì's daughter washed her hands by the steps,
ordering Yúnjǐng to fetch water.
Lady Wáng said:
"Let him go."
Only then did Yúnjǐng hurry away.
(Ming manuscript: Guō family's old history written as Guō family's old official.)
In the first year of Yǒngtài,
Púgù Huái'ēn died.
Various foreign tribes invaded the capital region.
Zǐyí led troops to resist them.
Reaching Jīngyáng,
the enemy had already assembled.
Zǐyí led two thousand armored soldiers in and out.
The enemy saw and asked:
"Who is that?"
The reply came:
"Lìnggōng Guō."
The Huíhé said:
"Is Lìnggōng still alive?
(Original had 'yuē' for 'hū';
amended according to the Ming manuscript.)
Huái'ēn told us
the Heavenly Khān had abandoned the realm,
Lìnggōng had passed away,
and China had no ruler,
so we came.
Now Lìnggōng is here,
is the Heavenly Khān alive?"
Zǐyí replied:
"The Emperor lives ten thousand years without end."
The Huíhé all said:
"Huái'ēn deceived us."
Zǐyí sent someone to explain.
The Huíhé said:
"If Lìnggōng is truly here,
how can we see him?"
Zǐyí went out.
The generals all said:
"The barbarians cannot be trusted.
We beg you not to go."
Zǐyí said:
"The enemy outnumbers us dozens of times.
Our strength cannot match them now.
What can we do?
But utmost sincerity moves even gods,
let alone barbarians."
The generals requested selecting five hundred armored cavalry as escort.
Zǐyí said:
"That would only cause harm."
When the call went out:
"Lìnggōng is coming!"
At first they doubted.
All held weapons and watched intently.
Zǐyí then slowly emerged with several dozen riders,
removed his helmet, and greeted them:
"Are you well?
We long shared loyalty and righteousness,
how did it come to this?"
The Huíhé all laid down their weapons and dismounted, saying:
"He is our father."
Zǐyí was over six feet tall,
with handsome and outstanding appearance.
In Língwǔ, he was appointed Píngzhāng Shì (Participant in Determining Government Matters),
enfeoffed as Prince of Fényáng,
and made Zhōng
(Original had 'píng' for 'zhōng';
amended according to the Ming manuscript.)
shū Lìng.
His portrait was placed in the Língyān Gé,
he was given the title Shàngfù,
and was enshrined in the Dàizōng temple.
He had eight sons,
seven sons-in-law,
all holding high offices.
His son Guō Ài
married Princess Shēngpíng.
He had several dozen grandchildren.
Whenever the students came to pay respects,
he merely nodded.
He served his sovereign with utmost loyalty,
and was lenient and generous to his subordinates.
Whenever a city or town surrendered,
he always achieved his aims wherever he went.
He repeatedly suffered from the slanders of favored ministers like Chéng Yuánzhèn and Yú Cháo'ēn,
who accused him in countless ways.
At times when he commanded strong armies,
or faced enemies on the battlefield,
if an imperial edict summoned him,
he never hesitated due to personal danger.
He also enjoyed heavenly fortune,
He ultimately avoided calamity.
Tián Chéngsì was then acting arrogantly,
ruthless and insolent, showing no courtesy.
Guó Zǐyí once sent an envoy to Wèizhōu,
and Chéngsì would gaze from afar and bow,
pointing to his knee and saying to the envoy:
"This knee has not bent to anyone for so many years,
yet today it bows for you, sir."
Among his veteran generals, such as Lǐ Huáiguāng and others, numbering several dozen,
all were nobles and high-ranking officials,
yet Zǐyí directed them with a wave of his hand, advancing or retreating as if they were servants or slaves.
Initially, he and Guō Zǐyí were equally renowned.
Although his military prowess and strategy were not as evident,
his generosity and magnanimity won people over even more.
His annual official salary amounted to 240,000 strings of cash,
not including his private income.
His residence was in the Qīnrén Ward,
occupying one-fourth of the area,
with access to a long alleyway.
His household consisted of three thousand people,
and those coming and going
could not tell where he lived.
Emperor Dàizōng did not address him by name,
but referred to him as "the great minister."
For nearly twenty years, the safety and stability of the empire hinged on his survival.
He served as Zhōngshū Lìng for twenty-four years.
His power overshadowed the entire realm, yet the court harbored no jealousy;
his achievements surpassed his generation, yet the sovereign harbored no suspicion;
he indulged in the extremes of human desires, yet gentlemen did not condemn him.
Wealth, honor, longevity, and prosperity,
flourishing and peaceful,
throughout his life, the pinnacle of human relations was complete without deficiency.
He passed away at the age of eighty-five.
From "Tán Bīn Lù."
Sòng Zé
Sòng Zé's household servant, while handling a crossbow, had the string snap,
accidentally killing Sòng Zé's son.
Sòng Zé did not punish him.
From "Dú Yì Zhì."
Lù Xiàngxiān
Táng dynasty Lù Yǎngōng Xiàngxiān served as the prefect of Tóngzhōu.
A household servant encountered a military advisor without dismounting from his horse.
The military advisor wanted to make an issue of it,
whipped the servant's back until it bled,
and said:
"This lowly official has offended you, sir.
I request to be dismissed."
Yǎngōng calmly said to him:
"When a servant sees an official and does not dismount,
you may beat him, or
you may not beat him.
Now that you, the official, have beaten him,
you may leave, or
you may not leave."
The military advisor, unable to fathom his meaning, withdrew.
From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ."
Yuán Zǎi
Yú Cháo'ēn sat on a high seat in the Guózǐ Jiàn to lecture on the "Yì Jīng,"
exhaustively discussing the "Dǐng" hexagram,
in order to humiliate Yuán Zǎi and Wáng Jìn.
That day,
all the officials were present.
Jìn could not bear the insult,
but Zǎi remained composed and cheerful.
Cháo'ēn later remarked:
"Anger is a common emotion,
but laughter is unfathomable."
From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ."
Dǒng Jìn
Dǒng Jìn and Dòu Shēn served together as officials.
At that time, political decisions rested with Dòu Shēn,
while Jìn merely obeyed imperial decrees and assented.
Later, Dòu Shēn became arrogant and overstepped his authority, offending the emperor.
Emperor Dézōng gradually grew to dislike him.
Shēn hinted to Jìn,
asking him to petition for the appointment of Dòu Shēn (the imperial attendant) as Vice Minister of Personnel.
The emperor sternly said:
"Was it not Dòu Shēn who sent you to submit this petition?"
Jìn dared not conceal the truth.
The emperor then inquired about Shēn's faults,
and Jìn reported them in detail.
Within ten days,
Shēn was demoted.
Jìn repeatedly submitted memorials resigning from office,
was relieved of his position as chancellor,
and appointed Minister of War.
Soon after, he was assigned as the留守 (commander) of the eastern capital.
At that time, the military governor of Biànzhōu, Lǐ Wànróng, was gravely ill,
and his son instigated a rebellion.
Jìn was appointed as the military governor of Biànzhōu.
After receiving the appointment,
he took only a dozen or so aides and attendants,
and did not summon any troops.
Upon reaching Zhèngzhōu,
no military officers or officials from Biànzhōu had come to meet him.
Jìn's aides and the officials of Zhèngzhōu were all fearful,
and together they advised Jìn, saying:
"The capital commissioner, Dèng Wéigōng, should have come to welcome you.
Taking advantage of Wànróng's critical illness,
he has assumed command of military affairs.
Now that you, sir, have arrived here,
he still does not send anyone to welcome you.
What are his intentions? It is impossible to guess.
We fear you should temporarily avoid him
and wait to see how the situation develops."
Jìn said:
"I have received an imperial decree to serve as military governor of Biànzhōu,
and I am to proceed to my post in accordance with the decree.
How can I act recklessly and delay?"
Everyone worried about unforeseen dangers,
but Jìn alone remained calm and unperturbed.
When they were still several dozen lǐ from Biànzhōu,
Dèng Wéigōng finally came to welcome them.
Jìn allowed him to remain on horseback.
After entering the city,
he still entrusted military affairs to Wéigōng.
Wéigōng tried to gauge Jìn's disposition,
but could not fathom his depth.
Initially, after Wànróng had expelled Liú Shìníng,
he succeeded him as military governor
and entrusted military authority to Wéigōng.
When Wànróng fell critically ill,
Wéigōng intended to submit to the court.
Wéigōng believed he should rightfully succeed to the position,
so he did not send officials to welcome Jìn,
hoping to intimidate and unsettle him,
and make him afraid to advance.
He did not expect Jìn to arrive so quickly.
Jìn's swift arrival
(The Ming manuscript does not include the four characters "Jìn's swift arrival.")
stayed nearby.
Only then did he come to welcome him,
but he remained resentful in his heart.
Wéigōng, due to his arrogance and disregard for the law,
secretly plotted treason.
He was exiled to Lǐngnán.
The court, fearing Jìn was too gentle and weak,
soon appointed Lù Chángyuán, the prefect of Rǔzhōu,
as Jìn's行军司马 (military advisor).
Jìn was generous and tolerant,
humble, respectful, simple, and frugal.
He often followed established practices, which was mostly acceptable,
and the military was relatively stable.
Chángyuán, however, was increasingly ostentatious in his actions,
requesting to change old regulations
and insisting on strict and harsh measures.
Jìn initially agreed to everything,
but once the documents were prepared,
he would then postpone the changes.
He also entrusted financial and grain management
(计 originally written as 许,
corrected according to the "Táng Shū," biography of Dǒng Jìn, vol. 155.)
to his aide Mèng Shūdù,
who was frivolous
and enjoyed belittling and insulting soldiers,
so everyone despised him.
Jìn died in office.
Ten days after his death,
Biànzhōu fell into great turmoil.
Chángyuán and Shūdù were killed,
and the soldiers cut their bodies into pieces and ate them.
Chángyuán was frivolous in speech and lacked dignified bearing.
From the time he arrived in Biànzhōu,
he was not respected by the military and the prefecture.
When Dǒng Jìn was critically ill,
he ordered Chángyuán to take over his duties.
Chángyuán then publicly declared:
"Many civil and military officers are negligent and disrespectful.
They cannot uphold laws and regulations.
They must all be disciplined according to the law."
Thus, everyone resented and feared him.
Shūdù was also harsh by nature,
and indulged in sensual pleasures.
He frequently visited the entertainment quarters,
frolicking with various women,
and called himself "Brother Mèng."
Thus, people looked down on him and despised him.
From "Tán Bīn Lù."
Péi Dù
Peì Jìngōng Dù served as Vice Director of the Chancellery,
passing by the Ministry of Personnel where officials were being selected.
He said to the Supervising Secretary who was passing by with him:
"We have been exceedingly fortunate,
while these people merely gain an extra rank or half a rank—
what is there to inquire about?
One's lifetime is predetermined, never to be reconsidered."
The Duke did not believe in divination or numerology,
nor did he favor consuming elixirs.
He often told people:
"Chicken, pork, fish, garlic—
when encountered, eat them;
birth, aging, sickness, death—
when the time comes, proceed."
His broad-mindedness and magnanimity were all of this kind.
From Yīnhuà Lù.
Also, when Duke Jìn was in the Secretariat,
his attendants suddenly reported that the official seal was missing.
Those who heard this all turned pale.
Dù immediately ordered a banquet to be laid out and music to be played.
People did not understand the reason,
and secretly found it strange.
In the middle of the night, as the banquet was in full swing,
the attendants again reported that the seal was present.
Dù did not reply,
and the festivities concluded with great joy.
Someone asked Dù about the reason,
and Dù said:
"This was merely the work of clerks stealing the seal to stamp documents.
If handled slowly, it would be preserved;
if pressed urgently, they would throw it into fire or water,
and it would never be recovered."
People at the time admired his magnanimity,
his unwavering composure in handling affairs.
From Yùquánzǐ.
Yú Dí.
Zhèng Tàimù, a Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel, served as Prefect of Jīnzhōu.
He sent a letter to Minister of Works Yú Dí of Xiāngyáng.
Zhèng was arrogant and self-assured,
as if showing no respect due to a regional governor.
The letter said:
"Your Excellency is the great roc of the southern seas,
a pillar supporting the heavens.
When you soar, the sun and moon darken;
when you stir, mountains and peaks crumble.
Truly the talons and teeth of the Son of Heaven,
the mirror and model for the feudal lords.
Tàimù, with over two hundred dependents, young and old,
suffers hunger and cold in the two capitals.
The salary of a small prefecture is meager,
yet I must manage food and clothing frugally.
Grant me one thousand strings of cash,
one thousand bolts of silk,
one thousand taels of utensils,
one thousand shí of rice,
and ten male and female servants each.
And I say:
'Take one leaf's shade from a thousand trees—
it still forms dense shade.
Subtract a few drops of water from the four seas—
it still becomes abundant moisture.'"
Duke Yú read the letter,
yet showed no surprise or dismay.
He said:
"What Governor Zhèng requests,
I will grant half of each amount stated,
as in this time of military expenses,
I cannot fully satisfy his original hopes."
There was also the hermit Fú Dài of Mount Lú,
who sent a young boy with a letter several feet long,
begging for a million cash to purchase a mountain.
The Duke then gave it to him,
along with items like paper, ink, and clothing.
There was also Scholar Cuī Jiāo, who resided by the Hàn River,
well-versed in literature and arts,
yet his family resources were exhausted.
Before long, he had an affair with his aunt's maid,
often indulging in unrestrained passion like Ruǎn Xián.
The maid was graceful and beautiful,
richly talented in music and performance,
the most exquisite in the region south of the Hàn River.
His aunt was poor,
and sold the maid to the Regional Commander,
who adored her.
Considering her peerless,
he paid four hundred thousand cash,
and his fondness for her grew ever deeper.
Jiāo longed for her incessantly,
and boldly approached the commander's residence,
hoping to see her once.
The maid happened to go out during the Cold Food Festival,
and encountered Jiāo standing under the shade of a willow.
From her horse, she wept continuously,
vowing love as enduring as mountains and rivers.
Cuī composed a poem for her, saying:
"Princes and nobles pursue the dust behind her,
Lǜ Zhū sheds tears upon her silk scarf.
Once entering the noble's gate, deep as the sea,
from then on, Xiāo Láng is but a stranger."
Someone who envied Jiāo
wrote the poem on a seat.
Duke Yú saw the poem,
and ordered Cuī to be summoned.
His attendants could not fathom the reason.
Jiāo was deeply anxious and regretful,
yet had nowhere to hide.
When he met Jiāo,
Yú shook his hand and said:
"'Once entering the noble's gate, deep as the sea,
from then on, Xiāo Láng is but a stranger.'
Is this your composition?
Four hundred thousand is trivial—
why begrudge a letter,
not showing it to me earlier?"
He then ordered the maid to return with him.
As for the curtains, boxes, and toiletries,
he had them all enhanced and adorned,
modestly enriching Cuī.
Earlier, a guest came from Línglíng,
praising a skilled singer at Governor Róng Yù's banquet.
The Duke of Xiāngyáng immediately ordered her summoned.
Governor Róng did not dare disobey,
and she arrived after over a month.
When she arrived,
he ordered her to sing.
The song turned out to be Governor Róng's poem bidding farewell to the entertainer.
The Duke said:
"A true man cannot achieve meritorious deeds
to be praised by later generations—
how could he seize another's beloved companion
for his own amusement?"
He then gave her much silk and fabric for her journey,
and personally wrote a letter apologizing to the Governor of Línglíng.
Yún Xīzǐ said:
"Wáng Dūn drove away female entertainers to supply his soldiers;
Yáng Sù returned Dé Yán's wife.
Those who are not greedy with wealth
and not stingy with beauty are rare."
People of the time regarded this as an elegant tale.
Reviewing the outstanding heroes among chancellors,
none compare to the Duke of Xiāngyáng.
Governor Róng's poem said:
"Precious hairpins, fragrant moth-eyebrows, kingfisher skirt,
adorned, she hides tears, about to drift like clouds.
Earnestly seek to please the King of Xiāng's intent,
do not dream of the governor at the sunny terrace."
From Yún Xī Yǒu Yì.
Wǔ Yuánhéng.
When Vice Director of the Chancellery Wǔ went to Xīchuān,
a grand banquet was held.
Attendant Yáng Sìfù, wild with drink,
pressured Yuánhéng to drink a large goblet.
When he refused to drink,
Yáng poured wine over him.
Yuánhéng clasped his hands and remained motionless.
After the dousing,
he slowly rose to change clothes,
and never called for the banquet to end.
From Gān Zǎizǐ.
Lǐ Shēn.
Chancellor Lǐ Shēn was stationed in Huáinán.
Court Gentleman Zhāng Yòuxīn had been dismissed from his post in the southern commandery,
and there had long been a rift between him and Lǐ,
the details of which are recorded elsewhere.
At that time, while traveling on the Jīng River, he encountered a storm,
and his two sons were swept away and drowned.
In the midst of his grief and sorrow,
he also feared that Lǐ would seek revenge against him.
He therefore sent a lengthy letter to confess and apologize.
Lǐ deeply pitied him,
and replied in a letter:
"As for the uncompromising words at Duān Creek,
I, in my foolishness, bear no grudge.
Regarding the tragic disaster of drowning at Jīng Bank,
I, in my humble way, am truly filled with compassion."
He then treated Zhāng with great kindness,
showing not the slightest hint of resentment.
Zhāng, moved to tears, expressed his gratitude,
and his worries dissipated as if they were old friends again.
Whenever Lǐ feasted and drank with Zhāng,
he would ensure they reached the peak of joy and intoxication.
Zhāng had once served as an assistant in Guǎnglíng,
where there was a singing girl who had shown him affection,
but he ultimately did not take her as his own.
Now, twenty years later,
she was still present at the banquet.
Gazing at Zhāng with melancholy,
she seemed on the verge of tears.
Lǐ rose to excuse himself,
and Zhāng dipped his finger in wine,
writing a verse on the tray.
The girl understood it perfectly.
When Lǐ returned,
Zhāng held his cup, looking unhappy.
Lǐ noticed this,
and immediately ordered the girl to sing to accompany the wine.
She then sang these lines:
"Like clouds and rain, we parted for twenty years;
back then, seeking dreams, I could not sleep.
Now, with hair turned white, we meet again,
and still ascend King Xiāng's tortoiseshell feast."
Zhāng returned home drunk,
and Lǐ commanded the girl to go with him.
From "Běnshì Shī".
Also, Minister Shàngshū Liú Yǔxī was dismissed from Hézhōu
and appointed Gentleman of Receptions.
Academician of the Jíxián Institute, Lǐ Shēn, having left his military command, was in the capital.
Admiring Liú's reputation,
he once invited him to his residence,
and lavishly prepared food and drink.
When the wine was flowing freely,
he ordered a beautiful singing girl to perform to accompany the drinking.
Liú, from his seat, composed a poem:
"Hair coiled high in palace style, adorned with makeup,
a spring breeze melody of Dù Wéiniáng.
To the Minister of Works, such sights are commonplace,
yet they break the heart of this Jiāngnán Prefect."
Lǐ then gave the girl to him as a gift.
The character "䰀鬌" can also be written as "浮喧".
Both are read with rising tones.
According to ancient and modern commentaries,
it refers to the lingering image of a 'fallen horse' hairstyle.
From "Běnshì Shī".
In "Běnshì Shī", "浮喧" is written as "低墮".
Lú Xié
The late Chancellor Lú Xié, while serving as Investigating Censor,
on the day Vice Censor-in-Chief Guī Rénshào first took up his post,
sent a message to Lú, saying:
"When you returned from handling affairs east of the Zhè River,
how did forty bolts of damask come to be in your saddlebag?
Please leave the Censorate."
Later, Lú was appointed Magistrate of Luòyáng County,
then soon transferred to be Prefect of Zhèngzhōu,
and was summoned to the capital as Remonstrance Advisor.
Upon reaching the capital,
he was appointed Vice Minister of War,
and then became Chancellor.
It was one hundred days from his appointment in Luòyáng to becoming Chancellor.
A few days later,
he asked why he had not seen Vice Minister Guī,
and someone replied:
"The Grand Councillor has taken leave for the grand ceremony."
Lú immediately appointed Guī Rénshào as Minister of War,
greatly pleasing public sentiment.
From "Wén Qí Lù".
Guī Chóngjìng
Guī Chóngjìng was successively promoted to Director of the Bureau of Provisions,
and was appointed as Envoy to Confer the Title on the King of Xīnluó.
While in the middle of the sea,
the waves became swift and fierce,
and the ship began to leak and break.
Everyone was terrified,
and the sailors requested to transfer to a small boat.
Guī Chóngjìng said:
"There are several dozen, even a hundred, people on this ship.
How could I cross alone?"
After a short while,
the waves gradually subsided,
and the entire ship was ultimately spared from disaster.
From "Tán Bīn Lù".
Xiàhóu Zī.
There was a certain Mr. Wáng who was with Xiàhóu Zī in the examination halls.
Mr. Wáng had a high contemporary reputation,
while Xiàhóu Zī was not his equal.
Once, having failed the exams,
they traveled together to Fèngxiáng, west of the capital.
The regional commander provided them lodging.
One day,
an Assistant invited them to a banquet.
When they were merry with drink,
(Míng manuscript adds 'wine' before 'merry'.)
the Assistant made a wish with dice, saying:
"If both you scholars pass the exams next year,
may the dice show the 'Hall Seal'."
Mr. Wáng, proud of his talent and elegance,
wore a look of anticipated success,
and angrily said:
"Am I truly so shallow
as to be in the same year as Xiàhóu Zī?"
He left displeased.
Xiàhóu Zī passed the exams,
and rose through the ranks to become Chancellor.
Mr. Wáng, in the end, never achieved any renown.
When Xiàhóu Zī was in Pǔjīn,
Mr. Wáng's son, unaware of the past circumstances,
happened to obtain over ten letters and notes documenting the past interactions and courtesies between Xiàhóu Zī and his father,
all in Xiàhóu Zī's own handwriting.
Delighted, he took them to visit Xiàhóu Zī.
Xiàhóu Zī received him,
asked what he desired,
and granted all his requests.
He then summoned his various Assistants,
and told them the story.
From "Yù Quán Zǐ".
Chén Jìngxuān
Grand Preceptor Chén Jìngxuān, although he rose improperly to high position,
possessed considerable magnanimity.
From the time he governed Western Chuān,
he entrusted administrative affairs to his secretarial staff,
and military matters to his guard commanders.
Daily, he consumed one steamed dog
and one pot of wine.
He held six formal banquets each month.
He also had five lifelong drinking companions with whom he was intimate.
A single bowl of pickled vegetables
cost thirty thousand cash.
There was once an accusation that the banquet official had stolen money;
he brushed aside the petition and paid it no heed.
There was a camp courtesan named Yù'ér.
The Grand Preceptor offered her a cup of wine,
but she refused to drink it,
and accidentally spilled it on the Grand Preceptor,
staining his head and face.
He promptly rose to change clothes.
Those around him were alarmed and worried,
expecting Yù'ér to be immediately ground to mincemeat.
After changing, he came out,
resumed his seat,
and again offered her wine.
Yù'ér begged for punishment,
but he laughed and pardoned her.
His tolerance and generosity were generally of this kind.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Gě Zhōu
When the Later Liang's Attendant-in-ordinary Gé Zhōu was stationed in Yǎnzhōu,
he once visited this pavilion.
The Duke had a guard named Jiǎ,
a vigorous young man, unmarried, of striking appearance,
skilled in horsemanship and archery,
with courage and strength surpassing others.
Once, while reporting on a matter,
Duke Gé summoned him in.
At that time, all his concubines were attending by his side.
Among them was a beloved concubine,
a woman of peerless beauty,
who enjoyed exclusive favor and was very pleased with herself,
and was often at the Duke's side.
Jiǎ caught sight of the beloved concubine,
and could not stop gazing at her.
When Duke Gé asked him questions,
even repeatedly,
Jiǎ was still casting sidelong glances at the extraordinary beauty,
and ultimately forgot to reply.
The Duke merely lowered his head.
After the audience concluded,
the Duke gave a slight, knowing smile.
Someone informed Jiǎ of this,
and Jiǎ became fearful,
only saying his mind was confused,
and he also could not recall the instructions the Duke had given.
For several days,
he worried about incurring an unpredictable punishment.
The Duke knew he was deeply anxious,
and received him with a gentle countenance.
Not long after,
an imperial edict ordered the Duke to campaign,
to resist the Táng army by the river.
At that time, they engaged the enemy in a decisive battle.
After several days of fighting,
the enemy army held its formation firm and unmoving.
As dusk fell,
the soldiers were hungry and thirsty,
their faces almost devoid of color.
The Duke then summoned Jiǎ and said to him:
"Can you break this enemy formation?"
Jiǎ said:
"Yes."
He immediately took the reins, mounted his horse,
and with several dozen cavalry charged towards the enemy army,
decapitating several dozen men.
The main army followed,
and the Táng army was utterly defeated.
When Duke Gé returned in triumph,
he said to his beloved concubine:
"He has achieved great military merit,
and deserves a reward.
I shall give you to him as his wife."
The beloved concubine wept and declined the command,
but the Duke urged her, saying:
"To be someone's wife,
is that not better than being someone's concubine?"
He ordered lavish dowry preparations,
worth several thousand strings of cash.
He summoned Jiǎ and told him:
"You performed meritorious service by the river.
I know you are unmarried.
Now I give you So-and-so as your wife,
and additionally appoint you to a ranked position.
This woman is the one you gazed upon."
Jiǎ firmly pleaded guilty to a capital offense,
not daring to accept the command.
The Duke insisted on giving her to him,
and he finally accepted.
Alas!
In ancient times there were ministers whose hat tassels were cut off or who stole horses,
but could they surpass this?
Duke Gé was a famous general of Liáng,
his prestige and fame renowned among the enemy.
A Héběi proverb says:
"In Shāndōng there is a Gé;
if nothing's wrong, don't go provoking him," or so it is said.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà" (Jade Hall Casual Conversations).
General Account of the Jìnshì Examination
The Jìnshì examination,
began during the Suí dynasty's Dàyè era,
and flourished during the Zhēnguàn and Yǒnghuī periods of the Táng.
Even if a gentleman achieved the highest ministerial rank,
if he did not come through the Jìnshì examination,
it was ultimately not considered admirable.
Consequently, the annual tribute of candidates
never fell below eight or nine hundred.
Regarding its esteem,
they were called "white-robed high ministers,"
or also "first-rank white gowns."
Regarding its difficulty,
it was said, "Thirty is old for a Míngjīng,"
"Fifty is young for a Jìnshì."
Those who possessed untrammeled talent,
adaptable methods,
the debating skills of Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí,
the courage of Jīng Kē and Nìè Zhèng,
the martial prowess of Zhòng Yóu,
the strategic planning of Zhāng Liáng,
the bookkeeping and calculation of Sāng Hóngyáng,
or the wit and humor of Dōngfāng Shuò—
all these were obscured by this examination.
They cultivated their persons and acted cautiously,
surpassing even virgins in restraint.
There were those who grew old and died in the examination halls,
yet harbored no regret.
Therefore, there is a poem that says:
"The Tàizōng Emperor's plan was truly far-sighted;
he tricked all the heroes until their hair turned white."
Lǐ Zhào said:
"The Jìnshì has long been esteemed by the age.
Therefore, outstanding men who emerge from it
remain literary men for life.
Thus, the struggle for fame is often intense,
a flaw of the times.
The metropolitan gathering place was called the Examination Grounds;
the general term was Xiùcai;
submitting one's card was called Local Tribute;
obtaining a degree was called Former Jìnshì;
mutual respect and deference was called Seniority;
achieving success together was called Same-Year;
those who recently passed the examination,
but had not yet passed the Guānshì,
were all called Newly Passed Jìnshì.
Therefore, Vice Censor-in-Chief Hán Yí,
often upon hearing that someone had recently passed the Guānshì,
would compose a poem to mark the occasion, saying:
"The short document is handed over to the Three Selection Boards;
do not vex Bìxiān with your new title.
Today you may be called a Former Jìnshì;
better save the spring scenery for next year."
The Ming manuscript has "yì" as "yí".
Also, the Ming manuscript and the Xǔ block-print edition have "jì zhī rì" as "jì zhī yuē",
"zhóu" as "nà",
"jiē" as "shī".
The examining officials were called Masters;
those examined and promoted by the Jīngzhào Prefecture
were called Ranked Candidates;
those presented from outer prefectures without examination
were called Selected Recommendations;
however, Selected Recommendations also required pre-arranging someone to compose the verses,
it was not an unsponsored recommendation.
Mutual guarantees before the examination
were called Joint Guarantee;
gathering privately to compose poems
was called Private Examination;
visiting and petitioning powerful officials
was called Making Connections;
boosting one's reputation and value
was called Networking.
After success,
listing names on the pagoda of Cí'ēn Temple
was called Inscribing Names;
the grand banquet at the Qǔjiāng Pavilion
was called the Qǔjiāng Gathering;
the Qǔjiāng Grand Gathering was after the Guānshì,
and was also called the Good News Banquet.
Later, the Same-Year graduates each went their separate ways,
which could also be called the Farewell Gathering.
The Ming manuscript has "wén" as "guān".
Registration and entry into selection
was called the Spring Tribulation;
getting drunk and full after failure
was called Beating the Felt;
anonymously creating ranked lists
was called Nameless Ones;
withdrawing to study further
was called Passing the Summer;
taking one's studies out
was called Summer Lessons;
smuggling notes into the examination
was called Strategy Diagrams:
this is the general outline.
Its customs depended on the senior graduates,
its regulations resided with the officials.
Nevertheless,
the worthy grasped its greater purpose,
so those who reached the highest ministerial rank
were often two or three out of ten;
those who attained prominent positions were six or seven out of ten.
And among them were Yuán Lùshān and Zhāng Suīyáng,
Liú Guān,
the National History Supplement has "Guān" as "Pì"
Yuán Xiū were among them.
From "Guóshǐ Bǔ" (Supplement to the National History).
The Jìnshì Examination under the Ministry of Rites
The categories such as Jùnxiù and others,
were all administered by the Bureau of Evaluation.
In the twenty-fourth year of the Kāiyuán era,
Assistant Minister Lǐ Áng, by nature intolerant of others,
gathered the tribute scholars and made an agreement with them, saying:
"The beauty or ugliness of the essays,
I am fully aware of.
The evaluation and selection process,
rests upon utmost fairness.
If anyone seeks favor through personal connections,
they shall all be failed."
Lǐ Áng's father-in-law was neighbors and on good terms with Jìnshì Lǐ Quán,
so he spoke to Áng on Quán's behalf.
Áng indeed became angry,
gathered the tribute candidates,
and enumerated Quán's faults.
Quán apologized, saying:
"Someone perhaps knew me superficially,
and privately mentioned me to you,
it was not something I sought."
Áng then said:
"Observing the essays of you gentlemen,
they are indeed beautiful.
However, as the ancients said,
'The flaw is not concealed by the gem,'
is an expression of loyalty.
If there are any phrases that are not elegant,
shall we discuss them together in detail?"
All said:
"Yes."
Quán went out and said to the crowd:
"What he said just now,
his intention was directed at me.
Áng's intention lies here,
I will certainly fail,
so what use is there in relying on this?
He then secretly sought out Áng's flaws.
Another day,
Áng indeed picked out minor flaws in Quán's sentences,
and posted them on the main thoroughfare to humiliate him.
Quán advanced with hands clasped,
and said to Áng:
"Courtesy values reciprocity.
The lack of merit in my humble writing,
I have already heard about.
But your esteemed self, in the past with your elegant compositions,
they were once heard on the roads,
I, in my foolishness, wish to切磋,
may I?"
Áng angrily replied:
"What is there that cannot be done!"
Quán said:
"Ears washed by the clear Wèi River,
heart inclined to the idle white clouds,"
are these not your esteemed self's words?"
Áng said:
"They are."
Quán said:
"In ancient times, Táng Yáo grew old and weary,
tired of ruling the world,
and wished to abdicate to Xǔ Yóu.
Yóu detested hearing of it,
therefore he washed his ears.
Now the Son of Heaven is in the prime of his life,
he is not abdicating to you, sir,
so why do you wash your ears?"
Áng heard this and was alarmed and frightened,
he complained to the authorities,
saying Quán was狂妄 and disrespectful,
and subsequently handed Quán over to the officials.
Initially, Áng was strong and upright,
and did not accept entreaties or requests.
But when he gained powerful position,
(Míng抄本 has 'powerful position' as 'official opinion')
those who sought favors he did not refuse.
Because of this, the court discussion held that the position of a ministry郎官 was too lowly,
and insufficient to command the respect of the many scholars,
so they ordered the Vice Minister of Personnel to take exclusive charge.
From "Zhìyán"
Prefectural Recommendation
Recommendation and dispatch by the Jīngzhào Prefecture,
from the time between the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras.
Generally, the top ten candidates,
were called the 'ranked list'.
They necessarily sought those whose reputation and reality matched,
to nourish the source of education and transformation.
The Vice Minister of Rites relied on this to select them,
and sometimes they all passed the examination.
If not,
seven or eight out of ten succeeded.
If it differed from this,
then they would often send a document to the Examination Bureau,
requesting the reason for the failure.
By the Xiántōng and Qiánfú eras,
it was then吞并 and临制 by powerful families,
almost等同于 passing the examination.
Those who obtained it first boasted and bragged to each other,
their carriages and clothing were大多奢侈 and extravagant,
not considering it presumptuous,
and they still gathered people for social events,
true scholars were no longer considered.
The reason it was abolished and reinstated不定,
was due to this duty.
From "Zhìyán"
Recommendations from Various Prefectures
Recommendations from Tónghuà were no different from Jīngzhào,
if one was首送,
none failed to succeed.
During the Yuánhé era,
Línghú Chǔ governed Sānfēng,
at the time of the autumn examination.
He posted an announcement:
"Specially establishing a five-session examination."
That is, poetry, song, prose, rhapsody, and帖经 made five.
In normal years, those seeking recommendation with清要 poetry topics,
generally numbered no less than ten or more people.
That year, none came,
although some came from afar, a thousand miles away,
hearing this, they all withdrew.
Only Lú Hóngzhèng独自 went to Huà to request examination.
The Duke ordered tents, wine, and food to be provided,
more extravagant than in the past.
The寄客 of Huà all watched from the side.
Hóngzhèng considered himself peerless.
Chǔ ordered one session examined per day,
emphasizing excellence over speed.
Hóngzhèng had already taken two sessions,
when Mǎ Zhí submitted his recommendation状.
Zhí was the son of a military family,
the attendants all secretly laughed.
Chǔ said:
"This cannot yet be known."
Subsequently, they examined the "Rhapsody on Climbing the Mountain to Gather Pearls".
It roughly said:
"The patterned leopard is moreover different from the black dragon,
gathering this is疏矣.
The white stone is also distinct from the old蚌,
cutting cannot obtain it."
Chǔ greatly admired its precision and aptness,
and thus took away Hóngzhèng's position as解头.
Later, Hóngzhèng himself, from Assistant Minister, was appointed to judge the盐铁 monopoly,
and shortly after was supplanted by Zhí.
Hóngzhèng戏弄 Zhí with a handwritten note, saying:
"In former days at Huà,
I already suffered a毒手.
Now coming to the盐务,
I am again hit by an old fist."
(Fist originally written as 'power',
changed according to Míng抄本.)
During the Dàzhōng era,
Hégàn Jùn and Wèi Zhēng contended for the prefectural first place,
and Hégàn屈居 below him.
The next day,

Examination in Miscellaneous Writings
In the first year of the Chuígōng era (685),
Wú Dàogǔ and twenty-six others passed the imperial examination.
After the results were posted, an imperial edict commented:
"A brief review of their policy essays
shows that none are entirely satisfactory.
If we strictly followed the regulations,
only one person should have passed.
However, wishing to select broadly,
we have allowed both the competent and the stagnant to pass."
Later, in the second year of the Tiáolù era (680),
the Vice Director of the Bureau of Evaluation, Liú Ēn
(In the Táng dynasty's "Zhíyán," volume one, "Ēn" is written as "Sī")
submitted a memorial proposing to add examinations on the Confucian classics and miscellaneous writings,
with those excelling in writing being admitted to the policy essay examination.
Soon, due to Empress Wǔ Zétiān's change of dynasty,
the old practices were resumed.
It was not until the second year of the Shénlóng era (706)
that the three-stage examination was implemented.
Hence, poetry and fu topics were regularly listed on the announcement board.
From "Zhíyán."
Topics Issued from the Palace
During the Kāichéng era (836–840),
Gāo Xiè presided over the examinations.
The palace issued the topic "Rhapsody on the Rainbow and Feather Garment Dance,"
and the poem "On the Establishment of the Stone Classics at the Imperial University."
The practice of testing jìnshì candidates with poetry and fu
began from this time.
From "Lú Shì's Miscellaneous Tales."
Posting the Miscellaneous Writings Results
When Cháng Gǔn served as Minister of Rites,
he commented after posting the results for the miscellaneous writings examination:
"On the day they achieve prominence,
their ambition knows no bounds.
Through the night they write without cease,
yet regret remains abundant."
Those who passed the miscellaneous writings examination
typically did not exceed one hundred.
When Chief Libationer Bào Fáng served as Minister of Rites,
he failed many in the classics examination.
The contemporaries called it "Cháng's Miscellaneous, Bào's Classics."
From "Anecdotes and Historical Facts."
Posting the Results
In the early years of the Zhēnguàn era (627–649).
On the day the results were posted,
Emperor Tàizōng privately visited the Duānmén gate,
and saw the jìnshì candidates filing out beneath the announcement board.
He joyfully said to his attendants:
"All the heroes under heaven have entered my trap!"
At the top of the jìnshì announcement board,
four sheets of yellow paper were pasted vertically.
Using a felt brush and light ink,
the characters "Lǐbù Gòngyuàn" (Ministry of Rites Examination Hall) were written in a swirling script.
Some say
Emperor Wénhuáng once wrote them with flying silk.
It is also said
this symbolized the state of yin receiving yang.
According to old practice for the jìnshì examination,
the candidates were examined at the Imperial Examination Hall in the Department of State Affairs,
and the results were posted at the Southern Court.
The Southern Court was where the Directors of the Ministry of Rites received and handled documents.
All board templates and various regulations
were mostly displayed there as examples.
(In the Ming manuscript copy, "example" is written as "list.")
The wall for posting the announcements
was the eastern wall of the Southern Court.
A separate wall over ten feet high was built there,
with an outer low wall.
Before daybreak,
the announcement would be brought from the Northern Court
to be posted at the Southern Court.
In the sixth year of the Yuánhé era (811),
a National University student named Guō Dōnglǐ broke through the thorn fence,
which was located beneath the low wall.
There was also one outside the main gate of the Southern Court.
He tore the announcement,
so thereafter, a dummy announcement was often issued from the Department of State Affairs gate,
while the real announcement was posted somewhat later.
From "Zhíyán."
Also, when Zhèng Xūn presided over the examinations,
on the day the results were posted,
only Secretariat Drafter Bì Xián came to his residence to give thanks.
By the time Xiāo Fǎng posted the results,
not even high-ranking officials in red or purple robes came to his door.
Contemporary opinion ridiculed this.
From "Lú Shì's Miscellaneous Tales."
The Five Elders List
In the first year of the Tiānfù era (901),
under the list announced by Dù Déxiáng,
Cáo Sōng, Wáng Xīyǔ, Liú Xiàng, Kē Chóng, and Zhèng Xīyán passed the examination.
At that time, the emperor had recently quelled internal troubles,
and upon hearing of the new jìnshì graduates,
was greatly pleased.
He decreed that among the selected, those who were orphaned, poor, or wronged
should have their names reported,
and they would be specially appointed to office by decree.
Therefore, Déxiáng submitted the names of Sōng and the others to fulfill the decree,
and each was appointed as a Collator.
The decree roughly stated:
"Considering you achieved success in the examinations
during the year of Our restoration.
Special favor shall be granted,
and each shall receive an honorable appointment."
Sōng was from Shūzhōu.
He studied poetry under Secretary Jiǎ,
but had no other talents.
His petitions were mockingly called "Presenting Lamb Trotters Memorials."
Xīyǔ
was from Shèzhōu,
and was accomplished and learned in literary arts.
Sōng and Xīyǔ were both over seventy years old.
Xiàng
was from Jīngzhào;
Chóng and Xīyán
were from Mǐn.
They all passed based on their poetry portfolios,
and were also all over sixty years old.
They were called the "Five Elders List."
From "Zhíyán."
Giving Thanks
After the results were posted,
the zhuàngyuán (top graduate) and those below him
went to the residence of the chief examiner.
Dismounting, they stood in a file,
presented their name cards for announcement,
and the gatekeeper
(According to "Zhíyán," volume three, "gatekeeper" is written as "entering the gate.")
arranged them standing below the steps,
facing east with the north as the upper position.
The chief examiner laid out mats and cushions,
facing west with the east as the upper position.
The Director of the Ministry of Rites ushered the zhuàngyuán and others to bow to the examiner.
After bowing,
the zhuàngyuán stepped forward to deliver a speech of thanks,
then retreated back into line,
and each bowed again,
with the examiner returning the bow.
After bowing,
the examiner said:
"Please, gentlemen, state your family and maternal relations."
The zhuàngyuán and the others,
each in order of age,
then gave thanks.
The others followed the same ritual as the zhuàngyuán.
After the ritual,
the Director said:
"Please, zhuàngyuán, express detailed thanks
("Xiè" was originally written as "móu,"
corrected according to "Zhíyán," volume three.)
for your ranking,
and the person of such rank thanks for the robe and alms bowl.
"Robe and alms bowl" refers to obtaining the same rank as the examiner.
If someone had the same rank as the examiner's ancestor,
he would give thanks for the "great robe and alms bowl."
If it was a hereditary success,
he would thank with tears of emotion.
After giving thanks,
they ascended,
and the zhuàngyuán sat facing the examiner.
At that time, ministers and high officials came to watch,
and all sat in order facing south.
After several rounds of wine,
they rose
and proceeded to the Assembly Hall.
Some say
this ritual was not constant in the Ministry of Rites.
Sometimes thanks were given at the Department of State Affairs,
and when ministers and high officials came to watch,
they might not sit but immediately turn their horses back.
(In the Ming manuscript copy, "bù" is written as "jí.")
Three days later,
they gave detailed thanks again.
On that day,
the examiner would speak one by one of the recommendations and guidance given,
so that each could thank for the support received.
Even if someone was specially selected for exceptional talent,
it was also necessary to mention it.
From "Zhíyán."
Assembly
After expressing gratitude,
they proceeded to the assembly hall.
