Generally, before the imperial edict was issued,
they gathered daily.
Twice a day, they visited the examiner's residence.
However, after three days,
once the examiner firmly declined further visits,
they stopped.
When the same cohort first arrived at the assembly place,
the officials in charge
(The original text had "國" for "團,"
corrected based on Tang "Zhiyan" 3.)
paid respects to the top graduate,
(The original text had "輦" for "輩,"
corrected based on Tang "Zhiyan" 3.)
and then to the other gentlemen.
After the salutations,
an official suddenly announced in the courtyard:
"Gentlemen, please take your seats,
in pairs, east and west."
On that day, many fines were imposed
(The characters "日醵" were missing in the original,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript.)
for drinking.
Additionally, name card money was collected,
ten strings of cash per person.
When presenting name cards,
upon seeing the top graduate,
three to five individuals were suddenly selected from the crowd,
and this money was thereby collected.
(Tang "Zhiyan" 3 uses "驀" for "騫.")
Foundation money.
From the top graduate downward,
each person contributed thirty strings of cash.
From "Zhiyan"
Hall Attendance
After the edict was issued,
the newly passed *jinshi* attended the hall.
On that day,
the assembly officials
(The original text had "園日" for "團司,"
corrected based on the Ming manuscript.)
first set up tents in the eastern corridor inside the Guangfan Gate,
(The character "廊" was missing in the original,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript.)
preparing wine and food.
The cohort waited here for the prime minister to ascend the hall,
while the examiner also summoned two or three acquaintances
to meet elsewhere.
This banquet incurred many fines.
Once the prime minister had assembled,
a hall official came to request name cards.
The students followed their examiner to the Secretariat,
where the prime minister stood in a row,
and they lined up inside the main hall door.
The hall official announced:
"The Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, [surname], leads the newly passed *jinshi* to see Your Excellency."
Suddenly, an official
loudly invited the examiner forward.
Upon ascending the steps,
he made a deep bow and withdrew.
Standing by the door,
facing east.
Then, from the top graduate downward, they lined up on the steps.
The top graduate stepped forward,
and delivered a speech:
"On such-and-such day of this month,
the Ministry of Rites released the results,
and we are fortunate to have achieved success,
all under Your Excellency's guidance and cultivation,
overwhelmed with gratitude and awe."
If the top graduate was on the left or right,
he would say "mèng qú."
(Tang "Zhiyan" 3 uses "慶懼" for "夢瞿.")
After speaking, he bowed and withdrew to his position.
Then, from the top graduate downward,
each announced his name in turn.
The hall official said:
"No further
(The Ming manuscript uses "與" for "典,"
Tang "Zhiyan" 3 uses "無" for "典.")
guests."
The examiner bowed again,
and led the students to withdraw.
They proceeded to the Secretariat Drafters' Office,
where the examiner entered directly.
The drafters, in official robes and slippers,
received the examiner.
However, the drafters' courtesy and respect were even greater.
Wine was served as appropriate.
Then, mats were spread on the steps,
the drafters ascended the mats,
and all the students bowed,
(The character "拜" was missing in the original,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript.)
with the drafters returning the bow.
The top graduate stepped forward to deliver a speech,
and they answered with a bow.
They bowed again as before,
then departed.
Waiting under the corridor for the examiner to emerge,
they exchanged only a single bow.
At that time, visiting residences to express gratitude
also involved hosting banquets.
From "Zhiyan"
Inscription of Names
Since the Shénlóng era,
after the Xìngyuán Garden banquet,
they all inscribed their names beneath the Cí'ēn Pagoda,
selecting one skilled calligrapher from the cohort.
If any among them later became generals or ministers,
their names were written in vermilion.
After passing the examination,
if acquaintances encountered places where names were inscribed before achieving success,
they would add the character "前" (former) in front.
Thus, an old poem says:
"Where names were once inscribed, 'former' is added;
those seeing them off outside the city beg for old robes."
From "Zhiyan"
Pass Examination
The Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel administered two sections of judgment writing at the Southern Bureau,
and after the examination, spring passes were issued,
called the pass examination.
The students expressed gratitude,
and on that day, they were called disciples,
known as "one-day disciples."
From then on, they fell under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Personnel.
(The source was missing in the original,
now seen in "Zhiyan" volume 3.)
Banquet Gathering
The pavilions at Qǔjiāng,
before the Ān-Shǐ Rebellion,
were possessed by various government offices,
lined up along the riverbank.
After the imperial journey to Shǔ,
they were all reduced to ashes by the flames of war.
Only the pavilion of the Department of State Affairs remained.
When the Presented Scholars held their banquet,
they often borrowed it.
After the feast was cleared,
they would move the music to boats for a cruise,
which became the established custom.
Several days before the banquet,
the market bustled side by side at the river's edge.
"Edge" originally read "bank";
changed according to Táng Zhíyán 3.
On that day,
the families of high officials and nobles would flock here to watch in full force,
with about eight or nine out of ten being those selected as sons-in-law.
Carriages adorned with gold and pearl curtains
arrived in close succession.
It is said that
during the Qiánfú era,
Xuē Néng served as the Grand Governor of the Capital,
and Yáng Zhīzhì was about to take his family on an outing.
He sent a letter to Néng,
asking to borrow a boat.
But it had already been borrowed by the new graduates.
Néng replied in writing:
"It has already become the dwelling of forty fledglings."
Zhīzhì received the letter,
and angrily said:
"A mere official from yesterday,
how dare he be so disrespectful!"
Néng had been appointed from Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel to Junior Governor of the Capital,
acting as Grand Governor.
In the fifth year of the Kāichéng era,
Lǐ Jǐngràng passed the examination.
At that time, the emperor was in mourning,
so the new graduates were allowed to go on outings and banquets,
usually engaging in refined drinking.
The poet Zhào Gǔ sent him a poem that said:
"High in the heavens, the moon's cassia groves abound,
clearly thirty-one branches sway in the wind.
Spring's full colors stir toward people,
blossoms blocking the path greet horses with red.
The crane carriage drifts far beyond clouds and rain,
the Lán Pavilion lies not within pipes and strings.
Truly these are matters of former worthies,
why must green towers lean against emerald skies?"
During the Bǎolì era,
Yáng Sìfù, under his parents' blessings,
successively released two lists of graduates.
At that time, Yú Líng came from the Eastern Capital for an audience,
and Sìfù led the students to welcome him at Tóngguān.
Afterward, a grand banquet was held at the residence in Xīnchāng Ward,
where Yú Líng and those he held in esteem sat in the main hall,
while the Duke led the students to sit in rows along the two sides.
At that time, Yuán Zhěn and Bái Jūyì were both present,
and all composed poems at the banquet.
Only Vice Minister of Justice Yáng Rǔshì finished his poem last.
Yuán and Bái looked at it and turned pale.
The poem said:
"Sitting apart, one should be granted the imperial screen,
all the immortal
"Immortal" originally read "tenant";
changed according to Táng Zhíyán 3,
the Ming manuscript reads "first."
writings enter the lofty heavens.
The old worth of literature remains at the Duckweed Office,
peach and plum's new shade lies in the Carp Court.
For two years, students present a congratulatory feast,
all fine historians of the time spread its fragrance.
Though Shū Guǎng and his nephew were said to flourish then,
how could they have such a feast with fine wine?"
Rǔshì got heavily drunk that day.
Returning home, he said to his disciples:
"Today, I have overshadowed Yuán and Bái."
From Zhíyán.
Dù Zhèngxuán
During the Rénshòu era of Suí,
Dù Zhèngxuán, Zhèngzàng, and Zhènglún
all passed the examination as Xiùcái.
In the Suí dynasty, those presented as Jìnshì
totalled only ten people,
and the Dù family had three of them.
From Tánbīn Lù.
Lǐ Yìchēn
In the fifth year of Wǔdé,
Lǐ Yìchēn, along with his younger brother Yìyǎn,
and their third cousin Shàngdé, three of the same year, became Jìnshì.
Yìchēn and others were from Lǒngxī,
their family long residing in Yèchéng.
In the early days of the state, when things were still unsettled,
their household was poor,
and they lived together with Shàngdé,
serving their paternal aunt,
attending to her as if she were their own mother.
While traveling for the examination to Tóngguān,
they encountered heavy snow,
and the inn could not accommodate them.
A merchant from Xiányáng saw them and took pity,
inviting them to share his room.
After several days,
the snow cleared and they departed.
Chēn and the others discussed selling their donkey
to buy a drink to thank him.
The merchant secretly learned of this,
and left without saying goodbye.
He had even given them grain beforehand.
Later, when Chēn became magistrate of Xiányáng,
he summoned the merchant.
He treated him with equal courtesy and closeness.
Chēn rose to the positions of Vice Minister of Justice and Chief Administrator of Yōngzhōu.
Yìyǎn served as chancellor under Emperor Gāozōng,
and Shàngdé became Director of the Bureau of Gates.
From Zhíyán.
Chén Zǐ'áng,
a man of Shèhóng in Shǔ,
lived in the capital for ten years
without being known to anyone.
At that time, in the Eastern Market, there was a seller of a barbarian lute,
priced at a million coins.
Daily, the rich and noble would pass it around to look,
but none could appraise it.
Zǐ'áng suddenly stepped forward from the crowd,
and said to those around him,
"Bring a thousand strings of cash to buy it."
Everyone asked in surprise:
"What will you use it for?"
He replied:
"I am skilled at playing this instrument."
Some curious person said:
"May we get to hear it?"
He replied:
"I live in Xuānyáng Ward.
Pointing to his residence,
he said, "I also have wine prepared.
Tomorrow I will specially await you.
Not only is it an honor for you gentlemen to visit,
but each should also invite and summon those known for their discernment to come together.
Then it will be a fortunate encounter."
The next morning,
about a hundred people gathered,
all esteemed figures of the time.
Zǐ'áng laid out a grand banquet,
with rare delicacies.
After eating,
he stood up, holding the barbarian lute,
and addressed the gathering:
"I, Chén Zǐ'áng of Shǔ, have a hundred scrolls of writings,
rushing about the capital's streets,
toiling in the dust,
unknown to anyone.
This instrument is the tool of a lowly artisan—
how could a fool like me care for it?"
With that, he lifted it and threw it away.
Then he brought out two tables of literary scrolls
and gave them to all present.
After the gathering dispersed,
within a single day,
his reputation spread throughout the capital.
At that time, Wǔ Yōuyí was Prince of Jiàn'ān,
and he recruited Zǐ'áng as his secretary.
Later, Zǐ'áng was appointed Reminder.
Returning home for a visit,
he was harmed by Duàn
"Duàn" originally read "Jiǎ";
changed according to the Old and New Tángshū biographies of Chén Zǐ'áng.
Jiǎn.
From Dúyì Zhì.
Wáng Wéi
Wáng Wéi, the Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, was not yet twenty years old when
he gained fame for his literary works.
He had a natural affinity for music,
and was exceptionally skilled at playing the pipa.
Moving among the circles of the nobility,
he was particularly favored and esteemed by Prince Qí.
At that time, the presented scholar Zhāng Jiǔgǎo enjoyed a widespread reputation.
A guest who frequented the princess's residence,
acting on his behalf,
had the princess send a written request to the examination officials in the capital,
instructing them to appoint Jiǔgǎo as the top candidate.
Wáng Wéi was about to take the imperial examination,
so he spoke to Prince Qí,
seeking his protection and assistance.
Prince Qí said:
"The princess's
"Princess" originally written as "student",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
influence is strong;
we cannot contend by force.
I shall devise a plan for you.
Select ten of your old poems that are pure and lofty,
and compose a new, sorrowful and poignant tune for the pipa.
Return to me in five days."
Wáng Wéi complied with the order,
and arrived as scheduled.
Prince Qí said to him:
"If you, a literary scholar, request an audience with the princess,
through which gate could you gain entry?
Can you follow my instructions?"
Wáng Wéi said:
"I will respectfully obey your command."
Prince Qí then brought out brocade garments,
bright, splendid, and extraordinary,
and had Wáng Wéi put them on.
He also instructed him to bring his pipa,
and together they went to the princess's residence.
Prince Qí entered and said:
"Having learned that Your Highness has emerged from the inner quarters,
I have brought wine and music to offer a feast."
He immediately ordered a banquet to be set,
and various musicians entered in succession.
Wáng Wéi, in his youth, was fair-skinned,
with an elegant and handsome demeanor.
Standing in the row,
he caught the princess's eye.
She asked Prince Qí:
"Who is this person?"
He replied:
"A connoisseur of music."
She then ordered him to perform the new tune alone.
The melody was mournful and poignant,
moving everyone present.
The princess inquired herself:
"What is the name of this piece?"
Wáng Wéi rose and said:
"It is called 'The Robe of Melancholy'."
The princess was greatly astonished by him.
Prince Qí then said:
"This young man excels not only in music,
but also in literary composition;
none surpass him."
The princess found him even more extraordinary.
She then said:
"Do you have any of your writings?"
Wáng Wéi then took out a scroll of poems from his bosom and presented it to the princess.
After reading them,
the princess exclaimed in astonishment:
"These are all poems I have recited and studied,
always thinking they were excellent works by ancient masters.
Could they actually be your compositions?"
She then ordered him to change his clothes
and seated him in the place of honor among the guests.
Wáng Wéi was cultured and refined,
his speech witty and humorous,
greatly admired and noticed by all the nobles.
Prince Qí then said:
"If the capital prefecture could have this young man as the top candidate this year,
it would truly be a glory for the state."
The princess then said:
"Why not have him take the examination?"
Prince Qí said:
"This young man will not sit for the exam
unless he is recommended as the top candidate.
However, I have heard that Your Highness has already recommended Zhāng Jiǔgǎo."
The princess laughed and said:
"What does that have to do with me?
I was merely acting on another's request."
Turning to Wáng Wéi, she said:
"If you truly wish to take it,
I will certainly use my influence to secure it for you."
Wáng Wéi rose and modestly declined.
The princess then summoned the examination officials to her residence,
and sent palace maids to convey her instructions.
Wáng Wéi thus became the top candidate,
and passed the examination in one attempt.
Later, when he served as Assistant Director of the Imperial Music Bureau,
he was involved with musicians performing the dance of the Yellow Lion,
and was dismissed from office because of it.
The Yellow Lion dance
could not be performed without a specific person.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
when Ān Lùshān first captured the Western Capital,
Wáng Wéi, along with Zhèng Qián, Zhāng Tōng, and others,
were all trapped in the rebel court.
After the recovery
they were all imprisoned in the former residence of Yáng Guózhōng on Xuānyáng Lane.
Cuī Yuán then summoned them to his private residence,
ordering them to paint several walls.
At that time, everyone considered Cuī Yuán's merit and status to be unrivaled,
and hoped he would rescue them,
so they applied their minds with exquisite skill,
displaying exceptional ability.
"Ability" originally written as "all",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
Later, because of this matter,
they all received lenient sentences;
even when demoted,
they were assigned to favorable locations.
The current private residence of Chancellor Dòu Yìzhí on Chóngyì Lane
was originally Cuī Yuán's old residence,
and the paintings are still there.
Wáng Wéi later served as Supervising Secretary.
Ān Lùshān forced him to accept a false official post.
After the rebellion was pacified,
Wáng Jìn served as Deputy Garrison Commander of the Northern Capital,
and requested to redeem him with his own official rank and title,
thus sparing him from death.
He eventually rose to become Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs.
He established a country estate in Lántián,
where he devoted himself to Buddhist scriptures.
From *Jíyì Jì*
Yáng Xuān
Yáng Xuān, son of Yáng Guózhōng,
took the examination for the *Míngjīng* degree.
The Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, Dáxī Xún, graded him,
but he failed to meet the standard.
He was about to be rejected,
but Xún, fearing Yáng Guózhōng, did not dare to decide.
At that time, the emperor was at the Huáqīng Palace.
Xún's son, Fǔ, was the magistrate of Huìchāng.
Xún urgently summoned a messenger,
and sent a letter to Fǔ,
instructing him to wait for Yáng Guózhōng
and explain the situation in detail.
When Fǔ arrived at Yáng Guózhōng's private residence,
just as the fifth watch had begun and he was rising,
torches lined the gates,
and he was about to hasten to court.
Carriages and canopies crowded like a market,
and Yáng Guózhōng was just mounting his horse.
Fǔ hurried in
and paid his respects under the candlelight.
Yáng Guózhōng thought his son must have been selected,
and seeing Fǔ's faint smile,
his expression was very pleased.
Fǔ then reported:
"By my father's order,
I inform you that your son did not pass the exam,
but we dare not reject him."
Yáng Guózhōng stepped back, stood up, and shouted loudly:
"Why should I worry about my son not attaining wealth and honor?
How could he rely on a mere title,
and be sold out by petty men!"
He immediately
"Immediately" originally written as "indeed",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
turned away without a glance,
and rode off on his horse.
Fǔ was terrified,
and rushed back to report to Xún, saying:
"Yáng Guózhōng relies on his power and acts arrogantly due to his high status.
He can alter a person's misery or comfort
in an instant.
How can we argue right and wrong with him?"
Thus, Xuān was placed among the top candidates.
Later, when Xuān became Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue,
Xún had only just been transferred from Vice Minister of Rites to Vice Minister of Personnel,
and they served together.
Xuān spoke to his close associates,
still lamenting his own slow advancement,
while remarking on Xún's rapid promotion.
From *Mínghuáng Zálù*
Xiāo Yǐngshì
Xiāo Yǐngshì passed the imperial examination in the twenty-third year of the Kāiyuán era.
He was arrogant and looked down on others,
believing no one could compare to him.
He often carried a pot of wine with him to roam the scenic outskirts,
and once rested at an inn,
drinking and reciting poetry alone.
Suddenly, a storm arrived,
and an old man in purple robes led a young servant to take shelter from the rain there.
Yǐngshì saw the old man’s disheveled appearance
and was quite rude and insulting.
After a short while,
the wind calmed and the rain cleared,
and a carriage and horses suddenly arrived.
The old man mounted the horse
and departed with attendants clearing the way.
Yǐngshì hurriedly inquired about him,
and his attendants said:
“It is Minister Wáng of the Ministry of Personnel.”
The minister’s name was Qiū.
Yǐngshì had often visited his residence,
but had never met him in person,
so he was extremely shocked.
The next day,
he prepared a long letter and went to the minister’s residence to apologize.
Qiū ordered him to be led to the side hall,
where he sat and reprimanded him,
saying:
“It is a pity that you and I are not relatives,
or I would discipline you as a father would.”
After a moment, he added:
“You carry a reputation for literary talent,
yet you are so arrogant and careless.
Will you be content with just passing the examination?”
Yǐngshì ultimately only served as a Registrar in Yángzhōu.
From “Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Mínghuáng.”
Qiáo Yí,
during the provincial examination in Jīngzhào Prefecture,
there were two examiners.
Yí knocked on the door at noon,
and the examiners had him brought in,
but he was already heavily drunk.
He looked at the topic, “Ode to the Secluded Orchid,”
and refused to write, saying:
“Two men facing each other,
how can they write on this topic?
Change it quickly.”
So it was changed to “Ode to the Wòwā Horse.”
He said:
“This will do.”
He then picked up his brush and finished it in a moment.
A striking couplet read:
“Four hooves trailing silk,
churning the startling waves of the vast sea.
One snort stirs the wind,
scattering the disordered leaves of the Xiāng Mountains.”
They immediately wanted to rank him first.
But the Jīngzhào official said:
“Qiáo Yí is too outstanding;
it would be better to recommend him as the second-place candidate.”
From “Whispers from the Secluded Lane.”
Xǔ Mèngróng
Xǔ Mèngróng passed the Jìnshì examination,
and also passed the Xuéjiū examination,
earning the nickname “a brocade robe worn over a grass coat.”
Cài Jīng was the same as Mèngróng.
From “Records of Gathered Sayings.”
Zhāng Zhèngfǔ
Chancellor Lǐ Jiàng’s
ancestor served as a Military Supervisor in Xiāngzhōu.
When Jiàng was about to take the imperial examination,
he sought a provincial recommendation.
At that time, Fán Zé, the Minister of Works, served as the Military Governor,
and Zhāng Zhèngfǔ, the Palace Attendant, served as his assistant.
He was in charge of provincial recommendations.
Zhāng knew Jiàng had a promising future,
so he informed the Minister of Works, saying:
“None of the candidates can compare to Scholar Lǐ.
I request that we recommend only him.
The funds for the others
should all be given to him.”
The Minister of Works happily agreed.
He also recommended Jiàng’s younger brother as an Attendant in the same department.
Jiàng deeply felt Zé’s extraordinary kindness.
Within ten years, Jiàng rose to a high position,
and Zé’s son, Zōngyì, became a court official.
When people asked Jiàng about Zōngyì’s literary talent,
Jiàng jokingly replied:
“Unmatched in his generation.”
People then used “unmatched in his generation” as a catchphrase.
When they met to discuss literature,
they would inevitably ask:
“Is this perhaps Lǐ Sān, the one unmatched in his generation?”
When Jiàng served as Vice Minister of Revenue,
Zhāng Zhèngfǔ was the Director of the same ministry.
During a gathering,
he raised his cup and asked the Vice Minister to sing.
Lǐ never sang but only smiled,
causing the entire table to burst into laughter.
From “Records of Refined Conversations.”
Yán Jìměi,
in the previous dynasty, the Duke, the Minister, and the high-ranking officials had promised and determined his fate,
but he was single-minded
(Míng manuscript: "zhì" reads as "wàng").
and did not pursue it,
so he took the imperial examination three times before passing.
The first time,
he failed in the miscellaneous essays under Vice-Minister Liú Dān;
the second time,
he sat for the examination under Vice-Minister Wáng
(Míng manuscript: "Wáng" reads as "zhǔ").
and failed in the miscellaneous essays.
At that time,
his age was already advanced,
and he often went to Master Qīn at Jìngshān via Jiāngjī to inquire about the Dharma.
That spring,
after he had failed the examination,
he was about to leave the capital.
Thus, he presented a six-rhyme regulated poem to the chief examiner:
"Loyal and upright are the king's ministers,
cultured and magnanimous in full measure.
Gazing at the furnace, gold leaps on its own,
reflecting objects, how can the mirror be biased?
The secluded depths of the southern states are exhausted,
the rites and music of the eastern hall are proclaimed.
Now
(Original text: "zhuǎn" reads as "lún",
changed according to Táng Shī Jì Shì.)
I wander among extraordinary scholars,
returning to the utmost fairness of past years.
Fragrant trees rejoice in the new scenery,
blue clouds weep under the evening sky.
Only worried about bowing at the Phoenix Pond,
who will pity this lonely and lowly one?"
The chief examiner read it.
He asked him,
"Who was rejected this year?"
He truthfully reported.
When the list of failures was announced first,
the chief examiner blushed and changed expression,
deeply sighing over the waste of talent.
Then he said,
"The six-rhyme poem you submitted,
will surely show its effect later.
You go south,
do not doubt matters of the future."
He then left the capital.
In the autumn,
he sought recommendation in Jiāngdōng,
and after his name reached the ministry,
examinations were held in both capitals,
and the chief examiner was already in Luòyáng.
By the time he arrived in Luòyáng,
he had no acquaintances,
so he lodged at a shop in Qīnghuà Lǐ.
As prices were soaring at the time,
he had only five bolts of silk in his bag,
and a lame donkey to ride.
There was an examinee, Lú Jǐngzhuāng, who had already received the top recommendation from the eastern prefecture,
and was staying in the same place.
His servants and horses were very impressive,
and he exchanged bows with him,
but did not speak a word.
After a long while, he asked him:
"Where has Master Yán come from?"
He replied:
"From Jiāngdōng."
He served him respectfully and did not dare neglect.
One evening, Jǐngzhuāng returned drunk,
and suddenly asked about his ranking,
saying:
"Yán the twentieth,
the news is extremely good,
Jǐngzhuāng is in great danger."
He replied:
"Not so,
you must have received the top recommendation from the grand prefecture first.
Your reputation has already shaken the capital and Luòyáng,
while I, a candidate from a distant place,
how dare I hope for success?"
Jǐngzhuāng said:
"You are sure to pass."
In the latter part of the eleventh month,
they took the miscellaneous essays examination.
On the third day of the twelfth month,
the list for the miscellaneous essays was posted at Tiānjīn Bridge.
Jǐngzhuāng and he both passed.
That day was bitterly cold,
and on the fourth day of that month,
the scripture memorization test was held at Tiānjīn Bridge.
Jǐngzhuāng was soon eliminated,
and he went forward to tell the chief examiner:
"I have long focused on literary composition,
and am not skilled at scripture memorization,
I fear I will not pass."
The chief examiner said:
"Don't you know the practice of the examination hall?
It also allows poetry to redeem the test."
After he spoke,
there was much commotion about staying or leaving.
He hurried forward again to tell the chief examiner:
"Vice-Minister, you have opened a path of encouragement,
allowing poetry to redeem the scripture test,
but the topic has not been announced."
The chief examiner said:
"Compose a poem on 'Viewing the Remaining Snow on Luòyáng City from Tiānjīn Bridge.'"
He only managed twenty characters.
His poem said:
"After the fresh clearing at Luòyáng's edge,
a thousand households' accumulated snow is cold.
The pure forbidden colors not yet gathered,
linger especially on the remnants of Shàngyáng."
When he heard the chief examiner urgently催促 for the poem,
and the day was growing late,
he told the chief examiner,
"The weather is cold and the ink frozen,
I cannot write properly."
Then he heard the chief examiner instruct,
"Bring what lines you have now."
The chief examiner glanced at what was submitted,
praised it repeatedly,
and announced his passing.
That evening,
Jǐngzhuāng congratulated him, saying:
"Earlier, I shared a desk with you,
during the test on the 'Rhapsody on Praying to the Heavenly Ancestor on La Day,'
I secretly saw you used Lǔ Qiū
(Original text: "qiū" reads as "xuè",
changed according to the Míng manuscript)
paired with Wèi Cì.
According to the meaning,
Wèi Cì is Zǐgòng,
but you wrote Wèi Cì as 'sì mǎ' (four horses),
I only worried about this for you."
Hearing this,
he reflected on it,
indeed he had written 'sì mǎ',
and felt very alarmed.
When the list came out,
he undeservedly passed,
and together with the top candidate, paid respects to the chief examiner.
The chief examiner said:
"On the examination day, gentlemen,
the weather was cold and time short,
writing the miscellaneous essays hastily,
some may not have followed the rules.
Now, fearing the documents will reach the Western Capital,
and must be presented to the prime minister,
I ask you, seniors, to each buy good paper,
come again to request the seal,
copy them neatly according to the rules and submit them,
and I will withdraw the rejected copies."
Everyone was delighted.
When his draft was taken out,
the character 'sì' had a very large red dot on it.
On the day the chief examiner returned to the capital,
he alone bowed forward and said:
"In spring, I let slip
(Original text: "yí" reads as "qiǎn",
changed according to the Míng manuscript)
a talent,
the six-rhyme poem you submitted,
I did not dare forget in shame,
this merely fulfills my simple promise."
From "Gàn Zǎizi"
Pān Yàn
Vice-Minister Pān Yàn,
the jìnshì list had six oddities:
Zhū Suì became Crown Prince Zhū Tāo;
Wáng Biǎo became Lǐ Nà's son-in-law,
and in that army was called the imperial son-in-law;
Zhào Bóxuān became the Yì
(Original text: "yì" reads as "yì",
changed according to the Xǔ manuscript)
dìng garrison commander;
Yuán Tóngzhí entered the foreign lands as a master;
Dòu Cháng was called a former jìnshì for twenty years,
and Xī Mǒu also had an incident.
At the time, it was called the six discrepancies.
Dòu Cháng had newly passed the examination,
and at the residence of Supervising Secretary Xuē Mǒu, he met Sāng Dàomào.
The Supervising Secretary said:
"Scholar Dòu has newly passed,
when will he obtain an official post?"
Sāng Dàomào said:
"He will obtain an official post only after twenty years."
Everyone present laughed,
not believing it.
But indeed, five times an official post was petitioned for him,
each time the imperial decree did not come down,
and he only acted in several posts temporarily.
What can one do about fate?
From "Jiāhuà Lù"
Línghú Huàn
In the fourteenth year of the Dàlì era, the reign title was changed to Jiànzhōng.
Under the supervision of Vice Minister of Rites Línghú Huàn,
twenty-two candidates passed the imperial examination.
At that time, among the high-ranking officials, there was anger over recommendations and requests that were not followed,
and the situation seemed on the verge of collapse.
Huàn was extremely fearful,
so he presented his private correspondence.
The emperor considered Huàn disloyal,
and on the day the results were posted, he was exiled,
not allowed to meet with his students.
Ten years later,
his disciple Tián Dūn became the prefect of Míngzhōu,
and Huàn was transferred to serve as Assistant Officer in the same prefecture.
Only then did Dūn arrange for him to express gratitude for the imperial favor.
From *Zhíyán*.
Xíong Zhíyì
Xíong Zhíyì was well-versed in the principles of the *Book of Changes*.
In the fourth year of Jiànzhōng,
Vice Minister Lǐ Shū tested candidates on the topic "Understanding Difficulties and Obstacles Through Simplicity."
Zhíyì sat upright and analyzed the topic thoroughly,
captivating the entire examination hall,
and passed in one attempt.
From *Guóshǐ Bǔ*.
Cháng Gǔn
When Emperor Dézōng of the Táng dynasty first ascended the throne,
Chancellor Cháng Gǔn served as the Surveillance Commissioner of Fújiàn, governing the region.
Gǔn valued literary talent,
and even among the common people in villages and counties,
those who could read, write, and compose literary works
were personally treated with the courtesy of a guest.
During outings, banquets, and feasts,
he would always summon them to join.
In a short time,
the local customs were transformed harmoniously.
At that time, Ōuyáng Zhān stood out prominently,
and Gǔn showed him particular respect and affection,
earning the admiration of all scholars.
People from Mǐnyuè (modern-day Fújiàn) began taking the imperial examinations,
starting with Zhān.
Zhān died while serving as an Assistant Instructor in the Directorate of Education,
and Lǒngxī native Lǐ Áo wrote his biography,
while Hán Yù composed a lament for him.
From Hán Yù's "Preface to the Lament for Ōuyáng Zhān."
Sòng Jì
Emperor Dézōng of the Táng dynasty traveled incognito,
and one summer day, he arrived at Xīmíng Temple.
At the time, Sòng Jì was spending the summer in the monks' quarters.
The emperor suddenly entered Jì's room,
where Jì was sitting by the window,
wearing a
"calf"
—originally written as "special,"
amended according to the Ming dynasty manuscript—
nose-shaped linen cap and copying texts.
The emperor said:
"Please serve a bowl of tea."
Jì replied:
"The water is boiling in the cauldron,
and there is tea here.
Please help yourself."
The emperor then asked:
"What do you do for a living?"
and also inquired about his surname and background.
Jì said:
"My surname is Sòng, and I am the fifth in my family,
preparing for the imperial examination."
The emperor asked again:
"What do you study?"
Jì replied:
"I write poetry."
The emperor continued:
"I hear the current emperor enjoys writing poetry.
What do you think of it?"
Sòng Jì said:
"The emperor's intentions are unfathomable"—before he could finish,
suddenly a carriage arrived in haste.
The attendants called out: "Your Majesty, Your Majesty!"
Jì, terrified, awaited punishment.
The emperor said:
"Sòng the Fifth is quite straightforward."
Later, when the Ministry of Rites posted the examination results,
the emperor ordered a eunuch to check if Jì's name was on the list.
The eunuch returned and reported that his name was not there.
The emperor said:
"Sòng the Fifth is straightforward again."
From *Lúshì Xiǎoshuō*.
Once, someone mocked Sòng Jì, saying:
"Why are there so many white-robed scholars?"
Jì replied:
"They are all striving for the red and purple robes of officials."
From *Guóshǐ Bǔ*.
Niú Xīshù
Niú Xīshù was by nature quiet, retiring, and had few friends,
and had repeatedly failed the imperial examinations.
In the first year of the Zhēnyuán era,
he consulted a fortune-teller,
who said:
"You will achieve the top rank in next year's examination."
Xīshù only hoped to pass at all,
and did not believe it at all.
It was already the eighth month,
and the chief examiner had not yet been appointed.
By chance, he passed by the residence of Junior Guardian Xiāo Xīn,
just as Xīn was leaning on his cane,
about to take a solitary stroll in the southern garden.
Xīshù encountered him,
quickly presented his name card,
and offered his writings as a gift.
Xīn, living alone,
had been longing for friends and guests,
and was very pleased.
He invited him in for a conversation.
After reviewing his writings,
he repeatedly praised them.
Then he asked:
"Who do people outside say will be appointed chief examiner?"
Xīshù replied:
"Your Excellency is fair-minded,
and will surely be appointed for another year."
Xīn said:
"I will certainly not be appointed.
But if that happens,
you will be the top candidate."
Xīshù stood up and bowed in gratitude.
Before he could sit back down comfortably,
suddenly the sound of galloping horses and announcements was heard:
"The Minister has been appointed chief examiner!"
Xīn quickly stood up.
Xīshù bowed again and said:
"Your Excellency has just promised me.
Heaven and earth
have heard these words."
Xīn said:
"What I said earlier stands."
The following year, Xīshù indeed achieved the top rank.
From *Yìshǐ*.
Cuī Yuánhàn
Cuī Yuánhàn was recommended by Yáng Yán,
who wanted to appoint him as a Reminder.
But Cuī earnestly requested:
"I wish to take the imperial examination," and thus stood out uniquely in the examination hall.
However, he was unfamiliar with the examination procedures,
and sought to obtain the topics in advance to prepare.
Cuī Áo learned of this.
At dawn,
when the examination hall first opened,
Áo, with an imposing manner, said to the chief examiner:
"If the topic 'White Clouds Rise from Within the Seals' is given,
I, Áo, will withdraw."
The chief examiner, caught off guard by his words,
was startled and changed the topic.
That year,
both Cuīs passed the examination.
From *Guóshǐ Bǔ*.
Zhàn Bēn
Péng Kàng and Zhàn Bēn were both from Yíchūn, Yuánzhōu.
Kàng's wife was also Bēn's aunt.
Kàng passed the imperial examination with high honors,
while Bēn was still a minor county clerk.
The wife's family held a celebration banquet,
attended by officials and renowned scholars.
Kàng sat in the seat of honor,
and the entire gathering admired him.
When Bēn arrived,
he was told to eat in the back room,
and he showed no sign of difficulty.
His wife angrily rebuked him:
"A man who cannot motivate himself,
enduring such humiliation—
what face is there to show?"
Bēn was moved by her words
and devoted himself diligently to his studies.
Within a few years,
he passed the examination in one attempt.
Kàng had often belittled him.
At that time, Kàng was riding a donkey,
roaming freely in the outskirts of the city.
Suddenly, a servant rushed to report:
"Master Zhàn has passed the examination!"
Kàng cried out in shock and fell off his donkey.
Thus, the people of Yuánzhōu joked:
"Zhàn Bēn passes the examination,
Péng Kàng falls off his donkey."
From *Zhíyán*.
Yǐn Jí
In the seventh year of the Zhēnyuán era,
Dù Huángcháng served as the chief examiner.
He heard that Yǐn Jí
(The Yùquánzǐ records "Jí" as "Shū")
(same below)
was widely renowned at the time,
so he disguised himself in plain clothes to visit him,
asking about the famous scholars in the examination hall.
Jí merely gave vague replies.
Huángcháng then fully disclosed:
"I am this year's chief examiner,
having received the appointment long ago,
but I have only found one worthy candidate.
I am unable to know all the others,
so I dare to ask for your recommendation."
Jí, startled, apologized:
"Since you have condescended to inquire,
how dare I conceal anything?"
He then mentioned that among the younger generation, there was Cuī Yuánlüè,
and among the solitary scholars, there were Mù
(In the Ming manuscript copy and Xǔ's edition, "Mù" is written as "Xiū";
Qīng Xú Sōng's Táng Dēngkē Jì Kǎo, volume 12, records "Mù" as "Lín")
Zǎo and Línghú Chǔ, among a few others.
Huángcháng was greatly pleased.
That year, Jí achieved the top rank as zhuàngyuán.
The examination topic was "Rhapsody on the Pearl Returning to Hépǔ."
When Zǎo completed his rhapsody,
he suddenly dozed off
and dreamed that someone told him:
"Why not describe the pearl's journey of departure and return?"
Upon waking,
he revised several lines,
and later expressed gratitude.
Huángcháng said to Zǎo:
"Your description of the pearl's journey
seems divinely aided."
From Mǐn Chuān Míngshì Zhuàn.
Lǐ Chéng
Lǐ Chéng, during the Zhēnyuán era, took the examination on the rhapsody "The Sun's Five Colors."
Initially, his name was omitted from the posted list.
Just after the examination,
Yáng Yúlíng, returning home from his official residence,
encountered Chéng at the ministry gate
and inquired about his examination.
Chéng retrieved his draft from his boot shaft
and showed it to him.
Its opening lines were:
"Virtue stirs Heaven's mirror,
Auspiciousness unveils the sun's splendor."
Yúlíng read it
and said to Chéng:
"You must become the zhuàngyuán this year."
The next day,
Chéng's name was absent from the list of successful candidates in the miscellaneous writings.
Yúlíng felt deeply indignant.
He then copied the rhapsody at the end of an old booklet
(Originally "mò" was written as "wèi,"
corrected according to Táng Zhíyán)
and transcribed it,
concealing the author's name,
and took it to visit the chief examiner.
Calmly deceiving him, he said:
"Your Excellency, this year's new rhapsody examination—
how could you use an old topic?"
The chief examiner denied this.
Yúlíng said:
"Not only the topic,
but someone previously wrote a rhapsody on this,
with identical rhyme words."
The chief examiner was greatly astonished.
Yúlíng then produced Chéng's rhapsody to show him.
The chief examiner praised it endlessly.
Yúlíng said, "If such a rhapsody appeared in the current examination,
how would Your Excellency treat it?"
The chief examiner replied:
"If none existed, it would be one thing;
if there were one, it would undoubtedly deserve the zhuàngyuán rank."
Yúlǐng said:
"If so,
Your Excellency has overlooked a worthy candidate,
for this was written by Lǐ Chéng."
He urgently requested to retrieve Chéng's submitted paper for comparison,
and not a single character differed.
The chief examiner then expressed his gratitude
and consulted with Yúlíng.
Consequently, Chéng was promoted to zhuàngyuán,
and the previous list was not reinstated.
Some say the list was reposted to include him.
Later, when Chéng was stationed in Dàliáng,
he heard that Hào Xūzhōu was taking the Hóngcí examination,
again on this topic.
He worried that Hào might surpass him,
so he specially sent a messenger to fetch the original.
Upon its arrival,
as he was about to open the letter,
he still wore a concerned expression.
But upon seeing Hào's opening lines:
"The radiant sun shines gloriously,
holding auspicious light within,"
Chéng joyfully said:
"Lǐ Chéng remains superior."
From Zhíyán.
Cài Nánshǐ
In the twelfth year of Zhēnyuán,
Imperial Son-in-Law Wáng Shìpíng and Princess Yìyáng had a falling-out.
Cài Nánshǐ and Dúgū Shēnshū composed a musical piece about it,
titled Yìyángzǐ,
featuring songs like "Gathering Snow" and "Scattering Snow."
Emperor Dézōng heard of this and was angered,
intending to abolish the imperial examinations.
Later, he only exiled and denounced Nánshǐ, and the matter ended there.
From Guóshǐ Bǔ.
Niú Sēngrú
When Niú Sēngrú first sat for the jìnshì examination,
he left his qin and books in the Bà-Chǎn area.
First, he presented his literary works to Hán Yù and Huángfǔ Shí for review.
At that time, he first visited Yù,
but Yù was away,
so he merely left his scroll.
Not long after,
Yù went to visit Shí.
At that moment, Sēngrú also arrived at the gate.
The two esteemed scholars, upon reading his name card, were pleased
and jointly agreed to receive him,
inquiring where he was staying.
He replied:
"I have just presented my humble skills and trivial compositions to masters of the craft;
whether to advance or withdraw is entirely at your command.
My single bag remains outside the capital gate."
The two gentlemen unrolled his scroll;
at the beginning was a chapter discussing music.
Before even reading the content,
they immediately said:
"This is elevated writing.
And what do you call the clappers?"
He replied:
"They are called 'musical phrases.'"
The two looked at each other, greatly delighted, and said:
"This is undoubtedly elevated writing."
Sēngrú then sought advice on accommodation.
The two pondered for a long while
before saying:
"You may rent a temple courtyard among the guest households."
Sēngrú followed their advice.
He visited to express thanks,
and the two further instructed him:
"On a certain day, you may visit Qīnglóng Temple.
Return at dusk."
The two rode side by side to that place
and wrote largely on his gate:
"Hán Yù and Huángfǔ Shí jointly visited the several officials but did not meet them."
The next day,
renowned scholars throughout the capital came to see it.
The fame of Qízhāng [Niú Sēngrú]
thus became resounding.
After Sēngrú passed the examination,
during the ceremonial hall visit,
the Prime Minister said to him:
"I have cleaned the hall to await you."
Sēngrú alone stepped forward and said:
"I dare not accept such honor."
The crowd was astonished and regarded him as exceptional.
From Zhíyán.
Yáng Yúqīng
After Yáng Yúqīng passed the jìnshì examination,
he took the Hóngcí examination,
became a collator,
and traveled to Huáinán to marry into Lǐ Yōng's family.
He encountered the former jìnshì candidate Chén Shāng,
who pleaded for help in extreme poverty.
Yúqīng did not know him previously.
Upon hearing his plight,
he emptied his purse to aid him.
From Zhíyán.
Miáo Zuǎn
Miáo Càn's son Zuǎn was sitting for the examination,
while Càn, suffering from a stroke, had slurred speech,
yet was extremely anxious in heart.
As the examination approached,
Càn's illness worsened critically.
Zuǎn then wrote a petition,
asking whether he could be permitted to enter the examination.
Càn could still grasp a brush
and wrote with pale ink:
"Enter! Enter!"
Such was the depth of their father-son affection.
That year,
Zuǎn passed the examination.
From Jiāhuà Lù.
Fèi Guànqīng
Fèi Guànqīng passed the imperial examination in the second year of the Yuánhé era.
Because his official salary could not benefit his parents,
he forever harbored a sense of boundless regret.
Thus, he retired to Jiǔhuá Mountain in Chíyáng.
During the Chángqìng era,
Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ Lǐ Xíngxiū recommended Guànqīng for his filial virtue,
and he was summoned and appointed as Yòu Shíyí.
The imperial edict stated:
"Former Jìnshì Fèi Guànqīng once participated in the examinations
and passed through literary merit.
His salary could not bring glory to his parents' support,
so regret accumulated in his eternal thoughts.
Thereupon, he withdrew to the hills and gardens,
cutting off all traces of official advancement.
He maintained his utmost nature
for fifteen years.
His lofty integrity is unmatched,
his pure reputation naturally far-reaching.
Now, commending filial conduct and promoting recluses
serves to enrich customs and emphasize moral teachings.
It is fitting to proclaim high praise,
to admonish the shallow-minded.
Promoted to the honor of serving closely,
we await the effect of transferring loyalty:
He may be appointed Yòu Shíyí."
Guànqīng ultimately did not accept the summons.
From *Zhíyán*.
Lǐ Gùyán
Lǐ Gùyán was born in a village estate in Fèngxiáng.
His nature was simple and honest,
unaccustomed to paying visits.
When he first sat for the Jìnshì examination,
he stayed at the capital residence of his relative, the Liǔ family.
The Liǔ brothers,
mostly fond of jesting,
seeing that Gùyán was unskilled in social matters,
tricked him into practicing the rituals of bowing and greeting.
While he was bowing deeply,
they secretly pasted a note on his headscarf that read:
"Rooms for rent here."
Gùyán was unaware.
When he went out,
court officials saw it and laughed at him.
Xǔ Mèngróng was Yòu Chángshì.
At that time, this post was looked down upon in the court,
nicknamed "sable's foot,"
and was rather incapable of promoting the reputations of younger scholars.
Gùyán initially sought an audience with his writings,
consulting the Liǔ brothers.
They directed him where to submit his portfolio,
first instructing him to present it to Chángshì Xǔ.
Gùyán indeed went to see him.
Mèngróng declined, saying:
"My post is idle and obscure,
insufficient to enhance a gentleman's brilliance.
Nevertheless,
I will keep it in mind."
Noticing the writing on his headscarf,
he realized Gùyán's simple and honest nature.
Not long after,
the following year, Xǔ oversaw the examination bureau,
and he made Gùyán the top candidate.
From *Zhíyán*.
Yīn Yáofān
In the ninth year of Yuánhé,
under the list of Wéi Guànzhī,
Yīn Yáofān failed the miscellaneous essays.
Yáng
(Míng manuscript note: "Yáng" is written as "Yáng.")
Hàn Gōng was a disciple from Guànzhī's previous list.
He strongly spoke of Yáofān's injustice,
and Guànzhī re-admitted him.
From *Zhíyán*.
Shī Jiānwú
Shī Jiānwú passed the examination in the tenth year of Yuánhé.
Considering Xīshān in Hóngzhōu
as the place where the Twelve True Lords achieved ascension,
with spiritual traces fully preserved,
he admired their true demeanor
and retired there in seclusion.
He once composed a hundred-couplet heptasyllabic poem on leisurely living and expressing sentiments,
which became widely circulated in the world.
From *Zhíyán*.
Zhāng Zhèngfǔ
Zhāng Zhèngfǔ was Governor of Hénán.
Péi Dù was commissioned to campaign against Huáixī,
and a banquet was set at the West Pavilion of the prefectural office.
Péi mentioned a candidate's literary skill,
Zhāng sternly said:
"What is Your Excellency's purpose on this campaign?
Why compete to remember Hénán's provincial top candidate?"
Péi showed a ashamed expression.
From *Zhíyán*.
(Míng manuscript note: From *Yōuxián Gǔchuī*.)
Féng Táo
Féng Sù's three sons, Táo, Tāo, and Tú,
passed the Jìnshì examination in consecutive years,
and passed the Hóngcí examination in consecutive years.
Such flourishing at one time
was unmatched in their generation.
Around the beginning of the Tàihé era,
those of the Féng clan who passed the Jìnshì examination
numbered ten throughout the land.
And from their own family, brothers, uncles, and nephews were eight.
From *Chuánzǎi Gùshí*.
Zhāng Huán
Zhāng Huán and his six brothers all passed the Jìnshì examination together.
From *Tánbīn Lù*.
Yáng Sānxǐ
Yáng Jìngzhī was appointed Guózǐ Sīyè.
His second son, Zài, passed the Jìnshì examination,
and his eldest son passed the Three Histories examination.
At the time, it was called "Yáng's Three Joys."
From *Zhíyán*.
Lǐ Féngjí
In the eleventh year of Yuánhé,
the cyclical year being Bǐngshēn,
Lǐ Féngjí's list of thirty-three candidates all came from humble backgrounds.
A saying of the time went:
"In the Yuánhé emperor's Bǐngshēn year,
Thirty-three men attained immortality together.
Robes like gleaming silver, writings like brocade,
Together they ascend to the blue sky in broad daylight."
Lǐ Déyù notably opened paths for humble scholars.
When he was demoted and sent south,
someone wrote a poem:
"Eight hundred lonely and cold ones shed tears together,
At once turning their heads to gaze toward Yázhōu."
From *Zhíyán*.
Zhāng Xiàobiāo
Zhāng Xiàobiāo failed the examination in the thirteenth year of Yuánhé.
Many of his contemporaries wrote poems satirizing the chief examiner,
but Zhāng alone wrote a "Returning Swallows" poem,
which he left as an offering to Vice-Minister Yǔ Chéngxuān.
Chéngxuān, upon receiving it in time,
repeatedly recited and pondered it,
truly regretting the overlooked talent.
He then awaited the autumn examination period,
determined to recommend him.
Yǔ indeed again presided over the examination bureau,
and Xiàobiāo passed the examination the following year.
Public opinion held that twenty-eight characters had secured a great success,
so the path to fame could be followed,
and they encouraged each other to strive diligently.
The poem said:
"The old nest on the perilous eave, its mud already fallen,
This year I return before the altar as before.
The towering cloud-high mansions have no perch for me,
Toward whose gate and door shall I fly now?"
From *Yúnxī Yǒuyì*.
Liú Kē
Liú Kē admired Mèng Kē's writings,
hence he adopted the name.
In his youth, he was a monk,
dwelling in the Guǒyuán of Gāo'ān in Yùzhāng.
Later, he sought the arts of Huáng-Lǎo,
and retired to Lúshān.
Subsequently, he passed the Jìnshì examination.
His literary works were considered equal to those of Hán and Liǔ.
From *Zhíyán*.
Cuī Qún
Cuī Qún, during Yuánhé, oversaw the examinations as Zhōngshū Shèrén.
His wife, Lady Lǐ, during leisure,
once urged him to establish manors and fields
as an estate for their descendants.
He laughed and said:
"I have thirty fine manors and good fields,
scattered throughout the land.
Why should you worry, madam?"
Lady said:
"I have not heard of you possessing such estates."
Cuī said:
"The thirty men I placed on the spring list the year before last,
are they not fine fields?"
Lady said:
"If that is so,
were you not a disciple of Chancellor Lù Zhì?"
He said:
"Yes."
Lady said:
"In previous years, when you held authority over the examinations,
you had someone instruct his son, Jiǎnlǐ,
not to sit for the test.
If you consider them fine fields,
then one of the Lù family's manors lies fallow."
Cuī retreated in shame,
and for several days did not eat.
From *Dúyì Zhì*.
The Daughter of Lǐ Áo
Lǐ Áo served as a prefect in the Jiānghuái region.
There was a presented scholar, Lú Chǔ, who submitted his examination papers.
Áo treated him with courtesy
and placed the literary scrolls on his desk.
Then he went out to attend to official duties.
His eldest daughter, who had reached the age of capping (i.e., marriageable age),
was leisurely walking in front of the bell tower
when she saw the literary scrolls.
After reading through them several times,
she said to her young maid:
"This man is sure to become the top graduate (zhuàngtóu)."
When Áo returned from his duties,
he heard of this
and was deeply struck by her words.
He then sent an assistant to the postal station
to fully explain the matter to Lú
and selected him as a son-in-law.
Lú modestly declined for a long time,
but in the end could not refuse his intention.
After a month, he went to the capital for the examinations.
The following year, he indeed achieved top graduate honors.
As soon as he passed the palace examination,
he went straight to the wedding ceremony.
His "Urging the Bride to Make Up" poem reads:
"In former years, I was about to journey to the Jade Capital;
The foremost immortal promised me the top graduate title.
Today, fortunate to join in this Qín-Jìn union,
May the phoenix descend early from her dressing tower."
Later, when Lú was residing in his official quarters,
he went to fetch his wife.
Seeing courtyard flowers in bloom,
he inscribed a poem:
"Peonies, freshly planted,
A few blossoms open in the courtyard.
The east wind restrains itself,
Awaiting the arrival of my lady."
That which is predetermined in life
is certainly not accidental.
From "Lyric Poems"
Hè Bá Jì
Wáng Qǐ, during the Chángqìng era, presided over the examinations for the second time.
He intended to make Bái Mǐnzhōng the top graduate,
but was troubled by his association with Hè Bá Jì.
Jì was talented but unconventional and unrestrained.
Thus, Qǐ secretly had a close acquaintance convey his intention,
urging Mǐnzhōng to break off with Jì.
The acquaintance again
Míng manuscript has "again" as "conveyed"
made the agreement,
and Mǐnzhōng readily agreed,
complying with all instructions.
Soon after, Jì came to visit.
The attendants deceived him, saying Mǐnzhōng had gone elsewhere.
Jì lingered a while, then left without a word.
Moments later, Mǐnzhōng rushed out,
repeatedly calling for his attendants to summon
"Summon" added based on "Táng Zhìyán."
Jì.
He then told him the whole truth.
And said:
"What rank could I not attain?
But how could I lightly betray a close friend?"
They drank together until thoroughly drunk
and slept under the sun.
When the acquaintance saw this,
he left in great anger.
He reported to Qǐ,
saying:
"It cannot be guaranteed."
Qǐ said:
"I originally only wanted Bái Mǐnzhōng;
now I must also take Hè Bá Jì."
From "Zhìyán"
Lǐ Zōngmǐn
When Lǐ Zōngmǐn oversaw the imperial examinations,
his successful candidates were mostly elegant, handsome, and outstanding.
Táng Shēn, Xuē Xiáng, Yuán Dū, and others
were called the "Jade Shoots Class" at the time.
"Jade Shoots Class" originally missing;
added based on the Huáng edition.
From "Yīnhuà Lù"
Yǔ Chéngxuān
Yǔ Chéngxuān presided over the examinations, and six or seven years later
he was finally awarded the gold seal and purple ribbon.
By then, his disciple Lǐ Shí had already received such an honor from the inner court.
When Chéngxuān first received his appointment,
Shí presented his own purple robe and gold fish tally to his examiner as an offering.
From "Zhìyán"
Zhāng Hù
Zhāng Hù, during the Yuánhé and Chángqìng eras, was greatly appreciated by Líng Hú Chǔ.
When Chǔ was stationed in Tiānpíng,
he personally drafted a recommendation memorial, ordering Hù to submit three hundred new and old regulated poems along with it.
The text roughly stated:
"All his pentasyllabic compositions
encompass the Six Principles.
Recently, many have been unrestrained and wild,
lacking a master to emulate.
The aforementioned person has long been among the rivers and lakes,
and has diligently practiced poetry since early on.
His study is profound and earnest,
his exploration
"Exploration" originally "mutual";
corrected per the Míng manuscript.
is quite deep.
Praised by his peers,
his style is rarely matched.
I respectfully have him record three hundred new and old regulated poems,
to be presented from the Guāngshùn Gate,
hoping they may be proclaimed and handed over to the Secretariat."
Hù arrived in the capital
just as Yuán Zhěn was serving in the inner court.
The emperor summoned him to inquire about Hù's literary quality.
Zhěn replied:
"Zhāng Hù's works are mere ornamental trifles;
what a true man would be ashamed to do.
If encouraged,
I fear it may alter Your Majesty's customs and teachings."
The emperor nodded,
and thus Hù returned disappointed.
Hù lamented in a poem:
"Hè Zhīzhāng's praise was in vain;
Mèng Hàorán's fate leaves no further doubt."
From "Zhìyán"
Lú Qiú
Among the second list of candidates under Yáng Sìfù was Lú Qiú,
the son-in-law of Lǐ Áo.
Previously, when Áo was prefect of Héféi,
a Daoist visited him and spoke of extraordinary matters.
Later, when Áo served in Chǔzhōu,
or perhaps Guìzhōu,
the man came again.
That year, Sìfù oversaw the examinations,
and Qiú failed.
Sìfù
was Áo's brother-in-law.
Thus, Áo felt somewhat embarrassed.
He consulted the Daoist,
who said:
"A minor matter;
I can also draft a memorial."
He prepared an inkstone, paper, and brush,
and also placed several measures of fine wine beside him.
The man drank a large cup to the brim,
slept briefly and awoke,
awoke and drank until the wine was finished,
then straightened his clothes and cap, bowed northward,
and quickly wrote two sealed letters at the desk.
At dawn, he handed them to Áo, saying:
"This autumn, there will be an examiner;
open the small scroll then.
Next year, when the list is posted,
open the large scroll."
Áo followed his instructions.
Soon, news arrived
that Sìfù would again preside over the examinations.
He opened the small scroll.
It read:
"Peí at the head, Huáng at the tail;
three Qiús and six Lǐs."
Áo found it strange
and sent it to Sìfù.
Sìfù already had his own list
and suspected a leak.
When the list was posted,
he opened the large scroll:
the entire list matched perfectly,
without a single error.
That year,
Peí Qiú was the top graduate,
Huáng Jià was last on the list,
and next was Lú Qiú.
The rest all matched.
Later, when Áo governed Xiāngyáng,
the man came again.
Áo regarded him with even greater respect and awe.
The man said to Áo:
"I have come again
out of admiration for your governance."
He then asked to see Áo's sons.
After looking them over carefully,
he said none would inherit Áo's
Táng "Zhìyán" eight has "inherit" as "match."
achievements.
Áo then had his daughters come out to bow to him.
He said:
"In the future, three of the Minister's grandsons
will all rise to the positions of Chief Ministers."
Later, Qiú's son Xié, Zhèng Yà's son Tián, and Dù Shěnquán's son Ràngnéng
all became generals and ministers.
From "Zhìyán"
Dù Mù
After Vice Minister Cuī Yǎn received his appointment,
he went to the Eastern Capital
(The Tang dynasty "Records of the Imperial Examinations" uses "capital" instead of "commandery.")
to administer the provincial examinations for the candidates.
The high-ranking officials from the three bureaus
all gathered to see him off at the Chánglè postal station.
The assembly of officials and their carriages was so grand
that it was rarely surpassed.
At that time, Wú Wǔlíng held the position of Erudite of the Grand Academy.
He arrived riding a lame donkey.
Cuī Yǎn, hearing of his arrival,
was slightly surprised.
When he left his seat to speak with him,
Wú Wǔlíng said:
"Your Excellency, with your lofty virtue and great reputation,
is selecting talented individuals for our enlightened Son of Heaven.
How dare I, Wú Wǔlíng, not offer my humble assistance, like dust and dew?
Recently, I happened to see several dozen students of the Grand Academy
raising their eyebrows and clapping their hands while reading a certain literary work.
I approached to look at it,
and it turned out to be the 'Rhapsody on the Ēpáng Palace' by the presented scholar Dù Mù.
As for this man,
he truly possesses the talent to assist a king.
Your Excellency holds a high office and is likely busy,
so I fear you may not have had time to peruse it."
Thereupon, he straightened his official tablet,
and recited it aloud once.
Cuī Yǎn was greatly impressed by it.
Wú Wǔlíng then requested:
"Your Excellency, please award him the top rank (zhuàngtóu)."
Cuī Yǎn said:
"That position is already taken."
Wú Wǔlíng said:
"If not,
then the third rank."
Cuī Yǎn said:
"That is also taken."
Wú Wǔlíng said:
"If there's no other choice,
then the fifth rank."
Before Cuī Yǎn could respond,
Wú Wǔlíng said:
"If not,
then I ask to take this rhapsody back."
Cuī Yǎn replied immediately:
"I respectfully comply with your instruction."
After returning to his seat,
he announced to the assembled officials:
"Just now, Erudite Wú has generously offered me the fifth rank."
Someone asked:
"For whom?"
He said:
"Dù Mù."
Among the crowd, someone raised the issue of Dù Mù's disregard for minor proprieties.
Cuī Yǎn said:
"I have already promised Master Wú.
Even if Dù Mù were a dog butcher,
I cannot change it."
Cuī Yǎn announced the results in the Eastern Capital,
and the successful candidates proceeded to the Western Capital for the final ceremony.
Dù Mù (styled Zǐwēi) wrote a poem:
"The list announced in the east, before flowers bloom,
Thirty-three men ride their horses back.
The youths of Qín land brew much wine,
Ready to bring the spring scenery through the pass."
From "Records of the Imperial Examinations"
Liú Fén
In the second year of the Tàihé era (828 AD),
Péi Xiū and twenty-two others passed the special decree examination.
At that time, Liú Fén submitted a policy response of over ten thousand characters,
deeply exploring the roots of order and chaos.
He also extensively cited the great principles of the Spring and Autumn Annals,
such that even Gōngsūn Hóng and Dǒng Zhòngshū could not surpass him.
From Péi Xiū down,
all were filled with respect.
However, because he pointedly criticized powerful and favored individuals,
showing no regard for taboos,
the officials in charge knew his worth but did not select him.
A fellow candidate who passed, Lǐ Shào
(The Ming manuscript has "Shào" written as "Hé".)
went to the palace and submitted a memorial,
requesting to exchange his own success
for Liú Fén's failure.
The memorial was submitted but kept in the palace without response.
Within a month,
Liú Fén's reputation for being wronged spread throughout the land.
From "Records of the Imperial Examinations"
Liú Fén was a disciple of Yáng Sìfù.
After his straightforward words caused offense,
the palace eunuchs were particularly resentful and angry.
The Palace Army Commander Qiú Shìliáng said to Yáng Sìfù:
"How could you use a state examination
to pass this madman?"
Yáng Sìfù, afraid,
replied:
"When Sìfù passed the examination with Liú Fén in the past,
he was not yet mad."
From "The Jade Spring Master"
Xuē Bǎoxùn
Xuē Bǎoxùn was fond of submitting large scrolls of writing,
and styled himself the "Vajra Pestle."
During the Tàihé era (827-835 AD),
the number of tribute scholars was no less than a thousand,
and the gates of the high ministers
were piled high with scrolls and volumes,
which were used to pay for the gatekeeper women's candles and cosmetics.
Therefore, those who were easygoing would say:
"If it's Xuē Bǎoxùn's scroll,
then the payment received will be double the usual."
From "Records of the Imperial Examinations"
Jiǎ Dǎo
Jiǎ Dǎo was not good at taking examinations.
Every time he took a test,
he would fold a sheet of paper for himself.
Patrolling the examination hall
(The original text has "捕" (arrest),
changed to "铺" (post/booth) according to the Ming manuscript.)
he would tell people:
"You fellows who start with '原夫' (yuánfū, a conventional essay opening),
give me a couplet,
give me a couplet."
From "Records of the Imperial Examinations"
Bì Xián
In the year Bì Xián passed the imperial examination,
he went with one or two others
to listen for divinatory sounds.
The night was late and people sparse,
and for a long time they heard nothing.
Suddenly, they encountered someone throwing a bone on the ground,
and a pack of dogs rushed to compete for it.
One of them then said:
"The one coming later is sure to snatch it."
From "Records of the Imperial Examinations"
Péi Déróng
Péi Déróng's taboo name was Gāo.
It happened that Gāo Kǎi was the chief examiner,
and Péi went to take the examination.
The chief examiner said:
"His taboo name is Gāo.
If I
(The Ming manuscript has "向" (towards) for "某" (I);
the Xu manuscript has "某" (I) for "棋" (chess).)
allow him to take the examination and pass him,
it will trouble him for a lifetime."
Later, he was appointed Assistant Minister of the Bureau of Imperial Farms.
At that time,
(The original text has "將" (about to),
changed to "時" (at that time) according to the Ming manuscript.)
Lú Jiǎnqiú was the Vice Director of the Right.
Péi went with another newly appointed vice director to pay a courtesy call.
Upon arriving at the residence,
Vice Director Lú first invited the other man in.
After a leisurely while,
the other man mentioned:
"I and the newly appointed Assistant Minister Péi of the Bureau of Imperial Farms
are both waiting to pay our respects to you, Vice Director.
Assistant Minister Péi has been waiting outside the gate for a long time."
Lú immediately had an attendant convey a message:
"Under whom did Assistant Minister pass the examination?
I happen to have some business
and cannot receive him."
Péi, flustered and confused,
mounted the other man's horse and rode out the gate.
From "Miscellaneous Stories of the Lú Family"
Péi Sīqiān
In the first examination list presided over by Gāo Kǎi,
Péi Sīqiān obtained the top position through the influence of Qiú Shìliáng.
Kǎi reprimanded him in the courtyard,
but Sīqiān turned back and said sternly:
"Next year, I will take the top position by my own merit."
The following year,
when Kǎi was in charge of the examinations,
he warned his subordinates not to accept any letters of recommendation.
Sīqiān personally carried a letter from Shìliáng into the examination hall.
After changing into purple robes,
he hurried to the steps below
and said to Kǎi:
"The Military Commissioner has a letter,
recommending the scholar Péi Sīqiān."
Kǎi had no choice
and thus accepted it.
The letter requested a high rank for Sīqiān.
Kǎi said:
"The top candidate has already been chosen.
Apart from that, we can comply with the Military Commissioner's wishes."
Sīqiān said:
"This humble official personally received instructions from the Military Commissioner:
if Péi Sīqiān is not the top candidate,
please do not release the list, Minister."
Kǎi lowered his head for a long while and said:
"Then I must at least meet Scholar Péi."
Sīqiān said:
"This humble official is he."
Sīqiān was a man of imposing stature,
and when Kǎi saw him, his expression changed.
Having no alternative,
he complied.
From "Zhì Yán."
Lǐ Gōng
In the autumn of the first year of the Kāichéng era,
Gāo Kǎi again oversaw the examination register.
The Emperor said:
"The imperial clan members are the pillars of the state,
the main branches for a hundred generations.
Their titles and enfeoffments should be appropriate,
and they must not be allowed to fall into disuse.
In previous years, those recommended by the Imperial Clan Court
may have been frivolous and shallow,
thus disgracing the examination honors.
You must meticulously select those with true talent and ability,
and not obstruct the path of the worthy.
For the fu they are to compose,
follow the usual conventions;
for the shi poetry, adopt the style of the Qí and Liáng dynasties."
Thus, they were tested on the fu "Qín Sè Hé Zòu" and the shi "Nícháng Yǔyī Qǔ."
The examiners first presented five shi poems,
the best being by Lǐ Gōng,
followed by Wáng Shōu.
By the time the sun was setting, the fu was presented—
it was the "Xuě Yuè Fù" from the Wén Xuǎn.
Moreover, Gōng was of the imperial clan,
his moral conduct was consistently exemplary,
and both his talent and character were excellent.
How could I not be impartial,
lest I betray the Emperor's instruction?
Thus, he was ranked first on the list and passed.
The shi "Nícháng Yǔyī Qǔ,"
by Lǐ Gōng, reads:
"In the peaceful times of Kāiyuán,
all states celebrated the abundant year.
The Líyuán presented old melodies,
the jade throne flowed with new compositions.
Phoenix pipes played in harmonious discord,
rainbow garments swayed in unison.
After the feast, the waterside palace stood empty,
following the imperial carriage, spring grass grew fine.
Matters of Pénglái have long passed,
yet the immortal music's merit remains undiminished.
How could one refuse to listen to these lingering sounds?
The sagely and wise know well how to carry on."
The Emperor read it and said:
"Among my close relatives, is there anyone like Gōng
who would bring disgrace?
With the discernment of Liú Ān,
he could be ordered to write books;
upholding the correctness of Mǎ Fú,
he could serve as an official historian.
Qín
(Original text had 'zòu' for 'qín',
corrected per "Yúnxī Yǒuyì.")
The Yíng clan ruled all under heaven,
yet their sons and brothers were like common men.
When the roots are not deep and firm,
how could Cáo Jiǒng not criticize it?"
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì."
Sū Jǐng, Zhāng Yuánfū
During the Tàihé era,
Sū Jǐngyìn and Zhāng Yuánfū
were masters of the Hànlín
(The character 'lín' was originally missing,
supplemented from the Ming manuscript copy.)
Academy.
Yáng Rǔshì and his brothers Yúqīng and Hàngōng
were especially
(Original text had 'xiān' for 'yóu',
corrected per Ming manuscript copy.)
regarded as models in the literary world.
(Original text had 'shì' for 'shì' [model],
corrected per Ming manuscript copy.)
Therefore, later scholars said among themselves:
"If you wish to enter the examination grounds,
first inquire of Sū and Zhāng.
Sū and Zhāng are manageable enough,
but the three Yángs will be the death of me."
During the Dàzhōng and Xiántōng eras,
it was widely said that Minister Cuī Shèn
(Ming manuscript copy has 'Shènyóu' after 'Shèn'.)
often sent letters to those he knew.
Some said,
"Wáng Níng, Péi Zàn, and my younger brother Ānqián—
in the court, no one addresses them by their courtesy names among acquaintances;
in their offices, there are absolutely no guests for whom they would remove their boots."
Níng ended his career as Governor of Xuānchéng;
Zàn became Minister of Rites;
Ānqián became a Palace Attendant.
The two families of Wáng Chóng and Dòu Xián of Tàipíng
both relied on the examination system as capital,
sufficient to elevate or sink later scholars.
Therefore, examination candidates said among themselves:
"Without having seen Wáng and Dòu,
your journey is but a futile effort."
From "Zhì Yán."
Later, there were eastern and western second-rank lists,
the eastern calling the western the 'Vast and Unskilled Brigade,'
meaning they had no talent.
From "Lú Shì Zá Shuō."
During the Kāichéng and Huìchāng eras,
it was also said:
"Zhèng, Yáng, Duàn, Xuē—
so powerful you can feel the heat from their hands."
There were also frivolous fellows
who often belittled and insulted others.
Therefore, Péi Mì, when taking the examinations,
composed the "Rě Měi Rén Fù" to satirize them.
There were also greater and lesser second-rank lists;
also the Wāng-Jǐ list;
also the 'Four Characters,'
meaning profound influence within the court.
Also the 'Four Villains' list.
Also the 'Ten Sages of Fānglín,'
referring to those who associated with palace eunuchs,
such as Liú Yè, Rèn Xī, Jiāng Jì, Lǐ Yánshì, Cái Chán, Qín Tāoyù, and their like.
Chán and Yánshì
each carried recommendation letters from two armies,
seeking the top position.
They were called at the time 'Army-Paired Top Candidates.'
During the Tàihé era,
there were also Dù Yǐ, Dòu Xún, Xiāo Jí who enjoyed contemporary fame,
and were leaders for later generations.
Emperor Wénzōng once spoke of the flourishing state of the jìnshì examinations.
The chief minister at the time replied:
"In the examination grounds, they say themselves:
'A provincial tribute jìnshì
is not worth a prefect of an upper prefecture.'"
The Emperor laughed and said:
"There's nothing to be done about it either."
From "Lú Shì Zá Shuō."
Cuī Lǐ
During the time when Cuī Lǐ of the Tang dynasty served as Zhìzhìgào,
his mother, the Grand Lady, passed away,
and he resided at his private residence in the Eastern Capital.
At that time, he still upheld a life of purity, hardship, and frugality.
Gifts sent from all directions
consisted only of tea and medicine;
he did not accept gold or silk.
Thus, the households of court worthies were no different from those of humble commoners.
Even his beloved concubines and children
wore neither light nor fine garments.
When Cuī Lǐ had set a date for the burial,
one day,
a scholar from his clan came to request an audience with Lǐ.
The gatekeeper refused him,
saying:
"The master is in mourning
and does not receive any guests."
The scholar then said:
"I am a descendant of the Cuī clan,
and I know that the day for the distant burial of your esteemed mother has been set.
I wish to see the master once."
Upon hearing this,
Cuī Lǐ invited him in and spoke with him.
The scholar said directly:
"I know that you, sir, while serving among the officials,
are pure and frugal.
The expenses required for the Grand Lady's funeral
cannot be without cost.
As I am of the unworthy generation of grandsons and nephews,
and moreover, my financial means are somewhat sufficient,
I wish to contribute three million coins to assist you in this great matter."
Lǐ, seeing his generosity,
was deeply impressed by him.
However, he only praised and accepted his intention,
ultimately declining and not accepting the money.
This scholar had long failed in the imperial examinations,
and there was considerable sympathy for his plight.
Not long after, Cuī Lǐ completed his mourning period,
was appointed Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
and oversaw the imperial examinations for the Ministry of Rites.
This scholar took the examination,
and Lǐ placed him as the top candidate (zhuàngyuán).
Many were quite surprised.
They said that Lǐ, as the chief examiner,
should select scholars based on fairness,
and that Cuī's literary skill
had earned him fame through its high quality.
Passing the examination was acceptable,
but being ranked first was not appropriate.
Because of this, some people questioned Lǐ.
He replied:
"Cuī Mǒu certainly deserved to pass the examination,
but his position as top candidate was due to my personal gratitude."
He then explained the previous incident to them.
Thereupon, both inside and outside the court, people began to be convinced,
and his reputation grew even greater.
From "Zhītián Lù".
Lú Zhào
Lǐ Déyù suppressed the frivolous and shallow,
and promoted the isolated and humble.
At that time, the powerful at court formed cliques,
which Déyù broke up.
As a result, he incurred resentment,
and cut off all associations,
so that no guests came to his gate.
Only the jìnshì Lú Zhào,
a native of Yíchūn,
who had extraordinary talent,
was known to Déyù from when Déyù had served as a minor official in Yíyáng.
Zhào had submitted his literary works to him,
and thus became known.
Later, when Zhào went to the capital for the examinations,
each time he paid a visit,
he was treated with great courtesy.
According to old practice:
The Ministry of Rites would present the list of successful candidates
to the Prime Minister first.
In the third year of the Huìcháng era,
Wáng Qǐ was in charge of the examinations.
He asked Déyù whom he desired to pass.
Déyù replied:
"Why ask about my desires?
As for Lú Zhào, Dīng Léng, Yáo Hú,
how could they not be granted the jìnshì degree?"
Qǐ then released the list according to this order.
From "Yùquánzǐ".
Dīng Léng
When Lú Zhào and Dīng Léng passed the jìnshì examination,
according to precedent, after the list was posted,
they had to pay respects to the Prime Minister.
The introductory speech,
was to be delivered by the top candidate (zhuàngyuán).
The pace and manner of delivery,
required particular care and precision.
At that time, Zhào was the top candidate,
but due to an unavoidable circumstance, he could not attend.
The next in line was Léng.
Léng stuttered,
and was also short and unimpressive in appearance.
When it was time for the audience,
he bowed and began his speech.
He intended to say "Léng and others have passed the examination,"
but Léng turned red and broke into a sweat.
After bowing for a while,
he finally said:
"Léng and others have passed,
Léng and others have passed."
In the end, he could not utter the rest of the words and stopped.
Those present all laughed.
The next day,
someone teased him, saying:
"I heard you are skilled at playing the zhēng,
may I hear it?"
Léng said:
"I am not."
The friend said:
"Yesterday I heard 'Léng and others have passed, Léng and others have passed,'
wasn't that the sound of a zhēng?"
From "Yùquánzǐ".
Gù Fēixióng,
son of Kuàng,
was witty and fond of debate,
often offending the arrogant sons of powerful families,
and was thus resented by many.
Having been ostracized,
Fēixióng remained in the examination halls for nearly thirty years,
and the sound of his grievances filled people's ears.
During the Huìcháng era,
when Chén Shāng posted the list of successful candidates,
the Emperor noticed Fēixióng's name was missing.
He summoned the officials to retrieve the list,
and Fēixióng was granted the jìnshì degree.
At that time, all the humble scholars in the empire
were encouraged by this.
The poet Liú Dérén wrote a congratulatory poem:
"Even when I was a child,
I already understood and recited your poetry.
Now that you have achieved a high rank late in life,
it must be because you met a wise ruler who recognized you."
From "Zhíyán".
Lǐ Déyù
Lǐ Déyù, because he himself had not advanced through the imperial examinations,
constantly resented those who took the jìnshì examinations.
When he held the position of Prime Minister,
he strictly restrained his sons.
Déyù had once served as an assistant in a regional government office,
and a fellow official, Lǐ Píngshì, had advanced through the literary examinations,
and happened to hold the same rank as Déyù.
At that time, an examination candidate submitted a scroll of writings,
and mistakenly gave it to Déyù.
Realizing his mistake,
the candidate requested it back, saying:
"My scroll was meant for the successful candidate Lǐ Píngshì,
not for you, sir."
From then on, Déyù was determined to suppress such candidates.
From "Yùquánzǐ".
Zhāng Fén
Zhāng Fén achieved the top rank (zhuàngyuán) in the fifth year of Huìcháng under the examiner Chén Shāng.
The Hànlín Academy reviewed the results,
and Fén and seven others were removed from the list.
Zhào Zhòunán sent Fén a poem:
"Do not complain to the spring breeze over a cup of wine,
The banished immortal truly has immortal talent.
Still worthy of being an auspicious sign for the world,
For you have once reached the summit of Pénglái Mountain."
From "Zhíyán".
Emperor Xuānzōng
Emperor Xuānzōng was extremely fond of those who passed the jìnshì examinations.
Whenever he faced his court ministers, he would ask about their examination success.
If anyone replied that they had passed the examinations,
he would be greatly pleased,
and would then ask about the topics of the poetry and fu they had written,
