and the names of the chief examiners.
If someone of decent appearance and talent
happened not to pass,
he would sigh with regret for a long time.
He often wrote inside the palace, "Provincial Tribute Jìnshì Lǐ Dàolóng".
From "Lúshì Záshuō".
Lú Wò
Lú Wò, the Surveillance Commissioner of Shǎnzhōu in the Táng dynasty,
enjoyed a great reputation in the examination circles.
Once, at an inn by the Chǎn River,
he encountered Emperor Xuānzong traveling incognito.
Suspecting him to be a nobleman,
Lú respectfully stepped aside to avoid him.
The emperor greeted him and they met.
Lú then introduced himself as the presented scholar Lú Wò.
The emperor asked for his collection of poems,
tucked it into his sleeve,
and rode away on his mule.
Some days later, while speaking with his chief ministers,
the emperor mentioned Lú Wò
and ordered the chief examiner to grant him a passing grade.
Lú felt uneasy,
fearing the disgrace of an undeserved honor.
The chief minister asked Lú what connection he had with the emperor.
Lú then explained the circumstances in detail,
and at the time, it was not considered shameful.
Thus, he also achieved success in his career.
Later, Lú Wò entered the court from his post as Surveillance Commissioner
and served as chief examiner.
When the Huáng rebels attacked the capital,
he was unable to complete the examination session.
Grand Master Zhào Chóng teased him, saying:
"He is an examiner who does not nurture those from his own womb."
However, the Lú family had never before served as chief examiner;
Chief Minister Lú Xié felt ashamed of this
and promoted him to be in charge of literary affairs,
but it did not come to fruition.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Liú Tuì
In Jīngnán, the provincial examination was notoriously called "the barren land."
In the fourth year of the Dàzhōng era,
Liú Tuì passed the metropolitan examination as a candidate from that prefecture.
At the time, Cuī Xuàn was the military governor there
and awarded Tuì seven hundred thousand coins for "breaking the barren land."
In his letter of thanks, Tuì wrote briefly:
"For fifty years,
it was due to human neglect;
a thousand miles away,
how could it be called a barren land?"
From "Zhí Yán".
Miáo Táifú and Zhāng Dú
Miáo Táifú could compose literary works at the age of six,
and was exceptionally intelligent.
By his teens, he had read extensively through many books
and authored thirty volumes of "Huáng Xīn."
He passed the imperial examination at the age of sixteen.
Zhāng Dú was also skilled in poetry and prose from a young age,
and passed the examination at eighteen.
They were both presented scholars in the same year,
and later served together as aides to Junior Mentor Zhèng Xūn in the Xuānzhōu administration.
The two often inscribed their names on the eastern corridor of the Xīmíng Temple.
Someone secretly annotated it, saying:
"A pair of former presented scholars,
two little children."
Táifú died at seventeen without holding office,
while Dú rose to the position of Vice Minister of Rites.
From "Zhí Yán".
Xǔ Dàomǐn
When Xǔ Dàomǐn was first recommended by his prefecture,
he gained the favor of the then chief minister.
That winter,
the chief examiner was about to oversee affairs at the examination hall
and paid a visit to the chief minister's residence.
The chief minister highly praised Dàomǐn's outstanding literary skills,
saying he deserved to be selected in the public examination.
The chief examiner accepted the instruction and left.
Dàomǐn secretly learned of this intention,
so he honed his skills in preparation,
counting down the days until the examination,
and his name was widely talked about.
Soon, Vice Director Zhāng Xīfù married into the family of Chief Minister Qízhāng Gōng.
On the wedding night,
Dàomǐn was invited to serve as the ceremonial attendant.
Seized by the joyous atmosphere,
Dàomǐn drank freely and composed impromptu verses,
swaying his jade pendant and speaking loftily,
ending the night in great merriment.
Not long after,
the chief minister's memorials failed to meet the emperor's approval,
and he was transferred to another commandery.
Fearing a change in circumstances,
the chief examiner did not dare to rank Dàomǐn among the top candidates.
From then on, Dàomǐn fell into obscurity and hardship,
and never regained his former prominence.
Later, he encountered family misfortunes,
and for twenty years he was out of step.
It was not until the sixth year of Dàzhōng, when Cuī Yù served as chief examiner,
that he was finally selected with a high rank.
At that time, his fellow candidate Zhāng Dú succeeded in one attempt,
at the age of nineteen.
This was the winter when Dàomǐn failed at the brink of success,
serving as attendant for the son of Zhāng Xīfù,
who was born of Lady Niú.
From "Táng Quē Shǐ".
Cuī Yīnmèng
was a disciple of his clansman Cuī Yáo.
He was the son of Guīcóng, the military governor of Yímén,
and topped the list of successful candidates in the same year as Rǎng.
Míng Chāo Běn notes: "Rǎng" is written as "Rǎng".
The same below.
Rǎng said to Yáo:
"A man of reputation
adorns his life and background to appear admirable,
but others should not be treated equally.
In recent years, within the capital examination,
many have used false names
to seek opportunities elsewhere,
which is utterly meaningless.
Now I beg you, Vice Minister,
not to follow this old practice."
Yáo greatly agreed.
One day,
Rǎng and others gathered with their fellow candidates to pay respects to Yáo.
After they were seated,
Yáo smiled and said to Rǎng and the others:
"Yesterday, I received a letter from the Grand Councilor of Dàliáng,
who wishes for Senior Cuī to visit once.
With a swift horse and sturdy servants,
the round trip should not cause delay.
I hope you seniors will take note."
Bound by his examiner's command,
Rǎng had no choice but to comply.
From "Yù Quán Zǐ".
Yán Biāo
When Vice Minister Zhèng Xūn served as chief examiner,
among the candidates was one named Yán Biāo.
Xūn mistakenly thought he was a descendant of Duke Lǔ.
At that time, the Xú region was not yet pacified,
and Xūn aimed to encourage loyalty and valor,
so he ranked Biāo as the top candidate.
On the day of giving thanks,
Xūn casually asked about his ancestral temple,
to which Biāo replied:
"I am a humble candidate
and have never had an ancestral temple."
Only then did Xūn realize his mistake,
and he fell silent in embarrassment.
Soon after, an anonymous person mocked him, saying:
"The examiner's mind is too muddled,
mistaking Yán Biāo for Duke Lǔ."
From "Zhí Yán".
Wēn Tíngyún
Wēn Tíngyún never drafted his compositions by lamplight;
he would merely tuck his hands into his sleeves and lean on the desk.
Each time he composed a rhyme,
he would chant it only once.
Thus, in the examination hall, he was called "Wēn the Eight-Chanter."
From "Zhí Yán".
Lú Càn
In the year Cuī Hàng passed the examination,
he served as the disciplinary officer.
His fellow candidate Lú Càn, as the banquet near the palace gate approached,
insisted on taking leave
to return to Luòyáng to celebrate.
However, he delayed for a long time,
and when his fellow candidates held a banquet at the Qǔjiāng Pavilion,
Lú arrived in a carved carriage with courtesans,
wearing plain clothes and loosely holding the reins,
observing from the side.
He was promptly reported by the banquet officials,
and Hàng delivered a judgment,
which read in part:
"Deeply hidden under a traveler's hat,
closely screened by a felt-covered carriage.
Seeking spring on the purple paths,
he is separated from his fellow candidates' faces;
having found his way to the blue clouds,
his future intentions can be known."
From "Zhí Yán".
Wēng Yànshū
was a native of Sūzhōu
who sat for the jìnshì examinations.
There was a monk from the same hometown as Yànshū
who frequented the household of the former chancellor Péi Yuán
("Yuán" is written as "Tǎn" in Yùquánzǐ),
and the same below.
He was allowed entry.
Because of his advanced age, they treated him with kindness and indulgence,
so even the inner gates
did not restrict his comings and goings.
He held prayer beads in his hand,
reciting Buddhist scriptures with his eyes closed;
except when eating or sleeping,
he never stopped.
When Yuán was in charge of the examinations
and entered the examination hall,
his sons, Xūn and Zhì,
would daily discuss the ranking list in their private chambers.
The monk was often present among them,
and the two sons did not suspect him.
The names they deliberated on,
along with decisions on promotions and demotions,
the monk became thoroughly familiar with them all.
Returning to the temple, Yànshū visited him.
The monk asked Yànshū about his prospects for success or failure.
Yànshū replied in detail that he had no hope of achievement.
The monk said:
"What rank must you achieve to become successful?"
Yànshū thought the monk was teasing him,
and replied:
"The eighth place would be enough."
The monk then went again to the Péi household.
The two sons were discussing as before,
when the monk suddenly opened his eyes and said to them:
"Is the Vice-Minister in charge of the examinations, or
are you young masters in charge?
The imperial examinations are a grave matter of the state.
The court entrusted them to the Vice-Minister,
intending for him to eradicate previous malpractices,
so that the isolated and impoverished
("impoverished" originally written as "píng,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript)
may find a path.
Yet now, promotions and demotions
are entirely decided by you young masters.
Is the Vice-Minister merely a puppet?
Moreover, those you associate with
are nothing but the children of the powerful and wealthy.
You have never considered a single impoverished
("impoverished" originally written as "píng,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript)
scholar of talent.
Is this acceptable, young masters?"
He then bent his fingers,
counting from first to last,
without missing a single person.
The intricate details of the powerful families and private connections
all hit upon what the two sons wished to conceal.
Xūn and the others were greatly frightened.
They immediately asked the monk what he desired,
and tried to bribe him with gold and silk.
The monk said:
"This poor monk is old;
what use have I for gold and silk?
There is a fellow townsman named Wēng Yànshū
who only wishes to pass the examinations."
Xūn and the others said:
"Then we will place him in the third class."
The monk said:
"It must be the eighth place, nothing else."
Xūn had no choice but to agree.
The monk said:
"Give this poor monk a written pledge."
Yànshū passed that year,
exactly as predicted.
From Yùquánzǐ
Liú Xūbái
Liú Xūbái and Péi Yuán had shared a study desk early on.
When Yuán presided over the examinations,
Xūbái was still a candidate.
On the day of the miscellaneous writings examination,
he presented a quatrain before the curtain:
"Twenty years ago on such a night as this,
the same lamps, the same breeze.
Who knows how many years remain,
yet still in hemp robes I serve the impartial lord."
Mèng Qǐ was older than Duke Wèi.
On the day the results were posted,
Qǐ went to offer his thanks in person.
Hàng wept and said:
"You, senior, are my teacher."
As Hàng wept,
Qǐ also wept.
Qǐ had been involved in the examination circuit for thirty years.
Chángsūn Jí was an old friend of Lord Zhāng.
The lord addressed Jí as elder brother.
The lord once urged him to change his plans.
Jí said:
"If I hear the Way in the morning,
I may die content in the evening."
From Zhìyán
Fēng Dìngqīng
After the Dàzhōng era,
jìnshì candidates were especially numerous.
Fēng Dìngqīng and Dīng Màoguī—
candidates who associated with them
would inevitably pass first,
yet these two gentlemen each took twenty attempts before achieving success.
Why such a disparity in advancement and setback?
Previously, the four gentlemen Lǐ Dū, Cuī Yōng, Sūn Huáng, and Zhèng Yú
—those who received their favor thereby advanced.
Thus it was said:
If you wish your fate to prosper,
ask Huáng, Yú, Dū, and Yōng.
From Běimèng Suǒyán
Féng Zǎo
Táng dynasty's Féng Zǎo
was the son of the Regular Attendant Féng Sù
and uncle to Féng Juān,
their family having a tradition of examination success.
Zǎo's literary talent was not high,
yet he was intensely fond of scholarly rank.
He had already attempted fifteen times.
An acquainted Daoist priest told him:
"I once entered meditation to observe:
in this life you will not achieve examination rank,
but you will hold official positions."
He did not believe it.
He attempted ten more times,
making twenty-five attempts in total.
His relatives urged him to give up the examinations
and seek an official post instead.
Zǎo said:
"Suppose even after a lifetime I achieve nothing,
I vow to attempt five more times."
Achieving nothing,
he thus made thirty attempts
before finally taking up an official career.
He served as a chief minister, supervisor, and prefect of Xiá,
ending his days in the Imperial Secretariat.
From Běimèng Suǒyán
Zhào Cóng
Zhào Cóng's father-in-law was a senior general in Zhōnglíng.
Cóng, having long accompanied the examinations without success,
was in extreme poverty and distress.
His wife's family treated him with increasing contempt,
and even his wife's parents could not help but do the same.
One day,
during a grand military banquet
that the prefecture called
("called" originally written as "invited,"
corrected according to Yùquánzǐ)
a spring feast,
the families of senior generals set up tents in rows to watch.
Though his wife was poor,
she could not avoid attending.
However, her clothes were old and shabby,
so the crowd separated her with a curtain.
Just as the feast was in full swing,
the Surveillance Commissioner suddenly sent a clerk galloping to summon the general.
The general was startled and afraid.
Upon arrival,
the Commissioner stood before the hall,
holding a document in his hand, and said with a laugh:
"Is Zhào Cóng not your son-in-law?"
He replied:
"He is."
Then he informed him:
just now a report arrived,
stating he had passed the examinations.
He then handed over the document he held,
which was the official ranking list.
The general immediately rushed back with the list,
shouting:
"Young Master Zhào has passed!"
His wife's family at once removed the curtain barrier,
shared the same mat with her,
and vied to present hairpins, robes, and congratulatory gifts.
From Yùquánzǐ
Liú Yè
Liú Yè, styled Hànfān.
During the Xiántōng era,
he was summoned from his post as assistant at Chángchūn Palace to serve within the inner court.
He was specially granted jìnshì status.
Wéi Bǎoyì, because his elder brother held the position of chancellor,
was unable to pass the examinations,
so he was specially granted jìnshì status
and promoted into the inner court.
From Zhìyán
Yè Jīng
was a native of Jiànzhōu
and had an extremely renowned reputation for literary talent.
He once traveled to Dàliáng,
where he often attended official banquets,
and thus became acquainted with the military supervisor.
By the time he reached the capital, he had already passed the imperial examination,
and was riding side by side with his fellow graduates.
When he encountered that person on the main thoroughfare,
he bowed to him from horseback.
Because of this, slanderous discussions erupted,
and later he fell into considerable obscurity.
He ended his career as a Doctor of the Imperial Academy.
From "Zhìyán"
Lǐ Āi
Lǐ Āi diligently prepared for the examinations,
and was exceptionally quick-witted and brilliant,
so people called him "the hawk with clipped wings."
He passed the examination in the second year of the Xiántōng era.
From "Lúshì Záshuō"
Fáng Xǔ,
a native of Hénán,
was the grandson of the Grand Commandant.
In the fourth year of the Xiántōng era, he was on the verge of success but failed.
Earlier, his ranking had already been determined;
however, while writing his examination,
mud fell from above,
overturning his inkstone,
and staining his examination paper.
Since Fáng Xǔ was in a highly regarded position among his maternal relatives,
and they had recommended only him,
the officials in charge had no choice
but to allow him to proceed.
Fáng Xǔ, facing the dawn,
requested a replacement examination paper.
The examiner did not consent,
so he withdrew.
From "Zhìyán"
Wāng Zūn
Xǔ Táng,
a native of Jīng County, Xuānzhōu,
had long pursued the path of imperial examinations.
A fellow villager, Wāng Zūn, had been a minor clerk since childhood.
By the time Xǔ Táng had taken the examination over twenty times,
Wāng Zūn was still among the clerks and subordinates.
However, he excelled at composing quatrains,
which were profound and obscure.
One day, he resigned from his duties to take the examinations.
It happened that Xǔ Táng was seeing off guests at Bàchǎn,
when he suddenly encountered Wāng Zūn on the road.
Xǔ Táng inquired of him:
"Wāng Dū,
Dū
was how clerks were addressed.
What brings you to the capital?"
Wāng Zūn replied:
"I have come to take the examinations."
Xǔ Táng angrily said:
"A petty clerk has no manners."
And indeed, Wāng Zūn ended up sharing the same examination hall with Xǔ Táng,
who greatly looked down upon him.
Later, Wāng Zūn achieved fame five years
before Xǔ Táng passed the examination.
From "Zhìyán"
Liú Yǔnzhāng
Liú Yǔnzhāng's examination topic was "Rhapsody on the World as One Family."
The Supervising Secretary Dù Yìtǐ
According to the Tang "Zhìyán" volume thirteen, "tǐ" is written as "xiū."
submitted a memorial discussing it.
Although the matter was not carried out,
it was considered appropriate at the time.
Cuī Dàn's "Rhapsody on the Most Benevolent Attacking the Unbenevolent,"
also attracted considerable contemporary criticism.
Xuē Dān's "Rhapsody on Flourishing Virtue Renewing Daily,"
with the rhyme foot:
"Follow without cease."
Liú Zǐzhèn submitted a petition,
requesting to change it to the character "xiū,"
and it was corrected at the time.
From "Lúshì Záshuō"
Wáng Níng
Wáng Níng, from a distinguished clan and of great virtue,
was unparalleled in his time.
Whenever he went to sleep,
he would always lie with his hands clasped,
perhaps fearing he might see his ancestors in his dreams.
He once served as prefect of Jiàngzhōu.
At that time, Sīkōng Tú was preparing for the imperial examinations,
and came from his country villa to the prefectural seat.
After paying his respects,
he did not visit any relatives or friends;
the gatekeeper hastily reported that Scholar Sīkōng had left the city.
If he entered the city to visit relatives or friends,
he would not go to the prefectural office.
Wáng, learning of this,
said that he was singularly respectful,
and esteemed him even more.
When Wáng served as examiner,
Sīkōng passed in one attempt,
ranking fourth among the successful candidates.
His fellow graduates were surprised that his name was rather obscure
and that he had succeeded so quickly.
Some frivolous people nicknamed him "Sītú Kōng."
Wáng heard of this talk.
He then summoned all the successful candidates of that year to a banquet,
and declared to the crowd:
"I have presumptuously held the literary authority;
this year's list of successful candidates
was entirely for Senior Sīkōng alone."
From then on, Sīkōng Tú's reputation and brilliance grew even more.
From "Běimèng Suǒyán"
Lú Shàngqīng
In the eleventh year of the Xiántōng era,
because Páng Xūn had rebelliously occupied Xúzhōu,
troops were stationed there for a long time,
and supplies were transported year after year,
resources were depleted.
Therefore, an edict was issued to temporarily suspend the imperial examinations for one year.
That year,
Jìnshì Lú Shàngqīng traveled from afar to the capital,
but upon hearing the edict, he turned back.
He then composed a poem on returning eastward, which said:
"From the ninefold heavens, the crimson edict descends to the dusty world,
Deep within the literary chambers, the selection of talent ceases.
Let the cassia trees grow to shade the moon,
The apricot garden will wait until next year to bloom.
Since discussions of war were held in the jade tent,
No one is allowed to come to the golden gate to remonstrate on hunting.
Today, crossing over Bàlíng Bridge,
The guards must laugh at my return before the year's end."
From "Niánhào Jì"
Lǐ Yáo
When Lǐ Yáo passed the examination,
he was in a subordinate position,
close to attending the celebratory banquet.
The continuous rain did not stop,
so he sent for rented oiled cloth curtains to be spread
(pronounced with a falling tone)
overhead.
Lǐ Yáo's former residence was on Shēngpíng Lane,
and altogether, seven hundred strings of cash were spent.
From his residence, they extended along the main thoroughfare for over a li,
with attendants and guards numbering no less than a thousand people.
Saddled horses and carriages
filled the lanes and gates,
and those coming and going were not drenched.
Moreover, the golden decorations shone brilliantly,
creating a particularly splendid scene.
At that time, Lǐ Yáo was entrusted by Chancellor Wéi Bǎohéng,
intervening in government affairs,
and was called Lǐ Bā Láng.
His wife was also the daughter of Wéi Zhòu from Nánhǎi,
who constantly supplied him with gold and silk,
beyond measure.
From "Zhìyán"
Gāo Shí
In the twelfth year of the Xiántōng era (871 CE),
Vice Minister of Rites Gāo Shí served as chief examiner.
Among the candidates listed, those who were orphaned and impoverished
("pín" originally written as "píng",
corrected according to the Ming manuscript copy)
included Gōngchéng Yì, who had composed three hundred fu rhapsodies,
which many people inscribed on walls.
Xǔ Táng's poem "Dòngtíng" was particularly exquisite,
earning him the contemporary nickname "Xǔ of Dòngtíng."
The most notable was Niè Yízhōng,
who experienced poverty and hardship in his youth
and excelled in ancient-style poetry.
His poem "The Young Master's Household" reads:
"Flowers planted fill the western garden,
Blooms line the paths by the pleasure towers.
Beneath a flower, a single grain sprout grows—
Plucked away as a vile weed."
Another poem, "On Farming Families," says:
"The father plows the fields on the plain,
The son clears the wasteland below the mountain.
In the sixth month, the grain has yet to ripen,
But the official's granary is already repaired."
And also:
"Hoeing the field under the midday sun,
Sweat drips onto the soil beneath the grain.
Who considers that the meal upon the plate,
Each grain, each morsel, comes from toil and pain?"
And further:
"In the second month, sell the new silk;
In the fifth month, sell the new grain.
To heal the festering sore before the eyes,
They cut away the flesh from the heart in vain.
I wish the sovereign's heart
Would transform into a bright candle's flame,
Not shining on feasts in silken gowns,
But on the homes of those who flee in shame."
This is what is called "words simple, meaning profound,"
in harmony with the spirit of the Three Hundred Songs.
From *The Record of the Selected*.
Gōngchéng Yì,
a man of Wèi,
was renowned for his ci and fu compositions.
By the thirteenth year of Xiántōng (872),
he had already attempted the examinations nearly thirty times.
Once, he fell gravely ill,
and his fellow villagers mistakenly spread word of his death.
His wife came from Héběi to fetch his coffin for burial.
It happened that Yì was seeing off a guest at the foot of a slope
when he encountered his wife.
Initially, husband and wife had been separated
for over ten years.
Yì, on horseback at the time,
saw a woman coarsely dressed, riding a donkey,
who vaguely resembled his wife,
and thus could not stop glancing at her.
His wife did the same.
He then sent someone to inquire,
and it indeed was Yì.
His wife and he held each other and wept.
Passersby marveled at the scene.
Ten days later,
Yì passed the imperial examination.
From *The Record of the Selected*.
Sūn Lóngguāng
achieved the top rank of zhuàngyuán under examiner Cuī Yīnmèng.
The year before,
he had dreamed of hundreds of piled logs,
with Lóngguāng treading back and forth upon them.
Later, he asked a recluse named Lǐ to interpret the dream.
The recluse said:
"I congratulate you, sir.
I rejoice, for next year you will surely be zhuàngyuán.
Why?
Because you already stand above all other timber."
From *The Record of the Selected*.
Wáng Lín
in Chángshā could draft ten thousand words in a day's examination.
Wáng Lín's literary talent was abundant,
not accumulated through prolonged study.
Vice Director Cuī, while on an inspection tour,
submitted a memorial recommending him to the court.
First, he tested him in the commissioner's office.
Lín requested ten clerks,
each provided with a desk and inkstone.
Lín, clad in light summer silk and stroking his belly,
paced about dictating,
while the ten clerks wrote without pause.
The first topic was the "Rhapsody on the Yellow River,"
three thousand characters completed in a few moments.
Then, thirty poems on "Birds Scatter, Remaining Blossoms Fall,"
written out with a flourish of the brush.
Suddenly, a storm arose,
and several sheets were swept up by the whirlwind,
splattered with mud,
rendered impossible to smooth and roll.
Lín said:
"Do not retrieve them.
Just bring more paper."
Again, he wielded his brush with a sweep,
and in an instant produced over ten more pieces.
By midday,
he had already accumulated over seven thousand words.
Commissioner Cuī said to the examiners:
"The ten-thousand-word limit is not binding for this test.
Simply invite him to come for a drink."
The "Rhapsody on the Yellow River" also contained over a hundred obscure characters;
he asked Lín to recite it aloud before the assembly,
which Lín did as if no one else were present.
Upon reaching the capital,
Lù Yán was then in power.
He sent a messenger to summon him.
Lín, intending to provoke and stir attention,
said:
"I request to wait until I can see the Emperor."
Yán heard of this,
was greatly angered,
and hastily ordered a memorial to abolish the ten-thousand-word examination category.
Lín leaned on his staff and returned home,
indulging freely in wine,
mixing even with butchers and wine-sellers without distinction.
From *The Record of the Selected*.
Jiǎng Níng
During the Qiánfú era (874–879),
Jiǎng Níng sat for the Hóngcí examination
("hóng" originally written as "chǒng",
corrected according to the Ming manuscript copy).
He composed a fu rhapsody that stopped at only four rhymes,
then announced he was finished and left.
The examiners did not believe him,
insisting he produce what he claimed.
Níng told them the truth.
Later, when compared with the others,
Níng wore an expression of virtuous satisfaction.
The examiners sighed in admiration for a long time.
In a mere moment,
his name spread by word of mouth.
Some praised him, saying:
"A face fully adorned with white-haired floral hairpins
cannot match Empress Xú's half-applied makeup."
From *The Record of the Selected*.
Wú Róng
Wú Róng, styled Zǐhuá,
during the Guǎngmíng and Zhōnghé eras (880–885), long bore a reputation of being wronged.
Although he had not yet passed the examinations,
his peers mostly took gifts to visit him
as they would a senior scholar.
There was one Wáng Tú, skilled in ci and fu,
who submitted his writings for about a month.
After Róng met him,
he said nothing at all about the quality of Tú's work.
He only asked Tú:
"Have you
(Ming manuscript copy has "xiàng" for "lì")
received any news from Lú Xiū?
Why does he stubbornly remain in seclusion and not rise?
A pity!
What I have gained is not equal to his."
Xiū
was a cousin of Tú's,
excelling in the eight-rhyme form,
and had once shared a study desk with Róng.
In his later years, he abandoned official life
and retired to his villa by the lake.
From *The Record of the Selected*.
Lú Guāngqǐ
Lú Guāngqǐ's ancestors were executed according to the law,
so Lú Guāngqǐ and his brothers groomed themselves to attend the imperial examinations.
He said to his relatives and friends:
"This is like opening up wasteland."
However, his nature was meticulous and prudent.
He wrote a volume titled *Chū Jǔzǐ*,
which dealt with matters of advancement and success;
all his endeavors were of this kind.
After his name was listed among the successful candidates,
he served in various high offices in the central government.
He gained the appreciation of Zhāng Jùn, the Commissioner of Revenue and Supplies.
When Zhāng Jùn went on a campaign to Bìngzhōu and Fénzhōu,
Lú would send him letters and memorials,
with each matter written on a separate sheet.
Officials at court still emulate this practice today,
as the method of using separate overlapping sheets
originated with Lú Guāngqǐ.
In the late Táng dynasty, examination candidates,
regardless of their conduct or literary talent,
were diligent only in paying visits and seeking connections,
which was called "being precise and earnest."
They all followed Lú Guāngqǐ's example.
His cousin Lú Rǔbì once served as Zhāng Jùn's administrative assistant during the campaign.
When they issued proclamations to all regions,
one passage read:
"Causing the common people to wander displaced,
began with the turmoil of the Zhūyé."
He said to others:
"Heaven created the Zhūyé common people
to supply my brush."
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Wáng Yànchāng
Wáng Yànchāng was from Tàiyuán.
His family for generations had worn official hats and ribbons,
and he was ranked among the top three in the palace examination.
In the Guāngmíng era, when the imperial carriage fled to Western Shǔ,
he was granted the *jìnshì* degree by imperial decree.
Later, he served as administrative assistant to Prince Xuē Zhīróu.
When Emperor Zhāozōng fled to Shímén,
the chief ministers and academicians could not follow the imperial carriage.
Zhīróu, as the Governor of the Capital Prefecture, acted as the head of the Secretariat,
handling affairs close to the emperor.
Memorials arrived continuously,
and he diligently wrote replies.
Zhīróu recommended Yànchāng by name,
and so he was appointed acting academician.
After half a year,
he was appointed Governor of the Capital Prefecture,
and additionally appointed Left Regular Attendant and Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
Implicated by a clerk of the court,
he was demoted to the south.
From *Zhí Yán*.
Dù Shēng
Dù Shēng's father, Xuānyóu, died in Wǎnlíng.
Shēng had literary talent.
In the Guāngmíng era,
Sū Dǎo, the Supervising Secretary, was appointed Prefect of Jiànzhōu,
and Shēng served as a soldier.
When the imperial carriage fled to Western Shǔ,
he was granted an audience according to precedent.
He was specially granted the crimson robe by imperial decree.
Dǎo soon entered the inner court,
and Wěi, the Secretariat Director, was appointed chief examiner from the Hanlin Academy.
Shēng had by then been appointed a minor remonstrance official,
but he submitted a memorial requesting to take the examination,
which was granted.
A few days after passing the examination,
an imperial decree restored his former position and
"and" originally read "appointed";
amended according to the Ming manuscript and Chén's collated edition.
his official robe color.
Commentators considered this an honor.
From *Zhí Yán*.
Shēng was granted the crimson robe as a Reminder,
yet he took the examination and passed,
and again became a Reminder,
so he was called the crimson-robed *jìnshì*.
From *Lúshì Zá Shuō*.
Zhèng Chāngtú
In the Guāngmíng era,
before Vice Commissioner of Fèngxiáng, Vice Minister Zhèng Chāngtú had passed the examination,
he considered himself broad-minded and magnanimous,
not拘泥于小节,
coming and going, traveling and staying,
he indulged his feelings completely.
When public opinion became clamorous,
he considered giving up the examination.
At that time, a servant from a relative's household in the same neighborhood,
coming from a manor in Sòngzhōu and Bózhōu,
told his master:
"Yesterday, passing through Luòjīng,
by the Gǔshuǐ Inn,
I met two yellow-clad messengers coming from the west,
and I traveled with them.
When we reached the front of the Huàyuè Temple,
the two yellow-clad messengers bid me farewell,
and we bowed to each other behind the inn.
They said to me:
'Is your young master taking the *jìnshì* examination?'
"无" originally read "元";
amended according to the Ming manuscript and Chén's collated edition.
The servant said:
'My master's official position is already high,
and the young masters are currently studying.'
They asked again:
'Are there no relatives' sons taking it?'
He said:
'There are.'
The messengers said:
'We two are the messengers delivering the list this year,
coming from Mount Tài to the Jīntiān Temple,
to affix
"affix" originally read "suppress";
amended according to the Ming manuscript.
the seal to the list.
It is fortunate we met you.'
The servant then asked to secretly peek at the list.
The messengers said:
'That cannot be,
but you can memorize it.'
So they drew on the ground and said:
This year's top graduate's surname
has the radical '阝' on the side,
and his given name has two characters,
the last character has a '口' in it.
The last person on the list's surname
also has this '阝' radical on the side,
his given name has two characters,
and the last character also has a '口' in it.
Remember it, remember it!'
Then they left.
Zhèng's relative found this matter quite strange,
so he visited the Vice Commissioner of Qí and told him everything.
He urged him to take the examination.
That year, Chāngtú was the top graduate,
and the last on the list was Zōu Xīhuí.
The strokes and dots of their names were the same.
From *Yùtáng Xián Yǔ*.
Also, in the Xiántōng era,
because *jìnshì* candidates' carriages and clothing were excessively extravagant,
they were not allowed to ride horses.
At that time, there were no fewer than a thousand people in the examination grounds,
and even those with powerful and influential connections
all rode donkeys.
Someone mocked them, saying:
This year by decree all ride donkeys,
short sleeves and long whips fill the nine avenues.
The slim young men can still manage,
but among them, poor Zhèng Chāngtú is most distressed.
The Minister was very stout,
hence this line.
From *Zhí Yán*.
Chéng Hè
In the Táng dynasty, Vice Minister Cuī Yà governed Méizhōu.
Chéng Hè served as a hall attendant through local corvée duty,
and his younger brother was a minor clerk in the prefectural office.
Cuī noticed that Hè's demeanor resembled that of a scholar,
so he questioned him:
'Do you read books?'
Hè descended the steps and replied:
'I have dabbled slightly in the arts and letters.'
Cuī pointed to an object
and asked him to compose a poem about it.
It was quite elegant and meaningful,
so he told him to return home.
On a selected day,
Hè dressed properly, brought his writings as gifts,
and Cuī praised him highly,
allowing him to be called a *jìnshì* candidate,
and to attach himself to Cuī's household,
not seeking other paths.
After twenty-five attempts, he finally passed the examination.
Every time he went to the capital,
he stayed at Cuī's residence,
always grateful for the favor of being promoted.
When Cuī Yà died,
Hè wore mourning clothes for him for three years.
People all praised him for this.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Chén Qiáo
Chén Qiáo paid a visit to Zhèng Chéng in Ānlù.
After three years,
they finally met face to face.
Casually, Chéng said to Qiáo:
'Do you know Mǐn Tíngyán?'
Qiáo said:
'I happen not to have heard of him.'
Chéng said:
'It would be good to associate with him;
his writing resembles that of the Western Hàn.'
From *Zhí Yán*.
Qín Tāoyù
Qín Tāoyù frequented Tián Lìngzī's household.
When the imperial carriage fled to Shǔ,
Tāoyù had already been appointed as a vice-director
and oversaw the salt monopoly.
When Xiǎo Guīgōng presided over the examinations,
Tāoyù was permitted by imperial decree to pass,
and was still listed in the ranking of that year.
Tāoyù sent a letter thanking the new graduates,
addressing them all as fellow graduates.
It roughly said:
"Beneath the three candles,
though I was barred from the literary gates,
by the wall several ren high,
I was fortunate to share the same ground of favor."
From *Zhìyán*.
Lù Yǐ
Lù Yǐ sat for the jìnshì examination.
It happened that Emperor Xīzōng fled to Liángyáng.
He followed the imperial carriage to the temporary capital,
and stayed at the same inn as the Secretariat Drafter Zhèng Sǔn.
Yǐ was recognized by the chancellor Wéi Zhāodù,
and wished to settle his own affairs quickly.
He repeatedly informed Zhāodù,
who said:
"But it is already deep summer;
whom else can we appoint as chief examiner?"
Yǐ suggested Zhèng Sǔn.
Zhāodù agreed.
He then ordered Yǐ to convey the message.
The ranking list and notices were all determined by Yǐ himself.
That year in the sixth month,
he achieved top honors as zhuàngtóu.
Later, while serving in the Hanlin Academy,
he was suffering from the intense heat.
His colleagues teased him, saying:
"Today is a fine day to compile the rankings."
However, Yǐ's reputation was foremost for a time.
There were three brothers,
called the Three Lùs of the time,
being Xīshēng and Wēi.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Zhāng Shǔ
Zhāng Shǔ and Cuī Zhāowěi
sat for the examinations together in Xīchuān in the early Zhōnghé era.
They went together to consult a fortune-teller about their fates.
At the time, Shǔ, relying on his considerable talent and fame,
was regarded by everyone as the future zhuàngyuán.
Cuī was also considered to be beneath him.
Not long after,
the fortune-teller paid no attention to Shǔ at all,
but only looked at Cuī and said:
"You will achieve the highest rank with complete success."
Shǔ showed a displeased expression.
The fortune-teller said:
"You, sir, will also pass,
but you must wait until Cuī becomes chancellor.
You will pass through the hall at that time."
Later, Shǔ indeed did not finish the examination due to mourning obligations,
while Zhāowěi took first place that year.
Shǔ wrote a poem satirizing him, saying:
"A thousand li in Jiāngxī, trailing the steed's tail,
At the fifth watch, a gentle wind lost the dragon's scales.
Last night's rain on Huànhuā Creek,
For whom are the green willows and fragrant grass?"
Cuī was very displeased.
Once during a night drinking session,
Cuī offered Zhāng a huge cup of wine.
Zhāng declined repeatedly.
Cuī said:
"Just drink it.
Wait until I become chancellor,
I will get you the zhuàngtóu position."
Zhāng flicked his sleeves and left,
and from then on they were greatly at odds.
Seven years later,
Cuī was appointed chancellor from the inner court.
Zhāng later passed under Péi Zhì.
He indeed passed through the hall under Cuī.
From *Zhìyán*.
Cuī Zhāojǔ,
achieved zhuàngyuán under Péi Zhì in the Dàshùn era.
The next day,
his elder brother Zhāowěi was appointed to office.
Wáng Tì,
son of Chancellor Lǔgōng Sǔn.
Tì passed the examination.
The next day,
Sǔn was appointed to office.
Tì passed through the hall for a separate audience.
Guī Diǎn
Note: In the Tang *Zhìyán*, volume eight, "Diǎn" is written as "Àn".
He personally went to greet and bow at the mat, saying:
"Zhuàngyuán has passed the examination,
the patrol under the rankings list.
A month after doffing mourning white,
he died without illness."
From *Zhìyán*.
Jiǎ Yǒng
Jiǎ Yǒng's father, Xiū, had a reputation for righteousness.
Yǒng was落魄 (down and out),
and not constrained by minor details.
He once served as an aide to a military officer in Jìnzhōu.
At the time, Emperor Zhāozōng had fled to Shǔ.
Péi, the chancellor Zhì,
who was then the former Vice Director of Receptions,
was traveling as a guest and arrived at the commandery.
Yǒng received him with an arrogant, sidelong glance.
Péi once visited Yǒng wearing his official cap and tablet.
Yǒng, in military attire, gave a single bow and said:
"The Prefectural Lord, the Director, has invited me to fly kites.
Do not take offense."
He withdrew in such a hurried manner.
Péi Zhì harbored considerable resentment towards him.
Later, when Péi presided over the examinations three times,
Yǒng failed twice under Péi.
Afterwards, Péi said to his disciples:
"Old Jiǎ Yǒng is pitiable in his落魄 (down and out state).
I should repay him with virtue."
He then allowed him to pass.
From *Zhìyán*.
Emperor Zhāozōng
Emperor Zhāozōng
made considerable efforts to open paths for孤进 (isolated, unsupported scholars).
Cuī Níng conducted re-examinations.
However, for those who were子弟 (sons of officials),
regardless of the quality of their essays,
most were rejected.
Many worthy men were wronged among them.
Among the孤寒 (isolated and poor scholars),
apart from Chéng Yàn and Huáng Tāo who excelled in the examination hall,
the rest, based on their submitted examination papers,
there were also many who undeservedly passed.
However, the regulated verse of Wáng Zhēnbái and Zhāng Pín,
and the ancient-style poems of Zhào Guānwén,
all reached the threshold of the前辈 (earlier masters).
From *Zhìyán*.
Wéi Zhēn
Wéi Zhēn had passed the examination,
his position was certainly secure.
But he did not yet know the exact ranking,
and could not avoid feeling anxious.
Suddenly, he heard something on South Street in Guāngdé Ward.
He suddenly saw a person knocking very urgently on a plank door.
After a long while,
the door creaked open.
A voice called out:
"The thirteenth official, may your honored self enjoy ten thousand blessings."
Later, Zhēn indeed was the thirteenth.
From *Zhìyán*.
Liú Zuǎn
Liú Zuǎn
was the son of Liú Tuì of Shāngzhōu,
and was also skilled in writing.
During the Qiánníng era,
he lived in poverty in the capital.
By chance, he became neighbors with a physician.
Zuǎn treated him with utmost courtesy,
often lending him money.
This man was a disciple of the Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner.
Later, Prince Xuē became the Grand Governor of the Capital,
and the physician thus came to diagnose Zhīróu's pulse.
During a leisurely moment,
he spoke at length about Zuǎn's poverty and frustration.
Zhīróu paid close attention.
When the examination officials reported the ranking list of recommended candidates,
they sought instructions from Zhīróu.
Zhīróu thought Zuǎn was someone mentioned by the physician from the Prince's household,
and assumed it must be the Prince's intention
that he must be the top recommended candidate.
Thus, Zuǎn was placed first for recommendation,
though Zuǎn himself did not know the reason.
From then on, Zuǎn failed several examinations,
before he finally realized the truth.
In the end, he had no way to clear himself.
From *Zhìyán*.
Zhōng Fù
During the Tang dynasty, after the chaos of the Gēngzǐ year in the Guǎngmíng era,
in the Jiǎchén year,
a great famine swept the land.
The imperial carriage fled again to Qíliáng.
Corpses of the starved were seen everywhere,
and the commanderies and princedoms largely paid no heed to the tribute scholars.
The military governor of Jiāngxī, Zhōng Fú, rose from a righteous militia,
swiftly took possession of the territory,
filled the court with his reports of duty,
and became a model for the feudal lords.
Yet he diligently prioritized the recommendation of worthy men.
Even commoners from within his prefecture,
if they sought recommendation from the authorities with even a scrap of writing or a single character,
were all received with the utmost courtesy.
When the time for examinations arrived,
he would host feasts and set up tents,
surpassing all in peace and order.
He performed the Rites of the District Libation,
often leading his aides to personally oversee it,
with a genuinely joyful expression.
Later, he held grand farewell banquets for them,
and beyond the gift boxes,
he generally provided them with funds for cinnamon and jade.
The top graduate (Jièyuán) received three hundred thousand,
the second-place graduate (Jièfù) two hundred thousand,
and the rest no less than one hundred thousand each.
For nearly thirty years,
this commitment never waned.
At that time, candidates would seek the foremost recommendation from high ministers through connections,
traveling thousands of *li* without regard for the distance,
and there were never fewer than several such individuals each year.
Lú Wénhuàn,
who achieved the top rank in the imperial examinations in the second year of the Guānghuà era,
was quite eager to host feasts and collect contributions.
When it was his turn to host a feast in the prefectural office,
his fellow graduates all worried about their poverty,
being unable to afford it.
One day, he tricked them into visiting the pavilion of Duke Qíguó,
and once there, they all relaxed and loosened their belts.
Huàn then ordered the banquet manager to lead in a donkey.
At that time, Liǔ Cǎn told Wénhuàn
that the following donkey was not his own.
Wénhuàn said:
"If the medicine does not cause dizziness,
the illness will not be cured."
Cǎn harbored deep resentment for this.
Four years later,
when Cǎn rose to power,
Wénhuàn's worries and distress increased daily.
Whenever Cǎn encountered him, he would say:
"If the medicine does not cause dizziness,
the illness will not be cured."
From *Zhíyán*.
Zhào Guāngféng
In the second year of Guānghuà,
Zhào Guāngféng passed Liǔ Cǎn in the examinations.
Guāngféng did not receive a promotion for three years afterward.
At that time, Cǎn was appointed to a high position from the inner court,
and only then was Guāngféng summoned to the capital as Left Assistant Director.
Not long after,
Cǎn was convicted of a crime and executed.
Guāngféng was entrusted with important duties,
holding a key position for over ten years.
He submitted a memorial requesting retirement due to old age,
and retired with the honorary title of Minister of Works.
Two years later,
he was again summoned and appointed as Chief Minister.
From *Zhíyán*.
Lú Yánràng
Lú Yánràng passed the examinations in the third year of Guānghuà.
Previously, Yánràng had studied poetry under Xuē Néng,
but his diction and ideas tended toward eccentricity,
and many people of the time laughed at him.
Wú Róng had previously served as Attendant Censor,
and was posted out to the Xiá region.
Yánràng was then traveling modestly in Jīngzhǔ,
poor and without scrolls of his writings,
and had not found the opportunity to present himself.
It happened that Wú Róng's maternal cousin, Téng Jí,
accidentally obtained a hundred of Yánràng's poems.
After Róng read them,
he found them extraordinarily remarkable.
He said:
"These have no other distinction,
except that the language is unusual."
He then praised them to his superior, Chéng Ruì.
At that time, the former Chief Minister, Lord Zhāng, was serving in that region,
and often used Yánràng as a subject of ridicule.
But after Róng spoke of him,
everyone's view changed.
As a result, Yánràng received substantial provisions for his journey to the capital.
Yánràng was deeply grateful.
However, due to his straitened circumstances,
they never actually met face-to-face.
When Róng was urgently summoned to the capital,
he soon entered the inner court,
and diligently praised Yánràng incessantly among the high officials.
In the Wùwǔ year of Guānghuà,
Yánràng came from south of Xiāng.
Róng, upon seeing him, felt as if they were old acquaintances.
Yánràng choked with emotion and shed tears,
and so, rolling up his sleeves, Róng helped him succeed.
From *Zhíyán*.
Wéi Yífàn
Luó Yǐn and Gù Yún
were both recognized by Chief Minister Línghú Táo.
Although Gù was the son of a salt merchant,
his demeanor was refined and proper.
Luó was also from Qiántáng,
but his local accent was harsh and grating.
Whenever the Chief Minister's sons held banquets,
only Gù was invited to participate.
His graceful demeanor and witty conversation
made it impossible to tell he was from a humble background.
Gù's literary compositions and rhapsodies were praised by contemporaries,
and he was keen on achieving fame.
He once submitted a petition to an acquaintance,
stating he only hoped to be placed at the very end of the third-class list,
but he ended up ranked just before the tail.
Luó, having repeatedly met with disappointment,
became quite resentful,
and was eventually ostracized by the sons of noble families,
parting ways and returning east.
After the Huang Chao rebellion was pacified,
court worthies discussed summoning him back.
Wéi Yífàn opposed it, saying:
"I was once on the same boat with him,
though we were not acquainted.
The boatman announced:
'There is a court official here.'
Luó said:
'What kind of court official is that?
I can hold a brush between my toes,
and still outdo several of his kind.
If he indeed passed the exams and entered the register,
then we, his peers, are nothing but chaff.'"
Consequently, the summons did not materialize.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Yáng Xuántóng In the Tiānyòu era of the Tang,
the Jìnshì Yáng Xuántóng from Hézhōng had grown old in the examination halls.
That year, he was also quite anxious.
With no inkling of his prospects,
he decided to seek an auspicious dream
to divine his future.
That night,
he dreamed of a dragon flying to the heavens,
but it had six feet.
When he saw the results list,
his name was sixth.
Thus he knew it was truly predetermined.
From *Yùtáng Xiánhuà*.
Fēng Shùnqīng Fēng Shùnqīng oversaw the examinations during the Liáng dynasty.
Later, his protégé Zhèng Zhìyōng received an appointment alongside him,
entering the Hànlín Academy as an Academician.
Zhìyōng possessed outstanding talent,
while Shùnqīng's literary skill was clumsy and halting.
When they were tested on five topics,
Shùnqīng, unable to bear the difficulty,
entrusted Zhìyōng to wield the brush for him.
Those who knew of it at the time
considered it a disgrace for an examiner to be shamed by his own protégé.
In the early Tóngguāng era, he retired from service.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Gāo Niǎn
The Yáng clan,
since Yáng Zhèn was known as the Confucius West of the Pass,
was buried at Tóngguān Pavilion.
Now, over seven hundred years later,
his descendants still reside in the old family home in Wénxiāng.
It is simply a case of one family under heaven.
From Guóshǐ Bǔ.
Lǐ Yì
Minister Lǐ Yì had a clansman, a Junior Supervisor, who shared the same name.
Both were descendants of the Duke of Gūzāng.
People of the time called the Minister "Lǐ Yì of Literary Works",
and the Junior Supervisor "Lǐ Yì of the Family Lineage".
However, the Minister also possessed a distinguished family background.
Once, at a ceremonial gathering among relatives by marriage,
the Minister returned home
and laughingly said to his family:
"It was extremely amusing.
At today's banquet seating,
two seats of honor
were both occupied by Lǐ Yì."
From Yīnhuà Lù.
Consort of Crown Prince Zhuāngkè
Emperor Wénzōng was selecting a consort for Crown Prince Zhuāngkè.
Daughters from the families of court officials
(Míng manuscript: "daughters from the families" reads as "have daughters").
were all submitted by name,
causing unease among both officials and commoners.
The Emperor learned of this
and summoned his chief ministers, saying:
"I wish to arrange a marriage for the Crown Prince.
Originally, I sought a bride from the distinguished families of the Rǔ and Zhèng clans.
(Míng manuscript: after "bride" there are nine characters: '扶出來田舍齁齁地如'.)
I have heard that court officials outside
are all unwilling to form marriage ties with Us.
(Míng manuscript: "ties" reads as "family".)
Why is this?
We are from a family of officials for several hundred years."
Not long after, Shén Yáo struck
(Míng manuscript: "struck" reads as "took Us").
the family Luóhē away.
Consequently, the selection was halted.
From Lúshì Záshuō.
Bái Mǐnzhōng
When Bái Mǐnzhōng served as chancellor,
he once wished to take the former jìnshì Hóu Wēn as his son-in-law.
The date was nearly set
when his wife, Madame Lú, said:
"As the chancellor,
many wish to become your son-in-law.
You are already surnamed Bái (White).
If you also take a son of the Hóu (Marquis) family as son-in-law,
people will surely call you 'Marquis White'."
Mǐnzhōng stopped because of this.
When Mǐnzhōng first married,
he already held high office (red and purple robes).
He once jokingly called his wife a "foot-propping wife".
Also, when his wife went out,
he always had a horse led for her.
His wife resented his words,
so whenever she went out,
she would order the horse removed,
saying:
"I am a foot-propping wife;
what use do I have for a horse?"
From Yùquánzǐ.
The official families of Rǔzhōu
were all prominent clans,
and many had sons and daughters.
There was a military advisor in Rǔzhōu also from a respected clan.
He sought a marriage alliance with one family,
but that family refused, saying:
"Our family tradition is not to form marriage ties with families of high officials."
From Lúshì Záshuō.
Huáng Shēng
There was a man named Huáng Shēng
who passed the jìnshì examination.
Someone asked if he had shared an examination cell with (someone named) Pō.
He replied:
"A separate cave."
Huáng was originally a prominent surname from the溪洞 (stream caves) region.
Shēng therefore answered this way.
Although people laughed at him,
they also appreciated his straightforward honesty.
From Shàngshū Gùshí.
Cài Kuò
During the reign of Emperor Fèi of the Sòng,
Cài Kuò was appointed Minister of Personnel.
The Director of the Department of State Affairs, Xú Xiànzhī, said to the Palace Secretary, Fù Liàng:
"From the Palace Attendants downward,
all can be entrusted to Cài;
we need not concern ourselves.
From this rank upward,
we should still deliberate together on agreements and differences."
Kuò heard this and said:
"I cannot sign at the tail of documents for Xú Xiànzhī."
He thus declined the appointment.
From Jiànkāng Shílù.
Xiè Zhuāng
Xiè Zhuāng of the Sòng, styled Xīyì,
was the son of Palace Attendant Xiè Wēi,
and grandson of Palace Attendant Xiè Sī.
He was handsome in appearance,
skilled in discourse,
proficient in calligraphy and literary composition,
and fond of discussing metaphysical principles.
In his youth, he was admired by Emperor Wén.
Whenever the Emperor saw him,
he would sigh and say:
"Does Lántián produce beautiful jade?
Surely it is not in vain!"
Zhuāng succeeded Yán Jùn as Minister of Personnel.
Jùn had a stern and severe countenance,
often with an unapproachable demeanor.
Zhuāng was gentle and graceful in bearing.
When people came with noisy complaints,
he would often answer them with laughter.
Therefore, people of the time said:
"Minister of Personnel Yán glares and grants official posts;
Minister of Personnel Xiè smiles and does not grant official posts."
Zhuāng was promoted to Palace Secretary and Palace Attendant,
and was posthumously titled Xiàn.
In Zhuāng's family lineage, none lived to fifty.
Zhuāng died at forty-two,
his grandfather at forty-seven,
his great-grandfather at forty-three,
and his great-great-grandfather at thirty.
His sons, Fěi and Yuè,
were both well-known.
From Tán Sǒu.
Liú Línfǔ
In the early Wǔdé era of the Táng,
following the old Suì system,
official selections began in the eleventh month
and stopped by spring.
By the second year of Zhēnguān,
Liú Línfǔ was Vice Minister of Personnel.
Considering the selection period too short,
and many matters not thoroughly handled,
he petitioned to allow selections throughout the four seasons,
with appointments made as candidates arrived.
This was considered convenient at the time.
From Táng Huìyào.
Zhāng Yuè
In the seventh year of Wǔdé,
Emperor Gāozǔ said to Vice Minister of Personnel Zhāng Yuè:
"Among this year's selection candidates,
surely there are those of talent and ability.
You may examine and select them for the future,
as I wish to bestow upon them good ranks."
Thereupon, Yuè presented several individuals, including Zhāng Xíngchéng and Zhāng Zhīyùn, in response.
He was considered perceptive in recognizing talent at the time.
From Táng Huìyào.
Wēn Yànbó
In the first year of Zhēnguān,
Wēn Yànbó was Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
overseeing selections.
His intent was to weed out,
so he rejected and suppressed many.
Those who failed were不服 (not convinced),
and noisy disputes filled the court.
Yànbó merely engaged in arguments with them,
leading to clamorous disturbances all day.
This was rather ridiculed by those with discernment.
From Táng Huìyào.
Dài Zhòu
In the fourth year of Zhēnguān,
Dù Rúhuì, on his deathbed,
requested that selection affairs be entrusted to the Minister of Revenue, Dài Zhòu.
Thus, Dài was also appointed Acting Minister of Personnel.
When overseeing selections,
he rather suppressed literary elegance and promoted legal officials,
which was not suited for practical administration.
Public opinion
(The character "議" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Míng manuscript.)
criticized him for this.
From Táng Huìyào.
Táng Jiǎo
In the eighth year of the Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty, in the eleventh month,
Táng Jiǎo was appointed as Vice Minister of Personnel.
He often summoned candidates for official appointments,
asking them which region would be convenient and suitable for them.
Someone said:
"My family is in Shǔ,"
so he assigned him to Wú.
Another said:
"My elderly parents
previously lived in Jiāngnán,"
so he appointed him to Lǒngyòu.
Observers could not fathom his intentions.
There was a man from Xìndū who desired Hèshuò,
so he deceitfully said:
"I wish to be assigned to Jiānghuái,"
and was consequently appointed as a county lieutenant in Héběi.
From then on, he was greatly deceived by the false statements of the selected candidates.
From "Táng Huìyào"
Yáng Shīdào
In the seventeenth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Yáng Shīdào served as Minister of Personnel.
As a noble scion,
he was not thoroughly familiar with the talents across the realm,
and thus many of his appointments were not suited to the individuals' abilities.
He strongly suppressed powerful nobles and their relatives and cliques,
intending to avoid suspicion.
Contemporary critics ridiculed him.
From "Táng Huìyào"
Gāo Jìfǔ
In the seventeenth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Vice Minister of Personnel Gāo Jìfǔ oversaw the selection process.
All his evaluations and appointments
were praised at the time as fair and appropriate.
By the eighteenth year, while solely managing selection affairs in the Eastern Capital,
the emperor bestowed upon him a golden mirror,
to commend his clear discernment.
From "Táng Huìyào"
Xuē Yuánchāo
In the first year of the Yǒnghuī era,
Secretariat Drafter Xuē Yuánchāo was fond of promoting humble and talented individuals.
He once submitted a memorial recommending Rén Xīgǔ, Gāo Zhìzhōu, Guō Zhèngyī, Wáng Yìfāng, Mèng Lìzhēn, and over ten others.
Contemporary opinion praised him.
From "Táng Huìyào"
Yáng Sīxuán
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era,
Vice Director of the Bureau of Appointments Yáng Sīxuán, relying on his status as a maternal relative of the imperial family,
treated many candidates rudely and excluded them.
He was accused by candidate Xiàhóu Biāo,
and Censor-in-Chief Láng Yúqìng impeached him, resulting in his dismissal.
At that time, Secretariat Director Xǔ Jìngzōng said:
"I knew Minister of Personnel Yáng would fail."
When asked why,
he replied:
"One tiger and one wolf,
together preying on a sheep—
how could he not fail?"
From "Táng Huìyào"
Zhāng Rénhuī
In the second year of the Zǒngzhāng era of the Táng dynasty, in the eleventh month,
Vice Minister of Personnel Lǐ Jìngxuán delegated affairs to Vice Director Zhāng Rénhuī.
Possessing insight, strategy, and capability,
he first created surname registers,
and revised procedures for evaluating and replacing officials.
Jìngxuán employed Rénhuī's methods,
and the selection process became orderly.
Rénhuī, moved by being entrusted as a pillar of the state,
ultimately exhausted himself mentally,
vomited blood, and died.
From "Táng Huìyào"
Péi Xíngjiǎn
In the second year of the Xiánhēng era,
there were Yáng Jiǒng, Wáng Bó, Lú Zhàolín, and Luò Bīnwáng,
all renowned for their literary talents.
Vice Minister of Personnel Lǐ Jìngxuán praised them all,
and introduced them to Péi Xíngjiǎn.
Xíngjiǎn said:
"They possess talent and fame,
but official rank and emolument will likely be scarce.
Yáng may reach the position of county magistrate,
the others will scarcely achieve a good end."
At that time, Sū Wèidào and Wáng Jù were not yet known,
but due to the selection process,
they were deeply respected and treated exceptionally by Xíngjiǎn.
He then said to them:
"I have sons born late,
and regret I may not see them grow up.
You two gentlemen will in a dozen years hold high office;
I hope you will recognize these individuals." [Míng manuscript note: "recognize these individuals" reads as "entrust this to them"]
Later events indeed turned out as he said.

Among the subordinate generals Xíngjiǎn had recommended were Chéng Wùtǐng, Zhāng Qiánxù, Cuī Zhìdōng, Wáng Fāngyì, Dǎng Jīnpí, Liú Jìngtóng, Guō Dàifēng, Lǐ Duōzuò, and Hēichǐ Chángzhī, all of whom became famous generals.
From "Táng Huìyào"
Comparison of Three Men's Merits
In the second year of the Chángshòu era,
Péi Zǐyú served as county lieutenant of Hù.
His colleagues Lǐ Yǐncháo and Chéng Xíngchén were both noted for their legal expertise,
while Zǐyú alone was known for his literary scholarship.
Someone asked the Senior Administrator of Yōngzhōu, Chén Chóngyè,
which of the three was superior?
Chóngyè said:
"They are like spring orchids and autumn chrysanthemums,
both indispensable."
Liú Qí
In the first year of the Zhèngshèng era,
Liú Qí served as Vice Minister of Personnel.
He appointed Zhāng Wéncháng [Note: "Táng Huìyào" 75 has "cháng" as "chéng"]
and Sīmǎ Huáng as Investigating Censors.
The two men expressed thanks through Shēntú Yáng.
Qí sternly said:
"Recommending the worthy is inherently selfless;
why are you two gentlemen thanking me?"
From "Táng Huìyào"
Dí Rénjié
At the beginning of the Shènglì era,
Dí Rénjié served as Head of the Chancellery.
He took considerable pride in his discernment of talent,
and thus recommended Huán Yànfàn, Jìng Huī, Cuī Xuánwěi, Zhāng Jiǎnzhī, and Yuán Shùjǐ, five individuals.
All later achieved great merit.
He also recommended dozens including Yáo Yuánchóng, all of whom became chief ministers or high officials.
During the Shènglì era,
Empress Zétiān ordered each chief minister to recommend one Departmental Director.
Rénjié alone recommended his own son, Dí Guāngsì,
who was thereby appointed Vice Director of the Ministry of Revenue,
and performed his duties with acclaim.
Zétiān said to him:
"Qí Xī recommended from within his family,
and indeed obtained the right person."
From "Táng Huìyào"
Zhèng Gǎo
In the second year of the Shènglì era,
Vice Minister of Personnel Zhèng Gǎo
appointed Hán Sīfù as Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and Yuán Xīshēng as Registrar of the Capital Prefecture.
He once said to others:
"This year in charge of selections,
having obtained these two gentlemen, Hán and Yuán,
the Ministry of Personnel has not failed the court."
From "Táng Huìyào"
Xuē Jìchǎng
In the third year of the Cháng'ān era,
Empress Zétiān ordered the Senior Administrator of Yōngzhōu, Xuē Jìchǎng,
to select subordinate officials suitable to serve as censors.
Jìchǎng consulted Administrative Assistant Lú Qíqīng,
who recommended the county lieutenant of Cháng'ān, Lú [Note: Original text has "Lú" as "chù", corrected per "Táng Huìyào" 75]
Huáishèn,
and Lǐ Tǐguāng [Note: "Táng Huìyào" has Lǐ Xiūguāng].
County lieutenant of Wànnián, Lǐ Yì,
and Cuī Shí;
Assistant Magistrate of Xiányáng, Ní Ruòbīng;
County lieutenant of Zhōuzhì, Tián Chóngbì;
and county lieutenant of Xīnfēng, Cuī Rìyòng.
All later attained high office.
From "Táng Huìyào"
Dèng Kě
In the first year of the Hóngdào era, in the twelfth month,
Vice Minister of Personnel Wèi Kèjǐ, after completing the evaluation and selection of candidates,
posted a long list,
thereby announcing the names of those who passed and those retained.
Consequently, there was uproar in the streets,
and he was greatly criticized and denounced by the winter assembly candidates [Míng manuscript note: "criticized" reads as "supported"].
He was demoted to Advisor to the Heir Apparent,
and was replaced by Secretariat Drafter Dèng Xuántǐng.
He also lacked discernment,
and suffered from diabetes (xiāokě),
so candidates nicknamed him "Dèng the Thirsty."
From "Táng Huìyào"
Lǐ Zhìyuǎn
In the second year of the Jǐngyún era (711 AD),
Lú Cóngyuàn served as Vice Minister of Personnel.
Dù Xiān, from his post as Military Advisor in Wùzhōu, was transferred to the capital for assignment,
and was appointed as Defender of Zhèng County.
Later, when Dù Xiān became Minister of Revenue,
and Lú Cóngyuàn returned to court from his post as Chief Administrator of Yìzhōu,
Dù stood above Lú in rank
and said to him:
"How did that official selection turn out?"
Lú replied:
"It was also due to my humble discernment
that Your Excellency was able to fully display your talents over a thousand li."
From "Táng Huìyào"
Wèi Zhīgǔ
In the first year of the Xiāntiān era (712 AD),
the Palace Attendant Wèi Zhīgǔ once submitted a memorial recommending Huánshuǐ County Magistrate Lǚ Tàiyī, Púzhōu Military Administration Officer Qí Hàn, and Right Inner Guard Cavalry Officer Liǔ Zé.
When he later became Minister of Personnel,
he also promoted Mì County Defender Sòng Yáo,
Left Reminder Yuán Huī and Fēng Xīyán,
and Yīquē County Defender Chén Xīliè.
Afterwards, they all held important and prestigious positions.
From "Táng Huìyào"
Lú Qíqīng
In the first year of the Kāiyuán era (713 AD),
Lú Qíqīng served as Governor of Yōuzhōu.
At that time, Zhāng Shǒuguī was a Military Officer,
and Lú treated him with special courtesy.
He said to him:
"Within ten years, you will become a Military Commissioner."
This indeed came true as he predicted.
From "Táng Huìyào"
Wáng Qiū
In the seventh month of the eighth year of Kāiyuán (720 AD),
when Wáng Qiū was Vice Minister of Personnel,
he promoted Shānyīn Defender Sūn Tì, Táolín Defender Zhāng Jìngwēi, Húchéng Assistant Magistrate Zhāng Jìnmíng, Presented Scholar Wáng Lěngrán, Lǐ Áng, and others.
Within a few years,
they passed the imperial examinations,
and took charge of drafting imperial edicts.
From "Táng Huìyào"
Cuī Lín
In the twelfth month of the eleventh year (723 AD),
when Vice Minister of Personnel Cuī Lín was conducting the selection process,
he accepted over ten candidates who had previously failed selection, such as Lú Yí, Péi Dūnfù, and Yú Hàoqīng.
Not long after,
they all entered the central government offices.
People considered him skilled at recognizing talent.
From "Táng Huìyào"
Péi Guāngtíng
In the eighteenth year of Kāiyuán (730 AD),
Sū Jìn served as Vice Minister,
while the Palace Attendant Péi Guāngtíng, whenever reviewing official appointments,
for those who should be rejected,
would merely point at the register before the crowd
and mark them with a red brush dot.
Sū then posted a notice in the selection office:
"Those marked with a dot by the Chancellery
shall be reconsidered for appointment."
Péi felt insulted
and was displeased.
At that time, there was a Chancellery Clerk Yán Línzhī,
who was Péi's confidant,
and solely handled the Personnel Ministry's appointment reviews.
Whenever Yán made a decision,
Péi would immediately write it down.
People at the time said:
Yán's mouth,
Péi's hand.
From "Táng Huìyào"
Xuē Jù
During the Kāiyuán era,
Xuē Jù, relying on his talent and reputation,
participated in the selection at the Ministry of Personnel,
requesting to be appointed as Registrar of Wànnián County.
All the non-official clerks jointly appealed to the chief ministers, saying:
"The registrar is a prestigious position for us low-ranking clerks.
Now a Presented Scholar wants to take it,
then what are we lowly people
to do?"
Thus, the appointment was canceled.
From "Zhíyán"
Lǐ Línfǔ
Starting from the twentieth year of Kāiyuán (732 AD),
the Ministry of Personnel established the Southern Court,
and began posting long lists
to determine who would stay or be released.
At that time, Lǐ Línfǔ was in charge of the selection.
Prince Níng privately visited Lǐ and said:
"Among them, I ask for one person."
Lǐ reprimanded him.
He then posted a notice:
"Based on his written examination and judgment,
he should by rights be retained.
However, because he is connected to Prince Níng,
he is temporarily released to await the winter selection."
From "Guóshǐ Bǔ"
Zhāng Yuè
Secretariat Drafter Zhāng Jūn was in charge of evaluations,
while his father, Left Councilor Zhāng Yuè, was in charge of evaluating capital officials.
He specially noted:
"A father teaching his son loyalty
is a good teaching from ancient times.
Qí Xī recommended his own son,
acting righteously without seeking private gain.
As for embellishing the king's words,
and implementing the emperor's deeds,
the principles are based on ancient classics,
and the precedents transcend ordinary merit.
Having respectfully learned from former worthies,
this duty is especially difficult.
How could personal suspicion
dare to disrupt law and order?"
He evaluated him as Upper-Middle grade.
From "Xuánzōng Shílù"
Zhāng Shì
When Miáo Jìnqīng oversaw the selection,
the son of Vice Censor-in-Chief Zhāng Yǐ, named Zhāng Shì, participated in the selection.
Miáo, wishing to please Zhāng Yǐ,
graded a total of sixty-four candidates,
placing Zhāng Shì at the top.
Sū Kǎoyùn, who was Magistrate of Jì County,
reported this selection matter to Ān Lùshān.
Ān Lùshān memorialized it to the emperor.
Emperor Xuánzōng then gathered those who had passed the examination in front of the Huā'è Tower for a re-examination,
and less than ten or twenty percent achieved a passing grade.
Zhāng Shì held the examination paper,
but by the end of the day, he had not written a single word.
People at the time called it "dragging a blank."
The emperor was furious,
and demoted Zhāng Yǐ.
The imperial edict stated:
"Within your own household,
you failed to properly instruct your son;
during the selection process,
you instead relied on connections, making yourself a laughingstock in the empire."
Miáo Jìnqīng was demoted to Ānkāng.
From "Lúshì Záshuō"
Yáng Guózhōng
In the eleventh month of the tenth year of Tiānbǎo (751 AD),
Yáng Guózhōng served as Right Councilor,
concurrently holding the post of Minister of Personnel.
He petitioned that candidates from the two capitals,
on the day of selection, should immediately be decided as retained or released,
and regardless of age, each should be summoned to his residence for appointment.
The Guóguó sisters watched from behind a curtain.
If there were any old, sick, or ugly candidates,
they would point at them by name and laugh.
Even scholar-officials suffered humiliation.
According to precedent,
after the Ministry of War and Ministry of Personnel completed appointments,
they had to be reviewed by the Palace Attendant and Supervising Secretaries at the Chancellery.
Those not passed were called "rejected for reconsideration."
When Yáng Guózhōng made appointments,
he summoned Left Councilor Chén Xīliè to a corner seat,
and had the Supervising Secretaries line up in front, saying:
"Since we have already discussed the appointments,
that means they have passed the Chancellery."
Chén and the others could only harbor silent resentment.
Vice Ministers Wéi Jiànsù and Zhāng Yǐ, both wearing purple robes,
along with the Ministry's Directors and Vice Directors,
arranged documents outside the screen,
hurrying about to report matters.
Yáng then said to the Yáng sisters behind the curtain:
"How about those two purple-robed officials in charge?"
The Yáng sisters then laughed heartily.
A candidate named Zhèng Fū
(The character "Fū" was originally missing in the text,
supplemented based on the Ming dynasty manuscript copy)
curried favor with his intentions,
and along with over twenty others, pooled money to hold a vegetarian feast at the Qínzhèng Tower,
and also
("also" originally written as "curtain,"
corrected based on the Ming dynasty manuscript copy)
erected a stele for Yáng Guózhōng south of the Department of State Affairs.
Regarding the appointments for the three selection categories of the Ministry of Personnel,
he was solely preoccupied with busyness,
unable to attend to them personally,
and delegated them all to clerks and record-keepers.
Yáng Guózhōng merely stamped one character,
and even that could not cover everything.
From "Táng Xù Huìyào"
Lù Zhì
In the spring of the eighth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
Lù Zhì, the Vice Director of the Secretariat and a participant in determining governmental matters,
first restored the order for the Ministry of Personnel to assemble candidates for official selection each year.
According to old practice,
the Ministry of Personnel assembled candidates annually.
Later, this was changed to holding selections only once every three or four years.
Candidates would all arrive at once,
resulting in a large volume of documents,
making it impossible to thoroughly examine them.
Genuine and fraudulent materials became mixed together,
allowing clerks to engage in widespread deceit and trickery.
If a candidate made a single misstep,
they might wait ten years without receiving an official post.
Meanwhile, official vacancies
sometimes remained unfilled for years.
Lù Zhì ordered the Ministry of Personnel to divide all officials, both central and local, into three groups,
calculating vacancies and assembling candidates accordingly,
making this the regular annual practice.
This eliminated seventy to eighty percent of the previous abuses.
The entire realm praised him.
From the *Táng Huìyào*.
Regarding Zhèng Yúqìng,
Liú Yǔxī said:
"When Chancellor Zhèng of Xuānpíng was in charge of official selection,
candidates congratulated each other
upon entering his selection process."
Liú Yǔxī also said:
A younger cousin of mine was selected under Zhèng's administration.
He was appointed as a county lieutenant in Húzhōu.
He answered the roll call and was about to leave.
Zhèng called him back and said,
"Judging by your examination performance,
there were no more than five or six men in the entire session who matched it.
To accept the first appointment called out—
if such conduct is not rewarded,
what is the purpose of selection?
What post would you prefer,
one that is stable and convenient for your family?"
My cousin replied:
"My family resides in Chángzhōu."
He was then appointed as county lieutenant of Wǔjìn County.
The candidates were unanimously
in awe and admiration of him.
Later, when he became chancellor,
his handling of official appointments was again ranked first,
showing he had worthy successors in Lǔ.
It is also said:
(Note: The character '云' (said) was originally written as '去' (go);
corrected according to the Ming dynasty manuscript copy.)
Chén Fěng and Zhāng Fùyuán were each appointed to counties near the capital.
They requested to exchange their posts,
and he approved.
Shortly after, Zhāng requested not to exchange after all.
By then, Zhèng had already posted the list.
(Note: The character '了' (completed) was originally written as '子' (child);
corrected according to the Ming dynasty manuscript copy.)
He summoned Zhāng, but as soon as Zhāng entered the door,
he stated the decision was already fixed and could not be changed.
Contemporaries admired him for this.
From the *Jiāhuà Lù*.
Regarding Péi Zūnqìng,
after Péi Zūnqìng left the chancellorship,
he took charge of official selection.
The court, honoring his age and virtue,
allowed him to conduct the appointment of officials from his own residence.
From Xuānpíng Ward, he posted the list and summoned scholars,
all the way to the two streets of the Eastern Market.
People of the time considered it a grand event.
From the *Guóshǐ Bǔ*.
Regarding Lǐ Jiàng,
In the early years of the Chángqìng era,
Lǐ Jiàng, the Minister of Personnel, proposed appointing ten vice directors
to separately adjudicate cases in the Southern Bureau,
which inconvenienced the clerks.
Within ten days, he was sent out to serve as the Defender of the Eastern Capital.
From then on, the selection process became standardized,
and was often completed swiftly.
From the *Guóshǐ Bǔ*.
Regarding Lǐ Jiàn,
When Lǐ Jiàn served as Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
he often said:
"The outstanding talents of today
all come from the Presented Scholar examinations.
If I could have my way,
I would have those who pass the examinations in a given year
assemble at the Ministry of Personnel
and be appointed as lieutenants in strategically important counties;
after their term ends, assemble them again,
and appoint them as lieutenants in prominent counties;
after that term, appoint them as lieutenants in capital-area counties,
and then promote them to court positions.
Generally speaking, for men of average ability,
they would achieve fame at thirty,
and by forty reach pure and esteemed ranks.
This pace would be appropriate.
Once they pass the examinations,
they receive official salary;
once they receive salary,
they inevitably aspire to court positions—
who would not desire this?
There would be no lingering idleness while adhering to fixed limits,
no contentious scrambling to seek rapid advancement.
Lower offices would get their orderly promotions,
and higher positions would get their further refinement.
Considering it overall,
the benefits are very extensive."
Many commentators approved of his proposal.
From the *Guóshǐ Bǔ*.
Regarding Cuī Ānqián,
When Cuī Ānqián oversaw selection in the Eastern Capital Luòyáng,
a candidate who could not make his own name known
secretly submitted a petition written by Gù Yún.
Cuī was unaware of this,
greatly admired and praised it,
summoned the man for an audience,
and immediately appointed him as a county magistrate with a promotion exceeding normal ranks.
Later, someone informed him of the truth,
and only then did Cuī regret his action.
From the *Lúshì Záshuō*.
Regarding Chancellors,
The ceremony for appointing a chancellor
halts all regular court processions.
The metropolitan prefecture and counties transport sand to pave the road,
from the chancellor's private residence all the way to the eastern street of the inner city,
called the "sand causeway."
If the chancellor is on mourning leave
or is ill and receiving inquiries,
all officials go to his residence.
The relevant office sets up a curtained enclosure,
and officials line up in ranks.
On New Year's Day, the winter solstice, and when ceremonial guards are posted,
high officials all have jade-decorated canopies prepared,
with five or six hundred torches arranged in rows,
called the "fire city."
When the chancellor's fire city approaches,
all others extinguish theirs to yield precedence.
The chancellor adjudicates matters from all regions at the Dūtáng (Hall of All Affairs);
his instructions to various offices are called tángtiě (hall notes);
the signature at the bottom is called a huāyā (flourished mark).
After the yellow imperial edict is issued,
minor corrections or additions are called huángtiě (yellow notes).
The chancellor is addressed as "Tánglǎo" (Elder of the Hall).
Originally, all officials waiting for morning court
would stand with their horses outside the Jiànfú and Wàngxiān Gates.
The chancellor alone waited in the carriage workshop of the Guāngzhái Palace,
to shelter from wind and rain.
In the early Yuánhé era,
the Waiting-for-Dawn Court was first established.
From the *Guóshǐ Bǔ*.
Regarding Assuming Office,
All officials of the Secretariat and the Chancellery
assume their duties at the Western Department,
for the sake of ceremonial propriety.
For those of the fifth rank and above,
the chancellor escorts them to assume office,
and then all ministers pay their respects.
From the *Guóshǐ Bǔ*.
Regarding Sū Guī,
In the third year of the Jǐnglóng era,
Sū Guī was appointed as Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
At that time, newly appointed high ministers and senior officials
customarily prepared a feast for presentation,
called "burning the tail."
Sū Guī, while attending an inner palace banquet,
was addressed by the Minister of Works Zōng Jìnqīng:
"You have been appointed Vice Director,
yet you ultimately did not 'burn the tail,'
is that not improper?"
The Emperor remained silent.
Sū Guī memorialized:
"Your servant has heard that the chancellor
presides over the forces of yin and yang,
assisting Heaven in ordering all things.
