Now grain prices are soaring,
and the common people lack sufficient food.
Your servant has seen guards of the palace,
some going three days without eating.
In my foolishness, I feel unworthy of my post,
therefore I dare not 'burn the tail.'"
From the *Tánbīn Lù*.
The Two Departments
Remonstrance officials do not enter without reason:
Whenever they enter the bureau,
there are four roasted meats from the kitchen.
Secretaries of the Secretariat were then called the chief minister's administrative officers;
if the chief minister had a personal conflict,
they would not appoint them as drafters of edicts, considering them as stepping stones.
It is also said:
"Those who do not go through the three-character process,
but are directly appointed as secretaries of the Secretariat,
are called 'forehead-tapping and head-wrapping.'
The origin of drafting edicts
comes from the words of the sovereign,
all done by the ruler.
Thus, during the time of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn,
Dìwǔ Lún served as overseer of coin casting,
and upon seeing an imperial edict, he sighed:
'This is a sage and enlightened ruler;
one look and I am decided.'
Recently, all edicts and decrees
are blamed on the subordinates.
Words of praise and blame
are what wise kings are cautious about.
All the various officials,
princes, dukes, ministers, and scholars—
when first praised, they are said to be like jade tablets of exceptional quality,
with goodness that cannot be surpassed;
but soon, when demoted or dismissed,
they are compared to petty talents of little measure,
with crimes that cannot be excused.
For the same person's
("person" originally written as "character,"
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy)
actions,
though they come from the ruler's words,
wisdom and foolishness arise in an instant,
right and wrong change in a moment.
For the Son of Heaven has no jesting words;
if his words are mistaken,
then he incurs blame from all under heaven.
From "Miscellaneous Stories of Lú."
Dúgū Jí
Dúgū Jí sought to become a drafter of edicts,
and went to see Yuán Zǎi for an interview.
Yuán knew what he wanted,
and greeted him, saying:
"Who is suitable for drafting edicts?"
Jí, knowing in his heart that it would not be given to him but to another,
recommended Lǐ Shū.
At that time, Yáng Yán was in the cabinet,
and, jealous of Jí's arrival,
Yuán obstructed him,
which was the effort of both men.
From "Records of Fine Conversations."
The Deliberation Bureau
In the early Chángqìng era,
Emperor Mùzōng regarded criminal law as important.
Whenever there was a major case,
the responsible officials would decide the punishment,
and then order the supervising secretaries and secretaries of the Secretariat to deliberate on the details,
so all the offices called it the Deliberation Bureau.
From "Supplement to the National History."
Yáng Chéng
Yáng Chéng lived in Xiàxiàn,
and was appointed remonstrance official;
Zhèng Gù lived in Wénxiāng,
and was appointed reminder;
Lǐ Zhōunán lived in Qǔjiāng,
and was appointed proofreader.
People at the time said that the farther away one lived, the higher the appointment;
the closer one lived, the lower the appointment.
From "Supplement to the National History."
Lǚ Wēn
When the usher announced an edict,
it was an old practice to have the reminder assist in punctuating and holding the hemp paper,
because the ushers were illiterate,
and often mispunctuated,
so reminders were used to lower their voices and punctuate to assist them.
When Lǚ Wēn became a reminder,
he was called to hold the hemp paper,
but he refused to go.
Thus, it became a precedent.
That reminders do not hold hemp paper
began with Lǚ.
At the time, Liǔ Zōngyuán teased Lǚ, saying:
"Fortunately, you know a character or half a character;
why not help him hold it?"
From "Records of Fine Conversations."
Wéi Xuàn
At the end of the Kāichéng era,
Wéi Xuàn was promoted from left rectifier to diarist.
At that time, Emperor Wénzōng revered antiquity and valued culture,
often implementing policies from the Zhēnguàn and Kāiyuán eras.
He carefully selected left and right historians,
appointing Wèi Mó as right historian,
who soon also served as grand remonstrator,
entering the cabinet to wield the brush.
His upright reputation spread far,
and the emperor relied on him as a future minister,
expecting it to happen soon.
He offered advice and remonstrance,
and whether major or minor, his suggestions were implemented.
His public reputation and fine deeds
made the court watch eagerly,
hoping to see the demeanor of Duke Wénzhēn.
But then Emperor Wénzōng passed away,
and as circumstances changed,
this was interrupted.
At that time, Xuàn had already been appointed diarist,
and Yáng Sìfù first reported to the emperor:
"Left rectifier Wéi Xuàn has newly been appointed diarist;
he has not yet expressed gratitude in person;
I report this for your decision."
The emperor nodded.
Lǐ Guī beckoned and led him,
and Xuàn placed his brush and paper on the stone railing of the jade steps,
quickly approached, and offered his thanks with bows and gestures.
The left historian expressing gratitude in person
—from the mid-Kāichéng era until Emperor Wǔzōng ascended the throne—
they would retreat with the imperial guard,
and no longer had the duty of wearing the hairpin brush.
When wearing the hairpin brush,
they could closely approach the emperor's face,
so people at the time called the two bureaus the attendants' ranks,
and those selected were considered quite prominent.
From "Records of Fine Conversations."
Lǐ Chéng
Lǐ Chéng was a Hanlin academician,
and used the shadow of the bricks in front of the steps as the time to enter.
Chéng was lazy by nature,
and every time he entered, it was always after eight bricks,
so he was called the Eight-Brick Academician.
From "Transmitted Records."
Miscellaneous Stories
Officials of the two bureaus call each other "cabinet elders,"
ministers and vice-ministers call each other "section chiefs,"
and vice-directors, censors, and reminders call each other "bureau chiefs."
Higher ranks can address lower ranks,
but lower ranks cannot address higher ranks.
Investigating censors call each other "upright gentlemen."
From "Supplement to the National History."
Censors
According to censor tradition,
during grand court assemblies, the supervising censor leads the procession;
during regular court sessions, the palace censor divides the ranks;
when entering the cabinet, the investigating censor supervises memorials.
Because Hányuán Hall is the farthest,
an eighth-rank official is used; Xuānzhèng Hall is next,
using a seventh-rank official; Zǐchén Hall is the closest,
using a sixth-rank official. The palace censor can stand on patterned bricks,
wearing green robes and using purple desk cushions, etc.,
and is called one of the seven nobles.
The supervising censor bureau chief and others in the same bureau observe strict etiquette,
and it is said:
"Serve the chief as you serve the upright."
When entering the hall, all conversation and laughter cease;
if something is unbearable,
and the chief of the miscellaneous bureau laughs,
then everyone in the hall laughs,
which is called "warming the hall."
Warming the hall is not penalized.
When the censor-in-chief or deputy censor-in-chief enters the three bureaus,
all penalties are suspended.
The severity of penalties
depends on
("depends on" originally written as "suspended,"
changed according to "Supplement to the National History")
the clerks,
but major cases are recorded in yellow scrolls.
When the three bureaus enter the hall,
those with new appointments cannot finish their meal.
Only the director of the Ministry of Justice can finish it.
From "Supplement to the National History."
The Tóngzhōu Censor
A certain Wáng said:
In past years, when I served as an official in Tóngzhōu,
I saw a censor come to investigate a case,
return and stay at the prefectural courier station,
and stay overnight without leaving.
Suddenly, he demanded miscellaneous case files,
and also took the seal register,
locking the courier station gate urgently,
causing great disturbance in the entire prefecture.
An old clerk secretly laughed,
and through a cook, contacted the censor's clerk,
promising a gift of a hundred bolts of silk.
The next day, before dawn,
the censor had already opened the courier station gate,
returned all the documents,
and rode away on horseback.
From "Supplement to the National History."
Cuī Wěi
Cuī Wěi served as a Supervising Censor.
While inspecting prisoners, he went to the Divine Strategy Army,
where he was entrapped by the clerks.
He entered under a canopy,
and also hinted for the army to provide wine and food,
intending to foster goodwill.
Dòu Wényáng was angered,
and immediately memorialized
(The original text had "memorialized immediately";
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
an edict ordering him to be flogged at the Censorate's duty hall and then exiled.
From then on, inspections of prisoners did not extend to the imperial guard armies.
From "Supplement to the National History"
Yán Wǔ
In the second year of the Bǎoyìng era,
Grand Master Yán Wǔ memorialized that it was inappropriate for newly appointed censors outside the capital
to lodge and eat in private residences.
From then on, they were provided with official carriages.
During the Yuánhé era,
Yuán Zhēn served as a Supervising Censor.
He contested a courier station hall with a palace eunuch envoy,
and was humiliated by him.
This led to an edict:
When a military commissioner, observation commissioner, or censorate official and a palace eunuch envoy
arrive at a courier station,
whoever arrives first gets the superior hall.
This became the established rule.
From "Supplement to the National History"
Leading the Formation
For all grand court assemblies,
if there are insufficient Supervising Censors to lead the formation,
then junior Investigating Censors are used,
and those presenting memorials at court act in their stead.
From "Supplement to the National History"
Censorate Gate
The gate of the Censorate opens to the north,
likely taking the meaning of sternness and alignment with the yin principle.
Therefore, the gates of the capital's Censorate open north.
According to the records of Yè Commandery:
The Censorate was located southwest of the palace city,
and its gate opened north.
The old city's Censorate in history also opened north.
During the Lóngshuò era,
the Guì Bureau was established,
serving as the disciplinary office for the Eastern Palace,
and its gate also opened north.
However, the gate of the Metropolitan Censorate opens south.
Those who constructed it at the time were not well-versed in tradition,
acting contrary to precedent,
and aligning with other departments.
Was this perhaps a temporary expedient?
From "Records of the Censorate"
Regarding the north-opening gates,
some say
that when the capital was moved early in the Suí dynasty,
the Minister of War Lǐ Yuántōng, who also served as Censor-in-Chief,
wanted it to be convenient and close to the Department of State Affairs,
so he had the north gate opened.
From "Tán Bīn's Records"
Serving in All Five Bureaus
According to Censorate protocol,
from the Censor-in-Chief down to the Supervising Censors,
they are collectively called the Five Bureau Censors.
In our dynasty, only three men have served successively in all five bureaus:
Lǐ Shàngyǐn, Zhāng Yánshǎng, and Wēn Zào.
From "Anecdotes from the Department of State Affairs"
Hán Gāo
When Hán Gāo served as Vice Censor-in-Chief,
whenever he had matters to present,
he would always do so at the Zǐchén Hall,
addressing all officials to make his request,
and never went to the informal audience hall.
The Emperor said to him:
"When I speak with you,
if matters are not fully discussed here,
you may come to the Yányīng Hall,
where I can converse with you at leisure,
so that no matters are left unresolved."
Relatives and friends said to Hán Gāo:
"Since the Qiányuán era,
when officials present matters,
they all go to the Yányīng Hall,
only then can things be discussed in detail.
Why do you alone present matters in the outer court,
before all the officials?
Does this not risk compromising secrecy and caution?"
Hán replied:
"The Censorate upholds fairness for all under heaven.
To break
(The original text had "authority";
changed according to the Xǔ printed edition.)
rigidity and straighten wrongs,
one must only act for the public good.
Regarding the matters I speak of,
it is good for people to know them.
Why should I seek an audience in the informal hall,
avoiding others and whispering in secret,
thereby privatizing the laws of the state?
Moreover, the establishment of the Yányīng Hall
was because Emperor Sùzōng, considering Miáo Jìnqīng was old and had difficulty walking,
set it up.
Later, officials who gained access to the informal hall
often used it for private gain,
seeking favor and grace,
wishing to exhaust their personal ambitions.
How can one aspire to such a thing!"
From "Transmitted Records"
Miscellaneous Sayings
Due to the nature of submitting memorials,
the worries and hardships of the Remonstrance Bureau are largely similar.
The Censorate focuses on investigation and impeachment.
The Department of State Affairs has many affairs,
with varying aims and directions,
hence it is said that Remonstrators and Supplements cherish each other,
Censors detest each other,
and Bureau Directors look down on each other.
From "Supplement to the National History"
Commissioner Posts
Before the Kāiyuán era,
outside the capital, one was appointed as an envoy;
otherwise, one held a regular office.
After establishing eight military commissioners and ten investigation commissioners,
there began to be sedentary commissioners.
Thereafter, the titles proliferated further.
Consequently, holding a commissioner post became prestigious,
while holding a regular office became slighted.
Thus, by the end of the Tiānbǎo era, some wore up to thirty seals,
and during the Dàlì era, some requested salaries of up to a thousand strings of cash.

Currently, within the court: the Grand Pure Temple, Grand Subtlety Temple, Revenue Commissioner, Salt and Iron Commissioner, Transport Commissioner, Park Superintendent, Pasturage Superintendent, Left and Right Patrols, Branch Investigators, Supervising Censors, Courier Stations Superintendent, Granary Superintendent, Treasury Superintendent, Left and Right Streets.

Outside posts: Military Commissioner, Observation Commissioner, Various Armies, Tribal Pacification Commissioner, Defense Commissioner, Militia Training Commissioner, Planning Commissioner, Garrison Suppression Commissioner, Pacification Commissioner, Salt Monopoly Commissioner, Land and Water Transport Commissioner, Army Farms Commissioner, Supply Commissioner, Pastures Superintendent, Chángchūn Palace.
Some are established temporarily:

such as Grand Ceremonies Commissioner, Rituals Commissioner, Alliance Commissioner, Editorial Commissioner, Three Departments Commissioner, Evaluation Commissioner, Touring Commissioner, Pacification Commissioner, Review Commissioner, Selection Commissioner, Ceremonial Assembly Commissioner, Investiture Commissioner, Condolence Commissioner, Army Supply Commissioner, Provisions Commissioner, Grain Purchase Commissioner.
This is the general outline.
Those established in the past but now abolished are not recorded.
Officials
(The original text had "officials";
changed according to "Supplement to the National History.")
both inside and outside the palace are all called commissioners.
Previously controlled by powerful ministers,
and administered by prefectures and counties,
now some belong to the palace eunuchs.
From "Supplement to the National History"
The Department of State Affairs
Traditions of the Bureau Directors:
The Bureau of Personnel has two halls for Directors:
first, the minor selection hall,
then the regulations hall;
two halls for Vice Directors:
first, the southern section,
then the abolition and establishment section.
The Bureau of Justice is divided into four reviews;
the Bureau of Revenue is divided into two tax sections.
This system is long-established.
According to old sayings,
the Bureau of Personnel is the eye of the department,
the Bureau of Rites is the lodgings of the southern department,
the Bureau of Evaluation and the Revenue Bureau are the bustling offices,
and the Bureau of Comparison gets meals
(The original text had "corridor";
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
from the corridor below.
They feed their attendants with the rice,
called the comparison plate.
The twenty-four bureaus call the Left and Right Offices the chief gentlemen.
A saying in the department goes:
The rear bureaus (rites and army farms)
are not as good as the middle bureaus (justice and revenue);
the middle bureaus (justice and revenue)
(The Ming manuscript copy has "revenue" for "bureau.")
are not as good as the front bureaus (personnel and war).
From "Supplement to the National History"
Cuī Rìzhī
Cuī Rìzhī served in various posts both in and out of the capital,
but regretted never reaching one of the eight high ministerial positions.
When he became Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
he built a tower behind the hall of the metropolitan temple,
directly facing the Department of State Affairs.
People of the time called it Cuī's Gaze-at-the-Department Tower.
From "Strange Compilations of National History"
Revenue Commissioner
According to the old system,
in the Bureau of Revenue,
the Langzhōng handled income,
the Yuánwài handled expenditures,
and the Shìláng only oversaw and signed off on the cases.
After the Zhēnyuán era,
it began to be designated as a commissioner post.
When a Lang official was on duty,
issuing imperial decrees was a weighty matter.
Once, the Water Department Yuánwàiláng Liú Yuē was on night duty,
when prisoners from Héběi were to be exiled to Lǐngnán.
The decree was issued at night,
and the duty clerk was inexperienced;
he only sent it
(The character "下" was originally missing,
added based on the Ming manuscript copy)
to Lǐngnán,
and not to Héběi.
A month later,
the original province reported the matter,
and Liú Yuē was consequently dismissed from his post.
From "Supplement to the National History"
Liǔ Bì
In the Archives of the Ministry of Personnel, there were several hundred forged yellow documents from Zhū Cǐ's rebellion.
Officials in the ministry often took them for amusement,
and later stored them away.
When Liǔ Bì was in charge of the Archives,
he first reported to the senior officials,
then gathered the eight high-ranking ministers and their assistants in the main hall and burned them.
From "Supplement to the National History"
The Ministry Bridge
At the southeast corner of the Department of State Affairs, on the main road, there is a small bridge,
commonly called the "Twisted Neck Bridge."
It is said that when Investigating Censors and Palace Attendants who have served long terms reach this point,
they inevitably twist their necks to look south toward the Southern Palace.
East of the path by the south gate of the main hall, there is an ancient pagoda tree,
whose spreading shade is very broad.
Legend has it that late at night, the sound of string and wind instruments can be heard,
and when a ministry official is about to become a chancellor,
it is called the "sound of music."
The Bureau of Sacrifices is called the "Water
(pronounced with a departing tone)
Office,"
meaning it is pure and cold.
From "Records of Conversations"
The Palace Library
In the early Táng,
the Palace Library was only responsible for copying, storing, collating, and proofreading books.
Consequently, its gates were so deserted one could spread nets,
and it had no subordinate officials under its jurisdiction.
Though its reputation was pure and elegant,
it was not actually a crucial or busy office.
The sons of powerful families and those fond of profit and ostentation generally did not favor this post.
Common parlance called the Director's position the "convalescent home for chancellors,"
the Vice Director's the "convalescent home for Jǐshìzhōng and Zhōngshū Shèrén,"
the Assistant's and Editorial Director's the "convalescent home for Department of State Affairs officials,"
and the Librarian's and Assistant Editorial Director's the "convalescent home for Investigating Censors."
This meant that those unable to handle heavy duties in their posts
would be transferred to this bureau.
However, its duties involved maps and histories,
and it was no longer a
(The Ming manuscript copy has "humble" instead of "noisy.")
lowly place,
so noble scholars who disliked competition and strife
also sought this position.
From "Records of the Two Capitals"
The Fish Pouch
According to court ceremonial, the ornament for the fish pouch
was only of two grades: gold and silver.
By Empress Wǔ's time,
it was changed to copper for the fifth rank.
When Emperor Zhōngzōng was restored,
the old system was reinstated.
From "Strange Compilations of National History"
The Sedge Office
In the administrative offices of the Jīngzhào Prefecture,
it is specifically called the Western Legal Scholars.
These two offices had many affairs.
The Eastern Legal Scholars Office
was nicknamed the "Rosary Office,"
because it handled one hundred and eight cases;
the Western Legal Scholars Office was called the "Sedge Office,"
as there was sedge in front of the office,
about fifteen paces around.
In the Jīngzhào Prefecture,
it was said that the Prefect did not stand for two county magistrates,
nor sit for two Vice Prefects.
When the two counties' horses arrived at the prefecture gate,
the gate was reported.
When the two Vice Prefects entered the hall,
the Prefect also went to the hall;
he did not wait for the two Vice Prefects to sit before leaving,
nor did he wait for them to stand before leaving.
The importance of the Jīngzhào Prefecture and its counties
also demonstrated the Prefect's dignity.
The clerks of the Jīngzhào Prefecture
were called by contemporaries "ministry officials leaning on the circle."
The Registrar's office in Hézhōng Prefecture also had green sedge.
In the past, enthusiasts took turns watering it.
After the Tiānyòu era,
it was removed by those who were not enthusiasts.
From "Records of Hearing Strange Things"
Zhāng Yìzhī
When Zhāng Yìzhī and Zhāng Chāngzōng
first entered the court,
their official positions were still low,
yet flatterers called them Fifth and Sixth Young Masters.
Thereafter, this became customary.
Zhāng Chāngyí and his brothers, relying on the favor of Yìzhī and Chāngzōng,
lived in extravagant luxury,
surpassing even princes.
In their later years,
someone wrote on their gate:
"A skein of silk,
how long can it be spun?"
Chāngyí saw it,
and immediately took a brush to add below:
"A single day is enough."
Not long after, disaster befell them.
When Zhāng Chāngzōng was prominent,
Wǔ Sānsī said he was the reincarnation of Prince Jìn,
and wrote a poem to present to him;
the poem still exists today.
From "Strange Compilations of National History"
Wáng Zhǔn
Wáng Hóng's son, Wáng Zhǔn, was a Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
who came and went in the palace,
amusing the Emperor with cockfighting.
At that time, Lǐ Línfǔ was wielding power and relying on his influence.
Lǐ Línfǔ's son, Lǐ Xiù, was the Director of the Directorate for the Palace Buildings,
and also served within the imperial quarters.
Xiù was often bullied by Zhǔn,
yet dared not utter a word.
One day, Zhǔn led all his followers to the private
(Originally "弘",
changed according to the Xǔ printed edition)
residence of the Imperial Son-in-Law Wáng Yáo.
Yáo, seeing the dust, hurried forward to bow,
but Zhǔn shot a pellet,
hitting Yáo's turban,
breaking his jade hairpin,
and taking it
(The "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng" has "took" instead of "hairpin")
for amusement.
Then they set out wine and music,
and Princess Yǒngmù personally served with a spoon.
The Princess was the Emperor's eldest daughter,
benevolent, filial, dignified, and virtuous,
highly regarded among the imperial relatives,
and especially beloved by the Emperor.
After Zhǔn left,
someone said to Yáo:
"Although those vermin rely on their father's power,
the Eldest Princess
is the Emperor's beloved daughter.
If you treat her with any disrespect,
would the Emperor not mind?"
Yáo replied:
"The Son of Heaven's anger
holds no fear for me;
but my life is tied to Seventh Young Master,
how dare I not do so?"
At that time, many called him Seventh Young Master.
Such was the fear of his rampant power and tyranny.
From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng"
Wáng Máozhòng
Wáng Máozhòng was originally a Goryeo man.
When Xuánzōng was still a prince,
Wáng Máozhòng and Lǐ Yídé served diligently by his side,
and the emperor cherished them both.
Whenever they attended banquets,
they shared a couch with Jiāng Jiǎo,
sitting before the emperor.
Later, relying on his seniority, Wáng grew arrogant and presumptuous,
increasingly engaging in unlawful acts.
The emperor often tolerated him with indulgence,
frequently sending palace eunuchs to inquire after him.
After receiving the imperial command,
if Wáng Máozhòng was even slightly displeased,
he would invariably vent his humiliation upon them
before sending them back.
Gāo Lìshì and Yáng Sīxù deeply resented him,
but never dared speak of it to the emperor.
When Wáng Máozhòng's wife, née Lǐ, had given birth three days prior,
the emperor ordered Gāo Lìshì to bestow upon her generous gifts of wine, food, gold, and silk,
and further commanded that her son be appointed to the fifth rank.
After Gāo Lìshì returned,
the emperor asked:
"Is Máozhòng pleased?
Did he have anything else to say?"
Gāo Lìshì replied:
"He brought the child out to show your servant,
gazing intently at the swaddled infant and saying:
'Could this child not even merit a third-rank official?'"
The emperor was furious and said:
"In the past, when we executed the Wěi clan,
this traitor was still wavering,
avoiding involvement and refusing to enter,
yet I never spoke of it.
Now he dares to resent me over an infant?"
From then on, the emperor's favor and goodwill toward him increasingly declined.
From the time the emperor assumed the throne during the Xiāntiān period, over the subsequent fifteen years,
only four individuals reached the rank of Kāifǔ.
They were the empress's father Wáng Rénjiǎo, Yáo Chóng, Sòng Jǐng, and Wáng Máozhòng, and that was all.
From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Minghuáng"
Lǐ Línfǔ
While Zhāng Jiǔlíng served as chancellor,
he possessed an honest and forthright loyalty, unwavering in his devotion.
As Xuánzōng's reign grew long,
he gradually neglected the affairs of government.
Whenever Zhāng Jiǔlíng saw the emperor,
he would exhaustively discuss the successes and failures of governance.
Lǐ Línfǔ, who was then a fellow minister,
upon discerning the emperor's inclinations,
secretly sought to undermine him.
At that time, there was a proposal to grant a substantive fief to Niú Xiānkè, the military commissioner of Shuòfāng.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng argued that it was inadvisable,
which greatly displeased the emperor.
On another day,
Lǐ Línfǔ requested an audience
and repeatedly asserted that Zhāng Jiǔlíng harbored considerable slanderous intent.
It was then autumn,
and the emperor ordered Gāo Lìshì to take a white feather fan and bestow it upon Zhāng,
intending to convey a message.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng was alarmed and fearful,
and consequently composed a rhapsody to present;
he also wrote a "Returning Swallow" poem to present to Lǐ Línfǔ.
The poem read:
How insignificant the sea swallow,
riding the spring but briefly coming.
How could it know the mud's low worth,
only seeing the jade hall's opening.
Through embroidered doors at times in pairs they enter,
to splendid carriages daily several times they go.
Without a heart to strive with creatures,
eagles and hawks, do not suspect me.
When Lǐ Línfǔ read it,
he knew Zhāng would certainly withdraw,
and his anger somewhat subsided.
On the day Zhāng Jiǔlíng and Péi Yàoqīng were dismissed from their posts,
as they proceeded from the Zhōngshū Province to the Yuèhuá Gate,
about to take their places in the ranks,
the two men bowed humbly and deferentially,
while Lǐ Línfǔ stood between them,
swaying with self-satisfaction.
Onlookers secretly remarked it was like a hawk clutching two rabbits.
Soon an edict appointed Zhāng and Péi as Left and Right Vice Directors of the Department of State Affairs respectively,
relieving them of administrative duties.
When Lǐ Línfǔ saw the edict,
he said angrily:
"Are they still to be Left and Right Chancellors?"
The two men hurried to their original positions in the ranks,
and Lǐ Línfǔ watched them go.
All the ministers and officials below watched this,
and could not help but tremble in fear.
From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Minghuáng"
Lú Xuàn
Emperor Xuánzōng held a banquet beneath the Qínzhèng Tower,
and the streets were empty of residents.
After the banquet concluded,
the emperor still watched from behind a lowered curtain.
The Vice Minister of War, Lú Xuàn, believing the emperor had returned to the palace,
let his whip hang and held his reins,
riding crosswise beneath the tower.
Lú Xuàn bore a reputation for refinement and elegance,
and moreover possessed a pure and distinguished demeanor.
The emperor saw him once,
and unconsciously followed him with his gaze.
He asked his attendants:
"Who is that?"
A close minister fully replied with Lú Xuàn's name.
The emperor repeatedly praised his refined and restrained bearing.
At that time, Lǐ Línfǔ was wielding power and envying talent.
The emperor's favored attendants close to him
he invariably bribed heavily with gold and silk.
Thus, there was no action or stillness of the emperor
that Lǐ Línfǔ did not know of.
The next day,
Lǐ Línfǔ summoned Lú Xuàn's sons and said to them:
"Your esteemed father, with his pristine reputation and high esteem,
is now needed in the south.
The Holy Emperor has an assignment for Jiāozhōu and Guǎngzhōu.
Would that be acceptable?
If he fears that distant region,
he should immediately request retirement due to age.
If not,
then as a Bīnzhàn official with duties divided to the Eastern Capital Luòyáng,
that would also be a command showing favor to a worthy man."
The sons returned and fully reported the proposal, seeking their father's decision on its feasibility.
Thereupon, Lú Xuàn requested the post of Bīnzhàn.
Lǐ Línfǔ, fearing to disappoint public expectation,
had him appointed as Prefect of Huàzhōu.
Within less than a month,
he falsely accused him of being ill
and unfit to govern the commandery,
appointing him instead as Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent,
an extra-compensatory placement.
From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Minghuáng"
Lǐ Fǔguó
When Emperor Xuánzōng was the Retired Emperor,
he resided in the Xìngqìng Palace.
After long rains had just cleared,
he visited the Qínzhèng Tower.
The market people below the tower and those coming and going in the streets,
overjoyed and with tears in their eyes, said:
"We never expected to see the Son of Heaven of peace again today."
They shouted "Long live!" ten thousand times,
the sound shaking heaven and earth.
At that time, Emperor Sùzōng was unwell,
and Lǐ Fǔguó falsely memorialized, saying:
"These are all the seditious plots of Jiǔ Xiānyuán, Gāo Lìshì, and Chén Xuánlǐ."
He issued a forged edict to move the Retired Emperor to the Western Palace,
and cut off
Míng transcript: "cut off" for "provided"
his retinue and personal troops,
leaving no more than twenty or thirty old and weak men.
When they reached the middle of the road,
a forest of blades gleamed in the sunlight,
with Lǐ Fǔguó commanding them.
The Retired Emperor was startled,
and nearly fell from his horse several times,
relying on his attendants to support him before he could mount.
Gāo Lìshì spurred his horse forward
and said in a stern voice:
"Fifty years a peaceful Son of Heaven!
Lǐ Fǔguó, you are his former subject.
It is not fitting to show such disrespect.
Lǐ Fǔguó, dismount!"
Lǐ Fǔguó unconsciously dropped his reins and dismounted.
He then proclaimed the Retired Emperor's decree:
"The officers and soldiers shall each be treated with kindness."
Míng transcript: "be treated with kindness" for "be well"
Thereupon, Lǐ Fǔguó ordered the soldiers to sheathe their blades in their scabbards,
and they shouted in unison:
"May the Retired Emperor enjoy boundless happiness!"
For a moment, they bowed and performed the dance of celebration.
Gāo Lìshì then said:
"Lǐ Fǔguó, lead the horse!"
Lǐ Fǔguó then put on his boots,
stepped forward to lead the horse,
and along with the soldiers, escorted and attended the Retired Emperor,
safely arriving at the Western Palace.
After Lǐ Fǔguó led the multitude away and withdrew,
the Retired Emperor, weeping, held Gāo Lìshì's hand and said:
"Without you, General,
Āmán would already be a ghost slain by soldiers."
Soon after, Jiǔ Xiānyuán, Gāo Lìshì, and Chén Xuánlǐ
were exiled to distant and harsh places,
all due to Lǐ Fǔguó's forged edicts.
At that time, Emperor Sùzōng was critically ill,
and Lǐ Fǔguó monopolized court affairs,
fearing further incidents in the Western Palace.
From "Leisurely Conversations in the Army Tent"
Wéi Qúmóu
In the final years of the Zhēnyuán era,
Grand Steward Wéi Qúmóu, Imperial Guard Commander Lǐ Qíyùn, Revenue Commissioner Péi Yánlíng, and Capital Prefect Shìdàowáng Shí,
all enjoyed imperial favor and influence,
and their recommendations often secured high positions for others.
At the time, Liú Shīlǎo and Mù Jí were both candidates for official posts.
Qúmóu supported Mù Jí,
while Qíyùn supported Shīlǎo.
Once, when Qíyùn attended court for an audience,
the emperor sighed at his frail appearance
and granted him permission to retire.
Consequently, Shīlǎo lost his chance for appointment.
Thus, an anonymous person wrote:
"The Grand Steward ascends to heaven and elevates Old Mù;
The Minister falls to the ground and drops Master Liú."
On another occasion, Qúmóu was in audience with Emperor Dézōng,
who asked him:
"I intend to appoint Zhèng Yīn as chancellor.
What do you think?"
Qúmóu replied:
"If you employ this man,
he will surely ruin Your Majesty's affairs."
When the emperor asked again another day,
he gave the same response.
The emperor said:
"I have decided to use Zhèng Yīn.
Do not speak of this further."
Zhèng Yīn was the Duke of Zhāoguó and Minister of Education.
He served twice as chancellor,
and was known for his integrity, frugality, and literary talent,
reputed as a worthy minister—
a reputation that endures to this day.
Thus, Qúmóu's slander was baseless.
From the "Jiāhuà Lù."
Yú Cháo'ēn
Yú Cháo'ēn wielded power arbitrarily and acted with arrogance,
so that the high ministers dared not look him in the eye.
When the chancellor and ministers decided on government affairs
without consulting him,
he would glare and say:
"Are not all matters under heaven
subject to my will?"
Thus, the emperor grew to detest him.
Cháo'ēn's youngest son, Lìnghuī,
was fourteen or fifteen years old
and had just begun serving in the inner palace.
Due to Cháo'ēn's influence,
the emperor specially granted him the green robe [of a low-ranking official].
Before a full month had passed,
a fellow eunuch who held a higher rank than Lìnghuī,
while lining up in front of the hall,
fearing he would arrive late,
pushed ahead to get in line.
Not long after,
he accidentally bumped Lìnghuī's arm.
Lìnghuī rushed home
and told Cháo'ēn
that because his rank was lower,
he had been bullied by his colleague.
Cháo'ēn was furious.
The next day,
he petitioned the emperor:
"Your subject's young son, Lìnghuī,
holds a rank lower than all his colleagues.
I beg Your Majesty to specially bestow upon him a golden seal,
so that he may rise above his peers."
Without even mentioning the crimson robe, he directly requested the purple robe [of high rank].
Before the emperor could speak,
Cháo'ēn had already ordered his subordinate
to bring forth a purple robe.
Lìnghuī immediately expressed his gratitude before the hall.
Though the emperor knew this was improper,
he reluctantly said to Cháo'ēn:
"Your son wearing the ceremonial robe
is most fitting."
The Yú family acted in court without the slightest fear or restraint;
all their actions were like this.
As for that fellow eunuch,
he was soon exiled to the distant southern region.
When Cháo'ēn was later executed,
there was no one in the land who did not rejoice.
From the "Dūyáng Zábiān."
Yuán Zǎi
While Yuán Zǎi served in the Secretariat,
his father-in-law came from Xuānzhōu, having sold his property to seek him out,
hoping to obtain an official post.
The Secretariat assessed that the man lacked the ability for such a position,
so they gave him a letter addressed to Héběi and sent him away.
The father-in-law was resentful and angry,
but having no choice,
he took the letter and left.
When he reached Yōuzhōu,
he thought of how he had bankrupted himself to come here,
only to receive a single letter.
If the letter was earnest,
there might still be hope.
So he opened and read it,
only to find it contained not a single word—
just a signature.
Greatly regretting his actions,
he angrily considered turning back.
But reflecting that he had already traveled several thousand li,
he decided to try visiting the local government office.
The office staff asked him:
"Since you are the father-in-law of the Grand Councilor,
surely you have a letter of introduction?"
He replied:
"Yes, I do."
The assistant magistrate was greatly astonished
and immediately ordered a messenger to report to his superior.
In a short while,
a senior officer arrived carrying a box
and requested the letter.
Once the letter was presented,
they lodged him in the finest guest quarters
and entertained him for several months.
When he took his leave,
they presented him with a thousand bolts of silk.
From the "Yōuxián Gǔchuī."
Also, Yuán Zǎi's son, Bóhé, wielded immense influence both in and out of court.
The Military Commissioner of Fúzhōu sent him ten female musicians as a gift.
After they arrived,
for half a year he could not get them presented to Bóhé.
The messenger watched those who frequently entered and exited the household,
and found that a pipa player named Kāng Kūnlún was the most familiar [with the family].
He bestowed generous gifts to seek an introduction.
After the musicians were presented,
Bóhé had them perform once,
and then gave them all away.
Previously, there was a monk named Duàn who excelled at playing the pipa
and had composed the piece "Xīliángzhōu."
Kūnlún had asked for it but was refused.
Now, he gave half of the musicians to the monk,
who then taught him the piece.
The present-day tune "Liángzhōu" is this very piece.
From the "Yōuxián Gǔchuī."
Lù Yán
When Lù Yán was appointed to govern the southwestern region,
he opened a central road,
but was wantonly pelted with tiles and stones [by the people].
The former Capital Prefect, Wēn Zhāng,
was an associate of his sons' faction.
Yán had appointed Xuē Néng from a ministry post to act as Capital Prefect,
upon the recommendation of Lǐ Pín.
At this time, Yán said to Néng:
"As I depart, I am wearied by the farewell of tiles and gravel."
Néng slowly raised his tablet and replied:
"According to precedent,
when a chancellor leaves to govern a region,
the capital offices have no established practice of sending people for protection."
Yán showed a ashamed expression.
In the later years of Emperor Yìzōng's reign,
the court administration was fragmented among many factions.
Yán, though young, clung firmly to his position.
By chance, he attained this status,
but once he lost power,
those at the crossroads [of decision]
were largely his enemies.
Those who attached themselves
(pronounced lí)
to him
angled to gauge the current climate,
their aim being flattery and sycophancy,
echoing the same words in unison.
Rumors seethed within and outside the court,
though the reality was not so.
Initially, while in Huáinán, Yán served as an assistant under Cuī Xuàn.
He was promoted to Investigating Censor.
In less than ten years,
without even leaving the city gates,
he rose to the position of a minister and chancellor.
Things forbid excessive flourishing;
a sudden rise to greatness is inauspicious—
truly, there is reason for this!
Earlier, Xuàn had believed Yán would certainly achieve high rank.
He often said:
"Lù Shí will eventually attain that position."
When Yán moved from Investigating Censor into the Hanlin Academy,
Xuàn was still in Huáinán.
Upon hearing this, he said:
"If Lù Shí is entering the Hanlin Academy now,
how will he manage in his old age!"
All turned out as he said.
From the "Yùquánzǐ."
Gāo Xiāng
In the early Yuánhé era, eight Simǎs were demoted:
Wéi Zhíyí to Yázhōu,
Hán Tài to Qiánzhōu,
Liǔ Zōngyuán to Yǒngzhōu,
Liú Yǔxī to Lǎngzhōu,
Hán Yè to Ráozhōu,
Líng Zhǔn to Liánzhōu,
Chéng Yì to Liǔzhōu.
By the Xiántōng era,
when Wéi Bǎohéng and Lù Yán served as chancellors,
they removed ten Sīhùs who did not align with them:
Cuī Hàng to Xúnzhōu,
Lǐ Dú to Xiùzhōu,
Xiāo Gòu to Bōzhōu,
Cuī Yànróng to Léizhōu,
Gāo Xiāng to Gāozhōu,
Zhāng Yán to Pānzhōu,
Lǐ Kuàng to Qínzhōu,
Dù Yìxiū to Duānzhōu,
Zhèng Yànchí to Yìzhōu,
Lǐ Zǎo to Fèizhōu.
Among them, the three assigned to Xiùzhōu, Pānzhōu, and Léizhōu never returned.
Initially,
Gāo Shí and his younger brother Xiāng had been at odds since youth.
In the late Xiántōng era,
after Xiāng was sent to Gāozhōu,
Shí, who was on good terms with Lù Yán,
visited Yán
and pretended to plead for Xiāng.
Yán said:
"Both you and I are among those who bore the cangue in the Jīngzhào Prefecture."
Previously, Liú Zhān had intended to remove Yán,
and Wēn Zhāng, currying favor,
had dozens of new cangues specially made in anticipation.
Zhān, believing people supported him,
was not very discreet,
and his plan leaked.
Thus, after Yán took office,
when Shí was appointed examiner,
he asked Yán whom he wished to recommend.
At the time, Yán had halted the examinations the previous year,
and had already secretly memorialized,
fearing oversight,
requesting ten additional candidates;
he then entrusted five to Shí.
Shí, pleased with the small number,
showed it in his words and expression.
Within days,
an edict for ten candidates was issued,
which Shí did not yet know.
Yán held the edict
and said to Shí with a laugh:
"The former five
were by your grace, Vice-Minister.
These ten now
are my own doing."
Shí ultimately passed exactly that number.
When Xiāng took up his post,
he resented Shí for not aiding him,
and once composed a poem saying:
"Only Gāozhōu is my true home."
From "Yùquánzǐ"
Lú Yǐn
Lú Yǐn and Lǐ Qiào were both protégés of the Huá commander Wáng Duó,
and had been demoted or disgraced several times.
Public opinion held that Yǐn and Qiào
were morally deficient in their private conduct.
Yǐn, because his cousin Lú Xié was chancellor,
was specially appointed Right Vice-Director of the Bureau of Operations.
Right Vice-Minister Cuī Hàng refused to let Yǐn assume his post in the department,
and then went to see Xié at his private residence.
Xié, unaware of the matter,
came out cheerfully.
Hàng said:
"When Vice-Director Yǐn entered the department the other day,
public criticism had not yet subsided.
Now he is again appointed Vice-Director of the Bureau of Review,
the department certainly dares not refuse,
according to Sòng Wáng Dǎng's 'Táng Yǔlín' 7, 'refuse' is written as 'comply'
but for other bureaus, it is as you command, Chancellor."
Xié flew into a rage,
rushed in and said:
"My younger cousin has been greatly wronged;
I shall immediately submit a memorial."
After the memorial was submitted,
Hàng then requested leave.
Xié immediately replaced Hàng's position.
Hàng remarked to others:
"I have seen a Vice-Minister remove a Department Vice-Director,
but never a Department Vice-Director remove a Vice-Minister."
Yǐn was initially appointed Vice-Director of the Bureau of Waterways from the post of Tàicháng Doctor,
but was obstructed by Right Vice-Minister Lǐ Jǐngwēn.
When the appointment to Right Vice-Director of the Bureau of Operations came,
it was on Jǐngwēn's recommendation.
Thus, he achieved his ambition.
At that time, some remonstrance officials also submitted memorials criticizing this,
to which Xié said:
"Remonstrance officials are like dogs—
when one barks,
they all make noise for a while."
From "Yùquánzǐ"
Guān Yǔ
The Shǔ general Guān Yǔ was good at caring for his soldiers but looked down on scholar-officials;
Zhāng Fēi respected scholar-officials but neglected his troops.
Both generals failed to strike a balance,
and both met unnatural deaths.
From "Dú Yì Zhì"
Jiǎnwén
Jìn Emperor Jiǎnwén commented on Emperor Guāngwǔ:
"Among the heroic and bold, Hàn Shìzǔ [Emperor Guāngwǔ]
possessed the most outstanding and refined demeanor,
the air of a worthy and enlightened man.
Emperor Gāozǔ [of Hàn] was untrammeled and broad-minded,
while Wèi Wǔ [Cáo Cāo] was suspicious, jealous, and narrow-minded."
From "Jiǎnwén Tán Shū"
Lǐ Mì
Táng Gāozǔ wrote a letter in reply to Lǐ Mì, saying:
"Heaven gives birth to the multitudes,
and there must be those who govern them.
To be the governor of the present age,
who else but you?
This old man is past the age of knowing fate,
and my wishes do not extend this far.
I joyfully support you, my esteemed younger brother,
clinging to your scales and attaching to your wings.
I only hope you will soon receive the mandate and charts,
to bring peace to the myriad people.
As the elder of our ancestral alliance,
I am content to be included in the registry.
To be enfeoffed again in Táng,
this honor is sufficient.
To slay the Shāng tyrant Xīn at Mùyě,
is something I cannot bear to speak of;
To capture Zǐyīng in Xiányáng,
is a command I dare not hear."
Lǐ Mì was very pleased upon receiving the letter,
and showed it to his subordinates, saying:
"With Táng Gōng supporting me,
it will not be difficult to secure all under heaven."
Later, Lǐ Mì's army was defeated,
and Wáng Bódāng defended Héyáng.
Lǐ Mì returned to him with a light cavalry,
and said to Bódāng:
"The army is defeated,
and I have long caused you all hardship.
I will now take my own life,
to apologize to the multitude."
Bódāng embraced Lǐ Mì and wailed.
Lǐ Mì then said again:
"If you gentlemen are fortunately unwilling to abandon me,
we should all return to Guānzhōng together.
Although I, Mì, am ashamed to have achieved no merit,
you gentlemen will surely preserve your wealth and honor."
Bódāng approved of his plan.
Those who followed him into Guānzhōng still numbered twenty thousand men.
Gāozǔ sent envoys to welcome and console them,
lining the roads.
Lǐ Mì was greatly delighted,
and said to his followers:
"Although my undertaking did not succeed,
I have won the affection of the common people.
East of the mountains, there are several hundred connected cities.
When they learn of my arrival,
they will all submit to Táng.
Compared to Dòu Róng,
my merit is also not small.
Would they not appoint me to a high ministerial position?"
When he reached the capital,
the courtesies grew increasingly sparse,
and those in power came to demand wealth,
which greatly displeased him.
Soon he was appointed Minister of the Imperial Household,
and enfeoffed as Duke of Xíngguó.
Not long after,
he heard that the generals and commanders under his former command
were all unwilling to submit to Wáng Shìchōng.
Gāozǔ again sent Lǐ Mì to lead his original troops to Líyáng,
to recruit his former officers and soldiers.
In order to strategize against Wáng Shìchōng,
Wáng Bódāng was made Left Guard of the Martial Guards,
and also ordered to assist Lǐ Mì.
When they reached Táolín,
Gāozǔ summoned him again.
Lǐ Mì grew fearful,
and plotted rebellion.
Bódāng tried to stop Lǐ Mì,
but he would not listen.
Lǐ Mì occupied the county town of Táolín,
driving off and plundering livestock,
and headed straight for the southern mountains,
advancing eastward through treacherous terrain.
He sent a messenger to inform Zhāng Shànxiāng,
ordering him to provide support.
At that time, Shǐ Wànbǎo remained to guard Xióngzhōu,
and sent Shèng Yànshī to lead several tens of thousands of infantry and cavalry in pursuit.
At a location seventy *lǐ* south of Lùhún County,
Yànshī set an ambush in the mountain valley.
When half of Lǐ Mì's army had crossed,
he attacked them from the side,
and thus beheaded Lǐ Mì.
He was thirty-seven years old.
At that time, Xú Jì was in Líyáng,
holding firm for Lǐ Mì.
Gāozǔ sent an envoy with Lǐ Mì's head to summon him,
Jì held a funeral and observed mourning,
performing the full rites between ruler and minister,
and submitted a memorial requesting to collect and bury him,
with great ceremony and dignity.
The entire army wore mourning white,
and he was buried five *lǐ* south of Líyáng Mountain.
His old acquaintances wept for him,
and many vomited blood.
From *Tán Bīn Lù*.
Liú Wénjìng
Liú Wénjìng was the magistrate of Jìnyáng.
He was implicated for having marriage ties with Lǐ Mì,
and the Suí Emperor Yáng imprisoned him in the commandery jail.
Tàizōng believed Wénjìng could be consulted on plans and discussions,
and entered the prison to see him.
Wénjìng was greatly pleased and said:
"All under heaven is in great chaos,
and without talents like Tāng, Wǔ, Gāozǔ, and Guāngwǔ,
it cannot be settled."
Tàizōng said:
"How do you know there is no such person?
My coming to this prison is not for sentimental worries like between children.
I have come to discuss a grand plan with you."
Wénjìng said:
"Take advantage of the void to enter Guānzhōng,
issue commands to all under heaven,
and in less than half a year,
imperial enterprise can be achieved."
Tàizōng laughed and said:
"Your words exactly match my thoughts."
Later, he was sent as an envoy to the Turks,
and Wénjìng said to them:
"I hope to join forces with the Qaghan's troops and horses to enter the capital together.
The people and land will go to Táng Gōng,
while the wealth, silks, gold, and treasures will go to the Turks."
They immediately dispatched two thousand cavalry,
to follow Wénjìng back.
Gāozǔ often invited important ministers to sit and eat together.
Wénjìng memorialized, saying:
"The imperial throne is exalted in position,
and the emperor's seat is solemn and weighty.
To have the sun condescend to be equal to the myriad things
causes your ministers to tremble with fear,
and leaves us no place to stand."
From *Tán Bīn Lù*.
Lǐ Jīncái
Tàizōng once advised Gāozǔ, saying:
"It is passed down through generations that the Lǐ surname will receive the mandate and charts.
Lǐ Jīncái held a high position and enjoyed great prestige,
yet his entire clan was exterminated in a single day.
If you, sir, accept the command to suppress the rebels,
can you avoid this?
Even if you truly pacify the bandits,
your merit will again be such that it cannot be rewarded.
To seek exemption from punishment on this basis,
can it be obtained?"
Gāozǔ said:
"I have thought it over all night,
and your words make great sense.
Today, the destruction of my family and my own death will be because of you,
and transforming the family into a state will also be because of you."
From *Tán Bīn Lù*.
Lǐ Jìng
In the fourteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Hóu Jūnjí, Xuē Wànjūn, and others defeated Gāochāng,
and its king, Qū Zhìshèng, surrendered.
They captured him
and presented the victory at the Guāndé Hall.
That land was made Xīzhōu,
and Jiāohé, Liǔzhōng, and other counties were established.
Its borders extended eight hundred *lǐ* east to west,
and five hundred *lǐ* north to south.
This was the territory of the Han dynasty's Wù-Jī Colonel.
Initially, the Turks stationed troops at Fútú City,
acting in concert with Gāochāng.
By this time, they grew fearful and came to surrender,
and their land became Yán
(Míng manuscript has "Yán" as "Tíng")
Prefecture.
The Turkish Qaghan, Xiélì, sent Zhíshī Sīlì to the court to apologize for his crimes,
requesting to become a vassal.
Tàizōng sent Táng Jiǎn and others as envoys beyond the frontier to pacify them.
Lǐ Jìng and Zhāng Gōngjǐn plotted in Dìngxiāng, saying:
"When the imperial envoy reaches there,
the barbarians will certainly let down their guard.
Select elite cavalry,
carrying twenty days' rations,
and take advantage of the opportunity to launch a surprise attack.
If we encounter their scouts,
take them all captive,
and then swiftly arrive and launch an assault."
Thus they destroyed their state.
They captured Princess Yìchéng,
and took captive one hundred thousand men and women.
Xiélì fled on a thousand-*lǐ* horse to the western regions.
Zhāng Bǎoxiāng, the campaign commander of Língzhōu,
captured him and presented him.
From *Tán Bīn Lù*.
Guō Qízōng
Emperor Gāozōng asked:
"In military treatises, it is said:
Heaven formation, Earth formation, and Human formation—
what does each refer to?"
Yuán Bànqiān stepped forward out of turn and replied:
"Your servant has perused the records;
this matter is mentioned many times.
Some say Heaven formation refers to the solitary and empty positions of the constellations;
Earth formation refers to the orientation and topography of mountains and rivers;
Human formation refers to the organization and seamless coordination of troops."
Guō Qízōng replied:
"In your servant's humble opinion, it is not so.
When an army marches forth with righteousness,
it is like timely rain—
this is obtaining the Heaven formation.
The military relies on sufficient food and ample troops,
farming while fighting—
this is obtaining the advantages of the land,
which is the Earth formation.
When the soldiers are swift and effective,
and the generals and commanders are harmonious—
this is the Human formation.
If in employing troops,
one discards any one of these three,
how can one fight?"
Emperor Gāozōng sighed in admiration
and promoted him to the post of Left Guard Armory Officer.
From "Lúshì Záshuō" (Miscellaneous Stories of Mr. Lú).
Táng Xiūjǐng
When the various tribes of the Western Tūjué were in discord,
they raised armies to attack each other.
The Ānxī route was cut off,
and memorials arrived one after another.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān ordered Táng Xiūjǐng to discuss the situation with the ministers.
In a short while, he drafted a memorial,
which was implemented.
More than ten days later,
memorials from the various prefectures of Ānxī reported that the schedules for troop movements and support
were exactly as Táng Xiūjǐng had planned.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān said to Táng Xiūjǐng:
"I regret employing you so late."
She then appointed him as a minister.
From "Tánbīn Lù" (Records of a Guest's Conversations).
Lǐ Jìnzhōng Lǐ Jìnzhōng During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān of the Táng,
the Qìdān leader Lǐ Jìnzhōng
and Wàn Róng attacked and captured the camp headquarters,
imprisoning several hundred Hàn captives in an underground prison.
Hearing that Má Rénjié and other armies were about to arrive,
they ordered the Xí guards watching the prisoners to deceive them, saying:
"Our families are starving and cold,
unable to survive.
We beg to wait until the imperial troops arrive,
and then we will surrender."
The prisoners were given one meal of porridge each day,
and were brought out and comforted, being told:
"We here have no food to feed you,
nor can we bear to kill you.
How about we release you all?"
The captives all bowed and begged for their lives.
They were then deceived and released.
Upon reaching Yōuzhōu,
they recounted in detail their hunger, cold, and delays.
When the soldiers heard this,
they all vied to be the first to advance.
When they reached Huángzhāng Valley,
the rebels again ordered the elderly to surrender to the government troops,
and left old oxen and emaciated horses by the roadside.
Má Rénjié and the other three armies,
abandoning their infantry,
took their cavalry and rushed ahead to enter,
where they were ambushed and cut off by the rebels.
The generals were ensnared with ropes,
and Má Rénjié and others were captured alive.
The dead filled the valleys,
with hardly anyone left.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi" (Records from Court and Country).
Fēng Chángqīng
Fēng Chángqīng was thin and had a small, blemished eye,
with short legs and a limp.
Gāo Xiānzhī was the Chief Military Commander under Fūméng Língchá,
and Fēng Chángqīng served as Gāo Xiānzhī's attendant.
It happened that the Dálǎn tribes all rebelled,
heading north from the Black Mountains,
west towards Suìyè.
Gāo Xiānzhī was ordered to intercept them with two thousand cavalry.
Fēng Chángqīng secretly drafted a victory report in the tent;
everything Gāo Xiānzhī wished to say
was covered thoroughly.
Gāo Xiānzhī was amazed.
When the army returned,
Gāo Xiānzhī met with administrative officers Liú Tiào and Dúgū Jùn,
who asked:
"Who wrote the previous victory report?
How does the Deputy Commander-in-Chief have such a person?"
Gāo Xiānzhī said:
"It was my attendant Fēng Chángqīng,
who is now outside by the horses."
Liú Tiào and others bowed to Gāo Xiānzhī,
and ordered Fēng Chángqīng to enter, sit, and converse with them,
as if they were old acquaintances.
Later, when Gāo Xiānzhī became Military Commissioner of Ānxī,
he recommended Fēng Chángqīng to be his administrative officer.
Whenever Gāo Xiānzhī went on campaigns,
he often put Fēng Chángqīng in charge of rear affairs.
Fēng Chángqīng was talented, learned,
and resolute.
Gāo Xiānzhī's foster brother Zhèng Déquán was already a colonel,
and his prestige moved the entire army.
Zhèng Déquán saw that Fēng Chángqīng had risen from his household,
and had always looked down on him;
he rode his horse and rushed past Fēng Chángqīng.
Fēng Chángqīng went to the commissioner's office,
ordered his attendants to secretly bring Zhèng Déquán to the hall,
and after passing through several gates,
each was closed behind them.
Fēng Chángqīng rose from behind the desk and said to him:
"I, Chángqīng, rose from humble origins,
and was appointed as the attendant of the Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Had the Vice Censor-in-Chief not accepted me twice,
would the colonel not know this?
Now, due to the Vice Censor-in-Chief's excessive trust,
I have been appointed as the acting commissioner.
How dare the colonel be so disrespectful,
insulting me in front of the imperial envoy?"
He then shouted at him,
ordered him to be turned back,
and immediately had him beaten sixty strokes,
leaving him face down on the ground before being dragged out.
Gāo Xiānzhī's wife and foster mother
wailed outside the gate trying to save him,
but to no avail.
Later, when Gāo Xiānzhī saw Fēng Chángqīng,
he did not say a word,
and Fēng Chángqīng did not apologize either.
Later, Fēng Chángqīng served as Military Commissioner of Ānxī.
In the fourteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
he went to court at Huáqīng Palace.
Emperor Xuánzōng asked him about the rebellious affairs,
and what strategy should be adopted.
Fēng Chángqīng then spoke grandly to comfort Emperor Xuánzōng, saying:
"Your servant requests to take a horsewhip and cross the river,
and within days take the head of the rebel leader,
hanging it beneath the palace gate."
Emperor Xuánzōng was worried but admired his bold words.
Upon reaching the eastern capital,
within a month,
he recruited sixty thousand men.
After repeated unsuccessful battles,
he retreated with Gāo Xiānzhī to defend Tóng Pass.
Gāo Xiānzhī served as deputy to Prince Róng Wǎn, leading fifty thousand men to advance and attack.
On the tenth day of the twelfth month, they reached Shǎnzhōu.
On the eleventh day, Fēng Chángqīng was defeated at the eastern capital,
and on the thirteenth day, Ān Lùshān entered the eastern capital.
Fēng Chángqīng fled to Shǎnzhōu.
Seeing that the rebel vanguard was unstoppable,
he burned the Tàiyuán granary,
led his troops back towards Tóng Pass,
and repaired the defensive structures.
The rebels soon reached the pass,
but could not enter—
thanks to Gāo Xiānzhī's efforts.
Fēng Chángqīng was then stripped of his official rank,
and ordered to serve as a commoner in Gāo Xiānzhī's army.
The supervising eunuch Biān Lìngchéng interfered in every matter,
but Gāo Xiānzhī often did not comply.
Biān Lìngchéng went to report to the emperor,
detailing the situation of their flight and defeat.
Emperor Xuánzōng was furious,
and sent Biān Lìngchéng to execute him.
Fēng Chángqīng submitted a memorial before his execution.
After he was executed,
his body was placed on a reed mat.
Biān Lìngchéng said to Gāo Xiānzhī:
"Your Excellency, there is also an imperial decree for you."
Gāo Xiānzhī hurried down to where Fēng Chángqīng had been executed.
Gāo Xiānzhī said:
"If I am guilty of retreating,
I dare not refuse death.
But if I am accused of embezzling military provisions and imperial gifts,
then that is slandering me."
He said to Biān Lìngchéng:
"Above is heaven,
below is earth,
and the soldiers are all here—
do they not know?"
The soldiers shouted in unison:
"Wronged!"
Their voices shook the ground.
Gāo Xiānzhī looked at Fēng Chángqīng's corpse and said:
"Fèng Èr,
you rose from obscurity to prominence;
I promoted you,
and you succeeded me as military commissioner.
Today, I die here with you—
is this fate?"
He was then executed.
From "Tánbīn Lù" (Records of a Guest's Conversations).
Lǐ Guāngbì
Lǐ Guāngbì campaigned against Shǐ Sīmíng.
His army was at Yěshuǐ Crossing,
and as evening fell, he withdrew his main force,
leaving behind a thousand soldiers.
He said to Yōng Hào:
"The enemy generals Gāo Huī, Lǐ Rìyuè, and Yù Wénjǐng
are all warriors who can match ten thousand men.
Sīmíng is sure to send one of them to raid us.
I will now leave,
and you, sir, lead the troops and await the enemy here.
When they arrive, do not engage them in battle;
if they surrender, bring them all with you."
That day,
Sīmíng summoned Rìyuè and said:
"Lǐ Jūn has led his troops to Yěshuǐ;
this is a chance to capture him.
You take cavalry and cross by night,
and seize him for me."
He ordered:
"You must capture Lǐ Jūn;
otherwise, do not return!"
Rìyuè led five hundred cavalry
and pressed upon Hào's army at dawn.
Hào held the moat and rested his troops,
humming and whistling as they watched each other.
Rìyuè found this strange
and asked:
"Is the Grand Commandant here?"
The reply was:
"He left last night."
"How many troops are there?"
The reply was:
"A thousand.
Who is the commander?"
"It is Yōng Hào."
Rìyuè pondered for a long time
and said to his subordinates:
"I received orders to capture Lǐ Jūn.
Now if I capture Hào,
it will not fulfill this expectation,
and I will surely be harmed.
It would be better to surrender to him."
He then requested to surrender.
Hào went with him together.
Guāngbì also once stationed troops to guard Héyáng,
facing off against Shǐ Sīmíng for a year.
Sīmíng had a thousand warhorses,
which he washed daily south of the river,
to show off their numbers.
Guāngbì then gathered five hundred mares from the various camps
and waited until Sīmíng's horses reached the water's edge,
then drove them all out.
With foals tethered in the city,
the mares neighed incessantly,
without pause,
and Sīmíng's warhorses
all swam across the river.
Guāngbì drove them all into his camp.
Guāngbì was also once in Héyáng
when he heard that Shǐ Sīmíng had crossed the river
and was heading straight for the Eastern Capital.
Upon arrival,
he said to the留守 Wéi Zhì:
"The enemy, taking advantage of our army's defeat,
will be difficult to confront head-on.
Luòchéng has no grain,
and cannot be held.
What is your plan, sir?"
Zhì said:
"Reinforce Shǎnzhōu
and retreat to defend Tóngguān."
Guāngbì said:
"This is the usual military approach,
not a strategy of surprise.
It would be better to move the army to Héyáng,
block the north from Zé-Lù,
and hold the three cities to resist them.
If we win, we capture them;
if we lose, we defend ourselves.
With interior and exterior supporting each other,
the enemy will not dare invade west.
This is the posture of an ape's arm."
When Sīmíng reached Yǎnshī,
Guāngbì ordered his officers and men to head to Héyáng,
while he alone, with over five hundred cavalry under his command, served as the rear guard,
blocking the road at the stone bridge,
holding torches and advancing slowly.
The enemy did not dare press him.
He reached the city in the second watch of the night.
At dawn,
Sīmíng attacked with all his forces.
The various generals fought to the death,
killing over ten thousand enemy troops,
capturing eighty alive,
and seizing tens of thousands of weapons and grain stores.
They captured his great generals Xú Huáng and Wáng Lǐ Qín.
Note: According to the "New Book of Tang," biography of Lǐ Guāngbì, volume 136, it reads "Xú Huángyù, Lǐ Qínshòu."
Sīmíng was greatly frightened
and retreated to build fortifications to resist.
Guāngbì was about to engage in battle
and said to those around him:
"All battles are perilous affairs,
with victory or defeat hanging in the balance.
I, Guāngbì, hold the rank of one of the Three Dukes;
I cannot die at the hands of the enemy.
If the battle is not won,
I vow to throw myself into the river."
As the river was somewhat far from the city walls,
he feared that in an emergency it might be difficult to reach,
so he placed a sword in his boot,
resolved to die if necessary.
When the battle was won,
he faced west from the city, bowed and danced,
deeply moving the three armies.
He was transferred to garrison Línhuái,
carried on a litter due to illness,
and went straight to Sìzhōu.
Before Guāngbì reached Hénán,
after Tián Shéngōng pacified Liú Zhǎn,
he lingered in Yáng Prefecture.
Shàng Héng and Yīn Zhòngqīng attacked each other in Yǎn-Yùn,
and Lái Tiǎn led his troops back to Xiāngyáng.
The court was troubled by this.
When Guāngbì reached Xúzhōu,
Shǐ Cháoyì retreated,
and Tián Shéngōng hastily returned to Hénán.
Shàng Héng, Yīn Zhòngqīng, and Lái Tiǎn, all fearing his formidable reputation,
successively went to the capital.
When the Tibetans were about to attack the capital,
an imperial edict summoned Guāngbì to lead his troops to Cháng'ān.
Guāngbì was at odds with Chéng Yuánzhèn
and, observing the changes in the realm,
delayed and did not go.
Initially, Guāngbì commanded his troops with strict discipline,
and the realm submitted to his formidable reputation.
All his orders
were such that the generals did not dare look up at him.
But when he had armies like Tián Shéngōng's,
they did not accept his control.
Because of this, he became frustrated,
and shame and humiliation led to illness.
He died in Xúzhōu,
at the age of fifty-seven.
His mother was old and frail,
and the庄宅使 Yú Cháo'ēn came to offer condolences.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Mǎ Suì
During the Táng dynasty, the Southern Mán tribes invaded and harassed Xīchuān,
and the region suffered from a lack of border defenses.
After the Xiántōng era,
Jiànnán was severely troubled by them.
When Minister Niú Cóng was stationed there as governor,
he was overwhelmed by the Mán bandits,
unable to resist them.
Later, Gāo Pián was transferred from Dōngpíng to take charge of Chéngdū.
The Mán were still harassing
("Harassing" originally written as "spreading,"
corrected based on the Míng dynasty manuscript copy)
the city of Shǔ.
Gāo Pián first selected brave and elite troops for emergency relief.
Each soldier carried a divine talisman on his back.
When the Mán scouts learned of this,
they fled at the mere rumor of his approach.
Later, when Emperor Xīzōng fled to Shǔ,
he deeply suspected the Mán of causing trouble,
so he agreed to offer a princess in marriage.
The Mán king, delighted to form a marital alliance with the great empire,
was overjoyed beyond measure.
He then ordered his chancellors Zhào Lóngméi, Yáng Qíkūn, and Duàn Yìzōng to come to the imperial temporary residence to pay homage,
and to welcome the princess.
Grand Marshal Gāo sent an urgent memorial from Huáihǎi, stating:
"The heart and vitals of the Southern Mán
are only these few men.
I request that they be detained and poisoned."
Until Emperor Xīzōng returned to the capital,
the southern borders remained secure,
all thanks to Gāo's strategy.
Men like Yáng Qíkūn were all gifted with literary talent.
A poem composed on his journey reads:
"Waves in the wind blow white again and again;
Shadows in the rain wash clear, then clear once more.
Where river gulls gather, seen before the window;
When forest monkeys cry, heard upon the pillow."
The verses are exceptionally pure and beautiful.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Zhāng Jùn
Chancellor Zhāng Jùn was rich in strategic cunning,
but he had never known military affairs.
During Emperor Zhāozōng's reign,
he personally led the imperial guard's six armies
to campaign against Tàiyuán,
but suffered a defeat,
and his deputy commander, Vice-Minister Sūn Kuí, was captured.
Soon, he planned to withdraw the troops,
passing through Píngyáng on the route.
Píngyáng was a subordinate commandery of Pú,
and its governor, surnamed Zhāng,
was a senior officer under Wáng Kē, the military governor of Pú.
Wáng Kē was treacherous and unpredictable,
and Zhāng Jùn also feared that as the army passed through,
they might fall victim to his cunning schemes.
So Zhāng Jùn set out several stages ahead,
and lodged at the official guesthouse in Píngyáng.
The six armies followed in succession,
advancing through the Yīndì Pass.
Zhāng Jùn deeply distrusted the governor of Jìn,
but dared not remove him.
Governor Zhāng welcomed him at the outskirts, one stage away.
After they settled at the postal station,
Zhāng Jùn invited Governor Zhāng to ascend the hall.
Tea, wine, and food were served.
Afterward, he ordered more tea and wine,
not allowing him to rise even briefly,
and further detained him for an evening meal.
After the meal,
it was already late afternoon,
and still he was not permitted to rise,
so several more bowls of tea were served.
Only when lamps were lit
was he allowed to take his leave.
From morning until dusk,
not a single word was exchanged.
Zhāng Jùn merely chewed on something small in his mouth,
and from a distance, it appeared as if they were engaged in conversation.
Wáng Kē was highly suspicious by nature,
and his actions were always under surveillance.
At the time, his spies had already secretly reported to him, saying:
"The imperial commissioner and the chancellor engaged in secret conversation all night long."
Wáng Kē indeed grew suspicious,
summoned Governor Zhāng, and asked him:
"What did you and the chancellor
talk about from morning until dusk?"
He replied:
"We did not exchange a single word."
Wáng Kē utterly refused to believe him,
accusing him of dishonesty,
and had him executed.
The six armies then passed through safely on their return to the capital,
completely free of any worries.
Later, when Zhāng Jùn was in charge of state finances,
the various provinces each presented him with silks and brocades.
He refused to accept them,
instead ordering a special envoy to deliver them back in person, saying:
"Convey my intentions:
use these items to cover the expenses for military campaigns instead.
Cooking pots, tents, cloth, troughs, and horse medicine—
all these are common local products—
I request that they be prepared."
Thereupon, the various military governors gladly complied,
so that even with an army of a hundred thousand,
all necessary supplies were met without shortage,
all planned with ingenuity.
Liáng Tàizǔ feared him,
and secretly ordered an assassin to kill him at his estate in Chángshuǐ.
From "Yù Táng Xián Huà."
Liú Xún
When the Jìn Prince of Later Táng entered Wèibó,
the Liáng general Liú Xún had first stationed his troops at Huánshuǐ,
where it was silent as if no one was there.
He ordered scouts to investigate,
and they reported:
"There are banners moving back and forth on the city walls."
The Jìn Prince said:
"Liú Xún is full of schemes;
we must not advance lightly."
He ordered further careful reconnaissance,
and it turned out that straw dummies had been tied up,
with banners attached to them,
and donkeys were made to carry them,
circling along the battlements,
so the banners appeared to move ceaselessly around the city.
When they asked the weak and sick left in the city,
they said:
"The army left two days ago."
Indeed, they had hurried toward Huángzé,
intending to attack Tàiyuán,
but were unable to advance due to heavy rains and flooding.
Such were his stratagems.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Zhāng Qíng
When Wáng Jiàn, the founding ruler of Former Shǔ, first besieged Chéngdū,
he could not capture it for three years.
Among his household servants,
there were about a hundred reckless, fearless, and fierce men
whom no one could match.
Wáng Jiàn once tempted them with sweet words, saying:
"Xīchuān is known as the Brocade Flower City.
Once we capture it,
the treasures, silks, and beautiful women
will be yours to enjoy as you please."
Later,
Chén Jìngxuān and Tián Lìngzǐ surrendered the city.
The next day, they entered the prefectural headquarters.
Wáng Jiàn preemptively warned his arrogant and violent sons:
"I have fought alongside you for years,
through life and death.
From tomorrow onward, we will be one family.
After entering the city,
you may enjoy wealth and honor,
but you must not act recklessly or tyrannically.
I have just appointed Zhāng Qíng as the Commissioner for Executing Offenders on Horseback and Foot,
and entrusted him with this responsibility.
You must not violate his authority.
If you are brought before me,
there may still be room for mercy,
but if you are executed on the spot,
I will not be able to save you."
Upon hearing this warning, his sons all took care to restrain themselves.
Yet, Zhāng Qíng had people beaten in the chest,
and their bodies piled up in the main thoroughfares,
so that no one dared to transgress.
Discerning individuals regarded Wáng Jiàn as capable of both warning and cherishing,
not letting people fall into punishment,
a comparison to benevolence and forgiveness.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Wáng Jiàn
Between Qióng and Lí, there were the Qiǎn Mán,
who inherited royal titles from generation to generation,
such as King Liú, King Yáng, and King Hǎo.
Each year, they received three thousand portions of clothing and supplies from Xīchuān,
so that they could spy on the movements of Yúnnán;
Yúnnán, in turn, used them to observe the strengths and weaknesses of Chéngdū.
They played both sides to seek profit.
Whenever a new military governor took office,
they would lead the chieftains from the border to visit the governor's office,
calling it "paying respects to the military governor."
The governor, hearing of this, would believe it was due to his own authority and benevolence,
but before they paid their respects,
they would secretly report to the chief military inspector,
waiting to see what was permissible.
If the military governor, in comforting and pacifying his generals,
acted even slightly inappropriately,
they would immediately stir up trouble.
At that time, most of the military governors were scholars,
unwilling to cause trouble.
Because of this, the chief military inspector relied on them,
and also sought to appease them.
The Mán and Dàn tribes took advantage of this,
and there was no defense against their encroachments,
all because of this.
When Wáng Jiàn first governed Shǔ,
he cut off their old subsidies,
and executed the chief military inspector, Shān Xíngzhāng, to make an example of them.
South of Qióng and Xiá,
not a single watchtower was erected,
nor a single soldier stationed.
For ten years, they did not dare to invade the border.
In his later years,
he ordered the general Xǔ Cún to campaign against the Mán,
but the three kings leaked military secrets.
So he summoned the three kings and executed them.
At the time, this was called "the decisive action."
In the past, the trouble caused by the three kings
was not unknown,
but the timing was not favorable.
Therefore it is said:
"To achieve extraordinary feats,
one must be like Lord Xǔ."
Earlier, during the Xiántōng era of the Táng,
there was a monk from Tiānzhú, a Tripitaka master,
who passed through Chéngdū.
He was versed in the languages of the Five Indias and the Hú
"Hú" originally written as "Hú" (lake),
corrected according to the Míng manuscript
regions,
and proficient in the scriptures, vinaya, and treatises of both the Mahayana and Hinayana traditions.
Since North Tiānzhú bordered Yúnnán,
he wanted to pass through to return home.
He was recognized by Shǔ's intelligence agents,
detained in the Chéngdū prefectural office,
and all the documents he had recorded regarding the imperial court's affairs were obtained,
revealing that he had once entered the inner court's Buddhist sanctuary.
This shows that among those who come to the court from foreign lands,
who knows if they are not spies?
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Emperor Tàizǔ of Wèi
When Emperor Wǔ of Wèi was young,
he and Yuán Shào both enjoyed being knights-errant.
Once, while observing a wedding,
they sneaked into the host's garden,
and at night shouted:
"There are thieves here!"
Everyone in the house came out to look,
and the Emperor then drew his sword to seize the bride,
and fled with Yuán Shào.
They lost their way,
and fell into a thorny thicket,
where Yuán Shào could not move.
The Emperor again shouted loudly:
"The thief is here now!"
Yuán Shào, in panic, threw himself out,
and both escaped.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi also once said
that whenever someone intended to harm him,
he would feel a stirring in his heart.
So he told a trusted servant:
"If you come to me secretly with a weapon,
my heart will surely stir,
and I will kill you.
But do not say anything,
and I will reward you later."
The servant believed him,
and was subsequently executed.
Those plotting rebellion were thus discouraged.
Also, when Yuán Shào was young,
he once sent someone at night to throw a sword at Emperor Wǔ of Wèi,
but it fell slightly short.
The Emperor deduced that the next throw would be higher,
so he lay flat on the bed,
and the sword indeed went higher.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi also said:
"When I am asleep, do not approach me recklessly.
If you come near, I will cut you down,
without even being aware of it myself.
All of you around me should be careful."
Later, he pretended to be cold,
and a favored servant
secretly covered him with a blanket,
whereupon he immediately killed him.
From then on, no one dared to approach him.
From "Xiǎoshuō"
Village Woman
After Emperor Zhāozōng was forcibly relocated by the Liáng ruler,
the regions of Qí and Fèng
"Qí Fèng" originally written as "Jùn Fèng",
corrected according to the Míng manuscript
and other prefectures
amassed large numbers of armored soldiers,
who plundered freely to sustain themselves.
In Chéng Prefecture, there was a remote village estate
with substantial accumulated goods.
The commanding general sent over twenty cavalrymen to plunder it at night.
Arriving suddenly,
no one dared to resist.
The men of the household were tied up and imprisoned,
while all their goods were searched out,
bagged, and stored.
Then pigs and dogs were cooked,
and the women of the household were ordered to prepare the meal,
allowing the soldiers to eat and drink freely.
The family had once collected henbane seeds,
and the women took many of them, roasting and pounding them
until they resembled chili powder.
They placed this in the food,
and then served the soldiers turbid wine.
When the drug took effect,
the soldiers drew their swords from their waists and dug at the ground, saying:
"The horses have gone underground!"
Some wanted to jump into fire or water,
staggering before collapsing.
Then the women freed their husbands from their bonds,
slowly took the knights' swords,
and one by one cut their throats and buried them.
The horses were driven onto the main road,
whipped and sent off,
with no one the wiser.
Later, when the land changed hands,
the matter was revealed.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Zāiqiū Xīn
During the Zhou dynasty,
in the eastern sea region,
there was a brave man named Zāi Qiū Xīn, renowned throughout the land for his courage.
Passing by the Divine Spring,
he ordered his horse to drink.
His servant said:
"Any horse that drinks from this spring
will surely die."
Qiū Xīn said:
"Let it drink, on my word."
His horse indeed died.
