Qiū Xīn then stripped off his clothes, drew his sword, and plunged into the spring.
For three days and three nights
he fought, emerging only after slaying two water-demons and one dragon.
The Thunder God pursued and struck him,
for ten days and ten nights,
blinding his left eye.
Yào Lí heard of this and went to see him.
Qiū Xīn was out attending a funeral.
Yào Lí went to see Qiū Xīn at the gravesite and said:
"The Thunder God struck you,
for ten days and ten nights,
blinding your left eye.
Heaven's wrath is not delayed by a day,
nor man's wrath by a single step.
Yet to this day you have not sought revenge.
Why is that?"
He then berated him and left.
Countless spirits at the gravesite trembled with indignation.
Yào Lí returned home
and said to others:
"Zāi Qiū Xīn is the bravest man in the world.
Today I insulted him before a crowd.
He will surely come to kill me.
At dusk, I will not bolt my gate;
at night, I will not lock my door."
Qiū Xīn indeed came at midnight.
Drawing his sword and resting its point against his own neck, he said:
"You have committed three capital offenses:
insulting me before a crowd—
that is the first;
leaving your gate unbolted at dusk—
that is the second;
leaving your door unlocked at night—
that is the third."
Yào Lí said:
"Wait until I have spoken one word before you kill me.
You came without announcing yourself—
that is your first failing;
you drew your sword but did not strike—
that is your second;
you brandished the blade first and spoke afterwards—
that is your third.
If you kill me now,
it would be like dying from poison."
Qiū Xīn sheathed his sword and left, saying:
"Alas!
In all the world, the only one I cannot match
is this man."
From *Dú Yì Zhì*.
Zhū Zūn
During the Hàn dynasty, Zhū Zūn served as a Gōngcáo in his commandery.
When Gōngsūn Shù usurped the imperial title,
Zhū Zūn rallied the people of the commandery and refused to submit.
Shù attacked him,
and Zūn led troops to resist.
He buried his chariot wheels and hobbled his horses, then fought to the death.
Emperor Guāngwǔ posthumously honored him as Fǔhàn Jiāngjūn,
and Wú Hàn petitioned to have a shrine built for him.
Another account says:
Zhū Zūn had lost his head,
but retreated to this spot.
After hobbling his horse,
he reached to touch his head,
only then realizing it was gone.
Moved by his righteousness, the local people
built a shrine for him,
naming it the Jiàn'ér Miào (Shrine of the Stalwart).
It was later renamed the Yǒngshì Cí (Shrine of the Brave Warrior).
From *Xīnjīn Xiàn Tújīng*.
Zhào Yún
Shǔ's Zhào Yún,
courtesy name Zǐlóng,
was eight chǐ tall
with a majestic and imposing appearance.
While serving as Liú Bèi's vanguard,
he was surrounded by Lord Cáo's forces.
He then flung his gates wide open
and lowered his banners, silencing the drums.
Lord Cáo led his troops away,
suspecting an ambush.
Yún shot arrows at them from behind,
throwing Cáo's army into great panic
and causing many casualties.
The next day, Bèi himself came
and surveyed the previous day's battlefield.
He said:
"Zǐlóng is all courage, from head to toe."
From *Zhào Yún Biézhuàn*.
Lǚ Méng
Wú's Lǚ Méng followed his brother-in-law Dèng Dāng to attack bandits
when he was only sixteen.
Shouting and cursing, he charged forward,
and Dāng could not restrain him.
Returning home, he told his mother:
"Poverty and lowly status are hard to endure.
If I achieve merit,
wealth and honor can be attained."
He also said:
"If you do not enter the tiger's lair,
how can you catch the tiger's cub?"
He indeed achieved great fame.
From *Dú Yì Zhì*.
Wèi's Rénchéng Wáng
Wèi's Rénchéng Wáng, Cáo Zhāng,
was a son of Emperor Wǔ.
From youth he was resolute and strong-willed.
He studied the arts of yīnyáng and divination,
and could recite several thousand words from texts like the *Liù Tāo* and *Hóng Fàn*.
When Emperor Wǔ planned to attack Wú,
he consulted Zhāng,
seeking his decisive judgment on the campaign's advantages.
The Prince was skilled at shooting left and right-handed,
fond of fencing,
and could hit a hanging hair from a hundred paces.
When the state of Yuèjīng presented a striped tiger,
its patterns like brocade,
it was kept in an iron cage.
Even the most valiant warriors
dared not approach it lightly.
Zhāng grabbed the tiger's tail and wrapped it around his arm;
the tiger fell silent.
All were awed by his divine courage.
Another time, Nányuè presented a young white elephant.
Before the Emperor,
Zhāng struck its trunk with his hand,
and the elephant knelt motionless.
Emperor Wén had a ten-thousand-jūn bell cast and placed before the Chónghuá Hall.
When they wished to move it,
a hundred strong men
could not pull it.
Zhāng then carried it on his back and ran.
When the four quarters heard of his divine courage,
they all laid down their arms and fortified themselves.
The Emperor said:
"With the Prince's martial might, swallowing up Wú and Shǔ
would be like an owl carrying off a rotten rat."
When Zhāng died,
he was buried with rites like those for the Hàn dynasty's Dōngpíng King.
As the funeral procession departed,
the sound of hundreds weeping was heard in the air.
Those attending the funeral all said
that in past chaotic battles, the wounded and slain had lacked coffins.
Through the Prince's benevolence and kindness,
their decayed bones were gathered.
The dead rejoiced in the underworld,
and their spirits knew of his compassionate feelings.
Thus people praised the Prince's virtue.
The state historians compiled *Rénchéng Jiùshì* in two volumes.
By the early Eastern Jìn,
it was stored in the Imperial Archives.
From *Shí Yí Lù*.
Huán Shíqián
Jìn's Huán Shíqián was talented and capable,
agile and peerlessly nimble.
He followed his father, Huò, in Jīngzhōu.
During a hunting encirclement,
they saw a fierce beast lying subdued, pierced by several arrows.
The various commanders, knowing of his bravery,
jokingly ordered him to pull out the arrows.
Shíqián swiftly went forward,
pulled out one arrow,
and the fierce tiger leapt up.
Shíqián also jumped,
even higher than the beast.
He then pulled out another arrow and returned.
At that time, when people fell ill,
they would say,
"Huán Shíqián is coming!" to frighten them,
and the sick would often recover.
From *Dú Yì Zhì*.
Yáng Dàyǎn
Yáng Dàyǎn of the Later Wèi Dynasty
was the grandson of Wǔdū Dí Nándāng.
From a young age, he possessed great courage and spirit,
and could leap and run as if flying.
When Emperor Gāozǔ campaigned south,
Lǐ Chōng was in charge of selecting officers for the expedition.
Dàyǎn sought a position.
Chōng did not grant it.
Dàyǎn said:
"Since the Minister does not recognize my abilities,
I will perform a feat for the Minister."
He then took a rope thirty feet long,
tied it to his topknot, and ran.
The rope stretched straight as an arrow,
and even a galloping horse could not catch up.
All who saw it were amazed and sighed in admiration.
Chōng said:
"For a thousand years,
there has never been a talent as extraordinary as this."
He was then appointed as an army commander.
Later, he was promoted to General Who Supports the State.
When Wáng Sù first returned to the state,
he said to Dàyǎn:
"In the south, I heard of your name,
and thought your eyes were like cartwheels.
Now
"Now" originally written as "order";
changed according to the Ming manuscript, Xǔ block-printed edition, and Huáng block-printed edition
seeing you,
they are no different from ordinary people's eyes."
Dàyǎn said:
"If we face each other across battle flags and drums,
when I glare and rouse myself,
it is enough to make you lose your soul and courage.
Why must they be as large as cartwheels?"
His contemporaries praised his valor and decisiveness,
considering even Zhāng Fēi and Guān Yǔ could not surpass him.
From "Tán Sǒu"
Mài Tiězhàng
was a man from Wēngyuán, Sháozhōu.
He possessed great courage and strength,
and could travel five hundred lǐ in a day.
He initially served the Chén dynasty,
often holding an umbrella and following the imperial carriage.
After nightfall,
he would frequently sneak away to Dānyáng Commandery to commit theft.
By dawn,
he would return to his post under the imperial guard to perform his duties.
The round trip was over three hundred lǐ,
yet no one noticed.
Later, Dānyáng repeatedly reported the traces and causes of thefts.
The last ruler of Chén suspected him,
but valued his abilities,
so he pardoned him and did not question him.
After the fall of Chén, he entered the Suí dynasty,
and pledged his service to Yáng Sù.
When Sù was about to pacify the various commanderies south of the Yangtze,
he sent Tiězhàng to swim across the Yángzǐ River at night.
He was captured by patrols.
Men were assigned to guard him,
and he was sent to Gūsū.
Upon reaching Lǐngtíng,
they stayed overnight.
Waiting until the guards were sound asleep,
he stole their weapons,
killed all the guards, and fled back.
He then held two heads in his mouth,
grasped a sword, and swam back across the great river.
He was highly rewarded and employed by Yáng Sù.
Later, he rose to the position of Grand Administrator of his commandery.
Today, there are many people surnamed Mài in Nánhǎi,
all of whom are his descendants.
From "Lǐngbiǎo Lù Yì"
Péng Lè
Péng Lè, a general of the Northern Qí, was peerlessly brave and fierce.
At that time, Emperor Shénwǔ led Lè and over a hundred thousand others
to battle Yǔwén Hù at Shāyuàn.
At the time, Lè had been drinking,
and in his drunkenness, he charged deep into the enemy lines.
He was stabbed, and his liver and intestines spilled out.
He could not stuff them all back in,
so he cut off the excess
and rejoined the battle.
Hù's troops were then defeated,
with over thirty thousand corpses piled upon each other.
From "Dú Yì Zhì"
Gāo Kāidào
At the end of the Suí dynasty,
Gāo Kāidào was struck by an arrow.
The arrowhead lodged in his bone.
He ordered a physician to extract it,
but he could not.
Kāidào asked him why,
and he replied:
"I fear Your Majesty will feel pain."
Kāidào beheaded him.
He summoned another physician, who said:
"I can extract it."
Using a small axe,
he struck the area around the wound,
drove the arrowhead an inch deeper into the bone with a small stick,
and then pulled it out with pliers.
Kāidào ate and drank as usual,
and rewarded the physician with three hundred bolts of silk.
Later, he was killed by his general Zhāng Jīnshù.
From "Dú Yì Zhì"
Dù Fúwēi
At the end of the Suí dynasty, during the Dàyè era,
Dù Fúwēi battled Chén Léng at Qízhōu.
A subordinate general shot Fúwēi in the forehead.
Enraged, he said:
"If I do not kill the shooter,
I will never pull out this arrow."
Thereupon, he charged forward,
captured the one who had shot him,
and ordered him to pull out the arrow,
then beheaded him.
Léng was then utterly defeated.
From "Dú Yì Zhì"
Yùchí Jìngdé
Wáng Shí's nephew Wǎn was sent as an envoy to Dòu Jiàndé's army.
He rode the fine horse once used by Emperor Yáng,
and his armor was very splendid.
Emperor Tàizōng said:
"The horse he rides is truly an excellent steed."
Yùchí Jìngdé requested to go and seize it.
He was given three cavalrymen,
charged straight into the enemy army, captured Wǎn,
and led his horse back.
None among the enemy troops dared to oppose him.
Jìngdé once attended a banquet at Qìngshàn Palace.
At the time, someone was seated above him in rank.
Jìngdé angrily said:
"What merit do you have
that you should sit above me?"
Rénchéng Prince Lǐ Dàozōng was seated below him
and tried to explain and persuade him.
Jìngdé flew into a rage,
punched Dàozōng with his fist,
nearly blinding him in the eye.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Chái Shào's Younger Brother
A younger brother of Táng dynasty's Chái Shào
possessed great strength and ability.
He was agile, nimble, and swift,
leaping upward
as if flying straight up,
covering over ten paces before stopping.
Emperor Tàizōng ordered him to fetch Duke Zhào Zhǎngsūn Wújì's saddle and saddle blanket,
and first informed Wújì,
telling him to be on guard.
That night,
he saw something like a bird
fly into the residence,
cut off the pair of saddle flaps, and leave.
He could not catch up in pursuit.
He was also sent to fetch Princess Dānyáng's gold-inlaid box pillow.
He flew into the inner chamber,
sprinkled dirt on the princess's face with his hand.
As she raised her head,
he immediately replaced it with another pillow and left.
It was not until dawn that she realized it.
He once wore Jímò boots and ran up a brick city wall,
reaching the parapet,
without using his hands to pull himself up.
He also stepped on a pillar of a Buddhist hall with his feet,
reached the eaves,
and grabbed the rafters to climb onto the roof.
He leaped over hundred-foot towers and pavilions,
completely unimpeded.
Tàizōng found him remarkable and said:
"This man cannot remain in the capital city."
He was sent out to serve as an external official.
People of the time called him the "Wall Dragon."
Tàizōng once bestowed upon Zhǎngsūn Wújì a seven-treasure belt
worth a thousand pieces of gold.
At that time, a great robber named Duàn Shīzi descended from a hole between the rafters on the roof into the room
and, drawing his sword, said to him:
"Move and you die."
He then took the belt from the pillow box and left,
propped his sword on the ground,
and leaped up through the hole between the rafters.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Qín Shūbǎo
Whenever Emperor Tàizōng of Táng personally went into battle,
seeing the enemy's valiant generals and fierce warriors,
displaying their men and horses,
coming and going freely,
he was greatly troubled by this.
He would then order Qín Shūbǎo to capture them.
Shūbǎo, accepting the command, would leap onto his horse,
carry his spear and charge forward,
inevitably stabbing them amidst the myriad troops,
causing both man and horse to fall.
Later, when Shūbǎo lived at home, he suffered from many illnesses.
He said to people:
"From my youth, I grew up amidst warhorses,
experiencing over two hundred battles in total,
repeatedly suffering severe wounds.
I estimate the blood I have lost amounts to several hú.
How could I not be ill?"
From "Tán Bīn Lù".
Xuē Rénguì
When Emperor Tàizōng of Táng campaigned against Liáodōng,
he halted his carriage at the battle array.
Xuē Rénguì, dressed in white,
grasping his halberd with quiver and bow-case,
drew his bow and gave a great shout,
and wherever he went, the enemy crumbled.
Emperor Tàizōng said to him:
"It is not capturing Liáodōng that pleases me,
but gaining you, my minister."
Later, he led troops to attack the Turks in Yúnzhōu.
The Turks first asked who the Táng general was.
The reply was:
"It is Xuē Rénguì."
The Turks said:
"We heard Xuē Rénguì was exiled to Huìzhōu and died there.
How can he have come back to life?"
Rénguì removed his helmet and showed himself.
The Turks looked at each other, their faces losing color,
dismounted and bowed in a circle,
then gradually fled.
From "Tán Bīn Lù".
Gōngsūn Wǔdá
Gōngsūn Wǔdá, Great General of the Left Martial Guard of Táng, possessed great physical strength.
Once he encountered bandits,
who had plundered all his clothes and belongings,
and forced Wǔdá to hand over his boots.
Wǔdá offered his foot to them.
As the bandit bent down to pull off the boot,
Wǔdá struck him,
killing him with his own hands.
Using the bandit's own weapons, he fought off the remaining robbers,
and thus escaped.
From "Tán Bīn Lù".
Chéng Zhījié
When Péi Xíngyǎn of Táng fought against Wáng Chōng,
he first galloped towards the enemy,
was hit by a stray arrow,
and fell to the ground.
Chéng Zhījié went to rescue him,
killed several men,
and Chōng's army crumbled.
Zhījié then lifted Xíngyǎn,
mounted together on a single horse, and turned back.
Pursued by Chōng's cavalry,
a lance thrust pierced through him.
Zhījié turned his body,
snapped the lance shaft,
killed the pursuer,
and both he and Xíngyǎn escaped.
From "Tán Bīn Lù".
Táng Qìbì Ā
The Míng manuscript copy writes "Ā" as "Hé" (何),
same below.
Lì campaigned against Liáodōng.
With eight hundred cavalry,
he met the enemy and joined battle,
was struck in the waist by a lance,
and was hard-pressed by the enemy.
Shàngniǎn Fèngyù Xuē Wànbèi, alone on his horse, charged in and killed the enemy cavalry,
rescuing Ā Lì from amidst the horde of enemies,
and came out together with him.
Ā Lì's strength was exhausted,
but he bound his wound and fought on,
and the enemy then retreated.
From "Tán Bīn Lù".
Lǐ Kǎigù
Lǐ Kǎigù
During the reign of Empress Tiānhòu of Táng,
General Lǐ Kǎigù,
a Qìdān man,
was skilled at using lassos.
After Lǐ Jìnzhōng was defeated,
Má Rénjié, Zhāng Xuányù and others were all captured by lasso.
Whether muntjac, deer, fox, or rabbit,
he would gallop and intercept them,
cast his lasso and snare them,
missing not one in a hundred.
On horseback, he wielded bow, arrows, spear, and lance,
appearing like a flying immortal.
Empress Tiānhòu, valuing his talent,
did not kill him,
but employed him as a general.
Somewhat greedy for wealth and fond of women,
he was sent out as Commandant of the Qiáokǒu Garrison in Tánzhōu,
where he died of resentment and anger.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi".
Wáng Jūn
Wáng Jūn of Táng, acting as Vice Censor-in-Chief,
concurrently administered the affairs of Liángzhōu Military Governor.
Emperor Xuánzōng, at the Guǎngdá Tower,
summoned Jūn and his wife Xià Shì to a banquet,
and bestowed gold and silk upon them.
Xià Shì was also brave and decisive.
Whenever Jūn went into battle,
Xià Shì also achieved military merit.
In Liángzhōu, there were the Huíhé, Qìbì, Sījié, and Zhèn
The Míng manuscript copy writes "Zhèn" (陣) as "Zhàn" (戰).
According to the "Old Book of Táng: Biography of Wáng Jūn", "Zhèn" is written as "Hún" (渾).
four tribes, and he was their chieftain.
When Jūn was in humble circumstances, he traveled to and from Liáng Prefecture,
and was looked down upon by the Huíhé.
When Jūn became Military Governor of Héxī,
the Huíhé and others were discontented,
ashamed to be under his command.
Jūn memorialized that the Huíhé and other tribes were difficult to control,
secretly plotting rebellion,
and thus detained the four tribal commanders.
Later, the four tribes conspired to rebel against Jūn to settle their grievance.
It happened that the Tibetans were taking a byway to go to the Turks.
Jūn led elite cavalry to Sùzhōu to attack them by surprise.
Returning to the Gǒngbǐ Post Station south of Gānzhōu,
the four tribes' ambush troops suddenly rose up.
Jūn fought strenuously with the bandits,
from morning until late afternoon,
his attendants all perished,
and they finally killed Jūn.
From "Tán Bīn Lù".
Sòng Lìngwén
Sòng Lìngwén of Táng possessed divine strength.
At Chándìng Temple, there was an ox that gored people;
no one dared approach it,
so they built a pen to confine it.
Lìngwén, curious about the reason,
stripped to the waist and entered.
The ox raised its horns and charged forward.
Lìngwén grabbed both horns and pulled,
the ox fell as his hands moved,
its neck bones all broken, and it died.
Also, using five fingers, he pinched the mortar pestle's tip,
and wrote a forty-character poem on the wall.
As a student of the National University, he once lifted a lecture hall pillar with one hand,
and had a fellow student's clothes placed under the pillar to press them,
promising a lavish feast of wine,
before he would lift it to retrieve them.
Lìngwén had three sons:
the eldest, Zhīwèn, had literary fame;
the second, Zhīxùn, was skilled at calligraphy;
the third, Zhītì, possessed courage and strength.
Zhītì was later demoted to Zhūyuān.
It happened that bandits captured Huānzhōu.
Zhītì was appointed Commander-in-Chief to attack them.
He recruited strong men and obtained eight.
Zhītì himself was eight chǐ tall,
clad in heavy armor,
charged straight forward and shouted loudly:
"Lǎo bandits,
move and you die!"
The seven hundred bandits
were all cut down in an instant,
and he routed them completely.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi".
Péng Bótōng
Péng Bótōng of the Táng dynasty was
a man from Héjiān,
standing eight chǐ tall.
Once, on the steps of a lecture hall,
he stood at the edge of the steps.
Taking a pair of shoes,
he clamped them under his arm,
and had a strong man pull them from behind.
The shoe soles snapped in the middle,
yet Bótōng’s feet never moved.
When an ox-drawn cart was moving forward,
Bótōng grabbed the tail of the cart and pulled it backward,
retreating several tens of steps,
and wrenched the cart’s axle so deeply that it sank two chǐ into the ground,
causing it to crack and split in all directions.
Once, while traveling on the Guābù River,
a strong wind filled the sail,
but Bótōng grabbed the stern cable and pulled it back,
preventing the boat from advancing.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi".
Lǐ Hóng
Lǐ Hóng, Duke Dìngxiāng of the Táng dynasty,
was the son of the Prince of Guó.
He stood eight chǐ tall.
Once, while hunting,
he encountered a tiger and wrestled with it.
He fell and lay on the ground,
with the tiger sitting on top of him.
His servant rode past on horseback,
and the tiger leaped up and seized the servant’s rear saddle.
Hóng got up,
drew his bow, shot the tiger, and killed it.
Neither Hóng nor his servant suffered any injury.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi".
Xīn Chéngsì
Xīn Chéngsì, a Loyal and Martial General of the Táng dynasty, was agile and swift.
Once, he untied the saddle and hobbled his horse,
took off his clothes, and lay down to rest.
He ordered a man to ride a horse from a hundred paces away,
charging toward him with a spear.
Chéngsì then saddled his horse, untied the hobble,
put on his clothes and armor,
mounted his horse, twirled his spear,
charged forward to meet the oncoming horse,
captured the man, and returned.
Later, Chéngsì was galloping with General Yuánshuài Jiǎng.
With one hand gripping the saddle horn,
he lifted both feet straight up like a dragonfly,
and rode for twenty lǐ.
Once, he and Vice Commander Péi Shàoyè
were surrounded by the Tibetans at Qīnghǎi.
He said to Shàoyè:
"General, follow me and we will break out together."
Shàoyè was afraid
and did not dare.
Chéngsì said:
"Let me try it for you, General."
He rode alone with his spear,
and wherever he charged, the enemy scattered.
He then turned back and escorted Shàoyè out.
Chéngsì’s horse was hit by an arrow,
so he jumped down,
seized a strong horse from the enemy, and rode it,
suffering no injuries at all.
Péi Mín campaigned north with Yōuzhōu Governor Sūn Quán
and was surrounded by the Xī bandits.
Mín stood up on his galloping horse,
whirled his sword like thunder,
and arrows flew like shooting stars,
all cut down by his blade.
The bandits dared not approach him
and scattered like tumbleweed.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi".
Lái Tiàn
Lái Tiàn of the Táng dynasty
rose to the rank of Zan4shan4 Da4fu1 during the Tiānbǎo era,
but was not yet widely known.
When Ān Lùshān rebelled,
an edict ordered court officials to recommend individuals with wisdom, strategy, decisiveness, and the talent to command troops.
Left Reminder Zhāng Hào recommended Tiàn for his strategic and tactical brilliance.
The memorial was submitted,
and he was summoned for an audience the same day.
His words pleased the emperor,
and he was appointed as the Prefect of Yǐngchuān,
serving concurrently as the Recruitment and Pacification Commissioner.
He repeatedly reported military achievements.
When Emperor Sùzōng succeeded to the throne,
due to Tiàn’s military prowess,
he was especially entrusted with important duties.
He recaptured the north, including Héluò,
but as bandits rose like swarming bees,
they frequently attacked,
yet all were defeated by Tiàn.
The bandits feared him
and called him "Lái the Iron-Chewer".
From "Tánbīn Lù".
Gēshū Hàn
Gēshū Hàn of the Táng dynasty defended against the Tibetans.
The enemy forces descended from the mountain in three continuous columns.
Gēshū Hàn wielded a broken half-section of a spear,
charged forward and struck them,
and none could withstand his assault.
Hàn entered the fray,
skilled in using the spear.
When he caught up with fleeing enemies,
he would place his spear on their shoulders and shout.
Startled, they would look back,
and Hàn would then thrust his spear into their throats,
sending them flying three to five zhàng high before they fell.
His servant Zuǒ Chē, fifteen years old,
would follow him into battle each time,
dismount, and behead the enemies.
From "Tánbīn Lù".
Mǎ Lín
In the first year of the Guǎngdé era of the Táng dynasty,
the Tibetans retreated from Cháng'ān to Fèngxiáng.
Military Commissioner Sūn Shǒuzhí closed the city gates and resisted them.
After several days of siege,
it happened that Zhènxī Military Commissioner Mǎ Lín led over a thousand elite cavalry,
returning from rescuing Yáng Zhìliè in Héxī,
and brought his troops into the city.
At dawn,
he rode out alone with a fully drawn bow,
charging straight into the enemy ranks.
Over a hundred horsemen on his left and right wished to follow him.
Lín fought fiercely and shouted loudly,
causing the enemy to scatter in disarray,
with none daring to stand against him.
The next day,
he again pressed the enemy and challenged them to battle.
They all said:
"This general does not fear death,
we cannot withstand him,
let us avoid him."
From "Tánbīn Lù".
Bái Xiàodé
Bái Xiàodé of the Táng dynasty served as a deputy general under Lǐ Guāngbì.
Shǐ Sīmíng attacked Héyáng,
and dispatched his valiant general Liú Lóngxiān with five thousand cavalry
to approach the city walls and issue a challenge.
Lóngxiān, relying on his own agility and bravery,
lifted his foot and rested it on his horse's mane,
insolently cursing Guāngbì.
Guāngbì ascended the city wall and looked at him,
then turned to his generals and said:
"Who can take him?"
Púgù Huáisī volunteered to go,
but Guāngbì said:
"That is not a task for a senior general;
let us select from the ranks below."
Those around him said:
"Xiàodé can do it."
Guāngbì summoned Xiàodé forward,
and asked him:
"Can you?"
He replied:
"I can."
Guāngbì asked how many additional men he would need to succeed.
Xiàodé said:
"Going alone is feasible;
adding more men would likely not work."
Guāngbì exclaimed:
"How valiant!"
Finally, he asked what Xiàodé desired.
Xiàodé replied:
"I wish to have fifty cavalrymen stationed at the army gate,
waiting to follow and advance after I enter,
and I request the main force to beat drums and shout to bolster morale;
nothing else is needed."
Guāngbì patted him on the back and sent him off.
Xiàodé, gripping two spears,
urged his horse and crossed the river, cutting through the current.
When he was halfway across,
Huáisī congratulated him, saying:
"He will prevail."
Guāngbì asked:
"It is not over yet;
how do you know he will prevail?"
Huáisī replied:
"Observing how he handles the reins and moves with agility,
I can see he is fully prepared."
When Lóngxiān first saw him coming alone,
he thought it very easy,
and did not lower his foot from the horse's mane.
As Xiàodé drew closer and Lóngxiān made to move,
Xiàodé waved his hand to stop him,
as if telling him not to move,
and Lóngxiān could not fathom his intent.
Xiàodé again signaled Lóngxiān to stop.
Xiàodé then said:
"The Imperial Attendant has sent me to deliver a message,
nothing more."
When Lóngxiān was thirty paces away,
Xiàodé spoke to him,
but Lóngxiān continued his vulgar insults as before.
Xiàodé waited for an opportunity,
then glared fiercely
The character "瞋" (glare) was originally written as "瞑" (close eyes).
Corrected according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.
and shouted:
"Do you recognize me, rebel?"
Lóngxiān said:
"Who are you?"
Xiàodé replied:
"I am the great general of the state, Bái Xiàodé."
Lóngxiān said:
"Is that a pig or a dog?"
With a fierce roar,
he raised his spear and charged forward.
Drums beat and shouts rose from the city walls,
and the fifty cavalrymen also advanced in support.
Lóngxiān had no time to shoot his arrows;
he fled along the embankment,
with Xiàodé in pursuit.
Xiàodé beheaded him and carried the head back.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Lǐ Zhèngjǐ
In the Táng dynasty, Lǐ Zhèngjǐ was originally named Bào Yù.
Hóu Xīyì was the commander of the Pínglú Army,
and Xīyì's mother was Zhèngjǐ's aunt.
Later, he went with Xīyì to Qīngzhōu,
where he proved valiant and strong, with great courage and strength.
During the Bǎoyìng era,
the army was mobilized to suppress Shǐ Cháoyì,
and reached Zhèngzhōu.
The Huíhé were then powerful and arrogant,
and all the military governors submitted to them.
Zhèngjǐ, then a military officer,
alone wished to overwhelm them with his spirit.
He thus competed with them in a race,
with all the troops gathering to watch.
They agreed:
"Whoever falls behind will be slapped."
He then raced ahead and won,
whereupon Zhèngjǐ seized his opponent by the collar and slapped his forehead,
causing the Huíhé man to lose control of his bowels and bladder.
The troops shouted in excitement,
and from then on, the Huíhé did not dare to act violently.
Later, when the soldiers mutinied against Xīyì,
and Xīyì fled,
the troops established Zhèngjǐ as their commander,
and the court accordingly appointed him as the military governor of Pínglú.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Lǐ Sìyè
In the Táng dynasty, Lǐ Sìyè commanded the Ānxī-Běitíng campaign army,
often serving as the vanguard general.
He would charge with a club,
and the enemy forces would scatter before him.
While besieging the rebels with nine other military governors,
he was struck by a stray arrow.
After several days, the wound was nearly healed.
As he lay in his tent,
he suddenly heard the chaotic sound of gongs and drums.
Upon inquiry,
he learned that a battle was underway.
He became agitated,
and blood gushed from his wound like a fountain.
He died shortly after.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Mǎ Xūn
When Emperor Dézōng of the Táng dynasty intended to travel to Liángyáng,
Yán Zhèn dispatched five thousand troops to Zhōuzhì to await the emperor's southern journey.
His general Zhāng Yòngchéng secretly plotted rebellion,
pledging allegiance to Lǐ Huáiguāng,
which caused great concern at court.
At that time, the Liángzhōu general Mǎ Xūn arrived,
and the emperor met with him in the palace hall to devise a plan.
Xūn said:
"I request to travel to Shānnán within a set number of days,
obtain the governor's tally to summon him;
if he refuses the summons,
I will behead him and report back."
The emperor was pleased and asked:
"How many days will it take to arrive?"
Xūn calculated the time and reported it,
and the emperor encouraged and sent him off.
After obtaining Zhèn's tally,
Xūn set out with fifty strong warriors through the Luò Valley.
Yòngchéng, unaware that his plot was known,
met Xūn with several hundred cavalry.
Xūn went with him to the relay station.
Yòngchéng's guards stood densely around.
Xūn said:
"It is cold; let us rest."
The soldiers on both sides withdrew,
and Xūn then had men light many fires with grass to lure them,
and the soldiers crowded around to warm themselves.
Xūn then calmly
took the tally from his bosom, showed it, and said:
"The Grand Master summons you."
Yòngchéng, terrified, tried to flee,
but the strong warriors seized him from behind and bound his hands.
Unexpectedly, Yòngchéng's son, who was at the rear,
drew his sword and struck at Xūn.
Xūn's attendants quickly grabbed his arm
The character "臂" (arm) was originally written as "背" (back).
Corrected according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.
so the sword did not descend fully,
only slightly wounding Xūn's head.
They then killed the son,
and threw Yòngchéng to the ground,
ordering a strong warrior to straddle his abdomen,
and held a blade to his throat, saying:
"Make a sound and you die!"
Xūn then rode swiftly to Yòngchéng's camp,
where the soldiers were already armored and armed.
Xūn declared loudly:
"Your parents, wives, and children are all in Liángzhōu.
If you abandon them to follow a rebel,
do you wish to have your clans exterminated?
The Grand Master sent me to capture Zhāng Yòngchéng;
you are not implicated.
What are you doing?"
The crowd trembled and submitted.
They then bound Yòngchéng
and sent him to Yángzhōu,
where Zhèn had him beaten to death with a staff.
Xūn appointed two deputies to command the troops.
He treated his head wound with medicine,
and returned to report,
delayed by half a day.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Wāng Jié
Tàiwēi Village is located five li northwest of Jìxī County.
In the village, there was a man named Wāng Jié.
His mother, while avoiding malaria, rested under the Vajra statue at Fútián Temple west of the village.
As she dozed off,
she conceived and gave birth to Jié.
Jé possessed divine strength.
He went to Cháng'ān,
and upon arriving at the Dōngwèi Bridge,
he saw a stone lion beside the bridge,
weighing a thousand jin.
Jé pointed at it and told the people:
"I can lift this and throw it."
The crowd did not believe him.
Jé then lifted the lion and threw it over a zhang away,
leaving the crowd utterly astonished.
Later, when dozens of people could not move it back,
they bribed Jié to request his help,
and Jié lifted it and returned it to its original place.
Soon after, he was recommended to join the Imperial Guard,
and appointed as a Shéncè General.
Once, in the presence of the emperor,
he bent down and carried a stone roller on his back,
placed a two-zhang-long square beam on the roller,
and on the beam, he set a bed,
on which a group of Kuīcí musicians sat,
playing a piece until the end before descending,
showing no sign of strain from the weight.
Emperor Dézōng greatly favored and cherished him,
repeatedly bestowing rewards.
Even the strength to uproot mountains or drag oxen
could not surpass his.
From "Shèzhōu Tújīng"
Péng Xiānjué
In the Táng dynasty, Péng Xiānjué's paternal uncle, Péng Bótōng, possessed extraordinary physical strength.
Once in Cháng'ān, he competed in strength with the strongmen Wèi Hóngzhé, Sòng Lìngwén, and Féng Shīběn.
Bótōng lay firmly on his back,
challenging the three to snatch the pillow from under his head.
The three exerted their utmost strength,
causing the bed legs to break completely,
yet the pillow remained unmoved.
Spectators climbed over the host's walls,
causing the buildings to collapse entirely,
and his fame shook the capital.
Once, while drinking with my father,
as dusk fell,
he alone carried two beds down the steps,
and moved them into the courtyard under the moonlight.
The wine and dishes,
were not spilled in the slightest.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì"
Wáng Páiyōu
During the Qiánfú era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Wáng Páiyōu from Miánzhú who possessed immense strength.
Whenever the prefecture held banquets for the army or guests,
he would first perform various acrobatics.
Wáng would carry a boat on his back,
with twelve people aboard,
and dance to the tune of "Hé Chuán,"
showing no sign of fatigue.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Zhōng Fù
In Ānlù Commandery, there was a retired scholar surnamed Mǎ (his given name forgotten),
who claimed to be from Jiāngxià.
In his youth, he traveled around Hú and Xiāng,
and later stayed in Zhōnglíng for over a decade.
He once spoke of Jiāngxī's Zhōng Fù,
originally from Yùzhāng,
who was unrestrained and unconventional in his youth,
and renowned in his hometown for his bravery and strength.
He did not engage in farming,
but was always fond of hunting.
Whether bears, deer, or wild beasts,
he never failed to capture any he encountered.
One day,
while attending a gathering with relatives for food and drink,
Fù, who was always a capable drinker,
became heavily intoxicated that day.
Only a young servant accompanied him,
and they did not return until dusk.
About two or three li from home,
in a deep and secluded valley,
a tiger with black stripes on a blue-gray body,
a round white patch on its forehead,
emerged from the forest, glaring fiercely.
From a hundred paces away,
it looked ahead and approached.
The servant trembled with fear upon seeing it,
and said to Fù:
"Quickly climb a large tree
to save your life."
Fù, at the height of his drunkenness,
felt his courage grow even bolder.
Taking the white stick carried by the servant,
he stood firm like a mountain to confront it.
The tiger charged straight at Fù,
and Fù leaped left and right,
swinging his staff to strike it.
The tiger crouched low,
and Fù also squatted down.
After a moment,
they engaged in grappling again.
This happened several times.
The tiger placed its front paws
on Fù's shoulders,
and Fù immediately wrapped his arms around the tiger's neck,
holding on for a long time.
The tiger could not use its claws and teeth effectively,
and Fù's bravery could not fully deploy his tactics.
The two were locked in a stalemate,
while the servant could only scream and cry beside them.
Fù's family, wondering why he had not returned as night fell,
took up swords and went to meet him.
Upon seeing the struggle,
they swung their blades forward and hacked at the tiger.
Once the tiger's back was broken,
Fù was finally spared.
Several years later,
when Jiāngnán was in turmoil,
and bands of robbers gathered from all directions,
Fù, famed for fighting the tiger,
was revered by the masses,
who elected him as their chieftain.
He eventually rose to the position of military commander,
governing Zhōnglíng.
He pacified the region,
and brought peace to six commanderies.
During the reigns of Emperors Xīzōng and Zhāozōng of the Táng dynasty,
his fame shook Jiāngxī.
He rose to the office of Zhōngshū Lìng.
From "Ěrmù Jì"
Mò Jūnhé
Mò Jūnhé of Zhēndìng,
was called Sānwàng in his childhood.
His family had been poor and lowly for generations,
making a living by slaughtering livestock.
When his mother was pregnant with him,
she once dreamed of a foreign monk bringing a young child,
whose face was bright and dark in complexion,
and handing him over, saying:
"I give you this child as your son,
in the future he will surely be of great help."
After he was born,
his eyebrows and eyes were angular and prominent,
and his skin was like iron.
At the age of fifteen or sixteen,
when Zhào Wáng Lǐ Róng had just succeeded to the throne,
he once saw him,
and pleased, asked:
"How did we get a Kūnlún child here?"
He asked for his surname,
and as it matched his appearance and physique,
he immediately called him Mò Kūnlún,
and thus bestowed upon him black clothing.
At that time, the towns and counties of Chángshān were repeatedly invaded and plundered by the central army of Bìngzhōu,
and the generals and soldiers of Zhào were exhausted from fighting the enemy,
so they urgently sought help from Yān Wáng Lǐ Kuāngwēi,
who led fifty thousand troops to rescue them.
The Bìng people had captured several cities.
When Yān Wáng heard this,
he personally led fifty thousand cavalry,
and directly engaged the Jìn army at Yuánshì.
The Jìn army was defeated.
Zhào Wáng, grateful for Yān Wáng's kindness,
slaughtered cattle and prepared wine,
and held a grand feast at Gǎochéng.
He presented two hundred thousand in gold as a token of gratitude.
When Yān Wáng returned to his state,
upon reaching the border,
he was blocked by his younger brother Kuāngchóu.
The people of Zhào, considering that he had been kind to them,
then built the Dōngpǔ estate for him to live in.
Yān Wáng, feeling that he had lost his state,
and seeing that the ruler of Zhào was still young,
plotted against him.
He then arranged for armed men to lie in ambush from below.
The Ming manuscript version writes "suì yǐ fú bīng" instead of "suí cóng xià yǐ shàng fú jiǎ",
and "yǐ" is suspected to be a variant of "yǐ".
He waited until Zhào Wáng arrived in the morning,
and immediately had him captured.
Zhào Wáng pleaded:
"I have inherited the foundation built by my ancestors,
ruling over these mountains and rivers,
and have often been invaded and harassed by neighboring enemies,
struggling to defend them.
Relying on Your Majesty's military prowess,
we have repeatedly thwarted the enemy's advance,
and managed to preserve our ancestral temple,
truly owing to your grace and strength.
Considering my youth and weakness,
I have long held humble sincerity,
hoping that you will not act hastily,
so that we may engage in mutual yielding.
I wish to return to the government office together with Your Majesty,
and the military headquarters will certainly not refuse or oppose."
Yān Wáng thought this reasonable,
and thus rode side by side with Zhào Wáng as they advanced.
Suddenly, a strong wind and dark clouds arose over the city.
Soon after, heavy rain fell,
with thunder and lightning striking.
When they reached inside the eastern corner gate,
a brave man with bared arms came from the side,
and punched Yān's armored soldiers.
He then carried Zhào Wáng on his back,
leaped over the wall, and fled.
Thus, they managed to return to the government office.
The king asked for his name,
but Jūnhé, fearing it would be hard to remember,
only said:
"The thing in the inkstone,
may Your Majesty keep it in mind."
The soldiers on both sides,
seeing that their lord had escaped danger,
then pursued Yān Wáng.
Yān Wáng retreated to the Dōngpǔ estate,
where the people of Zhào surrounded and killed him.
The next day,
Zhào Wáng, dressed in plain clothes, wept in the courtyard,
and also ordered that he be encoffined with full rites.
He then sent word to the ruler of Yān.
Kuāngchóu, enraged by his brother's killing,
immediately led his entire army to attack the eastern border of Zhào.
Intending to vent his anger,
he sent a letter containing ten points of suspicion.
Zhào Wáng sent his secretary Zhāng Zé to reply with the facts.
The gist of it was:
"The generals and soldiers in the camp,
perhaps they can be pursued;
but the thunder and lightning in the sky,
who can control it?"
The rest of the text is not recorded here.
After Zhào Wáng escaped the danger from Yān Wáng,
he summoned Mister Mò and rewarded him with a thousand pieces of gold,
along with a top-grade estate,
ten thousand mǔ of fertile land,
and also pardoned him from ten death sentences,
and petitioned to appoint him as Grand Master of Imperial Entertainments.
Throughout the reign of Zhào Wáng,
for forty years,
he enjoyed wealth and honor.
At that time, among the common folk,
if a child was born with a dark and ugly face,
many would say:
"Do not consider him ugly,
how do you know that in the future he will not be like Mò Kūnlún?"
From "Liú Shì Ěrmù Jì".
Zhōu Guīyòu
Zhōu Guīyòu, an old general of Yān,
during the upheaval at Jìmén,
was stabbed through the heart with a sword,
the blade coming out from his back, yet he did not die.
He fled to Liáng,
and became the vanguard of the cavalry general.
For fifteen years,
he fought a hundred battles along the river,
and the wound that pierced through him,
he often encountered.
When Later Táng Zhuāngzōng entered Luò,
an enemy made him sit on the ground in a hunting field,
drew the bow to its full,
and shot him, the arrow passing through his armpit,
but the wound healed and he remained unharmed.
He served up to the position of Acting Military Governor of a Prefecture.
In the end, he died peacefully at home.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Wáng Zǎi
In the year Dīngchǒu,
the Shǔ army was garrisoned at Gùzhèn.
There was a powerful commander named Fèi Tiězuǐ,
originally a general under the Green Forest bandits
the Ming manuscript version writes "lǜ" instead of "zú".
This man
often sent people to rob and took their goods.
One day,
he dispatched a commander to lead men to attack Héchí County.
There was a man named Wáng Zǎi
his given name is lost
who was young, strong, and brave,
and was staying at the government office with only a dozen or so servants.
A group of bandits arrived at night,
and Zǎi opened the door and waited for them,
fighting for several hours.
Zǎi was hit by an arrow and in great distress,
and the bandits were about to cross the threshold.
A young servant, holding a short spear,
leaned against the door and stood,
hitting three or four leaders in a row,
all of whom fell at the blade's edge,
their intestines and stomachs spilling on the ground.
The bandits then carried the corpses and fled.
Another day,
Tiězuǐ again raided a village,
just as night fell,
the bandits arrived at the village.
Some pushed open the doors and entered,
others broke through the walls from all sides and entered.
The lights in the people's homes were still bright.
The men all fled,
only a woman remained, using a ladle to splash boiling water from a pot at them,
a dozen or so bandits had no way to handle it,
and those who intended harm all fled in disarray.
The woman simply held the ladle and guarded the pot,
suffering no harm at all.
A month later,
several people within Tiězuǐ's ranks,
had faces as if scarred by leprosy,
and Fèi felt lifelong shame over it.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà".
Lǐ Tíng
Lǐ Tíng, a young man from Màolíng in Hàn times, loved to race swift hounds,
chasing cunning beasts.
Sometimes he used hawks and sparrowhawks to chase pheasants and rabbits.
He gave them all fine names:
the dogs had names like Xiūháo, Líjié, Báiwàng, Qīngcáo;
the hawks had names like Qīngchì, Huángmóu, Qīngmíng, Jīnjù;
the sparrowhawks had names like Cóngfēng, Gūfēi.
From "Xījīng Zá Jì".
Qiúrán Kè
When Emperor Suí Yángdì toured Jiāngdū,
he ordered Minister of Works Yáng Sù to guard Xījīng.
Sù was arrogant and esteemed,
and moreover, due to the chaotic times,
those in the world with great power and high prestige
were none like me.
He indulged in luxury and extravagance,
and his rituals differed from those of a subject.
Whenever high officials came to speak with him,
or guests paid their respects,
he would always receive them while reclining on his couch,
having beautiful women escort them in,
with maidservants lined up in rows,
quite exceeding the propriety of a subject.
In his later years, this became even more pronounced.
One day,
Lǐ Jìng, the future Duke of Wèi, came to pay his respects as a commoner,
offering an ingenious strategy.
Sù also received him while reclining.
Jìng stepped forward, bowed, and said:
"The world is in chaos,
heroes are rising in competition.
You are a senior minister of the imperial house,
you should focus on recruiting talented heroes,
it is not appropriate to receive guests while reclining."
Sù composed his expression and rose,
spoke with him and was greatly pleased,
accepted his strategy, and then dismissed him.
While Jìng was eloquently debating,
there was a courtesan of exceptional beauty,
holding a red whisk,
standing in front,
who alone fixed her gaze on Jìng.
After Jìng had left,
the whisk-bearing courtesan went to the balcony,
pointed and asked an attendant:
"Which among the scholars who just left was that?
Where does he live?"
The attendant answered in detail,
and the courtesan nodded and left.
Jìng returned to his inn.
That night, just at the fifth watch,
he suddenly heard a low knocking at the door.
Jìng rose and asked who it was,
and it was a person in purple clothes wearing a hat,
carrying a bag on a staff.
Jìng asked:
"Who is it?"
The reply came:
"I am the red whisk courtesan of the Yáng household."
Jìng hastily invited her in.
She removed her outer clothes and hat,
revealing herself to be a beautiful woman of eighteen or nineteen.
With a plain face and splendid attire, she bowed.
Jìng was startled.
She replied:
"I have served Minister Yáng for a long time,
and have seen many people in the world,
but none like you.
The silk vine does not grow alone,
I wish to entrust myself to a tall tree,
thus I have come to you."
Jìng said:
"Minister Yáng holds great power in the capital,
what about that?"
She said:
"He is but a corpse with lingering breath,
not worth fearing.
Many courtesans know he will not succeed,
and many have left.
He does not pursue them much either.
I have considered this carefully,
I hope you have no doubts."
He asked her surname,
and she said:
"Zhāng."
He asked her birth order among siblings,
and she said:
"The eldest."
Observing her skin, appearance,
speech, and temperament,
she truly seemed a heavenly being.
Jìng had not expected to gain her,
and felt both joy and fear,
his thoughts in turmoil,
and he kept glancing at the door, unable to keep his feet still.
After several days,
they heard sounds of pursuit and inquiry,
but the intent did not seem severe.
So they dressed in male attire, mounted horses,
pushed open the gate and left.
They intended to return to Tàiyuán,
and stopped at an inn in Língshí.
After setting up the bed,
with meat cooking in the stove and nearly done,
Lady Zhāng, with her long hair trailing to the ground,
stood combing it before the bed;
Jìng was brushing the horses.
Suddenly there was a man,
of medium build,
with a red beard that was curly,
riding a lame donkey,
threw a leather bag in front of the stove,
took a pillow and reclined,
watching Lady Zhāng comb her hair.
Jìng was very angry.
Before he could decide,
he continued brushing the horses.
Lady Zhāng carefully observed the man's face,
with one hand holding her hair,
and with the other hand behind her back, she gestured,
signaling Jìng not to be angry.
Hastily finishing combing her hair,
she straightened her sleeves and stepped forward to ask his surname.
The reclining guest said:
"My surname is Zhāng."
She replied:
"I am also surnamed Zhāng,
so I should be your younger sister."
She promptly bowed to him,
and asked his birth order?
He said:
"Third."
She asked her younger sister's birth order?
He said:
"The eldest."
Then he happily said:
"Today is most fortunate.
I have met a younger sister."
Lady Zhāng called from a distance,
"Lǐ Láng, come and pay respects to Third Brother."
Jìng quickly bowed.
Then they sat in a circle.
He said:
"What meat is cooking?"
They said:
"Mutton,
it should be done by now."
The guest said:
"I am very hungry."
Jìng went out to buy flatbread,
the guest drew a dagger,
and they cut the meat and ate together.
After eating,
he cut the remaining meat haphazardly in front of the stove and ate it,
very quickly.
The guest said:
"Observing Lǐ Láng's circumstances,
you are a poor scholar,
how did you obtain such an extraordinary person?"
Jìng said:
"Although I am poor,
I am also a man of ambition.
If others asked,
I certainly would not speak.
But since you, brother, ask,
I will not hide it."
He recounted the whole story,
and the guest said:
"Then where are you going?"
Jìng said:
"We intend to take refuge in Tàiyuán."
The guest said:
"However, I am not someone you can bring along."
He said:
"Is there wine?"
Jìng said:
"To the west of the innkeeper's place is a wine shop."
Jìng fetched a dou of wine.
After the wine had been passed around,
the guest said:
"I have a little something to go with the wine,
can Lǐ Láng share it with me?"
Jìng said:
"I dare not refuse."
Then he opened the splendid bag,
and took out a human head along with a heart and liver.
He put the head back into the bag,
and with the dagger, cut the heart and liver, and they ate together.
He said:
"This is the heart of a faithless man in the world,
I have borne a grudge for ten years,
and only now have I obtained it,
my regret is now resolved."
He also said:
"Observing Lǐ Láng's appearance and bearing,
you are truly a great man.
Do you also know of any extraordinary people in Tàiyuán?"
Jìng said:
"I once saw one person,
whom I privately consider a true man,
the rest are merely generals and ministers."
"What is that person's surname?"
Jìng said:
"The same surname as mine."
"How old?"
Jìng said:
"Nearly twenty."
"What is he doing now?"
Jìng said:
He is the beloved son of the provincial governor.
He said:
"He seems to be the one,
but I must see him for myself.
Can you, Lǐ Láng, arrange a meeting for me?"
Lǐ Jìng replied:
"I have a friend named Liú Wénjìng who is close to him.
We can meet him through Wénjìng.
What do you intend to do, brother?"
He said:
"An observer of auras said there is a remarkable aura over Tàiyuán,
so I have come to investigate.
Lǐ Láng, you depart at dawn;
when will you arrive in Tàiyuán?"
Lǐ Jìng calculated:
"I should arrive on such-and-such day."
He said:
"On the day after your arrival, at daybreak,
I will wait for you at the Fényáng Bridge."
Having said this,
he mounted his donkey and rode off as if flying,
and looking back, he was already far away.
Lǐ Jìng and Zhāng shì were both astonished and fearful.
After a long while, they said,
"A heroic man does not deceive others,
so there is certainly nothing to fear,
but let us whip our horses and hurry on."
On the appointed day,
they entered Tàiyuán,
met him as arranged,
and were overjoyed.
Together they went to see Liú shì.
They pretended to say to Wénjìng:
"We long to meet the gentleman because of our admiration for him."
He welcomed them.
Wénjìng had always considered this man extraordinary,
and just as they were discussing how to assist
"Assist" originally written as "厈",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy
and support,
upon hearing that a guest knew someone remarkable,
his feelings can be imagined.
He promptly arranged a banquet to entertain them.
Soon, Tàizōng arrived,
neatly dressed nor wearing shoes,
coming in a fur coat draped open,
his spirit soaring,
his appearance different from ordinary people.
Qiúrán sat silently at the end of the seat,
and upon seeing him, felt utterly defeated.
After several rounds of drinks,
he rose and beckoned to Lǐ Jìng, saying:
"He is the true Son of Heaven."
Lǐ Jìng told Liú,
and Liú became even more pleased and proud of himself.
After they left,
Qiúrán said:
"Having seen him,
I am eighty or ninety percent certain;
but my Daoist brother must also see him.
Lǐ Láng should return to the capital with Yīmèi.
On such-and-such day, at noon,
look for me at the tavern east of Mǎháng.
Below it, there will be this donkey and a lean mule,
which means I and my Daoist brother are both there."
When Lǐ Jìng arrived,
he immediately saw the two mounts,
lifted his robe and ascended the tavern,
where Qiúrán and a Daoist priest were drinking together.
Upon seeing Lǐ Jìng, they were pleasantly surprised,
invited him to sit,
and drank more than ten rounds together.
He said:
"In the cabinet downstairs, there are a hundred thousand coins.
Choose a secluded and hidden place,
settle Yīmèi there,
and on such-and-such day, meet me again at the Fényáng Bridge."
On the appointed day, he ascended the tavern,
and the Daoist priest and Qiúrán were already seated.
Together they went to see Wénjìng.
At that time, he was playing chess.
They bowed and began to speak from the heart.
Wénjìng quickly sent a letter inviting Wénhuáng to watch the game.
The Daoist priest played chess against him.
Qiúrán and Lǐ Jìng stood by as attendants.
Soon, Wénhuáng arrived,
bowed deeply and sat down,
his spirit clear and bright,
bringing a refreshing breeze to the entire gathering,
his gaze sharp and commanding.
At the sight of him, the Daoist priest looked dismayed,
set down a chess piece, and said:
"This game is lost,
lost.
To lose the game here,
how extraordinary.
There is no way to salvage it,
what more is there to say?"
He stopped playing and asked to leave.
After they left,
he said to Qiúrán:
"This world is not your world;
you may seek your fortune elsewhere.
Strive hard,
do not dwell on this."
Thus, they all entered the capital together.
Qiúrán said:
"Calculating Lǐ Láng's journey,
you should arrive on such-and-such day.
On the day after your arrival,
you and Yīmèi can come to a small residence in such-and-such alley.
I am ashamed that Lǐ Láng has traveled back and forth with me,
and Yīmèi has been living in poverty.
I wish to have my wife pay her respects,
discuss matters at leisure,
and not let you hesitate."
Having said this,
he sighed and left.
Lǐ Jìng also whipped his horse and hurried on his journey,
soon arriving in the capital.
He went with Zhāng shì,
and they came to a small wooden gate.
Knocking on it,
someone responded and bowed, saying:
"Sānláng has ordered us to wait for Lady Yī and Lǐ Láng for a long time."
They were led through inner gates,
and the gates grew increasingly magnificent,
with over thirty servants lined up in front.
Twenty servants led Lǐ Jìng into the eastern hall,
which contained objects not of this world.
After washing, dressing, and combing,
they were asked to change clothes,
and the clothes were also rare and exquisite.
After this was done,
it was announced that Sānláng had arrived.
It was Qiúrán,
wearing a gauze cap and a fur coat,
with the bearing of a dragon and tiger.
They met joyfully,
and he urged his wife to come out and bow.
She was indeed a heavenly beauty.
They were then invited into the central hall,
where the banquet spread was so lavish
that even the households of princes and dukes could not match it.
The four of them sat facing each other.
After the feast was served,
twenty female musicians were presented,
performing in front of them.
It seemed as if they had descended from heaven,
and the music was not of this world.
After the meal, wine was served,
and servants carried out twenty trays from the western hall,
each covered with an embroidered silk cloth.
Once presented,
the cloths were removed,
revealing account books and keys.
Qiúrán said to them:
"These are all records of treasures and wealth.
Everything I possess
I give to you as a gift.
Why?
I originally intended to seek achievements in this world,
perhaps engage in battles for two or three years,
and establish some merit.
But now there is already a ruler,
so what is the point of staying?
Lǐ shì of Tàiyuán is truly an heroic ruler.
Within three to five years,
there will be peace.
Lǐ Láng, with your outstanding talent,
assisting a wise and peaceful ruler,
devoting yourself wholeheartedly,
will surely reach the highest ranks of ministers.
Yīmèi, with your heavenly beauty,
possessing unparalleled wisdom,
will share in your husband's nobility,
reaching the pinnacle of honor and glory.
Without Yīmèi, you would not have recognized Lǐ Láng;
without Lǐ Láng, you would not have met Yīmèi.
When sages rise from obscurity,
their meeting is timely,
like a tiger's roar summoning the wind,
or a dragon's ascent gathering clouds.
This is only natural.
Take what I have given you
and offer it to the true ruler,
to support his achievements.
Strive hard!
In more than ten years,
there will be extraordinary events several thousand li to the southeast,
which will be the time of my success.
You and Lǐ Láng may pour wine to congratulate me then."
He turned to his attendants and said:
"Lǐ Láng and Yīmèi
are now your masters."
Having said this,
he and his wife mounted horses in military attire,
with one servant following on horseback,
and within a few steps, they vanished from sight.
Lǐ Jìng took possession of the residence,
Thus he became a wealthy and powerful family,
and was able to provide funds to assist Emperor Wén in establishing the foundation,
thereby supporting the great enterprise.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
Lǐ Jìng's rank reached that of Chief Minister.
The southern barbarians submitted a report, saying:
"There are sea bandits with a thousand ships,
gathering armor and a hundred thousand men,
who have entered the country of Fúyú,
killed its ruler and established themselves,
and the country is now pacified."
Lǐ Jìng knew that Qiúrán had succeeded,
and returning home, he told Lady Zhāng,
prepared ceremonial gifts to congratulate him,
and poured wine to the southeast to offer blessings and bow in reverence.
Then he realized that the rise of a true sovereign
is not something that heroes can aspire to,
let alone those who are not heroes?
For ministers to mistakenly think of rebellion
is like a mantis trying to stop a rolling cart wheel.
Some say
that Duke Wèi's art of war
was half transmitted by Qiúrán.
From "The Tale of the Curly-Bearded Man"
Péng Tà and Gāo Zàn
During the Táng Zhēnguàn era,
in Héngzhōu, there were Péng Tà and Gāo Zàn,
two men who competed in extravagance.
At that time, there was a grand feast,
and two teams in the arena vied for victory.
Tà caught a pig alive,
bit it from head to crown,
released it on the ground,
and it still ran away.
Zàn took a kitten and ate it from the tail,
consuming all its intestines and stomach,
and it still cried out without ceasing.
Tà was then utterly convinced and submitted.
From "Records of Court and Country"
The Rope Trick of Jiāxīng
During the Táng Kāiyuán era,
imperial edicts frequently granted grand feasts to prefectures and counties.
Jiāxīng County used various performances
to compete with the supervisory officials in skill and artistry.
The supervising official was particularly eager.
The jailer in charge spoke to those in the prison, saying:
"If any of our performances are inferior to those of the county officials,
we will surely be severely reprimanded.
However, if any of us can perform even one act that is somewhat impressive,
we will gain wealth and benefits,
but alas, we have no such ability."
Then they asked each other,
and even skills like juggling tiles or climbing trees
were all sought out and recruited.
A prisoner in the jail laughed and said to the jailer:
"I have a clumsy skill,
but being confined,
I cannot even briefly demonstrate it."
The jailer exclaimed in surprise:
"What can you do?"
The prisoner said:
"I know rope tricks."
The jailer said:
"If so,
I will speak on your behalf."
He then fully reported the prisoner's ability to the supervising official.
The official summoned him and asked about the severity of his crime,
and the jailer said:
"This prisoner is burdened by others,
owing a marriage payment that has not been paid,
with no other matters."
The official said:
"Rope tricks are common,
so what is so remarkable about them?"
The prisoner said:
"What I do
is slightly different from others."
The official asked again:
"How so?"
The prisoner said:
For most people's rope tricks,
they tie both ends,
and then walk, stand, and maneuver on it.
I only need one rope,
as thick as a finger,
fifty feet long,
without tying it to anything,
throw it into the air,
leaping and somersaulting,
and there is nothing I cannot do."
The official was greatly astonished and pleased,
and ordered him to be registered.
The next day,
the jailer led him to the performance ground.
After various performances had begun,
it was this person's turn,
and he was ordered to perform the rope trick.
He then held a coil of rope,
about a hundred feet long,
placed it on the ground,
took one end,
and threw it into the air with his hand,
as straight as a brush.
At first, he threw it twenty or thirty feet high,
then forty or fifty feet,
standing straight as if pulled by someone,
to the great astonishment of the crowd.
Later, he threw it over two hundred feet high,
looking up, the end could no longer be seen.
This person followed the rope with his hands,
his body and feet leaving the ground,
throwing the rope into the void,
his posture like a bird,
flying sideways far away,
and he vanished into the sky.
He escaped from prison
on that very day.
From "Records of Original Transformations"
The Woman in the Carriage
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
a man from Wújùn went to the capital to take the míngjīng examination.
Upon arriving in the capital, he was strolling idly through the city lanes.
Suddenly, he encountered two young men wearing large hemp-cloth robes.
They bowed to him as they passed,
their demeanor extremely humble and respectful,
yet they were not old acquaintances.
The examination candidate thought they had mistaken him for someone else.
Several days later,
he met them again.
The two said:
"Since you arrived in this realm
(Míng manuscript note: 'realm' written as 'end')
we have not yet acted as hosts.
Today we were just about to come and welcome you,
and this chance encounter
truly gladdens our hearts."
They bowed to the candidate and began to walk.
Though he was very suspicious and puzzled,
he reluctantly followed them.
After passing several wards,
within a small lane of the Eastern Market,
there were several shops facing the road.
Together they went straight inside;
the building was very neat and orderly.
The two men led him up into the hall,
where a lavish feast was laid out.
The two men and the guest sat down on rope-seated chairs.
Before the seats,
there were several more young men, each over twenty years old,
their manners quite respectful.
They went out the door several times,
as if waiting for an honored guest.
After noon,
they finally said, "She is coming."
They heard a carriage coming straight to the gate.
Several young men followed behind it,
and it proceeded directly to the front of the hall.
It was an ornate carriage.
The curtain was rolled up,
and they saw a young woman emerge from the carriage,
aged about seventeen or eighteen,
with a very beautiful appearance.
Her hair was fully adorned with floral ornaments,
and her clothes were of fine white silk.
The two men bowed in greeting,
but this woman did not acknowledge them;
this man (the candidate) also bowed to her,
and only then did the woman return the greeting.
She then bowed and invited the guest inside.
The woman then ascended to the seat of honor,
taking the central position and sitting down.
She bowed to the two men and the guest,
who then bowed and sat down.
There were also more than ten other youths, all dressed in light, new clothing.
Each paid their respects,
and sat in rows below the guest.
Delicacies were presented;
the food was extremely exquisite and pure.
After several rounds of drinking,
it came to the woman.
Holding her cup, she looked at the guest and asked:
"I have heard the two gentlemen speak of you,
and am now delighted to meet you.
I understand you possess marvelous skills;
may we observe them?"
The man humbly declined, saying:
"From childhood to adulthood,
I have only studied Confucian classics.
As for stringed instruments, pipes, singing, and such,
I have never learned them."
The woman said:
"What we study is not those things.
Think carefully, sir:
what is it you were first able to do?"
The guest pondered deeply for a long time and said:
"When I was in the schoolhouse,
I could walk several steps on the wall wearing boots.
Aside from such playful feats,
I have never done anything else."
The woman said:
"What we request is precisely that.
Please, guest, perform it."
So he walked several steps on the wall.
The woman said:
"That is also a very difficult feat."
She then looked back at the various youths seated there,
and ordered each to present his skill.
They all rose and paid their respects.
Some walked on the walls,
others walked gripping the rafters with their hands.
These agile, nimble feats,
each presented in several variations,
were like flying birds.
The man clasped his hands in astonishment and fear,
not knowing what to do.
After a short while, the woman arose,
took her leave, and departed.
The examination candidate was amazed and sighed,
feeling dazed and unhappy.
After several days,
he saw the two men again on the road, who said:
"We would like to borrow your fine team of four horses,
may we?"
The candidate said:
"Certainly."
The next day,
he heard that items were missing from the palace grounds.
A search was conducted but the thieves escaped,
only some horses were recovered—
these were the ones used to carry the stolen goods.
Upon investigating the horses' owner,
they arrested this man.
He was taken into the Palace Domestic Service for interrogation,
and driven through a small gate.
An official pushed him from behind,
and he fell down into a deep pit several zhàng deep.
Looking up, the roof was seventy or eighty zhàng above,
and he saw only a single opening,
barely more than a chǐ wide.
From morning until mealtime,
he saw a rope lowering a vessel of food.
The man was desperately hungry,
so he took it and ate.
After he finished eating,
the rope was pulled back up.
Late at night,
the man was filled with indignation,
lamenting bitterly with no one to appeal to.
Looking upwards,
he suddenly saw something like a bird flying down.
He felt it reach his side—
it was a person.
Placing a hand on the man,
she said to him:
"I imagine you are very frightened,
but with me here, have no worries."
Listening to her voice,
he realized it was the woman he had met before.
"I will take you out."
She tightly bound a silk cloth around the man's chest and shoulders,
with one end tied to her own body.
The woman leaped upward,
flew out of the palace city,
and descended several tens of lǐ beyond the gates.
She said:
"You should return to Jiānghuái for now.
As for your plans to seek office,
I hope you will wait for another day."
The man was overjoyed.
He traveled on foot, moving stealthily,
begging for food and lodging along the way,
until he reached the land of Wú.
Afterwards, he never dared to go west to the capital again to seek fame.
From "Yuánhuà Jì".
Kūnlún nú
During the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a young man named Cuī.
His father was a prominent official,
and was close friends with a meritorious minister of the highest rank, a peerless figure of the age.
At that time, the young man served as a Qiānniú guard.
His father sent him to inquire after the First-Rank Minister's illness.
The young man was in his youth,
his appearance as flawless as jade,
his nature upright and principled,
his demeanor calm and composed,
his speech refined and elegant.
The First-Rank Minister ordered a singing girl to roll up the curtain
and summoned the young man into the chamber.
The young man bowed and conveyed his father's regards.
The First-Rank Minister was pleased and fond of him,
inviting him to sit and converse.
At the time, there were three singing girls of peerless beauty.
They stood before him,
splitting cherries stored in a golden bowl
and serving them drenched in sweet cream.
The First-Rank Minister then ordered the girl dressed in red silk
to hold a bowl for the young man to eat.
Being young and shy in the presence of the girls,
he ultimately did not eat.
The First-Rank Minister ordered the girl in red silk to feed him with a spoon,
and the young man, having no choice, ate.
The girl smiled at him,
and he then took his leave and departed.
The First-Rank Minister said:
"Young master, in your leisure time,
you must pay me a visit;
do not distance yourself from this old man."
He ordered the girl in red silk to escort him out of the courtyard.
As the young man turned to look back,
the girl held up three fingers,
then turned her palm over three times,
and finally pointed to the small mirror on her chest, saying:
"Remember this."
Nothing more was said.
The young man returned home,
conveyed the First-Rank Minister's sentiments.
Back in his study,
his spirit was bewildered, his mind captivated,
his words grew few, his countenance downcast,
lost in deep contemplation,
he ate nothing all day,
only reciting a poem:
"By mistake I wandered to the peak of Péngshān to roam,
The jade maiden with bright earrings stirred her starry eyes.
Vermilion gates half-shut, the moon in deep palace glooms,
Should shine on snow-bright sorrow of the jasper orchid blooms."
Those around him could not fathom his meaning.
At the time, there was in the household a Kūnlún slave named Mólè.
He observed the young master and said:
"What troubles your heart,
that you harbor such endless regret?
Why not tell this old slave?"
The young man said:
"What could you people understand,
asking about the matters within my bosom?"
Mólè said:
"Just speak,
and I shall explain and resolve it for the young master.
Whether near or far, I will surely accomplish it."
Startled by his extraordinary words,
the young man told him everything.
Mólè said:
"This is a trivial matter.
Why didn't you speak of it earlier,
and torment yourself so?"
The young man also explained the hidden message.
Mólè said:
"What is so difficult to understand?
Holding up three fingers means
the First-Rank Minister's residence has ten courtyards of singing girls;
this refers to the third courtyard.
Turning the palm over three times
counts fifteen on the fingers,
corresponding to the fifteenth day.
The small mirror on her chest—
on the fifteenth night, the moon is round like a mirror,
telling the young master to come."
The young man was overjoyed beyond measure,
and said to Mólè:
"What plan can guide me to dispel my pent-up
"[pent-up]" character originally missing,
supplemented according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy
frustration?"
Mólè laughed and said:
"The night after next is the fifteenth night.
Please procure two bolts of dark blue silk
for me to make close-fitting clothes for the young master.
The First-Rank Minister's residence has a fierce dog
guarding the gate of the singing girls' courtyard.
No ordinary person can enter casually;
if one enters, it will surely bite them to death.
Its vigilance is god-like,
its ferocity like a tiger.
It is the dog of Mèng Hǎi from Cáozhōu.
In this world, none but this old slave can kill this dog.
Tonight I shall beat it to death for the young master."
He was then feasted with wine and meat.
At the third watch,
he went carrying an iron chain and hammer.
After the time of a meal, he returned and said:
"The dog is already dead;
truly there is no obstacle now."
That night at the third watch,
he dressed the young man in dark clothes,
then carried him on his back and leaped over ten layers of walls,
entering the singing girls' courtyard,
stopping at the third gate.
The embroidered door was unbolted,
a golden lamp dimly lit,
only the sound of the girl sighing deeply as she sat,
as if waiting for something.
Her jade-green hairpins newly removed,
her rosy face just relaxed,
her jade-like sorrow lacking its usual beauty,
her pearl-like melancholy turning more luminous.
She only recited a poem:
"Deep in the cave, orioles weep, resentful of Ruǎn Láng,
Who stole beneath the flowers to untie her pearl earrings.
Azure clouds drift away, news and letters severed,
Vainly leaning on jade flute, she grieves for the phoenix."
The guards were all asleep,
the surroundings utterly silent.
The young man then slowly lifted the curtain and entered.
After a long while,
she verified it was the young man.
The girl leaped down from the couch,
took the young man's hand and said:
"I knew the young master was clever and perceptive,
and would surely understand in silence,
hence the hand signals.
But I did not know what divine skill the young master possesses,
that enabled you to come here?"
The young man told her all about Mólè's plan,
and how he had carried him here.
The girl said:
"Where is Mólè?"
He said:
"Outside the curtain."
She then summoned him in,
and poured wine from a golden bowl for him to drink.
The girl said to the young man:
"My family was originally wealthy,
and lived in the northern regions.
My master, a military commander,
forced me to become his singing girl and servant.
Unable to end my own life,
I have merely survived.
Though my face is adorned with powder and rouge,
my heart is deeply troubled.
Even when jade chopsticks lift delicacies,
and golden censers waft fragrance,
behind cloud-patterned screens, adorned in fine silks,
sleeping under embroidered quilts, bedecked with pearls and jade—
none of this is my desire;
it is like being in shackles.
Since your capable helper possesses divine skills,
why not help me escape this prison?
If my wish is granted,
even death I would not regret.
I ask to be your servant,
wishing to attend upon your radiant presence.
But I do not know what the young master's noble intention might be?"
The young man looked solemn and did not speak.
Mólè said:
"Since the young lady is so resolute,
this too is a trivial matter."
The girl was overjoyed.
Mólè asked to first carry the girl's baggage, trunks, and cosmetic cases for her,
and did this three times back and forth.
Then he said:
"I fear dawn will come soon."
He then carried the young man and the girl on his back,
and flew out over more than ten layers of high walls.
The guards of the First-Rank Minister's household
gave no alarm,
so they returned to the study and hid her.
When morning came,
the First-Rank Minister's household only then realized.
Seeing also that the dog was dead,
the First-Rank Minister was greatly alarmed and said:
"The walls and gates of my residence
have always been deep and secure,
bolted and locked very strictly.
To move with the momentum of flight,
leaving no trace or sound—
this must be the work of a knight-errant who took her.
Let there be no further noise about this,
lest it only bring calamity."
The girl hid in Cuī's household for two years.
During the flower season,
she rode in a small carriage to visit Qǔjiāng,
and was secretly recognized and noted by a servant of the First-Rank Minister's household,
who then reported it to the First-Rank Minister.
The First-Rank Minister found it strange,
summoned Cuī and questioned him about the matter.
Fearing and not daring to conceal it,
he then explained the whole matter in detail,
all because the slave Mólè carried her away on his back.
The first-rank official said:
"This maid has committed a great crime,
but since you, sir, have employed her for over a year,
I cannot inquire into right or wrong.
I must rid the world of this menace.
He ordered fifty armored soldiers,
strictly armed and surrounding Cuī Shēng's courtyard,
to capture Mólè.
Mólè then grasped a dagger,
flew out over the high wall,
a glimpse like wings and feathers,
swift as a hawk or falcon.
Arrows gathered like rain,
but none could hit him.
In an instant,
no one knew where he had gone.
Thus, the Cuī family was greatly shocked.
Later, the first-rank official regretted and feared,
every night,
he often had household servants hold swords and halberds to guard himself,
and only after a full year did this stop.
More than ten years later,
someone from the Cuī family
saw Mólè selling medicine in the Luòyáng market,
his appearance unchanged as before.
From "Chuánqí"
Hóu Yí
During the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a Wànnián county captain named Hóu Yí who admired loyalty and righteousness,
and once hid a state criminal.
The investigating censor interrogated him exhaustively,
but he never revealed the criminal's whereabouts.
The censor said:
"The criminal is under your left and right kneecaps."
Hóu Yí then lifted the step bricks,
struck his own kneecaps,
turned and showed the censor, saying:
"Where is the criminal?"
The censor said again:
"Under the left kneecap."
He struck again and showed.
The censor then used a brazier filled with fierce fire,
placed it on his abdomen.
Smoke and flames blazed,
those around could not bear to watch.
Hóu Yí angrily shouted:
"Why not add more charcoal!"
The censor found him extraordinary,
and reported it to the emperor.
Emperor Dàizōng summoned him and said:
"Why hide the criminal,
bringing such suffering upon yourself?"
Hóu Yí replied:
"I did indeed hide the criminal.
Having already promised someone,
I would rather die than reveal it."
He was then demoted to captain of Gāoyào county in Duānzhōu.
From "Dúyìzhì"
The Monk Bandit
In the early Jiànzhōng era of the Táng dynasty,
a scholar named Wéi Shēng moved his family to Rǔzhōu.
On the way, he met a monk,
and they rode side by side,
conversing quite congenially.
As dusk approached,
the monk pointed to a fork in the road and said:
"A few miles ahead is this humble monk's temple.
Would you, sir, care to visit?"
The scholar agreed,
and had his family go ahead first.
The monk then instructed his attendants,
to prepare tents and food.
After traveling over ten miles,
they still had not arrived.
Wéi Shēng asked about it,
and the monk pointed to a grove with smoke and said:
"That's it."
When they reached it,
they went further ahead.
Night had already fallen,
and Wéi Shēng grew suspicious.
Skilled in using a slingshot,
he secretly took out his slingshot from his boot,
and placed over ten copper pellets in his lapel.
Then he reproached the monk:
"I, your disciple, have a schedule to keep.
Just now, indulging in your esteemed discourse,
I reluctantly accepted your invitation.
Now we have traveled twenty miles,
why have we not arrived?"
The monk only said to keep going.
As the monk walked ahead over a hundred paces,
Wéi Shēng knew he was a bandit,
and shot at him.
The pellet hit the monk squarely in the head.
At first, the monk seemed not to notice.
After five shots hit him,
the monk finally touched the spot,
and slowly said:
"Sir, please don't play such pranks."
Wéi Shēng knew there was nothing he could do,
