and did not shoot again.
After a long while,
they arrived at a manor villa,
where dozens of people lined up with torches to welcome them.
The monk invited Wéi Shēng to sit in a hall,
and said with a smile:
"Sir, do not worry."
He then asked his attendants:
"Is the lady's accommodation properly arranged?"
He added:
"Sir, please reassure them yourself,
then come back here."
Wéi Shēng saw his wife and daughter in another place,
with lavish provisions,
and they looked at each other, weeping.
He then returned to the monk.
The monk stepped forward, took Wéi Shēng's hand, and said:
"I am a bandit monk,
and originally had no good intentions.
I did not know you, sir, possessed such skill.
If not for me, no one else could have withstood it.
Today, I certainly have no other intentions,
I hope you do not doubt me.
The pellets you shot at me earlier are all here."
He then raised his hand and pressed the back of his head,
and five pellets fell out.
After a while, a feast was laid out,
with a steamed calf,
over ten knives stuck into the calf,
surrounded by pickled cakes.
He bowed and invited Wéi Shēng to sit,
then said:
"I have several sworn brothers,
and wish to have them pay their respects."
After speaking,
five or six men in red robes with wide belts
lined up below the steps.
The monk called out:
"Bow to the gentleman!
If any of you had encountered him,
you would have been turned to dust."
After the meal,
the monk said:
"I have long been in this profession,
but now I am growing old,
and wish to reform my past wrongs.
Unfortunately, I have a son whose skill surpasses mine.
I would like to ask you, sir, to decide this for me."
He then called Fēifei to come out and meet the gentleman.
Fēifei was only sixteen or seventeen,
wearing a green robe with long sleeves,
his skin and flesh like cured meat
(Míng manuscript note: "cured meat" written as "fat")
The monk said:
"Go to the back hall and wait for the gentleman."
The monk then gave Wéi a sword and five pellets,
and said:
"I beg you, sir, to use all your skill to kill him,
so as not to burden this old monk."
He led Wéi into a hall,
and then locked the door from outside.
In the hall, there were only
bright lamps in the four corners.
Fēifei stood in the hall holding a short whip.
Wéi shot with his slingshot,
thinking he would surely hit.
The pellet was knocked away,
and before he knew it, Fēifei had leaped onto the beam,
walking lightly along the wall,
agile as a monkey.
When the pellets were exhausted,
he still had not been hit.
Wéi then wielded his sword to chase him,
but Fēifei dodged swiftly,
staying within a foot of Wéi.
Wéi cut his whip into several sections,
but ultimately could not injure him.
After a long time, the monk opened the door,
and asked Wéi:
"Have you rid me of this menace?"
Wéi told him everything.
The monk was disappointed,
looked at Fēifei, and said:
"The gentleman has confirmed you as a bandit,
what more can be done?"
The monk spent the whole night discussing swordsmanship and archery with Wéi.
As dawn approached,
the monk escorted Wéi to the road,
presented him with a hundred bolts of silk,
and parted in tears.
From "Táng Yǔlín",
Míng manuscript note: from "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Cuī Shènsī
Cuī Shènsī of Bólíng,
during the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty, went to the capital to take the imperial examinations.
Having no residence in the capital,
he often rented vacant courtyards to live in.
The owner of one house lived in a separate courtyard;
there were no men there at all,
only a young woman over thirty years old.
Peeking at her, she was also quite beautiful,
and she had only two maidservants.
Shènsī then sent word expressing his intentions,
seeking to take her as his wife.
The woman said:
"I am not from an official family,
and I am not your equal.
We should not create regret for the future."
He then asked to take her as a concubine,
and she agreed,
but refused to state her surname.
Shènsī then took her in.
After more than two years,
whatever Cuī needed and took,
the woman showed no sign of weariness.
Later, she gave birth to a son.
When the child was several months old,
one night,
Cuī was asleep,
and after the doors were closed and curtains drawn,
by midnight,
he suddenly realized the woman was gone.
Cuī was alarmed,
thinking she must have a lover,
and felt quite angry.
He then got up
and paced anxiously in the front hall.
The moonlight was hazy and dim,
when suddenly he saw the woman descend from the roof,
her body wrapped in white silk,
a dagger in her right hand,
and a human head in her left.
She said that her father had been wrongfully killed by the prefect in the past,
and she had entered the city to seek revenge.
Several years had passed,
but she had not succeeded;
now that she had accomplished it,
she could not stay long,
and asked to take her leave from then on.
She then tightened her attire again,
placed the head in an ash bag, and carried it.
She said to Cuī:
"I have been fortunate to be your concubine for two years,
and we already have a son.
The house and the two maidservants were all acquired by myself,
and I give them all to you,
to raise the child."
Having spoken, she bid farewell,
leapt over the wall, and left the house.
Shènsī was still sighing in astonishment
when, after a short while, she returned,
saying:
"Just now, as I left,
I forgot to nurse the child a little."
She then entered the room.
After a long while, she came out and said:
"I have finished feeding the child;
now I will leave forever."
After a long time, Shènsī
found it strange that he did not hear the infant crying.
Looking at the child,
he found that she had already killed it.
She killed her son
to sever her own attachments.
Even the ancient knights-errant could not surpass this.
From "Yuánhuà Jì"
Niè Yǐnniáng
Niè Yǐnniáng was
the daughter of Niè Fēng, a general of the Wèibó region during the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty.
When she was just ten years old,
a nun came begging at General Niè's residence.
Upon seeing Yǐnniáng, she took a liking to her
and said:
"May I ask the General to give me this girl to teach?"
Niè Fēng was furious
and shouted at the nun.
The nun said:
"Even if you lock her in an iron cabinet,
I will still steal her away."
That night,
Yǐnniáng indeed vanished without a trace.
Niè Fēng was greatly alarmed
and ordered a search,
but there was no sign or sound of her.
Her parents often thought of her,
but could only weep together in sorrow.
Five years later,
the nun brought Yǐnniáng back.
She told Niè Fēng:
"Her training is complete. You may take her back now."
Then the nun vanished in an instant.
The family was both sad and overjoyed.
When asked what she had learned,
Yǐnniáng said:
"At first, I just chanted scriptures and incantations. Nothing else."
Niè Fēng did not believe her
and pressed for details.
Yǐnniáng said:
"If I tell the truth, I fear you won't believe me. What should I do?"
Niè Fēng said:
"Just tell the truth."
She said:
"When the nun first took me,
I didn't know how many miles we traveled.
By dawn,
we reached a large stone cave, hollowed out for several dozen paces.
It was desolate, with no inhabitants,
but many gibbons and monkeys,
and dense with pine vines and moss.
There were already two other girls there,
each also ten years old,
both intelligent, graceful, and beautiful, and they did not eat.
They could run and leap on steep cliffs,
like agile monkeys climbing trees,
never slipping or falling.
The nun gave me a pill of medicine
and also had me constantly hold a precious sword,
about two feet long,
sharp enough to slice a hair blown against its edge.
I followed the two girls climbing,
and gradually felt my body become as light as the wind.
After a year,
I stabbed gibbons and monkeys
without a single miss out of a hundred.
Later, I stabbed tigers and leopards,
always cutting off their heads and returning.
After three years, I could fly,
and was sent to stab eagles and falcons,
never missing.
The blade of my sword gradually shortened by five inches.
When birds encountered it,
they did not know where it came from.
In the fourth year,
she left the two girls to guard the cave
and took me to a city market.
I didn't know where it was.
Pointing at a person,
she listed his faults one by one, saying:
'Go and cut off his head for me. Do not let him notice.
Steady your courage; it will be as easy as catching a flying bird.'
She gave me a horn-handled dagger,
three inches wide.
So I stabbed that person in broad daylight in the city market,
and no one could see me.
I put the head in a bag,
returned to the master's dwelling,
and used medicine to dissolve it into water.
In the fifth year,
she said again:
'A certain high official has committed crimes,
killing many people without cause.
At night, enter his chamber
and cut off his head.'
Again, I took the dagger and entered the room,
slipping through the door crack
without any obstruction,
and hid on a beam.
When it grew dark,
I took his head and returned.
The nun was furious, saying:
'Why are you so late!'
I said:
'I saw him playing with a child, who was so adorable I couldn't bear to strike immediately.'
The nun scolded:
'In the future, when you encounter such people,
first kill what they love,
then kill them.'
I bowed in apology.
The nun said:
'I will open the back of your skull to hide the dagger,
without causing injury.
When needed, you can draw it out.'
Then she said:
'Your skills are complete. You may return home.'
So she sent me back,
saying we could meet again in twenty years.
Niè Fēng was very frightened upon hearing this.
Afterwards, she would disappear at night
and return by dawn.
Niè Fēng no longer dared to question her,
and because of this, he did not cherish her much.
One day, a young mirror-polisher came to the door.
Yǐnniáng said:
'This man can be my husband.'
She told her father,
who did not dare to refuse,
so she married him.
Her husband only knew how to temper mirrors
and had no other skills.
Her father then provided them with ample clothing and food,
and they lived in a separate house.
Several years later,
her father passed away.
The military governor of Wèi gradually learned of her extraordinary abilities
and hired her with gold and silk to serve as a close attendant.
Several more years passed like this.
During the Yuánhé era,
the Wèi governor was at odds with Liú Chāngyí, the military governor of Chénxǔ.
He sent Yǐnniáng to assassinate him.
Yǐnniáng took leave of the governor and went to Xǔ.
Liú, who possessed divine foresight,
already knew of her coming.
He summoned his officers
and ordered them to go early the next morning north of the city
to await a man and a woman,
each riding a white and a black donkey.
At the gate,
they would encounter a magpie cawing in front of the man.
The man would shoot it with a pellet bow but miss;
the wife would take the bow from her husband
and kill the magpie with one pellet.
They were to bow and say:
'Our lord wishes to meet you, hence we have come from afar to respectfully welcome you.'
The officers received these instructions
and encountered them.
Yǐnniáng and her husband said:
'Minister Liú is indeed a divine man.
Otherwise, how could he have seen through our plans?
We wish to see Lord Liú.'
Liú welcomed them.
Yǐnniáng and her husband bowed, saying:
'We deserve ten thousand deaths for betraying the Minister.'
Liú said:
'Not so.
Each is loyal to their own lord—this is the common way of people.
How is Wèi different from Xǔ now?
I ask you to stay here; do not doubt.'
Yǐnniáng thanked him, saying:
'The Minister has no one by his side.
We wish to leave him and serve here,
in admiration of your divine insight.'
She knew the Wèi governor was no match for Liú.
Liú asked what they required.
She said:
'Only two hundred copper coins daily will suffice.'
He granted her request.
Suddenly, the two donkeys vanished.
Liú sent people to search for them
but could not find where they had gone.
Later, he secretly looked inside a cloth bag
and saw two paper donkeys,
one black and one white.
Over a month later,
she told Liú:
'He does not yet know we have stayed.
He will surely send someone else.
Tonight, I request to cut my hair,
tie it with a red silk ribbon,
and place it on the Wèi governor's pillow,
to show I will not return.'
Liú agreed.
At the fourth watch, she returned and said:
"I have delivered the letter,
and later tonight, Jīngjīng'ér will surely come to kill me,
as well as the head of the rebel commander.
At that time, I will also devise a myriad of plans to kill him,
so I beg you not to worry."
Liú was open-minded and magnanimous,
showing no sign of fear.
That night, candles were lit brightly,
and after midnight,
indeed, two banners, one red and one white,
fluttered as if clashing at the four corners of the bed.
After a long while,
they saw a person fall from
(The character "zì" was originally missing,
added based on the Ming manuscript copy)
the air,
with his body and head separated.
Yǐnniáng also emerged and said:
"Jīngjīng'ér is already dead."
She dragged him out to the hall below,
and using medicine, dissolved him into water,
leaving not even a single hair behind.
Yǐnniáng said:
"Later tonight, Miàoshǒu Kōngkōng'ér will follow.
The divine skill of Kōngkōng'ér
is such that no one can perceive his methods,
and no ghost can track his traces.
He can enter the void from emptiness,
adept at vanishing without form or shadow.
My own skill
cannot reach his level,
so this will depend on the commander's fortune.
However, if you wrap your neck with Khotan jade,
cover yourself with a quilt,
I will transform into a midge,
sneak into the commander's intestines to listen and watch,
leaving no other place to escape."
Liú did as she said.
By the third watch,
before his eyes were fully closed in sleep,
he indeed heard a clanging sound on his neck,
which was very sharp.
Yǐnniáng leaped out from Liú's mouth.
She congratulated him, saying:
"The commander is safe now.
This person is like a swift falcon;
if he fails in one strike,
he will soar far away,
ashamed of his failure.
In less than a watch,
he was already a thousand miles away."
Later, when they examined the jade,
indeed, there was a slash mark from a dagger,
the cut more than a few fen deep.
From then on, Liú treated her with even greater generosity.
From the eighth year of Yuánhé,
when Liú went from Xǔ to the capital for an audience,
Yǐnniáng did not wish to follow.
She said:
"From now on, I will seek out mountains and rivers,
and visit enlightened beings,
but I only ask for a nominal salary for my husband."
Liú complied with her request.
Later, gradually, no one knew where she went.
When Liú died while serving as commander,
Yǐnniáng also rode her donkey to the capital once,
wept bitterly before the coffin, and then left.
During the Kāichéng era,
Chāngyì's son Zòng was appointed as the prefect of Língzhōu.
When he reached the plank roads of Shǔ,
he encountered Yǐnniáng,
whose appearance was as it had been in the past.
They were very pleased to see each other,
and as before, she was riding a white donkey.
She said to Zòng:
"Young master, a great disaster is coming;
it is not suitable for you to go here."
She took out a pill of medicine,
and told Zòng to swallow it.
She said that next year he must urgently resign from his post and return to Luò,
only then could he escape this calamity.
The power of my medicine can only protect against the disaster for one year.
Zòng did not fully believe her,
and offered her silk and brocade,
but Yǐnniáng accepted none of it,
only leaving in a deep drunken state.
A year later,
Zòng did not resign from his post,
and indeed died in Língzhōu.
From then on, no one saw Yǐnniáng again.
From "Chuánqí"
Hóngxiàn
In the Táng dynasty, the military governor of Lùzhōu, Xuē Sōng, had a maidservant named Hóngxiàn who was skilled at playing the yuánxián (a plucked string instrument),
and was also well-versed in the classics and histories.
Sōng thus put her in charge of his correspondence and documents,
calling her the "Inner Secretary."
During a grand banquet in the army,
Hóngxiàn said to Sōng:
"The sound of the jiégǔ drum
is quite sorrowful and poignant;
the person playing it must have some trouble."
Sōng, who was always knowledgeable about music theory,
said:
"It is as you say."
He then summoned the drummer and questioned him.
The drummer said:
"My wife passed away last night,
but I did not dare to ask for leave."
Sōng immediately sent him home.
At that time, after the Tōngdé era, the Héběi and Hénán regions were not yet pacified.
With Fúyáng as his garrison,
Sōng was ordered to hold firm,
controlling and suppressing Shāndōng.
In the aftermath of the killings and injuries,
the military headquarters was newly established.
The imperial court ordered Sōng to send his daughter to marry the son of Tián Chéngsì, the military governor of Wèibó,
and also ordered Sōng's son to marry the daughter of Línghú Zhāng, the military governor of Huábó.
The three garrisons thus became related by marriage,
with envoys coming and going daily.
However, Tián Chéngsì often suffered from a lung ailment,
which worsened in the heat.
He would often say:
"If I were to move my garrison to Shāndōng,
to enjoy its cool climate,
I could extend my life by several years."
He then recruited men from the army who were ten times braver and stronger,
obtaining three thousand men,
calling them the "Outer Residence Men,"
and provided them with generous provisions.
He often had three hundred of them stand guard at the prefectural residence at night,
and he divined to select an auspicious day
to annex Lùzhōu.
When Sōng heard of this,
he worried day and night,
muttering to himself,
unable to devise a plan.
One night, as the water clock was about to mark the hour,
and the gate of the camp was already closed,
he leaned on his staff in the courtyard,
with only Hóngxiàn accompanying him.
Hóngxiàn said:
"For the past month, my lord,
you have had no time for rest or food.
Your mind is preoccupied with something;
is it not the neighboring region?"
Sōng said:
"This matter concerns safety and danger;
it is not something you can fathom."
Hóngxiàn said:
"Although I am of lowly status,
I can also resolve my lord's worries."
Sōng, hearing her unusual words,
then said:
"I know you are an extraordinary person;
I have been ignorant."
He then told her the whole story, saying:
"I have inherited the legacy of my ancestors,
and have received great favor from the state.
If I lose this territory even for a day,
then centuries of merit and achievements will be lost."
Hóngxiàn said:
"This is easy to handle;
it is not worth troubling my lord with worry.
Allow me to go to Wèichéng for a while,
to observe the situation there,
and spy on their activities.
I will set out at the first watch,
and can return with a report by the second watch.
Please first arrange for a mounted messenger
and prepare a letter of greeting.
The rest can wait until I return."
Sōng said:
"But if this matter fails,
and instead hastens disaster,
what then?"
Hóngxiàn said:
"My journey this time
will not fail."
She then entered her chamber,
and prepared for her journey.
She combed her hair into a Wūmán bun,
fastened it with a golden sparrow hairpin,
wore a purple embroidered short robe,
tied on black silk light shoes,
carried a dragon-patterned dagger at her chest,
and wrote the name of the Tàiyī deity on her forehead.
She bowed twice and departed,
vanishing in an instant.
Sōng then turned back, closed the door,
and sat upright with his back to the candle.
Normally when drinking,
he would not exceed a few cups.
But that night, raising his cup,
he drank more than ten without getting drunk.
Suddenly, he heard the morning horn chanting in the wind,
and a leaf falling with dew.
Startled, he rose and asked,
and it was Hóngxiàn returning.
Sōng joyfully greeted her and said:
"Was the matter successful?"
Hóngxiàn said:
"I dare not have failed the mission."
He asked again:
"Was there any injury or killing?"
She said:
"It did not come to that;
I only took the golden box from the head of the bed as proof."
Hóngxiàn said:
"Before midnight, two marks past,
I reached Wèichéng.
Passing through several gates,
I arrived at the sleeping quarters.
I heard the Outer Residence Men resting in the corridors,
their snores like thunder.
I saw the soldiers of the central army
pacing in the courtyard,
their calls carried by the wind.
I then opened the left door,
and reached the sleeping tent.
The elder relative-by-marriage Tián was inside the tent,
sleeping soundly with his legs crossed,
his head resting on a patterned rhinoceros-horn pillow,
his hair tied with a yellow silk wrap.
Before his pillow lay a star-patterned sword,
and in front of the sword lay an open golden box.
Inside the box was written his birth date and time,
along with the name of the Běidǒu deity.
Fragrant incense and beautiful pearls
were scattered over it.
Thus, though he displayed his might in the jade tent,
his heart was open and carefree in life;
sleeping deeply in the orchid hall,
he did not realize his life hung by a thread in my hands.
There was no need for capture or release,
only added sighs of pity.
At that time, the candle wax was faintly smoking,
the incense in the burner had turned to ashes,
attendants were spread out on all sides,
and weapons were crisscrossed.
Some had their heads against the screen,
snoring and drooping;
some held towels or dusters,
asleep and stretched out.
I then pulled out their hairpins and earrings,
and tied their robes and skirts,
but they were like the sick or drunk,
and none awoke.
So I took the golden box and returned.
Exiting the west gate of Wèichéng,
and about to travel two hundred lǐ,
I saw the high tower of Tóngtái,
the Zhāng River flowing eastward,
morning roosters stirring in the fields,
and the slanting moon among the trees.
Anger gone, joy on the return,
I suddenly forgot the toil of the journey.
Feeling gratitude and repaying kindness,
I merely fulfilled my duty.
Thus, in three watches of the night,
I traveled seven hundred lǐ round trip,
entering a dangerous state once,
passing through five or six cities,
hoping to lessen my lord's worries,
daring not speak of the hardship."
Sōng then sent an envoy to Wèi,
delivering a letter to Tián Chéngsì that said:
"Last night, a guest came from Wèi and said
that he obtained a golden box from the head of the marshal's bed.
Not daring to keep it,
I respectfully return it sealed."
The special envoy galloped like a shooting star,
arriving around midnight.
He saw them searching for the golden box,
the whole army anxious and suspicious.
The envoy knocked on the gate with his horsewhip,
requesting an audience at an unusual hour.
Chéngsì hurried out,
and the envoy handed him the golden box.
When he received it,
he was shocked and overwhelmed.
He then detained the envoy,
keeping him in the residence,
entertaining him intimately with banquets,
and bestowing many gifts.
The next day,
he specially sent an envoy bearing thirty thousand bolts of silk, two hundred famous horses, and various rare treasures,
to present to Sōng, saying:
"My head
depends on your personal favor.
I should know my fault and reform,
and not bring further trouble upon myself.
I will specially follow your commands."
I dare not discuss marriage alliances.
That
According to the Gān Zé Yáo, "that" is written as "service"
I should have held the chariot's axle and followed behind,
coming before your whip and horse,
the retainers and outsiders I appointed
were originally meant to guard against other bandits,
and were not intended for any other purpose.
Now I have removed their armor and garments,
and sent them back to their fields."
Thus, within a month or two,
messengers from Héběi and Hénán came and went frequently.
Suddenly one day,
Hóngxiàn bid farewell to leave.
Sōng said:
"You were born in my household,
where do you intend to go now?
Moreover, I still rely on you—
how can you speak of leaving?"
Hóngxiàn replied:
"I was originally a man in a past life,
traveling and studying among rivers and lakes,
reading Shénnóng's medical texts
to save people from calamities and illnesses.
At that time, there was a pregnant woman in the village
who suddenly suffered from a parasitic disease.
I administered yuánhuā wine to her,
but both the woman and the two children in her womb died.
Thus, with one act, I killed three people.
The underworld punished me,
reducing me to a woman,
making me live as a lowly servant,
with a common and vulgar disposition.
Fortunately, I was born into your household,
and now it has been nineteen years.
My body has grown weary of silks and satins,
my mouth has tasted all manner of delicacies.
You have shown me increasing favor and care,
and the honors I have received are great indeed.
Moreover, the state has established its rule,
and celebrations are boundless.
To remain here would be to defy heaven,
and in principle, I should bring all to an end.
Yesterday, I went to the state of Wèi
to repay your kindness.
Now both lands have preserved their cities and walls,
and tens of thousands have been spared their lives.
I have made rebellious ministers know fear,
and loyal warriors plan for peace.
For a woman like me,
this achievement is not insignificant.
It should suffice to redeem my past sins
and restore my original form.
Thus, I shall withdraw from the dusty world,
dwell with my heart beyond material concerns,
purify my single breath,
and exist eternally beyond life and death."
Sōng said:
"Not so—
let me provide a thousand in gold for your mountain retreat."
Hóngxiàn replied:
"This matter concerns the next life;
how can it be planned in advance?"
Sōng knew he could not keep her,
so he prepared a grand farewell feast,
gathering all his guests and friends
for a night banquet in the central hall.
Sōng offered a song to accompany wine for Hóngxiàn,
inviting the seated guest Lěng Cháoyáng to compose the lyrics.
The lyrics said:
"The song of plucking water chestnuts grieves on the magnolia boat,
sending off the guest, soul vanishing from the hundred-foot tower.
Like the Luò River goddess riding the mist away,
the azure sky boundless, the waters flow in vain."
When the song ended,
Sōng could not contain his sorrow,
and Hóngxiàn bowed and wept.
Then, feigning drunkenness, she left her seat,
and vanished without a trace.
From the Gān Zé Yáo
Hú Zhèng
Táng dynasty minister Hú Zhèng was imposing in stature,
with extraordinary physical strength.
He was the same age as Duke Jìn, Péi Dù.
Once, while carousing together,
they were harassed by over ten strongmen from two military units,
and the situation grew perilous.
Péi Dù secretly sent a messenger
to seek help from Hú Zhèng.
Hú Zhèng, dressed in black sable with a golden belt,
burst through the door and entered.
The strongmen glanced at him and turned pale.
Hú Zhèng drank the wine that had been poured,
downing three cups in one go,
amounting to several shēng,
leaving not a drop in the cups or plates.
After a moment,
the host brought out lamps.
Hú Zhèng stood up,
took an iron lamp stand,
removed its branches and leaves, and joined its base,
laying it across his knee.
He said to the crowd:
"This humble man proposes an impromptu change to the drinking rules:
each must drink three full cups,
three rounds in one go,
the wine must be finished completely,
and not a single drop may remain.
Whoever breaks the rule will receive one strike from this iron
—referring to the lamp stand."
Hú Zhèng then downed three cups again in one go.
Next, it was the turn of a wrestler.
After three rounds of three cups,
he could not finish the wine,
and it spilled nearly onto the neighboring seats.
Hú Zhèng raised the lamp stand to strike him,
and all the troublemakers rose and bowed in apology,
kowtowing and begging for their lives,
calling him a divine being.
Hú Zhèng said:
"You vermin dare to act like this?
I spare your lives today as a favor."
He shouted at them to leave.
From the Zhí Yán
Féng Yān
Féng Yān of the Táng dynasty was
a man of bold spirit from Wèi,
his father and grandfather being unknown.
In his youth, Yān was chivalrous and acted on impulse,
devoted to polo and cockfighting.
Once, in the market of Wèi, there was a fight over money,
and when Yān heard of it,
he intervened and killed the unjust party.
He then hid in the countryside,
but as the authorities pursued him urgently,
he fled to Huá.
There, he became even more acquainted with the young men of the Huá army through cockfighting and polo.
At that time, the Chancellor Jiǎ Dān was stationed in Huá,
and recognizing Yān's talent,
he kept him in the army.
One day, while walking through the neighborhood,
he saw a woman standing by a doorway, hiding her face with her sleeve and gazing out,
her appearance exceedingly alluring.
He made someone convey his interest to her,
and eventually took her as his mistress.
Her husband was Zhāng Yīng, a general of Huá,
who often drank with his companions.
Seizing the opportunity,
Yān lay down in her bed again,
and barred the bedroom door.
When Yīng returned,
his wife opened the door to let him in,
using her skirt to conceal Yān.
Yān crouched and crept toward the cover,
then hid behind the door panel,
but his headscarf fell under the pillow,
close to his dagger.
Yīng, drunk, closed his eyes,
and Yān pointed to the headscarf,
signaling his wife to fetch it.
Instead, she handed him the dagger.
Yān stared intently,
then cut her throat,
took his headscarf, and left.
The next morning, when Yīng awoke,
he saw his wife killed,
and was stunned.
He wanted to go out and explain himself,
but his neighbors, believing he had truly killed her,
detained and bound him.
They hurriedly informed his wife's family,
who all came and said:
"He always envied and beat our daughter,
and now he falsely accuses her of wrongdoing.
Today, he has murdered her—
what other explanation could there be?
If someone else killed her, how could he alone survive?"
Together, they struck Yīng with more than a hundred blows from stones and whips,
until he could no longer speak.
The authorities arrested him on murder charges,
with no one to defend him,
and he was forced to confess to the crime.
The judicial officer and dozens of bailiffs with rods
led Yīng to the marketplace for execution,
surrounded by over a thousand onlookers.
One man pushed through the crowd and came forward,
shouting:
"Do not let an innocent man die!
I seduced his wife and then killed her—
I should be arrested."
The officers seized the man who confessed,
and it was Yān.
Together with Yān, they appeared before Dān,
and Yān confessed everything in detail.
Dān then reported the case,
requesting to surrender his official seal
to redeem Yān from death.
The emperor, moved by his sense of justice,
issued an edict
pardoning all death sentences in Huá City.
From Shěn Yàzhī's "Biography of Féng Yān"
The Old Man of the Western Capital Inn
Wéi Xíngguī of the Táng dynasty once recounted:
In his youth, while traveling west of the capital,
he stopped at an inn at dusk,
intending to continue onward.
An old man in the inn, busy with his work,
said to him:
"Traveler, do not journey by night—
there are many bandits here."
Wéi replied:
"I am skilled with bow and arrow,
and have nothing to fear."
He then traveled several dozen lǐ.
As darkness fell,
someone emerged from the grass and followed him.
Wéi shouted, but there was no response;
he shot arrow after arrow, hitting the figure,
yet it did not retreat.
When his arrows were exhausted,
Wéi, terrified, fled.
After a while,
wind and thunder gathered,
and Wéi dismounted,
leaning against a large tree.
He saw flashes of lightning chasing each other in the sky,
like polo mallets,
gradually closing in on the treetop.
He felt objects falling profusely before him.
Looking closely,
they were wood chips.
In moments,
the chips piled up, burying him to his knees.
Wéi, frightened,
threw down his bow and arrows,
and begged for mercy toward the sky.
After dozens of bows,
the lightning gradually rose and vanished,
and the wind and thunder ceased.
Wéi looked at the large tree—
its branches and trunk were stripped bare.
His saddle and pack were gone,
so he returned to the previous inn.
There, he saw the old man making a barrel.
Realizing he was no ordinary man,
Wéi bowed and apologized.
The old man laughed and said:
"Traveler, do not rely solely on bow and arrow—
you must understand swordsmanship."
He led Wéi to the backyard,
pointed to his saddle and pack,
and said he could take them back,
as it had merely been a test.
He then produced a piece of barrel wood,
on which all the arrows from the previous night
were embedded.
Wéi begged to serve him and learn,
but the old man refused;
however, he subtly demonstrated swordsmanship,
from which Wéi gleaned a thing or two.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
The Old Man of Lánlíng
During the Táng Dynasty, Lí Gàn served as the Governor of the Capital.
At Qǔjiāng, a dragon was painted to pray for rain,
with thousands of spectators gathered.
When Lí arrived,
only an old man remained standing with his staff, refusing to make way.
Furious, Lí struck him with his staff,
but it felt as if hitting tanned leather.
The old man shook his arm and left.
Lí suspected he was no ordinary person,
and ordered an elderly ward guard to find him.
They arrived south of Lánlíng Lane,
entered a small gate,
and heard the old man loudly say:
"I have suffered great humiliation and distress,
prepare hot water for me."
The ward guard hurried back to report to Lí,
who was greatly alarmed.
He then changed into plain clothes
and went with the ward guard to that place.
By then, it was already dark.
The ward guard entered directly,
announced Lí's official title,
and Lí, bowing respectfully, hurried in
and prostrated himself, saying:
"Earlier, I failed to recognize your esteemed appearance,
and deserve death ten times over."
The old man exclaimed in surprise:
"Who brought the Governor here?"
He then led him up the steps.
Lí knew he could reason with him,
and said calmly:
"As the Governor of the Capital,
if my authority is slightly diminished,
official governance will suffer.
You, venerable sir, hide your true form among the common crowd,
and without discerning eyes,
one could not possibly know.
If you hold this against me,
it would be fishing for fame at my expense,
which is not the heart of a righteous man."
The old man laughed and said:
"This old man was at fault."
He then prepared wine,
laid out mats on the ground,
and invited the ward guard to sit as well.
Late into the night,
they spoke of nurturing life,
and his words were concise and reasoning clear.
Lí grew even more respectful and fearful.
The old man then said:
"This old man has a skill,
allow me to demonstrate it for the Governor."
He then went inside,
and after a long while,
dressed in purple and red,
he held seven swords of varying lengths
and danced in the central courtyard.
Leaping and brandishing them in succession,
the flashing blades sparked like lightning.
At times horizontal like cutting silk,
at times swirling like circling fire.
Among them was a short sword over two feet long,
which frequently came close to Lí's lapels,
causing Lí to kowtow and tremble in fear.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
he threw the swords to the ground,
arranged in the shape of the Big Dipper.
Turning to Lí, he said:
"I was just testing the Governor's courage."
Lí bowed and said:
"From today onward, my life
is a gift from you, venerable sir.
I beg to serve by your side."
The old man said:
"The Governor's bone structure lacks the aura of the Way,
and cannot be hastily instructed.
Another day, we shall meet again."
He bowed to Lí and went inside.
Lí returned home,
his complexion as if ill.
Looking in the mirror,
he realized over an inch of his beard had been cut off.
The next day, he went back,
but the room was already empty.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Lú Shēng
During the Yuánhé era of the Táng Dynasty,
in Jiānghuái, there was a mountain recluse named Táng who was well-versed in historical texts,
devoted to the Dao,
and often lived in famous mountains.
He claimed to excel in "shrinking tin,"
and many sought to learn from him.
Later, at an inn in Chǔzhōu, he met a man named Lú Shēng,
and they found common ground in temperament.
Lú also spoke of alchemical practices.
He said the Táng clan was his maternal relatives,
so he addressed Táng as "uncle."
Táng could not bear to part with him,
and invited him to travel together to Nányuè.
Lú also mentioned he had relatives in Yángxiàn,
whom he intended to visit,
but for now, he would gladly accompany his uncle on his mountain journey.
Along the way,
they stopped at a temple.
In the middle of the night,
as their conversation grew lively,
Lú said:
"I know you, uncle, excel in shrinking tin,
could you give a general overview?"
Táng laughed and said:
"I followed a master for decades,
and only obtained this art.
How could I speak of it lightly?"
Lú pleaded with him repeatedly.
Táng declined, saying his master had set a time for transmission,
and it could be passed on once they reached Nányuè.
Lú then changed his expression:
"Uncle, you must transmit it tonight,
do not treat this lightly."
Táng rebuked him:
"You and I are as unrelated as horse and ox.
I never expected to meet you in Xūyí,
and truly admired your gentlemanly demeanor.
How could you sink to the level of a lowly guard?"
Lú rolled up his sleeves and glared,
staring at him for a long time before saying:
"I am an assassin.
If I do not obtain it,
you, uncle, will die here."
He then drew from his bosom a black leather pouch,
pulled out a dagger,
its blade curved like a crescent moon.
Holding it over the lamp flame, he heated a dipper
and sliced through it as if cutting paper.
Trembling with fear, Táng recounted everything in detail.
Lú then laughed and said to Táng:
"I almost mistakenly killed you, uncle.
Your technique is only fifty or sixty percent correct."
He then apologized:
"My master is an immortal,
who ordered ten of us
to seek out and kill those who recklessly transmit the arts of alchemy.
As for adding gold or shrinking tin,
those who transmit it must also die.
I have long mastered the art of riding the wind."
He then bowed to Táng
and suddenly vanished.
Afterward, whenever Táng met fellow Daoists,
he would recount this story to warn them.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
The Righteous Knight
There was once an official who served as a county captain in the capital region,
often in charge of the bandit affairs section.
There was a bandit who had been shackled and imprisoned,
but the case had not yet been concluded.
This official was sitting alone in the hall
when the bandit suddenly said:
"I am not a bandit,
and I am quite different from ordinary people.
If you, sir, can release me from my crime,
I will repay you one day."
This official saw that his appearance was extraordinary,
and his words were eloquent and upright.
He had already decided to agree,
but pretended not to.
After nightfall,
he secretly called the jailer to release him,
and also ordered the jailer to flee.
When day broke,
the prisoner was missing from the jail,
and the jailer had also run away.
The government office merely reprimanded and punished him.
Later, when his term of office ended,
he traveled as a guest for several years,
living a rather wandering life.
Arriving at one county,
he suddenly heard that the county magistrate had the same name as the prisoner he had released.
He went to visit him,
and had his name announced.
This magistrate was shocked and fearful,
and immediately came out to greet him with a bow.
It was indeed the man he had released.
The magistrate then kept him in the hall,
and they slept facing each other on couches.
They enjoyed each other's company for over ten days,
during which the magistrate did not enter his residence.
Suddenly, one day, he returned home.
This guest then went to the toilet.
The toilet and the magistrate's residence
were separated only by a wall.
While in the toilet,
the guest heard the magistrate's wife ask:
"What guest do you have,
that you haven't entered the house for ten days?"
The magistrate said:
"I owe this man a great debt of gratitude.
My life was once in his hands,
and even now,
I don't know how to repay him."
His wife said:
"Haven't you heard the saying,
'A great debt of gratitude goes unpaid'?
Why don't you seize the opportunity to act?"
The magistrate fell silent.
After a long while, he said:
"You are right."
Upon hearing this, the guest
returned and told his servants,
mounted his horse, and fled immediately,
leaving his clothes behind in the hall.
By nightfall,
he had traveled fifty or sixty li,
leaving the county's borders,
and stopped to rest at a village inn.
The servants only wondered at the hasty escape,
not knowing the reason.
When this man had settled down,
he told them about the bandit's betrayal.
After speaking, he sighed deeply.
While the servants were all weeping,
suddenly, a man from under the bed
emerged holding a dagger and stood up.
This guest was greatly frightened.
The man said:
"I am a righteous warrior.
The magistrate sent me to take your head,
but just now, hearing your story,
I realized that this magistrate is ungrateful.
Otherwise,
I would have wrongfully killed a virtuous man.
I, as a man of righteousness, cannot let this man go.
Please, sir, do not sleep yet.
In a little while,
I will bring you this magistrate's head
to avenge your grievance."
This man was both afraid and grateful, and thanked him.
The warrior, holding his sword, went out the door as if flying.
By the second watch, he had returned,
calling out:
"The bandit's head is here."
They lit a torch to look,
and it was indeed the magistrate's head.
The swordsman bid farewell and left,
and no one knew where he went.
From "Yuán Huà Jì"
Tián Péngláng
Emperor Wénzōng of the Táng dynasty once treasured a white jade pillow,
which was a tribute from the Kingdom of Yútián during the reign of Emperor Dézōng.
It was exquisitely carved and ingeniously crafted,
truly a rare treasure of the age.
It was placed within the curtains of the imperial bedchamber.
One day, it suddenly disappeared.
However, the palace guards were strict and vigilant,
and no one except favored consorts and attendants could enter.
Numerous precious items were displayed there,
but nothing else was missing.
The emperor was shocked and alarmed for a long while,
and issued an edict to search for the thief throughout the capital.
He secretly said to his close advisors and the commanders of the Left and Right Divine Strategy Armies:
"This was not the work of an outsider breaking in;
the thief must be within the palace walls.
If we fail to apprehend him,
I fear other troubles may arise.
While the pillow itself is not worth regretting,
you, my ministers, are tasked with guarding my imperial palace,
and must ensure the criminal is captured.
Otherwise,
the security around the Son of Heaven
will henceforth be useless."
The palace officials trembled with fear and apologized,
requesting ten days to search and capture the thief.
A large reward of gold and silk was offered,
but there was no trace of any clue.
As the imperial decree grew increasingly urgent and severe,
more and more people were arrested and detained.
Throughout the wards, alleys, and neighborhoods,
no place was left unsearched.
There was a second-generation general of the Dragon Martial Army named Wáng Jìnghóng, who kept a young servant,
just eighteen or nineteen years old,
with a bright and sharp demeanor,
and whom he sent on errands that were always accomplished.
Jìnghóng once attended a banquet with his peers at the Wēiyuǎn Army barracks,
where there was a serving girl skilled at playing the húqín.
As the guests at the four tables grew tipsy with wine,
they requested she play a tune.
She declined, saying her instrument was not excellent,
and that she needed her usual one to play it.
The night watch drum had already sounded,
and there was no time to fetch it,
so she stood up to loosen her belt.
The young servant said:
"If you want a pipa,
I can have it here in a moment."
Jìnghóng said:
"The curfew drum has just sounded,
the army gates are already locked.
Usually, I don't see you getting up early,
how can you be so mistaken?"
After a few more rounds of drinking,
the young servant arrived with a pipa in an embroidered bag,
and the guests laughed joyfully.
The Southern Army barracks were over thirty lǐ from the Left Divine Strategy Army,
a round trip of more than thirty lǐ.
At night, there were no troops moving about,
yet he had gone and returned in an instant.
Jìnghóng was astonished, as if he had lost something.
At that time, the search for the thief was also intense and urgent,
so he began to suspect the young servant of the theft.
After the banquet ended at dawn,
he hurried back to his residence.
Summoning the servant, he asked:
"I have employed you for years,
yet I never knew you were so nimble and swift.
I have heard there are knights-errant in the world;
are you perhaps one of them?"
The young servant apologized and said:
"It is not as you say,
I am merely able to walk fast."
He then mentioned that his parents were both in Sìchuān,
and he had come to the capital by chance some years ago.
Now he wished to return to his hometown,
but there was one matter he wanted to do to repay his master's kindness.
He already knew the name of the person who stole the pillow,
and within a few days would have him confess his crime.
Jìnghóng said:
"If this is the case,
it is no ordinary matter,
and it would spare many lives.
I do not know where the thief is;
can you report it to the authorities to capture him?"
The Ming manuscript notes: "存" is written as "府".
"獲" is written as "捕".
The young servant said:
"The thief is Tián Péngláng.
He moves between the marketplaces and army barracks,
with no fixed whereabouts,
possessing extraordinary strength,
and is skilled at leaping and climbing.
Unless his leg is broken on the spot,
even with a thousand soldiers and ten thousand cavalry,
he would still manage to flee.
Two nights from now,
wait for him at the Wàngxiān Gate,
and seize him when the opportunity arises—it is certain.
General, follow me to observe;
this matter must still be kept secret."
At that time, it had not rained for ten days,
and by dawn, the dust was quite thick.
Carriages and horses stirred it up,
so that people could not see each other even a step away.
Péngláng and several young men,
arm in arm, were about to enter the army gate
when the young servant struck him with a polo mallet,
and suddenly his left leg was broken.
Looking up, Péngláng said:
"I stole the pillow,
and I fear no one else,
only you.
Now that we have met like this,
what more is there to say?"
He was then carried to the Left and Right Divine Strategy Armies,
where he confessed with a single interrogation.
The emperor was pleased to have captured the thief,
and upon learning he was apprehended within the imperial guards,
he summoned Péngláng before the palace hall for questioning.
Péngláng explained in detail that he often moved about within the barracks.
The emperor said:
"This man belongs to the class of knights-errant,
not an ordinary thief."
Hundreds of people were imprisoned both inside and outside the palace,
and they were all ordered to be pardoned.
Once the young servant had captured Péngláng,
he informed Jìnghóng of his intention to return to Sìchuān.
He could not be found afterward,
so only Jìnghóng was rewarded.
From "Jùtán Lù".
The gatekeeper of Xuāncí Temple.
The gatekeeper of Xuāncí Temple, whose surname is not recorded,
judging by his character,
was a man of righteous chivalry.
In the second year of the Qiánfú era of the Táng dynasty,
Wéi Zhāofàn passed the Hóngcí examination.
Zhāofàn was a close relative of Yáng Yán, the Commissioner of Revenue.
For the banquet, items such as tents, canopies, and utensils
were borrowed from the Revenue Department,
and Yáng Yán further ordered the supply from the commissioner's treasury.
In the third month of that year,
the banquet was held at the Qǔjiāng Pavilion.
The splendor of the feast arrangements
was rarely matched.
At that time, the jìnshì candidates were holding a banquet on the same day.
Many people from the capital came to watch.
Just as the drinking was reaching its peak,
suddenly, a young man was seen arriving on a donkey,
his arrogant and unruly demeanor
showing no regard for anyone around.
He then pressed close to the banquet tables,
widening his eyes
Míngchāo edition reads "long ears" for "widening his eyes"
stretching his neck and shoulders,
and even used a large whip to poke and prod, urging others to drink.
His lewd and mocking words
were unbearable to hear.
While everyone was shocked and stunned,
suddenly, someone from the crowd slapped his face,
and he fell to the ground with the blow.
Then, they proceeded to beat him repeatedly,
seized the whip he was holding,
and whipped him over a hundred times.
The crowd grew furious,
tiles and stones rained down,
and he was nearly beaten to death.
At this moment,
the gate of Zǐyún Tower creaked open,
and several attendants in purple robes rushed out, shouting:
"Stop beating him!"
Their calls echoed one after another.
Another high-ranking eunuch arrived with a grand entourage,
galloping on horseback to rescue him.
The gatekeeper again raised the whip to strike back,
and those hit all fell face-first to the ground.
Even the imperial envoy was whipped.
Soon after, the gatekeeper galloped back on horseback,
his followers accompanying him as they entered the gate,
and the gate closed behind them.
The guests at the banquet were both pleased and ashamed,
but they could not guess where he had come from,
and they feared the incident might involve the palace,
bringing disaster upon them in an instant.
So they gathered money and silk,
summoned the one who had carried out the beating, and questioned him:
"Who are you?
Which of these gentlemen are you acquainted with,
that you would act so bravely on their behalf?"
He replied:
"I am the gatekeeper of Xuāncí Temple,
and I am not acquainted with any of these gentlemen.
I simply could not bear the rudeness of their subordinate."
Everyone praised and admired him,
and they all gave him money and silk.
Then they said to one another:
"This man must flee,
otherwise,
he will surely be captured."
About ten days later,
many of the guests from the banquet passed by the gate of Xuāncí Temple,
and the gatekeeper recognized them all,
showing them nothing but respect.
In the end, no one heard of any pursuit or inquiry regarding him.
From "Zhíyán"
Lǐ Guīshòu
Táng Jìngōng Bái Mǐnzhōng,
during the reign of Emperor Xuānzōng, served as chancellor for a second term
The previous two sentences originally read "Táng Jìngōng Wáng Duó during the Xīzōng reign served as chancellor for a second term."
According to "Xù Tánzhù," this was an error made during the compilation of "Guǎngjì."
The original text should read: "Maternal grandfather, Zhōngshū Lìng, Duke of Pǔ, during the Xuānzōng reign, reopened the Yellow Pavilion."
This refers to Bái Mǐnzhōng,
but during revision, it was mistakenly changed to Wáng Duó.
Now, based on historical facts and the meaning of the text, it has been restored
He did not collude with those in power,
but governed with fairness and integrity.
When requests came from all directions,
if they conflicted with virtue and conduct,
he would firmly oppose and refuse them.
Because of this, military governors resented him.
Yet he cherished classical texts,
and though his gate had barriers for carriages
and his courtyard displayed ceremonial bells,
he never tired of studying and pondering.
At his residence in Yǒngníng Ward, he built a separate study.
Every day after court,
he would stay there alone,
finding great joy in it.
One day,
as he was about to enter his study,
only his beloved short-legged dog, Huāquè, followed him.
As soon as he opened the door,
Huāquè began barking incessantly,
tugging at his robe to pull him back.
He scolded the dog, but it returned again.
Once inside the study,
Huāquè looked up,
barking even more urgently.
Bái also grew suspicious,
so he drew a precious sword from its case,
and laid it across his knee.
Then he prayed to the air:
"If there are any strange beings or hidden creatures,
show yourselves.
I am a true man—
how could I be intimidated by vermin and allow them to threaten me?"
As soon as he finished speaking,
suddenly, something fell from the beam to the ground—
it was a person.
With a red beard,
wearing a short jacket,
and appearing dark and thin.
He kowtowed repeatedly,
only saying, "I deserve death."
Bái stopped him
and asked about his origins and name.
He replied:
"I am Lǐ Guīshòu,
from Lúlóng Pass.
Someone offered me a large bribe
to harm you.
But Guīshòu was moved by your virtue,
and was also startled by Huāquè,
so I could no longer hide.
If you spare my life,
I vow to serve you for the rest of my days."
Bái said to him:
"I grant you your life."
He then ordered his trusted guard, Fù Cúnchū, to take him under custody.
The next morning at dawn,
a woman arrived at the gate,
dressed in simple, tight clothing,
dragging her shoes and holding an infant in swaddling clothes.
She pleaded with the gatekeeper:
"Please, call Lǐ Guīshòu for me."
When Guīshòu came out,
it was his wife.
She said:
"I was worried you were delayed,
so I came from Jì last night at midnight to find you."
After Bái
"Bái" originally read "Duó,"
corrected based on the surviving text of "Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú"
passed away,
Guīshòu and his entire family disappeared.
From "Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú"
In the capital, a gallant gentleman named General Pān lived in Guāngdé Ward.
His given name is forgotten;
the crowd called him Pān Gǔlù.
His family originally came from the region between Xiāng and Hàn.
He often traveled by boat to seek profit,
and once moored by the riverbank.
A monk came begging for food,
and stayed for several days.
Pān served him with utmost devotion and almsgiving.
When the monk departed,
he said to Pān:
"Observing your appearance, bearing, and capacity,
you are unlike other merchants.
As for your wife and children,
they will all enjoy great fortune."
He then left a string of jade prayer beads as a gift,
saying, "Treasure these, for they will not only bring wealth,
but in the future, you will also attain official rank and emolument."
After several years of trade and relocation,
his wealth indeed equaled that of Táo Zhūgōng and Dèng Tōng.
Later, he held a post in the Imperial Guards,
and established a residence in the capital.
He always treasured the prayer beads,
storing them in an embroidered pouch inside a jade box,
which he placed in a chapel.
On the first day of each month, he would take them out and pay homage to them.
One day, upon opening the box and the pouch,
he found the beads were gone.
Yet the seals remained intact as before,
and nothing else was missing.
He was utterly devastated and spiritless,
believing it to be an omen that his household would be ruined.
There was a steward in his household
who was acquainted with Wáng Chāo, a bailiff in the Metropolitan Prefecture's detention office.
Chāo was nearly eighty years old,
so the steward secretly told him of the matter.
Chāo said:
"How strange!
This is no ordinary theft.
I shall try to search for it,
though I do not know if I will succeed."
Another day, Chāo passed by the northern street of Shèngyè Ward.
It was early spring, just after the rain had cleared,
and he saw a young woman with her hair in three loops,
about seventeen or eighteen years old.
Her clothes were ragged,
and she wore wooden clogs.
She stood under a locust tree by the roadside.
Just then, some young soldiers were playing kickball,
and she caught the ball and kicked it back,
sending it soaring several zhang high.
Gradually, a crowd gathered to watch.
Chāo alone found this extraordinary.
He followed her to a narrow alley at the north gate of Shèngyè Ward,
where she lived with her mother.
They made a living by sewing and needlework.
Chāo, using some other pretext, gradually became familiar with them,
and eventually they acknowledged each other as uncle and niece.
Their dwelling was very poor;
she slept on an earthen bed with her mother.
Often, for days on end,
no smoke rose from their stove.
Yet sometimes they would set out sumptuous dishes,
with delicacies from land and sea.
When the first batch of Dòngtíng oranges arrived from Wúzhōng,
aside from those bestowed upon the chief ministers by imperial favor,
none were yet available in the capital.
She secretly gave one to Chāo, saying:
"Someone brought this out from the palace."
Moreover, her nature was resolute and decisive,
which made Chāo deeply suspicious.
Thus a year passed with their comings and goings.
One day, Chāo brought wine and food and conversed leisurely with her.
Gradually, he said:
"Your uncle has a sincere matter
he wishes to tell his niece.
What do you think?"
She replied:
"I have always felt deeply grateful for your kindness,
and regret having no way to repay it.
If there is anything within my power,
I will surely go through fire and water for you."
Chāo said:
"General Pān has lost his jade prayer beads.
Do you happen to know of it?"
She smiled and said:
"How did you know?"
Chāo sensed that she was not trying very hard to conceal it,
so he added:
"If my niece could find them,
he would richly reward you with silks and brocades."
The young woman said:
"Do not speak of this to anyone.
I happened to play a prank with some friends,
and always intended to return them,
but procrastinated and never found the time.
Uncle, come tomorrow at dawn
and wait for me in the pagoda courtyard of Cí'ēn Temple.
I know someone has left the beads there."
Chāo went as scheduled,
and she arrived in an instant.
At that time, the temple gate had just opened,
but the pagoda door was still locked.
She said to Chāo:
"In a moment, look up at the pagoda,
and you will see something."
Having said this, she dashed away,
swift as a flying bird.
Suddenly, from atop the spire, she raised her hand to show Chāo,
then swiftly descended with the prayer beads, saying:
"You may take these back now.
Do not concern yourself with rewards of wealth or silk."
Chāo delivered them to Pān
and recounted the whole story.
Pān then secretly prepared gifts of gold, jade, silks, and brocades
to present to her.
But when he went to visit her the next day,
the room was already empty.
Féng Jiǎn, the Supervising Secretary, had once heard that the capital harbored many chivalrous individuals.
When he became the Metropolitan Governor,
he secretly inquired among his subordinates.
They brought
"Brought" originally read "recounted";
emended based on the Ming manuscript.
Chāo to fully recount the story.
What General Pān said
matched Chāo's account exactly.
From *Jùtán Lù*.
The Merchant's Wife
In the Táng dynasty, Wáng Lì of Yúgān County was awaiting reassignment,
and rented a place to live in Dàníng Ward.
Due to an error in his documents,
he was rejected by the supervising official.
His wealth was completely depleted,
his servants and horses were lost,
and he became extremely destitute,
often begging for food at Buddhist temples.
One evening, as he was walking home,
he happened to walk alongside a beautiful woman.
They walked together, sometimes one ahead, sometimes the other.
He sincerely spoke to her,
and they got along very well.
Wáng Lì then invited her to his residence,
and their affection grew deep and harmonious.
The next day, she said to Wáng Lì:
"Your life,
how difficult it is!
I live in Chóngrén Ward,
and my resources are somewhat sufficient.
Would you be willing to come live with me?"
Wáng Lì was both delighted with her
and grateful for her support,
so he immediately said:
"My misfortunes
have brought me to the brink of the gutter.
For you to be so diligent and caring,
I would never have dared to hope for such kindness.
But how do you make a living?"
She replied:
"I was originally the wife of a merchant.
My husband passed away ten years ago,
but within the market,
I still have the old business.
I run the shop by day and return home by night,
earning three hundred coins daily,
which is enough to get by.
Since the time for your official appointment has not yet come,
and you lack the funds to travel,
if you do not look down on me,
we can simply live together until the winter reassignment period."
Wáng Lì then moved in with her.
He saw that her home
was neither too lavish nor too frugal, just right.
As for the keys and locks,
she entrusted them all to Wáng Lì.
Every time she went out,
she would first prepare a day's worth of meals for Wáng Lì,
and upon returning,
she would bring rice, meat, money, and silk to give to him.
Not a single day was missed.
Wáng Lì, moved by her diligence,
suggested hiring a servant.
The woman refused, citing other matters,
and Wáng Lì did not press her.
After a year,
she gave birth to a son,
and only returned at midday to nurse him.
In total, she lived with Wáng Lì for two years,
when suddenly one night she returned,
looking anxious and flustered.
She said to Wáng Lì:
"I have a grievance and enmity,
which has pained me to the bone
for a long time.
I waited for an opportunity to take revenge,
and now I have succeeded.
I must leave the capital immediately.
You must take care of yourself.
This residence
was purchased for five hundred strings of coins;
the deed is inside the screen.
All the assets and supplies in the house
I give to you.
I cannot take the infant with me,
but he is also your son.
Please remember that."
After speaking,
she wiped her tears and bid farewell.
Wáng Lì could not stop her.
He then noticed the leather bag she was carrying—
it contained a human head.
Wáng Lì was greatly shocked.
The woman laughed and said:
"Do not worry too much;
this matter will not involve you."
She then took the bag, leaped over the wall, and left,
her body moving like a flying bird.
Wáng Lì opened the door to see her off,
but she was already gone.
As he was pacing in the courtyard,
he suddenly heard her return.
Wáng Lì went to the door to welcome her,
and she said:
"I want to nurse the baby once more
to ease the pain of parting."
She then went to comfort the child.
Soon, she left again,
merely waving her hand.
Wáng Lì turned up the lamp and lifted the bed curtain—
the child's head and body were already separated.
Wáng Lì was terrified
and stayed awake until dawn.
He then used the money and silk to buy servants
"Buy servants" originally read "servants buy,"
changed according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy
and a carriage,
traveling to a nearby town
to await news of the matter.
After a long time,
he heard nothing at all.
That year, Wáng Lì received an official post,
so he sold the residence and returned to his duties.
After that, he never heard any news of her again.
From "Jíyì Jì"
Jīng Shísānniáng
In the Táng dynasty, the presented scholar Zhào Zhōngháng, whose family was from Wēnzhōu,
was known for his chivalrous and heroic deeds.
When he arrived in Sūzhōu,
he stayed at the Zhīshān Chányuàn monastery.
In the monks' quarters, there was a female merchant named Jīng Shísānniáng,
who was holding a grand memorial ceremony for her late husband.
Admiring Zhào,
she traveled with him back to Yángzhōu.
Zhào, in his chivalrous spirit, spent Jīng's wealth freely,
but she did not mind at all.
His friend Lǐ Zhèngláng's younger brother, the thirty-ninth son, had a beloved courtesan,
but the courtesan's parents
took her away and gave her to Zhūgě Yīn.
Lǐ was deeply distressed.
At that time, Zhūgě Yīn and Lǚ Yòngzhī were deceiving Grand Marshal Gāo Pián,
abusing their power and acting arbitrarily.
Lǐ feared disaster,
and could only weep in secret.
He happened to mention this to Jīngniáng,
who also felt indignant and resentful.
She said to Lǐ, the thirty-ninth son:
"This is a small matter;
I can avenge it for you.
Please cross the river tomorrow
and wait for me at Rùnzhōu's Běigù Mountain at noon on the sixth day of the sixth month."
Lǐ followed her instructions.
At the appointed time,
Jīng arrived with a bag containing the courtesan,
along with the heads of the courtesan's parents,
and returned them to Lǐ.
She then went with Zhào into Zhèzhōng,
and no one knew where they ended up.
From "Běimèng Suǒyán"
Xǔ Jì
In his youth, Xǔ Jì of Shǔ dwelled on Sìmíng Mountain,
studying the Book of Changes under Jìn Zhēngjūn.
One day, a couple came together to his mountain abode,
carrying a pot of wine.
Jì questioned them,
and they replied:
"We left Shàn County today."
Jì said:
"The road is very long;
how could you reach here in a single day?"
He found this quite strange.
The husband was rather young,
while the wife's appearance surpassed his,
her demeanor resolute and taciturn.
That evening,
they invited Xǔ to share the wine with them.
The husband produced a clapper board,
studded all over with copper nails.
Then he raised his voice and sang loudly,
the lyrics all expressing the essence of swordsmanship.
Suddenly, he drew two objects from his sleeve,
unfurled them with a shout,
and they became two swords.
He leaped up,
and the swords circled and clashed above Jì's head,
leaving Jì utterly terrified.
Soon, he sheathed them back into their case,
and after drinking, they retired to sleep.
By dawn,
only an empty bed remained.
At noon,
a mendicant monk came seeking the couple.
Jì recounted everything to him.
The monk said:
"I am one of them;
can you, a Daoist, learn this?"
At that time, Jì was wearing Daoist robes.
Jì declined, saying:
"Since youth, I have revered mystical studies,
and have no wish for this."
The monk laughed arrogantly,
then took Jì's clean water to wash his feet.
In a moment of wandering, he vanished.
Later, Jì encountered him again in Huàyīn,
and only then realized he was a xiá (knight-errant).
When Dù Guāngtíng traveled from the capital to Shǔ,
he lodged at the Zǐtóng government office.
A monk arrived afterward,
and the county magistrate, a certain Zhōu, who was acquainted with him,
said:
"He came from Xīngyuán today."
Dù found this strange.
At daybreak,
the monk departed ahead.
The magistrate told Dù:
"This monk practices Lùlúqiāo (a form of Daoist walking technique),
and is also of the xiá kind."
The poet-monk Qíjǐ, under a pine tree on Wéi Mountain,
personally encountered a monk
who drew two swords from beneath his fingernails,
leaped, and soared into the sky, departing.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Dīng Xiùcai
The Lǎngzhōu Daoist Luó Shǎowēi once stayed at Zǐyáng Temple on Máo Mountain.
A scholar named Dīng also lodged at the temple,
his demeanor and style
no different from ordinary people,
yet he showed no eagerness for official advancement.
He lingered for several years,
and the temple's abbot treated him well.
On a winter night,
when sleet and snow were falling heavily,
two or three Daoists gathered around the stove,
yearning for fat lamb and fine wine.
Dīng said:
"Obtaining these is not difficult."
At the time, they thought he was joking.
Suddenly, they saw him open the door, roll up his sleeves, and leave.
By midnight,
he returned covered in snow,
carrying a silver flask of wine
and a whole leg of cooked lamb,
saying they were from the kitchen of the Zhè military governor.
Thus amazed and overjoyed,
they brandished swords and danced,
then he leaped and vanished,
with no one knowing where he went.
Only the silver flask remained.
The abbot reported the incident to the county officials.
The poet-monk Guànxiū wrote in his "Xiákè" poem:
"At dusk, wind and rain dark as a millstone;
he bid me farewell, none know where he went."
Could it be that he had heard of this event in the Jiānghuái region and conceived the idea?
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Dōng Wén Shuò
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
there once appeared a one-legged crane.
No one knew what it was,
considering it an oddity.
Dōngfāng Shuò memorialized:
"This is the Bìfāng bird mentioned in the 'Shānhǎi Jīng'."
Upon verification, it indeed was.
Thus, the emperor ordered court officials to study the "Shānhǎi Jīng".
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" was authored by Bó Yì,
compiled and prefaced by Liú Xiàng.
Bó Yì is also called Bó Yì.
The "Shū" says:
"Yì oversaw my gamekeepers."
He followed Yǔ in controlling floods,
gathered the wonders of mountains and seas,
and thus completed the book.
From "Shàngshū Gùshí"
Liú Xiàng
Èrfù's minister named Wēi,
together with Èrfù, killed Yàyǔ.
The Emperor then bound him on Shūshǔ Mountain.
Shackling his right foot,
tying his hands behind his back along with his hair,
and fastening him to the mountain,
northwest of Guāntí,
as noted by Guō Pú.
Emperor Xuān of Hàn sent men to excavate a boulder in Shàngjùn,
and within a stone chamber, they found a man,
completely naked,
with disheveled hair and hands bound behind his back,
and one foot shackled.
When questioned,
none of the ministers knew.
Liú Xiàng explained based on this account.
Emperor Xuān was greatly astonished,
and from then on, people vied to study the "Shānhǎi Jīng".
From "Shānhǎi Jīng"
Hú Zōng
Hú Zōng was erudite and knowledgeable.
During Sūn Quán's reign in Wú,
someone excavated a copper box 2.7 chǐ long,
with a glass lid,
carved and engraved on top,
containing a white jade rúyì scepter,
the handle carved with dragons, tigers, and cicada shapes.
At the time, no one could discern its origin.
Quán, knowing Zōng was versed in past matters,
sent someone to ask him.
Zōng said:
"Long ago, Qín Shǐhuáng traveled east,
and because Jīnlíng had an imperial aura,
he changed the county's name.
He also excavated lakes and rivers,
leveled hills and mounds,
and everywhere buried treasures
to suppress the kingly earth's energy.
This is recorded in the Qín annals;
this likely is one such item."
All marveled at his extensive knowledge,
and were left in怅然自失 (chàngrán zìshī, dismayed and at a loss).
From "Zōng Biézhuàn"
Zhāng Huá
During the Wei period,
the bell in front of the palace suddenly rang loudly,
shaking and alarming the government offices.
Zhāng Huá said:
"This is because the copper mountain in Shǔ has collapsed,
and the bell is resonating in response."
Soon after, Shǔ reported the matter,
and indeed it was said that the copper mountain had collapsed.
The timing matched exactly what Huá had said.
From "Xiǎoshuō" (Anecdotes).
Also, during the Jin dynasty, Lù Shìhéng once sent Zhāng Huá some preserved food.
At that time, the guests filled the seats.
Huá opened the container
and immediately said:
"This is dragon meat."
Although everyone usually admired Huá for his vast knowledge,
they were still skeptical and did not fully believe him.
Huá said:
"Try pouring vinegar on it,
and something unusual will surely happen."
When they tried it,
a five-colored light rose from it.
Shìhéng then inquired thoroughly about its origin.
The maker of the preserved fish said:
"In my garden, under a pile of thatch,
I found a white fish.
Its substance and appearance were extraordinary,
and when made into preserved fish, it was exceptionally delicious,
so I sent it to Lù."
From "Shìshuō" (A New Account of the Tales of the World).
Also, during the Middle Jin period,
someone owned a copper washbasin
that would constantly ring morning and evening as if someone were striking it.
They reported this to Zhāng Huá.
Huá said:
"This basin is harmoniously tuned in pitch with the bell in Luòyáng.
The bell in the palace is struck morning and evening,
so the sounds resonate with each other.
If you file it down to make it lighter,
its pitch will change,
and the ringing will stop on its own."
They followed his advice,
and it no longer rang.
From "Xiǎoshuō" (Anecdotes).
Also, inside the imperial armory, there was a male pheasant,
and people at the time all considered it an anomaly.
Huá said:
"This is transformed from a snake."
He immediately ordered a search of the armory,
and indeed, the shed skin of a snake was found.
From "Xiǎoshuō" (Anecdotes).
Also, in Wújùn, the Línpíng riverbank collapsed,
revealing a stone drum
that made no sound when struck.
They asked Huá about it.
Huá said:
"You can take tóng wood from Shǔ,
carve it into the shape of a fish,
and strike it, and it will sound."
They followed Huá's advice,
and the sound could be heard for dozens of miles.
From "Xiǎoshuō" (Anecdotes).
Also, during Emperor Huì's reign,
someone obtained a bird feather several zhang long.
Huá saw it and sighed, saying:
"This is what is called a sea fú bird feather.
When this feather appears, the world will collapse."
It indeed turned out as he said.
From "Yìyuàn" (Garden of Marvels).
Also, in Luòyáng, there was a cave of immeasurable depth.
A woman wanted to kill her husband
and said to him:
"I have never seen this cave."
The husband went over to look at it.
When he reached the cave,
the woman pushed her husband, and he fell into the cave.
Reaching the bottom,
the woman threw down food
as if offering a sacrifice.
The man, dazed from the fall,
regained consciousness after a long while.
He ate the food
and regained some strength.
Anxiously searching for a way out,
he found another passage.
Crawling through it,
he twisted and turned through rugged terrain.
After traveling dozens of miles,
the passage widened slightly,
and there was a faint light.
He then reached a broad, flat, and expansive area.
Walking over a hundred miles,
he felt what he stepped on was like dust,
and he smelled the fragrance of rice.
Tasting it, it was sweet and delicious,
more than enough to satisfy his hunger.
He then wrapped it up as provisions
and continued along the cave, eating as he went.
When this substance was exhausted,
he encountered something like mud,
which tasted similar to the earlier dust.
He also took it with him.
The journey was dark and long,
and the distance was hard to measure.
When he reached a bright, open area and had eaten all his provisions,
he entered a city:
Its outer walls were well-built,
and its palaces and buildings were magnificent.
Pavilions, terraces, and houses
were all adorned with gold and silver.
Although there was no sun or moon,
the brightness surpassed that of the three luminaries.
The people were all three zhang tall,
wearing feathered garments,
and playing extraordinary music
unheard of in the mortal world.
He pleaded with them, begging for mercy.
The tall people told him to go forward,
and he obeyed, continuing on his way.
In total, he encountered nine such places.
At the last place he reached,
he earnestly complained of hunger.
A tall person went inside
and pointed to a large cypress tree in the courtyard,
nearly a hundred arm-spans around.
Beneath it was a goat.
He was told to kneel and pluck the goat's beard.
The first time, he obtained a pearl,
which the tall person took.
The second time he plucked, it was taken again,
and the third time, he was told to eat it,
which cured his hunger.
He asked for the names of the nine places
and begged to stay and not leave.
The reply was:
"Your fate does not permit you to stay.
Go back and ask Zhāng Huá, and you will understand everything."
The man then followed the cave back
and emerged in Jiāojùn.
After about six or seven years of traveling back and forth,
he returned to Luòyáng
and asked Huá,
showing him the two things he had obtained.
Huá said:
"The dust-like substance is the saliva of the Yellow River dragon;
the mud is the mud from beneath Kūnlún Mountain;
the nine places are the dwellings of earthly immortals, called the Nine Lodges;
the goat is the foolish dragon;
the first pearl,
if eaten, grants a lifespan equal to heaven and earth;
the second prolongs life,
and the last merely satisfies hunger."
From "Yōumíng Lù" (Records of the Hidden and Visible Worlds).
Also, in Yùzhāng, there was a burning stone
that would become hot when water was poured on it.
It could be used for cooking,
allowing food to be prepared.
When the heat was exhausted,
pouring cold water on it would make it hot again.
This could be repeated endlessly.
People valued it for its peculiarity
but could not identify its name.
Léi Huàn, during the Yuánkāng era, went to Luòyáng
and brought it to show Huá.
Huá said:
"This is what is called a 'burning stone.'"
From "Yìwù Zhì" (Records of Extraordinary Things).
Also, north of Sōnggāo Mountain, there was a large empty cave,
its depth immeasurable.
Common people would often visit it during festivals.
In the early Jin dynasty,
someone accidentally fell into the cave.
His companions, hoping he might still be alive,
tried throwing food into the cave.
The fallen man used it as provisions
and proceeded along the cave.
After about ten days,
he suddenly saw a bright, open space.
There was a thatched cottage,
inside which two people
sat facing each other, playing wéiqí.
Under the board was a cup of white drink.
The fallen man told them of his hunger and thirst.
The players said:
"You may drink this."
The fallen man drank it
and gained ten times his strength.
The players asked:
"Do you wish to stay here?"
The fallen man replied:
"I do not wish to stay."
The players said:
"Go westward for several dozen paces,
and there will be a well.
Inside are many strange things,
but do not be afraid.
Just throw yourself into it,
and you will emerge.
If you are hungry,
you may take what is in the well and eat it."
The man who fell did as he was told.
The well had many flood dragons,
but when they saw the man who fell,
they would avoid his path.
The man who fell walked along the well.
There was something in the well like blue mud,
and the man who fell ate it.
He no longer felt hunger at all.
After about half a year,
he emerged in Shǔzhōng.
He then returned to Luòxià,
and asked Zhāng Huà about it.
Huà said:
"This is an immortal's abode.
What you drank was jade nectar,
and what you ate was the marrow of dragon-cave stone."
From Xiǎoshuō.
Shù Xī
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn asked the Imperial Secretary Zhì Zhòngyě:
"On the third day of the third month, the winding water feast—
what is the meaning and purpose of this?"
He replied:
"During the reign of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
Xú Zhào of Píngyuán had three daughters born at the beginning of the third month,
and by the third day, all had died.
The whole village considered it an omen,
so they went together to the water's edge to wash,
and thus let wine cups float on the flowing water.
The meaning of the winding water feast
likely originated from this."
The Emperor said:
"If it is as you say,
then it is not an auspicious matter."
The Imperial Secretary Shù Xī stepped forward and said:
"Zhòngyě is young and inexperienced,
and cannot know of this.
I beg to explain its origins.
In the past, the Duke of Zhōu built the city of Luòyì,
and used flowing water to float wine cups.
Thus, a lost poem says:
'Feathered cups follow the east'
The Míng manuscript has 'east' as 'àn'.
The Tàipíng Yùlǎn, vol. 30, quotes 'east' as 'shuǐ ān'.
flow.'
Also, King Zhāo of Qín, on the third day of the third month, set out wine at the river bend,
and saw a golden man emerge from the depths,
presenting a Water-Heart Sword, saying:
'Now you rule over Western Xià,
and Qín will dominate the feudal lords.'
Thus, this place was established as the winding water site.
The two Hàn dynasties continued this tradition,
and it became a grand ceremony."
The Emperor said:
"Excellent."
He awarded fifty catties of gold,
and demoted Zhòngyě to Magistrate of Yángchéng.
From Xù Qíxié Jì.
Shěn Yuē
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng was fond of testing knowledge with questions.
Once, someone presented chestnuts an inch in diameter,
and the Emperor tested Shěn Yuē on matters concerning chestnuts:
the Emperor came up with over ten items,
while Yuē came up with nine.
After Yuē left,
people asked why he had not won today.
Yuē said:
"This man dislikes being outshone;
if I did not yield, I fear he would die of shame."
At another time, they tested knowledge on brocade quilts.
From Lúshì Záshuō.
Also, in the fifth year of Tiānjiàn,
a pottery object was found south of Dānyáng Mountain,
five feet high,
four feet in circumference,
pointed at the top and flat at the bottom,
with a lid like a box.
Inside was found a sword,
and several dozen porcelain vessels.
People at the time did not recognize it.
Shěn Yuē said:
"This is an Eastern Barbarian burial urn.
In burials, it is used in place of a coffin.
Its small size
reflects the customs of that time.
