The Eastern Barbarians bury their dead in a seated position."
Emperor Wǔ admired his broad knowledge.
Recorded in Jiāngyòu
The Míng manuscript has 'yòu' as 'zuǒ'.
miscellany.
From Shǐ Xì.
Yú Shìnán
Emperor Tàizōng of Táng ordered Yú Shìnán to copy the Biographies of Exemplary Women,
and the screen was already mounted,
but before he could obtain the original text,
he wrote it from memory,
without a single character missing.
From Guóshǐ Yìzuǎn.
Also, when Tàizōng often traveled,
officials requested to bring reference books along.
The Emperor said:
"No need.
Yú Shìnán is the walking library on this trip."
Fù Yì
During the Zhēnguàn era of Táng,
a Brahmin monk claimed to have obtained a Buddha's tooth,
which could break anything before it.
Thus, men and women flocked to see it,
and the area outside was like a market.
Fù Yì was lying ill at the time,
and heard of this.
He said to his son:
"It is not a Buddha's tooth.
I have heard that diamond is the hardest substance,
and nothing can withstand it,
except antelope horn, which can break it.
You may go and test it."
The monk kept it tightly sealed,
but after persistent requests,
he finally showed it after a long while.
He took out the horn and struck it,
and it shattered at the touch,
so the onlookers dispersed.
It is now used by those who work with pearls and jade.
From Guóshǐ Yìzuǎn.
Hǎo Chǔjùn
Emperor Tàizōng of Táng asked a certain Wéi, the Minister of the Imperial Banquets,
to obtain fat mutton without fat for medicine.
Wéi did not know where to get it,
so he went to the residence of the Palace Attendant Hǎo Chǔjùn to ask.
Chǔjùn said:
"The Emperor values life,
and would certainly not do such a thing."
He then submitted a memorial himself, stating:
To obtain fat mutton without fat,
one must take fifty fat sheep,
and slaughter them one by one in front of each other.
The sheep become terrified,
and their fat disperses into the meat.
Take the last sheep slaughtered,
and it will be extremely fat but without fat.
The Emperor could not bear to do this,
and so stopped.
He praised Chǔjùn for his broad knowledge.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Mèng Shēn
Mèng Shēn of Táng
was from Píngchāng.
His father, Yào, passed the imperial examination in the classics
and was appointed an academic official.
Shēn was intelligent and perceptive from a young age,
widely learned and full of remarkable knowledge,
unequaled in his time.
He passed the imperial examination as a jìnshì,
and began his career as the County Lieutenant of Chánglè,
rising through the ranks to become a Secretary in the Phoenix Pavilion.
At the time, the Vice Minister of the Phoenix Pavilion, Liú Yīzhī, was bedridden with illness,
and Shēn went to inquire after him.
Yīzhī kept him for a meal,
and served yogurt in a golden bowl.
Shēn looked at it in surprise and said:
"This is medicinal gold,
not gold extracted from ore."
Yīzhī said:
"It was bestowed by the Emperor,
so it cannot be false gold."
Shēn said:
"Medicinal gold is used in immortal recipes,
so it is not false."
Yīzhī said:
"How do you know this?"
Shēn said:
"If you burn medicinal gold,
it emits a five-colored vapor."
They immediately burned it,
and indeed it did.
Yīzhī reported this.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān, considering him a close minister,
should not have dabbled in unorthodox arts,
demoted him to Sima of Táizhōu,
and he later rose to become Prefect of Tóngzhōu.
In each of his official posts,
he imposed many burdensome policies,
and the people and officials could hardly bear it.
He treated his wife with little regard,
often saying
that a wife could be cooked to serve to guests.
Many people criticized him for this.
From Yùshǐ Tái Jì.
Emperor Wénzōng of Táng
Emperor Wénzōng of the Táng dynasty, during his leisure from governance,
extensively read various books.
One day,
during an audience at the Yányīng Hall, he asked his ministers,
"The Máo Shī says:
'The deer call out to each other, yōu yōu,
eating the píng in the wild.'
What kind of grass is píng?"
At that time, the chancellors Lǐ Jué, Yáng Sìfù, and Chén Yíxíng looked at each other but did not reply.
Jué said:
"Your servant, according to the Ěryǎ,
states that píng is lài xiāo."
The emperor said:
"I have read the Máo Shī commentary,
which says píng has round leaves and white flowers,
growing in clusters in the wild,
so it is not lài xiāo."
Another day, he asked his ministers,
"An ancient poem says:
'A light robe sets off the tiàotuō.'
What is a tiàotuō?"
The ministers did not reply.
The emperor said:
"It is what we now call a wrist bracelet.
The Zhēn Gào states that
Āngū had a tiàotuō made of carved gold,
which was an arm ornament."
From the Lú Shì Zá Shuō.
Jiǎ Dān
Jiǎ Dān of the Táng dynasty was fond of geography.
Envoys from all directions,
especially
Míng manuscript has "zì nǎi" instead of "nǎi shì"
those from foreign tribes,
he would sit with them,
asking about the geography of their lands, the mountains and rivers from beginning to end.
Over thirty years,
what he heard became comprehensive,
so he compiled the Hǎinèi Huáyí Tú.
He inquired with people from those regions,
and all obtained accurate information,
with no false statements.
From the Lú Shì Zá Shuō.
Duàn Chéngshì
Duàn Chéngshì of the Táng dynasty was learned in literature and widely read,
proficient in the three teachings;
moreover, he had a strong memory,
and whenever he read texts,
even if they were tens of thousands of words long,
he would glance over them without missing anything.
Once, while digging a pond at his private residence,
workers found a piece of iron in the soil.
Finding its unusual quality strange,
they brought it to present to him.
Chéngshì had it measured with a ruler,
and after measuring its circumference,
he smiled without saying a word.
He then prepared a quiet room,
hung the iron on the north wall of the room.
Afterward, he sealed the door with mud,
only opening a window a few inches square,
which he also locked.
Occasionally, he would open the window with close relatives to peek inside,
and there were two characters written in gold,
marking the twelve double-hours.
Such was the breadth of his knowledge.
From the Nánchǔ Xīnwén.
Also, Chéngshì was excessively fond of hunting,
which troubled his father, Wénchāng.
Moreover, because of his son's age,
he did not reprimand him face-to-face for his faults,
but asked his staff to speak to him.
The aides then went together to the study,
fully conveying the chancellor's intent,
but Chéngshì only meekly apologized.
The next day,
he went hunting again in the suburban fields,
with even more falcons and hounds.
Afterward, he sent each of the aides a pair of rabbits,
and in the accompanying letters, he cited classical allusions,
with not a single instance repeated.
The aides were astonished,
admiring his extensive knowledge of historical典故.
They then went together to Wénchāng,
each showing him the letters.
Only then did Wénchāng realize his son's literary and artistic talents were vast.
Shǎn Jiǎn once said:
"By the age of forty,
I was still not recognized by my family."
This case is quite similar.
From the Yùtáng Xiánhuà.
The Jiānglíng Scholar
Outside the south gate of Jiānglíng,
within the Yōng Gate,
under the eastern wall, there was a small tiled room,
about a foot high,
complete in form but miniature.
Inquiring with the locals,
they said:
"This is Xìrǎng."
Asked about its origin,
they said:
Several hundred years ago,
this region was suddenly flooded by great waves,
with only two or three planks left unsubmerged.
The regional commander was terrified,
not knowing what to do.
Suddenly, someone informed him that,
in the suburban estates of the region,
there was a scholar who had read extensively,
with exceptional talent and wisdom.
They requested to summon and consult him.
When summoned and asked,
he said this was the land of Xìrǎng,
located at the south gate.
"I have read the Xìrǎng Jì, which says:
When Yǔ controlled the floodwaters,
there was a sea eye here.
It overflowed unpredictably,
so Yǔ carved stone,
built a dragon's palace chamber,
placed it in the cavity,
to block the water veins.
Later, I heard that when building this city's walls,
they destroyed the old structure,
hence this inundation disaster occurred.
Please dig and search for it."
Sure enough, under the eastern wall,
after digging several feet,
they found a stone palace chamber,
already damaged.
The Jīng commander then had it repaired,
and covered it with thick soil.
The floodwaters then ceased.
Now, a building has been erected over it,
marking the location.
Checking it against the Xìrǎng Jì,
it was not mistaken.
From the Yùtáng Xiánhuà.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú of the Hàn dynasty composed rhapsodies,
which contemporaries praised as classical and beautiful,
so much that even the works of poets
could not surpass them.
Yáng Zǐyún said:
"Chángqīng's rhapsodies seem not to come from the human world;
are they the result of divine transformation?"
Zǐyún studied Xiàngrú's rhapsodies but could not equal them,
so he deeply admired him.
When Xiàngrú composed the "Shànglín Rhapsody,"
his thoughts were detached and free,
no longer concerned with external matters.
He controlled and drew upon heaven and earth,
interweaving past and present.
Suddenly he would fall asleep,
and abruptly rise again.
It took nearly a hundred days to complete.
His friend Shèng Lǎn, styled Chángqīng
Míng manuscript has "tōng" instead of "qīng"
a famous scholar from Zāngkē,
once asked him about composing rhapsodies.
Xiàngrú said:
"Weaving patterns to form the text,
arranging brocade and embroidery as the substance,
one warp and one weft,
one gōng and one shāng note,
this is the outward form of the rhapsody.
A rhapsodist must encompass the cosmos,
survey all figures,
this is what is grasped internally,
and cannot be obtained through extensive reading alone."
Shèng then composed the "Hézǔ Gē" and "Lièjǐn Fù" and withdrew.
For the rest of his life, he dared not speak of the heart of rhapsody composition.
From the Xījīng Zá Jì.
Xiè Tiǎo
Emperor Gāozǔ of the Liáng dynasty valued the poetry of Xiè Tiǎo from Chénjùn.
He often said:
"If I don't read Xiè's poetry for three days,
I feel my mouth stinks."
From the Tán Sǒu.
Shěn Yuē
In the Liáng dynasty, Wú Jūn, who held the position of Fèngcháoqǐng, possessed talent and ability.
He once composed a poem titled "Mounted Swordsman," which read:
"When shall I see the Son of Heaven,
And sketch a plan to seize Guānxī?"
Emperor Gāozǔ said to him:
"The Son of Heaven is before you now,
But where is Guānxī to be taken?"
Wú Jūn fell silent and had no reply.
Wú Jūn also wrote a poem that said:
"Autumn wind ripples the clear water,
Wild geese leave prints on the yellow sand."
Shěn Yǐnhóu Yuē remarked to him:
"The phrase 'prints on the yellow sand' is too perilous."
Wú Jūn said:
"I have also seen Your Excellency's poem that says,
'Mountain cherries bloom as if about to ignite.'"
Yuē replied:
"I merely intended 'as if about to ignite,'
But you have already 'printed' it."
From Tán Sǒu.
Yǔ Xìn
When Yǔ Xìn of the Liáng dynasty first arrived from the Southern Dynasties,
Many northern literati looked down upon him.
Yǔ Xìn showed them his "Rhapsody on the Withered Tree,"
After which no one dared speak disparagingly.
At that time, Wēn Zǐshēng composed the "Stele of the Hánlíng Mountain Temple."
Yǔ Xìn read it and copied the text.
Southerners asked Yǔ Xìn:
"How do the northern literati compare?"
Yǔ Xìn replied:
"Only the stone tablet at Hánlíng Mountain is worth discussing.
Xuē Dàohéng and Lú Sīdào have some slight skill with the brush.
As for the rest, their braying and barking
Are merely clamor to the ears."
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Wáng Bó
Táng dynasty Wáng Bó, whenever composing stele inscriptions or eulogies,
Would first grind several shēng of ink,
Pull the quilt over his face, and lie down;
Suddenly he would rise,
Write it out in a single stroke,
Without any initial corrections.
People of the time called this "drafting from the belly."
From Tán Sǒu.
Lú Zhàolín
Táng dynasty Lú Zhàolín, courtesy name Shēngzhī,
Was from Fànyáng.
At the age of twenty,
He was appointed Diǎnqiān in the princely establishment of Prince Dèng,
And all the administrative documents of the princely household
Were entrusted to him.
The prince possessed twelve cartloads of books,
Which Zhàolín comprehensively perused
And could largely memorize.
Later, he served as County Lieutenant of Xīndū County in Yìzhōu.
After his term ended,
He lingered in the Shǔ region,
Indulging freely in poetry and wine.
Thus, the world spoke of Wáng, Yáng, Lú, and Luò.
Hearing this, Zhàolín said:
"I am pleased to be placed after Wáng,
But ashamed to be ranked before Luò."
At that time, Yáng, in his writing,
Was fond of stringing together the names of ancient people,
Such as "Zhāng Píngzǐ's brief discussion,"
"Lù Shìhéng's recorded words,"
"Pān Ānrén would surely find it crude,"
"Zhòng Chángtǒng, what would he know?"
It was dubbed the "Register of Ghosts."
Luò Bīnwáng's writing favored numerical parallelism,
Such as "The Qín land's strategic passes, one hundred and two,"
"The Hàn dynasty's detached palaces, thirty-six."
People of the time called him "Doctor of Calculations."
As for Master Lú's writings,
People of the time could not assess their merits and flaws.
Alas,
Unfortunately, he suffered from the illness of Rǎn Gēng,
And composed Yōuyōuzǐ to vent his indignation.
His collected works comprise twenty volumes.
From Cháoyě Qiānshì.
Cuī Róng
Táng dynasty Guózǐ Sīyè Cuī Róng composed the edict for Empress Wǔ,
But fell ill
("Illness" originally written as "mat";
Corrected according to the Ming manuscript copy)
And died.
People of the time considered it a text unmatched in two hundred years.
From Guóshǐ Zuǎnyì.
Zhāng Yuè
Táng dynasty Zhāng Yuè and Xú Jiān served together as Jíxián Academy scholars for over ten years.
Their tastes and preferences were quite similar,
And they were congenial and compatible.
At that time, many of the scholars had passed away,
Leaving only Yuè and Jiān.
Yuè wrote down the names of the various scholars
And viewed the list together with Jiān.
Jiān said to Yuè:
"These gentlemen all possessed outstanding talent in their time.
May I ask about the relative merits of their literary arts?"
Yuè said:
"The writings of Lǐ Qiáo, Cuī Róng, Xuē Jǐ, and Sòng Zhīwèn
Are all like fine gold and beautiful jade,
Suitable for any application.
The writings of Fù Jiāmó
Are like a solitary peak or sheer cliff,
Standing ten thousand rèn tall,
With dense clouds gathering,
And thunderclaps erupting together.
Truly remarkable, are they not?
But if applied in the court and temple,
They would be alarming.
The writings of Yán Cháoyǐn
Are like a beautiful woman in splendid attire,
Dressed in embroidered silks,
Singing Yān songs and dancing Zhào dances,
Causing viewers to forget their worries.
Yet, compared to the Odes and Elegantiae,
They are merely theatrical."
Jiān also asked:
"Among the later scholars of today,
Whose literary compositions are worthy?"
Yuè said:
"The writings of Hán Xiū
Are like grand sacrificial broth and dark wine.
Though elegant and canonical,
They are lacking in flavor.
The writings of Xǔ Jǐngxiān
Are like plump, smooth flesh.
Though lush and lovely,
They lack strength of character.
The writings of Zhāng Jiǔlíng
Are like light silk and plain silk.
Truly useful for the times,
But constrained in breadth.
The writings of Wáng Hàn
Are like jade forests and jade cups.
Though brilliantly precious,
They often have flaws and defects.
If one can admonish their shortcomings
And supplement their strengths,
They too can be outstanding talents of the age."
From Dàtáng Xīnyǔ.
Cuī Shǔ
Táng dynasty Cuī Shǔ sat for the Jìnshì examinations.
He composed a poem on the fire pearl of the Mingtáng,
Continuing
(Ming manuscript copy has "to redeem the examination section" three characters)
With an excellent couplet that read:
"Last night, twin moons were full;
After dawn, a single star remains alone."
These lines were deeply admired and praised by literary scholars.
After his untimely death,
He left a daughter named "Xīngxīng" but no son.
People of the time all found this remarkable.
From Mínghuáng Zálù.
Wáng Wéi
Táng dynasty Wáng Wéi was fond of Buddhism,
Hence his courtesy name Mójié.
His nature was lofty and refined.
He acquired Sòng Zhīwèn's estate at Wǎngchuān,
Where the mountains and waters were supremely beautiful.
It is the present-day Qīngliáng Temple.
Wéi was renowned for his poetry,
But he was fond of adopting others' lines.
For example, "Walking to where the water ends,
Sitting to watch the clouds rise"—
People thought these were lines from the Hányīng collection.
"Vast, misty paddy fields where white egrets fly;
Dark, shady summer woods where yellow orioles sing"—
These were actually lines from Lǐ Jiāyòu's poem.
From Guóshǐ Bǔ.
Lǐ Hàn
Táng dynasty Lǐ Hàn's writings, though broad and fluent,
Were composed with great difficulty and labor.
In his later years, residing in Yángdí,
He often sought music from the county magistrate Huángfǔ Céng.
When his thoughts ran dry, he would play music;
When his spirit was restored, he would resume writing.
From Guóshǐ Bǔ.
Gù Kuàng
Táng Bái Jūyì had a singing girl named Fán Sù who excelled at singing,
and Xiǎo Mán who excelled at dancing.
He once wrote a poem that said:
"Cherry-like are Fán Sù's lips,
willow-like is Xiǎo Mán's waist."
As he grew old,
while Xiǎo Mán remained plump and beautiful,
he expressed his feelings through a poem about willows:
"A tree in the spring breeze with countless branches,
tender as gold, softer than silk.
In the southeast corner of Yǒngfēng Ward,
all day long, to whom does it belong?"
During the reign of Emperor Xuānzōng,
the court musicians sang this poem.
The emperor asked whose poem it was,
and where Yǒngfēng was located.
His attendants provided the answers.
Thereupon, through an envoy to the east,
he ordered two branches of the Yǒngfēng willow to be taken
and planted within the palace grounds.
Bái Jūyì, feeling that the emperor knew his name
and appreciated elegance,
composed another poem,
whose final lines read:
"Surely from now on, within the celestial patterns,
two stars will be added among the light of the Willow Constellation."
Later, he was appointed Prefect of Sūzhōu,
and traveled downstream through the gorges to assume his post.
At that time, Fán Zhīyī of Zǐguī County,
hearing that Bái Jūyì would pass by Wūshān,
first inscribed in large characters on the white wall of the Goddess Temple:
"The Prefect of Sūzhōu is a man of talent today;
arriving at Wūshān, he must compose a poem.
To inform the Goddess of Gāotáng,
swiftly arrange clouds and rain to await his pure verses."
Bái Jūyì saw the inscription and was pleased,
inviting Fán Zhīyī to come and saying:
"Liú Yǔxī, the Vice-Director from Lìyáng,
governed Báidì for three years
and wished to write a poem here,
but held back and did not compose it.
After leaving his post and passing through,
he removed over a thousand poems,
leaving only four pieces.
These four pieces
are masterpieces from ancient to modern times,
and people should not rashly attempt to match them.
Shěn Quánqī's poem says:
'Wūshān's peaks reach boundless heights,
layered and wondrous in form.
Dark valleys seem filled with wind and rain,
secluded cliffs like ghosts and deities.
Moonlight brightens the Three Gorges at dawn,
spring tides fill the Nine Rivers.
I ask the visitor to the Sunny Terrace,
surely he knows the one who enters dreams.'"
Wáng Wújìng's poem says:
"'The goddess faces Gāotáng,
Wūshān beneath the setting sun.
Lingering, she brings the traveling rain,
gracefully following the King of Jīng.
Lightning flashes before the river falls,
thunder echoes beyond the gorge.
After rain, clouds have no fixed place,
the terrace hall at dawn lies vast and gray.'"
Lǐ Duān's poem says:
"'Wūshān's twelvefold peaks,
all stand in the azure void.
Clouds conceal the sun as they circle,
misty rain carries the wind.
Gibbon cries chill the crossing waters,
tree colors merge with dusk's sky.
Sorrowful, I head toward Gāotáng,
where Chǔ's palace appears after a thousand autumns.'"
Huángfǔ Rǎn's poem says:
"'Wū Gorge appears in Bādōng,
towering into the half sky.
Clouds hide the goddess's lodge,
rain reaches the King of Chǔ's palace.
Morning and evening, the sound of springs falls,
warmth and chill share the same tree hues.
The clear gibbon cries are unbearable to hear,
especially in mid-autumn.'"
Bái Jūyì chanted these four poems
and traveled together with Mr. Fán,
yet ultimately did not compose one himself.
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì."
Yuánhé Monk
During the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
in Cháng'ān, there was a monk
whose name is not recorded,
skilled at finding faults in people's writings,
especially adept at pinpointing where phrasing and meaning coincided.
Zhāng Jí was quite annoyed by him
and searched his mind even more intently.
He thought of a couplet:
"Often at the place where I see others off,
I recall the time I left home."
He went straight to boast about it.
The monk said:
"This probably doesn't match the ideas of the ancients."
The monk smiled and said:
"Someone has already said this."
Zhāng Jí asked:
"Who said it before?"
The monk chanted coolly:
"Seeing his peach and plum trees bloom,
I recall the spring in the back garden."
Zhāng Jí then clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
From "Zhíyán."
Dù Mù
When Bái Jūyì first became the Prefect of Hángzhōu,
he ordered a search for peony flowers.
Only the monk Huì Chéng of Kāiyuán Temple had recently obtained some from the capital.
He first planted them in the courtyard,
with very dense railings and gates,
and no other place had them.
At that time, spring scenery was at its peak,
and Huì Chéng set up oiled curtains to cover them.
From then on, peonies were propagated and planted in the eastern Yuè region.
It happened that Xú Níng came from Fùchūn,
not yet acquainted with Bái,
and first inscribed a poem, saying:
"This flower, known to be hard to grow in southern lands,
shames the monk for idly tending with care.
Sea swallows, understanding pity, frequently glance askance,
while foreign bees, unfamiliar, wander even more.
Vainly born peonies labor in vain with envy,
shy roses dare not bloom.
Only a few red buds remain wrapped,
holding fragrance, waiting just for the court official to come."
Bái later went to the temple to see the flowers
and invited Xú to get drunk together before returning.
At that time, Zhāng Hù arrived by boat,
appearing quite aloof and unconventional.
However, the two scholars Zhāng and Xú were not accustomed to seclusion,
and each hoped to be recommended first.
Bái said:
"You two gentlemen discussing literature
is like Lián Pō and Bái Qǐ fighting in a rat hole—
victory or defeat depends on a single battle."
Thus, they were tested with the fu "Long Sword Leaning Beyond the Sky"
and the poem "Remaining Clouds Scatter into Brocade."
After the examination was concluded and the candidates were sent off,
Xú was ranked first,
and Zhāng second.
Zhāng said:
"My poem has 'The land's momentum distantly honors the mountain,
the river's flow yields sideways to the pass.'
Many scholars compare it to Chén Hòuzhǔ's 'The sun and moon glorify heavenly virtue,
mountains and rivers magnify the imperial abode.'
This merely has former fame."
Also, Zhāng's poem on Jīnshān Temple says:
"Tree shadows appear midstream,
bell sounds are heard on both banks."
Although Qímǔ Qián said,
"Pagoda shadows hang in the azure sky,
bell sounds harmonize with white clouds,"
this line is not considered excellent.
Bái also remarked that Zhāng's palace lyrics,
with numerical parallelism in all four lines,
what is so remarkable about them?
Yet none match Xú's lines:
"Ancient and modern, ever like a white silk flying,
a single line breaks the green mountain's hue."
Zhāng sighed:
"Honor and disgrace are entangled—
how constant are they?"
Thereupon, he departed singing as he walked,
and Xú also rowed back home.
From then on, the two scholars spent their lives in reclusion,
never again participating in provincial examinations.
Earlier, Lǐ Línzōng and Dù Mù
had competed in literature with Bái in the capital.
"Wén" originally written as "zhī,"
corrected according to "Yúnxī Yǒuyì."
They fully discussed how Yuán Zhěn and Bái Jūyì's poetic styles were flawed and mixed,
and were mocked by those of pure and austere taste,
hence there was resentment.
When Bái was Governor of Hénán,
and Lǐ was Magistrate of Hénán,
they met on the road.
The Governor rode a horse,
while the Magistrate was carried in a sedan chair,
seemingly contrary to the etiquette of attending to duties.
Lǐ once called Bái "Mumbling Lord,"
and those who heard it all laughed.
Thus, Lètiān's reputation diminished somewhat.
Bái said:
"Lǐ Zhímù
(Línzōng's style name)
is my mad dog—
his edge cannot be withstood."
Later, when Dù Mù served as Prefect of Qiūpǔ,
he became a poetic and drinking companion of Zhāng Hù,
passionately reciting Zhāng's palace lyrics.
He also knew that during Bái's time in Qiántáng,
Bái had made disparaging remarks about Zhāng,
and often felt indignant about it.
Thus, he composed two poems to elevate Zhāng, saying:
"Who can compare to Master Zhāng,
with a thousand poems lighter than a marquisate of ten thousand households?"
And also:
"How is it that for a homeland three thousand li away,
empty songs fill the six palaces?"
Zhāng's poem says:
"A homeland three thousand li away,
deep in the palace for twenty years.
One sound of 'Hè Mǎnzǐ,'
and twin tears fall before the lord."
This is Zhāng's most得意 line.
After Lǐ and Dù,
many praised its beauty,
wishing to differ from Bái and fully support Zhāng.
Therefore, Dù also wrote a critique,
saying that recently there were Yuán and Bái,
fond of licentious and vulgar language,
stirring up frivolous clamor.
"I regret being in a low position,
unable to discipline them according to law."
This also served to assist Zhāng.
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì."
Tiānqiáo Wanderer
Mágū Mountain,
with its splendid valleys,
has many rare plants and trees.
There was a Dèng Xiān
(Míng manuscript has "Xiān" as "Xiān")
guest who arrived at Yánkāng,
whose family for four or five generations served as state Taoist masters,
and were bestowed purple robes.
Upon his death,
he was returned from the capital to be buried on this mountain,
said to have achieved liberation from the corpse.
Yet all became mounds and ridges,
with pines and cypresses in view.
Literati passing by
would inevitably compose poems,
amounting to nearly a thousand.
Suddenly, a youth
casually inscribed a quatrain,
not stating his name,
only calling himself Tiānqiáo Wanderer.
Later visitors read what he had written.
No more writings were added.
And the Dèng family's fame
thereby diminished somewhat.
The poem says:
"Cranes grow old in mushroom fields, chickens are in cages;
the Upper Pure realm is not the same as worldly dust.
Since it is said he ascended to immortality in broad daylight,
why is there a burial palace in the human world?"
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì."
Tán Zhū
Zhēnniáng was
a beauty of the Wú state,
compared to Sū Xiǎoxiǎo of Qiántáng.
She was buried beside the Wú palace.
Travelers, moved by her splendor,
competed to inscribe poems on the trees by her tomb,
as dense as fish scales or comb teeth.
There was a candidate named Tán Zhū,
an outstanding scholar of Wú,
who thus wrote a quatrain.
Later visitors,
seeing his inscription,
gradually ceased writing.
The poem says:
"Below Wǔqiū Mountain, mounds are piled high;
pines and cypresses, desolate, all evoke sorrow.
Why do people in the world so favor beauty,
that on Zhēnniáng's tomb alone they inscribe poems?"
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì."
Zhōu Kuāngwù
Zhōu Kuāngwù, style name Jǐběn,
was from Zhāngzhōu.
In the twelfth year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
he passed the imperial examination under the list of Wáng Bō.
At that time, he was famous for his songs and poems.
Initially, due to family poverty,
Zhōu traveled on foot to take the examinations,
down and out in the dusty world,
carrying his name card but meeting no success.
Passing by the Qiántáng River,
he lacked the money to hire a boat,
and for a long time could not cross.
Thus, he inscribed a poem at the official lodge:
"Vast and boundless, the natural moat stretches far;
why did Qín Shǐhuáng not build a bridge?
At the mouth of the Qiántáng River, without money to cross,
again blocked by the two tidal letters of Xīlíng."
The prefect saw it when he went out,
and reprimanded the ferry officer.
To this day, at ferries across the land,
this poem is still recited and chanted.
Boatmen not daring to take money from examination candidates
began from this.
From "Mǐnchuān Míngshì Zhuàn."
Wáng Bō
Táng Wáng Bō was orphaned and poor in his youth.
He once lodged at the Huìzhào Temple’s Magnolia Courtyard in Yángzhōu,
taking meals with the monks.
Later, the monks grew weary of him,
so they would strike the bell only after the meal was over.
Twenty-four years later,
Wáng Bō, having attained a high position,
was appointed to govern that very region.
He thus revisited his old haunts.
The poems he had once inscribed
were now all covered with green gauze.
Wáng Bō then added two quatrains:
"Thirty years ago I roamed this courtyard;
Magnolias bloomed, the halls were newly built.
Now I return to tread the paths once more:
The trees are old, flowerless; the monks, white-haired."
"To the hall I went—
Míng manuscript reads 'had' for 'not'
—before all scattered east and west;
Ashamed before the abbot's 'after-meal bell.'
For thirty years, dust shrouded my face;
Only now does green gauze veil my verse."
From *Zhíyán*.
Zhū Qìngyú
In the Táng, Zhū Qìngyú met the Vice Minister of the Waterways Department, Zhāng Jí, who recognized his talent.
Zhāng requested several collections of Zhū’s new and old poems,
chanted and revised them, keeping only twenty-six pieces.
Zhāng carried them close and praised them highly.
As Zhāng enjoyed great renown at the time,
people all copied and recited them,
and so Zhū passed the imperial examination.
Initially, Zhū Qìngyú, still modest and reserved,
composed a poem titled "A Bride’s Thoughts,"
presenting it to Zhāng:
"Last night in the bridal room, red candles burned;
At dawn she waits to greet his parents in the hall.
Makeup done, she whispers to her husband:
'Are my brows drawn too dark or light—in fashion now?'"
Zhāng replied:
"A Yuè maiden, freshly adorned, steps from the mirror—
Míng manuscript reads 'presented' for 'mirror'
—heart;
Knowing her own bright beauty, she still hesitates.
Even Qí’s fine silk is not the world’s true treasure;
One song of water-chestnut girls is worth ten thousand gold."
Thus Zhū’s fame as a poet
spread throughout the land.
From *Yúnxī Yǒuyì*.
Emperor Xuānzōng of Táng
During the reign of Emperor Xuānzōng of Táng,
the former *jìnshì* Chén and two others sat for the Doctor of Letters examination.
The officials determined their rankings, along with their poems, fu, and essays.
The Emperor summoned the Secretariat Drafter Lǐ Fān and others to the Yányīng Hall and asked:
"In general examinations,
how is the reuse of characters viewed?"
Lǐ Fān replied:
"In *fu*, one should avoid lopsidedness and vulgar mixture;
in essays, losing praise, blame, and judgment is a flaw;
in poetry, one follows the topic and matches the rhyme.
Following the topic—
as in the poem 'White Clouds Rise from Within the Feng,'
the original 'Within the Feng, white clouds rise' is an example.
Note: *Yúnxī Yǒuyì* Vol. 7 lacks the character 'original.'
As for reusing characters within,
it is acceptable,
and there are established precedents."
The Emperor asked further:
"Whose poem reuses characters?"
He replied:
"Qián Qǐ’s poem 'Xiānglíng Plays the Se' says:
'Skilled she plucks the cloud-harmony se,
Often heard is the Princess’s spirit.
Féngyí dances in vain,
The Chǔ traveler cannot bear to listen.
Unfettered tones harmonize with metal and stone,
Clear notes arise from the distant gloom.
From Cāngwú comes sorrowful longing,
White zhǐ herbs stir fragrant scents.
Flowing water carries them past Xiāng’s shores,
Sad winds cross Dòngtíng Lake.
The song ends, the person unseen,
On the river, several peaks stand green.'
It contains two instances of the character 'not.'"
The Emperor said:
"Although Qián Qǐ reuses characters,
others’ poems seem inferior to Qǐ’s.
Even though Xiè Tiǎo wrote:
'Dòngtíng, land where music spread,
Xiāoxiāng where the Princess roamed.
Clouds depart, Cāngwú grows distant,
Waters return, Jiānghàn flows on'—
none can compare."
Those in the Doctor of Letters examination who reused characters in their poems passed.
Qǐ’s poem was then entrusted to the Historiography Office for selection.
From *Yúnxī Yǒuyì*.
Also, Emperor Xuānzōng, on the occasion of the Double Ninth Festival,
feasted all his officials,
and composed a royal poem.
It read in part:
"Pacifying the frontier, the cavalry soon returns;
Making peace with the tribes, we entrust to temple worthies.
With wholehearted trust we lean on them,
Joining forces to secure the border."
All ministers and below composed matching poems in response.
The Emperor said:
"The poem by Chancellor Wèi Mó stands out the most.
Its two couplets read:
'From four quarters, no troubles depart;
Divine joy arrives with deep autumn.
Eight rivers’ cold light rises,
A thousand mountains’ clear colors unfold.'"
The Emperor praised and admired it for a long time.
Wèi danced with joy and bowed in thanks.
All officials gazed up in awe;
Wèi wore a look of virtuous pride,
and the feast ended in great joy.
From *Shūqíng Shī*.
Wēn Tíngyún
Táng Wēn Tíngyún, courtesy name Fēiqīng,
was formerly named Qí.
He was equally famous with Lǐ Shāngyǐn,
and at the time they were called "Wēn-Lǐ."
His talent and thoughts were brilliant and beautiful,
and he excelled at composing short fu.
Each time he entered the examinations,
he would compose a fu using the official rhyme scheme.
He would merely cross his hands eight times and the eight rhymes would be completed.
He often ghostwrote for neighboring examinees,
earning the nickname "Savior of the Failing."
However, his conduct as a scholar was flawed,
and the gentry looked down upon him.
Lǐ Yìshān (Lǐ Shāngyǐn) once said to him:
"Recently I composed a couplet:
'From afar, like Duke Zhào,
thirty-six years as chief minister.'
But I haven't yet found a matching line."
Wēn replied:
"Why not say:
'In recent times, like Minister Guō,
twenty-four evaluations as Secretariat Director.'"
Emperor Xuānzōng once tested poetic skill,
providing the line "golden bùyáo (hairpin that sways with steps),"
but could not find a matching line.
He sent for jìnshì candidates to provide one.
Tíngyún then supplied "jade tiáotuō (bracelet)" to complete it.
Emperor Xuānzōng was pleased.
Also, there is a medicine named "white-headed old man" (báitóuwēng),
to which Wēn matched "cocklebur seed" (cāng'ěrzǐ).
Other examples were all of this kind.
Emperor Xuānzōng loved singing "Bodhisattva Barbarian" lyrics.
Chancellor Lìng Hú Táo had him compose some,
secretly presented them to the emperor,
and warned him not to divulge it to others.
But Wēn immediately told people,
and because of this, the chancellor became distant from him.
Wēn also had a saying:
"A general sits within the Secretariat."
This mocked the chancellor for being unlearned.
Emperor Xuānzōng enjoyed traveling incognito.
He encountered Wēn at an inn.
Wēn did not recognize the imperial countenance
and arrogantly questioned him, saying:
"Aren't you someone like a Chief Clerk or an Aide?"
The Emperor said:
"No."
Wēn asked again:
"Could it be you are something like a Senior Advisor, Registrar, or Captain?"
The Emperor said:
"No."
He was demoted to the position of Captain of Fángchéng.
The demotion edict stated:
"For scholars, moral conduct comes first,
literary talent is secondary.
Since you have nothing to offer in moral conduct,
how can your literary talent compensate?
You merely possess an unbridled talent,
rarely of any timely use."
He ultimately drifted into obscurity and died.
When Duke Bīn, Dù Cóng, was transferred from Xīchuān to Huáihǎi,
Tíngyún visited the Lín family's pavilion at Wéiqǔ
and left a poem, which said:
"Before Zhuō's furnace, golden-thread willows;
by the Suí dynasty embankment, brocade-sailed breeze.
Greedy to be the timely rain for two lands,
you do not see the pond lotus reflecting red in the water."
Upon hearing this, Duke Bīn
sent him a thousand bolts of silk.
Shěn Huī of Wúxīng said:
"Wēn was once caned by a relative in Jiānghuái,
and because of this he changed his name to Tíngyún.
Also, each year at the examination grounds,
he often ghostwrote for candidates."
When Vice-Minister Shěn Xún presided over the examinations,
he set up a separate mat
for Tíngyún,
not placing him adjacent to the other candidates.
The next day,
he requested Tíngyún before the curtain and said:
"Those who have succeeded in the past
all entrusted their literary compositions to you, Academician.
This year in the examination hall,
there will be no such entrustment.
You, Academician, should strive on your own."
He then dismissed him,
and because of this, Wēn was disheartened.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Lǐ Shāngyǐn
Táng Lǐ Shāngyǐn, courtesy name Yìshān,
served as an aide to Lord Péngyáng, Lìng Hú Chǔ.
Lìng Hú Chǔ's son, Lìng Hú Táo,
later achieved high ministerial rank like Wéi and Píng,
but seemed to distance himself from Shāngyǐn,
never showing him favor.
On the Double Ninth Festival,
Shāngyǐn visited his residence
and left an inscription in the main hall.
It roughly said:
"For ten years beneath the springs, no news;
on the ninth day before the cup, thoughts arise.
The young master, his office weighty, has barricades deployed;
the eastern pavilion offers no chance to peer within again."
The Chancellor saw it
and could only feel ashamed and regretful.
He then locked this hall,
and never used it again for the rest of his life.
Original source missing;
now seen in "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán", Volume 7.
Liú Zhuàn
Táng Liú Zhuàn, courtesy name Zǐquán.
He studied diligently from childhood,
able to compose prose,
his literary talent and elegance being abundant.
In the early Dàzhōng era,
he became a Hanlin Academician.
At that time, Héhuáng had just been recovered,
and military affairs on the frontier were somewhat frequent.
It happened that many academicians in the institute were on leave,
so Zhuàn alone handled drafting edicts.
One day he drafted nearly a hundred documents,
his brush never ceasing,
the wording and reasoning precise and fitting.
Late at night,
the Emperor again summoned him before the throne,
ordering him to draft an edict proclaiming to the realm.
Zhuàn moistened his brush and gave thought,
and in a moment it was completed.
At dawn he was summoned for an audience,
and the Emperor greatly praised and rewarded him.
He then bestowed upon him in person the robes of gold and purple.
Zhuàn was recognized for his literary talent,
and within a few years,
he eventually rose to high office.
His proclamation edict said:
"Since ancient times, when imperial kings have possessed the state,
have they not always used civility to preserve achievement,
and martial prowess to accomplish affairs?
Combining these two instruments,
they bring about great peace.
We unworthily bear the great plan,
thinking to expand the glorious enterprise.
Anxious, diligent, cautious, and vigilant,
for four years now it has been thus.
Ever mindful of the Héhuáng territory,
stretching vast and far.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
the Dog Rong (Tibetans) took advantage of our many troubles;
having no strength to resist the traitors,
they then gave free rein to the stench of mutton,
not far from the capital city.
Events passed through ten reigns,
time drew near to a hundred years.
Ministers and scholars offered their abilities,
none failing to exhaust their best strategies.
The court deliberated below,
and also listened to their forthright words.
All took 'not provoking border incidents' as the eternal plan,
and 'guarding the old territory' as clear principle.
Thus time drifted by,
with no means of recovery.
Now Heaven and Earth store auspicious signs,
our ancestors bestow protection.
Generals and soldiers alike combed by wind and rain,
exposed in the wilds.
Clearing thorns and brambles, night watches strict;
driving out jackals and wolves, dawn breaks their tents.
Every action met their wish,
unmatched in antiquity.
Considering this sincere diligence,
they should receive added favor and reward."
The text is not fully recorded here.
From the "Liú Zhuàn Stele" composed by Zhèng Chùhuì.
Zhèng Tián
At the Mǎwéi Buddhist temple,
the place where Consort Yáng was strangled.
Afterwards, when talented scholars passed by,
those who composed poems to express her hidden sorrow
were too many to record.
All spoke of kingfisher feathers and fragrant hairpins,
cast into dust and mud,
of crimson grief and azure lament,
causing people sorrow and sadness.
Though the tone was bitter and the words pure,
none escaped this sentiment.
When Chancellor Zhèng Tián served as an aide in Fèngxiáng,
he inscribed a poem, which said:
"Sùzōng turned his horse, Consort Yáng died;
though clouds and rain perished, sun and moon renewed.
After all, it was an affair of the sage court's Son of Heaven;
what of the one at the Jǐngyáng Palace well?"
Readers considered it a verse truly befitting a pillar of the state.
From "Quē Shǐ" (Incomplete History).
Sīkōng Tú
During the Tang Dynasty, Duke Jìn of the State of Táng, Péi Dù, campaigned against Huáixī,
and inscribed his name on the gate tower of the Huàyuè Temple.
Later, Sīkōng Tú composed a poem to commemorate this, saying:
"Before Mount Huà, a great army marched to Huáixī,
from then on, the Central Plains ceased the drums of war.
Do not let moss grow upon the stone tower,
clearly recognize the inscription of Duke Jìn."
From "Zhíyán"
Gāo Chán
The poetic thoughts of Táng poet Gāo Chán, though pure,
strove for the bizarre and perilous,
with sparse meaning and scant reasoning,
truly a sinner against fēngyǎ.
Xuē Néng said to others:
"If I were to meet this gentleman,
I would wish to present him with a slap."
However, his poem on failing the imperial examination reads:
"In heaven, green peaches are planted with dew,
by the sun's side, red apricots lean against clouds to grow.
The lotus blooms upon the autumn river,
not blaming the east wind for its late blooming."
This is because he adhered to his humble station,
without a heart of restless competition,
and was thus praised among the high officials.
Earlier, Hú Zēng had a poem that said:
"When did the Hànyuàn ever
(Míng Dynasty manuscript has 'shí' instead of 'céng')
cease marrying off daughters,
when will the Wénchāng stop bearing sons?
The new cassia in Shànglín blooms year after year,
yet commoners are not allowed to pluck a single branch."
Luó Yǐn also wrote many poems of grievance and satire,
which made the sons of those in power resent him,
and thus only Chán achieved success in the examinations.
The elder poet Lǐ Hè's songs and verses,
displayed extraordinary talent and bizarre peril.
Even so,
I have often doubted their lack of reason.
Dù Mù once said:
"If Chángjí (Lǐ Hè) had added a bit more reason to his works,
he could have made even the poets of Sāo his servants."
From this, we know that sound criticism is not far off.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Lǐ Wèi
When Táng Chancellor Lǐ Wèi was stationed in Huáinán,
he had an old friend from humble days, a retired scholar Sūn,
who traveled a thousand miles without regard for distance,
coming directly to pay his respects.
Wèi kept him for a full month of leisurely stay.
One day, Sūn announced his departure,
and Lǐ, honoring their old friendship,
saw him off with a river excursion.
As they passed under a bridge,
the waves were swift and fierce,
and the boatman, turning the boat,
raised his pole and splashed water,
drenching the robes of a singing girl seated nearby
especially severely.
Lǐ grew very angry,
ordered the boatman seized,
and handed over to the authorities.
The retired scholar clasped his hands and stepped forward, saying:
"Because of this lavish farewell,
the fault is mine.
I dare to request brush and inkstone,
to briefly express my rustic thoughts."
Lǐ agreed,
and so he composed a "Willow Branch Lyric":
"Half-forehead adorned with delicate gold, gown of golden thread,
jade hairpins sway, paired phoenixes take flight.
Even if water splashes, dampening her silken skirt,
say instead she returns from morning rain's journey."
Lǐ read it,
his anger dissolved into joyful laughter,
and all the guests and attendants praised it.
He ordered musicians to sing the lyrics,
and they drank merrily until dusk,
with the boatman pardoned.
Furthermore, Lǐ Róng presented a poem that said:
"The rooster-tree's mist holds auspicious air congealed,
the phoenix-pool's waves await the jade mountain's clarity.
The state's people long lean on the eastern pass, gazing,
planning to build a sand causeway to Guǎnglíng."
He later indeed became chancellor.
From "Shūqíng Shī"
Lú Wò
Táng Left Chancellor Lú Wò,
the splendor of his carriages and official caps,
was unmatched in recent times,
with all four brothers occupying prominent positions.
In the early Qiánfú era,
after the mourning period for his mother ended.
Wò, from his former post as Zhōngshū Shèrén, was appointed Observation Commissioner of Shǎn Prefecture.
Ten days later,
his younger brother Shào, from his former post as Magistrate of Cháng'ān, was appointed Jǐshìzhōng.
Another ten days later,
his younger brother Hàng, from his former post as Collator at the Jíxián Academy, was appointed Left Shíyí.
Another ten days later,
his younger brother Zhǎo, from his post as a county official near the capital, was promoted to Investigating Censor.
Imperial edicts arrived in succession,
bringing honor to the scholar clans.

In the Táng dynasty, Hán Dìngcí served as secretary to Wáng Róng, military governor of Zhènzhōu.
He was sent on a diplomatic mission to Liú Réngōng, military governor of Yān,
and lodged at the guesthouse.
Liú ordered his staff member Mǎ Huò
(according to Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán, "Huò" is written as "Yù")
(the same below)
to receive and entertain him.
Mǎ presented a poem to Hán, which read:
"Amidst the燧forest and fragrant grass, thoughts linger endlessly;
All day we stroll together, ascending the splendid tower.
After parting, gazing from the heights of Kuánwù Mountain,
I envy you, who may yet again see Wáng Qiáo."
Though Mǎ's poem was elegant and refined,
its intent was to test Hán's learning.
Hán also responded with a poem at the banquet:
"A celestial guest upon the Chóngxiá Terrace,
Skilled in discerning the痴dragon, his arts are most profound.
With noble virtue, he excels in the银笔technique
(Míng manuscript reads 'technique' as 'narration')
His beautiful verses are worthy of Xuě'ér's songs."
All the guests present admired and marveled at the exquisite lines,
yet they were also puzzled by the obscure reference to the "silver brush."
Some days later,
Mǎ was again sent by the Yān military governor
on a return mission to Chángshān,
and Hán Dìngcí was ordered to receive him at the official guesthouse.
At that time, there was a courtesan named Zhuǎnzhuǎn,
whom Hán favored.
Whenever they were at a banquet,
Mǎ would frequently glance at her.
Hán said:
"In the past, Jìn Wéngōng gave Jì Wěi to Zhào Cuī,
and Sūn Bófú yielded Xiǎo Qiáo to Gōng Jǐn,
allowing beauty to be presented to men of renown.
Yet I fear this courtesan may not be worthy of a worthy man's regard.
I hope you will bestow a verse upon her,
so that I may present it to her."
Mǎ took up his brush,
and without pause,
composed a rhapsody on Zhuǎnzhuǎn.
The text was exceedingly beautiful,
and all admired its cleverness and elegance.
It subsequently spread far and wide.
Mǎ then casually asked Hán about the matters of Xuě'ér and the silver brush.
Hán replied:
"In the past, when Emperor Yuán of Liáng was still Prince of Xiāngdōng,
he was fond of learning and writing.
He often recorded loyal ministers, righteous men, and beautiful writings,
using brushes of three grades.
Some were adorned with gold and silver,
others were made of mottled bamboo for their shafts.
Those who were both loyal and filial were recorded with gold-shafted brushes;
those of pure and unsullied virtue were recorded with silver brushes;
and those with rich and beautiful writings were recorded with mottled bamboo brushes.
Thus, the reputation of the Prince of Xiāngdōng
spread throughout the region south of the Yangtze. As for Xuě'ér,
she was the beloved concubine of Lǐ Mì,
skilled in singing and dancing.
Whenever she saw writings by guests or colleagues
that were exceptionally beautiful and to her liking,
she would immediately set them to music and sing them."
Mǎ then asked from where the "痴dragon" originated.
Dìngcí said:
"There is a cave beneath Luòyáng.
Once, someone accidentally fell into it.
After walking several miles,
he gradually saw brightness and open space.
He saw palaces and people in nine places.
He also saw a large sheep.
The sheep had pearls on its beard,
which the man took and ate,
not knowing where he was.
Later, after emerging, he asked Zhāng Huá about it,
who said: 'This is the land of the nine immortal halls.
The large sheep
is called the痴dragon.'"
Dìngcí then asked Mǎ,
"Where exactly is Kuánwù Mountain?"
Mǎ replied:
"This is an old tale from the Suí lord,
why do you humble yourself to ask?"
From then on, the two admired and respected each other,
formed a friendship, and parted.
From Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán.
Yáo Yánjié was
a descendant of Duke Liáng, Yuán Chóng.
As a child, he was exceptionally intelligent and perceptive,
and by his youth, he was thoroughly versed in the ancient classics.
He admired Bān Gù and Sīmǎ Qiān in his writing,
and was regarded as a great scholar of his time.
He often indulged in poetry and wine, wandering freely in the Jiāngzuǒ region,
and was especially unrestrained in belittling his predecessors,
acting as if no one else was around.
During the Qiánfú era of the Táng dynasty,
Yán Biāo governed Póyáng Commandery.
When the鞠field and official buildings were first constructed,
he asked Yánjié to record the event.
The essay was completed,
brilliantly spanning over a thousand words.
Biāo wanted to delete a word or two,
but Yánjié flew into a rage,
and Biāo could not tolerate him.
By then, the stone had already been engraved,
so Biāo ordered the stele to be overturned on the ground
and the text ground away.
Yánjié composed a poem to record this:
"To inform Lord Yán, do you know me?
My heart is only in harmony with heaven.
Worldly matters before my eyes stir little emotion;
after wine, green mountains enter my dreams
(Míng manuscript reads 'dreams' as 'thoughts')
often.
Tián Zǐ, do not resent the弹铗lament;
Nìng Qí, cease singing the饭牛song.
If the sage court cares for the common people,
it should send its carriage to the薜萝vines."
When Lú Zhào governed Shèzhōu,
Yánjié was in Wùyuán.
He first sent his writings to Zhào.
Knowing that Yánjié was prone to drunken arrogance,
Zhào wrote a letter praising him
and sent him bolts of silk as gifts,
saying:
"After the ravages of war,
the commandery is in decline and impoverished,
unable to properly welcome a great worthy."
Yánjié then sent a long letter provoking him,
and Zhào had no choice
but to receive him at the commandery residence,
treating him with the courtesy due to a high official.
Yet Yánjié soon became increasingly arrogant and contemptuous toward Zhào.
Zhào once boasted to Yánjié with a verse:
"The bright moon shines upon the sky of Bā."
Yánjié laughed heartily and said:
"The bright moon shines upon the entire sky;
why mention only the sky of Bā?"
Zhào gradually grew displeased.
Not long after,
they met at a riverside pavilion.
At the time, Kuǎi Xīyì was also present.
Lú proposed a drinking game:
take something currently in sight as the theme,
with the name of a musical instrument at the end.
Zhào began with:
"Gazing afar at the fishing boat,
not wider than a chǐbā."
Yánjié immediately drank a vessel of wine,
leaned against the railing, and retched.
A moment later,
he returned to his seat
and responded with:
"Leaning on the railing, one retch,
already leaves the throat empty."
Such was his insolence and arrogance.
From Zhí Yán.
Dí Guīchāng.
When Emperor Xīzōng of Táng fled to Shǔ,
a poet inscribed a poem at the Mǎwéi Station:
"The misty willows of Mǎwéi linger tenderly,
as the imperial carriage returns to Shǔ once more.
Below the springs, Ā Mán surely has words:
this time, do not trouble Yáng Guìfēi again."
The name was not given,
and people admired the extraordinary talent.
This was actually the poem of Vice Minister Dí Guīchāng.
From Shū Qíng Shī.
Dù Xúnhè.
The Táng poet Dù Xúnhè once chanted a couplet:
"Old clothes, like ash and floc, floc;
new wine, from bamboo strainers,篘篘."
Someone mentioned this to Wéi Zhuāng,
who said:
"I would say: seals, with golden locks,锁锁;
curtains, with jade hooks,钩钩."
Later, Zhuāng became chancellor in Western Shǔ.
From Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán.
Military officers with literary talent: Cáo Jǐngzōng.
Liáng's Cáo Jǐngzōng repeatedly achieved military merits.
In the early years of Tiānjiàn,
he was summoned to serve as General of the Right Guard.
Later, after defeating the Wèi army and returning triumphantly,
the Emperor held a banquet at Huáguāng Hall with linked verse composition.
Left Deputy Shěn Yuē assigned the rhyme words,
but Cáo Jǐngzōng did not receive one,
appearing displeased in expression and demeanor,
and requested permission to compose a poem.
The Emperor said:
"You possess many skills and talents,
your abilities are outstanding and exceptional,
why must you limit yourself to just a poem?"
Cáo Jǐngzōng was already drunk,
and persistently begged to compose one.
An edict ordered him to compose using the two characters "jìng" and "bìng."
Cáo Jǐngzōng then took up the brush and completed it, saying:
"When leaving, children and wives grieve,
upon return, reed pipes and drums compete;
May I ask the passerby on the road,
How does this compare to Huò Qùbìng?"
The Emperor was endlessly delighted,
and thereupon promoted him to the rank of Duke.
From "The Biography of Cáo Jǐngzōng."
Gāo Áng
In Northern Qí, Gāo Áng, styled Áocáo,
surpassed others in courage and strength,
and his appearance and bearing were extraordinary.
His father, Cìtóng,
sought a strict teacher to instruct him.
Áng did not follow the teacher's teachings,
devoting himself entirely to galloping about.
He often said that a true man should roam freely under heaven,
seizing wealth and honor for himself;
who could sit properly reading books,
becoming an old academician?
His father, because of his proud and lofty demeanor,
thus named him so.
At the end of Eastern Wèi,
when Qí's Shénwǔ Emperor raised the banner of righteousness,
Áng wholeheartedly attached himself to him,
thereby aiding in the establishment of the hegemon's enterprise.
He was appointed Palace Attendant and Minister over the Masses,
concurrently Commander-in-Chief of the Southwest Circuit.
Yet Áocáo was passionately fond of composing poetry,
elegantly possessing emotional depth,
and was praised by contemporaries.
Once while accompanying the army,
he composed "The Road Is Hard" with Xiàngzhōu Governor Sūn Téng, saying:
"Rolling armor, driving far without rest,
six days and six nights, eating but three times.
At first they said we'd halt at Hǔláo,
then were redeployed north of Héqiáo.
Looking back, hope cut off, all turns bleak,
sorrow comes, wiping snowy tears, still I restrain myself."
He also had a campaign poem that said:
"A thousand sheep raised in the pen,
a hundred jars of wine by the spring.
Each morning encircling hills for the hunt,
every night welcoming a new bride."
Shortly after,
his younger brother Jìshì became Governor of Qí Prefecture,
and Áocáo sent a relay station messenger urging him to drink.
He then presented a poem, saying:
"Missing you, pitying you, longing stops me dead,
in heaven or on earth, nothing can compare.
Galloping by the sea, shooting roaming deer,
sitting askance on a rock, plucking the singing pheasant.
In former times, a Regional Governor aspired to the Three Excellencies,
today, the Minister over the Masses envies a Prefectural Governor."
There were many other pieces,
not recorded here.
From "Tán Sǒu."
Hèruò Bì
Suí's Hèruò Bì, styled Fǔbó,
had great ambitions from youth.
Brave and fierce, skilled with bow and horse,
capable of literary composition,
well-read in records and texts,
he held a renowned reputation.
When Suí Wén received the abdication,
he secretly harbored the ambition to pacify Jiāngnán.
Seeking someone capable of the task,
Gāo Jiǒng recommended Bì for his civil and military talents,
and he was appointed Commander-in-Chief,
entrusted with the matter of pacifying Chén.
Hèruò Bì gladly accepted it as his own responsibility.
Together with Shòuzhōu Commander-in-Chief Yuán Xióng, they formed key strongholds.
Hèruò Bì sent a poem, saying:
"At Jiāohé, the Cavalry General's tent,
at Hépǔ, the Wave-Quelling General's camp.
Let not the Qílín Pavilion above,
lack the names of us two men."
He presented ten strategies for pacifying Chén,
which met the Emperor's approval.
In the ninth year of Kāihuáng,
a grand campaign was launched against Chén,
with Hèruò Bì as Field Army Commander-in-Chief,
and he captured Chén Shūbǎo.
From "The Biography of Hèruò Bì."
Lǐ Mì
Suí's Lǐ Mì
was the son of Duke of Púshān, Kuān.
Initially appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Personal Guard,
it was not to his liking,
so he pleaded illness and returned home.
During the Dàyè era,
he assisted Yáng Xuángǎn in raising troops.
After Xuángǎn's defeat,
Mì traveled covertly into the passes,
fleeing until he reached Píngyuán.
The rebel leader Hǎo Xiàodé did not treat him with respect,
and encountering famine,
he resorted to scraping tree bark for food.
He then went to Suīyáng,
lodging in a village,
changing his name to Liú Zhīyuǎn,
gathering disciples to teach.
After several months,
finding no satisfaction,
he composed a five-character poem, saying:
"The golden wind stirs the autumn season,
jade dew withers the evening woods.
This night, a scholar at road's end,
pent-up sorrow wounds the inch-heart.
Gazing and listening, much indeed to feel,
impassioned, alone, I wet my lapel.
Wetting my lapel, for what purpose?
Melancholy, cherishing thoughts of antiquity.
Qín's customs are not yet pacified,
Hàn's way—on what can I hope?
Fán Kuài was a market butcher,
Xiāo Hé a clerk with knife and brush.
Once the time and fortune joined,
for ten thousand ages their names were passed down.
A message for the heroes of this world:
to live in vain is truly shameful."
When the poem was finished,
tears fell in several lines.
In the first year of Yìníng,
Mì usurpatively occupied Luòkǒu,
assembling a host of bandits a million strong,
built an altar and proclaimed himself Duke of Wèi.
In the second year of his reign period,
Mì, from Gǒngluò,
advanced with drums against Suí.
His army defeated, he submitted to Táng,
and was appointed Minister of the Imperial Household.
From "Records of Héluò."
Gāo Chóngwén
Táng Chancellor Gāo Chóngwén was originally a fierce general from Jìmén.
For his merit in suppressing Liú Pì,
he was appointed Military Commissioner of Xīchuān.
One day during heavy snow,
his various aides were chanting and admiring poems.
Chóngwén abruptly arrived at the drinking party,
and said with a laugh:
"You gentlemen enjoy yourselves,
yet pay no regard to this rustic fellow.
This rustic fellow is a military man,
but also has a poem on snow."
He then improvised orally:
"Chóngwén esteems war, not culture,
taking up spear, leaving the frontier, long following the army.
It's like a northern lad shooting flying geese,
white feathers falling thick and fast through the empty sky."
The poem hit the mark well,
and all said it was comparable to Northern Qí's Áocáo.
Grand Marshal Pián,
was his grandson.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Wáng Zhìxīng
Táng Dynasty Imperial Attendant Wáng Zhìxīng,
initially served as Military Commissioner of Xúzhōu,
possessing outstanding military strategy and heroic distinction,
enjoying a reputation that commanded the age.
Once his headquarters was established,
all those he recruited were renowned scholars.
One day, his staff officers were feasting together at the commissioner's compound,
composing poems with guests and friends.
This soon reached Wáng.
Wáng then summoned the Army Supervisor and they came together.
The staff officers consequently put away their writing materials,
and only used cups and trays to receive them.
After a long while, Wáng asked them:
"I just heard that the Administrative Aides and various worthies were composing poems;
why did you stop upon seeing me?"
He immediately ordered them to fetch brushes and inkstones again,
and had several sheets of colored paper laid out on the mat.
All the guests looked at each other with doubt.
After the wine was passed around and music began,
he said again:
"My original intention was to observe your literary compositions,
not to focus on drinking."
At that time, a minor clerk also placed paper and writing implements before Lord Wáng,
and the staff officers politely yielded with gestures of deference.
Wáng said:
"I rose from a military background,
and have never paid attention to literary composition.
Today, accompanying and serving you brilliant talents,
I cannot avoid also presenting my clumsy sincerity."
Thereupon, he took paper and grasped a brush,
and finished in a moment, saying:
"For thirty years, a veteran soldier am I,
Now forced by officials to compose poetry.
The flowers and willows of Jiāngnán you may sing of,
But the smoke and dust of Sàiběi, I alone know."
All those seated looked at it,
and were endlessly amazed and sighed.
At that time, the literatus Zhāng Hù also attended this banquet.
The Army Supervisor said to him:
"Witnessing this grand occasion,
how can you be without words?"
Hù immediately composed a poem at the banquet to present, saying:
"For ten years, entrusted with command, guarding the frontier regions,
Filial devotion and loyal principles, both you have in excess.
Who would believe that beyond the general's platform and excellent governance,
Lie Líng's verses and Yòujūn's calligraphy you possess."
Zhìxīng read it and laughed, saying:
"These words of praise and embellishment,
can be said to be excessive."
Those around him said:
"Scholars of that sort
are always given to flattery and sycophancy."
Zhìxīng rebuked them, saying:
"If someone spoke ill of me,
would you all be willing then?
Scholar Zhāng is a famous scholar within the seas,
how can one say he is easily obtained?"
When people under heaven heard of this,
they all considered Wáng Zhìxīng to delight in goodness.
He stayed for several weeks,
and upon parting, gifted him a thousand bolts of silk.
From "Jùtán Lù"
Gāo Pián
Táng Dynasty's Gāo Pián loved composing poetry from childhood,
elegantly possessing remarkable literary talent.
When expressing emotions and composing verses,
he surpassed the ordinary stream,
and those of his time who wielded the brush mostly could not match him.
Therefore, in the latter part of the Lǐ clan's reign,
when speaking of meritorious officials with literary skill,
Pián was foremost among them.
His collected works, encountering turmoil, were mostly lost;
those that survive today are widely circulated in his time.
His self-composed "Yánhuái Shī" says:
"I regret lacking a strategy to pacify the barbarians,
Ashamed to ascend the platform for appointing generals.
Holding the golden battle-axe feels heavy,
Wearing the iron armor, my body feels the cold.
With a sage ruler, aiding and supporting is easy,
With deep favor, repaying and serving is difficult.
The three frontiers are still not peaceful,
How dare I simply retire from office?"
His "Èrnǚ Miào Shī" says:
"Emperor Shùn went south on tour and did not return,
The two consorts' hidden sorrow lies between water and clouds.
How many pearly tears were shed back then?
Even until now, the bamboo still bears spots."
Also, his "Yǒng Xuě" says:
"When the sixth month's flowers drift into the door,
Sitting, I watch the tall bamboo turn into jade branches.
Hesitant, I'd better go up the high tower to gaze,
Covering all the evil forks in the paths of the human world."
Also, his "Tīng Gē" poem:
"The young lord invites joy under the moon-filled tower,
The beautiful woman raises the tune, singing Yīzhōu.
Then from the banquet mat, the autumn wind arises,
Reaching all the way to the water's end at Xiāoguān."
Also, his "Jì Sēng Qióngzhúzhàng Shī" says:
"Firm and light, the Qióng bamboo staff,
One staff has nine joints.
I send it to the monk of Wòzhōu,
For leisurely strolling under the autumn mountain moon."
From Xiè Pán's "Záshuō"
Luó Zhāowēi
Liáng Dynasty's Prince of Yè, Luó Zhāowēi, came from a family of military men for generations,
possessing courage and decisiveness,
but he admired and esteemed literature,
and was fond of Confucian scholars.
Beside his main hall,
he separately established a study hall,
inviting and hosting wandering scholars from all directions,
placing them within it,
and treating them with kindness and courtesy.
Every morning, during leisure from attending to affairs,
he would discuss the meanings of the classics with the various Confucians.
He amassed over ten thousand volumes of books,
and beside the study hall,
built a library tower,
allowing Confucian scholars to browse freely,
while he himself also diligently recited and read.
Among the regional governors of that time,
he gained the greatest reputation for literary composition.
Whenever he ordered his staff to draft letters and proclamations for the four directions,
if they slightly failed to meet his intent,
he would tear them up and discard them,
then fold paper and draft himself,
wielding the brush to complete the text.
Although lacking an ornate and beautiful style,
his staff mostly could not match him.
He was also particularly fond of seven-character regulated verse;
at every singing, drinking, banquet, or gathering,
or while strolling and sightseeing at ponds and pavilions,
he would invariably compose verses,
and inscribe them on the walls of buildings.
In Jiāngnán, there was one Luó Yǐn,
who served as a staff officer under Qián Liú of Liǎngzhè,
and possessed literary talent.
Zhāowēi specially sent envoys with gifts to establish relations and exchange visits,
expressing the respect of Nán Ruǎn.
Yǐn sent all his written essays, poems, and rhapsodies in return to Zhāowēi.
Zhāowēi greatly admired and yearned for him,
and even named his own composed poems "Luó Jiāngdōng."
Now among the people of Yè,
there are those who recite them.
He once wrote a "Tài Tīng Jì" himself,
which also has some merit worth viewing.
From "Luó Zhāowēi Zhuàn"
Zhào Yánshòu
The false Liáo Prime Minister Zhào Yánshòu,
son of Déjūn,
served the Táng as Chief Military Commissioner.
At the end of the Qīngtài era,
he fell captive from Tàiyuán,
and Yēlǜ Déguāng employed him as false Prime Minister,
overseeing state affairs.
When the young ruler of Jìn lost proper governance,
Yánshòu guided the barbarian king to create disorder.
Within just several years,
they unlawfully possessed central Xià,
which was truly achieved through Yánshòu's supportive efforts.
Yánshòu was the son of a military family,
trained in military strategy from childhood.
During leisure from military duties,
he would occasionally turn his mind to composing poetry,
and also possessed considerable elegance.
He once composed a poem in the barbarian court, saying:
"Yellow sand, wind-swept, tossed into the half sky,
Clouds shift over Yīnshān, snow fills the outskirts.
Water-searchers return, moving tents closer,
Arrow that shot the eagle falls, picked up with the bow.
Birds encountering frosty fruit, hungry still peck,
Horses crossing icy rivers, thirsty themselves gallop.
Having secured the high plain's fertile grassland,
Deep at night, they make fire, breaking off treetops."
Southerners who heard it
often passed it on.
From "Zhào Yánshòu Zhuàn"
Shàngguān Yí
Emperor Gāozōng, succeeding the Zhēnguàn era,
when all under heaven was without incident,
Shàngguān Yí alone held the reins of state.
Once, entering court at early dawn,
patrolling the dikes of the Luò River,
strolling under the moon, leisurely holding the reins,
he chanted a poem, saying:
"Silently, the broad river flows,
Driving my horse, I pass through the long isle.
Magpies fly, mountain moon dawns,
Cicadas drone, wild wind autumn."
The sound and rhythm were clear and bright,
and the assembled lords gazed at him as if he were an immortal.
From "Guóshǐ Yìzuǎn"
Dōngfāng Qiú
Left Scribe Dōngfāng Qiú often said:
"Two hundred years from now,
I beg to be paired with Xīmén Bào."
He was especially skilled in poetry.
Shěn Quánqī was famous for his skill in poetry,
Duke of Yān Zhāng Yuè once said to him:
"Brother Shěn the Third's poetry,
truly must be returned to him as the best."
From "Guó Shǐ Yì Zuǎn"
Sū Tǐng
Sū Tǐng was intelligent and talented from a young age,
able to read a thousand words at a glance.
On the second day of the sixth month in the second year of Jǐnglóng,
just after the internal crisis had been settled,
only
Míng transcript: "only" is used.
Tǐng served as a Secretary of the Central Secretariat,
in the rear pavilion of Tàijí Hall.
At that time, Tǐng was still young,
just beginning to take on heavy responsibilities,
with official documents and edicts piling up,
amounting to tens of thousands,
and sometimes people worried he couldn't handle it.
But Tǐng handled them orally and in writing,
without the slightest error.
Chief Clerks Hán Lǐ and Tán Zǐyáng transcribed the draft edicts,
and repeatedly said to Tǐng:
"We beg you to slow down a bit,
we can't keep up with the writing,
we fear our wrists will be worn out."
Secretariat Director Lǐ Qiào saw this,
and sighed:
"The Secretary's thoughts flow like a spring.
It is beyond what Qiào and others can fathom."
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Lǐ Yōng
Lǐ Yōng came to the capital from his post as a provincial governor to report on his administration.
Yōng had long been renowned for his talent,
but was frequently demoted and dismissed.
This was because Yōng was skilled in literature and supported scholars,
like Jiǎ Yí and Lord Xìnlíng.
Those in power envied his superiority,
and kept him relegated to provincial posts.
He had long enjoyed a fine reputation among the people,
but later generations did not know him.
In the capital's streets, crowds gathered to look at him,
thinking he was an ancient figure,
or that his appearance was extraordinary.
People in official attire, hearing of his fame,
sought out his home and lane to visit.
Moreover, palace eunuchs came to inquire,
asking for his new writings.
Yet he was again secretly slandered by others,
and ultimately could not advance or be reassigned.
In the early Tiānbǎo era,
he served as Prefect of Běihǎi in Jí Commandery.
His nature was extravagant
Míng transcript: "extravagant" is "refined"
and he did not bother with minor details of conduct,
indulging in hunting and unrestrained leisure.
Later, when Liǔ Jī was imprisoned,
Jí Wēn ordered Jī to implicate Yōng,
discussing matters of fortune and misfortune.
He had given generous bribes,
and the statements and charges implicated him.
An imperial decree initially
Míng transcript: "initially" is "Qí"
ordered Shùnzhī to handle it.
Luó Xīshì rushed there,
and executed him in the commandery.
Yōng had early on gained fame for his talent,
and was especially skilled at composing stele inscriptions.
The works he produced before and after,
amounted to several hundred pieces;
he received gifts and payments,
which also reached enormous sums.
Since ancient times, those who sold their writings for wealth,
none were like Yōng.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Lǐ Huá
Lǐ Huá was renowned for his literary talent by the end of the Tiānbǎo era.
During the Zhìdé era,
from his former post as Vice Director of the Bureau of Honors,
he was appointed as an assistant to Chancellor Lǐ Liánggōng Xiàn,
serving as Acting Vice Director of the Bureau of Appointments.
At that time, Chén Shǎoyóu was stationed in Wéiyáng,
and particularly admired his reputation.
One day,
the city gate officer reported that Huá had entered the prefecture.
Shǎoyóu was overjoyed,
and waited for him with his official cap and tablet ready.
After a short while,
it was reported again:
"He has already visited Xiāo, the Registrar."
Xiāo Yǐng was a Registrar.
From "Zhí Yán"
Lǐ Bái
When Lǐ Tàibái first arrived in the capital from Shǔ,
he stayed at an inn.
Hè Jiàn Zhīzhāng, hearing of his reputation,
was the first to visit him.
Marveling at his demeanor,
he then requested to see his writings.
Bái presented "Shǔ Dào Nán" for him to read.
Before even finishing it,
Zhīzhāng praised it repeatedly,
hailing him as a "banished immortal."
Bái was extremely fond of wine,
so Zhīzhāng took off his golden tortoise ornament to exchange for wine,
and they drank until thoroughly drunk.
They met almost daily without interruption,
and from then on, Bái's fame shone brilliantly.
Hè also saw his "Wū Qī Qū,"
and, sighing in admiration while reciting it with deep feeling, said:
"This poem could move ghosts and gods to tears."
The poem reads:
"When crows roost on the Gūsū Terrace,
the King of Wú's palace sees Xīshī drunk.
Wú songs and Chǔ dances, joy not yet ended,
the western hills still hold half the sun.
Golden pot, ding-ding, the water-clock runs much;
rising to see the autumn moon sink in river waves,
the east grows brighter—what can be done about this pleasure?"
Some say this is "Wū Yè Tí,"
and it is unclear which of the two pieces it is.
Also, "Wū Yè Tí" says:
"By the city walls of yellow clouds, crows wish to roost,
returning flying, caw-caw, crying on the branches.
At the loom weaving brocade, a woman of Qínchuān,
green gauze like mist, speaks through the window.
Stopping her shuttle, she asks about her former husband,
wishing to speak of Liáoxī, tears fall like rain."
Bái's talent was extraordinary and his spirit lofty,
his fame equaled that of Chén Shíyí Zǐ'áng,
and they shared virtue in succession.
His discourse on poetry stated:
"Since
[The character 'Liáng' was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy]
Liáng and Chén dynasties,
frivolous elegance has reached its extreme.
Shěn Xiūwén further valued tonal rules,
but to restore the ancient way,
who but me can do it!"
Emperor Xuánzōng heard of this
and summoned him to the Hànlín Academy.
Considering his literary talent surpassing others
and his capability and insight both abundant,
he placed him in a high position,
thus not appointing him to an official post.
Once, during palace entertainment,
he said to Gāo Lìshì:
"Facing such fine hours and beautiful scenes,
how can we entertain ourselves only with music and performers?
If we could sometimes get a talented poet to compose verses,
it could be boasted of to later generations."
So he ordered Bái summoned.
At that time, Prince Níng had invited Bái to drink,
and he was already drunk.
Upon arrival,
he bowed unsteadily.
The emperor, knowing he disdained tonal rules,
thought it not his strength,
and ordered him to compose ten five-character regulated poems on palace entertainment.
Bái kowtowed and said:
"Prince Níng bestowed wine upon your servant,
and now I am drunk.
If Your Majesty grants me fearlessness,
then I can fully employ my slight skill."
The emperor said:
"Granted."
Then he sent two eunuchs to support him by the arms,
ordered ink ground and brushes moistened for him,
and commanded two others to spread red-ruled paper before him.
Bái took the brush and expressed his thoughts,
hardly pausing,
and ten pieces were completed at once.
Without further revision,
the brushstrokes were vigorous and sharp,
like a phoenix alighting or a dragon seizing,
the tonal patterns and parallel couplets
were all exquisitely perfect.
The first piece reads:
"Willow colors, tender as gold,
pear blossoms, white as snow, fragrant.
Jade towers nest kingfishers,
pearl halls lodge mandarin ducks.
Selecting courtesans to follow carved chariots,
summoning songs from inner chambers.
Who ranks first in the palace?
Flying Swallow in Zhāoyáng."
Emperor Xuánzōng treated him with extreme favor and courtesy,
but Bái, with his unrestrained talent and conduct,
free-spirited and candid,
begged to return to his native mountains.
Xuánzōng also considered him unfit for court office,
and graciously issued an edict permitting it.
He once had a drunken poem:
"If heaven did not love wine,
the wine star would not be in heaven.
If earth did not love wine,
earth should have no Wine Spring.
Since heaven and earth both love wine,
loving wine, why feel ashamed?
Three cups connect to the great Way,
five pecks accord with nature.
Just grasp the delight within wine,
do not transmit it to the sober."
He also recalled Hè Jiàn Zhīzhāng in a poem:
"Wishing to go southeast,
with whom shall I raise my cup?
Mount Jīshān has no old Hè,
so I turn my wine boat back."
Later, in Xúnyáng,
he was again received by Prince Yǒng Lín,
and was repeatedly banished to Yèláng.
At that time, Dù Fǔ presented Bái a poem of twenty couplets,
mostly narrating these events.
Bái was later released and returned,
traveling to enjoy the landscapes south of the Yangtze.
He died at Cǎishí in Xuānchéng,
and was buried at Xiè Gōng's Green Mountain.
Fàn Chuánzhèng, as observation commissioner of Xuānshè,
erected a stele for him,
to mark his tomb path.
Initially, Bái loved wine from childhood;
while studying in Yǎnzhōu,
he drank often in daily life.
He also built a wine tower in Rénchéng County,
daily
[The character 'daily' was originally 'three,'
changed based on the Ming manuscript copy]
indulging in wild feasts there with like-minded friends,
rarely sober.
The locals, valuing Bái's great reputation,
respected him all the more for his weighty name.
From "Běnshì Shī."
Fáng Guǎn
Sūzhōu's Dòngtíng,
Hángzhōu's Xīngdé Temple.
Grand Councilor Fáng Guǎn said,
"Without visiting Xīngdé and Dòngtíng,
one has not seen fine places."
Shòu'ān County has the Spouting Jade Spring and Stone Stream,
both supremely scenic landscapes.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Guǎn, as a guest, declined a county magistrate post,
and cleared away overgrowth,
opening paths and tunnels,
amazing people who heard of it.
Early in the Tàihé era,
Cuī Méng of Bólíng served as chief clerk,
marking standards along the roads,
and people then began to visit.
Also, Grand Preceptor Yán Zhēnqīng carved his name on stone,
sometimes placing it atop high mountains,
sometimes sinking it to the depths of great isles,
saying,
"Who knows if there won't be changes of hill and valley?"
From "Zhuànjì."
Hán Yù
Hán Yù was fond of the extraordinary;
he and a guest climbed to the highest peak of Huà Mountain.
Realizing they could not return,
he wept wildly in distress,
and wrote a letter left
[The characters 'wrote a letter left' were originally 'left a letter,'
changed based on the Ming manuscript copy]
for the Huàyīn magistrate.
The magistrate devised every means to retrieve them,
and only then did they descend.
Also, a son of the Lǐ family served as Qiānniú Guard,
and with his companions climbed the pagoda of Cí'ēn Temple.
Reaching extreme heights and dangers,
he leaped outside the railing,
lost his footing and fell,
but his belt caught on a nail,
swayed by the wind,
and he hung for a long time without falling.
His climbing companions fainted inside the railing,
unable to rise again.
Monks in the courtyard saw from afar and urgently shouted;
the whole temple came out to rescue him,
tying clothes into a rope,
and after a long time brought him down.
He revived after a night.
From "Guóshǐ Bǔ."
Lǐ Yuē
Lǐ Yuē, the Vice Director of the Ministry of War,
was the son of Duke Qiān.
As a close relative of the prime minister's son,
he was elegantly fond of profound mysteries.
Serene and transcendent,
his moral conduct was excellent.
He also possessed the charm of mountains and forests,
and his skills in qin, wine, and poetry
were all unparalleled for a time.
Throughout his life, he never approached women,
