and he enjoyed receiving and guiding people,
but disliked vulgar conversation.
In the morning, he would wrap his head in grass,
face his guests with a frown,
and pass the entire day.
He collected many ancient artifacts;
in Rùnzhōu, he once obtained an ancient piece of iron,
which produced a clear and resonant sound when struck.
He also kept a gibbon named Shēnggōng,
often taking it with him.
On moonlit nights, he would drift on the river,
climb Jīnshān,
strike the iron and play the qin,
and the gibbon would always howl in harmony.
He would empty his wine pot until dusk,
without waiting for external guests,
and would not stop until he was drunk.
Yuē once served as an aide to the rebel Lǐ Qí in Zhèxī.
When Yuē first arrived in Jīnlíng,
he repeatedly praised the elegance of Zhāoyǐn Temple
while seated with his lord, the rebel Qí.
One day,
the rebel held a banquet at the temple.
The next day,
he said to Yuē:
"You often praised Zhāoyǐn Temple,
but after visiting and feasting there carefully yesterday,
how is it any different from the prefecture?"
Lǐ laughed and said:
"What I appreciate is its rustic wildness.
If distant mountains are covered with green curtains,
ancient pines are wrapped in colorful objects,
the deer's spring is stained with foul odors,
and music disrupts the songs of mountain birds,
then it truly is no better than being in my uncle's great hall."
The rebel laughed heartily.
Yuē also had a strong fondness for tea.
He could brew it himself.
He once said to others:
"Tea must be roasted over a slow fire
and brewed with a lively flame.
A lively flame refers to the flame of charcoal."
When guests arrived,
he would serve unlimited cups of tea,
holding the tea utensils tirelessly all day long.
Once, while on a mission, he passed east of Xiáshí County,
and, captivated by the clear flow of the canal water,
he forgot to depart for ten days.
From "Yīnhuà Lù."
Lù Hóngjiàn
Lù Hóngjiàn, the Erudite of the Crown Prince,
was named Yǔ.
His origins are unknown.
A monk surnamed Lù from Lónggài Temple in Jìnglíng
found a newborn baby on an embankment,
took him in and raised him,
and thus gave him the surname Lù.
When he grew up,
he was intelligent, handsome, and knowledgeable,
with extensive learning and elegant speech,
witty in conversation and debate,
like Dōngfāng Shuò and his peers.
Hóngjiàn had a strong fondness for tea
and pioneered the method of brewing tea.
To this day, tea merchants
make pottery statues of him
and place them among tin utensils,
believing it brings good fortune and profit for tea.
During the Tàihé era,
an old monk in Fùzhōu,
who claimed to be a disciple of Monk Lù,
often chanted a song:
"I do not envy piles of gold,
nor do I envy jade cups of white.
I do not envy entering the ministry in the morning,
nor do I envy entering the court at dusk.
I only envy the waters of the Xī River,
which once flowed beneath the walls of Jìnlíng."
Hóngjiàn also wrote the two-volume "Chá Jīng,"
which circulated in his time.
Today, those who make statues of Hóngjiàn
(in the Ming manuscript, it says "appearance")
regard him as the Tea God.
When transactions are made, tea is offered to him,
or boiling water is poured over him.
From "Chuánzǎi."
Dúgū Jí
Dúgū Jí of Chángzhōu
developed a particular fondness for playing the qin in his later years.
When he suffered from an eye disease, he ignored it,
intending to focus solely on listening.
From "Chuánzǎi."
Dù Jiān
Dù Jiān once collected ten thousand volumes of books.
At the end of each volume, he would inscribe:
"Copied with my salary and proofread by my own hand,
you who read this will understand the way of the sages.
To lose or sell it is unfilial."
From "Chuánzǎi."
Lǐ Déyù
Lǐ Déyù was amiable with his colleagues.
When someone asked about his preferences,
Déyù said:
"I enjoy seeing new books and strategies I have never heard of."
Duke Cuī Xuàn of Wèi loved to eat fresh steamed buns,
considering them a delicacy.
When hosting a banquet,
(the character "cóng" was originally missing,
"kāi" was originally "wén,"
amended according to "Běimèng Suǒyán")
the day before,
he would always go to the envoy's office to request
("suǒ" was originally "àn,"
amended according to "Běimèng Suǒyán")
freshly steamed buns.
Duke Dù Cóng of Yīn ate steamed rice and dried meat every morning.
Cuī Ānqián, the Palace Attendant, enjoyed watching bullfights.
Although each had their own preferences,
they were not driven by profit.
Compared to those who tally with ivory chips and line up gold,
or are obsessed with money and piles of grain,
are they not far superior?
From "Běimèng Suǒyán."
Pān Yàn
During the Xiánhēng era,
Pān Yàn of Bèizhōu was fond of shuānglù (a board game).
Wherever he went,
he never left the game board behind.
Once, while sailing at sea,
he encountered a storm and the boat wrecked.
Yàn held a plank with his right hand,
clutched the shuānglù board with his left,
and held the shuānglù dice in his mouth.
After two days and a night, he reached the shore.
His hands were worn to the bone,
but he never let go of the board,
and the dice remained in his mouth.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi."
Sòng Zhīsōng
Sòng Zhīsōng, the Assistant Magistrate of Luòyáng County, had a fondness for singing.
He was appointed as the Military Advisor of Liánzhōu.
The prefect, Chén Xīgǔ,
was a mediocre man.
He ordered Zhīsōng to teach the maidservants to sing.
Every day, Zhīsōng would stand in the courtyard holding his tablet,
singing softly.
The maidservants would harmonize with him from behind the window,
and those who heard it could not help but laugh.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi."
Zhū Qiányí
Zhū Qiányí, the Director of the Ministry of War, was ugly in appearance,
but his wife was beautiful.
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
at a wine shop west of Zhíyè Ward in Luòyáng,
there was a maidservant with disheveled hair and a dirty face,
hunched shoulders and a protruding belly—
a repulsive appearance
unmatched in the world.
Yet Qiányí was greatly pleased by her,
almost forgetting to eat and sleep.
This shows that the ancient tale of Sùliú being loved
is indeed not false.
How varied are the desires of people in this world!
I have heard that King Wén of Zhōu loved chāngpú (calamus),
the King of Chǔ loved celery pickles,
Qū Dào loved water caltrops,
Zēng Xī loved jujubes,
and Liú Yōng of Sòng loved scabs.
The biography states:
"Yōng visited the former Wúxīng Prefect Mèng Língxiū.
When Língxiū removed his socks,
a roasted scab fell to the ground.
Yōng bent down, picked it up, and ate it."
Emperor Míng of Sòng loved honey-preserved wasps,
eating several shēng at a time.
This shows that the tale of chasing foul odors by the sea
and the story of Lord Chén loving ugliness—
how strange they are!
Heaven grants such obsessions.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi."
Xiānyú Shūmíng
Xiānyú Shūmíng, the military governor of Jiànnán Dōngchuān, was fond of eating stink bugs,
which people at the time called "pán chóng."
Each time he held a gathering,
he would have people gather three to five sheng of them,
then float them in lukewarm water
to draw out all their odor.
He would then fry them with butter and various seasonings,
roll them in a pancake, and eat them,
claiming their flavor was truly excellent.
From "Gānzǐ."
Quán Chángrú
At the end of the Chángqìng era,
Quán Chángrú, former magistrate of Fújiàn County
(Míng manuscript: "County" as "Court")
was exiled and demoted for committing an offense.
Later, because he was a close relative of the former Minister of Rites and Chancellor Déyú,
he was granted amnesty and had his official status restored.
He lingered in Guǎnglíng for many days,
and when he met with guests and officials,
they all looked down on him.
As he was about to go to the capital to seek an official post,
before his departure,
a group of gentlemen held a farewell banquet for him at the Chánzhì Temple.
The eccentric scholar Jiǎng Chuán knew that Chángrú had a fondness for human fingernails.
So, from soldiers and various laborers,
he paid a small fee
to obtain several liǎng of trimmed fingernails.
Some were not thoroughly cleaned,
so he wrapped them in paper.
Waiting until Chángrú was deep in his cups, he presented them, saying:
"Your Honor is traveling far,
and I have nothing to offer as a farewell gift.
Now I have a small delicacy
that I dare to present."
He then offered them to Chángrú.
Chángrú looked at them,
beaming with delight,
as if he had received a gift of a thousand gold pieces.
Saliva flowed from his lips,
and he scooped them up and ate them continuously,
looking utterly content.
Everyone present was astonished.
From "Gānzǐ."
Zhū Qiányí
Zhū Qiányí, a Vice Director of the Ministry of War, was ugly in appearance,
but his wife was beautiful.
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
at a tavern west of the Zhíyè Ward in Luòyáng,
there was a maidservant with disheveled hair and a dirty face,
hunched shoulders and a bulging belly—
a repulsive sight
unmatched anywhere in the world.
Yet Qiányí was greatly fond of her,
nearly forgetting to eat or sleep.
This shows that the ancient tale of the hunchbacked woman winning love
is indeed not false.
Human desires in this world—
how strangely they differ!
I have heard that King Wén of Zhōu loved pickled fish,
the King of Chǔ loved celery pickles,
Qū Dào loved water caltrops,
Zēng Xī loved jujubes,
and Liú Yōng of Sòng loved scabs.
The biography states:
"Yōng visited the former Governor of Wúxīng, Mèng Língxiū.
When Língxiū removed his socks,
a roasted scab fell to the ground,
and Yōng bent down, picked it up, and ate it."
Emperor Míng of Sòng loved honey-preserved cicadas,
eating several shēng each time.
This shows that the tale of the man who chased after foul odors by the sea,
and the story of Lord Chén's fondness for ugliness—
how bizarre they are!
Heaven grants such peculiarities.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi."
Xiānyú Shūmíng
Xiānyú Shūmíng, the military governor of Jiànnán Dōngchuān, was fond of eating stink bugs,
which people at the time called "pán chóng."
Each time he held a gathering,
he would have people gather three to five sheng of them,
then float them in lukewarm water
to draw out all their odor.
He would then fry them with butter and various seasonings,
roll them in a pancake, and eat them,
claiming their flavor was truly excellent.
From "Gānzǐ."
Quán Chángrú
At the end of the Chángqìng era,
Quán Chángrú, former magistrate of Fújiàn County
(Míng manuscript: "County" as "Court")
was exiled and demoted for committing an offense.
Later, because he was a close relative of the former Minister of Rites and Chancellor Déyú,
he was granted amnesty and had his official status restored.
He lingered in Guǎnglíng for many days,
and when he met with guests and officials,
they all looked down on him.
As he was about to go to the capital to seek an official post,
before his departure,
a group of gentlemen held a farewell banquet for him at the Chánzhì Temple.
The eccentric scholar Jiǎng Chuán knew that Chángrú had a fondness for human fingernails.
So, from soldiers and various laborers,
he paid a small fee
to obtain several liǎng of trimmed fingernails.
Some were not thoroughly cleaned,
so he wrapped them in paper.
Waiting until Chángrú was deep in his cups, he presented them, saying:
"Your Honor is traveling far,
and I have nothing to offer as a farewell gift.
Now I have a small delicacy
that I dare to present."
He then offered them to Chángrú.
Chángrú looked at them,
beaming with delight,
as if he had received a gift of a thousand gold pieces.
Saliva flowed from his lips,
and he scooped them up and ate them continuously,
looking utterly content.
Everyone present was astonished.
From "Gānzǐ."
Liú Xiànzhī
Liú Xiànzhī of the Northern Wèi dynasty was studious from a young age,
especially proficient in the "Book of Songs" and its commentaries,
and widely read in the works of various philosophers and histories.
When he came across the writings of the Legalist school,
he closed the scroll and laughed, saying:
"If figures like Yáng Zhū and Mòzǐ
had not written such books,
who would know, even after a thousand years, how little they amount to?"
He also said to those close to him:
"Reading Qu Yuán's 'Lísāo,'
it is clear he was a madman—
what a pity his death was!"
When people came to study under him,
Xiànzhī would say:
"Though there are a hundred paths to establishing oneself,
measured against the four categories of virtue,
moral conduct must come first.
If you can practice filial piety at home and brotherly respect outside,
be loyal, trustworthy, benevolent, and yielding,
then even without stepping out your door,
the world will know of you.
If you cannot do this,
even if you study behind curtains, prick your thigh to stay awake,
or tread in the footsteps of teachers,
you will only gain broad knowledge and a strong memory.
At most, you will be like a clay dragon praying for rain—
deceiving future generations.
What good is that for establishing oneself in life?
Even the disciples of Confucius
did not understand this at first.
It was only after hearing the sigh of Wúqiū
that they returned home to care for their parents.
Alas!
How late these early sages came to learn this!"
As a result, scholars from all directions admired him.
He sighed and said:
"I am far inferior to Zhuāng Zhōu, who was as useless as a rotten tree."
Thus, he firmly declined on grounds of illness.
From "Tán Sǒu."
Lú Jǐngyù
Lú Jǐngyù of Fànyáng
was the son of Tàicháng Jìng
and the nephew of Minister Tóng.
From a young age, he enjoyed quiet and solitude,
immersing himself in the classics and histories.
He upheld the Way with reverence and simplicity,
never harboring thoughts of glory or profit,
and was thus known as a "recluse."
Early on, a tuft of white hair grew on his head,
numbering forty-nine strands,
which is why he particularly favored the "Lǎozi" and "Yìjīng."
He wrote commentaries on them.
He died at the age of forty-nine,
hence his childhood nickname "White Head."
He was upright and cautious by nature;
even in a dark room,
he maintained a dignified demeanor.
During the hottest months,
he never bared his body.
Even when facing his wife and children,
he was as formal as with honored guests.
He served as Vice Director of the Secretariat.
From "Tán Sǒu."
Xiāo Déyán
Xiāo Déyán of the Tang dynasty was steadfast in his dedication to learning.
Whenever he opened the Five Classics,
he would wash his hands, tidy his attire,
and sit upright to face them.
His wife said to him:
"You do this all day long—
is it not too tiring?"
Déyán replied:
"To revere the words of the ancient masters,
how could I fear such effort!"
From Tán Bīn Lù.
Zhāng Chǔjīn
Zhāng Chǔjīn and Yuè Shí were both candidates for the provincial recommendation for the jìnshì examination.
The provincial officials intended to dismiss Yuè Shí and recommend Chǔjīn instead.
Chǔjīn declined, saying:
"In terms of seniority, Yuè Shí is the elder;
in terms of talent, I, Chǔjīn, am not his equal."
He firmly requested that both be withdrawn.
Lǐ Jì, serving as military governor,
sighed and said:
"The purpose of recommending scholars is to seek both virtue and talent.
To defer to each other like this—
why hesitate to recommend both?"
He then recommended them, and both passed the examination.
From Tán Bīn Lù.
Shěn Yuē
Wáng Yún of Liánglángyá, from a young age, was pure and outstanding,
with literary talent that was extraordinary and brilliant,
and was admired by Shěn Yuē.
When Shěn served as President of the Department of State Affairs,
Yún was a court gentleman.
Shěn said to Yún:
"In the past, I, along with various worthies like Wáng and Xiè,
enjoyed gatherings for literary appreciation.
Since their passing,
decline and illness have followed one after another.
The pleasures of my lifetime
have nearly all ceased.
Yet the composition of prose and poetry,
this pursuit has not waned.
I did not expect that in my weary old age,
I would again encounter such splendid virtue.
Cài Yōng, upon seeing Wáng Càn, sighed and said:
'This is the grandson of Lord Wáng.
I have ten thousand volumes of books at home;
I must share them with him.'
Though I am not talented,
I wish to emulate these words."
Whenever they deliberated on historical texts,
perused
(The character "liú" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy)
literary works,
they would continue until deep into the night,
considering it a delight of fulfilled aspirations.
Yún later held positions including Left Chief Clerk of the Minister over the Masses and Minister of Revenue.
From Tán Sǒu.
Táng Gāozōng
Hú Chǔbīn was swift in composing texts,
often writing only after drinking to mild intoxication.
Whenever Emperor Gāozōng ordered him to write,
he would have wine served in gold and silver cups.
He would order him to drink,
and then bestow the cup upon him.
From Tán Bīn Lù.
Empress Tiānhòu
When Empress Wǔ Zétiān visited Lóngmén,
she ordered her attending officials to compose poems.
The Left Historiographer Dōngfāng Qiú finished his poem first,
and Zétiān bestowed a brocade robe upon him.
When Sòng Zhīwèn completed his poem,
Zétiān praised its diction as even loftier,
and took back the robe to bestow upon him.
From Tán Bīn Lù.
Yuán Qiányào
Yuán Qiányào, because his memorials pleased the emperor,
gained the emperor's favor.
He was then rapidly promoted,
serving successively as Vice Minister of Revenue, Governor of the Capital Prefecture, and up to Chancellor.
One day,
the emperor spoke privately with Gāo Lìshì, saying:
"Do you know why I promoted Qiányào so quickly?"
Lìshì replied:
"I do not know."
The emperor said:
"It is because his appearance and speech resemble Xiāo Zhìzhōng's,
so I employed him."
Lìshì responded:
"Did Zhìzhōng not once betray Your Majesty?
Why does Your Majesty remember him so fondly?"
The emperor said:
"Zhìzhōng made erroneous plans only in his later years.
At the beginning of his court service,
could he not be called a worthy chancellor?"
The emperor's love for talent and forgiveness of faults
moved all who heard of it to admiration and joy.
From Guó Shǐ Bǔ.
Zhāng Jiànfēng
Cuī Yīng was by nature unruly.
Zhāng Jiànfēng admired his literary talent,
took him as a guest,
and brought him along on military campaigns.
One night, Cuī Yīng shouted loudly, alarming the army.
The soldiers were furious,
wanting to devour his flesh.
Jiànfēng hid him.
The next day, a banquet was held.
The army supervisor said:
"I have an agreement with you, Minister:
neither shall go against the other."
Jiànfēng said:
"Agreed."
The supervisor said:
"I have a request:
hand over Cuī Yīng."
Jiànfēng said:
"As agreed."
He hesitated.
Then Jiànfēng said:
"I also have a request:
I ask for Cuī Yīng back."
Everyone at the banquet laughed.
Cuī Yīng was thus spared.
From Guó Shǐ Bǔ.
Lǐ Shí
Lǐ Shí served as Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries,
pressing urgently for the collection of official land taxes.
Xiāo Yòu was in mourning,
and failed to deliver his payment on time.
Lǐ Shí was angry
and summoned him.
Just then, the cart carrying the tax grain arrived,
so Yòu avoided punishment.
It happened that there was an imperial bestowal,
requiring a letter of gratitude.
The usual writer was unavailable due to some reason.
Lǐ Shí, in a hurry,
said:
"Summon the one wearing the coarse mourning clothes."
Yòu arrived
and immediately drafted the letter.
Lǐ Shí was greatly pleased
and recommended him at the Yányīng Hall.
Emperor Dézōng ordered an inquiry into the mourning period,
counting the days until its end.
The day after Yòu completed mourning,
he was appointed from a common scholar to Reminder.
Yòu was skilled in literature,
good at painting,
and fond of playing the qín.
His promotion, however, was rather fortuitous.
From Guó Shǐ Bǔ.
Hán Yù
Lǐ Hè, styled Chángjí,
was a descendant of the Tang imperial clan.
His father, Lǐ Jìnsù,
served as an official on the frontier.
At the age of seven,
Hè gained fame in the capital for his poems in irregular meter.
At that time, Hán Yù and Huángfǔ Shí admired Hè's literary works,
marveling at them but not knowing the man himself.
They thus said to each other:
"If he were an ancient,
it would be understandable that we do not know him.
But if he is a contemporary,
how could there be any reason for us not to know him?"
It happened that someone spoke of Jìnsù's whereabouts,
so the two gentlemen rode together to his door,
requesting to see his son.
Soon, a boy with hair tied in two tufts and wearing a lotus-leaf garment came out.
The two gentlemen did not believe it was him,
and thus tested him on the spot with a composition.
Hè received the command with delight,
took up his writing brush and ink,
as if no one else were present.
He then titled it "Gāo Xuān Guò" (The Grand Carriage Passes By).
It read:
"Silken robes woven with emerald green like scallions,
Golden rings press the reins, tinkling with a delicate sound.
The horses' hooves rumble faintly, their tread resounding,
Dismounting at the gate, their aura like a rainbow.
They say these are talents from the Eastern Capital,
Masters of literature, grand and profound.
The twenty-eight constellations arrayed within their breasts,
Composing rhapsodies before the palace, their voices grind the sky.
Their brushes mend creation, Heaven's work surpassed,
The primal essence shines brightly, piercing through the core.
This bushy-browed scholar, moved by autumn's withered grass,
Who knew dead straw could be revived by glorious winds?
Now I, with drooping wings, bear the heavenly swan,
But in days to come, I'll feel no shame—a snake shall become a dragon."
The two gentlemen were greatly astonished,
and then, with the horses they had ridden,
invited him to ride side-by-side back to their residence,
personally tying up his hair.
Before he reached the age of twenty,
he observed mourning for his mother's passing.
Later, when he sat for the imperial examinations,
some slandered Hè for not avoiding his family's taboo name.
Master Wén (Hán Yù) at that time wrote an essay disputing taboos.
Unfortunately, Hè died before reaching the prime of his life.
From "Zhí Yán" (Collected Sayings).
Furthermore, Hán Yù, in guiding later generations,
recommended them for the examinations,
and many sent letters seeking his advice.
Contemporaries called them "Disciples of Hán's School."
Later, when he held high office,
he no longer engaged in this.
From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ" (Supplements to the National History).
Yáng Jìngzhī
Yáng Jìngzhī loved talent and was fair-minded.
He once recognized a scholar from the Jiangnán region named Xiàng Sī,
and presented him with a poem that read:
"Everywhere I see your poems, each one excellent,
But upon meeting your character, it surpasses even the verse.
All my life I've never known how to conceal others' merits,
Wherever I go, I speak of Xiàng Sī."
Because of this, Xiàng Sī achieved high rank in the examinations.
From "Shàngshū Gù Shí" (Old Stories of the Department of State Affairs).
Lú Zhào
Wáng Liáo was richly talented,
yet failed the examinations multiple times.
His disciple Lú Zhào and others
recommended him to the Ministry of Rites, saying,
"If allies do not succeed one another,
the worthy are ridiculed.
Seeing a son bearing firewood,
even a fine minister invites mockery."
They then praised Liáo's fine lines:
"Striking a stone easily yields fire,
but knocking on a person's heart is hard to move.
Those today within vermilion gates,
once hated how deep those gates were."
His reputation flourished abundantly.
Indeed, he was selected for the highest rank.
From "Shūqíng Shī" (Lyrical Poems).
Líng Hú Táo
When Emperor Xuānzong held court,
and the officials in turn approached before him,
he would always wait until their breath was calm and even,
before then inquiring about matters.
Líng Hú Táo recommended Lǐ Yuǎn for the post of Prefect of Hángzhōu.
Emperor Xuānzong said:
"I have heard Lǐ Yuǎn's poem says,
'Long days are spent only on a single game of chess.'
How can he be entrusted with governing a commandery?"
Táo replied:
"A poet's words
are not necessarily grounded in reality."
He further recommended Yuǎn as incorruptible and fit for the task,
and the emperor consented.
From "Yōu Xián Gǔchuī" (Leisurely鼓吹).
Cuī Xuàn
Shàngshū Zhèng Yú,
a native of Guǎngzhōu,
achieved the jìnshì degree.
The character 'shì' originally followed 'dì' (degree),
deleted according to "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán" (volume 3).
He served in prominent and illustrious posts.
His reputation was high, and he had a fondness for splendor,
using brocade to make a half-sleeved jacket.
When Duke Wèi, Cuī Xuàn, governed Jīngnán,
Zhèng Yú was appointed Military Commissioner of Guǎngnán.
Passing through Zhǔgōng on his route,
Xuàn received him with ordinary courtesy.
When Zhèng was a jìnshì candidate,
he had never presented his writings at Duke Wèi's door,
but now he offered his works as a gift.
Duke Wèi read them,
and deeply sighed in admiration, saying:
"This truly deserves the half-sleeved jacket."
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán" (Trivial Words from a Northern Dream).
Kǒng Zhìguī
Kǒng Zhìguī of Qí, from Kuàijī,
was the son of Guānglù (Minister of Imperial Banquets) Língchǎn,
grandson of Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) Dàolóng,
and the younger brother of Zhāng Róng's wife.
Zhìguī was deeply learned,
and maintained gentlemanly friendships with Lù Sīxiǎo and Xiè Yuè.
Guī took no pleasure in worldly affairs;
the weeds in his courtyard grew tall enough to hide a person.
To the south were mountain ponds,
where frogs croaked in spring.
Púyè (Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat) Wáng Yàn once visited him with sounding pipes and drums,
and hearing the chorus of frogs,
Yàn said:
"These are quite clamorous to the ear."
Guī replied:
"When I listen to your '鼓吹' (processional music),
it hardly compares to this."
Yàn wore a look of shame.
Guī served successively as Zhānshì (Supervisor) of the Crown Prince's Household.
He was posthumously granted the title Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Imperial Banquets).
From "Tán Sǒu" (A Bag of Conversations).
Lǐ Yuánchéng
Lǐ Yuánchéng of Běi Qí, from Zhàojùn,
was the grandson of Jùlù Zhēn Gōng (Duke Zhēn of Jùlù) Huī,
and great-grandson of Jùlù Jiǎn Gōng (Duke Jiǎn of Jùlù) Língzhī.
The original text had 'zhī gōng' for 'Língzhī',
amended according to "Běi Qí Shū" (vol. 22, Biography of Lǐ Yuánzhōng).
Great-grandson.
His nature was unrestrained and unconventional;
he cared not for worldly affairs,
considering drinking his primary occupation.
While serving as Tàicháng Qīng (Minister of Imperial Sacrifices),
Tàizǔ (Emperor) intended to appoint him as Púyè (Vice Director),
but doubted his excessive drinking.
His son Sāo admonished him,
but Yuánchéng said:
"I say being Púyè is not as enjoyable as drinking.
You
The original had 'ěr' (ear),
amended according to the Ming manuscript copy.
if you value the Púyè post,
should refrain from drinking."
Xíngtái Shàngshū (Secretary of the Mobile Secretariat) Sīmǎ Zǐrú and Sūn Téng
once visited Yuánchéng.
His courtyard was overgrown and desolate,
the surrounding walls dilapidated and crumbling.
He was beneath a tree,
wrapped in a quilt,
facing a single pot alone,
immersed in blissful contentment.
Then they saw
The character 'jiàn' (saw) was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Ming manuscript copy.
his wife,
her garments not even touching the ground.
She removed the sitting mat,
pawned it for wine and meat,
to fulfill their joyful intentions.
The two gentlemen sighed in admiration,
each providing provisions and gifts,
which he accepted without refusal,
but distributed among relatives and friends.
Yuánchéng was also named Yuánzhōng.
He was appointed Yítóng (Equal in Honor to the Three Excellencies),
concurrently commanded the Wèiwèi (Palace Guard),
and was enfeoffed as Duke of Jìnyáng.
Upon his death, he was posthumously granted the title Sītú (Minister of Education),
with the posthumous name Wénxuān.
From "Tán Sǒu" (A Bag of Conversations).
Táo Hóngjǐng
Táo Hóngjǐng of Dānyáng was intelligent from a young age,
and widely versed in the classics and histories.
Upon reading Gé Hóng’s Biographies of Divine Immortals,
he became determined to cultivate life.
He often said that gazing up at the azure clouds and bright sun
did not seem distant to him.
Initially, he served as Study Companion to the Prince of Yídū,
and later was promoted to Court Attendant.
During the Yǒngmíng era
(Originally written as “Shuǐpíng”;
according to the Biography of Táo Hóngjǐng in Liangshu, juan 51, he submitted a memorial resigning his salary in the tenth year of Yǒngmíng,
hence corrected)
he resigned his post and retired to Mount Máo.
This mountain is a cavern-heaven of Jīnlíng,
with a circumference of one hundred and fifty li,
named the Huāyáng Cavern-Heaven.
It contains the residence of the Three Máo Directors of Fate,
hence it was called Mount Máo.
Thereafter, he called himself the Huāyáng Recluse,
and in all correspondence with the secular world,
he used this name instead.
He was like Xuán Yàn of Shì’ān
or Bàopǔ of Zhìchuān.
He especially loved forests and springs,
and was particularly fond of writing.
Officials and commoners who revered the Way and admired him,
following his influence and emulating his style,
traveled a thousand li to visit him.
The master once said:
“I have read fewer than ten thousand volumes of secular books;
even including esoteric texts,
it is only a modest achievement.”
Emperor Gāozǔ of Qí asked him:
“What is there in the mountains?”
Hóngjǐng replied with a poem,
the words of which were:
“What is there in the mountains?
On the ridges, many white clouds.
They can only delight myself;
I cannot take them to give to you.”
Emperor Gāozǔ admired it.
From Tán Sǒu.
Tián Yóuyán
In the Táng, Tián Yóuyán was repeatedly summoned for his Confucian learning but did not respond,
instead retiring with his mother to Mount Sōng.
During the Gānlù era,
Emperor Zhōngzōng visited the Central Peak,
and upon visiting his dwelling,
Yóuyán came out to pay respects.
An edict ordered Vice Director of the Secretariat Xuē Yuánchāo to enter and inquire after his mother,
and the emperor inscribed on his gate:
“Dwelling of Recluse Tián Yóuyán.”
He was summoned and appointed Erudite of the Hóngwén Academy.
From Hànlín Shèngshì.
Zhū Táozhuī
was a man of Shǔ.
He was indifferent and non-active,
living in seclusion without taking office.
Clad in fur and rope belts,
he drifted among the human world.
When Dòu Guǐ governed Yìzhōu,
he heard of him and summoned him.
He sent him clothing
and pressured him to become a village head.
Táozhuī withdrew without a word,
fleeing into the mountains.
In summer he went naked,
in winter he covered himself with tree bark.
All gifts presented to him
he utterly refused.
He wove straw sandals
and left them on the road.
Those who saw them said,
“These are Master Zhū’s sandals.”
They would sell them for rice
and place it at the original spot.
Táozhuī would fetch it at dusk,
but was never seen by anyone.
When Gāo Shìlián assumed office,
he deeply honored him with courtesy.
Summoned to meet him,
Shìlián descended the steps to speak with him.
Táozhuī answered once,
then immediately left.
Shìlián often praised him as exceptional,
and the people of Shǔ considered it a fine tale.
From Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ.
Lú Hóng
Emperor Xuánzōng summoned Lú Hóng, a recluse of Mount Sōng,
and only after three edicts did he come.
At the audience,
he did not bow,
only bending slightly at the waist.
Asked the reason,
Hóng replied:
“Your servant has heard Lǎozǐ say,
‘Ritual is the thinning of loyalty and trust,
not worth relying on.’
Your mountain servant Hóng
dares to offer loyalty and trust to Your Majesty.”
Xuánzōng found him remarkable,
summoned him to a banquet,
appointed him Reminder,
and bestowed court robes,
all of which he declined and did not accept.
He was given a hundred shí of rice
and a hundred bolts of silk,
and sent back to his hermitage.
From Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ.
Yuán Jié
During the Tiānbǎo rebellion,
Yuán Jié led his neighbors from Rǔ Fén
south to Xiāng-Hàn in great numbers,
preserving over a thousand households.
He then raised a righteous army between Wǎn and Yè,
displaying the strength to defend cities and resist bandits.
Jié studied under Zhōng Xíngzǐ during Tiānbǎo.
First, in the Shāngyú mountains, he called himself Yuánzǐ;
fleeing troubles, he entered the Yīyú mountains and called himself Yīyúzǐ,
or sometimes Làngshì.
Fishermen called him the Old Man.
Drinkers called him the Unrestrained Old Man.
When he became an official,
he was called the Unrestrained Gentleman.
From Guóshǐ Bǔ.
Hè Zhīzhāng
Hè Zhīzhāng was unrestrained by nature,
eloquent and witty in conversation,
admired by all worthies of his time.
Lù Xiàngxiān was Zhīzhāng’s maternal cousin,
and Zhīzhāng was especially close to him.
Xiàngxiān said to others:
“Brother Hè’s speech and demeanor
truly make him a man of refined grace.”
In his later years, he became unrestrained and eccentric,
with no more restraint or discipline.
He called himself the Mad Guest of Sìmíng,
and after getting drunk, composing verses,
they readily formed chapters and scrolls,
written without corrections,
all quite commendable.
He was also skilled at cursive and clerical script,
and enthusiasts passed them around as treasures.
He requested to become a Daoist priest and return home,
donating his residence as a temple,
which the emperor permitted.
He also had his son appointed as Sima of Kuàijī Commandery.
The emperor composed a poem to send him off.
From Tán Bīn Lù.
Gù Kuàng
Gù Kuàng’s aspirations leaned toward detachment and freedom,
close to those beyond the世俗.
A certain chief minister once summoned him,
intending to offer him a good official post.
Kuàng replied with a poem:
“All under heaven is now at peace;
why does the minister summon this madman?
This body still resembles a crane in a cage,
gazing east toward the vast sea, crying out a few times.”
Later, in Wúzhōng, it was said that Kuàng attained the Way and transformed, departing this world.
From Shàngshū Gùshí.
Chén Shū was
the son of Chén Hóng.
Hóng, together with Bó Jūyì, transmitted the "Song of Everlasting Sorrow."
His literary style was of the highest order,
truly a fine historian.
During the Xiántōng era (860-874),
he served as an aide in the administration of Guō Chángshì Quán, the Surveillance Commissioner, in Xúzhōu.
His nature was particularly upright and principled;
he would not associate with those he deemed unworthy.
In the same office, there was a minor clerk surnamed Wǔ,
also a descendant of Chancellor Wǔ Yuánhéng,
and indeed a son-in-law of the Fényáng Prince (Guō Zǐyí).
Chén Shū felt this situation was unjust,
so he took his family and settled at Máo Mountain.
He lived separated from his wife and children by the mountain,
wearing short coarse garments tied with a cord,
burning incense and practicing meditation, nothing more.
Perhaps once a year or half a year,
he would briefly meet his wife and children.
During his time in office,
only the elder monk of Liúgōu Temple associated with him intimately,
and they also met wearing short coarse garments.
He himself composed three volumes of the *Zàn Sūtra*,
which are now in the canon.
Before departing,
he left a poem for that monk, which said:
"Moving is like a one-wheeled cart,
ever fearing it will overturn on the great road.
Stopping is like a round-bottomed vessel,
ever fearing other things will topple it.
Since movement and stillness are thus,
how can one not leave the vulgar world?"
During the Qiánfú era (874-879),
his younger brother Chén Liǎn again served as an aide in Xuē Néng's administration in Xúzhōu.
Chén Shū rowed a small boat from Dānyáng to Péngmén,
to see his brother.
Lord Xuē esteemed his character,
and invited him to enter the city.
He firmly refused, saying:
"I have already made a vow,
not to set foot in the gates of officialdom."
Xuē then took a boat to visit him,
and they talked of the Way the whole day,
but he did not stay overnight and left.
Such was the lofty and reclusive nature of his aspirations.
From *Yùtáng Xiánhuà* (Idle Talk from the Jade Hall).
Kǒng Zhěng
When Vice-Director Kǒng Zhěng was a Reminder and Supplements Official,
he was once returning from court when it rained,
and he had no rain gear,
so he took shelter under the eaves of someone's house.
Past mealtime,
the rain grew heavier,
and the family invited him into the main hall.
An old man came out to greet him very respectfully;
the wine and food provided were also extremely abundant and clean,
surpassing even those of ducal households.
Zhěng thanked him apologetically,
and asked to borrow rain gear.
The old man said:
"I live in idleness,
and do not involve myself in human affairs.
Cold, heat, wind, or rain,
I have never ventured out in them.
Why would I keep such things here?"
He instructed someone to borrow some from elsewhere to offer him.
Zhěng withdrew and sighed in admiration,
as if forgetting his official ambitions.
He told others:
"This is a great recluse indeed."
From *Běimèng Suǒyán* (Trifling Words of Northern Dreams).
Shùn's White Jade Guǎn
In the time of Shùn,
the Queen Mother of the West came to present a white jade *guǎn* (pitch-pipe).
During the reign of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
Xī Jǐng, a scholar from Línglíng, obtained a white jade *guǎn* (sheng pipe) at the foot of Shùn's temple in Lěngdào.
The ancients knew that *guǎn* were made of jade;
later they were changed to bamboo *guǎn*.
Using jade to produce sound,
thus spirits and men were harmonized,
and phoenixes appeared.
From *Fēngsútōng* (Comprehensive Meaning of Customs).
Shī Yán
Shī Yán was
a musician of the Yīn (Shāng) dynasty.
Since the time of Fúxī,
his family had followed this profession for generations.
As for Shī Yán, he thoroughly understood yin and yang,
was versed in the images of the heavens and astrology,
yet in the end, none could fathom his true nature.
Generations passed distantly,
and he would sometimes appear, sometimes hide.
In the time of Xuānyuán (the Yellow Emperor),
he served as Director of Music.
By the time of the Yīn dynasty,
he was comprehensively revising the music of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.
Strumming a single-stringed qin,
then the earth spirits would all ascend.
Blowing the jade pitch-pipes,
then the heavenly spirits would all descend.
During Xuānyuán's time,
he was already several hundred years old.
He listened to the music of all states,
to discern the signs of the rise and fall of generations.
At the end of the Xià dynasty,
he embraced his musical instruments and fled to Yīn.
King Zhòu was licentious in sounds and sensual pleasures,
so he confined Shī Yán within the Dark Palace,
intending to inflict extreme punishment.
The Dark Palace was a place for imprisoning people.
After Shī Yán was imprisoned,
he performed music in the *shāng* mode, the flowing *zhǐ* mode, and the *jué* mode.
The jailer reported this to Zhòu,
who still complained, saying:
"This is the pure, ancient, distant music,
not what I can enjoy listening to."
He still did not release him.
Shī Yán then changed and performed tunes that bewildered the soul and corrupted the spirit,
to provide pleasure for the long night's revelries,
and thus avoided the punishment of the roasting pillar.
Hearing that King Wǔ of Zhōu was raising an army,
he then crossed the Pú River and vanished.
Some say
he originally died in the water realm.
Therefore, the people of Jìn and Wèi carved stone, cast metal, and painted to depict his likeness,
and established shrines without cease.
From *Wángzǐ Nián Shíyí Jì* (Records of Omissions by Prince Nián).
Shī Kuàng
Shī Kuàng,
some say he appeared during the time of Duke Líng of Jìn.
As the chief music official,
he exquisitely distinguished musical tones and pitches,
and composed ten thousand chapters of military texts.
People of his time did not know his ancestry,
his appearances and disappearances were difficult to ascertain.
During the time of Duke Píng of Jìn,
with his knowledge of yin and yang studies,
he was prominent in his era.
He then smoked his eyes to become blind,
to cut off and block all distractions.
He concentrated on astrology, calculation, and music,
examining bells and pitch-pipes to determine the four seasons,
without the slightest error.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* do not record from which emperor's time Shī Kuàng came.
Kuàng knew his life was about to end,
so he composed one hundred volumes of the *Bǎofú*.
By the time of the Warring States' division and strife,
his book was lost and extinct.
Duke Píng of Jìn ordered Shī Kuàng to perform the *qīngzhǐ* mode.
Shī Kuàng said:
"The *qīngzhǐ* is not as good as the *qīngjué*."
The Duke said:
"May I hear the *qīngjué*?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"Your virtue is shallow,
you are not worthy to hear it.
If you hear it, I fear there will be ruin."
The Duke said:
"I am old,
what I love is music.
I wish to hear it nonetheless."
Shī Kuàng had no choice but to play.
At the first playing,
clouds arose from the northwest;
at the second playing,
a great wind arrived,
and heavy rain followed.
It tore the curtains and drapes,
shattered the sacrificial vessels,
and made tiles fall from the corridor roofs.
Those seated scattered and fled;
Duke Píng was terrified,
and prostrated himself in the corridor chamber.
Jìn suffered a great drought,
the land was barren for three years,
and Duke Píng himself fell ill.
From *Wángzǐ Nián Shíyí Jì* (Records of Omissions by Prince Nián).
Shī Juān
Shī Juān lived during the time of Duke Líng of Wèi.
He was able to transcribe the music of successive dynasties,
excelled at composing new melodies,
and used them to replace ancient tunes,
thus creating music for the four seasons.
In spring, there were songs such as "Lí Hóng," "Qù Yàn," and "Yìng Pín";
in summer, there were tunes like "Míng Chén," "Jiāo Quán," "Zhū
The original text had 'Zhī' for 'Zhū,'
corrected based on the Ming manuscript
Huá," and "Liú Jīn";
in autumn, there were melodies such as "Shāng Biāo," "Bái Yún," "Luò Yè," and "Chuī Péng";
in winter, there were compositions like "Níng Hé," "Liú Yīn," and "Chén Yún."
When these seasonal melodies
were performed for Duke Líng,
he became deeply indulgent and mentally confused,
neglecting governmental affairs.
Qú Bóyù admonished him, saying:
"Although these tunes may stimulate the spirit and rhythm,
they ultimately constitute decadent and effeminate music,
unfitting for the refined and elegant,
and are not what a subject should recommend to his lord."
Duke Líng then abandoned the new music and attended to governmental duties,
earning the praise of the people of Wèi for his transformative governance.
Shī Juān regretted having strayed from the principles of the Yǎ and Sòng,
failing in his duty as a subject,
and subsequently withdrew into seclusion.
Bóyù burned his musical instruments at the crossroads of nine roads,
fearing they might be passed down and imitated by later generations.
His songs were lost,
and as generations passed into distant memory,
only the general themes of their titles were recorded.
From "Wáng Zǐnián Shíyí Jì"
During the time of King Huái of Chǔ,
the Dòngtíng Mountains floated on the water,
with hundreds of golden halls beneath,
where the daughters of the emperor resided.
Throughout the four seasons, the sounds of stone chimes, metal bells, silk strings, and bamboo flutes echoed to the mountaintops.
In the era of King Huái of Chǔ,
he and a gathering of talents composed poetry by the water's edge.
Thus it is said
that the music of Xiāoxiāng and Dòngtíng
could make listeners feel ageless,
surpassing even "Xiánchí" and "Xiāosháo."
During each of the four mid-season festivals,
the king would tour and feast around the mountains.
They would each evoke the essence of the mid-seasons
to create musical compositions.
In mid-spring, when the pitch corresponded to Jiázhōng,
they composed poems of gentle flowing water,
feasting on the southern side of the mountain.
When mid-summer arrived, corresponding to Ruíbīn,
they created the melodies "Hào Lù" and "Qiū Shuāng."
Later, King Huái favored promoting treacherous and ambitious individuals,
causing the virtuous to flee.
Qū Píng, loyal but rejected,
went into hiding between the Yuán and Lǐ rivers.
Pursued relentlessly by the king,
he eventually threw himself into the clear, cold depths.
The people of Chǔ, longing for him,
called him the Water Immortal.
From "Wáng Zǐnián Shíyí Jì"
In the Xiányáng Palace of Qín,
there were twelve bronze figures
The original text had 'cast bronze,'
corrected based on the Ming manuscript
each seated about three to five feet tall.
Arranged on a single mat,
they held qín, zhù, yú, and shēng instruments,
each grasping their own.
All were adorned with colorful silk ribbons,
appearing as lifelike as living people.
Beneath the mat were bronze pipes,
with openings several feet above.
One of these pipes was hollow,
containing a rope as thick as a finger inside.
When one person blew into the hollow pipe,
and another pulled the rope,
the qín, sè, yú, and zhù would all play,
indistinguishable from real music.
From "Xījīng Zá Jì"
Emperor Wén of Suí
In the fourteenth year of the Kāihuáng era of Emperor Wén of Suí,
fourteen jade chimes were discovered at Díquán.
They were hung in the courtyard,
where two plain-robed divine beings came to strike them,
producing sounds of exquisite beauty.
From "Qiàwén Jì"
Emperor Tàizōng of Táng
Emperor Tàizōng of Táng paid close attention to refined correctness,
diligently promoting cultural education.
He ordered Grand Minister of Ceremonies Zǔ Xiàosūn to standardize the musical notes,
Court Diarist Lǚ Cái to study phonology,
and Harmonizing Official Zhāng Wénshōu to examine the pitch pipes.
They rectified the scattered and excessive elements,
striking a balanced compromise.
They composed music to invoke deities,
created the Nine Merits Dance,
and the whole empire turned toward this cultural influence.
Initially, Xiàosūn found that the old music of Liáng and Chén mixed with sounds of Wú and Chǔ,
while the old music of Zhōu and Qí often involved techniques of northern tribes.
Thus, he carefully blended northern and southern styles,
referencing ancient tones,
to create the Great Táng Refined Music.
Using the twelve pitch standards,
each aligned with its corresponding month,
they rotated to serve as the tonic.
As stated in the "Lǐjì,"
"Great music harmonizes with heaven and earth."
The "Shī Xù" says,
"The music of peace is tranquil and joyful,
reflecting harmonious governance."
Therefore, they established the Twelve Harmonies music,
combining thirty melodies and eighty-four modes.
For sacrifices at the circular mound, Huángzhōng served as the tonic;
for the square marsh, Dàlǚ served as the tonic;
for ancestral temples, Tàicù served as the tonic.
For the five suburban sacrifices and welcoming ceremonies,
the tonic varied according to the month's pitch standard.
Initially,
during Suí, only the Huángzhōng tonic was used,
with only seven bells struck.
The remaining five hung unused.
After Xiàosūn devised the method of rotating tonics,
all bells were struck,
leaving none unused.
At that time, Zhāng Wénshōu excelled in music theory.
Finding Xiāo Jí's music scores insufficiently detailed,
he drew from historical developments,
cut bamboo into twelve pitch pipes to blow,
fully mastering the principles of rotating tonics.
Emperor Tàizōng also summoned Wénshōu to the Court of Ceremonial Music,
ordering him to collaborate with Xiàosūn in finalizing the refined music.
Among the ancient bells of the grand music,
twelve were commonly called mute bells,
as no one could make them sound.
Wénshōu adjusted them by blowing the pitch pipes,
and their tones became clear and resonant.
Those knowledgeable in music all admired his skill,
and he was appointed Harmonizing Official.
After Xiàosūn's death,
Wénshōu further studied the Three Ritual Classics,
implemented additional reforms,
and thus greatly perfected musical education.
From "Tánbīn Lù"
Additionally, twelve jade chimes were obtained in Rùnzhōu and presented as tribute.
Zhāng, the Director of the Music Bureau, struck one and said:
"This was made in a certain year of Jìn.
That year had an intercalary month,
and the chime maker followed the lunar count,
so there should be thirteen chimes.
One is missing,
likely buried nine feet east of the Huángzhōng position.
It will surely be found there."
They searched,
and indeed found it as he said.
From "Guóshǐ Yì Zuǎn"
Also, during the Zhēnguàn era,
auspicious clouds appeared,
and the river waters cleared.
Zhāng, the Director of the Music Bureau, composed the "Jǐngyún Héqīng Gē,"
named Yānyuè music,
which is now the first piece performed at the New Year's court assembly.
From "Guóshǐ Yì Zuǎn"
Also, after Emperor Tàizōng pacified Liú Wǔzhōu,
the scholars and commoners of Hédōng sang and danced in the streets,
and the soldiers together composed the tune "Qínwáng Pòzhèn Yuè."
Later, it was incorporated into the Music Bureau repertoire.
Also, the "Pòzhèn Yuè"
featured armored performers holding halberds,
symbolizing warfare.
The "Qìngshàn Yuè"
featured long sleeves and trailing slippers,
symbolizing civil virtue.
When Duke Zhèng saw the "Pòzhèn Yuè" performed,
he would bow his head and not watch;
but for the "Qìngshàn Yuè,"
he would enjoy it without tiring.
From "Guóshǐ Yì Zuǎn"
Wèi Dàobì and Cáo Shàokuí
The musician Wèi Dàobì,
was someone no one in the world could deceive with sounds.
Cáo Shàokuí and Dàobì served together as Grand Musicians,
performing together at the northern suburban sacrifice.
The Censor was angry with Shàokuí,
and wanted to accuse him of disharmony in the music.
He randomly struck the bells and chime stones,
making Shàokuí listen,
but when summoned, he made no mistakes,
which instead made the Censor sigh in admiration.
In Luòyáng, there was a monk
whose chime stone in his room would sound by itself at midnight.
The monk thought it strange,
and, frightened, fell ill.
He sought out magicians,
tried a hundred methods to stop it,
but ultimately could not make it cease.
Shàokuí was on good terms with the monk,
and came to inquire about his illness.
The monk told him everything.
Soon, the fasting bell was struck,
and the chime stone sounded again.
Shàokuí laughed and said:
"Tomorrow, prepare a lavish feast,
and I will rid you of it."
Although the monk did not believe Shàokuí's words,
he hoped they might be effective,
so he prepared a feast and waited for him.
After Shàokuí finished eating,
he took out a file from his bosom,
filed the chime stone in several places, and then left.
The sound then ceased.
The monk earnestly asked him the reason,
and Shàokuí said:
"This sound harmonizes with the bell's pitch;
when one is struck, the other responds."
The monk was overjoyed,
and his illness was also cured.
From "Guó Shǐ Yì Zuǎn"
Péi Zhīgǔ
When Péi Zhīgǔ performed music,
he said to Yuán Xíngchōng:
"The metal and stone instruments are harmonious;
there should be an auspicious and celebratory event,
and it will be among the descendants of the Táng imperial house."
That same month,
Emperor Zhōngzōng ascended the throne.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Also, Zhīgǔ served in the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and once encountered a man riding a horse on the road.
Hearing the sound,
he secretly said:
"This man will fall from his horse."
Curious onlookers followed and watched,
and before he had traveled half a ward,
the horse startled and he nearly died.
He also once observed a wedding procession,
and upon hearing the sound of the bride's jade pendants, said:
"This bride will be unlucky for her mother-in-law."
That day, the mother-in-law fell ill,
and eventually died.
He was skilled in nurturing life,
and in the twelfth year of the Kāiyuán era,
he died at the age of one hundred.
From "Guó Shǐ Yì Zuǎn"
Lǐ Sìzhēn
The Táng dynasty inherited the chaos following the Zhōu and Suí,
and the musical instruments were scattered and lost,
leaving only the note Zhǐ missing.
This was a deficiency related to the imperial surname,
and those who knew did not dare to speak openly about it.
In the late years of Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
the Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Sìzhēn secretly searched for it but could not find it.
One autumn morning, clear and crisp,
he heard the sound of a fulling stone at what is now the Crossbow Camp,
which was the former residence of Duke Yīng.
Several more years passed,
with no way to obtain it.
Later, Xú Yè rebelled,
and Empress Wǔ flooded his palace.
Sìzhēn then managed to obtain a funeral cart bell,
entered and shook it in the southeastern corner,
and indeed, there was a response.
So he dug there,
and found a piece of stone,
which he cut into four parts,
mending the deficiency in the musical set.
Later, when sacrifices were made at the ancestral temple and to Heaven,
the ones hung on the stands
were those obtained by Sìzhēn.
From "Dú Yì Zhì"
Sòng Yǎn
Sòng Yǎn served as the Grand Music Director,
and his understanding of music was unmatched in recent times.
The Court of Imperial Sacrifices had long lost the Zhǐ mode,
and Yǎn, through examining bells and pitches, recovered it.
From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ"
Yǎn served as an Assistant at the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Once, early one morning, while waiting for the dawn at the Guāngzhái Buddhist Temple,
he heard the sound of wind chimes on the pagoda,
and listened intently for a long time.
After returning from court,
he again stopped at the temple quarters.
He asked the temple's head monk:
"Venerable monk, do you know the origins
of all the bells on your pagoda?"
The monk said:
"I do not know."
Yǎn said:
"Among them, one is an ancient piece.
I request to climb the pagoda once,
follow the metal chains,
and try striking them in sequence to identify it.
May I?"
The monk was initially reluctant but later agreed,
and Yǎn struck and identified it.
The people in the temple
then said that it often swayed without wind,
producing a clear, audible sound—
was it not this one?
Yǎn said:
"That's it.
It must be because during sacrificial ceremonies,
when the main set of bells is struck, it responds."
He insisted on taking it down to examine it,
and said:
"This is a Biānzhōng bell of the Gūxǐ note.
I ask to temporarily hang it alone
(Note: In the *Jíegǔ Lù*, 'temporarily hang' is written as 'temporarily attach')
in the temple courtyard."
Returning to the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
he ordered musicians to go with the monk to the site.
Coordinating the timing,
when they struck
(Note: The original text had 'zhī' (know); changed to 'kòu' (strike) according to the Ming manuscript copy)
the main set,
this one indeed responded.
They then purchased and obtained it.
He also once saw off a guest at the Tōnghuà Gate,
and encountered the Commissioner of Finance transporting a cart.
He stopped his horse for a moment,
then suddenly hastily bid farewell to his guest.
He then followed the cart,
identified one bell,
and said it was also a Biānzhōng.
Others only noticed its casting was uniquely fine,
not matching the others in quality,
but did not know the rest.
He then matched it to the set,
and its sound and form both fit the scale.
How extraordinary!
This too is an example of recognizing the Zhǐ note in metal performances, is it not?
From "Jíegǔ Lù"
Wáng Rényù
When the Jìn dynasty had its capital at Luòyáng,
in the spring of the Bǐngshēn year.
The Hanlin Academician Wáng Rényù was on night duty,
and heard the palace bell,
each time it sounded,
as if striking between the neck and brain.
The bell suddenly began making a rustling sound,
as if cracking,
and this continued for over ten days.
Each time, he silently discussed it with his colleagues,
but none knew what omen it signified.
That year in mid-spring,
the Jìn Emperor indeed went to Liángbiàn.
The imperial library and stables
were moved to the Snow Palace,
and it has been thirteen years to this day.
The rustling omen
was truthful and had a sign.
From "Yù Táng Xián Huà"
Lǐ Shīhuì
Lǐ Shīhuì was the grandson of Lǐ Jiàn, who painted foreign horses.
He served as an aide to Liú Cóngjiàn in Lùzhōu.
Knowing that Cóngjiàn was plotting treason,
he retired to live in seclusion on Líchéng Mountain.
After Lùzhōu was pacified,
the imperial court commended him
and appointed him as a county magistrate.
He once obtained a piece of meteorite from a patch-robed monk.
The monk said:
"While traveling early on the Shǔ road,
I saw a star fall in front of me.
I then dug it up
and found a piece of stone,
like a broken chime stone.
One end of the stone was carved with the head of a suānní,
also like a chime stone.
It had a hole,
and the area where the cord was threaded was still smooth.
Could it be that a celestial musical instrument broke and fell?"
This stone later passed into the residence of Lǐ Fǔ in Ānyì.
From "Shàngshū Gùshí."
Yúfán Music
In the Xiányáng Palace of Qín, there was a qín six feet long,
fitted with thirteen strings
and twenty-six markers.
All were adorned with the seven treasures,
and it was inscribed "Yúfán Music."
From "Xījīng Zá Jì."
Liú Dàoqiáng
Liú Dàoqiáng of Qí was skilled at playing the qín
and could perform melodies of solitary ducks and lone cranes.
Listeners all felt sorrow
and could not control themselves.
From "Xījīng Zá Jì."
Empress Zhào
Empress Zhào had a precious qín called "Phoenix,"
all decorated with dragons, phoenixes, chī dragons, and luan birds in relief with gold and jade,
depicting ancient sages and virtuous women.
She was also skilled at playing the compositions "Returning Phoenix" and "Sending Off Afar."
From "Xījīng Zá Jì."
Mǎ Róng
Mǎ Róng served in two commanderies and two counties,
governing with non-action
and following simplicity in affairs.
In Wǔdū for seven years
and in Nánjùn for four years,
he never once sentenced anyone to punishment or execution.
He had a fondness for music
and was skilled at playing the qín and blowing the flute.
Each time he exhaled, the sound harmonized with the chirping of crickets.
From "Shāng Yún Xiǎoshuō."
Yáng Xiù
Yáng Xiù, the Prince of Shǔ and son of Emperor Wén of Suí,
once made a thousand qín,
which were scattered among the people.
From "Shàngshū Gùshí."
Lǐ Miǎn
Lǐ Miǎn, the Duke of Qiān of Táng, loved elegant qín.
He once took the finest parts of tóng and zǐ wood
and pieced them together to make qín,
calling them
the phrase "calling them" was originally missing.
According to the Ming manuscript edition, it is supplemented.
"Patchwork qín."
He used snail shells as markers.
Among them, three sides were particularly extraordinary,
collectively called "Xiǎngquán" (Echoing Spring) and "Yùnqìng" (Resonant Chime).
Once the strings were put on,
they could last for ten years without breaking.
From "Shàngshū Gùshí."
Furthermore, Miǎn also made qín using lacquered bamboo tubes,
producing as many as several hundred,
and gave them to those who requested them.
Among them were peerless ones:
one named "Xiǎngquán,"
another named "Yùnqìng,"
which he treasured in his home.
Also, in the capital, the qín of the Fán and Lù families were considered the best.
The Lù family had a stone pillow of Grand Guardian Fáng,
with a damaged spot they cherished and did not repair.
In Shǔ, the Léi family crafted qín
and often graded them themselves.
The highest grade used jade markers,
the next used precious markers,
and the next used markers of gold, snail, or clam.
Zhāng Hóngjìng
Minister Zhāng Hóngjìng held a night gathering of renowned musicians,
watching Zhèng Yòu tune two qín with extreme precision.
Each was placed on a separate stand.
When he played a gōng note, the other responded with gōng;
when he played a jué note, the other responded with jué.
If it was slightly imprecise,
there would be no response.
Yòu studied under Dǒng Tínglán,
who was especially skilled in
according to Wú Céng's "Nénggǎi Zhāi Mànlù," volume five, "fàn" is written as "chén."
floating tones and zhù tones.
From "Guóshǐ Bǔ."
Dǒng Tínglán
"Xiǎngquán" and "Yùnqìng"
originally belonged to Minister Fán Zé's household,
later were at the Zhūyá residence,
and then at Zhāng Yànyuǎn's residence.
Now it is unknown where they have ended up.
In recent times, playing the qín has been praised as reaching the level of Hè Ruòyí and Gān Dǎng.
Earlier, there were Dǒng Tínglán and Chén Huáigǔ.
Huái was capable of kuàng
kuàng is suspected to be fàn.
See the earlier entry on Zhāng Hóngjìng for details.
and zhù, two types of tones,
referring to the large and small Hújiā.
Xiāo Gǔ was also skilled at the qín,
saying the fourth section of Hújiā
infringes upon the wúyì shāng mode,
and thus used its tones to create Xiāo's Nine Pieces.
From "Lúshì Záshuō."
Cài Yōng
While Cài Yōng was in Chénliú,
a neighbor invited him for food and drink.
By the time he arrived, the drinking party was already in full swing,
and a guest was playing the qín.
Yōng reached the door
and listened stealthily, saying:
"Alas,
I was invited with music, yet there is a murderous intent—
why is that?"
He then turned back.
The messenger informed the host,
who hurriedly chased after him and asked the reason.
Yōng told him everything.
The qín player said:
"Just now while plucking the strings,
I saw a mantis facing a singing cicada.
The cicada was about to leave,
and the mantis moved back and forth because of it.
In my heart, I only feared the mantis would lose the cicada.
Could this have been the murderous intent reflected in the sound?"
Yōng sighed and said:
"That is sufficient to explain it."
From "Hànshū."
The Ming manuscript edition says from Huá Shè's "Hànshū,"
suspected to be Huá Qiáo's "Hòu Hànshū."
Yú Dí
Minister Yú Dí often had guests play the qín.
His sister-in-law, who had an understanding of music,
listened from behind the curtain.
She sighed and said:
"Of the three parts,
one part is the sound of the zhēng,
two parts are the sound of the pipa.
There is no authentic charm."
From "Guóshǐ Bǔ."
Hán Gāo
Hán Gāo was born with an innate understanding of music.
He once watched someone play the qin,
and when it came to the piece "Zhǐxī,"
he sighed and said:
"How marvelous,
this is what Jī Kāng created."
It was during the time between the Wèi and Jìn
(The original text had "Wèi" written as "Wèi."
Changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
dynasties,
and its musical mode was based on Shāng.
Shāng is the sound of autumn.
Autumn is the season
when heaven causes things to wither and decay, turning harsh and severe—
is it not the year's end?
Moreover, Jìn inherited the musical influence of metal.
This is how one knows that it was the end of Wèi,
and that Jìn was about to replace it.
Slowing the Shāng string
to match the Gōng note in pitch
signifies a minister usurping the ruler's rightful place.
This is how one knows that the Sīmǎ clan was about to seize power.
Sīmǎ Yì received the dying entrustment of Wèi Míngdì,
yet later harbored intentions of usurpation.
After executing Cáo Shuǎng,
his rebellious nature became increasingly apparent.
Wáng Líng was the military governor of Yángzhōu,
and plotted to install King Chǔ, Cáo Biāo.
Wǔqiū Jiǎn, Wén Qīn, and Zhūgě Dàn,
successively served as military governors of Yángzhōu,
and all had plans to restore the Wèi house.
They were all killed by Yì and his sons.
Jī Kāng, considering Yángzhōu the ancient territory of Guǎnglíng,
and those four men
all being civil and military ministers of the Wèi house,
who all met their defeat and dispersal in Guǎnglíng,
therefore named this piece "Guǎnglíng Sàn."
It signifies the dispersal and fall of the Wèi house,
which began from Guǎnglíng.
As for "Zhǐxī,"
it means that although Jìn rose violently,
it would ultimately cease and end here.
The sounds of sorrow, indignation, grief, misery, pain, urgency, and distress
are all contained within it.
The chaos of the Yǒngjiā era
was its fulfillment, was it not?
Jī Kāng composed this,
intending to leave it for future generations who understood music,
and also to avoid disaster from Jìn,
hence he attributed it to ghosts and spirits.
Gāo's understanding of music
can be said to have reached the utmost.
From "Lúshì Záshuō."
Wáng Zhōngsàn
During the Táng dynasty's Qiánfú era,
when Huáng Cháo illegally occupied the two capitals,
many scholar-officials from Cháng'ān fled north to avoid the turmoil.
At that time, there was a former Hànlín Academy attendant named Wáng Jìng'ào,
a man of Cháng'ān.
He was skilled at both wéiqí and the qin,
and his demeanor was pure and lofty.
Initially, he traveled from Púbǎn to Bīngzhōu.
The military governor of Bīngzhōu, Zhèng Cóngdǎng,
held the title of Xiàngguó and governed Fén and Jìn.
Ào paid him a visit,
but was not treated with courtesy.
Later, he went to Yè,
at a time when Luó Shàowēi
(Ming manuscript copy has "wēi" instead of "wēi.")
had newly established himself,
and was just then pacifying his soldiers,
focusing on warfare.
Jìng'ào stayed in Yèzhōng for several years.
At that time, Lǐ Shānfǔ's literary style was vigorous and powerful,
and he was famous throughout the region.
By chance, at a Dàoguàn temple,
he met Jìng'ào.
There was also a retired scholar, Lǐ, who was also skilled at playing the qin.
Shānfǔ said to the two guests:
" 'Yōulán' and 'Lǜshuǐ'—
may we hear them?"
Jìng'ào immediately complied and played them,
the sound clear, the melody ancient.
It moved the spirits.
(The Xǔ printed edition has the character "shuǎng" after "shén.")
When the piece ended,
Jìng'ào secretly turned his sleeve and said:
"I recall in the Xiántōng era,
in the autumn night at the imperial court,
when I served His Majesty—
I never imagined I would be wandering in exile here."
Retired Scholar Lǐ also played the piece "Báihè."
Shānfǔ took up his brush, gathered his thoughts,
and presented them with a poem, saying:
" 'Yōulán' and 'Lǜshuǐ' shine with pure tones, /
I sigh that you, sir, have wasted your heart. /
When in this world has antiquity ever been truly cherished? /
Before others, why must you bitterly wet your lapels?"
The remaining lines were not completed.
Shānfǔ himself also felt downcast,
saddened by his lack of recognition.
Wáng then played another tune,
and the seated guests became even more awed and respectful—
it was no ordinary composition.
Shānfǔ then ordered wine and stopped the strings,
and each drank several full cups,
soon all collapsing like jade mountains.
When they sobered up,
Shānfǔ leisurely asked:
"What piece did you play earlier?
It is not found elsewhere."
Wáng said:
"My family practices orthodox music,
passed down through generations.
Since the Dézōng and Shùnzōng reigns,
we have served as attendants at the Golden Gate,
for four generations now.
The pieces I usually play
are known to many.
Only the tune that Jī Zhōngsàn received from Líng Lún—
everyone says it was cut off at the Eastern Market of Luòyáng,
and they do not know there is someone who transmits it.
I received it from my ancestors,
and named it 'Guǎnglíng Sàn.'"
Shānfǔ had earlier suspected its melody
was almost divinely crafted;
now hearing Wáng's explanation,
he realized the ancient "Guǎnglíng Sàn"
might indeed have been transmitted in the world.
He then completed a four-rhyme poem,
which was included in his poetry collection.
In Shānfǔ's collection today,
it only mentions Retired Scholar Lǐ,
probably due to a copying error.
From then on, Lord Lǐ often referred to Attendant Wáng as Wáng Zhōngsàn.
Wáng later traveled to Chángshān.
At that time, the military governor Wáng Róng was still young,
newly wielding military authority.
He was just then recruiting many scholars
to enhance his good reputation.
At the time, there were Lǐ Xiòng Láng
(The original had "láng" written as "jí."
Changed according to the Ming manuscript and Xǔ printed editions.)
Zhōng, Mò Yòuxuán the Secretary, Xiāo Xiàng the Vice Director, Zhāng Dàogǔ, and other talented and learned scholars of outstanding ability,
all gathered from the four directions at the Wénhuá Hall.
Thus, Attendant Wáng's skills in qin and wéiqí
were also treated with respect on the guest couch.
Throughout the year, the provisions supplied
were all generous and ample.
Whenever Wáng [Róng] ordered him to pluck the strings and move the bridges,
he would surely bestow generous gifts.
He stayed in Chángshān for over ten years,
receiving great courtesy and treatment.
Jìng'ào often wore a tall hat
and high clogs,
leisurely whistling, singing, and reciting poetry.
Even in winter, he wore a coarse hemp scarf and single-layered clothes,
his body without any silk wadding,
daily getting cheerfully drunk in the market,
and people all found him strange.
Hearing that Emperor Zhāozōng had been restored to the throne,
he bid farewell and returned to the imperial capital,
and later, no one knew his end.
Jìng'ào could also cut paper into bees and butterflies within his sleeves,
then raise his sleeve to make them fly,
filling the entire room.
Some would fly into people's lapels and sleeves,
and if one tried to catch them,
they would return to their original place.
People at the time often suspected he possessed immortal arts.
Zhāng Dàogǔ was on good terms with him,
always admiring his skills and arts.
He once wrote "The Biography of Wáng the Recluse,"
for this reason.
Dàogǔ's given name was Xiàn,
and he was widely learned.
He excelled in ancient prose,
having read ten thousand volumes,
but did not enjoy writing poetry.
Once, at Zhāng Chǔmèng's gathering,
there had been a long drought,
when suddenly heavy rain fell.
All the guests were delighted and composed poems about it.
Dàogǔ was the last to finish, finally completing a quatrain:
"Excessive sunshine has lasted long indeed, /
Joyful rain pours down from the clouds. /
Not a single drop falls askew, /
For a very long time, it comes straight down."
The seated guests respected his literary reputation,
but laughed at the clumsiness of his poem.
From "Ěrmù Jì."
Sè
Vice Censor-in-Chief Lú Mài possessed four precious sè,
each worth several hundred thousand.
They were named Hányù, Shíqìng, Xiǎngquán, and Hézhì.
From "Zhuànjì."
Ruǎnxián
When Attendant Yuán Xíngchōng was serving as Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
someone obtained a bronze object from an ancient tomb that resembled a pipa but had a perfectly round body,
and no one could identify it.
Yuán looked at it and said:
"This is a musical instrument created by Ruǎn Xián."
He then ordered craftsmen to remake it using wood,
and its sound was clear and elegant.
What is now called the "ruǎnxián" is precisely this instrument.
From Guóshǐ Yìzuǎn.
Additionally, the Jìnshū states that Ruǎn Xián was skilled at playing the pipa.
Later, someone excavated Ruǎn Xián's tomb
and found a pipa made of earthenware.
People at the time did not recognize it,
but since it was obtained from Ruǎn Xián's tomb,
they named it "ruǎnxián."
In recent times, there have been many capable individuals
who have harmonized it with the qin,
often achieving similar results.
From Lúshì Záshuō.
Grand Banquet
During the reign of Emperor Xuánzong of Táng in Dōngluò,
a grand banquet was held beneath the Wǔfèng Tower.
He ordered magistrates and prefects within a three-hundred-li radius
to lead their musicians to the imperial court.
It was said that they were to compete for victory or defeat, with rewards and penalties accordingly.
At that time, the governor of Hénèi Commandery had several hundred musicians on carts,
all dressed in brocade and embroidery;
the oxen harnessed to the carriages
were covered with tiger skins,
and some were made to resemble rhinoceroses and elephants,
astonishing the spectators.
Meanwhile, Yuán Lǔshān sent dozens of musicians who joined sleeves and sang "Yúwěi,"
which was a composition by Yuán Lǔshān.
Emperor Xuánzong heard this and found it remarkable,
inquiring about the lyrics,
then sighed and said:
"These are the words of a worthy man."
Afterward, the emperor said to his ministers:
"The people of Hénèi
must be suffering in hardship."
He urgently ordered their recall
and granted them honorary positions.
Whenever banquets and feasts were held,
the emperor would preside over them at the Qínzhèng Tower.
The Imperial Guards and soldiers of the Four Armies
would array their formations before dawn,
displaying banners in great numbers,
all clad in golden armor
and wearing short embroidered robes.
The Court of Imperial Sacrifices would present music,
while the Palace Guards set up curtains behind.
Various tribal chieftains dined with prefectural officials.
The Imperial Music Academy presented grand displays:
mountain carts and land boats,
pole-climbing and tightrope walking,
ball juggling, swordplay, and wrestling,
as well as horse performances and cockfighting.
They also ordered several hundred palace ladies adorned with pearls and jade,
dressed in brocade and embroidery,
to emerge from behind curtains
and strike thunder drums,
performing "Music of the Victorious Formation," "Music of Great Peace," and "Music of the First Principle."
They also led elephants and rhinoceroses into the arena,
which would bow and dance,
moving in rhythm with the music.
Every year on the night of the first full moon,
the emperor would also ascend the Qínzhèng Tower to watch musical performances.
Nobles and imperial relatives
were provided with viewing towers by the court.
Late into the night,
palace ladies would be sent to sing and dance in front of the towers for their entertainment.
From Mínghuáng Zálù.
Líyuán Music
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Emperor Xuánzong ordered several hundred palace ladies to become disciples of the Líyuán,
all residing in the northern courtyard of Yíchūn.
The emperor was well-versed in music theory,
and at the time, Mǎ Xiānqī, Lǐ Guīnián, and Hè Huáizhì all had deep understanding of musical scales.
When Ān Lùshān came from Fànyáng for an audience,
he also presented several hundred white jade flutes and pipes,
all displayed in the Líyuán.
From then on, the music sounded almost otherworldly.
From Tánbīn Lù.
Consort Tàizhēn
Consort Tàizhēn was skilled in many performing arts,
excelling particularly in playing the qìng.
The sounds she produced
were clear and melodious, often with new tunes,
and even the talented musicians of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices and the Líyuán
could not surpass her.
Emperor Xuánzong ordered the procurement of Lántián green jade to carve into qìng stones,
and the Imperial Workshop crafted stands, crossbeams, and tassels,
all adorned with gold inlays, pearls, jade, and other rare treasures.
They also cast two golden lions,
depicted in a pouncing and leaping posture,
each weighing over two hundred catties,
to serve as pedestals.
The other decorations were colorful and ornate,
the craftsmanship exquisite and marvelous,
unmatched at the time.
When the emperor returned to the capital after his journey to Shǔ,
many musical instruments had been lost,
but the jade qìng happened to remain.
The emperor looked at it with sorrow,
unable to bear keeping it before him,
and urgently ordered it sent to the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
To this day, it is stored in the Zhèngshēng Repository of the Grand Music Office.
From Kāitiān Chuánxìn Jì.
Tiānbǎo Musical Compositions
During the Tiānbǎo era,
musical compositions were often named after border regions,
such as "Liángzhōu," "Gānzhōu," "Yīzhōu," and the like.
These pieces were rich
(the original text had "xì" but was changed to "fán" according to the Ming manuscript)
in melody,
and their names included the term "pò."
Later, these regions were all conquered by the Western Barbarians,
which was seen as an omen.
From Chuánzǎi Lù.
Wéi Gāo
When Wéi Gāo governed Xīchuān,
he presented a sacred musical composition to the court,
along with the dancers' score.
Upon arrival in the capital,
it was rehearsed and reviewed at the lodging residence,
and several members of the Imperial Music Academy secretly observed it,
thus gaining an advance preview.
From Lúshì Záshuō.
Yú Dí
Minister Yú Dí, inspired by Grand Commandant Wéi's presentation of sacred music,
also composed "Shùnshèng Music" and presented it.
At every banquet,
he would have it performed.
When the piece reached its midpoint,
all the dancers in the rows would kneel,
and one person would dance in the center.
His advisor Wéi Shòu joked:
"Why exhaust troops for a solo dance?"
Though humorous,
each remark carried its own meaning.
Yú also had female performers dance in rows,
their movements vigorous and magnificent,
and the piece was named "Sūn Wǔ Shùnshèng Music."
From Guóshǐ Bǔ.
Emperor Wénzōng
Emperor Wénzōng was skilled at playing the small pipe.
At the time, the monk Wén Xù was a great virtue admitted to the inner court,
but one day he offended the emperor and was exiled.
His disciples entered the inner court
to gather the belongings from his residence that were to be confiscated,
and they still imitated the master's lecturing voice.
The emperor adapted this sound into a melody,
naming it "Wén Xùzǐ."
From Lúshì Záshuō.
Shěn Āqiào
During Emperor Wénzōng's reign,
there was a palace lady named Shěn Āqiào who performed the dance "Hémǎnzǐ" for the emperor.
Her voice, lyrics, grace, and demeanor
were all smooth and expressive.
After the performance,
the emperor bestowed upon her a golden armlet
and immediately asked about her background.
Āqiào replied:
"I was originally a courtesan of Wú Yuánjì.
After Wú Yuánjì's defeat,
I entered the palace as a maid due to my musical skills."
She then presented a white jade fāngxiǎng,
saying:
"This originally belonged to Wú Yuánjì."
It was bright, pure, and cool to the touch,
able to illuminate over a dozen steps.
She mentioned that its mallets were made of rhinoceros horn,
and whenever an object produced sound,
it would resonate within.
The frame was said to be made of sandalwood,
with patterns like clouds and rosy clouds,
and its fragrance clung to people,
lingering for a full month without dispersing.
Its construction was exquisite and marvelous,
truly not something found within the Central Plains.
The emperor then ordered Āqiào to perform "Liángzhōu Melody,"
its tones clear and transcendent,
leaving all listeners deeply moved.
The emperor said to her:
"This is music from the heavens."
He then selected palace ladies
to become Āqiào's disciples.
From Dùyáng Zábiān.
Emperor Yìzōng
One day, Emperor Yìzōng summoned the musicians.
Just as they were performing the melody "Dàodiào Nòng,"
the emperor began to clap along.
So the musicians followed his rhythm,
playing the tune,
which was then named "Dàodiàozi."
The various princes of the Ten Mansions
mostly understood music.
They had singers, actors, and miscellaneous performers,
prepared for when the emperor visited their residences,
to welcome the imperial carriage with music.
In the palace, they were called "yīnshēng lángjūn."
From "Lúshì Záshuō"
Wáng Lìngyán
When Suí Yángdì traveled to Jiāngdū,
the musician Wáng Lìngyán's son returned from the palace.
Lìngyán asked his son:
"What tune was performed today?"
He replied:
"Ān Gōngzǐ."
Lìngyán had his son play it,
then said:
"You need not follow the imperial carriage.
This tune lacks the gōng note,
so the emperor will certainly not return."
It turned out just as he said.
From "Lúshì Záshuō"
Níngwáng's Presentation
The custom in Xīliáng Prefecture favored music,
and a new tune called "Liángzhōu" was composed.
During the Kāiyuán era,
it was presented to the emperor.
The emperor summoned the princes to a side hall to watch together.
When the tune ended,
the princes bowed in congratulations,
dancing and praising it,
but only Níngwáng did not bow.
The emperor turned to ask him,
and Níngwáng stepped forward, saying:
"Although this tune is excellent,
I have some observations.
Music begins with the gōng note,
disperses through the shāng note,
and is completed with the jué, zhǐ, and yǔ notes.
All are rooted and follow gōng and shāng.
In this tune,
gōng is sparse and scarce,
while zhǐ and shāng are chaotic and overly forceful.
I have heard that gōng represents the ruler,
and shāng represents the ministers.
If gōng is not dominant, the ruler's authority is weakened;
if shāng is excessive, the ministers' affairs become presumptuous.
Weakness oppresses those below,
presumption offends those above.
Arising from subtle beginnings,
it takes form in music;
spreading through song,
it manifests in human affairs.
I fear that one day there may be the calamity of exile
and the peril of rebellion,
all foretold by this tune."
