Upon hearing this, the emperor fell silent.
When the Ān-Shǐ Rebellion erupted,
the land was thrown into turmoil,
demonstrating Níngwáng's profound understanding of music.
From "Kāitiān Chuánxìn Jì"
Wáng Rényù
In the early years of Hòutáng's Qīngtài era,
Wáng Rényù served in Liángyuàn,
under Fàn Yánguāng as his commander.
In the first month of spring,
when the countryside was still cold,
he led his staff officers
to bid farewell to a court guest at the Zhéliǔ Pavilion.
The music was in the yǔ mode,
but the iron instruments alone sounded the gōng note.
When they tried to play together,
it was completely discordant.
Wáng alone was astonished,
privately telling Military Judge Lǐ Fūshì and Secretary Táng Yuánwài:
"Today there will surely be an alarming event,
for the music is not harmonious.
Now all the instruments play yǔ,
but only the metal ones strike the gōng note.
Moreover, yǔ corresponds to water,
gōng corresponds to earth,
and water and earth conflict—
could there be no cause for worry?"
After the banquet ended,
the court guest departed westward.
Fàn led his guests,
with hawks and hounds,
to hunt north of Wángpó Diàn.
He was thrown by a galloping horse
and lay unconscious in the wild marsh.
From mid-morning until afternoon,
he revived after seeming lifeless.
Music foretold it first—
truly remarkable.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Qín Qīng and Hán É
Xuē Tán studied singing under Qín Qīng.
Before mastering Qīng's skill,
he thought he had learned everything,
so he bid farewell and prepared to return home.
Qín Qīng did not stop him.
Seeing him off at the suburban crossroads,
he beat time and sang a mournful song,
its voice shaking the trees,
its echoes halting the drifting clouds.
Xuē apologized and begged to return,
never again daring to speak of leaving.
Qín Qīng turned to his friend and said:
"Long ago, Hán É traveled east to Qí
and ran out of provisions.
Passing Yōngmén,
she sang for food.
After she left, her lingering notes circled the beams,
not fading for three days,
and those nearby thought she had not gone.
At an inn,
the innkeeper insulted her.
Hán É then drew out her voice in sorrowful weeping;
for three days, the entire village, old and young, wept in shared grief,
unable to eat.
They hurried after her to apologize,
and É again drew out her voice in a long song,
whereupon the whole village, old and young, joyfully danced and clapped,
unable to restrain themselves.
They then gave her generous gifts and sent her off.
Thus, the people of Yōngmén
to this day excel at singing and weeping,
imitating the lingering sounds of É."
From "Bówùzhì"
Lady Qī
Hàn dynasty Lady Qī was skilled at dancing with raised sleeves and bent waist,
singing the tunes "Chūsài," "Rùsài," and "Wàngguī."
Hundreds of attending maidservants joined her,
and the rear palace sang in unison,
the sound often reaching the clouds.
From "Xījīng Zá Jì"
Lǐ Guīnián
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the court musicians, the three brothers Lǐ Guīnián, Lǐ Péngnián, and Lǐ Hènián, were all talented and learned, enjoying great fame.
Péngnián excelled at dancing,
while Hènián and Guīnián were skilled singers,
and were especially superb at composing the "Wèi Chuān" melody.
They received exceptional favor and patronage,
and grand mansions were built for them in the Eastern Capital.
Their extravagance and excess
surpassed even that of dukes and marquises.
Their residence was located in Tōngyuǎn Lane of the Eastern Capital;
the scale and design of its central hall
were unmatched in the capital.
Today, Duke Péi of Jìn has moved it to a villa south of Dìngdǐng Gate,
named the Lǜyě Hall.
Later, Guīnián fell into destitution south of the Yangtze.
Whenever he encountered fine days and beautiful scenery,
he would sing a few songs for people.
Those who heard him in their seats
would all cover their faces and weep, putting down their wine cups.
Dù Fǔ once presented him with a poem,
which says: "In Qí Wáng's mansion we often met;
Before Cuī Jiǔ's hall I heard you sing.
Now, with the scenery south of the Yangtze at its best,
I meet you again as the flowers fall."
Cuī Jiǔ refers to Cuī Dí, the Palace Attendant, younger brother of Cuī Shí, the Secretariat Director.
From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Mínghuáng."
Also, during the Kāiyuán era,
the palace first prized the tree peony,
which is today's peony.
The "Record of Flowers and Trees of the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo Eras" states
that in the palace, tree peonies were called peonies.
They obtained four plants,
red, purple, light red, and pure white.
The Emperor then had them transplanted in front of the Chénxiāng Pavilion east of Xīngqìng Pond.
It happened that the flowers were in full bloom.
The Emperor rode his horse Zhàoyèbái,
and Consort Tàizhēn followed in a palanquin.
He decreed a special selection of the finest performers from the Líyuán troupe,
yielding sixteen musical ensembles.
Lǐ Guīnián, renowned at the time for his singing,
holding sandalwood clappers in hand,
led the musicians forward
and was about to sing.
The Emperor said:
"Appreciating famous flowers
and facing my consort,
why use old song lyrics?"
He then ordered Guīnián to take a gold-flowered paper
and summon Lǐ Bái to bestow an imperial command,
demanding the immediate composition of three stanzas for the "Qīngpíng Melody."
Bái gladly accepted the decree,
though still suffering from the lingering effects of a hangover.
He then took up his brush and composed them.
The lyrics said:
"Her robe is like a cloud, her face a flower;
Spring breezes caress the rail, dew-drenched blooms abound.
If not seen atop the Jade Mountain peak,
Then surely met beneath the moon at Jasper Terrace."
"A branch of red enchantment, dew congeals its fragrance;
Clouds and rain over Wū Shān—in vain heartbreak yearns.
I ask, within the Hàn palace who could compare?
Poor Fēiyàn, leaning on her fresh-made adornment."
"Famed flower and kingdom-toppling beauty, both bring joy,
Ever winning the monarch's gaze, wreathed in smiles.
To dispel spring wind's boundless regret,
By the Chénxiāng Pavilion's north rail she leans."
Guīnián promptly presented the lyrics.
The Emperor ordered the Líyuán musicians
to roughly tune their string and wind instruments,
then urged Guīnián to sing.
Consort Tàizhēn held a seven-jeweled glass cup,
poured wine from Xīliángzhōu,
and smiled, deeply appreciating the song's meaning.
The Emperor accompanied the melody with a jade flute,
and as each section was about to change,
he would linger on the notes to charm her.
After Consort Tàizhēn finished her drink,
she straightened her embroidered kerchief and bowed deeply again to the Emperor.
Guīnián often spoke to the Five Princes,
recalling that among his singing triumphs,
none surpassed this occasion,
indeed it was the pinnacle of that era.
From then on, the Emperor regarded Imperial Academician Lǐ
with exceptional distinction compared to other scholars.
Later, Gāo Lìshì ultimately considered the boot-removal incident a deep humiliation.
Another day,
when Consort Tàizhēn recited the previous lyrics again,
Lìshì jested:
"These lyrics express the Consort's resentment toward Lǐ Bái,
deep to the marrow.
Why then do you cherish them so?"
The Consort, startled, said:
"How could an Imperial Academician insult someone to such a degree?"
Lìshì replied:
"Using Fēiyàn to refer to the Consort
is an extreme insult."
The Consort rather deeply agreed with this.
The Emperor thrice intended to appoint Lǐ Bái to an official post,
but was each time obstructed by those within the palace and stopped.
From "Records from the Pine Window."
Lǐ Gǔn
Lǐ Gǔn was an excellent singer south of the Yangtze,
his fame stirring the capital.
When Cuī Zhāo came to court,
he secretly brought Gǔn with him.
He then invited guests
and requested the foremost musical troupe and famous performers from the capital
for a grand gathering.
Zhāo mentioned he had a cousin
and asked that he be given the lowest seat.
He had Gǔn appear in shabby clothes,
eliciting sneers and laughter from the entire assembly.
Shortly after, wine was served.
Zhāo said:
"Please ask my cousin to sing."
Those seated laughed again.
But when his voice poured forth in song,
the musicians were greatly astonished, saying:
"This is Lǐ Bā Láng!"
They surrounded him and bowed.
From "Supplement to the National History."
Hán Huì
Hán Huì was an excellent singer,
absolutely superb.
Among his renowned peers, he was called one of the Four Kuí,
with Huì as the head Kuí.
From "Supplement to the National History."
Mǐ Jiāróng
The excellence of song and music
has a long history.
During the Yuánhé era,
national musicians included Mǐ Jiāróng and Hé Kān,
and more recently, Chén Bùxián.
Bùxián's son, Yìnú—
for the past ten or twenty years, no one has heard of truly good singing;
instead, "beat-playing" has become prevalent in the world.
Beat-playing originated with Lǐ Kějiǔ.
Míng manuscript copy: 'jiǔ' written as 'jí'.
During Emperor Yìzōng's reign, favored tunes included
"Farewell to Zhào Shí" and "Lament for Zhào Shí."
Secretary Liú Yǔxī's poem "To Mǐ Jiāróng" says:
"For three reigns Mǐ Jiāróng served the court,
Able to transform new sounds into old.
Nowadays juniors look down on seniors;
Better to dye your beard and serve the young."
Also, upon returning to the capital from his place of exile,
his "Hearing Hé Kān Sing" says:
"Twenty years since I left the imperial city,
Hearing celestial music again overwhelms my heart.
Of the old crowd, only Hé Kān remains;
I earnestly ask him to sing 'Wèichéng' once more."
From "Miscellaneous Tales of the Lú Family."
Zhāohuá Pipe
In the Qín dynasty's Xiányáng Palace, there was a jade flute two feet three inches long,
with twenty-six holes.
When played, one could see carriages, horses, mountains, and forests
appearing faintly in succession.
When the playing ceased, they also vanished.
It was named the Zhāohuá Pipe.
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital."
Táng Xuánzōng
Emperor Xuánzōng once, while holding court,
pressed his abdomen up and down with his fingers.
After court was dismissed,
Gāo Lìshì approached and said:
"Your Majesty repeatedly pressed your abdomen with your fingers earlier;
could it be that the imperial body is slightly unwell?"
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"No.
Last night I dreamed of traveling to the Moon Palace,
where the various immortals entertained me with the music of Shàngqīng.
It was flowing, bright, clear, and transcendent,
almost beyond what mortals could hear.
After being deeply intoxicated for a long time,
they performed a pure melody together
to send me back.
That tune was poignant and moving,
lingering faintly in my ears.
I just now sought it out with my jade flute,
and have captured it all.
During court,
fearing I might forget it,
I kept the jade flute with me,
and from time to time sought the tune by pressing up and down.
It was not discomfort."
Lìshì bowed again in congratulation and said:
"This is an extraordinary event.
I wish Your Majesty would play it once for your servant."
The Emperor tried playing it;
its sound was vast and sparse,
indescribable.
Lìshì again bowed and
requested its name.
The Emperor smiled and said:
"This piece is called 'Zǐyún Huí' (Purple Clouds Return)."
It was recorded in the music archives,
and now the Tàicháng Temple has it engraved on stone.
From *Kāitiān Chuánxìn Jì* (Records of Messages from the Kaiyuan and Tianbao Eras).
Hànzhōng Prince Yǔ
Hànzhōng Prince Yǔ served as a high minister.
Rising early for court,
he heard someone in Yǒngxīng Lane playing a flute,
and asked if it was a musician from the Tàicháng Temple.
The reply was:
"Yes."
Later, while reviewing music, he summoned the musician
and asked:
"How is it that on a certain day you were lying down playing the flute?"
From *Zhuànjì* (Biographical Records).
Lǐ Mó
Lǐ Zhōu, a man fond of curiosities, once obtained some bamboo smoked in a village hut,
cut it to make a flute,
which became as hard as iron or stone.
He gave it to Lǐ Mó.
Mó played the flute,
and was the best in the land.
One moonlit night, boating on the river,
he played for his fellow passengers;
the sound was clear, bright, and soaring.
Suddenly, a stranger on the bank
called to the boat, asking for passage.
Once aboard,
he requested the flute and played it,
with such exquisite skill
it could have cracked mountains and rocks.
Mó had never seen the like in his life.
When he reached the *pò* section (the climactic, rapid part of the piece),
with intense breath and vigorous fingering,
the flute shattered in response to his fingers.
The guest departed,
and no one knew where he went.
The boatman recorded the event,
suspecting he was a flood dragon.
Mó once played his flute on an autumn night at Guāzhōu,
on a narrow, crowded boat.
When he first began the melody,
all movement ceased;
after several phrases,
a gentle breeze suddenly arose.
After a while,
among the merchants and travelers on the boat,
there were sounds of lament, sighing, and weeping.
From *Guóshǐ Bǔ* (Supplement to the National History).
Also regarding Mó:
During the Kāiyuán era, he was the foremost flute player,
unmatched in recent times.
Due to some matter,
he took leave from the Jiàofāng (Music Academy) and went to Yuèzhōu.
Both official and private banquets were held in succession,
so people could witness his marvelous skill.
At the time, there were ten candidates from the prefecture sitting for the imperial examinations,
all with some means.
They pooled two thousand coins for a gathering at Jìnghú Lake,
hoping to invite Master Lǐ to play his flute on the lake,
imagining his elegant style
would be particularly inspiring and divine.
Since the cost was high and attendees few,
they agreed each would invite one guest.
One among them,
remembering only late in the day,
had no time to invite anyone else.
His neighbor was an old man named Dúgū,
who had long lived in the countryside,
unaware of social affairs,
with just a few thatched huts,
and was usually called Elder Dúgū.
So he was invited to fulfill the obligation.
At the gathering place,
the clear waves stretched ten thousand *qǐng*,
the scenery was extraordinary.
Master Lǐ prepared his flute,
and the boat gradually moved to the center of the lake.
Light clouds veiled the sky,
a gentle breeze rippled the waves,
and suddenly the water grew choppy.
Master Lǐ held up his flute;
after the sound began,
the gloom lifted entirely,
the water and trees stood starkly serene,
as if spirits and ghosts had arrived.
All the seated guests praised and marveled at it,
thinking even the music of heaven could not surpass it.
Only Elder Dúgū said not a word,
which angered the others.
Master Lǐ felt slighted,
and was quite resentful.
After a long while,
he quietly concentrated and played another piece,
even more exquisitely marvelous,
leaving all in admiration and awe.
Elder Dúgū again remained silent.
The neighbor who had invited him felt deeply ashamed and regretful,
and explained to the crowd:
"Elder Dúgū lives secluded in a village,
rarely comes to the city walls.
As for music and such,
he is largely unfamiliar."
The gathered guests all joined in mocking and reproaching him.
Elder Dúgū did not reply,
only smiled faintly.
Master Lǐ said:
"Sir, acting like this,
are you being disrespectful?
(Míng manuscript note: 'disrespectful' written as 'skill')
Or are you perhaps an expert yourself?"
Elder Dúgū then said slowly:
"How do you know, sir, that I cannot play?"
All the guests changed their expressions on Master Lǐ's behalf and apologized to him.
Elder Dúgū said:
"Please try playing 'Liángzhōu'."
When the piece ended,
Elder Dúgū said:
"You are indeed quite skilled and marvelous,
but the melody is mixed with foreign music;
could it be you have a Qiūcí (Kucha) companion?"
Master Lǐ was greatly astonished,
rose and bowed, saying:
"Elder, your perception is divine!
I myself was not aware,
but my original teacher was indeed a man of Qiūcí."
Elder Dúgū continued:
"In the thirteenth *dié* (section/variation), you mistakenly entered the *shuǐdiào* mode;
are you aware of this?"
Master Lǐ said:
"I am dull and ignorant,
and truly did not notice."
Elder Dúgū then took the flute and played.
Master Lǐ had another flute,
which he wiped and offered.
Elder Dúgū looked at it and said:
"This one is quite unsuitable,
barely passable for a beginner."
He then switched to his own, saying:
"This one, when we reach the *pò* section,
will certainly split;
I hope you won't mind?"
Master Lǐ said:
"I dare not."
So he played.
The sound soared into the clouds,
shaking all present with awe.
Master Lǐ shrank back, not daring to move.
At the thirteenth *dié*,
he pointed out the erroneous passage,
and Master Lǐ, filled with respect, prepared to bow in submission.
When they reached the *pò* section,
the flute indeed burst and split,
and the piece could not be finished.
Master Lǐ bowed repeatedly.
All were utterly subdued,
and then dispersed.
The next morning,
Master Lǐ and all the guests went to visit him,
but upon arrival found only the thatched hut remaining;
Elder Dúgū was nowhere to be seen.
Those in Yuèzhōu who knew of this sought him,
but ultimately did not discover where he had gone.
From *Yìshǐ* (Lost Histories).
Xǔ Yúnfēng was a flutist among the court musicians.
In the early years of the Zhēnyuán era,
Wéi Yìngwù was transferred from the position of Lántái Láng to become the Prefect of Hézhōu.
This was not what he desired,
and he was quite disheartened.
Sailing eastward on a light boat,
he moored for the night at Língbì Post Station.
At that time, the sky had just cleared,
and the autumn dew was cold and congealing.
In the boat, he chanted poems (Míngchāo edition: "chanted poems" is written as "fēng";
it is suspected it should be "fēng" [to chant]),
intending to compose verses.
Suddenly, he heard the sound of Yúnfēng's flute
and sighed in admiration for a long while.
Wéi was thoroughly versed in musical theory
and said that the sound of the flute
closely resembled that played by Lǐ Mó of the Líyuán Fǎqǔ during the Tiānbǎo era.
He then summoned Yúnfēng to inquire,
and it turned out he was Lǐ Mó's grandson.
Yúnfēng said:
"I am from the old land of Rènchéng,
and I have not returned for many years.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era,
I was just one month old.
At that time, the emperor was returning from the eastern fēng sacrifice,
and the imperial procession stopped at Rènchéng.
My grandfather heard of my birth
and was very pleased to see me.
He then carried me to Academician Lǐ Bái,
requesting him to bestow upon me a fine name.
Lǐ was just then sitting in a tavern,
loudly calling for wine.
The woman tending the stove, a Ms. Hèlán, was nearly ninety years old
and invited Lǐ to drink upstairs.
My grandfather offered wine,
and Lǐ, holding a brush, drunkenly wrote on my chest:
'Under the tree, who is that person?
Not speaking is truly my delight.
If words reach the midday sun,
mist and haze thank and form a treasure.'
My grandfather declined, saying:
'I originally came to Lǐ to request a name,
but now I do not understand what is written.'
Lǐ said:
'The name is contained within.
"Under the tree, a person" is "mù zǐ" (木子),
and "mù zǐ" forms the character Lǐ (李).
"Not speaking" is "mò yán" (莫言),
and "mò yán" is Mó (謨).
"Delight" is "nǚ zǐ" (女子),
and "nǚ zǐ" means grandson.
"If words reach the midday sun" is "yán wǔ" (言午),
and "yán wǔ" is Xǔ (許).
"Mist and haze thank and form a treasure" is "yún chū fēng zhōng" (雲出封中),
which is Yúnfēng (雲封).
Thus, it is Xǔ Yúnfēng, grandson of Lǐ Mó.'
Afterward, I was named accordingly.
When I was just ten years old,
I was left orphaned.
Taking advantage of a post-horse,
I went west to Cháng'ān.
My grandfather, pitying me for coming from afar,
had me join my uncles in their studies.
He said I had a natural understanding of music
and taught me to play the transverse flute.
Every time I mastered a tune,
he would pat my back in appreciation and admiration.
At that time, the Fǎbù of the Líyuán established a minor musical troupe,
with over thirty members in total,
all under fifteen years of age.
On a day in the sixth month of the fourteenth year of Tiānbǎo,
when the imperial cortege was stationed at Líshān,
it was the birth anniversary of the Noble Consort.
The emperor commanded the minor musical troupe
to perform at the Chángshēng Hall.
They played a new composition,
which had no name yet.
It happened that litchis were presented from the South Sea,
so the tune was named 'Lìzhī Xiāng.'
Those present cheered with joy,
their voices shaking the mountains and valleys.
That same year, Ān Lùshān rebelled,
and the imperial carriage returned to the capital.
Afterward, I encountered continuous turmoil and chaos,
drifting to the South Sea
for nearly forty years.
Now I have recently visited my relatives
and am about to reach Lóngqiū."
Wéi said:
"I have the son of my wet nurse,
named Qiānjīn,
who once studied the flute under Lǐ the Court Musician during the Tiānbǎo era.
He died just as his art was perfected,
which I have always lamented.
The flute he used to play
was bestowed by Master Lǐ."
He then took out the old flute from a bag.
Yúnfēng knelt, received it with sorrow,
stroked it, examined it, and said:
"It is indeed a fine flute,
but it is not the one my grandfather played."
He then explained to Wéi:
"Bamboo grows south of Yúnmèng,
and is selected under the Kē Pavilion.
If it sprouts before the full moon of the seventh month this year,
it should be cut before the full moon of the seventh month next year.
If cut after this period,
its sound will be stifled.
If cut before the time,
its sound will be hollow.
Hollow means glossy on the outside but dry inside;
dry means it has not received the vital energy fully.
If the vital energy is not full, the bamboo is stunted.
Generally, to produce a single note,
it requires nine breaths in and out.
For the supreme music of antiquity,
one movement had twelve sections,
and one section had twelve beats.
As for the famous music of today,
such as the lingering melody of 'Falling Plum Blossoms,'
which moves the travelers of Jīngǔ Garden,
or the sentiment conveyed by 'Breaking the Willow,'
which saddens the garrison soldiers at Yùguān Pass—
though truly clear and resonant,
they are different from the supreme music
and cannot be used to summon spirits or pray for blessings.
A stunted bamboo,
when confronted with supreme music, is bound to break.
That is how I know this is not the flute my grandfather played."
Wéi said:
"I wish to test your judgment;
the flute breaking would not matter."
Yúnfēng then held the flute and played 'Liùzhōu Biàn.'
Before one movement was finished,
it suddenly split in the middle with a crack.
Wéi marveled for a long time
and then appointed Yúnfēng to the musical department.
From 'Gānzé Yáo.'
Lǚ Xiāngyún, a merchant from Dòngtíng, often traded goods between Jiāngxī
(Míng manuscript: Jiāngxī written as Shānhǎi)
and various other places,
seeking a profit of ten percent.
Any surplus beyond this profit,
he would immediately give to his impoverished relatives,
then to other poor people,
keeping nothing extra stored away.
He was skilled at playing the flute.
Whenever he encountered beautiful landscapes,
he would always moor his boat to explore them,
playing his flute before departing.
Once, during a mid-spring moonlit night,
he anchored beside Jūnshān.
He poured himself wine and drank alone,
taking a sip and then playing several tunes on his flute.
Suddenly, he saw a fishing boat approaching over the waves.
As it drew closer,
he saw it was an old man with white hair and eyebrows,
whose demeanor was extraordinary.
Xiāngyún set aside his flute and stood up,
welcoming him onto his boat.
The old man moored his fishing boat to Xiāngyún's vessel and came aboard.
They inquired about each other's well-being.
The old man said:
"I heard your flute's clear and resonant sound,
and its extraordinary melodies,
which is why I came."
Xiāngyún offered him several cups of wine.
The old man said:
"In my youth, I also practiced the flute.
Would you be willing to learn from me?"
Xiāngyún had always been deeply fond of the flute,
so he rose and bowed,
expressing his desire to become a humble student.
The old man then produced three flutes from within his sleeves.
The first was as large as joined arms could encircle;
the second was the size commonly used by ordinary people;
the third was extremely small, like a thin brush handle.
Xiāngyún bowed again and asked the old man to play one.
The old man said:
"The largest one cannot be played.
The second one is also the same.
I will play a tune for you on the smallest one.
But I do not know if I can finish it."
Xiāngyún said:
"I wish to hear why the others cannot be played."
The old man said:
"The first one is for the various heavens,
facing the various Heavenly Emperors,
or the Primordial Sovereign,
or the Lady of the Upper Prime,
playing in harmony with the music of the heavens.
If played in the human world,
people would vanish and the earth would split,
the sun and moon would lose their light,
the five planets would fall out of order,
mountains and peaks would collapse,
let alone speak of the other consequences.
The second one is for the various cave-dwelling immortals, the immortals of Pénglái and Gūyè, the Queen Mother of Kūnqiū, and the various Perfected Sovereigns,
playing in harmony with immortal music.
If played in the human world,
sand would fly and stones would roll,
birds in flight would fall to the ground,
running beasts would have their heads split open,
the five planets would become internally disordered,
the young would be shaken to death,
and people would stumble on the roads,
let alone speak of the other consequences.
As for the smallest one,
it is what I and my companions can enjoy for pleasure.
If various beings listen to it together,
playing it may not be safe.
(Míng manuscript: 安 written as 妨)
I do not know if I can finish the tune."
After speaking,
he took out the flute and blew three notes.
The wind stirred on the lake,
waves surged and swelled,
and fish and turtles leaped and spouted.
Xiāngyún and his servants were terrified and trembling.
At the fifth and sixth notes,
the birds and beasts on Jūnshān cried out,
the moonlight grew dim,
and those on the boat were greatly frightened.
The old man then stopped.
He drank several full cups of wine
and then chanted:
"On the lake, an old man reads Huáng-Lǎo,
holding a purple vine, sitting on emerald grass.
Spring arrives, unaware of the depth of the Xiāng River;
dusk falls, forgetting the road to Bālíng."
He drank several more cups
and said to Xiāngyún:
"Next year, at the Shè festival,
I will meet you here."
He then rowed his fishing boat away,
gradually disappearing into the waves.
By the following autumn,
Xiāngyún waited for him for a hundred days at Yúnshān,
but he never appeared again.
From "Bóyì Zhì"
Lǐ Wèi
During the Xiántōng era,
when Chancellor Lǐ Wèi assumed his high office,
he moved from Dàliáng to govern Huáihǎi.
Reports of his administrative achievements spread daily.
Before a full year had passed,
he was honored with additional responsibilities over the land and water,
transforming customs and practices,
greatly satisfying the sentiments of the people.
After the turmoil in Péngmén,
when the military governors' wounds had not yet healed,
Lǐ Wèi governed with restraint and humility.
He mended what was broken and decaying,
repaired damaged systems,
and achieved daily successes.
Because the commandery lacked scenic spots for enjoyment,
and its breeze pavilions and moon-viewing towers
had already fallen into desolation;
while its flower gardens and fishing terraces
did not fully satisfy his deeper intentions.
One day,
he ordered that west of Xìmǎ Pavilion,
connecting to the Yùgōu Xié road,
a pond be excavated,
and pavilions and towers be constructed and repaired.
Once the construction was completed,
it was named "Shǎngxīn" (Heart's Delight).
Flowers and trees were cultivated,
and rare birds and exotic animals from distant lands
were all gathered there.
During the ninety days of fragrant spring,
the men and women of the city could visit and enjoy the view.
One day,
he heard that a minor officer from Zhèyòu, Xuē Yángtáo,
was supervising the transport of tax rice into the city.
Lǐ Wèi was pleased by his name,
which was the same as that of a former attendant of Chancellor Lǐ of Zhūyá.
He ordered an inquiry to be made,
and indeed, it was the same person.
Lǐ Wèi was overjoyed,
as if he had obtained an ancient artifact.
He then ordered a minor officer from his yamen to take over the supervision of the grain transport,
and had Xuē Yángtáo stay at a separate guesthouse.
One day,
Lǐ Wèi invited Xuē Yángtáo for an outing
and inquired about what he had heard,
as well as past matters regarding the reed pipe.
Xuē then presented a scroll of songs composed by Chancellor Lǐ of Zhūyá, Lù Chàng, Yuán Zhěn, and Bái Jūyì.
Lǐ Wèi was even more delighted.
Next, Xuē produced a reed pipe
and played it in the pavilion.
The pipe was extremely delicate.
Often, within a single bìlì,
it could accommodate three pipes.
(Míng manuscript: 三 written as 一)
Its sound seemed to come naturally from the horizon,
with a relaxed and leisurely sentiment.
Lǐ Wèi greatly admired it
and also composed a poem for him, though not all is recorded.
The final lines read:
"Hollow-hearted, slender, like a wild goose carrying a remnant,
even the phoenix's call or dragon's chant surely cannot compare."
(Míng manuscript: 終 written as 全)
He then bestowed generous rewards upon him.
He brought out his two sons
and appointed them to positions overseeing salt production.
Initially, after Lǐ Wèi completed the pond and pavilion,
it had no fine name.
He thus named it "Shǎngxīn."
His subordinates, considering that the character "shǎng" contained the character "shàng,"
which was part of his personal name to be avoided,
objected. Lǐ Wèi said:
"Confucius said that one avoids the given name but not the homophone,
and avoids the homophone but not the given name.
Moreover, unless one is a palace eunuch or concubine,
why avoid such suspicions?"
Thus, he did not change it.
After the rebellion of Qín Yàn,
the pavilion became a pasture for livestock.
Alas!
The Eastern Pavilion of Gōngsūn Hóng
later became a stable under Liú Qūmáo.
How is this any different?
From "Guìyuàn Cóngtán"
Jiégǔ
The jiegǔ drum originates from foreign music.
Because it is a drum of the Róng and Jié peoples,
it is called the jiegǔ.
Its pitch is based on the tàicù mode.
The character "均" was originally written as "云",
and was changed according to the Jiegǔ Lù and Tàipíng Yùlǎn, volume 538.
It was used by the Qiūcí, Gāochāng, Shūlè, and Tiānzhú divisions.
It ranks below the dūtán drum and the dálà drum.
The dūtán drum
is shaped like a waist drum but smaller.
The dálà
is the kāigǔ.
It ranks above the jīlóu drum.
It is like a lacquered bucket.
Made of mountain mulberry wood,
it is supported below by an ivory stand,
and played with two sticks.
Its sound is sharp, piercing, and intense,
especially suitable for brisk
("brisk" was originally written as "but," changed according to the Jiegǔ Lù)
melodies and rapid breaks,
played with continuous, fragmented strikes of the sticks.
It is also fitting for enjoying scenery from high towers,
under bright moonlight and clear breezes,
soaring through the air and carrying far,
distinctly different from other instruments.
The sticks are made of wood such as huángtán, gǒugǔ, and huājiāo.
They must be extremely dry and firm,
completely free of moisture yet still soft and smooth.
Dryness ensures clarity and resonance,
while smoothness ensures agile and vigorous playing.
The hoops are made of hard iron,
which must be finely refined,
and the hoops must be perfectly even.
If not hard,
the tension will vary,
causing constant slackening and tightening.
If uneven,
the drumhead will be loose or tight inconsistently,
similar to the flaws of uneven frets on a qín.
From the "Jiegǔ Lù"
Xuánzōng
Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng possessed profound insight into musical tones and rhythms,
a talent bestowed by nature.
Regarding all wind and string instruments,
he inevitably grasped their subtleties.
If composing tunes and melodies,
he could create them at will.
He did not adhere to fixed rules or measures,
but adapted them to suit the short and long;
the notes produced by his fingers, whether plucked or open,
all hit the precise points.
As for the transformations between clear and turbid tones,
the summoning of the twelve pitch standards,
the relationships between ruler and minister, things and affairs,
mutually governing and employing each other—
even the ancient masters Kuí or Kuàng
could not surpass him.
He especially loved the jiégǔ drum,
often saying:
"It is the leader among the eight classes of instruments,
no other music can compare."
Once, at the beginning of the second month,
at dawn.
Just after finishing his morning toilette,
the overnight rain had just cleared,
the scenery was bright and beautiful.
In the small hall's inner pavilion,
willows and apricots were about to bud.
Seeing this, he sighed and said:
"Facing such scenery,
how can I not judge it with something?"
His attendants exchanged glances,
preparing to order wine to be served,
but only Gāo Lìshì sent for the jiégǔ drum.
The Emperor promptly commanded it,
and by the pavilion, freely played a piece,
named "Chūnguāng Hǎo" (Spring Scenery Fine).
He had composed it himself.
His spirit and thoughts were content.
When he looked back at the willows and apricots,
they had all burst into bloom.
Pointing, he laughed and said to the palace ladies and eunuchs:
"In this matter,
wouldn't you call me the Lord of Heaven?"
All shouted, "Long live the Emperor!"
He also composed "Qiūfēng Gāo" (Autumn Wind High),
and whenever the autumn sky was clear and distant,
with not a wisp of cloud,
he would play it.
Then a gentle breeze would surely come from afar,
and courtyard leaves would slowly fall—
such was its wondrous, divine perfection.
From "Jiégǔ Lù" (Record of the Jié Drum).
Emperor Xuánzōng once observed the various princes.
Prince Níng, in summer sweating, was stretching leather on a drum.
The book he was reading was a musical score from Qiūcí (Kucha).
The Emperor learned of this.
He said happily:
"The brothers of the Son of Heaven
should fully enjoy this music."
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ" (Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang).
Also, Prince Rǔyáng, Jìn,
was the eldest son of Prince Níng.
His appearance was elegant and beautiful,
outstanding among the princely households.
Emperor Xuánzōng particularly doted on him,
personally instructing him.
And because of his intelligence, quick-wittedness, and keen understanding,
he excellently grasped the essence,
so whenever the Emperor traveled for pleasure,
he would not part from him for a moment.
Jìn once wore a polished silk cap while playing a piece,
and the Emperor himself plucked a red hibiscus flower
and placed it on the cap.
Both objects were extremely smooth,
and only after a long time did it settle.
He then performed the piece "Wǔ Shānxiāng" (Dancing Mountain Fragrance),
and the flower did not fall.
This is what is inherently called "steady head and neck"—
the difficulty lies in not shaking.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and laughed,
bestowing golden vessels.
He then praised him, saying:
"Huā'nú (Jìn's childhood name),
Jìn's childhood name
has a luminous and radiant disposition,
with skin and hair fine and glowing,
he is not a mortal man,
he must be an immortal banished from heaven."
Prince Níng modestly declined,
and subsequently criticized him.
The Emperor laughed and said:
"Elder brother need not worry excessively.
Ā Mán (the Emperor's childhood name) naturally understands physiognomy.
The appearance of an emperor
must have an aura of outstanding and extraordinary prowess;
if not,
then a profound, encompassing tolerance.
Huā'nú is merely a handsome and exceptional man,
entirely lacking these qualities,
so there is certainly no cause for suspicion.
Moreover, his demeanor is refined and elegant—
he should instead gain fine repute among the ministers and nobility."
Prince Níng thanked him again.
And said:
"In this regard,
I concede to him."
The Emperor said:
"In this one matter,
Ā Mán also concedes to elder brother."
Prince Níng again modestly declined.
The Emperor laughed and said:
"Ā Mán wins in many aspects.
Elder brother also need not bow and yield."
All present joyfully congratulated them.
Emperor Xuánzōng had a bold and unrestrained nature,
and intensely disliked the qín (zither).
Once, while listening to someone play a proper piece,
before it was finished,
he shouted at the qín player:
"Attendant, get out!"
He said to the eunuchs:
"Quickly summon Huā'nú to bring the jiégǔ drum,
to cleanse me of this foulness."
Also, Huáng Fānchuò was also knowledgeable in music.
The Emperor once sent someone to summon him,
but he did not arrive promptly.
The Emperor grew angry,
and dispatched messengers one after another to search for and apprehend him.
When Chuò arrived,
reaching the side of the hall,
he heard the Emperor practicing the drum,
so he firmly stopped the usher,
not allowing him to announce.
After a short while,
the Emperor asked the attending official again:
"Has that fellow come yet?"
Chuò again stopped him.
When the piece ended,
and the Emperor changed to another piece,
after only thirty or so notes,
Chuò immediately walked in.
The Emperor asked where he had come from,
and he said:
"A relative or old friend was traveling far,
I saw him off outside the city walls."
The Emperor nodded.
After the drumming finished,
the Emperor said to him:
"Fortunately you were slightly delayed.
My earlier angry mood—
had you arrived then, disaster would surely have befallen you.
Just now I was thinking,
you have been in long-term service for over fifty days,
taking one day off to go out—
I cannot not allow you to go east or west to attend to matters."
Chuò bowed and gave thanks.
Some eunuchs were whispering and laughing to each other.
The Emperor questioned them,
and they fully recounted how Chuò had arrived early,
listened to the drumming, and waited for the right moment to enter.
The Emperor asked Chuò,
and Chuò described how the Emperor had been angry,
and the moment when his anger subsided—
all without the slightest error.
The Emperor found this remarkable,
and again said to him sternly:
"Matters beneath my heart, spleen, and bones—
how could a mere attendant fellow, listening to a small drum, predict them?
Now, tell me, what am I thinking?"
Chuò then descended the steps,
faced north and bowed deeply,
and said loudly:
"By imperial decree, supervise
(Míng manuscript copy: supervise as 'erect')
the golden rooster."
The Emperor laughed heartily and let it go.
Both from "Jiégǔ Lù" (Record of the Jié Drum).

When he first received imperial favor,
he discussed drum matters with Xuánzōng, saying:

then it is the huāwèng from Lǔshān.

the raindrops signify rapidity.

because it was slightly more elegant and refined compared to the Hànzhèn.
The Kāifǔ's family passed it down entirely.
The grandmother of Dōngdū Liúshǒu Zhèng Shūmíng,

It is said that in the Zhèng residence at Zūnxián Lane, there is a small tower,

Lǐ Guīnián
Lǐ Guīnián was skilled at the jiégǔ.
Xuánzōng asked, "How many sticks have you played, Minister?"
He replied:
"Your subject has played fifty sticks."
The Emperor said:
"You are far from it;
I have played through three vertical cabinets."
Several years later,
he heard that he had played one vertical cabinet,
and therefore bestowed upon him a fúméi jiégǔ juǎn.
From "Zhuànjì"
Cáo Wáng Gāo
Sì Cáo Wáng Gāo had ingenious ideas,
and was skilled in the use of utensils.
When he was Jīngzhōu Jiédùshǐ,
there was a traveling scholar who carried two juǎn,
wishing to seek an audience.
He first announced at the guest residence,
and those who saw it were surprised, saying:
"Is this really worth valuing?"
The scholar said:
"Just announce it;
the Shàngshū will understand."
When they met,
Gāo held them and sighed, saying:
"I never thought I would encounter a treasure today."
He pointed out their firm and even shape.
The guests in their seats merely assented,
some inwardly disagreeing.
Gāo said:
"Gentlemen may not believe it."
He ordered a food tray to be brought,
and selected the most level one himself.
Then he placed the two juǎn in the center of the tray,
poured oil into the juǎn until full,
and the oil did not seep through,
showing how perfectly they fit together.
Gāo said:
"These must be juǎn presented to the Emperor during the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras;
otherwise, they could not be like this."
He asked where they came from,
and the guest said:
"My late father was in Qián,
and obtained them from the household of Gāo Lìshì."
Only then did everyone deeply admire them.
Source originally missing;
according to book volume 231, from "Jiégǔ Lù"
Lǐ Wǎn
During the Guǎngdé era,
a visitor from Shǔ, former Shuāngliú County Deputy Lǐ Wǎn, could also do it.
He was transferred to Cháng'ān,
and lived on Wùběn Lane.
Once he heard jiégǔ at night,
the melody was quite exquisite.
He walked under the moon to find it,
and arrived at a small house,
with a very low and narrow door.
He knocked and requested an audience,
and said to the drummer:
"What you are playing,
is it not 'Yé Pó Sè Jī'?
One version writes 'Yé Pó Suō Jī'
Although it is extremely skillful,
why is there no ending?"
The drummer was greatly surprised and said:
"You are certainly one who understands music;
no one knows about this matter.
I am a worker from the Tàicháng Temple;
my grandfather passed down this art,
and he was especially skilled at this piece.
Recently, when Zhāng Rú entered Cháng'ān,
his family scattered,
my father died west of the river,
and this piece was thus lost.
Now I only follow several old scores to search for it,
but ultimately cannot find the concluding sound,
so I seek it every night."
Wǎn said:
"Does the piece's meaning end there?"
The worker said:
"It ends."
Wǎn said:
"If the meaning ends, then the piece ends.
What more is there to seek?"
The worker said:
"But what about the sound not ending?"
Wǎn said:
"It can be said:
For pieces like this,
they must be resolved with another piece,
only then can the sound be fully expressed.
For 'Yé Pó Suō Jī', one should use the 'Qū Zhè Jí Biàn' to resolve it."
The worker followed his instruction,
and indeed it harmonized perfectly,
both sound and meaning fully expressed.
Just as 'Zhèzhī' uses 'Hún' to resolve,
and 'Gānzhōu' uses 'Jíliǎo' to resolve, and the like.
Míng manuscript copy writes jíliǎo as jízǐ
The worker wept and thanked him.
He then spoke to the temple minister,
who recommended him as Zhǔbù.
Later, he rose through official ranks to become Tàicháng Shǎoqīng and Zōngzhèng Qīng.
From "Jiégǔ Lù"
Dù Hóngjiàn
During the reign of Emperor Dàizōng,
Prime Minister Dù Hóngjiàn was also skilled at playing the jiegǔ drum.
In the Yǒngtài era, he served as the
Deputy Commander-in-Chief and Military Governor of Xīchuān.
When he arrived in Chéngdū,
Lǐ Wǎn had a carved drumstick in Shǔ,
which he presented to Hóngjiàn.
Hóngjiàn obtained it and
showed it to the crowd, saying:
"This is a rare treasure,
which must have been stored in clothing and quilts for a long time."
The craftsman said:
"I kept it in the ridge groove for ten years."
When he left
Shǔ and reached the western border of Lìzhōu,
he looked toward the Jiāyì post road entering Hànchuān.
Coming from the southwest,
he finally reached the Jiālíng River,
where the landscape scenery was quite beautiful.
That night, the moonlight was also splendid,
so he climbed the post tower with his subordinates Yáng Yán and Dù Cóng
to gaze at the river and the moon.
"Today, having emerged from hardship and suspicion,
externally, I have not disgraced the court's command,
and internally, I have avoided disaster from subtle matters.
Since I have secured this peaceful journey
and now behold this extraordinary scenery,
how can I not congratulate myself?"
He then ordered his servant to fetch the drum, clappers, and flute,
and played several tunes with the drumstick he had obtained.
Birds and monkeys in the surrounding mountains
all flew away in alarm or fled screeching.
His subordinates were all astonished and said:
"In ancient times, when Kuí played the drums,
all the beasts danced in the courtyard.
Is this any different?"
Hóngjiàn replied:
"If someone like me,
who has only made slight efforts in this art
and has not yet reached perfection,
can still achieve this,
then how much more so when a sage rules the world
and virtuous ministers examine music?
How could flying and running creatures not be moved?"
He then mentioned that he had a villa near the Huāyán Pavilion,
and whenever the weather was clear and bright,
he would sometimes climb the pavilion to play there.
At first, he saw a flock of sheep grazing in the river valley below,
and suddenly several of them began to prance about incessantly.
He did not think it was because of the drumming.
But when he stopped drumming, they also stopped,
and when he resumed, they resumed as well.
He then varied the tempo and pitch to rhythmically accompany them,
and they responded to every change.
Soon, two dogs came running from their home, barking.
When they reached the side of the flock,
they gradually stopped barking, raised their heads,
and seemed to be listening.
After a short while,
they also bent their necks and wagged their tails,
following the changes in rhythm.
Thus, it is clear that leading them in dance is not difficult at all.
Recently, few among the literati practice this,
except for the Minister Hán Gāo, who is skilled
but rarely displays it.
When he served as the Military Governor of Èzhōu,
it was said he practiced only once or twice at the Huánghè Tower.
From "The Record of the Jiegǔ Drum"
Bronze Drum
Among the music of the southern barbarians,
there is the bronze drum.
It is shaped like a waist drum,
but with a face on one end,
the drum face about two feet in diameter.
The face and body are connected,
cast entirely from bronze.
The body is adorned with patterns of insects, fish, flowers, and grass,
evenly distributed across the surface,
and about two fen thick.
The craftsmanship of the casting
is truly ingenious and exquisite.
When struck, it produces a resounding sound,
no less loud than the bellowing of an alligator.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
when the state of Piào presented music,
there were jade conch shells and bronze drums.
The jade conch shells are white conch shells,
not carved from jade.
Thus, it is known that the chieftains of the southern barbarians
all possess such drums.
Zhāng Zhífāng
At the end of the Xiántōng era,
Zhāng Zhífāng of Yōuzhōu was demoted to serve as the Prefect of Gōngzhōu.
After assuming his post,
he repaired the city walls,
and while digging,
he unearthed a bronze drum.
When his term ended,
he transported it back to the capital.
Upon reaching Xiāng-Hàn,
he considered it a useless object
and donated it to the Yánshòuqìng Monastery,
where it was hung in the meditation hall as a large wooden fish.
It remains there to this day.
Also from "The Record of Strange Things from South of the Passes"
Zhèng Xù
During the reign of Emperor Xīzōng,
when Zhèng Xù was stationed in Pānyú,
a man named Lín Ăi served as the Prefect of Gāozhōu.
A shepherd boy, while herding cattle,
heard a frog croaking in the fields.
The shepherd boy tried to catch it.
The frog jumped into a hole,
which, when dug, turned out to be deep and large—
the tomb of a barbarian chieftain.
The frog had disappeared without a trace,
but in the hole, he found a bronze drum.
Its color was emerald green,
with several areas corroded and damaged by soil.
On its surface, raised patterns
depicted many frogs and toads.
It was suspected that the croaking frog
was the spirit of the drum.
He then reported the circumstances
to the Governor of Guǎng,
and it was hung in the armory,
where it remains to this day.
From "The Record of Strange Things from South of the Passes"
Luó Hēihēi
During the reign of Emperor Tàizōng,
a western country sent a foreigner skilled at playing the pipa,
who performed a tune
with exceptionally thick pipa strings.
The Emperor, not wanting foreigners to surpass the Chinese,
held a grand banquet
and had Luó Hēihēi listen from behind a curtain.
After hearing it once, she mastered it.
The Emperor said to the foreigner:
"This tune, my palace maidens can play it."
He fetched a large pipa
and placed it behind the curtain.
He ordered Hēihēi to play it,
and she did so without missing a single note.
The foreigner thought she was a palace maiden
and left in astonishment and admiration.
When the western countries heard of this,
dozens of them submitted.
From "Records of Court and Country"
Péi Luò'ér
During the Zhēnguān era,
Péi Luò'ér, a pipa player, was the first to abandon the plectrum and use his hands,
which is what is commonly known today as plucking the pipa.
From "The Collection of Unusual Historical Records"
Consort Yáng
During the Kāiyuán era,
the eunuch Bái Xiùzhēn returned from a mission to Shǔ
and presented a pipa as a gift.
Its body and frame were made of sandalwood,
warm and smooth as jade,
gleaming and reflective.
It had golden threads and red patterns,
forming the shadow of a pair of phoenixes.
Consort Yáng often held this pipa
and performed in the Líyuán.
The music was clear and melancholic,
floating as if beyond the clouds.
The princes and noble ladies,
from Guóguó Fūrén onward,
vied to become Consort Yáng's pipa disciples.
Each time they finished learning a tune,
they presented her with lavish gifts.
From "The Record of Tán Bīn"
Duàn Shī
In ancient times, pipa strings were made from the sinews of the kūnjī bird.
During the Kāiyuán era,
Duàn Shī, a skilled pipa player,
used leather strings.
When Hè Huáizhì tried to play it with a broken plectrum,
he could not produce any sound.
From "The Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng"
Hànzhōng Wáng Yǔ
Hànzhōng Wáng Yǔ saw Kāng Kūnlún playing the pipa,
and said, "There are many 'pí' sounds,
but few 'pá' sounds.
(The characters 'pá sounds' were originally missing,
and have been supplemented based on the Chuánzǎi.)
Moreover, one cannot play the fifty-four-string large string instrument either.
Moving from bottom to top is called 'pí,'
and moving from top to bottom is called 'pá.'
From the Chuánjì.
(The Ming manuscript states it is from the Chuánzǎi.)
Wéi Yìngwù
Wéi Yìngwù served as the governor of Sūzhōu.
He had a subordinate official who,
due to the Jiànzhōng Rebellion,
obtained the guqin, se, and pipa of the court musician Kāng Kūnlún.
These were then sent to the authorities,
and a memorial was submitted to present them to the palace.
From the Guóshǐ Bǔ.
Sòng Yǎn
Sòng Yǎn, the grandson of Sòng Jǐng, was knowledgeable in music theory.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
he presented two volumes of music books,
which Emperor Dézōng read and praised.
Learning that he was the grandson of Sòng Jǐng,
the emperor summoned him for an audience,
discussed music with him,
and was pleased.
A few days later,
he was summoned again to Xuānhuī Hall,
where music was performed for him to observe.
The emperor said,
"If there are any errors or irregularities,
you may point them all out."
Sòng Yǎn replied,
"Allow me to discuss and deliberate with the music officials,
and then submit a detailed memorial."
The emperor ordered the Xuānhuī envoy and the Jiàofāng to consult with the music officials.
After several days, they submitted a report,
in which many musicians claimed that Sòng Yǎn did not understand musical tones,
was unfamiliar with rhythm,
and was also hard of hearing,
making him unfit to discuss music.
The emperor found this strange
and summoned him again for an audience.
Sòng Yǎn replied,
"I am old and often ill,
and my hearing is indeed impaired.
However, when it comes to music theory,
I am not without skill."
The emperor then had him perform music.
After the piece ended,
he asked about its merits and flaws.
Sòng Yǎn responded slowly and hesitantly,
and many musicians laughed at him.
Sòng Yǎn looked around, smiled,
then became angry and said with a stern expression,
"Although the music is exquisite,
there are aspects within it that are unacceptable."
The emperor, surprised, asked him to explain.
He immediately pointed to a pipa player and said,
"This person has committed a grave and cruel act of treason,
and will soon face the law.
He should not be in the presence of Your Majesty."
He then pointed to a shēng player and said,
"This person's spirit has already wandered to the grave,
and he should no longer be allowed to serve."
The emperor was greatly alarmed
and ordered the authorities to secretly observe them.
Soon after, the pipa player was accused by his peers,
who claimed that six or seven years earlier,
his father had hanged himself
for unknown reasons.
Upon investigation,
he confessed to the crime.
The shēng player, overwhelmed with worry and fear, stopped eating
and died within ten days.
The emperor then held Sòng Yǎn in even greater esteem,
personally bestowed upon him ceremonial robes,
and frequently summoned him for audiences.
Whenever he was asked to observe music performances,
the musicians would tremble with fear, holding their breath,
and dared not look directly at him.
Fearing he would incur disaster,
Sòng Yǎn pleaded illness and retired.
From the Jiégǔ Lù.
Huángfǔ Zhí
The Shǔ general Huángfǔ Zhí had a discerning ear for music.
By striking pottery,
he could tell the season and month.
He enjoyed playing the pipa.
During the Yuánhé era,
he once composed a melody.
While enjoying the cool breeze
by a pond, he played it.
Originally in the Huángzhōng key, the sound shifted to Ruíbīn.
He changed the strings
and played it several times,
but the sound remained in Ruíbīn.
Huángfǔ Zhí was deeply puzzled and displeased,
thinking it an ill omen.
The next day, he played by the pond again,
and the sound was the same.
When he tried playing elsewhere,
it returned to Huángzhōng.
Huángfǔ Zhí then tuned the strings precisely to Ruíbīn
and played by the pond again at night.
He noticed ripples near the shore,
as if something was stirring the water like a fish leaping,
but when he stopped playing, it disappeared.
Huángfǔ Zhí then gathered guests to drain the pond,
exhausting the mud at the bottom.
After searching for several days,
they found a piece of iron buried more than a zhang deep in the mud.
It turned out to be a Ruíbīn iron from a fāngxiǎng.
From the Yǒuyáng Zázǔ.
Wáng Yí
Wáng Yí had never understood string instruments in his life.
One morning, he suddenly fell asleep
and did not wake until night.
He then asked for a pipa, strummed it,
and composed several pieces.
One was called "The Sparrow Pecking the Snake,"
another "The Hu King's Melody,"
and another "The Hu Melon Garden."
No one had heard these pieces before,
and those who listened were moved to tears.
His younger sister asked to learn them,
and he taught her a few notes,
but she forgot them almost immediately,
unable to recreate the melodies.
From the Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Guān Biéjià
At the end of Emperor Zhāozōng's reign,
the famous courtesans and entertainers of the capital
were all taken by powerful feudal lords.
Among the pipa musicians serving the court,
one was known as Guān Biéjià.
Xiǎohóng was her nickname.
Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng
(Originally "zong," corrected to "zǔ" based on the Ming manuscript)
sought her out.
After she arrived,
he said to her,
"Do you know how to play 'Shǒu
(Ming manuscript has 'yáng' instead of 'shǒu')
Bù Cǎi Sāng'?"
Guān bowed and played it.
Afterward, she was also asked by close associates
to play while they drank.
As a result, she became disheartened
and died not long after.
There was also a pipa player named Shí Cóng, known as Shí Sīmǎ.
He claimed that earlier, he had been appreciated by the chancellor Lìnghú Táo,
who allowed him to adopt a name alongside his sons Huàn, Fán, and others.
After the turmoil, he went to Shǔ,
but was not registered as a musician.
He often visited the homes of high officials,
where he was treated as a guest.
One day, he attended a gathering with several military officers
who were drinking and making merry.
Shí Cóng, with his húqín, noticed that those present were not connoisseurs of music,
as they were chatting and laughing loudly,
paying little attention to his playing.
Shí Cóng then struck the sandalwood frame and angrily said,
"I once performed for a chancellor of the central court,
yet today I play for soldiers who do not listen to me.
How bitter this is!"
Those who understood sighed in amazement at his words.
From the Běimèng Suǒyán.
Wáng Shì Nǚ
Wáng Shǔ Qiánnán Jiédùshǐ Wáng Bǎoyì,
had a daughter who was betrothed to Gāo Cónghuì's son Bǎojié of Jīngnán.
Before the marriage took place,
she temporarily adopted Daoist attire.
She was intelligent and quick-witted,
and skilled at playing the pipa.
Because she dreamed of extraordinary beings,
she was frequently taught musical compositions.
The beings who taught her
appeared sometimes as Daoists, sometimes as laypeople,
and wore robes either purple or yellow.
There were nights when she was taught several pieces,
and pieces she could remember after just one hearing.
Their sound was clear and transcendent,
different from the ordinary,
resembling the celestial family's "Zǐyún" and similar pieces.
She then said,
"Please have my eldest brother compose a preface for these musical scores,
and have them engraved on stone in the direction of Jiǎyǐn."
Her elder brother was Jīngnán Tuīguān and Junior Supervisor Wáng Zhēnfàn,
who composed the preface and had them engraved on stone.
The pieces transmitted included
the gōng mode pieces: "Dàodiào Gōng", "Yùchén Gōng", "Yízé Gōng", "Shénlín Gōng", "Ruíbīn Gōng", "Wúyì Gōng", "Xuánzōng Gōng", "Huángzhōng Gōng", "Sǎnshuǐ Gōng", "Zhònglǚ Gōng".
The shāng mode pieces:
"Dúzhǐ Fàn Qīngshāng", "Hǎoxiān Shāng", "Cè Shāng", "Hóngxiāo Shāng", "Fèng Mǒ Shāng", "Yùxiān Shāng".
The jué mode pieces:
"Shuāngdiào Jué", "Zuìyín Jué", "Dàlǚ Jué", "Nánlǚ Jué", "Zhōnglǚ Jué", "Gāodàzhí Jué", "Ruíbīn Jué".
The yǔ mode pieces:
"Fèngyín Yǔ", "Bèifēng Xiāng", "Bèinán Yǔ", "Bèipíng Yǔ", "Yìngshèng Yǔ", "Yùgōng Yǔ", "Yùchén Yǔ", "Fēngxiāng Diào", "Dàlǚ Diào".
The names of the pieces were the same as those in the human world,
such as "Liángzhōu", "Yīzhōu", "Húwèi Zhōu", "Gānzhōu", "Lǜyāo", "Mòdá", "Xiàng
Míng chāo běn xiàng zuò qǐng.
Yí dāng zuò qīng
pén Lè", "Ān Gōngzǐ", "Shuǐgǔzi", "Ā Làn Fàn" and the like,
totaling over two hundred pieces.
What was different was that
among the zhǐ mode pieces were "Xiāngfēi Yuàn" and "Kū Yánhuí".
At that time, the huqin did not play in the zhǐ mode.
Wáng married into the Gāo family,
but died after several years.
Could it be that she was a banished immortal who had fallen to earth?
Sūn Guāngxiàn's daughter-in-law
fù yuán zuò fù.
Jù míng chāo běn gǎi
was Wáng's niece,
and remembered one or two pieces.
I once heard her play them,
which was also an extraordinary matter.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Zhào Pì
Zhào Pì played the five-stringed lute.
Someone asked
huò wèn yuán zuò wén wú,
jù míng chāo běn gǎi
about his technique.
Pì said:
"Regarding the five-stringed lute,
at first I encountered it with my spirit,
and in the end, heaven followed along.
When I am in a vast and expansive state,
my ears are like eyes,
my eyes are like nose,
I do not know whether the five-stringed lute is Pì,
or Pì is the five-stringed lute."
From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ".
Xú Yuèhuá
Wèi Gāo Yáng Wáng Yōng's beauty Xú Yuèhuá could play the horizontal konghou,
producing the sounds of Míngfēi's departure to the frontier.
There was a Tián Sēngqǐ who could play the reed pipe, performing "Zhuàngshì Gē" and "Xiàng Yǔ Yín".
When General Cuī Yánbó went out with his troops,
each time he faced the enemy,
he would have Sēngqǐ perform the "Zhuàngshì" sounds,
and then he would charge alone into the enemy formation.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ".
Ancient Script
Regarding the Ancient Script,
it was created by Huángdì's historian Cāngjié.
Jié had four eyes on his head,
and communicated with the divine and enlightened.
He looked up to observe the curved patterns of the Kui constellation,
and looked down to examine the markings on turtle shells and the traces of birds.
He broadly collected various beauties,
combined them to form characters,
which are called Ancient Script.
"Xiàojīng" quotes "Shén Qì" as saying:
"The Kui constellation governs literature,
and Cāngjié imitated its forms."
From "Shū Duàn".
Large Seal Script
Regarding the Large Seal Script,
it was created by Zhōu Xuānwáng's Grand Historian Shǐ Zhòu.
Some say
the Pillar Historian first altered the Ancient Script,
sometimes identical, sometimes different,
and called it Seal Script.
Seal (zhuàn) means to transmit (chuán),
transmitting the principles of things,
applying them endlessly.
Zhēn Fēng established the Six Scripts,
the third being Seal Script.
Among the Eight Script Styles of calligraphy,
the first is Large Seal Script.
Also, the "Hànshū‧Yìwénzhì" lists
"Shǐ Zhòu" in fifteen chapters,
which is this same script.
It was created by this official,
used for teaching,
and called Historian's Script,
totaling nine thousand characters.
From "Shū Duàn".
Zhòu Script
Created by Zhōu's Grand Historian Shǐ Zhòu,
it differs slightly from Ancient Script and Large Seal Script.
Later people named the script after him,
calling it Zhòu Script.
"Qī Lüè" says:
"'Shǐ Zhòu' is
the script used by Zhōu dynasty historians to teach children to write,
and its style differs from the Ancient Script found in the walls of the Kǒng family.
Zhēn Fēng established the Six Scripts,
the second being the Curious Script, which is this."
From "Shū Duàn".
Small Seal Script
Small Seal Script
was created by Qín Chancellor Lǐ Sī.
He added to and subtracted from the Large Seal Script,
differing from and agreeing with the Zhòu Script,
and called it Small Seal Script.
It is also called Qín Seal Script.
From "Shū Duàn".
Eight-Part Script
Regarding the Eight-Part Script,
it was created by Wáng Cìzhòng of Shànggǔ during the Qín dynasty.
Wáng Yīn said:
"Wáng Cìzhòng began by making ancient script square and broad,
with few wave-like strokes."
During the Jiànchū era,
he used clerical script and cursive script to create a standard method,
with characters square and eight parts,
meaning they had a model standard.
Shǐhuáng obtained Cìzhòng's script.
It was simple and concise,
suited for urgent and speedy use.
He was very pleased.
He sent an envoy to summon him,
but after three summonses, he did not come.
Shǐhuáng was greatly angered,
ordered a cage cart to send for him,
but on the way, he transformed into a large bird and flew away.
From "Shū Duàn".
Clerical Script
Regarding Clerical Script,
it was created by Chéng Miǎo of Xiàguī during the Qín dynasty.
Miǎo, styled Yuáncén,
initially served as a county clerk.
He committed an offense,
and Shǐhuáng imprisoned him in Yúnyáng jail.
He pondered deeply for ten years,
enhancing the square and round aspects of Small Seal Script,
and created three thousand characters of Clerical Script,
which he presented.
Shǐhuáng approved of it,
and employed him as a Censor.
Because memorials and affairs were numerous and complex,
and Seal Script characters were difficult to complete,
they then used Clerical Script characters.
As it was used by clerks to assist in writing,
it was called Clerical Script.
From "Shū Duàn".
Draft Cursive Script
Regarding zhāngcǎo (draft cursive script),
it was created by Shǐ Yóu, a Clerk of the Yellow Gate during the Hàn dynasty.
Wèi Héng and Lǐ Dàn both stated:
"There was a method for cursive script in the early Hàn,
but it is not known who created it."
Xiāo Zǐliáng stated:
"Zhāngcǎo
was started by Dù Cāo, Chancellor of Qí during the Hàn,
who first transformed the draft method."
This is incorrect.
Wáng Yīn stated:
(The character "yún" (stated) was originally missing here,
added based on the Ming manuscript copy)
"During the time of Emperor Yuán
(The original text had 'zhāng' (chapter) for 'dì' (emperor),
corrected based on the Ming manuscript copy)
Shǐ Yóu composed the *Jíjiù Zhāng* (Quick Access Chapter).
He loosened the structure of the clerical script,
writing it roughly.
Due to the Hàn custom of simplicity and indolence,
it gradually came into use. This is correct."
From *Shū Duàn* (Judgments on Calligraphy).
Xíngshū (Running Script)
Regarding xíngshū (running script),
it was created by Liú Déshēng of Yǐngchuān during the Later Hàn dynasty.
Xíngshū is a minor variation of zhèngshū (standard script),
(The original text had 'wěi' (false) for 'biàn' (change),
corrected based on the Ming manuscript copy)
aiming for simplicity and ease,
suitable for correspondence and popular circulation,
hence it is called xíngshū (running script).
Wáng
(The original text had 'yún' (stated) for 'wáng',
corrected based on the Ming manuscript copy)
Yīn stated:
"Since the Jìn dynasty,
most skilled calligraphers have become famous for their xíngshū.
Zhōng Yuáncháng (Zhōng Yáo) excelled at xíngshū.
Afterwards, Wáng Xīzhī and Wáng Xiànzhī
both brought it to its ultimate perfection."
From *Shū Duàn*.
Fēibái (Flying White)
Regarding fēibái (flying white script),
it was created by Cài Yōng, a Left Gentleman of the Palace during the Later Hàn dynasty.
Wáng Yǐn and Wáng Yīn both stated:
"Fēibái is a transformation of the regular script style.
It was originally used for inscribing palace plaques.
The brushwork was vigorous,
but the characters were appropriately light and not fully saturated,
hence named fēibái (flying white)."
Wáng Sēngqián stated:
"Fēibái is a lighter form of bāfēn script.
Cài Yōng was at the Hóngdū Gate,
when he saw a craftsman applying whitewash with a broom,
and thus conceived the idea."
From *Shū Duàn*.
Cǎoshū (Cursive Script)
Regarding cǎoshū (cursive script),
it was created by Zhāng Bóyīng (Zhāng Zhī), a Recluse-Scholar of the Later Hàn dynasty.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, in his *Cǎoshū Zhuàng* (Description of Cursive Script), said:
"Cài Yōng stated,
In the past, during the Qín era,
the feudal lords contended for supremacy.
Urgent military dispatches were transmitted,
watching beacon fires and rushing couriers.
As seal and clerical scripts were difficult,
and could not meet urgent needs,
they consequently created a script for hastening urgency,
which is essentially today's cǎoshū."
From *Shū Duàn*.
Jízhǒng Texts (Texts from the Jí Tomb)
These were from the time of King Ānxī of Wèi.
A farmer from Jí County in Wèi Commandery
discovered them in an ancient tomb.
They were bamboo slips with lacquer writing in kēdǒu (tadpole) script,
containing miscellaneous writings of classics and histories.
Compared with modern editions for verification,
there were many differences and similarities.
The farmer's surname was Bù.
The character 'bù' is pronounced as Biāo.
His given name was Huái.
From the *Postface to the Chūnqiū* and annotations in the *Wénxuǎn*.
From *Shàngshū Gùshí* (Anecdotes from the Past).
Lǐ Sī
Lǐ Sī, Chancellor of Qín, said:
"In high antiquity, the great seal script was created,
and was quite prevalent in the world.
However, being ancient and remote,
most people could not comprehend it in detail.
Now, I have deleted and simplified the complex forms,
taking those with unified structure,
and devised the small seal script."
Sī was skilled in calligraphy.
From Zhào Gāo downwards,
all submitted to him.
Inscriptions on famous mountains,
stele seals and bronze figures,
were all written by Sī's brush.
When inscribing the stone commemorating his achievements at Qínwàng,
he said:
"Five hundred and thirty years after my death,
there will be a person
to succeed my traces."
From Méng Tián's *Bǐ Jīng* (Classic of the Brush).
Sī excelled at seal script,
first simplifying and reforming it into the small seal script,
composing
(The original text had 'zhě' (one who) for 'zhù' (compose),
corrected based on the Ming manuscript copy)
the seven chapters of the *Cāngjié Piān*.
Although the substance and refinement of emperors and kings
underwent additions and reductions through the ages,
ultimately refinement replaced substance,
gradually becoming shallow and diluted.
Thus, the knotted cords of the Three Sovereigns,
the symbolic images of the Five Emperors,
and the corporal punishments of the Three Kings—
Sī's case can be compared to these.
Ancient script can be considered high antiquity,
great seal script as middle antiquity,
small seal script as lower antiquity.
The three antiquities represent the substance,
while cursive and clerical scripts represent the refinement.
Those who reached the ultimate in refinement were Xī (Wáng Xīzhī) and Xiàn (Wáng Xiànzhī);
those who exhaustively mastered the substance were Zhòu (Shǐ Zhòu) and Sī (Lǐ Sī).
The First Emperor had the Héshì Jade
carved to make a seal,
and ordered Sī to inscribe its text.
The present steles on Mount Tài, Mount Yì, and at Qínwàng, etc.,
are all his surviving works.
They are also called the magnificent treasure transmitted through the state,
a model for a hundred generations.
Sī's small seal script entered the divine class,
his great seal script entered the marvelous class.
Lǐ Sī's calligraphy
is known
(The Ming manuscript copy has 'rú' (like) for 'zhī' (known))
to be preeminent,
is it not difficult to surpass?
From *Shū Píng* (Calligraphy Critique) and also from *Shū Duàn*.
Xiāo Hé
Xiāo Hé of the Former Hàn was skilled in seal and zhòu scripts.
When the front palace hall was completed,
he pondered deeply for three months
before inscribing its plaque.
Spectators flowed like a stream.
Hé used a worn-out brush to write.
From Yáng Xīn's *Bǐzhèn Tú* (Diagram of the Brush Battle Array).
Cài Yōng
Cài Yōng of the Later Hàn, styled Bójiē.
He was from Chénliú.
His appearance was exceptionally imposing,
deeply filial and widely learned,
capable in painting and skilled in music,
and understood astronomy and numerology.
He was accomplished in calligraphy,
his seal and clerical scripts were peerless in his time.
He particularly grasped the subtleties of bāfēn script,
his style and method underwent a hundred transformations,
exhausting the numinous and reaching the ultimate in marvel,
standing alone past and present.
He also created fēibái,
marvelously without equal.
Bójiē's bāfēn and fēibái entered the divine class,
his great seal, small seal, and clerical scripts entered the marvelous class.
His daughter, Yǎn, was very virtuous,
and also skilled in calligraphy.
Bójiē entered Mount Sōng to study calligraphy.
Inside a stone chamber, he obtained a plain book,
with eight corners and dangling radiance,
written in seal script describing the brush techniques of Lǐ Sī and Shǐ Zhòu.
Bójiē obtained it,
and for three meal times did not eat,
then cried out loudly in joy,
as if facing several tens of people.
Bójiē consequently read and recited it for three years,
and then marvelously comprehended its essential principles.
Bójiē personally wrote the Five Classics at the Imperial Academy,
spectators crowded like a market.
From Yáng Xīn's *Bǐfǎ* (Brush Methods).
Cài Yōng's calligraphy
has bone-force and wind-penetration,
its essence and spirit enter the divine class.
From Yuán Áng's *Shū Píng* and also from *Shū Duàn*.
Cuī Yuàn
Cuī Yuàn, styled Zǐyù,
was a native of Ānpíng.
His great-grandfather was Méng,
and his father was Yīn.
Zǐyù served as Chancellor of Jìběi,
and his literary works were unparalleled in his time.
He excelled in zhāngcǎo script.
He studied under Dù Dù,
surpassing him in graceful charm,
with dots and strokes exquisitely refined,
and divine transformations unimpeded.
Like fine metal refined a hundred times,
or beautiful jade with heavenly grace,
he could be said to surpass his master.
Yuán Áng remarked:
"Like a perilous peak blocking the sun,
or a solitary pine with a single branch."
Wáng Yǐn called him the "Sage of Cursive."
His zhāngcǎo script reached the divine level,
and his small seal script reached the marvelous level.
From *Shū Duàn*.
Zhāng Zhī
Zhāng Zhī, styled Bóyīng,
had a natural fondness for calligraphy.
All the silk fabrics in his household
were first written on and then bleached.
He particularly excelled in zhāngcǎo script,
and was also skilled in clerical script.
Wéi Zhòngjiāng called him the "Sage of Cursive."
It was also said,
"The Cuī family's flesh,
the Zhāng family's bones."
The characters in his zhāngcǎo script piece *Jí Jiù Zhāng*
were all completed in a single stroke.
Bóyīng's zhāngcǎo script reached the divine level,
and his clerical script reached the marvelous level.
From *Shū Duàn*.
Bóyīng's calligraphy
was like Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's love for the Way,
soaring in emptiness, desiring immortality.
From Yuán Áng's *Shū Píng*.
Zhāng Chǎng
Zhāng Chǎng, styled Wénshū,
was Bóyīng's youngest brother.
He served as Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gates,
and particularly excelled in zhāngcǎo script.
His calligraphy resembled Bóyīng's,
and contemporaries called him the "Second Sage."
Wénshū's zhāngcǎo script reached the divine level,
his bāfēn script reached the marvelous level,
and his clerical script reached the capable level.
From *Shū Duàn*.
Liú Déshēng
Liú Déshēng, styled Jūnsì,
was a native of Yǐngchuān.
During the reigns of Emperors Huán and Líng, he gained fame for creating the running script.
Even when creating cursive script,
he achieved great beauty.
Elegant and graceful,
he stood alone in his time.
Hú Zhāo and Zhōng Yáo
both studied his method.
It is said in the world that Zhōng Yáo excelled in informal running script.
Hú's calligraphic style was plump,
while Zhōng's was lean,
yet each possessed Jūnsì's beauty.
From *Shū Duàn*.
Shī Yíguān,
a native of Nányáng.
Emperor Líng loved calligraphy,
and summoned several hundred skilled calligraphers from across the land to the Hóngdū Gate.
In bāfēn script, Yíguān was considered the best,
writing large characters up to a zhang in size,
and small ones fitting a thousand words within a square inch.
He was very proud of his ability and had a fondness for wine.
Sometimes he would arrive empty-handed at a tavern,
and write on its walls to sell his calligraphy,
drawing crowds of spectators.
When he sold enough to buy wine,
he would scrape off the writing.
Later, he wrote the stele for Gěng Qiú, a general under Yuán Shù in Jùlù.
The stele erected by Shù
was inscribed by Yíguān.
From *Shū Duàn*.
Yíguān's calligraphy
was like an eagle's wings in restless motion,
soaring gracefully away.
From Yuán Áng's *Shū Píng*.
Liáng Hú
Liáng Hú, styled Mènghuáng,
was a native of Wūzhī in Āndìng.
From a young age, he loved calligraphy,
and studied under Shī Yíguān.
He became known for his skill in bāfēn script,
was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt and appointed as a Gentleman,
and also served at the Hóngdū Gate,
later promoted to Selection Bureau Gentleman.
Emperor Líng held him in high esteem.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi greatly admired his calligraphy,
often hanging it in his tent,
and also nailing it to walls,
believing it surpassed Yíguān's.
At that time, Hándān Chún also mastered Cìzhōng's method,
with Chún excelling in small characters,
and Hú excelling in large characters,
but Chún did not match Hú's mastery of brushwork and expression of momentum.
From *Shū Duàn*.
Zuǒ Bó
Zuǒ Bó, styled Zǐyì,
was a native of Dōnglái.
He specialized in bāfēn script,
and his reputation ranked alongside Máo Hóng,
differing slightly from Hándān Chún.
He also gained fame in the late Hàn dynasty,
and was highly skilled in papermaking.
With the rise of the Hàn dynasty,
paper began to replace bamboo slips.
By the time of Emperor Hé,
Cài Lún had perfected its production,
but Zǐyì achieved even greater excellence.
Thus, Xiāo Zǐliáng wrote in reply to Wáng Sēngqián:
"Zǐyì's paper
is exquisite, marvelous, and radiant;
Zhòngjiāng's ink
is as dark as lacquer with a single dot;
Bóyīng's brush
exhausts sound and thought."
These marvelous objects are now distant,
far beyond reach.
From *Shū Duàn*.
Hú Zhāo
Hú Zhāo, styled Kǒngmíng,
was a native of Yǐngchuān.
From a young age, he was widely learned,
and did not seek fame or wealth.
He possessed the integrity of Bóyí and the recluse Hè,
and was highly skilled in zhòu script,
with exceptional regular and running scripts.
Wèi Héng said:
"Hú Zhāo and Zhōng Yáo
both studied under Liú Déshēng,
and both excelled in cursive and running scripts.
Hú's style was plump, Zhōng's was lean,
and their correspondence
often served as models."
Yáng Xīn said:
"Hú Zhāo acquired Zhāng Zhī's bones,
Suǒ Jìng acquired his flesh,
and Wéi Dàn acquired his sinews."
Zhāng Huá said:
"Hú Zhāo excelled in clerical script.
Màoxiān, together with Xún Xù, organized records and texts.
He also established a Calligraphy Erudite,
appointed disciples to teach and practice,
using Zhōng and Hú as models,
truly a scholar of profound learning."
From *Shū Duàn*.
Zhōng Yáo
Wèi Zhōng Yáo, courtesy name Yuáncháng.
In his youth, he followed Liú Shèng into the Bàodú Mountains,
studying calligraphy for three years.
Thereafter, he discussed brush techniques with Tàizǔ of Wèi, Hándān Chún, Wéi Dàn, and others.
Yáo then inquired about "Cài Bójiē's brush method" from Wéi Dàn,
but Dàn, reluctant to share, did not give it to him.
Yáo then beat his own chest until he vomited blood,
and Tàizǔ saved his life with Wǔlíng Dān.
When Dàn died,
Yáo had someone secretly dig up his tomb,
and thus obtained it,
from which time Yáo's brushwork became even more marvelous.
Yáo devoted himself to studying calligraphy with intense concentration,
lying down to practice until his brush pierced through the quilt cover,
and forgetting to return even after spending entire days in the privy.
Whenever he saw all manner of things,
he would depict their forms in writing.
Yáo excelled at three styles of script,
the most superb being the eight-part script.
From Yáng Xīn's "Bǐzhèn Tú."
Yáo was especially skilled in calligraphy
(The Ming manuscript copy lacks the character for "calligraphy.")
surpassing Cáo Xǐ, Cài Yōng, and Liú Déshēng.
His regular script was peerless in the world,
perfectly combining strength and suppleness.
Between the dots and strokes,
there was often extraordinary charm.
It can be said to be profound and boundless,
with abundant classical elegance.
Since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
he alone stands as such.
Even if ancient benevolent governance and enduring affection
captured people's hearts,
it would not be enough to surpass this;
how virtuous indeed!
As for his running script,
it was second only to Wáng Xīzhī and Wáng Xiànzhī.
His cursive script ranked below Wèi and Suǒ.
For eight-part script, there is the Wèi Shòushàn Bēi,
considered the finest example.
He died in the fourth year of the Tàihé era,
having reached eighty years of age.
("Years" originally written as "nián,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
Yuáncháng's clerical and running scripts entered the divine class,
his cursive and eight-part scripts entered the marvelous class.
From "Shūduàn."
Zhōng's calligraphy has twelve kinds,
unexpectedly clever and exquisite,
truly also full of wonders.
From Yuán Áng's "Shūpíng."
Zhōng Huì
Zhōng Huì, courtesy name Shìjì,
was the son of Yuáncháng.
Skilled in calligraphy,
he had his father's style.
Gradually developing bone and sinew,
he excelled in both running and cursive scripts,
and was especially adept at clerical script.
Graceful and free, soaring and ethereal,
he possessed an ambition that reached the clouds.
He was also what is called "the sword is like Gānjiàng and Mòyé."
Huì once forged a letter in Xún Xù's handwriting,
and went to Xù's mother, Madame Zhōng, to obtain a precious sword.
The brothers spent tens of millions to build a residence,
but had not yet moved in.
Xù then secretly painted a portrait of Yuáncháng,
and when the Huì brothers entered and saw it,
they were greatly moved and wept bitterly.
Xù's calligraphy was also of Huì's kind.
Huì's clerical, running, cursive, and draft cursive scripts all entered the marvelous class.
From "Shūduàn."
Wéi Dàn
Wèi Wéi Dàn, courtesy name Zhòngjiàng,
was from Jīngzhào,
the son of the Grand Coachman,
and rose to the position of Palace Attendant.
He deeply admired Zhāng Bóyīng,
and also mastered the methods of Hándān Chún.
