He excelled in all scripts,
and was especially superb at inscribing signboards.
When Emperor Míng's Língyún Tower was first completed,
he ordered Zhòngjiàng to inscribe the plaque.
Due to varying preferences regarding height,
he was to approach and correct the dotting.
Because of the danger and fear,
he warned his descendants,
not to take up the standard method for large characters.
Yuán Áng said:
"Like a dragon seizing and a tiger crouching,
swords drawn and crossbows tensed."
Zhāng Màoxiān said:
"Jīngzhào's Wéi Dàn, Dàn's son Xióng, Yǐngchuān's Zhōng Yáo, Yáo's son Huì, all excelled in clerical script."
Initially, during the Qīnglóng era,
in the three capitals of Luòyáng, Xǔ, and Yè,
when the palaces and towers were first completed,
an edict ordered Zhòngjiàng to extensively inscribe signboards,
to establish a permanent standard.
He was provided with imperial brushes and ink,
but none were suitable for use.
He thus memorialized:
"Cài Yōng prided himself on his calligraphic skill,
mastering both the methods of Lǐ Sī and Cáo Xǐ,
and would not casually wield his brush except on fine white silk.
To excel at a task,
one must first sharpen one's tools.
If one uses Zhāng Zhī's brushes, Zuǒ Bó's paper, and my ink,
combining these three things,
and also gains my hand,
only then can one unleash the momentum of characters spanning ten feet,
writing a thousand words within a square inch.
However, the excellence of cursive traces
is second only to Suǒ Jìng."
He died in the fifth year of the Jiāpíng era,
at seventy-five years of age.
Zhòngjiàng's eight-part script, clerical script, draft cursive script, and flying white script entered the marvelous class,
his small seal script entered the capable class.
His elder brother Kāng, courtesy name Yuánjiàng,
was skilled in calligraphy.
His son Xióng, courtesy name Shǎolǐ
(The Ming manuscript copy has "jì" instead of "lǐ.")
was also skilled in calligraphy.
People of the time said,
"Sons of famous fathers,
can master both affairs."
The world praised this.
From "Shūduàn."
It is also said:
When Emperor Míng of Wèi's Língyún Tower was completed,
the plaque was mistakenly nailed up first,
before being inscribed.
They placed Dàn in a cage,
and using a long rope on a pulley, hauled him up,
to have him inscribe the plaque.
It was two hundred and fifty feet from the ground,
and Dàn, in fear and danger,
warned his descendants,
to abandon this standard method.
From "Shǔfǎ Lù."
Wáng Xīzhī
Jìn Wáng Xīzhī, courtesy name Yìshǎo,
was the son of Kuàng.
At seven years old, he was already skilled in calligraphy.
At twelve,
he saw the previous generation’s *Bǐ Shuō* (Treatise on the Brush) inside his father’s pillow,
and secretly read it.
His father said:
"Why have you come to steal my secret?"
Xīzhī smiled but did not answer.
His mother said:
"He is looking at the method of using the brush."
His father, seeing he was young,
feared he could not keep it secret,
and said to Xīzhī:
"Wait until you are an adult,
then I will teach you."
Xīzhī bowed and pleaded,
"Let me use it now.
If I must wait until adulthood,
I fear it will obscure my youthful talent."
His father was pleased,
and so gave it to him.
In less than a month,
his calligraphy greatly advanced.
When Madame Wèi saw it,
she said to the Grand Ceremonialist Wáng Cè:
"This child must have seen the secrets of brushwork.
Recently seeing his writing,
it already possesses the wisdom of maturity."
Shedding tears, she said:
"This boy will surely overshadow my fame."
During the time of the Jìn Emperor,
for the text of the sacrifice to the northern suburbs,
the prayer tablet was replaced.
When the workman planed it,
the brushstrokes had entered the wood three-tenths of an inch.
At thirty-three, he wrote the *Lántíng Xù* (Preface to the Poems Composed at the Orchid Pavilion).
At thirty-seven, he wrote the *Huángtíng Jīng* (Yellow Court Classic).
After finishing the writing,
a voice spoke from the air:
"Your writing moves me,
how much more so people?
I am the Wéntái
(*Shuōfú* 92 has 'wén' as 'zhàng')
Immortal."
He himself said his work truly surpassed Zhōng Yóu's.
Xīzhī's calligraphy often varied in style.
From Yáng Xīn's *Bǐzhèn Tú* (Diagram of the Brush Formations):
Yìshǎo was skilled in cǎoshū, lìshū, bāfēn, fēibái, and zhāngxíng scripts.
He mastered all styles with excellence,
forming his own school of method.
A thousand changes, ten thousand transformations,
achieved through divine skill.
Yìshǎo's lìshū, xíngshū, cǎoshū, zhāngcǎo, and fēibái—all five scripts reached the 'divine' grade.
His bāfēn reached the 'marvelous' grade.
His wife, Lady Xī, was also very skilled in calligraphy.
They had seven sons,
Xiànzhī being the most famous.
Xuánzhī, Níngzhī, Huīzhī,
and Cāozhī were all skilled in cǎoshū.
From *Shū Duàn* (Judgments on Calligraphy)
Also, Xīzhī
once wrote a reply to Yǔ Liàng in zhāngcǎo script.
He showed it to Yì,
and when Yì saw it,
he sighed in admiration.
Thereupon, he wrote to Xīzhī, saying:
"I formerly had eight sheets of Bóyīng's zhāngcǎo,
but during the crossing of the river in turmoil,
they were lost.
I have often lamented that such marvelous traces were forever gone.
Suddenly seeing your reply to my elder brother,
brilliant as if by divine intelligence,
instantly restored my former vision."
When Xīzhī left Kuàijī,
he stayed at the foot of Jí Mountain.
One morning he saw an old woman
holding about ten six-cornered bamboo fans to take to market.
Wáng casually asked:
"Are you planning to sell these?
How much for one?"
She replied:
"About twenty cash."
The Right General (Wáng) took a brush and wrote on the fans,
writing five characters on each fan.
The old woman was greatly distressed and lamented:
"This old woman's
(The character 'fù' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Ming manuscript copy)
entire family's morning meal
all depends on these.
Why did you ruin them?"
Wáng replied:
"It is no loss.
Just say it is the calligraphy of Wáng Yòujūn,
and ask for one hundred cash."
Once she entered the market,
people vied to buy them.
A few days later,
she came again with several fans,
asking him to write more.
Wáng smiled but did not answer.
It is also said
that Xīzhī once personally wrote a memorial to Emperor Mù,
with focused spirit and free intent.
The Emperor then ordered paper of similar color,
length, width, and narrowness,
to match Wáng's memorial.
He had Zhāng Yì copy and imitate it,
without the slightest difference,
then inscribed a reply on the back.
Xīzhī initially did not notice,
but later looked at it again,
and sighed, saying:
"How this petty person has confused the genuine!"
Xīzhī was fond of geese by nature.
In Tányàn Village of Shānyáng, there was a Daoist priest who kept over ten fine geese.
Wáng, early one clear morning, took a small boat
and purposely went to see them.
His desire and delight were great,
so he asked to purchase them.
The Daoist priest would not give them.
Despite a hundred methods of persuasion,
he could not obtain them.
The Daoist priest said he was fond of the Dào by nature,
and had long wished to transcribe the *Lǎozǐ* of Héshàng Gōng,
having prepared the silk fabric long ago,
but there was no one able to write it.
"If you, Prefect, can personally write the *Lǎozǐ*
(Original text had 'qū' for 'Lǎozǐ',
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy)
*Dàodé Jīng*, two chapters each,
then I will gather the whole flock and present them."
Xīzhī stayed for half a day,
and finished writing it.
He caged the geese and returned,
greatly pleased.
He also once visited the home of a disciple,
where fine food was prepared and offered.
Feeling very grateful,
he wished to repay with his calligraphy.
Seeing there was a new catalpa wood table,
extremely smooth and clean,
Wáng then wrote on it,
half in cǎo and half in zhèng script.
The disciple escorted Wáng back to the commandery.
By the time he returned home,
his father had already scraped it all off.
When the son went back to look,
he was shocked and regretful for days.
From *Túshū Huìcuì* (Compendium of Books and Paintings)
Also, in the ninth year of the Yǒnghé era of Jìn Emperor Mù (353 CE),
on the third day of the third month in late spring, he once traveled to Shànyīn.
With Tàiyuán Sūn Tǒng Chénggōng, Gōngsūn Chuò Xìnggōng,
(The character 'gōng' was originally missing,
supplemented according to *Fǎshū Yàolù*)
Guǎnghàn Wáng Bīnzhī Dàoshēng, Chénjùn Xiè Ānshí, Gāopíng Xī Tán Chóngxī, Tàiyuán Wáng
(The character 'wáng' was originally missing,
supplemented according to *Fǎshū Yàolù*)
Yùn Shūrén, the monk Zhī Dùn Dàolín, and Yìshǎo's sons Níng, Huī, Cāozhī, and others—forty-one people in total—
they performed the purification ritual of Fúxì.
Wielding the brush, he composed the preface,
and with heightened joy, wrote it.
Using silkworm cocoon paper and a mouse-whisker brush,
vigorous, graceful, powerful, and robust—
unmatched for all time.
In all, twenty-eight lines,
three hundred and twenty-four characters.
Characters that were repeated all had variant forms,
among which the character 'zhī' was the most numerous.
From *Fǎshū Yàolù* (Essential Records of Calligraphy)
Wáng Xiànzhī
Wáng Xiànzhī, styled Zǐjìng,
was particularly skilled in cursive and clerical script.
In his youth, he studied under his father,
and learned from Zhāng Zhī.
Thereafter, he altered the established conventions,
creating his own methods.
He followed his own heart with ease,
yet mysteriously conformed to the natural principles.
Initially, Xiè Ān invited him to serve as Chief Clerk.
During the Tàiyuán era,
the new Tàijí Hall was built.
Ān wanted Zǐjìng to inscribe the plaque,
considering it a treasure for ten thousand generations,
but found it difficult to broach the subject.
So he recounted the story of Wéi Zhòngjiāng inscribing the Língyún Terrace.
Zǐjìng understood his intent,
and said with a stern expression:
"Zhòngjiāng was a high minister of Wèi,
how could such a thing have happened?
If it did happen,
it shows that the virtue of Wèi would not last long."
Ān then did not press him further.
When Zǐjìng was five or six years old and learning calligraphy,
the Right Army General (Wáng Xīzhī) stealthily tugged his brush from behind,
but could not pull it away.
He then sighed and said:
"This child is destined for great fame."
Subsequently, he wrote the "Essay on Yuè Yì" and gave it to him.
His studies ultimately reached the pinnacle.
His small regular script can be said to have penetrated the subtle and entered the realm of the sage;
its sinews and bones were tight and dense,
not inferior to his father's.
However, his large characters were especially straight and lacked variety,
how could they be compared?
Only between running and cursive scripts,
his untrammeled spirit surpassed.
As for discussing various scripts,
he was mostly inferior to the Right Army General.
In summary,
the difference was like that between Jì and Mèng.
Zǐjìng's five scripts—clerical, running, cursive, draft cursive, and flying white—
all entered the divine class.
His eight-part script entered the capable class.
From "Shū Duàn"
Also, when Xīzhī was in Kuàijī,
Zǐjìng went out to play.
He saw the newly whitewashed earthen wall of the northern lodge,
white and clean, lovely.
Zǐjìng had someone fetch a broom,
dipped it in muddy water,
and used it to write on the wall.
He wrote a character one zhang square,
radiant and splendid,
extremely powerful and fine.
Day after day, spectators formed a market crowd.
Xīzhī later saw it,
marveled at its beauty,
and asked who had done it.
The reply was:
"The Seventh Young Master."
Xīzhī then wrote a letter to a close acquaintance, saying:
"Zǐjìng's flying white script has greatly advanced,
according to Shuō Fú 92, there is an additional character 'advance' below
it was precisely planned for this wall."
Zǐjìng loved calligraphy,
encountering and creating profound artistry wherever he went.
There was a young man fond of such things,
who intentionally made a fine, white paper garment,
and wore it to visit Zǐjìng.
Zǐjìng then took the garment and wrote on it,
cursive and regular scripts, all styles complete,
covering both sleeves and the collar almost entirely.
He sighed to himself about the serendipity of this northern visitor.
The young man noticed that Wáng's attendants had a look of wanting to seize it,
so he snatched the garment and ran.
The attendants indeed chased him to outside the gate,
struggled and tore it apart,
the young man barely obtained one sleeve.
When Zǐjìng served as Governor of Wúxīng,
Yáng Xīn's father, Bùyí, was Magistrate of Wúchéng.
Xīn was about fifteen or sixteen at the time,
and his calligraphy already showed promise.
Zǐjìng became aware of him,
and went to the county.
He entered Xīn's study,
where Xīn was sleeping in the daytime wearing a new white silk skirt.
Zǐjìng then wrote on the skirt's panels and sash,
Xīn awoke delighted,
and treasured it,
later presenting it to the imperial court.
From "Túshū Huìcuì"
Also, Xiànzhī once wrote over ten sheets for Emperor Jiǎnwén.
At the end, he inscribed:
"This writing of your humble official is quite well done,
I hope it may be preserved."
This writing was treasured by Huán Xuán.
Xuán loved and valued the Two Wángs,
unable to put them down.
He then selected the most beautiful examples of their regular and running scripts on silk and paper,
and bound them into one volume.
He often kept it by his side,
and when he fled south,
although in great狼狈,
he still carried it with him.
As he faced defeat,
it was lost in the river.
From "Fǎshū Yàolù"
Wáng Xiū
Wáng Xiū, styled Jìngrén,
was the son of Zhòngzǔ,
and rose to the position of Editorial Director.
In his youth, he had a reputation for brilliance and excellence,
at sixteen, he wrote the "Essay on Virtuous Magistrates."
Liú Zhēncháng saw it,
and sighed in admiration endlessly.
He was skilled in clerical and running scripts,
and once requested calligraphy from the Right Army General.
The latter then wrote the "Eulogy on Dōngfāng Shuò's Portrait" for him.
Wáng Sēngqián said:
"Jìngrén's calligraphy nearly exhausts its subtleties,
every time Wáng Zǐjìng looked at it,
it was咄咄逼人."
He died in the first year of Shēngpíng,
at twenty-four years of age.
Initially, Wáng Dǎo loved Zhōng Yáo's calligraphy,
and amidst the chaos and狼狈 of the upheavals,
he still carried the "Imperial Edict"
originally 'play',
corrected according to the Ming manuscript
hidden in his clothing belt.
After crossing the river,
he gave it to Yìshǎo (Wáng Xīzhī).
Yìshǎo begged for it for Jìngrén.
When Jìngrén died,
his mother, seeing that this writing was his lifelong favorite,
placed it in his coffin.
Jìngrén's clerical and running scripts entered the marvelous class,
Yīn Zhòngkān's calligraphy
was also second to Jìngrén.
From "Shū Duàn"
Xún Yú
Xún Yú was capable in calligraphy,
he once wrote the "Prescription for Fox Bone."
The Right Army General traced it,
and to this day it is called the "Fox Bone Manuscript."
From "Shàngshū Gùshí"
Xiè Ān
Xiè Ān, styled Ānshí,
studied regular script under the Right Army General.
The Right Army General said:
"You are one who understands calligraphy,
but know
originally 'zhi',
corrected according to the Ming manuscript
that understanding calligraphy is difficult."
Ānshí was especially skilled in running script,
also like Guard Captain Wèi,
a refined and famous scholar,
admired throughout the land.
Wáng Sēngqián said:
"Xiè Ān entered the record of capable calligraphers."
Ānshí's clerical, running, and cursive scripts all entered the marvelous class.
His elder brother Shàng, styled Rénzǔ, and Wànshí,
"Fǎshū Yàolù" writes Wànshí as younger brother Wàn, styled Ānshí
were both skilled in calligraphy.
From "Shū Duàn"
Wáng Yì
Jìn's General Who Pacifies the South and later Palace Attendant Wáng Yì,
was the Right Army General's uncle,
skilled in clerical and flying white scripts,
he followed and elaborated on the methods of Zhāng and Wèi.
He also had a sheet by Suǒ Jìng dated the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month,
which he always treasured and enjoyed.
During the Yǒngjiā upheavals,
he folded it four times and sewed it into his clothing to cross the river.
Now, Dòulú Qì, Magistrate of Sāngquán in Púzhōu, obtained it,
the fold marks are still visible.
From "Túshǐ Yìzuǎn"
Dài Āndào, Kāng Xīn
The monk Zhì Yǒng of the Yǒngxīn Temple,
was a distant descendant of Master Yǒng's ancestor, Yì Shǎo.
He devoted himself exclusively to calligraphy for many years,
rising through the ranks with diligence,
and was fully committed to cursive script.
Zhì Yǒng's zhāngcǎo and cursive script reached the level of "marvelous,"
while his running script was considered "capable."
His elder brother, Zhì Kǎi, was also skilled in calligraphy,
and Dīng Chān excelled in clerical script.
People of the time said:
"Dīng excels in clerical script, Yǒng in cursive."
From "Shū Duàn"
Also, Zhì Yǒng once studied calligraphy in an upper room,
and did not descend until his studies were complete.
From "Guó Shǐ Zuǎn Yì"
Liáng Zhōu Xìngsì compiled and arranged the Thousand Character Classic,
but there was a certain Wáng Yòujūn,
whose identity was unclear to everyone.
It began when Emperor Wǔ of Liáng taught calligraphy to the princes,
ordering Yīn Tiěshí to select one thousand non-repeating characters
from the calligraphy of the Great Master,
each character on a separate piece of paper,
scattered and disordered.
Emperor Wǔ summoned Xìngsì and said to him:
"You possess talent and thought,
arrange these into rhyme for me."
Xìngsì compiled and presented it overnight,
his hair turning completely white,
and he was richly rewarded.
The Zen master Zhì Yǒng, grandson of Yòujūn,
personally copied eight hundred copies,
distributing them to others,
with each temple in Jiāngnán keeping one copy.
Master Yǒng resided at the Yǒngxīn Temple in Wúxīng,
accumulating his study of calligraphy,
later having ten jars of worn-out brush tips,
each jar containing several thousand.
People came seeking his calligraphy,
and those requesting inscribed plaques were as numerous as in a marketplace.
The threshold of his dwelling was worn through,
so he wrapped it with iron sheets,
calling it the "iron threshold."
Later, he buried the brush tips,
naming it the "Retired Brush Tomb,"
and composed an epitaph himself.
From "Shàng Shū Gù Shí"
He often stayed in the pavilion of Yǒngxīn Temple practicing calligraphy,
and the discarded brush tips
were placed in large bamboo baskets.
Each basket could hold over one dàn,
and five baskets were all filled.
From "Fǎ Shū Yào Lù"
Monk Zhì Guǒ
The Suí dynasty monk Zhì Guǒ of Yǒngxīn Temple,
was from Kuàijī.
Emperor Yáng held him in high regard.
He excelled in carving inscriptions on stone,
his style lean and vigorous,
difficult to imitate in haste.
He once said to Master Yǒng:
"The venerable monk has obtained the flesh of Yòujūn,
while Zhì Guǒ has obtained the bones.
For sinews and bones are hidden within skin and flesh,
just as mountains and waters never tire of height and depth.
Yet this gentleman somewhat lacks clarity and depth,
marred by shallowness and exposure.
Like the battles of the Wú people,
advancing lightly and retreating easily,
possessing courage and strength but not martial prowess,
empty boasting and ostentation—
is this not the way of a petty Confucian?"
Zhì Guǒ's clerical, running, and cursive scripts were considered "capable."
From "Shū Duàn"
Táng Tàizōng
In the fourteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era of Táng Tàizōng,
he personally wrote a screen in regular and cursive script,
to show his ministers.
The brushwork was powerful and vigorous,
unmatched at the time.
He once said to his court officials:
"The study of calligraphy is a minor art,
not an urgent matter from the start.
Yet if one occasionally pays attention to it,
it is still better than wasting days.
In all arts and skills,
there is none that cannot be mastered through learning;
the fault lies in laxity of mind and effort,
and inability to concentrate fully."
He also said:
"When I study the calligraphy of the ancients,
I do not merely imitate their form and posture,
but focus on the bone strength.
Once bone strength is attained,
form and posture naturally arise."
He once summoned officials of the third rank and above,
and held a banquet at the Xuánwǔ Gate.
The Emperor took up a brush to write in feibái script,
and the ministers, emboldened by wine,
competed to take it from Tàizōng's hand.
The Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Liú Jì,
climbed onto the imperial couch and reached out his hand,
and only then obtained it.
Those who did not get it
all declared that Jì had climbed onto the couch,
a crime deserving death,
and requested he be handed over to the law.
Tàizōng laughed and said:
"In the past, I heard of the palace lady refusing the imperial carriage;
today, I see the Cavalier Attendant climbing onto the couch."
From "Shàng Shū Gù Shí"
Purchasing the "Lántíng Preface"
Wáng Xīzhī's "Preface to the Poems Composed at the Orchid Pavilion".
The monk Biàncái, a disciple of the monk Zhìyǒng,
once had a hidden compartment
chiseled into a roof beam in his sleeping chamber,
to store the "Orchid Pavilion" scroll.
He cherished and guarded it even more dearly than when his master was alive.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
Emperor Tàizōng, in his leisure from attending to state affairs,
devoted himself passionately to calligraphy.
He copied Wáng Xīzhī's authentic running and cursive script models,
collecting and copying them exhaustively,
but had yet to obtain the "Orchid Pavilion".
Investigating the whereabouts of this work,
he learned it was in Biàncái's possession.
He then issued an edict summoning the master monk into the inner palace chapel to receive offerings,
bestowing generous favors and gifts upon him.
After several days,
during conversation,
he brought up the subject of the "Orchid Pavilion",
skillfully and persuasively probing,
leaving no stone unturned.
Biàncái firmly stated that in the past, while attending his late master,
he had indeed often seen it,
but since his master's passing,
having experienced successive periods of turmoil and disorder,
it had been lost and he no longer knew its location.
Since he could not obtain it,
the Emperor subsequently released him to return to Yuèzhōng.
Later, upon further investigation,
it was confirmed the scroll had not left Biàncái's vicinity.
Another edict summoned Biàncái to the palace,
to question him again about the "Orchid Pavilion".
This happened three times,
yet he stubbornly refused to produce it.
The Emperor said to his attending ministers:
"Of Wáng Xīzhī's calligraphy,
I have a particular treasure.
Among these, the work of Yìshǎo (Wáng Xīzhī),
none compares to the 'Orchid Pavilion'.
My desire to see this work
troubles my waking and sleeping hours.
This monk is advanced in years,
and the scroll is of no use to him.
If we could find a man of wisdom and strategy,
to devise a plan and obtain it, we would surely succeed."
The Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Fáng Xuánlíng, said:
"Your servant has heard that the Investigating Censor Xiāo Yì,
is the great-grandson of Emperor Yuán of Liáng.
His current registered residence is in Shēn County, Wèizhōu.
He possesses talent and skill,
and is full of resourceful schemes.
He could undertake this mission,
and would certainly achieve the goal."
Emperor Tàizōng then summoned Xiāo Yì for an audience.
Yì memorialized, saying:
"If I go as an official envoy,
in principle, I will not succeed.
I request to travel there privately.
I will need several examples of miscellaneous calligraphy models by the two Wángs."
Tàizōng granted his request and provided them.
Yì then changed his headgear and dressed in plain clothes,
traveling to Luòtán.
He boarded a merchant vessel,
and sailed down to Yuèzhōu.
He wore a yellow gown,
extremely loose, long, and casual,
assuming the manner of a scholar from east of the mountains.
At dusk, he entered the temple,
strolling along the corridors to view the wall paintings.
Passing by Biàncái's courtyard,
he stopped before the gate.
Biàncái saw Yì from a distance,
and asked:
"Where are you from, lay devotee?"
Yì stepped forward, bowed, and said:
"Your disciple is from the north,
come to sell a small amount of silkworm eggs.
While touring the temple at leisure,
I am fortunate to encounter you, Chan Master."
After exchanging pleasantries,
their conversation immediately found common ground.
Biàncái then invited him into his room,
where they played weiqi and plucked the qin together,
engaged in pitch-pot and board games,
and discussed literature and history,
finding great mutual satisfaction.
Biàncái then said:
"Some remain strangers though their hair turns white together;
others become like old friends from the moment their carriage canopies meet.
From now on, let there be no formality between us."
He then had Yì stay overnight,
setting out jar-surface medicinal wine, fruits, and other refreshments.
In Jiāngdōng they say 'jar-surface',
just as in Héběi they say 'jar-head',
referring to newly matured wine.
After becoming merry with drink,
they invited each other to compose poems.
Biàncái drew the rhyme character 'lái' (來),
and his poem read:
"Uncorking a jar of first-brewed wine,
A new friend comes from ten thousand miles away.
Dispelling clouds, we share this solitude;
Strolling beneath the moon, we wander together.
Late into the night, a lone qin stirs thoughts;
The long wind carries the lament of migrating geese.
Were it not for your secret art,
Who could illuminate the unburning ashes?"
Xiāo Yì drew the rhyme character 'zhāo' (招),
and his poem read:
"By chance, we share this fine night;
Gratefully, I receive your gracious invitation.
Vast as heaven, yet instantly we are as old friends;
The initial stage—how could it seem distant?
Wine dregs tilt and still float;
The restless mind-monkey seems soothed.
Who pities the wing that has lost its flock,
Long suffering, tossed by the winds of karma?"
Their poetic skill was roughly equal.
Reciting each other's verses,
they regretted not having met sooner.
They enjoyed themselves thoroughly all night,
and Yì left the next day.
Biàncái said:
"Lay devotee, come again whenever you are free."
Yì then brought wine to visit him.
Inspired, they composed poems;
this happened several times.
Poetry and wine became their main pursuits,
and their rapport grew seamless.
After about a month,
Yì showed the master a self-written copy of "Illustrated Tributary States" by Emperor Yuán of Liáng.
The master praised it endlessly.
As they discussed calligraphy,
Yì said:
"Your disciple previously received instruction in the regular script methods of the two Wángs.
Since childhood, I have been fond of studying them,
and I now carry several models with me."
Biàncái said happily:
"Come tomorrow,
and you can bring them for me to see."
Yì went as scheduled,
and produced his models to show Biàncái.
Biàncái examined them carefully and said:
"They are indeed authentic,
but they are not the finest examples.
This humble monk possesses a genuine masterpiece,
which is quite extraordinary."
Yì asked:
"Which model?"
Biàncái replied:
"The 'Orchid Pavilion'."
Yì laughed and said:
"After so many periods of chaos and separation,
how could the genuine masterpiece still exist?
It must be a traced copy or a forgery."
Biàncái said:
"My master cherished and guarded it in his lifetime.
On his deathbed,
he personally entrusted it to me.
The transmission was orderly and clear;
how could there be any discrepancy?
You may come tomorrow to see it."
When Yì arrived,
the master himself retrieved it from the compartment in the roof beam.
Yì examined it.
Then, deliberately finding faults and pointing out flaws, he said:
"It is indeed a traced copy."
They argued back and forth without resolution.
After showing it to Yì,
Biàncái no longer returned it to the hidden beam.
Together with Xiāo Yì's models by the two Wángs,
he left them all on his desk.
Biàncái was over eighty years old at the time.
Every day, by the window, he would copy it several times—
such was his fervent devotion even in old age.
From then on, as Yì's visits became frequent,
the young novices and others no longer harbored any suspicion.
Later, when Biàncái went out to attend a vegetarian feast at the home of Yán Qiān south of the Yìsì Bridge in the town,
Yì came privately to his room.
He said to the novice:
"I left a piece of silk on the bed."
The novice immediately opened the door for him.
Yì then went to the desk,
took the "Orchid Pavilion" and the imperial collection's models by the two Wángs,
and went straight to the Yǒng'ān Postal Station.
He informed the station chief, Líng Sù, saying:
"I am a censor,
sent here by imperial decree.
I now have an imperial edict in my own hand;
you must report this to your commander."
The commander, Qí Shànxíng, heard this
and rushed to pay his respects.
Xiāo Yì then proclaimed the imperial decree,
and explained the whole matter.
Shànxíng immediately sent someone to summon Biàncái.
Biàncái was still at Yán Qiān's home and had not returned to the temple.
Startled by the sudden summons,
he did not know the reason.
The messenger added:
"The Investigating Censor must see you."
When the master came to see the imperial censor,
it turned out to be Xiāo Yì from the room.
Xiāo Yì reported:
"I was dispatched by imperial decree to retrieve the 'Lántíng,'
and now the 'Lántíng' has been obtained.
Therefore, I summoned you, Master, to bid farewell."
Upon hearing this, Biàncái fainted on the spot,
and it took a long while before he regained consciousness.
Yì then hastened by post relay southward
(the Fǎshū Yàolù records 'south' as 'and')
to depart,
arriving at the capital to present it to the emperor.
Tàizōng was greatly pleased.
Because Fáng Xuánlíng had recommended the right person,
he was rewarded with a thousand bolts of brocade;
Yì was promoted to the position of Yuánwàiláng,
elevated to the fifth rank,
and bestowed with a silver vase, a gold-inlaid vase, an agate bowl, all filled with pearls.
Two fine horses from the imperial stables,
along with exquisitely decorated saddles and bridles.
A residence and an estate, each one.
Initially, Tàizōng was angry at the old monk for his secretive stinginess,
but soon, considering his advanced age,
he could not bear to impose punishment.
Several months later,
he still bestowed three thousand bolts of silk,
three thousand shi of grain,
and ordered Yuèzhōu to distribute them.
Biàncái dared not use them for himself,
so he built a three-story pagoda.
The pagoda was extremely exquisite and splendid,
and it still exists to this day.
The old monk, due to shock and fear, fell seriously ill,
unable to eat solid food,
only consuming porridge,
and passed away a little over a year later.
The emperor ordered the court calligraphers Zhào Mó, Hán Dàozhèng, Féng Chéngsù, and Zhūgě Zhēn, four in total,
each to make several copies,
to bestow upon the crown prince, various princes, and close ministers.
In the twenty-third year of Zhēnguàn,
the emperor's health declined,
and he stayed at the Hánfēng Hall of the Yùhuá Palace.
On his deathbed,
he said to Gāozōng:
"I wish to ask you for one thing.
You are truly filial;
how could you go against my heart?
What do you think?"
Gāozōng choked with sobs and shed tears,
leaning in to listen and receive the command.
Tàizōng said:
"What I desire is the Lántíng;
you may take it with me."
Later, it followed the immortal carriage into the mysterious palace.
Today, the copies made by Zhào Mó and others
are still worth tens of thousands of coins each.
From the "Fǎshū Yàolù."
Another account says that Wáng Xīzhī once wrote the "Lántíng Gathering Preface."
At the end of the Suí dynasty,
a monk in Guǎngzhōu who was fond of curiosities obtained it.
The monk had three treasures,
which he cherished and kept.
The first was Wáng Xīzhī's calligraphy of the "Lántíng";
the second was a divine turtle,
made of bronze.
The turtle's belly could hold one shēng.
When water was stored in it,
the turtle would move its four legs and walk.
It could go wherever it was placed.
The third was a rúyì scepter.
It was patterned with iron.
Bright and transparent.
Its color was like crystal.
Tàizōng was particularly skilled in calligraphy,
and upon hearing of Wáng Xīzhī's authentic Lántíng manuscript,
he sought it and obtained other copies,
but the first copy,
he knew was with the monk in Guǎngzhōu,
yet it was difficult to obtain by force.
So he sent someone to deceive the monk,
and indeed obtained the manuscript.
The monk said:
"The first treasure is lost;
what use are the others?"
Then he struck the rúyì against a stone,
breaking and discarding it;
he also threw the turtle, injuring one of its legs,
and from then on it could no longer walk.
From the "Jì Wén."
Hàn Prince Yuánchāng
Táng Hàn Prince Yuánchāng,
son of Shényáo,
excelled in running script calligraphy.
Among the various princes, the middle and younger ones all had reputations for ability;
Prince Hán and Prince Cáo,
were also his peers.
Prince Cáo was especially skilled in "flying white" script,
while Prince Hán excelled in cursive and running script.
Prince Wèi and Prince Lǔ,
were also of the same caliber as Prince Hán.
From the "Shū Duàn."
Ōuyáng Xún
Táng Ōuyáng Xún, courtesy name Xìnběn,
was well-read in ancient and modern works,
and served as Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū and Shuàigēng Lìng.
In calligraphy, he mastered all eight scripts,
with a vigorous and sharp brushwork.
Gāolì admired his calligraphy,
and sent an envoy to request it.
Shényáo sighed and said:
"I never expected Xún's fame in calligraphy
to spread so far to foreign tribes."
He passed away in the fifteenth year of Zhēnguàn,
at the age of eighty-five.
Xún's "flying white," clerical, running, and cursive scripts were exquisite,
while his large seal and draft cursive scripts were proficient.
From the "Shū Duàn."
Also, Shuàigēng once went on a journey,
and saw an ancient stele inscribed by Suǒ Jìng.
He halted his horse to observe it,
and after a long while, left.
After a few steps,
he dismounted again and stood still.
When tired, he spread a rug and sat to observe,
eventually staying overnight beside it,
and departed only after three days.
The inscription on the Kāitōng Yuánbǎo coin,
cast in the fourth year of Wǔdé,
was written by Ōuyáng Shuàigēng.
From the "Guó Shǐ Yì Zuǎn."
Ōuyáng Tōng
Táng Ōuyáng Tōng,
son of Ōuyáng Xún.
Skilled in calligraphy,
his style was thin and delicate
(the Míng manuscript notes 'thin and delicate' as 'following the method')
of his father.
He often prided himself on his calligraphy skills,
always using ivory or rhinoceros horn for brush handles;
with wildcat hair as the core;
covered with autumn hare hair;
pine soot for ink,
mixed with musk at the end;
and only using paper that was firm, thin, white, and smooth for writing,
showing his great respect for his own calligraphy.
Xuē Chúntuó also imitated Ōuyáng's cursive script,
but suffered from being too plump and blunt,
and was also considered Ōuyáng Tōng's peer.
From the "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi."
Yú Shìnán
Yú Shìnán, courtesy name Bóshī,
was from Kuàijī,
and served as a Mìshū Láng in the Suí dynasty.
Emperor Yáng knew of his talent,
but resented his uprightness,
so he remained in the seventh rank for over ten years.
In the Táng dynasty, he served as Mìshū Jiān.
Emperor Wén said:
"Shìnán alone
possesses five outstanding qualities.
First, broad learning;
second, virtuous conduct;
third, calligraphy;
fourth, literary talent;
fifth, loyalty and integrity.
Possessing even one of these
is enough to be called a renowned minister,
yet Shìnán possesses all of them."
In running and cursive scripts,
he was particularly skilled.
He originally studied under the monk Zhìyǒng,
and in his later years,
added strength and elegance to his style.
He passed away at the age of eighty-nine.
Bóshī's clerical, cursive, and running scripts were exquisite.
From the "Shū Duàn."
Chǔ Suìliáng,
a native of Hénán.
His father, Liàng,
served as Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Suìliáng rose to the position of Vice Director of the Left.
He excelled at calligraphy.
In his youth, he deeply admired Yú Jiàn,
and in his maturity, he took Wáng Xīzhī as his master.
His regular script particularly captured an elegant charm.
He died during the Xiǎnqìng era,
at the age of sixty-four.
Suìliáng's clerical and running scripts reached the sublime level.
He had also studied under Shǐ Líng.
However, Shǐ's style also possessed an archaic straightforwardness,
though it suffered from being somewhat sparse and thin.
From "Shū Duàn."
Also, Chǔ Suìliáng once asked Yú Jiàn:
"How does my calligraphy compare to that of Monk Zhìyǒng?"
Yú replied:
"I have heard that a single character of his is worth fifty thousand coins.
Could an official's work ever command such a price?"
Chǔ asked:
"How does it compare to Ōuyáng Xún's?"
Yú said:
"I have heard that Xún could achieve his intent regardless of the paper or brush he used.
He could always realize his aims.
Could an official's work ever be like that?"
Chǔ said:
"If that is so,
why should I devote any more attention to this?"
Yú said:
"If one's hand and brush are in harmony,
and one encounters a work of true synthesis,
that too is profoundly worthy of esteem."
Chǔ was pleased and withdrew.
From "Guó Shǐ Yì Zuǎn."
Xuē Jì,
a native of Hénán,
rose to the position of Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
He studied calligraphy under Chǔ,
particularly favoring a gorgeous and charming beauty.
He attained about half of his master's flesh and substance,
truly a worthy disciple of the Duke of Hénán.
His work was highly treasured and esteemed in his time.
Jì's clerical and running scripts reached the capable level.
From "Shū Duàn."
Also, the household of Xuē Jì's maternal grandfather, Wèi Zhēng,
was rich in books and records,
and possessed many old works by Yú and Chǔ.
Jì diligently and meticulously imitated them,
achieving a brush manner that was vigorous and beautiful.
No one at the time could match him.
He was also skilled at painting.
The original text had "shū" (writing);
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy to "huà" (painting).
He extensively collected ancient traces,
rivaling the Imperial Library.
From "Tán Bīn Lù."
Gāo Zhèngchén,
a native of Guǎngpíng,
rose to the position of Minister of the Court of the Imperial Guard.
He practiced the method of Wáng Xīzhī.
Emperor Ruìzōng admired his calligraphy.
Earlier, Zhāng Huáisù
was an old acquaintance of Gāo's.
Court officials would go to Gāo to request his calligraphy,
and sometimes relied on Zhāng to write it.
Gāo once wrote fifteen sheets for someone.
Zhāng then playfully swapped five of the sheets,
and had them shown to Gāo again.
Gāo looked twice but did not realize the switch.
A guest said:
"Someone has swapped your calligraphy."
Gāo laughed and said:
"It must be Lord Zhāng."
He then examined them carefully,
and identified three of the sheets.
The guest said:
"There are still some left."
Gāo looked at them again,
but in the end could not distinguish them.
Gāo once promised someone a calligraphy screen,
but when the time passed, the person had not received it.
That person was then sent on a mission to Huáinán.
At parting,
he was deeply regretful and disappointed.
Gāo said:
"My old friend Zhèngchén is in Shēnzhōu.
His calligraphy is exactly of the same category as mine.
You may go there and request it from him."
He then immediately wrote a note to convey this intention.
Lù Jiǎnzhī once wrote an official appointment document for Gāo.
Gāo always disliked it,
and did not include it in his official portfolio.
Later, it was damaged by a rat.
Gāo took it to show Lord Zhāng, saying:
"This rat understood Zhèngchén's intentions very well."
When style and temperament do not match,
it can reach such an extent.
Zhèngchén's clerical, running, and cursive scripts reached the capable level.
From "Shū Duàn."
Wáng Shàozōng
Wáng Shàozōng, styled Chéngliè,
rose to the position of Vice Director of the Palace Library.
He traced his lineage back to Wáng Xiànzhī and admired Lù Jiǎnzhī.
His small regular script among these
was particularly extraordinary in form and appearance.
His running script and draft cursive
were next to his regular script.
He often wrote to others, saying:
"My humble calligraphy is not skillful;
it is merely due to the accumulated habit of ink and water.
I constantly concentrate my mind and follow my intent,
emptying my spirit and calming my thoughts to attain it."
Whenever he discussed this art with the official Lù from Wúzhōng,
by the next morning, he would invariably find himself having improved without realizing it.
Lù later secretly inquired and learned of this,
and expressed no small amount of admiration and praise.
"He compared me to Yú Shì'nán,
because Yú also did not practice by copying,
but only mentally measured and visually contemplated.
I heard that Yú, while lying under a cloth quilt,
would constantly trace characters on his belly with his hand.
That is exactly the same as what I do."
Chéngliè's clerical, running, and cursive scripts reached the capable level.
From "Shū Duàn."
Zhèng Guǎngwén
Zhèng Qián served as Erudite of the Guǎngwén College.
He studied calligraphy but was troubled by the lack of paper.
Learning that the Cí'ēn Temple had several rooms' worth of persimmon leaves,
he borrowed a monk's cell to reside there.
Each day he took red leaves to practice calligraphy on,
and over the years, he nearly used them all.
Later, he himself wrote out the poems he had composed along with a painting,
binding them together into one scroll to present.
Emperor Xuánzōng inscribed with his imperial brush at the end:
"Zhèng Qián's Three Perfections."
From "Shàng Shū Gù Shí."
Lǐ Yángbīng
Lǐ Yángbīng excelled at small seal script.
He himself said that after the venerable Lǐ Sī,
and
the original text had "ěr" (merely);
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy to "qiě" (and).
down to this minor student,
Cáo Xǐ and Cài Yōng were not worth mentioning.
During the Kāiyuán era,
Zhāng Huáiguàn compiled "Shū Duàn,"
but neither Yángbīng nor Zhāng Xù were included in it.
In Jiàngzhōu, there were seal characters different from the ancient ones,
quite strange and unusual.
Lǐ Yángbīng saw them,
and lay down beneath them,
unable to leave for several days.
Examination showed the writing was from the early Táng,
but the name of the calligrapher was not recorded.
The stele had the two characters "Bìluò,"
so people of the time called it the Bìluò Stele.
From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ."
Zhāng Xù
Zhāng Xù mastered the brush technique of cursive script,
which was later transmitted to Cuī Miǎo and Yán Zhēnqīng.
Xù said:
"Initially, I heard of a princess and a porter contending for the road,
and from this I grasped the intent of brush technique;
later, I saw Gōngsūn perform the sword dance and thereby attained its spirit."
When drunk, he would always write cursive script,
waving his brush and shouting loudly.
He would dip his head into the ink and write with it,
so the world called him Zhāng the Madman.
After sobering up and looking at his own work,
he considered it divinely extraordinary,
impossible to recreate.
Among later generations discussing calligraphy,
there were Ōu, Yú, Chǔ, and Xuē.
Some held differing opinions,
but regarding the Chief Secretary, there were no dissenting words.
From Guóshǐ Bǔ.
Also, after Zhāng Xù first took office, he served as the Deputy Magistrate of Chángshú County in Sūzhōu.
Not long after assuming his post,
an old man came with a petition,
which he adjudicated and dismissed.
After a few days, the old man came again.
Xù became angry and reprimanded him, saying:
"How dare you repeatedly disturb the official gate
with trivial matters."
The old man replied:
"I am truly not here to discuss any matter,
but merely because I have seen Your Honor's brushwork, which is marvelously exquisite,
and I treasure it as a precious item for my chest."
The Chief Secretary found this strange,
and thus inquired how he came to love calligraphy.
He answered:
"My late father studied calligraphy,
and also left writings."
The Chief Secretary took and examined them,
and indeed they were the work of a master calligrapher of the realm.
From then on, he fully grasped the subtleties of brush technique,
becoming the foremost of his time.
From Yōuxián Gǔchuī.
Monk Huáisù
The monk Huáisù of Chángshā was fond of cursive script,
claiming to have attained the essence of the Sage of Cursive.
He piled up discarded brushes
and buried them at the foot of a mountain,
calling it the "Brush Tomb."
From Guóshǐ Bǔ.
From Chéng Miǎo onward
Chéng Miǎo, a prison officer of the Qín, excelled in Large Seal script.
Having offended Emperor Shǐhuáng,
he was imprisoned in Yúnyáng.
He modified the forms of Large Seal script,
removing their complexity and redundancy.
Emperor Shǐhuáng approved of it,
releasing him and appointing him as a Censor.
This script was named "Clerical Script."
Cáo Xǐ of Fúfēng,
a man of the Later Hàn,
his official position is unknown.
He excelled in Seal and Clerical scripts,
slightly differing from Lǐ Sī,
and was revered as a teacher in his time.
Cài Yōng of Chénliú,
a man of the Later Hàn,
served as General of the Gentlemen of the Left.
He excelled in Seal script,
adopting Cáo Xǐ's methods.
The inscription on the Zhífù Stele of Zhēndìng
is still transmitted in the world,
and Seal script practitioners take him as their master.
Chén Zūn of Dùlíng,
a man of the Later Hàn,
his official position is unknown.
He excelled in Seal and Clerical scripts,
and whenever he wrote,
everyone present would be astonished.
People of the time called him "Chén the Astonisher."
Wáng Cìzhòng of Shànggǔ,
a man of the Later Hàn,
created the Eight-Fen Regular method.
Shī Yíguān,
of the Later Hàn,
his origins are unknown.
Yíguān could write large characters one zhàng square,
and small characters one cùn square containing a thousand words.
The Gěng Qiú Stele is Yíguān's writing.
He was very proud and guarded of his skill.
Sometimes he would go empty-handed to a tavern,
first writing on its walls,
whereupon spectators would gather like clouds,
and the wine would consequently sell greatly.
After drinking his fill,
he would scrape off the writing and leave.
Liáng Hú of Āndìng,
a man of the Later Hàn,
rose to the office of Minister of Selections.
He studied Yíguān's methods.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi esteemed him,
often hanging his calligraphy inside his tent.
Inscriptions on palace halls
were mostly by Hú's hand.
From Wáng Sēngqián's Míngshū Lù.
From Hándān Chún onward
Hándān Chún of Chénliú served as Literary Attendant to the Marquis of Línzī of Wèi.
He mastered Cìzhòng's method,
(The character for "method" was originally missing,
supplemented according to Fǎshū Yàolù.)
His fame came after Hú's.
Máo Hóng,
was Hú's disciple.
The Secretariat's Eight-Fen script
all transmitted Hóng's method.
There was also Zuǒ Zǐyì,
who differed slightly from Chún,
and was also renowned.
Dù Dù of Jīngzhào served as Chancellor of Qí under Wèi,
and was the first to gain fame for cursive script.
Cuī Yuàn of Ānpíng,
Chancellor of Jìběi in the Later Hàn,
also excelled at cursive script.
When Fú Jiān pacified [the region],
he obtained a traced copy of Cuī Yuàn's calligraphy.
Wáng Zǐjìng remarked,
it greatly resembled Zhāng Bóyīng's.
Yuàn's son, Cuī Shí, rose to the office of Minister,
and could also write cursive.
Zhāng Zhī of Hóngnóng, noble and unworldly, did not serve as an official.
He excelled at cursive script,
refined and vigorous, peerless.
The silk cloth in his household
was always written on first before being boiled and bleached.
Practicing calligraphy by the pond,
the pond's water turned entirely black.
Whenever he wrote, he would say,
"In haste, no leisure for cursive."
People of the time called him the "Sage of Cursive."
Zhī's younger brother, Zhāng Chǎng,
a Gentleman of the Yellow Gate in the Hàn,
could also write cursive.
What people nowadays call Zhāng Zhī's calligraphy
is mostly Chǎng's.
From Wáng Sēngqián's Míngshū Lù.
From Jiāng Xǔ onward
Jiāng Xǔ, Liáng Xuān, Tián Yànhé, and Situ Wěi Dàn,
all were disciples of Bóyīng,
and all excelled in cursive script.
Dàn was the most outstanding;
the precious vessels in the palaces and halls of Wèi
were all inscribed by Dàn.
Emperor Míng of Wèi constructed the Língyún Tower,
and mistakenly had the plaque nailed up first
before it was inscribed.
They placed Dàn in a cage,
hoisted him up with a pulley to write on it,
at a height of twenty-five zhàng from the ground.
Dàn was extremely fearful,
and thereafter warned his descendants
to abandon this standard method.
His son, Shào Jì, was also praised for his ability.
Luó Huī and Zhào Gōng—their origins are unknown—
were contemporaries of Bóyīng,
and were praised in Xīzhōu.
However, they were boastful and self-aggrandizing,
which greatly perplexed people.
Bóyīng wrote in a letter to Zhū Kuān, narrating himself:
"Compared above to Cuī and Dù, I am inadequate;
compared below to Luó and Zhào, I am more than sufficient."
Zhāng Qǐ from Héjiān was also skilled in cursive script,
but not equal to Cuī and Zhāng.
Liú Déshēng excelled at running script,
but his origins are unknown.
Zhōng Yáo from Yǐngchuān
served as Grand Commandant of Wèi.
Hú Zhāo from the same commandery was summoned by the official carriage;
both families studied under Déshēng.
However, Hú's calligraphy was plump,
while Zhōng's was lean.
There are three styles:
the first is called inscription stone script,
the most exquisite;
the second is called formal document script;
the third is called informal script,
used for correspondence.
Yáo's son, Huì,
served as General Who Guards the West.
He was extremely adept at imitating others' calligraphy;
he altered the memorial submitted by Dèng Ài,
and no one knew of the matter.
Wèi Jì from Hédōng
(Míng manuscript: Wèi written as Wèi)
Jì,
served as Imperial Secretary of Wèi.
He excelled in cursive script and ancient script,
nearly mastering their subtleties;
his cursive style was slightly lean,
and his brushwork was refined and fluent.
Jì's son, Guàn, served as Grand Guardian of Jìn,
adopting the methods of Zhī,
and blending them with Jì's methods.
He further developed draft cursive,
which is the script used for correspondence.
Guàn's son, Héng, was also skilled in calligraphy,
and widely knowledgeable in ancient scripts.
Suǒ Jìng from Dūnhuáng,
a descendant of Zhāng Zhī's elder sister,
served as Marshal Who Conquers the West of Jìn,
and was also skilled in cursive script.
Hé Yuángōng from Chénguó was also skilled in cursive script.
Huáng Xiǎng from Wú excelled in cursive script,
praised by the world as steady and exhilarating.
Chén Chàng from Xíngyáng
(Original text: Chén written as Jiě,
corrected according to Fǎ Shū Yào Lù)
Chàng,
served as Secretary of the Imperial Library of Jìn,
and excelled in clerical script.
From Míng Shū Lù
Wáng Xīzhī
Wáng Xīzhī's "Oath Declaration",
what is transmitted today is its draft version.
It does not include the year, month, day, or first day of the month.
The authentic version was dated the tenth year of Yǒnghé, third month, guǐmǎo day, ninth month, xīnhài day.
Liú Yǔxī's Jiā Huà Lù records guǐmǎo day as the first day of the month, ninth day as xīnhài day,
indicating omissions or errors here
and the calligraphy is also authentic.
In the early years of Kāiyuán,
when the lecture hall at Wǎguān Temple in Jiāngníng County, Rùnzhōu was being repaired,
a craftsman found it inside a bamboo tube within the roof ridge ornament,
along with a Buddhist monk.
By the eighth year,
the county assistant magistrate Lǐ Yányè obtained it.
He presented it to Prince Qí,
who in turn offered it to the emperor.
It was kept in the palace and not released.
Some say
it was later lent back to Prince Qí.
In the twelfth year,
the prince's residence caught fire,
and all the books and paintings turned to ashes;
this work was also burned.
From Guó Shǐ Yì Zhuàn
Wáng Yì,
was the uncle of Xīzhī,
skilled in calligraphy and painting.
He once said to the Right Army General:
"My other affairs are not worth mentioning,
only calligraphy and painting are worthy of emulation."
Emperor Míng of Jìn studied his painting,
and the Right Army General studied his calligraphy.
From Shàng Shū Gù Shí
Lú of Lùzhōu
In recent years, when the Fángqiū Hall was constructed in the Eastern Capital,
many stone classics inscribed by Cài Yōng at the Hóngdū Academy were excavated,
and later, households in Luòzhōng often possessed them.
Wáng Xīzhī's "Borrowing a Boat Note"
is an exceptionally fine piece of calligraphy.
Thus, Lú Kuāng from north of the mountain
treasured and cherished it for years.
Lord Lú sent a letter to borrow it,
but was unsuccessful.
It was said:
"It can only be viewed on-site,
and has never been lent to anyone."
When Lú was appointed to Lùzhōu,
with his ceremonial banner en route,
just a few stages into the journey,
someone suddenly approached Lú with the calligraphy note for sale.
Upon examining it,
it was indeed the "Borrowing a Boat Note".
Astonished, he inquired about it,
and was told:
"The young master of the Lú family needed money,
so he sent it to be sold."
Lú sighed in amazement for a while,
did not ask the price,
and returned it.
Later, it was unknown who acquired it.
In the capital, there was a calligraphy dealer named Sūn Yíng,
who was quite famous.
Yíng's father, named Zhòng Róng,
also appraised calligraphy and paintings,
excelling in evaluation and categorization.
The treasures of wealthy families
often passed through his hands,
and authenticity could not escape his discernment.
The "Borrowing a Boat Note"
was in Sūn Yíng's collection;
people sought it with high prices,
but without success.
Lord Lú, seizing the moment of urgency,
reduced the price and provided relief,
and after a long time, when it reached a hundred thousand,
he finally obtained it.
Lord Lú was the maternal grandson of Hán Tàizhòng,
thus he had seen and recognized
many of the finest calligraphies and paintings.
From Shàng Shū Gù Shí
Huán Xuán
In the Jìn Shū, there is a food named "hánjù",
but no explanatory annotation is found.
Later, it was found in Qí Mín Yào Shù and Shí Jīng,
which is what is now called "jiānbǐng".
Huán Xuán once displayed a grand collection of calligraphy and paintings,
inviting guests to view them.
A guest ate hánjù
and handled the calligraphy and paintings without washing his hands,
causing stains;
Xuán was displeased.
From then on, hánjù was not served when entertaining guests.
From Shàng Shū Gù Shí
Chǔ Suìliáng
In the tenth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Emperor Tàizōng said to Wèi Zhēng:
"Since Shì Nán passed away,
there is no one with whom I can discuss calligraphy."
Zhēng replied:
"Chǔ Suìliáng is a later master of calligraphy,
and his work is highly methodical."
Thus, he was summoned for an audience.
Emperor Tàizōng once purchased Wáng Xīzhī's calligraphic works with gold and silk,
and people from across the land vied to present ancient writings,
bringing them to the palace to offer as tribute.
At that time, no one could distinguish their authenticity.
Suìliáng exhaustively discussed their origins,
providing evidence for each,
without a single error.
On the twenty-third day of the fourth month in the fourteenth year,
Emperor Tàizōng created a screen with standard and cursive script calligraphy,
which he displayed to his assembled ministers.
The brushwork was vigorous and sharp,
unsurpassed in that era.
He sought and acquired authentic running script from among the people,
amounting to two hundred and ninety sheets in total,
bound into seventy scrolls.
There were also twenty sheets of cursive script,
bound into eighty scrolls.
Whenever he had leisure from attending to governance,
he would peruse them.
He once said to his court officials:
"The study of calligraphy is a minor art,
and not initially an urgent matter.
Yet if one occasionally pays attention to it,
it is still better than idling away the days.
In all arts,
there has never been one that cannot be mastered through learning.
The fault lies in the laxity of mind and effort,
and the inability to concentrate and refine one's skill.
People today study the calligraphy of the ancients,
but they do not merely learn its form and appearance;
they seek its underlying bone strength.
Once the form is grasped,
the brush strength naturally emerges."
From Tán Bīn Lù.
The Authentic Lántíng Manuscript
Emperor Tàizōng was an avid student of calligraphy.
He possessed three thousand six hundred sheets of authentic works by the Great Master,
typically mounted as scrolls each measuring one zhang and two chi.
Among these treasures, the Lántíng Preface was the most cherished.
He placed it beside his seat,
viewing it morning and evening.
One day,
he whispered into Emperor Gāozōng's ear:
"After I pass away a thousand autumns and ten thousand years from now,
the Lántíng Preface shall go with me."
When the time of mourning came,
it was stored in a jade casket
and interred in the Zhāolíng tomb.
From Shàngshū Gùshí.
Wáng Fāngqìng
In the second year of the Lóngshuò era, fourth month,
Emperor Gāozōng personally wrote to the various generals in Liáodōng.
Xǔ Jìngzōng said:
□□□□□□□□□□□□□□ The Emperor said to the Vice-Minister of the Phoenix Pavilion, Wáng Fāngqìng:
"Your family must possess calligraphic works."
Fāngqìng memorialized:
"My tenth-generation granduncle, Xīzhī,
originally had over forty sheets.
In the twelfth year of Zhēnguàn,
my late father presented them.
There is one scroll
that I recently presented.
My eleventh-generation ancestor, Dǎo,
tenth-generation ancestor
The four characters 'Dǎo tenth-generation ancestor' were originally missing,
supplemented according to Fǎshū Yàolù.
Qià,
ninth-generation ancestor Xún,
eighth-generation ancestor Tánshǒu,
seventh-generation ancestor Sēngchuò,
sixth-generation ancestor Zhòngbǎo,
fifth-generation ancestor Qiān,
great-great-grandfather Guī,
great-grandfather Bāo,
along with my ninth-generation granduncle, the Jin Dynasty Secretariat Director Xiànzhī.
The calligraphy of the following twenty-eight individuals,
totaling ten scrolls,
is currently in my possession."
The Emperor summoned his ministers to the Wǔchéng Hall,
took the works, and viewed them.
He then ordered the Phoenix Pavilion Secretary Cuī Róng to compose a preface,
personally titled it the Bǎozhāng Collection,
and bestowed it upon Fāngqìng,
bringing honor to both court and commoners.
From Tán Bīn Lù.
Authentic Works of the Two Wángs
In the sixteenth year of the Kāiyuán era, fifth month,
authentic works of the Two Wángs, along with calligraphy by Zhāng Zhī, Zhāng Chǎng, and others,
totaling one hundred and sixty scrolls,
were brought out from the inner palace and entrusted to the Jíxián Academy.
They were ordered to compile characters and make two ink rubbings to present,
which were then bestowed upon the various princes.
These calligraphic works were all those from the Zhēnguàn period,
whose authenticity had been determined by Emperor Tàizōng's order through Wèi Zhēng, Yú Shìnán, Chǔ Suìliáng, and others.
Of the works by the Right Army General,
a total of two hundred and ninety sheets of authentic running script were obtained,
bound into seventy scrolls;
two thousand sheets of cursive script,
bound into
Note: The twenty-five characters from 'Of the works by the Right Army General' to 'bound into' were originally missing,
supplemented according to Fǎshū Yàolù.
eighty scrolls.
The works of the Junior Master, Zhāng Zhī, and others,
were each bound into volumes according to quantity.
The characters "Zhēnguàn" were used as a seal,
stamped on the seams and at the beginning and end of each scroll.
For the cursive works,
Chǔ Suìliáng was further ordered to write small standard script characters,
pasted onto the paper to trace their shadows.
Among these ancient versions,
some were official copies from the Liáng and Suí dynasties.
The Liáng copies bore the signatures of Mǎn Qiān, Xú Sēngquán, Shěn Chìwén, and Zhū [surname],
while the Suí copies bore those of Jiāng Zǒng, Yáo Chá, and others.
Emperor Tàizōng also ordered Wèi and Chǔ, among others,
to further inscribe their names at the end of each scroll as a record.
The Lántíng manuscript,
is said to be in the mysterious chamber of the Zhāolíng tomb.
The Yuè Yì Lùn,
during the Cháng'ān period, was borrowed by Princess Tàipíng for rubbing and copying outside the palace,
and consequently its whereabouts were lost.
In the fifth year,
an edict ordered Lù Yuántì, Wèi Zhé, Liú Huáixìn, and others to inspect and replace the mountings.
Each scroll was divided into two,
resulting in a total of eighty scrolls currently extant,
the rest being lost.
Yuántì also cut off the previous dynasty's inscriptions,
replacing them with his own name.
Emperor Xuánzōng personally wrote the two characters "Kāiyuán"
to use as a seal impression.
There were one hundred and thirty scrolls by the Right Army General in total,
twenty-eight scrolls by the Junior Master,
and one scroll each by Zhāng Zhī and Zhāng Chǎng.
Of the Right Army General's authentic running script,
only scrolls such as Huáng Tíng and Gào Shì, among others, remain.
Additionally, the Right Army General's Shàn Shàng Zhēn Shàngshū Xuān Shì,
which was in the collection of a family from Huázhōu, was obtained,
along with two scrolls of the Junior Master's running script, such as Bái Qí Suì.
These works bore the old woven label with the characters "Zhēnguàn year."
From Tán Bīn Lù.
The Eight Script Styles
Zhāng Huáiguàn's Shū Duàn states:
"Seal script, large seal script, clerical script, official script, draft cursive script, cursive script, flying white script, and running script
are collectively called the eight styles,
and the Right Army General excelled in all, placing him in the divine category.
The Right Army General once wrote several characters while drunk;
the dots and strokes resembled dragon claws,
leading to the later creation of dragon claw script.
Styles such as tadpole script, jade chopstick script, and reclining wave script,
amount to twenty-five varieties among various masters."
From Shàngshū Gùshí.
Lǐ Dū
When Lǐ Dū served as an attendant in Jīngnán,
he was familiar with court officials.
A letter sent from the capital
had extremely poor handwriting.
Lǐ sent a playful poem in reply:
"A grass-script letter travels a thousand li to Jīngmén,
its draft cursive script sprawling freely as it pleases.
One should laugh at Zhōng [Yáo] and Zhāng [Zhī] for their futile efforts,
making Xī [zhī] and Xiàn [zhī] labor their spirits in vain.
It can only be cherished as a precious treasure,
not dared to be passed down to mislead descendants.
Deeply grateful for the old friend's great kindness,
allowing me to swallow this seasonal affliction from heaven's course."
From Shūqíng Shī.
The Eastern Capital Beggar
During the Dàlì era,
there was a beggar on the Tiānjīn Bridge in the Eastern Capital
who had no hands.
Using his right foot to hold a brush,
he copied scriptures to beg for money.
When he wished to write,
he would first toss the brush over a foot high,
catch it with his foot,
and never drop it.
His calligraphy surpassed that of official scribes.
From Yǒuyáng Zázǔ.
Lú Hóngxuān
Xiè Hè said:
"Among the painters of Jiāngzuǒ, Wú's Cáo Bùxīng,
using five thousand feet of silk to paint a single image,
with a quick mind and swift hand,
completed it in an instant.
The head, face, hands, and feet,
the chest, shoulders, and back,
did not miss a single measurement.
This is what is difficult,
and only Bùxīng could do it."
Xiè Hè of the Chén dynasty was skilled in painting.
He once examined the secret archives,
and marveled at the dragon head painted by Cáo Bùxīng,
believing it to be as if he had seen a real dragon.
From Shàngshū Gùshí.
Wèi Xié
Wèi Xié of the Jìn dynasty.
The Bàopǔzǐ says:
"Wèi Xié and Zhāng Mò were both painting sages.
In Sūn Hóng's Painting of the Shànglín Garden,
Xié's traces are the most marvelous.
Also, in the Painting of the Seven Buddhas,
people did not dare to dot the eyes."
Kǎizhī discussed painting, saying:
"The Seven Buddhas and the Virtuous Women,
are both works by Xié,
majestic and full of emotional power.
The Painting of the North Wind from the Book of Songs is also by Xié's hand,
intricate and skillful in its emotional depth."
This painting is a short scroll,
mounted to a length of eight-tenths.
Zhāng Yànyuǎn inscribed it, saying:
During the Yuánhé era,
a clansman, Wéi Sù, brought it forth.
My grandfather offered in exchange a famous horse and two hundred bolts of fine silk.
Wéi Sù later intended to sell it to Hán Yù.
Hán's son, Chǎng, lent it to Chancellor Duàn Wénchāng,
who then returned a copy to Chǎng.
In the first year of the Huìchāng era, I saw the Duàn family's version.
Later, while serving in Xiāngzhōu, I saw the Hán family's version.
Xiè Hè said:
"Ancient paintings were all sketchy,
but from this point onward, they became refined.
The Six Principles were quite well integrated,
and although not fully achieving formal likeness, they possessed spirit and resonance,
surpassing all other masters.
A peerless masterpiece for the ages.
Ranked below Cáo Bùxīng in the first class,
and above Zhāng Mò and Xún Xù."
From Mínghuà Jì.
Wáng Xiànzhī
Wáng Xiànzhī of the Jìn dynasty, styled Zǐjìng,
was renowned from a young age,
elegant and lofty in demeanor.
In cursive and clerical script, he continued the excellence of his father,
and was also skilled in painting.
Huán Wēn once requested a painted fan from him.
When he made a mistake with his brush,
he turned it into a black-and-white spotted cow,
which was extremely marvelous and exquisite.
He also wrote the Ode to the Spotted Cow on the fan,
and this fan still existed during the Yìxī era.
From Mínghuà Jì.
Gù Kǎizhī
Gù Kǎizhī, styled Chángkāng,
with the childhood name Hǔtóu,
was a native of Jìnlíng.
He possessed abundant talent and spirit,
and was especially skilled in painting,
portraying forms and postures
with unsurpassed excellence.
Xiè Ān once said to Chángkāng:
"Your paintings are unmatched since the beginning of humanity."
He also said:
"Your paintings are profound and majestic,
unprecedented since ancient times."
He once temporarily entrusted a cabinet of paintings to Huán Xuán,
all of which were treasured masterpieces of his finest works,
sealed and labeled.
Later, Huán Xuán heard about them and took them,
falsely claiming they were not opened.
Kǎizhī, unsuspecting of theft,
simply said:
"Exquisite paintings communicate with the divine;
they transform and fly away,
just as humans ascend to immortality."
Kǎizhī had three peerless qualities:
peerless talent, peerless painting, and peerless naivety.
He once admired a courtesan,
so he painted her image on a wall,
and drove a nail into her heart.
The woman suffered heart pain,
and informed Chángkāng,
who then removed the nail.
She then recovered.
He also once wished to paint a portrait of Yīn Zhòngkān,
but Zhòngkān had long suffered from an eye ailment,
and firmly declined.
Chángkāng said:
"Your Excellency has no ailment;
if I clearly dot the pupils,
and apply 'flying white' strokes over them,
it will be like light clouds obscuring the sun."
When painting figures,
he would often leave the eyes undotted for years.
When asked the reason,
he replied:
"The beauty or ugliness of the four limbs
is fundamentally unrelated to the essence of excellence.
Conveying spirit and capturing likeness
lies precisely in these [the eyes]."
He also painted a portrait of Péi Kǎi,
adding three hairs on his cheek.
He said:
"Kǎi is a handsome gentleman,
possessing discernment.
With these added,
viewers will certainly find it exceptionally superior."
Jī Kāng presented him with a four-character poem,
which he depicted as a painting.
He often said:
"'Wielding the five strings with the hand' is easy;
'following the returning goose with the eyes' is difficult."
He also painted Xiè Yòuyú amidst a cliff,
and when asked the reason,
he said:
"With his love for hills and valleys,
this
(Míng Chāo edition adds 'is called' here)
gentleman should be placed amidst cliffs and valleys."
Chángkāng also once painted the layman Vimalakīrti in the northern hall of the Wǎguān Temple.
After completing the painting,
it glowed brilliantly for over a month.
The "Records of Temples in the Capital" states:
During the Xīngníng era,
when the Wǎguān Temple first established its monastic community,
a temple fair was held,
inviting court officials and commoners to announce pledges and solicit donations.
At that time, no scholar-official pledged over one hundred thousand,
but Chángkāng alone pledged one million.
Chángkāng was always poor,
so everyone thought it was an empty boast.
Later, the temple monks asked him to fulfill his pledge,
and Chángkāng said:
"Prepare a wall for me."
He shut himself indoors
(original: 'went back and forth',
corrected per Míng Chāo edition)
for over a month,
until the painting of Vimalakīrti was completed.
When about to dot the pupils,
he told the monks:
"On the first day of viewing,
ask for a donation of one hundred thousand;
on the second day,
ask for fifty thousand;
on the third day,
let them donate as they wish."
When the doors opened,
light illuminated the entire temple.
Donors crowded in,
and soon the amount reached one million.
Liú Yìqìng's "A New Account of the Tales of the World" states:
Grand Marshal Huán often invited Chángkāng and Yáng Xīn to discuss painting and calligraphy,
forgetting fatigue throughout the night.
From "Records of Famous Paintings."
Also, the "Painting of a Clear Night Excursion to the Western Garden,"
painted by Gù Chángkāng.
There is a colophon by various princes of the Liáng dynasty stating:
Several people in the painting all dine at the Imperial Kitchen.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
inscriptions by Chǔ Héngōng and other worthies are all present.
Originally collected by the Zhāng Wéisù family,
it passed to Chancellor Zhāng Gōng Hóngjìng.
During the Yuánhé era,
Xuānzong summoned Wéisù along with Zhōng Yuáncháng's transcription of the "Dàodé Jīng,"
and both were entered into the palace.
Later, the powerful eunuch Cuī Tánjùn took it out from the palace,
and it circulated again among the people.
Wéisù's son, Zhōu Fēng, formerly an assistant in Jīngzhōu, was in the capital.
One day, someone brought this painting seeking to sell it.
Zhōu Fēng was astonished,
and quickly exchanged several bolts of silk for it.
After a year,
he suddenly heard urgent knocking at the door.
Upon inquiry,
he saw several people together claiming:
"Commandant Qiú wishes to exchange three hundred bolts of plain silk
for your 'Clear Night Painting.'"
Zhōu Fēng, intimidated by their coercion,
hastily handed over the painting.
The next day,
they indeed delivered the silk.
Later, he realized it was a deception;
it was actually a powerful figure seeking appointment as the Grand Supervisor of Jiānghuái.
At that time, Wáng Huái was in charge of the Salt and Iron Monopoly,
and was an avid lover of calligraphy and painting.
He told this person:
"If you obtain this painting for me,
I will grant your request."
Hence, they devised a plan to acquire it.
After the Wáng family's affairs arose,
it flowed again to a cosmetics shop.
The gatekeeper of Vice-Minister Guō Chénggǔ purchased it for three hundred coins.
After Guō's death,
it circulated again to the Húlìng family.
Emperor Xuānzong once asked the Chancellor what famous paintings he had,
and the Chancellor mentioned this painting in reply.
It was later entered into the palace.
From "Anecdotes from the Department of State Affairs."
Gù Guāngbǎo
Gù Guāngbǎo was skilled in painting.
In Jiànkāng, there was a Lù Gài
who suffered from malaria for a year.
Medical treatments were all ineffective.
Guāngbǎo once visited Gài,
who received him by his bedside,
and said to Guāng:
"I have suffered from this illness for a long time,
and it cannot be cured.
Do you know of it?"
Guāngbǎo did not know of Gài's illness,
and said to Gài:
"You suffer from this,
I truly did not know.
If I had heard,
how could I have come to your chamber?"
He then took up a brush,
and with ink painted a lion,
instructing it to be posted outside the door.
He told Gài:
"This, once done, will have spiritual efficacy.
You must sincerely pray with all your heart,
and there will be results tomorrow."
Gài had it displayed outside,
and sent family members to burn incense and bow to it.
That very night at midnight,
there were rustling sounds outside,
which lasted a long time,
then ceased.
The next day,
the painted lion
had blood dripping from its mouth and chest,
and bloodstains
were also scattered outside the door.
Gài's illness then healed,
astonishing people of the time.
From "Records of Paintings of the Eight Dynasties,"
(Míng Chāo edition states: from "Records of Marvels from the Eight Dynasties")
Wáng Yì
Jìn Wáng Yì, styled Shìjiàng,
was from Lángyá Línchuān
(Míng manuscript;
Xǔ printed edition has Chuān as Yí)
He excelled at composing prose,
and was skilled in calligraphy and painting.
After crossing the river,
he became the foremost painter and calligrapher of the Jìn dynasty.
He mastered all the subtleties of music and rhythm.
During the reign of Emperor Yuán, he served as General of the Left Guard,
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Wǔkāng.
At that time, General Zhènjūn Xiè Shàng built the East Pagoda at the Lè Temple in Wǔchāng,
and Dài Ruòsī built the West Pagoda.
Both invited Yì to paint for them.
From the "Records of Famous Paintings"
Wáng Méng
Jìn Wáng Méng, styled Zhòngzǔ,
was from Jìnyáng.
Unrestrained and unconventional,
his calligraphy was comparable to Yì
(in the "Records of Famous Paintings Through the Ages," volume five, Yì is written as Yǔ)
Yì.
His painting was exceptionally skillful,
and he aspired to lofty and distant ideals.
He once went to a donkey market to paint a hearse.
He said of himself:
"I am fond of wine, good meat, and skilled in painting.
As long as people have food, drink, fine wine, and exquisite silk,
what can I not do?"
He was particularly adept at pure conversation,
and was highly regarded in his time.
From the "Records of Famous Paintings"
Dài Kuí
Jìn Dài Kuí, styled Āndào,
was from Zhì County, Qiáo Commandery.
From a young age, he was intelligent and fond of learning,
skilled in the qín and painting.
As a child,
he mixed white tile fragments with egg white to create a stele for Zhèng Xuán,
which was praised as absolutely marvelous at the time.
Yǔ Dàojì saw it
and said to Kuí:
"The spirit is still too vulgar;
you have not yet perfected it."
Kuí replied:
"I only strive for appropriateness,
to avoid such criticism from you."
From the "Records of Famous Paintings"
Also, when Dài Āndào was young,
he painted inside the Wǎguān Temple.
Prefect Wáng saw it and said:
"This child is not only capable of painting,
but will also eventually achieve fame.
It is only a pity that I am old
and will not live to see his glory."
From "Miscellaneous Writings of Shì Shuō"
Zōng Bǐng
Sòng Zōng Bǐng, styled Shǎowén,
was skilled in calligraphy and painting,
and loved mountains and rivers.
He traveled west to Jīng and Wū,
and climbed Héngyuè in the south.
He built a dwelling on Héng Mountain,
but returned to Jiānglíng due to illness.
He sighed and said:
"Old age and illness have both arrived,
and I fear I can no longer travel to all the famous mountains.
I should purify my mind to contemplate the Way,
and travel while lying down."
All the places he had visited,
he depicted on his walls,
and he would sit or lie facing them.
From the "Records of Famous Paintings"
Huánghuā Temple Wall
Liáng Táo Hóngjǐng, courtesy name Tōngmíng,
was proficient in many arts,
skilled in calligraphy and painting.
Emperor Wǔ once sought to recruit him for official service.
The recluse painted two oxen:
one with a golden nose ring being led,
the other meandering freely towards water and grass.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng understood his meaning,
and thus did not force him with official titles or ranks.
From "Míng Huà Jì" (Record of Famous Paintings).
Zhāng Sēngyóu of Liáng,
was a man of Wú.
During the Tiānjiàn era,
he served as General of the Wǔlíng Prince's State and Prefect of Wúxīng.
Emperor Wǔ renovated Buddhist temples,
often commissioning Sēngyóu to paint for them.
At that time, the various princes were stationed outside the capital,
and Emperor Wǔ missed them.
He sent Sēngyóu to sketch their portraits,
so that facing the paintings was like facing them in person.
At the Tiānhuáng Temple in Jiānglíng,
established by Emperor Míng,
there was a Cypress Hall inside.
Sēngyóu painted an image of Vairocana Buddha and the Ten Philosophers of Confucius.
The Emperor found it strange and asked:
"Why paint Confucius within a Buddhist temple?"
Sēngyóu replied:
"In the future, we will rely on this."
Later, when the Later Zhōu dynasty suppressed Buddhism,
burning temples and pagodas across the land,
only this hall, because it contained the image of Xuānní (Confucius),
was not destroyed or dismantled.
Also, at the Ānlè Temple in Jīnlíng, he painted four dragons,
but did not dot their eyes.
He often said:
"If I dot them, they will fly away."
People thought this was absurd,
and thus urged him to dot them.
In a moment,
thunder and lightning shattered the wall,
and two dragons rode the clouds and soared into the sky.
The ones whose eyes were not dotted remain to this day.
Earlier, Cáo Bùxīng of Wú had painted a dragon of the Qīngxī stream,
which Sēngyóu saw and scorned,
so he expanded its image at the Lóngquán Pavilion.
His painting was kept in the Imperial Archives,
but was not highly regarded at the time.
During the Tàiqīng era,
thunder struck the Lóngquán Pavilion.
The wall painting was then lost,
and only then did people realize its divine wonder.
He also painted "Two Foreign Monks from India".
Due to the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng,
the painting was separated into two parts.
One monk was treasured by Lù Jiān, the Right Regular Attendant of the Táng dynasty.
When Lù Jiān was critically ill,
he dreamed of a foreign monk telling him:
"I have a companion,
separated for many years,
now in the Lǐ family in Luòyáng.
If you seek to reunite us,
I will use my spiritual power to aid you."
Lù used money and silk,
sought at that place,
and indeed purchased it.
His illness soon recovered.
Liú Chángqīng recorded this story.
All the spiritual responses of Zhāng's paintings
cannot be fully recorded.
From "Míng Huà Jì" (Record of Famous Paintings).
Also, at the Xīngguó Temple in Rùnzhōu,
doves and pigeons nesting on the beams soiled the revered images.
Sēngyóu then painted a hawk on the east wall.
And a sparrowhawk on the west wall.
Both looked sideways out from under the eaves.
From then on, doves and pigeons dared not come again.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi" (Records from Court and Country).
Gāo Xiàohéng
Gāo Xiàohéng of Northern Qí,
the second son of Shìzōng,
was enfeoffed as Prince of Guǎngníng Commandery, Grand Minister over the Masses, and Governor of Tóngzhōu.
He was broadly learned and multi-talented.
Once he painted a gray eagle on a hall wall,
viewers suspected it was real,
and turtledoves and sparrows dared not approach.
He also painted "Portrait of Court Officials",
which was exquisitely superb for its time.
Captured by the Zhōu army,
he was appointed Kāifǔ,
and enfeoffed as a County Marquis.
Xiàohéng was also skilled in music.
Emperor Wǔ of Zhōu held a banquet for the ruler and ministers of Qí,
personally playing the pipa,
and ordered Xiàohéng to play the flute.
From "Míng Huà Jì" (Record of Famous Paintings).
Yáng Zǐhuá
Yáng Zǐhuá of Northern Qí,
during the reign of Shìzǔ,
served as General of the Direct Gate and Vice Gentleman-in-Attendance of the Right.
He often painted horses on walls.
At night, listening,
one could hear them neighing and whinnying,
as if seeking water and grass.
He painted a dragon on plain silk,
and when unfurled, clouds and mist would gather around it.
Shìzǔ valued him greatly,
having him reside within the palace.
The world called him the Painting Sage.
Without an imperial edict,
he was not allowed to paint for outsiders.
At that time, there was Wáng Zǐchōng, skilled in chess to a divine level,
and they were called the "Two Unsurpassed".
From "Míng Huà Jì" (Record of Famous Paintings).
