Liú Shāguǐ
Liú Shāguǐ of Northern Qí was a contemporary of Yáng Zǐhuá,
and Shìzǔ valued them both.
He painted fighting sparrows on a wall.
The Emperor saw them,
thought they were alive,
and only realized they were paintings when he brushed against them.
He often stayed within the palace,
receiving immense rewards.
He served as Governor of Liángzhōu,
and his name appears in the History of Northern Qí.
From "Míng Huà Jì" (Record of Famous Paintings).
Zhèng Fǎshì
In Suí, Tián, Yáng, and Zhèng Fǎshì together painted a small pagoda at the Guāngmíng Temple in the capital.
Zhèng painted the east and north walls,
Tián painted the west and south walls,
and Yáng painted the outer four sides.
This was called the "Three Unsurpassed".
Yáng used a bamboo mat to screen his painting area.
Zhèng secretly observed it,
and said to Yáng:
"Your painting is ultimately impossible to learn.
Why trouble to screen it off?"
Zhèng proposed a marriage alliance,
establishing a close relationship as neighbors,
and further requested Yáng's painting models.
Yáng led Zhèng to the court hall,
and pointing to the palaces, official robes and caps, people, horses, and carriages, said:
"These are my painting models."
From then on, Zhèng was deeply convinced.
The Guāngmíng Temple was renamed Dàyún Temple,
located in the Huáiyuǎn Ward of Cháng'ān.
From "Míng Huà Jì" (Record of Famous Paintings).
Yán Lìdé
In the third year of the Zhēnguàn era of Táng,
Xiè Yuánshēn, a chieftain of the Eastern Man tribes, came to court.
He wore a crown of black bear skin,
with a gold headband,
a fur cloak for a skirt,
leg bindings for travel,
and shoes.
Yán Shígǔ, Vice Director of the Secretariat, memorialized:
"In the past, King Wǔ of Zhōu brought about great peace,
and distant states submitted.
The Zhōu historians then compiled these events into the 'Chapter of Royal Gatherings'.
Now, due to the Sage Virtue's reach,
ten thousand states come to court.
Those in plant-fiber garments and bird-patterned robes
all gather at the Man lodges.
This truly can be painted and left for posterity,
to manifest the virtue of cherishing the distant."
The Emperor agreed,
and thus ordered Lìdé and others to paint it.
Also, Lǐ Sìzhēn of Zhàojùn, in his "Discourse on Painting",
ranked it third in the highest category,
and in the preface concerning the paintings of the Right Minister, Bólíngzi Yán Lìběn,
and his elder brother, Minister of Works, Duke of Dà'ān, Yán Lìdé, said:
"Dà'ān and Bólíng,
are brothers hard to rank.
Since Lù and Xiè of the South perished,
and Zǐhuá of the Northern dynasties passed away long ago,
the wonder of figure painting
truly experienced a revival with them.
As for the ten thousand states coming to court,
presenting jade and silk as at Túshān,
the hundred Man tribes paying tribute,
receiving their positions at the Yìng Gate,
their turns and movements, square and round,
the rituals of straightening hairpins and holding tablets,
the strange and bizarre customs of nose-drinking and head-flying tribes—
all were captured down to the finest detail,
and their spirit fully obtained."
From "Tán Bīn Lù" (Records of Conversations with Guests).
Yán Lìběn
During the reign of Emperor Tàizōng of the Táng dynasty,
his official rank was very high,
and he was equally famous as his elder brother Lìdé.
He once received an imperial edict to paint Emperor Tàizōng's portrait.
Later, skilled artists
copied and displayed it in the front chamber of the eastern hall of Xuándū Temple,
to suppress the energy of the Jiǔwǔ Ridge,
allowing people to still look up to the majestic and heroic might.
Lìdé created the "Tribute Bearers Painting,"
depicting figures from foreign lands
with bizarre and strange appearances.
Lìběn's draft paintings of kings circulated among the people.
Even the renowned artists of the former Northern and Southern dynasties
could not surpass them.
At that time, fierce beasts in the southern mountains harmed people,
and Emperor Tàizōng sent brave warriors to capture them,
but they failed.
Guówáng Yuánfèng, loyal and righteous,
went to capture them himself
and killed one with a single arrow.
Emperor Tàizōng admired his bravery,
and ordered Lìběn to paint the scene.
The saddled horses and attendants
were all painted true to life,
and everyone marveled at his skill.
He also painted works such as "The Eighteen Scholars of the Qín Palace" and "The Meritorious Officials of Língyān Pavilion,"
which also shone brilliantly, surpassing the ancients.
Only paintings like "Tribute Bearers" and "Imperial Procession"
were created together with Lìdé.
It is commonly said that the paintings of meritorious officials at Cí'ēn Temple
were colored by various hands,
and his original traces are not seen.
His depictions of figures, saddled horses, crowns, chariots, and robes
are all divine.
Lǐ Sìzhēn said:
"He studied under Zhèng Fǎshì,
but in reality, he surpassed him.
Later, Wáng Zhīshèn followed his example,
and his brushwork was very powerful.
Yán's paintings are of divine quality."
From Táng's "Huà Duàn"
Emperor Tàizōng once boated with his attendants in the spring garden,
and an exotic bird in the pond floated gracefully with the waves.
Emperor Tàizōng repeatedly admired it,
ordered those present to compose poems,
and summoned Yán Lìběn to paint it.
Outside the pavilion, a call was announced:
"Painter Yán Lìběn."
At that time, he served as the Director of the Bureau of Honors,
yet he hurried over, sweating,
bent over the pond's edge,
wielding his brush and paints,
unable to bear the shame.
Afterward, he warned his son:
"In my youth, I loved reading,
and fortunately avoided ignorance.
I dabbled in writing and painting,
and was somewhat among my peers,
but I became known only for painting.
To personally engage in such menial tasks
is a great disgrace.
You should take this as a serious warning,
and not learn this craft."
By the reign of Emperor Gāozōng,
Yán Lìběn served as Right Chancellor,
while Jiāng Kè, having achieved military merits as a frontier general, served as Left Chancellor.
Due to famine that year,
students of the Imperial Academy were sent home,
and clerks were required to master one classic.
People at the time said:
"The Left Chancellor displays might in the desert,
the Right Chancellor earns fame with painting.
Students of the three academies are dispersed,
clerks of the five bureaus master the classics."
The characters "míng jīng" originally read "jīng míng,"
corrected according to the Míng dynasty manuscript.
From "Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ"
The Yán family excelled in painting for generations.
When Lìběn visited Jīngzhōu,
he saw the old works of Zhāng Sēngyáo and said:
"He must have gained his fame undeservedly."
The next day, he went again,
and said:
"He is still a fine artist of recent times."
The next day, he went once more,
and said:
"A famous master is truly not undeserving."
He sat and lay down to observe them,
stayed overnight beneath them,
and could not leave for ten days.
Also, Liáng dynasty's Zhāng Sēngyáo painted "Drunken Monk."
Taoist priests often used this to mock the monks,
and the monks felt ashamed.
So they pooled hundreds of thousands in cash,
commissioned Yán Lìběn to paint "Drunken Taoist."
Both paintings are now passed down through the ages.
From "Guó Shǐ Yì Zuǎn"
Xuē Jì
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
he held the position of Junior Guardian.
His literary and scholarly achievements
were the foremost of his time.
He studied calligraphy under Chǔ Hé'nán.
It was said at the time:
"Buy Chǔ, get Xuē, no loss in quality."
The phrase "Buy Chǔ, get Xuē, no loss in quality" was originally missing,
added according to a noted manuscript.
His painting followed Yán Lìng.
In the Imperial Library, there is his "Painting of Cranes,"
considered a unique masterpiece of the time.
While traveling in Xīn'ān Commandery,
he met Lǐ Bái.
They lingered together,
and he inscribed the plaque for Yǒng'ān Temple,
and painted a mural of a Western Buddha.
His brushwork was free and unrestrained,
his style elegant and spirited,
second only to Cáo and Zhāng.
Traces of these two wonders,
with inscriptions and praises by Lǐ Hànlín, still exist.
It is also said that in Shǔ Commandery, there are many paintings of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and green oxen,
all of divine quality.
From "Táng Huà Duàn"
Yùchí Yǐsēng
Táng dynasty's Yùchí Yǐsēng
was a foreigner from Tukhāra.
In the early Zhēnguàn era,
his country, due to his exquisite painting skills,
recommended him to the imperial court, saying:
"His country also has an elder brother, Jiǎsēng,
but no one has seen his paintings."
Yǐsēng painted the merits and virtues in the central front of the pagoda at Cí'ēn Temple,
and
the Míng manuscript has "yòu" instead of "chā"
concave and raised flowers,
and the Thousand-Armed, Thousand-Eyed Bodhisattva in the central west side,
extremely exquisite and marvelous.
At Guāngzhái Temple, behind the Seven Treasures Terrace, he painted a subduing demons image,
with thousands of strange and myriad forms,
truly a wondrous work.
However, his paintings of merits, figures, flowers, and plants
all bear the appearance of foreign lands,
lacking the virtues of Chinese rituals, music, and dignified bearing.
From "Táng Huà Duàn"
Wáng Wéi
Táng dynasty's Right Assistant Secretary Wáng Wéi lived at Yùshān in Lántián,
and roamed about in Wǎngchuān.
He and his brother were preeminent in the imperial examinations and literature of their time,
so it was said: "At court, the Left Chancellor's calligraphy;
in the world, the Right Assistant Secretary's poetry."
His paintings of landscapes, pines, and rocks
resembled living forms,
yet his style was uniquely outstanding.
Today, at the Western Pagoda Courtyard of Qiānfú Temple in the capital, there are screens:
one painting of a maple fort,
one painting of Wǎngchuān.
The mountain valleys are lush and winding,
clouds and waters seem to fly and move,
the conception transcends the mundane world,
strangeness springs from the tip of his brush.
He often inscribed his own poem:
"In past lives, a mistaken poet;
in a previous life, surely a painter."
Such was his self-regard.
In the eastern courtyard of Cí'ēn Temple,
together with Attendant Bì and Guǎngwén Zhèng,
each painted a small wall mural.
They were called the "Three Wonders" of the time.
At the residence of Assistant Secretary Yǔ,
there was a landscape mural with inscriptions,
also a marvelous work of that era.
In landscapes, pines, and rocks,
he was of the highest, supreme grade.
From "Táng Huà Duàn"
Also, Wáng Wéi once visited the residence of Yǔ Jìngxiū in Zhāoguó Ward,
and saw a painting of "Musicians Playing" on the wall.
Wáng Wéi looked closely and laughed.
When asked why,
Wáng Wéi said:
"This is the first beat of the third sequence of the 'Rainbow and Feather Garments Dance'."
Enthusiasts gathered musicians to verify it,
and not a single detail was off.
From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ"
Lǐ Sīxùn
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the various guard general Lǐ Sīxùn,
and his son Zhāodào, who was a Palace Secretary,
both excelled in the wonders of landscape painting.
People of the time said:
"General Lǐ the Elder" and "General Lǐ the Younger."
Sīxùn's style and quality were lofty and extraordinary,
his mountains and rivers sublimely perfect.
Birds, beasts, plants, and trees,
were all within his skill.
The paintings of the Palace Secretary
of landscapes, birds, and beasts,
were exceedingly intricate and clever.
His intellectual conception and brushwork could not be matched.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Emperor Xuánzōng summoned Sīxùn
to paint the walls of the Dàtóng Hall along with a screen.
Another day, during an audience,
the Emperor's edict stated:
"The screen painted by you,
at night one can hear the sound of water.
You are an excellent hand whose work connects with the divine,
the foremost in landscape painting of our dynasty."
Sīxùn is of the Divine Class.
Zhāodào is of the Sublime Upper Class.
From "Judgments on Táng Painting"
Hán Gàn
Hán Gàn of the Táng dynasty,
was a man of Jīngzhào.
During the Tiānbǎo era of Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng, he was summoned to serve in the palace.
The Emperor ordered him to study under Chén Hóng in painting horses,
but found it strange that his style differed.
The Emperor therefore questioned him.
He replied:
"I have my own teacher.
The horses in Your Majesty's inner stables,
are all my teachers."
The Emperor thought this very remarkable.
Afterwards, he was indeed able to capture the substance of flying dragons,
and exhaust the wonder of jade-spurting steeds.
His discernment was as refined as that of Jiǔfāng Gāo,
and his eye as complete as that of Bólè.
Moreover, among ancient paintings of horses,
there is "King Mù of Zhōu's Painting of the Eight Steeds";
in our dynasty, Yán Lìběn painted horses,
seeming to imitate Zhǎn Zǐqián and Zhèng Fǎshī.
They often showed sinews and bones,
and all enjoyed fame for a time,
but none possessed sublime skill for the ages.
After the Kāiyuán era,
the land was peaceful and orderly.
Famous horses from foreign lands,
arrived in succession through multiple translations.
However, the sandy deserts were distant,
and their hooves and nails were mostly thin.
Emperor Xuánzōng then selected the best among them,
and together with the fine steeds of the Central Kingdom,
issued decrees on horse administration.
From then on, the inner stables had steeds such as "Fēihuáng," "Zhàoyè," "Fúyún," and "Wǔfāng."
Their coats were strange, their forms extraordinary,
their sinews and bones were robust
Robust originally written as 'same',
changed according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy
their hooves and nails all thick.
Driving them through perilous places,
was as comfortable as riding in a carriage,
galloping and charging responded to the heart's intent,
matching the rhythm of Sháo and Huò music.
Therefore, Chén Hóng depicted them first,
and Hán Gàn continued afterwards.
He captured the form of the Wòwā horse,
though it was not in the water.
He transferred the shape of the Yǎoniǎo steed,
as if it came from heaven.
Thus Hán is placed in the Divine Class.
Chén also painted portraits,
and is placed in the Sublime Upper Class.
The deity at the triple gate of Bǎoyìng Temple,
the Northern Heavenly King in the western courtyard,
the Bodhisattva in front of the Buddha hall,
the Buddha image in the western courtyard,
and the Twenty-Four Sages in the northern courtyard of Bǎoshèng Temple, etc.,
are all his traces.
His paintings of horses, the Bodhisattva at the Gāohuì, and the ghosts and deities in the western courtyard are of the Divine Class.
From "Judgments on Táng Painting"
Also, while Gàn was at leisure,
suddenly a man in vermilion clothes and a black cap arrived.
Gàn asked:
"How did you get here?"
He replied:
"I am a ghost messenger.
Hearing that you are skilled at painting fine horses,
I wish you would bestow one upon me."
Gàn immediately painted one and burned it.
A few days later, while going out,
someone bowed and thanked him, saying:
"Thanks to your gift of a swift steed,
I am spared the toil of trekking over mountains and rivers,
and I also have something to repay you."
The next day,
someone sent a hundred bolts of plain white silk,
but its origin was unknown.
Gàn accepted and used it.
From "Records of Unique and Strange Things"
At the beginning of the Jiànzhōng era,
someone once led a horse to visit a horse doctor,
saying the horse had a problem with its leg,
and offered two thousand coins for treatment.
The horse's coat color and bone structure
were something the horse doctor had never seen before.
He laughed and said,
"Your horse looks exactly like one painted by Hán Gàn.
Among real horses, there certainly is none like it."
He then asked the horse owner to lead the horse around the market gate once,
and the horse doctor followed.
Suddenly they encountered Hán Gàn.
Gàn was also startled and said,
"This is truly one I painted and colored."
Only then did he realize that what he had casually crafted,
must have mysteriously matched a likeness.
He then stroked the horse,
and the horse seemed to stumble,
injuring its front leg.
Gàn found this strange.
Upon returning home,
he looked at his original painting of the horse,
and saw a spot of black missing on the leg.
Only then did he know that the painting had connected with the numinous. The money the horse doctor received,
after passing through several owners,
turned into clay coins.
From "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng"
Wú Dàoxuán
Táng Wú Dàoxuán, styled Dàozǐ,
was a native of Yángdí.
He was orphaned and impoverished in his youth.
Endowed by nature with talent,
before reaching the age of twenty,
he had mastered the subtleties of painting.
Wandering to the eastern capital Luòyáng,
Emperor Xuánzōng learned of his fame
and summoned him to serve in the palace.
Broadly speaking, he took Zhāng Sēngyóu as his master, achieving a myriad of forms and variations,
surpassing him in boldness and freedom.
In the temples and monasteries of the two capitals,
he painted murals on over forty
(Míng manuscript: 'forty' as 'hundred')
walls.
Though the transformations of images were similar,
the appearances and strange forms of the figures
were never identical.
Among the marvelous works still extant and seen by people:
At the Imperial Annotated Diamond Sutra Hall of the Xìngtáng Temple in the upper capital,
he also inscribed the sutra text himself.
At the Cí'ēn Temple pagoda, the front depicted Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra,
the west side showed the subjugation of demons and coiling dragons, etc.
Also, the bodhisattva on the front gate of the small hall,
the hell scenes, Indra, dragon deities at the Jǐnggōng Temple,
and the two deities on the central gate at the Yǒngshòu Temple—
all were supremely exquisite for their time.
Zhū Jǐngxuán said:
"There was an old family servant, Yǐn Lǎo, over eighty years old,
who once said:
'I saw Wú Shēng painting the deity inside the central gate;
the halo was done last,
completed in a single stroke.
At that time, hundreds of old and young from the wards and markets
gathered daily
to eagerly await and watch.
Barriers were set up.
They offered money and silk, piling them as high [as the barrier].
When he finally wielded his brush,
the onlookers stood like a wall.
Like wind falling and lightning turning,
the circle formed like the full moon,
and the clamor of shouts
shook the entire ward and city.
Some said it was divine.'" Also, the old monk Xuán Zòng of Jǐnggōng Temple said:
"After Wú Shēng finished painting these hell scenes,
the people of the capital all came to see,
and, fearing retribution for sins, cultivated goodness.
The butchers and wine sellers in the two markets
could no longer sell their meat and fish."
Also, during the Kāiyuán era, the emperor traveled to the eastern capital Luòyáng.
Wú Shēng met with Péi Mín and Zhāng Xǔ,
and each displayed his skill.
Péi performed a sword dance,
Zhāng wrote a wall of calligraphy,
and Wú painted a wall.
The gentry and people of the city
in a single day
witnessed these three masterpieces.
He also painted the Xuányuán Temple,
"The Five Sages and a Thousand Officials."
The palaces and official headdresses
had a momentum that overwhelmed clouds and dragons,
as if conceived by the Creator.
Thus, Assistant Minister Dù Fǔ's poem says:
"Exquisitely marvelous, they stir the palace walls."
Also, during the Tiānbǎo era of Emperor Xuánzōng,
he suddenly thought of the landscape of the Jiālíng River in Shǔ,
so he provided Wú Shēng with post-horse relay,
ordering him to go and sketch it.
Upon his return,
the emperor asked about its appearance.
He replied:
"Your subject has no preliminary sketches,
but has committed it all to memory."
Sent to depict it in the Dàtóng Hall,
he completed the three-hundred-li landscape of the Jiālíng River
in a single day.
At that time, General Lǐ was renowned for landscape painting,
and he also painted a wall in the Dàtóng Hall,
taking several months to finish.
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"Lǐ Sīxùn's work of several months
and Wú Dàoxuán's work of a single day
are both supremely marvelous."
He also painted five dragons inside the hall.
Their scales and armor seemed to flutter and move.
Whenever heavy rain was imminent,
they would emit mist.
Wú Shēng often recited the Diamond Sutra,
and from this recognized his original self.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
there was Yáng Tíngguāng who rivaled his fame.
Secretly, he painted a portrait of Wú Shēng during a lecture gathering.
Amidst the crowd,
he led Wú to see it.
Wú saw it and was startled,
saying to Tíngguāng:
"This old man is decrepit and ugly;
why paint him?"
Thereupon, he sighed in admiration.
His paintings of figures, Buddha images, ghosts and spirits, birds and beasts, landscapes, terraces and halls, plants and trees
were all divine and marvelous.
He was the foremost of the dynasty.
Zhāng Huáiguàn said:
"Wú Shēng's painting
is the rebirth of Zhāng Sēngyóu."
This statement is fitting.
From "Táng Huà Duàn."
Also, during the Kāiyuán era,
General Péi Mín was in mourning for his mother.
He visited Dàozǐ,
requesting him to paint several walls of ghosts and deities at the Tiāngōng Temple in the eastern capital,
to aid the deceased.
Dàozǐ replied:
"I have long ceased painting.
If the General is willing,
for my sake, tie up your hair,
and perform a sword dance.
Perhaps through such fierce inspiration,
I may connect with the unseen realm."
Péi then removed his mourning garments,
dressing in his usual attire.
He galloped like flying,
spinning left, drawing right,
and threw his sword into the clouds.
It soared several tens
(Original: 'tens' as 'thousands',
corrected per Míng manuscript)
of zhàng high,
like lightning descending.
Péi stretched out his hand, holding the scabbard to catch it;
the sword pierced through the scabbard and entered.
Spectators numbered in the thousands,
all trembling with awe.
Dàozǐ then took up his brush and painted the wall;
a swift wind arose,
creating a spectacle unparalleled in the world.
Among all Dàozǐ's lifetime paintings,
none surpassed this in satisfaction.
From "Dú Yì Zhì."
Also, Dàozǐ visited a monk to request tea.
The monk showed no courtesy,
so he asked for brush and inkstone.
On the wall, he painted a donkey and left.
One night,
all the furniture in the monk's room was trampled and broken;
he was harassed unbearably.
The monk realized it was Dàozǐ,
and earnestly invited him back to the monastery to plead.
Then he erased the painted area.
From "Lú Shì Zá Shuō."
Also, Xīmíng and Cí'ēn Temples had many famous paintings.
On the front wall of the Cí'ēn pagoda were a wet-eared lion and a lotus seat flower,
highly esteemed at the time.
Shèngshàn and Jìng'ài Temples
also had ancient paintings.
The wooden pagoda courtyard of Shèngshàn Temple had many paintings and calligraphies by Zhèng Guǎngwén.
The mountain pavilion courtyard of Jìng'ài Temple had pheasant tail feathers so lifelike,
and on the sand was the inscribed name of Jìnshì Fáng Lǔ.
Later, someone wrote a poem:
"The Yáo family's new son-in-law is Master Fáng,
not yet understanding her lovely face, his heart runs wild.
They say he's skilled at shooting feathered arrows;
don't let him shoot through the temple's wall."
In the northwest corner of the temple was the Sick Dragon Courtyard, also with paintings by Wú.
From "Lú Shì Zá Tán."
Féng Shàozhèng
During the Táng Kāiyuán era,
Guānfǔ suffered a great drought.
The capital especially lacked rain.
The emperor urgently ordered high officials to pray widely among mountains and marshes, but there was no response.
The emperor had a new hall built
by the Dragon Pool.
He then summoned the Director of the Imperial Workshops, Féng Shàozhèng,
ordering him to paint a dragon on each of the four walls.
Shàozhèng first painted a plain dragon on the west wall.
Its strange form writhed,
as if about to leap.
Before the painting was half done,
it seemed as if wind and clouds were born from his brush.
The emperor and his attendants watched below the wall;
the scales appeared damp,
and before the coloring was finished,
a white vapor emerged as if from the eaves and corridors,
entering the pool.
Waves surged violently,
and thunder and lightning followed.
Several hundred attending officials all saw a white dragon from the waves
riding the clouds and mist upward.
Soon, dark clouds spread everywhere,
and a storm arose violently.
Before the day ended, sweet rain spread throughout the capital region.
From "Mínghuáng Zálù."
Zhāng Zǎo
Zhāng Zǎo of the Táng dynasty was a man of literary and refined bearing,
a renowned figure of his time.
In painting pines, rocks, and landscapes,
he excelled and gained fame in his era.
His pine trees in particular stood out, surpassing both ancient and contemporary works.
He was skilled with the brush,
often holding two brushes in his hand,
using both simultaneously.
With one, he painted lush, living branches;
with the other, withered, dead branches.
Their spirit was haughty as mist and smoke,
their force surpassing wind and rain.
The rugged, scaly, and wrinkled texture of the bark
he rendered freely and unrestrainedly.
The living branches were moist, harmonizing with spring's bounty;
the withered branches were parched, cracked like autumn wind.
As for the appearance of his landscapes,
the heights and depths were supremely elegant and secluded,
with profound weight conveyed within a foot's space.
Rocks jutted out as if about to fall,
springs gushed forth with a roar.
Those nearby felt imposing and chill-inducing,
those distant reached the pure clarity of the sky's limit.
His painted screens and barriers were most numerous among men.
Today, the landscape with pines and rocks in the western courtyard of Bǎoyìng Temple
still bears his inscription.
It is a work of exquisite craftsmanship.
His pines, rocks, and landscapes
all rank among the divine class.
From "Huà Duàn".
Furthermore, a later scholar's family possessed a pine-and-rock screen by Zhāng Zǎo.
The scholar said:
"Lǐ Yuē, Vice Director of the Ministry of War, had a passion for painting bordering on obsession.
Upon learning of it, he sought to purchase it.
But the family's frail wife
had already bleached it for use as clothing lining.
Only two panels were obtained,
featuring a pair of cypresses and one rock.
He sighed with regret for a long time."
From "Míng Huà Jì".
Chén Hóng
Chén Hóng of the Táng dynasty
was from Kuàijī.
Skilled in painting portraits, figures, and beauties,
he was recommended by his local circuit
and summoned to serve during Emperor Xuánzōng's Kāiyuán era.
He was often commanded to paint imperial portraits,
which were supremely exquisite for the time.
Emperor Xuánzōng hunting boars, deer, and hares, handling falcons, etc.
Míng Chāo Běn reads "etc." as "zither"
and also portraits of dancers and true likenesses,
all were commissioned to be painted by him.
Also, the true portrait of Emperor Sùzōng in Tàiqīng Palace.
Not only did it capture the dragon-head and phoenix-bearing demeanor,
the sun-horn and moon-forehead features.
But the brushwork was vigorous and lush,
the bearing heroic and untrammeled,
matching auspicious signs and correspondences.
Heaven had bestowed this ability upon him.
After Lord Yán Lìnggōng of our dynasty,
he was the only one.
Today, in the Hall of the Heavenly Venerable at Xiányí Temple, the painting of the upper immortals and the true portraits of the Daoist priests serving at that time,
are all his works.
He also once painted two processional banners depicting the life story for the late Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, Xú.
There was a woman who could weave them,
supremely exquisite without equal.
Only in painting true portraits, divine figures, and beauties, etc.,
was he of the highest rank among the marvelous class.
From "Huà Duàn".
Wéi Wútiǎn
Wéi Wútiǎn of the Táng dynasty
was from Jīngzhào.
During Emperor Xuánzōng's reign,
he gained fame for painting horses and extraordinary beasts.
It was said at the time that Wéi's paintings of four-legged creatures
were all supremely wonderful.
He once depicted a lion presented as tribute from a foreign country,
strikingly lifelike.
Later, the lion was released and returned to its native land,
only the painting remained,
and people would view it from time to time.
All beasts that saw it were afraid.
Also, once during an imperial hunt by Emperor Xuánzōng,
a single arrow struck two wild boars.
He was commanded to paint this at the north gate of Xuánwǔ Gate.
Copies circulated among the people,
of supremely heroic and wonderful quality.
Now, considering the nature of the hundred beasts:
some are the majestic and peerlessly swift steeds,
some are the gentle and tame fine ones.
Their claws and hooves already differ,
their fur and manes are each distinct.
Previous masters might depict anger with an open mouth,
docility with a lowered head.
But to distinguish their temperament with a single brushstroke,
to know their name by the flourish of a single hair—
this was never achieved in ancient times,
but Lord Wéi could do it.
His "Picture of Extraordinary Beasts" was divided and distributed.
People's households often possess them.
In the capital's temples and monasteries, there is no place without his paintings.
His paintings of beasts, etc., rank highest among the marvelous class.
From "Huà Duàn".
Lú Léngjiā
Lú Léngjiā of the Táng dynasty
was a disciple of Wú Dàoxuán.
His painting style resembled Wú's,
but his talent and strength were limited.
He was quite capable of detailed painting.
Within a foot's space, landscapes appeared vast and open,
with objects and forms exquisitely complete.
Illustrations of sūtras and Buddhist subjects
were his specialty.
Wú once painted the triple gate of Zǒngchí Temple in the capital,
earning great wealth from the crowd.
Léngjiā then secretly painted the triple gate of Zhuāngyán Temple.
With sharp thought and expansive execution,
he quite reached the marvelous.
One day,
Wú suddenly saw it,
and exclaimed in astonishment:
"This man's brush strength
usually does not match mine,
but now it resembles mine.
This man,
his vital essence is entirely spent here."
After one month,
Léngjiā indeed died.
From "Míng Huà Jì".
Bì Hóng
Bì Hóng of the Táng dynasty,
in the second year of the Dàlì era, served as Jǐshìzhōng.
He painted "Pines and Rocks" on the wall of the Left Department hall,
which enthusiasts all composed poems about.
He was changed from Deputy Governor of Jīngzhào to Right Tutor.
He gained fame in his generation for trees and rocks.
Changing the manner and transforming the ancient style in painting trees
began with Hóng.
From "Míng Huà Jì".
Jìngyù Temple
was the residence of the Great Mù Empress of the Táng dynasty.
A temple monk said:
"Outside the gate of the Three Stages Courtyard
is where Shényáo Emperor shot a peacock."
Inside and outside the gate of the Meditation Courtyard,
"Yóumù

corrected according to "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"

Wáng Zhāoyǐn painted on the inner west side of the gate, Héxiūjí Dragon King possessing spiritual power.
West inside the gate,
Fire-Eyed Yakṣa and the Northern Heavenly King are extremely fierce and mighty.
East inside the gate,

with ghost heads and coiled snakes,

The eastern corridor has perilously strange trees and rocks.
The eminent monk is also strange.

The western corridor temple

Inside the gate of the Bodhisattva Hall, on the south wall,
Huángfǔ Zhěn painted ghosts and spirits and a carving.
Hawk

the wall.
Zhěn was contemporary with Wú Dàoxuán.
Wú, feeling his art threatened his own,
hired someone to kill him.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ".
From the sentence beginning with Wáng Zhāoyǐn, originally missing ninety-eight characters.

Zīshèng Temple
On the doors and windows of the main gate of Zīshèng Temple,
Wú Dàozǐ painted "Eminent Monks."
Wéi Shù composed the eulogy,
and Lǐ Yán wrote the calligraphy.
On the upper level of the two sides outside the middle triple gate,
it is unknown who painted the figures,
but they somewhat resemble Yán Lìběn.
In the northwest corner of the temple's western corridor,
Yáng Tǎn painted "Heavenly Maidens Near the Pagoda."
Their bright eyes seem about to blink.
The original text had "dance picture" for "blink,"
but it was changed according to *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
In the northern hall of the pagoda courtyard, there is an iron Guānyīn statue over three *zhàng* tall.
In the Guānyīn Hall, the two corridors feature "Forty-Two Sages,"
painted by Hán Gàn,
with a eulogy by Yuán Zǎi.
On the northern side of the eastern corridor, "Loose Horses,"
unexpectedly, when seen, they appear as if about to neigh and prance.
Among the holy monks, Lóngshù and Shāngnà are harmoniously and exquisitely rendered.
The bodhisattvas on the pagoda
were painted by Lǐ Zhēn.
The flowers and birds on all four sides
were painted by Biān Luán.
The lush sunflowers atop the bodhisattva on the medicine altar are especially fine.
Inside the pagoda, a thousand copies of the *Lotus Sutra* are stored.
Poets composed linked verses about these paintings,
in the Bóliáng style.
Wú's paintings show valor, spears and halberds clustered,
displaying wondrous transformations, myriad postures.
Vast and eerie, ghostly figures fill the layered walls,
seeing them suddenly makes one's hair stand on end.
Léngjiā imitated but strained his strength,
Lǐ Zhēn and Zhōu Fǎng, which is superior, hard to judge.
Living birds and running beasts, Biān Luán excels,
flowers fresh and colors tender, still not dry.
Hán Gàn's transformations like rushing rapids.
Alas, the wall paintings' momentum not exhausted,
later people's new paintings, how crude and sprawling.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*
In the eastern commandery
(Míng manuscript says "capital")
on Běimáng Mountain, there is Xuányuán Temple.
South of the temple is a Lǎojūn shrine.
Its platforms and halls are lofty and spacious,
overlooking the Yī and Luò rivers below.
The immortal clay statues
were all made during the Kāiyuán era by Yáng Huìzhī.
Ingenious, exquisite, and meticulously crafted,
beholders feel increased reverence.
On the walls are Wú Dàoxuán's paintings of the portraits of the Five Sages and scenes from *Lǎozǐ's Conversion of the Barbarians*,
the painting supremely marvelous,
unmatched in past or present.
Dù Gōngbù's poem says:
"Aligned with the pole, Xuándū's mystery secluded,
leaning on heights, forbidden gardens long.
Ancestral guardians strict in ritual observance,
sceptre-holders secure the extraordinary.
Green tiles beyond the early cold,
golden stem beside the single breath.
Mountains and rivers support embroidered doors,
sun and moon near carved beams.
Immortal Lǐ's roots coil great,
elegant orchid's leaves shine bright.
Noble lineage leaves old histories,
the Dàodé entrusted to the present king.
Painting masters look to predecessors,
Wú Shēng far excels in the field.
Dense arrays turn the earth's axis,
supreme marvels stir the palace walls.
Five Sages linked in dragon robes,
a thousand officials arrayed like wild geese.
Royal caps all elegant and striking,
banners and flags all flying high.
Green cypress deeply retains the scene,
red pear distantly gains frost.
Wind bells blow on jade pillars,
dew wells freeze silver beds.
Retiring, humble before the Zhōu house,
scriptures passed on, honoring the Hàn emperor.
If the valley spirit does not die,
where better to nurture simplicity?"
From *Jùtán Lù*
The Golden Bridge Painting
When Xuánzōng returned from sealing Tàishān,
the imperial procession stopped at Shàngdǎng.
The elders of Lù,
carrying burdens, pots and broth,
came from near and far to welcome and pay respects.
The emperor personally inquired after them.
He accepted their offerings,
and bestowed rewards accordingly.
Among the elders were those who had previously known the emperor,
to whom he granted wine and food,
and reminisced with them.
Thus, in every village passed,
he ordered inquiries about families with orphans, elderly, bereaved, or ill,
and increased condolences and aid.
The elders were joyful,
all gazing with admiration,
knocking and begging him to stay.
When the imperial carriage crossed the Golden Bridge,
(the bridge is in Lùzhōu)
the imperial road winding around,
the emperor saw for thousands of *lǐ*,
banners fresh and clean,
guards in orderly array.
He said to his attendants:
"Zhāng Yuè said I commanded three hundred thousand troops,
banners spanning a thousand *lǐ*,
from Shǎnxī to Shàngdǎng,
all the way to Tàiyuán.
I see the Hòutǔ stele.
Truly a man of talent."
The attendants all shouted "Long live!"
The emperor then summoned Wú Dàoxuán, Wéi Wútì, and Chén Hóng.
He ordered them to jointly create the "Golden Bridge Painting."
The imperial portrait and the emperor's steed, "Shining Night White,"
were overseen by Chén Hóng.
The bridge, landscape,
carriages and figures,
grass, trees, hawks, and birds,
vessels, staffs, and curtains,
were overseen by Wú Dàoxuán.
Dogs, horses, donkeys, mules,
cattle, sheep, camels,
cats, monkeys, pigs, badgers—
all four-legged creatures—
were overseen by Wéi Wútì.
When the painting was completed,
it was called the "Three Perfections."
From *Kāiyuán Chuánxìn Jì*
Cuī Yuán's Walls
When Ān Lùshān captured the two capitals,
Wáng Wéi, Zhèng Qián, and Zhāng Tōng all found themselves in the rebel court.
Upon recovery,
they were imprisoned in Yáng Guózhōng's former residence.
Chancellor Cuī Yuán then summoned them to his private residence,
ordering them to paint several walls with famous scenes.
At that time, all considered Cuī Yuán's merit and status second to none,
and hoped he would rescue them.
Thus they applied profound thought,
fully exerting their skill.
Consequently, they all received lenient sentences.
Even when demoted,
they were assigned to favorable places.
From *Mínghuáng Zálù*
Bǎoshòu Temple
Bǎoshòu Temple was originally Gāo Lìshì's residence.
In the ninth year of Tiānbǎo,
he donated it to become a temple.
When the bell was first cast,
Gāo Lìshì held a vegetarian feast to celebrate,
the entire court attended.
One strike [for donations] yielded hundreds of thousands.
Someone gauging his intent,
struck twenty times in succession.
The sutra repository's structure was perilously ingenious,
its two pagodas' fire pearls holding over ten *hú*.
Héyáng assistant official Lǐ Zhuó had a curious, antiquarian nature,
and was friendly with a monk.
Once they went together to this temple to view old objects in the storehouse.
Suddenly, from a broken jar, they found something like a covering,
its fabric torn, dirty and dusty,
touching it raised dust.
Lǐ Zhuó examined it slowly,
and realized it was a painting.
He exchanged it for three local maps and thirty bolts of fine silk.
He had his family mount and restore it;
it was over ten panels large.
He inquired of Attendant-in-ordinary Liǔ Gōngquán,
and only then learned it was "Stone Bridge Painting" by Zhāng Xuān.
Xuánzōng had bestowed it upon Gāo Lìshì,
hence it remained in the temple.
Later, art dealer Zōng Mù reported it to the Left Army.
Soon, a minor envoy led several dozen soldiers to the residence,
announcing an imperial edict to take it.
That same day it was presented.
The emperor, fond of antiquity,
saw it and was greatly pleased,
ordering it displayed in Yúnsháo Hall.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*
Xiāntiān Bodhisattva
There is a painting of the Primordial Bodhisattva,
which originated from Miàojī Temple in Chéngdū.
In the early years of the Kāiyuán era,
there was a nun named Wèi Bāshī who often recited the Great Compassion Mantra.
A commoner from Shuāngliú County named Liú Yì, also known as Yì’ér,
at the age of eleven,
wished to serve Nun Wèi.
The nun tried to send him away, but he refused to leave.
He once meditated in a secluded room.
He once told Wèi:
"The Primordial Bodhisattva has manifested in this place."
He then sifted ashes in the courtyard.
One night,
there appeared giant footprints several feet long,
with wheel-like patterns fully formed.
He then sought out painters,
asking them to apply colors as they wished,
but none satisfied him.
There was a monk named Yáng Fǎchéng who claimed he could paint.
Yì’ér would often clasp his hands and pray upward,
then instruct him,
over nearly ten years.
Only then did the painter apply the final touches.
The Primordial Bodhisattva had a total of 242 heads.
Each head resembled a pagoda,
with arms branching like vines.
There were fifteen scrolls of the painting design.
Liǔ Qīshī, a nephew of Cuī Níng,
took three scrolls
and brought them to the capital to circulate.
At that time, Wèi Fènggǔ served as Chief Clerk,
and he presented them.
Later, on the eighth day of the fourth month, they were bestowed upon Gāo Lìshì.
The version now in Chéngdū is a secondary copy.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
Wáng Zǎi
In the Táng dynasty, Wáng Zǎi lived in Western Shǔ.
During the Zhēnzhī era,
Wéi Gāo treated him with the courtesy due a guest.
He painted landscapes, trees, and rocks,
transcending mere form.
Thus, Dù Fǔ wrote a poem praising him:
"Ten days to paint a single pine,
five days to paint a single rock.
A master's work cannot be rushed;
only then will Wáng Zǎi consent to leave a true masterpiece."
I once saw a screen painting in Xí Kuí’s hall.
It depicted
"depicted" originally written as "líng,"
corrected based on the Ming manuscript copy.
two pines and one cypress by the river,
entwined with ancient vines.
Above, they coiled halfway to the sky;
below, they touched the water's surface.
Thousands of branches and leaves,
intertwined and winding,
were distributed without clutter.
Some withered, some lush,
some drooping, some upright.
Leaves layered a thousandfold,
branches spreading in all directions.
Such refinement is hard for ordinary people to achieve,
and common eyes cannot discern it.
I also saw a four-season screen painting at Xìngshàn Temple,
as if moving creation itself.
Winds, clouds, and scenery,
the eight solar terms and four seasons,
all within a single screen,
were exquisitely rendered.
His landscapes, pines, and rocks
are all of the highest grade.
From *Huà Duàn*.
Yáng Yán,
a chancellor during the Táng dynasty's Zhēnyuán era.
The Ming manuscript copy adds "exiled to Yázhōu" after "chancellor."
His spirit rivaled Wáng and Hán,
the Ming manuscript copy writes "wind and clouds" instead of "Wáng and Hán."
and his literary talent matched Yáng and Mǎ.
He painted pines, rocks, and landscapes,
surpassing ordinary people.
Initially known as a recluse scholar,
he visited Attendant Huángmén Lú,
who hosted him generously.
Knowing of Yáng's painting skill,
Lú wished to request a painting,
but dared not speak of it.
When Yáng insisted on leaving,
Lú earnestly urged him to stay.
Knowing Yáng’s family was in Luòyáng,
struggling with food and clothing,
Lú felt uneasy.
He secretly sent someone with hundreds of thousands of cash to Luòyáng to provide for them.
He brought back a letter from Yáng’s family
and showed it to Yáng.
Yáng was deeply moved.
Unsure how to repay him,
Lú then casually
mentioned wanting a painting,
to treasure for his descendants.
Yáng still found it difficult.
After over a month, he completed a screen painting.
Pines, rocks, clouds, and scenery
seemed to move creation itself,
unseen by the world before.
His work is of the highest grade.
From *Táng Huà Duàn*.
Gù Kuàng
In the Táng dynasty, Gù Kuàng, styled Būwēng.
In leisure from literary pursuits,
he also practiced small brushwork painting.
He once sought appointment as supervisor of Xīntíng.
Someone questioned him about it.
He replied:
"I want to depict the mountains in the sea."
He then appointed the painter Wáng Mò as his deputy.
From *Shàngshū Gùshí*.
Zhōu Fǎng
In the Táng dynasty, Zhōu Fǎng, styled Jǐngxuán,
was from Jīngzhào.
Descended from a military governor,
he loved learning,
and excelled in painting.
Moving among ministers and nobles,
he was a nobleman.
His elder brother, Zhōu Hào, excelled in archery and horsemanship,
and accompanied Gēshū in the campaign against Tǔbō.
After capturing Shíbǎo Fortress,
he was awarded the position of Commandant of the Capital Guards.
When Emperor Dézōng built Zhāngjìng Temple,
he summoned Hào and said:
"Your brother Fǎng is skilled in painting.
I wish to commission him to paint the deities for Zhāngjìng Temple.
Please convey this to him."
After several days,
the emperor requested again,
and only then did he begin.
Initially, the painting was screened off,
but people from the capital came to view it.
The temple faced the city gate,
so both wise and foolish visited.
Some praised its excellence,
others pointed out flaws,
and he revised it daily.
After over a month,
criticism ceased,
and all marveled at its perfection.
Only then did he finalize the painting.
It was considered the finest of its time.
Also, Marshal Guō’s son-in-law, Vice Minister Zhào Zòng, once had Hán Gàn paint his portrait,
which everyone praised.
Later, he asked Fǎng to paint another portrait.
Both were renowned for their skill.
The marshal once displayed both paintings side by side,
unable to decide which was superior.
When Zhào’s wife returned for a visit,
the marshal asked her:
"Who is this?"
She replied:
"My husband, Zhào."
"Which one looks most like him?"
She said:
"Both resemble him,
but the later one is better."
He asked further:
"Why do you say that?"
"The first painting only captures Zhào’s appearance,
while the later one also conveys his spirit, emotions, and the grace of his speech and laughter."
The marshal asked:
"Who painted the later one?"
She replied:
"Zhōu Fǎng."
That day, the superiority of the two paintings was settled,
and the marshal sent Fǎng several hundred bolts of silk.
In the capital today, there is a painting of the Bodhisattva of Compassion,
which people call "Water and Moon,"
a walking monk in front of the western Buddha hall at Dàyún Temple,
and two deities in front of the Buddha hall at Guǎngfú Temple,
all exceptionally exquisite.
Later, as Assistant Prefect of Xuānzhōu,
he painted the Northern Heavenly King at Chándìng Temple.
He often saw its image in dreams.
His paintings of women and children were unmatched in ancient or modern times.
He painted *Minister Hún’s Banquet*, *Liú Xuānwǔ Directing a Dance*, and *Consort Dúgū Directing Music* (draft).
Also *Confucius Inquiring About Rites*, *Descent of the Immortals*, *Five Planets*, and *Catching Butterflies*,
along with portraits of various immortals and the ten disciples of Confucius,
amounting to many scrolls.
At the end of the Zhēnyuán era,
someone from Xīnluó in the Jiāng-Huái region
purchased dozens of scrolls at high prices.
Before leaving,
he noted that the paintings of Buddhas, immortals, figures, women, and children
were all divine.
Only the horses, birds, beasts,
bamboo, rocks, plants, and trees
lacked exhaustive detail.
From *Huà Duàn*.
At Yúnhuā Temple, there was a Hall of Sacred Paintings.
In Cháng'ān, it was called the "Paintings of the Seven Sages."
Initially, after the hall's structure was completed,
the temple monks summoned painters.
They intended to commission them to apply colors and decorations.
However, the painters demanded a high price,
which did not meet the monks' expectations for payment.
Eventually, they left.
A few days later,
two young men came to the temple to pay a visit and said:
"We are skilled painters.
Now we have heard that this temple intends to commission painters.
We dare not seek profit for our work.
May we offer our labor instead?"
The temple monks wanted to first see their works.
The young men said:
"We are seven brothers in total,
and we have never painted in Cháng'ān before.
How could we have any existing works?"
The monks thought they were speaking nonsense.
They began to challenge them.
The young men said:
"Since we are not accepting payment from you,
if our work does not meet your expectations,
you can simply order the walls to be plastered over.
That would not be too late."
The monks, attracted by the fact that there was no cost,
agreed to their proposal.
The next day,
the seven men indeed arrived.
Each carried colored paints,
and they were about to enter the hall.
They said to the monks:
"From now on, for seven days,
be careful not to open our door,
and there is no need to provide us with food or drink.
This is because we fear the erosion of wind and sunlight.
You may seal our door with mud,
ensuring there is not the slightest gap.
Otherwise,
we will not be able to perform our miraculous work."
The monks followed their instructions.
Thus, for six days,
there was complete silence, with no sound heard.
The monks said to each other:
"These must be some kind of monsters,
and we cannot simply abide by the agreement."
So they jointly broke the seal.
Once the door was opened,
seven doves fluttered out,
flying into the sky.
Inside the hall, the colored paintings
were vividly arrayed in all four corners,
only the northwest wall remained unfinished in its decoration.
Later, when painters came and saw it,
they were greatly astonished and said:
"This is truly a divine and marvelous brushwork."
From then on, no one dared to continue the coloring.
From "Xuānshì Zhì"
Lián Guǎng
Lián Guǎng
was a man from Lǔ.
While gathering herbs,
he encountered wind and rain on Tàishān,
and took shelter under a large tree.
By midnight, the rain cleared.
He walked aimlessly.
Suddenly, he met a person
who resembled a recluse.
He asked Lián Guǎng:
"Why are you here so late at night?"
They then sat together under the trees.
After talking for a while,
he suddenly said to Lián Guǎng:
"I can paint,
and I can teach you the method."
Lián Guǎng assented.
The man then said:
"I will give you a brush,
but you must keep it hidden.
Then, paint as you wish,
and it will become spiritually potent."
He then took a five-colored brush from his bosom and gave it to him.
Lián Guǎng bowed in thanks,
and the man suddenly disappeared.
Afterward, the brush proved quite effective.
But he kept the matter secret,
not daring to paint lightly.
Later, when he went to Zhōngdū County,
the magistrate Lǐ, who was fond of painting,
learned of this matter
and summoned Lián Guǎng.
Over drinks, he casually inquired about it.
Lián Guǎng kept it secret and did not speak.
Lǐ persistently pressed him.
Lián Guǎng had no choice
and painted over a hundred ghost soldiers on the wall,
appearing as if they were going into battle.
The county captain Zhào learned of this
and also firmly requested it.
Lián Guǎng again painted over a hundred ghost soldiers
on the wall in Zhào's office,
appearing as if they were preparing for battle.
That night,
the ghost soldiers from both places went out to fight.
Lǐ and Zhào, seeing this strange occurrence,
did not dare to keep the paintings.
So they both destroyed the painted ghost soldiers.
Lián Guǎng, also frightened, fled to Xiàpī.
The magistrate of Xiàpī learned of this matter
and earnestly requested Lián Guǎng to paint.
Lián Guǎng then told him:
"I once met a deity at night,
who transmitted to me the art of painting,
but I often dare not wield the brush.
For it often causes supernatural disturbances.
I hope you will understand."
The magistrate did not listen.
He said to Lián Guǎng:
"If painting ghost soldiers makes them fight,
then painting other things surely will not cause battles."
He then ordered him to paint a dragon.
Lián Guǎng reluctantly painted it.
As soon as he finished the brushstroke,
clouds gathered and mist rose,
and a sudden gust of wind arrived.
The painted dragon suddenly rode the clouds upward.
This led to torrential rain,
which continued for days without stopping.
The magistrate feared the flooding would damage the town.
He also suspected Lián Guǎng of using demonic arts,
so he arrested Lián Guǎng and threw him into prison,
interrogating him thoroughly.
Lián Guǎng claimed he had no demonic arts.
As the rain still had not stopped,
the magistrate grew very angry.
Lián Guǎng wept and wailed in prison,
pleading with the mountain deity.
That night,
he dreamed of a divine being who said:
"You should paint a large bird,
shout at it, and ride it to fly away.
Then you will be spared."
At dawn, Lián Guǎng
secretly painted a large bird.
He tried shouting at it,
and indeed it spread its wings.
Lián Guǎng mounted it,
and it flew far away.
He went straight to Tàishān and descended.
Soon he saw the deity again.
The deity said to him:
"You revealed the secret to the human world,
so you inevitably faced calamity.
I originally gave you a small brush,
intending to bring you fortune,
but you instead brought misfortune upon yourself.
You should return it to me."
Lián Guǎng then took the brush from his bosom and returned it.
The deity soon disappeared.
From then on, Lián Guǎng could no longer paint.
The dragon painted in Xiàpī
eventually became a mud wall.
From "Dà Táng Qí Shì"
Fàn Shānrén
Lǐ Shūzhān once knew a Fàn Shānrén,
who stayed at his private residence.
Whenever he spoke of fortunes and misfortunes, he was always accurate.
He was also skilled in divination and incantations.
After half a year,
he suddenly said to Lǐ:
"I am about to leave,
and I have one skill
that I wish to offer as a farewell gift.
It is what is called water painting."
He then asked to dig a square pool in the back hall, one zhang in size,
and over a foot deep.
He plastered it with hemp ash.
Every day, he filled it with water.
When the water no longer diminished,
he prepared paints, ink, and inkstone.
First, he took up the brush, tapped his teeth for a long time,
then released the brush onto the water's surface.
Upon looking,
one could only see the water's color, murky and indistinct.
After two days,
he pressed four pieces of fine silk onto it.
After about the time of a meal,
he lifted them out to look.
Ancient pines, strange rocks,
figures, houses, and trees—
all were complete.
Lǐ was amazed and astonished,
and pressed him for an explanation.
He only said that he was skilled in controlling the colors,
preventing them from sinking and scattering.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Wéi Shūwén Wéi Shūwén, a Presented Scholar of the Táng dynasty, was skilled at painting horses.
During his leisure time,
he happened to paint two horses on silk but had not yet applied color.
While traveling to take the imperial examinations,
he passed in front of the Huàyuè Temple.
Suddenly, as if in a dream,
he saw someone from the temple approach him and say:
"The Golden Heavenly King summons you."
Shūwén unconsciously dismounted and entered,
ascending to the hall to see the King.
The King said:
"I know you have two excellent horses.
I now seek them from you.
Next spring, you will change your name and pass the examinations."
Shūwén replied:
"I only have the horse I ride."
The King said:
"You do have them.
Think carefully."
Shūwén silently thought of his two painted horses
and immediately responded:
"I have horses,
but their coats are not yet finished."
The King said:
"You may bestow them as a favor."
Shūwén said:
"Agreed."
After leaving the temple,
he hurriedly added color to the painting at an inn and offered it.
The following spring, he changed his name and passed the examinations.
From "Records of Hearing Marvels."
Guànxiū Guànxiū, a Buddhist monk of the Táng dynasty,
was originally from Lánxī in Wùzhōu.
He was skilled in poetry, calligraphy, and exquisite painting.
When the Wáng family established their state,
he came to reside at the Lónghuá Monastery in Shǔ.
Wielding his brush freely,
he painted sixteen arhats along with one Buddha and two great bodhisattvas in ink wash.
Massive rocks entwined with clouds,
withered pines draped with vines.
Their ancient appearances
differed from paintings by others.
Some said:
"He saw them in a dream,
and after waking, depicted
(The original text had '圓',
changed to '圖' based on the Ming manuscript copy)
them.
They were called 'Dream-Responsive Arhats'."
His disciples Tányù and Tánfú,
greatly treasured and kept them secret.
The ruler of Shǔ once summoned him to the palace.
Marveling at the wild and untrammeled quality of his brushwork,
he had them venerated for a full month
before ordering them returned to the monastery.
The Hanlin Academician Ōuyáng Jiǒng also viewed them.
He presented a song, which said:
"The high monk of the Western Peak is named Guànxiū,
His solitary spirit, steep and lofty, surpasses the clear autumn.
Heaven decreed ink-wash paintings of arhats,
Majestic ancient visages born from his brush tip.
At times discarding large silks to daub high walls,
Eyes closed, burning incense, sitting in the meditation chamber.
Perhaps in a dream he sees their true forms,
Casts off his kasaya, dips the divine brush.
Lifts high his wrist, flicks it through the air,
A rustling from the brush tip, given to wild abandon.
In a moment, two or three figures appear,
Unlike painters who vainly waste their days.
Strange rocks arranged, jagged and desolate.
True monks sit in rows, legs crossed in lotus posture.
Forms like lean cranes, spirits vigorous,
Crowns like crouching rhinoceroses, skulls coarse.
Leaning on pine roots,
beside rocky crevices,
Twisted waists and bodies seem about to move.
The scripture-reading disciple seems about to hear a sound,
The dozing mountain boy suspects he's in a dream.
Unaware how many summer retreats have passed,
One hand props the cheek, one shoulder bared.
Mouths open as if speaking with someone,
Bodies still, again seeming newly seated in meditation.
Before the dais, a reclining elephant's trunk hangs low,
On the bank, a playful ape stretches its arm askew.
Among banana blossoms, a light red is brushed,
Within moss patterns, a deep green is suffused.
Hard bamboo staffs,
low pine beds,
Snow-white eyebrows an inch long.
Opened sutra cords reveal two or three leaves,
Thread-mended patchwork robes, a thousand, ten thousand lines.
In the woods, scattered leaves fall in profusion,
A seal of remaining incense, the smoke and fire cut off.
Leather-pierced wooden clogs never dragged,
Bamboo-woven rush mats constantly sat upon.
Master Xiū, Master Xiū,
Your transcendent art none can surpass,
Your fame resounds loudly across the seas and shores.
Five- and seven-character verses, a thousand poems,
Large and small seal scripts, thirty masters' worth.
The Táng dynasty had many renowned scholars in succession,
Xiāo Zǐyún along with Wú Dàozǐ.
If comparing calligraphy and painting to you, Master Xiū,
I fear they merely lived and died in vain back then.
Master Xiū, Master Xiū,
First you came from Jiāngnán to enter Qín,
Now in Shǔ you have no close kin.
Your poetic fame and painter's hand are both wondrous and peerless,
Gazing at you, how can ordinary folk be considered human?
The Vimalakīrti in the Wǎguān Temple,
The Pratyekabuddha in the city of Śrāvastī.
If one compares and measures this painting,
It stands as the foremost in the human world."
From "Idle Talk of a Rustic."
Chǔ'ān The monk Chǔ'ān of the Shèngshòu Temple in Western Shǔ was a marvelous painter of landscapes,
and his details were extremely fine.
Even on a foot of plain silk,
mountains, rivers, trees, and forests,
cavern dwellings, peaks, and ridges,
temples, monasteries, misty vapors, and figures,
all were present.
Each time he painted a small round fan,
he would place the Gūsū Terrace or paint the Téngwáng Pavilion within it,
such that myriad mountains and rivers all lay before one's eyes.
However, it required about a season
to complete a single fan.
At that time, various princes and chief ministers vied to commission him.
Those who obtained his works presented him with substantial gifts,
while those who failed to get a painting were resentful.
Chǔ'ān said that this mountain monk merely used it to suit his own fancy.
After his passing into stillness,
there were connoisseurs
who often collected traces of his brush.
Some called them "ink treasures."
From "Idle Talk of a Rustic."
The Three Peerless Talents of Yìngtiān
In the year when Emperor Xīzōng of the Táng dynasty made his imperial journey westward,
a hermit from Kuàijī Mountain named Sūn Wèi followed the imperial carriage and stopped in Shǔ.
Wèi possessed skills in the Daoist arts,
and was also accomplished in calligraphy and painting,
both of which he executed with exquisite brushwork.
Once, on the left wall of the gate of Yìngtiān Temple, he painted a scene of the Heavenly King,
surrounded by a retinue of ghosts and deities.
The strangeness and wonder of it remained,
with brushstrokes wild and unrestrained,
unmatched by any.
For over thirty years, no one could rival it.
Jǐng Huàn, his predecessor, also specialized in calligraphy and painting.
He once formed a carefree friendship with Academician Ōuyáng Jiǒng of the Hànlín Academy.
One day, they rode together to visit this temple,
and by chance painted a Heavenly King on the right wall to match it.
Bó Hǎi, who was beside them
(the two characters "beside them" were originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition),
observed its unrestrained vigor,
and further composed a gēxíng poem to commemorate it.
Later, the cursive-script monk Mèng Guī arrived.
He was also invited to inscribe it on the corridor wall.
Thus, the painting, calligraphy, and gēxíng poem
were completed in a single day.
The entire city came to see it,
filling the temple to capacity,
the people of Chéngdū.
Hence, it was called the "Three Marvels of Yìngtiān."
The gēxíng poem is now also recorded and attached as follows:
"In the golden land northeast of Brocade City,
who, in times past, raised this temple?
The white-browed elder, renowned among gentlemen,
once knew the hermit of Kuàijī Mountain.
On the left wall of the temple gate, the Heavenly King is depicted,
with majestic retinue—from whence do they come?
Ghosts and strange beings scurry across the wall,
beneath the eaves, autumn light rustles and gleams.
I hear the Heavenly King governs the four realms,
his crystal palace roofed with glazed tiles.
Colorful banners at times sweep past, adorned with gems,
golden whips frequently urge on qílín steeds.
How glorious is the great image of Vaiśravaṇa,
holding aloft a giant pagoda, soaring through the clouds.
Earth deities emerge in pairs, bearing precious vases,
heavenly maidens wear golden-threaded robes turned inside out.
In the Táng dynasty, famous gentlemen's paintings are spoken of,
Zhōu Fǎng, with his brush tip, excelled at depiction.
Zhāng Sēngyáo was a man of divine skill,
Wú Dàozǐ is hailed as unmatched.
How wondrous, the marvelous hand passed down to Lord Sūn,
able to leave divine traces in this place.
Leaning askew, a small ghost glares with furious eyes,
straight-backed, a Yuè wolf stands tall, chest high.
The jeweled crown trembles
(shǎngshēng)
imposing dignity arises,
attendants hasten left and right, bowing in reverence.
Arms outstretched like eagle claws, sharp and slender,
waist wrapped
(qùshēng)
in tiger skin, mottled red.
Floating, as if about to ascend into the clouds,
striding, still seeming to return to the eastern sea.
Python dragged along, its whole body drooping,
spirits grasped, their eyes hollowed out.
At that time, such artistry was truly rare,
enshrined in this precious temple, hailed as immortal.
The east side painted, the west side left empty,
left for later generations to challenge.
Those who see it later are all struck with awe,
all defer to the famous master, daring not contend.
Who would have thought, not yet thirty years passed,
perhaps an extraordinary man came to intervene.
The Kuāng Mountain hermit, named Pǔ,
his skull lofty and strange, connecting the Five Peaks.
Once held an ivory tablet, served as an official repeatedly,
also often held a snake pearl in his grasp.
In past years, elders encountered wondrous traces,
today, the temple master recognizes Jǐng Gōng.
Inspired, he requested to plaster the high wall,
wildly seizing
(qùshēng)
the brush tip like a swift wind.
How chaotic and unrestrained the retinue appears,
scattered strange forms all surge forth.
Weapons crisscross, filling the empty space,
two sides suddenly as if locked in combat.
The sage king, with angry visage, surveys east and west,
with a sweep of his sword blade, all fall into order.
On his wrist, a lion bites golden armor,
beneath his feet, a yakṣa holds up laced boots.
Horse heads robust, with many sinews and joints,
beaks curved like rings, as if forged iron bent.
All over their bodies, snakes and serpents wildly crisscross,
around their necks, skulls dry and cracked.
Thick brows, glaring eyes, hair like awls,
so bizarre, it leaves one bewildered.
Bare-headed giant soldiers seem about to birth ghosts,
half-faced young girls cradle small children.
Moreover, it is said this temple was first established,
its geomantic veins deep and aligned with righteous energy.
How could it invite two mountain hermits,
whose brushstrokes both achieve timeless deeds?
Have you not seen,
in the Tiānbǎo era of Emperor Míng,
painting dragons to summon rain was no accident.
Embracing all phenomena within the heart,
manifesting a hundred transformations before the eyes.
Later, among ranked paintings of worthy sages,
only these two can stand shoulder to shoulder.
In the mortal world, all things can be sought,
but where can such a model be passed on?
I once feared clouds and mist would rise from the wall's base,
lifting the temple gate up to the heavens."
From "Yěrén Xiánhuà"
The Eight Immortals Painting
The Dàoist priest Zhāng Sùqīng of Western Shǔ
was a man of divine immortality.
Once, at Zhàngrén Temple on Qīngchéng Mountain,
he painted the true forms of the Five Peaks and Four Rivers, along with several walls of the Twelve Stream Maidens.
His brushwork was vigorous and robust,
the essence vivid and lifelike.
Those who saw it felt their hearts tremble and spirits stir,
their feet unable to advance.
Truly a rare and exceptional work in painting.
The ruler of Shǔ repeatedly dispatched Assistant Director of the Palace Library Huáng Quán to obtain a model.
But upon descending the mountain,
it ultimately bore no resemblance.
On his birthday,
someone obtained eight portraits of the true forms of the Eight Immortals painted by Sùqīng,
and presented them to Mèng Chǎng.
Observing the forms of the ancients,
seeing the exquisite brushwork of the ancients,
he delighted in appreciating them for a long time.
And said:
"If not a man of divine immortality,
one could not capture the essence of the immortals."
He bestowed generous gifts.
One day,
he ordered the pseudo-Hànlín Academician Ōuyáng Jiǒng to compose praises for them in sequence,
and also dispatched Vice Director of the Waterways Bureau Huáng Jūbǎo to inscribe them in bāfēn script.
Whenever he viewed the paintings,
he sighed at the freedom and unrestraint of the brushwork;
reading the praises,
he admired the lofty antiquity of the literary style;
looking at the calligraphy,
he cherished the grandeur of the strokes.
Thus, it was deemed the "Eight Immortals,"
not inferior to the "Three Marvels."
The Eight Immortals are:
Lǐ Jǐ, Róng Chéng, Dǒng Zhòngshū, Zhāng Dàolíng, Yán Jūnpíng, Lǐ Bābǎi, Chángshòu, and Gě Yǒngguī.
From "Yěrén Xiánhuà"
Huáng Quán
In the past, there was a painting of Zhōng Kuí by Wú Dàozǐ,
depicting him wearing a blue robe,
with one foot booted,
one eye blind,
a tablet at his waist,
and his hair wrapped in a turban, with disheveled locks hanging down his temples.
In his left hand, he was seizing a ghost,
while using the second finger of his right hand to gouge out the ghost's eye.
The brushstrokes were vigorous and powerful,
truly embodying the divine skill of the Táng dynasty.
The person who acquired it intended to present it to the ruler of the false Shǔ state,
who cherished it greatly.
It was often hung in the inner chamber.
One day,
he summoned Huáng Quán and had him look at it.
Upon seeing it,
Quán praised it as absolutely marvelous.
After expressing his gratitude,
Chǎng said to him:
"If this Zhōng Kuí were to gouge out the ghost's eye with his thumb,
it would appear even more forceful.
Try to alter it for me."
Quán requested to return to his private residence.
For several days, he studied it intently.
He prepared another piece of silk,
and painted a Zhōng Kuí,
using the thumb to gouge out the ghost's eye.
Together with Wú's original, he presented both at once.
Chǎng asked:
"I instructed you to alter it,
why did you paint a separate one?"
Quán replied:
"In Wú Dàozǐ's painting of Zhōng Kuí,
the strength of his entire body,
his expression and the look in his eyes,
all reside in the second finger,
not in the thumb.
Therefore, I dared not make any rash changes.
As for the painting I have now created,
though it may not match the ancients,
the strength of the entire body,
the intent and spirit are all concentrated in the thumb."
Chǎng was greatly pleased,
and praised Quán's ability.
He then rewarded him with colored silks and silver vessels,
to commend his exceptional insight.
From "Yěrén Xiánhuà"
Miscellaneous Compilation
At the Jìng'ài Temple, there is also a "Sick Dragon with Pheasant Tail,"
but no one knows who painted it.
The painting is exquisitely clever,
all traces of divine skill.
The pheasant tail is in the Guānyīn Hall of the east corridor,
among the retinue of the Heavenly Kings.
A crimson-clad deity holds a wild pheasant in his arms,
and upon close inspection,
it appears as if about to take flight.
(Originally, "Heavenly King" was written as "Great King,"
and "holds" was written as "body."
Changed according to the Jù Tán Lù.)
(Originally, the source was missing;
the Ming manuscript says it comes from the Shàngshū Tán Lù,
but it is now known to come from the Jù Tán Lù.)
Lǐ Sìzhēn of our dynasty commented on paintings, saying:
"Gù's paintings are relegated to second place."
However, Hǔtóu (Gù Kǎizhī) also admired Wèi Xié's painting "North Wind."
This painting was once in the home of Hán Lìbù (Hán Yù).
Zhāng Hóngjìng's residence in Píngkāng Ward
was originally the old mansion of Cuī Sīyè (Cuī Róng).
The place where Sīyè inscribed the wall still remains.
(From Shàngshū Gùshí)
Monk Dào Fēn,
from Kuàijī.
Zhèng Dīng from Xíngyáng.
Recluse Liáng Qià.
Recluse Xiàng Róng.
Recluse Wú Tián from Qīngzhōu,
also named Fén,
courtesy name Jiànkāng.
All of the above painted landscapes.
Dào Fēn's style is lofty.
Zhèng Dīng's is elegant and subtle.
Liáng Qià's is beautiful and refined.
Xiàng Róng's is rugged and austere.
Wú Tián's is perilous and clever.
He had a painting record titled "Shānshuǐ Lù,"
recording over a hundred of his paintings on silk and plain cloth.
It was passed on to enthusiasts.
He himself said:
"Initially, I dreamed of a deity instructing me in painting techniques."
Tián liked to paint rugged rocks,
with a profound and perilous atmosphere,
capable of conveying the mood of clouds and rain.
There was also Wáng Mò,
a disciple of Xiàng Róng,
who was eccentric and fond of drink.
Although his pines and rocks were lofty and extraordinary,
they were favored by the common people.
After getting drunk, he would use his hair bun to press against the silk or cloth.
Wáng Mò learned brush techniques from Táizhōu's Zhèng Qián in his early years.
At the end of the Zhēnyuán era,
he passed away in Rùnzhōu.
When his coffin was lifted, it felt empty,
and many people at the time said he had transformed and departed.
Many strange events occurred in his life.
When Gù Zhùzuò (Gù Kuàng) was the supervisor of Xīntíng,
Mò requested to be the patrol officer of the sea.
When asked his intention,
he said:
"I want to see the mountains and waters of the sea."
He held the position for half a year before resigning.
After that, his brushwork gained a wondrous charm.
He was a disciple of Xiàng.
My elder cousin, Investigating Censor Hòu,
told me all about this.
However, I do not particularly find Mò's paintings wondrous.
(From Mínghuà Jì)
There was another painter
who visited a temple with others.
Looking at a set of wall paintings depicting music
(originally written as "scroll,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript),
he said:
"This is the Xth movement of 'Liángzhōu.'"
Others did not believe him,
so they summoned musicians to play "Liángzhōu."
When they reached the painted scene,
his pointing matched without discrepancy.
(From Lúshì Záshuō)
Former Dézhōu Governor Wáng Yǐ's family had a brush about an inch long,
thicker than commonly used brushes,
with each end extending about half an inch.
In the middle was carved a set of "Cóngjūn Xíng."
(Originally written as "scroll,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript.)
Human figures, horses, hair, houses, trees, pavilions, terraces, and distant waters—
all were exquisitely rendered.
Each scene was carved with two lines from "Cóngjūn Xíng,"
such as "Before the courtyard, the qí trees are already climbable,
Beyond the frontier, the soldiers have yet to return."
It seemed beyond human skill.
The carved lines were like powdered traces,
visible only when held up to the light.
It is said
to have been carved with a mouse's tooth.
Thus, Cuī Lángzhōng (Cuī Yán)'s text
includes the "Wángshì Bǐguǎn Jì."
It resembles Hán Wéngōng's "Huà Jì."
Yǐ,
son of Xuánzhì and grandson of Shào,
was refined, broad-minded, and knowledgeable about antiquity,
skilled in playing the qín and ruǎn.
My old residence was on South Street of Guīdé Ward in East Luòyáng.
The beams of the main hall were made of apricot wood.
On the west wall were seven scattered horses painted by Wéi Mín Lángzhōng,
and on the east wall were several lines of Zhāng Xù's cursive script.
Xù was known in his time as "Zhāng the Madman."
The orchard east of the residence
was, according to the Liǎngjīng Xīnjì, the old mansion of Mǎ Zhōu.
(From Lúshì Záshuō)
When Xíngyáng's Deputy Magistrate Zàn served as magistrate of Wànnián,
there was a man in cangue who was called a thief.
He claimed to have once deceived a woman
(originally written as "stole,"
changed according to the Táng Quēshǐ)
to buy a horse painting.
Zàn reprimanded him
and ordered the painting brought for inspection.
It was old silk, darkened with smoke,
three or four panels joined together.
The mounting was of fine barbarian felt,
with a spotted sea turtle skin roller.
Zàn said:
"This is a painting."
It was treasured by Grand Commandant Lǐ Gōng,
bearing the seal script of the Zànhuáng collection.
Someone offered seventy thousand to purchase it for a salt-making official,
who obtained a deputy position overseeing the canal's crossbeam.
He then brought out a courtesan from his chambers.
The painting fell into common hands again.
It was said that the thief took advantage of the woman's lack of discernment
to buy it at a low price.
When the courtesan returned from elsewhere and filed a complaint,
she requested that the deficit in price be recorded as his crime.
Zàn could not decide the case.
At that time, in Yánshòu Ward, there was a recluse Lǐ who specialized in ink painting,
known for his discerning judgment of paintings among nobles and officials.
He was summoned to examine it.
Staring wide-eyed, he sighed three times and said:
"This is a superior work by Hán Gàn or Zhǎn Zǐqián."
The truth of the yellow sand (the cangue) was already clear,
but the judgment of the red brush (the verdict) remained doubtful.
Then, someone arrived from the imperial army with a register to claim it.
Zàn, considering it different from ordinary theft,
and not wishing to detain it harshly,
sent the painting along with the man.
After that, all trace of it was lost.
(From Táng Quēshǐ)
For works before the Jìn dynasty, unseen by the eye,
it is difficult to comment fairly.
From the Jìn dynasty onward,
where traces survive,
they can be discussed.
Gù Chángkāng (Gù Kǎizhī), Zhāng Sēngyóu, and Lù Tànwēi
emerged as extraordinary talents,
forming the three patriarchs.
Although there were later artists,
none could surpass them.
In the past, Emperor Wǔ of Liáng, being erudite and fond of antiquity,
collected paintings.
He ordered court officials skilled in painting
to examine the names
and determine their ranks,
storing them in the imperial repository
for appreciation.
During the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng,
Emperor Yuán moved the capital.
The imperial collection of paintings
was all transported to Jīngzhōu.
When the Zhōu army came to attack,
the emperor burned them all.
Through the Zhōu, Suí, and into our dynasty,
efforts were made to repurchase and recruit,
and gradually they reappeared.
Not long after,
the imperial repository was filled again.
At the beginning of the Cháng'ān era,
Zhāng Yìzhī petitioned to summon famous artisans from across the land
to restore the paintings.
Secretly, using old silk of the same color,
he had each artisan employ their strengths
to jointly recreate a work.
The original mounting and rollers
were kept unchanged,
making it impossible to distinguish.
Thus, he secretly swapped them.
After Zhāng's execution,
the paintings were collected by Junior Guardian Xuē Jì.
After Xuē's downfall,
they all went to Prince Qí.
Initially, this was not reported to the emperor.
Fearing discovery,
they were burned again.
Thus, the wondrous traces of painting
were utterly lost without a trace.
(From Tánbīn Lù)
Zhèng Xuán
Zhèng Xuán of the Hàn dynasty studied under Mǎ Róng.
For three years, they did not meet,
with only the senior disciples imparting instruction.
When Mǎ Róng often calculated celestial phenomena but could not make the results align,
he asked his disciples about it,
but none could solve it.
Someone mentioned Xuán.
Róng summoned him and ordered him to calculate,
and with a single turn, he resolved it.
Everyone was astonished and impressed.
When Xuán completed his studies and bid farewell to return home,
Róng harbored jealousy in his heart.
Xuán also suspected there might be pursuers,
so he sat beneath a bridge,
resting on clogs above the water.
Róng indeed performed a divination to pursue him.
He told his attendants:
"Xuán is on earth below and water above, resting on wood—
this surely means he is dead."
Thus, he ceased the pursuit.
Xuán ultimately escaped harm.
Another account says:
"Zhèng Kāngchéng studied under Mǎ Róng,
but for three years, he showed no notable achievements.
Róng looked down on him and sent him away.
Xuán passed under the shade of a tree and dozed off.
He saw an old man
who cut open his abdomen with a knife
and said to him:
'Now you are ready to learn.'
Thereupon, he awoke and immediately returned.
Subsequently, he mastered the classics thoroughly.
Róng sighed and said:
'The Shī, Shū, Lǐ, and Yuè
have all gone east.'
He secretly intended to kill Xuán,
but Xuán, aware of this, secretly left.
Róng used divination to calculate Xuán's whereabouts,
and Xuán was predicted to be on earth and wood.
Róng personally rode a horse to ambush him.
Xuán entered beneath a bridge
and crouched against a pillar.
Róng hesitated beside the bridge, saying:
'Between earth and wood—
this would be correct,
but with water, it is not.'
He then returned from there.
Thus, Xuán escaped harm.
From Yì Yuàn.
Also, Zhèng Kāngchéng was born on the Wùyín day of the seventh month in the second year of the Yǒngjiàn era.
By the age of eight or nine, Xuán could perform multiplication and division calculations.
At eleven or twelve, he followed his mother back to her family home.
During the Là festival banquet,
about ten people of similar age were all dressed in fine clothes and adorned splendidly,
engaging in lively conversation.
Xuán alone remained indifferent,
appearing as if he did not measure up.
His mother privately urged and scolded him.
He then said:
'This is not what I aspire to.'
From Xuán Lièzhuàn.
Zhēn Xuántù
Huángfǔ Sōng of Āndìng in the Hàn dynasty, Zhēn Xuántù,
Cáo Yuánlǐ,
were all skilled in arithmetic,
and were contemporaries during Emperor Chéng's reign.
Zhēn once calculated his own lifespan to be seventy-three years,
and predicted he would die at the Bū hour on the twenty-fifth day of the first month in the first year of the Suīhé era.
He wrote this on the wall of his house to record it.
He died at the Bū hour on the twenty-fourth day.
His wife said:
'When I saw him calculating, he often
(Míng manuscript note: often is written as long)
added one tally.
I wanted to tell him,
but feared it might be inappropriate,
so I did not inform him.
Now, indeed, it was one day earlier.'
Zhēn also said:
'Four zhàng west of the solitary catalpa tree on the green mound at Běimáng,
dig down seven chǐ.
I wish to be buried there.'
When Zhēn died,
they went to dig as instructed
and found an ancient empty outer coffin,
so they buried him there.
