From Xījīng Zá Jì.
Cáo Yuánlǐ
Cáo Yuánlǐ once visited his friend Chén Guǎnghàn, who was a friend of Zhēn Xuántù.
Guǎnghàn said:
'I have two granaries of rice,
but I have forgotten their exact measures.
Please calculate them for me.'
Yuánlǐ used chopsticks to count over ten times and said:
'The eastern granary contains seven hundred forty-nine dàn, two dǒu, and seven gě;
the western granary contains six hundred ninety-seven dàn and eight dǒu.'
He then wrote these numbers largely on the granary doors.
Later, when the rice was taken out,
the western granary had six hundred ninety-seven dàn, seven dǒu, and nine shēng.
There was a rat inside,
large enough to hold one shēng.
The eastern granary was not off by even a guǐ or gě.
Yuánlǐ met Guǎnghàn again the following year,
and Guǎnghàn told him the rice quantities.
Yuánlǐ struck the bed with his hand and said:
'I did not know the rat had eaten the rice—
I might as well peel off my face!'
Guǎnghàn then fetched wine for him
and several slices of dried deer meat.
Yuánlǐ calculated again and said:
'Twenty-five plots of sugarcane
should yield one thousand five hundred thirty-six stalks.
Thirty-seven mǔ of taro
should yield six hundred seventy-three dàn.
One thousand cows will produce two hundred calves.
Ten thousand chickens will hatch fifty thousand chicks.'
Sheep, pigs, geese, and ducks—
he stated all their numbers.
Fruits, nuts, and delicacies—
he knew exactly where they were.
He then said:
'With such vast resources,
why is the hospitality so meager?'
Guǎnghàn said sheepishly:
'There are hasty guests,
but no hasty hosts.'
Yuánlǐ said:
'There is a steamed pig's head on the chopping board,
and a plate of lychees in the kitchen—
both can be served.'
Guǎnghàn bowed twice in apology,
went inside to fetch them,
and they enjoyed themselves all day.
His methods were later passed down to Nán Jì.
Nán Jì passed them to Xiàng Tāo.
Xiàng Tāo passed them to his son Lù.
They all grasped the calculations,
but lost the profound essence.
From Xījīng Zá Jì.
Zhào Dá
In the second year of the Tàipíng era of Wú,
there was a great famine in Chángshā.
Countless people were killed.
Sūn Quán ordered Zhào Dá to divine the cause, and he said:
'Heaven, earth, rivers, and marshes are interconnected,
like the four limbs of a person.
When the nose bleeds, applying moxibustion to the foot can cure it.
Now, at the mouth of the Yúgān River,
a sandbar often
(The character "often" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Míng manuscript)
suddenly rises.
It is shaped like a turtle,
consuming the vital energy of that commandery.
You can make offerings and then dig it up.'
Quán then sent people to offer a Tàiláo sacrifice
and cut its back.
As the old saying goes,
the famine then ceased.
That water is in Yúgān County of Ráozhōu.
From Qià Wén Jì.
Zhēnguǎn Mì Jì
During the Táng dynasty's Zhēnguǎn era, a secret record stated:
'After three generations of the Táng dynasty,
a female ruler with the surname Wǔ will replace and possess the empire.'
Emperor Tàizōng secretly summoned Lǐ Chúnfēng to inquire about it.
Chúnfēng reported:
'Based on celestial signs,
I have already calculated and determined.
That person has already been born within Your Majesty's palace.
From now, in less than forty years,
she will possess the empire
and nearly exterminate your descendants.'
Tàizōng said:
'What if we kill all suspected individuals?'
Chúnfēng replied:
'Heaven's mandate
cannot be averted by any means.
A destined ruler will not die,
and killing would only harm the innocent.
Moreover, according to the divination, she has already grown up
and is among Your Majesty's palace household.
In another forty years, she will be old,
and old age brings benevolence.
I fear she will not kill many of Your Majesty's descendants.
If you kill her now, it will create enmity,
and she will be reborn young and vigorous,
certain to be more ruthless and cruel,
causing even greater harm.'
Thus, they stopped.
From Gǎn Dìng Lù.
Yī Xíng
The monk Yī Xíng,
whose secular surname was Zhāng and given name Suì,
was the great-grandson of Duke Tán, Gōng Jǐn.
He left home to become a monk at a young age,
and was esteemed by his contemporaries
for his intelligence, diligence, and virtuous conduct.
Emperor Xuánzōng ordered him to revise the calendar in the Guāngdà Hall.
Later, he was moved to the Lìzhèng Hall,
where he collaborated with scholars to review and correct it.
Yī Xíng then compiled the *Kāiyuán Dàyǎn Calendar* in one volume,
*Calendar Discussions* in ten volumes,
*Completion of the Calendar* in twelve volumes,
*Calendar Books* in twenty-four volumes,
and *Long Calendar of the Seven Luminaries* in three volumes.
In total, five works comprising fifty volumes.
He passed away before they could be presented to the throne.
Zhāng Yuè presented them on his behalf,
and an imperial decree ordered their implementation.
Initially,
Yī Xíng constructed a movable ecliptic armillary sphere and presented it.
The emperor personally composed
composed originally presented,
changed according to *New Tales of the Great Táng*
the *Inscription for the Armillary Sphere* and entrusted it to the Directorate of Astrology,
to be placed on the Spirit Terrace,
for use in celestial observations.
He dispatched Grand Astrologer Dà Xiàng Yuántài and others
by post-horse to Ānnán, Lǎng, Yǎn, and other prefectures,
to measure the sun's shadow.
They measured at noon on the equinoxes and solstices,
taking the shadow lengths,
which took several years to finalize.
In Ānnán, the polar altitude was 21 degrees and 6 fen;
the winter solstice shadow length was 7 chi, 9 cun, and 3 fen;
the spring and autumn equinox shadow length was 2 chi, 9 cun, and 3 fen;
at summer solstice, the sun was 3 cun and 1 fen south of the gnomon.
In Wèi Prefecture's Héngyě Army, the polar altitude was 40 degrees;
the winter solstice shadow length was 1 zhang, 5 chi, and 8 fen;
the spring and autumn equinox shadow length was 6 chi, 6 cun, and 2 fen;
at summer solstice, the shadow was 2 chi, 2 cun, and 9 fen north of the gnomon.
These two locations represented the northern and southern extremes of the central lands.
In Lǎng, Yǎn, Tàiyuán, and other prefectures,
the measurements varied and differed.
Using the gougu method, it was calculated:
"The approximate distance between the north and south poles
is only a little over 80,000 li."
Calendar compiler Chén Xuánjǐng was also skilled in calculation.
He sighed and said:
"The ancients said,
'Viewing the sky through a tube,
measuring the sea with a ladle.'
They believed it impossible to achieve.
Now, using methods of zhang and chi to measure the vastness of heaven and earth,
how could it be possible?
If we rely on this to speak,
then how can heaven and earth be considered vast?"
Later, when reviewing Yī Xíng's *Calendar Classic*,
it was found to be precise and thorough,
and it remains in use to this day.
From *New Tales of the Great Táng*
Xíng Hé Pú
Xíng Hé Pú was fond of the teachings of Huáng-Lǎo
and excelled in mental calculation.
He authored the *Yǐngyáng Book Commentary*.
There were tales of him knocking and strangely entering emptiness,
or that he had herbs,
though none had ever seen them.
Duàn Chéngshì heard from the mountain hermit Zhèng Fǎng:
"A certain Sīmǎ Cuī was residing in Jīngzhōu,
and was an old acquaintance of Xíng's.
Cuī had been ill for years and was near death,
often thinking of Xíng in his heart.
One day, Cuī heard digging sounds
from the north wall of his bedroom.
He ordered his attendants to look,
but they saw nothing.
He lay in the empty room to the north,
where his family resided.
This continued for seven days,
the digging unceasing.
Suddenly, the wall became transparent,
bright as a grain of millet.
He asked his attendants,
but again they saw nothing.
After a day,
the hole was as large as a plate.
Cuī peered through it.
Outside the wall was the wilderness.
Several people carrying spades and hoes
stood beside the hole.
Cuī asked them:
They all said,
"The Perfected Person Xíng ordered this opened.
Sīmǎ's misfortune is heavy,
requiring double the effort."
After a while,
five or six outriders appeared.
All wore flat caps and red robes.
They announced:
"The Perfected Person has arrived."
They saw Xíng in a carriage,
wearing a white headcloth with hanging ribbons,
holding a five-brightness fan,
with dozens of guards.
He stopped a few paces from the hole.
He said to Cuī:
"Your allotted lifespan is exhausted,
but I have pleaded on your behalf repeatedly,
gaining an extension of twelve years.
From now on, you will have no troubles."
After speaking,
the wall closed as before.
In ten days, Cuī recovered from his illness.
Xíng had also once lived on Zhōngnán Mountain.
Many Daoist enthusiasts built huts to be near him.
Cuī Shǔ, while young, also followed him there.
Chopping firewood and drawing water,
all were renowned scholars.
Xíng once said to his disciples:
"In three to five days, an unusual guest will arrive.
Each of you should prepare one dish for me."
Several days later,
with all kinds of land and sea delicacies prepared,
they set up a feast in a pavilion.
Xíng warned them not to peek recklessly.
Everyone closed their doors,
not daring to make a sound.
Xíng went down the mountain to invite a guest.
The guest was five chi tall,
three chi broad,
with his head occupying half his height.
He wore loose crimson robes
and held an ivory tablet horizontally.
His eyelashes were sparse and long,
his complexion like a peeled melon.
He stroked his beard and laughed heartily,
the corners of his mouth reaching his ears.
He engaged in lively conversation with Xíng,
mostly about matters not of this world.
Cuī Shǔ grew impatient
and ran across the courtyard.
The guest stared intently,
then turned to Xíng and said:
"Is this not the Tàishān Teacher?"
Xíng replied, "Yes."
The guest said again:
"One more turn and he would have been lost
lost originally first,
changed according to the Ming manuscript
by a thousand li—
a pity."
At dusk, the guest departed.
Xíng told Cuī Shǔ:
"That guest was a jester of the Heavenly Emperor.
He mentioned the Tàishān Teacher—
do you remember at all?"
Cuī shed tears and said:
"I am indeed the later incarnation of the Tàishān Teacher,
but I no longer remember."
He had often heard his elders speak of it.
Grand Marshal Fáng Guǎn once asked Xíng to calculate his lifelong affairs.
Xíng said that if he traveled from the southeast to the northwest,
his official salary and life would end.
The place where his soul would descend
would be neither an inn nor a temple,
neither a road nor an office.
The illness would arise from fish soup,
and the coffin would be made of Qiūcí wood.
Later, Fáng was transferred from Yuán Prefecture to Hàn Prefecture.
After leaving his post and returning,
he reached Láng Prefecture
and lodged at the Zǐjí Palace.
Coincidentally, carpenters were working on wood there.
Fáng was puzzled by the wood's grain pattern.
He asked about it,
and a Daoist priest said:
"Several months ago,
a merchant donated several sections of Qiūcí wood boards.
Now we are making them into a túsū hut."
Fáng then remembered Xíng's words.
After a while,
the prefect invited Fáng to a feast featuring finely sliced fish.
Fáng sighed and said:
"Master Xíng is indeed a divine man."
He explained everything to the prefect
and entrusted the Qiūcí wood boards to him.
That evening,
Fáng fell ill from the sliced fish and died.
From *Miscellaneous Morsels from Yóuyáng*
Mǎn Shī
In the Fǎshòu Temple of Tàipíng Ward in the Western Capital, there was a monk named Mǎn who excelled in the Nine Palaces divination.
Minister of Justice Wáng Xuán once consulted him.
The monk said:
"You will change your official position in a certain month,
likely to a post in the Secretariat-Chancellery,
very close to the jade steps."
Xuán thought to himself that the position of Vice Director of the Chancellery was beyond his reach,
and that the posts of Supervising Secretary and Reminder were already past.
Later, he was indeed appointed as General of the Imperial Guards,
often attending near the jade steps.
Monk Mǎn also said:
"The entire family of Wáng Hóng will turn into white bones."
All his predictions came true.
Mǎ Chùqiān
Mǎ Chùqiān of Fúfēng suffered from blindness,
so his father had him study the Book of Changes,
to make a living.
He once practiced divination in Ānlù to support himself.
A man came to consult him,
and said to Mǎ:
"Your divination has not yet reached its peak.
I have a secret method;
will you learn it from me?"
Mǎ then followed him.
Within the commandery, there was a Táo Xiān Temple,
where he received the secrets of astral calculations,
totaling seventeen lines.
He then asked for the man's name and hometown.
The man replied:
"My surname is Hú, and my given name is Tián."
He cautioned him:
"You will have an official career,
but it will end at the age of fifty-two.
Please do not reveal my whereabouts to the gates of nobles and princes."
After Mǎ obtained the secret method,
his predictions became highly accurate.
When Zhào Kuāngmíng abandoned Jīngzhōu and entered Shǔ,
Mǎ followed him to Chéngdū.
Former Sovereign Wáng once ordered Dù Guāngtíng
to secretly inquire about his lifespan.
Mǎ replied:
"The Sovereign has received the energy of primordial yang,
amounting to four catties and eight taels."
Indeed, he passed away at seventy-two.
Four catties and eight taels
equals seventy-two taels.
Mǎ rose to the position of Palace Attendant with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon,
and also died at fifty-two.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Yuán Hóngyù
Yuán Hóngyù of the Later Táng served as an assistant in Yúnzhōng,
excelling especially in calculations.
A colleague in the office asked him to count the leaves on a paulownia tree in the courtyard.
He immediately measured the tree himself,
seven feet above the ground,
and took its circumference.
Using the circumference and diameter, he performed calculations.
After a long while, he said:
"So many leaves."
No one could verify it.
They then had twenty-two leaves shaken off,
and asked him to calculate again.
He said:
"It is now twenty-one leaves fewer than before."
Upon close inspection,
two leaves were slightly smaller,
counting as only one leaf.
Military Commissioner Zhāng Jìngdá had two jade bowls.
Hóngyù measured their width and depth,
and calculated:
"These bowls will break at the sì hour on the sixteenth day of the fifth month next year."
Jìngdá, upon hearing this, said:
"If I store them carefully,
can they still break?"
He then ordered them placed in a large basket,
padded with cotton wadding,
and locked in the treasury.
When the time came,
a beam in the treasury collapsed,
landing directly on the basket,
and both bowls shattered.
Vice Minister of the Imperial Stud Xuē Wénměi, who served in the same office, witnessed this personally.
From "Jī Shén Lù"
Guǎn Lù
Guǎn Lù was profoundly knowledgeable in divination arts.
Once, a woman lost her ox
and came to him for a divination.
He said:
"Look in the grave mound to the east;
the ox is hanging upward there."
Soon, it was indeed found.
The woman, however, suspected Guǎn Lù,
and reported him to the authorities for investigation.
Only then did they realize it was deduced through divination.
Another time, a man in Luòyáng lost his wife.
Guǎn Lù told him to fight with a pig carrier at the Dōngyáng Gate.
The pig ran into a house,
breaking through the wall.
His wife emerged from inside.
In Guǎn Lù's hometown, Fàn Xuánlóng suffered from frequent fires.
Guǎn Lù said:
"A scholar wearing a square scarf and riding a black ox
will come from the east
[Note: Original text had "gù chē" for "from the east," corrected to "cóng dōng" based on the Ming manuscript.]
and arrive.
You must insist he stay overnight."
Later, such a scholar indeed came,
and Xuánlóng persuaded him to stay.
The scholar urgently wanted to leave,
but Xuánlóng did not listen,
so he stayed.
The host retired to his room.
Fearing a plot against him,
the scholar took a knife and stood outside the door,
leaning against firewood and pretending to sleep.
Suddenly, a creature appeared,
blowing at the fire with its mouth.
Startled, the scholar struck and killed it.
Upon looking, it was a fox.
From then on, there were no more disasters.
Another time, a man caught a deer,
but it was
stolen by someone.
He went to Guǎn Lù for a divination, who said:
"At the third house in the east alley,
wait until no one is around,
remove the seventh rafter from the roof,
and place a tile under the rafter.
By mealtime tomorrow,
it will be returned to you."
That night, the thief's father suffered a headache,
and also came for a divination.
Guǎn Lù told him to return the deer.
The illness then healed.
Another case involved an official who lost something.
Guǎn Lù told him to wait until it was quiet,
at the temple gate,
and point to the sky, draw on the ground,
and gesture toward the four directions.
That evening, the item was indeed found in its original place.
From "Yì Yuàn"
Another account: Tàishǒu Liú Bīn of Píngyuán placed a pheasant feather in a container
and asked Guǎn Lù to divine it.
Guǎn Lù said:
"High mountains, towering and steep,
a bird with vermilion body.
Feathers dark and yellow,
its crow never misses the dawn.
This is a pheasant feather."
From "Yì Yuàn"
Chúnyú Zhì
Bào Yuàn's family suffered many deaths and illnesses,
so Chúnyú Zhì performed a divination for them.
After the hexagram was formed, he said:
"Go several dozen steps into the market gate,
where a man holds a thorn horsewhip.
Buy it from him,
and hang it on the mulberry tree to the northeast.
There will be no more illness,
and within three years, wealth will come."
They followed his advice.
Later, while digging a well, they found coins
and bronze vessels worth two hundred thousand.
From "Dú Yì Zhì"
Liǔ Línzǔ
There was a diviner named Liǔ Línzǔ who excelled in divination.
His wife once suffered from a rodent ulcer,
which did not heal for years.
Gradually, her condition worsened
[Note: Original text had "yīn" for "worsened," corrected to "kùn" based on the Ming manuscript.]
and she was near death.
Línzǔ then performed a divination,
obtaining the hexagram "Yí" changing to "Fù".
Interpreting the hexagram, he said:
"You should find someone with the surname Shí to treat it,
and you will recover after catching and moxibusting a rat."
Later, in the village, there was a lowly family
indeed surnamed Shí.
They claimed they could cure this illness.
They then applied moxibustion to three points on the patient's head.
She felt better.
Soon, a rat appeared,
yellow and sleek,
coming straight forward.
It crouched motionless, making faint sounds.
They called a dog to bite it to death.
Upon inspecting the rat's head,
there were three moxibustion marks.
The patient recovered on her own.
From "Dòng Lín"
Wěi Zhāo
Jìn Wěi Zhāo was skilled in the Yìjīng.
On his deathbed, he told his wife and son:
"Even if there is a great famine in the future,
do not sell the house.
Five years from now,
an imperial envoy named Gōng will owe me gold.
Show him the wooden board I have written."
Later, it happened as he said.
His wife took the board to see him.
The envoy was bewildered,
pondering but not understanding.
He took yarrow stalks and performed a divination.
When the hexagram was formed, he said:
"How marvelous, Wěi Zhāo!
I do not owe you gold.
Your worthy husband hid the gold himself,
waiting for peaceful times.
Knowing I am skilled in the Yìjīng,
he wrote on the board to convey his meaning.
There are five hundred catties of gold,
contained in a green-glazed vessel,
buried in the main hall.
One zhàng from the wall,
nine chǐ underground."
His wife dug it up,
and indeed found the gold.
From Guó Shǐ Bǔ Yí,
the Ming manuscript copy says from Xì Méng.
Guō Pú
Gù Qiú, the Biéjià of Yángzhōu, had a younger sister who fell ill at the age of ten,
and remained so until over fifty.
He asked Guō Pú to divine for her.
He obtained the hexagrams "Dà Guò" changing to "Shēng."
The interpretation said:
"The meaning of the Dà Guò hexagram is not auspicious,
withered poplars by the grave mound lack splendor.
Stirring the wandering soul, a dragon chariot appears,
the body bears heavy burdens, afflicted by celestial evil.
The cause lies in felling a tree
(the original text had 'sacrifice' for 'tree,'
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy)
and killing a spiritual snake,
not her own fault but the ancestors' flaw."
Considering the hexagram, what could be done?
Qiú then investigated the family's past.
An ancestor had once cut down a large tree,
found a large snake and killed it.
The girl then fell ill.
After she fell ill, thousands of birds circled over the house,
which everyone found strange,
not knowing the reason.
A county farmer passing by the house,
looked up
and saw a dragon pulling a chariot,
dazzling with five colors.
It was extremely large and extraordinary.
After a while, it vanished.
From Sōu Shén Jì.
Cài Tiě
During the Sòng dynasty, while Nánjùn Prince Yì Xuān was stationed in his commandery,
there was a clerk in his administration named Cài Tiě who was skilled in divination.
The Prince once saw a white mouse running along a roof beam in his inner study,
and ordered his attendants to shoot it down.
He placed it in a box,
and ordered Tiě to divine what was inside the box.
After the hexagram was formed, Tiě laughed and said:
"I've got it."
The Prince said:
"Describe it."
"A white mouse with its back to the bright window,
a curved bow shot it,
severing its left thigh.
The mouse is pregnant with five offspring,
three males and two females.
If you don't believe it,
cut open its belly and you'll know immediately."
The Prince then cut it open.
It was exactly as Tiě had said.
He rewarded him with ten thousand coins.
From Zhǔ Gōng Jiù Shì.
The Sound-Discerner from Wúzhōng
In the late years of the Later Wèi,
a scholar from Wú arrived in the northern regions.
He was blind but excelled at discerning voices.
Chancellor and heir to the Bóhǎi princedom, Chéng, had him tested.
Hearing Liú Táozhī's voice, he said:
"He will be a nobleman of his time, but kings, marquises, generals, and ministers will die by his hand.
However, he is like a hawk or hound,
merely used by others."
Hearing Zhào Dàodé's voice, he said:
"He is also a nobleman."
Hearing the voice of Tàiyuán Duke Yáng, he said:
"He will become a ruler."
Hearing Chéng's own voice,
he remained silent.
Cuī Xiān secretly pinched him,
so he falsely said:
"He is also a king."
The Prince said:
"Even the slaves in my household
are destined for extreme nobility,
let alone myself."
Later, when various princes and ministers of the Qí dynasty were ordered to die,
many were strangled by Táozhī.
And Chéng ultimately met his end due to Lán Jīng.
Yáng received the abdication,
becoming Emperor Wén Xuān.
From Sān Guó Diǎn Lüè.
Wáng Zǐzhēn
During the Zhēn Guān era of the Táng dynasty,
in Gǔchéng County, Dìngzhōu, there was a man named Wèi Quán whose family was wealthy.
His mother suddenly lost her eyesight.
He consulted the diviner Wáng Zǐzhēn.
Zǐzhēn divined for her and said:
"Next year, someone wearing blue clothes will come from the east.
On the first day of the third month, he will come to treat her,
and she will surely recover."
When the time came,
they watched and saw a man wearing a blue silk jacket,
so they invited him in and prepared a lavish meal.
The man said:
"I don't understand medicine,
I only know how to make plowshares.
I'll make one for the master."
Taking an axe, he walked around the house looking for a plow beam,
and saw a crooked mulberry branch overhanging the well.
He then cut it down.
His mother's eyes suddenly became clear and she could see.
This was caused by the crooked branch's leaves covering the well.
From Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi.
Zhāng Jǐngcáng
Zhōu Lángzhōng Péi Guī's concubine, Madame Zhào,
was a great beauty.
She once went to Zhāng Jǐngcáng to have her fate divined.
Cáng said:
"Madam, your eyes are long and gaze slowly.
According to physiognomy texts,
a 'pig's gaze' indicates licentiousness.
If a woman's eyes show white in four directions,
five husbands will guard the household.
Madame will ultimately be ruined due to adultery,
you should be careful."
Zhào laughed and left.
Later, she indeed committed adultery,
and was confiscated into the palace servants.
From Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi.
The Diviner from Còu Prefecture
Dù Jǐngquán,
a native of Xìndū,
originally named Yuánfāng,
changed his name to Jǐngquán during the Chuí Gōng era.
He was upright, stern, and just,
passed the imperial examinations as a Jìnshì.
Later, he became Luán Tái Shìláng and Píng Zhāng Shì.
At that time, Nèishǐ Lǐ Zhāodé, due to his uprightness, was imprisoned.
Jǐngquán declared in court that he was fair, pure, upright, and honest.
Zétiān was angered,
considering it deception to her face.
He was demoted to
(the Ming manuscript copy has 'Zhēn' instead of 'Còu',
same below)
Prefect of Còu Prefecture.
When he first went to Còu Prefecture,
he met a skilled diviner on the road,
who said he would return to become Chancellor again,
attaining the third rank but not wearing the purple robe.
That summer, when his term ended,
he died wearing a purple gown.
From Yù Shǐ Tái Jì.
Cài Wēiyuǎn
Zhāng Huàilǐ, the Magistrate of Ān County in Yíng Prefecture,
and Jìn Xíngzhōng, the Magistrate of Gōnggāo in Cāng Prefecture,
went to Cài Wēiyuǎn for divination.
After performing the divination ritual,
he said to Lǐ:
"You will be very close to the emperor,
reaching the position of a Regional Governor."
To Zhōng he said:
"You will obtain a capital post,
but your official salary will end this year.
It would be best to retire."
Both men were candidates for official selection.
(The Ming manuscript copy has 'selection' instead of 'recommendation')
Huàilǐ was appointed Zuǒ Bǔ Quē,
and later became Prefect of Hé and Fù Prefectures.
Xíngzhōng was appointed Chéng Mén Láng,
and died that autumn.
From Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi.
Chē Sān
Chē Sān was a
Huàyīn native,
skilled in divination and physiognomy.
Jìnshì Lǐ Méng passed the special examination in ornate prose,
and went to the capital to receive his official appointment.
Arriving at Huàyīn,
the county magistrate ordered Chē Sān to see him.
He deceived him, saying he was Lǐ Yì.
Chē said:
"I do not see you receiving an official salary at all."
The gentlemen said:
"It must be because you did not state your real name,
so it was not accurate.
This is Lǐ Méng,
who passed the special examination in ornate prose,
and is about to go receive his official appointment.
What office can you see him obtaining?"
Chē said:
"What office does the gentleman wish to hold?"
Méng said:
"I would love Huàyīn County."
Chē said:
"This office exists,
but I see that you, sir, do not have the fortune for it.
What
can be
done?"
None of them believed it.
When they reached the capital,
he was indeed appointed as the County Lieutenant of Huàyīn.
They celebrated with a banquet on a boat at Qǔjiāng.
The gentlemen asked Méng to compose a preface.
By evening, the preface was finished.
Shǐ Huì stood up first,
and took the preface from Méng's hand to read.
Péi Shìnán and over ten others
also scrambled to stand up and read the preface.
The boat tilted,
and then capsized.
Lǐ Méng, Shìnán, and others
all drowned and died.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù".
Lǎo Lǐ
During the Kāiyuán era,
there was a man surnamed Liú, whose given name is unknown.
He sought an official post through hereditary privilege,
but for several years had no success.
Suddenly, one year after the selection examinations concluded,
he heard that at the West Market there was an old man named Lǐ skilled in divination,
so he went to visit and ask him.
The old man said:
"This year, an official post will not materialize for you."
The young man said:
"Someone secretly informed me,
expecting that I would certainly succeed.
Why is it not so?"
The old man said:
"This year it certainly will not happen.
Next year, you will obtain it without even seeking it."
The young man did not believe it.
Indeed, he was implicated by his guarantor,
and his application was rejected.
The young man then believed in the old man's supernatural ability.
When the examinations concluded the following year,
he judged his own written answers and judgments to be rather poor,
and thought he would not succeed.
He asked old man Lǐ again.
Old man Lǐ said:
"Do not worry.
You will certainly obtain an official post.
Your salary will be in Dàliáng.
Once you get it,
come see me again."
He was indeed appointed as the County Lieutenant of Kāifēng.
He visited the old man again.
The old man said:
"In your official post,
you need not be pure and frugal.
Feel free to seek and take.
When your term is near completion,
request to be sent into the city as an envoy.
I will make another divination for you then."
The young man arrived at the prefecture,
and was indeed entrusted by the prefect.
Remembering old man Lǐ's words,
he took large amounts of wealth and bribes.
When his term was complete,
he had amassed tens of millions.
He then petitioned the prefectural general,
requesting to serve as a transport commissioner.
The prefectural general dispatched him to escort his prefecture's taxes to the capital.
He saw old man Lǐ again.
Old man Lǐ said:
"You are about to be promoted."
The young man said:
"I am now awaiting selection after my term is complete.
What time is it now?
How could there be another official post?"
The old man said:
"Within three days you will obtain an official post.
The post should also be obtained in that commandery.
We will meet again."
The young man was skeptical,
and left.
The next day,
while delivering the prefectural taxes to the Left Treasury,
it happened that a phoenix was seen at that place.
An imperial decree stated:
"The first to see it shall be granted a change of office."
The young man had been the first to see it,
so he was promoted and appointed as Assistant Magistrate of Jùnyí County.
The young man respected old man Lǐ even more.
He asked again about the method of being an official.
He said:
"Exactly as before."
When his term was complete that year,
he again obtained tens of millions.
He returned to his hometown and lived for several years,
then was again called up for assignment,
and visited old man Lǐ once more.
Old man Lǐ said:
"Now you should obtain a district magistracy.
You must not act recklessly.
You must definitely be careful."
The young man was indeed appointed as Magistrate of Shòuchūn.
Before his term of office was over,
he was dismissed for corruption.
He came again to ask old man Lǐ.
The old man said:
"Now I shall tell you.
There is no need for shame or concealment.
Your ancestor was once a great merchant,
with assets of twenty million,
who died in Biànzhōu.
His wealth was scattered among people.
Therefore, you have recovered it here.
It was not taken unjustly.
Thus, you incurred no blame.
The people of this district
do not owe you wealth.
How can you demand excessively?"
The young man was greatly convinced.
From "Yuán Huà Jì".
Two Dàoshi During the Kāiyuán Era
In the second year of Kāiyuán,
Liángzhōu dàoshi Liáng Xūzhōu used the Nine Palaces method to calculate for Zhāng Zhuó, saying:
"The Five Ghosts press upon your year,
Tiāngāng approaches your fate,
this is a great calamity in your life."
He divined using the Zhōuyì.
He obtained "Guān" changing to "Huàn",
indicating alarm and fear.
Later, wind moving over water,
means the matter will disperse.
Also, Ānguó Temple dàoshi Lǐ Ruòxū, without giving his name,
secretly had a divination performed for him.
It said:
"This person this year is in the Celestial Prison,
bearing the crime of capital punishment,
yet can be spared.
Otherwise,
he will die of illness,
with no means of rescue."
Indeed, he was accused of a crime by Censor Lǐ Quánjiāo,
and an imperial decree ordered his execution.
But Ministers of Justice Lǐ Rìzhī, Vice Directors of the Department of State Affairs Zhāng Tíngguī and Cuī Xuánshēng, and Vice Minister Chéng Xíngmó all pleaded for him,
so he was spared death.
He was exiled to Lǐngnán.
The words of the two dàoshi
were indeed verified.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi".
Jiǎng Zhí
In the twelfth year of Tiānbǎo,
Yǒngjiā native Jiǎng Zhí said:
"Within the commandery city there are white curtains.
Prefect Lǐ Jiāng will suddenly go into mourning."
Lǐ wished to return north of the river.
Jiǎng also said:
"When you reach Jìnyún Commandery, you will be interrogated.
There will be one person in crimson, one in green, and one in blue-green who will come to investigate and press charges against you,
but in the end nothing will happen."
Later, indeed, Investigating Commissioner Zhāng Yuàn, wearing crimson,
Dàlǐ Sīzhí Dù Qiáo, wearing green,
and Judge Officer Zhāng Lín, wearing blue-green,
came to investigate.
He encountered an amnesty and it stopped.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù".
Shěn Qī
There was a man named Shěn Qī,
from Yuèzhōu,
who was skilled at divination.
Attendant Lǐ Dān said to him:
"I have heard news
that Vice-Director Lǐ is to take charge of government affairs,
and I am to receive the post of Supervising Secretary.
What do you think?"
Shěn Qī said:
"Vice-Director Lǐ will soon be summoned,
and will not get to eat the sacrificial meat on the She Festival day.
After this, he will have no official salary.
You, sir, will also not be transferred,
and will not receive the post of Supervising Secretary."
At that time, it was only fourteen days until the She Festival.
Sure enough, an imperial edict arrived summoning Vice-Director Lǐ.
He set off on the journey two days before the She Festival,
and died in Biàn.
Lǐ also did not receive the post of Supervising Secretary.
From "Dìngmìng Lù" (Records of Fixed Fate).
Also, in the fourteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
Wáng Zhū was to take the imperial examinations
and wanted to go to the capital.
He sought divination from Shěn Qī in Yuèzhōu.
He obtained the pure Qián hexagram,
with the fourth line from the bottom changing,
transforming into the Guān hexagram.
Shěn said:
"You are now taking the examinations,
and have obtained this hexagram.
'Contemplating the glory of the state'
and 'It is beneficial to be a guest of the king'
are originally auspicious signs.
However, the lines are changing;
all the yin lines are responding to the yang.
The lower trigram becomes Qián,
and the upper trigram changes up to the fourth line,
but does not reach the fifth.
The fifth is the ruler's position;
you have not yet obtained the benefit of seeing the great man.
I fear that on this journey,
you will not reach the capital but will turn back."
Indeed, he reached the Eastern Capital.
But then Ān Lùshān rebelled.
He fled and returned to Jiāngdōng.
From "Dìngmìng Lù".
The Diviner of Yǐngyīn
Chén Shù was the governor of Yǐngyīn.
When Ān Lùshān rebelled,
he dispatched a county captain surnamed Sūn to the Eastern Capital.
Sūn was unwilling to go.
Chén, angry, had him flogged
(the original text had 'urged',
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy)
When Sūn reached the Eastern Capital,
he met Lùshān,
who asked him to go to Yǐngyīn to fetch Chén Shù's head.
Lùshān appointed Sūn as governor of Yǐngyīn,
bestowed upon him crimson robes,
and had him lead over twenty men to capture Shù.
Shù heard they were about to arrive.
As dusk approached,
he left the city and fled.
The Registrar seized his horse's bridle and ordered him to return.
Shù was worried and distressed.
He took diarrhea medicine, feigning illness.
He ordered a diviner to perform a divination for him.
The diviner said:
"From now, in five days,
there will be a family matter,
but they will not capture you, sir.
However, you have the salary of five hundred carts,
so you certainly will not die.
By the mealtime on the seventh day,
you, sir, will be unharmed.
But you must leave this place;
you will not be able to stay."
After five days, Sūn arrived.
Chén then secretly gave treasury goods to various yamen personnel.
After nightfall,
he forged an imperial edict,
summoning him to the capital.
He ordered that two postal stations to the west,
men be sent to meet him.
At midnight, the edict arrived.
The next morning,
he assembled the officials to announce the edict.
He then ordered them to personally execute
(Ming manuscript copy has 'use force',
same below)
Sūn in the guesthouse,
and personally executed over twenty men.
He killed the Registrar.
Captain Sūn had previously sent men to fetch his wife and daughter, etc.,
who arrived together at midnight.
The next day at dawn,
he killed them all.
He ordered the superior to stay and manage the prefectural affairs,
then set off for the capital.
He rewarded the diviner with five bolts of official silk.
From "Dìngmìng Lù".
Wáng Qīyán
Wáng Qīyán, from Xiāngchuān, resided at Lùbái Lake in Jiānglíng.
He was skilled in studying the Yì,
and thoroughly understood the arts of pitch-pipes, seasons, yin and yang.
Around his dwelling, he personally planted peach and apricot trees, forming several tens of rows,
enclosing his house on four sides.
People of the time compared him to Dǒng Fèng.
Qīyán laughed and said:
"I only value their blossoms and kernels
for dispelling wind and guiding qi.
Why should I follow the traces of ancient men's trivial matters?"
Every clear morning, he would lay out the yarrow stalks
to decide matters for people.
Once he had taken enough fees to sustain himself for the day,
he would close his studio and tend his garden.
During the Dàlì era,
an old man once came with a hundred coins seeking a divination.
After the hexagram was formed,
he cross-checked the year.
Qīyán said in alarm:
"How far is your home?
Go quickly, old man.
Otherwise,
you will collapse on the road."
The old man left.
Qīyán looked at the hundred coins,
and they were paper.
Realizing the time verified by the divination
was his own jiazi year,
he sighed and said:
"Although I studied the Yì from a young age,
I did not expect to be able to penetrate the scrutiny of ghosts.
What regret is there in death?"
He then bathed and put on new clothes,
bade farewell to his wife and children.
A short while later, he died.
From "Zhǔgōng Jiùshì" (Old Stories from the Riverside Palace).
Lù Shēng
Zhào Zìqín, when once awaiting appointment,
sought divination from Lù Shēng in Cháng'ān County.
Lù said:
"Your official appointment,
if not on a 'double day',
will be on a 'double mouth'."
Later, on the sixth day of the sixth month, he divined again.
Lù said:
"Your official appointment,
if not issued on the ninth day,
will be issued on the twelfth day."
On the ninth day,
the Prime Minister indeed requested the personnel records from the Ministry of Personnel.
On the twelfth day, the edict was issued,
appointing him as Left Reminder.
The characters for "Reminder"
each contain one "mouth".
Also, Supplemental Omissioner Wáng Huǎng,
in the seventh month, sought divination from Lù Shēng.
Lù said:
"In the ninth month, you will enter a ministry,
and the official title will have the character 'Lǐ'."
At that time, Vice-Director Táo Hàn of the Ministry of Rites was present,
and said:
"You, sir, will be my replacement."
In the ninth month,
Táo fell ill and requested leave.
An imperial edict appointed Wáng as Vice-Director of the Ministry of Rites.
Later, he again asked for a divination.
Lù said:
"You will certainly be appointed to an official post with the character 'cāng'."
Indeed, he was demoted to Granary Supervisor of Wēnzhōu.
Afterwards, Lù Shēng entrusted his two sons to Huǎng.
Huǎng asked again:
"After all, what will happen?"
Lù said:
"The reason I have entrusted my sons to you, sir,
its meaning can be understood."
Zōu Shēng
During the reign of Emperor Wǔzōng,
the chancellor Lǐ Huí was originally named Lǐ Chán.
He had attempted the imperial examinations multiple times without success.
Once, while traveling to Luòqiáo,
he encountered two diviners.
One practiced divination by stalks,
the other by tortoise shells.
He first consulted the stalk diviner, saying:
"I wish to change my name before taking the examinations.
What do you think?"
The stalk diviner replied:
"Changing your name is very good.
If you do not change it,
you will never succeed."
He then consulted the tortoise-shell diviner, Master Zōu.
Master Zōu said:
"For this journey of yours, sir,
be careful not to change your name.
Your name will spread far and wide.
However, after you achieve success,
you will inevitably change your name after twenty years.
This has already been reflected in the celestial signs.
In time, you will understand my words."
As Lǐ was about to depart,
Master Zōu further cautioned him:
"You, young master, are certain to achieve glorious fame
and will later hold important responsibilities.
When dealing with those who come after you,
do not create rifts with common scholars.
If you do, it will surely lead to deep trouble in the future."
In the second year of the Chángqìng era,
Lǐ passed the imperial examinations.
When Emperor Wǔzōng ascended the throne,
because his name was the same as the emperor's,
he finally changed it to Huí.
Counting from the xīnchǒu year to the gēngshēn year,
exactly twenty years had passed.
He then said:
"Divination by stalks is short-sighted; divination by tortoise shells is far-sighted.
Master Zōu's words have come true."
After Lǐ Gōng became a vice-minister,
Wèi Mó served as a supervising secretary.
During an official gathering,
Wèi said to Huí:
"In the past, when I sought recommendation for the prefectural examination,
you, Vice-Minister, were the examiner.
You recommended one hundred and two candidates,
yet I alone did not receive a single recommendation.
Today, I am still unworthily wearing the golden seal,
standing among all you gentlemen."
Everyone present was shocked by these words,
expecting Lǐ to yield and apologize.
But Huí replied:
"If you were to take off your purple robe now
and call yourself Scholar Wèi again,
and I were the examiner,
I still would not recommend you, just as before.
Why do you bring up old matters to challenge me?"
Huí later gained sole authority,
and the three highest ministries stood in awe of him.
He was promoted to the position of chancellor.
But three to five years later,
Wèi Gōng also became chancellor, entering from Tóngzhōu,
while Huí was repeatedly demoted and exiled.
Wandering through rivers and lakes,
he sighed deeply and said:
"The warning from the master at Luòqiáo—
I brought this trouble upon myself.
Yet it was also the pull of fate."
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì"
by Wǔmíng Dàoshì
During the Chángqìng era,
in Yèzhōng, there was a Daoist priest named Wǔmíng, whose origins were unknown.
He excelled in the arts of yīn-yáng and calendrical calculations,
and was particularly skilled in divination.
Tián Hóngzhèng, the military governor of Chéngdé, governed his subordinates with some leniency,
but he was greedy for wealth and bribes,
incessantly demanding and extorting.
The people harbored deep resentment and lamented.
At that time, Wáng Tíngcòu was a subordinate general,
and he sent an envoy to Yèzhōng.
Upon arrival,
the envoy suddenly fell slightly ill.
After several days,
seeking medical treatment failed to cure him.
He therefore went to see Wǔmíng,
to inquire about his lifelong fortunes and misfortunes.
The Daoist priest immediately performed a divination for him.
When the hexagram was formed, three coins danced together,
taking a long time to settle.
And all six positions were heavy.
The Daoist priest said:
"This hexagram is pure Qián,
transforming into Kūn.
Kūn represents earth,
the land.
You, sir, will soon hold the command banner,
and will also have a share of the land, mountains, and rivers.
Matters are about to come together,
you should return quickly."
When Tíngcòu heard these words,
he immediately covered his ears.
That night,
he dreamed of a white-bearded old man with a majestic and extraordinary appearance,
attended by more than ten followers,
each holding a small jade axe.
They summoned Lord Wáng forward,
(the character 'forward' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
and said to him:
"Calamity is about to befall,
you cannot stay long."
After waking,
Tíngcòu felt suspicious and fearful,
and immediately took leave of the military governor of Wèi and returned.
By the time he reached home,
not even ten days had passed,
when a great mutiny broke out among the soldiers and people.
Hóngzhèng was killed by the rebellious troops.
The officials, scholars, generals, and officers
together recommended Tíngcòu.
Tíngcòu repeatedly declined and yielded,
but the crowd would not listen,
and they coerced and forced him to take the position.
The next day,
urgent memorials were sent to the court.
The imperial court was greatly alarmed upon hearing this,
and mobilized troops to attack and suppress.
They appointed Péi Dù as commander-in-chief.
The people of Zhào resisted the imperial orders for two years.
The imperial army could not subdue them.
Soon after, Emperor Jìngzōng passed away,
and Emperor Wén succeeded to the throne.
An edict stated:
"Considering the people,
who have long suffered devastation,
although the chief culprit is guilty,
what fault have the innocent commoners?
All should be pardoned and forgiven.
Additionally, grant them military command."
It was also decreed that Tíngcòu's son, Yuándí, enter the court to serve.
Consequently, he was married to Princess Shòuchūn.
After Tíngcòu was established,
he gained a good reputation for governance,
and was praised by the imperial court.
He died after thirteen years in power.
He was posthumously awarded the title of Grand Preceptor.
His son Yuándí succeeded him,
and his official rank reached Grand Commandant.
He died after twenty-six years.
The eldest son, Shàoyì, succeeded but after two years,
due to his debauchery, tyranny, and disorder,
the assembly decided to depose and kill him.
They installed his younger brother Shàodǐng.
Shàodǐng died after six years in power.
His son Jǐngchóng succeeded and ruled for thirteen years,
his official rank reaching Secretariat Director.
He was enfeoffed as Prince of Chángshān and died,
his son Róng succeeded,
who was the Prince of Zhào.
Later, he acted recklessly, tyrannically, and unrighteously,
and was killed by his subordinates.
He had been in power for forty-one years.
From Tíngcòu to Róng,
there were altogether five generations and six rulers,
lasting over a hundred years before their line ended.
Initially, when Tíngcòu was established,
he sent someone to Yèzhōng,
to fetch Wǔmíng and place him in his residence.
He built a lodging for him,
named "The Courtyard of Master Wǔmíng."
The lord once leisurely asked him:
"I have now undeservedly become a feudal lord,
regarding future emolument and longevity,
please divine further for me."
The Daoist said:
"Thirty years.
I hope Your Excellency will exhaust your loyalty in serving the king,
love the people and show compassion for all things.
Next, preserve your spirit and cherish your energy,
always keeping purity and frugality in mind.
You will certainly enjoy extraordinary longevity.
Your descendants will include two kings,
all resulting from the accumulated blessings you leave behind.
As the *Spring and Autumn Annals* says: 'For five generations they will flourish,
and after eight generations,
none can compare with them.'"
The lord said:
"I have already been fortunate in many matters,
and originally had no merit or virtue,
such words are beyond my hopes."
He then offered several hundred gold pieces as a gift for longevity.
The Daoist firmly declined to accept.
The lord also firmly insisted on giving them,
and had them carried to his chamber.
After a few days, he distributed them all,
keeping nothing for himself.
The two kings:
Jǐngchóng was enfeoffed as Prince of Chángshān.
Róng became Prince of Zhào.
From *The Record of Things Seen and Heard*
Huáng Hè
During the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Huáng Hè,
who claimed to be from Gǒngluò.
To avoid the turmoil of war, he traveled
across the Yellow River and wandered to Zhào,
eventually settling in Chángshān,
where he made divination his profession.
His predictions of fortune and misfortune always proved accurate.
At that time, Prince Zhào Wáng Róng was still young,
and the Yān army was invading the northern borders.
The prince was selecting generals to resist them.
Two brave warriors, Chén Lì and Liú Gàn, submitted their names at the military headquarters,
volunteering to lead five hundred men to test the enemy’s strength,
vowing to capture the enemy leader and present him bound.
The prince, impressed by their courage, granted their request.
The next day,
the two men led their troops out
and attacked the Yān encampment at night.
News of a great victory soon spread.
The Yān soldiers, terrified, fled in retreat.
Chén Lì died in the midst of battle,
while Liú Gàn returned triumphantly.
The prince was pleased
and rewarded him with several fine horses from the imperial stables
and an equivalent amount of gold and silk.
Soon after, a eunuch slandered him, saying:
“This was all Chén Lì’s achievement,
not Liú Gàn’s.”
The prince’s mother, Lady Hé, heard this and said:
“It is not necessary to die for one’s lord.
(Míng manuscript note: ‘lord’ is written as ‘loyalty.’)
It is better to preserve one’s life for the sake of the state.”
She then bestowed upon him brocade robes and a silver belt,
added two hundred thousand coins,
and promoted him to the position of Zhōngjiān Wèi.
Earlier, Liú Gàn had once visited Huáng Hè for a divination.
After the hexagram was formed, Huáng told Gàn:
“This hexagram is
‘Fire over Water, Not Yet Crossing.’
In the end, there will be establishment.
The movement of the second nine line,
‘dragging the wheel, upright and auspicious.’
By correcting and rescuing from difficulty,
you will achieve merit.
Changing to the hexagram Jìn,
‘brightness emerges from the earth.’
You will shine brilliantly,
and favor will follow.
Your orders will be carried out,
advantageous for resisting invaders,
and you will achieve great victory and celebration.
The prince will bestow upon you chariots and horses.
There may be minor conflicts,
but they are not worth worrying about.”
The army commander Lù Yàn
once went to the latrine at night,
and a thief was hiding there.
Yàn suddenly felt a premonition,
took a candle to illuminate the area,
and the thief immediately spoke up:
“Please do not be alarmed.
I have been ordered to do this.
Observing your fairness and integrity,
I cannot bear to harm you.”
He then sheathed his sword and left.
From then on, Yàn remained vigilant day and night,
preparing for unexpected events.
He summoned Huáng Hè to divine for him.
After the hexagram was formed, Huáng said:
“Crying out in alarm at dusk and night,
there is an enemy, but do not worry.
Examining the images and interpreting the words,
someone intended to harm you.
However, the danger has already passed.
Just maintain your uprightness,
and please set your worries aside.”
Yàn ultimately encountered no further trouble.
Also, Zhànhuáng County Captain Zhāng Shī had been bedridden for a year.
Each day he felt increasingly critical,
and skilled physicians stopped prescribing medicine.
He requested Huáng Hè to divine for him.
After the hexagram was completed,
Huáng told him:
“This is an unexpected illness;
without medicine, there will be joy.
Please cease all treatments for five days,
and you will surely recover greatly.”
Shī indeed recovered as predicted.
Several decades later,
Shī dreamed of a white bird flying
and falling beyond the clouds.
Upon waking,
he felt unsettled and confused.
He summoned Huáng Hè to divine for him.
Huáng immediately interpreted the hexagram
and asked Shī with a sorrowful expression:
“This morning upon resting,
did you not have a dream?
If you did dream,
was it of a flying bird?
Moreover, thunder shakes the mountain,
a bird falls beyond the clouds,
both sound and traces vanish,
never to be seen again.
I urge you to take care of yourself,
and accept fate with contentment.”
Zhāng Shī never rose from his bed again
and passed away at the age of seventy-one.
There was also a man named Duàn Huì,
who served as the commander of Hàochéng Garrison.
Once, while staying overnight at a postal station,
his horse broke its reins and ran away,
and for several days, no one knew where it had gone.
He sent someone to Huáng Hè’s shop to divine.
Huáng said:
“According to the hexagram, it is Kuí.
The movement of the first nine line
indicates a loss.
Could it be that you lost a horse?
Do not chase it; it will return on its own.
Someone will surely tie it up and bring it back.”
Before the messenger had even returned home,
a rough youth from the border region
had already led the horse back.
Huáng Hè’s divinations
were all of this kind.
People of the time called him “Yì Shèng Gōng” (the Sage of the Yì).
Liú Yán once visited him.
Huáng told him:
“In the future, you will certainly achieve greatness,
but do not resent the spring days.”
At first, Yán did not understand the meaning,
but when he grew old, he realized
it referred to a slow, gradual process.
From “Ěrmù Jì.”
The Diviner of Dèngzhōu
There was a scholar living in Dèngzhōu.
Once, he traveled to the southern part of the commandery
and did not return for several months.
His family went to a diviner to inquire about him.
The diviner examined the hexagram and said:
“Very strange.
I cannot fully comprehend it;
please repeat the prayer.”
After the prayer,
he wiped the turtle shell and applied heat again.
Then he said:
“The traveler you inquired about
shows signs of being ill but not ill,
of being dead but not dead.
He will return on his own after a year.”
Indeed, half a year later,
the scholar returned and said:
“I wandered into a deep cave in a certain mountain,
and encountered a creature hibernating.
It was as if I fell ill;
my limbs could not move,
and I felt dazed as if half-drunk.
I saw a creature enter the cave from the light,
then turn back.
After a long while, it came again,
directly approaching my body,
stretching its neck toward my mouth and nose.
Looking closely,
it was a giant turtle.
It stayed for about ten breaths before leaving.”
The scholar calculated the time,
and it matched the moment his family had consulted the diviner.
From “Yǒuyáng Zázǔ.”
Huà Tuó
Wèi Huà Tuó was skilled in medicine.
Once, a commandery governor was gravely ill,
and Huà Tuó passed by him.
The commandery governor ordered Huà Tuó to examine his condition.
Huà Tuó withdrew
and said to his son:
"Your father's illness is unusual;
he has accumulated stagnant blood in his abdomen.
He must be provoked to extreme anger and vomit blood,
then he can be cured.
Otherwise, he will not survive.
If you can fully recount all the faults your father has committed in the past,
I will list them and reprimand him."
His son said:
"If he can be cured,
why would I not speak?"
Thereupon, he detailed all the mistakes his father had ever made
and showed them all to Huà Tuó.
Huà Tuó left a letter reprimanding and scolding him.
The father grew furious,
sent officers to arrest Huà Tuó.
Huà Tuó did not come,
and the governor vomited over a shēng of black blood,
after which his illness was cured.
There was also a woman of extreme beauty,
who remained unmarried past the proper age.
She constantly suffered from a sore on her right knee,
with pus and fluid that never ceased.
Huà Tuó passed by.
Her father asked him about it,
and Huà Tuó said:
"Have someone ride a horse,
lead a chestnut-colored dog for thirty lǐ,
then return and immediately cut off its right leg,
and prop it against the sore."
Soon, a red snake emerged from the sore
and entered the dog's leg,
and her illness was then cured.
From "Dú Yì Zhì"
Also, at the end of the Later Hàn,
someone suffered from an abdominal mass illness,
with sharp pain day and night.
On his deathbed,
he instructed his son:
"After I stop breathing,
you may cut me open and look."
His son could not bear to disobey his words,
cut him open,
and found a copper vessel,
capable of holding several gě or so.
Later, Huà Tuó heard of his illness and understood it.
He then took medicine from his handkerchief box
and threw it into the vessel,
whereupon the vessel turned into wine.
From "Zhì Guài"
Zhāng Zhòngjǐng
Hé Yóng was exceptionally skilled in judging people.
Once, when Zhāng Zhòngjǐng was still a youth, he visited Yóng.
Yóng said to him:
"Your thinking is meticulous and precise,
but your spirit is not lofty;
you will become a fine physician."
Zhòngjǐng later indeed possessed remarkable skills.
When Wáng Zhòngxuān was seventeen, he visited Zhòngjǐng.
Zhòngjǐng said to him:
"Your body has an illness;
you should take the Wǔ Shí Tāng.
If not treated,
by the time you reach thirty,
your eyebrows will fall out."
Zhòngxuān, considering it distant, did not treat it.
Later, when he reached thirty,
indeed his eyebrows began to fall out.
His insight was such,
that everyone marveled at Yóng's ability to judge people.
From "Xiǎoshuō"
Wú Imperial Physician
In Wú, Sūn Hé favored Lady Dèng.
Once, while drunkenly dancing with a rúyì scepter,
he accidentally injured Lady Dèng's cheek,
causing it to bleed.
Her delicate distress was profound.
He ordered the imperial physician to prepare medicine.
It was said that with white otter marrow, mixed jade, and amber powder,
the scar could be eliminated.
Hé purchased a white otter for a hundred gold pieces
and prepared the ointment.
Too much amber was used,
and when it healed,
the scar did not disappear;
instead, there was a red dot on her left cheek like a mole.
From "Yǒu Yáng Zá Zǔ"
Gōulí Visitor
During the Wèi period, there was a Gōulí visitor skilled in using needles.
He would take a strand of hair an inch long,
cut it into over ten segments,
and thread them with a needle,
saying the hair was hollow inside.
His skill was this marvelous.
From "Yǒu Yáng Zá Zǔ"
Fàn Guānglù
There was a Fàn Guānglù who fell ill,
with both feet swollen,
unable to eat or drink.
Suddenly, a man appeared.
Without introducing himself,
he directly entered the study.
He sat beside Guānglù.
Guānglù said to him:
"I do not know you;
why have you come to see me?"
He replied:
"The Buddha sent me to treat your illness."
Guānglù then removed his clothes to show him.
He then took out a needle
(Original text: "took out a knife,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
and needled the swollen area.
In an instant,
he swiftly needled both feet and the bladder over a hundred times,
releasing about three shēng of yellow pus and fluid, then left.
By the next day,
there were no needle wounds, and the ailment gradually healed.
From "Qí Xié Lù"
Xú Wénbó
Sòng Xú Wénbó once accompanied Emperor Shào of Sòng out of the Lèyóu Garden gate,
when they encountered a pregnant woman.
The emperor was also skilled in diagnosis,
and after examining her, he said:
"It is a girl."
He asked Wénbó,
and Bó said:
"One boy and one girl.
The boy is on the left side,
bluish-black in color,
and smaller in form than the girl."
The emperor, being impatient by nature,
ordered the woman to be cut open.
Wénbó, feeling compassion, said:
"Your subject requests to use acupuncture on her;
the fetus will certainly fall."
He then needled the foot Tàiyīn meridian
and supplemented the hand Yángmíng meridian.
The fetus fell in response to the acupuncture,
and indeed it was as he said.
Wénbó was learned and virtuous,
not yielding to high officials,
and did not take medicine as his profession.
He was esteemed by Zhāng Róng
and served successively as the prefect of Tàishān.
Wénbó's grandfather, Xīzhī, was fond of Huáng-Lǎo teachings
and lived in seclusion on Qínwàng Mountain.
A Dàoshi passed by and begged for a drink,
leaving behind a gourd, saying:
"Your descendants should use this art to save the world,
and they will attain the rank of two thousand shí."
Xī opened it and looked inside,
and it was a scroll of the medical classic of Biǎn Què.
He then studied it diligently,
and his fame spread throughout the land.
He served as the prefect of Púyáng.
His son, Qiūfū, was the magistrate of Shèyáng.
Once, there was a ghost moaning,
its voice very mournful and pained.
Qiūfū asked:
"You are a ghost;
what do you need?"
The ghost said:
"My surname is Húsī,
and my home is in Dōngyáng.
I suffered from back pain and died.
Although I am a ghost,
the pain is still unbearable.
I have heard that you are skilled in the art,
and I wish for your relief."
Qiūfū said:
"You are a ghost,
without form;
how can I treat you?"
The ghost said:
"Just bind straw to make a human figure.
According to the acupuncture points
(the character for 'points' was originally written as 'fixed,'
corrected based on the Ming manuscript copy)
needle it."
Qiūfū did as he said,
needling four places,
and also needling the Jiānjǐng point in three places,
then setting up an offering and burying it.
The next day,
he saw a person come to thank him, saying:
"I am grateful for your treatment of my illness,
and also for setting up the offering,
relieving my hunger and curing my illness.
My gratitude is truly great."
Suddenly, he disappeared.
His contemporaries admired his ability to communicate with spirits.
From "Tán Sǒu."
Also, a palace lady of Emperor Míng of Sòng suffered from back pain that affected her heart,
and when it flared up, she would lose consciousness.
Many physicians thought it was a flesh mass.
Xú Wénbó said:
"This is a hair concretion."
He poured oil into her,
and she then vomited an object like hair.
Gently pulling it out,
it was three chǐ long,
and the head had already become a snake.
It could move,
and when hung on a pillar,
after the water dripped away,
it was just a strand of hair.
The illness was then cured.
From "Tán Sǒu."
Xú Sìbó
Xú Sìbó, styled Déshào,
was skilled in pure conversation
and excelled in medical arts.
Once there was an old woman
who suffered from stagnation and stasis,
which did not heal for years.
Sìbó diagnosed her illness, saying:
"This is corpse infestation;
you must boil and take a dead person's pillow to be cured."
So he obtained a pillow from an ancient tomb,
the pillow being half rotten and broken,
and after taking it, she was cured.
Later, a man from Mòlíng named Zhāng Jǐng, aged fifteen,
had a swollen abdomen and a yellow face,
and many physicians could not cure him.
He asked Sìbó,
and Sìbó said:
"This is a stone roundworm;
you must boil and take a dead person's pillow."
Following his words,
he boiled the pillow and took it,
resulting in a great purge,
expelling
(the character for 'expelling' was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy)
roundworms,
with heads as hard as stone, about five or six shēng,
and the illness was cured.
Later, Shěn Sēngyì had eye pain
and often saw ghostly things.
He asked Sìbó about it,
and Sìbó said:
"Evil qi has entered the liver;
you can seek a dead person's pillow, boil it, and take it.
Afterward,
you can bury the pillow back in its original place."
Following his words, he was cured again.
Wáng Yàn, hearing of this, asked him:
"The three illnesses are different,
yet all were treated using a dead person's pillow,
and all were cured. Why?"
He replied:
"Corpse infestation
is ghostly qi.
It lies dormant and does not rise,
thus causing people to sink into stagnation.
Using a dead person's pillow urges it,
causing the soul qi to fly away,
no longer attaching to the body,
so corpse infestation can be cured.
As for stone roundworms,
medical treatment becomes ineffective.
The roundworms become hardened,
and worldly medicine cannot remove them,
so it is necessary to use ghostly things to drive them away,
after which they can disperse.
As for evil qi entering the liver,
it causes eye pain and makes one see demons.
It is necessary to use an evil object to lure out the qi,
thereby removing it,
which is why we order it to be buried back in its original place."
Yàn deeply admired his divine skill.
From "Nán Shǐ."
Abdominal Concretion Illness
Once there was a person
who, together with a servant, simultaneously contracted an abdominal concretion illness.
After the servant died,
he ordered the abdomen to be cut open for examination,
and they found a white turtle.
They then tried pouring various medicines on it,
and also placed medicine inside its abdomen,
but none caused any damage or movement.
So they tied the turtle to a bed leg.
Suddenly, a guest came to see it.
He rode a white horse,
and then the horse's urine splashed on the turtle.
The turtle became terrified
and quickly tried to avoid it.
Since it was tied,
it could not leave,
so it retracted its head, neck, and feet.
The sick person observed this
and said to his son:
"My illness might be curable."
He then tried pouring white horse urine on the turtle.
In a moment, it dissolved into water.
The sick person then immediately drank over a shēng of white horse urine,
and the illness was completely cured.
From "Xù Sōushén Jì."
Lǐ Zǐyù
Xǔ Yǒng served as the Inspector of Yùzhōu,
stationed at Lìyáng.
His younger brother fell ill,
with severe pain in his chest and abdomen.
One night,
he suddenly heard a ghost speaking from behind the screen:
"Why not kill him quickly?
Tomorrow,
Lǐ Zǐyù will strike you with a red pill,
and you will die immediately."
At dawn,
he sent someone to fetch Zǐyù.
Upon his arrival,
the patient suddenly heard groaning sounds from within his abdomen.
Zǐyù then took an eight-poison red pill from his medicine box and administered it to him.
In a short while,
there was a rumbling and twisting
in his abdomen.
After a significant bowel movement,
the illness was cured.
From "The Continued Records of Searching for the Divine."
Xú Zhīcái
Xú Zhīcái, the Right Deputy Director of the Northern Qí, was skilled in medicine.
At the time, someone suffered from swelling and pain in the heel,
which none of the other doctors could diagnose.
He examined it and said:
"This is a clam spirit illness.
It must have been contracted while riding a boat into the sea,
with feet dangling in the water."
The patient said:
"That is indeed what happened."
He performed surgery,
and extracted two clam larvae,
resembling elm seeds.
From "The Stories of Tàiyuán."
Zhēn Quán
Zhēn Quán meticulously studied medicine,
and was considered the best in the world.
At the age of 103,
Emperor Táng Tàizōng visited his residence,
and appointed him as a Court Advisor.
From "The Records of Tán Bīn."
Sūn Sīmiǎo
Táng Dèngwáng Lǐ Yuányù,
the eighteenth son of Emperor Gāozǔ.
He was fond of learning,
skilled in discussing principles of names,
and formed a commoner's friendship with the diǎnqiān Lú Zhàolín.
He often praised him, saying:
"He is my Sīmǎ Xiàngrú."
Lú Zhàolín was from Fànyáng.
He served as the wèi of Xīndū,
but contracted a severe
severe originally written as illness,
amended according to the Míng manuscript
illness,
and resided on the Jùcí Mountain in Yángdí.
He wrote the "Explaining Illness Essay" and "Five Sorrows."
He truly possessed the style of a Sāo poet,
and ultimately drowned himself in the Yǐngshuǐ River and died.
Lú Zhàolín lived in the abandoned mansion of Princess Póyáng in the capital city.
In the third year of the Xiǎnqìng era,
an imperial edict summoned the hermit Sūn Sīmiǎo from Tàibái Mountain.
He also resided in this mansion.
Sūn Sīmiǎo was from Huáyuán,
over ninety years old,
yet his sight and hearing had not declined.
Lú Zhàolín was just at the age of strong service,
but was afflicted with a severe illness and exhausted,
so he composed the "Puncture Vine Tree Rhapsody,"
to lament the differences in their innate endowments.
The language was very beautiful.
Sūn Sīmiǎo possessed the arts of calendrical calculation and life cultivation.
Lú Zhàolín, along with the then-famous scholars Sòng Lìngwén and Mèng Shēn,
all performed the rites of a teacher-student relationship.
They once asked Sūn Sīmiǎo:
"Famous physicians cure illnesses.
What is the principle behind it?"
Sūn Sīmiǎo said:
"I have heard that those who are good at speaking of heaven,
must base it on humanity.
Those who are good at speaking of humanity,
must base it on heaven.
Thus, heaven has four seasons and five phases,
the sun and moon alternate,
cold and heat succeed each other.
Their movement and transformation
harmonize to become rain,
anger to become wind,
disperse to become dew,
chaos to become fog,
condense to become frost and snow,
spread to become rainbows.
These are the constant patterns of heaven.
Humans have four limbs and five organs,
waking and sleeping,
breathing in and out,
essence and energy flowing back and forth.
Flowing to become yíng and wèi,
manifesting to become complexion,
issuing to become sounds and voices,
these are also the constant patterns of humanity.
Yang uses its essence,
yin uses its form.
This is what heaven and humanity share.
When they go awry,
rising heat becomes fever,
stagnation produces cold,
coagulation forms tumors and growths,
blockage becomes abscesses and ulcers,
rushing leads to panting and exhaustion,
depletion results in withering and dryness.
Diagnosis appears on the face,
changes manifest in the form.
Extending this to heaven and earth,
it is also like this.
Thus, the five planets expand and contract,
stars stray from their courses,
solar and lunar eclipses occur,
comets and shooting stars fly.
These are the dangerous signs of heaven and earth.
Untimely cold and heat,
these are the rising and stagnation of heaven and earth.
Stones standing and earth surging,
these are the tumors and growths of heaven and earth.
Mountains collapsing and earth sinking,
these are the abscesses and ulcers of heaven and earth.
Rushing winds and violent rains,
these are the panting and exhaustion of heaven and earth.
Rainfall not descending,
rivers and marshes drying up.
These are the withering and dryness of heaven and earth.
A good physician guides with medicines and stones,
saves with acupuncture and moxibustion.
A sage harmonizes with utmost virtue,
assists with human affairs.
Thus, the body has illnesses that can be eliminated,
heaven has disasters that can be eliminated.
This is understanding the patterns."
Lú Zhàolín asked:
"What about human affairs?"
Sūn Sīmiǎo said:
"The gallbladder should be large and the heart should be small,
wisdom should be round and conduct should be square."
Lú Zhàolín asked:
"What does that mean?"
Sūn Sīmiǎo said:
"The heart is the ruler of the five organs.
The ruler prioritizes reverence and compliance,
thus the heart should be small.
The gallbladder is the general of the five organs.
The general's duty is decisiveness,
thus the gallbladder should be large.
The wise move like heaven,
thus should be round.
The benevolent are still like earth,
thus should be square.
The Book of Songs says:
'As if facing a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice,'
this is being small-hearted.
'Valiant warriors,
bulwarks of the lords,'
this is being large-bellied.'"
The Zuo Zhuan says:
'Not turning back for profit,
not feeling guilt over righteousness,'
this is the squareness of benevolence.
The Book of Changes says:
'Act upon seeing the signs,
do not wait all day,'
this is the roundness of wisdom.'"Lú Zhàolín asked again:
"Regarding the way of nurturing life,
what are its essentials?"
Sūn Sīmiǎo said:
"The way of heaven has fullness and deficiency,
human affairs often have difficulties and adversities.
If one is not cautious and can overcome adversity,
such a thing has never existed.
Thus, those who nurture life
first know self-caution.
Self-caution
always takes worry and awe as its foundation.
The Classic says:
'If people do not fear authority,
heaven's authority will arrive.'
Worry and awe
are the gate of life and death,
the reason for survival and perish,
the root of fortune and misfortune,
the source of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.
Thus, if scholars lack worry and awe, benevolence and righteousness will not be established;
if farmers lack worry and awe, crops will not flourish;
if artisans lack worry and awe, rules and compasses will not be set;
if merchants lack worry and awe, goods and wealth will not increase;
if sons lack worry and awe, filial piety will not be sincere;
if fathers lack worry and awe, kindness and love will not be evident;
if ministers lack worry and awe, merit and achievement will not be built;
if rulers lack worry and awe, the state will not be secure.
Thus, those who nurture life,
if they lose their worry and awe, their hearts will be chaotic and ungoverned,
their forms agitated and unsettled,
their spirits scattered and energy dissipated,
their wills dissipated and minds confused.
What should live dies,
what should survive perishes,
what should succeed fails,
what should be auspicious becomes inauspicious.
Worry and awe
are like water and fire, not to be forgotten even momentarily.
If people lack worry and awe,
their children and younger brothers become formidable enemies,
their wives and concubines become bandits and foes.
Therefore, the highest is to fear the Way,
next to fear heaven,
next to fear things,
next to fear people,
next to fear one's own body.
Those who worry about their bodies
are not constrained by others;
those who fear themselves
are not controlled by others.
Those cautious in small matters
do not fear great ones;
those warned by nearby things
do not fear distant ones.
Those who can understand this,
when traveling by water, flood dragons cannot harm them;
when traveling by land, tigers and rhinos cannot injure them.
Weapons cannot reach them,
epidemics cannot infect them.
Slanderers cannot defame them,
poisonous stings cannot harm them.
Knowing this, human affairs are complete."
Sūn Sīmiǎo was soon appointed Chéngwùláng,
directly serving in the Imperial Pharmacy Bureau.
He died at the beginning of the Yǒngchún era,
leaving orders for a simple burial.
No burial objects were to be set,
and sacrifices were to be without livestock.
He had been dead for over a month.
His complexion did not change.
They lifted the corpse into the coffin.
It was as if it were merely empty clothing.
He compiled the thirty-scroll "Qiānjīn Fāng" (Thousand Gold Prescriptions), which circulated in his era.
From "Tán Bīn Lù" (Records from the Guest of Tan).
Xǔ Yìzōng
Xǔ Yìzōng was a physician of divine skill.
People said to him:
"Why don't you write a book,
to pass on to future generations?"
Yìzōng replied:
"Medicine is about intent,
it lies in a person's contemplation.
Moreover, the signs of the pulse are subtle and profound,
very difficult to distinguish.
What the mind comprehends,
the mouth cannot fully express.
The skilled masters of old
excelled precisely in discerning the pulse.
Once the pulse is precisely distinguished,
then one can recognize the illness.
For an illness and its medicine,
there are those that match perfectly.
One only needs to use a single ingredient,
directly attacking that illness,
and recovery is immediate.
Nowadays, those who cannot distinguish the pulse,
who fail to recognize the source of the illness,
rely on guesswork and estimation,
and often add many medicinal ingredients.
It is like hunting:
not knowing where the rabbit is,
they dispatch many men and horses,
vainly spreading out to encircle a vast area.
Hoping that one person might happen upon it by chance.
To treat illness in this manner,
is it not too crude?
The profound essence of pulse diagnosis,
since it cannot be put into words,
is why I cannot compose writings."
From "Tán Bīn Lù".
Qín Mínghè
Emperor Gāozōng of Táng suffered from wind dizziness,
his head and eyes unable to see.
He summoned the attending physician Qín Mínghè to examine him.
Qín said:
"Wind toxin is attacking upwards.
If the head is pricked to release a little blood,
you will recover."
The Empress (Wǔ Zétiān) angrily said from behind the curtain:
"This man should be beheaded!
On the Son of Heaven's head,
how could that be a place for bleeding?"
Mínghè kowtowed, pleading for his life.
The Emperor said:
"A physician discusses illness;
by principle, he should not be punished.
Moreover, my head is heavy and stifled,
almost unbearable.
Bleeding might not be bad.
My mind is made up."
He ordered the procedure.
Mínghè pricked the Bǎihuì and Nǎohù points to draw blood.
The Emperor said:
"My eyes are clear now!"
Before he finished speaking,
the Empress from behind the curtain performed a gesture of reverence to thank him, saying:
"This is a teacher bestowed by Heaven upon me."
She personally carried silk and treasures to give to him.
From "Tán Bīn Lù".
Lú Yuánqīn
In Quánzhōu, there was a traveler named Lú Yuánqīn who contracted severe leprosy,
only the root of his nose remained unaffected.
It happened to be the fifth day of the fifth month,
officials were procuring python gallbladders to present as tribute.
Someone said the meat could cure leprosy,
so he took a section of snake meat and ate it.
Within three to five days, he rapidly improved,
and recovered fully in a hundred days.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi" (Unofficial Records from Court and Country).
Also, in Shāngzhōu, a man suffered from severe leprosy.
His family despised him,
and built a thatched hut for him in the mountains.
A black snake fell into his wine jar.
The patient, unaware,
drank the wine and gradually recovered.
Seeing snake bones at the bottom of the jar,
he then realized the cause.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi".
Zhōu Yǔnyuán
During Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
the Vice Minister of the Secretariat, Zhōu Yǔnyuán, entered the palace chambers after court.
Princess Tàipíng summoned a physician to enter through the Guāngzhèng Gate.
He saw a ghost grabbing Yǔnyuán's head,
with two other ghosts holding clubs following behind,
going straight out the Jǐngyùn Gate.
The physician reported this to the Princess,
and the Princess memorialized it.
The Emperor ordered an attendant to observe and inquire.
Yǔnyuán was in the chambers without incident,
ate a meal and returned to his room,
then went to the latrine in the afternoon.
A senior attendant found his prolonged absence strange,
and thought to check on him.
Yǔnyuán was found fallen face-down on the latrine,
eyes staring straight ahead, speechless,
with saliva dripping from his mouth.
The attendant reported this.
The Emperor asked the physician:
"How much longer does he have?"
He replied:
"If slow, three days;
if urgent, one day."
The Emperor covered him with a brocade quilt,
and had him carried home on his bed.
He died just past midnight.
The Emperor personally composed a poem to mourn him.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi".
Yáng Xuánliàng
During the Jiǔshì era,
a man from Xiāngzhōu named Yáng Xuánliàng, over twenty years old,
was laboring at the Wénshān Temple in Qiánzhōu.
One day he dreamed of the Heavenly Sovereign (Tiānzūn) saying:
"My hall is damaged;
if you repair it for me,
I will grant you the ability to cure all illnesses."
He awoke and spoke of it.
When he tried healing, there was no case he did not cure.
The village head of Gànxiàn County had a swelling on his back,
as large as a fist.
Liàng cut it open with a knife,
and it healed completely in a few days.
He earned ten thousand cash daily from healing.
After the Heavenly Sovereign's hall was completed,
his healing gradually lost its efficacy.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi".
Zhào Xuánjǐng
During the Rúyì era,
a man from Luòzhōu named Zhào Xuánjǐng fell ill and died,
but revived after five days, saying:
He saw a monk who gave him a piece of wood over a foot long.
The monk instructed:
"When people are ill,
if you touch them with this wood, they will recover."
Xuánjǐng saw a ruler on a loom,
which was exactly what the monk had given him.
He tried using it to heal illnesses,
and touching them brought immediate recovery.
Hundreds of people came to his door daily.
The Censor Mǎ Zhījǐ, considering this gathering of crowds,
arrested him and confined him in the Left Censorate.
The sick filled the Censorate gates.
When Wǔ Zétiān heard of this,
she summoned
Summoned (original text said 'pursued',
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy)
him into the inner palace.
When palace ladies fell ill,
touching them cured them immediately.
He was released,
and allowed to heal commoners.
After several months,
he had earned over seven hundred strings of cash.
Later, its efficacy gradually faded,
and it ceased.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi".
Zhāng Wénzhòng
In Luòzhōu, a scholar suffered from an echo illness,
