where whatever he said was echoed in his throat.
He asked the skilled physician Zhāng Wénzhòng about it.
Zhāng pondered it all night,
and finally devised a method.
He took the "Běncǎo" (Materia Medica),
and had the man read it aloud.
Everything was echoed,
but when he reached the entries the illness feared,
there was no echo.
Zhōng then noted down those medicines,
combined and prepared them into pills.
After taking them,
the echoing stopped immediately.
Another account says
he consulted the physician Sū Chéng.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi".
Hǎo Gōngjǐng
Hǎo Gōngjǐng went to Mount Tài to gather herbs,
passing through the market.
There was someone who could see ghosts,
and it was strange that all the ghosts, upon seeing Gōngjǐng,
fled to avoid him.
He then took the herbs and made them into Ghost-Killing Pills.
Those who were ill
recovered after taking them.
From Records of Court and Country.
Cuī Wù
Cuī Wù from Dìngzhōu fell from a horse and broke his leg.
A doctor instructed him to take copper filings,
mix them with wine, and drink it,
and he recovered completely.
More than ten years after his death,
when his grave was moved,
it was seen that at the fracture site of his shinbone,
copper filings bound it together.
From Records of Court and Country.
Zhōu Guǎng
During the Kāiyuán era,
there was a famous doctor named Jì Míng,
a man from Wú.
He once taught secret techniques to the recluse Zhōu Guǎng.
By observing a person’s complexion and conversation,
he could discern the severity of their illness.
His descriptions were precise and detailed,
without the need for diagnosis.
The emperor heard of his reputation
and summoned him to the capital.
He ordered those with illnesses in the inner palace to be brought forth,
so Zhōu could examine them.
There was a palace maid
who, every day at dusk, would laugh, sing, weep, and shout,
as if afflicted by madness.
Moreover, her feet could not touch the ground.
Zhōu observed her and said:
"This must be because she ate to fullness,
and then exerted great force,
and shortly after fell to the ground, causing this condition."
Zhōu then gave her mica soup to drink.
After she drank it,
he had her sleep deeply.
When she awoke,
her suffering had vanished.
He asked her about it.
She then said:
"Once, during the three-day celebration of the birth of the Grand Huá Palace Princess,
the palace held a grand display of singing and music.
I was the lead singer,
and I feared my voice would not be clear.
So I often
often originally written as 'cháng' (long),
changed according to the Ming manuscript
ate pig trotter soup,
soup originally written as 'měi' (delicious),
changed according to the Ming manuscript
and thus
Ming manuscript has 'shèn' (very) instead of 'suì' (thus)
became full.
And then at the banquet, I sang several
Ming manuscript has 'dà' (large) instead of 'shù' (several)
songs.
After finishing the songs,
I felt very hot in my chest,
and I playfully jumped down from the high platform.
Before reaching halfway,
I was pushed by someone coming from behind,
and thus fell to the ground.
After a long time, I regained consciousness but was afflicted with madness,
and because of this, my feet could not touch the ground."
The emperor was greatly amazed by this.
There was a eunuch who had been on a mission,
returning from Jiāoguǎng,
and was paying respects at the foot of the palace steps.
Zhōu looked at him and said:
"This man has a flood dragon in his abdomen,
and tomorrow it will give birth to a child,
then he cannot survive."
The emperor, alarmed, asked the eunuch:
"Do you have any illness?"
He replied:
"When I was riding fast over Dàyǔ Ridge,
the weather was extremely hot,
and I was both exhausted and thirsty,
so I drank from wild water by the roadside,
and since then, my abdomen has felt hard and lumpy like a stone."
Zhōu immediately used saltpeter and realgar,
boiled them, and gave him the decoction to drink.
He immediately vomited a creature,
not several inches long,
as thick as a finger.
Upon closer inspection,
it was fully covered in scales and armor.
it grew to several feet in length in a short while.
Zhōu quickly doused it with vinegar,
and it returned to its original shape.
He covered it with a vessel.
The next day,
a dragon had already grown inside the vessel.
The emperor treated him with great respect,
and wanted to bestow upon him an official title.
Zhōu firmly requested to return to Wúzhōng.
The emperor did not oppose his wish,
and thus allowed him to return to his hometown.
Liú Fù, Vice Director of the Ministry of Waterways, wrote a biography for Zhōu,
which described him in great detail.
From Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Ming.
Bái Cén
Bái Cén once met an extraordinary man who taught him a prescription for treating back abscesses,
which was completely effective.
Cén flaunted it to seek profit.
Later, as a minor general in Huáinán,
the military governor Gāo Shì forced him to hand it over.
However, the prescription was not very effective.
Cén reached Jiǔjiāng and was eaten by a tiger,
and the postal station clerk found the genuine version in his bag.
Wáng Shēngzhī from Tàiyuán copied it to spread it.
From Supplements to the National History.
Zhāng Wànfú
When Liǔ Fāng was a department director,
his son, Liǔ Dēng, was seriously ill.
At that time, the famous doctor Zhāng Wànfú had just been appointed to Sìzhōu.
As he was an old friend of Fāng,
Fāng went to congratulate him,
and told him about his son's illness.
He relied entirely on his old friend for a visit.
Zhāng visited Fāng the next morning,
and Fāng immediately led him to see Dēng.
From a distance, seeing Dēng's head, he said:
"With such a skull,
what is there to worry about?"
He then felt his pulse for five or six breaths.
And said again:
"Not mistaken,
he will live past eighty."
He then left a prescription of several dozen characters for Fāng.
And said to Dēng:
"Even without taking this, it's fine."
Later, Dēng became an assistant director,
and lived to ninety.
From Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang.
Wáng Yànbó
Wáng Yànbó, a Taoist from Jīngzhōu, was naturally skilled in medicine,
especially in pulse diagnosis.
In determining life, death, longevity, or premature death,
he was never off by one in a hundred.
Minister Péi Zhòu had a son
who suddenly fell seriously ill.
All the doctors could do nothing.
Someone suggested Yànbó,
and he was urgently invited to examine him.
After feeling the pulse for a long time,
he said:
"There is no illness at all."
He then boiled a few herbs into a powder,
and upon taking it, the boy recovered.
Péi asked about the condition,
and Yànbó said:
"He was poisoned by a boneless carp."
His son had indeed fallen ill from eating sliced raw fish.
Péi initially did not believe it,
so he had a boneless carp sliced,
and ordered his attendants to eat it.
They all developed the same illness.
Only then was he greatly astonished.
From Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang.
Also, Yànbó himself said:
"The way of medicine is about to be practiced."
He set up three or four stoves,
and boiled medicine in the courtyard.
Old and young crowded his door seeking treatment.
Yànbó pointed and said:
"Those with heat drink this,
those with cold drink this,
those with wind drink this,
those with qi disorders drink this."
Each brought money and silk to repay him,
and there was no case that was not effective.
From Supplements to the National History.
Lǐ Yòu's Wife
Lǐ Yòu was a general of Huáixī.
In the thirteenth year of the Yuánhé era,
he surrendered and pledged allegiance to the state.
Péi Dù defeated Wú Yuánjì,
and entered his city.
Among the government troops, there were those who stripped women's clothes, leaving them naked.
Lǐ Yòu had a new wife, née Jiāng,
who was five months pregnant.
She was seized by the disorderly soldiers,
who cut open her abdomen with a knife.
Née Jiāng fainted and collapsed to the ground.
When Lǐ Yòu returned and saw her,
her abdomen was split open over a foot wide.
He then took off his own robe to wrap her.
By evening, she revived.
Applying a miraculous medicine, she healed.
After a full ten months,
she gave birth to a son.
The imperial court, in recognition of Lǐ Yòu's merit in surrendering to the state,
granted an official post to one of his sons.
The son was named Lǐ Xíngxiū.
When he was over thirty years old,
he served as Military Governor of Nánhǎi.
After leaving his post and returning,
he died on the journey.
From Dú Yì Zhì.
Yuán Háng
In the Táng capital, there was a physician whose name has been forgotten.
Among Yuán Háng's relatives,
there was a woman who followed her husband to the south,
and once accidentally swallowed an insect.
She was constantly troubled by this suspicion,
and as a result fell ill,
with frequent treatments proving ineffective.
She requested a consultation.
The physician understood her ailment.
He then asked for one of the most discreet maidservants in the household,
and warned her in advance, saying:
"Now I will administer medicine to induce vomiting and diarrhea.
Just catch it in a basin or bowl.
When she vomits,
just say that a small frog jumped out and ran away.
But you absolutely must not let the patient know this is a deception."
The maidservant complied,
and the illness was permanently cured.
There was also a young man,
who constantly saw a small mirror in his eye.
He had the physician Zhào Qīng examine him.
Zhào Qīng made an appointment with the young man,
inviting him to come the next morning for a meal of sliced raw fish.
The young man arrived at the appointed time.
He was invited inside,
and told to make himself comfortable.
He would be attended to after the other guests had left.
Soon a table was set,
with only a bowl of mustard vinegar placed on it,
and no other flavors.
Zhào Qīng had not yet appeared.
By late morning,
he had waited a long time without arrival.
The young man grew very hungry,
and smelling the vinegar's aroma,
he couldn't help but take a small sip.
After a while, he sipped again.
He felt a sudden clarity in his chest,
and the mirror in his eye vanished.
He then drained the bowl, sipping it all.
Zhào Qīng, knowing this had happened,
finally came out.
The young man, ashamed for having drunk the vinegar, apologized.
Zhào Qīng said:
"Young master, you previously ate too much sliced raw fish,
and the soy sauce and vinegar did not digest properly.
There was also a fish scale stuck in your chest,
which caused the mirror vision.
The soy sauce and vinegar I prepared earlier
were precisely so that you, feeling hungry, would sip it.
It indeed cured this ailment.
The promise of a fresh fish feast
was merely a ruse.
Please go and plan your morning meal."
Many of his other ingenious cures were of this kind.
From Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán.
Liáng Gé
Liáng Gé, a Cavalry Officer of the Imperial Guards, possessed the skills of Hé and Biǎn.
In the early Tàihé era,
he served as Patrol Officer of Wǎnlíng.
The Surveillance Commissioner Yú Áo had a maidservant named Liánzǐ,
for whom he cared deeply.
One day, due to a jest, she offended him,
and was expelled and put up for sale.
The market official set the price at seven hundred strings of cash.
An Attendant Censor named Cuī heard of this and summoned her,
requesting Liáng Gé to examine her pulse.
Liáng Gé felt her pulse and said:
"This is a person without illness for twenty springs."
Cuī was pleased and kept her,
sending the payment to Yú Áo.
Yú Áo, though he had always cherished her deeply,
in a moment of anger had driven her out,
and selling her to someone unknown was final.
Hearing that Cuī favored her displeased him,
and his feelings showed on his face.
However, since she was already gone,
it was difficult to recall her,
though he often kept her in his thoughts.
Within a year,
Liánzǐ suddenly died.
Liáng Gé happened to be on an official trip outside the city.
Returning and seeing the city gate,
he encountered a funeral carriage,
with Cuī's attendants holding the cords.
He asked who was being buried,
and was told:
"It is Liánzǐ."
He called for the carriage to turn back,
and rushed to inform Cuī, saying:
"Liánzǐ is not dead;
it is merely a corpse syncope.
Just now, as I entered the city,
I encountered her coffin.
I have had it brought back and request permission to revive her."
Cuī was angry at Liáng Gé's earlier diagnosis,
and grieved Liánzǐ's sudden death.
Furiously, he said:
"You are a mere commoner,
who deluded the nobles with false claims,
and thus gained rank among the officials.
You said she was without illness for twenty springs,
yet she died within a year.
Now she is already buried.
You summon her coffin back.
If you cannot bring her to life,
how will you face me?"
Liáng Gé said:
"She is certainly not dead;
it is merely a corpse syncope.
If I cannot revive her,
then my art is unworthy in the world.
I would rather die to atone for my mistaken words."
He then ordered the coffin opened and her body taken out.
He then needled her heart and below her navel at several points each,
extracted one of her teeth,
and placed a small dose of medicine in her mouth.
He dressed her in a single garment,
laid her on an empty bed,
bound her hands and feet with plain silk,
and placed a low fire beneath the bed.
He said:
"When this fire dies down,
Liánzǐ will come to life.
And instruct your attendants
to prepare scallion congee and wait.
When her vital energy circulates, she may become frenzied.
Be careful not to let her rise.
After a while, she will calm down on her own.
Once calm, she will be exhausted.
When exhausted, untie her bonds,
and feed her the scallion congee.
Then she will be revived.
If she is frenzied and allowed to rise,
the consequences are beyond my knowledge."
Having said this,
he returned to the official residence and told Cuī:
"Liánzǐ will soon be alive."
Cuī greatly released his anger,
and invited him to stay in the main hall.
Soon, Liánzǐ sat up, talking and laughing.
The border official reported to Yú Áo.
Yú Áo swiftly sent a letter to Cuī,
asking how Liánzǐ had revived,
and by what method.
He then came with Liáng Gé to Cuī's place.
Upon entering the gate, Liánzǐ came to greet them.
Yú Áo was greatly amazed.
Moreover, Liánzǐ's service to Cuī
was not her original wish.
He therefore advised giving her to Liáng Gé.
Cuī also disliked her missing tooth,
and out of respect for Yú Áo,
he gave her to Liáng Gé.
Liáng Gé obtained her,
applied a divine medicine to her tooth,
and within a month, her tooth grew back as before.
In the rénzǐ year of the Tàihé era,
he was transferred to be a Cavalry Officer of the Imperial Guards,
and lived in the capital with Liánzǐ.
That autumn,
Gāo Sǔnzhī, whose maternal uncle was the Minister of Personnel,
immediately made his acquaintance,
and thus knew the story well and related it.
From Xù Yì Lù.
The Ming manuscript edition cites it from Xù Xuán Guài Lù.
Liáng Xīn and Zhào È
During the Táng dynasty, Cuī Xuàn governed Zhǔgōng.
There was a wealthy merchant who lived on his boat.
In the middle of the night, he suddenly fell ill and was near death.
By dawn,
he was still barely breathing.
In a neighboring cabin was a physician from Wǔlíng named Liáng Xīn, who heard about this.
He went to examine him and said:
"This is food poisoning.
In the past two or three days, did he eat anything outside?"
The servant replied:
"My master seldom leaves the boat,
and he doesn't eat food from others."
Liáng Xīn asked:
"What does he usually like to eat?"
The servant said:
"He loves eating bamboo partridges,
consuming no fewer than several hundred each year.
Recently, he bought bamboo partridges
and prepared them for a meal."
Liáng Xīn said:
"Bamboo partridges eat bànxià (Pinellia ternata).
It must be bànxià poisoning."
He ordered ginger to be pounded and its juice extracted,
then pried open the merchant's teeth and poured it in.
Thus, the merchant revived.
Cuī Xuàn heard of this and was amazed.
He summoned Liáng Xīn,
comforted and praised him.
He provided him with servants, horses, money, and silk to go to the capital,
and wrote letters to court officials on his behalf.
Liáng Xīn's reputation grew greatly.
He rose to the position of Shàngyào Fèngyù (Imperial Medicinal Attendant).
A court official once visited him.
Liáng Xīn said:
"Why didn't you come to see me earlier?
Your wind-stroke illness is already severe.
Please return home quickly,
settle your family affairs,
and resign yourself to fate."
The court official heard this and hurriedly took his leave in alarm,
galloping back on his horse.
At that time, there was a horse doctor from Fūzhōu named Zhào È,
who had recently arrived in the capital.
He posted his name on the main streets,
claiming expertise in medicine.
This court official dismounted and told him his situation.
Zhào È also said the illness was critical,
agreeing with Liáng Xīn's assessment.
He told him:
"There is one method:
I urge you, sir, to eat as many pears as possible,
without limit.
If you cannot chew them all,
extract the juice and drink it.
Perhaps there is a slim chance of recovery."
The court official again galloped back on his horse.
He used a book tube as collateral to obtain pears,
and ate them while riding.
By the time he reached home,
for ten days he ate only pears.
Gradually, he felt refreshed and clear-headed,
and his illness did not recur.
He later visited Zhào È to thank him,
and also visited Imperial Attendant Liáng,
telling him how he had been saved by Zhào È's advice.
Liáng Xīn was astonished,
and said:
"A great state must have someone to carry on the legacy."
He then summoned Zhào È,
provided him with servants, horses, money, and silk,
and widely praised him.
Zhào È eventually rose to the position of Tàipú Qīng (Minister of the Imperial Stud).
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Also, Vice Director Zhāng Tíngzhī fell ill
and visited Zhào È.
As soon as he took his pulse,
Zhào È said his illness required a cup of ginger wine
and a cup of dìhuáng (rehmannia) wine.
He also consulted Liáng Xīn,
who said the same thing,
both stating that if he missed this, he would die.
After drinking this wine,
his illness soon subsided.
Another day, a powerful minister forced him to drink a cup of wine,
and he could not refuse.
That night, he died.
Contemporary opinion regarded them as two marvels.
From "Wén Qí Lù."
Gāo Pián
in the Jiānghuái region,
had extremely strict fire regulations,
and offenders were shown no mercy.
Because many houses were made of bamboo,
if care was not taken,
fires could reduce hundreds or thousands of houses to ashes in an instant.
In the year Gāo Pián governed Wéiyáng,
a household of a magician caused a fire,
burning thousands of homes.
The authorities recorded the case,
and he was sentenced to death.
As he was about to be executed,
he said to the supervising officer:
"My crime is grave,
and death alone cannot atone for it.
However, I possess a humble skill
that I can pass on to one person,
so that they may save others in the future.
Then I would die without regret."
At that time, Gāo Pián eagerly sought practitioners of esoteric arts,
always craving them like hunger and thirst.
The supervising officer immediately postponed the execution,
and rushed to report to Gāo Pián.
Gāo Pián summoned the magician,
and personally questioned him.
He said:
"I have no other skill,
only that I am adept at treating severe wind-stroke diseases."
Gāo Pián said:
"We can verify this."
He replied:
"Just select the most severe patient from the charity hospital,
and I can test it on him."
They did as he said.
They placed the patient in a sealed
(The original text said "gap,"
but was changed according to the Ming manuscript copy)
room,
gave him several shēng of mastic wine to drink,
and he fell into a daze, unconscious.
Then, with a sharp knife, they opened the seam of his skull.
They extracted worms that filled a handful,
each about two cùn long.
Then they sealed the wound with a plaster,
gave him other medicine to take,
and regulated his diet and activities.
After more than ten days,
the wound healed completely.
In just one month,
his eyebrows and beard had regrown,
his flesh was smooth and clean,
as if he had never been ill.
Gāo Pián treated the magician as an honored guest.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà."
Tián Lìngzī
In the days when Cháng'ān was at its peak of prosperity,
there was a household in the Western Market that sold medicinal decoctions.
They used ordinary herbs,
no more than a few varieties,
and were not versed in medical theory or pulse diagnosis.
Regardless of what ailment one suffered from,
they would sell one dose for a hundred coins.
A thousand kinds of illnesses
would be cured upon taking it.
They often placed a large cauldron in a spacious house,
chopping and brewing day and night,
unable to keep up with the demand.
People came from near and far
to obtain it,
crowding the market and filling the streets,
creating a clamor throughout the capital.
Some even brought gold to wait at the door,
yet for five to seven days
they still could not receive their dose.
The profits were immense.
At that time, Tián Lìngzī fell ill,
and physicians from across the land were summoned.
Even imperial physicians and court-appointed doctors
could find no remedy.
Suddenly, an acquaintance said to Tián:
"The decoction from the Western Market—
why not try it?"
Tián Lìngzī replied:
"Very well."
He then sent a servant
galloping on horseback to fetch it.
The servant obtained the medicine
and whipped the horse to return.
As he neared the residential ward,
the horse stumbled and the medicine spilled.
Fearing his master's severity,
the servant dared not go back for more.
He then went to a dye workshop,
begged for a bottle of dye sediment,
and presented it to his master.
After taking it,
his illness was immediately cured.
Tián only knew his illness was cured
and had no idea where the medicine came from,
so he richly rewarded the medicine seller.
The reputation of the decoction seller
soared even higher.
This was indeed a physician blessed by fortune.
In recent years,
there was a certain Zhāng Fúyī in Yèdū who was also like this.
He amassed great wealth,
gained fame from it,
and was taken by a foreign prince beyond the frontier.
From *Jade Hall Casual Talk*.
Yú Gòu
In recent times, the Secretariat Drafter Yú Gòu
once suffered from gu poison,
and no physician could cure it.
He thus took long leave
and gradually planned to travel far in search of treatment.
One day,
he leaned on his cane and sat outside the central gate.
Suddenly, a tinker saw him
and asked:
"What affliction has left you so gaunt and weary?"
Yú then explained his condition.
The tinker said:
"I too once suffered from this,
but met a skilled craftsman
who used tweezers to extract a snake and cured me.
I also learned his technique."
Yú was overjoyed
and begged for his help.
The tinker said:
"This is a small matter.
Tomorrow morning, please refrain from eating,
and I will come."
The next day, he indeed arrived.
He asked Yú to stand under the eaves of the house,
face the light, and open his mouth.
Holding tweezers, he waited.
Just as he was about to clamp,
he stumbled and missed.
He then arranged to return the following day.
After another night, he came again.
Focusing intently, he waited,
and with one clamp, he succeeded.
The snake was already about two inches long,
red in color,
and as thick as a hairpin.
He quickly ordered it burned with fire.
Yú was then cured.
He was repeatedly appointed to office,
rising to the position of Zǐwēi before passing away.
The tinker accepted no gifts,
saying only:
"I have vowed to save people."
He merely drank a few cups of wine and departed.
From *Jade Hall Casual Talk*.
Yán Suì
In the capital and various prefectures and commanderies, within the markets,
there were physicians who could extract gu poison,
and many witnessed their effectiveness firsthand.
People were often perplexed,
thinking it mere illusion,
and that deep-seated ailments
could not be removed.
A certain Attendant Gentleman Yán Suì
had a maidservant in his household suffering from this illness.
She often felt something gnawing at her heart and liver,
causing unbearable pain.
After years of suffering, she grew emaciated,
skin clinging to bones,
and her shins like withered wood.
By chance, he heard of a skilled physician
who gathered large crowds in the market
to treat this illness.
Yán tried summoning him.
The physician saw her and said:
"This is snake gu poison,
and it can be extracted immediately."
He first ordered a fire with ten to twenty catties of burning charcoal,
then administered medicine.
After a long while,
the physician held small tweezers at the ready.
At that moment, she felt something moving in her throat,
fainted, and then revived.
Shortly after,
he told her to open her mouth
and used forceps to extract a small snake, five to seven inches long,
quickly throwing it into the burning charcoal to be incinerated.
The snake writhed in the flames,
and after a while turned to ashes,
its stench reaching neighbors and relatives.
From then on, her illness was cured,
and she never again suffered the gnawing pain in her heart.
Thus, we know that tales of reviving the dead and regrowing flesh and bones
are not unfounded.
From *Jade Hall Casual Talk*.
Shēn Guāngxùn
In recent times, Shēn Guāngxùn, the Surveillance Judge of Cáozhōu,
said his family was from Guìlín.
There was an official named Sūn Zhòng'áo
who resided in Guì,
a man from Jiāo and Guǎng.
Shēn went to visit him
and was invited into his bedroom.
Sūn met him wearing his official cap and hairpin, saying:
"It is not that I am lazy about grooming,
but rather that I suffer from a headache."
He then ordered over a liter of strong wine,
mixed with spicy ingredients such as pepper and dried ginger, about half a cup,
and blended it with warm wine.
He then took a black lacquered tube from his pillowcase,
similar to today's reed pipe,
placed it in his nostril,
and inhaled it all.
Only then did he rest on his pillow.
He broke into a sweat,
and his illness was immediately cured.
This is likely a practice of the nasal-drinking barbarians of the south.
From *Jade Hall Casual Talk*.
Sūn Guāngxiàn
For burns, nothing surpasses vinegar mud—
it is very effective.
Sūn Guāngxiàn once had a family member making pancakes,
and a maidservant holding a child near the stove
accidentally dropped a piece of burning charcoal on herself.
She immediately applied vinegar mud to it,
and by morning, she felt no pain
and had no scar.
This shows that folk remedies should not be dismissed out of hand.
From *Beimeng Suoyan*.
The Fisherman's Wife
In Guā Village, there was a fisherman whose wife contracted a consumptive disease.
It spread contagiously,
claiming several lives.
Someone said:
"If you nail the sick person alive into a coffin and abandon them,
the disease can be cut off."
Shortly after,
his daughter fell ill,
so he immediately nailed her alive into a coffin
and set it adrift on the river.
When it reached Jīnshān,
a fisherman saw it and found it strange,
so he pulled it to the shore.
Opening it to look inside,
he saw the girl was still alive,
so he took her and placed her in his fishing hut.
He often caught many eels and blackfish to feed her,
and after a long time, her illness was cured.
She then became the fisherman's wife,
and to this day remains well.
From "Jìshén Lù"
Chén Zhài
Chén Zhài was
a shaman from Jìnjiāng, Quánzhōu,
skilled in the arts of incantations and blessings.
When treating people's illnesses,
many were cured.
There was a man named Sū Měng, an innkeeper from Zhāngzhōu,
whose son was afflicted with madness.
No one could cure him,
so he went to invite Chén.
When Chén arrived,
Sū's son saw him
and pointed his fingers like halberds, cursing loudly.
Zhài said:
"This illness has entered the heart."
He then set up an altar in the hall
and warned people not to peek.
When night fell,
he took Sū's son
and split him into two pieces,
hanging them on the east wall of the hall,
while the heart was hung under the north eaves.
As Zhài was performing his rituals in the hall,
the hanging heart
was eaten by a dog.
Zhài searched for it but could not find it,
and in his panic and fear,
he took a knife and writhed on the ground,
then left through the door.
The master of the house did not know what had happened,
thinking he was merely performing his rituals.
After about the time it takes to eat a meal,
he returned holding the heart
and placed it into the patient's abdomen.
With disheveled hair, he chanted incantations repeatedly,
and the abdomen closed up.
Sū's son then regained consciousness.
But he kept shouting, "Relay station,
relay station!"
His family could not understand what he meant.
It turned out that on that day, several miles from their home,
a postal courier holding an official document
had died by the roadside.
Originally, on the southern postal routes,
a relay station was set up every twenty lǐ.
The postal courier would hold the official dispatch
and pass it on in sequence.
When approaching the next station,
he would shout repeatedly to alert them.
Thus, Zhài had taken the heart of the postal courier to revive Sū.
Sū then recovered as before.
From "Jìshén Lù"
Táo Jùn
In Jiāngnán, Zhāng Yàoqīng, the Prefect of Jízhōu,
had a servant named Táo Jùn, who was cautious and upright by nature.
He had once served in the army during the campaign in Jiāngxī,
where he was struck by a flying stone,
resulting in ailments in his waist and legs,
so he always walked with a cane.
Zhāng ordered him to guard a boat at the river mouth of Guǎnglíng.
While there, he went to Báishā Market,
and took shelter from the rain in a tavern.
Many people were standing together there.
Two scholars passed by in front,
and they alone took notice of Jùn.
They said to each other:
"This man has a good heart;
we should cure his ailment."
They then called Jùn over
and gave him two pills of medicine, saying:
"Take these, and you will recover."
Then they left.
Jùn returned to the boat and swallowed them.
After a while,
he felt severe pain in his abdomen,
but shortly after, the pain stopped,
and his ailment was largely cured.
Handling the pole and managing the ropes,
he felt especially light and agile.
Báishā was eighty lǐ from the city,
yet he could make the round trip in a single day,
without feeling tired.
Later, he tried to find the two scholars,
but he never saw them again.
From "Jìshén Lù"
Zhāng Yì
In Jiāngnán, Zhāng Yì, a Vice Director in the Ministry of Justice, lived in Zīchuān in his youth.
He fell ill with a fever,
and was extremely weak and distressed.
In his delirium, he saw a divine being, about a few inches tall,
standing by his pillow.
Holding three pills of medicine, it said:
"Swallow these, and you will recover."
Yì took them and hastily swallowed them,
but while two went down,
one fell onto the mat with a sound.
He got up to search for it but could not find it.
His family, startled, asked what he was doing,
and he recounted what he had seen.
His illness was immediately cured.
That day, he went in and out of the village lanes,
completely free from any discomfort.
From "Jìshén Lù"
The Carpenter of Guǎnglíng
In Guǎnglíng, there was a carpenter
who, due to illness,
had his hands and feet curled up
(Originally written as "raised,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript copy)
and shrunken,
unable to hold an axe again.
Leaning on a stick, he begged as he walked,
until he reached in front of the Hòutǔ Temple,
where he met a Daoist priest.
Tall and dark-skinned,
he had an extraordinary demeanor.
Calling him over, he asked about his illness,
then gave him several pills of medicine, saying:
"Take these, and you will recover.
Tomorrow at dawn,
meet me here again."
The carpenter declined, saying:
"I cannot walk;
my home is far from here.
Even if I start early tomorrow,
I may not be able to reach here in time."
The Daoist said:
"Do not worry;
just come here early."
Then he bid farewell and left.
After the carpenter returned home,
he took the medicine.
After a while,
he felt severe pain in his hands and feet,
which stopped around midnight,
and he was able to sleep.
At the fifth watch, he awoke,
feeling his hands and feet very light,
so he got out of bed
and walked and ran as before.
He immediately hurried to the front of the Hòutǔ Temple.
After a long time,
he saw the Daoist leaning on his staff, standing there.
He bowed twice and expressed his gratitude.
The Daoist said:
"I will teach you a method
to save people from suffering and illness.
Do not remain a carpenter."
The carpenter bowed twice again and received it.
He then asked for his name and residence.
The Daoist said:
"I am at Zǐjí Palace;
if you have matters, you can visit me there."
Then he left.
The carpenter obtained the method
and used it to treat illnesses,
and there was no one he did not cure.
He went to Zǐjí Palace to visit him,
but never saw him again.
Later, there was a woman with a long-standing illness
who also met a Daoist priest,
and after taking his medicine, she recovered.
When she described his appearance,
it was the same as the one the carpenter had seen.
Guǎnglíng soon fell into chaos,
and the carpenter ultimately disappeared without a trace.
From "Jìshén Lù"
Flying Gu Poison
In the region between the Jiāng and the mountains, there are flying gu poison.
When they come, there is a sound,
but their form is not seen,
like the chirping and twittering of birds.
If they strike a person, it causes dysentery,
with bloody stool.
Most medicines do not cure it.
Within ten days, the person is inevitably beyond saving.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Fungus Poison
In the customs of Lǐngnán,
many make poisonous drugs.
They make an old slave eat yěgě (Gelsemium elegans) and die,
then bury him.
On the earth mound, a fungus grows.
If it grows directly above the abdomen,
eating it causes immediate death.
If it grows on the hands, feet, or forehead,
death occurs the same day.
If it grows slightly to the side,
death occurs in several days.
If it grows farther away,
it may be one or two months.
If it grows very far away,
it may be two or three years.
None survive.
Only the medicine of Chén Huáiqīng's household can counteract it.
Some also smear the fungus poison on the head of a horsewhip or on the horse's bridle;
if it brushes against the hand, it poisons,
if it wipes against the mouth, it kills.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Tián Chéngzhào
Tián Chéngzhào, a general of the Shǔ kingdom of Wáng, once led cavalry to garrison Fèngxiáng.
He then stealthily led his cavalry out,
unsaddled, and rested under a grove of trees.
Suddenly before him, in a quiet patch of ground several feet square,
he saw a small tree, a single stem several feet tall.
It had no branches or leaves,
standing straight and upright,
exceptionally smooth.
Zhào approached it to play with it,
stroking it up and down with his hand.
In a moment,
his fingers felt as if poisoned,
the pain unbearable.
He then whipped his horse and returned to camp.
Upon arrival,
his arm was already as thick as a barrel.
At that time, there was an old village woman skilled in exorcism,
living deep in the mountains.
He urgently sent someone to summon her,
but he was already nearly beyond saving.
The old woman said:
"This is where a seven-inch fetal snake was playing;
it sprayed its venom among the trees.
If someone touches it, the tree branch immediately closes,
causing sudden death.
Zhào said:
"That's right."
He urgently sent someone to dig there.
Sure enough, they caught two snakes,
six or seven inches long.
They killed them.
The old woman then performed an exorcism.
Starting from his upper arm, she drove
gradually down to his wrist,
and then together drove it into his index finger.
When it reached one joint of the index finger,
she could not drive it out.
It shrank into a ball of flesh about the size of a pellet.
So they used a sharp knife to cut off that joint,
and only then was the affliction removed.
The severed joint
was as large as a blown-up ball.
From Yùtáng Xiánhuà.
Snake Venom
Zhào Yánxǐ said:
"Where one is bitten by a venomous snake,
apply a moxa cone,
and moxibustion should be performed right on the spot;
it will cure immediately.
Otherwise, death ensues.
Whenever bitten by a snake, one should immediately
(The characters 'immediately should' were originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy)
perform moxibustion
('Moxibustion' originally written as 'long,'
corrected based on the Ming manuscript copy)
on the spot,
to draw out the venom,
and it will stop.
The source was originally missing;
now seen in Yùtáng Xiánhuà.
Yěgě and Zhèn
Eating yěgě (Gelsemium elegans) causes immediate death.
Where there is yěgě,
there are white wisteria flowers,
which can counteract yěgě poison.
Where the zhèn bird drinks water,
there are rhinoceroses.
If a rhinoceros does not wash its horn in that water,
any creature drinking it will surely die,
because the zhèn bird eats snakes.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Miscellaneous Notes on Medicine
Medical texts say that when a tiger is struck by a poisoned arrow,
it eats clean mud;
when a wild boar is struck by a poisoned arrow,
it digs up qíngní (Adenophora trachelioides) and eats it.
When a pheasant is injured by a hawk,
it applies dìhuáng (rehmannia) leaves to the wound.
Also, yùshí (arsenic ore) can kill rats.
Zhāng Zhuó once tried it;
the rat was poisoned as if drunk,
and did not recognize people,
yet still knew to fetch muddy water to drink,
and shortly recovered.
Birds, beasts, insects, and creatures
still know to detoxify,
how much more should humans!
Those bitten by silkworms
should apply powdered jiǎchóng (a type of beetle);
those bitten by a horse
should burn a whip sheath to ashes and apply it.
This is probably based on mutual subjugation.
Those bitten by a spider
should apply powdered xiónghuáng (realgar);
if a tendon is severed and needs reconnection,
take xuánfùgēn (Inula japonica root), extract its juice by twisting,
align the tendon ends,
apply the juice and bind it,
and it will reconnect as before.
When Shǔ child slaves ran away,
they often cut their tendons;
using this method to reconnect them,
there was not a single failure out of a hundred.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
The Monk from Jiàngzhōu
During the Yǒnghuī era,
in Jiàngzhōu, there was a monk suffering from dysphagia,
unable to swallow any food.
This went on for several years.
As he approached his end,
he told his disciple:
"After I breathe my last,
you may open my chest and throat,
to see what is inside;
I wish to know the root cause."
Having spoken, he died.
The disciple followed his words and opened him to look.
In his chest, he found a creature,
shaped like a fish but with two heads,
its entire body covered in fleshy scales.
The disciple placed it in a bowl,
where it jumped about incessantly.
Playfully, they put various foods into the bowl;
though it was not seen eating,
in a short while,
they all turned into water.
They also put various poisons into it,
and all dissolved away.
At that time, it was midsummer when the indigo plant was ripe;
the monastery community was making dye by the water.
One monk went there,
and put a little indigo dye into the bowl.
This creature became terrified,
ran frantically around the bowl,
and in a short while turned into water.
It is passed down that indigo water can cure dysphagia.
From Guǎng Wǔxíng Jì.
Cuī Shuǎng
During the Yǒnghuī era,
there was a man named Cuī Shuǎng.
Every time he ate raw fish,
he needed three dǒu to be satisfied.
Later, when hungry,
while sliced raw fish was being prepared but not yet ready,
Cuī Shuǎng, unable to bear the hunger,
vomited out a creature,
shaped like a toad.
From then on,
he could no longer eat sliced raw fish.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Liú Lùshì
There was a man named Liú, a former clerk from Hézhōu.
During the Dàlì era, he was dismissed from his post
and lived in a county adjacent to Hézhōu.
He could eat as much as several people combined,
and was especially fond of eating sliced raw fish.
He once said that he had never felt fully satisfied by the taste of sliced fish.
A guest from the county then caught over a hundred catties of fish
and gathered with others in a country courtyard,
to watch him wield his chopsticks.
Liú initially ate several plates of sliced fish,
when suddenly he seemed to have a slight choke,
and coughed up
(The original text had "ké";
amended according to the Míng manuscript copy)
a bone bead the size of a bean.
He then placed it in a teacup
and covered it with a plate.
Before he had finished half his meal,
he noticed strangely that the plate covering the cup was tilting.
Lifting it to look,
he saw that the bone bead had already grown several inches long, taking on a human shape.
The guests at the table all rushed to look,
and it grew as they watched,
in a moment reaching human size.
It then grabbed Liú,
and they fought each other until blood was drawn.
After a long while, they separated and ran off,
one heading west along the hall,
the other turning left at the hall,
both reaching the back door,
where they collided,
merged into one person,
who was Liú.
His spirit seemed addled,
and it took half a day before he could speak.
When asked about what had happened,
he remembered nothing of it.
From then on, Liú detested sliced fish.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Jùróng Deputy Clerk
The deputy clerk of Jùróng County could eat dozens of catties of sliced raw fish
and was always insatiable.
The county magistrate, hearing of his prodigious appetite,
had a hundred catties prepared.
The clerk happily ate it all.
Then he felt stifled and breathless.
After some time,
he vomited out an object
shaped like the sole of a hemp shoe.
The magistrate ordered it washed and
placed it where the sliced fish was;
the sliced fish all turned into water.
Repeated inquiries with doctors and practitioners of esoteric arts
yielded no one who could name it.
The magistrate sent a minor clerk to take it to Yángzhōu to sell it,
hoping someone might recognize it.
He instructed him:
"If there is a buyer,
just keep raising the price,
see how high it goes."
The man arrived in Yángzhōu,
and after four or five days,
a foreigner sought to buy it.
Starting at one thousand cash,
he repeatedly increased the price.
When it reached three hundred strings of cash,
the foreigner would still return it.
There was initially no negotiation.
Someone said to the foreigner:
"This is from the household of the Jùróng County magistrate.
If you must buy it,
you should follow him back."
The foreigner thus followed him to Jùróng.
The county magistrate asked what this object was.
The foreigner said:
"This is the essence of a fish-dissolver;
it can also dissolve lumps and illnesses in a person's abdomen.
For someone suffering from such, take a piece the size of a fingertip,
tie it with a string,
and place it on the affected area.
The lump will then dissolve.
I am the crown prince of my country.
In my youth, I suffered from this illness.
My father sought a cure,
offering a reward of a thousand pieces of gold.
If you are willing to sell it,
you shall gain great profit."
The magistrate eventually sold half of it to him.
From "Guǎng Yì Jì"
Cuī Róng
Cuī Róng, Director of the Imperial Academy and Drafter of Edicts in the Táng dynasty, was ill for over a hundred days.
Worms gnawed in his abdomen, causing unbearable pain.
A creature resembling a gecko
emerged from his lower body,
and shortly after, he died.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Diāo Jùncháo
Diāo Jùncháo, an entertainer from Ānkāng,
had a wife from Bā who had a goiter on her neck.
At first, it was as small as a chicken egg,
gradually growing as large as a three- or four-sheng jar.
After five years,
it became as big as a several-hú cauldron,
so heavy she could not walk.
Inside, there were sounds like those of qín, sè, shēng, qìng, xūn, and chí instruments.
Listening closely,
they seemed to harmonize musically,
clear and delightful.
After several years,
tiny holes like needle tips appeared on the surface of the goiter,
countless in number.
Whenever rain was about to fall,
white smoke would blow from the holes,
drifting like fine silk threads.
Gradually rising and spreading,
it condensed into gathering clouds,
and rain would immediately fall.
Her family, young and old, were afraid of it,
and all urged that she be sent far away to a cave.
Jùncháo, deeply attached, could not bear it.
He said to his wife:
"Pressed by everyone's opinion,
I fear I can no longer protect my spouse.
Shall I send you to an uninhabited place?
What do you think?"
His wife said:
"This illness of mine is truly detestable.
Sending me away means death,
cutting it open also means death.
You should cut it open for me,
and see what is inside."
Jùncháo then sharpened a blade,
and was about to approach his wife with it.
Suddenly, there was a loud sound from within the goiter,
and it split open into four parts.
A large macaque
leaped out and bounded away.
They immediately wrapped the area with cloth and cotton,
and though the goiter was instantly cured,
she fell into a deep, comatose decline.
The next day,
a Daoist priest knocked on the door and said:
"I am the macaque that emerged from the goiter yesterday.
I am originally a monkey spirit,
capable of summoning wind and rain.
Somehow, I became associated with the old flood dragon of the Hànjiāng Ghost Sorrow Pool.
We often watched for boats approaching,
causing them to capsize,
to obtain the food provisions on board,
to nourish my offspring.
Recently, the Great One executed the flood dragon,
and was searching for its accomplices.
So I borrowed your wife's swan-like neck
to hide and preserve my life.
Although we are unrelated,
I have burdened you greatly.
Now, from the mountain god of Fènghuáng Shān,
I have obtained a small amount of miraculous ointment.
Please apply it for her,
and she should recover immediately."
Jùncháo applied it as instructed,
and the wound closed instantly.
Jùncháo then invited the Daoist priest to stay,
cooking chicken and preparing a meal.
After eating,
they bought wine to drink.
The Daoist priest then sang with a melodious voice,
and produced sounds like stringed, wind, and jade instruments,
all resonant and delightful.
Then he bid farewell and left,
and no one knew where he went.
This happened during the Dàdìng era.
From "Xù Xuánguài Lù"
Mr. Lǐ
During the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a Mr. Lǐ from Lǒngxī who, from a commoner's status, was selected for appointment as a military advisor in Guìzhōu.
After assuming his post,
he suffered from a feverish illness for over ten days.
He felt unbearable pain in his left breast,
and upon looking,
it was swollen as if with an abscess.
He summoned a doctor to examine his pulse.
The doctor said:
"There is nothing wrong with your internal organs,
but it seems there is something in your chest cavity,
using its beak to attack your breast,
causing the pain. If it becomes an abscess, it will be untreatable."
After another ten or so days,
his condition worsened.
One day, the abscess burst,
and a pheasant
suddenly flew out from his left breast,
disappearing to an unknown place.
That evening, Mr. Lǐ died.
From "Xuān Shì Zhì"
Wèi Shū
During the Dàlì era (766-779 CE),
Yuán Chá served as the Prefect of Qióngzhōu.
In the prefectural city, there was a man named Wèi Shū,
who was large and robust in physique,
just forty years old,
with elderly parents and a young wife.
Suddenly, he contracted a strange illness.
He felt no pain or bitterness,
but his daily food intake diminished,
and his body wasted away day by day.
Doctors and practitioners of esoteric arts
could only stand by helplessly, at a loss.
Before a full cycle of seasons had passed,
he had become like an infant,
unable to walk, sit, or speak.
His mother and wife
took turns carrying and holding him.
On the day of Wèi Shū's birthday,
the family invited monks to hold a vegetarian feast.
His wife then used a hairpin to prop open his mouth and feed him.
In a short while,
he could finish a small bowl.
From then on, his daily food intake increased,
and his body gradually grew as well.
In less than half a year,
he had returned to his original state.
Yuán Chá then reinstated him to his former post.
His energy and strength for running errands
showed no difference from before.
More than ten years later,
he fought against the Mán tribes
and died in battle.
From *Jíyì Jì* (Records of Collected Marvels)
Huángfǔ Jí
There was a man named Huángfǔ Jí.
His father was the Deputy Governor of Tàiyuán
and doted on him greatly.
Jí was born like an ordinary child.
By the year Rénchén of the Xiántōng era (872 CE),
he was fourteen years old
when he suddenly contracted a strange illness.
It did not involve any piercing pain to the muscles and bones,
but he simply grew violently.
Over time, his height exceeded seven chǐ,
and his waist grew to several arm-spans in girth.
His eating and drinking,
moreover, tripled compared to before.
In the autumn of the following year,
he passed away without any illness.
From *Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú* (Minor Records from Sānshuǐ)
Wáng Bù
During the Yǒngzhēn era (805 CE),
a commoner named Wáng Bù from the Eastern Market was literate,
possessed tens of millions in cash,
and was often hosted by traveling merchants.
He had a daughter, fourteen or fifteen years old,
beautiful and intelligent.
From each of her nostrils hung a polyp,
like the seed of a Chinese honey locust,
with roots as fine as hemp thread,
about an inch long.
Touching them caused pain that pierced to the heart and marrow.
Her father spent millions in cash to treat her,
but she did not recover.
Suddenly, one day,
a foreign Buddhist monk came begging for food
and asked Wáng Bù:
"I know your daughter has a strange illness.
If I may see her once,
I can stop it."
Wáng Bù, upon hearing this, was overjoyed.
He immediately presented his daughter.
The monk then took out some medicine, pure white in color,
and blew it into her nostrils.
After a short while, he plucked them out.
A small amount of yellow fluid emerged,
and she felt no pain at all.
Wáng Bù rewarded him with a hundred gold pieces.
The foreign monk said:
"I am a man who cultivates the Way;
I do not accept lavish gifts.
I only ask for these polyps."
He then bade farewell and left,
swift as if flying.
Wáng Bù also thought he must be a sage.
Estimating the monk had gone five or six blocks away,
block (original text had "cut,"
emended based on the Ming manuscript copy),
another youth appeared,
handsome as jade on a cap,
riding a white horse.
He knocked on the door and said:
"Did a foreign monk just come here?"
Wáng Bù hastily invited him in
and recounted the matter of the foreign monk in detail.
The man sighed with displeasure and said:
"My horse stumbled slightly,
and I ended up behind that monk."
Wáng Bù, astonished,
asked him the reason.
He said:
"The Lord of Heaven lost two music deities.
Recently, I learned they were hiding in your daughter's nostrils.
I am a celestial being,
sent to retrieve them.
I did not expect this monk to take them first.
I will surely be reprimanded."
As Wáng Bù began to bow in respect,
the man raised his hand and vanished.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ* (Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng)
Hóu Yòuxuán
Hóu Yòuxuán, a retired scholar from Jīngzhōu,
once went to the outskirts
and relieved himself on a desolate grave mound.
When he climbed down,
he fell and injured his elbow,
and the sore was severe.
After walking several hundred paces,
he met an old man.
The old man asked what troubled him.
Yòuxuán told him everything
and showed him his elbow.
The old man said:
"I happen to have a good medicine.
I can apply it for you.
Do not open it for ten days,
and it will surely heal."
Yòuxuán did as he was told.
When he unwrapped it to look,
his entire arm had fallen off.
Hóu Yòuxuán had five or six brothers, and they all fell ill in turn.
Each illness inevitably involved bleeding for over a month.
Yòuxuán once saw his elder brother's arms
suddenly break out in six or seven sores.
The smaller ones were like elm seeds,
the larger ones like coins,
and all had human faces.
Ming manuscript copy: This entry and the next are connected and both from *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*, scroll 15.
Also, in the Jiāngbiǎo region, there was once a merchant
who had a sore on his left arm.
It entirely resembled a human face
but caused no other suffering.
The merchant playfully dripped wine into its mouth,
and the face also turned red.
If he fed it with things,
it would eat anything.
If it ate a lot,
he felt the flesh inside his arm swell up,
suspecting the stomach was inside.
If he did not feed it,
then that arm would become emaciated.
A skilled physician
taught him to try various medicines one by one.
Metals, stones, plants, and trees—he tried them all.
When he reached fritillary bulb (bèimǔ),
the sore frowned and closed its mouth.
The merchant happily said:
"This medicine must cure it!"
He then used a small reed tube to pry open its mouth
and poured the medicine in.
After a few days, it scabbed over.
And thus he was healed.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*
Lǐ Yánjí
Cuī Yáofēng, the Defense Commissioner of Jīnzhōu, had a nephew named Lǐ Yánjí.
Suddenly, the eyelid of his left eye itched,
and a small sore grew.
It gradually grew as large as a duck egg,
with a root like a bowstring.
It constantly pressed on his eye, preventing him from opening it,
which troubled Yáofēng greatly.
One day, he made Yánjí drink wine
until he was heavily drunk,
then cut it off.
Yánjí was unaware.
When the growth was cut open,
inside was a yellow sparrow,
which chirped noisily and flew away.
From *Wénqí Lù* (Records of Hearing Marvels)
Kuǎi Liàng
Recluse Kuǎi Liàng
spoke of someone he knew who had a tumor on the forehead.
A doctor cut it open,
and inside was found a black Go stone.
Even when struck with a heavy axe,
it remained undamaged and unbroken.
There was also a man with a tumor on his shin.
While visiting a close relative’s home,
he was bitten by a rabid dog,
which happened to bite right into the tumor.
Inside, over a hundred needles were found,
all of them usable,
and the illness was cured as well.
From *Jīshén Lù* (Records of the Supernatural).
Yuán Tiāngāng was a native of Chéngdū in Shǔjùn.
His father Yuán Jī served as Controller of the Granaries of Liángzhōu.
His grandfather Yuán Sōng served as Prefect of both Púyáng and Pújiāng in Qiánwéi Commandery and as General of Chariots and Cavalry during the Zhōu dynasty.
His great-grandfather Yuán Dá served as Inspector of both Jiāng and Huáng Provinces during the Liáng dynasty,
and as Prefect of both Tiānshuǐ and Huáirén Commanderies during the Zhōu dynasty.
Tiāngāng was orphaned and impoverished in his youth.
He was fond of the arts of the Way and excelled in physiognomy.
During the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty, he served as Magistrate of Huǒjǐng.
In the sixth year of the Zhēnguān era, his term of office ended and he entered the capital.
Emperor Tàizōng summoned him for an audience
and said to Tiāngāng:
"In ancient times, Bā-Shǔ had Yán Jūnpíng.
Now I have you.
How do you compare yourself to him?"
Tiāngāng replied:
"He did not meet with the right times.
Your servant has encountered a sage ruler.
Your servant should surpass him."
At the end of the Suí dynasty's Dàyè era,
Dòu Guǐ was traveling as a guest in Déyáng County, Jiànnán,
and stayed overnight with Tiāngāng.
He asked about his fate due to his poverty and hardship.
Tiāngāng said:
"Your Honor's forehead has a rhinoceros horn bone running through to the Jade Pillow,
and the auxiliary angles are also well-formed.
From now, in ten years,
you will certainly attain wealth and honor,
becoming an excellent assistant to the sage court.
The right auxiliary angle is prominent,
and moreover is clear and bright.
You should achieve great distinction in merit and fame within the domains corresponding to Liáng and Yì Provinces."
Guǐ said:
"If it truly is as you say,
I dare not forget your virtue."
Initially, he became Vice Director of the Branch Department of State Affairs of Yìzhōu.
Upon arriving,
he summoned Tiāngāng and said:
"We met before in Déyáng County.
Surely you have not forgotten."
He treated him with great courtesy
and further requested a detailed examination.
Tiāngāng observed him for a long time and said:
"Your bone structure is well-formed,
no different from before.
However, the color of your eyes is red, piercing through the pupils,
your speech is frivolous and your face is flushed.
As a general, you will kill many people.
I hope you will deeply caution yourself."
Later, he indeed carried out many killings.
In the ninth year of Wǔdé,
Guǐ was summoned to the capital.
He said to Tiāngāng:
"What further office will I obtain?"
Tiāngāng replied:
"The 'Family' area on your face
(Míng manuscript variant: 'Family' as 'Home')
shows your seated position will not move.
The right side of your auxiliary angle is radiant,
and moreover shows a joyful countenance.
Upon reaching the capital, you will certainly receive the sage emperor's favor
and return to this post."
That year, he was indeed reappointed as Military Governor of Yìzhōu.
When Tiāngāng first arrived in Luòyáng,
he settled in the Qīnghuà Ward.
People from court and commoners gathered around him,
and his place was always full of visitors.
At that time, Dù Yān, Wáng Guī, and Wéi Tǐng, three men, came to see him.
Tiāngāng said to Yān:
"Your Lántái area is well-formed,
and your Xuétáng area is broad and wide."
He said to Guī:
"Your Honor's Fǎlìng area is well-formed,
and the Tiāndì areas face each other.
From now, in ten years,
you should obtain an important fifth-rank position."
He said to Tǐng:
"Your Honor's face resembles the face of a great beast.
The Wénjiǎo area is well-formed.
You will certainly receive support and connection from noble persons.
Initially, you will be a military officer."
He further said to Dù Yān:
"Beyond twenty years,
I fear the three worthies will together be reprimanded and dismissed.
It will be temporary; you will leave and soon return."
Yān soon was promoted to Attendant Censor.
During the Wǔdé era, he served as Military Administrator and Literary Academy Scholar of the Tiāncè Mansion.
Wáng Guī served as Palace Secretary of the Heir Apparent Yǐn.
Wéi Tǐng, since the end of the Suí,
was recommended by the Heir Apparent Yǐn to serve as Director of the Watch.
In the sixth year of Wǔdé,
they were all exiled to Juànzhōu.
When Yān and the others reached Yìzhōu,
they saw Tiāngāng and wept, saying:
"Master Yuán's words previously in Luòyáng
all came true as your lofty prediction indicated.
Now the situation is like this.
Please examine us once more."
Tiāngāng said:
"Your bone structures
are greatly superior to before.
You will return not long from now,
and in the end will all enjoy glory and honor."
By the sixth month of the ninth year,
they were all recalled to the capital.
Passing through Yìzhōu again,
they visited Tiāngāng.
Tiāngāng said:
"Upon reaching the capital, Master Dù
will obtain an important third-rank position.
His lifespan is not something Tiāngāng knows.
Masters Wáng and Wéi,
later on, should obtain third rank,
and moreover will have longevity.
However, their later paths will not be deeply fulfilled,
Master Wéi especially so."
When Yān reached the capital,
he was appointed Grand Master of Remonstrance
and concurrently Minister of Personnel.
He presented a poem to Tiāngāng, which said:
"Yī and Lǚ are deeply admirable,
Sōng and Qiáo are certainly illusory.
To tie the wind is ultimately impossible,
to cast off sandals—where would one go?
For now, cherish the beauty of fine silk,
and should distance oneself from ivy and vines.
Having met a Yáng Déyì,
no longer will one dwell in idleness long."
Wáng Guī soon became Palace Attendant
and was sent out as Prefect of Tóngzhōu.
Wéi Tǐng served successively as Prefect of Méngzhōu,
and both died in office,
all as Tiāngāng had said.
During the Zhēnguān era,
an imperial edict summoned him to the Jiǔchéng Palace.
At that time, the Secretariat Drafter Cén Wénběn
had him examine him.
Tiāngāng said:
"The Drafter's Xuétáng area is well-formed,
his eyebrows moreover extend past his eyes.
His literary talent resonates throughout the realm.
His head has raw bone,
yet it is not fully matured.
Looking from behind, he shows no sign of third rank at all.
Looking from the front, third rank can be obtained.
However, his four limbs are weak and frail,
his bones and flesh are not proportionate.
Obtaining third rank
is likely an omen of shortened lifespan."
Later, Wénběn's office reached Secretariat Director,
and he soon died.
Fáng Xuánlíng and Lǐ Shěnsù together saw Tiāngāng.
Fáng said:
"Lǐ relies on his talent and is arrogant toward others.
Sir, first examine what office he will obtain."
Tiāngāng said:
"Fifth rank is not seen.
If it is a pure and important office of sixth rank or below, he has that."
Lǐ did not ask further,
saying:
"Examine what office Master Fáng will obtain."
Tiāngāng said:
"This man will have great wealth and honor.
If you, Sir, wish to obtain fifth rank,
then seek it from this man."
Lǐ did not believe him.
Later, Master Fáng became Prime Minister.
Lǐ died while serving as Reminder.
Emperor Gāozōng heard of the earlier words
and ordered Fáng to grant him a fifth-rank office.
Fáng petitioned to grant him the post of Grand Master of Remonstrance.
Duke Shēn, Gāo Shìlián, said to Tiāngāng:
"What further office will you, Sir, obtain?"
Tiāngāng said:
"I know my own physiognomic fortune is already exhausted.
It is not fitting to obtain more.
I fear a great calamity this year in the fourth month."
He did not pass the fourth month and died.
Jiǎng Yǎn, Prefect of Púzhōu,
in his childhood,
Tiāngāng made a prediction for him, saying:
"This child will suffer many years of imprisonment.
Later, he will have great wealth and honor.
Starting from a certain office, he will reach the position of Prefect.
He will live to eighty-three.
In that year, on the fifth day of the eighth month, at the noon hour, his official salary will end."
Yǎn later campaigned against Liáodōng,
was captured by the enemy,
and imprisoned in an underground pit for seven years.
After Gāolì was pacified and he returned,
he obtained offices exactly as Tiāngāng had said,
reaching Prefect of Púzhōu.
At eighty-three,
he said to his family:
"Lord Yuán said that on the fifth day of the eighth month, my official salary would cease,
and I would die."
He set out wine and food,
and bid farewell to his relatives and old friends.
Indeed, an imperial edict arrived,
granting him retirement,
and thus his salary stopped.
He passed away several years later.
Lǐ Yìfǔ was residing in Shǔ,
when Tiāngāng saw him and, finding him extraordinary, said:
"This gentleman will reach the highest rank among ministers,
but his lifespan will not be long."
He then requested to lodge with him,
entrusting his son to Lǐ, saying:
"This child has the appearance of a seventh-rank official,
I hope you will support and promote him."
Yìfǔ agreed.
He then asked Tiāngāng about his own lifespan,
to which he replied:
"Beyond fifty-two,
I do not know."
Later, Yìfǔ was successively recommended by the Pacification Commissioner Lǐ Dàliàng, Palace Attendant-in-ordinary Liú Jì, and others.
Summoned for an audience,
he was tested by being ordered to compose a poem "Chanting on the Crow."
He completed it instantly.
His poem said:
"In daylight, it flutters with morning hues,
Amidst the zither, it accompanies night's cries.
How many trees are there in the Shanglin Park?
Yet not a single branch is lent for it to perch."
Tàizōng deeply admired it, saying:
"I will lend you the entire tree,
not just a single branch."
From the position of a ceremonial officer in the Chancellery,
he was exceptionally promoted to Investigating Censor.
His subsequent lifespan and rank
all matched Tiāngāng's words.
Duke of Zànhuáng, Lǐ Qiáo, showed exceptional talent from a young age.
Among his five brothers,
none lived past thirty,
only Qiáo had already grown to adulthood.
His mother grew increasingly worried
and visited Tiāngāng.
Tiāngāng said:
"The young master's spirit and energy are pure and refined,
but his lifespan is unfortunately not long,
I fear he may not pass thirty."
His mother was greatly distressed by this.
Qiáo was already renowned at the time,
and everyone expected him to achieve high status and prosperity.
Hearing this, he did not believe it.
His mother then invited Master Yuán,
prepared a meal, and requested a diagnosis.
He said:
"It is certain."
She further requested that he share a connected couch in the study to sit and sleep.
Yuán got on the bed and slept soundly,
while Lǐ alone could not sleep.
At the fifth watch, he suddenly fell asleep,
and Yuán happened to wake up.
Observing Lǐ Qiáo, he saw no breath,
and checking with his hand,
found no breath under his nose.
Initially greatly shocked and puzzled,
after a long while of careful observation,
he discovered his breath entering and exiting was actually from his ears.
Patting him, he announced:
"I have found it."
He then rose and congratulated his mother, saying:
"I checked several times,
but could not find it.
Now I have finally seen it.
The young master is destined for great nobility and longevity.
This is 'turtle breath,'
signifying nobility and longevity but not wealth."
Later events indeed matched his words.
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign, he was appointed Chancellor,
yet his household was constantly poor.
At that time, the Emperor frequently visited the residences of chancellors.
Seeing Qiáo sleeping under a plain black silk canopy,
the Emperor sighed and said:
"For a State Chancellor to be like this
is unbefitting of a great nation's dignity."
He then bestowed upon him an imperial embroidered silk canopy.
Qiáo slept under it,
but until dawn felt uneasy,
and his body began to feel ill.
He then personally memorialized, saying:
"When I was young, a physiognomist told me
I should not have extravagance.
Therefore, I cannot sleep peacefully under it."
The Emperor sighed for a long time,
and allowed him to use the old one as he wished.
Qiáo was short in stature,
and his nose and mouth lacked signs of fullness or prosperity.
At the time, people did not expect him to receive high salaries.
While he was in Rùn Prefecture,
serving as an envoy to mine silver in the mountains of Xuān Prefecture,
false rumors spread of his sudden death.
The entire court mourned and lamented.
Vice Minister of the Ministry of Works Zhāng Xúngǔ,
was Qiáo's maternal uncle.
Hearing this, he was deeply worried
and sent relatives to inquire about the truth.
It happened that a southern envoy said:
"He is truly dead."
Xúngǔ shed tears of sorrow,
and many court officials came to console him.
At that time, there was a man
known for his skill in bone physiognomy,
who had largely mastered Yuán Tiāngāng's techniques.
Many court nobles secretly consulted him.
This man said:
"I have long known that Secretariat Drafter Lǐ's official salary and rank are rather meager."
Everyone listened intently.
The man continued:
"Although Secretariat Drafter Lǐ possesses talent and literary brilliance,
his appearance, crown, ears, eyes, nose, and mouth
show almost no signs of great achievement.
Recently, seeing him promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-ordinary,
I already worried for him."
Everyone agreed.
Qiáo eventually held the position of Chancellor three times,
reaching the utmost nobility among ministers.
Thus, Qiáo's physiognomy was difficult to discern,
yet Tiāngāng succeeded.
Also, Wáng Dāng, Prefect of Shǎn Prefecture, had a daughter.
He gathered the civil and military officials of the prefecture and county,
and ordered Tiāngāng to select a son-in-law.
Tiāngāng said:
"There is no noble son-in-law here.
I only recognize a certain Commandant Yáo,
who will have a noble son.
You can marry her to him.
You will surely gain strength from it."
Dāng followed his advice and married her to him.
People at the time all laughed at this,
but this was Yuánchóng.
He was twenty-three at the time,
fond of hunting,
and had not yet studied books.
Once, while visiting a relative for a drink,
he encountered a physiognomist who said to him:
"You will attain wealth and nobility later."
Having said this, he left.
Yáo chased after him and asked,
the physiognomist said:
"You are very noble,
and will become Chancellor."
Returning home, he told his mother,
who urged him to study.
Chóng then gave up his hawks and falcons,
changed his ways, and diligently pursued learning.
He entered official service as a funeral attendant,
and eventually rose to the position of Chancellor.
Tiāngāng had a son named Kèshī,
who inherited his father's profession,
and his predictions were also accurate.
Kèshī held the office of Superintendent of the Granaries and Sacrifices.
During the Xiǎnqìng era,
he served alongside Jiǎ Wéntōng.
Emperor Gāozōng placed a mouse in a silver box,
and ordered various diviners to guess its contents.
All said there was one mouse.
Kèshī also said it was a mouse,
but that it entered as one and would exit as four.
The mouse had entered the box,
and had already given birth to three offspring,
so indeed there were four.
Kèshī once crossed a river with a scholar.
Boarding the boat,
he looked at the complexions of all the people on board,
and said to his companion:
"We cannot depart quickly."
So they led each other ashore.
Privately, he said:
"I see several dozen people on the boat,
all with black qi beneath their noses,
signifying a great calamity soon.
How can we knowingly follow them?
Let us just wait a little."
Before the boat departed,
they suddenly saw a man.
His spirit and expression were lofty and bright,
though he limped on one foot,
carrying a load and driving a donkey onto the boat.
Seeing this man, Kèshī
then said to his companion:
"We can go now.
A noble person is aboard,
we have nothing to worry about."
They boarded the boat and set off.
In midstream,
wind and waves suddenly arose.
Though the danger and fear were extreme,
they ultimately crossed safely.
Inquiring about the man who drove the donkey,
it turned out to be Lóu Shīdé.
He later rose to the position of Palace Attendant-in-ordinary.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù" (Records of Fixed Fate).
Zhāng Jiǒngcáng
Zhāng Jiǒngcáng was skilled in physiognomy,
and was as famous as Yuán Tiāngāng.
There was a certain Péi from Hédōng,
who at fifty-three was still a Sānwèi (Three Guardsman).
During the summer rotation,
he entered the capital and stopped at a shop west of the Chǎnshuǐ to buy a meal.
An old man sitting with him said to Péi:
"Noble sir."
Péi replied:
"I am fifty-three this year,
still a mere Sānwèi.
How could I hope for official rank?
Why do you, old father, call me a noble sir?"
The old man smiled and said:
"You simply do not know yourself.
Twenty-five days from now,
you will obtain a third-rank office."
Having said this, he bid farewell.
It was Zhāng Jiǒngcáng.
When Péi reached the capital,
twenty-one days of his rotation had already passed.
It happened that Tàizōng's qì illness flared up.
Famous doctors and excellent medicines
were administered, but none were effective.
He could not sit, lie down, sleep, or eat in peace.
An edict was issued ordering all Sānwèi and above,
and court officials and below,
to submit prescriptions.
Péi, following the example, submitted a prescription:
milk decocted with bìbá (long pepper) was taken,
and the illness was immediately cured.
An imperial order was sent to the Secretariat,
instructing them to grant him a fifth-rank office.
The Chief Ministers hesitated,
not daring to propose a candidate.
After a few days,
Tàizōng's qì illness flared up again,
and again he took bìbá and recovered.
He then asked what office the former Sānwèi had received?
The Secretariat replied:
"It has not yet been determined whether to grant him a fifth-rank civil or military post."
Tàizōng angrily said:
"He cured an emperor who brings order from chaos and saved my life.
Why has he not been given an office?
If he had cured a Chief Minister's illness instead,
he would surely have gotten the office the same day."
That very day,
by special grace, he was granted a third-rank substantive capital post,
and appointed Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglú Qīng).
He was promoted several times, eventually becoming Prefect of his home province.
Liú Rénguǐ
was from Wèishì.
When he was seven or eight years old,
Jiǒngcáng passed by his gate and saw him.
He said to his parents:
"This child's bone structure is most extraordinary;
he is destined for noble rank and emolument.
You should nurture and instruct him well."
Later, when Rénguǐ was serving as Deputy of Chéncāng,
Jiǒngcáng, having been exiled to Jiànnán at the time,
was passing through Qízhōu.
Féng Chángmìng was Prefect of Qízhōu,
and had Jiǒngcáng examine the officials from the Administrative Assistants down,
but none were fated to reach the fifth rank.
Coming out, he met Rénguǐ
and suddenly changed countenance, looking awed.
Turning back, he said to Prefect Féng:
"I have found a noble man."
He then examined him carefully.
Later, Rénguǐ rose to become Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Púyè).
Jiǒngcáng said to him:
"Twenty years ago,
I saw a child in Wèishì.
His bone structure was similar to yours, sir.
I did not ask his name at the time,
and did not know who it was."
Guǐ (Rénguǐ) laughed and said:
"That child from Wèishì
was none other than I, Rénguǐ."
Jiǒngcáng said:
"You, sir, will not exceed the fourth rank.
But if you commit a great crime,
you will then reach the third rank or above."
Later, Rénguǐ went from being a Supervising Secretary to serve as Prefect of Qīngzhōu,
overseeing maritime transport.
He encountered a storm and lost ships.
He was slandered by Duke Héjiān, Lǐ Yìfǔ.
Censor Yuán Yìshì was dispatched to investigate him.
The Court of Judicial Review sentenced him to death,
but by special decree he was spared death and stripped of his rank.
He served with merit in Liáodōng,
then entered the court as Chief Censor (Dàsīxiàn),
and ultimately rose to the position of Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Zuǒ Púyè).
Lú Jiāyáng had estate lands in Xǔzhōu,
adjacent to those of his maternal elder, a certain Zhāng from Héqīng.
Zhāng held the post of Investigating Censor,
and was in mourning for a parent.
When the mourning period ended,
he took Jiāyáng with him to visit Zhāng Jiǒngcáng.
At that time, Jiāyáng was still a young boy.
Zhāng went in to see Jiǒngcáng,
leaving Jiāyáng standing outside the middle gate.
Zhāng said to Jiǒngcáng:
"My mourning is over; I wish to see the Chief Ministers.
How do you think it will go?"
Jiǒngcáng said:
"You, Censor, will retain your current post.
Even if promoted,
you will not exceed a Bureau Director."
Having said this,
Jiǒngcáng escorted him out the door.
Suddenly, he saw Jiāyáng.
He said to Zhāng:
"Your official rank and nobility will not match this child's.
This child is destined for great nobility and long life;
he will govern over ten commanderies or more."
Later, Jiāyáng served as Prefect of ten commanderies,
and lived to eighty.
Duke Wèiqí, Yuán Zhōng,
when young, once visited Jiǒngcáng.
Jiǒngcáng treated him very coldly.
Yuán Zhōng inquired about his future prospects,
but Jiǒngcáng gave no answer.
Yuán Zhōng angrily said:
"I have traveled a thousand *li* not sparing provisions,
not merely walking,
certainly believing you, illustrious sir, had something to teach me.
Yet you hold a wooden tongue,
not expressing your earnest intentions.
Moreover, adversity, success, poverty, and lowliness
are determined by Heaven.
What concern is it of yours?"
With that, he flicked his sleeves and left.
Jiǒngcáng quickly rose and said:
"Your destiny for rank and emolument
lies precisely in this anger.
In the future, you will reach the highest position among subjects."
Gāo Jìngyán served as Legal Advisor of Yōngzhōu.
Jiǒngcáng wrote of him:
"From this, he will become Vice Director in the Ministry of Justice, then Supervising Secretary, and later Prefect of Guǒzhōu.
After ten years,
he will then serve as Vice Minister of Justice and Vice Minister of Personnel.
After two years, he will suffer from wind illness,
and be transferred to be Prefect of Guózhōu.
This will be his final substantive post.
He will live to seventy-three."
When he became Supervising Secretary,
and was on duty,
Zétiān asked Gāo Shìlián:
"What relation is Gāo Jìngyán to you?"
Shìlián said:
"He is my nephew."
Later, Zétiān asked Jìngyán.
Jìngyán said:
"My native place is Shāndōng.
Shìlián is a meritorious noble.
We share the same clan name,
but he is not a close relative of mine."
Zétiān told Shìlián what he said.
Shìlián said:
"Jìngyán lacks virtuous conduct.
I once reprimanded him angrily,
so now he does not acknowledge me."
Zétiān was displeased and angry,
and sent him out to be Prefect of Guǒzhōu.
Shìlián's princess (wife) was still alive.
When Jìngyán went to bid farewell,
the princess was angry and refused to see him.
Thus, he could not get a transfer.
After nine years,
both the princess and Shìlián had died.
Later, the court realized he had been wronged,
recalled him to the capital, and made him Vice Minister of Justice.
He rose to Vice Minister of Personnel.
Suddenly, he suffered from wind illness.
Zétiān ordered him to be given a small, nearby prefecture to recuperate,
and he was appointed Prefect of Guózhōu.
He died at seventy-three.
All was as Jiǒngcáng had said.
Yáo Yuánchóng, Lǐ Jiǒngxiù, and Dù Jǐngquán, the three of them,
went together to visit Jiǒngcáng during the selection process.
Jiǒngcáng said:
"You three gentlemen will all become Chief Ministers.
However, Yáo will be the most wealthy and noble,
entering and leaving the post of Chief Minister several times."
Later, it all happened as he said.
From *Dìngmìng Lù* (Records of Fixed Destiny).
Zhāng Jiǎnzhī
When Zhāng Jiǎnzhī served as the deputy magistrate of Qīngchéng County,
he was already sixty-three years old.
A skilled physiognomist said:
"Later, you will reach the highest position among ministers."
No one believed it.
Later, he took the imperial examination and failed.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān was surprised that so few candidates had passed,
and ordered a review among those who had failed.
The officials reported that one candidate had excellent answers,
but because his handwriting did not meet the standards,
he was rejected.
When Wǔ Zétiān read his answers,
she considered him a rare talent.
She summoned him for an audience,
questioned him about the matters in his answers,
and found him extraordinary.
She immediately granted him a top rank,
and appointed him as the county captain of Wángwū.
Later, he rose to become chancellor,
and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Hànyáng.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Lù Jǐngróng
Lù Jǐngróng served as the magistrate of Xīnzhèng.
A visitor told him:
"Thirty years from now,
you will become the prefect of this prefecture,
but you will sit in the office of the legal affairs department."
Lord Lù did not believe it.
At the time, Lord Lù noted that there was a paulownia tree in the courtyard of the legal affairs department.
Thirty years later, he indeed became the prefect of Zhèng Prefecture,
and in front of the hall where he sat, there was a paulownia tree.
He then inquired about it,
and was told:
"This hall was originally the office of the legal affairs department.
In previous years, the prefect found the residence too narrow,
so he merged the legal affairs department's office into the prefect's hall."
Only then did he realize the prophecy had come true.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Chéng Xíngchén
Chéng Xíngchén was sixty years old when he served as the county captain of Chénliú.
His colleagues, considering him old and holding a low position,
often mocked him.
Later, an old man came to visit,
and spoke of his official career and lifespan.
Soon, the county officials all arrived,
and continued to mock and tease him.
The old man said:
"None of you gentlemen will match Lord Chéng in official career or lifespan.
None of you gentlemen will match Lord Chéng in official career or lifespan.
From now on,
Lord Chéng will hold thirty-one official posts,
and live beyond ninety years of age.
He will rise to the position of Censor-in-chief,
and will face a crisis when he becomes Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs."
No one believed it.
