At that time, Chéng Xíngchén's brother-in-law had just been appointed as a county magistrate in Jiàng Prefecture,
and his sister was about to join her husband at his post.
She asked the old man to divine whether it would be good or bad.
The old man saw her and said:
"Your husband is already ill now.
Eighty lǐ from Jiàng Prefecture,
you will surely receive bad news."
His sister, worried and distressed, set out.
Eighty lǐ from the prefecture,
the bad news indeed arrived.
Later, Chéng Xíngchén became Censor-in-chief,
and died in his nineties.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and Right Chancellor,
exactly as predicted.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Wèi Yuánzhōng
Chancellor Wèi Yuánzhōng
and Minister of Rites Zhèng Wéizhōng were both from Sòng.
Both possessed talent and ability,
and had been close friends since youth.
Approaching thirty years of age,
they had not yet established their reputations.
A skilled physiognomist saw them
and treated them with exceptional respect.
He said to himself:
"The ancients said that like attracts like—
is it true?
Lord Wèi will reach the highest position among ministers,
with resounding fame and glory.
His heart is loyal and upright,
honest and unwavering.
He will surely become a pillar,
the chief assistant to the state.
Noble he will be, indeed,
but his fate will be full of hardships and setbacks.
There will be times of worry and fear,
but all these will occur before he becomes chancellor.
They are nothing to worry about.
He need only act when the situation arises,
and respond when he hears advice."
To Lord Zhèng he said:
"You, sir, will wear the golden seal and purple ribbon,
with boundless official fortune and emolument.
You will enter the third rank,
and also rise to the eight high ministerial positions.
You will never be demoted or dismissed from office,
and your lifespan will be long and far-reaching."
Wèi Yuánzhōng further asked:
"In what year will my emolument begin?
And in what place will my official career end?"
The physiognomist replied:
"If you submit a memorial this year,
your emolument will then advance.
After you cease to be chancellor,
you will travel to inspect the river borders,
and there your official career will end."
Thus, that same year,
he submitted a memorial at Liáng Palace stating his views.
For a long time, there was no response or decision,
and when his provisions ran out, he returned.
On the road, he met an old friend,
who kindly gave him silk fabric.
When he returned to Liáng Palace,
an imperial edict had already been issued summoning him for an audience.
He was appointed as a proofreader,
and later promoted to Vice Censor-in-chief and Grand Master.
In between, he offended the emperor's wishes and transgressed against powerful figures,
repeatedly suffering reprimands and censure,
and was imprisoned for thorough interrogation.
Whenever he considered ending his own life,
he would recall the physiognomist's words,
and again console himself.
Instead, he became even more outspoken in stating his views,
never bending his will or suppressing his words.
In the end, he escaped disaster
and rose to become chancellor.
After being exiled from the position of Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs to the southern commandery,
he traveled by river for several days
and fell seriously ill.
He then said:
"Will I end here?"
And indeed, he died.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Péi Guāngtíng
Yáo Yuánchóng
served as Secretariat Director at the beginning of the Kāiyuán era.
A skilled physiognomist came to see him,
and Yuánchóng had him secretly observe at the court hall.
He was to identify
He was to identify
Originally written as "zì" (self), corrected according to the Ming manuscript.
which officials would later become chancellors.
He pointed out Péi Guāngtíng.
At that time, Guāngtíng was a military officer.
Yáo had him come to his residence to speak with him,
and again had the physiognomist observe him carefully from behind a curtain in the hall.
After Guāngtíng left,
the physiognomist said:
"It is certain."
Yáo said:
"A chancellor
assists heaven in transforming the world.
Without the right person, the position cannot be held.
Just now, speaking with Péi,
he did not seem like a man capable of handling affairs,
and his literary learning is also lacking.
How could he have such fortune?"
The physiognomist said:
"What you speak of, sir, is talent,
while what I speak of is fate.
Talent and fate are fundamentally different."
Yáo fell silent, unconvinced.
Later, Péi indeed became chancellor for several years,
and while serving in the court,
he was also known as a famous chancellor.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Ān Lùshān
Emperor Xuánzōng was at the Qínzhèng Tower,
where various performances were staged below.
He had Ān Lùshān seated in the eastern compartment to watch.
Emperor Sùzōng remonstrated, saying:
"Throughout history, both ancient and modern,
there has never been a subject who sat together with the sovereign to watch performances."
Emperor Xuánzōng replied:
"He has an extraordinary appearance;
I wish to ward off misfortune, hence this arrangement."
On another occasion, he once feasted with him at night.
Lùshān, drunk, lay down to sleep
and transformed into a pig with a dragon's head.
His attendants hurriedly reported this.
The Emperor said:
"He is a pig-dragon;
he can accomplish nothing."
In the end, he did not have him killed.
Initially, Lùshān served as a minor clerk under Duke Hán, Zhāng Rényuàn.
Rényuàn often had Lùshān wash his feet.
Rényuàn had a black mole on the sole of his foot.
While washing, Lùshān secretly peered at it.
Rényuàn looked back and said with a laugh:
"This black mole is a sign of my noble destiny.
You alone are peeking at it;
could it be that you also have one?"
Lùshān replied:
"I am a lowly man,
yet unfortunately, I have them on both feet.
Compared to the General's, mine are darker and larger.
I truly do not know what omen this signifies."
Rényuàn observed this and found it remarkable,
thereafter treating him with even greater closeness and favor.
He pledged to take him as his sworn son
and further promoted him with special favor.
From "Dìngmìng Lù."
Sūn Sīmiǎo
Sūn Sīmiǎo was over a hundred years old
and skilled in medical arts.
He said to Gāo Zhòngshū:
"You bear the signs of nobility;
you will serve as Prefect several times.
If you become Prefect of Qízhōu,
I have a son serving as a Commandant there,
who will be under your administration.
Although he may deserve caning,
I hope you will remember this old man's words
and be willing to pardon him."
Later, it happened as he said.
After the son had already been stripped for punishment,
Gāo suddenly remembered,
and thus released him.
From "Dìngmìng Lù."
Master Sūn
There was a certain Master Sūn (his given name not recorded)
who was skilled in physiognomy.
When he arrived at Mùzhōu,
the Commandery Governor ordered him to examine all the officials.
At that time, Fáng Guǎn served as Registrar,
and Cuī Huàn was Commandant of Wànnián,
demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Tónglú County.
Master Sūn said:
"These two gentlemen will reach the positions of Chief Ministers.
However, Fáng—
his spirit and energy are of great treasure,
destined to be held within the palm of authority.
Cuī will later become Prefect of Hángzhōu.
Although I may not witness it,
I shall still receive his kindness."
Later, Fáng indeed carried the imperial edict
from Shǔ to Língwǔ to present to Emperor Sùzōng.
Cuī indeed became Prefect of Hángzhōu.
Upon taking office, he sought out Master Sūn,
only to find he had already passed away some ten days earlier.
He then appointed Master Sūn's son as a Staff Officer
and bestowed silk and gifts to support his family.
From "Guǎngdé Shényì Lù."
The Héng Physiognomist
During the Kāiyuán era, there was a physiognomist whose name was unknown.
He claimed to have come from Héng Mountain,
so people called him the Héng Physiognomist.
He resided in the Xuānpíng Ward of the capital.
At that time, Lǐ Línfǔ served as Tutor to the Heir Apparent.
He went to see him.
Upon entering the gate,
he found Zhèng Shǎowēi and Yán Gǎo already in the central courtyard.
The physiognomist invited them to sit
and said to Lǐ:
"Since I arrived here,
I have seen many people,
but none as noble as you, sir.
Moreover, as the state places great importance on penal law,
you, sir, will hold the office of Minister of Justice.
As the court prioritizes the selection of officials,
you, sir, will assume the duties of Chief Minister.
Furthermore, you will wield the vermilion brush of authority,
and be chosen for military command.
Added to this, you will be enfeoffed with lands and titles,
reaching the pinnacle of glory and splendor.
The sovereign's favor will be deep and enduring,
and your influence will be extensive.
You will also hold concurrent posts in the Southern Department,
with ranks increasing fourfold.
Grasping the affairs of the central administration,
your tenure will span eighteen years.
Officials will look up to your authority,
and the common people will benefit from your kindness.
This will be unprecedented in history."
Turning to Yán and Zhèng, he said:
"To hear this in advance
is not unfortunate.
You two gentlemen should treat him with respect and deference;
otherwise, regret and misfortune will arise."
At that time, Yán and Zhèng each possessed reputations for talent,
while Lǐ's fame was not yet established.
The two gentlemen harbored feelings of rivalry,
and upon hearing the physiognomist's words,
considered them utterly unfounded.
They assented vaguely and rose,
asking nothing further.
Lǐ then took his leave.
Later, when Lǐ was appointed as Secretariat Director,
Zhèng was then serving as Vice-Minister of Justice.
Recalling past events,
Lǐ said to Zhèng:
"That physiognomist from Xuānpíng back then—
everyone thought his words were absurd,
yet they have proven slightly accurate."
Not long after,
Zhèng was sent out as Prefect of Qízhōu.
He spoke of this matter with his close associates.
Before a year had passed,
he was further demoted to Military Aide of Wànzhōu.
Yán, from his post as Department Director,
was also sent to govern a distant commandery.
From "Dìngmìng Lù."
Also, Lǐ Línfǔ was orphaned young
and was raised by his maternal aunt of the Yuán family,
living in Yīchuān.
At that time, Línfǔ was ten years old
and was playing with other children by the roadside.
An old man sighed and gazed at him intently.
People asked him why.
The old man said:
"Wealth and honor truly are unknowable."
Pointing at Lǐ, he said:
"This child will later become Secretariat Director,
for a full twenty years.
My sigh was because who could distinguish him from ordinary children at play?"
From "Dìngmìng Lù."
Mǎ Lùshī
Wǔgōng's physiognomist Mǎ Lù was skilled in fortune-telling.
Xiāo Xuánxuán, the Registrar of Cháng'ān, along with the County Commandants Lǐ Qiáo and Lǐ Quánchāng, went together to seek his judgment.
Mister Mǎ said:
"All three of you will achieve nobility and prominence.
The elder Commandant Lǐ,
will reach the highest position among ministers,
his fame and reputation will be resplendent,
no appointment in the Southern Department will be merely nominal for him,
and he will enter the Secretariat three times.
The younger Commandant Lǐ,
will also have a distinguished official career,
obtaining important positions of the fifth rank or above,
and will ultimately reach the rank of a Chief Minister or Director.
Registrar Xiāo will experience obscurity in middle age,
but will achieve great wealth and honor later in life.
From now on, in ten years,
your family will suffer a great calamity,
your brothers will all be exiled,
only you and one younger brother will be spared.
Then, after another ten years,
you will finally obtain an official post.
When the elder Commandant Lǐ is serving at court,
you should receive his recommendation and appointment.
When the younger Commandant Lǐ enters the Department as an official,
he will make the decisive judgment for you."
Later, Xiāo left his post in Cháng'ān
and became a Gentleman of the Palace Library.
After Empress Wǔ Zétiān gained power,
Empress Wáng was destroyed.
Xiāo Xuán was related to her by marriage,
so his entire family was exiled.
Six brothers in total,
were sent to Lǐngnán.
Only Xiāo and his younger brother Xuàn
were sent to Liáodōng.
Not long after, an envoy was dispatched to deal with the exiles.
Those in Lǐngnán all perished,
only those in Liáodōng were spared.
The two brothers
thus lived as fugitives for over ten years.
By the beginning of the Shénlóng era,
they finally received pardon.
At that time, Lǐ Qiáo was serving as Chancellor.
He suddenly encountered Xiāo on the street.
He sent someone to ask if it was Gentleman Xiāo of the Palace Library,
and then said to him:
"Have you forgotten the words of Wǔgōng's Mister Mǎ?"
Thereupon, he promoted and employed him.
At that time, the younger Commandant Lǐ was serving as Vice Director of the Ministry of Justice,
and passed judgment to restore his family.
Lord Xiāo ultimately served in both central and provincial prestigious and important posts,
reaching high-ranking positions,
holding third-rank offices for over ten tenures.
From "Dìngmìng Lù"
Lǐ Hánzhāng
When Cuī Yuán was still obscure,
he wished to sit for the jìnshì examinations.
In Wèi County, he met the Market Director Lǐ Hánzhāng, who said:
"You are destined to enter officialdom through military service,
and your promotions will not stop,
until you become Chancellor."
In the twenty-third year of the Kāiyuán era,
he sat for the military command examination.
He also served as a tribute scholar from Hénán Prefecture.
On that day, he was taking the examination at Fútáng Temple,
when an imperial edict arrived,
summoning generals right in the examination hall.
He was appointed as a Halberdier and Military Advisor for Héxī.
When taking the examination,
he sat in the same hall and next to Dòu Gōnghéng, the County Commandant of Shàn County, Yuèzhōu,
who personally witnessed this event.
Afterwards, his promotions never stopped,
and within less than twenty years,
he was appointed Secretariat Director and Duke of Zhàoguó,
with an actual fief of five hundred households.
Also, when Cuī Yuán was about to become Vice Director of the Bureau of Honors,
after the mourning period, he went to visit Master Kèshèn at Huìchāng Temple.
The master laughed and said:
"Others all move from the Censorate to the Departments,
but you, sir, will move from the Departments to the Censorate.
From now on, you will often walk among spears and halberds,
and later you will achieve great honor."
Not long after, he became Vice Director of the Ministry of Justice and concurrently Investigating Censor,
serving as Acting Military Governor of Jiànnán.
After entering Jiànmén,
his travels were often accompanied by armed conflict.
Within less than a year,
he achieved meritorious deeds.
When Cuī first entered Shǔ,
he often told his relatives and friends this story himself.
From "Dìngmìng Lù"
Shàng Héng
When Shàng Héng, later Vice Censor-in-Chief, was a child playing games,
he once took off his blue-green robe,
wearing only a purple robe.
A skilled physiognomist saw him and said:
"This child, in the future,
will surely take off blue-green and put on purple."
Later, Héng served as Assistant Magistrate of Púyáng.
When Ān Lùshān rebelled,
he maintained his integrity and did not accept office from the rebels.
A certain general ordered Héng to wear the crimson robe and fish-bag,
and provisionally appointed him to an office,
but Héng refused, saying:
"I am destined to take off blue-green and put on purple;
this is not my robe."
Before even a month had passed,
there was
The character 'yǒu' originally had the character 'wèi' above it,
deleted according to the Xǔ edition
an imperial edict changing his office and bestowing the purple robe.
Thus, he took off blue-green and put on purple.
Héng himself also said:
"I should serve seventy tenures."
Now he has served over ten tenures,
and has already become Vice Censor-in-Chief and Grand Master.
From "Dìngmìng Lù"
Liǔ Fāng
Liǔ Fāng once sat for the jìnshì examinations,
failing for several consecutive years.
He attended a banquet of court officials,
where eight or nine guests all wore red sashes,
and some were officials from the capital or its environs.
Fāng sat at the very end,
and his clothes were coarse and old,
so all the guests looked down on him.
There was a skilled physiognomist present,
whom everyone paid attention to.
The character 'zhī' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Míng manuscript copy
He alone said to Fāng:
"You, Master Liǔ, have no brothers or sisters,
no manors, fields, or assets,
you are utterly alone,
and have suffered much hardship as a traveler.
In two years, you will pass the examinations,
and afterwards, your official salary and rank will not cease.
Among all the guests here,
in terms of lifespan and official salary,
none will match you."
None of the other guests believed him.
Two years later, he indeed passed the examinations,
and served successively as Collator, Commandant of a capital district, and Assistant Prefect,
traveling between Liáng and Sòng.
When a vacancy arose for a Court Gentleman of the Grand Temple,
Vice Minister of Works Wéi Shù, knowing his talent,
his thorough understanding of genealogy and official ranks,
and his knowledge of ancient and modern rituals and regulations,
recommended him to the Chief Ministers.
By imperial grace, he was appointed Court Gentleman of the Grand Temple.
By then, six or seven of the fellow guests from that time
had already passed away.
From "Dìngmìng Lù"
Chén Zhāo
The Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Fáng Guǎn and the Chancellor Cuī Huàn had both been demoted to serve as officials in Mù and Shè Prefectures.
At that time, a man from Wùzhōu named Chén Zhāo saw them and said:
"Later, both of you gentlemen will become Chancellors,
however, Lord Cuī will come to Jiāngnán
as a high-ranking commissioner."
By the beginning of the Tódé era,
when the Retired Emperor entered Shǔ,
Lords Fáng and Cuī
were simultaneously appointed Chancellors.
Cuī later became Commissioner of Selection and Recruitment,
inspecting Jiāngdōng.
When he reached the Sū-Háng region,
Lord Cuī told this story himself.
From "Dìngmìng Lù"
Lú Qíqīng
Lú Qíqīng had the ability to discern people's fates.
When he was six or seven years old, his temperament was careless and unrestrained,
so his uncles often had a servant follow him.
By the age of fifteen or sixteen, he enjoyed getting up at night
and sitting in the empty courtyard of the rear garden.
The servant saw many torches,
with numerous guards,
and someone holding a canopy over him.
He reported this to the uncles,
who thought it was a demon or spirit causing mischief.
A shaman taught them to use moxibustion on the center of his palm.
When Yuán Tiāngāng saw him,
he was greatly astonished and said:
"This person was originally destined to know three lifetimes,
but because his palm was damaged by moxibustion,
he lost knowledge of two lifetimes,
and now only knows the present lifetime."
From then on, whenever he made predictions,
none failed to come true.
He rose to the position of Director of the Palace Library.
When Zhāng Jiāzhēn was appointed as chancellor,
someone lodged a complaint against him.
Fearing demotion,
he asked Qíqīng to examine his fate.
Qíqīng did not give a definite answer,
but when Zhāng was about to attend court,
he wrote the character "Tái" on his ceremonial tablet,
and had Zhāng see it.
Zhāng thought it meant he would not leave the chancellor's seat,
but when the imperial decree was issued,
he was demoted to Prefect of Táizhōu.
Zhāng Shǒuguī,
a man from Héběi,
served under the county sheriff Liáng Wànqǐng.
Wànqǐng ordered him to catch a horse,
but he lost his grip on the horse's mane,
and was beaten as punishment.
Angered by this, he joined the army
and became a military officer in Yōuzhōu.
Qíqīng often invited him to sit and said:
"You will later attain wealth and honor,
and wield military authority."
Shǒuguī was flustered,
not expecting such a prediction.
He stepped down and bowed.
Before Lú left Yōuzhōu,
Shǒuguī had already become a general and military governor.
Liáng Wànqǐng was the sheriff of Hénán County,
and his initial term had just ended.
Shǒuguī summoned him for a meeting,
and Wànqǐng was very afraid,
but Shǒuguī bore no grudge against him.
He said:
"If not for your reprimand back then,
I would not have been driven to achieve success."
He then gave him money and goods,
so he could treat his illness.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Liáng Shí'èr
There was a man named Liáng Shí'èr, also known as Liáng Zhīrén.
He went to Sòngzhōu,
where the prefect Sīmǎ Quán wrote a letter,
recommending him to Lǐ Wúyán, the prefect of Sūzhōu.
It said:
"Liáng Shí'èr is the Guǎn Lù of today."
Lǐ Wúyán had him brought to his residence at dusk,
and Wúyán wore yellow clothes,
while having a guest wear purple,
posing as Wúyán,
to test him.
Liáng said to the guest:
"I just heard your voice,
and you have no official rank.
But I heard the voice of the man in yellow,
which is that of a third-rank official.
Now your robes are different,
so perhaps my observation was mistaken."
Wúyán believed him,
and confessed the truth:
"I had some matters recently,
and I feared being reported unfavorably by the imperial inspector.
What do you think?"
Liáng said:
"You are destined to be promoted to a higher prefect."
Later, he was indeed appointed Prefect of Mùzhōu,
and Wúyán gave him two hundred strings of cash.
Liáng said:
"When you arrive at that prefecture,
you will face a great calamity.
I will perform a ritual for you to avert it,
but you must scold me angrily,
saying I am a liar,
and whip my back ten times,
and you must not let your wife and children know."
Wúyán repeatedly refused,
but Liáng insisted,
so Wúyán reluctantly agreed.
The next morning,
Lǐ publicly ordered Liáng to be whipped ten times,
but a young servant ran to tell his wife.
When Wúyán returned home,
his wife asked:
"Why did you beat Liáng?"
Wúyán regretted it, saying:
"I forgot he said not to let the family know."
Soon after, Liáng rang the bell,
requesting to see Wúyán, and said:
"Why did you let your wife know?
The calamity cannot be avoided now.
Since you forcibly gave me two hundred thousand cash,
I will do one thing to repay your kindness.
Although the calamity cannot be avoided,
I will ensure you obtain two thousand strings of cash,
to enrich your family,
and taking it will bring no harm."
While in office,
Wúyán indeed obtained two thousand strings of cash before he died.
Liáng Shí'èr also said to Lú Wéiyǎ, the registrar of Dāntú:
"You will become a Palace Receptionist."
And so it happened.
Later, he met him in the capital.
He said:
"In a certain year,
your wealth and estates will be lost.
If you give me fifty thousand cash,
I will teach you how to avoid it."
Lú did not believe him,
and did not give him the money.
In that year,
Lú indeed lost all his estates
due to gambling.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Féng Qī
The presented scholar Lǐ Tāng was traveling to the capital for an official appointment,
hoping to secure a position.
On his way to the capital, he reached Biànzhōu,
where a fortune-teller named Féng Qī told him:
"This year you will be retained,
and appointed as a sheriff three thousand li southeast."
Lǐ did not believe it, saying:
"If I am retained after four selection rounds,
my position should not be lowly.
A collator or proofreader,
even if only for one or two terms,
is what I hope for.
How could it be a sheriff?"
Féng said:
"Just remember this:
after this, you will serve as a county sheriff,
and then you will not stop riding official horses."
He also asked if Lǐ was married,
and Lǐ said:
"Not yet,
but I have an aunt at home."
Féng said:
"From now on, you will never see her again."
When Lǐ reached the capital,
he was indeed retained.
Due to the Ān Lùshān Rebellion,
he did not want a capital post,
and requested a collator position,
but was not granted.
He requested the sheriff position of Wúchéng County in Húzhōu.
After one year,
the surveillance commissioner recommended him as sheriff of Dānyáng,
and he became an assistant,
often riding official horses without stopping.
After the rebellion,
roads were cut off,
and he indeed never saw his aunt again.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Mǎ Shēng
In the fourteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
Zhào Zìqín was due for an official assessment.
A blind man from Dōngyáng County named Mǎ Shēng told him:
"You will certainly not go,
and even if you do, you will return.
Your official fortune here is not yet exhausted,
and later you will reach the third rank,
wearing purple."
He also said:
"From the sixth rank, you will directly rise to the third rank."
That year, Zìqín indeed did not go for the assessment.
By winter,
he received an imperial decree granting him purple robes.
In the second year of the Qiányuán era, in the ninth month,
Mǎ Shēng came again.
Zìqín initially deceived him, saying:
"Páng Cāngcáo's family summoned you."
When he arrived, Mǎ felt Zìqín's skull and said:
"You should be of the fifth rank,
and your bone structure resembles that of Prefect Zhào."
His predictions about lifespan and official career
were the same as before.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù"
Sāng Dàomào
When General Lǐ Xīpíng Shèng was in service,
he once visited Sāng Dàomào.
Dàomào said:
"General, in the future you will become the Governor of the Capital,
please be cautious and avoid excessive killing."
Xīpíng replied:
"How could a military man ever aspire to become the Governor of the Capital?"
Later, after the recovery of Xìngyuán,
Xīpíng concurrently served as the Governor of the Capital.
At that time, Master Sāng was among the captives,
and at the moment of sentencing,
he addressed General Xīpíng:
"Have you forgotten the words about avoiding excessive killing?"
Xīpíng released him.
From "Chuán Zǎi"
Wéi Xiàqīng
Wéi Xiàngōng Xiàqīng possessed the insight to recognize talent,
though others were unaware of it.
Once, after retiring from court,
he encountered his second cousin Zhíyí on the street,
along with his cousins Qúmóu and Zhōu.
All three were the twenty-fourth in their generation,
and all served as court officials.
After gathering their horses for a while,
Xiàngōng said:
"Today I have met the three twenty-fourth gentlemen,
and I feel compelled to assess their futures."
He said to Zhíyí:
"You will certainly become a chancellor,
but take good care of your later years."
To Qúmóu, he said:
"You, my brother, will receive special favor from the sovereign,
and swiftly rise to the ranks of dukes and ministers."
To Zhōu, he said:
"Among the three of you,
you, my brother, will have the most enduring career.
And you will reach the highest military rank."
In the end, it all turned out as he said.
From "Chuán Zǎi"
Luò Shānrén
Wáng Tíngcòu was first born at a villa in Shíyì, thirty li southwest of Héng Mountain.
After his birth,
there were often dozens of turtledoves
that gathered in the courtyard trees in the morning
and roosted under the eaves at night.
A villager named Lù Débō found this strange.
When he grew up, he had fused ribs,
and was skilled in the texts of the Yīnfú and Guǐgǔ.
He served in military posts,
and won the hearts of his soldiers.
In the spring of the first year of the Chángqìng era, in the second month, he was sent to Héyáng,
and on his return, he reached Yǎnshuǐ.
Drunk and weary,
he slept by the roadside.
Suddenly, a man carrying a staff passed by,
looked at him intently, and said:
"You are destined to be enfeoffed as a lord,
no ordinary man."
His attendant, Dòu Zàiyīng, woke up
and told Tíngcòu.
Tíngcòu galloped several li to catch up with him,
paid his respects, and inquired.
The man said:
"I am Luò Shānrén from Jìyuán.
Just now, I saw the breath from your nostrils:
the left like a dragon, the right like a tiger.
When dragon and tiger breaths intertwine,
you will become king this autumn.
Your descendants will succeed you,
for a full hundred years.
I have read the faces of many men,
but never seen one like yours."
He added:
"In the courtyard of your home, there must be a large tree
that reaches the hall—
this is an omen."
After Tíngcòu returned,
he encountered the disaster of Tián Hóngzhèng.
In the middle of the night,
soldiers knocked at his door,
falsely calling out official titles.
Tíngcòu trembled with fear and wanted to flee,
but Zàiyīng said:
"The words of Luò Shānrén have come to pass."
That night was the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month,
and Tíngcòu's mind was put at ease.
When he became the military governor,
he later returned to his villa
and saw the tree in his courtyard—
it had grown luxuriantly, shading the northern rooms.
West of the villa was the shrine of the Flying Dragon Mountain deity,
and Tíngcòu went to offer sacrifices.
When he was a hundred paces from the gate,
he saw a man dressed in official robes
bowing deeply to him.
Tíngcòu asked his attendants,
but none of them had seen it.
When he entered the temple,
he found the deity's statue sitting sideways,
which astonished everyone.
He then ordered a hall to be built facing east,
which still exists today.
He soon invited Débō as an honored guest,
and placed Zàiyīng at the head of his officers.
He sought out Luò Shānrén,
and after a long search, finally found him.
He treated him with the utmost respect,
and even built a separate pavilion for him.
When Luò was away, he would hang up the couch,
and named it the "Luò Pavilion,"
in gratitude for the past.
From "Táng Nián Bǔ Lù"
Lǐ Shēng
Dù Cóng had long enjoyed high status and wealth.
Among his followers was a fortune-teller named Lǐ Shēng,
whom Cóng treated generously.
When Cóng served as the military governor of Xīchuān,
Mǎ Zhí was dismissed from Qiánnán and headed to the capital,
passing through Xīchuān.
As soon as the fortune-teller Lǐ saw Zhí,
he said to Cóng:
"I have long received your grace,
and have been thinking of how to repay it.
Now I have something to report.
Vice Censor-in-Chief Mǎ from Qiánzhōng is no ordinary man.
You should treat him with great kindness."
Cóng did not believe him at first.
One day, Lǐ secretly said to Cóng:
"You, sir, are about to face a great calamity,
and only Vice Censor-in-Chief Mǎ can save you.
I beg you to form a close bond with him."
Only then did Cóng become alarmed and believe him.
On the day of departure,
he gave Zhí generous gifts.
He also ordered his estate officer to buy a house for Zhí in the capital,
ensuring that all his living expenses were covered.
When Zhí arrived at the capital and learned of this,
he was moved but did not understand Cóng's intention.
Soon, Zhí was appointed Minister of the Imperial Granaries,
and when the notice reached Shǔ,
Cóng said to Lǐ Shēng:
"The honorable man has arrived at the capital
and become the Minister of the Imperial Granaries."
The fortune-teller said:
"Wait a little longer."
Soon, Zhí was promoted to Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
then further promoted to Vice Minister of Justice,
and appointed as Commissioner of Salt and Iron.
Cóng began to feel alarmed and worried.
Before long, Zhí became chancellor.
When Empress Yì'ān died mysteriously during Emperor Xuānzōng's reign,
Cóng was her son-in-law.
Suddenly, one day,
an imperial order was issued demanding an investigation into the case of the former chancellor Yuán Zǎi,
and Zhí conveyed the emperor's intent.
The next day,
in the Yányīng Hall before the emperor,
he exhaustively pleaded for mercy.
He was eloquent and persuasive,
and managed to change the emperor's mind,
so the matter was dropped.
From "Qián Dìng Lù"
Wáng È
Wáng È served as a deputy general under Xīn Gǎo,
who was then commanding in Chángshā.
One day, while playing polo,
they were galloping vigorously.
È exhaled toward the sky,
and his breath rose several zhàng high,
like a strip of white silk soaring upward.
Gǎo said to his wife:
"This is an extremely noble sign."
He then married his daughter to È.
È eventually became a general and chancellor.
From "Dú Yì Zhì"
Dòu Yìzhí
Chancellor Dòu Yìzhí,
was named Mì in his youth.
His family was poor,
so he attended a village school.
The old teacher there possessed mystical arts,
though people were unaware of it.
One day, as evening approached,
a fierce wind and snowstorm suddenly arrived.
The schoolchildren could not return home,
so they stayed overnight in a leaky house.
In the cold, they all huddled around the fire for warmth,
only Dòu slept on a couch,
and did not wake until deep into the night.
The old man patted Dòu and urged him to rise, saying:
"Dòu Mì,
you will later become a high minister,
reaching the pinnacle of nobility and longevity.
Strive hard and take care of yourself."
When Emperor Dézōng fled to Fèngtiān,
Dòu was just sitting for the imperial examinations,
and he also followed the imperial carriage westward.
Riding a lame donkey, he arrived at Kāiyuǎn Gate,
where the crowd was dense and the road narrow,
and the gate was about to close.
Dòu feared the situation would prevent him from passing through.
Suddenly, he heard someone shout at the donkey,
and also whip it from behind,
allowing it to gallop swiftly out.
Looking back, he saw a soldier dressed in black,
who called out to him:
"Scholar,
do not forget this kindness in the future."
Later, when Dòu rose to high office,
he sought out the soldier's son,
repeatedly promoting him until he achieved honor and prominence among officials.
From "Yīnhuà Lù".
Lǐ Tóng
When Wéi Chǔhòu was in Kāizhōu,
two examination candidates, Lǐ Tóng and Cuī Chōng, once came to visit him,
and stayed for over a month.
It happened that a passing traveler, a certain military officer from Xīchuān skilled in physiognomy,
said at a banquet:
"Lǐ Tóng will face a tiger-related calamity within three days."
Three days later,
Wéi Chǔhòu went with several guests to visit a mountain temple,
descending from the upper hall to the lower hall,
as evening had already fallen.
Lǐ went down first,
followed later by Cuī Chōng.
Cuī loudly called out to Lǐ:
"Wait for Chōng,
wait for Chōng!"
Hearing the cry "wait for Chōng,"
Lǐ thought a tiger had arrived.
He stumbled and fell,
tumbling down and injuring his toes.
He lost consciousness but later revived,
and recovered after several days.
When the military officer returned,
he said to Lǐ:
"Your calamity has passed."
From "Chuánzǎi".
Jiǎ Sù
When Jiǎ Sù was still a commoner,
he visited Jiǎ Dān, the military governor of Huátái.
As Jiǎ Sù was a clansman,
and Jiǎ Dān further admired his literary talent, which was exceptionally profound and rich,
he therefore extended even greater hospitality to him.
Suddenly one day,
during a large gathering of guests,
a skilled physiognomist present at Jiǎ Dān's side,
after Jiǎ Sù withdrew, said:
"The young master Jiǎ just now had an aura of brilliance and elegance;
he is destined to reach the highest ministerial rank.
However, it is a pity that
during his time in power,
the court will undergo subtle
(Míng dynasty manuscript note: "subtle" is written as "thorough")
changes.
When that time comes,
all of you gentlemen should take early precautions to avoid it."
Jiǎ Dān nodded in agreement,
even to the point of showing emotion.
By the end of the Tàihé era,
Jiǎ Sù held the reins of power.
Those who knew of this prophecy hid away in mountain valleys,
amounting to ten or twenty or thirty or forty percent.
From "Dùyáng Biān".
Lóu Qiānbǎo
Lǐ Bāo, the Governor of Zhèdōng, heard that in Wù Prefecture there were two men, Lóu Qiānbǎo and Lǚ Yuánfāng, who possessed extraordinary arts.
He dispatched a messenger to summon them.
After they arrived,
Governor Lǐ ordered them to be lodged in the Office of the Aides.
An aide asked them:
"Our lord holds the rank of Eight Seats;
what further office might he attain?"
Yuánfāng replied:
"Just now we saw the Minister,
but he will likely remain the former Military Governor of Zhèdōng;
I fear he will receive no other appointment."
Qiānbǎo's statement was the same.
The aide fell silent and ceased his questioning.
When they later met Governor Lǐ again,
he asked:
"What will become of me in the future?"
The two masters of arts said:
"Mount Jī stands lofty and green,
the lakeside willows hang their shade.
Your Excellency, with a hundred painted pleasure boats,
is perfectly suited for sightseeing excursions.
As the ancients said, a human life is but a generation,
like light dust settling on grass.
Why speak of future glory or decline?
Glory and decline are fixed by fate;
we dare not state it to your face."
He then asked about the various gentlemen in his staff.
Yuánfāng said:
"Deputy Commissioner Cuī Chúyán
and Investigating Judge Lǐ Zhèngfàn
are similar in capacity and bearing.
They will only become Department Directors,
stopping at the rank of Prefect.
Regimental Training Judge Lǐ Fúgǔ,
from now on, will only get thoroughly drunk a few more times;
what need to speak of office?
Observation Judge Rèn Gǔ
will stop at the post of Junior Remonstrator,
and will not exchange his red robe [for a higher purple one].
Assistant Yang Sǔn, the Court Reviewer,
though his frame is thin and frail,
among all the guests in this staff,
none will match his fortune and longevity.
Judge Lú Xūn,
though his appearance is radiant and glossy,
compared to Regimental Training Judge Lǐ Fúgǔ,
his remaining time in this world is slightly longer,
but his longevity will also not match [Yang Sǔn's].
The Deputy Commissioner and the three—Yang, Lǐ [Fúgǔ], and Lǐ [Zhèngfàn]—
their official ranks and emoluments will differ."
What the two masters of arts said,
none believed at the time,
but they silently noted it for verification.
After this, Lǐ Fúgǔ passed away within five days.
Truly, he only got thoroughly drunk a few more times.
Minister Lǐ and his various aides,
verifying their predictions,
revered them as divine.
At that time, Vice-Director Luó Shàoquán was departing to take up his post in Míng Prefecture,
and Shàoqīng Dòu Hóngyú,
son of Dòu Cháng,
was going to Tāi Prefecture.
Governor Lǐ, at a banquet,
asked about the futures of these two Prefects.
Lóu Qiānbǎo said:
"Prefect Dòu will surely get drunk again at the Wanghai Pavilion;
as for Prefect Luó, on this departure,
he will then seek the Way on Mount Sìmíng,
and will not wander the dusty world again."
Later, Shàoqīng Dòu was dismissed from his prefecture,
and came again to the Governor's residence,
which was the predicted second drunkenness.
Vice-Director Luó perished on a sea island,
hence the prediction that he would seek the Way,
knowing he would not return.
Minister Lǐ returned to Yìxīng,
and before long passed away,
confirming he received no other appointment.
Inspector and Collator Lú Xūn
died the following year at the Wǎnlíng administrative office,
his official life slightly longer than Lǐ Fúgǔ's,
as he was younger.
Judge Rèn Gǔ only became a Supplements Editor,
then retired to his gardens and fields,
never attaining the purple robes.
Director Cuī Chúyán stopped at the prefecture of Wúxīng.
Director Lǐ Fàn stopped at Jiǔjiāng.
Both gentlemen went from the Southern Palace to become Prefects of famous commanderies,
thus their ranks and emoluments were comparable.
Only Minister Yang Sǔn, for over thirty years,
twice served as Supervising Secretary,
twice as Capital Governor,
defended the Three Peaks,
became Military Governor of Qīng Prefecture,
passed the age of sixty,
and held offices across the frontier commands.
Among all the gentlemen of the same office in Zhèdōng,
none matched his fortune and longevity.
All this accorded with the words of Lóu and Lǐ.
When Supervising Secretary Dù Shèng was in Háng Prefecture,
he asked Qiānbǎo:
"What about my becoming Chancellor?"
He replied:
"It is like divining and obtaining the Zhèn hexagram:
there is sound but no form.
At that time,
you might be slandered by a woman,
and if you are appointed to a major commandery,
you will surely become ill from worry and depression,
but you can perform rites to avert it."
Later, Dù served as Vice-Minister of Revenue,
with hopes of direct promotion,
and the draft edict awaited proclamation.
The office clerks had already erected a plank house at Dù's gate,
preparing to spread the sand path.
Suddenly, a swift rider from the Eastern Gate
memorialized citing a minor fault,
and by imperial order, Vice-Minister Jiǎng Shēn was appointed Chancellor instead.
Dù was sent out to govern Tiānpíng,
and left depressed and unhappy,
his hopes dashed.
He then sighed:
"The words of Mount Jīnhuá's recluse Lóu indeed came true."
He wanted to summon Qiānbǎo and Yuánfāng.
But then said:
"The two scholars Lóu and Lǚ,
like solitary clouds and wild cranes,
who knows where they perch and roost?"
Minister Dù soon also passed away in Yùn Prefecture.
Junior Supervisor of the Household Zhōnglí Yòu,
in past years while living in retirement in Dōngyuè,
witnessed these extraordinary arts.
He often sought the two scholars,
but could not find them.
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì"
Dīng Zhòng
The Recluse Dīng Zhòng was skilled at reading people's physiognomy.
Imperial Son-in-law Yú Cóng was then serving as Salt and Iron Commissioner,
and there were frequent rumors of him becoming Chancellor.
At the time, Lù Yán held power and authority,
and was at odds with him.
One day, Zhòng came to Lù's private residence at Xīnchāng,
just as Yú happened to arrive.
Lù said:
"He and I are friends;
(Míng manuscript variant: friends as 'cóngróng' [companionable])
Master, please lower the screen and observe him carefully:
will this man ultimately become Chancellor or not?"
He prepared food and drink,
and detained them for several hours.
After they left,
he asked Zhòng:
"What did you see?"
Zhòng said:
"He will certainly become Chancellor,
and within ten days to a month."
Yán laughed and said:
"He is seen as a noble relative,
and is also serving as Salt and Iron Commissioner."
Zhòng said:
"Not so.
May I ask, how does Yú's imperial favor
compare to Commandant Zhèng in Emperor Xuānzōng's reign?"
Yán said:
"How could they even be compared?"
Zhòng said:
"Zhèng was long favored by Emperor Xuānzōng,
yet ultimately never became Chancellor.
Can such matters be decided by human deliberation?
I was not previously well acquainted with Vice-Minister Yú,
but seeing him today,
observing his bone structure,
he is truly a noble man.
Moreover, his demeanor is elegant and proper,
his manners humble and deferential.
He is like a vessel capable of holding a hundred hú,
yet still half empty of what it can contain;
how could his rank and emolument not increase?
If he does not enter the court as a high minister within a month,
I will never again come to your gate."
Yán said:
"Master, your words
can be said to be far-sighted."
Within ten days after that,
Yú indeed ascended to the position of Chancellor.
Yán, whenever he met court worthies,
praised Zhòng greatly.
From this, Zhòng's reputation stirred the capital,
and carriages and horses came calling in great numbers.
In all his predictions,
his words proved true.
Later, he lived in the Zhōngnán Mountains,
and those fond of such matters also went to his place.
From "Jùtán Lù"
Xiàhóu Shēng
Liú Chóngguī, the Minister of Works of Guǎngnán, often had hopes of becoming a chief minister,
believing that once he left his military post,
he would ascend directly to that position.
Xiàhóu Shēng, a hermit of Luófú, possessed the Way,
and Chóngguī esteemed him,
thus inquiring about future events.
Xià Shēng said he would not become a chief minister,
and that after traveling three thousand lǐ,
an unforeseen event would occur.
When he returned to the capital,
midway on the journey,
he fell ill and died.
Liú Shānfǔ also received predictions from Xià Shēng,
who foretold his actions over five years.
Everything came to pass,
truly, one's fortune in life is predetermined.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Vice-Director Xuē
Dǒng, the Military Commissioner's Judge of Jīngnán (in Oūyáng Xiū's "History of the Five Dynasties: Annals of the Prince of Nánpíng," Dǒng is written as Xūn,
same below)
along with Dù Wúyǐn of Jīngzhào,
who was the son of the Regular Attendant Dù Tāo of Huátái,
and Liáng Zhèn of Shǔ, all called themselves jìnshì.
They paid a visit to Chief Minister Chéng,
hoping for recommendation.
There was a Vice-Director Xuē,
who had traveled from Shǔ downstream to Zhǔgōng.
The three worthies often visited him.
One day,
Xuē said to Dǒng:
"You, sir, and the one from Jīngzhào,
should not seek fame,
for you will certainly not succeed,
and Dù will not live long.
Only the great worthy will unexpectedly be restrained by others,
attaining high office with purple and crimson robes.
As for Scholar Liáng, he will surely succeed in this examination,
but after passing,
he will not receive even a minor appointment."
Later, all came to pass as he said.
Liáng later wished to return to Shǔ,
and came again to Zhǔgōng.
The river route was blocked and chaotic,
and he could not travel west upstream.
The Huái army invaded Jiānglíng,
and the Prince of Bóhǎi invited him to his official residence.
He was asked to draft a proclamation,
and was offered a position in the prefectural staff.
He firmly held to his resolve not to serve,
and the Prince of Bóhǎi respected his decision.
For twenty-four years he lived there,
ultimately remaining a commoner in hemp clothes.
Vice-Director Xuē's words indeed proved true.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Zhōu Xuánbào
Zhōu Xuánbào of the Later Táng was from Yān.
In his youth, he became a monk.
His master had the insight to judge people.
Xuánbào followed and studied with him for ten years,
enduring hardships without complaint,
and thus inherited his secrets,
then returned to his hometown and resumed secular life.
Lú Chéng became a Daoist priest,
and with two companions visited him.
Xuánbào later said to someone:
"The two gentlemen just now,
when flowers bloom next year,
will both be deceased.
Only that Daoist priest
will in future years become very noble."
The following year,
the two indeed died.
Lú indeed rose to high office,
later returning to Jìnyáng.
Zhāng Chéngyè had Míngzōng change his clothes
and stand among the junior officers.
When someone else asked about him,
Xuánbào said:
"This is not he."
Xuánbào pointed to Míngzōng at the end of the line and said:
"His bone structure is extraordinary;
is this the Grand Guardian of the Inner Guard?"
When asked about his future,
he only said he would later become a military governor.
Míngzōng's Empress Xià was then serving as a lady-in-waiting;
sometimes she would disobey orders
and was severely caned.
Xuánbào said:
"This person has the status of a feudal lord's wife
and will bear a noble son."
His words indeed came true.
In all his predictions of fortune and misfortune,
none failed to hit the mark with divine accuracy;
many events are not recorded here.
When Míngzōng entered the capital from his post as military governor,
he said to his attendants:
"Zhōu Xuánbào once spoke of my affairs,
and it was quite prophetic.
He may be summoned from Běijīng and sent to the capital."
Zhào Fèng said:
"Predictive arts like those of Yuán and Xǔ are Xuánbào's expertise.
If he is summoned to the imperial carriage,
people will compete to ask about fortune and misfortune,
which may border on sorcery and delusion."
So it was agreed to bestow gold and silk upon him instead.
He attained the office of Minister of the Imperial Granaries,
and lived to the age of eighty before passing away.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Chéng Xùn
Chéng Xùn, the Minister of Ceremonies of Jìn, had tortoise-shell patterns on the soles of his feet.
He once summoned a physiognomist to examine them.
The physiognomist told him:
"You will ultimately meet with the calamity of drowning."
Later, when he was sent as an envoy to Zhèyòu,
he was ultimately buried in the belly of a sea fish.
It is often
(The character "常" was originally missing;
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy)
said that according to "The Biography of Lǐ Gù,"
Lǐ Gù had tortoise-shell patterns on the soles of his feet,
yet he attained the position of one of the Three Excellencies,
and ultimately suffered no harm from water.
The same sign but with different outcomes.
From "Yù Táng Xián Huà".
Wáng Zhèngjūn
Wáng Zhèngjūn, the aunt of Hàn's Wáng Mǎng, was betrothed for marriage.
Each time the date arrived for her to depart,
her husband-to-be would die.
This happened twice.
She was then presented to the Prince of Zhào,
but before he could take her, he also passed away.
Later, someone friendly with Zhèngjūn's father, Zhìjūn, came to read Zhèngjūn's physiognomy and said:
"She will be honored as the mother of the realm."
At that time, it was the reign of Emperor Xuān,
and Emperor Yuán was the crown prince.
Zhìjūn then, through the Commandant of Wèi Commandery, presented her to the crown prince.
The crown prince favored her,
and she bore a son.
When Emperor Xuān passed away,
the crown prince established Zhèngjūn as empress,
and her son became crown prince.
When Emperor Yuán passed away,
the crown prince ascended the throne,
becoming Emperor Chéng.
Zhèngjūn became empress dowager,
ultimately becoming the mother of the realm.
From "Lùn Héng".
Huáng Bà
Huáng Bà was a patrol officer in Yángxià.
He traveled in the same carriage with a skilled physiognomist.
They saw a woman of about seventeen or eighteen years old.
The physiognomist pointed at her and said:
"This woman will become greatly wealthy,
the wife of a marquis."
Huáng stopped the carriage
and examined her carefully.
The physiognomist said:
"If this woman does not become wealthy and noble,
then physiognomy books are useless."
Huáng asked about her,
and she turned out to be the daughter of a shaman from a neighboring village.
He then married her as his wife.
Later, Huáng indeed became greatly wealthy and noble,
rising to the position of Chancellor,
and was enfeoffed as a marquis.
From "Lùn Héng".
The Dough Cake Seller Granny
Mǎ Zhōu of the Táng Dynasty, styled Bīnwáng,
was orphaned and impoverished in his youth,
yet well-versed in the Book of Songs and its commentaries.
He was down-and-out and did not engage in productive work,
and was not esteemed by his local community.
He was appointed as an assistant instructor in Bózhōu,
but spent his days drinking.
The prefect Dáxī became angry,
and repeatedly reprimanded and blamed him.
Mǎ Zhōu then brushed off his sleeves and traveled south to the regions of Cáo and Biàn.
Because he offended the magistrate of Jùnyí, Cuī Xián, while drunk,
he again encountered blame and humiliation.
He traveled west to Xīnfēng,
and lodged at an inn.
The innkeeper only provided for the various merchants and peddlers,
and paid no attention to Mǎ Zhōu.
Mǎ Zhōu then ordered a dou of wine,
and drank alone.
With the leftover wine he had drunk,
he took off his boots and washed his feet,
which secretly astonished the innkeeper.
Subsequently, he arrived in the capital,
and stayed at an old woman’s shop that sold duī (steamed cakes).
After several days,
he sought a place to serve as a resident guest,
and the old woman led him to the home of the General of the Household, Cháng Hé.
When the old woman first sold duī,
Lǐ Chúnfēng and Yuán Tiāngāng once encountered her and found her remarkable.
They both secretly said:
"This woman will achieve great nobility;
why is she here?"
Lord Mǎ later took her as his wife.
Later, an edict was issued
requiring civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above
to each submit memorials on state affairs.
Mǎ Zhōu drafted twenty proposals on beneficial policies,
and had Cháng Hé submit them.
These included the request to establish street drums,
and regulations on the colors of official robes—scarlet, purple, blue, and green—for civil and military officials,
as well as rules for entering and exiting through the left and right sides of city gates.
All these matters aligned with the emperor’s intentions.
Emperor Tàizōng, surprised, asked Cháng Hé what he had observed,
and Cháng Hé replied:
"It was done by my resident guest, Mǎ Zhōu."
The emperor summoned Mǎ Zhōu for an audience and conversation,
and appointed him to the Chancellery.
He also ordered Fáng Xuánlíng to test him on the classics and policy questions,
and conferred upon him the title of Rúlín Láng,
appointing him as Investigating Censor.
Because Cháng Hé had recommended such a capable person,
he was rewarded with one hundred bolts of silk.
Mǎ Zhōu later served as Junior Supervisor of the Secretariat and Secretariat Drafter,
possessing wit and eloquence,
and was skilled in presenting memorials.
He had deep insight into matters,
and his actions never missed the mark.
Cén Wénběn, upon seeing him, said:
"When I see Lord Mǎ,
he makes one forget fatigue.
However, with his hawk-like shoulders and fiery complexion,
he will rise swiftly,
but I fear he may not last long."
Within a few years,
he rose to the position of chancellor,
and the old woman also became a lady of rank.
Later, as Minister of Personnel,
he suffered from wasting-thirst illness (diabetes),
which did not heal for a full year.
He died at the age of forty-eight.
He was posthumously honored as Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs and Duke of Gāotáng.
From "Records of Fixed Fate"
The Sū Family’s Daughter
A certain Sū,
a wealthy man of Xìndū,
had ten daughters,
and sought to select good sons-in-law for them.
Zhāng Wénchéng went to see him,
and Sū said:
"Although this man has talent,
he will not attain wealth or nobility.
If he is fortunate enough to reach the fifth rank,
he will die immediately."
Wèi Zhīgǔ had already passed the imperial examinations at that time,
but did not yet hold an official post.
Sū said:
"Although this man’s appearance is dark and small,
he is certain to achieve high rank."
He then married his eldest daughter to him.
This daughter had hair seven feet long,
black and glossy like lacquer,
which none of her younger sisters could match.
A physiognomist said:
"This woman will be wealthy,
and will not eat leftover food from the previous day."
The younger sisters teased Zhīgǔ, saying:
"It’s just that when a poor man gets rice, he cooks it immediately,
so there’s no leftover rice."
Later, Wèi became chancellor,
and whenever he ate,
everything was supplied by the official provisions.
From "Records of Fixed Fate"
Empress Wǔ
When Wǔ Shìhuò served as the military governor of Lìzhōu,
an imperial decree summoned Yuán Tiāngāng to the capital.
Passing through Lìzhōu on his journey,
Shìhuò had him read the physiognomy of his wife, Lady Yáng.
Tiāngāng said:
"Madam’s bone structure is extraordinary;
she is certain to bear noble sons."
He then summoned all her sons,
and was asked to read the physiognomy of Yuánqìng and Yuánshuǎng.
He said:
"They can reach the rank of prefect,
but will ultimately face hardship and obstruction."
When he saw the Lady of Hánguó,
he said:
"This woman’s husband will be noble,
but she will bring misfortune to her husband."
Empress Wǔ at that time was dressed in boys’ clothing,
and was held in the arms of her wet nurse.
Tiāngāng, greatly astonished, said:
"This young gentleman,
with his profound and clear spirit,
is not easy to discern."
He then had her try walking under the bed,
and Tiāngāng, greatly astonished, said:
"With a sun-horned forehead and dragon-like countenance,
dragon eyes and a phoenix neck—
this is the physiognomy of Fúxī,
the pinnacle of nobility."
He then had her turn and viewed her from another angle,
and again exclaimed in astonishment:
"If this is a girl,
she will become the ruler of the world."
From "Records of Tán Bīn"
Lǐ Chúnfēng
When Empress Wǔ was summoned into the palace,
Lǐ Chúnfēng memorialized:
"There is an imperial aura in the rear palace."
Emperor Tàizōng summoned the palace women for inspection,
ordering them into groups of one hundred.
He asked Chúnfēng,
and Chúnfēng said:
"She is in a certain group."
Tàizōng then divided them into two groups,
and Chúnfēng said:
"She is in a certain group;
I ask Your Majesty to select her yourself."
Tàizōng could not identify her,
and wanted to kill them all.
Chúnfēng advised against it, saying:
"If Your Majesty spares her,
although the imperial lineage may be temporarily interrupted,
the state will endure longer.
If Your Majesty kills her,
she will be reborn as a man,
and then the imperial clan will be utterly destroyed."
Tàizōng then desisted.
From "Records of Fixed Fate"
Consort Yáng
When Consort Yáng was in Shǔ,
a rustic named Zhāng saw her and said:
"She is destined for great wealth and nobility;
why is she here?"
Someone asked if she would become a lady of the third rank.
Zhāng said:
"No."
"First rank?"
He said:
"No."
"Then, an empress?"
He said:
"Also not,
but her nobility and prominence will be equal to that of an empress."
When he saw Yáng Guózhōng,
he said:
"You, sir, will also attain wealth and high rank,
and will wield the empire’s power for several years."
Later events all turned out as he said.
From "Records of Fixed Fate"
Jiāng Jiǎo
Before Jiǎng Jiǎo rose to prominence,
he enjoyed archery and hunting.
Returning from a hunt and entering his gate,
he saw a monk.
Jiǎng said:
"What kind of monk is here?"
The monk said:
"Begging for food."
Lord Jiǎng ordered meat and food to be given to him.
The monk finished eating and left,
but the meat remained entirely untouched.
Lord Jiǎng sent someone to chase after and question him,
the monk said:
"You, sir, will attain great wealth and honor."
Jiǎng said:
"How can I attain wealth and honor?"
The monk said:
"When you see the True Man, you will attain wealth and honor."
Jiǎng said:
"When will I get to see the True Man?"
The monk raised his eyes, looked, and said:
"You will see the True Man today."
Jiǎng had a sparrowhawk on his arm,
worth a full twenty thousand coins.
He followed the monk on horseback out of the city,
and by chance encountered the future emperor, who was also hunting,
at that time he was the Prince of Línzī.
Seeing the sparrowhawk, he recognized it and said:
"Is this my sparrowhawk?"
Jiǎng said it was.
Thus, he accompanied him on the hunt.
Soon after, the monk was nowhere to be found.
Later, a female shaman arrived,
Jiǎng asked her:
"Look and see who will come today."
The female shaman said:
"The Son of Heaven will come today."
Jiǎng laughed and said:
"The Son of Heaven sits in his palace,
how could he come to see me?"
Soon there was a knock at the door, someone saying:
"Sānláng is here."
Jiǎng went out to see,
and it was the future emperor.
From then on, he was doubly respectful and cautious,
providing money and horses as needed,
never daring to be sparing.
Later, when the future emperor departed from Lù Prefecture,
all the officials, relatives, and old friends came to see him off,
only Jiǎng was not seen.
The future emperor found it strange.
Traveling to the north of the Wèi River,
by the roadside,
he alone saw Lord Jiǎng had prepared a tent,
and grandly awaited him.
The future emperor joyfully bid him farewell,
thus establishing the distinction between ruler and subject.
Later, Jiǎng indeed attained wealth and honor.
From "Dìngmìng Lù"
Cháng Gǔn
When Cháng Gǔn was in Fújiàn,
there was a certain monk skilled in reading complexions,
his predictions were as if divine.
Gǔn, pitying the monk's old age,
ordered his disciple to learn his art.
The monk said:
"This matter is innate,
it cannot be rashly transmitted.
I have seen among those around you,
one person who can be taught."
They searched everywhere,
and found a minor clerk named Huáng Chè.
Gǔn ordered him to study.
The old monk then, in a dark room,
placed five-colored silks on a frame,
and told him to take them himself.
He said:
"People in the world all fail to fully use their eyesight,
but if you look at them intently,
after ten days,
you will vaguely recognize the white ones.
After half a year,
you will see the five colors.
Then you will achieve clear insight."
He instructed him, saying:
"Using your ability to see the five colors in the dark,
apply it to reading people's complexions in broad daylight."
Thus, he transmitted his methods and secrets,
and said that later generations would likely not surpass him.
Lǐ Jífǔ said:
"Huáng Chè's readings
are second only to Yuán and Xǔ."
From "Chuánzǎi"
Liú Yǔxī
Guest Minister Liú Yǔxī served as Vice Director of the Bureau of Imperial Farms.
At that time, political affairs were somewhat unusual,
and he had the momentum for rapid advancement day and night.
Knowing a monk whose divination arts were extremely refined,
on a day when he was on duty at the ministry,
he invited him to the ministry.
Just as he was about to ask about his fate,
it was reported that Scholar Wěi was at the gate.
The lord had no choice but to see him first,
and had the monk sit behind a curtain.
After Scholar Wěi presented his scroll,
Liú glanced over it briefly,
his demeanor was particularly aloof.
Wěi sensed this,
and left.
Then he spoke with the monk,
the monk, having no choice,
sighed for a long while,
then said:
"If I speak,
you, Vice Director, will certainly be displeased,
what should I do?"
The lord said:
"Just say it."
The monk said:
"After your promotion, Vice Director,
you will become a regular Director in your current bureau.
However, you must wait until Scholar Wěi, who just came, attains a position handling seals."
The lord was greatly angered,
and bowed him out.
Within ten days, he was demoted.
Scholar Wěi was none other than Chancellor Wěi Chǔhòu.
More than twenty years later,
while serving in the Secretariat,
he promoted Liú to Director of the Bureau of Imperial Farms.
From "Yōuxián Gǔchuī"
Zhèng Lǎng
When Chancellor Zhèng Lǎng first took the examinations,
he met a monk skilled in reading complexions.
Who said to him:
"You, young master, will reach the pinnacle of officialdom,
but you do not have the fate to pass the jìnshì examination.
If you do pass,
then your whole life will be fraught with difficulties."
Soon after, he passed as top graduate,
congratulatory guests filled his gate,
only this monk did not come.
When he failed the re-examination and was demoted,
many came to offer condolences,
but this monk alone came to congratulate him, saying:
"Wealth and honor lie within."
Later, it indeed turned out as he had divined.
From "Zhíyán"
Línghú Táo's Resident Monk
When Duke Línghú Táo of Zhào served as Chancellor,
Mǎ Jǔ was a minor officer in Zélù.
Having come to his residence on official business,
it happened the Duke had a resident monk,
skilled in reading voices and complexions.
Catching a glimpse of him by chance,
he said to the Duke:
"Just now, a military officer came to see you, Chancellor,
who is he?"
The Duke told him Mǎ Jǔ's name,
the monk said:
"I secretly observed this man,
one day he will succeed you, Chancellor, as a Regional Military Governor."
The Duke said:
"He is a minor border officer,
even if he achieves military merit,
he will at most command a single fortress on the frontier.
How could he succeed me?"
The monk said:
"If you, Chancellor, summon him again to speak,
this poor monk will observe him carefully."
The Duke agreed.
After he left,
the monk said:
"Today's observation is even clearer,
I'm afraid it might even be Yángzhōu or Biànzhōu."
The Duke then began to treat him with more regard.
In the ninth year of the Xiántōng era, when the Duke governed Wéiyáng,
Mǎ Jǔ achieved merit by defeating Páng Xūn.
Previously, Emperor Yìzōng had personally promised him,
that upon achieving success,
he would grant him Yángzhōu.
But then it became difficult to break his word,
so instead he appointed Jǔ as Military Commissioner of Huáinán.
Upon hearing this,
the Duke immediately instructed his subordinates
to prepare to welcome the new commissioner.
His subordinates all said:
"This is just a Military Commissioner."
The Duke then explained the matter to them.
It indeed turned out as the monk had said.
From "Zhíyán"
Monk Chǔhóng
Monk Chǔ Hóng practiced meditation at Wǔdāng Mountain.
When Wáng Jiàn was still obscure, he sold salt between Jūnzhōu and Fángzhōu,
and also engaged in petty theft,
earning the nickname "Thief Wáng Bā."
Chǔ Hóng saw him and urged him:
"You will one day reach the highest rank among ministers.
Why not join the army
to pursue achievements elsewhere?
Instead, you roam at night and hide by day,
staining yourself with the name of a thief?"
Wáng Jiàn was moved by this,
enlisted in the Zhōngwǔ Army,
and later, when Wáng Jiàn was in Shǔ,
Chǔ Hóng led his disciples into Shǔ.
Wáng Jiàn built a fine residence to settle him,
which became the Hóngjué Chán Monastery.
Jiāngxī's Zhōng Fù, when still obscure, also made a living selling salt.
He met the Shànglán Monk, who taught him to become a 'bandit' and capture Hóngjǐng.
From then on, he revered the monk even more,
to the extent that in major military and government affairs,
this monk was consulted.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Nun Fàn
During the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a nun surnamed Fàn,
who came from an official family,
and could foretell people's fortunes.
She was a relative of Lǔ Gōng Yán Zhēnqīng's wife's family.
When Lǔ Gōng served as a commandant at Lǐquán,
he went to Nun Fàn to ask about his fate:
"I wish to take the special examination.
I beg you, Master Aunt, to say a word."
Nun Fàn said:
"Yán Láng, your affairs will surely succeed.
Within a month or two, you will receive a court appointment.
But within half a year,
be careful not to contend with foreigners,
lest you face demotion."
Lǔ Gōng also asked:
"Will my official rank
reach the fifth rank?"
Nun Fàn laughed and said:
"Close to the first rank!
Yán Láng, your aspirations
are so humble!"
Lǔ Gōng said:
"If my official rank ends
at the fifth rank,
wearing crimson robes,
bearing a silver fish tally,
with my son appointed as a temple attendant,
my hopes would be fully satisfied."
Nun Fàn pointed to the purple silk tablecloth on the seat and said:
"Yán Láng
(The character 'láng' was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy)
Your robe's color will be like this,
and your achievements, fame, and integrity will match it.
You will live past seventy.
Do not ask further questions hereafter."
Lǔ Gōng pressed her repeatedly,
and Nun Fàn said:
"Yán Láng, you are exceedingly intelligent;
there is no need to inquire to the very end."
Over a month later, during a grand feast,
Lǔ Gōng passed the special examination with high honors that day,
and was appointed Commandant of Cháng'ān.
Within a few months,
he was promoted to Investigating Censor.
While supervising the court assembly,
there was someone who made excessive noise:
he ordered a clerk to record and memorialize it.
It was Gēshū Hàn.
Hàn had recently achieved merit by capturing the Shíbǎo Fortress,
and tearfully complained to Emperor Xuánzōng.
Emperor Xuánzōng charged Lǔ Gōng with disrespecting a meritorious official,
and demoted him to Granary Supervisor of Púzhōu.
These events unfolded exactly as foretold,
clear as if seen.
When Lǔ Gōng became Grand Preceptor,
and was sent as an envoy to Càizhōu,
he sighed:
"Nun Fàn's words
mean my life is surely in the hands of the rebels!"
From "Róng Mù Xián Tán."
Rèn Zhīliáng
Rèn Zhīliáng sat for the imperial examination,
but did not pass.
He rested and ate at a Guāndōng inn.
He met a Daoist priest also coming from the west,
staying at the same inn.
Zhīliáng spoke with him,
asking where he came from.
The priest said:
"Now you should have fame and satisfaction.
Why not return to the capital?"
Rèn declined, citing lack of funds and provisions,
and having no place to stay in the capital.
The Daoist then provided money and goods,
and gave him a note,
instructing him to stay at the main courtyard of the Sùmíng Temple.
Zhīliáng reached the capital,
went to the temple to settle.
By chance, he saw a Daoist priest reading scriptures,
who said to him:
"The Supreme Elderly Lord was born on the fifteenth day of the second month."
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial,
requesting lanterns be lit on the birthday of the Mysterious Origin Emperor.
The retired emperor read the memorial and approved,
ordering the Secretariat to summon him for examination,
to grant him an official post.
Lǐ Línfǔ objected,
so he was given an official status by special decree.
From "Dìng Mìng Lù."
Yīn Jiǔxiá
Vice Minister Zhāng served as an aide to Wū Chóngyì in Héyáng,
where all colleagues in the same office were renowned figures.
A Daoist named Yīn Jiǔxiá came from Qīngchéng Mountain,
possessing the insight to judge people.
Lord Wū asked about his own lifespan and official fortune,
to which Jiǔxiá replied:
"Your Excellency holds a noble post as a regional governor,
and what is hoped for is that you will grasp the reins of power,
and be enfeoffed with land.
It only depends on preserving your ordinary achievements,
and storing up benevolence and righteousness.
Your enjoyment of blessings will be abundant and profound,
truly without limit."
Then he asked about all the guests and aides,
and Jiǔxiá said:
"Among them, there must be one who will become a chief minister."
At that time, Lord Wū valued a Deputy Commissioner Péng,
and responded immediately:
"Is Deputy Péng the future prime minister?"
Jiǔxiá said:
"If we speak of current human affairs,
it should be as Your Excellency says.
But from what I observe,
it is not him."
At that time, the future Chancellor Xiàhóu Zī was an inspector of post stations,
and moreover, his appearance and bearing were humble and unrefined.
Lord Wū thus joked:
"Could it be Inspector Xiàhóu?"
He replied:
"What Your Excellency says is correct."
Lord Wū clapped his hands and laughed:
"Venerable Master, are you not mistaken?"
Jiǔxiá said:
"I am a man of the mountains and wilds,
who long ago cultivated the straightforward path,
with no desire for fame, office, gold, or jade.
It is merely based on what I see,
that I speak truthfully and straightforwardly."
Lord Wū said:
"If so, then this is beyond my understanding.
But who among them will next achieve nobility and prominence?"
He said:
"Although Commissioner Zhāng will not reside in the imperial court,
his career will follow a pure path,
and he will also attain honor and distinction."
After leaving,
he then went to Vice Minister Zhāng's residence,
and leisurely said to him:
"Commissioner, your spirit and bone structure are pure and refreshing,
your aura and bearing are lofty and transcendent.
If you burden yourself with official robes and caps,
you will only dwell in the mundane world for twenty or thirty years.
If you can shake off the clamor of the vulgar world,
follow me to study the Dao,
then within twenty years you will ascend to heaven in broad daylight.
My journey this time,
is not due to worldly concerns,
but is truly to seek out those who cultivate the true way.
However, I have observed many people,
and none compare to you, Commissioner."
Zhāng considered his words grandiose and exaggerated,
and merely assented vaguely.
As he was about to leave, he came back again,
his sentiment very earnest and sincere.
Seeing clearly that Zhāng's mind would not turn,
he sighed with deep regret.
Then he left several pills of medicine,
along with a letter written on yellow paper, and bid farewell, saying:
"Taking this medicine can prevent illness;
the letter records the achievements of your official career.
Each time you are transferred or promoted,
secretly open it.
When the writing is exhausted,
you will naturally remember me."
Later, Duke Qiáo achieved a brilliant and illustrious reputation,
and twice held the position of chief minister.
Zhāng indeed entered the ranks of court officials,
moving in and out of the imperial departments,
wearing the crimson and purple robes of high office,
and served as an inspector in several prefectures.
The words recorded in the letter
were all accurate and detailed.
When he reached the age of thirty-six years,
he was serving as Vice Minister of Revenue.
The paper that remained
was also nearly gone.
Although his name and position were prominent and illustrious,
his teeth and hair were declining.
He often spoke of the Daoist's matters
to relatives and friends,
recalling his demeanor with longing,
feeling that none could match it.
From "Jù Tán Lù"
Yǔ Dàomǐn Who Reads Handheld Tablets
Sòng Shānyáng's Wáng Xiūyòu repeatedly offended the Emperor with his words.
There was a man named Yǔ Dàomǐn who was skilled at reading handheld tablets.
Xiūyòu gave him a tablet, claiming it belonged to someone else.
Yǔ said:
"This tablet signifies nobility,
but it causes its bearer to give frequent offense."
Xiūyòu, because Chǔ Yuān was careful and meticulous,
then exchanged tablets with him.
Another day,
Chǔ referred to himself as "this humble official" before the Emperor,
which greatly displeased the Emperor.
From "Yǒu Yáng Zá Zǔ"
Attendant Official Lǐ
In the Táng dynasty, there was an Attendant Official Lǐ who was skilled at reading tablets,
knowing good and bad fortune with certain verification,
and everyone called him Lǐ the Tablet Reader.
The salt and iron office official Lù Zūn showed him his tablet.
He said:
"The Investigating Magistrate's son will arrive."
Lù Zūn laughed and said:
"Is it my nephew?"
He said:
"It is the Investigating Magistrate's son."
Lù said:
"You have lost your reputation,
for I have no son."
He then took it out again and looked at it under the curtain:
"It must be
(Míng manuscript has 'will not')
wrong."
Lù thought very little of him,
considering it a fraud.
Lù previously had a singing girl at his post,
and that month she became pregnant,
and gave birth to a boy indeed.
Original source missing,
Míng manuscript states: From "Yì Shǐ"
Lóng Fùběn
During the Kāichéng era,
there was a man named Lóng Fùběn who was blind,
skilled at judging by voice and feeling bones.
Whenever he spoke of good or bad fortune,
it was always accurate.
For any ivory tablet or bamboo tablet,
by rubbing it with his hand,
he would certainly know the official fortune and lifespan.
Sòng Qí, a Rectifier of Omissions, had great fame in the world,
and officials and gentry all looked up to him.
Counting on fingers and standing on tiptoe,
they anticipated his noble rise.
At that time, the Chancellor from Yǒnglè, Xiāo Zhì, also served in the remonstrance office,
and they went together on the same day to see him,
giving him the bamboo tablets they held.
Fùběn held Chancellor Xiāo's tablet for a long time,
placed it on the table and said:
"A prime minister's tablet."
Next, when it came to Rectifier Sòng, he said:
"A chief official's tablet."
Sòng was unhappy upon hearing this.
Xiāo said:
"Baseless words,
why should they concern you."
After a little over a month,
they stood together in the Secretariat waiting to see the prime minister.
At that time, Lǐ Déyù was in power,
his authority overawing the court and the country.
While waiting to be received,
they stood chatting idly.
There was mutual joking and banter.
In a moment, the Prime Minister suddenly came out,
and Sòng covered his face with his tablet,
still laughing.
Lǐ Déyù looked at him,
turned to his attendants and said:
"What is Rectifier Sòng laughing at me about?"
Those who heard it all felt their hearts chill and their legs tremble.
Within ten days,
he was sent out to be the magistrate of Qīnghé County.
A little over a year later,
he died in that post.
Afterwards, Chancellor Xiāo advanced through pure official paths,
from Military Governor of Zhèxī he entered to head the Ministry of Revenue,
and not long after, he resided in the imperial court.
All was as Fùběn had said.
From "Jù Tán Lù"
The Kingdom of Yīnzhī
In the fifth year of King Chéng of Zhōu,
the state of Yīnzhī, located ninety thousand lǐ from the royal capital,
sent a tribute of a female artisan.
She was exceptionally skilled and dexterous,
with a light and graceful figure.
She wore garments of fine silk gauze and embroidered crepe,
with long sleeves and flowing skirts.
When the wind blew, she would tie her sash,
fearing she would be blown away and unable to stop herself.
She was skilled in weaving,
placing multicolored silk threads into her mouth,
then drawing and knotting them,
to create patterned brocade.
Her people also presented Yúnkūn brocade,
whose patterns resembled clouds emerging from mountain peaks;
Lièdié brocade,
whose patterns resembled clouds and mist covering city walls and watchtowers;
Zázhū brocade,
whose patterns resembled strings of pearls;
Zhuànwén brocade,
whose patterns resembled large seal script characters;
and Lièmíng brocade,
whose patterns resembled rows of lamps and candles.
Each bolt was three chǐ wide.
The men of that state
were all diligent in farming.
In one day, they could hoe one hundred qǐng of land.
They also presented auspicious grain,
a single stalk of which filled a cart.
Thus, a popular four-character verse of the time said:
"Diligently hoeing a hundred qǐng,
one can obtain auspicious ears."
From Shíyílù.
Gě Yóu
was a Qiāng person from Shǔ.
He could carve wood into sheep and sell them.
One morning, he rode a sheep into the city of Shǔ,
and the wealthy nobles of Shǔ
followed him up Suí Mountain.
Suí Mountain is lofty and steep,
located west of Éméi.
Those who followed him all attained the Way,
and never returned.
Thus, a local saying goes:
"Obtain a peach from Suí Mountain,
even if you cannot become immortal,
you will still be exalted."
Many shrines were erected at the foot of the mountain.
From Fǎyuàn Zhūlín.
Lǔ Bān
was from Dūnhuáng,
though his exact era is unknown.
His skill rivaled that of nature.
In Liángzhōu, he built a pagoda
and made a wooden kite.
Each time he struck the wedge three times,
he would ride it home.
Not long after,
his wife became pregnant.
His parents questioned her,
and she explained the reason.
Later, his father waited for the kite,
struck the wedge over ten times,
and rode it,
eventually arriving at Wúkuài.
The people of Wú thought he was a demon,
and killed him.
Lǔ Bān then made another wooden kite and rode it,
retrieving his father's body.
Resenting the people of Wú for killing his father,
he made a wooden immortal south of Sùzhōu city,
with its hand raised,
pointing southeast.
As a result, the land of Wú suffered a great drought for three years.
Divination revealed
it was Lǔ Bān's doing.
They offered him thousands in goods as an apology.
Lǔ Bān then severed one of the wooden immortal's hands,
and that month, heavy rain fell in Wúzhōng.
At the beginning of the dynasty,
locals still prayed to that wooden immortal.
During the Warring States period,
Gōngshū Bān also made a wooden kite
to spy on the Sòng city.
From Yǒuyáng Zázǔ.
The Bowmaker
When Duke Jǐng of Sòng commissioned a bow,
it took nine years to complete and present it.
The bowmaker returned home
and died three days later.
It seems the craftsman had exhausted all his heart and strength on this bow.
Later, the duke ascended the terrace of the animal enclosure
and used this bow to shoot.
The arrow flew over the Xībà Mountains,
east of Péngchéng,
and its remaining force pierced a rock, embedding the feathers.
From Huáinánzǐ.
The Clever Man of Yān
The King of Yān sought a man skilled in clever techniques.
One man claimed he could carve a mother monkey on the tip of a thorn.
When the mother monkey was completed,
the clever man said:
"If Your Majesty wishes to see it,
you must not enter the palace for half a year,
nor drink wine or eat meat.
Then, on a clear day at sunrise,
view it in the dim light between shadow and light,
and the mother monkey on the thorn tip
will become visible."
The King of Yān, indulging in comforts,
could not see it.
From Yìwén Lèijù.
Yúnmíng Terrace
Emperor Qín Shǐhuáng built Yúnmíng Terrace,
gathering precious woods from all four directions
and skilled artisans from across the land.
From the south, he obtained Yānqiū jade-green trees,
Lìshuǐ burning sand,
Bēndū vermilion clay,
and Yúngāng plain bamboo;
from the east, Cōngluán brocade cypress,
Piǎosuì dragon fir,
Hánhé starry mulberry,
and Wánshān cloud catalpa;
from the west, Lòuhǎi floating gold,
Làngyuān feather jade,
Tiáozhāng rosy mulberry,
and Shěntáng round bamboo;
from the north, Míngfù dry lacquer,
Yīnbǎn catalpa,
Qiānliú black amber,
and Ànhǎi fragrant jade.
Rare and exotic materials were thus assembled.
