Two men, both light as air, tread upon the rafters,
wielding axes and adzes among the clouds.
They began work at midnight,
and by noon, it was already completed.
The people of Qín called it the Zǐwǔ Terrace,
also saying it was built on the zǐwǔ axis.
Each built one terrace.
The two accounts are doubtful.
From Shíyílù.
Yínyuān Bank
South of Rìnán,
there is the marsh of Yínquán.
It is said that its water seeps and oozes from the ground,
forming a deep pool,
hence it is called Yínquán.
Some say this spring's water is sweet and soft;
if men and women drink it, they become licentious.
In narrow places, the water is shallow enough to wade across with lifted garments,
while in broad areas, boats can sail along it, going upstream or downstream,
following the twists and turns of the current.
The sound of the water striking against rocks
resembles human singing and laughter.
Those who hear it feel stirred to licentiousness,
so it is commonly called Yínquán.
At times, there are wild ducks and geese
with golden-colored feathers,
flying in flocks and frolicking on the sandy shoals.
When hunters catch them,
they turn out to be real golden ducks.
Long ago, when the tomb at Lìshān was broken into,
travelers in the wilderness saw golden ducks flying southward,
all the way to Yínquán.
In the first year of the Bǎodǐng era,
Zhāng Shàn served as the governor of Rìnán.
A local obtained a golden duck
and presented it to Governor Zhāng Shàn.
Shàn was knowledgeable and well-versed;
examining its date,
he concluded it was indeed the golden duck from the tomb of Qín Shǐhuáng.
In the past, when Shǐhuáng built his tomb,
he gathered rare treasures from across the land
and buried craftsmen alive as sacrifices.
He poured exotic treasures from distant places into the tomb.
He created models of rivers, seas, streams, and mountain ranges.
Using sandalwood and eaglewood for boats and oars,
gold and silver for ducks and geese,
and colored glaze and assorted gems for turtles and fish.
He also placed jade elephants and whale-like fish holding fiery pearls in the "sea" to serve as stars,
replacing oil lamps.
Light emanated from the tomb,
a marvel of spiritual essence.
All the skilled craftsmen were buried alive inside the tomb.
Rows of lamps and candles shone like bright suns.
The craftsmen buried earlier in the tomb
were still alive when it was opened.
These skilled men inside the tomb
carved stone into images of dragons, phoenixes, and immortals,
and composed inscriptions and eulogies.
When this tomb was excavated in the early Hàn dynasty,
checking historical records,
none mentioned the creation of immortals, dragons, or phoenixes,
so it was realized these were made by the buried craftsmen.
Later people copied these inscriptions,
and the words were full of bitter grievances,
so they were called "Grievance Steles."
The Historical Records omitted and did not record this.
From "Records of Omitted Tales"
Xīnfēng
After Gāozǔ established Xīnfēng,
he also relocated the old community.
The streets, lanes, and buildings
looked exactly as before.
Men, women, old, and young,
walking hand in hand to the road's end,
each recognized their own homes.
Dogs, sheep, chickens, and ducks released onto the main roads and paths
also competed to find their own households.
This was the work of the craftsman Cháo Kuān.
The relocated people were delighted by the resemblance and moved by it,
so they vied to give rewards and gifts,
amassing hundreds in gold within a month.
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Zhāng Héng
Zhāng Héng, styled Píngzǐ, of the Later Hàn dynasty,
created the seismoscope.
It was cast from refined bronze,
with a diameter of eight feet,
its lid arched and raised,
shaped like a wine vessel,
adorned with seal script and patterns of mountains, turtles, birds, and beasts.
Inside was a central pillar,
with eight channels extending sideways,
equipped with mechanisms and triggers.
On the outside were eight dragon heads,
each holding a bronze ball in its mouth,
with toads below,
their mouths open to catch them.
The intricate gear mechanisms
were all concealed inside the vessel,
covered tightly without gaps.
If an earthquake occurred,
the vessel would shake, triggering the mechanism,
causing a dragon to spit out its ball, which the toad would catch.
The vibration would be intense,
allowing the observer to detect it.
If one dragon triggered its mechanism
while the other seven remained still,
by checking the direction,
one could know where the earthquake occurred.
The instrument's accuracy was almost divine;
according to all written records,
nothing like it had ever existed.
Once, a dragon triggered its mechanism, but no earthquake was felt.
Scholars in the capital
initially doubted its reliability.
A few days later, a courier arrived,
reporting that an earthquake had indeed occurred.
Then everyone admired its miraculous precision.
From "Book of the Later Hàn"
Wáng Sù
Wáng Sù created a rat-repelling ball.
It was made of bronze,
rotating on its own day and night.
From "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng"
Língyún Tower
The towers and pavilions of Língyún Tower were exquisitely crafted.
First, the materials were weighed to balance them perfectly,
ensuring appropriate lightness and heaviness,
before construction began.
Thus, there was not the slightest imbalance.
Although the tower was lofty and steep,
it constantly swayed with the wind,
yet never collapsed.
When Emperor Míng of Wèi ascended the tower,
fearing its precarious state,
he ordered large timbers to support it.
The tower immediately crumbled.
Commentators said it was due to the imbalance of weight.
From "A New Account of the Tales of the World"
Prince Sī of Chén
Prince Sī of Chén of Wèi possessed divine ingenuity.
He made a duck-head ladle that floated on a winding wine pool.
Wherever the prince intended to urge someone to drink,
the duck head would turn in that direction.
He also made a magpie-tail ladle,
with a long, straight handle.
Wherever the prince's intention focused,
by spinning it on the wine vessel,
the magpie would point there.
Lady Wú
Lady Zhào, consort of the Lord of Wú,
was the younger sister of Zhào Dá.
She excelled at painting,
and her skill was matchless.
Between her fingers,
she could weave colored silk into brocade depicting clouds, dragons, coiling phoenixes,
ranging from over a foot in size
down to a square inch.
In the palace, it was called "the ultimate loom work."
Sūn Quán often lamented that Wèi and Shǔ had not yet been pacified,
and during lulls in military campaigns,
he wished to find a skilled painter
to create images of mountains, rivers, terrain, and military formations.
Zhào Dá then presented his sister.
Sūn Quán ordered her to depict the landscapes of the Nine Provinces, rivers, lakes, and the Five Sacred Mountains.
Lady Zhào said:
"The colors of painting
fade and vanish easily,
and cannot be treasured for long.
I am skilled at embroidery."
She arranged all the states on a square piece of silk,
embroidering the forms of the Five Sacred Mountains, rivers, seas, cities, and military formations,
and presented it to the Lord of Wú.
People of the time called it "the ultimate needlework."
Even the thorn-carved monkeys and wooden birds,
or cloud ladders and flying kites,
could not surpass its beauty.
Sūn Quán resided in the Zhāoyáng Palace,
and wearied by the summer heat,
he lifted the purple gauze curtains.
Lady Zhào said:
"This is not precious enough."
Sūn Quán asked her to explain her idea,
and she replied:
"I wish to exhaust my thoughts and efforts
to create a silk curtain that, when lowered, allows cool breezes to enter naturally,
with no obstruction to the view outside.
Those standing in attendance will feel a refreshing coolness,
as if riding the wind."
Sūn Quán praised the idea.
Lady Zhào then split strands of hair
and joined them with divine glue.
This divine glue came from the country of Yùyí,
used to reconnect broken bowstrings.
No matter how many breaks, it could mend them all.
She wove it into a fine gauze,
taking months to complete,
and tailored it into a curtain.
Viewed from both inside and out,
it fluttered like mist lightly stirring,
and the room became naturally cool.
At that time, Sūn Quán was still on military campaigns,
and he often carried this curtain with him,
using it as his campaign tent.
Unfurled, it spanned several zhang in width and length;
rolled up, it could fit inside a pillow.
People of the time called it "the ultimate silk."
Thus, Wú possessed three ultimate arts,
and none in the world could rival their marvel.
Later, those who coveted favor and sought to flatter
claimed that Lady Zhào showed off too much before the ruler,
leading to her dismissal.
Although she fell under suspicion and was demoted,
records of her exquisite craftsmanship were preserved.
When Wú perished,
her whereabouts became unknown.
From Wáng Zǐnián's *Shíyí Jì*
Ōu Chún
During the Dàxīng era,
Ōu Chún of Héngyáng created a mouse market.
It was over four square zhàng in size,
with four gates opened,
each gate guarded by a wooden figure.
When four or five mice were released inside,
and tried to exit through a gate,
the wooden figure would strike them with a mallet.
From *Jìnyáng Qiū*
The Water Lily Tilt Vessel
Emperor Wén of Western Wèi crafted two tilt vessels.
One depicted two immortals
holding a bowl together,
placed on a single tray.
There was a mountain cover,
and the mountain emitted a fragrant aroma.
Another immortal held a golden vase,
positioned above the vessel,
pouring water onto the mountain.
The water would then flow from the vase into the vessel,
with mist rising from the mountain.
This was called the "Immortal Tilt Vessel."
The other depicted two lotus flowers,
placed on a single tray,
spaced about a foot apart.
In the center was a lotus blossom,
hanging down over the vessel.
When water was poured into the lotus, it would fill the vessel.
It was also adorned with ducks, geese, and toads,
and was called the "Water Lily Tilt Vessel."
Each tray had a stand and a bowl;
the bowl was round, and the stand was square.
Figures were placed within,
representing the three realms of heaven, earth, and humanity.
The vessel was shaped like a gōng cup,
level when full,
and tilting when overflowing.
It was placed in the front hall
to warn against excess.
The original source is missing;
the Ming manuscript cites it from *Sānguó Diǎnlüè*
Prince of Lánlíng
The Prince of Lánlíng of Northern Qí had ingenious ideas
and created a dancing húzi figure.
Whenever the prince intended to offer a toast,
the húzi would hold up a cup and bow.
No one knew how it worked.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*
Monastery Língzhāo
In Northern Qí, there was a monk named Língzhāo who possessed great ingenuity.
Emperor Wǔchéng ordered him to build a floating cup stream in a mountain pavilion.
Each time a cup boat reached the emperor,
he would reach out to take the cup,
and the boat would stop by itself.
Above, a small wooden child would clap its hands,
harmonizing with the music of strings and pipes.
After drinking, when the cup was set down,
a wooden figure would push it back.
If the emperor did not finish his drink,
the boat would not leave.
Not long after,
Língzhāo suddenly clutched his chest,
as if stabbed by a knife,
and shortly after vomited blood and died.
Seven-Treasure Mirror Stand
Empress Dowager Hú ordered Língzhāo to create a seven-treasure mirror stand.
It had thirty-six compartments in total,
with a separate figure of a woman,
each holding a lock.
As soon as one latch was lowered,
all thirty-six doors would close simultaneously.
If this latch was pulled,
all the doors would open,
and the women would each step out before their doors.
From *Huánglǎn*,
*Yùlǎn* 717 cites it from *Sānguó Diǎnlüè*
Illustrated Manual of Water Features
Emperor Yáng additionally ordered Academician Dù Bǎo to compile the *Illustrated Classic of Water Ornaments* in fifteen volumes,
newly completed.
On the third day of the third month,
he assembled his ministers at the Qūshuǐ [Winding Stream]
to view the water ornaments.
There was a divine turtle emerging from the river bearing the Eight Trigrams,
presenting
The character "presenting" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy.
them to Fúxī;
a yellow dragon emerging from the river bearing a chart;
a dark turtle emerging from the Luò River with a tally in its mouth;
a great carp emerging from the waters of Cuìguī with a register chart in its mouth,
both presented to the Yellow Emperor;
the Yellow Emperor fasted at Xuánhù,
and a phoenix descended upon the Luò River;
a red-armored numinous turtle emerged from the Luò River with a writing in its mouth, presenting it to Cāngjié;
Yáo and Shùn sat in a boat on the river,
a phoenix bearing a chart;
a red dragon emerging from the river carrying a chart,
both presented to Yáo;
a dragon-horse emerging from the river with patterned armor in its mouth, presenting it to Shùn;
Yáo and Shùn traveled on the river,
encountering five old men;
Yáo met the Four Masters on the south bank of the Fén River;
Shùn fished at Léizé;
made pottery by the riverbank;
a yellow dragon emerged from the river bearing a yellow tally, seal, and chart, presenting it to Shùn;
Shùn harmonized in song with the hundred artisans,
and fish leaped in the water;
a white-faced tall man with a fish body,
presented the River Chart to Yǔ,
danced and entered the river;
Yǔ regulated the waters,
Yìnglóng used its tail to draw on the ground,
guiding where the floodwaters should be channeled;
he cut through the Lóngmén [Dragon Gate] to dredge the river,
Yǔ crossed the Jiāng,
a yellow dragon bore his boat;
the Xuányí Cāngshuǐ envoy presented Yǔ with the *Classic of Mountains and Seas*,
he encountered two goddesses by a spring;
Emperor Tiānyǐ viewed the Luò,
two yellow fish leaped together,
transforming into black jade with red markings;
Jiāngyuán stepped into the footprints of a giant by the riverbank,
abandoned Hòujì on the cold ice,
birds covered him with their wings and trod upon him;
the King sat by the Spirit Pond,
full of leaping fish;
Crown Prince Fā crossed the river,
a white fish with red markings leaped into the king's boat;
King Wǔ crossed Mèngjīn,
wielding a yellow battle-axe to command the waves of Yánghóu;
King Chéng performed the rites of Shùn,
glorious radiance covered the river;
King Mù of Zhōu performed the music of the heavens at Xuánchí,
hunted at Zǎojīn,
capturing a dark raccoon dog and a white fox;
toasted the Queen Mother of the West above the Jade Pool,
crossed the Jiǔjiāng,
giant turtles forming a bridge;
the state of Túxiū presented King Zhāo with a green phoenix and red crane,
they drank at Yùxī;
Prince Jìn played the shēng on the Yī River,
a phoenix descended;
Qín Shǐhuáng entered the sea,
saw the sea god;
Hàn Gāozǔ hid in the marshes of Mángdàng Mountain,
purple clouds above;
Emperor Wǔ sailed a tower ship on the Fén River,
toured the Kūnmíng Pond,
removed the hooks from the big fish
The character "hooks" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Huáng manuscript copy.
toured the Luò,
the water god presented luminous pearls and dragon marrow;
Emperor Huán of Hàn toured the river,
encountered a green ox emerging from the river;
Cáo Mān bathed in the Qiáo River,
struck a water dragon;
Emperor Wén of Wèi raised an army,
reached the river but did not cross;
Dù Yù completed the construction of a river bridge,
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn attended the gathering,
raised his wine cup to toast Dù Yù;
five horses floated across the Jiāng,
one horse transformed into a dragon;
an immortal drew water from the Sweet Spring;
a golden man rode a golden boat;
a dark turtle with green markings emerged from the Luò River with a writing in its mouth,
a green dragon emerged from the river bearing a writing,
both presented to the Duke of Zhōu;
Lǚ Wàng fished at Pánxī and obtained a jade tablet,
also
"Also" originally written as "text",
corrected based on the Ming manuscript copy.
fished at Biànxī and caught a great carp,
found military tallies inside its belly;
Duke Huán of Qí asked Yúgōng his name;
the King of Chǔ crossed the Jiāng and obtained a duckweed fruit;
King Zhāo of Qín feasted at the river bend,
a golden man holding a water-heart sword came to him;
the Great Emperor of Wú stood at the fishing terrace looking at Gě Xuán;
Liú Bèi rode his horse across Tánxī;
Dāntái Zǐyǔ crossed the Jiāng,
two dragons flanked his boat;
Zīqiū Xīn battled the water god;
Zhōu Chǔ beheaded a dragon;
Qū Yuán encountered a fisherman;
Biàn Suí threw himself into the Yǐng River;
Xǔ Yóu washed his ears;
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ encountered the ferryman's daughter;
Confucius encountered a woman bathing in the river;
Qiū Hú's wife threw herself into the water;
Kǒng Yú released a turtle;
Zhuāngzǐ and Huìzǐ observed fish;
Zhèng Hóng, while gathering firewood on the path, had the wind return.
Zhào Bǐng crossed the Jiāng under a canopy;
the Yánggǔ maiden bathed the sun;
Qū Yuán drowned himself in the Mìluó River;
Jùlíng split the mountain;
a giant whale swallowing a boat—all such scenes totaled seventy-two tableaus,
all carved from wood.
Some rode boats,
some rode mountains,
some rode flat islets,
some rode massive rocks,
some rode palaces.
The wooden figures were about two feet tall,
clothed in fine silks,
adorned with gold and jade.
And the various birds, beasts, fish, and fowl that were made,
all could move as if alive,
proceeding along the winding stream.
Also interspersed were pleasure barges,
arranged in sequence with the water ornaments,
also made as twelve barges.
The barges were one zhàng long and six chǐ wide.
Wooden figures played music,
struck chime stones and bells,
plucked the zhēng and played the sè,
all capable of producing complete melodies.
And they performed various entertainments,
juggling swords and dancing wheels,
ascending poles and throwing ropes,
all indistinguishable from living performers.
These pleasure barge water ornaments,
were also exquisitely carved and decorated.
Circling the winding pond,
they were all operated by hydraulic mechanisms.
Their wondrous and fantastical strangeness,
exceeded all expectations.
Also made were small boats eight chǐ long,
seven vessels.
Wooden figures about two feet tall,
rode these boats to serve wine.
On each boat,
one person holding a wine cup stood at the bow,
one person holding a wine jar stood next,
one person steered the boat at the stern,
two persons rowed in the center,
circling the winding water pond.
At the turns of the winding course,
sat the banquet guests in attendance.
These wine-serving boats,
moved along the bank,
traveling faster than the water ornaments.
The water ornaments circled the pond once,
while the wine boats completed three circuits,
before they would stop together.
Whenever a wine boat reached a guest's seat, it would stop,
the wooden figure holding the wine on the bow would extend its hand.
When offered wine,
the guest would take the cup and drink.
After returning the cup,
the wooden figure would receive the cup,
turn towards the person with the wine jar to take a ladle and fill the cup with wine.
The boat would then proceed according to its pattern,
and whenever it reached a guest's seat,
the procedure was as before.
All this was achieved by mechanisms installed along the bank in the water,
such marvelous ingenuity,
all originated from the ideas of Huáng Gǔn.
Dù Bǎo at that time received the imperial order to compile the *Illustrated Classic of Water Ornaments*,
and to supervise the fine craftsmen's drawings.
Once completed and presented to the throne,
he was ordered to collaborate with Huáng Gǔn.
They constructed these water ornaments within the imperial park,
thus allowing him to observe them in detail.
Huáng Gǔn's ingenious nature,
is rarely matched in past or present.
From *Records of Omitted Matters of the Great Enterprise Era*
Guānwén Hall
Emperor Suí Yángdì ordered the construction of the Guānwén Hall.
In front, two side wings served as book halls,
each with twelve bays.
In front of the halls, a connecting corridor ran through.
Supporting the hall,
each bay had twelve precious cabinets.
In front, square five-incense layered beds were set,
also adorned with gold and jade.
In spring and summer, nine-curved
The character "curved" was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition.
elephant mats were spread;
in autumn, phoenix-patterned silk flower cushions;
in winter, then added cotton-stuffed Sumeru felt.
When the emperor visited the book hall,
sometimes to read books,
within those twelve bays,
north and south were connected by lightning windows.
Lattice cages faced each other,
the craftsmanship of carving,
reached the pinnacle of wondrous skill.
Golden fittings and jade inscriptions,
ornate caissons and painted rafters,
shone brilliantly, dazzling the eyes.
Every three bays opened a square door,
with brocade curtains hanging over the doors.
Above were two flying immortals,
at the ground by the door, a mechanism was installed.
When the imperial carriage was about to arrive,
then palace maidens would hold incense burners,
walking ahead of the carriage.
One zhàng away from the door,
stepping on the mechanism triggered it,
the immortals then descended from the pavilion,
holding the curtains as they rose,
the door leaves immediately opened,
the book cabinets also unlocked,
as if naturally,
all by the force of a single mechanism.
When the imperial carriage departed,
the curtains hung down and closed as before.
The doorways of all the rooms,
were of identical style.
The books compiled there,
in wording and arrangement of events,
were systematic and orderly,
the writing concise and reasoning smooth,
mutually illuminating and clarifying.
As for the accuracy of transcription,
between the characters,
there were no errors of alteration or deletion.
The binding was splendid and clean,
could be said to be unmatched in past and present,
a renowned treasure of an age without peer.
From the Hàn dynasty onward until the Liáng,
literary talents and gifted scholars,
all their writings and compositions,
none could match these.
The titles of the new books,
mostly were created by the emperor himself,
each time a book was presented,
rewards were surely bestowed.
From "Dàyè Shíyí Jì"
Liú Jiāo
Liú Jiāo of Yōuzhōu,
carried a long pole seventy chǐ high,
lifting it up and down by himself.
He had a daughter, twelve years old and very comely,
stationed atop the pole,
standing alone on a tray,
onlookers could not bear to watch,
yet the girl showed no fear.
Later, she eventually fell and was killed.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Zhāng Chóng
Táng dynasty craftsman Zhāng Chóng could make gray-painted belt hooks and fittings.
Each piece,
as large as a coin.
Gray-painted and fired,
upon seeing fire, patterns would subtly rise.
Shapes of dragons, fish, birds, and beasts,
all were fully represented.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Twelve Zodiac Carriage
During the Rúyì era of Wǔ Zétiān,
Hǎizhōu presented a craftsman,
who made a twelve zodiac carriage.
When the shafts turned due south,
then the noon gate would open,
and a horse-headed man would emerge.
Turning in all directions,
not deviating by the slightest.
Also made a wooden fire tube,
an iron cup holding fire,
rolling and turning without spilling.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Bronze Zūn
Hánwáng Yuánjiā had a bronze zūn vessel,
with wine stored on its back and standing on one leg.
When full, it stood upright;
when not full, it tilted.
Also made a bronze dove,
rubbed on felt until hot, it would chirp,
like the sound of a real dove.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Yīn Wénliàng
Yīn Wénliàng of Luòzhōu once served as a county magistrate,
ingenious by nature and fond of wine.
Carved wood into figures,
clothed in silk colors.
Pouring wine and passing cups,
all in proper order.
Also made singing girls,
singing songs and playing sheng pipes,
all able to keep rhythm.
If the drink was not finished,
the wooden boy would refuse to hold the cup;
if drinking was not completed,
then the wooden singing girls would urgently urge with song and pipe,
this too was unfathomably divine and marvelous.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Yáng Wùlián
The Minister of Works Yáng Wùlián had great ingenious ideas.
Often in Qìnzhōu city carved wood into a monk,
holding a bowl in hand,
able to beg on its own.
When the bowl was full of coins,
a mechanism suddenly triggered,
naturally making a sound saying "alms."
Marketers vied to watch,
wanting it to make the sound.
Daily alms soon exceeded several thousand.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Wáng Jū
Wáng Jū, Prefect of Chēnzhōu, carved wood into an otter,
sank it in water to catch fish.
It would raise its head and emerge,
for in the otter's mouth was placed bait with a turning mechanism,
weighted with a stone to sink it,
fish taking the bait,
the mechanism would trigger,
the mouth closing would then hold the fish,
the stone releasing would make it float up.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Xuē Shènhuò
Xuē Shènhuò was skilled at pitch-pot.
Like a dragon leaping, a falcon flying,
nimble without missing an arrow.
Placing the pot behind his back,
then turning to throw arrows backward at it,
a hundred shots, a hundred hits.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Mǎ Dàifēng
In the early years of the Kāiyuán era, when the imperial carriage was being refurbished,
Mǎ Dàifēng from Dōnghǎi was capable of mastering ingenious craftsmanship.
Thus, for items such as the south-pointing chariot, the mileage drum, and the wind-direction bird,
Dàifēng made modifications and repairs,
their ingenuity surpassing that of ancient times.
Dàifēng also crafted a dressing set for the empress,
in the center of which stood a mirror stand,
with two layers beneath the stand,
each having doors.
When the empress was about to comb her hair and wash,
after opening the mirror case,
the doors below the stand would open,
and a wooden woman’s hand would extend, holding a comb.
After the empress took it,
the wooden figure would immediately withdraw.
As for facial cream, makeup powder,
eyebrow ink, and hair flowers,
all the items needed for use,
were held by wooden figures.
They would arrive in succession,
and after being taken, would immediately withdraw,
with the doors closing again.
In this manner, all provisions were supplied by wooden figures.
After the empress finished her makeup,
all the doors would close,
and then the set would be taken away.
The dressing stand was adorned with gold, silver, and colorful paintings,
and the wooden women’s clothing and decorations
were of the utmost exquisiteness and refinement.
After Dàifēng had crafted the imperial procession equipment,
he also made a dressing stand for the empress,
and so several years passed.
An imperial decree only provided for his expenses,
but ultimately did not grant him an official post,
which Dàifēng found humiliating.
He further petitioned to create items such as the tilting vessel, wine mountain, and coin jar,
and was permitted to do so.
All were crafted from silver.
Within the wine mountain and coin jar,
there were mechanisms in motion.
Sometimes openings were made on all sides,
to admit air currents.
The air currents would rotate,
with yīn and yáng orientations.
This caused external springs to flow and spout,
to fill wine cups.
The wine’s flow in and out
all appeared natural.
Its ingenuity surpassed even that of nature.
After completion, it was presented to the emperor.
But just then, there were matters in the palace,
and ultimately he was not summoned for an audience.
Dàifēng resented his repeated misfortunes,
so he changed his name,
and hid in the mountains of Xīhé.
By the end of the Kāiyuán era,
Dàifēng came from Jìnzhōu.
He called himself the Daoist Wú Cì.
He often abstained from eating grains.
Together with Lǐ Jìn, the magistrate of Cuīyì, he crafted a wine mountain, coin jar, tilting vessel, and other items.
The wine mountain stood on a tray,
the tray having a diameter of four feet five inches,
with a large turtle beneath supporting the tray,
all mechanisms being inside the turtle’s belly.
On the tray stood a mountain,
three feet high,
with exceptionally beautiful peaks and ridges.
The tray was made of wood,
lacquered on the outside,
the turtle and mountain were also lacquered cloth hollow structures,
with colorful paintings on the outside.
The mountain was hollow inside,
able to hold three dǒu of wine.
Around the mountain were arranged wine pools,
outside the pools there were more mountains encircling them.
In the pools grew lotuses,
the flowers and leaves all made of wrought iron.
When the flowers bloomed and leaves unfolded,
they served as plates and leaves,
with dried meats, pickled foods, rare fruits, and other accompaniments for wine placed among the flowers and leaves.
On the southern half of the mountain was a dragon,
half-hidden within the mountain,
opening its mouth to pour wine.
Beneath the dragon, in a large lotus leaf,
there was a cup to catch it,
the cup holding four hé.
The dragon would pour wine until eight-tenths full and then stop,
and the one to drink would take it.
If drinking was delayed,
on the mountain top was a double pavilion,
the pavilion door would open,
and a wine-urging figure, fully dressed and holding a tablet, would come out.
Then, after returning the cup to the leaf,
the dragon would refill it,
the wine attendant would withdraw,
and the pavilion door would close.
If there was further delay,
the figure would emerge as before.
Until the banquet ended,
there were never any mistakes.
On all four sides of the mountain, east and west, dragons poured wine.
Even if wine overflowed into the pool,
there were holes in the pool,
secretly channeling the wine from the pool back into the mountain.
By the time the banquet ended and drinking finished,
there was no wine left in the pool either.
There were two tilting vessels,
on the left and right of the wine mountain,
into which dragons poured wine.
When empty, they tilted,
when half-full, they leveled,
when full, they overturned.
This is the so-called admonishing vessel placed beside the seat in the Lǔ temple.
Gentlemen use it to warn against excess,
and Confucius observed it as a caution.
Dù Yù attempted to make a tilting vessel but failed,
as recorded in previous histories.
But as for Wú Cì,
he crafted it as if it were an ordinary vessel.
From “Jì Wén.”
Huáqīng Pool
Emperor Xuánzōng newly expanded a pool at Huáqīng Palace,
its construction grand and magnificent.
Ān Lùshān, from Fànyáng, crafted fish, dragons, phoenixes, and wild geese from white jade stone,
and also presented a stone bridge and stone lotus flowers.
The carving was exquisitely skillful,
almost beyond human capability.
The emperor was greatly pleased,
and ordered them placed in the pool,
with the stone bridge spanning across it,
and the lotus flowers emerging from the water’s edge.
When the emperor visited Huáqīng Palace,
he went to that spot.
Undressing to enter,
he saw the fish, dragons, phoenixes, and wild geese all as if raising scales and wings,
appearing ready to fly and move.
The emperor was very frightened,
and hastily ordered them removed,
though the lotus flowers and stone bridge remained.
He also once built several dozen long hot spring pools in the palace,
with surrounding buildings.
They were paved with patterned stone.
Silver-inlaid lacquer boats and sandalwood-scented boats
were placed within them.
Even the oars and paddles were adorned with pearls and jade.
Also, in the hot spring pools,
he piled sapphires and sandalwood to form mountains,
resembling Yíngzhōu and Fāngzhàng.
From “Tán Bīn Lù.”
Chóngmíng Pillow
In the eighth year of the Yuánhé era,
the state of Dàzhěn presented a Zhòngmíng pillow and a divine brocade quilt.
It is said that their state is located thirty thousand lǐ to the southeast of the sea,
in the position of the Zhěn constellation,
hence it is called "Dàzhěn State."
Héqiū Yúhāo Mountain,
"Héqiū Yúhāo Mountain,"
is mentioned in the Classic of Mountains and Seas.
The Zhòngmíng pillow is one chǐ and two cùn in length,
and six cùn in height.
It is pure white, surpassing crystal.
Inside, there are structures resembling towers and pavilions,
with ten Daoist priests holding incense and tablets on all four sides,
circling endlessly,
referred to as "Daoist Realms of Practice."
The tiles, wood, and pigments of the towers and pavilions,
as well as the hairpins and robes of the Daoist priests,
are all meticulously depicted,
transparent and clear as if viewing objects through water.
The divine brocade quilt is woven from the silk of water silkworms,
measuring two chǐ square,
and one cùn thick.
On it are dragon patterns and phoenix colors,
almost as if not made by human hands.
In their state, they use five-colored stones to line ponds,
and gather large leaves of the paper mulberry tree.
They raise silkworms in the ponds.
When they first hatch, they are as small as
The character "rú" was originally missing,
and has been added based on the Míng manuscript, Xǔ manuscript, and Huáng manuscript.
the eyelash of a mosquito,
swimming within.
When they grow, they can reach five or six cùn in length.
In the ponds, there are upright lotuses,
which remain unmoved even when blown by fierce winds,
with the largest spanning three or four chǐ.
After fifteen days, the silkworms leap into the lotuses,
to form their cocoons.
The cocoons are shaped like square dippers,
naturally in five colors.
The people of the state reel the silk,
to weave the divine brocade.
It is also called "Língquán silk."
When the emperor first examined the brocade quilt,
he laughed with his consorts and said:
"This is not even enough to serve as swaddling clothes for an infant,
how could it cover me?"
The envoy said:
"The silk of this brocade
comes from water silkworms,
and expands when exposed to water.
Water and fire counteract each other,
so it shrinks when exposed to fire."
Then, before the emperor,
he ordered four officials to stretch it out,
and with a spray of water,
it expanded to two zhàng square,
radiant with five colors,
surpassing its previous appearance.
The emperor sighed and said:
"What originates from heaven is close to the heavens,
what originates from earth is close to the earth.
Is this not so!"
He then ordered it to be shrunk with fire,
and in a moment, it returned to its original state.
From the Dùyáng Biān.
Hán Zhìhé
During the reign of Emperor Mùzōng,
there was a flying dragon craftsman named Hán Zhìhé,
originally from the state of Wō.
He excelled at carving wood,
creating shapes of luan, cranes, crows, and magpies,
which drank, pecked, and cried mournfully,
indistinguishable from real ones.
He placed mechanisms inside their bellies,
and when activated, they would soar into the air and flap their wings,
reaching heights of up to one hundred chǐ,
and flying one or two hundred steps away,
before descending again.
He also carved wooden cats to catch sparrows and mice,
and the Flying Dragon Envoy marveled at his ingenuity.
He reported this to the emperor,
who was delighted upon seeing them.
Zhìhé further carved a footstool several chǐ high,
adorned with gold, silver, and colorful paintings,
calling it the "Dragon-Revealing Stool."
When left untouched, the dragon shape was invisible,
but when stepped on, its scales, mane, claws, and horns would all emerge.
When first presented,
the emperor stepped on it with his foot,
and the dragon writhed as if amidst clouds and rain.
The emperor grew fearful,
and ordered it removed.
Zhìhé prostrated himself before the emperor,
claiming his own ignorance,
and that he had inadvertently startled the emperor.
He expressed his wish to present another humble skill,
to entertain the emperor's eyes and ears,
and to atone for his capital offense.
The emperor laughed and said:
"What skill do you possess?
Try performing it for me."
Zhìhé then took from his bosom a square box made of paulownia wood, several cùn in size.
Inside were creatures called "fly tigers,"
numbering no less than one or two hundred.
They were all red in color,
said to be due to being fed cinnabar.
He divided them into five groups,
and ordered
The Míng manuscript uses "hé" instead of "lìng."
them to perform the "Liángzhōu" dance.
The emperor summoned the court musicians,
to play the accompanying music.
The fly tigers swirled and twirled,
never missing a beat,
and whenever there was a lyrical passage,
they emitted faint buzzing sounds like flies.
When the music ended,
they retreated in an orderly manner,
as if there were ranks of seniority and hierarchy.
Zhìhé placed a fly tiger on his finger,
and hunted flies within several steps,
like a sparrowhawk catching a sparrow,
rarely missing its target.
The emperor praised his skill as somewhat remarkable,
and bestowed upon him assorted silks and silverware.
But Zhìhé, upon leaving the palace gates,
gave them all away to others.
Within a year,
no one knew where Zhìhé had gone.
The emperor planted thousand-petaled peonies in front of the palace hall,
and when they bloomed,
their fragrance was overwhelming.
Each flower had a thousand petals,
large and bright red.
Whenever the emperor beheld their splendid beauty,
he marveled that nothing like it existed in the mortal world.
From then on, every night in the palace,
tens of thousands of yellow and white butterflies
would gather among the flowers,
their glow illuminating the surroundings,
and depart only at dawn.
The palace maids vied to catch them with silk handkerchiefs,
and none failed to capture some.
The emperor ordered nets to be set up in the palace,
and they caught hundreds.
Inside the hall, he allowed the consorts to chase and catch them,
as a form of entertainment.
At daybreak, when they looked at them,
they had all turned into gold and jade.
Their craftsmanship was exquisite,
beyond compare.
The palace ladies competed to tie silk threads around their feet,
to wear them as hair ornaments,
and at night, they glowed inside their cosmetic cases.
That night, when they opened the treasure cabinet,
they saw that the gold and jade dust stored inside
was about to transform into butterflies,
and the palace finally realized the truth.
From the Dùyáng Biān.
Dū Jūnmó
In the late Suí dynasty, there was a man named Dū Jūnmó who excelled at shooting with his eyes closed.
If he aimed for the eye, he would hit the eye.
If he aimed for the mouth, he would hit the mouth.
A man named Wáng Língzhì learned archery from Jūnmó.
Believing he had mastered all the subtleties,
he wanted to kill Jūnmó,
so he alone could possess this skill.
Jūnmó held a short dagger,
and whenever an arrow came, he would cut it down.
Only one arrow remained.
Jūnmó opened his mouth and caught it.
Then, biting the arrowhead, he laughed and said:
"You have studied archery for three years,
but I never taught you the method of biting arrowheads."
In the "Lièzǐ,"
there is a story about Gǔ Zhīgōng, an ancient master archer.
His disciple was named Fēi Wèi,
whose skill surpassed his master's.
Jǐ Chāng then learned archery from Fēi Wèi.
Using a bow made of horn from a young deer,
and arrows made of northern bamboo,
he could shoot through the heart of a louse.
After mastering all of Fēi Wèi's techniques,
he reckoned that in all the world,
only one person could rival him.
So he plotted to kill Fēi Wèi.
They met in the wilderness,
and the two shot at each other.
Their arrowheads collided,
falling to the ground without raising a speck of dust.
Fēi Wèi's arrows were exhausted first,
while Jǐ Chāng had one arrow left.
When he shot it,
Fēi Wèi blocked it with the tip of a thorny branch,
without the slightest error.
Then the two men wept, threw down their bows,
and pledged to be as father and son.
They carved an oath on their backs,
vowing never to reveal their skills to others.
Mèngzǐ said:
"Féng Méng learned archery from Yì,
and mastered all of Yì's techniques.
Thinking that only Yì surpassed him,
he then killed Yì."
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ."
Lǐ Qīnyáo
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a cavalry general named Lǐ Qīnyáo,
whose skill with bow and arrow was unparalleled.
Through his merits, he rose to the position of prefect,
and concurrently served as Censor-in-Chief.
During the Zhìdé era,
he served under Lín Huái,
and faced off against Shǐ Simíng in Shǎnxī.
One morning, as the battle was about to begin,
Lín Huái deployed his troops and advanced slowly.
While still about ten lǐ from the enemy,
suddenly a fox appeared in front of the army,
stumbling along as if leading the way.
It seemed like a guide.
Lín Huái, displeased, said:
"The King of Yuè saluted an angry frog,
but that was to inspire his officers and soldiers.
A fox is a suspicious and demonic creature—
how can it lead the vanguard?"
He immediately gave Qīnyáo three arrows,
ordering him to shoot the fox.
Qīnyáo accepted the order and galloped off.
There happened to be a patch of shallow grass, about twenty or thirty mǔ in size.
The fox ran into it.
Qīnyáo pursued it,
when suddenly a wild pheasant startled from under his horse's hooves
and flew straight into the clouds.
Qīnyáo turned and shot upward,
bringing it down with a single arrow.
Then, cracking his whip, he chased the fox,
and within ten paces,
picked up an arrow and shot it, hitting his target.
Thus, he returned with both creatures to report his success.
The entire army cheered,
their voices shaking the mountains and valleys.
At that time, the Huíhé cavalry had arrayed themselves on the northern plain,
their leaders numbering only one or two hundred.
They abandoned their troops and galloped over,
vying to praise Qīnyáo,
as if he were a divine marvel.
They then said:
"You must be a descendant of the Huíhé.
Otherwise,
how could your skill with bow and arrow
be so extraordinary?"
From "Jíyì Jì."
The Wandering Monk of Sūzhōu
One corner of the pavilion at Chóngxuán Temple in Sūzhōu suddenly sank.
Estimating the cost of repairs,
it would require several thousand strings of cash.
A wandering monk said:
"There is no need to trouble others.
Just give me one man,
and I will cut wooden wedges
to fix it."
The temple abbot agreed.
After each meal, the wandering monk
would take dozens of wedges,
carry an axe, and climb the pavilion,
hammering them into place.
In less than ten days,
all the pillars of the pavilion were straightened.
An old tale says that Shèngshàn Temple always stored ten jars of vinegar in its pavilion,
fearing that dragons might hide there
and cause thunderstorms.
From "Guóshǐ Bǔ."
The Jiāngxī Man
A man from Jiāngxī was skilled at splitting bamboo,
using just a few sections to make utensils.
Another man could juggle gourds,
saying flipping gourds was easier than flipping a ball.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ."
Monk Líng Jiàn
At the end of the Zhēnyuán era,
Monk Líng Jiàn of Láng Prefecture was skilled at slingshot.
He often made his own pellets,
and his pellets were square.
He used three catties of soil from the shore of Dòngtíng Lake,
three liǎng of charcoal powder,
one liǎng of alum powder,
half a liǎng of elm bark,
two spoons of rice water sediment,
two liǎng of purple mineral,
three fēn of fine sand,
five sheets of rattan paper,
half a gě of dried mulberry juice,
mixed the nine ingredients and pounded them three times,
then shaped them into pellets,
and dried them in the shade.
When Zhèng Huì was the prefect,
he had a relative named Yín,
who was well-read and fond of drinking,
and Huì held him in high regard.
Yín often competed with Líng Jiàn in slingshot.
Yín pointed to a tree knot,
several tens of paces away,
and said:
"Hit it and win five thousand."
Yín shot once and hit it,
but the pellet bounced back without breaking.
Líng Jiàn drew his sling,
hitting the target every time,
each pellet embedding in the knot and shattering.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ."
Zhāng Fēn
Zhāng Fēn once served as a行军 under Wéi Gāo,
and his miscellaneous skills surpassed others.
He could lift a seven-foot stone tablet,
and stop a double-wheeled water mill.
He often played kickball at Fúgǎn Temple,
kicking it as high as half the pagoda.
His slingshot required a draw weight of five dǒu.
He would select giant bamboo shoots facing the sun,
weave bamboo cages around them,
and as they grew, he would continually add soil,
always leaving about an inch exposed.
When the bamboo cage reached four feet in height,
he would let them grow freely.
In late autumn,
he would remove the cage and cut the bamboo.
Each foot had ten nodes,
and its color was like gold.
He used it to make bows.
Whenever he whitewashed a wall of one square zhàng,
he would use his slingshot to write the characters "天下太平" (peace under heaven).
The characters were upright and elegant,
as if shaped by hand.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ."
The Héběi General
At the beginning of the Jiànzhōng era,
there was a general from Héběi surnamed Xià,
who could draw a bow weighing several hundred catties.
Often on the polo field,
he would stack more than ten coins,
gallop on horseback,
and strike them with his polo mallet.
With each strike, a coin would fly up,
reaching a height of sixty or seventy feet—
such was his skill.
He would also plant dozens of thorns in a newly plastered wall,
take some boiled beans,
stand one zhàng away,
and throw the beans to impale them on the thorns,
missing not one in a hundred attempts.
He could also write a page of characters while galloping on horseback.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ."
The Western Shǔ Traveler
Also, when Zhāng Fēn was in Wéi Gāo's staff,
a guest at a banquet
used mung beans from a counting bowl to hit flies,
never missing once in ten attempts.
Everyone at the table was amazed and laughed.
Fēn said:
"Don't waste my beans."
He then pointed and caught flies,
pinching their hind legs,
with hardly any escaping.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Monk of the Zhìqǐ Temple
The monk Nàzhào of the Zhìqǐ Temple in Jīngzhōu was skilled at archery,
and often spoke of methods for aiming by light.
Generally, light that is long and flickering indicates a deer;
light that clings to the ground, brightening and dimming, indicates a hare;
light that is low and unmoving indicates a tiger.
He also said that when fighting a tiger at night,
one must see three tigers coming together.
The narrow one is the tiger's power (wēi),
and one should stab the middle one.
When the tiger dies,
its power (wēi) enters the ground,
and obtaining it can ward off all evils.
When the tiger first dies,
remember the place where its head rested,
and wait for a moonless night to dig there.
When about to dig,
tigers will certainly come roaring and throwing themselves about before and after,
but there is no need to fear,
for these are the tiger's ghosts.
At a depth of two feet,
one should obtain an object like amber,
which is formed when the tiger's gaze sinks into the earth.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Yáng Xuánbǎo
Emperor Wén of the Sòng dynasty was skilled at playing chess,
and often played chess with Tàipíng's Yáng Xuánbǎo.
Xuánbǎo won the governorship of Xuānchéng through a playful wager in chess,
and an imperial decree was issued to grant it as an empty appointment.
From "Tán Sǒu"
Wáng Jīxīn
When Emperor Xuánzōng traveled south,
all officials rushed to the imperial temporary residence,
and Wáng Jīxīn, a skilled chess player from the Hànlín Academy, followed.
The roads in Shǔ were narrow and treacherous.
Whenever travelers stopped to rest,
the postal stations and houses along the way
were mostly taken first by high-ranking or powerful officials.
Jīxīn had nowhere to stay,
so he followed a stream deep into the distance,
and lodged for the night in the home of an old widow in the mountains.
There were only a woman and her mother-in-law,
and they both closed their doors,
providing only water and fire.
As soon as it grew dark,
the woman and her mother-in-law both closed their doors and rested.
Jīxīn stayed under the eaves,
unable to sleep late into the night.
Suddenly, he heard the mother-in-law inside the hall say to the woman:
"On such a fine night, with nothing to amuse ourselves,
shall we play a game of chess for fun?"
The woman said:
"Yes."
Jīxīn privately found this strange:
there had been no lamps or candles in the hall,
and the woman and her mother-in-law were each in separate rooms to the east and west.
Jīxīn then pressed his ear against the door.
Soon, he heard the woman say:
"I place a stone at east five, south nine."
The mother-in-law replied:
"I place a stone at east five, south twelve."
The woman said again:
"I place a stone at west eight, south ten."
The mother-in-law replied again:
"I place a stone at west nine, south ten."
Each time they placed a stone,
they pondered for a long time.
As the night approached the fourth watch,
Jīxīn secretly recorded each move,
and they had placed only thirty-six stones in total.
Suddenly, he heard the mother-in-law say:
"You have lost,
I have won by only nine points."
The woman also accepted this gracefully.
At dawn,
Jīxīn dressed formally and requested instruction.
The old widow said:
"You may set up the board and place stones according to your own ideas."
Jīxīn then took out the board from his bag,
and arranged stones using all the secret techniques he had learned in his life.
Before he had placed even ten stones,
the old widow turned to the woman and said:
"This fellow can only be taught common strategies."
The woman then pointed out methods for attack, defense, capture, rescue, response, and resistance,
but her explanations were very brief.
Jīxīn asked for further elaboration,
but the old woman laughed and said:
"Even with just this, you will be unbeatable among mortals."
Jīxīn thanked them reverently and departed.
After walking a dozen steps,
he turned back to look,
but the house and gate he had seen earlier were gone.
From then on, Jīxīn's skill
was unmatched by anyone.
He set up the board according to the moves he had recorded from the woman and her mother-in-law's game,
exhausting all his mental effort,
trying to understand the nine-point victory,
but he never succeeded.
Thus, he named it the "Dèng Ài Invades Shǔ Formation,"
and it remains in chess manuals to this day,
yet no one in the world has ever been able to solve it.
From "Jíyì Jì"
Yīxíng
Yīxíng originally did not understand chess,
but once, while at Yān Guógōng's residence,
he watched Wáng Jīxīn play one game,
and then became his match.
He laughingly said to Yān Guógōng:
"This is merely about seizing the initiative.
If one remembers my four phrases on multiplication and division,
then everyone can become a national master."
Jìn dynasty's Luóshí, when playing chess with others,
would pick up the opponent's dead stones,
leaving empty spaces in the shape of dragons and phoenixes.
Some say that when Wáng Jīxīn played chess against Emperor Xuánzōng,
after the game ended,
he took all the stones away.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Wéi Yányòu
Wéi Yányòu played chess
as an equal match against Lǐ Shìxiù.
Shìxiù valued his reputation,
and refused to make the first move.
He would rather lose points to Yányòu,
and always conceded two lines.
Yányòu was originally supposed to take the imperial examination in the classics,
and passed through Dàliáng on his way.
The local military commander there knew he was skilled at chess.
He recommended him to the court.
Thus, it was said that there were many skilled chess players in Jiānghuái,
among whom those who played chess and understood the classics were often highly perceptive.
From "Jiāhuà Lù"
The Japanese Prince
During the Dàzhōng era,
a prince from the Kingdom of Japan came to court,
presenting precious vessels and musical performances.
The emperor arranged a variety of entertainments and delicacies to honor him.
The prince excelled at Go,
so the emperor ordered the court attendant Gù
("Gù" originally written as "Yán,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript copy) Shīyán to play against him.
The prince produced a catalpa-jade Go board
and warm-and-cool jade Go stones.
He said:
"Thirty thousand li east of our country,
there is Jízhēn Island.
On the island stands the Níngxiá Terrace,
and on the terrace lies the Shǒután Pool.
From this pool emerge jade stones—
not crafted by human hands,
yet naturally distinct in black and white.
They are warm in winter and cool in summer,
hence called 'warm-and-cool jade.'
There is also catalpa-jade,
which resembles catalpa wood in appearance.
Carved into a Go board,
it becomes so smooth and lustrous it can serve as a mirror."
When Shīyán played against him,
by the thirty-third move,
the outcome remained undecided.
Fearing to disgrace the emperor's command,
Shīyán wiped his sweaty hands and pondered deeply
before daring to place his stone.
This move was called "suppressing the divine head,"
resolving a double-ko situation.
The prince stared wide-eyed and withdrew his arm,
already acknowledging defeat.
Turning to the Court of State Ceremonial, he asked:
"What rank is this attendant?"
The official deceitfully replied:
"He is the third best."
In truth, Shīyán was considered the national champion.
The prince said:
"I wish to see the first."
The reply was:
"If you defeat the third,
you may see the second;
if you defeat the second,
you may see the first.
Now, to rashly demand to see the first—
how could that be possible?"
The prince covered the board and sighed:
"The best of a small kingdom
is no match for the third best of a great kingdom.
How true!"
Even now, enthusiasts still possess Gù Shīyán's "Diagram of the Thirty-Third Move Suppressing the Divine Head."
From the Dùyáng Biān.
Emperor Chéng of Hàn
Emperor Chéng of Hàn enjoyed cùjū (ancient football).
His ministers argued that cùjū was physically strenuous
and unsuitable for someone of his exalted status.
The emperor said:
"I enjoy it.
Find something similar but less taxing and present it to me."
Liú Xiàng presented dànqí (a table game) as an offering,
and the emperor was pleased.
He bestowed upon him a black lambskin robe and purple silk shoes,
which Liú wore for court audiences.
From the Xiǎoshuō.
Emperor Wén of Wèi
Dànqí was a game played with decorated pieces in the Wèi palace.
Emperor Wén was exceptionally skilled at it,
able to flick the pieces with the corner of a handkerchief
and never miss.
A guest claimed he could do the same,
so the emperor had him demonstrate.
The guest lowered his head and flicked the pieces with the corner of his hemp scarf,
his skill nearly surpassing the emperor's.
From the Shìshuō.
Emperor Wén also once said:
"Among other amusements and pastimes,
I have little interest,
but in dànqí I have somewhat grasped its subtleties.
In my youth, I once composed a rhapsody about it.
In the past, the capital had two master craftsmen:
the Marquis Héqīng, Dōngfāng Shì'ān, and Zhāng Gōngzǐ.
I have always regretted not being able to play against them."
In dànqí, twenty-four pieces are used,
their colors indicating rank.
Also, the Wèi method of play:
first, one piece is placed in the center of the board,
the others, alternating black and white, encircle it,
and eighteen moves complete the setup.
From the Shìshuō.
Cánggōu (Hidden Hook)
Traditionally, it is said that cánggōu originated with Gōuyì,
based on Xīn's Sānqín Jì, which states:
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's consort, Lady Gōuyì, kept her hand clenched.
People of the time imitated her,
calling it "hiding the hook."
Yīn Jìngshùn's Jìngxùn says:
"Gōu" is the same as "kōu."
People divide into teams,
hide an object in their hands,
and try to guess its location.
Also, in playing cánggōu,
if there is one extra person,
that person moves between the two teams,
called the "owl."
The Fēngtǔ Jì says:
"In the game of cánggōu,
players divide into two teams to compete.
If the number is even, they face off directly;
if odd,
one person becomes a floating participant,
attached either to the upper team or the lower team,
called the 'flying bird.'"
Also, this game must be played
during the first month.
According to the Fēngtǔ Jì,
it takes place after the year-end sacrifice.
Yǔ Chǎn's "Rhapsody on Cánggōu" says:
"After the year-end sacrifice,
I ordered both inside and outside the palace to play the hook-hiding game."
From the Yǒuyáng Zázǔ.
Huán Xuán
Yīn Zhòngkān and Huán Xuán played cánggōu together,
with one hundred tallies per team.
Huán's team was about to lose,
with only the "tiger's probe" left.
Gù Kǎizhī served as Yīn Zhòngkān's military advisor
and was ill, resting in his office.
Huán sent a messenger
to request Gù to rise from his sickbed
and have him guess the "tiger's probe."
Gù came and,
after sitting down,
Huán said to him:
"You may try to find the hook."
Gù replied:
"If you reward me with a hundred bolts of cloth,
I will retrieve the hook."
Huán's team then won.
From the Zhǔgōng Gùshì.
Gāo Yìng
An old saying claims that playing cánggōu causes separation among people,
or that predictions made during the game come true.
The scholar Gāo Yìng
was exceptionally skilled at guessing in cánggōu.
Duàn Chéngshì often played cánggōu in Jīngzhōu,
with over fifty people per team,
and Gāo guessed correctly nine out of ten times.
Even when his teammates hid the hook, he knew its location,
leading others to suspect he used some special technique.
When asked,
Yìng said he merely observed their demeanor, speech, and expressions,
like detecting a thief by watching closely.
From the Yǒuyáng Zázǔ.
Shí Mín
The hermit Shí Mín was especially adept at guessing in cánggōu.
He was friends with Zhāng Yòuxīn and his brothers.
One leisurely evening while entertaining guests,
they decided to test his guessing skill,
and every time he focused, he guessed correctly.
Zhāng then hid the hook in the folds of his turban.
After a long while, Mín smiled and said:
"You're all holding empty fists."
A moment later, he pointed out the hook
in the left flap of Zhāng's headwrap—
such was his remarkable skill.
Mín later lived in Yángzhōu,
where Duàn Chéngshì came to know him.
Duàn once asked to learn his technique.
Shí told Duàn he should first paint several dozen human heads,
with features from different regions like the Hú and Yuè,
and then he would teach him how to distinguish them.
Suspecting he was being deceived,
Duàn never got around to painting them.
From the Yǒuyáng Zázǔ.
Miscellaneous Games
During Emperor Wǔ's reign,
Guō Shèrén excelled at pitch-pot.
He used bamboo arrows,
not thornwood ones.
In ancient pitch-pot,
the aim was to land the arrow in the pot without it bouncing out,
so they placed small beans inside
to prevent the arrows from leaping out.
Guō Shèrén, however, would propel the arrow to make it bounce back,
with one arrow rebounding over a hundred times—
this was called "xiāo".
It was likened to the "xiāo" piece in board games,
meaning the most outstanding among its kind.
Whenever he performed pitch-pot for Emperor Wǔ,
he was often rewarded with gold and silk.
From *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital*.
Among minor games,
there was one played on a single board,
each side placing five pieces,
contesting speed—
named "cù róng".
Duàn Chéngshì, reading the inscription on his desk,
called it "cù róng".
From *Miscellaneous Morsels from Youyang*.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Dǒng Shūrú presented a game board and a scroll of rules,
which had considerable novelty
but did not become popular at the time.
Magistrate Cuī Shīběn of Luòyáng also favored the ancient game "chū pú".
Its method:
divide the 360 pieces into three parts,
limited by two gates,
each player holds six horses,
with five dice.
The upper side is black,
the lower side white.
On the black side, two are carved as calves;
on the white side, two are carved as pheasants.
When thrown,
all black is called "lú",
scoring sixteen;
two pheasants and three black is "pheasant",
scoring fourteen;
two calves and three white is "calf",
scoring ten;
all white is "white",
scoring eight—
these four are the noble scores.
"Kāi" is twelve;
"sāi" is eleven;
"tǎ" is five;
"tū" is four;
"xiāo" is two;
"juē" is three.
Two and six are mixed scores.
With a noble score, one can throw again,
strike the opponent's horse,
and pass through gates—
other scores do not allow this.
Newly added are the "liù" and "liǎng" scores.
From *Supplements to the National History*.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
there was Dù Quàn, who loved chángxíng.
All had fine names,
each noted for their lightness and elegance.
Those used in summer were called "cold pieces",
named for their resemblance to the lightness and sturdiness of banana fiber cloth.
From *Record of Refined Conversations*.
Among present-day board games,
chángxíng is the most popular.
It has a board and pieces,
with fifteen black and fifteen yellow pieces each,
and two dice for throwing scores.
The method originated from wòshuò,
evolving from shuāngliù.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān once dreamed of losing at shuāngliù,
and Dī Liánggōng said it meant there were no sons in the palace.
Later innovations
gave rise to chángxíng.
There are also names like xiǎo shuāngliù, wéitòu, dàdiǎn, xiǎodiǎn, yóután, and fèngyì,
but none match chángxíng.
Those who gauge risks and ease
use it as a metaphor for current affairs.
Those who adapt to change
compare it to the symbols of the *Book of Changes*.
Nobles and high officials
often indulge in it,
to the point of neglecting celebrations and condolences,
forgetting sleep and food.
When gamblers use it,
they fiercely compete for victory,
calling it "liáo líng".
Borrowing and dividing stakes
is called "náng jiā".
The náng jiā takes one-tenth,
called "qǐ tóu".
Some battle all night,
some lose their fortunes.
Among the skilled, recently Tán Gǎo and Cuī Shīběn stand out.
Wéiqí comes next to chángxíng,
with Wéi Yányòu and Yáng Pēng recently excelling.
Games like tánqí are very ancient;
though rules exist,
few play them.
Among the skilled, recently Jí Dá
and Gāo Yuè stand out.
From *Supplements to the National History*.
King Mù of Zhōu
During King Mù of Zhōu's time,
the Western Róng presented a jade cup
that illuminated the entire room.
Placed in the central courtyard,
it filled with water by the next day.
The cup was fragrant and sweet—
truly an immortal's vessel.
From *Records of the Ten Continents*.
King Líng of Zhōu
In the 23rd year of King Líng of Zhōu, the Kūnyáng Terrace was built.
The state of Qúxū presented a jade camel five feet tall,
an amber phoenix six feet tall,
and a fire-mirror three feet tall—
in darkness, it made objects visible as if in daylight,
and facing the mirror, shadows responded to sound.
The people of Zhōu regarded it as divine.
By the end of King Líng's reign,
it was gone, no one knew where.
From *Wáng Zǐnián's Records of Omitted Affairs*.
Wáng Zǐqiáo
Wáng Zǐqiáo's tomb is at Jīnglíng.
During the Warring States period,
someone tried to rob it.
They found nothing inside,
except for a single sword hanging in the burial chamber.
When they tried to take it, the sword made sounds like a dragon and tiger,
so they dared not approach.
Soon, it flew straight up to heaven.
The *Scripture of Immortals* says:
When a true person passes away,
they often leave a sword in their place.
After five hundred years,
the sword can also become spiritual.
This is proof of it.
From *A New Account of the Tales of the World*.
Fāngzhàng Mountain
Fāngzhàng Mountain is also called Luánzhì.
To the east is a dragon arena a thousand *li* wide,
with forests of jade and precious stones.
Dragons often fought here,
their fat and blood flowing like water.
The black fat,
upon touching the ground, solidified like lacquer,
and emitted a purple light—
it could be made into precious vessels.
From *Wáng Zǐnián's Records of Omitted Affairs*.
Kūnwú Mountain,
beneath it lies abundant red gold,
its color like fire.
In ancient times, the Yellow Emperor battled Chīyóu,
deploying troops in this place.
They dug a pit a hundred fathoms deep,
yet still did not reach the spring,
only seeing fiery light like stars.
Within the earth is much cinnabar,
smelted stone yields copper.
The copper is green in color and sharp,
the spring water is red.
The mountain's plants and trees are all sturdy and sharp,
the soil is also hard and fine.
By the time of King Gōujiàn of Yuè,
he sent craftsmen to sacrifice white oxen and horses to the deity of Kūnwú.
They mined gold and cast it,
to create eight swords.
The first was named Yǎnrì (Eclipse Sun);
pointing it at the sun caused daylight to darken.
Gold is a thing of yin,
when yin flourishes, yang perishes.
The second was named Duànshuǐ (Sever Water);
drawing it across water,
the water parted and did not close again.
The third was named Zhuǎnpò (Turn Soul);
pointing it at the moon,
caused the toad and rabbit to turn aside.
The fourth was named Xuánjiǎn (Hanging Shears);
flying birds and swimming insects,
if they touched its blade,
were as if cut in two.
The fifth was named Jīngní (Startle Whale);
sailing the seas with it,
caused whales to dive deep.
The sixth was named Mièhún (Destroy Soul);
carrying it while traveling at night,
one would not encounter ghosts and demons.
The seventh was named Quèxié (Repel Evil);
if there were evil spirits,
upon seeing it they would cease.
The eighth was named Zhēngāng (True Hardness);
using it to cut jade or sever gold,
was like carving wood or earth.
They were forged in response to the qi of the eight directions.
From "Wáng Zǐnián's Records of Omitted Affairs"
The Great Emperor of Hàn
When the Great Emperor of Hàn was in humble circumstances,
he often wore a dagger three feet long.
Upon it was an inscription,
the characters of which were difficult to recognize,
suspected to be from the time when King Gāozōng of Yīn campaigned against the Guǐfāng.
This object was made then.
The Great Emperor was traveling in the mountains and marshes of Fēng and Pèi,
in a remote valley there was a man, Ōuyě, forging.
The Great Emperor rested beside him,
and asked:
"What weapon are you forging?"
The craftsman laughed and replied:
"Forging a sword for the Son of Heaven,
do not speak of it."
The Great Emperor thought it was a jest,
showing no sign of doubt.
The craftsman said:
"The iron being forged now,
is difficult to temper into steel.
If I could obtain the dagger at your waist,
mix it in and smelt it together,
it would become a divine weapon,
capable of conquering and pacifying the realm.
The essence of stars will assist,
to exterminate the three cunning ones.
Water wanes, fire prospers,
this is an extraordinary omen."
The Great Emperor said:
"I have this object,
named a dagger,
its sharpness is unmatched.
In water, it severs hornless dragons;
on land, it beheads tigers and rhinoceroses.
Ghosts and demons,
dare not encounter it.
It carves jade and engraves gold,
its edge never dulls."
The craftsman said:
"If I cannot obtain this dagger to blend in the forging,
even if Ōuyě devotes all his skill,
and Yuè craftsmen hone the edge,
it will ultimately be an inferior weapon."
The Great Emperor then untied the dagger from his waist,
and threw it into the furnace.
Instantly, smoke and flames shot toward the sky,
and the sun darkened in daytime.
When the sword was completed,
they sacrificed three kinds of livestock and consecrated it with blood.
The forger asked the Great Emperor:
"When did you obtain this dagger?"
He replied:
"During the time of King Zhāoxiāng of Qín,
while I was traveling,
I met a rustic on the road.
He gave it to me, saying:
'A spiritual object from the Yīn era,
passed down through generations.'
Upon it is ancient writing,
recording its year and month."
When the sword was finished,
the craftsman examined it,
the inscription was still present,
confirming the previous suspicion.
The craftsman then took the sword and presented it to the Great Emperor,
who bestowed it upon Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ wore it on his person for a long time,
and with it exterminated the three cunning ones.
After the realm was pacified,
he gave it to Empress Lǚ,
who stored it in the treasure vault.
The keeper saw white vapor like clouds,
issuing from outside the door,
resembling dragons and snakes,
so they renamed the vault "Spiritual Gold Repository."
When the various Lǚs usurped power,
the white vapor also vanished.
When Emperor Huì ascended the throne,
he used this vault to store forbidden weapons,
renaming it the Spiritual Gold Inner Treasury.
From "Wáng Zǐnián's Records of Omitted Affairs"
Also, the Hàn emperors passed down the white jade seal
The phrase "passed down the white jade seal" originally had missing characters;
amended and supplemented based on the Ming manuscript.
presented by Prince Yīng of Qín,
and Gāozǔ's sword that beheaded the white serpent.
The sword was adorned with seven-colored pearls
The four characters "shàng jiē yòng qī" and the character "zhū" were originally missing;
supplemented based on the Huáng manuscript.
and nine-flower jade as ornaments,
mixed with five-colored glass for the sword scabbard.
When the sword was in the chamber, its light
The four characters "shì zhōng qí guāng" were originally missing;
supplemented based on the Huáng manuscript.
still shone outward,
no different from holding the sword unsheathed.
"Shū" originally read "mèi";
amended based on the Ming manuscript.
Every twelve years it was polished once,
the blade always appearing as if frosted
The four characters "shàng cháng ruò shuāng" were originally missing;
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript.
with snow.
Opening the case or drawing the sheath,
always produced a gust of wind,
its radiance dazzling to behold.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
In the Sui dynasty, there was a man named Hóu from Fényīn,
a remarkable scholar of the world.
Wáng Dù often treated him with the respect due to a teacher.
On his deathbed,
he presented Dù with an ancient mirror, saying:
"Hold this, and all evil will stay far from you."
Dù accepted it and treasured it.
The mirror's horizontal diameter was eight inches,
with a knob in the shape of a crouching qílín.
Around the knob were arranged the four directions,
with the turtle, dragon, phoenix, and tiger,
each positioned according to its direction.
Outside the four directions, the eight trigrams were also set,
and beyond the trigrams were placed the twelve earthly branches, each accompanied by its corresponding animal.
Outside the branches and animals,
there were also twenty-four characters,
encircling the perimeter.
The script resembled clerical script,
with every stroke complete,
yet they were not characters found in any dictionary.
Hóu said:
"These are the symbolic forms of the twenty-four solar terms."
When held up to the sunlight,
the patterns and inscriptions on the back
would appear in the shadow cast by the mirror,
without the slightest discrepancy.
When lifted and tapped,
it produced a clear, lingering sound,
which would resonate for an entire day before fading.
Alas,
this was not something ordinary mirrors could match.
It was fitting that it was appreciated by noble sages
and deemed a spiritual object.
Hóu often said:
"In the past, I heard that the Yellow Emperor cast fifteen mirrors.
The first had a horizontal diameter of one chi and five cun,
following the measure of the full moon.
Based on this difference,
each subsequent mirror was one cun smaller.
This is the eighth mirror."
Although the ages have passed far into the past,
and records are scarce,
the accounts handed down by lofty individuals
cannot be dismissed as false.
In the past, when the Yáng family received the jade rings,
blessings extended for generations.
When Lord Zhāng lost his sword,
his life also came to an end.
Now, Dù lives in a time of turmoil and unrest,
often feeling depressed and discontent.
The royal house is like a raging fire,
where in this world can one find a place?
The precious mirror is also gone,
how lamentable!
Now, I shall record its extraordinary traces,
listing them after this lament.
Thousands of years from now,
should someone obtain it,
they may understand its origins.
In the seventh year of the Dàyè era, in the fifth month,
Dù, having resigned from his post as Censor, returned to Hédōng,
and it happened that Hóu passed away, leaving him this mirror.
In the sixth month of that year,
Dù returned to Cháng'ān.
Upon reaching Chánglè Slope,
he stayed overnight at the home of his host, Chéng Xióng.
Xióng had recently taken in a maidservant entrusted to him,
who was quite dignified and beautiful,
named Yīngwǔ.
After Dù had settled in,
as he was about to adjust his hat and shoes,
he took out the mirror to look at himself.
Yīngwǔ saw it from a distance,
and immediately kowtowed until her head bled, saying,
"I dare not stay."
Dù then summoned the host to ask the reason,
and Xióng said:
"Two months ago,
a traveler came from the east with this maidservant.
At the time, the maidservant was gravely ill,
so the traveler left her here,
saying he would come back for her later.
He has not returned since,
and I do not know this maidservant's background."
Dù suspected she was a spirit or demon,
and held the mirror up to her.
She then said:
"I beg for my life."
And immediately transformed.
Dù covered the mirror and said:
"First, tell your story,
then transform.
I will spare your life."
The maidservant bowed twice and confessed:
"I am a thousand-year-old fox from under the tall pine tree in front of the temple of the Lord of Huàshān.
I have greatly practiced transformation and deception,
a crime deserving death.
I was then pursued and captured by the Lord,
and fled to the area between the Hé and Wèi rivers.
I became the adopted daughter of Chén Sīgōng of Xiàguī,
who raised me with great kindness.
He married me, Yīngwǔ, to a fellow villager named Chái Huá.
Yīngwǔ and Huá were not compatible,
so I fled east to Hánchéng County.
There, I was seized by a traveler named Lǐ Wú'ào,
a rough and violent man.
He then took Yīngwǔ traveling for several years.
Yesterday, I followed him here,
and was unexpectedly left behind.
I never imagined I would encounter the Heavenly Mirror,
leaving me no way to hide my form."
Dù then said to her:
"You were originally an old fox,
"fox" originally written as "fox,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript.
Transforming into a human,
how could you not harm people?"
The maidservant said:
"Transforming to serve people
is not harmful.
But fleeing, hiding, and practicing illusions
are despised by the divine way,
and for that, I deserve death."
Dù then said to her:
"If I wish to spare you, is it possible?"
Yīngwǔ said:
"I am honored by your generous offer,
how could I dare forget your kindness?
However, once illuminated by the Heavenly Mirror,
I cannot escape my form.
But having long taken human form,
I am ashamed to revert to my original body.
I beg you to seal the mirror in its case,
and allow me to drink to my fill before I die."
Dù then said to her:
"If I seal the mirror in its case,
will you not flee?"
Yīngwǔ laughed and said:
"You have just spoken kindly,
promising to spare me.
If I were to flee after the mirror is sealed,
would that not betray your grace?
But once the Heavenly Mirror is present,
there is no path to escape.
I only hope for a few moments of life,
to enjoy the last joys of my existence."
Dù immediately placed the mirror in its case,
and also brought wine.
He summoned all the neighbors of Xióng's household,
and they feasted and joked together.
The maidservant soon became heavily intoxicated.
She shook her sleeves, rose to dance, and sang:
"Precious mirror, precious mirror,
how lamentable is my fate.
Since I left my original form,
how many generations have passed?
Though life may be joyful,
death need not be sorrowful.
Why cling to attachment,
guarding this one corner?"
After finishing the song, she bowed twice,
transformed into an old fox, and died.
Everyone present gasped in amazement.
In the eighth year of the Dàyè era,
on the first day of the fourth month,
the sun was eclipsed.
Dù was on duty at the office at the time,
resting in the hall during the day.
He noticed the daylight gradually dimming,
and the clerks informed him that the solar eclipse was severe.
As he straightened his clothes,
he took out the mirror,
and noticed that the mirror itself had also grown dim,
losing its luster and color.
Dù thought that the creation of this precious mirror
aligned with the profound principles of yīn and yáng and the interplay of light and shadow.
Otherwise,
how could it be that when the sun lost its brilliance, the precious mirror also lost its light?
He marveled at this strange phenomenon.
Soon, the mirror's radiance returned,
and the sun also gradually brightened.
By the time the sun was fully restored,
the mirror was again as clear and bright as before.
From then on,
whenever the sun or moon was partially eclipsed,
the mirror would also grow dim.
In the eighth month of that year, on the fifteenth day,
a friend named Xuē Xiá obtained a bronze sword four chǐ long.
The sword was connected to its hilt,
which was carved with dragons and phoenixes.
On the left side, the pattern resembled flames,
and on the right, like rippling water.
It shone brilliantly,
clearly no ordinary object.
Xiá brought it to Dù and said:
"I have often tested this sword.
On the fifteenth day of each month, when the heavens and earth are clear,
if placed in a dark room,
it naturally emits light,
illuminating several zhàng around."
The swordsman had possessed it for many days and months.
Your Excellency, being fond of the extraordinary and cherishing antiquity,
is like one hungry and thirsty.
I wish to test it with you this very evening."
Wáng Dù was greatly pleased.
That night, indeed, the heavens and earth were clear and serene.
He tightly closed a room,
leaving no gaps for escape,
and stayed overnight with the swordsman.
Wáng Dù also brought out his precious mirror,
placing it beside his seat.
Soon, the mirror emitted light,
brightly illuminating the entire room.
They could see each other as if in daylight.
The sword lay beside it,
but no longer shone with brilliance.
The swordsman was greatly astonished and said:
"Please put the mirror back into its case."
Wáng Dù followed his words.
Only then did the sword emit light,
but it extended no more than one or two feet.
The swordsman stroked the sword and sighed:
"Even divine objects under heaven
have the principle of mutual subjugation."
After this, every time the full moon arrived,
he would take the mirror out in a dark room,
and its light would often shine for several zhang.
But if moonlight entered the room,
then it would emit no light.
Could it be that the radiance of the great sun and great moon
cannot be rivaled?
That winter,
he concurrently held the post of Zhùzuò Láng.
He received an imperial edict to compile the state
(The Ming manuscript has "Zhōu" instead of "state").
history,
and intended to compose a biography for Sū Chāo.
Wáng Dù had a servant named Bào Shēng, seventy years old,
originally a retainer of the Sū family.
He was quite familiar with historical texts,
and somewhat understood literary composition.
Seeing the draft of Wáng Dù's biography,
he became overwhelmed with grief.
Wáng Dù asked him the reason,
and he said to Wáng Dù:
"Bào Shēng once received generous treatment from Lord Sū.
Now seeing Lord Sū's words proven true,
this is why I grieve.
The precious mirror you possess, sir,
was left to Lord Sū by his friend Miáo Jìzǐ from Hénán.
Lord Sū cherished it greatly.
In the year Lord Sū was nearing death,
he was sorrowful and unhappy.
He often summoned Master Miáo and said:
'I reckon my time of death is not far off,
I do not know into whose hands this mirror will fall.
Now I wish to divine a hexagram using yarrow stalks,
I beg you, sir, to observe it.'
Then he told Bào Shēng to fetch the yarrow stalks,
and Lord Sū himself arranged the stalks and cast the hexagram.
The divination completed.
Lord Sū said:
'More than ten years after my death,
my family will lose this mirror,
and its whereabouts will be unknown.
However, as a divine object of heaven and earth,
its movements and stillness have signs.
Nowadays, in the region between the rivers,
there often appears an aura of treasure matching the hexagram's omen.
Perhaps the mirror will go there?'
Jìzǐ said:
'Will it also be obtained by someone?'
Lord Sū further examined the hexagram and said:
'First it will enter a marquis's household,
then return to the Wáng family.
Beyond that,
its whereabouts cannot be known.'" Bào Shēng finished speaking and wept.
Wáng Dù inquired of the Sū family,
and indeed they said they formerly had this mirror.
