After Lord Sū passed away,
it too was lost, its whereabouts unknown,
just as Bào Shēng had said.
Therefore, when Wáng Dù wrote Lord Sū's biography,
he also fully recounted this matter in the final chapter.
The discussion that Lord Sū's divination was peerless,
silently and uniquely applied,
refers to this.
On the first morning of the first month in the ninth year of the Dàyè era,
a foreign monk came begging to Wáng Dù's house.
His younger brother, Wáng Jì, came out to see him,
sensing his divine bearing was not ordinary.
He further invited him into the house,
and prepared food for him.
They sat and talked for a long time.
The foreign monk said to Wáng Jì:
"It seems your household possesses a peerless precious mirror;
may I see it?"
Wáng Jì said:
"How did the Dharma Master come to know of it?"
The monk said:
"This humble monk has received secret arts of illumination and records,
and can somewhat recognize auras of treasure.
Above your residence,
every day there is often a continuous emerald light,
and crimson vapor connecting to the moon;
this is the aura of a precious mirror.
This humble monk has observed it for two years.
Now, having chosen an auspicious day,
I specifically wish to see it."
Wáng Jì brought it out.
The monk knelt, held it, and rejoiced with excitement.
He also said to Wáng Jì:
"This mirror has several divine manifestations,
all of which you have likely not yet seen.
If you apply gold ointment to it,
and polish it with pearl powder,
then hold it up to the sun,
its light will surely penetrate walls."
The monk also sighed and said:
"If further magical methods are applied,
it should illuminate the internal organs.
The regret is the sudden lack of medicine.
But if you fumigate it with golden smoke,
wash it with jade water,
then again apply gold ointment and pearl powder,
polishing it according to the method,
and store it in mud,
it will also not lose its luster."
He then left behind the methods for golden smoke and jade water, etc.
Practicing them, all proved effective without fail.
And the foreign monk was never seen again.
That autumn,
Wáng Dù was appointed concurrently as magistrate of Ruìchéng County.
In front of the magistrate's hall was a jujube tree, its trunk several arm-spans around,
no one knew how many hundred years old.
Previous magistrates upon arrival
all made offerings and paid respects to this tree;
otherwise, calamity would immediately befall them.
Wáng Dù believed that supernatural phenomena arise from people,
and improper sacrifices should be stopped.
The county clerks all kowtowed, pleading with Wáng Dù.
Wáng Dù, having no alternative,
performed the sacrifice for them.
However, he secretly thought that this tree must harbor some spirit or demon,
which people could not eliminate,
allowing its power to grow.
So he secretly hung this mirror among the tree's branches.
That night, around the second watch,
they heard a crashing sound in front of the hall,
like thunder.
He then rose to look,
and saw wind, rain, darkness,
swirling around the tree.
Lightning flashed and flickered,
now rising, now falling.
By dawn,
there was a large snake,
with purple scales and a red tail,
a green head and white horns,
and the character for 'king' on its forehead.
Its body bore several wounds,
and it lay dead by the tree.
Wáng Dù then took down the mirror,
ordered clerks to remove the snake,
and burned it outside the county gate.
He then had the tree dug up.
In the tree's heart was a cavity,
which widened toward the ground.
There were traces of a giant serpent coiled there.
Afterward, they filled it in,
and the supernatural phenomena ceased.
That winter,
Wáng Dù, as Censor, concurrently served as magistrate of Ruìchéng.
Holding credentials, he traveled the Héběi Circuit,
opening granaries,
to provide relief to Shǎndōng.
At that time, there was a great famine in the land,
and the people suffered from illness.
Between Pú and Shǎn,
pestilence was especially severe.
There was a man from Héběi named Zhāng Lóngjū,
a minor clerk under Wáng Dù.
His household, high and low, numbered several tens of people,
all fell ill at once.
Wáng Dù took pity on them,
and brought the mirror into their home,
having Lóngjū hold the mirror and shine it at night.
All the sick people, seeing the mirror,
rose in alarm, saying:
"We saw Lóngjū holding a moon coming to shine upon us;
where its light reached,
it was like ice touching the body,
chilling through to our internal organs."
Immediately their fever subsided,
and by evening all were cured.
Considering it harmless to the mirror,
yet greatly beneficial to the multitude,
he ordered it to be secretly carried,
and circulated among all the people.
That night,
The mirror in the case rang out clearly on its own,
its sound penetrating and far-reaching,
and only after a long while did it cease.
Wáng Dù found this strange in his heart.
The next morning,
Lóngjū came and said to Dù:
"Last night, Lóngjū suddenly dreamed of a person,
with a dragon's head and a snake's body,
wearing a vermilion crown and purple robes.
He said to Lóngjū,
'I am the essence of the mirror,
named Zǐzhēn.
I have often shown virtue toward your household,
so I have come to entrust you with a message:
thank Duke Wáng for me.
When the common people have committed offenses,
Heaven afflicts them with illness.
How can you make me oppose Heaven to save them?
Moreover, by next month,
the illness will gradually heal.
Do not trouble yourself on my account.'"
Dù, moved by its spiritual wonder,
thus recorded this.
By the following month,
the illness indeed gradually healed,
just as had been said.
In the tenth year of the Dàyè era,
Dù's younger brother, Jì,
resigned from his post as Magistrate of Liùhé and returned home.
He then planned to travel extensively through mountains and rivers,
intending it as a long-term strategy for withdrawal.
Dù tried to stop him, saying:
"Now the world is heading toward chaos,
bandits and thieves are everywhere.
How can you seek peace?
Moreover, you and I are of the same flesh and blood,
and have never been far apart.
This journey of yours
seems like you intend to become a recluse.
In the past, Shàng Zǐpíng wandered the Five Peaks,
and no one knew where he went.
If you are to follow in the footsteps of such worthies,
I cannot bear it."
He then wept facing Jì.
Jì said:
"My mind is already made up,
and I certainly cannot stay.
Brother, you are a man of understanding now,
and should comprehend all things.
Confucius said:
'One cannot deprive even a common man of his will.'
A human life spans a hundred years,
passing as swiftly as a glimpse through a crack.
To fulfill one's desires is joy,
to lose one's aspirations is sorrow.
To allow one to follow one's desires
is the principle of the sages."
Dù, having no alternative,
bid him farewell.
Jì said:
"Upon this parting,
I also have a request.
The mirror you treasure, brother,
is no ordinary object.
Jì intends to uphold my aspirations along the cloudy paths,
and dwell amidst the mists and rosy clouds.
I wish for you to give this to me as a gift."
Dù said:
"How could I begrudge you anything?"
He immediately gave it to him.
Jì, having obtained the mirror, then departed,
not saying where he was going.
In the summer, the sixth month of the thirteenth year of Dàyè,
he finally returned to Cháng'ān,
bringing the mirror back.
He said to Dù:
"This mirror is truly a treasure.
After taking leave of you, brother,
I first traveled to Shàoshì on Sōng Mountain.
Descending a stone bridge,
I sat upon a jade altar.
As dusk approached,
I came upon a crevice in the cliff.
There was a stone chamber that could hold three to five people,
and Jì rested there.
After the second watch on a moonlit night,
there were two men.
One had the appearance of a foreigner,
with white beard and eyebrows, and was thin,
calling himself Shāngōng.
The other had a broad face,
with long white beard and eyebrows,
dark and short,
calling himself Máoshēng.
They said to Jì:
'What manner of person resides here?'
Jì said:
'One who seeks the secluded, explores caves, and visits the wondrous.'
The two sat down,
and talked with Jì for a long time,
often expressing extraordinary meanings beyond their words.
Jì suspected they were spirits or monsters,
reached his hand behind his back,
opened the case, and took out the mirror.
As the mirror's light shone forth, the two men cried out and prostrated themselves.
The short one transformed into a turtle,
the foreign-looking one transformed into an ape.
Jì hung the mirror until dawn,
and both bodies perished.
The turtle's body had green fur,
the ape's body had white fur.
He then entered Jī Mountain,
crossed the Yǐng River.
Passed through Tàihé,
and viewed the Jade Well.
Beside the well was a pool,
its water deep and green.
He asked a woodcutter,
who said:
'This is the Spiritual Pool.
The villagers make offerings at each of the eight solar terms,
to pray for blessings and protection.
If a single offering is missed,
black clouds and large hailstones emerge from the pool water,
flooding the banks and destroying the mounds.'
Jì took out the mirror and shone it upon it,
the pool water boiled and surged,
and thunder rumbled as if shaking the earth.
Suddenly the pool water surged upward,
leaving not a single drop in the pool.
After traveling over two hundred paces,
the water fell to the ground.
There was a fish,
about ten feet long,
its girth larger than an arm.
Its head was red, its forehead white,
its body mottled with blue and yellow,
scale-less and slimy,
dragon-shaped with snake-like horns.
Its mouth was pointed,
shaped like a sturgeon,
and it glowed when it moved.
Lying in the mud and water,
it was stranded and unable to go far.
Jì thought it was a jiāo,
helpless without water.
He cut it up and roasted it,
it was very fatty and flavorful,
and served as food for several days.
He then emerged at Sòng and Biàn.
At the home of a Biàn host named Zhāng Qí, there was a girl who was ill.
At night,
the sounds of her agony
were truly unbearable.
Jì asked the reason,
and was told the illness had persisted for years;
during the day she was fine,
but at night it was always like this.
Jì stayed for one night,
and upon hearing the girl's cries,
he opened the mirror and shone it.
The one in pain said:
'The crowned gentleman has been killed.'
Under the sick girl's bed,
a large rooster lay dead—
it was the host's seven- or eight-year-old rooster.
He traveled to Jiāngnán.
About to cross the Yángzǐ River at Guǎnglíng,
suddenly dark clouds covered the water,
a black wind whipped up waves,
the boatman lost his composure,
fearing capsizing.
Jì carried the mirror onto the boat,
shone it upon the river for several paces,
and it became clear and bright to the bottom.
The wind and clouds scattered in all directions,
and the waves then calmed.
In a short while,
they crossed the natural moat.
He climbed Shè Mountain,
headed toward
"headed toward" originally written as "qū" but
according to the Ming manuscript copy, changed to "qū".
Fāng Ridge.
Sometimes he climbed the highest peaks,
sometimes entered deep caves.
He encountered flocks of birds circling and screeching around people,
and several bears squatting blocking the path.
Waving the mirror at them,
the bears and birds fled in terror.
At that time, he advantageously crossed the Zhèjiāng River,
encountering the tide coming in from the sea.
The roar of the waves
could be heard for hundreds of miles.
The boatman said:
'The tide is already near,
we cannot cross south.
If we do not turn the boat back,
we will surely be buried in the bellies of fish.'
Jì took out the mirror and shone it,
The river waves ceased to advance,
standing tall like clouds.
On all four sides, the river water opened up for over fifty paces,
the water gradually became clear and shallow,
and giant turtles and crocodiles scattered and fled.
Hoisting the sails, they sailed gracefully,
directly entering Nánpǔ.
Then, looking back,
they saw the surging waves,
tens of zhang high,
reaching the place they had just crossed.
Thereupon, they ascended Tiāntāi Mountain,
touring the caves and ravines all around.
Traveling at night, they carried it through the mountain valleys;
a hundred paces away from their bodies,
light illuminated all directions,
revealing even the tiniest details.
Birds roosting in the forest,
startled, flew about in chaos.
Returning, they passed through Kuàijī.
They met an extraordinary man named Zhāng Shǐluán,
who taught Jì the matters of the "Zhōu Bì" and "Nine Chapters" as well as the "Míngtáng Liùjiǎ."
Together with Chén Yǒng, they returned,
and further traveled to Yùzhāng.
They met a Daoist priest named Xǔ Cángmì,
who said he was a seventh-generation descendant of Jīngyáng,
possessing the arts of chanting spells to tread on knives and walk through fire,
and spoke of the hierarchy of demons and monsters.
He further mentioned that the family of Lǐ Shèn, the granary superintendent of Fēngchéng County, had three daughters afflicted by a bewitching illness,
which no one could recognize,
and Cángmì's treatments were ineffective.
Jì, through an old acquaintance named Zhào Dān, who had talent and capability,
and served as the county captain of Fēngchéng,
Jì thus visited him.
Dān ordered an attendant to guide Jì to his lodging place,
and Jì said to him:
"I wish to stay at the home of Granary Superintendent Lǐ Jìngshèn."
Dān promptly ordered Jìng to act as host.
Jì asked about the reason,
and Jìng said:
"The three daughters live together in a small room within the main hall.
Every day as evening approaches,
they dress up beautifully and wear dazzling clothes.
After dusk,
they return to their small room,
extinguish the lamps and candles.
Listening,
one can hear them secretly talking and laughing with someone,
until dawn when they sleep.
They do not wake unless called,
growing thinner day by day,
unable to eat.
If we try to prevent them from dressing up,
they immediately want to hang themselves or throw themselves into a well.
What can be done about it?"
Jì said to Jìng:
"Show me the place of the small room."
To the east of the room was a window.
Fearing that the door was firmly closed and difficult to open,
he first cut four window lattice bars during the day,
then propped them up with something to look as before.
When dusk arrived,
Jìng reported to Jì:
"They have dressed up and entered the room."
At the first watch,
listening,
the talking and laughter were natural.
Jì removed the window lattice bars,
took the mirror, entered the room, and shone it.
The three girls cried out:
"You have killed my husband!"
At first, nothing was visible,
but when the mirror was held until dawn,
there was a weasel,
with head and tail measuring one chi three or four cun long,
its body hairless and toothless.
There was also a rat,
also hairless and toothless,
its plump body weighing possibly five jin.
There was also a gecko,
as large as a human hand,
its body covered in scales and armor,
glittering with five colors,
with two horns on its head,
about half a cun long,
its tail over five cun long,
the tip of its tail one cun in length, white in color,
all dead before the hole in the wall.
From then on, the illness was cured.
Afterward, seeking truth, he reached Lúshān,
lingering for several months.
Sometimes resting in the deep forests,
sometimes sleeping in the open among the grasses.
Tigers and leopards followed behind,
jackals and wolves left continuous tracks.
Raising the mirror to look at them,
none failed to flee and hide.
Lúshān recluse Sū Bīn,
a man of extraordinary insight,
profoundly understood the principles of the Yì,
preserving the past and knowing the future.
He said to Jì:
"Divine objects of the world
will surely not remain among humans for long.
Now the universe is in chaos and disorder,
other lands may not necessarily be safe to stay.
As long as you, sir, still have this mirror,
it is sufficient to protect you.
I urge you to quickly return to your hometown."
Jì agreed with his words,
immediately headed north to return,
and then traveled to Héběi.
At night, he dreamed the mirror said to him:
"I have received your elder brother's generous courtesy.
Now I must leave the human world and go far away.
Wishing to bid farewell once,
I ask you, sir, to return to Cháng'ān early."
Jì promised in the dream.
Upon waking at dawn,
sitting alone and thinking of it,
he felt dazed and his heart trembled.
Immediately, he set out westward on the road to Qín.
Now that I have seen you, elder brother,
Jì has not broken his promise.
Yet I fear this spiritual object may also not remain in your possession."
Several months later,
Jì returned to Hédōng.
In the thirteenth year of the Dàyè era,
on the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
a mournful cry came from the case,
its sound faint and distant.
Suddenly it gradually grew louder,
like the roar of a dragon or the roar of a tiger.
After a long while, it finally settled.
Opening the case to look,
the mirror was already gone.
From "Yì Wén Jí."
Zhāng Huà
Jìn Dynasty's Zhāng Huà,
born with outstanding intelligence and wisdom.
He enjoyed studying extraordinary charts and weft texts,
collecting lost and scattered works from across the land.
From the beginning of written records,
he examined and verified supernatural and strange tales,
as well as stories told in villages and alleys,
compiling the "Bówù Zhì" in four hundred volumes,
which he presented to Emperor Wǔ.
The Emperor said:
"Your talent surpasses that of ten thousand generations,
your breadth of knowledge is unparalleled.
However, in recording events and collecting sayings,
much is exaggerated and unfounded.
You should delete and trim the unsubstantiated parts,
to achieve a polished work.
In the past, Confucius edited the Book of Songs and Documents,
not
The character "not" was originally missing,
supplemented based on "Shí Yí Jì"
including matters of ghosts and spirits, the obscure and dark,
he did not speak of strange forces and chaotic spirits.
Now seeing your work,
it astonishes with what has never been heard,
and amazes with what has never been seen,
which will overwhelm the ears and eyes.
You may further cut away the exaggerated and doubtful,
dividing it into ten volumes."
Immediately, in front of the imperial presence, he bestowed a green iron inkstone.
This iron was presented by the Kingdom of Yútián,
cast into an inkstone.
He also bestowed a lín horn brush tube,
this was presented by the Kingdom of Liáoxī.
Ten thousand sheets of cèlǐ paper,
presented by Nányuè.
In Hàn language, it is called "zhìlí,"
"zhìlí" and "cèlǐ" are easily confused.
Southern people use seaweed to make paper,
its texture crisscrossing diagonally and sideways,
hence it is named accordingly.
From "Wáng Zǐnián Shí Yí Jì"
Jìn Emperor Huì
In the third year of Yuánkāng of Jìn Emperor Huì,
the imperial armory caught fire.
It burned the sword with which Hàn Emperor Gāozǔ beheaded the white serpent and the shoes of Confucius.
All saw this sword pierce through the roof and fly away,
no one knew where it went.
From "Yì Yuàn"
Xǔ Xùn
In the late Western Jìn dynasty,
there was a county magistrate of Jīngyáng named Xǔ Xùn,
who attained the Way at Western Mountain in Yùzhāng.
In the river, a flood dragon and giant clam were causing trouble.
Jīngyáng dove into the water,
drew his sword and slew them,
and afterward was never seen again.
Later, a fisherman caught a stone in his net,
which made a loud sound.
When struck,
the noise could be heard for tens of lǐ.
During the Táng dynasty, Prince Zhào, serving as governor of Hóng Prefecture,
broke it open,
and obtained a pair of swords.
Looking at their inscriptions,
one had the characters "Xǔ Jīngyáng",
and the other had "Wàn Rèn".
Thus, one "Wàn Rèn Master" emerged.
From "Records from Court and Country".
Táo Zhēnbái
The "Tàiqīng Scripture" authored by Liáng dynasty's Táo Zhēnbái,
also called the "Sword Scripture".
All who study Daoist arts
must have good swords and mirrors with them.
It also says
that the swords Gānjiàng and Mòyé
were both cast from bronze,
not iron.
From "Veritable Records of the Secretariat".
Also, Zhēnbái lived in seclusion in Bèidū Mountain.
He once kept two swords,
one named Shànshèng,
the other named Bǎoshèng.
They would often fly away.
When people saw them,
they resembled two green snakes.
His official biography fully records this.
From "Records of Zhītián".
Zhāng Zǔzhái
During the Qiánfēng era of the Táng dynasty,
someone east of the wilderness in Zhèn Prefecture
spotted two white rabbits.
Trying to catch them,
they suddenly retreated into the ground
and vanished without a trace.
Digging at the spot where they disappeared,
only about three chǐ deep,
he obtained a pair of bronze swords,
of ancient and exquisite craftsmanship.
At the time, Senior Clerk Zhāng Zǔzhái reported this.
From "Records from Court and Country".
Táng Yí
During the Shàngyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
officials of the ninth rank and above were ordered
to wear pouches for knives and whetstones.
The colored silk ribbons were shaped like fish,
made of knotted silk.
Taking the image of fish
(Míng manuscript: "the image" reads as "many carp")
as an omen of strength.
This practice ceased by Empress Tiānhuò's reign.
After the Jǐngyún era,
the previous adornments were restored.
From "Records from Court and Country".
Emperor Táng Zhōngzōng
Emperor Táng Zhōngzōng ordered Yángzhōu to craft a square-zhàng mirror.
A cassia tree was cast in bronze,
with golden flowers and silver leaves.
The emperor would often ride his horse and look at himself in it,
with both man and horse reflected in the mirror.
From "Records from Court and Country".
Sòng Qīngchūn
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the Héxī cavalry commander Sòng Qīngchūn was brave, resolute, and fierce,
esteemed by his troops.
The Western Róng tribes would invade the border yearly.
Whenever Qīngchūn went into battle,
he would always wield his sword alone, shouting loudly,
and return with severed enemy ears,
never once struck by blade or arrow.
The Western Róng feared him,
and the entire army relied on him.
Later, the Tǔbō suffered a major defeat,
and thousands of captives were taken.
The army
(Original text: "army" was written as "lǐ",
corrected per the Míng manuscript.)
commander ordered an interpreter to ask those wearing tiger skins,
"Why couldn't you harm him?"
They replied:
"We only saw a blue dragon charge through the formation,
wherever its blade reached,
it was like striking bronze or iron.
We thought a deity was aiding the general."
Only then did Qīngchūn realize his sword's spiritual power.
After Qīngchūn's death,
the sword was obtained by Guā Prefecture governor Lǐ Guǎngchēn.
Sometimes after wind and rain,
light would burst from the room,
illuminating an area of one square zhàng.
Gēshū Hàn, garrisoning Xīliáng,
learned of this.
He sought to exchange it for other treasures,
but Guǎngchēn refused.
He thus presented him with a poem:
"Carving the boat to seek it has already vanished,
plucking the sword-hilt, yet kindness remains unrequited."
From "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng".
Wǔ Shèngzhī
In the late Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Tàiyuán's Wǔ Shèngzhī served as Sīshì of Xuān Prefecture,
overseeing Jìngjiāng affairs.
Suddenly, in the rapids, he saw the Thunder God treading on faint clouds chasing a small yellow snake,
coiled around the rapids.
A Jìngjiāng laborer playfully threw a stone at it,
hitting the snake,
which produced a metallic clang.
The Thunder God then flew away.
Sending someone to look,
they obtained a bronze sword.
On it was a seal script inscription: "Xǔ Jīngyáng's third sword for slaying the flood dragon."
From "Extensive Records of the Strange".
Lǐ Shǒutài
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month in the third year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
a water-heart mirror was presented from Yángzhōu.
It measured nine inches in both length and width,
and its blue-green luster shone brilliantly in the sun.
On its back was a coiled dragon, three feet, four inches, and five fen in length,
so lifelike it seemed to move.
Emperor Xuánzōng examined it and was astonished.
The official who presented the mirror, Lǐ Shǒutài, a military advisor from Yángzhōu, said:
"When the mirror was being cast,
an old man appeared,
claiming his surname was Lóng and his given name Hù.
His beard and hair were pure white,
his eyebrows like silk threads,
hanging down to his shoulders,
and he wore a white robe.
He was accompanied by a young boy,
ten years old,
dressed in black.
Lóng Hù called him Xuánmíng.
They suddenly arrived on the first day of the fifth month,
their divine aura extraordinary,
and no one recognized them.
He said to the mirror craftsman Lǚ Huī,
'Old man, I live nearby.
Hearing that you, young man, are casting a mirror,
I have come for a brief look.'
The old man understood how to create a true dragon
and wished to make one for you, young man,
which should greatly please the emperor.'
He then had Xuánmíng enter the furnace room,
locked the doors and windows,
and allowed no one else inside.
After three days and three nights,
the left door was found wide open.
Lǚ Huī and twenty others searched the courtyard,
but Lóng Hù and Xuánmíng had vanished.
In front of the mirror furnace, they found a sheet of plain paper
with small clerical script that read:
'The mirror dragon is three feet, four inches, and five fen long,
modeled after the Three Powers.
It symbolizes the Four Qi,
and embodies the Five Elements.
Its nine-inch length and width
resemble the nine provinces and their celestial divisions.
The mirror's knob is like a bright moon pearl.
Since the Kāiyuán Emperor is sagely and spiritually perceptive,
I have descended to bestow blessings.
This mirror can ward off evil
and reflect all things.
Even Qín Shǐhuáng's mirror
cannot surpass it.
A song says:
"Coiled dragon, coiled dragon,
hidden within the mirror.
Its divisions have form,
its transformations endless.
It summons clouds and exhales mist,
brings rain and generates wind.
An immortal from the highest purity
comes to offer it to the sage's ear."'" Lǚ Huī and the others then moved the mirror furnace onto a boat,
and at noon on the fifth day of the fifth month,
they cast it on the Yángzǐ River.
Before the casting began,
heaven and earth were serene and still.
During the casting process,
the river water on both sides suddenly rose over thirty feet high,
like snowy mountains floating on the river.
They also heard dragon roars,
like the sound of reed pipes,
reaching for dozens of miles.
Consulting the elders,
since the beginning of mirror casting,
there had never been such marvels."
The emperor ordered the relevant officials
to specially oversee this mirror.
By the seventh year of Tiānbǎo,
a great drought struck Guānzhōng.
From the third month to the sixth month, no rain fell.
The emperor personally visited the Dragon Hall to pray,
but there was no response.
He asked the Dàoshì Yè Fǎshàn from the Hàotiān Temple:
"I have reverently served the spirits and deities
to bring peace to the people.
Now, with such scorching sun,
I am deeply worried.
I personally came to pray,
yet why is there still no rain?
Have you, sir, ever seen a true dragon?"
He replied:
"I have indeed seen a true dragon.
I have heard that if a painted dragon's limbs and joints
even partially resemble a true dragon,
it will elicit a response.
If used for prayer,
rain will immediately fall.
The reason it is not efficacious
may be because it does not resemble a true dragon."
The emperor then ordered the palace envoy Sūn Zhīgǔ
to lead Yè Fǎshàn to inspect the inner treasury thoroughly.
Suddenly, they saw this mirror,
and Fǎshàn returned to report:
"The dragon on this mirror is a true dragon."
The emperor went to the Níngyīn Hall
and summoned Fǎshàn to pray to the mirror dragon.
In moments,
two streams of white vapor were seen from the hall's beams,
descending close to the mirror dragon.
White vapor also rose from the dragon's nostrils,
ascending near the beams.
Soon, it filled the hall and courtyard,
spreading throughout the city.
Sweet rain poured heavily,
lasting for seven full days before stopping.
Guānzhōng had a bountiful harvest.
The emperor ordered the court academician Wú Dàozǐ
to paint the mirror dragon
and present it to Fǎshàn.
From *Yìwén Lù*.
Chén Zhònggōng
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Chén Zhònggōng whose family lived in Jīnlíng.
He possessed much gold and silk.
Zhònggōng was fond of learning,
but his literary studies were not yet complete.
Carrying several thousand gold pieces,
he went to Qīnghuà Lane in Luòyáng,
where he rented a residence.
There was a very large well there,
which often drowned people,
and Zhònggōng also knew this.
However, as he had no wife or family,
he was not afraid.
Zhònggōng often studied and did not go out.
After more than a month,
there was a girl from a neighboring family who fetched water, about ten-something years old.
Strangely, she came to the well every day,
and would linger for a long time without leaving.
Suddenly, she fell into the well and died.
The well water was deep,
and it took until the next day
before her body was finally retrieved.
Zhònggōng found this strange.
On a free day,
he peered into the well,
and suddenly saw a woman in the water.
Her appearance was young and beautiful,
adorned in the fashion of the time.
She looked at Zhònggōng,
and as she gazed intently,
she used a red sleeve to half-cover her face and smiled.
Her enchanting and alluring demeanor
was beyond anything in this world.
Zhònggōng felt his spirit and soul grow faint and confused,
as if he could not support himself.
He then sighed and said:
"This is the reason people drown."
So he paid no further attention and withdrew.
Several months later, during a scorching drought,
the water in this well did not decrease.
Suddenly, one day, the water dried up completely.
Early in the morning,
someone knocked at the door, saying:
"Jìng Yuányǐng requests an audience."
Zhònggōng ordered her to enter,
and it was the woman he had seen in the well.
She wore crimson and green garments,
and her makeup and powder
were all in the current style.
Zhònggōng sat with her
and inquired:
"Why do you kill people?"
Yuányǐng said:
"I am not the one who kills people.
There is a poisonous dragon in this well.
Ever since the Hóu of Jiàng in the Hàn dynasty lived here,
this well was dug.
Within Luò City, there are five poisonous dragons,
and this is one of them.
Because it has befriended the attendant dragons of Tàiyī,
it is often shielded and concealed.
When Heaven commands its summons,
it often makes excuses and does not attend the assemblies.
It is fond of drinking human blood.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
it has killed three thousand seven hundred people,
yet the water never dries up or diminishes.
I only fell into this well at the beginning of the current dynasty,
and was then enslaved by the dragon.
I bewitch and lure people,
to provide them for the dragon to eat.
It is extremely arduous,
and not something I willingly do.
Yesterday, because the Tàiyī envoys were changing shifts,
all the dragon gods of the world had to gather for the imperial procession.
Last night at the zǐ hour,
it already went to court before Tàiyī.
Additionally, because Hénán is suffering from drought,
it will be investigated and reprimanded for several days before returning.
Now there is no water left in the well.
If you, noble sir, can truly order workmen to dredge it,
then I can escape this hardship.
If so,
I wish to serve and support you for the rest of your life.
There is nothing in worldly affairs that I cannot accomplish."
When she finished speaking,
she vanished from sight.
Zhònggōng immediately ordered workmen at that time,
and commanded a trusted confidant
to enter the well with the workmen.
He instructed them:
"If you see anything unusual, collect it immediately."
At the bottom, there was nothing else,
only an ancient bronze mirror was retrieved,
seven cun and seven fen in width.
Zhònggōng ordered it washed clean,
and stored it in a case.
He burned incense to honor it,
for this was the so-called Jìng Yuányǐng.
After the first watch,
Yuányǐng suddenly entered through the door,
went straight before the candle and performed a bow.
She said to Zhònggōng:
"I thank you for the grace of giving me life,
and illuminating me from beneath the muddy filth.
I was originally the seventh of the twelve mirrors cast by Master Kuàng.
When they were cast,
all were made according to the sun and moon, with differences in size.
I, Yuányǐng, was cast at noon on the seventh day of the seventh month.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
I was dropped into the well by Lántiáo, a maidservant of Xǔ Jìngzōng.
Because this well water was deep,
and additionally troubled by the poisonous dragon's aura,
people who entered would suffocate and perish,
so I could not be retrieved,
and thus I was enslaved by the poisonous dragon.
Fortunately, I encountered you, a noble and upright gentleman,
and have been able to see the human world again.
However, before tomorrow morning,
I hope you, noble sir, will move out of this residence."
Zhònggōng said:
"I have already used money to rent this place.
If I move out now,
how will I find a place to set my feet?"
Yuányǐng said:
"Just please prepare your belongings, noble sir,
and have no worries at all."
As she was about to bid farewell and leave,
Zhònggōng detained her again.
He asked:
"How is it that you have the appearance of wearing rouge, green, and powder?"
She replied:
"I can transform without constancy,
which cannot be fully described."
When she finished speaking,
she was nowhere to be seen.
The next morning,
suddenly a broker knocked at the door,
and also led the owner of the residence to visit.
"visit" originally read "said",
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy.
Zhònggōng,
and then requested to move residences,
with both laborers and means fully provided.
Before the mealtime,
they arrived at a residence in Lìdé Ward.
Its size and price
were exactly the same as the one in Qīnghuà.
The broker said:
"The price and deed documents,
are completely without omission."
And the handover was completed.
Three days later,
the well at the Qīnghuà residence
collapsed without reason.
Moreover, it extended to the eastern wing of the main hall's corner,
causing the ground to sink all at once.
Later, Zhònggōng repeatedly succeeded in the literary examinations,
and became a high official.
Whenever he had important matters,
it was always as effective as when he moved residences.
On the back of the mirror were twenty-eight
"twenty-eight" originally read "thirty",
changed according to the "Bó Yì Zhì".
characters,
all in tadpole script.
Pushing and transcribing them into modern script, it read:
On the seventh day of the seventh month at noon, in the second year of the Duke of Xīn of Jìn,
this mirror was cast before Shǒuyáng Mountain at White Dragon Pool.
For a thousand years in the world.
Circling the back in writing,
each character governs an astronomical constellation.
Arranged according to their directions,
then the sun is on the left and the moon on the right.
The Black Tortoise, Azure Dragon, White Tiger, and Vermilion Bird,
are all in their proper positions.
Inscribed around the four sides of the knob, it said:
The mirror of Yízé.
From the "Bó Yì Zhì".
Cáowáng Gāo.
Táng Sì Cáowáng Gāo possessed ingenious ideas,
and was highly skilled in the use of tools and implements.
When he served as the military governor of Jīng
(Jīng was originally written as Xíng,
0 corrected according to the entry for Cáowáng Gāo in volume 25 of this book.)
zhōu,
there was a traveling scholar who carried two jiégǔ drum hoops,
and wished to seek an audience.
He first announced himself at the guest office,
where all the observers were surprised and remarked:
"Is this really worth valuing?"
He replied:
"Just announce me,
and the Minister will understand."
When he was received,
Gāo held them and sighed, saying:
"I never expected to encounter such a treasure today."
He pointed out the evenness of their steel,
and the aides and assistants merely assented,
some inwardly disagreeing.
Gāo said:
"Do you gentlemen not believe in your hearts?"
He ordered a food tray to be brought,
and personally selected the most perfectly level one.
He then had the hoops placed in the center of the tray,
and poured oil into the hoops.
The hoops filled, yet not a single drop of oil leaked out.
Gāo said:
"These must be tribute hoops from the Kāiyuán or Tiānbǎo eras,
otherwise they could not be like this."
He asked where they came from,
and the scholar said:
"My late father was in Qiánzhōng,
and obtained them from the household of Gāo Lìshì."
Only then did everyone deeply admire them.
The guest office then secretly asked the scholar,
"How much should be paid?"
The scholar said:
"No more than thirty thousand."
When gold, silk, and vessels were given,
their value indeed matched that amount.
From "The Record of the Jiégǔ Drum"
The Fisherman
Sūzhōu's Tài Lake enters the mouth of the Sōng River.
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
a fisherman carried
(The Míng manuscript has "carried" as "for".)
a small net.
Several boats, over ten people in total,
cast their nets to catch fish,
but caught nothing at all.
In the net, they found an object,
which turned out to be a mirror, though not very large.
The fisherman, angry at catching no fish,
threw the mirror into the water.
They moved the boat and cast the net again,
and again caught this mirror.
The fishermen found this strange,
so they took the mirror to look at it.
It was only seven or eight inches across.
When they looked into it, they could see all their bones, muscles, and internal organs,
clearly visible and repulsive.
The person fainted and fell,
and everyone was greatly alarmed.
Those who had taken the mirror to look at themselves
immediately all fell down,
vomiting in disarray.
One remaining person,
dared not take it to look,
and immediately threw the mirror into the water.
After a long while,
they helped the fallen and vomiting ones to wake up,
and then they all returned home together,
considering it a monster.
The next day, when they sorted their nets,
the fish they caught were several times more than usual.
Those among them who had pre-existing illnesses
were all cured from then on.
Inquiring among the elders,
they learned that this mirror appears in rivers and lakes
once every few hundred years.
People have often seen it,
but they do not know what kind of spirit relies on it.
From "Records of Original Transformations"
Fú Zài
In the Táng dynasty, Fú Zài excelled in both literature and martial arts.
He once kept a sword
whose divine light turned night into day.
While traveling as a guest to Huái and Zhè,
he encountered a large merchant fleet
that was obstructed by a flood dragon,
unable to proceed.
He drew the sword and swung it once,
blood rained down,
and the boats sailed safely away.
Later, during the Cold Food Festival,
he was at someone's home wrapping zòngzi,
which were as thick as barrels.
The kitchen knife was unusable,
so he used this sword to cut them.
After that, the sword lost its light,
becoming like dull iron,
and was of no further use.
The ancients said:
"A thousand-jūn crossbow
should not be triggered for a mere mouse."
Is this not what is said of this sword?
From "Records of Zhītián"
The Mountain-Splitting Sword
In recent times, a scholar plowed his land and found a sword.
He polished it and took it to the market.
A foreigner sought to buy it,
initially offering one thousand,
then gradually raising the price to a hundred strings of cash,
but the scholar refused.
The foreigner followed him to his home,
admiring and fondling it, unwilling to part with it,
and eventually offered a million.
They agreed that the next day he would bring the money to take the sword.
That night, under a beautiful moon,
the scholar and his wife held the sword and looked at it together.
They laughed and said:
"What is so special about this,
that it commands such a high price?"
In the courtyard was a stone for pounding cloth.
Pointing the sword at it,
the stone immediately split in two.
By dawn,
the foreigner arrived with his money.
He took the sword and looked at it,
sighed, and said:
"The sword's light is already exhausted,
how could this have happened?"
He no longer wanted to buy it.
The scholar questioned him,
and the foreigner said:
"This is a mountain-splitting sword,
and can only be used once.
I intended to use it to split a treasure mountain,
but now its radiance is suddenly gone,
I suspect it has been triggered."
The scholar and his wife were filled with regret,
and told the foreigner what had happened.
The foreigner bought it for ten thousand cash and left.
From "Extensive Records of the Strange"
Yángzhōu Tribute
Yángzhōu used to present Jiāngxīn mirrors as tribute,
cast on the fifth day of the fifth month
in the Yángzǐ River.
Some say they were not refined a hundred times,
but only sixty or seventy times.
They were easily broken and difficult to perfect,
and often made a ringing sound.
From "Supplement to the National History"
Zhèng Yúndí
In the Táng dynasty, Zhèng Yúndí obtained a sword in his youth.
Its scales and blade shone like stars,
and it sometimes roared.
He often lived in his country residence,
resting it across his knee while admiring it.
Suddenly, a person descended rustling from a tree in the courtyard,
wearing purple clothes and a red headband,
with disheveled hair and a drawn sword, standing there.
Black qi surrounded his body,
like a thick fog.
Zhèng was always courageous,
and pretended not to see him.
The person then said:
"I am from the upper realm,
and I know you possess an extraordinary sword.
I wish to borrow it for a look."
Zhèng said to him:
"This is just ordinary iron.
You reside in the upper realm,
how could you need this?"
The person persisted in his request.
Zhèng waited for an opportunity for a long time,
then suddenly struck at him,
but missed.
The black qi was struck and fell to the ground,
and only dispersed after several days.
From "Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng"
Zhāng Cún
Duan Chengshi of the Tang Dynasty,
his friend Wen Jie said:
During the Dàlì era,
a commoner named Zhāng Cún from Gāoyóu made a living by treading lotus roots.
Once in a pond, he saw a dried lotus root as thick as an arm,
so he dug with all his might,
reaching a depth of two zhang,
until it was as large as an armful.
Unable to reach the end,
he cut it off.
Inside, he found a sword two chi long,
blue in color and without an edge.
Zhāng Cún did not treasure it.
A townsman who knew its value
acquired it for ten bundles of firewood.
The lotus root had no fibers.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Lily Flower
At the end of the Yuánhé era of the Tang Dynasty,
a lily flower grew in front of the courtyard of Xiàhóu Yī in Hǎilíng,
several times larger than usual,
which he found strange.
So he dug beneath it,
and found thirteen nested arm-sized boxes,
each containing a mirror.
Up to the seventh,
the light did not touch,
and when shone upon sunlight, it formed a halo of one zhang.
The others were merely ordinary bronze.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Fisherman from Zhèyòu
Lǐ Déyù of the Tang Dynasty,
during the Chángqìng era,
served as an inspector in Zhèyòu.
A fisherman happened to cast his net deep in the Qínhuái River,
when he suddenly felt it unusually heavy,
different from usual.
When he hauled it to the water's edge,
he caught not a single scale,
but only an ancient bronze mirror about a chi long,
its light floating on the waves.
The fisherman took it to look,
and could clearly see all his internal organs,
blood vessels and pulses moving,
which terrified him.
In his trembling hand, he dropped it.
The fisherman mentioned it casually to a neighbor,
and it eventually reached Lǐ Déyù.
For a whole year,
he exhausted all means to search the river bottom,
but never found it again.
From "Sōngchuāng Lù"
Yuán Zhěn
When Chancellor Yuán Zhěn of the Tang Dynasty governed Jiāngxià,
he once ascended the Huánghè Tower on an autumn evening.
Gazing at the riverbank in the distance,
he saw a light like a fading star,
so he ordered a trusted subordinate to go and investigate.
The man rowed a small boat,
straight to where the light was,
which turned out to be a fishing boat.
He asked the fisherman,
who said:
"I just caught a carp,
but there is no light."
The man then brought the carp back.
Once they ascended the tower,
the lord ordered the cook to cut it open.
Inside its belly, they found two mirrors,
as large as coins,
and facing each other.
On the back, two dragons were faintly raised,
though small, their scales, manes, claws, and horns were all complete.
Exquisitely crafted and lustrous,
they often emitted a radiant light.
The lord treasured them,
placing them in a handkerchief box in his bedroom.
When the chancellor passed away,
the mirrors also vanished.
From "Sānshuǐ Xiǎolù"
Lǐ Déyù
Grand Commandant and Duke Wèi Lǐ Déyù of the Tang Dynasty,
once had an old man visit his gate.
Leading five or six people carrying a huge mulberry wood, he requested an audience,
and the gatekeeper could not refuse him.
Lǐ Déyù, finding it strange, came out to meet him.
The old man said:
"This wood has been treasured by my family for three generations.
I am now old,
moved by your benevolence and virtue,
and knowing you appreciate curiosities,
I thus present it.
Inside the wood is a rare treasure;
if someone skilled cuts it open,
they will surely gain something.
In Luòyì, there is a craftsman,
but considering his age, he may already be old,
or perhaps already deceased.
His descendants should still know the technique.
If not the Luò craftsman,
no one else can cut it open."
The lord followed his words,
inquired in Luòxià,
and found the craftsman had already died.
His son came with the messenger.
After examining it for a long time, he said:
"It can be cut slowly."
He then split it into two pipa soundboxes,
naturally forming a white dove,
with wings, beak, and feet,
all details complete.
The craftsman's calculation was slightly off,
the thickness uneven,
so one dove lacked a wing.
The lord presented the intact one,
and kept the other for himself.
It is still among the people today.
Vice Minister of Water Resources Lú Yánràng,
saw the grand commandant's grandson,
and recounted this story.
From "Lùyì Jì"
Monk of Gānlù Temple
A monk of Gānlù Temple in Rùnzhōu during the Tang Dynasty was of lofty conduct,
renowned in Jiāngzuǒ.
When Lǐ Déyù, Duke Wèi, served as inspector,
he often associated with him.
Upon leaving his post,
he left a square bamboo cane as a gift.
Square bamboo comes from Dàyuān country,
solid and perfectly square,
with nodes, eyes, and whiskers,
protruding symmetrically on all four sides,
truly treasured by Duke Wèi.
When he returned to govern Zhèyòu again,
the monk was still there.
The duke asked:
"Is the bamboo cane I presented earlier still intact?"
The monk replied:
"I have already rounded it and lacquered it."
The duke sighed with regret all day.
From "Guìyuàn Cóngtán"
Lìng Hú Táo
Chancellor Lìng Hú Táo of the Tang Dynasty, while discussing strange objects,
produced an iron tube himself,
less than a cun in diameter,
four cun long.
Taking out a small scroll inside and viewing it in sunlight,
it contained the Nine Classics in full.
The paper was waxed cattail matting,
the text evenly small.
The beginning and end were similar,
its exquisiteness beyond words.
Then he poured out its contents,
and unfurled a bolt of light silk.
Measuring it, it was four zhang without shortage,
weighing only half a liang,
appearing as if not of this world.
Note: Many characters are missing after "suǒ."
The text after "fǎn bào" seems to belong to the latter half of the entry about the Prefect of Qiánzhōu,
with four entries including Péi Yuè missing in between.
Returned to report,
the prefect was afraid.
He pursued the old man intending to punish him,
but the old man said:
"I beg Your Excellency not to act hastily.
I am literate;
people like Chǔ only need such a brush.
I beg to first see the chancellor's handwriting,
and then create it."
The prefect showed it to him,
and the old man laughed:
"If it is like this,
you need not spend thirty coins,
and I will send fifty more brushes.
If they are not satisfactory,
I willingly accept the punishment of the cauldron."
He still requested to be shackled,
awaiting the messenger's return.
The prefect's anger slightly subsided,
and he recounted the old man's story.
Saying:
"Having seen the chancellor's divine calligraphy,
such brushes are appropriate."
The chancellor's residence received them,
tested them with ink, and found them excellent.
He replied in writing:
"The brushes are very satisfactory,
the craftsman should be generously rewarded."
The prefect was pleased,
and sent the old man off with a bundle of silk.
From "Zhītián Lù"
Zhōu Hán
Táng Zhōu Hán traveled downstream from Shǔ,
and once purchased a slave,
named Shuǐjīng,
who was skilled at diving,
being of the Kūnlún Báishuǐ variety.
Hán, suspicious of the depth of the Qútáng Gorge,
ordered Shuǐjīng to explore it.
After some time, he emerged,
saying:
"There is a gate below,
impossible to cross,
but I only obtained some gold and pearls."
Whenever encountering deep pools or caves,
he would order the slave to explore them,
and they often acquired many treasures.
Hearing that the Bājiǎo Well in Biànzhōu was frequented by dragon spirits,
and that strange hands sometimes appeared on the water's surface,
he wanted to send Shuǐjīng to investigate,
but hesitated and did not proceed.
His friend Shào Zé possessed a sharp sword,
which he often regarded as divine.
He unsheathed the sword and handed it to the slave,
sending him into the well.
Hán and Zé waited outside,
but after a long silence,
they suddenly saw Shuǐjīng leap high out of the well,
before he could reach the bank,
a large golden hand seized him and pulled him back in,
and both the sword and the slave were lost from then on.
Hán grieved for his Shuǐjīng,
Zé lamented his precious sword,
but they never fully understood what had happened.
Some time later,
someone said to Hán:
"This well is the dwelling of dragon spirits,
a sacred abode of the water realm.
How could you rashly violate it?
You should make an offering and apologize."
Hán then made an offering and apology before leaving.
From "Yuánhuà Jì",
the Ming manuscript copy says from "Lùyì Jì",
"Lèishuō" volume thirty-two cites it as from "Chuánqí".
Zhēnyáng Guàn
In Xīnzhè Xiàn, there is a Zhēnyáng Guàn,
which is the place where the disciple of Xǔ Zhēnjūn, Zēng Zhēnrén, attained the Way.
The temple had permanent estate lands,
which were largely encroached upon by local villagers.
During the reign of Emperor Xīzōng of the Táng dynasty,
Nánpíng Wáng Zhōng Chuán controlled the lands of eight prefectures in Jiāngxī.
At that time, while the temple was conducting a Yuánzhāi ceremony,
suddenly an incense burner descended from the sky.
The burner was three feet tall,
with a tray beneath it.
From the tray emerged a lotus flower,
with twelve petals.
Between the petals faintly appeared objects,
which were the twelve zodiac animals.
On top of the burner was an immortal,
wearing a distant travel cap,
clad in clouds and mist garments,
with a dignified and graceful appearance.
His left hand supported his chin,
his right hand rested on his knee,
sitting on a small flat rock.
On the rock were carvings of flowers, bamboo, flowing water, pines, and junipers,
exquisitely carved and strangely marvelous,
beyond human craftsmanship.
When it first descended,
whenever villagers encroached upon the temple's estate lands,
it would fly to the fields,
emitting a great radiance.
The villagers, frightened,
would immediately return the lands to the temple,
not daring to linger.
Nánpíng Wáng, hearing of its miraculous nature,
sent an envoy to fetch the burner,
and brought it to Jiāngxī for veneration.
Suddenly one night, the burner disappeared,
and upon searching, it was found to have returned to the old temple.
Both clergy and laity regarded it as an auspicious burner.
When the former Chancellor, Lè'ān Gōng Sūn Wò, was exiled south,
he passed by this temple.
He left an inscription.
The final lines read:
"How lovely, on a moonlit night of celestial steps,
the auspicious burner flies down before the altar of offerings."
The auspicious burner was golden in color,
its weight unfixed.
Normally lifting it,
one could only manage six or seven catties.
Once a thief tried to steal it,
but even several people could not lift it.
It remains in the temple to this day,
but it no longer flies.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà".
Pí Hú Fisherman
Between Xú and Sù lies Pí Lake, spanning several hundred li.
The reeds, rushes, and lotus plants of the two prefectures
rely on it for sustenance.
During the Tiānyòu era of the Táng dynasty,
a fisherman caught an iron mirror in his net,
not very rusty,
its surface still reflective,
about five or six inches wide,
and he took it home.
Suddenly a monk arrived at his door,
saying to the fisherman:
"You possess a strange object,
may I see it?"
The fisherman replied:
"I have nothing."
The monk said:
"I heard you obtained an iron mirror,
that is the object."
So he brought it out.
The monk said:
"Just take it back to where you found it and shine it,
see what appears."
He did as instructed and shone it,
seeing countless armored soldiers in the lake.
The fisherman was terrified,
and threw it back into the water.
The monk also disappeared.
According to elder lore,
the lake was formed by the sinking of Pí Prefecture,
though no records document it.
Originally missing source,
the Ming manuscript copy says from "Yùtáng Xiánhuà".
Wén Gǔ
Wén Gǔ, a literary figure of the pseudo-Shǔ state,
was a scholar fond of antiquity.
Once visiting the Secretariat Drafter Liú Guāngzuò,
he happily said:
"Today I have arranged to meet with two guests,
to show them my peach pit cup."
Wén was about to ask the reason,
when the guests arrived.
The first was Liú Yún, a Taoist from Qīngchéng Shān,
the second was Shěn Mò, a guest from Shēng Palace.
Liú said to them:
"Literary Attendant Wén is also an extraordinary man."
He then had the peach pit cup brought out for viewing.
The cup was over a foot wide,
with brilliant patterns,
truly the fruit of a flat peach.
Liú said:
"In my youth,
I often traveled to Huà Mountain.
I met a Taoist there,
who used this pit to fetch waterfall water for washing,
and I was astonished to see it."
The Taoist laughed and said:
"Do you desire it?"
And gave me half of it.
I have treasured it for years."
Taoist Liú Yún produced a white stone,
round like a chicken egg.
On it were patterns,
faintly appearing like a painting,
depicting two boys,
holding scepters leading an immortal,
with eyebrows, eyes, hair,
hats, shoes, and robes,
all finely detailed.
He said:
"I obtained this from a stone cave in Má Gū Cave."
Shěn Mò also produced a stone,
about an inch wide,
two and a half inches long.
On it faintly appeared a coiled dragon,
with scales, horns, claws, and mane,
all complete.
He said:
"I obtained this from the mountains of Wūxiá Gorge.
Wén Gǔ, in one day, saw all these wondrous objects,
how fortunate."
From "Yěrén Xiánhuà".
Qiānrìjiǔ
Once there was a man named Xuánshí,
who bought wine from a tavern in Zhōngshān.
The tavern owner gave him Thousand-Day Wine,
but forgot to tell him its potency.
Upon returning home, he fell into a drunken slumber
and did not wake for several days.
His family, unaware of the situation,
thought he had died
and prepared a coffin to bury him.
When the tavern owner reached the thousandth day,
he remembered that Xuánshí had come earlier to buy wine
and should have sobered up by then.
He then went to Xuánshí’s home to inquire,
and was told:
"Xuánshí passed away three years ago,
and the mourning period has now ended."
So he went with the family to Xuánshí’s grave,
dug it open, and looked inside.
Xuánshí finally awoke
and rose from the coffin.
From *Records of Diverse Matters*
Qínjiān Wine
Liú Báiduò from Hédōng was skilled at brewing wine.
In the heat of the sixth lunar month,
Liú would store the wine in jars
and expose them to the sun.
After ten days,
the wine’s flavor remained unchanged,
and it tasted fragrant and delicious,
but once drunk, it was hard to sober up.
When nobles from the capital traveled to other commanderies,
they would send this wine as gifts
over distances exceeding a thousand *lǐ*.
Because it could travel far,
it was called "Crane Goblet,"
also known as "Donkey-Riding Wine."
During the Yǒngxī era,
Máo Hóngbīn, the Governor of Qīngzhōu, took this wine with him to his post.
On the road, he encountered bandits at night,
and after drinking the wine, they all became drunk,
allowing them to be captured.
Hence, it was renamed "Qínjiān Wine" (Wine for Capturing Villains).
Wandering knights would say:
"We fear not drawn bows or drawn swords,
only Báiduò’s spring brew."
From *Records of Buddhist Temples*
Ruòxià Wine
*Gazetteer of Regions* states:
Villagers took water from Ruòxià to brew wine,
which was mellow and delicious.
It was commonly called "Ruòxià Wine."
As Zhāng Xiéshì said:
"Wūchéng in Jīngzhōu,
Zhúyè in northern Yù."
This refers to it.
From *Records of Ten Circuits*
Kūnlún Goblet
Wèi Jiǎ Cóng’s family amassed great wealth,
and he was widely learned and skilled in writing.
He had a servant who was adept at distinguishing water,
often sent on a small boat into the Huáng Hé.
Using a gourd to collect water from the river’s source,
he could gather no more than seven or eight *shēng* a day.
After a night,
the water in the vessel turned crimson.
Using it to brew wine,
it was named "Kūnlún Goblet,"
and the wine’s fragrance and flavor
were unparalleled in the world.
He once presented thirty *hú* of it to Emperor Zhuāng of Wèi.
From *Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng*
Bìtóng Wine
North of Lìchéng was Shǐjūn Forest.
During the Zhèngshǐ era of Wèi,
Duke Zhèng Gōngquè, in the hottest days of summer,
would often lead guests and colleagues to escape the heat there.
They would take large lotus leaves and place them on inkstone racks.
Filling them with three *shēng* of wine,
they would pierce the leaf with a hairpin,
making it connect with the stem.
Bending the stem
(Original text had "jìng" for "stem,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy)
upwards,
it coiled like an elephant’s trunk.
Passing it around to drink from,
it was called "Bìtóng" (Green Tube).
People in Lìxià imitated this,
saying the wine’s flavor mingled with the lotus scent,
its cool fragrance surpassing ice.
From *Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng*
Nine-Ferment Wine
After Zhāng Huá became prominent,
an acquaintance from his youth came to visit him.
Huá drank Nine-Ferment Wine with him,
and they became thoroughly intoxicated,
falling into a drunken sleep that night.
Huá often drank this wine,
and after falling asleep drunk,
he would order his attendants
to turn him over until he awoke.
That evening,
he forgot to give the order.
The attendants, as usual, turned Lord Zhāng over,
but no one did so for his friend.
By dawn,
the friend still had not risen.
Huá exclaimed:
"He must be dead!"
He had someone check,
and indeed, the wine had corroded his intestines and flowed out,
flooding beneath the bed.
From *A New Account of the Tales of the World*
Intestine-Corroding Wine
Zhāng Huá made a strong wine,
boiling three kinds of vetch to soak the yeast and malt.
The malt came from the Western Qiāng,
and the yeast from the Northern Hú.
Among the Hú was "Pointing Star Wheat,"
harvested and eaten
when Mars appeared in the fourth month.
The malt was soaked in water,
and after three nights, the wheat sprouted.
It was used at dawn when the roosters first crowed,
commonly called "Rooster-Crowing Wheat."
Used to brew wine,
it was clear, delicious, and aromatic.
Holding it in the mouth too long could loosen teeth,
and if one became heavily drunk without moving,
it could cause liver and intestines to rot,
hence it was called Intestine-Corroding Wine.
Some said
this strong wine could provide all-night pleasure.
The two interpretations share the same name but refer to different things.
From *Records of Forgotten Events by Prince Nián*
Qīngtián Wine
In the Wūsūn Kingdom, there was a Qīngtián nut,
though no one knew the tree or its fruit.
The nut was as large as a five- or six-*shēng* gourd,
and when hollowed out and filled with water,
it would quickly turn into wine.
Liú Zhāng once obtained two of them,
and when he hosted guests with them,
they could serve twenty people.
As soon as one nut was emptied,
the wine in the other nut
was ready to drink again.
However, it could not be stored long,
as it would become bitter and hard to drink.
Thus, the nut was called "Qīngtián Gourd,"
and the wine "Qīngtián Wine."
From *Annotations on Past and Present*
Sticky Rain Wine
Shí Hǔ built a tower in front of the Dàwǔ Hall,
forty *zhàng* high.
Pearls were woven into curtains,
adorned with five-colored jade pendants.
Above was a bronze dragon,
hollow inside,
holding several hundred *hú* of wine.
Hú people were made to spray the wine from the tower,
and when the wind blew,
it looked like clouds and mist.
It was named "Sticky Rain Terrace,"
used to sprinkle and settle dust.
From *Records of Forgotten Events*
Wine Names:
Fùshuǐ from Yǐng,
Ruòxià from Wūchéng,
Tǔkūchūn from Xíngyáng,
Shídòngchūn from Fùpíng,
Shāochūn from Jiànnán,
Gānhépútáo from Hédōng,
Língxībóluó from Lǐngnán,
Jiǔyùn from Yìchéng,
Pénshuǐ from Xúnyáng,
Xīshìqiāng from the capital,
Lángguānqīng from Hámálíng.
From Héhàn—
*Supplement to the National History* reads "From Héhàn—Āpóqīng, also"
Sānlèjiāng,
its method originating from Persia.
The three *lè* refer to
Ānmólè, Pílílè, and Hēlílè.
From *Supplement to the National History*
Southern Wines
Xīnzhōu has many fine wines.
In the south, wine is not made using yeast;
instead, rice is pounded into powder,
mixed with the juice of various herbs and leaves, especially húmàncǎo.
Southerners call "wild kudzu" húmàncǎo.
The mixture is shaped into balls as large as eggs,
placed among mugwort and sheltered in the shade,
and left to ferment for a month.
This is then combined with glutinous rice to make wine.
Therefore, after heavy drinking,
even when sober,
one's head remains feverish and damp with sweat,
due to the poisonous herbs.
In the south, after the wine is heated,
the jar is filled to the brim,
sealed with mud on top,
and heated over fire until fully cooked.
Otherwise,
it is not fit to drink.
Once heated, the jar is opened to release pressure,
but the mud seal remains intact.
Buyers cannot tell the quality of the wine,
so they drill a small hole in the mud, large enough for a chopstick,
insert a thin tube into the hole,
and suck on the tube
to taste the wine.
This is commonly called "dīlín."
Rogues enter the market empty-handed,
going from wine shop to wine shop to sample through dīlín,
claiming none are satisfactory,
and return home drunk.
When a southern family has a daughter a few years old,
they brew a large quantity of wine.
After filtering,
they wait until winter when the pond water recedes,
place the wine jars,
seal them tightly,
and bury them in the pond.
When spring arrives and the water rises,
they are not retrieved.
When the daughter is about to marry,
they drain the pond,
retrieve the wine to serve to congratulatory guests.
Southerners call this "nǚjiǔ."
It tastes exceptionally fine,
and is not usually available.
From Tóuhuāng Zálù.
Lǐ Jǐngràng
During the Dàzhōng era,
at a banquet for officials,
Jiǎng Shēn was present.
Suddenly, he poured a cup and said:
"Whoever at this table is filial at home,
loyal to the state,
and renowned in their time,
drink this cup."
Everyone was solemn,
and no one dared to raise it.
Only Duke Lǐ Jǐngràng stood up and took the cup.
Jiǎng said:
"This is only fitting."
From Lúshì Záshuō.
Xiàhóu Zī
When Cuī Yìng served as the Capital Governor,
the Three Commissioners held a banquet for officials at Yǒngdá Pavilion.
Cuī, under the influence of wine, barged in to drink,
and everyone invited him to stay.
At the time, Duke Xiàhóu Zī was the Commissioner of Revenue.
He asked:
"Have you ever served as a Secretary or Advisor?"
Cuī said:
"No."
Duke Xiàhóu said:
"If you have never served as a Secretary or Advisor,
the Capital Governor should not intrude on a banquet for officials.
Bring the wine for penalties,
call for tallies,
and drink the penalty cup."
He took three large vessels,
filled them to the brim, and drank.
After a long while, he finally rose.
From Lúshì Záshuō.
Sūn Huìzōng
Táng Dynasty Minister Sūn Huìzōng,
the great-grandfather of Minister Wò,
once hosted a banquet at his home for relatives, both internal and external.
A nephew who served as a court official
arrived late.
As he reached the inner gate,
he saw an official in crimson robes,
his front lapel stained with wine,
storming out angrily.
He did not recognize him.
Shortly after taking his seat,
he mentioned it to the host.
The host was surprised, as there was no such official.
After pondering,
they realized it was when wine was being poured
on the steps as a libation,
carelessly splashed.
From then on, every time a libation was poured,
they only bowed respectfully to the side,
and poured a single libation.
This began with the Sūn family.
Nowadays, pouring three libations is incorrect.
From Běimèng Suǒyán.
Lù Yǐ
When Chancellor Lù Yǐ was appointed to Yílíng,
a scholar came to pay his respects.
The Chancellor spoke with him leisurely
and offered him wine.
The scholar declined, saying:
"I am naturally unable to drink."
The Chancellor said:
"If what you say is true,
you have already reduced it by half.
For the regrets and troubles in life amount to ten parts;
not being troubled by wine
naturally reduces them by half."
From Běimèng Suǒyán.
Shān Tāo
Shān Tāo, courtesy name Jùyuán,
could drink up to eight dǒu of wine.
Emperor Wǔ wanted to test him,
so he secretly had someone keep count.
He became drunk only after reaching his limit.
From Jìnshū.
Zhōu Yǐ
Zhōu Yǐ, courtesy name Bórén,
could drink up to one dàn of wine.
After crossing the river,
though he drank daily,
he often regretted having no match.
Once, a visitor from the north returned,
and Yǐ met him,
feeling delighted.
He set out two dàn of wine for them to drink together,
and both became heavily drunk.
When Yǐ woke up,
he sent someone to check on the guest,
only to find he had died from a ruptured liver.
From Jìnshū.
Péi Hóngtài
Pei Hongtai: During the Tang Dynasty, when Pei Jūn was stationed in Xiāngzhōu,
Pei Hongtai served as the patrol officer of the Zhèng-Huá courier station.
He was sent on a diplomatic mission to Hànnán.
Encountering a grand banquet,
he was overlooked by the guest administration.
When the banquet was being set up,
Pei Jūn ordered someone to quickly invite Patrol Officer Pei from Zhèng-Huá.
Pei Hongtai rushed over,
and Pei Jūn was displeased.
He reprimanded him, saying:
"Why have you arrived so late?
This is highly disrespectful.
The penalty wine for latecomers
has already been poured into the disciplinary tally cup."
Pei Hongtai apologized, saying:
"I truly did not receive any notice of the banquet from the guest office,
and I dared not be negligent.
If Uncle would pardon my offense,
I request that all the silver vessels at the banquet
be filled to the brim with wine.
Each vessel shall be given to Hongtai after I drink from it.
Is that acceptable?"
All those present admired his boldness,
and Pei Jūn also agreed.
Pei Hongtai proceeded to lift the small cups on the banquet table in order,
up to the large wine vessels.
He drank each one dry,
and as soon as he finished drinking,
he immediately placed them in his bosom.
In a short while, his bosom was full.
On the banquet table, there was a large silver wine vessel,
capable of holding over a dou.
The wine inside it was also full.
Pei Hongtai lifted it with both hands and drank,
finishing it.
He then glanced at the attendants,
overturned the vessel onto the ground,
stepped on it with his foot,
rolled it up, embraced it, and walked out,
immediately calling for his horse to return to the courier station.
Pei Jūn, seeing that Pei Hongtai had taken quite a few drinking vessels,
looked unhappy.
After the banquet ended in the afternoon,
Pei Jūn thought again of Pei Hongtai's drinking,
fearing that he must have been harmed by excessive alcohol,
and was worried about him.
By evening,
he sent someone to see what Pei Hongtai was doing after drinking.
The messenger saw Pei Hongtai wearing a gauze cap,
in the hall of the Hànyīn courier station,
sitting with his legs stretched out casually.
He had summoned a craftsman to weigh the vessels,
which totaled over two hundred liǎng.
Pei Jūn couldn't help but laugh heartily.
The next day, they drank again,
and on the day of his return journey,
Pei Jūn bestowed generous gifts upon him.
From "Qián Cuàn Zǐ."
Wáng Yuánzhōng,
during the reign of Emperor Wénzōng, served as the Hanlin Academician Recipient of Edicts.
On a leisurely day,
he was playing cùjū with his brothers at his residence in Tàipíng Lǐ.
The ball was kicked up,
accidentally hitting Wáng Yuánzhōng's forehead,
causing a slight injury.
Shortly after, there was an urgent summons.
When he arrived,
the emperor was surprised.
Wáng Yuánzhōng reported the whole matter to the emperor,
and the emperor said:
"You are truly harmonious with your family."
He ordered two trays of wine to be bestowed upon him,
each tray containing ten golden bowls,
each bowl holding about a shēng.
The emperor decreed that the bowls be given to him as well.
Wáng Yuánzhōng drank all the wine without leaving a drop,
showing no sign of drunkenness.
From "Zhí Yán."
Xú Miǎo
Xú Miǎo, styled Jǐngshān, of the Wèi state,
served as a Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat.
At that time, alcohol was prohibited,
but Xú Miǎo drank privately and became heavily intoxicated.
His subordinate Zhào Dá asked him about official matters,
and Xú Miǎo said:
"I have become a 'sage.'"
Zhào Dá reported this to Tàizǔ,
and Tàizǔ was very angry.
Xiānyú Fǔ said:
"Drunkards call clear wine 'sage'
and turbid wine 'worthy man.'
Xú Miǎo is by nature cautious and disciplined,
and this was merely a drunken remark."
Thus, he was spared punishment.
From "Yì Yuàn."
Liú Líng
Liú Líng often rode in a deer-drawn carriage,
carrying a pot of wine,
and had someone follow him with a spade.
He said:
"Bury me where I die."
Such was his disregard for his physical form.
Once, he was extremely thirsty
and asked his wife for wine.
His wife had hidden the wine and discarded the vessels,
admonishing him:
"This is not the way to nurture life;
you should quit."
Liú Líng said:
"Good.
I should pray to the gods and spirits and make a vow.
You may prepare wine and meat for the offering."
His wife complied.
Liú Líng knelt and prayed:
"Heaven gave birth to Liú Líng,
who takes wine as his name.
He drinks one dàn at a time,
and five dǒu sober him from a hangover.
The words of a woman
must never be heeded."
Thereupon, he drank the wine and ate the meat,
and once again became thoroughly drunk.
From "Jìn Shū."
The Stench of Wine
At the beginning of the Yìníng era,
there was a county magistrate who was a descendant of an official family.
In his youth,
he was exceptionally handsome and elegant.
He was well-read in history and literature,
and also possessed literary talent.
Later, he became addicted to alcohol,
and as he aged, his addiction grew even stronger.
He drank several shēng daily,
with almost no sober moments.
When he fell ill and was nearing death,
the stench of wine could be smelled from several lǐ away,
astonishing people near and far,
who did not know the cause.
After about ten days like this,
the man passed away.
Therefore, Buddhist scriptures warn against alcohol,
saying it causes confusion and folly.
Now, the stench of wine at the moment of death
reveals that he entered an evil path.
From "Wǔ Xíng Jì."
Wú Zhuàn
Wújùn presented four bottles of dried minced sea miǎn fish,
each bottle containing one dǒu.
Soaking one dǒu
can yield several plates a foot in diameter.
Along with it, a memorial was submitted detailing the method of making dried minced fish.
The emperor showed it to his assembled ministers, saying:
"In the past, the magician Jiè Xiàng once fished a sea fish in the palace courtyard—
that was mere illusion.
What is so extraordinary about it?
Today's minced fish,
however, is made from real sea fish,
coming from thousands of miles away,
and is indeed an exceptional delicacy of the time."
Yú Shìjī replied:
"Since the magician's fish was illusory,
his minced fish was certainly not real either."
Several plates were taken out and bestowed upon the high-ranking officials.
The method for making dried minced fish:
During the hottest days of the fifth and sixth months,
catch miǎn fish from the sea.
The larger ones are four to five chǐ long,
with fine scales and purple color,
and have no fine bones or fishy smell.
Once caught,
prepare the minced fish right on the sea vessel.
Remove the skin and bones,
take the lean meat and shred it finely.
As it is prepared, dry it in the sun immediately.
After three or four days,
it must be thoroughly dried,
then placed in a new white porcelain bottle
that has never held water.
Seal it with mud,
ensuring no air enters.
After fifty or sixty days,
it will be no different from fresh fish.
When ready to eat,
open the container of dried minced fish,
wrap it in cloth,
soak it in a large jar filled with water.
After the time it takes for three kè, remove it,
and with the cloth still wrapped, drain the water away—
then it becomes bright and clear.
Scatter it on a plate,
indistinguishable from fresh minced fish.
Finely chop fragrant ròu leaves and spread them on top,
then mix evenly with chopsticks before serving.
Sea fish inherently lack a fishy smell,
and the meat of the fān miǎn fish is soft and white.
After drying and mixing with green leaves,
it becomes bright and extremely palatable.
Also presented were thirty sticks of sea shrimp roe.
Each stick is one chǐ long,
one cùn wide,
and about one cùn thick,
exquisitely fine.
The method of making it:
Take sea white shrimp that carry roe,
place three to five dǒu of them in a tightly woven bamboo basket,
and rinse them with water in a large basin.
The roe is under the shrimp's abdomen,
red like fùpénzi berries,
and it falls through the basket's holes with the water.
In total, for one dàn of shrimp,
one can obtain five shēng of roe,
which is then filtered out from the basin.
Sew cloth into small bags,
about the size of a half-cùn diameter bamboo tube,
two chǐ long.
Fill these bags with the shrimp roe,
tie the openings tightly,
and depending on the number of bags,
cover them with fine salt,
several cùn thick all around.
After one day and night, take them out to dry in the sun.
At night, press them with flat boards.
The next day, take them out to dry again.
After pressing for ten days until dry,
break open the bags
to remove the shrimp roe sticks.
Their color is like red glass,
translucent and rich in flavor,
several times saltier than zī fish.
Also presented were a thousand heads of miǎn fish with intact bellies,
extremely fine and excellent.
The method of making them:
During the hottest days of the sixth and seventh months,
take miǎn fish about two chǐ long,
remove the scales and wash them clean.
Let them sit for two days,
waiting until the bellies swell,
then pull out the intestines from the mouth,
remove the gills but keep the eyes.
Fill the belly completely with salt,
then cover the entire fish with fine salt,
several cùn thick.
After one night,
wash it clean with water.
Dry it in the sun during the day,
and bring it back indoors at night.
Place it on a flat board,
and press it with another board and stones.
The next day, dry it again in the sun,
and press it again at night.
After five or six days like this, when dry,
place it in a dry porcelain jar,
and seal the opening.
After twenty days, take it out.
The skin becomes glossy and translucent,
like yellow oil,
and the meat resembles qiǔ.
It is also like the crispiness of shāqí,
slightly salty and flavorful,
tastier than shíshǒu fish with intact bellies.
However, shíshǒu fish with intact bellies are also presented annually,
but their meat is tougher and inferior.
This method originated from the Imperial Flavor Commissioner, Grand Commander Dù Jì,
a native of Kuàijī,
who could distinguish flavors,
and was skilled with salt and vinegar.
He was like the ancient Fú Láng,
or the modern Xiè Fěng.
From "Dàyè Shíyí Jì."
Also, Wújùn presented six bottles of dried minced Sōngjiāng perch,
each bottle containing one dǒu.
The method for making minced fish
is the same as for miǎn fish.
However, to make minced perch,
it must be during the eighth and ninth months when frost falls.
Catch perch under three chǐ in length to make dried minced fish.
After soaking,
wrap it in cloth and drain the water completely,
then scatter it on a plate.
Take fragrant ròu flowers and leaves,
chop them finely and intersperse them,
mixing them evenly with the minced fish.
Perch after frost
has meat as white as snow,
with no fishy smell.
This is the so-called "golden relish and jade minced fish,"
a delicacy of the southeast.
Purple flowers and green leaves,
interspersed with plain minced fish,
are also fresh and pleasing to the eye.
Wújùn also presented three thousand honey crabs,
made using the method for sugar crabs.
And four jars of honey yōngjiàn.
Yōngjiàn resembles a crab but is smaller,
with two disproportionately large claws.
This is what "The Rhapsody on Wújùn" refers to as "the inkfish and yōngjiàn."
From "Dàyè Shíyí Jì."
Imperial Kitchen
When the imperial kitchen presented dishes,
all utensils were supplied by the Shàofǔ Jiān.
For the nine-dish meal,
nine ivory plates were used,
arranged with various foods.
Placed before the emperor,
it was also called "viewing food."
According to people from the capital,
whenever the two armies marched and provisions were presented,
or during banquets,
they often ate chickens and geese.
Among these, they particularly favored young geese,
each worth two to three thousand coins.
Whenever a feast was held,
geese were taken according to the number of people.
Singe off the feathers,
remove the internal organs,
and stuff with meat and glutinous rice,
seasoned with five flavors.
First, take a whole sheep,
also singed and skinned,
and remove its intestines and stomach.
Place the goose inside the sheep,
sew it up, and roast it.
When the mutton is cooked,
remove the sheep.
Take the goose and eat it whole—
this was called "hún yáng mò hū."
Whenever the Hanlin Academicians were bestowed food,
there was a dish resembling bìluó,
large and coarse in shape,
but fragrant and delicious in flavor,
called "zhūwáng xiūshì."
From "Lúshì Záshuō."
Wǔhóu Qīng
Lóu Hù, styled Jūnqīng,
frequented the households of the Five Marquises.
Every morning,
each of the Five Marquises' households would send him food.
Jūnqīng grew weary of the flavors,
so he tried combining the mackerels sent by the Five Marquises and ate them,
finding them exceptionally delicious.
What the world calls the "Five Marquises' Mackerel"
was created by Jūnqīng.
From *Yǔlín*.
Some say,
Hù was equally favored by all Five Marquises,
and did not show partiality in his eating.
Therefore, he combined them to make the mackerel.
From *Shìshuō*.
Also, the Five Marquises were not on good terms with each other,
and their guests were not allowed to interact.
Lóu Hù, with his eloquent words,
mediated among the Five Marquises.
He won the favor of each,
and they vied to present him with rare delicacies.
Hù then combined them to make mackerel,
which the world called the "Five Marquises' Mackerel,"
considering it a rare delicacy.
From *Xījīng Zájì*.
Liú Xiàoyí.
Liáng's Liú Xiàoyí, while eating mackerel and fermented fish, said:
"The Five Marquises and Nine Chiefs,
now all are summoned."
Wèi envoys Cuī Jié and Lǐ Qiān were present.
Jié said:
"The duty of the Imperial Censor,
should not yet involve dividing Shǎn."
Qiān said:
"If so,
the Imperial Censor's four territories,
should extend to Mùlùlíng."
Xiàoyí said:
"The deer tail from Yèzhōng,
