is the finest among wines and dishes."
Jié said:
"Raw fish and bear's paw,
were praised by Mencius.
Chicken feet and orangutan lips,
were mentioned in *Lǚshì*.
Deer tail indeed has a rare flavor,
yet it is not recorded in books,
which I always regret."
Xiàoyí said:
"It truly is so,
perhaps preferences differ between ancient and modern times.
Liáng's Hè Jì said:
'The crab roe from Qīngzhōu,
was recorded by the Zhèng family.'
This item is not written about,
I do not understand why."
Qiān said:
"Zhèng also mentioned Yìzhōu deer meat,
but it was not the tail."
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
Discussion on Shàn.
Hé Yìn was extravagant in his tastes,
his meals always filled a square zhang.
Later, he wished to remove the most excessive items,
but still ate white fish, shàn cured meat, and candied crab,
and had his disciples discuss it.
Academician Zhōng Huì discussed:
"The shàn being cured,
suffers in its bending and stretching;
the crab being candied,
is even more agitated.
A benevolent person's consideration,
deeply holds compassion.
As for clams, ark shells, and oysters,
their features are internally lacking,
ashamed of the wonder of wholeness.
Their lips are sealed externally,
not as cautious as the golden man.
Neither flourishing nor withering,
they are even less than plants and trees;
without fragrance or odor,
how do they differ from tiles and gravel.
Therefore, they should long fill the kitchen,
forever be food for the mouth."
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
Memorial on Shàn.
Later Liáng's Wéi Lín,
a man from Jīngzhào.
He moved south to Xiāngyáng,
and during the Tiānbǎo era, served as a secretary.
He was well-read and talented,
skilled in witty conversation.
He once wrote a "Memorial on Shàn" to satirize the people of his time.
Its text said:
"Your subject Shàn states:
'I humbly observe the appointment document,
appointing me as General of Sǎn'ào,
Commandant of Oil-Steaming,
and Governor of Hóu Prefecture.
My position as cured meat remains unchanged.
Respectfully receiving the command,
I hold my breath with ashes in my mouth,
leaning against the cage, facing the cauldron,
trembling with fear.
Your subject's beauty is inferior to summer sturgeon,
my flavor shamed by winter carp.
I often fear the ridicule of a bulging belly,
dreading to incur the mockery of turtle cliffs
(pronounced wǔgān fǎn).
Therefore, I gargled at the bottom of the lake,
and rested my head on stones in the mud.
Unexpectedly, a high reward specially arrived.
I was graciously selected,
and thus was elevated to the fine mat,
shamefully placed on the jade plate,
far positioned at the tortoiseshell feast.
I was humbly bestowed ivory chopsticks,
my purple belly bathed in favor,
my yellow belly graced with kindness.
Just as ginger and cinnamon are stirred,
and perfumed with basil and pepper.
A light ladle's movement,
makes the plate swirl like smoke.
When the thick broth pauses briefly,
orchid-like dishes array in rows.
Twisting within green pickles,
roaming freely inside red lips.
Bearing favor and tasting grace,
I would not refuse even nine deaths.
With utmost sincerity and trepidation,
I respectfully approach the bronze pot gate,
presenting this memorial to express gratitude for your attention.'"
The edict replied:
"We have reviewed your memorial and understand fully.
You, a distinguished gentleman of ponds and marshes,
an outstanding talent of banks and channels.
Passing through reeds and entering water plants,
your plumpness and smoothness are well-known.
You are truly worthy of this selection,
no need to trouble yourself with thanks."
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
Rèluòhé.
Emperor Xuánzōng ordered hunting officials to shoot a fresh deer,
take its blood to fry
(Míng manuscript has "fry" as "fresh").
deer intestines.
("Intestines" originally written as "bestow,"
corrected according to Míng manuscript.)
and eat it,
calling it "Rèluòhé,"
and bestowed it upon Ān Lùshān and Gēshū Hán.
From *Lúshì Záshuō*.
Famous Foods.
Nowadays, among distinguished families, famous foods include:
the Xiāo family's wontons,
strained out,
their broth not greasy,
suitable for brewing tea;
the Yǔ family's zongzi,
white and translucent like jade;
Hán Yuē could make cherry bìluó,
their color unchanging;
he could also prepare cold hútū,
sliced snakehead fish breast,
and continuously steamed roe deer skin noodle soup.
General Qū Liánghàn could roast donkey tail and camel hump.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
Ruined Saddle Blanket.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a general's household that served meals.
He often said:
"Nothing is inedible,
it only depends on the heat control,
and skillfully balancing the five flavors."
He once took a ruined saddle blanket and a foreign case,
prepared and ate them,
finding their flavor excellent.
From *Yǒuyáng Zázǔ*.
Shàngshílìng.
Féng Jǐshì entered the Zhōngshū Province to wait upon the prime minister,
where he saw an old official dressed in crimson robes,
standing at the gate of the Zhōngshū,
awaiting an announcement.
At that time, Xià Sōnggōng was serving as prime minister,
and he kept Féng seated for a long discussion.
When Féng emerged,
the sun was already setting,
and the old official was still there.
Féng then sent someone to ask what official he was.
The official approached and said:
"I have recently been appointed as the Director of the Imperial Food Bureau,
and I have matters to discuss with the Prime Minister."
Féng then ordered a provincial official to announce him.
The official entered,
and Féng happened not to have left yet.
After the official met with the prime minister,
he came out and thanked Féng, saying:
"If not for your kindness,
I would have had no chance to meet the Prime Minister.
I am the pastry chef of the Imperial Food Bureau,
and I wonder where your residence is?"
Féng replied:
"In the Qīnrén Ward."
The official said:
"I wish to demonstrate my humble skill,
but I do not know when you will be at home?"
Féng said:
"I will await you tomorrow.
However, if you wish to visit,
what items do you need?"
The official replied:
"A large tray,
thirty to fifty wooden wedges,
an oil cauldron and charcoal fire,
one or two dou of fine sesame oil,
and a small amount of southern dates and soft dough."
Féng had always been skilled in culinary arts,
so upon returning home, he immediately arranged everything.
He also hung a curtain,
and his family watched together.
At daybreak,
the official indeed arrived with a bamboo slip.
After sitting and drinking a cup of tea,
he rose and went out to the hall.
He removed his robe, boots, and belt,
his small cap,
his green half-sleeve garment,
Ming manuscript: "肩" written as "臂"
three-paneled trousers,
a floral apron,
and brocade arm guards.
He then inspected the tray from all sides,
and wherever it was uneven,
he filled it with a wedge,
until it was perfectly level.
He then took the oil cauldron, soft dough, and other ingredients and prepared them.
From his apron, he took out a silver box,
a silver comb, and a silver strainer.
When the oil was hot,
he took the pastry filling from the box.
"豏" originally written as "𨃰",
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
He kneaded it with his hands in the soft dough,
and dough oozed out between his five fingers.
He scraped it off with the comb,
then placed the pastry into the cauldron.
When it was cooked,
he strained it out with the strainer.
After soaking it in freshly drawn water for a long time,
he returned it to the oil cauldron,
boiling it three to five times before taking it out.
He tossed it onto the tray,
where it spun without stopping,
because it was so perfectly round.
Its flavor was crispy and delicious,
beyond description.
From "Lúshì Záshuō"
Large Pancake
During the Wángshǔ period,
there was a man named Zhào Xióngwǔ,
known by everyone as Zhào Dàbǐng (Large Pancake).
He served successively as the administrator of famous commanderies,
and was one of the wealthiest men of his time.
He maintained a strict and clean personal life,
and was highly skilled in culinary arts.
In daily life, he did not employ cooks;
among his six bureaus,
two maids performed duties,
and there were always more than fifteen kitchen staff,
all dressed in neat, narrow-sleeved clothing.
For a single meal,
when inviting a guest,
he would ensure both land and sea delicacies were provided.
Even the households of princes and marquises
could not match him.
He was skilled at making large pancakes,
each made from three dou of flour,
larger than several rooms.
Whether for palace banquets
or grand feasts in wealthy households,
he would often present one among the guests.
It would be cut and served,
and there would still be leftovers.
Even among close friends and relatives,
no one knew the method of making it,
and thus he earned the nickname "Large Pancake."
From "Běimèng Suǒyán"
Fàn Wāng
Jìn Dynasty's Fàn Wāng could eat raw plums.
Someone once gave him a hú of plums,
and Fàn Wāng ate them,
finishing them in a short while.
From "Jìnshū"
Sòng Míngdì
Sòng Míngdì Wéi Yù
could eat honey-pickled sturgeon,
consuming several shēng in one meal.
He ate roasted pork,
often up to two hundred pieces.
From "Sòngshū"
Fú Jiān's Three Generals
Fú Jiān appointed Qǐhuó Xià Mò as Left Garrison Commander,
the Hu man
"人" originally written as "又",
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
Hù Mónà as Right Garrison Commander,
and the eunuch Shēn Xiāng as Canopy Commander.
All three were ten feet three inches tall,
strong and skilled in archery.
The three of them ate,
per meal, one shí of rice
and thirty jīn of meat.
From "Qiánqín Lù"
Máo Róng
Later Hàn's Máo Róng, courtesy name Jìwěi,
once hosted Guō Línzōng overnight.
The next morning,
Máo Róng killed a chicken to prepare a meal,
and Guō Línzōng initially thought it was for him.
However, Máo Róng served it only to his mother,
while he himself ate vegetables with the guest.
Guō Línzōng then rose and bowed to him, saying:
"How virtuous you are!"
He encouraged him to pursue studies,
and Máo Róng eventually achieved moral excellence.
From "Chénliú Qíjiù Zhuàn"
Lù Jī
Lù Jī visited Wáng Wǔzǐ,
who had several hú of goat cheese.
Pointing to it, Wáng said to Lù:
"In Jiāngdōng, you have nothing
Ming manuscript: "無" written as "何以" two characters
to rival this."
Lù replied:
"We have thousand-mile water shield soup,
only it lacks salted fermented beans."
From "Shìshuō"
Yáng Màn
Jìn Dynasty's Yáng Màn served as Dānyáng Governor.
At that time, when court officials crossed the river,
upon first receiving an appointment,
they would always prepare lavish feasts.
When Yáng Màn was appointed Dānyáng Governor,
guests who arrived early received fine dishes,
but as the day wore on, the food gradually ran out,
and no more delicacies were served.
He treated guests according to their arrival time,
regardless of their status.
There was a man named Yáng Gù who was appointed Línhǎi Prefect.
He prepared a feast,
and all day long, the food was exquisite.
Even those who arrived late
still enjoyed sumptuous dishes.
Commentators said that Yáng Gù's lavishness
was not as good as Yáng Màn's sincerity.
From "Jìnshū"
Zōng Shìlín
In the late Hàn dynasty,
Zōng Shìlín of Nányáng was a contemporary of Wèi Wǔ,
but he despised Wǔ's character,
and did not associate with him.
When Wǔ Dì was appointed as Minister of Works,
and took control of the court's governance,
he casually asked Zōng:
"Can we associate now?"
Zōng replied:
"My resolve, like that of the pine and cypress, remains unchanged."
Thus, he offended the emperor's wishes and was distanced,
his position not matching his virtue.
Yet, Wén Dì and his brothers, whenever they visited his home,
would invariably bow before his couch.
Such was the depth of their respect for him.
From *Shì Shuō*.
Mí Héng
Mí Héng, styled Zhèngpíng,
in his youth formed a close friendship with Kǒng Wénjǔ, addressing each other informally.
At that time, Héng was not yet twenty,
while Wénjǔ was already over fifty.
From *Běn Zhuàn*.
Xún Jùbó
Xún Jùbó traveled from afar to visit a sick friend,
and encountered Hú bandits attacking the commandery.
His friend said to Jùbó:
"I am about to die;
you should leave."
Jùbó said:
"I came from afar to see you;
to abandon you and flee now that you face peril—
how could that be the conduct of Jùbó?"
When the bandits arrived,
they said to Jùbó:
"Our great army has come here,
and the entire commandery is empty.
Who are you,
that you alone remain?"
Jùbó said:
"My friend is ill;
I cannot bear to abandon him.
I would rather give my own life in place of my friend's."
Hearing his words,
the bandits were astonished.
They then said to each other:
"We are unrighteous men,
yet we have entered a land of righteousness."
Thereupon, they withdrew and retreated,
and the entire commandery was preserved.
From *Yīn Yún Xiǎoshuō*.
Guǎn Níng
Guǎn Níng of Wèi was a close friend of Huà Xīn.
Once, they were hoeing vegetables together in a garden
when they saw a piece of gold on the ground.
Guǎn swung his hoe without a glance,
treating it no differently from tiles or stones;
Huà picked it up and then threw it away.
Another time, they were reading together on the same mat.
A person riding in a carriage with official headgear passed by the gate.
Guǎn continued reading as before,
but Huà set aside his book and went out to look.
Guǎn cut the mat and separated their seats, saying:
"You are not my friend."
From *Shì Shuō*;
the Ming manuscript copy states it is from *Yīn Yún Xiǎoshuō*.
The Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove
Ruǎn Jí of Chénliú, Jī Kāng of Qiáoguó, and Shān Tāo of Hénèi—
these three were close in age.
Joining this fellowship were
Liú Líng of Pèiguó, Ruǎn Xián of Chénliú, Xiàng Xiù of Hénèi, and Wáng Róng of Lángyá.
The seven often gathered beneath a bamboo grove,
indulging freely in unrestrained merriment.
The world called them the Seven Worthies of the Bamboo Grove.
From *Shì Shuō*.
Jī Kāng
Jī Kāng had long been friends with Lǚ Ān.
Whenever one missed the other,
he would order a carriage to travel a thousand *lǐ* for a visit.
Once, when Ān came,
Kāng happened to be away.
His elder brother, Jī Xǐ, came out to greet him,
but Ān did not proceed forward.
Instead, he wrote the character "phoenix" (鳳) on the gate and left.
Xǐ did not understand.
When Kāng returned, he said:
"A phoenix (鳳) is just a common bird (凡鳥)."
From *Yǔ Lín*.
Shān Tāo
Shān Tāo, upon meeting Jī [Kāng] and Ruǎn [Jí] just once,
formed a bond as strong as gold and orchid.
Shān's wife, née Hán, sensed that Tāo's friendship with these two was extraordinary,
and asked him about it.
Tāo said:
"In this present age, the only ones worthy of being my friends
are these two men."
His wife said:
"The wife of Fù Jī
also personally observed Zhào Dūn and Hú Yǎn.
I wish to take a look at them;
may I?"
Tāo said:
"You may."
Another day, when the two men came,
she urged Tāo to have them stay overnight,
and prepared wine and food.
She peered at them through a hole in the wall
until dawn, forgetting to return.
Tāo entered and asked:
"What are they like?"
She said:
"Your talent and grace are not equal to theirs;
it is only in insight and breadth of mind that you are their match."
Tāo said:
"They also consider my insight and breadth of mind to be superior."
From *Shì Shuō*.
Wáng Ānqī
In the Jìn dynasty, the Grand Tutor, the Prince of Dōnghǎi, Sīmǎ Yuè,
was stationed in Xǔchāng.
He appointed Wáng Ānqī as his Record Office Army Advisor,
and held him in high esteem and deep regard.
He instructed his heir, Sīmǎ Pí, saying:
"What one gains from study is shallow;
what one embodies and finds comfort in is deep.
To idly practice ritual forms
is not as good as observing exemplary demeanor.
To recite and ponder the words of the past
is not as good as personally receiving instruction from a master.
Army Advisor Wáng is a model among men;
you should take him as your teacher."
From *Shì Shuō*.
Wáng Dūn
Yǔ Liàng saw Wáng Dūn and asked:
"I have heard you have four friends;
who are they?"
He replied:
"Your family's Zhōngláng [Yǔ Kūn],
my family's Tàiwèi [Wáng Yǎn], Ā Píng [Wáng Chéng],
and Húwú Yànguó.
My Ā Píng is certainly the least among them."
Yǔ said:
"It seems he is not the least."
He then asked who ranked highest among them.
Wáng said:
"There is naturally someone."
Yǔ said:
"Who is it?"
Wáng said:
"Ah,
my left and right are treading; Lord Yǔ knows when to stop."
The Ming manuscript copy lacks the characters "zhī zú" (知足);
"zhī yí" (知疑) should be read as "zhī" (之).
Then he stopped.
From *Shì Shuō*.
Sūn Bóyì
Sūn Bóyì of Tàiyuán in Qí was poor,
and once read by the light reflected from snow.
He gave free rein to his spirit beyond worldly affairs,
and lodged his aspirations among hills and valleys.
With Minister Wáng Liàng and General Fàn Yún,
he formed an intimate, inseparable friendship.
After Wáng and Fàn served in two successive courts,
they wished to secure official positions for him.
Bóyì said:
"A human life lasts a hundred years at most,
like a candle in the wind.
One should delight the spirit and nourish one's nature,
entrusting one's feelings to the zither and wine.
How can one toil and labor restlessly like this?
What Jī Kāng could not endure,
I am also unable to endure."
From *Tán Sǒu*.
Xiāngdōng Prince Yì
Liáng's Prince of Xiāngdōng, Xiāo Yì,
was widely read in all books,
and his talent and eloquence were unmatched in his time.
He did not care for music or women,
but cherished and esteemed famous worthies.
With Péi Zǐyě of Hédōng and Xiāo Zǐyún of Lánlíng,
he formed a friendship as commoners.
From *Tán Sǒu*.
Táng Huòwáng Yuánguǐ,
the fourteenth son of Gāozǔ,
was modest, cautious, and self-restrained,
not casually associating with scholars.
While in Xúzhōu,
he formed a humble, commoner's friendship with the retired scholar Liú Xuánpíng.
Someone once asked Xuánpíng
about the prince's strong points.
Xuánpíng said:
"None."
The questioner, finding this strange, pressed him for an explanation.
Xuánpíng said:
"A person has shortcomings,
and it is through these that one sees their strengths.
As for Huòwáng,
he lacks nothing,
so how can I possibly praise him?"
From the *Tán Bīn Lù*.
Wáng Fāngyì
Liángzhōu Chief Clerk Zhào Chímǎn,
was a relative of Zhǎngsūn Wújì.
After Xǔ Jìngzōng had framed Wújì,
fearing Chímǎn would become a problem for him,
he falsely accused Chímǎn of conspiring in the rebellion.
Chímǎn was brought to the capital and interrogated under torture.
He sighed and said:
"My body can be killed,
but my words cannot be dishonored."
The clerks composed a confession on his behalf and submitted it,
and he subsequently died in prison.
His corpse was left outside the western wall of the city,
and none of his relatives dared to go and see it.
Wáng Fāngyì sighed and said:
"Luán Bǔ weeping for Péng Yuè
was an act of great righteousness.
Zhōu Wén covering the decaying bones
was the ultimate benevolence.
To sever the obligations of friendship,
to obstruct the sovereign's benevolence,
how can one serve one's lord with such conduct?"
He then arranged a proper burial for him.
Gāozōng considered this righteous and did not question him.
From the *Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ*.
Wú Shàowēi,
a man from Dōnghǎi,
was gifted with literary talent from a young age,
and was a close friend of Fù Jiāmó.
Shàowēi passed the jìnshì examination
(The seven characters "yǒushàn shàowēi jìnshì jí" were originally missing;
supplemented based on *Táng Shī Jì Shì*, 6.)
and,
after successive appointments, served as Wèi of Jìnyáng (Tàiyuán),
and was appointed Censor.
At the time, Jiāmó died of illness,
and Shàowēi wrote a text mourning him.
Its words
(The ten characters "Jiāmó jí zú wéi wén kū zhī qí cí" were originally missing;
supplemented based on *Táng Shī Jì Shì*, 6.)
said:
"On the guǐchǒu day of the third month,
Fù Jiāmó of Hénán passed away.
At that time, he lay ill in the northern wards of Luòyáng.
Hearing
(The nine characters "shí qǐn jí yú Luòyáng běi lǐ wén" were originally missing;
supplemented based on *Táng Shī Jì Shì*, 6.)
the news, I threw aside my pillow
(The character "zhěn" was originally missing;
supplemented based on *Táng Shī Jì Shì*, 6.)
and rose,
tears soaking my lapel
("Lèi zhān hū rèn" originally read "jí xíng hū shān";
corrected based on *Táng Shī Jì Shì*, 6.)
and mat.
I crawled to the outer door of his chamber,
but my illness prevented me from rising.
Looking up to heaven, I cried out:
'Heaven, oh Heaven,
with whom shall I befriend?
Where are the standards?
Where can I see them again?'
I suppress this writing,
to preserve my grief."

The Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, Lord Xú; the Governor of Fūzhōu, Lord Yǐn; the two Secretaries of the Secretariat, Xú and Yuán; and the Director of the Ministry of War, Zhāng Shuō,
whenever they met me at court, could not help but sigh.
Moved by sorrow,
I compose a poem to honor the departed.
Its words say:
"Had my friend not died,
alas, he would have been a pillar of the state.
His straightforward salary brought no personal gain,
he constantly sought to shelter others greatly.
Yet he lacked a position at Chéngmíng,
and met this spring of Dūnzāng.
Medicine and illness, how fearsome they are,
the August Vault was thus unkind.
In times past, with you, sir,
who could say our bond was not heavenly?
Sharing the same ailment, one is lost,
vast and boundless, never to be told again.
Your writings remain,
their novelty nearly that of Master Ni.
Their vigor stirs rivers and mountains,
their true words sting ghosts and spirits.
Pitiable, yet imperishable,
the eastern hearse vanishes in wild thickets.
A sage ruler treasures the worthy as jewels,
alas, this great state is impoverished."
Men of letters all sighed in admiration.
Later, when Shàowēi's illness became critical,
he sighed deeply and said:
"Life and death are the great divide for man,
what have I to regret?
Yet, I have not accomplished even one-tenth of my official duties,
and so it has come to this?"
He passed away with passionate resolve.
From the *Yùshǐ Tái Jì*.
Zhāng Shuō
When Zhāng Shuō was exiled to Yuèzhōu,
he was often depressed and unhappy.
The chief ministers at the time, because of Shuō's quick wit, talent, and strategic ability,
mutually excluded and rejected him.
Sū Tǐng was then being greatly employed,
and Zhāng Shuō was on good terms with Guī.
Zhāng therefore composed the "Ode to the Five Gentlemen",
and sent a letter,
enclosing the poem to give to Tǐng.
He instructed his messenger:
"Wait for the anniversary of his father's death,
and deliver it near dusk."
When the messenger arrived,
on that death anniversary,
he brought the letter to Tǐng's gate.
It happened that overcast weather had persisted for several weeks,
and near dusk,
condolence visitors arrived,
many being former colleagues of Tǐng's late father.
Tǐng, upon reading the poem,
sobbed and shed tears,
overcome with grief.
The next day,
he submitted a sealed memorial.
He strongly advocated that Shuō was loyal, upright, and outspoken,
had labored diligently for the royal house,
and was also someone the people looked up to,
and should not be left languishing in a distant region.
The Emperor then issued an imperial edict to console and inquire after him,
and soon after transferred him to be Chief Clerk of Jīngzhōu.
Because of this, Lù Xiàngxiān, Wéi Sìlì, Zhāng Tíngguī, and Jiǎ Zēng,
all of whom had been demoted and exiled for years,
were consequently selected and recalled.
Tǐng, because Shuō
was a close friend of his father,
served him with great respect.
And Shuō, valuing Tǐng's talent and capacity,
deeply respected and admired him.
From the *Mínghuáng Zálù*.
Liǔ Fāng
Liǔ Fāng and Wéi Shù were close friends,
both being historians.
After Shù's death,
the books he had been writing but had not finished,
Fāng mostly completed.
From the *Guó Shǐ Bǔ*.
Dù Yòu
Liú Yǔxī said:
"Minister Dù Yòu regarded Mù Zàn
like the child of an old friend."
Yòu saw that Zàn, as a Censorate official, had repeatedly submitted impeachments,
and therefore admonished him about the matter, saying:
"I have one piece of advice,
for your long-term benefit, young sir:
it would be better to make fewer enemies in the future."
Mù deeply accepted this advice,
and as a result tempered his imposing manner
(From "Tái chéng" to "jì wēi" above,
the original text was illegible;
... one piece of advice,
for ... young sir long ... ... ... shield as jade tablet,
Mù ... accepted it,
friend ... imposing manner.
Now supplemented and corrected based on Sòng Qián Yì's *Nánbù Xīnshū*, 10.)
From the *Jiā Huà Lù*.
Lǐ Zhōu
Lǒngxī Lǐ Zhōu was a close friend of Qí Yìng.
Yìng became a general and chancellor,
while Zhōu remained a commoner.
Zhōu sent a letter to Yìng,
based on friendship, not on status.
At that time, Yìng had been demoted to Kuí.
The letter read:
"To the Thirty-Third Official,
in recent years,
when chief ministers govern the state,
they often sever ties with old friends according to ritual.
If I treated you with ritual propriety,
since you are a senior,
my heart could not bear it.
If I treated you as an old friend,
then I fear the common people
would consider me sycophantic.
I have often wished to write,
but hesitated until now.
Suddenly I learned that you have been appointed to guard Kuí State.
For the hopes of the common people,
this is
(Míng manuscript: 'this is' reads 'then it is')
not unfortunate;
but for your own plans,
to achieve fame and then retire,
this is indeed difficult.
I, who understand
(Míng manuscript: 'understand' reads 'am ignorant of')
the times,
respectfully offer my congratulations.
However, between Póyáng and Yún'ān,
the road is treacherous and long.
News is scarce and silent,
and gazing into the distance only deepens my sighs.
I am afflicted with a chronic illness,
and am now leading my children in farming diligently,
withdrawn from the world.
How can you not also become distant from me?
You have always been known to me,
and regarding gain and loss,
you are naturally serene.
Yet among court ministers, few are like you.
How could the enlightened ruler fail to recognize this?
Only, eat well and take care of yourself,
treasure yourself, treasure yourself."
From *Zhí Yán*.
Bái Jūyì
Junior Tutor Bái Jūyì
was a close friend of Chancellor Yuán Zhěn.
They were renowned for their poetic craft,
and were called Yuán-Bái.
In his collection is the poem "Mourning Chancellor Yuán":
"Facing each other, covering tears, both wordless;
Who knows the heart's other sorrows?
I imagine the trees on the plains of Xiányáng,
Have already sprouted white poplar branches three zhang long."
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Xǔ Táng
Xǔ Táng long struggled in the examination arena.
At the end of the Xiántōng era,
Mǎ Dài served as aide in the Dàtóng Army headquarters.
Táng went to visit him,
and they became like old friends at first sight.
He stayed for several months,
with only poetry and wine,
and Dài never asked what he desired.
Suddenly one day, during a large gathering of guests and friends,
Dài ordered a messenger to deliver a letter from Táng's family to him.
Táng was shocked,
unaware of its origin.
Upon opening the letter,
he realized Dài had secretly sent a servant
to provide relief to his family.
From *Zhí Yán*.
Lù Guīméng
Lù Guīméng, styled Lǔwàng, was from Wú Commandery.
His father, Bīnyú, passed the imperial examination with top honors,
served as an assistant in Zhèdōng,
and settled in Sūtái.
Guīméng was proficient in the Six Classics from childhood,
and devoted himself to literature as he grew.
He formed beneficial friendships with Yán Ráo, Pí Rìxiū, Luó Yǐn, and Wú Róng.
He was noble and pure in character,
but his family was poor,
and he longed for an official salary to support his parents.
He served as deputy to Zhāng Tuán in Lújiāng and Wúxīng commanderies.
Chancellors Lǐ Wèi and Lú Xí esteemed him highly.
Luó Yǐn's poem "Sent to Guīméng" reads:
"The dragon tower's Chancellor Lǐ,
(The five characters 'The dragon tower's Chancellor Lǐ' were originally missing,
supplemented from the Huáng manuscript.)
In past years admired your lofty writings.
Now the yellow pavilion has no master,
Yet the green hills, after all, were not burned."
This suggests there had been an intention to summon him to office.
At the end of the Táng,
he was offered the post of Left Reminder.
On the day the edict arrived,
he passed away from illness at home.
He was a poetic friend of Pí Rìxiū.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Yán Ráo
When Attendant Yán Ráo was demoted,
he died beyond the lakes.
Before the news spread,
he wrote his own epitaph.
He was impatient by nature,
and intolerant of others.
The epitaph text read:
"Residing in Eastern Wú,
I formed a friendship in poetry and prose with Lù Guīméng of Wú Commandery,
unwavering for twelve years.
When Guīméng died,
I attended to his coffin until burial,
fulfilling both affection and propriety.
Afterwards, the late Reminder Gāo Chéngzhī and the late Chancellor Lù Yǐ
remained unchanged towards me until death.
All other face-to-face friendships
were like joining hands to cross the market:
seeing profit, they would release hands and leave.
None truly knew me.
Later, there were three gentlemen:
Minister of Personnel Xuē Yíjù, Vice Minister of War Yú Jīng, and Secretariat Drafter Zhèng Zhuàn
(Míng manuscript: 'Zhuàn' reads 'Zhuàn')
—these three,
up to this day, have not changed towards me.
I do not know how they will treat my orphaned children
after my bones are gone.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
King Fūchāi of Wú
King Fūchāi of Wú built the Gūsū Terrace,
which took three years to complete.
It wound around intricately,
spanning five lǐ in width.
The construction was lavishly decorated,
exhausting human resources.
There were a thousand palace courtesans,
and he also established a separate Chūnxiāo Palace
for all-night drinking,
and crafted a thousand-dàn wine bell.
He also built a large pool,
in which a blue dragon boat was placed,
with courtesans and music arranged,
and daily he engaged in water games with Xī Shī.
Furthermore, within the palace, he built the Língguǎn Hall and Wá Pavilion,
with bronze fittings and jade balustrades.
The palace railings
were all adorned with pearls and jade.
From *Shù Yì Jì*.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn
During the time of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
the country of Shéndú presented linked bridles,
all made of white jade,
with agate stones for the bits,
and white luminous glass for the saddles.
In a dark room,
they would often illuminate over ten zhàng,
bright as daylight.
From then on, Cháng'ān began to richly adorn horses and saddles,
competing in carved embellishments.
Sometimes the ornaments for a single horse were worth a hundred gold pieces,
all using white clams from the southern sea as ornaments,
and purple gold for flowers,
to decorate them.
Yet they still worried about the lack of sound.
Sometimes bells were added,
adorned with tassels,
so that when moving, they sounded like bells and chimes,
and fluttered like flying banners.
Later, they obtained the Heavenly Horses of Èrshī,
often using rose quartz for saddles,
inlaid with gold, silver, and brass,
and with green-ground five-colored brocade as mudguards.
Later, they gradually used bear and brown bear skins for these,
the bear fur having a green glow,
all three chǐ long,
worth a hundred gold pieces each.
Zhuō Wángsūn had over a hundred pairs,
and an imperial edict ordered him to present twenty pieces.
From *Xī Jīng Zá Jì*.
Dīng Yuàn
In Cháng'ān, there was a skilled artisan named Dīng Huǎn,
who made a "constant-full lamp,"
adorned with seven dragons and five phoenixes,
intermingled with lotus flowers and lotus roots.
He also created a reclining-mat incense burner,
also known as a "within-the-quilt incense burner."
It originally came from Fángfēng,
but its method was later lost,
until Huǎn revived it.
He installed mechanical rings,
allowing it to rotate in all directions,
while the burner itself remained level,
so it could be placed in bedding,
hence the name "within-the-quilt."
He also made a nine-layer Bóshān incense burner,
carved with strange birds and beasts,
exhausting all manner of wondrous creatures,
all capable of moving naturally.
He also created a seven-wheel fan,
each wheel about a foot in diameter,
connected in succession,
operated by one person,
filling the entire hall with a chilling breeze.
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Línchí Pond
In the first year of the Yuánshǐ era of Emperor Zhāo of Hàn,
the Línchí Pond was excavated,
spanning a thousand paces wide.
Within it were planted branching lotuses,
each stem bearing four leaves.
They resembled paired canopies,
and when the sun shone, the leaves lowered to shade the roots,
like sunflowers protecting their stems,
hence named "low-light lotuses."
Their seeds were like black pearls,
suitable for adorning pendants.
When the flowers and leaves withered together,
their fragrant scent permeated over ten miles.
Eating them kept one's breath constantly fragrant,
and improved one's complexion.
The palace ladies prized them,
and whenever they went out for excursions or banquets,
they would chew them,
or cut them to make clothing,
or pluck them to shade from the sun,
playing with each other.
The "Chǔcí" speaks of plucking lotus leaves to make clothing,
referring to this.
There were also upside-growing water chestnuts.
Their stems were like tangled silk,
each flower with ten leaves,
roots floating on the water,
seeds sinking into the mud,
the mud being purple in color,
hence called "purple-mud water chestnuts."
Eating them prevented aging.
At times, water games were ordered,
with excursions and banquets lasting all day.
A craftsman presented a huge trough,
and the Emperor said:
"Pine boats with oars,
I find them heavy and crude,
let alone this trough—
how could one possibly ride in it?"
So he ordered a boat made of patterned catalpa wood,
with magnolia wood for oars.
Carved with flying phoenixes and soaring egrets,
adorning the bow.
Drifting lightly with the wind,
they forgot to return even as the sun set,
continuing until deep into the night.
He had the palace ladies sing,
the song going:
"In autumn's clear scene, vast waves surge,
who says skilled hands pluck lotus leaves?
Chilly winds rise as oar songs are sung,
dawn breaks through clouds, the moon sinks low by the river,
ten thousand years of joy—how could it be too much?"
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and built the Yóushāng Tower by the pond.
But in his later years,
admonishers grew numerous.
So he reduced his extravagant wanderings,
filled in the towers and ponds,
and the phoenix boats and lotus leaves
were abandoned and destroyed over time.
Now no trace of the tower remains,
and the pond has been leveled.
From "Records of Omissions"
Huò Guāng's Wife
Huò Guāng's wife of the Hàn dynasty gave Chúnyú Yǎn twenty bolts of grape-pattern brocade
and twenty-five bolts of scattered-flower damask.
The damask came from Chén Bǎoguāng of Jùlù,
whose wife passed down the technique.
Huò Xiǎn summoned her into the residence,
and had her produce it.
The loom used one hundred twenty treadles,
taking sixty days to complete one bolt,
worth ten thousand coins.
She also gave her a peck of Yuè pearls strung together,
seven hundred bolts of green damask,
worth a million coins,
and a hundred taels of gold.
She also built a mansion for her,
with countless servants.
Yet Yǎn still complained it was meager, saying:
"After all I accomplished for you,
is this how you repay me?"
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Hán Yān
Hán Yān enjoyed shooting pellets,
often using gold pellets,
losing over ten in a single day.
The people of Cháng'ān had a saying about him:
"Suffering hunger and cold,
chase the gold pellets."
Whenever the children of the capital heard Yān was out shooting,
they would follow him.
Watching where the pellets fell,
they competed to pick them up.
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Yuán Guǎnghàn
Yuán Guǎnghàn, a wealthy man of Màolíng, amassed immense wealth,
with eight to nine hundred household servants.
He built a garden at the foot of Běimáng Mountain,
four li from east to west,
and three li from north to south.
He channeled water to flow within it,
constructed stone mountains,
over ten zhang high,
stretching for several li.
He kept white parrots and purple mandarin ducks,
yaks and green hares
("Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital" says three hares, or rhinoceroses).
Strange birds and beasts
accumulated within.
He piled sand to form islets,
and churned water to create waves.
There he raised river gulls and sea cranes,
which bred and hatched chicks,
spreading through the forests and ponds.
Rare trees and exotic plants
were all cultivated there.
Pavilions and interconnected buildings,
linked by long corridors.
Walking through them took hours,
unable to cover it all.
Later, Yuán Guǎnghàn was convicted and executed,
and his property was confiscated by the state.
The birds, beasts, plants, and trees from his garden
were all transplanted to the imperial Shangyuàn Garden.
From "Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital"
Xiāoyóu Palace
Emperor Chéng of Hàn enjoyed traveling incognito.
By the Tàiyè Pond, he built the Xiāoyóu Palace,
using lacquer for its pillars,
and spreading black silk curtains.
Utensils, garments, and carriages
all favored the color black.
He delighted in moving in darkness,
and detested the illumination of lamps and candles.
The beautiful consorts in the palace
all wore black garments.
From Bān Jī down,
they all wore dark-colored ribbons.
Their clothing and pendants
(Míngchāo edition: "clothing and pendants" reads as "veils and coverings")
were adorned with brocade and embroidery,
and further covered with magnolia gauze and silk.
Only upon reaching the Xiāoyóu Palace
would they light torches and candles.
When feasts and visits concluded,
drums fell silent and covers were removed,
yet footsteps raised no dust.
He enjoyed going out for evening excursions,
and had a "Flying Palace" built, one zhàng square,
like today's imperial carriage.
He selected warriors from the Qīmén and Yǔlín guards,
who carried it as they ran.
The Emperor, seated in the carriage,
felt as if he heard the sounds of wind and thunder in his ears.
Due to its speed,
it was also called the Yúnléi Palace.
Wherever it passed,
felt and silk were laid on the ground,
as he disliked the noise of wheel ruts and hoofprints.
Although he was infatuated with incognito travels and intimate feasts,
the people bore no hardship or resentment.
Whenever the imperial carriage returned to the palace,
he would have his beloved consorts
distribute precious garments and fine food
along the roadside.
The impoverished elderly of the nation
all cried out, "Long live the Emperor!"
Thus, during the Hóngjiā and Yǒngshǐ eras,
the state was wealthy and families prosperous,
and weapons were long stored away.
Therefore, Liú Xiàng and Gǔ Yǒng privately offered pointed admonitions,
whereupon he burned the Xiāoyóu and "Flying" palaces,
and ceased the pleasures of feasting and idleness.
As the saying goes, "Following the plumb line makes it straight,"
like turning a ball.
From *Shíyílù*.
Shātáng Boat
Emperor Chéng of Hàn often, on leisurely autumn days,
would frolic with Fēiyàn on the Tàiyè Pond.
They used shātáng wood for boats,
valuing its unsinkable nature.
They adorned the prow with mica,
calling it the "Cloud Boat."
They also carved large paulownia wood into coiling dragons,
carved and decorated to resemble real forms,
to flank the Cloud Boat as it moved.
They used purple-grained cassia for oars and rudders.
Whenever they gazed at the clouds and rowed on water,
or played and plucked water chestnuts in the channels,
he worried that the gentle rocking might startle Fēiyàn.
He ordered Yìfēi warriors
to secure the Cloud Boat with golden chains,
having the Yìfēi pull it from beneath the water.
When a light breeze arose at times,
Fēiyàn nearly drifted with the wind,
and followed the wind into the water.
The Emperor tied Fēiyàn's skirt with a green silk ribbon,
and they returned only after tiring of play.
Fēiyàn later gradually fell out of favor,
and often lamented resentfully:
"With my humble status,
when will I ever again join in ribbon-skirt excursions,
or float the Cloud Boat upon the waves?"
The Emperor was disheartened by this.
Today, in the Tàiyè Pond, there still remain Emperor Chéng's Wind-Sheltering Terrace and the place where Fēiyàn tied her skirt.
From *Shíyílù*.
Zhào Fēiyàn
Zhào Fēiyàn became Empress.
Her younger sister, the Zhāoyí, in the Zhāoyáng Hall, sent Fēiyàn a letter saying:
"On this fine morning,
my esteemed elder sister is honored to receive the grand decree.
I present as tribute
(Míngchāo edition: "tribute" reads as "flint")
thirty-five items,
to express my utmost joy:

a gold-flower purple silk hat, a gold-flower purple gauze face veil, a woven lower skirt, a同心七宝钗 (tóngxīn qībǎo chāi),七宝綦履 (qībǎo qí lǚ), jade rings, five-colored patterned ribbons, a mandarin duck mattress, a mica screen, a colored glaze screen, a mica七宝扇 (qībǎo shàn), an amber pillow, a turtle-patterned pillow, a gold-inlaid embroidered dāng,琉璃玛瑙彄 (liúlí mǎnǎo kōu), coral jué, a gold bùyáo hairpin, a gold Bóshān incense burner, a seven-branch lamp, a Huífēng mat,
a茅叶席 (máoyè xí), gold蒲圆璫 (pú yuán dāng), a peacock fan, a五明扇 (wǔmíng shàn), a九华扇 (jiǔhuá shàn),同心梅 (tóngxīn méi),合枝李 (hézhī lǐ),三清木香 (sānqīng mùxiāng),螺卮 (luózhī)
from the螺田 (luótián) in the southern regions,
musk,沉水香 (chénshuǐxiāng),九真黄 (jiǔzhēn huáng), mandarin duck jackets and quilts."
From *Xījīng Zájì*.
Guō Kuàng
Guō Kuàng of the Hàn dynasty
was the brother of Emperor Guāngwǔ's Empress.
He amassed gold worth billions,
with four hundred household servants.
He used gold for utensils and vessels,
and the sounds of casting and smelting
reached both the capital and the outskirts.
People of the time said of the Guō household:
"It thunders without rain,"
meaning the sounds of smelting were overwhelming.
In his courtyard, he built a tall pavilion,
placing weighing stones upon it
for measurement.
Below was a vault for storing gold,
guarded by rows of warriors.
He adorned his terraces and pavilions with assorted treasures,
and hung bright pearls between the beams and pillars.
Their radiance dazzled the eyes.
("Their radiance dazzled the eyes" – these five characters were originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition.)
By day, they looked like stars;
by night, they shone like the moon.
A local saying went:
"In Luòyáng, the Guō house has abundant wealth,
with night moons and day stars
("house with night moons and day stars" – these five characters were originally missing,
supplemented according to *Shíyíjì*, chapter six.)
Its riches are hard to match."
His favored inner attendants
all used jade vessels for their meals.
Thus, in the Eastern Capital, the Guō household was called the "Jade Kitchen and Golden Vault."
Kuàng was cautious and prudent;
though he possessed wealth and influence,
he remained behind closed doors, living in leisurely ease,
and never meddled in worldly affairs,
earning the recognition of his time.
From *Shíyílù*.
Emperor Líng of the Later Hàn
In the third year of the Chūpíng era of Emperor Líng,
ten Naked Pleasure Pavilions were built in the Western Garden.
Green moss was gathered to cover the steps,
and canal water was channeled to wind around the terraces.
The water flowed clear and pure all around;
one could ride in small boats to drift and wander.
Palace women would ride them,
selected for their jade-like complexion and slender bodies to hold the poles and oars,
rocking and drifting along the canals.
The water was clear and shallow,
and during the height of summer,
they would deliberately capsize the boats
to gaze upon the jade-like beauty of the palace women.
They would perform the "Zhāoshāng" song in seven-character verses
to invite cool air.
The song went:
"Cool winds arise, oh, sunlight shines on the canal;
green lotus leaves lie by day, spread by night.
Only the day is not enough, joy is abundant;
clear strings and flowing pipes sing of jade ducks,
for a thousand years, ten thousand ages, happiness is hard to change."
In the canals, lotus plants were grown with leaves as large as canopies,
their stems ten feet long,
presented as tribute from the southern lands.
Their leaves spread at night and curled by day;
a single stem bore four lotus flowers clustered together,
named "Night-Spreading Lotus."
It was also said that when the moon rose, the leaves would spread,
so it was also called "Moon-Gazing Lotus."
The emperor would escape the summer heat in the Naked Pleasure Pavilions,
feasting and drinking through the long nights.
The emperor sighed and said:
"If it could be like this for ten thousand years,
then I would be an immortal."
Palace women aged fourteen and above,
and eighteen and below,
all adorned themselves beautifully and removed their upper garments,
sometimes bathing naked together.
Yīnchí incense, presented as tribute from the Western Regions,
was boiled to make bathing water,
which the palace women used for bathing.
After bathing,
the leftover liquid flowed into the canals,
named "Flowing Fragrance Canal."
He also wanted the eunuchs to imitate rooster crows,
so a Rooster-Crowing Hall was built north of the pavilions,
where many roosters were kept.
Whenever drunk with pleasure,
oblivious to the break of dawn,
the eunuchs would compete to crow like roosters,
to confuse the real sounds.
Torches were then thrown beneath the hall,
and the emperor would awaken with a start.
When Dǒng Zhuó sacked the capital,
he seized the beauties,
and burned the halls and pavilions.
During the Xiánxī era of the Wèi dynasty,
at the spot where the former emperor had thrown the torches,
a faint light like stars shimmered,
and later generations regarded it as divine light.
A building was erected on this site,
named the Lingering Light Shrine,
to pray for blessings.
By the end of the reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
it was cleared away.
From "Wáng Zǐnián's Records of Omitted Tales"
Shí Chóng
Jìn dynasty's Shí Chóng and Wáng Kǎi vied in extravagance.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn
was Wáng Kǎi's nephew,
and once gave Kǎi a coral tree,
about two feet tall,
with luxuriant, spreading branches,
rarely matched in the world.
Kǎi showed it to Chóng.
After looking at it,
Chóng raised an iron ruyi scepter and smashed it,
shattering it into pieces with a single strike.
Kǎi was deeply regretful,
and thinking Chóng envied his treasure,
his voice and expression grew fierce.
Chóng said:
"No need for regret,
I'll repay you now."
He then ordered his attendants
to bring out all his coral trees.
Some were three feet tall,
with branches and trunks of extraordinary beauty,
six or seven of them dazzlingly brilliant.
Those comparable to Kǎi's were numerous.
Kǎi was disheartened and felt a sense of loss.
From "Shì Shuō"
Wáng Dūn
When Wáng Dūn first married the princess,
he went to the toilet
and saw a lacquered box filled with dried dates.
Originally meant to block the nose from odors,
Wáng thought they were fruits for the toilet,
and ate them all.
After returning,
a maid held a golden basin filled with water,
and a glass bowl containing bath beans.
He poured them into the water and drank it,
causing all the maids to cover their mouths in laughter.
From "Shì Shuō Xīn Shū"
Wèi's Gāoyáng Prince Yōng
In the Later Wèi, Gāoyáng Prince Yōng resided a few lǐ outside the Qīngyáng Gate,
west of the imperial road,
the finest mansion in Luòyáng.
During the Zhèngguāng era,
Yōng served as chancellor.
He was granted feather canopies and ceremonial music,
and a guard of a hundred tiger warriors with decorated swords.
Noble to the highest rank among officials,
wealthy as the mountains and seas combined.
His residence rivaled the imperial palace,
with white walls and red railings,
elegantly stretching continuously,
soaring eaves and splendid halls,
interconnected and winding throughout.
He had six thousand servants,
and five hundred singing girls.
Pearls like Suí's shone in the sunlight,
silks and gauzes fluttered in the wind.
Since the Hàn and Jìn dynasties,
among all princes and their extravagance,
none had matched this.
When he went out, mounted escorts cleared the imperial road,
ceremonial objects formed rows,
cymbals and drums resounded,
the character "發" was originally missing,
supplemented based on "Luòyáng Qiélán Jì."
reed pipes wailed mournfully;
when indoors, singing girls and dancers played the zhù and blew shēngs,
while string and wind instruments played in turns,
continuing day and night.
Bamboo groves and fish ponds
matched the imperial gardens.
Fragrant grasses lay like carpets,
rare trees formed continuous shade.
After Yōng passed away,
all the singing girls were ordered to become nuns,
and some took monastic vows.
The beauty Xú Yuèhuá excelled at playing the kōnghóu,
and could perform the song of Míngfēi leaving the frontier.
Listeners were invariably moved.
During the Yǒng'ān era,
she became the concubine of General
the character "衛" was originally written as "衙,"
corrected based on "Qiélán Jì"
Yuán Shìkāng.
Shìkāng's residence was also near the Qīngyáng Gate,
where Xú played the kōnghóu and sang,
her mournful voice reaching the clouds.
Passersby who listened
soon formed a crowd like a market.
Xú often told Shìkāng:
"The prince had two beautiful consorts,
one named Xiūróng,
the other named Yànzī.
Both had moth-like eyebrows and gleaming teeth,
with pure beauty that could topple cities.
Xiūróng could perform the 'Green Water Song.'
Yànzī excelled at the 'Chasing the Phoenix Dance.'
Both were beloved in the inner chambers,
favored above all other consorts."
Hearing this,
Shìkāng often had Xú sing the tunes of "Green Water" and "Literary Phoenix."
From "Qiélán Jì"
Yuán Chēn
In the Later Wei dynasty, the princes, marquises, and imperial relatives,
monopolized
("Monopolized" originally read "blocked,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy)
the wealth of the mountains and seas,
occupying the abundance of rivers and forests.
They vied to build gardens and residences,
competing in extravagance.
With grand gates and lavish rooms,
adjoining doors and connected chambers,
flying pavilions that caught the wind,
and towering buildings that rose into the mist.
High terraces and fragrant trees
were built in every household.
Flowering groves and winding ponds
were found in every garden.
Without exception, peach and plum trees were lush green in summer,
while bamboo and cypress remained evergreen in winter.
Among them, Prince Chén of Héjiān was the most extravagant,
often competing with Prince Yōng of Gāoyáng.
He constructed the Wénbǎi Hall to resemble the Huīyīn Palace.
He installed jade wells and golden jars,
using five-colored silk as ropes.
He kept three hundred courtesans, all of exceptional beauty,
and had a maid named Zhāoyún who excelled at playing the chí flute,
capable of performing the "Tuánshàn Song" and the melodies of Lǒngshàng.
When Chén served as the governor of Qín Prefecture,
the various Qiāng tribes rebelled,
and repeated campaigns failed to subdue them.
Chén ordered Zhāoyún to disguise herself as a poor old woman
and beg while playing the chí flute.
When the Qiāng people heard it,
they were all moved to tears,
and said to one another:
"Why have we abandoned our ancestral graves and wells
to become bandits in the mountains and valleys?"
They then surrendered one after another.
The people of Qín said:
"Swift horses and strong warriors
are no match for an old woman playing the chí flute."
During Chén's tenure in Qínzhōng,
he achieved little in governance.
He sent envoys to the Western Regions to seek famous horses,
traveling as far as Persia.
He obtained a thousand-li horse,
named "Wind-Chasing Red."
Next, he acquired more than ten seven-hundred-li horses,
each with its own name.
He used silver for their troughs
and gold for their halters and chains.
The other princes admired his wealth and extravagance.
Chén once said to others:
"Shí Chóng of the Jìn dynasty,
merely a commoner,
could still wear pheasant-head fur and fox-axilla garments,
and decorate eggs and carve firewood.
How much more should I, a heavenly prince of the great Wei,
not indulge in splendor and extravagance?"
He built the Yíngfēng Pavilion in his rear garden.
On its windows,
were arranged coin patterns and green latticework,
with jade phoenixes holding bells in their beaks
and golden dragons spitting out streamers.
White crabapples and red plums
extended their branches into the eaves.
Courtesans sat in the pavilion and plucked the fruit to eat.
Chén once hosted a gathering of the imperial clan,
displaying various precious vessels.
There were over a hundred golden bottles and silver urns,
with an equal number of cups, trays, and boxes.
Among the other drinking vessels,
were dozens of crystal bowls, agate and glass bowls, and red jade zhī cups.
Their craftsmanship was exquisite and marvelous,
unseen in the Central Plains,
all brought from the West.
He also displayed female musicians and various famous horses.
He further led the princes on a tour of his treasury,
filled with brocades, woolen carpets, pearls, and jade,
icy silks and mist-like gauzes,
piled high within.
Chén said to Prince Róng of Zhāngwǔ:
"I do not regret that I never saw Shí Chóng;
I regret that Shí Chóng never saw me."
Róng was by nature greedy and violent,
with insatiable desires.
Upon seeing this, he sighed in admiration,
and unconsciously fell ill.
Returning home,
he lay in bed for three days, unable to rise.
Prince Jì of Jiāngyáng came to visit him in his illness,
and advised him:
"Your wealth and property
should be comparable to his.
Why sigh in admiration
to such an extent?"
Róng replied:
"I always thought that only Prince Yōng of Gāoyáng
had more treasures than I.
Who would have known that Prince Chén of Héjiān
surpasses even him?"
Jì said:
"You wished to be like Yuán Shù in Huáinán,
unaware that there was still a Liú Bèi in the world."
After the rebellion of the Ěrzhū clan,
the mansions of princes and marquises
were mostly converted into temples and monasteries.
In the neighborhoods of Shòuqiū Lane,
temples stood in rows, facing one another.
Monasteries rose in abundance,
with pagodas towering high and grand.
On the eighth day of the fourth month,
the gentry and women of the capital
often visited the Héjiān Temple.
Viewing the beauty of its halls and corridors,
they all sighed in admiration,
thinking that even the immortal chambers of Pénglái
could not surpass it.
From "A Record of Buddhist Monasteries"
Emperor Yáng of Suí
Emperor Yáng of Sui toured the northern frontier,
and had a Great Traveling Palace with a Seven-Treasure Canopy constructed.
It could accommodate several hundred people,
was adorned with rare jewels,
and its brilliance was utterly dazzling.
He invited Qǐmín Kèhán of the Xiongnu
to feast within it.
The Kèhán was dazed,
doubting such a thing could exist in the mortal world.
A knowledgeable person remarked:
"This Great Traveling Palace
is an inauspicious omen.
This is not comparable to Wáng Mǎng's light carriage.
This truly stems from the will of Heaven,
and is not a matter of human affairs."
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Also, in the early Zhēnguàn era of the Táng,
the realm was peaceful and secure,
the common people were prosperous and well-supplied,
and there were few matters of public or private concern.
It was the time of New Year's Eve.
Emperor Tàizōng lavishly decorated the palace precincts,
brightly lit lamps and candles,
and every chamber within the halls was exquisitely beautiful.
The empress, consorts, and ladies-in-waiting all wore splendid garments,
their gold and kingfisher feathers dazzlingly resplendent.
Torches were set up in the courtyard below the steps,
making it as bright as day.
Grand music and songs were performed.
He then invited Empress Xiāo of Sui
to view it with him.
When the music ended,
the Emperor said to Empress Xiāo:
"How do my arrangements compare with those of the Sui sovereign?"
Empress Xiāo smiled but did not answer.
He pressed her,
and she said:
"He was a ruler who lost his state,
while Your Majesty is a founder of a dynasty.
Matters of extravagance and frugality
are naturally different."
The Emperor said:
"What was the Sui sovereign like?"
She replied:
"The Sui sovereign reigned for over ten years,
and I was often in attendance.
I witnessed his wanton extravagance.
Every New Year's Eve,
extending to the night of the year's end,
in the various courtyards before the halls,
he would set up several dozen 'volcanoes'
made entirely of aloeswood roots.
For each mountain, several cartloads of aloeswood were burned.
When the flames dimmed,
he would douse them with jiǎjiān oil,
causing flames to leap up several zhàng high.
The fragrance of aloeswood and jiǎjiān oil
could be smelled for dozens of lǐ around.
In a single night,
he would use over two hundred cartloads of aloeswood
and two hundred dàn of jiǎjiān oil.
Furthermore, within the halls and chambers,
no oil lamps were lit;
instead, one hundred and twenty large pearls were suspended to provide illumination,
their light comparable to the bright day.
There were also 'Bright Moon' treasures and 'Night Shining' pearls,
the largest being six or seven cùn,
the smallest still three cùn.
The price of a single pearl
was worth tens of millions.
Observing Your Majesty's arrangements,
I see none of these things.
What is burned before the halls
is all firewood.
What illuminates within the halls
is all oil.
One merely feels the smoke irritating the eyes,
and truly does not see such splendor.
However, the affairs of a lost state
are something I also wish Your Majesty to keep far from."
Tàizōng remained silent for a long while.
His words criticized her extravagance,
but in his heart, he admired its magnificence.
From *Jì Wén*.
Empress Zétiān
had the Mingtáng constructed.
On its roof, she cast an iron yuèzhuó bird,
two zhàng tall,
adorned with gold,
poised as if about to take flight.
Several years later,
a great wind blew it down,
but its base remained.
She further cast a large 'Fire Pearl' from bronze,
adorned with gold,
brilliantly dazzling the sun,
which is still seen today.
She also had the Tiānshū (Celestial Pivot) monument erected at the Dìngdǐng Gate,
funded by contributions totaling millions and billions from foreign envoys and Hu merchants.
It was ninety chǐ tall.
Its base used iron mountains as feet.
Two qílín were cast from bronze
to guard the four directions.
On top was a bronze plate,
three zhàng in diameter.
A jiāolóng stood in human form,
its two feet holding up a large fire pearl,
appearing from a distance like the rising sun.
An inscription was carved on the pillar, reading:
"The Great Zhōu's Tiānshū, Proclaiming Virtue to All Nations."
Later, during the Kāiyuán era, it was toppled,
and the bronze was taken into the imperial stores.
From *Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ*.
Xǔ Jìngzōng
of the Táng was extravagant and ostentatious.
He once built seventy 'flying towers' (multi-story structures),
and had courtesans ride horses atop them
for amusement.
From *Dú Yì Jì*.
Zhāng Yìzhī
had a Seven-Treasure Canopy made for his mother, Ā Zāng.
Gold, silver, pearls, jade, precious shells, and the like—
nothing was omitted, all gathered together.
Since ancient times,
such a thing had never been heard of or seen.
An ivory bed was laid,
a mat woven from rhinoceros horn,
a mattress of sable and marten fur,
a felt rug of qióng-wén pattern,
and mats made of Lóngxū grass from Fénjìn and Fènghé feathers from Línhé.
Ā Zāng had an illicit affair with Vice-Minister Lǐ Jiǒngxiù of the Fènggé Department,
which she forced upon him.
They drank together from a pair of 'Mandarin Duck' cups,
symbolizing constant companionship.
Jiǒngxiù feared her powerful influence
and disliked her old age.
So he indulged in unrestrained drinking,
devoted to drunken stupor,
often not rousing despite frequent calls.
He was sent out to serve as Prefect of Héngzhōu.
When Zhāng Yìzhī fell from power,
Ā Zāng was confiscated into government service.
Jiǒngxiù was implicated,
and demoted to Senior Clerk of Wèizhōu.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Zōng Chǔkè
built a new mansion.
All its beams were made of patterned cypress.
The walls were plastered with aloeswood mixed with red powder,
so that upon opening the door, a rich fragrance burst forth.
The steps and floors were paved with polished patterned stone,
so slippery that those wearing jímò boots
would slip and fall.
Chǔkè was investigated by Prince Jiànchāng for accepting bribes exceeding ten thousand strings of cash,
and he and his brother were exiled.
Princess Tàipíng went to see his mansion
and sighed, saying:
"Looking at his living quarters,
we have lived in vain and will die for nothing!"
A year later,
he was recalled to serve as Vice-Minister of the Fènggé Department.
During the Jǐnglóng era,
he became Zhōngshū Lìng.
He was executed following the downfall of the Wěi clan.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Princess Ānlè
At the Zhāochéng Buddhist Temple in Luòzhōu,
there was a hundred-treasure incense burner made by Princess Ānlè.
It stood three feet high,
with four doors opening.
With crimson bridges and railings,
flowers, plants, flying birds, and running beasts,
heavenly musicians and entertainers,
qílín, luán phoenixes,
white cranes, and flying immortals.
Threads came and went,
ghosts emerged and spirits entered.
Carved in relief and openwork,
graceful and delicate.
Pearls and agate,
liúlí and amber,
crystal and coral,
chēqú and wǎnyǎn,
all kinds of treasures,
costing thirty thousand strings of cash,
the treasury’s stores
were exhausted for this.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Also, Princess Ānlè was later demoted to a rebellious commoner.
She seized commoners’ manors and fields,
and built the Dìngkūn Pond, forty-nine lǐ in circumference,
stretching directly to the Southern Mountains,
modeled after the Kūnmíng Pond.
Rocks were piled to form mountains,
to resemble Huà Mountain.
Water was channeled to form streams,
to resemble the Tiānjīn River.
Soaring pavilions and covered walkways,
slanting walls and stone steps,
draped with brocade and embroidery,
painted with vermilion and azure,
adorned with gold and silver,
gleaming with pearls and jade.
Also, a nine-bend floating cup stream was made,
with a stone lotus flower platform,
from which a spring flowed.
It exhausted the grandeur under heaven,
impossible to describe fully.
After her rebellion failed,
it was allocated to the Ministry of Agriculture.
Every day, men and women came to visit and view it,
carriages and horses clogging the roads.
By imperial decree,
those who went without permission—
officials were dismissed from their posts,
commoners were given one flogging—
only then did it stop.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Also, Princess Ānlè made a skirt of hundred-bird feathers,
after which officials and commoners’ households imitated it.
Strange birds and beasts from mountains and forests
were hunted across valleys and hills,
swept clean without remainder.
As for nets and snares,
countless were killed or captured.
During the Kāiyuán era,
treasure vessels were burned before the palace hall,
and people were forbidden to wear pearls, jade, gold, silver, gauze, or silk.
Only then did the hunting and capturing cease.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Yáng Shènjiāo
During the Jǐnglóng era,
imperial consorts and princesses’ households vied in extravagance.
Imperial sons-in-law Yáng Shènjiāo and Wǔ Chóngxùn even used oil to sprinkle the ground,
to build a polo field.
From Guóshǐ Yìzuǎn.
Táng Emperor Ruìzōng
On the nights of the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth of the first month in the second year of the Xiāntiān era of Táng Emperor Ruìzōng,
outside the Ānfú Gate in the capital,
a lantern wheel twenty zhàng high was erected.
Draped with brocade and silk,
adorned with gold and silver.
Fifty thousand lanterns were lit,
all
the character “all” originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition.
standing like flowering trees.
Thousands of palace maidens,
clad in silk and gauze,
trailing brocade and embroidery,
glittering with pearls and jade,
applied fragrant powder.
One floral crown,
one scarf or cape,
each cost up to ten thousand strings of cash.
To attire one courtesan,
cost up to three hundred guàn.
Over a thousand young women from Cháng’ān and Wànnián counties were exquisitely selected,
their clothing, hairpins, and ornaments equally splendid.
For three days and nights, they sang and danced under the lanterns.
The height of viewing pleasure,
unprecedented.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Emperor Xuánzōng
Emperor Xuánzōng visited the Huáqīng Palace.
New hot spring pools were expanded,
constructed with grand magnificence.
Ān Lùshān from Fànyáng
carved fish, dragons, wild ducks, and geese from white jade stone,
and also offered stone bridges and stone lotus flowers.
The carving was exquisitely skillful,
almost beyond human effort.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
ordering them placed in the hot springs.
Also, stone bridges spanned the springs,
with lotus flowers just emerging from the water’s edge.
When the Emperor visited the Huáqīng Palace,
upon reaching the spot,
he undressed to enter.
But the fish, dragons, ducks, and geese
all seemed to flare scales and raise wings,
as if about to fly and move.
The Emperor was greatly frightened,
and hastily ordered them removed.
The lotus flowers remain to this day.
Also, he once built several dozen long hot spring chambers in the palace,
encircled and paved with patterned stone.
Silver-inlaid lacquer boats and white sandalwood boats
were placed within.
Even the oars and rudders
were adorned with pearls and jade.
Also, in the hot springs,
sapphires and aloeswood were piled to form mountains,
resembling Yíngzhōu and Fāngzhàng.
When the Emperor was about to visit the Huáqīng Palace,
Guìfēi and her sisters vied in adorning their carriages and attire.
For one calf-drawn carriage,
adorned with gold and kingfisher feathers,
interspersed with pearls and jade,
the cost of one carriage
was no less than several hundred thousand guàn.
Eventually, they became too heavy,
and the oxen could not pull them.
Therefore, it was reported to the Emperor,
requesting to each ride horses instead.
Thus, they vied to purchase famous horses,
with bits and stirrups made of gold,
the character “stirrups” originally missing,
supplemented according to the Míng transcript edition.
and embroidered saddle cloths as mudguards.
They gathered at Yáng Guózhōng’s residence,
to enter the palace together.
Brilliantly shining and illuminated,
onlookers crowded like walls.
From Yáng Guózhōng’s residence to the southeastern corner of the city,
servants, drivers, carriages, and horses
milled about in confusion.
Yáng Guózhōng sat with guests at his gate,
pointing and saying to them:
“My family rose from humble origins,
through connection as relatives of the imperial consort,
to reach this state.
I now do not know where my final resting place will be,
thinking I can never achieve a good reputation.
I should simply seek pleasure in wealth and honor.”
Hence, attitudes of arrogance, extravagance, and presumption became rampant,
and they were blind to the way of maintaining fullness and guarding abundance.
Princess Tàipíng’s jade-leaf crown,
Lady Guó’s luminous night pillow,
Yáng Guózhōng’s chain-link curtain,
were all rare treasures of their time,
their value incalculable.
From Mínghuáng Zálù.
Lady Guó
Lady Guóguó, the elder sister of Consort Yáng Guìfēi,
enjoyed exceptional favor for a time.
She undertook a grand construction of her mansion,
and the magnificence of its buildings
was unmatched by any.
The site she occupied was the old residence of the Wéi family.
("Sì" originally written as "fù",
corrected according to the Huáng edition.)
The sons of the Wéi family were resting at midday in the halls and corridors
when they suddenly saw a woman wearing a yellow gauze shawl and gown
descend from a palanquin.
She had several dozen maidservants,
and she chatted and laughed with perfect composure.
She said to the Wéi sons:
"I hear this residence is for sale.
What is the price?"
The Wéi sons descended the steps and said:
"This is our ancestors' old home,
which we cannot bear to part with."
Before they had finished speaking,
several hundred workmen
climbed onto the eastern and western wings
and began tearing off the tiles and timbers.
The Wéi sons then led their household servants,
gathered their lutes and books,
and abandoned them in the middle of the road.
Lady Guóguó granted the Wéi family a dozen or so *mǔ* of vacant land with a pond,
but gave no compensation whatsoever for the residence itself.
After Lady Guóguó's central hall was completed,
she summoned craftsmen to plaster it.
She awarded them two million cash as payment,
and additionally gave them a reward of three *dǒu* of gold dust and turquoise.
Later, a violent storm once uprooted trees,
which fell onto her hall.
When she went to look afterwards,
it was completely undamaged.
When the tiles were removed to inspect it,
it was found that they were all wooden tiles.
The exquisite craftsmanship of its construction
was all of this kind.
Whenever Lady Guóguó entered the palace,
she often rode a piebald horse,
driven by a young eunuch.
The piebald horse's strength and vigor,
and the young eunuch's handsome elegance,
were both considered the finest of the time.
From *Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Mínghuáng*.
Wéi Zhì
and Wéi Bīn, though born into a noble family,
were by nature quite honest and sincere.
However, their family's status and reputation had always been lofty,
and their official caps and robes were particularly splendid,
though the family customs were somewhat extravagant.
Yet Bīn, when serving at court, was dignified and upright,
his demeanor and bearing were solemn and imposing,
possessing the bearing of a high minister.
Whenever attending court assemblies,
he never chatted or laughed with his colleagues.
According to old regulations,
when officials stood in the palace courtyard
and it happened to rain or snow,
they still did not move to stand under the corridors.
One day, heavy snow suddenly fell.
From the Three Excellencies downwards,
none did not shake the snow from their caps and robes,
or change their standing positions.
Only Bīn's expression and demeanor grew even more reverent.
Soon the snow piled up to his knees.
After the court session concluded,
Bīn extricated himself from the snow and departed.
Those who saw this all sighed in admiration and respect.
Bīn's elder brother, Zhì,
had early on become famous in his time for his literary talent, knowledge, and judgment.
He was skilled at composing essays
and excelled at cursive and clerical script calligraphy.
He moved in and out of high and prestigious offices,
treading a path of honor and nobility.
Considering his family background and literary brilliance,
But in his interactions with others, he was curt and arrogant,
never engaging in intimate conversation with anyone.
His clothing, carriages, and horses
were especially luxurious.
Maidservants and eunuch attendants
constantly numbered several dozen around him.
Sometimes he would lean on an armrest, propping his chin, passing the days,
too lazy to utter a single word.
Regarding food and delicacies,
he was particularly fastidious about their refinement and cleanliness,
even using bird feathers to select rice grains.
After each meal,
looking at what was discarded in the kitchen,
it was worth no less than ten thousand cash.
If he was a guest at a banquet hosted by high officials,
even if all manner of land and sea delicacies were arrayed,
he would still not pick up his chopsticks.
He often had his maidservants handle his correspondence,
drafting replies to letters.
He never wrote them himself,
merely conveying his intent.
The weight and phrasing of the wording
always perfectly matched Zhì's intentions.
And the calligraphic style was vigorous and skillful,
all conforming to standard models.
Zhì would only add his signature.
He often said that the character "Zhì" he wrote
resembled five clouds.
Many people at the time imitated it,
calling it "Duke Xún's Five-Cloud Style."
He often used five-colored paper for sealing and addressing letters.
His extravagance and self-indulgence
were all of this kind.
However, his household discipline was strict and orderly.
His son, Yǔn,
was assigned to study the classics and histories.
He was daily instructed and encouraged,
and even at midnight, someone was sent to check on him.
If Yǔn studied and read without stopping,
and paid his morning and evening respects,
his father's expression would certainly be pleased.
If he showed the slightest laziness or neglect,
he would immediately send someone to stop him,
order him to stand in the main hall,
and sometimes not speak to him for ten days.
Though Zhì had several dozen household servants,
for receiving guests at the gate,
he always made Yǔn do it.
This continued without cease in both heat and cold,
earning considerable praise at the time.
However, Zhì ultimately, due to his curt arrogance and exceptional talent,
was often resented by those in power.
From *Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng*.
The Yúnhuī Hall
Yuán Zài built the Yúnhuī Hall in his private residence.
Yúnhuī is the name of a fragrant herb,
originating from the country of Yútián.
Its fragrance is pure and white like jade.
When buried in the earth, it does not rot or decay.
It is pounded into powder,
and used to coat the walls,
hence the name Yúnhuī.
Furthermore, beams and pillars were made of chénxiāng wood,
and doors and windows were made of gold and silver.
Inside were hung a Xuánlí screen and a purple xiāo silk curtain.
The screen was originally a treasure of Yáng Guózhōng.
On it were carved images of beautiful women and musicians from previous dynasties.
Externally, it was inlaid with tortoiseshell and crystal,
and adorned with pearls and sè-sè stones.
Its exquisite craftsmanship
was almost beyond human capability.
The purple xiāo silk curtain was obtained from a tribal chieftain of the southern sea region,
belonging to the jiǎo-xiāo type.
It was light, loose, and thin,
as if there were no obstruction.
Even during severe cold,
the wind could not penetrate it;
in the height of summer, coolness naturally arrived.
Its color was faintly discernible,
so that sometimes one did not even realize a curtain was there,
and people said there was a purple aura in Zài's sleeping chamber.
The rest of his clothing, ornaments, and extravagant luxuries
generally imitated those of the imperial household.
In front of the Yúnhuī Hall was a pond,
its banks paved with patterned stones.
In it grew Píngyáng flowers,
also resembling white duckweed,
their flowers red and large,
as if they were peonies.
There were also green lotus flowers,
fragrant, pure, and blooming,
more magnificent than ordinary ones.
Zài, on a leisurely day,
leaned on the railing to gaze at them.
Suddenly he heard a song, clear and bright,
as if sung by a girl of fourteen or fifteen.
The tune was "Jade Tree Backyard Flowers."
Zài was startled and amazed,
unable to tell where it came from.
Upon listening carefully,
he realized it was from within the lotus flowers.
Bending down to look,
he heard the sound of breathing.
Zài was greatly disturbed,
so he cut open the flower,
but found nothing inside.
He then kept it secret and did not let anyone speak of it.
After Zài was executed,
a runaway servant became a soldier in the Pínglú army,
so people finally learned the truth.
Zài had a dragon-whisker duster,
purple in color like overripe mulberries.
It was about three chǐ long,
with a handle carved from crystal,
and a ring knob carved from red jade.
When wind, rain, or darkness came,
or when it was dipped in flowing water and became damp,
its radiance would shimmer and sway,
flaring up as if in anger.
Placed in the hall,
at night mosquitoes and gnats could not approach;
when waved to make a sound,
chickens, dogs, oxen, and horses would all flee in alarm;
if hung over a pond or deep pool,
then scaly and shelled creatures
would all come bowing and prostrating;
if water was drawn into the air with it,
it would immediately form a waterfall three to five chǐ long,
without ever breaking off;
if roasted meat was used to fumigate it,
it would billow forth as if generating clouds and mist.
Later, the emperor learned of its marvels,
and Zài had no choice but to present it to the palace.
Zài himself said
he obtained it from the Dòngtíng Daoist priest Zhāng Zhīhé.
From the "Dūyáng Biān."
Also, Zài's wife, née Wáng, styled Yùnxiù,
was the daughter of Wáng Jìn.
Initially, when Wáng Jìn governed Běijīng,
he married Yùnxiù to Yuán Zài.
As years passed, she was looked down upon and treated with contempt.
Yùnxiù said to her husband:
"Why not increase your studies?
I have dowry and trousseau assets,
which can all be used for paper and brush expenses."
Whether Wáng's parents knew or not—
the Ming manuscript reads "or knew of it"—
relatives, considering Zài and his wife both beggars,
despised and scorned them greatly.
Yuán then traveled to Qín,
and composed a poem parting from Yùnxiù:
"In recent years, who does not weary of decline?
Even within noble gates, I seem unwelcome.
Behold the cold, verdant trees of sea and mountain,
Bitterly enduring frost and hail until the spring wind."
His wife requested to accompany him, saying:
"We'll sweep the road of hunger and cold's traces,
Heaven pities those of lofty ambition.
Cease shedding these parting tears,
Hand in hand we enter western Qín."
After Zài arrived in the capital,
he repeatedly presented proposals on current affairs,
which deeply accorded with the emperor's wishes.
Emperor Sùzōng promoted him to Zhōngshū.
Wáng shì was delighted that her husband Yuán had become chancellor,
and sent a poem to her sisters:
"The Chancellor has followed the Qílín Pavilion to honor,
Our family's tradition foremost is the poems of the Right Assistant.
Since hair-pinning age I laughed at the loom-weaving wife,
Ashamed to see Sū Qín in his hour of wealth and rank."
Zài served as chancellor under both Emperors Sùzōng and Dàizōng,
unparalleled in nobility and influence.
He extensively built pavilions and terraces,
associated with noble families,
and guests awaiting at his gate
were often delayed or obstructed.
Wáng shì again composed a piece to admonish him:
"Chǔ bamboo, Yān songs stir painted beams,
Spring orchids again change dance costumes.
Lord Sūn opened his mansion to welcome honored guests,
Knowing that floating glory does not long endure."
Zài then slightly reduced [his excesses].
Relatives from inside and outside Tàiyuán all came to pay respects and offer congratulations.
Yùnxiù settled them in a secluded courtyard.
Suddenly, taking advantage of clear weather,
she had forty blue and purple silk ribbons,
each thirty zhàng long,
all adorned with luó, wán, qǐ, and embroidered decorations.
Beneath each ribbon,
were arranged twenty gold and silver incense burners,
all burning rare incense.
The fragrance reached their clothing.
She then invited the relatives to stroll in the western courtyard.
Yùnxiù asked what these things were.
A maidservant replied:
"Today the Chancellor and his lady are airing their night clothes."
Wáng shì said to the relatives:
"Who would have thought the wife of a beggar
still possesses two sets of covering garments and coarse clothes?"
At this, the relatives were ashamed and blushed,
and gradually took their leave.
Yùnxiù often distributed clothing and ornaments to others,
but did not give to her own flesh and blood who had been too unkind.
She often said:
"It is not that I, your child, am disrespectful to aunts and sisters,
but what can I do about the insults I suffered then!"
Later, Zài's heart became greedy and willful,
and he ultimately brought upon himself criminal guilt.
The emperor, detesting him, ordered his execution,
and his family was destroyed.
Yùnxiù had insight and judgment from youth,
and her integrity and principles were also lofty.
After Zài was executed,
the emperor ordered her to enter the palace.
Intended for the duty of admonition with the red-tube brush,
she sighed and said:
"I, the twelfth daughter of the Wáng family,
for twenty years daughter of the Tàiyuán military governor,
for sixteen years wife of a chancellor—
