who could bear to record the affairs of Chángxìn and Zhāoyáng Palaces?
Death would be fortunate indeed!"
She firmly refused the command.
Some say
the emperor pardoned her crime.
Others say
the Jīngzhào prefectural authorities flogged her to death.
Zài's favored concubine Xuē Yáoyīng could compose poetry and write,
excelled at singing and dancing,
and had an immortal's grace and jade-like purity.
Her skin was fragrant and her body light,
so that even Xuánbō, Yíguāng,
Fēiyàn, or Lǜzhū
could not surpass her.
Yáoyīng's mother, Zhào Juān,
was also a beloved concubine of the Prince of Qí—
the original text had "courtesan" for "Qí,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
Later she left to become the wife of a man named Xuē,
and gave birth to Yáoyīng.
From infancy, she was fed with fragrances,
hence her fragrant skin.
After Zài took her as a concubine,
he housed her in a golden-thread curtain
and a Chénchén mattress.
It came from the country of Gōulí.
It is said to be made from the fur of the Chénchén beast,
its color deep red,
lustrous and soft beyond compare.
She wore garments of dragon xiāo silk;
one set weighed no more than two or three liǎng,
and when grasped, it did not fill a handful.
Because Yáoyīng's body was so light,
Zài felt she could not bear heavy clothing,
Therefore, he sought her in foreign lands.
Only Jiǎ Zhì and Yáng Yán were on friendly terms with Zǎi,
so they often had the chance to see her dance and sing.
Jiǎ Zhì thus presented a poem to her, which said:
"Her dance timid, her gauze robe heavy,
Her smile like a peach blossom blooming.
Only then did I realize why Emperor Wǔ of Hàn
Built the Wind-Avoiding Terrace in vain."
Yáng Yán also composed a long song praising her beauty,
the gist of which was:
Her snow-white face and delicate brows, a heavenly maiden,
With phoenix flute and simurgh wings, about to take flight.
Jade hairpins tilted, her steps on jade are dustless,
Her slender waist like willow, unable to bear the spring.
Yáoyīng excelled at charming with cleverness,
and Zǎi was infatuated with her,
neglecting his duties as chancellor.
Yáoyīng's father was named Zōngběn,
her elder brother was named Cóngyì,
and they took turns coming and going with Zhào Juān.
They engaged in bribery,
which was called "pulling strings."
They further conspired with Zhūo Qiàn, the chief clerk of the Secretariat, and others as their confidants.
Whenever Zōngběn and his ilk reported matters to him,
Zǎi never failed to comply.
Throughout the land, those who offered goods to seek official positions
all relied on Zǎi's powerful influence,
pointing to Xuē and Zhūo as their intermediaries.
After Zǎi's death,
Yáoyīng became the wife of a local man.
Commentators believed that Yuán Zǎi's loss of virtuous conduct
was caused by a single woman.
From "Dū Yáng Biān"
Péi Miǎn
When Péi Miǎn succeeded Péi Hóngjiàn in governance,
a minor clerk presented him with the salary ledger.
Miǎn looked at his family members,
his joy evident on his face—
such was his greed for wealth.
Miǎn was inherently extravagant,
fond of fine carriages and robes.
He had famous horses worth several hundred in gold
(The Ming manuscript lacks the character "cast";
"worth" is written as "often")
ten of them.
Whenever he entertained guests,
the variety of delicacies
included many whose names were unknown.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi",
the Ming manuscript states: from "Lú Shì Zá Jì"
Yú Dí
When Yú Dí was in Xiāngzhōu,
he lit mountain lanterns,
using two thousand shi of oil at once.
When Lǐ Chāngkuí was in Jīngnán,
he went hunting,
lavishly adorning himself.
His wife, Dúgū shì,
also led a female troop of two thousand,
all dressed in crimson purple embroidered jackets with brocade saddles and saddlecloths.
Thus, the commandery was depleted.
From "Zhuàn Zǎi"
Wáng Yá
During Emperor Wénzōng's reign,
the chancellor Wáng Yá was extravagant and luxurious.
In his courtyard, he dug a well,
with gold and jade as its railings
(the Ming manuscript reads "combined to form a jade cabinet" for "gold and jade as its railings")
and secured it with strict locks.
All the precious jades and pearls under heaven
were thrown into it.
He drew water from it
for his own consumption.
Not long after, he broke the law,
was executed by the army,
and his clan was exterminated.
Wáng Yá's flesh and bones all appeared golden in color.
From "Dú Yì Zhì"
Lǐ Déyù
During Emperor Wǔzōng's reign,
the chancellor Lǐ Déyù was extravagant.
For each bowl of soup he consumed,
the cost was about thirty thousand.
It was made by mixing pearls, jade, treasures,
realgar, cinnabar,
and boiling them into a juice.
After three boilings, the dregs were discarded.
From "Dú Yì Zhì"
Yáng Shōu
During the Xiántōng era,
Cuī Ānqián was known for his pure virtue and lofty reputation.
To rectify the customs of the time,
the chancellor Yáng Shōu held him in high esteem.
Wishing to invite him to a meal,
Yáng found no way to approach him.
He first sought out Cuī's disciples,
asking them to speak on his behalf,
repeatedly,
but Cuī ultimately refused.
Yáng's determination grew stronger.
Gradually, rumors began to spread,
and someone advised Cuī:
"One should not firmly refuse the current chancellor."
Reluctantly, Cuī agreed.
Yáng was overjoyed,
immediately ordering preparations,
and then invited Cuī to attend on the appointed day.
Earlier, a relative of Cuī's,
who was also an old acquaintance of Yáng's,
wished to seek a favor,
asking Cuī to speak on his behalf,
but found it difficult to broach the subject.
As Cuī was about to attend Yáng's invitation,
he said to his relative:
"Xiūxíng (Yáng Shōu) has invited me to a meal today.
Tomorrow,
you simply wait nearby,
and I will surely bring it up then.
If he wishes to see you,
you must come immediately."
When Cuī arrived at Yáng's residence,
he saw the halls and rooms lavishly decorated,
with attendants on both sides wearing double buns adorned with pearls and jade.
Cuī was displeased.
The food and drink included rare delicacies from land and sea.
On the table in front, there was an incense burner,
from which smoke rose, forming the shape of a pavilion.
Cuī detected another fragrance,
which seemed not to come from the incense burner or the pearls and jade.
Finding it strange,
he looked around from time to time,
but could not identify the source of the fragrance.
After a while,
Yáng said:
"Does Your Excellency seem to be looking for something else?"
Cuī replied:
"I notice an unusually intense fragrance."
Yáng glanced at his attendants,
ordering them to fetch from the gilded table in the eastern chamber
a white horn tray,
holding a lacquered ball.
He presented it to Cuī, saying:
"This is incense from Jìbīn Kingdom."
Cuī was greatly astonished.
After the banquet, he returned home,
ultimately failing to mention his relative's request.
According to "Tàizōng Shílù Yún",
Jìbīn Kingdom presented Jūwùtóu flowers,
whose fragrance could be smelled for several li—
this is likely similar.
Also, according to Yáng's disciples,
whenever the chancellor returned from court,
he often played with a jade Brahmin figurine.
Several inches tall,
it was translucent, exquisite, and adorable,
said to be from the inner treasury of the King of Yútián.
From "Lú Shì Zá Shuō"
Princess Tóngchāng
In the ninth year of the Xiántōng era,
Princess Tóngchāng was married.
Her residence was established in Guǎnghuà Ward,
and she was granted five million strings of cash.
Moreover, the treasures of the inner treasury were exhausted
to furnish her residence.
As for the rooms, doors, and windows,
all were adorned with numerous precious gems.
Further, well railings and medicine mortars were made of gold and silver,
along with food cabinets and water troughs.
Pots, cauldrons, basins, and jars of various kinds,
and ladles, baskets, and winnowing fans were inlaid with gold.
Beds were crafted from crystal, firestone, colored glaze, and tortoiseshell,
supported by golden turtles and silver deer.
Moreover, vessels and utensils were carved from five-colored jade,
and a round table was assembled from a hundred treasures.
She was bestowed with several hu of golden wheat and silver millet,
all of which were tributes from Tiáozhī during the reign of Emperor Tàizōng.
In the hall were hung curtains of linked pearls,
curtains that warded off cold,
rhinoceros-horn mats and ivory mats,
and embroideries of dragons and phoenixes.
The curtains of linked pearls
were made by stringing together genuine pearls.
The curtains that warded off cold
resembled the mottled patterns of tortoiseshell,
with a purple hue,
and were said to be crafted from the bones of the cold-warding bird.
However, it was unknown from which country they originated.
There were also partridge pillows, kingfisher boxes, and divine silk embroidered quilts.
The pillows were made by combining seven treasures into the mottled pattern of a partridge,
and the boxes were adorned with kingfisher feathers.
The divine silk embroidered quilt
featured three thousand mandarin ducks,
interspersed with exotic flowers and rare leaves,
so exquisite and magnificent
that one could well imagine.
It was further embellished with spirit-millet pearls as small as millet grains,
radiant in five colors.
There were also grudge-dispelling rhinoceros horn and wish-fulfilling jade.
The rhinoceros horn was round like a pellet,
and did not decay when buried in the earth;
wearing it
dispelled one’s anger.
The wish-fulfilling jade resembled a pillow,
though according to the Dùyáng Zábiān, “pillow” is written as “peach,”
and in the Ming manuscript copy, “head” is written as “fruit.”
It had seven holes,
said to symbolize clarity and illumination.
There were also curtains of green-blue stone,
patterned cloth towels, fire silkworm floss, and nine-jade hairpins.
The curtains were the color of green-blue stone,
three chi wide,
and one hundred chi long,
light, translucent, and thin,
beyond compare.
When hung in the air,
their sparse and clear patterns
resembled green threads strung with pearls.
Even under heavy rain,
they would not become damp,
said to be because they were coated with mermaid incense ointment.
The patterned cloth towels were hand towels,
pure white as snow,
exceptionally smooth and soft,
absorbing water without becoming wet,
and even after years of use,
they never became soiled.
These two items were said to have come from the country of Guǐgǔ.
Fire silkworm floss came from the land of fire,
and a single set of clothing
required only one liang;
if slightly exceeded,
the scorching heat would become unbearable.
The nine-jade hairpin was engraved with nine phoenixes,
each in nine colors,
and bore the inscription “Yù’ér,”
so exquisite and marvelous
that it seemed not of human craftsmanship.
It was obtained by someone in Jīnlíng,
who then presented it as a tribute.
The princess rewarded him generously.
One day while napping,
she dreamed of a servant in crimson clothes delivering a message:
“Pān Shūfēi of the Southern Qí has taken the nine-phoenix hairpin.”
Upon waking,
she recounted the dream to her attendants.
When the princess passed away,
the hairpin was nowhere to be found.
The Wéi family found this strange,
and thus truthfully told their disciples.
Some said:
“Yù’ér was the childhood name of Consort Pān.”
As for the other rare treasures,
they cannot all be recorded.
Since the Han and Táng dynasties, no princess’s marriage
had ever been so lavish.
The princess rode in a seven-treasure palanquin,
with five-colored brocade sachets hung from its four corners.
The sachets contained evil-warding incense, auspicious unicorn incense, and golden phoenix incense,
all tributes from foreign lands.
They were also mixed with borneol and gold dust,
and carved from crystal, agate, and dust-repelling rhinoceros horn into shapes of dragons, phoenixes, flowers, and trees.
These were all adorned with genuine pearls and tortoiseshell,
and further embellished with golden tassels,
and carved light jade that seemed to float.
Whenever she went out,
the fragrance filled the streets and alleys,
and the crystalline light dazzled under the sun,
dazzling the eyes of onlookers.
Once, a palace eunuch
was buying wine at the Guǎnghuà tavern,
when he suddenly remarked to his companions:
“Why is the fragrance here
so extraordinary?”
A companion at the same table said:
“Could it be borneol?”
He replied:
“No.
In my youth, I served in the consorts’ palace,
so I often smelled such scents.
I wonder how it has come to be here today.”
He then inquired with the tavern keeper,
who said:
“A bearer of the princess’s palanquin
pawned his brocade robe here for wine.”
The eunuch and his companions asked to see it,
and were even more amazed.
Daily, the emperor bestowed imperial delicacies and medicinal soups,
and messengers on the road were continuous.
The delicacies included spirit-dissipating roast and red dragon jerky.
The wines included dew-condensing nectar and osmanthus-fermented brew.
The teas were named green flower and purple blossom.
The spirit-dissipating roast
used only four liang of meat from a whole sheep,
and even in the heat of summer,
it never spoiled or turned foul.
The red dragon jerky
was not actually dragon meat.
When placed on a plate,
the strands stood firm like red silk,
rising one chi high;
when pressed with chopsticks,
it would shrink to three or four fen,
but upon release, it would return to its original height.
As for the other delicacies,
no one else could identify them.
Yet the princess’s household consumed them
as if they were chaff and husks from the village.
One day, a grand gathering of the Wéi clan was held in Guǎnghuà Ward,
with jade-like delicacies arrayed.
As the summer heat grew intense,
the princess ordered the clear-water cloth to be soaked
and hung in the southern pavilion,
filling the entire gathering with a feeling of warmth as if wrapped in silk floss.
The clear-water cloth was eight or nine chi long,
resembling cloth but finer,
translucent and thin enough to reflect light.
It was said to contain ambergris,
which is why it could dispel the summer heat.
The members of the Wéi clan enjoyed playing leaf games,
and at night, the princess would use a red glass tray
to hold luminous pearls,
ordering the monk Qí to hold it in the hall,
making it as bright as day.
When the princess first fell ill,
she summoned the sorcerer Mǐ Bīn to perform exorcisms,
and gifted him fragrant candles.
Mǐ’s neighbors
noticed an extraordinary fragrance,
and some came to his door to inquire about it.
Bīn truthfully explained the matter.
He produced the candles,
which were two cun square
and over a chi long,
adorned with five colors.
When lit,
they burned through the night without extinguishing.
Their rich and intense fragrance
could be smelled from over a hundred paces away.
The smoke that rose from them
formed shapes of towers, pavilions, and palaces.
Some said
the candles contained clam fat.
As the princess’s illness worsened,
healers sought rare medicines,
and submitted a memorial stating:
“If red honey and white ape ointment can be obtained,
consuming them may cure her.”
The emperor ordered the inner treasury inspected,
and several dan of red honey were found,
originally a tribute from the country of Dōulí.
Several jars of white ape ointment were also found,
originally presented from the Southern Sea.
Despite daily administration of medicines,
there was no improvement,
and the princess passed away.
The emperor was grief-stricken,
and personally composed elegiac verses.
He ordered the court officials to compose matching poems.
At the ancestral temple ceremony,
all the officials and palace attendants
used gold and jade to adorn their carriages, clothing, and playthings,
which were then burned in the Wéi family courtyard.
The Wéi family scrambled for the ashes to sift out the gold and treasures.
When she was buried in the eastern suburbs,
the Emperor and the Shū Concubine watched from the Yánxīng Gate.
From the inner treasury, they brought out golden camels, phoenixes, and qílín, each several feet tall,
to serve as ceremonial attendants.
Their clothing and playthings
were no different from those of humans.
Each type of item amounted to as many as one hundred and twenty carriages.
They carved wood into numerous halls,
with countless images of dragons, phoenixes, flowers, trees, people, and animals.
Using crimson silk and embroidered brocade,
strung with gold beads and gemstones,
they made a thousand teams of canopies and curtains.
Their banners, parasols, and canopies
filled the streets and blotted out the sun.
The flags, jade ornaments, and ceremonial guards
were mostly of a higher grade.
He ordered Buddhist nuns and female Daoist priests to serve as attendants and guides.
They burned the Shēngxiāo Bǎilíng incense
and struck the Guītiān Zǐjīn chimes.
The splendor and brilliance
stretched for nearly twenty *li*.
The Emperor also bestowed one hundred *hú* of wine
and thirty camel-loads of cakes and pastries,
each two feet in diameter,
to feed the laborers.
The scholars and commoners of the capital abandoned their work to watch, their sweat flowing continuously,
each fearing they would fall behind.
When the hearse passed the Yánxīng Gate,
the Emperor and the Shū Concubine wept bitterly.
Those who heard of it, both inside and outside the palace,
were all grieved and pained.
On the same day, the wet nurse was buried,
and the Emperor further composed "Elegy for the Wet Nurse."
The words were plain but the sentiment sincere,
and many people recited it.
Thereafter, the Emperor was preoccupied day and night.
Lǐ Kějí presented the "Lament for a Hundred Years" song,
its melody and lyrics mournful and plaintive.
Those who heard it could not help but shed tears.
He further taught several dozen people to perform the "Lament for a Hundred Years" dance.
They took treasures from the inner treasury and carved them into head ornaments,
and used eight hundred bolts of silk to paint designs of fish, dragons, and waves,
to serve as a floor covering.
At the end of each dance,
pearls and jadeite lay scattered all over the ground.
Kějí held the office of General-in-Chief,
and was rewarded with tens of thousands.
He was utterly without propriety.
The Left Army Supervisor Xīmén Jìxuán was always quite upright and outspoken.
He thus said to Kějí:
"You indulge in clever flattery to delude the Son of Heaven;
the extermination of your clan is not far off."
Kějí, relying on the Emperor's favor,
did not change in the slightest.
Kějí was skilled at twisting his tongue,
and before the Son of Heaven,
he would roll his eyes and nod his head,
continuously uttering words,
singing
[Míng manuscript adds "miscellaneous sounds" after "sing"]
songs.
In a moment,
he would assume hundreds of different expressions without cease.
At that time, the unruly youths of the capital imitated him,
calling it "pāi tán"
[departing tone]
One day, Kějí requested leave to marry off his son.
The Emperor said:
"I shall immediately send wine, flour, and rice
to assist in your joyous ceremony."
When Kějí returned home,
soon a palace eunuch supervised the delivery of two silver jars, each over two feet tall,
proclaiming them as gifts to Kějí.
At first, he thought it was wine,
but upon opening them,
they were both filled with gold and treasures.
The Emperor bestowed upon Kějí a silver *qílín* several feet tall.
Kějí took an official treasury cart
to transport it to his private residence.
Xīmén Jìxuán said:
"Today you receive gifts using an official cart;
another day, when your household is ruined,
you will also have to cart them back to the inner treasury.
Not to mention receiving rewards,
you merely tire the oxen's legs."
Later, Kějí was indeed exiled to Lǐngbiǎo,
and all the precious playthings previously bestowed upon him
were taken back.
Gentlemen said that Jìxuán had foresight.
From "Dū Yáng Biān"
Lǐ Zhāng
Lǐ Jiàng's son Zhāng served as Observation Commissioner of Xuānzhōu.
When Yáng Shōu first completed building a pavilion of white sandalwood,
he gathered relatives and guests to view it.
Earlier, Zhāng had secretly sent someone to measure its dimensions,
wove a carpet accordingly,
and presented it that day.
When Shōu fell from power,
Zhāng was also implicated.
From "Dū Yáng Biān"
Prefect Lǐ
During the Qiánfú era,
there was a Prefect Lǐ who, having completed his term as a regional governor and returned,
resided in the eastern part of Luòyáng.
Deeply grateful for past kindness from a noble family,
he wished to invite their sons for a leisurely gathering.
There was a monk named Shènggāng from the Jìng'ài Temple,
with whom he often associated.
Lǐ thus told him about preparing a banquet.
The monk said:
"I have been their disciple for a long time.
Every time I observe their meals,
they exhaust the flavors of land and sea.
Their regular meals must be cooked with charcoal,
yet they are often dissatisfied.
This is because arrogance and indulgence have become their nature.
Is it appropriate for you, Prefect, to invite them?"
Lǐ said:
"If it were vermilion elephant marrow or white gorilla lips,
I fear I could not obtain them.
But merely preparing a fine, small banquet
should not be difficult."
Thereupon, he extensively sought rare delicacies,
and had his wife and children personally oversee the cooking.
He set out exquisite mats and carved plates,
selected a day, and invited them.
The brothers sat in a row,
reserved and solemn as ice and jade.
Each time a dish was served,
they did not partake.
The host repeatedly urged them,
but they only tasted the fruits.
When the meal of ice was served,
each put a spoonful into his mouth,
exchanged glances for a long while,
all as if chewing gall or swallowing needles.
Lǐ could not fathom the reason,
and only apologized for the poor cooking.
The next day, he saw Shènggāng again
and described in detail the demeanor of the sons.
The monk said:
"What I said earlier was not mistaken."
Then he went to their door and asked:
"Prefect Lǐ specially prepared a banquet;
the dishes could be said to be sumptuous and clean.
Why did you not somewhat accept his好意?"
The sons said:
"The roasting, grilling, frying, and seasoning were not done properly."
The monk said:
"Even if other things were inedible,
what could you possibly find objectionable about the charcoal-cooked meal?"
They then said:
"Reverend, you do not know.
Whenever cooking with charcoal,
[Míng manuscript has "rice" instead of "food"]
one must first burn
[Original has "nuǎn" (warm); changed according to Míng manuscript]
it until well done.
This is called 'refined charcoal,'
and only then can it be used for cooking.
Otherwise, it still has smoke.
The charcoal at Prefect Lǐ's residence was not refined,
hence it was difficult to eat."
The monk clapped his hands and laughed loudly:
"This is beyond what this humble monk knows."
When the rebel Huáng Cháo's forces captured Luò,
their property was all plundered and exhausted.
The several brothers
then fled together with Shènggāng.
Hiding in mountain valleys,
they went without food for up to three days.
As the rebel front moved somewhat farther away,
they walked on foot toward Héqiáo.
A small shop along the way had just opened,
selling meals of coarse millet.
The monk had several hundred coins in his bag,
and bought some to eat together from earthenware cups.
Their stomachs were extremely empty;
even fine delicacies could not compare.
The monk laughed and said to them:
"This was not cooked with refined charcoal.
I wonder if it is fit for you gentlemen to eat?"
They all hung their heads in shame and embarrassment,
and had no words to reply.
From "Jù Tán Lù"
Liú Lóngzǐ
During the reign of Emperor Gāozōng of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Liú Lóngzǐ who spread heretical teachings to deceive the masses.
He made a golden dragon head and hid it in his sleeve,
using a sheep's intestine filled with honey water,
which he wound around and tied.
Whenever he gathered a crowd,
he would bring out the dragon head,
claiming that the holy dragon spat water,
and drinking it would cure all illnesses.
He then transferred the water from the sheep's intestine into the dragon's mouth,
giving it to people to drink,
and they all falsely claimed their illnesses were cured.
He received countless donations.
He then plotted rebellion,
but the affair was exposed, and he fled.
He was tracked down and captured,
executed in the marketplace,
along with more than ten of his accomplices.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Guō Chún
Guō Chún, a filial son from Dōnghǎi, lost his mother.
Whenever he wept, flocks of crows would gather in great numbers.
An investigation found this to be true,
so his household was honored with a commemorative plaque.
Later, it was discovered
that the filial son, each time he wept,
would scatter cakes on the ground,
and flocks of crows would compete to eat them.
After this happened several times,
the crows, hearing his weeping, took it as a signal,
and all rushed to gather.
It was not due to any spiritual power.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Wáng Suì
In the household of Wáng Suì, a filial son from Hédōng,
cats and dogs nursed each other's young.
The local authorities reported this,
and he received an honorific plaque.
It turned out that the cats and dogs had given birth at the same time,
so he placed the kittens in the dog's den,
and the puppies in the cat's nest.
They suckled from each other's mothers,
and this became habitual,
hardly something to be considered extraordinary.
We know of connected trees, twin melons, forked wheat stalks, and grains sharing the same ear—
things of a similar kind arise,
and indeed, their numbers are many.
All are man-made,
and not worth marveling at.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Táng Tóngtài
Táng Tóngtài found a white stone with purple markings in the Luò River,
inscribed: "The Holy Mother approaches the water,
Míng manuscript note: "water" is written as "person"
eternally prospering the imperial enterprise."
He presented it,
and was appointed to the fifth-rank military post of Guǒyì,
and Yǒngchāng County was established.
It turned out that characters had been carved into the stone,
and filled with a mixture of purple stone powder and adhesive.
Later, in Wénshuǐ County of Bìngzhōu, a stone was found in a valley,
similarly inscribed,
with the characters "Wǔ Xīng,"
and Wénshuǐ was renamed Wǔxīng County.
From then on, such things were often fabricated,
but later, when their falseness was known,
they were no longer adopted,
and the practice ceased.
From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ,"
note: see "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi," volume three
Hú Yánqìng
Hú Yánqìng of Xiāngzhōu obtained a turtle,
and wrote on its belly in red lacquer:
"The Son of Heaven for ten thousand years."
He presented it,
but the Vice-Minister of the Secretariat, Lǐ Zhāodé, scraped it all off with a knife.
He petitioned for Hú to be punished,
but Empress Wǔ Zétiān said:
"This was not done with ill intent."
She pardoned him and did not pursue the matter.
From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ,"
note: see "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi," volume three
Zhū Qiányí
Empress Wǔ Zétiān was fond of auspicious signs.
The Reminder, Zhū Qiányí, recounted a dream, saying:
"Wǔ Zétiān's white hair turned black again,
and her lost teeth grew anew."
He was immediately appointed Director of the Bureau of Honors.
The Court of Judicial Review held over three hundred prisoners.
After the autumn equinox,
they could think of no plan.
So, beside the outer wall of the inner prison,
they made a saint's footprint five feet long.
At midnight,
all the prisoners shouted at once.
The eunuch officials investigated,
and they replied:
"Last night, a saint appeared,
ten feet tall,
with a face of golden color.
He said:
'You are all wronged,
do not worry.
When the Son of Heaven reigns for ten thousand years,
there will be an amnesty to release you.'"
Torches were lit to inspect,
and a giant footprint was seen.
An amnesty was immediately declared throughout the land,
and the era name was changed to Dàzú, first year.
From "Táng Guó Shǐ,"
Míng manuscript note: from "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Prince Níng
Prince Níng once hunted within the boundaries of Hù County.
Searching the woods,
he suddenly saw a chest in the grass,
securely locked.
He ordered it opened,
and inside was a young woman.
Asked where she came from,
she said her surname was Mò,
and her father had also served as an official.
The previous night, she had encountered a gang of bandits,
two of whom were monks.
They had abducted her and brought her here.
With a pained expression, she pleaded her case,
her charming manner overflowing.
The prince, surprised and delighted,
had her ride in his carriage.
At that time, they had just hunted a bear,
so he placed it in the chest,
locking it as before.
It happened that the emperor was seeking women of exceptional beauty.
Since Mò was the daughter of an official family,
the prince submitted a memorial that very day recommending her,
and explained the circumstances.
The emperor appointed her as a Cáirén.
Three days later,
the Jingzhào Prefecture reported:
In a food shop in Hù County,
two monks
had paid ten thousand cash to rent a room for a day and a night.
They said they were performing a religious ceremony,
and only carried a chest into the shop.
Late at night,
there were thumping sounds.
The shopkeeper, finding it strange that they did not open the door by daybreak,
removed the door to look,
and a bear charged out and ran away.
The two monks were already dead,
their bones exposed.
When the emperor learned of this,
he laughed heartily.
He wrote to Prince Níng:
"Elder brother, you certainly knew how to deal with these monks."
Mò was skilled at creating new melodies,
and was known at the time as Cáirén Mò's Trill.
From "Yǒuyáng Zázǔ"
Ān Lùshān
Emperor Xuánzōng doted on Ān Lùshān,
calling Ān Lùshān his son.
Once, in a side hall, he was feasting with Consort Yáng,
and whenever Ān Lùshān approached,
he would bow not to Emperor Xuánzōng but to Consort Yáng.
The emperor thus asked him:
"This barbarian bows not to me but to the consort.
What is the meaning of this?"
Ān Lùshān replied:
"I am a barbarian.
We only know our mothers,
and do not know our fathers."
The emperor laughed and let it pass.
Ān Lùshān was portly with a large belly.
The emperor once asked him:
"What is in this barbarian's belly,
that it is so large?"
Ān Lùshān answered immediately:
"There is nothing else in your servant's belly,
only a loyal heart."
Taking his words as sincere,
the emperor grew even more fond and trusting of him.
From "Kāitiān Chuánxìn Jì"
Bái Tiěyú
Bái Tiěyú was a
Jīhú from Yánzhōu,
who deluded the masses with heterodox teachings.
First, he buried a bronze Buddha statue under a cypress tree deep in the mountains.
After several years,
grass grew over it.
He deceived the villagers, saying:
"Last night, as I passed by the foot of the mountain,
I saw a Buddha's radiance."
He then selected an auspicious day to hold a vegetarian feast,
intending to unearth the holy Buddha.
When the day arrived,
he gathered several hundred people
and ordered them to dig at a spot where nothing was buried,
so they found nothing.
He then deceitfully said:
"All of you are not sincere enough in your almsgiving,
so the Buddha cannot appear."
That day,
men and women scrambled to donate over a million [coins].
He then had them dig at the actual burial site,
and they retrieved the bronze statue.
The villagers regarded him as a sage,
and word spread far and wide,
with everyone eager to see it.
He proclaimed:
"Those who see the holy Buddha
will be cured of all illnesses."
Thereupon, Bái Tiěyú deceived hundreds of li, with old and young, men and women, all coming to him.
He then used dark purple, crimson, scarlet, and yellow damask silk
to make dozens of layers of bags,
in which he placed the Buddha statue.
When people came to view it, they would remove one layer,
each time making a donation,
earning him tens of millions [of coins],
before finally seeing the statue.
After one or two years of such fraud,
the villagers submitted to him,
and he eventually rebelled.
He proclaimed himself the Radiant King,
according to the Examination of Discrepancies in the Zizhi Tongjian, the Radiant King is recorded as the Moonlight King
appointed officials,
established administrators,
and caused trouble for several years.
General Chéng Wùtǐng was ordered to suppress and execute him.
From Records of Affairs from Both Official and Unofficial Sources
Lǐ Qìngyuǎn
Captain Lǐ Qìngyuǎn was cunning, deceitful, frivolous, and treacherous.
Initially serving the Crown Prince,
he frequently came and went [in the palace].
Whenever he stepped outside temporarily,
he would presume upon his authority.
Everyone from the Grand Councilors down
called him an important person.
Just as the councilors were about to eat, he would arrive.
When they invited him to sit,
he would immediately send someone outside the gate to urgently call out:
"His Highness summons you."
He would then hurriedly spit out his food and leave.
He used this trick in all the government offices,
seeking audiences and entrusting matters.
He sold official posts and tampered with lawsuits,
and whatever he sought was invariably achieved.
Later, the Eastern Palace gradually distanced itself from him.
He still sneaked into the guards' quarters,
and ate the food of the attendant officers.
One evening, after going out,
he suffered a severe stomachache.
Yet he deceitfully claimed:
"The Crown Prince bestowed melons,
I ate too many of them,
hence this illness."
Shortly after, he had a sudden bout of cholera.
He vomited the coarse rice that the guards ate,
and yellow, foul-smelling leek paste, making a mess.
Generally, when petty men gain favor,
they often behave like this.
From Records of Affairs from Both Official and Unofficial Sources
Liú Xuánzuǒ
At the Xiàngguó Temple in Biànzhōu,
it was said that the Buddha statue was sweating.
Military Commissioner Liú Xuánzuǒ immediately ordered his carriage,
and personally brought gold and silk to donate.
By noon,
his wife also arrived.
The next day, he again set up a vegetarian feast venue.
Thereupon, officers, officials, and merchants
hurried along the roads,
fearing only that they could not deliver their goods in time.
He then ordered officials to keep records,
registering all donations.
After ten days, he closed the temple,
saying:
"The Buddha's sweat has stopped."
He obtained tens of thousands in cash,
which were used for military supplies.
From Supplements to the National History
Zhāng Hù
After Jìnshì candidates Cuī Yá and Zhāng Hù failed the imperial examinations,
they often traveled in the Jiāng-Huái region.
They were fond of drinking
and insulting and mocking their contemporaries.
Sometimes, riding on their drinking enthusiasm,
they would proclaim themselves gallant knights.
As the two shared the same tastes,
they got along very well.
Cuī once wrote a poem about a knight-errant, which said:
"On Tàiháng Ridge, three feet of snow;
In Cuī Yá's sleeve, three feet of steel.
If one day I meet a man of purpose,
I leave my home, bidding wife and children farewell."
Hence, it was often circulated among people, saying:
"Cuī and Zhāng are true knights-errant."
Therefore, many people prepared feasts to entertain them,
allowing them to praise each other.
Later, Zhāng presented a poem to the Salt and Iron Commissioner,
who appointed his son to a minor post in the canal administration,
in charge of a dam named Winter Melon.
Someone teased him, saying:
"Your worthy son is not suited for this position."
Zhāng replied:
"Winter melon naturally produces Hù seeds."
Those joking with him burst into loud laughter.
Over a year later,
he had accumulated modest wealth and influence.
One evening,
a man of unusual appearance, dressed very martially,
with a sword at his waist and a bag in his hand,
arrived. In the bag was an object,
with blood seeping darkly through.
Entering the gate, he said:
"Is this not the residence of Knight-errant Zhāng?"
Zhāng replied:
"It is."
He bowed to the guest very respectfully.
After sitting down,
the guest said:
"I have held a grudge against an enemy
for ten years,
and tonight I have caught him."
Overjoyed, he could not contain himself,
and pointing to the bag, said:
"This is his head."
He then asked Zhāng:
"Is there a tavern?
Fetch some wine to drink."
After drinking, he said:
"Three or four li from here lives a righteous man
whom I wish to repay.
If I can manage it tonight,
then all the kindness and grudges of my life will be settled.
I have heard of your noble spirit and righteousness;
could you lend me a hundred thousand strings of cash?
I wish to repay him immediately.
If this wish of mine is fulfilled,
henceforth, even if I must go through fire and water,
I swear I will not fear."
Zhāng was deeply pleased by his words
and was not stingy.
He immediately emptied his coffers under the candlelight,
calculated the medium-grade silks and other goods,
and measured out what he could give.
The guest said:
"Splendid!
I have no regrets!"
He then left the bag with the head behind and departed,
promising to return.
After he left,
when the appointed time arrived
"appointed time" originally read "his" in the text,
corrected according to the Ming manuscript.
he did not come.
When the fifth watch drum fell silent,
there was still no trace of him.
Zhāng also worried that the head in the bag might be discovered,
becoming a burden to himself.
Since the guest was not coming,
he could think of no plan,
so he sent a servant to open the bag and look inside—
it was a pig's head.
From then on, his gallant and chivalrous spirit suddenly declined.
From Guìyuàn Cóngtán
Dà'ān Temple
Emperor Yìzōng of the Táng dynasty governed the realm with culture and reason,
bringing peace and order throughout the land.
He often changed his attire to travel incognito to Buddhist and Daoist temples.
Among the common people, there were cunning and deceitful individuals.
Hearing that in the Dà'ānguó Temple,
a tribute official from Jiānghuái had deposited a thousand bolts of Wú silk in the monastery,
they secretly gathered their gang.
From among them, they selected one who resembled the emperor in appearance,
dressed him in the clothes the emperor wore for private outings,
heavily perfumed him with various scents like lóngnǎo,
and led by two or three young attendants,
they stealthily entered the monastery where the silk was stored.
At that time, one or two beggars arrived,
and the impersonator gave them alms before they left.
In a short while,
beggars of all kinds,
arriving one after another,
were given alms without pause.
The impersonator said to the monastery monks:
"What items are there in the monastery
that can be lent to me?"
Before the monks could respond,
the young attendants cast meaningful glances at them.
The monks, startled and fearful, said:
"In the cabinet, someone has deposited a thousand bolts of silk;
we are at your command."
Thereupon, they opened the cabinet,
emptied it, and gave everything to him.
The young attendants said to the monks:
"Come early tomorrow morning
to the palace gate to meet us;
we can escort you inside,
and the reward will not be light."
The impersonator then mounted a donkey and departed.
From then on, the monks spent days searching at the palace gates,
but saw nothing at all.
Only then did they realize that the group of beggars were all accomplices of the deceitful men.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Prefect Wáng
When Vice-Minister Wáng Níng was inspecting Chángshā,
there was a certain newly appointed Prefect Wáng of Liǔzhōu,
of unknown origin,
who was about to assume his post.
He arrived at the Xiāng River.
He paid a visit to Níng.
Níng invited him to a banquet with his aides.
Wáng
(Míng manuscript note: "Níng invited him to a banquet with his aides, Wáng" reads as "Wáng Jūn requested the protocol officer to present him")
addressed Níng, saying:
"I am a nephew
(Míng manuscript note: "nephew" reads as "courtyard")
of the Vice-Minister,
and should receive your bow."
Níng quickly asked:
"Since you are of my clan,
what is your childhood name?"
He replied:
"My name is Tōngláng."
Níng then said to his attendants:
"Quickly summon my son here."
In a short while,
his son arrived.
Níng questioned him:
"Is there anyone named Tōngláng in our family register?"
His son pondered for a moment,
then said:
"There is,
he should be my elder brother."
Níng then ordered Wáng Jūn to be invited,
and received him with the courtesy due to a nephew.
Casually, he asked:
"What was your previous post?"
He replied:
"I recently left my position at the Běihǎi Salt Bureau,
and soon after received this appointment."
Upon hearing this,
Níng was displeased.
After he withdrew,
Níng summoned his son again and said:
"The Wáng Jūn who came earlier
has a rather mixed background;
he is definitely not a branch of our family."
He immediately checked the clan register,
traced the lineage,
and found that there was indeed a Tōngláng,
but he had already passed away on a certain day in a certain year.
Níng saw this and became angry.
The next day,
he prepared a feast in the hall and invited him.
Wáng Jūn, upon seeing Níng,
intended to kneel.
Suddenly, he was seized and supported by two strong men,
unable to bow.
Níng stepped forward and said:
"Prefect, you are not of my clan.
Yesterday, I mistakenly accepted your bow;
today, I respectfully return it."
He then bowed to him the same number of times.
The two strong men withdrew,
and he was invited to sit and dine.
Níng further said to him:
"In this current era of peace and order,
you must not recklessly enter other people's homes again."
All the clerks and soldiers in the courtyard laughed.
Wáng Jūn was ashamed and flushed,
unable to eat or drink.
After a short while,
he left in embarrassment.
From "Nánchǔ Xīnwén"
Liú Chóngguī
Liú Chóngguī prided himself on being pure and frugal,
which attracted much public criticism.
Once, he invited his colleagues to dine on bitter vegetable dumplings.
A court official, knowing this was an affectation,
secretly asked a young servant:
"What did the Vice-Director eat for breakfast?"
The servant truthfully replied:
"He ate raw fish."
When this was heard in the court, people sneered at him.
When he governed a distant region,
relatives in the capital who were poor and needy
awaited his aid.
He merely painted a "Lychee Picture"
and composed a rhapsody to give to them.
Later, he died in Lǐngbiǎo,
and when his body was returned for burial,
passing through Zhǔgōng,
his family sold sea pearls and jadeite in the market.
This was despised by people at the time.
From "Běimèng Suǒyán"
Lǐ Yánzhào
When Wáng Zōngchóu, a general of the Shǔ kingdom of Wáng, commanded Nánliáng,
he gathered provisions and stationed troops.
Daily, he initiated labor projects,
cutting through mountains and felling trees,
hardly ever pausing.
Transporting grain by boat,
the soldiers complained of exhaustion.
The people of Mín and É
were deeply devoted to Buddhism.
In the army, all held weapons in their right hands
and Buddhist scriptures in their left.
The sounds of recitation and study
mingled with the night watches.
At that time, there was a strong soldier named Lǐ Yánzhào,
who had served for years in the area from Sānquán to Hēishuǐ,
cutting and gathering timber.
Exhausted and emaciated,
he could no longer bear the work.
So he deceitfully submitted a petition, stating:
"Recently, I have repeatedly seen the Buddhas and Tathāgatas,
riding in carriages and on elephants,
moving among the cliffs and rocks,
soaring above the pines and cypresses."
Such reports were frequent.
"Although I am in the military,
I have long embraced Buddhism.
Because my recitations are sincere,
I have had such spiritual responses.
Now I beg to be removed from the military register,
and to have my foot cut off to serve the Buddha,
so that in the future I may hope to attain the supreme fruit."
Zōngchóu ruled:
"Though he is in the military register,
his heart is in the Buddhist gate.
Cultivating his mind amidst the ranks,
comprehending truth beyond illusions and bubbles.
Devoting his heart to follow the Buddha,
cutting off his foot to serve the King of Emptiness.
How valiant, this warrior!
How fiercely determined!
His great vow is hard to hinder;
his sincerity is praiseworthy.
According to the petition, hand him over to his own unit,
remove his name from the register.
Then dispatch an officer
to oversee the amputation of one foot. After completion,
send him to Zhēnyuán Temple to be assigned sweeping duties."
Yánzhào
(Original text: Yánzhào originally read as "Fénxiū,"
corrected according to the Míng manuscript.)
He had intended to deceive and avoid his duties through falsehood,
but when facing the amputation,
his fear grew intense.
Thus, he delayed for over ten days,
wailing and writhing in agony,
avoiding the blade.
Zōngchóu heard of this,
laughed heartily, and did not punish him.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
The Beggars of Chéngdū
In Chéngdū, there was a beggar who pretended to be a fallen scholar-official.
Wearing tattered, ragged clothes,
he often wandered through the markets of Chéngdū.
Whenever he saw someone, he would extend his hand, hoping for a single coin, saying:
"I have lost my official documents,
and failed to secure an official post."
People all pitied him,
because his speech was sorrowful and hoarse,
and his appearance haggard and worn.
He lived by the side of Zǎoqiān Bridge.
Later, a powerful family,
building a garden pavilion next to his dwelling,
wishing to expand their pond and grounds,
forcibly purchased it.
When they opened his humble door,
they saw two large rooms,
all filled with scattered coins.
The amount totaled tens of millions.
None of the neighbors had known of this.
People in Chéngdū uniformly call those seeking official posts "begging scholars."
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi";
the Ming manuscript version states from "Wángshì Jiànwén."
The Xuē Brothers
There were two sons of the Xuē family living in the countryside of Yīquē.
Their ancestors had once governed large commanderies,
so their wealth and resources were abundant.
One day,
as the tree shade was just becoming lush,
and the clear, mild season had arrived,
someone happened to knock at their gate.
Opening it to look,
they saw it was a Daoist priest.
Wearing straw sandals with a snow-white beard,
his demeanor was pure and ancient.
He said:
"On the road, I fell ill with thirst;
I beg for a cup of water."
The two brothers invited him to the guest seat.
He engaged in elegant conversation and lofty discourse,
deeply savoring the richness of the Dao.
He also said:
"I am not truly one who craves water.
Passing by here with my staff,
I noticed the aura is exceptionally fine.
A hundred paces southeast from here,
are there five coiled, reclining pine trees within your boundaries?"
They replied:
"That is our fine farmland."
The priest became even more pleased,
and then, sending others away, said:
"Beneath this lies a hundred catties of gold,
and two precious swords.
Their energy faintly emanates,
floating between the Zhāng and Yì constellations.
Zhāng and Yì mark the celestial division corresponding to Luò.
I have been searching for this for a long time.
The gold can be distributed to aid impoverished relatives.
The Dragon Spring swords you should wear yourselves;
you will then reach the highest official positions.
I ask for one of them,
to perform demon-slaying arts."
The two brothers were greatly astonished.
The priest said:
"Have your servants and hired laborers
prepare baskets and spades in full,
and wait for an auspicious day to break ground.
Then you can see it with your own eyes.
However, without a method to control it,
it will flee and hide in the yellow earth,
never to be pursued again.
Now, wait for a fine night,
clear a square area to build an altar,
sprinkle it with ritual water,
and it will be unable to escape.
Also, instruct the servants
not to leak this."
Asked what was needed for the altar,
he said:
"Three hundred feet of black ropes,
that is, red and black cords.
A great deal of colored and plain silk according to the directional colors,
along with tables, incense burners, mats, and cushions."
And he said:
"I am not one who seeks profit,
but borrow these for the ritual.
Also, use ten sets of sacrificial offerings,
with wine and tea accompanying them.
The vessels must be made of fine gold."
The two brothers then exerted all efforts to prepare these.
Still lacking some items,
they borrowed from relatives and friends.
He also said:
"I am skilled in the art of transmutation,
viewing gold and silver as dirt,
and always make it my duty to relieve people's urgent needs.
Now, I have bags and chests stored at Tàiwēi Palace,
and wish to temporarily deposit them here."
The two brothers agreed.
He immediately summoned people to carry them over.
There were four large cases,
so heavy they could barely be lifted,
sealed very securely,
entrusted to them for safekeeping.
Soon the auspicious day arrived.
He grandly set up the ritual implements among the five pines,
had the two brothers bow and offer prayers,
then urgently ordered them to return home,
close the doors and wait,
warning them not to peek through cracks.
"I will perform Jǐngchún's technique of loosened hair and sword in mouth.
If someone peeps,
disaster will immediately strike.
Wait until the ritual is complete;
I will raise a torch to summon you.
Then lead your servants,
bring baskets and spades,
and by night, dig it up.
I hope you can quietly behold the supreme treasure."
The two brothers followed his instructions.
From midnight, they sat upright vigilantly,
intently watching for torchlight,
but none appeared at all.
Unable to bear it,
they opened the door to spy,
finding all silent with no trace.
Walking to the trees,
they saw cups overturned and vessels upturned,
food and drink scattered in disarray.
The colored silks and vessels
had all been taken away.
Wheel and hoof tracks
crisscrossed the spot.
They suspected he had used the black ropes to bind and secure things before fleeing.
Upon opening the deposited cases,
they were filled with tiles and rubble.
From then on, their family property was greatly depleted,
and they lost trust among people.
Stunned, worried, and ashamed,
they remained silent, unable to complain.
From "Táng Guóshǐ";
the Ming manuscript version states from "Táng Shǐ Wài Bǔ,"
note: see "Táng Quēshǐ," scroll lower part.
The Man from Qínzhōng
In Qínchuān, there was a wealthy young man skilled in seeking profit, who had amassed millions in silver.
One day, as night fell,
a letter was dropped at his door.
A servant picked it up and brought it in.
The young man opened the seal,
and found it was written on rush paper sealed with wax,
with faint ink and slanted brushstrokes,
purportedly left by his late father.
It said:
"The profits you have gained
are due to my assistance from the netherworld.
Now a great disaster is about to befall you,
but I have already pleaded with the underworld authorities.
On the morning of the first day of the month,
you should fast, purify yourself, and dress in clean clothes,
then go to the inn outside the Chūnmíng Gate.
Prepare fine silk,
matching your age,
which is thirty-five.
Wait until midnight and go to the Bà River Bridge.
Walk to the stone bank,
and when you see someone in yellow, place the silk before them,
bow respectfully and retreat.
The disaster may then be averted.
If you encounter no one,
take the silk back with you,
quickly settle your family affairs,
and prepare to flee.
The disaster will come without delay."
The young man, holding the letter, was terrified.
The whole household dressed in plain clothes and wept,
focusing only on the first day of the month.
He abandoned all other matters,
straightened his cap and smoothed his clothes,
and stayed at the inn outside the Chūnmíng Gate,
solemn and unable to sleep.
Respectfully waiting until midnight,
he then took a servant and a horse,
galloped to the Bà Bridge,
fearing only that he would see nothing.
Upon arrival, there was indeed a figure,
with a strange and eerie form,
disheveled hair and dressed in yellow,
arms crossed and knees bound,
leaning against a pillar and sitting,
head bowed as if asleep.
The young man, both startled and delighted,
placed the silk before it,
prayed and bowed,
not daring to look back,
and hurriedly drove back.
Returning home, they celebrated together,
thinking they had narrowly escaped disaster.
Only the servant suspected something was amiss.
Before even ten days had passed,
another letter was thrown in.
The servant immediately captured the person,
who turned out to be a young scholar from the neighboring house.
Opening the letter,
it was rush paper sealed with wax and faint ink, just like before.
The words said:
"Your disaster is very great;
the silk offered before
has not blocked the source of the calamity.
You should take another thirty-five bolts of silk
and place them again at the river bridge."
The family then wrote a detailed account of the events,
and reported it to the authorities.
After interrogation, the scholar confessed fully,
and was punished according to the law.
At that time, the Attendant-in-Ordinary Lǐ Cóng was the magistrate of Wànnián,
and the legal documents were still preserved for several years.
From "Quē Shǐ"
Lǐ Quángāo
The Protector-General Lǐ Quángāo,
after leaving his post as Supervisor of Huáihǎi,
stayed at the Kāiyuán Temple.
Due to the difficulties and obstacles in the court,
he had not yet been able to return west.
One day,
a minor officer brought a Daoist,
claiming to be skilled in alchemical matters.
Lǐ Quángāo then invited him in and treated him with respect,
and from then on, they became close.
One day, they discussed the art of alchemy,
and the Daoist said:
"Only I am quite capable of achieving it.
You can seek an iron cauldron,
with a capacity of five or six shēng or more,
and over twenty liǎng of gold as the base material.
Provide mercury and medicines daily,
and when the time is sufficient, exchange it.
Do not count the months and years,
but start over again and again."
Lǐ was very pleased with this idea.
Looking into his bag, he had a gold belt,
which could match the amount,
and gave it to the Daoist.
Once all the medicines were prepared,
after the day the fire was started,
he personally inspected it daily.
After a few days, feeling slightly tired,
he ordered a trusted family member to guard it.
When the appointed number of days was fulfilled,
he purified himself and then opened it to look.
The gold was brilliantly shining,
truly not false.
Lǐ bowed and believed in him.
Within three days,
the additions and exchanges showed evidence.
One day, the Daoist did not come,
and the medicine furnace remained as before.
In the midst of suspicion and alarm,
two nights passed in a flash.
After waiting long and wondering why he had not come,
Lǐ had no choice
but to open the furnace and look inside.
The gold was nowhere to be seen.
The matter involved the minor officer who had introduced him,
who compensated for the gold and that was the end of it.
The Daoist had completely vanished without a trace.
From "Guìyuàn Cóngtán"
There was a young man
(Míng manuscript: "zǐ" written as "shì")
surnamed Wén,
whose given name is not recorded,
who lived in Hànzhōng.
He often visited the mansions of nobles in the Two Shǔ regions,
making a living by alchemy.
All those who paid attention to furnace alchemy
were deceived by him.
There was a wealthy merchant named Lǐ Shíwǔláng,
who had accumulated much wealth.
He was deluded by Wén,
and within three years,
his family wealth was completely exhausted.
He was also ridiculed by those who knew better,
pursued and shamed,
to the point of hanging himself.
There was also a great general of Shǔ,
who was stationed with troops in Hànzhōng,
and was also deluded by him.
In Huáyáng ward, there was a newly built mansion of Grand Commandant Chéng, which was unoccupied,
and also quiet and empty.
So he sought out the caretaker,
rented it to burn medicines.
Due to a fire starting, the mansion was burned down,
spreading to the entire ward,
leaving it completely empty and quiet.
Wén then fled at night,
intending to take the Sānglín road westward,
then head east toward Xiégǔ Valley,
to escape with his life.
As soon as he left the gate, he was chased by a fierce tiger,
and could not go west.
So he went north into the mountain streams and valleys of Wángzǐshān.
The tiger followed him,
never leaving even a step away.
In desperation,
he climbed up a tree,
tying himself with a belt to a high branch.
The tiger circled the tree, roaring.
At dawn,
the officials pursuing him arrived under the tree,
and the tiger slowly left.
They then captured him from the tree,
and executed him at the place where he had burned the medicines.
From "Wángshì Jiànwén"
Ān Lùshān
Emperor Xuánzōng ordered the Crown Prince to meet Ān Lùshān,
but Ān Lùshān did not bow.
He then addressed the Emperor, saying:
"Your subject is a Hu man,
unfamiliar with the laws of the state,
and does not know what official the Crown Prince is?"
Emperor Xuánzōng said:
"He is the heir apparent.
After I pass away,
he will rule over you in my place."
Ān Lùshān said:
"Your subject is ignorant;
until now, I have only known of Your Majesty,
and did not know of the Crown Prince."
Those around him ordered him to bow,
and Ān Lùshān then bowed.
Emperor Xuánzōng praised his sincere devotion,
and especially pitied him.
From "Tánbīn Lù"
Chéng Jìngqí
Chéng Jìngqí possessed outstanding talent,
and could compose essays with immediate success.
He served as a Dàlǐ Zhèng,
and was related by marriage to Yáo Chóng.
Once, when Chóng was bedridden with illness,
Jìngqí visited his residence to inquire after his health.
Facing Chóng, he wept,
then took several live sparrows from his bosom,
holding them out one by one,
and asked Chóng to hold them in his hand before releasing them.
He prayed, saying:
"I wish for Your Excellency to recover swiftly."
Chóng reluctantly complied.
After Jìngqí had left,
Chóng was disgusted by his fawning flattery.
He said to his family members:
"Where did those tears come from?"
From then on, he no longer received him.
From "Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ"
Chén Shàoyóu
In the Táng dynasty, Chén Shàoyóu served as Acting Jiǎnxiào Zhífāng Yuánwàiláng,
and was appointed as an envoy to the Huíhé.
The position of Jiǎnxiào official began with Shàoyóu.
In governance,
Shàoyóu excelled in expedient adaptability,
and was praised by his contemporaries for his competence.
However, he heavily exacted wealth and goods,
and associated with powerful figures.
Soon, he was appointed Guǎnguì Guāncháshǐ.
At that time, the eunuch Dǒng Xiù was in power,
so Shàoyóu stayed overnight in the neighborhood.
Waiting for the moment Xiù finished his duty,
he visited him alone.
Casually, he said:
"How many people are in Seventh Gentleman's household,
and what are the daily expenses?"
Xiù said:
"Having long held a position close to the emperor,
my burdens are heavy.
Moreover, as the price of goods is soaring,
I require over a thousand strings of cash per month."
Shàoyóu said:
"Based on these expenses,
your salary is insufficient to cover the amount.
Beyond that, you must constantly seek help from others
to make ends meet.
If someone sincerely offers support,
just take care to shield and protect them,
and it will certainly be easy to manage.
Although I, Shàoyóu, am untalented,
I ask to personally bear Seventh Gentleman's expenses alone.
Each year, I am willing to send fifty thousand strings of cash.
I currently have more than half on hand,
please accept it now.
The remainder will be sent after I take up my official post,
sparing you the trouble and worry.
Wouldn't that be acceptable?"
Xiù, having received more than he expected,
was extremely pleased,
and thus became close with him.
After Shàoyóu finished speaking,
he wept and said:
"The southern regions are plagued by poisonous miasma and are remote,
I fear I may not return alive,
to see your face again."
Xiù promptly said:
"Vice Censor-in-Chief, with your fine talent,
you should not serve in a distant post.
Wait calmly for ten days or so,
I hope to exhaust my humble efforts."
At that time, Shàoyóu had already bribed Yuán Zǎi's son, Yuán Zhòngwǔ.
Xiù and Zǎi recommended him from inside and outside the court.
A few days later,
he was appointed Xuānshè Guāncháshǐ,
then changed to Zhèdōng Guāncháshǐ,
and promoted to Huáinán Jiédùshǐ.
Over more than ten years,
he governed three major frontier commands.
He levied exactions and engaged in trade,
with hardly a day of respite,
amassing wealth and treasures,
accumulating to an immense sum of billions.
He regarded refined and upright scholars
with contempt.
Initially, he befriended Yuán Zǎi,
presenting him with a hundred thousand strings of cash annually.
Later, as Zǎi gradually became jealous and suspicious,
Shàoyóu also gradually distanced himself from him.
When Zǎi's son, Yuán Bóhé,
was demoted to Yángzhōu,
Shàoyóu outwardly maintained a deep friendship with him,
but secretly sent people to watch for his faults,
and secretly reported them to the emperor.
Emperor Dàizōng considered him loyal,
and treated him even more generously.
Guān Bō once served as a guest under Shàoyóu,
and Lú Qǐ in his early years
served with him in Púgù Huái'ēn's headquarters,
so he rapidly promoted their official ranks.
After Emperor Dézōng fled to Fèngtiān,
Shàoyóu seized eight million strings of cash from Bāo Jí's treasury.
He also sent his staff advisor Wēn Shù
to pledge allegiance to Lǐ Xīliè, saying:
"For Háo, Shū, Lú, and other prefectures,
I have already ordered the dismantling of fortifications,
storing away weapons and armor,
awaiting your command."
Later, when the imperial carriage returned to the capital,
Bāo Jí entered the court,
and fully reported the situation regarding the finances.
Shàoyóu submitted a memorial,
claiming that the funds he had taken
were all used for military expenses,
and now requested to return the amount accordingly.
He then heavily taxed the people within his jurisdiction to submit the funds.
Later, when Liú Qià governed Biànzhōu,
he obtained Lǐ Xīliè's diary of daily activities:
on a certain month and day,
Chén Shàoyóu submitted a memorial pledging allegiance.
When Shàoyóu heard of this,
he died of shame.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Péi Yánlíng
In the Táng dynasty, Péi Yánlíng was successively promoted to Vice Minister of Revenue and Agriculture,
and soon was appointed as acting Commissioner of Finance and Revenue in his current official capacity.
Knowing himself to be unfamiliar with matters of food and currency,
he devised schemes,
summoned veteran clerks from the Finance and Revenue Bureau to consult with them,
seeking favor and attention.
He then memorialized:
"The funds and goods entering and leaving the empire,
with new replacing old in succession,
constantly amount to no less than sixty to seventy million strings of cash,
all stored in a single treasury.
Discrepancies and losses,
cannot be known.
I request that within the Left Treasury, separate storage be established,
the Ming manuscript notes 'storage' as 'store.'
Separate treasuries for deficits, debts, wastage, and surpluses should be built.
And for seasonal and monthly disbursements,
various types of money and goods should be deposited."
Emperor Dézōng complied.
But he merely valued creating impressive titles,
to confuse the emperor's hearing.
In reality, the money and goods did not increase at all,
only wasting the efforts of clerks and record-keepers.
He also petitioned,
ordering the Jīngzhào Prefecture's twice-a-year tax and green sprout money,
to purchase one million bales of hay,
and deliver them to the imperial gardens.
The chief ministers deliberated:
considering that if one million bales of hay were purchased,
then the common people of that region,
from winter through summer,
would be unable to transport them all,
and it would also hinder and seize agricultural work.
The matter was thus halted.
West of the capital, there were low-lying, damp marshes,
where reeds grew densely,
covering no more than a few acres.
Yánlíng suddenly memorialized:
"Stable horses in winter should be fed in their stalls,
but in summer they must have grazing grounds.
I recently inquired and found within the boundaries of Cháng'ān and Xiányáng counties,
a hundred qǐng of marshland,
I request it be used as grazing land for the imperial stables.
Moreover, it is only a dozen or so lǐ from the capital."
Emperor Dézōng believed him,
and spoke to the chief ministers.
The chief ministers firmly insisted:
"We fear this certainly does not exist."
When officials were dispatched to inspect,
it was all false.
Yánlíng was both ashamed and angry,
and again during an audience,
Emperor Dézōng said:
"One beam in the courtyard of my bath hall palace,
due to its age, has become damaged,
and has not yet been replaced."
Yánlíng said:
"Ancestral temple affairs are important,
palace beams are minor.
Your Majesty has your own rightful funds."
Emperor Dézōng exclaimed in surprise:
"What are these rightful funds called?"
He replied:
"This is according to the classics.
Foolish Confucians of ordinary talent,
are not worth discussing this with.
Your Majesty should rightly ask me,
I can understand it.
According to the Classic of Rites:
The empire's taxes,
are divided into three parts.
One part fills the sacrificial vessels;
one part is for guests,
one part fills the ruler's kitchen,
the sacrificial vessels supply the ancestral temples.
Now Your Majesty serves the ancestral temples,
though with utmost solemnity, abundance, and generosity,
still cannot use one part of the financial resources.
Just as the Court of State Ceremonial entertains guests,
the various foreign envoys,
even including the horse payments to the Huíhé,
using one part of the funds,
still leaves a great surplus.
Moreover, Your Majesty's imperial kitchen,
is extremely frugal and simple,
beyond what is used,
what is given to the hundred officials as salaries and meal allowances, etc.,
still cannot exhaust it.
Based on this,
the kitchen's expenses,
their amount is still small,
all are Your Majesty's rightful share.
Using it to repair ten palaces,
should not be doubted,
let alone a single beam."
The Emperor said:
"The classics say so,
but people have never mentioned it,"
and merely nodded.
Later, when estimating materials for building the Shénlóng Temple,
pine logs seventy chǐ long were needed.
Yánlíng memorialized:
"I recently in Tóng Prefecture,
inspected a valley,
where there were several thousand trees,
all seventy to eighty chǐ long."
Emperor Dézōng said:
"People say,
during the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras,
seeking five or six zhàng long timber nearby,
was still not easily obtained,
all had to be felled and prepared in Lán and Shèng Prefectures.
Why now is such timber available nearby?"
Yánlíng replied:
"Precious treasures and rare things for the worthy,
exist everywhere,
but appear only when encountering a sage ruler.
Now these trees grow near the capital region,
precisely because of the sage ruler,
how could the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo eras have had them?"
Yánlíng, being keen on harshness,
considered oppressing the people and flattering the ruler as achievements.
During memorials and audiences,
he freely indulged in bizarre and false statements,
what others dared not say,
Yánlíng said without hesitation,
also things people had never heard.
The Emperor quite wished to know external affairs,
so treated him with special favor.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Xuē Yíngzhēn
Yáo Nánzhòng was military governor of Zhèng-Huá.
At that time, the army supervisor Xuē Yíngzhēn relied on his power,
interfering and seizing military administration.
Nánzhòng did not comply,
and was repeatedly slandered to the Emperor by Yíngzhēn,
the Emperor became quite suspicious.
Later, Yíngzhēn sent a minor envoy Chéng Wùyíng,
riding swiftly to present a memorial accusing Nánzhòng of unlawful acts,
the slander and fabrication were severe.
Nánzhòng's deputy general Cáo Wénqià,
at the time was going to the capital to report matters.
He secretly learned the contents of Yíngzhēn's memorial,
Wénqià privately felt angry.
Thereupon, traveling day and night, he pursued Wùyíng,
reaching Chánglè Station,
caught up with him,
and stayed in the same lodging.
In the middle of the night, he killed Wùyíng.
Sank Yíngzhēn's memorial in the latrine.
Then committed suicide.
When the sun was high,
the station officer opened the door,
saw blood covering the ground.
Beside it were two letters from Wénqià,
one letter accusing Yíngzhēn of crimes;
one letter pleading Nánzhòng's innocence,
and also apologizing for killing Wùyíng.
Emperor Dézōng heard of the incident,
was quite shocked and moved.
"Shocked and moved" originally read "disagreeing and surprised,"
according to the Ming manuscript changed.
Nánzhòng, fearing deep trouble,
then went to court.
Upon arrival,
the Emperor said:
"Yíngzhēn harassed you greatly."
Nánzhòng said:
"Yíngzhēn did not harass me,
he himself undermined Your Majesty's laws.
With people like Yíngzhēn present,
even if Yáng and Dù were reborn,
to comfort the people,
command the three armies,
they certainly could not achieve benevolent parental governance,
or the discipline and good formations of an army."
Emperor Dézōng remained silent for a long time.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Painting a Vulture
Péi Yánlíng, relying on favor, was frivolous and rash,
his colleagues feared him,
only Gù Shǎolián did not avoid him.
Yánlíng once painted a vulture,
with a flock of birds clamoring at it.
He presented it,
Emperor Dézōng understood the public anger,
and trusted him even more.
From "Tán Bīn Lù"
Féng Dàomíng
Yǒng Táo
was a man of Shǔ.
He passed the imperial examination as a jìnshì.
Later, he gradually became distant from his relatives and friends.
His maternal uncle, Liú Jìngzhī of Yún'ān, having failed the imperial examinations,
returned to the mountains,
and had always been devoted to writing poetry.
He reproached Táo for not sending him letters, saying:
"Though the mountains near Héngyáng have few geese,
the waters connecting Bā and Shǔ surely have fish?"
Táo, upon receiving the poem, felt ashamed and blushed,
and only then did he have thoughts of sending a letter.
Later, when he served as Prefect of Jiǎnzhōu,
he compared himself to Xiè Xuānchéng and Liǔ Wúxīng.
When guests arrived, he would belittle and snub them,
and even the gatekeeper became negligent,
so those presenting their credentials rarely gained an audience.
Suddenly, a certain Féng Dàomíng, having failed the imperial examination, requested an audience, saying:
"I am an old acquaintance of the Attendant."
The gatekeeper reported Dàomíng's words to him,
and when he was admitted,
Táo scolded him:
"I have never met you before,
how can
"方" originally written as "妨",
corrected according to the Ming manuscript.
we be acquainted?"
Dàomíng said:
"I recite the Attendant's poems,
and admire the Attendant's virtue;
I see you daily in your poetry collection.
How can you say we have never met!"
He then recited:
"Standing amidst green grass, people see you first;
approaching white lotuses, the fish remain unaware."
He also said:
"The sound of the river enters the temple in autumn;
the dampness of rain invades the tower at night."
And also:
"With doors closed, guests arriving often suspect illness;
the courtyard full of blooming flowers does not seem like poverty."
Upon hearing the recitation, Táo was delighted,
and treated Dàomíng as an old friend.
Gentlemen considered Yǒng Jūn to be arrogant yet fond of flattery,
and Master Féng to seek recognition without genuine talent;
both were at fault.
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì"
Grand Master Dù Xuānyóu
"閩" originally written as "陶",
corrected according to "Yùquánzǐ"
was appointed from Mǐn to Xuānchéng,
through the influence of the palace eunuchs.
Each circuit annually presented castrated men,
the so-called "private whites",
with Mǐn being the foremost.
Moreover, many were appointed to positions.
Therefore, the hometowns of the great eunuchs and below
were mostly in Mǐn.
At the time, it was considered a breeding ground for eunuchs.
After Xuānyóu arrived at his post,
every Cold Food Festival,
he would dispatch officers and clerks,
carrying food and drink,
to make offerings at the tombs of the various eunuchs.
This was called "sweeping and cleaning",
hence he was nicknamed "the imperial envoy who tends graves".
From "Yùquánzǐ"
Lǐ Déyù
Lǐ Déyù governed Yángzhōu.
The supervising army commissioner, Yáng Qīnyì, was recalled to the capital,
and was certain to become a close minister in the Privy Council.
Yet Déyù treated him with ordinary courtesy,
not exceeding the usual norms,
which Qīnyì resented in his heart.
One day,
a banquet was set in the central hall,
with no other guests.
Several tables were arranged with precious vessels and paintings,
all of exceptional quality.
The service and hospitality throughout the banquet
were also extremely gracious.
After the banquet,
all these items were given to him as gifts.
Qīnyì was overjoyed beyond expectation.
Ten days later,
as he traveled west to Biànzhōu,
an edict ordered him back to supervise Huáinán.
Qīnyì immediately returned,
and presented all the previously gifted items back to Déyù.
Déyù laughed and said:
"These are not worth much;
why refuse them?"
He returned them all to him.
Qīnyì felt several times more grateful.
Later, Qīnyì indeed became the Commissioner of the Privy Council,
and the authority throughout Emperor Wǔzōng's reign of the Táng
was all due to Qīnyì.
From "Yōuxián Gǔchuī"
Hán Quánhuì
Emperor Zhāozōng of the Táng, because the eunuchs clung to power,
were arrogant and unruly, difficult to control,
often harbored intentions to eliminate them.
The chancellor Cuī Yìn was especially jealous and resentful.
The emperor instructed Yìn
that whenever he had a secret memorial,
he should present it in a sealed bag,
and not report it orally in the informal hall.
Thus, the eunuchs could not learn of them.
Hán Quánhuì and others then sought out several dozen beautiful women from the capital to present to the emperor,
secretly seeking to uncover palace intrigues.
The emperor did not realize this,
and Yìn's plans gradually leaked.
The eunuchs used heavy bribes and sweet words
to request military governors to serve as their shields,
regarding Cuī Yìn with eyes
"眥" originally written as "皆",
corrected according to "Běimèng Suǒyán"
filled with hatred.
At that time,
"時" originally written as "肘",
corrected according to the Ming manuscript.
during winter and summer festival gatherings,
they would face each other and shed tears,
their words fawning and obsequious.
When the people of Biàn invaded Tónghuà and learned of Cuī Yìn's plans,
Hán Quánhuì then led the imperial guards,
deployed troops in ambush,
and forced the emperor to flee to Fèngxiáng.
Later, Cuī Yìn conspired with Liáng Zǔ
to eliminate the eunuchs.
Not long after,
disaster also befell him,
leading to the extermination of his clan.
Discerning people blamed Cuī Yìn.
Earlier, his younger uncle, Cuī Ānqián, often said to his close ones:
"The one who will destroy our clan
is surely the 'black-robed child'."
"Black-robed child" was Yìn's childhood name.
Lǐ Kèyòng, the Prince of Jìn of Hédōng, upon hearing of Yìn's actions,
said to his advisors:
"The one who
"助" character originally missing,
supplemented according to "Běimèng Suǒyán".
aids the bandits in their cruelty,
must be Cuī Yìn.
The one who will ruin the state and destroy families
is surely this man."
From "Běimèng Suǒyán"
Sū Xún
At the end of the Táng dynasty,
Secretary Sū Xún was obsequious and opportunistic,
despised by Liáng Tàizǔ.
One day, he went to Bīngzhōu
to pay respects to the Prince of Jìn.
At that time, Zhāng Chéngyè was intent on restoring the dynasty.
Yet Xún suddenly presented the Prince of Jìn with a pair of painted imperial decree brushes,
making Chéngyè despise him even more.
From "Tángshū",
the Ming manuscript cites "Běimèng Suǒyán"
Sū Kǎi
Emperor Zhāozōng was initially posthumously honored as "Shèng Mù Jǐng Wén Xiào Huángdì",
with the temple name Zhāozōng.
The起居郎 Sū Kǎi and others disputed this,
requesting to change it to "Gōng Líng Zhuāng Mǐn Huángdì",
with the temple name Xiāngzōng.
Sū Kǎi
was the son of the Minister of Rites, Sū Xún.
In the second year of Qiánníng, he sat for the jìnshì examination.
Kǎi was unattractive in appearance
and moreover lacked virtue.
Emperor Zhāozōng disliked his undeserved advancement,
and personally demoted him.
From then on, he harbored resentment,
and took pleasure in the disasters of the state.
His father, Xún,
was treacherous and sycophantic,
with no good reputation at the time.
Thus, he curried favor to advance opportunistically.
Liáng Zǔ recognized his sinister and perverse nature,
grew increasingly displeased,
and he was greatly despised by Jìng Xiáng and Lǐ Zhèn.
When Liáng Zǔ established his reign title,
he issued an edict stating:
"Sū Kǎi, Gāo Yíxiū, and Xiāo Wénlǐ
are all unattractive in appearance
and should not defile the ranks of officials.
All are to be dismissed from their current posts
and sent back to their hometowns.
Sū Xún is ordered to retire."
The scholars of Héshuò
regarded Sū Kǎi as an owl or jìng among the gentry.
From "Běimèng Suǒyán"
Yuè Péngguī
According to old custom,
scholars did not associate with palace eunuchs.
The military commissioner of the Ten Armies, Tián Lìngzī, wielded the power to overturn heaven.
When Emperor Xīzōng of Táng was forced to flee,
and the procession reached Yángyuán,
the officials had not yet all assembled,
and there was a lack of someone to draft imperial proclamations.
The Vice-Minister Yuè Péngguī
also reached the temporary imperial residence.
He then paid a visit to the Palace Army Commander,
and still requested to serve both inside and outside the palace.
Because of this, he was recommended
to fill the post of Hanlin Academician.
Chancellor Zhāng Jùn, appointed from a retired scholar to the position of Qǐjūláng,
also came from Tián Lìngzī's patronage,
and both expressed respect for both inner and outer court affairs.
When the imperial carriage arrived in Shǔ,
the court officials had all gathered.
One day,
the Palace Army Commander held a banquet for the chancellor,
and the Academician along with Qǐjūláng Zhāng both attended.
Zhāng, ashamed to bow before the crowd,
first went to pay his respects to the Palace Army Commander.
He intended to express his gratitude for the wine in advance,
which surprised the Commander.
Soon the guests arrived,
and everyone took their seats.
The Commander announced to all the officials:
"I and the Qǐjūláng
are of different streams, clear and turbid.
I once received respect regarding both inner and outer affairs.
Since I fear being tainted,
why hesitate to make changes?
Today, secretly thanking for the wine
is not acceptable."
Zhāng was overwhelmed with shame and fear.
From then on, he was greatly despised by the talented crowd.
Yuè passed the imperial examinations,
and when first submitting his petition,
he paid a visit to Vice-Minister Lǐ Zhāo,
promoting himself by saying:
"Apart from the Nine Classics, historical texts, and the Lǎozǐ, Zhuāngzǐ, and the eight
"Eight" originally written as "line",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.
capitals rhapsodies,
I have authored eight hundred volumes of books.
I request a comparative examination."
He truly had learning,
but his draft proclamations were not very concise or appropriate.
Some people of the time did not approve of him.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Kǒng Qiān
In the early days of Later Táng Emperor Míngzōng's accession to the throne,
he executed the Tax Commissioner Kǒng Qiān, Guīdé
"Dé" originally written as "dé",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.
Army Jiedushi Yuán Xíngqīn, Dèngzhōu Jiedushi Wēn Tāo, Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent Duàn Níng, Biànzhōu Quwù Xīn Tíngwèi, Lǐ Jìxuān, and others.
Kǒng Qiān was a clerk in Wèizhōu,
and when Emperor Zhuāngzōng sought hegemony,
he supplied military provisions.
Kǒng Qiān contributed to this effort,
and later became the Tax Commissioner.
He curried favor with the emperor's favorites,
usurped the chancellor's power,
and focused entirely on extortion,
exploiting the people in countless ways,
