thus incurring public wrath and being executed.
Yuán Xíngqīn was a beloved general of Emperor Zhuāngzōng,
coming and going from the palace without restriction.
He had killed Emperor Míngzōng's son Cóngjǐng,
and for this was executed.
Duàn Níng served the Liáng,
advancing through flattery and deceit.
He rose to military governor,
and in his later years held military authority,
but surrendered helplessly to the court.
Wēn Tāo was vicious and cruel,
desecrating the imperial tombs of the Western Capital.
When Emperor Zhuāngzōng restored the dynasty,
he did not punish his crimes;
instead, Wēn Tāo bribed musicians and eunuchs heavily,
and both he and Duàn Níng were granted the imperial surname,
some even receiving command insignia.
Emperor Míngzōng listened to public opinion and executed them.
Xīn Tíngwèi was a subordinate general of Kāifēng Administrator Wáng Zàn.
During Zhū Yǒuzhēn's time,
Tíngwèi relied on Zàn's influence to pervert the law and disrupt governance,
earning the hatred of the people of Biàn.
Lǐ Jìxuān was the son of Biàn general Mèng Shěnchéng,
who fled and submitted to Emperor Zhuāngzōng.
Empress Liú adopted him as a son.
At that time, within the palace,
scandalous rumors spread.
These four villains
were despised by the emperor when he was still a prince for their conduct,
so he executed them all.
Emperor Zhuāngzōng avenged the Táng's disgrace,
and was hailed as a restorer of the dynasty.
Yet Wēn Tāo had destroyed and looted the imperial tombs,
and deserved severe punishment.
Instead, he was granted the imperial surname
and given military command.
From this, it is clear that the claim of restoration is false.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Zhào Yuánkǎi
Zhào Yuánkǎi was the Grand Commander of the Jiāohé Circuit Campaign.
At that time, Hóu Jūnjí was the commander-in-chief.
Jūnjí's horse had a sore on its forehead,
and Yuánkǎi dipped his finger in the pus and smelled it,
to flatter Jūnjí.
He was impeached by the censor,
and demoted to prefect.
From "Tán Bīn Lù".
Yán Zhīwēi
Táng Minister of Rites Yán Zhīwēi made peace with Mòchuò,
with Sībīnchéng Tián Guīdào as his deputy.
Upon reaching the tent,
Zhīwēi performed a dance,
bent down and hugged Mòchuò's boot, smelling its tip.
Tián Guīdào alone made a deep bow without prostrating.
Mòchuò was furious,
hung him upside down,
and left him there overnight.
The next day, he intended to kill him,
but Yuánzhēn advised:
"He is an envoy of a great kingdom for peace marriage;
killing him would be inauspicious."
Thus he was released.
Later, Guīdào argued with Zhīwēi in the court hall,
saying that Mòchuò would certainly not keep the peace,
while Zhīwēi stubbornly insisted on peace.
Mòchuò indeed rebelled,
capturing Zhào and Dìng.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān then executed Zhīwēi's entire clan,
and appointed Guīdào as Vice-Minister of War.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi".
Zhèng Yīn
Táng Vice-Minister of Personnel Zhèng Yīn first attached himself to Lái Jùnchén.
After Jùnchén was executed,
he attached himself to Zhāng Yìzhī.
After Yìzhī was killed,
he attached himself to Empress Wéi,
and later to Prince Qiáo.
He was eventually executed.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi".
Xuē Jì
Táng Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent Xuē Jì, Yōngzhōu Chief Administrator Lǐ Jìn, Secretariat Director Cuī Shí, Xiāo Zhìzhōng, Cén Xī, and others,
all outwardly displayed loyalty and integrity,
but inwardly harbored flattery and sycophancy.
They hunched their shoulders and held their breath,
licking hemorrhoids and breaking limbs,
currying favor with Princess Tàipíng.
They all soared high on the path of clouds,
each thinking they had achieved their ambitions,
as secure as Mount Tài.
On the third day of the seventh month,
their families were destroyed and they were killed.
How different is this from a wren nesting on reed flowers,
when a great wind suddenly rises,
the nest breaks and the eggs are destroyed.
Gentlemen of later times,
can you not take this as a warning!
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi".
Lǐ Qiáo
In the Tang Dynasty, Lǐ Qiáo was gifted with talent from a young age,
and his family passed down Confucian learning through generations.
He successively held the positions of Chancellor of the National University and Minister of Personnel,
three times participated in governance affairs,
and was enfeoffed as Duke of Zhèng.
In the third year of the Chángshòu era,
Empress Wǔ Zétiān requisitioned over 500,000 catties of copper from across the empire,
and over 1.3 million catties of iron,
as well as 20,000
("Wàn" originally written as "bǎi",
corrected according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
7,000 strings of cash.
Inside the Dìngdǐng Gate,
they cast an eight-sided bronze pillar,
ninety feet tall,
with a diameter of twelve feet.
It was inscribed with the words "The Celestial Pivot of the Great Zhōu, Proclaiming Virtue to All Nations."
It proclaimed the merits of the revolution,
and disparaged the virtue of the imperial house.
Beneath the Celestial Pivot, an iron mountain was placed,
with bronze dragons bearing the weight,
surrounded by lions and qílín.
Above, there was a cloud-shaped canopy,
on which coiled dragons were arranged,
supporting a fiery pearl.
The pearl was ten feet tall,
with a circumference of thirty feet,
radiant with golden brilliance,
its light rivaling the sun and moon.
Wǔ Sānsī composed the inscription for it,
and court officials who presented poems
were too numerous to count.
Only Lǐ Qiáo's poem was considered the best of the time.
The poem reads:
"The tracks of chariots shine in the western hills,
merits and achievements recorded in the northern Yān.
How does it compare to this gathering of all nations,
proclaiming virtue before the nine gates?
Brilliantly facing the Yellow Path,
stretching far into the purple mists.
The immortal plate drips dew,
the lofty pillar seeks to support heaven.
Mountains resemble clusters of clouds rising,
the pearl seems like a great fire suspended.
Voices flow, dust becomes kalpas,
deeds solidify, seas turn to fields.
The sage's grace pours like Yáo's wine,
the fragrant wind enters Shùn's strings.
Joyful to encounter a lower birth,
coinciding with the years of the supreme emperor."
Later, the Censorate exposed Lǐ Qiáo for currying favor with Wéi Shùrén,
and he was demoted to Vice Prefect of Chúzhōu.
Later, during the Kāiyuán era,
an edict was issued to destroy the Celestial Pivot,
sending laborers to melt it down,
but even after a full month, it was not completely destroyed.
Lǐ Xiūliè, the Magistrate of Luòyáng, then composed a poem to chant about it:
"At the eastern
(Ming manuscript copy has "zhōng" instead of "dōng")
end of Tiānmén Street, the Celestial Pivot topples,
urgently, the fiery pearl must first be removed.
Since a single silk thread can pull it,
why trouble two counties to demand men to push?"
Previously, there was a ballad that said:
"A single silk thread pulls the Celestial Pivot."
It meant that it would not last long,
hence Lǐ Xiūliè's poem alluded to it.
Common scholars all recited it.
To the north of the Celestial Pivot,
Wéi Shùrén later built another tower,
which was demolished earlier.
From "The New Account of the Great Táng"
Lǐ Yìfǔ
In the Táng Dynasty, Lǐ Yìfǔ appeared gentle and respectful in demeanor,
and when speaking with people,
he would always smile cheerfully,
yet he was narrow-minded, jealous, and treacherous.
Once in a position of power,
he wanted others to side with him,
and those who slightly opposed him would be framed and overthrown.
Thus, people at the time said that Lǐ Yìfǔ had a knife hidden behind his smile.
Yáng Xíngyǐng submitted a memorial detailing Lǐ Yìfǔ's crimes,
and an imperial order commanded Liú Xiángdào to jointly investigate the matter.
Lǐ Jī supervised the case,
and upon investigation, the accusations were substantiated.
He was exiled to Xīzhōu.
Some wrote: "Liú Xiángdào defeated the great thief of the copper mountain,
Lǐ Yìfǔ issued a public proclamation."
It said: "Mixing up slaves and maids and releasing them in disorder,
each recognizing their own home and competing to enter."
From "Records of Tán Bīn"
Hóu Sīzhǐ
In the Táng Dynasty, Hóu Sīzhǐ was impoverished
and unable to manage a livelihood,
so he attached himself to Gāo Yuánlǐ, a参军 of Héngzhōu.
He was unscrupulous and cunning,
unmatched by anyone.
At that time, Péi Zhēn, the Prefect of Héngzhōu, caned a判司.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān was about to act against the imperial house,
and those who fabricated charges were already active.
The判司 said to Hóu Sīzhǐ:
"Now, many of the princes have been executed;
why not accuse them?"
Hóu Sīzhǐ then requested a written accusation,
and accused Prince Shū and Péi Zhēn of plotting rebellion.
An imperial order was issued to investigate,
and both were executed along with their clans,
while Hóu Sīzhǐ was appointed as a游击将军.
Gāo Yuánlǐ, fearful, sought to flatter him,
invited him to sit together,
and addressed him as "Big Brother Hóu," saying:
"The state appoints people regardless of rank;
if someone says Big Brother Hóu is illiterate,
you can reply:
'The xièzhì beast is also illiterate,
yet it can gore the wicked.'"
Empress Wǔ Zétiān indeed said:
"I intend to make you a Censor,
but people say you cannot read."
Hóu Sīzhǐ responded with the xièzhì example,
and Empress Wǔ Zétiān was greatly pleased,
immediately appointing him.
Gāo Yuánlǐ further instructed him:
"The Holy Emperor knows Big Brother Hóu has no residence;
if she offers to lend you a confiscated official residence,
you should decline with thanks.
The Holy Emperor will surely ask why,
and you can reply:
'The residences of rebels and traitors,
I detest their names,
and do not wish to reside within them.'"
It happened as predicted,
and Empress Wǔ Zétiān was again greatly delighted,
bestowing generous favors and rewards.
From "Records of Tán Bīn"
Lú Cángyòng
Lú Cángyòng was summoned and appointed as Left Reminder,
then promoted to Vice Minister of Personnel and Secretariat Drafter.
He served as Vice Minister of the Imperial Secretariat,
concurrently as Academician of the Zhāowén Institute,
and transferred to Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
He was on friendly terms with Chén Bóyù and Zhào Zhēngù.
During his days as a recluse,
he often boasted of his integrity and purity,
traveling between the Shàoshì and Zhōngnán mountains,
earning him the contemporary nickname "fake recluse."
After joining the court,
he became extravagant, corrupt, and unrestrained,
with lavish carriages and attire.
He was obsequious and deceitful,
devoted solely to currying favor with the powerful.
Public opinion then exposed his disgraceful conduct.
For currying favor with Princess Tàipíng,
he was exiled to Lǒngzhōu.
From "Records of Tán Bīn"
Zhào Lǚwēn
In the Táng Dynasty, Zhào Lǚwēn served as Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries,
flattering and serving Princess Ānlè.
His influence could move mountains and seas,
his breath could change frost and snow.
Someone asked Zhāng Wénchéng:
"What kind of person is Minister Zhào?"
He replied:
"A rampant petty man.
His heart is flattering and treacherous,
his conduct perverse and arrogant.
He bows to powerful clans,
and licks the hemorrhoids of influential families.
Servile to those above,
haughty to those below.
Fierce as a raging tiger,
greedy as a starving wolf.
His nature loves to devour others,
but in the end, he will be devoured by others."
He seized commoners' fields and gardens for the princess,
constructing the "Dìngkūn Pond,"
claiming it would "rival the Son of Heaven's Kūnmíng Pond."
He used hundreds of millions in treasury funds.
With his purple robe hitched up askew,
he pulled the princess's golden calf-drawn carriage from behind.
Such were his treacherous and wicked deeds.
During the suppression of the rebellious Wéi faction,
the Emperor ascended the Chéngtiān Gate.
Zhào Lǚwēn feigned joy,
dancing and shouting "Long live!"
The Emperor ordered him beheaded,
swords and blades fell chaotically,
and he was executed along with his sons.
People each cut a slice of his flesh,
until his bones and flesh were completely gone.
From "Records of Affairs Within and Outside the Court"
Zhāng Jí
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān of the Táng dynasty,
Zhāng Jí flattered and served Preceptor Xuē.
He held up a yellow turban and followed behind Preceptor Xuē,
prostrating himself beside the horse to serve as a mounting block for Preceptor Xuē's stirrup.
Attendant Censor Guō Bà tasted the excrement of Lái Jùnchén,
and Sòng Zhīwèn held the chamber pot for Zhāng Yìzhī.
All of them sought favor through fawning and sycophancy,
truly they were criminals against the teachings of propriety.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Jí Xū
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
Jí Xū, a Tàicháng Academy Doctor,
had a father named Zhé,
who served as Governor of Yìzhōu,
and was sentenced to death for corruption.
Xū intercepted the Imperial Secretary, Prince Wèi Wǔ Chéngsì,
south of the Tiānjīn Bridge,
prostrating himself and declaring his crime deserving death.
Chéngsì asked him why,
and he said:
"I have two younger sisters fit to serve Your Highness."
Chéngsì agreed,
and they were brought in by ox-cart.
For three days they did not speak.
When Chéngsì asked the reason,
they replied:
"Our father violated the state's laws,
we are worried,
and have no peace of mind."
Chéngsì then secured a pardon sparing their father from execution.
He promoted Xū to Supervisor of the Imperial Stables,
and soon Xū was further promoted to Vice Minister of the Censorate and Vice Minister of Personnel.
His rise was not due to talent,
but through the request of his two sisters.
Original source missing;
the Míng dynasty manuscript states it is from "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Zōng Chǔkè
Zōng Chǔkè, Imperial Secretary under Empress Wǔ Zétiān of Táng, had a sycophantic and flattering nature.
At that time, Preceptor Xuē enjoyed favor akin to Lào'ǎi,
so Chǔkè composed a two-volume biography for him,
discussing Preceptor Xuē's sageliness,
claiming he descended from heaven,
and his origins were unknown from which era.
He was like Śākyamuni reborn,
or Guānyīn returning to life.
Within a year,
Chǔkè rose to the position of Imperial Secretary.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Cuī Róng
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign, Prince Liáng Wǔ Sānsī of Táng composed a biography for Zhāng Yìzhī,
claiming he was the reincarnation of Prince Zǐ Jìn,
and established a shrine for him on Gōushì Mountain.
Literary talents and sycophants wrote poems praising him,
among them, Secretariat Drafter Cuī Róng was the foremost.
Later, when Yìzhī's entire clan was executed,
the sycophants were all exiled to Lǐngnán.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Cuī Shí
Cuī Shí, son of Cuī Yì of Táng,
Huán Jìng, fearing slander from Wǔ Sānsī,
recruited Shí as his eyes and ears.
Shí, however, secretly reported Huán Jìng's plans to Sānsī,
and soon became Secretariat Director.
Shí further advised Sānsī
to kill all five princes,
eliminating any hope of their return.
Previously, Shí served as Vice Minister of War,
while his father Yì was Vice Minister of Rites.
Father and son both held vice-ministerial positions in the Southern Department,
something unprecedented
since the establishment of the Táng dynasty.
Shàngguān Zhāoróng frequently went out,
and Shí flattered and attached himself to her.
After Emperor Xuánzōng executed Xiāo Zhìzhōng,
the authorities reported: "The palace woman Yuán shì confessed
that she and Shí had secretly plotted to administer poison."
Shí was then ordered to commit suicide,
at the age of forty.
Initially, Shí had a feud with Zhāng Yuè.
When Yuè became Secretariat Director,
commentators believed Yuè had framed him.
Shí was handsome in appearance,
and gained a reputation for talent early on.
His younger brothers Yè and Dí, and his cousin Lì,
were all accomplished in literature,
and held prestigious and important positions.
During private banquets,
he compared his family to the Wáng and Xiè clans.
He told people:
"My family background, initial appointment, and official career
have always been first-rate.
A true man should seize key positions to control others,
how can he silently be controlled by others!"
Thus he pursued advancement relentlessly,
but did not meet a good end.
Furthermore, Shí flattered and served Zhāng Yìzhī and the commoner consort Wéi.
After Wéi was executed,
he attached himself to Tàipíng Princess.
He enjoyed favor like Féng Zǐdū and Dǒng Yǎn.
His wife was beautiful,
and both she and his two daughters were presented to the crown prince's palace,
enabling him to become Vice Director of the Secretariat and Participating in Determining Governmental Matters.
A placard was posted about him:
"Placing mediocre talent in the prince's residence,
presenting seductive women to the spring palace."
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Employing Foreign Generals
When Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng first ascended the throne,
he employed Guō Yuánzhèn and Xuē Nè;
eight years later he employed Zhāng Jiāzhēn and Zhāng Yuè;
five years later Dù Xiān was promoted;
three more years and Xiāo Sōng was promoted;
twelve more years and Lǐ Shìzhī was promoted.
All were great generals directly appointed to the three highest offices.
Lǐ Línfǔ, having learned from the troubles with Shìzhī,
then changed the old system.
He requested that foreigners be appointed as generals,
wishing to consolidate his own power.
He once memorialized to the Emperor:
"With Your Majesty's heroic talent,
combined with the state's wealth and strength,
the reason the various foreign tribes remain unsubdued
is because civilian officials serve as generals,
they are timid and cowardly, unfit for military affairs.
If Your Majesty truly wishes to destroy the barbarians on all sides,
and awe the land within the seas,
there is none better than military officers,
and among military officers, none better than foreign generals.
Foreign generals are born with fierce spirits,
raised on horseback from youth,
seeking battle on the front lines as they grow,
this is their innate nature.
If Your Majesty shows them favor and appoints them as generals,
making them willing to die for you,
then the barbarians will not be difficult to subdue."
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
First he employed Ān Lùshān,
Ān Lùshān achieved merit;
he employed Gēshū Hàn for his bravery;
he employed Ān Sīshùn for his military ability;
he employed Gāo Xiānzhī for his skill in warfare.
Lùshān ultimately became the leader of the rebellion,
this was Línfǔ's crime.
From "Records of Tán Bīn"
Zhāng Yuè
Zhāng Yuè, Duke of Yān of Táng,
was a sycophantic man.
Previously, as Governor of Bìngzhōu,
he flattered and served the Specially Advanced Wáng Máozhòng.
He presented him with gold and treasures,
countless in number.
Later, when Máozhòng was touring the border,
he met Yuè at a grand banquet in the Tiānxióng Army.
As the wine flowed freely,
an imperial edict suddenly arrived:
appointing him Minister of War and Joint Manager of Affairs with the Secretariat-Chancellery.
After Yuè bowed in gratitude,
he immediately took Máozhòng's hand and danced,
and even smelled the tip of his boot.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Chéng Bóxiàn
General Gāo Lìshì of Táng enjoyed special favor and宠爱 from Emperor Xuánzōng.
When his father died,
Left Imperial Guards General-in-Chief Chéng Bóxiàn and Junior Palace Superintendent Féng Shàozhèng,
went directly before the funeral,
loosened their hair and wept,
more grievously than for their own kin.
The court and the public heard of this,
and could not help but laugh.
From "Records of Tán Bīn"
Yáng Guózhōng
Emperor Xuánzōng said to his attending ministers:
"I wish to do something
that no emperor in history has ever done.
I intend to abdicate the throne to Sùzōng."
When the edict was issued,
Yáng Guózhōng was greatly terrified,
and his speech became incoherent.
Returning home, he said to the Yáng sisters:
"Ladies,
what need is there for us to continue living?
If the Crown Prince assumes regency,
my sisters and I will surely die."
They gathered together and wept.
Lady Guó entered to conspire with the Noble Consort.
The Consort, holding earth in her mouth, pleaded
and the matter was halted.
Gēshū Hàn was at Tóngguān,
and some advised him to request Yáng Guózhōng's execution
to please the masses,
but Gēshū Hàn did not listen.
Ān Lùshān set out from Fànyáng,
and every day before his tent he sighed, saying:
"Yáng Guózhōng's head,
why does it come so slowly!"
Yáng Guózhōng's wife, Péi Róu,
was a great courtesan of Shǔ.
Yáng Guózhōng also served as the military governor of Jiànnán.
He urged Emperor Xuánzōng to enter Shǔ,
appointed his relatives to office,
and spread them throughout Shǔ and Hàn.
From the Tán Bīn Lù.
Tàizhēn Consort
The Tàizhēn Consort once, due to jealousy,
spoke words that offended the Emperor.
The Emperor was extremely angry.
He ordered Gāo Lìshì to send her back to her family in a curtained carriage.
The Consort, remorseful and weeping bitterly,
took a knife and cut off her hair,
handing it to Gāo Lìshì, saying:
"Pearls, jade, and rare treasures,
are all bestowed by His Majesty,
and are insufficient as an offering.
Only this hair is given by my parents,
and can convey my feelings.
I hope you will express even a ten-thousandth part of my sincere longing and devotion."
When the Emperor received the hair,
he shed tears and was moved.
The character "潣" was originally missing,
and is supplemented based on the Ming manuscript.
Thus.
He immediately ordered Gāo Lìshì to summon her back.
From the Guìfēi Zhuàn.
The Ming manuscript states it is from the Kāiyuán Zhuàn,
and is also seen in the Kāitiān Chuánxìn Jì.
Lǐ Línfǔ
When Emperor Xuánzōng was in the Eastern Capital,
there were strange occurrences in the palace.
The next day,
he summoned the chancellors,
intending to travel west.
Péi Yàoshān and Zhāng
"Zhāng" originally written as "Xī",
corrected according to the Guóshǐ Bǔ.
Qūjiāng advised:
"The common people have not yet finished their harvests in the fields and gardens;
please wait until winter."
At that time,
Lǐ Línfǔ had just been appointed chancellor.
Secretly knowing the Emperor's intention,
after the audience ended,
he pretended to walk with a limp.
The Emperor asked:
"Why do you have a foot ailment?"
He replied:
"Your servant is not ill in the foot,
but wishes to report matters alone."
He then said that the two capitals are Your Majesty's eastern and western palaces.
If you wish to travel there,
why choose a time?
If it hinders harvesting,
simply exempt the road taxes.
Your servant requests to announce to the relevant offices,
and depart west today."
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
From then on, he traveled to Cháng'ān,
and never went east again.
Within ten days,
Yàoqīng and Jiǔlíng were both dismissed,
and Niú Xiānkè was promoted.
From the Guóshǐ Bǔ.
Also, Lǐ Línfǔ held the chancellorship for nineteen years,
eliminating men of reputation throughout the land.
From the Crown Prince down,
none dared not hold their breath in fear.
In the early Kāiyuán period,
Yáo, Sòng, and a few other senior ministers
often offered advice on governance,
contending for the greater good of the empire.
Once the empire was well-governed,
the Emperor's mind was also at ease.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng was promoted by the Emperor,
but was somewhat looked down upon as a junior.
Jiǔlíng was especially outspoken,
frequently offending the Emperor,
and the Emperor angrily dismissed him.
The Emperor, with his great talent and broad-mindedness,
trusted people without suspicion.
Later, he obtained Lǐ Línfǔ,
who nurtured the Emperor's desires,
never speaking words that grated on the ears,
and the Emperor loved him.
Thus, the Emperor secluded himself in high comfort,
enjoying his wealth and honor.
Ministers and below
rarely had audiences,
and matters great and small
were entrusted to Lǐ Línfǔ.
Although Lǐ Línfǔ was not cultured,
he was astute in administrative affairs,
strictly upholding laws and regulations.
Officials not following the usual path
had no means of advancement.
Yet he was treacherous and ruthless,
never showing favor or dislike in his expression.
Even the Emperor's attendants, down to cooks and servants,
were all bribed by him,
so he knew of every movement.
When Lǐ Shìzhī first became chancellor,
he was careless and not discreet,
and Lǐ Línfǔ betrayed him.
He then said:
"At the foot of Huàshān, there is a gold mine.
Mining it could enrich the state.
The Emperor does not yet know of it."
Shìzhī thought his words good,
and another day,
casually reported it,
and the Emperor was pleased.
He then consulted Lǐ Línfǔ,
who said:
"Your servant has known of it for a long time.
But Huàshān is Your Majesty's life-mountain,
the location of the royal aura,
and must not be disturbed.
Therefore, your servant dared not speak of it."
The Emperor then looked down upon Shìzhī.
And said:
"From now on, when reporting matters,
first discuss them with Lǐ Línfǔ,
and do not be rash."
From then on, Shìzhī was restrained.
Those not introduced by him
were all executed on charges.
His authority shook the land,
and remonstrance officials merely held their salaries and maintained their positions,
none daring to discuss affairs.
Only the supplementary official Dù Zhōngyóu submitted two memorials again.
The next day,
he was demoted to magistrate of Xiàguī.
Lǐ Línfǔ summoned the remonstrance officials and said:
"Now, with a wise ruler above,
ministers should follow and assist without delay;
what need is there for many words?
Have you not seen the ceremonial horses?
Silent all day,
they eat third-grade fodder;
but once they neigh,
they are dismissed.
Even if they wish to neigh again,
how could they?"
Thus, the path of remonstrance was cut off.
In his later years, he had many enemies,
and feared retaliation.
He went out with a large carriage and attendants,
with imperial guards clearing the streets,
and a vanguard a hundred paces ahead.
At home, he built walls with bricks
and covered them with wooden boards.
His family guarded him
as if against a great enemy.
Such were his self-protective measures.
According to precedent,
chancellors rode with only
three to five attendants.
Commoners did not avoid them on the road.
But now, he rode with over a hundred attendants,
forming left and right wings,
and officials below the highest rank hurried to avoid him—
this began with Lǐ Línfǔ.
From the Tán Bīn Lù.
Wáng Chéngxiū
Wáng Chéngxiū was a eunuch of the Later Shǔ ruler Wáng Yǎn.
The Later Ruler favored him for his amusing jokes and intimate familiarity.
He was handsome,
and often attended the young ruler while he slept and rested,
eventually monopolizing his favor.
Chéngxiū frequently used depraved and obscene matters to flatter his lord,
and the lord favored him even more.
He and Hán Zhāo were sworn friends,
and their schemes always complemented each other.
One day, Chéngxiū requested to select strong soldiers from the various armies,
obtaining several thousand brave and fierce men,
who were named the Dragon Martial Army.
Chéngxiū himself became their commander,
and they were specially granted extra clothing and rations,
receiving generous daily provisions.
He then requested to be appointed Military Commissioner of Qínzhōu,
and said:
"I wish to gather beauties for Your Majesty in Qínzhōu.
Moreover, it is said that the local conditions of Qínzhōu
produce many women of surpassing beauty.
I further request Your Majesty to visit Tiānshuǐ."
The young ruler was very pleased,
and immediately sent him with authority to take up his post.
All the selected elite troops of the Dragon Martial Army
served as his guard and accompanied him.
Upon arriving at his regional command and taking up his post,
he immediately dismantled the government office courtyard that very day,
conscripted laborers to gather timber and stone,
and built a new official residence and governor's mansion,
making it entirely in the style of a palace.
Moreover, with severe punishments and harsh laws,
even women were not exempt from construction labor.
He also secretly ordered the forcible seizure of young people from among the commoners,
Ming manuscript note: 'young people' is written as 'young women'.
to have them taught singing, dancing, and musical arts.
Those who were captured
had their portraits painted by artists and their names recorded,
and were urgently sent by courier to Hán Zhāo.
Zhāo then secretly presented them to the young ruler.
When the young ruler saw them,
he could not help but become wildly excited.
He then decided on the plan to visit Qín,
and consequently issued an edict stating:
"We have heard that former kings conducted inspection tours,
observing the hardships and ease of the land,
and successive generations made provincial inspections,
to comfort the expectations of the common people.
The western region of Qín, its territory
lies far in the borderlands.
Our late father the emperor delineated these rivers and mountains,
campaigning year after year,
and although they have submitted to royal rule,
the gentle breeze of beneficence has not yet permeated them.
Now farming has been established for years.
The soldiers and people have rather expressed their hope for a royal visit,
to thereby pacify the border regions.
We shall therefore deliberate on a provincial inspection,
and We have selected the third day of the tenth month this year to visit Qínzhōu.
This is announced to all within and without the court,
so that all may hear of it."
Because of this, urgent remonstrances from both inside and outside the court were disregarded.
The Empress Dowager wept to stop him,
even to the point of refusing food.
The former Administrative Assistant of the Qínzhōu Military Commissioner, Pú Yǔqīng, kowtowed before his horse until he wept blood,
and submitted a memorial of remonstrance saying:
"Your servant has heard that Yáo had a drum for courageous remonstrance,
Shùn had a pillar for criticism,
Tāng had officials who pointed out faults,
and Zhōu had a drum of warning and caution.
This is because the enlightened rulers of antiquity,
who were able to fully realize the Way of the Emperor,
wishing to know their own faults,
sought to accept honest words.
They would summon blame and reproach themselves,
hoping thereby to govern the people and cultivate virtue.
Since Your Majesty inherited the ancestral temple and received the registry,
assuming the rightful position under Heaven,
You have loved to hear loyal words that grate on the ear,
and have often risked offending Your countenance with straightforward admonition.
Moreover, our late father the emperor started his rise in Xǔchāng,
and began his ascent in Làngyuàn,
enduring hardships amidst chaos and obscurity,
facing dangers in times of fierce contention.
His hands and feet were calloused from armor and weapons,
he slept and woke amidst wind and frost,
he exerted military force to capture enemies on the plains,
and established battle merits to pacify many strongholds.
He sacrificed his life,
served his lord and aided the king with diligence,
only then was he able to establish his family,
and ultimately found the state.
Today the great foundation is vast and flourishing,
the grand enterprise is mighty and lofty.
The territory reaches Yōng and Liáng,
the borders connect north and south.
Virtue reaches Wú and Yuè,
authority pacifies the barbarian frontiers.
Commanderies and prefectures are quite numerous,
passes and rivers gradually expand.
The people are elegant and beautiful,
the land is prosperous and splendid.
In an age when the empire was torn asunder,
he accomplished the enterprise of a dragon's rise for ten thousand generations.
Your Majesty was born into wealth and honor,
and obtained the world without effort.
But You only delight in pleasure and amusement,
giving no thought to critical changes.
Your servant wishes that Your Majesty
would use the teachings of reputation to restrain Yourself,
and use ritual and music to guard Yourself.
Follow the norms of the Way and virtue,
receive the instruction of teachers and mentors.
Know that the altars of state are not easily maintained,
and think of how difficult farming is.
Cherish the foundation established by the High Ancestor,
and emulate Tàizōng in governing.
Esteem the worthy and be indifferent to beauty,
and be diligent and earnest in heart.
Do not listen to unsubstantiated words,
do not employ plans that have not been consulted upon.
Listen to the five notes and accept remonstrance,
use the three mirrors to reflect upon Yourself.
Rest less in the various forest pavilions,
read more of the classics and histories of former kings.
Cultivate superior virtue separately,
to plan for the distant future.
Do not let Yourself be deluded by sensual pleasures,
nor let wine confuse You.
Always attend to affairs of government personally,
and do not indulge in idle wandering.
Your servant has privately heard that Your Majesty wishes to leave Chéngdū,
to go on an inspection tour of the border fortifications.
Moreover, Tiānshuǐ is a distant place,
with steep and treacherous terrain difficult to travel.
Dangerous plank roads lean against the clouds,
perilous peaks pierce the Milky Way.
A light rain will cause the gallery roads to collapse,
a little mud will make the mountain paths slippery and obstructed.
How can the imperial carriage bells be sounded there?
How can the charioteer be urged on?
Furthermore, the enemy capital is close at hand,
the border towns are desolate and bleak.
The people are intermingled with barbarian tribes,
the land is full of miasmic vapors.
There are no other splendid sights or unusual scenery,
no place to select for scenic beauty or seek seclusion.
The sound of the Lǒng River is mournful,
the melody of the barbarian reed pipe is choked with sobs.
The camps contain only armored soldiers,
the city walls are manned by people who sleep with their weapons.
Watching for enemy scouts on solitary peaks,
they are suspicious and anxious every morning.
Observing signal flags on steep ridges,
they are on guard every day.
This is a land of many mountains and abundant rivers,
precisely a place easily stirred and difficult to pacify.
The Màijī Cliff offers nothing worth longing for,
how can the Mǐgǔ Gorge be considered comparable?
Ming manuscript note: 'comparable' is written as 'like'.
The roads encounter sighing mountains,

It is the land where Duke Mù of Qín corralled horses,

Therefore, when one person travels,
a hundred officials follow in attendance,
a thousand groups gather like mist,
ten thousand masses move like shooting stars.
The prefectures and counties along the route will be devastated,

finding lodging will still be difficult,

Even if arrangements are made from within,

Considering this discussion,
it is not fitting to act lightly.
It is like a black dragon emerging from the sea,

How can one expect the waves to be calm and the wind tranquil?
One will surely see seedlings injured and crops damaged.
Therefore, the imperial carriage must halt,

Moreover, in recent years the imperial carriage
only went as far as Shānnán,
and still did not involve mobilizing troops.
This time, going all the way to Tiānshuǐ,

Ever since we initially captured the city of Liángyuán,
plundered the population of Yìníng,
those whose wrists were cut off were not few,

This not only stirred the hearts of those people,

Now we are not far from the Luò capital,
and they will hear again of the imperial carriage coming.
If they have premeditated schemes,
then we must immediately launch a punitive campaign.
Moreover, Fèngxiáng has long been an advancing enemy,
and must harbor treacherous plots.
I deeply fear that baselessly concocting sinister words
may lead to the creation of conflicts and rifts.
Moreover, Your Majesty has just begun to establish friendly relations with the Tang ruler,
with tokens of trust and gifts exchanged back and forth.
Yet I worry that upon hearing of Your Majesty’s personal journey,
he may harbor suspicion and jealousy,
and will surely specially dispatch an envoy
to request a meeting with Your Majesty at the border for an alliance.
I am uncertain whether Your Majesty’s person should go or not?
If you go, it would resemble the struggle for supremacy between Qin and Zhao,
where neither side could easily yield;
if you do not go,
it would immediately be akin to the discord between Lu and Wei.
Warfare would soon arise.
Considering what has not yet sprouted,
anticipating what may come first.
I beseech Your Majesty to ponder this.
Your servant has heard that since ancient times, emperors and kings
toured the provinces and inspected the domains,
comforted the people and punished the guilty,
displayed righteousness and observed customs,
and only then returned to the ninefold palace,
bringing peace to the myriad clans.
Now, Your Majesty has repeatedly traveled,
yet I have not heard of a single edict or decree.
It is merely traversing mountains and rivers,
driving and galloping

Broad-minded and magnanimous,

How can you bear to let the ancestral teachings be severed?

the Way cut off,

Your Majesty, blessed by fortune for a thousand years,

Civil virtue and martial prowess,

Examination surpassing Shùn,
benevolence exceeding Tāng.
All virtues complete,

Intelligent and broadly knowledgeable,

I wish Your Majesty
Would slightly open the path of remonstrance,

The Later Ruler ultimately did not heed this.

On the third day of the tenth month,
They departed from Chéngdū,

He said:
"I just want to personally witness the battle,

Ascending Zǐtóng Mountain,
The Young Ruler composed a poem:
"Tall cliffs cluster with cold mist,

Looking down upon Éméi Ridge,

it was already heard that the eastern army had captured Gùzhèn.
Within ten days,
news came again of the defeated troops from Jīnniú,
blocking the gorge as they arrived.
At that time, the Shǔ army numbered over a hundred thousand,
stretching over a thousand lǐ from Miánhàn to Shēndù,
forming a continuous line from front to rear,
yet none had the heart to fight the enemy.
When envoys were sent to press them,
they turned their spears and stabbed, saying:
"Summon the Lóngwǔ Army to fight.
Not only are they brave,
but they also receive extra provisions and supplies.
We have been selected out as unfit;
how can we fight?"
Truly, there was no other choice.
On the twenty-ninth day of the tenth month, they retreated in disarray.
Through the perilous plank roads, steep ravines, and deep valleys,
traveling day and night without rest,
they returned to Chéngdū.
Kāng Yánxiào and Prince Wèi followed closely behind,
and the young ruler then surrendered.
Before the eastern army entered,
Wáng Zōngbì killed Hán Zhāo, the Privy Councilor Sòng Guāngsì, Jǐng
Note: The characters "sì jǐng" were missing in the original,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition.
Rùnchéng, the Xuānhuīzhōu
Note: The Míng manuscript lacks the character "zhōu."
Commissioner Lǐ Zhōulù, Ōuyáng Miǎn
Note: The Míng manuscript writes "Miǎn" as "Huǎng."
and others.
Wáng Chéngxiū held a strong army in Tiānshuǐ,
yet did not raise a weapon.
Upon learning that the eastern army had entered Shǔ,
he gathered his troops and over ten thousand women and children,
along with gold, silver, silk, and cloth,
and bought passage back to Shǔ from the western tribes.
Along the way, they were plundered by the tribes,
and traversing streams and mountains,
they froze, starved, and trampled each other to death.
By the time they reached Shǔ,
only a little over a hundred remained,
and only he and Tián Zōngruì, among others, escaped and arrived.
Prince Wèi sent someone to question him, saying:
"You personally commanded a strong army;
why did you not fight?"
He replied:
"I feared Your Highness's divine might
and dared not face your vanguard."
The prince asked:
"Why did you not surrender earlier?"
He replied:
"Because the royal army had not entered our territory,
and there was no way to submit."
The prince asked:
"How many people traveled with you when you first entered the tribal lands?"
He replied:
"Over ten thousand."
"How many remain now?"
He replied:
"Only about a hundred."
Prince Wèi said:
"You must repay the lives of those ten thousand."
And so, he had them all executed.
The Shǔ army did not fight,
and their downfall came without resistance,
largely due to the actions of Wáng Chéngxiū and Hán Zhāo.
Few people knew of this.
From the "Wángshì Wénjiàn Lù."
The Governor of Yìzhōu
In the Táng dynasty, Yìzhōu annually presented mandarin oranges,
each wrapped in paper.
Once, the governor found this disrespectful
and replaced the paper with fine cloth.
Later, he constantly worried that the oranges might be damaged by the cloth,
and each year he was filled with anxiety.
Suddenly, an imperial censor named Gān Zǐbù arrived.
The governor thought he was investigating the cloth-wrapped oranges matter
and was greatly frightened, saying:
"It is indeed being investigated."
When Zǐbù arrived at the post station,
the governor explained that wrapping oranges in cloth was a sign of respect.
Zǐbù initially did not understand,
but after a while, he realized the misunderstanding.
Those who heard of it could not help but laugh.
Zǐbù was studious,
possessed literary talent,
and was well-known in his time.
From the "Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ."
Xiāo Yǐngshì
In the early Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
Xiāo Yǐngshì traveled to Língchāng.
He went as far as twenty lǐ south of Zuòxiàn.
There was a Hú inn,
and many people at the inn were surnamed Hú.
Yǐngshì departed from the county late in the day,
and the county officials feasted him for a long time.
It was nearly dusk when he set out.
Three to five lǐ south of the county,
it grew completely dark.
A woman of about twenty-four or twenty-five,
wearing a red blouse and green skirt,
rode a donkey,
with clothes on the donkey,
spoke to Yǐngshì:
"My home is directly south, twenty lǐ away.
Now, returning at night,
traveling alone is frightening.
I wish to ride alongside you."
Yǐngshì asked the woman her surname.
She replied:
"Surname Hú."
Yǐngshì had often heard tales of wild foxes
that could take the form of men
or women,
seducing people at dusk.
Suspecting this woman was a wild fox,
he spat and scolded her:
"You dead wild fox,
dare to seduce Xiāo Yǐngshì!"
He then whipped his horse and galloped south,
rushing to the host's inn,
where he rested and removed his clothes.
After a while,
he heard a woman
leading a donkey through the gate.
The old innkeeper asked:
"Why are you traveling so late at night?"
She replied:
"Traveling late is one thing,
but I just encountered a mad scholar
who called me a wild fox
and nearly spat me to death."
The woman was the innkeeper's daughter.
Yǐngshì could only feel ashamed.
From the "Biànyí Zhì."
Xī Áng
In the Táng dynasty, Xī Áng was good friends with Wéi Zhì.
While discussing the dynasty's chancellors,
they wondered who was the most virtueless.
Áng mistakenly replied:
"Wéi Ānshí."
Then, startled, he ran away.
On the street, he met Jí Wēn.
Wēn asked why he was in such a panic.
He replied:
"Just now, while discussing with Minister Wéi which chancellor was the most virtueless,
I meant to say Jí Xū,
but mistakenly said Wéi Ānshí."
After saying this,
he whipped his horse and rode off again,
arriving at Chancellor Fáng's residence.
Fáng Guǎn held his hand and comforted him,
but Áng again mistakenly named Fáng Róng.
Áng was once highly regarded,
but in one day, he offended three people.
The entire court sighed in regret,
and only Wéi Zhì severed ties with him.
From the "Guó Shǐ Bǔ."
Administrator Zhāng
Lǐ Huí, the magistrate of Línjì County in the Táng dynasty,
had a wife, née Zhāng.
Her father was the senior administrator of Lúzhōu,
who had retired due to old age.
Because Huí treated his daughter poorly,
he went to Línjì to berate him,
but mistakenly arrived at Quánjié County.
He asked the gatekeeper:
"Is the magistrate in?"
The gatekeeper said, "He is."
Zhāng then entered to the front of the hall
and began shouting insults.
Zhào Zǐyú, the magistrate of Quánjié, did not know the reason,
so he secretly peeked through the door
and saw an old man cursing incessantly.
In the county, there were often foxes causing
trouble,
so Zhāng was mistaken for a fox.
He secretly summoned his officers to seize and whip him.
Zhāng still did not realize
and continued cursing recklessly.
Only when he was beaten to exhaustion
did they ask who he was,
daring to curse like this.
He then said, "I am Lǐ Huí's father-in-law.
Huí mistreats my daughter,
so I came to vent my anger on him."
Only then did the Quánjié magistrate realize his mistake.
He placed him in a guesthouse
and provided medical treatment.
Zhāng's servant fled at night to Línjì
and reported to Huí.
Huí was furious
and dispatched several hundred officers
to attack Quánjié and assault the magistrate.
The magistrate, frightened,
closed the gates and defended himself.
Huí then went to the commandery to lodge a complaint.
The grand administrator summoned the magistrate and reprimanded him,
but forgave his mistake.
He ordered him to pay two hundred thousand coins to Senior Administrator Zhāng to reconcile.
Huí then welcomed him to the county,
and Zhāng was pleased with Huí's retaliation.
In the end, he did not mention Huí mistreating his daughter
and returned home.
From *Jì Wén*
Xiāo Fǔ
In the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Xiāo Fǔ had just passed the imperial examination.
At that time, the imperial physician Wáng Yànbó lived in Tàipíng Ward,
next door to the supervising secretary Zhèng Yúndá.
Fǔ suddenly fell ill with chills and fever,
so he went early to Yànbó's residence seeking diagnosis,
but mistakenly entered Yúndá's house.
It happened that the gatekeeper was away,
and Yúndá was standing in the central courtyard.
Fǔ hurried forward and said:
"I have recently passed the examination,
and have duties for the scheduled gathering,
but suddenly fell ill."
He described his symptoms in detail.
Yúndá ordered a servant to invite him to sit,
then felt his pulse and said:
"According to the pulse,
this is a heart-related heat wind.
My surname is Zhèng.
If you are looking for the imperial physician Wáng Yànbó,
he is the neighbor to the east."
Fǔ blushed with embarrassment and left.
From *Gàn Zǎizi*
Cuī Qīng
In the Táng dynasty, Cuī Qīng was appointed prefect of Háozhōu,
replacing Lǐ Xùn.
Qīng took leave from Vice Minister of Revenue Lǐ Xùn,
who asked him to stay and chat.
Qīng pointed to the man he was replacing, Lǐ Xùn, and said:
"I have no idea why Lǐ Xùn simply doesn't understand about leaving office."
He repeated this several times.
Xùn said:
"Lǐ Xùn is right here,
it's just that he alone doesn't meet your expectations."
Only then did Qīng realize his mistake,
and left in shame.
From *Jiā Huà Lù*
Hé Rúliàng
The Táng dynasty presented scholar Hé Rúliàng came from an outer prefecture to the capital
to visit his paternal uncle.
He mistakenly went to the residence of Vice Director Zhào Xū,
claiming to be his nephew from the same branch of the family.
It happened to be the Winter Solstice,
and Xū was preparing a family banquet.
In haste,
he said:
"Since we are of the same branch,
let him join the banquet."
All the aunts, sisters, wives, and children were present.
After Rúliàng finished eating,
he slowly left.
Upon closer inspection,
they realized he was a son of the Hé family,
and Xū laughed heartily.
Rúliàng did not dare to go out for over a year.
People in the capital at the time
thus called him Hé Xū, the Vice Director.
From *Guó Shǐ Bǔ*
Yú Dí
Táng dynasty Minister of Works Yú Dí thought the musical piece *Xiǎng Fū Lián* (Longing for the Husband)
had an inelegant name
and intended to change it.
A guest laughed and said:
"In the Southern Dynasties, the chancellor's residence
once had auspicious lotuses,
so the song was called *Xiàng Fǔ Lián* (Chancellor's Residence Lotus).
Later generations corrupted the pronunciation."
So he did not change it.
From *Guó Shǐ Bǔ*
Also, according to an old saying,
at Dǒng Zhòngshū's tomb,
disciples upon arrival
would all dismount from their horses.
It was called 'Xiàmǎlíng' (Dismount Mound),
but the pronunciation was corrupted to 'Hámálíng' (Toad Mound).
Now, people in Jīngxiāng
call 'dī' (embankment) 'tí';
people in Liújiàng
call 'fǔ' (cauldron) 'fù'.
According to *Guó Shǐ Bǔ*, it should be 'people in Jìnjiàng',
'call 'léng' (ridge) 'shēng'',
people in Guānzhōng call 'dào' (rice) 'tǎo',
call 'fǔ' (cauldron) 'fù',
so there are omissions and errors here.
These are all corruptions from habitual usage.
From *Guó Shǐ Bǔ*
Yuàn Zhòu
Táng dynasty Minister Péng Zhòu was stationed in Jiānglíng
and had an old acquaintance with Yuàn Lùn.
After Lùn passed the examination,
they never met again,
only communicating by letters.
Lùn's younger brother
Chōu was about to take the examinations,
passed through Jiānglíng,
and went to pay respects to the local authority.
The guest, upon seeing the name Chōu, said:
"Although the scholar's name
is written with a different character,
it will be difficult to present yourself before the Minister.
What should we do?"
It happened that Chōu had an old name card of Lùn in his pocket,
so he said to the usher:
"I have another name."
The usher, seeing it was getting late,
hurriedly took the name card inside.
Zhòu happily said:
"Yuàn Dà is here!
Invite him in!"
When Chōu reached the middle
of the courtyard,
Zhòu saw his appearance was different.
After he sat down,
Zhòu bowed and asked:
"Which rank are you?"
Chōu replied:
"The fourth."
Zhòu asked:
"How are you related to Yuàn Dà?"
Chōu said:
"He is my elder brother."
Zhòu asked again:
"What is your formal name?"
Chōu replied:
"My name is Lùn."
Zhòu said:
"Did your worthy brother change his name?"
Chōu said:
"My elder brother is also named Lùn."
All the officers and clerks in the hall
burst into laughter.
When he was shown to his seat,
he then stated his original name was Chōu.
After lingering in the side courtyard,
soon everyone near and far knew about it.
From *Gàn Zǎizi*
Lǐ Wénbīn
The jǔrén Lǐ Wénbīn was appreciated by the secretary Hégàn Quán.
("Hégàn" was originally written as "Jìyú",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy,
same below.
Note: "Quán" should be "Gāo",
see the collation note in volume 178 of this book, under the entry for prefectural examination candidates.)
At that time, Hèlán Jì, the deputy registrar of the Jīngzhào prefectural government, died.
Wénbīn then went to visit the Zǐwēi (i.e., Hégàn Quán, who held the Zǐwēi Shìláng post).
The Zǐwēi asked:
"Is there any news today?"
Wénbīn said:
"I just passed by the prefectural office,
and heard that Hégàn Jì has died."
Quán said:
"Are you sure you're not mistaken?"
Wénbīn said:
"I am not mistaken."
Quán said:
"You sound like you're talking to a ghost."
He flicked his sleeves and went inside.
Wénbīn then realized his mistake:
both men shared the same surname,
and also the same given name,
so he had answered incorrectly.
From "Qí Wén Lù".
Sū Zhěng
During the Guānghuà era of the Táng,
Sū Zhěng lived together with his fellow villager Chén Dí.
Zhěng, upon first discussing clan relations with Sū Pú, the Kǎogōng Lángzhōng,
established their ancestral connection.
Pú was the son of the former Fèngcháng, Sū Dí.
After Zhěng had presented his gifts (as a disciple),
he soon submitted a letter of introduction along with sample writings for review.
He had Chén Dí seal the envelope,
and Dí mistakenly wrote his own name on it.
When Pú received it,
he was furious.
Zhěng heard this and was flustered,
so he sent another letter to apologize.
Wú Zǐhuá heard about this and said:
"This letter must have been a mistake."
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán",
(the Ming manuscript copy states it is from "Zhí Yán").
Dòu Shǎoqīng
There was a Dòu Shǎoqīng who lived in the old capital.
He was traveling
(Ming manuscript copy has "suǒ" for "sù")
through the various prefectures north of the Wèi River,
and arrived at a village inn.
One of his attendants fell ill,
so he left him with the innkeeper and went on ahead.
He passed through Fū, Yán, Líng, and Xià,
and did not return for a year.
In the meantime, his attendant died at the inn.
As this man was dying,
the innkeeper asked him:
"What is your name?"
The servant only managed to say the three words "Dòu Shǎoqīng",
and then fell silent and passed away.
The innkeeper then dug a grave by the roadside and buried him,
erecting a marker facing the road that read:
"Tomb of Dòu Shǎoqīng".
Someone who knew Dòu passed by.
He was greatly surprised,
and asked the innkeeper about it.
The innkeeper said:
"The name is on the marker,
so it cannot be wrong."
Later, another person who knew Dòu passed by,
and felt deep sorrow and regret.
A close relative reported this to Dòu's family.
They sent family members to examine the marker,
and indeed it was not mistaken.
The family then began mourning, donned mourning garments,
held successive vegetarian feasts for the deceased,
and went to fetch the traveling coffin for burial.
Relatives, near and far,
all came to offer condolences.
Over a month after the burial,
a letter from Dòu arrived at his home,
saying his return journey was nearing the commandery,
and reporting that all was well.
His family was greatly shocked,
and did not believe it,
thinking someone had fraudulently written this letter.
Then someone else reported:
"I saw his appearance on the road,
and he looked very healthy and well."
His family became even more perplexed.
They sent someone to secretly intercept him,
and peeked at him from the side of the road,
suspecting he was a ghost.
When he arrived home,
his wife and children all thought his spirit had returned.
Dòu explained the details in a low voice,
and only then did they realize the buried person was his attendant,
and that the innkeeper had made an error in erecting the marker.
From "Wángshì Jiàn Wén".
Zhāng Lìshè
In the Táng, Zhāng Lìshè was very forgetful.
After taking office as a参军 in Huáizhōu,
whenever he was invited to gatherings,
he would always note it on his hu tablet.
Once, the magistrate of Hénèi, Gěng Rénhuì, invited him,
and wondered why he did not come.
He personally went to his door to invite him.
Lìshè looked at his hu and said:
"Why have you come to see me?
Your name is not on my hu."
Another time, he woke up startled from a daytime nap,
called for his horse, and rode to the prefecture office.
He knocked on the door of the prefect Dèng Yùn,
bowed and apologized, saying:
"I heard you intended to reprimand me,
for which I deserve death?"
Dèng Yùn said:
"There is no such thing."
Lìshè said, "Sīgōng so-and-so told me."
Yùn was furious,
and summoned the prefectural officials for a whipping,
(Ming manuscript copy has "jí" for "chuí")
and interrogated that person about sowing discord.
He was about to cane him,
when the man bitterly pleaded that he had never said such a thing.
Lìshè stepped forward and requested:
"I hope you will spare him.
I'm afraid I might have heard it in a dream."
From then on, people all knew about his muddled and confused nature.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi".
Yán Xuányī
In the Táng, the magistrate of Sānyuán county, Yán Xuányī, was very forgetful.
Once he went to the prefecture,
and sat in the host's residence.
A prefectural assistant official passed by in front of him,
and he thought it was a county clerk.
He called out, intending to cane him.
The clerk said:
"I am a prefectural assistant."
Xuányī was ashamed, apologized, and stopped.
Shortly after, a county clerk arrived.
Xuányī suspected he was a prefectural assistant,
and took his hand, leading him to sit down.
The clerk said:
"I am a county clerk."
Again he felt ashamed and stopped.
Once, someone brought a letter from his elder brother,
and waited at the foot of the steps.
Soon, a village officer arrived with a registered person.
Xuányī called for a cane.
("Cane" was originally written as "support",
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
He then whipped the letter carrier several times.
The man did not know why,
and asked about it.
Xuányī said:
"I made a big mistake."
He turned to the duty clerk,
and told him to fetch a cup of wine from the house to comfort the wound.
After a long while,
the clerk brought the wine.
Xuányī had already forgotten about fetching the wine,
and also forgotten about the man who had been caned.
So he simply gave the wine to the duty clerk to drink.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi".
Guō Wùjìng
In the Táng, Guō Wùjìng, the county丞 of Nánpí county in Cāngzhōu,
had just taken up his post.
The clerk Wáng Qìng was handling a case with him.
Wùjìng asked:
"What is your surname?"
Qìng said:
"Surname Wáng."
A moment later,
Qìng came again.
He again asked what his surname was.
Qìng again said:
"Surname Wáng."
Wùjìng was strangely astonished for a long time,
then looked up at Qìng and said:
"Do all the assistant clerks in Nánpí have the surname Wáng?"
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi".
Zhāng Shǒuxìn
In the Táng dynasty, Zhāng Shǒuxìn served as the prefect of Yúháng.
He was on good terms with Zhāng Yáo, the district defender of Fùyáng.
He treated Yáo with favor,
but Yáo did not know the reason.
So he sent the recorder-adjutant Zhāng Yù
to convey his intentions to Yáo,
planning to marry his daughter to him.
Yáo was delighted,
and an auspicious date was set.
However, this was communicated privately;
the prefecture and district were unaware of it.
Shǒuxìn prepared the dowry for his daughter.
The daughter's nurse asked:
"To whom are you planning to marry your daughter?"
Shǒuxìn told her.
The nurse said:
"The son-in-law's surname is Zhāng,
but what is the surname of your daughter?
I am privately puzzled."
Only then did Shǒuxìn realize,
and he urgently stopped the arrangement.
From "Jì Wén"
Lǐ Xiàn
In the Táng dynasty, the palace attendant censor Lǐ Féngnián, after being demoted,
was gradually promoted to magistrate of Luò County in Hàn Prefecture.
Féngnián had talent as an official,
and the inspector of Shǔ often entrusted him with judicial investigations.
Féngnián's wife
was the daughter of the vice censor-in-chief Zhèng Fǎng.
Their temperaments were incompatible,
so he divorced her.
While in Shǔ City,
he said to the registrar of Yì Prefecture, Lǐ Xiàn:
"Féngnián's household lacks a mistress,
and it is desolate and unbearable.
The children are growing up,
and it is proper to arrange marriages for them.
Since you and I are close,
I hope you can find a wife for Féngnián.
Among the daughters or sisters of officials in this capital,
even if they are remarried,
it can be considered.
Please pay attention to this."
Xiàn said:
"Agreed."
Later, he inquired with Xiàn again.
Xiàn was a careless person,
so he went to Féngnián and said:
"The military officer Lǐ Zhá
is from a very distinguished family.
Zhá's younger sister is very beautiful,
renowned in Shǔ City.
She was previously married to a man of the Yuán family,
but
"Shì qí" originally read "mín mò,"
amended according to the Míng dynasty manuscript.
her husband soon died.
Her dowry is also substantial,
with nearly twenty maidservants accompanying her.
Can you, elder brother, marry her?"
Féngnián agreed,
and instructed Xiàn to inform Lǐ Zhá.
Zhá personally visited Féngnián to express his gratitude.
The next day,
he invited Féngnián to his residence.
That night,
Féngnián was overjoyed.
He rose before dawn while still in bed.
After dressing formally,
he paced the steps and muttered to himself:
"Lǐ Zhá's younger sister,
her family background is like this.
Although she was previously married,
she is young and beautiful.
Her family is also wealthy and noble.
What fortune this is!"
After repeating this several times,
he suddenly exclaimed in alarm:
"Lǐ Xiàn has made a mistake,
and I have been misled!
Now, regarding this proposed marriage,
what is her surname again?
How strange!"
He then rode his horse to the prefectural office.
Lǐ Xiàn approached and said:
"Elder brother, are you visiting Zhá's sister today?"
Féngnián did not respond.
Xiàn said:
"Something has changed."
Féngnián said:
"Are you thinking of Zhá's sister?
What is her surname again?"
Xiàn was startled and withdrew.
He encountered Lǐ Zhá,
who said:
"Did the attendant censor visit today?
I have already prepared the ground."
Xiàn said:
"I have made a grave error.
I only thought of finding a good son-in-law,
but completely forgot to consider the surnames."
Zhá was greatly shocked,
and deeply regretted it.
From "Jì Wén"
Zhāng Cángyòng
In the Táng dynasty, Zhāng Cángyòng was the assistant magistrate of Línqú in Qīng Prefecture.
His nature was dull-witted,
and he was also weak-minded.
Once he summoned a carpenter,
but after ten summonses, the carpenter did not come.
Cángyòng was furious,
and sent someone to apprehend him.
When the carpenter arrived,
it happened that the magistrate of a neighboring county
sent a person with a letter
to deliver to Cángyòng.
Cángyòng had just calmed his anger,
and the carpenter ran off again.
After reading the letter,
he ordered the messenger who delivered the letter to be flogged.
He was caned up to ten strokes,
and the messenger protested the beating.
He pleaded:
"I am delivering a letter for you, my lord.
Even if the letter writer's intentions offended you, my lord,
what crime has the messenger committed?"
Only then did Cángyòng realize his mistake.
He apologized:
"I was angry with the carpenter just now,
and inadvertently caned you by mistake."
He ordered the village head to fetch a vessel of drink,
to give to the messenger.
Then he returned to his duties.
Suddenly seeing the village head,
he pointed to the wine and asked:
"What is in this?"
The village head said:
"Wine."
Cángyòng said:
"Why not drink it?"
The village head bowed and drank it.
Cángyòng then went inside.
The messenger ultimately did not get the wine,
and returned leaning on his cane.
From "Jì Wén"
Péi Mínglǐ
In the Táng dynasty, Péi Mínglǐ,
a man from Hédōng.
He was skilled at managing livelihood.
He collected discarded items from people,
accumulated and sold them,
thereby amassing a fortune of millions.
Also, outside the Jīnguāng Gate,
he bought barren land.
It was full of rubble,
and not valuable.
So at the edge of the land, he erected a pole,
hung a basket from it,
and rewarded with money anyone who hit it,
but only one or two out of a hundred succeeded.
Before long,
the rubble in the land was all gone.
Then he lent it to shepherds for grazing sheep,

Hé Míngyuǎn
In the Táng dynasty, Hé Míngyuǎn of Dìngzhōu was extremely wealthy,
