and kept several hundred fugitives,
who would raid and plunder wherever they went.
If the matter was exposed, he would kill them.
In the end, he did not meet a violent death,
but was implicated for his cruelty and excesses.
From "Jì Wén"
Péi Jí
Péi Jí of the Táng dynasty once recounted that
when he was young, his uncle-in-law was a court official
with a noble reputation.
Jí went to his residence
and met him after he returned from court.
His uncle-in-law sighed deeply and said:
"Who is this Cuī Zhào,
that everyone praises him so?
He must be offering bribes.
How can there be no chaos like this?"
Before he finished speaking,
the gatekeeper announced:
"Cuī, the prefect of Shòuzhōu, requests an audience."
His uncle-in-law was angry,
scolded the gatekeeper,
and was about to whip him.
After a long while,
he reluctantly straightened his attire and went to meet him.
Shortly after,
he urgently ordered tea,
then wine and food,
and then a meal.
Jí's aunt said:
"Why were you so arrogant before and so respectful now?"
When he entered the room,
he had a pleased expression.
He waved
(Míng manuscript note: "waved" originally written as "bowed")
to Jí and said:
"Rest in the study."
Before Jí descended the steps,
his uncle-in-law took out a piece of paper from his bosom,
which was a gift of a thousand bolts of official silk.
From "Guóshǐ Bǔ"
Yuán Zǎi
When Yuán Zǎi of the Táng dynasty had his household confiscated,
the inventory of his property
included nine hundred dàn of pepper.
From "Shàngshū Gùshí"
Zhāng Yánshǎng
When Zhāng Yánshǎng of the Táng dynasty was about to assume the post of Commissioner of Finance,
he learned of a major case with considerable injustice,
which often filled him with indignation.
Upon taking office,
he summoned the prison warden,
sternly admonished him,
and said:
"This case has dragged on for too long;
it must be concluded within ten days."
The next morning, when he went to his office,
he found a small note on his desk that read:
"Thirty thousand strings of cash,
begging you not to pursue this case."
Yánshǎng was furious
and pressed even harder
("pressed" originally written as "feared,"
corrected according to the Míng manuscript)
for its resolution.
The next day,
he saw another note that said:
"Fifty thousand strings of cash."
Yánshǎng grew even angrier
and ordered the case to be concluded within two days.
The following morning,
he found yet another note on his desk:
"One hundred thousand strings of cash."
Yánshǎng then stopped pursuing the case.
His subordinates took the opportunity to inquire about it,
and he said:
"When the money reaches one hundred thousand strings,
it can move even the gods.
There is nothing that cannot be overturned.
I fear disaster,
so I have no choice but to accept it."
From "Yōuxián Gǔchuī"
Lú Áng
Lú Áng of the Táng dynasty was in charge of the salt and iron monopoly in Fújiàn.
When his corruption was exposed on a large scale,
a large turquoise pillow, half a dǒu in size, was discovered,
placed on a golden stand.
The Vice Censor-in-Chief, Mèng Jiǎn, investigated for months
before it could be presented.
Market appraisers were summoned to evaluate it:
some said it was a priceless treasure,
while others said it was just a beautiful stone,
not genuine turquoise.
From "Guóshǐ Bǔ"
Cuī Xián
Cuī Xián, a Secretariat Drafter of the Táng dynasty, once received the favor of a high-ranking official.
When the official reached the age of retirement,
he submitted a memorial requesting to step down.
Cuī, then serving as Director of the Bureau of Honors,
out of gratitude for the official's kindness,
praised him lavishly.
He was ordered to draft the proposal for implementation,
but as there were no strong supporters,
the request was approved in a single memorial.
Two or three months later,
the official's residence grew increasingly quiet and desolate,
and his family secretly complained.
He later deeply regretted it
and told his subordinates:
"For important matters,
be careful not to discuss them with young men."
From "Yōuxián Gǔchuī"
Cuī Yuǎn
When Cuī Yuǎn of the Táng dynasty was about to retire,
his close friends and relatives all urged him to stay.
His eldest daughter, who was virtuous
and well-read,
was the only one who advised him to retire.
The Councilor thus decided to step down.
Within a year or two,
he grew restless and bored in his idleness.
Turning to his sons and nephews, he said:
"I haven't received any gold or bronze tea caddies from the provinces lately;
recently, they've all been withheld."
He then resumed his official post.
From "Yōuxián Gǔchuī"
A Merchant from Jiānghuái
A merchant from Jiānghuái hoarded rice to wait for prices to surge.
(The character "price" was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Míng manuscript.)
He drew a picture of a person
holding one dǒu of rice,
selling it for one thousand coins,
and hung it in the market.
Yú Càn, the deputy military commissioner of Yángzǐ,
had him beaten to death.
From "Guóshǐ Bǔ"
Lóng Chāngyì
In the year of Wùzǐ, there was a drought.
A man from Lúlíng named Lóng Chāngyì had several thousand hú of rice for sale.
Soon after, the price of rice fell somewhat.
Chāngyì then composed a text,
prayed at the Shéngāng Temple,
and begged that it would not rain for another month.
After the prayer,
on his way back,
he rested in a pavilion.
Suddenly, a patch of black cloud
emerged from behind the temple.
In a moment,
thunder and rain arrived in force,
and Chāngyì was struck dead by lightning outside the pavilion.
When the officials examined him,
they removed his headscarf
("scarf" originally written as "shēn,"
corrected according to the Ming manuscript.)
and found a paper note in his topknot,
which was the text of his temple prayer.
Chāngyì had a grandson
who was about to take the child prodigy examination.
The villagers reported the incident to the authorities,
and he was not allowed to be recommended.
From "Records of the Spirits"
Ān Zhòngbà
Ān Zhòngbà, the prefect of Jiǎnzhōu in Shǔ, was insatiably greedy for bribes.
Among the prefecture's people was an oil merchant surnamed Dèng,
who was skilled at chess
and whose family was also well-off.
Zhòngbà summoned him for a match,
but only allowed him to stand and serve.
Each time Dèng placed a piece,
he was made to retreat and stand under the northwest window.
"Wait until I calculate my moves,"
only then could he approach again.
Thus, in a whole day, no more than a dozen pieces were placed.
Dèng grew weary from standing and hungry,
almost unbearable.
The next day, he was summoned again.
Someone hinted to Dèng,
"This lord loves bribes;
he isn't really here for chess.
Why not offer a bribe and ask to be excused?"
Dèng agreed,
and presented three ingots of medium-grade gold.
He was then spared.
From "Beimeng Suoyan"
Zhāng Qiánjiàn
Zhāng Qiánjiàn was very greedy.
When he governed Cāngzhōu,
due to severe drought and famine among the people,
he opened the granaries to provide relief.
When the matter was reported to the emperor,
he was greatly praised and rewarded.
Later, after the autumn harvest,
he collected double the amount in taxes.
He often said he felt his actions contradicted his words,
but whenever he saw wealth,
he could not restrain himself.
People of the time laughed at him.
From "Beimeng Suoyan"
Shí Miáo
In the Hàn dynasty, Shí Miáo was the magistrate of Shòuchūn.
He went to visit the assistant prefect Jiǎng Jì,
but Jì was drunk
and refused to see him.
Returning home, Miáo carved a wooden figure
and wrote "Drunkard Jiǎng Jì" on it.
He then shot it with bow and arrows.
When the governor heard of this,
he could not control him.
From "Duyi Zhi"
Wáng Sī
Wáng Sī had an impatient temperament.
Once while holding a brush to write,
a fly landed on the tip of the brush.
He shooed it away, but it returned.
Sī grew furious,
got up to chase it himself,
but could not catch it.
He then took the brush, threw it to the ground,
and trampled it to pieces.
From "Weilue";
the Ming manuscript cites "Weishu."
Lǐ Níngdào
Lǐ Níngdào, the magistrate of Lóngyóu County in Qúzhōu during the Táng dynasty, had a narrow and impatient nature.
His sister's son, seven years old,
purposely annoyed him.
He immediately went to chase the boy,
but could not catch him.
He then lured him with a cake and caught him,
biting his chest and back until they bled.
His sister rescued the boy, saving him.
Another time, while riding a donkey in the street,
a man on horseback
brushed his knee with his boot tip.
Níngdào flew into a rage, cursing loudly,
and was about to beat him.
But the man galloped away, and he could not catch up.
Unable to vent his anger,
he gnawed on thorns by the roadside until his mouth bled.
From "Chaoye Qianzai"
Yáo Jūnqīng
During the Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty,
Yáo Jūnqīng, an assistant magistrate of Wǔqiáng in Jìzhōu, lost a horse.
After catching the thief,
he had him caged but not yet sentenced.
Jūnqīng pointed at the thief's face and scolded,
"You old thief,
you must have eaten tiger's gall!
How dare you steal my things!"
The thief raised his cage and struck him with it,
and Jūnqīng's skull shattered instantly, killing him.
From "Chaoye Qianzai"
Xiāo Yǐngshì
Xiāo Yǐngshì of the Táng dynasty
passed the imperial examination at the age of nineteen during the Kāiyuán era.
By his twenties,
he was well-versed in the teachings of the three schools.
But his temperament was irritable, angry, and harsh,
unmatched by anyone.
He often employed a servant named Dù Liàng.
Every time he punished him severely,
once Liàng had recovered after recuperating,
he would follow Xiāo's orders as before.
Someone advised Liàng,
"You are a servant;
why not choose a better master
and suffer like this?"
Liàng said,
"Do you think I'm foolish and unaware?
But I admire his profound talent and learning,
and because of that, I cannot bear to leave."
In the end, it led to his death.
From "Chaoye Qianzai"
Péi Shū
In Hédōng, there was a man named Péi Shū, whose courtesy name was Huánzhōng.
His youngest uncle, Péi Yàoqīng,
during the reign of Emperor Xuánzōng of the Táng dynasty,
rose to the position of Chancellor.
In the twenty-first year of the Kāiyuán era, he submitted a memorial
(Originally, "submitted" was written as "spring,"
corrected based on the Míng manuscript copy.)
proposing the opening of river transport
to supply the state's needs.
The emperor deeply praised and adopted his proposal.
Péi Shū's maternal aunt's husband, Xuē Yōng, who served as a Secretariat Drafter,
at the time had news of being appointed as the chief examiner for the imperial examinations.
On New Year's Day,
he came to visit Péi Shū's family.
He then said:
"Does my sister have any arrangements
(The character "arrangements" was originally left blank,
supplemented based on the Huáng manuscript.)
among relatives and old acquaintances for recommending candidates?"
His relative pointed at Péi Shū.
Xuē Yōng straightened his attire, respectfully held his official tablet, and replied:
"The thirty-sixth young master
is naturally a talent accumulated through public selection;
he does not require any special arrangements.
I fear there may be other young relatives."
Péi Shū immediately responded:
"My aunt's husband has spoken improperly."
He then poured wine on the ground,
and swore:
"If Uncle Xuē becomes the chief examiner,
I, Shū, will vanish from sight and hide my form,
never to set foot in human society again."
His relative sternly reprimanded him,
ordering him to bow and apologize to Xuē Yōng,
but Péi Shū remained unyielding.
In the second year of the Yǒngtài era,
when Vice Minister Jiǎ Zhì served as chief examiner,
Péi Shū passed the examination on his first attempt.
Later, in the second year of the Dàlì era,
Xuē Yōng finally became chief examiner.
After Péi Shū passed the examination,
he returned to Dānyáng Lane,
and did not associate with miscellaneous crowds.
Also, when Wéi Yuánfǔ was appointed to this prefecture,
it was expected that the day after his arrival in the commandery,
he should come to pay respects to his relatives.
The day after Wéi Yuánfǔ arrived in Dānyáng,
he specially sent an envoy to deliver clothing, letters, and gifts.
Péi Shū angrily refused to accept them.
Three days later,
Wéi Yuánfǔ personally rode with his entourage to Péi Shū's villa.
Péi Shū instructed his servants
not to announce him.
Wéi Yuánfǔ's carriage and attendants were kept waiting for a long time,
unable to proceed.
Wéi Yuánfǔ was not angered,
but only said:
"Lord Péi is too narrow-minded.
I have just arrived,
and must acquaint myself with the military officials and army supervisors.
To be so severely reproached like this,
I dare not accept it."
Péi Shū's relative then sent a maidservant to relay a message,
inviting Wéi Yuánfǔ into the main hall,
and set out wine.
Wéi Yuánfǔ discussed official matters,
and only then did Péi Shū come out to converse cheerfully.
From "Qián Zhuàn Zǐ."
Cuī Gǒng
In the Táng dynasty, Cuī Gǒng served as the留守 (Liúshǒu) of the Eastern Capital,
overseeing the affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Secretariat Drafter Cuī Jīng served as a minor official,
and went on official business to visit Cuī Gǒng,
but Cuī Gǒng refused to see him.
Cuī Jīng then sought someone who was on close and friendly terms with Cuī Gǒng,
to inquire on his behalf.
Cuī Gǒng became increasingly angry.
Another day,
while drinking merrily,
he questioned him again.
The留守 (Liúshǒu) grew even more indignant and said:
"I, Gǒng, swear never to meet this man face-to-face.
Moreover, when people write literary compositions,
their words and phrases are limitless;
how could he use my brothers as a false antithesis?"
Cuī Jīng still did not understand,
and his relatives all grew anxious and uneasy.
Among his nephews, there was one who was perceptive,
who searched through the collected writings,
and discovered the reason.
It turned out that when drafting the imperial edict,
demoting Cuī Qiú to the position of Assistant Prefect of Fǔzhōu Commandery, it said:
"Relying on the order of wild geese,
he fanned the flames of frivolous customs."
Cuī Jīng consequently fell ill.
From "Zhī Tián Lù."
Hán Gāo
In the Táng dynasty, Hán Gāo
was appointed from Secretariat Drafter to Censor-in-Chief.
According to the old practice of the Western Department,
when a senior official changed positions, the draft of the appointment document,
was to be sent to the next-ranking Drafter.
At that time, Lǚ Wèi was drafting the edict,
and Hán Gāo, feeling apprehensive,
asked:
"Why am I being transferred?"
Lǚ Wèi did not tell him.
Hán Gāo pressured him, saying:
"Will you be demoted together with me?"
Lǚ Wèi grew anxious,
and finally told him.
Hán Gāo also wanted to appeal to the newly appointed Chancellor,
but Lǚ Wèi restrained him.
He seized his boots and official tablet.
After much clamoring,
he finally stopped.
From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ."
Dù Yòu
In the Táng dynasty, Yáng Màoqīng traveled as a guest to Yángzhōu,
and wrote a letter to Dù Yòu.
The wording was full of rhetoric and persuasion,
alluding to the story of the Duke of Zhōu spitting out food and holding back hair to receive worthy men.
Dù Yòu was surprised by it.
At the time, Liú Yǔxī was present,
and Dù Yòu also had Yáng summoned,
to drink together.
Dù Yòu handed Yáng Màoqīng's letter to Liú Yǔxī and said:
"Please, man of letters, read this for us."
After finishing,
Dù Yòu asked:
"What do you think?"
Liú Yǔxī said:
"Generally, scholars without official rank
all need to use rhetoric and persuasion,
to move the hearts of the noble and powerful."
Dù Yòu said:
"Enough, enough,
this business of rhetoric and persuasion is rotten.
Have you not seen Wáng Shě?
He used rhetoric and persuasion with Chén Shàoyóu,
and Shàoyóu cut off his head.
Now, I am giving you and me a meal to eat.
Going too far is as bad as not going far enough."
The next day,
Yáng left without saying goodbye.
From "Jiā Huà Lù."
Huángfǔ Shí
Táng Huángfǔ Shí was of stern appearance and rigid temperament,
his literary style ancient and elegant,
relying on his talent to look down upon others,
and his nature further being prejudiced and straightforward.
(Míng manuscript copy has "急" [impatient] for "直" [straightforward])
While serving as a court gentleman,
under the influence of wine, he gave vent to his temper and offended his colleagues.
Upon sobering up,
he felt ill at ease,
and requested a transfer to the Eastern Capital, Luòyáng.
It happened that the Yī and Chán rivers had years of poor harvests,
and he remained stagnant in his post without promotion,
his official salary meager,
leaving him in dire poverty and distress.
Once, due to accumulated snow,
there were no footprints at his gate,
and no smoke rose from his kitchen chimney.
Péi Dù, who was then overseeing the security of Luòyáng,
with fine words and generous gifts,
recruited him as an assistant in the留守府 (Liúshǒu Fǔ).
Shí was simple and informal, lacking in courtesy,
but Dù tolerated him generously.
Previously, when Dù was suppressing the Huáixī rebellion,
he received immense imperial rewards,
stored in his private residence at the Jíxián Academy.
Dù believed in Buddhism,
and mindful of the many lives taken,
feared it would bring calamity.
Therefore, he donated the spoils from suppressing the Huáixī rebellion
to rebuild the Fúxiān Buddhist Temple.
It was made extremely magnificent,
and the completion date was near.
He was about to write to Bái Jūyì,
requesting him to compose the stele inscription.
Shí, who was present,
suddenly flared up in anger and said:
"You disregard me nearby and seek Bái from afar;
truly, I have incurred your displeasure.
My writing, if
(The character "若" was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng manuscript.)
compared to Bái's works,
is like comparing precious qín and jade sè to the vulgar songs of Sāngjiān and Púshàng.
However, which gate cannot accommodate long robes?
I hereby bid you farewell and withdraw."
The guests were all shocked and fearful.
Dù apologized with gentle words,
and said:
"Initially, I dared not trouble you, esteemed sir,
fearing rejection by a great literary master.
Now that it has come to this,
it is exactly what I wished for."
Shí's anger subsided slightly,
and he requested a dou of wine before returning home.
Upon reaching home,
he drank half of it alone,
and, riding on his drunkenness, wielded his brush,
completing the text in one go.
The next day,
he presented a clean copy.
The literary conception was ancient and profound,
and the characters were also strangely unconventional.
Dù pondered over it for a long time,
unable to discern its punctuation and phrasing.
Finally, he sighed and said:
"He is of the same caliber as Mù Xuánxū
and Guō Jǐngchún, masters of rivers and seas!"
Thereupon, with precious carriages and famous horses,
silks, colored fabrics, vessels, and curios,
worth approximately over a thousand strings of cash,
along with a letter,
he sent a junior officer to Shí's residence to reward him.
Shí, upon reading the letter, flew into a rage,
threw the letter to the ground,
and said to the junior officer:
"Convey my thanks to the Shìzhōng,
but why is his treatment of me so shabby?
My writing
is not the writing of ordinary people.
Apart from once composing a collection preface for Gù Kuàng,
I have never rashly agreed to write for anyone.
Now, I agreed to compose this stele inscription
solely because I have received deep kindness.
The stele inscription is about three thousand characters;
each character is worth three bolts of silk,
not a single cash less."
The junior officer, both frightened and angry,
returned and reported everything in detail.
The subordinates and ranked officers
all clenched their wrists in indignation and resentment,
wishing to slice his flesh.
Dù heard this and laughed, saying:
"He truly is a rare talent."
He immediately sent someone to reward him according to the amount.
From the留守府, the official's residence, and the neighborhood,
carts carrying the rewards were seen in succession.
The people of Luòyáng gathered to watch,
comparing it to the boat-ferrying operation of Yōng Jiàng.
Shí accepted it all without a trace of shame.
Moreover, his impatient and irritable nature
was uniquely different from others.
Once, he was stung on the finger by a bee,
and became greatly agitated and impatient.
He ordered his servants and the children from the neighborhood
to gather bee nests with dustpans,
purchasing them at good prices.
In a short while, they piled up like a mountain in the courtyard.
He then ordered them crushed on a chopping block,
pulverized in a mortar,
and the juice squeezed out,
to repay the pain.
He also once ordered his son Sōng
to copy several poems.
If a single character was slightly wrong,
he would curse, scold, and even jump about.
When his hand couldn't reach with a cane,
he would bite his own wrist until it bled.
His narrow-minded and impatient nature
was often like this.
From "Quē Shǐ" (Missing History),
(Huáng manuscript says from "Guó Shǐ" [National History])
Duàn Wénchāng
Táng Chancellor Duàn Wénchāng had an upright and narrow-minded nature.
At banquets with guests,
if there was the slightest mistake in etiquette,
he would inevitably express surprise and blame.
While in Xīchuān,
there was a Jìnshì named Xuē Dàbái,
who drank too much and called out names excessively,
and the next day was never invited again.
From "Yīn Yǔ Lù" (Record of Casual Talk)
Liú Yǔxī
(The three characters "Liú Yǔxī" were originally missing,
supplemented according to the Míng manuscript copy.)
During the Tàihé era of the Táng, he served as a Bīnkè (advisor),
at the same time Lǐ Déyù held a concurrent appointment in the Eastern Capital.
Yǔxī, while paying a visit to Déyù, asked:
"Have you recently obtained Bái Jūyì's collected works?"
Déyù replied:
"They have been shown to me repeatedly,
and I have separately ordered them stored away,
but I have never once opened them.
Today, for your sake, I will look at them."
Upon fetching them to look,
the boxes and chests were overflowing,
covered in dust.
After opening them, he rolled them back up again,
and said to Yǔxī:
"I have long been dissatisfied with this man;
why should I read his writings?
I only fear it might turn my refined and exceptional mind,
which is why I do not wish to look at them."
This is how he suppressed talent.
Initially, Emperor Wénzōng ordered Déyù to report on factions in the court,
and he first named Yáng Yúqīng and Niú Sēngrú.
Yáng and Niú were Bái's close friends.
His not supporting or assisting them
was all of this kind.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán" (Idle Talk of Northern Dreams)
Lǐ Pān
Táng Lǐbù Shìláng Lǐ Pān once compiled Lǐ Hè's song-poems,
intending to write a collection preface for them,
but did not complete it.
Learning that Hè had a maternal cousin,
who had shared writing brush and inkstone with Hè,
he summoned him for an audience,
entrusting him with searching for any遗漏 (missing works).
The man respectfully declined,
and requested:
"I remember what he wrote,
and have also often seen his many revisions.
Please let me see what you have compiled,
and I will make corrections."
Pān was pleased,
and handed them all over.
For a full year, the man left no trace.
Pān, angry,
summoned him again to question him.
The man said:
"Hè and I are related through our mothers' families,
and from childhood spent much time together.
Resenting his arrogance and neglect,
I have long thought of repaying him.
The song-poems I obtained,
together with the old ones I had,
I threw them all into the latrine at once."
Pān was furious,
shouted at him to leave,
and lamented with regret for a long time.
Therefore, few of Hè's song-poems have been passed down.
From "Yōu Xián Gǔchuī" (Leisurely鼓吹)
Lú Hǎn
During the Tang Dynasty, Lǐ Nè was appointed to Zhèdōng.
On his journey, he passed through Huáichǔ,
where Lú Hǎn served as the prefect.
After Lǐ Nè arrived,
it happened to be the Yuǎn Rì festival.
Lú Hǎn ordered a vegetarian meal to be prepared and sent to Lǐ Nè.
Lǐ Nè was initially pleased upon seeing it,
but upon reading the accompanying note,
he discovered that the sender’s name was identical to his father’s taboo name.
Originally, the text read "Xiè" for "Lǐ Nè’s father,"
but according to the Yùquánzǐ, it has been amended to "Nè’s father."
The name was the same.
Lǐ Nè,
the son of Jiàn,
was by nature narrow-minded and irritable.
He flew into a rage.
Early the next morning,
he had already ordered the boat to set sail and depart.
When Lú Hǎn heard of this,
he hastily ordered a carriage and hurried to the scene,
but the boat was already moving.
Lú Hǎn learned the reason
and apologized profusely for a long time,
explaining that it was due to his own carelessness,
and even had the responsible person flogged.
However, Lǐ Nè’s resolve to leave only grew firmer.
Seeing that he could not be persuaded to stay,
Lú Hǎn angrily said:
"Many people, great and small, are named Jiàn.
Why are you so deeply angered by this!"
With that, he flicked his sleeves and left.
From the Yùquánzǐ.
Wáng Gǒng
Wáng Zhù, a Jǐshìzhōng of the Tang Dynasty,
was a scion of a distinguished family
and prided himself on his upright and unyielding character.
Before the Huáng Cháo rebellion,
he governed Chángzhōu.
Amid the chaos and turmoil in the capital,
he wandered the rivers and lakes,
earning considerable contemporary renown.
When he was summoned back by imperial decree,
he passed through Shǎn.
At that time, Wáng Gǒng was the military governor there,
a man of considerable brutality.
Nevertheless, knowing that Wáng Zhù would likely hold a high court position in the future,
he treated him with due courtesy.
Wáng Zhù, however, despised the man
and refused to lower himself to engage with him.
Wáng Gǒng then prepared a lavish banquet in his inner hall,
complete with musicians and courtesans.
With a solemn expression, he addressed Wáng Zhù:
"Although I am a man of lowly station,
I have been undeservedly entrusted with military authority.
Today, I am most fortunate
to have your esteemed presence passing through.
If you do not spurn my humble lineage,
I wish to be counted among your nephews."
Wáng Zhù firmly refused.
Wáng Gǒng’s face flushed with anger, and he said:
"The Jǐshì’s official schedule is tight;
I dare not detain you."
Shortly after, the banquet was concluded,
and he ordered his officers to swiftly request that Jǐshì Wáng leave the guesthouse.
Secretly conveying his intentions,
he ordered them to kill him.
Wáng Zhù’s entire family was thrown into the Yellow River,
and all their belongings were seized.
It was reported to the court that they had drowned in a boating accident.
The court was preoccupied with numerous troubles,
so the matter was dropped and not investigated.
At that time, Wáng Zhù had a son
who was traveling to Xiāngzhōu.
He also inexplicably threw himself into a well and died.
From the Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán.

Yàn Yīng
Qí’s Yàn Yīng was short in stature.
He was sent as an envoy to Chǔ.
The people of Chǔ built a small gate next to the main gate
and invited Yànzǐ to enter through it.
Yàn Yīng refused to enter,
saying:
"When one is sent to a dog state,
one enters through the dog gate.
Now I am an envoy to Chǔ;
it is not fitting for me to enter through a dog gate."
The King said:
"Is there no one in Qí?"
He replied:
"Qí sends its worthy envoys to worthy kings,
and its unworthy envoys to unworthy kings.
I am unworthy,
therefore I was sent to you, O King."
The King said to his attendants:
"Yàn Yīng is skilled in debate;
I wish to wound him."
After they were seated,
a bound man was brought in.
The King asked:
"What is he accused of?"
The attendants replied:
"A man of Qí, accused of theft."
The King looked at Yàn Yīng and said:
"Are the people of Qí skilled at theft?"
He replied:
"I have heard that oranges grown south of the Jiāng
become trifoliate oranges north of the Jiāng.
Their leaves and branches are similar,
but the taste of their fruit is quite different.
This is due to the difference in soil and water.
Now, this man was born in Qí
and did not know how to steal.
Upon entering Chǔ, he became a thief.
The nature of the fruit is different;
the soil and water made it so."
The King laughed and said:
"I have only brought ridicule upon myself."
From the Qǐyán Lù.
Dōngfāng Shuò
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn once asked Dōngfāng Shuò, saying:
"Sir, what kind of ruler do you consider me to be?"
Shuò replied:
"Since the times of Táng and Yú,
and even during the era of Chéng and Kāng,
none would suffice for comparison.
Your servant humbly observes Your Majesty's merits and virtues,
which surpass those of the Five Emperors,
and stand to the right of the Three Kings.
It is not merely this alone.
Truly, you have obtained the worthy scholars of the realm,
and the high ministers in office
are all the right men for their positions.
For instance, taking Zhōu Shào as Chancellor,
Kǒng Qiū as Grandee Secretary,
Tàigōng as General,
Bì Gōnggāo to gather oversights from behind,
Biàn Yánzǐ as Commandant of the Guards,
Gāo Yáo as Chief Judge,
Hòu Jì as Minister of Agriculture,
Yī Yǐn as Superintendent of the Lesser Treasury,
Zǐ Gòng as envoy to foreign states,
Yán Mǐn as Erudite,
Zǐ Xià as Grand Master of Ceremonies,
Yì as Governor of the Right Fúfēng,
Jì Lù as Commandant of the Capital,
Qì as Superintendent of State Visits,
Lóng Páng as Director of the Imperial Clan,
Bó Yí as Governor of the Capital District,
Guǎn Zhòng as Governor of Féngyì,
Lǔ Bān as Director of Palace Buildings,
Zhòngshān Fǔ as Superintendent of the Imperial Household,
Shēn Bó as Grand Coachman,
Yánlíng Jìzǐ as Director of Waters and Parks,
Bǎilǐ Xī as Superintendent of Dependent States,
Liǔxià Huì as Grand Prolonger of Autumn,
Shǐ Yú as Rectifier,
Kǒng Fù as Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent,
Qú Bóyù as Grand Tutor,
Sūn Shū'áo as Chancellor of the Feudal Lords,
Wáng Qìngjì as Leader of the Palace Guard,
Zǐ Chǎn as Commandery Governor,
Xià Yù as Tripod Officer,
Yì as Banner-Head,
Yì was skilled at archery.
Sòng Wàn as Marquis of the Road-Clearing." The Emperor then laughed heartily,
and asked again:
"Now, men like Chancellor Gōngsūn, Grandee Ér, Dǒng Zhòngshū, Xiàhóu Shǐchāng, Sīmǎ Xiàngrú, Wúqiū Shòuwáng, Zhǔfù Yǎn, Zhū Mǎichén, Yán Zhù, Jí Àn, Jiāo Cāng, Zhōng Jūn, Yán Ān, Xú Lè, Sīmǎ Qiān—
all are eloquent, wise, broad-minded, and penetrating,
overflowing with literary talent.
Sir, how do you view yourself?
How do you compare with them?"
He replied:
"Your servant observes that they have teeth set in jaws,
cheeks and chins planted,
their voices altered.
They protrude lips and mouths,
stretch necks and chins,
join thighs and feet,
connect buttocks and rumps,
dragging their tracks in a winding manner,
walking with a Yǔ-like gait.
Your servant Shuò, though unworthy,
can still encompass the qualities of these several men."
Shuò's manner of advancing and retreating with calm words
was always of this kind.
The Emperor once had several experts perform divination by covering objects,
placing a gecko under a basin.
They divined,
but none could hit upon it.
Shuò volunteered, saying:
"Your servant once studied the Changes,
allow me to divine it."
He then separately arranged yarrow stalks and cast a hexagram, replying:
"Your servant thinks it is like a dragon yet has no horns,
called a snake yet has feet.
Creeping and gazing, adept at climbing walls—
if not a gecko, then it is a lizard."
The Emperor said, "Excellent,"
and bestowed ten bolts of silk,
then had him divine other objects.
He hit upon them repeatedly,
and was each time bestowed silk.
At that time, there was a favored entertainer, Guō Shèrén, endlessly witty,
often attending by the Emperor's side.
He said:
"Shuò just got lucky with a wild guess,
it was not the ultimate skill.
Your servant wishes to have Shuò divine again.
If Shuò hits upon it,
your servant will take a hundred strokes.
If he cannot hit upon it,
your servant should receive silk."
So he covered a tree parasite,
and had Shuò divine it.
Shuò said:
"It is a 'poor man's nest'."
Shèrén said:
"Indeed I knew Shuò could not hit upon it."
Shuò said:
"Fresh meat is minced meat,
dried meat is jerky.
Attached to a tree it is a parasite,
under a basin it is a 'poor man's nest'."
The Emperor ordered the entertainer superintendent to flog Shèrén,
Shèrén could not bear the pain,
and cried out.
Shuò laughed at him, saying:
"Tut!
Mouth without hair,
voice crying 'áo áo',
rump getting higher."
Shèrén angrily said:
"Shuò has presumptuously slandered and deceived an official of the Son of Heaven,
he should be executed in the marketplace."
The Emperor asked Shuò:
"Why did you slander him?"
He replied:
"Your servant did not dare slander him,
I was merely making a riddle with him."
The Emperor said:
"What is the riddle?"
Shuò said:
"Now, 'mouth without hair'—
is a dog's hole.
'Voice crying 'áo áo''—
is a bird feeding its chicks.
'Rump getting higher'—
is a crane bending to peck."
Shèrén was not convinced,
and thus said:
"Your servant wishes to ask Shuò another riddle,
if he does not know it, he should also be flogged."
He then arbitrarily made up a rhyming phrase, saying:
"Lìng hú jǔ,
lǎo bǎi tú,
yī yōu yà,
yí hōu yá.
What does it mean?"
Shuò said:
"'Lìng' means command,
'hú' is that which contains.
'Jǔ' means uneven teeth,
'lǎo' is what people respect.
'Bǎi' is the court of ghosts,
'tú' is a muddy path.
'Yī yōu yà'—
are words not yet exhausted
(the character for 'exhausted' was originally left blank,
supplemented according to the Ming manuscript copy)
'Yí hōu yá'—
are two dogs fighting."
Whatever Shèrén asked,
Shuò responded immediately,
with clever changes and sharp retorts emerging,
and none could exhaust him.
The attendants were greatly astonished.
The Emperor appointed Shuò as a Regular Attendant Gentleman,
and thus he gained favor and closeness.
After a long time,
on the day of the Fú sacrifice, an edict bestowed meat upon the attending officials.
The Grand Provisioner's assistant did not come until late in the day.
Shuò alone drew his sword,
and said to his colleagues:
"On Fú day one should return early,
allow me to receive the bounty."
He then took the meat and left.
The Grand Provisioner reported this.
Shuò entered,
and the Emperor said:
"Yesterday, when meat was bestowed,
you did not wait for the edict,
but cut the meat with your sword and left.
Why?"
Shuò removed his cap and apologized.
The Emperor said:
"Sir, rise and censure yourself."
Shuò bowed twice and said:
"Shuò came, Shuò came,
receiving bounty without waiting for the edict—
how lacking in propriety!
Drawing a sword to cut meat—
how heroic!
Cutting not too much—
how frugal!
Returning to give it to my wife—
how benevolent!"
The Emperor laughed and said:
"I had the sir censure himself,
but instead he praised himself."
He further bestowed one dàn of wine,
and a hundred catties of meat,
for him to take back to his wife.
Biān Sháo
In the Later Hàn dynasty, there was a man named Biān Sháo, courtesy name Xiàoxiān,
who taught several hundred students.
Once, he dozed off during the daytime,
and his students privately mocked him, saying:
"Biān Xiàoxiān,
with a bulging belly,
too lazy to read books,
only wanting to sleep."
Xiàoxiān overheard this in secret
and responded:
"Biān is my surname,
Xiào is my courtesy name.
A bulging belly—
a repository of the Five Classics.
Only wanting to sleep—
pondering the affairs of the classics.
In sleep, I communicate with Duke Zhōu in dreams;
in stillness, I share the same thoughts as Confucius.
If a teacher can be mocked,
from which classic or record does this come?"
The mocker was greatly ashamed.
The original source was missing;
the Míng dynasty manuscript version cites it from "Qǐyán Lù" (Records of Amusing Tales).
Yuán Cìyáng
In the Later Hàn dynasty, Yuán Cìyáng's wife
was the daughter of Mǎ Jìcháng of Fúfēng.
At the beginning of the marriage, her dowry was extremely lavish.
Cìyáng said:
"A wife's duty is merely to serve with broom and dustpan—
why such excessive splendor and beauty?"
She replied:
"My loving parents bestowed this out of affection,
and I dared not disobey their command.
If you, sir, admire the lofty virtues of Bào Xuān and Liáng Hóng,
I, your humble wife, shall also strive to follow the examples of Shào Jūn and Mèng Guāng."
Cìyáng asked further:
"For a younger brother to marry before his elder brother
is considered laughable by the world.
Now, my elder sister remains unmarried;
is it proper for me to proceed first?"
She said:
"My elder sister's conduct is lofty and exceptional,
and she has not yet encountered a suitable match.
Unlike my lowly and shallow self,
who merely marries hastily."
Cìyáng fell silent,
unable to refute her.
Those listening outside the curtain felt ashamed.
From "Běn Zhuàn" (The Original Biography).
Yī Jí
The First Ruler of Shǔ appointed Yī Jí as Gentleman of the Household of the Left General and sent him to Wú.
Sūn Quán, hearing of his talent and eloquence,
wanted to挫折 his arguments in advance.
As Yī Jí entered to pay respects,
Sūn Quán said:
"You labor in serving a ruler without the Way."
Yī Jí immediately replied:
"One bowing down and one rising up—
hardly counts as labor."
The Lord of Wú was greatly ashamed
and had no words to reply.
From "Sānguó Zhì" (Records of the Three Kingdoms).
Zhāng Yì
Zhāng Yì of Shǔ was the Grand Administrator of Yìzhōu
and was captured by a commandery man, Yōng Kǎi, who bound him and sent him to Sūn Quán.
Wǔ Hóu (Zhūgě Liàng) sent Dèng Zhī as an envoy to Wú,
instructing him to request Zhāng Yì from Sūn Quán during their conversation.
Since arriving in Wú,
Zhāng Yì had been moving about in exile and hiding in concealment.
Sūn Quán was unaware of this,
so he agreed to Dèng Zhī's request to send him back.
Just before Zhāng Yì's departure,
Sūn Quán summoned him for an audience.
He asked Zhāng Yì:
"In Shǔ, the widowed daughter of the Zhuō family
fled to elope with Xiàngrú.
What is the custom in your esteemed land
that it should be like this?"
Zhāng Yì replied:
"In my foolish opinion, the widowed daughter of the Zhuō family
is still more virtuous than the wife of Mǎi Chén."
From "Qǐyán Lù" (Records of Amusing Tales).
Zhāng Yù
□□□□□ When Liú Zhāng met at Fú,
Zhāng Yù was then an Attendant Clerk,
attending the seated gathering.
The man had a luxuriant beard.
The First Ruler mocked him, saying:
"In my county of Zhuō, there are especially many with the surname Máo (hair).
East, west, south, and north—
all are various Máo.
The Magistrate of Zhuō exclaimed:
'The various Máo surround and dwell at Zhuō (涿, homophone for "penis")!'"
Yù immediately replied:
"In the past, there was one who served as Chief of Lù in Shàngdǎng
and was promoted to Magistrate of Zhuō.
Upon leaving office and returning home,
when people wrote to him,
if they addressed him as 'Lù,' they would miss 'Zhuō,'
and if they addressed him as 'Zhuō,' they would miss 'Lù.'
So they addressed him as 'Lord Lùzhuō (潞涿, homophone for "露涿" meaning exposed penis).'"
The First Ruler laughed heartily.
The First Ruler had no beard,
hence Yù's remark alluded to this.
"Yìwén Lèijù" (Classified Anthology of Literary Works), vol. 25, cites "Shǔ Zhì" (Records of Shǔ). The text in "Shǔ Zhì," biography 12 of Zhōu Qún, is roughly the same;
it is suspected to be from "Qǐyán Lù" (Records of Amusing Tales).

"Shouldn't you also mock your state of Wú (吳)?"

Thereupon, all those seated laughed joyfully,
and Fèng had nothing to reply.

Fèi Yī
Sūn Quán once hosted a feast for the Shu envoy Fèi Yī,
and beforehand ordered his officials:
"When the envoy arrives,
remain seated and eating, do not rise."
When Yī arrived,
Quán stopped eating to greet him,
but his officials did not rise.
Yī mocked them, saying:
"When the phoenix comes soaring,
the qilin stops chewing;
donkeys and mules, unaware,
keep eating as before."
Zhūgě Kè said:
"We planted the parasol tree,
to await the phoenix.
What kind of swallow-bird is this,
claiming to come soaring?
Why not shoot it down,
and send it back to its homeland?"
All praised his reply.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù".
Wáng Róng's Wife
Jìn dynasty's Wáng Róng had a wife.
She addressed Róng as "qīng".
Róng said to her:
"How can a wife address her husband as 'qīng'?
It is improper according to ritual."
She replied:
"Because I am fond of you and love you,
therefore I call you 'qīng';
if I do not call you 'qīng',
who should call you 'qīng'?"
Róng laughed and then allowed it.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù".
Dèng Ài
Dèng Ài had a stutter,
when speaking he would say "Ài... Ài..."
Jìn Wénwáng teased him, saying:
"When you say 'Ài Ài', how many Àis is that?"
He replied:
"'Fèng xī, fèng xī' (Oh phoenix, oh phoenix),
is still just one phoenix."
"Tàipíng Yùlǎn" vol. 464 cites this from "Yǔ Lín",
and vol. 466 cites it from "Shì Shuō",
the text is the same.
The Ānlíng Person
Jìn dynasty's Zhōng Yù and his brothers were exceptionally sharp-witted,
whenever they engaged in banter,
they were never at a loss.
Once they heard it said,
that there was a woman skilled at witty repartee,
and went to observe her.
So they dressed elaborately and rode together in a carriage,
traveling to the West Gate.
A woman laughed and said:
"The center of the carriage is especially high."
Yù and the others initially didn't notice,
a disciple behind the carriage said:
"You've just been mocked."
Zhōng was startled.
The disciple said:
"'The center is high,
the two ends are low' —
she is referring to a ram (dī)."
The brothers had thick beards, hence the remark.
Yáng Xiū
Jìn dynasty's Yáng Xiū was nine years old,
and very intelligent.
Kǒng Jūnpíng visited his father,
who was not home.
Yáng Xiū at the time served Jūnpíng.
There was fruit, bayberries,
Jūnpíng showed them to Xiū and said:
"This is truly your family's fruit."
Xiū immediately replied:
"I have never heard that the peacock is the Confucian gentleman's family bird."
From "Qǐ Yán Lù".
Sūn Zǐjīng
Jìn dynasty's Sūn Zǐjīng in his youth wanted to become a recluse,
and said to Wáng Wǔzǐ:
"I shall 'pillow on stone and rinse with stream'."
But mistakenly said "rinse with stone and pillow on stream."
Wáng said:
"Can a stream be pillowed on?
Can stone be rinsed with?"
Zǐjīng said:
"The reason for pillowing on the stream,
is to wash my ears;
the reason for rinsing with stone,
is to sharpen my teeth."
From "Shì Shuō Xīn Yǔ",
the Ming manuscript copy cites it from "Qǐ Yán Lù".
Cài Hóng
Jìn dynasty's Cài Hóng went to Luòyáng,
where people in Luòyáng asked him:
"The recruitment office has just opened,
and the lords are appointing men.
Seeking outstanding talents from humble places,
gathering worthy men from mountain caves.
You are a scholar from Wú-Chǔ,
a remnant of a fallen state,
what exceptional talent do you have,
to respond to this summons?"
Cài replied:
"The pearl of night's radiance,
need not come from the Mèngjīn River;
a jade disc filling the grasp,
need not be gathered from the Kūnlún Mountains.
The Great Yǔ was born among the Eastern Barbarians;
King Wén was born among the Western Qiāng.
Where sages and worthies emerge,
why must it always be the usual places?
In the past, King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
and moved the stubborn people to Luòyì.
Could it be that you gentlemen are their descendants?"
From "Qǐ Yán Lù".
Lù Jī
Lù Jī visited Wáng Wǔzǐ,
Wǔzǐ had a hundred hu of goat cheese.
Pointing at it, he said to him:
"What in your Eastern Wú can match this?"
Lù said:
"We have thousand-mile water shield soup,
only it hasn't had fermented beans added yet."
While Jī was seated,
Pān Ān arrived,
and Lù immediately stood up.
Ānrén (Pān Ān) said:
"When the clear wind arrives,
disorderly things rise."
Lù immediately replied: "A flock of birds gathers."
From "Qǐ Yán Lù".
Cài Mó
Jìn dynasty's Wáng Dǎo had a jealous wife,
Dǎo kept several concubines in a separate residence,
his wife found out,
and grabbing a kitchen knife, was about to go there.
The lord hastily ordered his carriage,
worried the ox was slow,
he took a fly-whisk in hand,
and used its handle to help whip the ox.
Cài Mó heard of this,
and later, visiting Wáng, said to him:
"The court wishes to bestow upon you the Nine Bestowals."
Wáng began to modestly decline,
Cài said:
"I haven't heard of the other items,
only of the short-shaft calf-cart,
and the long-handled fly-whisk."
Dǎo was greatly ashamed.
From "Jìn Shǐ".
Zhūgě Huī
Jìn dynasty's Zhūgě Huī and Chancellor Wáng Dǎo
argued over whose family name came first.
Wáng said:
"Why not say 'Gě Wáng',
but instead say 'Wáng Gě'?"
He replied:
"It's like saying 'donkey-horse' —
does the donkey possibly surpass the horse?"
From "Qǐ Yán Lù".
Zhōu Yǐ
Jìn dynasty's Yǔ Liàng visited Zhōu Yǐ.
Yǐ said:
"Why are you so happy and suddenly fat?"
Yǔ said:
"Why are you so worried and gaunt?"
Zhōu said:
"I have nothing to worry about,
it's just that purity and emptiness increase daily,
and filth and dregs depart daily."
From "Nán Shǐ".
Hán Bó
Hán Bó, the Attendant Gentleman of the Jin dynasty official Zhāng Tiānxī,
presented a memorial along with a covenant document.
Bó was eloquent,
and Huán Wēn greatly praised him.
Once at a grand gathering,
Wēn had his Marshal Diāo Yí say to Bó:
"You are a descendant of Hán Lú."
Bó replied:
"You are a descendant of Hán Lú."
Wēn laughed and said:
"Diāo, because your surname is Hán,
naturally asked you that.
Others have the surname Diāo,
how could they be descendants of Hán Lú?"
Bó said:
"Your Excellency has not thought it through,
the short-tailed one is Diāo."
The entire assembly sighed in admiration.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Xí Zàochǐ
When Fú Jiān of the Qin state captured Xiāngyáng,
he captured Xí Zàochǐ and the monk Shì Dào'ān.
At that time, Zàochǐ suffered from a foot ailment,
Jiān saw him,
and after speaking with him was greatly pleased.
He sighed and said:
"In the past, when Jin pacified Wu,
the gain was in the two Lùs;
now breaking the southern lands,
I have obtained one and a half scholars."
This was mocking his lameness.
Earlier, Zàochǐ once visited Dào'ān for discussion,
and praised himself saying:
"Throughout the four seas, Xí Zàochǐ."
Ān responded immediately:
"Filling the heavens, Shì Dào'ān."
All considered it an elegant rejoinder.
From "Jìn Chūnqiū"
Sūn Shèng
Jin dynasty's Sūn Shèng and Yīn Hào engaged in debate,
their back-and-forth was intense and arduous.
Host and guest were uninterrupted,
attendants brought food,
but it grew cold and was reheated four times.
They both vigorously waved their yak-tail whisks,
until all the hairs fell out,
covering the entire meal.
Host and guest thus forgot to eat until dusk.
Yīn then said to Sūn:
"Don't be a stubborn-mouthed horse,
or I'll twist your nose."
Sūn said:
"Haven't you seen a nose-ringed ox,
someone will soon yoke your neck."
From "Nán Shǐ"
Zǔ Nà
Zǔ Nà of the Eastern Jin, an Imperial Household Grandee, was orphaned and impoverished in his youth,
and was extremely filial by nature.
He often personally cooked meals for his mother.
Wáng Píng heard of his fine reputation,
"fine reputation" originally written as "dwelling," amended according to "Shì Shuō."
and knowing he personally attended to her support,
gave him two maidservants,
and subsequently made him an official.
Someone teased him,
saying a male slave's price is double that of a maid.
Zǔ replied:
"Was Bǎilǐ Xī necessarily worth less than five ram skins?"
From "Shì Shuō"
Hǎo Lóng
Jin dynasty's Hǎo Lóng served as a Southern Barbarian Army Consultant.
On the third day of the third month he composed a poem:
"Jūyú fish leap in the clear pond."
Huán Wēn asked what that was,
he replied:
"The barbarian name for fish is jūyú."
Huán said:
"Why use barbarian language?"
Lóng said:
"I traveled a thousand lǐ to serve you, Sir,
and only obtained a barbarian prefecture consultant post,
how could I not speak barbarian language?"
From "Shì Shuō"
Luó Yǒu
Jin dynasty's Luó Yǒu's family was poor,
and he sought an official salary from Huán Wēn.
Although Wēn treated him well for his talent and learning,
he considered him unrestrained and eccentric,
unsuited for governing the people,
and promised but did not employ him.
Later, a colleague in the same office obtained a commandery post,
and Wēn held a drinking gathering to bid farewell.
Yǒu was also commanded to attend,
but arrived especially late.
Wēn asked him why,
he replied:
"Your servant yesterday received your command and left,
but on the way encountered a ghost who mocked me, saying:
'I only see you seeing others off to their commandery,
why don't I see anyone seeing you off to your commandery?'
Your servant felt ashamed throughout,
and had to turn back to resolve it.
Unwittingly, I incurred the fault of delay."
Wēn laughed at his wit,
and felt rather ashamed himself.
Later, he appointed him as Grand Administrator of Xiāngyáng.
From "Zhǔ Gōng Jiù Shì"
Zhāng Róng
Song dynasty's Zhāng Róng once requested leave to return home,
the Emperor asked where he lived.
He replied:
"Your servant lives on land but not in a house,
lives on a boat but not on water."
The Emperor did not understand,
and asked Zhāng Xù.
Xù said:
"Róng is near the Eastern Hills,
and has no fixed dwelling.
He temporarily pulled a small boat ashore,
and lives inside it."
The Emperor laughed heartily.
Emperor Tàizǔ once promised Róng in person the post of Chief Clerk to the Minister of Education,
but the edict never appeared.
Róng rode a very thin horse,
Tàizǔ said:
"Why is your horse so thin?
How much grain do you give it?"
Róng said:
"One dàn per day."
The Emperor said:
"Why is it so thin then?"
Róng said:
"Your servant promises but does not give."
The next day,
he was appointed Chief Clerk to the Minister of Education.
Róng and Xiè Bǎojī
"Xiè Bǎojī" should be "Bǎojī Xiè,"
Bǎojī was Róng's sixth younger brother,
see the basic biography in "Nán Shǐ."
went together for an audience with Tàizǔ,
and Róng passed gas in front of the Emperor.
Bǎojī rose and apologized, saying:
"My elder brother has offended Your Majesty."
The Emperor laughed and did not inquire further.
Shortly after, food arrived,
Róng pushed Bǎojī aside,
refusing to eat with him.
The Emperor said:
"Why not eat with your worthy brother?"
Róng said:
"Your servant cannot share a plate with a mouth that apologizes for gas."
The Emperor laughed heartily.
From "Tán Sǒu"
Hé Chéngtiān
Hé Chéngtiān of Dōnghǎi in the Song dynasty,
was the nephew of Xú Guǎng.
He was appointed Assistant Editorial Director,
but was already advanced in years.
The other Assistant Directors were all young men from famous families,
and Xún Bózǐ of Yǐngchuān mocked him,
calling him "wet nurse."
Chéngtiān said:
"You should know the phoenix leads nine chicks,
what's wrong with being a wet nurse?"
From "Tán Sǒu"
Wáng Xuàn
Jin dynasty's Wáng Xuàn,
was the son of Wáng Yù.
At six years old,
his maternal grandfather Hé Shàngzhī
particularly admired and valued him.
He was studying the "Analects,"
and reached the line "How cultured and elegant!"
Shàngzhī joked:
"You could change it to 'How cultured and elegant, yéyé!'"
People of Wú and Shǔ
call father "yé."
Xuàn clasped his hands and replied:
"An elder's name,
how can it be joked about?
One could also say 'The grass, when the wēng wind blows, must bend to the jiù.'"
The "Analects" says,
"The grass, when the wind blows upon it, must bend."
Wēng refers to Wáng Xuàn's maternal grandfather Hé Shàngzhī,
Jiù refers to Shàngzhī's son Hé Yǎn.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù,"
after the characters "wēng jí" originally had the three characters "wēng jí zài,"
deleted according to the Ming dynasty manuscript.
Hé Xù
Sòng Jiāngxià Wáng Liú Yìgōng was fond of antiques,
and often sought them from court officials.
Attendant-in-Chief Hé Xù had already presented some,
but the prince kept demanding more.
Hé was greatly displeased.
Once, while traveling,
he saw a dog collar and a calf-nosed loincloth on the road.
He ordered his attendants to pick them up and bring them back.
He then sent them in a box,
with a note that read:
"I have heard you again require ancient objects;
now I present Lǐ Sī's dog collar,
and Xiàngrú's calf-nosed loincloth."
From "Yīnhuà Lù".
Xiè Língyùn
Mèng Yǐ, the governor of Kuàijī during the Sòng dynasty, was devout in his Buddhist practice,
but Xiè Língyùn looked down on him.
He said to Yǐ:
"Attaining the Way requires wisdom and karma;
you, sir, may ascend to heaven before Língyùn,
but you will certainly achieve Buddhahood after Língyùn."
Yǐ deeply resented this.
From "Nán Shǐ".
Liú Huì
Qí's Liú Huì served as the governor of Nánkāng commandery.
A resident of the commandery, Zhì Lèi, lived in a place
called Filthy Village.
Huì teased him, saying:
"What filth do you possess,
that you live in Filthy Village?"
He replied:
"I do not know what fault Kǒng Qiū had,
that he lived in Quē Village."
Huì admired his clever reply.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Xú Xiàosì
Qí's Minister of Works, Xú Xiàosì of Dōnghǎi, renovated and maintained Gāozuò Temple,
and often rested there.
Master Fǎyún also frequented Xiāo Temple day and night, each visiting their own.
The two temples were adjacent,
but they did not visit each other.
Xiàosì once said to Fǎyún:
"Master, you often reside on the high seat,
yet you do not visit Gāozuò Temple."
He replied:
"Patron, since you serve the Xiāo family,
why do you not go to Xiāo Temple?"
From "Tán Sǒu".
Shěn Wénjì
When Qí's Tàizǔ was Prince of Qí,
he hosted a drinking feast for entertainment.
Cuī Sīzǔ of Qīnghé attended the banquet,
and said to Attendant-in-Chief Shěn Wénjì:
"Thick soup and minced fish are praised by both north and south."
Wénjì replied:
"Thick soup and minced fish are actually Wú cuisine,
not something you would know."
Sīzǔ said:
"Roasted turtle and minced carp—
these seem not to be poems of Gōuwú."
Wénjì said:
"Water shield soup from a thousand lǐ away—
how could it concern the gentlemen of Lǔ and Wèi?"
The emperor praised him, saying:
"The water shield soup should indeed be credited to Shěn."
From "Tán Sǒu".
Shěn Zhāolüè
Qí's Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Shěn Zhāolüè of Wúxīng,
was the son of Attendant-in-Chief Shěn Wénshū.
He was wild and talented,
indulging in drink and acting on impulse,
so court officials often feared yet tolerated him.
Once, while drunk,
he leaned on a staff and arrived at Wúhú Garden,
where he met Wáng Yuē of Lángyá.
Staring wide-eyed, he said:
"Are you Wáng Yuē?
Why so fat and foolish?"
Yuē replied:
"Are you Shěn Zhāolüè?
Why so thin and mad?"
Zhāolüè clapped his hands and laughed loudly, saying:
"Thin is already better than fat,
and mad is again better than foolish."
Yuē
was the son of Wáng Jǐngwén.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Hú Xiézhī
Qí's Hú Xiézhī of Yùzhāng initially served as the Records Officer of Jiāngzhōu,
and Tàizǔ entrusted him with responsibilities.
Because his family spoke with a Xī accent,
and their pronunciation was not standard,
the emperor sent several palace attendants
to Xiézhī's home
to teach his children.
After two years,
the emperor asked him:
"Has your family's pronunciation been corrected?"
He replied:
"The palace attendants are few,
while my family members are many.
Not only did they fail to correct our pronunciation,
but they even made the palace attendants pick up the Xī accent."
The emperor laughed heartily;
he told all the court officials about it.
Xiézhī later served as Minister of Revenue and Governor of Yùzhōu.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Liáng Wǔ
Liáng's Gāozǔ once composed a five-character stacked-rhyme verse:
"Behind the window, there are pomegranates and willows."
He ordered the court officials to compose similar verses.
Liú Xiàochuò said:
"Liáng Wáng is strong and healthy."
Shěn Yuē said:
"Sleeping tilted against the side of the boat."
Yǔ Jiānwú said:
"Carrying a spoon often obstructs the dam."
Xú Chī said:
"Yesterday, I sacrificed at Yǔ's temple,
and there were six hú of leftover cooked venison."
Hé Xùn, using Cáo Mán's old story, said:
"Gazing at the withered Sūgū hut."
Wú Jūn pondered for a long time,
but ultimately said nothing.
Gāozǔ looked displeased and unhappy.
Soon, an edict was issued:
"Wú Jūn is not equitable,
Hé Xùn is not modest;
they should be handed over to the Commandant of Justice."
From "Tán Sǒu".
Liǔ Xìnyán
Liáng's Prince of Ānchéng, Xiāo Chì, was erudite
and skilled in writing.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he was the leading literary figure of his generation,
exclusively in charge of profound and elegant decrees.
He served as Attendant-in-Chief, Minister of Works, and Head of the Secretariat,
with a collection of thirty volumes,
and authored the one-hundred-volume "History of Liáng".
Initially, Chì was renowned for his literary talent,
and the only one who could rival him
was Liǔ Xìnyán of Hédōng.
However, although Liǔ inwardly did not concede,
he could not compete.
Upon hearing of Chì's death,
Liǔ was then serving as Minister of Personnel.
Guests came to visit him,
and saw him hopping on one foot,
repeatedly exclaiming:
"Walking alone now,
walking alone now!"
All the guests danced and clapped,
treating it as a joke and amusement.
From "Zhǔgōng Jiùshì".
Xú Chī
Liáng's Attendant-in-Chief Xú Chī of Dōnghǎi
was the son of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Xú Chāo.
He was erudite and talented,
fond of novel changes,
and not constrained by old styles.
He once described someone suffering from an ulcer:
"Crimson blood flows at night,
yellow pus drains by day.
Looking askance, purple lungs;
gazing straight, red liver."
He also said:
"A curtain hanging on the door,
clearly known to be bamboo.
Fish swimming fear the net,
surely seeing the weir."
And also:
"Not shaped like a swift horse,
yet hooves tread in succession.
Unlike a scholar's mat,
but lying long with a scripture belt."
Chī's son, Xú Líng,
served as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
He was sent as an envoy to Wèi.
Wèi's Receptionist, Wèi Shōu, said:
"Today's heat
must be because Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary Xú has come."
Líng replied:
"In the past, Wáng Sù came here,
and began establishing rituals for Wèi.
Now that I have come on this mission,
I make you aware of cold and heat again."
Shōu was unable to reply.
From "Tán Sǒu".
Xú Líng
Lǐ Táotú
When a Chén envoy was sent to Qí,
he saw someone with a red beard at court.
Turning to the Imperial Attendant Lǐ Táotú of Zhàojùn, he asked:
"What about the red-bearded one?"
Táotú replied:
"Girded with a sash and standing at court,
he can be made to converse with guests."
Táotú was then assigned to receive guests.
From Tán Sǒu.
Lú Sīdào
When Běi Qí's Lú Sīdào was sent as an envoy to Chén,
the Chén ruler ordered high-ranking court officials to prepare wine and food
and hold a banquet with Sīdào,
composing linked-verse poetry together.
One person began first,
and took the opportunity to mock the northerners, saying:
"Elms grow to fill the Hàn men,
grass grows to fatten the donkeys."
This was because northerners ate elms,
and the Wú region had no donkeys,
hence this verse.
Sīdào took up the brush and immediately continued:
"Sharing a steamer, they cook rice separately,
rice originally written as water,
changed according to the Míng manuscript.
in the same pot, each boils his own fish."
This was because southerners lacked affection and righteousness,
sharing a stove but eating different dishes,
hence Sīdào's verse.
The Wú people were greatly ashamed.
Also, the Commandant of the Guards, Dù Táiqīng of Jīngzhào,
was playing shuò with the Central Army Adjutant Cuī Biāo of Qīnghé.
They had bet ten coins from Chéngdū,
but only wagered one pheasant.
Lú Sīdào said:
"Even with all of Chéngdū,
it's no more than one pheasant."
Biāo also said to Sīdào:
"Last night there was great thunder,
but I slept through it."
Sīdào said:
"Such thunderous noise,
yet it couldn't stir the hibernating insects."
The Crown Prince's Household Manager, Lú Shūhǔ of Fànyáng, had ten sons.
The eldest was named Chùshēng,
and was the most talented.
Sīdào said to others:
"My uncle has ten sons,
but none can compare to Chùshēng."
Shūhǔ was the grandson of the Director of the Bureau of Receptions, Zé.
The Imperial Attendant Xīn Déyuán of Lǒngxī said to Sīdào:
"Yesterday I composed a poem about a Qiāng old woman,
but only got five words:
'Black scarf drapes the shoulder well.'
I struggled to find a matching line."
Sīdào immediately responded:
"Why not 'Yellow thing
Míng manuscript has thing as yáng
stuck in the forehead.'" Sīdào once said to the Attendant-at-Arms Fēng Xiàoqiān of Bóhǎi:
"Since your surname is Fēng,
you must be descended from the great boar."
Qiān replied:
"You
The words 'you' are supplemented according to the Míng manuscript.
since your surname is Lú,
must be descended from the black hound."
From Tán Sǒu.
Shí Dòngtǒng
Emperor Gāozǔ of the Northern Qí once held a banquet to entertain his close ministers for amusement.
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"I will present you all with a riddle,
and you may all try to guess it.
'Zúlǜ gědá.'" None of the others could guess it.
Someone said,
"It is a 'xiāozi' arrow."
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"That is not it."
Shí Dòngtǒng said:
"Your servant has guessed it."
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"What is it?"
Dòngtǒng replied:
"It is a fried pancake."
Emperor Gāozǔ laughed and said:
"Dòngtǒng has guessed correctly."
Emperor Gāozǔ then said:
"All of you,
make a riddle for me,
and I will guess it for you."
Before anyone else could compose one,
Dòngtǒng made a riddle.
He again said, "Zúlǜ gědá."
Emperor Gāozǔ could not guess it,
and asked:
"What is this thing?"
The reply was:
"It is a fried pancake."
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
"I just made that one,
why are you making it again?"
Dòngtǒng said:
"Taking advantage of Your Majesty's hot griddle,
I made another one."
Emperor Gāozǔ laughed heartily.
Emperor Gāozǔ once ordered someone to read from the "Wénxuǎn".
When it came to Guō Pú's "Roaming Immortal" poem,
he sighed in admiration and praised it.
All the scholars said:
"This poem is extremely skillful,
truly as Your Majesty's judgment indicates."
Dòngtǒng immediately stood up and said:
"What ability does this poem have?
If Your Majesty ordered me to compose one,
it would surpass his by double."
Emperor Gāozǔ was displeased.
After a long while, he said:
"Who are you,
to claim that your poem would surpass Guō Pú's by double?
Is that not deserving of death?"
Dòngtǒng immediately said:
"If Your Majesty orders me to compose one now,
and it does not surpass his by double,
I willingly accept death."
He was then ordered to compose it.
Dòngtǒng said:
"Guō Pú's 'Roaming Immortal' poem says:
'Green stream, a thousand rèn high,
in its midst is one Daoist priest.'
My composition says: 'Green stream, two thousand rèn high,
in its midst are two Daoist priests.'
Does that not surpass his by double?"
Emperor Gāozǔ then laughed heartily.
The Ming Dynasty manuscript copy has 748 more characters after "laugh",
up to "Emperor Gāozǔ laughed heartily at Dòngtǒng",
which are now supplemented accordingly.
Additionally, the missing characters are collated and supplemented using the Dūnhuáng manuscript version
of the "Qǐyán Lù".
Also, Emperor Wénxuān of Qí said:
"If you pardon your servant from ten thousand deaths, it can be done."
The Emperor said:
"Good."
He said:
"Your servant yesterday □□□□□□□□□ fell into a sealed jar,
your servant for Your Majesty managed to return and ascend to heaven again □□□□□□□□□ truly?"
The reply was:
"Your servant last night dreamed of following Your Majesty,
fell into a latrine and came out.
□□□□□ licked it."
The Emperor was greatly angered,
and ordered the authorities to execute him.
He said:
"Your servant requests to speak one word before dying."
The Emperor said.
□□□ Your Majesty obtaining your servant's head is utterly useless,
your servant losing his head □□□.
He laughed and spared him.
Gāo □□□ held a vegetarian assembly,
where the Great Virtue Dharma Master gave a lecture.
When Daoist and lay followers had doubts,
or points of stagnation,
they would engage in debate and discussion.
Citing great principles,
expounding the Dharma gate,
the discourse was profound and abstruse,
all being elegant and orthodox.
Dòngtǒng was the last to engage in discussion,
and said to the Dharma Master:
"Allow me to ask the Dharma Master a small question:
What does the Buddha usually ride?"
The Dharma Master replied:
"Sometimes he sits on a thousand-petaled lotus,
sometimes he rides a six-tusked white elephant."
Dòngtǒng said:
"The Dharma Master does not read the sutras nowadays,
and does not know what the Buddha rides."
The Master then asked:
"Does the donor read the sutras?
What does the Buddha ride?"
The reply was:
"He rides an ox."
The Dharma Master said:
"How do you know?"
"The sutra says,
'The World-Honored One is most extraordinary,
he rides an ox.'"
The entire assembly laughed heartily.
He also said to the Dharma Master:
"Since the Dharma Master does not know the Buddha usually rides an ox,
I now have another question on Dharma meaning for the Master.
In every sutra it is always said to be worth a hundred thousand taels of gold;
I wonder, how many catties is a hundred thousand taels of gold in total?"
Thus, he had no reply.

at that time a Dharma Master first established the principle of "no one, no two, no right, no wrong".
Gāo □ ascended the high seat to lecture,
and again had him expound the old principle,
summoning Confucian scholars and academicians,

Though the principles and meanings were a hundredfold intricate,
none could match him.
Dòngtǒng then engaged in debate to challenge this monk, determined to make him speechless.

there should not be one foot.

can the Dharma Master still say there is no one?

can the Dharma Master still say there is no two?
Now the Emperor's virtue is vast and luminous,

insects, grass, and trees
all attain life;
can the Dharma Master still say there is no right?
Now the four seas are one family,

Thereupon the monk fell silent with no response,
and Emperor Gāozǔ clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
Emperor Gāozǔ also often gathered Confucian scholars for lectures,
"the responses and challenges were not few."
Dòngtǒng came later and said to the assembled scholars:
"Do you gentlemen know what surname Heaven has?"
A Doctor of the Five Classics said Heaven's surname is Gāo,
Dòngtǒng said:
"The Son of Heaven's surname is Gāo,
so Heaven's □ must be surnamed Gāo.
This is just imitating that Shǔ minister Qín Mì,
and is not a new idea at all.
In the orthodox classics,
There is the surname Tiān.
Sir, you may cite the main text,
without needing to rely on old stories."
The academician said,
"I don't know which classic
mentions the surname Tiān."
Shí Dòngtǒng said:
"Sir, you have not read books at all;
even the Classic of Filial Piety says that Tiān is originally a surname.
Sir, have you not seen the Classic of Filial Piety state,
'The way of father and son
is the nature of Tiān!'
Is that not the surname Tiān?"
The High Ancestor laughed heartily.
Shí Dòngtǒng
(The above is supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy.)
He also once observed an academician discussing in the National Academy:
"Among Confucius's disciples,
seventy-two were accomplished."
Shí Dòngtǒng then asked:
"Among the seventy-two accomplished ones,
how many had already worn caps,
and how many had not yet worn caps?"
The academician said:
"The classics and commentaries have no record."
Shí Dòngtǒng said:
"Sir, when you read books,
how could you not understand?
Among Confucius's disciples,
thirty had already worn caps,
and forty-two had not yet worn caps."
The academician said:
"On what text do you base this distinction?"
He replied:
"The Analects says,
'Five or six capped men.'
Five times six is thirty men.
'Six or seven boys.'
Six times seven is forty-two boys.
Is that not seventy-two people?"
Everyone present was greatly amused,
and the academician had no reply.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Xú Zhīcái
Xú Zhīcái of Gāopíng, King of Xīyáng of Qí, was knowledgeable
and eloquent.
His father Xióng,
grandfather Chéngbó,
both excelled in
(The Ming manuscript copy has a blank space after "excelled in";
according to the "Běi Qí Shū" biography of Xú Zhīcái,
it is suspected to be the character "yī" [medicine].)
Their skills were passed down through the family.
The advisor Zǔ Xiàozhēng teased him,
calling him "Shīgōng" [Master-Father].
Zhīcái said:
"Since I am your master,
and also your father,
in the principle of the three [relationships],
I occupy two at once."
Xiàozhēng was the son of the minister Yíng.
Zhīcái once engaged in witty banter with minister Wèi Shōu.
Shōu stared at him and said:
"Your face resembles a commoner's fāngxiàng [exorcist figure]."
Zhīcái replied:
"If so,
then it is your burial implement."

From "Sān Guó Diǎn Lüè"
Hóu Bái
During the Sui dynasty, there was a man named Hóu Bái.
He was recommended by his prefecture as a xiùcái,
and came to the capital.
He was quick-witted and eloquent,
unmatched by anyone at the time.
Once, he was riding side by side and chatting with the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Duke Yuèguó Yáng Sù.
Beside the road stood a pagoda tree,
withered and dead.
Sù then said:
"Scholar Hóu, your reasoning surpasses others.
Can you make this tree come back to life?"
He replied:
"I can."
Sù said:
"What method will bring it back to life?"
He said:
"Take the seeds of the pagoda tree and hang them on the branches,
and it will revive itself."
Sù said:
"How can that make it live?"
He answered:
"Haven't you heard the Analects say,
'While the Master (Zǐ) is alive,
how dare Huí die?'" Sù laughed heartily.
During the Kāihuáng era,
there was a man whose surname was Chū,
and his given name was Liùjīn.
Wishing to visit Sù,
he brought his name card to the gate of the ministry.
He encountered Bái
and asked him to write his surname.
Bái then wrote:
"Liùjīnbàn (Six and a half jīn)."
After the name was submitted,
Sù summoned the man and asked:
"Is your surname Liùjīnbàn?"
He replied:
"It is Chū Liùjīn."
Sù said:
"Why is it written as Liùjīnbàn?"
He said:
"Earlier, I asked Scholar Hóu to write it;
he must have made a mistake."
Sù immediately summoned Bái.
He said to him:
"Why did you mistakenly write the man's name?"
Bái replied:
"It is not a mistake."
Sù said:
"If it's not a mistake,
why is it that his surname is Chū, his name Liùjīn,
and when he asked you to write it,
you wrote Liùjīnbàn?"
Bái replied:
"Earlier at the ministry gate,
I happened to be in a hurry and had no means to weigh it.
Upon hearing it was Chū Liùjīn,
I estimated it should be six and a half jīn."
Sù laughed heartily at this.
Sù was from Guānzhōng,
while Bái was from Shāndōng.
Sù often posed sudden, difficult questions to him,
hoping he would have no reply.
Now, the local dialect of Guānzhōng
pronounces "water" (shuǐ) as "bà."
In Shāndōng, they also say "qié jiāng qù" for "carrying something away," pronounced as "jié"
(the sound is like its initial and final,
meaning "carrying a knife away").
Sù once teased Bái, saying:
"Shāndōng certainly has much benevolence and righteousness;
they borrow one thing and get two."
Bái asked:
"How do they get two?"
Sù answered:
"When someone asks to borrow a bow from them,
they say:
'Carry the knife away (jié dāo qù).'
Isn't that borrowing one thing and getting two?"
Bái immediately replied:
"The people of Guānzhōng are also very clever;
they ask about one and know two."
Sù said:
"How do you know that?"
Bái said:
"If someone asks,
'Lately there has been much rain;
has the Wèi River risen?'
They answer:
'Bà has grown (bà zhǎng).'
Isn't that asking about one and knowing two?"
Sù was then convinced of his quick-witted eloquence.
Bái held a sinecure post,
subordinate to Yáng Sù,
who admired his ability for witty conversation.
On each of his duty days,
Sù would order him to engage in amusing talk.
Sometimes from morning until evening,
he was only then able to return.
Just as he exited the ministry gate,
he happened to meet Sù's son, Xuǎngǎn.
Xuǎngǎn then said:
"Scholar Hóu,
you can surely tell Xuángǎn a good story."
Bái was detained,
unable to refuse.
He then said:
"There was a great tiger
who wanted to go into the wild to look for meat.
He saw a hedgehog lying on its back,
and thought it was a piece of meat.
As he was about to pick it up in his mouth,
he was suddenly coiled around the nose by the hedgehog.
Startled, he ran away,
not knowing to rest.
He ran straight into the mountains,
exhausted,
and unconsciously fell into a deep sleep.
The hedgehog then released his nose and left.
The tiger suddenly got up, overjoyed,
and walked to the foot of an oak tree.
Looking down, he saw an acorn cup,
and turning sideways, he said to it:
'This morning I had the honor of meeting your esteemed father;
I beg you, young master, to please step aside.'" Sù and Bái were engaged in witty conversation,
when Sù said:
"Suppose there is a deep pit now,
perhaps several hundred feet deep.
If you, sir, were to fall into it,
how would you get out?"
Bái said:
"I wouldn't need anything else inside,
just a needle and I could get out."
Sù said:
"What would you use the needle for?"
Bái replied:
"I would use the needle to bore a hole and fill the pit with water,
then float and paddle out."
Sù said:
"Where on the needle's head is there that much water?"
Bái said:
"If there isn't that much water,
why would I be willing to go into such a deep pit?"
Sù also said to Bái:
"I shall make a riddle for you, sir.
You must guess it,
without delay,
or you must be fined with wine."
Sù said:
"The head is one fēn long,
the eyebrows one cùn long.
Before midday arrives,
it has already been beaten twice."
Bái immediately replied:
"This is a dàorén (a Taoist priest)."
Sù said:
"Now you, sir, must make a riddle,
also without delay."
Bái then said:
"The head is one fēn long,
the eyebrows one cùn long.
Before midday arrives,
it has already been beaten twice."
Sù said:
"Why are you copying my riddle about the dàorén?"
Bái said:
"This is ālì (a donkey)."
Sù laughed heartily.
Bái served in the Táng dynasty,
and once made riddles with others.
Bái said:
"The riddle must be about a real object;
you cannot fabricate an explanation.
If you mislead everyone,
and after the solution is given,
no such object exists,
then you must be punished."
Bái then said:
"Its back is about the size of a house,
its belly about the size of a bowl,
its mouth about the size of a cup."
No one could guess it.
They all said:
"Where in the world is there an object
with a mouth the size of a cup,
yet a back the size of a house?
Certainly, no such thing exists.
We must make a bet."
After Bái made the bet with everyone,
he explained:
"This is a swallow's nest."
Everyone laughed heartily.
On another occasion, he came upon a banquet,
and everyone laughed at Bái for arriving late.
They all ordered him to make a riddle,
stipulating it must not be obscure and difficult to recognize,
nor crafty and bizarre,
nor artificially combined to form something
that people have never seen.
Bái immediately replied:
"There is a creature as big as a dog,
Its appearance greatly resembles an ox.
What is this thing?"
Some said it was a river deer,
some said it was a deer,
but all were told they were wrong.
Then he ordered Bái to explain,
and Bái said:
"This is a calf."
Bái and Sù also encountered a Hu man on the road,
carrying green grass as he walked.
Sù said:
"On the road to Cháng'ān,
one can even see the Green Grass Lake."
Moments later,
there were two drunken Hu men.
Wearing heavy mourning garments,
they rode horses and galloped away.
Soon, one Hu man fell off his horse.
Bái said:
"Truly what is called filial piety,
only filial piety has this."
Bái was not yet famous at first,
in his hometown.
When the county magistrate first arrived,
Bái went to pay his respects.
He said to his acquaintances:
"I can make the magistrate bark like a dog."
They said:
"How could the magistrate be made to bark like a dog?
If it truly happens as you say,
we will treat you to a meal.
If it is false,
you shall treat us."
Thereupon he entered to pay his respects,
while his acquaintances waited outside the gate.
The magistrate said:
"What brings you here,
that you come again to see me?"
Bái said:
"Your Honor has just arrived,
and there are inconveniences among the people,
so I wish to consult you.
Before Your Honor arrived,
there were many thieves and robbers.
I request that every household be ordered to keep dogs,
so that their barking will startle them,
and naturally the thefts and robberies will cease."
The magistrate said:
"If so,
my household must also keep a dog that can bark,
how can I obtain one?"
Bái said:
"My home has a new pack of dogs,
their barking is different from other dogs."
The magistrate said:
"How do they sound?"
Bái replied:
"Their barking goes 'yōu yōu'."
The magistrate said:
"You know nothing about good dog barks.
A good dog's bark
should go 'háo háo'.
The 'yōu yōu' sound
is not at all from a dog that can bark."
Those listening outside heard this,
and none could help but cover their mouths and laugh.
Bái knew he had won,
and then said:
"If you seek such a barker,
I shall go out and find one."
Then he bid farewell and left.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Lú Jiāyán
In the Suí dynasty, Lú Jiāyán went to a temple to pay respects,
and entered the monks' quarters.
One monk was skilled in debate,
so Jiāyán began conversing with him.
They started teasing each other,
and this monk was at a loss for arguments.
Two other monks sitting nearby
immediately helped this monk respond.
After several rounds back and forth,
all three monks were at a loss.
Jiāyán then laughed and said to them:
"Three reverend masters,
none of you understand chūpú."
The monks did not understand,
so Jiāyán immediately explained:
"Haven't you heard chūpú players say,
'Three bald heads,
cannot match one Lú'?"The onlookers laughed heartily,
and the monks had no reply.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Lù Cāo
In the Suí dynasty, Lù Cāo, Minister of the Seven Military Departments from Héjiān, was not handsome,
but was eloquent.
Once, when he had just married,
Lǐ □, Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent from Zhàojùn, said to him:
"Repeatedly encountering pheasant shooting,
several times it brings a smile to one's face."
Cāo replied:
"Xī Guī's two sons,
neither spoke nor laughed."
From "Tán Sǒu"
Xuē Dàohéng
In the Suí dynasty, former Vice Director of the Secretariat Xuē Dàohéng ate a mixture of sweet wine and wheat porridge,
and said to Lú Sīdào:
"In the application of the rites,
harmony is prized.
The way of the former kings,
this was considered beautiful."
Sīdào replied:
"To know harmony and pursue harmony,
without regulating it with the rites,
is also not permissible."
From "Tán Sǒu"
In the Suí dynasty, Liú Zhuòzhī
from Héjiān Commandery
and his nephew Liú Xuàn were both Confucian scholars,
and both broke the law and were imprisoned.
The county clerks did not know
that they were great scholars,
and put cangues on them both.
Zhuò said:
"Sitting all day in the cangue,
yet not seeing home."
Xuàn said:
"Also carrying the cangue all day while sitting,
yet not seeing my wife."
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
The Shāndōng Man
A man from Shāndōng married a woman from Pǔzhōu,
where many suffer from goiters.
His mother-in-law had a very large goiter on her neck.
Several months after the wedding,
the wife's family suspected the son-in-law was not clever.
The father-in-law held a banquet,
gathering many relatives,
intending to test him.
He asked:
"Our son-in-law studied in Shāndōng,
so he should understand principles.
Why do swans and cranes cry?"
He replied:
"Heaven made them so."
He asked again:
"Why do pines and cypresses stay green in winter?"
He replied:
"Heaven made them so."
He asked again:
"Why do trees by the roadside have knobs?"
He replied:
"Heaven made them so."
The father-in-law said:
"Our son-in-law understands no principles at all,
why then did he idly dwell in Shāndōng?"
Then, teasing him, he said:
"Swans and cranes cry because their necks are long;
pines and cypresses stay green in winter because their hearts are strong;
trees by the roadside have knobs
because carts have scraped them.
How could it be that Heaven made them so?"
The son-in-law said:
"Allow me to respond with what I have heard and seen,
I wonder if it is permitted?"
He said:
"You may speak."
The son-in-law said:
"Frogs can croak,
is it because their necks are long?
Bamboo also stays green in winter,
is it because its heart is strong?
Your wife's goiter under her neck is so large,
is it because a cart scraped her?"
The father-in-law was ashamed,
and had nothing to reply.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Eater
