In the Suí dynasty, there was a man who was quick-witted and intelligent,
but he had a stutter.
Yáng Sù, whenever he was idle and bored,
would summon him for lively conversation.
Once, at the end of the year with nothing to do, they sat facing each other,
and Yáng Sù teased him, saying:
"There is a large pit, one zhàng deep.
It is also one zhàng square.
If you were sent into it,
by what method could you get out?"
The man lowered his head for a long while,
then asked:
"Is there a ladder to get out?"
Yáng Sù said:
"We are only discussing the scenario without a ladder.
If there were a ladder,
why would I need to ask?"
The man again lowered his head for a long while,
and asked:
"Is it d-d-d-daytime,
or n-n-n-nighttime?"
Yáng Sù said:
"Why mention daytime or nighttime?
How would you get out?"
The man then said:
"If it weren't nighttime,
and my eyes weren't blind,
why would I f-f-f-fall into such a place?"
Yáng Sù laughed heartily.
He asked again:
"Suppose you were suddenly appointed as a military commander,
defending a small city.
Your troops number no more than a thousand,
and you have only a few days' worth of provisions.
Outside the city, you are surrounded by tens of thousands of enemy troops.
If you were sent into the city,
what strategy would you devise?"
He lowered his head for a long while,
then asked:
"Is th-th-there any r-r-reinforcements?"
Yáng Sù said:
"Precisely because there are no reinforcements,
that is why I am asking you."
After pondering for a long while,
he raised his head and said to Yáng Sù:
"If it is r-r-really as you say,
then defeat is unavoidable."
Yáng Sù laughed heartily.
He asked again:
"I reckon you are highly capable.
There is nothing you do not understand.
Today at home,
someone was bitten on the foot by a snake.
How would you treat it?"
The man immediately replied:
"Take s-s-snow from under the south wall on the fifth day of the fifth month and a-a-apply it,
and it will be cured."
Yáng Sù said:
"Where can you find snow in the fifth month?"
He replied:
"If there is no snow on the fifth day of the fifth month,
then where are there snake bites in the twelfth month?"
Yáng Sù laughed and sent him away.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Zhào the Little Boy
In the Suí dynasty, there was a Tripitaka Master.
His father was originally a Sogdian merchant,
and the Master was born in China,
but his appearance and features
still resembled those of a foreigner.
His conduct and practice were extremely lofty,
and he was also eloquent and quick-witted.
Once, on the eighth day of the fourth month, he held a vegetarian feast and gave a lecture.
At that time, over a thousand people, including court officials, Daoists, and laypeople, came to watch.
Eminent monks of great virtue,
and officials known for their eloquence,
more than ten in total, engaged in debate with him one after another.
The Master responded to each challenge as it came,
and his arguments were inexhaustible.
Finally, there was a little boy surnamed Zhào,
thirteen years old,
who stepped forward from the crowd.
The Master's eloquence and quick-wittedness were already exceptional,
and moreover, all those who had debated before were venerable elders of high repute.
Suddenly seeing this boy wanting to engage in debate,
the crowd all found it strange and laughed.
The boy remained calm and composed,
and took his seat.
He said loudly to the monk:
"In the past, the Wild Fox Monk had his own scriptures.
I am not clear: when a fox serves as an ācārya,
from which canonical text does that come?"
The monk said:
"This young
man (original text had '即',
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy)
has a loud voice but a small body.
Why not use your voice to supplement your body?"
The boy immediately replied:
"Since the Master says that your disciple has a loud voice but a small body,
and asks why not use the voice to supplement the body,
then the Master has deep-set eyes and a long nose.
Why not cut off your nose to supplement your eyes?"
Everyone was astonished,
stood up, and laughed heartily.
It was the hot summer month then,
and the Master held a ruyi scepter in his left hand,
while fanning himself with a fan in his right hand.
Before the laughter had subsided,
the Master was again thinking of a reply.
Using the fan he was waving,
he covered his face and lowered his head.
The boy again said loudly:
"Round like the full moon,
it does not hide the Jade Rabbit,
but instead covers the male fox."
The crowd laughed uproariously.
The Master then put down the fan,
and pointed with the ruyi scepter,
intending to pose another question.
But before he could finish speaking,
suddenly the head of the ruyi scepter fell off.
The boy immediately stood up and said to the Master:
"Since the ruyi is broken,
the edge of your arguments is also blunted."
Then, before the seat,
he made a deep bow and left.
The monk was both angry and ashamed,
and had nothing more to say in response.
All who witnessed it were amazed, sighed in admiration, and laughed.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Zhǎngsūn Wújì
Emperor Tàizōng of the Táng dynasty was feasting with his close ministers,
and they were teasing and joking with each other.
Duke Zhào, Zhǎngsūn Wújì,
mocked Ōuyáng Xún, saying:
"Hunching your shoulders forms the character 'mountain',
burying your head, it does not emerge.
On whose Pavilion of Imperial Favor
is such a macaque painted?"
Ōuyáng Xún responded:
"Tucking
your head in warms your back (original text had '索',
changed according to the Ming manuscript copy),
a thin robe fears the cold of the belly.
Only because the mind is muddled,
therefore the face is round and plump."
The Emperor assumed a stern expression and said:
"Ōuyáng Xún,
are you not afraid that the Empress will hear?
Duke Zhào is the Empress's elder brother."
From "Guócháo Zá Jì"
Rén Guī
In the Táng dynasty, Duke Guǎn, Rén Guī, was terribly afraid of his wife.
Emperor Tàizōng, in recognition of his merits, bestowed upon him two maidservants.
Rén Guī bowed in thanks,
but did not dare take them home.
Emperor Tàizōng summoned his wife
and bestowed wine upon her.
He said to her:
"A woman's jealousy
is grounds for the seven reasons for divorce.
If you can reform your behavior and cease being jealous,
then you need not drink this wine.
If not,
you may drink it."
She said:
"Your concubine cannot reform her jealousy,
I request to drink the wine."
She then drank it.
When she returned home drunk,
she bid farewell to her family as if facing death.
But in fact, it was not poisoned wine,
so she did not die.
Another day,
Dù Zhènglún teased and mocked Rén Guī.
Rén Guī said:
"There are three reasons why a man should fear his wife.
When first married,
she sits properly like a Bodhisattva.
Is there anyone who does not fear a Bodhisattva?
After she bears children,
she becomes like a tiger raising its cubs.
Is there anyone who does not fear a tiger?
When she grows old, her face wrinkled,
she resembles a demoness.
Is there anyone who does not fear a demon?
For these reasons to fear one's wife,
what is so strange about it?"
Those who heard this were delighted.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì"
Cáo
In the manuscript copy, "Cáo" is written as "Táng".
Left Department Director Fēng Dàohóng,
was tall in stature,
and had an exceptionally broad buttocks.
When Dàohóng was about to enter the chamber to present a report,
Duke Yīng Lǐ Jì was behind him
and said to Dàohóng:
"Fēng Dàohóng,
your buttocks should just be enough to sit on—why do they need to be so large?"
From "Qǐyán Lù"
Lǐ Róng
In the Táng dynasty, there was a monk named Fǎguǐ,
who was short and small in stature.
While lecturing at the temple,
Lǐ Róng went to debate with him.
They went back and forth several rounds.
The monk had previously composed a poem mocking Róng,
and recited it from the high seat:
"Your surname is Lǐ, so you must be a plum (Lǐ);
you claim to be glorious (róng), yet you are not glorious."
Before the monk could finish the next line,
Lǐ Róng immediately responded:
"Your body is only three and a half chǐ tall,
and the hair on your head hasn't even grown yet."
The entire audience was delighted,
and admired his wit and quickness.
From "Qǐyán Lù"
Línghú Défēn
In the Táng dynasty, Zhào Yuánkǎi and Línghú Défēn accompanied the emperor to Shǎn.
Yuánkǎi invited Défēn to view the Dǐzhù stone in the river,
but Défēn did not go,
so Yuánkǎi went alone.
When he returned,
Défēn asked:
"What did the Dǐzhù stone say to you?"
Yuánkǎi replied:
"The Dǐzhù stone sent its respects to you."
Défēn immediately responded:
"Stones cannot speak,
but perhaps spirits inhabit them."
At the time, all the officials considered this an excellent retort.
From "Qǐyán Lù"
Cuī Xínggōng
In the Táng dynasty, Cuī Xínggōng and Jìng Bō were teasing each other.
Bō wore a dagger with a palm wood hilt,
and Xínggōng asked Bō:
"What kind of wood is this?"
Bō replied:
"It is palm wood (bīnglǘ mù)."
Xínggōng said:
"I was only asking about the dagger,
not about the person wearing it."
From "Qǐyán Lù"
Biān Rénbiǎo
In the Táng dynasty, Sìmén Assistant Instructor Hóng Chuò was debating with his student Biān Rénbiǎo.
When Hóng Chuò was about to be defeated in the argument,
he raised his voice in anger.
Biān then retorted:
"Sir, you become angry as soon as you hear reason;
how can you be called 'broad-minded' (Hóng)?
Everything about you is 'broad' (hóng, meaning 'loud' or 'boastful')."
Hóng responded:
"My surname is indeed Hóng."
Biān immediately replied:
"Although you are called Hóng,
your reasoning is never 'sufficient' (chuò)."
The audience burst into laughter,
and Hóng was ultimately defeated and left.
From "Qǐyán Lù"
Xīn Yù
In the Táng dynasty, Xīn Yù,
a native of Guǎnchéng,
was originally named Tàigōng.
At the age of twenty,
he encountered Emperor Tàizōng while traveling.
The emperor asked who he was,
and he replied:
"Xīn Tàigōng."
Emperor Tàizōng said:
"How do you compare to the former Tàigōng?"
Yù replied:
"The former Tàigōng
was eighty when he first met King Wén.
I am now just eighteen,
and have already met Your Majesty.
Thus, I surpass him by far."
Emperor Tàizōng was pleased,
and appointed him to serve in the Zhōngshū Department.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì"
Yǐn Jūn
In the Táng dynasty, Yáng Zuǎn,
a native of Huàyīn,
rose through the ranks to become Chief Administrator of Yōngzhōu
and later Minister of Personnel.
While Zuǎn was in Yōngzhōu,
Judicial Officer Yǐn Jūn had previously served as Registrar of Fāngzhōu.
When a directive ordered the procurement of dùruò herbs,
Yǐn Jūn wrote a response:
"Fāngzhōu has never had dùruò herbs,
as everyone in the world knows.
The directive suddenly requires this;
it must be due to misreading Xiè Tiǎo's poem.
If officials in the ministry handle matters like this,
aren't they afraid the Twenty-Eight Constellations will look down and laugh at them?"
He became known for this.
Later, while serving as Judicial Officer in Yōngzhōu,
there was a case of a foreigner stealing in the Jīnchéng ward.
Zuǎn ruled:
"All foreigners in the capital should be detained and interrogated."
Yǐn Jūn disagreed, saying:
"Criminals come in endless varieties,
and deceit takes many forms.
There are foreigners wearing Hàn hats,
and Hàn people wearing foreign boots.
We must also search among the Hàn people,
not just among the foreigners.
I request that only foreigners in the West Market be detained;
the rest should not be interrogated."
Zuǎn was angry and refused to accept the differing opinion.
He quickly took up his brush,
but after a moment of hesitation,
he ruled:
"Zuǎn concedes one point;
the rest is approved as requested."
When Emperor Tàizōng heard of this, he laughed and said:
"I appointed Yáng Zuǎn,
and now I hear he concedes one point upon hearing reason.
How many points should I concede?"
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì"
Péi Xuánběn
In the Táng dynasty, Péi Xuánběn enjoyed jesting
and served as Director of the Revenue Department.
At the time, Left Vice Director Fáng Xuánlíng was gravely ill,
and the department officials were going to visit him.
Xuánběn joked:
"If the Vice Director is ill,
we should visit him.
But if he is already gravely ill,
what's the point of visiting?"
Someone leaked his words.
Later, when he went with the others to see Xuánlíng,
Xuánlíng smiled and said:
"Director Péi has come;
it seems Xuánlíng will not die after all."
From "Dà Táng Xīnyǔ"
Zhǎngsūn Xuántóng
Táng Chángsūn Xuántóng was witty and eloquent from a young age,
and whenever he engaged in spirited conversation at gatherings,
there was no one who did not laugh with joy.
During the Yǒnghuī era,
he attended a banquet in the capital.
The conversation turned to matters among the common people,
and one person said:
"Lǐquán County is not far from the capital,
yet the people there practice gu poison.
This county should be exiled to a distant place;
how can we allow it to remain nearby?"
Another person then said:
"If the place of exile still has people,
and this person practices gu poison again,
wouldn't it still harm others?"
The first person said:
"If that's the case,
where do you suggest we place them?"
Xuántóng immediately said:
"If you let Xuántóng arrange it,
I will surely find them a suitable place."
Everyone was delighted,
and together they asked him.
He replied:
"Simply send all those who practice gu poison
to Mòlízhī to serve as cooks."
(Míng manuscript has "cooks" as "sons.")
Everyone laughed heartily.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
he once attended a banquet hosted by several nobles,
and no one could match him.
Princess Gāomì then said:
"My Duàn family also has talented men."
She immediately sent for Duàn Kè to come
and face Xuántóng.
Although Duàn Kè was somewhat articulate,
he was short in stature.
When summoned,
as soon as he entered the door,
Xuántóng said:
"The sun has already grown dim."
The princess and others were all greatly surprised and said:
"It's only the hour of fasting;
why do you say it's dim?"
Xuántóng then pointed at Duàn Kè and said:
"If the sun weren't dim,
how could a short man walk?"
Everyone at the gathering laughed loudly.
Duàn Kè's face turned bright red,
and he had nothing to say in reply.
When Xuántóng first took office,
a meal was set in the government office.
The granary officer was from Wú,
and his speech carried a strong local accent,
calling "flour porridge" "manure porridge."
At the time, all the dishes were laid out,
and steamed and roasted meats were served.
The granary officer said:
"Why not bring the manure porridge first?"
Everyone at the table laughed at him.
Xuántóng said:
"The granary officer is a descendant of dukes and marquises;
he must be returning to his origins.
Why are you all laughing?"
Everyone at the table laughed again.
Xuántóng served as an advisor to Prince Jīng,
and the authorities assigned him to act as the sacrificial officer for the community altar.
While purifying himself at the altar site,
Xuántóng sat inside a tent.
A dog came
and defecated on the wall.
Xuántóng then took a brick used to prop up the bed
and threw it at the dog himself.
Those nearby were surprised by his impulsiveness
and asked:
"Why did you take the brick propping up your bed to hit the dog?"
Xuántóng said:
"Haven't you heard?
If it benefits the state,
one may act on their own authority."
From "Qǐyán Lù."
Wáng Fúzhì
Táng Wáng Fúzhì was known for his virtuous and respectful conduct,
and he successively served as prefect of Qí and Zé prefectures.
His generation was praised for talent and learning.
His sons Miǎn, Jù, and Bó
were all renowned throughout the land for their literary skill.
Fúzhì was acquainted with Hán Wǎn's father.
Fúzhì married a woman from the Cuī family
and had a son named Bó.
(Original text has "Bó" as "Quàn," corrected according to the Míng manuscript.)
He once wrote to Hán's father:
"Miǎn, Jù, and Bó's writings are all elegant and brilliant;
even the youngest seems quite promising."
Hán replied:
"Wáng Wǔzǐ had a fondness for horses,
and you, sir, have a fondness for praising your sons.
Are the Wáng family's fondnesses
not a bit excessive?
I must see their writings
before I can judge."
Fúzhì then sent his sons' writings,
and Hán, along with other notable figures, read them and said:
"To have sons like these,
one can indeed boast."
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì."
Xǔ Jìngzōng
Táng Vice Minister of Personnel Yáng Sīxuán, relying on his status as a relative of the imperial family,
treated many candidates rudely
and excluded them.
He was accused by candidate Xiàhóu Biāozhī,
and Imperial Censor Zhōngchéng Láng Yúqìng impeached him, leading to his dismissal.
Grand Councilor Xǔ Jìngzōng said:
"I always knew the Vice Minister of Personnel Yáng would fail."
Someone asked him why,
and Jìngzōng said:
"One tiger and one wolf,
both preying on a sheep—
how could they not fail?"
Jìngzōng was frivolous and arrogant by nature,
and he often forgot people after meeting them.
Some said he was not sharp,
but he said:
"You yourselves are hard to remember.
If I met Hé, Liú, Shěn, or Xiè,
I could recognize them even groping in the dark."
From "Guócháo Zá Jì."
Gāo Cuīwéi
Táng entertainer Gāo Cuīwéi was skilled at playing the fool.
Tàizōng ordered an attendant to press his head underwater,
and after a long while, he emerged laughing.
The emperor asked why,
and he said:
"I saw Qū Yuán, who said,
'I met the unprincipled King Huái of Chǔ,
so I drowned myself in the Mìluó River.
You have met a wise and enlightened ruler;
why have you come here?'"
The emperor laughed heartily
and rewarded him with a hundred bolts of silk.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi."
Yuán Jìn
Táng Cáo Huáishùn
was from Jīnxiāng.
His father, Wéishū
(Míng manuscript has "Wéishū" as "Jìnú," same below),
died in service to the state
and was posthumously awarded the title of General Yúnhuī.
Huáishùn was appointed Guerrilla General while still in swaddling clothes
and served in various civil and military positions.
Empress Zétiān said:
"Huáishùn has long served in civil posts,
yet he is now relegated to a military position."
He was promoted from Left Yīngyáng Guard Colonel to Right Yùqián Guard General.
There was a Sīmǎ of Sòng Prefecture named Cáo Yuánběn, whose father was named Qǐbó.
Yuán Jìn, a county magistrate of Míngjí,
enjoyed conversation
and often spoke with wit and insight.
Someone asked Yuán Jìn
about Yuánběn,
saying, "He is Huáishùn's paternal uncle."
Yuán Jìn immediately replied:
"Although they share the same hall,
they are not of the same clan."
People were puzzled and asked why,
and Jìn said:
"Yuánběn is the son of Qǐbó,
while Huáishùn is the son of Jìshū.
From this, you can understand."
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì."
Zhào Qiānguāng
Among Táng dynasty officials,
those who were promoted to vice director without first serving as assistant director
were called "mountain-top fruit inspectors."
This meant they were directly appointed to high positions,
similar to conscripted soldiers
being appointed as frontier fruit inspectors.
Zhào Qiānguāng was promoted from Military Administrator of Péng Prefecture to Chief Judge of the Dàlǐ Temple,
and then to Vice Director of the Ministry of Revenue.
The Assistant Director of the Ministry of Revenue, Hè Suìshè, composed a poem:
"The assistant director has always been fine,
but the vice director's prospects are not superior.
Who would have thought that in the powder office,
one would become a mountain-top fruit inspector?"
Zhào Qiānguāng replied with a poem:
"The brocade tent is set as one pleases,
the golden censer burns as one wishes.
The only worry is the assistant director's placement—
(Míng manuscript has "placement" as "office")
it should not be among the constellations."
People considered this an extraordinary line.
From "Tán Bīn Lù."
Shěn Quánqī
In the Táng dynasty, Shěn Quánqī was demoted due to an offense.
When he encountered an imperial amnesty, his official rank was restored,
but he had not yet regained the crimson robe.
During an inner court banquet,
all the ministers sang the "Huíbōlè" lyrics and danced,
and many used this to seek promotion.
Quánqī's lyrics said:
"Huíbō, at this time Quánqī,
flowed to beyond the ridges, yet returned alive.
My person and name have already been recorded,
but robe and tablet have not restored the ivory crimson."
Emperor Zhōngzōng then bestowed upon him the crimson fish pouch.
From "Běnshì Shī"
Cuī Rìyòng
Cuī Rìyòng served as Vice Censor-in-Chief,
and was granted the purple robe.
At that time, wearing the fish tally required a special favor.
Also during a banquet,
the emperor ordered the ministers to compose lyrics.
Rìyòng said:
"The mice in the Censorate must be well-versed indeed,
confidently leaping up to the wall niche.
They knock over the lamp grease and stain Zhāng the Fifth,
then come back to gnaw the belt and report to Hán the Third.
Do not speak recklessly,
it's truly a royal minister.
If His Majesty must painfully bestow a golden turtle,
I'll sell off the cat to reward him."
Emperor Zhōngzōng bestowed upon him a golden fish.
From "Běnshì Shī"
Péi Tán
During the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng of Táng,
the Grand Censor-in-Chief Péi Tán revered Buddhism.
His wife was fierce and jealous,
and Péi Tán feared her as if she were a stern father.
At that time, Empress Wéi rather inherited Empress Wǔ Zétiān's style,
and Emperor Zhōngzōng gradually came to fear her.
During an inner court banquet,
someone began singing the "Huíbō Cí",
and an entertainer's lyrics said:
"Huíbō, at this time the basket,
fearing one's wife is also very good.
Outside there is only Péi Tán,
inside there is none surpassing
(The character 'guò' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Míng manuscript copy.)
Old Lǐ."
Empress Wéi looked pleased and self-satisfied,
and bestowed bolts of silk upon him.
From "Běnshì Shī"
Lǐ Zhèn'è
In the Táng dynasty, Lǐ Zhèn'è
was the father of Duke Zhào, Lǐ Jiào.
He was selected and appointed as the magistrate of Zǐzhōu Qí County,
and wrote to a friend:
"The prefecture bears the name 'Zǐ' (son),
the county bears the name 'Qí' (wife).
These have never belonged to this old man;
they are all the offices of wife and children."
From "Chuánzǎi"
Lú Yì
In the Táng dynasty, the Palace Attendant Lú Yì upheld the law meticulously,
and even with close friends or powerful figures,
he showed no favoritism.
His demeanor was leisurely and elegant,
always observing carefully before acting.
Once at Jǐnglóng Temple,
he supervised the officials performing incense offerings.
The various censors of the Right Censorate also participated.
Within the Censorate, the Right Censorate was previously nicknamed "Gāolì monks".
At that time, a foreign monk was loitering in the front courtyard.
The Investigating Censor of the Right Censorate, Huáng Shǒulǐ, pointed at him and said:
"What is this foreign monk doing here?"
Lú Yì slowly said to him:
"There are also Gāolì monks;
why single out and find the foreign monk strange?"
Everyone laughed heartily.
Lú Yì and Lǐ Shē were both poor archers.
Once during the Yuánrì ceremonial archery,
though Lǐ Shē drew the bow fully and shot,
the arrows all fell short of the target.
They bantered
(The original character was 'xuán';
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy.)
about each other's skill,
and Lǐ Shē joked:
"Shē and Lú's arrows both go thirty paces."
Those around did not understand.
Lǐ Shē said:
"Shē's arrow lands thirty paces from the target;
Lú's arrow lands thirty paces from himself."
They laughed for a long time.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì"
Sōng Shòu
In the Táng dynasty, Wéi Qìngběn's daughter was selected as a consort,
and he went to the court hall to give thanks.
Now, Wéi Qìngběn's ears were curled forward beforehand,
and many court officials called him "Juǎn'ěr" (Curled Ears).
At that time, Duke Cháng'ān, Sōng Shòu,
saw Qìngběn and congratulated him.
He then said:
"I always knew your daughter would become a consort."
Qìngběn said:
"How did you know?"
Sōng Shòu then touched his own ears and curled them forward, saying:
"'Curled Ears' is the virtue of a queen consort."
From "Qǐyán Lù"
Fēng Bàoyī
In the Táng dynasty, Fēng Bàoyī served as the Deputy Magistrate of Jiǔlǒng in Yìzhōu.
He was playing a game and betting money with his colleagues.
Several hundred coins were on the table,
and he had almost
(The original character was 'kè';
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy.)
lost them all,
so he wanted to withdraw.
Someone beside him said:
"Why not play another
(The character 'xì' was originally missing;
supplemented according to the Míng manuscript copy.)
round to win back your money?"
Bàoyī then raised his hand, touched the money, and said:
"It's all
(The Míng manuscript copy has 'cì' instead of 'tóng'.)
gone; how dare I hope to get it back?"
In Shāndōng dialect, 'jìn' (all gone) is pronounced 'cì',
hence he said 'cì'.
From "Qǐyán Lù"
Yǐn Shéntóng
In the Táng dynasty, the child prodigy Yǐn often said:
Bó Lè ordered his son to take the "Horse Classic" illustrations to seek a horse,
but after a year, he found none that resembled them.
He returned and told his father,
who ordered him to search again.
He went out and saw a large toad,
and said to his father:
"I found a horse
somewhat similar,
but not fully matching."
Bó Lè said:
"How so?"
He replied:
"Its skull is prominent, eyes sunken, back hunched and contracted,
only its hooves are not like piled copper coins."
Bó Lè said:
"This horse is good at jumping and kicking;
it's no good."
His son laughed and stopped.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Dí Rénjié
In the Táng dynasty, Vice Minister of Justice Dí Rénjié
(Note: There seems to be a missing character before 'qiū'.)
said to Vice Minister of Justice Lú Xiàn:
"If your honor is matched with a horse, it becomes a donkey."
Lú Xiàn said:
"If your surname is split down the middle,
(The character 'xìng' was originally missing;
supplemented according to the Míng manuscript copy.)
it becomes two dogs."
Dí Rénjié said:
"The character 'Dí' is 'dog' beside 'fire'."
Lú Xiàn said:
"A dog beside fire
is a cooked
(The Míng manuscript copy has 'rè' instead of 'shú'.)
dog."
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Sū Wèidào
In the Táng dynasty, Chancellor Sū Wèidào
and Zhāng Chānglíng were both famous.
Meeting on a leisure day,
they boasted and teased each other.
Zhāng Chānglíng said:
"The reason my poetry does not match Your Excellency's
is because it lacks 'silver flowers merge'."
Sū had a poem "Viewing Lanterns" that said:
"Fiery trees with silver flowers merge,
star bridges with iron locks open.
Hidden dust follows the horses away,
bright moonlight chases people here."
Sū Wèidào said:
"Your poetry may lack 'silver flowers merge',
but it still has 'golden copper nails'."
Zhāng Chānglíng's poem for Zhāng Chāngzōng said:
"In the past, Fúqiū Bó,
today, same as Dīng Lìngwēi."
They then clapped their hands and laughed.
From "Běnshì Shī"
The Attendant Censor
Táng Jīng served as a Censor in the Western Corridor of the Censorate,
which was nicknamed the "Horizontal Split Room."
Anyone assigned to this room
was first required to host a lavish feast for the entire Censorate,
and only then could they occupy it.
It originally had no window,
but a later occupant had one installed.
During the Shénlóng era,
when the Palace Attendant Yáng Zàisī also held the post of Censor-in-Chief,
all the chief ministers escorted him to his inaugural duty.
The Secretariat Director Wèi Yuánzhōng had once served as a Censor,
and was thoroughly familiar with the old customs of the Censorate.
He jokingly pointed at the room and said:
"This is the Horizontal Split Room."
The chief ministers asked the reason,
and Yuánzhōng explained its origin in detail.
A Censor said:
"Has this room been assigned to anyone recently?"
He replied:
"It hasn't been assigned to anyone else."
"Assigned" was originally written as "selected",
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
Yuánzhōng said:
"They probably opened a window to let the air out,
so it hasn't been assigned."
Those present laughed heartily, almost unable to contain themselves.
Moreover, as Censors investigate commanderies and offices,
and oversee all administrative affairs,
they are truly resented by all officials.
Censors are reviled as 'cold and severe',
and the Turks call Censors 'Tudun'.
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
when foreign envoys came to court,
the Tudun stood alone and did not join the ranks.
The Advisor to the Heir Apparent Zhāng Yuányī was known for his
"wit" was originally written as "uniformity",
changed according to the Ming manuscript
humor and wit.
He asked the foreign envoy:
"Who is this person standing alone?"
The interpreter said:
"Tudun,
that is a Censor."
Yuányī
"Yī" was originally written as "Zhōng",
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
said:
"People say the Censors of our court are uniquely cold and severe,
it seems this foreign Censor is also quite cold and severe."
The entire court erupted in laughter.
From "Records of the Censorate"
Lǐ Ānqī
Táng Dynasty Vice Minister of Personnel Lǐ Ānqī,
grandson of Suì Dynasty Palace Secretary Délín,
and son of Duke Ānpíng Bǎiyào.
He was clever and quick-witted.
Once, a candidate who had failed the selection
complained, saying:
"I am ashamed to return the way I came."
Ānqī asked:
"Which pass did you come through?"
He said:
"I came through the Pújīn Pass."
Ānqī said:
"Then take the Tóng Pass road back."
The candidate said:
"I am ashamed to face my wife and children."
Ānqī said:
"Your good wife surely knows you well,
she probably won't laugh."
Another candidate was being evaluated for appointment,
Ānqī looked at his examination essay and said:
"Your calligraphy is somewhat weak."
The candidate replied:
"I fell from a horse yesterday and injured my foot."
Ānqī said:
"How does an injured foot prevent you from writing well?"
He then read the essay aloud and said:
"Looking at your
"Your" was originally written as "the",
changed according to the Ming manuscript.
essay,
it seems not only was your
The Ming manuscript has "injured" instead of "hurt"
foot hurt,
but you must have internal injuries as well."
The man left in shame.
Another candidate, named Dù Ruò,
was appointed to an official post in Fāngzhōu.
The man was ashamed and protested.
Ānqī said:
"Haven't you heard, 'On the fragrant isle there is dùruò'?"
The man said:
"It can be presented to a renowned gentleman."
Ānqī said:
"This 'qī' is not that 'qī'."
Ruò said:
"This 'ruò' is not that 'ruò'."
Ānqī laughed,
and had his appointment changed.
Another candidate from Wú,
had a record of drunkenness from his previous post.
Ānqī said:
"Your record is not good."
The Wú man said:
"I know a hidden spear has already struck."
Ānqī said:
"I will pull out that hidden spear for you."
The man replied:
"Alas, the fair maiden."
The Ming manuscript lacks the character for "maiden".
Ānqī said:
"If you are selected with spirit,
I will give you a good post."
He replied:
"No wonder you are late."
Ānqī laughed and gave him an official post.
From "Records of Court and Country"
Dèng Xuántǐng
Táng Dynasty Dèng Xuántǐng entered a temple to offer incense,
and went with some monks to the garden,
to view the planted vegetables.
He saw a waterwheel with wooden buckets connected together,
drawing water from a well.
He then said:
"Venerable masters, if you tread this wheel yourselves,
it must be very laborious."
They replied:
"We have servants pull it."
Dèng immediately responded:
"Venerable masters, if you don't tread it yourselves,
what is the use of so many wooden buckets?"
The monks were stunned and pondered,
then realized Xuántǐng was using 'wooden buckets' as a pun for 'bald heads'.
Once, he was shooting arrows with Xiè Yòu,
and first boasted of his own nimble skill.
But when they faced each other to shoot,
he missed the target dozens of times.
Yòu then said:
"It's simply because the arrows are bad,
this has never happened to me before."
Xuántǐng immediately retorted:
"You should blame your own shooting,
why fault the arrows?"
Everyone laughed heartily,
considering him eloquent and quick-witted.
When Quán Xuánfú was in charge of the Xiāojī bureau,
he kept the Directors and Vice Directors waiting,
and only allowed them to leave very late.
A small date tree had sprouted in front of a Director's hall, right by the steps,
piercing through the brick pavement as it grew.
Everyone was surprised,
and went to look.
Xuántǐng, then serving as a Vice Director, said:
"This tree fears not the Xiāojī bureau,
so it just pierces the brick and puts forth dates."
The Vice Minister of War Wéi Shèn was extremely short in stature,
and people mocked him as a dwarf.
After Xuántǐng first obtained the post of Vice Director,
the Directors and Vice Directors all came to see him.
Wéi Shèn said:
"Shèn, with my mediocrity and vulgarity,
presumptuously holds the post of a Director.
You, with your great talent,
have further become a green-robed Vice Director."
Dèng immediately replied:
"A green-robed Vice Director,
how
The character for "how" was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Ming manuscript.
could he compare to a dwarf Director?"
Everyone laughed uproariously.
From "Records of Sparkling Wit"
Yuán Fúqìng
Táng Dynasty Yuán Fúqìng,
a man from Hénán,
was appointed Right Terrace Censor.
Along with Wéi Xūmíng and Rèn Zhèngmíng, he was quite haughty and aloof.
The Palace Censor Zhū
The character "Zhū" was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Ming manuscript.
Píngzhī composed a verse about them:
"Wéi is solemn and secretive,
Rèn is blunt and wild;
Pitiful Yuán Fúqìng,
also learns to sit on the fool's bench."
Zhèngmíng heard this,
and changed his own line to 'handsome and strong'.
From "Records of the Censorate"
The position of Secretary in the Department of State Affairs,
since the Two Han Dynasties,
has always been filled by exceptional individuals.
From the Wǔdé and Zhēnguàn eras of the Táng Dynasty onward,
this post was held in particularly high regard.
The Ministry of Personnel and the Ministry of War were considered the foremost departments,
and were the most crucial and demanding.
Officials transferred from the less important departments into these
were all considered to have received excellent appointments.
The Vice Director of the Bureau of Evaluations was solely responsible for the imperial examinations for selecting candidates.
Among the Vice Directors, the most prestigious posts were in the Bureau of Gates and the Bureau of Waterways.
The Bureau of State Farms, the Bureau of Forestry and Hunting, and the Bureau of Waterways,
along with the Bureau of Provisions and the Bureau of Receptions,
were all considered rear departments,
leisurely and simple with little to do.
People of the time had a saying:
"The Bureau of Gates and the Bureau of Waterways,
seldom set foot in the main ministry compound."
In a wrestling performance,
actors impersonated a Clerk from the Ministry of Personnel and a Clerk from the Bureau of Waterways meeting.
They suddenly both fell to the ground.
After a long while, they got up and said:
"The clash of heat and cold
caused us to take ill like this."
During the Xiāntiān era,
Wáng Shàngkè served as Attendant Censor.
Considering himself talented, reputable, refined, and elegant,
he fully expected to be transferred into a ministry bureau,
and often looked forward to a post in a foremost department.
He was suddenly appointed Vice Director of the Bureau of Provisions,
and felt somewhat disappointed and regretful.
Zhāng Jìngzhōng, a Director in the Ministry of Personnel, teased him with a verse:
"He disdains the Ministry of War,
and focuses solely on the Bureau of Evaluations.
Who would have thought his steps would falter,
nearly landing him east of the ministry wall?"
The Bureau of Provisions was located in the northeasternmost corner of the ministry compound,
hence this line.
From "Records of the Two Capitals"
Acting Censors
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng Dynasty, the position of Acting Censor was established,
with no fixed number of posts.
There were Acting Censors,
Acting Attendant Censors,
Acting Palace Censors,
and Acting Investigating Censors.
They were not yet regular officials.
In the Censorate, they were mocked with a verse:
"Though at the pillar's base he serves as clerk,
within the Censorate, he's not yet an official.
When will we hear 'it must be so',
and soon see Rén Duān?"
Rén Duān refers to the Attendant Censor Rén Zhèngmíng.
From "Records of the Censorate"
Yáo Chóng
In the Táng Dynasty, Yáo Chóng served as Head of the Secretariat.
By convention, the Secretariat provided duty lodgings,
and did not defer to the Chief Ministers.
Yáo Chóng, being advanced in both age and rank,
did not follow the old practice of requesting it.
A clerk brought the duty roster to him,
and Yáo Chóng wrote on it:
"Inform the duty clerk,
sent away, yet you return again.
If you insist on taking me,
you are like the Controller of Fate.
An old man's years,
are ultimately unfit for such duty."
The various department officials saw it and laughed,
and did not press him further.
Thus, the practice of Chief Ministers staying on duty was halted.
From "New Accounts of the Great Táng"
Huáng Fānchuò
Emperor Xuánzong of Táng was fond of playing polo.
The horses kept in the imperial stables
still did not quite satisfy him.
Once, while bantering with Huáng Fānchuò in jest,
he said:
"I have long desired fine horses,
but who is well-versed in equine lore?"
Fānchuò replied:
"Your servant knows."
And added:
"Now, the three Chief Ministers are all experts in equine lore."
The Emperor said:
"Apart from discussing affairs of state with the three Chief Ministers,
I have thoroughly inquired into their other fields of knowledge.
I have not heard that any of them is versed in equine lore.
How do you know this?"
Fānchuò said:
"Your servant daily walks upon the sandy causeway.
I see the horses the Chief Ministers ride
are all fine steeds.
Therefore, I know they must be versed in equine lore."
The Emperor then laughed heartily and spoke of other matters.
Emperor Xuánzong once ascended the northern tower of the imperial park,
gazing at the Wèi River.
He saw a drunkard lying down by the water,
and asked his attendants who it was.
The attendants did not know.
As he was about to send someone to inquire,
Fānchuò said:
"Your servant knows.
That is a Clerk whose term has expired."
The Emperor said:
"How do you know?"
He replied:
"With one more turn, he enters the stream."
The Emperor laughed loudly.
On another occasion, he was dining with the imperial princes.
Prince Níng, facing the imperial seat,
spurted a mouthful of rice,
directly onto the Emperor's face.
The Emperor said:
"Brother Níng, why did you choke?"
Fānchuò said:
"This was not choking,
it was a sneeze."
From "Miscellaneous Records from the Pine Window" and "Records of Casual Talk"
Yáng Guózhōng
Yáng Guózhōng of Táng once gathered his relatives for a meeting.
At the time, he was in charge of personnel selection for the Ministry of Personnel.
Wishing to create great amusement to entertain them,
he called out the names of candidates
and had them brought into the central courtyard.
Without inquiring into their qualifications or seniority,
he appointed the short ones as Military Advisors of Dàozhōu,
(Ming manuscript note: "Dàozhōu" is written as "Zhūzhōu" in some versions.)
(Note: According to "Records of Refined Conversation," it is "Military Advisor of Dàozhōu.")
and those with beards as Instructors of Húzhōu.
Those behind the curtains roared with laughter.
From "Records of Refined Conversation"
Liú Zhāoxiá
In the early Tiānbǎo era of Táng,
Emperor Xuánzong visited the Huáqīng Palace.
Liú Zhāoxiá presented his "Rhapsody on the Imperial Visit to the Hot Springs",
its style and tone were untrammeled and unrestrained,
mixed with jest and humor.
The text is mostly not recorded here,
but the beginning of the rhapsody roughly says:
Now, in the second year of Tiānbǎo,
after the tenth month, before the twelfth.
The officials prepared the provisions,
and the imperial carriage set out for the hot springs.
The heavenly gates creaked open,
blocked by a throng of immortals;
the imperial carriage swept forth,
driving armored guards in dense array.
One troop in blue, another in yellow,
bears beating chests, leopards seizing backs;
one cluster of pearls, another of embroidery,
jade-inlaid bridles, gold-chased saddles.
Later, describing the imperial virtue, it says:
"Straight obtained the marrow of Pángǔ,
pinched the nipples of Nǚwā.
Never mind your thousand emperors of antiquity,
how could they compare to our Sānláng of today?"
His self-description says:
"Furthermore, I am poor and strange, stumbling and faltering,
having lost my way, running wild.
Though my frame is short,
my skills are long.
In dreams, several times I attained wealth and honor,
upon waking, still distressed and anxious as before.
It's only a once-in-a-thousand-years chance to kowtow,
don't make it at odds and ends."
The Emperor read it and found it remarkable,
intending to bestow special rewards.
He ordered Zhāoxiá to change the words "at odds and ends."
Zhāoxiá memorialized:
"Your servant composed this rhapsody
as if aided by spirits."
He claimed the text needed no editing,
the brush never ceasing to write,
and was unwilling to change it.
The Emperor heard this,
looked at his attendants and said:
"Truly a man of meager fortune."
He then appointed him
(The character "yǐ" was originally missing here,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript.)
to a minor post in the palace guards and that was all.
From "Records of Transmitted Tales from the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo Eras"
Yáo Zhēncāo
Yáo Zhēncāo of the Táng dynasty said:
"Since I entered the Censorate as a Reviewing Clerk,
Hóu Chéngxùn followed in succession.
After this, they continued one after another without end,
thus I know it is like pulling up weeds and bringing along the roots."
Hán Wǎn considered this incorrect,
for since Empress Zétiān favored law,
the Ministry of Justice has been esteemed above the Nine Courts.
Because of this, many Reviewing Clerks entered the Censorate,
and it has become an elegant precedent up to now.
How could the prestige of the Reviewing Clerk
have originated from Zhēncāo?
Xū Yì joked, saying:
"There are six paths for a Capital District Lieutenant:
entering the Censorate is the Buddha's path,
becoming a Reviewing Clerk is the immortal's path,
becoming a Capital District Lieutenant is the human path,
becoming a Capital District Assistant is the sea of bitterness path,
becoming a County Magistrate is the animal path,
and becoming a Section Administrator is the hungry ghost path.
Thus, the prestige of the Reviewing Clerk
arose from the ruler of the time favoring law;
it is not something Zhēncāo could elevate or diminish."
From "Records of the Censorate"
Péi Xǔ
Péi Kuān's son Péi Xǔ of the Táng dynasty again served as Governor of Hénán.
Péi Xǔ had always been fond of jesting.
Once, someone submitted a petition
and mistakenly wrote on the back of the paper.
Péi Xǔ ruled:
"This side resembles that side,
that side resembles this side.
I do not refuse to rule for you,
but it makes the boot-wearing fellow at the gate laugh himself to death."
Also, two women jointly submitted a petition disputing over a cat.
The petition stated:
"If it is a male cat,
then it is a male cat.
If it is not a male cat,
then it is not a male cat."
Péi Xǔ laughed heartily
and ruled on the petition:
"The cat does not recognize its master,
and catches mice at the neighbor's house.
The two families need not dispute;
bring it to Péi Xǔ."
He then took the cat.
The disputants also ceased.
From "Records of Trusted Accounts from the Kāiyuán and Tiānbǎo Eras"
Zhāng Wénchéng, Vice Director of the Bureau of Gates of the Táng dynasty, was fond
fond originally written as "superior,"
corrected according to the Míng dynasty manuscript.
of composing humorous poems and rhapsodies,
which circulated in his time.
At that time, General-in-Chief Hēichǐ Chángzhī
was about to go on an expedition.
Someone encouraged him, saying:
"Your official rank is low;
why not follow along?"
Wénchéng said:
"I would rather drink wine with red lips,
who would chase after you, Hēichǐ Chángzhī?"
From "Records of the Censorate"
Dòu Xiǎo
Dòu Xiǎo of the Táng dynasty was short in stature
with large, bulging eyes;
Yuè Yànwěi was tall with protruding teeth.
Yànwěi first teased him, saying:
"Your Excellency possesses great merit."
Those nearby wondered why,
Yànwěi said:
"Already short of flesh,
yet again diligent and advancing.
Is that not great merit?"
Dòu immediately retorted:
"Your Excellency yourself has great merit;
why mention Xiǎo?"
People asked the reason,
Dòu said:
"Yuè has been a lifelong vegetarian."
They asked the meaning of "lifelong vegetarian,"
Dòu said:
"So tall in stature,
with teeth even like cliffs.
Is that not 'long abstinence'?"
Everyone laughed heartily.
From "Records of Raising a Laugh"
Dù Yányè
Cuī Sīhuì, Magistrate of Huáyuán in the Táng dynasty, stuttered.
He often engaged in mutual teasing with his younger cousin Dù Yányè.
Dù often said to Cuī:
"Yányè can make you, elder brother, crow like a rooster.
But whenever I ask something,
you must answer immediately."
Someone nearby said:
"His mouth should be free;
how can you order him about?
If he refuses to do it,
how can you make him?"
Dù then said:
"I can."
Then the bystanders made a private bet with Dù.
Dù brought a handful of grain before Cuī and said:
"What is this?"
Cuī said:
"Gu gu."
The bystanders laughed heartily,
and thus lost the bet to Yányè.
From "Records of Raising a Laugh"
Lù Lìxíng
When Lù Lìxíng of the Táng dynasty first assumed the post of Assistant Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
relatives and acquaintances all came to congratulate him.
After they were seated,
one person said:
"Now that you, elder brother, hold an important post,
all your relatives rejoice."
As the proverb says:
"One person at court,
a hundred loosen their belts."
Is that not a good thing?"
He replied:
"Not only do they loosen their belts,
they must also remove their headscarves!"
Everyone laughed heartily.
From "Records of Raising a Laugh"
Xiāo Chéng
When Xiāo Chéng of the Táng dynasty was first appointed Vice Director,
he was composed and at ease among the court officials.
Attendant Censor Wáng Xù said:
"Master Xiāo is calm and perceptive."
Hán Wǎn immediately replied:
"When Xiāo served as Recorder,
he had long been exempted from caning.
How could it be only today that he becomes perceptive of flogging?"
Those who heard burst into laughter.
From "Records of the Censorate"
Emperor Dézōng
When the grandson of Mǎ Suì of the Táng dynasty was born,
Emperor Dézōng named him Jìzǔ.
After retiring, he laughed and said:
"This has two meanings;
the intention is to say 'to continue with a rope.'"
From "Supplement to the National History"
During the Táng dynasty, Zhōu Yuàn
once served as an envoy to Wèizhōu.
Military Governor Tián Jì'ān rode alongside him, their horses abreast.
On the road, they saw an extremely fat donkey.
Jì'ān pointed at it and said to Yuàn:
"This creature belongs to Dàwáng Shìchōng."
In response,
[The original text here is missing nine characters;]
supplemented based on Yīnhuà Lù]
Yuàn replied:
"It's always the little Dòu
[The character 'Dòu' is missing in the original;]
supplemented based on Yīnhuà Lù]
Jiàndé."
Lǐ Xùn had a stern and severe temperament,
and did not enjoy jokes or laughter.
At that time, Yuàn
[The original text here is missing eight characters following 'stern and severe';]
supplemented based on Yīnhuà Lù]
was appointed to oversee the salt and iron affairs in Héxī,
and was about to arrive.
Lǐ warned his staff:
"Zhōu is fond of jesting and teasing,
being presumptuous and disrespectful.
I hope you all can be somewhat more solemn in order to
[The original text here is missing fifteen characters following 'Zhōu is fond...';]
supplemented based on Yīnhuà Lù]
receive him."
When Yuàn arrived,
several banquets were held.
Apart from exchanging pleasantries about the weather,
Lǐ did not speak to him,
and Zhōu
[The original text here is missing seven characters following 'pleasantries about the weather';]
supplemented based on Yīnhuà Lù]
also had no opportunity to initiate conversation.
One day,
while hosting relatives and guests at a feast,
Yuàn was also present.
An old friend's son came to seek Lǐ's help,
[The original text here is missing eight characters following 'Lǐ had';]
supplemented based on Yīnhuà Lù]
being down on his luck and idle.
Lǐ asked him about all the old villas and skilled household servants.
Books and paintings of repute
[The original character for 'skill' was '之';]
[the original character for 'repute' was '笞';]
[the characters '者圖' are missing in the original.]
Corrected and supplemented based on Yīnhuà Lù]
he replied that they had all been sold off.
Lǐ reproached him:
"Even if your family is poor and you hold no office,
and you sell off your property,
how could you go so far as to
[The character '至' is missing in the original;]
supplemented based on Yīnhuà Lù]
sell even the books and ancient paintings?"
He lamented this for a long time.
Then he asked again:
"There is one volume of the Shàngshū handwritten by Yú Yǒngxīng—
is this one still around?"
The man, ashamed and fearful,
did not dare say it had been sold,
and said:
"I temporarily pawned it for money."
Yuàn suddenly spoke up:
"This Shàngshū has met with great misfortune."
Lǐ completely forgot his earlier resolve to reject his jesting and
thus asked:
"What misfortune has the Shàngshū met?"
Yuàn said:
"It has already suffered the hardships of the 'Yáo Diǎn' and 'Shùn Diǎn,'
and now it is 'diǎn' (pawned)."
[In the Ming manuscript, '之苦' is written as '又被'.]
[In the Ming manuscript, '而即' is written as '兒郎'.]
Lǐ's face broke into a broad smile,
and from then on, he never again kept his distance.
[The source was originally missing;]
now seen in Yīnhuà Lù, volume four]
Also, Lù Chángyuán, due to his longstanding virtue, served as the marching
[The character '軍' is missing in the original;]
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript]
administrator of the Xuānwǔ Army,
while Hán Yù served as patrol officer,
both working in the same commissioner's office.
Some mocked the wide gap in their ages and seniority,
but Yuàn said:
"The tiger and the rat
are both among the twelve zodiac animals—
what is so strange about that?"
Within ten days, this remark spread throughout Cháng'ān.
From Guóshǐ Bǔ
Liú Yǔxī
During the Táng dynasty, Liú Yǔxī governed Liánzhōu,
succeeding Gāo Yù.
Later, Yù became a general of the Imperial Guard,
and from the capital, he sent a letter saying:
"Due to your gracious care,
I have been promoted to take your place."
Liú replied in a letter:
"In the past,
[The four characters '答書云昔' are missing in the original;]
supplemented based on the Huáng manuscript]
there was a tale:
Once, an old woman was walking in the mountains
when she saw a tiger, weak and taking small, hesitant steps, unable to advance,
as if injured in its foot.
The woman looked at it,
and the tiger then raised its foot to show her.
There was a thorn stuck in its paw,
so she pulled it out for him.
Soon, the tiger leaped and roared vigorously, expressing its gratitude.
Afterward, it would toss deer, elk, foxes, and rabbits into her courtyard,
never missing a day.
The woman climbed the wall to look,
and it was indeed the previously injured tiger.
She then told her relatives the whole story,
and they found it remarkable.
One day,
it suddenly threw a dead person,
bloody and mangled,
and the woman was then arrested and interrogated by the village officer.
The woman explained the reason in detail,
and only then was she released from bondage.
The woman then climbed the wall,
waited for the tiger to arrive, and said to it:
'I am grateful,
I kowtow to you, Great King.
But from now on, please don't throw any more dead people over.'"
From Jiāhuà Lù
Yuán Déshī
During the Táng dynasty, Yuán Déshī of Rǔnán
was the son of the late Imperial Advisor Gāo.
He once bought the former garden of Lóu Shīdé in the Eastern Capital
and built a library tower there.
The people of Luòyáng said:
"In the past, it was Lóu Shīdé's garden;
now it is Yuán Déshī's tower."
[The source was originally missing;]
the Ming manuscript states it is from Jiāhuà Lù]
Lǐ Chéng
Liú Yǔxī of the Táng dynasty said:
"The twenty-sixth Chancellor, Lǐ Chéng, was fond of jesting.
While stationed in Xiàkǒu,
a guest came to take his leave.
Lǐ said:
'Stay another couple of days.'
The guest said:
'I am already set to depart;
the boat is already at Hànkǒu.'
Lǐ said:
'Just stay and trust me;
that Hànkǒu is not to be trusted.'
The guest covered his mouth, chuckling, as he withdrew.
Also, once while drinking wine at an inn with his cousin
[The original text has '裳以' for 'cousin';]
corrected based on the Ming manuscript]
the Chancellor and Garrison Commander Shí,
Shí collected the dice,
and the overseer penalized him.
Shí said:
'What penalty is there?'
Chéng said:
'In your busy commotion,
you took away his chancellor's seal;
what excuse do you have then?'
Wine shops call double fours 'the chancellor's seal,'
which was a jab at Shí.
In the winter of the ninth year of Tàihé,
during a time of court affairs,
he was promoted and employed."
From Jiāhuà Lù
Yáng Yúqīng
Táng Dynasty official Zhāng Yòuxīn
was a close friend of Yáng Yúqīng of Qiánzhōu,
and they were equally renowned.
Yáng's wife, née Lǐ,
was the daughter of Chancellor Lǐ of Fūzhōu,
virtuous but plain in appearance.
Yáng never minded this
and treated her with exceptional respect.
Zhāng once said to Yáng:
"I achieved a fine reputation while young,
so I have no worries about my career.
Only by obtaining a beautiful wife
would my lifelong wishes be fully satisfied."
Yáng replied:
"If you must seek such a match,
just share my taste,
and I will surely fulfill your desire."
Zhāng deeply believed him.
After the marriage,
he was utterly dissatisfied.
Yáng tapped him with his official tablet and said:
"Why are you so foolish!"
He repeated this several times.
Zhāng, unable to bear his anger,
retorted:
"We are close friends without secrets,
so I confided in you sincerely.
You have misled me so badly—
why am I the fool?"
Yáng then recounted step by step how he had pursued fame and office,
saying:
"Wasn't it all the same as your path?"
Zhāng said:
"Yes."
"Then since I got an ugly wife,
how could yours be any different?"
Zhāng's expression softened,
and he asked:
"How does your wife compare to mine?"
Yáng said:
"Far worse."
Zhāng laughed heartily,
and their friendship resumed as before.
After Zhāng had established his household,
he composed a poem:
"A single peony is worth a thousand gold,
thought to be the deepest hue of all.
Today the railings brim with blooms like snow—
a lifetime's longing for flowers, all in vain."
From "Běnshì Shī"
Shěn Yàzhī
Táng Dynasty's Shěn Yàzhī often traveled as a guest.
Once, he was tested by some juniors,
who said:
"We'll change the drinking game:
compose two lines each, mixing elegance and vulgarity:
'Chopping wood, ding-ding;
birds chirping, ying-ying.
Going east, going west;
encountering rice, encountering soup.'"
Yàzhī replied:
"As cutting and filing,
as carving and polishing.
Bullying guests, beating wives—
shouldn't act so slyly."
From "Zhíyán"
Zhāng Hù
Táng Dynasty's Zhāng Hù was a guest in the Huáinán administrative office.
Attending a banquet,
where Secretariat Drafter Dù Mù served as censor,
a courtesan present called for dice to gamble over drinks.
Mù murmured softly:
"The dice are swiftly snatched and hidden in hand,
no chance to glimpse those slender jade fingers."
Hù responded immediately:
"Just let it be known her golden hairpin fell—
perhaps then we'll see fingertips brushing the path."
Hù had not yet met
Bái Jūyì.
When Bái was Governor of Sūzhōu,
Hù first went to pay his respects.
As soon as they met,
Bái said to him:
"Long have I admired your great reputation,
and I recall your 'Interrogation Head' poem."
Hù, startled, said:
"What does the Drafter mean?"
Bái said:
"'Where have you tossed the mandarin-duck inlaid belt?
To whom did you give the peacock-patterned silk gown?'
If that's not 'Interrogation Head,' what is it?"
Zhāng lowered his head, smiling slightly,
then looked up and replied:
"I also recall the Drafter's 'Mùlián Transformation'."
Bái said:
"What is that?"
Hù said:
"'Searching above the azure sky, below the Yellow Springs,
both places vast and empty, nothing to be seen.'
If that's not 'Mùlián Transformation,' what is it?"
Thereafter, they feasted joyfully all day.
When Duke Zhào, Lìng Hú Táo, governed Wéiyáng,
Hù often joined in intimate banquets.
The Duke, having observed Hù closely,
changed the drinking game, saying:
"A boat sailing upstream,
the wind too fierce.
The man beneath the sail,
must stand firm."
Hù replied:
"A boat sailing upstream,
the hull springs a leak.
Dear guest, take care,
do not lean on the rudder."
From "Zhíyán"
Travelers of Jiāo and Guǎng
Travelers between Jiāozhōu and Guǎngzhōu
each sought travel passes.
Wherever they went, they received lavish welcomes,
with farewell gifts of ten thousand cash at each stop.
Guǎngzhōu Governor Lú Jūn was well aware of this abuse.
To all who requested travel passes,
he directed:
"Along the route, post stations
shall provide only vegetables and rice."
A traveler carrying such a pass arrived at a station,
and the station officer, following the pass, provided the meal.
The traveler did not depart.
The station clerk said:
"I fear later envoys may come,
the next station is far,
this is no place to lodge."
The traveler said:
"How will the food provision be handled?"
The clerk said:
"Only vegetables and rice are provided."
The traveler said:
"The vegetables and rice are served,
now return my 'only' to me."
The station clerks
looked at each other,
uncertain what to do.
The traveler pressed urgently,
and with no alternative,
the clerk asked:
"I don't know what 'only' is."
The traveler said:
:"Larger than a donkey,
smaller than a mule.
If you cannot provide it,
just repay me its value."
The station clerk asked:
"For each 'only',
what is the price?"
The traveler said:
"Three to five thousand."
The station clerks hastily collected and handed over the cash.
From "Lúshì Záshuō"
Lú Zhào
When Táng Dynasty's Lú Zhào first took the examinations,
some senior candidates asked where he was from.
Zhào said:
"I am from Yuánzhōu."
Someone said:
"Does Yuánzhōu produce examination candidates?"
Zhào replied:
"Yuánzhōu producing candidates
is like Yuánjiāng producing turtle shells—
those with nine ridges are exceedingly rare."
Also, when Zhào took the provincial examination in Jiāngxī,
he was placed last by the examiner.
Zhào submitted a thank-you note stating:
"The giant turtle, mighty and imposing,
tops the list at Péngshān."
The examiner said to him:
"Yesterday, constrained by quotas and crowding,
though I managed to extend the list,
I am deeply ashamed to have sullied the ranking.
How then can you speak of 'topping the list at Péngshān'?"
Zhào said:
"I knew you would inquire.
Generally, when a dull stone is above,
a giant turtle carries it.
Is that not 'topping the list'?"
Everyone present
heard this and laughed heartily.
From "Zhíyán"
Zhāng Xiàobiāo
In the Táng dynasty, after Zhāng Xiàobiāo passed the imperial examination,
he sent a poem to Lǐ Shēn in Huáinán, which read:
"Passing the exam surpasses ten terms as an official;
Having crossed the Jīntāng Pass, I leave Cháng'ān.
My horse's head gradually enters Yángzhōu's outer walls;
I report to the people of the time to wash their eyes and see."
Lǐ Shēn promptly replied with a quatrain:
"Fake gold only needs real gold to plate it;
If it were real gold, it would not need plating.
After ten years in Cháng'ān, you've gained one exam success;
Why must you have an empty stomach yet lofty ambitions?"
From *Zhíyán*.
Nán Zhuó
In the Táng dynasty, the Vice Minister Nán Zhuó
was a cousin of Lǐ Xiūgǔ.
Lǐ had a迂僻 (pedantic and eccentric) nature,
and Nán often looked down on him.
Lǐ was soon appointed as an assistant in Xǔzhōu,
and when the official appointment decree arrived,
the military governor of Xǔzhōu was hosting a grand banquet.
Suddenly, a sealed document was delivered,
containing a letter from Nán to Lǐ.
Lǐ then held the letter and joyfully reported to the governor:
"I and Nán are twenty-third cousins,
and he often looked down on me.
Today, I am humbly serving as a guest advisor to the Minister,
and now the appointment decree has arrived;
he suddenly sends me a letter—
this is most strange."
When he opened the envelope, it read:
"On this day, old Nán is not dead yet,
and gets to see Lǐ Xiūgǔ receive an appointment."
Míng manuscript note: "因" is written as "目".
The governor asked to see the letter,
and everyone at the banquet burst into laughter.
Lǐ Xiūgǔ was deeply ashamed.
From *Lúshì Záshuō*.
Wáng Zhìxīng
In the Táng dynasty, Wáng Zhìxīng held the titles of Commissioner and Palace Attendant,
and was returning to the capital after leaving his military governorship.
A relative sought Wáng's recommendation for an official selection matter,
but Wáng firmly refused.
The relative then requested a letter to the Vice Minister of Personnel.
The Vice Minister of Personnel wrote at the end of the document:
"The candidate's name and title have been respectfully noted."
Wáng said:
"It seems even a Palace Attendant has his uses."
From *Lúshì Záshuō*.
Lú Fā
In the Táng dynasty, the Secretariat Director Bái Mǐnzhōng was governing Jīngnán,
while Dù Yùn was inspecting Chángshā.
Dù requested his assistant Lú Fā to deliver a formal invitation.
Lú, intoxicated with wine, looked around arrogantly.
Bái was slightly displeased,
so he improvised a verse, saying:
"The sixth of the ten Hu surnames,
I too once managed the imperial furnace in the golden pavilion.
A young assistant boasting of his family background—
do not show a rough demeanor before the wine cup."
Lú replied:
"The sixth of the ten Hu surnames,
my literary talent and official rank surpass those of Cuī and Lú.
Temporarily stationed beyond the pass to share worries and duties,
I do not deserve such rough words at the guest banquet."
Bái was greatly pleased, and the gathering ended.
From *Zhíyán*.
Péi Xiū
The Qūjiāng Pond was originally the Qǐzhōu of the Qín dynasty.
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
it was dredged and developed into a scenic spot.
To the south were the Zǐyún Tower and the Lotus Garden,
to the west were the Apricot Garden and the Cí'ēn Temple.
Flowers and plants surrounded it,
the misty waters were bright and beautiful,
and the capital's people visited for enjoyment.
It was most bustling during the Zhōnghé and Shàngsì festivals.
Banquets were granted to officials,
gatherings were held in mountain pavilions,
and music from the Tàicháng and Jiàofāng offices was bestowed.
The pond was equipped with colorful boats,
but only the Chancellor, the Three Commissioners, officials of the Northern Departments, and Imperial Academy scholars could board them.
This stirred the entire imperial city,
and was considered a grand spectacle.
When Péi Xiū was appointed Inspector of Xuānchéng,
before leaving the capital,
he encountered the lotus flowers in full bloom at Qūjiāng Pond,
and went sightseeing with renowned scholars from the same departments.
Starting from the Cí'ēn Temple,
each dismissed their attendants,
bringing only a young servant,
and walked to the Zǐyún Tower.
They saw several people sitting by the water's edge,
and Péi and the court officials rested nearby.
Among them was a man in yellow robes, half-drunk,
proud and composed,
pointing at the others and speaking with frivolous laughter.
Péi felt slightly indignant,
bowed, and asked him:
"What official position do you hold, sir?"
The man replied casually:
"Well,
I dare not claim to be a gentleman
Míng manuscript note: "郎" is written as "即",
same below
I dare not,
I have newly been appointed Magistrate of Guǎngdé in Xuānzhōu."
He then asked Péi in return:
"What position do you hold, Commander?"
Péi imitated him, saying:
"Well,
I dare not claim to be a gentleman,
I have newly been appointed Surveillance Commissioner of Xuānzhōu."
At this, the man fled in panic,
and his companions also scattered.
The court officials clapped their hands and laughed heartily.
Within a few days,
the story spread throughout the capital.
Later, when inquired at the Personnel Bureau,
it was said:
"The Magistrate of Guǎngdé requested a transfer to Luójiāng."
When Emperor Xuānzōng was still a prince, he heard this story,
and often joked about it with the other princes.
Later, when he ascended the throne,
Péi became Chancellor.
While drafting the appointment edict,
he turned to the close advisors and said:
"Well,
I dare not claim to be a gentleman,
I have newly been appointed Secretariat-Chancellery Grand Councilor."
From *Sōngchuāng Zálù*,
Note: Also seen in *Jùtán Lù*, Volume 2.
Féng Gǔn
In the Táng dynasty, Féng Gǔn governed Sūzhōu.
Beyond the river, life was leisurely and comfortable,
and on idle days, he often indulged in drinking and gambling.
Once, while gambling with guests and colleagues,
Féng suddenly won,
and distributed his winnings equally among everyone present.
He then recited:
"An eight-foot gaming table shines like new,
a thousand gold coins tossed in a bet stir the spirit.
When it's time to gamble, one must gamble;
it's no harm to turn back and beg from the idle."
Later, while heavily intoxicated,
he teased a courtesan.
But the military deputy was enamored with her,
and she appeared listless and uninterested.
Féng glanced at him and said:
"This old man's teasing is excessive,
I can do nothing about it."
The deputy straightened his clothes and apologized.
Féng then recited:
"Drunken eyes follow her a hundred glances askew,
she belongs to him, she belongs to him.
Whispering, let the Taoist know,
across the seat, I just tossed a cardamom flower."
From *Shūqíng Shī*.
Neighbor's Husband
A man observed that his neighbor's husband and wife were harmonious.
When the husband returned from outside,
he saw his wife blowing on the fire,
and gifted her a poem:
"Blowing on the fire, her vermilion lips move;
adding firewood, her jade wrists slant.
Gazing from afar at her face in the smoke,
she greatly resembles a flower in the mist."
His own wife also waited for her husband to return,
and told him:
"Every time I see the neighbor's husband and wife,
they are extremely affectionate.
Just now, the husband saw his wife blowing on the fire
and composed a poem praising her.
Can't you learn from him?"
The husband said:
"What did his poem say?"
She recited it.
The husband said:
"You blow on the fire,
and I'll compose a different one."
The wife also imitated blowing on the fire,
and he composed a poem:
"Blowing on the fire, her blue lips move;
adding firewood, her black wrists slant.
Gazing from afar at her face in the smoke,
she exactly resembles a Jūpánchá demon."
From *Xiàoyán*,
Míng manuscript note: Appears in *Xiàolín*.
Guān Tú
In the Táng dynasty, Jīngzhōu
was a gathering place for the elite,
but each year when it sent candidates for the imperial examinations,
few ever achieved success,
earning it the nickname "Heaven's Barren Prefecture."
When Liú Tuì passed the examination as a candidate from Jīngzhōu,
it was called "Breaking Heaven's Barrenness."
Since then, Guān Tú and Cháng Xiāo, both natives of Jīngzhōu,
possessed outstanding literary talent
and successively passed the highest levels of the examinations.
Guān Tú was the son of a military officer.
Upon passing the examination and returning to his hometown,
the local garrison commanders held a banquet in his honor.
Pointing to a sauce jar on the table,
he jokingly said to an old officer:
"This must have been made by a low-ranking soldier."
The man then presented a vinegar jar and replied:
"This one was also 'made by a low-ranking soldier.'"
The entire banquet erupted in laughter.
Guān Tú's wife,
who was Cháng Xiāo's younger sister,
was a woman of literary talent.
Her "Elegy for My Husband" circulated widely.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
In the Táng dynasty, during the Xiántōng era
(The character "xián" was originally missing;
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy.)
of the reign,
(The character "zhōng" was originally missing;
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy.)
Yáng Xuányì was angered by the excessive luxury of the candidates' carriages and attire
and wanted to make them ride donkeys.
A poem from that time said:
"This year,
(Originally read as '□有看三字';
corrected based on the Ming manuscript copy.)
the decree orders all to ride donkeys,
purple shafts and red felt fill the nine avenues.
The lean and thin young men can still manage,
but among them, Zhèng Chāngtú is utterly distressed."
From "Lú Shì Zá Shuō."
Péi Qìngyú
In the Táng dynasty, Péi Qìngyú,
toward the end of the Xiántōng era,
served as an aide to Lǐ Wèi, the military governor of Huáinán, at the northern gate.
He often traveled by river.
Once, a boatman poling the boat
accidentally splashed water with the bamboo pole,
wetting a courtesan's clothes.
Lǐ Wèi's expression changed with displeasure.
Péi Qìngyú immediately requested a piece of colored paper
and composed a quatrain:
"Her forehead adorned with moth-like gold, clad in golden-threaded garments,
kingfisher feathers flutter, jade hairpins hang low.
Even if water splashes and wets her silk skirt,
one knows she returns from rain-making at Wūshān."
Lǐ Wèi read it and was greatly amused,
ordering the entertainers to perform it.
From "Zhí Yán."
Zhào Chóng
Although the Lú clan was prominent among the elite,
for generations, none had ever presided over the imperial examinations.
During the Qiánfú era,
Lú Xié served in the Secretariat,
and because no member of his clan had ever held authority over literary affairs,
he promoted his relative Lú Wò, the surveillance commissioner of Shǎn-Guó,
to oversee the examination hall.
That autumn,
Huáng Cháo attacked the capital,
and Emperor Xī fled,
causing the examination candidates to scatter like stars.
By the time the capital was recovered,
Péi Zhì had presided over three consecutive examinations,
and Lú Wò showed envy.
Zhào Chóng teased him, saying:
"Your Excellency is what they call 'one whose belly produces no offspring to serve as chief examiner.'"
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Zhèng Guāngyè
had a cousin who was also taking the examinations.
At that time, candidates typically covered their desks with white paper,
and Zhèng Guāngyè secretly wrote a verse about it:
"Newly pasted desk,
white as silver.
Entering the exam, leaving the exam.
For a thousand springs, ten thousand springs."
Zhèng Guāngyè and his brothers
shared a large leather trunk.
Whenever fellow candidates submitted their writings,
if the verses were laughable,
they would toss them into the trunk,
calling it the "Sea of Bitterness."
When the brothers were at leisure,
they would use it for amusement.
They would order two servants
to carry the "Sea of Bitterness" before them,
each reading one piece,
and all would laugh heartily before finishing.
Zhèng Guāngyè often spoke of the year he passed the examination.
On the night of the policy exam,
a fellow candidate suddenly entered his exam booth.
Speaking in the Wú dialect,
he said to Zhèng Guāngyè:
"Honored sir, honored sir,
may I share your space?"
Zhèng Guāngyè gave up half of his booth for him.
The man then said:
"Honored sir, honored sir,
may I trouble you for a ladle of water?"
Zhèng Guāngyè fetched it for him.
The man then said:
"And may I also ask you to brew a bowl of tea?"
Zhèng Guāngyè gladly brewed it for him.
Two days later,
Zhèng Guāngyè achieved the top rank as zhuàngyuán.
That man was the first to submit a congratulatory letter,
recounting in detail the kindness shown that night.
It roughly said:
"You not only fetched water for me,
but also brewed tea.
At the time, I did not recognize your noble status,
my eyes were those of a commoner.
Now, suddenly, I am your junior,
a wretched and lowly bone."
From "Zhí Yán."
Lǐ Yào
In the Táng dynasty, Minister Lǐ Yào left his post in Shèzhōu
and was replaced by Wú Yuán.
There was a courtesan named Mèichuān who served wine,
clever and quick-witted.
Lǐ Yào was quite fond of her,
but he had already taken the courtesan Sháoguāng into his household,
so he entrusted Mèichuān to his successor,
asking him to care for her.
At the farewell banquet,
overwhelmed by parting emotions,
he composed a poem:
"For years governing the prefecture, few joys I found,
amidst military affairs, I drank with companions.
Today, as I depart, I hand over everything,
clearly entrusting the pearl that is Mèichuān."
Wú Yuán replied:
"Strolling leisurely, daily joys abound,
yet speaking of virtue brings tears profound.
Sháoguāng has already taken the lead,
now I hold the pearl in my palm to heed."
From "Shū Qíng Shī."
Wáng Duó
In the Táng dynasty, the Secretariat Director Wáng Duó
held a high position and enjoyed great prestige,
all due to his literary elegance,
but he lacked the talent to quell rebellion.
He was stationed at Zhǔgōng
(Originally written as "qīng";
corrected based on the Xǔ manuscript copy.)
as military commander
to defend against Huáng Cháo.
He brought his concubines to his post,
but his wife was jealous.
Suddenly, news arrived that his wife had left the capital and was on her way.
Wáng Duó said to his aides:
"Huáng Cháo seems to be advancing from the south,
and now my wife is coming from the north.
How am I to find peace
in such a situation?"
A staff member joked:
"Why not surrender to Huáng Cháo?"
Wáng Duó also laughed.
After Jīngzhōu fell,
he defended Tóngguān Pass.
Huáng Cháo sent a message:
"Your Excellency is a scholar,
no match for me.
Please withdraw voluntarily,
lest you stain the blade's edge."
So he abandoned the pass
and followed Emperor Xī in his flight to Shǔ.
He was again appointed military commander
to recover the capital,
but he failed to achieve great merit
and ultimately met an untimely death.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Xuē Zhāowěi
In the Táng dynasty, before Xuē Zhāowěi passed the imperial examination,
he went to a shop to buy shoes.
The shopkeeper asked:
"What size are your feet, scholar?"
He replied:
"My feet came with me.
I've never ranked them by size."
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Kǒng Wěi
Kǒng Wěi, a chancellor of the Táng dynasty, once received an official appointment.
Performers from the Jiàofāng troupe came one after another seeking congratulatory gifts.
One performer, Shí Yězhū, arrived alone first.
When given some gifts,
Kǒng Wěi said to him:
"My household is quite lacking,
so I cannot give generously.
If you see the other 'wild boars',
please do not tell them."
Another performer arrived later.
Kǒng Wěi summoned him to bend down by the steps,
asked for his flute,
pointed to a finger hole and asked:
"Which one is the 'Huàn Xī Shā' hole?"
The performer laughed heartily at this.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Yǔwén Hàn
Chéng Zǐxiāo, a Táng dynasty Daoist priest, once climbed to the summit of Huà Shān
and happened to take a tumble.
Imperial Secretary Yǔwén Hàn sent him a letter teasing him:
"We don't know if you made it up or not,
but we find it strange that you were 'hanging' yet again."
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
A Petition to the Village Elders Written in Phrases from the Thousand Character Classic
Respectfully addressed to the Village Chief and the Three Elders:
We have earnestly heard that governance is rooted in agriculture,
and one must devote oneself to these farming tasks.
If clouds do not rise to bring rain,
how can we pay taxes on ripe grain and offer up the new harvest?
Our Sage Emperor has subdued the barbarian tribes,
cherishing and nurturing the common people.
Thus, he can use the intercalary days to complete the year,
and harmonize the pitch pipes to adjust the yang energy.
We, the undersigned,
all admire and follow the virtuous,
cultivating our virtue to establish our reputation.
Therefore, we have spread mats and set out seats,
to perform the seasonal sacrifices.
We strum the zither and blow the sheng,
singing to strings and feasting with wine.
Superiors and inferiors live in harmony,
joyful, happy, and healthy.
Rituals distinguish the noble from the humble,
music varies for the esteemed and the lowly.
Wine flows like an unceasing river,
meat is as fragrant as orchids.
Not only are vegetables like mustard and ginger valued,
but fruits like plums and crabapples are also prized.
All raise their heads and stamp their feet,
together raising cups and goblets.
This is not merely to dispel sorrow and invite joy,
but truly because fortune favors the good and celebrates virtue.
However, I, so-and-so, live in solitude and idle leisure,
isolated, inexperienced, and ill-informed.
Although I have occasionally eavesdropped over walls,
I have never held office or participated in governance.
I cannot steadfastly maintain noble conduct,
for my desires chase after material things and my mind is easily swayed.
Thinking of home, I grasp something hot yet wish for coolness;
yearning for wine is like wanting a bath when covered in grime.
The elders are satiated with sumptuous feasts,
while I, so-and-so, am hungry and weary of husks and chaff.
Admiring your virtue is like an echo in an empty valley;
looking up to your kindness is like listening intently in a vacant hall.
If I may receive your benevolent compassion and pity,
perhaps there will be aid for the weak and support for the falling.
I hope you will deign to consider and reply in detail,
and I wish for all to receive your dripping grace, like lotus leaves gathering dew.
I, so-and-so, hereby kowtow and bow again.
Ultimately, I hope to inscribe this on a stele and engrave it in bronze,
but I only know fear and trepidation,
truly as if standing on the edge of an abyss or treading on thin ice.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
The Shāndōng Clerk
In the Táng dynasty, there was an old clerk in Shāndōng
whom all the county magistrates before and after
could not avoid being insulted by.
His family became extremely wealthy.
When a new magistrate first arrived,
he would test him with official documents,
to immediately gauge his strength or weakness.
There was a magistrate who had just arrived.
The clerk was tasked with compiling a register of adult laborers for corvée duty,
and he personally went through the list.
There were names like Xiàng Míngfǔ (Magistrate Xiàng), Sòng Lángjūn (Young Master Sòng), Chéng Lǎoshǔ (Rat Chéng), and Zhāng Pòdài (Torn Sack Zhāng).
This clerk intentionally jumped out of order,
grouping these names together,
to observe the magistrate's strength or weakness.
He first called out: "Zhāng Pòdài, Chéng Lǎoshǔ, Sòng Lángjūn, Xiàng Míngfǔ."
The county magistrate merely nodded,
showing no intention to question it.
The clerk went out and happily said:
"What's under the official hat is now clear."
He eventually went and sold [the position?].
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Luó Yǐn
Luó Yǐn of the Táng dynasty was close friends with Zhōu Yáo.
Zhōu Yáo said to Luó Yǐn:
"Your Honor has an excellent poem about a painted screen,
it is truly a masterpiece."
Luó Yǐn didn't understand what he was referring to.
Zhōu said:
"If taught to speak, she would topple kingdoms;
Even devoid of feeling, she still stirs the heart."
This was Luó Yǐn's poem about flowers.
Luó Yǐn clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
From "Shū Qíng Shī"
Lú Yánràng
Lú Yánràng of the Táng dynasty studied poetry
and only passed the imperial examinations on his twenty-fifth attempt.
Among his examination papers were the lines: "A fox darted across the official road;
A dog bumped the shop door open."
Zhāng Jùn, the Commissioner of Finance, personally witnessed these events
and often praised these lines.
He also had the lines: "A hungry cat peers into a mouse hole;
A greedy dog licks the fish-cutting block."
which were admired by Chief Minister Chéng Ruì.
And also: "Chestnuts popping burst the felt;
A cat leaping overturned the cauldron."
which were admired by Shǔ King Wáng Jiàn.
Lú said to others:
"In my life, I have sought audiences with high officials and nobles;
I never imagined my success would come from cats, mice, and dogs."
People heard this and laughed at him.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Performers
During the Xiántōng era of the Táng dynasty,
the performer Lǐ Kějí was witty and humorous in his acts,
standing out among his peers.
