Although his performances could not convey profound moral lessons,
his cleverness and quick wit
were nonetheless rare.
Once, on Yánqìng Festival,
after Buddhist and Daoist monks had finished their lectures,
it was the turn of performers to put on a show.
Kějí, dressed in a wide robe with a broad sash,
lifted the hem of his garment and ascended the stage,
proclaiming himself a "Debater of the Three Teachings."
Someone seated nearby asked him:
"Since you claim mastery of the Three Teachings,
tell me, who was Shìjiā Rúlái (Śākyamuni Buddha)?"
He replied:
"A woman."
The questioner, startled, said:
"How so?"
Kějí said:
"The *Diamond Sūtra* states:
'*Fū zuò ér zuò* (He spread out his seat and sat).'
If he were not a woman,
why would he need a *fū* (husband) to sit before his *ér* (child) could sit?"
The Emperor smiled at this.
He was asked again:
"Who is Tàishàng Lǎojūn (the Supreme Venerable Sovereign)?"
He said:
"Also a woman."
The questioner was even more puzzled.
Kějí then said:
"The *Dàodé Jīng* states:
'I have a great affliction
because I have a body.
When I have no body,
what affliction do I have?'
If he were not a woman,
why would he worry about having a *shēn* (body/pregnancy)?"
The Emperor was greatly amused.
He was asked yet again:
"Who is Wénxuān Wáng (Confucius)?"
He said:
"A woman?"
The questioner said:
"How do you know that?"
He replied:
"The *Analects* says:
'Sell it!
Sell it!
I am waiting for the right price.'
If he were not a woman,
why would he be waiting to *jià* (be married/for a price)?"
The Emperor was extremely pleased,
and bestowed generous rewards upon him.
From *Táng Quē Shǐ*.
Also, in the first year of the Tiānfù era,
Lǐ Màozhēn of Fèngxiáng requested an audience to present matters to the court.
Emperor Zhāozōng received him at Ānfú Tower.
Màozhēn tearfully presented words about saving and aiding the state.
At the time, Chancellor Cuī Yìn secretly memorialized, saying:
"This man is treacherous,
not to be trusted.
Your Majesty should maintain a broad mind while dealing with him."
The next day,
a banquet was held at Shòuchūn Hall.
Màozhēn arrived in a sedan chair, wearing coarse clothing
(Míng manuscript note: 'sedan chair' as 'riding';
'coarse clothing' as 'armor'
entered through the Jīnluán Gate,
and changed clothes to attend the banquet.
All considered such arrogance unprecedented
in previous dynasties.
At that time, the eunuch Hán Quánhuì had formed a deep alliance with Màozhēn.
Chancellor Cuī, fearing him,
from then on also allied himself with Zhū Quánzhōng.
This eventually led to Quánzhōng bringing his army from Biànzhōu to escort the emperor,
marking the beginning of the forced relocation of the court to Luòyáng.
Using
(Míng manuscript note: 'beginning using' as 'calamity indeed')
the example of Wángzǐ Dài summoning the Róng barbarians,
Cuī Yìn was compared to him.
Previously, when Màozhēn entered the passes,
he set fire to the imperial palaces in the capital,
leaving almost no inhabitants.
At this banquet,
the court performer Ān Pèixīn,
nicknamed Màozhēn "Fire Dragon's Son."
Màozhēn, ashamed and fearful, bowed his head.
But secretly he angrily said:
"One day I will kill this brat."
Ān heard of this,
and requested leave,
traveling to Qíxià to pay his respects to Màozhēn.
When Màozhēn saw him,
he cursed loudly:
"How dare this actor show his face here?
He must be here to beg."
Ān said:
"I only wished to pay my respects,
not daring to impose."
Màozhēn said:
"If you are so poor and destitute,
why don't you beg?"
Ān said:
"Recently in the capital, one only needs to sell bran and charcoal
to make a living for life.
Why would one need to beg?"
Màozhēn laughed heartily and bestowed generous gifts upon him.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Also, during the Guānghuà era,
Zhū Pǔ was appointed Chancellor from the position of *Máoshī* (Classic of Poetry) Erudite.
Pǔ, relying on his eloquence,
believed he could easily bring about peace and prosperity.
Introduced by a feudal prince,
he came to the attention of Emperor Zhāozōng,
and thus received this appointment.
On the day of his audience,
he presented several proposals,
each time saying, "Your servant will certainly achieve this for Your Majesty."
Once he held great power,
he accomplished nothing at all.
From then on, the emperor's favor towards him waned daily,
and criticism rose both inside and outside the court.
On a day of an inner-palace banquet,
the performer Mù Dāolíng, dressed as a scripture-reciting ascetic,
came forward and declaimed clearly:
"If you see Minister Zhū,
that is seeing a non-minister (or: that is an illusion)."
The next day, he was dismissed from the palace.
People of the time said:
"Becoming Chancellor has happened since ancient times.
A gentleman is not ashamed that his words are not put forth,
but ashamed that his respectful actions do not match them."
Moreover, before
(Míng manuscript note: 'before' as 'now')
the collapse and chaos,
with armed conflict throughout the land,
even one endowed with extraordinary talent
could not devise a plan.
And Zhū Pǔ was merely a Confucian scholar,
relying on meager eloquence,
wanting to bring order to chaos—
he only brought humiliation upon himself.
It was fitting that before his fine plans could be fully presented,
dismissal and exile had already arrived.
Thus he was greatly ridiculed by those with discernment.
From *Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán*.
Also, when Tàizǔ (Liáng Tàizǔ, Zhū Quánzhōng) went to pay homage to Zhāoxuān (Emperor Āi, also known as Zhāoxuāndì, the last Táng emperor).
Emperor Zhāozōng held a banquet.
When all were seated,
musicians and various performers were present.
A performer constantly praised [text missing] the sage.
First, he extolled the emperor's virtue,
then spoke of the achievements of the Prime Minister, Prince of Liáng, saying:
"Our Prime Minister, Prince of Liáng,
is a worthy born once in five hundred years."
The Senior Court Musician-Historian Hú Zǎn responded:
"Exactly so.
[Text missing several characters] surely taught the court... [text missing] all the ministers attending the banquet turned pale,
but Liáng Tàizǔ only laughed.
Emperor Zhāozōng was displeased,
but could do nothing.
Zǎn himself was fond of board games.
He often rode a single donkey,
going daily to an old friend's house to play chess,
mostly leaving early and returning late.
Over the years,
he never once stopped.
Every time he arrived at the house,
the host would invariably instruct his servant boy:
"Take care of the Superintendent's donkey in the backyard."
Zǎn was very grateful for this.
At night, he would ride it back.
One day, he was summoned unexpectedly,
and Zǎn hurriedly asked for his donkey.
When it was led forward,
he noticed it was panting,
its whole body sweating,
for it had just been pulling the millstone for the host.
Only then did Zǎn realize his donkey had been pulling the mill for them all along.
The next morning,
he walked on foot to the house again.
The host also said:
"Take care of the Superintendent's donkey."
Zǎn said:
"The donkey happens to be unavailable today."
The host said:
"Why is that?"
Zǎn said:
"Ever since returning home yesterday,
it has suffered from dizziness and nausea,
unable to get up or move about.
I beg leave for it to rest and recuperate."
The host also laughed heartily.
Thus, although Zǎn was cunning like this,
he remained unaware of what his mount had been doing.
For years, it had been turning the mill for others, sharing the profits,
and he was also repeatedly teased by his colleagues about this.
From *Yùtáng Xiánhuà*.
Wángshèchéng
The false Shu king, the Former Ruler,
before establishing the state,
a monk from the Western Regions arrived in Shǔ.
The people of Shǔ gazed upon him with reverence,
as if seeing Śākyamuni.
He stayed at the Dàcí Sānxuéyuàn,
and the Shu ruler again paid him a visit, sitting in the hall.
The entire city's scholars and women
came to the monastery, not prevented from doing so
(The false Shu king, the Former Ruler, to "came to the monastery, not prevented from doing so" — forty-five characters missing from the original text,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition
Women lined up to pay their respects,
when the performer Wángshèchéng joked, saying:
"These female disciples diligently and earnestly pay their respects,
hoping that in their next life, their faces
will all resemble the monk's."
The Shu ruler laughed heartily.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Gù Xiòng
The false Shu king, the Former Ruler, rose from Lì and Làng,
and established the Qīnqí Army,
all composed of brave and strong men.
Four hundred men were divided... carrying purple banners.
In every battle formation,
if the front army was about to be defeated,
they would wave the purple banners to reinforce it,
and none... would not collapse.
Like thunder startling and stars scattering,
they never suffered defeat.
The officers and soldiers of this regiment often achieved high rank,
some reaching the rank of general... down to scattered personnel,
also enjoying official salaries.
By relying on them to secure hegemony,
they all benefited from fortunate men.
At that time... the southern Hēiyún Dū,
were all of the purple banner type.
These troops each had their own names,
at that time Gù... also once governed a commandery,
often mixing in jokes and banter.
He once organized a military examination,
assisted by... Vice-Minister Lǐ Zhāzhā, who passed the jìnshì examination,
three... Hānzi, Jiāng Làizi, Zhāng Dǎxiōng, Cháng Xiǎo... Xǔ... Lǐ Kèqū, Lǐ Pòlè, Lǐ Jíliǎo, Fán Hūléi, Rìyóushén, Wáng Hàotuó, Hǎo Niúshǐ,... Gòng, Chén Bōsī, Luó Mánzi.
They were tested on "Fu on Fleeing to the Mountains and Marshes" and "Poem on Grass Not Growing Anywhere".
These were also of the caliber of Mài Tiězhàng and Hán Qínhǔ.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Bùtiàozǐ
There was a Bùtiàozǐ,
who always engaged in jesting.
Among his peers, those who were clever and sharp-witted,
alert and perceptive by nature,
were all tricked and made fun of by him.
Once, he traveled by boat with a scholar,
sailing on a river.
When they were about to disembark,
a fellow passenger had a thin and weak donkey,
with a crooked tail.
Bùtiàozǐ strongly urged the scholar to buy it.
The scholar despised its thinness and weakness,
but Bùtiàozǐ encouraged him, saying:
"This donkey has extraordinary features,
different from ordinary ones."
Reluctantly,
the scholar bought it at a high price.
After leaving the boat and embarking on the road,
the donkey was indeed frail and weak,
unfit for riding.
The scholar bitterly complained about it.
Bùtiàozǐ said:
"Don't regret it,
this one is different from others."
That evening,
it suddenly snowed.
Bùtiàozǐ said:
"Now I've got it.
Please buy three or five cups of wine,
and then I will tell you the story behind it."
The scholar again reluctantly bought wine and drank with him.
When raising his cup,
Bùtiàozǐ said:
"Haven't you heard Dù Xúnhè's poem:
'Buying fish from the boat, the tail is especially fine
(Míng manuscript note: 'fish' as 'donkey',
'fine' as 'tail'
Buying wine in the snow, the fragrance is doubly strong'?
The reason I asked you to buy the donkey and buy wine
is precisely because Dù's poem mentions it;
it's not without evidence."
The scholar had been tricked and made fun of,
completely unaware,
and only then did he realize it.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà".
Sīmǎ Dū
Former jìnshì Sīmǎ Dū resided in Qīngqiū.
Once, he entrusted twenty thousand coins
to a military officer under commander Wáng Shīfàn to buy silk.
After a year,
both the silk and the money were embezzled.
Sīmǎ Dū went to the commander's office at the beginning of the month
to pay respects to Lord Wáng.
He happened to see this person
and questioned him.
The man's appearance
was imposing, with a thick beard,
fierce and stubborn, and he flew into a rage,
wanting to throw himself into a well.
Sīmǎ Dū calmly said:
"Why go to such extremes?
You, with a fistful of beard,
your expression shows it;
gazing into a thousand-xún jade well,
there is someone in the well."
Lord Wáng learned of this
and had the military officer executed on a withered tree.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Wú Yáoqīng
In the Táng dynasty, Wú Yáoqīng's family was in Guǎnglíng.
Initially, he worked as a servant in an inn.
Skilled in writing and accounting,
he thus gained access to government offices,
and became known among the officials.
He started as a minor clerk in the salt and iron administration.
Quick-witted and eloquent by nature,
regarding the advantages and disadvantages of matters,
he could memorize and adjust them all,
pleasing people's eyes and ears.
Therefore, Chancellor Lǐ Wèi, recognizing his ability,
personally appointed him from the start.
Gāo Pián then appointed Wú Yáoqīng to administer the Sìzhōu office,
concurrently overseeing the Lìguó supervision,
and soon recommended him as prefect.
Before the imperial order was issued,
a military mutiny occurred,
and he returned to Guǎnglíng.
Shortly after,
he administered the Zhèxī office,
but was dismissed after a few months.
He then administered the Yángzhōu office,
concurrently serving as the quèdiào commissioner.
The false court appointed Wú Yáoqīng as Yùshǐ Dàfū.
Wú Yáoqīng attached himself to the powerful,
regardless of their status,
if there was any opportunity,
even with servants and lowly people,
he would straighten his robes and use gold and jade as bait for them.
If they slightly lost power,
even if they had sworn lifelong friendship,
he would sit facing them all day
without speaking to them again.
So much did he pursue profit and betray righteousness.
The powerful and noble all associated with him through bribery.
Thus, without leaving Huái and Sì,
he usurped high office,
soiling the government offices.
Within a few years,
he embezzled six hundred thousand strings of salt and iron money.
At that time, Wáng Qǐ was in charge of the affairs of the two commissions,
and had Wú Yáoqīng imprisoned,
intending to investigate the matter thoroughly.
But he was protected and saved by Zhūgě Yīn.
When the city fell,
soldiers who recognized Wú Yáoqīng
all requested to eat him.
Bì Shīduó did not allow it,
and at night ordered Wú Yáoqīng to escape in different clothes.
He reached Chǔzhōu, where a disturbance occurred,
and he was killed by an enemy,
his corpse abandoned in the street.
His wife wrapped him in a paper-and-reed coffin,
but before it could be buried,
someone fond of mischief wrote on it:
"A parcel,
to be delivered to Avīci Hell;
please remove the diagonal seal,
and deliver it to King Yánluó."
People at the time considered it a joke.
From "Yāoluàn Zhì"
Lǐ Rèn Wéi Fù
In the Tiānchéng era,
Lú Wénjìn was stationed in Dèng.
Once, when he went out of the city,
his guests and attendants all accompanied him.
The secretary Wéi Jí was also summoned.
He was old,
and lacked the strength to control his horse.
Already drunk,
his horse bolted,
galloping east and west among the mulberry groves.
He was caught by a horizontal branch, which tore off his scarf and cap,
exposing his bald head as he dashed about.
By the time his servant caught up,
he had already fallen off.
He had a chronic lung condition,
and dark, itchy rashes on his nose.
He lay by the roadside.
None of the staff could help but laugh.
The assistant ordered the Left Department Director Lǐ Rèn
and the Sacrificial Bureau Vice-Director Rèn Yáo
to each compose a poem using a single rhyme.
One verse read:
"When the servants secretly peeked,
and the officers all looked on,
he was shouting in the wheat fields,
and tumbling down by the mulberry grove.
His blue, hooked nostrils
were truly like a hammer of raw iron;
his ashamed, hanging skull
resembled a pot of cooked copper."
The rest is not recorded.
All who heard it couldn't help but laugh.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà".
Chéng Jìmíng
Jìn dynasty Chéng Jìmíng's poem mocking a summer guest said:
"In the hottest days of the year,
no carts travel the roads.
People stay indoors, avoiding the heat, lying down,
not visiting each other.
Nowadays, foolish people
brave the heat to visit others' homes.
When the host hears a guest has come,
he frowns—what can he do?
Thinking the guest should get up and leave,
he sits properly, sighing deeply.
Nothing said is urgent,
so why all this endless chatter?
Waving the fan makes the wrist ache,
sweat pours down in torrents.
Don't say it's a small matter,
it is also a human flaw.
I advise all friends,
those who go out in the heat deserve scolding."
From "Qǐyán Lù".
Zhūgě Kè
The King of Wú invited the Shǔ envoy Fèi Yī to drink,
and had Zhūgě Kè supervise the drinking.
Kè struck Yī's back with a horsewhip,
causing great pain.
Yī addressed the King of Wú:
"The Shǔ chancellor is compared to the Duke of Zhōu,
the protector lord is compared to Confucius;
now there is a boy,
a whip-wielding attendant."
Kè responded:
"You, coming to a great state,
are arrogant against heaven's norms;
striking you with a whip,
what harm is there in principle?"
Everyone laughed heartily.
Also, when Zhūgě Jǐn was Governor of Yùzhōu,
he said to his Assistant Biéjià Xiàng Tái,
saying:
"My son knows how to converse,
you may speak with him."
Xiàng went north to visit Kè,
but did not get to see him.
Later, they met at Zhāng Zhāo's gathering.
The Assistant called to Kè:
"Hey,
young master!"
Kè then mocked him:
"Yùzhōu is in chaos,
what's with the 'hey'!"
He replied:
"With a sage ruler and worthy ministers,
I have not heard of chaos."
Kè said again:
"In ancient times, Táng Yáo was above,
and the Four Fiends were below."
He replied:
"Not only the Four Fiends,
but also Dān Zhū."
From "Qǐyán Lù",
the Ming manuscript divides this into two entries.
"The King of Wú invited the Shǔ envoy" is from "Qǐyán Lù".
"Zhūgě Jǐn was Governor of Yùzhōu" is from "Shìshuō".
Zhāng Zhàn
Jìn dynasty Zhāng Zhàn liked to plant pines and cypresses in front of his study.
Yuán Shānsōng, when traveling,
often liked to have his attendants sing funeral dirges.
People of the time said:
"Zhāng displays corpses under his roof,
Yuán conducts funerals on the road."
From "Shìshuō".
Hè Xún
Jìn dynasty Grand Tutor Hè Xún served as Governor of Wú Commandery.
At first, he never went out.
The powerful clans of Wú looked down on him,
and wrote on his office gate:
"A Kuàijī chicken,
cannot crow."
Hè heard of this,
so he went out,
turned back at the gate,
asked for a brush, and replied:
"If it could crow,
it would kill the Wú boys."
Thereupon, he went to the various garrisons and storehouses,
inspected the troops under the Gù and Lù families and those hiding fugitives,
and reported everything to the emperor.
Many were punished.
Lù Kàng was then the Governor of Jiānglíng Commandery,
so he went to petition Sūn Hào himself,
and only then were they released.
Original source missing,
the Ming manuscript cites "Shìshuō".
Lù Shìlóng
Jìn dynasty Lù Shìlóng and Xún Mínghè
did not know each other.
They met at Zhāng Màoxiān's place
(Ming manuscript adds 'at Zhāng's gathering' after 'Xiān')
and were told to converse,
as both had great talent,
they should avoid commonplace talk.
Lù raised his hand and said:
"Lù Shìlóng among the clouds."
Xún said:
"Xún Mínghè under the sun."
Lù said:
"Since the blue sky has opened,
and a white pheasant is seen,
why not draw your bow,
and set your arrow?"
Xún said:
"I thought it was a majestic cloud dragon,
but it turns out to be a mountain deer, a wild elk.
The beast is small, but the crossbow strong,
hence the delayed shot."
Zhāng simply clapped and laughed heartily.
From "Shìshuō".
Fán Qīn
Wèi dynasty Fán Qīn mocked Dù Jùmíng, saying:
"Dù Bó's distant descendant, styled Zǐjù,
his imperial ancestor was cruel and violent, shot to death;
the spirits did not heed,
heaven and earth did not grant;
at birth,
he looked like a field mouse,
his nature pestilent and harmful,
neither cultured nor martial;
roughly remembered, roughly noted,
cannot be fully listed."
From "Qǐyán Lù".
Liú Dàozhēn
Jìn dynasty Liú Dàozhēn, during the turmoil,
was pulling a boat by the river with others,
when he saw an old woman handling the oar.
Dàozhēn mocked her:
"Woman, why not adjust the loom and play the shuttle?
Why are you by the river handling the oar?"
The woman replied:
"Man, why not ride a horse and wield the whip?
Why are you by the river pulling the boat?"
Also, once sharing a simple meal in a thatched hut,
he saw a woman passing by with two small children,
both dressed in black clothes.
He mocked them:
"A black sheep leading two lambs."
The woman said:
"Two pigs sharing one trough."
Dàozhēn had no reply.
From "Qǐyán Lù".
Zǔ Shìyán
Jìn’s Zǔ Shìyán and Zhōng Yǎ mocked each other.
Zhōng said:
“We from Rǔyǎn are sharp as awls,
you from Yāndài are dull as mallets.”
Zǔ said:
“With my dull mallet,
I strike your sharp awl.”
Zhōng said:
“I have a divine awl,
which cannot be struck.”
Zǔ said:
“Since there is a divine awl,
there is also a divine mallet.”
Zhōng then conceded defeat.
From “Qǐyán Lù.”
Gāo Shuǎng
Gāo Shuǎng was eloquent, knowledgeable, and talented.
At the time, Liú Qiàn was the magistrate of Jìnlíng.
Shuǎng passed by and visited him,
but Liú did not receive him at all,
which Shuǎng deeply resented.
Soon after, Shuǎng replaced Qiàn as magistrate.
Qiàn hurried to welcome him,
offering generous gifts,
all of which Shuǎng accepted.
In his reply, he wrote:
“Gāo Jìnlíng replies on his own behalf.”
In the Ming manuscript, “zì” is written as “bái.”
Someone asked him the reason,
and he said:
“Liú Qiàn sent gifts
The character “xiǎng” was originally missing,
added based on the Ming manuscript
to the magistrate of Jìnlíng,
what does that have to do with Shuǎng?”
Later, he was promoted to assistant instructor at the Imperial Academy.
When Sūn Yì was the magistrate of Lánlíng,
Shuǎng visited him again,
but Yì showed no regard for their old friendship.
Shuǎng left and passed by the pavilion,
took a brush, and wrote on the drum face:
“The body is eight spans around,
the belly lacks an inch of guts,
the face is so thick,
beaten but never finished.”
Yì was stout and robust,
with a waistband ten spans around,
so Shuǎng used this to provoke him.
From “Tán Sǒu.”
Xú Zhīcái
In Northern Qí, Xú Zhīcái was enfeoffed as the King of Xīyáng.
At the time, Wáng Xīn and Zhīcái mocked each other. Zhīcái mocked Wáng’s surname, saying:
“The character for ‘Wáng,’
with words becomes ‘kuáng’ (deceitful),
near a dog becomes ‘kuáng’ (mad),
adding a head and feet becomes ‘mǎ’ (horse),
adding a tail and horns becomes ‘yáng’ (goat).”
Xīn had no reply.
On another occasion, during a banquet with guests,
Lú Yuánmíng was present,
and he teased Zhīcái about his surname, saying:
“Your surname, Xú,
is
Originally written as “dāo,”
corrected based on the Ming manuscript
not yet entered into people.”
Zhīcái then mocked Yuánmíng’s surname, Lú, saying:
“With ‘ān’ gone, it becomes ‘nüè’ (tyranny),
with ‘qiū’ added, it becomes ‘lǘ’ (donkey),
bearing a son becomes ‘lǔ’ (slave),
paired with a horse becomes ‘lǘ’ (donkey).”
He also mocked the characters “Yuánmíng”:
“Removing the head becomes ‘wù míng,’
extending the neck becomes ‘wú míng,’
halving it becomes ‘wú mù,’
changing the sound becomes ‘wú máng.’”
Yuánmíng also had no reply.
From “Qǐyán Lù.”
Sīmǎ Xiāonán
Zhōu’s Sīmǎ Xiāonán defected to Chén with Ānlù,
and Emperor Xuān treated him very generously,
appointing him as Minister of Works.
Seeing that court officials all valued scholarship,
accumulating classics and histories,
Xiāonán deeply admired this.
So he rolled up many sheets of yellow paper,
added red rollers,
and pretended they were ancient texts,
to show off to his colleagues.
The Minister of Works, Jìyáng’s Jiāng Zǒng, teased him, saying:
“Yellow-paper Five Classics,
red-roller Three Histories.”
Xiāonán
was the son of Qí’s Minister of Works, Zǐrú.
From “Tán Sǒu.”
Mǎ and Wáng
In Suí, two men surnamed Mǎ and Wáng once gathered for a banquet and joked.
Mǎ then mocked Wáng, saying:
“Wáng is you,
originally your surname was two,
because you wandered over,
they nailed a ‘dīng’ to your nose.”
Wáng said:
“Mǎ is you,
originally your surname was Kuāng,
they cut off your tail,
and on your back, you carry Wáng Láng.”
From “Qǐyán Lù.”
Wine Shop
During the Suí dynasty,
several people entered a wine shop.
The wine tasted sour and weak,
so they all mocked it.
One person said:
“Wine,
where have you wandered from,
steaming hot, you’ve lost the ‘yǒu.’”
The others asked:
“What does this mean?”
He replied:
“There’s water left.”
The next person said:
“Wine,
its head looks like an ā làn duī head.”
The others asked:
“Why does wine resemble an ā làn duī head?”
He replied:
“It’s not a quail head.”
Another person said:
“Wine,
when you get its head from over the fence,
its four legs touch the ground, yet it sleeps alone.”
The others said:
“What does this mean?”
He replied:
“There’s no other meaning.”
The others laughed together and said:
“This mockery is the most beanless.”
He immediately replied:
“If I had beans,
I’d go home to make sauce.
Why would I come here to drink vinegar?”
Everyone laughed heartily.
From “Qǐyán Lù.”
Lú Sīdào
Suí Dynasty Lú Sīdào once composed poetry together with Shòuyáng's Yǔ Zhīlǐ.
Yǔ had already finished, but Lú Sīdào had not yet completed his.
Yǔ said:
"Why is Lú's poem so spring-like?"
Lú Sīdào replied:
"I consider myself swift at weaving mats,
but find his brocade weaving too slow."
When Lú Sīdào first arrived in the capital from Wǔyáng,
the inner attendant Lǐ Délín bowed to Lú Sīdào.
Lú Sīdào said to others:
"Délín, when in Qí,
always bowed to me.
Now that his official rank is high,
although he bowed just now,
it
(Míng Dynasty manuscript note: 'it' is written as 'still')
resembled a kneeling posture."
Lú Sīdào once stood under the sun at the guest gate,
and Lǐ Délín said to him:
"Why not move to the shade of the tree?"
Lú Sīdào said:
"Hot it may be,
but I cannot stand under the trees."
Lú Sīdào wrote "On the Rise and Fall of Zhōu and Qí,"
in which Emperor Wǔ and Emperor Xuān of Zhōu
all received bad reputations;
while Emperor Gāozǔ and the Retired Emperor of Qí
were without good praise.
Lú Sīdào once paid a visit to the Crown Prince,
and the Crown Prince said to him:
" 'On the Rise and Fall of Zhōu and Qí'—
was it written by you?"
Lú Sīdào said:
"Yes."
The Crown Prince said:
"For those who serve as your lord,
is it not difficult?"
Lú Sīdào could not reply.
Emperor Wén of Suí, because Xú Líng was eloquent and quick-witted,
and no one could match him in debate,
felt deeply ashamed.
He then inquired among the court officials:
"Who can confront the envoy?"
At that time, they recommended Lú Sīdào,
and Emperor Wén was very pleased.
He immediately ordered Lú Sīdào to confront the southern envoy,
and all the court officials went along.
Xú Líng saw from a distance that Lú Sīdào was the smallest,
and laughed, saying:
"This gentleman is very small."
Lú Sīdào responded from afar:
"Because you, sir, are a small
(Note: The character 'small' was originally missing,
added based on the Dūnhuáng manuscript of 'Qǐ Yán Lù')
subject,
there is no need for the elder to trouble himself."
Shortly after they were seated,
Xú Líng said to Lú Sīdào:
"In ancient times, the Yīn moved stubborn people,
who originally lived in this city.
Those who remain today are all such people."
Lú Sīdào responded with a laugh:
"In ancient times, during the Yǒngjiā crossing south,
they all lived east of the river.
Among those who remain today,
you are the only one."
Everyone laughed heartily.
Xú Líng had nothing to say in reply.
Also, the Suí court ordered Lú Sīdào to be an envoy to Chén,
and the Chén ruler commanded all places along the road
not to engage in conversation with him,
to prevent any loss of opportunity.
After Lú Sīdào crossed the river,
he passed by a temple.
The monks prepared a meal for Lú Sīdào,
but did not dare to speak,
only providing food and drink.
Then they offered honey-soaked yìzhì fruit,
urging Lú Sīdào to taste it.
Lú Sīdào laughed and said:
"The master has long consumed it without reason,
why trouble yourself to urge others with this?"
The monk, having violated the command,
lost the opportunity and was afraid.
When Lú Sīdào arrived in Chén,
he held the national credentials,
(Note: Originally written as 'ruler,'
corrected based on the Dūnhuáng manuscript of 'Qǐ Yán Lù')
and after the Chén ruler saw Lú Sīdào,
he used words from the "Guānshìyīn Sūtra" to mock Lú Sīdào, saying:
"What merchant is this,
carrying heavy treasures?"
Lú Sīdào immediately responded,
also using the "Guānshìyīn Sūtra,"
replying:
"Suddenly encountering a fierce wind,
drifting and falling into the land of the rākṣasa ghosts."
The Chén ruler was greatly ashamed,
and had nothing to say in reply.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Lǐ Yǐn
After the mountain tomb of Emperor Gāozǔ of Wèi was completed,
an edict ordered Wèi Shōu, Zǔ Xiàozhēng, Liú Tì, Lú Sīdào, and others
each to compose ten elegiac songs.
The Minister of Works, Yáng Zūnyàn, evaluated them,
and four of Wèi Shōu's,
two each of Zǔ and Liú's were selected,
while Lú Sīdào alone had eight chosen,
so people of the time called him "Eight Odes Láng."
Lú Sīdào once was at Wèi Shōu's banquet,
raising a toast to urge Liú Tì to drink.
Wèi Shōu said:
"Is Lú the Eighth urging Liú the Second?"
The Secretariat Gentleman, Lǐ Yǐn of Zhàojùn,
also teased him, saying:
"Lú the Eighth inquires after Liú the Second."
Liú Tì harbored resentment over this.
Later, when Lǐ Yǐn was punished by flogging for some offense,
Liú Tì teased him, saying:
"Two heavy blows with the mallet,
one hundred lashes with the whip—
how does that compare to saying 'inquire after Liú the Second' back then?"
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Xuē Dàohéng
Suí Dynasty Xuē Dàohéng was sent as an envoy to the south,
and in the Southern Dynasty, regardless of whether they were monks or laypeople,
as long as they were quick-witted and eloquent,
they were conveniently arranged to meet Xuē Dàohéng.
One monk was particularly eloquent and quick-witted,
and he was ordered to read the "Lotus Sūtra" in the Buddha hall of the temple,
while Xuē Dàohéng was led to pay respects at the temple.
When they reached the door of the Buddha hall,
the monk loudly read from the "Lotus Sūtra," saying:
"The Kumbhāṇḍa ghost
is now outside the door."
Xuē Dàohéng immediately responded, also using the "Lotus Sūtra,"
replying:
"The Piśāca ghost
is actually inside."
The monks felt ashamed and convinced,
and had nothing more to say.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Explaining Ridicule
At the end of the Suí dynasty,
Liú Hēità held several prefectures,
indulging in his cruel tyranny.
Those who pleased him were richly rewarded,
while those who opposed him were slaughtered and mutilated.
Once during his leisure,
he sought out a man skilled at jesting.
Summoned into the courtyard to stand before him,
after a short while,
a water-owl flew past,
and he ordered the man to jest about it.
The man immediately said:
"Water-owl,
head like a sickle-ladle, tail like a chisel,
catching fish in the river without a single miss."
Liú Hēità was greatly pleased.
He then ordered him to jest about a camel.
The jest went:
"Camel,
neck bent green,
hooves
In the Dūnhuáng manuscript of Qǐ Yán Lù, 'bèi' is written as 'bō'.
The Míng manuscript copy writes it as 'pō'.
carried by it,
bearing many loads."
Liú Hēità then laughed heartily,
and bestowed fifty bolts of silk upon him.
After bowing in thanks,
he carried the silk on his left shoulder and walked out.
Before reaching the halberd gate,
he fell to the ground and could not rise.
Liú Hēità sent someone to ask:
"Why have you fallen to the ground?"
He replied:
"Because the load is uneven."
Liú Hēità then ordered another fifty bales of silk floss,
to be placed on his right shoulder and taken away,
telling him to come again the next day.
Upon returning to his village,
he met an acquaintance on the road,
who asked:
"Where did you get this silk floss and silk?"
He recounted the whole affair.
The acquaintance then begged to hear these jests,
and also asked about the reason for falling down.
Overjoyed, he returned home,
and said to his wife:
"I will certainly get silk floss and silk tomorrow."
At dawn

he went to the gate,
saying:
"I am extremely skilled at jesting."
Liú Hēità was greatly pleased,
and ordered him brought in.
It so happened that a macaque was in the courtyard,
and he was ordered to jest about it.
He immediately said:
"Macaque,
head like

According to the Míng manuscript copy, supplemented.
a sickle-ladle, tail like a chisel,
catching fish in the river without a single miss."
Liú Hēità was already suspicious,
but still did not reprimand him.
Then an owl flew past,
and he was again ordered to jest about it.
He again said:
"Old owl,
neck bent green,
hooves carried by it,
bearing many loads."
At this, Liú Hēità became furious,
and ordered one of his ears cut off.
As he walked out to the courtyard,
he immediately fell to the ground again.
Ordered to ask him,
he again said:
"The load is uneven."
Liú Hēità then ordered his other ear cut off.
Returning home,
his wife came to meet him and asked about the silk floss.
He replied:
"Silk floss?
Both ears cut off,
only face left."
From Qǐ Yán Lù.
Xīn Dǎn
In the Suí dynasty, Xīn Dǎn served as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel.
A candidate for office posted a notice about him,
roughly saying:
"Mr. Hánghèn (Harboring Resentment) of Bùshēn Village, Qūzhì Township, Yì County, Wǎng Prefecture,
asked Suí Vice Minister of Personnel Xīn Dǎn:
'The Son of Heaven today is sage and enlightened,
and all officials carry out his commands.
He expands the territory on all four sides,
and harmonizes the seven administrative affairs within.
Yet you, sir, hold a position of authority and balance,
with duties befitting a clear mirror.
You stand at the forefront of promotions and demotions,
grasping the power of praise and censure.
You ought to recognize right from wrong,
know the stagnant and the subtle,
so that the talentless lie buried,
and the capable soar like clouds.
How can you instead hold a sinecure and feed on empty fare,
wrongfully occupying a high office,
demoting and promoting without principle,
damaging and crippling the selection and appointment process?
Petty men hold positions,
while gentlemen are rejected and impeached.
None do not tremble with anxiety on your behalf,
yet how can you alone remain at ease?'
Xīn Dǎn replied:
'The sons of the common people,
the people of ten thousand states—
I cannot know them all.
Who is close, who is kin?
Those rewarded by a tyrant like Jié—
cannot but be pleased;
those blamed by a sage like Yáo—
how could they not be angry?
Those who gain office appear joyful,
those who lose office appear resentful.
Examining it in detail,
it is not my fault.'
Mr. Hánghèn said:
'What kind of illness is this?
What kind of illness is this?
If you do not know them, why not inquire their names?
If offices are few, why not select the finest?
Carefully examine their records and deeds,
and you will fully recognize the legal experts;
carefully examine their judgments and verifications,
and you will fully recognize the literary talents.
Do you not know that jade comes from stone, gold comes from sand?
Measuring your talent,
gauging your wisdom,
you should only be cast out to the four wilds,
to ward off demons and goblins.
Complaints and laments are many,
truly harming harmonious energy.'
Xīn Dǎn bowed twice and apologized, saying:
'Fortunately, sir, you have reproached me,
I truly feel I have many faults.
I shall earnestly scrape my flesh and penetrate my bones,
reform my errors and punish my wrongs.
I beg you, sir, to allow me to cultivate myself,
and spare me punishment.
If I err again,
I willingly submit to the axe and halberd.'
Mr. Hánghèn said:
"Men like you,
are as many as carts can carry and dippers can measure.
The court has many
The Míng manuscript copy writes 'rén' (people) for 'shǎo' (few).
who can immediately replace you.
How can the Office of Heaven's Officials long remain vacant,
waiting for you to reform yourself?
Leave quickly, leave quickly,
do not stay long!
Summon the shamans and priests,
but there is no place for you to go back.'
Xīn Dǎn covered his face and wept, saying:
'I brought this guilt upon myself,
I shall destroy and dissolve myself.
How dare I again present this face
to defile the sage court?'
Mr. Hánghèn dragged his staff and sang:
'Xīn Dǎn departs,
the Ministry of Personnel becomes clear.
Open the path for the worthy,
encounter peace and prosperity.
This year it is certain you cannot obtain it,
next year as scheduled you may again enter the capital.'"
From Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi.
Niú Hóng
In the Suí dynasty, Niú Hóng served as Minister of the Ministry of Personnel.
There was a candidate for office named Mǎ Chǎng,
whose appearance was extremely ugly.
Niú Hóng looked down on him,
and reclining on his side while eating fruit,
mocked Chǎng, saying:
"I have heard of the Fúfēng horse,
said to descend from heaven.
Now I see the Fúfēng horse—
getting a donkey wouldn't be a bad deal either."
Chǎng replied immediately:
"I have heard of the Lǒngxī ox,
a thousand shí yet no yoke needed.
Now I see the Lǒngxī ox—
lying on the ground chewing grass."
Niú Hóng rose in surprise,
and subsequently gave him an official post.
From Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi.
Hóu Bái
The Chén dynasty once sent an envoy to the Suí dynasty,
but they did not know the depth of the envoy's wit and eloquence,
so they secretly ordered Hóu Bái to change his appearance,
put on old, tattered clothes,
and serve as a lowly attendant.
The envoy thought he was of humble status,
and looked down on him greatly,
so he lay down beside him and spoke to him while passing gas.
Hóu Bái felt quite indignant.
The envoy asked him:
"Are horses expensive or cheap in your country?"
He replied:
"Horses come in several grades,
with varying prices:
If they are skilled,
with strong tendons and legs,
and a decent appearance,
capable of being ridden,
they are worth over twenty thousand;
If they are sturdy in appearance,
though lacking skill,
but can carry loads,
they are worth over four or five thousand;
If they have a scruffy tail and hooves,
pronounced bó jié fǎn
scruffy tail and hooves,
utterly lacking skill,
lying down and passing gas,
they are not worth a single coin."
The envoy was greatly astonished,
asked his name,
and upon learning it was Hóu Bái,
he finally felt ashamed and apologized.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Zhào Shéndé
In the early Táng dynasty,
Liáng Bǎo enjoyed teasing and joking.
Once, while on official business, he arrived at Bèizhōu,
and rested at a guesthouse.
Casually asking the assistant officials of Bèizhōu,
he said:
"In this prefecture, there is a Zhào Shéndé,
who is very skilled at mockery."
He immediately ordered him summoned.
Liáng Bǎo's face was very dark,
and he leaned on a desk in the hall, waiting.
Shortly after, Shéndé entered,
both of his eyes were red.
As he reached the steps,
Liáng Bǎo immediately said:
"Zhào Shéndé,
since there are no clouds in the sky,
why is the lightning so erratic?"
He replied:
"Just now, upon entering the door,
behind the desk, I only saw a stick of ink."
Liáng Bǎo then said:
"The government allocates cinnabar,
half an eye is enough for an entire country."
He replied again:
"Grind your little finger,
and it could paint the north of the Great Altar."
Liáng Bǎo had nothing more to say in response,
and, ashamed, he apologized and sent him away.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Jiǎ Jiāyǐn
In the Táng dynasty, Jiǎ Jiāyǐn, at the age of seven,
was summoned for an audience as a child prodigy.
Chángsūn Wújì and Xú Shìjì
stood talking in the court hall.
Xú teased him, saying:
"What kind of tree am I leaning against?"
He said:
"A pine tree."
Xú said:
"This is a locust tree,
how can you call it a pine?"
Jiǎ Jiāyǐn said:
"With 'Duke' (公) paired with 'wood' (木),
how can it not be 'pine' (松)?"
Chángsūn asked him again:
"What kind of tree am I leaning against?"
He said:
"A locust tree."
Chángsūn said:
"Aren't you going to correct yourself?"
Jiǎ Jiāyǐn said:
"Why bother correcting the answer?
Just take 'ghost' (鬼) paired with 'wood' (木)."
At the age of eleven or twelve,
during the Zhēnguàn era, he was recommended for office.
Though he was eloquent and witty,
his appearance was ugly.
Once, while awaiting instructions in the court hall,
the court officials had finished court and were all leaving,
and they came over to look at him.
Before anyone else could speak,
the Duke of Yīngguó, Lǐ Jì,
first said to the high-ranking ministers:
"This child looks just like a Liǎo face,
how could he be clever?"
Before anyone could respond,
Jiǎ Jiāyǐn immediately answered:
"Even a barbarian-headed man can become a chancellor,
why should a Liǎo-faced man be denied cleverness?"
The entire court burst into laughter.
From "Guó Shǐ Zuǎn Yì",
the Ming manuscript version cites "Jiā Huà Lù"
Ōuyáng Xún
In the Táng dynasty, Duke Sòng, Xiāo Yǔ, did not know how to shoot arrows.
On the ninth day of the ninth month, archery was bestowed as a gift,
but Yǔ's arrows all missed the target,
and he gained nothing.
Ōuyáng Xún composed a poem mocking him:
"A swift wind blows on slow arrows,
Weak hands驾驭 strong bows.
Wanting to go high, they instead fall down,
Should go west, yet turn east again.
All ten times they hit the ground,
Both hands are left holding empty air.
May I ask who is responsible for this?
It must be Duke Sòng."
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Gāo Shìlián
In the Táng dynasty, Gāo Shìlián was in charge of official selections.
He was advanced in years.
There was a candidate
who claimed to be skilled at mockery and jest.
Shìlián was wearing wooden clogs at the time,
and ordered him to mock them.
The candidate immediately responded:
"Pricking the nose, yet never sneezing,
Stepping on the face, yet never getting angry.
Mr. Gāo has two teeth,
and considers himself a winner."
Shìlián laughed and recommended him.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi"
Péi Lüè
In the early Táng dynasty,
Péi Lüè had completed his term as an imperial guard,
and the Ministry of War tested his judgment in writing,
but he failed because of one wrong character.
This man then went to the Chief Minister Wēn Yànbó to plead his case.
Yànbó was sitting with Dù Rúhuì at the time,
and paid no attention to his plea.
The man then said:
"Since I was young,
I have prided myself on being eloquent and discerning,
to the point of being able to relay messages,
fit to serve as a Receptionist,
and also capable of writing essays,
as well as skilled at mockery and jest."
Only then did Yànbó turn his attention and speak with him.
At that time, there was bamboo in front of the hall,
and Yànbó ordered him to mock the bamboo.
The man immediately mocked it, saying:
"Bamboo,
the wind blows, green and rustling.
In deep winter, its leaves do not wither,
through spring, its seeds do not ripen.
Hollow-hearted, it cannot await men of talent,
on its surface, why must there be nodes?"
Yànbó was greatly pleased,
and said:
"Since you understand relaying messages,
you can convey a message to the screen wall in front of the hall."
The man walked to the screen wall,
and said loudly:
"Nowadays, the sage emperor is wise,
opening the four gates to welcome scholars.
What thing are you,
staying here so long, blocking the path of the worthy?"
And then he pushed it over.
Yànbó said:
"This meaning hits 'Bó' (博)."
The man said:
"Not only does it hit 'Bó' (膊),
it also hits 'Dù' (肚)."
Because Dù Rúhuì was present,
he said this.
Yànbó and Rúhuì both laughed heartily,
and immediately ordered him sent to the Ministry of Personnel to be given an official post.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Liú Xíngmǐn
In the Táng dynasty, there was a man surnamed Cuī.
Returning home drunk, he violated the curfew,
and was captured and bound by the military patrol.
By the time of the fifth watch,
he still had not been released.
Liú Xíngmǐn, the magistrate of Cháng'ān,
heard the drum signaling the approach of morning court,
and encountered him at the head of the street.
Only then did he order him untied.
Thereupon, he composed a verse about it:
"Cuī the man broke curfew on his way,
The patrol was strictly keeping watch.
His turban fell beneath their fists,
His high topknot held in their palms.
(The character for 'held' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Míng dynasty manuscript copy.)
The marks of the staff emerged upon his chest,
The rope's pattern grew behind his wrists.
The sorrowful man cares not for the night,
At will, he'll see the dawn stars cross the sky."
Duke Wǔlíng, Yáng Wénguàn,
served as Vice Minister of Revenue.
Because he could drink well,
he was ordered to host a banquet for the foreign guest, Prince Hún.
But he mistakenly held the banquet for the Yántuó tribesman instead.
Xíngmǐn composed a verse:
"Duke Wǔlíng respects and loves his guests,
At the banquet's end, he knows no fatigue.
Sent to drink with Prince Hún,
He mistakenly feasted the Yántuó lad.
First recognized by the Court of State Ceremonial,
Finally known to the Censorate.
Since his spirit is already thus,
Why sigh long and grieve?"
Lǐ Shūshèn and Hèlán Sēngqié
had very dark faces;
Dù Shànxián, serving as magistrate of Cháng'ān,
was also dark.
Xíngmǐn composed a verse about them:
"Shūshèn rides a black horse,
Sēngqié grasps a lacquer bow.
Summon the magistrate of Cháng'ān,
Let's hunt the bears of North Mountain together."
From "Qǐ Yán Lù" (Records of Cheerful Banter).
Dòu Fǎng
In the Táng dynasty, Xǔ Zǐrú formerly held the post of Libationer.
During the Yǒnghuī reign period,
the Imperial Academy was being constructed.
Zǐrú was in charge of the rituals,
and there should have been steps/terraces,
but later he did not get the steps/rank.
Dòu Fǎng composed a verse about it:
"Unable to specialize in mastering rites,
With a hollow heart, he forcibly sought rank.
For one year, he declined the ceremonial cap,
For half a year, he wore hemp shoes.
With bad tiles, he was often 'guóed'
(Pronunciation: guó)
With a weak wall, he was repeatedly 'chāi-ed'.
(Pronunciation: chāi, both initial sounds).
Against a tree, he would promptly sleep sideways.
Passing a cabinet, he would immediately act perversely.
At year's end, his fine work complete,
He said he surpassed his peers.
Today, an imperial edict descended,
Only then did he realize his foolish plan was awry.
(Pronunciation: wāi, initial 'k-' and final '-huái')."
From "Qǐ Yán Lù".
Dí Rénjié
In the Táng dynasty, Dí Rénjié was untrammeled and unrestrained.
He once held the post of Vice Director of the Court of the Imperial Granaries.
Whenever he handled official matters,
he often had disagreements with the Chief Minister.
Rénjié was discontent about this,
so he wrote a judgment:
"The Vice Director is like a concubine,
The Chief Minister occupies the position of the principal wife.
It is difficult to serve the lady of the house with such twists,
In the end, one never receives her favor."
The Chief Minister was also rather ashamed and fearful.
At that time, Wáng Jíshàn and Dòulú Qīnwàng
were appointed Left and Right Chancellors.
Rénjié, based on his talent and reputation, was the one public opinion favored for the post,
and he rather hoped for this appointment.
He often teased Wáng and Dòulú,
showing not the slightest deference.
Wáng and Dòulú were both skilled at the board game 'chángxíng'.
After their appointment,
they said to the current chief ministers:
"We have no talent or virtue,
yet undeservedly received this appointment."
Dí said to them:
"You two gentlemen are both capable at 'chángxíng' (long journey/enduring conduct),
how can you say you have no talent or virtue (cáixíng)?"
Someone mentioned a matter for the Left Chancellor,
saying it had just been reported to the Right Chancellor.
Dí said:
"I'm not sure if he should be called Right Chancellor (Yòuxiàng),
but rather should be called 'Having Fortune' (Yǒuxiàng)."
Wáng and Dòulú asked the reason,
Dí said:
"Haven't you gentlemen heard,
'A clever son is not as good as a fortunate son'?
You two gentlemen can be called fortunate sons."
The two gentlemen forced a smile,
but their hearts were also depressed.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì" (Records of the Censorate).
Yáng Màozhí
In the Táng dynasty, Yáng Màozhí served as Reminder.
There was a Rectifier surnamed Wáng,
proficient in the Nine Classics,
but not versed in current affairs.
He often claimed to understand the Three Teachings.
At that time, there was a monk named Dào Rú,
who spread heresies and falsehoods.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān pursued and arrested him very urgently.
Notices were posted everywhere saying:
"Seeking the monk Dào Rú."
Màozhí and Xuē Jiānjīn teased him, saying:
"The edict seeks the monk Dào Rú,
how can you, sir, remain at ease?"
He said:
"What does that have to do with me?"
Màozhí said:
"You, sir, understand the Three Teachings.
'Sēng' is the Buddhist teaching,
'Dào' is the Daoist teaching,
how is it not related to you?"
Only then was he startled and afraid.
He became restless, unable to sleep or eat,
and dared not return home,
lodging in the government office for several nights.
He begged his colleagues to investigate
(Original text had 'shèn' for 'investigate',
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy.)
the matter's intent.
They again jointly deceived him,
and his worry and fear did not cease.
Whenever he met anyone, he would just say:
"I truly do not understand matters of the Three Teachings."
Only then did Màozhí and the others comfort him, saying:
"They are seeking another person,
it's not about the Three Teachings."
Then he dared to go out.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì".
Left and Right Terrace Censors
During the Xiàohé reign of the Táng dynasty,
among the Censors of the Left and Right Terrain,
three were transferred to the Southern Department while still serving as Internal Attendants,
and five were appointed by informal imperial edict.
The Censorate ridiculed them as the "Five Ink [Edict] and Three Still [Attendants]".
The Left Terrace called the Right Terrace the "Gāolì monks",
saying they followed
(Original text had 'Suí' dynasty,
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy.)
the Hàn monks to the vegetarian feast,
not chanting prayers or intoning hymns,
but only eating, drinking, and receiving alms.
This ridiculed them for managing the Outer Terrace,
and in the capital having nothing to impeach or criticize,
yet receiving the same salary.
Transferring from the Right Terrace to the Left Terrace
was called "going out to the foreign tribes";
transferring from the Left Terrace to the Right Terrace
was called "submerging into the foreign tribes".
Whenever they met,
they would inevitably tease and mock each other endlessly.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì".
Dù Wénfàn
In the Táng dynasty, Dù Wénfàn
was from Xiāngyáng.
Starting as a Captain of Cháng'ān, he took the examinations,
passed with distinction,
and was appointed Investigating Censor.
Selected for the Palace Administration,
he was appointed Vice Director of the Ministry of Justice,
and by special appointment as Attendant Gentleman, he was made a Secretary of the Western Terrace.
Previously, he and Gāo Shàngzhì both served in the Palace Administration.
They were oppressed and harassed by the Attendant Censors Zhāng Yóugǔ and Sòng Zhīshùn,
and along with Shàngzhì, were transferred to Vice Director posts.
After fifty days,
Yóugǔ and Zhīshùn finally entered the Ministry.
Wénfàn said to them in front of the crowd:
"Censors Zhāng and Sòng,
are both men of outstanding talent."
Yóugǔ asked him about it;
he replied:
"If they were not men of outstanding talent,
how could they, riding an earthen ox for fifty days,
catch up to the Palace Administration?"
The entire assembly laughed heartily.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì".
Supernumerary Censor
When Empress Wǔ first proclaimed the Zhōu dynasty,
fearing that the people's hearts were not yet settled,
she ordered officials to recommend themselves for court positions,
and many supernumerary posts were established beyond the regular quotas.
There was a clerk of the Censorate
who, while entering the Censorate,
encountered several supernumerary censors
standing gathered inside the gate.
The clerk did not dismount from his donkey and charged straight through.
The censors were furious
and were about to cane him.
The clerk said:
"Today's offense
truly lies with this donkey.
I beg you to first reprimand it,
and then I will accept my punishment."
They agreed.
He said to the donkey:
"Your skills are evident,
your spirit dull and stupid.
What kind of donkey beast are you,
that you dare to 'walk among the censors'?"
At this, the censors were ashamed and stopped.
From "Miscellaneous Records of the State"
Zhāng Yuányī
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān of Zhōu,
foreigners who submitted memorials
were often given offices and rewards;
some even became Right Terrace censors.
Once, Wǔ Zétiān asked Vice Director Zhāng Yuányī:
"What amusing things are happening outside?"
Yuányī replied:
"Zhū Qiányí wears green,
Dí Rénjié wears vermilion.
Yán Zhīwēi rides a horse,
Mǎ Jífǔ rides a donkey.
Taking the given name as the surname—Lǐ Qiānlǐ,
taking the surname as the given name—Wú Qīwú.
Left Terrace Censor Hú,
Right Terrace Censor Hú."
Censor Hú refers to Hú Yuánlǐ.
Censor Hú refers to a foreigner who became a censor;
he was soon transferred to another post.
When Zhōu replaced the Táng,
a provincial graduate from Bèizhōu named Zhào Kuò,
who was short and slight,
began his career as an Investigating Censor.
People of the time called him "the Censorate's filth."
Lǐ Zhāodé cursed him as "a bundle of frost-bitten grain."
Yuányī dubbed him "an owl on an eagle's perch."
At that time, Lǔ Kǒngqiū from Tóngzhōu served as a Reminder;
he had the air of a military man,
and people of the time called him "the commander of the external armies."
Yuányī dubbed him "a waterfowl entering the Phoenix Pool."
Sū Wèidào had talent, learning, insight, and bearing,
and was widely respected;
Wáng Fāngqìng had a crude and vulgar physique,
his speech was dull and clumsy,
his wisdom did not surpass the ordinary,
his talent was not exceptional,
yet both served as Vice Ministers of the Phoenix Pavilion.
Someone asked Yuányī:
"Which is more worthy, Sū or Wáng?"
He replied:
"Sū is a falcon touched by September frost,
Wáng is a fly frozen in October."
When asked the reason,
he answered:
"The frost-touched falcon is swift and keen,
the frozen fly is stubborn and timid."
People of the time admired his ability to capture the essence of things.
When the rebel Sūn Wànróng of Qìdān invaded Yōuzhōu,
Prince Héneì Wǔ Yìzōng was made marshal
and led troops to Zhàozhōu.
Hearing that the enemy leader Luò Wùzhěng
was approaching from the north with several thousand cavalry,
the prince abandoned his weapons and armor
and fled south to Xíngzhōu
(Míng manuscript note: Xíng is written as Xíng)
Zhōu,
leaving military supplies and equipment
scattered along the road.
Upon hearing the enemy had retreated,
he then advanced again.
When the army returned to the capital,
a grand banquet was held.
Yuányī mocked Yìzōng before the Empress:
"Long bow, short-range arrow,
Shǔ horse, mounting the steps lame,
seven hundred *lǐ* from the enemy,
hiding by the wall, fighting alone.
Armor and weapons all cast aside,
riding a pig, fleeing straight south."
(Míng manuscript note: 掾 is written as 猭)
The Empress said:
"Yìzōng has a horse;
why would he ride a pig?"
He replied:
"Riding a pig means 'running while clasping a pig'
(Original text: 夾 was written as 來,
corrected per Míng manuscript)
—that is 'fleeing'."
The Empress laughed heartily.
Yìzōng said:
"Yuányī prepared this in advance;
it's not improvised."
The Empress said:
"Then you set a rhyme for him."
Yìzōng said:
"Please use the *běng* rhyme."
Yuányī responded immediately:
"Inside, utterly slovenly,
brushing the temples, not neat.
Never seen a peach-blossom face,
vainly making almond-shaped eyes."
Wǔ Zétiān was greatly amused,
and the prince was deeply ashamed.
Yìzōng was short and ugly,
hence "long bow, short-range arrow."
Princess Jìnglè of Zhōu,
younger sister of Prince Héneì Yìzōng,
was also short and ugly.
Among the Wǔ clan women, she was the eldest,
and was called "Big Brother" at the time.
Once, the princess was riding side-by-side with Wǔ Zétiān.
The Empress ordered Yuányī to compose a verse:
"Horse adorned with peach-blossom brocade,
skirt trimmed with green grass gauze.
Surely beneath that curtained hat,
her looks resemble Big Brother."
Wǔ Zétiān laughed heartily,
and the princess was mortified.
The Palace Secretary Lóu Shīdé was tall, large, and dark,
and lame in one foot.
Yuányī dubbed him "the walking hearse demon"
and also called him "Duke Wèi Líng,"
meaning the demon guarding the spirit bier.
Vice Minister of Personnel Jí Xū was tall and large,
prone to walking with head held high,
gazing loftily into the distance.
He was dubbed "the camel gazing at willows."
Palace Censor Yuán Běn had hunched shoulders and a stooped body,
dark and thin,
and was dubbed "the examination official from Lǐngnán."
Vice Director of the Bureau of Equipment Zhū Qiányí was stout, dark, fat, and short,
his body grimy and greasy.
He was dubbed "the steward of the Imperial Banquets."
Dōngfāng Qiú had a long body and short gown,
bony face and coarse brows.
He was dubbed "the sergeant of the external armies."
Táng Bōruò was short and squat,
and was dubbed "the stunted Shǔ horse."
He called Lǐ Zhāodé "the sharp-toothed macaque of Suì"
(Note: 卒 pronounced as *zú*, with the meaning of 銳)
Academician of Letters Mǎ Jífǔ was blind in one eye,
and was called "the arrow-straightening master."
Vice Director's son Cháng Rúzǐ had a sunward gaze,
and was called "the vinegar-sipping fellow."
Magistrate of Sìshuǐ Sū Zhēng had frivolous and flighty manners,
and was called "the mouse that lost its hole."
From "Records from Court and Country"
Jí Xū
During Zhōu, Zhāng Yuányī had a thick belly and short legs,
a retracted neck and drooping eyes.
Jí Xū dubbed him "the upstream frog."
From "Records from Court and Country"
Zhū Suíhóu
During Zhōu, Magistrate Zhū Suíhóu of Qǔjiāng County, Sháozhōu,
his son-in-law Lǐ Tì,
and a traveler Ěrzhū Jiǔ
all had somewhat charming appearances.
People of Guǎngzhōu called them "the three woodcutters"
(pronounced *qiáo*).
A song circulated:
"By decree, chasing three woodcutters,
Suíhóu runs by the roadside,
turns his head to call Master Lǐ,
'Go fetch Ěrzhū Jiǔ!'"
Zhāng Zhuó called Suíhóu "a stew of chaotic dirt with an owl."
From "Records from Court and Country"
Lǐ Xiáng
Zhōu Lǐ Xiáng was a person from Hénèi.
He was chivalrous and resolute by nature.
Initially, he served as the Deputy Sheriff of Zǐzhōu.
During the performance evaluation,
the Prefect asked if it was fair.
Only Xiáng said:
"It is not fair."
The Prefect said:
"If it's not fair,
you take the pen and write the evaluation."
Xiáng said:
"Allow me to evaluate Your Excellency."
He then wrote:
"You handle major matters poorly,
yet are meticulous about trivial details;
you conceal your own faults,
but suspect others of being corrupt.
Evaluation: Below Average."
The Prefect fell silent and ended the matter.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Zhāng Zhuó
When Empress Wǔ Zétiān changed the dynasty,
she appointed officials without examination for those recommended,
so many rose from commoners to become Censors, Reviewers, Reminders, and Supplements,
their numbers beyond count.
Zhāng Zhuó composed a satirical verse:
"Supplements fill carts in a row,
Reminders are measured by the peck.
Censors are scraped together with a rake,
Proofreaders are molded like bowls."
At that time, there was a man named Shěn Quánjiāo,
arrogant and unrestrained,
who flaunted his talent and promoted himself.
Wearing a tall hat
and a long cloth gown,
he chanted this verse in the Southern Court,
adding four more lines:
"Reviewers don't read the laws,
Scholars don't seek the classics.
The Pacification Commissioner is blind,
and the Divine Empress closes her eyes."
He was then arrested by Censor Jì Xiānzhī,
who took him to the Right
(Míng manuscript note: Right should be Left)
Censorate for interrogation and impeachment.
Jì accused him of slandering court policies
and corrupting the nation's customs,
requesting that he be caned in the court
before being handed over to the law.
Empress Wǔ laughed and said:
"As long as you officials are not corrupt,
why worry about what the people say?
No need to punish him;
release him at once."
Xiānzhī was then
(original: shǒu, corrected to hū per Míng manuscript)
left pale-faced.
Táng Dynasty Yùzhāng Magistrate Hè Ruò Jǐn
had taut eyelids
and a thick neck.
Zhāng Zhuó nicknamed him "The Well-Fed Calf."
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Shí Bàozhōng
Shí Bàozhōng served as Acting Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
along with Vice Ministers Liú Qí and Zhāng Xúngǔ,
overseeing official selections.
Bàozhōng was never known for integrity, Liú Qí had long been renowned for fairness, and Xúngǔ married into a prominent family.
When assignments were being distributed,
people said:
"With money, Shí's office is best;
without money, Liú's office is best;
for scholars and officials, Zhāng's office is best."
This saying proved true.
Later, he served with Xǔ Zǐrú in selections,
while Liú Qí alone was praised for impartiality.
Bàozhōng, Shī Fàn, and Zǐrú
often relied on clerks for decisions.
Each time they appointed an official,
they would ask:
"Is the clerk's decision ready?"
People then composed another verse:
"The learned emulate Liú,
the Confucian scholars follow the
(original: yǔ, corrected to diǎn per Míng manuscript)
classics' words."
Bàozhōng was later executed alongside Liú Qí.
Candidates who were rejected or suppressed
composed another verse:
"This year, persimmons all suffer frost;
advise the pomegranates to be picked early."
While in Shǐpíng,
Bàozhōng once wrote a humorous poem:
"At dawn I depart from Shǐpíng,
by dusk I reach Hécéng.
Towers greet the morning clouds,
ponds reflect the bright night moon.
On the plank bridge, I meet the Chief Clerk;
outside the Língxīng Gate, I bow to the Military Officer.
A group of county deputies, donkeys and mules in a row;
several assistants, geese and ducks in line."
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì"
Zhèng Yīn
In the Táng Dynasty, Zhèng Yīn once insulted a candidate as a "foolish man."
The candidate replied:
"I am a foolish man from Wú,
but the 'man' here refers to you."
Yīn ordered him to compose a poem about foolishness.
The man from Wú said:
"Elm son and elm wife,
building houses and making carts.
On the seventeenth, eighteenth, or nineteenth night,
still borrowing and returning books."
Yīn's original surname was Mào,
but he changed it to Zhèng.
People at the time called him Mào Zhèng.
From "Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi"
Sòng Wùxiān
In the Táng Dynasty, there was a Censor who was unskilled in writing
but loved composing incessantly.
Since he held a powerful position,
many flattered him,
and he remained unaware.
Each of his compositions was inscribed by Sòng Wùxiān to glorify the Censorate.
His monthly salary was nearly exhausted.
His wife said to him:
"You are a scholar by training,
never skilled in literary composition.
The poems you praise
are not circulated outside.
This must be your colleagues mocking you,
deducting your salary to fund their kitchen.
Why endure their ridicule?"
Afterward, though he continued composing,
he no longer paid for the glorification.
When asked,
he repeated his wife's words.
The Censors later said among themselves:
"He has someone advising him;
we can no longer mock him."
And they stopped.
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì"
Fù Yán
Fù Yán of the Táng Dynasty,
from Wèizhōu,
originally named Fó Qìng.
He once served in the Left Censorate,
overseeing the Zhongliu sacrifice,
but the Zhongliu offering was meager,
lacking proper sacrificial animals.
Upon returning,
he lamented:
"The first sacrifice of the year,
yet it was so neglected."
Diànzhōng Liáng Zàiyán composed a poem about it:
"I heard he oversaw Zhongliu,
said to be a grand sacrifice.
Hurriedly seeking relay horses,
rushing out of Ānhuī.
The guards had no canopies,
the offerings lacked fresh meat.
His appearance gaunt and worn,
he returned
(original: róng, corrected to kōng per Míng manuscript)
empty-handed."
From "Yùshǐ Tái Jì"
Hóu Wèixū
Táng Dynasty Household Department official Hóu Wèixū authored the *Hundred Officials Materia Medica*,
describing the Censor as:
"Extremely hot,
and toxic."
It also states in red ink:
"Extremely hot and toxic.
Primarily dispels evil and flattery,
blocks treacherous circuits,
redresses grievances and stagnation,
stops excessive indulgence,
especially attacks greed and corruption.
Regardless of rank, all are confronted;
the Capital District Commandant and Registrar serve as its assistants.
It fears being recalled as an envoy,
detests explosive forthrightness,
and avoids confronting powerful magnates.
Originates from the various counties of Yōng and Luò prefectures;
those produced from outer prefectures
are especially usable.
Those sun-dried until hard are of good quality.
Taking it
enhances vitality,
reduces charm and allure.
Long-term use
makes one cold and stern.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*;
the Ming manuscript copy states it is from *Yùshǐ Tái Jì*.
Jiǎ Yánzhōng
Táng Dynasty Jiǎ Yánzhōng compiled the *Supervisory Materia Medica*, stating:
"Taking it causes heartache and worry,
frequent palpitations and fright,
and promotes white hair."
Shí Yì said:
"Those serving as probationary or acting officials
are like closed-mouth peppers,
most toxic.
Supervisory officials are like open-mouth peppers,
their toxicity slightly diminished.
Palace officials are like radishes,
also called ginger;
though pungent, they cause no harm.
Attendant Censors are like crisp pears,
gradually entering pleasant flavor.
Promotion to Vice Director is like sweet oranges,
suitable for long-term use.
Some say closed-mouth peppers are slightly toxic while crisp pears are toxic;
this is because toxicity manifests upon contact,
and also lacks constant nature.
Only upon appointment as Vice Director
is it called having the poison removed.
Joy and regret are half and half,
happy about the promotion,
yet regretful about losing the authority."
From *Yùshǐ Tái Jì*.
Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn
Táng Dynasty Lú Cángyòng
initially lived in seclusion on Zhōngnán Mountain.
During the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng,
he repeatedly held important positions.
The Daoist priest Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn
was summoned to the capital by Emperor Ruìzōng,
and was about to return to office.
Lú Cángyòng pointed to Zhōngnán Mountain and said to him:
"There are many excellent scenic spots here;
why must you go far away?"
Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn slowly replied:
"From what I observe,
it is merely a shortcut to officialdom."
Lú Cángyòng showed a look of shame.
From *Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ*.
Lǐ Jìngxuán
Táng Dynasty Secretariat Director Lǐ Jìngxuán served as commander-in-chief,
campaigning against Tǔbō,
reaching Shùdūn City.
Upon hearing that Minister Liú had perished among the Tǔbō,
he could not put on his boots,
and fled in disarray.
Wáng Gǎo
The Ming manuscript copy has "General Shí" before Wáng.
Gǎo written as Guǒ.
and Deputy Commander Cáo Huáishùn and others retreated in panic.
They abandoned their wheat rations,
stretching for a thousand *li* from start to end,
over a foot deep on the ground.
A military ballad of the time said:
"Lǐ Āpó of Táohé,
Wáng Bómǔ of Shànzhōu,
seeing the enemy dare not fight,
all because of Cáo Xīnfù."
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Gé Fǔyuán
Táng Dynasty Gé Fǔyuán was appointed Supervisory Censor,
then promoted to Palace Censor.
While on a mission,
he encountered bandits at Lóngmén,
losing all his traveling gear,
and sat wrapped only in a quilt.
Supervisory Censor Dù Yìjiǎn
playfully composed a verse about him:
"Shamefully lodged at Lóngmén,
his spirit first dimmed
Ming manuscript copy: dimmed written as dawned.
and muddled.
Eyes sunken, nearing the inn,
snoring resounds through distant woods.
Gathering his sack, he meets old acquaintances,
wrapped in a quilt, unlike a new marriage.
Who would say the envoy on the piebald horse
has turned into a hibernating bear crouching."
From *Yùshǐ Tái Jì*.
Zhù Qīnmíng
Táng Dynasty Minister of Rites Zhù Qīnmíng was quite versed in classics and history,
but unfamiliar with current affairs,
solely
Ming manuscript copy: solely written as broadly.
corpulent and plump,
stubborn, sluggish, and suspicious.
Minor clerks in the Censorate
nicknamed him "the meat lump."
A meat lump
is a lump of flesh,
without seven orifices.
It was obtained by a rustic during the time of Duke Mù of Qín.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Jiāng Shīdù
During the Xiāntiān era of the Táng Dynasty,
Jiāng Shīdù dug canals within Cháng'ān city,
circling the court halls, wards, and markets,
reaching everywhere.
The emperor ascended the western tower to view it;
Jiāng Shīdù dammed the rushing water,
letting rafts of firewood float down,
and was subsequently appointed Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries.
Afterwards, when water rose it would surge violently,
and when water receded it would dry up completely.
He also earlier diverted the Huáng Hé,
channeling water toward Dìzhōu,
expending immense labor and resources.
The people suffered from the flooding,
and laborers were again conscripted to block the river mouth.
In the sixth year of the Kāiyuán era,
the water overflowed,
the dam at the river mouth broke,
and the people of Dìzhōu
were almost entirely drowned.
Jiāng Shīdù considered it an achievement,
and his official rank advanced further.
There was also Fù Xiàozhōng who served as Director of the Imperial Observatory,
claiming to understand celestial phenomena,
and exclusively engaged in deceit and trickery.
A saying in the capital went:
"Jiāng Shīdù focuses solely on the ground,
Fù Xiàozhōng gazes with both eyes at the sky."
When Emperor Shénwǔ ascended the throne,
he recognized their deceit,
and had both executed.
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Jiāng Huì
Táng Dynasty Jiāng Huì served as Vice Minister of Personnel,
his eyes unable to recognize characters,
his hands incapable of writing,
yet he indiscriminately oversaw official selection,
making no distinctions whatsoever.
Selected candidates sang:
"This year's selection numbers happen to match,
all because the examiner lacks literary skill.
Behind the desk sits a lump of frozen pork,
hence he is called Vice Minister Jiāng."
From *Cháoyě Qiānzǎi*.
Wèi Guāngchéng
Yáo Yuánchóng, the Minister of War of the Tang Dynasty,
was tall and walked hurriedly;
Wèi Guāngchéng nicknamed him "the snake-chasing stork."
Lú Huáishèn, the Vice Director of the Chancellery, liked to look at the ground,
and was nicknamed "the mouse-peeking cat."
Jiāng Jiǎo, the Palace Attendant, was fat and dark,
and was nicknamed "the mulberry-satiated sow."
Ní Ruòshuǐ, a Secretary in the Secretariat,
was dark and had no beard or sideburns,
and was nicknamed "the drunken tribal spirit"
(the Ming manuscript notes "spirit" as "inspector")
Secretary Qí Chùchōng liked to squint at the sun,
and was called "the old mother searching for lice under a dim candle."
Secretary Lǚ Yánsì was tall and had little hair,
and was nicknamed "the envoy from Japan."
He also nicknamed Secretary Zhèng Miǎn "the drunken Goguryeo."
He nicknamed Reminder Cài Fú "the small-town medical doctor,"
pretending to be knowledgeable about medicinal properties.
There was also a Palace Censor who was short, ugly, and dark,
and was nicknamed "smoke-smoked earth fungus."
He nicknamed Censor Zhāng Xiàosōng "the village exorcist."
He nicknamed Secretary Yáng Shēnsì "the monkey on a hot griddle."
He nicknamed Supplemenator Yuán Huī "the zither-playing doctor at the prince's gate."
He nicknamed Vice Director Wèi Tián "the rain-praying Brahmin."
He nicknamed Lǐ Quánjiāo "the ranked official attendant."
He nicknamed Vice Director of the Chancellery Lǐ Guǎng "the water-satiated frog."
Because of this, he was charged with evaluating court officials in this manner,
and was demoted from Left Reminder to the position of County Lieutenant of Xīnxīng County in Xīn Prefecture.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Shào Jǐng
Shào Jǐng of the Tang Dynasty,
was from Ānyáng.
He passed the imperial examination and was appointed as the Lieutenant of Fényīn,
later transferred to the position of Granary Supervisor of Shè Prefecture,
and promoted to Right Censorate Investigating Censor and Vice Director of the Bureau of Evaluations.
When Emperor Shénwǔ ascended the throne,
Jǐng, along with Palace Censors Xiāo Sōng and Wéi Kēng,
were all promoted to perform duties in the palace,
though their responsibilities differed.
When the edict was issued,
Jǐng and Sōng were both appointed as Grand Masters of Court Discussion,
but Kēng received no appointment.
Jǐng and Sōng resembled foreigners in appearance,
with Jǐng having a high nose and Sōng having a thick beard.
They both wore crimson robes,
standing opposite each other in the courtyard.
Kēng alone secretly peeked from behind a screen and composed a poem about them:
"A pair of bearded men in crimson robes,
one with a thick beard, the other with a high nose.
Standing opposite each other in the hall, pressing down and
(pronounced with a falling tone)
standing,
ashamed of their worldly, hairy appearances."
The entire court joyfully recited it.
Another day,
when Emperor Ruìzong was at Chéngtiān Gate,
with all officials lined up,
Kēng suddenly fainted from dizziness.
Kēng was fat and short,
and Jǐng composed a poem about him:
"A sudden whirlwind rises in a swirling dance,
falling to the ground like a sticky rice dumpling with legs.
No wonder he performs duties emptily in the palace,
for he was never fit for the fifth rank's talent."
From "Records of the Censorate"
Huáng Fānchuò
Liú Wénshù, a Tang Dynasty general from Ānxī, was eloquent,
skilled in responding to the emperor,
and often praised by Emperor Xuánzong.
Wénshù had a beard growing under his chin,
and his appearance resembled a monkey.
The emperor ordered Huáng Fānchuò to mock him.
Wénshù deeply disliked being called a monkey,
so he secretly bribed Fānchuò
not to mention it.
Fānchuò agreed but proceeded to mock him:
"Poor, good Liú Wénshù,
your beard and chin live separately.
Wénshù's face does not resemble a monkey's,
but a monkey's face strongly resembles Wénshù's."
The emperor knew he had been bribed,
and laughed heartily.
From "Records of the Kaiyuan and Tianbao Eras"
Hè Zhīzhāng
Hè Zhīzhāng, the Tang Dynasty Director of the Palace Library, was highly renowned.
He requested to retire and return to Wúzhōng in his old age,
and Emperor Xuánzong praised and esteemed him,
showing him exceptional favor in all matters.
As Zhīzhāng was about to leave,
he tearfully bid farewell.
The emperor asked what he desired,
and he said:
"Your subject has a son,
who has not yet been given a formal name.
I hope Your Majesty will bestow one upon him,
so that I may return home with the honor of my hometown."
The emperor said:
"The essence of the Way
lies in nothing more than trustworthiness.
'Fú' means trust.
To act with trust and think of compliance—
your son must be a trustworthy and compliant person.
It is fitting to name him 'Fú.'"
Zhīzhāng bowed twice and accepted the command.
Later, he said to others:
"How the emperor teases me!
I am truly a man of Wú.
'Fú' is 'claw' (zhǎo) with 'child' (zǐ) underneath—
is he not calling my son 'claw-child' (zhǎozǐ)?"
From "Records of the Kaiyuan and Tianbao Eras"
Wáng Wéi
Wáng Yú, a Tang Dynasty chancellor, enjoyed writing epitaphs for others.
Those who sent payment for his writing
mistakenly knocked on the door of Vice Director
(the original text had "chancellor" after "director,"
deleted according to the Ming manuscript)
Wáng Wéi.
Wéi said:
"The great writer is over there."
From "Miscellaneous Stories of the Lu Family"
Gān Qià
Gān Qià and Wáng Xiānkè of the Tang Dynasty were close friends.
They mocked each other based on their surnames.
Qià said:
"Wáng,
I reckon your surname should be Tián.
Because your face is like a scraped otter,
with the sides stripped away."
Xiānkè retorted:
"Gān,
I reckon your surname should be Dān.
Because your head doesn't bend,
so your feet turn upward."
From "Records of Making People Laugh"
Qiáo Lín
When Zhū Cǐ first rebelled during the Tang Dynasty,
Yuán Xiū, Yáo Lìngyán, and others
collected books and records,
stored grain in warehouses,
emulating Xiāo Hé's achievements.
Xiū later said to the false Vice Director of the Chancellery Jiǎng Liàn:
"If we assess our talents,
then I am Xiāo Hé,
and Yáo is Cáo Shēn."
Those who heard this
thought Xiū could not handle his official position.
Qiáo Lín had a fondness for jesting,
and said to his old colleagues:
"Lord Yuán is truly what you'd call a 'fire-pressed Marquis of Cuó.'"
From "New Accounts of the Great Tang"
Qìliè Tū
In the Tang capital, there was a monk
who was very clever and perceptive,
but suffered from a foot ailment.
Someone saw him on the road
and mocked him:
"The Dharma Master is from Yúnzhōng Commandery."
The monk said:
"I did not know you before,
why do you insult this poor monk as 'qìliè tū'?"
The person feigned ignorance and said:
"Yúnzhōng Commandery means the Dharma Master is lofty and distant,
how is that an insult?"
The monk said:
"Yúnzhōng Commandery means 'Heavenly Prefecture,'
which translates to 'stealing felt'—
that means 'fur thief.'
'Fur thief' translates to 'ink trough,'
beside which there is a curved iron,
translating to 'qìliè tū.'
Why go to such lengths to insult me?"
The previous person then felt ashamed and submitted.
From "Records of Making People Laugh"
Sòng Jì
In the Táng dynasty, Xǔ Mèngróng and Sòng Jì were friends from humble backgrounds.
When Xǔ became an examination official,
Sòng did not pass the exam.
After the results were posted,
Xǔ felt quite ashamed,
and repeatedly asked others to convey his apologies,
also sending his own students to visit him.
Sòng, having no other choice,
then went to see him.
Xǔ merely explained himself and admitted his fault,
then ordered wine, and after drinking freely,
said:
"Even so,
this year I selected ministers and chancellors for the state.
At that time, there was Yáo Sìqīng who passed the exam,
but died the very next day."
Sòng then rose to console Xǔ, saying:
"It is the nation's misfortune
that Minister Yáo has passed away."
Xǔ was greatly ashamed.
From "Lú Shì Zá Shuō".
The Deputy Clerk of Ānlíng
In the Táng dynasty, the people of Ānlíng were skilled at mockery.
Every county magistrate who arrived
was inevitably mocked with cryptic jokes.
There was one magistrate
who had not a single tooth in his mouth,
and often feared being mocked.
When he first arrived,
he said to the county clerks:
"I hear Ānlíng is very fond of ridicule;
you must not continue the old ways."
At his first session,
he adjudicated three cases.
A deputy clerk, holding the documents behind him, said:
"Your Honor writes very swiftly."
The man did not realize this was mockery,
but thought he was being praised for his skill,
and thus trusted him greatly.
After several months,
an enemy of the deputy clerk reported:
"The one who said 'Your Honor writes very swiftly'
was mocking Your Honor."
The magistrate asked:
"What does that mean?"
He replied:
"'Writes very swiftly'
means 'rushing ink',
'rushing ink' reverses to 'north gate',
'north gate' means 'lacking behind',
'lacking behind' reverses to 'mouth cavity',
this mocks having no teeth."
Only then did the magistrate understand,
and had the deputy clerk flogged before releasing him.
From "Qǐ Yán Lù".
Cuī Hù
Liú Yǔxī of the Táng dynasty said:
Cuī Hù did not pass the imperial examination,
and was angry at his examiner Miáo Dēng,
who was actually Cuī's maternal uncle three times removed.
So he privately wrote a mock judgment,
slandering his uncle, saying:
"On his back, he has the peculiarity of pig skin."
Someone asked:
"Why not remove it?
There must be a reason for it."
His judgment said:
"When the people of Cáo bared Zhòng'ěr's back,
his fused ribs were seen again.
When Xiànglǐ bared Miáo Dēng's back,
pig skin was revealed."
Earlier, when Miáo Dēng was a commandant in the eastern capital region,
Xiànglǐ Zào was the prefect.
He once wanted to cane him,
and when his back was bared,
there was a pig-
Míng manuscript note: 'pig' is written as 'zhì',
should be 'mole'
-with hairs several inches long.
Therefore, it was also said:
"In times of peace,
it lies dormant and useless;
in times of burrowing and feeding,
