the character 'shí' (feed) was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Míng manuscript
then it stirs and seeks."
All referring to its tail.
From "Jiā Huà Lù".
Lú Mài
Táng chancellor Lú Mài did not eat salt or vinegar.
His colleagues asked him:
"If you don't eat salt or vinegar,
how can you bear it?"
Lú smiled and replied:
"You eat salt and vinegar all day long,
how can you bear that?"
From "Guó Shǐ Bǔ".
Liǔ Zōngyuán
In the Táng dynasty, Liǔ Zōngyuán and Liú Yǔxī
passed the imperial examination in the same year.
They inscribed their names on the Cí'ēn Pagoda,
with Tán Yuánmào wielding the brush.
At the time, they did not want their names to be
'be' originally written as 'author',
corrected based on the Míng manuscript
too prominent,
saying:
"Those whose names are on the seam boards
mostly do not achieve high status,
or soon pass away."
Liǔ drafted the list,
secretly deliberating over it,
but from Zhāng Fù onward,
the names of Mǎ Zhēng and Dèng Wénzuǒ
were all placed on the boards.
The inscribed names all used their clan's prestige,
but for Xīn Nánróng,
no one knew his.
Yuánmào set down his brush and said:
"I ask Senior Xīn to state his clan's prestige."
Xīn happened to be elsewhere,
so Liǔ said:
"He is from the Eastern Sea."
Yuánmào asked:
"How do you know?"
Liǔ replied:
"The Eastern Sea is vast,
there is nothing it does not contain."
Soon after, Xīn arrived,
and when asked about his clan's prestige,
he said:
"Bóhǎi."
Everyone laughed heartily.
The practice of inscribing names at Cí'ēn
began with Zhāng Jǔ,
who originally was idly wandering in the temple
and inscribed the names of his examination cohort.
People then followed it as a tradition.
From "Jiā Huà Lù".
Lù Chàng
In the Táng dynasty, Lù Chàng:
When Princess Yúnyáng married Commandant Liú,
court officials recommended him as an attendant.
The palace ladies, because Lù spoke the Wú dialect,
and he was quick-witted and agile,
for every jest made,
he responded fluently.
They also mocked him with poems,
and Lù replied in kind.
The entire palace was delighted.
There were over ten pieces in total.
The palace ladies all recited them.
As an exception,
he was specially bestowed ten bolts of palace brocade,
a Léngqié vase and spittoon,
as rewards.
A palace lady's poem said:
"Twelve-story towers lean against the azure sky,
phoenixes stand opposite each other by the paulownia tree.
Shuāngchéng runs to report to the gate guards:
Do not let Wú songs enter the Hàn palace."
Some say it was composed by the palace scholars Sòng Ruòlán and Ruòzhāo sisters.
Lù replied:
"A powdered-face immortal lad chosen for the sacred court,
by chance meets the Qín maiden learning to play the flute.
He must make the kingfisher hear the Queen Mother,
but cannot bear the crows cawing at the Magpie Bridge."
From "Yún Xī Yǒu Yì".
Píng Zēng
Táng Píngzēng, relying on his talent, was arrogant and conceited,
often violating taboos and prohibitions.
When Deputy Chief Xiè Píng was appointed to govern Zhèxī,
Píngzēng went to pay his respects,
but the reception was somewhat cold.
So he left a poem to satirize the situation, saying:
"Climbing mountains and sailing seas, how rugged the journey,
I came to pay respects to Minister Xiè in Jīnlíng.
When your beard and hair bristle, one hastens before your sword and halberd;
where your robes and crown are solemn, one bows to the ice-pure vessel.
I truly know these two scrolls are not pearls or jade,
deeply ashamed of the three bolts of silk to aid my travels.
Today, the wind on the Chǔ River is just right,
no need to turn my head to gaze toward Jùwú."
Upon hearing this, Xiè
sent an official to chase after him and bring him back,
detaining him for several days.
Píngzēng then presented the poem "Tethering the White Horse," which said:
"The white horse's flowing mane like a roll of silk,
today tethered, finding it hard to proceed.
Released in the snow, its tracks vanish in vain;
led under the moon, only the saddle is seen.
Facing north, its long neigh reaches beyond the heavens;
against the wind, the slanting bridle brings chill to the ears.
Knowing its own hair and bones are still extraordinary,
it further invites Sūnyáng to examine carefully."
Xiè, upon reading the poem, said:
"If we do not tether the traveling carriage,
how can we observe its hair and bones?"
He then treated Píngzēng with exceptional courtesy.
Later, while traveling in Shǔ,
he paid respects to Junior Mentor Lǐ Gùyán.
At that time, the staff officers were all famous scholars,
and Píngzēng often engaged in discussions with the various guests,
laughing and talking all day long,
attending at Lǐ's side.
He acted lightly and without fear,
and then presented the "Rhapsody on Snowy Mountains," stating:
"Though the snowy mountains have this pure white appearance,
with layered peaks and clustered summits,
cool and clear in summer,
yet without lush grasses and trees,
they are plucked by people."
This was because Lǐ rarely composed literary works,
focusing instead on specialized classics.
Lǐ read the rhapsody
and ordered him expelled.
Not more than ten days later,
Píngzēng presented the "Rhapsody on the Pufferfish,"
saying, "This fish, upon touching something, becomes angry,
turns over and rides the waves,
only to be caught by kites and hawks—
what can the bream and chub do about it?"
Lǐ read the rhapsody and laughed, saying:
"Even the wild simplicity of Zhào Yuánshū in the past,
or the wit and quickness of Yuán Yànbó,
could not surpass this."
Yet he admired Píngzēng's literary talent.
Among those presenting their writings, none surpassed Píngzēng,
and though he might offend,
he was not deeply punished.
He also composed the "Rhapsody on Tóng Pass,"
satirizing the central court,
"This pass leans against Tàihuà,
overlooking the Yellow River.
Though those who come and go are the same,
their sighs differ."
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì."
Monk Língchè
In the Táng dynasty, the military governor of Jiāngxī, Wéi Dān,
and the Dōnglín monk Língchè
shared a carefree friendship,
exchanging poems and matching verses,
four or five times a month.
The preface states:
"Recently, Chègōng sent me the 'Seven Odes of Kuānglú,'
and upon reciting them,
I found them exceptionally beautiful in the literary garden.
Namely, Lotus Flower Peak, Stone Mirror, Tiger-Spring, Clever Water, White Deer Cave, Iron Rainbow Bridge, and King Kāng's Temple
are the seven odes.
These seven odes
(the character 'ode' was originally missing;
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy)
make me even more eager to return.
Moreover, during fragrant seasons with excellent companions on outings,
with two or three Daoist friends,
we must climb the thousand-ren peaks
to view the waters of the Nine Rivers.
(The character 'water' was originally missing;
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy.)
At that time,
we drift away freely,
not hoping for a glance from Jīngkǒu;
we wander in silence,
not needing a farewell at the east gate.
Heaven and earth become a single morning,
all things subject to molding.
The two forests, majestic and grand,
with secluded pine paths,
then why must we set foot in crimson clouds
or let our hearts race to ancient times?
Occasionally, I composed a quatrain on 'Longing for Return,'
to send to the venerable monk,
hoping my Dharma friend will first grasp its profound meaning."
The poem says:
"Official duties in chaos leave no free days,
this floating life drifts softly like clouds.
Already planning for Píngzǐ's retirement,
before the Five Elders' Cliff, it shall surely be heard."
Chè replied:
"Aged and idle, with no external affairs,
hempen robes and grass seats also shelter the body.
Meeting, all speak of resigning from office,
yet beneath the woods, has one ever been seen?"
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì."
Sū Yún
In the Lǐngbiǎo region, many act as temporary officials,
and the lanes and alleys regard them as commissioners,
yet there are many who are poor and travel on foot.
During the Yuánhé era,
jìnshì Sū Yún lingered in the southern regions,
and once wrote a poem:
"Within the walls, many banyan trees,
on the streets, plenty of commissioners."
Lǐ Huán
In the Táng dynasty, Lǐ Huán governed Jìnzhōu.
His cousin Wǔ Gōng had an absurd and delusional nature.
He also claimed to love the Dào,
and collected ancient objects.
On the occasion of Huán's birthday,
having no gift to offer,
he brought an old black robe in a box to Huán,
saying:
"This was worn by Commandant Lǐ when he recaptured the capital.
I hope your achievements, Minister,
will resemble those of Xīpíng."
Huán thanked him.
Later, hearing it was Gōng's birthday,
Huán brought a tattered and worn hat in a box as a gift to Gōng, saying:
"Knowing my elder brother deeply admires lofty transcendents,
I obtained the hat that Hóngyá Xiānshēng wore when he first attained immortality.
I hope my brother attains the Dào like Hóngyá."
The guests and staff all laughed heartily.
From "Yīnhuà Lù."
Wáng Fán
In the Táng dynasty, Wáng Fán
was appointed Right Assistant from the post of Governor of Hénán.
As soon as the appointment document arrived,
Vice Governor Hóu Jì held a banquet
and invited him by letter.
Wáng wrote a response on the letter:
"Though the new appointment is heard,
the old title still remains.
To hastily issue an invitation
is fit for the 'Forest of Laughs.'"
In the central capital
("Yùquánzǐ" records the central capital as "Luòzhōng")
this became a subject of ridicule.
According to precedent:
the Vice Governor and the Governor
have separate protocols for social gatherings and banquets;
even after a new appointment,
one must await the official decree to cease duties.
From "Yīnhuà Lù."
Wéi Chán
Assistant Wéi Chán arrived at Chánglè Station,
saw the inscribed name of Attendant Lǐ Yáng,
and quickly wrote beside it:
"Wèi River and Qín Mountains shine bright before the eyes,
why does Xīrén lack poetic feeling?
Only because he learned from Yú Jī's husband—
in writing, he can barely remember names."
From "Zhíyán."
Fēng Bàoyī
In the Táng dynasty, Fēng Bàoyī served as the Sheriff of Yuèyáng.
A guest visited him,
who was short in stature,
and also suffered from eye problems and a stuffy nose.
Bàoyī used phrases from the "Thousand Character Classic" to mock him.
The poem said:
"Face like 'Heaven and Earth Dark,'
nose has 'Wild Goose Gate Purple,'
since lacking 'Left Reaching Receive,'
why trouble 'Do Not Talk That'?"
From "Qǐyán Lù."
Cuī Yá
Cuī Yá of the Táng dynasty was
a wild scholar from Wú and Chǔ.
He was equally famous as Zhāng Hù.
Whenever he inscribed poems in brothels,
they would all be recited on the streets.
If he praised someone, carriages and horses would follow in succession;
if he slandered someone, cups and plates would be thrown into disarray.
He once mocked a courtesan, saying:
"Though she has obtained sapanwood,
she still covets tortoiseshell.
After carrying the pregnancy for ten months,
she gives birth to a Kūnlún child."
Also:
"A cloth robe, a padded jacket, and a felt burned by fire,
a paper-patched konghou with hemp-repaired strings.
Add a pair of leather clogs,
clattering and clacking as she steps out the door."
He also mocked Lǐ Duānduān:
"At dusk, silent, not knowing where to go,
her nose like a chimney, her ears like tripods.
Alone, she inserts an ivory comb into her hair,
like the newborn moon over Mount Kūnlún."
After Duānduān received the poem,
her heart was as troubled as if she were ill.
Returning from drinking at the government office,
she saw the two men from afar,
walking in clogs.
She then bowed repeatedly by the roadside,
trembling with fear, saying:
"Duānduān only awaits the Third and Sixth Gentlemen,
I beg for your mercy."
He then composed another quatrain to embellish her:
"Finding a yellow steed saddled with embroidered trappings,
I fetch Duānduān from Shànhé Ward.
In Yángzhōu recently, all is awry,
but one white peony can still walk."
After this, wealthy and powerful men
once again flocked to her door.
Someone teased her, saying:
"Lady of the Lǐ family,
just emerged from the ink pond,
now ascends the snowy peak.
Why is it that in one day, black and white are uneven?"
The pleasure quarters regarded her as a courtesan,
and none were unafraid of his mockery and ridicule.
Hù and Yá stayed in Wéiyáng for a long time.
The world was peaceful and clear,
their verses were free and unrestrained,
the noble and powerful respected and feared them,
their influence spread like the wind.
Lǐ Xuāngǔ
At a banquet in Lǐ Prefecture during the Táng dynasty,
the wine overseer, Cuī Yúnniáng, was thin and emaciated in appearance.
Whenever she joked and teased,
she would impose penalties on all the guests,
and she also relied on her singing voice,
considering herself as marvelous as the singers of Yǐng.
Lǐ Xuāngǔ composed a poem at the banquet,
which immediately silenced her.
The poem said:
"What is the most sorrowful thing?
Yúnniáng's head is truly strange.
Her thin fists hastily issue penalties,
her long mouth sings songs slowly.
One only sees her shoulders encroaching upon her temples,
and worries that her bones will pierce her skin.
There's no need to stand before the door,
for on her head is Zhōng Kuí."
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì."
Dù Mù
When Dù Mù of the Táng dynasty left his post in Xuān Prefecture,
he passed through Shǎn,
where there was a wine overseer
who was fat and stout but timid in speech.
Dù Mù presented her with a poem:
"Pángǔ in ancient times had a distant descendant,
who still today flaunts the family's prestige.
A cart of white soil to plaster the neck,
ten red banners to patch the torn trousers.
At Wěiguān Temple, traces of her passing are met,
before Mount Huàyuè, palm prints are seen.
There's no need to weep, worrying about being hard to marry off,
wait until I send a letter to ask Yuè
(Míng manuscript: 'ask Yuè' reads 'report to Lè.')
Yúnxī Yǒuyì is the same.
the gods."
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì."
Lù Yánmèng
Lù Yánmèng of the Táng dynasty
composed a poem at a banquet in Guì Prefecture, presenting it to a Hú girl:
"She claims her charm is beyond reach,
but how can one bear her furrowed brow and haggard face?
Her eyes are deeper than the Xiāng River's waters,
her nostrils higher than Mount Huàyuè.
Her dancing posture surely cannot be held in the palm,
her singing voice likely does not linger around the beams.
Since Mèng Yáng died nearly a thousand years ago,
there are still beauties seeking to come and go."
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì."
Lǐ Yuǎn
The Táng dynasty jìnshì Cáo Táng's "Poems on Roaming Immortals"
were ethereal in talent and sentiment.
Lǐ Yuǎn, the prefect of Yuèyáng, often recited his poems and thought of the man.
One day,
when Cáo went to visit him,
Lǐ hurriedly welcomed him, even putting his shoes on backwards.
Cáo was imposing and robust in appearance,
and Lǐ teased him, saying:
"Before, I had not seen your distinguished appearance,
and thought you could ride phoenixes and cranes.
Now that I have met you,
who would have thought even a strong water buffalo might not bear your weight!"
People of the time laughed upon hearing this.
The world said that Hún's poems and Yuǎn's rhapsodies
were better left unwritten.
This was not to say they lacked literary talent,
but to scorn their lack of moral instruction.
From "Běimèng Suǒyán."
Lǐ Déyù
Lǐ Déyù, Duke Wèi of the Táng dynasty,
served as chancellor during Emperor Wǔzōng's reign,
wielding power that overshadowed the court and the common people.
After he was convicted and exiled,
someone composed a poem about him:
"Artemisia and thorns
(Original text: 'thorns' was written as 'là,'
corrected according to the Míng manuscript) deeply guard the gates of Wèi,
for nine years here, he stole the universe.
Two lines of secret memorials toppled the realm,
one night of conspiracy reached the sovereign.
His gaze made officials drop their chopsticks,
his aura devoured colleagues, chilling their warmth.
Who at that time received imperial favor?
Behind him, ripples reached the village of ghosts."
Also:
"His power aspired to touch the clouds, his might struck heaven,
belittling all under heaven, his strength pushed mountains aside.
For three years, some clung to the phoenix's tail,
in one day, the dragon's beard had no path to climb.
Painted pavilions unopened, the beams' swallows depart,
vermilion gates unswept, fledgling crows return.
A thousand cliffs and ten thousand valleys should feel sorrow,
the flowing water slants and spills out of Wǔ Pass."
From "Lúshì Záshuō."
Xuē Zhāowěi
Xuē Bǎoxùn of the Táng dynasty,
during the Dàzhōng reign,
was especially frivolous and impudent.
Because of this, he insulted and bullied his uncles,
and thus was demoted from Assistant Secretary of the Bureau of Operations to Military Administrator of Lǐ Prefecture.
His son, Zhāowěi,
quite resembled his father's style.
He once served as Vice Director of the Bureau of Sacrifices.
At that time, Lǐ Xì served as Vice Director of the Bureau of Rites,
and Wáng Ráo served as Vice Director of the Bureau of Receptions.
After the New Year's Day court assembly disbanded,
Zhāowěi loudly chanted:
"To the left, the golden crow; to the right, the jade rabbit—
the Son of Heaven's banners and flags."
Ráo hastily asked for the next line,
and he replied without hesitation:
"Above, Lǐ Xì; below, Wáng Ráo—
the ranks of petty men."
Those who heard it could not help but laugh heartily.
During the Tiānfù era,
he was repeatedly demoted from a Censorate position to Military Administrator of Dēng Prefecture.
The Secretariat Drafter Yán Ráo drafted the edict,
which roughly stated:
"Trampling over his uncles,
his descendant inherits his viciousness."
From "Zhíyán."
Cuī Shènyóu
During the Dàzhōng to Xiántōng reigns of the Táng dynasty,
Bái Mǐnzhōng became chancellor.
Subsequently, Bì Xián, Cáo Què, and Luó Shào,
who held provisional concurrent chancellorships,
also ascended to the highest ministerial positions.
Chancellor Cuī Shènyóu remarked:
"It is time to retire.
Recently, the Secretariat
has been filled entirely with foreigners."
This was because he considered the surnames Bì, Bái, Cáo, and Luó to be of foreign origin.
When Jiǎng Shēn first rose to high office,
Lǐ Jǐngràng of Xīchuān, upon reading the official announcement,
sighed and said:
"I cannot serve under this man."
He promptly feigned illness and left his post.
There is a poem that says:
"Chéngdū's hundred thousand households,
cast aside like a goose feather."
This expresses the same sentiment as Cuī Shènyóu's criticism.
When Grand Master Zhào Chóng passed away,
Vice-Minister Wú Xióng sighed:
"I had expected him to achieve the status of Bì and Bái,
how could he have fallen so short of expectations!"
He lamented
the character 'lamented' was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Xǔ edition
that Zhào did not attain the chancellorship,
and was also criticizing the situation of his time.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Zhèng Xūn
In the Táng dynasty, Yán Biāo,
during the Xiántōng reign,
was placed first in the imperial examinations by Zhèng Xūn.
Previously, there had been a rebellion by the Xú bandits.
Zhèng Xūn, wishing to encourage heroic deeds,
believed Yán Biāo to be a descendant of Duke Lǔ (Yán Zhēnqīng),
and therefore ranked him as the top candidate.
Later, he inquired about Yán's ancestral temple.
Yán replied:
"I am of humble origins,
and have no ancestral temple in the capital."
Only then did Zhèng Xūn realize his mistake,
and he remained silent for a long time.
An anonymous person at the time mocked:
"The examiner's head is utterly muddled,
mistaking Yán Biāo for Duke Lǔ."
From "Zhí Yán".
Táng Wǔjīng
During the Xiántōng reign of the Táng dynasty,
a scholar from Jīngzhōu was known as "Táng Wǔjīng".
He was profoundly learned and erudite,
truly a great Confucian scholar.
His ideals were lofty,
and he was admired as a teacher by many.
He gathered five hundred disciples,
supporting himself with their tuition fees.
He lived leisurely throughout his years,
embodying the style of Xīhé and Jǐnán's ancient masters,
and many officials associated with him.
He often said to people:
"Unworthy descendants undergo three transformations:
The first transformation is into locusts,
meaning they sell their estates to eat.
The second transformation is into bookworms,
meaning they sell their books to eat.
The third transformation is into tigers,
meaning they sell their slaves and maidservants to eat."
Such people who live off these three resources—
in which era are they absent?
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
The Guest at Qīnglóng Temple
Towards the end of the Qiánfú reign of the Táng dynasty,
a guest was lodging at the Kāiyuán Temple in Guǎnglíng.
During a literary gathering, he recounted:
"Some time ago, while staying at the Qīnglóng Temple in the capital,
a visitor once called upon the monk in charge of affairs.
Due to the monk's haste,
he had no time to entertain him.
The visitor came again the next day,
but encountered important court officials.
When he returned later,
he was again hindered by other matters.
Greatly angered,
he wrote on the temple gate before leaving:
'The dragon in the niche has gone to the eastern sea,
The sun and moon hide as the west slopes.
Jìngwén is not here today,
Broken stones enter the flowing sand.'"
The monks could not decipher it.
The character 'decipher' was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Míng manuscript copy.
A novice monk understood it quite well.
When everyone asked him the reason,
he said:
"'The dragon in the niche has gone'—
leaves the character 'hé' (合).
'The sun and moon hide'—
leaves the character 'sì' (寺).
'Jìngwén is not here'—
leaves the character 'gǒu' (苟).
'Broken stones enter the sand'—
leaves the character 'zú' (卒).
These are disrespectful words,
insulting us."
The monks, suddenly realizing, pursued and searched for the visitor,
but he had vanished without a trace.
The guest inquired about the novice monk,
and it turned out he was the供奉 Yún Hào from Emperor Yìzōng's reign.
From "Guì Yuàn Cóng Tán".
Luó Yǐn
In the Táng dynasty, Péi Jūn married the daughter of Xiāo Gòu.
Not long after the betrothal,
he passed the imperial examinations as a Jìnshì.
Luó Yǐn wrote a quatrain satirizing him,
which roughly said:
"Looking closely, the moon's disk still has intent,
I believe the green cassia knows it is near Héng'é."
From "Zhí Yán".
Cuī Dàn
In the Táng dynasty, Cuī Dàn
set an examination question: "Rhapsody on the Most Benevolent Attacking the Most Unbenevolent".
At that time, Huáng Cháo's rebellion was at its peak.
Consequently, an anonymous person mocked:
"What grievance does the examiner hold against our emperor,
that he compares Huáng Cháo to King Wǔ?"
From "Zhí Yán".
Pí Rìxiū
In the Táng dynasty, Pí Rìxiū once called upon Guī Rénshào,
but went several times without being received.
Pí, feeling resentful,
gave voice to his thoughts
and composed a poem on the tortoise:
"Your hard bones and misshapen form, who knows for how many autumns?
A corpse in the end is not elegant.
After death, your stubborn shell will be drilled through everywhere,
all because in life you never stuck your head out."
At that time, Rénshào also had sons, Yì and Xì,
who were in the same examination hall as Pí Rìxiū,
and heard of this immediately.
Waiting for Pí's next visit,
they wrote a poem beneath the character 'Pí' (皮) on his name card
and presented it to him:
"Eight sharp pieces cut to make a ball,
Exploded in fire, kneaded in water.
If a pack of idle air remains within,
It will invite kicks and punches endlessly."
People of the time felt that while Pí Rìxiū was frivolous and mocking,
Guī Rénshào was also shallow and impetuous.
From "The Collected Works of Pí Rìxiū".
Xuē Néng
In the Táng dynasty, Zhào Lín was petty and ugly in appearance and bearing.
After achieving fame, he took a wife,
and Xuē Néng served as the groomsman.
He then composed poems to mock and tease him,
roughly saying:
"Patrolling the pass, he often leans by the dice game board,
Gazing at the moon, he still climbs the Qǐqiǎo tower.
First, don't let the beauty be too proud,
For along a man's girdle she'll reach his head."
Another said:
"Not knowing he was originally within the saddle frame,
He thought he was carrying an empty hat back on the mat."
And another:
"Standing upright on the heated brick bed,
He serves as his lady's dressing mirror stand."
From "Shū Qíng Shī".
Zhōu Yǐ
In the Táng dynasty, the retired scholar Zhōu Yǐ was a great Confucian of profound learning.
He happened to fail the imperial examinations,
and traveled to Zhèxī.
While joyfully drinking with colleagues,
he was ignorant of the drinking game rules,
and everyone at the banquet teased him.
A guest composed a poem for him:
"For ten years you labored, turning tail at the dragon's ford,
Your reputation then vied with the moon's height.
Only the rouge-adorned ones, with dancing hands turned back,
Seem to wield twin blades against the gibbons."
Zhōu replied:
"For ten years in the literary arena, dare I fear the toil?
In Sòng's capital, the returning quail fled the high wind.
Today I gladly let the flowering branches laugh,
Let them say before the winecup I love to bind the gibbon."
From "Shū Qíng Shī".
Rén Gǔ
Táng Rèn Gǔ was well-versed in the Confucian classics,
and lived in Huáigǔ.
He awaited the imperial summons, but the carriage with rushes did not arrive.
So he entered the capital to seek out his close friends.
A court official playfully presented him with a poem, saying:
"The clouds and forests must wonder why the crane missive is late;
since entering the capital, he has come to inquire about matters.
From now on, when he sees mountains, he must close his eyes,
for the mountains have deceived him for far too long."
Later, he rose to the position of Bǔgǔn.
From "Yōuxián Gǔchuī."
Wáng Huī
In the Guǎngmíng year of the Táng dynasty,
Xuē Néng lost control of Xǔchāng due to military failure,
and the general Zhōu Jí replaced him.
The following year,
the chancellor Wáng Huī passed through Xǔ,
and said to Jí:
"I once heard that in your domain there was a commander named Zhōu Zhuàngzi;
could it be you, Sikōng?
How did you come by this title?"
Jí blushed with shame for a long time,
and replied:
"Jí rose from the ranks of foot soldiers,
but truly harbored great ambition.
Whenever there was a campaign,
I never shied from the edge of the blade,
charging left and right,
and repeatedly achieved minor merits,
which is why the army gave me this nickname."
Wáng laughed,
and said to Jí again:
"Back then, when you fell into the Huó River,
was it because you couldn't 'zhuàng' (collide) with it?"
Jí had once led the troops of Xǔ
to campaign against Xúfāng,
but was defeated by the rebels,
and fell into the Huó River.
Someone rescued him, and he barely escaped.
Hence these words.
From "Sānshuǐ Xiǎodú."
Shāndōng Rén
A man from Shāndōng came to the capital.
His host often cooked vegetables for him,
but he found none of them delicious.
(The original text had "gēng" (broth),
changed according to the Ming manuscript.)
He often thought of elm leaves,
and cooked them himself.
The host then teased him, saying:
"I heard that Shāndōng people cook cart hub juice to eat,
because it has the flavor of elm."
He replied:
"I heard that people in the capital cook donkey axles to eat;
is that true or false?"
The host asked:
"What do you mean by that?"
He said:
"Because it has the flavor of alfalfa."
The host was greatly ashamed.
From "Qǐyán Lù."
Zhāng Dēng
In the Táng dynasty, Zhāng Dēng from Nányáng passed the imperial examination.
He was thin and gaunt in appearance,
and arrogant in temperament, looking down on others.
Péi Shū was his teacher and friend.
When Shū served as Sīxūn Yuánwài,
he gathered a group of officials to submit their writings.
Shū had just criticized their flaws and errors.
Dēng, who had come to the city from the Jiānglíng salt and iron office for accounting,
went straight into the Sīxūn hall,
and said with a cold laugh:
"Péi Thirty-Six,
there is something truly laughable."
Shū then asked Dēng the reason for the laughter.
Dēng said:
"I laugh at you, the donkey tooth broker,
haggling over horse prices."
This became a joke.
From "Gānzǎizi."
Zhū Zé
In the Táng dynasty, Wáng Xuān wrote poetry from a young age,
and was quite talented.
Traveling on the West Xiǎo River,
he moored his boat at Zhùluó Chuān,
and inscribed on the Xīshī Stone:
"On the ridge, a thousand peaks stand elegant;
by the river, fine grass greets the spring.
Today I meet the washing stone,
but see no washerwoman."
Soon, he saw a woman,
shaking her jade pendants,
leaning on a stone bamboo shoot,
and lingering as she thanked him:
"I returned from the Wú palace to the Yuè kingdom,
in plain clothes, unrecognized for a thousand years.
Back then, my heart was firmer than metal or stone;
today, with you, it cannot remain firm."
After their joyful encounter,
there were also words of regret at parting.
Later, Guō Níngsù from Xiāoshān,
hearing of Wáng Xuān's encounter,
would pass by Huànshā Xī every day,
chanting long into the evening,
and repeatedly inscribing poems on the stone.
But it was silent, with no one there,
so he returned dejected.
The jìnshì Zhū Zé mocked him,
and those who heard it all laughed scornfully.
Níngsù felt ashamed inwardly,
and never made such a journey again.
The poem says:
"The peach and plum blossoms of spring are naturally silent,
but are tormented by the sunset clamor of birds and sparrows.
May I ask, how does the eastern neighbor imitating Xīzǐ
compare to Guō Sù imitating
(The original text had "Níngsù,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript.)
Wáng Xuān?"
From "Yúnxī Yǒuyì."
Xú Yànruò
During the Qiánníng era of the Táng dynasty,
Chéng Ruì of Jīngnán had once been a monk,
and usurped control of Zhǔgōng.
Soon after, he submitted to the imperial court.
In his later years,
he often engaged in sophistry.
Initially, because Lǐ and Lǎng were under his jurisdiction,
but were occupied by the local strongman Léi Mǎn,
he petitioned to have them transferred.
The chancellor Xú Yànruò was in the Zhōngshū Province,
and did not handle the matter,
which caused Ruì to bear a grudge.
When Yànruò went out to govern Fānyú,
he passed through Zhǔgōng.
Although Ruì received him,
he was often discontented.
After the meal,
they moved to another seat,
and sophistry arose sharply.
Xú said:
"Your Excellency holds a high position and governs a region,
comparing yourself to Huán and Wén.
Léi Mǎn
is merely a fire-starting grass bandit in a remote prefecture.
Your Excellency cannot send troops against him,
yet you resent the court?"
Chéng blushed and yielded.
Xú was elegant and highly cultured,
and spoke tirelessly.
Although Chéng greatly respected and feared him,
he still joked about the yellow thatch miasma beyond the mountains,
which causes hair loss in sufferers,
saying:
"The yellow thatch miasma—
I hope Your Excellency takes care."
Xú said:
"The yellow thatch miasma of the South Sea
does not kill Monk Chéng."
This mocked Chéng for having once been a monk.
Chéng felt ashamed and humiliated for the rest of the banquet.
From "Běimèng Suǒyán."
Féng Juān,
a renowned scholar of the old Táng dynasty,
possessed profound talent and deep learning.
He passed the imperial examinations and earned the jìnshì degree,
and his career experience was already distinguished.
When the Táng emperor traveled to Liáng and Yáng,
Juān accompanied the imperial carriage.
Upon reaching Hànzhōng,
he was appointed by imperial decree as the prefect of Méi Prefecture.
While traveling to assume his post,
he was blocked by troops in Shǔ,
and Wáng shì forcibly detained him in his military headquarters.
His nature was upright and unyielding,
and he relied on his talent to look down upon others,
which made him very incompatible with the ruler of the false Shǔ state.
Knowing that Wáng shì harbored rebellious ambitions,
he consistently refused to comply.
If someone presented him with silk fabrics,
he would certainly lock them in a chest,
and inscribe upon it the words "bandit goods."
Although the ruler of Shǔ was aware of this,
he admired Juān's literary and artistic talents,
and often forcibly tolerated him.
At times when it became intolerable,
he would repeatedly bow and escort him out of the compound.
Even when intending to have him beaten to death,
Juān showed not the slightest trace of fear.
Later, when the Later Liáng dynasty sent an envoy to deliver a letter to Shǔ,
the ruler ordered his various aides, such as Wéi Zhuāng and others,
to draft a reply and present it to him,
but none were satisfactory.
His attendants said:
"Why not order the former Investigating Judge to do it?"
The ruler of Shǔ again showed an ashamed expression.
As the Liáng envoy was about to return with a reply,
having no alternative,
he then requested Juān to resume his duties.
Juān promptly composed a reply,
writing it out in a single stroke,
which greatly met the ruler's wishes.
Thereupon, their previous rapport was restored.
Consequently, he summoned all the officials of the various bureaus for a joint banquet.
During the drinking,
Juān straightened his robes and said:
"I happen to recall a story,
and wish to tell it to Your Majesty.
May I?"
The ruler permitted it.
He said:
"When I, Juān, was young,
I often traveled to visit various feudal lords.
Each time I journeyed,
I would certainly carry a great many books and writings,
loaded on a donkey,
and also loaded on a horse.
At the start of the journey,
the donkey brayed, jumped, and pranced,
vying with the horse for the road and going ahead,
and nothing could control it.
After traveling for half a day,
we reached a slope.
Exhausted and footsore,
its entire body streaming with sweat,
it turned its head to look at the horse and said:
'Brother Horse, Brother Horse,
I can go no further.
Could you carry the books for your younger brother?'
Brother Horse agreed,
and so they were all placed on the horse.
The horse then turned its head and said to the donkey:
'Donkey brother,
I thought you had so many tricks,
but in the end, you still have to load them onto your elder brother?'"
The ruler of Shǔ laughed heartily.
All his colleagues in the headquarters suffered such humiliation and bullying.
When the false Shǔ state was established,
he ultimately refused to serve as prime minister.
From "Wáng shì jiàn wén lù" (Wáng shì's Record of Things Seen and Heard).
Zhāng Jùn's Actor
Táng dynasty chancellor Zhāng Jùn
once viewed peonies with court officials at Wànshòu Temple while drinking.
Suddenly rain began to fall,
and by dusk it had not ceased,
yet the assembled gentlemen, deeply intoxicated, had not ended their revelry.
The attending actors were all from the First Troupe of the Imperial Presence,
and, relying on imperial favor, they acted wildly and recklessly,
without any fear or restraint.
Among them was one named Zhāng Yǐn,
who suddenly leaped out,
raised his voice, and recited a verse:
"Your position, contrary to harmonizing, has caused injury and ruin;
the four walls of enclosure are unbearable to behold.
Just when it is the season of flowers, one ought to shed tears—
why must the Chancellor still pursue pleasure?"
Having finished speaking, he then departed.
The entire gathering was stunned;
they looked at each other, their faces pale,
and dispersed all at once.
Zhāng could only feel shame and resentment.
From "Nán Chǔ xīn wén" (News from Southern Chǔ).
Fēng Shùnqīng
Zhū Liáng's Fèng Shùnqīng possessed exceptional literary talent,
excelling in both ability and background,
and he relied on his intelligence and brilliance.
He was often frivolous and disrespectful.
Emperor Liáng Zǔ sent him on a diplomatic mission to Shǔ.
At that time, Qí and Liáng were at odds,
and the mountain passes were blocked,
so he traveled upstream along the Hàn River.
His route passed through Quán
(Míng manuscript note: Quán is written as Jīn,
same below.)
Prefecture,
where a local man, Quán Zōngcháo
(Míng manuscript note: Cháo is written as Lǎng,
same below.)
served as military governor.
When Fèng arrived at the prefecture,
Zōngcháo hosted a banquet at the official office.
Fèng had always looked down upon this mountainous region,
often displaying arrogance and disdain,
and none of the people of Quán dared not to serve him respectfully.
When it came time to raise the cup and request a tune,
he said:
"Play 'Mài Xiù Liǎng Qí'."
The musicians looked at each other in astonishment:
"We have never heard of it,
so let us substitute another tune of a similar kind."
Fèng shook his head and said:
"No."
He then
(Originally written as 'wén',
corrected according to the Míng manuscript)
said:
"'Mài Xiù Liǎng Qí'."
Again, they had no way to proceed.
The host felt humiliated and grew resentful,
caning the leader of the musicians.
After setting down the cup for a while,
hesitating,
with the cup in hand again,
he once more said:
"'Mài Xiù Liǎng Qí'."
Since they could not obtain it,
he called the musicians forward and said:
"Although you are mountain folk,
you should also have heard
(Originally written as 'mén',
corrected according to the Míng manuscript)
the music of the great court, right?"
The people of Quán felt deeply ashamed.
Next, he reached Hànzhōng.
The musicians there had already learned of the incident in Quán Prefecture,
and were worried.
During the drinking gathering,
he again said:
"'Mài Xiù Liǎng Qí',"
just like at the banquet in Quán,
but after three calls, they still could not respond.
A musician leader named Wáng Xīn stepped forward and said:
"I humbly request that the Vice Minister sing it once."
Before Fèng had finished singing it,
it was already under the fingers of the musicians.
Because of this, he was greatly pleased,
and they played this tune,
not changing it for the rest of the banquet.
The musicians reported to the governor, saying:
"This is a newly composed piece from Dà Liáng,
and even Xī Shǔ has not yet heard it.
Please allow us to copy the score."
They urgently sent it into Shǔ,
fully describing the events that occurred in the two prefectures.
By the time Fèng arrived in Shǔ,
a banquet was arranged.
After the performance of the cān
(Originally written as 'sān',
corrected according to the Míng manuscript)
jūn act,
they played 'Mài Xiù Liǎng Qí' at length in front of the hall,
setting up tools for weeding wheat,
leading several dozen poor children,
dressed in ragged clothes,
carrying boys and holding girls,
holding baskets to gather wheat,
and singing in unison.
The lyrics were mournful and bitter,
expressing their poverty and hardship,
which was unpleasant for people to hear.
Fèng looked at it,
his face turning ashen,
and in the end, he had not a single word to say.
Ashamed and resentful, he returned,
and then reported back on his mission.
Traveling through the circuits of Liáng, Hàn, Ān, Kāng, and others,
he did not dare to mention the words "liǎng qí" again.
The people of Shǔ ridiculed him.
From "Wángshì Jiànwén"
Fèng Shùnqīng
Yáo Jì
Táng's Péi Tíngyù, styled Yōngyú,
during the Qiánníng era,
served in the inner court.
He was swift and agile in handling documents,
and was nicknamed "Downstream Boat".
When Liáng Tàizǔ accepted the abdication,
Yáo Jì served as an academician.
Once, during a leisurely moment,
the Emperor asked about Tíngyù's whereabouts.
Jì replied:
"In recent years, he was demoted,
and now I hear he is staying in Héngyǒng."
The Emperor said:
"I have heard that his talent and quick thinking are quite remarkable."
Jì replied:
"When he was in the Hànlín Academy,
he was nicknamed 'Downstream Boat'."
Tàizǔ immediately responded to Jì, saying:
"Then you, sir, are the 'Upstream Boat'."
Jì smiled faintly,
deeply showing a look of shame.
Commentators considered Jì to be an "Upstream Boat on a Rapid Shoal".
From "Zhíyán"
Lǐ Táixiá
In the pseudo-Shǔ state, Hán Zhāo served the Wáng family as Minister of Rites,
and Grand Academician of the Lìwén Hall.
He had a rudimentary grasp of literature,
and as for skills like the qín, chess, calligraphy, arithmetic, and archery,
he dabbled in them all,
thereby gaining favor from the later ruler.
Court official Lǐ Táixiá said:
"The skills of Minister Hán
are like the threads of a torn sock—
not a single one is long."
People of the time considered this apt.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán"
Brocade Weaver
A man named Lú of the Táng dynasty failed the imperial examinations,
and walked to the eastern gate of the capital.
That day, the wind was bitterly cold,
so he sought lodging at an inn.
Soon, another person arrived after him,
and warmed himself by the fire for a long time.
Suddenly, he recited a poem:
"My skill in weaving liáo líng is not yet great,
Haphazardly throwing the shuttle, missing the loom's beat.
Do not let masters of palace brocade see this,
Lest they laugh themselves to death at this writing."
He also said:
"Nowadays, literary matters are not valued,
Do not boast of literary skill to others."
Lú was astonished,
recalling that this was a poem by Bái Jūyì,
and so asked his name.
He replied:
"My surname is Lǐ,
and for generations, my family has woven damask and brocade.
Before the turmoil of war,
I belonged to the Eastern Capital's official brocade workshop as a skilled craftsman weaving palace brocade.
I offered my modest skills to this trade.
Everyone said:
'Nowadays, the patterns and styles
are different from before.'
It is not that craftsmen who seek to sell their skills through literary elegance
are not valued by the world,
so I am returning east."
From "Lúshì Záshuō"
Lǐ Zhǔbù
Táng Fāng Gān had the appearance of a rustic from the mountains and wilds,
and moreover had a harelip,
yet he was fond of insulting others.
There was a certain Registrar Lǐ of Lóngqiū,
though it is not known from where he hailed,
who happened to meet Gān at an acquaintance's place,
and they passed cups of wine to each other.
Lǐ of Lóngqiū had a cataract in his eye.
Gān altered the drinking game rule to mock him, saying:
"Gān alters the rule:
all
(The original text had 'wèi' here.
Changed according to Zhíyán, juan 13.)
people shall follow the host's
(The original text had 'yún' here.
Changed according to Zhíyán, juan 13.)
lead.
The village chief drinks wine with a pinch of salt
(The original text had 'jiān' here.
Changed according to Zhíyán, juan 13.),
the military officer drinks wine with a dab of sauce
(The original text had 'jiāng' here.
Changed according to Zhíyán, juan 13.),
I only see a fence placed outside the door,
but have never seen a barrier installed in the eye."
Lǐ of Lóngqiū replied:
"The village chief drinks wine with a pinch of salt,
(The original text had 'jiān' here.
Changed according to Zhíyán, juan 13.)
the servant drinks wine with a piece of pickled fish,
(Gān was fond of pickled fish.)
I only see a half-sleeve robe worn over a gown,
but have never seen lips split open like a crotch."
The whole company roared with laughter.
From "Zhíyán".
Chén the Leper
In Yíngqiū during the Táng, there was a wealthy commoner surnamed Chén,
who hoarded countless strings of cash,
but contracted leprosy.
Everyone called him Chén the Leper.
As for his own lifestyle,
it was certainly not frugal,
yet he absolutely detested the word 'leper'.
If his family members, wife, or children
accidentally uttered it,
they would inevitably incur his wrath,
sometimes even to the point of being beaten.
If guests remarked that his affliction seemed to be subsiding,
he would entertain them with wine and food,
treating them with exceptional lavishness.
If they said it was worsening,
he would glare at them with the whites of his eyes.
There was a wandering visitor
who coveted the potential benefits,
yet could not restrain his tongue,
so he paid Chén a visit.
Initially, he said:
"Your ailment, sir,
has recently diminished considerably."
Chén was also pleased,
ordering wine and food to receive him,
and subsequently gave him five strings of cash.
As the guest was about to leave,
Chén asked him again:
"Has my ailment truly receded?"
The guest said:
"This is also an ailment of addition and subtraction."
Chén asked:
"What do you mean?"
The guest said:
"The addition is the addition of pustules on your face,
the subtraction is the subtraction of your nostrils."
With a deep bow, he departed.
For several days, Chén was displeased.
Furthermore, every year in the fifth month,
on the occasion of his birthday,
he incurred considerable expense.
He would summon Buddhist monks and Daoist priests to hold a vegetarian feast.
Performers and all manner of entertainers were fully prepared.
After the feast,
the performers were given tens of thousands in cash.
At that time, there was a bald performer named Hé Àn,
who was not very sharp-witted.
Having left, he re-entered,
and said:
"I am grateful for your generous favor,
words cannot express my gratitude.
However, I happened to recall a couplet from the final lines of a poem by the short-statured Minister Lǐ,
which deeply accords with the host's magnificent virtue."
Chén said:
"Please recite it."
At that time, Chén was in the central hall,
seated within a green gauze curtain,
with attendants standing to his left and right,
several of them holding light bamboo-handled white whisks.
The performer said:
"The poem says:
'For thirty years, Chén the Leper,
only now gets a green gauze covering.'" [Chén] drove him away with loud curses.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà".
The Man Afflicted with Eyes and Nose
One man suffered from a squinting eye with a cataract,
another suffered from a blocked nose,
and they both used lines from the "Thousand Character Classic" to compose poems mocking each other.
The man with the blocked nose first mocked the squinting man:
"The eye can hold sun and moon full,
because old roots lie entangled."
The eye-afflicted man continued the next lines:
"Unable to distinguish orchids thus,
all due to the Yànmén purple."
From "Qǐyán Lù".
The Hunchback
There was a man afflicted with a bent, hunched back,
who always walked with his head lowered.
Someone beside him mocked him with a poem:
"A walking stick would be like 'nǎi',
holding a tablet would be like 'jí';
walking against wind and driving rain,
face dry, top of forehead wet;
sitting on the bed to put on clothes,
belly slack, back skin tight;
the city gate is so high,
yet you naturally crawl in on all fours."
From "Qǐyán Lù".
Old Woman Tián
In the capital city during the Táng,
there was a woman surnamed Tián,
who was old
and toothless.
She had taken a daughter of the Zhāng family from the same ward as a wife for her son.
On a festival day, the Zhāng family prepared a lavish feast,
invited Old Woman Tián to eat and drink,
and upon seeing her off,
the hostess said:
"I am ashamed,
there was nothing to chew on,
sending my kinswoman mother-in-law to come empty-mouthed,
and leave empty-mouthed."
This happened several times,
but Tián never caught on.
Returning home, she told her husband:
"Mother Zhāng called
(The original text had 'qù' here.
Changed according to the Ming manuscript copy.)
me over,
there was plenty of food and drink,
but upon parting she said:
'I am ashamed,
kinswoman mother-in-law came empty-mouthed,
and left empty-mouthed.'
I don't understand why?"
Her husband said:
"This is making fun of you for having no teeth.
Mother Zhāng has scarred pockmarks on her face,
the skin under her eyes is tight,
and it's extremely sticky and unsightly.
If she says this again,
you can reply:
'It's just that the area under your eyes is tight.'" Tián privately memorized this.
After a few days,
the Zhāng family again invited Tián.
As she was about to leave, [the hostess] again said:
"I am ashamed,
you came empty-mouthed,
and leave empty-mouthed."
Old Woman Tián then stared intently at the hostess's eyes,
but after a long while, she forgot "the area under your eyes is tight".
She said directly:
"It's that your eyelids are sticky and unsightly."
The whole family burst into laughter.
From "Qǐyán Lù".
The Wèi Man Drilling for Fire
A man of Wèi fell suddenly ill at night,
and ordered his servant to drill for fire.
That evening was dark and overcast.
He urged and pressed quite urgently.
The servant angrily said:
"Your demand is utterly unreasonable.
It's as dark as lacquer now,
why don't you hold a torch to light my way?
Then I could find the fire-drilling tools,
and afterwards it would be easy to get."
Kǒng Wénjǔ, hearing of this, said:
"One should demand things from others according to proper method."
From "Xiàolín".
The Qí Gentleman
The Book of Han, in its "Eulogy of Wáng Mǎng," states:
"Purple is not a true color; the croaking of frogs is not a true sound;
they are but leftover fragments and intercalary positions."
This means using the false to disrupt the true.
Yán Zhītuī once said:
"Recently, I was reading with someone,
and when we talked about Wáng Mǎng's appearance,
a talented scholar who prided himself on his knowledge of history,
and whose reputation was very high,
said:
'Wáng Mǎng not only had owl-like eyes and a tiger-like mouth,
but also had a purple complexion and a frog-like voice.'"
From The Family Instructions of Master Yán.
A Minister of the Northern Wei
During the Northern Wei dynasty,
while in the capital Luòyáng,
there was a high-ranking minister of great learning
who had newly acquired a pronunciation guide for the Records of the Grand Historian,
but it contained many errors.
When he saw the character for Zhuānxū written as Xǔ Lǜ,
he mistakenly read it as Xǔ Yuán.
This man then told the court officials:
"The long-standing erroneous pronunciation 'Zhuān Xù'
should actually be 'Zhuān Piāo.'"
Since this man was previously held in high esteem,
everyone readily believed and followed him.
After a year,
there came
there came originally written as "shǐ,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript
a great Confucian scholar,
who painstakingly investigated and debated,
and only then did they realize the mistake.
From The Family Instructions of Master Yán.
A Gentry Clan of Bìngzhōu
During the Northern Qí, there was a gentry clan in Bìngzhōu
who enjoyed writing ridiculous poems and rhapsodies,
looking down upon figures like Xíng Shào and Wèi Shōu.
Everyone mocked him.
If anyone falsely praised him,
he would surely slaughter an ox, brew wine, and invite them.
His wife was a discerning person,
and she tearfully advised him.
This man sighed and said:
"My talent is not tolerated even by my wife
"tolerated" originally followed by the character "yǔ,"
deleted according to the Ming manuscript
let alone
"let alone" originally written as "xiōng,"
changed according to the Ming manuscript
by passersby."
He remained unaware until his death.
From The Family Instructions of Master Yán.
Gāo Áocáo
Gāo Áocáo once wrote three "Miscellaneous Poems," which said:
"Grave mounds hold dice on the ground,
Stars play weiqi in the sky.
Open the jar, it gapes wide,
Roll up the mat, the bed is skinned."
Another:
"Seeing off, seeing off again,
Seeing off all the way to the bridgehead.
Piled up, two streams of tears,
Hard to press down the sorrow filling my chest."
Another:
"Peaches grow furry pellet sons,
Gourds grow club-like children.
Walls lean, bellies press against each other,
Rivers freeze, water grows a skin."
From The Records of Opening Laughter.
A Powerful Official of the Liáng Dynasty
During the Liáng dynasty, there was a powerful official
who read a faulty edition of the "Rhapsody on the Shu Capital,"
where the annotation for "dūn chī"
meaning "taro"
was mistakenly written as "sheep."
Later, someone sent him mutton as a gift.
He wrote a reply:
"Thank you for your gift of dūn chī."
The entire court was shocked and bewildered,
unable to understand the meaning.
After a long time, upon careful consideration,
they finally realized what had happened.
From The Family Instructions of Master Yán.
Liǔ Qiǎnzhī
Liǔ Qiǎnzhī of Hédōng, a secretary in the Suí dynasty's Imperial Secretariat,
was prone to making mistakes when reporting matters.
Once, a princess of the Zhōu family
submitted a petition to become a nun.
Qiǎnzhī reported:
"The Zhōu family princess has submitted a petition,
requesting to become a dàorén."
The emperor laughed heartily.
After he left,
Minister Yú Qìngzé asked him:
"How did you make a mistake in your report?"
Qiǎnzhī mistakenly replied again:
"The Zhōu family princess
wishes to return to secular life."
Qiǎnzhī later served as Minister of the Imperial Banquets.
Ruǎn Sōng
During the Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty,
Ruǎn Sōng, the magistrate of Guìyáng,
had a wife named Yán,
who was extremely jealous.
Once, while Ruǎn was hosting guests and drinking in the hall,
he summoned a maidservant to sing.
Lady Yán, with disheveled hair, bare feet, and bared arms,
rushed into the banquet with a knife.
The guests scattered in fright,
Ruǎn hid under the bed,
and the maidservant fled in panic.
The provincial governor Cuī Miǎo wrote Ruǎn's performance evaluation as follows:
"The wife is strong, the husband weak;
firm inside, soft outside.
If he cannot control even one wife,
how can he govern the people?
Since the wife lacks cultivation in ritual propriety,
where is the husband's spirit?
Evaluation: Fail."
Following official orders,
he was dismissed from his post.
From Records of Court and Country.
Hǎo Xiàngxián
Hǎo Xiàngxián of the Táng dynasty
was the grandson of Grand Councilor Hǎo Chǔjùn
and the son of Nánróng, the magistrate of Dùnqiū.
He was around twenty years old.
His friends gave him the courtesy name Chǒngzhī,
and they often referred to him by this name in front of his father.
His father tricked him, saying:
"Your friends are extremely virtuous.
I will prepare a feast for you;
you may invite them."
The next day,
Xiàngxián invited over ten people.
Nánróng welcomed the guests and drank with them,
saying:
"As the proverb goes:
'After three generations of high officials,
come dead dogs.'
My son is indeed foolish,
but troubling you all to create a courtesy name for him—
harming Nánróng's reputation is still tolerable,
but how can it extend to the Grand Councilor?"
He then wept,
and the guests left in shame.
"Chǒngzhī,"
when reversed in pronunciation, means "idiot seed."
From Records of Court and Country.
Zhū Qiányí
Zhū Qiányí of the Zhōu dynasty was shallow, dull, and ignorant,
with an extremely ugly appearance.
He submitted a memorial saying:
"I dreamed that Your Majesty would live eight hundred years."
He was immediately appointed as a Reminder,
and soon promoted to a Langzhōng.
Upon returning from a mission,
he submitted another memorial:
"I heard Mount Sōng shout 'Long live!'"
He was immediately granted the crimson robe and fish pouch.
Not yet having reached the fifth rank,
he wore it over his green official robe.
Everyone at court and among the people found it bizarre and laughed.
Later, when the Qìdān rebelled,
an edict was issued that any capital official who provided a horse for the army
would be rewarded with the fifth rank.
Qiányí bought a horse and submitted it,
then petitioned for the crimson robe.
The emperor was angry
and wrote on his petition:
"Dismiss him and send him back to his village."
He died of anger and resentment.
From Records of Court and Country.
Zhāng Yóugǔ
In the Táng dynasty, Zhāng Yóugǔ had administrative talent but lacked scholarly learning,
and successively held positions in the central government offices.
Once, in front of a crowd,
he sighed that Bān Gù was highly talented,
yet his writings were not included in the *Wénxuǎn*.
Someone said to him:
"The 'Rhapsody on the Two Capitals,' 'Inscription on Yān Mountain,' 'Diǎnyǐn,' and others
are all included in the *Wénxuǎn*.
Why do you say they are not?"
Yóugǔ replied:
"These are all writings by Bān Mèngjiān.
What does that have to do with Bān Gù?"
Those who heard this covered their mouths and laughed.
He also said to his colleagues:
"Yesterday I bought the *Collected Works of Wáng Sēngrú*,
which is actually Sēngrú.
It makes a lot of sense."
Dù Wénfàn knew he was mistaken
and responded immediately:
"Wénfàn also bought the *Collected Works of Fóbāo*,
which is far superior to the *Collected Works of Sēngrú*
('rú' originally written as 'rú,'
corrected according to the Xǔ edition
Yóugǔ remained completely unaware.
He was eventually promoted to the position of Sījì Yuánwài.
Later, he was exiled to Tíngzhōu for a crime.
At that time, the Zhōngshū Lìng Xǔ Jìngzōng was overseeing the handling of imperial edict cases.
He summoned Yóugǔ by official notice.
Yóugǔ was pleased,
but upon arrival, he was reprimanded.
Frightened, his hands trembled,
his hu tablet fell to the ground,
and he was unable to speak.
Earlier, when he served as Diànzhōng Zhèngbān,
he saw a Shàngshū Láng standing in the wrong position
and said to the Yǐnjià official:
"These Yuánwài Láng youngsters are hard to talk to;
you can punch them right in the face."
Court officials despised him.
From *Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ*
Hóu Sīzhèng
In the Táng dynasty, Hóu Sīzhèng came from a lowly servant background.
His pronunciation was incorrect.
He was appointed Shìshū Yùshǐ for reporting a rebellion.
When handling cases under imperial edict,
he became increasingly harsh and cruel.
Once, while interrogating Zhōngchéng Wèi Yuánzhōng, he said:
"Quickly confess to Bái Sīmǎ,
otherwise,
you'll taste Mèng Qīng."
Bái Sīmǎ refers to
a slope in Luòyáng
called Bái Sīmǎ Slope.
Mèng Qīng refers to
a general named Mèng Qīng,
who once beat Lángyá Prince Chōng to death with a staff.
Sīzhèng was a commoner from the alleys
and often used these words to intimidate prisoners.
Yuánzhōng remained unyielding in his tone,
so Sīzhèng angrily dragged him backward.
Yuánzhōng slowly stood up and said:
"I have bad luck,
like riding a bad donkey and falling off,
with my foot caught in the stirrup
(the character 'dèng' was originally missing,
supplemented from the Míng manuscript
and thus being dragged by the villain."
Sīzhèng grew furious
and dragged him again, saying:
"You are resisting an imperial envoy;
I will memorialize to have you executed."
Yuánzhōng said:
"Hóu Sīzhèng,
you are now a state Yùshǐ.
You must understand the proprieties of rank and importance.
If you need Wèi Yuánzhōng's head like this,
why not just saw it off!
Don't force me to confess falsely.
How can you wear the crimson sash
and personally bear the imperial mandate,
yet fail to act with proper integrity?
Instead, you speak of Bái Sīmǎ and Mèng Qīng—
what kind of talk is that?
If it weren't for Wèi Yuánzhōng,
no one would teach you this."
Sīzhèng startled and stood up,
trembling with fear
(the character 'zuò' was originally missing,
supplemented from the Míng manuscript
) and said:
"Sīzhèng deserves death;
I truly did not understand.
Fortunately, the Zhōngchéng has instructed me."
He then led Yuánzhōng up the steps,
seated him with respect, and questioned him.
Yuánzhōng calmly took his seat, composed as ever.
Also, Sīzhèng's pronunciation was incorrect.
At that time, there was a ban on slaughter.
Sīzhèng said:
"Now that slaughter is banned,
chicken
(pronounced 'gǔ lí' in reverse),
fish
(yú),
pork
(jì),
donkey
(lóu),
all
(jū)
cannot be eaten
(pronounced 'kǔ chǐ' in reverse),
meaning
(the character 'wèi' was originally missing,
supplemented from the Míng manuscript
empty eating of rice
(mǐ),
noodles
(pronounced with the departing tone of 'miè'),
like
how can one be full with only pickles?"
Shì Yùshǐ Huò Xiànkě laughed at him.
Sīzhèng complained to Zétiān.
Zétiān angrily said to Xiànkě:
"I know Sīzhèng is illiterate,
but I have already employed him.
Why are you laughing?"
Xiànkě recounted the incident about the chicken and pork,
and Zétiān also laughed heartily.
Sīzhèng once ordered steamed buns to be made
and said
(the character 'wèi' was originally missing,
supplemented from the Míng manuscript
) to the cook:
"Make me some steamed buns,
but chop the scallions finely.
Compared to market steamed buns,
which have lots of scallions but little meat,
I order you to chop the scallions finely and add more meat."
People at the time called him the "Finely-Chopped-Scallions Shì Yùshǐ."
At that time, Lái Jùnchén abandoned his former wife
and petitioned to forcibly marry the daughter of Tàiyuán's Wáng Qìngshēn.
Sīzhèng also petitioned to marry the daughter of Zhàojùn's Lǐ Zìyì.
An edict ordered the matter to be discussed by the government.
Fènggé Shìláng Lǐ Zhāodé clapped his hands and said to the ministers:
"Most laughable,
most laughable."
The ministers asked him why,
and Zhāodé said:
"In previous years, the villain Lái Jùnchén seized Wáng Qìng
(the character 'qìng' was originally missing,
supplemented from the Míng manuscript
)shēn's daughter,
which already greatly disgraced the state.
Today, this slave again requests to marry
(the character 'qǔ' was originally missing,
supplemented from the Míng manuscript
)Lǐ Zìyì's daughter.
Is this not another disgrace to the state?"
The matter was then dropped.
Sīzhèng was eventually beaten to death by Lǐ Zhāodé.
From *Yùshǐ Tái Jì*
Wáng Jíshàn
In the Táng dynasty, Wáng Jíshàn had mediocre talent and conduct
and a dull, muddled demeanor.
When he served as Nèishǐ,
people called him "A Magpie Gathering in the Phoenix Pond."
Soon, he was promoted to Wénchāng Yòuxiàng.
He implemented no significant policies,
but only prohibited clerks
('zhī' originally written as 'shuāng,'
corrected according to the Míng manuscript
) from bringing donkeys into the office.
He spent all day chasing them away,
never taking a break.
People at the time called him the "Donkey-Chasing Zǎixiàng."
From *Cháoyě Qiān Zǎi*
Lù Rénjié
In the Zhōu dynasty, there was Lù Rénjié,
a native of Héyáng.
Starting as a clerk in the Ministry of Revenue, he rose to become a Secretary in the Department of State Affairs,
where he revised the nationwide accounting system.
It became extremely intricate and detailed,
and the laws and regulations grew increasingly complex.
In every village, a community official was established,
and three additional officers for fairness and integrity were appointed,
responsible for managing records and documents,
and equipped with locks and keys.
With too many shepherds for the sheep,
the people scattered and fled.
However, the prime minister, being short-sighted,
believed this system could be implemented for generations to come,
and appointed Lù Rénjié as a Director in the Ministry of Revenue.
After several years,
the people suffered greatly from it,
and the system was eventually abolished.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Yuán Yǎn
Yuán Yǎn, a clerk in the Bureau of Evaluations during the Zhōu dynasty,
on a day of national mourning,
when everyone gathered,
served as the recorder in charge.
He then wrote a judgment:
"The government offices are bustling and noisy,
with no moment of respite.
If not for this day of national mourning,
there would be no opportunity to express joy and laughter."
Everyone present mocked him.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Sayings from the Censorate
Hóu Zhīyī, a Vice Minister of the Ministry of War during the Zhōu dynasty,
was old,
and an imperial decree allowed him to retire.
He submitted a memorial refusing to comply,
and in the court hall, he leaped and ran about,
to demonstrate his agility.
Zhāng Cóng was in mourning for his parents,
yet he requested to resume his official duties.
Gāo Yún, a Secretary in the Ministry of Personnel,
upon his mother's death,
had relatives come to mourn.
Gāo Yún said:
"I cannot play the filial son."
Yuánwàiláng Zhāng Qīzhēn,
facing a lawsuit,
falsely claimed his mother had passed away,
and refused to appear in court.
At that time, the Censorate circulated a saying:
"Hóu Zhīyī refuses to retire.
Zhāng Cóng requests to resume his duties.
Gāo Yún refuses to be filial.
Zhāng Qīzhēn willingly claims mourning.
None are men of proper teachings,
all are beyond the king's transformation.
Beasts in human form—
is this not indeed the case?"
From "Records from Court and Country"
Shěn Zǐróng
Shěn Zǐróng, a candidate for official selection during the Zhōu dynasty, had memorized two hundred model judgments.
On the day of the examination, he could not write a single word.
When asked why,
Shěn Zǐróng said:
"It is simply fate.
Today, among the judgments I have memorized,
none match the topic.
There is one that is somewhat similar,
but the names are different."
The following year, during another selection,
the judgment topic was about a water mill.
Again, he could not write.
When asked why,
he said:
"The water mill judgment I memorized
was about Lántián,
but now the question is about Fùpíng.
How can I write?"
Those who heard this could not help but clap their hands in laughter.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Wǔ Yìzōng
During the Zhōu dynasty, Empress Wǔ Zétiān was hosting a banquet in the inner court with great merriment,
when Prince Héneì, Wǔ Yìzōng, suddenly stood up and reported:
"A subject urgently informs his ruler,
a son urgently informs his father."
Wǔ Zétiān was greatly alarmed,
summoned him forward, and asked him,
to which he replied:
"The goods from my fief,
were previously collected by my own estate.
Recently, an imperial decree ordered the prefectures and counties to collect and deliver them,
resulting in significant losses."
Wǔ Zétiān was furious,
looked up at the roof beams,
and after a long while said:
"I am here enjoying a banquet with my relatives,
and you, a prince,
for the sake of a fief of two or three hundred households,
almost frightened me to death.
You are unworthy of being a prince."
She ordered him dragged away.
Wǔ Yìzōng removed his cap and prostrated himself in apology.
The other princes interceded for him, saying:
"Yìzōng is foolish and dull-witted,
he meant no harm."
The Empress then released him.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Zhāng Héng
Zhāng Héng of the Zhōu dynasty
started his career as a clerk,
rose to the fourth rank,
and was due for a promotion of one grade,
which would have placed him in the third rank.
The list had already been finalized.
However, after leaving court one day,
he saw freshly steamed cakes by the roadside,
bought one,
and ate it on horseback.
He was impeached by a censor for this.
Wǔ Zétiān issued a decree:
"Those of non-official background
are not permitted to enter the third rank."
Thus, his name was removed from the list.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Lǐ Liángbì
Lǐ Liángbì, a Reminder of the Right during the Zhōu dynasty,
was proud of his eloquence,
fond of discussing metaphysical principles,
and requested to be sent as an envoy to the northern barbarians to persuade Gǔdǔlù.
The Xiongnu served him feces on a wooden tray,
and held a white blade to his face.
Lǐ Liángbì, in fear,
ate the entire trayful,
and only then was he released to return.
People mocked him, saying:
"Reminder Lǐ can indeed pick up what the Turks leave behind."
He was later appointed Magistrate of Zhēnyuán,
and upon completing his term,
returned to Yíng Prefecture.
He encountered Sūn Wànróng, a rebel leader of the Qìdān,
who sent Hé Āxiǎo to capture Cāng, Yíng, and Jì
Jì was originally written as 'fèn' (dung),
corrected according to the Ming manuscript
all entered
The Ming manuscript lacks the character 'rù' (enter)
Lǐ Liángbì said to Lǐ Huáibì, the Magistrate of Lùchéng:
"Sūn means macaque,
that is, a monkey,
difficult to withstand.
The character 'wàn' (萬) has grass above it.
That means hiding in the grass.
He urged Lǐ Huáibì to surrender."
Hé Āxiǎo appointed Lǐ Huáibì as a General of the Third Rank.
When Hé Āxiǎo was defeated,
Lǐ Huáibì and Lǐ Liángbì, along with his two sons,
were all executed by Prince Héneì, Wǔ Yìzōng.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Lái Zǐxún
Lái Zǐxún of the Táng dynasty,
was entrusted by Wǔ Zétiān with investigating political cases,
often catering to her intentions.
He was granted the surname Wǔ,
with the courtesy name Jiāchén.
He resumed his post during mourning for his father,
and was successively promoted to Commandant of Mobile Guards and General of the Right Guard of the Feathered Forest Army.
He often wore a brocade half-sleeve jacket,
talking and laughing as if nothing was amiss.
Court officials ridiculed him.
Zhāng Yuányī, an Exhorter of the Heir Apparent who enjoyed mocking and jesting,
said:
"How can a son of the Wǔ family
wear mourning clothes for your Lái family's old man?"
From "Records of the Censorate"
Yán Zhīwēi
Zhōu Chūnguān Shàngshū Yán Zhīwēi was mediocre, trivial, and cowardly.
Sent as an envoy to the foreign tribes,
he accepted Mòchuò's appointment as the "Hàn Kèhán."
When the bandits invaded Héngdìng,
Zhīwēi was dispatched ahead to Zhàozhōu to appease them.
General Chén Lìngyīng and others were guarding the western side of the city.
Zhīwēi said to Lìngyīng:
"General Chén, why not surrender early?
If you surrender only after the Kèhán's troops arrive,
not a blade of grass will be left."
Lìngyīng did not reply.
Beneath the city, Zhīwēi
(The original text had "chéng" [成],
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy)
joined hands and danced in a circle, singing,
chanting "Wànsuì Lè" (Long Live Music).
Lìngyīng
(The original text had "bīng" [兵],
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy)
said:
"As a Shàngshū, one of the eight high ministers of the state,
the responsibility entrusted to you is not light.
Yet you turn to dance and sing for the bandits—
have you no shame?"
Zhīwēi then sang:
"Wànsuì Lè,
Wànsuì nián (Long Live years),
bù zìyóu (not free),
Wànsuì Lè."
People of the time despised him.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Cuī Shí
In the Táng dynasty, Cuī Shí served as Lìbù Shìláng (Vice Minister of Personnel)
and was greedy and unrestrained.
Elder brothers relied on their younger brother's influence,
fathers wielded their sons' authority.
All accepted requests and solicitations,
and their corrupt practices were in utter disorder.
His father, Cuī Yì,
served as Sīyè (Director of the Imperial Academy),
and accepted money from a candidate for office.
Shí was unaware of this.
When the long list of appointments was released,
that person complained:
"Your own relative took the bribe—
why was I not given an official post?"
Shí said:
"Which relative?
I will seize him and whip him to death."
The person said:
"If you whip him, you will bring mourning upon yourself."
Shí was greatly enraged and ashamed.
The Emperor, considering Shí's father old,
and melons having just ripened,
bestowed one upon him.
Shí gave the melon to his concubine,
and did not share it with his father.
Both court and commoners ridiculed him.
At that time, Cuī, Cén, and Zhèng Yīn
all served in the Ministry of Personnel.
A ballad circulated in the capital:
"Cén Yì is the descendant of a Liáo tribesman,
Cuī Shí is the grandson of a Lìnggōng.
These three men compared side by side—
Mòhèduō is the most muddled."
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Quán Lóngxiāng
Táng Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Quán Lóngxiāng was narrow-minded and impatient,
and often boasted of his poetic talent.
During the Tōngtiān era,
he served as Cāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Prefect of Cāngzhōu).
Upon first arriving,
he composed a poem to present to the local officials:
"Gazing afar at Cāngzhōu city,
willows lush and green.
In the center, a group of men,
gather sitting, clinking wine cups."
The gentlemen thanked him:
"Your Excellency possesses extraordinary talent."
Xiāng said:
"I dare not claim that—
merely fitting the rhyme."
Again in autumn,
he wrote "Shùhuái" (Expressing My Feelings):
"Before the eaves, seven hundred fly,
snow-white behind the garden wall.
Full-bellied, lying inside the room,
household dung gathers wild dung beetles."
The Cānjūn (Military Advisor) did not understand,
and asked for an explanation.
Xiāng said:
"A sparrowhawk flies before the eaves.
It's worth seven hundred coins.
Washed clothes hung in the back
(The original text had "bǐ" [彼],
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy)
garden,
dry and white as snow.
Full-bellied, lying on my side in the room,
at home
(The original text had "xiāng" [襄],
changed according to the Míng manuscript copy)
I relieve myself,
and gather wild marsh dung beetles."
Those who heard of it laughed at him.
At a banquet hosted by the Crown Prince,
he composed a poem in summer:
"Severe frost, vast and white,
bright moon, round and red."
The Crown Prince took up a brush and wrote a comment:
"Lóngxiāng, man of talent,
a native of Qínzhōu.
The bright moon shines at noon,
severe frost rises in summer.
Such poetic verses—
merely fitting the rhyme."
Due to his involvement in Zhāng Yìzhī's affair,
Xiāng was demoted to Róngshān Fǔ Zhéchōng (Commander of Róngshān Garrison).
During the Shénlóng era, he was recalled to the capital,
and presented a poem:
"With nothing to do, I went to Róngshān,
today I head east to the capital.
His Majesty ordered me to come in,
now I serve as Yòu Jīnwú (Right Imperial Guard General)."
He also wrote a "Joyful Rain" poem:
"When it darkens, there is no rain,
when it brightens, there are no clouds.
The sun blazes forth,
the ground turns green and misty."
While serving as Governor of Yíngzhōu,
just after the New Year,
several people from the capital sent him letters saying:
"The change of year brings many feelings,
I respectfully imagine you share the same."
He immediately summoned his officials and declared:
"There is an edict changing the reign title to 'Duōgǎn' (Many Feelings) First Year."
He presented the letters to his deputies and below.
Everyone laughed heartily.
Lóngxiāng then listened intently,
wondering why the pardon edict was late.
Gāoyáng and Bóyě counties
were disputing over land and submitted petitions.
Lóngxiāng then rendered a judgment:
"Two counties dispute land,
without the prefecture, it cannot be decided.
Since it involves two counties,
in principle, it is not improper to refer it to the office.
Quán Lóngxiāng instructs."
The clerk said:
"In the past, when superiors rendered judgments,
they never wrote their surname."
Lóngxiāng said:
"Others might not understand.
If I don't write my surname,
who would know which family's stray donkey I am?"
Lóngxiāng did not know about death anniversaries.
He asked a government clerk:
"What is a 'private忌' (private taboo)?"
The reply was:
"On the day one's parents died,
one requests leave,
and sits alone in one's room without going out."
When the day arrived, Xiāng
sat quietly in his room.
A black dog suddenly rushed in.
Lóngxiāng was furious and said:
"It has broken my忌 (taboo observance)."
He then submitted another petition,
changing it to the next morning,
to properly observe the death anniversary.
Those who heard of it laughed at him.
From "Cháoyě Qiānzǎi"
Sū Wèidào
When Táng Sū Wèidào was first appointed Chancellor,
a disciple asked him:
"With all the pressing affairs under heaven,
how will Your Excellency harmonize them?"
Wèidào said nothing,
but only rubbed the edge of his bed with his hand.
Thus, he was called the "Rubbing-the-Edges Chancellor."
From "Lúshì Zájì"
Lǐ Shīdàn
Lǐ Shīdàn of the Táng dynasty
was a native of Xīnfēng.
He served as a commandant in Kuàijī.
On a national day of mourning, when official duties were suspended,
he drank wine, sang songs, and caned people,
and was thus impeached by his subordinates.
The investigating censor Sū Wèidào examined the case,
but Lǐ did not confess or admit anything.
Wèidào sternly said to him:
"You are an official;
how can you not abide by the law
and commit such violations?"
He was about to punish him,
but Shīdàn requested to be questioned further,
then sighed and said:
"Drinking wine is not prohibited by law,
let alone medicinal wine.
Singing dirges is merely an expression of grief.
Caning subordinates is due to urgent official matters.
Why should the investigating censor reprimand me for this?"
Wèidào said:
"This man turns white into black;
I cannot discipline him."
From "Records of the Censorate"
Huò Xiànkě
Huò Xiànkě of the Táng dynasty
was a native of Guìxiāng.
His father, Huò Yù,
served as a judicial officer in Qízhōu.
Xiànkě was well-versed in literature
and enjoyed jesting.
He was promoted repeatedly, eventually becoming a left department vice director of the investigating censor.
As Empress Wǔ Zétiān's laws were severe,
many could not ensure their own safety
and competed to curry favor to show their loyalty.
Xiànkě knocked his head against the jade steps,
requesting the execution of Dí Rénjié and Péi Xíngběn.
Péi was Xiànkě's maternal uncle.
After injuring his forehead,
he wrapped it with green silk under his headscarf
and often let it show,
hoping that Wǔ Zétiān would consider him loyal.
People at the time compared him to Lǐ Zǐshèn.
Zǐshèn,
during Wǔ Zétiān's reign, falsely accused his uncle
and was promoted to mobile corps general.
When his mother saw him wearing crimson official robes,
she covered her face with the bedcovers
(in some versions, "covered her face with the bedcovers" is written as "covered her face with a quilt"),
and wept uncontrollably, saying:
"Is this dyed with your uncle's blood?"
From "Records of the Censorate"
Yuán Shǒuyī
Yuán Shǒuyī of the Táng dynasty was shallow and impulsive in nature,
and people at the time nicknamed him "the fighting duck old rooster."
He served as a commandant in Wànnián.
The chief administrator of Yōngzhōu, Dòu Huáizhēn, often wanted to flog him.
So, at the residence of the secretariat director Zōng Chǔkè,
he presented fresh vegetables as a gift
and was appointed as a investigating censor.
Huáizhēn was unaware of this.
Zhēn greeted him with a high bow and said:
"The carriage is about to depart;
why are you conducting such inspections?"
Yuán Shǒuyī immediately impeached him.
After over a month,
Huáizhēn was appointed left censor-in-chief.
Shǒuyī requested leave,
not daring to appear,
and begged to be dismissed.
Huáizhēn called him and comforted him,
but Shǒuyī remained fearful and uneasy.
When Chǔkè learned of this,
he appointed Shǒuyī as a right censor.
In the court hall, Shǒuyī confronted Huáizhēn and said:
"I am your 'luóshī.'"
"Luóshī"
is street slang,
meaning "having no connection."
Not long after,
Chǔkè was executed for rebellion,
and Shǒuyī, as his associate,
was exiled to Duānzhōu.
From "Records of Court and Country"
Cuī Tàizhī
Cuī Tàizhī, a vice director of the imperial secretariat in the Táng dynasty, wrote a poem mourning the death of the special advanced grand master Lǐ Qiáo:
"The tower was a place of immortals,
the robes and caps a gentleman's realm.
Yesterday we still sat facing each other,
today you are suddenly said to be gone.
Your soul follows the ghost of fate,
your spirit chases after King Yán.
Now laughter ceases here,
never again to face the court hall."
From "Records of Court and Country"
Lù Yúqìng
Lù Yúqìng, a vice director of the department of state affairs in the Táng dynasty, was transferred to serve as chief administrator of Luòzhōu.
His son mocked him with a verse:
"Lù Yúqìng,
your brush is weak but your mouth is tough.
Once
(some versions have 'yá' instead of 'cháo')
you receive litigation cases,
ten days pass without a verdict."
He placed it under the desk mat.
Yúqìng found it and read it, saying:
"It must be that dog!"
He then chased and caned him.
From "Records of Court and Country"
Sūn Yàngāo
Sūn Yàngāo, prefect of Dìngzhōu during the Zhōu dynasty,
was besieged by the Turks with dozens of layers around the city.
He did not dare to go to the official hall;
documents requiring mobilization
were passed through a small window,
and he locked the gates of the prefectural residence.
When the enemy scaled the walls,
he hid inside a cabinet,
instructing his servant:
"Hold the keys tightly;
if the enemy asks for them,
be sure not to give them."
Once there was a fool
who went to the capital for an official selection,
and his leather bag was stolen by a thief.
The man said:
"The thief stole my bag,
but he will never be able to use my things."
When asked why,
he replied:
"The key is now on my belt;
what will he use to open it?"
Sūn Yàngāo is of this sort.
From "Records of Court and Country"
Emissary Censors
When Táng dynasty censors were on missions,
they long abstained from flavorful food.
Upon arriving at a relay station,
some would secretly place dried meat in their meal,
pretend to scold the attendant to remove it,
and after the attendant left, slowly eat it.
This often occurred,
greatly compromising their dignity.
Once there was a censor
who left very little,
unaware that the attendant had seen it.
The attendant replied:
"The station has plenty of dried meat;
please, sir, keep it."
The censor felt deeply ashamed.
