There were also cooks who boiled meat until tender,
using the broth to make soup,
and the censor would pretend not to know and eat it.
If he encountered meat in the soup,
he would reprimand the cook.
If it was a new cook
unfamiliar with how to respond,
he would only apologize, saying it slipped through the sieve,
meaning it leaked through the sieve filter.
During the Shénlóng era,
Hán Wǎn, Lù Yuánké, and Zhèng Yuánfù served as assistant judges.
When they reached Láizhōu,
they witnessed this incident firsthand
and looked at each other and laughed.
The vice director of the department of state affairs, Wèi Yuánzhōng, who was then serving as vice censor-in-chief,
said to Wǎn:
"When Yuánzhōng served as a investigating censor,
upon arriving at a relay station,
I ate dried meat and eggs together,
which did not diminish the dignity of the censorate.
But secretly stealing deeply compromises the integrity of a state scholar."
Lord Wèi's words were apt;
if one neither eats nor steals,
wouldn't that be even better?
From "Records of the Censorate"
Hán Wǎn
Táng Hán Wǎn, together with Zhāng Chāngzōng and Wáng Běnlì,
visited the Imperial Academy together.
There was a professor surnamed Zhāng,
who was Zhāng Chāngzōng's paternal uncle,
well-versed in the Five Classics,
but ignorant of current affairs.
He kept a rooster,
calling it "Young Master Bó,"
and doted on it endlessly.
Whenever he lectured on the classics,
the character for "classics" was originally missing,
supplemented based on the Ming manuscript copy
it would gather among the students
originally written as "towel,"
corrected based on the Ming manuscript copy
Sometimes it would snatch and tear books;
whenever anyone chased it away,
they would inevitably be scolded angrily:
"This creature possesses the Five Virtues;
how dare you disrespect it?"
Zhāng Chāngzōng once received caning because of this rooster.
Wáng Běnlì and Hán Wǎn
felt quite indignant about this,
saying:
"This pedantic scholar doesn't understand matters;
we'll kill this rooster for you."
Professor Zhāng often collected leftover food from the students.
Wáng Běnlì, being the senior student,
was asked whether this was permissible.
Wáng Běnlì said:
"If there is a written record, it's fine."
Professor Zhāng was pleased,
and every day when he received the food,
a written record was made.
One day,
Professor Zhāng requested leave.
Wáng Běnlì submitted a document,
listing the rooster's crimes,
killed it, and ate it.
When Professor Zhāng returned to the academy,
he could not find the rooster.
Startled, he exclaimed:
"Where is my Young Master Bó?"
Those around him reported that Wáng Běnlì had killed it.
Furious, he said:
"Bring the record!
Bring the record!"
Seeing the list of the rooster's crimes,
he said:
"Even so,
it still shouldn't have been put to death."
Wáng Běnlì said:
"A rooster is not like a person;
it cannot be punished with flogging or caning,
so execution was precisely appropriate."
Professor Zhāng repeatedly slapped the table with his hand and said:
"Young Master Bó,
when there's a written record,
what more can be said?"
At that time in Cháng'ān,
whenever there was a written record,
people would readily say it was factual.
Thus we know that those immersed in studying the classics and histories
should also be well-informed about current affairs.
Otherwise,
why were the ancients called foolish scholars, simple scholars, pedantic scholars, or petty scholars?
This can also serve as a warning for later generations.
From "Records of the Censorate"
Zhào Rénjiǎng
Táng dynasty's Zhào Rénjiǎng,
a native of Hénán,
made a living by selling goods north of Wáng Róng's tomb in the Zhíyè ward.
He was skilled at singing "The Yellow Roe Deer,"
and had old connections with eunuchs.
Relying on these connections,
during the Jǐnglóng era,
he carried firewood to the imperial court,
and thus gained an audience.
He said:
"I carry firewood to assist the state in governing."
That very day he was appointed as a censor.
During Emperor Ruìzōng's reign,
he was demoted to Shàngcài County Assistant Magistrate.
When sent to the capital,
he sought out his old colleagues in the Censorate,
acting presumptuously and familiar.
Censor Ní Ruòshuǐ said to Yáng Màozhí:
"This mediocre fellow
acts so presumptuously and incompetently."
He then memorialized against him.
Grand Secretary Yáo Chóng said:
"Is this the 'Yellow Roe Deer' fellow?"
He was appointed as Xīdāng Deputy Sheriff of his home prefecture,
and dispatched by post relay.
While in the Censorate,
Zhào Rénjiǎng had no other abilities,
relying solely on "The Yellow Roe Deer" to show off.
Sòng Wùxiān inscribed a verse about him:
"Zhào Jiǎng emerged from Wáng Róng's shadow,
entered Zhū Bó's Censorate hall.
Abandoning that firewood-carrying,
he ascended to stand among these cypresses.
Pedestrians do not avoid his piebald horse,
guests seated only hear 'The Yellow Roe Deer.'"
At that time, Cuī Xuānyī was on a mission to the capital.
Zhào Rénjiǎng entrusted a letter to his home with him,
addressed as:
"Letter from Censor Zhào of the Western Capital.
Deliver to the first shop north of Wáng Róng's tomb in the Zhíyè ward, Luò Prefecture.
To my wife, Yīniáng."
Cuī Xuānyī showed the letter to court officials.
When he was first demoted to Shàngcài,
Pān Hǎolǐ was promoted from Shàngcài Magistrate to Censor.
Zhào Rénjiǎng presented him a poem:
"The Magistrate leaves on his piebald horse,
the Assistant Magistrate doffs his embroidered robes to come."
People were astonished at the time,
some thinking it was ghostwritten.
When Zhào Rénjiǎng was first appointed Investigating Censor,
he thanked the high court officials,
merely saying:
"I am fortunate to grasp your lordships' horse hooves."
Court officials were accompanying him at the time.
They encountered a foreigner carrying two bundles of firewood.
He said:
"This foreigner deserves appointment as Palace Attendant."
Someone asked why,
he replied:
"Zhào Rénjiǎng carried one bundle and was appointed Investigating Censor;
this man carries two bundles,
so surely he deserves appointment as Palace Attendant."
From "Records of the Censorate"
Jiāng Shīdù
Táng dynasty's Jiāng Shīdù was fond of strange and crafty schemes.
While serving as Prefect of Cāng Prefecture,
concurrently as Surveillance Commissioner,
he constructed spear-carts to transport grain,
dug canals and built dams,
throwing the prefectures and counties into turmoil.
Within the boundaries of Lǔchéng,
he planted rice and established military colonies.
Crabs ate up all the rice ears,
so he conscripted laborers to catch crabs.
The people suffered bitterly,
singing:
"In Lǔ land they planted rice once,
all of it covered by water foam.
Every year they press for crab catchers,
the common folk cannot survive."
Later, as Prefect of Shǎn Prefecture,
to transport rice from the Yǒngfēng Granary,
he levied an extra three coins per unit,
calculating it as a fee.
One evening he suddenly claimed to have found a solution:
he erected a pouring tower,
built a chute from the granary,
straight to the river,
several thousand zhàng long.
He then ordered the rice poured down it.
Where it didn't flow smoothly,
they used large rakes to push it,
causing the rice to suffer losses,
much turning to powder.
Moreover, the wind blew it about;
each container lost about a hundred dàn of rice,
and each operation involved tens of thousands.
He made the granary overseers compensate for it,
exhausting their family fortunes.
He then ordered the households delivering grain to measure it themselves,
some having to compensate dozens of hú.
It greatly harmed the people,
and was only then stopped.
From "Records of Affairs Within and Outside the Court"
Chéng Jìngqí
Táng Chéng Jìngqí possessed outstanding talent.
During the Tiāncè era,
he went to the imperial court to present himself,
requesting to be tested daily with thirty essay topics.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān then ordered Wáng Bó
(Míng manuscript copy: Bó written as Jù)
to test him,
and he was appointed as a proofreader.
He was successively promoted to Censor, Chief Minister of Justice,
and became related by marriage to Privy Councilor Yáo Chóng.
Once, when Chóng was ill,
Jìngqí visited his residence to inquire after him,
and wept tears before Chóng.
He had several live sparrows hidden in his bosom,
which he then took out one by one,
asking Chóng to hold them in his hand before releasing them.
He prayed, saying:
"I wish for Your Excellency to recover quickly."
Chóng reluctantly complied.
After Jìngqí left,
Chóng despised his flattery and sycophancy,
and said to his family members:
"Where did these tears come from?"
From then on, he no longer treated him with respect.
From "Records of the Censorate"
Shí Huìtài
Shí Huìtài, an adjutant in the household of Prince Qí of the Táng dynasty,
wrote a poem to Censor Lǐ Quánjiāo, which said:
"The Censor does not hold his post long,
nor does the Adjutant remain for long.
Once you are transferred and promoted,
this position will come back to me."
They then competed in sending official documents back and forth,
and Quánjiāo wrote over ten pages of judgments in response,
which were actually composed by Reminder Zhāng Jiǔlíng on his behalf.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Féng Guāngzhèn
Féng Guāngzhèn, a military officer in the household of the Crown Prince's guard during the Táng dynasty, entered the Jíxián Academy
to collate the "Wénxuǎn."
He once annotated "dūn chī" as:
"The 'dūn chī'
is today's taro,
which is essentially a hairy radish."
When Xiāo, the Director, heard this,
he clapped his hands and laughed heartily.
From "Records of Tán Bīn"
Lǐ Jǐndù
Lǐ Jǐndù, a Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Táng dynasty,
was recommended by Sòng Jǐng.
When his mother passed away,
he refused to announce the mourning.
When the obituary arrived,
he hid it.
His colleagues, troubled by his uselessness,
instructed his native place, Yíngzhōu,
to report that Jǐndù's mother had died.
The Department of State Affairs then sent a document to the Censorate,
and only then did he weep.
His mediocrity and vulgarity were all of this kind.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Three Filths
During the Táng dynasty, Wáng Yí served as Vice Censor-in-Chief,
the filth of the Censorate;
Jiāng Huì served as Vice Minister of Personnel,
the filth of the Ministry of Personnel;
Cuī Tàizhī served as Vice Minister of the Chancellery,
the filth of the Chancellery;
they were called the Three Filths of the Capital.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Yáng Tāo
Yáng Tāo of the Táng dynasty served as a Secretary in the Secretariat.
Once, when urgently ordered to draft an imperial decree,
the clerk holding the key to the archives had gone elsewhere,
and there was no old copy to consult.
So he broke a window to retrieve it.
People at the time called him the Window-Breaking Secretary.
From "Records from Court and Country"
Cháng Dìngzōng
Xīn Hóngzhì, Director of the National Academy during the Táng dynasty, wrote a poem:
"You are the grass by the river,
meeting spring, your heart grows abundantly.
I am the mirror on the stand,
reflecting only when it becomes clear."
His fellow academician Cháng Dìngzōng
changed the word "shǐ" (始, begin) to "zhuǎn" (转, turn),
and they disputed over this poem.
Both claimed to have written it.
So a document was submitted,
and they went to see Doctor Luó Dàozōng,
who judged:
"In the past, five words determined a memorial,
valued for their logical precision.
Now, a single word competes in a poem,
and the one with more words is considered the author.
The poem belongs to Hóngzhì,
but 'zhuǎn' is returned to Dìngzōng.
Let this be known through the document,
and let it serve as public
(original text had the character 'zhī' after 'gōng,'
deleted according to the Míng manuscript copy)
evidence."
From "Records from Court and Country"
Zhāng Xuánjìng
Zhāng Xuánjìng of the Táng dynasty,
a native of Shǎn,
was promoted from a warehouse officer in the Left Guard to Censor.
His nature was not honest and sincere.
He advanced by currying favor with Mùróng Bǎojié.
At the time, there were two Censors named Zhāng,
so Xuánjìng was called Little Zhāng.
When he first entered the Censorate,
he addressed his older colleagues as "elder brother."
But after being selected for the Palace Administration,
he no longer called them "elder brother."
After Bǎojié was executed,
he felt quite uneasy,
and resumed calling his former colleagues "elder brother."
Censor Dù Wénfàn,
upon returning from a mission,
met Zhèng Réngōng, who was just about to leave on a mission.
When asked about affairs in the Censorate,
Gōng replied:
"After Bǎojié's downfall,
Little Zhāng has started calling us 'elder brother' again."
People at the time found this amusing.
From "Records of the Censorate"
The Gōngyáng Commentary
There was a man, A, who wanted to visit the county magistrate.
He asked those around him:
"What does the magistrate enjoy?"
Someone told him:
"He enjoys the 'Gōngyáng Commentary.'"
Later, when he went to see the magistrate,
the magistrate asked:
"What books do you read?"
He replied:
"I only study the 'Gōngyáng Commentary.'"
The magistrate tested him, asking:
"Who killed Chén Tuó?"
After a long pause, A replied:
"I have never killed Chén Tuó in my life."
The magistrate, realizing his mistake,
teased him further, saying:
"If you didn't kill Chén Tuó,
then who did?"
A was terrified,
and ran out barefoot.
When people asked him the reason,
he exclaimed loudly:
"When I met the magistrate,
he immediately questioned me about a murder case.
I dare not go back again.
I'll only come out when there's an amnesty."
From "Forest of Laughs"
Lǐ Wénlǐ
Lǐ Wénlǐ of the Táng dynasty,
a native of Dùnqiū,
was studious and talented in writing.
He was successively promoted to the position of Military Administrator of Yángzhōu,
but his nature was slow and sluggish,
and not very meticulous.
At the time, he was in Yángzhōu.
A clerk returned from the capital,
bringing a letter from the Chief Administrator's family,
which said that his elder sister had died,
and requested him to choose a day for the funeral.
When Wénlǐ suddenly heard that his elder sister had died,
he wailed and wept bitterly.
The clerk, seizing an opportune moment,
informed him again:
"It was the Chief Administrator's elder sister."
After a long while, Wénlǐ slowly asked:
"It was the Chief Administrator's elder sister?"
The clerk said:
"Yes."
Wénlǐ said:
"I don't have an elder sister,
no wonder I found it strange earlier."
From "Records of the Censorate"
Yīn Ān
Táng Dynasty recluse Yīn Ān,
a native of Xìndū, Jìzhōu.
Said to Attendant Gentleman Huángmén Xuē:
"Since ancient times, the sages and worthies,
number no more than five.
Fúxī with the Eight Trigrams,
exhausted the principles of Heaven and Earth.
That is the first."
Then he bent one finger.
"Shénnóng planted the hundred grains,
saving the lives of myriad people.
That is the second."
Then he bent two fingers.
"Duke of Zhōu established rites and music,
practiced for a hundred generations.
That is the third."
Then he bent three fingers.
"Confucius foreknew the boundless,
and understood the limitless.
Standing out from the crowd,
rising above his kind.
That is the fourth."
Then he bent four fingers.
"After this,
there is no one worthy of bending a finger for."
After a long pause, he said:
"Including me, that makes five."
Then he bent all five fingers.
And he slighted and scorned the high ministers.
His son Zhēng admonished him:
"The high ministers are respected,
Father should show them some respect."
Ān said:
"You too are fit to be a chancellor."
Zhēng said:
"How would your son dare?"
Ān said:
"You with your fat head and big face,
ignorant of past and present,
a glutton
(pronounced tóng)
who eats without wit or wisdom,
if you don't become a chancellor, what will you be?"
His contempt for others was all of this kind.
A Person Surnamed Fáng
In the Táng, there was a person surnamed Fáng,
fond of boasting about his family background.
Whenever there was an official surnamed Fáng,
he would claim them as a relative.
His acquaintances, annoyed by this,
said to him:
"The Duke Minister of Fēngyì
(Fēngyì ward is in the upper capital,
it is a funeral shop,
where exorcists come from)
what relation is he to you?"
He said:
"He is
(The original text below had the character for 'surname'.
Deleted according to the Ming manuscript copy)
my second cousin's paternal uncle."
People laughed heartily and said:
"Since you are the nephew of an exorcist,
you're only fit to scare ghosts."
From "Qǐ Yán Lù"
Yuánzōng Kuí
In the Táng, Yuánzōng Kuí was the Sīmǎ of Guǒzhōu.
A maidservant died,
and he instructed the duty clerk:
"An old maidservant of the Kuí household has died.
She served for a long time,
so find a coffin to bury her.
When Kuí first arrived home, he was poor,
and couldn't afford a new one.
Just get one that has been used before,
that will suffice.
Also, no need to say Kuí bought it,
just say your own family needed it."
The duty clerk went out and talked about it,
and the whole province took it as a laughingstock.
From "Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ"
Dúgū Shǒuzhōng
In the Táng, Hángzhōu Cānjūn Dúgū Shǒuzhōng was leading a tax grain shipment to the capital.
In the middle of the night,
he urgently summoned the boatmen.
He had nothing else to say,
but then said:
"Against the wind, you must not raise the sails."
Everyone laughed heartily at him.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi"
Wáng Xióng
In the Táng, Wáng Xióng was the Dūdū of Zézhōu.
The prefectural Legal Officer judged a case of grain thieves,
sentencing each
(Ming manuscript copy has 'according to statute' instead of 'sentencing each')
to one hundred strokes of the cane,
and reported for joint judgment.
Xióng said:
"How many thieves in total?"
The Legal Officer said:
"Seven thieves."
Xióng said:
"Seven thieves
(The five characters 'Xióng said seven thieves'
are added according to the Ming manuscript copy)
should receive seven hundred strokes in total."
The Legal Officer rendered a wrongful judgment,
and the prefectural office imposed punishment.
People of the time laughed at him.
The previous Dūdū, Yǐn Zhèngyì,
was fair and just.
Later, Xióng came to replace him.
The commoners sang a song:
"First we got Yǐn the Buddha-child,
then we got Wáng the mangy otter.
Judging cases like a donkey biting a melon,
summoning people like an ox chewing iron.
Seeing money, his face beams with joy,
no cash, he shouts from the start.
Often meeting a hungry yaksha,
the commoners cannot survive."
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi"
Qū Chóngyù
A poem by Táng Jìzhōu Cānjūn Qū Chóngyù, "Sending off the Sīgōng to the Capital", said:
"Chóngyù has the fortunate chance,
to encounter the bright journey.
The Sīshì goes to the capital,
the wilds echo with mournful cries."
The Sīgōng said:
"A great talent!
Who, sir, is your teacher?"
He said:
"A Wú scholar,
taught me these rhymes."
The Sīgōng said:
"A wise teacher makes a perceptive student."
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi"
Liáng Shìhuì
Táng Huázhōu Língchāng Wèi Liáng Shìhuì,
the office requisitioned crow feathers,
but the village headman did not deliver them.
He wrote a judgment on the document:
"The office summons crow feathers.
What kind of village headman,
does not deliver crow feathers?"
His assistant said:
"Your judgment is excellent,
but there are too many 'crow feathers'."
Huì took up his brush and wrote:
"The office summons crow feathers.
What kind of village headman,
does not deliver goose wings?"
People of discernment,
heard of it and laughed.
From "Cháo Yě Qiān Zǎi"
Zhāng Huáiqìng
In the Táng, Lǐ Yìfǔ once composed a poem:
"Carving the moon to make a song fan,
cutting clouds to make a dance gown.
Pitying my own snow-whirling shadow,
I'd best return to Luòchuān."
There was a Zǎoqiáng Wèi, Zhāng Huáiqìng, who loved plagiarizing famous scholars' writings.
He then made a poem:
"Born of feeling, carving the moon to make a song fan,
Inspired, cutting clouds to make a dance gown.
Looking in the mirror, pitying my own snow-whirling shadow,
When I come, I'd best return to Luòchuān."
People of the time said of him:
"Skinning Wáng Chānglíng alive,
swallowing Guō Zhèngyī whole."
From "Dà Táng Xīn Yǔ"
Kāng Tóng
After Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng appointed Niú Xiānkè as chancellor,
he was quite worried that contemporary opinion would not be in harmony.
Therefore, he consulted Gāo Lìshì:
"Regarding the appointment of Xiānkè as chancellor,
what is the opinion outside the court?"
Lìshì said:
"Xiānkè comes from a petty clerk background;
he is not the material for a chancellor."
The Emperor flew into a rage and said:
"Then I should appoint Kāng Mài."
This was merely the Emperor's angry words in the heat of the moment,
mentioning the most unsuitable candidate.
Someone secretly reported this to Mài,
saying that the Emperor's favor towards him
was quite deep,
and he would soon be made chancellor.
Upon hearing this,
Mài believed it to be true.
The next day,
he dressed in his finest court robes and hurried to court.
Once he had taken his place in the ranks,
he craned his neck gazing northwards,
hoping for the official appointment.
Those who saw him could not help but cover their mouths to laugh.
However, contemporary opinion also regarded him as a man of integrity.
Mài served as the Minister of Works;
he was full of ingenious ideas,
and was especially skilled in geomancy.
He once said to someone:
"Since I live in this residence,
how could I not become chancellor?"
Those who heard this laughed at him even more.
The current residence of Chancellor Niú in the northwest of Xīnchāng Ward
was originally Mài's house.
From "Miscellaneous Records of Emperor Míng Huáng"
The Recluse
During the reign of Emperor Sùzōng of Táng,
there was a competition for virtuous and talented men.
An edict was issued to search the mountains, forests, marshes, and wilderness,
for those who possessed talent and virtue or could assist the times and strengthen the state.
All such men could be enfeoffed and appointed.
A recluse came from Língwǔ,
wearing clothes of grass,
and straw sandals on his feet.
He arrived at the capital gate.
Emperor Sùzōng was delighted to hear of it and said:
"Indeed, a worthy scholar has answered the summons!"
He then summoned him for an audience,
and inquired about the successes and failures of current affairs.
In the end, the man said not a single word.
He only repeatedly gazed at the Emperor's face and finally addressed him, saying:
"Your humble servant has an observation;
does Your Majesty know of it?"
The Emperor replied:
"I do not know."
The man addressed him:
"Your servant sees that Your Majesty's sacred countenance
is thinner than when you were in Língwǔ."
The Emperor said:
"Toiling late into the night and rising early has led to this."
Some of the attending officials could not help but stifle their laughter.
When he withdrew,
he said nothing further.
The Emperor knew he was a foolish man,
but fearing to block the path for future worthies,
he reluctantly appointed him as a district magistrate.
When the Cold Food Festival was approaching,
the Jīngzhào Prefecture officials demanded almonds from each county
to prepare tribute offerings.
Upon hearing this,
he considered it highly improper,
and single-handedly opposed it.
He then went to the palace to request an audience.
The Jīngzhào officials also feared this recluse might have some unusual opinion;
what were they to do?
When he was summoned for the audience,
he addressed the Emperor:
"Your Majesty wants almonds for the Cold Food Festival.
Now your servant has knocked them and brought them;
how can I present whole almonds again?"
The Emperor chuckled and dismissed him,
and in the end did not punish him for his crime.
From "Idle Talk from the Jade Hall"
Lǐ Zuǒ
Lǐ Zuǒ of the Táng dynasty
was from a prominent clan in Shāndōng.
In his youth, due to the Ān-Shǐ Rebellion,
he lost his father.
Later, Zuǒ passed the imperial examinations as a Jìnshì,
gained a good reputation,
and served as Deputy Governor of the Capital Prefecture.
He secretly searched for his father.
An acquaintance informed him afterwards,
and he went to welcome him from a family that sold funeral objects.
He brought him home and provided for him.
This continued for many months.
One day,
his father summoned Zuǒ and said to him:
"Your filial piety is unparalleled.
However, I have been among this group for thirty years.
Since I came with you,
I have not yet bid farewell to my companions.
You should prepare five large pigs,
several hú of white wine,
several jars of garlic paste,
and ten platters of thin cakes.
Set up a feast in the central hall,
so that I may have one final gathering with my group to express our feelings.
Then I will have no regrets."
Zuǒ respectfully obeyed his instruction,
and after several days everything was prepared.
His father summoned a hundred skilled singers of funeral dirges from both markets.
At first, they sat in rows in the hall.
After a long while, they began singing mixed songs.
By evening, they were all drunk.
The crowd helped Zuǒ's father onto a couch.
Then, with one cry of a funeral dirge,
all hundred joined in harmony.
Suddenly, they supported his father and left,
and no one knew where they went.
Tens of thousands of passersby watched.
The next day,
Zuǒ abandoned his family and entered the mountains,
and died after a few days.
From "Records of Unique Events"
Yuán Zǎi and Cháng Gǔn
Emperor Dàizōng of Táng entrusted all governmental affairs to his chancellors.
Yuán Zǎi monopolized power,
further corrupting the laws of the state.
Without fine gold and heavy bribes,
or resorting to crooked paths and hesitation,
one could not gain access to the court.
When Cháng Gǔn became chancellor,
although bribery did not occur,
he was obstinate and self-willed,
lacking in discernment.
Therefore, promotions and demotions were often mistaken.
If his colleagues submitted proposals somewhat frequently,
he would call them "repetitive old men."
At that time, a saying circulated in the capital:
"Cháng has no discernment, Yuán loves money;
the worthy become fools,
the fools become worthy."
Cuī Yòufǔ was always fair and upright.
Amidst the crowd, he proclaimed loudly:
"The court, from top to bottom, deceives one another;
good and evil are treated alike.
Pure offices and lofty ministries
serve only as places for petty men to accumulate seniority and qualifications.
How can this benefit the imperial transformation?"
From "The Dūyáng Miscellany"
Cuī Qiān
When Emperor Shùnzōng of Táng was Crown Prince,
Wěi Qú recommended Cuī Qiān.
He was appointed Tutor [Yùdé]
and served as Calligraphy Instructor.
Qiān was utterly ignorant of affairs.
Addressing the Crown Prince, he said:
"Your subject is a rustic from the mountains and wilds;
I am unfamiliar with court rituals.
When I see Your Majesty, should I refer to myself as 'chén' (your subject)?"
The Crown Prince said:
"You are an official of the palace establishment;
you should naturally know this."
From "Records of Refined Conversation"
Lí Gàn
During the reign of Emperor Dàizōng of Táng,
the Capital Prefecture Governor, Lí Gàn, due to a prolonged drought,
prayed for rain at the Zhūquè Gate Street.
He constructed an earthen dragon,
summoned all the shamans and sorcerers in the city,
and had them dance around the dragon.
Gàn himself took turns dancing with the shamans and sorcerers,
causing the spectators to be shocked and to laugh.
After a full month without rain,
he also requested to pray at the temple of King Wénxuān [Confucius].
The Emperor heard of this and said:
"Qiū has been praying for a long time."
He ordered the earthen dragon destroyed,
the rain prayers stopped,
reduced his meals and practiced frugality,
to await Heaven's mandate.
Thereupon, ample sweet rain fell.
From "Miscellaneous Stories of the Lú Family"
Cuī Shūqīng
When Dù Yòu of the Táng dynasty governed Huáinán,
he presented one hundred poems by Cuī Shūqīng [to the throne].
Emperor Dézōng said to the messenger:
"These are terrible poems;
what use is presenting them?"
People of the time called them "the officially decreed bad poems."
From "Supplement to the National History"

and was further besieged by Zhū Cǐ's troops,

Cuī Sǔn
During the Táng, Cuī Sǔn
was extremely cautious by nature.
Every time he responded to the emperor's questions,
he did not dare to express any personal views.
He held all the important and prestigious posts in the two central departments,
serving in each one,
yet during his tenure, he earned no praise from others.
He occupied the position of chief minister.
His mother was buried in the wilderness,
yet he never spoke of visiting her grave,
nor discussed moving her remains for proper burial

Zhāng Màozhāo
During the Táng, when Zhāng Màozhāo served as a military governor,

someone among the officials asked him:
"I've heard that while governing, Your Excellency enjoyed human flesh;
is it true or false?"
Màozhāo laughed and said:
"Human flesh is rank and tough,
how could one bear to eat it?"

From "Lúshì Záshuō"
Lǐ Xiùcai
When Táng Dynasty official Lǐ Bō was serving as prefect of Qízhōu,
a certain Lǐ, claiming to be a candidate for the imperial examinations, came to pay him a visit.
It happened that Bō was ill,
so his sons received the visitor.
Looking over the poetry collection he presented,
they found it was entirely Bō’s own work.
After the visitor had left,
they showed it to Bō.
Startled, he said:
“This is the very collection I submitted when I sat for the examinations long ago,
only the name has been changed.”
The next day,
he sent his son to invite Mr. Lǐ over,
and calmly questioned him, saying:
“On my father’s behalf, I must ask:
is this collection not something you, sir, composed yourself?”
Upon hearing this, Mr. Lǐ
changed color and said:
“This is the product of a lifetime of my earnest labor;
it is no falsehood.”
The son then said:
“This is my father’s collection from his own examination days.
Moreover, the handwriting has not been altered.
I must ask you, sir, not to speak falsely.”
Immediately he said:
“I have indeed been deceitful all along.
Twenty years ago,
I actually bought this in a bookstore in the capital
for a hundred coins.
I truly did not know it was the fine work of your esteemed father, the Director.
I am overwhelmed with fear and trepidation.”
The son reported this back to Bō,
who laughed and said:
“This is surely a man of no ability.
What is strange about that?
To be so poor and hungry
is truly pitiable.”
He then provided him with provisions
and had his son invite him to dine in the study.
A few days later,
as Mr. Lǐ was taking his leave to go elsewhere,
Bō gave him some silk.
On that day, Bō finally granted him an audience.
Mr. Lǐ bowed in thanks for the previous matters, then
added:
“I have been carrying your esteemed collection, Director,
traveling between the Jiāng and Huái regions
for twenty years now.
Now I wish to beg you to bestow it upon me.
May I?
What I value is that it will bring glory to my travels.”
Bō said:
“This is something I kept from my youthful, unsuccessful years.
Now that I am old and serving as a prefect,
it is of no use to me.
I can simply present it to you.”
Showing no sign of shame,
he promptly tucked it into his sleeve.
Bō then asked:
“Where does the candidate plan to go now?”
The man said:
“I am going to Jiānglíng
to pay a visit to my maternal uncle, Minister Lú.”
Bō asked:
“What office does your esteemed uncle hold?”
He replied:
“He currently serves as Military Commissioner of Jīngnán.”
Bō said:
“What is his name?”
He answered:
“His name is Lú Hóngxuān.”
Bō clapped his hands and laughed heartily, saying:
“Candidate, you are mistaken again!
Minister Lú of Jīngmén
is my own maternal uncle.”
The man, ashamed and flustered, lost his composure.
He then pressed on, saying:
“If what you, Director, say is true,
then I will take the Jīngnán uncle as well,
for the time being.”
Thereupon he bowed twice and hurried out.
Bō sighed:
“How can there be such a man in this world!”
In Qízhōu, everyone talked about it as a joke.
From *The New Account of the Great Táng*.

Wáng Chū and His Brother
During the Chángqìng and Tàihé eras of the Táng Dynasty,
Wáng Chū and Wáng Zhé
both achieved success in the imperial examinations.
Their father, Wáng Zhòngshū, was prominent at the time.

they did not serve in the Imperial Library

("Saying" was originally written as "and";

From *Records of Unique Events*.
Lǐ Jù
Lǐ Jù of the Táng Dynasty
was the nephew of Chancellor Lǐ Jiàng.
He grew up in luxury.
He had never studied,
and obtained the post of Assistant Magistrate of Miǎnchí through hereditary privilege.
During the New Year festival,
he demanded fish but could not get any.
Angry, he summoned the fisherman.
The fisherman said:
“Because otters are rampant,
I dare not catch fish.”
Lǐ Jù wrote his judgment:
“As we approach the New Year,
fierce beasts alarm people.
The fishing net is extremely wide;
loose yet nothing slips through.
Dismissed.”
Also, when a subordinate requested leave,
he wrote his judgment on the petition:
“You must arrive by dusk of the day you leave,
and be released by dawn of the night you return.”
The subordinate ultimately did not dare to go.
He also passed judgment on the subordinate:
“So foolish and stubborn;
how could he deserve a beating?
Sentence: five strokes.”
Someone remarked:
“'How could he deserve a beating?'
means he should not be sentenced.”
Lǐ said:
“What do you understand?
'How could' is an auxiliary word;
what difference is there from 'zhi', 'hu', 'zhe', 'ye'?”

Zhèng Guāng
Táng Dynasty: Zhèng Guāng was appointed Military Commissioner of Hézhōng.
Emperor Xuānzōng asked him:
"When you were in Fèngxiáng,
who was your Administrative Assistant?"
Guāng replied:
"Féng Sān."
The Emperor did not understand.
The Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs reported:
"It is Féng Yǎn.
I once served as an envoy there,
so I know."
The Emperor said:
"Then make Féng Sān his Deputy Commissioner."
Later, when Guāng was relieved of his post in Hézhōng and returned,
he was summoned for an audience again.
The Emperor said:
"Your administration in Hézhōng was excellent."
Guāng replied:
"I had to 'open and begin' to achieve it."
When discussing other matters further,
he said:
"It wouldn't do;
I had to 'tear and begin' to achieve it."
The Emperor laughed heartily.
Afterwards, whenever court officials attended the Yányīng Hall,
entering the pavilion to await audience,
they often used "open and begin" as a catchphrase.
At that time, Vice-Director Péi Sīqiān served as Sectional Administrator.
He had once been a guest in Hézhōng.
When he arrived at the commissioner's office,
Péi said:
"My
(Original text: '其',
changed according to the Xǔ version)
official titles and ranks
have all been stripped away by the Department Head."
This was said because he was not addressed by his proper title.
When Guāng was in Hézhōng,
on state memorial days for incense-offering,
he would invite his Administrative Assistant and various guests to feast and drink at the temple.
They played drinking games with commands.
At the time, Reminder Xūe Bǎoxùn
was among the guests present.
Guāng raised his cup and said:
"I'll change the command:
name a fruit from something on your body."
He said:
"Belly-button."
The others all pondered but couldn't figure it out.
When it was Xūe's turn to give a command,
he said:
"Foot apricot."
The whole room burst into laughter.
From "Lú Shì Zá Shuō".
Zhèng Tián and Lú Xié
Táng Dynasty: Chancellors Zhèng Tián and Lú Xié were close relatives,
and both served in the Secretariat.
Due to disagreements over official matters,
they exchanged insults
(The character for 'insult' was originally missing,
added according to the Huáng version)
even to the point of throwing inkstones at each other.
Contemporaries called it "Chancellors Brawling."
Because of this, both were sent out of the capital.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Zhèng Qǐ
Táng Dynasty: Chancellor Zhèng Qǐ, though famous for poetry,
originally had no aspirations for high office.
At that time, imperial discipline was already in disarray,
and troubles arose from all directions.
Since his talent was not exceptional,
his words were inevitably ambiguous.
When the Tàiyuán army reached the north of the Wèi River,
the Son of Heaven was terrified,
desperately seeking strategies to defeat the rebels.
Qǐ memorialized:
"I request adding the character 'zhé' to the posthumous title of Confucius."
This was typical of his proposals.
His colleagues, considering him unworthy,
often mocked and belittled him.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Zhèng Zhǔn
Táng Dynasty: Zhèng Zhǔn of Xíngyáng relied on his literary skills to serve Chéng Ruì in Jīngzhōu.
He often wished to emulate Chén Lín and Ruǎn Yǔ,
compiling his own writings into ten volumes,
titled "Liú Biǎo's Military Documents".
However,
(The characters 'shū ér' were originally reversed,
changed according to Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán, ch. 7)
his literary style was inelegant.
For example, in a letter congratulating a court dignitary, he wrote:
"The Secretariat Drafter drafts the edict,
the Receptionist says it's acceptable."
Also, in a letter congratulating Zhào Hóngsì of Xiāngzhōu on inheriting his post, he wrote:
"Without bathing and wearing jade like Shí Qí's omen,
nor climbing mountains to retrieve tallies like Wú Xù's enfeoffment."
This clearly implied the recipient's humble origins.
For the poetry scroll submitted during the examinations,
his poem titled "Water Buffalo" said:
"Guarding its calf, it stands blocking the way;
meeting people, it lifts its tail and jumps."
Court officials found this highly amusing.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
The Zhāng Family Son
Táng Dynasty: Zhāng Tí had five sons:
Wénwèi, Yíxiàn, Jìměi, Rénguī,
all achieved fame in the examinations,
rising to the positions of Chancellor, Vice-Chancellor, or Directors.
One son's name is forgotten.
In his youth, he heard it said
that silverfish entering Taoist scripture boxes,
because they gnawed on the characters for 'immortal',
their bodies turned multicolored.
If a person could catch and swallow such a silverfish,
they would become an immortal and ascend.
The Zhāng son was moved by this tale.
He then wrote the characters for 'immortal',
cut them up and placed them in a bottle,
caught silverfish and put them in,
hoping they would gnaw on the characters.
He also intended to swallow them,
but this led to a mental disorder.
Each time it flared up,
he would not eat for a whole month,
his speech became crude and foul,
with no sense of propriety.
His family would lock him up and guard him,
waiting for his recovery.
Once recovered, he was normal,
but would eat double the usual monthly ration,
requiring fine delicacies to satisfy him.
He died after many years.
This shows that the mind is a spiritual entity;
once the vital spirit is injured,
even good intentions cannot help,
let alone evil ones?
Just as Liú Pì swallowed people,
the Zhāng son swallowed immortals.
Though good and evil differ,
the harm done is the same.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Liú Yìfāng
Táng Dynasty: Liú Yìfāng,

with the rhyme scheme based on "judging its thickness".
After Yìfāng completed his rhapsody
(The character for 'rhapsody' was originally missing,

"For the 'thick' rhyme,
I have a couplet that hits the mark."
Then he recited:
"Hanging it on the wall,
it resembles a helmet;
wearing it on the head,
it is again like a straw hat."
(Note: 'Mò hòu fǎn' likely indicates a pronunciation or tonal note, possibly for the character 帽 (mào) meaning 'hat'.)
Everyone found it hilarious.
Zhèng Qúnyù
In the Eastern Market of the Táng dynasty, there was an ironware shop.
There lived a diviner named Fàn,
who would predict the success or failure of candidates in the imperial examinations.
Each divination cost one bolt of silk.
A xiùcai

His family lived by the seaside,

When he came to present his compositions,
he looked down upon his peers,
[The two characters "tóng bèi" were originally missing,

His servants and horses were splendidly adorned.
So he brought three thousand strings of cash,

Fàn was delighted by the unusual gifts,
and after casting the divination, he said:
"Xiùcai, you are assured of complete success."
Qúnyù's confidence grew even higher.
When he entered the examination hall,
he brought many more precious items,
cooked them and sat enjoying them,

Seeing the examination papers of others,
he noticed many
[The character "duō" was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition.]

[The character "dǎ" was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition.]

At daybreak,

From "Gàn Zuǐ Zǐ."
Méi Quánhéng
In the Táng dynasty, Méi Quánhéng
was a man from Wú.
He entered the examination without bringing any books or notes,
and everyone considered him a prodigy.
When the prefectural examination topic was "Rhapsody on the Green Jade Table,"
with the rhyme scheme based on "yóu rán yì zhí zǐ liàng zhī xīn,"
the candidates in the hall debated how to rhyme the character "liàng."
Quánhéng, under a tree in the courtyard,
used a short whip to sketch his draft on the ground.
By late afternoon,
Quánhéng had completed his poem and rhapsody.
Zhāng Jìxiá stepped forward
and asked Quánhéng how he had rhymed the character "liàng" in the rhapsody he submitted,
wishing to take it as a model.
Quánhéng then said loudly:
"Rhyming requires deliberation;
why compete in the jìnshì examination?"
Jìxiá modestly claimed his own inadequacy,
and led several dozen people to seek further instruction.
Quánhéng said:
"This rhyme is difficult to handle.
Gentlemen, please sit in the hall
and listen to whether my rhyming makes sense."
Then he chanted clearly:
"Dim and dark,
within it there is substance;
Dark and dim,
within it there is 'liàng';
A dog crouches beside it,
an owl flaps above it."
Quánhéng further explained:
"The green jade table
is a dining table,
hence the line 'a dog crouches beside it,
an owl flaps above it.'"
The crowd burst into laughter.
From "Gàn Zuǐ Zǐ."
Lǐ Yúnhàn
During the Xiántōng reign of the Zhōu [Táng] dynasty,
jǔrén Lǐ Yúnhàn composed a "Rhapsody on Lip Balm,"

"Before the window, distant peaks hang with raw jade-green;

"Yán Huí is like the blue sky,"

Among the candidates, there were those who annually composed anonymous satires,

The year Xiāo Xiàng presided over the examinations,

That year,
Lú Yōng wept for half a day in front of the temple of King Xuān of Wén.

Hán Jiǎn
In the Táng dynasty, military governor of Wèi-Bó, Hán Jiǎn, was crude and simple by nature.
Whenever he faced literary scholars,
he could not understand their discussions,
and often felt ashamed in his heart.
So he summoned a xiàolián to lecture on the "Analects."
When they reached the "Wéi Zhèng" chapter,
the next day he said to his staff:
"I have recently learned that the ancients were simple and honest;
only at the age of thirty
were they able to walk and stand."
Those who heard this outside
could not help but laugh uproariously.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Hú Lìng
In Fèngxiān County, there was a magistrate,
surnamed Hú,
whose given name is forgotten.
He was greedy for wealth and stingy with food,
and had a peculiar fondness for board games.
A visiting official named Zhāng Xúnguān,
sharing the same hobby,
often interacted with him quite amiably.
Every time they played chess,
it would last from morning till dusk.
Their skill levels were evenly matched,
so they never grew tired of it.
However, Magistrate Hú would occasionally go inside his inner quarters,
and after a short while,
return to continue the game.
This happened day after day—
he would arrive early and leave late—
yet he never offered Zhāng any food,
leaving him unbearably hungry and cold.
Zhāng secretly realized
that Hú was going inside to eat before coming back out.
One evening, as Zhāng took his leave, he said:
"I must go now;
this is truly 'tāo tiě.'"
Hú merely nodded in agreement.
After Zhāng left,
Hú suddenly pondered and said:
"This man said upon parting:
'This is truly tāo tiě.'
What kind of literary allusion is that?"
He urgently ordered someone to bring Zhāng back.
When Zhāng arrived,
Hú asked:
"Sir, you just said 'this is truly tāo tiě.'
What does it mean?"
Zhāng sat back down comfortably
and said to him:
"Does Your Honor not know what tāo tiě is?"
Hú replied:
"I do not."
Zhāng said:
"Have you ever seen blacksmiths
place a long iron rod in the forge?
That is exactly it.
When the fire in the furnace is blazing fiercely,
and the iron has not yet fully melted,
they use this rod to stir the fierce fire in the furnace,
then take it out;
after a while, they stir the fierce fire again,
then take it out.
That is precisely tāo tiě."
Having said this, he left.
Hú went into his room
and told his wife and children about it.
After pondering it repeatedly,
he finally realized it was a satire on his habit of going inside every day,
stirring the fierce fire (i.e., eating),
then coming back out to play chess.
For those who are stingy with food and tire out their guests,
people of the time often used this phrase to mock them.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"

Xiè Chái Shū
In the Táng dynasty, there was a high-ranking palace official who learned to write in a peculiar style.
The military governor of Fèngxiáng sent him several cartloads of firewood,
and in his reply, he wrote:
"I am grateful for the gift of so much 'yú'."
From "Lúshì Záshuō"
During the Tang dynasty, a young man from a wealthy family was appointed as the regional governor.
The local people went to great lengths to welcome and await his arrival.
The outgoing governor arranged a handover ceremony for him.
The ceremony was conducted without any omissions.
Two ceremonial assistants, wearing official hats and ceremonial robes,
guided the host and guest through the rituals,
including ascending and descending steps, bowing, and yielding.
However, the new governor appeared awkward and uneasy,
composing his expression and lowering his gaze,
not daring to face the ceremonial assistants directly.
After the ceremony concluded,
he repeatedly sent messengers to convey his words,
expressing gratitude and appreciation,
but no one could fully grasp his intentions.
The next day,
he summoned the ceremonial assistants to his inner chamber.
The assistants were extremely apprehensive,
unsure of how to conduct themselves.
Once seated,
the governor, with a furrowed brow, whispered,
"Is your esteemed father well?"
The assistants merely murmured in agreement.
He continued,
"In recent years, when handling important matters,
I have greatly troubled your esteemed father's mind and efforts."
The assistants were left bewildered.
After they were dismissed,
a close acquaintance inquired in detail,
and the governor explained,
"These ceremonial assistants are descendants of the Fangxiang family.
In the past, I once employed their father,
hence my repeated expressions of gratitude.
Moreover, among the scholarly class, there are those who deliberately act frivolously,
and there are also those who are ignorant and unable to distinguish properly.
This is indeed true."
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Zhāng Xiánguāng
During the Liáng dynasty's Lóngdé era,
there was a poor scholar named Zhāng Xiánguāng,
who wandered about begging without restraint.
Between the regions of Liáng and Sòng,
there was also a man named Liú Yuèmíng,
who was similar to Xiánguāng.
He often carried a spoon and chopsticks with him.
Whenever he visited the homes of the wealthy,
he would be subjected to playful harassment.
Just as he was about to eat, his spoon and chopsticks would be snatched away,
but he would then produce another set from his sleeve and continue using them.
Wēn Jī, the son-in-law of the Liáng emperor and an advisor,
was temporarily serving as the administrator of Kāifēng Prefecture.
Xiánguāng suddenly went around bidding farewell to all the wealthy families.
When asked where he was going,
he replied,
"I am going to seek out Advisor Wēn."
When asked what recommendation he had to present,
he answered,
"In recent years, I have greatly benefited from his records.
This visit is sure to be met with generous treatment.
The great advisor once composed the 'Ridgepole Raising Text for the Hidden Dragon Palace on Jiéshān,'"
which said:
"The steamed buns are as big as bowls,
the flatbreads are like sieves.
They delight Liú Yuèmíng, the registrar,
and thrill Zhāng Xiánguāng, the scholar.
From this, I know I will surely receive his favor."
Those who heard this were utterly amused.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
The Long-Bearded Monk
In the region of Sānshǔ, there was a long-bearded elder monk
who claimed to be the son of the chancellor Kǒng Qiān,
though no one knew who he really was.
He did not shave his hair or beard,
which flowed white down to his abdomen.
Leading a following of over a hundred people,
he entered Shǔ from the Jiāng-Hú region.
Wherever he went, the common people,
astonished by his appearance,
competed to rush forward and bow at his feet.
In every place he passed through,
the entire city would turn out to see him.
With his deep-set eyes and wide mouth,
people found him unfathomable.
Upon reaching Shǔ,
he was welcomed with conch shells and cymbals.
He first paid a visit to the Privy Councilor Sòng Guāngsì,
who asked him,
"Master, why do you not shave your beard?"
He replied,
"Shaving the head removes烦恼,
but keeping the beard signifies manhood."
Sòng, greatly annoyed, said,
"I have no beard. Does that make me an old woman?"
He then had him escorted out,
instructing him to return only after shaving his beard for an audience.
Since his followers were numerous,
he lingered for about ten days,
but eventually had no choice but to shave his beard and enter.
His followers, ashamed of his loss of integrity,
all dispersed and left him.
The ruler of the pseudo-Shǔ state asked him,
"From afar, I have heard of the master's reputation for having a long beard.
How did it come to be like this?"
He replied,
"When I was in the Jiāng-Hú region,
I heard that Your Majesty had already attained the fruit of Srotāpanna,
so I came with my beard intact.
Now, seeing that Your Majesty is about to attain the fruit of Anāgāmin,
I have shaved my beard to appear before you."
The young ruler did not understand at first,
but after nodding in agreement,
and upon explanation by his close ministers,
he burst into hearty laughter.
Later, the monk became the abbot of Jìngluàn Temple.
He was frequently involved in disputes with the congregation.
One of his senior disciples
was punished for impropriety.
A performer named Zàng Kēqǔ deeply admired the Buddhist monastic life
but was unaware of its sordid details.
Believing it to be pure and serene,
he renounced secular life and shaved his head.
He diligently attended to his alms bowl and robes,
but gradually witnessed corruption and depravity.
Cursing, he left,
hanging his monastic robe on the temple gate, saying,
"I had grown weary of the mundane world
and sought refuge in a place of purity
to cleanse my karmic obstructions.
But now, the master's gate
is worse than the brothel district.
I cannot be part of this."
He then returned to his life as a performer.
The people of Shǔ said of the monk,
"One thing is lacking in the south,
and the long beard is shorn."
From "Wángshì Jiànwén"
The Daoist
□□□□□ served as a military judge in Xìngyuán.
Having left his hometown in Qínzhōu,
not even a year had passed
when someone suddenly came looking for him as a teacher.
This person brought a sealed letter from his relative, Liú Jiān, the prefect of Shīzhōu,
and arrived wearing purple robes,
also mentioning that he was going to Yángzhōu to seek something.
When asked about his background,
he said,
"I am fortunate to share a hometown connection.
Previously, I entered the Daoist order at the Xīshēng Temple in Qínzhōu
and have been a Daoist for many years."
The judge pondered this deeply,
recalling that when he left his hometown,
there was no such Daoist at the temple.
He was deeply suspicious of the man's official robes and his requests.
The man also passed through in a hurried manner.
Within a month,
he returned from Yángyuán,
having obtained a small amount of goods.
His intention to bid farewell
was also expressed with great haste.
The judge then devised a plan to detain him,
preparing a bed and inviting him to stay.
In the stillness of the night,
after plying him with several bowls of strong wine,
he slowly inquired,
"Venerable Master, where did you obtain the purple sash you wear?
You should tell me truthfully."
The man replied,
"This is the official robe of my late master,
passed down for me to wear.
I was originally a disciple of the purple-robed monk at Guǎngxiū Temple.
After my master passed away,
I left the Buddhist order
and joined the Xīshēng Temple to become a Daoist.
I then wore this purple robe."
He claimed to have inherited his master's robe and bowl,
but how could a Daoist steal the purple robe of his former
Buddhist master?
Such a thing had never been heard of before.
From "Yùtáng Xiánhuà"
Three Foolish Men
When Sūn Guāngxiàn was in Shǔ,
he once went to Zīzhōu,
where he met Lǐ Dàoshi of Yìngzhēn Temple.
He mentioned that in the prefecture there was a man surnamed Zhào,
who secluded himself and kept his gate closed,
aspiring to serve in the imperial court.
The capital military commissioner Yán Pǔ, finding this remarkable,
personally went to pay him a visit.
Yán was a tall and sturdy man.
When Zhào greeted him at the door,
he stared in astonishment for a long time,
then bowed deeply and exchanged pleasantries, saying:
"I humbly greet the fierce beast."
Yán then inquired of the person who had introduced him,
asking him to find out what this meant.
Zhào said:
"If one speaks of bears and panthers,
that requires the talent of a prime minister
to warrant such a description.
Commissioner Yán, being only a capital commander,
should merely be called a fierce beast."
When people heard this, they all laughed at him.
Another scholar, who called himself Attendant Zhāng,
complained to Guāngxiàn, saying:
"My elder brother uses sorcery to bewilder my mind."
Guāngxiàn asked him:
"Could it be the art of gu poison or curses?"
Zhāng said:
"No,
it is using the Guǐgǔzǐ's methods of opening and closing,
to split and break my mind and spirit,
so that I still suffer from uncontrollable mental agitation."
Also, in Jiānglíng, there was a man named Yán Yún,
who happened to acquire Zhūgě Liàng's book on military strategy.
He claimed he could command an army of a hundred thousand,
and conquer the entire realm.
Whenever he discussed military affairs,
he would roll up his sleeves and shout fiercely,
as if facing a formidable enemy.
People at the time called this "wrestling by the manual."
At that time, there was an army deputy commander named Wáng,
a veteran general from Yōuyān,
renowned throughout the land.
Yán Yún went to pay his respects,
claiming to be a fellow enthusiast,
and said that his great ambitions remained unfulfilled
(the character for 'fulfilled' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
and that he had lost a good friend,
so he often wept bitterly over it.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Zhōu
(the character 'Zhōu' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
Wéi Xùn
was the son of Grand Commandant Zhāodù.
He was weak, cowardly, dull, and obtuse,
and was entirely governed by maids and old women.
He served under the Wáng clan of the false Shǔ regime,
and due to past connections, they treated him leniently,
so he rose to the rank of a high minister.
Sometimes he was ridiculed by his colleagues,
who said:
"A dead rat comes out from the gate of the Three Excellencies."
Xùn retorted:
"The Three Excellencies come out from the gate of a dead rat."
Zhōu was the son of the Shǔ chancellor Zhōu Bóyǎ,
and served as the Wáng clan's Commandant of the Imperial Guards.
His nature and understanding were vulgar and base.
After the state fell,
he associated with poor beggars.
He would have one person go ahead to announce his titles and hometown in the markets and taverns,
and those who pitied him
would give him two or three hundred coins a day.
He would then just drink and eat with his companions.
Everyone sighed over this.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán."
Not Recognizing a Mirror
There was a commoner's wife who did not recognize a mirror.
Her husband bought one and brought it home.
The wife took it and looked into it,
then exclaimed in surprise to her mother:
"My husband has brought another woman home."
Her mother also looked into it and said:
"And he's brought his mother-in-law along too."
From "Xiào Lín."
Biting Off a Nose
A and B got into a fight,
and A bit off B's nose.
When the officials wanted to decide the case,
A claimed that B had bitten it off himself.
The official said:
"A person's nose is high and the mouth is low;
how could one bite one's own nose?"
A said:
"He stepped on a stool to reach it and bit it off."
From "Xiào Lín."
Assisting with Funeral Rites
Someone went to offer condolences at a funeral
and wanted to bring something to assist the family.
He asked someone:
"What can I give?"
The reply was:
"Money, cloth, or silk—
whatever you have."
So he brought a hu of soybeans,
placed them before the filial son,
and said:
"I have nothing else,
so I'll help you with this hu of soybeans."
The filial son wept, saying, "What can a lonely, poor man do?"
The man said:
"Make fermented beans
(the character for 'fermented beans' was originally written as 'drum,'
corrected according to the Huáng edition)."
The filial son again wept about being poor and alone,
saying:
"Just when I thought it couldn't get worse,
you send me another stone."
From "Xiào Lín."
Returning from Studies Elsewhere
A's parents were alive.
He went away to study for three years and then returned.
His maternal uncle asked him what he had gained from his studies
and also inquired about his long separation from his father.
He replied:
"My longing for my uncle surpasses even that of Qín Kāng for his."
Later, his father scolded him:
"What good did your studies do you?"
He replied:
"I lacked my father's instruction from a young age,
so my studies were of no benefit."
From "Xiào Lín."
Attending a Funeral
Some rustic folk wanted to attend a funeral together,
but none knew the proper etiquette.
One said he was somewhat familiar with it
and told his companions:
"Just follow my lead."
When they arrived at the funeral,
the one who claimed familiarity went first,
prostrated himself on the mat,
and the others, one by one, prostrated behind him, pressing against his back.
The leader,
kicking with his foot, cursed:
"You fools!"
The others thought this was part of the ritual,
so each in turn kicked and said:
"You fools!"
The last one was near the filial son,
so he also kicked the filial son and said:
"You fool!"
From "Xiào Lín."
The Foolish Son-in-Law
There was a foolish son-in-law.
When his father-in-law died,
his wife taught him how to perform the mourning rites.
On the way, he encountered water,
so he took off his socks to cross,
but
(the character 'but' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
he left one sock behind.
Then he heard a turtledove in the woods calling:
"Gūgū gūgū."
He silently recited this
and completely forgot the mourning etiquette.
When he arrived,
he stood on one foot with a sock on,
tucking the bare foot up,
and just said:
"Gūgū gūgū."
The filial sons all laughed.
He then said:
"Don't laugh, don't laugh.
If you find my sock,
return it to me."
From "Xiào Lín."
The Man from Lǔ Holding a Pole
In Lǔ, there was a man holding a long pole trying to enter the city gate.
At first, he held it vertically,
but could not get it through;
he then held it horizontally,
but still could not enter.
He was at a loss for a solution.
Soon an old man arrived and said:
"I am not a sage,
but I have seen many things.
Why not saw it in half and then enter?"
So he followed the advice and cut it.
From Xiào Lín.
A Man from Qí Learns the Sè
A man from Qí went to a man from Zhào to learn the sè,
and because the latter had already tuned it beforehand,
he glued the tuning pegs and returned home.
For three years, he could not play a single tune.
The man from Qí found it strange.
When someone came from Zhào,
he asked about the reason,
and only then realized the foolishness of that man.
From Xiào Lín.
Buying a Horse
In Luòyáng, there was a high official
whose family had long been wealthy and noble.
He could not distinguish between male and female.
Once he bought a horse,
and had no idea whether it was good or bad.
He was deceived by a horse dealer
(the character 'suǒ' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
who said:
"This horse is not only gentle and tame,
but also over twenty years old.
It is worth the price of two horses.
Moreover, when it walks, it doesn't stir up dust—
truly the epitome of gentleness."
So he paid a large sum to buy it.
The dealer thus doubled his profit.
As he was leaving, he added:
"This horse even has quince-like teeth protruding."
The official was overjoyed.
The next morning, he rode it out,
and it walked like a goose or duck.
When he returned home,
he boasted proudly:
"This horse is not only gentle and well-trained,
but also comes with two extra fruit-like teeth."
He summoned the dealer again,
and gave him an additional twenty coins.
From Yùtáng Xiánhuà.
The Scholar of Zhāoyìng
During the Táng dynasty, an imperial decree was issued
to seek out those with talent and virtue who did not pursue fame or advancement.
Someone in Zhāoyìng
encountered a scholar
hurrying into the capital.
When asked what he was seeking,
he replied:
"I am going to take the 'Not Seeking Fame or Advancement' examination."
From Yīnhuà Lù.
Liú Jièzhī
During the Tiānshòu era of the Táng dynasty,
Liú Jièzhī of Péngchéng,
coarse and reckless, ill-mannered,
spoke both lofty and vulgar words,
insulted superiors and disregarded inferiors,
extorted money and goods,
had no restraint in speech,
and spread false rumors of disasters.
He demanded one hundred thousand coins
from Cháng Yànwěi, the county captain of Wànnián,
saying:
"I am Liú Guǒyì,
and I will bring you wealth and honor."
Yànwěi submitted a report accusing him.
The emperor ordered two attendants to first enter Yànwěi's room,
lower the curtain, and sit by the window to listen.
After a while,
Jièzhī and Lú Qiānrèn arrived,
sat in the hall,
and conversed.
Yànwěi led them to discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the state,
with no restraint or taboo,
and the attendants recorded everything in writing to present to the emperor.
The emperor was enraged
and ordered the imperial guards to arrest them.
He personally interrogated them,
and they confessed fully.
Jièzhī was then cut in half at the waist,
Qiānrèn was sentenced to hanging,
and Yànwěi was appointed as a palace censor.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Zōng Xuánchéng
In the Táng dynasty, Lǎo Sānwèi Zōng Xuánchéng,
a native of Nánhé, Xíngzhōu.
His grandfather was a deputy director of the imperial secretariat.
Xuánchéng was by nature crude and violent,
endowed with a fierce and domineering temperament,
oppressing the villages,
and running rampant through the prefectures and counties.
When Prince Jì was the prefect of Xíngzhōu,
Xuánchéng acted defiantly against him.
Lǐ Bèi was the magistrate of Nánhé,
and upon hearing of this,
he would descend the steps to receive him,
treating him as an equal,
striving to win him over,
thus nurturing his wickedness.
When a famine struck Héshuò,
granaries were opened for relief,
and Xuánchéng, relying on his influence,
asserted his authority in the countryside,
forcibly demanding one shí of grain.
Bèi was with a guest and did not summon him,
so Xuánchéng raised his voice outside the gate,
rolled up his sleeves, and barged straight in.
Bèi gathered over a hundred clerks and officials inside the gate,
drafted a document to investigate thoroughly,
and confirmed the forced demand as true.
First, he ordered a chain placed around his neck,
then a cangue placed over the chain.
Once the legal documents were complete,
he was sentenced to sixty strokes,
and died under the beating.
No one dared to speak of it.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Mèng Shénshuǎng,
a native of Yángzhōu,
was by nature cruel and vicious,
with a heart as poisonous as a venomous bird.
Patrolling the market to demand goods,
they would come at his call;
entering an inn to demand money,
it would arrive with his words.
Prefects and county magistrates
would bow deeply to him,
while assistant magistrates and clerks
would merely nod.
When Zhāng Qián became the prefect of Yángzhōu,
he heard of his violent and lawless behavior,
and ordered the magistrate of Jiāngdū County to arrest him at an inn.
Dragged into the prefectural gate,
a loud order was given to quickly hand him over to Legal Officer Lǐ Guǎngyè for interrogation.
The secret matters were all false,
and according to the imperial decree, he was sentenced to one hundred strokes,
dying under the beating.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
The Imperial Guardsman at the Banquet
When Wǔ Zétiān deposed the Lǔlíng Prince,
over ten imperial guardsmen were drinking together in a guesthouse quarter.
One of them said:
"Had I known there would be no reward today,
I would not have helped to support the Lǔlíng Prince."
One person at the banquet stood up and left,
went to the north gate to submit a report accusing him.
Before the banquet ended,
all were arrested and sent to the imperial guards.
Upon interrogation, it was all confirmed true.
The accuser was granted the fifth rank,
the speaker was beheaded,
and the others who knew of the rebellion but did not report it
were sentenced to hanging.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Hán Lìngguī
The Zhou dynasty clerk Hán Lìngguī was shameless and thick-skinned,
with a fierce and domineering appearance.
He would address dukes and nobles
by their birth order.
Even if he had never met someone before,
he would still force himself upon them.
Once during an official selection,
he was conducting the evaluation under Lù Yuánfāng.
At the time, the Secretariat Drafter Wáng Jù was in mourning leave but had been recalled to duty,
and was sitting in the same hall as Lù.
Guī feigned surprise and said:
"I haven't seen Wáng the Fifth."
Jù then descended the steps
(The original text had "皆" for "steps,"
corrected to "steps" based on the Huáng edition)
looking distressed
(The original text had "silent" for "distressed,"
corrected to "distressed" based on the Huáng edition)
while Lìngguī frowned and knitted his brows,
offering condolences before leaving.
Lù and Wáng were old acquaintances,
so Lù stopped Wáng right there
and asked:
"Who is this Jù?"
He did not recognize him at all.
Later, when his intimidation tactics were exposed,
he was sentenced to caning in the court hall.
From afar, he called out to the Prince of Hénèi, saying:
"Big brother, why won't you save me?"
Yìzōng glared at him and said:
"I don't know you."
The caning was hastened, and he was brutally whipped,
dying under the blows.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Lǐ Hóng
Lǐ Hóng of the Táng dynasty
was from Jùnyí in Biànzhōu.
He was vicious, rebellious, and shameless.
Cruel and merciless.
He often rode tall horses with high saddles,
patrolling the wards and visiting shops,
intimidating officials in charge of corvée labor, taxes, and grain transport,
extorting hundreds of strings of cash at a time.
He forcibly borrowed tens of thousands from merchants,
never repaying a single coin.
Merchants and travelers were terrified,
and transport officials trembled with fear.
When Rèn Zhènglǐ became the Prefect of Biànzhōu,
within ten
(The original text had "下" for "ten,"
corrected to "ten" based on the Huáng edition)
days or so,
he sent officers to arrest him,
sentenced him, and ordered sixty strokes of the cane.
He died under the blows.
Artisans, merchants, and travelers
drank joyfully in celebration.
Those near and far who heard of it
all expressed their delight.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Zhǎngsūn Xīn
Zhǎngsūn Xīn of the Táng dynasty
was the brother-in-law of the Empress.
Along with his wife's cousin Yáng Xiānyù and over twenty horsemen,
they formed a line
(The two characters for "formed a line" were originally missing,
supplemented based on the Huáng edition)
and whipped their horses,
riding through the streets.
The Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Jié was inside a ward visiting his aunt,
with his servants waiting outside the gate.
Xīn and Xiānláng
ordered their slaves to beat Lǐ Jié's attendants.
When Jié came out,
they also assaulted and subdued him.
Shortly after,
the Imperial Guards and officials from Wànnián County arrived,
and took them to the county jail.
Xīn's father-in-law, the Duke Wáng Kāifǔ,
led two hundred horsemen
to forcibly rescue Xīn and the others.
Jié, along with the Imperial Guards and Wànnián County,
reported the matter to the Emperor.
An edict was issued to execute Xīn,
and after receiving several hundred strokes of the cane, he died.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
The Zhāng Yìzhī Brothers
The Zhāng Yìzhī brothers were arrogant and noble,
forcibly seizing manors, houses, slaves, and concubines,
too many to count.
Once, Chāngqī was riding along a street in Wànnián County
when he encountered a woman
walking with her husband, who was carrying their child.
Chāngqī used his horsewhip to flick off her headscarf,
and the woman cursed at him.
Chāngqī turned to his slave and said:
"Carry her away by force."
The husband submitted three or four petitions to the complaint box,
but none received a response.
Chāngqī had him arrested and sent to Wànnián County,
falsely accusing him of another crime,
and had him executed.
Chāngyí often said to people:
"A real man should be like this.
Nowadays, even a thousand people pushing cannot topple me,
but when I fall from power,
ten thousand people lifting cannot raise me up."
Soon afterward, their crimes were exposed,
and both brothers were beheaded.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Quán Huái'ēn
Quán Huái'ēn, the Prefect of Xíngzhōu in the Táng dynasty,
was shameless.
He was appointed as the Chief Clerk of Luòzhōu.
The prefecture sent the Military Advisor Liú Quǎnzi to welcome him.
When they met on the road at Huáizhōu, Quǎnzi bowed.
Huái'ēn rushed past him
without saying a word.
Quǎnzi followed on foot for over two hundred paces,
but Huái'ēn still did not offer him a horse to ride.
Quǎnzi sensed something was amiss,
so he mounted his own horse and rode ahead.
When they reached the relay station,
Huái'ēn ordered him to remove his boots,
and then asked:
"How many Military Advisors are there in Luòzhōu?"
Quǎnzi replied:
"Six regular ones,
and one supernumerary."
Huái'ēn asked:
"How can there be a supernumerary?"
Quǎnzi replied:
"There is one extra
sent to remove the boots for the Chief Clerk."
Huái'ēn was shocked and asked:
"Whose son are you?"
Quǎnzi replied:
"My father is the Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs."
Huái'ēn, stroking his beard, left in embarrassment.
The Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Liú Rénguǐ, said to him:
"You were just a prefect from the countryside;
now that you've come to the capital,
you must not act recklessly.
Although a Military Advisor is lowly
(The original text had "維" for "lowly,"
corrected to "lowly" based on the Huáng edition)
how could you order him to remove your boots?"
Huái'ēn felt ashamed,
requested leave and did not appear again,
and within ten days, he was appointed as the Prefect of Yìzhōu.
From "Records of Affairs from Court and Country"
Sòng Zhīsūn
In the Táng dynasty, Sòng Zhīqiàn was a chéng of Luòyáng,
the younger brother of Sòng Zhīwèn, who was a zhǔbù in the Tàicháng Temple.
He framed and killed the imperial son-in-law Wáng Tóngjiǎo.
Initially,
Zhīqiàn had flattered and attached himself to the brothers Zhāng Yìzhī,
and was sent out to serve as a sīcāng in Yǎnzhōu.
He then fled and returned,
and Wáng Tóngjiǎo hid him in a small room.
Tóngjiǎo was a man of passionate spirit,
who resented the rebellious Empress Wěi and Wǔ Sānsī for bringing chaos to the state.
He would discuss this with one or two close associates,
often gnashing his teeth in anger.
Zhīqiàn eavesdropped from behind the curtain,
and sent his nephew Sòng Tán
to submit a written accusation,
hoping to gain Empress Wěi's favor.
Wǔ Sānsī and others were indeed greatly enraged,
and petitioned to execute Tóngjiǎo and his faction.
The brothers were both appointed to fifth-rank offices:
Zhīqiàn became a guānglù chéng,
Zhīwèn became a hónglú chéng,
and Tán became a shàngyī fèngyù.
The people of the realm resented them,
and all said to each other:
"The crimson robes of Zhīwèn and his kin
are dyed with the blood of Wáng Tóngjiǎo."
After the rebellious Empress Wěi was executed,
Zhīqiàn and others were exiled to Lǐngnán.
A guest asked Fúxiūzǐ:
"What about men like Lái Jùnchén?"
He replied:
"Long ago, the lion king in the deep mountains
caught a jackal,
and was about to eat it.
The jackal said:
'I beg to offer the king two deer to redeem myself.'
The lion king was pleased.
After a full year had passed,
and there was nothing left to offer,
the king said:
'You have killed many living creatures,
now it is your turn.
What will you do about it?'
The jackal fell silent and had no reply,
so he was bitten to death.
Men like Jùnchén,
how are they different from jackals?"
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Zhāng Gàn and Others
In the markets of the capital, there were wicked youths
who typically shaved their heads and tattooed their skin,
depicting all sorts of shapes and forms.
Relying on military connections,
they would raise their fists and commit strong-arm robbery,
even going so far as to use snakes to sell wine,
or grabbing sheep shoulder armor to strike people.
The Jīngzhào yǐn Xuē Yuánshǎng,
upon taking office for three days,
ordered village heads to secretly arrest them,
capturing over thirty men,
all of whom he had beaten to death with rods,
and their corpses displayed in the market.
Any market-goer with blue tattoos
had them burned away.
At that time, a strongman named Zhāng Gàn from Dàníng ward,
had tattooed on his left arm: "In life, I fear not the Jīngzhào yǐn,"
and on his right arm: "In death, I fear not Yánluó Wáng."
There was also Wáng Lìnú,
who paid five thousand coins to hire a tattoo artist,
to cover his chest and abdomen with a mountain pavilion garden, ponds, terraces, plants, trees, birds, and beasts,
all meticulously detailed,
as fine as painted colors.
Lord Xuē had them all beaten to death with rods.
Also, the bandit Zhào Wǔjiàn,
had one hundred and six tattoos of foreign seals, coiled magpies, and the like.
On his right arm was inscribed:
"On the wild chicken beach I lodge,
each dawn the falcon strikes.
Startled, I fly into the water,
my life preserved until this morning."
Also, from Gāolíng county, they captured a tattooed man named Sòng Yuánsù,
with seventy-one tattoos.
On his left arm was inscribed:
"In days gone by, before my family fell poor,
I spared no thousand in gold to befriend kin.
But when distressed I sought a true friend,
through passes and mountains, not a single one was found."
On his right arm was tattooed a gourd,
with a human head emerging from it,
like the Guōgōng in puppet shows.
The county clerks did not understand,
and asked him about it.
He said it was a gourd spirit.
From Yǒuyáng Zázǔ.
Péng Xiānjué
In the Zhōu dynasty, the yùshǐ Péng Xiānjué
was shameless.
During the Rúyì period,
the prohibition on slaughter was extremely strict.
Xiānjué was in charge of inspection duties.
At Dìngdǐng Gate, a cart of hay overturned,
revealing two carcasses of sheep.
The gatekeepers reported it to the yùshǐ.
Xiānjué submitted a memorial requesting:
"The Hé Gōng wèi Liú Miǎn, responsible for slaughter,
failed to detect this.
He should be sentenced to one round of beating with rods.
The meat should be given to the officials of the Southern Office to eat."
Miǎn was terrified,
and sewed new trousers in preparation for punishment.
The next day,
Wǔ Zétiān commented:
"Yùshǐ Péng Xiānjué
petitioned to punish Liú Miǎn.
It is unnecessary.
The meat should be given to Miǎn to eat."
The entire court praised this.
Xiānjué was thus ashamed.
From Cháoyě Qiānzǎi.
Zhōu Chángshòu
During the Zhōu Chángshòu period (these three characters were originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
the prohibition on slaughter was extremely severe.
The left shíyí Zhāng Dé
had a wife who gave birth to a son.
He secretly slaughtered a sheep to feast guests.
On the day
of the feast (these three characters were originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
he invited various yí and bǔ officials.
Dù Sù privately pocketed a piece of meat,
and submitted a memorial accusing him.
The next day,
in court
(these two characters were originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
before
the assembly, Wǔ Zétiān said to Zhāng Dé:
"Your wife has borne a son,
great joy."
Dé bowed in thanks.
Zétiān then said to him:
(these three characters were originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
"But where did you get the meat?"
Dé kowtowed, pleading guilty to a capital offense.
Zétiān said:
"I have prohibited slaughter,
but this does not apply to auspicious or inauspicious occasions.
When you
(these two characters were originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
invite guests,
you must also choose your company carefully.
Unscrupulous people
should not be gathered together."
She then showed Sù's memorial to him.
Sù sweated profusely, drenching his back.
The entire court spat in his face.
A Scholar Swallows a Relic
In Luòyáng during the Táng dynasty,
in recent years there was a monk
who
(this character was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
kept several grains of what are called relics
stored in a glass vessel,
with incense and lamps burning day and night.
Offerings from devotees
never ceased for a day.
There was a scholar, hard-pressed by cold and hunger,
who approached the monk,
wishing to obtain a relic,
to hold it and look at it
(this character was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
The monk then took out the bottle and gave it to him,
whereupon he immediately swallowed it.
The monk was as frantic as if mad,
and further feared the news would spread.
The scholar said:
"Give me some money,
and I will take medicine to pass it out."
The monk was delighted to hear this,
and gave him two hundred strings of coins.
He then took croton seeds.
The monk collected
(these two characters were originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition)
what was excreted, washed it, and retrieved it.
From Shàngshū Gùshì.
Liú Zǐzhèn was
a man from Pú.
He was quite learned,
but lacked understanding of the greater principles,
and was especially fond of bullying his peers,
defaming and attacking high officials.
He felt no shame in seeking favors from prefectural and county authorities;
if they showed the slightest inattention,
he would immediately create trouble for them.
Thus, when he attended examinations at the imperial court,
even in crowded gatherings,
few would stand and converse with him.
During the year when Liú Yǔnzhāng oversaw the examinations,
concerned about the excessive number of scrolls submitted by candidates,
he posted a notice:
"Submitted scrolls must not exceed three volumes."
Zǐzhèn, however, submitted forty scrolls.
As a result, he garnered a terrible reputation.
The original source was missing;
now it is found in *The Collected Sayings*.
The Tattoo Seller in Jīngzhōu
During the Zhēnyuán era in Jīngzhōu,
there was a tattoo seller in the market,
who used stamps
with clusters of needles arranged into shapes of various objects,
such as toads, scorpions, birds, and beasts,
according to the customer's desire.
With one stamp,
brushed with graphite,
after the wound healed,
the mark was finer than those made by Suí Yǒng's stamps.
From *Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng*.
Marriage Customs of the Southern Barbarians
Among the southern barbarians when taking a wife,
if a man fancied a girl from another household,
he would lead a group of youths,
armed with knives and clubs,
to wait along a deserted road to spy,
