and when she passed by,
they would seize and bind her,
and carry her back to be his wife.
After a month or two,
he would go with his wife
to confess the crime to her father and brothers.
This custom was called "the son-in-law who binds the woman."
Unless there was a parental funeral,
he would not return to her family home.
From *Miscellaneous Records of Exile to the Wilderness*.
Zhào Gāo
Lǐ Yíjiǎn
was in Shǔ at the end of the Yuánhé era.
A Shǔ market man named Zhào Gāo loved to fight
and had once been imprisoned.
His entire back was tattooed with the image of Vaiśravaṇa,
and when the jailers intended to cane his back,
upon seeing it, they would stop.
Thus he became a menace to the neighborhoods and markets.
His subordinates reported this to Lǐ,
who was greatly angered,
captured him and brought him before the hall,
demanded a newly made sinew cudgel,
three inches in diameter,
and ordered the caners to strike the heavenly king,
continuing until it was finished,
over thirty strikes, yet he did not die.
After about ten days,
he merely bared his back and went door to door,
begging for money to repair the damaged merit.
From *Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng*.
Wéi Shǎoqīng
The minor Shǔ general Wéi Shǎoqīng
was the cousin of Wéi Biǎowēi.
From youth he disliked books,
but was fond of green tattoos.
His uncle once made him remove his clothes to look:
on his chest was tattooed a tree,
with dozens of birds gathered on its branches.
Below hung a mirror,
its
the character here was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Huáng edition
nose tied,
with a person standing beside pulling it.
His uncle did not understand,
and asked about it.
Shǎoqīng laughed and said:
"Uncle, have you ever read the poem by Zhāng Yàngōng?
It says, 'Pulling the mirror, cold crows gather.'"
From *Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng*.
Gě Qīng
The street tough Gě Qīng of Jīngzhōu,
brave,
from the neck down,
was entirely tattooed with poems of Bái Jūyì.
Duàn Chéngshì once went with a Jīngzhōu guest named Chén Zhì
to call and see,
making him explain himself.
He could even recite from memory the ones on his back.
Reaching back to point at the tattooed spots,
when it came to "Not that among flowers I especially love the chrysanthemum,"
there was a person holding a cup facing a chrysanthemum cluster.
"Yellow patterned silk nests, cold with leaves,"
then showed a tree,
with patterned silk hanging from the tree,
the patterns of the silk nests exquisitely fine.
In all, over thirty poems were tattooed,
leaving no patch of skin untouched.
Chén Zhì called him the walking poetry illustration of Secretary Bái.
From *Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng*.
The Three Princes
When Yáng Yúqīng served as the Capital District Governor,
in the market quarter there were three men called "prince,"
whose strength could lift giant stones.
Their bodies were covered with tattoos,
leaving no patch of skin untouched.
They had previously deserved death several times over,
but each time hid in the army to escape.
It happened they committed an offense,
and Yáng ordered several officers to capture them,
shut the gates and caned them to death.
The judgment read:
"Tattooed on all four limbs,
calling themselves princes—
what need for further interrogation?
They duly deserve punishment."
From *Miscellaneous Morsels from Yǒuyáng*.
Lè Cóngxùn
When Wáng Duó was removed as Commander-in-Chief
and appointed Military Governor of Huázhōu,
he was soon relieved of his command.
As Héběi was peaceful,
and he had an old acquaintance with Yáng Quánjiǔ,
he moved to Fúyáng to avoid trouble.
He traveled with his staff,
all scholars from the court.
When passing through Wèi,
Lè Yànzhēn treated him with utmost courtesy.
Duó's luggage was extremely lavish,
with attendants and concubines in tow,
displaying the former extravagant airs of the capital's peace.
Yànzhēn had a son named Cóngxùn,
always a scoundrel,
who coveted his carriages, horses, and concubines,
and consulted his father's advisor Lǐ Shānfǔ.
Moreover, during the Xiántōng era,
Shānfǔ had repeatedly failed the examinations,
and harbored deep resentment toward the powerful at court.
Thus he urged Cóngxùn to plot against Duó.
When Duó reached Gānlíng,
Cóngxùn led several hundred light cavalry,
looted all his baggage, concubines, and servants, and returned,
and the guests were all killed.
When reporting to the court, it was said:
"Received report from Bèi
Bèi originally written as Jù,
corrected according to the Xǔ edition
Prefecture that
on a certain day, a man was killed,
surnamed Wáng,
named Lord Wáng."
Such was their vicious audacity.
Yànzhēn and his son
were soon killed by mutinous soldiers.
From *Trifling Words from a Northern Dream*.
Zhāng Cónghuì
When Liáng Tàizǔ was scheming to establish his hegemony,
Jiāng Yànwēn, the governor of Shòuzhōu, surrendered his commandery to our side.
Therefore, (Liáng Tàizǔ) dispatched his trusted subordinate Zhāng Cónghuì to reward his diligence.
However, Cónghuì was a scoundrel who indulged in heavy drinking.
There was a drinking companion named Hé Cángyào who accompanied him,
and they were very intimate.
Cónghuì delivered his message in the commandery.
Yànwēn prepared a grand feast with music,
but the invitation was not accepted.
(Cónghuì) instead dined with Cángyào at the home of the commanding general.
Yànwēn indeed grew suspicious and fearful, saying:
"The Prince of Biàn is plotting against me.
If not,
why would the envoy act like this?"
He then killed his commanding general,
executing several dozen people in connection,
and reported the matter in writing.
Later, he again grew suspicious
(The character for 'suspicious' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Xǔ edition) and fearful, saying:
"If I expose my innermost thoughts,
it will destroy my clan."
He then hanged himself and died.
Liáng Tàizǔ was greatly enraged,
investigated the matter,
and had Cónghuì
waist-
(The characters for 'matter' and 'waist' were originally missing,
supplemented according to the Xǔ edition) chopped.
He detained Hé Cángyào,
shattered his shackles and fetters,
and executed him in the market of Shòuchūn.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Lǐ Rénjǔ
During the reign of Emperor Míngzōng of Later Táng,
Dǒng Zhāng was appointed to Dōngchuān
and harbored intentions of becoming defiant.
At that time, (the court) dispatched the Commissioner of Guest Reception, Lǐ Rénjǔ, on a mission to Tóngzǐ.
Rénjǔ was originally a minor officer under a military commissioner,
but suddenly rose to an inner court position.
His nature was fond of debauchery.
The regional commander prepared a feast,
but (Rénjǔ) declined due to illness and did not attend.
Instead, he held a private banquet with camp courtesans.
Zhāng heard of this and was very angry.
He called for his horse and went to the guesthouse,
intending to harm him immediately.
Rénjǔ, barefoot and holding his tablet upright, greeted him at the gate.
Zhāng's anger subsided slightly.
Later, when (Dǒng Zhāng) rebelled,
and both Chuān regions raised troops,
it was all because Rénjǔ had offered plans to Ān Zhònghuì.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Lǐ Hǎnzhī
was from Héyáng.
In his youth, he was a Buddhist monk,
but was a scoundrel
and was not tolerated wherever he went.
He once begged for food in Suānzǎo County, Huázhōu.
From morning until evening,
no one gave him anything.
He threw his alms bowl on the ground,
destroyed his monk's robes,
and joined Zhūgě Shuǎng in Héyáng as a soldier.
Hǎnzhī was his monastic name,
and he then used it as his personal name.
He was inherently very strong.
Sometimes when fighting with others,
if he was struck on the left cheek,
blood would flow from his right cheek.
Shuǎng soon appointed him as a minor officer.
Whenever he was sent to suppress bandits,
he never failed to capture them.
North of Pú and Jiàng,
there was Móyún Mountain.
A fort was built on top,
called Móyún Stronghold.
Previously, no one could capture it,
but at that time, Hǎnzhī took it.
From then on, he was called "Lǐ Móyún".
He successively served as a commandery lord, Governor of Hénán, and military commissioner,
rising to the position of Shìzhōng.
He died
(The character for 'died' was originally missing,
supplemented according to Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán) in Biànzhōu.
He was also of the same ilk as Chéng Ruì of Jīngnán.
He served the Liáng after the Táng.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Hán Shēn
There was a man named Hán Shēn,
from Qúzhōu.
He was skilled at drinking and gambling,
and proficient in scorching turtle shells (for divination).
He visited the gates of the powerful nobles,
always carrying a turtle shell with him.
The night before, he would scorch a shell first.
If the omen for the next day was auspicious,
he would gamble;
if inauspicious, he would stop.
Also, if it indicated that going to a certain direction was auspicious,
he would go there;
no one from any direction could drag him away if it was not.
When he took people's money and goods,
it was like collecting a blood debt.
Sometimes he would forget his home for a year and not return,
often falling into destitution among flowers and willows (brothels).
His wife was extremely angry
and would occasionally come herself in shame and distress,
driving and chasing him to return together.
Such incidents happened frequently.
He once traveled to visit in Dōngchuān,
and did not return for a year.
Suddenly one day,
he gathered his gambling companions
and arranged a secret rendezvous with singing girls for drinking.
During the night's merrymaking and revelry,
his wife again came secretly from home with one or two maidservants.
Hiding in the neighboring house,
she waited until the night banquet was in full swing,
then held a club, lying in wait in a dark place.
Shēn was unaware,
and with a drawling voice sang "Chí Shuǐ Qīng",
his voice unceasing,
when a blow from a club landed on the back of his head,
knocking off his headscarf
and extinguishing the lamps and candles.
Shēn immediately hid under the dining couch.
A fellow guest sitting there
received a beating with whips in the dark.
Unable to bear the pain,
... afterwards, (she) dispatched two maidservants
to grab him by the topknot and drag him away,
dealing a blow with a club at each step,
scolding:
"This old man,
... so destitute and not returning home!"
Not long after,
(The character for 'after' was originally missing,
supplemented according to the Xǔ edition) when dragged under the candlelight for inspection,
it turned out to be the fellow guest.
Her husband was still ... head hidden under the dining couch.
The people of Shǔ found this greatly amusing,
and his contemporaries called Hán "Chí Shuǐ Qīng".
From "Wángshì Jiàn Wén".
Lǐ Lìng
In Zhǔgōng, there was a certain Lǐ Lìng,
who had served as a magistrate in Yán'ān.
He was originally a cunning fellow,
forcing himself to compose literary pieces to seek patronage.
At that time, there was a Guī Píngshì
who was in charge of the salt bureau in Jiānglíng,
and often had a mind to sympathize with scholars.
After Lǐ Lìng became acquainted with Guī Jūn,
he repeatedly sought loans and assistance,
all of which were promised.
He also said:
"I am seeking relatives beyond the lakes,
and wish to borrow lodging to settle my family."
Guī Jūn also kindly agreed.
Lǐ then departed by boat.
Not twenty days later,
his wife sent servants to beg for dry rations,
and Guī also relieved their destitution.
Lǐ suddenly sent a letter to the salt bureau,
its sentiments intimate and earnest,
unusual compared to normal.
In the letter was a poem dedicated to his wife and others,
intending to entrap Guī Jūn.
Guī Jūn was filled with regret and resentment but could not clear himself.
He took up duties in Wǔlíng and Qújiāng
to make a living.
The presented scholar Shěn Zhuó often recounted this among the guests of the same bureau,
using it as a warning to be cautious.
The poem Lǐ Lìng sent to his wife reads:
"Someone advises me toward Héngyáng,
Each thought of return breaks my heart anew.
Tell my beautiful wife and young daughter,
To seek for me the Lǎngzhōu post."
From "Yún Xī Yǒu Yì".
Mèng Hóngwēi
Táng Dynasty Vice Director Mèng Hóngwēi was wildly unrestrained.
During Emperor Xuānzōng's reign,
he once addressed the emperor during an audience, saying:
"Why does Your Majesty not know of your subject,
and not summon me for service with literary talents?"
The emperor angrily replied:
"Who are you, sir?
My ears are cold,
how could I not know of you?"
The next day,
the emperor said to the chief ministers:
"This man is clamorous and presumptuous,
desiring to become a Hanlin Academician—
is that so easy to achieve!"
(The character "zāi" was originally missing,
added according to the Xǔ edition.)
Thereupon, the chief ministers returned to the Secretariat,
demoted his official rank,
as a minor punishment.
He also once acted in a fit of rage,
pushing his younger brother into a well,
causing public outcry.
He then wrote a letter to inform his relatives and friends:
"Hanging halfway in the well,
rumors are boiling.
A foot of water stirs waves ten feet high—
such is common throughout the ages."
He lived next to Zhèng Fěng,
who served as an assistant in Nánhǎi.
Due to a collapsed wall,
Mèng encroached five or six zhàng into Zhèng's boundary.
The property manager submitted a petition,
requesting the return of the encroached land.
Mèng wrote his judgment on the petition:
"An assistant in remote coastal regions
seldom returns alive.
The land's terrain is steep and slanted,
the wall was squeezed in."
His lifelong conduct and actions
were mostly like this.
That he was not cast aside
was indeed fortunate.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Sēng Luán
Sēng Luán possessed outstanding talent but was unrestrained.
In his early years, he held a local title,
and visited Xuē Néng in Jiāzhōu.
Xuē, considering him eccentric and rash,
found him unsuitable as an examination candidate,
so he later became a monk,
shaving his head before a hundred-foot statue himself,
unwilling to take an ordinary monk as his master.
Later, he went to the capital,
served as an Attendant for Literary Compositions,
and was granted purple robes.
Liǔ Pín greatly admired his talent,
and the Commissioner of Revenue Zhāng Jùn
also showed him respect,
strongly recommending him for important office.
Thus, he returned to lay life,
adopting the name Xiānyú Fèng,
and prepared a name card to visit Liǔ.
Liǔ despised him and refused to receive him.
He then visited Zhāng,
who also rejected him.
Disappointed by this,
he became an assistant to Lǐ Tíng in Jiāngxī,
later serving as a minor general in the Western Battalion,
and was eventually killed in Huángzhōu.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Lù Déyán
Assistant Magistrate Lù Déyán of Hézhōng,
nephew of Chancellor Lù Yán,
son of Lù Yuè,
was regarded as talented and outstanding at the time.
He passed the imperial examination,
and served on the staff of Prince Xīpíng Zhū Yǒuqiān,
but was unrestrained, arrogant, and contemptuous,
though his lord tolerated him.
When Zhū Yǒuqiān rebelled against the Liáng,
he sought refuge in Jìnyáng.
Just as envoys from the rival state arrived,
and Zhū was treating them with careful courtesy,
Lù spoke about the matter during a banquet.
Zhū Yǒuqiān, worried and angered,
threw Déyán into the Huáng Hé
to avert disaster.
Previously, a senior servant near the assistant magistrate's quarters had requested
to change rooms,
as sworn brothers sharing a residence
did not wish to hear the official's vulgar talk.
Was Lù not such a person?
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
Xiāo Xīfǔ
Xiāo Xīfǔ passed the imperial examination,
possessing literary talent, eloquence,
and much cunning.
During the Liáng dynasty, unsuccessful,
he abandoned his mother and wife, crossed the river,
and changed his name to Huángfǔ Xiàoshū.
When Emperor Zhuāngzōng ascended the throne in Wèizhōu,
he summoned Xīfǔ to serve as Drafter.
After Emperor Zhuāngzōng pacified Biàn and Luò,
Xīfǔ was ordered to pacify Qīng and Qí,
only then learning his mother had died and his wife remarried.
He then wore mourning in Wèizhōu.
Contemporaries mockingly quoted Lǐ Líng's letter:
"The aged mother passed away in the hall,
the living wife left the chamber."
Later, he became Reminding Advisor.
By nature narrow-minded and irritable,
eager for advancement,
he submitted memorials criticizing Chief Ministers Dòulú Gé and Wéi Shuō,
leading to their demotion.
Again, for slandering the chancellor,
he was demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Lánzhōu.
From "Běi Mèng Suǒ Yán".
I have heard that among book collectors there is a Sòng edition missing seven volumes.
For three of them, I have recovered about seventy percent,
and have already sent them for printing.
For the remaining four volumes, only twenty to thirty percent remains.
Learned gentlemen, please clearly inform me,
so that it may become a complete work.
Written on the first day of the seventh lunar month in the autumn of the first year of the Lóngqìng reign, by Tán Kǎi of Shíshān.
Liú Xiáng was a native of Dōngguǎn Jǔ.
During the Sòng dynasty,
he began his career as an Attendant Officer under the Western Expeditionary Commander.
From a young age, he was fond of literature and learning,
but his temperament was rigid and unrestrained.
He spoke lightly and acted recklessly,
showing no deference to superiors or inferiors.
When the Minister of Education Chǔ Yuān entered the court,
he used a waist-fan to shield himself from the sun.
Liú Xiáng, passing by his side, remarked:
"To behave in such a manner,
ashamed to show your face to others,
what good does shielding with a fan do?"
Chǔ Yuān retorted:
"An impoverished scholar shows no respect."
Liú Xiáng replied:
"If you cannot kill Yuán and Liú,
how can you avoid being called an impoverished scholar?"
In the early years of the Yǒngmíng era,
he was promoted to Advisory Officer of Chángshā.
He compiled the History of the Sòng Dynasty,
in which he satirized and criticized the dynastic transition.
Wáng Jiǎn secretly reported this to the emperor,
who harbored resentment but did not investigate.
His elder brother, Liú Zhěng,
died while serving as an official in Guǎngzhōu.
Liú Xiáng went to his brother's wife to demand the return of his assets.
He composed a series of linked verses,
often filled with ridicule and slander.
When this came to light,
the emperor separately sent an edict to Liú Xiáng, stating:
"You have always lacked proper conduct,
as is well known both in the court and among the people.
You lightly abandoned your own flesh and blood,
and insulted your elder brother and his wife.
These are shortcomings in your family conduct,
and have nothing to do with others.
As for your talent and knowledge,
they are hardly worth discussing.
Your position involves a clear and honorable path,
and in terms of your duties, you are not wronged.
Why do you recklessly utter harsh words,
defaming court officials?
Whenever you speak at gatherings,
you invariably use criticism and judgment as your pretext.
I had hoped that, given your advanced age,
you would be able to reflect and motivate yourself,
and daily I looked forward to your reform.
Yet, from what I have heard,
you have instead grown worse.
You clamor and criticize the court,
showing no respect for your superiors and teachers.
You speak with extreme recklessness,
publicly exposing matters for all to hear.
Recently, I saw your linked verses,
in which you conveyed ideas of rebellion and arrogance.
This trend must not be allowed to continue.
I spare your life,
and send you ten thousand lǐ away to reflect on your faults.
If you can reform,
I will allow you to return."
Later, in Guǎngzhōu,
he indulged in drinking all day long
and died of illness.
Liú Xiáng of Dōngguǎn,
relying on his talent, looked down on everyone.
He once said to a donkey:
"If you worked as hard as your kind,
you would already be a high minister."
He also composed linked verses to satirize the court,
and was soon executed.
Liú Xiàochuò was a native of Péngchéng.
From childhood, he was intelligent and quick-witted,
able to compose essays by the age of seven.
His maternal uncle, the Court Secretary Láng Wáng Róng, deeply admired and regarded him as exceptional,
often saying that in the world of literature,
if it were not for himself,
it should belong to Āshì.
Āshì was Liú Xiàochuò's childhood name.
He was on friendly terms with Dào Qià,
and together they served in the Eastern Palace.
Liú Xiàochuò believed his own talent surpassed Dào Qià's,
and at banquets and gatherings,
he often ridiculed and belittled Dào Qià's writings.
Dào Qià harbored resentment.
When Liú Xiàochuò served as the Chief of the Court of Judicial Review,
he brought his concubine into the government office,
while his mother remained in their private residence.
Dào Qià, as the Imperial Censor,
impeached him for this,
and he was dismissed from his post.
When Emperor Gāozǔ composed a poem for the Jíyòng ceremony,
dozens of people were ordered to compose matching verses,
and Liú Xiàochuò's was particularly skillful.
That very day, he was ordered to be reinstated as an Advisory Officer,
and later promoted to Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate.
He was demoted
after being impeached for accepting bribes, as reported by the briber.
Liú Xiàochuò enjoyed great fame from a young age,
but he relied on his temperament and talent,
often acting arrogantly and disrespectfully toward others.
If anything did not suit his liking,
he would speak extremely harshly, defaming and slandering.
The General of the Army Zāng Dùn and the Minister of the Imperial Treasury Shěn Sēngguǒ,
both favored by the times,
were particularly looked down upon by Liú Xiàochuò.
At court assemblies,
while among the high officials,
he would not speak with them,
but instead call out to the attendants,
asking about trivial matters on the roads.
Because of this, he often offended others.
Liú Xiàochuò of the Liáng dynasty was frivolous and disrespectful toward Dào Qià.
Dào Qià originally came from a gardening background.
Dào Qià said to Liú Xiàochuò:
"There is a good plot of land east of my residence.
I intended to buy it,
but the owner refused.
How can I obtain it?"
Liú Xiàochuò replied:
"Why don't you cart more manure and pile it under his wall to trouble him?"
Dào Qià resented this deeply.
Liú Xiàochuò ultimately suffered harm because of it.
Xǔ Jìngzōng was a native of Xīnchéng.
In the early years of the Wǔdé era, Emperor Tàizōng heard of his reputation
and summoned him to serve as an Academician.
When Empress Wéndé passed away,
all officials wore mourning garments.
The Director of the Palace Timing Ōuyáng Xún,
whose appearance was exceptionally ugly,
was pointed at by everyone.
Xǔ Jìngzōng saw this and laughed heartily,
for which he was impeached by the censors
and demoted to the position of Military Advisor of Hóngzhōu.
He was later promoted to the post of Attendant Gentleman
and concurrently served as the Minister of Rites and compiler of the National History.
He married his daughter to the son of the tribal chieftain Féng Àng,
accepting much gold and treasure in return,
for which he was impeached by the relevant authorities
and demoted to the position of Prefect of Zhèngzhōu.
During the Yǒnghuī era,
he was again appointed Minister of Rites.
When the emperor intended to install the Zhāoyí as empress, the senior ministers strongly advised against it.
Xǔ Jìngzōng, secretly gauging the emperor's intentions,
recklessly stated:
"A peasant who harvests an extra ten hú of wheat
still considers replacing his old wife.
The Son of Heaven, who possesses all under heaven,
installing one empress—
what is there to say about it?"
The emperor's mind was thus made up.
His residence was extravagantly and presumptuously built,
even to the extent of constructing connected towers,
where he had courtesans run about,
indulging in drinking and music for his own amusement.
When he died,
the Erudite Yuán Sīgǔ proposed:
"Jìngzōng rose to his position through talent,
and held high-ranking posts throughout his career.
However, he abandoned his eldest son in a remote borderland
and married his young daughter to a barbarian tribe.
The learning of poetry and rituals
ceased at the threshold of his home.
The exchange of betrothal gifts and inquiries about names
were only heard of in the context of bribery.
I request that he be given the posthumous title 'Mù' (Erroneous)."
Xǔ Jìngzōng of the Táng dynasty had a frivolous nature.
He often forgot people upon meeting them,
and some said he was not intelligent.
He replied:
"You yourselves are difficult to recognize.
If it were Cáo, Liú, Shěn, or Xiè,
I could recognize them even by groping in the dark."
Yíngchuān County Magistrate Yáng Jiǒng
was from Huàyīn.
In his youth, he was intelligent and widely learned.
He was recommended as a child prodigy.
He was equally famous with Wáng Bó, Lú Zhàolín, and Luò Bīnwáng.
He once said to others:
"I am ashamed to be ranked before Lú,
and humiliated to be placed after Wáng."
At the time, people agreed with this.
He was appointed Collator in the Imperial Library,
and became a Scholar of the Chóngwén Hall.
At the beginning of Empress Zétiān's reign,
he was demoted to Judicial Officer of Zǐzhōu due to an incident,
and after his term ended,
he was appointed Magistrate of Yíngchuān County.
Yáng Jiǒng governed with cruelty,
and whenever officials or people did not act as he wished,
he would flog them to death.
Moreover, the official residence where he lived
had many pavilions and terraces for scholars,
all of which he inscribed with plaques,
giving them elegant names,
which made him widely mocked by people near and far.
Yáng Jiǒng
was from Huàyīn.
In his youth, he was intelligent and widely learned.
He was recommended as a child prodigy.
He was equally famous with Wáng Bó, Lú Zhàolín, and Luò Bīnwáng.
He once said to others:
"I am ashamed to be ranked before Lú,
and humiliated to be placed after Wáng."
At the time, people agreed with this.
He was appointed Collator in the Imperial Library,
and became a Scholar of the Chóngwén Hall.
At the beginning of Empress Zétiān's reign,
he was demoted to Judicial Officer of Zǐzhōu due to an incident,
and after his term ended,
he was appointed Magistrate of Yíngchuān County.
Yáng Jiǒng governed with cruelty,
and whenever officials or people did not act as he wished,
he would flog them to death.
Moreover, the official residence where he lived
had many pavilions and terraces for scholars,
all of which he inscribed with plaques,
giving them elegant names,
which made him widely mocked by people near and far.
Táng Dynasty Yíngchuān County Magistrate of Qúzhōu, Yáng Jiǒng,
excelled in literary studies,
but relied on his talent and was arrogant and aloof,
making him unwelcome in his time.
Whenever he saw court officials,
he called them "qílín xuàn" (unicorn stuffings).
When asked why,
Yáng said:
"Nowadays, those who perform with fake unicorns
carve horns and heads,
adorn them with fur,
cover a donkey with it,
and parade it around the arena.
But when the hide is removed,
it's still just a donkey.
Those without virtue yet dressed in red and purple robes—
how are they different from a donkey covered in unicorn skin?"
Cuī Shí
was the son of Cuī Rénshī.
His younger brothers Chéng and Yè,
and his elder brother Lì,
were all talented in literature,
and held high-ranking, prestigious positions.
During private banquets,
they compared themselves to the Wáng and Xiè families.
He once said to others:
"Our family background and the official positions we have held
have always been of the highest rank.
A true man should seize key positions to control others,
how can he silently be controlled by others?"
When Cuī Shí was in power,
he was thirty-six years old.
Once, he went out of Duānmén at dusk,
descended to Tiānjīn Bridge,
and composed a poem on horseback:
"Spring returns to the Shànglín Garden,
flowers fill the city of Luòyáng."
Zhāng Yuè saw it and sighed:
"Literary talent and official rank can be achieved,
but his youth cannot be matched."
Later, he attached himself to Empress Wéi,
served as chancellor,
and then attached himself to Princess Tàipíng.
A guest presented "The Seagull Ode" to satirize him,
but Cuī Shí praised it without reforming.
When Xiāo Zhìzhōng was executed,
Cuī Shí was exiled beyond the mountains and ordered to commit suicide.
When Cuī Shí served as Zhōngshū Lìng,
Zhāng Jiāzhēn was a Shèrén.
Cuī Shí looked down on him,
often calling him "Zhāng Dǐ."
Later, Zhāng Jiāzhēn handled several matters,
all of which surpassed others' expectations.
Cuī Shí was amazed and admired him for a long time,
saying to his colleagues:
"Did you know? Zhāng Dǐ is actually one of us,
this position will ultimately be his seat."
More than ten years after Cuī Shí's death,
Zhāng Jiāzhēn from Hédōng indeed became Zhōngshū Lìng.
Dù Shěnyán
was from Xiāngyáng.
He passed the imperial examination
and became the Wèi of Xíchéng.
Relying on his great talent,
he was resented for his arrogance.
When Sū Wèidào served as Tiānguān Shìláng,
Dù Shěnyán submitted his judgments and said to others upon leaving:
"Sū Wèidào will surely die."
People asked in surprise why,
and he replied:
"When he sees my judgments,
he will surely die of shame."
He also once said to others:
"My essays should have Qū Yuán and Sòng Yù serve as my subordinates,
my calligraphy should make Wáng Xīzhī bow in respect."
His boastfulness was like this.
Later, when he was gravely ill,
Sòng Zhīwèn and others visited him,
and he replied:
"I am greatly tormented by the whims of fate,
what more is there to say?
However, as long as I am alive,
I have long suppressed all of you.
Now that I am about to die,
it is indeed a great relief,
only I regret not seeing a successor."
Dù Shěnyán first passed the imperial examination,
and relying on his talent, he was arrogant and aloof,
greatly envied by his contemporaries.
When Sū Wèidào served as Tiānguān Shìláng,
Dù Shěnyán participated in the selection examination,
and after submitting his judgments, he said to others:
"Sū Wèidào will surely die."
When asked why,
Dù Shěnyán said:
"When he sees my judgments, he will surely die of shame."
He also said to others:
"My essays deserve to have Qū Yuán and Sòng Yù as my subordinates,
my calligraphy deserves to make Wáng Xīzhī bow in respect."
His boastfulness was like this.
He was demoted to Registrar of Jízhōu.
Sīmǎ Zhōu Jìchóng and Assistant Registrar Guō Ruònè together fabricated accusations against Dù Shěnyán,
imprisoning him,
intending to kill him over the matter.
Later, when Zhōu Jìchóng and others were feasting and drinking,
Dù Shěnyán's son Dù Bìng, aged thirteen,
concealed a dagger and attacked Zhōu Jìchóng,
who died from his wounds,
and Dù Bìng was also killed by the attendants.
Dù Fǔ was the grandson of Dǔ Shěnyán.
In his youth, he was poor and unable to support himself,
wandering as a guest between the regions of Wú, Yuè, Qí, and Zhào.
He sat for the imperial examinations but did not pass.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he presented three rhapsodies,
and the emperor, impressed by them,
had him wait for appointment at the Jíxián Academy.
He submitted rhapsodies and eulogies several times,
taking the opportunity to speak of his own talents,
and stated that since his ancestors Dù Yù and Dù Yù,
they had upheld Confucian learning and held official posts for eleven generations.
By the time of Dù Shěnyán, who gained fame through literary works,
he himself relied on this inherited legacy,
and had been composing since the age of seven,
for nearly forty years.
Yet his clothes did not cover his body,
and he often relied on others for food,
secretly fearing he would die in a ditch.
He humbly hoped the emperor would take pity on him,
and if allowed to follow the precedent of his ancestors,
then his writings,
though not sufficient to propagate the Six Classics,
in terms of depth, melancholy, and rhythmic force,
and timely responsiveness,
could match Yáng Xióng and Méi Gāo.
With a subject like this,
how could Your Majesty bear to abandon him?"
When Ān Lùshān rebelled,
and the emperor fled to Shǔ,
Dù Fǔ took refuge and fled to Sānchuān.
It happened that Yán Wǔ was appointed military commissioner of Jiànnán,
so Dù Fǔ went to rely on him.
Yán Wǔ, due to their long-standing family friendship,
treated Dù Fǔ very well,
and personally visited his home.
When Dù Fǔ saw him,
he was sometimes improperly dressed.
Moreover, his temperament was narrow-minded, irritable, arrogant, and unrestrained.
Once, while drunk, he climbed onto Yán Wǔ's bed,
stared at him and said,
"Yán Tǐngzhī actually has a son like this."
Yán Wǔ was also fierce and violent,
and though outwardly he did not show offense,
he harbored resentment inwardly.
Dù Fǔ enjoyed discussing major affairs of the state,
but his views were lofty and impractical.
However, having experienced multiple rebellions and invasions,
he maintained his integrity without being tainted.
In his poetry,
his feelings never forgot his sovereign.
People pitied him for his loyalty.
Dù Fǔ, the Minister of Works, was in Shǔ.
Once, drunk, he climbed onto Yán Wǔ's desk,
and sternly asked Yán Wǔ,
"Are you Yán Tǐngzhī's son or not?"
Yán Wǔ's expression changed,
and Dù Fǔ then said,
"I am Dù Shěnyán's son."
Yán Wǔ's anger subsided slightly.
Chén Tōngfāng passed the imperial examinations in the Zhèngyuán era,
in the same year as Wáng Bō.
Wáng Bō was fifty-six years old,
while Chén Tōngfāng was very young.
During a gathering,
he patted Wáng Bō's back and said,
"Old Wáng, I present you with this degree."
Meaning that he was at the end of his road,
and passing the examination was like being granted an official post.
Wáng Bō resented this.
Later, Chén Tōngfāng faced family difficulties,
and endured great hardship.
Wáng Bō excelled in three examinations,
became a senior official,
and was appointed to oversee the salt and iron monopoly.
When Chén Tōngfāng, impoverished and distressed, sought his help,
Wáng Bō did not provide much assistance.
At the time, Lǐ Xūzhōng was the deputy commissioner,
and Chén Tōngfāng used a poem to seek his recommendation, saying:
"Think of the haggard bird by the roadside,
once fortunate to migrate with the tall trees."
Wáng Bō had no choice but to recommend him as an official in the Jiāngnán bureau.
Chén Tōngfāng was from Mǐn County.
He passed the imperial examinations under Gù Shǎolián in the tenth year of Zhēnyuán.
At that time, the path of fairness was wide open,
and solitary talents were selected.
Chén Tōngfāng was twenty-five years old
and placed fourth in the examinations.
Due to his youth and high reputation,
he was frivolous and self-assured.
He was in the same year as Wáng Bō.
Wáng was fifty-six at the time,
and Chén Tōngfāng looked down on his late achievement.
Later, during a gathering, he jokingly patted his back and said,
"Old Wáng, old Wáng,
I present you with this degree."
Meaning that he was at the end of his road,
and passing the examination was like being granted an official post.
Wáng said,
"I intend to sit for three more examinations."
Chén Tōngfāng added,
"Old Wáng, once is enough,
how could there be a second time?"
Wáng harbored this in his heart.
Chén Tōngfāng soon encountered family difficulties and returned home.
Wáng indeed repeatedly excelled in the higher examinations,
and his official career gradually advanced.
Later, Chén Tōngfāng, seeking employment, entered the capital,
by which time Wáng had become a senior official overseeing the salt and iron monopoly.
Chén Tōngfāng, impoverished and distressed, with few connections,
unaware that Wáng still bore a grudge over his words,
turned to him for help.
His fellow examinee Lǐ Xūzhōng was then the deputy commissioner,
and Chén Tōngfāng also sent him a poem,
seeking his recommendation, saying:
"Think of the haggard bird by the roadside,
once fortunate to migrate with the tall trees."
Wáng had no choice but to appoint him as an official in the Jiāngxī bureau.
Before he reached his post,
he was reassigned to the Zhèdōng bureau.
When he was only halfway there,
he was again reassigned to the Nánlíng bureau.
This happened four or five times in succession.
His hardships grew increasingly severe.
Reflecting on his mistake,
he said to his nephews and nieces,
"I merely joked,
not knowing that Wáng would harbor such deep resentment.
One must be careful with words—how can they be spoken lightly?"
Soon after, Wáng was formally appointed to a high position,
and the gap in status became vast.
With no way to apologize,
he gazed in regret and died of illness.
Lǐ Hè was a descendant of the Táng imperial clan.
At the age of seven,
during the Yuánhé era,
he was already famous for his poetry.
Hán Tuìzhī and Huángfǔ Shí read Lǐ Hè's works and were amazed,
saying to each other,
"If this were an ancient,
there might be some we do not know.
But if this is a contemporary,
how could we not know of him?"
They then rode together to his door to request a meeting.
Lǐ Hè, still a youth with hair tied in tufts and wearing simple clothes, came out.
The two gentlemen tested him on the spot with a composition.
Lǐ Hè accepted the task cheerfully,
took up his brush and ink,
as if no one else were present,
and titled it "Gāo Xuān Guò."
The two gentlemen were greatly astonished
and rode back side by side on their horses.
Yuán Zhěn had passed the examinations in the míngjīng category
and wished to befriend Lǐ Hè.
Lǐ Hè, upon seeing his name card, said,
"You passed the míngjīng examination—
what business do you have coming to see Lǐ Hè?"
Yuán Zhěn left in shame.
Not long after, Yuán Zhěn passed the policy examination,
became an official in the Ministry of Rites,
and raised the issue that Lǐ Hè's father's name was Jìn,
which, by taboo, disqualified him from taking the imperial examinations.
His contemporaries followed suit in excluding him,
and Lǐ Hè ultimately never passed the examinations.
According to records, during the Tang Dynasty, Lǐ Gōngfān once compiled the song-poems of Hè,
and began writing a preface for them but did not complete it.
He learned that Hè had a maternal cousin
who had shared a writing-brush and inkstone friendship with Hè in the past.
Summoning him for an audience,
Gōngfān entrusted him with the task of searching for and collecting Hè's lost works.
The man agreed,
and furthermore requested:
"I remember all of Hè's poems and songs,
but there are many places with smudges and corrections.
I wish to have the collection you have compiled to look over,
and I will make the necessary corrections."
Gōngfān was pleased,
and handed everything over to him.
For a full year, the man disappeared without a trace.
Summoned again and questioned,
he then said:
"I was Hè's cousin,
and we grew up together since childhood.
I resented his arrogance and neglect,
and often thought of taking revenge.
Now, fortunately, I have obtained the works you collected,
along with the old ones I had,
and have thrown them all into the weir."
Gōngfān was greatly enraged,
and shouted at him to leave.
During the Yuánhé era,
Jìnshì Lǐ Hè was skilled at composing song-poems.
Hán Yù deeply recognized and valued him,
and among the officials often praised and recommended him,
so his fame and reputation became very widespread.
At that time, Yuán Zhěn was young,
having achieved first place by passing the míngjīng examination,
and he devoted himself to literary composition.
He often sought to associate with Hè.
One day, holding a gift, he visited Hè's home.
Hè, after reading his name card, did not immediately allow him to enter.
A servant said to him:
"You passed the míngjīng examination—
what business do you have coming to see Lǐ Hè?"
Zhěn could not express his feelings further,
and withdrew in shame and anger.
Later, having passed the special decree examination from the position of Left Reminder,
and holding an important post daily,
when he became a Vice Director of the Ministry of Rites,
he raised the issue that Hè's grandfather's personal name was Jìn,
and thus it was improper for Hè to take the examinations;
Hè was also ostracized by his contemporaries for being frivolous,
and consequently met with hardship and obstruction.
Hán Yù, pitying his talent,
wrote the "Discussion on Taboos" to clarify the matter,
but in the end Hè did not achieve fame.
Lǐ Qúnyù
was from Lǐzhōu.
He enjoyed playing the shēng,
and often had his household servants play it.
By nature, he liked to eat goose.
When he was appointed Collator,
he immediately returned to his hometown.
Lú Zhào sent him a poem which said:
"Your marvelous playing surely answers the phoenix;
your skilled writing certainly obtains the goose."
His poem inscribed at Huánglíng Temple reads:
"Before Huánglíng Temple, spring has already emptied;
the cuckoo cries blood, tears in the spring wind.
I do not know where the pure spirit has fallen;
I suspect it is amidst the autumn colors of the passing clouds."
Qúnyù himself felt that 'spring emptied' immediately led to 'autumn colors,'
and hesitated, wanting to change it,
when suddenly it was as if something
told him this was an omen of two years.
Arriving at Xúnyáng,
he recounted the entire matter to Duàn Chéngshì.
After Qúnyù's death,
Chéngshì wrote a poem mourning him, which said:
"Thirty years amidst wine and poetry,
reckless and abrupt in a clamorous world.
In enlightened times, not dying like Mí Héng,
having scorned all the high officials, you return to the Nine Springs."
Lǐ Qúnyù, styled Wénshān,
was by nature frivolous and hasty,
often mocking and teasing people.
He once borrowed a letter from a clerk in Jiānglíng to seek alms from the Prefect of Lǐzhōu, Ài Yǐ.
Lǐ said to Ài:
"This humble student is gravely ill,
I beg Your Excellency to compassionately save me."
Lǐ was mocking his eccentric nature.
Qúnyù, due to his frivolous and unrestrained behavior, did not receive generous assistance.
Féng Juān: In the fourth year of the Dàzhōng era,
Jìnshì Féng Juān passed the examinations,
and his literary reputation was the highest among those on the list.
That year, the kingdom of Xīnlóo built a tower,
and generously presented gold and silk,
requesting in a memorial that he compose a record for it,
which his contemporaries considered an honor.
He initially held office as Adjutant of the Capital Prefecture,
and his patron was none other than Chief Minister Dù Shěnquán.
When Dù received the appointment to Jiāngxī,
before the imperial decree was issued,
he first summoned the Duke of Chánglè for a confidential talk,
extending an offer of appointment on his staff,
intending to entrust him with the responsibility of drafting memorials in Nánchāng,
and admonished him not to divulge it.
The Duke of Chánglè bowed in thanks,
took his leave and exited the residence,
and hurried home with whip in hand.
On the main thoroughfare, he met his friend Zhèng Cóng,
who saw the joy apparent on his face,
stopped his horse, and earnestly questioned him.
Chánglè promptly told him about his patron's offer of appointment.
The man from Xíngyáng soon afterward, holding a name card, went to the gate of the Capital Prefect to offer congratulations,
and fully stated that he had learned of it from Senior Féng.
The Capital Prefect sighed in vexation,
and despised his shallowness and indiscretion.
When the decree was issued and the administration was established,
Féng was not included.
His mind was anxious and doubtful,
not knowing the reason.
On the day the carriage of the Surveillance Commissioner departed,
he rode in a sedan chair from Bà Bridge,
and his disciples were all at Chánglè to bid farewell.
The Duke, the Capital Prefect, bowed with hands clasped to Féng and said:
"Do your best!"
From then on, a reputation for boastfulness and superficiality
spread among the officials,
and he ultimately did not attain high office.
In the interim, he was also involved in associating with powerful palace eunuchs,
which further attracted criticism from pure opinion,
and his offices stopped at Vice Director of the Ministry of Sacrifices and Prefect of Méizhōu.
He served in Shǔ,
rising to the position of Censor-in-chief.
Wēn Tíngyún
was from Tàiyuán.
In the early Dàzhōng era,
he sat for the jìnshì examinations.
He diligently studied at his desk,
and excelled at poetry and rhapsodies.
However, his conduct as a scholar was worldly and mixed,
and he did not attend to his appearance.
He could follow the sounds of strings and winds,
composing ornate and sensuous lyrics.
He associated with the idle sons of high officials like Péi Chéng and Línghú Gǎo and their ilk,
gambling and drinking together,
drunk and besotted all day long,
and as a result, for years he did not pass the examinations.
When Xú Shāng governed Xiāngyáng,
Tíngyún went to rely on him,
and was appointed Patrol Officer.
During the Xiántōng era,
disappointed, he returned east of the river.
Passing through Guǎnglíng on his journey,
he bore resentment in his heart that when Línghú Táo was in power,
he had not helped him achieve fame.
After arriving,
he wantonly roamed with newly advanced young men, acting the gallant,
and for a long time did not present his card for an audience.
He also begged for provisions at the Yángzǐ Bureau.
Drunk, he violated the night curfew.
He was detained by the patrol officer,
his face injured and teeth broken,
only then was he released to Yángzhōu.
He complained to Línghú Táo,
who had the patrol officer arrested and punished.
The officer spoke exhaustively of Tíngyún's dissolute and disgraceful conduct.
From then on, his sullied behavior became known in the capital.
During the Kāimíng era,
Wēn Tíngyún was renowned for his literary talent,
yet he rarely adhered to minor proprieties,
using his writings as commodities,
which earned him the disdain of discerning individuals.
Before long, among the high officials, there were also malicious memorials accusing Tíngyún of disrupting the examination halls,
and he was appointed as the Deputy Magistrate of Fāngchéng County in Suízhōu.
At that time, the Secretariat Drafter Péi Tǎn was drafting the appointment edict,
and he hesitated, holding his brush for a long while.
An old clerk happened to be present,
so Péi inquired about promotions and demotions.
The clerk replied:
"Should the Drafter compose a reproachful text?
Why?
A Presented Scholar who passes the palace examination is of equal rank to the Chief and Assistant Officials of a Prestigious Prefecture."
Tǎn was relieved,
hence the comparison to the exile of Jiǎ Yì to Chángshā by the riverbank.
When Tíngyún assumed his post,
literati vied to compose poems to send him off,
but only Jì Tángfū captured the essence, writing:
"Why weep over jade so often in this enlightened age?
In Cháng'ān, the apricot garden's spring is unseen.
Though the phoenix decree bestows a humble fate,
the parrot's lofty talent brings only burden to its frame.
Drink now the green ale to dissolve accumulated regrets;
do not decline the yellow绶, brushing off the journey's dust.
If Fāngchéng seems farther than Chángshā of old,
a thousand mountains and myriad streams will part our wanderings."
As for Chén Pánsǒu,
his father's name was Hù,
who was known for his literary learning,
and was particularly devoted to Buddhist scriptures.
During the Chángqìng era,
he once annotated the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* and presented it to the throne,
receiving an imperial decree,
ordering that he be given a good official post.
The high officials argued that Hù had presented the sutra through a temple monk,
and thus suppressed him considerably,
granting him only a minor position.
Pánsǒu was short in stature,
with a long beak-like mouth and sparse teeth.
He was exceptionally learned in literature.
He prided himself on having the talent to assist a king.
Boasting and engaging in grand debates,
even when facing ministers,
he acted as if no one else was present.
Furthermore, he judged himself unfit for the Confucian order,
and at the age of twenty, he became a Daoist priest,
registered at the Hàotiān Temple.
During the Xiántōng era,
on the emperor's birthday,
a debate between the two teachings (Buddhism and Daoism) was held,
and the Daoists repeatedly fled in defeat.
The emperor was slightly displeased.
An edict was issued,
ordering that among the newcomers to the inner Daoist assembly,
anyone capable of refuting the Buddhists
should recommend themselves.
Pánsǒu straightened his robes and accepted the decree.
At that time, the Buddhists were leading the debate,
and mistakenly cited a commentary on the *Nirvana Sutra*.
Pánsǒu immediately rebuked them, saying:
"The emperor is hailed with great celebration,
and the master offers words of longevity,
yet you cite the *Nirvana Sutra*,
committing a grave act of disrespect."
Since the monk thought Pánsǒu was unfamiliar with Buddhist texts,
he was taken aback,
nearly stumbling and falling.
From then on, Pánsǒu defeated several opponents in succession,
greatly pleasing the emperor,
and those around shouted "Long live!"
That day, before the curtain, he was bestowed a set of purple robes.
Thereafter, Pánsǒu became increasingly arrogant and contemptuous,
much to the dismay of many eminent and virtuous figures,
who secretly reported to the emperor,
saying:
"Pánsǒu is from an official family,
and does not wish to remain in priestly robes;
he rather desires to govern a county to prove his worth."
Thus, by imperial decree, he was appointed Magistrate of Zhìdé County.
Pánsǒu assumed his duties,
but before completing even one assessment period,
he abandoned his post,
and went to the capital to submit a sealed memorial.
Liú Gōng of Tōngyì took him under his wing,
and he was summoned for an audience at an unusual time, lasting several hours.
Pánsǒu presented several dozen points,
criticizing the maladies of the times.
He further said:
"If Your Majesty permits me to confiscate Biān Jiān's family property,
it could sustain the army for one or two years."
The emperor asked:
"Who is Biān Jiān?"
He replied:
"He is a close subordinate of Chancellor Lù Yán."
This greatly angered Yán.
The next day,
an edict was issued accusing Pánsǒu of deceiving the emperor
and slandering high officials.
He was stripped of his official status and made a commoner,
and exiled to Àizhōu.
Although Pánsǒu faced such a downfall,
he never compromised his principles.
He had long suffered from a severe ailment,
and when visiting various regional governors,
he often had himself carried in a sedan chair to their official residences,
and wherever he went, he was highly regarded.
After Yán was demoted,
Pánsǒu was allowed a mitigated transfer to become the Military Advisor of Dèngzhōu.
At that time, following the Gēngzǐ year of Guāngmíng,
Liú Jùróng rose from a Xúzhōu general
to seize Xiāngyáng,
but he did not recognize Pánsǒu's worth,
treating him merely as a subordinate official of a prefecture.
Pánsǒu traveled south along the Hàn River,
and on the way, he wrote to Jùróng's staff officer:
"I have left a land of discourtesy,
and am gradually entering a realm of carefree ease."
Jùróng was greatly angered upon reading this,
and dispatched over ten strong foot soldiers,
sending documents to Tán and È prefectures,
to pursue and capture Pánsǒu.
At that time, the empire was in chaos,
with no one to maintain order,
and soon he was assaulted by soldiers.
His entire family fled upstream along the Hàn River,
reaching Jiǎqiàn,
where over thirty members of his household
were slaughtered, leaving none alive.
Xuē Néng
was a Presented Scholar during the Huìcháng era,
and he held himself in excessively high regard.
While serving in Xīchuān,
he often belittled Zhūgě Liàng's achievements,
writing a poem that said:
"Who would approve of his battle formations?
I mock the temple's solemn appearance."
He also said:
"Better to burn the books of Shǔ and not read them,
for Marquis Wǔ cannot discipline my person."
He ridiculed Lǐ Bái, saying:
"Had I been born in the Kāiyuán era,
how could the name 'Lǐ Hànlín' have been so renowned?"
He also said:
"Lǐ Bái ultimately has nothing to offer,
and Táo Qián is certainly not worth emulating."
He inscribed his own collection with these lines:
"From which era did the source of poetry lose its clarity?
Everywhere, wild waves taint the later generations.
Often I grieve, solitary in the Way, shedding tears as I chant,
yet because the wind ruins, my words lack feeling.
Hard to bear that wicked youths bully Hán Xìn,
in vain was Mí Héng slain by the feudal lords.
Even if I reached Gōushān, it would be of no avail,
for all around, the interconnected croaking of frogs is heard."
Such was his unrestrained and eccentric nature.
Later, during a military mutiny, he was killed.
Xuē Néng prided himself on his literary talent,
yet he was repeatedly assigned to military frontier posts,
often sighing in melancholy,
hence he wrote "A Poem of Thanks for the Tiānzhù Tea Sent from Huáinán."
Its closing lines read:
"This crude official post, given to me, I'd gladly cast aside,
but for my poetic sentiment, which allows me to savor it."
He meant that a military governor was a "crude official."
While stationed in Xǔchāng,
when all his staff officers were gathered,
he had his son, armed with bow and quiver, greet the various guests,
which startled and perplexed them.
Néng said:
"To ward off disasters for him."
People of the time considered him frivolous and disrespectful.
Gāo Féngxiū looked at Gù Yún,
during the Dàshùn era,
an imperial decree ordered him, along with Yáng Zhāoyè and eight others, to compile history.
Yún was in the Jiāng-Huái region,
when he encountered Reminder Gāo Féngxiū.
At that time, Attendant-in-ordinary Liú Zǐcháng enjoyed a pure reputation and elegant renown,
filling the ranks of officials.
His younger brother, Liú Chóngwàng, was also in the Secretariat.
Yún, knowing that Féngxiū was an old friend of Zǐcháng,
planned to visit his door,
hoping to secure an introduction.
Féngxiū had agreed for a long time.
When the time came, Yún requested a letter.
Féngxiū handed him a sealed letter,
quite hastily drafted.
Yún felt slightly suspicious,
so he secretly opened and read it.
It was a single sheet,
and it did not mention Yún at all,
but only said:
"Yáng Zhāoyè intends to use his one-foot-three-inch sweaty feet
to tread upon the burnt remnants of the dragon-tail path.
Although Emperor Yìzōng was of shallow virtue,
he did not deserve to be ensnared by the aforementioned person.
Those who hold great power are also far too negligent."
Yún could only sigh.
Jí Shī
was a man from Huázhōu.
He was appointed Investigating Censor from the position of Lìshuǐ County Defender.
At that time, Grand Master Lǐ Qiányòu was the Magistrate of Wànnián County.
Shī was investigating the county's prison cases.
Qiányòu came out late due to some mishap.
Shī became angry,
and left without even looking at him.
He harbored resentment.
Qiányòu soon became an Inspector.
Wéi Wùjìng was from the same hometown as Shī,
and served as Qiányòu's Administrative Assistant.
When an imperial decree appointed Qiányòu as Palace Aide to the Censor-in-chief,
Qiányòu looked at Wùjìng and said:
"Your townsman can leave now,
and you, sir, may enter."
Shī was then demoted to Magistrate of Xīnlè.
His nature was rash and impulsive.
Once, the Duty Officer Lǐ Chōngjì,
who was a cousin of Emperor Gāozōng,
committed a minor offense.
Shī was about to impeach him and spoke to him,
calling Chōngjì "younger brother."
Chōngjì said to him:
"Chōngjì is the emperor's cousin.
Your surname is Jí.
What relation are you to the imperial family,
that you call me 'younger brother'?"
Shī, ashamed, stopped.
Once, while supervising the sacrifices at the Grand Temple,
he reprimanded an official in charge,
intending to impeach him.
The official watched for his mistake all night.
Jí, wearing red ceremonial shoes, went to the toilet.
They jointly exposed him,
and he stopped.
Cuī Pián, Lǐ Déyù, after retiring from court and returning home,
often joked intimately and informally with his relative Péi Jǐng,
and inquired of Lǐ about new affairs inside and outside the court.
Lǐ asked if there was any other news.
Péi said:
"Nothing else new,
but yesterday, a group of court officials gathered at the slope to send off a certain official appointed to a regional post,
holding a farewell feast at the relay station.
There were many guests.
Bái, the Vice Director of the Bureau of Revenues, arrived last.
Cuī Pián, Director of the Bureau of Revenues, acted as the master of ceremonies,
and assigned four tallies of drink.
Bái, considering his low rank,
and feeling intimidated by others,
did not dare to firmly decline.
The first round served four large vessels.
Bái drained three vessels in succession,
held the remaining one,
and asked the name of the fourth vessel.
Director Cuī said:
'Nothing else,
but why must you try to get out of it everywhere?'"
At that, Bái staggered and fell from his lower seat,
and ultimately left without drinking.
Some at the table laughed,
others shrank their necks in fear,
but who knows if that official managed to get up today?"
Lǐ, hearing this, became furious,
and said:
"How can this be endured?
Is it true that such words were spoken?"
He replied:
"Certainly."
Lǐ then asked if his brother knew where Vice Director Bái resided.
Jǐng said:
"That man lives in such-and-such ward, such-and-such lane."
Lǐ said:
"Please convey a message to Vice Director Bái for me,
and ask him to come to my residence."
Bái, receiving the summons, was both worried and fearful.
When he arrived,
Lǐ said:
"I have long wished to have a leisurely chat with you,
but affairs both inside and outside have been pressing.
However, for the next ten days to a month, do not involve yourself in others' matters."
Soon after, Bái was appointed Hanlin Academician.
Cuī Pián was made Prefect of Fénzhōu,
later changed to Prefect of Míngzhōu,
wandering in provincial posts,
never again serving in the ministries.
He ended his career as Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial.
People of Xīchuān and Shǔdōng, the people of the Eastern and Western Chuān,
often looked down upon each other.
People of Xīchuān said:
"Zǐzhōu
is merely the grass market at our eastern gate.
How can it be considered our equal?"
Military Governor Liǔ Zhòngyǐng heard this,
and said to his staff:
"I have served at court for thirty years,
experiencing all the pure and illustrious posts,
and today I finally get to be the market supervisor for Xīchuān."
Those who heard it all laughed.
Therefore, it is said that people of the Eastern and Western Chuān are often scornful.
Liú Zhān's father, Liú Jǐng, a staff member in Hézhōng,
was from Liánzhōu.
In his youth, he drafted documents for Minister Zhèng of Hànnán.
Once, he inscribed a poem on a spring and rock beside the Shāngshān relay station.
Zhèng was greatly impressed.
He encouraged him to pursue advancement,
had him change into hemp clothes at the previous station and present gifts to meet him,
later recommended him for the examinations,
and he passed the Jìnshì examination,
serving in various ministries.
Zhān was orphaned and poor but talented.
Although he passed the examinations,
he did not join the fast stream.
While serving as Reviewer in the Court of Judicial Review,
he often lacked even gruel to eat.
He once sought a meal from a monk he knew at Ānguó Temple,
leaving several scrolls of his writings on the monk's table.
The retired Army Supervisor Liú Xuányì visited the temple,
saw Zhān's literary scrolls,
was greatly impressed,
and pitying his poverty,
generously aided and relieved him.
Knowing he was from Liánshān,
and had no powerful connections at court,
he said to the monk:
"Although he is currently idle and neglected,
I will surely help this man become Chancellor."
Later, Zhān was appointed Junior Administrator of Hézhōng.
Among his staff were some arrogant and frivolous nobles,
who looked down upon him.
One day, an order came summoning him to the capital.
The Prefect saw him off.
The previously scornful staff member addressed Zhān as "Administrator."
He said:
"What official position will you hold upon returning to court?"
Zhān replied:
"If I find the way, I will become Chancellor."
His colleagues in the office laughed at him,
though some at the gathering were surprised by his words.
Zhān subsequently became Drafter of Edicts from the position of Vice Director of the Bureau of Waterways,
soon entered the Hanlin Academy,
and eventually became Chancellor.
Cuī Zhāofú and Pí Rìxiū
were students of Zhèng Yú from Nánhǎi.
During the Spring Imperial Examination, they once feasted at Qǔjiāng,
and Pí Rìxiū, drunk, slept on a separate couch.
His clothing bags and book cases,
arranged beside him,
were all newly adorned.
Cuī Zhāofú, a fellow candidate,
son of Cuī Liáo,
had always looked down upon him,
and was also drunk.
While changing clothes, he saw Rìxiū
and, thinking him someone familiar and close,
immediately watched and inquired,
intending to tease him.
Rìxiū’s servant hurried forward to call him.
Zhāofú, knowing it was Rìxiū,
said:
“Don’t call him;
he is holding a clan gathering right now,
because his bags and cases are all made of ‘pí’ (leather).”
People of the time spread this as a subject of ridicule.
Rìxiū once traveled between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
while Liú Yǔnzhāng governed Jiāngxià.
In his staff was a Judge Mù,
a relative of Yǔnzhāng,
and someone slandered Rìxiū for treating him disrespectfully.
Yǔnzhāng was often prone to drunken anger;
one day during a feast,
he suddenly angrily said:
“Why do you disrespect Judge Mù?
Do you know where you come from?
The Parrot Isle is here,
the place where Huáng Zǔ drowned Mí Héng.”
The entire gathering feared for him,
but Rìxiū only shed tears to the south.
Another account says Liú Yǔnzhāng, the Eastern Capital’s military governor,
a master of literature,
was quite haughty and aloof.
Ordinary scholars of later generations
rarely dared to approach his gate.
During the Xiántōng era,
he was appointed as the observation commissioner of Èzhōu from the post of Vice Minister of Rites.
The following year, Pí Rìxiū passed the imperial examination,
and was returning to pay respects at Sūtái.
Passing through Jiāngxià,
he was in distress and sent in his name card.
Liú treated him very generously,
even providing extra provisions.
He stayed for several days.
Liú then held a feast at the Yellow Crane Tower in his honor,
after the supervising army commissioner and staff had all gathered,
Rìxiū finally arrived for the summons,
already heavily intoxicated.
Upon ascending the tower,
Liú, because of his late arrival
and his drunken compliance with the summons,
inwardly disdained him.
After several rounds of drinking,
Rìxiū’s speech became disorderly and contentious,
abruptly losing all courtesy and respect.
Liú, with a changed expression, said to him:
“Young man from Wú, do not rely on your trivial talent;
you may preside over the feast.”
Rìxiū replied:
“Sir, are you perhaps one of the Liú clan from Nányuè?
Why are you so arrogant and haughty?”
Liú grew furious,
pointed accusingly from afar and scolded:
“Pí Rìxiū,
do you know that Parrot Isle is where Mí Héng died?”
Rìxiū dared not reply,
only stood unsteadily as if drunk,
and the host’s attendants helped him out.
The next day, he disguised himself and fled to the east of Zhèjiāng.
Wēn Dìng, in the fourth year of the Qiánfú era,
at the Qǔjiāng spring banquet for new jìnshì,
surpassed previous years in splendor.
There was a Wēn Dìng,
long frustrated in the examinations,
unrestrained and self-indulgent by nature,
particularly resentful of the frivolity of the times,
who devised an unusual plan to mock them.
On that day,
he covered himself with a cloak and rode in a shoulder carriage,
with gold and jade ornaments,
strikingly standing out from the crowd,
and his maidservants were similarly adorned,
lingering under the willow shade.
Soon, the gentlemen moved their music from the open pavilion to the bow of the boat.
Then, thinking this was a noble and wealthy person,
whose entourage must include beautiful women,
they urged their boats forward,
all gazing intently in that direction,
some endlessly bantering and teasing.
As the group’s excitement peaked,
Dìng then let his foot and knee hang from behind the curtain,
revealing an extremely large and hairy shank.
The crowd suddenly saw it,
and all covered their sleeves, urgently ordering their boats to turn away.
Someone said:
“This must be Wēn Dìng.”
Yáo Yánjié
was a descendant of Duke Liáng Yuánchóng.
In childhood, he was exceptionally intelligent and perceptive.
By his capping age, he was broadly versed in the classics,
admiring the ways of Bān Gù and Sīmǎ Qiān,
and was called a great Confucian scholar of his time.
He often roamed east of the Jiāng with poetry and wine,
especially unrestrained in disparaging his elders,
acting as if no one else was present.
During the Táng Qiánfú era,
Yán Biāo governed Póyáng commandery,
and when the official grounds and polo field were first constructed,
he invited Yánjié to record the event.
The essay completed,
brilliantly over a thousand words long,
Biāo wanted to delete two characters,
but Yánjié refused.
Biāo grew angry;
by then, the stone had already been engraved,
and he ordered the stele smashed.
Yánjié commemorated this with a poem:
“To inform Lord Yán, do you know me?
My heart is only with Heaven, that’s all.
The vulgar matters before me stir great feelings,
After wine, the green hills enter my thoughts more.
Féng Xuān often resents strumming his sword hilt with regret,
Níng Qì should cease singing the ‘Ox-Feeding Song.’
If the sage court plans for the common people,
A public carriage should come to the ivy and vines.”
Lú Zhào governed Shèzhōu,
while Yánjié was in Wùyuán,
and first sent his writings to Zhào.
Zhào knew he was prone to drunkenness,
so he wrote a letter praising him,
and sent cloth and silk as gifts.
The message said:
“After the ravages of war,
the commandery is in decline and destitution,
and has nothing with which to welcome a great worthy.”
Yánjié again provoked him with a long letter.
Zhào had no choice,
and welcomed him to the commandery residence,
treating Yán with the courtesy due to a high minister.
But Yáo remained arrogantly self-assured.
Zhào boasted to Yánjié with a poetic line:
“The bright moon shines on the land of Bā.”
Yánjié laughed and said:
“The bright moon shines on the whole sky;
why do you only say ‘the land of Bā’?”
Zhào was greatly ashamed.
Not long after,
they met at a riverside pavilion,
with Kuǎi Xīyì also present.
Lú proposed a drinking game using current sights,
ending with the name of a musical instrument.
Zhào gave the challenge:
“Gazing at distant fishing boats,
not even a chǐbā (an 18-inch ruler, also a flute) apart.”
Yánjié then drank a full cup of wine,
leaned on the railing and retched.
Shortly after,
returning to his seat,
he gave his challenge in return:
“Leaning on the railing, one retch,
already feels the throat empty.”
Such was his insulting and arrogant manner.
Court officials on a mission to Shuòfāng
... jumping ropes and various acrobatic performances were all presented.
The envoy watched as if he did not see them.
... thinking it insufficient for amusement ... separately ... not ... Húténg. The envoy looked up at Tuòbá,
then glanced sideways at Húténg.
Then he straightened his lapels respectfully ... his position, looking as if ashamed ... appearance.
The dance soon ended.
Hurrying forward, he thanked them:
“I have already been honored by Your Excellency’s arrangement of the banquet feast,
with various performances for entertainment.
Please do not trouble your worthy son ... singing and dancing quite ... repeatedly declining with thanks.”
It seemed he saw among the Tuòbá someone resembling Húténg in nose,
so he called him “worthy son,”
using this to slight him.
Xuē Bǎoxùn was
the son of a distinguished family.
Relying on his talent and status,
he freely evaluated and ranked others.
Scholars’ reputations rose or fell based on his judgments,
earning him the contemporary label of being frivolous and shallow.
Chancellor Xiàhóu Zī particularly despised him.
His paternal cousin, named Bǎohòu to distinguish himself,
caused a rift between them.
His wife, Madame Lú,
shared similar principles and conduct
with her husband, Bǎoxùn.
When his younger uncle, Supervisor Xuē, came for a visit,
Madame Lú went out to greet him.
After he left,
she ordered water to wash the threshold.
Supervisor Xuē learned of this and was greatly angered.
He submitted a memorial to the chancellor,
and as a result, Bǎoxùn was demoted to the position of Sima of Lǐzhōu,
where he remained for seven years without replacement.
When Duke Xiàhóu left the capital to govern a province,
and Chancellor Wèi Mó rose to power,
Bǎoxùn was about to be recalled for an appointment
but passed away in the commandery.
I once read several of his refined writings,
one of which said:
"Bidding farewell to relatives and friends at Bàshàng,
I stayed at an inn
and saw several figures resembling people.
When spoken to, their mouths moved,
and they all claimed to be officials from prefectures and counties in Jiāng, Huái, and Lǐngbiǎo.
Alas,
are the people born under heaven
to be flogged by such individuals?"
Another piece, "Watching a Performance," said:
"A red-bearded barbarian pushed the magistrate,
who stumbled out clumsily.
Everyone laughed,
but Bǎoxùn did not."
His irreverent and unrestrained nature was often like this.
When Lú Qiánguàn was dismissed from Kuízhōu,
as a close relative,
he went directly to Lǐzhōu to console and visit [Bǎoxùn].
Returning to a courier station,
he looked back and wept, saying:
"Who would have thought that Xuē Bǎoxùn
would one day receive Military Judge Lǐ
and perform 'Beating the Willow Branch'?"
Xuē Zhāowěi,
a Tang dynasty figure,
was the son of Xuē Bǎoxùn.
Relying on his talent, he looked down on others,
inheriting his father's style.
Whenever he entered the court or government offices,
he would toy with his official tablet while walking,
as if no one else was around.
He also enjoyed singing the lyrics of "Washing Sand Creek."
After overseeing the imperial examinations,
one of his disciples bid farewell to return to his hometown.
At the parting, the disciple offered advice, saying:
"Your Excellency is of great virtue,
and I have received your kindness.
If hereafter you refrain from toying with your tablet and singing 'Washing Sand Creek,'
I would be most fortunate."
Contemporaries considered this profound advice.
There was a minor clerk
who once imitated his walking and bowing mannerisms.
When Xuē learned of this,
he summoned the clerk and said:
"Try to imitate me in the courtyard.
If you succeed,
I will forgive your offense."
He then lowered the curtains
and watched with his concubines.
The clerk calmly and arrogantly
performed movements strikingly similar to his,
so Xuē laughed and let him go.
When Lù, the Palace Attendant, was in Shǔ,
he once sought coolness on a summer day in the ball field hall.
A minor clerk from the administrative office, Luó Jiǔgāo,
wrapped in a headscarf and walking with a stride,
resembled Péi Tiáo.
The Palace Attendant saw him from afar and urgently summoned him,
but only upon closer inspection did he realize it was not him.
He then had the clerk flogged.
Also, when Xuē Zhāowěi was sent as an envoy to the State of Liáng,
to convey the intention of abdication,
Liáng Zǔ ordered his guest general to intercept and turn him back.
Xuē then said to the receptionist:
"My sovereign has given orders.
I cannot turn back."
He swiftly urged his horse forward.
Upon reaching Yímén,
Liáng Zǔ had no choice but to come out and receive him.
Seeing Xuē's elegant demeanor and eloquent speech,
he began to change his opinion of him.
From then on, during banquets and meetings,
he treated him with utmost sincerity.
One day,
when Liáng Zǔ spoke of hawks and falcons,
Xuē enthusiastically praised the prowess of birds of prey.
Liáng Zǔ was pleased
and thought Xuē also enjoyed falconry.
After returning to his lodgings,
[Liáng Zǔ] sent him a falcon as a gift.
Xuē wrote a letter of thanks,
and in front of the messenger, instructed his servant:
"What His Excellency has bestowed
must be cherished.
You may wrap it in paper
and place it in the falconry bag."
Those who heard of this laughed at him.
Jù Yàn
was from Púbǎn.
He excelled at composing elegant and proper poetry.
At that time, Wáng Chóngróng governed Hézhōng,
only to the state gate to pay respects to the Three Dukes fourteen characters originally left blank,
and Chóngróng treated him with great respect and courtesy.
As a person,
he often acted unrestrainedly.
He bullied and oppressed the various assistants.
Ultimately, he met with the disaster of Zhèngpíng.
Wéi and Xuē looked down on the Gāo family.
In the late Tang dynasty, Gāo Jìchāng of Jiānglíng served as the military governor of Jīngnán.
At that time,
the chancellors Wéi Shuō and Zhèng Jué
were related by marriage as uncle and nephew.
During the reign of Emperor Tàizǔ of the Later Liáng,
they both attained
control over regional affairs.
Gāo, as a nobleman’s son, was appointed as the military secretary,
(the text here is missing a character)
and hosted banquets with wine and delicacies
to entertain these gentlemen.
They gathered frequently for feasts,
making constant demands,
and Gāo treated them all with great courtesy.
Later, when Zhuāngzōng crossed the Yellow River,
he swiftly seized the Central Plains,
causing fear throughout the land.
Prince Gāo rode alone to pay homage,
while Wéi and Zhèng,
having ascended to high positions,
along with many scions of the central court’s noble families,
failed to grasp the changing times.
They maintained their old attitudes.
Xuē Zé was appointed as a Reminder,
and Wéi Jīng was appointed as a Doctor of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
both granted crimson robes,
and they all wore expressions of self-satisfaction.
Hastily preparing their belongings,
they awaited their return to the court,
looking down upon the military secretary.
Lǐ Zàirén, the nephew of Wéi Shuō,
was appointed as a secretary in the Imperial Library.
Liú Shēn, the brother-in-law of Zhèng Jué,
was appointed as a Doctor of the *Book of Songs*,
and granted a crimson robe.
Afterward, Wéi repeatedly urged Lǐ to go to the capital,
but Gāo wished to promote and employ him.
Lǐ Zàirén delayed,
citing the admonitions of his ancestors,
and did not wish to rely on his uncle,
though he could not say so openly.
In the end, he did not leave Gāo’s household.
Liú Shēn had no other talents or reputation,
was fond of drinking,
and though he accepted the new appointment,
showed no intention of leaving.
Day after day, he remained with Gāo,
his affection and respect undiminished,
likely drawn by the fine wine and plump lamb.
Not long after,
he died of illness.
Gāo provided for his orphaned family,
with considerable care and thoroughness.
Before long,
turmoil arose in Luòyáng,
and Míngzōng ascended the throne.
The powerful lords of the south
were appeased with concessions,
and both Chancellors Wéi and Zhèng were dismissed.
Wéi and Xuē still lingered in Jīngchǔ.
The following year,
when Bǎozuì succeeded to the position,
he appointed Lǐ as his secretary.
Later,
he married his eldest son to Lǐ’s daughter,
and had all three of Lǐ’s sons appointed to official posts.
Thus, the entire family was adorned with crimson and purple robes.
Liú Shēn’s three sons
were successively employed and favored,
and his three granddaughters married into the Gāo family.
For nearly thirty years,
they enjoyed official salaries,
which was indeed commendable.
Wéi Jīng lived in obscurity
and died in solitude,
while Xuē Zé served as an acting official until his death.
Was this brought upon themselves,
or was it fate?
Hú Huì
There was a man named Hú Huì,
who served as an aide in a major military command,
renowned for his literary talent,
skilled at drafting military documents,
all of which met with approval.
At that time, the imperial court had moved west,
and the Central Plains were garrisoned with troops.
The two commands of Qí and Qín
were the most formidable bulwarks.
Their urgent dispatches and proclamations
circulated throughout the realm,
and none could match his pen and tongue.
The commanding general was young at the time,
and the power over life and death
rested with the deputy commander,
Zhāng Yún.
His authority was comparable to that of the governor of Jīngzhōu.
Zhāng Tóng
served as an inspector.
Hú often belittled his commander,
and looked down upon his peers without showing them respect.
The commander,
valuing his talent,
did not severely reprimand him,
but only admonished him.
Yet Hú remained frivolous and unrestrained.
Once, during an official banquet,
Hú, intoxicated, shouted
at Zhāng Yún,
“Zhāng Shíliù!”
Zhāng Shíliù was Zhāng Yún’s informal name based on his birth order.
He repeatedly insulted Zhāng Yún with his words,
and though the commander tolerated it,
Zhāng harbored resentment.
Another day, Hú went to Jīngzhōu to visit Zhāng Tóng.
Zhāng Tóng’s servant did not recognize him,
and asked
his attendants,
who said:
“It is Grand Master Hú Huì.”
By the time he reached the hall,
he had already removed his outer robe.
When Zhāng Tóng heard Hú had come,
he wished to treat him generously,
so he ordered
his household to prepare an elaborate feast.
Zhāng Tóng hurried out to greet him,
but suddenly it was reported:
“The Grand Master has already left.”
Zhāng Tóng then
walked to the hall,
only to find that Hú had left behind filth between two chairs and departed,
without leaving a single word.
Zhāng Tóng also
laughed but harbored resentment.
Zhāng Yún could do him no harm.
Later, the commander sent Hú on a mission to Dàliáng.
Hú was accompanied by a guest of his, a certain Judicial Reviewer Chén.
Zhāng Yún secretly bribed Chén,
instructing him to watch for any misconduct by Hú.
In Liáng, Hú indeed acted recklessly and boastfully,
and some reported what they observed secretly to the Prince of Liáng.
All of this was recorded by Chén in a memorial.
Upon his return,
the commander knew of his arrogance and rashness,
but still treated him leniently.
Chén, following instructions,
fabricated accusations against him,
compiling a record of his eccentric and improper drafts,
and presented it to the commander.
The commander was intoxicated at the time,
and upon hearing this, flew into a rage.
He then had Hú and his entire family taken out
and executed at the mouth of Píngróng Valley,
leaving no survivors.
When the commander sobered up and learned of this,
he was greatly shocked,
and lamented for a long time.
After deep thought, he said:
“It was the deputy commander who killed you,
not I.”
Later, when military documents were drafted but failed to meet his expectations,
he would weep and think of Hú.
This fault did not lie with Zhāng Yún alone,
for Hú brought it upon himself.
Wáng Rényù once passed by Píngróng Valley
and composed a poem mourning him:
“Halting my horse in the desolate wilds, my eyes filled with sorrow,
What crime did this man commit to die in these wooded hills?
The wind howls through ancient trees, eternal grief remains,
Rain dampens the cold sedge, tears silently flow.
Do not say his writings aroused the envy of the crowd,
Only his frivolousness became the enemy of his own life.
If not for his spirit resting beneath the solitary mountain,
This place could be named Parrot Isle.”
Frivolous Scholars
In the Táng dynasty, there was a frivolous scholar-official who was appointed as the prefect of a commandery.
The local people gathered singers, musicians, and all sorts of performers to welcome him.
There were even sword-swallowers and sword-vomiters,
those who played bamboo and string instruments, those who walked on balls and jumped through hoops, singers with beautiful voices and dancers with slender waists—yet he seemed not to see any of them.
The people of the prefecture said:
"Our Prefect is austere and stern;
there is nothing to please him."
They looked at each other with worry and distress.
Suddenly one day,
in the height of summer, he ascended the tower
and abruptly ordered music to be performed.
The local people joyfully said:
"So our Prefect is not averse to music after all."
When the performers arrived below the tower,
