he then ordered each type to be brought up one by one.
The various string, wind, and percussion instruments were presented in succession,
but he scolded them all away, refusing to use them.
There was a shēng player
who arrived last.
The Prefect happily said:
"I only want this one kind."
He asked:
"What is this thing called?"
They replied:
"It is called a shēng,
it can be blown."
The musician looked very pleased with himself.
Just as he was about to play and adjust it,
after a few notes,
the Prefect abruptly stopped him, saying:
"Don't move your fingers,
just blow it straight through."
The musician complied.
He then ordered him to blow it long by the railing,
from noon until late afternoon.
Then he called his attendants,
ordered that wine be bestowed and the musician dismissed,
saying:
"Who needs melodies?
I just used you to summon the wind."
Another day, he went into the mountains and summoned musicians.
When they arrived,
he became angry,
glared and scolded them, saying:
"I only want tall women."
The music troupe hurriedly withdrew in confusion,
not understanding the reason.
So they sent six or seven women with bound,
long
feet, entered with drums and flutes.
He then looked at the women and had them climb a large tree,
each holding
a basket, and ordered them to pick the tree's fruit.
Such
frivolous and shallow acts
by this kind of person were very numerous.
Zhāng Áo
During the Qiánníng era of the Táng dynasty,
Chén Fán, the Prefect of Sùzhōu, rose from a military background
and arbitrarily exercised severe judgment.
Jìnshì Zhāng Áo, relying on his talent, looked down on everyone.
At a banquet, he flirted with Chén Fán's favorite courtesan, Zhāng Xiǎotài.
Chén Fán became angry,
had him seized and handed over to the clerks,
accusing him of impropriety.
The accusation stated:
"There is a Zhāng Áo,
who dwells in Huáiyīn,
coming to this splendid feast,
he indulges his whims without restraint."
Chén Fán grew even angrier and said:
"Based on this analysis,
how many strokes should he receive?"
Zhāng Áo also said:
"For just these two lines,
he should receive three or five strokes;
yet truly seeking a smile,
should cost a thousand or ten thousand in gold."
In the end, he was flogged on the back and died.
From Liú Shānfǔ's "Xián Tán",
the full text is not recorded here.
Lú Chéng
Lú Chéng passed the jìnshì examination
and served as Hézhōng Judge under Emperor Zhuāngzōng,
and after the founding of the state, was appointed Chancellor.
He had no other talent or achievement,
only relying on his clan lineage to look down on others.
Rèn Yuán once went to visit him on official business.
Lú Chéng, wearing his black gauze cap and leaning on his desk,
said to Rèn Yuán:
"You are an insect,
how dare you come and be presumptuous."
Rèn Yuán was ashamed and shocked,
and quickly reported it to Emperor Zhuāngzōng.
The Emperor was furious,
ordered him killed,
but he was saved through Lú Zhì's intervention and plea.
From then on, he was dismissed from the Secretariat,
and people of the time gnashed their teeth at him.
Jiānglíng, during the Táng era,
was known as a gathering place for the cultured elite.
People said there were more pipas than rice steamers,
and more poor scholars than crucian carp.
There was a District Magistrate, Mr. Lú,
who frequently requisitioned boats from Zhījiāng County to travel to the prefectural seat,
much to the boatmen's distress.
One day, during the military turmoil of Wáng Xiānzhī,
Mr. Lú had his tendons pulled out by the boatmen,
tied to the gunwale of the boat,
and set adrift to die.
Generally, those young men without skill,
mostly relied on their family status to act frivolously and arrogantly.
During the Guǎngmíng disturbances,
many suffered such fates,
all brought upon themselves.
Cuī Mì
In the second year of the Tiānchéng era,
Pān Huán was appointed Prefect of Dìzhōu due to military merit.
He normally had few guests.
Someone recommended Cuī Mì,
a scholar from Bólíng,
whose demeanor was refined and elegant,
and whose literary compositions were also skillful.
Pān was very pleased upon meeting him,
prepared a superior guesthouse to host him,
but after a night, Cuī did not return.
Pān sought him but could not find him.
Later, he engaged another scholar who then went.
Afterwards, the recommender saw Cuī and questioned him.
Cuī said:
"Although Lord Pān is diligent and sincere,
to the left of his nose bridge there is a sore,
constantly oozing pus and blood.
Every time I was near, the stench assailed me,
the foul odor was unbearable.
I regard him as a 'white-dead man'."
The recommender laughed heartily.
Cuī disregarded reputation and substance to act frivolously,
indeed.
It was because Pān had once been struck in the face by a stray arrow,
the arrowhead embedded in the bone,
hence he suffered a severe wound.
Medical treatment lasted a full
year.
The arrowhead came out by itself,
the wound became a fistula,
and never healed for the rest of his life.
King Xiānzhǔ Suffers Frivolity
When Wéi Zhāodù was recruiting to campaign against Chén Jìngxuān,
Supplemented according to the Huáng edition.
Shǔ commander Gù Yànhuī served as deputy,
and King Xiānzhǔ
served as Chief Commandant.
The three headquarters each appointed staff officers,
all of whom were sons of prominent court officials,
and they looked down on King Xiānzhǔ.
King Xiānzhǔ's attendants
had shaven heads,
tattooed faces and bound wrists,
like a troop of ghosts and spirits.
Those men competed in solemnity with King Xiānzhǔ.
Lord Gù was calm and unhurried,
but momentarily lost his composure and laughed, and they dispersed.
King Xiānzhǔ returned to camp,
his attendants spoke of this matter,
and he himself also laughed heartily.
Later, when he captured Qīchéng,
those frivolous staff officers
were all killed.
Jiǎng Yígōng
The Investigating Commissioner of the Zhōu, Suǒ Yuánlǐ,
was called Commissioner Suǒ by people of the time.
When interrogating prisoners, he would make an iron cage head,
place it over the prisoner's head,
then add wedges,
often until the skull split and brains spilled out.
He also devised methods like "phoenix drying its wings" and "monkey drilling fire,"
where he would bind the hands and feet with rafters and twist them.
He would also grind
the bones until they shattered.
He would also hang prisoners from a beam,
with stones tied to their heads.
Such were his cruel methods.
Yuánlǐ was originally a Hu man,
the adoptive father of Xuē Shī.
Later, he was convicted of bribery and corruption,
exiled to Lǐngnán, where he died.
Framing People
Zhōu's official Lái Jùnchén framed people for crimes,
always first submitting a memorial,
receiving an imperial edict approving the report,
and then confiscating their property.
Xú Yǒugōng, when releasing death-row prisoners,
would also first submit a memorial,
stating that someone's crime deserved pardon,
receive an imperial edict of approval,
and only then overturn the verdict.
Yǒugōng was fond of exonerating crimes,
but he always acted upon prior imperial instruction,
not on his own authority.
Zhāng Tāng probed the ruler's intentions;
this was likely the reason.
Yuánkǎi
Táng's Yǔlín General Yuánkǎi
gained office through three generations of informing.
His son Yànwěi
informed against Liú Chéngzhī, ruining his family,
and Yànwěi was appointed Attendant Censor.
In the second year of the Xiāntiān era,
on the third day of the seventh month,
Yuánkǎi was executed for treason,
and his family was exiled to Lǐngnán.
This is what is called the family that accumulates evil
will surely have leftover calamity.
Wǔ Chéngsì
Zhōu's Supplémentor Qiáo Zhīzhī had a maidservant named Bìyù, beautiful and charming,
skilled in singing and dancing,
and literate.
Zhīzhī favored her especially,
and for her sake did not marry.
The false Prince of Wèi, Wǔ Chéngsì, temporarily borrowed her to teach his concubines makeup and hairstyling.
He then kept her,
and would not return her.
Zhīzhī then composed "Lament of Lǜzhū" to send to her.
The lyrics said:
"In the Shí family's Jīngǔ, a new melody arose,
Ten hú of bright pearls bought a graceful beauty.
On this day, pitiable, she pledged herself alone,
In this moment, her song and dance won people's hearts.
Your family's inner chambers have never been seen,
Yet you gladly lend your song and dance for others to watch.
Arrogant and domineering, without reason or right,
Proud and powerful, they interfere by force.
To leave you, my lord, in the end I cannot bear,
Vainly I hide my sleeves, grieving over leaden powder.
A century's parting sorrow in a high tower,
A lifetime's beauty exhausted for you, my lord."
Bìyù received the poem,
wept silently and did not eat for three days,
then threw herself into a well and died.
Chéngsì had her corpse retrieved,
and found the poem on her skirt belt.
Furious,
he then insinuated to the framers to accuse him.
Subsequently, he had Zhīzhī beheaded at the southern market,
and his family was ruined and property confiscated.
The Zhāng Yìzhī Brothers
Zhōu's Zhāng Yìzhī was Director of the Control Crane Bureau,
his younger brother Chāngzōng was Director of the Palace Library,
and Chāngyí was Magistrate of Luòyáng.
They vied in extravagance and luxury.
Yìzhī made a large iron cage,
placed geese and ducks inside it,
lit a charcoal fire in the middle,
with a bronze basin holding a five-flavor sauce.
The geese and ducks walked around the fire,
drinking the sauce when thirsty,
roasted by the fire, they turned in pain,
until cooked through and through,
feathers all fallen off,
and the flesh red and sizzling before they died.
Chāngzōng tied a live donkey in a small room,
lit a charcoal fire,
placed the five-flavor sauce,
using the same method.
Chāngyí took iron stakes and hammered them into the ground,
tied a dog's four feet to the stakes,
released hawks and falcons,
which pecked at and ate its flesh alive,
until the flesh was gone but the dog was not yet dead,
howling in agony,
too painful to hear.
Yìzhī once visited Chāngyí,
and craved horse intestines.
Chāngyí took a horse from his retinue,
broke its ribs to extract the intestines,
and it took a long time before it died.
Later, when Yìzhī, Chāngzōng, and others were executed,
the people carved up their flesh,
which was plump and white like lard,
and fried or roasted it to eat.
Chāngyí had his legs broken by beating,
then his heart and liver were gouged out before he died.
His head was cut off and sent to the capital.
People of the time said it was retribution for the dogs and horses.
Hǎo Xiàngxián
was the grandson of Hǎo Chǔjùn.
Empress Wǔ held a long-standing grudge against his grandfather,
and the killing extended to his grandson.
As Xiàngxián faced execution,
he cursed vehemently and died.
From then on, the judicial authorities, fearing this,
when about to execute someone,
would first stuff a wooden ball into their mouth,
and then carry out the punishment.
Zhōu Xīng
Zhōu's Vice Minister of Justice Zhōu Xīng conducted investigations with cruelty,
inflicting torment beyond the law,
stopping at nothing.
People of the time called him "Ox-Headed Granny."
The common people resented and criticized him.
Xīng then posted a judgment on his door, saying:
"Those accused,
when questioned, all claim innocence.
After beheading,
all become silent."
Hóu Sīzhǐ
Zhōu's Attendant Censor Hóu Sīzhǐ
was a pancake seller from Lǐquán.
Through false accusations,
he was rewarded according to precedent with the fifth rank.
He requested the position of Censor before the Emperor,
who said:
"You do not know how to read."
He replied:
"Does the xièzhì know how to read?
It only butts against criminals for the state."
He was then granted the post.
Whenever he conducted investigations,
he killed a great many people,
with hardly any other words.
He only said to the prisoners:
"I don't need your written statements or eloquent words,
just give me back my White Simǎ.
If you won't come to Jùn,
then I'll give you Mèng Qīng."
Many suffered unjust torment,
and those who died unnaturally were countless.
"White Simǎ" refers to
the White Simǎ Slope on Mount Běimáng.
"Come to Jùn" refers to
Vice Censor-in-Chief Lái Jùnchén.
"Mèng Qīng" refers to
General Mèng Qīng's club.
Later, he was convicted of privately hoarding brocade,
and was executed by beating in the court assembly hall.
Lái Jùnchén was a native of Yōngzhōu.
His father, Cāo,
served as the Chief Secretary of Sōngzhōu.
In his youth, Jùnchén was cunning and unscrupulous,
treacherous and deceitful,
cruel and depraved,
unparalleled in the world.
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
he fabricated accusations against various princes and high-ranking ministers,
and was appointed Gentleman for Court Discussion,
promoted to Attendant Censor,
and put in charge of the special prison.
Anyone who did not comply with his wishes
would inevitably be implicated,
and over time, entire clans were executed,
with over a thousand families exterminated.
The court was filled with fear,
and no one dared to speak out.
People on the streets communicated only with their eyes.
He was close confidants with Attendant Censors Wáng Hóngyì and Hóu Sīzhǐ.
They fabricated accusations against officials,
without regard for the seasons.
Executions were continuous.
At that time, a special prison was established inside the Lìjǐng Gate,
also known as the Newly Opened Gate.
Once one entered the Newly Opened Gate,
fewer than one in a hundred survived.
Hóngyì jokingly called the Lìjǐng Gate the "Gate of Certain Death,"
meaning that entering this gate meant certain death.
Jùnchén, along with his accomplices such as Zhū Nánshān and over ten others,
composed a manual of dozens of words on fabricating accusations and entrapment,
all with systematic organization and supporting evidence.
They would arrange the details and origins of the accusations,
then have their accomplices report them.
Sometimes they would submit them through the petition box to make them known.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān often entrusted Jùnchén with interrogations.
Jùnchén created a special cangue,
called the "Earth-Shaking Roar."
Those subjected to this cangue
would be spun on the ground,
quickly losing consciousness.
He also made ten types of cangues,
and a club named "Confess on Sight."
There was also an iron hoop head cage;
when interrogating prisoners,
a wedge would be driven into the hoop.
There were dozens of other such devices,
generally of this nature.
Regardless of whether the prisoners were noble or common,
they would first
have the cangue and club laid out on the ground,
and then be summoned forward and told:
"These are the tools."
Upon seeing them, their souls would flee in terror,
and none failed to falsely confess.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān rewarded him generously with titles and riches,
so others competed to be even more cruel!
As a result, informants filled the streets,
and prominent figures lived in constant fear,
counting their days.
Court officials, while attending court,
would silently be ambushed,
leading to the extermination of their clans.
When parting from their families, they would say:
"I don’t know if we will ever meet again."
During the Tiānshòu era,
Minister of Rites Dí Rénjié, Vice Minister of Personnel Rèn Lìnghuī, Vice Director of the Right of the Secretariat Lú Xiàn, and others,
five men in total,
were all falsely accused by him.
Jùnchén, having made exterminating families his achievement,
wanted to force them to confess to rebellion,
so he petitioned for an imperial decree.
According to the rule, if one confessed during the first interrogation, it would be treated as a voluntary confession,
and the death penalty could be reduced.
He used this to coerce Dí Rénjié and the others,
forcing them to confess to rebellion.
Rénjié sighed and said:
"With the Great Zhōu dynasty’s revolution,
all things are renewed.
As an old minister of the Táng court,
I deserve execution;
rebellion is true."
Jùnchén then relaxed his treatment slightly.
His deputy, Wáng Déshòu, said to Rénjié:
"Your situation is already like this, Minister,
and you may yet avoid death.
I am now under orders,
and I wish to seek a small promotion.
Could you,
Minister, implicate Yáng Zhíróu?"
Rénjié said:
"What do you mean?"
Déshòu said:
"When you were previously in the Ministry of Rites,
Zhíróu served as a Vice Director in a bureau;
you could implicate him."
Rénjié said:
"By Heaven and Earth,
would Dí Rénjié do such a thing!"
He struck his head against a pillar,
blood streaming down his face.
Déshòu, frightened, apologized.
After Rénjié confessed to rebellion,
the authorities awaited the execution date
and no longer guarded him strictly.
He managed to ask for writing materials from the jailer.
He tore a piece of cloth from his bedding and wrote on it,
detailing his grievances and suffering,
and placed it inside a padded garment.
He told Déshòu:
"The weather is hot now.
Please have my family remove the padding."
Déshòu did not suspect anything.
Rénjié’s family found the letter inside the garment,
and his son, Dí Guāngyuǎn, presented it, claiming an injustice,
and was granted an audience.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān read it with dismay
and summoned Jùnchén to ask:
"You said Dí Rénjié and the others confessed to rebellion,
so why are their children now appealing their innocence?"
Jùnchén said:
"How could such people voluntarily admit their crimes?
I treat them very leniently;
they even keep their caps and belts."
Empress Wǔ Zétiān ordered the Court Usher, Zhōu Chēn, to go and inspect.
Jùnchén then ordered the prisoners
to put on caps and belts for Rénjié and the others,
and had them stand in the west.
He ordered Chēn to look.
Chēn, fearing Jùnchén,
dared not look westward,
but only glanced eastward and mumbled in agreement.
Jùnchén had Chēn stay briefly
and then submitted a report.
He then ordered his deputy to forge a petition of gratitude for death on behalf of Rénjié and the others,
signed it for them, and submitted it.
The son of Vice Director of the Secretariat of State Affairs, Yuè Sīhuì,
was eight or nine years old.
His family had already been exterminated,
and he was enslaved to the Court of the Imperial Granaries.
He submitted a petition and was granted an audience,
stating that Jùnchén and others were cruel and vicious,
and asking Her Majesty to write a sample confession of rebellion and give it to them;
then, regardless of the crime’s severity, all would confess accordingly.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān’s anger slightly subsided,
and she summoned Rénjié and the others to ask:
"Why did you confess to rebellion?"
Rénjié and the others said:
"If we hadn’t confessed then,
we would have died under the cangue and club!"
Empress Wǔ Zétiān said:
"Then why did you submit a petition of gratitude for death?"
Rénjié and the others said:
"We did not."
She then showed them the petition,
and they realized it had been forged.
Thus, these five families were released.
Jùnchén then accused Grand General Zhāng Qiánxù
and Grand General Attendant Fàn Yúnxiān
in Luòyáng
at the Pasture Office.
Qiánxù and others,
unable to endure the torture,
pleaded that they had contributed to the state,
their words rather forceful.
Jùnchén ordered guards to hack them to death with random blows;
Yúnxiān also said he had served the previous dynasty
and complained of injustice and suffering from the authorities.
Jùnchén ordered his tongue cut out.
Officials and commoners were terrified,
and no one dared to speak out.
Jùnchén was repeatedly convicted of corruption,
demoted to Military Advisor of Tóngzhōu,
forcibly seized the wife of a fellow Military Advisor,
and even insulted her mother,
with no one daring to speak out.
Soon, he was appointed Captain of Hénán,
and repeatedly promoted to Minister of the Imperial Stud.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān awarded him ten male and female slaves,
to be allocated by the Court of the Imperial Granaries.
At that time, the Western Barbarian chieftain and Grand General Húsèluó
had a young maidservant skilled in singing and dancing.
Jùnchén temporarily halted the allocation by the Court of the Imperial Granaries
and had his accomplices falsely accuse Húsèluó of rebellion,
intending to seize the maidservant.
Dozens of chieftains went to the palace,
cutting their ears and slashing their faces
to appeal the injustice,
and thus Húsèluó’s clan was spared extermination.
At that time, Qílián Yào and Liú Sīlǐ and others were conspiring;
the Captain of Cháng'ān, Jí Xū, knew of this
and told Jùnchén.
Jùnchén exposed it,
implicating dozens of clans who were executed.
Jùnchén, relying on his achievements,
Again, Lái Jùnchén framed Jí Xū.
Jí Xū managed to get an audience and appealed his case in court,
barely escaping punishment.
Jùnchén had previously coerced and taken
the daughter of Tàiyuán's Wáng Qìngshēn.
Jùnchén had long been acquainted with Hédōng's Wèi Suìzhōng.
Although Suìzhōng's reputation and conduct were not distinguished,
he was fond of learning
and eloquent in speech.
Once, while drunk, he went to visit Jùnchén.
Jùnchén was at that time feasting with his wife's family.
The gatekeeper falsely claimed that he was out.
Suìzhōng, knowing it was a lie,
entered his house
and insolently cursed and insulted him.
Jùnchén, feeling shamed before his relatives,
ordered him beaten and bound with his hands behind his back.
Later, he released him,
but from then on, a rift formed between them.
When Jùnchén was about to frame and accuse the various false princes of the Wǔ clan, as well as Princess Tàipíng and Zhāng Yìzhī, among others,
Suìzhōng exposed him.
Zétiān repeatedly protected him,
but the various members of the Wǔ clan and the princess, filled with fear,
jointly slandered him,
and he was executed in the marketplace.
People throughout the country, young and old alike, resented and hated him,
vying to slice flesh from his body.
In a moment, it was all gone.
Zétiān then came to her senses
and issued an edict, saying:
"Lái Jùnchén,
a petty man from the alleys,
has long been frivolous and treacherous.
Because he somewhat carried out investigations and impeachments,
it was thought he showed slight loyalty and sincerity.
Yet the various princes, as pillars and branches of the imperial clan,
he certainly sought to ruin and destroy.
The civil and military generals and ministers of the Northern and Southern Offices
he all plotted to overthrow and endanger.
He should be punished with the extermination of his clan,
to assuage the anger of the common people."
After his clan was exterminated,
regardless of scholar, commoner, man, or woman,
all celebrated together on the roads.
They all said:
"From now on when we lie down,
our backs can finally rest on the bed.
Otherwise,
we could not plan from morning to evening!"
Jí Xū
Jí Xū, Captain of Zhōu Míngtáng,
once stayed overnight with Investigating Censor Wáng Zhù.
Because they were relatives,
Wáng Zhù told him about Qílián Yào's sons, Dàjué and Xiǎojué,
saying they corresponded to the 'two-horned qílín'.
Yào's style name was Guāngdí,
which was interpreted as 'illuminating and residing over the world'.
The next day, Jí Xū recorded the account and handed it to Lái Jùnchén.
By imperial order, Hénèi Prince Wáng Yìzōng was assigned to investigate,
resulting in the execution of Wáng Zhù and forty others,
all of whose families were ruined.
Later, when Jùnchén committed offenses
and the Department of Punishments sentenced him to death,
the submitted judgment was not issued for three days,
causing astonishment both at court and among the populace.
When the Emperor entered the imperial park,
Jí Xū held his horse.
The Emperor asked if anything was happening outside.
Jí Xū reported:
"I am fortunate to serve in the Kòng Hè Guard,
acting as Your Majesty's eyes and ears.
Outside, people only wonder why Lái Jùnchén's judgment has not been issued."
The Emperor said:
"Jùnchén has rendered service to the state;
I am thinking about it."
Jí Xū reported:
"Yú Ānyuǎn accused Huǐ Zhēn of rebellion,
and the facts were all verified.
Now Zhēn serves as a Clerk in Chéng Prefecture.
Jùnchén gathered and assembled the unscrupulous,
falsely implicated the virtuous and good,
and amassed bribes like a mountain.
The roads are filled with wronged souls.
He is a traitor to the state;
why is he worth pitying?"
The Emperor then ordered the judgment issued,
and Jùnchén was executed at the Western Market.
By edict, Yú Ānyuǎn was recalled
and appointed Chief Steward of the Imperial Kitchen.
Jí Xū had a hand in this.
He was appointed Vice Censor-in-Chief
and granted crimson robes.
Jí Xū, considering his handling of the Qílián Yào affair as his own merit,
was appointed Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel and Participating in Determining Governmental Matters.
He contended with the Hénèi Prince,
was sent out as Military Aide of Wēn Prefecture, and died there.
Prince Chéng, Qiānlǐ
Táng Prince Chéng, Qiānlǐ, on a mission to Lǐngnán,
captured a large snake,
eight or nine feet long.
He bound its mouth with a rope
and laid it across the threshold.
When officials from the prefectures and counties came to pay their respects,
he would call for them to enter.
They, only looking straight ahead,
without looking down,
would step on the snake and be startled,
terrified and falling stiffly.
The snake would coil around them several times,
and only after a long while would it be released,
all for his amusement and laughter.
He also obtained turtles and soft-shelled turtles,
ordering people to undress,
then setting the turtles to bite their bodies.
The creatures would not let go until death.
The victims, in sore pain, would scream and cry,
unable to speak further.
The Prince and his concubines would watch together,
considering it entertainment.
Afterwards, they would poke the turtles' mouths with bamboo sticks,
whereupon the turtles would bite the bamboo and release the person.
They would also apply moxibustion to the turtles' backs,
and the pain from the moxibustion would make them release their bite.
Those who were frightened
all lost their spirits,
and until death they did not recover peace.
Zhāng Dǎn
Táng Commander-in-Chief of Shuòfāng, Zhāng Dǎn, was fond of killing.
At that time, there were Tūjué who surrendered and submitted.
Dǎn then composed a proclamation,
insulting Mòchuò,
using extremely disrespectful language.
He wrote it on their bellies and backs,
carving into their skin and flesh,
tattooing it with ink,
and cauterizing it with fire.
Unable to bear the agony,
they cried day and night like insects and birds.
Then he sent them to Mòchuò.
After the words were announced,
he cut them into pieces and killed them.
The Xiōngnú resented this,
and did not dare to surrender.
Wáng Xù
Táng Palace Censor Wáng Xù
searched for women in his own residence and other houses based on rumors and appearances.
Those who did not confess
he would bind their private parts with a rope,
ordering strong men to strike them with bamboo rods,
causing unbearable sore pain.
He once suspended a woman upside down,
tying a stone to her hair,
forcing her to testify to adultery with Cháng'ān Commandant Fáng Héng.
After three days, she still did not confess.
The woman said:
"Censor, with such cruel torture,
if I die,
I will certainly appeal to the underworld courts.
If I am assigned to the palace,
I will surely report to the sovereign;
I will never let you go."
Xù, ashamed and afraid,
then released her.
The Three Leopards of the Capital
During the Tang dynasty, the Investigating Censor Lǐ Sōng, Lǐ Quánjiāo, and Palace Attendant Wáng Xù
were known in the capital as the "Three Leopards."
Sōng was called the Red-Spotted Leopard,
Quánjiāo the White-Browed Leopard,
and Xù the Black Leopard.
They were all cruel, tyrannical, and lawless,
poisonous and without propriety,
wild and unrestrained in nature,
and brutal and harsh in spirit.
Whenever they interrogated prisoners,
they would spread thorns for them to lie on,
shave bamboo into splinters to thrust under their fingernails,
use square beams to press on their thigh bones,
and pile broken tiles under their knees.
They forced them into positions called "Immortal Presenting Fruit," "Jade Maiden Ascending Ladder," "Calf Suspended by the Neck,"
"Donkey Pulling the Stake," "Phoenix Drying Its Wings," "Macaque Drilling Fire," "Upper Wheat Rope," and "Lower Penitentiary."
People could not survive,
and prisoners all begged for death.
They indulged in fabricating charges,
turning truth into falsehood.
They arbitrarily pointed and commanded,
transforming emptiness into substance.
Even Zhōu Gōng and Kǒngzǐ
would have been forced to confess to murder;
Bó Yí and Shū Qí
would have been made to admit to robbery.
If they interrogated a dry moat,
water would surely appear on schedule;
if they examined wet mud,
not even dust could avoid entering.
Lái Jùnchén begged to become their disciple,
and Suǒ Yuánlǐ sought to be their student.
Those pursued all said to each other:
"Leading a sheep to a tiger,
there is no hope of escape.
Tying a mouse to a cat,
there is never a day of release.
Wives and children part forever.
Friends bid long farewell."
People in the capital made pacts,
swearing an oath:
"If we betray our hearts and break our teachings,
may we suffer the Three Leopards."
Such was their venomous harm.
Zhāng Xiàosōng
was from the capital region, a Gāolì who came from a poor family.
He worked at the Censorate delivering documents on behalf of minor officials.
At that time, a clerk forged a warrant,
gave it to Gāolì to pursue someone,
intending to extort money.
When the affair was exposed,
the clerk fled,
and efforts to apprehend him failed.
Censor Zhāng Xiàosōng seized Gāolì and tortured him,
until his kneecaps fell to the ground,
and both feet became crippled.
He then forced him to confess to forging the warrant in the clerk's stead.
According to the law, he was sentenced to death.
The Minister of the Court of Judicial Review submitted a memorial.
According to precedent,
following the statutes on names and examples,
those with severe disabilities should not be subjected to additional punishment.
Xiàosōng flushed with anger and said:
"How does being crippled prevent one from forging documents?"
He ordered two men
to carry him to the market and behead him.
Wáng Hóngyì
was from Héngshuǐ.
He reported a rebellion and was appointed as a Guerrilla General.
During the Tiānshòu era,
he was made a Censor,
and together with Jùnchén, he falsely accused scholars and officials.
When Jùnchén fell,
Hóngyì was also exiled to Lǐngnán.
He falsely claimed to be pursuing an imperial edict.
At that time, Hú Yuánlǐ, serving as a Censor, was on a mission to Lǐngnán.
Stopping at Xiāng and Dèng,
he met Hóngyì and interrogated him.
Hóngyì, having exhausted his excuses,
then said to him:
"You and I are of the same kind."
Yuánlǐ replied:
"In the past, you served as a Censor,
and I served as the Commandant of Luòyáng;
now I serve as a Censor,
and you are an exiled prisoner.
What kind of sameness is there?"
He then had him beaten to death.
Whenever Hóngyì imprisoned people in the summer months,
he would place them in a small room,
piled with mugwort and covered with felt mats.
Those subjected to this
would soon be on the verge of suffocation.
If they falsely confessed or implicated others,
they would be moved to another room.
Jùnchén often issued official documents,
and the prefectures and counties trembled in fear.
He boasted to himself:
"My documents
are like wolf's bane and poisonous vines."
Hóngyì once asked a neighbor for some melons from their garden.
The melon owner was stingy and refused.
Hóngyì then filed a report,
claiming there was a white rabbit in the melon garden.
The county officials gathered people to chase and capture it,
and in no time, the melon vines were all destroyed.
The Palace Secretary Lǐ Zhāodé said:
"In the past, I heard of the 'Grey Falcon' prison officials;
now I see the 'White Rabbit' Censor."
Xiè Yòu
was the Military Governor of the Qián Prefecture under the Zhōu. He was vicious, treacherous, cruel, and ruthless.
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
Prince Cáo was exiled to Qiánzhōng.
Yòu threatened him, saying:
"Empress Wǔ Zétiān has granted you permission to end your own life.
I have personally received the order,
and there is no other decree."
The prince, terrified, hanged himself.
Later, Yòu was sleeping on a flat pavilion,
with over ten concubines sharing the room.
At night, without anyone noticing, an assassin cut off Yòu's head and took it away.
Later, when Prince Cáo's household was destroyed,
during the inventory of assets,
Yòu's head was found, lacquered,
inscribed with the characters "Xiè Yòu,"
and used as a chamber pot.
Only then was it known that the prince had ordered an assassin to kill him.
Prince Hénèi Wáng Yìzōng
During the Zhōu, when the Mòchuò rebels captured Héng and Dìng Prefectures,
the peace envoy Yáng Qízhuāng,
who had been appointed to the third rank by decree,
entered the territory of the Xiōngnú
and was subsequently captured by the rebels.
As they approached Zhào Prefecture,
the Duke of Xiāng, Duàn Guǐ, who was also captured,
called Qízhuāng to escape together.
Qízhuāng was afraid and did not dare to act,
so Guǐ returned first alone.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān rewarded him,
restoring him to his former position.
Qízhuāng arrived shortly after,
and by decree, he was handed over to Prince Hénèi Wáng Yìzōng for interrogation.
Qízhuāng said:
"Once, someone read my physiognomy,
saying I would reach the third rank,
but would face danger from blades and arrows.
I escaped and was pursued,
chopped and shot at but did not die,
and managed to get away.
I beg Your Highness to have pity on me."
Yìzōng was by nature cruel and ruthless.
He memorialized that Qízhuāng had initially been hesitant,
and requested his execution.
The decree approved.
He was led to the south of the Tiānjīn Bridge,
and on the drum rack of the guards' post,
his hands and feet were bound and stretched apart.
Duàn Guǐ was ordered to shoot first.
Three arrows all hit their mark.
Then Duàn Jǐn shot and hit him as well.
Then all the officials of the various departments were ordered to shoot.
The arrows were as dense as porcupine quills,
and he still twitched slightly, breathing faintly.
Immediately, a knife was plunged straight down into his heart,
splitting him open down to the groin,
his heart was gouged out and thrown to the ground,
where it still jumped and twitched several dozen times.
Such was Yìzōng's cruelty and ruthlessness.
Cruel Officials
Lái Jùnchén, Hóu Sīzhǐ, Wáng Hóngyì, Guō Bà, and several dozen others,
served as investigating officials.
Lái Jùnchén's father was named Cāo.
He was on good terms with his fellow villager Cài Běn.
Běn gambled with Cāo,
and lost several hundred thousand in cash to him.
Běn had no way to repay.
So he handed over his wife, Féng, as compensation.
By the time she arrived at Cāo's home,
she was already pregnant,
and gave birth to Jùnchén in Hézhōu.
Jùnchén committed theft,
and then took advantage of secret denunciations.
Empress Zétiān considered him loyal,
and repeatedly promoted him to Attendant Censor.
When handling cases under special imperial decree,
he never failed to meet her expectations,
and was appointed Left Terrace Vice Censor-in-Chief.
People on the roads dared only exchange glances.
Together with Hóu Sīzhǐ and others,
he used denunciations to fabricate charges.
Zétiān established a separate investigation bureau beside the Lìjǐng Gate,
a separate investigation court,
and ordered Jùnchén and others to handle cases there.
Anyone who entered the Newly Opened Gate
rarely came out alive, not one in a hundred.
Hóngyì jokingly called it the "Gate of Case Conclusion."
Jùnchén, along with his associate Zhū Nánshān and others,
compiled a one-volume "Manual of Fabricated Charges."
Whenever interrogating prisoners,
regardless of the severity of the crime,
they would first pour vinegar into their noses,
then imprison them in underground cells.
They would surround them with fire,
cut off their food supply,
and often pull out cotton wadding from their clothes for them to eat.
Whenever an amnesty was about to be issued,
they would first kill all the prisoners.
They also made ten types of large cangues.
Those subjected to these cangues
would suffocate and writhe on the ground,
and none failed to falsely confess.
Zétiān especially rewarded them.
Court officials, whenever they went to court,
often bid farewell to their wives and children.
When they imprisoned Dí Rénjié,
Rénjié placed a letter inside his padded garment,
and requested a prison guard to deliver it to his family.
His family received it,
and appealed to Zétiān.
Zétiān ordered an investigation,
and indeed found him wronged.
She asked Rénjié why he had falsely confessed,
to which he replied:
"If I had not admitted to rebellion,
I would already have died from the cangue and beatings."
Jùnchén was later implicated for corruption,
and censors impeached him.
He was removed as Palace Attendant,
but was again appointed Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Again implicated for corruption,
he was sent out as Adjutant of Tóngzhōu,
where he seized the wife of a fellow adjutant.
Soon he became Commandant of Héguan,
and was again appointed Magistrate of Luòyáng.
He further coveted the maidservant of the Western Tribes chieftain Āshǐnà Húsèluó,
and accused him of plotting rebellion.
Húsèluó's followers cut their faces and appealed at the palace gate,
and he was spared.
When Jùnchén planned to accuse the various Wǔs and Princess Tàipíng,
he was instead exposed by them,
and executed in the marketplace.
People vied to slice flesh from his body.
Emperor Zhōngzōng issued an edict that cruel officials be exiled to distant, harsh places,
and their descendants barred from official service.
Zhōu Xīng repeatedly served as Vice Minister of Justice,
and submitted a memorial requesting the removal of the Lǐ family from the imperial clan register.
Later, he was exiled to Lǐngbiǎo,
and killed by an enemy.
Fù Yóuyì was appointed Left Rectifier of Omissions,
and submitted a memorial discussing the Wǔ clan's revolution.
He was appointed Imperial Secretary,
and also became Participating Chancellor of the Phoenix Pavilion.
In the first year of the Tiānshòu era,
he changed his surname to Wǔ.
He dreamed of ascending the Zhànlù Hall,
and told his close associates.
When the matter came to light, he was executed.
Within one year, Yóuyì
cycled through all the official robe colors—green, dark green, crimson, and purple—
and was called the "Four Seasons Official."
He requested that Zétiān establish Six Circuit Commissioners,
and after his death, his suggestion was eventually followed.
Thus, Wàn Guójùn and Qiū Shénjì were both cruel and brutal.
Sīzhǐ accused Prince Shū, Yuánmíng, of rebellion,
and was appointed Commandant of Mobile Cavalry.
Initially, Yuánlǐ taught Sīzhǐ,
that if the Emperor asked if the Marquis was illiterate,
he should simply say:
"Does the xièzhì beast know characters?
It can only gore the wicked."
When the question was indeed asked, he so replied,
and Zétiān was greatly pleased,
appointing him Left Terrace Attendant Censor.
He was further taught,
that if the Emperor asked about a desirable residence,
and he was granted one confiscated from an official,
he should simply say:
"Your servant detests its name,
and does not wish to reside there."
The Emperor was again pleased.
Once, when interrogating Wèi Yuánzhōng, he said:
"Quickly confess to Bái Sīmǎ,
or else you'll taste Mèng Qīng."
Mèng Qīng
was surnamed Mèng, named Qīng,
the one who killed Lángyé Prince Chōng.
Bái Sīmǎ
was the name of a slope.
Sīzhǐ was a vulgar slave,
and often used this phrase to intimidate Yuánzhōng.
Yuánzhōng did not yield,
so Sīzhǐ, claiming he resisted an imperial order, dragged him backwards.
Yuánzhōng said:
"It is as if I fell from a bad donkey,
and got caught in the stirrup."
Sīzhǐ grew angry again,
and wanted to memorialize for his execution.
Yuánzhōng said:
"You are a Censor,
you must understand etiquette.
If you want Yuánzhōng's head,
just take it,
why must you saw it off?"
Sīzhǐ was startled and fearful,
and sat with him.
Sīzhǐ's speech was not standard,
and Huò Xiàn laughed at him.
Sīzhǐ was angry,
and reported him.
When Zétiān learned of it,
she also laughed heartily.
At that time, Jùnchén forced a marriage with the daughter of Tàiyuán's Wáng Qìngshēn,
and Sīzhǐ also memorialized to marry the daughter of Zhàojùn's Lǐ Zìyì.
Lǐ Zhāodé clapped his hands and said to the various chancellors:
"In previous years, the bandit Lái Jùnchén seized Wáng Qìngshēn's daughter,
already greatly shaming the state.
Now this slave again requests Lǐ Zìyì's daughter,
is this not another disgrace?"
In the end, Sīzhǐ was beaten to death by Zhāodé.
Wàn Guójùn investigated Lǐngnán,
where over three hundred exiles
were gathered at the water's edge,
and he killed them all at once.
Lái Zǐxún was appointed Right Terrace Investigating Censor.
At that time, if court officials appeared at court without wearing boots and belts,
he would certainly impeach them, saying:
"Your servant has heard that one should stand at court properly dressed and belted."
The entire court roared with laughter.
Later, he was granted status as a retainer of the Wǔ family,
and often handled cases under special decree.
He often wore a brocade half-sleeved jacket.
Guō Bà passed the examination for the revolution,
and became an Investigating Censor,
and then Attendant Censor.
Seeing Zétiān, he said:
"In previous years, campaigning to eliminate Jìngyè,
your servant wished to pull out his sinews, eat his flesh, drink his blood, and suck out his marrow."
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
People called him "Guō the Four Its."
When Grand Censor-in-Chief Wèi Yuánzhōng fell ill,
Bà requested to taste his feces.
Yuánzhōng refused,
but Bà eventually tasted it, saying:
"If the taste is bitter,
the illness will be cured."
Yuánzhōng considered him sycophantic,
and greatly detested him.
Once, when interrogating Fāngzhōu Prefect Suǒ Sīwēi,
Wēi could not endure the beatings and torture and died.
Later, Bà repeatedly saw Sīwēi.
So he held vegetarian feasts and recited sutras.
Soon he saw Sīwēi standing in the courtyard, saying:
"You framed me,
now I have come to take you."
Bà was terrified,
and cut open his own abdomen and died.
At that time, the Luò Bridge had just been completed,
and people found it convenient.
Zétiān asked someone:
"What good news is there outside?"
Secretary Zhāng Yuányī, always a humorist,
said:
"We rejoice at the completion of the Luò Bridge,
and are glad that Guō Bà is dead."
Yáng Wùlián
Lú Qǐ
Palace Censor-in-ordinary Zhèng Zhān was close friends with Zhāng Yì.
Whenever he noticed Lú Qǐ taking a midday nap,
he would go to see Yì.
Qǐ became aware of this.
One day,
Qǐ pretended to be fast asleep,
and sure enough, Zhān came to visit.
Knowing that he was having a private conversation with Yì,
Qǐ hurried to Yì’s chamber,
and Zhān rushed to hide.
Qǐ then began discussing confidential matters.
Yì said:
"Palace Censor-in-ordinary Zhèng is here."
Qǐ feigned surprise and said:
"What I just said
is not for others to hear."
Later, he severely impeached Zhān for his crimes,
in order to oust Yán Yǐng.
While the Three Judicial Commissioners were still investigating the two men,
and the case had not yet been concluded,
Qǐ had already memorialized to have Zhān executed and Yǐng dismissed.
Both inside and outside the court, people regarded him with fear and resentment.
The Xiāngyàng Military Governor
The people of Xiāngyáng were skilled at making lacquerware,
which was emulated throughout the empire,
and called "Xiāngyàng."
When Minister of Works Yú became Military Governor,
he was extremely cruel;
and when Zhèng Yuán governed Hézhōng,
he was also cruel,
so people near and far called them "Xiāngyàng Military Governors."
Shǐ Móu
Shǐ Móu managed the salt monopoly in Xiè County,
and initially reformed the monopoly laws
to please the court.
He had a nephew over ten years old
who followed Móu to inspect the salt fields
and picked up a single salt crystal to take home.
When Móu found out,
he immediately had him beaten to death.
His sister came crying to rescue him,
but it was already too late.
Lǐ Shēn
Lǐ Shēn, as a former Chief Minister governing a region,
wielded his authority arbitrarily.
Even when executing the guilty,
he would wait until the autumn equinox,
but Wú Xiāng, younger brother of the Wèi County Magistrate of Yǒngníng,
was unjustly killed in the height of summer.
Cuī Yuánzǎo resented Lǐ Déyù for dismissing him,
so he reversed his testimony,
claiming that when the investigating censor returned from reviewing the case,
he should have reported directly to the Emperor,
to clarify right and wrong.
But Déyù’s power overshadowed the empire,
preventing him from doing so,
and the case was not handed over to the judicial authorities;
instead, Shēn’s memorial alone was used to condemn Xiāng to death.
At that time, Déyù had already lost power,
and the former faction of Lǐ Zōngmǐn—Líng Hú Táo, Cuī Xuàn, and Bái Mǐnzhōng—
were all in influential positions.
Seizing this opportunity to vent their grudges,
they bribed and incited Yuánzǎo and others
to have the Three Judicial Commissioners implicate Shēn,
accusing him of wielding authority as a military governor,
brutally killing good and innocent people,
and citing the Shénlóng era edict
that when cruel officials die,
their official titles and ranks are to be revoked,
and their descendants barred from holding office.
Although Shēn was already dead,
they requested that he be treated like those executed under the Spring and Autumn Annals,
An edict was issued stripping Shēn of three official ranks,
barring his descendants from office,
and demoting Déyù and others.
Rǔ Nà was promoted to Left Reminder,
and Yuánzǎo was made Magistrate of Wǔgōng.
Initially, Shēn was employed for his literary talent and moral integrity,
but wherever he served, he insisted on severity,
sometimes descending into cruelty,
which ultimately led to his downfall over the Wú Xiāng injustice.
After Táng Lǐ Shēn took charge of Huáinán,
he adjudicated the Wú Xiāng case.
He enforced the law harshly,
showing no mercy to offenders.
Cunning clerks and powerful bullies went into hiding.
However, acting on his own judgment,
his subordinates dared not speak up.
Reviewer Lǐ Yuánjiàng’s younger brother, Zhòngjiàng, was residing in Jiāngdū.
When Lǐ was traveling in his youth,
he often stayed with Yuánjiàng and addressed him as "Uncle."
After achieving honor and status,
Yuánjiàng addressed himself as "younger brother" or "nephew," but Lǐ was displeased;
only when he called himself "grandson"
did Lǐ seem to accept it.
There was also Inspector Cuī, who lived in Zhèng Garden
and was an old acquaintance of Shēn from the same examination year.
He came specially to visit.
Just as he arrived at the lodging,
his servant got into a dispute with a townsman.
When questioned about it,
the servant said:
"I am under Inspector Cuī of the Xuānzhōu post station."
Both the servant and the townsman were given the severest punishment.
Shēn then had Cuī arrested and brought before him, saying:
"I used to know you;
why didn’t you come see me when you arrived?"
Cuī kowtowed and apologized:
"I had just settled at the inn,
and it was already late.
Your Excellency is of high status;
I did not dare to present myself at an inappropriate time to pay my full respects.
I beg for your pity,
and to be allowed to return to my hometown."
Shēn then had him detained,
sentenced him to twenty lashes,
and sent him past Mòlíng.
Cuī looked ashen-faced,
but dared not weep aloud.
People at the time said to each other:
"Lǐ’s clan uncle has been turned into a grandson,
and an old friend suddenly became a banished prisoner."
Thus, local residents and commoners,
fearing unpredictable calamities,
crossed the Jiāng and Huái rivers in great numbers.
The chief clerk reported:
"A significant number of households have fled."
Shēn said:
"Have you not seen wheat being winnowed?
The good grains stay below,
while the chaff floats away—no need to report it."
Suddenly, a young man,
appearing somewhat casual and informal,
introduced himself as the son of the Xīn family
and requested an audience with Shēn.
During their conversation, he was not particularly respectful.
Previously, Minister Bái had sent a poem to Minister Yuán that said:
"Bored, I urge the pedantic Xīn to drink;
leisurely, I recite the short Lǐ’s poetry."
This referred to Xīn Qiūdù, who was pedantic and fond of wine,
and Lǐ Shēn, who was short but skilled in poetry.
This young man was Qiūdù’s son.
He said to Lǐ:
"I often recall the poem by the venerable Bái Twenty-Second:
'Bored, I urge the wine of bygone days;
leisurely, I recite the poetry of the twenty-zhàng.'"
Lǐ laughed and said:
"Xīn the Elder has such an insolent son;
how dare I not preserve old ties?"
All the official families
mutually praised the Xīn son’s ability to defy and mock.
Even the Chief Minister suffered such insults;
his stern nature was momentarily subdued.
Another official, upon assuming his post,
had a demeanor quite similar to the Prefect.
Lǐ saw him and took a dislike to him.
He wrote a description of him:
"Dressed in blue, holding a tablet,
he also requests his salary.
Seeing this figure,
is truly lamentable."
Those around him all secretly laughed.
Also, when a veteran general committed an offense and requested punishment,
Shēn said:
"This old soldier relies on his age to avoid punishment.
If this were at the army gate,
he would receive a hundred strokes."
In the end, he did not escape the cane.
Hú Zhè
Seventy li south of Pānzhōu, one arrives at Bànzhōu, which is Língshuǐ Commandery.
The governor of Bànzhōu was named Hú Zhé,
formerly a soldier under Wú Shàochéng of Huáixī.
Like an owl spreading its wings in a remote corner,
he largely emulated the actions of the rebellious generals of Héshuò.
Moreover, he was fond of cuju (kickball).
Horses in the south are small and weak,
not adept at galloping.
Zhé would often summon his officers and officials to play cuju,
and being troubled that the horses were unaccustomed to it,
he would then order over a dozen local tribesmen to carry a sedan chair.
Zhé, riding in the sedan, would brandish a stick,
and the carriers would run while being struck,
circling around like the wind.
If they slacked slightly,
Zhé would immediately tap their backs with his whip,
urging them to run faster under the lash,
using this for amusement and laughter.
Alas!
Zhé was merely a rebellious soldier.
Those tribesmen,
are still the people of the Son of Heaven.
Could it be Heaven's will that those who deserve to be enfeoffed suffer poison and pain from those who deserve execution?
Zhé's wickedness,
shooting people and cutting open pregnant women,
is close to such acts.
Could it be that those appointed as officials treat distant peoples as straw dogs?
Why employ such a man to poison and torment the people of an entire region?
A year later,
Zhé's crimes were reported,
and an imperial decree exiled him to Jiǔzhí.
Fifty li from Bànzhōu, one reaches Luózhōu, which is Zhāoyì Commandery.
The commandery borders the sea,
and there are three sea-salt boiling fields along the coast.
However, the commandery's people secretly boil salt,
and it cannot be prohibited.
The commandery abounds in honey,
pure white as snow.
Wéi Gōnggàn
Forty li southeast of Cuīzhōu, one reaches Qióngshān Commandery.
The grand administrator commands five hundred soldiers,
concurrently serving as the pacification commissioner of the five commanderies: Dān, Yá, Zhèn, Wàn, and Ān.
All taxes and levies from the five commanderies,
are supplied entirely to the pacification commissioner.
The other four commanderies are subordinate to Qióng,
and Qióng is subordinate to Guǎnghǎi Circuit.
The annual taxes from the five prefectures,
not a single string of cash may be taken by the surveillance commissioner,
all are given to Qióng.
Military expenditures and provisions,
still rely on supplies from the commanderies north of the sea.
Whenever Guǎngzhōu changes its military governor,
an additional five hundred thousand coins are bestowed as a reward for orderly governance.
Although the grand administrator of Qióng is on a sea island,
the annual monetary income,
cannot be matched even by the military commissioner of the southern frontier.
The grand administrator, Wéi Gōnggàn,
was greedy and cruel,
seizing children from good families to be slaves,
as if driving dogs and pigs.
He had four hundred female slaves,
the majority engaged in labor,
some weaving patterned silk and gauze, some stretching horns into vessels, some smelting and forging gold and silver, some crafting rare woods into utensils.
His household was like a marketplace,
with daily inspections and monthly assessments,
fearing only that quotas were not met.
Gōnggàn previously served as grand administrator of Àizhōu.
Within the territory was the bronze pillar of Mǎ Yuán,
Gōnggàn had it melted down,
and sold to foreign merchants.
The local people did not know it was cast by Fúbō (Mǎ Yuán),
and moreover considered it a sacred object,
crying out:
"If Your Excellency truly destroys this,
we will be killed by the sea god."
Gōnggàn did not listen,
and the common people rushed to complain to the Protector-General Hán Yuē.
Yuē sent a letter reprimanding and shaming him,
and only then did he stop.
After governing Qióng,
he found much ebony and qūtuó wood,
all rare timbers.
Gōnggàn forced carpenters to explore and cut along the coast,
to the extent that some, failing to meet the quota, killed themselves with axes.
The year before,
Gōnggàn, being replaced by Hán Yuē's son-in-law,
ordered two large boats,
one loaded with ebony utensils mixed with silver,
one loaded with qūtuó wood utensils mixed with gold,
to sail east across the sea.
And he ordered strong soldiers to escort them.
Just before reaching Guǎngzhōu,
the wood being hard and dense,
and the gold heavy,
not a few hundred li out,
both boats capsized,
a loss of who knows how many tens of thousands.
The Book says:
"Wealth gotten by wrongdoing departs by wrongdoing."
Gōnggàn, unprincipled,
harming people to obtain goods,
draining the fat and blood of the tribesmen to enrich himself,
only sullied his name,
and never gained even a little benefit.
Hidden calamity and concealed evil,
if he escapes human punishment,
surely ghosts will exact it.
Zhào Sīwǎn
The treacherous minister Zhào Sīwǎn, from inciting rebellion to defeat,
altogether ate the livers of sixty-six people.
Without exception, he sliced them open face-to-face and minced them,
and when about to finish eating,
the victims were still writhing and screaming.
And those he slaughtered numbered ten to twenty thousand.
Alas!
If not for the imperial authority wielded by famous generals to suppress him,
then who could have exterminated this yàyǔ (monstrous beast) among the black-haired people?
Ān Dàojìn
There was a man named Ān Dàojìn,
the younger brother of the former Yúnzhōu commander Zhòng Bà,
a native of Ādōng,
whose nature was vicious and treacherous.
When Zhuāngzōng was still a hidden dragon (i.e., before ascending the throne),
Ān served as a minor officer,
often wearing a sword among the imperial guards.
Suddenly one day, he drew his sword and toyed with it,
saying to others:
"This sword
can slice through bells and cut jade;
who dares to stand against its blade?"
A man beside him said:
"What kind of sharp weapon is this,
that you boast so wildly?
Even if I were to stretch out my neck to receive it,
could it sever it swiftly?"
Dàojìn said:
"Would you truly stretch out your neck?"
The man thought it was a jest,
so he stretched out his neck and leaned forward,
whereupon Dàojìn swung the sword and severed it.
The bystanders all fled in terror.
Dàojìn took his sword
and galloped south day and night,
defecting to the Liáng ruler.
The Liáng ruler admired his boldness,
and assigned him to garrison duty in Huái.
There was a granary clerk
to whom Ān said:
"The ancients said that piercing seven layers of armor was a feat;
my sharp arrows
can penetrate ten layers.
How could you people understand this?"
The clerk scoffed at him, saying:
"If I were to open my robe and await it,
could it pierce through my belly?"
Ān said:
"Do you dare to open your robe and try?"
The clerk immediately opened his robe,
and Dàojìn shot an arrow that killed him,
the sharp arrow passing straight through
and embedding itself in the wall.
Ān kept a dog and a maidservant,
and with them he fled south.
By day, he hid among the reeds and rushes;
by night, he fled by the light of the stars.
He also often observed the divine light in his eyes;
where the light was abundant was a favorable direction,
where it was scarce was unfavorable.
Since he could control his breath,
he abstained from food.
After some time, he reached the region of the rivers and lakes,
carrying the maidservant on his left
and the dog on his right,
and floated across the water,
suffering no harm at all.
The Huái commander, upon receiving him,
promoted him to deputy general.
He was richly rewarded.
At that time, his elder brother Zhòng Bà served Shǔ,
also as a ranked officer.
Hearing that his brother was in Wú,
he reported to the king.
The Shǔ king, Wáng, praised his intention,
and sent an envoy to request his brother.
Upon arriving in Shǔ,
he also became a chief general,
later leading troops to garrison at Tiānshuǐ Camp in Chángdào County.
Zhòng Bà served as the cavalry and infantry commander of the expedition,
stationed in Qíntíng County.
A commoner had a beloved son,
whom he entrusted to Ān,
calling him the hall attendant.
Dàojìn happened to be going outside the door,
and the hall attendant accidentally passed in front of his bedroom.
Ān grew suspicious,
flew into a rage,
and cut him in half at the waist, throwing him into a well.
The family cried out and appealed to Bà,
who forwarded the case to Commander Wáng.
When it reached Nánliáng,
Commander Wáng could not bear to harm him,
and submitted a petition to spare his life.
Later, bearing a grudge against his elder brother,
he also sought to harm his family.
His brother's family fortified their doors and divined for protection.
When Shǔ fell,
Dàojìn returned east.
Míngzōng appointed him as the commander of the cavalry and infantry of various prefectures.
Later, he committed an offense,
was flogged on the back, and died.
This volume is missing in the Sòng edition;
I have examined the books in my family collection and found eleven individuals to supplement it,
the remaining missing text still awaits another day.
Tán Kǎi of Shíshān records,
Xiǎn Shì.
A native of Gāoliáng.
For generations, her family were chieftains of the Nányuè,
with a tribe of over a hundred thousand.
From a young age, she was wise and intelligent;
while still in her parents' home,
she was able to pacify and govern the tribal masses,
subduing the various Yuè peoples.
Féng Bǎo, the governor of Gāoliáng, heard of her character and conduct,
and took her as his wife.
Often with her husband Bǎo,
she participated in deciding legal cases,
and government orders were carried out in an orderly manner.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
the regional commander Xiāo Bó conscripted troops for reinforcement,
and sent the prefect Lǐ Qiānrén to summon Bǎo.
Bǎo intended to go,
but Xiǎn Shì suspected it was a rebellion,
and stopped him.
It later indeed turned out to be a rebellion.
After Bǎo's death,
the region south of the mountains fell into great chaos,
but Xiǎn Shì pacified and united it,
and the hundred Yuè tribes lived in peace.
Her son, Féng Pú, was still young,
but due to Xiǎn Shì's achievements, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xìndū,
and an imperial edict appointed Xiǎn Shì as Grand Lady of Gāoliáng Commandery,
bestowing upon her an enclosed carriage with embroidered curtains, oiled cords, and a team of four horses,
along with musical bands, command banners, and ceremonial insignia,
in the manner of a prefect.
Féng Pú later died.
The hundred Yuè tribes addressed the lady as the Holy Mother.
When Wáng Zhòngxuān rebelled,
the lady led troops and defeated him.
She personally donned armor and rode a horse,
touring and pacifying the various prefectures,
and the region south of the mountains was completely pacified.
She was enfeoffed as Lady of Qiáo.
The command headquarters established a chief clerk,
and officials were provided with seals,
authorizing them to act according to circumstances.
The empress bestowed upon her a set of head ornaments and banquet attire.
At that time, the governor of Fānzhōu, Zhào Nà, was greedy and cruel,
and many Lí and Liáo people fled or rebelled.
The lady submitted a sealed memorial discussing this,
and an imperial decree ordered the lady to summon and pacify them.
The lady personally carried the imperial edict,
calling herself an envoy,
traversed over ten prefectures,
proclaiming the imperial virtue and intentions,
and wherever she passed, all submitted.
Emperor Wén bestowed upon the lady the district of Línzhèn as her estate.
Upon her death, she was posthumously honored as Chéngjìng.
Xiǎn Shì was a native of Bǎoníng in Gāozhōu.
She was seven feet tall,
highly resourceful and strategic,
possessing the strength of three men,
with breasts over two feet long.
Sometimes, when traveling far in the heat,
she would sling her breasts over her shoulders.
During the chaos at the end of the Qín dynasty in the Five Ridges region,
Xiǎn Shì mustered military conscripts,
firmly protecting her hometown,
and the chieftains of the barbarian tribes did not dare to invade.
When Zhào Tuó declared himself king,
dominating the region south of the mountains,
Xiǎn Shì then presented two hundred loads of military equipment and supplies as tribute.
Zhào Tuó was greatly pleased.
When discussing current affairs and military strategy with her,
her wisdom and eloquence were overwhelming,
and Tuó ultimately could not refute her.
He entrusted her with governing Gāoliáng,
where her kindness and authority inspired awe among the people.
Neighboring commanderies relied on her.
Today, there are many with the surname Xiǎn in the southern regions,
mostly descendants of her lineage.
The wife of Wèi Jìngyú
was sixteen when her husband died.
Her parents and in-laws wished to remarry her,
so she cut off her ear to swear an oath
and refused.
At the house, there was a nesting swallow
that always flew in pairs;
later, it suddenly flew alone.
The woman, moved by its solitary perch,
tied a thread to its leg as a marker.
The following year,
this swallow indeed returned,
still bearing the thread from before.
The wife composed a poem, saying:
"In years past, you left without a mate;
this spring, you return alone again.
The kindness and devotion of an old friend are deep—
I cannot bear to see you fly in pairs once more."
The wife of Zhōu Dí, a certain woman.
Dí was skilled in trade
and traveled to and from Guǎnglíng.
During the rebellion of Bì Shīduó,
people were abducted and sold for food.
Dí was starving and near death,
and his wife said:
"If we wish to return now,
we cannot both survive.
Your parents are still alive—
you cannot die with me.
I ask to be sold to aid your journey."
Dí could not bear it,
but his wife insisted and went with him
to the marketplace,
where she was sold for several thousand coins, which she gave to Dí.
When they reached the city gate,
the guards questioned them,
suspecting deceit,
and took Dí to the marketplace to inquire.
There, they saw his wife's head already displayed on a pole.
Dí wrapped her remaining body and returned to bury her.
The wife of Zōu Dàizhēng, Bó,
was the daughter of Zìmù, the Wǔkāng County Captain.
She accompanied Dàizhēng to his post in Jiāngyīn.
During the rebellion of Yuán Cháo,
Dàizhēng abandoned his official seal and fled into hiding.
Bó was captured by the rebels,
who intended to violate her,
but she refused.
She told an elderly servant of the household
to report to Dàizhēng, saying:
"I will not submit to dishonor."
Then she died in the water.
After the rebels left,
her body was recovered,
and her righteous reputation stirred the region south of the Yangtze.
The scholar Lǐ Huá composed "The Lament for the Chaste Woman," saying:
In years past, hordes of bandits
rose together,
rampaging through the coastal regions of Zhè.
The ten thousand households of Jiāngyīn
were transformed into coagulated blood.
No stone was left unburned,
no jade unbroken.
Lofty and pure was Lady Bó,
resplendent in name and integrity.
Daughter of Zìmù,
wife of Zōu Dàizhēng.
With virtue like jade, grace like orchids—
a heroine among women.
Zōu, avoiding disaster,
hid in the wild thickets.
His gentle and noble wife—
who made her a captive?
Crawling through mud and sand,
gazing afar, seeing nothing.
She entrusted the official's proclamation
to a white-haired old woman.
The old woman, moved by the lady,
then reached Master Zōu.
When the troops dispersed, he sought her body,
there by the riverbank.
Sorrowful winds arose, forming continuous waves;
anguished breath congealed into solitary clouds.
Wild ducks and geese cried mournfully for her,
the sun and moon grew dim and dusky.
Her upright standard casts a shadow, ever straight;
her steadfast fragrance pierces the frost, still enduring.
To know a child, none surpass the father—
truly, the words of an elder.
In Fèngtiān County, the two daughters of the Dòu family, Bóniáng and Zhòngniáng,
though raised in a rustic village,
were of firm resolve from a young age.
Their home bordered Bīn Prefecture.
During the Yǒngtài era,
several thousand bandits armed with weapons
entered their village,
plundering and robbing.
Hearing that the two sisters were beautiful,
the elder sister being nineteen
and the younger sixteen,
they hid in a cave among the rocks.
The bandits intended to force and violate them,
first dragging Bóniáng out
and walking several tens of paces,
then dragging Zhòngniáng out.
The bandits looked at each other, congratulating themselves.
As they approached a deep valley,
Bóniáng said:
"I will not suffer defilement by bandits."
And she threw herself into the ravine.
While the bandits were still shocked,
Zhòngniáng also threw herself into the ravine.
The ravine was several hundred feet deep.
The elder sister soon perished,
while Zhòngniáng suffered broken legs and a battered face,
her body covered in flowing blood.
She lost consciousness for a long time before reviving.
The bandits, moved by their righteousness, departed.
The Capital Governor Dìwǔ Qí, stirred by their chastity and fortitude,
reported it to the court.
An imperial decree honored their household with a commemorative gate,
exempting them from corvée labor in perpetuity,
and the burial expenses for the two sisters were provided by the state.
The Capital Governor Cáo Lùhǎi
was the first to compose a rhapsody praising them.
The virtuous woman was surnamed Dòu,
with the childhood name Guìniáng.
Her father, Liáng,
served as the Registrar of Households in Biànzhōu at the beginning of the Jiànzhōng era.
Guìniáng was beautiful in appearance,
and well-read and literate.
When Lǐ Xīliè captured Biànzhōu,
he sent armored soldiers to Liáng's gate to seize Guìniáng and take her away.
As she was about to leave the gate,
she turned to her father and said:
"Do not grieve excessively.
I will surely be able to destroy the rebel,
and enable you, Father, to obtain wealth and honor from the Son of Heaven."
After Guìniáng came to be by Lǐ Xīliè's side due to her talent and beauty,
she was further able to skillfully and subtly gain his trust.
All of Xīliè's secrets,
even those unknown to his wife and children,
she was able to hear about.
When Xīliè returned to Càizhōu,
Guìniáng said to Xīliè:
"In loyalty and courage,
no one in the entire army compares to Chén Xiānqí.
His wife is also surnamed Dòu,
and Xiānqí dotes on and trusts her.
I wish to be able to interact with her,
treating each other as sisters according to age,
and gradually persuade her,
to strengthen Xiānqí's resolve."
Xīliè agreed.
Thus, she served Xiānqí's wife as an elder sister.
Once, she took an opportunity to say to her:
"The rebel is cruel and unprincipled,
and will surely fall sooner or later.
Sister, you should therefore plan early for a place to preserve your lineage."
Xiānqí's wife agreed.
In the fourth month of the first year of the Xīngyuán era,
Xīliè died suddenly.
His son did not announce the mourning,
but wished to exterminate all the old generals and officers,
replacing them with younger men.
Before the plan was decided,
someone presented cherries.
Guìniáng said:
"Xīliè's son wishes to share and send some to Xiānqí's wife."
And also to show outwardly that nothing was amiss.
She therefore wrote a letter on waxed silk, saying:
"He died the day before yesterday,
and the coffin is in the rear hall.
He intends to kill the senior ministers.
You must make your own plans."
She then coated a silk pellet with red dye to resemble a cherry.
Xiānqí opened the pellet and saw it,
and said to Xuē Yù:
"For two days he has claimed illness,
but it is strange that music and songs are mixed and played,
ceaselessly day and night.
This means there is a plot not yet settled,
showing leisure outwardly.
The matter leaves no room for doubt."
The next day,
Xiānqí and Xuē Yù each led their troops to clamor at the yamen gate,
requesting to see Xīliè.
Xīliè's son was forced to come out and bow,
expressing willingness to abandon the false title,
just like Lǐ Nà.
Xiānqí said:
"You are a rebel and traitor,
by the Son of Heaven's command."
He then beheaded Xīliè's wife and son, placed their seven heads in a box, and presented them,
displaying the corpses in the marketplace.
Two months later,
Wú Shǎochéng killed Xiānqí,
learned of Guìniáng's plot,
and therefore killed her as well.
In the fifth year of the Dàzhōng era,
the daughter of Zhèng Shénzuǒ from Xiáqiū County, Yǎnzhōu,
aged twenty-four,
had previously been betrothed to Lǐ Xuánqìng, an officer of the Chíxióng army.
Shénzuǒ was also a government soldier,
garrisoned in Qìngzhōu.
At that time, the Dǎngxiàng rebelled,
and Shénzuǒ died in battle.
Her mother had already died earlier,
and there were no sons.
The daughter, because her father had died in battle at a border city,
with no means to have him returned,
cut her hair and marred her appearance,
and went herself to Qìngzhōu,
to escort her father's remains back.
Arriving at Mǎqīng Village in Jìnxián Township, Xiáqiū County,
she buried him together with her mother.
She then built a hut by the gravesite,
planted pines and junipers with her own hands,
and vowed not to marry anyone.
The military governor Xiāo Chù submitted a report to the throne, stating:
"I humbly submit that within villages and neighborhoods,
few understand ritual teachings.
In the nature of women,
understanding of righteousness and principle is especially obscure.
The Zhèng family's daughter, her grief knots in the deep springs,
her sorrow profound as ascending the rugged hill.
She threw herself into the sandy wastes,
to retrieve her father's remains.
From the distant borderlands,
she managed to return to her village.
Moved by the 'Lù É' poem, she harbors accumulated sorrow,
guarding the grave mound, she pledges her heart.
She manifests the virtue of filial principle,
sufficient to encourage the integrity of chastity and righteousness."
An imperial edict ordered the honoring of her family gate.
□The Eulogy states:
When governance and teaching flourish in peace,
men are loyal and women chaste.
They use ritual to guard themselves,
and righteousness to avoid living ignobly.
The vermilion brush shines brightly,
the orchid chamber resounds with her fame.
"The Guan Ju" harmonizes with elegance,
beginning to be called civilized.
Lady Lú
was the wife of Fáng Xuánlíng.
When Xuánlíng was in humble circumstances,
he fell ill and was near death.
He entreated her, saying:
"My illness is critical.
You are young,
you should not remain a widow.
Serve well the one who comes after."
Lady Lú wept, entered behind the curtain,
gouged out one of her eyes and showed it to Xuánlíng,
to demonstrate she had no other intention.
It happened that Xuánlíng recovered fully,
and he honored her for the rest of his life.
□According to the "Record of Jealous Wives".
There are also wives
who are virtuous in humble times but become jealous in glory and prominence?
I therefore have feelings about this.
Yùyīng
was the wife of Fú Fèng in the Táng dynasty,
exceptionally beautiful.
Fèng was exiled to Dānzhōu for a crime.
Upon reaching the Southern Sea,
he was killed by Lǎo bandits,
who forced Yùyīng to submit to them.
She replied:
"One woman is not enough to serve many men.
I request you choose one elder among you."
The bandits agreed,
and she then asked to change clothes.
After a short while,
she stood on the boat in full ceremonial attire,
and cursed, saying:
"To suffer insult by bandits
is worse than death."
She then threw herself into the sea and drowned.
Xǔ Shēng's wife, née Lǚ, was named Róng.
Shēng was a gambler in his youth,
and paid no heed to moral conduct.
Róng personally toiled diligently in managing the household,
to support and care for her mother-in-law,
and repeatedly urged Shēng to pursue his studies.
Whenever he did something improper,
she would weep and offer admonitions.
Róng's father, harboring deep resentment and hatred toward Shēng,
summoned Róng,
intending to have her remarry.
Róng sighed and said:
"Such is the fate I have encountered;
in righteousness, there can be no separation or betrayal."
In the end, she refused to return home.
Shēng, moved and inspired,
then sought a teacher and traveled far to study,
and thus achieved fame.
Soon, he was summoned to office by his home province,
but on his way to Shòuchūn,
he was killed by bandits.
The provincial inspector Yǐn Yào captured the bandits and apprehended them.
Róng went to meet the funeral procession on the road,
and upon hearing the news, went to the provincial office,
requesting to personally take revenge on the enemy.
Yào granted her request.
Róng then personally beheaded him,
to offer sacrifice to Shēng's spirit.
Later, the commandery was attacked by bandits,
who sought to violate her.
Róng climbed over the wall and fled.
The bandits drew their swords and pursued her.
The bandits said:
"If you submit to me, you will live;
if not, you will die."
Róng said:
"In righteousness, I cannot allow my body to be dishonored."
The bandits then killed her.
On that day,
there was a fierce wind and torrential rain.
Thunder, lightning, and darkness descended,
and the bandits, terrified,
kowtowed and begged for forgiveness,
then buried her with proper rites.
Yīn Bǎohuì's wife
was a granddaughter of Fēng Áo,
named Xuàn, courtesy name Jǐngwén,
skilled in writing prose, poetry, and calligraphy in cursive and clerical scripts.
Bǎohuì served as a collator in the imperial library.
When Huáng Cháo entered Cháng'ān,
they hid together in Lánlíng Lane.
The next day,
Bǎohuì fled.
The bandits, captivated by Fēng's beauty,
wanted to take her,
but she firmly refused.
The bandits tried to entice and persuade her with countless words,
but she did not respond.
The bandits, enraged, said furiously:
"Submit and live;
otherwise,
you will only grease my sword."
Fēng cursed them, saying:
"I am the daughter of a high official;
to die upholding righteousness
is still life."
In the end, she did not submit to the rebel's hand,
and was thus killed.
When Bǎohuì returned,
his attendants said:
"Your wife is dead."
Bǎohuì wailed and died of grief.
Gāo Mǐn's daughter was named Mèimei.
Her father, Gāo Yànzhāo,
served under Lǐ Zhèngjǐ,
and when Lǐ Nà rebelled against the court,
he took Yànzhāo's wife and children as hostages,
sending him
to guard Púyáng.
In the second year of the Jiànzhōng era,
he led the city to surrender to the Henan commander Liú Xuánzuǒ.
Lǐ Nà slaughtered his family.
At that time, the girl was seven years old.
Her mother, Lǐ, pitied her youth,
and pleaded for her life to be spared to serve as a slave,
which was granted.
The girl refused, saying:
"If my mother and brothers cannot escape death,
what use is it for me to live on?"
As her mother and brothers were about to be executed,
they bowed in all four directions.
The girl asked why,
and they replied:
"We are praying to the gods."
The girl said:
"My family is being executed for loyalty and righteousness;
what do the gods know that we should bow to them?"
She asked where her father was,
then faced west and wept,
bowed twice, and went to her death.
Emperor Dézōng was astonished and sighed in admiration,
and issued an edict for the Court of Imperial Sacrifices to bestow upon her the posthumous title "Mǐn."
Many scholars vied to write eulogies for her.
Yànzhāo followed Xuánzuǒ to rescue Nínglíng,
recaptured Biànzhōu,
and was appointed prefect of Yǐngzhōu.
The court recorded his loyalty.
He remained in the prefecture for twenty years without transfer,
and upon his death was posthumously awarded the title of military governor of Shǎnzhōu.
In Mǐnzhōng, within the territory of Dōngyuè, there was a mountain called Yōnglǐng,
tens of *li* high.
In the low-lying northern marshes below it,
there was a giant serpent,
seventy to eighty *zhàng* long,
and one *zhàng* in girth.
The local people were constantly afraid.
Many commandants of Dōngyě and officials of the subordinate cities had died.
They sacrificed oxen and sheep to it,
but still received no blessings.
Sometimes it appeared in people's dreams,
or communicated through shamans and priests,
demanding to devour young girls aged twelve or thirteen.
The commandants and magistrates were troubled by this.
Together, they sought slave-born girls from households and daughters from families of criminals to raise.
On the morning of the eighth month,
they would send them as sacrifices to the serpent's cave entrance.
The serpent would then emerge at night and devour them.
This went on for many years.
Nine girls had already been used.
One year, as the sacrifice time approached,
they had not yet found a girl through recruitment.
In Jiànglè County, Lǐ Dàn's family had six daughters and no sons.
His youngest daughter was named Jì,
and she volunteered to go.
Her parents would not allow it.
Jì said:
"Parents, do not keep me.
Now you have only given birth to six daughters,
not a single son.
Having us is like having none.
I, as a daughter, lack the merit of a Tí Yíng in aiding my parents.
Since I cannot provide for you,
I only waste food and clothing.
My life brings no benefit;
it would be better to die early.
Selling my body
could bring a little money to support my parents.
Would that not be good?"
Her parents, out of love and pity, still would not let her go.
But in the end, they could not stop her.
Jì then set out,
requesting a good sword and a dog trained to bite serpents.
On the morning of the eighth month,
she went to the temple and sat there.
She carried the sword and led the dog.
First, she prepared several *shi* of rice cakes sweetened with honey and placed them at the cave entrance.
The serpent emerged at night,
its head as large as a granary,
its eyes like two-foot mirrors.
Smelling the fragrance of the cakes,
it first devoured them.
Jì then released the dog,
which went to bite and attack it.
Jì struck from behind.
The serpent thrashed out,
and died in the courtyard.
Jì entered the cave to look,
and found the skulls of the nine girls.
She brought them all out.
Exclaiming, she said:
"You were timid and weak,
and were eaten by the serpent—
truly pitiable!"
Then, Jì walked slowly back home.
The King of Yuè heard of this,
took Jì as his queen,
appointed her father as magistrate of Jiànglè County,
and bestowed rewards upon her mother and sisters.
From then on, in Dōngyě, there were no more demonic practices.
The songs and ballads about this survive to this day.
In Hànyuán County, there was a woman, the wife of Yìchéng,
who in her prime had no children.
When her husband died and was about to be buried,
at the time of the initial encoffining,
she took poisoned wine,
and just before the coffin was lowered into the tomb,
she caressed the coffin, swallowed the poison, and died.
Thus, she was buried together with him.
The circumstances were reported to the authorities at the time,
