and an imperial edict granted her silk.
This event is recorded in Cháng Hǔ's *Guózhì*.
Wèi Zhīgǔ, the Minister of Works of the Táng dynasty,
was upright and refined in character,
and skilled in literary composition.
At the age of seventy,
he died while still in office.
His wife, Madame Sū, did not weep.
When the time came,
she bathed with perfumed water,
and after the enshrouding and dressing were completed,
she let out one cry of grief and died.
She was buried together with the Minister on the same day.
People at the time marveled at her integrity,
believing it to be unprecedented in previous eras.
In the first year of the Zhìdé era,
when Shǐ Sīmíng had not yet been pacified,
in Wèizhōu, there were three women, including Hóu Sìniáng,
who pricked their fingers to write in blood and petitioned before the army,
expressing their wish to join the volunteer camp to fight the rebels.
Among the brothers of the Zhèng Lù family, one served as an official beyond the river.
He moored his boat on a riverbank.
A group of thieves suddenly arrived,
so he laid out all his gold and silk on the shore,
and allowed the bandits to take them freely.
The bandits did not touch any of it,
saying:
"We only wish to have the young lady of the Shìyù."
Their daughter was of great beauty,
and the bandits had secretly learned of this.
The family members looked at each other,
not knowing how to respond.
The daughter cheerfully offered to go.
The bandits then prepared a small boat,
and took her away.
She said to the bandits:
"Although you are thieves,
surely you have a home and relatives?
However, my family is of scholarly and official lineage.
Since I am to be your wife,
how can I be forced without propriety?
If we reach your dwelling place,
let me meet my relatives once,
so that I may entrust myself to a proper match."
The bandit said:
"Agreed."
She also pointed to the two maids who had accompanied her and said:
"Since you are known as thieves,
these maids should not remain.
For your sake,
it would be better to send them back to my home."
The bandit, captivated by her beauty,
and finding her words reasonable,
saw no reason to refuse,
so he rowed the boat himself,
and took the two maids away.
The young lady then threw herself into the river and died.
In the year Rénwǔ of the Lóngdé era at the end of the Liáng dynasty,
Zōu Jǐngwēn, in charge of military affairs in Xiāngzhōu, was transferred to Xúzhōu,
where he also took charge of military affairs.
He had a strong servant,
who relied on his own strength and bravery,
and traveled alone with his wife on a donkey.
When they reached the Mángdàng marshes east of Sòngzhōu,
an area notorious for bandits,
if travelers were alone,
few escaped unharmed.
That day, he and his wife rested under a pair of willow trees halfway up a slope,
and he shouted loudly:
"I've heard this place is full of bold fellows—
is there not one who dares to challenge me to a contest?"
As soon as he finished speaking,
five or six bandits leaped out from the thicket,
one man grabbed him from behind with both arms,
wrestled him to the ground,
and his companions quickly choked his throat,
drawing a short blade to cut it.
This servant's own weapons
were of no use at all,
as he was caught off guard.
Only his wife was by his side,
showing no sign of panic,
but instead cried out loudly:
"Splendid!
Today, my shame is finally avenged.
I, a woman from a good family,
was captured and seized by him,
and brought to this state.
Who says there is no divine justice!"
The bandits, thinking her sincere, did not kill her,
and took the luggage and the two donkeys, heading south.
After nearly fifty or sixty *lǐ*,
they reached the northern border of Bózhōu,
and stopped south of an isolated village.
At the village gate, there were weapons and armor,
likely belonging to nearby garrison patrols.
The woman went straight into the main hall of the villagers,
while the bandits thought she was seeking food,
and did not suspect her.
She then tearfully bowed to the village chief,
and reported how her husband had just been murdered.
Upon hearing this,
the chief secretly summoned his men,
and they captured and bound the bandits at once,
with only one bandit managing to escape.
They were shackled and sent to Bó City,
where all were executed in the market.
The woman returned to Xiāngyáng,
shaved her head to become a nun,
and vowed to remain so for the rest of her life.
In the southern regions, there was a powerful commander,
who inherited his noble rank,
but was quite arrogant and tyrannical.
There was a skilled singer
who came from the north with her husband,
and she was very beautiful.
The commander heard of her and summoned her.
Each time she entered,
she came with her husband,
and they sang in turns, harmonizing beautifully,
their melodies full of grace.
The commander desired to have her for himself,
but the woman refused and would not consent.
The commander secretly sent someone to kill her husband and placed the woman in a separate chamber,
adorned her with pearls and jade,
to win her favor.
After a year, he went to visit her,
and the woman received him cheerfully,
her demeanor gentle and affectionate.
But as he approached the bed,
the woman suddenly drew a white blade from her sleeve,
grabbed the commander and tried to stab him.
The commander broke free and fled,
with the woman chasing him.
Fortunately, two servants were in front and closed the door,
so he escaped.
He immediately sent people to seize her,
but she had already cut her own throat.
Talent Lady Xú
Madame Xú, named Huì,
was the daughter of Xú Jiān,
and could speak at five months old.
Emperor Tàizōng of Táng made her a Talent Lady,
and specially promoted her to Chōngróng.
When military campaigns were still unsettled,
she submitted a memorial advising against building palaces,
and her words were elegant and beautiful.
The emperor approved.
Madame Lú
When Dí Rénjié served as chancellor,
he had a maternal aunt of the Lú family who lived in a villa south of Wǔqiáo.
This aunt had only one son,
who had never visited his relatives in the capital.
At every seasonal festival, at the end and beginning of each month,
Dí Rénjié would perform the proper rituals with great reverence.
Once, during a holiday after a snowfall,
Dí Rénjié went to inquire after Aunt Lú's well-being.
It happened that his cousin was returning home,
carrying a bow and arrows, with pheasants and hares he had hunted.
He presented the game to his mother for a meal,
then turned and gave Dí Rénjié a casual salute,
his attitude very offhand and disrespectful.
Dí Rénjié then said to his aunt:
"I now serve as chancellor.
If my cousin has any aspirations he wishes to pursue,
I am willing to exert my full efforts to help him achieve his aims."
His aunt replied:
"The chancellorship is your own high office.
Your aunt has only this one son.
I do not wish for him to serve a female sovereign."
Dí Rénjié was greatly ashamed and withdrew.
Dǒng Shì
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
Lái Jùnchén, the Minister of Imperial Stud, was extremely powerful.
Court officials dared not look at him directly, treating him with fear and caution.
Hóu Mǐn, the Director of the Imperial Parks, went out of his way to serve him.
His wife, Dǒng Shì, admonished him to stop, saying:
"Jùnchén is a traitor to the state.
His power will not last long.
Once his affairs collapse,
his faction of villains will be the first to suffer.
You should show him respect but keep your distance."
Hóu Mǐn gradually began to withdraw from him.
Lái Jùnchén became angry
and had him appointed as Magistrate of Wǔlóng County in Fúzhōu.
Hóu Mǐn wanted to resign from his post and return home.
Dǒng Shì said:
"Leave quickly.
Do not seek to stay."
So they departed.
Upon reaching the prefecture,
he presented his name card to pay respects to the prefectural general.
He mistakenly wrote on a piece of paper,
and when the prefectural general unrolled it to look,
there were characters written at the end.
He became furious and said:
"You cannot even write your name properly;
how can you serve as a county magistrate?"
He did not allow him to take up his post.
Hóu Mǐn was endlessly worried and distressed.
Dǒng Shì said:
"Just stay.
Do not seek to leave."
They remained for fifty days.
Bandits from Zhōngzhōu attacked Wǔlóng,
killed the former county magistrate,
and plundered and killed his entire household.
Hóu Mǐn, because he had not been allowed to take up his post, was spared.
Later, when Lái Jùnchén was executed,
his faction was exiled to Lǐngnán,
and Hóu Mǐn was again spared.
Gāo Ruì's Wife
Qín Shì, the wife of Gāo Ruì, Governor of Zhàozhōu.
When the bandit Mòchuò's forces breached the Dìngzhōu region
and reached Zhàozhōu,
all officials from the Chief Administrator down
opened the gates and admitted the bandits.
Gāo Ruì could think of no plan,
so he and his wife Qín Shì took poison and feigned death.
They were carried to where Mòchuò was.
After a long while,
Mòchuò showed them a golden lion belt and a purple robe, saying:
"Surrender,
and I will give you office.
If you do not surrender, you will die."
Gāo Ruì looked but said nothing,
only glancing at his wife, Qín Shì.
Qín Shì said:
"We have received the state's grace.
Repaying it lies here.
To receive a first-rank title from bandits today—
how could that be considered an honor?"
They both closed their eyes and spoke no more.
After two days,
the bandits, seeing they could not be subdued,
killed them.
Cuī Jìng's Daughter
In the Táng dynasty, Jí Miǎn, Chief Administrator of Jìzhōu,
wanted his son Jí Xū to marry the daughter of Cuī Jìng, Assistant Magistrate of Nángōng County.
Cuī Jìng refused.
Later, due to certain circumstances,
Jí Miǎn pressured him to agree to the marriage alliance.
Cuī Jìng, afraid, consented.
A day was chosen, and the betrothal gifts were sent.
Along with the decorated wedding carriage,
they abruptly arrived at the gate.
Cuī Jìng's wife, Zhèng Shì, initially did not know.
She hugged her daughter and wailed, saying:
"Our family has never had a son-in-law from the Jí family."
The daughter lay firmly in bed and refused to rise.
Her younger daughter then said to her mother:
"Our father is in dire straits.
We should risk our lives to save and resolve it.
Even if I were to become a maid,
I should not refuse.
Our family is one of reputable surname and standing.
What is there to be ashamed of?
If elder sister cannot do it,
I will take her place."
She then mounted the carriage and left.
Later, Jí Xū was promoted to Vice Director of the Secretariat.
His worthy wife, who understood principle,
was praised as honorable by those who spoke of her.
Jí Xū was implicated in a dispute with Prince Wǔ Yìzōng of Hénèi
and was sent out to serve as Military Advisor of Wēnzhōu, where he died.
Lǐ Yú's Mother
The mother of Investigating Censor Lǐ Yú was pure, frugal, chaste, and upright.
When Lǐ Yú received his official grain stipend,
the rice was delivered to his residence.
His mother had it measured,
and there was an excess of three dàn.
She asked the reason.
The clerk said:
"It is the custom for Investigating Censors not to have their grain leveled off."
She asked further:
"What about the cart
and the porterage fee?"
He also said:
"It is the custom for Investigating Censors not to repay cart and porterage fees."
His mother became angry
and ordered the excess rice and the porterage fee to be sent back, using this to reprimand Lǐ Yú.
Lǐ Yú then pursued the granary officials to punish them.
All the other Investigating Censors looked ashamed.
Lú Xiàn's Daughter
The second daughter of Lú Xiàn, Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs,
was first married into the Zhèng family.
Her husband died early,
and she vowed not to remarry.
She was dignified and beautiful in appearance,
and her character and bearing were very lofty.
Her brother-in-law, General Lǐ Sīchōng of the Imperial Guard,
after his wife (her elder sister) died,
petitioned to continue the marital alliance by marrying her.
Permission was granted.
Her brothers did not dare to tell her.
Lǐ Sīchōng chose a day and prepared the ceremonies,
with betrothal gifts of great abundance.
He personally went to the residence to present them.
The Lú lady barred the gate
and loudly cursed him, saying:
"You old slave,
I am not your match."
She then climbed over the wall to a relative's house
and cut off her hair.
Lǐ Sīchōng reported this to the throne.
An imperial decree was issued not to force her against her will.
Later she became a Buddhist nun
and pursued her practice with great diligence.
Dèng Lián's Wife
In Cāngzhōu, Lǐ Shì, daughter of Dèng Lián of Gōnggāo,
was married less than a year when Lián died.
Lǐ was eighteen years old,
and she preserved her chastity,
setting up a spirit table,
offering food three times daily and weeping before it,
wearing plain clothes and eating simple fare for six or seven years.
Suddenly one night she dreamed of a man.
His appearance and demeanor were most elegant,
and he sought to take Lǐ Shì as his mate.
In her sleep, Lǐ Shì did not consent.
After this, she saw him in dreams every night,
but Lǐ Shì ultimately did not accept him.
Considering him a spirit or demon,
she wrote talismans and incantations to exorcise him,
but in the end could not stop him.
Lǐ Shì sighed and said:
"I have vowed not to change my chastity,
yet I am troubled by this—
it must be because my appearance is not yet faded."
So she took a knife and cut off her hair,
wore unwashed hemp garments,
left her disheveled hair uncombed,
and smeared her face and body with dirt.
The ghost then apologized to Lǐ Shì, saying:
"Madam, your integrity like bamboo and cypress
cannot be shaken."
From then on, he no longer appeared in her dreams.
The commandery governor honored her household with a plaque,
and to this day there remains a "Chaste Widow Lane."
Princess during the Reign of Emperor Sùzōng
Emperor Sùzōng held a banquet in the palace,
where female performers put on a play.
There was one dressed in green holding a tablet, playing the role of Cānjūn.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
the foreign general Ābù'ēn was executed,
and his wife was consigned to the Yètíng,
being skilled in performance.
Thus she was assigned to the musicians,
and so was ordered to play the role of Cānjūn.
The princess admonished, saying:
"There are many courtesans in the palace;
why must this person be used?
If Ābù'ēn was truly a rebel,
then his wife is also a criminal,
and should not be allowed near Your Majesty's presence.
If he was wrongly accused,
how can we bear to have his wife mingle with the performers,
becoming an object of laughter and jest?
Although I am most foolish,
I deeply believe this is not right."
The emperor was also moved with pity,
and so canceled the play and pardoned Ābù'ēn's wife.
From this, the princess was esteemed for her virtue.
Pān Yán's Wife
Vice Minister Pān Yán
was a Hànlín Academician during the reign of Emperor Dézōng,
and received exceptional favor and grace.
His wife was the daughter of Liú Yàn.
A certain Capital Governor had some business and waited for an audience,
but for days could not gain an audience.
So he gave the gatekeeper three hundred bolts of silk.
When the wife learned of this,
she said to Pān:
"How can it be that as a subject,
when the Capital Governor wishes for an audience,
he must give your servant three hundred bolts of silk?
The peril is evident."
She urgently advised Pān to resign from his post.
Their son,
Mèngyáng, initially served as Vice Minister of Revenue.
His mother was worried and fearful,
and said to him:
"With your talent,
to hold the position of Vice Minister—
I fear disaster is sure to come."
The Minister of Revenue tried to explain and reassure her repeatedly,
so she said:
"If not,
try gathering your colleagues,
and let me observe them."
So he invited all his close acquaintances.
When the guests arrived,
the mother watched them from behind a curtain.
After the gathering ended,
she said happily:
"They are all your peers,
so there is no need to worry."
Then she asked:
"Who is that somberly dressed young man in the last seat?"
He replied:
"Reminder Dù Huángcháng."
The mother said:
"This man is completely different;
he is sure to become a famous minister or chancellor."
Empress Liú
After the incident at Shàngyuányì in Zhōuzhōu during the Later Táng Tàizǔ's time,
Tàizǔ was furious and resentful,
and wanted to turn the army back to attack.
Empress Liú was accompanying the army at the time,
and said to Tàizǔ:
"You are campaigning against rebels for the state,
yet because of a private grievance over a cup of wine,
if you attack the city,
then the fault lies with us.
Better to withdraw the army;
the court will have its own deliberations."
Thus the army was withdrawn.
During the Tiānfù era,
Zhōu Déwēi was defeated by the Biàn army,
and the three armies scattered in disarray.
The Biàn army pressed their advantage,
and Tàizǔ was in peril and fear.
He discussed with Déwēi about withdrawing to defend Yúnzhōu.
Empress Liú said:
"I hear you wish to abandon the city and retreat to a border region.
Who proposed this plan?"
He replied:
"It was suggested by Cúnxìn and his ilk."
Empress Liú said:
"Cúnxìn was originally a shepherd boy from the northern tribes;
how could he consider success or failure?
You often laughed at Wáng Xíngyú for abandoning his city,
losing power,
and being slaughtered.
Now you wish to imitate him?
In recent years, when you took refuge among the Dádá,
you nearly met with disaster.
It was only because the court had many troubles
that you were able to return.
Now, once you leave the city,
unforeseen changes will occur.
How could you reach the northern tribes?"
So he stopped.
After a few days,
the scattered soldiers regrouped,
and the military city was secure.
This was due to Empress Liú's efforts.
The Woman from Héchí
The year Liángzǔ attacked and besieged Qílǒng,
he led his troops to Fèngxiáng.
The Qín commander Lǐ Màozhēn
sent his officer Lǐ Jìlǎng to lead troops to rescue it.
Upon arrival, they achieved a great victory,
capturing over seven thousand alive.
When returning with the army,
they seized a young woman in Héchí County,
who was very beautiful.
Jìlǎng was pleased with her,
and had her stay in his military tent.
After traveling westward over fifteen stages,
each time he tried to force himself on her,
she would say:
"My mother-in-law is strict and my husband jealous;
I beg to die instead."
The commander grew angry,
threatening her with force and intimidation,
but ultimately could not break her will.
The commander laughed and pitied her,
and in the end did not violate her.
He sent someone to escort her back to her home.
Hè Shì
In Yǎnzhōu, there was a woman from a commoner family surnamed Hè,
whom the villagers called the Weaving Maiden.
Her parents made their living by farming.
Her husband, however, carried loads and engaged in trade,
traveling back and forth to the commandery.
When Hè first became a wife,
before even ten days had passed,
her husband went away.
Each time he left,
it would be several years before he returned,
and upon returning, he would leave again after just a few days.
The profits he gained
he used to keep another woman elsewhere,
not contributing a single coin to support his family.
Hè knew of this,
yet whenever her husband returned,
she served him joyfully,
never letting her feelings show on her face.
The husband, feeling ashamed and uneasy,
would instead unreasonably beat and curse her,
but the wife never retaliated.
Her mother-in-law was already old and ill,
suffering bitterly from cold and hunger.
Hè worked as a weaver for hire to support her,
and all the wages she earned
she gave entirely to her mother-in-law,
while she herself endured cold and hunger.
The mother-in-law was also unkind,
daily subjecting her to abuse.
Hè only became more respectful,
speaking softly and gently,
to please her mother-in-law's wishes,
never once complaining or sighing.
The husband once brought the woman he loved home,
and Hè addressed her as "younger sister,"
showing not the slightest trace of anger.
Hè was a wife for over twenty years,
during which her husband spent less than half a year at home,
yet she diligently served and supported the family,
remaining without resentment from beginning to end.
She can truly be called virtuous and filial.
Xiè Dàoyùn
Xiè Dàoyùn was the wife of Wáng Níngzhī.
Once, Wáng Xiànzhī was losing a debate on principles with a guest,
when Xiè Dàoyùn sent a maidservant to announce:
"I request to relieve my brother-in-law from his siege."
She then set up a blue silk screen to conceal herself
and debated with the guest,
who was unable to defeat her.
Yáng Rónghuá
Yáng Rónghuá was the niece of Yáng Yíngchuān.
From a young age, she excelled at composing writings.
She once wrote a poem titled "New Makeup,"
which was widely circulated by enthusiasts.
The poem reads:
"The roosting birds, startled from sleep, have ceased;
The room's windows open with the dawn's light.
Phoenix hairpins, gold threaded fine,
A phoenix mirror, its stand of jade so bright.
Her makeup seems as if by the pond applied,
Herself, one might suspect, from the moon has glided.
Pitying that ultimately she remains unseen,
Wishing to leave, yet again she lingers between."
Shàngguān Zhāoróng
When Táng's Shàngguān Zhāoróng was still in the womb,
her mother, Lady Zhèng, dreamed that a deity gave her a large steelyard,
saying with this she could weigh the world.
When the child was one month old,
Lady Zhèng teased her, saying:
"Aren't you the one who will weigh the world?"
The baby gurgled in response:
"Yes."
While still in swaddling clothes, she encountered family misfortune
and entered the palace precincts.
At the age of fourteen,
she was intelligent, perceptive, and sharp-witted,
with unparalleled literary talent.
The Empress Wǔ heard of her and tested her,
whereupon she took up the brush and completed compositions instantly,
all as if prepared long in advance.
From the Tōngtiān era onward,
until before the Jǐnglóng era,
she consistently managed the imperial writings.
The strategic plans for military and state affairs,
the great authority over life and death,
were often decided by her.
As for seeking out outstanding talents,
and fostering literary elegance,
the state had scholars fond of literature,
and the court lacked ministers who did not study.
For twenty years,
there were no talents left neglected in the countryside,
all due to her efforts.
However, in her later years, she rather extensively formed external cliques,
lightly toying with power and influence,
so that the court officials feared her.
When Emperor Xuánzōng quelled the troubles,
she was executed.
Lady Zhāng
The Duke Wénzhēn of Yān, Zhāng Yuè,
had a daughter who married into the Lú family.
Once, she asked her father-in-law to seek an official post for her husband,
and waited for her father to return from court to inquire about it.
Her father did not speak,
but only pointed to the turtle-shaped support of his bed and showed it to her.
The daughter bowed and returned to her room,
telling her husband:
"Father-in-law has obtained the position of Zhǎnshì."
Dù Gāo's Wife
Dù Gāo's wife, née Liú, was skilled at poetry.
Dù Gāo repeatedly took the imperial examinations but failed to pass,
so he returned home.
As he was about to reach home,
his wife first sent him a poem, which said:
"My husband truly possesses rare talent,
Why is it that year after year he is sent back?
Now my face feels shame before your face,
When you arrive, let it be near the night's embrace."
Dù Gāo saw the poem,
immediately turned back,
and eventually passed the examinations.
Zhāng Kuí's Wife
During the Huìcháng era,
the border general Zhāng Kuí had been stationed on defense for over ten years.
His wife, née Hóu,
embroidered a reversible-pattern poem in the shape of a turtle
and presented it at the palace.
The poem reads:
"Parted already for ten autumns strong,
Facing the mirror, how can I reapply makeup long?
Hearing wild geese, how many times I've written letters anew,
Seeing frost, I first make clothes for you.
Opening the chest, folding silk, tears first fall,
Sweeping the pestle, tuning the block, heartbreak befalls all.
Embroidered as a turtle shape to the Son of Heaven presented,
I pray the campaigning guest soon be homeward sent."
An imperial decree awarded her three hundred bolts of silk,
to commend her talent and beauty.
Guān Tú's Younger Sister
Guān Tú had a younger sister who was exceptionally intelligent and talented,
skilled in literature and letter writing,
all of which moved people deeply.
Guān Tú often said to his colleagues:
"In my family, there is a jìnshì,
only regrettably she is not a man."
Later, he resided in Jiānglíng.
There was a salt merchant named Cháng,
who had amassed a fortune of a thousand gold pieces,
a man from Sānxiá,
who also made his home in Jiānglíng.
He deeply befriended and entrusted himself to Guān Tú,
and Guān Tú also treated him as an elder.
After several years,
Cháng passed away.
He left a son,
whose appearance and demeanor carried an air of scholarly elegance,
and who had some knowledge of literature and writing.
Guān Tú eventually married his sister to him.
This was Cháng Xiū.
Guān shì then studied with Xiū,
practicing for over twenty years,
until his talent and learning became excellent and extensive,
surpassing his peers.
In the sixth year of the Xiántōng era, he passed the imperial examination,
with the chief examiner being Minister of Works Lǐ Wèi.
Earlier, when Luó Yǐn from Jiāngdōng failed the examination and returned east,
he composed a poem bidding farewell to Xiū, which said:
"Six years of toil in the capital's streets,
now seeking a different path east to the Five Lakes.
Ashamed of the laurel branch in the garden,
I recall the red sails on Sōngjiāng's boats.
In this fleeting world, one must follow one's nature,
why must a man always achieve success?
Only Bào Shū truly understands me,
someday, with a hundred-foot wind in the sail."
Also, "Reading the Three Poems Composed by Xiū on a Guǎnglíng Autumn Night,"
he chanted again, sending it to Xiū:
"Three poems from Shǔ back to Wú,
treasured in my box, more precious than a teacher.
At Jiànguān, reading at night, even Xiàngrú would listen,
at Guābù, chanting in autumn, even Emperor Yáng would grieve.
Scenes and objects know they lose to your mighty brush,
who in these times does not praise the high branch?
Next year in February, in the east wind,
on the river island, a leisurely man consoles his thoughts."
Cháng Xiū's fame and reputation were such,
and Guān shì also contributed to it.
After Xiū passed away,
Guān shì herself wrote a eulogy for him.
People of the time eagerly copied and circulated it.
Yú Xuánjī
The female Taoist priest Yú Xuánjī, styled Huìlán,
was highly talented and thoughtful.
During the Xiántōng era,
she married Lǐ Yì, a Bǔquē official.
Later, as his affection waned, she left the mountain,
and became a Taoist priest at Xiányí Temple.
Her poem says:
"Easy to find a priceless treasure,
hard to find a man with a sincere heart."
She also wrote:
"Huìlán withers and returns to the spring garden,
willows east and west tangle the traveler's boat."
From then on, she indulged her passions,
becoming a courtesan.
Eventually, she killed her maidservant,
and was executed by the Capital Governor Wēn Zhāng.
Her collected works circulated in the world.
Niú Sù's daughter
Niú Sù's eldest daughter was named Yìngzhēn,
who married Yáng Tángyuán of Hóngnóng.
From a young age she was intelligent and quick-witted,
able to recite anything she heard.
By the age of thirteen,
she had already recited over three hundred volumes of Buddhist scriptures,
and several hundred more volumes of Confucian classics, philosophical works, and histories,
astonishing her relatives.
Initially, Yìngzhēn had not read the *Zuǒzhuàn*.
Just as her father was planning to teach it to her,
one night, as she first fell asleep,
she suddenly began reciting the *Chūnqiū*.
Starting from "Duke Huī of Xī's consort Mèngzǐ died,"
and ending with "Zhì Bó, greedy and returning,"
"thus Hán and Wèi turned against him and caused his downfall,"
she recited all thirty volumes,
without missing a single word,
and finished by daybreak.
While reciting,
it was as if there were
someone teaching her,
or engaging in dialogue with her.
Her father was shocked and alarmed,
and called out to her several times,
but she did not answer at all.
After finishing the recitation, she awoke,
and when asked why she had done it,
she also did not know.
When tested by opening the text,
she was already thoroughly familiar with it,
but when questioned, she did not answer.
She wrote over a hundred literary pieces.
Later, she mastered the teachings of the Three Schools,
and was broadly learned and multi-talented.
Often, in the middle of the night while deeply asleep,
she would discuss literature with scholars,
all of whom were famous figures from antiquity,
engaging in back-and-forth debates,
sometimes mentioning names like Wáng Bì, Zhèng Xuán, Wáng Yǎn, Lù Jī,
with arguments flaring up intensely;
sometimes she would discuss literature with scholars,
all of whom were famous figures from antiquity;
sometimes they would discuss essays, talk about principles and logic, often continuing for several nights without end.
She died at the age of twenty-four.
Now, I have selected her piece "Rhapsody on the Specter Questioning the Shadow."
It is included in her collected works.
Its preface says:
In the year Gēngchén,
I was afflicted with a severe illness,
and for a hundred days I could not rise.
My spirit was broken and weary,
my body emaciated and haggard.
Medicines and treatments were applied,
but instead of improving, they only worsened.
Moved by Zhuāngzǐ's allegory of the specter reproaching the shadow,
I borrowed this theme to compose a rhapsody,
hoping it might alleviate my illness.
The specter questioned my shadow, saying:
"You, a person of outstanding talent,
a child of keen intelligence,
your learning encompasses the Six Arts,
your writing embraces the Hundred Schools,
you delve into the secret words of Daoism,
and explore the profound meanings of Buddhist teachings;
you are devout in your domestic duties,
and you admire the histories of the past;
you do not distort principles to seek fame,
nor do you destroy things to achieve your own ends.
With such virtuous conduct,
surely your spirit is something to rely on.
Why then is your appearance so emaciated,
your spirit so downcast,
troubled and pained upon your pillow and mat,
haggard in your clothes and headscarf?
You rely solely on the form,
and the form is intimate with you.
Why not instruct it to uphold virtue,
and teach it to cultivate itself?
Unlike Lái Qī, who found joy in the Way,
or Hóng Fù, who was content in poverty.
Is it that a chronic illness leaves no hope for life,
or that lowly status makes you wish to forget yourself?
Now the seasons change, the year turns,
winter ends and spring begins.
Bright sunlight shines over the suburbs and fields,
warm air stirs among the plum and willow trees.
Melting ice flows around the veranda,
a gentle breeze enters through the window.
Surely one could dispel
worries and relieve illness,
soothe the spirit and nurture longevity.
Why are you silent and without ambition,
bringing such misfortune upon yourself?"
I then responded with sudden vigor:
"You dwell in a land without people,
roaming in the realm of specters and demons.
Your form is depicted on the Xià Tripod,
and your name is recorded by Master Zhuāng.
How can your knowledge be anything but shallow,
your discourse anything but limited?
The shadow depends on the sun to exist,
the image appears because of the person.
How can mere words make it understood,
or distinguish the changes of the seasons?
It appears and vanishes with darkness and light,
changes and shifts with the physical form.
When a foolish man fears his shadow,
his ignorant nature is revealed;
when a wise man observes the shadows,
his sense of aging becomes apparent.
Good and evil lie within oneself,
what fault has the shadow to be reproached?
Moreover, I have heard that the essence of the supreme Way is profound and obscure,
the ultimate of the supreme Way is dim and silent.
The enlightened entrust themselves to the length of their lifespan,
the noble accept the fortunes and misfortunes of the times.
Regrets cannot entangle them,
glory cannot delude them.
Loss is not regarded as loss,
gain is not regarded as gain.
Why then, noble sir, do you resent me for not admiring the fragrant spring,
or blame me for not valuing ornate adornments?
Moreover, my principles and conduct,
how can your wisdom possibly fathom them?"
Before the words were finished,
the specter became alarmed and startled,
sighed and rose, saying:
"I was born beyond the farthest borders,
and grew up in remote and desolate lands,
never understanding how the wise conduct themselves,
which is why I came to you to question the shadow.
Now that I have heard such profound and wondrous discourse,
I shall withdraw and hide for the rest of my life."
Initially, Yìngzhēn dreamed of tearing
books and eating them,
and each time she dreamed of eating several dozen volumes,
her literary style would change.
This happened not just once,
and she eventually became skilled at writing rhapsodies and eulogies.
Her collected works are titled *Yífāng*.
Shěn Shì
was the daughter of a Confucian family from Běilíng Qiántíng.
Yán Guànfū, a scholar of the Three Histories, met her while traveling,
and they formed a marital bond,
returning together to Qíchūn.
After more than ten years without bearing children,
Guànfū seized upon her faults and divorced her,
ordering her to return to Èrzhè.
Shěn Shì, filled with emotion, boarded the boat,
as relatives gathered by the river to see her off.
She then composed a poem to bid farewell to Guànfū.
When Guànfū read it, he was deeply moved and saddened,
and thereafter treated her as his wife again, as before.
Shěn Shì's poem reads:
"Our shared feelings from back then are already connected,
yet like rain scattering and clouds flying, they vanished in a moment.
Now I must set sail alone from here,
unable to bear climbing the Husband-Gazing Mountain once more."
Xuē Yuán
There was a man from Háoliáng named Nán Chǔcái who traveled to Chényǐng.
After a long time,
the governor of Yǐng admired his demeanor and bearing,
and intended to marry his daughter to him.
Chǔcái had a wife at home,
but because he had gained the favor of the Yǐng governor,
he suddenly disregarded righteousness,
and hastily agreed to the proposal.
He then sent a servant home to fetch his qin and books,
as if he had no intention of returning to his former life.
Some said he sought the Way at Qīngchéng,
or visited monks at Héngyuè,
and no longer cared for fame and officialdom.
His wife Xuē Yuán was skilled at calligraphy and painting,
and excelled in composing literature.
She also subtly understood his intentions.
So she faced a mirror and painted her own portrait,
along with a poem of four couplets to send to him.
When Chǔcái received his wife’s portrait and poem,
he felt deeply ashamed,
and promptly made a noble gesture of yielding like Juàn Bùyí,
and the couple grew old together.
A local saying goes:
"In the past, wives abandoned husbands;
today, husbands abandon wives.
If she had not wielded the brush,
she would have been left alone in an empty room."
Xuē Yuán’s poem "Painting My Portrait to Send to My Husband" reads:
"Before I lower my painting brush,
I first hold up the precious mirror.
Already my face looks weary and pale,
gradually I feel my temples fading and thinning.
Tearful eyes are easy to depict,
but sorrowful heart is hard to convey.
I fear you may forget me completely,
so from time to time unfold this portrait and gaze."
Lady Sūn
Lady Sūn of Lèchāng,
wife of the presented scholar Mèng Chāngqī,
was skilled at poetry.
One day, she burned her entire collection,
believing that talent and thought were not matters for women.
From then on, she devoted herself solely to wifely duties and domestic management.
Lady Sūn’s poem "Presenting White Candles on Behalf of My Husband" reads:
"Brighter than silver lamps, fragrant as orchids,
a strip of white jade chills the beholder.
One day in the Forbidden Palace on a spring breeze night,
drunkenly drafting imperial edicts, examine it closely."
Another poem, "Hearing the Qin," reads:
"Jade fingers on vermilion strings, plucking clear and pure,
the sorrowful lament of the Xiāng consorts hardest to bear.
At first I thought it the rustling of cool winds stirring,
then like the pattering of evening rain falling.
Near, it resembles flowing springs from emerald peaks,
far, like dark cranes descending from azure skies.
Deep in the night, when the playing ends, melancholy reigns,
mist dampens clustered orchids, moonlight fills the courtyard."
Another poem, "Thanking Someone for Sending Wine," reads:
"Poems and clear wine sent to a sorrowful soul,
limpid, sweet, fragrant, the flavor true.
Perfect for a green-windowed, breeze-and-moonlit night,
one cup swirling and swaying fills the heart with spring."
Yíguāng
Yuè plotted to destroy Wú,
gathering the world’s rare treasures, beautiful women, and exotic delicacies
to present to Wú.
They obtained the jade of Yīnfēng,
the steeds of ancient emperors,
and the eels of Xiāng and Yuǎn;
there were also beautiful women,
one named Yíguāng,
the second named Xiūmíng,
who were offered as tribute to Wú.
Wú housed them in a pepper-blossom chamber,
strung fine pearls to make curtains and drapes,
lowered in the morning to block the light,
rolled up at evening to await the moon.
The two sat side by side before the window,
arranging mirrors and applying makeup within the pearl curtains.
Those who stole a glimpse were all stirred in heart and soul,
calling them "goddesses."
When King Fūchāi of Wú looked upon them,
they were like a pair of phoenixes in light mist,
or autumn lotuses rippling on still waters.
Bewitched and infatuated deeply,
he neglected state affairs.
When Yuè troops entered the kingdom,
he fled the Wú gardens holding the two women.
After the Yuè army entered,
seeing the two beneath bamboo and trees,
all exclaimed "goddesses."
They gazed but did not approach.
Now, inside the Shémén gate of Wú City, there is a broken tree stump,
still a place where goddesses are worshipped.
Lìjuān
A palace lady favored by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
named Lìjuān,
was just fourteen years old.
Her jade-like skin was soft and tender,
her breath fragrant as orchids.
Her body was delicate and frail,
she disliked having clothing or tassels brush against her,
fearing they would leave marks.
Whenever she sang,
Lǐ Yánhé would harmonize.
Beside the □zhī Shēng Hall,
she sang the "Song of the Whirling Wind,"
and the trees in the courtyard shed their leaves in response.
She was often placed in a glass-beaded canopy,
for fear dust might soil her body.
Often,
he would tie her robe with a sash,
and enclose her within layered curtains,
fearing she might be carried away by the wind.
Lìjuān
wore amber as a pendant,
hidden inside her garment hem,
so no one would know.
She then claimed her joints rang of themselves,
and people thought it supernatural.
Zhào Fēiyàn
Hàn’s Zhào Fēiyàn had a light body and slender waist,
skilled in walking, advancing and retreating.
Her younger sister, the Lady Zhāoyí,
could not match her.
But she had delicate bones and plump flesh,
and was especially fond of laughter and talk.
Both had complexions like red jade,
unsurpassed in their time,
uniquely outstanding.
They enjoyed favor in the rear palace.
Xuē Língyún
The beauty Xuē Língyún, beloved by Emperor Wén of Wèi,
was a native of Chángshān.
Her father’s name was Yè,
who served as the village head of Cuó Township.
Her mother, née Chén,
lived with Yè in a house beside the village station.
Born into poverty and low status,
by night,
she would often gather with neighboring women to spin,
using
hemp stalks for light.
When Língyún reached the age of fifteen,
her beauty was unparalleled in the world.
Young men from the neighborhood often came by night to peek at her,
but in the end, none ever succeeded in seeing her.
In the first year of Xiánxī,
Gǔ Xí was appointed as governor of Chángshān Commandery.
He heard that the village head had a beautiful daughter, but the family was very poor.
At that time, Emperor Wén was selecting daughters from good families
to enter the six palaces.
Xí used a thousand pieces of gold as a precious betrothal gift to secure her.
Once he obtained her,
he promptly presented her to Emperor Wén.
Upon hearing she was to part from her parents,
Língyún wept and sighed for days on end,
her tears soaking her clothes.
When the time came to mount the carriage and set off,
she used a jade spittoon to catch her tears,
and the vessel immediately turned as if red.
After departing from Chángshān,
and upon reaching the capital,
the tears in the vessel had congealed like blood.
The emperor dispatched ten carriages
to welcome Língyún.
The carriages all had wheels carved with precious designs,
and their hubs were painted crimson.
Before the yoke were assorted treasures,
forming dragons and phoenixes holding hundred-bell chimes,
which jingled harmoniously,
their sound echoing through forests and fields.
They were drawn by blue-green paired-hoofed oxen,
which could travel three hundred lǐ in a day.
These oxen were tribute from the country of Shītú,
their hooves resembling those of horses.
Along the roadside, Shíyè incense was burned.
This stone is layered,
resembling mica in appearance.
Its fragrance wards off malignant diseases;
it was tribute from the country of Fùtí.
When Língyún was still several tens of lǐ from the capital,
the light of torches and candles
stretched continuously without extinguishing.
Carriages and attendants choked the road,
dust rose and blotted out the stars and moon.
People of the time called it “dusty skies.”
They also built an earthen platform,
with a foundation thirty zhàng high.
Candles were arranged below the platform,
and it was named the “Candle Terrace,”
looking from afar like stars fallen to earth.
Moreover, along the sides of the main road,
at every lǐ, a bronze marker was erected,
five chǐ high,
to mark the distance in lǐ.
Hence travelers sang:
“Green locusts line the road, much dust in the air,
dragon towers and phoenix gates loom grand and fair.
Clear breeze and fine rain mingle with fragrant scent,
earth yields metal, fire lights the terrace there.”
At that time, bronze pillars were erected
to mark the distance along the roadside;
this is the meaning of “earth yields metal.”
As for the candles placed at the terrace,
it signifies fire beneath the earth.
The Hàn dynasty ruled by the virtue of Fire,
the Wèi by the virtue of Earth.
Fire is subdued and Earth rises.
Earth yielding metal
means Wèi perishes and Jìn rises.
When Língyún was still ten lǐ from the capital,
the emperor rode in a jade-carved carriage,
gazing upon the grandeur of the carriages and attendants.
He sighed and said:
“In the past, it was said, ‘Morning brings traveling clouds,
evening brings traveling rain.’
Now it is neither cloud nor rain,
neither morning nor evening.”
Thus he changed Língyún’s name to “Yèlái.”
Upon entering the palace, she received great favor.
When a foreign state presented hairpins of fire-pearl dragons and simurghs,
the emperor said:
“Pearls and kingfisher feathers are already too much,
how much more the weight of dragons and phoenixes!”
So he stopped and did not accept them.
Yèlái was exceptionally skilled at women’s work.
Even within deep curtains and layered canopies,
without using lamps or candles,
she could cut and sew garments instantly.
If it was not sewn by Yèlái,
the emperor would not wear it.
In the palace, she was called “Divine Needle.”
Sūn Liàng’s concubine Cháoshū
Sūn Liàng made a green glass screen,
very thin and crystal clear.
He would often unfold it under the moonlight on clear nights.
He once favored four concubines,
all of them beauties surpassing ancient times:
the first named Cháoshū,
the second Lìjū,
the third Luòzhēn,
the fourth Jiéhuá.
He would have the four sit behind the screen,
and looking from outside,
it was as if there were no barrier,
only the fragrance did not pass through.
He blended four scents for the four of them.
This incense was tribute from distant, exotic lands.
Wherever they trod or rested over the years,
the fragrance would cling to their clothes,
growing stronger with each passing year,
and not fading even after a hundred washings.
Thus it was named “Hundred-Wash Incense.”
Sometimes it was named after people,
hence there were Cháoshū, Lìjū, Luòzhēn, and Jiéhuá incenses.
Whenever Liàng went on outings,
these four would always accompany him at the banquet,
summoned to attend.
They were seated in order according to the names of their scents,
and this order could not be disrupted.
The chamber where they resided was called “Thought-of-Fragrance Alluring Bedchamber.”
Shǔ’s Empress Gān
Empress Gān of the former ruler of Shǔ
was from Pèi,
born into lowly circumstances.
A fortune-teller in her village said:
“This girl will later attain nobility,
reaching the highest position in the palace.”
When the empress was born, her physique and appearance were extraordinary.
By the age of eighteen,
she had jade-like skin and soft flesh,
with a charming demeanor and enchanting beauty.
The former ruler placed the empress behind a white silk curtain,
and those looking from outside
saw her like snow gathered under moonlight.
When Hénán presented a jade figurine,
three chǐ tall,
he placed the jade figurine beside the empress.
By day, he would discuss military strategies,
and by night, he would embrace the empress while admiring the jade figurine.
He often said that the value of jade
lies in comparing its virtue to that of a gentleman.
How much more so when it takes human form—
how could one not admire it?
Empress Gān and the jade figurine were equally pure white and lustrous,
so that viewers were almost confused between them.
Those who sought favor were not only jealous of Empress Gān
but also envious of the jade figurine.
The empress often wished to have it carved and destroyed,
so she admonished the former ruler, saying:
“In ancient times, Zǐhǎn did not consider jade a treasure,
and the Spring and Autumn Annals praised him for it.
Now Wú and Wèi are not yet destroyed;
how can you indulge in such bewitching playthings?
All such delusions breed suspicion.
Do not bring them forth again.”
The former ruler then removed the jade figurine,
and those who sought favor all withdrew.
The gentlemen of the time regarded Empress Gān as a woman of divine wisdom.
Shí Chóng’s maid Xuānfēng
The beloved maidservant of Shí Jìlún,
named Xuānfēng,
was bought from among the Hu people
at the end of the Wei dynasty.
She was just ten years old at the time,
and was raised within the inner chambers.
By the age of fifteen,
none could compare to her appearance,
and she was especially admired for her graceful demeanor.
She excelled at distinguishing the sound of jade
and could discern the quality of gold.
The wealth of the Shí family
rivaled that of the royal house,
and their extravagance was unmatched in their time.
Precious gems and rare treasures
were regarded as mere tiles and pebbles,
gathered like dirt and dust,
all obtained from distant, foreign lands.
No one could identify their origins,
but Xuānfēng could distinguish them by their sound and color
and knew exactly where they came from.
She would say:
"Jade from the west and north
has a deep, heavy sound and a warm, smooth nature;
wearing it benefits one's spirit.
Jade from the east and south
has a clear, pure sound and a cool, refreshing nature;
wearing it sharpens one's mind."
The Shí family had thousands of beautiful attendants,
but Xuānfēng was the most beloved for her literary talent.
Shí Chóng often said to her:
"After my death,
I will point to the bright sun
and have you buried with me."
She replied:
"To love in life and part in death
is worse than no love at all.
If I am to be buried with you,
how could my body ever decay?"
Thus, she was cherished even more.
Shí Chóng often selected several dozen women with similar beauty and appearance,
dressed them in identical clothes,
all of the same size,
so that at a glance they could not be distinguished,
and had them constantly attend at his side.
He had Xuānfēng select jade for the craftsmen
to make pendant ornaments in the shape of descending dragons,
twisted gold into phoenix crown hairpins,
carved jade into the posture of descending dragons,
and cast gold into the form of phoenixes.
With sleeves linked, they danced around the pillars,
day and night without pause,
which was called the "constant dance."
If someone was summoned,
names were not called;
instead, they listened to the sound of the pendants
and observed the color of the hairpins.
Those with lighter jade sounds stood in front,
those with brighter gold colors stood behind,
forming a procession in this order.
He had several dozen women each hold a different fragrance in their mouths,
so that when they walked and laughed,
the scent would drift with the wind.
He also sifted agarwood incense into fine dust
and spread it on the ivory bed.
If the beloved could tread on it without leaving a trace,
she would be rewarded with a hundred pearls;
if there were traces,
her food and drink would be restricted
to make her body light and frail.
Thus, the women in the inner chambers joked among themselves:
"If you are not fine-boned and light-bodied,
how can you earn a hundred pearls?"
When Xuānfēng reached the age of thirty,
the younger, more beautiful women grew jealous of her,
some saying, "A Hu woman should not be among us,"
and they vied to slander and disparage her.
Shí Chóng, influenced by their insinuations,
demoted Xuānfēng to the role of chamber matron,
tasking her with overseeing the younger women.
Filled with resentment, she composed a five-character poem,
which read:
"Who does not admire spring blossoms?
Yet they grieve when autumn falls;
Choking back tears, I weep alone,
Did I expect such disgrace and dismissal?
The cassia's fragrance only invites moths,
Losing favor lies in the moth-brow beauty;
Sitting idle, I watch my prime fade,
Haggard and worn, I mock myself in vain."
The women of the Shí household sang this as a melody for their amusement,
and it continued until the end of the Jin dynasty.
The Dancers of Zhèdōng
In the second year of the Bǎolì era,
Zhèdōng presented two dancers as tribute:
one named Fēiyàn,
the other named Qīngfēng.
They had slender eyebrows and jet-black hair,
with an orchid-like fragrance about them.
In winter, they wore no padded clothes;
in summer, their bodies never sweated.
Their diet consisted mostly of lychees, torreya nuts,
gold flakes, borneol, and the like.
They wore crowns of light gold,
and their gauze robes were seamless.
The weaving was exquisitely intricate,
beyond anyone's comprehension.
The light gold crowns were woven from gold threads
into the shapes of swallows and cranes,
adorned with multicolored fine pearls,
delicately linked together,
standing about a foot tall,
yet weighing no more than two or three qián.
On top, carved jade hibiscus flowers were set as ornaments.
When the two women sang and danced on stage,
every night as soon as their performance began,
their voices sounded like those of phoenixes,
and all kinds of birds would flock and hover above them,
even gathering in the courtyard.
Their dance movements were enchanting and ethereal,
unlike anything found in the mortal world.
After each song,
the emperor ordered the palace ladies to hide them in golden chambers and precious curtains,
for fear of exposure to wind and sun.
Thus, the women in the palace would say:
"Behind fragrant, layered precious curtains,
a pair of red hibiscus flowers."
The Wife of Chē Wǔzǐ
As the popular tale goes,
the wife of Chē Wǔzǐ was extremely jealous.
Once, when her brother came to stay overnight,
she took a crimson skirt
and hung it on the screen.
His wife, drawing a knife, rushed straight to the bed,
pulled back the covers,
only to find it was her brother.
Ashamed, she withdrew.
Duàn Shì
In Línjì, there was a Ford of the Jealous Wife.
It is said that during the Tàishǐ era of the Jin dynasty,
Liú Bóyù's wife, Duàn Shì, styled Míngguāng,
was of a jealous nature.
Bóyù once recited the "Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luo River" in front of his wife.
He said to her:
"If I could have a wife like this,
I would have no regrets."
Míngguāng replied:
"How can you praise the water goddess's beauty and slight me?
If I die,
why worry that I won't become a water goddess?"
That night, she drowned herself.
Seven days after her death,
she appeared to Bóyù in a dream, saying:
"You wished for a goddess;
now I have become one."
Bóyù then never crossed the water again for the rest of his life.
Whenever women crossed this ford,
they would dishevel their clothes and mess up their makeup
before daring to cross.
Otherwise,
storms would suddenly arise.
Even if an ugly woman
crossed with full makeup,
the goddess would not be jealous.
If a woman crossed the river without wind or waves,
it was assumed she was too ugly to attract the water goddess.
Ugly women, ashamed of this,
would all disfigure their appearances
to avoid being mocked.
Thus, the people of Qí would say:
"If you seek a beautiful wife,
stand at the ford.
By the water's edge,
beauty and ugliness reveal themselves."
The Wife of Wáng Dǎo
Wáng Dǎo's wife, Madame Cáo, was extremely jealous and possessive.
She forbade the Prime Minister from having any concubines or attendants,
even extending to the lowliest servants.
If there were any young and beautiful women,
she would inevitably reprimand and punish them.
So, Wáng Dǎo secretly established a separate residence,
where he assembled a host of concubines,
and fathered several sons.
When Madame Cáo found out,
she was greatly shocked and enraged.
She then led twenty eunuchs and maidservants,
each armed with a kitchen knife,
intending to go out and hunt them down.
Lord Wáng hastily ordered his carriage prepared.
Worried it would be too slow,
he personally used the handle of his yak-tail fly whisk to help the driver whip the oxen,
fleeing in a frantic,狼狈 (disheveled) gallop,
and thus managed to arrive first.
When Minister of Education Cài Mó heard of this,
he went to see Wáng and said to him:
"The court intends to bestow upon you the Nine Bestowals,
are you aware?"
Wáng began recounting his modest achievements.
Cài said:
"I haven't heard of the other items,
only of a short-axle calf-cart
and a long-handled yak-tail whisk."
Dǎo was greatly ashamed.
Dù Lánxiāng
Dù Lánxiāng descended to visit Zhāng Shuò.
Shuò's wife had no sons,
so he took a concubine.
His wife's jealousy knew no bounds.
Shuò said to Xiāng:
"What can be done about this?"
Xiāng said:
"This is easy to remedy."
As soon as she finished speaking, Shuò's wife fell ill with sores and became bedridden.
Shuò said:
"What if my wife is going to die?"
Xiāng said:
"These sores are to cure her jealousy.
Once the sores heal, she should recover."
Within a few days,
the sores diminished and his wife lost her jealous heart.
She subsequently gave birth to several sons.
Rén Guī's Wife
In the early Táng dynasty,
Rén Guī was Minister of War.
By imperial decree, he was granted two palace ladies,
both women of surpassing beauty.
His wife was jealous
and burned off all the hair of the two women, leaving them completely bald.
Emperor Tàizōng heard of this
and ordered a senior official to take a golden foreign flask of wine to bestow upon her, saying:
"Drinking this will cause immediate death.
Guī holds the third rank,
and is entitled to have concubines.
If you are not jealous hereafter,
you need not drink it;
if you are jealous, then drink it."
Madame Liǔ received the decree and said:
"I and Guī are husband and wife since youth,
both coming from humble origins.
We supported each other,
and thus achieved honored office.
Guī now has many favored women inside.
I would truly rather die."
She then drank it all.
However, it was not poison.
After she awoke from sleep,
the Emperor said to Guī:
"Her nature is like this,
even I must fear her."
Thereupon he issued an edict concerning the two women,
ordering them to be settled in a separate residence.
Also, Fáng Xuánlíng's wife was extremely jealous.
Emperor Tàizōng intended to bestow a beauty upon him,
but she repeatedly declined to accept it.
The Emperor then ordered the Empress to summon the wife
and explain to her that the ranks of concubines and attendants
have regular regulations.
Moreover, the Minister of Works was nearing old age,
and the Emperor wished to show him special favor.
The wife remained steadfast and would not relent.
The Emperor then ordered someone to say to her:
"Would you rather live without jealousy,
or die with jealousy?"
She said:
"I would rather die with jealousy."
He then sent someone to pour a cup of wine and give it to her, saying:
"If so,
you may drink this cup of poison."
She raised it and drank it all in one go,
without any hesitation or difficulty.
The Emperor said:
"Even I fear to see this,
how much more so Xuánlíng?"
Yáng Hóngwǔ's Wife
Yáng Hóngwǔ was Vice Minister of the Ministry of War.
Emperor Gāozōng said to him:
"For what reason was a certain person
so readily appointed to this position?"
He replied:
"My wife, Madame Wéi, has a fierce and stubborn nature.
Yesterday she urged this appointment upon me.
If I did not comply,
I feared there would be future trouble."
The Emperor praised him for not hiding the truth
and dismissed him with a laugh.
Fáng Rúfù's Wife
Fáng Rúfù's wife, Madame Cuī, had a jealous and possessive nature.
The maidservants around her were not allowed to appear before her with heavy makeup or high hairdos.
They were allotted one bean's worth of rouge
and one coin's worth of powder.
There was a newly bought maidservant
whose makeup was slightly better.
Madame Cuī angrily said to her:
"You like to make up, do you?
I shall do your makeup for you."
She then ordered her eyebrows carved out,
filled in with blue pigment,
heated a lock and crossbar in the fire,
and burned the corners of her eyes.
The skin curled up from the scorching,
and she applied cinnabar over it.
When the scabs fell off,
the scars resembled makeup.
Lǐ Tíngbì's Wife
Lǐ Tíngbì sat for the examinations for twenty years
before finally achieving success in Shǔ.
His song lyrics were exquisite and beautiful,
his poetry rhymes refined and skillful.
He once served as Assistant Military Commissioner of Shùzhōu.
His wife was suspicious and jealous.
One day, there were consecutive banquets at the government offices,
and for three nights he did not return home.
His wife sent word that
if he came, she would surely knife him.
He tearfully reported this to the Prefect,
moved to reside in a Buddhist temple,
and hid his traces for twelve days.
Thereupon he composed a poem titled "Chanting on Sorrow":

"Arriving, hard to dispel; leaving, hard to detain, / It clings to the bone, sticks to the heart, all matters cease. / Pān Yuè's sorrow-sprouting strands within his temples grow, / The Lady Bān's sad hue upon her eyebrows shows. / On the long road, poems spent, in vain I ride my horse; / The distant wild geese's first call, alone I lean on the tower. / And still there is longing, yet we do not meet— / Sober from wine, lamp at my back, the moon like a hook."
Zhāng Hè's Wife
When Minister Zhāng Hè was governing Jìnzhōu,
he kept a beloved courtesan outside,
who bore him a son.
His wife, Madame Sū, was jealous,
so he dared not bring the child home.
He thus gave the boy to his friend, the Recluse Zhāng, to raise as his own,
and they lived by the riverbank.
Zhāng Hè often sent letters,
inquiring about the child’s well-being,
and provided money and silk.
As the boy gradually grew up,
he was taught to read.
Someone told him he was not the Recluse’s son,
and that his father was a high-ranking official at court.
The boy then secretly took the letters between his father and the Recluse,
and without saying goodbye, fled to the capital.
By then, Zhāng Hè had already died.
Arriving at the mansion gate,
none of the servants recognized him;
they only called him “the young master from Jiānghuái.”
His brothers were all astonished.
His legal mother, Madame Sū, wept and said to her sons:
“It is true that there was such a child;
I knew of him.
In my youth, I acted without reason,
causing father and son to be separated in life and death forever—
it is my fault.”
The whole household wept together,
took him into the mansion,
placed him among his brothers in age order,
and named him Rén Guī.
He was learned in literature,
polished his writing, and took the imperial examination,
passed it,
and served as Attendant Censor.
He died while on a mission to Jiāngzhè.
Wú Zōngwén
Wú Zōngwén of the Shǔ Kingdom,
through his achievements, successively governed famous commanderies.
Young and wealthy,
he had over ten concubines, maids, and singing girls at home,
all carefully selected.
His wife was jealous,
and he was often discontented and frustrated.
One day,
he set out for court at the drum’s signal,
and after passing several wards,
suddenly received word that “court was canceled.”
He then secretly ordered his attendants,
slipped back home,
and slept with them all in succession.
After more than ten such encounters,
he clutched his stomach and died.
A Shǔ Meritorious Official
There was a meritorious official in Shǔ whose name is forgotten;
his wife was jealous.
The household kept many singing girls,
but ordinarily he was kept apart from them.
When there was a banquet,
they would play music from behind a curtain,
so he never saw them.
Around his wife,
he was always served by old and ugly women.
He often lived alone,
with no attendants at all,
yet his residence, utensils, and clothing were extremely lavish.
Later, his wife fell gravely ill,
and said to her husband:
“When I die,
if you approach the maids and concubines,
I will immediately come for you.”
After she was buried,
he summoned all the singing girls,
and day and night drank and reveled with them.
There was a maid in charge of clothing
whom he especially favored,
and he slept with her.
Just as he was resting,
suddenly there was a sound like thunder,
the bed curtains all tore apart,
and he was so frightened he fell ill and died.
A Qín Cavalry General
There was a cavalry general of Qín named Shí,
who had considerable military achievements.
His wife was fierce and jealous,
and Shí often suffered because of it.
Later, when his wife was alone,
he sent someone at night to assassinate her.
The wife caught the blade with her hands,
and screamed for help.
The maids and concubines together attacked the assassin,
who then broke the sword guard and fled,
ultimately unable to harm her.
The woman’s ten fingers were all injured.
Several years later,
after Qín fell and he entered Shǔ,
Shǔ sent General Shí with troops,
stationed at Bāoliáng.
He again recruited a knight-errant from the army,
to go to his home and assassinate her.
Bāo and Shǔ were several thousand lǐ apart.
The knight-errant, carrying a blade,
and holding a letter from home,
arrived at her door and said:
“A letter has arrived from Bāo,
and I am to deliver it to the lady in person.”
The wife happily came out to see him.
The knight-errant bowed and handed her the letter;
as she reached out to receive it,
he swung his blade and struck her.
The wife had a daughter who leaped out,
raised her hands to catch the blade,
and held it off for a long time,
so he ultimately could not harm her.
Outsiders heard and came to rescue them,
and the girl’s ten fingers were all injured.
Ten years later,
when Shǔ fell,
they returned to the region of Qín,
and in the end, she grew old together with her husband,
and died peacefully at home.
Zhōu Hào
The Grand Coachman Minister Zhōu Hào,
a son of a noble family,
possessed great strength and a proud spirit.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
when Hào was young,
he often gathered companions for visits to the pleasure quarters,
ultimately harboring fugitives.
He sought out famous courtesans in the city,
like flies drawn to meat,
and there was none he did not obtain.
At that time, in Jìnggōng Ward, there was a courtesan named Yèlái,
young, with a charming smile,
peerless in song and dance,
for whom noble young masters bankrupted themselves to welcome her.
Hào, along with several wealthy men, took turns monopolizing her favor.
One day,
her mother said to Hào:
"On such-and-such a day is Yèlái's birthday,
how can it be allowed to pass quietly?"
Hào and those who associated with him
vied to procure rare treasures,
pooling several hundred thousand coins,
to hold a feast at her home.
The musicians Hè Huáizhì and Jì Háihái,
were both unrivalled masters of the time.
Just as the doors were closed and the gathering began,
suddenly they heard the sound of urgent pounding at the gate.
Hào warned those inside not to open it,
but after a long while,
the gate was broken down and they entered.
There was a young man in purple robes,
with several dozen mounted attendants,
who berated the mother;
he was the son of General Gāo Lìshì.
The mother and Yèlái wept and bowed in apology,
and the guests were about to disperse.
Hào, then in the full vigor of youth,
and relying on his strength,
saw that the attendants were no match for him.
He therefore stepped forward, reproaching the young man for relying on his power,
and rolling up his sleeves, struck him.
The purple-robed youth fell beneath his fist,
and his jawbone was broken.
Severely injured and bleeding,
Hào then rushed out.
At that time, Wèi Zhēn, the official in charge of the Metropolitan Courier Station,
was a man of principle and feeling,
fond of sheltering private guests,
and Hào, confiding his situation, sought refuge with him.
Zhēn then hid him among his wife and daughters.
As the authorities were urgently pursuing and seizing him,
Zhēn, fearing the trail would be exposed,
prepared baggage by night,
and tucking several ingots of white gold at his waist,
said to Hào:
"In Biànzhōu there is Zhōu Jiǎnlǎo,
a righteous man,
and moreover a member of your own clan,
you may now rely on him.
You must be humble and respectful without fail."
Zhōu Jiǎnlǎo was indeed a great knight-errant.
Upon seeing Wèi Zhēn's letter,
he was greatly pleased.
Hào therefore paid respects to him as an uncle,
and then related his circumstances.
Jiǎnlǎo had him stay in a boat,
warning him not to venture out recklessly,
and provided for him most generously.
After residing there for over a year,
Hào suddenly heard the sound of weeping from a boat.
He secretly peered out,
and saw a young woman,
in plain white garments and very beautiful,
being comforted by Jiǎnlǎo.
That evening,
Jiǎnlǎo suddenly came to Hào's place,
and asked:
"Are you married, sir?
I have a cousin's daughter,
who was married to a certain man.
That man died without sons,
and now she has nowhere to return to.
She could serve you, sir."
Hào bowed in thanks.
That very evening,
his cousin's daughter was given to Hào.
She had two daughters,
and one son,
who were still in the boat.
Jiǎnlǎo suddenly said to Hào:
"The matter has now blown over.
Your appearance is plain,
certainly no one will recognize you.
You may travel in the Jiāng-Huái region."
He then gave him over a hundred thousand coins,
and they parted with loud weeping.
Thus he escaped.
Lǐ Xiùlán
Lǐ Xiùlán was famous as a woman of talent.
When she was five or six years old,
her father held her in the courtyard,
and she composed a poem chanting about roses.
Its final lines were:
"Past their time, not yet trellised,
my heart's thoughts run wild and tangled."
Her father angrily said:
"This girl will in the future be rich in literary talent,
but she is sure to become a woman of loose conduct."
It turned out just as he said.
Also, Xiùlán once met with various worthies at the Kāiyuán Temple in Wūchéng County.
Knowing that Liú Chángqīng from Héjiān suffered from a scrotal ailment,
she said to him:
"The mountain air is fine, day and night."
Chángqīng replied:
"All birds rejoice, having found their perch."
The whole company laughed heartily,
and commentators praised both lines.
Xiùlán had a poem that reads:
"Distant waters float an immortal's boat,
cold stars accompany the envoy's carriage."
This is indeed fine imagery within a five-character line.
Compared above to Bān Jī she may fall short,
but compared below to Hán Yīng she has surplus,
truly a poetic heroine among women.
She once composed a song, "Gaining the Theme of the Flowing Springs of the Three Gorges", which says:
"My home was originally beneath the clouds of Wū Mountain,
The flowing waters of Wū Mountain I often heard of myself.
The jade zither's playing turns vast and distant,
Just like listening in a dream of times past.
The Three Gorges stretch on for thousands of miles,
In a moment, their flow enters the deep women's quarters.
Huge rocks, rushing rapids, born beneath the fingers,
Flying waves, racing billows, rise from the strings.
At first I suspect a gushing surge containing thunder and wind,
Then again it seems a sobbing flow, blocked and不通.
Swirling eddies, rushing over shallows, their force about spent,
Now and again dripping onto the level sand.
I recall long ago Ruǎn Jí composed this tune,
It could make Ruǎn Xián listen without satisfaction.
One playing finished, yet another begins.
May it with the flowing springs forever continue."
Dù Mù
Dù Mù, a Secretariat Drafter of the Táng dynasty,
possessed extraordinary talent from a young age,
composing poetry as soon as he put brush to paper.
At the age of twenty, he passed the imperial examination and became a Presented Scholar,
and later excelled in the special decree examination.
Dù Mù was brilliant in his youth,
but his nature was unrestrained and dissolute.
Although he tried to restrain himself,
he could not control his impulses.
It happened that Chancellor Niú Sēngrú was appointed to govern Yángzhōu.
He recruited Dù Mù to serve as his military secretary.
Outside of his official duties,
Dù Mù devoted himself solely to feasting and pleasure-seeking.
Yángzhōu was a renowned scenic place.
Every evening when the inner city gates closed,
atop the courtesans' towers,
there were often tens of thousands of crimson silk lanterns,
shining brilliantly in the sky,
along the nine-li and thirty-step street.
Adorned with pearls and jade, the area was packed and bustling,
like a distant fairyland.
Dù Mù often roamed and galloped about in these places.
Not a single evening was missed.
Moreover, there were thirty soldiers
who changed their clothes and followed him,
secretly protecting him—
this was Niú Sēngrú's covert instruction.
Yet Dù Mù believed he had gotten away with it.
No one else knew.
Wherever he went, he found joy,
and nothing failed to satisfy his desires.
This went on for several years,
until he was summoned to the capital and appointed as Investigating Censor.
Niú Sēngrú held a farewell banquet for him,
and took the opportunity to admonish him, saying:
"With the bearing and drive of an Investigating Censor,
you should naturally tread a smooth path.
However, I often worry that your romantic passions are unchecked,
which may harm your noble health."
Dù Mù then falsely replied:
"I am fortunate to have always exercised self-restraint,
and would not cause you such concern."
Niú Sēngrú smiled without answering,
and immediately ordered a servant girl
to fetch a small book chest.
Opening it in front of Dù Mù,
it contained the secret reports from the street patrols.
There were several hundred in total,
all reading:
"On such-and-such night,
Dù Mù went to such-and-such place,
and did such-and-such."
Dù Mù was ashamed and thanked him.
After Dù Mù became a censor,
he was later assigned to duty in Luòyáng.
At that time, Minister of Works Lǐ Yuàn had retired from his military governorship and was living in leisure.
His singing girls and luxurious lifestyle
were unmatched at the time.
The famous scholars of Luòyáng
all paid him visits.
Lǐ then held a grand banquet,
to which all the high-ranking officials and eminent figures of the time
were invited.
Because Dù Mù held a censorial position,
they dared not invite him.
Dù Mù sent a message through a guest,
expressing his wish to attend the gathering.
Lǐ had no choice but to send a swift letter of invitation.
Dù Mù was then drinking alone,
already quite intoxicated.
Upon receiving the invitation, he hurried over.
By the time he arrived, the banquet was already underway,
with over a hundred female entertainers,
all possessing exceptional skills and extraordinary beauty.
Dù Mù sat alone in the southern row,
staring intently,
drank three full cups,
and asked Lǐ:
"I've heard there is one named Zǐyún—which one is she?"
Lǐ pointed her out.
Dù Mù gazed at her for a long time and said:
"Her reputation is well-deserved.
You should give her to me."
Lǐ bowed his head and laughed,
and all the entertainers also turned around and broke into smiles.
Dù Mù drank three more cups himself,
then stood up and recited loudly:
"Today in this splendid hall, a lavish feast unfolds;
Who summoned the Investigating Censor from his duties?
Suddenly uttering wild words that startle the entire gathering,
Two rows of rosy faces turn back at once."
His demeanor was calm and carefree,
as if no one else was present.
Dù Mù also felt that he was gradually aging,
and often composed poems reminiscing about the past, such as:
"Downcast, I roamed the rivers and lakes, carrying wine with me,
Entranced by slender waists of Chǔ, light enough to dance in the palm.
Ten years in Yángzhōu seem but a dream upon waking,
Winning only the name of a heartless man in the blue towers."
And also:
"A boat with a single oar empties a hundred percent of cares,
Ten years of youth did not betray you.
Today, with temples graying, I keep company with a meditation couch,
As tea smoke drifts lightly in the breeze scattering fallen blossoms."
In the late Tàihé era,
Dù Mù again left his post as Investigating Censor to serve under Shěn Chuánshī in the administrative offices of Jiāngxī and Xuānzhōu.
Although he traveled wherever he went,
he never found anyone to his liking,
as none suited his tastes.
Upon hearing that Húzhōu was a famous commandery,
with beautiful scenery and pleasant climate,
and many extraordinary beauties,
he eagerly decided to visit.
The prefect of Húzhōu, a certain Mr. Yǐ,
was someone Dù Mù had long been close to,
and he understood Dù Mù's intentions quite well.
When Dù Mù arrived,
he often arranged private banquets and escorted him on tours.
All the skilled courtesans and singing girls
that could be procured by any means
were presented to him.
Dù Mù stared intently and said:
"They are beautiful!
But not yet perfect."
Yǐ again tried to discern his wishes,
and Dù Mù said:
"I would like to organize a water festival,
so that all the people of the prefecture can watch.
Wait until crowds gather from all directions,
and I will stroll among them to look around.
I hope that on this occasion,
I might find someone to my liking."
Yǐ was delighted,
and acted accordingly.
On the day of the event,
spectators lined both banks like walls.
As evening approached,
he still had found nothing.
Just as they were about to moor the boat and return to shore,
among the dense crowd,
an old woman from the village appeared, leading a young girl with her hair in twin buns,
about ten years old.
Dù Mù examined her closely and said:
"This is truly a beauty fit for a nation!
All the earlier ones were merely placeholders."
He then sent someone to speak to her mother,
proposing to bring the girl onto the boat.
Both the old woman and the girl were frightened.
Dù Mù said:
"I will not take her immediately,
but will set a later date."
The old woman said:
"If you break your promise in the future,
what should we do then?"
Dù Mù said:
"Within ten years,
I will certainly become the prefect of this commandery.
If I do not come within ten years,
then she may marry whomever she pleases."
The mother agreed,
and Dù Mù gave her generous gifts to secure the promise,
making a pledge before parting.
Therefore, after Dù Mù returned to the capital,
he often thought of Húzhōu.
However, because his official rank was still low,
he did not dare to make the request.
He was successively appointed to Huángzhōu, Chízhōu,
and then transferred to Mùzhōu,
none of which were to his liking.
Dù Mù had long been on good terms with Zhōu Chí.
When Zhōu Chí became chancellor,
Dù Mù submitted three petitions to him,
requesting to be appointed prefect of Húzhōu,
citing his younger brother Dù Yǐ's
eye disease
as a pretext, hoping to seek treatment south of the Yangtze River.
In the third year of the Dàzhōng era,
he was finally appointed prefect of Húzhōu.
By the time he arrived at the commandery,
fourteen years had already passed.
The girl he had pledged to marry
had been married to someone else for three years
and had given birth to three children.
After Dù Mù assumed his duties,
he immediately sent for her.
Her mother, fearing he would take her by force,
brought the young children along.
Dù Mù questioned the mother:
"You promised her to me before—
why have you gone back on your word?"
The mother replied:
"We agreed on ten years.
If you did not come within ten years, she would marry someone else.
She has been married for three years now."
Dù Mù then took out the written pledge and examined it.
He bowed his head for a long while and said:
"Her words are fair.
Forcing her would bring ill fortune."
He then gave them generous gifts and sent them away.
Thus he composed a poem to lament his own situation, saying:
"I went seeking spring, but arrived too late;
No need for sorrow, no need to blame the season of blossoms.
The fierce wind has stripped away the deep crimson hues,
Green leaves now form shade, and fruits fill the branches."
Liǔ Yǔxī
Liǔ Yǔxī was traveling to assume his post in Gūsū,
and passed through Yángzhōu.
The regional governor, Dù Hóngjiàn, treated him to wine,
and he returned to the post station utterly drunk.
Upon sobering up a little,
he saw two women by his side,
and was startled, as they were not his own.
He then said:
"At the banquet, the Minister of Works and I exchanged poems,
and he specially ordered these two singing girls to attend me through the night. As for the poem composed in my drunken state,
I have no recollection of it at all."
The next morning,
he wrote a letter of apology and thanks.
Dù also treated him with leniency.
Now, Liǔ Yǔxī, as a court official and regional governor,
lightly offended a high minister of state;
was this not excessive?
The poem says:
"High chignons, cloud-like hair, palace-style makeup,
A song of spring breeze, Dù Wéiniáng.
What the Minister of Works is accustomed to is an ordinary affair,
Yet it breaks the heart of the Governor of Sūzhōu."
Lǐ Féngjí
Prime Minister Lǐ Féngjí
was by nature stubborn, obstinate, deeply suspicious, and greatly jealous,
fond of endangering others,
showing not the slightest trace of shame.
After he became the garrison commander,
Liǔ Yǔxī had a singing girl of exceptional beauty,
known to all.
Relying on his prestige and influence,
Lǐ acted arbitrarily, wielding power and dispensing favors.
Officials serving in the capital
had no time to do anything but seek his favor.
One day,
he secretly plotted to seize her.
He issued an invitation, saying:
"On such-and-such a day, a banquet will be held in the main hall of the Imperial City.
All court worthies and their favored companions
are requested to attend the gathering early."
Those with even slightly pleasing appearances
gathered like clouds on the appointed day.
He ordered the gatekeeper:
"First admit Liǔ's singing girl through the gate."
The entire capital was astonished,
but no one dared speak.
Liǔ could devise no plan,
and in his distress and confusion, he swallowed his voice.
The next day,
he went with several close friends to pay a visit.
But Lǐ met them as usual,
and after a long, leisurely conversation,
