he still said nothing about the reason for the gathering.
Silence reigned among the guests,
they merely exchanged glances.
After the visit concluded,
they bowed once and withdrew.
Liǔ returned sighing in amazement,
helpless,
and so, filled with indignation, he composed four stanzas,
modeled after the "Four Sorrows." They are as follows:
"The jade hairpin rejoined, yet both are without fate,
The fish is in the deep pool, the crane in the sky.
The delighted purple phoenix, cease dancing before the mirror;
The eloquent azure bird, stop carrying letters.
The golden basin, once overturned, cannot gather the water back;
The jade zither bridge,
long cast aside, cannot rejoin the string.
If you pass by the foot of Míwú Mountain,
from afar shed crimson tears upon the remote spring."
"Where does the phoenix, flying to distant trees, perch?
The phoenix, having gained a new nest, has already left its heart behind.
The red wall still flows with a faint, lingering fragrance;
The azure clouds have just broken,
the message sinks deep.
Knowing well the jade is sullied, cast into the mud,
Yet still I strive to earn gold for a bought smile.
Henceforth, the human-shaped stone upon the mountain peak
will bear the deep tear-stains of a husband's form!"
"Where can one go to seek her again?
Though a living separation, it is like death itself.
By the tree where smiles were bought, the flowers are already old;
Under the window where brows were painted, the moon still wanes.
Clouds hide Wū Gorge, voice and face are severed;
The road is cut by the Star Bridge, passage is hard.
Do not wonder that the poem is finished without a drop of tears—
Even if the Eastern Sea were poured out, it would surely run dry!"
"The three mountains unseen, the sea lies deep and still,
How could there be any trace of immortals left to seek?
When the azure bird departed, the cloud-path was cut;
Where Cháng'é returned, the Moon Palace is deep.
Through the gauze window, I wistfully think of spring and remember;
By the study curtain, who pities my solitary chant at night?
I imagine the heavenly mirror that comes by night
shines only to illuminate the hearts of two people."
A Luòyáng Examination Candidate
A certain examination candidate,
a resident of Luòyáng,
happened to become acquainted with a singing girl named Mào Yīng.
Yīng was very young.
Later, when the candidate traveled beyond the river,
he happened to meet her at a drinking party.
He therefore presented her with a poem, saying:
"I recall in the past, passing by the Willow Tower,
Mào Yīng was young and still coy with shyness.
Through the window, I never quite heard her lofty speech;
Before the mirror, I once glimpsed her learning to dress her hair.
After parting in the Central Plains, both have aged;
Coming south again, I see her graceful charm.
Plucking strings, pouring wine, we speak of times gone by.
Scattered azure clouds bring evening melancholy."
The candidate then paid a visit to the military governor,
and lingered as a guest for several months.
The governor treated him with great generosity.
Banquets and drinking were frequent,
and he became quite familiar and playful with the wine stewardess.
One day, he announced his departure.
The governor generously provided gold and silk for his journey,
and again held a farewell banquet.
He secretly left a quatrain for the stewardess, saying:
"Fewer flowers in your hair, fewer tallies laid down,
Beware your companions' jealousy of your charm.
If in the seat a guessing game is played,
Unless it's the Minister, do not nod your head."
He then arranged a dance tune and presented the poem.
The governor took it and read it,
and immediately had someone deliver it to the candidate's location.
Cài Jīng
When Cài Jīng, Military Commissioner of Yōngnán, passed through Yǒngzhōu,
the Prefect of Yǒngzhōu, Zhèng Shǐ, who was Cài's examination cohort,
repeatedly invited him for wine and music.
Among the company was one named Qióng Zhī,
beloved by Zhèng,
and the most beautiful at the feast.
Cài forcibly seized her and took her away.
Zhèng could not prevail against him.
The actions of the Yōngnán Commissioner
were mostly of this kind.
Those who valued virtue and righteousness despised him,
yet he never reformed to the end.
Later, when the Yōngnán Commissioner failed in military command and discipline,
he was executed.
The Wǔchāng Singing Girl
Wéi Chán was inspecting Ēzhōu,
and upon concluding his term,
his guests and subordinates lavishly prepared a farewell feast.
Chán then wrote a line from the *Wén Xuǎn*:
"No sorrow is greater than the sorrow of parting in life,
Climbing mountains, facing waters, I send you on your return."
He handed brush and paper to his guests and attendants,
asking them to continue the verse.
Those seated looked on wistfully,
but none could compose a suitable line.
After a moment's hesitation,
a singing girl rose with tears in her eyes and said:
"I have little talent,
and dare not stain the brush,
but I would like to improvise two lines orally."
Wéi was greatly astonished,
and told her to speak them at once:
"Wǔchāng's newly planted willows are without limit,
But I see no willow catkins flying to meet my face."
None among the guests failed to praise and sigh in admiration.
Wéi had her sing it as a "Willow Branch Song,"
and they parted in great joy.
He gave her several bolts of silk,
which she accepted.
The next day, they departed together in the same carriage.
Wéi Bǎoqú
Wéi Bǎoqú once visited a friend,
and just as he was sitting down,
Lǐ Jù, who had newly passed the imperial examination,
also arrived afterward.
Because Wéi Bǎoqú had arrived first,
he hid behind the curtain.
After entering, Lǐ Jù said:
"Is there a guest?"
The friend replied:
"It is Scholar Wéi Bǎoqú.
May he come out?"
Lǐ Jù, having newly passed the examination,
was very proud of himself,
and said slowly:
"What harm is there in him coming out?"
Wéi Bǎoqú ultimately did not come out.
Later, when Wéi Bǎoqú married the princess and became chancellor,
Lǐ Pín was stationed in Qíxià,
and Lǐ Jù, who had previously served in Shānběi, was appointed there.
Earlier, after Wéi Bǎoqú had passed the examination,
Dúgū Yún was appointed to Dōngchuān,
and recruited him to serve in his staff.
Among the courtesan musicians, there was one who assisted with drinking,
and Deputy Official Lǐ Jiǎ was fond of her.
At the time, as she was about to be sent elsewhere,
he made a private arrangement with her,
planning to take her as his own later.
When Wéi Bǎoqú arrived,
he was unaware of this,
and pleaded with Dúgū Yún,
asking to remove her from the courtesan registry.
When Lǐ Jiǎ arrived,
he was extremely displeased,
and at every banquet,
he would insult Wéi Bǎoqú with his words.
Wéi Bǎoqú could not tolerate this,
so he took the courtesan and left.
Lǐ Jiǎ became even angrier,
and repeatedly complained to Dúgū Yún.
Dúgū Yún had no choice,
and ordered a swift dispatch to recall her.
Not long after,
an official dispatch summoned Wéi Bǎoqú to the capital,
as he was to marry Princess Tóngchāng.
Lǐ Jiǎ was deeply afraid of him.
A few days later,
Wéi Bǎoqú returned to the Hanlin Academy,
and when Lǐ Jiǎ heard this,
he died on the spot.
Cáo Shēng
When Attendant-in-Ordinary Lú Pī
was governing Lújiāng,
the chancellor entrusted him with a certain Cáo Shēng,
ordering him to be appointed to a prefectural post,
so he had no choice but to comply.
Cáo Shēng was fond of a courtesan named Dānxiá,
but Lú Pī discouraged him and did not permit it.
Once, while bidding farewell to a court official at a short pavilion,
Cáo Shēng presented a poem:
"Bidding farewell to guests at the Jade-Worshiping Pavilion, busy,
At this moment, loneliness and regret stir thoughts of home.
Recalling the past affair of the severed cap tassel,
How could I weep through the long night at the vermilion gate?"
Lú Pī composed a long verse,
harmonizing with it and encouraging him:
"The mulberry finches dart, the hundred-tongues busy,
Hearing music at the ancestral pavilion doubles thoughts of home.
Before the cup, regrets shame the lowly official,
On the mat, no loneliness with lovely adornments.
Do not let wild flowers cloud your vision,
Seek the true principle to steady your heart's king.
When will the wandering bees cease their gathering?
Only fear that many words will discuss shortcomings."
Luó Qiú
Luó Qiú was richly gifted in literary talent,
and was equally famous with his clansmen Luó Yǐn and Luó Yè.
During the Xiántōng and Qiánfú eras,
they were known as the "Three Luós."
After the chaos of the Guāngmíng Gēngzǐ year,
he went to serve Lǐ Xiàogōng in Fūzhōu.
Among the courtesan musicians was one named Hóng'ér,
skilled in music,
who was often favored by the deputy commander.
Once, when the deputy commander was visiting a neighboring region,
Luó Qiú requested Hóng'ér to sing,
and gave her silk as a gift.
Lǐ Xiàogōng, because she was favored by the deputy commander,
did not allow her to accept it.
Luó Qiú became angry,
shook his sleeves, and stood up.
The next morning,
he killed Hóng'ér with his own hands.
Later, thinking of her,
he composed a hundred quatrains,
titled "Poems Comparing to Hóng'ér,"
which became widely popular at the time.
Xú Yuèyīng
In the region between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
there was one named Xú Yuèyīng,
a famous courtesan.
Her poem bidding farewell to someone reads:
"Melancholy, all things in this world go awry,
Two went together, one returns alone.
How I detest the water in the Píngwàng Pavilion—
How can it bear to reflect mandarin ducks flying apart?"
Another poem reads:
"Tears on the pillow and rain before the steps,
Through the window, they drip until dawn."
She also had a poetry collection.
The young masters of the Xú family in Jīnlíng
favored a courtesan,
and when she died, they cremated her.
Xú Yuèyīng attended the funeral
and said to Master Xú:
"This lady was charming all her life,
even in death, she carries flames."
It was praised as witty
and playful at the time.
The Face Powder Girl
There was a very wealthy family
with only one son,
who was excessively indulged.
While wandering the market,
he saw a beautiful girl
selling foreign face powder
and fell in love with her.
Having no way to express his feelings,
he pretended to buy powder,
going to the market daily.
He would take the powder and leave.
At first, he said nothing,
but as time passed,
the girl grew deeply suspicious.
The next day, when he came again,
she asked:
"You buy this powder—
what do you intend to do with it?"
He replied:
"I admire and adore you,
but dare not express it directly.
Yet I always wish to see you,
so I use this as a pretext to gaze upon your beauty."
The girl, moved and melancholic,
then agreed to a secret rendezvous,
set for the following evening.
That night,
he rested in the main hall,
awaiting the girl's arrival.
At dusk, she indeed came,
and the young man, overwhelmed with joy,
took her arm and said:
"My long-held wish is finally fulfilled here!"
In his excitement, he suddenly died.
The girl, terrified and not knowing what to do,
fled,
and returned to the powder shop the next day.
By mealtime,
his parents wondered why he had not risen,
and upon going to check,
found him already dead.
When preparing for the funeral,
they opened his chests
and saw over a hundred packets of foreign face powder,
piled up in various sizes.
His mother said:
"The one who killed my son
must be linked to this powder."
She went to the market and bought foreign face powder from every shop,
until she came to this girl's shop.
Comparing the packets,
the handiwork matched the earlier ones.
She seized the girl and demanded:
"Why did you kill my son?"
The girl, hearing this, sobbed
and truthfully explained everything.
The parents did not believe her,
so they brought the case to the authorities.
The girl said:
"How could I fear death now?
I only beg to see his body one last time and express my grief."
The county magistrate permitted it.
She went straight to the body,
caressed it, and wept bitterly, saying:
"How unfortunate it has come to this!
If your soul in death has awareness,
what regret would remain?"
The young man suddenly revived,
and recounted the whole story.
They then became husband and wife,
and their descendants flourished.
Cuī Hù
Cuī Hù of Bólíng,
possessed exceptional talent and beauty,
yet was aloof and unsociable.
He passed the imperial examination.
On the Qingming Festival,
he wandered alone south of the capital city
and came upon a villager’s estate.
Enclosed within an acre of land,
it was thick with flowers, trees, and grass,
and as quiet as if no one was there.
He knocked on the gate for a long time.
A young woman peeked at him through a crack in the gate
and asked:
"Who is it?"
Cuī gave his name in reply
and said:
"I am wandering alone in search of spring,
and, thirsty from wine, I seek a drink."
The woman went inside
and brought a cup of water.
She opened the gate
and set out a stool, inviting him to sit.
She stood alone, leaning against a slanting branch of a small peach tree,
her demeanor exceptionally warm.
Her enchanting posture and charming manner
were overflowing with grace.
Cuī tried to engage her in conversation,
but she did not reply.
They simply gazed at each other for a long time.
When Cuī took his leave,
she saw him to the gate,
then went inside, seemingly unable to contain her emotions.
Cuī also looked back longingly as he departed.
After that, he never went back.
When the Qingming Festival arrived the following year,
he suddenly thought of her.
Unable to suppress his feelings,
he went straight there to find her.
The gate and courtyard were as before,
but they were locked shut.
Cuī then inscribed a poem on the left leaf of the gate:
"On this day last year, within this very gate,
A face and peach blossoms mirrored each other’s blush.
Where has that lovely face now gone?
The peach blossoms still smile in the spring breeze."
A few days later,
he happened to go south of the capital city again
and once more went to look for her.
Hearing crying from inside,
he knocked and inquired.
An old man came out and said:
"Are you not Cuī Hù?"
He replied:
"I am."
The old man cried out again:
"You have killed my daughter!"
Cuī was shocked and dismayed,
not knowing how to respond.
The father said:
"My daughter, of marriageable age and well-educated,
was not yet betrothed.
Since last year,
she had often been absent-minded, as if she had lost something.
The other day, I went out with her,
and when we returned,
we saw writing on the left leaf of the gate.
After reading it,
she fell ill upon entering the house
and, refusing to eat for several days, died.
I am old,
and she was my only daughter.
The reason I had not married her off
was to find a gentleman
to whom I could entrust my own future.
Now she has unfortunately perished.
Is it not you who killed her?"
He then clung to Cuī and wept bitterly.
Cuī was also deeply moved and grieved.
He asked to go inside to mourn her.
She lay as if in life upon the bed.
Cuī lifted her head and rested it upon his lap,
weeping and praying:
"I am here!"
After a moment, she opened her eyes.
Half a day later, she revived.
The old man was overjoyed
and subsequently gave his daughter to Cuī in marriage.
Wǔ Yánsì
During the Zǎichū era of Empress Wǔ of Táng,
the Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, Qiáo Zhīzhī,
had a maidservant named Yǎoniáng,
whose artistry and beauty were unmatched at the time.
Zhīzhī doted on her
and, for her sake, did not marry.
Wǔ Yánsì heard of her
and demanded to see her once.
His power was irresistible.
Once he saw her, he kept her,
with no intention of returning her.
Zhīzhī, in anguish and indignation, fell ill.
He then composed a poem,
wrote it on fine silk,
heavily bribed the gatekeeper,
and had it delivered to Yǎoniáng.
Yǎoniáng, upon receiving the poem, wept bitterly.
She tied three copies to her sash
and threw herself into a well, dying.
When Yánsì saw the poem,
he had cruel officials falsely accuse Zhīzhī,
ruining his family.
Zhīzhī’s poem reads:
"The Shí family’s Jīngǔ Garden favored new tunes;
Ten hú of bright pearls bought a graceful beauty.
In days past, you pitied and pledged yourself to me.
Now your song and dance please another’s heart.
Your family’s towers and pavilions were never hard to scale;
You gladly lent your song and dance for others to admire.
Wealth, power, and might are not rightfully yours;
Arrogance, luxury, and force intrude without cause.
Parting from you, leaving you—in the end, I cannot bear it.
In vain, I cover my sleeves, grieving for the fair one.
A lifetime’s parting in a lofty tower;
A generation’s beauty is spent for you."
The Kāiyuán Garment-Making Maiden
During the Kāiyuán era,
winter garments for border troops were issued,
made within the palace.
A soldier found a poem inside his short robe:
"A guest campaigning on the sandy battlefield,
How do you bear the bitter cold in sleep?
This battle robe, made by my own hand,
Who knows into whose possession it will fall?
With intent, I added extra thread;
With feeling, I added more wadding.
This life of mine has already passed;
Let us form a bond in the next life."
The soldier reported the poem to his commander,
who presented it upward.
Emperor Xuánzōng ordered the poem shown throughout the Six Palaces,
saying:
"Let the one who wrote it not hide;
I will not punish you."
One palace maiden confessed, saying she deserved ten thousand deaths.
Xuánzōng deeply pitied her
and married her to the soldier who received the poem.
He then said to her:
"I shall form a bond for you in this present life."
The border troops were all moved to tears.
Wéi Gāo
Wéi Gāo, the military governor of Xīchuān in the Táng dynasty, traveled to Jiāngxià in his youth,
and stayed at the residence of Prefect Jiāng.
Prefect Jiāng had a young son named Jīngbǎo,
who had already studied two Confucian classics.
Although he addressed Wéi as an elder brother,
he served him with the respect
due to a father.
Jīngbǎo had a young maidservant named Yùxiāo,
only ten years old,
who was often ordered to attend to Brother Wéi.
Yùxiāo also diligently served him.
Two years later,
Prefect Jiāng went to the capital to seek an official post,
but his family did not accompany him.
Wéi then moved to reside at the Tóutuó Temple.
Jīngbǎo would occasionally send Yùxiāo there to serve him.
As Yùxiāo grew older,
affection developed between them.
At that time, the Surveillance Commissioner Chén Chángshì received a letter from Wéi's uncle, which said:
"My nephew Gāo has been staying in your esteemed region for a long time,
and I earnestly hope you will send him back to visit his family."
The commissioner opened the letter,
provided him with a boat and supplies,
and, fearing he might linger,
requested not to meet him.
When the boat reached the riverbank,
he ordered the boatmen to hasten the departure.
Wéi, with tearful eyes in the dusk,
wrote a letter to bid farewell to Jīngbǎo.
Jīngbǎo arrived in an instant with Yùxiāo,
both sorrowful and joyful.
Jīngbǎo ordered the maidservant to accompany and serve him.
However, as Wéi had been away from his family for a long time,
he dared not take her with him,
and firmly declined.
He then made a promise with her:
"In as little as five years,
or at most seven,
I will come for Yùxiāo."
He left her a jade ring
and a poem as a parting gift.
When five years passed without his return,
Yùxiāo prayed silently at the Yīngwǔ Zhōu.
After another two years,
in the spring of the eighth year,
Yùxiāo sighed and said:
"The young master of the Wéi family,
it has been seven years since we parted,
and he is not coming!"
She then refused to eat and passed away.
The Jiāng family, moved by her fidelity,
placed the jade ring on her middle finger and buried it with her.
Later, when Wéi governed Shǔ,
three days after assuming his post,
he reviewed the cases of prisoners,
redressing wrongful convictions.
Those detained, whether for minor or major offenses,
numbered nearly three hundred.
Among them was one group
bound by five sets of shackles,
who stole glances at the courtroom
and whispered among themselves:
"The commander is the Brother Wéi from back then."
One then raised his voice and said:
"Commander, commander,
do you remember Jīngbǎo of the Jiāng family?"
Wéi replied:
"I remember him well."
"That is me!"
Wéi asked:
"What crime have you committed to be so heavily bound?"
He answered:
"After parting from you,
I soon passed the imperial examination in the míngjīng category,
and was appointed magistrate of Qīngchéng County.
However, my family accidentally burned down the government office, including the official seals and documents."
Wéi said:
"A crime committed by family members
is certainly not your fault."
He immediately cleared his name,
restored his official rank,
and recommended him for the post of prefect of Méizhōu.
The imperial decree was issued,
but before allowing him to assume the post,
Wéi had him placed under supervision.
He honored him with the crimson official robe
and kept him in his advisory staff.
At that time, following a major military campaign,
affairs were in disarray and numerous.
Only after several months
did Wéi ask about Yùxiāo's whereabouts.
Jiāng replied:
"On the evening of your departure by boat,
you made a promise with her.
The agreed period was seven years.
When you did not return after the time had passed,
she refused to eat and died."
He then recited the poem "Farewell Gift of the Jade Ring":
"The yellow sparrow brought it several springs ago,
left as a parting gift for the fair lady.
No letters have come from the Long River,
so I send my longing dreams into Qín."
Upon hearing this,
Wéi felt even more sorrowful.
He extensively sponsored the copying of scriptures and the creation of Buddhist statues
to repay his longstanding feelings,
yet his longing and thoughts
had no way to reunite them.
At that time, there was a hermit named Zǔ,
who possessed the arts of Shào Wēng,
capable of making the deceased appear to the living.
He only required the governor to observe a seven-day fast.
On a clear night,
Yùxiāo appeared.
She expressed her gratitude, saying:
"Thanks to the merit from your copying of scriptures and creation of statues,
I will be reborn in ten days.
Thirteen years from now,
I will again serve as your concubine,
to repay your great kindness."
Before leaving, she smiled and said:
"Men are fickle,
making life and death a separation!"
Later, due to his achievements in Lǒngyòu,
Wéi served until the end of Emperor Dézōng's reign,
governing Shǔ without interruption.
Over the years, he was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng,
with the entire realm responding to his authority,
and even Lú and Bó submitting willingly.
On his birthday,
the military governors sent congratulations,
all presenting rare treasures.
Only Lú Bāzuò of Dōngchuān sent a singing girl,
not yet of age,
also named Yùxiāo.
When Wéi saw her,
she was truly the Yùxiāo of the Jiāng family.
On her middle finger, a flesh ring protruded faintly,
no different from the jade ring left at parting.
Wéi sighed and said:
"Now I understand the distinction between life and death,
as one departs and another arrives.
Yùxiāo's words
have indeed been verified."
Ōuyáng Zhān
Ōuyáng Zhān, styled Xíngzhōu,
was a native of Jìnjiāng in Quánzhōu.
In his youth, he was capable of composing literary works,
his talents vast and boundless as if bestowed by heaven.
In the Zhēnyuán era,
he passed the imperial examination,
completed the official selection process,
and traveled to Tàiyuán.
Among the courtesan registers,
he found one he favored,
and their affection was mutual.
Upon his departure,
he made a vow to her, saying:
"When I reach the capital,
I will send for you."
With tears, they parted,
and he left her a poem:
"As my horse trots away, the distance grows,
I turn to see the long road's dust.
The high city walls are no longer in sight,
much less the one within the city.
My heart is unwilling to depart,
and staying would bring much sorrow.
From Wǔyuán northeast to Jìn,
a thousand li southwest to Qín.
One shoe never leaves the door,
one carriage never stops its wheels.
Like drifting duckweed or a tied gourd,
we shall reunite sooner or later."
Soon after, he was appointed as an assistant instructor at the Imperial Academy's Four Gates School,
and resided in the capital.
The courtesan missed him incessantly,
and after a year, fell gravely ill.
She adorned herself solemnly,
cut off her hair, placed it in a box,
and said to her younger sister:
"I am about to die.
If Ōuyáng sends a messenger,
this can serve as proof."
She also left a poem:
"Since we parted, my beauty has faded,
half from longing, half from resentment.
If you wish to see my former cloud-like coiffure,
open the gilded chest for me."
With these final words, she passed away.
When Ōuyáng's messenger arrived,
her younger sister followed her instructions,
took the box directly to the capital,
and recounted everything.
Ōuyáng opened the box and read the message,
then saw her poem,
and died of grief.
Thus, Mèng Jiǎn composed a poem mourning him,
with a preface stating:
"Among the talents of Mǐnyuè,
Ōuyáng stands alone,
He passed the examination through literary skill,
and began his official career.
He received a salary from the Imperial Academy,
assisted in its teachings,
and achieved commendable results.
In the year Jǐmǎo of the Zhēnyuán era of our Táng dynasty,
he submitted a memorial to the chancellor's office,
discussing important matters,
with elegant style,
and sincere, straightforward language.
At the time, military campaigns were underway in the east,
and the authorities had no time to acknowledge or recommend him.
After a while,
weary of his travels in Tàiyuán,
he returned to the imperial capital,
and died while serving at Língtái.
Alas!
Born into poverty,
for the sake of reputation,
he focused on diligence and frugality,
and knew nothing of sensual pleasures.
Upon taking office,
he was unaware of the temptations of beautiful women.
When he first arrived in Tàiyuán,
he attended a banquet hosted by a general,
where a courtesan,
a peerless beauty of the north,
repeatedly glanced at him,
and he was captivated.
He stayed for months, enjoying her company,
believing that the joys of romance
were all here.
Later, when he headed south,
the courtesan asked to accompany him.
He said:
'Under the gaze of many eyes,
one cannot be without fear.'
He declined,
but promised to send for her upon reaching the capital.
She agreed,
and he departed.
However, due to difficulties,
he could not keep his promise.
After the deadline passed,
he dispatched a messenger with a carriage,
to secretly bring her.
But she, consumed by longing, had fallen ill,
beyond recovery.
On the eve of her death,
she cut off her cloud-like hair,
and told her maid:
'My beloved will surely come for me,
give him this as a token.'
The messenger arrived and received it,
returning with an empty carriage,
and presented the hair to Ōuyáng.
Overwhelmed with grief and regret,
within ten days, he too passed away.
This is the Ōuyáng Zhān mentioned
in Hán Tuìzhī's letter to Hé Fān.
Hé nán's Mù Xuándào visited me,
often lamenting this story.
Alas!
The depth of love between a man and a woman
is such
that they would die for it,
a truth undeniable.
Generally, if one acts with restraint,
and resolutely,
not being swayed by beauty,
would such a thing happen?
The ancient ballad 'Huàshān Jī'
and 'Lújiāng Xiǎolì' from 'Yùtái Xīnyǒng'
tell of lovers dying for each other,
similar to this.
In my leisure,
I composed a poem to continue the tale:
A traveler not heading north,
rode his horse to Tàiyuán.
In Tàiyuán lived a beauty,
her divine charm outshone the clouds.
At the banquet, her glances turned,
her radiant gaze fixed on her lord.
Her lord's heart was stirred,
and that day they became lovers.
Their pledge was not mere words,
their vow bound them like the green hills.
In life or death, unchanged,
sincere and without discord.
He was a scholar of the Imperial Academy,
she belonged to the northern official's household.
At midnight, she wished to follow,
but the fortified city barred the way.
By day, she longed to live together,
but he feared the judgment of others.
Suddenly, like the waters of Lǒngtóu,
they sat, east
and west apart.
Startled, their hearts tied in knots,
tears fell, dimming both eyes.
He returned to the capital,
planning to fetch her later.
Their promise was broken by delay,
her sorrow had already taken hold.
Her high coiffure like a yellow oriole,
her delicate hair like jade cicadas.
With her own slender hands,
she cut it off with scissors.
Entrusting her tender feelings to her maid,
to deliver it to her beloved.
When her beloved's messenger came,
the maid stepped forward.
Wiping tears, she took the token,
earnestly begging it be delivered.
Sealed and sent to her lord,
hoping to comfort him beyond the grave.
The messenger returned with the news,
slowly, filled with grief.
Ōuyáng, eager for news,
rushed barefoot to greet him.
Kneeling, he listened, but before it ended,
shocked and wounded, tears streamed down.
He neither ate nor drank,
his heart broken in countless ways.
His spirit emptied overnight,
his vitality gone by dawn.
Alas, his noble spirit,
scattered, returned to the origin.
Though their lives were short and parted,
the long night holds no barriers.
Their souls will eventually reunite,
like two swords entwined.
Had the gentleman been more open-minded,
how could a charming smile have undone him?
Guarding oneself with austerity,
once gone, how to return?
Let later generations not be infatuated,
for infatuation loses one's true self.
Xuē Yǐliáo,
during the Huìchāng era, served as Left Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent.
He was appointed as the envoy to bestow imperial honors and gifts upon Xīnluó,
and set sail from Qīngzhōu.
The ship was repeatedly hindered by fierce winds and rain.
Upon reaching Dēngzhōu,
it was driven back,
returning to anchor at Qīngzhōu,
where they remained for a year, relying on postal stations.
The military governor Wū Hànzhēn treated him with exceptional hospitality.
Among the registered courtesan-entertainers was one named Duàn Dōngměi,
for whom Xuē developed deep affection.
The regional commander arranged for her to stay at the postal station.
On the day of Xuē's departure that spring,
at the farewell banquet, he choked with sobs and shed tears,
and Dōngměi did the same.
Thereupon, he left a poem on the banquet mat, which read:
"The mother's peach blossoms are just like brocade,
The noble's grass is precisely like mist.
No need to gaze further toward the vast sea;
Melancholy, our joyous love has lasted just a year."
Xuē arrived in the foreign land,
but before he could perform the ceremony of bestowing honors,
the tassels on his envoy's banner made sounds day and night.
Soon he fell ill,
and said to his assistant judge Miáo Jiǎ:
"Why does Dōngměi so frequently appear in my dreams?"
A few days later, he died.
Miáo acted as the chief envoy to perform the ceremony.
Xuē's coffin was soon returned,
and when it reached Qīngzhōu,
Dōngměi requested leave and went to the postal station.
Dressed in plain mourning clothes, she performed the libation,
wailed in grief while stroking the coffin,
and died from one burst of overwhelming sorrow.
Their feelings resonated with each other,
making it quite a remarkable tale.
Róng Yù
When Hán Jìngōng Huǎng governed Zhèxī,
Róng Yù served as a prefect within his jurisdiction.
In the commandery was a courtesan who served wine,
skilled in singing,
and of graceful and exquisite beauty.
Yù was deeply attached to her.
The music officer of Zhèxī, hearing of her talents,
reported to Huǎng,
who summoned her and registered her among his entertainers.
Yù did not dare to keep her,
but soon, on the lake, he composed a song lyric to present to her,
and said:
"When you arrive there and are ordered to sing,
you must first sing this lyric."
After she arrived,
Hán held a banquet,
personally raised his cup,
and ordered her to sing to send off the guests.
Thereupon, she sang Róng's lyric.
When the song ended,
Hán asked:
"Did Prefect Róng entrust his feelings to you?"
The courtesan, startled, stood up and said:
"Yes."
Tears fell as she spoke.
Hán ordered her to change clothes and await further instructions.
Those at the banquet felt anxious and concerned for her.
Hán summoned the music officer and reprimanded him:
"Prefect Róng is a renowned scholar.
He had affection for a commandery courtesan.
Why did you not know this and summoned her to be placed here,
causing me to commit this fault!"
He then had him flogged ten times.
He ordered that the courtesan be given a hundred bolts of fine silk
and sent back to him immediately.
The lyric reads:
"Farewell to the lakeside pavilion in the spring breeze,
Willow twigs and vine tendrils bind the heart's feelings.
The oriole, long dwelling here, is wholly attached;
About to part, it frequently sings four or five notes."
Wéi Táofú
During the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era,
in the capital region, there was a Wéi Gǔn,
who had a servant named Táofú.
Whenever they went on campaigns,
he displayed courage and strength.
Gǔn rose to the position of Vice Commander of the Left Guard.
Considering Táofú had long served him,
he freed him to become a commoner.
Fú's family had a yellow cow,
which he slaughtered and offered as a gift,
and then asked Gǔn to bestow a surname upon him.
Gǔn said:
"Simply take my surname and become Wéi."
Fú kowtowed and said:
"I dare not share the same surname as my master."
Gǔn said:
"You just follow this.
There is a profound meaning to it."
Hence, to this day, there are those known as "Yellow Calf Wéi,"
and Empress Wéi (Wéi Shùrén) was their descendant.
The reason for not allowing a different surname
was likely due to the concern that over many years and generations,
descendants might intermarry with the Wéi clan.
This was his intention.
Lǐ Jìng
Lǐ Jìng
was originally a servant of Xiàhóu Zī.
Zī long suffered setbacks in the examinations,
and Jìng endured all the hardships of poverty.
Sometimes, those of his own kind would persuade him:
"The officials who serve the court nowadays,
when at court become influential eunuchs,
and when sent out become imperial envoys.
Wherever they go,
they stir up storms.
Why don't you follow one of them?
Instead, you diligently serve a poor scholar—
what prospects for advancement are there?
Even if not that,
serving a high-ranking official
would mean ample clothing and food,
and success in every endeavor."
Jìng laughed and said:
"When my master passes the examinations,
he is still planning to become the military commissioner of Xīchuān."
Everyone ridiculed and laughed at him.
At that time, Zī overheard his words from behind a wall.
After more than ten years,
Zī left the Secretariat to take up a governorship in Chéngdū.
Before his departure,
some tried to entrust him with recommendations for official posts,
but he agreed to none.
Upon assuming his post,
he appointed Jìng to manage memorials and communications,
and Jìng became extremely busy and burdened.
Those who had previously laughed at him
mostly came to submit to Jìng.
Earlier, when Zī had not yet achieved success,
he struggled through hardships,
riding a lame donkey.
Once, for no reason, it fell into a well.
Whether at the gates of court officials
or at inns and lodgings,
he often faced difficulties and conflicts, so people of the time called him "the inauspicious scholar."
Yet he eventually rose to become a general and minister.
Wǔ Gōnggàn
Wǔ Gōnggàn often served the scholar Kuǎi Xīyì,
for over ten years,
exceptionally diligent and capable.
When Xīyì passed the examinations,
Gàn excused himself due to having parents at home,
and begged to return to care for them.
Xīyì tried to detain him but could not keep him.
Admiring his loyalty and filial piety,
he composed a poem to see him off,
which roughly said:
"On perilous mountains, you never lagged behind my horse;
Awakening from wine, I'd often find you by my bed."
Friends pooled silk to give him for the journey,
and all composed matching verses.
Wú Xínglǔ
Shàngshū Wú Xínglǔ
was from Péngzhōu.
In his youth, he served the eunuch official Xīmén Sīgōng,
being cautious and respectful.
Every night,
he would often warm the chamber pot and present it to him,
deeply winning the favor of the eunuch commander.
One day, while washing the eunuch commander’s feet,
the commander showed him the lines on the sole of his foot, saying:
"With lines like these,
how could one not become a military commissioner?"
Xínglǔ bowed and replied:
"This is also unreliable."
Xīmén asked:
"Why?"
Lǔ said:
"If that were the case,
I also have them,
so why am I always performing servant duties?"
He then took off his shoe and showed it.
Xīmén sighed in admiration,
and said to him:
"If you are loyal and filial,
I will help you succeed."
Afterward, he was given a military post,
and appointed as Prefect of Péngzhōu.
Lú Dān recommended him as Xīchuān March Field Officer;
he achieved merit in defending against the barbarians,
and served successively as military governor of Dōngchuān and Shānnán.
When Xínglǔ was in Dōngchuān,
Lì Túnán was Deputy Commissioner of Xīchuān,
and left office when his administration ended.
Xínglǔ wanted to recruit him.
Lì had always looked down on Xínglǔ;
hearing this, he laughed loudly and said:
"How could I shave my head and face,
to serve a mere soldier!"
He rode a horse from the official compound,
did not return to his private residence,
and went straight out the northern gate.
His family hastily packed and chased after him.
Zhāng Yún was Deputy Prefect of Chéngdū;
he often spoke carelessly,
and was poisoned to death by Xínglǔ.
Lǐ Gǔ
Lú Sù, son of Lú Jūn,
was upright and simple, possessing his father’s character.
In the early Guānghuà era,
he passed the imperial examination at the imperial temporary seat in Huázhōu.
Since the great rebels invaded the capital, for twenty years,
officials had all become impoverished.
When Sù first passed the examination,
suddenly a man named Lǐ Gǔ came to him,
offering to work as a servant.
Gǔ was skilled at managing profits;
in his spare time, he often even provided funds to Sù,
and beyond that, never concerned himself with his own needs.
Sù had an old estate in Nányáng,
and often sent Gǔ to collect rent.
Gǔ always arrived on time,
traveling back and forth over ten miles,
yet never embezzled a single coin.
After Sù passed the examination,
Gǔ continued to serve diligently as before.
When the spring affairs were completed,
Gǔ immediately took his leave.
Pěng Yàn
Pěng Yàn
was a houseboy of Péi Zhìdé.
His mother was named Chūn Hóng,
who was paired with the groom Gāo Fán and gave birth to him.
When he was one year old,
during a summer day while bathing him,
he was left naked lying in the corridor;
a short-legged dog named Qīnghuā
suddenly came.
It bit off the child’s genitals and ate them.
Chūn Hóng heard the crying,
hurried over in panic,
and found blood flowing all over the mat.
Thanks to Zhìdé having good medicine to apply,
after a hundred days, he recovered as before.
The next summer,
while sleeping in the front porch,
Qīnghuā waited for a gap when people were absent and came again,
and ate the remaining testicles completely.
He writhed on the ground and died,
but again the previous medicine was applied to him,
and after healing, he became a eunuch.
He was given the name Pěng Yàn,
and entrusted with the duties of a palace attendant.
By the bǐngwǔ year of Guāngqì,
he was over ten years old.
Péi sent him out on an errand,
and he encountered bandits in the outskirts of Zhèng and was killed.
Alas.
Pěng Yàn was just a young boy,
twice mutilated yet unharmed,
while Péi went out once and did not return—
what is the reason for this?
Pěng Jiàn
The Guō family of Xiányáng
was a wealthy household,
with many servants and maids.
Among them was a servant,
named Pěng Jiàn,
who did not engage in music,
but often gazed at water and clouds,
not obeying commands,
and though often whipped and beaten,
always remained contrary.
One day,
he suddenly composed a poem,
which made his master even angrier.
The poem said:
"A blue bird carries cattail and chrysanthemum,
flying up to the golden well rail.
The beauty fears startling it away,
daring not roll up the curtain to look."
Scholars heard of it and vied to see it,
considering it harmonious and lyrical.
His master then became somewhat tolerant.
Another poem, "On the Peony in the Back Hall," said:
"A kind of fragrance emerges from the back pavilion,
yet loses to peach and plum in gaining fine fame.
Who can speak to the celestial beings,
to transplant its roots near the highest purity?"
Pěng Jiàn privately told guests:
"I would rather be a ghost among the barbarians,
than be ashamed as a common servant."
Later, when about to flee,
he left another poem:
"Farewell, Fourth Gentleman Guō,
at departure, I cannot bid farewell.
The dawn water-clock stirs a parting heart,
the light carriage braves the remnant snow.
About to step out the master’s gate,
tears fall, silently sobbing.
Ten thousand miles separate the mountain passes,
my heart yearns for the Han moon."
Guī Qín
Shěn Xún had a favored concubine,
whom his wife resented,
and privately gave to the eunuch attendant Guī Qín,
which Xún could not prevent.
Afterward, the concubine still served within,
and Guī Qín felt ashamed of this,
so he took a blade, waited for an opportunity,
and killed Xún and his wife at the Zhāoyí Commissioner’s office.
That evening,
Xún had hosted a banquet for friends in his office,
and had sung a command as a drinking game:
"Do not strike the geese coming from the south,
let them fly northward.
If striking, strike both together,
do not let the pair be separated."
Upon returning home, husband and wife both met their fate.
This was in the fourth year of the Xiantong era.
Duàn Zhāng,
in the tenth year of the Xiántōng era,
served the Presented Scholar Sīkōng Tú.
Initially,
Zhāng worked as a hired driver,
no different from other servants.
That summer,
Tú had long returned to Pú,
and due to lack of resources,
was unable to provide adequate support,
so Zhāng took his leave and departed.
In the Gēngzǐ year of the Guǎngmíng era,
the twelfth month of winter,
bandits invaded the capital,
and Tú was residing in Chóngyì Lǐ.
On the ninth day,
from the home of the local magnate Yáng Qióng,
he moved to hide under the Chángpíng granary.
As he was about to leave,
a group of bandits arrived one after another.
One of them, holding a spear and blocking the door,
stared intently for a long time,
then approached and took Tú’s hand, saying:
"I am Duàn Zhāng,
captured and brought here,
unable to free myself.
Yet I remember your kindness in nurturing me,
and now we meet—
this is heaven’s will!
My master is General Zhāng,
who delights in treating scholars with respect,
and fortunately, he is away elsewhere,
so there will surely be no harm.
Thus, you can certainly avoid violence and injustice."
Tú vowed not to submit to humiliation,
and Zhāng, filled with sorrow, shed tears,
guided him to the main road,
and then parted ways.
Tú thus managed to flee through the Kāiyuǎn Gate under cover of night.
Upon reaching the Xiányáng Bridge,
he again encountered the posted official Hán Jūn, who aided him,
and so arrived at Hù Xiàn,
thereby reaching the imperial camp.
Shàngqīng
In the third month of spring in the rénshēn year of the Zhēnyuán era,
Chancellor Dòu Shēn was residing at his mansion in the Guāngfú Ward.
On a moonlit night,
he was strolling leisurely in the central courtyard.
A favored maidservant named Shàngqīng,
then said:
"I have something to report,
but I must reach the main hall before I dare speak."
Dòu hurriedly went up to the hall,
and Shàngqīng said:
"There is a person in the courtyard tree,
and I fear he may startle you, sir.
I beg you to be cautious and avoid him."
Dòu said:
"Lù Zhì has long desired to seize my power and position.
Now that there is someone in the courtyard tree,
it means my calamity is about to arrive.
Moreover, whether this matter is reported or not,
I will suffer misfortune,
and will surely be exiled and die on the road.
You are one of a kind among your peers,
but when I die and my family is ruined,
you will certainly become a palace maid.
If the Imperial Majesty should inquire,
please speak well on my behalf."
Shàngqīng wept and said:
"If it truly comes to that,
I will follow you in life and death."
Dòu descended the steps and shouted loudly:
"The person in the tree must have been sent by Lù Zhì.
If you can spare this old man's life,
how dare I not repay you generously?"
The person in the tree responded and climbed down.
It was a man wearing coarse mourning garments.
He said:
"My family has suffered a great bereavement,
and we are extremely poor,
unable to afford funeral rites.
I have heard that Your Excellency is sincere and aids others,
so I came by night to seek help,
and I beg Your Excellency not to take offense."
Dòu said:
"All I have
is a thousand bolts of silk from my official stipend.
I had intended to use it for repairing my family temple,
but today I can give it to you."
The man in mourning bowed in thanks,
and Dòu returned the courtesy appropriately.
The man then said:
"I shall now take my leave of Your Excellency.
Please have your attendants bundle the silk you bestowed,
and throw it over the wall.
I will wait for it in the street beforehand."
Dòu complied with his request.
He ordered his servants to watch until the man had been gone for a long time,
before he dared return to sleep.
The next day,
the Commander of the Capital Guards first reported the matter,
and then Dòu, in his turn,
also reported it.
Emperor Dézōng said sternly:
"You have been colluding with military governors,
harboring assassins and knights-errant.
Your position is as high as the Three Dukes,
what more do you desire?"
Dòu kowtowed and said:
"Your subject rose from humble beginnings as a minor clerk,
and my official rank has reached great honor,
all due to Your Majesty's encouragement and promotion.
I truly did not rely on others.
Now that I have unfortunately come to this,
it must be the work of my enemies.
If Your Majesty suddenly unleashes your thunderous wrath,
your subject deserves ten thousand deaths."
A palace eunuch descended from the dais and announced:
"You may return to your private residence for now,
and await further instructions."
After a month,
he was demoted to Assistant Prefect of Liǔzhōu.
It happened that the Xuānwǔ military governor Liú Shìníng established friendly relations with Liǔzhōu.
The Surveillance Commissioner submitted a detailed memorial informing the emperor.
Emperor Dézōng said:
"Colluding with military governors—
the evidence is credible and substantiated."
Dòu was exiled to Huānzhōu,
his family assets were confiscated,
and not a single hairpin was left on his person.
Before he even reached the place of exile,
an edict was issued ordering him to commit suicide.
Shàngqīng was indeed registered in the palace women's quarters for a long time.
Several years later,
because she was skilled in conversation,
could brew tea well,
she often found herself in the emperor's presence.
Emperor Dézōng said to her:
"There are many people in the palace.
You handle matters very competently.
How did you come to be here?"
Shàngqīng said:
"Your handmaid was originally a maidservant in the household of the late Chancellor Dòu Shēn.
Dòu Shēn's wife died early,
so I was able to accompany him in cleaning and sweeping.
When Dòu Shēn's household was ruined,
I fortunately entered the palace to fill its ranks.
Now that I serve before Your Imperial Majesty's countenance,
it is as if I am in heaven."
Emperor Dézōng said:
"Dòu Shēn's crimes
were not limited to harboring assassins.
He was also deeply corrupt,
and previously submitted an excessive amount of official silverware."
Shàngqīng said through tears:
"Dòu Shēn, from the time he served as Vice Censor-in-Chief,
through his successive posts as Commissioner of Finance, Commissioner of Revenue, and Salt and Iron Commissioner,
until he became Chancellor,
a period of six years in total,
his monthly income amounted to several hundred thousand.
The untimely rewards and gifts he received before and after
were surely beyond measure.
As for the silverware submitted by Chēnzhōu that was turned over to the government,
it was all bestowed by imperial favor.
On the day it was inventoried and recorded,
I was in Chēnzhōu,
and personally witnessed the prefectural and county officials, currying favor with Lù Zhì's intentions,
scrape off
the inscriptions of the military governors' official titles and names engraved on the submitted silverware,
falsely labeling them as illicit goods.
I humbly beg that an investigation be ordered to verify this."
Thereupon, an order was issued to retrieve the silverware confiscated from Dòu Shēn.
Upon re-examining the scraped areas,
it was exactly as Shàngqīng had said.
This was in the twelfth year of the Zhēnyuán era.
Emperor Dézōng then asked about the matter of harboring assassins.
Shàngqīng said:
"There was originally none.
This was entirely Lù Zhì's scheme to frame him,
having people fabricate it."
Emperor Dézōng finally understood completely.
He then became angry with Lù Zhì and said:
"That old southern barbarian slave!
I took off his green robe
and had him dressed in purple.
I even often called him 'Lù the Ninth'.
I appointed Dòu Shēn,
and just when I was satisfied with him,
I was made to have him killed.
And then power fell into his hands,
but he was so weak and ineffectual,
even softer than a lump of clay."
He then issued an edict exonerating Dòu Shēn of the false charges.
At that time, Péi Yánlíng, sensing that Lù Zhì had fallen out of favor,
freely slandered him,
and seized the opportunity to attack him.
Lù Zhì ultimately suffered condemnation and did not return to favor.
Shàngqīng was specially pardoned by imperial decree, her name removed from the palace registers,
and she became a Daoist nun.
She eventually married Jīn Zhōngyì.
As many of Lù Zhì's disciples and protégés held prominent and illustrious positions in the world,
and the world could not openly discuss it,
therefore this matter was almost completely unknown.
The Maidservant of Lǐ Qí
Lǐ Fú's wife, Madame Péi, was by nature jealous and suspicious.
Although there were many concubines and maids,
Fú never dared to show interest in any of them.
While stationed at Huátái,
someone presented him with a female slave.
Fú intended to have an affair with her but had not yet succeeded.
One day,
he seized an opportunity to say to his wife:
"Your husband has already risen to the rank of military governor,
yet those I can order about
are nothing but old servants.
Madam, is your treatment of me
not rather stingy?"
Madame Péi replied:
"Indeed.
I wonder whom my lord has in mind?"
Fú pointed out
the very female slave who had been presented to him.
Madame Péi agreed.
After that, however, the slave merely attended to his clothes and meals;
she never once enjoyed intimate relations with him.
Fú then instructed his wife's attendants:
"If Madame washes her hair,
you must immediately come and report it to me."
Soon enough, someone indeed came to inform him that Madame was washing her hair,
saying:
"Madame is washing her hair."
Fú immediately feigned a stomachache
and summoned that female slave.
After the slave had gone,
the attendants, considering that Madame Péi was in the midst of washing her hair
and it would be difficult for her to stop abruptly,
informed her of Fú's illness.
Believing it to be true,
Madame Péi hastily emerged from the hair-washing basin,
and barefoot, went to inquire about Fú's suffering.
Since Fú had already claimed illness,
he then acted as if in unbearable pain.
Madame Péi was extremely worried,
and consequently administered medicine mixed with a child's urine for him to drink.
The next day,
the supervising army commissioner and his staff
all came to inquire after his health.
Fú then told them the whole story,
and said with a laugh:
"Achieving nothing
was my destined lot.
What pains me
is having vainly swallowed a bowl of piss."
All who heard this burst into laughter.
Quèyào
The female slave of Lǐ Yǔ, the military governor of Húnán,
was named Quèyào.
She was beautiful in appearance and demeanor,
and skilled in speech.
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, when paying ritual visits to relatives by marriage,
only Quèyào was in charge.
Among Lǐ's several dozen maidservants,
none could match her.
Moreover, she was clever, charming, talented, and quick-witted,
able to cater to others' moods and expressions,
so she was also much loved by the relatives.
Lǐ had four sons:
the eldest named Yánxǐ,
the second Yánfàn,
the third Yánzuò,
and the so-called fifth son after the eldest.
All were young, wild, and dissolute,
and all desired to seduce Quèyào but could not.
Once during the Qingmíng Festival,
when the slender moon was lovely,
and courtyard flowers bloomed brilliantly,
the main hall had embroidered curtains hung,
all lit by silver lamps.
Quèyào encountered the eldest son amidst the shadows of cherry blossoms.
The eldest son then seized her, seeking intimacy.
Quèyào fetched a mat and handed it to him,
saying:
"You may wait in the southeastern corner of the courtyard.
Stand there and wait for me.
Once everyone in the front hall is asleep,
I will come."
After the eldest son left,
in the corridor,
she met the second son, who also propositioned her.
Quèyào again fetched a mat and handed it to him,
saying:
"You may wait in the northeastern corner of the hall."
After the second son left,
she encountered the third son, who grabbed her.
Quèyào again fetched a mat and handed it to him,
saying:
"You may wait in the southwestern corner of the hall."
After the third son left,
she met the fifth son,
who grasped her hand and would not let go.
Quèyào also fetched a mat and handed it to him,
saying:
"You may wait in the northwestern corner of the hall."
All four sons departed.
Yánxǐ, in a corner of the hall,
held his breath and waited.
The hall door was slightly ajar.
He saw his three younger brothers
arriving one after another,
each hurrying to a different corner.
Though surprised in his heart,
he dared not make a sound.
After a short while,
Quèyào secretly lit a torch,
swiftly approached the hall,
flung open both doors, and shone the light upon them,
saying to Yánxǐ and the others:
"You wretched beggars!
How dare you come here looking for a place to sleep!"
They all dropped what they carried,
covered their faces, and fled.
Quèyào then laughed at them from behind.
From then on, the sons felt ashamed
and dared not show her any disrespect.
King Zhāo of Zhōu
In the thirtieth year of King Zhāo's reign,
the king was sitting in the Hall of Reverent Brightness,
and dozed off during the day.
Suddenly, white clouds rose densely,
and a person appeared whose clothes were entirely made of feathers,
hence called a "feathered person."
The king spoke with him in his dream,
inquiring about the arts of becoming an immortal.
The feathered person said:
"Your Majesty's essence and wisdom are not yet awakened.
To seek long life and eternal vision
is impossible."
The king knelt as if requesting teachings on eliminating desires.
The feathered person then used his finger to draw on the king's heart,
and it split open at his touch.
The king awoke in alarm,
his sweat soaking his robe and mat.
He consequently suffered from a heart ailment
and abstained from meals and music.
After about ten days,
he suddenly saw the person from his dream arrive
and say to the king:
"I previously wished to change Your Majesty's heart."
He then produced a small green pouch,
inside which was medicine
named "Continuity Pulse Pills" and "Blood Essence Replenishing Powder."
He rubbed the king's chest with his hand,
and the king recovered shortly after.
The king then requested this medicine,
stored it in a jade jar,
and sealed it with a golden cord.
Applying it to one's feet
enabled flight beyond heaven and earth,
as if traveling within a foot's distance.
Those who obtained and consumed it
would die only after heaven perished.
Fūchāi of Wú
King Fūchāi of Wú dreamed at night of three black dogs howling,
to the south and to the north,
and a cooking steamer with no steam.
Upon waking,
he summoned his ministers to interpret the dream,
but none could explain it.
He then summoned Gōngsūn Shèng.
When Shèng received the summons,
he bid farewell to his wife, saying:
"He summons me for an ominous dream.
How could I, one who does not deceive his heart,
avoid being killed by the king?"
Thereupon, Shèng arrived,
and the king told him the dream.
Shèng said:
"The king will lose his state!
The howling dogs signify
the ancestral temple having no master;
the steamer with no steam means
there will be no food."
The king indeed grew angry
and killed him.
When the Yuè army arrived,
the king said to his attendants:
"I have acted without virtue,
killing Gōngsūn Shèng.
You may call out to him."
Thereupon, they called three times, and he answered three times.
Wú was ultimately destroyed by Yuè.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn dreamed of a great fish,
begging to have the hook removed from its mouth.
The next day, while boating on Kūnmíng Pond,
he saw a fish with a hook in its mouth.
The emperor removed the hook and released it.
Three days later,
a pair of bright pearls was found by the pond's shore.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú,
courtesy name Chángqīng.
He intended to present a rhapsody but did not know what to write.
He dreamed of an old man in yellow clothes who said to him:
"You may compose the 'Rhapsody of the Great Man,'
speaking of matters concerning immortals."
When the rhapsody was completed and presented,
the emperor greatly praised and rewarded him.
Noble Consort Yīn
Noble Consort Yīn of Emperor Míng of Hàn
dreamed of eating a melon that was extremely delicious.
At that time, Dūnhuáng presented a rare melon seed,
named Qiōnglóng.
The elders said:
"A Daoist priest obtained this seed from Pénglái;
eating it prevents hunger."
Zhāng Huàn
In the Later Hàn, Zhāng Huàn served as the Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi.
His wife dreamed that the emperor gave her an official seal and ribbon,
and she ascended a tower and sang.
Upon waking, she told Huàn.
Huàn ordered a divination.
It said:
"Your wife is about to give birth to a son,
who will also govern this commandery,
and whose life will end in this tower."
Later, she gave birth to a son named Měng.
During the Jiàn'ān era,
he became the Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi,
killed the Inspector Hándān Shāng,
and was urgently besieged by the provincial troops.
Měng felt ashamed to be captured,
so he ascended the tower and burned himself to death.
Zhèng Xuán
Zhèng Xuán studied under Mǎ Róng,
but for three years, he showed no notable achievements.
Róng sent him back.
Xuán dozed off under the shade of a tree,
and dreamed of a person
who cut open his heart with a knife,
saying:
"Now you can learn."
Thereupon, he awoke and immediately returned,
and subsequently mastered the classics thoroughly.
Later, when he returned east,
Róng said:
"The Books of Songs, History, Rites, and Music have all gone east."
Fàn Mài
In Línyì, purple refined gold was considered the finest gold,
commonly called Yángmài gold.
Fàn Mài's mother dreamed that someone spread a Yángmài gold mat,
and gave birth to her child upon it.
When the child was born, the mat's color was bright and clear.
Later, when she gave birth to a son,
she named him Fàn Mài,
who became the king of Línyì.
Xǔ Yōu
Xǔ Yōu dreamed of an official in black clothes,
presenting a lacquered tray,
on which were six sealed documents.
The official bowed and said:
"My lord, you shall become the Lord of the Northern Dipper.
Next year in July, there will be another tray
with four sealed documents,
saying:
Chén Kāng shall be the Registrar."
After waking,
it happened
that Kāng arrived,
saying:
"I have come now to pay my respects."
Yōu heard this and became even more fearful.
He asked Kāng:
"I, as a Daoist master,
would at most become a local earth god after death;
today I am to become the Northern Dipper Lord and Registrar—
this is an undeserved honor for me."
The following July,
the two died on the same day.
Xuē Xià
was a man of Tiānshuǐ,
of unparalleled broad learning.
When his mother was pregnant with Xià,
she dreamed that someone gave her a chest of clothes,
saying:
"Madam, you will surely give birth to a wise and brilliant son,
who will be revered by emperors and kings."
His mother recorded the time of her dream.
When Xià was born,
by the time he reached the age of twenty,
his talent and skill surpassed others.
Emperor Wén of Wèi engaged in discussions with him,
which lasted all day without cease.
His words were elegant and his meaning clear,
he responded as fluently as a flowing stream,
without any hesitation.
The emperor said:
"In the past, Gōngsūn Lóng was praised for his eloquence and quick wit,
but his arguments were far-fetched and deceitful.
Now, what you speak of—
if it is not the words of a sage, you do not discuss it—
then you are like Zǐyóu and Zǐgòng.
They could not surpass you.
If Zhòngní were in Wèi,
he would again have an 'inner chamber' disciple."
The emperor personally wrote a letter to Xià,
inscribed with the words "Inner Chamber Disciple."
He rose to the position of Assistant Director of the Palace Library.
He lived in great poverty,
so the emperor took off his own imperial robe and bestowed it upon him,
fulfilling the earlier dream.
His fame topped his time,
and he became a lofty scholar of his generation.
Jiǎng Jì
Jiǎng Jī of the Wèi state served as the Commander of the Imperial Guard.
His wife dreamed of their deceased son weeping and saying:
"The realms of the living and the dead are separate.
When I was alive, I was the descendant of a high minister,
but now in the underworld, I serve as a lowly constable under Mount Tài,
worn out and humiliated,
beyond words.
Now, west of the Grand Temple, there is a man named Sūn Ā,
who is about to be appointed as the Magistrate of Mount Tài.
I beg my mother to inform the Commander,
and ask Ā to transfer me,
so that I may find a better position."
After finishing his words,
the mother awoke in fright.
She told Jī about it,
and Jī said:
"Dreams are not to be trusted."
The next day,
the mother dreamed of him again,
and he said:
"I have come to welcome the new magistrate,
and am staying near the temple.
Before his departure,
I have a brief chance to return.
The new magistrate will depart at noon tomorrow,
and there will be many tasks before his departure,
so I will not be able to return here again.
I urge you to speak to him once more—
what harm is there in giving it a try?"
He then described Sūn Ā's appearance,
in great detail.
When day broke,
the mother spoke to Jī again, saying:
"Last night, I had another dream like this.
Although I know dreams are not to be trusted,
what harm is there in verifying it?"
Jī then sent someone to the area near the Grand Temple,
to inquire about Sūn Ā,
and indeed found him,
whose appearance matched the dream.
Jī wept and said:
"I almost failed my son."
He then went to see Sūn Ā,
and told him the whole story.
Ā was not afraid of impending death,
but was delighted to become the Magistrate of Mount Tài,
only worrying that Jī's words might not be true.
He said to Jī:
"If it truly is as you say,
it is my wish.
I wonder what position your son would like to have?"
Jī replied:
"Give him whatever position brings joy in the underworld."
Ā agreed.
After speaking, he was sent back.
Jī wanted to quickly know the outcome,
so from the gate of the Commander's residence to the temple,
he stationed one person every ten paces,
to relay news about Ā.
At the hour of Chén, word came that Ā had a heartache,
and at noon, word came that Ā had died.
Jī wept and said:
"Though I grieve for my son's misfortune,
I am glad to see that the dead have awareness."
Over a month later,
the mother dreamed again of her son coming to tell her:
"I have been transferred to serve as a clerk."
Zhōu Xuān
Zhōu Xuān of the Wèi state,
styled Kǒnghé,
was skilled in interpreting dreams.
Once, someone asked Xuān:
"I dreamed of a straw dog."
Xuān said:
"You will obtain delicious food."
Not long after,
the person again dreamed of a straw dog,
and Xuān said:
"You will fall from a carriage and break your foot."
Soon after, he again said he dreamed of a straw dog,
and Xuān said:
"There will be a fire disaster."
Later, all came true as he said.
The person asked:
"I actually did not have these dreams—
I was merely testing you!
Yet three interpretations were different,
and all were accurate.
Why is that?"
Xuān replied:
"Intentions take shape in words,
and from them, fortune or misfortune can be divined.
Moreover, a straw dog
is an object used in sacrifices to spirits.
Thus, when you first spoke of dreaming of it,
it meant you would obtain delicious food.
After the sacrifice is completed,
it is trampled upon,
so it meant falling from a carriage and injury.
After being trampled by the carriage,
it is carried away as firewood,
hence the prediction of fire."
Wáng Róng
Wáng Róng dreamed that someone gave him seven mulberries,
placing them in his lapel.
Upon waking, he found them there,
and interpreted it, saying:
"Mulberries
are the fruit of the mulberry tree."
Afterward, seven deaths occurred among his family, both male and female, young and old.
Zōu Zhàn
Zōu Zhàn dreamed of a person bowing to him,
calling himself Zhēn Zhòngshū,
and requesting burial.
Zhàn awoke,
thought about it, and said:
"This must be the person in the earthen mound west of my house."
He then retrieved and buried him.
Later, he dreamed of the person coming to bow in gratitude.
Chén Táo
Yú Fān annotated the *Book of Changes* and
submitted a memorial, saying:
"A clerk in my commandery, Chén Táo,
dreamed that I met a Daoist priest,
who, with disheveled hair and coarse fur,
handed me the six lines of the *Changes*.
He burned three of them
and gave them to me to drink.
I begged to swallow them all.
The Daoist priest said:
'The *Changes* is in heaven,
three lines
are enough.'
Could it be that I have received a mandate,
and am meant to understand this?"
Lǚ Méng
When Lǚ Méng entered Wú,
the king urged him to study.
He then extensively read various texts,
taking the *Book of Changes* as his foundation.
Once, while drunk at Sūn Cè's gathering,
he suddenly, in his sleep,
recited an entire volume of the *Book of Changes*,
and shortly after awoke with a start.
Everyone asked him about it.
Méng said:
"Just now, I dreamed of Fúxī, King Wén, and the Duke of Zhōu,
discussing with me matters of the rise and fall of dynasties,
and the principles of the sun and moon illuminating the world,
all of which were profoundly subtle;
I have not yet grasped the profound meaning,
so I merely recited the text aloud."
All those present knew that Méng had been reciting in his sleep.
Wáng Mù
Wáng Mù of Luòyáng raised an army in Jiǔquán,
to campaign westward against Suǒ Gǔ.
His Chief Clerk, Guō Yǔ, advised against it,
but he did not listen.
At night, he dreamed of riding a green dragon up to heaven,
but stopped at a roof.
Upon waking, he sighed and said:
"The character for 'roof' (屋) is composed of 'corpse' (尸) and 'arrive' (至).
A dragon flying to the roof means 'corpse arrives'—
I am going to die."
Later, it indeed came true.
From
Zhāng Tiānxī
Zhāng Tiānxī was in Liángzhōu.
He dreamed of a green dog,
very long,
coming from the south,
trying to bite Tiānxī.
He tried to avoid it on his bed,
but fell to the ground.
Later, Fú Jiān sent a man named Xún Cháng,
wearing a green-ground brocade robe,
coming from the south,
who attacked and entered the gate,
defeating him utterly.
Zhāng Jùn
Liáng Wénwáng Zhāng Jùn,
dreamed of a person with white hair and eyebrows,
who called himself Zǐ Yú,
saying:
"I entrust the affairs of the world above to you,
and the affairs of the underworld to me."
Upon waking, the king inquired about this,
and found that a certain Hóu Zǐyú had died earlier.
He then found Zǐyú's great-grandson Liàng,
who was serving as the magistrate of Qílián.
Suǒ Chōng and Sòng Tǒng
Suǒ Chōng dreamed of a captive,
who took off his upper garment and came to see Chōng.
Suǒ Dǎn interpreted it, saying:
"The character for 'captive' (虜) without its upper half
becomes the character for 'male' (男).
Captives are of the yin category,
so your wife will give birth to a boy."
Later, it indeed came true.
Also, Sòng Tǒng dreamed that inside there was a person wearing clothes,
and Tǒng grabbed two sticks with one hand,
beating him fiercely.
Suǒ Dǎn interpreted it, saying:
"A person inside
means 'meat' (肉);
the image of two sticks striking it
means beating meat to eat."
After three days,
he visited three households,
and in each, he obtained meat to eat.
Fú Jiān
Fú Jiān was about to launch a southern campaign,
when he dreamed of the city overflowing with vegetables,
and the land tilting to the southeast.
The interpretation said:
"An abundance of vegetables
makes it difficult to make sauce.
The southeast tilting
means Jiāngzuǒ cannot be pacified."
Later, Zhào Xuānxián
Five years after Xuānxián's death,
Shí Hǔ dreamed of Xián.
With tears and snivel, Xián entrusted his son Fèn,
saying:
"This is beyond what the mind can comprehend."
The words conveyed in the dream proved true:
"Where is Fèn now?"
Those around replied:
"He is the governor of Zhào Commandery."
Thereupon, he was immediately promoted to Court Justice,
and then became Minister of Ceremonies.
Though his talent was inferior to his father's,
he rose to the rank of minister due to his father's dream.
Zhāng Jiǎ
There was a man named Zhāng Jiǎ,
who was related to the Minister of Education Cài Mó,
and stayed temporarily at Mó's home.
He went away for a few nights,
but exceeded the deadline and did not return.
Mó was napping during the day,
when he dreamed of Jiǎ saying:
"I went away briefly,
but suddenly fell seriously ill,
suffering from heart and abdominal pain,
with bloating and inability to vomit or relieve myself,
and died at such-and-such time."
Mó asked:
"How can it be treated?"
Jiǎ said:
"Take a living spider, cut off its legs,
and swallow it to be cured."
When Mó awoke,
he sent someone to the place where Jiǎ had gone to verify,
and indeed, he was dead.
Zhāng Mào
Zhāng Mào from Kuàijī
once dreamed of a great elephant,
and asked Wàn Tuī about it.
He said:
"You will become a grand administrator,
but will not meet a good end.
A great elephant is a large beast;
taking its pronunciation,
'beast' (獸) sounds like 'to guard' (守).
An elephant is destroyed because of its tusks,
so you will surely be killed by someone later."
During the Yǒngchāng era, Mào
served as the governor of Wúxīng.
When Wáng Dūn coveted the throne,
Mào remained upright and unwavering,
so Dūn sent Shěn Chōng to eliminate him.
Jìn Míngdì
During the time of Jìn Míngdì,
a man offering a horse dreamed that the River God requested it.
When he arrived,
his dream matched the emperor's dream.
So the horse was thrown into the river to serve the god.
Earlier, Grand Tutor Chǔ Bāo
also favored this horse.
The emperor said:
"It has already been given to the River God."
After Chǔ Bāo died,
soldiers saw him riding this horse.
Féng Xiàojiāng
Guǎngpíng Governor Féng Xiàojiāng's
son, Mǎzǐ.
dreamed of a woman,
aged eighteen or nineteen,
who said, "I am the daughter of the former governor Xú Xuánfāng,
unfortunately, I died young,
and it has been four years since my death.
I was wrongly killed by a ghost.
According to the records of life,
I was supposed to live to over eighty.
Now I am allowed to be reborn,
and will become your wife.
Will you marry me?"
Mǎzǐ dug open the coffin to look,
and the woman had revived,
so they became husband and wife.
Xú Jīng
In the early years of the Xiánhé era of Jìn,
Xú Jīng traveled far away,
and dreamed of sleeping with his wife,
who became pregnant.
The following year, he returned.
His wife indeed gave birth.
Later, it happened as he said.
Shāng Zhòngkān
Shāng Zhòngkān was in Dāntú,
when he dreamed of a person saying:
"You have a heart to help others;
could you move me to a high, dry place?
Then your kindness will extend to dry bones."
The next day,
indeed, a coffin was floating down the river.
Zhòngkān retrieved it and buried it on a high ridge,
pouring a libation of wine.
That evening,
he dreamed of that person coming to bow in gratitude.
Shāng Língjūn,
during the Yìxī era,
dreamed of someone coming to bind him and take him away,
his body and spirit scattered.
Then another person said:
"Leave him for now;
when he becomes the governor of Héngyáng,
we will take him then."
Later, he was appointed governor of Héngyáng,
and though he declined, he could not avoid it.
Indeed, he died in office.
Huán Huò
Jīngzhōu Governor Huán Huò,
in his residence,
saw a person over ten feet tall,
who said in a dream:
"I am the mountain god of Lóngshān,
and I come with no good intentions.
Since you, Governor, are steadfast and firm,
I will leave on my own."
Sīmǎ Tián
In the new city of Jīngkǒu, there was a temple for Dèng Ài,
which had long been in ruins.
Jìn Qiáowáng Sīmǎ Tián, serving as military commander,
dreamed of a person calling himself Lord Dèng,
requesting the repair of his temple.
Tián then ordered it to be rebuilt.
Jiǎ Bì
Jiǎ Bì from Hédōng served as a military advisor in Lángyá.
One night, he dreamed of a man,
with a ruddy complexion, a large nose, and deep-set eyes,
who requested:
"I admire your appearance;
may I exchange heads with you,
is that acceptable?"
In the dream, he had no choice,
and thus his head was swapped.
When he awoke, everyone who saw him fled in terror.
Returning home,
his family members all hid.
From then on, he could laugh and cry with half his face,
and with both hands, feet, and mouth,
he could each hold a brush to write,
producing compositions of exceptional literary and calligraphic beauty.
Wáng Fèngxiān
After a nobleman passed away,
Wáng Fèngxiān, the magistrate of Yǒngxīng, dreamed of facing him as if in life.
Fèngxiān asked:
"Do you still have feelings and desires from afar?"
The reply was:
"On a certain day, I went to a certain household,
and asked the maid."
Later, upon waking,
he questioned the maid,
who said:
"On that day, I dreamed that the master came."
Zōng Shūlín
Zōng Shūlín, the governor of Jìnyáng, obtained ten turtles,
and instructed the cook:
"Make soup with two each day."
That night,
he dreamed of ten men,
dressed in black cloth garments and trousers,
kowtowing and pleading for mercy.
Unaware, he ate two.
The next night,
he dreamed of eight men begging for their lives,
and only then did he realize.
He then released them,
and later dreamed of the eight men coming to thank him.
Monk Fǎchēng
The Sòng dynasty monk Fǎchēng,
on his deathbed, said:
"There is Sōng.
A mountain hermit told me,
General Liú of Jiāngdōng is destined to receive the Mandate of Heaven.
I have thirty-two jade discs and one cake as tokens of proof."
The founder of Sòng heard of this,
and sent the monk Huìyì to Mount Sōng.
After seven days and nights of religious practice,
he dreamed of a long-bearded elder giving directions.
Upon waking,
he clearly remembered the location,
excavated, and obtained them.
Liú Mùzhī
Liú Mùzhī once crossed the Yángzǐ River and stayed overnight,
dreaming of joining two boats into a barge,
topped with a splendid canopy,
adorned with magnificent decorations,
ascending to heaven.
At dawn,
an old woman asked him:
"Did you have a good dream last night?"
Mùzhī then recounted it in detail,
and the old woman said:
"You will surely hold a high ministerial position."
After speaking, she vanished.
Later, he rose to the posts of Deputy Director and Governor of Dānyáng,
due to his great achievements.
Mùzhī also dreamed
that someone addressed him as Liú Zhènjūn coming to welcome him.
In the morning, he interpreted it:
"I am going to die,
for how could there be a Liú Zhènjūn now?"
Later, Emperor Wǔ of Sòng sent someone to welcome him,
and together they established the great enterprise.
Emperor Wǔ was then the General Who Guards the Army.
Xú Xiànzhī
Xú Xiànzhī served as a minor tutor and registrar for Wáng Xióng.
He dreamed his deceased father told him:
"From now on,
do not cross the Zhūquè Bridge,
and you will attain high status."
Later, Xiànzhī crossed halfway,
remembered his ancestor's dream,
and turned his horse back.
Because of this, he was dismissed from his registrar post,
and later indeed became prime minister.
Shěn Qìngzhī,
during the Yuánjiā era,
once dreamed of leading a procession of guards into a latrine,
though pleased by the cleared path,
he found it very distasteful.
Someone interpreted it for him:
"You will surely become noble,
but not yet.
The guard procession signifies
the appearance of wealth and honor;
the latrine
refers to the later emperor.
Your wealth and honor will not come under the current ruler."
Later, it indeed came to pass.
Míngzhī
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā,
Míngzhī, a military advisor in the northern expedition,
had a follower
who suffered a severe nightmare while sleeping at night.
Míngzhī went himself to wake him,
but for a while he could not respond.
Moreover, his hair bun was missing,
and he only awoke after three days.
He recounted:
"I was seized by the feet by three people,
and one of them took my bun.
Suddenly I dreamed of a Daoist priest,
who gave me a pill medicine,
like a tung seed,
and told me to take it with water."
Upon waking,
he found the medicine in his hand,
took it, and then recovered.
Liú Dàn
Liú Dàn of Jìnglíng,
while in Guǎnglíng,
had attendants on duty sleeping,
who dreamed someone told them:
"The official needs hair for spear tassels."
Upon waking, they found their hair already gone,
and this happened to dozens of people.
Yuán Mǐnsūn
Yuán Mǐnsūn,
when Shìzǔ appointed him as prefect of Hǎilíng,
dreamed of the sun falling upon his body.
Soon after, he was recalled,
and entrusted with confidential matters.
Monk Liú
Monk Liú lived in Péngchéng,
and died of illness.
His wife was poor and their child young;
when a violent storm struck,
the walls and house were damaged.
His wife wept, holding their young son, saying:
"If your father were still here,
how could it come to this!"
That night, she dreamed of Monk Liú leading dozens of people to repair the house,
and by the next day, it was restored.
Zhū Zhòngwù
Zhū Zhòngwù had a daughter named Xiǎnyí,
married to Mǐ Yuánzōng,
who died in childbirth at home.
Custom held that those who died in childbirth
should have ink dots marked on their faces.
Her mother could not bear to do it,
so Zhòngwù secretly dotted it himself,
unseen by anyone.
Yuánzōng served as deputy magistrate of Shǐxīn County.
He dreamed his wife came onto the bed,
clearly with a fresh white makeup and ink dots on her face.
Sūnshì
A certain Sūnshì sought an official post,
and dreamed of twin phoenixes alighting on his fists.
He asked the diviner Sòng Dǒng about it.
Who said:
"Phoenixes roost only on parasol trees,
and eat only bamboo seeds.
You will face great misfortune,
either a rough mourning staff
or a smoothed mourning staff."
Later, Sūnshì indeed encountered his mother's death.
Huán Shì
Xú Xiàosì,
courtesy name Shǐchāng.
While serving at the military headquarters,
he once lay sleeping by day beneath the northern wall.
He dreamed of two youths,
who urgently said:
"Move your bed."
Xiàosì awoke in alarm,
and the wall made a sound.
He had taken a few steps when the wall collapsed,
crushing the bed.
Liáng Jiāng Yān
Jiāng Yān, the Governor of Xuānchéng and a native of Jìyáng,
dreamed in his youth that someone gave him a five-colored brush,
and thus his literary talent flourished brilliantly.
Later, he dreamed of a man,
who called himself Guō Jǐngchún,
and said to Yān:
"I previously lent you a brush;
it can be returned now."
Yān reached into his bosom and found the five-colored brush,
and gave it to him.
From then on, Yān's literary compositions faltered.
Thus, people of the time spoke of his "talent being exhausted."
Emperor Dàizōng
Lǐ Fǔguó was arrogant and tyrannical, showing no respect for the sovereign,
and Emperor Dàizōng gradually came to detest him.
