While sleeping,
he dreamed of climbing a tower,
where he saw Gāo Lìshì leading several hundred armored cavalry.
They stabbed Fǔguó with halberds,
causing blood to spill on the ground.
Singing and shouting before and after,
they went away northward.
The emperor sent an attendant to ask the reason.
Lìshì said:
"It is by the order of Emperor Míng."
The emperor awoke.
He did not speak of it at once.
When Fǔguó was later killed by bandits,
the emperor found it strange,
and only then told his attendants about the dream.
Xú Shàn
Xú Shàn, a false Secretariat Drafter of Jiāngnán,
was orphaned in childhood
and his family lived in Yùzhāng.
When Yáng Wú captured Yùzhāng,
Shàn's younger sister was taken captive by a military officer.
After the situation stabilized,
the officer located Shàn
and requested to marry her with proper rites.
Shàn, considering himself from an old-established family,
felt it inappropriate to marry a military man,
and firmly refused.
The officer then forcibly sent betrothal gifts,
all of which Shàn threw away.
Even threatened with a naked blade,
he showed no fear,
but the officer ultimately abducted her and left.
Shàn then went to Yángdū,
seeking an audience with Wú Yáng Wò to plead his case.
At that time, Wò had just succeeded to the princely domain,
and his court was very strict,
usurping the protocols of a king.
Commoners and wandering scholars
could not gain an audience for months or years.
But as soon as Shàn arrived at Báishā,
Wò dreamed at night that someone came and said:
"There is a scholar from Jiāngxī named Xú Shàn,
who will come to see you.
He is now at an inn in Báishā;
he is a good man.
Moreover, he has a matter of grievance;
you should treat him generously."
Wò immediately sent riders to welcome him.
Upon his arrival,
he received him with great courtesy and hospitality.
Wò asked what he wished to say,
and Shàn fully explained the matter of his sister.
Wò then ordered her ransomed and returned to the Xú family.
At that time, Táo Yǎ, the Prefect of Shèzhōu, heard of this and found it remarkable,
and thus recruited him as an aide.
Emperor Wén of Suí
Before Emperor Wén of Suí attained high status,
he was once traveling by boat on the river.
During a night mooring,
he dreamed he had no left hand.
Upon waking,
he was greatly disturbed.
When he went ashore,
he visited a thatched hermitage.
Inside was an old monk
of very high attainment.
The emperor told him the dream in detail.
The monk rose and congratulated him, saying:
"To have no left hand
means a solitary fist (dú quán);
you shall become the Son of Heaven."
Later, the emperor had this hermitage rebuilt as the Jíxiáng Temple.
It was located thirty lǐ below Wǔchāng.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng
When Táng Tàizōng was the Prince of Qín,
at the age of eighteen,
on the night he first plotted with Liú Wénjìng, the Magistrate of Jìnyáng,
Emperor Gāozǔ dreamed of falling from his bed,
and saw his entire body being eaten by maggots and worms.
He found it very disturbing.
He consulted the Chan Master Zhì Mǎn of Ānlè Temple.
The master's secular surname was Jiǎ,
and he was from Xīhé.
His observance of precepts was lofty and pure.
The master said:
"This is something to be celebrated!
To be beneath the bed
means 'Your Majesty' (bìxià).
The masses of worms eating you
means that the multitude of living beings rely on one man to sustain them."
Emperor Gāozǔ praised his words.
He also said:
"This humble monk has studied the *Book of Changes* somewhat.
Judging by the hexagram images,
it is an omen of Míngyí.
According to the *Changes*, it says:
'Xùn (the Gentle) is beneath the bed;
in great number, there is no blame.'
But it is auspicious early and inauspicious late.
This enterprise is inherently grand;
it cannot be undertaken on a small scale.
Small scale will lead to failure.
Grand scale will bring success.
You can accomplish great deeds,
to aid the multitude of living beings.
Wherever you go, you will prosper;
you are sure to succeed."
Emperor Gāozǔ, moved, said:
"Though I have received your good guidance,
I dare not presume to accept."
The Chan Master glanced at the Prince of Qín and said:
"The young lord and his father both have dreams corresponding to omens.
This is called 'remedying the father's faults.'
The father's actions incur no blame.
Heaven's principle and human affairs
are clearly knowable.
You cannot stubbornly refuse;
it is Heaven's grant.
If Heaven grants and you do not take,
you will surely suffer misfortune.
Is that not inadvisable?"
Emperor Gāozǔ bowed and thanked him, saying:
"How fortunate is this disciple,
to be troubled again by your earnest and repeated admonition.
How dare I not respectfully comply?"
Dài Zhòu
Dài Zhòu had always been on good terms with Shǔzhōu Assistant Administrator Shěn Yù.
Zhòu died in the seventh year of the Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty.
By the eighth year, in the eighth month,
Yù was in the prefecture
when he dreamed that he was walking along the southwest street of the Yìníng ward in the capital.
Each time he saw Zhòu wearing old, tattered clothes,
his face and appearance extremely haggard,
and upon seeing Yù, he was both sorrowful and joyful.
He asked Yù, "In your lifetime, you cultivated blessings;
what are you doing now?"
Yù replied:
"I once mistakenly memorialized for someone's execution,
and after I died,
others killed a sheep to sacrifice to me.
Because of these two matters,
I have been arguing and answering with great hardship,
which cannot be fully described.
Now, the situation is also coming to an end."
He then said to Yù:
"In my lifetime, I was a good friend with you,
yet I ultimately could not advance your official position,
deeply regretting it in my heart.
Now you yourself have attained the fifth rank,
the documents have already passed through the Heavenly Ministry,
I assist and rejoice in your celebration,
therefore I came to inform you."
After he finished speaking, Yù awoke,
and told others about it,
hoping the dream would have an omen.
That winter,
Yù went to the capital to participate in the selection.
There was a penalty involving bronze,
and he did not obtain an official post.
He again told others that the dream had not been verified.
In the spring of the ninth year,
Yù was about to return to the region south of the Yangtze,
and when he reached Xúzhōu,
he received an imperial edict,
appointing him to the fifth rank,
as Assistant Administrator of Wùzhōu.
Lóu Shīdé
When Lóu Shīdé was still a commoner,
he once suffered from a severe illness,
and dreamed of a person dressed in purple,
who came before his bed and bowed twice, saying:
"Your illness is about to improve,
I am fortunate to accompany you and go together."
He then led the gentleman out.
Suddenly, he felt his strength very agile,
and thought himself cured of the illness.
After walking several li,
he saw an official office,
with clerks and guards on both sides,
and vermilion gates very high,
inscribed:
"Office of the Underworld."
He exclaimed in surprise:
"How can the Office of the Underworld be in the human world?"
The purple-clad person replied:
"The path of the underworld is indeed connected with human traces,
how could people in the world know of it?"
The gentleman entered the courtyard,
and the clerks and guards retreated in all directions.
He saw an empty room,
inscribed "Office of the Director of Fate."
He asked what its duties were.
The reply was:
"It is in charge of the registers of people's official salaries and lifespans in the world."
The gentleman then secretly looked inside,
and there were several thousand scrolls of books,
on the table.
Beside it was a green-clad person,
called the Record Clerk.
The gentleman ordered him to bring out his own register,
and the clerk took out one scroll and presented it.
The gentleman read it,
it recorded his name,
detailing his official salary, position, year, and month,
going through various prestigious posts,
entering and leaving the highest ministerial positions,
with a lifespan reaching eighty-five.
After reading it, he was delighted,
and said to the Record Clerk:
"I am merely a commoner,
to avoid hunger and cold is enough,
how dare I have other aspirations?"
Before he finished speaking,
suddenly a sound came down from the sky,
shaking and penetrating the eaves and roof.
The Record Clerk exclaimed in surprise:
"The heavenly drum is about to sound,
you should quickly return,
you cannot stay any longer."
Hearing the sound,
he then awoke with a start,
realizing it had been a dream journey.
At that time, dawn had already broken,
and to the east of his residence was a Buddhist temple,
striking the morning bell.
This was probably what the Record Clerk called the heavenly drum.
That day, his illness also improved.
Later, he entered officialdom and held various posts,
all exactly as recorded.
When he became the military governor of the Western Capital,
one day,
he saw a yellow-clad messenger arrive before the pavilion, saying:
"I am a minor official from the underworld path,
ordered to invite you."
The gentleman said:
"I once saw the register of the Director of Fate,
recording my position,
that I should reach the highest ministerial rank,
with a lifespan of eighty-five,
why am I suddenly being summoned?"
The yellow-clad person said:
"When you held a certain official post,
you once mistakenly killed an innocent person,
your position and lifespan were reduced by the managing official,
and now they are exhausted."
After speaking,
he suddenly disappeared.
From then on, he lay ill,
and after three days, he passed away.
Gù Cóng
Gù Cóng was serving as a Reminder,
when he once committed a crime and was imprisoned in the imperial prison,
and was to be executed.
One night, Cóng was worried and sorrowful,
and sat dozing off.
Suddenly, he dreamed of his mother's lower body,
and Cóng became even more frightened,
showing it on his face and expression.
His colleagues asked,
and Cóng told them the dream,
himself saying it was extremely inauspicious.
At that time, there was someone skilled in interpretation who congratulated him:
"You will probably be spared, won't you?"
He asked how he knew.
He said:
"Your mother's lower body,
is the path of life for you.
To see the path of life again,
what auspiciousness could compare?
This is why I congratulate you."
The next day,
Vice Director of the Chancellery Xuē Jì memorialized that the punishment was mistakenly imposed,
and he was eventually spared.
Cóng later rose to become Chancellor.
Empress Wǔ
Táng Empress Wǔ Zé once dreamed of a parrot,
with very magnificent feathers,
but both wings were broken.
She asked her chief ministers about it,
and all the lords were silent.
Palace Secretary Dí Rénjié said:
"The parrot represents Your Majesty's surname.
The two broken wings,
represent Your Majesty's two sons,
Lúlíng and Xiàngwáng.
If Your Majesty raises these two sons,
the two wings will be whole."
Wǔ Chéngsì and Wǔ Sānsī both flushed red down to their necks.
Later, the Qìdān besieged Yōuzhōu,
and issued a proclamation to the court, saying:
"Return our Lúlíng and Xiàngwáng to us."
Then Empress Wǔ remembered Dí Rénjié's words and said:
"You once interpreted a dream for me.
Now it has come true.
I wish to establish a crown prince,
which one would be appropriate?"
Jié said:
"Your Majesty has worthy sons within,
and worthy nephews without,
the choice requires careful consideration,
the decision lies in Your Majesty's wise judgment."
Empress Wǔ said:
"I have my own sage sons,
what are Chéngsì and Sānsī but scabies and ringworm?"
Chéngsì and others were frightened,
and covered their ears and left.
She then issued an edict to summon Lúlíng back,
established him as crown prince,
and appointed him as commander-in-chief.
Initially, when recruiting troops,
no one responded.
Upon hearing the crown prince was coming,
the northern Mángshān mountaintop was filled with soldiers,
leaving no room for people.
The rebels retreated and scattered on their own.
Xuē Jìchǎng
In the Táng dynasty, Xuē Jìchǎng served as the Chief Clerk of Jīngzhōu.
He dreamed of a cat crouching on the threshold of the hall,
with its head facing outward.
He asked the diviner Zhāng Yóu about it,
and Yóu said:
"The cat represents claws and teeth,
crouching on the threshold.
This pertains to matters beyond the inner gates—
you are sure to be entrusted with military affairs."
Within ten days,
he was appointed Military Commissioner of Guìzhōu and Pacification Commissioner of Lǐngnán.
Emperor Xuánzōng
once dreamed of falling from the palace hall,
and a filial son helped him up.
Later, he asked Gāo Lìshì about it,
and Lìshì said:
"A filial son in plain clothes—
this must refer to Wéi Jiànsù."
The emperor deeply agreed.
A few days later,
Wéi was promoted from Vice Minister of Personnel to Chancellor.
Another time, Emperor Xuánzōng dreamed of falling into a well,
and a soldier,
wearing red trousers,
carried him out on his back.
The next day,
he ordered a search among the soldiers,
but no such person was found.
Then he had the imperial gardens searched,
and they found a gatekeeper
wearing red trousers.
He was brought for an audience.
The emperor asked:
"What did you dream last night?"
He replied:
"I carried the sun out of a well on my back and ascended to heaven."
The emperor observed his appearance,
which matched the dream.
He then asked:
"Do you wish for an official post?"
The man answered:
"I do not understand how to be an official;
my family is poor."
So the emperor ordered him to be given five hundred thousand coins.
Wèi Réng
and Lǐ Guīnián were selected for office together.
They both had dreams.
Wèi dreamed that Vice Minister Lǐ Péngnián
sent someone to summon him,
and he listened with his ear against the gate of the selection office.
Guīnián dreamed someone reported to him,
"The Vice Minister has assigned you a county magistrate position in Jīzhōu."
The next day, they interpreted these dreams together,
thinking that "ear against the gate" formed the character 'wén' (闻),
which should correspond to Wénxǐ.
Sure enough, Wèi was appointed Magistrate of Wénxǐ,
and Lǐ Guīnián was indeed appointed County Magistrate of Qíxiàn in Qízhōu.
Later, Wèi was demoted to Assistant Magistrate of Huánggǎng in Qí'ān Commandery.
According to an imperial decree, he was allowed a reassignment.
He sought a dream for guidance,
and dreamed of picking up a hairy fly.
He discussed it with Lǐ Guīnián for interpretation,
who said:
"The character for 'hairy' (毛) has 'thousand' (千) above and 'seven' (七) below,
meaning you will be posted seventeen hundred lǐ away."
It turned out as he said.
Chén Ānpíng
The son of the Imperial Secretary Chén Ānpíng,
having reached the age for official selection,
slept beside his fellow villager Lǐ Xiānyào.
At night, he dreamed of raising silkworms in the eleventh month.
Xiānyào interpreted it, saying:
"Raising silkworms in the eleventh month
produces winter silk.
You will surely be sent to the Eastern Bureau."
A few days later,
he was indeed sent to the Ministry of Personnel.
Lǐ Qútán
Lǐ Qútán of Ráoyáng,
having completed his term as a merit official, was up for selection.
He dreamed at night of an enormous sow.
Lǐ Xiānyào interpreted it, saying:
"A sow
is the master of piglets.
You are sure to become a garrison commander."
A few days later,
it turned out exactly as he said.
Zhào Liángqì
Zhào Liángqì once dreamed of more than ten coffins,
lined up side by side.
Liángqì walked over them from the east,
and upon reaching the eleventh coffin, it broke,
and his foot sank into it.
Later, he indeed served eleven official posts,
and died while serving as a Secretary in the Secretariat.
Gāo Shì, while serving as Chief Clerk of Guǎnglíng,
once told someone:
"Recently, I dreamed of being in the main hall,
seeing coffins piled up,
from the ground to the roof ridge.
I also saw another coffin beside them,
extremely wide and large.
I entered it,
and it was not full on any side.
I wonder what this dream means?"
Afterward, he served in various positions successively,
and was later transferred to be the Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent,
which is indeed a broad and leisurely post.
Xī Zhì
Vice Minister Xī Zhì,
when young and not yet in office,
dreamed of having tea with over twenty court guests
in a hall.
It was extremely hot at the time.
Xī sat in the first seat on the east side.
The tea started from the west,
and passed from the south onward.
After two bowls had been served,
he still had not received his,
and Xī, unbearably thirsty,
could hardly endure it.
Suddenly, a clerk walked in,
stout and large,
carrying a ledger of nearly a thousand pages.
He placed a desk with brush and inkstone before him,
requesting a signature.
Xī, both hot and thirsty,
and disliking the clerk's stoutness,
became angry.
Standing up, he pushed the desk away, saying:
"Take this away for now."
Dark ink splattered from the inkstone,
landing right on the documents,
as well as on the clerk's face, hands, feet, and clothes—
all were stained.
Then he woke with a start.
That night, he fetched paper and brush to record the dream in detail,
and stored it in a box.
Fifteen years later,
he became Vice Minister of Personnel.
At that time, people were beginning to regard tea as a superior beverage,
and daily pursued refinement and elegance.
Xī, by nature extravagant,
had prepared a set of tea utensils beforehand,
which even other high officials did not possess.
With a wind stove and Yuèzhōu porcelain cups,
bowl stands and horn spoons,
all were exquisite.
The weather was already hot.
After the meal,
he invited his fellow vice ministers to a tea gathering in the hall.
Xī acted as host,
sitting in the first seat facing east.
There were over twenty guests seated.
Two cups were passed around slowly,
and the servings were also very small.
The tea was offered starting from the west,
mingled with conversation and laughter,
making the serving even slower.
Xī already suffered from diabetes,
and with the heat and exhaustion,
he still had not received his tea,
and grew extremely agitated and irritable.
After a while,
a clerk, stout and dark,
carrying a large ledger,
along with brush and inkstone,
his face dripping with sweat,
approached and asked for a signature.
Xī, filled with disgust and anger, could bear it no longer.
He pushed the desk on the steps, saying:
"Take this away for now."
Both the desk and its contents toppled over,
splattering right onto the clerk's face,
and the ledger was completely stained.
The seated guests burst into laughter.
Only then did Xī realize it was the dream from years before.
He told his colleagues in the ministry.
The next day,
he retrieved the recorded dream to verify it,
and found not the slightest discrepancy.
Zhāng Zhuó
Zhāng Zhuó once dreamed of a great bird,
purple in color,
with patterns of five colors,
flying down
and lingering before the courtyard, refusing to leave.
He told his grandfather about it,
who said:
"This is auspicious.
In the past, Cài Héng said:
'There are five types of phoenixes:
the red one with patterned feathers is the fèng,
the blue one is the luán,
the yellow one is the yuānchú,
the white one is the hónghú,
and the purple one is the yuèzhuó.'
This bird is an assistant to the phoenix,
and you will become an imperial aide."
Thus, he took it as his name.
When Zhuó first sat for the imperial examination,
upon reaching Huáizhōu,
he dreamed of auspicious clouds covering his body.
That year, in the policy examination,
the examination official Qián Wèidào
ranked him first in the empire.
Also, when he first served under Prince Qí,
he dreamed at night of wearing crimson and riding a donkey.
In his sleep, he found it strange,
thinking, "I wear green robes
and ride a horse;
why would I wear crimson and ride a donkey?"
That year, he passed the examination
and was appointed as an assistant in the Court of State Ceremonial,
receiving the fifth rank without undergoing an assessment.
This was the fulfillment of the dream.
Péi Yuánzhì
Péi Yuánzhì from Hédōng first sat for the imperial examination.
The results were to be announced the next morning,
but that night he dreamed of a dog emerging from a hole,
and he drew a bow to shoot it,
but the arrow veered off.
He considered this inauspicious
and asked Cáo Liángshǐ about it,
who said:
"On the night before the results were announced,
I also had this dream.
A deity explained it to me, saying:
'The dog represents the top part of the character dì (第),
the bow represents the body of the character,
the arrow is the vertical stroke,
and the veering stroke completes the character dì (第).'"
Soon after, the results were announced,
and it indeed matched the dream.
Pān Jiè
Pān Jiè claimed
that whenever he obtained an official position,
he would have a dream beforehand.
He and Zhào Zìqín were selected together,
and both had their names submitted to the higher authorities,
but the official appointments were delayed.
Later, Jiè said
he had already dreamed,
and the appointments would soon be issued.
He dreamed that he and Zìqín were both expressing gratitude for their appointments,
with Jiè walking ahead
and Zìqín following behind.
When they reached the place to give thanks,
Jiè stood on the east,
and Zìqín stood on the west,
and they looked at each other and smiled.
Three days later,
the appointments were indeed issued.
Jiè was made a censor,
and Zìqín was made a reminder official.
They expressed gratitude on the same day.
During the initial introduction,
Jiè walked ahead first,
and Zìqín followed behind.
Upon entering the court,
Jiè stood on the east,
and Zìqín stood on the west,
and the two looked at each other and smiled,
exactly as in the dream.
Fán Xì
Assistant Secretary Fán Xì,
one year before sitting for the examination,
once dreamed of passing.
When the results were posted,
Wáng Zhèngqīng was ranked first.
There were twenty-six people on the list.
The following year, when Xì sat for the examination,
after passing,
it was indeed Wáng Zhèngqīng who ranked first,
and the number of candidates was also the same.
Later, when Xì was transferred from the position of collator,
the Vice Minister of Personnel Dáxí Xún
held him in high regard
and appointed him as the captain of Jīnchéng County.
Xì declined the appointment.
Dáxí said:
"If a collator refuses the position of captain of Jīnchéng County,
what other position would you take?"
Xì replied:
"I dare not disdain a county captain near the capital,
but this position is not meant for me."
After over a month,
the personnel department had no other vacancies to offer,
so they pressed him to accept the appointment,
but Xì still refused.
At that time, Cuī Yì was appointed as the captain of Jīngyáng County in the eastern selection,
but due to it being an undesirable vacancy,
he did not accept it.
Yì
was the son of Minister Cuī Qiào.
He then sought another vacancy,
and it happened that Xì's appointment was still unsettled.
On the day the appointments were announced,
Dáxí said to him:
"If you won't take Jīnchéng,
I have changed your appointment.
What position do you think you deserve?"
Xì said:
"I dreamed that my official position should contain the character yáng (阳)."
Dáxí sighed and said:
"This is fate."
He then ordered the announcement to be read,
and it was indeed the captain of Jīngyáng County.
Lǚ Yīn
Lǚ Yīn once dreamed during the day that he was summoned by the underworld,
and he was brought before a judge.
The judge said:
"This man's achievements are great,
but he should not be taken."
Yīn then pleaded:
"My mother is old, and my children are young;
there is no one to take care of the family."
He pleaded earnestly,
and the judge ordered him to be taken before the king.
Soon after,
the attendants reported to the king:
"A replacement has been found for this man."
The king asked who the replacement was,
and they said it was Kuǎi Shì.
The king said:
"Kuǎi Shì is a renowned scholar,
and he is fit for the duty."
Thus, Yīn was released.
At that time, Yīn was staying with his brother-in-law Gù Kuàng.
Upon waking,
he told Kuàng about it.
Several tens of days later,
Shì was appointed as the acting assistant magistrate of Wú County,
and he was perfectly healthy.
Kuàng often teased Yīn about it
for amusement.
Over a month later, Shì left his position
and built a residence in the Jīshàn Lane of Wú.
Suddenly, a runner rushed in
and announced:
"Attendant Dīng sends word
to summon the third gentleman."
Shì said:
"I have never heard of an Attendant Dīng.
Who is he?"
The runner said:
"It is Xiānzhī."
Shì said:
"Xiānzhī died in Yúháng;
how can he be called an attendant?"
The runner said:
"He is an attendant in the underworld."
Shì was displeased and said:
"An attendant in the underworld—
why would he send word to the living?"
The runner said:
"He also orders your summoning,
not just sending word.
Your name is already registered,
and it cannot be changed."
Shì begged him to inform Attendant Dīng:
"I am not yet due to die;
please find a replacement for me."
The runner left and returned,
saying:
"The attendant does not permit it
and urges you to prepare quickly."
Shì then fell ill,
and died a few days later.
Zhāng Yì,
during the Dàlì era, served as Minister of Works and concurrently oversaw financial administration.
Because his memorials pleased the emperor,
Emperor Dàizōng personally promised him the position of chancellor,
showing him great favor.
Zhāng Yì eagerly anticipated this day after day,
but for several weeks there was no news.
Suddenly one night, he dreamed that someone hurriedly entered through the gate,
loudly proclaiming:
"Rèn Diào is appointed chancellor."
Zhāng Yì awoke in alarm,
pondering that there was no such person in or outside the court,
and could not decipher the meaning.
He had a nephew named Lǐ Tōnglǐ,
who was learned and wise.
Zhāng Yì summoned him and told him the dream,
asking him to analyze its meaning.
After deep thought for a long time,
Lǐ Tōnglǐ congratulated him, saying:
"Uncle, you will become chancellor."
Zhāng Yì immediately questioned him,
and Tōnglǐ replied:
"The reverse reading of 'Rèn Diào' sounds like 'ráo tián,'
and nothing is sweeter than licorice.
Licorice is a precious herb,
and the reverse reading of 'precious herb'
is exactly your name, Uncle."
Zhāng Yì was very pleased.
Soon, a messenger on horseback came to report:
"The imperial edict has been issued."
Zhāng Yì was appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat and participated in the administration.
Chǔ Shí
Chǔ Shí, an Assistant Editorial Director,
during the Dàlì era,
fell severely ill with a pestilential disease,
and for forty days was in a daze, unaware of his surroundings.
One day later,
he suddenly dreamed of a female Daoist in yellow robes coming to him,
saying to him:
"You have official rank and salary,
and it is not yet your time to die."
She then called for Fàn Zhèng to bring medicine.
Suddenly, a young boy appeared,
holding a glass bottle,
and poured medicine into a large horn bowl.
After drinking it, he recovered.
At dawn,
Xǔ Shūjì sent medicine over.
Chǔ Shí had been long afflicted by the illness,
and initially did not open his eyes.
When he saw the young boy and the bowl of medicine,
they were exactly what he had seen in his dream the previous night,
so he called the boy Fàn Zhèng.
Upon inquiry, it was confirmed.
His illness then healed.
Yáng Yán
The late Chancellor Yáng Yán, before taking office,
once dreamed of climbing to the peak of a high mountain,
looking down upon the human world below,
which was indistinct and unrecognizable.
Looking upward,
he saw an auspicious sun close at hand,
its red light blazing brilliantly,
illuminating everything for thousands of miles.
Yáng Yán raised both hands to hold it,
and the scorching heat
felt as if it were burning his heart and eyes.
After a long time, he awoke,
looked at his hands,
and they were still dripping with sweat.
He found this strange,
so he told others about it.
Someone interpreted it, saying:
"The sun
is a symbol of the sovereign.
Now you dreamed of climbing a mountain to hold the sun.
Does this not mean you will ascend to the position of chancellor and assist the sovereign?"
Later, Yáng Yán held various prestigious positions,
and indeed became chancellor,
fulfilling the auspicious omen of holding the sun.
Dòu Shēn
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Chancellor Dòu Shēn served as Vice Censor-in-Chief.
One night, he dreamed that Emperor Dézōng summoned him for an audience in a side hall,
inquiring about matters of state governance.
The emperor was pleased,
and bestowed upon him a half-sleeved brocade garment.
Upon waking,
he found the dream peculiar,
and silently pondered:
"'Bì' (arm) means protection,
and a great city protects my person.
Now dreaming of a half-sleeved garment
—could it be that His Majesty, considering my unworthy occupation of a prominent position,
intends to grant me half my salary
and have me retire from office?"
He remained troubled for a long time.
He then told others about the dream,
and a guest interpreted it, saying:
"Your dream is an auspicious sign.
Moreover, a half-sleeved garment
is clothing that covers the arms and shoulders.
Now you dreamed that the Son of Heaven bestowed it upon you.
Does this not mean that the sovereign will entrust you with the position of a key minister?"
The next day,
he was indeed appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat and participated in the administration.
Lǐ Féngjí
Before Lǐ Féngjí was in charge of drafting imperial edicts,
there was an old maidservant in his household who was fond of interpreting dreams,
and many of her interpretations later came true.
Lǐ Féngjí had long hoped for an official appointment,
so he consulted the maidservant.
One day,
the maidservant came looking sorrowful,
and when Lǐ Féngjí asked why,
she said:
"Last night, I had a bad dream about you, sir.
I would rather not say."
Lǐ Féngjí pressed her,
and the maidservant said:
"I dreamed that someone carried a coffin to the back of the hall.
Saying:
'Just place it here for now.'
Soon after, it was moved into the main hall.
This dream is probably not a good omen."
Upon hearing this, Lǐ Féngjí was very pleased.
Shortly after, he was appointed a Drafter of the Secretariat,
later served as examiner for the imperial examinations,
and before completing that duty, he became chancellor.
Wáng Bō
Wáng Bō was poor and lowly in his youth,
living in Yángzhōu,
with no one who recognized his talent.
Only one military officer often received and provided for him,
sparing no effort.
Vice Director Dù Yà was in Huáinán.
On the Dragon Boat Festival,
a grand boat race was held as entertainment.
Various prefectures summoned musicians and performers,
and the two counties competed for victory.
Colorful towers and viewing pavilions
illuminated the river waters,
something unseen for decades.
All guests in Yángzhōu,
whether worthy or unworthy, were invited to attend.
Only Lord Wáng was not invited,
leaving him disheartened and self-reproachful.
A clansman who was a military officer said:
"I have a pavilion,
and my family members are all there.
Eighth Brother, just watch from inside the pavilion—
it’s even better than sitting among the banquet tables."
Lord Wáng replied:
"Yes."
So he went to the pavilion.
It was summer at the time,
and the morning sun was just shining.
The clansman ordered a jug of fine wine to be sent.
He said:
"This is very good—
I just had it fetched."
Lord Wáng, feeling frustrated and resentful,
drank it all by himself.
As the sun grew hotter inside the pavilion,
the strong wine made him drowsy and weary,
so he lay down to rest.
As soon as he fell asleep,
he dreamed he was at the banquet,
sitting in Dù’s seat.
The administrative officers were below,
outnumbering those close to Lord Dù by nearly half.
After a long while, he awoke with a start,
but dared not speak of it to anyone.
Later, when he became chancellor,
he was about to be appointed to Huáinán,
concurrently serving as Salt and Iron Commissioner.
The imperial decree was long delayed,
and Lord Wáng was very troubled.
So he summoned his former subordinates who were in the city and said to them:
"My appointment to Huáinán as Salt and Iron Commissioner—
this is certain now.
Back then, in my dream, the number of administrative officers
exceeded half,
which corresponds to the additional Salt and Iron Commission staff."
A few days later, the appointment indeed arrived.
Later, during a banquet by the river,
with all guests and aides present,
Lord Wáng suddenly felt as if he had been there before.
Reflecting on it,
he realized it was the dream from years past.
The scenery and atmosphere
were entirely the same.
It was early May at the time.
Dòu Lú Shǔ,
originally named Fǔzhēn,
traveled to Qúzhōu in his youth.
Prefect Zhèng Shìzhān treated him generously.
He said to him:
"You have a compound surname,
so it is unsuitable to have a two-character given name.
Let me change it for you."
Then he wrote the three characters Shǔ, Zhù, and Zhù and gave them to him,
saying:
"I fear there may be someone among your clan with the same name,
so choose one yourself."
That evening,
he dreamed an old man told him:
"I heard the Prefect is changing your name.
You will achieve fame after four attempts at the examinations,
and the number four is very auspicious."
He also said:
"Twenty years from now, you will govern this prefecture."
Then he pointed to a piece of land and said:
"Here, you can build a pavilion."
After waking,
he accordingly changed his name to Shǔ.
Later, he failed the examinations twice,
then attempted two more times,
and again did not pass.
After two more attempts,
he finally achieved fame.
Indeed, it was four attempts after changing his name.
Twenty years later,
he indeed became Prefect of Qúzhōu,
and on the land from his dream, he built the Zhēng Mèng Pavilion.
Wéi Cí
In the sixth year of the Yuánhé era,
Wéi Cí of Jīngzhào served as an aide to Liánshǐ Fáng Wǔ of Wǎnlíng.
In the seventh month of autumn,
during a light rain,
Wéi Cí was at the official office
and took a nap during the day.
Suddenly, he dreamed that someone presented a name card.
Looking at it clearly,
he saw the characters written as:
"Lǐ Gùyán."
Shortly after, in a daze,
a voice from the air said:
"Next year, he will come first on the examination list."
At that time, early in the Yuánhé era,
there was a Lǐ Gùyán who passed the examinations,
and he found the matter very surprising.
For among names, few contained the character Gù,
so how could there be another Lǐ Gùyán?
In the eighth month of autumn,
a candidate for the examinations indeed presented a name card with his name,
exactly as in the dream,
except "Gù" was "Gù."
This was the present Western Commander Lord Lǐ.
Wéi Cí kept the dream a secret and did not reveal it,
but said:
"You will certainly pass the examinations next year,
and will rank first among all candidates."
That winter,
Vice Minister of War Xǔ Mèngróng presided over the examinations,
and indeed ranked him first on the list.
Earlier, Gùyán had dreamed of wearing Sòng Jǐng’s clothes.
After the tenth year of the Yuánhé era,
Jǐng became very prominent,
his reputation widespread,
and there were rumors of his appointment as a high-ranking censor.
But when Jǐng, from the position of Director of the Bureau of Justice, was appointed to oversee miscellaneous affairs
and sent out as Prefect of Zézhōu,
he soon passed away.
Gùyán felt suspicious about his dream.
Early in the Chángqìng era,
when Emperor Mùzōng performed ceremonies at the Circular Mound,
Gùyán was serving as Left Reminder.
According to old custom:
when remonstrance officials accompanied the emperor in ceremonies,
the Court of Imperial Sacrifices would issue each a set of ceremonial robes.
When Gùyán put his on,
he lifted the robe to look underneath,
and saw written:
"Left Supplementer Sòng Jǐng’s robe."
So he recounted this himself among his colleagues.
Huángfǔ Hóng
Huángfǔ Hóng applied for the imperial examination,
seeking recommendation in Huàzhōu.
He offended Prefect Qián Huī while drunk,
and was driven out.
Arriving in Shǎnzhōu to complete his recommendation process,
as he was about to pass through the city gate,
he heard that Qián himself had been appointed chief examiner from Huàzhōu.
Knowing he would certainly not pass,
he turned east to return home.
After traveling several stages,
he fell asleep
and dreamed of his deceased wife’s wet nurse, who said:
"Young Master Huángfǔ is sitting for the examination—
where are you going now?"
He explained in detail the rift with the chief examiner.
The wet nurse said:
"Young Master Huángfǔ must seek the Stone Granny deity."
Then they went together north of the inn,
walked several li through the grass,
and entered a small hut,
where they saw a broken stone figure.
Huángfǔ bowed to it.
The wet nurse said:
"My young lady’s husband, Young Master Huángfǔ, wishes to sit for the examination—
Granny, can you see if he will succeed?"
The stone figure nodded and said:
"He will."
The wet nurse said:
"Since Stone Granny says he will,
then he certainly will.
In the future, do not forget to repay with offerings."
Huángfǔ then bowed in thanks.
The wet nurse escorted him back to the inn gate.
He awoke with a start and said:
"My dream was so clear—
how could it not come true?"
So he re-entered the city to sit for the examination.
Vice-Minister Qián intended to thwart him.
He passed Huángfǔ’s miscellaneous essays,
but thought to himself:
"Everyone knows I am angry with Hóng—
if I now humiliate him in court,
that would not do.
Simply not letting him pass will suffice."
He then ordered the examination on the classics.
When the results were finalized and about to be posted,
Qián felt fearful—
he wanted to replace one candidate with another,
but could not decide.
Turning it over and pondering,
he remained sleepless until nearly the fifth watch,
then said to his attendants:
"Try fetching for me
a bundle of the candidates’ essays in order."
When opened,
it was Huángfǔ’s examination papers.
Master Qián said:
"This is surely ordained by Heaven."
So he made no changes.
After passing, Huángfǔ returned east,
and upon reaching Shǎnzhōu,
he asked the innkeeper:
"Is there nearby
a
Stone Granny deity?"
They all laughed and said:
"How do you know about that, young master?
It’s just a piece of dumb stone—
some cowherd boys
playfully chiseled it
into a human shape
and call it Stone Granny.
It’s only two or three li from the inn."
Huángfǔ then prepared wine and dried meat,
and went with the innkeeper—
it was exactly the place he experienced in his dream.
He made offerings, bowed to the stone figure, and returned.
Dù Mù
Dù Mù once sought the position of Junior Ceremonialist from the chief ministers,
but did not succeed;
he then requested the post of Junior Autumn Official.
Again he did not succeed.
He once dreamed someone said to him:
"Farewell to spring, not reaching autumn;
the foot of Kūn and the head of Jiē."
Later, he indeed obtained the position of Vice-Director of the Bureau of Evaluations.
Gāo Yuányù
Xiāngyáng Military Governor Gāo Yuányù,
in the third year of the Tàihé era,
served as Vice-Director of the Bureau of Honors,
lodging in the Southern Palace.
By day he dreamed someone told him:
"In ten years, you will be Governor of Xiāng."
After waking,
he vaguely recalled the figure’s demeanor—
a tall, handsome scholar.
Secretly finding it strange,
he took up a brush
and recorded it in cryptic language on the eastern pillar of the hall,
in a shaded spot,
writing:
"Great Three, awake, Xiāng Governor, ten years."
By the third year of the Kāichéng era,
he had become Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Since the earlier dream had not come true,
he thought dreams were indeed empty.
Thereafter, serving both in the capital and provinces,
he rose through noble positions,
enjoying pure reputation and great virtue,
leading the eminent figures of the time.
The whole realm looked up to him,
awaiting his ascent to the highest ministerial posts—
the governorship of Xiāng
seemed merely an act of honoring a worthy.
In the second year of the Dàzhōng era,
from the post of Minister of Personnel,
he received command of Hànnán,
twenty years after the earlier dream.
He thought the writing on the pillar
could no longer exist,
so he mentioned the matter to Dūguān Wéi.
Being a man fond of curiosities,
Wéi went to seek it.
Since Gāo’s inscription,
the office building had been repaired many times,
yet the brushstrokes remained vivid and alone preserved.
Was this not divine support clearly manifested today!
Gāo then counted on his fingers—
adding the ten years from before
to the present year
made exactly twenty years.
How hidden and subtle are the workings of unseen virtue,
yet so clearly understood when the time arrives!
Yáng Jìngzhī
Yáng Jìngzhī was born.
The Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngxī, Dài.
When Dài was taking the imperial examination in Jiāngxī,
Jìngzhī was older,
and his innate nature was especially earnest.
It was already late autumn,
when he suddenly dreamed of a new list of forty jìnshì,
each clearly countable.
As his eyes passed over half,
his son was among them.
His neighbor on the list had the surname Púyáng,
but the given name was indistinct.
After waking, he was overjoyed,
and inquired in the literary circles,
learning there was one named Púyáng Yuàn,
whose writing was very lofty,
and who already had a reputation.
At the time, the search for talent from the countryside was urgent,
and he was rightly among the selected.
So he sought his residence,
and it was said he was from Mǐn,
and had not yet reached the capital.
Lord Yáng admonished his son,
ordering him to listen.
Wait until he arrived in the capital,
and associate with him,
to correspond with this dream.
One day,
Lord Yáng was seeing off guests at Bàshàng,
and before the guests arrived,
he rested at an inn.
Seeing someone coming from afar,
he tried ordering an inquiry,
and it was a tribute scholar.
Investigating his origin,
he said:
"From Mǐn."
Asked his surname,
he said:
"Púyáng."
Ascertaining his name,
he said:
"Yuàn."
Lord Yáng said:
"Ah!
This is heaven's revelation.
How could one dream of him there,
and meet him here again?"
So he ordered them to meet.
Púyáng hesitated but could not decline,
and presented his writings.
First observing the man,
his brow was clear and bright;
next speaking with him,
his words and demeanor were calm and composed;
finally reading his writings,
the style and reasoning were profound and subtle;
asked where he was staying,
he said:
"Now I will rent a place."
Lord Yáng ordered all his belongings moved,
placed him in the school,
and ordered Jiāngxī to stay with him day and night.
That winter,
He greatly praised Púyáng's literary learning among the ministers,
public sentiment was unanimous,
and passing the examination was certain.
The examination date was set,
but one night the scholar suddenly died.
Lord Yáng lamented, grieved, and sighed in shock,
searched his bags for his meager possessions,
his hometown road was far,
so he strenuously managed the arrangements,
to return his bones to Mǐn.
Then he said to his son:
"My dream was not fulfilled,
your one name on the list,
also cannot be secured."
The next year,
his son passed the examination,
but among the same year's graduates, there was no Púyáng.
At the start of summer,
they were about to send the list to the Ministry of Personnel.
At the time, the prime minister said:
"The elders valued clan and reputation,
and lightly regarded official positions.
The Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove,
namely Ruǎn Jí from Chénliú, Liú Líng from Pèiguó, Xiàng Xiù from Héjiān,
can be spoken of as lofty scholars."
That year, the names inscribed at Cí'ēn Temple,
all used clan reputation.
After the inscription was finished,
Yáng strolled leisurely beneath the pagoda,
looked up and said:
"Yáng Dài from Hóngnóng,
Púyáng Wú Dāng."
Suddenly it was as if he saw what was in the dream.
Lú Zhēn's Nephew
The Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Shàngshū Lú Zhēn,
had a nephew who became a monk.
During the Huìcháng era,
when Buddhist monks were being purged,
he was expelled and returned home,
and by hereditary privilege was appointed as a参军 in the Prince of Guāng's residence.
One night,
he dreamed that the master he had served as a monk came to console him,
asking about his circumstances.
He repeatedly explained that Buddhism was in decline and broken,
and he had nowhere to return.
Now holding an official post,
he was merely passing the days.
He hoped to shave his head again,
to fulfill his aspiration.
He spoke while weeping.
After a long while, he said,
"If my aspiration is indeed aligned with the Buddha's teachings."
Before he finished speaking,
he saw troops stationed on all sides,
thousands of chariots and ten thousand cavalry,
banners like the sun and moon,
robes of brocade and embroidery,
guards and attendants surrounding them,
truly the great procession of the Son of Heaven.
Among the army, people were clamoring,
saying they were welcoming the Prince of Guāng.
The ranks were ordered,
and they proceeded forward in sequence.
Lú was just shocked and unable to comprehend,
when suddenly he awoke,
his soul trembling and sweating profusely,
and only after a long time could he speak,
but in the end did not dare reveal it to anyone.
Not long after,
Emperor Xuānzóng ascended the throne from the Prince of Guāng's residence,
and recorded the officials of the princely residence.
Lú, according to precedent,
was promoted outside the usual regulations,
and from then on, Buddhism gradually revived.
The old system of temples, monks, and nuns,
entirely matched the words in the dream.
Lú considered the so-called original master in the dream,
was probably the Prince of Guāng, the lord of the参军's residence.
Close as master and disciple,
thus he took it as a hidden omen.
Could it be the divine intent,
to reveal through such subtlety?
A National University Míngjīng
The year Liǔ Jǐng oversaw the examinations,
there was a National University míngjīng,
whose name is lost,
who dreamed during the day of lingering by the university gate.
There was a person
carrying a clothing bag,
who asked the míngjīng
his surname,
the míngjīng told him,
and the person laughed and said:
"You will pass the examination next spring."
The míngjīng then invited him into the Bìluó shop in Chángxīng Ward,
a place he often visited.
Outside the shop, dogs were fighting,
and he exclaimed in surprise:
"Wrong."
He awoke from the dream,
and immediately called several people from neighboring rooms,
and told them his dream.
Suddenly, he saw the shopkeeper from Chángxīng Ward enter the door and say:
"Young master, you and a guest ate bìluó,
totaling two jin,
why didn't you pay before leaving?"
The míngjīng was greatly alarmed,
took off his clothes to pawn for payment,
and went to verify the dream,
observing the couch and utensils,
and saw it was exactly as in the dream.
Then he said to the shop owner:
"The guest and I both came here in a dream,
could the guest have eaten?"
The shop owner said in surprise:
"At first, I thought it strange that the guest's bìluó was completely untouched,
and suspected he disliked the garlic placed on it."
The next spring,
the míngjīng and the three people from neighboring rooms whom he had visited,
all passed the higher level.
Xuē Yì
Secretary of the Palace Library, Xuē Yì from Hédōng,
whose brother-in-law Cuī Mì
served as the Deputy Magistrate of Tónglú.
Yì and his aunt Wéi Shì were guests
at Mì's home.
After a long time,
he contracted malaria,
which persisted for several months,
nearly causing his death.
Wéi Shì was deeply worried,
and one night she dreamed of a deity dressed in white robes and a single-layered garment.
Wéi Shì clasped her hands in reverence
and begged for Yì's illness to be cured.
The deity said:
"If this is not treated for a long time,
it will turn into a severe malaria,
and then it will be incurable."
He then gave Wéi Shì two talismans along with an incantation,
saying:
"'Severe malaria, severe malaria,
gods of the four mountains,
send me to bind you.
Messengers of the Six Dīng,
Generals of the Five Paths,
seize your vital energy,
capture your spirit and soul.
Leave quickly, leave quickly,
avoid meeting this person.
Swiftly, swiftly, as decreed by the law.'
Whenever the illness flares up,
recite this,
and hold the talismans,
and the illness will be cured."
At that time, Wéi Shì's youngest daughter,
aged seven,
also suffered from malaria.
Beside her, she saw something
resembling a black dog with coarse fur.
The deity said:
"This is what is making you ill.
Quickly capture and kill it,
and your illness will surely be cured.
Otherwise,
your two young maidservants
will also contract malaria."
Wéi Shì killed the dog in her dream.
When she awoke,
she passed the incantation to Yì,
who recited it with utmost sincerity.
His illness was then cured.
Wéi Shì's daughter was also cured.
Everything happened as foretold.
Zhèng Guāng
Minister Zhèng Guāng of Zīqīng,
in the spring of the sixth year of Huìchāng,
dreamed that he was driving an ox cart,
carrying a propitious sun in the cart,
its light illuminating heaven and earth.
He held the reins himself,
traveling along a broad road.
Suddenly, he woke in alarm,
and marveled at the dream.
Over a month later,
Emperor Xuānzōng ascended the throne.
Due to his status as the emperor's maternal uncle,
he was repeatedly appointed as Minister and Military Governor of Zīqīng.
This indeed matched his earlier dream.
Sòng Yán,
after nearly ten attempts at the imperial examinations, had yet to gain fame.
In the eleventh year of Dàzhōng,
he was about to take the prefectural examination.
Originally named Yuè,
he once dozed off during the day
and felt as if someone told him:
"If Scholar Sòng wears a mountain on his head,
he will never achieve fame.
But if he removes it,
success will naturally follow."
Upon waking, he thought of removing it,
but could not name himself Yù.
So he removed the two 'dogs' (犭犭),
and changed his name to Yán.
When he took the prefectural examination,
Vice-Minister Féng Yá served as the examiner,
and he was recommended as the top candidate.
At that time, the Governor of Jīngzhào, Zhāng Yìfū, accused Féng
The Military Advisor was found guilty of favoritism in recommending candidates,
and was demoted to Registrar of Lǐzhōu.
As a result,
Sòng was demoted from first place to sixty-fifth.
When friends came to console him,
Sòng said:
"Next spring's affairs,
I am resigned to the uncertainty."
When Examiner Lǐ Pān announced the results,
Sòng Yán placed fourth in the final list.
Cáo Què
Cáo Què served as Commissioner of Finance,
and was also seen as a candidate for high ministerial office.
Once he dreamed of shaving his head to become a monk,
which troubled him greatly.
There was a scholar
known for his accurate dream interpretations.
Què summoned him
and recounted his dream.
The scholar said:
"I congratulate the Vice-Minister in advance,
for you will soon be promoted to high office.
Becoming a monk is called 'tonsure' (剃度)."
Not long after,
Chancellor Dù was appointed to govern Jiāngxī,
and Què was indeed appointed Chancellor.
Liú Réngōng
In his humble days, Liú Réngōng of Liáng
once dreamed of a Buddhist banner flying from his fingers.
A dream interpreter said:
"When you are forty-nine,
you will surely attain high military rank."
Later, as predicted,
he indeed became the Military Governor of Yōu.
Emperor Xīzōng of Táng
Emperor Xīzōng ascended the throne as Prince of Jìn,
talented from a young age,
though he had never understood the game of Go.
One night,
he dreamed that someone burned three volumes of Go manuals and made him swallow them.
Upon waking,
he summoned Go masters to play,
and every move he suggested
was unexpectedly brilliant.
Liú Tán
Vice-Director Liú Tán of Wáng Shǔ, originally named Shěn Yì,
once dreamed of a filial son
leading him up a sandalwood tree,
saying:
"Climb quickly."
Liú then climbed.
The filial son took out a crimson robe from his bosom
and told him to wear it.
Upon waking,
he changed his name to Tán.
Within a year,
the Governor of Shǔ Commandery requested Dù, an Evaluator, to serve as Deputy,
and petitioned for him to be appointed Palace Censor with Internal Service,
granting him crimson robes.
When the decree arrived,
Dù went into mourning and could not take up the post.
Dù then recommended Liú to the Governor.
The Governor petitioned for Tán,
and the official appointment was the same as Dù's earlier one.
The petition and recommendation were identical.
At that time, Liú was living in leisure and facing financial difficulties,
so Dù gave him a new crimson official robe.
This indeed fulfilled the dream.
The Young Lord of Jìn
In the late winter of the year Jiǎchén of Kāiyùn,
the Emperor of Jìn sent a palace eunuch to the Imperial Academy,
announcing to the scholars:
"Last night, I dreamed of a jade plate,
containing a jade bowl and a jade belt,
all intricately carved,
glowing and lovely.
What omen is this?
Report your interpretation immediately."
Chief Scholar Lǐ Shènyí and his colleagues submitted a memorial of congratulations,
stating that jade is the treasure of emperors,
the belt symbolizes achievements and vows,
and the plate and bowl represent safeguarding the imperial regalia.
It was an auspicious dream,
and they dared not interpret it otherwise.
Xīn Yínxùn
Xīn Yínsùn, an Academician of the Later Shǔ,
once lived for several years on Qīngchéng Mountain.
His residence was an ancient Daoist temple,
situated atop a peak,
inside which was a statue of the Imperial Aunt,
who was a daughter of Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng.
One night,
he dreamed that the Imperial Aunt summoned him
and said:
"You may eat apricot kernels;
they will make you intelligent and sharp,
vigorous even in old age,
with a mind that never wearies,
and they will also contribute to your longevity.
You possess a nature inclined toward the Way,
but you will not remain here long;
you must go forth to assist in governing the present age."
In the dream, Yínsùn bowed and requested the method,
which turned out to be the same as that in Shēn Tiānshī's *Treatise on Nourishing the Spirit*.
Yínsùn then ate them daily,
which kept him light and healthy in old age.
He lived beyond the age of seventy,
and still produced many writings.
He also dreamed of an endless stream of grass in his palm,
Later, he drafted imperial edicts for several years.
He also oversaw official selections,
his mental energy never flagging.
Thus, it is known that the immortal prescriptions in Shēn Tiānshī's *Treatise on Nourishing the Spirit*
can indeed be verified.
Hé Zhìyōng
Hé Zhìyōng
was the son of a merchant.
From childhood, he was intelligent, handsome, and fond of learning.
Once, he accompanied his uncle
and moored their boat at Wǎnkǒu.
That night, his uncle dreamed of a man who looked like an official,
riding a horse followed by several attendants,
coming and going along the riverbank.
He inspected the number of boats and people on each.
Then another person called from behind:
"Vice Director Hé is here,
do not disturb him."
The man replied:
"Understood,
I dare not disturb."
After waking,
his uncle inquired among people on neighboring boats,
but none were surnamed Hé.
So they moved their boat into a deep inlet.
The next day,
a great storm arose with huge waves,
and all the boats that had been moored there sank,
only the Hé family's boat survived.
His uncle then said to Zhìyōng:
"Our family has been poor and lowly for generations,
and I am old now.
That Vice Director Hé must be you!
Take good care of yourself."
Later, Zhìyōng gained recognition in Húnán,
serving as Military Commissioner Judge.
When King Mǎ Yīn of Chǔ declared himself emperor,
he appointed Zhìyōng as Vice Minister of Revenue and Academician of the Hànlín Academy.
Zhìyōng believed he would become chancellor,
holding the position of a senior mentor.
Later, King Mǎ Xīfàn succeeded to the throne,
relinquished the imperial title,
and appointed Zhìyōng as Military Commissioner Judge and Acting Vice Director.
He eventually died in office.
Guō Rénbiǎo
Guō Rénbiǎo, a clerk in the Eastern Palace of the Wú Kingdom, lived in Yěchéng.
north of the city.
In the jiǎyín year,
he fell seriously ill with a persistent disease.
Suddenly, he dreamed of a Daoist priest wearing a golden-flowered purple cape,
followed by a young attendant,
entering through his gate
and sitting in his hall.
Rénbiǎo was not very respectful at first,
and asked when his illness might be cured.
The Daoist sternly said:
"It could be severe."
Upon waking,
his illness worsened.
Several nights later,
he dreamed the same Daoist came again,
so he kowtowed and apologized humbly.
After a while,
the Daoist's expression softened,
and he asked for paper and brush.
Rénbiǎo thought he would write a prescription,
so he knelt and presented them.
The Daoist wrote and handed it to him;
the text said:
"The raging wind and storm can be pondered,
The crane gazes at the nest gate, folds its wings and flies.
The orthodox core of our Way can be relied upon,
The numbers of all things' origins lie herein,
If you cannot practice this, what will you do?"
In the dream, he did not understand its meaning,
and was about to ask,
but the young attendant waved his hand and said:
"You may not."
He bowed in thanks,
and the Daoist departed toward the northwest.
Thereafter, his illness was cured.
Wáng Yú
Wáng Yú, a military governor of È for the Wú Kingdom, was a minor officer in his youth.
He followed the army besieging Yǐngzhōu.
One night, he dreamed a Daoist priest told him:
"Tomorrow, a meteor will fall to the ground.
If you can avoid it,
you will rise to the rank of general or chancellor."
The next day,
the troops attacked the city,
and arrows and stones rained down from the walls.
Yú, holding his sword,
leaned against a palisade stake while directing the battle.
Suddenly, a large stone
struck that very stake and Yú directly.
Half of his armor was shattered to pieces,
yet Yú was unharmed.
He sighed and said:
"So that was the meteor."
From then on, he became self-assured,
and eventually attained high office.
Xiè È
The presented scholar Xiè È
lived in Nánkāng.
In front of his house was a stream,
a place where he often played.
When È was a child,
he once dreamed of bathing in the stream,
and someone gave him a container of pearls, saying:
"If you swallow these, young sir,
you will gain clarity and understanding."
È thought the larger ones were too big to swallow,
so he swallowed over sixty of the smaller ones.
When he grew up,
he excelled at writing poetry.
The presented scholar Péi Shuō selected over sixty of his best poems,
which circulated in the world.
Cuī Wàn'ān
Cuī Wàn'ān, Vice Minister of Agriculture in Jiāngnán,
was assigned to duty in Guǎnglíng.
He often suffered from a painful spleen disorder with diarrhea,
which left him extremely debilitated.
His family prayed at the shrine of the Earth Goddess.
That night,
Wàn'ān dreamed of a woman
wearing pearl earrings and pearl shoes,
dressed in five layers of garments,
all woven from cowrie shells and pearls.
She said to Wàn'ān:
"This illness can be cured.
I will now give you a prescription:
Take equal parts of costus root and nutmeg,
mix with jujube pulp to form pills,
and take twenty pills with rice water."
She added:
"This medicine is very heating,
stop once the illness subsides."
He took it as instructed,
and recovered.
Lǐ Lìng of Jiāngnán
In Jiāngnán, there was a man named Lǐ Lìng,
who had served in succession as magistrate of large districts,
and was provisionally appointed to the rank of Píngshì.
In the chaos of the times and in his old age,
he no longer had any desire for official service,
so he built a house to the west of Fǎyún Temple in Guǎnglíng,
planning to spend his remaining years there.
Once he dreamed of bundling straw and placing it on his head,
with a knife in his mouth,
and a knife in each hand,
walking into the water.
He found this very strange.
Soon after, Sūn Rú captured Guǎnglíng,
and Sūn Rú’s general Lǐ Qióng stationed troops at Fǎyún Temple.
He often stayed at Lǐ Lìng’s house,
serving Lǐ Lìng as a father.
After Sūn Rú died,
Mǎ Yīn and Liú Jiànfēng, subordinate generals under Xuānchéng,
led their troops southward.
Lǐ Qióng then forced Lǐ Lìng to go with them.
When Mǎ Yīn seized Húnán,
Lǐ Qióng became the Guìguǎn Observation Commissioner.
He appointed Lǐ Lìng as magistrate of Lìpǔ.
This was the fulfillment of the earlier dream.
Máo Zhènfǔ
Máo Zhènfǔ of the pseudo-Wú state
had served as district magistrate multiple times.
When he was selected for assignment to Guǎnglíng,
he dreamed of swallowing the sun.
After waking up,
his abdomen still felt hot.
He asked the Attendant Censor Yáng Tíngshì about it.
Yáng said:
"This dream is extremely significant,
and not something you can bear.
But as far as you are concerned,
you should become an official at the Chìwū Field."
It turned out exactly as he said.
Xiāo Jí
During the Dàyè era,
someone dreamed of a phoenix perching on his hand,
and deeply considered it a good omen.
He went to Xiāo Jí to have it interpreted.
Xiāo Jí said:
"This is an extremely inauspicious dream."
The dreamer resented this,
and thought it was nonsense.
More than ten days later,
the dreamer’s mother died.
He sent a close acquaintance to ask Xiāo Jí for the reason,
and Xiāo Jí said:
"The phoenix will not perch except on a parasol tree,
and will not eat except bamboo seeds.
The reason it perched on your hand
is that your hand had the image of a parasol tree and bamboo.
The Book of Rites says:
'The mourning staff for a father is made of bamboo,
the mourning staff for a mother is made of parasol wood.'
Therefore, I knew there must be a grave sorrow."
Hóu Jūnjí
During the Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty,
Hóu Jūnjí conspired with the commoner Chéngqián,
and felt uneasy.
Suddenly he dreamed of two armored soldiers escorting him to a place,
where he saw a man wearing a tall hat with bristling whiskers,
who shouted to his attendants,
"Fetch Hóu Jūnjí’s commanding bone!"
Soon several men came with butcher knives,
opened his skull and right arm,
and each took out a piece of bone,
shaped like a fish tail.
He then woke up mumbling,
with his head and arm still aching.
From then on, his heart palpitated and his strength waned,
to the point where he could not draw a thirty-pound bow.
He wanted to confess,
but hesitated and was defeated.
Cuī Shí
Táng Right Assistant Lú Cángyòng and Secretariat Director Cuī Shí were part of the Tàipíng faction,
and were exiled to Lǐngnán.
When they reached Jīngzhōu,
Cuī Shí dreamed at night of sitting below a lecture seat listening to the Dharma while looking in a mirror.
He asked the skilled dream interpreter Zhāng Yóu.
Zhāng said to Assistant Lú:
"Director Cuī is in great danger.
Dreaming of sitting below listening to a lecture
means the Dharma comes from above.
The character for mirror (鏡) has the metal radical (金) and the character jìng (竟).
Does it end today?"
Soon, the Censor Lù Yímiǎn arrived with an imperial decree ordering Cuī Shí to commit suicide.
Lǐ Línfǔ
Lǐ Línfǔ dreamed of a person,
slender and tall with whiskers,
who pressed close to Lǐ Línfǔ,
and would not leave no matter how he pushed.
Lǐ Línfǔ woke up and said:
"This is Péi Kuān plotting to replace me."
Dù Xuán
Dù Xuán of Luòzhōu had an ox,
which he cherished greatly.
One night he dreamed the ox had two tails,
and asked the diviner Lǐ Xiānyào about it.
Lǐ said:
"The character for ox (牛) with two tails
becomes the character for 'lose' (失)."
After several days,
he indeed lost it.
Zhào Jiǎo
Ān Lùshān used the excuse of punishing the evil around the emperor
to blame the Yáng family,
submitting a memorial detailing their crimes,
and sent a dispatch to the Eastern Capital to deliver the memorial.
Those discussing it thought the wording was unfavorable to the Yáng family,
making it difficult to transmit.
They also feared that Ān Lùshān might later be executed,
so they sent the Dàlǐ Chief Clerk Zhào Jiǎo to deliver the memorial to the capital.
Emperor Xuánzōng read it and was displeased,
but only ordered Zhào Jiǎo to return.
Zhào Jiǎo left the Secretariat
and met Yáng Guózhōng,
who asked:
"Delivering the barbarian’s memorial,
wasn’t it exhausting?
Fortunately, it did not contain slanderous statements.
If there had been malicious words,
would you still have delivered it?"
He then shouted at him to leave quickly.
Zhào Jiǎo returned to Xìkǒu Station,
feeling very anxious.
He sat on a rope-seat chair in the hall,
and suddenly felt as if in a dream.
He suddenly felt the rope-seat chair rise several zhang off the ground.
Looking up,
he saw a man in armor standing in the middle,
shouting orders to over twenty attendants
to seize him.
Though he was being dragged,
another man in the hall,
wearing a short hat and purple clothes, came and said:
"This is not Jiǎng Qīng;
he should not be killed."
He was then released.
A few days later, Zhào Jiǎo returned to Luòyáng,
and the rebels soon arrived as well.
Zhào Jiǎo and several of his colleagues guarded the gate awaiting orders,
and were all captured and bound.
Zhào Jiǎo was tall,
with dignified bearing,
and stood at the front of the line
when they went to see the rebel general Tián Qiánzhēn.
Tián Qiánzhēn stood in armor,
exactly the man he had seen in the dream earlier.
The rebel shouted at Zhào Jiǎo:
"What kind of petty man are you,
daring to resist the imperial army?"
He ordered his attendants to beat him to death.
Just as the guards began to act,
Yán Zhuāng hurriedly came from below the hall and said:
"This is not Jiǎng Qīng;
he should not be punished."
Tián Qiánzhēn then asked his surname,
and he replied:
"My surname is Zhào."
Thus he was released.
Next came Jiǎng,
who was then killed.
Lǐ Shāoyún
Lǐ Shāoyún of Lǒngxī was the son-in-law of Lú Ruòxū of Fànyáng.
He was unrestrained and frivolous by nature,
fond of indulging in drinking and gathering for feasts.
One night, his wife dreamed of capturing Shāoyún and over a dozen others,
mixed with courtesans,
all with their hair disheveled and stripped to the waist,
bound together with a long rope,
and driven away in a line.
They wept and wailed, looking back at his wife to bid farewell.
Startled awake,
her tears soaked the pillow and mat,
and she told him about it.
Shāoyún had also dreamed the same,
exactly matching her account.
Greatly frightened and disgusted,
he then gave up meat and blood,
recited the Diamond Sutra,
and frequently invited monks for vegetarian feasts.
For three years, nothing happened.
Later, as the dream seemed increasingly unfulfilled,
he gradually became lax and indulgent again.
At a gathering with friends,
they pressured him with wine and roasted meat.
Shāoyún had never been restrained,
so he indulged in wine and meat as before.
The following year on the Shangsi Festival,
he went boating on the Qǔjiāng River with over ten others, including Lǐ Méng, Péi Shìnán, and Liáng Bāo.
They extensively selected famous courtesans from Cháng'ān
and greatly indulged in singing and entertainment.
Just as the wine was at its peak, the boat capsized,
and all drowned.
Lǐ Shūjì
Lǐ Shūjì, the Investigating Censor,
along with his elder brother Zhòngyún, both passed the imperial examinations as jìnshì
and were renowned in their time.
In the early Dàlì era,
Shūjì died.
Over a year later,
his brother-in-law was sleeping together with Zhòngyún
when he suddenly dreamed of Shūjì.
They met with lingering affection.
Speaking of Zhòngyún,
Shūjì’s voice and expression were sorrowful as he said:
"The realms of the living and the dead are utterly separate;
there is no way for us to reunite in joy.
Only after a hundred years
will we be able to gather again.
I have a poem
that you can recite and present to my elder brother.
The poem says:
'Suddenly parted without a set date,
In darkness, regret lingers on.
Though Cháng'ān is not far,
No letter can be sent across.'"
Several years later,
Zhòngyún also died.
Lǐ Sù
Liáng Wǔgōng Lǐ Sù,
as the son of extraordinary merit,
led the armies of the Yuánhé era,
captured Cài and broke Yùn.
Over years of campaigning,
capturing cities and taking fortresses,
he always prioritized benevolence and forbearance,
never unjustly killing a single person.
His sincere trust in dealing with others
stemmed from deep earnestness.
In the autumn of the first year of Chángqìng,
he was summoned back to the capital from his posts as Military Governor of Wèibó, Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and Participating in Determining Governmental Matters.
As he was about to enter Luòyáng,
his guard commander Shí Jìwǔ was already in Luòyáng.
Jìwǔ dreamed that Liánggōng was ascending the Tiānjīn Bridge from the north,
with Jìwǔ leading the way.
The procession of the宰相 was imposing, with shouts shaking the ground.
There were eight Daoist priests
on horseback,
holding crimson banners and streamers,
coming from the south intending to ascend.
The outriders shouted at them,
to which they replied:
"We are here to welcome the Immortal Lord;
what do we care about a宰相?"
They beckoned Jìwǔ to speak with them,
and Jìwǔ urged his horse forward.
The banner-holding Daoist priest said:
"Remember my words
and relay them to the相公."
His words were:
"Reining in the steed, I ascend the golden gate,
Riding the carriage, I board the Han raft.
Fleeting fame—what is there to cling to?
Soaring high, I enter the misty haze."
Jìwǔ originally could not read,
and his memory was poor,
but as he followed the Daoist priest and listened,
he grasped it upon hearing it a second time.
The Daoist priest said:
"You have remembered it;
you may first inform the相公."
Then he awoke with a start,
sweat drenching his body.
Delighted, he thought that even a相国 could ascend to immortality,
let alone ordinary officials!
Three days later,
Liánggōng indeed ascended the Tiānjīn Bridge from the north,
with Jìwǔ leading the way.
They then went to rest at Tiāngōng Temple,
and over a month later, he passed away.
People of the time believed that his benevolent, forbearing, upright, and sincere heart
was certainly in harmony with the Dao.
Who knows if he was not an exiled immortal whose time had come to return?
Xuē Cúnchéng
Xuē Cúnchéng, Vice Censor-in-Chief,
in the late Yuánhé era,
moved from the Censorate to the position of Supervising Secretary.
Before a full year had passed,
he returned as Deputy Head of the Censorate.
The Censorate was pure and strict,
rarely touched by worldly dust.
On the day of his return,
he felt a vast sense of leisure and openness.
Upon entering the hall, he chanted:
"Rolling up the blinds, I wonder if a guest has arrived;
Stepping inside, I feel like a monk returning home."
A month later,
the gatekeeper, not fully asleep during a daytime nap,
vaguely saw several dozen novice monks
holding incense, flowers, banners, and canopies,
chanting Buddhist hymns,
entering the Censorate one after another.
The gatekeeper shouted at them:
"This is the Censorate!
What religious ceremony is this,
entering with such loud voices?"
One of the monks identified himself:
"I am Shídá,
a disciple of the Vice Censor-in-Chief,
here to welcome my master.
My master is in the Censorate;
may we enter to greet him?"
The gatekeeper said:
"This Vice Censor-in-Chief
holds a high position in the Censorate
and is not a member of the clergy.
How dare you enter the Censorate gates?"
He was about to seize them.
Shídá said:
"The Vice Censor-in-Chief was originally the great virtuous arhat of the Jìngjū Temple on the eastern peak of Mount Sumeru.
Because he mistakenly spoke with heavenly beings,
his thoughts inclined toward the mundane,
he was exiled to the mortal world for fifty years.
His time is now complete and he must return,
so we have come to welcome him.
This is beyond your understanding."
As the gatekeeper was about to rush and report,
he suddenly awoke.
Several days later,
Xuēgōng fell ill in the Censorate and passed away.
Quietly calculating his age,
it was exactly fifty years.
Lǐ Bólián
Méi Bóchéng, a minor officer in the Wēiyuǎn Army, was skilled in interpreting dreams.
There was an entertainer named Lǐ Bólián who traveled to Jīngzhōu to beg for money
and obtained a hundred hu of rice.
Upon returning,
he sent his younger brother to fetch it,
but the brother did not arrive by the appointed time.
That night, Bólián dreamed of washing a white horse
and went to consult Bóchéng about it.
Bóchéng pondered and said:
"Entertainers often use reverse language.
'Washing a white horse'
means 'pouring out'
—white rice.
What you are worried about
might involve the perils of wind and water."
A few days later, his younger brother arrived
and indeed reported that the boat had capsized in the Wèi River,
with not a single grain remaining.
Zhāng Zhān
In the Jiānghuái region, there was a man named Wáng Shēng,
who advertised himself as an interpreter of dreams.
A merchant named Zhāng Zhǎn was about to return home.
He dreamed that he was cooking in a mortar,
so he went to ask Wáng Shēng about it.
Wáng Shēng said:
"When you return home, you will not see your wife.
Cooking in a mortar
means there is no pot."
When the merchant arrived home,
his wife had already passed away several months earlier.
Yú Jǐn
There was a man who dreamed of a pine tree growing in front of his door,
and another who dreamed of a jujube tree growing on his roof.
They went to ask the Reminder of Omissions, Yú Jǐn, about it.
Yú Jǐn said:
"Pine trees are planted in graveyards,
and the character for 'jujube' (棗) is composed of two 'come' (來) characters,
which symbolizes the repeated calling of the soul."
Later, both men died.
Lú Yànxù
Lú Yànxù, the Granary Officer of Xǔzhōu, had a latrine at his residence.
During a summer rainstorm,
water flooded it,
and in a moment, it all drained away.
Yànxù sent someone to investigate,
and they saw an ancient tomb below,
inside which was a pottery coffin.
Inside lay a woman,
around twenty years old,
pure white and serene,
with fingernails five or six inches long,
and more than ten golden hairpins in her hair.
An inscription stated:
"This is a person from the Qín dynasty.
A thousand years later, she will be opened by Lú Yànxù,
as fate dictates.
Closing it is auspicious,
opening it is inauspicious."
There was also a precious mirror,
with golden flowers on the back.
When held up to the sun,
the flowers appeared like golden wheels.
Yànxù took the hairpins, mirror, and several dozen other items,
and then closed the tomb.
That night, he dreamed of the woman saying:
"Why did you take my playthings?"
She had an angry expression.
After a year, Yànxù died.
Liǔ Zōngyuán
Vice Director Liǔ Zōngyuán was summoned to the capital from his post as Military Advisor of Yǒngzhōu,
hoping for an important reappointment.
One day,
he went to a fortune-teller to ask about his fate,
and told him about a dream,
saying:
"My surname is Liǔ (willow).
Last night, I dreamed of a willow tree falling to the ground.
Is this not an ill omen?"
The fortune-teller said:
"Do not worry,
but I fear you will be appointed to a distant post."
When asked to explain,
he said:
"In life, one plants a willow tree;
in death, one becomes willow wood.
The word for 'wood' (木) sounds like 'to govern' (牧).
Will you not be governing Liǔzhōu?"
It turned out exactly as he said.
Later, he died in Liǔzhōu.
Wèi Zhōngxíng
When Wèi Zhōngxíng was a Secretary in the Central Secretariat,
the son of an old friend came to seek an official appointment
and approached Wèi for help.
Wèi gladly agreed.
Just before the list of rejected candidates was to be posted,
the man suddenly dreamed of riding a donkey across water,
stumbling and falling into the water,
but climbing ashore with his boots not even wet.
The candidate was acquainted with the Archivist Hán Gāo,
so he went to visit him.
Hán was drunk,
and half-jokingly said:
"Your appointment this year will not go through!
According to the dream,
Wèi Zhōngxíng has betrayed you,
and your feet are not wet."
When the list was posted,
he was indeed rejected.
Hán was a learned man,
the nephew of Vice Director Hán.
Zhāng Shěnggōng
The magistrate of Zhījiāng County, Zhāng Tīng,
had a son named Shěnggōng.
After Tīng died,
Shěnggōng remained in Zhījiāng.
There was a man named Zhāng Chuí,
who had failed the imperial examination as a xiùcai,
and was staying in Shǔ.
He and Shěnggōng had never met.
In the eighth year of the Tàihé era,
Shěnggōng was napping during the day
when he suddenly dreamed of a man.
The man claimed to be from the same clan,
named Chuí,
and they interacted,
enjoying each other's company all day.
As he was about to leave,
he left behind a poem as a gift, which said:
"Sorrow upon sorrow,
the autumn hall bears the colors of a hundred years.
But I alone am lost in vastness,
encountering the Cold Food Festival in the desolate outskirts."
Shěnggōng woke with a start,
quickly wrote down the poem,
and died a few days later.
Wáng Yùn
The presented scholar Wáng Yùn
was elegant and talented in literary composition,
especially skilled at describing objects.
He wrote the "Rhapsody on Seeing You Off at the Southern Bank,"
which was praised by poets.
In the second year of the Huìchāng era,
his friend Lù Xiūfú suddenly dreamed of being taken to a place
where attendants stopped him outside a screen.
He saw what looked like dozens of petty officials,
with Wáng Yùn among them.
Lù tried to approach him,
but Yùn's face showed shame.
Lù insisted on speaking with him,
and Yùn said tearfully:
"I recently received an official post,
but I am ashamed for people to know."
Pointing to the others,
he said, "These are all colleagues of mine."
Xiūfú then woke up in a daze.
At the time, Yùn was living in Yángzhōu,
and his son was in Tàipíng.
Xiūfú, troubled by the dream,
at dawn
went to inquire for news from Yùn's family,
and received a letter saying Wáng had gone to Luò.
Seven days later,
the news of his death arrived.
Calculating the date of his death,
it turned out to be the night of Lù's dream.
Liǔ Líng
When the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries, Wéi Zhèngguàn, was taking the imperial examinations,
he once went to Rǔzhōu.
The Prefect of Rǔzhōu, Liǔ Líng, kept him on as a Military Judge.
Liǔ once dreamed of someone presenting a document
that stated he owed 1,700 bundles of firewood.
He asked Wéi to interpret it,
and Wéi said:
"Firewood
is fuel wood.
Does this mean you will not be here much longer?"
Over a month later,
Liǔ fell ill and died.
He had always been poor,
so Wéi made arrangements for him.
Rice, wheat, silk, and coins
had all been requested from the government months earlier.
Only the 1,700 bundles of firewood owed by the government remained.
When Wéi examined the documents,
he realized it matched Liǔ's earlier dream.
Cuī Xiá
The Secretariat Drafter Cuī Xiá's younger brother Cuī Gǔ
married the daughter of Lǐ Xù.
Lǐ was the Prefect of Cáozhōu,
and ordered the Military Commander Guó Shàonán to manage the wedding carriage barrier.
Later, while Shàonán was sleeping,
he suddenly dreamed of Cuī's daughter in a hall.
The girl stood on the west side of the bed,
while Cuī Gǔ was on the east side of the bed.
The girl held a red paper,
inscribed with a poem,
and smilingly handed it to Gǔ,
who then recited it aloud.
The poem said:
"Do not keep me for chastity's sake,
let him follow the strings and pipes.
Beauty cannot long endure,
who knows how many years remain?"
One year after the dream,
Cuī Gǔ's wife died.
Sū Jiǎn
Sū Jiǎn passed the imperial examination,
and returned to Wú to visit his family.
When he reached Chéngchéng County in Tóngzhōu,
he stopped at the county tower.
After getting drunk,
he dreamed that his wife took a brush and inkstone,
retrieved red paper from a case,
cut off several inches and composed a poem, saying:
"The Chǔ River water flat as a mirror,
white birds fly all around.
How much land is there in Jīnlíng?
Once gone, I know not when to return."
Jiǎn also cut Shǔ paper and composed a poem, saying:
"Returning to Wú, eastward I descend to Chéngchéng,
in the tower, the clear breeze, wine half-sober.
I think of reaching home as spring is about to...
dusk,
a thousand crabapple trees have already withered."
After the poems were finished,
they were both placed under the mat where he slept.
