He also saw his wife severely whipping the little maid Xiǎoqīng whom Jiǎn had brought along.
Upon waking,
he found the poems under the mat,
and looking at the red paper in the case,
there was also a cut mark.
That day, Xiǎoqīng suddenly fell seriously ill.
Then they traveled eastward,
and by the time they reached Èyuè,
they abandoned land and boarded a boat,
and Xiǎoqīng's illness worsened.
Thirty-some lǐ from home,
she died.
Xiǎoqīng said in a dream:
"Bury me behind the new grave on the northern bank."
When they buried her on the northern bank,
they encountered a new grave,
and buried her according to the agreement in the dream.
When he returned home,
his wife had already died.
Asking about the date,
it was the day of the dream in Chéngchéng County.
Visiting her grave,
it was in front of Xiǎoqīng's burial mound.
It was then late spring,
and all around the grave,
there were many crabapple flowers.
Wéi Jiǎn
Wéi Jiǎn sat for the imperial examination but did not pass.
He often had a beautiful concubine,
who one day clutched her chest and died.
Jiǎn grieved and mourned deeply,
almost unable to bear the sorrow.
Raising wine and reciting poetry,
his sadness and resentment were palpable.
Thus he chanted:
"The precious sword transforms into a dragon, returning to the azure heavens,
Cháng'é follows the moon down to the Yellow Springs.
A cup of wine faces the late spring,
lonely by the book window, I resent sleeping alone."
One day,
he suddenly dreamed that the concubine said:
"My life was limited in length,
unable to fulfill my duties as a wife,
tears streaming down,
there will be a later meeting.
Now I respond to your poem,
improvising:
'Spring rain misty, the sky unseen,
outside every home, willows and mist blend.
Now heartbroken, vainly shedding tears,
laughter and joy will be pursued again in another year.'"
Jiǎn remained sorrowful all day,
and later dreamed of the concubine again,
who said:
"We shall meet soon."
Upon waking, his spirit was dazed,
so he inscribed:
"White waves endlessly recede, never to return,
floating clouds vanish, the sun sets in the west.
On Qín Shǐhuáng's tomb, the thousand-year-old trees,
even silver ducks and golden mallards turn to ashes."
Later, he indeed passed away,
all matching the omens.
Junior Minister Zhū
During the Shǔ of Wáng,
there was a Junior Minister Zhū,
whose name is not recorded.
Poor and lowly, he was a guest in Chéngdū,
and slept at an inn.
In a dream, someone knocked on the door looking for Junior Minister Zhū,
the voice very stern.
Startled awake, he inquired about it,
but there was no trace or sound.
He slept again,
and in the dream, someone called out repeatedly.
Soon he saw a person,
holding a scroll in hand, saying:
"Is Junior Minister Zhū really here?"
Zhū said:
"My surname is the same,
but I am not the Junior Minister."
The person then rolled up both ends of the document,
leaving only one line,
covering the top and bottom with his hand,
and indeed there were the three characters "Zhū Shǎoqīng."
Then another person,
led a horse straight in from outside.
Saying:
"Junior Minister, receive this."
Zhū looked at it;
the horse had no front legs,
stumbling sideways with each step,
crawling forward,
its appearance extremely miserable.
Zhū was greatly alarmed and woke up,
and always felt troubled by it.
Later, when the King of Shǔ established his state,
relatives and acquaintances recommended him,
and he rose to the position of Junior Minister of the Court of the Imperial Granaries.
Not long after,
he developed sores on his knees,
and both legs fell off below the knees.
After suffering for ten days,
he died on the fifth day of the fifth month.
This was the omen of the horse dream.
Qín Zhì
Mèng Shǔ's Vice Minister of the Ministry of Works Liú Yìdù,
while serving as Prefect of Yún'ān.
There was a Commandant Qín Zhì,
who dreamed he was with his friend Hú Zhēn in front of a government office hall.
They saw several people
leading in Lord Liú,
who was bound with the five woods,
alone and silent,
explaining and analyzing the reasoning,
as if three or five people were confronting him.
After a long time, he withdrew,
and sat under the corridor,
seeing those bringing food,
all carrying fresh blood.
Qín then asked,
and someone nearby answered:
"It is because the lord made errors in sentencing,
and he has been summoned for several days already."
Then he awoke.
Early in the morning,
he told Hú Zhēn about it,
and Zhēn said:
"What I dreamed last night
completely matches yours.
Could it be we shared the same dream?"
Thus they kept it secret.
That day, Lord Liú indeed chanted a ten-verse "Poem of Reflections."
One of them said:
"Yesterday, I still wore a maiden's bun,
now my beard covers my jaw.
The Purple Pavilion holds no attraction for me,
the green mountains I intend to retreat to."
Now his poems are all engraved on stone,
and people are all surprised by their meaning.
Not many days later, he died.
Was it not because there were errors in his sentencing?
Mèng Déchóng
Mèng Déchóng, the Junior Minister of the Imperial Clan of the Shu state,
was the son of Yānwáng Yíyè.
Relying on his noble lineage,
he was unrestrained, arrogant, and eccentric.
Once, while offering incense at the Grand Temple,
he brought a courtesan along.
One night,
he dreamed of an old man reprimanding him,
who then took a brush from the table,
shouted at him to open his hand,
and wrote the characters "jiǔ shí" (ninety) in large script before he woke up.
The next day,
while speaking with guests about this matter,
he said himself, "The old man reprimanded me
because he cared for me.
Writing 'jiǔ shí'
means he bestowed upon me a lifespan of ninety years."
A guest named Fēng Liǎn teased him, saying:
"The characters 'jiǔ shí'
actually form the cursive character 'zú' (to die).
Is this not an ominous sign for you, Junior Minister?"
Within ten days,
he indeed passed away.
Sūn Guāngxiàn
When Jīngnán Jiéduìshǐ Gāo Bǎoróng fell ill,
his staff officer Sūn Guāngxiàn dreamed that he was sitting with colleagues by the pond at Zhǔgōng,
while Bǎoróng was alone in the western hall,
attended only by his concubines.
Soon, Gāo Bǎoróng's younger brother Bǎoxù summoned him onto a bridge,
handed him a brush and inkstone,
and ordered Guāngxiàn to direct troop movements,
while also sending two or three attendants from the hall to shield Guāngxiàn,
so that Bǎoróng would not see him from afar.
After a short while,
officers equipped with quivers and bows lined up awaiting orders.
Next, he saw the officer in charge of tallies, Yán Guāngchǔ, striding forward in leather armor,
holding two black objects in his hands:
one was shiny like black lacquered boots,
and the other was ordinary boots.
He said to Guāngxiàn:
"I once lost two sticks of ink,
and was demoted and reprimanded by the king for it.
Now I have finally found them."
After a long while, he woke from the dream.
The next day,
he recounted it to his colleagues.
A month later, Bǎoróng passed away.
The tally office officer Yán Guāngchǔ submitted a petition requesting instructions on reversing the tallies.
Guāngxiàn asked the military commander Wáng Jiǎ to adjudicate the matter.
Ink is a dark, black substance,
and tallies are also black,
which is close to an ominous sign.
This matched the earlier dream,
referring to the reversal of the two tallies.
Lù Jì
In the Jiangnán region, Lù Jì served as the Prefect of Chángzhōu,
but did not take up the post,
instead becoming the Deputy Commissioner of Huáinán.
His nature was gentle, refined, and dignified,
and he was highly esteemed by his contemporaries.
Deputy Commissioner Lǐ Chéngsì was especially close to him.
In the ninth month of the yǐchǒu year,
Chéngsì and several guests visited him.
Jì calmly said:
"At this time next year,
I will bid farewell to all of you."
Chéngsì asked the reason,
and he replied:
"I once dreamed that someone summoned me on horseback,
stopping west of Dàmíng Temple,
a few li away,
arriving at a large mansion
with a plaque reading 'Yángmíng Prefecture.'
Entering the gate, to the west,
there was another large gate facing east.
I dismounted and entered a room.
After a while,
an official led me to stand below the steps.
Inside the gate were two green-robed officials
holding a tray.
On the tray was a document.
A purple-robed official holding a tablet
took the document and proclaimed:
'Jì has been human for three lifetimes,
each time practicing kindness and filial piety.
Having achieved merit and success,
he is fit to receive this appointment.
He shall be appointed Vice Minister of Yángmíng Prefecture,
overseeing the affairs of the Nine Provinces.
On the seventeenth day of the ninth month next year,
he shall assume his duties in this prefecture.'
Then I was sent back on horseback,
and suddenly I awoke.
My spiritual fate is already determined,
and it cannot be changed."
All the guests laughed in disbelief.
By the ninth month of the following year,
they sent messengers daily to inquire about his well-being.
On the sixteenth day,
Chéngsì and the guests who had previously visited went to see him again,
saying:
"You are supposed to assume your duties tomorrow,
yet you seem perfectly fine now?"
Jì said:
"Everything in the prefecture is prepared,
and I will depart tomorrow."
Chéngsì said:
"I have always respected you as an elder,
but are you not speaking like a sorcerer now?"
Jì said:
"Only you and I are fated.
One day, we will surely be neighbors."
Chéngsì fell silent and left.
The next day, Jì indeed passed away
and was buried at Zhūyú Bay.
Later, Chéngsì served as the Prefect of Chǔzhōu and passed away,
and was buried north of Jì's grave.
Zhōu Yánhàn
Zhōu Yánhàn, a proofreader for the crown prince in the Jiangnán region,
was fond of Daoist practices
and diligently pursued elixir consumption.
He once dreamed that a deity handed him a scroll,
resembling a Daoist scripture,
with each line consisting of seven characters.
He only remembered the last line:
"Beside the purple beard lies cinnabar."
Yánhàn woke up delighted,
believing it foretold the efficacy of cinnabar.
He served in Jiànyè and passed away there,
buried beside the mausoleum of Emperor Wǔ of Wú.
He had no wife or children,
only a maidservant named Dānshā (Cinnabar).
Wáng Zhān
Wáng Zhān, the magistrate of Qiánhuà County, resigned and returned to Jiànyè,
anchoring his boat on the Qínhuái River.
He fell gravely ill.
He dreamed of a red-robed official holding a summons, saying:
"Your life has come to an end,
and you are now summoned."
Zhān said:
"I dare not refuse my fate,
but the boat is cramped.
I wish to request a reprieve
so that I may go ashore to arrange my residence,
with no fear."
The official agreed,
setting a five-day deadline,
and said, "At dawn on that day,
I will come for you."
After waking,
he was able to get out of bed,
rented a house himself,
prepared funeral items,
taught his son the rituals of mourning,
and summoned relatives to bid farewell.
When the day arrived,
he lay peacefully on his bed.
At dawn, he passed away.
Xíng Táo
Xíng Táo, a judicial officer in the Jiangnán region,
in the guǐmǎo year,
dreamed that someone told him:
"You will become the Prefect of Jīngzhōu."
Later, he was appointed magistrate of Jīng County in Xuānzhōu.
After his term ended,
he dreamed again of the same person telling him:
"All the officials in Xuānzhōu counties
will be replaced next spring,
but your official appointment will not arrive."
Xíng was deeply troubled by this.
By the following spring,
he was dismissed and returned.
Someone recommended Xíng for the position of Vice Director of the Water Bureau.
The appointment document was issued but lost by the responsible office.
After more than twenty days of requests,
he ultimately died before assuming the post.
Emperor Yáng
In the fourth year of the Wǔdé era,
after the pacification of the Eastern Capital,
the new books in the treasure repository of the Guānwén Hall, numbering about eight thousand volumes, were to be transported back to the capital.
Shàngguān Wèi dreamed of Emperor Yáng,
who loudly rebuked him, saying:
"Why are you taking my books to the capital?"
At that time, Sòng Zūnguì, the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury, was overseeing the transport,
managing the dispatch from the Eastern Capital.
He then loaded the books at Shǎnzhōu,
placing them on a large ship,
intending to transport them to the capital.
On the river, they encountered a storm and capsized,
and not a single volume survived.
Shàngguān Wèi again dreamed of the emperor,
who joyfully said:
"I have already recovered the books."
During his lifetime,
the emperor cherished books and historical records.
Although they accumulated like mountains,
not a single character was allowed to be taken out.
After his demise,
his spirit still clung to them with affection and reluctance.
As for the new books in the treasure repository,
they were all secret books from the Dàyè era.
Dòulú Róng
At the beginning of the Shàngyuán era,
Dòulú Róng died while serving as Deputy Prefect of Wēnzhōu.
Róng's wife was the daughter of Princess Jīnhé.
The princess had once married into the Bìyè tribe,
which had submitted to the empire.
After the king of Bìyè died,
the princess returned.
When Róng went to serve in Wēnzhōu,
the princess accompanied him and lived in the prefecture for several years.
At the beginning of the Bǎoyìng era,
the bandit Yuán Cháo from Línhǎi Mountain captured Táizhōu.
The princess's daughter dreamed at night of a person,
with disheveled hair and bleeding,
who said to her:
"Wēnzhōu will soon fall into chaos.
You should leave quickly.
If not,
you will surely suffer disaster."
When she awoke,
she recounted the dream.
The princess said:
"Dreams are often inverted and confused;
how can they be trusted?"
After a short while, she fell asleep again,
and the daughter dreamed of Róng,
who said:
"The person with disheveled hair just now
was me, your father-in-law.
I am now a general in the underworld.
Eastern Zhèjiāng is about to fall,
and I want my wife and daughter to leave.
You should heed this.
Do not cling to wealth and possessions."
The daughter again told the princess about it.
At that time, rice was expensive in Jiāngdōng,
but cheap in Wēnzhōu.
The princess had people purchase several thousand bolts of Wú silk,
so she was reluctant to leave.
Another day,
the daughter dreamed of her father, who said:
"The eight prefectures of Eastern Zhèjiāng
have been captured by Yuán Cháo.
If your mother does not leave soon,
she will surely suffer hardship."
As he spoke, he wept.
The princess then moved to Guāzhōu.
When Guāzhōu fell,
she fled with only her life,
exactly as foretold in the dream.
Yáng Zhāochéng
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
a man named Jiǎ from Luòyáng was appointed Magistrate of Shífāng in Guǎnghàn,
and he took his family to his post.
When they were about seven lǐ east of Báitǔdiàn,
his wife, Duàn shì,
was thrown from her horse into a pit and died.
She was buried in the mountains.
Two years later,
Yáng Zhāochéng from Hóngnóng, serving as Granary Officer of Yìzhōu,
traveled to Guǎnghàn.
Setting out at dawn,
his wife, Dòu shì, suddenly fell asleep on her horse
and leaned backward.
Zhāochéng dismounted to steady the horse
and repeatedly called to her,
but she remained unconscious
until they reached Báitǔ, where she awoke.
She said:
"Just now, I dreamed of a woman,
wearing a green single-layer skirt and a white cloth blouse,
about thirty years old,
with a beautiful and charming appearance.
She stopped my horse,
wept sorrowfully for a long time,
and said her surname was Duàn,
the wife of Magistrate Jiǎ of Shífāng.
She died here,
and her body remains in the mountains.
Her lonely soul wanders adrift,
unable to bear the solitude.
She said that if you, madam, return to the capital later,
she has an elder brother named so-and-so,
currently serving as Merit Officer in Jīngzhào.
Could you visit him
and ask him to retrieve her soul,
so it may return to her hometown?
She earnestly entrusted this to me,
and after speaking, she left."
That evening, Zhāochéng stayed at Báitǔ
and asked the innkeeper about the dream in detail.
The innkeeper said:
"The grave of Magistrate Jiǎ's wife
is about six or seven lǐ from here.
She fell into a pit and died,
and was buried in the mountains.
It has been two years already."
The details of the story
matched the dream.
Zhāochéng found this deeply strange
and recorded the event.
Later, when he went to the capital on official business,
he sought out the Duàn family
and told them the whole story.
The Duàn family wept in sorrow,
and they sent someone to retrieve the coffin,
burying it properly.
Magistrate of Fúgōu
A certain Magistrate of Fúgōu named Jì,
whose surname is unknown,
died in the second year of the Dàlì era.
Half a year later,
his wife dreamed of meeting Jì.
She asked him about the punishments and blessings in the underworld.
Jì said:
"In life, I was a Jìnshì,
but I fell into frivolity and disrespect.
Sometimes I slandered poetry and prose,
sometimes I disparaged people.
Now I am under the jurisdiction of the underworld.
Every day, two snakes and three centipedes are sent
to enter and exit through my seven orifices,
causing me immense suffering,
unbearable pain.
According to the law, I must endure this punishment for three hundred and sixty days.
After the punishment ends,
I may be reborn.
Recently, due to another matter,
I was stripped by King Yánluó,
and my old trousers were left in disarray,
making me a laughingstock.
Could you make a pair of trousers for me?"
His wife said:
"I have nothing to make them with."
Jì said:
"Previously, Gài Yòuxuán, the Captain of Wànnián, brought two bolts of silk.
How can you say there is nothing?"
He also asked her to cast a statue and copy the Lotus Sutra.
His wife agreed to everything,
and only then did he leave.
Wáng Zhū
During the Dàlì era,
Cuī Lì, the prefect of Qióngzhōu, had a nephew named Wáng Zhū,
whose family lived in Miánzhōu.
He traveled frequently between Qín and Shǔ,
and was quite familiar with affairs in the capital.
Once, when he went to the capital,
he became close friends with Zhào Yíng, a clerk in the Bureau of Granaries.
Whenever he brought goods from the left circuit,
such as silk and other items,
Yíng would handle everything for him.
When Zhū wanted to return home,
Yíng insisted on keeping him longer.
In the middle of the night,
Yíng said to Zhū:
"My eldest sister was married to the Chén family,
and she had only one daughter who has just come of age.
The year before last,
my eldest sister passed away.
As for my niece,
I have taken her in to raise her.
I cherish her intelligence and grace,
and do not wish to entrust her to anyone else.
Knowing your noble character,
I believe you can provide for her through hardship.
I do not seek a formal marriage alliance,
but only wish for her to serve you.
If you later marry with proper ceremony,
as long as this girl is well cared for,
and not left destitute,
that is all I hope for!
By forming this bond,
we can secure goodwill for the future."
Zhū replied:
"I am moved by your kindness,
how could I refuse?
I will certainly strive to grow old together with her!"
Zhū then prepared betrothal gifts and welcomed her.
Two years later,
he took Chén-shi back to Zuǒmián.
At that time, Cuī Lì was serving as the prefect of Qióngshāng,
and Zhū went to visit him.
Lì reproached Zhū for his wandering ways,
and worried that he was growing older without marrying.
Zhū explained the situation to his uncle.
Lì said:
"My youngest daughter is gentle and tolerant,
and I wish to form a marriage alliance with you.
She will surely accept the woman you have already taken in."
Chén-shi also said:
"How could I dare have other intentions?
As long as I have enough food and clothing,
and the lady does not resent or blame me,
that is all I desire."
Zhū then married his cousin.
After the marriage,
Cuī-shi had Chén-shi brought to live with them.
They got along well,
and there was not the slightest discord.
Lì ordered his son Cuī Kēng to go with Zhū to Jiānglíng to find a residence,
and they took gold and silk down the Three Gorges.
In the third month, Zhū set out.
In the fifth month,
Lì was replaced in his post,
and moved his entire household to Jiānglíng.
Zhū and Kēng had just bought a house,
and were repairing it.
At noon,
Zhū suddenly dreamed that Chén-shi appeared with disheveled hair.
She tearfully told him:
a lowly woman from another land.
Lady Cuī,
originally promised to care for me always,
but why, while washing my hair on the boat in the Three Gorges,
did she have someone push me,
causing me to fall into the raging torrents and drown,
forever buried in the bellies of fish and turtles!"
Her sorrowful tears soaked her sleeves.
Soon after, Kēng, sleeping in the eastern wing,
also dreamed that Chén-shi complained of injustice:
"Lady Cuī is unkind,
causing my death in the Three Gorges."
Kēng and Zhū were sitting together,
just marveling at this matter,
when that night,
both of them had the same dream again.
Kēng felt deeply ashamed,
and said to Zhū:
"My mother's temperament should not be like this,
how could such injustice occur!
Let us wait for news at the riverbank today,
if we hear that Chén-shi is not safe,
then it must be true!"
A few days later,
news indeed arrived,
saying that Chén-shi had drowned in the Three Gorges.
When Lì arrived at Zhū's home,
Zhū tearfully recounted what had happened.
Cuī-shi was reprimanded by her brother,
and unable to clear her name,
she cut her hair and died in silent grief.
Zhū also wandered off to other places.
Several years later,
suddenly in Xiàkǒu,
within the naval barracks at the eastern gate wing,
he saw a woman
whose appearance was exactly that of Chén-shi.
Zhū gazed at her for a long time.
The woman also looked at him intently,
and asked a servant:
"Does that gentleman not share the surname Wáng?"
The servant hurried to tell Zhū.
Zhū told his cousin,
and had him inquire about the details.
Chén-shi said:
"I was not actually pushed by Cuī-shi,
I accidentally fell into the Three Gorges,
and after two nights,
my body washed up on a shoal,
where I was found by Liáng Cǎn, a junior officer returning to Èzhōu.
At first, he intended to bury me,
but after I vomited endless water,
I suddenly revived.
Grateful for Liáng's great kindness,
I married Liáng Cǎn,
and have now given birth to two sons."
Zhū thus realized he had wronged Cuī-shi unjustly,
and entered Luófú Mountain to become a mendicant monk!
A Man from the Western Market
During the Jiànzhōng era,
a man from the Western Market in the capital suddenly dreamed that he was arrested by someone,
and taken to a government office,
which was very solemn.
The messenger made him stand outside the gate screen,
then left,
and he was not summoned.
He only heard sounds like a trial proceeding inside the gate,
and peeking through a gap in the screen,
he saw a nobleman in the hall,
wearing purple robes and seated behind a desk,
with three or four attendants in green robes holding documents.
In the courtyard,
Zhū Cǐ was shackled at the body and chained at the neck,
dressed in plain clothes with his head uncovered,
bowing as if pleading for vindication,
his words extremely earnest.
The official lowered his head to attend to matters,
paying him no heed at all.
After a long while, he finally said:
"You are fated for this matter,
the Emperor's decree has already been issued,
pleading will be of no use."
Cǐ kept pleading,
until he began to weep.
The official angrily said:
"Why do you not know the Mandate of Heaven?"
He ordered his attendants to open the two courtyards under the eastern corridor.
The sound of locks being opened was heard.
Inside the gate were over thirty people,
all dressed in red and purple robes,
lined up below the steps.
The nobleman pointed and said:
"These people await your rise to wealth and honor,
what use is refusing?"
The man looked,
and they were people like Lǐ, Shàng, Wéi, and Luò.
The group then re-entered the courtyard gate.
He then shouted at Cǐ to enter a courtyard in the western corridor.
The nobleman asked his attendants:
"When will this matter occur?"
They replied:
"In the tenth month."
He also asked where it would be appropriate to go.
They said:
"Fèngtiān."
Such questioning went on.
After a long while, it finally ended.
The arresting messenger from before came out again,
and said to the commoner:
"We mistakenly brought you here,
you may return quickly."
He found his way back.
Upon waking from the dream,
he told his close friends.
Later, the events indeed came to pass.
Wáng Fāngpíng
Wáng Fāngpíng of Tàiyuán was extremely filial by nature.
His father fell gravely ill.
Fāngpíng attended to him and administered medicine,
not loosening his belt for over a month.
Later, exhausted from nursing his father,
he dozed off while sitting by his father’s bed.
He dreamed of two ghosts talking,
wanting to enter his father’s belly.
One ghost said:
“How will you enter?”
The other ghost replied:
“Wait until he eats rice porridge,
then we can follow the porridge in.”
After they agreed,
Fāngpíng awoke with a start.
He made a hole in a bowl.
Blocking it with his finger,
he placed a small jar beneath it.
When his father sipped,
he removed his finger,
and the porridge flowed into the jar,
which he then covered.
He boiled it in a pot a hundred times,
opened it to look,
and found the jar full of flesh.
His father’s illness then healed.
Commentators believed this was due to his pure filial piety.
Zhāng Shēn,
during the Zhēnyuán era,
was transferred by the authorities from his former post as magistrate of Wángwū.
Suddenly he dreamed that a palace eunuch arrived,
and Shēn immediately prepared his official cap and tablet to welcome him.
The eunuch said to Shēn:
“There is an imperial edict summoning you,
you may come with me.”
Shēn was both startled and pleased,
thinking the emperor would employ him.
He immediately ordered his carriage,
and departed with the eunuch.
Outside the gate, he saw over ten clerks,
serving as escorts.
Shēn grew even more delighted,
and they exited the Kāiyuǎn Gate,
heading westward.
Along the road to the left were many clerks,
bowing repeatedly before him.
After nearly two hundred lǐ,
they reached a city,
bustling with carriages, horses, and people,
crowded along the roads,
with locust tree shadows towering on all sides,
and misty curtains stretching afar.
Several lǐ northwest of the city,
was another city.
Outside were several hundred armored men,
standing in rows to the left and right of the gate,
holding spears and halberds,
displaying banners and flags,
the guard was extremely strict,
as if it were a ruler’s residence.
Upon reaching the gate,
the eunuch ordered Shēn to dismount.
Shēn straightened his cap and tablet,
and the eunuch led him through the gate.
There were many soldiers.
He saw palaces, towers, and pavilions,
both lofty and magnificent.
They came to another gate,
where the eunuch led in over a hundred people,
all holding tablets and wearing ceremonial sashes,
arranged in the courtyard,
the ceremony very solemn and respectful.
There was also a towering hall,
resplendent with jade and brilliance,
truly an imperial hall.
To the left and right of the hall were several dozen guards,
armored and leaning on swords.
In the hall were many eunuchs in crimson and purple robes.
One person wore a tall crown,
draped in a dragon robe,
and sat leaning on a jade table in the eastern wing of the hall.
Another, dressed in a crown and robes,
with a face like a woman’s,
also leaned on a jade table in the western wing of the hall.
Several dozen palace ladies
stood in front.
The eunuch said to Shēn:
“The emperor is in the eastern wing,
you may approach and pay respects.”
Shēn hurried to the front of the eastern wing,
and bowed twice.
A crimson-robed eunuch,
standing in the front corridor of the hall,
proclaimed:
“You must now hasten to manage the affairs of my palace,
ensuring nothing is contrary to the law.”
Shēn again bowed twice and performed the ceremonial dance.
Then the eunuch led him to the western wing,
where the ceremony was like that in the eastern wing.
After bowing,
the eunuch led him out of the gate.
Shēn was extremely frightened,
and said to the eunuch:
“I have long served in the outer regions,
and have not seen the Son of Heaven.
The audience just now—
might it not have been improper in ritual?”
The eunuch smiled and said:
“Our lord is lenient,
do not fear.”
As he finished speaking, looking east,
several hundred soldiers galloped over.
The eunuch said to Shēn:
“These are the night patrol soldiers.
You must leave quickly,
do not violate the strict curfew.”
He then called clerks to prepare the carriage.
In his confusion, Shēn awoke.
Secretly finding the dream strange,
he dared not speak of it to anyone.
Several days later,
Shēn was appointed magistrate of Qiánlíng.
And everything he experienced
matched his dream.
Moreover, when Empress Wǔ Zétiān was buried alongside the emperor,
the eastern wing of the hall in Shēn’s dream—
the one wearing a tall crown and dragon robe—
was Emperor Gāozōng.
In the western wing of the hall,
the one dressed in crown and robes with a woman’s face,
was Empress Wǔ Zétiān.
Several months later,
when he went to Cháng’ān,
he stayed overnight with several friends,
and told them the whole story.
Someone showed Shēn portraits of past emperors,
and Emperor Gāozōng and Empress Wǔ Zétiān
were indeed those he had seen in the dream.
Má Ānshí,
during the Táng Zhēnyuán era, went to Shòuchūn,
to visit Prefect Yáng Chéng’ēn.
Ānshí was a Daoist practitioner,
skilled in astrology and divination,
and claimed that the prefect would receive a promotion in the fourth month,
and obtain a commander’s insignia.
That year,
three prefects from Wǔchéng—
Yī Shèn of Ānzhōu, Liú Yì of Sòngzhōu, and Yáng Huái of Shòuzhōu—were all promoted to Imperial Attendants.
Later, Ānshí suddenly dreamed at night.
In the hall within the west courtyard inside the inner city of Shòuzhōu,
he saw a deity wearing a crown and headcloth,
riding a white horse,
with a crimson tail and mane,
who claimed to be Emperor Wǔ of Sòng.
Calling Ānshí forward, he said:
“Yáng Chéng’ēn will not become a military governor,
you need not stay.”
At dawn,
he asked people about it,
and learned this was where Emperor Wǔ of Sòng ascended the altar to appoint generals,
with a record still existing.
Ānshí consulted dream interpretation books,
which said that seeing a crowned deity speaking to someone
means good or evil will occur as spoken.
He then repeatedly pleaded to resign,
and temporarily returned to the mountains.
That month,
he left Shòuzhōu.
Later, Yáng Chéng’ēn suffered a wind-stroke illness,
was dismissed and returned to the court,
which indeed verified the dream.
Yán Zhì
When Yán Zhì was young,
his father served as the Chief Clerk of Mìzhōu,
and Zhì accompanied his father to his post.
Once, while napping during the day,
he suddenly dreamed of a young woman,
about fifteen or sixteen years old,
with a beautiful and radiant appearance,
who came to meet him.
This happened over several months,
and whenever he slept, he would dream of her.
One day later,
he dreamed that the woman came to bid farewell,
her voice and expression filled with sorrow and despair.
She said:
"I am the daughter of the former Chief Clerk,
who died and was buried in the southeast corner of the city.
Your Excellency did not despise my obscure and lowly state,
and deigned to share a pillow and mat with me.
My elder brother will come tomorrow to retrieve my remains,
and we shall part forever,
how could I not feel deep regret?
Now I have a hundred thousand coins to give you,
to express my sincere affection."
After speaking,
she ordered a maid to place the money under the bed,
and then departed.
When Zhì awoke,
he looked under the bed,
and indeed there were a hundred thousand paper coins.
Liú Jǐngfù
The temple of Wú Tàibó
is located west of the Eastern Chāng Gate.
Every spring and autumn season,
the merchants and shops would gather their associates,
prepare sacrificial animals and wine,
and pray for blessings from the King of Three Concessions,
often presenting paintings of fine horses, colorful carriages, and women as offerings.
Even in months other than these,
there was not a single day without activity.
In the spring of the yǐchǒu year,
the head of the goldsmiths' guild gathered his followers,
and painted a beauty on silk,
holding a barbarian lute, with attendants following,
her appearance surpassing those in previous paintings.
They named the beauty Shèng'ér.
Indeed, among all the offerings previously presented on windows, walls, and doors,
none could match her.
A sorceress was just beginning to dance.
There was a Presented Scholar, Liú Jǐngfù,
who was seeing off a guest to Jīnlíng.
He set out wine at the Eastern Tōngbō Pavilion of the temple,
but felt weary and drowsy, longing to sleep.
So he went to the couch,
and just as he was falling asleep,
he saw a man in purple robes and cap say:
"The King of Concessions humbly requests your presence."
Liú followed him to the temple,
where they exchanged courtesies and sat down.
The king said to Liú:
"I have just received a barbarian lute player,
whose skill is exquisite and appearance exceptionally beautiful.
I know that you are skilled in song,
so I have invited you to compose a piece for the barbarian lute,
to honor her artistry."
At first, Liú was rather unwilling,
so he ordered a cup of mortal wine to be served to accompany his song.
Soon the wine arrived,
along with offerings.
Looking at it,
it was exactly the farewell feast from the pavilion.
Liú drank several cups,
and, intoxicated, composed a song:
"When the numerous strings have ceased and the varied winds fallen silent,
Shèng'ér plucks the Luòsuō tune to begin.
With four strings, she strums and twists three or four notes,
summoning the border winds to halt the cold moon.
Loud sounds surge and rush like roaring torrents,
waves churn and tumble, overturning the vast deep.
Soft strings whisper with plaintive sighs,
ghosts weep and spirits mourn in low, rustling sorrow.
With a slanting wrist, she swiftly plucks like a flash of lightning,
in autumn, striking straight like a soaring falcon.
The Hàn consort merely gained a name for grace,
the Qín maiden vainly boasted of immortal bones.
I have heard of events before the Tiānbǎo era,
when Liángzhōu was not yet a den of western tribes.
Those in hemp robes with right-lapped collars were all Hàn people,
unaware of the sudden surge of barbarian dust.
At the end of the Tàipíng era, wild barbarians brought chaos,
dogs and swine rampaged, wantonly assaulting.
Before Xuánzōng reached the Wànlǐ Bridge,
both the eastern Luòyáng and western capital fell at once.
Once Hàn people were captured as prisoners,
they swallowed their hatred and stifled their sobs in vain.
Often gazing at the Hàn moon, longing for Hàn skies,
their resentment soared to the stars, forming
comets.
Eight or nine garrisons west of the capital gates,
with high walls and deep moats, kept idle soldiers confined.
Though Héhuáng was within reach, it could not be reclaimed,
pushing carts and hauling grain was but futile toil.
Today, hearing the Liángzhōu melody played,
my heart and soul secretly soar with longing.
If Shèng'ér were to play this at the frontier fortress,
the soldiers' tears of blood would surely flow freely."
After the song was completed,
Liú, still intoxicated,
dashed off the lyrics on paper and presented them.
The king perused them several times,
then summoned Shèng'ér to bestow the song upon her.
One of the king's attendants was displeased,
and jealousy showed on her face as she sat.
The king,
relying on his drunkenness,
struck Shèng'ér on the head with a golden rúyì scepter,
blood drenching her collar and sleeves.
Liú then awoke in alarm.
The next day, looking at the silk painting,
he indeed found a damaged spot.
The song is now passed down in Wúzhōng.
Presented Scholar Lǐ
There was a jìnshì surnamed Lǐ,
whose given name is forgotten.
He once dreamed that several people came
and pursued him away.
They arrived at a city,
entered a gate where there was a hall,
with rooms and buildings vast and magnificent.
At first, he saw no one,
so Lǐ directly ascended the hall,
and sat sideways on the corner of a bed.
Suddenly, there was a person
who struck him with a staff,
cursing and saying:
"What kind of new ghost dares
to sit on the king's bed?"
Lǐ immediately ran out.
After a short while,
from inside the gate came the announcement that the king was coming out,
and then he saw a person in purple clothes ascend to take his seat,
with attendants leading people in.
The king asked:
"Why did you steal your brother-in-law's money?"
At first, he did not understand.
The king said:
"You sold a horse with him,
and should have received twenty-seven thousand,
but you instead
took thirty
thousand.
Isn't this theft?"
After a moment,
he saw a person in crimson clothes arrive,
who pleaded on Lǐ's behalf:
"This person still has life left,
and should not be detained here yet.
Why not just have him return the money?"
The king set a limit of fifteen days,
saying that if the matter was not settled,
he would be summoned again for questioning.
After Lǐ awoke,
he thought the dream was absurd,
and not credible.
More than ten days later,
a mirror polisher came to his home,
claiming to be skilled in divination.
The family members had him perform divinations, which proved accurate,
and they all reported this to Lǐ.
Lǐ personally went to where he was,
and asked:
"What kind of petty person
deceives and confuses my household?"
The mirror polisher angrily said:
"You stole money from selling a horse,
and the king ordered you to settle the matter.
Now the deadline is about to expire,
and you haven't returned a single coin.
The king will soon summon you.
How dare you insult a man of talent?"
Lǐ was shocked that this was the matter from his dream,
so he bowed and apologized,
asking how he knew about this.
The mirror polisher said:
"The person in red clothes who saved you yesterday
was your great-grandfather.
Fearing you would be summoned again,
he sent me to inform you."
Lǐ said his brother-in-law was already dead,
and there was no place to return the money.
The mirror polisher said:
"Just give it to the poor and beggars,
or distribute it among various temples,
saying it is an offering for your deceased brother-in-law,
and that will suffice."
Lǐ distributed the money as instructed,
and was not summoned again.
Hóu Shēng
Regarding Hóu Shēng from Shànggǔ,
he lived in Jīngmén.
Having passed the míngjīng examination, he entered official service,
and was appointed to Yúchéng County in Sòngzhōu.
He first married a woman from the Hán family of Nányáng,
and five years had passed.
Madam Hán once dreamed at night that several people in yellow clothes summoned her,
took her out of her gate,
and together they walked east for more than ten lǐ,
arriving at an official office.
In the courtyard below, there were several dozen clerks and guards,
with lofty buildings grand and magnificent,
and a great crowd of people.
They then led her to another courtyard,
where there was a person in black clothes,
wearing a tall hat and square shoes,
looking very stern and imposing.
Around him were several hundred attendants,
with desks, tables, cushions, and mats
arranged in rows before and behind.
Madam Hán bowed twice.
Suddenly, a woman around twenty years old appeared,
tall and voluptuously beautiful,
wearing a green jacket with crimson sleeves,
and adorned with gold and jade hairpins as head ornaments.
She came through the gate,
identifying herself as Madame Lú.
She said to Madam Hán:
"I have been your enemy for a long time.
Do you know this?"
Madam Hán replied:
"I am but a woman,
who has never left the inner chambers.
How could I have an enemy?"
Madame Lú, looking very angry, said:
"In my previous life, I was an official.
You falsely accused me of a crime and took my place,
causing me to be banished to the wilderness to die.
Is that not being an enemy?
Now I have appealed to the Heavenly Emperor,
and wish to clear the injustice of my previous life.
The Emperor has granted my request,
so your death is imminent."
Madam Hán grew even more fearful,
wanting to argue back with words,
but Madame Lú chattered on incessantly.
The person in black clothes said to Madame Lú:
"Your grievance is indeed as you say,
but Madam Hán certainly should not die now,
so this cannot be done."
He then ordered a clerk to bring out the records.
The clerk said:
"Madam Hán has one year of life remaining."
The person in black clothes said:
"Quickly send her back,
do not keep her here long."
He ordered her escorted to the gate.
She had not walked more than a few lǐ
when she suddenly woke up in fright,
and, disturbed, dared not speak of it.
From then on, her spirits were downcast and dejected,
as if she were ill.
Hóu Shēng inquired about it,
and she told him the entire dream.
Several months later,
Madam Hán again dreamed that Madame Lú came to her home,
and said to Madam Hán:
"You are about to die."
Madam Hán woke in alarm,
and from then on her illness worsened,
and she died a little over a year later.
Hóu Shēng secretly sighed in wonder,
but never told anyone.
Several years later,
while traveling in Xiāng-Hàn,
he passed through Fùshuǐ.
A commandery official, Xiāo Mǒu of Lánlíng,
admiring Hóu Shēng's virtues,
gave his daughter to him in marriage.
After Madame Xiāo married him,
she often wore crimson-sleeved green jackets,
adorned with gold and jade hairpins as head ornaments,
and moreover was tall and voluptuously beautiful,
exactly as in Madam Hán's earlier dream.
Hóu Shēng then told her about Madam Hán's dream.
Upon hearing this,
Madame Xiāo was very displeased,
and said:
"My maternal family name is Lú.
Since I was a child,
my maternal uncle cared for me
and treated me as his own daughter,
so he gave me the childhood name Lú.
Thus, your late wife's dream was true."
Yuán Jìqiān
Diànzhōng Shǎojiān Yuán Jìqiān,
served as the judicial officer of Yǎnzhōu.
To the east was the residence of Lǚ Jūn, the commander of the prison garrison.
Lǚ, finding his residence low and damp,
ordered soldiers to cut earth from beneath the inner city wall to raise it.
After much cutting,
it reached the main city wall,
gradually thinning it.
Yuán suddenly dreamed of riding a horse,
ascending the eastern gate tower of the inner city.
Someone conveyed a message,
inviting the judicial officer to ascend the tower.
He claimed to be the guardian of the inner city.
Exchanging courtesies with Yuán,
he then said to Yuán:
"Lǚ Jūn is renovating his private residence,
and cutting earth from the inner city wall—
this is absolutely unacceptable.
Why doesn’t the judicial officer speak up about it?"
Yuán replied:
"Although I serve as an advisor,
I have no authority over him."
The guardian said further:
"Since the judicial officer will not speak,
I will handle it myself."
Within a year,
Lǚ Jūn was pursued by the military garrison,
detained for offenses,
and after a long time, dismissed from his post.
His residence now belongs to the Yuán family,
and Zhāng Hàng once borrowed it to live in.
Shào Yuánxiū
Shào Yuánxiū, a Right Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel in the Jìn dynasty,
once spoke of a certain Pān, a reporting officer from Héyáng,
who was loyal, trustworthy, and wise.
Shào and
were close friends,
and once casually discussed matters of the underworld,
expressing doubts about their truthfulness.
They then made a pact:
"In the future,
whichever of us two passes away first,
must inform the other about the affairs of the underworld,
so that the living may have no doubts."
Later, Shào and Pān parted for several years.
Suddenly, Shào dreamed of arriving at a place,
and as he advanced slightly,
he saw beneath the eastern corridor,
bright and splendid curtains,
which was a guest reception area.
There were several guests,
and Pān was among them.
Among them, one person,
seemingly a high official,
dressed imposingly and sternly,
sat to the right of the guests.
Shào immediately stepped forward and bowed.
The high official invited Shào to sit.
Shào saw Pān also sitting below,
with a very respectful and cautious expression.
Shào then addressed the high official,
asking, "Do you know Pān from before?"
The high official merely nodded,
and soon ordered tea.
In response, tea appeared before all the guests,
with no one seen delivering it.
The tea set was very grand.
As Shào was about to drink,
Pān looked at Shào,
leaned over and waved his hand,
stopping Shào from drinking.
Shào understood his intention,
and refrained.
The high official then ordered wine,
which also appeared before the guests in response,
with no one seen holding the vessel.
The wine vessels were ancient in style and grand.
The high official toasted the guests and drank.
As Shào was about to drink,
Pān again leaned over, waved his hand, and stopped him,
so Shào also dared not drink.
The high official then served food,
and large pastries descended before the guests,
fragrant and rich.
As Shào was about to eat,
Pān stopped him again.
After a while,
Pān looked at Shào,
signaling him to leave.
Shào immediately took his leave.
Pān said to the high official:
"Shào and I are old friends,
and now I wish to see him off."
The high official nodded in approval.
The two left the official building together,
and spoke of their earlier pact about the underworld.
Shào then asked:
"What is the underworld like?"
Pān replied:
"Matters of the underworld
certainly cannot be dismissed as false.
Generally, it is like
the human world,
but dim, obscure, and sorrowful."
After speaking,
Shào bid farewell and left.
Upon waking,
he inquired about Pān's fate,
only to learn that Pān had already passed away.
Zhōu Ăi
In Xiānghú, there was a senior officer named Zhōu Ăi,
who was always very close to his fellow student and relative.
Often lamenting how people of the time failed to manage their affairs properly,
leading to unworthy sons fighting over wealth and quarreling,
ending up in court,
he took this as a cautionary tale.
Thus, they made an agreement:
"In the future, we
must not follow this path.
If anything should happen to us,
we must first divide our affairs,
so as not to expose ugliness and disgrace,
and burden our descendants."
Sometime later,
his fellow student was serving in Xiāng’s residence.
One evening,
Officer Zhōu dreamed of him weeping.
He told him:
"Brother-in-law, brother-in-law,
my earlier words have been broken,
for I am now a spirit.
Yesterday on the main road,
struck by a sudden gust of wind,
I was beyond saving.
But thinking of my family affairs,
I have now returned,
to briefly handle matters."
Officer Zhōu suddenly awoke,
and could not sleep the rest of the night.
At dawn,
he went to his home and recounted the dream.
His family had also dreamed of him,
and within ten days, news of his death arrived.
From then on, his spirit conveyed messages,
divided the property,
admonished his sons, and bade farewell to his wife,
speaking earnestly and kindly.
After about a month, he left,
and never returned.
Zhèng Qǐ
Jìnshì Zhèng Qǐ paid a visit to Jīngzhōu Jiédùshǐ Gāo Cónghuì,
and was lodged in an empty residence.
That night,
he dreamed of someone telling him:
"Clerk Yán Guāngchǔ has been disrespectful."
The tone was very indignant.
The next night, he dreamed again.
Zhèng found this strange,
summoned Yán, and told him about it.
Yán ordered shamans to pray and make offerings,
exhausting all methods,
but the reason remained unknown.
The following year,
as Zhèng was preparing for the imperial examinations,
Yán Guāngchǔ, fond of the residence’s small bamboo path,
made many efforts to obtain it.
Shortly after moving in,
he was soon punished for an offense, dismissed from his post,
and never learned the reason.
Zhū Zhěng
Zhū Zhěng, the former Registrar of Yùshān in the false state of Wú, was traveling to the capital for an official appointment selection
when he reached Yángzhōu.
He dreamed of entering a government office,
where a figure in purple robes was seated in the main hall,
with another in green robes beside him.
The purple-robed figure rose and bowed, saying:
"You must give me ten thousand coins."
Zhěng bowed in return and agreed.
Then he awoke.
Shortly after,
he was appointed Magistrate of Ānfú.
Upon arriving at his post,
he paid a visit to the City God temple.
The temple buildings and the deity statues
were exactly as in his dream.
Behind the deity's seat, the roof was leaking and the beams were damaged.
Zhěng sighed and said:
"Could the ten thousand coins be for this?"
He immediately used his own funds to repair it,
and the cost matched the amount exactly.
Wéi Jiàn
Wéi Jiàn, a military commander in Jiāngnán,
was transferred from his post as Commander-in-Chief to become Military Commissioner of Wǔchāng.
As he was about to depart,
he dreamed of a man in red robes,
attended by several dozen followers,
who came to Wéi and said:
"I hear you are about to govern Èzhǔ.
My dwelling is located there,
but its beams and roof are dilapidated and collapsing,
leaving me exposed to wind and rain.
No one but you can repair it for me."
Wéi agreed.
When he arrived at his post and inquired about it,
it turned out to be the temple of Sòng Wújí.
Looking at the statue,
it was exactly the figure he had seen in his dream.
Thus, he renovated the temple.
It is said that the temple then showed numerous efficacious responses to prayers.
Zhèng Jiù
Zhèng Jiù, a butcher from Shòuchūn, was extremely poor.
He often dreamed of a man
who called himself Lián Pō,
telling him:
"You may dig in the ground east of the house
to retrieve my precious sword,
and it will make you wealthy.
However, you must not change your former occupation." Jiù did as he was told,
and indeed found it.
Within a year, he became rich.
Later, he revealed the affair,
and then lost the sword.
Yīngtáo Qīngyī
In the early years of the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a man from Fànyáng named Lú,
who was in the capital to take the imperial examinations.
For years he had not passed,
and gradually became impoverished.
One evening, he was riding a donkey out for a stroll
when he saw a monastery
where a monk was delivering a lecture,
with a large audience listening.
Just as Lú was approaching the lecture hall,
he grew drowsy and fell asleep,
dreaming that he arrived at the monastery gate.
There he saw a maidservant
carrying a basket of cherries, sitting below.
Lú inquired whose household she belonged to,
and then shared the cherries with her.
The maidservant said:
"My mistress’s surname is Lú,
she married into the Cuī family,
and is now a widow living in the city."
Upon asking about her close relatives,
it turned out she was Lú’s paternal great-aunt.
The maidservant said:
"How can it be that your aunt is in the same city,
and you, sir, do not go to pay your respects?"
Lú then followed her.
Crossing the Tiānjīn Bridge,
they entered a ward south of the river,
where there was a residence
with a very tall and grand gate.
Lú stood beneath the gate.
The maidservant entered first.
After a short while,
four men came out the gate
and met Lú.
They were all the sons of his aunt.
One served as a Director in the Ministry of Revenue, one formerly as Simǎ of Zhèngzhōu, one as a Registrar of Hénán,
and one as a Doctor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Two wore crimson robes,
two wore green robes,
and their appearances were very handsome.
They met and conversed,
and it was extremely joyful.
Soon after,
they led him into the northern hall to pay respects to his aunt.
His aunt wore purple robes,
and was about sixty years old.
Her speech was lofty and clear,
and her demeanor was very stern and imposing.
Lú was afraid,
and dared not look up at her.
She invited him to sit,
inquired about all his relatives,
and was thoroughly familiar with the clans.
Then she asked whether he was married yet.
Lú said:
"Not yet."
His aunt said:
"I have a niece whose surname is Zhèng,
orphaned early,
and left to my younger sister to raise.
She is very beautiful,
and quite virtuous.
I shall arrange a match for you,
I am sure it will be successful."
Lú then bowed in thanks.
She then sent for her younger sister, Madame Zhèng.
After a while,
the whole family arrived together,
with very grand carriages and horses.
They then consulted the calendar to choose a date,
saying:
"The day after tomorrow is most auspicious."
Thus they settled the matter with Lú.
His aunt said:
"As for betrothal gifts, letters, and the wedding banquet,
do not worry at all,
I will handle everything.
Which relatives and friends do you have in the city?
Write down their names,
along with their households and ranks."
There were over thirty families in all,
all serving as officials in the central ministries, prefectures, and counties.
The next day, the invitations were sent,
and that evening the marriage was concluded.
Everything was splendid and magnificent,
almost as if not of this world.
The next day, the wedding banquet was held,
gathering all the relatives in the capital.
After the banquet ended,
they entered a courtyard.
The courtyard’s screens, curtains, beds, and mats
were all extremely rare and exquisite.
His wife was about fourteen or fifteen years old,
with a beautiful appearance,
as if she were a celestial being.
Lú was overwhelmed with joy,
and forgot all about his own family.
Soon it was again time for the autumn examinations.
His aunt said:
"The Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Rites is a relative of mine,
he will surely do his utmost,
so do not worry."
The following spring, he passed the examination.
He then took the special examination,
and his aunt said:
"The Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Personnel is a colleague and neighbor of your cousins,
their relationship is particularly close,
I will have him ensure you achieve a high rank."
When the results were posted,
he again passed with distinction,
and was appointed a Secretary in the Imperial Library.
His aunt said:
"The Governor of Hénán is my cousin’s son,
I will have him recommend you for a county magistrate position near the capital."
A few months later,
he was appointed Magistrate of Wángwū,
then promoted to Investigating Censor,
transferred to Palace Attendant,
and appointed Vice-Director of the Ministry of Personnel.
He was put in charge of the southern selection office,
and after the selection process was completed,
he was promoted to Director.
His other duties remained unchanged.
After several months as Drafter of Edicts,
he was confirmed as Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
For two years he oversaw the examinations,
his evaluations were fair and just,
and he was praised by the court.
He was transferred to Governor of Hénán, and soon after the imperial carriage returned to the capital,
he was promoted to Vice-Minister of the Ministry of War.
Accompanying the emperor to the capital,
he was appointed Governor of the Capital District.
He was then transferred back to Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Personnel.
For three years he was in charge of official selections,
and gained an excellent reputation,
so he was appointed Vice-Director of the Chancellery and Participating in Determining Governmental Matters.
Imperial favor was abundant,
and he received lavish rewards.
After serving as Chancellor for five years,
he offended the emperor with his blunt admonitions,
was demoted to Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and removed from governmental affairs.
A few months later,
he was appointed Defender of the Eastern Capital and Governor of Hénán,
concurrently holding the title of Censor-in-Chief.
From the time of his marriage
until now, twenty years had passed.
He had seven sons and three daughters,
all married and holding official posts,
and ten grandchildren in total.
Later, while traveling,
he happened to return to the monastery gate where he had once met the maidservant with cherries,
and again saw a lecture being held inside,
so he dismounted to pay his respects.
With the dignity of a former chancellor,
and the weight of his high office as Defender,
his entourage before and after him
was extremely grand and imposing.
He carried himself with lofty pride,
radiating brilliance all around.
Ascending the hall to worship the Buddha,
he suddenly felt dizzy and drunk,
and for a long time could not rise.
In his ears he heard the lecturing monk call out:
"Why does the benefactor not rise for so long?"
Suddenly he awoke from the dream,
and saw that he was wearing a plain white robe,
his clothing just as before,
and the officials before and after him
were gone without a trace.
Confused and bewildered,
he slowly walked out the gate,
and saw a young servant holding his donkey and hat, standing outside the gate,
who said to Lú:
"Both man and donkey are hungry,
why did you stay inside so long, sir?"
Lú asked what time it was,
and the servant said:
"It is almost noon."
Lú sighed in confusion:
"The glory and obscurity of human life,
wealth and honor, poverty and lowliness,
are all just like this.
From now on,
I will no longer seek official advancement!"
He then sought out immortals and studied the Way,
and vanished from the human world.
Dúgū Xiáshū
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Jìnshì Dúgū Xiáshū
lived in Chóngxián Ward of Cháng'ān,
having recently married a woman of the Bái family.
His family was poor, and he had failed the imperial examinations,
so he planned to travel to Jiànnán.
Bidding farewell to his wife, he said:
"I may be delayed for about a year before returning."
Xiáshū reached Shǔ,
but his stay was difficult and he found no success,
so it was over two years before he returned.
Arriving west of Hù County,
with about a hundred lǐ still to the city,
his longing to return home pressed him urgently,
and he aimed to reach home that very night.
He hurried along a side path, walking swiftly.
Both man and beast were exhausted,
and when he was five or six lǐ from Jīnguāng Gate,
the sky had already darkened.
There were absolutely no inns.
Only at the roadside corner was there a Buddhist hall,
so Xiáshū stopped there.
It was near the Qīngmíng festival,
and the moonlight was as bright as day.
He tethered his donkey outside the courtyard,
and entered the empty hall.
There were over ten peach and apricot trees.
Late at night,
he spread his quilt and curtain beneath the west window,
and lay down to rest.
Just as he was thinking of arriving home the next morning,
he recited an old poem:
"The closer to home, the more anxious the heart becomes,
not daring to ask the travelers I meet."
He remained awake until midnight.
Suddenly, he heard the calls of over ten people outside the wall,
sounding like village officers and old farmers.
They were preparing to serve and welcome someone.
In a moment,
several laborers appeared,
each holding baskets, spades, dustpans, and brooms,
cleaned up the courtyard,
and then left.
After a short while,
they returned carrying beds, mats, ivory trays, candles, and such,
along with wine vessels and musical instruments,
arriving in a bustling crowd.
Xiáshū thought it was a gathering of nobles for enjoyment,
and deeply feared being driven away.
So he hid, holding his breath,
and watched from the beam of the Buddhist hall.
After everything was arranged,
a group of about ten young masters and maidens appeared,
along with over ten attendants in black and yellow turbans,
walking slowly in the moonlight,
chatting and laughing merrily.
They then sat among the banquet mats.
Toasts were exchanged freely,
and shoes and slippers lay scattered.
Among them was a maiden.
Sorrowful and distressed,
she sat to the side, lower down.
Her demeanor resembled that of Xiáshū's wife.
Peeking at her, he was greatly startled.
After descending from the roof beam,
he moved slightly into a darker spot,
approached, and observed closely.
It was indeed his wife.
Just then he saw a
young man
raise a cup and urge her, saying:
"When one person faces the corner,
the whole gathering feels no joy.
I, though insignificant, presume to ask,
and wish to hear your golden, jade-like voice."
His wife, filled with grievance and sorrow,
as if with no one to appeal to,
was forced to sit among them.
So she raised a golden goblet,
held back her tears, and sang:
"What night is this night?
Do I live or have I perished?
My good man has gone to the ends of the earth,
the garden trees grieve—three times they have bloomed."
The entire gathering listened intently,
and the maidens turned their faces, wiping away tears.
One person said:
"Your good man is not far,
why speak of the ends of the earth!"
The young men looked at each other and laughed heartily.
Xiáshū, shocked and enraged for a long time,
could think of no plan.
So he went to the steps,
picked up a large brick,
and hurled it toward the gathering.
The brick had just hit the ground
when everything vanished silently into nothingness.
Xiáshū, disheartened and sorrowful,
thought his wife had died,
and hurriedly yoked
his carriage to return.
Looking ahead toward his home,
each step was filled with grief and sobs.
By dawn,
he reached his dwelling,
and sent a servant in first.
The household was all safe and sound,
so Xiáshū was astonished,
and rushed inside the gate.
A maid reported that the lady had just awoken from a nightmare.
Xiáshū went to the bedroom,
where his wife was still lying in bed, not yet risen.
After a long while, she said:
"Just now I dreamed I was with my sisters-in-law and their companions,
enjoying the moonlight together.
We went outside Jīnguāng Gate,
toward a wilderness temple,
when suddenly several dozen violent men
forced me to sit among them and drink."
She also recounted the conversations from the gathering in her dream,
which matched exactly what Xiáshū had witnessed.
She added:
"Just as we were drinking,
I suddenly saw a large brick come flying down,
and then I was so startled by the nightmare I nearly died.
I had just awoken when you arrived.
Could it have been stirred by hidden anguish?"
Yuán Zhěn
Chancellor Yuán Zhěn, while serving as Censor,
was trying a case in Zǐtóng.
At that time, Bái Jūyì was in the capital,
and with renowned companions visited Cí'ēn Temple,
drinking lightly beneath the flowers.
He composed a poem to send to Yuán:
"With flowers in bloom, together we dispel spring sorrow.
Drunk, we break off flowering branches
to use as wine tallies.
Suddenly I recall an old friend gone to the horizon's edge;
calculating his journey, today he should reach Liángzhōu."
At that time, Yuán indeed reached Bāochéng,
and also sent a "Dream Journey" poem:
"I dreamed of you, my brother, at Qǔjiāng's shore,
also wandering in Cí'ēn's courtyard.
The post-house officer called men to ready the horses to depart,
when suddenly, startled, I found myself in ancient Liángzhōu."
Souls communicated across a thousand lǐ,
matching like tally and token.
Duàn Chéngshì
Duàn Chéngshì often said:
"I have heard from physicians:
When yin dominates among the visceral energies, dreams are frequent;
when yang is robust, dreams are few,
and even those dreams are not remembered.
The blind have no dreams,
which shows it is a matter of habit for the perceptive."
Duàn Chéngshì's maternal cousin Lú Yǒuzé
dreamed of watching drums being beaten,
and upon waking,
his younger brother was playfully knocking on the door like a yamen drum.
Also, his brother-in-law Péi Yuányù said
that among his clan, there was one who admired a neighboring girl,
dreamed that a courtesan gave him two cherries,
and ate them.
Upon waking,
the pits had fallen beside his pillow.
Lǐ Xuàn, in his "Lǐ Zǐzhèng's Discourses,"
states that in dreams of the utmost essence,
one's dream-self can be seen by others.
As when Liú Yōuqiú saw his wife's body in a dream.
Thus we know dreams cannot be interpreted by a single principle.
Foolish people dream little—
not only the perfected person;
I have heard that among grooms and servants,
not one dream occurs in a hundred nights.
Xíng Fèng
In the tenth year of the Yuánhé era,
Shěn Yàzhī first served as a record-keeper in the army of the Duke of Lǒngxī at Jīngzhōu,
and all the worthy scholars of Cháng'ān came to be his guests.
On the eighteenth day of the fifth month,
the Duke of Lǒngxī arranged a banquet with his guests at the eastern pond's convenient lodge.
When the banquet was halfway through,
the Duke of Lǒngxī said:
"In my youth, I roamed with Xíng Fèng,
and I remember his strange experience.
Allow me to recount it."
The guests said:
"We wish to hear it."
The Duke said:
"Fèng was the son of a military family,
with no particular talents.
Later, he resided in the south of Píngkāng Ward in Cháng'ān,
where he spent a million coins
to buy a former mansion of a wealthy family with winding rooms and a cave-like gate.
One day, he lay down to nap in his bedroom,
and dreamed of a beautiful woman
who came from the western pillar,
walking gracefully in a circle,
holding a scroll and reciting,
dressed in ancient attire,
with high hair buns and long eyebrows,
wearing a square-collared robe with an embroidered sash,
and a short jacket with wide sleeves.
Fèng was greatly delighted and said:
'Where does such a beauty come from to visit me?'
The beautiful woman said:
'This is my home.
I am fond of poetry,
and often linger here.'
Fèng said:
'I am fortunate that you have stayed a while,
allowing me to observe and read.'
Thereupon, the beautiful woman handed him the poem,
and sat on the western bed.
Fèng unrolled the scroll,
looked at the first piece,
which was titled 'Chūnyáng Qǔ,'
and it ended with four lines.
The other pieces that followed
were all similar, with several tens of lines each.
The beautiful woman said:
'If you must transmit it,
do not let it exceed one piece.'
Fèng immediately rose,
went to the table under the eastern corridor,
took a colored paper,
and transcribed 'Chūnyáng Qǔ.'
The lyrics said:
'The young maidens of Cháng'ān enjoy the spring sun,
but where is the spring sun that does not break the heart?
The dancing sleeves and bow-like bends are all forgotten,
within the silk curtains, empty, passing the frosts of nine autumns.'
When Fèng finished reciting,
he asked:
'What is meant by "bow-like bends"?'
She said:
'In years past, my parents had me taught this dance.'
The beautiful woman then rose,
adjusted her clothes and spread her sleeves,
danced a few beats,
and assumed the shape of a drawn bow to show Fèng.
After finishing,
the beautiful woman lowered her head for a long while,
then took her leave.
Fèng said:
'I wish you would stay a little longer.'
In a moment, she was gone,
and Fèng soon awoke,
dazed, forgetting what he had remembered.
When he changed clothes,
he found the lyrics in his lapel and sleeve,
looked at them in surprise,
and recalled the dream.
This happened during the Zhēnyuán era,
and later Fèng told me this story."
On that day,
the army supervisor, the guests from the commandery's staff,
and those feasting—Dúgū Xuàn of Lǒngxī, Lú Jiǎncí of Fànyáng, Zhāng Yòuxīn of Chángshān, and Sū Dí of Wǔgōng—all sighed and said:
"This should be recorded."
Thus, Yàzhī withdrew and wrote it down.
The next day,
guests who arrived again,
Gāo Yuánzhōng of Bóhǎi, Wéi Liàng of Jīngzhào, Táng Yán of Jìnchāng, Lǐ of Guǎnghàn, and Yáo Hé of Wúxīng,
along with Yàzhī, gathered again at Míngyù Spring.
He then brought out his writing to show them.
Thereupon, Yáo Hé said:
"I have a friend, Mr. Wáng,
who in the early years of Yuánhé,
dreamed one night of traveling to Wú,
and serving the King of Wú.
After a long while,
he heard the palace carriage emerge,
with flutes playing and drums beating,
and it was said they were burying Xī Shī.
The king was endlessly grief-stricken,
and immediately ordered his guests to compose elegiac songs.
Mr. Wáng, in response to the command, wrote the lyrics:
'Gazing west at the King of Wú's palace,
cloud-written phoenix characters on the plaque.
Pearl curtains rise along the river,
choosing earth to bury the golden hairpin.
The ground covered with red-hearted grass,
three layers of jade-green steps.
The spring breeze has nowhere to go,
grief and regret unbearable to bear.'
When the lyrics were presented,
the king greatly praised them.
Upon waking,
he could remember the event.
Mr. Wáng was originally from Tàiyuán."
Shěn Yàzhī
In the early years of the Tàihé era,
Shěn Yàzhī was about to go to Bīn,
and upon leaving Cháng'ān City,
he lodged as a guest at the Suǒquán Inn.
It was springtime,
and during the day he dreamed of entering Qín.
The ruler, Nèishǐ Liào,
recommended Yàzhī
to the Duke of Qín.
Summoned to the front of the hall,
the Duke leaned forward on his knees and said:
"I desire to strengthen the state;
I wish to know the methods.
What can you, sir, teach me?"
Yàzhī responded with examples of Kūn, Péng, and Qí Huán,
and the Duke was pleased.
He then tested him by appointing him as a supplementary Zhōngjuān,
and sent him to assist Xīqǐ Shù in attacking Héxī.
Yàzhī led the troops forward,
capturing five cities.
Upon returning to report,
the Duke was greatly pleased
and rose to console him, saying:
"You, Grand Master, have truly suffered hardship;
now rest."
After a long while,
the Duke's youngest daughter, Nòngyù, whose husband Xiāo Shǐ had died earlier,
prompted the Duke to say to Yàzhī:
"Without you, Grand Master,
the five cities of Jìn would not be mine.
I am deeply grateful to you.
I have a beloved daughter,
and I wish to have you, Grand Master, attend to her sweeping and cleaning.
Is that acceptable?"
Yàzhī had been independent from a young age
and genuinely did not wish to be kept as a favored minister;
he firmly declined,
but his request was not granted.
He was appointed Zuǒshùzhǎng,
married the princess,
and was bestowed two hundred catties of gold.
Among the common people, she was still called Princess of the Xiāo Family.
That day, a eunuch in yellow clothing
urgently rode a horse to
invite Yàzhī into the palace.
It was very solemn.
The princess was called out;
her hair was black and thick,
she wore a garment with slanted sleeves,
her attire was not overly adorned,
yet her beauty was exceptionally radiant,
indescribable with a brush.
Attending maidservants
stood divided left and right, numbering in the hundreds.
Yàzhī was received in a convenient lodge,
and he resided in the palace,
the gate of which was inscribed "Cuìwēi Palace."
The palace people called it Shěn Láng's Courtyard.
Although he held the position of a lower-ranking grand master,
due to the princess's circumstances,
he could enter and exit the forbidden guards.
The princess enjoyed the phoenix flute;
whenever she played it,
it was always from the high tower of Cuìwēi Palace.
The melody carried far and wide,
capable of moving people to sorrow,
and listeners could not help but be deeply affected.
The princess was born on the seventh day of the seventh month,
and Yàzhī had nothing to offer as a birthday gift.
Nèishǐ Liào was present,
and because Qín had gifted female musicians to the Xīróng,
the Róng chieftain gave him a small box made of water-rhinoceros horn.
Yàzhī obtained it from Liào and presented it to the princess.
The princess was delighted, appreciated it greatly, and treasured it,
tying it to her skirt sash.
Duke Mù treated Yàzhī with the same courtesy as his peers,
and gifts of favor were frequently seen on the roads.
Another year passed, and in spring,
when the Duke was in Shǐpíng,
the princess suddenly died without illness.
The Duke grieved incessantly.
When she was to be buried on the Xiányuán Plain,
the Duke ordered Yàzhī to compose a funeral dirge.
In response to the command, he wrote:
"Weeping, we bury a branch of red,
alive together, but death parts us.
Golden hairpins fall in fragrant grass,
scented embroidery fills the spring breeze.
Where once the flute was heard,
the high tower stands beneath the moon.
On the Cold Food night with pear blossoms,
deep within Cuìwēi Palace, it is closed."
Presented to the Duke,
he read the verses and found them good.
At that moment, in the palace, there were sounds as if someone could not bear it,
and the Duke followed with tears.
He also had Yàzhī compose an epitaph inscription,
and he alone recalled the inscription as:
"White poplars weep in the wind, oh, stone wells overgrown with moss,
mixed flowers cover the ground, oh, spring colors misty and mild.
Pearls of sorrow scattered thin, oh, no brocade or silk grows,
deeply buried jade, oh, how endless is its regret."
Yàzhī also attended the burial on the Xiányuán Plain,
where fourteen people from the palace were sacrificed.
Yàzhī, due to excessive grief and sorrow,
fell ill.
He was still in Cuìwēi Palace,
but in a separate chamber outside the main hall,
not within the inner palace.
After more than a month,
his illness greatly subsided.
The Duke said to Yàzhī:
"Originally, I entrusted my young daughter to you for a long-term bond,
never expecting she would not be able to serve you fully,
but passed away first.
Our humble Qín is but a small state,
unworthy of troubling you, Grand Master.
However, whenever I see you,
I cannot help but grieve.
Why not go to a great state, Grand Master?"
Yàzhī replied:
"I, your servant, am unworthy,
yet my heart belongs to the ducal house.
I await punishment as Zuǒshùzhǎng.
Unable to follow the princess in death,
if you, my lord, pardon my offense,
and allow me to return my bones to my parents' state,
I will never forget your grace, bright as the sun."
As he was about to leave,
the Duke held a grand farewell banquet,
with Qín music played,
and Qín dances performed.
The dancers slapped their shoulders and thighs, humming,
yet the music held no joy,
the sound full of resentment.
The Duke held wine before Yàzhī and said:
"To your longevity.
I find this music somewhat lacking;
I wish for Shěn Láng to compose a song to fill the farewell."
The Duke ordered brush and inkstone to be brought quickly,
and Yàzhī, accepting the command,
immediately wrote the song lyrics:
"Slapping shoulders,
dancing,
regret fills the misty light, nowhere to place it.
Tears fall like rain,
trying to compose words, but speech fails.
Golden phoenix bearing red on old embroidered clothes,
how many times in the palace we watched dances together.
In the mortal world, spring days are full of joy,
but as dusk falls, where does the east wind go?"
When the song ended,
it was given to the dancers,
mingled with their voices as they sang it,
and all in attendance wept.
After bidding farewell again and preparing to leave,
the Duke ordered him to go to Cuìwēi Palace
to bid farewell to the princess's attendants.
Upon re-entering the hall,
he saw scattered pearls and jade fragments on the green steps below,
and the gauze curtains with sandalwood dots still as before.
The palace women wept facing Yàzhī,
and Yàzhī, deeply moved, choked with emotion for a long time.
He then inscribed a poem on the palace gate:
"The sovereign, filled with feeling, sends me eastward home,
from now on, the Qín palace will be seen no more.
Spring scenes grieve for Qín's lost mistress,
falling flowers like rain, tears of rouge."
Finally, he parted and left.
A carriage was ordered to escort him out of Hángǔ Pass.
Once beyond the pass,
the escorting official said:
"The Duke's orders end here;
please go on."
Yàzhī bid them farewell,
and before his words were finished,
he suddenly awoke with a start,
lying in the inn.
The next day,
Yàzhī recounted it all to his friend Cuī Jiǔwàn.
Jiǔwàn was from Bólíng
and well-versed in antiquity.
He said to me:
"The 'Huánglǎn' states,
Duke Mù of Qín was buried beneath the Qínián Palace at Tuóquán in Yōng.
Could it not be his spirit manifesting?"
Yàzhī further sought out Qín-era geographical records,
and said:
"As Jiǔwàn said.
Alas!
Since Nòngyù has already become an immortal,
how could she die again?"
Zhāng Shēng
There was a man named Zhāng Shēng,
whose home was at Chìchéng Slope, northeast of Zhōngmóu County in Biànzhōu.
Due to hunger and cold,
he once bid farewell to his wife and children to travel to Héshuò,
and only returned after five years.
On his way back from Héshuò to Biànzhōu,
he left Zhèngzhōu Gate late,
and by the time he reached Bǎnqiáo,
it was already dark.
He then left the main road,
taking a shortcut through the marshlands to return home.
Suddenly, amidst the thick grass,
he saw the flickering glow of lanterns.
Five or six guests
were in the midst of feasting and drinking.
Zhāng Shēng then dismounted from his donkey and approached them.
When he was about ten paces away,
he saw his wife also seated among them,
chatting and laughing warmly with the guests.
Zhāng Shēng then hid himself behind a white poplar tree
to spy on them.
He saw a long-bearded man holding a cup, saying:
"Please ask the scholar's wife to sing."
Zhāng Shēng's wife
came from a literary family,
had studied poetry and books since childhood,
and was quite skilled in composing verses.
Though she wished not to sing,
the guests at the table urged her insistently.
So she sang:
"Lamenting the withered grass,
the chirping of crickets is mournful.
My beloved has gone and never returns,
tonight I sit in sorrow, my hair as white as snow."
The long-bearded man said:
"A toast for your song."
She drank it down.
When the wine reached a fair-faced youth,
he also requested a song.
Zhāng's wife said:
"Once is already too much,
how can there be a second time?"
The long-bearded man picked up a tally stick and said:
"Let us set a penalty cup.
Anyone who refuses to sing when asked
must drink a cup.
If the song contains old lyrics with laughter,
the same penalty applies."
Thereupon, Zhāng's wife sang again:
"I urge you to drink,
do not decline.
Fallen flowers merely linger on branches,
flowing water never returns.
Do not rely on youth,
for how long does youth last?"
When the wine reached a man in purple,
he also raised his cup and requested a song.
Zhāng's wife was displeased,
pondered for a long while,
and then sang:
"Resentment fills the empty chamber,
even autumn days are slow to pass.
My husband has cut off news,
wild geese cross the distant sky in vain."
When the wine reached a black-clad foreigner,
he also requested a song.
Zhāng's wife had already sung three or four songs in a row,
and her voice and breath were failing.
While she was hesitating and had not yet sung,
the long-bearded man threw a penalty cup and said:
"It is not right to refuse."
He then poured a cup.
Zhāng's wife wept as she drank,
and sang again to toast the foreigner:
"The evening wind blows urgently,
dew moistens the courtyard grass.
My beloved has gone and does not return,
who knows of my weeping behind closed doors?"
When the wine reached a green-clad youth,
he raised his cup and said:
"The night is already late,
I fear we cannot linger.
We must part soon,
do not refuse one song,
I hope you will sing it."
She sang again:
"Fireflies flit through white poplars,
a mournful wind enters the wild grass.
I suspect I wander in a dream,
sorrow clouds the path to my old home."
When the wine reached Zhāng's wife,
the long-bearded man sang to toast her:
"We first met before the flowers,
and now we part beneath them.
Why speak of dreams,
when all of life is but a dream?"
When the wine reached the purple-clad foreigner,
he requested a song again, saying:
"It must have a romantic tone."
As Zhāng's wife lowered her head and had not yet sung,
the long-bearded man threw another penalty cup.
At this, Zhāng Shēng grew furious,
felt around on the ground and found a tile,
and hurled it.
It struck the long-bearded man on the head.
He threw another tile,
which struck his wife on the forehead.
Suddenly, everything vanished without a trace.
Zhāng Shēng thought his wife had died,
and wept bitterly all night as he returned home.
By dawn, when he reached his door,
his family, surprised and delighted, came out to greet him.
Zhāng Shēng asked about his wife,
and the maids and servants said:
"The mistress had a headache last night."
Zhāng Shēng entered the room.
He asked his wife about the cause of her illness.
She said:
"Last night, I dreamed of a place in the wild grass,
where there were six or seven people.
They made me drink all around,
and each requested a song.
I sang six or seven songs in total,
and a long-bearded man kept throwing penalty cups.
