Just as I was drinking,
tiles came flying from outside,
and the second one struck my forehead.
I woke up in shock,
and then had a headache."
Zhāng Shēng then realized that what he had seen the previous night
was his wife's dream.
Liú Dàojì
During the Guānghuà era,
there was a scholar named Liú Dàojì,
who stayed at Guóqīng Temple on Tiāntāi Mountain.
Once he dreamed of a woman,
who led him beneath a window,
where there were cypress trees and sunflowers,
and they became husband and wife.
Afterward, he frequently met her in dreams,
though he did not understand why.
Not long after,
in an ancient temple in Fènghuà County, Míngzhōu,
he saw a window,
with cypress trees and sunflowers,
exactly like the place he had visited in his dream.
There was a traveling official,
who was lodging in this room.
His daughter was talented and beautiful,
but poor and unmarried,
and recently she had fallen ill with lovesickness.
What Liú Dàojì had encountered
was the spirit of this young woman.
There was also a man named Liú from Péngchéng,
who dreamed of entering a brothel,
and indulged in drinking and revelry with the courtesans.
Afterward, whenever he dreamed,
he would return to that place.
He began to doubt it was merely a dream,
for the fragrance of the courtesan he met
often lingered on his clothes.
This too was caused by his own improper thoughts.
This story was heard from Liú Shānfǔ.
Zhèng Chāngtú
In the year Zhèng Chāngtú passed the imperial examination,
he was living in Cháng'ān.
One night, while enjoying the cool air in the courtyard,
he dreamed that he was beaten by someone,
dragged out through Chūnmíng Gate,
and only released at the stone bridge where the roads converged.
He was freed there.
He lost one of his purple silk shoes,
and ran back to his residence before waking up.
He was very exhausted,
and told his brothers about it.
Sure enough, one shoe was missing by his bed.
In the morning, he sent someone to search for it on the stone bridge,
and it was found.
Hán Què
In Yuèzhōu, there was a man named Lú Cè,
who had been recommended as a Xiùcai.
His family was poor,
and he had not yet gone to the capital.
He served as the weir keeper in Gùshù Village, Shānyīn County,
living together with his cousin Hán Què.
Since childhood, Hán had been fond of minced fish,
and he once asked a clerk to procure fish for him.
Hán was just falling asleep
when he dreamed that he had turned into a fish.
In the pond, he experienced the joy of forgetting everything.
Then he saw two fishermen
in a boat casting a net.
Unaware, he swam into the net,
was caught, and thrown into a bucket.
It was covered with reeds.
He then saw the clerk he had asked for help
come to the pond to negotiate the price.
The clerk immediately lifted him by the gills and strung him through with a cord,
causing such excruciating pain that it was almost unbearable.
When they arrived at the house,
he recognized his wife, children, and servants one by one.
After a while,
he was placed on a chopping block and butchered.
As he was being chopped,
the pain felt like his skin was being stripped away,
and only when his head fell off did he wake up.
He remained dazed for a long time.
Lú, alarmed, asked him what was wrong,
and Hán recounted the entire dream.
Lú immediately called the clerk
to inquire about where the fish had been purchased
and the appearance of the fishermen.
They matched the dream exactly.
Hán later became a Buddhist monk,
residing at Qíyuán Temple.
This happened in the second year of the Kāichéng era.
Master Shū Lǐ
In Bāqiū County, there was a shaman named Shū Lǐ.
In the first year of the Yǒngchāng era of the Jìn dynasty, he fell ill and died.
The local earth god was escorting him to Tàishān.
It was common custom to refer to shamans as "dàorén" (religious practitioners).
As they first passed by the "Blessed Abode" of the underworld court,
the earth god asked the gatekeeper:
"What place is this?"
The gatekeeper said:
"This is the dwelling for dàorén."
The earth god said:
"Shū Lǐ is a dàorén."
And so he handed him over.
Lǐ entered the gate
and saw hundreds and thousands of rooms,
all with curtains hung and beds placed.
Men and women were separated,
some were reciting scriptures,
some were chanting hymns,
and they ate and drank naturally,
enjoying a happiness beyond words.
Lǐ's name had already been sent to Tàishān,
but his person had not yet arrived.
Suddenly, he saw a being
with eight hands and four eyes,
holding a golden pestle, chasing Lǐ.
Terrified, Lǐ ran out.
The earth god was already outside the gate,
and he seized Lǐ and sent him to Tàishān.
The Lord of Tàishān asked Lǐ:
"What did you do in the human world?"
Lǐ replied:
"I served the thirty-six thousand gods,
performing sacrificial rites to dispel misfortunes for people."
The Lord said:
"You flattered the gods and killed living beings,
your crimes deserve severe punishment."
He ordered an officer to take him away.
Lǐ saw a creature
with an ox head and a human body,
holding an iron fork.
It grabbed Lǐ and threw him onto an iron bed.
His body was scorched and mangled,
and he longed for death but could not die.
After many nights,
he suffered extreme agony and injustice.
The Lord of Tàishān asked the officer in charge,
and learned that Lǐ's allotted lifespan was not yet exhausted,
so he ordered him released and sent back.
He also admonished him:
"Do not kill living beings or engage in improper sacrifices again."
After Lǐ revived,
he never worked as a shaman again.
The Female Shaman Qín Shì
In the fifth year of the Yìxī era,
when Emperor Wǔ of the Sòng dynasty campaigned north against the Xiānbēi,
he achieved a great victory
and advanced to besiege Guǎnggù.
The generals and officers in the army
then sent envoys with sacrificial animals and offerings
to pay respects at the Dàiyuè Temple.
There was a female shaman named Qín Shì,
a native of Fènggāo,
and the widow of a man named Suǒ from the same county.
She could summon spirits and convey teachings,
and her words never proved false.
The envoys set up prayers
and inquired about the date of their decisive victory.
Qín Shì then conveyed the divine teaching, saying:
"Heaven has bestowed a heroic assistant,
whom even demons and spirits cannot match.
There will be an expedition but no battle;
these petty, insignificant foes
are not worth subduing.
By the fifth day of the second month next year,
victory will be achieved."
As scheduled, the three Qí regions were pacified.
Yáng Lín
During the Sòng dynasty,
there was a cypress pillow in the Jiāohú Temple,
some called it the "jade pillow."
The pillow had a small crack.
At that time, a merchant from Shànfù County named Yáng Lín
came to the temple to pray.
The temple shaman said to him:
"Do you wish for a good marriage?"
Lín said:
"Very much so."
The shaman then had Lín approach the pillow.
As he entered the crack,
he saw vermilion towers and jade chambers.
There was a Grand Commandant named Zhào inside,
who married his daughter to Lín.
They had six sons,
all of whom became Secretarial Court Gentlemen.
Several decades passed,
and he had no thought of returning home.
Suddenly, it was as if he awoke from a dream,
and he was still beside the pillow.
Lín was sorrowful for a long time.
Lái Jùnchén
During the Zǎichū era of the Táng dynasty,
Lái Jùnchén fabricated charges
and accused the two sons of the former commoner Xián of sending shamans at night to pray to the stars and moon,
cursing and committing treason.
Under torture and severe pain,
and with slaves and maidservants giving false testimony,
the two sons falsely confessed,
and were both flogged to death.
The court and the common people were grieved and pained.
Fúxiūzǐ Zhāng Zhuó said:
"Common folk from the villages
often believe in curses and prayers;
children and women
place great importance on talismanic writings.
They harbor hidden evils,
turning falsehoods into realities.
Using blood in earthen pits
was indeed the deliberate act of Yī Lì;
digging the ground to bury a bronze figure
was the arbitrary fabrication of Jiāng Chōng."
Empress Wǔ of Táng
When Empress Wǔ of Táng was about to go to Luò,
upon reaching east of Wénxiāng,
her horse suddenly refused to advance.
She summoned a shaman to inquire,
and the shaman said:
"The Jìn dynasty General of Dragon Steeds, Wáng Jùn, says:
'My tomb lies south of the road,
and I am often troubled by woodcutters.
Hearing that Your Majesty's carriage is passing,
I have come to beg for mercy.'" The Empress issued an edict
that within a hundred paces of the tomb,
farming and planting were forbidden.
To this day, the area is densely overgrown with thorns.
Ā Lái
During the peak of Táng dynasty Consort Wéi's power,
she was fond of curses and prayers,
and even used a dim mirror to reflect upon people,
causing them confusion and disorder.
Together with the wicked folk sorceress Ā Lái from Chóngrén Ward,
she specialized in casting malevolent spells.
Prince Píng executed them.
Later, sorcery objects were often dug up in the palace halls,
the work of the rebellious Wéi faction.
Yōng Wénzhì
Táng Dynasty official Bái Xíngjiǎn,
during the early Tàihé era,
due to being heavily intoxicated,
dreamed that two men led him out through the Chūnmíng Gate.
They arrived at a new grave mound,
and as dawn was about to break, they returned.
Upon reaching the city gate,
there was a shop selling bótuō noodles.
Xíngjiǎn was extremely hungry,
and was just about to inform the two messengers when
he suddenly saw the shopkeeper’s wife holding an infant.
The messengers then handed Xíngjiǎn a small clod of earth,
instructing him to strike the child.
Xíngjiǎn did as told and threw it,
and the child immediately cried out in fright and fainted.
The shopkeeper’s wife said:
“The child has been struck by an evil influence.”
She had someone summon a female shaman.
The shaman burned incense,
strummed a pipa, and invoked spirits, saying:
“There is no other cause;
it is merely a minor demon causing trouble.
There are three individuals in total,
one is a living soul,
seeking wine and food,
not intending to cause harm.
Quickly prepare bótuō noodles
and fetch wine.”
In a short while, everything was set out.
The shaman paid her respects,
the two messengers and Xíngjiǎn took their seats,
ate their fill, and then rose.
The child returned to normal.
After Xíngjiǎn awoke,
he felt deeply disturbed by this,
and over ten days later, he passed away.
Xǔ Zhìyōng
Xǔ Zhìyōng’s wife, née Mǒu,
was dignified and elegant in appearance.
She died young,
and Zhìyōng deeply mourned her.
Whenever he encountered serene nights with beautiful scenery,
or gatherings with music and feasts,
he could not help but sigh and weep with sorrow.
On the night of the fifteenth day of the eighth month, Zhìyōng was playing the qin and admiring the moon in the courtyard.
After a long while,
he suddenly sensed someone moving behind the curtained screen,
sighing several times.
Zhìyōng asked:
“Who is there?
This must be something unusual.”
After a long pause,
he heard someone speak, saying:
“It is your deceased wife.”
She said:
“If you wish to see me again,
seek out Zhào Shísì.
Do not begrudge three strings and six hundred coins.”
Zhìyōng rose in shock and asked further,
but there was nothing to be seen.
From then on, he always remembered her words,
but did not know who Zhào Shísì was.
Several years later,
Zhìyōng was leisurely traveling in Sūzhōu.
It was springtime,
and he saw over ten youths,
all dressed in women’s attire,
boarding painted boats,
about to visit the Temple of Tàibó of Wú.
Xǔ Jūn then asked:
“Who are those people?
Why are their garments like that?”
Someone replied:
“In this prefecture, there is a male shaman named Zhào Shísì,
whose predictions are often accurate and who is revered by the locals.
These are all his disciples.”
Xǔ Shēng asked:
“What is Zhào Shēng’s special skill?”
They said:
“He excels at summoning people’s souls.”
Xǔ Shēng then realized this matched what his wife had said.
The next morning,
he went to see Zhào Shísì,
and fully explained his sincere wish.
Zhào Shēng said:
“What I can summon
are the souls of the living.
Now, to summon a dead soul,
and furthermore to allow a living person to see it—
I have not done this for a long time,
and do not know if I can succeed.
But knowing of your deep longing,
and that the divine principle has already made it clear,
how can I refuse to summon her for you?”
He then calculated the required expenses,
which indeed amounted to three strings and six hundred coins.
He then selected an auspicious day,
and within his residence,
swept clean, burned incense,
set up a bed and small table against the western wall,
and outside the eaves, arranged an altar,
offering wine and dried meat.
He chanted, danced, and bowed,
playing the húqín.
When evening came,
he had Xǔ Jūn wait in the eastern corner of the hall.
Zhào Shēng then lay down behind a curtain hung from the eaves,
and remained silent.
At the third watch,
he suddenly heard footsteps in the courtyard.
Zhào Shēng then asked:
“Is it perhaps the wife of Scholar Xǔ?”
After several sighs were heard,
a reply came:
“Yes.”
Zhào Shēng said:
“Due to the scholar’s sincere and earnest feelings,
I dared to invite you here.
Please do not take offense, Madam.
I ask Madam to enter the hall.”
After a moment,
it seemed someone lifted the curtain,
and Xǔ Shēng’s wife appeared.
Dressed plainly with light makeup,
she bowed to Zhào Shēng,
then slowly entered the hall,
and sat facing west.
Xǔ Shēng, weeping and sobbing, said:
“Since your departure,
have you suffered any wrongful injustice?”
His wife replied:
“All this is fate;
how could there be wrongful injustice?”
He then asked about their children, family, old friends, and neighborhood matters,
exchanging several dozen sentences.
Xǔ Shēng asked further:
“In the human world, Buddhist sutras are revered,
called ‘meritorious deeds.’
Is this truly effective?”
His wife said:
“Yes, it is.”
He asked again:
“What is most valued in the underworld?”
She replied:
“Offerings made during the Spring and Autumn seasons are all acceptable,
but what is most valued
is thin rice gruel.”
Zhào Shēng prepared it.
In a moment, the gruel arrived.
She brought it to her mouth as if to eat,
then set it aside,
and resumed as before.
Xǔ Shēng asked again:
“Do you need meritorious deeds?”
His wife said:
“I committed no evil in my lifetime;
how could I have any guilt?
The deeds you previously performed for me
have already been fully received.”
After a long while,
Zhào Shēng said:
“Madam should leave now,
lest staying too long brings punishment.”
His wife then went out.
Xǔ Shēng followed, weeping, and said:
“I beg you to leave me something
as a keepsake.”
His wife wept and said:
“In the netherworld, only tears can be passed on to the world of the living.
If you have a garment,
you may throw one item on the ground.”
Xǔ Shēng removed an undershirt
and placed it on the ground.
His wife picked it up,
and in front of a tree in the courtyard, she hung it on a branch,
covered her face with the undershirt,
and wept bitterly.
After a long while,
she waved her hand, bidding Xǔ Shēng farewell,
left the undershirt hanging on the tree branch,
and seemed to ascend into the air and depart.
Xǔ Shēng took the undershirt and looked at it;
the tear stains were all blood.
Xǔ Shēng grieved painfully,
and for several days could not eat.
Lú Qiú, who lived in seclusion in Sūzhōu,
knew Zhào Shēng.
Zhào Shēng’s given name was Hé,
and the people of Sūzhōu all passed down this story.
Wéi Jìn
Táng Dynasty Grand Minister of Imperial Stud Wéi Jìn desired to seek the position of military commissioner of Xiàzhōu.
There was a shaman who knew what he wished for,
and suddenly visited Wéi, saying:
"I am skilled at praying to the stars and constellations;
for all those seeking official positions,
I can certainly fulfill their wishes."
Wéi did not know he was deceitful and fraudulent,
and ordered him to select a date.
Late at night,
in the central courtyard, wine, fruit, incense, lamps, and other items were prepared.
The shaman arrived drunk,
requested Wéi to personally write down his official rank in one document,
and reverently present it at the altar.
Once he had obtained the handwritten official titles,
he raised his head to the sky and shouted loudly:
"Wéi Jìn harbors treacherous intentions,
ordering me to sacrifice to Heaven."
Wéi, along with his entire clan, bowed and pleaded:
"We beg the mountain hermit not to speak such words;
it would be the fortune of our hundred mouths."
All the valuables and wealth at hand
were given to him.
At that time, Cuī Kǎn served as the Metropolitan Governor of the capital.
There was a prisoner from the prefecture who had escaped from jail,
and it was said the shaman was one of his gang.
A local constable interrogated him about why his clothing had suddenly changed?
The shaman, in a desperate situation,
then said:
"Grand Minister of Imperial Stud Wéi Jìn,
once ordered me to sacrifice to Heaven.
I intended to report it,
but he used his family wealth to bribe me.
Isn't this theft?"
After this was reported to the throne,
Emperor Xuānzōng summoned Jìn to the front of the hall,
where the truth of his wrongful accusation became clear.
He then summoned his chief ministers and stated:
"Wéi Jìn is from a prominent clan south of the city,
a family of officials and nobility.
Recently, because he sought an official position,
he thus incurred slander and false accusations.
Do not allow harsh officials to impose crimes upon him."
That master shaman was then handed over to the Jīngzhào Prefecture to be executed,
and Wéi was demoted to Simǎ of Pānzhōu.
Gāo Pián
Táng Dynasty's Gāo Pián once instructed his sons, saying:
"You all must plan well for yourselves.
I certainly will not imitate vulgar people,
dying and being placed into four wooden planks,
thereby burdening you."
When he met his end in the disaster caused by Bì Shīduó,
he was buried in the same pit alongside his various nephews and nieces.
Only Pián was wrapped in an old felt blanket,
indeed matching his earlier words.
Later, when Lǚ Yòngzhī was executed,
a soldier excavated the central hall of his residence,
and found a stone casket.
Inside was a wooden figurine,
about three chǐ tall,
its body bound with fetters,
a long nail driven through its mouth,
and on its back was written Pián's native place, date of birth, official rank, and name,
performing a malevolent magical practice.
Because of this, Pián was often controlled by Yòngzhī,
as if he had assistance in doing so.
Method to Repel Thieves:
Take nine mice over seven days,
place them in a cage,
bury it in the ground,
weigh nine hundred jīn of soil to cover the pit,
each side two chǐ five cùn deep,
tamp it down to make it firm and solid.
The Miscellaneous Wǔxíng Texts state:
"Using earth from the Tíngbù area to plaster the stove,
prevents passage of water, fire, and thieves;
plastering the four corners of the house,
prevents mice from eating silkworms;
plastering the granary,
Yōng Yìjiān
Táng Dynasty's Yōng Yìjiān said:
"The incantation of the Lord of the Night deity,
reciting it brings merit,
when walking at night or sleeping,
it can stop terror and bad dreams."
The incantation says:
"Póshānpóyǎndǐ."
Sòng Jūshì
Táng Dynasty's Layman Sòng said,
the incantation for throwing dice is:
"Yīdìmídì,
Míjiēluódì."
Recite it one hundred thousand times while gambling,
and the winning combination will appear as called.
Kè Yǐnyóu
King Ānxī of Wèi watched soaring swans and delighted in them,
saying:
"If I could fly like these swans,
I would view the world as mere mustard seeds."
A wandering recluse named Kè Yǐnyóu heard this,
made a wooden swan and presented it to the king.
The king said:
"This has form but is useless.
To make useless objects
is the work of wicked people in the world."
He summoned Yǐnyóu,
intending to punish him.
Yǐnyóu said:
"Your Majesty knows the usefulness of the useful,
but has not yet realized the usefulness of the useless.
Now I ask to soar for Your Majesty."
He then took it and mounted it,
whereupon it flapped its wings and flew away,
and none knew where he went.
The Magician from Tiāndú Country
In the seventh year of King Zhāo of Yān,
the country of Mùgǔ came to court,
which is another name for Shēndú country.
There was a magician named Shīluó.
Asked his age,
he said:
"One hundred and forty years old."
Carrying a monk's staff and holding a bottle,
he said:
"I set out from my country five years ago,
and only now reached the Yān capital."
He delighted in dazzling magical arts.
From his fingertip,
emerged a pagoda of ten stories,
three chǐ high,
with all the heavenly immortals and deities,
exquisitely beautiful and extraordinarily fine.
Banners and canopies were arrayed, dancing and drumming,
circling the pagoda as they walked,
the figures all five or six fēn tall,
their singing voices
like those of real people.
Shīluó sprayed water to create mist and fog,
darkening an area of several lǐ.
Then he blew again to create a swift wind,
and the mist and fog all ceased.
He also blew on the pagoda on his finger,
and it gradually entered the clouds.
Then from his left ear emerged a blue dragon,
from his right ear a white tiger.
When they first emerged,
they were only one or two cùn,
gradually growing to eight or nine chǐ.
Soon wind arrived and clouds gathered,
then with one hand he waved them away,
and the dragon and tiger both re-entered his ears.
He also opened his mouth towards the sun,
then one could see people riding in feathered canopies,
driving chī-dragons and swans,
directly entering his mouth.
Again, pressing his hand on his chest,
one could hear from within his sleeve,
the rumbling sound of thunder.
Opening his mouth again,
then the previously seen feathered canopies, chī-dragons, and swans,
followed one another out from his mouth.
Shīluó often sat under the sun,
gradually feeling his form grow small,
sometimes transforming into an old man,
sometimes changing into an infant,
suddenly dying,
fragrance filling the room,
then a clear breeze would come,
blowing upon him to revive,
restoring his former shape.
His incantations and dazzling arts,
were divine and strange, endless and boundless.
The Painter from Qiānxiāo Country
The first year of Emperor Qín Shǐ Huáng's reign.
The state of Qiānxiāo presented a skilled jade-carving painter named Yì.
He could hold pigments in his mouth and spit them onto the ground,
whereupon images of demons, ghosts, and all manner of creatures would appear;
he could carve stone into the forms of a hundred beasts,
their fur and hair as lifelike as if they were real.
Each was inscribed on its chest,
recording the year and month.
The artisan could also paint on the ground with silk.
Within a square inch,
he could depict maps of the four great rivers, the five sacred mountains, and various states.
He also painted dragons and phoenixes,
soaring as if about to fly.
None were allowed to have eyes painted,
for if eyes were added, they would surely fly or run away.
Emperor Qín Shǐ Huáng sighed and said:
"How can mere painted forms
possibly fly or run away?"
He ordered pure lacquer to be used to dot a single eye on each of two jade tigers.
After ten days, they disappeared,
and no one knew where they had gone.
People from the mountains and marshes said:
"We saw two white tigers,
each missing one eye,
walking together.
Their fur color and appearance
were different from ordinary tigers."
The following year,
the western regions presented two white tigers,
both missing one eye.
Emperor Qín Shǐ Huáng had the cages opened to inspect them,
suspecting they were the ones previously lost.
He then had them stabbed to death,
and upon examining their chests,
found they were indeed the jade tigers carved in the first year.
The man from Yínglíng
In Hàn Dynasty Běihǎi, Yínglíng, there was a Daoist
who could make people see the already deceased.
A man from the same commandery,
whose wife had died several years earlier,
heard of this and went to see him, saying:
"I wish to see my deceased wife just once,
and I would die without regret."
The Daoist said:
"You may go see her.
But if you hear the sound of a drum,
leave immediately and do not linger."
He then explained the method for the meeting.
Thereupon, the man spoke with his wife, experiencing both sorrow and joy,
their affection as if she were alive.
After a long while,
he heard the drum sound,
but reluctantly could not bring himself to leave.
Just as he was exiting the door,
suddenly, the hem of her garment caught on the doorframe,
tore off, and he left.
More than a year later,
this man died.
When his family buried him
and opened the grave,
they saw the hem of a garment under the lid of his wife's coffin.
People of Fúlóu
In the southern borderlands was the state of Fúlóu.
Its people were skilled in ingenious transformations,
changing their forms and altering their attire.
They could become large enough to raise clouds and mist,
or small enough to enter the finest thread.
They adorned their clothing with gold, jade, feathers, and fur.
They could spew clouds and spit fire,
and drumming their bellies produced sounds like thunder.
Sometimes they took the shapes of giant elephants, lions, dragons, snakes, dogs, or horses.
Sometimes a human would emerge from a tiger's mouth,
or they would produce music of a hundred beasts within their palms,
twisting and bending between their fingers.
Human forms might be only a few tenths of an inch tall,
or again several inches,
spirits and monsters appearing and vanishing in an instant,
dazzling.
Splendid for their time.
The Music Bureau all transmitted these arts,
until the end.
Later generations still studied them,
some grasping the coarse, some the refined,
passed down unbroken through the ages,
commonly called the Póhóu arts,
which is a phonetic corruption of Fúlóu.
Xú Dēng
In Mǐnzhōng there was a man named Xú Dēng,
a woman who transformed into a man.
Together with Zhào Bǐng from Dōngyáng, both were skilled in occult arts.
At the time, due to military chaos,
they met by a stream,
each boasting of their abilities.
Xú Dēng first magically halted the stream so it ceased to flow,
then Zhào Bǐng magically caused a withered willow to sprout new shoots.
The two looked at each other and laughed.
Xú Dēng was older,
so Zhào Bǐng served him as a teacher.
Later, Xú Dēng passed away,
and Zhào Bǐng traveled east to Cháng'ān.
The common people did not yet know Zhào Bǐng,
so he ascended to a thatched hut,
and used a tripod cauldron to cook.
The owner was shocked and alarmed,
but Zhào Bǐng only laughed and did not respond,
and the hut remained undamaged.
He also once sought to cross a river,
but the boatman refused him.
Zhào Bǐng then opened a canopy and sat within it,
let out a long whistle to summon the wind,
and crossed the turbulent current.
Thereupon, the common people revered and submitted to him,
and followers gathered like returning home.
The magistrate of Cháng'ān, despising him, had him killed.
The people erected a shrine for him in Yǒngníng,
and mosquitoes and gnats could not enter it.
Zhōu Zhěn's slave
During the Wèi period,
among the Mán people in the northern mountains of Xúnyáng County,
there was a man with magic arts
who could transform people into tigers.
Their fur color, claws, and bodies were exactly like real tigers.
A villager named Zhōu Zhěn had a slave
whom he sent into the mountains to gather firewood.
The slave had a wife and a younger sister,
who went with him.
Upon reaching the mountains,
the slave said to the two women:
"You two go climb a tall tree,
I need to do something."
They did as he said.
He then entered the grass,
and moments later,
a large yellow-striped tiger emerged from the grassy hill,
leaping fiercely and roaring,
extremely terrifying.
The two women were greatly frightened.
After a long while, it returned to the grass,
and soon after returned as a human.
He told the two women:
"When you return home, be careful not to speak of this."
Later, they eventually spoke of it to others.
Zhōu Zhěn investigated further,
and had strong wine given to the slave to drink,
making him thoroughly drunk.
He had someone remove the slave's clothes,
then meticulously examined every part of his body,
finding absolutely nothing unusual.
Only within his hair knot did he find a piece of paper,
on which a tiger was drawn,
with a talisman beside the tiger.
Zhōu Zhěn carefully took and recorded it.
When the slave was awakened,
they questioned him.
Seeing the matter exposed,
he then fully explained the whole story, saying:
"Previously, I went to purchase grain among the Mán people,
and a Mán shaman said he had this talisman.
For three chǐ of cloth,
one dǒu of rice,
one chicken,
and one dǒu of wine,
I received this method."
Zhào Hóu
Marquis Zhào of Jìn was fond of various arts from a young age,
but his appearance was unimpressive and haggard,
standing no taller than a few chǐ.
He would place water in a basin to perform spells,
and fish and dragons would immediately appear.
The Marquis had white rice,
which was stolen by rats.
He then let down his hair and held a knife,
drawing a hell on the ground,
with gates on all four sides.
Facing east, he let out a shout,
and all the rats gathered.
He chanted a spell:
"Those who did not eat it may pass,
but the thieves must stay."
More than ten rats remained,
and when he cut open their bellies to examine their organs,
rice was found inside.
Once, needing sandals while barefoot,
he tilted his head and softly chanted,
and a pair of sandals came to him on their own.
When people laughed at his appearance,
he pretended to set up a spell,
using a wine cup to face the sun,
Immediately, their noses were covered and could not be removed,
so they kowtowed to apologize for their offense.
Their heads remained pressed to the ground, unable to rise.
In Yǒngkāng, there is Qíshí Mountain,
on which there are stone figures riding stone horses.
The Marquis pointed his seal at them,
and the heads of the figures and horses fell off at once,
and they remain at the foot of the mountain to this day.
The Indian Foreigner
During the Yǒngjiā era of Jìn,
an Indian foreigner came across the river to the south.
He possessed illusionary arts,
able to cut his tongue and spit fire,
attracting crowds of onlookers wherever he went.
Before cutting his tongue,
he would first show it to the crowd.
Then he would cut it with a knife,
and blood would flow and cover the ground.
He would then burn it and place it in a container,
passing it around for people to see.
When they looked,
half of the tongue was still there.
Afterward, he would retrieve it,
reattach it,
and in a moment, it was as before,
leaving people unsure whether it had truly been cut.
He once took a piece of silk cloth and had someone hold one end while he held the other,
then cut it in the middle.
Afterward, he took the two pieces,
chanted a spell over them,
and the silk cloth became whole again,
as if it had never been cut.
He also took paper, rope, and similar items,
threw them into the fire,
and everyone watched
as they burned completely to ashes.
Then he stirred the ashes,
lifted them out,
and the original objects were restored.
Jū Dàolóng
Gé Hóng said:
Among those I knew in my youth was Jū Dàolóng,
who excelled in illusionary arts.
He told me stories from ancient times.
There was a man from Dōnghǎi named Huáng Gōng,
who in his youth could ride dragons and tame tigers,
wearing red
gold as a knife,
and tying his hair with crimson silk.
Standing, he could summon clouds and mist;
sitting, he could create mountains and rivers.
But as he grew old and weak,
his strength waned,
and he drank excessively,
losing the ability to perform his arts.
At the end of the Qín dynasty,
a white tiger appeared in Dōnghǎi,
and Huáng Gōng tried to subdue it with his red knife,
but his arts no longer worked,
and he was killed by the tiger.
The people of Sānfǔ adopted this story as entertainment,
and the Hàn dynasty also incorporated it into wrestling performances.
The Scholar from Yángxiàn
During the Eastern Jìn dynasty, Xǔ Yàn of Yángxiàn was traveling through Suí'ān Mountain
when he encountered a scholar,
about seventeen or eighteen years old,
lying by the roadside,
who said:
"My feet hurt,
may I ride in your goose cage?"
Xǔ Yàn thought he was joking,
but the scholar entered the cage.
The cage did not grow larger,
nor did the scholar shrink.
He sat comfortably alongside the two geese,
and the geese were not startled.
Xǔ Yàn carried the cage and walked on,
feeling no extra weight.
When he rested under a tree ahead,
the scholar emerged from the cage.
He said to Xǔ Yàn:
"I would like to prepare a modest meal for you."
Xǔ Yàn replied:
"That would be wonderful."
The scholar then spat out a bronze tray and a small box from his mouth,
inside which were all kinds of delicacies,
a lavish spread of land and sea delicacies,
all served in bronze vessels,
with fragrant and delicious aromas,
rarely seen in the world.
After several rounds of wine,
the scholar said to Xǔ Yàn:
"I brought a woman with me earlier,
and now I would like to summon her for a moment."
Xǔ Yàn said:
"Very well."
The scholar then spat out a woman from his mouth,
about fifteen or sixteen years old,
dressed in elegant and beautiful clothes,
with peerless beauty,
and they all sat together feasting.
Soon, the scholar fell into a drunken slumber.
The woman said to Xǔ Yàn:
"Although I am with the scholar,
I actually have feelings for another.
I secretly brought a man with me earlier,
and now that the scholar is asleep,
I would like to call him out for a moment.
Please do not say anything."
Xǔ Yàn said:
"Very well."
The woman then spat out a man from her mouth,
about twenty-three or twenty-four years old,
also clever and charming,
and he exchanged pleasantries with Xǔ Yàn.
When the scholar began to stir from his sleep,
the woman spat out a brocade screen,
and the scholar remained with the woman to sleep.
The man said to Xǔ Yàn:
"Although this woman has feelings for me,
her heart is not entirely devoted.
She secretly brought another woman with her earlier,
and now I would like to see her for a moment.
Please do not reveal this."
Xǔ Yàn said:
"Alright."
The man then spat out another woman from his mouth,
about twenty years old,
and they drank and feasted together.
They flirted and joked for a long time,
until they heard the scholar stirring.
The man said:
"The two of them are waking up."
He then took the woman he had spat out
and put her back into his mouth.
Shortly after,
the woman with the scholar came out
and said to Xǔ Yàn:
"The scholar is about to get up."
She then swallowed the man from earlier,
and sat alone with Xǔ Yàn.
The scholar then said to Xǔ Yàn:
"I slept longer than intended,
leaving you sitting alone.
You must have been bored.
It is getting late,
so I will take my leave."
He then swallowed the woman again,
and all the bronze vessels were put back into his mouth.
He left behind a large bronze tray,
about two chǐ or more in diameter.
Bidding farewell to Xǔ Yàn, he said:
"Keep this as a memento,
to remember me by."
During the Tàiyuán era,
Xǔ Yàn served as Lántái Lìngshǐ,
and he gave the tray to Attendant-in-Waiting Zhāng Sàn as a gift.
Zhāng Sàn examined the inscription,
which stated it was made in the third year of the Hàn dynasty's Yǒngpíng era.
Hóu Zǐguāng
Hóu Zǐguāng from Āndìng,
in his youth was handsome in appearance.
He claimed to be the Buddha's son,
come from the Great Qín country,
destined to be king of the Lesser Qín country.
He changed his name to Lǐ,
and relied on Yīng.
He lodged at the home of Chìméi.
His strange abilities were quite apparent,
and his deeds showed slight evidence of efficacy.
Chìméi believed in him,
and gave him two daughters in marriage.
Spreading his influence and deluding others,
Fán Suí, Zhúlóng, and Chén from Jīngzhào,
Chén, Xiè Lè, and others,
gathered a crowd of several thousand at Dùyáng Mountain,
proclaiming himself the Great Emperor.
He changed the reign era to Lóngxīng,
and established officials.
General Zhènxī Shí Guǎng attacked and pacified them,
Zǐguāng's neck showed no blood,
and after more than ten days his complexion remained as if alive.
Sòng Zǐxián
In the ninth year of the Dàyè era of Emperor Yáng of Suí,
Sòng Zǐxián from Táng County was skilled in illusionary arts.
Every night there was light upstairs,
he could transform into the shape of a Buddha,
and claimed to be the Maitreya Buddha appearing in the world.
He also hung a mirror in the hall,
and the walls were filled with shapes of beasts.
When people came to pay respects and visit,
he would turn the mirror,
allowing them to see images of their next life,
sometimes appearing as snakes or beasts.
Zǐxián would then inform them of their sinful karma.
Only after further worship and recitation,
would he turn it to show a human shape.
People from near and far were deluded and believed,
gathering several thousand people,
and he secretly planned rebellion.
The affair was exposed.
Officials arrested him.
Arriving at night,
they surrounded his dwelling.
They only saw a pit of fire,
and the soldiers dared not advance.
Their commander said:
"This place has never had a pit,
it is merely demonic deceit."
Upon advancing,
there was again no fire,
and they captured and beheaded him.
The Hú Monk
During the Zhēnguàn era of Táng,
the Western Regions presented a Hú monk.
His incantation arts could kill people,
and could revive people.
Emperor Tàizōng ordered strong and brave men from the Feíqí cavalry to test him.
As he said, they died,
as he said, they revived.
The emperor informed Fù Yì, the Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
Yì said:
"This is evil magic.
Your servant has heard that evil cannot overcome the upright.
If he were to curse your servant,
it certainly would not work."
The emperor summoned the monk to curse Yì,
Yì faced him without any sensation.
After a moment,
the Hú monk suddenly fell down by himself,
as if struck,
and did not revive.
Zǔ Zhēnjiǎn
During the Xiánhēng era of Táng,
Zǔ Zhēnjiǎn of Zhàozhōu had demonic arts.
He hung a water jar from a beam,
struck it with a knife,
the rope broke but the jar did not fall.
Also, in an empty room with the door tightly closed,
he placed a jar of water,
and laid a knife across it.
After a long while, people entered to look,
and saw Jiǎn dismembered into five sections,
the water jar all bloody.
After people left,
he returned to normal as before.
In the extreme cold of winter,
when the stone mortar was frozen,
he chanted and pulled it out.
He sold divinations in the market of Xìndū,
earning a hundred coins daily,
following the method of Jūn Píng.
Later, he was accused by someone,
taken to the market for execution,
his expression composed,
showing no fear at all,
requested paper and brush to compose verses,
his spirit undaunted.
Dàoshi Yè
Dàoshi Yè of the Língkōng Temple in Táng,
enchanted knives.
He would strike a sick person's belly with full force,
place peach and willow branches across the abdomen,
the branches would break but the flesh remained unharmed.
Later, he used two knives to cut a woman,
she fell into two sections instantly,
blood flowing all over the ground.
Her family wailed loudly.
The dàoshi took and rejoined her,
sprayed water and chanted.
After a moment,
she recovered as before.
The Yāo Master of Hénán
In the Lìdé Ward and the Western Ward of the Southern Market of Hénán Prefecture in Táng,
there were Hú yāo spirit temples.
Each year,
Hú merchants prayed for blessings,
cooking pigs and slaughtering sheep,
playing pipa, drums, and flutes,
singing and dancing drunkenly.
After repaying the spirits,
they selected one Hú as the yāo master.
Spectators gave money to him.
The yāo master took a horizontal knife,
sharp as frost and snow,
a hair blown against it would not pass.
He stabbed the knife into his abdomen,
the blade emerging from his back,
then stirred his intestines and stomach, bleeding.
After the time of a meal,
he sprayed water and chanted,
recovering as before.
This was likely illusionary magic from the Western Regions.
The Yāo Master of Liángzhōu
At the yāo spirit shrine in Liángzhōu of Táng.
On the day of prayer,
the yāo master used sharp iron,
driving it from his forehead,
piercing straight through to under his armpit,
then went out the door.
His body light as if flying,
covering several hundred lǐ in a moment.
Arriving before the Western yāo spirit,
he performed a dance,
then returned to the original yāo place,
pulled out the nail,
completely unharmed.
He rested for over ten days,
then recovered as before.
No one knew how it was done.
Míng Chóngyǎn
Míng Chóngyǎn of Táng had magical arts.
Great.
The emperor tested him,
digging an underground cellar,
and had courtesans play music.
Summoning Yǎn,
said to him:
"This place often hears string and wind music,
what omen is this?
Can you stop it?"
Yǎn said:
"Yes."
Then wrote two peachwood charms,
nailed them above,
and the sounds ceased.
The emperor laughed,
called the courtesans to ask,
they said:
"We saw two dragon heads,
opening mouths downward,
so we were terrified and dared not play music."
The emperor was greatly pleased.
Liú Jìng's Wife
When Zhāng Shǒuguī was stationed in Fànyáng during the Táng dynasty,
the magistrate of Mìyún County in Tánzhōu had a daughter,
seventeen years old,
of extraordinary beauty.
The girl had been ill for over a year,
and no doctor could cure her.
In the northern mountains of Mìyún lived a Daoist,
dressed in yellow robes,
who had resided in the mountains for several hundred years
and was said to possess magical arts.
The magistrate personally went to the mountains to invite him.
After the Daoist arrived,
he provided a prescription,
and the girl’s illness was immediately cured.
The magistrate was overjoyed
and rewarded him generously with wealth.
After staying for over a month,
the girl, while sleeping at night,
found someone lying with her and engaging in intimacy.
Whenever this person came,
the girl would fall into a stupor.
When dawn came and the man left,
she would return to normal.
This happened for several nights,
and the girl, frightened, told her mother.
The mother informed the magistrate.
They then moved the bed closer to themselves
and kept watch at night.
Feeling the bed move,
they seized the moment,
captured a man,
and immediately called for a lamp.
It turned out to be the Daoist from the northern mountains.
The magistrate had him bound and interrogated.
The Daoist wept and said:
"My fate is at its end,
and I have been deluded to this extent.
I have lived in the northern mountains for over six hundred years
and have never ventured into the human world.
Now I am nearing a thousand years old.
Yesterday, I received a sincere invitation,
which is why I came to the county.
Upon seeing your daughter,
I was greatly captivated by her,
and though I tried to restrain myself, I could not,
so I came and went.
I possess magical arts,
and during the day, I can conceal my form,
which is why the household never saw me.
Now that I have encountered this calamity,
what more is there to say?"
The magistrate ultimately had him killed.
A Daoist Priest of Dōngmíng Temple
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
a beautiful woman in the palace
suddenly dreamed at night of being invited away,
where she indulged in secret meetings with wine,
returning after great joy,
always sweating and exhausted.
Later, she calmly reported this to the emperor.
The emperor said:
"This must be the work of a sorcerer.
If you go again,
secretly mark something as a clue."
That night, she fell into a deep sleep
and drifted away once more.
Half-drunk, the beauty
saw an inkstone in front of her
and secretly pressed her handprint onto the screen in the secluded chamber.
Upon waking, she reported everything in detail.
The emperor then secretly ordered a search,
instructing that it be conducted in all the temples and monasteries.
Sure enough, at Dōngmíng Temple, they found the screen
with the handprint still on it,
but the Daoist priest who lived there had already fled.
A Monk of Dōngyán Temple
Cuī Jiǎn of Bólíng was intelligent and clever from a young age,
fond of extraordinary arts.
He once met the Daoist priest Zhāng Yuánsù, who enlightened him with the essentials of the Dao,
enabling him to command divine beings
and effortlessly master transformations.
In the second year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty, he went to Shǔ Commandery.
In the commandery, there was a man named Lǚ Yì
who, upon meeting Cuī Jiǎn, generously offered him gifts,
intending to request something.
Cuī Jiǎn asked what he desired,
and Lǚ Yì replied:
"I have a daughter,
who has never been seen by others.
While secluded in her inner chambers,
she vanished one night.
I believe you, sir, possess extraordinary arts;
I wish to know how to capture her,
so that I may close my eyes without regret."
Cuī Jiǎn said:
"That is easy."
He then prepared a separate room,
set up a table and mat at night,
and burned fine incense to summon divine spirits.
Cuī Jiǎn instructed Lǚ Yì to hide with a sword by the door,
saying that if a foreign monk came, he should seize him and demand the girl,
but he must be careful not to harm him.
Cuī Jiǎn wrote a talisman and incanted over it,
and the talisman flew away.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
a wind arose, uprooting trees and tearing off roofs.
Suddenly, an armored soldier entered and reported:
"The divine troops are prepared,
awaiting your command, my king."
Cuī Jiǎn said:
"The master's daughter was lost on a certain day;
capture her and bring her here."
The soldier said:
"Only the ascetic on the eastern mountain
daily uses incantations and water to abduct people;
could it be him?"
Cuī Jiǎn said:
"If so,
capture him quickly and bring him here."
The soldier left
and returned shortly, saying:
"The ascetic on the eastern mountain was alarmed and angry upon hearing this,
and is about to send a Vajra warrior to attack you.
What shall we do?" Cuī Jiǎn said:
"Do not worry."
He wrote another talisman and sent it flying.
Suddenly, tens of thousands of divine troops appeared,
all with strange shapes and unusual appearances,
holding swords and halberds, arrayed in the courtyard.
Soon, a Vajra warrior was seen approaching from the northwest,
dozens of zhang tall,
glaring and shouting at Cuī Jiǎn's troops.
Cuī Jiǎn's troops
prostrated themselves, not daring to move.
Cuī Jiǎn paced with his sword before the altar,
and the divine troops suddenly vanished.
Immediately, the Vajra warrior appeared alarmed.
Ah!
After a long time, nothing was seen.
Suddenly, a creature appeared,
with a pig's head and a human body,
wearing leopard skin and water trousers.
It said:
"The ascetic wishes to pay his respects to the immortal official."
Cuī Jiǎn sat cross-legged
and commanded it.
A foreign monk in purple robes hurried in.
Cuī Jiǎn rebuked him:
"Monk, you stole the master's daughter;
how dare you recklessly employ divine beings!"
At first, the monk resisted and lied.
Suddenly, Lǚ Yì leaped out from behind the door,
seized him, and accused him.
The monk, under pressure, could no longer hide the truth
and said:
"I submit!
I, a humble monk, practice the Great Power Dharma,
but it was a sage who caused this,
not something I sought.
I will return her now,
so please do not press me harshly.
If not for the immortal official's command,
would you have hoped for this?
I ask that the sage bring her here."
In a moment,
the pig-headed creature was seen carrying the girl back,
unconscious as if asleep.
Cuī Jiǎn said:
"You should fetch well water and make peach soup,
wash her with it, and she will awaken."
The girl then recounted:
"At first, while sleeping,
I dreamed that a creature with a pig's head and a human body abducted me.
I did not know how far we traveled,
until we reached a small room,
where I saw the foreign monk assaulting me.
I asked where I was,
and he said it was heaven,
then confined me so I could not leave.
That night,
soldiers and cavalry arrived at the door,
and the pig-headed creature came again,
saying:
'Perfected Person Cuī has given an order.'
Only then was I able to return.
However, when I left,
I secretly smeared a little rouge powder on the monk's door,
leaving three fingerprints.
If you search based on this, you may find him."
Lǚ Yì generously rewarded Cuī Jiǎn
and secretly searched for the mark on the monk's door.
Several months later,
while visiting Dōngyán Temple,
he entered a winding room
and suddenly saw fingerprints on the right panel of the door.
He immediately pursued,
but the monk had already left the previous night,
and no one knew where he had gone.
The temple was
more than ten lǐ away from where Lǚ Yì lived.
The Jīng Sorcerer
During the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
a sorcerer from Jīng came from the south
and stayed at Zhìpǐ Temple.
He was fond of wine,
and was seldom sober.
During a grand vegetarian feast at the temple,
with a crowd of several thousand people,
the sorcerer suddenly said:
"I have a skill
that can replace
the joy of clapping and juggling pearls."
He then mixed colored pigments in a container,
paced with light steps and rubbed his eyes.
Slowly, he recited several dozen incantations,
drank water two or three times,
and spat it onto the wall.
It formed a transformation scene of Vimalakīrti visiting the sick,
with colors harmoniously blended,
as if freshly painted.
After half a day or more,
the colors gradually faded,
and by evening, they had completely vanished.
Only a single flower on the robe of the golden millet turban and the Kāśyapa garment
remained for two more days.
The Foreign Monk Nàntuó
The Tang dynasty chancellor, Duke Wèi, Zhāng Yánshǎng,
while in Shǔ,
encountered a foreign monk named Nàntuó who had attained the samādhi of illusion,
able to enter water and fire,
penetrate metal and stone,
and perform limitless transformations.
When he first entered Shǔ,
he traveled with three nuns.
Sometimes they would get heavily drunk and sing wildly,
and the garrison commander was about to have them executed.
But when the monk arrived,
he said:
"I have taken refuge in the monastic order,
but I also possess special medicinal arts."
He then pointed to the three nuns,
saying, "They excel at singing and playing instruments."
The garrison commander instead showed them respect,
and they lingered,
with wine prepared for them.
One night, during a gathering with guests and heavy drinking,
the monk borrowed a woman's jacket and headscarf,
bought lead powder and eyebrow pigment,
and adorned the three nuns.
Once seated,
they cast flirtatious glances and bantered,
their enchanting demeanor unparalleled in the world.
As the drinking was about to end,
the monk said to the nuns:
"You may perform the tune of Yāyá."
They then slowly advanced and danced in pairs,
their sleeves trailing like drifting snow,
swiftly moving and touching their feet,
their skill also peerless.
After a long while,
the music ended, but the dancing did not stop.
The monk shouted:
"Is this the manner of women?"
Suddenly, he rose and took the garrison commander's sword.
The crowd thought him drunk and mad,
and fled in panic.
The monk then drew the sword and struck them,
and they all fell to the ground,
blood spreading several feet.
The garrison commander was greatly terrified,
and called for his attendants to seize the monk.
The monk laughed and said:
"Do not act rashly."
Slowly, he lifted the nuns—
they were three bamboo staffs,
and the blood was merely wine.
On another occasion, during a drinking party,
he had someone cut off his head,
which was then nailed by the ear to a pillar,
with no blood.
His body sat on the mat,
and when wine was brought,
it was poured into the neck wound,
his face flushed as he sang,
his hands still keeping time.
When the party ended,
he stood up, took his head, and reattached it,
leaving no trace at all.
He often foretold people's misfortunes and declines,
all in cryptic language,
only understood after the events occurred.
A commoner in Chéngdū
provided for him for several days,
but the monk did not wish to stay.
The commoner shut the door to detain him,
so the monk walked into the wall.
The commoner hastily grabbed him,
but he gradually sank in,
leaving only a corner of his kasaya robe,
which soon also vanished.
The next day, there was a painting of the monk on the wall,
resembling his form,
but it gradually faded with each passing day.
After seven days,
only a black trace remained,
and by the eighth day,
even the black trace disappeared,
for he was already in Péngzhōu.
Later, no one knew where he went.
The Old Monk of Tàibái
During the Táng dynasty,
there was a son of the Lù family from Píngyáng,
who had a curious nature.
In his youth, he traveled with Daoist priests,
and later lived in seclusion on Mount Tàibái.
One day,
an old monk knocked on his door.
Mr. Lù invited him in to sit,
and they conversed for a long time.
The monk said:
"You, benefactor, are a curious person,
but you have yet to reach the essence of the profound mysteries.
It is futile to merely dwell deep in the mountains.
Would it not be better to don light furs,
ride swift horses,
and roam the bustling markets?
Would that not fulfill your lifelong aspirations?
How can you be content keeping company with deer?"
Mr. Lù replied:
"Your words, Master,
sound like those of a truly enlightened one.
Yet, if you cannot show me traces of the profound mysteries,
why do you boast with empty words?"
The monk said:
"Allow this disciple to show you my traces of the profound mysteries."
With these words,
he took out a small box from his robe,
about an inch in diameter,
black in color and gleaming.
Upon opening it,
he entered it with his body,
and in an instant transformed into a bird,
soaring into the sky.
Zhāng Hé
In the early years of the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a wealthy family in Shǔ Commandery,
whose riches rivaled those of Zhūo and Zhèng.
All the famous beauties of Shǔ
had been gathered without exception,
each sought according to portraits.
Matchmakers filled their gate,
yet they often lamented having no one who pleased them.
Someone said:
"The ward head Zhāng Hé
is a great gallant.
Secluded chambers and young maidens
—there is none he does not know of.
Why not sincerely seek his help?"
The scion of the wealthy family then took gold and silk by night to his dwelling and told him,
and Zhāng Hé gladly agreed.
Another day,
he and the scion both went out one post-station west of the outer wall,
entered an abandoned temple,
where a great statue stood majestically.
Together with the scion, he climbed onto the statue's seat.
Hé reached out and pressed the Buddha's breast, lifting it.
The breast broke open into a hole,
like a bowl.
He then straightened his body and entered the hole,
pulled the scion's arm,
and before they knew it, they were together inside the hole.
After walking several dozen steps,
suddenly they beheld high gates and lofty walls,
resembling a prefectural or county seat.
Hé knocked five or six times,
and a lovely child with hair in a round topknot came to greet them, bowing, saying:
"My master has long awaited your arrival, sir."
After a short while,
the master came out,
dressed in purple robes with a shell-adorned belt,
attended by over ten servants,
and treated Hé with great respect.
Hé pointed to the scion and said:
"This is a young gentleman.
You must serve him well.
I have urgent matters and must return;
I will not stay and take my leave."
Having said this,
Hé was already nowhere to be seen.
The scion found this strange in his heart,
but dared not ask.
The master invited him into the central hall,
where pearls, jades, and embroidered silks
were arrayed before his eyes.
He prepared a lavish feast of land and sea delicacies
and ordered wine to be poured.
Singing girls approached, their hair coiled and temples brushed,
ethereal as immortals.
Their games of dancing cups and flicking balls
were all novel and full of ingenuity.
There was a golden vessel,
holding several shēng,
with a cloud-shaped stem and a whale-shaped mouth,
inlaid with pearl granules.
The scion did not recognize it
and asked about it.
The master laughed and said:
"This is a vessel for spitting,
originally intended for Bóyǎ."
The scion still did not understand.
When the third watch arrived,
the master suddenly turned to the singing girls and said:
"Do not cease your merrymaking;
I shall briefly go elsewhere."
He bowed to the guest and rose,
his mounted retinue like that of a prefect,
and departed with a row of torches.
The scion then privately went to a corner by the wall,
and a singing girl somewhat older in years
hurriedly approached him and said:
"Alas!
How did you come to be here?
We have already been abducted,
intoxicated by his illusions,
and the road back is forever cut off.
If you wish to return,
just follow my instructions."
She gave him a seven-foot-long white silk ribbon,
admonishing him:
"Hold this,
and when the master returns,
pretend to have a request and bow to him.
The master will surely bow in return;
then use the ribbon to cover his neck."
As dawn approached,
the master returned.
The scion followed her instructions,
and the master fell to the ground, begging for his life, saying:
"That old hag betrayed me;
she has ruined my plans in the end.
I shall no longer dwell here."
He then galloped away on horseback.
The singing girl who had instructed him then lived with the scion.
After two years, he suddenly thought of returning home.
The singing girl did not detain him.
She prepared a grand feast with wine and music to bid him farewell.
When the drinking was done,
the singing girl herself took a spade,
opened a hole in the eastern wall,
also like the Buddha's breast,
and pushed the scion outside the wall.
It was beneath the eastern wall of Cháng'ān,
and he had to beg for food before finally reaching Shǔ.
His family had lost him for many years,
and they thought him a ghost,
but when he told his story from the beginning, they believed him.
Hú Mèi'ér
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
in the wards and markets of Yángzhōu,
suddenly there appeared a female performer.
She practiced magic and begged,
and no one knew where she came from.
She claimed her surname was Hú,
and her given name was Mèi'ér.
Her actions were rather bizarre.
After ten days,
spectators gradually gathered like clouds.
What she begged for
amounted to tens of millions daily.
One morning,
she took out a glass bottle from her bosom,
which could hold half a shēng.
It was transparent inside and out,
as if nothing separated them,
and she placed it on a mat.
She first said to the spectators:
"If someone fills this bottle with alms,
then it will be enough."
The mouth of the bottle was just as big as a reed pipe.
Someone gave her a hundred coins,
dropped them in,
and they clinked with a sound.
Then they saw the coins inside the bottle as large as millet grains.
Everyone found it strange.
Another person gave her a thousand coins,
and when dropped in, it was as before.
Yet another gave ten thousand coins,
and it was the same.
Soon, an enthusiast
gave her a hundred thousand or two hundred thousand,
and it was all the same.
Some even led horses or donkeys into the bottle,
and the people and horses inside appeared as small as flies,
moving about as usual.
After a short while,
a tax transport convoy from the revenue department,
from the Yángzǐ bureau,
arrived with dozens of carts of light goods.
They stopped to watch,
thinking that if they put them in all at once,
perhaps they could not later take other things away,
and moreover, they considered official goods not to be doubted.
They then said to Mèi'ér:
"Can you make all these carts enter this bottle?"
Mèi'ér said:
"If you allow it, then it can be done."
The convoy leader said:
"Then try it."
Mèi'ér then slightly tilted the bottle's mouth,
shouted loudly,
and the carts rumbled one after another,
all entering the bottle.
Inside the bottle, they were clearly visible like marching ants.
After a while,
they gradually disappeared from sight.
Mèi'ér then leaped into the bottle herself.
The convoy leader was greatly alarmed,
hurriedly grabbed and smashed the bottle,
but found nothing inside.
From then on, Mèi'ér was nowhere to be found.
Over a month later,
someone north of Qīnghé
encountered Mèi'ér,
leading a convoy of carts,
heading east toward Dōngpíng.
At that time,
Lǐ Shīdào was the military governor of Dōngpíng.
A commoner from the central region
In the early years of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man from Tiānshuǐ named Zhào Yún,
who was traveling as a guest in Fūzhì.
Passing through Zhōngbù County,
he attended a banquet hosted by the county officials.
An official had apprehended a man,
whose crime was not particularly serious,
and the officials intended to release him.
Yún, being drunk,
insistently urged that punishment be imposed,
and so the man was caned.
Several months later,
Yún journeyed beyond the frontier.
When he reached Lúzǐ Pass,
he encountered a man on the road,
who invited him to converse.
As dusk fell,
the man led Yún off the road to his residence.
After traveling several lǐ,
he ordered wine, and they drank together.
After a while, the man asked:
"Do you remember meeting me before?"
Yún replied:
"I have never traveled this way before,
and truly do not recall you."
The man continued:
"On such-and-such day of such-and-such month,
I encountered you in Zhōngbù.
I had suffered an unjust accusation,
and though I had no prior enmity with you,
why did you urge them,
causing me to receive severe punishment?"
Yún hastily rose and apologized.
The man said:
"I have long awaited you—
how could I have expected to avenge this small grievance here!"
He then ordered his attendants
to drag Yún into a room.
In the room was a large pit,
over three zhàng deep,
filled only with ten hú of distiller's grains.
They stripped off his clothes
and pushed Yún into it.
When hungry, he ate the grains;
when thirsty, he drank the liquid.
Thus, he remained in a daze for nearly a month,
after which they bound him and pulled him out.
They made someone pinch his nose and forehead,
twist and pull his limbs,
so that his fingers, shoulders, and thighs
all changed from their original form.
They then exposed him to the wind,
and in an instant, his form solidified.
Even his voice and speech had changed.
He was then kept as a lowly slave
and made to perform miscellaneous duties at the Wūyán post station.
After several years,
it happened that his younger brother, serving as a censor,
was dispatched to investigate cases in Língzhōu.
Yún secretly sent him a detailed account of what had happened.
His brother reported this to Surveillance Commissioner Lǐ Míng,
who then dispatched troops to search,
capturing all the evildoers
and exterminating their gang.
Before execution, they concealed nothing,
saying:
"For generations,
we have been transforming people in this manner!"
Bǎnqiáo Sānniángzi
West of Biànzhōu in the Táng dynasty, there was a shop at Bǎnqiáo.
The shopkeeper, Sānniángzi,
no one knew where she came from.
She was widowed,
over thirty years old,
with no children,
and no relatives either.
She had several rooms,
and made a living by selling meals.
Yet her household was quite wealthy,
with many donkeys and livestock.
For travelers on both public and private business,
if any were in difficulty,
she would lower her prices to help them.
People all said she was virtuous,
so travelers from near and far mostly stayed with her.
During the Yuánhé era,
a traveler from Xǔzhōu, Zhào Jìhé,
was heading to the Eastern Capital,
and stopped here to lodge.
There were six or seven guests who had arrived earlier,
all occupying the convenient beds.
Jìhé arrived later,
and got the innermost bed,
which was adjacent to the wall of the hostess’s room.
Afterward,
Sānniángzi provided the guests with generous hospitality.
Late at night, she served wine,
and drank merrily with the guests.
Jìhé usually did not drink,
but he also joined in the conversation and laughter.
Around the second watch,
the guests, drunk and weary,
each went to bed.
Sānniángzi returned to her room,
closed the door and extinguished the candle.
Everyone was fast asleep,
but Jìhé alone tossed and turned, unable to sleep.
Through the wall, he heard Sānniángzi rustling about,
as if making the sounds of moving objects.
By chance, he peeked through a crack,
and saw Sānniángzi take a candle from under a covered vessel
and light it.
Then from a chest,
she took out a set of plow and plowshare,
along with a wooden ox and a wooden puppet,
each about six or seven inches tall,
and placed them in front of the stove.
She took water in her mouth and sprayed it on them.
The two objects then began to move.
The little man led the ox and hitched it to the plow,
then plowed a patch of ground in front of the bed,
going back and forth several times.
Then from the chest,
she took out a packet of buckwheat seeds,
and gave them to the little man to plant.
In a short while, they sprouted,
bloomed, and the buckwheat ripened.
She ordered the little man to harvest and thresh it,
yielding about seven or eight pecks.
Then she set up a small millstone,
ground it into flour,
and put the wooden puppet back into the chest.
Then she took the flour and made several baked cakes.
After a while, the rooster crowed,
and the guests prepared to depart.
Sānniángzi got up first and lit the lamp,
placing the freshly made baked cakes on the dining table,
and served them to the guests as breakfast.
Jìhé, his heart stirred, hastily declined,
opened the door, and left,
then secretly watched from outside.
He saw the guests gathered around the table,
eating the baked cakes. Before they finished,
they suddenly all fell to the ground at once,
braying like donkeys,
and in a moment, all turned into donkeys.
Sānniángzi drove them all behind the shop,
and confiscated all their goods and money.
Jìhé did not tell anyone about this,
but privately admired her skill.
Over a month later,
Jìhé was returning from the Eastern Capital,
and as he approached the Bǎnqiáo shop,
he prepared some buckwheat baked cakes in advance,
of the same size as before.
Upon arrival,
he lodged there again,
and Sānniángzi was as cheerful as before.
That night, there were no other guests,
and the hostess treated him even more generously.
Late at night,
she earnestly asked what he desired.
Jìhé said:
“I will depart tomorrow morning,
please prepare some breakfast as usual.”
Sānniángzi said:
“That is no trouble at all,
just rest peacefully.”
After midnight,
Jìhé watched her,
and she did exactly as before.
At dawn,
Sānniángzi prepared a tray of food,
placing several baked cakes on the tray,
and went to fetch other things.
Jìhé seized the moment to go down,
and swapped one of the cakes with one he had prepared earlier,
without her noticing.
When Jìhé was about to depart,
and went to eat,
he said to Sānniángzi:
“It happens that I have my own baked cakes,
please take away the hostess’s cakes,
and keep them for other guests.”
Then he took his own and ate them.
Just as he was drinking,
Sānniángzi brought out tea.
Jìhé said:
“Please, hostess, try a piece of the guest’s baked cake.”
Then he picked the swapped cake and gave it to her to eat.
As soon as it entered her mouth,
Sānniángzi fell to the ground, braying like a donkey.
She immediately turned into a donkey,
very strong and healthy.
Jìhé then mounted it and departed,
also taking along the wooden puppet, wooden ox, and other items.
However, he could not master the technique,
and his attempts were unsuccessful.
Jìhé rode the transformed donkey,
traveling to various places,
never encountering obstacles or losses,
covering a hundred lǐ a day.
Four years later,
as he rode it into the pass,
about five or six lǐ east of Huàyuè Temple,
he suddenly saw an old man by the roadside,
clapping his hands and laughing loudly, saying:
“Sānniángzi of Bǎnqiáo,
how did you end up in this form?”
Then he grabbed the donkey and said to Jìhé:
“Although she was at fault,
she has suffered enough at your hands!
Have some pity,
and release her from now on.”
The old man then placed his hands on the donkey’s mouth and nose,
and pried them apart.
Sānniángzi jumped out from the skin,
restored to her original form,
bowed to the old man,
and then walked away.
No one knew where she went after that.
Guān Sīfǎ
In Yùnzhōu, there was a judicial officer named Guān.
He had a hired servant woman surnamed Niǔ.
Guān provided her with food and clothing,
to serve and be driven by him.
As she grew older,
she was called Granny Niǔ.
She also had a grandson,
named Wàn'er,
five or six years old,
who came with her.
Guān's wife also had a young son,
named Fēng Liù,
about the same age.
Guān's wife's son often played with Granny Niǔ's grandson.
Every time Fēng Liù had new clothes made,
his old ones were always given to Wàn'er.
One day,
Granny Niǔ suddenly became angry and said:
"They are both children,
what makes one noble and the other base?
That one's clothes are always new,
while my child gets the old ones!"
She was very displeased.
Guān's wife asked:
"This is my son,
your grandson is just a servant.
I consider that he is about the same age as my son,
so I give him clothes.
How can you not understand propriety?
From now on, he won't even get old clothes anymore!"
Granny Niǔ laughed and said:
"What difference is there between the two children?"
Guān's wife said again:
"How can a servant be the same as a good person's child?"
Granny Niǔ said:
"Are they really different?
Let me test it."
Then she led Fēng Liù and her grandson,
tucked them both under her skirt,
and pressed them to the ground.
Guān's wife, startled, jumped up to snatch them back,
but both children had become Granny Niǔ's grandsons,
identical in appearance and clothing,
indistinguishable.
She then said:
"Now they are the same!"
Guān's wife was greatly frightened,
and together with the judicial officer, they earnestly begged and pleaded,
saying:
"We did not realize a divine being was here."
From then on, the whole family served her respectfully,
not daring to treat her with the old manner.
After a long while,
she again placed the two children under her skirt and pressed them,
and each returned to his original form.
The Guān family then moved Granny Niǔ to live in a separate room,
treated her generously,
and no longer made her work.
After several years,
the Guāns grew rather weary and annoyed,
and secretly wanted to harm her.
They had the wife get her drunk with wine,
while the judicial officer hid by the door,
and struck her with a pickaxe,
hitting her squarely on the head.
There was a sound, and she fell.
Looking at her,
it was a chestnut wood log,
several feet long.
Husband and wife were overjoyed,
ordered it chopped with an axe and burned.
Just as it was about to burn up,
Granny Niǔ came out from the room and said:
"Why did you play such a cruel joke, sir?"
She spoke and laughed as before,
completely unperturbed.
The people of Yùnzhōu learned of this.
Guān, having no other choice,
was going to report it to the Surveillance Commissioner.
As he entered to see him,
suddenly there was another Judicial Officer Guān,
who had already seen the Commissioner and spoken,
identical in appearance.
Guān then returned home,
and upon arriving,
there was already another Judicial Officer Guān who had returned first in the main hall.
His wife and children could not tell them apart.
They again pleaded pitifully with Granny Niǔ,
weeping and bowing in supplication.
After a long while, they gradually drew closer,
and then became one person again.
From then on, the family no longer had any intention of harming her.
For several decades,
she was still in the Guān household,
and there was no further trouble.
A man from Chánglè Ward
In the Bǎolì era of the Táng dynasty,
at the gate of Chánglè Ward, there was a commoner who tattooed his arm,
with dozens of people gathered around watching.
Suddenly, a man,
wearing a white robe,
tilted his head, smiled slightly, and left.
Before he had gone ten paces,
the commoner's son bled from the tattoo as if from a nosebleed,
the pain piercing to the bone.
In the time it takes to eat a meal,
he had lost over a dou of blood.
The crowd suspected it was the doing of the man who had been watching earlier,
and had his father follow and beg him.
The man did not admit it,
but his father bowed dozens of times.
The man then pinched some dust from the wheel rut as if uttering a spell,
saying, "Apply this."
They did as he said, and the bleeding stopped.
Chén Wǔzhèn
In the Táng dynasty, there was a commoner of Zhènzhōu named Chén Wǔzhèn,
whose family wealth accumulated to tens of thousands in gold,
making him a great magnate of the seas.
He had hundreds of storehouses of rhinoceros horn, ivory, and tortoiseshell.
Previously, when merchants from the Western Regions drifted and were shipwrecked arriving there,
he thus acquired these goods.
The people of the sea were skilled in incantation arts,
commonly called 'Démóu methods'.
Whenever merchant ships traveled the sea routes,
far, far away from the five commanderies of the sea,
if unfortunately blown off course by the wind and losing their way,
entering the territory of Zhènzhōu,
the people of Zhènzhōu would climb a mountain, let down their hair, and chant curses.
They would raise winds and stir waves,
so the ships could not leave,
and would inevitably drift to the place they cursed and stop there.
Wǔzhèn became rich because of this.
The Pacification Commissioner Wéi Gōnggàn
treated Wǔzhèn as an elder brother.
When Wǔzhèn died,
Entering.
Gōnggàn's household was also exhausted.
Women of the Sea
The women of the sea were skilled in bewitching charms,
and men from the north sometimes took them as wives.
Even if disheveled and hunchbacked,
they could make men love them passionately,
unto death without regret.
If one abandoned her and tried to return north,
his boat would drift on the sea, unable to advance,
and he would have to return of his own accord.
A painter
The Táng dynasty scholar Zhào Yán,
obtained from a painter a soft screen,
depicting a woman of exceptional beauty.
Yán said to the painter:
"No such person exists in this world;
how can she be brought to life?
I wish to take her as my wife."
The painter replied:
"This is a divine painting,
and she too has a name,
called Zhēnzhēn.
Call her name for a hundred days,
ceaselessly day and night,
and she will surely answer.
Once she answers, pour into her mouth a wine made from the ashes of a hundred families' colored silk,
and she will certainly come to life."
Yán followed his words,
and called her name for a hundred days,
ceaselessly day and night.
Then she answered:
"Yes."
He hurriedly poured in the wine made from the ashes of a hundred families' colored silk,
and she came to life.
She stepped down, speaking and laughing,
eating and drinking as usual.
She said:
"Thank you for summoning me,
I wish to serve you as your wife."
After a year,
she bore a son.
When the child was two years old,
a friend said:
"This is a demon,
she will surely bring you calamity!
I have a divine sword,
with which you can slay her."
That evening,
he gave Yán the sword.
As soon as the sword reached Yán's chamber,
Zhēnzhēn wept and said:
"I am an earth immortal of Nányuè;
unexpectedly, someone painted my likeness,
and you called my name.
Since I did not oppose your wish,
now you doubt me,
I cannot stay."
With these words,
she took her child and returned to the soft screen,
vomiting out the wine made from the ashes of a hundred families' colored silk she had drunk earlier.
Looking at the screen,
only an additional child was seen,
all of it painted.
Hóu Yuán
Hóu Yuán was a woodcutter from a mountain village in Tóngdī County, Shàngdǎng Commandery.
His family was poor,
and he made his living solely by selling firewood.
In the yǐhài year of the Qiánfú era of the Táng dynasty,
he went to cut firewood in the mountains northwest of the county.
On his way back, he rested at the mouth of a valley.
Beside him was a massive rock,
towering like a grand house.
Yuán sighed deeply as he faced it,
lamenting his own toil.
Before his voice had faded,
the rock suddenly split open as if forming a cave.
Inside was an old man,
dressed in feathered robes and a black hat,
with a beard and hair as white as frost,
leaning on a staff as he emerged.
Yuán was startled and alarmed,
and he quickly rose to bow before him.
The old man said:
"I am a divine lord.
Why do you harbor so much discontent?
You may seek wealth through my methods.
Just follow me."
The old man reentered the cave,
and Yuán followed him.
After walking several dozen steps,
the space opened up, clear and bright.
The fields were level as a whetstone,
and there were many exotic flowers and fragrant grasses.
After a few miles,
they crossed a horizontal stream.
Its green rapids flowed over moss,
and mandarin ducks and egrets swam against the current.
Above it stretched a long, winding bridge,
like a rainbow on a clear day.
North of the stream,
tall pines and slender bamboos stood on both sides.
A grand gate painted in deep red,
with terraces and pavilions layered one upon another.
The old man led Yuán to a separate courtyard,
where they sat in a small pavilion.
The eaves, pillars, steps, and courtyard were all adorned with dazzling rare treasures.
When food and wine were served,
it was again something Yuán had never seen before.
After the meal, the old man withdrew.
A short while later,
two youths bowed to Yuán and invited him to a side chamber,
where they prepared a bath for him
and presented him with a new set of clothes.
Once he was dressed and capped,
they guided him back to the pavilion.
The old man emerged
and ordered a servant to lay a clean mat on the ground,
instructing Yuán to kneel upon it.
The old man then taught him tens of thousands of words of secret formulas,
all techniques for transformation, concealment, and manifestation.
Though Yuán had been dull and foolish by nature,
he now remembered everything after hearing it just once.
The old man admonished him:
"Though you possess a measure of fortune
and are suited to advance through these supreme methods,
you still bear an aura of ruin upon your face that has not yet been dispelled.
You must remain cautious and secretive, fortifying yourself.
If you plot treachery,
disaster will surely claim your life!
For now, return and reflect deeply.
If you wish to visit me again,
simply knock on the stone with a sincere heart,
and someone will answer the door."
Yuán then bowed in gratitude and departed,
with a youth escorting him out.
Once he exited the cave,
it closed up as before,
and he saw that his firewood and tools were gone.
When he returned home,
his parents and brothers were both shocked and overjoyed, saying:
"You've been gone for ten days—
we thought you had been torn apart by the jaws of tigers or wolves!"
Yet to Yuán, his time in the cave had felt like a single day.
They were also astonished by his splendid, clean clothing
and his spirited, vigorous demeanor.
Knowing he could not hide the truth,
Yuán told his family everything that had happened.
He then entered a quiet room
to practice and master the techniques.
After a month, his arts were perfected:
he could transform all manner of things,
summon and command ghosts and spirits,
and turn plants, trees, earth, and stones into foot soldiers, cavalry, armor, and weapons.
Thereupon, he gathered all the brave and fierce youths from his village to serve as his generals and soldiers.
When he went out, he displayed banners, flags, and canopies,
with drums and horns sounding,
his pomp rivaling that of the feudal states.
He proclaimed himself
"The Worthy Sage."
His officials bore titles such as the Three Elders, Left and Right Assistants, and Left and Right Generals.
On the first and fifteenth of each month,
he would dress in full splendor to visit the Divine Lord.
The Divine Lord always warned him not to raise arms,
saying that if he insisted on undertaking such endeavors,
he should wait for a sign from Heaven.
By the gēngzǐ year,
he had amassed several thousand troops.
Fearing rebellion, the county authorities
reported the matter up the chain of command.
