Gāo, the military governor of Shàngdǎng,
soon ordered a commanding officer to lead a brigade against him.
Yuán hurried to visit the Divine Lord to seek guidance.
The Divine Lord said:
"I have already spoken on this matter.
You should simply lower your banners and silence your drums in response.
When they see your military might as it is,
they will certainly not dare to press inward and attack us.
Remember this—
be careful not to engage them lightly in battle."
Though Yuán assented,
he thought to himself that his extraordinary arts were more than enough to handle them,
and that if he could not withstand a small force,
what would he do later against larger ones?
It would also show his followers that he lacked martial prowess.
After returning,
he ordered his followers to prepare for strict defense.
That night,
the troops from Lù Commandery camped thirty miles from the strategic point Yuán occupied.
They saw foot soldiers, cavalry, spears, and armor covering the mountains and marshes,
and found the situation very difficult.
At dawn, they advanced in a square formation.
Yuán led over a thousand men in a direct charge against them.
He prevailed at first but was later defeated,
and, in a drunken stupor, he was captured.
Taken to Shàngdǎng,
he was imprisoned in the prefectural jail,
with strict guards surrounding and watching him.
At daybreak, they looked inside the cangue—
only a lampstand remained,
and Yuán had disappeared.
By midnight, he had already reached Tóngdī
and went straight to the Divine Lord to apologize.
The lord angrily said:
"Foolish slave! You have ultimately disobeyed my teachings.
Though you have escaped today by luck,
the executioner's axe will soon be upon you.
You are no disciple of mine!"
Without another glance, he turned and went inside.
Dejected and melancholy, Yuán hurried away.
Later, when he tried to visit the Divine Lord again,
he knocked on the stone with a devout heart,
but the stone would not open for him!
Gradually, his arts began to fade,
yet he was still persuaded by his followers.
That autumn,
he led his band to plunder Dàgǔ in Bīngzhōu,
but the cavalry from Bīngzhōu happened to arrive
and surrounded them in multiple layers.
With his arts no longer divine,
he was beheaded on the battlefield,
and his followers scattered and returned to their villages.
Gōngdé Shān
When the Tang rebel Huáng Cháo's forces were about to throw the Central Plains into chaos,
in Biànzhōu there was a sorcerer-monk named Gōngdé Shān.
Buddhist monks from near and far all submitted to him.
As for the gentry and common folk,
there was none who did not surrender and join him.
He could paint demon soldiers on paper,
release them into people's homes,
and make them cause calamities and hauntings,
bewildering the inhabitants.
They would paint all through the night,
preventing people from sleeping peacefully,
or even causing them illness and suffering.
Only when people ordered Gōngdé Shān and paid him gold to perform rituals
would the affliction be immediately removed.
He also painted paper soldiers and armor,
which every night would neigh and clamor in the streets and neighborhoods,
trampling over the city walls,
vanishing by dawn without a trace.
He also painted many dogs,
burned them with incantations,
and at night they would bark and howl,
biting and fighting each other in the streets,
so that residents could not sleep peacefully.
When ordered and paid,
they would quietly disappear without a trace.
People, amazed by his arts,
flocked to him in ever greater numbers.
Also, in Huázhōu there was another monk
quite skilled in sorcery,
no different from Gōngdé Shān,
causing considerable trouble for both government and people.
At that time, the Secretariat Director Wáng Duó was garrisoning Huátái,
so he issued an order:
"The Nányàn region is afflicted by disaster;
it is fitting to perform proper exorcisms."
Thus, from the government offices,
down to the various military camps,
they opened a grand Buddhist ceremony,
inviting several thousand monks.
The number of monks was insufficient,
so they sent an official dispatch to Biànzhōu,
requesting
Gōngdé Shān and his entire group of followers to attend.
They were welcomed to Wèi with banners, flowers, conches, and cymbals.
On the evening they arrived for the ceremony,
the most eminent and virtuous among them were selected
to enter the government offices,
while the rest were dispersed to the various camps to perform penitential rites.
Once they entered the camps,
the gates were locked and they were buried alive in pits;
several thousand perished in their monastic robes.
In the offices, only Gōngdé Shān and his chief followers were kept,
interrogated,
and all were found to be part of Huáng Cháo's rebel faction,
planning to rise in mutual response from the two prefectures.
All were ordered executed.
The Old Man of Xiāngyáng
In the Tang dynasty, there was a man named Bìng Huá,
a butcher by trade in Xiāngyáng.
Once, while enjoying a spring outing,
he got drunk and lay down by the Hàn River.
An old man roused him with a shout,
saying:
"Judging by your appearance,
you are not meant for a life of mere gambling.
I have an axe to give you.
If you use it for crafting,
your work will surely be exquisitely skillful, even divinely inspired.
But in the future, be careful not to be burdened by women."
Huá bowed and accepted it.
After obtaining this axe,
whatever he crafted to fly would fly,
whatever he made to walk would walk.
As for building houses,
lofty towers and high pavilions,
they required no other tools.
Later, while traveling in the Ānlù area,
he stayed at the home of a wealthy man named Wáng Méi.
Méi, knowing of Huá's ingenious skill,
asked him to build a single-pillar pavilion over the water.
When the work was completed,
Méi brought out his entire household to see it.
Méi had a daughter,
who had been widowed and returned home.
Her beauty was extraordinary,
rarely matched.
Huá, upon seeing her, deeply admired her.
That night, he climbed over the wall and secretly entered her chamber.
The girl was greatly alarmed.
Huá said to her:
"If you do not consent,
I will surely kill you."
The girl gradually yielded and became willing.
Thereafter, every night,
he would secretly enter her room.
One day, Méi discovered this stealthily
and richly bribed Huá to send him away.
Huá, sensing his intention,
said to Méi:
"I have lodged in your home,
and received much kindness from you.
Now you further give me generous gifts;
I fear someday I will have no way to repay you.
I have a clever skill:
I shall make something to offer you."
Méi said:
"What thing?
If I have no use for it,
I certainly dare not keep it."
Huá said:
"I can make a wooden crane
that can fly.
If you ever have an emergency,
just mount this crane,
and you can reach a place a thousand *li* away."
Méi, having heard of such things before,
agreed.
Huá then brought out his axe and tools,
and crafted a pair of flying cranes from wood,
only leaving their eyes unfinished.
Méi, puzzled, asked why.
Huá said:
"You must fast and purify yourself,
then they can be completed and will fly.
If you do not fast,
they certainly will not fly."
Méi then began his fast.
That night,
Huá stole away with Méi's daughter,
and together
they mounted the crane and returned to Xiāngyáng.
At dawn,
Méi found his daughter missing.
Searching for her without success,
he secretly traveled to Xiāngyáng
and reported the matter to the prefect.
The prefect secretly ordered a search,
and indeed captured Huá.
The prefect, enraged,
had him beaten to death.
The crane he rode could no longer fly by itself.
The Dàoist of Qīngchéng
In the false Shu state, a Daoist priest from Qīngchéng Mountain was skilled in illusion techniques.
He often entered Jǐnchéng,
performed his magic,
and whenever he gained something,
he secretly carried it back to his cave dwelling.
Some heard that his conduct was very vile,
and among the officials, those who knew of him
greatly detested him.
Later, in Chéngdū, he enticed the sons of wealthy families and noble officials,
who all secretly followed him.
Sometimes in secluded and remote courtyards,
after sweeping, burning incense, and setting up couches,
he would hang curtains and drapes.
Then, alone inside the room, he performed his magic,
sometimes summoning the Queen Mother of the West, sometimes the Goddess of Wūshān, sometimes the immortals Mágū or Bàogū,
all of whom would arrive in response to his summons,
drinking, dining, and sleeping with him,
no different from living people.
He then ordered his disciples to peek through cracks to watch.
After the laughter and joy ended,
they would tiptoe away from before the curtains.
Suddenly, a golden tower would also appear in the city,
witnessed by all,
greatly bewildering the masses.
The young men among the common folk,
the pampered sons of wealthy families,
went mad throughout the city.
The young ruler, knowing he was a sorcerer,
secretly sent people to capture him,
but for months they could not catch him.
Later, someone reported:
"He has already left through the Zuóqiáo Gate."
So he sent people to pursue him,
taking pig and dog blood with them.
About thirty-some lǐ along the road to Qīngchéng,
they caught up with him,
and poured the blood over him.
Unable to perform his magic,
he was taken to prison and interrogated,
and he said:
"Every year, I take virgin girls from common families to live in the mountains,
to practice the Way of the Yellow Emperor."
Countless died in the rocky caves.
Many noble and wealthy families
suffered defilement and violation.
The confessions he made
implicated many high-ranking and powerful households.
The young ruler, not wishing to expose his evil deeds,
secretly had him killed.
A Woman of Shǔdū
Yuánhézi once, on a leisurely day,
went out the eastern city gate of Shǔdū,
and saw two men sitting on the riverbank,
arranging and preparing their boats,
angrily scolding the pole and oar handlers,
shouting and yelling.
Suddenly, a woman in a cloth jacket knelt before them,
begging for something.
The men, in a great rage,
shouted at her.
She lingered for a long time without leaving,
and as they were about to beat her,
the woman finally left.
She stood by the riverbank,
looking around for a long time,
then pushed her waist and took a step,
staring directly at the two guest boats.
The boats then seemed as if pulled by something,
drifting swiftly away,
straight to the great shore,
and instantly shattered to pieces,
with all goods and cargo sinking into the water.
The two men were terrified,
suspecting it was the woman's doing,
and wanted to seize her,
but she had already vanished.
Cài Dàn
Cài Dàn was fond of the Dao,
neglected his family's livelihood,
and day and night recited texts like the "Huángtíng," "Tàiqīng," "Zhōngjīng," "Guāntiān,"
and "Jiéjiě,"
believing the Dao was fully contained within them.
His family was troubled by this,
and he himself felt ashamed and regretful.
Suddenly, he abandoned his home,
saying:
"My immortal path is accomplished."
He then fled into the deep mountains,
selling firewood to exchange for clothes.
After three years, unable to bear the hardship, he returned home,
dark, thin, and gaunt,
deceiving his family by saying:
"I am only an earthly immortal,
of low rank,
herding several dozen dragons for Lǎojūn.
There was one multicolored spotted dragon
that Lǎojūn once gave me,
but later, while gambling with an immortal,
I lost this dragon.
For this, I was demoted,
sent to below Kūnlún to hoe three or four qǐng of zhīcǎo grass,
all growing among fine stones,
overgrown with weeds,
very bitter.
It was to be ten years before I could be pardoned.
Fortunately, Wòquán and Zǐqiáo came on an inspection tour,
I first pleaded my case to them,
and they both exerted effort for me,
so I was spared."
Xū Mànqīng
In Púbǎn, there was a man named Xū Mànqīng who said:
"After three years of intense meditation in the mountains,
an immortal came to welcome me,
and I rode a dragon to ascend to heaven.
The dragon flew very swiftly,
with its head raised and tail lowered,
making the person on it feel peril and terror.
Upon reaching heaven,
we first passed through the Purple Mansion,
with golden beds and jade tables,
dazzling and brilliant,
truly a noble place.
The immortal gave me a cup of liúxiá to drink,
and I immediately felt neither hunger nor thirst.
Suddenly, I thought of home,
and before the Heavenly Emperor, I bowed improperly,
and was reprimanded and sent back.
I was ordered to cultivate and reproach myself further,
then I could go again.
In the past, Liú Ān, the Prince of Huáinán,
ascended to heaven and saw the Supreme God,
but sat cross-legged and boasted arrogantly,
calling himself 'the solitary one,'
and was thus demoted
to guard the heavenly toilet for three years.
Who am I, then?"
In Hédōng, they therefore called Mànqīng the Reprimanded Immortal.
Prefect Mǎ
While Prefect Mǎ of Xīnggǔ was in office,
an old acquaintance sought him out,
asking for relief.
Mǎ then had this person stay outside,
falsely claiming:
"He is a divine Daoist priest,
who cures illnesses, all instantly healed by his hand."
He also had eloquent men travel around,
creating false fame for him,
saying:
"He can make the blind see,
and the lame walk immediately."
Thus, people gathered from all directions like clouds,
flocking to him as to a market,
and money and silk piled up like mountains.
He also instructed all who came for treatment:
"Even if you are not cured immediately,
you must tell others you are already cured,
and then you will surely be cured;
if you tell others you are not cured,
then you will never be cured later.
The Daoist method is exactly like this,
you must believe and comply."
So when later people asked those who came earlier,
they always said they were already cured,
and no one dared say they were not cured.
Within ten days to a month,
he thus amassed great wealth.
A Person from Yèchéng
During the Jǐngyún era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man with long hair named Hè Xuánjǐng,
who called himself the Virtuous One of the Five Precepts.
More than ten people joined him in practicing sorcery.
They built thatched huts in the Lùhún Mountains,
deceiving and deluding the foolish sons and daughters of common folk,
who exhausted their family fortunes to serve them.
They falsely claimed:
"Those who seek with utmost sincerity
will certainly attain Buddhahood."
Xuánjǐng wore a golden-threaded kasaya robe
and sat alone in a dark room.
He had the foolish secretly look in,
saying that the Buddha was emitting light,
and all were awed and submitted.
They lit a fire beneath a cliff,
and sent several people halfway up the cliff,
dressed in red and green gauze as immortal robes,
fluttering in the wind.
They made the crowd watch,
deceiving them, saying:
"These are immortals."
They told each person to put on immortal robes,
and if they could fly to them,
they would immediately attain the Way.
On an appointed day, they held a vegetarian feast,
putting henbane seeds in the drinks,
and had everyone consume them.
They cut off the hair of women who had beautiful locks,
shaving their heads.
Dressed in immortal robes,
they looked down from the cliff edge,
their vision blurred and dizzy,
and were pushed off the cliff bottom,
burned to death all at once.
Their wealth and possessions were seized.
When the affair was exposed,
officials came to investigate,
and found charred, curled-up corpses in the ashes.
Several hundred people
were executed by imperial decree, Xuánjǐng was sentenced to death,
and the county officials were demoted.
The Woman from Yíngzhōu
During the Jǐnglóng era of the Táng dynasty,
a woman was presented from Yíngzhōu,
on whose body appeared raised images of pagodas, temples, and various Buddhas.
The Surveillance Commissioner presented her,
and she was granted the fifth rank,
with the woman remaining in the Inner Dàochǎng.
After the rebellious Wěi clan died,
her whereabouts became unknown.
Xuē Huáiyì
In the first year of Zhèngshèng of the Zhōu dynasty,
the Teacher Xuē, named Huáiyì,
built a Merit Hall one thousand feet tall,
north of the Bright Hall.
Inside it was a great statue,
nine hundred feet high,
with a nose like a ship holding a thousand hu,
and a little finger large enough to seat several dozen people together.
It was lacquered with layered hemp cloth.
On the fifteenth day of the first month,
he held an unrestricted great assembly at the court hall.
They dug a pit five zhang deep,
using multicolored silk to make palaces, terraces, and pavilions,
bending bamboo as a frame,
and stretching and setting it up as a canopy.
They also made great statues of Vajra deities,
pulling them up from the pit,
falsely claiming they had emerged from the ground.
They also drew ox blood,
painting it to make a great statue head,
two hundred feet high,
falsely claiming it was made from Teacher Xuē's knee blood.
Spectators filled the city and overflowed the outer walls,
men and women gathering like clouds.
Coins were loaded inside and thrown,
people trampled over each other,
and not a few old and young died.
By the sixteenth day,
the statue was displayed south of the Tiānjīn Bridge,
and a vegetarian feast was set.
During the second watch,
the Merit Hall caught fire,
spreading to the Bright Hall,
flames shooting skyward,
lighting Luòchéng as bright as daytime.
The hall's construction was not yet half finished,
but it was already over seventy feet tall.
It also spread to burn the gold and silver treasury,
molten iron flowing like liquid,
over a foot deep on level ground.
People who mistakenly entered
were immediately scorched and mangled.
The hall was reduced to ashes,
not a single piece of wood remaining.
By dawn,
they held another assembly,
when a sudden violent wind arose,
tearing the blood-painted statue into several hundred pieces.
Fúxiūzǐ said:
"Emperor Wǔ of Liáng renounced the world at the Tóngtài Temple,
and officials emptied the treasury to redeem him.
That night, sudden lightning and thunderclaps,
wind, rain, and darkness fell.
The temple's pagoda and Buddha hall
were utterly destroyed in an instant.
Such unreasonable affairs—
could they be the original intent of the Tathāgata?"
The Foreign Monk Bǎoyán
During the Jǐngyún era of the Táng dynasty,
the Western Capital had continuous rain for over sixty days.
There was a foreign monk,
named Bǎoyán,
who claimed to have magical methods,
able to stop the rain.
He set up an altar,
reciting scriptures and mantras.
At that time, slaughter was prohibited,
but Bǎoyán used twenty sheep
and two horses for sacrifice.
After praying for over fifty days,
the rain became even heavier.
Then they beheaded and expelled the foreign monk,
and the rain subsequently stopped.
The Foreign Monk Hú Chāo
During the Shènglì era of the Zhōu dynasty,
in Hóngzhōu, there was a foreign monk named Hú Chāo,
who left home to study the Way,
secluding himself on White Crane Mountain.
He had slight magical arts,
and claimed to be several hundred years old.
Empress Zétiān ordered him to prepare an elixir of immortality,
costing an enormous sum,
and it took three years to complete.
He personally presented the medicine at the Sānyáng Palace.
Empress Zétiān took it,
considering it divine and marvelous,
hoping to live as long as Péngzǔ,
and changed the era name to the first year of Jiǔshì.
She released Chāo to return to the mountains,
bestowing generous rewards.
Two years after taking the medicine, Empress Zétiān passed away.
Training Cats and Parrots
During Zétiān's time,
she trained a cat and a parrot to eat from the same vessel,
ordering Censor Péng Xiānjué to supervise,
and displayed it to all officials and examination envoys from across the land.
Before the display was complete,
the cat grew hungry,
and bit the parrot to death to eat it.
Zétiān was greatly ashamed.
"Wǔ" being the imperial surname,
this was likely an inauspicious omen.
Luò Bīnwáng
During the Tang dynasty, Péi Yán served as the Chief Secretary of the Central Secretariat.
At that time, Xú Jìngyè intended to rebel.
He ordered Luò Bīnwáng to devise a plan
to win Péi Yán over to join the uprising.
Luò Bīnwáng leaned against a wall with his foot,
and after pondering for as long as it takes to eat a meal,
he composed a rhyme:
"One piece of fire,
two pieces of fire,
a child in crimson robes sits upon the hall."
He taught the children on Péi Yán's estate to chant it,
and soon all the children in the capital were singing it.
Péi Yán then consulted scholars, asking them to interpret it.
He summoned Luò Bīnwáng,
and repeatedly tempted him with treasures, brocades, and fine silks,
but Luò Bīnwáng said nothing.
He then bribed him with musicians, courtesans, and fine steeds,
but still he remained silent.
Then they looked together at portraits of ancient loyal ministers and martyrs.
When they came to Sima Xuānwáng,
Luò Bīnwáng suddenly rose and said:
"This is a heroic man."
He then spoke of how, since ancient times, great ministers who held power
often shifted the fate of the state.
Péi Yán was greatly pleased.
Luò Bīnwáng said:
"But I wonder what the prophecy in the rhyme means?"
Péi Yán explained the rhyme about the pieces of fire and the crimson robes.
Luò Bīnwáng immediately descended,
bowed facing north, and said:
"This is the true man."
Thus, he conspired with Xú Jìngyè and others.
When the troops rose in Yángzhōu,
Péi Yán acted as an insider.
He wrote a letter to Xú Jìngyè and the others,
which contained only the characters "青鵝" (qīng é).
Someone reported this,
but none of the court officials could decipher it.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān said:
"The character '青' (qīng)
means the twelfth month.
The character '鵝' (é)
means 'I myself will join.'"
Thus, she had Péi Yán executed,
and Xú Jìngyè and the others were soon defeated.
Féng Qīyí
was the younger sister of the rebellious Wéi clan during the Tang dynasty,
the wife of Féng Tàihé,
and was called Seventh Aunt.
She believed in heterodox views,
using a leopard-head pillow to ward off evil,
a Báizé pillow to dispel demons,
and making a crouching-bear pillow to ensure the birth of sons.
After Féng Tàihé died,
the heir to the Duke of Guó married her.
When the Wéi clan fell,
the Duke of Guó cut off Féng Qīyí's head and sent it to the court.
Thus it was known that the evil-warding pillows had failed.
Master Jiāng Fǔ
Master Jiāng Fǔ of the Tang dynasty
was of unknown origin.
He often wore Daoist robes and headgear,
claiming to be several hundred years old.
He held talismans,
along with medicines for longevity
and techniques for transcending the world.
People of the time called him Master Jiāng Fǔ.
Emperor Xuánzong ruled with lofty dignity,
his spirit dwelling beyond worldly things,
and he often spoke of ascending to immortality.
Jiāng Fǔ served in the palace,
receiving special favor.
When he went to various provinces to gather herbs and perform meritorious deeds,
the governors and magistrates of the provinces and counties
would rush to pay their respects amidst the dust.
Those who sought the Dao begged to be allowed to stand at his gate,
but could not gain entry.
There was a man named Jīng Yán,
who had failed the imperial examinations for forty years at the National University.
He retired to Sōngshǎo,
calling himself a mountain hermit.
He was quite knowledgeable about the histories of the Northern and Southern Dynasties
and familiar with recent notable figures.
He once visited Jiāng Fǔ,
but Jiāng Fǔ sat arrogantly and did not stir for him.
Jīng Yán then pressed forward.
He asked:
"How old are you, Master?"
Jiāng Fǔ replied:
"You are not a man of faith,
why bother asking my age?"
Jīng Yán said:
"Since you cannot state your birth year,
from which dynasty do you hail, Master?"
Jiāng Fǔ said:
"I am from the Liáng dynasty."
Jīng Yán said:
"The Liáng dynasty is quite recent,
so you cannot be a man of great longevity.
I wonder, Master,
did you serve as an official in the Liáng dynasty,
or did you live in seclusion?"
Jiāng Fǔ said:
"I was the military governor of Xīliáng Prefecture."
Jīng Yán rebuked him, saying:
"How can you speak such falsehoods?
You deceive the Son of Heaven above,
and mislead the people below.
The Liáng dynasty was south of the Yangtze River;
where was there a Xīliáng Prefecture?
There were only the Four Pacification, Four Security, Four Garrison, and Four Expeditionary Generals;
where were there military governors?"
Jiāng Fǔ felt ashamed and resentful,
and died a few days later.
Lǐ Mì
Lǐ Mì was given to empty boasts and pretensions.
Once, in front of a guest,
he instructed his family to clean and sweep,
saying, "Hóngyá will come tonight."
Someone sent him a jar of fine wine.
When a guest arrived,
he said:
"Mágū has sent wine;
let us drink together."
Before they finished drinking,
the gatekeeper reported:
"A certain vice-minister has come to retrieve the jar."
Lǐ Mì ordered it to be returned,
showing no sign of shame.
The Paper-Robe Master
During the Dàlì era,
there was a monk
renowned for his ascetic practices.
He did not wear silk, cotton, linen, or other fabrics,
but always wore paper robes.
People of the time called him the Paper-Robe Chan Master.
Emperor Dàizōng summoned him to the palace chapel,
where he was ordered to chant and meditate.
He was allowed to go out once a month,
and people revered him even more.
Later, he stole a golden Buddha from the palace.
When the matter came to light,
he was handed over to the Jīngzhào Prefecture for execution.
Míng Sīyuǎn
The Huàshān Daoist Míng Sīyuǎn
diligently practiced Daoist registers and rituals
for over thirty years.
He often taught people the "Method of Metal-Water Separation,"
along with breath retention and visualization.
He had many disciples.
During the Yǒngtài era,
tigers ran rampant in Huà Prefecture.
Míng Sīyuǎn told people:
"Tigers are not to be feared.
Just hold your breath and concentrate,
visualizing a lion emerging from each of your ten fingers.
If you send them forward,
the tiger will leave."
Once, Míng Sīyuǎn was traveling with others.
As dusk approached,
they encountered a tiger at the mouth of a valley.
His companions fled in terror,
but Míng Sīyuǎn remained composed,
holding his breath and concentrating.
Soon after, he was devoured by the tiger.
The next day, his disciples searched for him at the valley mouth,
but found only pine vines and a pair of shoes.
Zhōu Shìlóng
Zhōu Shìlóng was a man from Dōngyáng, Wùzhōu.
He was skilled in discerning mountain ridges
and divining locations for grave sites,
sharing equal fame with his paternal uncle.
Whenever the year and month were highly auspicious,
carriages and horses would crowd his gate like a marketplace.
People’s longevity, official positions,
good or ill fortune, benefit or harm—
he determined everything based on the land.
In the fifth year of the Dàlì era,
he arrived in Yèzhōng.
The Yèzhōng military commander Yáo Xīshèng had recently buried his mother in Qīngdū Village.
Shìlóng divined the grave site
and said, “Within a year, the entire family will be ruined.”
By the following year,
Xīshèng had committed an offense and was executed.
The people of Yèzhōng
were all astonished,
calling him a divine man.
There was also the military commander Lóu Guàn, who was planning a major undertaking.
He earnestly entreated Shìlóng to divine a site for him,
presenting over a thousand strings of cash in gifts.
Shìlóng was greatly pleased
and spent more than a month searching the mountains and plains.
Suddenly, he found a place,
describing its terrain as encircling and embracing,
like the belly of a dragon.
Within three years, he was sure to become a military governor.
Guàn also became self-assured because of this.
Within the year,
a military mutiny broke out in Yèzhōng.
Guàn, believing the terrain gave him support,
began to harbor rebellious intentions.
The plot was exposed,
and he was beheaded at the army gate,
with not a single member of his family spared.
Lǐ Chángyuán
Lǐ Chángyuán regularly practiced breath cultivation and guiding exercises,
and also studied the arts of Yǔ steps and occult techniques
for several decades.
He claimed to have attained spiritual essence and subtlety,
and that his path was complete.
Many from near and far revered him as a teacher.
One day in Hóngzhōu, a fire broke out.
The wind was fierce, the flames intense,
advancing from the north.
His family was in a panic,
wanting to tear down houses and fences
to cut off the fire’s path.
Chángyuán stopped them,
then climbed onto the roof and performed Yǔ steps with incantations to suppress it.
Suddenly, the fire grew even stronger.
Chángyuán chanted incantations loudly,
but then flying sparks burst forth,
first striking Chángyuán’s body,
causing him to fall from the roof.
The room where he lived
was completely burned to ashes.
Utensils, clothing, and playthings—
nothing remained.
All his charts, talismans, and ritual implements for chanting incantations
were reduced to ashes.
The Twin Sacred Lamps
Forty lǐ south of Cháng’ān,
there is a valley called Língmǔ Gǔ,
also known as Tàn Gǔ.
Five lǐ into the valley,
there is Huìjù Temple.
To the southwest of the temple, crossing
a stream,
the water follows the cliffside
for eighteen lǐ to a peak,
called the Língyìng Terrace.
On the terrace stands a pagoda.
Inside the pagoda is an iron statue of Guānshìyīn Bodhisattva.
The statue was made by Ān Tàiqīng, a dismissed general of the Six Armies.
It is widely said that Guānshìyīn Bodhisattva once manifested here on this terrace.
It is also said that the iron statue in the pagoda often emits a halo of light.
Common folk from Cháng’ān
competed to visit and pay homage,
each carrying rice, yeast, oil, soy sauce, and the like on their backs.
Below the terrace and around it are more than forty monasteries,
where monks and acolytes
have ample clothing and food.
On major fasting days when offerings are sent,
men and women number nearly a thousand,
never fewer than several hundred.
They stay overnight on the terrace,
performing rituals and chanting,
hoping to see the light.
It is also said
that sacred lamps often appear.
These lamps may be halfway up the mountain
or on level ground,
their height unfixed.
On the eighth night of the fourth month in the fourteenth year of the Dàlì era,
as the crowd chanted in unison,
a pair of sacred lamps appeared
southwest of the terrace, near it.
There was also a robust soldier from the Six Armies
who threw himself down,
calling out to Guānshìyīn Bodhisattva,
and step by step approached the sacred lamps.
Suddenly, he was dragged away by a tiger.
What they had seen were actually the tiger’s eyes glowing.
Lù Shéntōng
Lù Shéntōng, a groom under Duàn Chéngshì’s household,
could lift stones in military contests,
carrying a six-hundred-pound stone on a bamboo hat and straw sandals,
and biting through dozens of stone-like grains.
He had a tattoo of a heavenly king on his back
and claimed to have obtained divine power.
When he entered the arena, the spirit
assisted him,
and his strength would surge.
On the first and fifteenth days of each month,
he would prepare milky porridge,
burn incense, sit bare-chested,
and have his wife and children worship and make offerings to the tattoo on his back.
The Wǔfú Tower
In the early Yuánhé era,
diviners said the Wǔfú Tàiyǐ was in Shǔ,
so Liú Pì built the Wǔfú Tower.
Fú Zǎi composed an inscription for it.
Fish Eyes as Relics
The monk Hóngmì of Zézhōu requested a relic pagoda.
Hóngmì used Chán Buddhist riddles to stir up the ignorant masses,
claiming that relics emerged from his body.
Once, when he went to Tàiyuán,
wealthy locals welcomed and invited him,
with women bowing in rows.
After Hóngmì departed,
women picked up a hundred grains from where he had sat.
People examined them
and found they were all dried fish eyes.
When he was about to leave for the mountains,
he asked for over a dozen coarse felt mats.
In half a day, he received five hundred.
Such was his ability to deceive people.
Calling an Old Man a Child
During the prosperous era of Cháng'ān,
there was a man skilled in the Daoist arts,
who claimed to have mastered the wonders of cinnabar elixirs,
with a youthful appearance,
and boasted of being over three hundred years old.
The people of the capital greatly admired him.
As for those who offered goods and sought his elixirs,
or brought scriptures to request teachings,
his door was as bustling as a marketplace.
At that time, several court officials visited his residence,
and as they were drinking and feasting merrily,
a gatekeeper reported:
"Your son has come from the estate,
wishing to pay his respects."
The Daoist master changed his expression and scolded him.
Upon hearing this,
some of the seated guests said:
"Since your esteemed son has come from afar,
why not let him in?"
The Daoist frowned and hesitated for a while,
then said:
"Just let him in."
Soon, an old man appeared,
with hair as white as silver,
feeble and hunched over,
hurrying forward to bow.
After bowing,
he was scolded and sent into the inner gate.
The Daoist slowly said to the guests:
"My foolish son,
unwilling to take the cinnabar elixirs,
has ended up like this.
He is not even a hundred years old,
yet withered and aged like this.
I have long banished him to the countryside."
The guests revered him even more.
Later, someone privately questioned the Daoist's close acquaintances,
and it was revealed:
"The hunched old man was his father."
Those who admired the Daoist arts
were deceived and misled by him,
as if tricking infants.
Regarding Shìzūn
In the villages under the jurisdiction of Suízhōu,
there was a man surnamed Yú,
known as Shìzūn,
who, along with his daughter,
could foretell people's fortunes and misfortunes.
Several prefectures revered and worshipped them,
donating wealth that piled up like mountains.
They carved cliffs and walls,
arranging them into Buddha statues,
spending an incalculable amount.
The military governor Xǔ Cún,
considering them deceitful and delusional,
summoned them to the government office,
and had them perform divination.
When they failed,
he had them shackled and executed,
with no divine transformations occurring.
At their residence,
multicolored hemp ropes were found,
which required nearly a hundred oxen to carry,
and the amount of money and silk can be imagined.
Every night during gatherings,
they would impersonate Amitābha Buddha,
with palaces and ponds
resembling those of the Western Paradise.
Men and women gathered,
merely reciting Buddha's name.
These were also among the most foolish,
how could their arts be divine?
Or were they possessed by something?
The Incident of Capturing Buddha's Light
When Duke Gāo Yàn governed Shǔ,
monks from Dàcí Temple reported
that Buddha's light had appeared in the hall.
Duke Yàn decreed:
"Order the cavalry and infantry commander to capture the Buddha's light."
The authorities secretly investigated,
coaxed a young novice,
who confessed:
"The monks used a mirror to catch the sunlight through a crack,
reflecting it onto the Buddha statue."
Thus exposed,
they were captured and punished.
The Great Wheel Mantra
Among the five esoteric practices of Buddhism,
there is the Great
Wheel Mantra technique,
used to cure illnesses,
but it was not very effective.
However, it could capture people's spirits,
causing them to run wildly,
climb roof beams,
or bite porcelain bowls.
The common folk revered and worshipped it,
almost as if it were divine.
Those who practiced it thus amassed great wealth.
In Niúpí Village, Guìpíng County, Língzhōu, there was a man named Zhōu Dá,
who peddled this technique.
One day, he fried his genitals in boiling oil,
as an offering,
drawing a crowd of onlookers,
some shocked, some laughing.
At first, he forgot the pain,
but soon he died from it.
In between, the monk Zhāo Pǔ recounted
that in Lǎngzhōu, there was a monk known as Zhōu Dàbēi,
who practiced this mantra technique.
One day, he refined his genitals and died.
Why is it that the surname I witnessed matches exactly,
and their stories are so similar?
It seems that petty men use the Dao to deceive Heaven,
mutilating themselves as punishment.
Because their stories are alike,
I recorded them here.
Chancellor Chén
During the Táng dynasty, the military commissioner Tián Lìngzī wielded great power,
with the ability to overturn Heaven.
He once sent a letter to Xǔchāng,
requesting the position of military commander for his brother Chén Jìngxuān,
but the military governor, Chancellor Cuī Ānqián, refused.
Later, when Cuī was transferred to govern Xīchuān,
Chén Jìngxuān, along with Yáng Shīlì, Niú Xù, and Luó Yuángǎo,
competed in polo for control of the Three Chuān regions.
Chén Jìngxuān won first place,
and was appointed military governor of Yòushǔ by imperial decree,
replacing Cuī.
This shocked both the court and the public.
The official report stated it was Chancellor Chén's appointment,
but no one knew who was behind it.
A deceitful man in Qīngchéng County organized a Maitreya assembly,
seeing this opportunity,
he forged Chancellor Chén's travel documents,
claiming that
bandits had risen in Shāndōng,
and the emperor would surely seek refuge in Shǔ,
with Chancellor Chén rushing ahead to assume his post.
He appointed a leader,
and the deceitful followers supported him.
The military government, unaware of the truth,
also sent people to welcome him.
As they approached the post station,
a command was issued demanding four white horses.
The investigators sensed something amiss,
and detained them.
Before they could turn around,
the real Chancellor Chén arrived swiftly on horseback.
The deceitful men were all captured and bound, awaiting orders.
Yǐngzhōu ordered them to be secretly executed.
Those with insight said:
"Grand Tutor Chén rose to power through eunuch influence,
without the slightest merit.
Illegitimately occupying a military governorship,
he was first manipulated by deceitful forces,
and ultimately brought ruin upon himself.
His execution
was not unfortunate.
Xiè Yuánguī
The Daoist Xiè Yuánguī
was originally a junior officer under a Shǔ military commander.
When Emperor Míngzong ascended the throne,
he came from the west,
audienced in the side hall,
presented poems praising the emperor's virtue,
and claimed to be a Zhèngyī Daoist from Tàibái Mountain.
He submitted a memorial requesting the positions of Western Capital garrison commander and Three Chuān military commissioner,
intending to repair the Western Capital's palaces.
The emperor said to his attendants:
"This old man came from afar to court,
I expected some extraordinary insight,
but he only seeks fame and position,
which is quite laughable."
He was granted the title "Master Zhībái,"
and bestowed purple robes.
He was indeed an arrogant and delusional man.
Cài Tián
Táng Gāo Pián governed Chéngdū,
and was very fond of occult arts.
There was a recluse named Cài Tián,
who sought to impress him with alchemy.
Taking an earthen tile,
he ground a single cinnabar pellet,
smeared half of it, and placed it in the fire,
where it burned into half a piece of purple refined gold—
truly a marvelous feat.
Cài himself was poor,
yet everyone revered him,
considering him an earthbound immortal.
Lord Yàn sought his methods but could not obtain them.
After a long time, his deception was exposed:
he had actually acquired the drug from someone else,
using it to dazzle and show off,
and for this, the commander had him killed.
Zhāng Shǒuyī
Zhāng Shǒuyī
was a man from the fields of Cāngjǐng.
In his youth, he was idle and lazy,
attending to no livelihood.
He claimed to be able to transmute the five metals,
thereby enticing those greedy for profit.
Later, impoverished and destitute,
unable to support himself,
he carried a willow trunk on his back,
selling cosmetics to trade for food and clothing,
wandering between the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
Lǚ Yòngzhī, who was favored for his sorcery and deceit,
then came to Guǎnglíng,
and became a guest under Xiāo Shèng's roof.
Long unable to realize his ambitions,
he was about to leave Xiāo Shèng.
Yòngzhī heard of this
and stopped him, saying:
"A man who sincerely sets his heart on something,
why worry about lacking a kindred spirit?
If you can align with Yòngzhī,
then matters of wealth and honor
we shall strive for together."
Thus, he was recommended by Yòngzhī.
Gāo Pián, seeing his rustic simplicity,
often treated him as a true immortal.
Once he gained power,
though his extravagance did not match Yòngzhī's,
his greed and avarice were especially severe.
When the two capitals were established,
he was made Left Mòyé Army Commander,
and successively promoted to Acting Left Vice Director,
his status and respect second only to Yòngzhī.
Whenever they discussed the Way over drinks,
from morning till dusk,
they could not bear to part.
Their schemes of deception and delusion
often complemented each other,
so that for years their affairs remained undisclosed.
In the second year of the Guāngqì era,
the illegitimate court appointed Shǒuyī as Prefect of Dézhōu.
The following year,
Bóhǎi recommended Shǒuyī for Mǐnchuān,
but before the appointment was finalized, he fell from grace.
He then followed Yáng Xíngmì into the city,
and again requested to concoct the Grand Reverted Elixir for the generals.
Before the drug was completed,
there was a certain Kāng Zhīróu,
originally a household servant of Zhèng Chāngtú.
When Chāngtú oversaw the Ministry of Revenue,
he appointed Zhīróu as Transport Commissioner.
A minor clerk in the bureau, Wǔ Fěng,
had once offended Zhīróu,
and was flogged by him.
When Yáng Xíngmì entered the city,
Fěng then exposed over twenty instances of Zhīróu's corrupt practices.
At this point, both Fěng and Zhīróu
were imprisoned in the military jail.
Zhīróu had always been on good terms with Shǒuyī,
and said:
"I wish to offer wealth to redeem my crime."
Shǒuyī immediately reported this to Lord Yáng.
Lord Yáng considered that Shǒuyī, Zhīróu, and Fěng
were all beyond pardon for their deeds,
and thus ordered them executed in prison.
Lǚ Yòngzhī,
was a commoner from Ānrén Lane in Póyáng.
His nature was cunning and crafty,
and he had a rough knowledge of writing.
His father, Lǚ Huáng,
made a living by trading tea,
traveling between Huái and Zhè.
At that time, the four quarters were free from trouble,
and Guǎnglíng was a place of music and song,
where wealthy merchants and great traders
numbered over a hundred at a time.
Huáng was intelligent and quick-witted,
excelling in the rules of wine,
and often socialized with groups of merchants.
When Yòngzhī was twelve or thirteen years old,
his father took him along on his travels.
Being clever and perceptive,
he served the various merchants,
and won the favor of them all.
At times, he would straighten his shoes and wave a fan,
hiding at home and living among the servants.
After a few years,
Huáng died at home.
At the beginning of the Qiánfú era,
bands of bandits attacked and plundered the prefectures and villages,
so he went elsewhere.
Yòngzhī, now orphaned and impoverished,
was supported by his maternal uncle, Xú Lǔrén.
After a little over a year,
he had an affair with Lǔrén's wife,
and was driven out by Lǔrén.
He then served the Daoist priest Niú Hónghuī of Jiǔhuá Mountain.
Hónghuī claimed to be one who had attained the Dao,
and Yòngzhī humbled himself to become his disciple,
learning from him the arts of summoning and interrogating spirits.
After Hónghuī died,
Yòngzhī again became a guest in Guǎnglíng.
There, he wore a coarse headscarf and simple clothing,
using talismans and medicines to exchange for food and clothing.
After a little over a year,
Chancellor Liú Gōng was appointed military governor of the region east of the Huái,
and there were those who practiced sorcery and witchcraft,
who were urgently arrested.
Yòngzhī, fearing this,
then crossed southward.
Gāo Pián was stationed in Jīngkǒu,
and summoned masters of esoteric arts,
seeking the way of ascending lightly and achieving immortality.
Yòngzhī used his arts to gain access to the guest quarters.
After more than a month without being summoned,
he visited his relative Yú Gōngchǔ of Bóhǎi.
Gōngchǔ found him extraordinary,
and dressed him in Confucian robes,
calling him "Lǚ, the Patrol Officer of Jiāngxī,"
and thus took the opportunity to recommend him to Bóhǎi.
When he was summoned for a test,
Gōngchǔ and his attendants corroborated his arts,
and they proved effective.
Soon, he was appointed Observation Judge,
and his name was also regulated.
Thus, he was given the courtesy name Wúkě,
meaning "nothing is acceptable, nothing is unacceptable."
From then on, he came and went without restriction.
At first, he specialized in matters of medicines and incense.
The following year,
Bóhǎi was transferred to another command,
and Yòngzhī firmly requested military attire.
He was then appointed to a military position.
Yòngzhī had long been a peddler,
and had long been a guest in Guǎnglíng,
so he was thoroughly familiar with
both public and private advantages and disadvantages.
In his spare time from alchemical practices,
he recklessly discussed the successes and failures of current governance.
Bóhǎi found him even more extraordinary,
and gradually entrusted him with greater responsibilities.
Previously, Bóhǎi's old generals,
such as Liáng Zuǎn, Chén Gǒng, Féng Shòu, Dǒng Jǐn, Gōngchǔ, and Guī Lǐ,
were daily marginalized and pushed aside,
and Bóhǎi became isolated.
Yòngzhī then established his own faction,
watching every move.
Those who could not be removed,
he pleased with generous gifts of gold and treasures.
The petty men around him,
were all market-town folk,
who saw profit and forgot righteousness,
deceiving each other from top to bottom,
and greatly indulged in sorcery and falsehoods.
Immortal books and divine talismans,
appeared daily without fail,
and they took turns singing in harmony,
without any sense of shame.
From then on, bribery was openly practiced,
regulations and ordinances daily fell into disorder,
harsh punishments and heavy taxes,
were carried out arbitrarily.
The roads were filled with complaints and sighs,
and everyone harbored plans for rebellion.
Yòngzhī, fearing the outbreak of secret plots,
requested the establishment of an Inspectorate,
to gather secret information from within the city.
Bóhǎi then received an imperial commission as Censor-in-Chief,
and served as the Inspector-General of All Armies.
Thus, he recruited over a hundred former clerks and officials from the prefectures and counties who had previously been dismissed for crimes, cunning and crafty individuals,
providing them with generous salaries,
to be ready for his commands.
Each had over ten followers,
roaming freely through the lanes and alleys,
and they were called "Inspectors."
As for the households of scholars and commoners,
scolding wives and angry children,
secret words and hidden language,
nothing went unknown.
From then on, people on the roads communicated only with their eyes.
Those who opposed him,
even if cautious, quiet, upright, and silent,
could not escape disaster.
Hundreds of families were destroyed.
Among the officers and generals,
they stood on tiptoe and held their breath.
Zhūgě Yīn
Gāo Pián favored the clerk Zhūgě Yīn,
who was a member of the sorcerer Lǚ Yòngzhī's faction.
Initially from Póyáng,
he was about to go to Guǎnglíng.
Yòngzhī first said to Pián:
"The Jade Emperor, because Your Excellency has long served as a subject,
and your official duties have been somewhat neglected,
has incurred the censure of the current ruler.
He has therefore dispatched a deity from his side to serve as Your Excellency's protector on the way,
and he will soon descend."
Your Excellency should treat him well,
wishing him not to leave,
and you can also bind him with a high-ranking position in the human world.
The next day,
Yīn indeed arrived.
He then appeared before Pián in a headscarf and coarse clothes at the Bìyún Pavilion,
with a demonic form and ghostly demeanor,
his sophistry and deceit swarming like bees,
claiming he could summon immortals while seated,
and instantly change the cold and heat.
Pián could not fathom him,
and treated him as a divine being,
calling him General Zhūgě.
Often during leisurely banquets,
listening to his tales of ghosts and monsters,
he would forget fatigue for the entire day.
From then on, Yīn was repeatedly promoted to important positions in salt and iron administration,
amassing wealth amounting to hundreds of thousands of strings of cash.
His wickedness and dark sorcery,
Yòngzhī regarded as nothing.
There was a great merchant named Zhōu Shīrú,
whose residence had exotic flowers, trees, towers, and pavilions,
making it the finest mansion in Guǎnglíng.
Yīn desired it, but Shīrú refused.
One day,
Yīn said to Pián:
"Within the city walls,
a demon is about to arise.
If it achieves its ambitions,
it will not be comparable to floods, droughts, or wars."
Pián said:
"What should we do about it?"
Yīn said:
"We should build an altar beneath it,
and invite a divine official to suppress it."
Yīn then pointed to Shīrú's mansion as the location.
Pián ordered the military officers to drive out his family.
That day, rain and snow suddenly fell,
and the mud was at its worst.
The officials whipped and pressed them urgently,
Shīrú led his elderly and young,
crawling on the road,
and those who saw it were all astonished.
Yīn moved his own clan there.
and made it his home.
Yīn's feet had previously suffered from wind sores,
and by this time they had worsened.
Whenever they itched intensely,
he would order a maidservant,
to scratch them with both hands,
and only stop when blood flowed.
Pián had a strict and clean nature,
and even his nephews and nieces were not allowed to sit with him,
but only with Yīn did he engage intimately,
often to the point of forgetting to eat or sleep.
Sometimes they sat close together in secrecy,
sharing the same cup and utensils.
When Yīn's wind sores suddenly flared up,
he would scratch and rub them freely,
and between his fingers and nails,
pus and blood would stain.
Pián would drink and eat with him,
without ever showing any difficulty.
Those around him sometimes spoke about it,
but Pián said:
"Immortals often test people in this way.
Do not take it to heart."
Pián previously had a small dog,
and whenever it smelled Yīn's foul and filthy odor,
it would come close to him.
Pián found its familiarity strange.
Yīn laughed and said:
"I often saw it before the Jade Emperor in the Great Lofty Palace,
and though we parted hundreds of years ago,
it still recognizes me."
His empty boasts were mostly like this.
Gāo Yú often said to people:
"How do we know he is not the one who will bring ruin to our clan?"
Yīn had a violent and cruel nature,
and within two months of taking charge of the Yángzhōu bureau,
out of several hundred officials,
he had whipped the backs of nearly half.
In the second year of the Guāngqì era,
the false court appointed Yīn as concurrent Censor-in-Chief,
and bestowed upon him the golden and purple insignia.
When the city fell,
he fled to Wāntóu,
where he was captured by patrols.
Several catties of gold were found at his waist,
and two belts made of通天rhinoceros horn.
After being bound and brought into the city,
the common people gathered to watch,
spitting on his face one after another,
and plucking out his hair and beard,
until they were completely gone in an instant.
Once the trial was concluded,
he was executed south of the Xiàmǎ Bridge,
beaten with over a hundred strokes,
and strangled but not yet dead.
As Shī Duó's mother was returning home from the inner city,
passing by the execution site,
she helped him up and moved him aside,
and he revived under the bridge.
The executioner soon knocked him down with a large log.
After the carriage passed,
he was punished again as before.
From the beginning of Yīn's rise,
his reputation for arrogance and cruelty,
quickly spread far and wide.
His clansmen repeatedly warned Yīn to be humble and restrained.
Yīn said:
"A man's worry is not being able to fulfill his ambitions.
Once he achieves them,
he should live in wealth and honor.
How can a person die twice in life?"
By this time, he indeed faced execution twice.
When his corpse was abandoned by the roadside,
his enemies gouged out his eyes,
and cut off his tongue.
Children threw tiles and stones at him,
and in a moment, a mound formed.
Moreover, in Gāo Pián's later years,
he was deluded by the arts of immortality.
Lǚ Yòngzhī, Zhāng Shǒuyī, Zhūgě Yīn, and others,
all claimed they could command ghosts and deities,
and transform gold.
Pián deeply believed them,
and thus entrusted them with government affairs.
Yòngzhī and others brought in their cronies,
and acted lawlessly as they pleased.
Later, they also worried that talkative people might leak information,
so they said to Pián:
"The lofty immortals and supreme sages,
are not difficult to summon.
What is concerning is,
for those who study the Dao,
if their true energy is slightly depleted,
their divine incantations will cease."
When Pián heard this,
he believed it to be true,
and thus cut off all human affairs,
and dismissed his concubines.
Guests, generals, and officials,
could no longer see him.
If there was an unavoidable reason,
he would have the person first bathe and fast,
and go to the Zǐjí Palace to have a Daoist priest perform purification rituals to remove inauspiciousness,
called 'cleansing impurities,'
and only then would he see them.
As soon as the bows and greetings ended,
they were already led out again.
From then on, internal and external communication was blocked.
Discipline and order daily grew chaotic.
Yòngzhī and others thus greatly exercised their power,
as if no one else was around.
As time passed deeply,
their roots became firmly established.
Yòngzhī called himself the True Lord of Pánxī, Zhāng Shǒuyī called himself Chìsōngzǐ, and Zhūgě Yīn claimed the title of General.
There was one named Xiāo Shèng,
who was called the son-in-law of Duke Mù of Qín.
They all said they were sent by the Supreme God,
to be companions for Your Excellency on the Dao path.
Their vulgar and absurd claims,
were mostly like this.
In front of the Jiāngyáng County office, there was a small shrine to the earth deity.
When Yòngzhī was poor and lowly,
he often stayed there with his wife.
stopped at its.
lodging.
For all his actions,
he would pray before proceeding.
After achieving success,
he believed it was due to divine assistance,
and thus renovated and honored it.
Winding corridors and curved rooms,
dressing towers and sleeping halls,
amounted to over a hundred chambers.
The craftsmen and builders,
were the finest selections from the Jiangnan region.
Whenever there were major military affairs,
he would offer a shàoláo sacrifice there.
Yòngzhī and Shǒuyī,
both claimed to have encountered deities.
Whenever Pián had a secret request,
he would send these two to convey his intentions.
In the first year of the Zhōnghé era,
Yòngzhī, because immortals enjoy residing in towers,
He requested to build the Yíngxiān Tower north of the official residence,
spanning across the river.
The sound of axes and adzes
continued day and night without ceasing,
costing tens of thousands of strings of coins,
and it took half a year to complete.
From its completion to its downfall,
he never once visited it.
The locks and keys remained intact,
until it was reduced to ashes.
That winter,
he also constructed the Yánhé Pavilion west of the main hall,
comprising seven bays in total,
standing eighty feet tall,
all adorned with pearls and jade,
with elegant windows and embroidered doors,
almost as if not made by human hands.
Every morning,
he would burn rare incense
and display exotic treasures,
praying for the descent of the Queen Mother of the West.
When Bì Shīduó rebelled,
someone climbed up to it
and saw twenty-eight characters inscribed on the lotus-shaped caisson ceiling:
"The Yánhé Pavilion towers into the clouds,
even whispers are heard by Tàiyǐ.
Burning all the incense achieves nothing,
opening the door welcomes General Bì."
This was akin to poetic sorcery.
Lǚ Yòngzhī openly claimed:
"I communicate with the immortals."
Whenever facing Gāo Pián,
he would command wind and rain with shouts,
or bow to the air,
claiming to see groups of immortals passing by outside.
Gāo Pián would follow and bow to them.
Lǚ Yòngzhī gestured wildly,
showing no trace of shame.
If anyone around him expressed the slightest dissent,
they would meet death without delay.
Witnesses could not fathom the reason,
but could only beat their chests in silence, not daring to speak out.
Lǚ Yòngzhī suddenly declared:
"The spirit of the Hòutǔ Fūrén has sent an envoy to borrow troops and horses from me,
along with the Tàibái Yīn Jīng compiled by Lǐ Quán."
Gāo Pián immediately ordered two counties
to gather thousands of reed mats from the people,
painted to resemble armor and weapons,
and sent Lǚ Yòngzhī to burn them in the temple courtyard.
He also wrote ten copies of the Tàibái Yīn Jīng on multicolored paper,
placing them beside the deity's seat.
He also sculpted a young man in green robes in the Hòutǔ Fūrén's tent,
calling him Wéi Láng.
After the temple was completed,
someone inscribed a long poem on the beam of the western corridor:
"The turmoil across the land remains unsettled,
yet futile efforts are made in Huáihǎi to emulate rituals.
Even the Mysterious Maiden of the Nine Heavens lacks credibility,
how could the Hòutǔ Fūrén possess any spiritual power?
A strand of fine clouds tinges the temples green,
two rows of towering peaks brush the brows clear.
Wéi Láng, young and idle, indulges in trivial matters,
do not boast of the Tàibái Jīng on your desk."
Those fond of such matters eagerly circulated and recited it.
That year,
an imperial decree ordered the establishment of a living shrine for Gāo Pián in Guǎnglíng,
along with an engraved stone eulogy.
People from the prefecture were sent to Xuānchéng to quarry stone for the stele.
When it arrived at the Yángzǐ Courtyard,
Lǚ Yòngzhī secretly dispatched fifty strong oxen overnight to haul it to the south of the prefecture,
breached the wall, spanned the moat,
and moved it into the city.
By dawn,
the fences and barriers appeared untouched.
He then ordered the Yángzǐ County to report to the prefecture,
stating that the stele had mysteriously disappeared overnight.
A reward was offered for its recovery.
By evening, it was claimed
that deities had moved it to the marketplace.
Gāo Pián was greatly astonished
and erected a large wooden pillar beside it,
inscribed in gold with the words:
"Not by human effort,
it arrived naturally."
He then ordered troops from both capitals, armed with instruments and drums,
to welcome it into the Bìyún Pavilion.
At the bustling intersection of three bridges,
stones were deliberately buried to obstruct it,
and it was falsely claimed:
"Neither humans nor oxen can move it."
Gāo Pián then wrote a few characters in red seal script,
pasted them onto the stele,
and shortly after, the stones were removed, and it proceeded.
Onlookers whispered to one another:
"The stele is moving."
Those with insight despised it.
The next day,
an old village woman from Yángzǐ
went to the prefectural judge to submit a petition,
saying:
"Last night, the village officer borrowed my plow ox to haul the stele,
and accidentally injured its leg."
When this spread far and wide,
everyone burst into laughter.
By the time the city fell,
Bì Shīduó's troops
eventually breached the walls and entered.
Gāo Pián often clashed with Chancellor Zhèng,
and Lǚ Yòngzhī, aware of this,
suddenly said:
"I have just received a letter from an immortal,
stating that among the high officials,
there is someone secretly plotting against you, Lord.
A knight-errant will come,
arriving tonight."
Gāo Pián was terrified and anxious,
and sought advice from Lǚ Yòngzhī.
He replied:
"Master Zhāng Shǒuyī learned this art in his youth
from Madame Niè of Shēnjǐng Village.
I do not know if he still practices it these days.
If he does,
simply ask him to handle it,
and the plotter will surely be crushed to dust."
Gāo Pián immediately summoned Zhāng Shǒuyī and told him.
He replied:
"I have long ceased such performances,
and my skills have grown rusty.
However, for your sake, Lord,
why not?"
At the appointed time, he dressed in women's clothing
and hid in a separate room.
Zhāng Shǒuyī slept in Gāo Pián's bedroom.
At midnight,
he threw a piece of copper or iron onto the stone steps,
producing a clanging sound.
He then took pig's blood from a leather pouch
and splattered it around the courtyard, eaves, and pillars,
creating the appearance of a struggle.
The next day,
Gāo Pián tearfully thanked Zhāng Shǒuyī, saying:
"I owe you the grace of rebirth.
Truly, dry bones have been clothed with flesh again."
He personally presented gold, jade, and a Tōngtiān rhinoceros-horn belt as a reward.
The Jiangyáng County Captain Xuē,
whose given name is lost,
was also a follower of Lǚ Yòngzhī.
One day, he suddenly reported to Gāo Pián:
"Last night, while patrolling,
I arrived in front of the Hòutǔ Temple
and saw countless ghostly soldiers.
One among them said:
'Tell King Gāo for me,
the Lady has ordered me to lead millions of troops to patrol this region.
Rest assured, King, no other invaders will encroach.'
After speaking, he vanished."
The group of sorcerers heard this and rejoiced greatly,
competing to gift him gold and silk.
Not long after,
he was appointed Magistrate of Liùhé County.
Lǚ Yòngzhī also carved a large human foot out of wood,
three feet five inches long.
After a long period of rain had just cleared,
he stamped it overnight behind the Hòutǔ Temple in the cypress grove,
and in front of the Jiangyáng County office,
leaving marks resembling a contest of strength.
The next day,
Lǚ Yòngzhī told Gāo Pián:
"Last night, deities fought in the Lady's temple.
I dispatched ghostly soldiers overnight to drive them away,
and they have already crossed the river."
Otherwise,
Guǎnglíng would have nearly been engulfed by floods.
Gāo Pián was horrified.
He then gave twenty catties of gold
to reward Lǚ Yòngzhī.
Later, a beloved horse of Gāo Pián died.
The stableman, fearing punishment,
sought help from Lǚ Yòngzhī.
Lǚ Yòngzhī then went to see Gāo Pián and said:
"The Sui general Chén Gǎorén,
under my orders, has gone to Huáidōng.
Gǎorén complained about lacking a horse,
and your great black horse, Lord,
he hopes to borrow it."
Moments later,
the stable officer reported:
"The great black horse is sweating profusely."
Gāo Pián calmly replied:
"I have already lent it to the Grand Minister Over the Masses."
Soon after, it was reported dead.
Initially, Xiāo Shèng bribed Lǚ Yòngzhī,
seeking appointment as Salt Commissioner of Yánchéng.
Gāo Pián felt that the incumbent had performed well,
and was hesitant about replacing him.
Lǚ Yòngzhī said:
"Using Shèng as the salt city official,
is not for Shèng's sake.
Yesterday I received a letter from the Supreme Immortal stating:
'There is a precious sword in the well of the salt city,
which must be retrieved by a Spiritual Official.'
Because Shèng is a close associate of the Supreme Immortal,
I wish to send him there."
Pián bowed and agreed to it.
Shèng arrived at the salt works for several months,
then placed a bronze dagger in a box and presented it to Pián.
Yòngzhī kowtowed and said:
"This is what the Northern Emperor wears.
With it, within a hundred li,
no weapon of war dares to offend."
Pián found it very extraordinary,
and adorned it with precious jade,
often placing it by his seat.
At that time, Guǎnglíng had long been rainy,
and Yòngzhī said to Pián:
"This place is due for a fire disaster,
between the city walls and settlements,
all will turn to ashes.
Recently I dispatched a poisonous dragon under Jīnshān,
to moisten it with a little rain.
From now on, although there won't be large-scale burning,
there will inevitably be minor disturbances."
So Yòngzhī secretly sent people to set fires every night,
and desolate shrines and ruined buildings
were no longer preserved.
Pián was about to receive the secret methods of Daoism,
but Yòngzhī and Shǒuyī did not increase them.
So they carved a piece of green stone,
shaped like a hand tablet,
with faintly raised dragons and snakes,
nearly forming characters:
"The Jade Emperor bestows upon Báiyún Xiānshēng Gāo Pián."
They secretly had attendants place it on the incense table in the Dàoist temple.
When Pián saw it,
he was overwhelmed with surprise and joy.
Yòngzhī said:
"The Jade Emperor, due to Your Excellency's meritorious cultivation through burning incense,
specially issued this command.
I reckon his phoenixes and cranes
will descend soon.
Our period of banishment is already full,
and we should then accompany your banners and insignia,
returning together to the true realm.
In the future, at the feast by the Jasper Pool,
this will also be a tale from the mortal world."
After speaking,
they laughed joyfully without end.
Then together they ascended the Yánhé Pavilion,
ordered wine and delicacies,
and enjoyed themselves to the utmost before concluding.
Later, in the courtyard of the Dàoist temple,
they carved a crane from wood,
as large as a small steed,
with mechanisms set in the saddle and bridle;
if anyone approached it,
it would vigorously flap as if to fly.
Pián once, dressed in feather robes, mounted it,
gazing up at the open sky,
with thoughts of soaring freely.
From then on, he strictly observed fasts and performed rituals,
flying and refining the golden elixir.
The expenditure of resources and wealth
often exceeded tens of thousands.
Days and months passed,
yet there was no verification of its efficacy.
Dǒng Chāng
Before Dǒng Chāng usurped the throne,
an old man from Shānyīn County
falsely submitted a statement to Chāng, saying:
"Now Your Majesty's benevolent governance reaches the people,
I wish for you to be emperor for ten thousand years in Yuè,
to bring fortune to the multitudes.
Thirty years ago,
I already heard a ballad,
which exactly matches today,
hence I come to present it.
Its words say:
'If you wish to know the sage's surname,
a thousand li of grass is lush and green.
If you wish to know the sage's given name,
the sun person says it is born above.'" Chāng obtained it and was greatly pleased,
and therefore said,
saying:
"Heaven's mandate has long belonged to me,
what I do is great."
Then he rewarded the old man with a hundred bolts of silk,
and also exempted him from taxes and levies.
First, he sent the Dàoist priest Zhū Sīyuǎn to set up an altar,
to await the Supreme Emperor.
Suddenly one evening it was said
that a heavenly tally descended in the rain,
with green paper and red writing,
the text of which was again illegible.
Sīyuǎn said, "Heaven's mandate is bestowed upon the Dǒng clan."
There was also Wáng Shǒuzhēn,
whom some called Wáng Bǎiyì,
extremely ingenious.
Initially, he established a living shrine,
carving and sculpting images.
Modeling and continuing the officials and subordinates,
and setting up armed guards,
appearing like ghosts and deities,
all were done by Bǎiyì.
During the time of deceit and falsehood,
it was all caused by Bǎiyì's illusions and deceptions.
Chāng often said:
the prophecy of the rabbit ascending the golden bed refers to me.
I was born in the year of the rabbit,
next year the year is in the rabbit,
the second day of the second month is also rabbit,
that is the rabbit year, rabbit month, rabbit day,
and it should still be at the rabbit hour.
The enterprise of ten thousand generations,
its advantage lies herein."
In the second year of Qiánníng,
on the second day of the second month,
leading tens of thousands of soldiers and commoners,
usurping the imperial robes and crown with ceremonial guards,
he ascended the gate tower of the inner city,
granted amnesty within the territory,
changed the false reign name to Luópíng Kingdom,
era name Tiāncè,
calling himself the Sage.
And ordered the officials, subordinates, generals, and officers, etc.,
all to shout, "Long live the Sage!"
Bowing, he said.
After the speech,
he again wished to perform the ceremonial dance.
Chāng then repeatedly stopped him:
"You have spoken so many words,
they are pressing down on my head and giving me a headache."
When people of the time heard,
they all laughed at him.
Lóngmén Shān
Yǔ cut through the mountain of Lóngguān,
also called Lóng,
mén.
Reaching an empty cave,
several tens of li deep,
dark and obscure, impossible to proceed further.
Yǔ carried a torch and advanced.
There was a beast shaped like a pig,
holding a luminous pearl in its mouth,
its light like a candle.
There was also a green dog,
walking and barking ahead.
Yǔ reckoned he had traveled over ten li,
confused between day and night,
then gradually became aware of increasing brightness,
saw the former pig and dog
transformed into human form,
all wearing black clothes.
Also saw a deity with a human face and snake body.
Yǔ therefore spoke with him.
The immortal then showed Yǔ the diagram of the Eight Trigrams,
arranged on a golden plate.
There were also eight deities,
attending beside this diagram.
Yǔ asked:
"Huáxū gave birth to a sage son,
is that you?"
He answered:
"Huáxū is the ninth.
River goddess's daughter,
who gave birth to me."
Then he took out a jade tablet to give to Yǔ.
The tablet was one foot two inches long,
to match the number of the twelve hours,
enabling the measurement of heaven and earth.
Yǔ then held this tablet,
to pacify and regulate the waters and lands.
Bestowing the tablet and unfolding the diagram,
the snake-bodied deity
is the body of Fúxī.
Tàigōng Wàng
King Wén appointed Tàigōng Wàng as the magistrate of Guàntán.
After a year,
the winds did not rustle the branches.
King Wén dreamed of a woman of great beauty,
weeping in the middle of the road.
He asked her the reason,
and the woman said:
"I am the goddess of Mount Tàishān in the Eastern Sea,
married to the Western Sea.
I wish to return east,
but the magistrate of Guàntán blocks my path.
Tàigōng is virtuous,
so I dare not pass through with violent winds and torrential rain."
King Wén awoke from his dream.
The next day, he summoned Tàigōng.
For three days and three nights,
there were indeed violent winds and sudden rains that passed by,
all coming from the west.
King Wén then appointed Tàigōng as Grand Marshal.
The Four Sea Deities
King Wǔ attacked King Zhòu,
and established his capital at Luòyì.
The following year was overcast and cold,
with snow falling for over ten days,
accumulating more than ten feet deep.
At dawn on the jiǎzǐ day,
five men in a horse-drawn carriage,
accompanied by two riders,
stopped outside the king's gate.
Shī Shàngfǔ sent someone out with a bowl of porridge, saying:
"The great officers are inside,
currently facing the Son of Heaven.
There is no time to come out,
but please have some hot porridge,
to ward off the cold."
After they finished the porridge,
Shī Shàngfǔ said:
"The guests may now be received.
Five.
Carriage and two riders,
they are the deities of the Four Seas,
along with Hé Bó, Fēng Bó, and Yǔ Shī.
The deity of the Southern Sea is called Zhùróng, the Eastern Sea Gōumáng, the Northern Sea Zhuānxū, and the Western Sea Rùshōu.
As for Hé Bó, Fēng Bó, and Yǔ Shī,
please have the usher
summon each by their name."
King Wǔ then stood in the hall,
with the usher inside the gate below the hall,
leading Zhùróng forward.
The five deities were all startled,
looking at each other and sighing.
Zhùróng and the others all bowed.
King Wǔ said:
"You have come from afar on such an overcast day,
what instruction do you have for me?"
They all said:
"Heaven is attacking Yīn to establish Zhōu,
and we have respectfully come to confer the mandate."
They then instructed Fēng Bó and Yǔ Shī,
each to perform their duties.
Yán Juān
In the twentieth year of King Zhāo of Zhōu,
Dōng'ōu presented women,
one named Yán Juān,
the other Yán Yú.
Both were eloquent, beautiful, and clever with words,
skilled in singing and laughter,
leaving no footprints in the dust,
and casting no shadow at noon.
When the king traveled to the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
he drowned along with the two women.
Therefore, between the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
people remember them to this day,
and a shrine was erected by the river.
Ten years later,
people often saw the two women embracing the king, floating in a boat,
playing by the water's edge.
On the Shangsi day in late spring,
purification gatherings are held at the shrine.
Some use fresh seasonal fruits,
wrapped in fragrant orchids and azaleas,
and sink them into the water.
Some tie them with five-colored silk,
or attach gold or iron to them,
so that the flood dragons do not encroach.
Thus, the shrine is called the Zhāozhī Shrine.
Duke Huán of Qí
Duke Huán of Qí was traveling in the marshes,
with Guǎn Zhòng driving the carriage.
The duke saw something strange.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"In the marshes, there is a wēiyí,
as large as a hub,
as long as a carriage shaft,
wearing purple clothes and a red crown.
When it sees a person, it raises its head and stands;
one who sees it is likely to become a hegemon, is that not so?"
The duke said:
"This is what I saw."
Also, when Duke Huán campaigned north against Gūzhú,
arriving ten lǐ from the Bēi'ěr Stream,
he saw a person a foot tall,
yet fully human in form.
Complete.
With his right sleeve lifted,
he ran before the horses.
The duke asked Guǎn Zhòng about it,
and Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I have heard that among the mountain deities, there is one called Yú'ér,
a foot tall but fully formed in human likeness.
When a hegemon king arises,
the mountain deity appears.
Running ahead to guide.
Lifting the sleeve indicates water ahead.
Lifting the right sleeve shows to cross from the right."
It turned out as he said.
Duke Wén of Jìn
Duke Wén of Jìn was traveling,
when a large snake, as thick as an arch,
blocked the road.
Duke Wén then cultivated virtue,
and ordered an official to guard the snake.
The snake-guarding official dreamed that a heavenly envoy killed the snake,
saying:
"Why did the snake block the path of the sage lord?"
When he awoke and looked,
the snake had already rotted.
Duke Mù of Zhèng
Duke Mù of Zhèng was in the temple during the day,
when a deity with a human face and bird body,
dressed in plain clothes,
and of square, upright appearance,
appeared, frightening the duke greatly.
The deity said:
"Do not fear,
the Emperor values your bright virtue,
and grants you ten more years of life,
so that your state may prosper."
The duke asked the deity's name,
and it said:
"I am Gōumáng."
Duke Píng of Jìn
Duke Píng of Jìn was by the Kuài River,
when he saw a person arriving in a carriage drawn by eight white horses.
There was a creature with a wildcat's body and a fox's tail,
which left its carriage and followed the duke's carriage.
The duke asked Shī Kuàng,
and Shī Kuàng said:
"A wildcat's body with a fox's tail,
its name is the deity of Shǒuyáng.
It drank at Mount Huòtài and is returning,
meeting you, my lord, by the Kuài River.
You, my lord, shall have good fortune!"
Duke Jǐng of Qí
Duke Jǐng of Qí attacked Sòng,
passing by Mount Tàishān,
when he dreamed of two angry men.
The duke was afraid,
thinking they were deities of Mount Tàishān.
Yànzǐ explained that they were the ancestors of Sòng, Tāng
and Yī Yǐn,
describing their appearances:
Tāng had a fair complexion,
with a thick beard,
while Yī Yǐn was dark and short.
These matched the men in the dream.
Duke Jǐng advanced his army but did not heed [the warning].
The army's equipment was destroyed,
and the duke, afraid,
disbanded the army and did not attack Sòng.
The Shrine of the Jealous Woman
In the border area between Shí'ài and Shòuyáng counties of Bīngzhōu,
there is the Jealous Maiden Spring,
with a temple dedicated to its deity.
The spring water is deep and abundant,
clear and transparent for a thousand fathoms.
When worshippers throw coins or sheep bones into it,
they remain distinctly visible.
Folklore says the jealous maiden
was the sister of Jiè Zǐtuī.
In rivalry with her brother,
she decreed that within a hundred *li* of the spring,
no fires were to be extinguished during the Cold Food Festival,
a practice that persists to this day.
The maiden is dressed in bright, fresh brocade robes,
adorned in splendid attire.
And if someone takes from the mountain...
When cinnabar or lilies are carried past,
thunder, wind, lightning, and hail will surely strike to shake them.
Wǔ Zǐxū
Wǔ Zǐxū repeatedly admonished the King of Wú,
and was given the Zhǔlòu sword to die by.
Before his death,
he instructed his son, saying:
"Hang my head above the southern gate,
so that I may watch the Yuè troops arrive.
Wrap my corpse in sturgeon skin,
and cast it into the river.
I shall then ride the morning and evening tides,
to witness the downfall of Wú."
Ever since then, from the Hǎimén Mountain,
the tidal bore has surged hundreds of feet high,
passing through Yuè's Qiántáng and Yúpǔ,
before gradually subsiding.
It returns twice daily,
its roar like thunderous rage,
racing like thunder and lightning for over a hundred *li*.
At times, people have seen Wǔ Zǐxū riding a plain carriage with white horses amid the tidal bore,
and thus a temple was built to offer sacrifices to him.
On the bank of the Féi River within Lúzhōu city,
there is also a temple to Wǔ Zǐxū.
Every time the morning and evening tides come,
the waters of the Féi River
also swell and surge with fury,
rising up to the front of his temple.
They rise one or two feet high,
spreading over ten *zhàng* wide,
and only settle after about the time of a meal.
Common lore says:
This corresponds with the tides of the Qiántáng River!
Qū Yuán
Qū Yuán threw himself into the Mìluó River on the fifth day of the fifth month,
and the people of Chǔ mourned him.
On this day each year,
they would store rice in bamboo tubes,
and cast them into the water as offerings.
During the Jiànwǔ era of the Hàn dynasty,
a man named Ōu Qū from Chángshā
suddenly saw a scholar in broad daylight,
who claimed to be the Sānlǘ Dàfū,
and said to Qū:
"I have heard that you are about to make offerings,
which is very good.
However, the offerings made over the years
have often been stolen by flood dragons.
If you wish to bestow a favor now,
you may seal the top with chinaberry leaves,
and bind them with colored silk threads.
These two things are what flood dragons fear."
Qū followed his advice.
Nowadays, people make rice dumplings on the fifth day of the fifth month,
wrapping them with chinaberry leaves and five-colored silk threads,
all traditions inherited from the Mìluó River.
Lǐ Bīng
Lǐ Bīng served as the governor of Shǔ Commandery.
A flood dragon wreaked havoc every year,
causing widespread flooding and devastation.
Lǐ Bīng then entered the water to slay the flood dragon.
He transformed himself into the shape of an ox,
while the river god leaped like a dragon,
and Lǐ Bīng could not overcome it.
After emerging,
he selected several hundred of the bravest soldiers,
armed with strong bows and large arrows,
and made an agreement, saying:
"Earlier, I transformed into an ox,
and now the river god will surely also become an ox.
I will tie a long white silk ribbon around myself to distinguish me.
You must kill the one without the mark."
Then, with a roar, he charged back into the water.
In a moment, great thunder and wind arose,
and heaven and earth became one color.
When things settled slightly,
two oxen were seen fighting on the surface.
Lǐ Bīng's white silk ribbon was very long and bright,
so the warriors all shot at the river god,
and it was killed.
From then on, the people of Shǔ no longer suffered from floods.
Even today, when great waves surge,
as if about to reach his temple,
they all recede and flow away.
Thus, in spring and winter, ox-fighting performances are held,
which likely originated from this event.
South of the temple, several thousand households
live along the low riverbanks,
yet even during severe autumn floods,
they do not relocate.
There is a stone ox
in the temple courtyard.
In the fifth year of the Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty,
a great flood suddenly broke out.
Lǐ Bīng's spirit transformed into a dragon,
and fought again with a dragon at Guànkǒu,
still using a white silk ribbon as a marker.
The waters then surged downstream,
