flooding Zuǒmián, Zǐ, and Tóng,
overflowing rivers and gorges,
and damaging several dozen commanderies.
Only Western Shǔ remained unharmed.
The Earth Goat Deity
In Qiānyuán County of Lǒngzhōu,
there is a temple to the Earth Goat Deity.
Long ago, when Qín Shǐhuáng opened an imperial road,
he saw two white goats fighting.
He sent an envoy to chase them,
and they turned into earthen mounds here.
The envoy, frightened, returned.
Qín Shǐhuáng then visited the place,
where he saw two men bowing by the roadside.
The emperor asked them,
and they replied:
"We are not human,
but deities of the earth goats.
Because you have come here,
we have come to pay our respects."
After speaking, they vanished.
Qín Shǐhuáng immediately ordered a temple to be built,
and sacrifices have continued without interruption to this day.
Méi Gū
During the Qín dynasty,
by the lake in Dānyáng County,
there was a temple to Méi Gū.
During her lifetime, she possessed magical arts,
and could walk on water while wearing shoes.
Later, she violated Daoist laws,
and her husband, enraged, killed her,
throwing her corpse into the water.
It then drifted with the waves,
to the place where her temple now stands.
Shamans often gather there.
For burial,
no grave mound is needed,
as a square-headed lacquered coffin always appears in the ancestral hall.
On the last and first days of the lunar month,
one can sometimes see in the mist over the water,
a faint, shoe-wearing figure.
No fishing or hunting is allowed around the temple,
or one risks getting lost or drowning.
The shamans say:
"Since Méi Gū died a violent death,
she detests seeing killing and harm."
Qín Shǐhuáng
Qín Shǐhuáng built a stone bridge,
intending to cross the sea,
to observe the place where the sun rises.
It is said:
"At that time, there was a deity who could drive stones into the sea.
The eleven mountains of Yángchéng,
now all stood up,
towering and leaning eastward,
as if following one another.
It is also said:
When the stones moved too slowly,
the deity would whip them,
and they would all bleed,
turning completely red,
and remain so to this day.
Qín Shǐhuáng built a stone bridge in the sea,
and some say
it was not built by human effort,
but the sea deity erected its pillars.
The emperor, moved by its favor,
then paid respects to the deity,
seeking to meet it.
The deity said:
'My form is ugly;
if you promise not to depict my form,
I will meet with the emperor.'"
The emperor then entered the stone bridge for thirty lǐ,
and met the deity.
Among the emperor's attendants was a skilled man,
who secretly sketched with his foot.
The deity angrily said:
'The emperor has broken his promise;
you must leave quickly.'"
The emperor immediately turned his horse around.
The front hooves were still standing,
but the rear hooves collapsed,
and he barely managed to reach the shore.
The River Deity of Guāntíng
During the Qín dynasty,
there was a shrine altar for the River Deity of Guāntíng on the Qiānlǐ Shuǐ in Zhōngsù County.
Those who passed by without reverence
would inevitably run madly into the mountains,
transforming into tigers.
A resident of Zhōngsù County went to Luò,
and on the road,
encountered a traveler,
who entrusted him with a letter, saying:
'My home is in front of the Tíng Temple,
where vines hang among the rocks.
Just knock on the vines,
and someone will respond.'"
The man returned and did as instructed,
and indeed two people emerged from the water,
took the letter, and submerged.
Soon they returned, saying:
'The River Lord wishes to see you.'"
Without realizing it, the man followed them.
He then saw houses exquisitely beautiful,
with fresh and fragrant food and drink,
and conversations and interactions
no different from the mortal world.
Wǎnruò
Emperor Hàn Wǔdì built the Bǎiliáng Terrace to house Shénjūn.
Shénjūn was
a woman from Chánglíng,
who married and became a wife.
She gave birth to a son,
who died at a few years old.
The woman grieved deeply for him,
and within the year, she also died.
After death, she manifested spiritual power,
and her sister-in-law, Wǎnruò, established a shrine for her.
It was then said:
Wǎnruò acted as the medium,
and many people came to seek blessings,
discussing minor household matters,
with considerable efficacy.
Píngyuán Jūn also served her,
and his descendants later achieved honor and prominence.
Believing it was due to Shénjūn's power,
they revered her even more.
When Emperor Wǔdì ascended the throne,
the empress dowager welcomed her into the palace to make offerings.
They heard her words,
but did not see her person.
At this point, Shénjūn requested to leave,
so the Bǎiliáng Terrace was built to house her.
Initially, when Huò Qùbìng was still obscure,
he prayed to the deity several times.
Shénjūn then appeared to him in form,
adorned herself,
and sought to have relations with Huò Qùbìng.
Huò Qùbìng refused,
rebuking Shénjūn, saying:
'I believed Shénjūn was pure and chaste,
so I fasted and prayed for blessings.
Now you seek licentiousness;
this is not befitting a deity.'"
He severed ties and never went again,
and Shénjūn felt ashamed.
When Huò Qùbìng's illness became critical,
the emperor ordered prayers to Shénjūn.
Shénjūn said:
'General Huò's vital essence is depleted,
and his life will not be long.
I once intended to use the essence of Tàiyī to supplement him,
which could have extended his years.
General Huò did not understand this intention,
and severed ties.
Now he cannot be saved.'"
Huò Qùbìng eventually died.
One year before Crown Prince Wèi's downfall,
Shénjūn departed.
Dōngfāng Shuò took Wǎnruò as a concubine,
and they had three sons,
who died along with Shuò.
The Bamboo King
During the reign of Emperor Hàn Wǔdì,
the Bamboo King arose in
Tún Shuǐ.
There was a woman washing by the riverbank,
when a large bamboo with three sections
floated between her feet.
She pushed it, but it would not leave,
and she heard a sound.
She broke it open,
and found a baby boy inside.
When he grew up,
he became a leader among the Yí and Pú tribes,
taking Bamboo as his surname.
The damaged bamboo
grew into a forest overnight,
which is the Bamboo King's shrine grove.
The king once stopped with his followers on a large rock,
and ordered soup to be made.
A follower said:
'There is no water.'"
The king struck the rock with his sword, and water flowed out,
which is now called Bamboo King Water.
Later, when Táng Méng opened up Zāngkē,
he beheaded the Bamboo King.
The Yí and Lǎo tribes all resented this,
and because the Bamboo King was not born of flesh and blood,
they requested a shrine be established for him.
The emperor enfeoffed his three sons as marquises.
After their deaths,
they were enshrined alongside their father,
and now the Bamboo King's Three Lords Shrine venerates their spirits.
Liú Xiàng
Liú Xiàng, in the final years of Emperor Chéng's reign,
was collating texts in the Tiānlù Pavilion,
concentrating deeply and pondering intently.
At night, an old man dressed in black,
holding a green staff,
knocked on the pavilion and entered,
finding Xiàng sitting alone in the dark, reciting texts.
The old man then blew on the tip of his staff,
and a bright flame emerged,
illuminating Xiàng.
He spoke in detail about the time before creation.
Xiàng thus received the text of the "Wǔxíng Hóngfàn,"
with extensive and elaborate explanations,
so Xiàng tore his robe and used the silk to record the words.
At dawn, the old man departed,
and Xiàng asked his name.
He said:
'I am the essence of Tàiyī,
and the Heavenly Emperor heard that the descendant of Jīnmǎo had a profound scholar,
so I descended to instruct him.'"
He then took out bamboo tablets from his bosom,
containing texts on astronomy and geography.
'I will briefly impart them to you.'"
Xiàng's son, Xīn,
learned the arts from Xiàng,
but Xiàng never realized who this man was.
Hé Bǐgàn
Hé Bǐgān of Rǔnán
was well-versed in laws and statutes.
During the Yuánshuò era,
Gōngsūn Hóng appointed him as Tíngwèi Yòupíng.
Under his jurisdiction, no innocent people were imprisoned,
and he was called Lord Hé.
At the beginning of the Zhēnghé era,
he left office and stayed at home.
The sky was heavily overcast with rain,
and he was napping during the day,
dreaming of guests arriving in carriages and on horseback.
Upon waking, he saw an old woman over eighty years old,
her hair completely white,
seeking shelter from the rain.
The rain was pouring heavily,
yet the woman’s clothes and shoes were not wet.
Bǐgān found this strange,
and invited her to take a seat.
Shortly after, the rain stopped,
and the woman bid farewell to leave.
He escorted her out to the gate.
Kneeling, she said to Bǐgān:
“Your ancestors trace back to Hòujì.
From Yáo to the Jìn dynasty, they accumulated hidden virtue.
In your generation,
you alone are to inherit this.
Now Heaven bestows a register,
to expand your descendants.
Those who will wear official seals and ribbons
shall correspond to the tallies.”
It was nine inches long,
with a total of one hundred and ninety tablets.
She handed it to Bǐgān and said:
“For descendants who will wear official seals and ribbons,
they shall correspond to these tallies.”
The woman headed east,
and suddenly vanished.
Bǐgān was fifty-eight years old,
with six sons.
Three years later,
he had three more sons.
He moved to Pínglíng,
and eight sons left,
with one son remaining.
He often made offerings to the woman facing east,
and upon his death,
he left instructions to be buried with his head facing east.
From Bǐgān onward,
both the Hé and Zhāng families received spiritual blessings.
For generations, they were renowned clans.
An old saying in Sānfǔ states:
“The Hé family’s register,
the Zhāng family’s tallies.”
The Marquis Luán
In Hànzhōng, there was a ghost deity called the Marquis Luán.
He often stayed on the ceiling canopy,
enjoyed eating pickled fish and vegetables,
and could foretell good and bad fortune.
During the Gānlù era,
a great locust plague arose,
and wherever it passed,
the crops were completely devoured.
The Grand Administrator sent an envoy to inform the Marquis Luán,
offering pickled fish and vegetables in sacrifice.
The Marquis said to the official:
“Locusts are a trivial matter,
I shall eliminate them at once.”
As soon as he finished speaking,
he swiftly flew out.
The official vaguely saw his form resembling a turtledove,
with a voice like a water bird.
The official returned
and reported everything to the Grand Administrator.
Soon after, countless birds, numbering in the hundreds of millions,
came to eat the locusts,
and in a short while, they were all gone.
Yáng Qǐ
Yáng Qǐ of Hénán, styled Shèngqīng.
In his youth, he suffered from malaria.
At the village shrine, he obtained a scroll of writings,
the “Method of Reprimanding and Subduing a Hundred Ghosts.”
He served as Grand Administrator of Rìnán.
His mother went to the toilet
and saw a ghost
with a head several feet long.
She told Shèngqīng about it.
Shèngqīng said:
“This is the god of Sùshuāng.”
He subdued it and made it appear,
transforming its shape into that of a servant.
He sent it with a letter to the capital,
departing in the morning and returning by evening.
It could perform tasks requiring the strength of a thousand men.
There was someone who became angry and resentful toward him,
so Shèngqīng sent the deity to go at night,
approach the person’s bedside,
seize both hands,
open eyes glowing bright red,
stick out a tongue propped on the ground,
and the person was terrified nearly to death.
Ōu Míng
Ōu Míng, a native of Lúlíng,
followed merchants on a journey passing by Péngzé Lake.
Every time he passed,
he would take whatever he had on the boat,
more or less, and throw it into the lake.
He saw on the main road
several officials all dressed in black clothes,
riding in carriages and on horses,
saying they were envoys of Lord Qīnghóng,
inviting Míng to come.
Míng knew it was a deity,
yet he dared not refuse to go.
The officials took Míng in their carriage,
and soon they saw a mansion,
with officials and guards at the gate.
An official said:
“Lord Qīnghóng is moved by your courtesy,
hence he invites you.
He will give you valuable gifts,
but do not take any of them,
only ask for Rúyuàn.”
They left,
and indeed, they offered him silk and cloth as gifts,
but Míng did not accept them.
He only asked for Rúyuàn.
The deity was greatly astonished that Míng knew about this,
and was very reluctant to part with her,
but had no choice.
He called Rúyuàn
and sent her to follow Míng away.
Rúyuàn was
a maidservant of Lord Qīnghóng,
often sent to fetch things.
Míng took Rúyuàn home,
and whatever he needed, he would obtain it.
In a few years, he became a wealthy man.
Gradually, he grew arrogant and complacent,
and no longer cherished Rúyuàn.
On New Year’s Day,
at the first crow of the rooster,
he called Rúyuàn.
Rúyuàn did not get up immediately,
and Míng became furious,
wanting to beat her.
Rúyuàn then ran to the dung heap,
where there was a pile of firewood from the previous day’s year-end cleaning,
enough to conceal a person.
Rúyuàn then escaped there
and got away.
Míng thought she was hiding in the pile of firewood and dung,
so he used a stick to beat the dung, trying to force her out.
But she did not come out,
and he realized he could not get her back.
He then said:
“If only you would make me rich again,
I would not beat you.”
Nowadays, on New Year’s Day at the crow of the rooster,
people often go and beat the dung heap,
saying:
“Make me rich.”
Lǐ Gāo
During Wáng Mǎng’s time,
the Grand Administrator of Hànzhōng went to offer sacrifices at the temple at dawn,
and left behind his writing knife.
He sent the minor official Lǐ Gāo back to retrieve it.
Gāo saw the knife on the temple bed,
and there was a person
wearing a large hat and a crimson robe,
who said to Gāo:
“Do not speak of me,
and I will bless you!”
Later, Gāo rose to the position of Grand Administrator.
When he was over sixty years old,
he suddenly spoke of seeing the temple deity.
As soon as he finished speaking, this knife stabbed him in the heart,
and he died shortly after.
Wáng Mǎng heard of this and was greatly displeased.
Huáng Yuán
During the Hàn Dynasty,
there was a man named Huáng Yuán from Tàishān.
One morning as he opened his door,
he suddenly saw a black dog
lying outside the gate,
guarding it as if it were a household pet.
Huáng Yuán leashed the dog
and went hunting with his neighbors.
As the sun began to set,
they spotted a deer,
and he released the dog.
The dog moved very slowly,
and though Huáng Yuán chased after it with all his might,
he could not catch up.
After traveling several miles,
they came to a cave entrance.
Entering for over a hundred paces,
he suddenly found himself on a level road,
lined with rows of pagoda trees and willows,
surrounded by walls.
Following the dog through a gate,
he saw dozens of rooms in a row,
all occupied by women,
whose appearances were beautiful and charming,
their clothes bright and elegant.
Some were playing the qín or sè,
others were engaged in board games.
Reaching the northern pavilion,
there were three rooms,
with two attendants on duty,
as if waiting for something.
Upon seeing Huáng Yuán,
they looked at each other and smiled, saying:
"This is the fine son-in-law brought by the black dog for Miàoyīn."
One of them stayed,
while the other entered the pavilion.
Shortly after, four maidservants came out,
announcing: "Lady Tàizhēn informs Young Master Huáng
that she has a daughter,
who has just reached marriageable age.
By fate, she is destined to be your wife."
When evening fell,
they led Huáng Yuán inside.
There was a hall facing south,
with a pond in front of it,
and in the pond was a terrace.
At the four corners of the terrace were holes a foot in diameter,
from which light shone,
illuminating the curtains and mats.
Miàoyīn's appearance was gentle and exquisite,
and her maidservants were also beautiful.
After the wedding ceremony was completed,
they rested together as if they had long been married.
After several days,
Huáng Yuán wished to return home briefly to inform his family.
Miàoyīn said:
"The ways of humans and spirits are different;
this was never meant to last long.
Tomorrow,
we will part, removing our pendants and separating our sleeves.
At the steps, tears will flow,
for we shall never meet again.
I hold you in deep affection and respect.
If you long for me,
on the morning of the third day of the third month,
you may observe fasting and purification."
The four maidservants escorted him out the gate,
and in half a day, he was home.
His thoughts were in a daze.
Whenever that date arrived,
he would often see a carriage in the sky,
seeming to fly by.
Jiǎ Kuí
When Jiǎ Kuí died in Yùjùn,
his family came to take his coffin away.
After they left,
his form was often seen in Xiàngchéng.
The officials and people, believing he was attached to that place,
thus built a temple for him.
In front of the temple was a cypress tree.
Once, someone secretly came to chop it down,
but as soon as he swung his axe,
the blade stuck in the tree,
and the cut immediately healed over.
The people around Xiàngchéng
were all terrified.
Lǐ Xiàn
At Lóngshū Língtíng,
there was a large tree,
several dozen zhàng tall,
with over ten oriole nests in it.
At the time, there had been a long drought,
and the elders said to each other:
"That tree often has a yellow aura;
perhaps there is a divine spirit there
to whom we can pray for rain."
So they went with wine and dried meat.
In the pavilion lived a widow named Lǐ Xiàn.
One night, as she rose in her room,
she suddenly saw a woman in embroidered clothes, who said:
"I am the tree spirit.
Because of your pure nature,
I will assist you in making a living.
This morning, the elders all wished to pray for rain;
I have already requested it from the Emperor."
By noon the next day,
it indeed rained heavily,
and so they built a shrine for her.
Lǐ Xiàn said:
"All of you are here;
I live near the water,
and will bring some small carp."
As soon as she finished speaking,
several dozen carp
flew and gathered in the hall below.
Everyone present was astonished.
This went on for over a year.
The spirit said:
"There will be a great war;
I now bid you farewell."
She left behind a jade ring,
saying:
"Holding this can help you avoid disaster."
Later, when Yuán Shù and Liú Biǎo attacked each other,
the people of Lóngshū all fled,
but only Lǐ Xiàn's village was spared from the fighting.
Zhāng Pú,
courtesy name Gōngzhí,
whose origins are unknown,
served as the Grand Administrator of Wújùn.
On his way back after being recalled to the capital,
he passed by Lúshān.
His children went to view the temple shrine,
and a maidservant pointed at a statue, joking:
"This one shall be your match."
That night, Zhāng Pú's wife dreamed that the Lord of Lúshān came with a betrothal gift, saying:
"My humble son is unworthy,
but I am touched that you have chosen him,
and offer this small token of my regard."
When she woke, she found it strange.
The maidservant told her what had happened.
Frightened, the wife
urged Zhāng Pú to depart quickly.
Midstream,
the boat would not move.
Everyone on board was terrified.
They threw things into the water,
but the boat still would not go.
Someone said:
"Throw a daughter overboard, and the boat will advance."
Everyone said:
"The divine intent is clear;
but to sacrifice one daughter and doom the whole family—
what can we do?"
Zhāng Pú said:
"I cannot bear to see it."
So he went up to the cabin to lie down,
ordering his wife to drown their daughter.
The wife instead used the orphaned daughter of Zhāng Pú's deceased elder brother as a substitute.
Placing a mat on the water,
the girl sat on it,
and the boat was able to move.
When Zhāng Pú saw that his daughter was still there,
he angrily said:
"How can I face the world!"
So he threw his own daughter into the water as well.
After they had crossed,
they saw from afar both girls downstream.
An official stood on the riverbank,
saying:
"I am the Registrar of the Lord of Lúshān.
The Lord of Lúshān thanks you.
He knows that spirits and humans are not suited to be matched,
and he admires your righteousness,
so he returns both girls to you."
When asked,
the girls said:
"We only saw fine houses and officials,
unaware that we were in the water."
Luò Zǐyuān
During the Xiàochāng era of the Later Wèi,
there was a Tiger Guard named Luò Zīyuān,
who claimed to be from Luòyáng.
In the Xiàochāng era,
he was stationed in Péngchéng.
A fellow soldier from his camp, Fán Yuánbǎo,
obtained leave to return to the capital,
and Zīyuān entrusted him with a letter.
He said:
"My home is south of the Língtái,
near the Luò River.
Just go there,
and my family will come out to meet you."
Yuánbǎo did as he was told,
arriving south of the Língtái,
but saw no houses.
He lingered, about to leave,
when suddenly he saw an old man,
who asked:
"Where have you come from?
Why are you wandering here?"
Yuánbǎo explained everything to him.
The old man said:
"He is my son."
He took the letter
and led Yuánbǎo inside.
There he saw lofty pavilions and spacious halls,
with beautiful buildings.
After sitting down,
the old man ordered a maid to fetch wine.
Shortly after,
he saw the maid carrying a dead child past them,
which greatly puzzled Yuánbǎo.
Soon the wine arrived,
its color very red,
and exceptionally fragrant and delicious.
Alongside it were rare delicacies,
both from land and sea.
After drinking, Yuánbǎo announced his departure.
The old man saw him out, saying:
"It will be hard to meet again,
which fills me with sorrow."
Their parting was very earnest.
The old man went back inside.
Yuánbǎo could no longer see the gate or the lane.
He only saw high cliffs facing the water,
with green waves flowing eastward.
A boy, about fourteen or fifteen years old,
had recently drowned,
and blood was flowing from his nose.
Only then did Yuánbǎo realize that the wine he had drunk
was that boy's blood.
When he returned to Péngchéng,
Zīyuān was already gone.
Yuánbǎo had served alongside Zīyuān for three years,
unaware that he was the god of the Luò River.
Chén Yú,
styled Jūndù.
His wife was from the Dù clan of Lújiāng,
who often served the goddess Hārītī,
offering female musicians to entertain the deity.
One evening during a later gathering,
the strings and pipes fell silent,
and the singing voices were mournful and distressed.
Dù often dreamed of Hārītī,
who hurriedly wept and said:
"Evil men are coming.
The maidservant first colluded with outsiders,
using a ladder against the wall,
and they climbed over to enter.
The deity's garments were about to be stripped away completely,
and they took the image, burned and crushed it, then left."
Huáng Fān
In the first year of the Guānghé era of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
Huáng Fān, the governor of Liáoxī, submitted a memorial:
"There is a drifting corpse by the sea,
wearing an exposed cap and crimson robes,
with the body intact.
Fān was moved by a dream, saying:
'I am the younger brother of Bóyí,
a nobleman of Gūzhú.
The sea has damaged my coffin,
and I seek to be buried.'
The people mocked and looked at it,
and all fell ill and died."
Yáng Yōng
Yáng Yōng of Wèi,
from Luòyáng, Hénán.
He had six brothers,
and they made their living by hiring out their labor.
Yáng Yōng cultivated filial piety from a young age.
His reputation spread far and wide.
After his parents passed away,
and the funeral rites were completed,
he longed for and missed them deeply,
unable to bear the pain in his heart and mind.
So he sold his fields and house,
moved north to a place without water,
and settled below a steep slope on the main road.
Day and night, he carried water in a cart,
offering it to travelers,
and also repaired their shoes and sandals,
refusing any payment.
He continued this tirelessly for many years.
A heavenly deity transformed into a scholar and asked:
"Why don't you grow vegetables to support yourself?"
He replied:
"I have no seeds."
The scholar then gave him several shēng of seeds.
Yáng Yōng was overjoyed,
planted them,
and the roots turned into white jade discs,
while the rest became coins.
The scholar asked again:
"Why don't you seek a wife?"
He replied:
"I am old,
and no one is willing."
The scholar said:
"Seek a daughter from a renowned family,
and you will surely get one."
There was a Xú clan,
a prominent family in Yòuběipíng,
whose daughter was known for her virtue and conduct,
and many had sought her hand but were refused.
So he tried to seek her hand.
The Xú family laughed at him,
thinking him mad and eccentric,
but hearing of his goodness,
they jokingly told the matchmaker:
"If he can bring a pair of white jade discs
and a million coins,
we will agree to the marriage."
Yáng Yōng immediately delivered them.
The Xú family was greatly astonished,
and so gave him their daughter in marriage.
They had ten sons,
all virtuous and exceptionally talented,
who rose to the positions of ministers and chancellors.
The various Yáng families in Yòuběipíng today
are their descendants.
Qián Yòu
Qián Yòu, from Yúyáo, Kuàijī,
went out behind his house at night
and was taken by a tiger.
Eighteen days later, he returned on his own.
He said that when the tiger first took him,
he was brought to a government office,
where he saw a man sitting leaning on a table,
of imposing stature and appearance,
with forty attendants.
The man said to him:
"I wish to teach you the methods of numerology."
He was kept for fifteen days,
day and night being taught various essential techniques.
After Qián Yòu received the methods,
he was sent out by someone.
He was able to return home.
He became highly skilled in divination,
with no mystery he could not unravel.
After a year, he died.
Xú Láng
In Jīngkǒu, there was a man named Xú Láng,
whose family was very poor,
and he often gathered driftwood by the river.
Suddenly, he saw a fleet of boats on the river,
covering the water as they approached,
turning into the inlet,
and mooring opposite Xú.
An envoy was sent, saying:
"The heavenly maiden will now become Xú Láng's wife."
Xú hid in a corner of the house,
refusing to come out.
His mother, brothers, and sisters urged and forced him to go out.
Before reaching the boat,
he was first taken to a separate room to bathe.
The water was fragrant,
unlike anything in the mortal world.
He was given crimson silk garments.
Xú was only fearful,
kneeling on the edge of the bed,
and showed no courtesy of receiving her at night.
The maiden angrily sent him out.
He returned the gifted clothes and withdrew.
His entire family lamented, regretted, and angrily scolded him.
He then died in remorse and sorrow.
Dīng Shì Fù
In Huáinán Quánjiāo County,
there was a woman named Dīng Xīnfù,
originally a daughter of the Dīng family from Dānyáng.
At sixteen years old,
she married into the Xiè family of Quánjiāo.
Her mother-in-law was harsh and cruel,
assigning her chores with strict deadlines.
If she failed to meet them,
she would be whipped and beaten,
making it unbearable.
On the seventh day of the ninth month, she hanged herself.
Thereafter, her spiritual presence became known,
spreading among the people.
She spoke through a shaman, saying:
"I pity the women of households,
who toil tirelessly.
Let them refrain from work on the seventh day of the ninth month."
She appeared in form,
wearing a pale green robe,
with a blue head covering,
accompanied by a maidservant,
arriving at the Niúzhǔ ferry to seek passage.
Two men were together in a boat fishing,
and she called out, asking for a ride.
The two men laughed,
teasing and mocking her together,
saying:
"Become our wife."
They said:
"We'll ferry you across."
The Dīng woman said:
"I thought you were decent men,
but you know nothing.
If you are human,
I will make you sink into the mud and die.
If you are ghosts,
I will make you drown in the water."
She then retreated into the reeds.
Shortly after,
an old man appeared,
rowing a boat loaded with reeds,
and the woman asked him for passage.
The old man said:
"My boat has no shelter,
how can you cross exposed?
I fear it is not suitable for you."
The woman said:
"Do not worry."
The old man then removed about half of the reeds,
making a space for her.
She boarded the boat,
and he ferried her directly across,
reaching the southern bank.
Before leaving, she said to the old man:
"I am a spirit,
not a human,
and could have crossed on my own.
However, I wished to let the people know of my presence.
Your kindness,
in removing reeds to ferry me,
fills me with deep gratitude and shame,
and I must repay you.
Return quickly,
and you will surely see something,
and also gain something."
The old man said:
"I am ashamed I could not provide proper shelter,
how dare I accept thanks?"
The old man returned to the western bank,
and saw the two young men drowned in the water.
Advancing a few miles,
he saw thousands of fish,
leaping by the water's edge.
The wind blew them onto the shore.
The old man then discarded the reeds and loaded the fish to return home.
Thereafter, the Dīng woman returned to Dānyáng.
People south of the Yangtze River all called her Dīng Gū.
On the seventh day of the ninth month, no work was done,
and it became a day of rest.
Now, she is worshipped everywhere.
Ā Zǐ
In the world, there is the spirit of Zǐ Gū.
Since ancient times, it has been passed down that she was a concubine,
envied by the principal wife,
who often assigned her filthy tasks.
On the fifteenth day of the first month,
she died of grief and resentment.
Therefore, on that day, people make an effigy of her,
and at night, welcome her near the toilet or pigpen.
They pray, saying:
"Zǐxū is not here,"
which was her husband's name.
"Cáo Gū has also returned,"
referring to the principal wife.
"Little sister, you may come out to play."
If the one holding the effigy feels it grow heavy,
it means the spirit has arrived.
Offerings of wine and fruit are set out,
and her appearance seems to glow with color.
She then dances and leaps without stopping.
She predicts various matters,
divines the year's fortunes and silkworm harvest.
She is also skilled at shooting and fishing.
If pleased, she dances wildly;
if displeased, she lies on her back to sleep.
Mèng of Píngchāng always doubted this,
and personally tried to hold her.
She then leaped through the roof,
and was never seen again.
Duò Shuò Jūn
Yuán Shào was in Jìzhōu,
when a deity emerged from Hédōng,
named Dù Shuò Jūn,
for whom the common people erected a temple.
The temple had a chief clerk named Dà Fú.
Càiyōng from Chénliú served as the governor of Qīnghé,
and passed by to pay respects at the temple.
He had a son named Dào,
who had been deceased for thirty years.
Dù Shuò Jūn prepared wine for Yōng and said:
"Your noble son came here long ago,
and wishes to meet you."
In a moment, the son arrived.
Dù Shuò Jūn himself said:
"My father and grandfather once served in Yǎnzhōu.
A scholar came to pray for his ailing mother.
The chief clerk said:
'The lord has encountered a celestial scholar and asks you to wait.'"
Then, the sound of drums was heard from the northwest, and the lord arrived.
Shortly after,
a guest came.
He wore a black single-layered robe,
with multicolored hair on his head,
several inches long.
After he left,
another person arrived wearing a white cloth single-layered robe,
with a tall hat,
shaped like a fish head.
He said to the lord:
"Long ago, I visited Lúshān,
and ate white plums.
It feels like not long ago,
yet three thousand years have already passed.
Time flies so easily,
it makes one feel melancholy."
The lord said to the scholar:
"The one who came earlier was the Lord of the South Sea."
The scholar was a learned man,
and the lord was well-versed in the Five Classics,
especially proficient in the Book of Rites.
When he discussed rites with the scholar,
the scholar was not his equal.
The scholar begged to save his mother's illness.
The lord said:
"To the east of your residence, there is an old bridge,
which people have damaged.
This bridge is a pathway,
and your mother has offended it.
If you can restore the bridge,
she will recover."
When Cáo Cāo attacked Yuán Tán,
he sent someone to the temple to exchange for a thousand bolts of silk,
but the lord refused.
Cáo Cāo then dispatched Zhāng Hé to destroy the temple.
Before he had traveled a hundred lǐ,
the lord sent tens of thousands of troops,
advancing along the road.
When Hé was less than two lǐ away,
clouds and mist enveloped his army,
and he could no longer find the temple's location.
The lord said to the chief clerk:
"Cáo Cāo's energy is too strong,
it is better to avoid him."
Later, in the neighboring house of Sū Bìng, a deity descended,
recognizing the lord's voice,
and said:
"I once moved to the Hu region,
and we have been separated for three years."
Then he sent someone to communicate with Cáo Cāo:
"I wish to repair the old temple,
but the land has declined and is no longer suitable to live in,
so I would like to lodge elsewhere."
Cáo Cāo said:
"Very well."
He prepared the north tower of the city for the deity to reside in.
A few days later,
Cáo Cāo went hunting
and caught a creature,
as large as a fawn,
with big feet,
white as snow in color,
its fur soft, smooth, and lovely.
Cáo Cāo rubbed it against his face,
but could not name it.
At night, a cry was heard from the tower:
"My child went out and has not returned."
Tàizǔ (Cáo Cāo) clapped his hands and said:
"This creature matches
the description.
It is indeed the case."
At dawn, he led hundreds of dogs to surround the tower.
The dogs caught the scent,
charged,
and
rushed inside and out.
They saw a creature as large as a donkey,
which threw itself down from the tower.
The dogs killed it,
and the temple deity was no more.
Jiǎng Zǐwén was a native of Guǎnglíng.
He was fond of wine and women,
and unrestrained in his behavior.
He often said of himself that he had green bones,
and that after death he would become a deity.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
he served as commandant of Mòlíng.
While pursuing bandits to the foot of Zhōng Mountain,
he was struck on the forehead by the bandits.
He then untied his official seal ribbon to bind the wound,
and shortly afterward died.
At the beginning of the reign of the founding ruler of Wú,
a former subordinate saw Zǐwén on the road,
riding a white horse,
holding a white feather fan,
attended by followers as in his lifetime.
The one who saw him fled in fright.
Zǐwén pursued him
and said:
"I am to be the local deity of this land,
to bring blessings to your people.
You may announce to the commoners
to establish a shrine for me.
If not,
there will be great calamity."
That summer,
a great plague broke out.
The people were terrified and agitated,
and many secretly made offerings to him.
Zǐwén again spoke through a shaman:
"I will greatly aid and protect the Sūn clan.
You should establish a shrine for me.
If not,
I will send insects into people's ears as disaster."
Soon after, small insects like deer flies
entered people's ears, and they all died;
doctors could not cure them.
The people grew even more fearful.
Lord Sūn did not yet believe it.
Zǐwén spoke again through a shaman:
"If you do not sacrifice to me,
I will bring a great fire as disaster."
That year,
fires broke out frequently,
dozens of places in a single day.
The fire reached the ducal palace,
and Lord Sūn became concerned.
Advisors believed that if ghosts had a place to return to,
they would not cause harm.
It would be appropriate to appease him.
Thereupon, he sent an envoy to enfeoff Zǐwén as Zhōngdū Hóu,
and his younger brother Zǐxù as Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
both bestowed with official seals.
A temple hall was built,
and Zhōng Mountain was renamed Jiǎng Mountain.
This is the present Jiǎng Mountain northeast of Jiànkāng.
From then on, disasters and plagues ceased,
and the people greatly revered him.
Xiè Yù of Chénjùn
served as administrator of Lángyé.
He was in the capital.
That year, tigers were rampant,
killing many people.
There was a man
who carried a young woman in a small boat,
with a large knife inserted in the boat.
He arrived toward dusk.
A patrol officer came out and said:
"Recently, there have been many wild beasts here.
You are carrying a delicate person,
traveling so lightly.
This is very unsafe.
You may stop and lodge at the patrol station."
After they finished exchanging greetings,
the patrol officer had just turned to leave
when the woman went ashore
and was seized by a tiger.
Her husband pulled out the knife and shouted loudly,
intending to pursue it.
Having previously served Lord Jiǎng,
he called out for help.
After traveling about ten lǐ like this,
he suddenly felt as if a black-clad man was guiding him,
and he followed him.
After another twenty lǐ,
he saw a large tree,
and then reached a cave.
The tiger cubs heard footsteps
and thought their mother had returned.
They all came out.
The man killed them on the spot,
then hid by the tree with his knife.
After a long while,
the tiger finally arrived.
It set the woman down on the ground
and began to drag her into the cave.
The man cut the tiger in half at the waist with his knife.
After the tiger died,
the woman was still alive.
By dawn, she could speak.
When asked, she said of the tiger:
"When it first seized me,
it carried me on its back.
Only when it arrived did it set me down.
My limbs were unharmed,
only scratched by plants."
He helped her back to the boat.
The next night,
he dreamed that someone said to him:
"Lord Jiǎng sent help.
Do you know?"
When he returned home, he slaughtered a pig and made offerings.
In the eastern wilds of Màoxiàn in Kuàijī,
there was a girl
surnamed Wú,
named Wàngzǐ,
sixteen years old,
lovely in appearance.
In her village, there were drum dances to entertain the deities,
and she was invited to go.
Walking halfway along the embankment,
she suddenly saw a nobleman,
extremely handsome.
The nobleman was in a boat,
with more than ten attendants.
He sent someone to ask Wàngzǐ:
"Where are you going?"
She told him everything.
The nobleman said:
"I am heading there now.
You may board the boat and go together."
Wàngzǐ declined, not daring to,
and he suddenly disappeared.
Wàngzǐ then went to pay respects at the deity's seat.
She saw the nobleman from the boat earlier,
solemnly sitting upright.
It was the statue of Lord Jiǎng.
He asked why she had come so late
and threw two tangerines to her.
He appeared to her many times,
and their affection grew deep.
Whenever she desired something in her heart,
it would descend from the air.
Once she longed to eat sliced fish,
and a pair of fresh carp
came as she wished.
Wàngzǐ's fragrance
spread for several lǐ.
She had many spiritual experiences,
and the entire district served her.
After three years,
Wàngzǐ suddenly developed feelings for another.
The deity then ceased visiting.
During the Xiánníng era,
a son of Tàicháng Qīng Hán Bó,
a son of Kuàijī Nèishǐ Wáng Yùn,
and a son of Guānglù Dàfū Liú Chǒng
went together to the temple of Jiǎng Mountain.
In the temple were several statues of women,
very beautiful.
They were drunk
and each pointed at a statue, joking about matching with them.
That very night,
all three had the same dream.
Lord Jiǎng sent a messenger to inform them:
"My daughters are all plain,
yet you have graciously bestowed your regard.
I have set a certain date
to welcome you all."
They thought their dreams were unusually specific
and went to ask each other.
Indeed, each had the same dream,
perfectly matching.
They were greatly frightened
and prepared the three sacrificial animals,
going to the temple to apologize and beg for mercy.
They all dreamed again that Lord Jiǎng personally descended to them and said:
"Since you have already shown interest,
I truly desire this meeting.
The appointed date is near.
How can you now change your minds?"
After a short while,
they all died.
Liú Chìfù
dreamed that Lord Jiǎng summoned him to be his registrar.
The date was urgent,
so he went to the temple to plead.
His mother was old, his children young,
the situation was too pressing.
He begged for forgiveness and release.
Wèi Guò of Kuàijī,
talented and skilled,
was good at serving deities.
He requested to recommend Guò as his replacement
and kowtowed until he bled.
The temple priest said:
"We especially wish to trouble you.
Who is Wèi Guò,
And there was this event!"
Chìfǔ insisted on asking,
but in the end, he was not permitted.
Soon after, his father Fǔ died.
When Sūn Ēn rebelled,
Wúxīng was thrown into chaos,
and a man in a hurry rushed into the Jiǎng Temple.
As soon as he entered the gate,
the wooden statue drew a bow and shot him,
and he died immediately.
Passersby and temple guards all witnessed this.
Zhōngshū Láng Wáng Chángyù
had a fine reputation.
His father, Chancellor Dǎo,
cherished him deeply.
When Chángyù fell ill and his condition worsened,
Dǎo was especially worried and concerned.
He was sitting on the northern bed,
having not eaten for several days.
Suddenly, he saw a man
of very imposing stature,
wearing armor and holding a sword.
Wáng asked:
"Who are you?"
The man replied:
"I am Marquis Jiǎng.
Your son is not well,
and I wish to plead for his life,
so I have come.
Do not worry any further."
Wáng was overjoyed and moved,
and immediately asked for food.
He then ate several dǒu of food,
and no one inside or outside understood why.
After eating,
he suddenly became sorrowful again
and said to Wáng:
"The Zhōngshū's life is at its end;
he cannot be saved."
With these words, he vanished.
Gě Zuò
was the Tàishǒu of Héngyáng during the Wú period.
Within the commandery, there was a large raft blocking the water,
capable of causing supernatural harm.
The common people built a temple for it.
Travelers would pray and make offerings,
and then the raft would sink.
If they did not, the raft would float,
and their boats would be destroyed.
When Zuò was about to leave his post,
he prepared many axes and hatchets,
intending to rid the people of this burden.
He was to arrive the next day.
That night,
he heard clamoring human voices from the river.
Going to look,
he saw the raft had moved away,
floating downstream for several lǐ,
and came to rest in a bay.
From then on, travelers no longer suffered the danger of sinking.
The people of Héngyáng erected a stele for Zuò, saying:
"By upright virtue and earnest prayers,
the divine wood was moved."
Yú Dàoshī
Yú Dàoshī was traveling by carriage.
Suddenly, a man in black clothes came directly and boarded the carriage,
saying:
"I only ask to ride for about ten lǐ."
Dàoshī cautiously observed this person:
his head emitted light,
his mouth was entirely red,
and his face was covered with hair.
He found this strange.
At first, he did not dare to send him away.
After traveling about ten lǐ,
the man left as he had said.
Before parting,
he said to Dàoshī:
"I am the Great General of Exorcism.
I am grateful for your accommodation."
He gave Dàoshī a pair of silver bells and vanished.
Gù Shào
When Gù Shào was in Yùzhāng,
he promoted schools,
prohibited excessive sacrifices,
and moral transformation flourished.
He successively destroyed various temples.
When he came to the Lúshān Temple,
the entire commandery advised against it,
but he did not listen.
One night, he suddenly heard the sound of the main gate being pushed open.
Finding it strange,
he suddenly saw a person
who came straight forward through the gate,
appearing like a Fāngxiàng exorcist.
He claimed to be the Lord of Lú.
Shào faced him alone
and invited him to sit on the bed.
The ghost then entered and sat down.
Shào was well-versed in the *Zuǒ Zhuàn*,
so the ghost discussed the *Chūnqiū* with him.
They talked all night, neither able to best the other.
Shào admired his extensive arguments.
He said:
"The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* records the great demon that Duke Jǐng of Jìn dreamed of.
Does such a being exist in both ancient and modern times?"
The ghost laughed and said:
"Great ones exist today,
but demons like that do not."
When the lamp oil was exhausted,
Shào did not order more to be fetched.
Instead, he burned the *Zuǒ Zhuàn* to continue the light.
The ghost repeatedly asked to leave,
but Shào kept detaining him.
The ghost originally intended to overpower Shào,
but Shào's spirit was calm and composed,
leaving no opening to exploit.
The ghost instead became humble and polite,
begging for the temple to be restored,
his words sincere and earnest.
Shào smiled but did not answer.
The ghost left in anger.
Turning back, he said to Shào:
"Tonight I cannot take revenge on you,
but within three years,
you will certainly decline.
I will take my revenge then."
Shào said:
"Why be in such a hurry?
Stay a while longer and continue our discussion."
The ghost then vanished.
Looking at the gates,
they were all closed as before.
As predicted,
Shào indeed fell gravely ill.
He often dreamed this ghost came to attack him
and urged him to restore the temple.
Shào said:
"How can evil overcome good?"
He never consented.
Later, he died.
The Chén Family's Daughter
The Chén family of Wūshāng had a daughter.
She put on clogs and climbed to the top of a large maple tree,
showing no fear at all.
Looking around, she said:
"I am destined to become a spirit.
Now I shall depart forever.
Only when the left is blue and the right is yellow
shall I briefly return."
Her family all came out to see her.
She clasped her hands in farewell,
then floated lightly upward,
disappearing only when gazed at to the utmost distance.
People did not understand the meaning of "blue and yellow."
Each spring, they would use a blue dog,
and each autumn, a yellow dog,
to make offerings beneath the tree.
Wáng Biǎo
In Luóyáng County of Línhǎi, there was a spirit
who called himself Wáng Biǎo.
His speech, eating, and drinking
were no different from a human's,
yet his form was invisible.
He also had a maidservant
named Fǎng Jī.
That month,
they sent Zhōngshū Láng Lǐ Chóng
bearing the seal and ribbon of General Fǔguó, King of Luóyáng, to welcome Biǎo.
Biǎo went out with Chóng.
For the mountains and rivers they passed,
he would always send his maidservant to communicate with the local spirits.
When Biǎo arrived,
Quán established a residence for him outside the Cānglóng Gate.
Biǎo would speak of minor matters like floods and droughts,
and his words were often accurate.
The Stone Man Deity,
located south of Fēngchéng County.
The stone resembles a human form.
Originally, it was in the water beneath Luó Mountain,
and even during floods, it never submerged.
Later, someone was washing clothes by the water,
and hung them on its left arm.
Suddenly, heavy rain fell from the sky,
with thunder and lightning striking fiercely,
breaking the stone man's arm,
and it walked to the mountainside.
People at the time found it extraordinary,
so they jointly established a shrine for it,
and it often manifested spiritual efficacy,
earning the title "Stone Man Deity."
The Holy Maiden
At the border of Wúxīng Commandery,
there is Dòngtíng Mountain,
where the shrine of the Holy Maiden is located in the mountains.
The "Wúzhì" records:
The maiden's surname was Lǐ,
and she possessed magical arts,
capable of walking on water.
Her husband grew angry and killed her.
From her death until now,
nearly seven hundred years have passed,
yet her appearance remains as if alive,
lying peacefully on her side.
Those from near and far who come to pray,
if their hearts are sincere, they can reach the temple;
if their hearts are not sincere,
the wind will turn their boats away,
and none can arrive.
Now, on the first day of each month, she is bathed,
and her fingernails are trimmed.
She is adorned daily,
her body soft and delicate,
just like someone sleeping.
Perhaps she attained the Way.
Chén Mǐn,
during Sūn Hào's reign, served as the governor of Jiāngxià.
While traveling from Jiànyè to report on his duties,
he heard of the spiritual power of the Gōngtíng Temple deity,
so he detoured his boat to visit,
praying for safety and stability in his post,
and promised to offer a silver staff.
When his term ended,
he made the staff,
using bamboo as the core,
and covering it with silver.
Soon after, he was summoned to serve as a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and upon returning to the river mouth,
he sent the staff to the Gōngtíng Temple,
then continued on his journey.
As evening fell,
a spirit medium descended and proclaimed:
"Chén Mǐn promised me a silver staff,
but now he gives me a silver-plated staff.
Throw it into the water,
and I will return it to him.
The crime of deception and contempt
cannot be tolerated."
So the staff was placed on the water, floating,
drifting northward with the current,
swift as if flying,
straight to Chén Mǐn's boat,
hovering and refusing to leave.
Chén Mǐn grew fearful,
retrieved it,
and sent a minor official to the temple to apologize humbly.
As soon as the official departed,
a sudden fierce wind arose,
with towering waves reaching the sky,
and Chén Mǐn's boat capsized.
Only four minor officials survived.
Fèi Chángfáng
Fèi Chángfáng could command ghosts and spirits.
Later, the Lord of the Eastern Sea visited the Lord of Gěbēi,
and violated his wife.
Thereupon, Fèi Chángfáng ordered him imprisoned for three years,
causing a great drought in the Eastern Sea.
Fèi Chángfáng went to the Eastern Sea,
saw the Lord praying for rain,
and ordered the Lord of Gěbēi to release him,
whereupon heavy rain fell immediately.
Hú Mǔ Bān
Hú Mǔ Bān once traveled to the side of Mount Tài,
when suddenly among the trees,
he encountered a crimson-clad attendant,
who called out to Bān, saying:
"The Lord of Mount Tài summons you."
Mǔ Bān was startled and astonished,
hesitating without reply,
when another attendant emerged and called to him.
He then followed them for several dozen steps,
and the attendant requested Mǔ Bān to close his eyes briefly.
After a short while,
he beheld a palace,
with majestic and solemn ceremonies.
Mǔ Bān then entered the chamber to pay his respects.
The host prepared a meal for him,
and said to Mǔ Bān:
"I wish to see you for no other reason
than to entrust a letter to my son-in-law."
Mǔ Bān asked, "Where is your daughter?"
He replied:
"My daughter is the wife of the River Earl."
Mǔ Bān said:
"I will certainly deliver the letter,
but I do not know how to reach him."
The reply was:
"When you reach the middle of the river,
simply knock on the boat and call out 'Qīngyī,'
and someone will come to take the letter."
Mǔ Bān then bid farewell and departed.
The former attendant again instructed him to close his eyes,
and after a moment,
he suddenly found himself back on the original path.
He then journeyed westward,
and as instructed by the deity, called out "Qīngyī."
Shortly after,
a maidservant indeed emerged,
took the letter, and vanished.
After a short while, she reappeared and said:
"The River Earl wishes to see you briefly."
The maidservant also requested him to close his eyes,
and he then paid his respects to the River Earl.
The River Earl set out a lavish feast of wine and food,
speaking with earnest and sincere words.
As they parted,
he said to Mǔ Bān:
"I am grateful that you have traveled so far to deliver the letter,
but I have nothing to offer in return."
Thereupon, he ordered his attendants:
"Fetch my green silk shoes."
And presented them to Mǔ Bān.
Mǔ Bān departed,
closed his eyes, and suddenly found himself back on the boat.
He then spent a year in Cháng'ān before returning.
When he reached the side of Mount Tài,
he did not dare to pass by secretly,
so he knocked on a tree,
announced his name,
and said, "I have returned from Cháng'ān,
and wish to report the news."
Shortly after,
the former attendant emerged,
led Mǔ Bān forward using the same method as before,
and thus delivered the letter.
The Lord of the Mansion said:
"I shall send a separate reply."
After Mǔ Bān finished speaking,
he went to the restroom,
where he suddenly saw his father wearing shackles and performing forced labor,
among a crowd of several hundred people.
Mǔ Bān approached, bowed, and wept,
asking his father how he had come to this.
His father said:
"My death was unfortunate;
I was condemned to three years of labor,
and now two years have already passed!
The hardship is unbearable.
Knowing that you are now acquainted with the Lord of the Mansion,
you can plead on my behalf,
begging to be exempted from this labor,
so that I may become a local earth god."
Mǔ Bān then followed his father's instructions,
kowtowed, and pleaded.
The Lord of the Mansion said:
"The realms of the living and the dead are separate paths,
and they should not come close;
I have no personal attachment."
Mǔ Bān pleaded bitterly,
and only then was his request granted.
Thereupon, he bid farewell and departed.
After returning home for over a year,
his sons nearly all died.
Mǔ Bān was terrified,
and returned to Mount Tài,
knocking on the tree to request an audience.
The former attendant then welcomed him and led him in.
Mǔ Bān explained himself:
"Previously, my words were careless and foolish.
After returning home,
my sons died one after another.
Now I fear the misfortune is not yet over,
so I have come to report,
hoping for your compassion and rescue."
The Lord of the Mansion clapped his hands and laughed heartily, saying:
"This is precisely because I told you before,
'The realms of the living and the dead are separate paths,
and they should not come close.'"
He immediately ordered his attendants to summon Mǔ Bān's father,
who shortly arrived in the courtyard.
The Lord asked him:
"Previously, you requested to return to your village as an earth god,
to bring blessings to your household.
Yet your grandsons have all died.
Why is this?"
He replied:
"Having been away from my hometown for so long,
I was overjoyed to return,
and with ample wine and food,
I truly missed my grandsons,
so I summoned them to feast with me."
Thereupon, he was replaced.
His father wept and departed.
Mǔ Bān then returned home,
and his subsequent children were all safe and sound.
Zhāng Chéngzhī
Zhāng Chéngzhī of Wú County.
One night, he saw a woman
standing at the southeast corner of his house.
She raised her hand and beckoned to Chéng.
Chéng approached her.
The woman said:
"This place is your family's silkworm room.
I am the deity of this land.
On the fifteenth day of the first month next year,
you should prepare white congee,
pour oil over it,
and offer it to me as a sacrifice.
I will ensure your silkworm harvest increases a hundredfold."
After these words, she vanished.
Chéng did as instructed,
preparing the oil congee,
and from then on, his silkworm harvests were exceptionally abundant every year.
This is why people today prepare oil congee on the fifteenth day of the first month.
Wáng Yòu
The Gentleman Cavalier Attendant Wáng Yòu,
gravely ill,
bade farewell to his mother.
Soon after, he heard someone announcing a visitor:
"So-and-so from such-and-such village in such-and-such commandery."
He had once served as an Assistant Inspector,
and Wáng Yòu was also familiar with his name.
A moment later,
he suddenly arrived,
saying:
"You and I are of the same scholarly class,
bound by a natural affinity.
Moreover, we are from the same region,
so our feelings are naturally warm and congenial.
This year, the state has great affairs,
and has dispatched three generals,
who are deploying and conscripting troops.
More than ten of us
serve as aides to Prefect Zhào Gōngmíng.
Arriving here in haste,
I saw you have a grand gate and a large house,
so I came to seek lodging.
Getting along with you
would be most excellent."
Wáng Yòu knew he was a ghost or spirit,
and said:
"Unfortunately, I am gravely ill,
and death is imminent.
I have encountered you, yet you entrust your fate to me?"
He replied:
"In life, there is death;
this is an inevitable matter.
In death, one is not bound by the status of wealth or poverty held in life.
I now command a thousand soldiers,
and need you
to receive and manage the roster.
Such a position is hard to come by,
you should not decline it."
Wáng Yòu said:
"My aged mother is advanced in years,
and I have no brothers.
If I die suddenly,
there will be no one to care for her."
He then wept uncontrollably.
The man said sorrowfully:
"Your position is that of a constant attendant,
yet your family has no surplus wealth.
Earlier, I heard you bidding farewell to your honored mother;
your words were mournful and bitter.
Thus, you are a man of true worth to the state.
How can I let you die?
I shall help you."
He then rose to leave:
"I will come again tomorrow."
The next day, he came again.
Wáng Yòu said:
"You promised to save my life;
will you truly fulfill this kindness?"
He replied:
"This old man has already promised you;
would I deceive you again!"
Wáng Yòu saw his several hundred followers,
all about two *chi* tall,
wearing black clothes and military uniforms,
with red oil as their insignia.
Wáng Yòu's household beat drums and offered prayers.
The various ghosts, hearing the drumbeats,
all danced in rhythm,
shaking their sleeves with a rustling sound.
Wáng Yòu was about to prepare wine and food for them,
but he declined, saying:
"It is unnecessary."
He then rose to leave again,
and said to Wáng Yòu:
"Illness in the human body is like fire;
it should be extinguished with water."
He then took a cup of water,
opened the bedding, and poured it over him.
He also said:
"I have left more than ten red brushes for you
under the mat.
You can give them to people to carry,
to ward off evil and disaster when going out and coming in."
He then said:
"Wáng Jiǎ and Lǐ Yǐ,
I have given them to as well."
He then took Wáng Yòu's hand and bid farewell.
At that time, Wáng Yòu was sleeping peacefully,
but in the middle of the night, he suddenly awoke,
and called to his attendants,
ordering them to open the bedding:
"The spirit poured water on me;
it must be very wet."
They opened the bedding and indeed found water,
on top of the upper cover
and beneath the lower cover,
not soaking through,
like dew on a lotus leaf.
Measuring it, they found three *sheng* and seven *ge*.
Thereupon, his illness was two-thirds cured,
and within a few days, it was completely gone.
All those whom he had said would be taken
died,
only Wáng Wényīng died half a year later.
Those to whom he said he gave the red brushes
all experienced sickness and military turmoil,
yet all remained unharmed.
Earlier, there was a strange text that said:
"The Supreme Deity has sent the three generals Zhào Gōngmíng and Zhōng Shìjì,
each commanding tens of thousands of ghosts down to take people."
No one knew where they were.
After Wáng Yòu recovered from his illness,
he saw this text,
and it matched what was said about Zhào Gōngmíng.
Wēn Qiáo
According to an ancient and modern tradition:
If one uses fire to illuminate the water at night,
one can see all the ghosts and spirits.
When Wēn Qiáo pacified the rebellion of Sū Jùn,
and reached Pénkǒu,
he tried illuminating the water.
Indeed, he saw official temples resplendent and majestic,
with many people and followers;
he also saw a group of small children,
paired in twos,
riding in light carriages,
drawn by yellow goats,
their arrogant and hateful gaze.
Wēn then dreamed that a spirit angrily said:
"I shall make you know."
He then fell ill.
Dài Wénchén
Dài Wénchén of the Pei Kingdom lived on Yángchéng Mountain.
A spirit descended
and became his wife.
Dài suspected she was a demon,
and the spirit, already aware of this,
then departed.
He then saw her transform into a five-colored bird,
followed by several dozen white doves,
with clouds covering her,
and she was not seen again.
Huáng Shígōng
West of Yìzhōu,
east of Yúnnán,
there is a spirit shrine.
A chamber is carved into the mountain rock,
and below, people worship there.
He calls himself Lord Huáng.
It is thus said that this spirit
is the numinous essence of Huáng Shígōng, whom Zhāng Liáng received instruction from.
The practice is pure and abstains from cooking and killing.
Those who come to pray
bring one hundred coins,
a pair of brushes,
and an ink stick,
and make their requests before the stone chamber.
First, they hear a sound from within the stone chamber,
and after a short while,
they are asked what they desire.
After they speak,
they are fully told their fortune, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
without seeing its form.
It remains like this to this day.
Yuán Shuāng
In Dānyáng County, there is a temple to Yuán Shuāng.
He was the fourth son of Yuán Zhēn.
After Yuán Zhēn was executed by Huán Xuānwǔ,
he disappeared without a trace.
His spirit, during the Tàiyuán era,
manifested in Dānyáng,
requesting the establishment of a temple.
Before the construction was completed,
severe tiger disasters occurred.
Families who were harmed
would dream of Yuán Shuāng arriving,
urgently pressing for the work to be hastened.
The common people erected a shrine,
and thereafter the fierce attacks ceased.
Nowadays, both Daoists and laypeople often, on the last day of the second month,
beat drums and dance to pray and make offerings.
On that day,
wind and rain often suddenly arrive.
In the fifth year of Yuánjiā,
after the offerings were set out,
a villager named Qiū Dū
saw a creature behind the temple,
with a human face and the body of an alligator,
wearing a coarse headscarf,
its seven orifices well-formed,
yet carrying the smell of wine.
It is unknown whether this was the spirit of Yuán Shuāng,
or if it was some creature possessing the place.
In Shāngkāng,
at Biànshān in Wúchéng,
originally named Tǔshān,
there is a temple to Xiàng Jī.
He called himself the King of Biàn,
and thus the mountain was renamed.
At the foot of the mountain is a stone cabinet,
several feet high.
Yīn Kāng of Chénjùn,
once went to open it,
but wind, rain, and darkness descended,
so he stopped.
Jiǎ Chōng
When Jiǎ Chōng was campaigning against Wú,
he once stationed his troops at Xiàngchéng,
when suddenly Jiǎ Chōng went missing from the camp.
Zhōu Lè, a commander under Jiǎ Chōng's tent,
was napping during the day,
and dreamed of over a hundred people,
arresting Jiǎ Chōng,
leading him along a path.
Zhōu Lè awoke in alarm,
heard that Jiǎ Chōng was missing,
and went out to search for him.
Suddenly, he saw the path from his dream,
and proceeded along it to seek him.
Sure enough, he saw Jiǎ Chōng arriving at a mansion,
heavily guarded,
where the lord of the mansion sat facing south,
his voice and expression extremely stern,
and said to Jiǎ Chōng:
"You are the one who will bring chaos to my family's affairs,
along with Xún Xù.
You have already deluded my son,
and now you bring disorder to my grandson.
Previously, I sent Rèn Kǎi to dismiss you, yet you did not leave;
then I sent Yǔ Chún to reprimand you, yet you did not reform.
Now, with the Wú rebels about to be pacified,
you are just proposing to execute Zhāng Huá.
Your foolish obstinacy,
is all of this kind.
If you do not repent and act cautiously,
punishment will befall you day and night."
Jiǎ Chōng then kowtowed until his head bled.
The lord said:
"The reason you have prolonged your days and attained such rank and honors,
is due to your merit in defending the palace.
Yet, in the end, I will cause your grandson to die between bells and stands,
your eldest son to perish by poisoned wine,
and your younger son to be trapped beneath a withered tree.
Xún Xù's fate is roughly the same.
However, his ancestral virtue was slightly greater,
so his end will come after yours.
Within a few years,
the state's heir will also be replaced."
Having spoken, he ordered him to leave.
Jiǎ Chōng suddenly returned to camp,
his countenance haggard,
his spirit confused and lost,
and it took a full day for him to recover.
Later, his grandson, Jiǎ Mì, died beneath a bell.
Empress Jiǎ,
died after drinking poisoned wine,
and Jiǎ Wǔ was interrogated to death
using a large staff.
All transpired as foretold.
Wáng Wéndù
When Wáng Wéndù of Jin was stationed in Guǎnglíng,
he suddenly saw two grooms
holding a goose-head tablet summoning him.
Greatly alarmed,
Wáng asked the grooms:
"What office do I hold?"
The groom said:
"Your Honor holds the positions of General Who Guards the North and Inspector of Xú and Yǎn Provinces."
Wáng said:
"I already hold these offices;
why am I being summoned again?"
The ghost said:
"That is in the human realm;
the office you are now to assume is in the celestial bureaucracy."
Wáng was greatly frightened by this.
Soon, he saw welcoming officials in black robes and many minor clerks in goose-colored clothes,
and Wáng shortly fell ill and died.
Xú Cháng
Xú Cháng of Wúxīng long had a spiritual friendship with Bào Jìng,
who wished to impart secret arts to him.
First, Bào requested that Xú make a pledge,
vowing not to take office,
and only then transmitted the register to him.
Thereafter, Xú could often see eight great spirits by his side,
able to know the future and see the past.
His talents and knowledge grew daily more remarkable,
and he became the subject of admiring talk throughout his region and village.
They wished to appoint him as the Prefectural Registrar.
Xú was pleased in his heart.
One morning, seven of the eight spirits disappeared,
and the one remaining was arrogant and not as before.
Xú asked the reason,
and it replied:
"You have violated
your vow,
so we will no longer assist you.
I alone am left to guard the register."
Xú then returned the register,
and they departed.
Chén Xù
At the home of Chén Xù, a commoner of Xīnchéng County,
during the Yǒnghé era of Jin,
one morning they heard knocking at the gate,
and a voice announced itself:
"Commandant Chén."
Then came the sounds of a carriage and horses,
though no form was seen.
It proceeded directly inside,
called to the host and spoke with him, saying:
"I am fated to come here,
and shall temporarily reside in your home,
bringing you good fortune."
He instructed Chén Xù to set up a bed and curtains in the study.
Sometimes people would visit him,
bringing wine and gifts to the study to make requests and seek blessings,
and whatever he said would come true.
Whenever food and wine were presented,
he would have people kneel and bow,
then take it inside the curtains,
not allowing them to open and look.
There was also another being,
suspected to be something like a fox spirit,
who, while kneeling,
suddenly grabbed at it.
The creature retreated behind the bed,
and said angrily:
"How dare you suspect and test the Commandant?"
This person's heart ached as if he would die,
and the host kowtowed to apologize for him,
and only after a long while did the anger subside.
After this, no one dared offend again,
and Chén Xù's entire household remained unharmed,
with every matter becoming more prosperous,
and aside from this, there was little else, good or bad.
Bái Dàoyòu
To the west of Zhāng'ān County lies Chìchéng Mountain,
which spans thirty li in circumference,
with one peak exceptionally high,
reaching over three hundred zhang.
During the Tàiyuán era of the Jin dynasty,
there was a foreign monk,
named Bái Dàoyóu,
who resided on this mountain.
The mountain deity repeatedly sent wolves with strange forms and eerie sounds to frighten him,
but Dàoyóu remained unperturbed.
The mountain deity then personally visited him and said:
"The venerable monk's majestic virtue is profound,
so I now relinquish this mountain to you.
May I, your disciple, seek another place to dwell?"
Dàoyóu asked:
"What deity are you?
How long have you lived here,
and if you must leave now,
where will you go?"
The deity replied:
"I am the son of King Xià,
and have lived here for over a thousand years.
Hánshí Mountain is where my maternal uncle resides,
so I shall go there to rest temporarily.
In the future, I intend to return to the temple on Kuàijī Mountain."
Before departing,
he sent a messenger to present three boxes of incense.
He also came in person to bid farewell,
clasping hands regretfully,
with drums sounding and horns blaring,
he soared into the sky and vanished.
Gāo Yǎzhī
During the Tàiyuán era of the Jin dynasty,
Gāo Héng served as the governor of Wèijùn,
garrisoned at Shítóu.
His grandson, Yǎzhī,
was in the stable when
he said:
"A deity descended,
calling himself the White-Headed Lord,
his staff glowing brightly, illuminating the room.
He lifted Yǎzhī lightly and traveled by night,
reaching Jīngkǒu by dusk,
and returning by morning."
Later, Yǎzhī and his father
were exterminated by Huán Xuán.
Luó Gēnshēng
In Yùzhāng, there was Lúsōng Village.
A man from the commandery, Luó Gēnshēng,
came to cultivate wasteland beside this village,
planting melons and fruits.
In the garden, there was a divine altar.
As the melon vines began to spread,
he suddenly saw a new wooden board on the altar,
with ink writing saying:
"This is sacred land,
leave quickly."
Gēnshēng prayed:
"If this is truly a divine command,
I hope you will rewrite it in vermilion ink as a sign."
The next morning, he went to look,
and the board remained as before,
with all the characters now in vermilion instead of ink.
Gēnshēng apologized and left.
Shěn Zòng
Shěn Zòng, a man from Yúyáo,
came from a poor family.
Once, while returning from the mountains with his father,
before reaching home,
they saw a person
with an entourage of about four to five hundred attendants,
with chariot wheels and horse whips in front,
and ceremonial guards lining the road,
like those of a two-thousand-bushel official.
Seeing Zòng and his father from afar,
he called them to stop,
and lit a fire from Zòng's hand.
Zòng then asked what noble person he was.
The reply was:
"I am the King of Dòu Mountain,
located south of Yúháng."
Realizing he was a deity,
Zòng kowtowed and said:
"I hope you will bless and assist me."
Later, when he entered the mountains,
he found a jade pillow,
and from then on, everything went as he wished.
The Dài Family Daughter
In Yùzhāng, there was a daughter of the Dài family,
who suffered from a long illness that did not heal.
She saw a small stone,
shaped like a figurine.
The girl said to it:
"You have a human form,
are you perhaps a deity?
If you can cure my chronic illness,
I will honor you greatly."
That night, she dreamed someone told her:
"I will protect you."
From then on, her illness gradually healed.
So she built a shrine for it at the foot of the mountain.
The Dài family became shamans,
hence it was named the Dài Hóu Shrine.
Sūn Shèng
On Héng Mountain, there was the Báichá Shrine.
According to ancient legend:
In the past, there was a divine raft,
pure white in color,
and prayers to it were always answered.
When Sūn Shèng of the Jin dynasty governed the commandery,
he did not believe in ghosts or deities,
so he cut it down.
As the axe struck, it bled.
That night, the divine raft floated upstream with the waves,
and only the sounds of drums and horns were heard,
with no one knowing where it stopped.
It was abolished in the ninth year of the Kāihuáng era,
but the Báichá Village still exists today.
Zhàn Mǎn
On Jiāngláng Mountain in Xūjiāng County,
there once lived a Jiāng family at the foot of the mountain,
with three brothers,
who transformed into deities there.
Hence, there are three peculiar stone peaks.
There was a man named Zhàn Mǎn,
who also lived at the foot of the mountain.
His son served in Luòyáng,
but during the Yǒngjiā Rebellion,
he could not return.
Mǎn then had a prayer master speak to the spirits of the three stones,
promising that if they could bring his son back,
he would not spare any sacrificial offerings.
Within ten days,
Zhàn's son appeared by the Luòshuǐ River,
where he saw three youths,
who told him to close his eyes and crouch between the chariot railings,
and they departed like a swift wind.
In a moment,
he fell from the sky,
dazed and unaware of where he was.
After a long while,
he realized he was in his family's garden.
Zhú Tánsuì
In Tán County's western township,
there was a temple to Lord Yáng.
A man from the county had previously served it.
Later, he became a follower of the libationer Hóu Chǔ,
seeking to enter the Great Way.
He encountered Qiáo Commandery's Lóu Wúlǒng, who visited Chǔ,
and together they went to the temple's building.
They burned the vessels and robes from the god's seat.
Wúlǒng begged to take a fan.
After a year passed,
Wúlǒng heard a man on horseback calling "Lóu Wúlǒng" several times,
saying:
"Do you still not return Lord Yáng's fan?"
When he finished speaking,
he turned his horse and left as if departing.
Wúlǒng then contracted scrofula and died.
Lú Xún
In the fourth year of the Yìxī era,
Lú Xún was in Guǎngzhōu,
secretly planning rebellion.
He covertly sent a man to the temple in Nánkāng to pray and make requests.
After presenting the sacrificial animals and drums were played,
the envoy alone saw a man,
wearing a military cap and vermilion robes,
sitting in the middle of the mat, who said:
"If Field Pacifier Lú initiates his affair,
when he reaches here,
I will send him off with water."
In the spring of the sixth year,
Xún then led his forces straight to Chángshā.
He sent Xú Dàofù to cross the mountain range.
Arriving at Nánkāng,
they outfitted twelve warships,
with fighting towers over ten zhang high.
Just as the ships were fully equipped,
heavy rain fell for a day and a night,
raising the water by four zhang.
Dàofù rode the waves downstream,
and met Xún at Bālíng.
Upon reaching the capital, Xún was defeated in battle.
Unaware that the god would hasten his punishment,
the great flood's descent
was to make him deliver himself.
Chén Chén
Línchuān's Chén Chén's household was very wealthy.
In the first year of the Yǒngchū era,
while Chén was sitting in his study,
within his residence there was a patch of sinew bamboo.
In broad daylight, he suddenly saw a man over a zhang tall,
with a face like a Fāngxiàng exorcist,
emerge from the bamboo,
go straight to Chén Chén and say:
"I have been in this home for many years,
you did not know.
Now that I am leaving,
I will make sure you know."
About a month after he left,
a great fire broke out in the household,
the servants and slaves perished instantly,
and within a year they became greatly impoverished.
Zhāng Shū
Zhāng Shū of Chángshān,
on the 24th day of the second month in the ninth year of the Yuánjiā era, suddenly saw a man,
wearing vermilion robes and a flat-topped headcloth.
He held a green-handled horsewhip.
He said:
"You can be taught,
come with me now."
He saw a plain silk rope tied to a long ladder coming down.
Shū climbed the ladder,
and then reached a great city.
With elegant halls and deep chambers,
the ground was like gold.
There was a man, tall and large,
wearing no headcloth,
sitting alone within crimson gauze curtains,
who said to Shū:
"The master mistakenly fetched you,
so I bestow upon you secret arts of divination and prognostication.
Do not covet money and bribes."
Shū, without realizing it, accepted them.
Xiāo Huìmíng
In the Sòng, Xiāo Huìmíng was the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
Within the commandery's borders was Biàn Mountain.
At the mountain's foot was a temple to Xiàng Yǔ.
Tradition held that:
"Yǔ often resided in the commandery's main hall,
and successive Grand Administrators dared not enter it."
Huìmíng said to his chief clerk:
"Kǒng Jìgōng once governed this commandery,
and I have not heard of any disaster."
He then ordered a grand feast and couches to be set up.
Not long after,
Huìmíng suddenly saw a man,
over a zhang tall,
drawing a bow and aiming an arrow at him.
He then disappeared.
Consequently, a carbuncle erupted on Huìmíng's back,
and within ten days he died.
Liǔ Jī,
courtesy name Défēng.
He studied diligently and laboriously,
burning tree leaves at night to serve as a lamp.
At midnight,
he heard a call outside his window.
Jī went out and saw
five or six people.
Each carried a sack,
which they emptied beneath his house—
contents like elm seeds.
They said:
"We give you these as provisions for your studies.
Do not worry that your endeavor will not succeed."
The next day he looked,
and they were all ancient Hàn coins,
totaling one hundred and twenty thousand.
He thereby completed his studies.
During Emperor Míng of Sòng's reign,
he attained the office of Gentleman of the Heir Apparent's Household.
Zhào Wénzhāo
In the eighth month of the third year of the Yuánjiā era of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
Zhào Wénzhāo of Wú Commandery,
courtesy name Zǐyè,
served as Lecturer in Attendance to the Heir Apparent.
His residence was north of Qīngxī Bridge,
separated by a wall running north-south from the Minister of Personnel, Wáng Shūqīng.
Once on an autumn night,
facing the moon over the stream,
he sang the lyrics of "The Crow Rests,"
their tone leisurely and plaintive.
Suddenly, a woman appeared,
wearing robes of blue gauze,
exceedingly beautiful.
She said:
"The young lady of Minister Wáng
wishes to visit you."
Wénzhāo asked her reason,
and she replied:
"The young lady heard your singing,
which held the heart of one wronged and neglected,
bearing the sorrow of one desolate and cool.
Therefore, she has come wishing to offer her pillow and mat."
When she finished speaking, she arrived,
her beauty peerless in the world.
Wénzhāo, confused and dazed,
completely forgot all other intentions.
He bowed and welcomed her in.
At ease in a secluded chamber,
he ordered wine and set a feast.
They took turns singing to each other,
and then retired to bed.
At dawn she asked to leave.
The woman untied a golden tassel as a parting gift.
Wénzhāo gave her a glass cup in return.
Several nights later,
Wénzhāo could not cease thinking of her.
By chance, he visited the temple of the Qīngxī River Goddess.
Suddenly, he saw the glass cup he had given
behind the statue of the goddess.
And when he looked at the goddess herself,
and the painted attendant maidens,
they were the very ones with whom he had spent the night.
The River Earl
South of Yúháng County, there is an Upper Lake.
In the middle of the lake, an embankment was built.
There was a man who rode a horse to watch a performance,
then went with three or four others to Cén Village to drink.
Slightly intoxicated,
he returned in the evening.
As the weather was hot,
he dismounted and entered the water,
resting his head on a stone to sleep.
The horse broke free and ran home,
and his attendants all chased after the horse,
not returning by dusk.
When he awoke from sleep,
the sun was already approaching late afternoon,
and neither his attendants nor the horse were to be seen.
He saw a woman approaching,
about sixteen or seventeen years old,
who said:
"This young lady bows twice.
Since the day is already turning to dusk,
this place is quite frightening.
What plan do you have?"
He asked:
"What is the young lady's surname?
How is it that you suddenly address me?"
Then there was a youth,
about thirteen or fourteen years old,
very bright and alert,
riding in a new carriage,
with twenty people following behind the carriage. They arrived
and called for him to get in the carriage.
They said:
"Our master wishes to see you briefly."
So they turned the carriage around and departed.
Along the way, torches were held in an unbroken line.
They saw city walls and dwellings.
After entering the city,
they proceeded to the main hall,
where there was a banner of authority,
inscribed with the words "Hé Bó."
Soon they saw a man,
about thirty years old,
with features as beautiful as a painting,
and numerous guards and attendants.
Facing each other joyfully,
he ordered wine and roasted meat to be served,
and said:
"I have a young daughter,
quite intelligent,
whom I wish to give to you as your wife."
This man knew he was a deity,
and dared not refuse or oppose.
So he ordered preparations to be made,
instructing that the wedding be held in the official's residence.
It was reported that everything was ready.
They entered.
A silk cloth single-layer robe.
And lined jackets, silk skirts, gauze shirts and trousers, shoes and clogs,
all exquisitely fine.
He was also given ten minor officials
and several dozen attendants in black clothing.
The woman was about eighteen or nineteen years old,
graceful and charming in appearance.
Thus the wedding ceremony was completed.
On the third day,
a grand banquet was held for guests,
and they paid respects at the inner chamber.
On the fourth day, it was said:
"Since the wedding rites have their limits,
you should be sent off to depart."
The woman gave her husband a golden cup and a musk-scented pouch as farewell gifts,
