weeping as they parted.
She also gave him a hundred thousand coins and three volumes of medicinal prescriptions,
saying:
"These can be used to perform good deeds and spread virtue."
She also said:
"In ten years, I will come for you."
This man returned home,
and thereafter refused to marry anyone else.
He bid farewell to his family,
left home to become a Daoist monk.
The three volumes of prescriptions he obtained were:
one volume on pulse classics,
one volume on decoction formulas,
and one volume on pill formulas.
Traveling everywhere to provide relief and treatment,
all achieved miraculous efficacy.
Later, when his mother grew old and his elder brother died,
he returned to marry and take up an official post.
Shào Jìngbó
Ten lǐ west of Píngyuán County,
there was formerly a sacred grove.
During the reign of the Southern Yān's Tàishàng period,
there was a man named Shào Jìngbó,
who lived at Chángbái Shān.
Someone entrusted Shào Jìngbó with a letter,
saying:
"I am an envoy from Wú Jiāng,
ordered to deliver a message to Qí Bó.
I must now pass through Chángbái,
and I hope you can deliver it for me.
He then instructed Shào Jìngbó,
saying that upon reaching the sacred grove,
he should take a leaf from a tree and toss it into the water,
and someone would come out."
Shào Jìngbó followed the instructions,
and indeed saw someone who led him inside.
Jìngbó feared water,
so that person told him to close his eyes.
It felt as if he entered the water,
and suddenly there were grand and magnificent palaces.
He saw an old man,
about eighty or ninety years old,
sitting on a crystal bed.
He opened the letter and read it, saying:
"Yù Xìng Chāo is destroyed."
The guards all had round eyes,
and were fully armored.
Shào Jìngbó bid farewell and left,
and the old man gave him a dagger as a gift, saying:
"Go safely.
Just hold this dagger,
and you will have no trouble with water."
Shào Jìngbó exited,
returned to the sacred grove,
and his clothes were completely dry, not wet at all.
Indeed, that year, Emperor Wǔ of Sòng destroyed Yān.
Shào Jìngbó lived between two rivers for three years.
One night, a great flood suddenly occurred,
submerging the entire village.
Only Shào Jìngbó remained seated on a couch,
which by dawn had reached the shore.
Shào Jìngbó looked down at it,
and the couch turned out to be a large softshell turtle.
When Shào Jìngbó died,
the dagger was also lost.
It is said among the people that beneath the sacred grove lies the home of Hé Bó.
A Man from Wúxīng
During the Lóng'ān era of the Jìn Dynasty,
there was a man from Wúxīng,
about twenty years old,
who called himself Shènggōng,
with the surname Xiè.
He had been dead for a hundred years,
when he suddenly visited the Chén family residence,
saying:
"This is my former home,
you should return it to me,
or else I will burn you down."
One night, a great fire broke out,
burning.
Everything to ashes.
Because there were bird feathers stuck in the ground,
surrounding the residence in multiple layers,
the common people then built a temple.
Liú Zǐqīng
During the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
Huáng Miáo, a man from Pínggù in Nánkāng,
served as a clerk for the prefecture.
He overstayed his leave.
As he was traveling back to his post,
he passed by Gōngtíng Lake,
entered the temple and made a vow:
"I hope to avoid punishment for my offense,
and also wish to return home.
If both wishes are fulfilled,
I will offer pork and wine."
When Huáng Miáo reached the prefecture,
everything went as he wished,
so he returned home.
His funds and baggage were meager,
so he did not stop at the temple.
When he reached the capital's border,
he moored his boat with his companions to spend the night.
In the middle of the night,
the boat suddenly moved downstream by itself,
as swift as the wind.
At the fourth watch of the night,
Huáng Miáo arrived at Gōngtíng,
and only then did he realize.
He saw three men on the boat,
all dressed in black and holding ropes,
who seized and bound Huáng Miáo.
At night, they ascended the temple steps,
where he saw a deity, about forty years old,
with a yellow face,
wearing a brocade robe.
A pearl was suspended from a beam,
as large as a pellet,
its radiance illuminating the room.
A man outside the door reported:
"Huáng Miáo of Pínggù,
vowed to offer pork and wine,
but fled home.
By your order, he has been apprehended,
and is now here."
The deity sentenced him to three years of punishment,
requiring him to capture thirty people.
He sent an officer to escort Huáng Miáo deep into the mountains and forests,
where he was chained by the waist to a tree,
and fed raw meat daily.
Huáng Miáo grew dazed and anxious,
feeling only alternating chills and fever, with sores on his body,
and spots of fur growing all over.
After ten days,
fur covered his body,
claws and fangs grew,
and his nature became predatory and ravenous.
The officer unchained and released him,
following wherever he went.
In three years,
he had captured twenty-nine people in total.
Next, he was to capture a woman from Xīngàn,
but this woman was from a prominent family,
who initially never went out.
Later, she happened to go out the back gate with her sisters,
to visit relatives.
The woman was last in line,
so he captured her.
Because this woman was hard to capture,
it took five years,
before the required number was fulfilled.
The officer escorted him to the temple,
where the deity ordered his release and dismissal.
They then fed him salted rice and drink,
his body fur gradually fell off,
his beard and hair all grew back,
his claws and fangs dropped,
and new ones grew.
After fifteen days,
he returned to human form.
His mind and thoughts became normal again.
They sent him out to the main road.
The county magistrate summoned Huáng Miáo to provide a detailed account of the events,
verifying all the people he had captured before and after,
and questioned their families one by one,
all of which matched.
His thigh had been wounded by a halberd,
and the scar was still there.
Huáng Miáo returned home and lived for eight years,
then died of a seasonal illness.
Gōng Shuāng
In a village west of the Hàn River in Xiāngyáng,
there was a temple named the Lord of the Land,
whose deity was extremely efficacious.
At the end of the Yǒngyuán era of the Qí dynasty,
Gōng Shuāng served as the governor of Féngyì Commandery.
He did not believe in ghosts or deities,
and when passing by this temple,
he led men to burn it down.
Suddenly, a whirlwind twisted the flames,
and two creatures emerged,
transforming into a pair of blue birds,
which flew into Gōng Shuāng's eyes.
His eyes immediately began to ache,
and his whole body burned with fever.
By dawn, he was dead.
There was a severe drought in Liáng,
so an imperial edict was issued to pray for rain from the deity of the Jiǎngdì Temple.
After a hundred days with no rain,
the emperor grew angry,
loaded reeds onto a cart to burn down the temple,
along with the deity's image.
On that day, the sky was clear,
and they were about to set the fire.
Just above the deity,
suddenly clouds appeared like an umbrella canopy,
and in a moment, a torrential rain fell.
The palaces and halls in the imperial compound
all shook violently.
The emperor was terrified,
and hastily sent an edict to stop the burning.
Shortly after, everything calmed down.
From then on, the emperor's faith and sincerity deepened greatly.
Since ascending the throne, he had never visited the temple,
but now he prepared the imperial carriage,
and led his court officials to pay homage.
At that time, the Wèi general Yáng Dàyǎn
invaded Zhōnglí.
The deity of the Jiǎngdì Temple responded to the prayer,
promising to provide assistance.
Soon after, though there was no rain,
the water suddenly rose six or seven feet,
and they greatly defeated the Wèi army.
This was the power of the deity.
After the triumphant return,
the people and horses in the temple all had mud-stained feet,
which was witnessed by everyone at the time.
Línrǔ Hóu Yóu
Línrǔ Hóu Yóu, a member of the imperial clan,
served as the governor of Wúxīng.
He was unrestrained and unconventional by nature,
and befriended the deity of the Chǔ Temple,
drinking up to a hú of wine together.
Whenever he offered sacrifices in return,
he would enjoy himself to the fullest and get extremely drunk,
and the deity's image would also appear flushed with wine.
Every prayer he made was answered.
Later, he became the governor of Yìzhōu.
At that time, a man named Qí Gǒu'ér from Jiānglíng rebelled,
with a force of over a hundred thousand,
attacking the prefectural city.
Yóu's troops and provisions were exhausted,
and people were becoming disloyal,
so he prayed from afar, seeking rescue.
On that day,
an old farmer within the prefecture boundaries
encountered a rider in iron armor,
coming from the east,
who asked how many miles it was to the city.
The farmer replied:
"One hundred and forty miles."
The sun was already setting,
and the rider said to the farmer:
"If someone comes later,
tell them to speed up their horses,
as I wish to defeat the rebels before sunset."
Soon after, several hundred riders swept by like the wind,
and one of them still asked for a drink.
The farmer asked who they were,
and the reply was:
"The King of Chǔ from Wúxīng,
coming to rescue Línrǔ Hóu."
At that time,
prayers in the temple had not been answered.
Over ten days later,
it was seen that the clay attendants and statues in the temple were all muddy and damp, as if sweating.
On that day,
Yóu greatly defeated Gǒu'ér.
When Yóu passed away,
he was posthumously honored as "Líng" (Spiritual),
because of his friendship with the deity.
Yīn Zǐchūn
Liáng's Yīn Zǐchūn served as the governor of Dōngguǎn.
At that time, Wáng Shénniàn, the governor of Qīngzhōu,
destroyed the shrine of the Línhǎi deity.
There was a snake on the roof beam,
and the laborers did not capture it;
it escaped into the sea.
That night,
Zǐchūn dreamed of a person coming to his residence,
saying:
"Someone has suffered hardship,
their dwelling has been destroyed,
and now they have nowhere to rely on,
so they wish to rest in this region."
Zǐchūn secretly remembered this in his heart.
After some time,
he learned that Shénniàn had destroyed the temple.
He then prepared sacrificial animals and wine,
and built a shrine to worship the deity.
A few days later,
he dreamed of a person in red robes thanking him:
"For your great kindness,
I shall repay you with a governorship."
A little over a month later,
the Wèi ruler planned to attack Qúshān,
but Zǐchūn foresaw it,
set up an ambush, and crushed the attack.
Emperor Wǔ appointed him as the governor of Nánqīngzhōu.
Sūlǐng Temple
At the Sūlǐng Mountain Temple in Xiāngyáng,
the entrance is flanked by two stone deer,
so it is called Lùmén Mountain.
The Xí family records state:
"Xí Yù often served as a palace attendant,
and accompanied Emperor Guāngwǔ on a visit to Líqiū.
Yù and Emperor Guāngwǔ
both dreamed of the mountain deity of Sūlǐng,
so they had a temple built."
Guō Chóngchǎn's records state:
"The two stone deer stood on their own as if fighting,
and woodcutters often passed beneath them.
Sometimes the deer could not be seen.
From this, it was known there was a spiritual omen.
During the early Tiānjiàn era of Liáng,
a man from Bànghú Village
was hunting in these marshes.
He saw two extremely large deer,
unlike ordinary deer,
so he rode his horse to chase them.
The deer leaped across a stream,
heading straight toward Sūlǐng.
The man chased the deer to the deity's place,
where they suddenly vanished.
He only saw the two stone deer in front of the temple.
The hunter suspected these were the deer he had chased, now transformed,
so he turned back.
That night, he dreamed of a person,
wearing a simple headscarf,
and yellow cloth trousers,
who said:
'The governor sent me to herd horses;
why did you chase and harass me?
Fortunately, nothing happened,
but if there had been any harm,
how could I have remained unharmed?'"
Lú Yuánmíng
Běiqí's Lú Yuánmíng
was sent on a diplomatic mission to Liáng.
His wife rode in a carriage,
seeing him off to the riverbank.
Suddenly, they noticed an extraordinary fragrance from the water,
and looking back, they saw a water deity emerging from the waves.
The oxen were startled and bolted,
dragging the carriage into the river.
His wife drowned,
but his young nephew, Shízhù,
who was in the same carriage,
was thrown out and survived.
Dǒng Shèn
In the first year of the Dayè era of the Suí dynasty,
Dǒng Shèn, an assistant clerk in Yǎnzhōu,
was by nature fair and upright,
well-versed in legal principles.
From the governor down,
if anyone applied the law unjustly,
he would invariably risk offense by remonstrating.
Even if reprimanded,
he showed no fear,
insisting on withdrawing only after the punishment was rectified.
Once, while returning home to receive seasonal clothing,
he exited the prefectural gate
and encountered a messenger in yellow robes, who said:
"The Lord of Tàishān summons you to serve as recorder."
He then took out a document from his bosom to show Shèn.
The document read:
"Dǒng Shèn is renowned for his solid integrity
and excels in handling official documents.
To adjudicate doubtful legal cases,
we must await a capable person.
He is temporarily appointed as acting recorder of the Right Bureau."
The seal was very clear.
It was later signed:
"Jù."
Shèn said to the messenger:
"Since the prefect summons me,
how could I not go?
But I do not know the prefect's name—what is it?"
The messenger replied:
"Recorder, do not ask.
You will know upon taking up your post."
He then took a large cloth bag,
placed Shèn inside it,
carried him out of Yǎnzhōu's outer walls,
and set the bag down by the roadside.
Fetching water and mixing mud,
he sealed Shèn's eyes.
Shèn had no idea how far they traveled
when suddenly he heard a loud announcement:
"Fàn Shèn has brought Dǒng Shèn."
The messenger said:
"Acknowledged."
and hurried inside.
The prefect asked:
"Where is the recorder we summoned?"
The messenger replied:
"The underworld is secret and hidden;
I feared possible leaks,
so I requested a shadow-concealing bag from the Left Bureau to carry him."
The prefect laughed heartily and said:
"Fàn Shèn, who is already dead, fetching Dǒng Shèn,
using a Left Bureau bag to carry a Right Bureau recorder—
this can indeed be called careful precaution."
He then ordered Shèn to be taken out,
removed the mud from his eyes,
and bestowed upon him a blue silk robe, a fish-whiskered tablet, and leopard-skin boots,
all exquisitely patterned.
Inviting him to ascend the side steps,
he ordered attendants to bring a couch for him to sit,
and said:
"Because of your fairness and integrity,
I have made this request.
Now, there are six individuals, including Sīmǎ Línghú Shí of Mǐnzhōu,
who have been placed in the Avīci Hell.
According to a heavenly decree,
since Shí is a third-degree relative of Lady Tàiyuán,
he is to receive a three-degree reduction in punishment.
Yesterday, the criminal Chéng Zhù and 120 others
cited this precedent and clamored in protest,
unable to be stopped.
Their names have already been reported to the heavenly authorities.
The heavenly authorities, considering that doubtful punishments should be lightened,
also ordered a two-degree reduction.
I fear
that many will cite this precedent in the future.
What do you think should be done?"
Shèn replied:
"Water reflects beauty and ugliness without incurring resentment
because it is utterly clear and impartial.
How much more should heaven and earth's laws
avoid showing favor to the wicked?
However, I am merely a minor clerk,
untrained in literary composition.
Although I know it is wrong,
my words lack coherence.
In our prefecture, there is a xiùcai named Zhāng Shěntōng,
whose literary talent is outstanding,
fully capable of serving as your secretary."
The prefect ordered a summons to be issued.
Shortly after, Shěntōng arrived.
Shěntōng said:
"This is easy.
I will draft a judgment for submission."
The prefect said:
"Please compose a good argument for me."
He then appointed him as recorder of the Left Bureau,
bestowing robes similar to Dǒng Shèn's,
and gave each a black fox
to ride whenever they went out.
Shěntōng's judgment read:
"Heaven is inherently impartial;
laws should be uniform.
If favor is shown based on personal connections,
it encourages wicked conduct.
Línghú Shí's earlier sentence reduction
already amounted to a private plea;
Chéng Zhù's subsequent petition
differs from cases of doubtful guilt.
If a precedent for reduction is established,
it truly undermines public justice.
I request that they be returned to the Avīci Hell as before,
and the judgment be reported to the heavenly authorities."
Immediately, a person in yellow robes took the document and left.
After a short while,
he returned with a heavenly decree, which stated:
"The submitted document
raises many unorthodox arguments.
In serving one's lord,
one should simply comply.
The Zhōulǐ's Eight Considerations,
the first is 'consideration for relatives.'
Moreover, the Shìchōng Fú in the Yuánhuà Guì
also states 'there are none who are not relatives.'
Thus, the statutes are clear—
what is unacceptable about this?
How can Lady Tàiyuán's merits and virtues
fail to protect a third-degree relative?
Daring to persist in defiance
must be punished.
The prefect shall be penalized by not wearing purple for sixty jiǎzǐ cycles.
The rest shall be handled as before."
The prefect angrily said to Shěntōng:
"Your judgment
has caused me to be reprimanded."
He then ordered attendants
to cut a piece of flesh one cùn square
and plug one of his ears,
rendering him deaf on that side.
Shěntōng pleaded:
"I beg to draft another judgment for submission.
If it is not accepted,
I will willingly accept further punishment."
The prefect said:
"If you can remove my penalty,
I will give you an extra ear."
Shěntōng drafted another judgment:
"Heaven is vast, earth is vast—
they are fundamentally without relatives.
If they had relatives,
how could they achieve unity?
If laws are altered based on personal feelings,
it will indeed foster falsity and lose truth.
Before the great antiquity,
people were still utterly simple;
after the middle antiquity,
each began favoring their own relatives.
How can we let the nurturing heart of great antiquity
evoke Confucius's sigh while observing the Zhà sacrifice?
'There are none who are not relatives'—
this is not public justice;
why must it be cited?
I beg to pardon the offense of harsh words
and dare to offer medicine to cleanse the heart.
May this be examined for truth,
so that fairness may prevail.
For Línghú Shí and others,
I request
that they be dealt with according to proper law,
and the judgment be reported to the heavenly authorities."
The yellow-robed person took it away again.
After a short while,
another heavenly decree arrived, stating:
"Upon reviewing the resubmission,
it is very appropriate.
The prefect may be promoted to Deputy Chief Enforcer of the Six Heavens.
Línghú Shí, Chéng Zhù, and others
shall all be dealt with according to proper law."
The prefect then said to Shěntōng:
"Without you, this case could not have been rectified."
He ordered attendants to cut the flesh from his ear,
had a child shape it into an ear,
and attached it to Shěntōng's forehead.
He said:
"I plugged one of your ears;
now I give you three ears—
how about that?"
He also said to Shèn:
"I greatly relied on your recommendation of a worthy man
to accomplish this good deed.
However, I cannot keep you long.
I will add
one year to your lifespan as repayment.
Combined with your original lifespan,
It has been twenty-one years."
He was then sent back home.
The messenger again sealed the two men with mud,
and each was sent to his residence in a cloth sack.
Suddenly, as if poured out,
he turned to look at his wife and children.
His wife and children said:
"Your soul had departed,
for over ten days already."
From then on, Shèn indeed died twenty-one years later.
Shěntōng felt an itch on his forehead a few days later,
and another ear sprouted out,
making three ears in total,
with the newly sprouted one being especially sharp.
People of the time laughed and said:
"In heaven, there is the nine-headed bird;
on earth, there is the three-eared scholar."
He was also called the Cockscomb Scholar.
Shèn initially thought the Prefect called him "neighbor,"
but later realized that "jù" was actually the character for "neighbor."
Lǐ Jìng
Duke Wèi, Lǐ Jìng,
was initially trapped in poverty and low status.
While passing by the Huàshān Temple,
he complained to the deity,
and also requested to be informed of the official positions he would attain.
His words and expression were defiant and stern,
startling the onlookers.
He stood there for a long time,
then walked about a hundred steps out of the temple gate,
when he heard a loud voice from behind saying:
"Minister Lǐ, farewell."
He turned to look but saw no one.
Later, he indeed rose to the position of chief minister.
Dānqiūzǐ
At the end of the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era.
An old man visited Emperor Shényáo, the future Táng Gāozǔ,
his appearance was very unusual.
Shényáo respected and waited upon him,
leisurely serving wine.
After drinking to his fill,
he spoke of current affairs, saying:
"The Suí dynasty is about to perish,
and the Lǐ family is about to rise.
This is the mandate of heaven.
Does it rest with you?
I hope you will take care of yourself."
Shényáo was alarmed and felt lost,
and refused him.
The old man said:
"Since it is bestowed by the spirits,
how could you refuse?
The Suí dynasty, unheard of in previous eras,
succeeded the Zhōu and rose to power,
its achievements surpassing Jìn and Wèi.
Although it temporarily occupied the throne,
and pacified the southern lands,
it was merely clearing the way for you.
Heaven is about to reveal something."
Shényáo secretly rejoiced at his words,
and thus inquired about worldly affairs.
The old man said:
"You have accumulated virtue and entered the gate,
and also possess the appearance of utmost nobility.
If you respond to heaven and receive the mandate,
you will achieve stability without effort.
But it must be after Dānqiūzǐ."
The Emperor asked:
"Who is Dānqiū?"
The old man said:
"He is close to you in registry,
but you do not know him.
The divine vessel belongs to
only these two individuals.
However, Master Dānqiū
is detached from worldly affairs,
and I fear he will not burden his heart with worldly entanglements.
If he were to condescend,
and if you do not contend with him in the Central Plains,
you should serve as his assistant."
Shényáo said:
"Where is the Master now?"
He said:
"He lives in seclusion in the area of Hù Dù."
The Emperor then concealed a sword in his sleeve and went to visit him.
Although the Emperor's arrival
was intended to harm Dānqiū,
his virtue and Dao were profound and far-reaching,
his appearance like an ice jar,
and seeing his demeanor would surely awe and inspire reverence.
Upon arrival, he prostrated himself beneath the thatched hut.
The Master leaned on an armrest, resting his chin,
aloof and self-contained.
Before the Emperor could rise from his bow,
the Master abruptly said:
"I have long been weary of this turbid world.
You are entangled in the times.
Our paths of prominence and obscurity are already different.
I hope you will not hold it against me."
The Emperor was startled and apologized,
then knelt and rose, saying:
"The Suí dynasty is about to perish,
as the spirits have already foretold.
The one destined for the heavenly mandate
lies within my clan.
I
have long been aligned with hidden signs,
and believe the end of fate is approaching.
I secretly know that your Dao
will also align with the signs of heaven and humanity.
When two forces are evenly matched,
they must decide superiority through the edge of blades,
and flaunt intelligence through power and deceit.
If virtue is not cultivated and competed for,
I fear the Central Plains will long suffer the calamities of Liú and Xiàng.
My coming here
is indeed with intention,
to save the people from suffering.
Little did I know that you, Master, have abandoned the humility of Yáo and Shùn,
and followed the distant traces of Cháo and Xǔ.
I am what is called a vinegar fly or a summer insect,
insufficient to glimpse the great Dao."
The Master smiled and nodded.
The Emperor continued:
"With the vastness of the world,
how can one mind or one thought encompass it all?
I observe that the order or chaos of previous dynasties
lies in obtaining the right assistants.
If not for individuals like Yī, Zhōu, Gāo, and Kuí,
since the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
all have been trivial mediocrities not worth counting.
Emperor Hàn obtained Xiāo and Zhāng but did not fully utilize them,
which is lamentable.
Now, Master, you still refuse the positions of Yáo and Shùn,
so naturally you disdain Yī and Gāo.
A single word from you could bring about prosperous fortune.
Would you not have something to instruct me?"
The Master said:
"In the past, Táo Zhū, with the remaining five thousand troops of Kuàijī,
ultimately destroyed the powerful Wú.
Later, he left Yuè to serve as minister of Qí,
but in Qí, he was not noteworthy.
Was he wise in Yuè but foolish in Qí?
Achievements and deeds follow the times;
they cannot be recklessly attained.
Rise and fall already have their own numbers;
the goodness or badness of the times,
how can they be achieved by human effort?
And is this not my understanding?"
He then fell silent.
The Emperor knew he could not be swayed,
and returned disappointed.
In the early Wǔdé era,
he secretly sent Tàizōng to visit him in Hù Dù,
but his dwelling was already in ruins.
The God of the Vast Sea
Seventy li north of Bìngzhōu, there is an ancient tomb.
In the early years of the Zhēnguàn era,
every evening,
ghost soldiers numbering over ten thousand would appear,
their banners fresh and clean,
surrounding this tomb.
Shortly after,
several thousand ghost soldiers would also emerge from the tomb,
a mix of infantry and cavalry,
fiercely battling beside the tomb.
By night, they would each retreat,
and this continued for nearly a month.
Suddenly, one evening,
over ten thousand ghost soldiers appeared again,
arriving from the north,
and arrayed themselves several li away from the tomb.
A farmer saw this and fled in terror.
A ghost general
ordered over ten soldiers to capture him and bring him forward,
saying to him:
"Do not fear,
I am the God of the Hànhǎi.
A minor general stole my beloved concubine,
and fled into this tomb.
Lord Zhāng of this tomb
then lent him soldiers,
and fought fiercely against me.
I have been away from the Hànhǎi for over a month,
and have not yet captured this thief,
which deeply angers me.
You must go to this tomb and inform Lord Zhāng for me,
saying that I have come personally to retrieve the rebellious general.
Why does he hide him in the tomb?
Moreover, he even lends him troops to resist me.
He must quickly drive him out.
Otherwise,
I will surely kill you!"
He then ordered a hundred soldiers
to escort this farmer there.
When the farmer reached the front of the tomb,
he loudly relayed the message.
After a long while,
soldiers emerged from the tomb and formed a battle array.
There were two divine beings,
standing side by side on horseback under a large banner,
with swords and halberds like a forest on their left and right.
They quickly summoned the farmer forward,
and also ordered him to relay a message, saying:
"In life, I was a fierce general for thirty years,
and after death, I was buried here.
Those who follow me number over five thousand infantry and cavalry,
all of them elite and strong.
Now,
your minor general has come to me for refuge,
and I have already formed a bond with him and made an oath,
so I cannot refuse to assist him.
If you insist on fighting me with force,
I will ultimately defeat you,
and not allow you to return to the Hànhǎi.
If you wish to preserve your position,
you should retreat quickly!"
The farmer relayed this to the God of the Hànhǎi,
who became furious,
led his troops forward,
and ordered his men:
"If we do not destroy this tomb,
we must all die before it tonight!"
They then fought fiercely again,
suffering three defeats and rallying three times.
The battle lasted until early night,
when the soldiers from the tomb were defeated,
and the rebellious general was captured alive.
Upon entering the tomb,
they retrieved the beloved concubine,
detained her, and returned.
Lord Zhāng and his followers
were all beheaded before the tomb,
and the tomb was set ablaze.
The farmer was rewarded with a golden belt.
The next day, the farmer went to observe,
and the fire in the tomb was still not extinguished.
Beside the tomb, there were many dried bones and wooden figures.
Xuēyántuó
the Tūjué Shāduōmí Kèhán,
during the Zhēnguàn era,
ruled without benevolence toward his subjects,
frequently committing killings,
causing terror throughout the country,
and leaving everyone uneasy.
Once, a guest begged for food from a host,
who led him into his tent,
and ordered his wife to prepare a meal.
The wife looked at the guest,
and saw that he had the head of a wolf.
The host did not notice this.
The wife told her neighbors,
and they all looked together.
The wolf-headed man had already eaten his
host and left.
They chased after him together,
and when they reached the Yùdūjūn Mountain,
they saw two men.
The pursuers explained the reason.
The two men said:
"We are divine beings,
and Xuēyántuó is destined to perish.
We have come to take him."
The pursuers were frightened and returned.
Tàizōng ordered generals to attack him,
and his troops were thrown into panic and chaos,
causing great disorder among the various tribes.
Soon after, he was killed by the Huíhé,
and his clan was nearly exterminated.
Mù Rénqiàn
Táng Mù Rénqiàn was a man from Hándān in Zhàojùn.
In his youth, he studied the classics
and did not believe in ghosts and spirits.
He often wanted to test whether they existed or not,
so he sought out someone who could see ghosts.
He learned from him,
but for over ten years he was unable to see any.
Later, he moved his family to Xiàng County.
On the road, he saw a person
who looked like a high official,
with magnificent clothes and headgear,
riding a fine horse,
followed by over fifty horsemen.
He looked at Rénqiàn but did not speak.
Later, he saw him several times,
over a period of ten years,
meeting him dozens of times in total.
Later, the man suddenly halted his horse
and called out to Rénqiàn, saying:
"I have frequently seen you lately,
and my feelings are of fondness and admiration,
I wish to befriend you."
Rénqiàn immediately bowed to him
and asked, "Sir, who are you?"
He replied:
"I am a ghost.
My surname is Chéng, given name Jǐng,
originally from Hóngnóng.
During the Western Jìn dynasty, I served as Biéjià,
and now I hold the position of Chief Clerk of the Línhú Kingdom."
Rénqiàn asked where this kingdom was located,
and what the king's name was.
He replied:
"North of the Yellow River,
all belongs to the Línhú Kingdom.
The capital is northwest of Lóufán in the sandy desert.
The king is the former King Wǔlíng of Zhào.
He now rules this kingdom,
but overall is under the control of Tàishān.
Every month, each kingdom sends its chief minister to pay respects at Tàishān.
That is why I have come here several times and met you.
I can be of benefit to you,
enabling you to foresee disasters and difficulties and avoid them in advance,
thus sparing you untimely suffering.
Only the fate of life and death,
and the retribution of great fortune and misfortune,
cannot be altered."
Rénqiàn agreed to follow him.
Jǐng then ordered his attendant horseman, Cháng Zhǎngshì, to be given to him,
sending him to accompany Rénqiàn on his travels.
If anything happened, he would report it first;
if there was something he did not know,
he would come and inform me.
Thus they parted.
Zhǎngshì constantly followed him,
just like a personal attendant.
Whenever Rénqiàn asked about something,
there was nothing he did not know in advance.
At the beginning of the Dàyè era,
Cén Zhīxiàng from Jiānglíng served as the magistrate of Hándān.
His son, Cén Wénběn,
was not yet twenty years old.
Zhīxiàng invited Rénqiàn to teach Wénběn at home,
and Rénqiàn told Wénběn about this matter.
He then said to him:
"Chief Clerk Chéng told me,
'There is one thing I am ashamed to tell you.
But since I have befriended you,
I cannot but inform you.
In the realm of ghosts and spirits, there is also food,
however,
we cannot get full,
and often suffer from hunger.
If we obtain human food,
we can be full for a year.
Many ghosts steal human food.
Since I am of high status,
I cannot steal it,
so I ask you for a meal.'"
Rénqiàn had already told Wénběn.
Wénběn then prepared a feast,
setting out rare delicacies.
Rénqiàn said:
"Ghosts do not wish to enter human dwellings,
so we can set up a tent and mats by the water outside,
and arrange wine and food on them."
Wénběn did as he said.
When the time came,
Rénqiàn saw Jǐng arrive with two guests,
followed by over a hundred horsemen.
After they were seated,
Wénběn bowed twice toward the mats,
apologizing for the food not being exquisite,
and also conveyed Jǐng's words of thanks.
Earlier, when Wénběn was about to prepare the food,
Rénqiàn requested gold and silk to give as gifts.
Wénběn asked what kind of items these were.
Rénqiàn said:
"The items used by ghosts
are all different from those used by humans.
Only gold and silk
can be used universally.
However, counterfeit ones are even better.
Coating large tin pieces with gold to make 'gold,'
and using paper as silk fabric,
are considered the most valuable."
Wénběn did as he said and made them.
After Jǐng finished eating,
he ordered his horsemen to take turns sitting and eating.
Wénběn presented the gold coins and silk he had made as gifts.
Jǐng was very pleased,
and thanked him, saying:
"Because of Mùshēng, I have troubled you, young master, to provide for us.
Would you, young master, like to know your lifespan?"
Wénběn declined, saying:
"I do not wish to know."
Jǐng laughed and left.
Several years later,
Rénqiàn fell ill,
and not because of any severe hardship, yet he could not rise.
After over a month,
Rénqiàn asked Cháng
Zhǎngshì,
but Zhǎngshì did not know.
He then asked the Chief Clerk,
and the Chief Clerk reported:
"The kingdom does not know.
Next month, when I go to pay respects at Tàishān,
I will inquire about the news and report back to you."
The following month,
the Chief Clerk came to report:
"It is a fellow townsman of yours, a certain Zhào,
who serves as Chief Clerk of Tàishān.
There is a vacancy for one Chief Clerk position,
and he recommended you for this post.
Therefore, he prepared the documents,
arranging to summon you.
Once the documents are completed, you will die."
Rénqiàn asked what plan could be devised,
and Jǐng said:
"Your lifespan should be over sixty years,
and you are only forty now.
It is only because Chief Clerk Zhào has arbitrarily summoned you.
I will plead on your behalf."
He then said:
"Chief Clerk Zhào asked me to convey,
'Brother Mù and I were classmates in the past,
and our friendship was deep and profound.
Now, I am fortunate to serve as Chief Clerk of Tàishān.
It so happens that there is a vacancy for one official position.
The Prefect ordered me to select someone,
and I have already recommended you to him.
He has agreed to employ you.
Since you, brother, cannot attain immortality,
you are destined to die.
If death meets with such an opportunity,
it may not be a bad thing to hold office.
Why cling to ten or twenty years of ignoble life?
Now the documents have already been issued,
and cannot be stopped.
I hope you will decide to come,
without any doubts.'"
Rénqiàn became worried and fearful,
and his illness grew more severe.
Jǐng said to Rénqiàn:
"Chief Clerk Zhào is determined to bring you there.
You can go to Tàishān yourself,
and plead your case before the Prefect,
then you may be spared."
Rénqiàn asked how he could see the Prefect.
Jǐng said:
"Go east of the Tàishān Temple,
cross a small ridge,
and on level ground is his capital.
You
go there,
and you will naturally see him."
Rénqiàn told Wénběn about this,
and Wénběn prepared his traveling gear.
Several days later,
he again told Rénqiàn:
"The documents are about to be completed,
and I fear your plea may not be enough to avoid it.
Quickly make a statue of the Buddha,
and those documents will vanish on their own."
He told Wénběn,
and with three thousand coins, they had a statue painted on the west wall of the temple.
When it was finished, Jǐng came to report:
"You are spared."
Rénqiàn, by nature, did not believe in Buddhism,
and still had doubts in his mind.
He then asked Jǐng:
"Buddhist teachings speak of the causality of the three periods of existence—past, present, and future.
Is this true or false?"
He replied:
"All true."
Rénqiàn said:
"If that is so,
when people die they should be divided into the six paths,
how can they all become ghosts?
And King Wǔlíng of Zhào and you,
are you still ghosts now?"
Jǐng said:
"How many households are in your county?"
Rénqiàn said:
"Over ten thousand households."
He asked again:
"How many prisoners are in the jail?"
Rénqiàn said:
"Usually fewer than twenty."
He asked again:
"Within ten thousand households,
how many hold the fifth-rank office?"
Rénqiàn said:
"None."
He asked again:
"How many hold offices of the ninth rank or above?"
Rénqiàn said:
"Several tens."
Jǐng said:
"The division of the six paths,
is exactly like this.
Those who attain the heavenly path,
not one in ten thousand,
just as in your county there is not a single fifth-rank official;
those who attain the human path,
several out of ten thousand,
like the several tens of ninth-rank officials in your county;
those who fall into hell,
also several tens out of ten thousand,
like the prisoners in your jail;
only ghosts and beasts,
are the most numerous,
like the tax-paying households in your county.
Within this path,
there are further levels."
Then pointing at his attendants, he said:
"That person is far inferior to me,
and those inferior to him are even more numerous."
Rénqiàn said:
"Do ghosts die?"
He replied:
"Yes."
Rénqiàn said:
"When they die, into which path do they enter?"
He answered:
"I do not know,
just as humans know life but do not know death."
Rénqiàn asked:
"The Taoist rituals of offering petitions,
are they beneficial or not?"
Jǐng said:
"The Taoist Heavenly Emperor oversees the six paths,
this is the Heavenly Ministry.
King Yánluó,
is like the Son of Heaven in the human world.
The Lord of Mount Tài,
is like the Chief Secretary.
The gods of the five paths are like the various ministers.
As for our kingdom,
it is like a large prefecture.
Whenever there is a human affair,
Taoist priests submit petitions to request blessings,
like seeking the grace of the gods.
The Heavenly Ministry receives them.
They then instruct King Yánluó:
'On such and such a day and month,
we received such and such a petition.
You should handle it justly,
do not allow any wrongful punishment.'
King Yánluó respectfully receives and carries out the order,
just as humans obey an imperial decree.
If there is no reason, one cannot seek exemption;
if there is injustice, it will certainly be redressed.
How can it be said to be without benefit?"
Rénqiàn asked further:
"What about the Buddhists cultivating blessings?"
Jǐng said:
"The Buddha is a great sage,
he does not issue documents.
Those who cultivate blessings,
are revered by the heavenly gods,
and often receive leniency.
If one's blessings are abundant,
even if destined for an evil path,
the records cannot pursue and capture them.
This is beyond my understanding,
and I do not know the reason why."
Having said this, he departed.
After a day or two, Rénqiàn was able to rise,
and recovered fully.
Wénběn's father passed away,
and he returned to his hometown.
Rénqiàn sent a letter saying:
"Ghosts are certainly greedy and flattering.
In the past, wanting your food and drink,
they were so attentive.
Now knowing there is no more benefit,
their attitude has become quite indifferent.
However, the regular attendants still follow me.
Our county was overrun by bandits,
and almost everyone perished.
I was guided by the attendants,
thus
the bandits did not see me,
and I managed to survive intact."
On the eighth day of the ninth month in the sixteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era, civil officials were granted an archery event at the Xuánwǔ Gate,
Wénběn was then the Vice Minister of the Secretariat.
He himself told people this story.
A person from Yǎnzhōu.
There was a man from Zōu County, Yǎnzhōu in the Táng dynasty, surnamed Zhāng,
whose courtesy name is forgotten.
He had once served as a county captain.
In the sixteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era,
he intended to go to the capital to participate in the official selection.
While passing by Mount Tài,
he visited the temple to pray for blessings.
In the temple, the Prefect Lord, his wife, and all their sons,
all manifested their forms.
After Zhāng paid his respects to each,
he came to the side of the fourth son,
and saw that his appearance was elegant and handsome.
Among the five people traveling together,
Zhāng alone prayed, saying:
"If only I could befriend the Fourth Láng,
composing poetry and raising wine cups,
my life's purpose would be fulfilled.
What use is an official career?"
After traveling several lǐ,
suddenly several dozen horsemen,
wielding their whips, arrived,
and their attendants said it was the Fourth Láng.
He said:
"Earlier I saw my elder brother showing regard for me,
so I have come to pay my respects."
He also said:
"I understand you wish to participate in the selection,
but this year you are not fated to obtain an official post.
Furthermore, I fear you may encounter disaster on the road,
so it is best not to go."
Zhāng did not heed him,
and they parted ways.
After traveling over a hundred lǐ,
Zhāng and his companions were traveling at night
when they were robbed by bandits,
and all their belongings were taken.
Zhāng then prayed, saying:
"Would the Fourth Láng not help me?"
After a short while,
the Fourth Láng arrived with his chariots and horsemen,
and after expressing shock and lament for a long time,
he immediately ordered his attendants to pursue and capture them.
The bandits stumbled and became confused,
and returned to the original spot.
The Fourth Láng ordered them beaten with rods several dozen times.
Their thighs and arms were all mangled.
Soon after, they parted again.
The Fourth Láng pointed to a large tree,
saying, "On the day you return,
call for me here."
That year,
Zhāng indeed did not obtain an official post and returned.
When he reached the appointed place,
he called out loudly for the Fourth Láng.
Shortly after, the láng arrived.
He then led Zhāng, saying,
"Follow me to my residence."
Immediately, there were soaring towers and elegant pavilions,
loftily spanning the sky,
with stern and imposing guards,
resembling those of a king.
Zhāng then entered.
The Fourth Láng said:
"You must pay respects to the Prefect Lord,
before you can settle in."
He then led him inside.
Passing through over ten layers of gates,
they hurried forward,
and reached the great hall to pay their respects.
Zhāng saw the Prefect Lord was extremely imposing.
Zhāng trembled with fear,
not daring to look up.
The judgments seemed to be written in vermilion,
and the characters were all extremely large.
The Prefect Lord ordered a messenger to announce:
"You are able to befriend my son,
which is a very good path.
You should stay for a day or two to feast and gather,
and then depart as you please."
He then ordered him led out,
to a separate lodge.
A lavish feast of rare delicacies was set,
with both land and sea delicacies fully prepared.
Music filled the ears.
He then shared a room with the Fourth Láng to sleep.
After three nights had passed,
Zhāng, by the next morning,
was strolling and playing in the courtyard,
wandering back and forth,
when he peeked into another courtyard,
and saw his wife.
Before a crowd of officials, she stood wearing a cangue.
Zhāng returned,
feeling very unhappy.
The Fourth Láng, finding this strange, asked the reason.
Zhāng explained in detail.
The Fourth Láng was greatly surprised and said:
"I did not know sister-in-law had come here."
He immediately went himself to the Judicial Office.
There were several dozen of its kind,
and upon seeing the Fourth Láng arrive,
they all stepped down from the dais,
standing with feet together respectfully.
He gestured for one judicial officer to come forward,
and explained the matter in detail.
The judicial officer replied:
"I dare not disobey your command.
However, I must inform the Recorder."
He then summoned the Recorder,
and the Recorder agreed, saying:
"We must place this case among the other cases,
and handle it conveniently together with other judgments,
only then can it be done."
The judicial officer then ruled:
"This woman, upon investigation in another case,
often had merit from copying scriptures and maintaining vegetarian fasts,
so she should not die immediately."
She was then released and allowed to return home.
Zhāng parted from the Fourth Láng with tears,
who still said:
"Only by performing meritorious deeds
can one increase longevity."
Zhāng rode his original horse,
while his wife borrowed a horse from the Fourth Láng,
and they returned together.
Although his wife was a spirit essence,
her demeanor was as usual.
As they were about to reach home,
about a hundred paces away,
she suddenly disappeared.
Zhāng was greatly astonished and afraid.
He ran to his home,
and immediately encountered his children wailing,
and learned she had already been encoffined.
Zhāng immediately called his children,
hurried to open the grave,
opened the coffin,
and his wife suddenly sat up,
smiling broadly and saying:
"Because I missed the children,
do not blame me for going ahead."
Thus, after being dead for six or seven days, she revived.
This is what the people of Yǎnzhōu tell of it.
Liǔ Zhìgǎn
Liǔ Zhìgǎn of Hédōng in the Táng dynasty,
in the early years of the Zhēnguàn era, served as magistrate of Chángjǔ County.
One night, he suddenly died,
but revived the next morning.
He recounted:
"Suddenly, I was summoned by an underworld official.
An envoy from a great government office brought me to see him,
who said to me:
'There is now an official vacancy,
so I have wrongfully appointed you to it.'
Zhìgǎn declined, citing his elderly parents,
and moreover stated his own merits and blessings,
arguing that he should not die so soon.
The king ordered his records checked,
and it was indeed so.
He then said:
'You are not fated to die yet,
but may temporarily serve as a record judge.'
Zhìgǎn agreed and thanked him.
An official led him to a department,
where there were five judges,
and Zhìgǎn became the sixth.
The hall was a long building,
People sat in three sections,
each with a bed and desk,
and the work was extremely busy and crowded.
At the western end, one seat had no judge,
so the official led Zhìgǎn to the empty seat.
A group of officials brought documents and ledgers,
asking Zhìgǎn to sign them,
sign.
They placed them on the desk,
then retreated and stood below the steps.
Zhìgǎn asked them why,
and they replied:
'Our foul aura would oppress you, sir,
so we only answer matters from a distance.'
Zhìgǎn read and examined them,
finding them similar to those in the human world,
and thus began judging and writing.
After a while, food arrived,
and the other judges ate together.
Zhìgǎn also wanted to join them,
but the other judges said:
'Since you are only temporarily judging,
you should not eat this.'
Zhìgǎn complied.
At dusk,
an official escorted Zhìgǎn back home,
and he revived just as dawn broke.
He returned home.
At nightfall, the official came again to fetch him, and it was like this until dawn.
Therefore,
he realized that the underworld and the human world have opposite day and night cycles.
Thus, he judged underworld affairs at night
and attended to his county duties during the day.
After over a year,
while in the underworld department,
Zhìgǎn got up to go to the toilet
and saw a woman in the western part of the hall.
She appeared around thirty years old,
with graceful features,
wearing bright and beautiful clothes,
standing there wiping her tears.
Zhìgǎn asked who she was,
and she replied:
'I am the wife of the Sīcāng Cānjūn of Xīngzhōu.
I was brought here,
having just parted from my husband,
hence my sorrow.'
Zhìgǎn asked an official about her,
and the official said:
'She was brought here by the officials
for questioning
and to testify about her husband's affairs.'
Zhìgǎn then said to the woman:
'I am Liǔ Zhìgǎn, magistrate of Chángjǔ County.
If you are questioned, madam,
I hope you will answer for yourself.
Do not implicate the Sīcāng,
as it would be useless for both of you to die.'
The woman said:
'I truly do not wish to implicate him,
but I fear the officials will pressure me.'
Zhìgǎn said:
'Madam, please do not implicate him,
and you need not worry about being pressured.'
The woman agreed.
Later, when he returned to the prefecture,
he first asked about the Sīcāng's wife's health.
The Sīcāng said:
'My wife is young and has no illness.'
Zhìgǎn told him what he had seen,
describing her clothes and appearance,
and urged him to perform good deeds.
The Sīcāng hurried home,
saw his wife weaving at the loom,
and she was fine,
so he did not fully believe it.
Over ten days later,
the Sīcāng's wife suddenly died.
Only then did the Sīcāng become frightened and performed good deeds to ward off misfortune.
Also in Xīng
Two officials from the prefecture had completed their terms of service
and were about to go to the capital for reassignment.
They said to Zhìgǎn:
'Since you judge underworld affairs,
may we ask what posts we will be assigned?'
Zhìgǎn went to the underworld
and asked a minor record-keeper for their names.
He said:
'The name registers are sealed in boxes on the left and right,
and it will take two days to check.'
Two days later,
he fully informed the two men.
When the two men went to the capital for reassignment,
the Ministry of Personnel proposed posts for them,
but they were different from what had been reported.
The prefectural officials heard this
and told Zhìgǎn.
He later asked the minor record-keeper,
who rechecked the register
and said:
'It is exactly as checked,
no mistake.'
Later, when the candidates passed through the examination bureau,
the bureau reviewed and rejected them.
The Ministry of Personnel resubmitted their names,
and indeed, the posts matched what the register had reported.
Thus, everyone believed and was convinced.
Whenever Zhìgǎn saw the names and details of his relatives and acquaintances in the underworld register,
along with their dates of death,
he would inform them,
urging them to perform good deeds,
and many were spared.
After Zhìgǎn had temporarily judged for three years,
an official from the underworld came to tell him:
'We have already found Lǐ Sīhù of Lóngzhōu,
who will be appointed as the permanent official to replace you.
You will no longer judge.'
Zhìgǎn went to the prefecture
and informed the prefect Lǐ Défèng,
who sent someone to Lóngzhōu to investigate.
The Sīhù had already died.
When asked about his date of death,
it was exactly when the official had come to inform Zhìgǎn.
From then on, it ceased.
The prefectural office sent Zhìgǎn to escort prisoners
to the Fèngzhōu border.
All four prisoners escaped.
Zhìgǎn was worried and afraid,
and could not capture them.
One night, while staying at a relay station,
he suddenly saw his former subordinate official come to tell him:
'The prisoners have all been captured.
One is dead,
three are in the western valley of the southern mountain,
and all have been captured and bound.
Please do not worry, sir.'
After speaking, he bid farewell and left.
Zhìgǎn immediately requested to go together into the western valley of the southern mountain,
and indeed found the four prisoners.
Knowing they could not escape,
they came to resist.
Zhìgǎn fought them,
killed one prisoner,
and bound the other three,
exactly as had been reported.
Zhìgǎn is still alive today,
serving as Sīfǎ of Cízhōu.
Liǔ Hēng, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, told this story.
Hēng was prefect of Qióngzhōu,
met Zhìgǎn,
and personally asked him about it.
Moreover, the Censor Péi Tóngjié also said
that he had heard several people tell it this way.
Lǐ Bō
Emperor Gāozōng.
Intended to perform the fēng sacrifice at Mount Tài,
but there had been continuous rain for a long time.
The Emperor was doubtful about it,
and sent someone to ask the Huàshān Daoist priest Lǐ Bō,
to petition the Jade Capital Heavenly Emperor.
Bō
was the father of Lǐ Chúnfēng.
Thereupon, he dispatched the Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Liú Rénguǐ to Huàshān,
to ask Bō about the fēng and shàn sacrifices.
Bō said:
"We must wait and ask the Lord of Mount Tài's Prefecture."
He then ordered him to be summoned.
After a long while,
the Prefectural Lord arrived,
bowed in the courtyard,
with very respectful etiquette.
Bō said:
"The Táng Emperor wishes to perform the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
what do you think?"
The Prefectural Lord replied:
"It is appropriate to perform the fēng sacrifice,
and sixty years later,
it will be appropriate to perform another."
Bō bowed to him and he left.
At the time, Rénguǐ was standing by Bō's side,
and saw the Prefectural Lord repeatedly glance at him.
Bō called him back and said:
"This is the Táng Prime Minister,
he does not recognize the Prefectural Lord,
please do not take offense."
After he left,
Bō said to Rénguǐ:
"The Prefectural Lord was somewhat displeased that the Prime Minister did not bow,
and ordered his attendants to record this man's name,
fearing it might affect your great virtue.
That is why I called him back to handle the matter."
Rénguǐ was terrified and sweated for a long time.
Bō said:
"The matter has been handled,
there should be no suffering."
After that, the Emperor performed the fēng and shàn sacrifices.
Dí Rénjié
During Emperor Gāozōng's time,
Dí Rénjié served as Investigating Censor.
Temples to mountain and river spirits in the Jiāngnán and Lǐngnán regions,
were almost all burned down.
When he arrived at Duān Prefecture,
there was a southern barbarian deity,
and Rénjié wanted to burn its temple.
Anyone who entered the temple died immediately.
Rénjié recruited someone capable of burning it,
offering a reward of one hundred thousand cash.
At that time, two men came forward to answer the recruitment.
Rénjié asked what they needed to go and return,
the men said:
"We wish to have an imperial edict."
Rénjié gave them the edict.
The men took it and went,
arriving at the temple,
they announced there was an imperial edict,
then opened the edict and entered,
proclaiming it.
The deity did not move again,
and they then burned and destroyed it.
Later, when Rénjié returned to Biàn Prefecture,
he met someone who could see ghosts, who said:
"Behind the Censor there is a southern barbarian deity.
It says its dwelling was burned,
and constantly seeks revenge."
Rénjié asked:
"How will this matter end?"
The one who saw ghosts
said:
"The Censor is destined to become a chief minister,
and has over twenty spirits and ghosts following him.
What can that one possibly do?
After a long time,
that deity returned to Lǐngnán."
Wáng Wànchè
In the later years of Empress Dowager Wǔ,
many palace women died,
within one month,
already several hundred.
The Empress Dowager then summoned the ghost-summoner Wáng Wànchè,
to inspect the palace.
Chè reported:
"The Heavenly Emperor is displeased that Your Majesty has long ruled over the myriad states,
the spirits are not content,
and this is the cause."
The Empress Dowager said:
"What can be done?"
Chè said:
"Your servant can perform an exorcism."
He then laid out a mat in front of the hall,
grasped a knife, sprayed water,
and chanted incantations in all directions.
After a while, he said:
"The Emperor has arrived."
Chè then questioned the Emperor in the court:
"The Way of Heaven has its comings and goings,
the tides of fate have their decline and rise.
In the past, the Emperor assisted Your Majesty,
to motherly govern all within the seas,
greatly expanding the transformative influence of Jiāngyuán and King Wén's mother,
thus being supported,
with the myriad states submitting wholeheartedly.
This was Heaven's will,
not human affairs.
Your Majesty's sacred spirit is in Heaven,
separated by the principles of the hidden and manifest worlds,
how could you fail to recognize the opportunity,
and harm the living so cruelly,
to such an extent?"
The Emperor then spoke from the air, saying:
"It is hardly my intent,
this is because Empress Wáng's冤 grievance has been redressed.
It will not stop at the rear palace,
but will also bring harm to your ruler."
The Empress Dowager and those around her heard this clearly,
the Empress Dowager fell silent, her expression changed,
and she ordered the mat removed.
The next year, the Five Princes supported the installation of Emperor Zhōngzōng,
moved the Empress Dowager to the Shàngyáng Palace,
where she died in seclusion.
The Imperial Academy student Zhèng Shēng
During the Chuígōng era,
the imperial carriage was at the Shàngyáng Palace.
Zhèng Shēng, a Presented Scholar of the Imperial Academy, set out at dawn from Tóngtuó Ward,
riding under the waning moon,
crossed the Luò Bridge.
Below, there was a very sorrowful weeping sound,
Shēng immediately dismounted to investigate.
He saw a beautiful woman,
veiled and covering her face with her sleeve, who said:
"I was orphaned and raised by my elder brother and his wife,
my sister-in-law is cruel,
and makes me suffer.
Now I wish to throw myself into the water,
hence I linger here, grieving for a moment."
Shēng said:
"Can you follow me home?"
She replied:
"Even as a maid or servant, I would have no regrets."
So he carried her on his horse and took her to his dwelling.
She called herself Fánrén,
and could recite texts like the "Chǔcí," "Jiǔgē," "Zhāohún," and "Jiǔbiàn,"
and often composed lyrics and rhapsodies in the form of plaintive songs.
Her words were beautiful and ornate,
yet none could match them.
Thus she composed the "Fēngguāng Cí," which said:
"Lush past elegance, ah, shines in glorious times;
Sowing fragrant green, ah, gentle blossoms return.
In the old chamber, with tender shoots and nestled calyxes, ah,
Hidden deep within adorned chambers to embellish her grace.
Seeing the radiant beauty of youthful splendor, ah,
Veiled in long mists as if by curtains,
Intoxicated by melting light, ah, vast and boundless,
A thousand miles afar, ah, misty brows embraced.
Dawn brings joy, ah, dusk brings brightness,
Without the lush branches swaying gracefully, ah,
Slender and graceful, she moves with lingering pace.
Repaying the wandering countenance, ah, singing amidst蔓 flowers,
Gauze streams, charming lightning, ah, hair follows in gentle sway."
Shēng lived in poverty,
Fánrén once brought out a bolt of fine silk to sell,
and a foreign merchant paid a thousand in gold.
After living there for over a year,
Shēng planned to travel to Cháng'ān.
That evening,
she said to Shēng:
"I am the younger sister from the underwater dragon palace of the lake.
Banished, I followed you.
Now the term is fulfilled,
I cannot stay long by your side."
Then she bid farewell to Shēng.
Shēng tried to keep her but could not,
and she finally left.
More than ten years later,
Shēng's elder brother served as the Prefect of Yuèzhōu,
and on the Shangsi Festival day,
he climbed the Yuèyáng Tower with his family and retinue,
gazing toward Èzhǔ,
they set out a feast, music in full swing.
Shēng, feeling melancholy, chanted:
"Feelings boundless, ah, surging and vast,
Longing for a joyful reunion, ah, entrusted to the Three Xiāng."
Before his voice faded,
a painted pleasure boat came floating and rippling toward them,
in the middle was a colorful tower,
over a hundred feet high.
On it were curtains, railings, and cages,
all adorned with silk drapes.
There were those playing strings and blowing pipes,
all were immortals with delicate eyebrows,
clad in mist and lightning,
their skirts and sleeves were a full foot wide.
Among them, one person danced,
with a frown, full of resentment and longing,
her appearance resembling Fánrén.
Dancing, she sang:
"Against the spring tide, ah, by the river's bend,
Trailing lake waves, ah, my green skirt sways.
Lotus buds tightly curled, ah, now unfold,
If not to return together, ah, what then?"
When the dance ended,
she gathered her sleeves, desolate.
In a moment,
wind and waves roared furiously,
and then she was gone without a trace.
The Wife of the Military Advisor of Zhàozhōu
Lú, the Military Advisor of Zhàozhōu,
newly married, took up his post,
his wife was exceedingly beautiful.
After several years,
he ended his official term and returned to the capital.
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
his wife wanted to go to the market,
to seek longevity tokens,
to present to her parents-in-law.
The carriage was already at the gate,
when she suddenly suffered a violent heart pain,
and within the time of a meal, she died.
After Lú Shēng finished wailing and crying,
he went to see Remonstrance Grand Master Míng Chóngyǎn,
knocking on the door urgently.
Chóngyǎn, startled, said:
"This is the Duānwǔ Festival day,
such urgent knocking is ominous,
there must be an emergency."
He hurried out.
Lú bowed twice,
and told him everything.
the matter.
Míng said:
"This is the doing of the Third Prince of Tàishān."
Then he wrote three talismans and gave them to Lú:
"Return home and quickly burn the first talisman,
if after the time it takes to walk ten li,
she does not revive;
then burn the next one,
if she still does not revive;
then burn the third talisman.
If she died an untimely death, she will surely come back to life,
if she does not return, then she is truly dead."
Lú returned and did as told,
successively burning the three talismans,
and his wife then revived,
soon able to speak.
At first she said:
She was carried by carriage to the summit of Mount Tàishān,
where there were separate palaces and chambers,
she saw a young man,
who was said to be the Third Prince.
He ordered over ten maids to escort her into another chamber,
to attend to her makeup and hair.
The Third Prince was in the front hall,
playing backgammon with other young men,
waiting for her makeup to be finished,
then planning to hold a banquet.
The maids urged her to hurry with her makeup,
but because she was attached to her former husband,
she was still shedding sad tears.
After a while,
she heard someone knocking at the door, saying:
"I am the Merit Officer Shànglì,
just now received orders from the Capital Commissioner,
to ask the Third Prince,
why has he taken another man's wife?
She should be sent back immediately."
The Third Prince angrily said:
"I take another's wife myself,
what business is it of the Capital Commissioner!"
He scolded the Merit Officer and ordered him to leave.
They went back and forth,
the words becoming very harsh.
After a moment,
she heard knocking again, saying:
"I am the Straight Talisman Messenger,
the Capital Commissioner orders to take the woman of the Lú family."
The one playing backgammon with him urged him,
but he would not listen.
The backgammon player said:
"Not only will this bring trouble upon you,
it will also bring disaster upon me."
Still he would not listen.
Soon, a fierce wind arose,
blowing dark clouds from the cliff top,
the two messengers announced:
"The Great One's Straight Talisman,
is now about to arrive!"
The Third Prince showed fear.
The wind suddenly swept up the residence,
lifted it over a hundred zhang high and then dropped it,
people and objects were crushed to pieces,
only Lú's wife survived.
The three messengers escorted her back,
arriving at the hall,
she saw her body lying on the bed,
feeling deeply sorrowful and resentful,
she was pushed into her form,
and thus revived.
Wéi Āndào
Wéi Āndào of Jīngzhào,
was the son of Wéi Zhēn, a Gentleman of the Palace.
He sat for the imperial examinations,
but for a long time did not pass.
During the Dàdìng era of the Táng dynasty,
he went out early in Luòyáng,
reaching the west gate of Cíhuì Ward.
The morning drums had just begun,
when he saw in the middle of the thoroughfare armed guards,
like the retinue of an emperor.
Ahead were several dozen teams of armored cavalry,
followed by eunuchs,
holding large staffs,
wearing painted trousers and jackets,
clearing the way along both sides of the road,
also numbering several dozen.
He also saw a yellow-canopied carriage with a leftward-plumed banner,
bearing moon flags but no sun flags.
There were also close attendants, talented ladies, palace eunuchs, and the like,
also numbering several hundred.
Among them was a flying parasol,
beneath the parasol,
he saw someone wearing garments adorned with pearls and jadeite,
riding a large horse,
like an empress's
adornments,
beautiful and radiant,
her appearance captivating.
There were also following riders,
all women, talented officials,
holding battle-axes,
carrying bows and arrows,
riding on horseback in attendance,
also over a thousand people.
At that time, Empress Wǔ Zétiān was in Luòyáng,
and Āndào initially thought it was an imperial excursion by the Empress.
The sky was not yet bright,
so he asked his companions,
but they all said they saw nothing.
He also found it strange that the Golden Guards and street officials on the thoroughfare
did not clear the way.
After a long while, it gradually grew light,
and he saw one of the following riders, a palace eunuch,
galloping forward on horseback.
Āndào then stopped and asked him:
"Those who passed by earlier,
were they not the sovereign?"
The palace eunuch said:
"No."
Āndào requested to know the matter,
but the palace eunuch merely pointed to the west gate of Cíhuì Ward and said:
"Sir, just go from here,
through the ward gate,
follow the wall southward,
walk over a hundred paces,
and there will be a vermilion gate facing west.
Knock and inquire about the reason,
and you will naturally understand."
Āndào followed his words and knocked.
After a long while,
a red-robed official came out to answer the gate and said:
"Are you not Wéi Āndào?"
He replied:
"I am."
The official said:
"The Goddess of the Earth has been waiting for you for a long time."
He then invited him inside.
They saw a large gate like a ceremonial gate,
the official went in to announce,
and after a moment,
he was invited further inside.
A purple-robed palace eunuch
conversed with Āndào in the courtyard,
then led him into a palace chamber,
where bathing preparations were made.
After a moment,
a large chest was presented containing a set of fine garments,
among which were a blue robe, an ivory tablet, a sash, a headscarf, and boots, all complete,
and Āndào was ordered to put them on.
The palace eunuch said:
"You may go now."
He then mounted Āndào on a large horse,
with several female riders following as attendants.
The palace eunuch rode alongside Āndào,
they exited the west gate of Cíhuì Ward,
went southwest along the main street,
proceeded eastward from Tōnglì Street,
and exited through Jiànchūn Gate.
They then traveled northeast,
for about over twenty lǐ,
gradually seeing guards lining the road,
who bowed before the horse and then left.
After several such places,
they finally reached a large city,
heavily guarded by armored soldiers,
like a king's city.
Passing through several layers,
they saw soaring towers and connected pavilions,
below which was a large gate,
like the residence of a Son of Heaven,
with many palace eunuchs.
Āndào rode on horseback,
passing by emerald towers and vermilion halls,
and after over ten such places,
they entered through one gate.
Walking about a hundred paces,
there was another great hall,
inside which a grand banquet was laid out with abundant music,
wine vessels and food stands arrayed,
with nine performances and myriad dances,
like the music of Heaven.
Over ten beautiful women,
resembling imperial consorts and princesses,
stood arranged to the left and right of the banquet.
The palace eunuch who had accompanied him earlier
led Āndào up from the western steps.
After a moment,
a palace eunuch inside the hall, like a master of ceremonies,
ordered Āndào to stand facing east in the western chamber.
After a moment,
from the inner door of the hall,
guards and attendants were seen
first lining up in the hall,
and then the faint sound of jade pendants was heard.
A beautiful woman,
fully adorned with head ornaments and wearing ceremonial robes,
like garments for temple worship,
came to the western side of the hall,
standing opposite Āndào,
and she was the one he had seen beneath the flying parasol on the west street of Cíhuì Ward.
The palace eunuch then announced:
"The Goddess of the Earth
is fated by destiny to be your mate."
Āndào was ordered to bow,
and the Lady accepted it;
the Lady bowed,
and Āndào accepted it,
following the etiquette of host and guest in the human world.
They then removed their ceremonial garments,
and sat facing each other at the banquet.
The over ten beautiful women seen earlier
also sat in rows to the left and right,
music was played, and food and drink were served,
continuing until dusk, when it concluded.
That night, they became husband and wife,
and she was still a virgin.
This continued for over ten days,
and the clothing, equipment, food, and drink
were all like those of an imperial household.
The Lady then said to Āndào:
"I am your wife,
and you have parents.
To marry without informing them
cannot be called proper etiquette.
I wish to follow you home,
pay respects at the ancestral temple to your honored parents,
and complete the rites of a wife,
which would be fortunate."
Āndào said:
"Agreed."
She then gave orders,
for carriages and horses to be prepared that very day.
The Lady rode in a yellow calf-drawn carriage,
adorned with gold, jadeite, and precious jade,
what is called in the human world a 'storehouse carriage.'
Above it, a flying parasol provided shade,
with carriage attendants and escorts,
just as seen on the west street of Cíhuì Ward.
Āndào rode on horseback,
following the carriage,
with over ten attendants to his left and right,
all skilled officials and eunuchs.
After traveling over ten lǐ,
there was a vermilion-curtained city with prepared tents,
female officials lined up behind,
which was
the resting place of the traveling palace.
The Lady then entered the prepared tent,
ordering Āndào to stay with her,
and the food and drink served were exquisite.
After a while,
they departed again.
An order was given to reduce
the accompanying carriages and riders by seventy to eighty percent,
and after traveling another three or four lǐ,
another order was given to dismiss the attendants.
By the time they reached Jiànchūn Gate,
there were only about twenty riders and horses left,
like an excursion by a king.
After entering Luòyáng,
as they approached his home,
Āndào went in first,
and his family was astonished by the unusualness of his carriage and attire.
Āndào then went to see his parents.
His two parents were shocked and bewildered for a long time,
and said:
"We have not seen you for
It had been over a month,
where have you been?"
Āndào bowed and explained clearly:
"I was forced into a marriage by a certain family."
He said his new bride would arrive soon,
so he came to inform them first.
Before his parents could finish their shocked questioning,
carriages and horsemen were already at the gate.
Then came several dozen maidservants and eunuchs,
from the outer main gate,
spreading embroidered mats and fine mats,
arranging them in the courtyard,
and with green screens and painted curtains,
decorating the hall entrance,
placing a fine rope bed on each side,
inviting the parents-in-law to sit opposite each other.
Then from outside the gate,
they set up two brocade walking screens,
the lady, dressed in ceremonial attire,
entered with jade pendants hanging.
After completing the bride's rituals,
she presented green jade, gold, jade, silk, and fine silk,
amounting to over ten chests,
as congratulatory gifts from the human world,
placing them before her parents-in-law.
As for uncles, aunts, and other family members,
all received her gifts.
Then she said:
"The new bride requests to reside in the eastern courtyard."
Then again there were maidservants and eunuchs.
Holding room curtains and furnishings,
they placed them in the eastern courtyard,
decorating it very thoroughly,
and she then resided there.
His parents were worried and fearful together,
not knowing where she came from.
At that time, it was the court of Empress Tiānhòu,
where laws and decrees were strict and severe,
fearing disaster would befall them,
they fully reported the matter to the throne, requesting punishment.
Empress Tiānhòu said:
"This must be a bewitching creature,
you need not worry.
I have skilled spellcasters,
masters of the Buddhist sect,
the two monks Jiǔsī and Huáisù,
can rid you of this demon."
Thus she ordered Jiǔsī and Huáisù to go,
the monks said:
"This is nothing more than a type of demonic fox spirit,
easy to remove with our arts.
First have a feast set in the new bride's courtyard,
set seats,
request we come the next day."
Wéi Zhēn returned,
fully conveying the two monks' words to her,
the new bride accepted the command,
prepared the feast and set the seats,
showing no fear at all.
The next day,
the two monks arrived,
after finishing the meal and sitting upright,
they requested to meet the new bride,
intending to perform their arts.
The new bride quickly came,
and also paid respects to the two monks.
The two monks suddenly seemed struck by something,
prostrated themselves admitting guilt,
blood flowing from the corners of their eyes, noses, and mouths.
Again they fully reported the matter to the throne.
Empress Tiānhòu asked about it.
The two monks replied:
"The spells we use,
are only effective against demonic spirits and ghostly creatures,
this one, we do not know where she comes from,
we think we cannot control her."
Empress Tiānhòu said:
"There is the Grand Master of Remonstrance Míng Chóngyǎn,
who uses the extraordinary arts of the Great One to control and record all the gods and deities of heaven and earth,
he surely can handle this."
Thus she summoned Chóngyǎn.
Chóngyǎn said to Wéi Zhēn:
"You should tonight,
in the main hall of your residence,
sit with pure sincerity,
and watch above the room where the new bride resides,
waiting for any strange creature to arrive.
If it prevails, then it ends,
if it does not prevail,
then we must use other methods to control it."
Wéi Zhēn did as he said,
until the first watch.
At night,
he saw something like flying clouds,
red light like startling lightning,
from Chóngyǎn's residence,
flying and leaping to arrive.
When it reached the new bride's roof,
suddenly it seemed struck down by something,
and thus disappeared.
He sent someone to check on the new bride,
and she was safe and sound as before.
During the second watch,
he again saw something shaped like a red dragon,
snatching and spewing poison,
its sound like a multitude of drums,
riding on black clouds with light,
arriving at the new bride's roof,
again seeming struck by something,
with a shrieking sound, it vanished.
He sent someone to check on the new bride,
again she was as before.
Then at midnight,
he saw a creature with vermilion hair and saw-like teeth,
spinning an iron wheel,
riding on flying thunder,
the wheel's edges and horns roaring as it rushed forth,
once it reached her roof,
again it seemed killed by something,
admitting guilt before vanishing.
When dawn finally came,
Wéi Zhēn, strange and fearful,
did not know what plan to make,
again fully reported the matter.
Chóngyǎn said:
"The methods used before,
were the Great One talisman arts,
only capable of subduing fox spirits,
now since they are ineffective,
I request to try further."
Thus he performed altar rituals and registers,
summoning the eight directions and thick earth,
mountains, rivers, and streams,
hills, ruins, water, and trees,
all deities in charge of ghosts and spirits,
their number complete,
Chóngyǎn found it strange.
The next day,
he again summoned the gods of the human world, heavenly realm, and eight extremes,
their number complete.
Chóngyǎn said:
"If it is a deity causing the bewitchment,
then I can control it,
but if so,
then it cannot be known!
Let me try to see her myself and observe."
Thus he ordered a feast set in the new bride's courtyard,
inviting Chóngyǎn.
Chóngyǎn arrived and sat,
requesting to see the new bride,
the new bride was just solemnly replying,
about to bow to Chóngyǎn,
Chóngyǎn again suddenly seemed struck by something,
collapsing lifelessly,
admitting guilt and begging for his life,
blood from the corners of his eyes, nose, and mouth flowing on the ground.
Wéi Zhēn became even more shocked and fearful,
not knowing what to do.
His wife then said to Wéi Zhēn:
"This, Jiǔsī, Huáisù, and Míng the Grand Master of Remonstrance,
could not control,
what can be done about it?
I heard when Āndào first met her,
he said she was the Hòutǔ Fūrén,
though it is among the hundred arts of the human world,
none can control her.
Now observing her relationship with Āndào as husband and wife,
they also get along very well,
try having Āndào speak to her,
requesting she leave,
perhaps it can be done."
Wéi Zhēn then ordered Āndào to apologize to her, saying:
"I am of humble family,
the new bride is a noble spiritual deity,
now fortunately married to my son,
I dare not claim to be an equal match;
also, Empress Tiānhòu's laws are strict,
fearing disaster will befall us because of this,
I hope the new bride will temporarily return,
for the sake of her parents-in-law's plans."
Before he finished speaking,
the new bride said tearfully:
"I am fortunate to be matched with a gentleman,
serving my parents-in-law,
the way of a wife,
is to follow the commands of parents-in-law,
now since parents-in-law have commanded,
how dare I not respectfully obey."
Thus that same day she ordered her carriage and left,
then fully performed rituals to bid farewell below the hall.
Then she requested:
"The new bride is a woman,
I dare not return alone,
I wish to take Wéi Láng with me."
Wéi Zhēn happily agreed,
thus she and Āndào left together,
reaching outside the Jiànchūn Gate,
His former chariots and followers all arrived,
and the servants and guards in the city were all as before.
On the day after reaching the city,
the lady donned ceremonial robes,
and sat in the great hall,
like the image of a Son of Heaven holding court.
Then strange-looking and extraordinary people came to pay homage:
some were over ten feet tall,
all wearing ornate crowns and long swords,
and dressed in crimson and purple robes.
It was said they were the gods
of the mountains, rivers, and seas within the four seas.
Next came several thousand people,
said to be the gods of the forests and trees.
Then the kings of all the nations under heaven arrived.
At that time, Ān Dào and the lady sat to the side,
with a small couch placed
for him to observe from.
Finally, one person was announced,
saying:
"The Great Luótiān Nǚ."
Ān Dào looked and saw
it was the Empress.
The lady then smiled and said to Ān Dào:
"This is your local ruler;
step aside for a moment."
She had Ān Dào enter a small room inside the hall.
Soon after, the Empress bowed in the courtyard below,
with great reverence.
The lady then invited the Empress up,
and the Empress declined several times
before ascending the hall,
bowing twice, and taking a seat.
The lady said to the Empress:
"Due to a predestined fate,
I was to be paired with Wéi Ān Dào, a person within your domain.
Now that the predestined fate has ended,
we must part,
but I cannot be without affection for him.
This man suffers from a short lifespan.
I originally intended, while in his household,
to extend his life by three hundred years
and have him attain a third-rank official position.
However, due to the pressure from his respected parents,
