I could not remain long in the mortal world,
and thus could not accomplish this.
Now that you, Heavenly Maiden, have fortunately arrived,
I ask you to grant him five million coins
and an official position up to the fifth rank.
Do not exceed this,
for fear he cannot bear it—
Ān Dào's fate is thin."
She then summoned Ān Dào to come out
and bow to the Empress.
The lady said to the Empress:
"This man is under your jurisdiction;
he should receive his bow."
The Empress hesitated,
her expression seeming reluctant, but accepted it.
She then agreed and left.
The lady said to Ān Dào:
"Since you are skilled in painting,
I will enhance this art for you,
so you may achieve fame for a thousand generations."
She then placed Ān Dào in a small hall,
with curtains and screens hung,
and summoned before him the famous emperors and meritorious officials since ancient times,
instructing Ān Dào to paint them.
After more than a month,
he had captured all their likenesses,
compiling them into twenty scrolls.
Then Ān Dào requested to leave.
The lady ordered a carriage prepared,
and west of the city,
set up a farewell tent and feast,
bidding Ān Dào farewell.
Tears fell as they held hands,
overwhelmed with emotion.
She also gave him gold, jade, and jewels,
filling the carriage before he departed.
When Ān Dào reached the Eastern Capital,
entering through the Jiànchūn Gate,
he heard the Jīnyú guards relaying an order
to search for Wéi Ān Dào in Luòyáng City,
which had been ongoing for over a month.
Upon arriving,
he paid homage to the Empress.
She received him in a small hall,
and recounted her previous dream,
which matched what Ān Dào had described.
She then appointed Ān Dào as the Chief Clerk of the Wèi Prince's Mansion,
and bestowed upon him five million coins.
Taking the paintings of emperors and meritorious officials that Ān Dào had made,
she verified them against the old ones in the secret archives,
and they have been circulated ever since.
During the Tiāncè period,
Ān Dào eventually died in office.
Dù Péngjǔ
At the end of the Jǐnglóng era,
Empress Wéi held sole power.
The former Governor of Ānzhōu, posthumously honored as Grand Preceptor, Dù Péngjǔ,
was at the time serving as the District Defender of Jìyuán County.
He was summoned by the prefectural office to Luòchéng to compile household registers.
One evening, he suddenly died.
His relatives and friends were about to prepare for the minor encoffining.
His wife, Lady Yùchí,
a granddaughter of Yùchí Jìngdé,
was intelligent and resolute by nature.
She said:
"Your calculations are divinely accurate.
You yourself said you would rise to the rank of Regional Governor.
How could you now depart forever?"
She remained calm and did not weep.
After two days and three nights,
a slight warmth gradually returned to his chest,
and the next day he slowly revived.
Several days later, he finally spoke, saying:
"At first, I saw two men holding summons come to fetch me.
They then led me out through the Huī'ān Gate.
The gap in the gate was only an inch wide,
yet passing through it felt quite spacious.
Heading directly north to Mount Máng,
after about ten-some *lǐ*,
there was a large pit,
so deep the bottom could not be seen.
The messengers ordered me to enter,
and Péngjǔ was greatly afraid.
The messengers said:
'Close your eyes.'
Holding my hand, they flew,
and in a moment, my feet were already on the ground.
Following a small path eastward,
for several tens of *lǐ*,
the weather was gloomy and dismal,
like the frozen overcast of winter.
Then we arrived at an official building,
with grand and imposing walls and halls.
The messengers entered first.
An official in green robes came out,
hurriedly bowing with great deference.
After withdrawing, he led me inside.
The green-robed one sat leaning behind a desk,
summoned Péngjǔ forward,
and beside him was a dog.
A human voice spoke, saying:
'The name was mistaken; it's the same,
but this is not the official.'
He caned the messengers,
and changed the summons, ordering them to leave.
There was a horse,
with half a body and two legs,
leaping forward, saying:
'I was formerly killed by Dù Péngjǔ;
now I request justice for my grievance.'
Péngjǔ also clearly remembered it,
and pleaded, saying:
'I was once in charge of a courier station.
An imperial envoy brought the horse and ordered it killed;
it was not my wish.'
The green-robed one ordered a clerk to fetch the records.
Upon examination, it was confirmed,
and the horse then withdrew.
To the side, I saw a clerk,
waving his hand and moving his eyes,
instructing me on the proper procedure,
intending to shield and extricate me.
After the testimony was concluded,
he then bowed and saw me out.
The green-robed one bowed in farewell outside the gate.
He said:
'I am a living person,
a registered householder of Ānzhōu.
Your Honor will become the Governor of Ānzhōu,
so I offer my respects in advance.
I hope you will maintain yourself well.'
After he finished speaking,
the clerk who had earlier instructed me hurried out,
saying:
'My surname is Wéi, given name Dǐng;
I am also a living person.
I reside in Wùběn Ward in the Upper Capital.
I claim that I have just exerted some effort,
and request one hundred thousand cash.'
Péngjǔ declined, saying he could not provide it.
Dǐng said:
'Although I am a living person,
here we use paper money,
which is easy to obtain.'
Péngjǔ then agreed.
Dǐng also instructed, saying:
'When burning it, I hope you will place it on something,
so it fortunately does not touch the ground.
Also call out "Wéi Dǐng,"
and I will personally send someone to receive it.'
Dǐng also said:
'Since you have come here,
surely you wish to see the household register of your own family.'
He then led me into a courtyard,
inscribed as the Ministry of Revenue.
Corridors surrounded it on all sides,
with registers and account books piled mountain-high.
In the center were three bays,
with shelves and cabinets exceptionally tall,
covered with red-yellow curtains and cloths,
and a golden plaque reading *Imperial Registers*.
The rest were all open shelves,
often with boxes,
covered with purple lids.
Wéi Dǐng said:
'These are for the Chief Ministers.'
He then led me to the Dù family register.
The book label read *Púyáng Branch*.
There were four purple boxes.
Opening one volume,
Péngjǔ's three sons—
those not yet born at the time—
already had their names recorded in the register.
Then.
I asked for a brush,
and wrote their names on my arm.
My mind wished to linger,
desiring to look around further.
Wéi Dǐng said:
'Since you are not staying,
you should also return early.'
He then led me out,
and ordered a clerk to escort me back.
The clerk said:
'I am suffering from hunger.
If I do not take this opportunity,
I will have no way to get out.
I hope you will allow me to leave separately,
so I may seek a meal.
Just follow this path,
and you will reach your place on your own.'
He could not be detained.
Péngjǔ then proceeded westward.
To the left of the path, he suddenly saw a new city,
from which a wondrous fragrance could be smelled for several *lǐ*.
The city was encircled by armored soldiers holding weapons.
Péngjǔ asked them,
and the armored soldiers said:
'The Prince of Xiàng is here ascending to become the Son of Heaven,
with four hundred heavenly beings coming to escort him.'
Péngjǔ had once served as an official in the Prince of Xiàng's household,
and was pleased to hear this.
There was a large gap in the wall,
through which he could see clearly.
Several hundred heavenly beings
surrounded the Prince of Xiàng.
The ground was filled with colored clouds,
and all wore immortal garments,
just like in paintings.
Before the Prince of Xiàng was a woman,
holding an incense burner to lead the way.
Drawing closer to peek carefully,
the patterns on her skirt and sash seemed cut and torn,
exactly like the teeth of a wild goose.
The Prince of Xiàng wore a sun on his head,
radiant and brilliant,
nearly over ten feet in size.
Behind the Prince of Xiàng, there were a total of nineteen suns,
piled in rows,
all as greatly luminous as the one he wore.
In a moment,
a messenger on a piebald horse came to welcome him.
The armored soldiers ordered Péngjǔ to run,
so he reached the old path,
and without realizing it, had already arrived at the Huī'ān Gate.
The gate was closed, but passing through it
was also as easy as when he left.
He was blocked and bitten by a pack of dogs,
unable to advance.
Arriving home,
he saw his body lying on the bed,
leapt into it,
and then awoke.
The writing on his arm
was like characters carved on rotten wood,
yet the words were still clear.
He then burned one hundred thousand in paper money,
calling out to present it to Wéi Dǐng.
In his heart, he knew the number of the dynastic change
and the time of the restoration.
He then took leave on pretext,
and came to pay his respects to Emperor Ruìzōng.
The Emperor grasped his hand and said:
"How dare I forget your virtue?"
He sought out Wéi Dǐng,
who had just died.
When Emperor Ruìzōng ascended the throne,
he appointed Péngjǔ as Right Reminder.
The record states:
"His thoughts entered the realm of elegance,
his spirit communed with ghosts and deities."
He ordered several dozen palace ladies and imperial consorts,
to dress in the same attire.
He then told him to look at the one holding the incense burner.
Péngjǔ recognized her from afar—
it was none other than Princess Tàipíng.
When asked about the reason for her scorched skirt sash,
the princess replied:
"While ironing the dragon robe,
it suddenly caught fire,
and in the panic,
I inadvertently scorched my sash,
and in the rush, I had no time to change clothes."
The princess sighed and offered her congratulations, saying:
"The rise of a sage ruler
is indeed ordained by Heaven."
What Péngjǔ witnessed
occurred three years before Emperor Ruìzōng ascended the throne.
Therefore, Péngjǔ's epitaph states:
"When Emperor Ruìzōng ascended the throne,
hidden auspicious signs appeared.
The destined time of the sage was revealed in the transformations of the cosmos,
and the decree of success was determined by the mysterious workings of fate."
Later, he indeed became the military governor of Ānzhōu.
Another account says:
After Péngjǔ was released,
he entered another courtyard,
and asked who was behind the curtain.
The reply was:
"Wèi Yuánzhōng."
After a short while,
Jìng Huī arrived,
dismounted,
and everyone greeted him with bows.
It was said that he was the Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, there to conduct an investigation.
He saw Wǔ Sānsī wearing a cangue, and Wéi Wēn, Zōng Chǔkè, Zhào Lǚwēn, and others in chains.
Lǐ Qiào stood bareheaded with his belt loosened.
He heard Wèi Yuánzhōng and others say:
"This year, there will be a great reckoning."
Indeed, by the sixth month,
the rebellious Wéi clan was executed,
Zōng, Zhào, Wéi, and others were all beheaded,
and Lǐ Qiào was dismissed from office and returned home.
All turned out as he had said.
The Wife of the Hédōng County Captain
During the Jǐngyún era,
there was a certain Lǐ, the county captain of Hénán County in Hédōng,
whose wife, née Wáng,
was of exceptional beauty,
renowned throughout the three metropolitan regions.
One day, Lǐ went to his office and had not yet returned,
Wáng had just finished her makeup and was sitting leisurely, burning incense,
when suddenly she saw several eunuchs
driving an ox-drawn carriage
descending from the clouds to the hall.
Startled, Wáng asked what was happening.
They replied:
"The Lord of Huàshān
has sent us to respectfully welcome you."
Unable to refuse,
in haste, she prepared to leave.
She said to her family:
"How I regret not being able to bid farewell to Captain Lǐ."
With tears streaming down her face, she departed
and died beside the steps.
Soon after, a carriage, borne aloft by colorful clouds,
floated into the sky and gradually vanished.
When Lǐ returned from the prefecture,
and found his wife gone,
he caressed her corpse and wailed in grief,
fainting and reviving several times.
Shortly after,
someone came to the gate,
claiming he could revive the lady.
Lǐ bowed deeply in reverence,
begging for his protection and assistance.
The man sat on the bed,
seeking vermilion ink to write a talisman.
Before the vermilion ink arrived,
he wrote a talisman in black ink and sent it flying.
When it did not return promptly,
he sent another talisman flying.
Smiling, he said to Lǐ:
"Do not worry,
she will revive shortly."
After a while, Wáng revived.
Lǐ bowed in gratitude dozens of times,
and offered generous gifts with all his might.
The man laughed heartily and said:
"In rescuing from disaster and relieving suffering,
what use are material things?"
With that, he walked out the gate and vanished.
After Wáng regained consciousness,
she said:
"When I first arrived at Huàshān,
I met the lord,
who was very pleased.
He set up a feast on the mountain peak
and joyfully drank with his followers.
After the banquet and music ended,
just as we were about to become intimate,
while toasting with cups,
suddenly I saw a person
riding on a black cloud arrive,
saying:
'The Great One orders the summoning of Lady Wáng.'
The deity remained calm,
asking to wait until the gathering concluded.
Soon, another person arrived on a red cloud,
angrily saying:
'The Great One asks Huàshān why he has taken a living man's wife without permission?
If she is not returned immediately,
there will be severe punishment.'
The deity was greatly alarmed and fearful,
and immediately ordered her sent back home."
Sānwèi
In the early years of the Kāiyuán era,
a Sānwèi officer was returning from the capital to Qīngzhōu.
When he reached the front of the Huàyuè Temple,
he saw a maidservant dressed in blue.
Her clothes were old and worn.
She came forward and said:
"My lady wishes to see you."
She then led him forward.
He encountered a woman,
about sixteen or seventeen years old,
with a sorrowful and haggard appearance.
She said:
"I am not human.
I am the third daughter-in-law of the Huàyuè deity.
My husband is extremely cruel.
My family is in Běihǎi,
and for three years I have had no letters from them.
Because of this, I am especially despised by the Huàyuè family.
I heard that you are returning from afar,
and I wish to trouble you with a letter.
If you can deliver it for me,
my father will surely offer you a generous reward."
She then handed him the letter.
This man was also a trustworthy person.
He asked where in Běihǎi he should deliver it.
The woman said:
"At the second tree by the sea pool,
just knock on it,
and someone will respond."
After speaking, she bid farewell and left.
When he reached Běihǎi,
he delivered the letter as instructed.
After knocking on the tree,
he suddenly saw a vermilion gate appear beneath the tree.
Someone came out from the gate to receive the matter,
and the man handed him the letter.
After a short while inside,
the person came out and said:
"The Great King invites the guest to enter."
Following him for over a hundred steps,
they entered another gate.
There was a man dressed in red,
over ten feet tall,
with thousands of maidservants attending him on both sides.
After the guest was seated,
the man said:
"For three years, I have not received any letters from my daughter."
After reading the letter, he became furious
and said:
"How dare those slaves act like this!"
He then issued an order,
summoning his left and right Yúhóu officers.
They arrived in an instant,
all over ten feet tall,
with huge heads and large noses,
their appearances fearsome.
He ordered them to muster fifty thousand troops
and, by the fifteenth day,
march west to attack Huàshān,
ensuring they would not fail to win.
The two officers received the order and rushed out.
The man then said to the Sānwèi officer:
"I have nothing with which to repay you."
He ordered his attendants to fetch two bolts of silk as a gift for the messenger.
The Sānwèi officer was displeased,
resenting that only two bolts were given.
As they parted,
the man in red said:
"These two bolts of silk are worth twenty thousand strings of cash.
You must sell them for that price,
and be careful not to sell them cheaply to anyone."
After the Sānwèi officer left,
he wanted to verify the matter,
so he went again to Huàyīn.
On the fifteenth day,
as dusk fell,
he saw from afar a black aura like a canopy in the east.
It gradually moved westward,
with thunder rumbling and lightning flashing,
the sound audible for a hundred lǐ.
In a short while,
a great wind arose at Huàshān, breaking trees.
Blowing clouds from the west,
the cloud formations grew even more massive,
advancing directly toward Huàshān.
Thunder, fire, and clamor pressed close,
turning the entire mountain crimson,
and it took a long time before it subsided.
By dawn,
the mountain's color was scorched black.
The Sānwèi officer then went to the capital to sell the silk.
When buyers heard he was asking for twenty thousand strings,
they all scoffed in shock,
thinking him a madman.
A few days later,
a man on a white horse came to buy it.
He immediately paid the full twenty thousand strings
without any hesitation.
The money had already been locked away in the West Market.
The Sānwèi officer then asked what the buyer intended to use it for.
The man said:
"Now,
because the Wèichuān deity is marrying off his daughter,
this will be used as a gift.
In all the world, only Běihǎi silk is the finest.
I was just about to send someone to the market to buy it
when I heard you were selling Běihǎi silk,
so I came."
After the Sānwèi officer received the money,
he spent several months trading goods,
then headed east back to Qīngzhōu.
When he reached Huàyīn,
he saw the same maidservant in blue from before, who said:
"My lady has come especially to thank you for your kindness."
Then he saw a covered ox-drawn carriage
descending from the mountain,
with over ten attendants following on both sides.
When it arrived and she alighted,
it was the same young woman as before,
but now her appearance and attire were radiant,
her gaze clear and bright,
almost unrecognizable.
Seeing
the Sānwèi officer,
she bowed and said:
"Thanks to your great kindness,
my message reached my parents far away.
After the great battle,
the affection between us has deepened considerably.
I am only ashamed that I have nothing with which to repay you.
However, because you delivered the letter,
the third young lord has transferred his anger onto you.
He is now leading five hundred soldiers
to await you at Tóngguān.
If you go there,
you will surely be harmed.
You should return to the capital for now.
Soon, the imperial carriage will journey east.
Ghosts and spirits fear the drum carriage.
If you ride in the drum carriage,
you will have nothing to worry about."
After speaking, she disappeared.
The Sānwèi officer was greatly frightened
and immediately returned to the capital.
Several tens of days later,
it happened that Emperor Xuánzōng was traveling to Luòyáng.
The Sānwèi officer then gave money to the drummer
and followed the drum carriage out of the pass,
thus avoiding any trouble.
Lǐ Shí
Lord Zhào Lǐ Shí,
during the Kāiyuán era,
paid a visit to the Huà Mountain Temple.
Passing by the courtyard of the Three Ladies,
he suddenly saw that the goddesses were all living people.
They invited him into a precious tent,
where they enjoyed the utmost joy and harmony.
The three ladies took turns in sharing intimacy with him,
and after their conversation ended, he left.
At parting, they said to Shí:
"Every year from the seventh to the twelfth day of the seventh month,
the mountain god must ascend to heaven to present his accounts.
When that time comes, we will welcome you,
and you must not decline.
Our meeting today
also coincides with this time,
which is why we could fully enjoy ourselves."
From then on, for seven years,
every time he realized the date had arrived,
he would faint and lose his breath.
His family would watch over him,
and after three days he would awaken.
He recounted:
"Spiritual tents with tortoiseshell mats,
elegant seats and silk cushions.
Moon-shaped fans waved to cool the summer heat,
silk robes trailed, spreading fragrance.
Jade pendants clear and cool,
fragrant breezes wafting gently.
Awaiting Shí's arrival,
all smiled, their starry dimples opening,
flowers charming their jade-like faces.
Speaking of separation brought tears,
discussing newfound joy brought deep affection.
All three ladies were his.
Shí's talent surpassed his capacity,
and he was especially valued by them.
Each expressed their joy and affection to the fullest.
When it was time to return home,
all were sorrowful and sobbed,
lingering in the scene, reluctant to part."
After Shí awoke,
his appearance was drenched in sweat,
and he would fall ill for about ten days before recovering.
A practitioner of arts saw Shí and said:
"You are afflicted by an evil aura."
He wrote a talisman for him.
Afterward, even when they met again,
they could not draw close.
Two of the ladies, one surnamed Wáng and one surnamed Dù,
scolded him, saying:
"Cruel and without virtue,
why did you bring a talisman?"
The youngest lady, surnamed Xiāo,
was especially deep in affection and righteousness.
Tearfully looking at him,
she warned Shí not to speak of it for three years.
Speaking of it would not only harm you,
but also harm me."
Shí asked about his official career,
and she said:
"You are destined to pass the imperial examination as a jìnshì,
and end as a minor county magistrate."
All turned out as she said.
Yè Jìngnéng
At the beginning of the Kāiyuán era,
Emperor Xuánzōng, because the empress had no son,
ordered the Daoist priest Yè Jìngnéng
to submit a memorial to the Jade Capital Heavenly Emperor,
asking:
"Does the empress have a son or not?"
After a long time, the memorial returned,
with the comment: "No son,"
the traces very clear.
Wáng Chānglíng
During the Kāiyuán era,
Wáng Chānglíng of Lángyá,
traveled from Wú to the capital.
Sailing by boat to Mǎdāng Mountain,
taking advantage of favorable winds,
the boatman said:
"Noble guests who arrive here
are all asked to pay respects at the temple."
Chānglíng could not stop,
but he had already prepared offerings for praying to the gods.
Hearing the boatman's words,
he ordered an attendant to bring wine, dried meat, paper horses,
and present them at the temple,
along with straw sandals for the Lady.
He inscribed a poem:
"A dappled horse led from Kūnlún,
presented to the great king without taking money.
Only because fierce winds and waves rush swiftly,
do not blame Chānglíng for not disembarking."
After reading it, he passed by.
When buying the straw sandals,
he also bought a pair of gold-inlaid knives,
and stored them inside the sandals.
When praying to the gods,
he forgot to take them out.
Mistakenly, he sent them along.
Chānglíng, upon reaching his destination ahead,
searched for the inlaid knives,
and only then realized his mistake.
After traveling a few more miles,
suddenly a red carp,
about three feet long,
leapt into Chānglíng's boat.
He called his attendant to cook it.
After cutting open its belly,
he found the gold-inlaid knives,
exactly the ones mistakenly sent to the temple.
Zhāng Jiāyòu
During the Kāiyuán era,
Zhāng Jiāyòu served as the Prefect of Xiàngzhōu.
The official residence had long been haunted,
and as soon as Jiāyòu arrived,
a ghost began to haunt his household,
causing extreme disturbances.
Jiāyòu was not afraid.
In the small hall of the western courtyard, the furnishings,
along with other food items,
were overturned again.
Jiāyòu went to inspect it.
He saw a woman.
Jiāyòu asked the lady which deity she was.
The woman said:
"I am the daughter of the late Great General and Prefect of Xiàngzhōu, Lord Yùchí.
My family has suffered a great injustice,
and I wish to see Your Excellency to present our case."
Jiāyòu said:
"I respectfully await your arrival."
After a short while, she arrived,
her appearance and attire imposing,
her gaze lofty and distant.
She first paid her respects to Jiāyòu,
and Jiāyòu invited her to sit.
He asked her:
"In life, you were a virtuous person;
in death, you are a bright spirit.
Why do you lurk in the shadows of the night,
frightening children,
causing this prefecture
to be known far and wide as a haunted place?
Why would a righteous spirit act in such a manner?"
She replied:
"In the past, when the Zhōu dynasty was in decline,
and Yáng Jiān usurped the throne,
I, as a loyal subject of Zhōu,
could not bear to see the state collapse.
Therefore, to uphold my duty as a subject,
I took the lead in championing righteousness,
hoping to restore order to the realm
and preserve the legacy of Tàizǔ.
Wéi Xiàokuān, an old minister of Zhōu,
failed to rise up for righteousness;
instead, he accepted Yáng Jiān's bridle,
and was used by him.
With the forces of a single prefecture,
I faced the combined armies of the realm.
Though my sincerity sought to pierce the heavens,
no aid came from the four seas.
Soon, I lost my hold,
and my entire family was slaughtered,
the bones of over sixty members
lie beneath this hall.
As time passed,
my hidden grievances grew deeper.
I wished to depart but could not;
I wanted to speak to people,
but all feared death.
Having no one to appeal to, I have come here,
hoping for Your Excellency's compassionate attention.
If my remains are not discarded,
and my spirit is given a place to rest,
then even in death,
it will be as if I were alive."
Jiāyòu promised.
Another day,
he unearthed the accumulated bones
and buried them with proper rites behind the hall.
He then converted the hall into a shrine,
where offerings were made seasonally.
Jiāyòu had a daughter, eight or nine years old,
and whenever the family had questions,
they would have her relay them,
and the spirit would always respond.
When the spirit wished to speak to Jiāyòu,
she would also have the young girl come out to meet him.
This became the usual practice.
Afterward, whenever Jiāyòu's family members traveled,
the spirit would send hidden soldiers to escort them beyond the border.
Upon their return, the soldiers would report
where they had escorted them to.
Their westward escort never went beyond Héyáng Bridge.
A person from Rǔyīn.
In Rǔyīn there was a man surnamed Xǔ,
who was orphaned young.
He was fair-skinned,
handsome in appearance,
fond of fine clothes and good horses,
and unrestrained in his wanderings and gallops.
He often led a yellow hound,
chasing game through wild ravines,
and resting wearily beneath a great tree.
The tree was over a hundred chǐ tall,
several dozen arm-spans in girth,
with lofty branches stretching out on all sides,
their shade covering several mǔ.
Looking up among the branches,
he saw a five-colored silk pouch hanging there.
Thinking someone had mistakenly left it behind,
he took it home,
but the knot could not be undone.
He cherished it greatly, finding it strange,
and placed it in his cap-box.
As evening approached,
it transformed into a young woman,
who, holding a name card, stepped forward directly and said:
"The royal maiden sends word."
After delivering the card,
she departed.
After a short while,
a wondrous fragrance filled the room,
and gradually the sound of carriages and horses was heard.
Xǔ went outside,
and saw rows of torches lined up.
There was a young man,
riding a white horse,
with over ten horsemen following behind,
who came straight to Xǔ and said:
"My younger sister, though of humble family,
secretly admires your noble virtue,
and wishes to entrust a good match to you, sir.
What say you?"
Xǔ, considering them divine beings,
dared not refuse strenuously.
The young man immediately ordered his attendants
to sweep and clean a separate chamber.
In a moment,
the maiden's carriage arrived,
its light and fragrance filling the road.
There were several dozen maidservants on horseback.
All were of beautiful appearance,
holding screens,
and escorting the maiden as she alighted from the carriage.
They invited her into the separate chamber,
where curtains, canopies, mats, and cushions were all provided.
Xǔ's family was greatly astonished,
and looking, they all saw it.
The young man urged Xǔ to bathe,
presented him with new clothes,
and maidservants supported him into the maiden's chamber.
The maiden was sixteen or seventeen years old,
of unparalleled beauty and radiance,
wearing a dark blue robe,
adorned with pearls and jade, resplendent and intricate.
She descended the steps to return his bow.
After they ascended the hall together,
the young man then departed.
In the chamber, a mica screen was set up,
with lotus-patterned emerald curtains,
and walls screened with Lùruì brocade.
A grand feast of rare delicacies was laid out,
with many exotic fruits,
sweet, delicious, fresh, and fragrant,
unlike anything in the mortal world.
The vessels included seven-spiral shells, nine-branch trays, red spiral cups, and lotus-leaf bowls,
all with raised designs in gold,
inlaid with precious jade and greenstone.
There was a jade jar,
storing Chēshī grape wine,
fragrant and intensely potent.
On the seats were placed linked-heart candles,
all set on purple jade trays,
shining bright as day.
Xǔ had always been frivolous and unrestrained,
and now, dazzled by such sights,
his heart was greatly pleased.
Once seated,
Xǔ asked:
"This humble man is rustic and ignorant,
his thatched dwelling lowly and cramped.
I never imagined I would receive such deep regard from you.
Joy and delight mingle within me,
and I know not how to respond."
She replied:
"My father is the General of the Southern Region of Zhōnglè.
Not considering my lowly and humble station,
he wished to entrust me to you, sir,
that I may personally serve and support you.
Fortunately, we have this fine meeting;
my joyful wish is truly profound."
He asked further:
"What office does the General of the Southern Region hold now?"
She said:
"He governs a separate command under Sōng Jūn,
like the Four Garrison Generals of ancient times."
When the wine warmed them, she sighed and said:
"What night is this night?
That I see this good man.
Your words are clear and charming,
unlike anything I have heard or seen."
Then, taking up a zither, she played the tune "The Parting Swan and Crane,"
tilting her neck as she sang,
offering wine to Xǔ.
Her clear voice was plaintive and flowing,
her expression and manner enchanting and unrestrained,
almost beyond her own control.
Xǔ, unable to contain his feelings,
abruptly stepped forward and embraced her.
She then glanced sidelong and smiled, saying:
"Now I incur the poet's ridicule for loosening my sash,
and also disgrace the guest's laughter for snagging his cap string—
what is to be done?"
Thereupon, she turned and ordered the feast cleared,
the candles removed, and they retired to the bed-curtains.
They indulged in joyous intimacy;
her flesh was full, her bones delicate,
soft and smooth as malt sugar.
The next day,
she summoned all the household,
fully observed the rites of a wife,
and bestowed generous gifts upon them.
After three days had passed,
the young man from before came again and said:
"My father feels deeply grateful and ashamed,
and wishes to meet you.
He has sent me to respectfully welcome you."
So Xǔ went with him,
arriving at the former hunting place,
but the great tree was no longer there.
Instead, they saw vermilion gates and white walls,
like those of a great official's residence today.
Guards lined both sides,
all bowing in welcome.
The young man led him inside,
where he saw the Prefect Lord,
wearing a flat-heaven cap,
and a crimson gauze robe,
seated in a high hall.
In the courtyard, halberds were arrayed and banners set up.
Xǔ bowed in audience.
The Prefect Lord rose for him,
bowed and invited him up the steps,
and cordially inquired:
"My young daughter lost her support early.
Fortunately, she may entrust herself to your noble self.
My gratitude and joy are boundless.
Yet this is also a darkly appointed, divine union.
Had it not been for utmost purity resonating,
how could it have come to this?"
Xǔ expressed thanks,
and then entered the inner quarters with him.
The gateways and buildings were solemn and deep,
with winding corridors and curved pavilions,
interconnected throughout.
In the central hall, a grand gathering was held,
the feasting and revelry at its peak.
Thereupon, music was ordered.
Strings and bamboo instruments played in rich complexity,
the melodies novel and unusual.
There were several dozen singing girls,
all exquisitely beautiful, of the finest looks.
After the performance ended,
he bestowed generous gifts of gold and silk upon Xǔ,
and also provided servants and horses,
so that his household
was amply supplied.
Moreover, a mansion was built for him in the village,
all extremely lavish and splendid.
The maiden was especially skilled in the arts of Xuánsù and nurturing life,
and Xǔ's physical strength and vitality
became twice that of ordinary men.
From this, he knew she was truly a divine being.
Later, whenever he returned home,
the maiden always accompanied him,
and the Prefect Lord would send lavish gifts.
After several decades,
they had five sons,
yet her beauty remained undiminished.
Later, when Xǔ died,
she took the children and left together,
and none knew where they went.
Cuī Mǐnké
Cuī Mǐnqiào of Bólíng
was of an upright and straightforward nature,
unafraid of gods or ghosts.
At the age of ten,
he once died suddenly,
and remained dead for eighteen years before reviving.
He himself said he had been wrongly summoned,
and Cuī Mǐnqiào bitterly pleaded his case,
until after over a year he was released.
The King of the Underworld said to Cuī Mǐnqiào:
"You are due to return,
but your body has already decayed.
What is to be done?"
Cuī Mǐnqiào begged and insisted on returning.
The King said:
"You should be reborn instead,
with double the official rank and emoluments."
Cuī Mǐnqiào refused.
The King found it difficult to refute his reasoning,
and hesitated for a long time.
Cuī Mǐnqiào pleaded his grievance,
and the King had no choice.
He sent someone to the Western Regions
to seek the medicine of rebirth.
It took several years before they returned.
When the medicine was applied to the bones,
flesh grew all over,
except on the soles of the feet,
where the bones remained exposed.
Afterwards, his family frequently dreamed of Cuī Mǐnqiào saying:
"I have revived."
They then opened the coffin,
and at first there was breath,
and after nursing him for over a month, he recovered.
Cuī Mǐnqiào, while in the underworld,
had checked and found he was destined to serve as a provincial governor ten times,
so he repeatedly sought dangerous posts,
and treated ghosts and spirits with contempt,
yet fortunately remained unharmed.
Later, he became the governor of Xúzhōu.
No one dared to occupy the main hall,
as it was said
to be the former palace of Xiàng Yǔ.
When Cuī Mǐnqiào arrived in the province,
he immediately ordered it cleaned.
A few days after he began his duties,
a loud shout was suddenly heard in the air:
"I am Xiàng Yǔ, the Hegemon King of Western Chǔ!
Who is Cuī Mǐnqiào,
that he dares seize my dwelling!"
Cuī Mǐnqiào replied calmly:
"How petty, Xiàng Yǔ!
In life you could not contend with Hàn Gāozǔ for the empire,
and in death you compete with Cuī Mǐnqiào over a dilapidated house?
Moreover, you died at Wūjiāng,
your head traveled ten thousand lǐ,
even if some spirit remains,
what is there to fear?"
Then all fell silent,
and the hall was henceforth peaceful.
Later, he became the governor of Huàzhōu.
Beside the shrine of Huàyuè,
someone late one night
heard clamoring in the temple.
Looking in, he saw the courtyard torches blazing brightly.
Hundreds of soldiers were arrayed,
receiving orders:
"We are to accompany the Third Prince to fetch a bride."
Then it was said:
"Governor Cuī is in the province.
Do not recklessly stir up violent storms."
All replied:
"We dare not."
Once they went out,
nothing more was seen.
Zhāng Ān
During the reign of Emperor Xuánzōng,
an edict ordered that shrines be established to honor
meritorious officials, martyrs, chaste women, and filial wives.
In Jiāngzhōu, there was a man named Zhāng Ān,
of a free and unrestrained nature.
Sometimes he would get drunk alone,
singing loudly in the marketplace.
If people laughed at him,
he would become even more unrestrained,
to the point of dancing with hands and feet,
never feeling ashamed.
At other times, he would dress neatly,
carrying his name card to visit officials,
calling himself Fúshēngzǐ (the Drifter).
Later, he suddenly died without illness,
and his family buried him.
Every night,
his spirit would visit the governor,
requesting a shrine be built for him.
His words were impassioned,
no different from when he was alive.
At the time, Lǐ Xuán was governor,
a straightforward man who did not believe in supernatural nonsense.
But after repeatedly hearing his attendants report,
he put on his court robes and sat,
summoning and questioning the spirit,
which appeared upon being called.
Lǐ Xuán asked:
"You are already dead.
How can you manifest like a person?
Your speech is clear,
and you seek an audience with me.
By what means have you achieved this?
You must explain first,
then I will discuss the matter of a shrine with you."
The spirit said:
"Generally, the spiritual essence of humans
is unsurpassed.
The monstrous manifestations of creatures,
though they may possess some spiritual power,
are like clouds and mud in comparison.
Humans receive the harmonious and combined qi of heaven and earth
to be able to take form.
Thus, the human face bears the features of the Five Peaks and Four Rivers,
the head resembles the roundness of heaven,
the feet resemble the squareness of earth.
We inherently possess wisdom to comprehend all matters,
and courage to withstand all evils.
How could there be no spirit after death?
Moreover, during Fúshēngzǐ's life,
he did not regard life as life;
and at his death,
he did not regard death as death.
His life was already different from the masses,
and his death is also different from ordinary beings.
Today, hearing of Your Excellency's wisdom
and encountering the Emperor's grace,
if I do not seek a shrine,
later generations will laugh at Fúshēngzǐ for not being as worthy as the deceased women of former times.
I earnestly hope you will consider this carefully.
If a shrine is established by Your Excellency,
it would make Fúshēngzǐ's death more honorable than his life,
and also sufficiently show the error of human greed for life and fear of death."
The governor said:
"The Emperor establishes shrines for meritorious officials, martyrs, filial daughters, and chaste women of former times
to serve as encouragement and warning,
desiring later generations to emulate them.
If a shrine is established for you,
what would you have later generations emulate?"
The spirit said:
"Fúshēngzǐ has no merit, filial piety, or chastity to record.
Your Excellency does not realize that the Way of the enlightened
is loftier than merit, martyrdom, filial piety, or chastity."
The governor could not refute this,
and ordered a private shrine be built.
Qiú Jiāfú
Táng Qiú Jiāfú was a man from Fùpíng in Jīngzhào.
His home was in Bùtái Village.
He went to Luòyáng to take the imperial examinations.
Upon leaving the capital,
he encountered a young man
whose appearance resembled that of a king.
His fur robes, horse, and retinue were exceedingly grand.
Seeing Jiāfú, he appeared pleased
and asked where he was going.
Jiāfú said,
"I am going to the capital for the examinations."
The man said,
"I am also heading east.
I am delighted to have your company."
Jiāfú asked his surname,
and he replied,
"The surname is Bái."
Jiāfú secretly thought that there were no noblemen with the surname Bái in the imperial court
and felt somewhat suspicious.
After a day,
the man said to Jiāfú,
"Your donkey is weak
and cannot keep up.
Please ride in the carriage behind."
After several days,
they reached Huàyuè Temple.
The man said to Jiāfú,
"I am no ordinary person.
The Heavenly Emperor has sent me to investigate the ghosts and deities of the world.
Now I must enter the temple to conduct interrogations.
Your fate is intertwined with mine from past connections.
Since things have come to this,
would you enter the temple with me?
Once the matter is concluded,
we shall proceed to the capital together."
Jiāfú had no choice
and followed him into the temple gate.
Inside, he saw dark green curtains and somber clouds,
with furnishings arranged in great detail.
In front was a bed.
The nobleman sat before the table,
and Jiāfú was seated on a bamboo chair beside the bed.
Soon, an order was issued to summon the god of Mount Huà.
The god arrived and prostrated himself.
The nobleman called out and reprimanded him several times,
then ordered his attendants to drag him out.
He summoned all the deities of Guānzhōng,
calling their names and inspecting them.
When it came to the god of Kūnmíng Pond,
he was called up the steps to speak.
He requested that Jiāfú keep a slight distance
and not involve himself in this discussion.
Jiāfú went behind the hall into a curtained area,
where he heard sounds of agony outside the curtain.
Parting the curtain,
he saw his own wife's head hanging from a tree in the courtyard.
Realizing she must be dead,
he was overcome with grief and horror.
Shortly after,
the nobleman summoned him back.
Seeing Jiāfú's distressed expression,
he asked the reason.
Jiāfú told him everything truthfully.
The nobleman ordered another inspection,
and the report confirmed it was true.
The nobleman exclaimed in shock,
"Your wife is as my wife.
How could I not handle this?"
He then issued an order to summon the god of Mount Huà.
When the god arrived,
he was asked why he had taken the wife of Qiú Jiāfú from Bùtái Village,
causing her such torment.
The god initially claimed not to know.
A man in blue robes,
who was the investigating officer,
stepped forward and replied on his behalf,
"This matter was summoned by the Heavenly Court.
Now the written order is presented."
The nobleman ordered the case file brought forward,
sealed it with a command,
and said that when it reached the Heavenly Emperor's court,
it should be presented,
as he had already reported to the Emperor.
Turning to the god of Mount Huà,
he said, "Release her immediately."
He also said to Jiāfú,
"I originally intended to go to the capital,
but now it is not possible.
You should return quickly to Fùpíng."
Then, counting on his fingers to estimate the journey,
he said,
"It will take four days to arrive,
but I fear that will be too late.
I shall lend you a swift horse.
If you think of me later,
burn incense in a pure chamber,
and I will surely come."
With these words, he bid farewell and left.
Once outside the gate,
a divine servant arrived with a horse.
Jiāfú mounted the horse
and immediately reached his home.
His family was in sudden mourning and weeping.
Jiāfú went straight in,
removed the cloth covering his wife's face, and waited for her breath.
After a short while, she revived.
The whole family celebrated with joy.
The village elders
toasted with jugs of wine in congratulation,
and the festivities lasted for several days.
Four or five days later,
Jiāfú himself arrived riding his donkey,
accompanied by his servant.
His family could not distinguish between them.
When the one inside went out and met the one outside,
they merged into one,
and only then did they realize that the one who had returned earlier was his soul.
Over a year later,
Jiāfú again went to the capital for the examinations.
When he reached Huàyuè Temple,
he encountered the wife of Cuī, the judicial officer of Dèngzhōu, who had died suddenly.
The wailing was exceedingly sorrowful,
and Jiāfú felt deep compassion.
He personally went to Cuī
and told him to stop weeping,
promising to handle the matter.
Cuī was overjoyed.
Jiāfú burned incense in a pure chamber
and thought of the nobleman.
After a short while, he arrived.
After joyful greetings,
Jiāfú explained the reason.
The nobleman said,
"This was done by the god of Mount Huà.
It is indeed possible to save her.
I will obtain two hundred thousand coins for you.
First request the money,
then take action."
He then wrote nine talismans
and said,
"First burn three talismans.
If she does not recover,
burn the remaining six,
and she will return."
With these words, he flew away.
Jiāfú relayed the divine words to Cuī,
and Cuī did not dare to disobey.
He first burned three talismans,
but by evening, she had not recovered.
He then burned the remaining ones,
and shortly after, she revived.
Cuī asked his wife,
and she said,
"When I first entered the inn,
I suddenly saw a mica carriage at the steps,
with several hundred strong soldiers,
each holding weapons,
lined up on both sides.
A message was conveyed that the king had sent for me,
and in haste, I followed.
The king was pleased to see me
and was about to form a union,
when suddenly three men arrived and said,
'The Great Unity God asks why you have seized a living man's wife?'
The god was terrified
and held up a register, saying,
'Heaven destined her to be my wife;
I did not take her unjustly.'
Yet he refused to release me.
Shortly after,
five or six great gods arrived,
holding golden pestles,
and came to the king's hall.
The followers scattered in fear,
and the god stood alone under a tree,
begging for his life to be spared.
The king then brought me back."
From this, Jiāfú realized that the nobleman was the Great Unity God.
Afterward, whenever Jiāfú thought of him, he would surely come,
and he helped Jiāfú change five or six official posts,
greatly aiding him.
The man who ate mutton.
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
there was a man who was fond of eating sheep heads.
One morning, as he was going out,
he encountered a strange creature at his gate,
with a sheep’s head and a human body,
dressed in magnificent attire.
It addressed the man, saying:
"I am a spirit of the sheep,
belonging to the sheep kind.
Because you are so fond of eating sheep heads,
I have come to seek you out.
If you cease eating them, that will be the end of it;
if not,
I will kill you."
The man was greatly terrified,
and thereafter he never ate sheep heads again.
Wáng Jùn
Wáng Jùn possessed a majestic and imposing presence,
with the bearing of a dragon or tiger.
He recruited volunteers and inspired them with righteousness,
displaying the manner of the ancients.
He governed his subordinates with strict discipline,
and both the people and officials feared him yet respected his integrity.
After Wáng Jùn’s death,
Xìn’ān Wáng Lǐ Huī,
while campaigning against the Xī in Yōuzhōu and reporting a victory,
submitted a memorial stating
that the soldiers had all seen Wáng Jùn leading troops as the vanguard to attack the enemy.
The Vice Director of the Ministry of Revenue, Yáng Bóchéng, submitted a memorial
requesting that the burial mound of Wáng Jùn be expanded,
that an envoy be sent to offer sacrifices,
and that his descendants be granted special favors.
Emperor Xuánzōng complied with these requests.
Huángfǔ Xún,
courtesy name Jūnhé.
During the Kāiyuán era,
he was appointed as a military advisor in Huàzhōu.
He died suddenly,
and his soul seemed to be on a long, broad road,
lined with many locust trees on both sides.
He saw several officials holding brooms,
and Xún asked them about it.
They replied:
"The General of the Five Paths often rests his horses here."
Only then did Xún realize he was dead,
and he sighed as he walked on.
Suddenly, several officials in yellow robes appeared,
holding warrants,
saying they were summoned by the Celestial Ministry,
and they hurriedly forced him to a certain place.
The gate towers were very lofty,
resembling the Shàngdōng Gate,
and there was another gate,
similar to the gate of the Department of State Affairs.
There were many guards at the gate,
and they were just about to lead him in
when one official said:
"You hold an official position,
so you must be reported separately.
Wait for a break in the duties."
Xún stood respectfully, waiting.
After a short while,
he saw people on the street startled and making way.
Soon, several hundred riders approached from the east,
with spears and halberds leading the way.
Xún hid himself by the wall gate to peek.
As they drew nearer,
he saw an elderly woman,
under a large canopy,
driving a carriage pulled by four horses,
with a large retinue of riders.
Xún looked closely,
and it turned out to be his aunt by marriage, Madame Xuē.
Xún then hurried out and bowed down,
stating his name.
The aunt halted her horse and asked Xún:
"Who are you?
I don't remember at all."
Xún then called out his childhood name,
and the aunt said happily:
"How did you get here?"
Xún answered truthfully.
The aunt said:
"Among my nephews, you have the most blessings.
Coming here was a mistake.
Moreover, I have recently taken up a post here,
and I am busy with duties.
You may come to my residence to meet me."
After saying this, she passed by.
After a short while,
the judge called him in during a break in his duties.
Xún saw a man in official attire,
who haughtily greeted him,
and Xún pleaded with him pitifully.
The man said to Xún:
"Did you perform any virtuous deeds in the mortal world?"
Xún replied:
"Yes, I did."
The man lowered his head and laughed, saying:
"This is not a place for false words."
He turned to his attendants and said:
"Summon the castrator,
bring the castration tools."
Xún was terrified.
Suddenly, the sound of urgent news was heard,
that the king had sent a messenger,
and the judge hurried out,
bowing to receive the command.
Xún peeked and saw
a eunuch delivering the message,
who then left.
The judge bowed and saw him off outside the gate,
then returned
and said to Xún:
"Just now, the great envoy gave an order,
saying that you should not have come here,
and that the authorities made a mistake.
You may see the great envoy yourself,
and then you can return."
Several officials led him away,
and they traveled west for three or four lǐ,
arriving at a prefectural mansion,
with banners and flags crowding the gate.
Xún was ordered to enter.
Looking up,
he saw his aunt seated in the great hall,
who ordered him to sit.
Xún bowed and sat down,
with guards standing solemnly around.
Beside her was a monk sitting cross-legged on a precious seat,
with two attendants by his side,
and Xún also bowed to him.
His aunt then recounted the affairs of their family and relatives,
instructing Xún on the principles of benevolence and righteousness,
and explaining the workings of karma.
She then said:
"Child, have you not heard of hell?
This is the place,
and you must take a look at it."
His aunt turned to the monk and said:
"Please guide this child."
The monk then straightened his robes
and said to Xún:
"Follow me."
Xún followed behind him.
After walking about one or two lǐ,
they saw a black wind in the distance,
stretching from above to below,
with smoke billowing endlessly.
Within it was a black city,
with flames flying fiercely.
As they approached the city,
the black gas parted about ten feet away from the monk.
When they reached the city,
the gate opened by itself,
and they entered.
Inside, they saw sinners on both sides,
some being skinned alive and having their blood sucked,
others being chopped, stabbed, and crushed to pieces,
their cries of pain and resentment
echoing throughout the place,
too many to count,
and the sounds of agony shook the earth.
Xún trembled in fear and unease,
and begged to return.
Looking north, he saw another gate,
blazing with flames,
and the monk pointed and said:
"That is the gate to the Avīci hell."
Just as he finished speaking and was about to return,
they suddenly heard someone in the flames calling Xún.
Xún looked and saw
a monk sitting on an iron bed,
with an iron nail driven into his head,
blood flowing down to the ground.
Looking closely,
it was his disciple monk Hú Biàn.
Xún asked in shock,
and the monk said:
"In life, I drank and ate meat with others and with you.
Now, in this situation,
I regret it deeply.
Since you are now following the monk,
you will surely have great blessings.
Please, save me."
Xún asked:
"How can I save you?"
The monk said:
"Copy one volume of the Golden Light Sutra,
and build a stone pillar in the marketplace for me.
Only then can I be reborn as an animal."
Xún sadly agreed.
They then returned to the hall,
and Xún recounted everything he had seen.
His aunt said:
"Strive to do good,
and you will not end up like this."
She then said:
"Child, do you want to know about your future official positions?"
Xún said:
"I would like to know."
Soon, a yellow-robed official brought a document,
and she ordered it to be opened and read under the eaves.
Xún saw many capital official positions listed.
Another section
mentioned the Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury being demoted to Prefect of Miánzhōu,
but the rest was covered up.
The official said:
"You are not supposed to know this."
She then ordered two people to escort Xún back,
and he bowed twice before leaving.
After exiting the gate,
he asked the two officials for their surnames.
One was named Jiāo,
and the other was named Wáng.
They traveled west together for over ten lǐ.
A three-legged sheep appeared,
blocking the road and roaring,
cursing Xún:
"I have been waiting for you for a long time!
Why did you cut off one of my legs?"
Xún truly did not remember,
so he asked,
and the sheep said:
"On a certain day in a certain year,
in the hall of a certain county's deputy magistrate,
you boasted about your ability to cut off a sheep's leg.
At that time, there was no sheep,
so the deputy magistrate had a butcher
cut off one of my legs alive and take it away,
and I died from it."
I died because of you."
Xǔn then realized,
and humbly apologized,
explaining himself by claiming to be a butcher.
The two officials, Jiāo and Wáng,
also helped resolve the dispute.
The sheep stood blocking the road,
so Xǔn could not leave.
He then apologized and said:
"Shall I perform meritorious deeds for you?"
The sheep said:
"Quickly copy the Diamond Sutra for me."
He agreed,
and the sheep happily left.
The two officials also said:
"Fortunately, we were able to escort you,
and we too would like to share in your kindness,
each requesting one volume."
He agreed to both.
After walking another li or so,
the two officials said:
"We are only supposed to escort you this far.
You, sir, must find your own way from here.
Another li or two ahead,
there is a shop selling fermented drink.
Beside the shop, there is a slanted path.
Within a hundred paces,
you will reach home."
They then parted ways.
Xǔn walked alone,
suffering from exhaustion and thirst.
Sure enough, he came to a shop.
The shop had a water jar,
but no one was in sight.
Xǔn secretly took some drink,
when suddenly an old man shouted angrily,
holding a knife and chasing him,
cursing:
"You thief, drinking my drink!"
Xǔn was terrified and retreated,
but the old man came swiftly.
Xǔn looked back,
and suddenly fell into a pit,
and in a daze, he came back to life.
He had been in the coffin,
dead for five or six days.
Soon, his wife sensed something unusual,
opened the coffin to look,
and found him faintly breathing.
After a long time, he was able to speak,
and ordered three volumes of the Diamond Sutra to be copied urgently.
That night, they suddenly heard knocking at the door,
and a gust of wind blew.
A clear voice from the air said:
"Jiāo and Wáng,
thanks to your meritorious deeds,
have now ascended to heaven."
The whole family heard it.
More than a month later,
Master Hú Biàn came from the capital.
Xǔn found it strange,
and no longer drank with him.
The monk was very resentful.
Xǔn, in a quiet place,
briefly told him about seeing him in the underworld like this,
but the monk refused to believe it.
Later, when he went to Xìnzhōu,
he suddenly developed a head sore.
It quickly festered and ulcerated,
and he became critically ill.
The monk said:
"Was Xǔn's account divine?"
He died a few days later.
Xǔn then had a stone pillar erected in the temple.
When the pillar was just completed,
that day in the market, a pig gave birth to six piglets,
one of them white.
It went to the pillar on its own,
circled it for several days,
and then died from exhaustion.
The pillar still exists today.
Xǔn later indeed became Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Treasury,
was demoted to Prefect of Miánzhōu, and died there.
Wèi Tíngxùn,
from Hénán,
repeatedly failed the imperial examinations.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he devoted himself to music and wine,
and always treated others to drinks.
He often roamed the East Market,
where he met friends drinking at a tavern.
One day,
he happened to meet a fellow examination candidate,
and they hit it off very well,
so he invited him to drink.
Tíngxùn treated him again,
and this person became dazed and drunk.
Tíngxùn said:
"You haven't drunk much,
why are you drunk?"
He replied:
"I am not human,
but the deity of the Zǐtóng Temple in Huáyuán.
Yesterday, I passed by the tavern
and was already drunk on your wine.
So today I came to visit you,
and the drunkard was also moved by your sincerity.
Now I must return to the temple.
If someday you are in need,
you should come visit me."
After saying this, he left.
Ten days later,
Tíngxùn went to visit him.
Arriving at the temple,
the deity had already sent two attendants to welcome Tíngxùn inside.
Tíngxùn was about to bow,
but the deity said:
"I am young,
let us be brothers."
The deity then bowed to Tíngxùn as his elder brother,
and prepared wine, food, and music for him.
When evening came, Tíngxùn returned home.
The next day, he visited again,
and told the deity about his poverty.
The deity turned to his attendants and said:
"Look in Huáyuán County for a wealthy person whose fortune is declining,
and bring their living soul here."
The ghosts searched everywhere,
and found that the wife of the county magistrate, Wéi, was in decline,
so they took her soul.
They covered her heart,
and Wéi suddenly felt heart pain, nearly dying.
The deity said to Tíngxùn:
"You can go now,
and get two hundred thousand coins to cure her."
Tíngxùn then returned to his host,
and posted a notice himself, saying:
"Specializes in curing heart pain."
The magistrate summoned him.
Tíngxùn followed the deity's instructions,
demanded two hundred thousand coins,
and the magistrate agreed.
Tíngxùn administered the medicine,
and she recovered as before.
The children rejoiced,
and the magistrate was pleased,
giving him money for a feast.
From then on, he was drunk every day.
His host advised him:
"You should hide your poverty,
why do you spend so recklessly?"
Tíngxùn said:
"As long as the Zǐtóng deity is here,
why worry about poverty!"
The host reported this to the magistrate,
who summoned and questioned him,
and Tíngxùn told him everything truthfully.
The magistrate was furious,
expelled Tíngxùn, and burned down the Zǐtóng Temple.
Tíngxùn stayed overnight at a village inn,
when suddenly the Zǐtóng deity appeared and said:
"It was not your fault, elder brother,
but my own fate to decline.
I am now going to Zhuójǐn River to establish a temple,
which will be even more prosperous than before.
You can come visit me there."
After saying this, he disappeared.
Tíngxùn went to Zhuójǐn River,
and indeed found a new temple.
The deity appeared in the dreams of the locals,
telling them to invite Scholar Wèi to be the temple caretaker.
The next day,
the locals invited him to stay.
At the end of the year,
the deity said to Tíngxùn:
"I am going to the heavenly court,
to ask about your official salary and lifespan."
He left for several days and returned,
saying to Tíngxùn:
"Next year, elder brother, you will achieve fame,
and become the Registrar of Jīngyáng.
Before your term is completed,
someone will welcome you to serve as a judge."
The deity then prepared a farewell feast for him.
Arriving in the capital,
the following year, he indeed achieved fame,
and was appointed Registrar of Jīngyáng County.
After serving for two years,
during a leisurely moment in his duties,
he was standing alone in the main hall,
when a yellow-robed official
entered holding a document,
bowed, and said:
"By order of the heavenly court, you are appointed judge."
He died that very night.
Wéi Xiùzhuāng
During the Kāiyuán era,
Wéi Xiùzhuāng, the prefect of Huá Prefecture,
came to the city tower in his leisure time to gaze at the Yellow River.
Suddenly, he saw a person in the tower,
about three chǐ tall,
wearing purple clothes and a vermilion crown.
The figure announced his name and paid his respects.
Knowing he was not human,
Xiùzhuāng asked what deity he was.
The figure replied:
"I am the lord of the city god."
Xiùzhuāng asked further why he had come.
He answered:
"The god of the Yellow River
wants to destroy my city
to straighten the river's course,
and I firmly refuse.
In five days,
we will have a great battle by the riverbank.
I fear my strength is insufficient,
so I have come to seek your help, Governor.
If I can have two thousand men,
armed with bows and crossbows,
to assist me in various ways,
I will surely achieve victory.
This is your city,
so I leave it to you to consider."
Xiùzhuāng agreed,
and the deity vanished.
When the day arrived,
Xiùzhuāng led two thousand elite soldiers to the city wall.
Suddenly, the river became dark and gloomy.
After a short while,
a white vapor rose straight up over ten zhàng high,
while a blue vapor emerged from the tower,
and the two intertwined.
Xiùzhuāng ordered his archers to shoot wildly at the white vapor.
The vapor gradually shrank,
until it vanished,
leaving only the blue vapor,
which meandered like cloud-covered peaks
and returned into the tower.
Initially,
the Yellow River flowed close beneath the city walls,
but afterward, it gradually receded,
and to this day, it is five or six lǐ away.
Huà Yuè Shénnǚ
In recent times, there was a scholar who traveled to the capital to take the imperial examinations.
On his way, passing through Guānxī,
he stayed overnight in a small room at an inn.
Suddenly, several attendants of a noble person arrived,
saying:
"The princess is coming to stay here."
They enclosed the inn and four or five other nearby establishments with curtains.
The people inside were initially panicked,
and had no time to move elsewhere.
Soon after,
the sound of the princess's carriage arrived loudly,
and everyone alighted.
The people in the inn then shut their doors and went to bed,
not daring to come out.
The princess bathed in front of the door,
and ordered a search of the rooms.
A maidservant said:
"There shouldn't be anyone here."
But then they saw the scholar,
and the maidservants scolded him loudly.
The princess ordered him to be brought out,
and after looking at him carefully, she said:
"This scholar is quite pleasing to people's hearts;
he should not be humiliated."
She then ordered him to enter the room.
After bathing, she summoned him,
and their conversation was very agreeable.
She had her maidservants wash him,
and dressed him in beautiful clothes.
Then, she set up a crimson curtain,
spread out brocade cushions,
and other sleeping and playthings,
all of the utmost worldly luxury,
and treated him with great affection.
The next day, they returned to the capital together.
The princess's residence was in Huáiyuǎn Lǐ,
with several hundred male and female servants inside and out,
and its splendor and prosperity
were unmatched at the time.
The household addressed the scholar as the consort,
and the utensils, clothing, carriages, and horses he used when going out
were no different from those of princes and dukes.
The scholar had parents
living in their old home.
The princess sent maidservants to pay respects at their home,
delivering hundreds of millions in cash,
and other gifts in proportion.
The scholar's family thus became wealthy,
and flourished in honor and prosperity.
After seven years like this,
they had two sons and one daughter.
Suddenly, the princess said
she wanted to arrange a marriage for him.
The scholar was very surprised,
and wondered why she said this.
The princess said:
"I am not human by nature,
and it is not fitting for me to be your wife for long.
You should also have a marriage in your destiny.
Know that this is not due to a decline in affection."
Afterward, he indeed married another,
but his visits to the princess never ceased.
His wife's family, because he would often be gone for several days at a time,
sent someone to watch him.
They saw him constantly entering an abandoned residence,
and feared he was bewitched by ghosts or spirits.
One day,
they got him drunk,
and then had a sorcerer write talismans,
which they placed in his clothes,
covering his entire body.
Later, when the scholar went again to the princess's home,
she had her servants come out to stop him,
not allowing him to enter.
At first, he did not understand the reason,
and leaned against the door in melancholy.
Soon, the princess came out to the door,
and reproached him severely, saying:
"You were originally a poor scholar,
and I raised you up.
Now you are a noble man—
this is also no small favor to you.
Why did you let your wife's family write talismans to come between us?
Do you think I cannot kill you?
The scholar looked at his body,
and only then realized there were talismans.
He begged for forgiveness most earnestly.
The princess said:
"I also understand your feelings in this matter,
but the talisman's command has already taken effect,
and the situation cannot be maintained."
She called all their children,
and had them bid farewell to their father.
The scholar wept and sobbed.
The princess ordered her attendants to pack quickly,
and they left the city that same day.
The scholar asked where she lived,
and also requested her name.
The princess said:
"I am the third daughter of Huà Yuè."
After speaking, she bid farewell and left,
vanishing as soon as she stepped out the door.
Wáng Xiàn
Wáng Xiàn,
in his youth, sat for the examination to become an Imperial Messenger.
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
he entered the capital.
Upon reaching the west of the palace gates,
he rested beneath a locust tree,
and heard
the sound of an imperial proclamation being announced.
Suddenly, he saw several riders,
appearing like palace eunuchs,
who said to Xiàn:
"For the one being summoned,
you are truly an Imperial Messenger."
They then had Xiàn mount one of the horses behind them.
Xiàn did not know who they were,
but hastily followed along.
After a long time,
they arrived at the temple of the god of Mount Huà.
The messengers placed Xiàn in a separate courtyard,
admonishing him:
"Be careful not to look around privately."
They then entered the inner quarters.
Xiàn sat alone,
when he heard the sounds of beating and painful cries from caning,
so he went forward and secretly peeked.
He saw his wife, seized by the neck and tied to a tree by the officials,
being beaten with clubs.
Xiàn stood there in sorrow and distress.
A palace eunuch came out,
saw his grief, and asked the reason.
Xiàn wept,
and recounted the entire event.
The eunuch said:
"We originally intended to keep you here,
but since your wife has died,
it is not right for you to stay.
If you delay further,
and wait until after you return,
you will be unable to save her.
You should return quickly and open the coffin—
this will revive your wife."
He then ordered his attendants to fetch a post horse,
and sent off Messenger Wáng.
Suddenly, a fox appeared.
Xiàn, having no alternative,
mounted the fox and galloped off.
It was as swift as the wind,
and in two days, they reached his home.
The fox he rode was actually his soul.
Xiàn's physical body, ever since his soul departed,
had lost its voice and could not speak.
Once his soul arrived home,
his family was weeping in sorrow.
Xiàn ordered the coffin opened,
and his wife revived,
saying to Xiàn:
"How did you get here?"
The entire household rejoiced.
Ten days later,
his physical body finally arrived.
Word spread outside:
"Master Wáng has returned!"
He had been mute for over ten days.
His soul said:
"Master Wáng has arrived."
They went out the gate to welcome him,
and thus his soul merged with his body.
Hán Guāngzuò
Hán Guāngzuò, the magistrate of Táolín,
was taking his family to assume his post,
and along the way passed by the temple of Mount Huà.
He alighted from the carriage to pay his respects.
Upon entering the temple gate,
his beloved concubine suddenly died.
The magistrate summoned a shaman to inquire,
and the shaman said:
"The Third Lord fancies your concubine.
Since you have requested it, he will spare her for now,
but he will take her once you reach the county."
When Guāngzuò arrived at the county,
he summoned a goldsmith,
and had him cast a gold statue of Guānyīn Bodhisattva for the concubine,
but did not inform her of this.
Five days later,
the concubine suddenly died,
and after half a day revived,
saying:
"Just now, the Lord of Mount Huà
had carriages and horsemen prepared to welcome me.
As I went out the gate,
there was a monk,
golden in color,
who blocked the way in front,
and the carriages and horsemen dared not pass.
The god said:
'Leave her for now,
and welcome her again in three days.'" Guāngzuò understood the reason,
and again used one thousand coins
to commission an image of the Bodhisattva.
When the time came, she died again,
and after a while revived, saying:
"Just now, I was again welcomed,
but there were two monks present,
and before I could board the carriage,
the god said:
'She cannot be taken yet,
take her again in three days.'" Guāngzuò again used one thousand coins to summon the goldsmith,
ordering him to create another statue.
The craftsman took the money and left the county,
where he encountered someone holding a pig,
about to slaughter it.
The craftsman took pity,
and used all the money to redeem it,
so the statue was not made.
Yet the concubine died again,
and shortly after revived, saying:
"I have been spared.
Just now, I was again welcomed,
with even more carriages and horsemen,
but two monks guarded the gate,
and they could not enter.
There was a huge boar, as large as a horse,
that charged at the horsemen,
knocking down all in its path,
and the carriages and horsemen retreated.
The god sent word saying:
'Do not take her again.'
Thereupon, they dispersed."
Guāngzuò wondered how a pig could have repelled them,
and the goldsmith then explained the reason.
From then on, he truly believed in Buddhism.
The Registrar of Xuānzhōu
In Wú customs, people fear ghosts,
and every prefecture and county must have a City God.
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
the Registrar of Xuānzhōu died,
and was brought to see the City God.
The god's dwelling was deep and layered,
with lofty and imposing halls,
and stern, solemn guards armed with weapons.
After the Registrar entered,
the Prefectural Lord asked about his conduct throughout his life.
The Registrar declared himself innocent,
wrongfully seized.
The Prefectural Lord said:
"Indeed,
I shall let you go.
Do you recognize me at all?"
The Registrar said:
"I am lowly and ignorant,
and truly do not recognize you."
The Prefectural Lord said:
"I am Huán Yí, the Internal Historian of Xuānchéng during the Jìn dynasty,
and now serve as the god overseeing this commandery."
After reviving, the Registrar recounted this.
Cuī Yuán
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Cuī Yuán was in Yìzhōu.
On the third day of the third month in late spring,
he, along with dozens to a hundred guests and military officers,
prepared boats to cruise on the river,
while the city's people crowded the banks to watch.
On that day,
the breeze was gentle and pleasant,
the waves flowed calmly.
At the start of the banquet, music was played,
and the guests and attendants were orderly and respectful.
Suddenly, from over ten miles downstream,
the sounds of silk and bamboo instruments competed in performance,
laughter and chatter were boisterous,
carried by the wind and water,
as if just a short distance away.
In a short while, they gradually drew closer—
hundreds of tower-like ships,
blocking the river as they arrived.
All had brocade and embroidery for sails,
gold and jade adorning the boats,
with banners, canopies, and umbrellas,
flags, spears, and halberds,
dazzling in a riot of colors.
Among them were several dozen officials in crimson and purple robes,
and nearly a hundred courtesans in fine silks,
drinking and playing music in the midst of their revelry.
The other boats were lined with five or six thousand accompanying officials and armed guards, holding weapons and maintaining strict security.
They sailed up and down the midstream.
After a long while, they passed by.
Cuī Yuán immediately ordered inquiries to be made.
Following them for several miles,
they approached the boats,
when voices from the boats said:
"The Son of Heaven is about to visit Bājiàn,
and the various revered deities of Shǔzhōng
are relocating to avoid His Majesty's carriage.
We hope you do not find it too strange."
Cuī Yuán was shocked and astonished,
and thus ended the gathering.
At that time, the court was untroubled by affairs,
but from this point on, he began making preparations in advance.
The following year, the emperor made a southern tour,
and Cuī Yuán was able to respond promptly without any shortcomings.
Zhèng Rénjūn
was the son of Qīn Shuō.
He was erudite and well-informed,
possessing his father's demeanor.
Outside the Shàngdōng Gate of Luòyáng, he had a country villa,
where he lived with his younger brother and a maternal cousin.
His younger brother had a sister,
who was married to the son of Yáng Guózhōng.
At that time, the cousin had lost his sight due to a seasonal illness,
with long eyelashes drooping over his eyes.
Moreover, from his hairline,
down the center of his nose,
to his chin,
the left side was cold as ice and pale in color,
while the right side was hot as fire and flushed red.
His aunt and brother both pitied him,
but did not know what illness it was.
At that time, there was a man named Zhèng in Luòyáng,
known as a diviner.
Previously, the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Cuī Lín,
while on a mission to Héshuò,
passed through Luòyáng.
Knowing that Zhèng possessed special skills,
he summoned him to accompany him.
When the mission was completed and he returned,
they entered Luòyáng.
Zhèng was traveling behind,
and upon reaching the road by the Shàngdōng Gate,
knowing that Rénjūn’s villa was by the roadside,
he went to visit him.
Before entering the village gate,
Zhèng suddenly exclaimed that he deserved death,
or said he was fated to die,
his words and expression filled with fear.
Rénjūn asked him about it,
but Zhèng said nothing else,
only repeating that he was fated to die.
Rénjūn pressed him further,
and Zhèng said:
"I just passed by here,
and unfortunately, being hungry and thirsty,
I knew a member of my clan lived here,
so I rashly came as an uninvited guest.
Little did I know it was utterly inappropriate to come,
for this means I am fated to die today."
Rénjūn said:
"Only my aunt, my brother, and I are here,
there are no other strangers,
why are you so afraid?"
Zhèng trembled even more with fear.
Rénjūn initially did not consider his blind cousin
as someone to be reckoned with,
but suddenly remembered the strange condition of his illness, with its cold and hot sides.
How could he know that Zhèng was not concerned about this?
So he described his cousin's condition in detail.
Zhèng said:
"He is a judge of the heavenly court,
while I am a minor clerk in the underworld.
Today I happened to come here,
not because I intended to offend.
However, whether I pay my respects or not, I will die.
If I do not pay my respects, I will also die.
According to propriety, I must pay my respects."
He then wrote a name card, saying:
"Zhèng, law clerk of the underworld, pays his respects with a double bow."
At that time, Rénjūn's brother and cousin
were tossing coins as a game in the main hall.
Rénjūn then called Zhèng from behind the door screen
and read his name card to announce him.
Zhèng hurried in,
bowed twice to apologize, and then left.
The cousin looked back twice,
his long eyelashes fluttering,
as if he were angry.
Rénjūn apologized on his behalf, saying:
"He did not know you were here,
so he came.
I hope you can forgive his offense, is that possible?"
After a long while, the cousin clearly said:
"For my elder brother's sake, I forgive him."
Rénjūn questioned him repeatedly,
but he never spoke again.
His aunt heard of this,
summoned him behind the screen,
and tried to persuade him with maternal affection,
urging him to speak,
but he stubbornly refused to explain the reason.
Several years later,
he suddenly said to his mother:
"Quickly pack your belongings.
Troops will soon arrive here,
and both capitals will fall into chaos and turmoil.
Take me into the city,
and seek refuge with my sister, the Yáng family.
Ask for two or three hundred thousand cash,
and within ten days, we must plan to return east to the Jiānghuái region to avoid the chaos.
At that time, the entire Yáng family, all hundred members,
will be exterminated,
only my sister and her child
can be spared."
His mother had always found him unusual,
so they entered the capital
and stayed at the Yáng residence.
His mother told her daughter everything her cousin had said.
The sister had long known that her brother had spoken of Zhèng's words,
and upon seeing her cousin's appearance,
found it even more extraordinary.
She secretly informed her husband
and had him report it to his father.
Guózhōng angrily said:
"If in-laws need money,
why not say so directly?
Instead, you use ominous words to frighten us?"
In the end, he did not give them a single coin.
His daughter said to her mother:
"Empty all the trunks and boxes,
that should be enough to manage.
Why force my uncle?"
At that time, the mother and son had stayed at the Yáng residence
for four or five days already.
The cousin urged them, saying:
"Do not stay more than ten days."
His sister gathered two or three hundred thousand cash
and gave it to her mother as they left.
At parting,
the cousin said to his sister:
"Give me a short coarse garment as well.
a robe."
His sister made a short coarse garment with purple silk and short padding
and gave it to him before parting.
The following year,
Ān Lùshān rebelled.
The imperial carriage reached Mǎwéi,
and the soldiers exterminated the entire Yáng family,
leaving none alive, young or old.
His sister heard of the chaos
and fled to the back of an inn,
hiding in the grass to escape.
After the soldiers had left,
she emerged by the roadside
and saw the entire Yáng family
lying dead in heaps.
Among the chaotic corpses,
she found a nursemaid in green clothing,
who had already lost an arm
but could still speak.
The sister asked:
"Is my child alive?"
She replied:
"He is on the master's bed,
covered with that purple coarse garment from earlier."
The sister hurried to look
and found her child still sleeping.
She then carried him and fled east.
As the sister began to flee,
she suddenly noticed an old woman following closely behind,
saying:
"Yáng's daughter-in-law, walk slowly,
I wish to hide with you."
The sister asked who she was,
and she replied:
"I am the old woman who sold shoes at your gate in the past."
That the sister could escape after the soldiers dispersed and find her child
was all due to this old woman guiding and protecting her,
keeping her safe in the wilderness.
It was the blind cousin
who sent a being to protect her.
Otherwise,
how could only these two people
have been spared from a family that was exterminated?
Jì Guǎngchēn
West of the river there is a goddess.
When Jì Guǎngchēn was young,
he once traveled west of the river
and rested at an inn.
Sleeping during the day,
he dreamed of a cloud chariot
with several dozen attendants
descending from the sky,
claiming to be the goddess.
Two sisters came to visit.
Guǎngchēn was initially very pleased,
but upon waking and opening his eyes,
he vaguely saw them still there.
Chēn suspected they were demons,
so he drew a sword from his waist and struck them.
The goddess then scolded him:
"We came to you in goodwill for so long,
how could you bear such malice!"
Then she left.
Guǎngchēn told the innkeeper about it,
