and the innkeeper said:
"This is the goddess."
Chēn then went to the market himself to buy wine and dried meat for an offering,
intending to apologize for his earlier offense,
but the goddess remained displeased.
So Chēn wrote a poem on the wall,
but the ink did not form characters.
The following night,
he dreamed again of the goddess coming,
who angrily said:
"I will ensure you never receive a fiefdom in your lifetime."
Liú Kědà,
having passed the imperial examination during the Tiānbǎo era,
entered the capital.
Departing from the eastern capital,
on the road he met a young man
who looked like a noble son,
dressed in luxurious attire,
carrying a slingshot as he walked,
with a magnificent entourage.
At first, he became familiar with Kědà,
and they traveled together for several days.
Upon reaching Huàyīn,
he said:
"I have an estate east of the county."
He invited Kědà to go with him,
and they followed him to the estate.
The buildings were grand and imposing,
and he hosted Kědà in the hall.
After entering the room for a long time,
Kědà secretly peeked through the middle gate,
and saw a nobleman
handling affairs in the inner hall.
In the courtyard, there were many prisoners,
most of them being tortured,
their cries pitiful and sorrowful.
Kědà suspected this was not a human realm,
and grew fearful, wanting to leave.
Earlier, when the young man was about to enter,
he had told Kědà not to peek privately,
fearing it would cause trouble.
When he came out, he said:
"I just consulted and reported,
why did you break your promise?
But since this has happened, I can no longer hide it:
my father is the god of Huàshān.
As old friends,
I will ultimately ensure you benefit,
so do not fear."
Soon after, food was served,
and he turned to his attendants,
telling them to fetch human food for Scholar Liú.
When the food arrived, they faced each other,
each eating their fill,
They also shared wine and enjoyed themselves,
leaving nothing undone.
Kědà asked to check his own record,
to see how he would advance,
and what his prospects were for the year.
The young man looked back and ordered a yellow-robed clerk to check.
After a while, the clerk said:
"Liú Jūn will pass the imperial examination next year
and hold seven official posts."
Kědà earnestly requested the same for the current year,
and the clerk said:
"This year, you can only obtain one post as a county captain.
I regret this for you."
Kědà insisted on his request,
and the young man changed it for him again.
The clerk left,
repeatedly looking back with regret,
lamenting the reduction in his official salary.
Kědà feared the gods would not keep their word,
so he insisted again,
and later, because of this, he lost his position.
The following year, he bid farewell and left,
reached the capital and passed the examination,
and after several years, he was appointed captain of Xíngyáng County, where he died.
The servant Cāngbì
Chancellor Lǐ Línfǔ had a household servant,
named Cāngbì,
who was intelligent and clever by nature,
and Línfǔ was fond of him.
Suddenly one day, he died abruptly,
but revived after one night.
Línfǔ asked him about it,
and the servant said:
"When I died, I truly did not feel that I had died.
I only suddenly saw an honor guard in front of the gate.
They were escorting a noble person passing by,
who resembled Your Majesty.
Just as I was secretly peeking,
several people immediately rushed over and seized me.
I followed them,
arriving at a steep, towering, and extraordinarily beautiful mountain,
and soon reached the base of a large building.
After a short while,
three or four yellow-clad youths arrived,
urgently calling Cāngbì to enter.
Passing through seven layers of gates and courtyards,
we arrived at the base of a great hall.
The yellow-clad youths said:
'Stand here for now,
and await the lord's command.'
I saw a pearl curtain rolled up in the hall,
and a noble person sitting by the steps.
It seemed like he was handling matters of judgment.
In front of the hall, attendants and guards stood in formation to the east and west,
numbering about over a thousand.
There was a person in red robes,
carrying a document and reporting:
'These are Ān Lùshān, who has newly been ordered to bring chaos to the state and overthrow the throne,
along with the successive three dynasties' chaotic rulers.
Also included are the rebellious nobles of the same time, whose cases have been pre-determined.'
The person in the hall asked the red-robed one:
'Regarding the Táng ruler Lǐ Lóngjī,
the number of his years as ruler,
though nearly fulfilled,
what about the number of his lifespan?'
The red-robed one said:
'The ruler of the Great Táng,
being extravagant and lacking frugality,
originally should have his years reduced.
However, because he does not favor killing,
and possesses a benevolent heart,
his lifespan number remains intact.'
He asked again:
'After Ān Lùshān,
several people will usurp and falsely claim rulership,
slaughtering the common people.
This must be swiftly stopped,
do not let too many be killed,
lest it wound the heart of the Supreme Deity,
and we fear the crime will extend to our office.
When these events unfold,
they must be quickly halted.'
The red-robed one reported:
'Since the Táng ruler succeeded to the throne and began his reign,
the people of the world
have lived in peace and enjoyed their livelihoods,
and it has already been long.
According to the numbers of fate's shifts and changes,
the people of the world
are themselves destined to encounter turmoil and anxiety.
As for widespread harm to the common people,
it surely will not reach the point of wounding the Supreme Deity's heart.'
The person in the hall said:
'Then first summon Lǐ Línfǔ and Yáng Guózhōng.'
The red-robed one received the order and withdrew.
Soon, there was another red-robed person,
holding a document and arriving.
Presenting it, he said:
'This is the document of the Great Táng's sixth dynasty Son of Heaven's restoration to the throne,
along with the assisting ministers.'
The person in the hall said:
'It is a pity that Lǐ Shìmín of the Great Táng,
exerted himself with great toil,
only then achieving orderly rule of the realm,
yet today it falls into chaos again.
Although the successor ruler restores the throne,
even until the end,
it will ultimately not be well-governed.'
He said to the red-robed one:
'Just carry it out swiftly.'
The red-robed one withdrew again.
As dusk approached,
a youth came down,
urgently calling Cāngbì to have an audience.
Cāngbì then looked carefully,
and saw a person in the hall,
sitting on a jasper bed,
wearing Daoist robes,
and a white jade crown,
who said to Cāngbì:
'You should return now,
take a message to Línfǔ,
tell him to come quickly to my Purple Palace,
he should know the suffering of the human world.'
Cāngbì soon was released and returned."
Línfǔ knew that the world would soon fall into chaos,
and so secretly indulged in wine and sensual pleasures.
Nán Zuǎn
Táng Dynasty Guǎnghàn Prefect Nán Zuǎn,
often told people:
During the Zhìdé era,
there was someone appointed as the Dūyóu of Tóngzhōu,
surname Cuī,
his given name forgotten.
Traveling lightly on horseback to take up his post,
he exited the Chūnmíng Gate,
and saw a person in blue robes,
also riding out on horseback,
not knowing his name either,
they exchanged bows and traveled together,
gradually asking what office he held.
The blue-robed one said:
"Newly appointed as Dūyóu of Tóngzhōu."
Cuī said:
"I have newly received this appointment,
sir, might you not be mistaken?"
The blue-robed one laughed but did not answer.
They continued traveling together,
both saying they were going to take up their posts.
Several tens of lǐ from Tóngzhōu,
reaching a fork in the road,
there were officials bowing in welcome.
The blue-robed one said to Cuī:
"You are the Lùshì of the Yang Path,
I am the Lùshì of the Yin Path.
Our paths diverge here,
would you not see me off?"
Cuī found this strange,
and so rode side-by-side with him into the fork.
They then arrived at a walled city,
its streets and official buildings
were also very magnificent.
The blue-robed one went to the hall,
and sat together with Cuī.
After the Wǔbó notified the clerks, monks, and Daoists, etc.,
next they notified the litigants and prisoners,
among them was Cuī's wife.
Cuī was greatly startled,
and said to the blue-robed one:
"I don't know how my wife came to be here?"
The blue-robed one then withdrew behind the desk,
letting Cuī speak with his wife himself.
The wife said:
"I was summoned here,
it has already been several days,
you should plead with the Lùshì!"
Cuī then begged the blue-robed one,
who thus ordered a clerk to promptly release Cuī's wife to return.
Cuī's wife asked what crime she had committed to come here,
the blue-robed one said:
"Our jurisdiction is Tóngzhōu,
all deceased persons from Tóngzhōu
are examined in this hall.
It is because you govern the Yang Path,
and I govern the Yin Path."
Cuī lingered for half a day,
then requested to return,
the blue-robed one ordered the clerks to bow in farewell, saying:
"Though Yin and Yang differ,
yet we are both of Tóngzhōu,
how could we not bow in farewell to the Dūyóu?"
The blue-robed one also gave a farewell feast,
repeatedly earnest and warm, waving his sleeve,
and again had him leave from the fork in the road.
Cuī arrived at Tóngzhōu,
asked his wife,
who said she had been ill for seven or eight days,
unconscious and unaware of anything,
her spirit and consciousness revived only one day ago.
Cuī calculated it,
exactly the day she was released.
His wife had no memory of the Yin Path at all,
when Cuī told her about it,
she then realized it was like a dream,
but could not clearly recall it.
Wáng Cháng
Wáng Cháng was
a man of Luòyáng.
He was proud and righteous;
whenever he saw injustice done to others,
he would surely slay the offender with his own hand;
when he saw people suffering from hunger and cold,
he would go so far as to give them his own clothes and food,
showing not the slightest reluctance.
In the second year of the Zhìdé era of the Táng dynasty,
Cháng entered the Zhōngnán Mountains,
encountered wind and rain,
and lodged in the mountains.
As midnight approached,
the rain cleared,
the moon was bright and the wind calm.
He looked around with deep emotion and sighed, saying:
"I wish to pacify the calamities and chaos of the world,
yet I have no authority over a single person to assist me,
nor a foot of land enfeoffed to me to support my cause;
I wish to save the world from hunger and cold,
yet my own clothing and food are insufficient.
The Heaven, Earth, and deities bless the good—
it seems this cannot be trusted."
As soon as he finished speaking, a divine being descended from the sky
and said to Cháng:
"Why do you speak these words?"
Cháng, gripping his sword for a long while, replied:
"What I speak of
is the aspiration of my entire life."
The divine being said:
"I possess an art—
gold can be created,
mercury can be transformed.
Although it may not suffice to pacify calamities and chaos,
it can still relieve people's hunger and cold.
Are you willing to receive this art?"
Cháng said:
"I have heard that this is the art of immortals,
but it is merely an empty name;
I have never witnessed it.
I have only heard that Qín Shǐhuáng and Hàn Wǔdì were fond of this path,
yet they ultimately achieved nothing,
and were only ridiculed for millennia!"
The divine being said:
"In the past, Qín Shǐhuáng and Hàn Wǔdì
were emperors.
Occupying positions where they could save people,
they possessed their own methods to save people but did not implement them;
instead, they sought the art of immortals—
that was wrong.
You do not hold a position to save people,
yet you wish to save the people of the world;
therefore, you may practice this art."
Cháng said:
"Creating gold,
transforming mercury—
does this truly exist?"
The divine being said:
"Do not doubt.
Gold is born from mountain rocks;
initially, it is the essence and fluid of the rocks,
and after a thousand years, it becomes mercury.
Mercury receives the energy of the Great Yin,
thus it flows and drifts without solidifying.
If it occasionally encounters the pure Yang energy and combines with it,
it transforms into gold in an instant.
If one wishes to transform mercury into gold,
it is not necessary that it transforms only within the mountains,
nor that it fails to transform outside the mountains.
As long as it occasionally encounters and combines with the pure Yang energy,
it will transform.
You should receive it without doubt."
Cháng then bowed twice.
The divine being took a scroll of text from his sleeve
and handed it to Cháng.
Cháng knelt and received it.
The divine being admonished him, saying:
"On another day, you must pass this on to another person.
Do not bestow it lightly,
nor keep it secret forever;
do not give it to the noble and powerful.
They already possess their own methods to save people.
Do not give it to the unrighteous;
those who do not care about hunger and cold,
and who, beyond aiding others,
indulge in luxury and idleness.
If you do otherwise,
Heaven will take away your allotted lifespan."
Cháng bowed twice again and said:
"I wish to know which deity you are."
The divine being said:
"I am the mountain deity.
In the past, a Daoist priest hid this text in my mountain.
Now, encountering a righteous and heroic person like you,
I entrust it
to you."
Having spoken, he vanished.
Cháng obtained this text, studied it,
and mastered the art.
Thereafter, he traveled extensively throughout the world,
using gold to relieve the destitute.
Kāiyè Temple
In the second year of the Zhìdé era,
on the twenty-third day of the tenth month,
at the Kāiyè Temple in Fēnglè Ward,
there appeared divine footprints of great length,
stretching from the outer gate of the temple to the Buddha hall.
Previously, the gatekeeper had lodged beneath the gate
and dreamed of a person over two zhàng tall,
clad in golden armor and holding a lance,
standing outside the temple gate.
Suddenly, the figure pulled at the gate with his hand,
causing all the locks and bolts to come undone.
The divine being then stooped and entered the temple.
He walked to the Buddha hall,
looked around for a long time, and then vanished.
The gatekeeper awoke in fright,
and at dawn, when he inspected the gate,
it was already open.
He immediately reported the dream in detail to the temple monks.
The monks all went to look
and saw the footprints of the divine being.
They then reported it to the Jīngzhào authorities,
who informed the emperor.
Emperor Sùzōng dispatched a palace envoy to verify it,
and it was as described.
Goddess Nǚwā
When Emperor Sùzōng was about to reach a relay station on the way to Língwǔ,
at dusk,
a tall woman,
carrying two carp,
shouted at the camp gate, saying:
"Where is the emperor?"
The crowd thought she was mad.
The emperor ordered someone to secretly observe her movements.
The woman stopped under a large tree.
A soldier approached to look closely
and saw scales on her arms.
Soon, the sky darkened, and she vanished.
When the emperor ascended the throne
and returned to the capital,
Wáng Qíguāng, the prefect of Guózhōu,
submitted a memorial regarding the tomb of Nǚwā, stating:
In the thirteenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
during heavy rain and darkness, it suddenly sank.
On the first night of this month,
people by the river heard the sound of wind and thunder.
At dawn, they saw the tomb surge forth.
On it grew two willow trees,
over a zhàng tall,
with a large rock beneath them.
When the emperor first reclaimed the land,
he sent ritual officers to offer sacrifices at the site.
It was then that this was seen.
Many suspected that the woman from before was this deity.
Wáng Jí
Wáng Jí
was a clansman of Wáng Xuán, the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
During the Qiányuán era,
he was residing in Kuàijī.
His servant fell ill and died,
but after several days, he revived,
saying:
"I saw an official in the underworld,
who asked:
'Whose servant are you?'"
The servant told him everything.
The official said:
"Now I summon your master to serve as the General of the Five Paths.
Because I exerted effort on your behalf,
you were spared and allowed to return."
Along the way, he saw many banners and ceremonial processions.
The servant asked what this was for,
and was answered:
"We are welcoming General Wáng."
A few days after his return,
Jí died.
On the day of his death,
people saw carriages and horses in great profusion,
with countless ceremonial processions.
When asked the reason,
they were all people coming to welcome Jí.
Chàng Cuǐ
Chàng Cuǐ prided himself on his talent and ambition,
but he was already over sixty years old
before he became a county magistrate in the region between Xiàngzhōu and Wèizhōu in Héběi.
He often felt frustrated and indignant.
In the county, he sought out only fortune-tellers and diviners,
asking about his future prospects for poverty or success,
but he never encountered a true one.
Someone secretly told Chàng:
"Why search so far?
The bailiff in your own office
is a judge of the underworld."
Chàng was secretly delighted.
That day, when he entered,
he prepared his official cap and tablet,
summoned the bailiff,
ascended the steps to return his bow,
and invited him to sit and share a meal.
The bailiff was frightened and uneasy,
not knowing what was happening.
After a long while, Chàng said to him:
"I consider my own talent and achievements no worse than others',
yet I am already sixty years old,
and my official position is only that of a county magistrate.
I do not mind toiling away in this post,
but I fear I will never rise above the lower ranks.
I want to know what lies ahead for me.
If I can achieve success later in life,
I will continue to hold this post.
But if there is ultimately no hope,
I will resign my official seal and retire to the mountains,
to take elixirs and seek the Way.
Unable to decide,
I have learned that you are a master of the underworld.
Please give me a word."
The bailiff rose from his seat, looking distressed, and said:
"I am but a humble man, yet you have shown me such extraordinary courtesy.
If I conceal the truth from you today,
I will betray your deep kindness;
if I do not conceal it, I will suffer misfortune.
Yet, compelled by circumstances, I have no choice but to speak.
I am not a master of the underworld;
what I oversee is merely the bailiff's duties in the netherworld.
I only determine people's life and death by the number of strokes administered.
Whenever someone is about to face calamity,
they first receive a certain number of strokes.
Those who receive more than twenty strokes die,
while those who receive fewer than twenty
only suffer serious illness.
Based on this, I make judgments,
and though I often speak carelessly among the villagers,
I have never been wrong."
Chàng immediately pressed him further:
"Who is the current master?"
The bailiff replied:
"You must be extremely careful not to reveal this—
it is the magistrate of the neighboring county.
I hear he will soon come here.
You may seek him out yourself,
but you must never say you learned this from me."
Ten days later,
the magistrate of the neighboring county indeed arrived,
and together with Chàng, he went to the prefecture for a seasonal gathering.
Chàng went out early in the morning to welcome him from afar,
lodged him in the county residence,
and entertained him with exceptional hospitality.
When he arrived,
he turned out to be an old man
over seventy years old.
At that time, the empire was at peace,
and the clerks and deputies in Héběi
were all sons of wealthy and noble families.
Magistrates were carefully selected from among renowned scholars.
The old magistrate apologized to Chàng, saying:
"Your reputation is lofty,
while I am lowly and humble.
I rose to office through the legal examination,
and I am fortunate to serve in a neighboring district.
How dare I accept such preferential treatment?"
His words and expression showed gratitude and shame.
Then, he went with Chàng to the commandery.
Afterward, they returned together,
and Chàng lodged him again in the county residence,
where their rapport grew even more cordial.
The next day, as they were about to part,
that night,
Chàng invited him into a secluded room,
prepared his official cap and tablet, bowed twice,
and repeated the same questions he had asked the bailiff,
but with even greater earnestness.
The old magistrate said sternly:
"Who told you this?"
His expression and tone were furious.
He said:
"If you do not reveal who spoke,
I will never tell you anything."
This went on for a long time,
until Chàng, having no other choice,
finally revealed the bailiff's name.
Immediately afterward, the old magistrate lowered his head, suppressing his anger.
A moment later,
a clerk reported:
"The bailiff has suddenly died at the wine shop."
Upon hearing this, Chàng grew even more respectful and fearful,
and he pleaded with the magistrate, begging him earnestly.
The magistrate then slowly said to Chàng:
"I am ashamed of your deep sincerity and great courtesy,
so I cannot hide the truth from you.
You should sweep and clean a courtyard,
and wherever there are cracks or openings,
seal them all completely.
Strictly warn your family members
that they must not peek under any circumstances—
those who disobey will bring disaster upon themselves.
Set up a couch in the hall,
place a desk with brush and inkstone,
and seven or eight sheets of paper.
That evening, I will enter,
and you must personally lock the door.
At dawn,
bring the key here to meet me."
At daybreak, Chàng took his tablet and
opened the door to see him.
The magistrate emerged with a joyful expression on his face.
From a distance, he congratulated Chàng:
"Your official salary will be very high—
you have nothing to worry about."
Then, he left behind a letter, saying:
"You must not read it in advance.
Only after each event occurs,
and each time you are promoted to a new office,
should you open it and read."
Later, Chàng was recruited from this county to serve as an assistant,
appointed Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ,
entered the capital as a ministry official and Jiànyì Dàfū.
Each time he opened the letter,
he found that the dates of his appointments were never wrong.
When he was demoted to Chénzhōu Sīmǎ,
he took out the letter and read it, which said:
"You were demoted because of such-and-such matter."
Later, he was recalled as Zuǒ Chéng,
and finally became Gōngbù Shàngshū.
Everything recorded in the letter matched without discrepancy.
Qiáo Guīnián
Qiáo Guīnián was a man
skilled in seal script calligraphy.
He cared for his mother with great filial piety.
During the Dàlì era,
whenever he wrote large seal characters for others,
he would use the money earned to provide his mother with delicacies.
If he saw his mother lacking anything,
he would invariably weep and cry out to heaven,
lamenting his own poverty.
One summer month,
he went to the well himself
to draw fresh water for his mother.
Suddenly, a person in black garments
leaped out from the well,
stood beside it,
and said to Guīnián:
"Your poverty
was predetermined.
Why do you weep and cry out to heaven
every time your mother lacks something?"
Guīnián suspected this was a divine spirit,
so he bowed and replied:
"I often regret my inability to attain wealth and honor,
to provide abundantly for my mother's care.
Moreover, she is old,
and delicacies are often lacking.
Though I do not fear toil and hardship in my brushwork for hire,
the support I gain from it
is insufficient to meet our needs.
That is why I cannot help but weep and cry out to heaven."
The divine person said:
"Your filial piety has reached its peak;
Heaven above knows of it.
You should take from this well
one million coins—
a gift from Heaven."
Having spoken, he vanished.
Guīnián then took them,
obtaining one million coins.
He often prepared rare delicacies to serve his mother,
yet mostly refrained from visiting the gates of the noble and powerful.
Three years later,
his mother passed away,
and Guīnián's mourning and longing nearly destroyed him.
He still used all the remaining money for a lavish burial for his mother,
and once again became impoverished.
After several years,
while strolling leisurely,
he came to the well where he had previously obtained the money,
and said with melancholy:
"In the past when I was poor,
Heaven bestowed money upon me.
Today I am poor,
yet Heaven does not bestow it.
If Heaven gave it to me because I was a filial son,
am I not a filial son today?"
Soon after, the divine person leaped out from the well again,
and said to Guīnián:
"In the past, Heaven knew you were filially caring for your elderly mother,
so it bestowed money upon you,
for the purpose of providing delicacies,
not to relieve your poverty.
Today, there is no need for delicacies,
so how can you harbor resentment?
If so,
then your former intention was not for your parent,
but for yourself."
Guīnián was startled, ashamed, and fearful,
and once again bowed twice.
The divine person also said:
"Your past filial piety
was heard by Heaven above.
Your present lack of filial piety
is also heard by Heaven above.
You should exert yourself diligently;
otherwise,
you will freeze or starve to death.
Today's words
have already deepened your offense;
it cannot be undone."
Having spoken, he vanished again.
Guīnián indeed died in poverty and hardship.
Zhāng Guāngshèng
The treacherous minister Zhāng Guāngshèng,
his origins were very humble,
yet he had talent and ability,
and was unrestrained and fond of drink.
In his prime, he was a soldier at Tóngguān,
frequently whipped by his commanding officer.
While on duty to Huàzhōu,
driving hard in the intense summer heat,
he felt discontent.
Passing by a temple of the mountain deity,
he took off his clothes to buy wine,
and made an offering to the Golden Heavenly King,
declaring loudly:
"Zhāng Guāngshèng possesses talent and capability,
but has yet to meet one who recognizes it.
Whether I attain wealth and honor or remain poor and lowly,
I cannot foresee,
but with the deity's keen discernment,
you should grant me a truthful revelation."
After the offering,
he drank to excess and became heavily intoxicated,
sleeping by day in the stele hall.
Suddenly, he dreamed of a voice calling:
"Summon Zhāng Guāngshèng."
The urgency was pressing,
and he entered an official residence,
exceptionally solemn and deep.
A guide announced:
"Zhāng Guāngshèng has arrived."
After bowing and kneeling,
he saw from afar a noble person in the main hall,
resembling a king,
who said to him:
"If you wish to know your official rank and fortune,
only when Guāngshèng becomes chancellor
will the world be at peace."
Having spoken,
Guāngshèng woke in alarm, drenched in sweat,
and found it strange alone.
Later, he repeatedly achieved military merits,
and through accumulated service rose to the office of Minister of Agriculture.
By the Jiànzhōng era,
when Emperor Dézōng fled west,
Guāngshèng rushed to follow.
Upon reaching Kāiyuǎn Gate,
he suddenly said to fellow court officials traveling with him:
"Today's rebellious soldiers
are merely the troops from Jīngzhōu turning their spears!
They have no leader,
and are likely to just plunder and pass through.
If they gain a leader,
the disaster is unforeseeable.
Zhū Cǐ has long been in Jīngyuán,
and has always enjoyed the people's hearts.
Now he is in the city;
if he gathers the Jīngzhōu troops to support him,
he will be difficult to control.
Considering his haste and panic,
he may not yet have devised this plan.
If you gentlemen can follow me straight to Cǐ's residence,
and summon him to go west together?"
The officials hesitated,
but Guāngshèng immediately galloped to Cǐ and said:
"The sovereign has left the capital;
you, sir, as a high minister,
how can this be a time for leisurely repose?"
Cǐ said:
"I wish to go with you, sir;
let the carriage be prepared to depart."
But the Jīngzhōu troops had already gathered at his gate.
Guāngshèng intended to flee himself,
but was instead detained by Cǐ.
Nevertheless, he served Cǐ with great effort;
whenever there was battle,
he was often in the midst of it.
At the battle of Shéncè,
Cǐ appointed Guāngshèng as Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and Participator in Determining Governmental Matters,
commanding troops to go out and fight,
but was greatly defeated and returned.
Only then did he realize the divine revelation was an omen.
Huáinán army soldier
When Chén Shàoyóu was stationed in Huáinán,
he once dispatched a soldier named Zhào to the capital,
to deliver letters to the high officials.
Before he set off,
Chén admonished him:
"I have urgent matters,
and I await your return to report.
Because you are brave and strong,
I am sending you west.
You must not delay even a little;
if you do not arrive by the appointed day,
you will die."
Zhào traveled several hundred lǐ each day,
not daring to slacken.
When he reached Huàyīn County,
he lodged at an inn,
and before he had fallen deeply asleep,
he suddenly saw a man in green clothes,
who said to Zhào:
"I am an official under the Golden Heavenly King,
and the King has ordered me to summon you.
You should come quickly."
Zhào, not knowing what to expect,
immediately went with the messenger.
When they reached the front of the mountain temple,
the messenger entered and announced:
"Zhào has arrived."
Then he called Zhào,
who hurried forward and bowed at the foot of the steps.
In the hall, candles were arrayed,
and he saw a person seated behind a desk,
with stern guards in attendance.
The person slowly said to Zhào:
"I have a son-in-law,
who has been in Shǔ for several years.
I wish to send a messenger to visit him,
but there is no one suitable to send.
I have heard that you are good at traveling,
covering several hundred lǐ a day.
I intend to command you to go to Shǔ;
is that acceptable?"
Zhào declined, saying that the Prime Minister had ordered him to go west to Cháng'ān,
and there was a set date;
if he failed, he would die.
If he now went to Shǔ for the King,
that would be abandoning the Prime Minister's order,
and he truly dared not return to Guǎnglíng.
Moreover, his parents, wife, and children were all there,
and he could not bear to live without returning to his hometown.
He did not dare to refuse the order with other excuses,
but hoped the King would understand.
The King said:
"Go directly for me,
and it should not come to that.
Returning from Shǔ via Cháng'ān
will not be too late."
He then had Zhào stay in an empty room behind the temple,
and provided food and drink.
Zhào, worried and confused, dared not sleep.
If he went to Shǔ,
he feared punishment;
if he firmly refused to go,
he worried disaster would befall him.
He had not yet decided what to do.
Soon it gradually grew light,
and he heard noisy sounds from the temple.
He went out to look,
and saw tigers, leopards, elk, deer,
foxes, rabbits, birds,
nearly ten thousand in number.
There were also a thousand or so ghosts and spirits of strange forms,
lined up and bowing,
as if paying homage.
After a moment, several people with disputes entered together,
and the Golden Heavenly King judged their cases very clearly.
After a long while, they withdrew.
Then he told his attendants to call Zhào,
who responded and went.
The King ordered him to ascend the steps,
took out a letter from his sleeve,
and handed it to Zhào, saying:
"Take this for me to Shǔ Commandery,
find a man named Xiāo Jìngzhī in Chéngdū and give it to him.
I have many officials here,
but because the matter is confidential,
I fear it might be leaked,
so only a living person can deliver it.
You should return quickly in a day or two,
do not stay long."
He then gave Zhào ten thousand coins,
and Zhào bowed in thanks and left.
At the gate,
he told an official:
"The King gave me ten thousand coins,
but I am traveling on foot;
how can I carry them?"
The official said:
"Put them in your bosom."
Zhào then stored the coins in his bosom,
and they did not hinder him at all,
nor did he feel their weight.
After traveling less than a few lǐ,
he felt inside his clothes,
and they were all paper money.
He immediately discarded them by the roadside.
Soon someone came chasing after him,
and gave him several thousand coins,
saying:
"Earlier I mistakenly gave you money used in the underworld,
which is of no use there.
Now I give you this instead!"
Zhào accepted them,
traveled day and night without rest,
and in over ten days reached Chéngdū.
He sought out Xiāo Jìngzhī
and gave him the letter.
Jìngzhī opened and read it,
and was very pleased.
He then had a mat laid out,
and said to Zhào:
"I am a human,
my home is between Rǔ and Zhèng.
In past years, I went to the capital for an official assignment,
and on the way passed through Huàyīn,
where I was forced by the Golden Heavenly King to become his relative.
Now my wife is here,
and...
...no different from a living person.
Previously I earnestly sought an official post,
and now it has been granted.
That is why I had you rush to report."
He then kept Zhào for one day,
gave him several bolts of silk,
and sent him back with a reply letter.
Passing through Cháng'ān,
he delivered Chén Shàoyóu's letters.
Having obtained the reply,
he traveled day and night.
When he reached Huàyīn,
the Golden Heavenly King saw him and was greatly pleased,
and consoled him:
"No one but you could have been sent.
Now I send you back.
If the Prime Minister questions you,
just say you were sent by me.
I appoint you as a lieutenant general;
do not fear."
He then gave him several dozen bolts of silk,
saying:
"This is silk from the human world,
you can use it."
Zhào bowed in thanks and went straight back to Huáinán.
Chén Shàoyóu questioned him about his delay,
and Zhào told him everything that had happened.
Shàoyóu angrily did not believe him,
and had him imprisoned.
That night,
Shàoyóu dreamed of a person,
clad in golden armor and holding a sword, who said:
"The Golden Heavenly King informs the Prime Minister:
I indeed sent Zhào to Shǔ earlier.
Now I hear he has been punished;
I hope you will release him."
Shàoyóu woke in fright,
and marveled at it for a long time.
The next morning,
he spoke of it to his guests and subordinates,
and immediately ordered Zhào released,
appointing him as a lieutenant general.
During the Yuánhé era, he was still alive.
Yuán Zǎi, Zhāng Wèi
When Yuán Zài was still a commoner,
he was often friendly with the former Vice Minister of Rites, Zhāng Wèi.
Being poor, they had no servants or horses,
and traveled on foot in worn clothes through Chén and Cài.
One day as dusk fell,
suddenly there was a great wind and thunder,
and the wilderness grew dim and dark.
The two of them went together to a roadside temple to take shelter.
At that time, there were several bandits,
all armed with swords and bows and arrows,
hiding under the temple eaves.
When Yuán and Zhāng suddenly saw them,
they became even more frightened and alarmed,
and moreover feared they would be harmed by them.
The two then stood with their backs against the wall,
not daring to move.
Soon they heard someone in the temple call out:
"Chancellor Yuán and Vice Minister Zhāng have arrived;
the bandits should quickly depart,
and not harm the noble ones."
The bandits looked at each other in shock,
and then galloped away.
The two then congratulated each other:
"We were just now worried about starving to death;
today's words were truly those of a divine being."
They were both joyful and amazed.
Later, Yuán indeed became chancellor under Emperor Dàizōng.
Wèi ended his career as Vice Minister of Rites.
The Village Head of Yǐngyáng
The village head of Yǐngyáng—his name cannot be given—
once returned to his village while drunk,
and became drunk at the Shàofù Temple,
so he tied his horse and lay down under the temple gate.
After a long time, as he was about to wake,
he turned his head,
but was unable to get up.
He heard someone knocking on the temple gate,
the sound very urgent.
Soon he heard from inside asking who it was,
and the reply said it was the officer in charge,
ordering to find someone to make rain.
From inside the temple,
it was said:
"The whole family has gone to the Yuè Temple as guests,
and now there is no one else."
The person said:
"Just take the one lying under the gate; that will do."
From inside the temple,
someone said:
"This is a passing traveler,
how can we make him do it?"
But after much arguing it could not be avoided,
so they called him to get up.
He followed them to a place,
all misty and full of cloud vapor,
where there was a creature like a camel.
Someone lifted him onto the camel's back,
handed him a bottle,
and instructed him:
"Just hold the bottle upright,
do not let it tilt."
The creature then set off.
Water from the bottle scattered down in droplets,
as there had been a long drought.
Looking down, he saw his own dwelling,
and fearing the rain would not be enough,
he then tilted the bottle.
After the rainmaking was finished,
the officer in charge released him to return.
Arriving at the temple gate, he saw his own corpse in the water,
then went forward, entered it, and came back to life.
He rode his horse back home.
Because he had tilted the bottle,
his house was swept away by the flood,
and all the people in his household died.
From then on, he went mad,
and died a few months later.
Wáng Fǎzhì
Wáng Fǎzhì, a woman from Tónglú,
from childhood served the Lángzǐ deity.
During the Dàlì era,
she suddenly heard the deity speaking in a grown man's voice.
Fǎzhì's father asked:
"Are these words not from a sage?"
It replied:
"Indeed.
My surname is Téng,
given name Chuányìn.
I am originally from Wànnián in Jīngzhào,
my residence was in Chóngxián Ward.
Originally, I had a karmic connection with Fǎzhì."
Engaging in conversation with it,
it deeply understood the principles of things,
and was highly regarded by the local and provincial authorities.
The magistrate of Tónglú County, Zhèng Fēng,
a man fond of the unusual,
often summoned Fǎzhì to his residence.
He ordered her to invite Téng the Twelfth Gentleman,
and after a long while he arrived.
His eloquent responses in conversation
deeply reflected the style of a scholar,
and Fēng listened without tiring.
Whenever he met literary men,
he would discuss classics and recite poetry,
joyfully talking all day.
Once there was a traveling monk who came to Fǎzhì to beg,
and the deity conversed with him,
presenting a poem that said:
"Standing alone, not seeking fame, I left home;
long holding a fragment of ambition toward the azure mists.
Today the hero's spirit soars to the heavens;
who can long sit upon the precious lotus flower?"
He also once composed a poem to give to someone, saying:
"In this life, talent is insufficient;
in establishing oneself, sincerity is abundant.
I sigh that there is no great cause;
gentlemen, do not distance yourselves from me."
On the night of the twenty-fifth day of the second month in the sixth year,
Dài Fú, together with Left Guard Military Officer Xú Huǎng, Lóngquán Magistrate Cuī Xiàng, Dānyáng Assistant Magistrate Lǐ Cóngxùn, and locals Hán Wèi and Sū Xiū,
gathered at Fēng's residence.
When Fǎzhì arrived,
they ordered her to summon Téng Chuányìn.
After a long while he arrived,
and exchanged several hundred words of conversation with Huǎng and the others.
He then said to the assembled worthies:
"I ask each of you to recite one stanza."
After the recitations,
the group requested his poem.
Casually, he then recited two pieces, saying:
"At the river mouth, the tide comes, vast and wide at first;
the lotus boat sways, picking flowers is hard.
Spring feelings unsatisfied, I return empty-handed;
I'll wait for the tide to calm, then break one to view again."
He said:
"Everyone, don't laugh at me."
Then he recited another:
"Suddenly over the lake, a slice of cloud flies;
unnoticed in the boat, rain dampens my clothes.
Having broken a lotus, I completely forget;
only use the lotus leaf to cover my head on the return."
He said of himself:
"This work is also rather trivial."
He also instructed Fǎzhì's brother to exchange several hundred words with Fēng,
and then departed.
Lǐ Zuǒshí
Lǐ Zuǒshí, the county captain of Shānyīn,
in the second year of the Dàlì era encountered exhaustion,
and after being ill for several tens of days recovered,
traveling from Kuàijī to Lóngqiū.
There he met his clansman Lǐ Shù, who was the county magistrate,
and Zuǒshí stayed in the magistrate's office for several days.
One evening, he was again with a guest named Lǐ Jǔ,
sitting by a bright lamp.
Suddenly, he saw about twenty people dressed in crimson and purple garments,
all holding military weapons,
hurrying to pay their respects in the courtyard below.
Zuǒshí asked who they were,
and they replied:
"We are ghost soldiers.
The Great King has appointed you as a judge,
and we have been specially ordered to come and welcome you,
to serve under your command."
Zuǒshí said:
"I am currently in mourning,
so this is improper.
Moreover, how did the King come to know of me?"
They replied:
"It was Dòu Kān, the magistrate of Wǔyì County, who recommended you."
Zuǒshí said:
"I am not acquainted with Kān,
why would he recommend me?"
They replied:
"The gracious command has already been issued,
it is difficult to refuse."
Shortly after, Kān arrived,
paid his respects,
and was as refined as an ordinary person.
Sitting down, he said to Zuǒshí:
"The King is seeking a son-in-law,
and also wishes to marry into a prominent family,
hence I recommended you.
This is also due to karmic connections."
Zuǒshí firmly declined but to no avail.
Soon, the King's daughter also arrived,
fragrant and elegant,
with carriages and riders gathering like clouds.
Zuǒshí descended the steps to welcome and bow to her,
and upon seeing the lady's appearance, demeanor, and attire,
he felt quite pleased.
Kān said to Zuǒshí:
"Who among men does not die?
But one like you is rare.
You should not repeatedly refuse,
lest you provoke the King's anger."
Zuǒshí knew he could not ultimately avoid it.
After a while,
the King's daughter and Kān departed,
leaving over two hundred attendants
to serve the judge.
The next day,
Shù and his younger brother Zào
together visited Zuǒshí.
Zuǒshí then recounted the whole story,
saying:
"I am certainly not going to live,
so I ask for one last meal."
Shù prepared a lavish feast for him.
Zuǒshí was eating pheasant stew,
when suddenly he said:
"I don't see the bowl."
He scolded his attendants:
"Why have you taken away the stew?"
He collapsed onto the dining table,
and died.
His wife, Lady Zhèng, was in Kuàijī.
On the evening the funeral boat arrived,
a maidservant suddenly spoke in Zuǒshí's spirit voice, saying:
"The King's daughter has already married another,
but I have been sent to escort my wife back."
His words were filled with sorrow.
Wéi Gāo
Wéi Gāo initially traveled humbly beyond Jiàn,
and Zhāng Yánshǎng, the military minister and chancellor of the Xīchuān military command, married his daughter to him.
Later, however, he grew to dislike him,
and his feelings of contempt became increasingly apparent.
Gāo, depressed and unable to fulfill his ambitions,
would often enter the command headquarters,
socializing with guests and friends,
and venting his frustrations.
Yánshǎng disliked him even more for this,
and said to Gāo:
"The staff officers are all extraordinary talents of the time,
and even I, Yánshǎng, respect and stand in awe of them.
Young Master Wéi, since you have no duties,
there is no need for you to come here so often."
Such was his disdain for him.
Another day,
his wife felt especially sorry for him and said:
"A man should have ambitions that span the four directions.
Now, to be so despised and looked down upon, yet remain unaware,
and pass the days cheerfully—
how strange!
I left my family to serve you, my husband.
Even a thatched hut in a remote corner
would be your home;
cooking beans and making vegetable soup,
eating simple meals and drinking from a gourd,
would be your sustenance.
Why must you endure shame and force yourself to stay,
only to be laughed at by those with spirit?"
Thereupon, she went in to inform Zhāng of their intention to leave.
Yánshǎng gave them fifty bolts of silk as a parting gift.
His wife thought it meager,
but did not dare speak.
At that time, a sorceress was present.
Seeing Gāo enter the western courtyard,
she asked the lady:
"Who is that man in green who just entered the western courtyard?"
She replied:
"Young Master Wéi."
The sorceress said:
"This man is destined for extreme nobility,
his position will far surpass that of a chancellor.
His fortune is about to rise,
and before long he will also govern this region.
You should treat him exceptionally well."
When asked how she knew,
she said:
"Wherever a noble person goes,
there are sure to be underworld officials accompanying him.
A chancellor has only ten or twenty attendants,
but someone like Young Master Wéi
has over a hundred."
The lady was overjoyed to hear this,
and immediately told Yánshǎng.
Yánshǎng angrily said:
"If you thought the parting gift was too little, you could have asked for more.
Why resort to fabricating stories from a witch
to mock me?"
Wéi traveled for over a month and reached Qí.
The military governor of Qí, because Gāo was the esteemed son-in-law of Xīchuān,
invited him to join his staff,
and recommended him for the position of Dàlǐ Píngshì.
Soon, because he adjudicated cases fairly,
he was promoted to Jiānchá,
and following the death of the prefect of Lǒngzhōu, he was appointed to administer the prefecture.
Not long after, Zhū Cǐ rebelled,
and the imperial carriage fled to Fèngtiān.
In Lǒngzhōu, there were five hundred of Cǐ's former soldiers,
commanded by the military commander Niú Yúnguāng.
Yúnguāng plotted to start a rebellion,
but failed,
and led his troops to join Zhū Cǐ.
On the way, they encountered an envoy from Cǐ,
who brought a false edict appointing Gāo as Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Gāo accepted the appointment,
and said to Yúnguāng:
"Since I have accepted the command, there should be no suspicion.
You should surrender all your weapons,
to show that there is no deception between us."
Yúnguāng complied.
The next day, a great feast was held,
where hidden soldiers killed them all.
Gāo then set up an altar and swore an oath with his generals.
Cǐ again promised Gāo the position of military governor of Fèngxiáng,
but Gāo beheaded his envoy.
When the news reached the imperial camp,
everyone's morale was boosted.
He was then appointed prefect of Lǒngzhōu and military governor of the Fèngyì Army.
When the emperor returned to the palace,
he was appointed military minister and military governor of Xīchuān.
When Yánshǎng heard this,
he wanted to gouge out his own eyes,
to punish himself for failing to recognize talent.
Dòu Shēn
Dòu Cān once served as the magistrate of Púqí County.
In the county, there was a temple dedicated to a deity.
All the previous magistrates had offered sacrifices there.
Upon Dòu’s arrival, he intended to demolish it,
and the day for doing so had already been set.
He dreamed that the deity said to him:
"You wish to destroy my dwelling.
The reason I have not yet harmed you
is that you are destined to become a chancellor.
However, I hope you will spare it.
I am willing to associate with you,
and can foretell good and bad fortune for you."
Startled awake,
he personally entered the temple to offer wine and sacrifices,
treating the deity as an elder brother.
Afterward, whenever there was news of a promotion,
the deity would inform him in advance,
and they developed a rather close spiritual connection.
When the deity wished to meet him,
he would prepare a lavish feast in an empty room,
surrounded by curtains.
After Dòu entered,
those outside could hear the sounds of laughter and conversation between two people.
When Dòu served as the Deputy Administrator of Liǔzhōu,
there was an empty courtyard in the official residence,
which Dòu had closed off.
Suddenly, he heard calls three or four times,
but upon searching, found no one.
Feeling uneasy,
he put on formal attire and looked up to ask:
"Could it be my elder brother?"
The voice replied:
"It is indeed me.
You should quickly put your household affairs in order.
Within two or three days, an envoy from the north will arrive,
and you will not escape."
Dòu followed the advice and settled his affairs.
He sat waiting for the envoy.
A few days later,
imperial messengers hurriedly arrived,
and indeed, there was a subsequent order.
Lǐ Bóqín
In the fifth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
Lǐ Bó's son, Bóqín,
served as the salt purchasing official at the Xiàchǎng station of Xúpǔ under the Jiāxīng supervision.
Within the station's boundaries was the temple of Vice Minister Cài.
Bóqín paid a visit to the temple.
Glancing inside, he saw several goddesses,
among them a particularly beautiful one.
He jokingly remarked:
"If I could marry a woman like this,
it would be enough."
He then poured wine and made a toast to her.
A few days later,
while attending to official duties during the day,
he suddenly heard the sound of carriages and horses outside the gate.
Startled, Bóqín rose,
and after a long while,
dressed formally to welcome them at the gate,
he then turned and entered.
The clerks and subordinates were astonished,
not knowing the reason.
He ordered wine and food,
and after some time,
they respectfully conversed before departing.
Later, he announced that Vice Minister Cài had come.
The next day, he came again,
but those around him could not see him.
Bóqín welcomed him in the courtyard,
and they conversed, saying:
"I am fortunate to be remembered
and to serve your noble household."
He bowed twice and sat down,
and they drank and ate throughout the night before departing.
Bóqín then told his family:
"I have already promised Vice Minister Cài to discuss marriage."
He settled his household affairs,
bid farewell to relatives and friends,
and passed away a few days later.
Xiāo Fù's Younger Brother
Xiāo Fù's own younger brother
was devoted to Daoism from a young age and did not pursue an official career.
He consumed medicinal herbs and cinnamon,
could play the qin,
and was especially skilled at the "South Wind" melody.
While traveling in Héngshān and Xiāng River regions,
he moored his boat by the riverbank.
He saw an old man
carrying books and a qin.
Xiāo bowed and invited him to sit, saying:
"Do you, sir, play the qin
and know the 'South Wind' melody?"
The old man replied:
"I have long been skilled in this."
Xiāo then asked him to play it,
and it was exceptionally exquisite.
The old man then fully transmitted the method to him.
After drinking several cups of wine,
Xiāo asked where he lived,
but the old man only smiled without answering.
On his journey northward,
when he reached the mouth of the Yuán River,
he went ashore to practice the "South Wind" melody.
A young woman with double buns,
carrying a small bamboo basket, said:
"My mistress nearby loves the qin
and wishes to invite you."
Xiāo asked where she came from,
and she replied:
"I was just picking fruits."
She left for a moment and returned,
saying:
"My mistress summons you."
Having been on the boat for a long time,
Xiāo felt like taking a leisurely stroll,
so he agreed.
Soon, an old servant rowed a painted boat to fetch him.
Xiāo boarded it,
and after traveling over a li,
they arrived at a magnificent gate and hall.
He was invited to ascend the hall,
where he saw two beautiful women above,
and he bowed before them.
The beautiful women said:
"Do not be surprised by our invitation.
We know you are skilled in the 'South Wind' melody.
We have also long loved it,
but having not practiced for a long time,
we have forgotten half of it.
We hope you can teach us."
Xiāo then played for them,
and the women also ordered a qin to be brought.
After Xiāo finished playing,
the two women and their attendants all covered their faces and wept.
They asked from whom he had learned it,
and he mentioned the old man,
describing his appearance in detail.
The women shed tears and said:
"It was Shùn.
This was also arranged by the Heavenly Emperor for you to receive it
and transmit it to us.
We are Shùn's two consorts.
Shùn has served as the Minister of Works in the Ninth Heaven for a thousand years,
and he separately received this melody,
but over the years, much of it has been forgotten."
They then invited Xiāo to stay and drink several bowls of tea.
When Xiāo bid farewell to leave,
he said:
"I cherish your generous hospitality."
However, he did not wish to speak of this to others.
He then exited the gate,
boarded the painted boat again,
and returned to where he had played the qin.
The next day, when he went to look for the place,
it was nowhere to be seen.
Lǐ Nà
In the early years of the Zhēnyuán era,
Lǐ Nà, the military governor of Pínglú, fell gravely ill.
He dispatched his aide Wáng Yòu
to offer prayers at Mount Tài.
Wáng Yòu observed the purification rituals and set off.
When he reached the southwestern foothills of the mountain,
he saw from a distance four or five figures on the slopes,
dressed in green sleeveless jackets.
The other three or four,
in mixed-colored attire,
were their attendants.
The green-clad men held slingshots,
shooting at mountain birds in the ancient trees.
With a single shot, they hit one,
and the bird fell from the tree.
The attendants scrambled to catch it.
Wáng Yòu noticed that all the people arriving at the mountain's base
descended from their carriages, removed their canopies,
and bowed uniformly toward the mountain.
As Wáng Yòu was about to approach,
passersby stopped him and urged him to dismount:
"These are the Third and Seventh Young Masters."
He then bowed to the green-clad men.
The attendants motioned to the passersby,
instructing them to return to their carriages.
The passersby hesitated,
but the green-clad men waved their hands themselves,
again urging them to ascend.
Holding his slingshot,
one of them stood southwest of the temple hall,
tapping the ground with it while looking down intently,
as if waiting for something.
Seeing Wáng Yòu,
he summoned him forward and asked:
"Why have you come?"
Wáng Yòu explained in full.
The green-clad man said:
"Sir,
Your master has already arrived.
Why trouble yourself with this journey?
Do you wish to see your master?"
He then ordered one of his men:
"Take Wáng Yòu to see his master."
They opened the western courtyard gate and led him in.
There, he saw Lǐ Nà, wearing a cangue that covered his ears,
sitting on a mat in the courtyard.
Wáng Yòu, shocked and weeping, rushed forward and prostrated himself,
clutching Lǐ Nà's left foot
and biting his skin.
The guide said:
"Wáng Yòu, you may withdraw."
He was then led back out.
The green-clad man was still on the temple steps.
He said to Wáng Yòu:
"Do you wish to see the new master?"
He then summoned another man approaching from the east,
short and broad in stature,
with a charming and dignified bearing.
The green-clad man said:
"This is your new master."
Wáng Yòu bowed but remained silent.
He felt as if he needed to sneeze but was delayed for a long while.
Suddenly, everything vanished,
leaving only moss-covered pines and cypresses,
serene and solemn in the stillness.
He then performed the offerings and returned.
Upon seeing Lǐ Nà,
Lǐ Nà called him into the inner chamber.
He asked Wáng Yòu,
but Wáng Yòu only reported that the offerings were completed,
and that he had cast divination sticks,
obtaining auspicious omens to relay to Lǐ Nà.
Lǐ Nà said:
"Why does Wáng Yòu not speak truthfully?
Why did you bite my foot?"
He then raised his foot,
revealing the bite marks left by Wáng Yòu.
Wáng Yòu kowtowed
and confessed everything truthfully.
Lǐ Nà asked:
"Who exactly did you see as the new master?"
Wáng Yòu replied:
"I would recognize him if I saw him,
but I do not know his name."
Lǐ Nà then summoned three men to come forward.
When they reached Lǐ Shīgǔ,
he said:
"This is the one."
Lǐ Nà then entrusted him with his affairs,
and upon finishing his words, he passed away.
When Wáng Yòu first saw Lǐ Nà wearing the cangue,
he asked:
"Why is the Vice Director in such a state?"
Lǐ Nà replied:
"It is the fault of a lifetime as a subject,
unavoidable, what can be done?
What more is there to say today?"
Cuī Fén
Cuī Fén, a military officer of Lǐquán,
had his second elder brother residing in Chóngxián Ward in Cháng'ān.
One summer night,
he was enjoying the cool in the courtyard.
The moon was directly overhead,
when a breeze passed by,
carrying a strange fragrance.
Suddenly, he heard rustling from the southern wall,
and Cuī assumed it was a snake or rat.
Then, a Daoist priest appeared,
exclaiming loudly:
"What splendid moonlight!"
Cuī, frightened, retreated to avoid him.
The priest strolled leisurely in the courtyard.
He appeared to be around forty,
with a refined and ancient demeanor.
After a while,
over ten courtesans
pushed open the main gate and entered,
dressed in light silks with kingfisher hairpins,
their beauty unparalleled in the world.
Attendants laid out fragrant mats,
and they sat in a row under the moonlight.
Cuī suspected they were demons or spirits,
so he struck the door with a pillow to startle them.
The priest glanced briefly,
angered, and said:
"I came here for its quietness,
and to enjoy the moonlight.
I had no intention of lingering,
yet you dare to act so rudely."
He then raised his voice and demanded:
"Are there any local guardians here?"
Suddenly, two figures appeared,
only three feet tall,
with large heads and drooping ears,
prostrating themselves before him.
The priest gestured toward where Cuī was and said:
"This man should have relatives registered in the underworld.
Bring them here."
The two hurried off.
Soon, Cuī's parents and elder brother arrived,
escorted by several guards,
who pushed, dragged, and beat them.
The priest scolded:
"With me here,
how dare you let your son be so disrespectful?"
The parents kowtowed and said:
"The realms of the living and dead are separated,
we cannot instruct or reprimand him."
The priest shouted and dismissed them.
He then turned to the two demons and said:
"Seize this suspicious man."
The two demons leaped to the door,
and with a red object like a pellet,
hurled it from a distance into Cuī's mouth—
it was a thin red cord.
They then fished him out into the courtyard
and berated and humiliated him.
Cuī was too shocked to speak,
unable to defend himself,
while his servants and concubines wept.
The courtesans bowed in a circle and pleaded:
"He is but a mortal,
startled by the immortal official's sudden arrival,
it does not seem a grave offense."
The priest's anger subsided,
and he brushed his sleeves and left through the main gate.
Cuī fell ill as if possessed,
and only recovered after five or six days.
He then invited a priest to perform rituals and offer apologies,
but nothing further happened.
Earlier, Cuī had glimpsed his deceased elder brother through a crack,
wiping his lips with a cloth,
as if they were injured.
The servants were all surprised,
and one maid wept and said:
"When the young master was placed in the coffin,
the burial veil was forgotten to be opened for the mouth.
In haste, it was cut open,
accidentally injuring his lower lip.
No one else saw it then,
yet who knew that in the underworld for over twenty years,
he still suffers this pain."
Xīn Mì
After Xīn Mì passed the imperial examination in the Five Classics,
he went to Chángzhōu to attend a wedding.
When he reached Shǎn,
he rested under the shade of a tree.
Beside him sat a beggar, cross-legged,
his face covered in scabs and his clothes infested with lice.
The beggar inquired about Xīn Mì's journey,
but Xīn Mì did not respond and immediately left.
The beggar followed him.
Xīn Mì's horse was weak,
so he could not distance himself,
and the beggar kept talking incessantly.
Ahead, they encountered a person dressed in green,
and Xīn Mì greeted him, traveling together for over a li.
Suddenly, the green-clad person spurred his horse and galloped away.
Xīn Mì found this strange
and muttered to himself:
"Why did this person suddenly act like that?"
The beggar said:
"His time had come.
How could he have acted freely?"
Xīn Mì sensed something unusual in his words
and finally asked him:
"What do you mean by 'his time had come'?"
The beggar replied:
"You will understand shortly."
As they approached an inn,
they saw dozens of people crowding the entrance.
Upon inquiry,
they learned that the green-clad person had died.
Xīn Mì was astonished
and immediately treated the beggar with great respect.
He took off his own clothes to dress the beggar
and gave him his horse to ride.
The beggar showed no sign of gratitude at first,
but his words often carried profound meaning.
When they reached Biàn,
he said to Xīn Mì:
"I will stop here.
What is your destination?"
Xīn Mì told him about his marriage arrangement.
The beggar laughed and said:
"You are a scholar,
and your career cannot be hindered by this journey.
However, she is not your wife.
Your wedding is still far off."
A day later,
he carried a vessel of wine to bid farewell to Xīn Mì
and pointed to the pagoda of the Xiàngguó Temple, saying:
"It will catch fire by noon.
You may delay your departure until then to say goodbye."
As predicted,
the pagoda caught fire for no reason,
destroying its spire.
Before leaving,
he gave Xīn Mì a silk pouch,
which had a knot tied on it.
He told Xīn Mì:
"If you ever have doubts in the future,
open it and look inside."
More than twenty years later,
when Xīn Mì served as the magistrate of Wèinán,
he finally married a woman from the Péi family.
On Péi's birthday,
while hosting relatives and guests,
he suddenly remembered the beggar's words.
He untied the knot on the silk pouch
and found a piece of paper,
as large as a hand tablet,
inscribed with:
"Xīn Mì's wife, Péi of Hédōng,
born on such-and-such month and day."
It was indeed that very day.
Xīn Mì calculated that on the day he parted with the beggar,
his wife had not yet been born.
Recorded by Chén Yuánshēng.
In the early years of the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a man from Chénjùn named Yuán.
He once served as a military advisor in Táng'ān.
After his term ended, he traveled to Bāchuān,
staying at an inn.
Suddenly, a man
in white clothes came to visit.
After sitting down,
he said to Yuán:
"I am the son of the Gāo family,
and my home is in Xīnmíng County of this commandery.
In the past, I served in the military,
but now I am exempt.
Therefore, I am traveling here."
Yuán conversed with him,
and found him exceptionally intelligent, eloquent, and knowledgeable,
far surpassing ordinary people,
which amazed Yuán.
The man added:
"I am skilled in divination
and can analyze
the events of your entire life."
Yuán immediately inquired,
and the man recounted past events,
each one as if written down,
leaving Yuán greatly astonished.
That evening,
when the night was deep,
he secretly said to Yuán:
"I am not human.
I wish to confide in you, sir.
May I?"
Upon hearing this, Yuán became frightened
and immediately stood up, saying:
"You are not human?
Are you a ghost, then?
Do you intend to bring calamity upon me?"
Gāo replied:
"I am not a ghost,
nor do I intend to harm you.
The reason I have come
is to entrust something to you.
I am the deity of Chìshuǐ,
with a shrine south of Xīnmíng.
Last year, there was continuous rain for several months,
and the shrine collapsed entirely.
No one in the commandery has repaired it,
leaving me exposed to the wind and sun,
and daily subjected to the insults of woodcutters and herdsmen.
The villagers regard me as nothing more than a pile of earth.
Now I appeal to you.
If you agree, then speak;
if not, I shall leave.
I bear no resentment."
Yuán said:
"Since the deity has such a wish,
how could I refuse?"
The deity said:
"Next year, you will be appointed as the magistrate of Xīnmíng.
If you could rebuild my shrine for me
and offer sacrifices in due time,
that would be my greatest fortune.
I hope you do not forget."
Yuán promised.
Then the deity added:
"When you first arrive in the county,
you must come to visit me once.
However, there is a divide between humans and deities.
I fear your attendants might show disrespect toward me,
so you should dismiss your officials
and enter the temple alone.
I hope to speak with you fully."
Yuán said:
"I shall respectfully follow your instructions."
That winter,
Yuán was indeed appointed magistrate of Xīnmíng.
Upon taking office,
He inquired
and found there was indeed a Chìshuǐ deity shrine
several miles south of the county.
Over ten days later,
he went to visit it.
When he was still over a hundred paces away,
he dismounted and dismissed his carriage attendants,
entering the temple alone.
He saw the eaves and halls in ruins,
overgrown with wild grass.
He stood gazing for a long time
when a man in white clothes appeared from behind the temple—
it was Gāo.
He looked very pleased
and bowed.
He said to Yuán:
"You have not forgotten our previous agreement
and have come to visit me today.
How fortunate I am!"
They then walked together inside the temple.
Yuán saw an old monk under the steps and walls,
bound in shackles,
with several people standing beside him.
Yuán asked:
"What is this about?"
The deity said:
"This monk is Dàochéng, a master from the temple east of the county.
He has incurred calamity,
so I have bound him here for a year.
Every morning and evening, he is whipped.
In about ten more days,
he will be released."
Yuán asked again:
"Since this monk is still alive,
how can he be bound here?"
The deity said:
"By binding his living soul,
he naturally falls gravely ill,
and how could he know it is my doing?"
The deity then told Yuán:
"Since you have promised to rebuild my shrine,
please proceed quickly."
Yuán said:
"I dare not forget."
After returning,
he began planning the construction.
However, he was very poor
and had no funds.
He thought to himself:
"The deity said
that by binding Dàochéng's soul,
he would fall gravely ill.
He also said
that in about ten more days,
he would be released.
If I use another pretext
to have him build the shrine,
what doubt could there be?"
He then went directly to the temple east of the county to inquire,
and indeed, there was a Master Dàochéng
who had been bedridden for a year.
Dàochéng said:
"I am ill and near death,
and my whole body aches day and night."
Yuán said:
"Master, your illness is severe
and close to death,
but I can cure you.
Could you use funds to rebuild the Chìshuǐ deity shrine?"
Dàochéng said:
"If I am truly cured,
why would I hesitate to provide funds?"
Yuán then deceived him, saying:
"I am skilled in seeing ghosts.
Recently, I visited the Chìshuǐ deity shrine
and saw your soul
bound in shackles under the wall.
I summoned the Chìshuǐ deity to ask about it,
and he said:
'This monk has incurred past calamity,
so he is bound here.'
I pitied your suffering
and told the deity:
'Why bind a living person?
Release him quickly.
I will order this monk to rebuild the shrine,
so do not disobey.'
The deity happily agreed, saying:
'In about ten more days,
I will forgive his offense.'
That is why I tell you, Master, that your illness will soon be cured,
and you should repair the Chìshuǐ deity shrine.
Do not, once cured,
neglect this matter,
or calamity will befall you."
Dàochéng pretended to agree, saying:
"I respectfully accept your instruction." Over ten days later,
he indeed recovered.
He then summoned his disciples and said:
"In my youth, I left home
to study Buddhism,
and now I am fifty years old.
Unfortunately, I fell gravely ill.
Previously, Master Yuán told me:
'Your illness
is caused by the Chìshuǐ deity.
Once cured, you must repair his shrine.'
The purpose of establishing a deity shrine
is to protect the people
and respond to their prayers.
Now that it has harmed me,
how can I not remove it?"
He then led his disciples,
carrying shovels to the shrine,
completely destroying the deity statue and the shrine building,
leaving nothing behind.
The next day,
Dàochéng went to visit Yuán.
Yuán Shēng joyfully said:
"Has the master's illness truly recovered?
Was my statement perhaps false?"
Dào Chéng said:
"Indeed,
fortunately you saved me;
how dare I forget your kindness?"
Yuán Shēng said:
"You should quickly plan to repair the Chìshuǐ Shén Temple.
Otherwise,
I fear disaster will strike."
Dào Chéng said:
"The reason gods rely on humans
is because blessings can be extended,
and calamities can be averted.
During drought, they are prayed to for rain;
during floods, they are supplicated for clear skies.
Thus, the Son of Heaven decrees that throughout the empire's commanderies and fiefdoms,
even in a single town or village,
their shrines must be built.
This is done for the benefit of the people.
As for the Chìshuǐ Shén,
it brings no blessings to people
but instead harms them.
Should it not
be removed?
I have already completely destroyed its temple."
Yuán Shēng was both shocked and fearful,
and so he apologized.
Dào Chéng's vigor grew even stronger,
while Yuán Shēng became increasingly afraid.
A little over a month later,
a clerk committed an offense,
and Yuán Shēng punished him.
Not long after, the clerk died,
and his family appealed to the commandery.
As a result, Yuán Shēng was exiled to Duānxī.
While traveling through the Three Gorges,
he suddenly encountered a figure in white
standing by the roadside.
Looking closely,
it was the Chìshuǐ Shén.
It said:
"Earlier, I entrusted you with repairing my temple.
Why did you allow Dào Chéng to destroy my dwelling
and discard my image?
Leaving me suddenly without a home—
this is your crime.
Now that you are cast into this desolate exile,
it is my revenge upon you!"
Yuán Shēng then apologized, saying:
"It was Dào Chéng who destroyed you.
Why blame me?"
The god said:
"Dào Chéng's master possesses immense fortune;
I cannot move against him.
But now your prosperity and fate have declined,
so I am able to exact revenge."
Having spoken, it vanished.
Yuán Shēng was horrified by this,
and a few days later,
he ultimately died of illness.
Rǎn Suì
Rǎn Suì was a man from Qí.
His father served as a county magistrate.
Suì married Zhào Yù’s daughter from Chángshān.
After his father’s death,
Suì, being young and unintelligent,
was barely literate,
and had no means to advance,
so he took up farming in Chángshān.
His wife, née Zhào,
was beautiful in appearance
and of a frivolous nature.
One day, while wandering alone in the woods,
she saw a man dressed in brocade robes,
riding a white horse,
with over a hundred attendants,
all carrying swords and halberds, passing by.
Zhào said:
"If I could have such a husband,
I would die without regret."
The brocade-robed man looked back and smiled at her.
His attendants asked Zhào:
"Would you be willing to have him as your husband for a short while?"
Zhào replied immediately:
"If you would be my husband for a short while,
I would also cherish your kindness."
The brocade-robed man quickly dismounted
and entered the woods with her.
After parting,
he said to Zhào:
"You will give birth to a son
who will become a bright spirit.
Take good care of him."
Zhào indeed became pregnant,
and when the time came, she gave birth to a boy
with red hair, a green face,
and red hair covering his entire body.
He was only five inches long,
but his eyes shone brightly.
Suì found this very strange
and said:
"This must be a monster;
we should kill him."
Zhào said:
"This child was entrusted to you;
how could he be a monster?
Perhaps he is an extraordinary being.
Why kill him?
If you kill him, it may bring harm.
What should we do?"
Suì, frightened, stopped,
and Zhào hid the child in a secret room.
When he turned seven,
the boy suddenly grew to ten feet tall.
Soon, a large bird descended from the sky,
and the boy ran out,
leaped onto the bird's back, and flew away.
His mother wept for him day and night.
After several months,
the boy returned from outside,
wearing golden armor,
carrying a sword and a curved bow,
and leading over a thousand soldiers.
He entered the gate directly,
bowed to his mother, and said:
"I am the son of the Touring Inspector Envoy,
fortunate to have been entrusted to you.
I have received the grace of birth and nurturing,
but have not yet repaid it.
From now on,
I will come from time to time to pay my respects.
Once I have slightly repaid your kindness,
I will no longer come."
Zhào said:
"What kind of deity are you, my son?"
The boy replied:
"Mother, be careful not to speak of this.
I have been appointed as the Eastern Demon-Capturing General.
In the eastern lands,
those who do not revere the bright spirits
and dare to commit evil,
I am authorized to execute them all."
Zhào brought wine and roasted meat to feed him,
and said to her son:
"I do not have much wine or meat;
it cannot be enough for all your soldiers."
The boy smiled and said:
"Mother, simply sprinkle a cup of wine into the air,
and all the soldiers will drink."
His mother did as he said.
They saw wine falling from the sky like rain,
and the soldiers all lifted their faces to drink it.
The boy quickly stopped them and said:
"Drink sparingly."
Before parting,
he said to his mother:
"If you are ever in danger,
simply burn incense and call out to me from afar,
and I will come immediately."
After speaking,
he mounted his horse and left like wind and rain.
A year later,
Zhào's father passed away,
and Zhào went to bury him.
At her father's home,
every month, about a thousand ghost soldiers
would surround the residence.
A deity knocked on the door and said:
"I want to build a shrine here.
Your father has come to join me.
You should leave quickly;
otherwise,
I will kill you all."
Zhào suddenly remembered her son's parting words
and burned incense to call for him.
That evening,
her son arrived with over a thousand soldiers.
He sent an envoy to question the deity,
and the deity, bewildered, gathered his troops into formation
and bound himself before the boy.
The boy reprimanded him
and executed all his followers.
He said to his mother:
"This is not a deity
but a powerful ghost.
In life, he was a general under Shǐ Cháoyì.
After dying in battle, he had nowhere to go,
so he gathered the soldiers who had died in battle
and led them here,
intending to establish a shrine for himself."
His mother said:
"I just heard that
my father is already by my side.
Can you ask him?"
The boy ordered the deity to be seized and questioned:
"I know everything about your schemes;
there is no need to speak of them.
But why did you pursue Zhào Yù without cause?
Where is he now?"
The deity wept and replied:
"I beg the general for mercy.
In life, I was a general
but failed to achieve merit
and died on the battlefield.
After death, I sought to become a deity,
but again made poor plans.
Today, I have incurred your wrath.
If the general does not report this crime to heaven,
and allows me to serve under your command,
I will pledge my loyalty unto death."
The boy asked again:
"Where is Zhào Yù?"
The deity replied:
"He is hidden inside the tomb of Doctor Zhèng."
The boy immediately ordered Zhào Yù to be retrieved from the tomb,
and Zhào Yù soon revived.
Zhào earnestly urged her son to forgive the deity's crime,
so the boy released his bonds
and appointed him as a minor general under his command.
He then bid farewell to his mother,
weeping as he said:
"As a deity,
I should not frequently appear in the human world.
I will not come again.
Take good care of yourself, Mother."
He then departed like wind and rain,
and from then on, he never came again.
Wèi Dān
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Jízhōu Prefect Wèi Dān,
after leaving his post, resided in Luòyáng.
He had a daughter,
just sixteen years old,
of exceptional beauty.
One midsummer day,
they were enjoying the cool in the courtyard.
Suddenly, looking up, they saw the sky split open,
and a tall man descended from the rift,
coming straight before Dān.
He wore purple robes and gold ornaments,
was dark-skinned and bearded,
and said:
"My surname is Zhū,
and Heaven has sent me to be your son-in-law."
Dān dared not refuse,
but requested time to prepare,
and only after repeated pleas was permission granted.
They set a date for the following month,
and then he soared into the sky and departed.
Dān and his wife,
though deeply worried and distressed,
still prepared wine and food to await him.
Suddenly, a stableman rushed in and bowed to Dān.
Dān said:
"Why do you rush in without tending to the horses?
This is most improper."
The stableman said:
"I secretly observed that you, sir, look troubled,
so I beg to speak of this matter."
Dān said:
"Why should you need to know?"
The stableman insisted,
so Dān told him.
The stableman said:
"You, sir, need not worry;
this is a trivial matter."
Having said this, he left.
When the gold-adorned man arrived as scheduled,
the stableman rushed in again.
Upon seeing him,
the gold-adorned man hurriedly descended and bowed twice.
The stableman, with a stern expression, rebuked him:
"Heaven pardoned you,
sentencing you to live among humans;
how dare you disturb people like this again?"
He replied:
"I deserve death."
And bowed again.
The stableman then ascended the hall and sat down,
summoned the gold-adorned man to sit,
and ordered wine.
The stableman took a large bronze basin,
drank several vessels from it,
each vessel holding over three dǒu.
After drinking,
he took an iron pestle,
broke it and chewed it.
Then he offered the bronze basin to the gold-adorned man to drink from.
The gold-adorned man looked very fearful,
but drank it.
He only repeated, "I deserve death,"
and said nothing else.
The stableman said:
"I sentence you to one hundred days in the celestial prison."
Then he soared into the sky and departed.
The stableman said:
"I am your, sir, Beidǒu life-star.
You, sir Wèi, have devotedly practiced day and night,
and now I repay you.
That impudent one
is a rogue star,
now imprisoned.
Please dismiss your other worries."
Having said this, he left.
Lú Pèi
In the final years of the Zhēnyuán era,
Lǘ Pèi, the Deputy Magistrate of Wèinán County,
was by nature profoundly filial.
His mother had long suffered from ailments of the waist and legs,
and by this time her illness had grown severe,
confining her to bed for years on end,
unable to bear the pain day and night.
Lǘ Pèi thereupon resigned from his post,
escorted his mother back to Cháng'ān,
and took up residence in a separate estate within Chánglè Ward,
intending to exhaust his wealth to seek treatment from the imperial physician Wáng Yànbó.
Wáng Yànbó’s reputation and influence were immense,
making it impossible to see him on short notice;
day after day, Lǘ Pèi went to plead for an audience.
After more than half a year,
he was finally granted a single visit,
scheduled for a certain day at dawn.
On that day, by midday he still had not arrived;
Lǘ Pèi waited and watched at the gate,
his heart anxious, his gaze strained.
As the day gradually grew late,
Lǘ Pèi became increasingly disheartened.
Suddenly, he saw a woman in white robes,
of exceptionally beautiful appearance,
riding a fine horse,
accompanied by a young maidservant,
coming from the west of the lane,
swiftly galloping eastward past him.
After a short while,
she returned from the east,
halted her horse at Lǘ Pèi’s location,
and said to him:
"Observing your expression, you seem worried and dejected,
as if awaiting someone’s arrival;
may I inquire the reason?"
Lǘ Pèi’s thoughts were fixed on Wáng Yànbó,
and at first he did not notice the woman’s approach;
only after being repeatedly questioned
did he fully explain the situation to her.
The woman said:
"Wáng Yànbó is an imperial physician;
it is unlikely he will come here.
I possess modest skills,
no less than what Wáng Yànbó is capable of.
Allow me to see your honored mother once,
and I shall surely bring about her complete recovery."
Lǘ Pèi, overjoyed and astonished,
bowed before her horse’s head and said:
"If this truly comes to pass,
I beg to repay you by serving as your slave."
Lǘ Pèi then first went in to inform his mother,
who was at that moment groaning in agony;
hearing Lǘ Pèi’s words,
she suddenly felt slightly relieved.
He then led the woman to his mother’s presence;
the woman had only just raised her hand to examine her,
