when his mother was already able to move on her own.
Thereupon, the entire household rejoiced and leaped for joy,
vying to offer all the gold and silk they possessed
to present to the woman.
The woman said:
"This is not yet enough;
I must administer one dose of medicine,
which will not only completely eradicate the chronic illness
but also ensure she enjoys longevity."
The mother said:
"This old woman’s bones were nearing death;
you, celestial master, have given me rebirth.
I do not know by what means I may repay such complete virtue."
The woman said:
"If you do not disdain my humble status,
and permit me to serve as Jiǔláng’s wife,
so that I may constantly remain by your honored mother’s side, that will suffice;
how dare I speak of merit?"
The mother said:
"Lǘ Pèi was even willing to become your slave, celestial master;
now, on the contrary, he may become your husband—
what could be amiss with that?"
The woman bowed twice in gratitude,
then from her maidservant’s hand
took the small dressing case she carried,
extracted a dose of medicine the size of a knife-tip,
and mixed it to administer to the mother.
Once the medicine entered her mouth,
all the accumulated sufferings of years
dissipated and were instantly pacified.
They then fully arranged the six rites of marriage
and took her as wife.
The woman attended to her mother-in-law morning and night,
fulfilling wifely duties with strict diligence.
However, every ten days,
she would request to return once to her own home.
Lǘ Pèi wished to send a carriage to escort her,
but she firmly declined,
riding only her old horse
and accompanied by her maidservant,
coming and going swiftly,
leaving virtually no trace.
At first, Lǘ Pèi intended to accommodate her wishes,
and did not investigate further;
but as time passed,
he grew rather suspicious.
One morning,
waiting for her departure,
Lǘ Pèi secretly went to spy on her.
He saw her ride out through Yánxīng Gate,
the horse traveling through the air.
Startled, Lǘ Pèi asked passersby,
but none had seen it.
He then followed her to the burial grounds east of the city,
where a shaman had laid out wine and food offerings,
pouring libations of wine upon the ground in sacrifice;
there he saw the woman dismount
and approach to receive and drink it.
Her maidservant followed, gathering paper money,
loaded it onto the horse,
whereupon it transformed into copper coins.
He also saw the woman use her whip to draw on the ground,
and the shaman, following her indication, said:
"This may serve as the burial site."
Once the matter was concluded,
she mounted her horse and returned.
Lǘ Pèi felt deeply disturbed by this,
returned and fully reported it to his mother,
who said:
"I always knew she was a supernatural being;
what can we do about it?"
From then on, the woman never again returned to Lǘ Pèi’s household,
and Lǘ Pèi considered himself fortunate.
Several tens of days later,
as Lǘ Pèi was out on South Street,
he suddenly encountered the woman traveling with her entourage;
Lǘ Pèi called out:
"Why has my lady not returned for so long?"
The woman paid him no heed,
urged her horse forward, and departed.
The next day,
she sent her maidservant to convey a message to Lǘ Pèi:
"I am truly not your equal,
but moved by your filial conduct,
I therefore treated
your honored mother’s illness,
bringing about her peace and recovery.
You yourself requested and pledged to become husband and wife.
Now that you have grown suspicious,
it is indeed time to part."
Lǘ Pèi asked the maidservant:
"Where is my lady now?"
The maidservant said:
"My lady the day before yesterday has already remarried,
to the Advisory Secretary Jìng Gōnglǐ."
Lǘ Pèi said:
"Even if she wished to abandon me,
how could it be so swift?"
The maidservant said:
"My lady is an earth deity,
overseeing the burial sites of households within three hundred lǐ of the Jīngzhào Prefecture.
She must constantly dwell within the capital as the wife of a living man,
and cannot remain unattached."
The maidservant added:
"My lady will never be without a proper place,
but it is lamentable that Jiǔláng’s fortune and blessings were too meager;
had my lady remained his wife forever,
the entire household of Jiǔláng
would have become terrestrial immortals."
Lǘ Pèi was the ninth among his siblings.
Shěn Yù
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Shěn Huá,
a junior official,
retired and lived in Yǒngchóng Lane.
His son, Shěn Yù, served as a county lieutenant in Sānyuán.
He had long owned a separate estate,
located west of the county seat,
and because of his official duties, Yù took the opportunity to renovate it.
North of the manor,
on a plain over ten *li* wide,
he demolished an ancient burial mound to build a cattle barn.
When his term of office ended,
he returned to farming there.
One day,
while napping in the eastern pavilion of the hall,
he suddenly awoke with a start,
and saw two yellow-clad officials who said to Yù:
"The prefectural office summons you, sir.
Yù thought to himself that since his official duties had ended,
he had no business at the prefectural office,
so he refused and did not go.
The two officials insisted and called him urgently,
and Yù unconsciously followed them out.
He passed by his beloved relatives and family members,
waving and calling out to them,
but none responded.
The two officials drove him forward with great urgency,
and they proceeded north for about twenty *li*.
They arrived at a city office,
where the people were sparse,
and the roads were overgrown with weeds.
On the east street of the main government office,
two large gates faced each other, one to the north and one to the south, both open.
The officials led him through the north gate
and made Yù wait outside a screen.
They went in and announced,
"Shěn Yù has been brought here."
After a long while,
a statement was read in the hall,
and the case was handed over to the authorities for questioning.
Yù, terrified, fled,
not knowing where to go,
and so he rushed into the south gate.
Inside the gate was a hall,
with multiple layers of curtains and drapes.
In his desperate situation,
Yù went straight behind the curtains.
There he saw a nobleman in purple robes,
sleeping behind a writing desk.
Yù was glad to have found someone to turn to,
but he also feared the arrival of the two officials,
so he made noises to rouse him,
and the purple-robed man awoke.
He looked closely at Yù and said:
"Who are you?"
Yù immediately stated his official title and name.
The purple-robed man said:
"I am a relative and old acquaintance of yours,
do you know me?"
Yù, startled and confused, did not reply.
The man said again:
"Are you not the nephew of the Zhāng family?
I am your maternal granduncle.
While in the human world,
have you also heard of Vice Minister Zhāng Wèi?"
Yù said:
"I heard of him when I was young.
Our family has his collected works,
and I can still remember them."
The purple-robed man said happily:
"Try reciting some for me."
Yù recited: "The cherry blossoms understand how to knot and hang like pendant eaves; / The willow branches know how to bend low and enter the window."
The purple-robed man was greatly pleased.
The two officials hurried to the front courtyard and said:
"The Autumn Bureau summons Shěn Yù."
They then bowed from a distance,
and addressed the purple-robed man as "Sir Cáo,"
paying their respects with great deference.
The purple-robed man said to them:
"Shěn Yù is my grandson,
you can convey my wishes to the Autumn Bureau,
and ask them to delay the deadline."
The two officials accepted the order and left.
Soon they returned and said:
"We respectfully comply with your instruction."
The purple-robed man said:
"You are not dead yet,
you should return quickly."
Yù thanked him and took his leave,
and the officials waited for Yù at the gate.
They smiled and said to Yù:
"The kindness of Sir Cáo,
how could you forget it?"
They then led Yù southward.
Yù promised them generous rewards of wine, food, money, and silk.
Suddenly, it was as if he awoke from a dream,
and the sun had already set.
He did not tell anyone about this,
but immediately ordered offerings to be made to the two officials in the wilderness.
Yù remained unharmed.
Five days later,
Yù saw the two officials again in the evening at the manor gate, and they said:
"The grievances and accusations continue,
and we need you, sir, to testify."
Yù then inquired about the offense,
and the two officials said:
"You, sir, built a cattle barn,
and leveled ten ancient graves,
which has been strongly contested,
and we await your defense."
Yù said to them:
"This was the arbitrary decision of my servant, Yínyào."
The two officials looked at each other and said:
"If we summon the servant instead of you, sir,
that might suffice."
Then they suddenly disappeared.
That night,
Yínyào suffered a seizure and died.
A few days later,
Yù suddenly encountered the two officials again,
and they said to Yù:
"Yínyào claims that you, sir, instructed him,
and his plea is very earnest,
so you, sir, should go yourself."
Yù earnestly pleaded with them,
especially hoping they would report this to Sir Cáo once more.
The two officials agreed.
After a short while, they returned and said:
"Sir Cáo instructs you, sir, to go into hiding tonight,
and be careful not to reveal it.
Hide for three days,
and the matter will be resolved."
After saying this, they disappeared.
Yù then secretly selected a fast horse
and rode alone at night.
Yù had once lived and studied at the Fǎlún Temple in Tóngzhōu,
so he went there.
When he arrived,
He encountered a monk who was his friend coming out,
so he took shelter in his room.
After staying for several days,
fearing he would cause his strict father worry,
he went straight back to the capital,
not daring to tell the truth.
The manor steward came and said:
"A fire broke out the night before last,
and the cattle barn on the northern plain
has been reduced to ashes."
Yù ultimately escaped harm.
Dǎng Guóqīng
Twenty li southeast of Jìnyáng,
there is a Tái Tái temple,
located beside the Fén River.
During the Yuánhé era,
when Wáng È
was governing Hédōng,
there was a villager named Dǎng Guóqīng
who was skilled at building houses.
One evening,
he dreamed that a man dressed in black came to his door,
and said to Guóqīng:
"The Tái Tái deity summons you."
He followed him and left.
Exiting the city gate,
they walked twenty li,
arriving at the Tái Tái deity's temple.
Outside the temple gate were several dozen officials and soldiers,
clad in armor and holding weapons,
arrayed on both sides.
Guóqīng was terrified and dared not advance.
The messenger said:
"Do not be afraid."
Then he entered to pay his respects.
He saw over a hundred soldiers,
conducting the proceedings with great solemnity,
and then he bowed twice.
The Tái Tái deity summoned Guóqīng to ascend the steps and said:
"My temple is dilapidated and leaking,
damaged by wind and sun,
and whenever it rains,
my robes, tables, and mats get soaked.
Moreover, you shall seal its cracks for me,
so that I suffer no more from wind and rain."
Guóqīng said:
"I humbly accept your command."
Thereupon, he applied plaster and climbed onto the temple roof,
patching all the leaks.
When it was finished,
the deity summoned the man in black
to escort Guóqīng back.
Exiting the temple gate,
they headed northwest.
Before they had gone ten li,
they suddenly heard the sound of heralds shouting,
and the messenger and Guóqīng both hid by the side of the road.
Soon they saw over a hundred riders,
coming from the north toward the south,
with several dozen holding weapons and clearing the way.
There was one person wearing a crown and official headdress,
clad in purple robes with a golden pendant,
riding a white horse,
his demeanor imposing and grand,
with the most followers bringing up the rear.
The messenger said:
"That is the deity of Mójī Mountain.
He is to feast tomorrow at the Lǐ family's home,
so tonight he first came to pay his respects to my lord at the temple."
Guóqīng and the messenger entered the city gate together,
when suddenly he felt a slight sting in the corner of his eye.
As he scratched it,
he awoke with a start.
The next day,
he went to the Tái Tái temple,
and saw on the table traces where the roof had leaked and rain had dripped.
Looking at the roof,
there were indeed places that had been repaired.
On his way back,
before he had gone six or seven li,
he heard the sound of flutes and drums from a village fortress west of the road,
so he went to pay a visit.
He saw a feast set out,
with a shaman calling out and dancing,
performing a sacrificial ceremony to the deity.
Guóqīng inquired about it,
and was told:
"This is the Lǐ family's residence.
Lǐ Cúngǔ once served as a yájiàng,
but in previous years, Sītú Fàn punished him for neglecting the law.
Because he had military achievements,
he was spared death,
and banished to Yànmén Commandery.
In Yànmén, there is the deity of Mójī Mountain.
Cúngǔ often prayed at his temple,
wishing to return alive.
Recently, he was pardoned and allowed to return.
Cúngǔ believed it was due to the protection of the Mójī Mountain deity,
so he is now holding this sacrificial ceremony."
This indeed matched Guóqīng's dream.
A minor official in Tàiyuán
When Wáng È governed Tàiyuán,
one day around noon,
a minor official
saw a divine being,
over ten feet tall,
clad in golden armor and holding a sword,
walking slowly from the yámén.
Then he stood still for a long time,
as if waiting for something.
The minor official was very frightened upon seeing this,
and reported it to the yájiàng Jìn Tǎn and Zhāng Hé.
They went together to look,
and it was as the minor official had said.
Soon a violent wind arose,
and he suddenly disappeared.
A little over a month later, È passed away.
This was during the Yuánhé era.
Villager Old Man Chén
Between Yúnzhōu and Shuòzhōu, there was once a great drought,
and the summer heat was also severe.
Thousands of villagers fell ill from the heat.
There was a peasant named Old Man Chén,
who was walking alone in the fields
when he suddenly encountered a person
whose appearance was extraordinary.
He wore golden armor,
with a bow and arrows at his side,
held a long sword,
and rode a fine horse,
with a red tassel and golden pendant,
radiant and splendid,
whipping his horse to gallop swiftly.
He happened to meet Old Man Chén,
reined in his horse, and said:
"Are you not from this village?"
The old man said:
"I am a farmer,
and my family has lived here for many years."
The divine being said:
"I am a heavenly envoy.
The Supreme Deity sees that the people of your village are all suffering from heat illness.
Is it solely due to the blazing sun?
Moreover, there is a malevolent ghost in your village.
That is why many villagers are ill.
The Supreme Deity has ordered me to drive it away."
Then he disappeared.
Old Man Chén immediately reported the matter to the villagers.
From then on, between Yúnzhōu and Shuòzhōu,
all those suffering from heat illness recovered.
Yuè Kūn,
originally named Chōng,
repeatedly took the imperial examinations but did not pass.
In the twelfth year of Yuánhé,
he gave up the examinations and returned east,
arriving at Huàyīn.
At night, he prayed at the mountain temple,
to divine whether to advance or retreat.
In the middle of the night,
he suddenly dreamed of a man with a blue sash,
who checked the register and came to report:
"Next year, the name Yuè Kūn has already arrived,
but the register of the underworld does not show Yuè Chōng."
Chōng then changed his name to Kūn.
The following year, it happened as foretold.
After the spring examinations,
he passed by the mountain temple to give thanks,
and also prayed to learn what official rank he would attain.
In his dream, it was said that his official career would span four grades,
only reaching commandery governor,
and he would end his days in Yǐngzhōu.
The temple in Yǒngqīng County
In Fángzhōu's Yǒngqīng County,
120 li east of the commandery seat,
the mountain town lay in ruins,
its walls and streets desolate.
During Emperor Mùzōng's reign,
a magistrate had served for over a year
when his younger brother came to visit.
Startled by the desolation,
he was overcome with sorrow.
On a leisurely day,
he toured the four corners
and found nothing but brambles and thorns.
He saw a dilapidated temple standing tall,
with clay idols arrayed inside,
but no door plaque or inscribed tablet
to indicate whose temple it was.
Inquiring with the local clerks,
he was only told it was the Temple of the Great King of Yǒngqīng.
The magistrate's brother lingered there for a long time,
then drowsily fell asleep
and encountered the deity in a dream.
The deity said:
"My name and deeds have long been obscure.
I have yearned to recount my story,
but feared being labeled a monster.
Now that you inquire,
I can finally vent the grievances of many years.
I am from Pílíng.
My grandfather, Zǐyǐn,
has a biography in the Records of Wú.
He slew the tiger of the Southern Mountains,
beheaded the flood dragon of the Long Bridge,
rid the people of scourges,
and his hidden merits were illustrious.
I, too, always harbored lofty ambitions
to achieve merit and aid my time.
My name is Kuò.
Commissioned by the Supreme Deity,
I hunted fierce beasts
in the four commanderies of Jīn, Shāng, Jūn, and Fáng.
Within several years,
I exterminated countless
ferocious tigers,
bringing sudden peace to the living populace.
The leader of the tigers was in Xīchéng Commandery,
massive in form,
unusually swift and agile,
its body like white brocade,
with a round, mirror-like glow on its forehead.
It had harmed the most people,
and I also slew it.
The grateful residents
built a temple for me.
From north of Xiāng-Hàn
to south of Lánguān,
over thirty places in total
became my resting sites.
Over the long years of worship,
folk traditions have often erred,
mistaking me for the White Tiger Deity.
Fortunately, you inquired,
so I wish to clarify,
to correct this misconception."
Another day,
the magistrate's brother spoke of this to an official in Xiāngyáng,
who then wrote it on a wooden tablet placed in the temple.
Dust eroded and rain soaked it,
and the text was nearly obliterated
until the rénshēn year of the Dàzhōng era,
when Wáng Chéng, an observation judge of Xiāngzhōu,
had it carved in stone at the temple.
Cuī Zé
When Wáng È governed Tàiyuán,
there was a man from Qīnghé named Cuī Zé,
who served as prefect of Fǎngzhōu during the Chángqìng era.
Once, while escaping the heat in his courtyard
on a clear, moonlit night,
he suddenly saw a very tall man
with a high hat and wide sleeves
descend from the front corridor of the hall
and stand on the steps,
shouting loudly
three times before stopping.
The entire Cuī household witnessed it.
Zé was both frightened and repulsed,
ordering servants to approach him,
but the figure had already vanished.
That night,
Zé fell ill.
The next day,
he sent a messenger with a letter,
requesting to retire from office due to old age,
but the ministerial office did not permit it.
Over a month later,
he died in the commandery.
Hán Yù
The Vice Minister of Personnel, Hán Yù,
in the summer of the fourth year of Chángqìng,
fell ill and could not attend to duties.
By the ninth month of autumn, he was dismissed,
and his illness worsened.
In the eleventh month of winter,
he lay resting by day at Jìng'ān Ward.
He saw a divine being
over ten feet tall,
clad in armor and bearing a sword,
with bow and arrows at his side,
his appearance imposing and stern.
He entered the bedchamber
and stood before the couch.
After a while, he said to Hán Yù:
"The Emperor commands me to discuss matters with you."
Hán Yù hastily rose,
straightened his cap, and sat up, saying:
"I, your subject, am unfortunately ill,
and dare to..."
...appear before the King in a disrespectful posture."
The divine being said:
"The state of Wēicuìgǔjué
has long been an enemy of the Hán clan,
and now we wish to campaign against them but lack the strength.
What do you think?"
Hán Yù replied:
"I, your subject, am willing to follow the Great King in this campaign."
The divine being nodded and departed.
Hán Yù then wrote down these words
and placed them beside his seat,
unable to decipher them for several days.
By the twelfth month, he passed away.
Lǐ Féngjí
The former chancellor Lǐ Féngjí
once served as an assistant to the Minister of Works, Fàn Xīcháo, in the Shànyú Headquarters.
At that time, at Jīnchéng Temple, there was an elderly monk named Wúwéi,
over seventy years old.
One day, while sitting alone in his meditation chamber,
leaning against the wall,
with eyes closed and counting breaths,
he suddenly saw a figure clad in armor and holding a spear
enter from the temple.
After the time of a meal,
he heard the announcement that Assistant Lǐ was coming—
whenever Lǐ Féngjí was about to visit Jīnchéng Temple,
Wúwéi would always see that divine being arrive first,
and this became a regular occurrence.
The garrison commander Jiǎn Yǐng
was friendly with Wúwéi's disciple Fǎzhēn,
who often told Yǐng about this.
Fán Zōngxùn
West of Xiáshí County was a shrine to a holy goddess.
The county magistrate, Wéi Móu,
once visited there with the former magistrate Fán Zōngxùn.
Zōngxùn was by nature careless and unrestrained,
holding no regard for gods or spirits.
He scratched the walls with his whip,
picked at the sleeves of the deity's garments,
and spoke and laughed with irreverent levity.
Several days after returning,
a mad monk in the county
suddenly rushed into the county office gate, shouting loudly:
"The magistrate should uphold the law!
How can you let a wicked man run free,
allowing him to act with such reckless oppression?"
Móu had him driven out,
without understanding his meaning.
Over ten days later,
Móu's young daughter fell ill.
He summoned a shaman to examine her, who said:
"The Holy Goddess sends word to the Chief Official:
The local earth spirits
all hope for the Chief Official's protection.
How could you teach people to encroach and plunder?
Previously, she sent the Master to inform the Chief Official,
but you showed no understanding."
Magistrate Wéi said:
"Who is this wicked man?
I will have him captured at once."
The shaman said:
"It is the former magistrate, Fán Zōngxùn.
He has already departed,
so nothing can be done.
Henceforth, we hope the Chief Official will be mindful
and not allow such things.
Then your young daughter's illness will soon be cured."
Magistrate Wéi thanked him,
ordered incense burned and the place swept clean,
and the entire county grew more reverent and fearful.
His daughter recovered within a few days.
Péi Dù
When Péi Dù was young,
a fortune-teller said:
"Your fate is governed by the Lianzhen Star Deity of the Northern Dipper.
You should always maintain reverence,
and offer sacrifices with fruit and wine."
Péi Dù followed this advice,
serving the deity with great diligence.
When he became chancellor,
his official duties became numerous and complex,
and he eventually forgot about it.
Though he always felt something was lacking in his heart,
he never spoke of it to anyone,
and his sons also did not know.
A Daoist priest from the capital came to visit him,
and Péi Dù kept him to converse.
The priest said:
"In the past, sir, you revered and served the deity.
Why did you stop halfway?
If you had continued your devotion without cease,
it would also have moved you, sir."
Péi Dù only smiled.
Later, when he became military governor of Tàiyuán,
a family member fell ill,
so they summoned a female shaman to examine them.
The shaman plucked the huqin,
and after swaying for a long while,
she suddenly leapt up and said:
"I request Péi the chancellor.
General Liánzhēn sends a message: 'How utterly heartless,
do you not recognize me at all?'
The general is very angry.
Why does the chancellor not apologize to him?"
Péi Dù was greatly startled.
The shaman said:
"You should choose an auspicious day, purify yourself and fast,
burn incense in a clean courtyard,
and prepare wine and fruit.
General Liánzhēn also wishes to manifest his form to you, sir."
On that day,
Péi Dù bathed,
donned his official robes,
stood below the steps,
faced east, poured a libation of wine, and bowed twice.
He saw a man in golden armor holding a spear,
over three zhang tall,
standing facing north.
Péi Dù was drenched in sweat,
prostrated himself and dared not move.
After a short while, the figure vanished.
He asked his attendants,
but they all said they saw nothing.
From then on, Péi Dù revered and served the deity, not daring to neglect him.
Zhāng Zhòngyīn
The son of the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Revenue, Zhāng Pāng,
was named Zhòngyīn.
He was studying in the Nánshān mountains,
and thus befriended three or four young men of his time.
Zhòngyīn was also intelligent and sharp by nature,
but he did not devote himself to literary studies;
he preferred practicing archery and horsemanship.
At times, he and his companions would take their crossbows
and wander through the forests and marshes.
Several li from their lodging,
they saw an old man holding a bow,
chasing a deer around the woods.
With one arrow he hit it,
piercing its chest, and it fell.
Zhòngyīn was amazed and admiring.
The old man said:
"Can you do this?"
Zhòngyīn said:
"It is certainly something I enjoy."
The old man said:
"I have caught this deer,
but I have no use for it.
I offer it to you,
to cover the cost of a meal."
Zhòngyīn and the others thanked him respectfully.
The old man said:
"Can you come tomorrow to watch me shoot?"
The next day they arrived,
and again saw the old man chasing a deer.
He shot it again,
with no difference from before,
and again gave it to Zhòngyīn.
Zhòngyīn found it even more extraordinary.
After this happened three times,
Zhòngyīn bowed and begged to learn his archery method.
The old man said:
"Observing you, it seems you can be taught.
Meet me here again tomorrow,
and do not let others know."
So Zhòngyīn went to the place the day after tomorrow.
The old man also returned,
then led Zhòngyīn westward for four or five li,
entering the mouth of a valley.
The path gradually descended,
as if entering a cave.
The plants and trees were different from those of the human world,
and Zhòngyīn revered him all the more.
After walking about thirty li or more,
they reached a large estate,
like the country villa of a high minister or noble.
He had Zhòngyīn wait in the hall outside the central gate,
then the old man straightened his clothes and entered,
appearing to pay a formal visit.
He came out and said:
"My aunt knows you have come here.
Tomorrow you will go to see her."
Zhòngyīn respectfully agreed and stayed the night in the hall.
The next day,
he ordered servants to prepare bath water for Zhòngyīn,
and to change into new clothes.
The old man prepared a feast in the central hall,
and invited Zhòngyīn in to pay respects to his mother.
Zhòngyīn bowed below the hall,
but the mother did not rise,
nor did she offer any polite refusals.
The old man again invited him up into the hall to be seated.
Looking at her appearance,
it did not much resemble a human's;
perhaps it was due to extreme old age and change,
or it was like the form of an ape or macaque.
The food items laid out were very numerous.
While Zhòngyīn was eating,
he did not see the mother move her spoon or chopsticks,
yet in an instant, the meal was finished.
Gazing at her for a long time,
she sat collected as before,
and soon all the food was gone.
The old man again led Zhòngyīn out,
and in front of the hall under a tree,
set up a couch and sat down.
The old man then called for a bow and arrows.
He looked up,
pointed at a tree branch and said:
"With ten arrows, take one chi of this."
He then shot ten arrows,
shattering and shooting down ten segments of branch,
which joined together to make one chi.
He said to Zhòngyīn:
"How is this for precision?"
Zhòngyīn bowed below the couch and said:
"I am filled with admiration."
He then had ten needles placed on top of a wall,
stood thirty paces away,
and raised his first arrow.
Then he shot in order,
and every shot hit without fail.
He then taught Zhòngyīn the postures for bending, stretching, and positioning the feet.
He only emphasized aligning the bones of the arm and wrist.
When the arm and wrist bones supported each other,
the bow was already fully drawn.
Thus, regardless of strength,
it was not,
a matter of exertion.
After several days,
Zhòngyīn had grasped its subtleties.
The old man patted him
and said to Zhòngyīn:
"Stop here.
Strive to make a name with this skill.
Teach five thousand men on each side,
to save the troubled world."
He then led him back to the original place.
And Zhòngyīn's skill improved daily,
indeed gaining a reputation as an excellent archer.
Those who received his teaching,
even children and women,
could then discuss military arts.
Later, after his father died and the mourning period ended,
he happened to travel to the Dōngpíng army,
where he taught several thousand men before he died.
That old man was likely a mountain deity.
An expert archer must have agile limbs and connected arms,
hence his mother resembled an ape.
Líng Huá
In Hángzhōu's Fùyáng, there was a prison officer named Líng Huá,
whose bone structure was extraordinary.
He once met a fortune-teller named Shī Wēng, who said:
"If you can abandon your position as an officer,
you will become a great general."
Huá was a cruel and violent officer;
whenever there were prisoners,
he would strangle their throats and strike their hearts
to extort bribes.
In the early years of the Yuánhé era,
he fell ill and died one night.
As he was dying,
he saw a yellow-robed officer holding an edict.
Approaching him,
it proclaimed:
"By official decree, it is ordered
that Huá, having once governed a difficult county,
achieved notable merit.
However, later misconduct
ruined his success.
Demoted to serve in prison,
he was to await self-reflection and reform.
Yet he lost his way,
straying far from his original intent.
His noble jade-like skull,
was entrusted to a base and lowly man.
Considering this precious bone,
it must find its rightful place.
Now, the ministers suppressing rebellion in Zhènhǎi Army
are to become great generals.
Their bones are not yet solid and complete,
lacking in majestic authority.
They should be replaced with a suitable person,
to avoid leaving them in vain.
The department is ordered to seize Líng Huá,
extract his jade skull bone, and present it.
Furthermore, instruct the relevant office
to provide appropriate compensation."
Then, the yellow-robed man led him in.
Someone in green robes and a crown spoke from behind a curtain:
"Your coming today
is due to your lack of virtue.
To lose your noble fate over petty officers—
I privately lament for you."
He ordered attendants to bring pincers and hammers.
Shortly after,
three men in black robes with leopard-sleeves, holding axes, appeared.
The green-robed figure bestowed five cups of wine upon Huá,
and he fell into a drunken stupor.
He only heard the sound of chiseling his skull,
and when the noise ceased, Huá awoke from his drunkenness.
He was then made to wait on the western steps to receive further orders.
After a while,
an announcement was made:
"For one who has lost noble bones,
it is fitting to make amends.
His life shall be extended by half a cycle,
and he shall be granted ten thousand cash."
After the proclamation,
the green-robed figure invited Huá up the steps and said:
"I am one who lived in obscurity during the Hàn dynasty, fishing and butchering.
Seeking only to preserve my life,
I pursued minor gains.
After death,
I was assigned this post.
Low in rank and trivial in duty,
it is far from satisfying.
Sir, do not lament the loss of your noble bones;
this matter is somewhat significant,
and not unique to you alone."
He ordered wine and drank with Huá in farewell.
After several cups,
Huá fell into unconsciousness.
When he awoke,
he was lying on his old bed.
Feeling his head, the bone was gone;
his colleagues contributed funeral assistance,
totaling ten thousand cash.
He died fifteen years later.
Lǐ Huí
The former Táng chancellor Lǐ Huí,
in his youth, was long afflicted by illness.
His elder brother, Lǐ Pián,
summoned shamans and mediums,
set out wine and food in the courtyard,
to entertain the spirits.
Huí faced the wall and lay down,
when suddenly he heard noise in the courtyard.
Looking back,
he saw several dozen figures below the hall,
some in yellow, some in green robes,
scrambling to take the wine and food and eat.
After a long while, as they were about to disperse,
the shaman prepared to clear the offerings,
when suddenly a figure descended from the sky,
with wings on both sides.
All the ghosts retreated in fear,
exclaiming:
"The god of Grand Master Lù has arrived!"
The shaman also cried out in alarm:
"The god of Grand Master Lù is here!"
He immediately ordered more wine and food placed in the courtyard.
The god lowered his head to the feast,
ate almost everything,
then drank the wine.
Shortly after,
his face turned red,
as if drunk.
Then he flew away,
and the crowd of ghosts vanished with him.
Several days later,
Huí recovered from his illness.
Lǐ Xù
In the fourth year of the Yuánhé era,
in Huòqiū County, Shòu Prefecture, there was a man named Lǐ Liùláng,
who claimed to be the spirit-official Imperial Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Xù.
When speaking with people,
his form remained unseen.
There was a man named Wáng Yún
who served as his attendant.
After arriving in Huòqiū for over a month,
they rented a house to live in,
with no other possessions,
only a table, a chair, and a rope-bed.
Those who came to request matters
all submitted written petitions.
Wáng Yún would spread them beside the table,
and the writing would appear moist,
filling the paper in an instant.
He could write.
The characters were clear and distinct,
and predictions of fortune and misfortune all came true.
At that time, Chángsūn Yǐng from Hénán served as the garrison commander,
and initially did not believe it,
but after witnessing the reality,
he began to interact with them.
Previously, the backyard of the official residence was empty and spacious,
and after nightfall, owls would hoot and foxes cry,
frightening everyone, young and old.
So he ordered Lǐ Liùláng to manage and pacify it,
and Lǐ agreed.
Each time he moved,
it sounded like the rustling of wind and rain,
and soon the sound of whipping could be heard.
He sent them away, saying:
"Do not come again."
From then on, the backyard became peaceful.
At that time, Imperial Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Xiāng served as the prefectural governor,
and Attendant Censor Zhāng Zōngběn served as his deputy.
Over a year later,
Zōngběn was touring the county.
Having heard earlier of Lǐ Xù's extraordinary abilities but not believing them,
Chángsūn Yǐng summoned him,
and he arrived in an instant.
Zōngběn requested a written note,
intending to present it to the governor,
and took paper and brush to ask.
Xù said:
"Facing these gentlemen,
may I write now?"
Zhāng said:
"Yes."
At first,
there were three brushes on the table,
but suddenly one brush disappeared,
and soon writing filled the paper.
It concluded with:
"Imperial Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Xù bows his head."
Zōngběn was convinced,
returned and reported to Xiāng,
and Xiāng then sent an envoy to invite him.
Thus, they interacted for several days,
and he said:
"I am the younger brother of the god of the Five Sacred Mountains.
My seventh younger brother is in Qí Prefecture,
and I govern this commandery in the underworld."
He also drank wine,
his voice like a woman's,
his words precise and essential,
graceful, fluent, laughing, and chanting.
He often composed poems mocking shamans, such as:
"When have ghosts ever been seen?
The moment the head turns, the spirit descends.
Coveting his fine silk robe,
he falsely claims the great king is angry."
There were many such poems,
but not all are recorded.
Later, he said:
"I will temporarily go to Qí Prefecture to see my younger brother."
He arrived in Qí in mid-July,
and still had Wáng Yún deliver two pecks of new rice
and a letter
to Chángsūn.
Neighbors,
Nearby,
People of the prefecture
all sought predictions of fortune and misfortune from Lǐ Xù.
The places where he wrote critiques still remain.
Cài Róng
In Sānyì Township, Zhōngmóu County, there was a carpenter named Cài Róng
who had believed in and prayed to spirits since childhood.
Every time he ate, he would set aside a portion on the ground,
secretly offering it to the earth god,
and never forgot this even after growing up.
In the spring of the second year of Yuánhé,
he lay ill for six or seven days.
Just as evening fell,
a military officer came running
and said to his mother:
"Hide Cài Róng's clothes and utensils quickly,
do not let anyone see them,
and quickly dress him in women's clothing.
If anyone comes asking,
you must deceive them, saying:
'He has gone out.'
If they seek his whereabouts,
respond vaguely,
and do not let them know where he is."
After speaking, he ran off.
His wife and mother followed his words.
As soon as they finished,
a general on horseback,
followed by over ten men,
holding bows and arrows,
entered the hall directly,
and called for Cài Róng.
His mother, frightened, said:
"He is not here."
They asked:
"Where has he gone?"
She replied:
"Róng returned drunk,
neglected his work,
and I, an old woman, became angry and beat him.
Perhaps he secretly left,
and I do not know where he is;
it has been over ten days now."
The general sent officers to search,
and the searchers came out and said:
"There is no man in the room,
nor any male belongings."
The general repeatedly called for the local earth god.
The one who had instructed them to hide came out and said:
"Yes,"
and was reprimanded:
"Cài Róng has gone out;
how could you not know his whereabouts?"
He replied:
"He left in anger privately,
without telling anyone where he was going."
The general said:
"The king's rear hall has collapsed,
and we need this skilled craftsman.
The deadline is nearly upon us;
who can replace him?"
He replied:
"There is a man named Yè Gàn from Liángchéng Township,
who is more skilled than Cài Róng.
Calculating his allotted lifespan,
he is just due to be conscripted for service."
The general galloped away on his horse.
After a while,
the one who had instructed them to hide came again and said:
"I am the local earth god here.
Because Cài Róng always shares his food with me,
I returned the favor out of gratitude."
Then he left.
The mother looked at Róng,
and he was already drenched in sweat.
From then on, his illness was cured.
Soon, it was heard that Yè Gàn from Liángchéng Township had died suddenly.
Gàn's wife was a cousin of Róng's mother.
Upon checking the time of death,
it was exactly when Róng was dressed in women's clothing.
There was a man named Lǐ Fù,
whose maternal uncle Yáng Shǔ
served as a militia household head in Sānyì Township,
and he heard the whole story.
He went to summon Róng's mother to ask about it,
and she told him everything in return.
The virtue seen in his widespread offerings—
could this be the reason?
Liú Yuánhuán
Liú Yuánjiǒng was a
cunning and deceitful man.
He claimed to be able to refine mercury into gold,
and was also skilled at using ghostly arts to delude the masses,
many of whom were bewitched by him,
allowing him to amass wealth.
Lǐ Shīgǔ was the military governor of Pínglú,
who recruited scholars from all directions.
Anyone with a single skill who arrived
would receive generous treatment.
Yuánjiǒng thus used this technique to seek an audience with Shīgǔ.
Shīgǔ found him remarkable,
and personally tested his ability.
Whether ten zhū or five zhū,
he completed them all instantly.
This was because he had first placed gold flakes into the mercury.
Shīgǔ said:
"This is truly a supreme treasure.
What should it be used for?"
Yuánjiǒng, intent on perfecting his deceit,
without considering future harm,
replied:
"Mix it with other medicines,
slowly burn it for three years,
and one can become an immortal;
make it into eating utensils,
and it can ward off poison;
use it for playthings,
and it can repel evil."
Shīgǔ greatly revered him,
and said:
"The period for burning it again is somewhat long.
For now, you make ten jīn for me,
to prepare the utensils I urgently need."
Yuánjiǒng had originally boasted of this technique
to scheme for Shīgǔ's money and silk,
planning to delay and then flee.
But he was detained by Shīgǔ,
who ordered him specifically to refine gold.
The quantity demanded was extremely large,
and Yuánjiǒng had no way to produce it.
Thus, he used ghostly arts to persuade Shīgǔ, saying:
"You, sir, have succeeded and governed this region
for over thirty years.
Although in terms of military horses and granaries,
no one in the realm can compare with you,
yet if you wish to make all directions look up and submit to your might and virtue,
and to ensure your plans succeed,
you must borrow the power of the gods."
Shīgǔ was very pleased,
and thus inquired further.
Yuánjiǒng then said:
"The Heavenly Equal King of Mount Tài,
when Emperor Xuánzōng performed the eastern fēng sacrifice,
had his image carved from sinking incense wood.
That is why Emperor Xuánzōng enjoyed a long reign.
If you, sir, can exchange his image with other treasures,
then you will receive blessings equal to those of the Kāiyuán era."
Shīgǔ, arrogant and perverse,
strongly agreed.
Yuánjiǒng then said:
"To bring the entire body here,
I fear it cannot be accomplished hastily.
For now, use fifteen jīn of gold
to cast and exchange for its head.
That will surely secure divine protection."
Shīgǔ said:
"Then you first refine it for me,
and quickly accomplish this matter."
Yuánjiǒng laughed heartily and said:
"Although the Heavenly Equal is called a noble god,
he is actually of the ghostly kind.
If we use my gold for his head,
how could dark ghosts dare to rely on such a supremely spiritual object?
That would be to expel the Heavenly Equal;
how could we hope for his blessings?
Only by using pure gold from the mountains and marshes to exchange it
will it do."
Shīgǔ found him even more extraordinary,
and thus gave him twenty jīn of stored gold,
allowing Yuánjiǒng to act as he pleased.
He also ordered Yuánjiǒng to go to the temple on Mount Tài to make the exchange.
Yuánjiǒng then used a mixture of lead and tin,
melting it on the outside to make the exchange,
He
kept the real gold and returned,
making eating utensils for Shīgǔ,
completing everything without fail.
Shīgǔ treated him with even greater courtesy and respect,
serving him like an elder brother.
Silks, concubines, residences,
his support was extremely generous.
The following year,
Shīgǔ was feasting with his officials, officers, and subordinates
when suddenly a cook
came straight from the kitchen to Shīgǔ.
In the midst of the gathering,
he lifted himself over ten feet into the air,
stepped on emptiness and stood,
loudly cursing:
"I am the god of the Five Sacred Mountains.
What kind of thief
has damaged my form?
I appealed to the Emperor above,
and only returned after a year.
When I returned,
my armored soldiers and warhorses,
treasury stores and valuables,
were all plundered by Huáng Shígōng."
Then he cursed even more fiercely,
again raised himself several zhang high,
and after a long while landed on the ground.
Shīgǔ ordered him dragged away.
The cook regained no consciousness,
but remained as if heavily intoxicated for several days.
Shīgǔ then ordered paintings of war chariots and warriors,
spears, armor, banners, and flags,
along with several dozen carts of paper money and silk,
to be taken to Mount Tài and burned.
He still had not realized Yuánjiǒng's deceit.
Just as he was about to investigate the matter,
Shīgǔ suddenly developed a malignant ulcer.
Within a few days,
his brain festered and he died.
His younger brother, Shīdào, took over affairs,
and immediately ordered his administrative officers Lǐ Wénhuì and Yú Zǎo to investigate.
Yuánjiǒng, his arguments exhausted,
was executed in the marketplace.
Zhèng Jiǎn
When Emperor Mùzōng performed the southern suburban sacrifice,
he was about to pay homage at the Tàiqīng Palace.
Zhèng Jiǎn, the chief clerk of Cháng'ān County, was in charge of the labor.
In the western wing of the imperial compound,
he saw a white-clad old man who said:
"There is a well below here,
directly on the path the Yellow Emperor will pass.
You must quickly fill it in.
Otherwise,
the consequences will be unpredictable."
Jiǎn, alarmed and hurried,
had it repaired.
The spot had already sunk several feet;
when excavated, it was an ancient well.
In the moment of his startled glance,
the old man had already vanished.
The Merit Commissioner and Protectorate Army Supervisor Liú Hóngguī reported this.
The Emperor, after completing the court offerings at the palace,
proceeded to the southern suburb.
At the palace gate, he halted his horse.
The chief ministers and attending officials offered congratulations.
He then ordered the Hanlin Academician Wéi Chǔhòu to compose a record,
and commanded the起居郎 Liǔ Gōngquán
to inscribe it above the filled well,
titled "Record of Sacred Auspices and Responses."
He also bestowed crimson robes upon Zhèng Jiǎn.
Liǔ Xiè
Liǔ Xiè was poor in his youth,
and traveled to the Lingnan region.
Kǒng Kuí, the military governor of Guǎngzhōu,
treated him with great generosity,
gifting him over a hundred taels of gold,
and advising him to journey westward.
He then traveled north by boat with several scholars, including Yán Zhú and Céng Àn.
When they reached a point sixty li south of Yángshuò County,
they were gambling on the boat
when Liǔ Xiè suddenly pushed away the gaming board,
rose from his seat,
and caught something with his hand.
At first glance,
it appeared as if someone had handed him a name card.
He immediately hurriedly straightened his robe and belt,
anchored the boat, and disembarked.
Standing on the sandy shore,
he bowed with clasped hands and said:
"I am fortunate to have served alongside you all.
Although my summons has arrived,
I must first reach Guìzhōu.
However, regarding my journey,
you should wait for me ahead on the road."
Céng Àn and Yán Zhú, witnessing Liǔ Xiè's actions,
could not help but feel a chill,
and they too seemed to perceive something as if seeing a vision.
Liǔ Xiè then returned to the boat,
lay down sighing,
and after a long while said to his two friends:
"I have already been appointed as the Registrar of Mount Tài.
Just now, the carriages, officials, and attendants all arrived,
and I have arranged to meet them in Guìzhōu."
From then on, he no longer laughed or spoke,
nor did he fall ill.
However, every time they moored for the night,
he would sit cross-legged,
giving orders and making arrangements
in a manner unlike that of the living.
Yángshuò was still three days' journey from the prefectural seat,
and its fifty rapids
usually required the boatmen's utmost effort to pass through,
but this time they arrived in a single night.
Liǔ Xiè often saw two figures in purple,
fully armed,
holding hammers,
driving over a hundred soldiers
to push and pull his boat through the water.
When Liǔ Xiè reached Guìzhōu,
he had just finished writing a letter home when he died.
This occurred in the eighth month of the fourteenth year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty.
Mǎ Zǒng
Mǎ Zǒng served as the military governor of Tiānpíng.
One day, while leisurely writing a distant letter,
the diviner Chéng Jū was by his side.
Mǎ Zǒng leaned on his desk
and suddenly seemed to doze off,
but his expression turned pained and tense,
unlike his usual demeanor.
Chéng Jū did not dare to disturb him,
so he slowly rose
and went to inform his deputy, Xiàng Yuánfēng.
Shortly after, Mǎ Zǒng summoned Yuánfēng,
dismissed the others, and said to him:
"A strange thing, a strange thing!
I just went somewhere,
a place of solemn depth and majestic gates,
surpassing even a king's residence.
Someone led the way for me,
and I saw the late Minister of Revenue Dù,
who smiled, descended the steps, and greeted me, saying:
'I have long awaited you.
I am very pleased to see you.'
He then lingered and said:
'The position I hold here
is equivalent to that of a Secretariat Director in the human world.
All matters within the universe
pass through my hands.
However, having long been in such a demanding role,
my mind and strength are nearly exhausted,
and I seek a worthy successor.
Your insight and judgment
truly qualify you for great responsibility,
and moreover, we are close and old acquaintances,
which is why I have invited you here.
I respectfully offer this position to you.'
I then declined and withdrew,
even shedding tears.
After a long while,
Dù said:
'Since you are unwilling,
you may return for now.
However, in twenty years,
shall we meet again?'" After waking,
Mǎ Zǒng was greatly pleased at the prospect of such a long life.
Yet, he passed away two years later.
Could it be that Mǎ Zǒng misheard,
or perhaps Dù exaggerated the number of years
to please him?
Cuī Guīcóng,
in the third year of the Chángqìng era (823 CE),
served as a Dàlǐ Píngshì in Hézhōng Prefecture.
One evening,
he dreamed of entering an official compound with someone,
and upon reaching its courtyard,
he saw inside the hall a person sitting facing the sun,
with a grand and imposing retinue.
Another person sat to the side,
his appearance and attire roughly similar.
Both had prominent noses and wide-open eyes,
grasping brushes and examining documents,
as if deciding on matters.
He then hurriedly approached the steps,
bowed and withdrew.
As he walked to the western temple,
he looked between the windows under the corridor,
where documents and registers were piled on large shelves,
like the offices of today’s clerks.
A clerk emerged holding a case file,
so he approached and asked him:
"This must be the underworld office;
I wish to know how much official salary and lifespan I have."
The clerk replied:
"Both of you will later become the prefect of this prefecture;
there is no need to consult the registers."
Upon exiting the gate,
he saw a colleague from the same time,
sitting on the ground playing chūpú.
Returning, he awoke,
greatly astonished by it,
the scene still vivid before his eyes.
Only the person he had accompanied in the dream,
whom he had asked in the dream,
him,
his name was someone he often associated with,
but upon waking,
he forgot who it was.
The next day, upon entering the official compound,
he spoke of it to his colleagues in the residence,
and all considered it auspicious.
They interpreted it:
"You dreamed of seeing yourself,
and you also saw someone playing chūpú,
which is 'pú.'
You will later follow your lord,
govern Pú Prefecture with authority."
Afterward, whenever he entered a temple or shrine,
he would recall the dream,
and he often paid respects at the Hé Dú temple.
When he served as prefect of Huàzhōu,
he paid homage at the temple of the Western Peak,
but the deities and statues were not those he had seen in the dream.
During the Kāichéng era (836–840),
he was appointed from Vice Minister of Revenue
to serve as prefect of Xuānzhōu,
twenty years after the earlier dream.
In the fifth month, he arrived at the prefecture,
and the clerks informed him:
"The deity of Jìngtíng is sincerely revered by the people of this prefecture;
every year, regardless of status,
they must hold a ceremony there.
Other prayers and offerings of thanks occur without a single day’s break.
Therefore, the honest officials always prepare rituals to worship and pay respects."
Guīcóng was ill at the time,
and by autumn he recovered,
so he went to pay respects at the temple.
Upon reaching the gate, he was startled;
on the screen wall was a painted figure,
holding a case file and bowing respectfully,
exactly the clerk from his dream.
Everything he experienced upon entering the temple
matched the old dream,
except there was no companion.
He returned and told his wife and children.
The following year in the seventh month,
Guīcóng fell ill again,
suffering from severe diarrhea,
and especially disliked eating,
with symptoms worsening at night.
He then reflected on his earlier dream,
thinking, "What the clerk said—
will I end here?"
So he prayed in his heart.
After falling asleep,
he dreamed again of rising at dawn and handling affairs as usual.
As he was about to enter the side room,
approaching the side door,
a household clerk named Yáo Guī
whispered in his ear:
"The Lord of the Left has sent someone with a message."
Hearing this, his heart raced and his hair stood on end,
thinking it was no ordinary person.
Before he could sit down in the room,
a person
in military attire, carrying a knife,
rushed in.
He appeared tall and imposing,
with a dark face tinged with red,
unlike a human complexion.
His purple robe was peeling and discolored—
it was the clay statue from the steps of the Jìngtíng Temple.
Before he could speak,
Guīcóng sternly asked:
"How many years will I live?"
The figure immediately replied:
"Over sixty."
In the dream, he remembered these words,
but upon waking,
he forgot the exact number,
perhaps because the deity did not wish people to know their end in advance?
At dawn,
he composed a text to pray to the deity,
explaining everything in detail.
He ordered his sons and nephews to take wine and sacrificial animals to the temple to pray.
Earlier, when the illness struck,
doctors said it arose from cold,
and taking hot medicine worsened it.
So he sought a doctor from Zhèxī,
and physician Shěn Zhōngsuì arrived by post horse.
After taking his pulse,
he straightforwardly said that his illness
was due to excessive heat and blocked qi,
and should be treated with cooling methods,
with licorice and rhinoceros horn as the main ingredients.
Following his advice,
after about ten days he improved slightly,
and after a month he fully recovered.
Believing it must have been divine assistance,
he again composed a text to pray to the deity.
Using his personal salary,
he repaired the temple’s dilapidated parts,
added more clay statues,
and renewed all the paintings on the walls.
He held a grand music performance to honor the deity,
and even danced himself, waving his sleeves.
Back when he had the dream during the Chángqìng era,
he absolutely did not play the game of five dice,
but after arriving south of the river,
he began playing it again with his colleagues.
Guīcóng later became chancellor,
was demoted to Junior Guardian, and returned to Luòyáng.
He died in the seventh year of the Dàzhōng era (853 CE).
Jiǎng Chēn
A man from Zhà, Jiǎng Chēn,
was thoroughly versed in the two classics,
and often taught in his hometown.
Every autumn and winter,
in the middle of the Zhàxī and Tàihú waters,
he would set nets to provide food,
often catching a giant turtle.
Because its appearance was extraordinary,
he looked at it and said:
"Though you have entered my net,
I shall spare you the calamity of being gutted.
Since you are among the four divine creatures,
would you not feel ashamed before this humble old man?"
Then he released it.
The turtle, upon reaching midstream,
turned back to look six or seven times.
Over a year later,
one evening during a stormy, dark night,
he heard a tumultuous sound from the waves,
and the former turtle knocked against the boat, stood up like a human, and said:
"Tonight, the gods of Tàihú, Zhàxī, and Sōngjiāng are holding a gathering,
and the various river deities
have also been summoned.
Banquets are being prepared and seats arranged,
close to this fishing boat.
As you have lingered here,
casting nets for so long,
the fine-scaled fish and small-shelled creatures
have suffered from your frequent netting.
Those who escaped disaster
often harbor resentment.
I fear the water creatures may seize the opportunity
to vent their grievances.
The kindness you showed me in the past
has always been stored in my sincere heart,
and because of this,
I hope to repay you even a ten-thousandth of it.
Could you retreat a short distance to avoid harm?"
Chēn said:
"Yes."
Then, in calm waters,
he moored his boat and waited.
Not long after,
there were turtles, alligators, fish, and turtles,
too numerous to count,
surrounding an area of over two li,
pressing the waves to form walls,
and restraining the waves to create solid ground.
Three gates were opened,
and wide roads were laid out.
Over a thousand strange creatures,
all with human bodies and dragon heads,
holding spears and halberds,
formed ranks,
standing guard as if awaiting something.
Then, several dozen flood dragons and sea monsters
rushed in from east and west,
exhaling breath to form towers and pavilions,
jade palaces and pearl halls,
banquet tables and dance floors,
seats, couches, and cushions,
all completed in an instant.
The wine vessels, utensils, and playthings
were all things not found in the human world.
There were also several hundred divine fish,
spitting fiery pearls,
leading over a hundred armored soldiers,
escorting one in black robes and a black hat,
emerging from the southern ford of Zhàxī.
Then, several hundred water beasts were seen,
holding torches,
leading over two hundred iron-clad cavalry,
escorting one in red robes and a red hat,
coming from the middle of Tàihú.
Upon reaching the city gate,
they dismounted and exchanged greetings.
The Zhàxī god said:
"Not having seen each other,
for five cycles,
though letters have not ceased,
laughter and conversation have long been absent.
I have earnestly admired your great virtue,
and my heart aches with longing."
The Tàihú god said:
"My heart knows this too."
As they exchanged courtesies,
an old flood dragon stepped forward and announced:
"The King of Calm Waters is mounting his horse."
Then the two gods waited.
There appeared one dressed in tiger and leopard skins,
with a red forehead,
green feet,
holding a wax torch,
leading soldiers with banners, spears, and armor,
over a thousand in total,
escorting one in purple robes and a red hat,
arriving from the western branch of Sōngjiāng.
The two gods greeted him at the gate,
performing the rites with great reverence.
After exchanging pleasantries,
the Sōngjiāng god said:
"Ahead, there is one destined to become a prime minister crossing northward,
but his divine appearance is not yet revealed,
and his journey is very difficult.
I fear the gods are not,
aware and do not know,
so we must order Píngyì to still the winds,
and Féngyí to calm the waves.
This is also a standing command from the Heavenly Emperor,
and we should personally attend to it.
Awaiting your noble presence,
can we avoid being punished?
However, I have secretly brought Chancellor Fàn from the waterside,
which should suffice to make up for the oversight."
Then appeared one in coarse clothing,
holding a sword and stepping forward.
The Zhàxī and Tàihú gods said:
"We have long revered you."
Lord Fàn said:
"My meager virtue has not yet vanished,
and the people of Wú remember my kindness,
building a shrine by the river,
offering modest sacrifices in spring and autumn.
Intoxicated by village wine,
I was thus driven here by Lord Jiāng.
To intrude upon this grand banquet
only increases my shame and trepidation."
Then, after exchanging courtesies, they entered the gate.
Once seated,
the old flood dragon stepped forward and announced:
"The King of Xiāng is two li from the city."
Soon, the sound of carriages and horses was heard.
Then appeared one in green robes and a black hat,
of imposing stature and appearance,
with an escort of over a hundred.
Upon ascending the steps,
he met with the three gods.
He said:
"I have just come with Deputy Envoy Qū of Mìluó."
Then appeared one with haggard clothing and a sorrowful,憔悴 appearance,
hunched over as he advanced.
As he took his seat,
Chancellor Fàn said to Qū Yuán with a laugh:
"A banished minister, burdened by the hardships of the waves,
with slanderous marks and traces, your bones not yet dissolved—
with such a wretched face,
how dare you come hunting for cups and plates?"
Qū Yuán said.
"A lonely soul from the Xiāng River,
leftover flesh from a fish's belly,
how dare I use my tongue to respond to the Chancellor?
Yet I have heard that an arrow that can pierce seven layers of armor
does not shoot a bird in a cage;
a sword that can cleave a great bell
does not slice meat on a table.
Moreover, you destroyed Wú and made Yuè hegemonic,
achieved success and retired,
roaming freely over the Five Lakes,
shining brilliantly for eternity.
Thus, this humble man secretly admires your great virtue and renowned name,
and dares not treat you with ordinary regard.
Why today do you jest at this splendid feast,
showing arrogance toward a banished minister?
How is this different from shooting a sick bird in a cage,
or slicing rotten meat on a table?
I secretly regret for the gentleman the waste of golden arrowheads and sharp blades."
Then the Xiāng god's expression changed,
and he ordered wine to penalize Lord Fàn.
As Lord Fàn was about to drink,
several dozen female musicians appeared,
all holding their instruments at the dance floor.
A jester loudly announced:
"The white-haired beauty
sings the 'Song of Sir, Do Not Cross the River.'"
The lyrics were:
"Turbulent waves surge in the morning mist,
Sir, do not cross the river, yet you crossed after all.
The wind howls, the water rages, your cries unheard,
lifting your robe, watching you go into the midstream.
The current sweeps your robe away as you step into the depths,
your sinking corpse deep into the flood dragon's lair.
The flood dragons, all drunk, your blood dried up,
pushing you onto the yellow sand, your bones afloat.
When you died then, where could I go?
So I joined the waves to unite our souls.
Wishing to hold the heart of Jīngwèi carrying stones,
to exhaust all efforts,
to block the river's source and stem its springs."
After the song ended,
the jester announced again:
"Xiè Qiūniáng dances,
the 'Song of Picking Mulberries.'"
Over ten repetitions in total,
the melody mournful and plaintive.
Before the dance ended,
There was an announcement outside:
"Master Shentú has arrived from the river,
and Recluse Xú and Lord Chīyí have come from the seashore."
He then followed the guide and entered.
Jiāng Xī, Xiāng Hú,
received him with great courtesy.
Grand Master Qū said:
"Are you not one of those who tread the jar, embrace the stone, and support the eye?"
He replied:
"Indeed."
Qū said:
"I have found a companion."
Then crimson strings were elegantly strung,
and clear pipes slowly played.
They poured from jade goblets,
and flew jade wine vessels.
Land and sea delicacies,
nothing was not brought to the utmost.
After the dance ended,
the performers again proclaimed:
"Cáo É sings 'Resentful River Waves.'"
In all five stanzas,
Chēn only remembered three.
The lyrics said:
"The mournful wind rustles, oh, the waves stretch endlessly,
Reed flowers for ten thousand miles, oh, congeal into gray mist.
Dragons and serpents dwell in dens, oh, deep and mysterious,
Pushing waves and piling swells, oh, sink my sky.
What is covered is not whole, oh, how can my body be whole?
Hateful blood overflows my eyes, oh, only ripples endlessly.
I would take tender shoots to pry open the beaks of saw-toothed birds,
Empty the water palace and hide their fishy drool.
Dark brows and green moth-antennae, oh, sink by the riverbank,
Blue clouds and slanting moon, oh, vainly lovely.
Swallowing voice and drinking hatred, oh, words lack strength,
Only raising sorrow and resentment, oh, ascending the singing mat."
When the song ended,
all in attendance wore mournful expressions.
The River God held wine,
and the Tài Hú God danced and sang a song:
"White dew abundant, oh, the west wind high,
Blue waves for ten thousand miles, oh, churn with great swells.
Do not say the softest under heaven,
Bearing boats and capsizing boats are all us."
The River God emptied his cup,
danced and sang a song:
"Have you not seen,
Last night at the ferry, a thousand vessels crowded,
Within carrying the fat and grease of the myriad people.
When tall ships float upon piled waves,
Resent pearls and shells lighter than goose down.
Have you not seen again,
At high tide, the landing pavilion moors a small boat,
Within is a scholar in blue robe.
Heading to the auspicious day of his magistracy,
Enduring waves' roar and wind's howl.
Thus know that those drowned in fame and profit,
Cannot avoid becoming the fishy stench of the water palace."
The King of Xiāng held a cup,
and the Zhà Xī God sang:
"Mountain contours wind around, water veins divide,
Water's light and mountain's hue, emerald joining clouds.
All four seasons enter poets' chants,
Toiling to death the envoy Liǔ of Wúxīng."
When wine reached the Stream God,
the King of Xiāng sang:
"Vast misty waves connect to Jiǔyí,
How many passing here weep by the river fences.
Year after year, green waters and blue mountains' colors,
Unchanged since Chónghuá's southern hunt times."
Then Chancellor Fàn presented a poem on the border gathering night feast:
"Waves broad, waves clear, autumn air cool,
Deep, deep water palace, night just grown long.
Self-pitying the retired guest of Five Lakes,
How fortunate to accompany the King of Hundred Valleys.
Incense curls, blue clouds drift over mats and tables,
Goblets fly, white jade brims with pepper brew.
Wine-drunk, alone floating away in a small boat,
Laughing entering Qíngāo's deathless land."
Recluse Xú Yǎn presented "Border Gathering Night Feast and a Brief Poem for Fàn":
"Pearl light, dragon radiance, fire blazing bright,
Night receives dawn clouds, feast at the isle palace.
Phoenix pipes clear blow, mournful distant shores,
Crimson strings leisurely play, cold autumn sky.
Discussing hearts, lucky to meet friends returning together,
Measuring my portion, ashamed of no aiding merit.
Cloud and rain each fly after the true realm,
Cannot bear sorrowful wind rising on the waves."
Grand Master Qū held a cup in his left hand,
struck a plate with his right.
Clearly he sang a song:
"The phoenix soaring down with auspicious signs, oh,
Fears the pheasant's mingled flight.
Jade warm and gentle presenting vessels, oh,
Because flawed stones vie in brilliance.
When the noble's gates swing open on four sides, oh,
Block fine plans with heavy doors.
Since auspicious vessels find no use, oh,
Darkness and obscurity should mutually diminish.
Vainly hollowing stone to make a boat, oh,
But following the current, will goes astray.
Would carve wood to make wings, oh,
With leaping and soaring, principle is not so.
Proud, solitary in empty vastness,
oh,
No group's aid to rely upon.
Blood gushing and streaming profusely, oh,
Look to river fish's belly and shall return.
West wind soughing, oh, Xiāng waters long flowing,
White zhǐ fragrance fades, oh, river fences autumn.
Sun dim, oh, river clouds gather,
Oars rise on four sides, oh, sorrowful wind deep.
The wandering soul submerged, oh,
My name forever floats.
Though blue waves dry up, oh,
That praise long flows.
If earlier sweet words and顺从 had been followed in the past,
How could today I sit at the monarch's head?
Thus know that those greedy for fame, pursuing salary, following the age to be ground to dust,
Though dying in proper bed and,
dead, oh,
cannot be my companions.
At this excellent meeting of the tripod's feet, oh,
I gain to circle around you, noble lords.
Carved plates, jade vessels, oh, array rare delicacies,
Golden cups, jade beakers, oh, just now toasting.
Dare write my heart, oh, sing one song,
Do not mock me holding cup and lingering."
Master Shentú presented "Border Gathering Night Feast Poem":
"Traveling palace, autumn not yet late,
Water palace, wind just turning cool.
Who says in this midnight,
One can receive the journey of paying homage?
Divine alligator drums thump-thump,
Divine dragon shines dazzling bright.
Red tower presses waves rising,
Green canopies join clouds spreading.
Jade flute coldly chants autumn,
Jade zither clear holds shāng note.
Worthy gathered: river-lake old men,

Consider me, a man of declining customs,

Parting words from a chaotic age,

Lingering on secluded isles,

Since then, all flowing customs,
Hard to share pot and cup.
Today ascending splendid feast,
Slightly feel spirit soaring.
Just enjoying companions of blue waves,
Suddenly fear the white sun's light.
Before sea people's auspicious brocade,

Just sing of numinous border gathering,

Lord Chīyí, cup in mouth, sang a song:
"Clouds gather over great wilds, oh, blood waves surge and swell,
Dark and yellow clash in battle, oh, Wú without whole mound.
Since the hegemon's enterprise about to fall,
Fine plans should not be followed.
The state's steps stumble and fall, oh,
My way meets misfortune.
Placed in Chīyí's great distress,
Enter the ninefold depths of abyss springs.
The Lord on High pities my innocence, oh,
Makes the great river drum rage for my冤 traces.
Thus whipping wave mountains and swiftly driving wave peaks,
Also roughly enough to unfold my stifled郁闷 heart and chest.
At the numinous realm's fine feast, oh,
Mistakenly honored vessels accommodate me.
Strike flutes and drums, oh, clash singing bells,

Suddenly the army town's dawn drums thump-thump,

When the song ended,
Zhà commandery city tower's morning drums ceased,
Dòngtíng mountain temple's dawn bell tolled.
And a whirling wind arose mightily,
dark clouds gathered on four sides,
sounds of chariots and horses among waves still mingled and重叠.
In a moment,
nothing was seen.
Dawn's colors now divided,
the giant turtle again stretched its head in the midstream.
It glanced back at Chēn and left.
Zhāng Zūnyán
In Nányáng, there was a man named Zhāng Zūnyán,
who, having failed the imperial examination,
was traveling and stopped at a mountain lodge in the Shāng Mountains.
In the middle of the night, it was pitch dark,
so he got up in the hall to oversee the feeding of the horses.
He saw something under the eastern wall,
gleaming white and radiant.
He ordered a servant to look at it,
and it turned out to be a white dog,
as big as a cat,
with whiskers, eyelashes, claws, and teeth all like jade,
its fur glossy and smooth,
delightful and adorable.
Zhāng Zūnyán took pity on it and loved it,
naming it Jiéfēi,
meaning it could run faster than flying.
He was often together with it,
initially having his servant Zhāng Zhìchéng carry it in his sleeve.
Whenever he ate or drank,
he would always hold it before him.
If sometimes he had no appetite for food or drink,
he would make sure to find what it liked to eat and feed it.
If there was ever not enough,
Zhāng Zūnyán would rather go without his own meal
than let Jiéfēi go hungry.
After more than a year,
Zhìchéng grew tired of carrying it in his sleeve,
and his attention slackened.
From then on, whenever Zhāng Zūnyán traveled,
he carried it in his own sleeve.
He took even greater care with its food and drink,
sleeping with it at night,
staying together during the day,
for a full four years.
Later, Zhāng Zūnyán was traveling on the Liángshān road,
as the sun was setting,
and the sky was growing overcast.
Before he reached his destination,
a sudden storm of wind and rain arrived.
Zhāng Zūnyán and his servants took shelter under a large tree.
At that time, it was dark and gloomy,
and they could see nothing.
Suddenly, Jiéfēi was nowhere to be found.
Zhāng Zūnyán cried out in alarm,
ordering Zhìchéng and the others to search separately,
but before they could find it,
suddenly they saw a person,
dressed in white clothes,
over eight feet tall,
with a lovely appearance.
Zhāng Zūnyán felt as if he were standing in bright moonlight,
and everyone could see clearly.
He asked the white-clad person where he came from,
and what his surname was.
The white-clad person said:
"My surname is Sū,
and I am the fourth."
He said to Zhāng Zūnyán:
"I already know your name.
Do you know where Jiéfēi has gone?
I am it.
You are now facing a disaster and are fated to die.
Because of your deep kindness and love for me,
over the past four years,
you have kept me alive, even going without your own meals to feed me,
without the slightest regret.
I now vow to save you from this calamity.
However, it will require the loss of more than ten lives."
After speaking,
he mounted Zhāng Zūnyán's horse and rode off,
while Zhāng Zūnyán followed on foot.
After about ten lǐ,
they saw in the distance three or four people on a tomb mound,
dressed in white clothes and hats,
each over ten feet tall,
holding bows and arrows,
with majestic and imposing forms.
Seeing Sū the Fourth,
they stooped and hurried forward to bow,
and after bowing,
none dared to look up.
The Fourth asked why they had come to meet him.
The white-clad people said:
"We have received the Great King's warrant
to apprehend the scholar Zhāng Zūnyán."
After speaking,
they stole glances at Zhāng Zūnyán.
Zhāng Zūnyán was terrified,
about to fall to the ground.
The Fourth said:
"Do not be rude.
I am traveling with Zhāng Zūnyán.
You must leave with me now."
The four were distressed and wept.
Then the Fourth said to Zhāng Zūnyán:
"Do not worry or fear.
These people cannot harm me."
After traveling another ten lǐ,
they saw six or seven yakṣas,
all holding weapons,
with bronze heads and iron foreheads,
their appearances repulsive and vile,
leaping and prancing about,
advancing and retreating with ferocious violence.
Seeing the Fourth from afar,
they restrained their venomousness and stood trembling,
bowing in fear and trembling.
The Fourth shouted and asked:
"What brings you here?"
The yakṣas softened their fierce and venomous expressions into fawning smiles,
crawling forward on their elbows and saying:
"We have received the Great King's warrant
specifically to seize the scholar Zhāng Zūnyán."
They stole glances just as before.
The Fourth said:
"Zhāng Zūnyán is my old friend.
It is impermissible to take him."
The yakṣas immediately kowtowed until they bled and said:
"Earlier, the four white-clad ones
failed to apprehend Zhāng Zūnyán,
and the Great King has already ordered each of them to receive five hundred blows with an iron staff.
Whether they are dead or alive is still uncertain.
If the Fourth does not let us take him now,
we will all die.
We beg you to take pity on our lives
and temporarily send Zhāng Zūnyán with us."
The Fourth grew furious,
shouted at the yakṣas,
and the yakṣas recoiled,
collapsing dozens of steps away,
bleeding and jumping about,
weeping and speaking again.
The Fourth said:
"You little demons dare to act like this?
If not,
you will die quickly."
The yakṣas wept and whimpered as they left.
The Fourth then said to Zhāng Zūnyán:
"These sorts are very difficult to reason with.
Now that they have left,
what we are undertaking will succeed."
After traveling seven or eight lǐ,
they saw over fifty soldiers with weapons,
whose forms and spirits were like ordinary people,
who also lined up and bowed before the Fourth.
The Fourth said:
"Why have you come?"
Their reply was the same as the yakṣas'.
They also said:
"Earlier, the yakṣas Niú Shūliáng and six others
failed to apprehend Zhāng Zūnyán,
and all were dealt with according to the law.
We are terrified,
and do not know what method the Fourth has
to save our lives."
The Fourth said:
"Just follow me,
and perhaps there is hope."
Of the fifty people,
about half agreed.
In a short while,
they reached a large black gate.
After traveling a few more lǐ,
they saw a city wall with very strict defenses.
There was a person in full military attire,
who rode forward on horseback.
He conveyed the king's words:
"The Fourth has come from afar.
As my authority is limited,
by law I cannot welcome and bow to you on the road.
Please rest for a while at the southern lodge,
and I will soon invite you in."
Before they had settled in the lodge,
messengers arrived one after another to summon them,
also requesting the scholar Zhāng.
Soon they followed along,
and the palaces, halls, and official buildings
were all fit for a true king.
Entering the gate,
they saw the king wearing a royal robe and a crown with hanging beads,
who came forward to bow to the Fourth.
The Fourth returned the bow,
his demeanor very casual,
his words merely assenting.
The king performed all the proper courtesies,
stepped forward, bowed, and invited the Fourth to ascend the steps.
The Fourth also gave a slight bow and went up.
Turning back, he said to Zhāng Zūnyán:
"The duties of a host
cannot be neglected."
The king said:
"The front hall is humble and crude,
not a place for the Fourth to feast."
He bowed again to the Fourth.
They passed through three halls in total,
each hall furnished with tables, couches, dining utensils, and curtains.
They sat down only in the fourth hall.
The food they ate and the vessels used
were not of this world.
After eating,
King Yī invited Sìláng up to the Night-Bright Tower.
The four corner pillars of the tower
were adorned entirely with luminous pearls,
their light as bright as day.
He ordered wine and music prepared,
and after several rounds of drinking,
the king said to Sìláng:
"There is someone to assist with the drinking;
I wish to summon them."
Sìláng replied:
"Why not?"
There were seven or eight female musicians,
and over ten drinkers,
all with the appearance and adornments of immortals and celestial beings.
The king and Sìláng each wore casual attire,
and their laughter and conversation resembled that of young men in the mortal world.
After a while,
Sìláng teased a beautiful woman,
but she remained stern and did not respond.
Sìláng teased her again,
and the woman angrily said:
"I am the wife of Liú Gēn.
If not for the orders of the Primordial Lady,
why would I be here?
How can you, sir, be so presumptuous?
Once, during a gathering at the Cloud-Forest Palace of Lady Wáng,
the Chief Administrator Xǔ spoke lightly,
and I already admonished the sisters Dù Lánxiāng.
Even with the slightest words,
I dare not jest frivolously.
How can you, sir, be so presumptuous?"
Sìláng grew angry,
struck the wine cup against the ivory tray with a clang,
and the luminous pearls on the pillars
clattered down,
plunging everything into darkness.
After a long while, Zūnyán awoke dazed and confused,
finding himself back under the tree,
with Sìláng and the saddled horse beside him.
Sìláng said:
"You have passed through your ordeal,
and I must now bid you farewell."
Zūnyán replied:
"I have received the utmost kindness from you for saving my life.
Yet I still do not know Sìláng's origins,
nor where to direct my gratitude.
Moreover, for the rest of my life,
what else can I rely on?"
Sìláng said:
"I cannot speak of it.
But if you go to the old monk mending robes in the east corridor of Lóngxīng Temple in Shāngzhōu and ask him,
you will know."
With these words,
he soared into the sky and departed.
Dawn was approaching,
so Zūnyán adjusted his reins and headed for Shāngzhōu,
where he indeed found Lóngxīng Temple.
He saw the old monk mending robes
and bowed to him in respect.
At first, the old monk firmly refused Zūnyán,
but Zūnyán persisted in his pleas.
Late into the night, the old monk finally spoke:
"Since you, sir, insist so earnestly,
how can I not respond?
Sìláng Sū
is the essence of the Great White Star;
the Great King
is an exiled official from the immortal realm,
and now resides here."
When Zūnyán asked about other matters,
the old monk refused to answer further,
saying:
"I have already left this place."
He then urged Zūnyán to depart.
The next morning, when Zūnyán went to search for him,
he could no longer find the place.
Zhāng Wúpō
During the Chángqìng era,
Jìnshì Zhāng Wúpō,
resided in Nánkāng.
As he was about to set off for the imperial examinations,
he traveled to Pānyú seeking assistance.
It happened that the regional commander was being replaced,
leaving him with nowhere to turn.
Worried and ill, he lay in an inn,
and all his servants had fled.
Suddenly, he met a skilled diviner named Yuán Dàniáng,
who came to the innkeeper's house.
She stared at Wúpō and said:
"Are you destined to remain in such dire straits for long?"
She then took off her outer garment to buy wine and shared it with him,
saying:
"Since you are in such distress,
if you can follow a plan of mine,
in less than a month,
you will naturally become wealthy,
and even gain extended life."
Wúpō said:
"I am so beset by hardship and hunger,
how dare I not accept your instruction?"
Dàniáng said:
