"I have a small box of Jade Dragon Ointment.
It not only revives the dead,
but through it, you will also forever encounter a renowned beauty.
Simply put up a notice,
stating that
you can treat severe illnesses.
If ordinary people seek treatment,
just say it cannot be cured;
but if an extraordinary person requests it,
you must take this medicine and go once,
and you will naturally attain wealth and honor."
Wúpō bowed in thanks and accepted the medicine,
storing it in a warm golden box.
She said:
"When it is cold, simply bring out this box,
and the whole room will become warm,
without needing a stove or charcoal."
Wúpō followed her advice.
After posting the notice for several days,
indeed, a yellow-robed man resembling a eunuch
knocked urgently at the door,
saying:
"The Guanglì King knows you possess the ointment,
and therefore sends me to summon you for an audience."
Remembering Dàniáng's words,
Wúpō followed the messenger.
By the riverbank was a painted boat;
boarding it felt remarkably light and swift.
In the time it takes to eat a meal,
he suddenly saw towering city walls and buildings,
heavily guarded.
The eunuch led Wúpō through over ten gates
to the palace courtyard.
Many beautiful women were arrayed there,
their attire exceedingly splendid,
standing respectfully in attendance.
The eunuch hurried forward and announced:
"Zhāng Wúpō has been summoned and is here."
Then he heard the curtain on the hall being rolled up,
and saw a man
dressed in royal robes,
wearing a yuǎnyóu crown.
Two purple-clad maidservants
supported him as he stood by the steps.
He beckoned to Wúpō and said:
"Please, do not bow."
The King said:
"I know you, Xiùcai, are not from Nányuè,
and not under my jurisdiction,
so I hope you will not perform the formal rites."
Wúpō insisted on bowing.
The King bowed deeply in return and said apologetically:
"I, a man of little virtue,
have presumptuously invited a great worthy from afar,
all because my beloved daughter is ill.
My heart is wholly preoccupied with concern.
Knowing you possess a divine ointment,
if she can be cured and restored to health,
I would be profoundly grateful."
He then ordered two senior attendants
to lead Wúpō into the princess's quarters.
Wúpō passed through several more doors
to a small hall.
The corridors and buildings were adorned with luminous pearls;
green jade ornaments on the pillars and lintels
shone brilliantly as if inlaid with gold,
and an extraordinary fragrance
filled the courtyard and rooms.
Presently, two maids lifted the curtain
and summoned Wúpō inside.
He saw within a pearl-embroidered curtain
a young woman,
just of hair-pinning age,
wearing a green silk jacket woven with gold thread.
Wúpō felt her pulse,
and after a long while said:
"The illness afflicting Your Highness
stems from distress in her heart."
He then brought out the Dragon Ointment,
which she swallowed with wine,
and she was immediately cured.
The princess then took out a green jade hairpin with paired phoenixes and gave it to Wúpō,
gazing at him meaningfully for a long time.
Wúpō dared not accept it.
The princess said:
"This is insufficient to repay you, sir.
It merely expresses my feelings.
However, the King will surely have gifts for you."
Wúpō thanked her with embarrassment.
The attendants then led him to see the King.
The King presented Wúpō with a rhinoceros horn that startles chickens, a jadeite bowl, and beautiful luminous jades,
and bestowed them upon him.
Wúpō bowed in thanks.
The eunuch again escorted him to the painted boat,
and he returned to Pānyú.
His innkeeper was unaware of any of this.
Merely selling the rhinoceros horn
already yielded tens of thousands in cash.
Wúpō, having seen the princess's dazzling beauty,
thought of her often.
Over a month later,
suddenly a maidservant in dark clothing
knocked at the door and delivered a red letter.
It contained two poems,
with no name signed.
Wúpō received it.
The maidservant vanished in an instant.
Wúpō said:
"These must have been composed by an immortal maiden."
The verses read:
"Ashamed to remove bright earrings, seeking the Hàn river's shore;
Only relying on spring dreams to visit the world's far ends.
At red tower, dusk falls, orioles fly away;
Deep palace flowers fallen by the steps—sorrow slays."
And also:
"Swallows' chatter, spring mud falls on brocade mats;
Heartsick, listless, no mind to adjust floral hairpins.
Cold boudoir, leaning on pillow, dreams refuse to form;
Incense from golden censer curls its lonely smoke."
Soon after,
the eunuch from before arrived again,
and said to him:
"The King orders your summons once more;
the princess is ill as before."
Wúpō gladly went again.
Seeing the princess,
he began feeling her pulse once more.
Those around said:
"The Queen has arrived."
Wúpō descended the steps.
Hearing the sound of jade pendants,
he saw palace ladies and guards arrayed in rows.
He saw a woman,
perhaps around thirty years of age,
attired like a queen or imperial consort.
Wúpō bowed to her.
The Queen said:
"To trouble a worthy sage again
truly fills me with shame.
But what ailment afflicts my daughter this time?"
Wúpō said:
"It is the previous illness;
her heart has been stirred, and it has recurred.
If she takes the medicine again,
it should eradicate the root cause."
The Queen said:
"Where is the medicine?"
Wúpō presented the medicine box.
The Queen looked at it and fell silent,
her expression unhappy.
She comforted and instructed the princess, then left.
She then informed the King, saying:
"Our beloved daughter is not ill;
she has formed a private attachment to this Wúpō.
Otherwise,
how would the warm golden box from our palace
be in that man's possession?"
The King looked grave for a long time, then said:
"Is she to become another Jiǎ Chōng's daughter?
I too should carry on that affair and bring it to completion,
so she does not suffer long."
When Wúpō came out,
the King ordered him hosted in a separate lodge,
with lavish feasts and rewards.
Later, the King summoned him and said:
"I privately admire your character, sir,
and wish to entrust my beloved daughter to you.
What do you say?"
Wúpō bowed repeatedly in polite refusal,
though inwardly overjoyed beyond measure.
The King then ordered the officials
to select an auspicious day
and prepare the ceremonies to receive him.
The king and queen held Zhang Wúpō in higher esteem than their other sons-in-law,
so he stayed for over a month,
enjoying feasts and banquets to the fullest.
The king said:
"Sir Zhang, unlike my other sons-in-law,
must return to the human world.
Last night,
I checked with the underworld authorities,
and it is indeed fate's arrangement.
Since she is my daughter,
she will not suffer hardship.
Fānyú is nearby,
but I fear people of this time would find it strange.
Nánkāng is far away,
and moreover, it lies beyond our borders.
It would be most convenient to return to Sháoyáng instead."
Wúpō said:
"That is my intention as well."
They then prepared boats and oars,
along with rare and precious clothing and ornaments,
gold, pearls, and precious jade.
Wúpō said:
"Only the guards and attendants must be arranged by myself;
do not employ beings from the underworld,
as this would shorten one's lifespan."
He then bid farewell to the king.
The king said:
"Every three years, I will come to you once,
but do not speak of this to others."
Wúpō took his family and settled in Sháoyáng.
Few people knew of this.
After living there for over a month,
suddenly, Yuán Dàniáng knocked on the door to see Wúpō.
Wúpō was greatly surprised.
Dàniáng said:
"Sir Zhang, today you should fulfill your promise,
and the young lady should reward the matchmaker."
The two each presented her with treasures as a reward,
after which she took her leave.
Wúpō questioned his wife,
and she said:
"This is the daughter of Yuán Tiāngāng,
the wife of Master Chéng.
The Warm Gold Box is a treasure from my palace."
Thereafter, every three years,
King Guǎnglì would certainly visit Zhang's residence at night.
Later, people grew suspicious and astonished by Wúpō,
so he left,
and no one knew where he went.
Wáng Qí
Wáng Qí, the Assistant Magistrate of Tiānxīng,
during the Bǎolì era,
once traveled to Lǒngzhōu.
On the road, he rested under a large tree,
removed his saddle, spread out on the ground, and slept.
Suddenly, he heard the calls of riders on the road approaching from the west.
He saw a man in purple robes riding in a carriage,
followed by several riders.
The man ordered his attendants:
"Invite Assistant Magistrate Wáng here."
They led Qí forward,
and a tent with furnishings was already set up.
He sat and spoke with Qí for a long time.
Qí did not know why he had been summoned,
and each time he responded,
he was hesitant and flustered.
The man in purple noticed this
and said:
"I have been idle in this position for twenty years.
If you wish to address me,
you may simply call me 'King.'"
Qí said:
"I do not understand, Your Majesty, from where do you hail?"
He replied:
"I, Méng Tián, once built the Great Wall for Qín,
and for this small achievement,
I was repeatedly entrusted with important responsibilities.
After the First Emperor passed away,
I was framed by petty men,
and unjustly executed.
The Supreme Deity, considering the Great Wall project
laborious and harmful to the people,
assigned me to guard Wùyuè.
At that time, Wùshān had the title of a sacred mountain,
and everyone called me 'King.'
Later, the sacred mountain duties were transferred to Huàshān,
but my punishment period was not yet complete.
The official positions were shifted around,
leaving me with no one to oversee,
merely guarding an empty mountain.
Few people come here,
and it is quite lonely.
Moreover, because I already bear this empty title,
I cannot lower myself to take a minor position,
so to this day, I merely hold the false title of 'King.'
Meeting you here by chance,
I thought to have a brief, leisurely conversation."
Qí said:
"My name and reputation are obscure,
and my nature is timid and weak.
I am fortunate to receive your gracious attention,
but I do not know how I may be of service?"
Tián said:
"Originally, I wished to express my admiration
and behold your dignified demeanor.
How fortunate that you so generously extend your goodwill.
If there truly is a matter, then what of it?"
Qí said:
"That would be most fortunate."
Tián said:
"Having been idle for so long,
and scattered,
I long to be of some use.
Nowadays, soldiers and horses everywhere have their masters;
one cannot seize their authority.
Three years from now,
in Xīngyuán, there will be eight hundred masterless strong men.
If you plan early,
you can surely lead them.
What I must entrust to you
is to prepare ten thousand sheets of paper money.
With this, I can take action,
and then it will be accomplished."
Qí agreed and then awoke,
sweating profusely.
He then purchased ten thousand sheets of paper money and burned them.
This was in the fourth year of the Tàihé era.
The military governor of Xīngyuán, Lǐ Jiàng, was assassinated,
and later, the military governor Wēn Zào
executed the eight hundred members of the violent faction.
Mǎ Cháo
Mǎ Cháo was a foot soldier of the Tiānpíng Army.
In the early years of the Tàihé era,
Lǐ Tóngjié rebelled in Cāngzhōu,
and an imperial edict ordered the Yùn army to suppress him.
Cháo was among the troops.
When they reached the south of Píngyuán,
they faced the rebels for several weeks.
Cháo’s son, Shìjùn,
brought provisions from Yùn
and arrived at the camp.
As the battle was imminent,
Cháo, being old,
pleaded with his commander:
"My eldest son, Shìjùn,
is young and strong,
and skilled with bow and arrows.
For tomorrow’s engagement,
I beg to let him take my place."
The commander agreed.
When the battle began,
the Yùn army suffered a minor defeat,
and Shìjùn was severely wounded multiple times,
collapsing on the battlefield.
Late at night, he regained consciousness.
Suddenly, he heard calls and announcements,
the voices resembling those of a dozen officers.
With no light,
Shìjùn could not see them.
He only heard the rustling of ledgers
and the calling of names.
Soon it was his turn,
and they called "Mǎ Cháo."
Someone beside said:
"This is not the right person;
quickly summon the correct one."
With that, they passed by,
and as they moved away,
he could still hear them checking the roster.
Shìjùn, bewildered,
struggled to rise and slowly made his way back.
He reached the camp gate at the fourth watch,
and the camp officer admitted him,
helping him to his father’s quarters.
Cháo thought his son had died,
and upon seeing him, was both shocked and overjoyed.
He immediately washed the wounds and applied medicine.
Then he said:
"You should drink some wine and porridge
to help you sleep."
He then went out to fetch water.
At that time, the camp had an enormous number of soldiers and horses,
with every two or three hundred men
sharing a single well.
The well was surrounded by a hundred paces of tunnels,
gradually leading down to the spring,
so that many could draw water around it.
As Cháo was drawing water with a jar,
he slipped on the mud
while pulling the heavy load
and fell to the ground.
There happened to be a broken knife in the ground,
and it pierced Cháo right through the heart.
After a while, Shìjùn grew worried that his father had not returned
and told his comrades.
When they arrived, Cháo was already dead.
Shìjùn recovered after ten days.
Qiè Yuánwèi
Qiè Yuánwèi was an officer of the Hédōng garrison.
In the early years of the Tàihé era,
he was often sent on missions to the capital.
Once, while passing through Shāyuàn,
dusk fell.
He saw a man over ten feet tall,
dressed in purple with golden ornaments,
of majestic and imposing appearance.
He rode a white horse,
also over ten feet tall.
Nearly ten attendants followed him,
all of extraordinary appearance,
carrying bows and arrows,
coming from the south.
Yuánwèi was greatly astonished
and halted his horse to avoid them.
Suddenly, the divine figure raised his whip and pointed west,
as if seeing something,
and his attendants all looked in that direction.
Yuánwèi also looked west
but saw nothing.
When he turned back to look,
they had all vanished.
Yuánwèi broke into a cold sweat,
his legs trembling and heart pounding,
and he fell from his horse without realizing it.
He fell ill with fever
and was carried back in a sedan chair,
recovering after more than ten days.
At that time, the regional commander of Hédōng, the Minister of Works Lǐ Yuàn, had just passed away.
Xiàyáng’s Deputy Zhào
Xiàyáng, a subordinate county of Féngyì,
lies along the great river.
East of the county, there is a garden pavilion
facing Tàihuà
and Zhōngtiáo mountains,
where mist and haze
are visible morning and evening.
To the south, there is also a Fèn spring,
its water clear and pure,
with not a speck hidden.
During the Tàihé era,
a man named Zhào served as deputy in Xiàyáng.
One evening after the rain cleared,
Zhào and several friends
strolled together to admire the moon by the Fèn spring.
Suddenly, they saw a man,
very dark in appearance,
wearing a green robe,
floating in the water,
swimming along for a long time.
He chanted:
"The night moon shines bright and clear,
the green waves stretch empty and far."
Just as Zhào was startled,
the man suddenly looked back toward the shore,
as if afraid of something,
then submerged into the water,
only his head remaining visible,
and after a while, he disappeared entirely.
The next day, Zhào returned to the spring.
About several dozen paces from the bank,
there was a temple,
its gate inscribed "Fèn Water Deity."
Zhào entered the temple
and saw that to the left and right of the deity’s seat,
there were clay figurines,
one wearing a green robe.
Looking at its face,
it resembled the man they had seen in the water earlier.
Zhào said:
"This is just mud from the Fèn spring,
yet it can deceive the masses—
is this not strange?"
He intended to demolish the temple.
But a county clerk said:
"This is a divine temple,
and it can bring wind and rain to aid growth.
If we destroy its building,
it will only bring harm to the townspeople."
Thus, the demolition did not proceed.
Lú Sìzōng
At Pǔjīn, there is a temple to Shùn,
and also temples to Éhuáng and Nǚyīng,
located beside Shùn’s temple.
The clay statues are exquisitely beautiful.
During the Kāichéng era,
Lú Sìzōng of Fànyáng
was temporarily assigned to Pǔjīn.
One day,
he and several friends
visited Shùn’s temple.
When they reached the temples of Éhuáng and Nǚyīng,
Sìzōng joked:
"I wish to serve as a servant to the emperor’s daughters—
may I?"
He bowed repeatedly and prayed for a long time.
Everyone said to him:
"Such disrespectful words—
are you not defiling the deities?"
Sìzōng only laughed more heartily.
From then on, he often visited Éhuáng’s temple alone,
and when drunk,
he would utter many profane words.
Soon, he fell ill
and was carried back in a sedan chair.
He looked fearful and trembled,
his body drenched in sweat,
and died that very night.
His servants saw over ten people
seize and drag Sìzōng out the door,
heading toward Shùn’s temple.
When they examined Sìzōng’s corpse,
they found many red marks on his back,
as if he had been beaten.
The people of Pǔ all found this strange.
Wáng Shēng, Master of the Three Histories
There was a certain Mr. Wáng,
whose given name is not recorded.
He was a scholar of the Three Histories,
and his reading was extensive and profound.
By nature, he loved to boast and show off,
and his speech was exceedingly glib.
Whenever he debated about antiquity,
he often relied on subjective judgment.
If there were bystanders who disagreed,
he would certainly refute them with grand words.
Once, while traveling in Pèi,
he entered the temple of Emperor Gāozǔ in a drunken state.
Gazing at the spirit tablet,
he laughed and said:
"You who raised a three-foot sword,
destroyed the tyrannical Qín,
and annihilated the powerful Chǔ,
yet could not avoid your mother being called 'Wū Lǎo'.
You merely sang 'A great wind rises, oh! The clouds fly and scatter,'
how could you truly impose your might across the four seas!"
Pacing back and forth in the temple courtyard and corridors,
he gazed about for a long time,
then returned to his lodgings.
That very night, he had just fallen asleep when he died.
He saw over a dozen horsemen,
who seized him and brought him to the temple courtyard.
The Han Ancestor, gripping his sword, said in great anger:
"You have not even read a few pages of the historical records,
yet dare to profane a revered deity.
This talk of 'Wū Lǎo'.
From which classic does it originate?
If you have no basis for it,
your crime will be hard to escape."
Mr. Wáng kowtowed and said:
"Your subject has often read Your Majesty's 'Basic Annals' and seen that Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù state,
'Mother,
was Liú Āo.'
And the annotation states: 'pronounced like Wū Lǎo.'
The explanation says,
'It is a term for an old mother.'
I have seen it in history,
heard it from my teacher,
and it is recorded in the texts,
as clear and bright as the sun at noon.
It is not something your subject dared to invent from his own mind."
The Han Ancestor grew even angrier and said:
"On my ancestral tablet at the Sìshuǐ Village Chief Pavilion,
it is clearly and fully recorded.
How could you mistakenly call the Wēn clan of my maternal line 'Wū Lǎo'?
You have misread the book itself,
and furthermore failed to grasp its meaning,
yet you dared, relying on drunkenness, to clamor in the temple hall.
Hand him over to the authorities to be prosecuted for the crime of offending the sovereign."
Before he had finished speaking,
from the southwest came someone clearing the way,
announcing loudly that the Grand Sire had arrived.
Just as he reached the steps,
he looked at Mr. Wáng and said:
"Who is this person being so greatly insulted?"
The Han Ancestor descended the steps and replied:
"This is a false and insolent fellow.
His crime deserves beheading."
Mr. Wáng stared straight at the Grand Sire,
and then said in a stern voice:
"Your subject has read the historical records,
and seen that those who insulted and showed contempt to their sovereign and parents
were still not censured.
Yet now, a humble subject like me makes a jesting remark in a temple,
how could I expect to be executed in the marketplace?"
The Han Ancestor said angrily again:
"In the canonical records,
could there possibly be an account of someone insulting his sovereign and parents?
You must try to cite an example."
Mr. Wáng said:
"May your subject dare to cite Your Majesty as an example?"
The Han Ancestor said:
"Yes."
Mr. Wáng said:
"When the King ascended the throne,
assembled all his ministers,
and set out wine in the front hall,
toasting the longevity of the Supreme Emperor.
Did this happen?"
The Han Ancestor said:
"It did."
"After the toast,
you then said,
'Father, you always said I was good-for-nothing,
that I did not attend to property and livelihood,
and was not as capable as Zhòng.
Now, whose achievements are greater, mine or Zhòng's?'
Did this happen?"
The Han Ancestor said:
"It did."
"All the ministers in the hall shouted 'Long live the King',
laughing heartily in their merriment.
Did this happen?"
He said:
"It did."
Mr. Wáng said:
"That was insulting and showing contempt to your own parent."
The Grand Sire said:
"This man's reasoning cannot be refuted.
You should quickly drive him away.
If not,
you are sure to face a 'cup of broth' reproach."
The Han Ancestor remained silent for a long time, then said:
"To behead this creature
would soil my three-foot blade.
Order the one holding his hair to slap him."
With one slap, he came to his senses in a daze and revived.
The east was already bright.
Looking at his cheek in a mirror,
there was something like a finger mark,
which faded only after several days.
Mr. Zhāng
Jìnshì Zhāng Shēng,
skilled in playing the qin,
enjoyed reading the books of Mèng Kē.
Having failed the imperial examination, he traveled to Pǔ Guān
and entered Shùnchéng.
As the day was nearing dusk,
he pushed through the gate, raised his reins, and vied to enter,
causing his horse to stumble.
Soon after, the horse died,
and Shēng had nowhere to go.
He then went to the temple official,
asking to stay for one night.
The official let him stay under the eaves of the corridor, saying:
"Apart from this, there is nowhere else to go."
So he stayed there.
At the beginning of the night, just as he was about to sleep,
he saw two men in crimson robes,
who came forward and said:
"The Emperor summons the scholar."
Shēng hurriedly went,
and the Emperor asked:
"What profession and skills do you practice?"
Shēng replied:
"I am a son of the Confucian school,
often studying the books of Confucius and Mencius."
The Emperor said:
"Confucius is a sage,
I have long known of him.
Who is this Mèng?
How can he be spoken of in the same category as Confucius?"
Shēng said:
"Mèng also transmitted the ideas of the sage.
He upheld benevolence and righteousness,
established rites and music, and promoted moral education."
The Emperor said:
"Did he write books?"
Shēng said:
"He wrote seven thousand two hundred chapters,
which include difficult questions and answers with Confucius's disciples,
as well as the Lǔ Lùn and Qí Lùn.
All are excellent words."
The Emperor said:
"Do you remember his writings?"
Shēng said:
"Not only do I understand his writings,
but I also deeply grasp their meaning."
The Emperor then ordered Shēng to recite aloud,
and he listened attentively.
Shēng recited the "Wàn Zhāng Asks":
"Shùn went to the fields,
and cried out to Heaven.
Why did he cry out and weep?"
Mèngzǐ said:
"It was out of resentment and longing."
Wàn Zhāng asked:
"When parents love him,
he is joyful and never forgets;
when parents hate him,
he toils without resentment.
Then, did Shùn resent them?"
The answer was:
"Cháng Xī asked Gōngmíng Gāo."
Shùn went to the fields,
then I have heard the command.
Crying out to Heaven,
resenting his parents,
then I do not know."
The Emperor stopped Shēng's recitation,
sighed with disappointment and said:
"There are those who act without knowing,
and this is what it means.
I have been away from the world for one thousand eight hundred and twenty years,
the violent Qín usurped the throne,
poisoning and tormenting the four seas,
burning my classics and records,
obliterating my imperial plans,
obscuring the words of the masses,
and indulging in selfish desires.
A hundred generations later,
the classics and histories have become erroneous.
The words and meanings contradict each other,
bordering on absurdity.
I often hear praises of Táng Yáo's virtues, saying:
'He let his robes hang down and the world was governed,'
which illustrates that there was no trouble.
However, to pacify and distinguish the hundred surnames,
harmonize the myriad states,
and deal with the floods reaching the heavens, surrounding the mountains, and inundating the hills,
the common people lamented.
If so, then it contradicts the meaning of 'letting robes hang down.'
I also hear praises of my virtues, saying:
'He governed without action.'
Yet it is recorded in the classics, saying:
'He received guests at the four gates,
regulated the seven governments,
sacrificed to the Supreme Deity,
offered sacrifices to the six ancestral temples,
paid homage to the mountains and rivers,
honored all the spirits,
exiled Gònggōng,
banished Huāndōu,
executed Gǔn,
and drove away the Sān Miáo.'
If so, then it is far from the way of non-action.
Now I hear again of crying to Heaven,
out of resentment and longing,
which is not what I did.
That which is done without anyone doing it,
is Heaven;
that which comes without anyone bringing it,
is fate.
My weeping
was resentment of my own fate,
not harmonizing with my parents,
and I lamented to Heaven.
Why did Wàn Zhāng ask,
and Mèng Kē not know how to answer?
To transmit the sage's intentions,
should it be like this?"
He sighed incessantly,
and after a long while, said to Shēng:
"Do you study the qin?"
Shēng said:
"I am fond of it but not skilled."
The Emperor then looked to his attendants and had them bring a qin,
saying:
"If you have not heard the playing of the five strings,
or the song 'South Wind,'
how can it suffice to illuminate your return journey?"
He then played the qin and sang:
"The south wind is warm, oh, the grass is lush,
the wondrous sound returns to the clear strings.
The vast teachings come from nature,
the harmonious transformation completes my way.
Warm, oh, how are thoughts to be transmitted?"
After finishing the song,
he played the qin with "South Wind Melody."
The melody was clear and smooth,
refreshing to the heart and bones.
Shēng then spoke up and said:
"How wonderful!"
And so he awoke with a start.
Xiāo Kuàng
The hermit Xiāo Kuàng of Tàihé,
traveled east from Luòyáng.
Arriving at the Xiàoyì Lodge,
he rested at night in the Shuāngměi Pavilion.
The moon was bright, the breeze was clear.
Kuàng was skilled at the qín,
so he took his qín and played it.
At midnight,
the melody was very sorrowful.
Suddenly, from over the Luò River,
came the sound of a long sigh.
Gradually it drew near,
and it was a beautiful woman.
Kuàng then set aside his qín and bowed to her, saying,
"Who might you be?"
The woman said:
"I am the goddess of the Luò River's shore.
In the past, Prince Sī of Chén wrote a rhapsody about me,
do you not recall it?"
Kuàng said:
"Indeed."
Kuàng then asked further:
"Some have heard that the Luò River Goddess is actually Empress Zhēn,
who passed away.
Prince Sī of Chén encountered her spirit on the banks of the Luò,
and thus composed the 'Rhapsody on Moved by Zhēn'.
Later, realizing the affair was not proper,
he changed it to 'Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luò',
transferring the sentiment to the consort Fúfēi.
Is there truth to this?"
The woman said:
"I am indeed Empress Zhēn.
Because I admired the talent and bearing of Prince Sī of Chén,
Emperor Wén was angered and had me imprisoned until death.
Later, my essence and spirit encountered the Prince on the banks of the Luò,
where I recounted my grievance and oppression.
Moved, he composed the rhapsody.
Realizing the affair was not canonical,
he changed its title,
thus it is not mistaken."
Soon a maid with twin buns,
holding a mat and cushions,
arrived with wine and food all prepared.
She said to Kuàng:
"When I was a new bride in the Yuán family,
I was fond of playing the qín.
Whenever I played 'The Mournful Wind' or 'The Flowing Springs of the Three Gorges',
I would not stop until the night was spent.
Just now I heard the pure elegance of your qín's melody,
and I wish to hear it once."
Kuàng then played 'The Parting Crane Air' and 'The Mournful Wind'.
The goddess sighed deeply and said:
"Truly a peer of Cài Zhōngláng."
She asked Kuàng:
"What of Prince Sī of Chén's 'Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luò'?"
Kuàng said:
"It truly depicts things with lucid clarity,
and is a refined selection of Prince Zhāomíng of Liáng."
The goddess smiled slightly and said:
"Describing my bearing as 'fluttering like a startled swan,
graceful like a swimming dragon' —
is that not somewhat off the mark?"
Kuàng said:
"Where is the essence and spirit of Prince Sī of Chén now?"
The woman said:
"He is now the king of the Zhēxū Kingdom."
Kuàng said:
"What is the Zhēxū Kingdom?"
The woman said:
"Liú Cōng's son died and came back to life,
and told his father:
'Someone informed me,
the Zhēxū Kingdom has long been without a ruler,
awaiting your father to come and be its lord.'
That is this kingdom."
Soon a maid in blue,
leading another woman, said:
"The Lady Weaving Gauze has arrived."
The goddess said:
"She is the daughter of the Dragon King of the Luò River's shore,
skilled at weaving gauze in the water palace.
I just had her summoned."
Kuàng then spoke to the Weaving Gauze Lady, saying:
"Recently in the mortal world, some tell the story of Liǔ Yì's spiritual marriage,
is there truth to it?"
The woman said:
"Only four or five parts out of ten,
the rest are embellished words,
not to be deluded by."
Kuàng said:
"Some say dragons fear iron,
is there truth to that?"
The woman said:
"The divine transformations of dragons,
even iron, stone, gold, or jade,
can all be penetrated and passed through.
Why would they fear iron alone?
Those who fear it are the likes of jiāo and chī."
Kuàng also said:
"The son of the Léi family, wearing the Fēngchéng sword,
arrived at the Yánpíng Ford,
leaped into the water,
and transformed into a dragon.
Is there truth to that?"
The woman said:
"False.
Dragons
belong to the wood category.
Swords are of metal.
Metal overcomes wood,
and they do not generate each other.
How could they transform?
How could it be the same as sparrows entering water becoming clams,
or pheasants entering water becoming giant clams!
However, the treasured sword is a numinous object.
Metal and water generate each other,
and entering water generates thunder.
Naturally it cannot sink into the spring.
Believing their underwater search for the sword was fruitless,
they falsely claimed it became a dragon.
Moreover, Léi Huàn only said it transformed and left,
Minister Sīkōng Zhāng only said it would eventually reunite,
neither spoke of it becoming a dragon.
Regardless of the sword's spiritual anomaly,
and considering that humans smelted and forged it,
it is not a natural object.
Thus it is clear that it ultimately cannot become a dragon."
Kuàng also said:
"What of the shuttle transforming into a dragon?"
The woman said:
"The shuttle is wood.
Dragons originally belong to wood.
Its transformation returns to wood.
What is strange about that?"
Kuàng also said:
"The transformations of dragons are like the divine,
so why would they fall ill and seek Mǎ Shīhuáng to heal them?"
The woman said:
"Shīhuáng is a lofty transcendent of the upper realm.
Pitying horses for bearing heavy loads and pulling over long distances,
he thus became a horse doctor,
curing the illnesses of over ten thousand horses.
Heaven above looked down with discernment,
placing an illness between the lips of a dragon,
wishing to test Shīhuáng's ability.
The dragon later carried him and ascended to heaven,
Heaven lent him this.
It's not that dragons truly fall ill."
Kuàng also said:
"That dragons crave swallow's blood,
is there truth to that?"
The woman said:
"Dragons are pure and ethereal,
their drink and food are the vapors of dawn and night.
If they ate swallow's blood,
how could they act and withdraw?
Those who crave it are the likes of jiāo and shèn.
Do not believe fabricated tales;
they are all the absurd and false words of the Four Dukes of the Liáng dynasty."
Kuàng also said:
"What do dragons like?"
She said:
"They like to sleep.
For the great ones, up to a thousand years;
for the small ones, no less than several hundred years.
They recline in caves,
sand and dust gathering between their scales.
Sometimes birds carry tree seeds
and drop them upon them.
Then the scales split and trees grow,
until they are as thick as an armspan,
and only then does the dragon awaken.
Then it shakes itself vigorously and practices cultivation,
shedding its body and entering emptiness and nothingness,
clarifying its spirit and returning to extinction and stillness.
Naturally, its form and its vital energy
follow its transformative functions.
They disperse into the true void,
as if not yet an embryo,
as if not yet congealed.
Like things in a state of indistinctness,
subtle, marvelous, profound, and obscure.
At this time,
even its hundred bones and five limbs
can all enter within a mustard seed.
Following its movements,
there is nowhere it cannot go.
It naturally attains the art of returning to the origin and reverting to the root,
contending in achievement with the Creator."
Kuàng also said:
"In their cultivation practice,
through which gate do dragons attain it?"
The woman said:
"How does it differ from the arts cultivated by lofty transcendents?
Superior individuals who cultivate it
achieve both form and spirit;
middling individuals who cultivate it
transcend in spirit while their form sinks;
inferior individuals who cultivate it,
Both form and spirit have fallen into decay.
Moreover, when cultivating,
the vital energy is refreshing and the spirit is concentrated,
and something emerges.
This is what Lǎozi meant by "dim and dark,
within it there is something."
As for its profound subtleties,
I dare not reveal them,
fearing that I would be condemned by Heaven."
The goddess then ordered her attendants,
to pass the wine cups and converse.
The atmosphere was intimate and harmonious,
the orchid-like beauty was captivating,
as if standing between jade branches and jade trees,
lingering affectionately throughout the night,
deeply moved and opening the hidden heart.
Kuàng said:
"Meeting two immortal maidens here,
truly what one would call the Pavilion of Twin Beauties."
Suddenly, the crowing of a rooster was heard,
and the goddess left a poem, saying:
"Jade chopsticks congealed on cheeks, recalling the Wèi palace,
A single pluck of crimson strings washes the clear breeze.
Tomorrow morning, chasing after the beauty, I shall be filled with sorrow and solitude,
On the sandy isle, mist dissipates, emerald feathers vanish into emptiness."
Zhīxiāo's poem said:
"Weaving gauze beneath the spring, there is little joy,
I urge Xiāoláng once more to empty the wine jug.
Sorrowful to see the jade zither playing 'Parting Crane,'
Once again, clear tears drip like pearls."
Kuàng replied to the two maidens with a poem:
"Red orchids bloom brilliantly amidst peach blossoms,
I rejoice at having sought fragrance, my fortune already bestowed.
The pearl pendant and Magpie Bridge are severed from this moment,
In the distant sky, I vainly lament the lofty azure clouds."
The goddess then presented two items—a bright pearl and emerald feathers—to Kuàng, saying:
"These are as described in Prince Sī of Chén's rhapsody: 'Some gather bright pearls,
some pick emerald feathers.'
Therefore, I offer these gifts,
to complete the ode of the 'Rhapsody on the Goddess of the Luò River.'"
The dragon maiden presented a bolt of fine gauze to Kuàng, saying:
"If any foreigner seeks to purchase it,
nothing less than ten thousand gold will suffice."
The goddess said:
"You possess extraordinary bones and an unusual appearance,
destined to transcend the mundane world.
But you must embrace simplicity and reject vulgar tastes,
purify your heart and nurture your true nature,
and I shall secretly assist you."
Having spoken,
she soared lightly into the void and departed,
leaving nothing to be seen.
Later, Kuàng safeguarded the pearl and gauze,
often wandering among the Sōng and Yuè mountains.
A friend once encountered him,
and recorded the events in detail.
Now, he has withdrawn from the world and is no longer seen.
Shǐ Suì
During the Huìchāng era,
the minor eunuch Shǐ Suì,
retired to his home due to illness.
One day,
he suddenly summoned his relatives,
saying that when he first fell ill,
he saw a person dressed in yellow,
holding an official document, who said:
"The underworld has summoned your two souls for questioning.
One is to be detained,
the other remains to govern the body."
Unconsciously, he followed.
They exited the Tōnghuà Gate,
headed southeast into a desolate path,
crossed the Bà and Chǎn rivers.
Ascended Lántián Mountain.
After traveling about several dozen lǐ on the mountain,
suddenly, a rider holding a black banner appeared,
saying:
"The Great One has long been seated in the hall,
and the sinners have all been recorded.
Why are you so late?"
Urging them onward, they departed.
They arrived at a city,
with armored soldiers guarding the gates.
Heading directly north, they reached a palace,
where the palace gates were heavily guarded.
A clerk dressed in red
led the messenger inside together.
Between the screens,
a clerk emerged from within, saying:
"Receive the instruction, receive the instruction."
The messenger bowed and accepted the command.
It was proclaimed:
"Shǐ Suì, in a previous life, was an attendant to the Chief Recorder of Kuòcāng Mountain.
Initially, he was respectful and diligent,
but later became negligent and fell into decay,
and was demoted to serve as a eunuch,
in hopes that he would awaken and realize his errors.
Now that the Chief Recorder has resumed his position,
the attendant should be transferred,
and handed over to the relevant authorities to act according to the law."
Suì was then led to a courtyard,
where he saw a person,
with white beard and temples,
dressed in purple,
attended by over ten attendants on both sides.
After bowing, he looked up,
and it was Junior Tutor Bái Jūyì.
Suì had served as a minor clerk in the Hànlín Academy during the Yuánhé era,
so he asked:
"Why has the Junior Tutor come here?"
Bái, with a serene expression, said:
"Attendant, do you recall the past events?"
Suddenly, it was as if he awoke from sleep,
and his spirit and energy immediately returned to their former state.
The eunuchs, hearing of his recovery,
all came to visit him.
That evening,
Bái Jūyì passed away in Luòyáng.
On his deathbed,
he said to his relatives:
"Long ago, from Pénglái,
with the Emperor.
There was a cause in Jambudvīpa.
The Emperor, in Jambudvīpa, parted at the Lìndé Palace."
Having spoken, he passed away.
No one understood his words.
Comparing the dates,
at the time of his passing,
it was when the Emperor was feasting in the Lìndé Palace.
Tián Bù
The Tang Dynasty chancellor Cuī Xuàn was governing Huáinán.
Lú Dān had been dismissed from Zhèxī,
Zhāng Zé,
dismissed from Chángzhōu,
both passed through Wéiyáng,
and paid a visit to Xuàn.
Xuàn, on a day of leisure,
was playing chess with the two guests,
when a clerk reported that a female shaman and the former Wèibó military commissioner Tián Bù had arrived together,
staying at a certain pavilion in the inn.
Xuàn found this very strange,
and the clerk further said:
"Her manifestations are clear and proven,
different from other shamans,
I request that she be moved to the lodging of the capital patrol officer."
Xuàn hastily summoned the shaman to come,
and she then exchanged bows with the spirit,
saying:
"Thank you, Your Excellency."
Xuàn said:
"For what do you thank me?"
The spirit replied:
"Bù has an unworthy son,
who is insatiably greedy for wealth,
and does not govern the commandery affairs properly.
He was due to commit a capital crime,
but thanks to your hidden virtue, he was spared.
That the sacrificial offerings at Bù's family temple have not been cut off,
is due to your grace."
Xuàn was startled and said:
"How extraordinary.
When Xuàn was serving as chancellor,
the Xiàzhōu military commissioner reported that Yínzhōu prefect Tián Huì had committed a corruption crime,
privately manufacturing armor,
to exchange for horses, cloth, and silk at the border markets.
The Emperor was furious and said:
'Corruption is a separate matter for deliberation.
Moreover, he was entrusted with a border prefecture,
and should have been guarding against bandits.
To supply armor to the enemy,
is this not rebellion?'
He ordered the Secretariat to judge him according to the law,
intending to exterminate his clan.
The next day,
Xuàn spoke calmly to the Emperor, saying:
'Huì's corruption crime naturally has its statutes.
However, he is the grandson of Tián Hóngzhèng,
and the son of Tián Bù.
Hóngzhèng was the first from Héshuò to come to court,
and presented the registers of officials.
Bù also fulfilled his father's command,
continuing with loyalty and instruction,
and died by falling on his sword.
Now, if we enforce the law to secure the border defenses,
it would be better to grant a generous pardon in light of these circumstances,
to encourage loyalty and martyrdom.'
The Emperor's anger then subsided.
He only demoted him to a distant prefecture as a Simǎ.
And Xuàn had never once spoken of this to relatives or close associates,
and had nearly forgotten it.
Now the spirit's words,
precisely refer to this matter."
He then ordered a vegetarian meal in the corridor.
Dressed in plain clothes, he received them.
He said to the spirit:
"You died with righteous martyrdom,
why are you being driven by a mere foolish woman?"
The spirit said:
"Bù once owed this old woman eight hundred thousand coins,
and is now enduring the shame to repay her."
Xuàn, along with the two guests and the staff under the supervision of the army commissioner,
together paid the money for him.
The spirit then took his leave,
and consequently, the shaman's predictions ceased to be accurate.
Jìnshì Cuī Shēng,
traveling from Guāndōng to take the imperial examination,
set out early, more than ten lǐ beyond Tóngguān.
It was just the fifth watch of the night,
with no one else on the road,
only a servant, a carrying pole, and a donkey.
Suddenly he encountered a procession with torches and shouts clearing the way,
with banners, spears, and armor—
about two hundred people in all,
like a regional military governor’s entourage.
Shēng hid himself behind a tree.
After they passed,
he had not gone two or three lǐ further
when the vanguard of the procession turned back,
so he slowly followed them.
There was a swift-footed attendant in charge of tea utensils,
walking quite slowly,
so Shēng asked who they were.
He replied:
“The mountain god is welcoming the heavenly official Attendant Censor Cuī.
Since you, xiùcai, are about to take the examination,
why not pay him a visit
to divine your future?”
Shēng declined, saying he had no way to gain access,
and the swift-footed attendant promised to sound it out for him.
When they reached the temple gate,
dawn had not yet broken.
The attendant arranged for Shēng to wait by the gate.
After entering for a long while, he came out and said:
“I have informed the Attendant Censor.”
He promptly led Shēng in to meet him,
and he was very pleased.
Soon the mountain god arrived,
they stood talking,
then he invited Attendant Censor Cuī into the temple.
Curtains and canopies were set up,
with lavish feasts and music.
After a while,
music was played and wine served.
As Cuī was about to attend the banquet,
he instructed his attendants
to wait upon Shēng alone,
providing him with hot water, tea, and whatever he needed,
showing deep kindness.
As the drinking went on for some time,
Shēng grew tired
and strolled around to look,
unconsciously walking out the gate.
Suddenly he saw his maternal uncle,
grasped his hand, and spoke of old times.
His uncle’s face was haggard,
his clothes ragged.
Shēng said:
“Uncle, you left the human world long ago;
how did you come to be here?”
He replied:
“I departed the human world
fifteen years ago,
but have had no position.
Recently I became the god of the Fúshuǐ Bridge,
weary of greeting and sending off,
and hard-pressed for food and clothing.
The state of my poverty
is almost beyond relief.
Knowing that my nephew is on good terms with the heavenly official Attendant Censor,
and considering our shared surname and kinship,
he will surely recommend me,
so I have come to plead sincerely.
If I can obtain the position of god of the Nánshān Zuǐ,
I can roughly escape hunger and poverty.
After this transfer,
I may advance to a heavenly rank.”
Shēng excused himself, saying, “We have only just met;
I don’t know if I can really recommend you.
But I will try to speak of it.”
Soon the Attendant Censor also ended the banquet and returned,
saying to Shēng:
“You will pass the examination the year after next;
you may skip this year’s exam.
My official business will also be finished shortly,
and I must return at once.
The journey schedule is very tight,
so I cannot stay long.”
Shēng then told him of his uncle’s request.
The Attendant Censor said:
“The Zuǐ god position is like a selected appointment in the human world,
a very pure and prestigious post.
The Fúshuǐ Bridge god is lowly and miscellaneous;
how could he obtain it directly?
But I will try to speak of it;
the mountain god surely will not refuse.”
He then went again to attend upon the mountain god.
Shēng stealthily drew near to listen,
hearing the whole request,
and the mountain god indeed agreed.
He immediately ordered a document issued to appoint him.
Soon, the uncle received the document and came to give thanks,
with one or two hundred welcoming officials and officers,
his retinue very orderly.
Shēng then came out to congratulate him,
and the Zuǐ god wept, saying:
“Without my nephew’s help,
I could not have obtained this position.
After one more transfer,
I will enter the heavenly administration.
This year the Wèi River will flood,
and your estate will be washed away.
The damage along that stretch will affect three to five hundred households,
but I have already ordered protection for your estate;
by the fifth or sixth month, you will surely avoid this disaster.
Moreover, I will repay you with five hundred rolls of silk.”
In a moment,
the Zuǐ god departed with his entourage,
the Attendant Censor also set off,
and the mountain god came out to see them off.
Shēng alone remained in the temple,
suddenly as if awakening from a dream.
He went out to find his servant,
who was still at the inn,
having seen nothing.
Thereupon, Shēng did not proceed through the pass,
but returned to stay at his country villa.
That summer,
the Wèi River indeed flooded,
washing away and damaging much,
but only Cuī Shēng’s estate was spared.
In front of the estate, an empty boat came to rest;
after the waters receded,
the boat contained five hundred rolls of silk.
The next year, he indeed passed the examination.
Zhāng Yǎn
Jìnshì Zhāng Yǎn, on his way to take the examination,
reached the front of the Jīntiān Wáng Temple,
when he encountered heavy rain.
He took shelter from the rain at the temple gate,
but by evening it still had not stopped.
Unable to reach an inn,
he entered and stayed overnight inside the temple gate.
By the fourth watch,
he heard the sound of Jīntiān Wáng conducting official business,
shouting orders very sternly.
After a while,
he heard his name called:
“Tomorrow at noon,
when Zhāng Yǎn travels to such-and-such village,
he will be eaten by a red fox-tiger.”
Yǎn heard this and was terrified.
Waiting until the courtyard was quiet,
he crawled in through the gate
and announced his name, bowing.
Jīntiān Wáng said:
“You are a living man;
what brings you here?”
Yǎn then recounted what had happened.
Jīntiān Wáng said:
“Summon the tiger.”
Soon the tiger arrived.
Jīntiān Wáng said:
“Take two large beasts to eat instead of Yǎn.”
The tiger said:
“The fated one must be eaten;
another cannot substitute.”
Jīntiān Wáng said:
“Check when this tiger will die.”
An officer came and said:
“It will be shot to death by Wáng Cún of such-and-such village during the wèi hour.”
Jīntiān Wáng said:
“Order Zhāng Yǎn to proceed only after the time he was to be eaten has passed.”
When Yǎn traveled on to that road ahead,
he indeed saw a crowd clamoring.
He asked about it,
and they said:
“Wáng Cún of such-and-such village
shot and killed a red fox-tiger.”
It was exactly as Jīntiān Wáng had said.
Yǎn then bought wine himself,
obtained dried venison,
and personally went to the temple to give thanks.
The Péi Family Son
In Tiānshuǐ's Péngjùn, there was a son of the Péi family.
During the Xiántōng era,
he studied the Gūlín method in Dōngláng.
He committed adultery with a female relative from his maternal side.
When the affair was exposed, he was imprisoned.
Every day, his food and drink were provided,
all delivered by the deity of the Gūlín method.
The jailer found it strange and said to the deity:
"Since you are so divine and extraordinary,
why not spare him from this punishment?"
The deity replied:
"Those who receive my method
can only use it to protect themselves from harm
and to help others with skillful means.
Since he has violated the precepts and vows,
not only does the law of the land apply,
but even the deities will not tolerate it.
The diligence I show now
is to repay the merit of his incense offerings."
In the end, he was flogged to death.
Wéi Zōu
Wéi Zōu
was skilled in the five tones,
excelled at whistling,
and called himself the Unrivaled Young Master.
He took the imperial examination,
but after failing once, he gave up.
He said:
"A man should have ambitions to travel the world;
how could he bend his principles for worldly affairs?"
He traveled to Yuèyáng,
where the prefect of Yuèyáng, who knew him personally, recruited him.
After a few months, he resigned on grounds of illness and left.
Wéi Zōu's younger brother, Wéi Lái,
was traveling by boat
and drowned in Dòngtíng Lake.
Wéi Zōu wept bitterly by the shore.
He moved his boat to the foot of the lake god's temple
and wanted to burn it down,
saying:
"Wealthy merchants worth a thousand gold
cross safely and smoothly.
My poor and unfortunate brother
suffered such a calamity.
What use is your temple?"
Suddenly, while dozing off in the boat,
he dreamed of a deity in splendid attire coming to visit him,
who said to Wéi Zōu:
"On the paths of the underworld,
no one is wrongfully killed.
Your late father,
when he served as the city guard,
was known for his integrity and righteousness,
and even ghosts and spirits avoided him.
He demolished many illicit temples,
but two of them should not have been destroyed.
The two deities appealed to the Emperor,
who initially refused,
but after over ten years of persistent requests,
he granted them one of your father's descendants
as compensation to the lords of the two abolished temples.
However, it had to be someone who, in retreat, did not know the Way,
and in advancement, could not contribute to the times.
Thus, your worthy brother was chosen.
If you cannot recover his body,
it will be my fault,
and I will have the boatmen deliver his corpse to the lake shore."
Wéi Zōu awoke in shock,
and the matter was settled.
He then ordered fishing boats to cast hooks and nets,
and indeed retrieved his brother's body from the shore.
That evening,
he dreamed again of the deity expressing gratitude:
"Ghosts and spirits do not fear anger,
but they fear decisiveness,
because of its sincerity.
You are now a decisive person.
In the past, when music was performed in Dòngtíng,
it was under my jurisdiction.
I wish to repay your great kindness with sublime music,
hoping you will observe the rhythms of Xiánchí
and release the worries and troubles of this floating world."
Suddenly, he saw metal and stone instruments, feathers and flutes,
resounding and vibrating.
Wéi Zōu marveled greatly,
thinking it was not something he deserved,
and only awoke when the music ended.
A person from Chǔzhōu
Near the area between Chǔ and Sì,
a man left his wife and several servants in a village.
He traveled as a guest for several years,
and one day returned home.
The elders and youths of the village
came together with wine to visit him,
and he invited them in to drink together,
becoming very merry while intoxicated.
The villagers only played flutes to the tune of "The Music God's Melody."
They continued almost until dawn,
when suddenly a dancer in front was possessed by a deity, who spoke:
"The Great King wishes to meet with the master,
and desires to discuss kinship with him."
The man was greatly alarmed,
and rebuked:
"The ways of the gods are not deceitful;
I have no sons or daughters,
what kinship could I have with you,
what kinship?"
The deity said:
"I am to marry your wife,
so quickly have her dress and groom herself,
for I will come shortly to fetch her."
The man was furious,
and the villagers dispersed,
thinking the dancer was just a villager
speaking drunken nonsense.
Shortly after, dawn broke,
when suddenly the sound of horses neighing was heard outside the gate.
The man was greatly astonished,
and wanted to go out and shout at them.
Then he saw a foreign deity,
dressed in purple with a thick beard.
He was over ten feet tall,
his head appearing above the wall.
He called out:
"Madam, it is time to depart."
The man did not know what to do,
and his wife collapsed inside the room and died.
The Xiànhé Deity
The God of the Sunken River:
In Xīzhōu Xīxiàn, there lived an old couple named Zhāng Wēng,
who were childless in their old age.
The old man went to the valleys daily to gather firewood to support himself.
Not long after,
one day,
he cut his finger on a sharp rock in a cave.
His blood gushed out,
dripping into a stone crevice.
He plugged it with a leaf and returned home.
Another day, when he returned to the spot,
he pulled out the leaf to look,
and the blood had transformed into a small snake.
The old man picked it up in his palm,
and played with it for a while.
This creature lingered affectionately,
as if reluctant to leave,
so he cut a bamboo tube, placed it inside, and carried it in his bosom.
At home, he fed it various meats,
and it became very tame.
As time passed, it gradually grew.
After one year,
it began stealing chickens and dogs to eat at night.
After two years,
it stole sheep and pigs.
The neighbors were puzzled by the loss of their livestock,
but the old man and his wife said nothing.
Later, the county magistrate lost a Shǔ horse.
Following its tracks,
he entered the old man’s home,
pressed him for answers,
and discovered the horse had already been swallowed by the snake.
The magistrate was shocked,
and reprimanded the old man for keeping such a dangerous creature.
The old man confessed his guilt,
and the magistrate intended to kill the snake.
Suddenly, one night,
thunder and lightning struck violently,
and the entire county sank into a vast marsh,
stretching endlessly,
with only the old couple surviving.
Afterward, both the man and the snake disappeared,
and the county was renamed Xiànhéxiàn,
with the snake called Zhāng Èzǐ.
Later, Yáo Cháng traveled to Shǔ,
and upon reaching Zǐtóng Ridge,
he rested by the roadside.
A man in plain clothes approached,
and said to Cháng:
"You should return to Qín early,
for the people of Qín will soon be without a ruler.
Is it not you who will bring them peace and prosperity?"
When asked his name,
he replied:
"I am Zhāng Èzǐ.
Do not forget me in the future."
After Cháng returned,
he indeed proclaimed himself emperor in Cháng'ān.
He then sent an envoy to Shǔ to search for Zhāng Èzǐ,
but could not find him.
So he built a temple at the place where they had met,
which is the present-day Zhāng Xiànggōng Temple.
When Emperor Xīzōng fled to Shǔ,
the god emerged from the temple for over ten lǐ,
kneeling in welcome.
Amid the white mist,
his form could faintly be seen.
The emperor then bestowed upon him his own sword,
praying for his loyalty,
and setting a date for the rebellion to be quelled.
When the emperor returned,
he generously gifted precious treasures,
which no one dared to peek at.
Wáng Duó had a poem inscribed on stone:
"In night rain, the dragon casts aside a three-foot case.
In spring clouds, the phoenix enters the ninefold city."
Jiǎn Zōngrú
A military officer in Qiánnán surnamed Jiǎn,
whose original name is not recorded.
He was upright and outspoken,
poor yet content.
His home neighbored the Xuānfǔ Temple,
and whenever his family ate,
they would first offer food to the temple.
This continued for many years.
In the second year of the Xiántōng era,
when barbarian invaders encroached on the border,
the military inspector reviewed the troops,
but could not find a suitable general.
Jiǎn suddenly dreamed of a man,
dressed like a king,
who said to him:
"I am Zhòngní.
I am moved by your constant devotion to me,
and I shall assist you.
Change your name to Zōngrú,
and from then on, you shall attain wealth and honor."
Upon waking,
he joyfully volunteered for the mission,
and also requested a name change.
At that time, everyone else was reluctant,
but when they heard Zōngrú volunteer,
they sent him.
In one battle, he decisively defeated the barbarian invaders,
and the remnants fled.
The commander of Qián reported his achievements,
and he was appointed Prefect of Lǎngzhōu.
After his term ended, he went to the capital,
and was promoted to Minister of Agriculture,
receiving many rewards.
He died in office several years later.
Huá Néng
During the Xiántōng era of the Táng dynasty,
Huá Néng, a Hanlin Academician,
was the highest-ranked chess player.
There was a man named Zhāng,
around forty years old,
who came to challenge him to a game.
At first, Huá gave him a one-move advantage,
and pondered carefully for a long time.
Just as he placed a piece,
Zhāng responded immediately,
sometimes even strolling in the courtyard.
He waited for Huá to make another move,
and again responded instantly.
When the Huáng rebels attacked the capital,
and Emperor Xīzōng fled to Shǔ,
Huá intended to join the imperial entourage,
planning to take the Jīnzhōu route.
Zhāng said:
"There is no need to go forward.
I am not a chess player;
the Heavenly Emperor has sent me to take your chess skills."
Huá was shocked,
his wife and children wept,
and he passed away suddenly.
Liǔ Huì,
a native of Hédōng,
was gifted in literature from a young age,
and initially entered office through hereditary privilege.
By the end of the Xiántōng era,
he had risen to the position of Reminder.
After submitting a memorial that was ignored,
he resigned from office
and retreated to Zhōngnán Mountain.
One day, he entered the city
to visit an old friend in Xuānyáng Lane.
Suddenly, he encountered a man begging for food,
and Huì gave him some.
The man only sniffed it three times and stopped.
Huì, puzzled, asked him why,
and the man replied:
"I am an official of the underworld.
I am grateful for your offering,
and deeply touched.
In three years, you will become a chancellor."
With that, he disappeared.
Huì did not believe it.
When Huáng Cháo attacked the capital,
he sought someone skilled in writing proclamations,
and someone recommended Huì.
Cháo sent riders to fetch him,
forcing him to write a proclamation.
When the proclamation reached the imperial entourage,
Emperor Xīzōng recognized it as Huì’s work,
and said:
"Huì resigned on his own;
I did not abandon him.
Why does he slander me so harshly?"
After the rebellion was quelled,
it was decided not to pardon him.
Cháo appointed Huì as a Secretary in the Secretariat,
and soon made him a false chancellor.
Liú Shānfǔ
Liú Shānfǔ of Péngchéng in the Táng dynasty,
was from a prominent official family of the central court.
His father served as an official in Lǐngwài,
and as Shānfǔ accompanied him on the journey northward back home,
their boat reached Qīngcǎo Lake.
They went ashore,
and saw a shrine to the Northern Heavenly King.
They therefore went to visit it.
They saw the temple buildings in ruins and decay,
with incense offerings no longer continuing.
Shānfǔ had shown talent and thought from a young age.
He thus inscribed a poem, saying:
"The ruined walls have weathered wind and rain for many springs;
the courtyard overgrown with weeds is covered in a layer of dust.
It must be that the deity shows no divine response,
for how can rise and fall be up to humans?"
That night, he dreamed that he was reprimanded by the Heavenly King.
The deity declared:
"I am not the Heavenly King,
but the god of Nányuè.
I preside over this place—
why do you insult me?"
Soon after, he awoke in alarm.
Violent winds and waves arose,
nearly capsizing the boat.
He hastily rose to repent his fault,
ordering the poem plaque to be removed,
after which the storm calmed.
The Èrzhū Clan
During the Xiántōng era,
there was a man surnamed Èrzhū
who lived in Wūxiá.
Each year he traded along the banks of the Qútáng Gorge in Jīngyì.
There was a shrine to the White Horse Deity,
which Èrzhū often prayed at.
One day,
upon returning from Shǔ,
he again made offerings there,
when suddenly he heard the deity speak:
"I am ashamed of your friendship over the years.
I am about to leave this place,
so I speak plainly to bid you farewell."
The traveler asked in surprise:
"Where is the deity going?"
The reply came:
"I am to become the City God of Húnán.
The Supreme Deity, because I performed modest virtues for the people of the Three Gorges,
has thus promoted me.
However, the world will soon fall into chaos,
and the present Son of Heaven will not rule the world much longer either."
Èrzhū asked again in astonishment:
"Who will succeed him?"
The answer was:
"The Táng's virtue is still strong."
The traveler asked for the taboo name,
but the deity said:
"This certainly cannot be revealed."
The traveler pleaded earnestly,
and then the deity said:
"I recently saw the celestial mandate,
and it only had 'double suns'."
After speaking,
it said no more.
That year, Emperor Yìhuáng passed away,
and Emperor Xīzōng ascended the throne as the Prince of Jìn.
Lǐ Zhònglǚ
Lǐ Zhònglǚ of Gūzāng,
toward the end of the Xiántōng era,
was appointed magistrate of Lǔshān in Rǔzhōu.
He governed with clarity and competence,
and officials did not dare deceive him.
When drought struck,
he prayed to various local deities,
but none responded.
Zhònglǚ then purified himself and fasted,
and personally prayed at the Yáo Shrine on Lǔshān, twenty lǐ from the county seat,
offering his black horse and his groom Zhāng Hàn as sacrifices.
After the sacrifice,
as he was about to descend the mountain,
clouds and mist suddenly arose,
and by the time he reached the flat marshes, heavy rain fell.
Both the groom and the horse suddenly died.
Thereupon, Zhònglǚ performed another sacrifice,
and had images of the groom and horse painted on the eastern wall.
A Resident of Xīnchāng Ward
Near the north side of the western corridor of Qīnglóng Temple,
there was a painting of a Buddhist deity clan,
depicting the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
Its vividness made it seem alive,
and prayers and offerings gathered there like spokes to a hub.
There was a man living in Xīnchāng Ward
who, due to a seasonal epidemic,
became so weak in all his limbs
that he could not bear the weight of clothing,
and neither doctors nor shamans could cure him.
One day,
he declared that he wished to follow Buddhism,
and so he was carried on a shoulder-borne litter and placed beneath the painted wall.
He gave generous alms to the chief monk,
and ate and stayed in the temple's side rooms.
After more than ten days,
he dreamed of someone resembling the Heavenly King,
holding something like a rope made of sinews,
and feeding it to the sick man.
He also urged him on.
Chewing the tough and resilient substance,
he forcefully ate about a zhàng of it,
and suddenly felt his weak bones become strong and stiff.
The next day he could walk,
and the day after he could run.
Within a month, he became known for his strength.
Previously, the Imperial Guard had hung a six-jūn bow at the gate,
saying:
"Anyone who can draw it halfway
will have his grain ration doubled as a reward;
anyone who can draw it fully will have it doubled again."
The man answered the call,
drew it fully with ease,
and thus enjoyed a generous salary for the rest of his life.
The Pei Family Daughter
During the rebellion of Huáng Cháo in the Táng dynasty,
there was a court official named Péi
who took his wife and children
and hurried south toward Hànzhōng.
Just after leaving the capital,
his unmarried daughter suddenly died.
In the chaos and haste of the military turmoil,
they had no time to bury her.
When they reached Luògǔ,
at night they heard their daughter speaking,
though her form was not visible.
Her parents questioned her,
and the daughter said:
"I was assaulted by the son of the Chǎnshuǐ River God,
who lured me to his home.
His father angrily reprimanded him
for recklessly killing a living person,
and promptly caned him.
He also apologized and comforted me,
and had someone escort me back.
But for now, I have nowhere to rely.
I wish to follow you, father, southward.
Please pull up some cogon grass and place it in a box or basket for me to reside in,
so that my soul may have a place to rest."
Her eating, drinking, and speech
were no different from when she was alive.
Later, she said she had found a place to be reborn,
and with sorrowful sobs, bade farewell and departed.
Xiàhóu Zhēn
Sixty li west of Lǔshān County in Rǔzhōu,
within the small mountains stands a shrine,
called the Língnǚ Temple.
Its statue is solely of a maiden,
with lowered hairpins and knitted brows,
beautiful and alluring yet bearing an expression of sorrow and longing.
Behind the shrine lies flat ground,
spanning several acres to the left and right,
from which rise three peaks,
each over ten zhang tall,
majestic like Tàihuà Mountain.
The elders say,
in the early Dàzhōng era,
this place was suddenly struck by violent winds and torrential rain,
which ceased overnight,
and thus this mountain appeared.
The deity manifested herself to a woodcutter, saying:
"I am a daughter of Shāngyú,
the Emperor has commanded me to govern this hundred-li domain.
Inform the villagers
to erect a shrine before the mountain,
named Nǚlíng,
for I have brought it here."
At the end of the Xiántōng era,
the county registrar Huángfǔ Méi,
during a seasonal sacrifice,
went together with his friend Xiàhóu Zhēn.
After the sacrifice,
they toured the temple.
Zhēn alone lingered, unable to leave,
and requested a cup of wine to pour as a libation, saying:
"Xiàhóu Zhēn is young and without a partner,
today I have beheld your divine form,
and wish to serve as a humble sweeper in this temple."
After offering the wine, he returned.
That evening,
Xiàhóu Zhēn felt dazed and could not sleep,
as if afflicted by a dark force.
His servant came to report,
Méi hurried to see him,
and found him wide-eyed and speechless,
unable to speak.
Méi asked:
"Could it be the Nǚlíng deity?"
Zhēn nodded.
Méi ordered an official to pray, saying:
"Xiàhóu Zhēn, overwhelmed by the lingering effects of wine,
uttered disrespectful words,
defiling the deity's ears,
and now he is ill.
Is this a punishment from you?
Or is it the fulfillment of his request?
If it is a punishment,
would you destroy a scholar of the state over a single remark?
This would violate the virtue of cherishing life,
and incur the guilt of wanton slaughter.
Would the Emperor not observe this,
and allow a deity to wreak cruelty below?
If it is the fulfillment of his request,
then with a single word you would abandon the path of chastity and tranquility,
spreading a licentious wind;
thinking of Zhāng Shuò, you would stir your cloud chariot,
seeing Jiāofǔ, you would remove your bright jade pendant.
If the Nine Gates were to cry out,
it would surely bring blame for neglecting propriety.
Moreover, the world has many handsome men,
why must it be him?
May the deity hear this."
After the offering,
Xiàhóu Zhēn recovered as before.
Xú Huàn
To the southeast of Yìyáng Commandery,
lies the Black Water River,
on whose banks stands the shrine of the Black Water General.
During the Tàihé era,
Xuē Yòngruò, from the Ministry of Rites, was appointed to govern this commandery,
ruling strictly but not cruelly.
One evening,
he dreamed of an attendant announcing:
"The Black Water General has arrived."
He invited him in,
and saw a tall, imposing man,
with majestic beard and eyes,
clad in armor and armed.
After sitting,
he said:
"I once drowned in this river,
but because I upheld a heart of benevolence and righteousness,
I was able
to appeal to the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
'Your status in the underworld is rising,
thus I grant you this duty.' Sir, you may erect a shrine by the river,
and I will protect the people."
After speaking, he awoke.
He then ordered the shrine built and sacrifices offered,
and during floods, droughts, or disasters,
prayers to him were always answered.
Yòngruò possessed a Géxī precious sword,
and again dreamed that the general requested it,
so he presented it as a gift.
He then hollowed out a pillar before the deity,
placed the sword in a box inside,
and set up a small door outside,
securing it with a lock.
In the wùxū year of the Qiánfú era,
the Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Xú Huàn,
for his fair and just handling of cases,
was appointed to Yìyáng Commandery.
In the seventh month of autumn, he left the capital,
during a time of continuous rain,
and the eastern roads were muddy.
Passing through Xiáohán,
crossing Dōngzhōu,
and traveling via Xǔ and Cài,
there was hardly a clear day.
After crossing the Huái River,
he stayed at the Jiālù Lodge,
which lies in the western part of Yìyáng.
At the time, they suffered from bitter rain and bleak winds,
and the attendants were shivering with cold.
Huàn prepared wine and prayed,
and that evening the skies cleared.
From then on, Huàn revered the deity even more,
and personally attended the spring and autumn sacrifices.
In the tenth month of winter the following year,
several thousand bandits
attacked the commandery city.
Huàn defended firmly,
and the city could not be taken,
so the bandits led their troops west into Yìyáng.
At that time, a rogue
told a bandit lieutenant about the temple sword.
The lieutenant then led his men,
broke the pillar, and took it away.
Soon after, they went out at dawn to plunder,
but a dense fog enveloped them,
and they lost their way.
Suddenly, they encountered a woodcutter boy,
captured him,
and ordered him to lead the way.
After crossing the mountain, the fog lifted,
and they found themselves at the camp of Zhāng Zhōu in Yìyáng.
The soldiers clashed with the bandits,
killed them all,
and Zhāng Zhōu personally captured their leader,
retrieved the sword,
and returned it to the temple.
To this day, the sacrifices continue without cease.
Luó Hóngxìn
During the Zhōnghé era,
the military governor of Wèibó, Luó Hóngxìn,
initially served as a minor officer of foot archers in his army,
in charge of pasturing duties.
Once, he stayed outside the Guānyīn Temple in Wèizhōu,
where there was a shrine
commonly called the White-Bearded Elder.
A shaman named Zōng Gān
suddenly approached Hóngxìn and said:
"Last night, the deity suddenly spoke,
saying you will soon become the master of this land."
Hóngxìn angrily replied:
"Are you trying to endanger me?"
Another day,
he came again with the same message,
and Hóngxìn ordered him to keep it secret.
Within a year,
a military revolt indeed occurred,
and Hóngxìn was elected as commander.
Hóngxìn was tall and robust in appearance,
strong and skilled in archery,
and though his fame was not yet widespread,
the troops already respected him.
He was eventually promoted to the rank of Grand Commandant and Prince of Línhuái.
Lǐ Yáo
During the Qiánníng era of the Táng dynasty,
Liú Chāngměi served as the Prefect of Kuí Prefecture.
It happened during the summer floods,
when the gorge waters swelled, turbulent and treacherous.
A local proverb said:
"When Yànyù is as big as a horse,
one must not sail down Qútáng."
Therefore, travelers would cease boating and wait.
Scholar Lǐ Yáo,
with his family in tow,
was traveling downstream from Shǔ,
heading to Jiānglíng.
Chāngměi, seeing the water conditions were extremely dangerous,
urged him to stop.
Yáo, however, hastily proceeded.
Soon after, his boat capsized.
His entire family drowned.
Only one wet nurse,
pushed ashore by terrifying waves the next night,
revived. Earlier, Chén Xiǎonú, a salt-burner from Yǒng'ān,
was sailing an empty boat down Qútáng.
He saw a person under the cliff,
wearing a four-seamed hat,
a narrow white gown,
blue trousers,
and holding an iron caltrop.
He asked about Yáo's travel schedule,
claiming he was there to welcome him.
After the wet nurse revived,
she also reported to the Prefect,
saying Scholar Lǐ had arrived at an official bureau to handle affairs,
with vermilion gates and white walls,
and subordinates came to congratulate him.
She also heard it said,
"On this list, there is no name for a wet nurse,"
so she was sent out of the water.
Yáng Biāo
In the Táng dynasty, Yáng Biāo,
son of Chief Minister Yáng Shōu,
served as an assistant in Jiāngxī in his youth.
During the autumn sacrifice to the Great Gū Goddess,
Biāo admired the beauty of the deity's statue
and casually joked about it.
After the sacrifice, as his boat returned,
he saw within the clouds and mist in the sky
a woman,
of exceedingly beautiful appearance,
approaching Biāo.
She addressed him as "Young Master Yáng,"
saying:
"My elder sister is most fortunate
to have caught Young Master Yáng's fancy.
She hopes you will turn your boat around
to complete the wedding rites,
so I have come to welcome you."
Biāo, astonished,
replied:
"My earlier words were merely a jest."
The goddess said:
"My elder sister originally had no intention of admiring you, sir,
but Young Master Yáng spoke first.
If you were to break it off now,
I fear immediate harm would befall you."
Biāo, having no choice,
then consented.
He requested a month's grace
to settle his family affairs.
After returning home and arranging his final instructions,
he died suddenly,
as if fetched by ghosts or spirits.
Reminder Xiē Zé,
who was related by marriage to Biāo,
often recounted this story in great detail.
Recently, the late Shǐ Zàidé, Adjutant to the Military Commissioner of Dèng Prefecture and a Palace Gentleman,
had a son named Shǐ Guāngzé,
very intelligent and handsome,
who was preparing for the imperial examinations.
Returning from his country villa,
he entered the Tài Shān Temple while drunk
and said to the deity:
"How about I become your third son?"
From then on, he returned home in a dazed state,
as if being summoned,
and died within a month.
Zhāng Jǐng
Lúshān scholar Zhāng Jǐng,
during the Qiánníng era,
was traveling to Guì Prefecture for his studies.
Reaching Quǎn Háo Tān in Héng Prefecture,
he damaged his boat, went ashore,
and slept in a riverside temple,
where he was reprimanded by the temple deity.
Jǐng defended himself citing his scholarly vocation,
and the deity's expression softened.
He invited Jǐng to sit and spoke leisurely,
saying:
"There is a shaman named Lì Rén,
whose crimes warrant the extermination of his clan.
I, the temple deity, have pleaded his case to the Mountain Deity,
but there is no one to draft the memorial."
Jǐng drafted it for him.
After the memorial was submitted,
the Mountain Deity approved it.
The temple deity was pleased
and gave Jǐng ten ingots of white gold as a gift.
Liú Shānfǔ and Proofreader Liào Xùn
personally heard Jǐng narrate this story in great detail.
Attendant Cuī
Attendant Cuī from Fújiàn,
his name forgotten,
was upright and disciplined in conduct,
highly regarded by the military headquarters.
Sent on a mission to Hú-Xiāng,
upon his return journey,
he encountered bandits on the road.
His companions all died,
but Cuī, in his panic,
was suddenly led away by someone and escaped.
Mid-journey, he again fell ill with malaria,
and could find no medicine.
Passing by the Yánpíng Ford Temple,
he dreamed the temple deity bestowed upon him three pills of medicine.
After taking them,
he awoke with a start, completely cured.
Liú Shānfǔ of Péngchéng said himself that
his maternal relative Lǐ Jìngyí, a Palace Gentleman,
had a residence in the Yùcái Ward of the Eastern Capital,
where the local earth god was most efficacious.
A family servant named Zhāng Xíngzhōu
served him and received responses.
Before the great flood,
the god forewarned Zhāng in a dream,
requesting food and drink.
When the day came,
he led his kind to block the floodwaters,
ensuring the Lǐ residence was not breached or destroyed.
Wáng Shěnzhī
At the Huángqí shore of the Fúzhōu estuary,
lay a massive, jagged rock,
constantly a hazard to boats.
Wáng Shěnzhī, as Military Commissioner of Fújiàn,
wished to address this,
but dreaded the labor required.
During the Qiánníng era,
he dreamed of a golden-armored deity,
who called himself Prince Wú'ān,
and promised to assist in the excavation.
Upon waking,
he told his staff.
He then ordered Adjutant Liú Shānfǔ to perform a sacrifice.
Before the sacrifice concluded,
various sea spirits and apparitions appeared.
Shānfǔ rested at a monastery,
watching from a high vantage point.
A violent storm of wind and thunder arose.
He saw a creature,
neither fish nor dragon,
with yellow scales and red mane.
After three days,
the wind and thunder finally cleared.
A separate harbor had been opened,
greatly facilitating travel.
A memorial was sent to inform the court,
which bestowed the name "Gāntáng Harbor."
Liú Shānfǔ, an Adjutant in Mǐn,
was from an old clan of the central court.
He authored the twelve-volume *Jīnxī Xiántán*
which recorded these events in detail.
Zhāng Huáiwǔ
Nánpíng Wáng Zhōng Fù,
governed Jiāngxī.
He sent the Daoist priest Shěn Tàixū
to pray at the Jiǔtiān Shǐzhě Temple on Lúshān.
After Tàixū finished the ritual,
he sat at night in the corridor.
As if in a dream,
he saw a person from a mural painting
step forward and bow to Tàixū, saying:
"I am Zhāng Huáiwǔ,
once a general.
The Supreme Deity, because I had some small hidden merits benefiting others,
now assigns me to this temple as a spirit official."
After waking,
he rose to look at the mural,
which was labeled "Five Hundred Spirit Officials."
Tàixū returned
and told this to the presented scholar Shěn Bīn.
Twenty years later, Bīn
traveled to Lǐlíng,
where the county magistrate Lù Shēng hosted him.
While dining,
a military officer Xǔ Shēng arrived later,
and the conversation turned to Zhāng Huáiwǔ.
Bīn then asked about him.
Xǔ said:
"Huáiwǔ
was a deputy general under Cài,
and my chief clerk.
Recently, in the jiǎchén year, there was a great famine,
and we heard that only Yùzhāng had a good harvest.
So he and another general
each led their troops to flee to Yùzhāng.
Once on the road,
the two armies gradually became incompatible.
By the time they reached Wǔchāng,
a major conflict erupted.
They set a date for a decisive battle,
and no one could stop them.
Huáiwǔ then took his sword and climbed the watchtower,
removed the ladder,
and said to his followers:
'Our journey today
has no other purpose
but to save our lives.
Why can't we endure small grievances
and instead attack each other?
In battle,
surely the strong will be wounded and the weak will perish.
If so, then why leave our homeland
only to die on the road?
The reason the two armies are contending
is because of me, Huáiwǔ.
Now I will die for you all,
so the two armies may become one.
Do not create calamity.'
Then he cut his own throat.
Thereupon, the soldiers of both armies
all prostrated below the tower and wept bitterly.
Subsequently, they made peace and became kin.
By the time they reached Yùzhāng,
