not a single person had deserted."
Xǔ only cherished his old kindness,
and did not know about the spirit official matter.
Bīn thus recorded the account
to clarify it.
Could it be that Heaven's intent wished to stir feelings for righteous death,
and thus informed people through subtle signs?
Lǐ Méi
In the beginning of the Tiānyòu era,
in Shūzhōu, there was a granary official named Lǐ Méi,
who said that from a young age he had an illness,
and thus could see ghosts,
telling people fortunes and misfortunes,
often accurately.
The Huáinán general Zhāng Hào,
monopolized the power to depose and establish rulers,
and his might shook both court and country.
Méi was then staying overnight at the Sīmìng Zhēnjūn Temple on Qiánshān.
The next day,
with the Daoist priest Cuī Chǎnrán and several others,
he was about to enter the city.
Several li from the temple,
he suddenly stopped his companions by the roadside,
and hid behind a large tree to peer.
After a long while, he proceeded.
Chǎnrán said:
"Did you see a ghost again?"
Méi replied:
"Just now I saw a person,
heavily shackled,
escorted by several dozen officers and soldiers,
heading toward the temple.
He must certainly be summoned for trial by the True Lord.
Although his spirit is still present,
he cannot avoid his fate."
Someone asked who it was,
and after a long while he was willing to say:
"It was Zhāng Hào."
Those who heard were afraid,
and together kept it secret.
Within ten days, news came that Hào had been executed.
Lǐ Zōng completed the construction of Kāiyuán Temple,
and held a grand gathering of civil and military officials, monks, and Daoists in the temple.
After it ended,
Méi again said to Chǎnrán:
"Among the guests seated earlier,
one was firmly escorted away by two officers.
His time is not long."
He described the person's clothing and appearance,
and it was the drill inspector and patrol officer Chén Jiàng.
Within a few days,
Jiàng suddenly fell ill and died.
The Daoist priest Shào Xiūmò,
a disciple of Cuī,
witnessed this.
Zhào Yú
The presented scholar Zhào Yú,
a man from Lǔ,
repeatedly failed the examinations,
and was in extreme hardship.
Thus he traveled to Tàishān,
praying for death at the mountain temple.
As he was about to leave the temple,
suddenly a minor officer came from behind and said:
"The judge summons you."
Yú followed him.
Abruptly they arrived at a hall,
and someone from behind a curtain said:
"What people value is life;
why do you pray for death?"
Yú replied:
"I was recommended by my hometown,
but repeatedly failed the examinations.
I have no means to return to farming,
and am trapped in poverty and illness.
I no longer have the will to live,
hence I pray for death."
After a long while,
the sound of checking records was heard from behind the curtain.
Then it was said:
"Your fate is extremely meager;
you have no share in fame, rank, salary, or office.
Since you have come to tell this,
I should provide some aid.
Now I give you one medicinal prescription.
With this, you can sufficiently support yourself with food and clothing.
However, you must not establish a household;
if you establish a household, you will become poor."
Yú bowed in thanks and left.
Outside the gate,
a large paulownia leaf floated down from the air before Yú.
Looking at it,
he saw the prescription for Bādòu pills written on it,
identical to the prescription used in the human world.
Yú then claimed to be the former magistrate of Chángshuǐ,
and sold medicine in the Yímén market.
Those who took his medicine
were all cured of illness,
and he earned much profit.
The Daoist priest Lǐ Déyáng
personally saw his paulownia leaf,
which even after more than ten years,
still looked new.
Guān Chéngtuān's Wife
In Qīngchéng County, the Mínjiāng River suddenly flooded violently,
washing away and submerging people's homes.
Guān Chéngtuān's wife, Jì Shì, from the county,
had an infant child in her arms.
She climbed onto a wooden cabinet,
which was pushed and tossed into the great river by terrifying waves.
She only saw a man wearing a red turban and carrying a sword,
and another in red robes holding a tablet,
who protected her,
telling her to go to the county irrigation area.
So she floated along with the current,
reaching the county irrigation area,
where boatmen came to rescue her,
and both mother and child were unharmed.
Lǐ Bīng Shrine
In the summer of the seventh year of the Tiānyòu era,
there was heavy rain in Chéngdū.
The Mín River swelled,
threatening to breach the Jīngkǒu River irrigation weir.
At night, the sound of shouting and clamor was heard,
as if from thousands of people,
with countless torches arrayed.
Despite the fierce wind and rain, the torch flames did not extinguish.
By dawn,
the great weir had shifted several hundred zhang,
and the weir's water flowed into the Xīnjīn River.
The banners erected in Lǐ Yángbīng's temple were all soaked.
At that time,
the counties of Xīnjīn, Jiā, and Méi suffered especially severe flood damage,
yet the Jīng River did not overflow.
Zhèng Jūnxióng
Zhèng Jūnxióng was the prefect of Suízhōu.
One evening,
he suddenly saw several thousand soldiers
on the eastern bank of the river,
with banners, spears, and armor,
the figures clamoring noisily,
no different from a marching army.
He did not dare to question them,
only maintaining vigilance.
Before dawn,
he secretly sent scouts to investigate.
The large army had already departed,
leaving only three or five men behind.
The scouts asked them,
and they replied:
"We are the river... gods.
For several years, the region has been unsettled,
so we moved into the gorges.
Now that peace has returned near and far,
we are going back to the river plains."
Looking again,
there were traces of encampments and fire pits,
each detail verifiable.
The Temple of Zhōnglí Wáng
In Táng Village on the eastern bank of Suízhōu,
it is said
that long ago, a man
wearing large sleeves
and an ancient cap and headcloth
stood by the side of the road.
He said to the villagers:
"I am King Zhōnglí.
My former temple was located over ten lǐ downstream,
but it was damaged by the water.
Now my statue has drifted upstream and stopped here,
and it is about to arrive.
You may build a temple for me here."
The villagers went to the river to look,
and found a wooden figure,
several chǐ tall.
They then built a temple at the place where they had seen him,
calling it the Táng Village deity.
To this day, prayers and requests made there are answered.
Some say
that when first seen, he appeared like a Daoist priest.
The Temple of Pángǔ
In Guǎngdū County, there is a temple to Pángǔ Sānláng,
which is quite efficacious.
If commoners passing the gate
show even slight disrespect,
they are often beaten,
or stumble and fall on the road.
A county resident named Yáng Zhīyù,
who had received the Zhèngyī Míngwēi register,
was one night heavily drunk
and about to return home.
The road was long, the moon was dark,
and he had no companion for the journey home.
He wished for divine power
to show him the way back.
Suddenly, a torch flame
emerged from the temple gate
and led the way ahead to his home.
For over twenty lǐ,
though the path was narrow,
with bridges and woven paths,
he did not stumble or fall,
and then the torch flame was seen no more.
The local villagers were especially astonished.
The Temple of Dí Rénjié
The temple of Dí Rénjié in the southern outer city of Wèizhōu
is a temple erected during his lifetime.
During Empress Wǔ Zétiān's reign,
Dí Rénjié served as prefect of Wèizhōu
and implemented benevolent governance.
The officials and people erected a temple in his honor while he was alive.
After he entered the court in the capital,
the men and women of Wèizhōu
would, at the start of each month,
go to the temple to make offerings of wine.
Dí Rénjié was attending court one day,
and on that day he also appeared flushed as if drunk.
The Empress had long known that Dí Rénjié originally did not drink alcohol.
She questioned him,
and he related the matter in full.
The Empress sent someone to verify,
and then believed it.
When Zhuāngzōng observed and dominated Héshuò,
someone once lay drunk beneath the temple corridor.
He woke at midnight.
He saw a person below the hall steps,
bowing respectfully and consulting on a matter.
Someone in the hall asked him,
and he replied:
"I have received orders to requisition ten thousand men from Wèizhōu."
The voice in the hall said:
"This prefecture is depleted and exhausted,
with frequent disasters and calamities.
Transfer it elsewhere."
The man said:
"Understood.
I request to go and report this."
He then left.
After a short while he returned,
and said:
"The order has already been transferred to Zhènzhōu."
When he finished speaking, he vanished.
That year,
Zhuāngzōng divided his troops to attack Zhènzhōu.
When the city was finally taken,
the casualties on both sides were very numerous.
The Wife of the Gé Family
East of Yǎnzhōu, in Dōngchāo Village, there is a pavilion by the Sì River,
and below the pavilion is a temple to Tiānqí Wáng.
Within it is a shrine to a deity called Sānláng Jūn.
The shamans say
he is the beloved son of Tiānqí Wáng,
and his spirit is extremely potent and strange.
It is passed down that below Mount Dàizōng,
woodcutters' children and cowherds
sometimes encounter feather-clad hunters,
with splendid riders and attendants,
resembling
feudal lords or kings—
this is that very deity.
The people of Lǔ fear and revere him
even more than Tiānqí Wáng.
During the Later Liáng dynasty,
Gě Zhōu was stationed in Yǎnzhōu as military commissioner.
Once, he took all the women of his household to stroll at the Sì River Pavilion,
and they proceeded to the deity's temple.
Gě Zhōu had a twelfth son,
whose wife was beautiful in appearance and demeanor.
She bowed before Sānláng Jūn,
gazed intently, and withdrew.
Soon after, she fell ill with heart pain,
collapsed to the ground, and lay unconscious for a long time.
The whole clan was greatly alarmed,
and immediately prayed to the deity.
After a while, she recovered.
From then on, her spirit and mood were abnormal;
in dreams and trances she was vague and distracted,
and she often encountered the deity.
Her family, afraid,
sent the wife to the Eastern Capital to avoid him.
Not long after,
the deity also arrived there,
and said to the woman:
"I have searched for you for a long time,
and now we meet again."
After that, he came every other night.
Whenever the deity was about to arrive,
the woman would first stretch, yawn, and sneeze,
and say to her attendants:
"He has already come."
She would then rise and enter the curtains.
The attendants, pressing their ears close to listen,
would hear private whispers and laughter,
and after a while he would leave.
This became the regular routine.
Her husband, fearing the deity,
ultimately did not dare to share the bed with his wife.
After a long time, the woman died.
Mǎ Xīshēng
In Húnán, Mǎ Xīshēng
succeeded his father's position.
For consecutive years there was severe drought,
and prayers brought no response.
So he sealed off the Temple of the Heavenly King of the Southern Peak,
as well as all shrines within his territory.
Still, no rain came.
His elder brother, Xīzhèn,
went to admonish him,
and they drank wine until midnight before he left.
Hearing clamor in the front hall,
Xīshēng repeatedly summoned Xīzhèn back inside.
They saw Xīshēng standing upside down under the steps,
his clothes not draped properly,
his head already shattered.
He ordered his trusted aides to carry him up,
covering his head with silk.
The next day, mourning was announced,
and his younger brother Xīfàn succeeded to the position.
Earlier, the general Zhōu Dá,
upon returning from the Southern Peak,
saw in the mist and clouds over the river,
someone seizing Xīshēng and taking him away,
but he kept it secret and dared not speak of it.
That night, something like a black curtain
suddenly entered the empty hall,
and he died instantly.
Páng Shì
In the third year of the Chángxīng era of the Táng dynasty,
the presented scholar Páng Shì
pursued his studies beside the Sōngyáng Temple,
building a hut by the water to live in.
One day,
he went to the front village in the morning and had not yet returned.
In the hut was only Xuē Shēng,
a man from Dōngjùn,
young and pure-hearted,
who studied under Shì.
Rising in the morning,
he finished washing by the stream,
when he saw in the woods southeast of the hut,
five people,
all wearing star crowns and rainbow robes,
or garments with wide sleeves,
each in a different color,
with divine and handsome appearances,
clear and resonant voices,
piercing gazes,
and a fragrance perceptible from over ten paces away.
Xuē Shēng, astonished,
bowed to them all.
They asked Xuē:
"Who are you?"
Shēng answered in detail.
They asked again:
"Can you come with us?"
Xuē declined, citing his elderly parents,
hoping to do so another day.
They said:
"Since you will not go,
we shall write on your back to mark it."
They then had him bare his back.
He only felt a breeze-like sensation on his back,
and when the writing was done,
they retreated into the woods,
and the place vanished.
Shortly after, Páng Shì arrived,
and Xuē recounted everything,
showing him his back.
They saw a line of characters written in vermilion,
the script mixed with seal and ancient styles,
only two characters somewhat resembling the official script of noblemen,
the rest unrecognizable.
Xuē Shēng also touched them with his hand,
and several characters smudged and broke,
the color fresh as blood.
After several days,
the fragrance still had not faded.
Later, Páng Shì passed the imperial examinations,
and was appointed magistrate of Lèxiāng County,
but was killed by the rebel commander Ān Cóngjìn.
Xuē's son soon returned to Huátái,
and died at home.
Qīngtài Sovereign
The Táng Qīngtài Sovereign
was the elder brother of Jìn Gāozǔ's wife.
When Míngzōng first served as a general in Tàiyuán,
both sovereigns held low military ranks.
While playing polo,
they entered the temple of Zhào Xiāngzǐ,
and both saw the clay statues stepping aside from their positions to stand,
which greatly surprised them,
and they secretly felt自负.
When Míngzōng achieved great merit,
they often felt anxious and fearful.
The two sovereigns said:
"Can Zhào Xiāngzǐ ultimately bring us fortune?"
Afterwards, the two sovereigns successively enjoyed great positions.
Púyè Slope
In the year Yǐwèi,
the Khitan occupied Héshuò,
and the Jìn army resisted at Chányuān.
The land was in turmoil,
exhausted from warfare.
The Hanlin Academician Wáng Rényù
was sent on a mission to Féngyì,
passing through Zhèng on the way,
and crossed Púyè Slope.
He saw local people and women from military camps
crowding the roads,
all holding small colorful flags,
which they stuck into the slope,
countless in number.
Inquiring with the residents,
they all said:
"The people of Zhèng have been dreaming of Duke Wèi Lǐ, who said:
'Please make many banners and flags,
and place them on the slope.
I have gathered countless soldiers,
to eradicate the barbarian invaders for the Central Plains,
but what we lack are banners.'
That is why each household separately offered these flags."
At first, he did not believe it,
considering it superstitious talk,
but indeed, within a month,
they defeated the northern invaders.
Upon his return from the mission,
passing the slope again,
he had his servant go down the road,
to check among the grass,
and many still remained.
Lǐ Yǒng's Son
Shǔ's Dàlǐ Shǎoqīng Lǐ Yǒng
once returned to his villa in Píchéng.
Crossing a bridge,
he saw an infant,
wrapped in banana leaves.
Yǒng pitied its unusual appearance,
and nurtured it as his son.
After six or seven years,
he could write,
was good at conversation and laughter,
and his parents doted on him,
more than their own biological children.
By age twelve,
even unseen classics and histories,
he read as if long familiar,
and people called him divinely intelligent.
Once, while reading alone in a room,
his parents secretly peeked at him,
and saw a person holding a register,
with two童子 assisting to present it,
and their son wrote several lines in large characters,
then handed it back and it left.
His parents found it strange.
The next day,
while standing by in attendance,
Yǒng gently said to him:
"Last night, I secretly saw something.
Are you perhaps judging matters of the underworld?"
He said:
"Yes."
Further questions were met only with bows and no answers.
Yǒng said:
"The underworld and the human world
have different affairs and intentions.
I do not wish to press you,
you should take good care."
The son bowed again.
Six years later,
one morning he told his parents:
"I was only destined to be the son of the Shǎoqīng and his wife for eighteen years,
now the matter is concluded.
Tomorrow at the shēn hour,
I shall return to the underworld."
He wept for a long time,
and his parents also shed tears.
Yǒng asked:
"To what office will I rise?"
He answered:
"Only to Dàlǐ Shǎoqīng."
Indeed, the next day at the shēn hour,
his son died,
so Yǒng had the intention to retire.
Not long after,
he was dismissed due to an incident.
Qiáo Yìjùn
In Luójiāng County, there was a Daoist priest named Qiáo Yìjùn,
in the prime of his life.
Suddenly, he dreamed that the Lord of Mount Tài was summoning him,
bestowing upon him a yellow edict,
appointing him as a staff officer.
By day, he returned to the world of the living;
by night, he went to the underworld court.
This continued for over twenty years.
He often said that among the living, there were those whose allotted lifespan had not yet ended but who had committed evil deeds;
their living souls were summoned and flogged,
and the illness or poverty and begging of such persons in the world of the living were the result.
When he went and saw relatives or villagers being flogged,
the next morning he would go to visit them,
and it always proved true.
Yet he constantly wished to be released from this duty.
Suddenly, while in the underworld, he encountered a Daoist priest,
who did not give his name,
and said to him:
"Why do you not offer fine incense?
By day,
in the world of the living, appeal to the Southern Star and Northern Pole,
and you will surely be released."
Yìjùn followed this and devoutly prayed.
Suddenly, the Lord of Mount Tài recalled the yellow edict,
and from then on he was freed.
He then devoted himself to Daoist practice and the study of the Yìjīng,
living to over eighty years of age.
Liú Qiào
In the year Xīnyǒu,
Liú Qiào, the registrar of Jīnshuǐ,
while traveling on Yúndǐng Mountain,
saw in a mountain temple a lavishly decorated hall,
containing a clay statue,
dressed in red robes and seated on a saddle.
Qiào was surprised by this,
and questioned the mountain's master, Zhāo Nè, about it.
Zhāo Nè said:
"For three consecutive nights, I dreamed of the king,
who said that he had recently appointed a judge,
and that a hall should be set up,
with a red-robed official sculpted and worshipped.
That is why this was made."
Qiào did not believe it.
The following year, when his term of office ended,
he returned to Chéngdū,
and met the Vice Director of the Bureau of Honors, Sūn Féngjí.
He told him the story,
and Féngjí said:
"Recently, when Ān Zhònggǔ was on his deathbed,
he said to his family:
'The king of Yúndǐng Mountain has already prepared letters, horses, and betrothal gifts,
appointing me as judge.'
As soon as he finished speaking,
he sat upright and passed away."
An Elder of Yuánzhōu
In a village of Yuánzhōu, there was an old man,
cautious and honest by nature,
respected by the local community,
and his family was also quite wealthy.
One day, a youth in purple robes,
with a grand carriage and attendants,
came to his home seeking food.
The old man immediately invited him in,
provided a lavish meal,
and served all his followers as well.
The old man waited on him as he ate,
and thought to himself: when high officials or imperial envoys travel through the county,
there should be a place for them to rest,
but who is this person?
His expression showed deep suspicion.
The youth noticed this,
and said to him:
"You doubt me;
I can no longer hide it from you.
I am the god of Yǎngshān."
The old man, trembling with fear, bowed twice,
and said:
"The god of Yǎngshān is daily sated with sacrifices;
why then do you seek food?"
The god said:
"Whenever people sacrifice to me,
they all seek blessings from me.
For those whose strength I cannot grant blessings to,
or those who are not worthy to receive blessings,
I dare not accept their offerings.
Because you are a virtuous elder,
I have come to you seeking food."
After eating,
he bid farewell and left,
and then vanished.
Zhū Tíngyǔ
Zhū Tíngyǔ, a eunuch of Jiāngnán,
said that his relative, while sailing on the sea, encountered a storm,
and the boat was on the verge of capsizing several times.
The sea pilot said:
"The sea god desires something.
Quickly take what is loaded on the boat,
and throw it into the water."
When almost everything was gone,
a woman in yellow robes appeared,
of peerless beauty,
approaching by boat,
with four attendants in black clothes rowing the boat,
all with red hair and boar-like tusks,
their appearance extremely fearsome.
The woman came aboard,
and asked if there was a fine hairpiece,
which could be given to her.
The man, in panic and terror,
could not remember,
and only said:
"Everything is already gone."
The woman said:
"It is hanging on the wall at the back of the boat,
inside a box."
Following her words, they found it.
On the roof of the boat cabin, there was dried meat,
which the woman took to feed the four attendants.
Looking at her hands,
they were like black claws.
She took the hairpiece and left,
and the boat then reached safety.
Tíngyǔ also said
that another relative of his, traveling from Jiāngxī to Guǎnglíng,
brought along an eleven-year-old child.
When they reached Mǎdāng and moored,
they went ashore to enjoy the evening view.
Upon returning to the boat,
the child was missing.
They searched everywhere,
and found him in a dense forest,
already as if stupefied.
The next day,
he was able to speak.
He said:
"I was summoned by someone,
who taught me something."
Then he blew on his fingers and gave a long whistle,
and dozens to hundreds of mountain birds,
responding to the sound, arrived,
with strange and unusual plumage,
which no one could recognize.
From then on, as they sailed eastward,
whenever he whistled,
flocks of birds would surely come.
When they reached Báishā,
he no longer dared to do it.
They sought out physicians and shamans to treat him,
and only after a long time was he cured.
Monk Dé Lín
The monk Dé Lín from Western Zhèjiāng,
in his youth traveled to Shūzhōu,
and by the roadside saw a man
carrying a hoe to clear a square zhang of land.
For tens of li around, no dwellings were in sight.
He asked him about it,
and the man replied:
"Some time ago, I was traveling from Shū to Tóngchéng.
Upon reaching this place, I suddenly contracted malaria,
and could not go on,
so I lay down in the grass.
When I gradually regained consciousness,
it was already dusk.
Looking around in all directions, there was no sign of human habitation,
only the roars of tigers and leopards.
I thought for certain I would die.
Suddenly, there was a man
with attendants like a great general,
who dismounted here.
He sat on a folding chair.
After a long while,
he summoned two soldiers and said:
'Guard this man well,
and tomorrow escort him to the foot of Tóngchéng County.'
Then he mounted his horse and left,
vanishing in an instant,
leaving only the two soldiers behind.
I forced myself up and asked them,
and they replied:
'This is General Máo.
He often goes out at night to hunt tigers,
and was worried you might be harmed,
so he ordered us to protect you.'
I wanted to ask more,
but exhausted, I lay down again.
When I awoke,
the sun was already up.
The two soldiers were no longer to be seen,
so I got up and walked on,
feeling remarkably light and vigorous,
as if I had never been ill.
Upon reaching Tóngchéng,
my illness soon healed.
Therefore, at the place where I had this encounter,
I built a shrine to worship him."
Dé Lín went up to Shūzhōu for ten years,
and upon his return,
he found that villages everywhere had erected shrines to General Máo."
Sīmǎ Zhèngyí
Sīmǎ Zhèngyí,
in his early days, was a minor official.
While traveling on the road to Lìshuǐ,
still far from the next inn,
he grew very hungry and thirsty,
and was quite worried about it.
Suddenly, he came upon several newly built thatched inns,
where a lone woman welcomed guests,
and provided food and drink for him,
which was very abundant and clean.
Tiānyí thanked her,
and the woman said:
"When you reach the capital,
if there is good face powder and rouge,
it would be kind of you to bring me some as a gift."
Zhèngyí promised.
Upon arriving at Jiànyè,
he met an acquaintance who was going to Lìshuǐ,
so he bought powder and rouge and had them delivered to her.
He gave a detailed account of the location,
but when the acquaintance arrived,
the inn was no longer there,
only a goddess temple.
So he left the gifts there and departed.
Zhèngyí later became the magistrate of Lìshuǐ,
and according to legend,
people often encountered her,
though the truth of it is unknown.
Liú Xuān
In the year of Wùyín,
the Wú army campaigned against Yuè,
and was defeated at Lín'ān.
The deputy general Liú Xuān was severely wounded,
and lay among the dead.
When night fell,
several officials appeared,
holding registers,
and examined the dead one by one.
When they reached Xuān,
they helped him up, looked at him, and said:
"This fellow is not one of them."
They led him out over ten paces,
placed him by the roadside, and left.
The next day, when the enemy retreated,
Xuān was able to return.
Xuān was plump and pale like a gourd;
initially, he lay face down on the ground,
and a Yuè man cut flesh from his buttocks,
but Xuān dared not move.
Later, the wound healed,
but the flesh did not grow back,
leaving his buttocks slightly lopsided.
He died over ten years later.
Huáng Lǔ
Xú Sānhuì served as the Records Officer of Fǔzhōu,
and under him was a laborer named Huáng Lǔ,
a local man from the commandery.
He was young,
quite fair-skinned,
and had parents in his hometown.
Every few months, he would request leave to return home,
staying for about ten days before coming back.
One day,
he went home and did not return for over a month.
Sānhuì sent a clerk to his home to summon him.
His family said:
"He has not returned for a long time."
So they searched for him far and wide.
Another month passed,
and he was seen deep in the mountains,
wearing yellow clothes and straw sandals,
roaming with a slingshot.
With several other youths,
all similarly dressed.
They tried to capture him but failed.
Huáng Lǔ's family was wealthy,
so they hired many people,
who hid in the grass to wait for him.
After several days,
they finally captured him,
while the other youths all fled.
After bringing him back,
they asked him for the reason,
and he said:
"In the mountains, there is a family named Shí,
whose household is as grand as that of a prince.
They took me as their son-in-law."
He said nothing more.
After staying for a few days,
he disappeared again,
and they found him once more in the mountains.
This happened three times.
One day, he finally left,
and was never seen again.
They searched for the Shí family's residence,
but could not find it.
This mountain was a place where people from Línchuān quarried stone,
likely the abode of the stone spirit.
Zhāng Yán
Zhāng Yán
served successively as county magistrate,
and was praised for his integrity and uprightness.
Later, he became the magistrate of Péngzé,
and upon arriving at the county residence,
he found a shrine behind the main hall.
In front of the shrine were large trees forming a grove,
where crows and kites,
and wild birds
nested in flocks above,
and their droppings accumulated in the hall.
People feared the deity,
so no one dared to interfere.
Yán was greatly
disgusted by this,
and had a shaman pray to the deity, saying:
"As the local earth deity,
you should keep the county office clean,
to properly accommodate its residents.
How can you allow such filth and stench?
Within three days,
you must drive away all the birds.
Otherwise,
I will burn down the shrine and cut down the trees!"
After two days,
several large eagles
swooped down fiercely,
destroying all the nests.
The next day, heavy rain fell.
All the filth was washed clean.
From then on, the residence remained clean.
Guō Hòu
Lǐ Zōng was the prefect of Shūzhōu,
and he rebuilt the Kāiyuán Temple.
When the workers first gathered,
they were about to dredge an abandoned well.
The well,
"Bandits attacked the capital,
and the world fell into chaos.
The monks coveted my travel funds,
killed me, and threw me into this well.
Now my bones are here.
Please inform Lord Lǐ for me,
and I hope he will bury me,
and not abandon me."
The supervisor reported this to Zōng,
and the next day, he personally went to the well,
ordered it to be excavated,
and indeed found the bones.
He immediately prepared burial clothes, quilts, and a coffin,
held a sacrificial ceremony, and buried them.
On the day of the burial,
the guard fell to the ground again.
The ghost spoke,
Saying:
"Thank Lord Lǐ for me.
My lonely soul has been here
for thirty years.
Thanks to your kindness,
the local deities of the Nine Provinces
have now appointed me as the local earth god,
and I will receive offerings here."
The temple has worshipped him ever since.
Xúnyáng County Clerk
In the year Gēngyín,
Xú Zhījiàn, the military governor of Jiāngxī,
donated a million coins to the Messenger Temple on Lúshān.
The magistrate of Xúnyáng sent a clerk to oversee the matter.
This clerk once entered the city,
summoned a painter to go with him,
and the painter carried pigments and various materials, following him.
As soon as they left the city,
the clerk became dazed as if drunk,
took off his belt and threw it on the ground.
The painter thought he was drunk,
And followed him.
After a short while,
he took off his clothes and discarded his hat.
By the time they reached the mountain,
he was almost naked.
In the stream near the temple,
there was a soldier,
dressed in black,
with a white leather apron.
When the clerk arrived,
he seized him.
The painter tried to save him, saying:
"This man is drunk."
The soldier angrily said:
"Jumbled and confused,
who can understand?"
He captured him anyway,
and made him sit in the water.
The painter realized he was not human,
ran to the temple to inform others.
They rushed to look,
the soldier had already disappeared,
but the clerk was still sitting in the water,
already dead.
When they checked the disbursement records,
he had already embezzled more than half.
Jìnshì Xiè Yuè witnessed this personally.
Zhū Yuánjí
Zhū Yuánjí, the magistrate of Wūjiāng County,
said that someone he knew was boating to Cǎishí,
when they encountered a storm.
Several boats traveling together sank,
and after drowning,
he no longer saw water,
but a road like in the human world.
Someone drove him eastward,
and they arrived at the foot of a mountain on the eastern shore,
where there was a large government office.
Outside the gate, broken ship planks and wood were piled up like hills,
and many people were transporting the belongings of the drowned into a warehouse.
Entering the gate,
there was an official in the hall,
who summoned all the drowned,
and examined them against a register.
When it was his turn, he alone was told:
"This person should not have come,
send him back."
The clerk immediately led him away,
and they returned to the boat's location.
The belongings in the boat
were also returned to him.
In a daze, unaware of what was happening,
he emerged from the water,
and found himself on the sand of the western shore.
The entire boat was intact,
and nothing was wet.
Wine Seller Wáng
Behind the government office of Jiāngníng County in Jiànkāng,
there was a wine seller named Wáng,
known for his fairness and honesty.
In the year Guǐmǎo,
on the night of the sixteenth day of the second month,
the shopkeeper was about to close the outer door,
when suddenly several men in red clothes,
with numerous servants and horses,
abruptly arrived in front of the door,
and shouted:
"Open the door,
we will rest here for a while."
The shopkeeper hurriedly informed the owner.
When the owner came out to welcome them,
they had already taken their seats.
The owner then prepared ample wine and food,
and also rewarded the attendants,
for which the guests thanked him profusely.
After a while,
a servant brought hundreds of thousands of feet of rope,
and another brought hundreds of wooden stakes,
and stepped forward to report:
"Please set up the enclosure."
The man in purple agreed.
They went out,
drove the stakes into the ground,
tied the ropes to them,
and enclosed all the houses in the neighborhood.
After a long time, they reported the task completed,
and the man in purple stood up and went outside.
An attendant reported:
"This shop is also within the enclosure."
The man in purple said to the others:
"The host treated us very generously,
can we exempt this shop?"
They all said:
"Just one family,
why not?"
He immediately ordered the stakes moved,
placing the shop outside the enclosure.
Turning to the owner, he said:
"This is our repayment."
Then they left,
vanishing in an instant.
Looking back at the ropes and stakes,
they had already disappeared.
Soon after, patrol officer Ōuyáng Jìn was making his night rounds,
and arrived in front of the shop.
He asked why the door was open so late at night,
and why the lamps and candles were not extinguished.
The owner recounted everything he had seen,
but Jìn did not believe him.
He arrested him and threw him in prison,
intending to charge him with spreading rumors.
Two days later,
a great fire broke out in Jiànkāng,
from the west of Zhūquè Bridge to Fèngtáishān,
and nearly all the residents' homes were burned to ashes.
All the neighbors around this shop were reduced to rubble,
but the Wáng family alone was spared.
Bào Huí
Bào Huí
once went deep into the mountains to hunt,
and saw a young man,
lying naked under a large tree,
with hair trailing on the ground.
Huí was about to shoot him,
when the young man said:
"I am the mountain god,
and could not avoid you in time.
Do not kill me,
and I can bring you wealth and honor."
Huí stabbed his mouth with a blade,
and the blood flowed backward,
so he killed him.
Not long after, Huí died.
Liú Hào
Liú Hào, the Minister of the Imperial Clan of the Han dynasty,
suddenly dreamed of a person
holding a document in hand,
resembling an underworld official.
Thinking that he knew about human fate and fortune,
Hào questioned him,
hoping to learn about his own future prospects of poverty or success.
The official said:
"You will serve as the assistant to the Prince of Qí,
and later become the Minister of the Imperial Clan."
Hào, considering his own high official rank,
was displeased at the thought of serving as an official in a prince's residence.
Upon waking from the dream,
he remembered it vividly
and spoke of it to relatives and friends.
Later, while on a mission to Wúyuè,
he passed through Yùnzhōu,
and suddenly fell ill at the official lodge.
In his delirium, he recalled the dream of serving as the assistant to the Prince of Qí,
fearing it referred to the Prince of Tàishān,
the divine Prince of Qí.
He then ordered an attendant to go to the temple,
relate the dream,
and burn incense while casting divination blocks to seek confirmation.
The first cast indeed confirmed it.
The Minister, with family matters unresolved,
pleaded with the deity again,
asking to postpone until after returning from crossing the sea,
so he could then comply.
Repeated casts yielded no approval,
and he soon died at the postal station.
Cuī Liànshī
Cuī Liànshī, a female Daoist from Jìnzhōu,
her name forgotten,
and it is unknown which Daoist path she followed.
She kept a carriage,
hiring it out to support herself.
Occasionally, she performed small hidden acts of merit,
unnoticed by others.
One day,
the carriage ran over and killed a child on the road.
The child's parents filed a complaint with the authorities,
who arrested the carriage driver
and imprisoned him.
They intended to use his ox and carriage to compensate the child's family,
but the driver said:
"These items were rented from Cuī Liànshī."
The authorities summoned Liànshī
and also detained her.
The prefect, Luán Yuánfú,
dreamed at night of the underworld official Cuī, who said:
"Cuī Liànshī is my niece.
For what crime is she detained?"
Upon waking from the dream,
he summoned Liànshī
and told her the words from the dream.
Liànshī replied:
"Although I share the surname Cuī,
I do not know which elder relative this refers to."
Soon after, the dead child revived.
Emperor Gāozǔ of the Zhōu dynasty heard of this and found it extraordinary,
summoning Cuī Liànshī to the capital,
and selecting Daoist priests
to go to Jìnzhōu's Zǐjí Palace to perform rituals.
Líshān Temple
Líshān Temple in Jiànzhōu.
Local people say
it is the temple of the former chancellor Lǐ Huí.
Huí was demoted to the post of prefect of Jiànzhōu
and later died in Línchuān.
On the night of his death,
the people of Jiàn'ān all dreamed of Huí riding a white horse
into Líshān.
When news of his death arrived,
they erected a shrine there.
It is widely believed to be efficacious.
When Wáng Yánzhèng was in Jiàn'ān,
he had a conflict with Fúzhōu
and sent his general, a certain Wú,
to lead troops toward Jìn'ān.
Wú had newly forged a sword,
very sharp.
Before departing,
he took the sword to pray at Líshān Temple,
saying:
"I vow with this
sword
to personally kill a thousand people."
That night,
he dreamed of someone telling him:
"One should not make wicked vows.
I will protect you,
ensuring you do not die by another's hand."
After being defeated in battle,
his troops scattered in all directions.
As pursuing troops were about to catch up,
Wú, believing escape impossible,
used this sword to slit his own throat and die.
Wú Yántáo
In Guǎnglíng, there was a bean granary official named Wú Yántáo.
His younger brother had already reached the age of capping,
and he was about to seek a wife for him.
In the neighborhood, there was an old matchmaking woman
who had long been entrusted with tasks by the Wú family.
One day,
someone came to her door and said:
"The household of Minister Zhāng Sīkōng has sent me to summon you."
She followed him and went.
To the southeast of Zhèngshèng Temple,
there was a residence that was very grand and imposing.
The old woman said:
"I have never heard of a Lord Zhāng living here."
The person replied:
"The lord died in the battle of Lín'ān.
That is why few people know about him."
After a while,
The furnishings in the house were resplendent,
like those of a prince or noble family.
She saw an old lady,
who said she was the lady of the county,
and took a seat.
After a short while,
her daughter also came out.
The old lady said to the matchmaker:
"I heard that you are seeking a marriage for the Wú family.
I wish to have this daughter serve him."
The matchmaker said:
"The Wú family are minor officials from a poor household.
How could they be worthy of marrying a noble family?"
The daughter then spoke for herself,
She said:
"I have an elderly mother.
There are no brothers.
The family estate is large,
and matters must be entrusted to a good person.
I have heard that the Wú family's son is filial and diligent, worthy of service.
Why would I seek a high-ranking family?"
The matchmaker said:
"Very well,
I will ask them."
She returned and told Yántáo,
who found it strange.
He did not dare to speak of it.
A few days later,
suddenly several carriages arrived,
coming to the matchmaker's house.
It was the Zhāng family's daughter, along with two old maidservants.
They summoned Yántáo's wife to the gathering,
and prepared a lavish feast of food and drink,
all provided by the Zhāng family.
The daughter herself discussed the marriage proposal.
Yántáo's wife thought to herself,
although this girl was extremely beautiful,
she seemed to be over thirty years old.
Her young brother-in-law was much younger,
and he might not be pleased.
The girl immediately said:
"Husband and wife are all predestined.
If fate decrees a match,
what does age matter?"
Yántáo's wife was startled
and dared not say more.
The girl then brought out two bolts of red and white silk, saying:
"Take these as gifts.
There are many other presents as well."
By evening,
she invited the matchmaker to return with her to their home,
where she stayed for several nights.
She said to the matchmaker:
"My family is extremely wealthy,
but people do not know it.
One day, it will all belong to Wú Láng."
In the room, there were three large cabinets,
reaching up to the ceiling.
She opened them to show her.
One cabinet was filled with gold,
the second with silver.
She then pointed to the ground and said:
"There is money buried here."
She ordered it to be dug up,
and after digging a little over a foot deep,
they saw coins piled up densely.
They then went to the outer hall,
where a white horse with a red mane was tethered in the courtyard,
and beside it was a pig.
She said:
"These are all gifts."
To the west of the hall, there was also a large workshop,
fully equipped with tools for various crafts.
She said:
"This is also for making gifts."
At night, as they went to sleep,
they heard the pig as if startled,
and she called to the maidservants:
"This pig should not be left outside.
It must have been bitten by a snake."
The matchmaker said:
"Do snakes eat pigs?"
The girl replied:
"They are common here."
They then took candles to look,
and indeed saw a large red snake
emerge from the ground,
coil around the pig,
and then go back into the ground.
They rescued the pig, and it was spared.
The next day,
just as they were about to bid farewell to the matchmaker,
she suddenly summoned two maidservants in blue,
who stood by her side.
She said to the matchmaker:
"I have some business to attend to nearby.
I will return shortly."
She then rose into the air with the maidservants and flew away,
to the matchmaker's great astonishment.
Her mother said:
"My daughter has gone to heaven temporarily for accounting matters.
Just sit and wait,
do not worry."
After about the time it takes to eat a meal,
they saw her return from outside,
slightly smelling of wine.
She said:
"The immortals kept me to drink,
but since the matchmaker is here,
I firmly declined and returned."
The wife returned home,
Even more astonished and afraid, she dared not speak of it.
Over a month later,
the matchmaker was summoned again.
The lady of the county was critically ill,
and by the time she arrived,
the mother had already passed away.
The matchmaker attended the funeral,
which was held in the Xú family village north of Yángzǐ County.
The entire household gathered for the occasion.
The Xú family had a daughter,
about ten years old.
The Zhāng family's daughter patted her and said:
"This girl has the appearance of fortune.
She will become the wife of a military general in Huáiběi,
Treat her well."
After the burial,
she again gave gifts to the matchmaker.
The entire family then moved south,
and no one knew where they went.
The marriage proposal,
Ultimately did not come to pass.
The matchmaker returned
and visited their former residence,
but found only a few ordinary houses.
She asked the villagers,
and they said:
"They have lived here for a long time.
It is said to be the residence of Minister Zhāng Sīkōng,
but no one knows for sure."
Ten years later,
Guǎnglíng fell into chaos,
and Wú's younger brother returned to Jiànyè,
ultimately unharmed.
Yúguāng Shrine
In the third year of the Chūpíng era of Emperor Líng of Hàn,
the Luǒyóu Pavilion was built.
During the height of summer, to escape the heat,
they would drink and feast through the long nights until drunk,
losing track of the dawn.
A palace attendant would throw a giant candle onto the palace steps,
and only then would the emperor awaken with a start.
When Dǒng Zhuó sacked the capital,
he burned down the pavilion.
By the Xiánxī era of Wèi,
the place where the candle was thrown
would glow like a star in the dark of night.
People of the time considered it divine light
and built a shrine there,
naming it the "Yúguāng Shrine,"
to pray for blessings.
By the end of Emperor Míng's reign,
it gradually fell into disuse.
Shànfù Temple
At the Shítíng Dài in Kuàijī,
there was a large maple tree,
whose interior had rotted hollow.
Whenever it rained,
water would fill it.
A traveling merchant carrying live catfish arrived here,
and would release one into the hollow tree.
The villagers saw this,
and since catfish were not creatures of trees,
they all considered it divine.
They then built a shrine by the tree,
slaughtered animals for sacrifices,
which never ceased for a day,
calling it the Shrine of the Catfish Father.
Whether one prayed sincerely or acted disrespectfully,
fortune or misfortune would immediately follow.
Later, the merchant returned,
laughed heartily,
then sought the catfish, made a stew, and ate it,
and its divine power thus ended.
Lord Bào
In the past, there was a man in Rǔnán
who set a rope snare in his field
to catch deer.
Before the owner noticed,
a passerby saw it,
and thus secretly took the deer away.
Still feeling uneasy about taking it without waiting for the owner,
and having a salted fish,
he placed one in the snare and left.
The original owner came,
found the salted fish in the snare,
found it strange and considered it divine,
not daring to take it home.
Thereupon, the village collectively built a house and established a shrine,
naming it Lord Bào.
Later, more and more people came to worship it,
with red pillars and painted rafters,
and the sounds of bells and drums never ceased.
If a sick person occasionally recovered,
it was said the deity was responsible.
Travelers passing by
all visited the shrine.
After seven or eight years had passed,
the owner of the salted fish later passed by the shrine,
and asked about its origin.
People explained the whole story to him.
He then said:
"This is just my salted fish,
what divinity does it have?"
And so it ceased.
Zhāng Zhù
There was a man from Nándùn named Zhāng Zhù,
who was plowing in his field.
While planting grain,
he saw a plum pit,
and intending to take it home,
he dug it up,
wrapped its roots in damp soil,
placed it in a hollow mulberry tree,
and then forgot to retrieve it.
Zhāng Zhù later took a distant post,
and was not present.
Afterwards, people from the village saw a plum tree suddenly growing from the mulberry,
and called it divine.
Someone with sore eyes,
resting in the shade of this mulberry tree,
prayed to it,
saying, "If Lord Lǐ can cure my eyes,
I will offer a piglet in thanks."
His eyes happened to get better,
so he killed the piglet and sacrificed it.
The story spread with exaggeration,
and soon it was said this tree could make the blind see.
From near and far, people flocked together,
coming in turn to seek blessings.
Beneath it, carriages and horses were constantly packed,
with wine and meat flowing abundantly.
This went on for several years.
Zhāng Zhù, having left his post, returned,
saw this,
and said:
"This is just the plum pit I placed here long ago,
what divinity does it have?"
He then chopped it down.
The Stone Man with Cakes
Also, in Rǔyáng, there was a Péng family tomb,
near the main road,
at the tomb entrance stood a stone figure.
An old farming woman went to the market,
bought several rice cakes and was returning.
The weather was hot,
so she passed by and rested in the shade under a tree at the Péng tomb entrance,
and placed the cakes she had bought
temporarily on the stone figure's head.
When she left,
she forgot to take them.
Later passersby saw cakes on the stone figure's head,
sought answers and asked about it.
Someone joked, saying:
"This stone figure is divine,
it can cure illness.
Those who recover bring cakes to thank it."
This story was passed around,
and it was said:
"Those with headaches,
rub the stone figure's head.
Those with stomachaches,
rub the stone figure's stomach,
and also rub your own,
and none fail to recover."
Thus, people came from a thousand *li* to seek the stone figure for cures.
At first they prepared chickens and piglets,
later using cattle and sheep,
erected canopies and tents,
with music never ceasing.
This went on for several years.
The old woman who had forgotten the cakes heard of this,
and explained it to people,
after which no one went anymore.
The Ancient Tomb West of Luò
West of Luò there was an ancient tomb,
breached and ruined for a long time,
water filled the tomb,
containing much lime solution.
It was good for treating sores.
In summer, travelers
suffering from sores and feverish discomfort,
seeing the clear, good water in this tomb,
would wash themselves in it,
and their sores happened to heal.
Thereupon, various sick people heard of this,
and all went to wash themselves.
Further, some drank it to treat internal ailments.
People living near the tomb,
conveniently built a temple at the tomb site,
and sold this water.
Those going to buy it
would also make offerings at the temple.
Wine and meat offerings never ceased,
and the number of visitors grew.
When this water ran out,
the sellers would often secretly transport other water at night to replenish it.
Those from distant places who could not go themselves,
would rely on travelers,
or send vessels and messengers to buy it.
Thus, the sellers
of the water became very wealthy.
Some said it had no divine power,
the authorities prohibited it,
and so it was filled in,
and thus ended.
The Yùzhāng Tree
In Táng-dynasty Hóngzhōu, there was a Yùzhāng tree,
from the Qín dynasty to the present,
over a thousand years old,
revered from near and far.
Sometimes it demanded women,
sometimes pigs and sheep.
There was a Master Hú Chāo,
who lived in seclusion in the Báihè Mountains,
and occasionally visited Hóng Prefecture.
He saw pigs, sheep, and women arrayed before it,
who complained, saying this deity unjustly saw them killed.
Chāo then gathered firewood to burn it,
yet felt apprehensive.
In the tree were several dozen stork nests,
and three days before the intended burning,
the storks circled in the air,
hovering and not descending.
Also, the surrounding houses were densely packed,
all made of bamboo and wood,
and he feared the fire might spread.
At that time, a great wind arose,
blowing the flames straight upward,
causing no damage to the sides,
and so he petitioned to establish a Daoist temple on that site.
Dí Rénjié's Proclamation
In the fourth year of the Chuígōng era of the Táng dynasty,
the Pacification Commissioner Dí Rénjié
issued a proclamation to the generals and officers of the late King of Western Chǔ, Lord Xiàng Yǔ,
which read in summary:
"A great name cannot be falsely claimed,
and the sacred vessel cannot be seized by force.
Those who respond to Heaven receive the name of joyous support,
while those who defy the times are not rulers who perceive the signs.
Since the First Emperor ruled the realm,
he wantonly devoured the feudal lords.
He entrusted Zhào Gāo with authority,
and abandoned Méng Tián to the sword.
First, disaster struck at Shāqiū,
and later, destruction befell Wàngyí.
The ancestral temples crumbled,
and the people were slaughtered across the plains.
Birds long for stillness amidst flying dust,
and fish find no peace in boiling water.
Glorious was the great Hàn,
which received the mandate from the dark heavens.
It bore the true sign of the Red Emperor,
and aligned with the revered movement of the four auspicious creatures.
Bending to secure the earth's axis,
it displayed the auspiciousness of the phoenix's reign;
lifting to weave the celestial net,
it gathered the portents of the dragon's rise.
Yet you, Lord, lurked in the marshy lands,
gathering followers in the watery regions.
You boasted of the strength to lift a cauldron,
and flaunted the power to uproot mountains.
You failed to discern where the great mandate would converge,
and remained unaware to whom the celestial succession belonged.
Thus, you spread your wings in Guānzhōng,
only to have them clipped at Gāixià.
This was truly due to human affairs,
how could it be attributed to Heaven's will?
Though you commanded a million troops,
in the end, you abandoned your eight thousand sons.
Taking this as a warning from the Yīn dynasty,
is it not a pity?
You should thus hide your spirit in the eastern peaks,
and gather your soul at the northern pole.
How can you vainly receive temple offerings,
and wastefully consume sacrificial animals?
I, Rénjié, have received command over this region,
entrusted with the task of reform.
Now I order the burning of your temple,
and the leveling of your shrine platform,
so that the fragrant curtains vanish entirely,
and the feathered banners follow the smoke.
You, Lord, should depart swiftly,
and bring no harm to the people.
Upon receipt of this proclamation, comply as per the law."
The proclamation was swiftly posted at the mountain temple.
The main text is originally missing.
It comprised six lines in total.
Each line contained twenty-two characters.
The Painted Pípa
The first two lines are originally missing.
Each line contained twenty-two characters.
A boat was moored.
A scholar went up the mountain for a leisurely stroll.
After walking several dozen paces into the woods,
he came upon a slope.
He saw a monastic courtyard with its gate open,
and inside was a bed.
The bed was collapsed,
and outside were several small corridors,
beside which lay writing brushes and inkstones.
The scholar was skilled in painting,
so he took up a brush,
and on the plain wall of the room's door,
he painted a pípa,
its size no different from a real one.
After finishing the painting,
the wind calmed and the boat departed.
When the monk returned,
he saw the painted spot,
but did not know who had done it.
He then told the villagers:
"This might be the sacred pípa from Wǔtái Shān."
Though he likely said it in jest,
it was passed on by the villagers,
and people made offerings and prayed for blessings, which proved very effective.
The scholar then went to the Yáng family,
After spending a year in Wú,
he heard people say that in a monk's room on the Jiāngxī road,
there was a sacred pípa,
and its spiritual responses were numerous.
The scholar grew suspicious,
so when returning to Jiāngxī,
he ordered the boatman to moor the boat at that spot.
He went up to investigate,
but the monk was not there.
The painted pípa remained as before,
with banners, flowers, and incense burners placed before it.
The scholar fetched water and washed it all away,
and the monk still had not returned.
The scholar spent the night on the boat,
and went up again the next day.
The monk had returned during the night,
and noticed the pípa was missing.
He reported it,
and the neighbors gathered in large numbers,
lamenting together.
The scholar deliberately asked,
and they recounted the previous miracles,
saying that now someone must have offended it,
which was why the pípa had hidden itself.
The scholar laughed heartily,
and explained the reason for the painting,
as well as why he had wiped it away.
The monk and the villagers believed him,
and the spiritual miracles ceased thereafter.
The Mountain Deity of Bì Shān
In Hézhōu, there was a mountain deity of Bì Shān.
When the villagers made offerings,
they had to use a grand sacrifice of oxen,
otherwise disaster would ensue,
and the entire region feared this.
Every year, countless animals were slaughtered,
with no end in sight.
A Shǔ monk named Shàn Xiǎo,
who had previously served as a local official,
grew weary of the constant transfers and appointments,
so he shaved his head and became a monk,
strictly upholding the precepts,
and traveling to practice and pay respects.
Passing by this temple,
he said:
"Heaven, earth, and the altars of soil and grain
have proper rituals for offerings.
How can this ghost secretly claim a place among them?
Oxen are the foundation of agriculture,
yet you greedily demand them for your sacrifices—
is this not excessive?"
He then took an axe and smashed several of the clay idols,
leaving one remaining,
as the monk was exhausted from the effort.
After catching his breath slightly,
he was about to strike again.
The temple attendant pleaded with the monk:
"This deity has always been vegetarian,
so please spare it."
The military and civil authorities were astonished,
and reported the matter to their superiors,
but the monk remained unharmed.
Thus, by rebuking it with righteous principles,
even the deity dared not inflict harm.
Hán Zhòng
King Fūchāi of Wú,
had a young daughter named Yù,
aged eighteen.
A youth named Hán Zhòng,
aged nineteen.
Yù was fond of him,
and they privately exchanged messages and pledges,
promising to become husband and wife.
Zhòng went to study in the region between Qí and Lǔ,
and entrusted his parents to seek marriage on his behalf.
The king was furious and refused.
Yù, choked with sorrow, died,
and was buried outside the Chāngmén gate.
Three years later, Zhòng returned,
He asked his parents,
and his parents said:
"The king was greatly enraged,
Yù, choked with sorrow, died,
and has already been buried."
Zhòng wept in grief and sorrow,
prepared sacrificial offerings and went to mourn.
Yù appeared in form beside the tomb,
and said to Zhòng:
"After you departed before,
I had my parents seek the king's permission,
thinking our great wish would surely be fulfilled.
I never imagined that after parting,
I would meet such a fate—what could be done?"
Yù turned her head left, bent her neck gracefully, and sang:
On the southern mountain there is a bird,
on the northern mountain nets are spread.
My heart wished to follow you,
but slanderous words were many.
Grief choked me and brought illness,
I lost my life and entered the yellow earth.
My fate was unkind,
how can such injustice be?
The leader among feathered kinds,
is named the fènghuáng.
Once she loses her mate,
for three years she grieves.
Though there are many other birds,
none can match as a pair.
Thus I show my humble form,
meeting your radiant light.
Though bodies are far, hearts are near,
never for a moment have I forgotten."
When the song ended,
she sighed and tears flowed,
unable to contain herself.
She invited Zhòng to return to the tomb with her,
but Zhòng said:
"The living and dead walk different paths,
I fear there will be blame and transgression,
I dare not accept your request."
Yù said:
"I know as well
that the living and dead walk different paths.
But once we part, there will never be another meeting.
Do you fear that I, as a ghost, will bring you harm?
I wish to sincerely offer myself.
Can you not believe me?"
Zhòng was moved by her words,
and accompanied her back to the tomb.
Yù feasted and drank with him,
for three days and three nights,
fulfilling the rites of husband and wife.
As he was about to leave,
she took a pearl one cùn in diameter and gave it to Zhòng, saying:
"My reputation has already been ruined,
my hopes have been cut off,
what more is there to say?
I only wish that you, my lord,
take care of yourself.
If you go to my home,
pay respects to the great king."
After Zhòng left,
he went to the king and recounted the events.
The king was greatly enraged and said:
"My daughter is already dead,
yet Zhòng fabricates lies,
to defile and sully the departed spirit.
This is nothing but grave-robbing to obtain objects,
using ghosts and spirits as a pretext."
He ordered Zhòng seized,
but Zhòng escaped and fled,
going to Yù's tomb to tell Yù.
Yù said:
"Do not worry,
I will now go and explain to the king."
Suddenly, Yù appeared, dressed and groomed.
The king was startled, amazed, sorrowful, and joyful,
and asked:
"How have you come back to life?"
Yù knelt,
and said:
"Previously, the student Hán Zhòng came to seek my hand,
but you, great king, did not permit it.
Now my reputation is ruined and our bond severed,
I brought about my own death.
Zhòng returned from afar,
hearing I had died,
so he brought sacrificial offerings,
and came to the tomb to mourn.
Moved by his sincere devotion to the end,
I then met with him.
Thus I gave him the pearl,
it was not grave-robbing.
I beg you not to pursue and punish him."
The queen heard this,
came out and embraced her,
but she was exactly like smoke.
Gōngsūn Dá
Gōngsūn Dá of Rènchéng,
during the Gānlù era,
died in office in Chénjùn Commandery.
As they were about to encoffin him,
his sons and several dozen commandery officials attended the funeral.
Dá's five-year-old son
suddenly spoke in a spirit voice,
the tone and sound like his father's,
admonishing everyone to stop crying.
He then called his sons,
instructing and admonishing them in turn.
The sons were overcome with grief and sorrow,
and he comforted and encouraged them, saying:
"The cycle of the four seasons,
still has beginning and end.
Human lifespans differ in length,
but who does not come to this?"
He spoke over a thousand words,
all well-composed and literary.
His son asked further:
"When people die, they are all without awareness;
only you, father, are exceptionally intelligent and extraordinary.
Do you have divine powers?"
He replied:
"Matters of ghosts and spirits,
are not for you to know."
He then asked for paper and brush to write a letter,
filled with eloquent meaning,
then threw it down and was gone.
Xiānyú Jì
In the second year of the Jiànwǔ era of the Later Hàn,
Xiānyú Jì of Xīhé was appointed as the Grand Administrator of Qīnghé.
He undertook the construction of an official office building.
It was not completed when he died.
Later, the administrator Zhào Gāo,
calculated the construction cost as two million coins.
But the official Huáng Bǐng and the merit official Liú Shì said four million coins.
Then Jì appeared as a ghost,
entering the prefecture in broad daylight with attendants.
Together with Gāo and Bǐng and others,
he confronted and jointly examined the accounts,
determining that Shì and Bǐng had embezzled and concealed funds.
Jì then wrote a memorial to state his case,
its general meaning being:
"Gāo esteems trivial matters.
A man of the fields and ridges,
yet he usurps the position of his predecessor.
He scrutinizes minutiae but misses the larger opportunity.
His nature is that of a servant or concubine,
flattering the world to seek prominence,
stealthy, thieving, cruel, and base.
He brings disgrace to the office bestowed by heaven.
The Yìjīng ridicules one who bears a burden unfit for his station;
this truly describes Gāo.
I, your servant, cannot bear these ghostly words,
and respectfully report this via the thousand-lǐ relay stations,
entrusting Gāo to submit it."
Then he went northwest for thirty lǐ.
Carriage and horses all vanished.
He was seen no more.
Bǐng and others all fell to the ground and died.
Gāo reported the matter by memorial.
An imperial edict was issued,
returning Jì's fields, residences, wife, and children in Xīhé to him,
and additionally arranging a replacement,
to settle the lawsuit from the netherworld.
Lú Chōng
was a man from Fànyáng.
Thirty lǐ west of his home,
there was the tomb of Prefect Cuī.
Chōng was twenty years old.
One day during the winter solstice,
he went hunting west of his residence,
shot a river deer and hit it,
the deer fell but then got up,
and Chōng chased after it.
Unaware, he suddenly saw about a lǐ north of the road,
a tall gate with tiled roofs,
surrounded by buildings like a prefectural mansion.
He no longer saw the deer.
Inside the gate, a bell-ringer
announced the guest’s arrival,
and someone handed him a bundle of new clothes,
saying:
“The prefect sends these to you, sir.”
After putting them on, Chōng entered to meet him.
Prefect Cuī said to Chōng:
“Your esteemed father did not consider my humble family beneath notice.
Recently, I received a letter
asking for my young daughter’s hand in marriage for you,
so I have come to welcome you.”
He then showed the letter to Chōng.
When his father died,
Chōng, though young,
already recognized his father’s handwriting.
He sighed and did not refuse.
The prefect then ordered inside:
“Sir Lú has arrived.
Have my daughter dress and adorn herself.
Proceed to the eastern corridor.”
When dusk arrived,
it was announced from inside that the young lady was ready.
Cuī said to Chōng:
“You may go to the eastern corridor.”
When he arrived,
the young lady had already stepped down from her carriage,
standing at the head of the mat.
They bowed to each other,
and the ceremony lasted three days.
After three days of feasting,
Cuī said to Chōng:
“You may return home.
If she bears a son,
he shall be returned to you.
Do not doubt this.
If she bears a daughter, she shall stay and be raised here.”
He ordered a carriage prepared to send off the guest.
Chōng then took his leave and departed.
Cuī escorted him to the middle gate,
holding his hand with tears falling.
Outside the gate, he saw a calf-drawn carriage,
driven by a servant in dark clothes.
He also saw the clothes he had originally worn and his bow and arrows,
still lying outside the gate.
Soon, a messenger was sent with a man carrying a bundle of clothes for Chōng.
They conveyed the message:
“This marriage bond
has just begun,
yet parting brings such sorrow.
Therefore, we now send a set of clothes
along with matching bedding.”
Chōng boarded the carriage,
which sped away like lightning,
and in a moment, he reached home.
His mother saw him
and asked what had happened.
Chōng recounted everything in detail.
Four years later, in the third month,
Chōng was playing by the water
when he suddenly saw a calf-drawn carriage nearby,
now sinking, now floating.
Then it came ashore,
and all his companions saw it.
Chōng went and opened the carriage’s rear door,
seeing the Cuī maiden and a three-year-old boy inside.
The maiden handed the child to Chōng,
also giving him a golden bowl,
and presented a poem:
“Radiant as a numinous mushroom’s essence,
how splendid and lush its glow.
In bloom, its beauty shone in its time,
marvelous and wondrous, displaying divine wonder.
Holding splendor, not yet in full bloom,
midsummer met frost and withered.
Glory long vanished in darkness,
the worldly path forever barren.
Unaware of yīn and yáng’s workings,
a wise man suddenly came in grace.
Now, after this parting,
when shall we meet again?”
Chōng took the child, the bowl, and the poem,
and suddenly they vanished.
Later, Chōng took a carriage to the market to sell the bowl,
hoping someone might recognize it.
A maidservant recognized it
and reported to her mistress:
“In the market, I saw a man in a carriage
selling the bowl from the Cuī maiden’s coffin.”
The mistress was the Cuī maiden’s own maternal aunt.
She sent her son to see,
and it was just as the maidservant said.
He then boarded the carriage, exchanged names,
and said to Chōng:
“Long ago, my aunt married Prefect Cuī.
Her daughter died before she could wed.
Her family grieved deeply
and placed a golden bowl in her coffin.
Please tell me how you obtained this bowl.”
Chōng recounted the events.
The son was also moved to sorrowful tears,
took the story back, and told his mother.
The mother then sent him to Chōng’s home to bring the child back.
All the relatives gathered.
The child had the Cuī family’s appearance,
yet also resembled Chōng’s features.
Both the child and the bowl were verified.
The aunt said:
“This is my nephew.
His style name shall be Wēnxiū.”
Wēnxiū
means “hidden marriage.”
He later became an outstanding talent,
serving as a commandery governor.
His descendants have held high office to this day.
Among them was Lú Zhí, styled Gàn,
who became renowned throughout the land.
Tán Shēng
There was a man named Tán Shēng,
who was forty years old,
and had no wife.
He often devoted himself earnestly to studying.
Suddenly,
At midnight, a woman appeared,
who seemed to be about fifteen or sixteen years old,
with features and attire
unparalleled in the world.
She came to Shēng to become his wife.
Then
She said:
"I am different from ordinary people.
Do not shine a light on me.
Only after three years
may you do so."
They became husband and wife,
and had a son,
who was already two years old.
Unable to restrain himself,
one night, after she had fallen asleep,
he secretly lit a lamp to look at her.
Her waist had already grown flesh like that of a human,
but below the waist, there was only dried bone.
The woman awoke,
and then said:
"You have betrayed me.
I was on the verge of becoming fully alive.
Why could you not endure for one more year and instead shone the light on me?"
Shēng apologized.
She wept uncontrollably,
and said:
"Although I must part from you forever,
I still care for our son.
If you are too poor to support yourselves,
follow me for a moment,
and I will give you something."
Shēng followed her,
entering a magnificent hall,
where the rooms and furnishings were extraordinary.
She gave him a pearl-embroidered robe and said:
"This can sustain you."
She tore off a piece of his garment,
kept it, and departed.
Later, Shēng took the robe to the market,
where the household of the Prince of Suīyáng bought it,
paying him tens of millions in cash.
The prince recognized it and said:
"This is my daughter's robe.
This must be grave robbery."
He then had Shēng seized and interrogated.
Shēng told the whole truth,
but the prince still did not believe him.
He then went to inspect his daughter's tomb,
which was intact as before.
Upon opening it,
they indeed found a piece of garment under the coffin lid.
They called for Shēng's son,
who closely resembled the prince's daughter,
and only then did the prince believe it.
He immediately summoned Tán Shēng,
returned the robe to him,
and took him as his son-in-law.
He appointed Shēng's son as Shìzhōng.
Chén Fān
When Chén Fān was still obscure,
he once traveled and stayed overnight at the home of a host named Huáng Shēn.
Shēn's wife gave birth at night,
and Fān was unaware of it.
At the third watch of the night,
someone knocked at the door.
After a long while,
he heard someone inside respond:
"There is someone inside the gate,
you cannot come forward."
They told each other:
"Go through the back gate."
Soon, he heard the one who had gone return,
and the one inside the gate asked:
"What child did you see?
What is its name?
How long will it live?"
The one who returned said:
"It is a boy,
named Ānú,
who will live to fifteen years."
He asked again:
"How will he die later?"
The answer was:
"While building a house for someone,
he will fall to his death."
Fān heard this but did not believe it.
Fifteen years later,
when he was the governor of Yùzhāng,
he sent an official to inquire
about the whereabouts of the boy Ānú from back then.
The family said
he was helping the eastern neighbor build a house
and fell from a beam and died.
Liú Zhào,
during the Jiàn'ān era,
served as the governor of Héjiān.
His wife died.
Her coffin was buried in the government garden.
When the Yellow Turban rebels came,
Zhào abandoned the commandery and fled.
Later, when a new governor arrived,
he dreamed at night of a woman coming to him.
She later left him a pair of locks,
which the governor could not name.
The woman said:
"These are wēiruí locks,
connected with gold threads,
flexible and adjustable by hand,
truly precious objects.
I am about to leave,
so I give these to you as a farewell gift.
Be careful not to tell anyone."
Twenty days later,
Zhào sent his son to retrieve the coffin.
The governor then understood the situation.
When the son saw the locks, he was deeply moved and grieved,
unable to control himself.
Zhāng Hànzhí
Zhāng Hànzhí of Chénguó
went to Nányáng
to study the Zuǒzhuàn
under Yán Shūjiān, the governor of Jīngzhào.
Several months after he left,
a ghost possessed his younger sister,
speaking through her:
"I died of illness,
and my body lies on the roadside.
I often suffer from hunger and cold.
I have a pair or two of straw sandals,
hanging on the paper mulberry tree behind the house.
Fù Zǐfāng gave me five hundred coins,
which are under the north window.
I hope you will retrieve them.
Also, I bought a calf from Lǐ Yòu,
and the original contract is in the book chest."
They went to search,
and everything was as described,
even though Hànzhí's wife did not know about these things.
His sister had just returned home for a visit,
so she could not have known about them either.
The family was sorrowful,
and became even more convinced it was true.
His parents and brothers,
with their hair tied in knots, went to meet the funeral procession.
A few miles from the school,
they encountered Hànzhí walking with fellow students.
Hànzhí saw his family
and wondered why they were dressed like that.
When the family saw Hànzhí,
they truly thought he was a ghost.
After a moment of confusion,
Hànzhí came forward
and explained the whole story to his father.
Only then did they realize it was the work of a demon.
Fàn Dān
Fàn Dān of Wàihuáng, Chénliú,
courtesy name Shǐyún,
in his youth served as a minor clerk for a commandant,
and was sent with a dispatch to meet the Dūyóu.
Dān had high aspirations and integrity,
and was ashamed of being a lowly servant.
When he reached the great marsh in Chénliú,
he killed the horse he was riding,
discarded his official cap,
and pretended to have been robbed.
A spirit descended to his home and said:
"I am Shǐyún.
I was killed by robbers.
Quickly retrieve my clothes from the great marsh in Chénliú."
The family went and found a cap.
Dān then went south to Nánjùn,
and later moved to the Sānfǔ region.
He traveled and studied with worthy scholars.
Thirteen years later, he returned.
His family no longer recognized him.
The people of Chénliú admired his lofty aspirations and conduct,
and after his death,
they honored him as Zhēnjié Xiānshēng (the Virtuous and Upright Master).
Fèi Jì
Fèi Jì of Wú was a merchant who traveled for several years.
At that time, the roads were plagued by robbers,
and his wife often worried about him.
Jì once lodged at the foot of Lúshān with fellow travelers,
and they asked each other how long it had been since they left home.
Jì said:
"I have been away from home for several years.
Before leaving,
I bid farewell to my wife
and asked her for a gold hairpin to take with me,
wanting to test her feelings—
whether she would give it to me or not.
She gave me the hairpin,
but I placed it on the lintel of the door.
When I departed, I forgot to take it.
That hairpin must still be on the lintel."
That night,
his wife dreamed that Jì said to her:
"I encountered bandits on my journey
and have been dead for two years.
If you do not believe my words,
I took your hairpin
but did not take it with me.
I left it on the lintel.
You can go and retrieve it."
His wife awoke,
searched for the hairpin, and found it.
The family then held a funeral.
A little over a year later,
Jì returned home from his journey.
Zhōu Shì
Zhōu Shì of Xiàpī in the Hàn dynasty
once traveled to the Eastern Sea.
On the way, he encountered an official
holding a scroll of documents,
who asked to ride in his boat.
After traveling over ten lǐ,
the official said to Shì:
"I have a brief errand to attend to.
I will leave this document in your boat.
Be careful not to open it."
After the official left,
Shì secretly opened and looked at the document.
It contained records of various deceased persons,
and one entry listed Shì's name.
Shortly after, the official returned.
Shì was still looking at the document.
The official angrily said:
"I explicitly warned you,
why did you disregard it?"
Shì kowtowed until his head bled.
After a long while, the official said:
"I am grateful that you gave me a ride from afar,
but this document cannot be altered.
You must return home today
and not leave your house for three years.
Then you may be spared.
Do not mention that you saw this document."
Shì returned home and did not go out.
After more than two years,
his family found it strange.
When a neighbor suddenly died,
Shì's father, angered,
ordered him to go offer condolences.
Shì could not refuse.
As soon as he stepped out the door,
he saw the official.
The official said:
"I told you not to leave for three years,
yet now you have stepped out.
What can be done?
I could not find you,
and I was even flogged for it.
Now that I have seen you,
there is no other choice.
Three days from now at noon,
I will come for you."
Shì returned home weeping
and recounted everything.
His father still did not believe him.
His mother stayed with him day and night, weeping.
When noon arrived three days later,
they saw someone come to take him,
and he died.
Chén Ādēng
A man from Jùzhāng in Kuàijī during the Hàn dynasty
was returning from the eastern countryside.
As dusk fell and he could not reach the city gate,
he saw a small hut by the roadside with a light burning,
so he sought lodging there.
Upon arriving,
he found a young woman
who did not wish to share lodging with a man.
She called a neighbor's daughter to keep her company.
At night, they played the kōnghóu together
and sang:
"Like the tangled vines on the kudzu,
one loose, one taut.
If you wish to know my name,
I am Chén Ādēng."
The next day, he reached the outer eastern wall.
There was an old woman selling food in a shop.
The man sat down to rest
and recounted what he had seen the previous night.
The old woman exclaimed in surprise:
"That was my daughter.
She recently passed away
and is buried outside the city wall."
Wú Xiáng
Wú Xiáng, an official of Zhūjì County in the Hàn dynasty,
was weary and exhausted from his duties.
He decided to flee into the deep mountains.
On his journey, he came to a stream.
As dusk approached,
he saw a young woman
in colorful, beautiful garments,
who said:
"I live alone,
with no relatives or neighbors,
except for one old widow
who lives over ten paces away."
Xiáng was delighted to hear this
and immediately followed her.
After walking over a lǐ,
they arrived at the woman's home.
The house was very poor and humble.
She prepared food for Xiáng.
When the first watch ended,
he heard an old woman call out:
"Zhāng Gūzi!"
The woman replied:
"Yes."
Xiáng asked who it was,
and she answered:
"It is the old widow I mentioned earlier."
The two slept together until dawn.
When the rooster crowed, Xiáng left.
They were deeply attached to each other,
and the woman gave Xiáng a purple scarf as a gift,
while Xiáng gave her a cloth handkerchief in return.
When he reached the place where he had met her the previous night,
he tried to cross the stream,
but the water had suddenly surged during the night,
making it too deep to ford.
He turned back toward the woman's house,
but the place from the previous night was nowhere to be seen.
There was only a grave mound.
Zhōu Wēngzhòng
Zhōu Wēngzhòng of Rǔnán,
initially served as a clerk under the Grand Commandant.
His wife gave birth to a son.
Later, when he became Chancellor of Běihǎi,
there was a subordinate named Zhōu Guāng who could see ghosts.
Wēngzhòng appointed him as Registrar.
He sent him back to pay respects to the commandery and county of his origin,
and instructed him, saying:
"When your business is finished,
on the La Festival day, you may come with my young son to attend the sacrificial ceremony."
The Registrar finished his business and returned.
Wēngzhòng asked him about it.
He replied:
"I only saw a butcher.
Wearing ragged clothes and with a disheveled topknot, he was squatting on the god's seat,
holding a knife and cutting meat.
There were several men in official robes with black and green silk ribbons,
pacing back and forth in the eastern and western wings of the hall,
not daring to advance.
I don't know the reason."
Wēngzhòng then took up his sword and went into the hall.
He said to his wife:
"Why did you raise this son?"
The wife was greatly angered and said:
"You always said
that our son's appearance, demeanor, voice, and spirit were happily learning to resemble you.
Old man, are you about to die,
that you speak such mad words?"
Wēngzhòng told her the whole story.
"If the sacrificial ceremony is like this,
and you do not confess fully,
mother and son will be executed immediately."
The wife wept and said:
