"In the past, because I was older and had no son,
I felt uneasy.
In truth, I exchanged our daughter for the butcher's son.
I gave him ten thousand coins.
This son is now eighteen years old.
Send him back to his home.
Bring back our daughter,
who is now married to a cake seller as his wife."
Later, she married Lǐ Zhīsī of Xīpíng,
and Wénsī's official rank rose to Governor of Nányáng.
Tián Chóu
was a man of Běipíng.
When Liú Yú was killed by Gōngsūn Zàn,
Chóu's remembrance and admiration were endless.
He went to Yú's tomb,
set out offerings of chicken and wine, and wept for him.
The sound moved the forests and wilderness.
Soaring birds cried mournfully for him,
and running beasts wailed in sorrow.
Chóu lay down among the grass,
when suddenly someone announced:
"Liú Yōuzhōu has come,
wishing to speak with Tián Zǐtài about the events of his life."
Chóu, with his keen spiritual awareness and profound insight,
knew it was the spirit of Liú Yú.
He then advanced and bowed.
Chóu wept uncontrollably.
They then together offered chicken and wine.
Chóu became drunk.
Yú said:
"Gōngsūn Zàn is urgently seeking you with a reward,
you should hide and flee to avoid harm."
Chóu replied:
"The way between ruler and minister is such that
in life, one fulfills one's duty to the utmost.
Now that I have seen your spirit,
I wish to join you in the Nine Springs.
My bones will then be imperishable.
How could I flee?"
Yú said:
"You are a noble scholar for the ages.
Be deeply cautious of your conduct."
Suddenly, he vanished.
And Chóu's drunkenness also cleared.
Wén Yǐng
Wén Yǐng of Hànnányáng,
courtesy name Shūcháng,
during the Jiàn'ān era,
served as Assistant to the Prefect of Gānlíng.
While crossing the border, he stopped to lodge for the night.
At the third watch of the night,
he dreamed of a man kneeling before him, saying:
"In the past, my ancestors
buried me here.
Water came rushing to the tomb,
the coffin was submerged,
half soaked in the water.
Yet I have no means to warm myself.
Hearing that you are here,
I have come to rely on you.
I wish to trouble you tomorrow,
to stay briefly.
I beg you to move me to a high, dry place."
The ghost lifted his clothes to show Yǐng,
and they were all soaked.
Yǐng felt sorrow in his heart,
and immediately awoke.
He asked those around him about it.
They said:
"Dreams are empty illusions,
why consider this strange?"
Yǐng then went back to sleep.
Towards dawn,
he dreamed again.
The ghost said to Yǐng:
"I have told you of my hardship and suffering,
why do you not take pity on me?"
Yǐng asked in the dream:
"Who are you?"
He replied:
"I was originally a man of Zhào.
Now I belong to the deity of the Wāngmáng clan."
Yǐng said:
"Where is your coffin now?"
He replied:
"Very close, about a dozen paces north of your tent,
beside the water under a withered poplar tree,
that is me.
Dawn is about to break,
I can no longer be seen.
You must remember this."
Yǐng replied:
"Yes."
Suddenly, he awoke.
When day broke and it was time to depart,
Yǐng said:
"Although it is said dreams are not to be considered strange,
this one is too much."
Those around him said:
"Why begrudge a moment
to verify it?"
Yǐng immediately arose,
led a dozen men as guides,
and went upstream along the water.
Sure enough, they found a withered poplar.
He said:
"This is it."
They dug beneath it.
Before long,
they indeed found a coffin.
The coffin was very rotten and damaged,
half submerged in the water.
Yǐng said to those around him:
"Earlier, hearing from others,
I considered such things empty.
But traditions passed down among the common people
cannot be without verification."
They moved the coffin
and buried it before leaving.
Wáng Fán
The *Dūnhuáng Shílù* records:
When Wáng Fán died,
a grave robber opened his tomb.
He saw Fán playing liubo with someone,
and Fán offered wine to the robber.
The robber was terrified,
but drank it.
He saw someone lead a bronze horse out of the tomb.
That night, a divine being came to the city gate,
and announced:
"I am a messenger of Wáng Fán.
Now, there is one who opened a tomb.
I have marked his lips with wine.
When morning comes,
you can verify and capture him."
When the robber entered the city,
the gatekeepers bound and interrogated him.
It was just as the divine being had said.
Qín Jùbó
Lángyé's Qín Jùbó,
was sixty years old.
Once he was walking at night after drinking,
and passed by the Péngshān Temple.
Suddenly he saw his two grandsons coming to meet him.
They supported him for over a hundred paces,
then suddenly grabbed Bó by the neck, threw him to the ground, and cursed:
"Old slave,
you beat me on a certain day,
and now I shall kill you."
Bó thought to himself:
indeed, he had beaten this grandson at that time.
Bó then pretended to be dead,
and they left him there and went away.
Bó returned home,
intending to punish his two grandsons.
The grandsons were shocked and dismayed, kowtowing and saying,
"As your grandsons,
how could we possibly do such a thing?
It must have been ghosts or demons.
We beg you to test them again."
Bó then realized the truth.
A few days later,
he pretended to be drunk again,
and walked near that temple.
Once more, he saw his two grandsons coming to support him.
Bó quickly seized them.
They could not move.
When he reached home,
they turned out to be two strangers.
Bó lit a fire and burned them,
until their bellies and backs were scorched and cracked.
He then dragged them out into the courtyard,
but during the night they both escaped.
Bó regretted not having killed them.
A month later,
he again pretended to be drunk and walked at night,
taking a hidden knife with him,
but his family did not know.
When he did not return late into the night,
his grandsons feared he might be trapped by those ghosts again,
so they went together to meet him.
Bó then stabbed and killed them.
Zōng Dài
Zōng Dài served as the Governor of Qīngzhōu.
He prohibited improper sacrifices,
and wrote the "Treatise on the Nonexistence of Ghosts."
It was very profound,
and no one could refute him.
Neighboring regions were all influenced by him.
Later, there was a scholar.
Wearing a silk headscarf,
he prepared a name card and visited Dài.
They conversed for a long time,
but Dài's arguments remained unshaken.
When Dài's words were not fully articulated,
the scholar would elaborate for him.
When they came to the topic of the nonexistence of ghosts,
the scholar began to press Dài with difficult questions,
and Dài's arguments were on the verge of being refuted.
The scholar then straightened his clothes, stood up, and said:
"You have cut off our blood sacrifices for over twenty years.
You had a black ox and a bearded servant,
which prevented us from troubling you.
Now the servant has rebelled,
the ox has died,
and today we can finally subdue you."
As soon as he finished speaking,
the scholar vanished.
The next day, Dài died.
Zhèng Qí
During the Later Hàn dynasty,
there were ghosts and demons at the West Gate Pavilion in Rǔyáng, Rǔnán.
Many guests who stayed there died.
Some lost their hair or their vital essence.
The Commandery Attendant Clerk, Yílù's Zhèng Qí, was on leave.
About six or seven lǐ from the pavilion,
a beautiful woman begged for a ride.
Qí initially refused,
but then let her board the carriage.
Upon entering the pavilion,
she hurried to the upper floor.
The clerks and guards said the upper floor could not be accessed.
Qí said:
"I am not afraid."
It was already dark,
so he went upstairs.
He spent the night with the woman,
and left before dawn.
The pavilion guard went upstairs to clean,
and saw a dead woman.
Greatly shocked,
he ran to report to the pavilion chief.
Drums were beaten to gather all the officials,
and they examined her together.
She turned out to be the wife of the Wú family,
who had recently died,
and during the night vigil, the funeral fire went out,
and when the fire was relit, she was missing.
Her family immediately took her away.
Qí departed,
traveled several lǐ,
and felt abdominal pain.
When he reached the Lìyáng Pavilion in Nándùn,
his condition worsened and he died.
After that, no one dared to go upstairs again.
Zhōng Yáo
Zhōng Yáo suddenly stopped attending court meetings,
and his demeanor became unusual.
His colleagues asked him the reason,
and he said:
"A woman often comes to visit me,
beautiful beyond compare in the mortal world."
They said:
"She must be a ghostly creature,
you should kill her."
Later, she came and stopped outside the door,
saying:
"Why do you have the intention to kill me?"
Yuáncháng (Zhōng Yáo) said:
"I do not."
He warmly invited her in.
Feeling reluctant,
he only slightly wounded her,
and she then left.
She used new silk to wipe the blood,
all along the way.
The next day,
he sent someone to follow the trail,
which led to a large tomb.
Inside the coffin was a woman.
Her body was as if alive,
wearing a white silk shirt,
and a red embroidered waistcoat.
She had a wound on her thigh,
and had used silk from the waistcoat to wipe the blood.
After this, she never appeared again.
Xiàhóu Xuán
Xiàhóu Xuán was executed by Sīmǎ Jǐngwáng.
His clansmen held a sacrificial ceremony for him.
They saw Xuán come to the spirit seat,
remove his head and place it aside,
gather all the fruits, fish, wine, and meat offerings,
put them into his neck, and after finishing,
reattach his head.
Then he said:
"I have received permission from the Emperor.
Zǐyuán (Sīmǎ Shī) will have no heirs."
Soon after, the Yǒngjiā campaign occurred,
and when the army returned,
Shìzōng (Sīmǎ Shī) died without a son.
Jī Kāng
Jī Kāng was playing the qin by lamplight,
when suddenly there appeared a person,
over ten feet tall,
wearing a black unlined garment
and a leather belt.
Kāng stared at him intently,
then blew out the lamp, saying:
"I am ashamed to contend for light with a demon."
Once, while traveling,
he left the road.
Several tens of li away,
there was a pavilion named Yuèhuá.
He sought lodging at this pavilion,
which had a history of murders.
Kāng's spirit was calm and detached,
showing not the slightest fear.
At the first watch, he played the qin,
first performing several pieces.
The elegant sounds and transcendent melodies
drew praise from the air.
Kāng stroked the qin and called out:
"Who are you, sir?"
The reply came:
"I am a man of the past,
buried in obscurity here.
Hearing you play the qin,
the music pure and harmonious,
something I loved in life,
I came to listen.
I met an untimely, unjust death,
my body is mutilated and ruined,
unfit to meet a gentleman face to face.
Yet I love your qin playing,
and must meet you,
please do not find me strange or repulsive.
Could you play a few more pieces?"
Kāng again played the qin for him,
beating time.
He said:
"The night is already late.
Why not come forth?
Matters of physical form
are ultimately of little consequence."
The ghost then appeared, holding his own head, and said:
"Hearing you play the qin,
I felt my heart open and spirit awaken,
as if briefly brought back to life."
They then discussed the subtleties of music together,
his words exceptionally clear and eloquent.
He said to Kāng:
"Please, let me try your qin."
He then played "Guǎnglíng Sàn."
Kāng learned it from him then and there.
Indeed, he mastered it completely.
The pieces Kāng had learned previously
were far inferior.
The ghost made Kāng swear
not to teach it to anyone.
At daybreak,
he said to Kāng:
"Though our meeting was but this single night,
its resonance spans a thousand years.
Now we part forever here."
Overwhelmed with emotion,
Kāng was filled with melancholy.
Ní Yànsī
During the time of Wú,
in Jiāxīng, there was Ní Yànsī.
He lived in Yánlǐ, west of the county seat.
A ghost haunted his household.
It spoke with people,
ate and drank like a human,
but remained invisible.
Among Yànsī's servants,
if any secretly cursed their master,
it would say, "I will now report this."
Yànsī would then punish them,
so none dared insult him.
Yànsī had a concubine,
whom the ghost pursued and demanded.
Yànsī then invited a Daoist priest to exorcise it.
When wine and food were laid out,
the ghost took filth and weeds from the latrine
and scattered them over the offerings.
The priest vigorously beat his drum,
summoning and invoking the gods.
The ghost then took a tiger-shaped amulet
and blew on it from the altar, producing a horn-like sound.
After a while,
the priest suddenly felt a chill on his back;
startled, he rose and removed his clothes—
it was the tiger amulet.
Thereupon, the priest gave up and left.
Yànsī, at night under the covers,
secretly spoke with his wife,
sharing their troubles about this ghost.
The ghost, from the roof beam,
said to Yànsī:
"You and your wife are talking about me;
I will now cut your roof beam."
Immediately, a rumbling sound arose.
Fearing the beam would break, Yànsī
took a torch to look,
but the ghost extinguished the flame,
and the sound of the beam being cut grew more urgent.
Yànsī, afraid the house would collapse,
sent everyone, young and old, outside.
He fetched another torch
and saw the beam was as before.
The ghost laughed heartily
and asked Yànsī:
"Will you talk about me again?"
The Commandery Agricultural Officer heard of this and said:
"This 'deity' is surely just a fox creature!"
The ghost immediately went and said to the Officer:
"You took several hundred hu of government grain
and hid it in a certain place.
As an official, you are corrupt and filthy,
yet you dare to judge me?
I will now report to the authorities
and have men seize the grain you stole."
The Officer was terrified and apologized,
and thereafter no one dared speak of it.
After three years, it left,
and no one knew where it went.
Shěn Jì
Shěn Jì of Wúxīng,
in the second year of the Tiānjì era of Wú,
served as Governor of Yùzhāng.
One day,
in the main hall, he saw a person
wearing a yellow headscarf and a plain silk garment,
who claimed to be Xǔ Zǐjiāng from Píngxīng in Rǔnán,
requesting a reburial,
then vanished into thin air.
Jì searched for his remains
but could not find their location,
so he performed a funeral for the summoned spirit.
Mí Zhú
Mí Zhú employed the methods of Táo Zhūgōng,
increasing his profits by hundreds of millions daily,
his wealth rivaling that of princes and marquises.
He possessed a thousand treasure vaults.
Mí Zhú had a nature capable of reviving the dead and saving the living.
Beside the stable of his family home,
there was an ancient tomb,
within which lay a hidden corpse.
One night, Mí Zhú followed the sound of weeping,
and suddenly saw a woman
approaching with her back exposed,
who said:
"In the late Hàn dynasty, I was disturbed by the Red Eyebrows,
my coffin opened and my body stripped.
Now my flesh lies exposed on the ground,
for over two hundred years.
I come to you, General, to ask for a deeper burial,
and beg for tattered clothes to cover myself."
Mí Zhú immediately ordered a stone outer coffin and earthenware inner coffin to be made.
After the sacrificial rites were completed,
he placed a blue cloth jacket and skirt
on top of the tomb.
A year passed.
While walking along a winding road,
he suddenly saw the place where the woman was buried,
with a blue aura shaped like a dragon or serpent.
Someone asked Mí Zhú:
"Could it be a dragon monster?"
Mí Zhú then grew suspicious of this anomaly,
and asked his household servants,
who said:
"We sometimes see a blue reed staff
naturally entering and exiting the gate.
We suspect it is a spirit,
but dare not speak of it."
Mí Zhú was by nature highly suspicious,
and trusted practitioners of exorcism.
If anyone spoke against him,
he would immediately punish or execute them,
hence the servants remained silent.
Mí Zhú's wealth and loans piled up like mountains,
beyond calculation.
Inside, he used fāngzhū mirrors as utensils,
and large pearls as big as eggs
were scattered all over the courtyard,
so it was called the Treasure Courtyard,
and outsiders were not allowed to glimpse it.
A few days later,
he suddenly saw several blue-clad youths arriving, saying:
"Mí Zhú's household is about to suffer a fire calamity,
with nothing left behind.
But because you took pity on dry bones,
Heaven's way does not betray your virtue.
Thus, we have come to ward off this fire,
ensuring your wealth is not entirely lost.
From now on,
you should also take precautions."
Mí Zhú then dug ditches and channels
encircling his vaults.
Ten days later,
fire broke out from within the vaults,
burning his pearls and jades,
leaving only one-tenth remaining.
It was all due to the yangsuì mirrors attracting drought and scorching heat,
which spontaneously ignited the objects.
When the fire was at its peak,
he saw dozens of blue-clad youths arriving to extinguish it,
and a blue aura like clouds
covered the flames, which then died out.
The youths also said:
"Gather many birds like storks to ward off disasters,
as storks can gather water on their nests."
The family then collected thousands of jiāojīng birds,
raising them in ponds and channels,
to suppress fire.
Mí Zhú sighed:
"A person's wealth and fortune are limited,
and cannot overflow endlessly."
Fearing calamity for himself,
and with the three kingdoms at war at the time,
military expenses multiplied ten thousandfold.
He then donated his treasures, carriages, and garments
to assist the First Ruler.
One hundred million catties of gold,
brocades, embroideries, woolen carpets, and felt,
piled up like mountains,
and a thousand fine horses.
After Shǔ was conquered,
he had nothing left.
He died with regret.
Wáng Bì
Wáng Bì annotated the "Yìjīng,"
and often laughed at Zhèng Xuán as a pedantic Confucian scholar,
saying:
"The old man is clueless."
One night at midnight,
he suddenly heard the sound of clogs outside the pavilion,
and shortly after, someone entered,
claiming to be Zhèng Xuán,
who rebuked him:
"You are young,
how dare you recklessly distort the text
and falsely criticize and slander Lǎozi?"
He appeared extremely angry,
and after speaking, he left.
Wáng Bì was disturbed by this,
and later contracted a plague and died.
Chén Xiān
During the Wú period,
Chén Xiān worked as a merchant.
While driving his donkey,
he suddenly passed by an empty mansion,
with grand halls and vermilion gates,
but no one in sight.
Chén Xiān led his donkey inside to stay overnight.
At night,
he heard voices saying:
"You insignificant man, fearless,
dare to bring disaster upon yourself."
Then a person
approached Chén Xiān directly,
shouting at him:
"How dare you enter an official residence!"
The moonlight was dim at the time,
and he saw that the person's face was deeply pockmarked,
with eyes lacking pupils,
lips curled back and teeth exposed,
holding yellow silk in hand.
Chén Xiān fled to the nearby village,
and recounted the incident in detail.
The village elders said:
"There used to be an evil spirit there."
The next day,
they went to look at the site of the mansion,
and found only tall graves and deep pits.
Hú Xī
Hú Xī, Left Gentleman of the Palace and Chancellor of Guǎnglíng in Wú,
styled Yuánguāng.
His daughter was named Zhōng,
betrothed and about to be married.
But suddenly she became pregnant.
The girl herself was unaware of it.
Hú Xī's father, Xìn,
was strict and adhered to the law,
so he sent Hú Xī's wife, Dīng shì, to kill her.
Suddenly, a ghost spoke from within the womb,
its voice chattering:
"Why kill my mother?
I will be born on such-and-such month and day."
Those nearby were shocked and alarmed,
and reported it to Xìn.
Xìn went to listen himself,
and then spared her.
When the child was born and left on the ground,
it had no visible form,
only the sound of a baby could be heard
around them.
As it grew up,
its speech was like that of a human.
Hú Xī's wife set up a separate curtain for it.
It often said
it would reveal its form
for its grandmother to see.
Hú Xī's wife looked,
and inside the red curtain,
golden hairpins were pinned front and back,
with beautiful arms
skilled at playing the qín.
It often asked about its grandmother and mother's desires,
and would bring back wine, dried meat, dates, and the like.
When the mother sat sewing clothes,
the child would come, cling to her knees, climb onto her back, and play around.
Zhōng grew impatient with this,
and secretly thought angrily:
"How can a human family be accompanied by a ghost child?"
Immediately, the child beside her said angrily:
"I was just playing with Mother.
Yet you scold me as a ghost child.
Now I will enter Mother's finger,
and go into Mother's womb,
so she will know."
Her middle finger immediately straightened and hurt,
gradually moving up her arm and thigh,
as if pierced by something.
Soon she was near death.
Hú Xī's wife then set out offerings,
prayed and pleaded,
and after a while, it stopped.
When Sūn Quán fell ill,
a shaman revealed:
"There is a ghost wearing a silk turban,
resembling a former general or minister,
who scolds without regard,
and directly enters the palace."
That night,
Sūn Quán saw Lǔ Sù come,
his clothing and turban exactly as described.
Lù Jī
When Lù Jī first entered Luòyáng,
he stopped in Hénán.
Entering Yǎnshī,
the weather was overcast and gloomy,
and looking to the left side of the road,
he saw what seemed like a dwelling,
so he sought lodging there.
He encountered a young man,
whose demeanor was dignified and profound,
engaged in studying the *Book of Changes* and playing pitch-pot.
Conversing with Lù Jī,
he displayed profound and subtle insights.
Lù Jī inwardly admired his ability,
unable to match him in discourse.
At daybreak, he departed.
When he paid for lodging at the inn,
the innkeeper's wife said:
"For over ten miles east of here, there are no villages,
only the tomb of the Prince of Shānyáng."
Lù Jī went to look,
and found a desolate wilderness shrouded in clouds,
with towering trees blocking the sun.
Only then did he realize that the person he met the previous night
was indeed Wáng Bì.
Zhào Bólún
Zhào Bólún, a native of Mòlíng,
once traveled to Xiāngyáng.
The boatmen used a pig as an offering for prayer,
but when it came time for the sacrifice,
only a pig's shoulder remained.
That evening,
Zhào Bólún and others dreamed of an old man and an old woman,
their hair gray and white,
both dressed in plain cloth garments,
holding oars and paddles,
angry with them.
The next morning,
the boat repeatedly struck sandbars and rocks,
all beyond human control.
Only after offering a more substantial sacrifice
did they manage to proceed smoothly.
Zhū Yàn
Zhū Yàn of Yǒngjiā,
resided in Yǒngníng.
While clearing wilderness to build a house,
he immediately heard the sounds of string and wind instruments,
as well as the cries and shouts of children.
At night, he saw a person,
very large and strong,
blowing,
extinguishing his fire.
Zhū Yàn was naturally brave and daring,
and was not afraid,
so he did not move away,
and no further troubles occurred.
Huán Huí
Huán Huí, a sacrificial officer in Bīngzhōu,
in the third year of Liú Cōng's Jiànyuán era,
encountered an old man on the road.
He asked him, saying:
"There is,
the musician Chéng Píng,
what position does he hold now?
I have an old acquaintance with him,
and wish to engage in refined conversation,
so that he may be recommended as Xiàolián.
If you meet him,
let him know this news."
Huán Huí asked for his name,
and he said:
"I am Mázi Xuān of Wújùn."
After speaking, he disappeared.
Huán Huí saw Chéng Píng,
and fully conveyed the message,
Chéng Píng sighed and said:
"There was such a person in the past,
but he passed away nearly fifty years ago."
When the court gentleman Xún Yànshū heard of this,
he composed a prayer,
instructing Chéng Píng to prepare wine and food,
and offer sacrifices at a major crossroads.
Zhōu Zǐcháng
lived at the eastern ridge of Wǔdà Pǔ in Wǔchāng.
In the third year of the Xiánkāng era,
Zhōu Zǐcháng went to the Jī family at Hánxī.
The Jī family lived several miles from Wǔdà.
At dusk, returning to Wǔdà,
he had not yet arrived.
Previously an empty ridge,
he suddenly saw tiled houses encircling the road,
and a gate guard seized Zhōu Zǐcháng by the head.
Zhōu Zǐcháng said:
"I am a disciple of the Buddha,
why seize me?"
The officer said:
"If you are a disciple of the Buddha,
can you recite scriptures?"
Zhōu Zǐcháng previously could recite the scriptures of the Four Heavenly Kings and the Prince.
He recited them three or four times,
but they still did not release him,
so he scolded them, saying:
"Foolish ghosts of Wǔchāng,
I tell you,
I am a disciple of the Buddha,
and have recited several verses of scripture for you,
yet you still do not release me."
The captor then released him,
and the houses were no longer seen,
but the ghosts still pursued him.
Passing by his own house,
the ghosts blocked him from entering,
and he could not make a sound.
As he led the ghosts past the Hánxī Temple,
Zhōu Zǐcháng grabbed the ghost's chest, saying:
"I will take you before the monks in the temple."
The ghost also grabbed Zhōu Zǐcháng's chest,
and they dragged each other across the Wǔzhàng Pond,
heading west.
Later, one ghost said to the captor:
"Let go,
he is about to drag me into the temple."
The captor said:
"Once seized, I will not release."
Zhōu Zǐcháng then said to the one behind:
"There are bald ones in the temple,
are you still not afraid of them?"
Another ghost whispered:
"When you recently encountered the bald one east of the city,
why was your face defeated?"
They all laughed together.
By the time Zhōu Zǐcháng reached home,
it was already past the third watch.
Xún Zé
Xún Zé of Yǐngchuān
died during the Tàiyuán era.
He often appeared in form to return,
and with his wife, Kǒng shì of Lǔguó,
they were affectionate and intimate.
Thus, she became pregnant.
After ten months, she gave birth,
and what was born was entirely water.
In another room, they were making sauce.
Xún Zé said:
"I know a mourning household should not make sauce,
but you deliberately did so.
Now the officials above are holding me accountable for a few beans,
causing me such exhaustion I can no longer bear it."
Shortly after, he vanished.
Huán Gě,
during the Tàiyuán era, served as the governor of Bādōng,
and left his family in Jiānglíng.
His wife's wet nurse, surnamed Chén,
had a son named Dàoshēng,
who followed Huán Gě to the commandery,
but fell into a rapid and drowned.
Dàoshēng appeared in form, saying:
"Now I am in the service of the River Earl,
and have been granted twenty days of leave,
to return temporarily."
His mother was overcome with grief,
and Huán Gě had a black bird
that covered her mouth with its wings,
causing a tumor to grow on her tongue,
and from then on, she could no longer cry.
Zhū Zǐzhī
In Dōngyáng Commandery, there was a man named Zhū Zǐzhī.
A ghost
would constantly come to his house.
Zǐzhī's son fell ill with heart pain.
The ghost said to him:
"I will find a remedy for you."
It said:
"If you burn tiger pills and drink them, you will be cured.
Find a large halberd and give it to me,
and I will fetch them for you."
His family then took a halberd and gave it to the ghost.
The ghost took the halberd and left,
returning after a short while.
It placed the halberd in the courtyard,
threw the tiger pills onto the ground,
which were still warm.
Yáng Xiàn
In the last years of the Xiàowǔ Emperor's Tàiyuán era,
in Wú County, there was a man named Yáng Xiàn.
There was a creature resembling a monkey,
with a human face and hair.
Whenever Xiàn ate,
the ghost would constantly snatch his food.
Xiàn's wife was weaving at the loom.
Xiàn took up a knife to kill the ghost.
The ghost ran toward the loom.
His wife's form transformed into the ghost.
Xiàn then struck her down.
He saw the ghost leap out,
clapping its hands and laughing heartily.
After the ghost left,
Xiàn finally realized what had happened.
He looked at his wife, now in more than ten pieces.
She had been pregnant for nearly six months.
The hair of the child in her womb had already grown.
Xiàn, filled with grief and remorse, died.
Wáng Zhàozōng
Wáng Zhàozōng of Tàiyuán fell ill and died.
After his death, his form appeared
and spoke with his mother, Liú, and his wife, Hán.
He approached his mother and asked for wine.
She raised a cup and gave it to him.
He said:
"Good wine."
He said to his wife:
"I will be parted from you for only three years."
When the mourning period ended, his wife fell ill.
She said:
"The principle of sharing the same grave
has always been difficult to achieve in ancient times.
If we are fortunate enough to be together as if alive,
would that not be the greatest wish?"
She then refused to take medicine and died.
Zhāng Yǔ
During the Yǒngjiā era,
the Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, Zhāng Yǔ,
was once traveling through a great marsh.
The sky was dark and gloomy.
Suddenly, he saw the gate of a house wide open.
Yǔ then went forward to the main hall.
A maidservant came out and asked him,
Yǔ said:
"I encountered rain on my journey,
and wish to ask for lodging."
The maidservant went in to report,
soon came out,
and called Yǔ forward.
He saw a woman,
about thirty years old,
sitting inside a curtained bed,
with more than twenty attending maidservants,
all dressed in splendid and beautiful clothes.
She asked Yǔ what he desired.
Yǔ said:
"I have my own food,
I only need something to drink."
The woman ordered a pot to be given to him.
He then lit a fire to make soup.
Although he heard the sound of boiling,
when he touched it, it was still cold.
The woman said:
"I am a dead person.
In the realm of graves and tombs,
I have nothing to offer you,
only shame and regret."
Sobbing, she told Yǔ:
"I am the daughter of the Sūn family of Rénchéng County.
My father was the Grand Administrator of Zhōngshān.
I was married into the Lǐ family of Dùnqiū.
I had a son and a daughter.
The son was eleven years old,
the daughter seven.
After my death,
Mr. Lǐ favored my former maidservant, Chéng Guì.
Now my children are often beaten and whipped,
not even sparing their heads and faces.
My heart and marrow are constantly in extreme pain.
I wish to kill this maidservant.
However, the energy of the dead is weak.
I must rely on something.
I entrust you to assist me in this matter.
I will richly repay you."
Yǔ said:
"Although I sympathize with your words, Madam,
because killing a person is a grave matter,
I dare not accept this task."
The woman said:
"Why would I ask you to wield the blade yourself?
I only wish for you to speak to the Lǐ family on my behalf,
telling them what I have told you.
If the Lǐ family cherishes and pities Chéng Guì,
they will certainly perform exorcism rites.
You should tell them
that you claim to know methods for suppressing and cutting off such hauntings.
When the Lǐ family hears this,
they will surely have Chéng Guì oversee the ritual.
I will then seize the opportunity to kill her."
Yǔ agreed.
At dawn, he left
and went to tell the Lǐ family,
fully reporting to them what had been said.
The Lǐ family was shocked and alarmed,
and told Chéng Guì.
Greatly afraid,
she then sought help from Yǔ.
Soon after, Yǔ saw Madam Sūn coming from outside,
with more than twenty maidservants,
all holding knives to stab Chéng Guì.
She fell to the ground dead on the spot.
Not long after,
Yǔ again passed through the marsh.
This person sent a maidservant to present him with fifty bolts of assorted colored silks in repayment.
Shào Gōng
There was a man named Shào Gōng
who suffered from malaria,
which did not heal for a year.
Later, he was living alone at a country estate.
During an attack of malaria,
he saw several small children
holding his hands and feet.
Shào Gōng then pretended to close his eyes.
Suddenly rising,
he caught one of the children,
which transformed into a yellow otter.
The others all fled.
He then tied it up and took it home,
hung it by the window,
intending to kill and eat it.
By dawn,
the otter was gone from where it hung,
and his malaria was then cured.
At that time, those who suffered from malaria
would simply call out "Shào Gōng" and be cured.
Wú Shìjì
The Magistrate of Jiāxīng, Wú Shìjì,
once suffered from malaria.
While traveling by boat, he passed by the Wǔchāng Temple.
He then sent someone to offer apologies and thanks,
begging to sever the malaria ghost.
After leaving the temple for more than twenty li,
while resting,
he suddenly dreamed of a rider on an embankment pursuing him,
seeming very swift and urgent.
Seeing Shìjì, the rider dismounted.
Together with an officer, they entered the rear of the boat,
tied up a small child and took him away.
After that, his malaria was cured.
Zhōu Zǐwén
At the end of Emperor Yuán's reign.
There was a man named Zhōu Zǐwén from Qiáo Commandery.
His childhood name was Āshǔ.
His home was in Yánlíng County, Jìnlíng Commandery.
In his youth, he hunted with bow and arrow.
Once, while hunting in the mountains,
he became separated from his companions.
Suddenly, among the mountain peaks, he saw a person,
about five feet tall,
holding a bow and arrows.
The arrowheads were about two feet wide,
white as frost and snow.
This person suddenly called out:
"Āshǔ!"
Zǐwén unconsciously answered.
This person drew his bow to the full,
aimed at Zǐwén,
who then fell prostrate,
unable to move again.
Then this person disappeared.
His hunting companions searched for Zǐwén,
found him unable to speak.
They carried him back home,
and after several days, he died.
Wáng Gōngbó
In the Jìn dynasty, there was Wáng Gōngbó,
courtesy name Zǐshēng,
a man from Kuàijī,
handsome in appearance,
skilled at playing the qín.
He served as a Gentleman of the Eastern Palace.
He requested leave to rest in Wú.
Arriving at the postal station at Chāngmén,
he played the qín under the moonlight.
Soon, a woman appeared,
followed by a maid,
who said to Gōngbó:
"I have always loved the qín;
I wish to play it with you."
Her beauty was striking.
Gōngbó kept her overnight,
and at dawn they parted.
She left him an embroidered quilt and a scented sachet as keepsakes,
and Gōngbó gave her a jade hairpin in return.
Soon, day broke.
He heard that on a neighboring boat was the deceased daughter of Liú Huìjī, the magistrate of Wú County,
and that an embroidered quilt and scented sachet were missing from her bier.
Shortly after,
officials searched all the neighboring boats,
reaching Gōngbó's boat,
where they found the items.
Gōngbó, frightened,
explained the situation,
saying:
"I also gave her a jade hairpin."
Huìjī ordered it checked,
and indeed, it was found on the deceased girl's head.
Huìjī then wept bitterly,
and addressed Gōngbó with the rites due a son-in-law.
The girl's name was Zhìhuá,
who had died at the age of sixteen.
Lǐ Jīng
Lǐ Jīng, a man from Guìyáng,
was with...
Zhū Píng, carrying a halberd, pursued him.
After walking over a hundred paces,
he suddenly saw a ghost,
over ten feet tall,
who stopped him, saying:
"Lǐ Jīng is fated to live;
how can you kill him?
Do not proceed,
or you will surely injure your hand."
Píng, in his drunkenness,
went straight to Lǐ Jīng's house,
the ghost following him.
When Píng saw Jīng,
just as he was about to strike with his blade,
he suddenly stood rigid, unmoving,
as if bound,
and indeed injured the fingers of his left hand.
He then stood in the courtyard
until evening,
when he awoke and left.
The ghost said:
"I warned you earlier;
why did you not listen?"
With these words, it vanished.
Xiè Miǎozhī
When Xiè Miǎozhī was in Wúxīng Commandery,
a subordinate named Zōu Lǎn,
riding a firewood boat, fell behind the troops.
Arriving at Píngwàng Pavilion,
at night, with wind and rain,
the vanguard halted to rest.
Lǎn, in an open boat,
had no shelter for the night.
Noticing lamplight from a house below the embankment,
he went to seek lodging.
He reached a thatched hut,
inside which was a man,
about fifty years old,
On another bed was a child,
about ten years old.
Lǎn asked to stay overnight,
and the man gladly agreed.
The child wept and sobbed,
and though the man tried to soothe him, he would not stop,
crying until dawn.
Lǎn asked the reason,
and the man said:
"This is my son.
His mother is about to remarry,
so he weeps from sadness and attachment."
At dawn, Lǎn departed.
Looking back, he saw no sign of the hut,
only two graves,
overgrown with deep grass.
On the road, he met a woman in a boat,
who said to Lǎn:
"This is no place for people to travel;
why have you come out from there?"
Lǎn told her everything he had seen the previous night.
The woman said:
"That was my son.
I truly intended to remarry,
so I came to bid farewell at the grave."
She then choked with sobs.
She went to the grave and wailed,
and did not remarry.
Péng Hǔzǐ,
young and strong with great physical strength,
often claimed there were no ghosts or spirits.
When his mother died,
a local shaman warned him:
"On a certain day, the baleful spirit will return,
and it will kill again.
You should leave to avoid it."
All the weaker members of the family
fled and hid,
but Hǔzǐ alone stayed behind.
In the middle of the night,
someone pushed the door open and entered,
went to the east and west rooms,
but found no one.
Then they entered the central room,
heading toward the mourning chamber.
Hǔzǐ, panicked and with no plan,
saw a large jar by the bed,
climbed into it,
and covered his head with a board.
He felt his mother standing on the board.
Someone asked:
"Is there no one under the board?"
His mother said:
"No."
Then they left together.
Sīmǎ Tián
Dèng Ài's temple was in Jīngkǒu,
it had only...
a thatched hut.
Jìn's General of Northern Pacification, Sīmǎ Tián,
while ill, dreamed of an old man who said:
"I am Lord Dèng.
My dwelling is collapsing;
please repair it for me."
Later, he inquired about it,
and learned it was Dèng Ài's temple,
so he built a tiled house for it.
During the Lóng'ān era,
a man and a woman were meeting on the temple's altar seat,
when a snake came
and coiled around them several times.
The woman's family, searching for her, found them,
and made offerings of wine and dried meat to pray to the deity,
only then were they freed.
Ruǎn Dérú
once saw a ghost in the latrine.
It was over ten feet tall,
with dark skin and large eyes,
wearing a plain white robe
and a flat-topped headscarf,
standing just a few feet away.
Dérú remained calm and composed,
slowly smiled and said to it:
"People say ghosts are detestable,
and indeed they are."
The ghost blushed and retreated.
Chén Qìngsūn
In Yǐngchuān, behind Chén Qìngsūn's house stood a sacred tree.
Many people came to seek blessings from it,
so a temple was built
and named the Temple of the Heavenly Deity.
Qìngsūn owned a black ox.
The deity spoke from the air:
"I am the Heavenly Deity,
and I desire your ox.
If you do not give it to me,
on the twentieth day of next month,
I will kill your son."
Qìngsūn replied:
"A person's life is governed by fate,
and fate is not determined by you."
When the day arrived,
his son indeed died.
The deity spoke again:
"If you do not give it to me,
in the fifth month, I will kill your wife."
Again, he refused to give it,
and when the time came,
his wife indeed died.
The deity spoke once more:
"If you do not give it to me,
in autumn, I will kill you."
Still, he refused to give it,
and when autumn arrived,
he did not die.
The ghost then came to apologize:
"Your heart is upright,
and you are destined for great blessings.
I beg you not to speak of this matter,
for if Heaven and Earth hear of it,
my punishment will be severe.
I merely saw a minor ghost serving as a clerk in the Department of Fate,
and learned the predetermined lifespans of your wife and son.
I used this to deceive you and demand offerings.
I sincerely hope you will forgive me.
Your recorded lifespan is eighty-three years,
and your household will prosper as you wish,
with gods and spirits protecting and aiding you.
I too shall serve you as a slave."
Then, the sound of kowtowing was heard.
Zhēn Chōng,
courtesy name Shūràng,
was a man from Zhōngshān
and served as the magistrate of Yúnshè.
Before reaching Huìhuái County,
suddenly a messenger arrived,
saying:
"The Shèláng
will arrive shortly."
He was young,
handsome and clean,
and after exchanging pleasantries upon sitting,
he said:
"My father has sent me,
admiring your noble status,
and wishes to marry his sister to you.
Thus, I have come to convey this intention."
Zhēn was startled and said:
"I am already old,
and I already have a family.
How could such a proposal be made?"
The Shèláng replied:
"My sister is young,
and her beauty is unparalleled.
She must have an excellent match.
Why do you refuse?"
Zhēn said:
"I am an old man,
and I have a wife.
How could I overstep such boundaries?"
After several rounds of back-and-forth,
Zhēn remained unmoved.
The Shèláng showed an angry expression,
saying:
"My father will come himself,
and I fear you will not be able to refuse."
After he left,
Zhēn saw people on both banks wearing headscarves,
holding horsewhips,
lined up in rows,
with a large entourage.
The Shègōng soon arrived,
with a procession and attendants like a feudal lord,
riding in a horse-drawn carriage,
with green canopies and red tassels,
and several covered carriages.
The young lady rode in a four-windowed carriage,
with dozens of embroidered screens,
and eight maidservants
approached the carriage,
wearing clothes of patterns and colors
he had never seen before.
They set up a tented pavilion on the bank beside Zhēn,
spread out mats and cushions.
The Shègōng descended,
and sat with his knees hidden.
A small table was placed,
with a white felt cushion,
and a jade spittoon.
A tortoiseshell hand-towel holder,
and he held a white yak-tail whisk.
The young lady remained on the eastern bank,
with eunuchs holding white dusters standing on both sides of the carriage,
and maidservants in front.
The Shègōng led his officials forward to sit,
about sixty in number,
and ordered music to be played,
with instruments all made of glass.
The Shègōng said to Zhēn:
"I have an unworthy daughter,
whom I deeply cherish.
Admiring your noble character and virtue,
I desire to form a marital alliance.
Thus, I sent my son
to convey this intention."
Zhēn replied:
"I am already old and frail,
and I already have a family.
My sons are grown.
Though I covet such an honorable proposal,
I dare not accept."
The Shègōng said again:
"My daughter is just twenty years old,
graceful and virtuous,
fully accomplished in the four virtues.
She is now on the bank.
Do not trouble yourself further;
simply complete the ceremony."
Zhēn refused even more firmly,
suspecting this was an evil spirit,
so he drew his sword and laid it across his knees,
resisting unto death,
and spoke no more.
The Shègōng grew furious,
and summoned three leopards and two tigers with a breath,
their mouths gaping and crimson.
They roared, splitting the earth,
and leaped straight up.
This happened dozens of times,
and they stood guard until dawn,
but to no avail,
so they left.
They left a carriage
and several dozen attendants
to escort Zhēn.
Zhēn then moved to reside in Huìhuái County,
and the carriage and attendants sent to fetch him arrived at the gate.
A man wearing a plain robe and headscarf
bowed to them,
and they stopped there,
unable to proceed.
Zhēn stayed for over ten days
before daring to leave.
He saw two men wearing headscarves and holding horsewhips
following him home.
Shortly after returning home, he fell ill
with sickness
and eventually died.
Zhāng Zǐcháng
During the Jin Dynasty,
Wǔdū Commandery Administrator Lǐ Zhòngwén
lost his daughter while serving in Shào.
She was eighteen years old
and was temporarily buried north of Shào City.
Later, Zhāng Shìzhī succeeded him as the administrator of Shào.
Shìzhī had a son named Zǐcháng,
who was twenty years old
and served as an attendant in the official residence.
He dreamed of a young woman,
around seventeen or eighteen years old,
of extraordinary beauty.
She claimed to be the daughter of the former administrator,
who had unfortunately died young,
and said it was now time for her to return to life.
Feeling affection for him,
she had come to meet him.
After five or six nights like this,
she suddenly appeared during the day.
Her clothes were exquisitely fragrant,
and they became husband and wife.
When they slept together, stains appeared on her clothes
as if she were a virgin.
Later, Zhòngwén sent a maidservant to inspect his daughter’s grave
and, passing by, paid a visit to Shìzhī’s wife.
Upon entering the residence,
the maidservant saw one of the young woman’s shoes
under Zǐcháng’s bed.
She picked it up, weeping,
and cried out that the grave had been opened.
She took the shoe back
and showed it to Zhòngwén.
Zhòngwén was shocked
and sent someone to ask Shìzhī:
"How did your son obtain my deceased daughter’s shoe?"
Shìzhī called his son and questioned him.
The son explained everything in detail.
Both Lǐ and Zhāng found it strange.
They opened the coffin to look,
and found that the young woman’s body had grown flesh,
her appearance as it was in life,
but only her right foot wore a shoe.
Zǐcháng dreamed that the young woman said to him:
"I was on the verge of returning to life,
but now my grave has been opened.
From this moment on,
my flesh will decay and die,
and I can no longer be reborn.
What more can I say
of my endless regret?"
She wept and bid him farewell.
Huán Dàomǐn
During the Jin Dynasty, Huán Dàomǐn,
a native of Qiáo,
lost his wife in the fourth year of the Lóng'ān era.
He missed her deeply,
and his grief was unending.
That year,
as he was about to sleep at night,
he saw a hand
on the screen.
He rose, took a torch,
and shone it outside the screen,
only to find it was his wife.
Her appearance and attire were just as in life.
Dàomǐn felt no fear at all
and invited her to lie down with him.
They conversed back and forth,
discussing life and death.
Dàomǐn said:
"Since your passing, there has been no trace or sound of you.
How is it that you have suddenly returned tonight?"
She replied:
"How could I return so easily?
The ways of humans and spirits are different,
each governed by their own authorities,
and we act according to our own will.
In life,
I committed few other faults,
but I constantly suspected you of favoring the maidservants.
Because of this jealousy,
I suffered retribution in hell,
and only now have I been released.
I am now to be reborn as a human,
so I have come to bid you farewell."
Dàomǐn asked:
"Where will you be reborn?
Can I find you?"
She replied:
"I only know I will be reborn,
not where.
Once I become an ordinary person,
I will no longer remember past lives.
How could you seek me out?"
At dawn, she took her leave,
weeping as they parted.
Dàomǐn escorted her to the corridor before returning.
Only then did he feel great terror,
and he remained in a daze for a long time.
Zhōu Línhè
During the Jin Dynasty, a man surnamed Zhōu from Yìxīng,
in the Yǒnghé era,
went out of the city on horseback,
accompanied by two attendants.
Before reaching the village,
night fell.
By the roadside was a small, newly built thatched hut.
He saw a young woman come out and look around,
about sixteen or seventeen years old,
with a graceful and proper appearance,
and wearing bright, clean clothes.
Seeing Zhōu pass by,
she said to him:
"It is already dark,
and the next village is still far.
How could you reach Línhè?"
Zhōu then asked to stay overnight.
The young woman lit a fire and prepared food for him.
Around the first watch,
he heard a child outside calling for Ā Xiāng.
The young woman replied:
"Yes."
Soon, the voice said:
"The officials summon you to push the thunder chariot."
The young woman then bid farewell,
saying:
"I have matters to attend to and must leave."
That night, there was a great thunderstorm.
By dawn, the young woman returned.
Zhōu mounted his horse
and looked back at where he had stayed the night,
only to see a new grave,
with horse urine and leftover grass at its entrance.
Zhōu was greatly shocked and regretful.
Five years later,
he indeed became the Administrator of Línhè.
Hú Màohuí
During the Jin Dynasty, Hú Màohuí from Huáinán
could see ghosts.
Although he did not like seeing them,
he could not stop it.
Later, he traveled to Yángzhōu
and returned to Lìyáng.
East of the city was a shrine,
where villagers were performing sacrifices with shamans.
After a short while,
a group of ghosts shouted to one another:
"The superior official is coming!"
They all fled from the shrine.
Màohuí looked back
and saw two Buddhist monks approaching,
entering the shrine.
The ghosts,
clinging to each other in twos and threes,
hid in the grass beside the shrine.
When they saw the monks,
they were all terrified.
After the monks left,
the ghosts returned to the shrine.
From then on, Màohuí devoted himself sincerely to Buddhism.
Ruǎn Zhān
Ruǎn Zhān had always upheld the theory that ghosts do not exist.
Once, a ghost gave his name
and visited him as a guest.
They exchanged pleasantries,
engaged in casual conversation,
and
discussed philosophy and logic.
The guest was very talented,
but when the topic turned to ghosts and spirits,
they debated intensely.
The guest finally defeated him in argument
and, changing his expression, said:
"Ghosts and spirits have been passed down by sages and worthies throughout history.
How can you alone claim they do not exist?"
He then transformed into a strange shape
and vanished in an instant.
Ruǎn fell silent,
his expression turning very grim.
Over a year later, he fell ill and died.
Línxiāng County Magistrate
In the early years of the Lóng’ān era,
a man from the Yīn family of Chénjùn served as the magistrate of Línxiāng.
In the county, there was a ghost,
over three zhàng tall,
who would climb onto the roof,
yet its feet still dangled to the ground.
When Yīn entered,
it would come to summon him.
Whenever it shook the screen,
or moved the windows,
his illness would worsen.
His younger brother, Guān, also saw it,
and often stood by with a drawn knife,
arguing with it.
The ghost said:
"Do not curse me,
or I will break your mouth."
The ghost suddenly vanished,
and his mouth was struck until it bled.
Later, his mouth became crooked,
and he became a disabled person.
The Gù Family
A man surnamed Gù from Wúzhōng
went to his country house.
Traveling by day,
when he was over ten lǐ from the house,
he heard faint sounds from the northwest.
Raising his head,
he saw four to five hundred people,
all dressed in red,
two zhàng tall,
who suddenly arrived.
They surrounded him in three layers,
and Gù’s breath became stifled,
unable to move.
From dawn until dusk,
the encirclement did not disperse.
He could not speak,
but in his heart, he called upon the Big Dipper.
After another mealtime passed,
the ghosts said to each other:
"His heart is truly focused on the divine,
we should let him go."
Suddenly, they vanished like mist.
Gù returned to his house,
and fell seriously ill in bed.
That night,
in front of his door,
there was a great blaze that did not burn,
and ghosts gathered in chaos.
Some came and went,
calling Gù to talk,
some pulled off his blanket,
some climbed onto his head, light as a goose feather,
and vanished by dawn.
The Clerk of Jiāngzhōu
During the Jin dynasty, when Huán Bàonú was in Jiāngzhōu,
there was a clerk named Gān,
whose home was under the jurisdiction of Línchuān Commandery.
His son, thirteen years old,
fell ill and died,
and was buried among the graves east of the house.
Ten days later,
they suddenly heard drumming and music from the eastern road,
as if from about a hundred people,
who went straight to the Gān family,
asking:
"Is the clerk here?
We have come to visit.
Your worthy son is also here."
They only heard voices,
but saw no forms.
Then they brought out two jars of wine for them,
and in a moment, they vanished,
leaving both jars empty.
When the drumming was first heard,
the governor of Línchuān thought it was people performing,
and expected them to visit him.
But then it fell silent and they did not come.
Upon hearing Gān’s account,
he was greatly astonished.
Chén Sù
In the first year of Shēngpíng of the Jin dynasty,
Chén Sù of Shànxiàn was wealthy,
but after ten years of marriage, he had no son.
The husband wanted to take a concubine,
so the wife prayed to the deities,
and suddenly became pregnant.
A neighbor’s lowly wife was also pregnant,
and they made an agreement:
"If I give birth to a boy,
it is heaven’s will;
if it is a girl,
and yours is a boy,
we shall exchange them."
They both agreed.
The neighbor gave birth to a boy,
and this woman gave birth to a girl three days later,
so they exchanged them.
Chén Sù was overjoyed,
and raised the boy until he was thirteen.
During a sacrificial ceremony,
an old maidservant in the household,
who could see ghosts,
said:
"I saw the ancestors of the master’s family
come to the gate and stop.
But I saw a group of small people
come to the altar and eat the offerings."
The father was suspicious and alarmed,
so he summoned someone who could see ghosts.
During the sacrifice, he had him observe,
and his words matched exactly.
Chén Sù then went to question his wife,
and she, in fear,
confessed the matter.
They returned the boy to his original family,
and called their daughter back.
Hú Zhāng
Hú Zhāng of Tánxiàn
and Guǎn Shuāng of Shàngyú
shared a fondness for weapons.
After Shuāng died,
Zhāng dreamed of him,
leaping and playing with blades before him,
and awoke feeling very uneasy.
The next day,
he pasted a talisman on the wall.
When Zhāng was about to travel nearby,
and had already boarded a boat and readied the oars,
he suddenly saw Shuāng come to detain him,
saying:
"We were close friends,
our bond lasting a thousand years.
Last night, I came to play with you.
You were asleep,
so I left.
Why now do you use a talisman to repel me?
A true man does not understand the principles of the world—
do you think I fear a talisman?"
Sū Sháo,
styled Xiàoxiān,
was a man of Ānpíng.
He served as magistrate of Zhōngmóu
and died.
Sháo’s paternal uncle, Chéng,
died while serving as military supervisor to the General of the Southern Army.
His sons brought the coffin back
and reached Xiāngchéng.
The ninth son, Jié,
dreamed at night of a procession of guards and attendants,
its ranks extremely solemn.
He saw Sháo,
who had someone call Jié, saying:
“You have violated the procession;
your crime warrants the punishment of head-shaving.”
Jié bowed his head to receive the shaving,
awoke in alarm and touched his head—
and found his hair already cut off.
The next evening,
sleeping with others,
he dreamed that Sháo said:
“Your head-shaving is not yet finished.”
Again he was shaved as on the previous night.
That evening,
he prepared himself very carefully,
lit bright lamps,
set up talismans and incantations,
and again dreamed of Sháo.
He was shaved as on the previous night five times.
Jié had always had beautiful hair;
in five nights,
it was all gone.
After six or seven days,
he no longer dreamed of him.
Later, Jié was in a carriage
in broad daylight
when Sháo entered from outside.
He rode a horse,
wore a black cap,
a yellow single-layer robe of fine silk,
and white socks with dark shoes.
Leaning on the carriage shaft,
Jié said to his brothers:
“The magistrate of Zhōngmóu is here.”
His brothers all stared in astonishment
but saw nothing.
They asked Sháo:
“How have you come, sir?”
Sháo said:
“I wish to be reburied,
so I have come to ask you to go.”
He said:
“I shall come again.”
He went out the door and vanished.
After several days he came again.
The brothers then sat with Sháo,
and Jié said:
“If you must be reburied,
instruct your son separately.”
Sháo said:
“I shall write a letter.”
Jié offered him a brush,
but Sháo would not take it,
saying:
“The writing of the dead differs from that of the living.”
He wrote characters for Jié,
which emerged resembling barbarian script.
Then he laughed
and immediately called Jié to write, saying:
“In ancient times, Marquis Wǔ of Wèi
floated on the Western River
and, reaching midstream,
turned to Wú Qǐ and said:
‘How splendid is the firmness of these rivers and mountains—
they are the treasure of the state of Wèi.’
I have always loved the capital Luòyáng;
whenever I came and went, entering and leaving,
I gazed upon the heights of Mángshān.
How joyful—
a tomb for ten thousand generations!
To the north, it backs against Mèngjīn,
with its vast, flowing river;
to the south, it looks upon the heavenly capital,
with its abundant splendor.
Though I never spoke of this aspiration,
I engraved it in my heart.
I did not expect to pass away so suddenly,
and my wish was not fulfilled.
I have gone ahead.
In the tenth month,
quickly rebury me.
Beside the tomb of the military supervisor,
buy a few mǔ of land—
that will be sufficient.”
When Jié spoke with Sháo,
he only saw his mouth move;
though his voice was clear and loud,
it was never heard by those beside them.
They invited Sháo into the room,
set out a seat and made offerings to him,
but he would not sit.
Nor did he partake of any offering.
They said to Sháo:
“The magistrate of Zhōngmóu always loved wine and fish;
have a little to drink.”
Sháo took the cup in hand and drank it dry,
saying:
“Excellent wine.”
Jié looked at the cup—it was empty.
After Sháo left,
the wine in the cup was as before.
He came more than thirty times in all,
and the brothers grew familiar and playful with him.
Jié asked about his doubts,
and Sháo said:
“Even matters of heaven and earth
cannot all be known.
Yán Yuān and Bǔ Shāng
are now serving as Cultured Scholars.
There are eight Cultured Scholars in all—
they are sages among ghosts.
Now there are also Xiàng Liáng, Chéng Xiánzhě, and Wú Jìzǐ.”
Jié asked how death compares to life,
and Sháo said:
“There is no difference,
except that the dead are empty
and the living are solid—
that is the difference.”
Jié said:
“Why do the dead not return to their corpses?”
Sháo said:
“Suppose one of your arms were cut off and thrown to the ground,
then stripped of flesh—
would that trouble you?
The departure of the dead from their corpses
is like that.”
Jié said:
“With lavish burials and grave mounds,
do the dead take pleasure in this?”
Sháo said:
“It makes no difference.”
Jié said:
“If it makes no difference,
why rebury?”
Sháo said:
“Now I truly have no fixed abode,
but I merely wish to express my intention from life.”
A younger brother said:
“Your son is still young,
your wife is youthful,
and the household faces difficulties—
do you care for them?”
Sháo said:
“I no longer have such feelings.”
Jié said:
“Is there a lifespan?”
Sháo said:
“Each has one.”
Jié said:
“Do you know
the lifespans of us, Jié and the others?”
He said:
“I know, and I will tell you.”
Jié said:
“What of the great epidemic this year?”
Sháo said:
“Liǔ Kǒngcái became the Duke of Tàishān
and wished to rebel,
arbitrarily taking people to form his followers.
The Northern Emperor, knowing of Kǒngcái’s actions,
has now executed and eliminated him.”
Jié said:
“Previously I dreamed you cut my hair—
whose procession were you leading?”
Sháo said:
“The Prince of Jǐnán.
You were to die,
but I, thinking to protect you,
therefore sentenced you to punishment.”
Jié said:
“Can you benefit the living?”
Sháo said:
“If the dead, of their own will, think of benefiting the living,
then I can benefit you.
But if they themselves have no such feelings,
and the living make sacrifices to seek blessings,
it is of no benefit.”
Jié said:
“When I previously dreamed of you,
was it truly meeting you?”
Sháo said:
“When the living dream of the dead,
the dead see them.”
Jié said:
"Can the grudges from when one was alive
still harm them after death?"
Sháo replied:
"Ghosts are heavily restricted from killing,
they cannot act on their own."
Jié got off the carriage,
Sháo laughed heartily at Jié's short stature,
saying:
"He resembles Zhào Línshū."
Zhào Línshū was short and small,
he was Sháo's brother-in-law.
Sháo wished to leave,
but Jié detained him,
closing the door and locking it,
so Sháo stayed a little longer.
When Sháo left,
Jié saw the door was still closed,
but Sháo had already gone.
Sháo bid farewell to Jié, saying:
"I am now appointed as a Xiūwén Láng,
bound by my duties and cannot come again."
Jié grasped his hand,
the hand felt soft and weak,
and upon holding it, he realized,
then they parted.
From then on, they were completely cut off.
Xiàhóu Kǎi,
courtesy name Wànrén,
died of illness.
Gǒunú, a young clansman of the Xiàhóu family,
who often saw ghosts,
saw Kǎi return several times.
He wanted to take a horse,
and also take his younger brother Ruǎn Gōng away.
Ruǎn fled to Gǒunú's house,
where he was persuaded and consoled,
and by winter, it stopped.
Kǎi's eldest son Tǒng
told his family:
"Last night I dreamed someone was being tied up,
I struggled with great effort,
and only then was he freed."
As soon as he finished speaking,
suddenly there was a light in the room as bright as day,
and they saw Kǎi wearing a píngshàngzé headscarf and a single-layered garment,
entering and sitting as he did in life.
He sat on the large bed against the west wall,
sorrowful and laughing as when alive,
after his voice ceased,
he then gnashed his teeth, making a sound,
saying:
"Someone easily broke into my household,
falsely accused Tǒng of hiding someone.
With his shirt torn, he was bound,
but thanks to me sending someone to rescue him,
he was freed.
I lead several dozen people,
the older ones are outside,
eight rows follow Kǎi."
Ruǎn moved the bed away from the wall,
Kǎi saw and said to Ruǎn:
"Why move the bed?"
He also said:
"A home without a master
cannot be properly inhabited."
Ruǎn replied, why not take a wife.
Kǎi said:
"You have lived with me for so many years,
yet you speak such words.
Among the ghosts, there should be one who understands."
Ruǎn asked who,
Kǎi said:
"The younger generation's intentions,
are not worth being pleased with."
He called to see his grandson,
saying:
"The young one's vitality is weak,
do not let him come near me."
He also said:
"The eldest daughter has a promising appearance,
do not hastily marry her off."
Kǎi asked Ruǎn:
"If you wish to see your deceased daughter,
I can summon her."
Ruǎn said:
"My daughter has been dead for a long time,
I do not wish to see her."
Kǎi said:
"She often wishes to see her father,
but due to restrictions, she has not been able to."
He also said:
"I originally should not have died,
I still had nine years.
The official position of Jìshì was vacant,
they summoned ten people in total,
I did not recognize them,
my writing was not selected,
they all could leave.
My writing was selected,
so I was forced to stay and fill the vacancy."
Liú Tā
Liú Tā lived in Xiàkǒu,
suddenly a ghost came
to stay at Liú's house.
At first, because it was dark,
he vaguely saw a form like a human,
wearing white cloth trousers.
From then on,
it came every few days,
no longer hiding its form,
and would not leave.
It enjoyed stealing food,
which was not considered a serious problem,
but it was still troublesome.
At first, they did not dare to scold it.
Jí Yìzǐ,
a strong and stubborn man who did not believe in ghosts,
came to Liú's house.
He said to the host:
"Where is the ghost in your house?
Call it here,
I will scold it for you now."
Immediately, they heard a sound from the roof beam.
At that time, there were many guests,
they all looked up,
and something was thrown down chaotically,
landing right on Yìzǐ's face.
Looking at it,
it was the intimate undergarment of the host's womenfolk,
still soiled and worn.
Everyone laughed heartily for amusement,
Jí was greatly ashamed,
washed his face and left.
Someone told Liú,
this ghost steals food and eats it all,
it must be a tangible being,
so poison could be used against it.
Liú then went to another house to boil yěgé,
took two shēng of the juice,
and secretly brought it back.
Toward night,
he had congee made,
placed it on the table,
and covered it with a basin.
Later, they heard the ghost coming from outside,
lifting the basin to take the congee.
After eating it,
it threw the broken bowl and left.
After a short while,
they heard it vomiting on the roof,
extremely angry,
then it beat the windows with a stick.
Liú had prepared in advance,
and fought with it,
but it did not dare to enter the house,
until around the fourth watch,
then it finally ceased.
Wáng Róng
Ānfēng Hóu Wáng Róng,
once attended a funeral at someone's home.
The host had not yet finished preparing the coffin,
and the mourners
were all present,
in the main hall.
Ānfēng was lying in his carriage,
when suddenly he saw a strange object in the air,
like a bird,
which grew larger as he stared at it.
As it drew closer,
he saw a red horse-drawn carriage,
with a person inside,
wearing a red headscarf and red clothes,
holding an axe in his hand.
Upon reaching the ground, he got out of the carriage,
walked straight into Wáng's carriage,
and sat down facing him.
He said to Wáng:
"Your spirit is clear and bright,
nothing can be hidden from you,
and since you too have a body,
I have come to follow you.
However, I must give you a word of advice.
Whenever attending funerals and burials for others,
unless they are your closest relatives,
you must not rush to go.
If it is truly unavoidable,
you should ride a black ox,
and have a bearded servant drive it.
And if you ride a white horse,
then you can ward off evil."
He said to Róng:
"You will attain the position of one of the Three Excellencies."
After speaking for a long time,
when the host was about to place the coffin for burial,
all the guests entered,
and this ghost also entered.
Once inside the door,
the ghost took up his axe,
and walked along the coffin wall.
There was a relative who approached the coffin,
wanting to bid farewell to the deceased,
and the ghost struck him squarely on the forehead with his axe,
causing him to fall to the ground immediately,
and those around helped him out.
The ghost looked at Róng from atop the coffin and laughed,
which everyone saw,
and then the ghost also left with his axe.
Wáng Zhòngwén
Wáng Zhòngwén served as the Registrar of Hénán Commandery,
and lived north of Gōushì County.
Once, when he was on leave and returning home,
he passed by a marshy area,
and saw a white dog following behind him,
which Zhòngwén greatly adored.
He wanted to take it,
when suddenly it transformed into a human-like form.
It was six feet tall,
resembling a Fāngxiàng.
Its eyes were red like fire,
grinding its teeth and chewing its tongue,
appearing very hateful.
When he tried to strike it,
it either retreated,
or tried to get into the carriage.
Zhòngwén was terrified,
and ordered his servant to beat it,
but they could do nothing to it.
So he got out of the carriage,
and together with his servant, they struck it again,
but still could not stop it.
After exhausting their strength,
they could no longer strike,
and so they abandoned the fight and fled.
They reported to a household,
and gathered over ten people,
armed with knives and torches,
and went to look for it themselves,
but by then it had disappeared.
Over a month later,
Zhòngwén suddenly saw it again,
and he and his servant fled together,
but before reaching a household,
they fell to the ground and both died.
Cài Mó
Cài Mó was summoned to serve as Grand Master of Splendid Happiness,
and while at home,
he suddenly heard crying from the southeast,
as if someone had just died.
Then he saw a young woman,
and the deceased person, both crying separately.
Not understanding what was happening,
he thought it might be a family dispute.
Suddenly, he heard the call for the soul,
and then saw the living woman.
She ascended into the sky from the air,
which he found very disturbing.
Soon after, he fell ill,
and passed away.
Another account says,
Mó was sitting in the main hall,
when he suddenly heard the soul-summoning cries from the neighboring house.
He went out to the courtyard to look,
and saw the family of the newly deceased,
where an old woman,
wearing a yellow gauze half-sleeve top,
and a light blue skirt below,
floated up into the sky.
Each time she heard a call,
she would look back,
and after three calls, she looked back three times.
She lingered for a long time,
and when the calls ceased,
she was no longer seen.
When he asked the mourning family,
they said,
the deceased was dressed exactly like that.
Yáo Yuánqǐ
Yáo Yuánqǐ from Hénèi,
lived near a mountain forest,
and his whole family often went into the wild to farm.
Only his seven-year-old daughter stayed home to watch the house,
but she gradually grew thin,
so her parents asked her,
and the girl said:
"There is often a person,
over ten feet tall with four faces,
each face having seven holes.
He calls himself the Great General of the High Heavens,
and whenever he comes, he swallows me,
and then exits directly from below.
This has happened several times."
He said:
"Be careful not to speak of me,
if you speak of me,
I will stay in your belly forever."
The whole family was horrified and distressed,
so they moved away to avoid it.
Lǘ Jiǎo
Lǘ Jiǎo from Wǔtáng, Wúxīng,
heard clapping outside early in the morning,
and went out to look.
He saw two officials wearing black headscarves,
who took him directly to the shore,
saying:
"The authorities have ordered you to take a boat to deliver beans."
They then ordered Jiǎo to row,
while the two officials pulled the ropes.
When they reached Jiāxīng Commandery,
they stopped briefly at an inn.
It was at Píngwàng Pavilion,
where Jiǎo secretly escaped and returned home.
Over ten days later,
he heard calls from outside again,
and saw the two officials, who said:
"How dare you desert and betray us?"
They took him to the boat,
which was still loaded with beans,
and again ordered him to row the boat,
while the two officials pulled the ropes.
They first arrived at the old tomb of Jiālè,
and said to Jiǎo:
"We need to pass through
a place,
and will leave you behind,
so be careful not to run away again.
If there is food and drink,
we will call you ourselves."
After a short while,
one official called Jiǎo up.
He saw a tall gate and tiled house,
filled with joyous feasting.
They then ordered Jiǎo to serve wine,
and also gave him roasted meat to eat.
As dawn approached,
the two officials said:
"We are leaving now,
you stay here."
After a moment,
all he saw were tall graves and dense trees.
Jiǎo was confused and disoriented,
and his family searched for him,
finding him only after a full day.
Soon after, he developed a large sore and died.
Sūn Zhì
Sūn Zhì of Jìn,
styled Fǎhuī,
was a native of Pányáng County in Qí.
His father, Zuò,
served as Grand Master of the Palace in Jìn.
Zhì had followed the Buddhist teachings since childhood,
and at the age of eighteen,
he died in the eighth month of the first year of the Xiánkāng era.
Zuò.
Later, the family moved to Wǔchāng.
On the eighth day of the fourth month in the third year,
the monk Yú Fǎjiē was parading a revered statue.
As he passed by their home,
the entire family, husband and wife, came out to watch,
and they saw Zhì among the crowd,
following and attending the statue’s procession.
Seeing his parents,
he knelt and greeted them,
then returned home with them.
Zuò had been ill beforehand,
but after Zhì left,
there were no other misfortunes or hauntings;
it was merely due to a lack of self-care.
He would recover by the fifth month.
After saying this, Zhì bid farewell and departed.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month that same year, he returned again.
Kneeling and bowing in greeting,
he was exactly as he had been in life.
He said that his maternal grandfather served as the Lord of Mount Tài,
and when he saw Zhì,
he called his mother by name, saying:
“Are you so-and-so’s child?
It is not yet your time to come;
how have you arrived here?”
Zhì replied that his uncle was about to come,
intending to take his place in atonement,
but there was an order to interrogate him,
and they wanted to whip him as punishment.
Zhì intervened and secured his pardon.
Zhì’s elder brother, Róng,
styled Sīyuān,
was present at his side at the time.
Zhì said to him:
“Although I have left my former body,
I am in a place of bliss.
I only study scriptures,
with no other tasks.
I hope my elder brother has no worries.
If one diligently strives,
blessings will naturally follow.
After two years of study, I will complete my training,
and shall be reborn into a royal family.
There are five hundred of us in the same cohort,
now in the Hall of Blessings.
Once our studies are complete,
we shall all ascend to the sixth heaven.
I too was originally meant to ascend,
but because I rescued my ancestors,
I became entangled by karmic bonds,
and thus will be reborn alone into a royal family.
I will return again on the seventh day of the seventh month in the fifth year.”
He foretold that Zhūchéng would suffer invasion and calamity,
citing many such instances,
all of which came to pass as he said.
The family kept it secret,
so no one else spread the tale.
He also said:
“Our ancestors have many sins requiring atonement,
so we should perform meritorious deeds for them.
I am now reborn among humans,
and need not seek further for myself,
but only to rescue our ancestors.
I urge my father and brother to diligently accumulate merit,
and when preparing food offerings,
ensure they are fresh and pure.
Those who follow the Dharma in every detail will receive the highest blessings.
Those who follow less precisely will receive lesser blessings.
If this cannot be done,
it is merely a waste of offerings.
One must maintain equality,
with a mind free of self and other,
for then blessings will be abundant.”
At the time, Zuò had a maidservant.
Before Zhì returned,
she suddenly fell gravely ill, near death.
Her entire body was in pain.
Zhì said:
“This maidservant intended to flee,
and I earlier whipped her,
so she can no longer leave.”
When questioned, the maidservant confessed
that she had indeed planned to flee,
having set a date with someone,
but when the day approached, she stayed.
Suǒ Xùn
During the Shēngpíng era,
Suǒ Xùn, Governor of Xúzhōu,
traveled by boat to Jìnlíng.
As darkness fell,
after sailing several miles along the river,
someone asked for a ride,
saying:
“My home is at Hánzhǒng.
My feet hurt and I cannot walk;
may I ride in your boat?”
During the fourth watch,
they reached Hánzhǒng,
and the man departed.
Xùn and another were pulling the boat,
crossing a ford,
but found it unusually strenuous.
He cursed the man, saying:
“I carried you for several miles,
and you just leave,
not helping to pull the boat—
I ought to give you a painful beating.”
The man then returned
and helped pull.
Without seeming to exert effort, they crossed the ford,
and the man then went straight into the burial mounds.
Xùn suspected he was not human.
He sent someone to secretly follow and watch.
The man passed through the mounds
and then vanished.
Shortly after, he reappeared
and called out at a mound:
“Lord Zài.”
Someone emerged and answered.
The man said:
“I earlier rode in someone’s boat,
and because I didn’t help pull,
the fellow wanted to beat me.
Now I must go repay him.
I’d like to borrow Gān Luó for a moment.”
Lord Zài said:
“If you harm my Gān Luó,
it won’t do.
That man meant no harm;
I was just testing him.”
Hearing this, Xùn
immediately returned to the boat.
Shortly after,
something appeared on the shore.
Red as a hundred-hú granary,
about twenty feet long,
it came straight toward the boat.
Xùn then shouted loudly:
“You rode in my boat
and didn’t help me pull.
Not getting a beating was lenient enough,
yet you go and fetch Lord Zài’s Gān Luó.
Now you want to attack me?
Today I will surely smash you to pieces!”
Gān Luó suddenly vanished,
and so they proceeded.
Féng Shù
Féng Shù of Shàngdǎng,
during the Yuánxī era of the Jìn dynasty,
served as a general in the ministerial office.
While on leave at Hǔláo,
he suddenly encountered four men,
each holding ropes and staffs,
who approached Shù.
Shù spurred his horse to avoid them.
The horse refused to advance,
and the four men each seized one of the horse’s legs,
causing it to suddenly collapse by the river.
They asked Shù:
“Do you wish to cross?”
Shù replied:
“The water is deep and unfathomable.
Since there are no boats or oars,
how could I possibly cross?
Do you simply intend to kill me?”
The four men said:
“We will not kill you,
but we must take you to the authorities.”
Then they again grasped the horse’s legs
and waded north across the river.
Shù only heard the sound of waves,
but did not feel the water.
As they neared the shore,
the four men said to each other:
“This man is impure;
how can we take him?”
At that time, Shù was in mourning for his younger brother,
and deeply feared that if the ghosts abandoned him,
he would drown and die.
So he whipped his horse into motion
and hurriedly ascended the bank.
Shù expressed his gratitude, saying:
“Since I have received your grace,
how dare I trouble you further?”
Rén Huáirén
In the first year of the Shēngpíng era of the Jìn dynasty,
Rén Huáirén was thirteen years old
and served as a clerk in the imperial office.
In his hometown, there was a man named Wáng Zǔ who also served as a petty official,
and he often favored Huáirén.
By the time Huáirén was fifteen or sixteen,
he began to harbor unusual intentions,
and Zǔ bore a grudge.
When they reached Jiāxīng,
Zǔ killed Huáirén
and buried him in a coffin at the edge of the fields belonging to Xú Zuò’s family.
Later, when Zuò stayed overnight in the fields,
he suddenly saw a grave mound.
At the morning, noon, and evening meals,
he would always share food as an offering,
calling out:
“Ghost of the field’s edge,
come and eat with me.”
When it was time to sleep at night,
he would also say:
“Come and keep me company.”
This went on for a long time.
One night, the ghost suddenly appeared and said:
“My family will hold a memorial service tomorrow to mark the end of mourning,
and the offerings will be very lavish.
You should come with me tomorrow.”
Zuò said:
“I am a living person.
I should not meet with you.”
The ghost said:
“I will conceal your form myself.”
Zuò then followed the ghost.
After about the time it takes to eat a meal,
they arrived at the ghost’s home.
The house was full of guests.
The ghost led Zuò to the spirit seat,
and as the offerings diminished,
the whole family wept and wailed,
unable to control themselves,
believing their son had returned.
When they saw Wáng Zǔ arrive,
the ghost said:
“This is the man who killed me.”
Still afraid of him,
Zǔ immediately fled.
Zuò’s form then became visible,
and the family was greatly startled.
They questioned Zuò in detail,
and he recounted the whole story.
They then followed Zuò to retrieve the body.
Once they left,
the ghost ceased to appear.
Wáng Míng
Wáng Míng’ér of Dōnglái,
who lived in Jiāngxī,
had been dead for a year
when he suddenly appeared in form.
After returning home for a day,
he summoned his relatives and close friends,
reminisced about his life,
and said:
“The heavenly court has allowed me to return temporarily.”
When he spoke of his impending departure,
his words were filled with tears.
He inquired about his hometown,
expressing deep affection.
He instructed his son, saying:
“Since I left the human world,
a full cycle has passed,
and I long to see my homeland.”
He ordered his son to accompany him to view their hometown.
As they passed by Dèng Ài’s temple,
he ordered it to be burned down.
His son was greatly alarmed and said:
“Ài was a general of the eastern expedition during his lifetime,
and after his death, he became a spirit.
The people make offerings to him to pray for blessings.
Why burn it down?”
Angrily, he said:
“Ài is now polishing armor in the imperial workshop,
with his ten fingers worn down.
How could he possibly have divine power?”
He then said:
“General Wáng is also reborn as an ox,
driven until nearly dead.
Huán Wēn is a soldier,
suffering together in hell.
These individuals are all exhausted and at their wits’ end;
how could they bring benefit or harm to people?
If you wish to seek abundant blessings,
you must be respectful and cautious,
and fulfill loyalty and filial piety.
Do not harbor resentment or anger,
and goodness will flow endlessly.”
He also instructed that fingernails and toenails be kept,
as they could be used to redeem sins after death.
He also advised making high thresholds,
for when ghosts enter people’s homes
to record their wrongdoings,
if they trip over the threshold,
they will forget the matters.
Wáng Biāozhī
