Wáng Biāozhī of the Jìn dynasty,
when young and not yet an official,
once sat alone in his study,
with bamboo in front of him.
Suddenly, he heard a sighing voice,
and Biāozhī became alarmed.
It strangely resembled his mother’s voice,
so he went to look.
He saw his mother dressed as in the past,
and Biāozhī knelt and bowed, weeping.
His mother said:
“You are about to face a strange calamity.
From now on,
you will see a white dog every day.
If you can travel east for a thousand lǐ,
for three years,
then you will be spared disaster.”
Suddenly, she disappeared.
Biāozhī grieved and lamented until dawn.
When it grew light,
he saw only a white dog.
It constantly followed him wherever he went.
So he prepared his bamboo luggage
and set off for Kuàijī.
Once he had traveled beyond a thousand lǐ,
what he had seen vanished completely.
After three years, he returned
and again stayed in his former study.
Suddenly, he heard the earlier voice,
and went to see his mother as before.
She said:
“Because you followed my instructions,
I have come to congratulate you.
From now on,
you will live past eighty,
and hold a high position in the imperial court.”
Everything happened as his mother had said.
Wáng Níngzhī
Wáng Níngzhī of Lángyá, a left general of the Jìn dynasty,
had a wife, Madame Xiè,
who suddenly lost her two sons.
Overwhelmed with grief,
she wept for six years.
Later, she suddenly saw both sons return,
each wearing shackles.
They comforted their mother, saying:
“You must restrain your grief.
We both have sins for which we are being punished,
and you should perform good deeds on our behalf.”
Only then did she cease her mourning
and diligently seek blessings for them.
Yáo Niú
A commoner from Xū County named Yáo Niú,
was over ten years old.
His father had been killed by a fellow villager.
Yáo Niú once sold
his clothes
to buy swords and halberds,
planning to take revenge.
Later, he encountered the man in front of the county office gate.
He stabbed him to death in the crowd,
and the officials arrested him.
The magistrate deeply sympathized with his filial devotion,
so he delayed handling the case.
When an amnesty was issued, Yáo Niú was pardoned.
Moreover, the provincial and commandery authorities argued for his rescue,
so he ultimately faced no further consequences.
Later, when the magistrate went out hunting,
he chased a deer into the grass,
where there were several old, deep wells.
As his horse was about to rush toward them,
he suddenly saw an old man
raise his staff and strike the horse.
The horse, startled, swerved away,
and he failed to catch the deer.
The magistrate ordered his servant to draw his bow and shoot the old man,
but the old man said:
"There are wells here;
I was afraid you might fall into one."
The magistrate asked:
"Who are you?"
The old man knelt respectfully and said:
"I am the father of Yáo Niú.
I am grateful that you spared my son's life,
so I came to thank you."
With that, he vanished.
Huán Gōng
Huán Gōng served as an aide to Huán Shímín.
While in Dāntú,
his residence
had a small sunken pit in front of his bed.
Upon closer inspection, it turned out to be an ancient tomb,
and the coffin had already decayed.
Whenever Huán ate,
he would first toss some fish and rice into the pit,
and he did this for years.
Later, while sleeping, he awoke
to see a man standing before his bed, saying:
"Since my death,
over seven hundred years have passed.
My descendants have died out,
and no one offers sacrifices to me anymore.
Yet you consistently share your food with me;
I am endlessly grateful for your virtue.
According to your official record,
you are destined to become the Governor of Níngzhōu."
Later, it indeed happened as he said.
Ruǎn Yúzhī
In the tenth year of the Tàiyuán era of the Jìn dynasty,
Ruǎn Yúzhī lived in front of the Buddhist temple in Shǐxīng.
He had been orphaned young and lived in poverty, unable to establish himself,
and wept incessantly.
Suddenly, he saw a ghost
writing on a brick,
and placing it before him, saying:
"Your father has died and returned to the underworld;
why do you weep for so long?
Within the next three years,
your family will be able to establish itself.
I will temporarily reside in your home,
ensuring no losses occur.
Do not fear me as an evil spirit;
I intend to bring you good fortune."
Afterward, the ghost constantly stayed in his home.
Whenever the household needed something,
the ghost provided it.
After two or three years,
Ruǎn's situation improved slightly.
He prepared food for the ghost,
and they chatted, laughed, and conversed together.
Ruǎn asked for his name,
and the ghost replied:
"My surname is Lǐ, given name Liúzhī,
and I am your brother-in-law."
Ruǎn asked:
"How did you come here?"
The ghost said:
"My punishment has been completed,
and now I am temporarily in the ghost realm,
staying at your home for a while.
In four or five years, I will leave."
Ruǎn asked:
"Where will you go then?"
The ghost replied:
"I will be reborn into the human world."
When the time came,
he indeed bid farewell and left.
Liú Chéng
In the fifth year of the Yìxī era of the Jìn dynasty,
Liú Chéng from Péngchéng
often saw ghosts.
When he served as Left Guard Marshal,
his office was adjacent to that of General Cháo.
Liú Chéng would visit Cháo at night to sit and talk.
He saw a child in a reddish-brown garment,
holding a red banner,
round like a lotus flower.
A few days later,
Cháo's residence suffered a major fire.
Liú Dàoxī
Liú Dàoxī and his younger cousin Kāngzǔ
never believed in ghosts when they were young.
Their elder cousin Xīngbó,
however, had been able to see ghosts since childhood.
They would argue about it,
but neither could convince the other.
Once, at the eastern side of their residence by Chángguǎng Bridge in Jīngkǒu,
Xīngbó said:
"There is a murderous ghost
on the eastern fence."
Liú Dàoxī laughed
and asked for its exact location.
He dragged Xīngbó along with him,
grasping a large knife, intending to chop it.
Xīngbó called out from behind:
"The ghost is attacking you!"
Before Liú Dàoxī could reach the ghost,
he heard what sounded like a heavy staff striking.
Liú Dàoxī fell to the ground
and did not wake until the next day.
It took a full month for him to recover.
Later, Xīngbó said again:
"On the mulberry tree at the eastern end of the hall,
there is a ghost.
It still looks like a child,
but when it grows up, it will surely harm people."
Kāngzǔ did not believe him
and asked how high up in the tree it was.
Xīngbó pointed to the exact spot.
More than ten days later,
on the last evening of the month,
Liú Dàoxī sneaked over in the darkness
and stabbed the spot where the ghost resided with a halberd.
He then returned,
with no one knowing about it.
The next day,
when Xīngbó came early in the morning,
he suddenly exclaimed in surprise:
"How did someone manage to stab this ghost last night?
It is nearly dead,
completely unable to move,
and likely won't survive much longer."
Kāngzǔ laughed heartily.
Zhào Jí
The former Captain of Yè County, Zhào Jí,
often stayed in the fields.
Long ago, a lame man had died
and was buried by the path.
More than twenty years later,
a traveler from afar
passed by outside Zhào's gate.
After walking a dozen or so steps,
he suddenly began to limp.
Zhào, puzzled, asked him why,
and the traveler laughed and said:
"There was a lame ghost ahead,
so I imitated it as a joke."
Sīmǎ Lóng
In the Eastern Wei, there was a man named Xú,
whose given name is forgotten.
He returned to serve as a soldier in his native commandery.
His tomb is located on Líng Mountain in Dōng'ān.
The tomb was first opened by someone,
and the coffin was already damaged.
While Xiè Xuán was in Péngchéng,
Sīmǎ Lóng of Qí Commandery, his younger brother Jìn, and Wáng Xiāng of Dōng'ān, among others,
together took the damaged coffin
and divided it to make carts.
Shortly after, all three men fell ill,
passing the affliction among themselves,
with misfortunes unceasing.
Xiāng's mother, in a spirit-possessed state, told her descendants:
"Xiāng, along with Sīmǎ Lóng and his brother,
took the coffin from Prefect Xú's tomb to make carts.
The deaths and ruin of Lóng and the others
all stem from this."
Guō Fān
Guō Fān of the Jin dynasty,
styled Chángxiáng,
was from Wǔchāng.
He was a disciple of Jìng Yán.
He declined summons and appointments.
Several days after his death,
his youngest son suddenly seemed as if struck by a malignant influence,
no longer recognizing people,
and spoke in a spirit-possessed voice,
the tone and sound exactly like his father's.
He knew much about the underworld,
He answered all questions asked.
In the past, Yǔ Liàng had wished to recruit him as a senior aide,
but he did not accept.
His family asked:
"In life you possessed fine virtue,
and in death have become a divine spirit.
Do you now hold an official position?"
He replied:
"I originally had no ambition for official advancement.
Because,
Duke Yǔ wished to recruit me,
I was unwilling,
and was released.
I managed to escape.
Now I am again bound and fettered,
unable to follow my original wish,
hence this sorrow,
This sorrow."
They asked:
"What office does Yǔ hold now?"
He replied:
"He is employed by Heaven,
serving as General-in-Chief Who Pacifies the Army.
He currently resides,
east of the Eastern Sea,
commanding divine troops.
He took me as his Marshal.
He originally wished to appoint Xiè Rén for that selection,
but considered his qualifications and prestige insufficient.
Moreover, Marquis Jiǎng Dà had already taken him as Commandant,
therefore it was not possible."
Then,
They asked:
"What office does Grand Commandant Táo hold?"
He replied:
"Táo's hardship is indescribable.
He is currently in a period of punishment and exile.
After this,
he will be greatly reinstated and employed."
They asked further:
"What position does Chancellor Wáng hold now?"
He answered:
"Duke Wáng serves as a Gentleman in the Imperial Secretariat,
Greatly constrained, he manages myriad affairs.
Although his rank is not equal to when he was alive,
his nobility and influence are no different."
The people said:
"After death, do you still think of,
those left behind?"
Chángxiáng said:
"After death for a long time,
one no longer thinks of the living.
As for me, having just died,
personal feelings
have not yet ceased,
so I still have thoughts."
The spirit, speaking through the child,
requested paper and brush,
wishing to write a letter to relatives and old friends.
He took the brush to dictate,
The child wrote it down.
The writing was all horizontal,
resembling foreign script.
After completing one sheet,
he said:
"This is ghost script,
no human can recognize it."
He had someone hold the paper,
and dictated orally to compose the letter.
After finishing the letter,
the people said
that Sū Xiàoxiān often spoke like this for a long time.
Then he later composed and recited two poems, saying:
"My spirit scattered, ascending the lofty heavens,
My bodily form suddenly perished.
Recalling past,
former aspirations,
My essence and soul wander freely again.
Holding to my heart's intent, I could not follow the command,
Unable to avoid what the times demanded.
Briefly I tell my dear ones,
fearing,
they will call my words demonic and forget."
Greatly gone, without awareness; in the past there was Sū Sháo,
and then the voice ceased and he departed.
Wáng Yuànzhī
Wáng Yuànzhī of Guànghàn
served as Magistrate of Xìn'ān.
While in the county,
suddenly a ghost appeared,
claiming his surname was Cài and his given name Bójiē.
Soon he discussed poetry,
and his knowledge spanned past and present,
with nothing he was not versed in.
Asked if he was the former Cài Yōng,
he replied:
"No,
I merely share the same surname and style."
Asked where the former Bójiē is now,
he said:
"In heaven, he has become an immortal,
truly,
receiving blessings,
very happy.
He is no longer as he was in the past."
Qiānténg,
in the third year of the Xiánhé era, served as the Prefect of Pèi Commandery.
He often traveled without restraint.
He dreamed of a man in black clothes who told him:
"Why do you travel so incessantly?
You must only cut off the horse's hooves."
Later, when Qiānténg went on a journey,
the horse's hooves broke off on their own.
Once, while traveling near the outskirts of the city,
suddenly,
It grew dark,
and there appeared a man,
over ten feet tall,
wearing a black cap and white clothes.
From afar, he shouted at the carriage driver,
ordering him to make way.
Soon after,
The tall man approached,
struck the driver with a horsewhip,
and the driver immediately fell.
When dawn broke,
the attendants looked and found the carriage empty.
They searched for Qiānténg's whereabouts,
He was there,
walking sixty or seventy paces away.
They saw him in the thicket,
sitting leaning on a small table,
saying:
"I had no awareness of it at all."
Fifty days later, Qiānténg was executed.
The New Ghost
There was a newly deceased ghost,
whose form was emaciated and exhausted.
Suddenly, he saw a friend from his lifetime,
who had been dead for over twenty years,
looking plump and healthy.
They greeted each other, and the friend asked:
"Why are you like this?"
The new ghost replied:
"I am starving,
almost unable to endure it.
You know many methods,
so you must teach me a way."
The friend ghost said:
"This is very easy.
Just haunt people,
and they will be greatly frightened,
then they will give you food."
The new ghost went to the eastern end of a large village,
where there was a family devoted to Buddhism and diligent in practice.
In the western wing of the house, there was a millstone.
The ghost went and pushed it,
This millstone,
moved as if pushed by a person.
The head of the household said to his family:
"The Buddha pities our poverty,
and has sent a ghost to push the millstone.
Let us bring wheat for it."
By evening,
the ghost had ground several hu of wheat,
and left utterly exhausted.
He then scolded his friend ghost:
"Why did you deceive me?"
The friend ghost replied:
"Just go again,
and you will surely succeed."
He then went to a house at the western end of the village,
a family devoted to Daoism.
Beside the gate, there was a rice-pounding mortar.
The ghost climbed onto the mortar
and pretended to pound rice for them.
The master of the house said:
"Yesterday, a ghost helped so-and-so,
and now it has come to help us.
Let us bring grain for it."
He also had the maidservants winnow and sieve the grain.
By evening,
the ghost was utterly exhausted,
but received no food.
The ghost returned at dusk,
furious, saying:
"I am related to you by marriage,
unlike others.
How could you deceive me?
I helped people for two days,
but did not get even a bowl of food or drink."
The friend ghost said:
"It was just your misfortune.
These two families are devoted to Buddhism and Daoism,
and their hearts are hard to move.
Now, go and haunt an ordinary household,
and you will surely succeed."
The ghost went out again
and found a household
with a bamboo pole at the gate.
He entered through the gate.
Inside, he saw a group of women
eating together by the window.
He went into the courtyard.
There was a white dog,
so he picked it up and made it float in the air.
The family was greatly alarmed at the sight,
saying they had never seen such a haunting before.
A diviner said:
"There is a guest ghost demanding food.
You should kill the dog,
along with sweet fruits, wine, and rice,
and offer them in the courtyard as a sacrifice.
Then there will be no further trouble."
The family followed the diviner's instructions,
and the ghost indeed obtained a great deal of food.
From then on, he often haunted people,
all thanks to his friend ghost's teaching.
Liú Qīngsōng
Liú Qīngsōng of Guǎnglíng
woke up one morning
and saw a man in official attire
holding a tablet, who said:
"You are summoned to serve as the Prefect of Lǔ Commandery."
After speaking, he left.
After he left, he was never seen again.
The next day, he returned
and said:
"You must assume your post now."
Liú Qīngsōng knew he was destined to die,
so he went in to inform his wife and children
and arranged his family affairs.
He bathed and waited until late afternoon.
Then he saw carriages, horses, and officials waiting on him.
Liú Qīngsōng suddenly passed away.
His family all saw him ascend the carriage,
travel south for over a hundred paces,
gradually rise higher, and disappear.
Yǔ Liàng
When Yǔ Liàng was stationed in Jīngzhōu,
he once went to the latrine
and suddenly saw a creature inside.
It resembled a Fāngxiàng spirit,
with completely red eyes
and a glowing body,
slowly emerging from the ground.
Yǔ Liàng rolled up his sleeves,
struck it with his fist,
and with the impact, a sound was heard
as it shrank back into the ground.
After this, he fell ill
and eventually died.
Sīmǎ Yì
Sīmǎ Yì, a commander of the Imperial Guards, had a concubine named Bìyù
who was skilled in playing stringed instruments and singing.
During the Tàiyuán era, Sīmǎ Yì fell gravely ill
and said to Bìyù:
"After I die,
you must not marry another.
If you do, I will kill you."
She replied:
"I will obey your command."
After his burial,
a neighbor wanted to marry her,
and Bìyù was about to leave.
Suddenly, she saw Sīmǎ Yì riding a horse through the gate,
drawing his bow and shooting her,
hitting her directly in the throat.
Her throat immediately began to ache severely,
her demeanor became abnormal,
and she suddenly collapsed.
More than ten days later, she revived,
but could not speak.
Her limbs felt as if they had been beaten.
After a year, she was finally able to speak,
though still not clearly.
Bìyù was not particularly beautiful in appearance.
She had been taken in primarily for her voice.
After suffering this affliction,
she was unable to marry.
Lǐ Yuánmíng
In the former Tang,
Lǐ Yuánmíng,
was once lying on his bed,
in the middle of the night,
suddenly heard someone calling:
"Yuánmíng, Yuánmíng."
After a long time,
He then went out to respond,
and two people immediately seized him and took him away.
They entered under a house,
left him there,
and he did not know where he was.
After some time had passed,
finally,
He saw little.
Slowly feeling the bed he was sitting on,
it was a coffin,
and the four walls were all tombs.
Terrified and uneasy,
he wanted to leave,
but it was difficult,
As if ascending to heaven,
he could no longer get out.
His family searched left and right,
not knowing where he had gone,
so they led the servants,
Then they all loudly called his name,
Yuánmíng heard from within the tomb,
and distantly responded,
so they broke open the door and got him out.
Zhāng Kǎi
□ city Zhāng Kǎi,
in the second year of Jiànwǔ,
was returning home from the wilderness.
He saw a person lying by the side of the road,
asked him,
and he said:
"My foot is sick,
I can no longer go on,
my home is in Nánchǔ,
and I have nowhere to turn."
Kǎi pitied him,
and having a cart behind carrying goods,
he abandoned them to carry him.
Once they reached home,
this person showed no sign of gratitude,
and moreover said to Kǎi:
"Actually, I wasn't sick before,
I was just testing you."
Kǎi angrily said:
"Who are you,
that you dare to make a fool of me?"
He replied:
"I am a ghost,
sent by the Northern Terrace to come and collect you.
Seeing you are a respectable person,
I could not bear to take you,
so I pretended to be sick lying by the roadside.
You earlier abandoned your goods to carry me,
I truly appreciate this gesture.
However, I was ordered to come,
and have no freedom,
what can I do?"
Kǎi was shocked.
He asked the ghost to stay.
And offered a pig and wine to sacrifice to him.
The ghost shared in the libation.
Then, weeping,
he firmly begged for rescue,
the ghost said:
"Is there anyone with the same name as you?"
Kǎi said:
"There is a sojourner named Huáng Kǎi."
The ghost said:
"You can go to him,
I will go there myself."
Kǎi arrived at the home,
the host came out to see,
the ghost marked his head with a red marker,
then turned his hand,
and pierced his heart with a small dagger.
The host felt it,
the ghost then went out,
and said to Kǎi:
"You have a noble appearance,
I pity you for it,
so I have broken the law to help you.
However, the ways of the spirits are mysterious and secret,
and cannot be revealed."
Kǎi later left,
the host suddenly had heart pain,
and died by midnight.
Kǎi lived to sixty,
and reached the position of Guānglù Dàfū.
Yǔ Shàozhī
Jìn Xīnyě Yǔ Shàozhī,
childhood name Dàofù,
was the Tàishǒu of Xiāngdōng.
He and Nányáng Zōng Xié,
were cousins,
and their affection was deep.
Shào died of illness at the end of Yuánxīng,
during Yìxī,
he suddenly appeared in form to visit Xié.
His appearance and clothes,
were exactly as in life,
but his two feet wore shackles.
After arriving,
he removed the shackles, placed them on the ground, and sat.
Xié asked why he had come to visit,
he replied:
"I am temporarily granted leave to return,
and because of our close friendship,
I came to visit you."
Xié asked about matters of ghosts and spirits,
his words were vague and general,
not very detailed in response.
He only said:
"You should diligently strive.
Do not kill living beings,
if you cannot completely abstain,
do not slaughter oxen.
When eating meat,
do not eat the heart of creatures."
Xié said:
"The five organs and the meat,
are they different?"
He replied:
"The heart is the dwelling of the spirit.
Its sin is especially heavy."
He asked in detail about relatives.
Then they talked about worldly affairs.
Finally, he asked for wine,
Xié at the time had Zhūyú wine,
so he set it out for him.
When the wine came, he did not drink from the cup,
saying it had the smell of Zhūyú.
Xié said:
"Do you dislike it?"
He replied:
"All we officials fear it,
not just me."
Shàozhī as a person,
his speech was loud and strong,
when speaking now,
was no different from usual days.
After a while,
Xié's son Suìzhī came.
Shào heard the sound of clogs,
showed extreme fear,
and said to Xié:
"The vitality of the living oppresses me,
I can no longer stay.
I will part from you for three years."
Then he put on the shackles and stood up,
went out the door and vanished.
Xié later became Zhèngyuán Láng,
and indeed died after three years.
Wéi Shì
There was a man from Āndìng surnamed Wéi.
During the northern campaign against Yáo Hóng, he returned to the state.
Upon reaching the capital,
he stayed at the home of a relative or friend.
At that time, there was turmoil,
A guest from Qí came to visit him,
and Wéi said:
"Although I am now free from worries,
my body and energy are weak,
and I have no strength.
I long to make a soup,
but I am unable to do so,
which has brought me great sorrow.
In the middle of the night, I fell into a deep sleep."
Suddenly, someone knocked on the bed and came to tell him,
The person said:
"An official has given you money."
Startled, he went outside,
and suddenly, a thousand coins were there.
He also saw a black gauze cap.
A man wearing a headscarf and holding a tablet stood with his back to the door.
Wéi called the host to look together.
By the time they came, the man was no longer visible,
so they took the money,
and used it.
Hú Fùzhī
Hú Fùzhī of Shàngjùn
married a woman surnamed Lǐ.
For over ten years, they had no children, and then his wife passed away.
He wept bitterly:
"You have left no offspring;
how deep is my sorrow and bitterness?"
Suddenly, his wife sat up and said:
"Moved by your grief and mourning,
I have not yet decayed.
You may come in after nightfall.
Later, approach me.
As in life,
I will bear you a son."
After speaking, she lay back down.
Fùzhī did as she said,
not taking a lamp or candle.
He approached her in the darkness.
She spoke again:
"The dead have no life force.
You may build a side room to place me in.
Wait.
Observe until the full ten months have passed, then bury me."
Afterward, he felt his wife's body slightly warm,
as if she were not dead.
After ten months had passed,
she gave birth to a boy,
and the boy was named Língchǎn.
Jiǎ Yōng
Jiǎ Yōng, the governor of Yùzhāng,
possessed divine arts.
He went beyond the border to fight bandits,
was killed by them,
and lost his head.
He mounted his horse and returned to camp,
speaking from his chest:
"The battle did not go well;
I was wounded by bandits.
Gentlemen, do you think it is better to have a head,
or not to have a head?"
The officials wept and said:
"It is better to have a head."
Yōng said:
"Not so;
it is also good not to have a head."
After speaking, he died.
Sòng Dìngbó
Sòng Dìngbó of Nányáng,
when he was young,
encountered a ghost while walking at night.
He asked it,
and the ghost said:
"I am a ghost."
The ghost asked:
"And who are you?"
Dìngbó deceived it,
saying:
"I am also a ghost."
The ghost asked:
"Where do you wish to go?"
He replied:
"I wish to go to the market in Wǎn."
The ghost said:
"I also wish to go to the market in Wǎn."
So they walked several miles together.
The ghost said:
"Walking is too slow.
We could take turns carrying each other;
what do you think?"
Dìngbó said:
"Excellent."
The ghost first carried Dìngbó for several miles.
The ghost said:
"You are too heavy;
you are not a ghost."
Dìngbó said:
"I am a new ghost,
so my body is still heavy."
Dìngbó then carried the ghost,
and the ghost was almost weightless.
They did this several times.
Dìngbó said again:
"I am a new ghost,
and I do not know what things ghosts dislike or fear."
The ghost replied:
"They only dislike being spat on."
So they continued on together.
On the way, they encountered water.
Dìngbó told the ghost to cross first,
and listened as it crossed without making a sound.
Dìngbó crossed himself,
making splashing noises.
The ghost said again:
"Why are you making noise?"
Dìngbó said:
"I have just died,
so I am not used to crossing water.
Do not be suspicious of me."
As they were about to reach the market in Wǎn,
Dìngbó lifted the ghost onto his shoulder
and quickly seized it.
The ghost cried out loudly,
making a chattering sound,
and begged to be let down,
but Dìngbó paid no heed.
He went straight into the market in Wǎn,
set it down on the ground,
and it transformed into a goat.
He then sold it.
Fearing it might change back,
he spat on it.
He received fifteen hundred coins,
and then left.
At the time, people said:
"Dìngbó sold a ghost,
and got fifteen hundred coins."
Lǚ Guāng
In the first year of Chéngkāng under Lǚ Guāng,
a ghost cried out in the capital streets:
"Brothers destroy each other, and the people suffer."
Patrol officers searched for it,
but found nothing.
That year, Guāng died,
and his son Shào succeeded him.
Five days later,
Shào's half-brother Cuàn
killed Shào and took the throne himself.
Táo Kǎn,
courtesy name Shìzhú,
once went to the latrine
and saw several dozen people,
all holding large seals.
One man, wearing plain clothes and a flat-topped headscarf,
called himself the Hòudì,
and said:
"You are a noble man,
so I have appeared to you.
Do not speak of this for three years,
and you will attain the highest wealth and honor."
Kǎn then stood up,
and in an instant, they vanished.
There was a large seal with the character for "duke"
in the filthy place.
The Miscellaneous Five Elements Book says:
"The latrine deity is called Hòudì."
Xiè Shàng
Xiàhóu Hóng claimed to see ghosts,
and could speak with them.
The horse ridden by Xiè Shàng, General of the West, suddenly died,
causing him great distress and annoyance.
He said:
"If you can make this horse live again,
then you truly have seen ghosts."
Hóng left for a long while,
then returned and said:
"The temple god liked your horse,
so he took it.
It should revive."
Shàng sat facing the dead horse,
and in a moment,
the horse suddenly ran back from outside the gate,
reached the horse's corpse,
and then vanished.
Immediately, the horse could move and rise to walk.
Xiè said:
"I have no heir—
is this a punishment upon me alone?"
For a time, Hóng had nothing to report,
saying:
"What I have seen recently are only minor ghosts;
they certainly cannot discern the reason for this."
Later, he suddenly encountered a ghost
riding in a new carriage,
followed by about ten attendants,
dressed in blue silk cloth robes.
Hóng stepped forward and grasped the ox's nose.
The person in the carriage said to Hóng:
"Why do you block my way?"
Hóng said:
"I wish to ask something.
General of the West Xiè Shàng has no son.
This gentleman is refined and esteemed—
should he be left without descendants to carry on his sacrifices?"
The person in the carriage, moved, said:
"The one you speak of
is precisely my son.
In his youth,
he had relations with a maid in the household,
vowing not to marry anyone else, but then broke that vow.
Now that maid has died
and has brought a complaint against him in heaven.
That is why he has no son."
Hóng reported all of this in detail.
Shàng said:
"In my youth, I truly did have such an affair."
Hóng, while in Jiānglíng,
saw a large ghost
carrying a spear and halberd,
with several minor ghosts following.
Hóng, afraid,
stepped off the road to avoid them.
After the large ghost passed,
he caught one of the minor ghosts.
He asked what this thing was,
and it said:
"People are killed with this spear and halberd.
If it strikes the heart or abdomen,
none fail to die immediately."
Hóng said:
"Is there a remedy for this illness?"
The ghost said:
"Apply a black chicken to it,
and it will be cured."
Hóng also asked:
"Where are you going now?"
The ghost said:
"We are heading to the two provinces of Jīng and Yáng."
At that time, for days on end, heart and abdominal illnesses occurred,
and there were none who did not die.
Hóng then taught people to kill black chickens and apply them,
and in eight or nine out of ten cases, it worked.
Nowadays, when there is a sudden evil affliction,
they immediately use a black chicken application—
this originated from Hóng.
A soldier from Xiāngyáng,
Jìn Tài.
In the early Yuán period,
Fú Jiān sent his general Yáng Ān to invade Xiāngyáng.
One of the soldiers died in the army,
and a fellow townsman escorted the coffin back.
They were due to arrive home the next day.
That night, the deceased appeared to his wife in a dream and said:
"What they are sending is not my corpse.
In the granary,
the one under the happy-faced one is mine.
You once made a hair knot for me, and it is still there.
You can untie it and see, then you will know."
When dawn came,
the funeral procession indeed arrived.
The wife told her mother this,
but the mother did not believe it.
The wife herself went to Nánfēng to carefully examine
the corpse from another family.
The hair was as before, clearly showing it was his handiwork.
Lǚ Shùn
Lǚ Shùn lost his wife
and wished to marry her cousin.
He therefore built three tombs.
When the construction was nearly complete,
it repeatedly failed to be finished.
One day, Shùn was lying down during the day
when he saw his wife come to lie with him,
her body cold as ice.
Shùn, because of the separation between life and death,
told her to leave.
Later, the wife also appeared to her cousin,
angrily saying:
"There are countless men in the world;
why must you share a husband with me?
The tomb cannot be completed
because I am causing it."
Soon after, both husband and wife died.
Huán Gōng
Huán Gōng and Huán Ān,
served as army advisors,
stationed in Dānyáng.
In their residence,
there was a sunken hole in front of the bed.
Upon closer inspection, it appeared to be an ancient tomb;
looking inside, there was indeed a decayed coffin.
Every time Gōng ate,
he would first throw some rice into the hole.
After a year of this,
he suddenly saw a person in front of his bed,
who said:
"I have been dead for over seven hundred years;
my descendants have died out,
and no seasonal offerings are made to me.
I have often received food from you;
touched by your virtue,
I will repay you with the position of Prefect of Níngzhōu."
Not long after, he was indeed promoted.
Yǔ Chóng
Yǔ Chóng,
during the Jiànyuán era,
drowned in Jiāngzhōu.
That same day, he returned home in visible form,
just as in life,
often in the room of his wife, Lè shì.
At first, his wife was afraid,
and often called her female cousins to keep her company.
Gradually, the companionship became less frequent,
and sometimes they only came briefly.
The ghost would then angrily scold:
"You are greedy for contact with the living.
Instead, you suspect and dislike me—
does this match my intention in returning?"
Once, the female cousins were inside spinning,
when suddenly the spinning tools floated in the air,
something messed them up,
or threw them to the ground.
The cousins, terrified, all left,
and the ghost then appeared frequently.
There was a boy,
only three years old,
who went to his mother asking for food.
The mother said:
"We have no money—
how can we get food?"
The ghost then became sorrowful,
stroked his son's head, and said:
"I unfortunately died early,
leaving you in poverty.
I am ashamed and think of you—
how boundless are my feelings."
Suddenly, he placed two hundred coins in front of his wife,
saying:
"You can buy food for the child."
After a year of this,
the wife became increasingly poor and unable to sustain herself.
The ghost said:
"Since you have remained chaste,
yet are so poor and suffering,
I should just come to fetch you."
Not long after,
the wife fell ill and died,
and the ghost then became silent.
Cáo Gōng's ship
At the Rúxū estuary, there is a large ship,
which capsized and sank in the water.
When the water level is low, it becomes visible.
The elders say:
"This is Lord Cáo's ship."
Fishermen often spend the night beside it,
tying their boats to it.
They only hear the sounds of reed pipes, flutes, strings, and singing,
and an extraordinary fragrance,
which allows the fishermen to finally fall asleep.
In their dreams, someone drives them away, saying:
"Do not approach the official courtesans."
It is said that
Lord Cáo's ship carrying courtesans capsized here,
and it remains there to this day.
Wáng Zhìdū
Mǎ Zhòngshū and Wáng Zhìdū,
both from Liáodōng,
were the closest of friends.
Zhòngshū died first.
Years later, he suddenly appeared in form,
saying:
"I unfortunately died early,
and my heart constantly misses you.
Thinking that you have no wife,
I shall obtain a wife for you.
Expect her by the twentieth day of the eleventh month,
when she will be sent to your home.
Just clean up and prepare a bed with mats to await her."
When the day arrived,
Zhìdū secretly cleaned and prepared everything.
Suddenly, a great wind arose,
turning the bright day dark as night.
By evening, the wind ceased.
In the bedroom, a red curtain suddenly unfurled by itself.
Peering inside,
on the bed was a woman,
beautiful and dignified like a flower.
Lying on the bed,
she was barely breathing.
Relatives, both close and distant, were shocked and terrified,
none daring to approach,
only Zhìdū could go near.
Shortly after, she revived,
and sat up.
Zhìdū asked, "Who are you?"
The woman said:
"I am from Hénán,
my father is the governor of Qīnghé.
Just as I was about to be married,
I do not know how,
I suddenly found myself here."
Zhìdū explained everything in detail.
The woman said:
"Heaven must have destined me to be your wife."
Thus they became husband and wife.
They went to her family's home,
who were overjoyed,
also believing it was Heaven's gift,
and so they gave her to him.
They had a son,
who later became the governor of Nánjùn.
Táng Bāng
Héng,
Shāntáng Bāng,
during the Yìxī era,
heard someone knocking at the door.
Going out to look,
he saw two officials in red robes.
They said:
"The authorities want you."
They then took him to the tomb of Yīn Ān east of the county,
where someone inside the tomb said to the officials:
"We were supposed to fetch Táng Fú,
why did you wrongly take Táng Bāng?"
He ordered them whipped,
and sent them out.
Táng Fú died young.
Wáng Jǔ
Wáng Jǔ, governor of Héngyáng,
was appointed to Guǎngzhōu.
When Jǔ reached Chángshā,
he saw a man over ten feet tall,
wearing a plain white cloth robe.
Holding a tally, he stood on the shore,
calling out:
"Jǔ, my servant, come to me."
Jǔ examined the tally,
and it was for Dù Língzhī.
He boarded the boat to speak with him,
and they exchanged greetings after a long separation.
Jǔ asked:
"You are from Jīngzhào;
when did you depart?"
He replied to Jǔ, "I departed this morning."
Jǔ, puzzled, questioned him.
Dù said:
"It is the Jīngzhào of the heavens;
I am a ghost,
sent here to see you."
Jǔ was greatly frightened.
Dù then requested paper and brush,
saying:
"You certainly cannot read heavenly script,
so I will rewrite it."
He folded the document,
and asked Jǔ for a small box to contain it,
sealing it and handing it to Jǔ, saying:
"Do not open it now;
when you reach Guǎngzhōu,
you may look."
Several months after arriving in Guǎngzhōu,
feeling depressed and anxious,
Jǔ opened it to look.
The document stated:
"Summon Wáng Jǔ to serve as Assistant Registrar of the Left Director of Destinies."
Jǔ was deeply distressed,
and soon fell ill and died.
Zhōu Yì
Zhōu Yì of Rǔnán
married the granddaughter of Liú Dàn of Pèiguó.
Yì's younger brother, the magistrate of Ài County in Yùzhāng,
fell ill on the journey.
When they were still ten lǐ from the county,
Yì said:
"My brother will certainly not survive."
He left his family members behind,
and first went with his brother to the county.
After one night, the brother died.
When the wife arrived to face the corpse,
Yì raised his hand to bid farewell to his wife,
and she combed his hair for him.
He then pulled out her hairpin.
After the burial was completed,
when his wife was staying in her room,
Yì came up to the bed,
and said to his wife:
"Though our time together was short,
our affection for each other was deep.
It is unfortunate that it has come to this.
My elder brother was unkind,
separating husband and wife,
so that in the end I could not hold a proper farewell.
It is truly regrettable.
Earlier, I raised my hand in farewell,
and pulled out your hairpin,
intending to rise,
but there were many people and the atmosphere was oppressive, so I could not."
From then on, he came every evening to rest,
no different from when he was alive.
Yuán Qǐ
Yuán Qǐ of Wúxīng,
as his wife was nearing death,
took Qǐ's hand and said:
"After I die,
will you remarry?"
Qǐ said:
"I could not bear to."
Later, he did remarry.
One day, he saw his former wife in broad daylight, who said to him:
"You first made a vow;
why did you break your word?"
She then cut his genitals with a knife.
Although it did not cause death,
He was permanently incapacitated for marital relations.
Wáng Héngzhī
The Buddhist monk Fǎshī Zhú,
a native of Kuàijī,
was on very close terms with the Northern Central Gentleman Wáng Héng.
They
associated intimately,
and together discussed matters of life and death, sin and blessing, and retribution.
These matters were obscure and difficult to understand,
so they made an agreement:
whoever died first
should come and report.
Later, Wáng was in a temple
when he suddenly saw Fǎshī come and say:
"This humble monk passed away on such-and-such a day of such-and-such month.
Sin and blessing are not empty;
retribution is like shadow and echo.
You, the almsgiver, should diligently cultivate virtue and the Way,
so as to ascend and join the divine spirits.
I previously made an agreement with you
that whoever died first would report,
so I have come to tell you."
Having finished speaking,
he was seen no more.
Liú Dùn
During the Yìxī era of Emperor Ān,
Liú Dùn was at home observing mourning for his mother.
There was constantly a ghost
that came and stayed at Dùn's house.
It moved beds and small tables,
overturned vessels and utensils,
sang, wept, and cursed.
It was fond of speaking of people's private affairs,
and the servants dared not commit offenses.
Dùn ordered his younger brother to guard the house.
Dùn saw a rope tied around his brother's head,
suspending him from the roof beam.
In a flurry, he got him down,
and as a result, his brother lost his soul;
after more than a month, he recovered.
Whenever Dùn's cooking was about to be done,
it would always disappear.
Dùn secretly bought wild kudzu,
cooked it into a paste,
and the ghost again stole it.
North of the house, the sound of vomiting was then heard,
and from then on, it was silent and gone.
Hence, the world passed down the tale of Liú Dùn poisoning the ghost.
Dùn later became a staff officer under Liú Yì,
and was killed by Emperor Gāozǔ of Sòng.
Wáng Sīguī
Wáng Sīguī of Chángshā
served as magistrate of Hǎiyán.
Suddenly he saw a clerk.
Sīguī asked who it was.
The clerk said:
"I am ordered to summon you to serve as Registrar."
Thereupon, he produced a tablet and placed it before the bed.
The clerk also said:
"The deadline is distant,
in the tenth month.
If you do not believe me,
on the fifteenth day of the seventh month at midday,
look at the sky,
and you will see something."
Sīguī instructed his family
to look at the sky at the appointed time.
They heard the sound of weeping,
and saw people in the air,
with hanging banners arrayed in rows,
in the manner of a funeral procession.
Huá Yì
Huá Yì of Guǎnglíng,
who resided in Jiānglíng,
returned seven years after his death.
At first, his voice was heard,
but his form was not seen.
His family earnestly pleaded
until they managed to see him.
He replied:
"I am haggard and worn,
and cannot bear to let you see me."
Asked about the reason,
he said:
"Although my allotted lifespan was not long,
it should still not have been exhausted.
Because during my lifetime I punished and beat others improperly,
and also killed a mutinous soldier who was a servant,
my allotted span was reduced because of this."
He said:
"I have been sent on a mission to Chángshā,
and will pass by again on my return."
At the appointed time, he indeed arrived,
and instructed his two sons, saying:
"Since I died early,
you must diligently encourage and exert yourselves.
For the family to decline and fall—
how can that befit sons?"
He also reproached his elder brother for not providing instruction and guidance,
his expression very displeased.
Then he said:
"Mèng Yú's name is already registered in the death ledger;
he only has a few days left of his allotted time."
At that time,
Yú was vigorous and strong.
Later, when the predicted time arrived,
he died suddenly.
Zhāng Jūnlín
Zhāng Jūnlín of Wú County,
lived in Yáng Village in the eastern countryside.
During the Lóng'ān era,
a ghost suddenly came to assist with chores.
Lín originally had an old, broken steamer among his stored utensils,
which was already useless.
The ghost had him break the bottom of a jar to make a steamer.
By the time the family got up,
the rice was already cooked.
This ghost required nothing else,
only eating sugarcane.
It called itself Gāo Hè.
Some say
this ghost's name is a *fǎnyǔ* [reversal],
Gāo Hè is Gě Hào.
Mounds and graves accumulated there,
with especially many ancient tombs.
It is suspected this thing was a ghost from among them.
Lín alone could see it each time,
its form like a young maiden,
aged about seventeen or eighteen,
with a bluish-black face.
It wore blue-green clothes all over.
It then had the Zhāng family fetch a white jar,
fill it with water,
and cover its head.
The next morning, looking at it,
there was something inside.
The Zhāng family was originally poor,
and subsequently became wealthy.
It once said:
"Do not dislike me;
when the days and months are finished, I will leave of my own accord."
Later, it indeed left.
Mán Soldiers
The Mán soldiers of Nánpíng State,
at the beginning of the Yìxī era,
followed the multitude to Gūshú,
and then a ghost possessed them.
Its voice was faint, slender, and drawn-out,
sometimes at the edge of the eaves,
sometimes in the courtyard trees.
If predicting good or ill fortune,
it would first demand a *pípá*,
and speak while playing it.
At that time, Xì Yǐ was the Prefectural Chief Clerk.
He asked about promotion in office.
It said:
"Soon you will hold the tally and staff."
Shortly after, he became Colonel of the Southern Mán,
I was a Gentleman of the State,
and personally governed this region.
A common saying in Jīngzhōu states
it is made by rats,
and is called Ghost Hou.
Chén Gāo
Chén Gāo of Píngyuán,
during the Yìxī era,
went out by boat from behind Fán Liáng in Guǎnglíng.
Suddenly there was a red ghost,
about ten feet tall,
wearing a crimson cap on its head,
shaped like deer antlers.
It approached Gāo asking for passage,
and in an instant boarded the boat.
Gāo was originally skilled in breath control,
so he sang a common southern tune of the secular families.
The ghost then stuck out its tongue and opened its eyes wide.
He struck it with a staff-pole,
and it immediately scattered into sparks,
illuminating the wilderness.
Gāo died not long after.
Yuán Wújì
Yuán Wújì of Chén State in Jìn,
resided in Dōngpíng.
In the early years of Yǒngjiā,
he contracted a plague,
and of his household of over a hundred people,
nearly all had died.
They moved to avoid the large residence,
temporarily staying in a farmhouse.
There was a small cottage,
where the brothers slept together,
with several layers of wooden beds and straw mats.
When they slept at night until dawn,
the bed would end up outside the door,
and this happened repeatedly.
The brothers found it strange and frightening,
and could not sleep.
Later, they saw a woman,
who came before the door,
and knowing that Wújì and the others were not sleeping,
retreated outside the door.
At the time, the moon was bright before dawn,
and they all peeked at her:
she wore colorful clothes and white makeup,
with hair ornaments and silver hairpins and an ivory comb on her head.
Wújì and the others chased her together,
at first she ran around the house and fell,
her hair bun and ornaments all fell off,
Wújì picked them all up,
and she still went out the door and fled south.
By the road there was a well,
and she then entered it.
Wújì returned to sleep,
and at daybreak,
looking at the hair ornaments and ivory comb,
they were all real objects.
They then broke open the well,
and found a catalpa wood coffin,
already completely decayed.
So they changed the coffin and burial clothes,
moved it to a high, dry place and buried it,
and then it stopped.
Xīn Cài King Zhāo Píng
In the Jìn dynasty, Xīn Cài King Zhāo Píng,
had a calf cart in the main hall,
which at night for no reason entered the study room by itself,
bumped into the wall and then came out.
He also repeatedly heard shouting and attacking noises,
coming from all directions.
Zhāo Píng then gathered a crowd,
set up bows and crossbows for battle preparations,
aimed at the sounds and shot arrows,
but the ghosts responded to the sounds and caught the arrows,
several of which fell into the ground.
A Student Studying Afar
There was a student studying afar,
whose parents were working at night,
when the son suddenly arrived,
sighing and saying:
"Now I am only a soul,
no longer a living person."
The parents asked him,
and the son said:
"At the beginning of this month I fell ill,
and died at a certain time today,
now I am at Rén Zǐchéng's house in Lángyá.
Tomorrow I will be encoffined,
and have come to welcome my parents."
The parents said:
"It is a thousand li from here,
even if we rush,
how can we reach you in time!"
The son said:
"Outside there is a carriage,
just ride it,
and you will naturally arrive."
The parents followed him,
got on the carriage and suddenly felt as if asleep,
by the time the rooster crowed,
they had already arrived at the place,
looking at the carriage and horses,
they were only spirit carriages and wooden horses.
Then they met with the host,
faced their son with sorrow,
asked about the details of his illness,
and it was as he had said.
Zhāng Lóng
In the third year of Yǒngchū of Sòng,
at the home of Zhāng Lóng of Wú Commandery,
suddenly there was a ghost.
It said:
"If you give me food,
I will assist you."
Later, when food was prepared for it,
he used a large knife to chop where it had eaten.
Then he heard several dozen people crying,
crying very sorrowfully,
saying:
"How can we get a coffin when we die?"
And then he heard:
"The host's family has a broken boat,
the servant cherishes it greatly,
we should take it to make a coffin."
He saw them take the boat over,
and there were sounds of cauldrons and saws.
When it grew dark,
he heard calls to lift the corpses and place them in the boat.
Zhāng Lóng did not see any of it,
only heard the arrangements.
Then he saw the boat gradually rise into the air,
entering the clouds.
After it disappeared,
he again heard what seemed like several dozen people laughing loudly, saying:
"How could you kill me?
It was just because I disliked you before,
so I hid your boat."
Zhāng Lóng then changed his mind and served this ghost,
asking about good or bad omens and future plans,
and the ghost said to him:
"You can place a large jar in the corner of the wall,
and I will find things for you."
Every ten days he would pour it out,
and there would be money and gold, silver, copper, iron, fishy smells, and the like.
Jí Quèshí
Jí Mòhàn's younger cousin named Quèshí,
previously served as Cānjūn under Tán Dàojì.
Once he fell ill,
and saw a person in red clothes come forward,
bowing and saying:
"I have come specifically to welcome you."
Quèshí generously prepared a feast,
seeking to be spared.
The ghost said:
"I am moved by your hospitality,
I will wait a little while."
Then it was no longer seen.
Quèshí gradually recovered.
Later, during mourning,
he returned to Shòuyáng,
and again saw the ghost, saying:
"The envoy to welcome you will arrive soon,
you should prepare your belongings."
Quèshí said:
"You previously showed kindness by staying,
can you now show compassion again?"
The ghost said:
"Previously I summoned you to employ you,
so I waited.
Now Tàishān appoints you as Registrar,
and I am again sent to escort you,
you cannot refuse."
Then he saw carriages and horses delivering orders,
with oiled halberds arrayed in front,
he pointed them out to his family,
but no one else could see them.
Quèshí urgently wrote letters calling relatives and friends to bid farewell,
in the midst of conversation and laughter,
he suddenly passed away.
A Man from Fùyáng
In the early years of the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
a man named Wáng from Fùyáng
set up a crab trap in a remote stream.
One morning, when he went to check it,
he saw a piece of timber,
about two chǐ long,
that had split open inside the trap,
and all the crabs had escaped.
So he repaired the trap
and took the timber out onto the bank.
The next day, when he went to look again,
he saw the timber was back inside the trap,
and it was broken just as before.
Wáng repaired the trap again,
and when he went to check once more,
he saw the same thing as initially.
Wáng suspected this timber was a demonic anomaly,
so he took it and put it into a crab basket,
tied it to the end of his carrying pole, and headed home,
saying:
"When I get home, I'll chop it up and burn it."
Before he had gone three lǐ from home,
he heard a rustling movement inside the basket.
Turning to look,
he saw the former timber head transform into a creature
with a human face and a monkey's body,
having one arm and one leg.
It said to Wáng:
"I have a craving for crabs.
It was indeed I who entered the water and broke your crab trap.
I have wronged you many times over.
I hope you will forgive me.
Open the basket and let me out.
I am a mountain spirit,
and I will surely aid you,
making your trap catch many crabs."
Wáng said:
"You have violently trespassed against people,
not just once but repeatedly.
Your crime warrants death."
The creature grew increasingly agitated,
begging to be released,
and repeatedly asked what Wáng's name was.
Wáng looked back but did not answer.
As they drew closer to home,
the creature said:
"Since you won't release me,
and you won't tell me your name,
what recourse do I have left?
I can only await death."
When Wáng reached home,
he lit a fierce fire and burned it.
Afterward, all was quiet with no further anomalies.
Local custom calls this creature a shānxiāo,
saying:
"If it learns a person's name,
it can harm them.
The reason it persistently asked
was precisely to harm the person and save itself."
The Attendant
In recent times, there was a man who acquired a young attendant.
The attendant frequently asked to return home but was not permitted.
After a long time had passed,
this attendant was sleeping beneath the south window.
The man saw a woman in the doorway,
about fifty or sixty years old,
very stout,
and walking with difficulty.
The attendant had kicked off his covers in his sleep.
The woman went to the bedside
and took the blanket to cover him.
She then turned and went out the door.
The attendant turned over, and his clothes slipped off.
The woman came back and did the same as before.
The man found this strange.
The next day, he asked the attendant:
"For what reason do you ask to go home?"
The attendant said:
"My mother is ill."
He then asked about her appearance and age,
and it all matched what he had seen,
except the attendant said she was thin, which was different.
He asked further what ailment the mother had.
The attendant replied:
"She suffers from swelling."
He then immediately granted the attendant leave
and sent him off.
Soon after, a letter arrived from home saying:
"Your mother has passed away."
Recalling the stoutness he had seen,
it was actually her swollen condition.
Zhēn Fǎchóng
During the Sòng dynasty, Zhēn Fǎchóng,
in the Yǒngchū era,
served as magistrate of Jiānglíng
and governed with strict integrity.
At that time, a man named Miào from Nánpíng was magistrate of Jiāng'ān
and died in office.
A year later,
while Fǎchóng was in the hall,
he suddenly saw a person enter through the door,
saying:
"I am Miào, respectfully paying a visit."
Fǎchóng knew he was deceased,
so he asked why his appearance was so emaciated.
He replied:
"In life, my good deeds
did not outweigh my evil ones.
I suffer the torments of bondage,
and am further burdened with intense judicial matters."
He also said:
"A certain person from your county,
owes me over a thousand dàn of rice,
with no written contract.
He stubbornly refuses to repay.
Now my sons are repeatedly impoverished and destitute.
I beg you to issue a strict order."
Fǎchóng said:
"You may draft a petition."
Miào said:
"I have no paper at hand,
and moreover, I can no longer write."
Fǎchóng ordered a clerk to fetch a brush,
and recorded his statements.
Miào dictated orally,
and his words were clear and distinct.
When the petition was completed,
he gave thanks and departed.
Fǎchóng inquired about the matter with Miào's family,
and they said:
"This is true."
He immediately summoned the debtor for questioning.
The man who owed the rice was terrified
and repaid it in full according to the facts.
Xiè Huì
When Xiè Huì was in Jīngzhōu,
a red ghost appeared in the corner of his wall,
about three chǐ tall.
It came before him,
holding a bronze plate in its hands,
completely filled with blood.
What Xiè Huì received was actually a paper plate,
and it vanished after a short while.
Xiè Língyùn
In the fifth year of the Yuánjiā era, Xiè Língyùn
suddenly saw Xiè Huì,
holding his own head in his hand,
come and sit on another bed.
Blood dripped profusely,
too dreadful to behold.
Also, the marten fur robe he wore
was soaked with blood filling the chest.
When he later served as governor of Línchuān commandery,
large insects suddenly appeared in his rice.
He was subsequently executed.
Liáng Qīng
During the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty,
there was a man from Tiānshuǐ named Liáng Qīng,
whose home was in Xīntíng, the capital.
In the twelfth lunar month, as he was about to conduct a sacrifice,
he sent a maidservant to the kitchen to prepare food.
Suddenly, she felt something in the air
wielding a stick and striking her.
The maid fled and reported this to Liáng Qīng.
Liáng Qīng then went to investigate
and saw pots and utensils moving by themselves,
filling with drinks and ladling soup,
arranging themselves on the table,
while the sounds of eating and drinking could be heard.
Liáng Qīng said:
"Why not show yourself?"
Then a man appeared,
wearing a flat-topped headscarf
and black leather trousers and jacket.
He said:
"I am from Jīngzhào,
deceased and drifting without a home.
I heard that you are fond of scholars,
so I have come to follow you."
Liáng Qīng then sat on the ground with him,
setting out food and wine.
The ghost said:
"You have sacrificial matters to attend to, and so on."
Liáng Qīng was planning for a certain commandery appointment,
and first consulted the ghost about it.
The ghost said,
"What you seek will certainly come to pass."
On a certain month and day, the appointment was issued,
and indeed it happened.
The ghost said:
"The commandery is very leisurely,
I wish to accompany you there."
Liáng Qīng replied:
"Very good."
Later, when he moored his boat at Shítóu,
he waited for five days,
but the ghost did not come.
So he set out on the road,
reached Péngchéng,
and only then did the ghost arrive.
They stayed together in the commandery for several years,
and when he returned to the capital,
the ghost also followed him back.
Xú Dàoráo,
in the tenth year of the Yuánjiā era,
suddenly saw a ghost,
who claimed to be his ancestor.
At that time, it was winter,
and the weather was clear and bright.
The ancestor had previously stored rice under the house and said:
"Tomorrow you should sun the grain,
for heavy rain is coming,
and there will be no clear weather for a while."
Ráo followed his advice,
and the ghost also helped with the hauling.
Later, there was indeed continuous rain.
Some who saw it at the time
said its form was like a macaque.
Ráo went to a Daoist priest to request a talisman,
which he hung on the window.
The ghost then laughed loudly:
"You think this can stop me?
I can still enter through the dog hole."
Though he said this,
he did not come in again.
After several days,
he sighed and said:
"Xú Shūbǎo is coming,
I should not see him."
Two days later, he indeed arrived,
and after that, the ghost ceased to appear.
The Chén family of Dōnglái
In Dōnglái, there was a family named Chén,
with over a hundred members.
One morning, when cooking, the pot would not boil.
Lifting the steamer to look,
suddenly a white-haired old man
emerged from the pot.
They then went to a master,
who said:
"This is a great omen of misfortune,
and the entire family should be exterminated.
Go back and make many weapons,
and when the weapons are ready,
place them under the walls by the gate,
then firmly close the gate and stay inside.
If someone on horseback with banners and canopies comes knocking at the door,
be careful not to respond."
They returned,
worked together to make over a hundred weapons,
and placed them under the eaves by the gate.
Sure enough, someone arrived,
and when they called, no one answered.
The commander grew furious,
and ordered his men to climb over the gate to enter.
A follower peered inside the gate
and saw over a hundred weapons, large and small.
Coming out, he reported this,
and the commander was greatly alarmed and regretful.
He said to his attendants:
"Tell them to come quickly.
If they do not come quickly,
then not a single person here will be taken away,
how then will we atone for our crime?
From here, heading north,
about eighty li away,
there is a family of one hundred and three people.
Take them instead."
Within ten days,
all members of that family died.
That family was also named Chén.
Xiè Dàoxīn
In the Kuàijī commandery, there was often a great ghost,
several zhang tall,
with a waist dozens of arm-spans thick,
wearing a tall hat and dark robes.
Whether auspicious or inauspicious events would befall the commandery,
it would first show signs of sorrow or joy at the Thunder Gate.
For the Xiè clan,
it would always announce both sorrow and joy.
Several months before Xiè Hóngdào encountered his mother's passing,
the ghost came morning and evening.
Later, when he was about to be transferred to become Minister of Personnel,
it clapped its hands and danced in three sections,
from the main gate to the central courtyard,
and soon the news of his promotion arrived.
When Xiè Dàoxīn encountered a grave misfortune,
and went to the Lítáng area to visit the gravesite,
as night approached,
he saw two torches at Lítáng.
In a moment,
the fire suddenly entered the water,
then stretched out to several dozen zhang long,
white as silk.
Gradually, it turned red again,
scattering into several hundred torches,
chasing and following the carriage as it moved.
He clearly saw a ghost within the fire,
very tall and large,
with a head like a five-dàn winnowing basket,
looking like someone heavily drunk,
with small ghosts on both sides supporting it.
That year, Sūn Ēn started a rebellion,
and everyone in Kuàijī,
great and small, supported him.
At the time, it was believed that what Dàoxīn saw
was an omen of the rebellion.
When Yǔ assembled the feudal lords at Kuàijī,
it was the ghost of Fángfēng.
Shěn Jìzhī
Shěn Jìzhī of Wúxīng,
during the Yuánjiā era,
suddenly heard a ghost laughing and talking in the air.
Sometimes it sang, sometimes it wept,
and at night it was especially active.
Jìzhī had a spirit carriage,
and the ghost pulled it away with others,
damaging the carriage.
Jìzhī had a long knife,
which he then placed in a jar,
and a large mirror,
which he also put into a container.
Wáng Hú
Sòng Wánghú was
a man of Cháng'ān.
Several years after his uncle's death,
in the twenty-third year of the Yuánjiā era,
the uncle suddenly appeared in physical form and returned home.
He reprimanded Wánghú for lacking diligence and care,
and for neglecting household affairs,
and punished Wánghú with five strokes of the cane.
The bystanders and neighbors
all heard their conversation and the sound of the caning,
and later saw the cane marks,
but did not see the uncle's form.
Only Wánghú alone could see and interact with him.
The uncle said to Wánghú:
"I should not have died;
the divine order required me to calculate the registers of the various ghosts.
Now I have a large retinue of officers and soldiers,
and I fear startling and disturbing the neighbors,
so I did not bring them in."
Wánghú also saw many ghosts clamoring outside the village.
Soon, the uncle bid farewell, saying:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month next year,
I will return briefly again.
I intend to take you along,
to travel the dark paths,
so that you may know the retribution for sins and blessings.
There is no need for lavish preparations;
if you insist,
only tea and simple food will suffice."
When the time came, he indeed returned,
and said to Wánghú's family:
"I will now take Wánghú to tour and observe;
after the tour, he will return,
so there is no need to worry."
Wánghú then immediately fell onto his bed,
lifeless as if extinguished.
The uncle then took Wánghú to tour all the mountains,
where he fully observed the ghosts and monsters.
Finally, they reached Sōnggāo Mountain,
where the various ghosts entertained Wánghú,
and a feast was prepared,
the flavors of which were no different from those in the mortal world,
only the ginger was exceptionally crisp and delicious.
Wánghú wanted to take some back,
but the people around him laughed and said:
"You can only eat it here,
you cannot take it far away."
Wánghú also saw a place,
with magnificent and spacious buildings,
exquisite curtains and mats,
where two young monks resided.
Wánghú visited them,
and the two monks served him various fruits, betel nuts, and the like.
Wánghú traveled for a long time,
fully witnessing the retributions of sin, blessing, suffering, and joy.
When he bid farewell to return,
his uncle said to him:
"Now that you know that goodness should be cultivated,
return home and seek out Báizú Āliàn.
This person's precepts and conduct are pure and lofty,
and you can take him as your teacher."
The Cháng'ān monk's feet were white,
so people of the time called him Báizú Āliàn.
He was highly respected by the Wèi barbarians,
and the barbarian king served him as his teacher.
After receiving this instruction,
Wánghú then traveled and studied with the young monks on Sōnggāo Mountain.
Among the crowd, he suddenly saw the two monks,
and Wánghú was greatly surprised.
He recounted their long separation,
asking when they had come here.
The two monks said:
"We humble monks originally resided in this temple;
we had no intention of making your acquaintance in the past."
Wánghú again spoke of their encounter on Sōnggāo Mountain,
and the monks in the crowd said:
"You are mistaken, sir;
how could such a thing have happened?"
By the next day,
the two monks had left without saying goodbye.
Wánghú then fully informed all the monks,
recounting what he had seen on Sōnggāo Mountain in the past,
and everyone was astonished.
They immediately searched for the two monks,
but did not know where they had gone.
Táo Jìzhī,
towards the end of the Yuánjiā era, served as the magistrate of Mòlíng,
and once wrongfully killed a musician.
At night, he dreamed that the musician came and said:
"I was wrongfully killed before,
appealed to heaven and obtained justice,
so now I have come to take you."
He then jumped into Táo's mouth,
and fell into his stomach.
After a short while, he came out again,
and then said to himself:
"Now, if I take Táo of Mòlíng directly,
it would be of no use;
I should instead discuss taking the magistrate of Dānyáng."
After saying this, he disappeared.
Táo died not long after,
and Magistrate Wáng of Dānyáng indeed died.
Zhū Tài
Zhū Tài's home was in Jiānglíng.
During the Yuánhuī era of the Sòng dynasty,
he fell ill and died before being encoffined,
when suddenly his form appeared,
returning to sit beside his corpse,
comforting and encouraging his mother.
Everyone saw him,
directing the funeral arrangements,
insisting on frugality and simplicity.
He said to his mother:
"Our family has always been poor,
and now I have also died.
I will forever be separated from serving and caring for you;
how can we spend extravagantly on the funeral?"
Dài Chéngbó
Dài Chéngbó of the Sòng dynasty,
during the Yuánhuī era,
bought land from the Pípá Temple in the jurisdiction of Jīngzhōu,
mistakenly taking the empty land to the east as the site for his residence.
At dusk,
he suddenly heard angry cursing.
Getting up to look,
he saw a person of strange appearance.
Chéngbó asked him,
and he replied:
"My surname is Gōng,
and I originally lived on this land.
Why do you forcibly seize it?"
Chéngbó said:
"Dài Jǐn sold the land;
you should not blame me."
The ghost said:
"Benefiting yourself at the expense of others,
what does that have to do with Jǐn?
If you do not leave quickly,
I will make you know."
After saying this, he disappeared.
Chéngbó had a stubborn nature,
and was not moved by this.
Ten days later,
he suddenly fell ill and died.
Zhāng Shòu
Zhāng Shòu, a clerk of Dānyáng commandery,
was sent on a mission to Wú commandery,
passing through Pílíng.
There was a man,
over thirty years old,
wearing a yellow single-layer garment,
who asked Shòu to carry his bamboo case.
After traveling for several days,
he hardly ate anything.
Whenever they passed through villages,
he would wander around.
From the village, they would then hear calls for souls,
and after a long while, he would return to the boat.
Shòu became suspicious of him,
and waited until he left,
then opened his bamboo case.
Inside were several scrolls of documents,
all listing names of people from Wú commandery.
There were also several hundred needles,
and whenever he left, he would take one tube.
When he returned later,
he obtained over a shēng of wine,
and several slices of dried meat.
He said to Shòu:
"You know I am a ghost;
I troubled you to carry me along,
and I obtained a little wine,
to bid you farewell.
The reason I carry so many needles is that
when someone is ill,
I use the needles to needle their spirit.
Now, all the places I go are people from this commandery;
Dānyáng has another messenger going there.
This year, there is much illness;
do not go to the homes of the sick."
Shòu asked him for medicine,
and he replied:
"I can only spread illness and kill people;
I do not administer medicine to cure illness."
At the end of the Yuánjiā era,
there was a Cháng'ān monk named Shí Tánshuǎng,
who traveled to the region south of the Yangtze River,
and fully recounted it thus.
Shī Xù's disciple
In Wúxīng, there was a man named Shī Xù,
who had a disciple
who always upheld the theory that ghosts do not exist.
Suddenly, a guest wearing a single-layered white robe
came to converse with him,
and the topic turned to ghosts and spirits.
After a long while,
the guest found himself at a loss for words,
and finally said:
"Your arguments are clever,
but they lack sufficient reasoning.
I am a ghost myself,
so how can you say ghosts do not exist?"
The disciple asked why the ghost had come,
and it replied:
"I have been sent to fetch you,
and the deadline is tomorrow at mealtime."
The disciple pleaded bitterly,
and the ghost asked:
"Is there anyone who resembles you?"
He said:
"The commander under Shī Xù's tent
looks similar to me."
So they went together.
Sitting face to face with the commander,
the ghost produced an iron chisel from its hand,
about a foot long,
placed it on the commander's head,
and then raised a mallet to strike it.
The commander,
said:
"I feel a slight pain in my head."
Soon it became increasingly severe,
and after about the time of a meal, he died.
Zhāng Dàoxū
In Wújùn, there were Zhāng Dàoxū and Zhāng Shùn,
both well-known scholars,
who lived near the Chāngmén gate.
While in mourning for their mother,
they bought a new house.
At dusk,
they heard someone knocking at the door, saying:
"You are gentlemen,
so why do you endanger others for your own peace?"
They replied:
"We bought this house ourselves,
and found your coffin inside.
We moved it to the market and built a grave for it,
so what wrong have we done?"
The ghost said:
"You moved my body to the grave of General Wú,
and I am a humble person.
Day and night, we fight,
and I cannot bear it.
If you don't believe me,
you can follow me to see for yourselves."
Then the two Zhāngs, in a daze,
arrived outside the Chāngmén gate.
The two Zhāngs listened,
and only heard the sound of turbulent fighting and clashing from the grave.
The ghost then said:
"I will make sure you know."
Soon after, both brothers died.
Qín Shù
There was a man from Pèijùn named Qín Shù,
whose home was in Xiǎoxīn Village of Qū'ē.
Once, while returning from the capital,
when he was still about twenty lǐ away,
the sky grew dark and he lost his way.
Seeing a distant light,
he went toward it.
He saw a woman,
holding a candle, who came out and said:
"I am a weak woman living alone,
and cannot accommodate guests."
Qín Shù said:
"I wish to continue my journey,
but the night hinders me from going forward,
so I beg to stay outside."
The woman agreed.
After Qín Shù entered and sat down,
he thought that since this woman lived alone in one room,
he feared her husband might come,
and dared not sleep peacefully.
The woman said:
"Why be overly suspicious?
I assure you there is nothing to worry about,
and I will not mislead you."
She prepared food for Qín Shù,
but all the food was old and stale.
Qín Shù said:
"I understand you are not yet married,
and I am also unmarried.
I wish to form a marital bond with you.
Would you consider it?"
The woman smiled and said:
"I consider myself humble and unworthy,
how could I be your match?"
Then they slept together.
As dawn approached, Qín Shù prepared to leave,
and they both rose to bid farewell.
The woman wept and said:
"After this one meeting with you,
there may be no chance to see you again."
She gave him a pair of rings,
tied them to his belt,
and saw him out the door.
Qín Shù lowered his head and hurried away for several dozen steps,
then looked back at the place where he had stayed,
only to find it was a grave mound.
After a few days,
the rings disappeared,
but the knot on his belt remained as before.
Zhú Huìchì
The monk Zhú Huìchì
resided at the four-story Buddhist temple in Jiānglíng,
and died in the second year of the Yǒngchū era.
After his burial,
his disciples held a seven-day gathering.
The entire temple went out,
except for the monk Míng Dào, who was previously ill
and stayed behind alone.
Suddenly, he saw Zhú Huìchì,
who said to Míng:
"In life, I could not abstain from eating meat,
and now I have fallen into the Hungry Dog Hell.
Let this be known as retribution."
Guō Quán,
styled Zhòng Héng,
in the early years of the Yìxī era,
was killed for supporting Huán Xuán.
In the eighth year of the Yuánjiā era,
he suddenly appeared in a carriage with attendants,
manifesting himself to his son-in-law Liú Níngzhī, saying:
"I am under punishment,
and if you can gather forty monks for a ceremony,
I may be spared."
Also, his daughter dreamed that he said:
"I am under punishment,
and asked your husband to perform good deeds.
Why has it taken until now,
and the ceremony has not yet earned me mercy?"
The daughter asked where the vegetarian feast should be held,
and he replied:
"You may return to my home."
Then he vanished abruptly.
After the ceremony was completed,
someone claiming to be a messenger from Guō Quán
spoke to Liú Níngzhī, saying:
"I am grateful for your great kindness,
and the matter has finally been pardoned."
Hè Sīlìng
In Kuàijī, there was Hè Sīlìng,
who was skilled at playing the qín.
Once, he sat under the moonlight at night,
playing the qín in the breeze.
Suddenly, a person appeared,
of imposing stature,
wearing shackles and looking sorrowful,
arriving in his courtyard.
He praised Hè's playing,
and they began to converse.
He claimed to be Jī Kāng (Jī Zhōngsǎn),
and said to Hè:
"Your playing is extremely swift,
but it does not quite match the ancient methods."
Then he taught him the "Guǎnglíng Sàn."
Hè thus learned it,
and it has been passed down to this day without interruption.
Shāndū,
resemble Kūnlún people in form,
their bodies covered in hair,
when seeing people, they close their eyes and open their mouths as if laughing.
They prefer to dwell deep in the woods,
overturning stones to search for crabs to eat.
The "Shù Yì Jì" states,
in Nánkāng there is a spirit,
named Shāndū,
shaped like a human,
over two chǐ tall,
black in color with red eyes,
yellow hair covering the body.
They make nests in the deep mountain trees,
the nests shaped like eggs but sturdy,
about three chǐ long,
inside very smooth,
vivid in five colors.
Two are stacked together,
connected in the middle.
Local people say,
the upper one is the male dwelling,
the lower one the female chamber.
The sides all have openings like circles,
their substance light and hollow,
quite resembling wooden tubes,
in the center using bird feathers as bedding.
This spirit can transform and become invisible,
suddenly glimpsing its form,
it is likely of the same kind as Mùkè and Shānshēn.
Fifteen lǐ northwest of Gànxiàn,
there is an ancient pond,
named Yúgōng Táng.
Above it is a large catalpa tree,
about twenty arm spans around,
the old tree hollow inside,
contains a Shāndū nest.
In the first year of Sòng Yuánjiā,
county residents Dào Xùn and Dào Líng, two brothers,
cut down this tree,
took the nest home.
Shāndū appeared in form,
scolded the two men saying:
"I dwell in the wilderness,
what concern is it of yours?
Mountain trees are usable,
how could they be counted?
The tree had my nest,
so you cut it down.
Now I shall burn your house,
to repay your unrighteousness."
By the second watch,
inside and outside on the roof,
fires broke out simultaneously,
the entire household was completely destroyed.
Mùkè,
Dèng Démíng's "Nánkāng Jì" says,
Mùkè's head, face, and speech,
are not entirely different from humans,
but their hands and feet have claws like sharp hooks.
High cliffs and remote peaks,
there they then dwell.
They can cut planks,
tie them together and hang them on trees.
In the past, some wanted to buy planks from them,
first placed goods under the tree,
according to how much was placed, they took it.
If it suited their intention,
they would give the planks to the person,
if not taken, they would not forcibly offend either.
But they never face people or engage in market trade.
When they die, all are given burial.
Once someone went to see their burial,
using wine and raw fish meat as offerings to guests,
they themselves prepare food and drink,
ultimately never letting people see their form.
Burial coffin method,
often on high banks at tree tops,
or hidden in stone nests.
Nánkāng three battalions' shipbuilding soldiers say,
they went and personally witnessed the burial site,
the rhythm of dancing and singing,
though different from humans,
sounded like wind through forest echoes,
the sound similar to harmony of songs and music.
During Yìxī,
Xú Dàofù went south,
sent people to cut planks,
to build boat railings,
Mùkè then offered their planks but could not be seen.
Ōu Jìngzhī
Nánkāng county resident Ōu Jìngzhī,
in the first year of Sòng Yuánjiā,
with his son rode a boat together,
from the county going upstream.
Entering deep into a small stream,
remote, desolate, perilous and extreme,
where human footprints had never reached.
Evening, they went ashore,
stopped and rested in a hut,
Jìngzhī was struck by evil and suddenly died,
his son lit a fire to guard the corpse.
Suddenly heard distant crying,
calling "uncle."
The filial son was startled and suspicious,
in a moment,
the crier had already arrived.
Like a human tall,
hair draped to feet,
hair mostly covering the face,
the seven orifices not visible.
Then called the filial son's name,
consoling him.
The filial son afraid,
then gathered.
firewood to light a fire.
This creature said "I came to console you,
why should you fear?"
About to need to light fire,
this creature sat by the deceased's head crying.
The filial son secretly peeked in the firelight,
saw this creature press its face against the deceased's face,
the deceased's face soon cracked and peeled exposing bone.
The filial son terrified,
wanted to strike it,
had no weapon.
In a moment,
his father's corpse appeared as white bones connected,
while skin and flesh were all gone.
Ultimately could not discern what kind of spirit this creature was.
Liú Jùn
Early Yuánjiā,
Cavalry Regular Attendant Liú Jùn,
home in Dānyáng.
Later once encountered sudden rain,
saw three small children in front of the gate,
all about six or seven years old,
playing tricks together,
yet not at all wet.
Soon saw them fighting over a gourd bottle,
Jùn drew a slingshot and shot it,
hit the bottle squarely,
suddenly they disappeared.
Jùn got the bottle,
so hung it by the pavilion.
Next day,
a woman entered the gate,
holding the bottle weeping,
Jùn asked her,
she replied:
"This is my child's thing,
I don't know how it came to be here?"
Jùn explained the reason in detail,
the woman took the bottle and buried it before the child's grave.
After a day,
again saw the former children holding it coming by the gate side,
lifting it,
laughing and saying to Jùn:
"I have already gotten the bottle back."
Finished speaking and vanished.
Tán Dàojì
Tán Dàojì lived at Qīngxī,
the second son at night suddenly saw someone come to bind him,
wanted to shout but couldn't,
until dawn then released,
still saw rope marks there.
This residence was previously lived in by Wú general Bù Chǎn,
proverb says:
"Yángzhōu Qīng,
is a ghost camp."
Qīngxī Qīngyáng is this.
From Bù to Tán,
all were executed.
Shí Xiùzhī
Shí Xiùzhī of Dānyáng,
during the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
suddenly saw a person appear in his hall,
wearing a flat headscarf,
and black cloth trousers,
holding a tablet and approaching the door,
handed it over, saying:
"I have heard that your skill rivals that of Bān Chuí,
and your carving of boats is especially exquisite.
The Prefect of Tàishān therefore summons you."
Xiùzhī explained himself:
"I can only make carts;
my boat-making is not as good as Liú Rú of Gāopíng."
Suddenly, the man took the tablet
and vanished.
Liú Rú was then a court attendant,
appointed as the Deputy of Lìyáng Commandery,
and died within a few decades.
Xiàhóu Zǔguān
During the Yuánjiā era,
Xiàhóu Zǔguān served as the Governor of Yǎnzhōu,
stationed at Xiáqiū,
and died in office.
