Shěn Sēngróng succeeded him.
A year later,
Xiàhóu came to visit Sēngróng,
speaking as in life,
often discussing matters of the underworld.
On Sēngróng's bed was an ornate woven silk belt.
Xiàhóu said:
"Could you give it to me?
If you are willing to bestow it,
please have it burned."
Sēngróng ordered it burned in his presence.
Before the flames and smoke had dissipated,
he already saw Xiàhóu wearing the belt around his waist.
The following year, while Sēngróng was stationed there,
he held a nighttime banquet with female musicians.
Suddenly, a woman appeared outside the door.
Shěn asked her,
and she replied:
"I was originally Cǎizhī, a zheng-playing courtesan of Dù, the Governor of Qīngzhōu.
Dù gave me to Xiàhóu, the Governor of Yǎnzhōu, as a favored concubine.
I only wish for one of the courtesans here to accompany me in play."
She pointed to one playing the pipa below.
The courtesan wept, saying:
"Why does my lord suddenly give me to a ghost?"
The ghost said:
"Do not speak too much;
I will certainly not let you go."
She entered to bid farewell to her companions in the room.
Before the drinking was finished,
she died of heartache.
Just as her breath ceased,
her spirit had already taken human form again,
standing beside Cǎizhī.
Zhāng Chéngjí
Zhāng Yuánqìng, son of Zhāng Chéngjí of Wèijùn,
was twelve years old.
During the Yuánjiā era,
he saw a ghost,
three feet tall,
with one foot and bird-like claws,
and scales on its back.
It came to summon Yuánqìng,
who became dazed as if mad,
wandering aimlessly,
so his parents beat him.
Soon, a voice was heard in the air saying:
"It is I who taught him;
please do not punish him."
The Zhāng family had two scrolls of Yáng Zhōngjìng's calligraphy,
which suddenly went missing.
The ghost threw them back from the beam,
one scroll slightly torn,
and then repaired it.
When the Wáng family married off a daughter,
they borrowed something from Zhāng,
and the ghost requested paper and brush to reply on his behalf.
Zhāng was skilled in craftsmanship
and once made a catapult.
The ghost borrowed it,
returning it the next day,
but it was completely broken.
Liáng Qīng
Liáng Qīng of Āndìng in the Sòng dynasty,
courtesy name Dàoxiū,
lived in the former residence of the late Governor of Xúzhōu, Huán, located in the Right Imperial Workshop area of Yángzhōu.
In the fourteenth year of Yuánjiā, in the second month,
strange lights appeared repeatedly,
and the sound of splitting bamboo was heard.
He sent his maidservant Sōngluó to investigate.
She saw two people,
asked them;
they said:
"My surname is Huá, given name Fúróng,
sent by the Supreme Deity of the Six Jiǎ.
Accompanying an immortal from the Purple Chamber of the Great Subtlety,
I have come to visit my old dwelling."
They then stayed and did not leave.
Sometimes they appeared with bird heads and human bodies,
their faces covered in feathers.
Sōngluó was frightened.
She shot an arrow at them,
and they vanished with the twang of the bowstring,
leaving only crimson stains on the arrow.
She then saw another creature,
vaguely resembling a walking person,
hiding behind a tree.
She ordered someone to stab its thigh,
and it fell to the ground and sank away.
After a day,
it came limping from the roof,
approaching the maidservant to beg for food.
She gave it a ball of rice,
which it finished in one go, making two liters.
A few days later,
a crowd of ghosts arrived,
too hideous to describe.
They pulled down bed curtains,
stirring up dust and stones,
and the disturbance lasted for several mornings without ceasing.
The maidservant Cǎijú
encountered a ghost on the road,
wearing clothes and a headscarf,
riding a horse.
Attended by dozens of guards,
he said to Cǎijú:
"I am an immortal from heaven,
do not call me a ghost."
She asked why they constantly threw filth.
He replied:
"Filth and dirt symbolize wealth;
throwing it is an omen of rapid promotion."
Soon after,
Liáng Qīng indeed became General Yángwǔ and Governor of Běilǔ Commandery.
After enduring this torment for a long time,
Liáng Qīng called upon the foreign monk Bōluódié to chant incantations.
Seeing the ghosts terrified,
they fled by leaping over walls and burrowing through them,
all making bird-like sounds,
and thus it all ceased.
While in the commandery, not long after,
one night,
Sōngluó again saw ceremonial guards and instruments,
attended by dozens of people,
wearing headscarves.
They delivered a letter on coarse paper,
with about seventy characters,
the handwriting elegant and charming,
resembling that of Wáng Xīzhī and Wáng Xiànzhī from afar.
They also sang:
"Sitting in the Peacock Tower,
I hear the Phoenix Drum from afar.
Descending from my Zōu Mountain peak,
I seem to see Liáng and Lǔ."
The ghosts exchanged condolences,
no different from people in the world.
A ghost once asked Sōngluó for a letter,
addressed: "The late Kǒng Xiūzhī, guilty of death, respectfully submits this note."
To mourn his uncle's passing.
It expressed grief and sorrow,
with a very orderly arrangement.
It also said that he had recently gone west,
where he met a monk,
who called himself Dàmóshā,
inquired about your well-being,
and entrusted me with five fragrant pills to give to you.
Liáng Qīng had previously been sent to Dūnhuáng,
where he had seen this monk.
In Liáng Qīng's household, a maidservant gave birth,
and then it all ended.
Cuī Màobó
Cuī Màobó's daughter
was betrothed to Péi Zǔ'ér.
Their families lived over five hundred lǐ apart,
and for several years they had no communication.
In the eighth month,
Cuī's daughter suddenly died,
but Péi did not yet know.
As dusk approached,
the girl went to Péi's gate,
clapped her hands and asked to enter.
She carried a golden jar,
holding about two shēng.
She came to the front of the bed and stood there.
Péi invited her to sit,
and asked her reason for coming.
The girl said:
"I am the daughter of Prefect Cuī of Qīnghé.
I heard in my youth that my father had betrothed me to you,
but unfortunately I have died.
Our great bond was not fulfilled,
and though we never shared the marital cup,
our pledge of union is already firm.
That is why I have come to inform you."
She then gave Péi the golden jar as a parting gift.
After the girl left,
Péi reported the matter to his father.
His father wanted to send a messenger to inquire.
Péi said:
"I was betrothed to the Cuī family in my youth,
and now such a spiritual response has occurred.
I must go myself."
His father agreed.
When Péi arrived,
the girl was indeed dead.
They offered condolences.
Péi fully recounted the events,
and showed the jar to Màobó.
They first used this jar to accompany the girl in burial.
After seeing the jar,
Màobó went with Péi to the girl's grave.
When they were still over ten lǐ away,
Péi again saw the girl speaking at the grave.
Those nearby all heard her voice,
but could not see her form.
Péi's heart was knotted with grief,
and he fell ill and died.
Thus they were buried together.
The Cháo Family
During the Yuánjiā era,
the Cháo family of Tàishān,
who had previously served as magistrate of Xiāng County,
lived in Jìnlíng.
A maidservant of the household was gathering firewood
when suddenly a man pursued her.
It seemed they conversed,
and they developed mutual affection.
He followed the maidservant home,
and stayed, never leaving again.
Cháo, fearing this would bring disaster,
would send the maidservant out at night.
They heard him singing and talking with the maidservant.
Everyone, young and old, could hear it,
but no one could see him.
Only the maidservant could see him.
They constantly obtained money, goods, wine, and food,
and daily life became abundant.
Whenever they drank with him,
he would play the flute and sing.
His song went:
"In the quiet night, silence has turned clear,
The long flute shines and sings.
If you wish to know me,
My surname is Guō, my given name Chángshēng."
Hú Bìzhī
Hú Bìzhī of Yùzhāng in the Sòng,
once served as Assistant Prefect of Wǔchāng Commandery.
In the twenty-sixth year of Yuánjiā, when he entered his official residence,
there was already a ghost there.
In the midnight hazy moonlight,
with the doors and windows slightly ajar,
someone could be seen leaning outside the door,
appearing like a child.
When the door closed,
they would hear footsteps,
like the sound of wooden clogs.
Looking, they would see nothing.
This happened very frequently.
In the second month of the twenty-eighth year,
the entire family fell ill with a seasonal disease.
Tiles and stones were thrown from the air,
or sometimes dry earth.
By midsummer, the sick had all recovered,
but the throwing became even fiercer.
They then invited a Daoist priest to fast, chant scriptures,
but the objects came down doubly hard like rain,
only not hitting the priest or the scripture scrolls.
By autumn and winter, sounds gradually appeared.
When tiles and stones hit people,
their flesh would turn dark blue,
and it was also very painful.
There was an old maidservant
who liked to curse.
The ghost would loudly frighten her from nearby.
Bìzhī invited a Jìjiǔ to submit a petition,
and used talismans to drive it out.
Gradually it ceased.
By the twenty-ninth year,
the ghost returned,
more severe than before.
The next year,
the assistant's residence caught fire four times in succession.
They struggled to douse the flames, and all were extinguished.
The ghost often made sounds like a dog.
The family often called it "chī lǎn".
Later, it suddenly spoke in a voice resembling Wú dialect.
At the third watch, it knocked on the door.
Bìzhī asked:
"Who is it?"
It replied:
"Chéng Shàolíng."
Taking a torch, he went out to look,
but saw nothing at all.
A few days later,
in the middle of the third watch,
it again knocked on the outer door.
He then cursed it again.
It replied:
"Sir, do not curse me.
I am a good spirit,
not one of those who came before or after.
Censor Táo sent me to inform you."
Bìzhī said:
"I do not know any Censor Táo."
The ghost said:
"Táo Jìngxuán,
you associated with him in the past."
Bìzhī said:
"When I was with him in the capital,
we served under Héngyáng,
and he was not usually a censor."
It said:
"Táo now resides in a blessed land,
serving as a heavenly censor.
The disturbances before and after
were caused by Lord Shěn.
This residence was originally Shěn's house.
He came to look at the house,
and merely played some mischievous tricks, throwing things.
Your angry exorcisms were too excessive,
even reaching the point of cursing.
You ordered maidservants to be disrespectful toward him,
and again had the Jìjiǔ submit petitions,
accusing him of crimes.
The matter reached the heavenly offices.
Shěn is now...
Tiānrán Jūn.
You are a disciple who has taken the Three Refugees in Buddhism.
Why did you not seek blessings from the Buddhist teachings,
but instead had the Jìjiǔ submit petitions?
From now on, I only hope you will sincerely devote yourself to the Dharma.
There is no need to confront evil ghosts."
Bìzhī then invited Buddhist monks to chant scriptures and complete fasting.
After one night passed,
he again heard outside the door the censor communicating:
"To Assistant Hú:
Now Shěn is pleading his case very bitterly.
As he says,
you were rather unreasonable.
If you can sincerely turn to the true enlightenment,
study scriptures and uphold precepts,
then all evil will be repelled.
Remembering our past affection,
I therefore inform you."
Suǒ Yí
Sòng Xiāngchéng's Suǒ Yí,
his father was a man
who did not believe in demons and evil spirits.
There was a house rumored to be haunted,
where anyone who lived there would die.
His father bought it and moved in,
and for many years it was peaceful and auspicious,
his descendants flourished,
and he rose to the rank of two thousand shi.
When he was about to move his family to take up his official post,
just before leaving,
he invited all his relatives, both inner and outer, to a gathering.
After the wine and food were served,
his father then said:
"Does the world truly have auspicious and inauspicious places?
This house was always said to be inauspicious,
yet since I have lived here,
it has been peaceful and auspicious for many years,
and I have even been promoted.
Where are the ghosts?
From now on,
this shall be considered an auspicious residence,
and there is no need to avoid living here."
After speaking, he went to the toilet.
A moment later,
he saw something in the wall,
as large as a rolled-up mat,
about five feet tall.
Yí's father,
immediately went back to fetch a knife and hacked at it,
cutting it in half,
whereupon it transformed into two beings.
He slashed at it horizontally again,
and it became four beings.
They then seized the knife,
turned it on Suǒ,
and killed him.
Carrying the knife to the seat,
they hacked and killed his sons and brothers.
All those surnamed Suǒ were doomed to die,
only those with different surnames were spared.
Yí was still young,
and his wet nurse carried him out the back door,
hid him in another household,
so only he alone survived.
Yí, styled Jǐngzhēn,
rose to the position of Prefect of Xiāngdōng.
Wáng Chěngzhī
Lángyé's Wáng Chěngzhī's wife,
of the Xiè family from Chénjùn,
gave birth to a son,
whose childhood name was Núzi.
After a year,
Wáng took the maidservant Zhāolì as his concubine,
and Xiè died of illness in the eighth year of Yuánjiā.
Wáng's tomb was in Kuàijī,
but she was temporarily buried at Dōnggāng in Jiànkāng.
After the burial and the return ceremony,
when the spirit tablet was brought into the house,
the table suddenly fell from midair to the ground.
An angry voice then said:
"Why was no funeral dirge sung,
leaving me to depart in silence?"
Chěngzhī replied:
"Since this is not the permanent burial,
the full rites were not prepared."
Mèng Xiāng,
styled Bǎochēng.
In the eleventh year of Yuánjiā,
he served as Magistrate of Wúníng.
His wife, née Cài,
died in the county.
Not long after,
suddenly there was pushing on windows and pounding on doors,
long howls and singing,
and dry soil being thrown about.
Then, in midair, knives and spears were brandished,
as if about to attack people.
Fires broke out repeatedly,
sometimes inside chests and boxes,
where clothes were scorched without any external signs.
It then pretended to speak in Cài's voice,
exactly as she had in life.
Xiāng then asked:
"Why did you die so young?"
She replied:
"It was fate.
However, I had one sin:
when I was a girl, I once slaughtered a chicken,
and for that I was summoned to hell for three days.
I heard people say
that casting a bronze statue could bring redemption,
so I took off a pair of gold rings to contribute,
and thus obtained release."
At the time, there was a shaman in the county,
and Xiāng summoned him to investigate.
The ghost immediately trembled in fear.
After a long while,
the shaman said:
"I see two beings,
one like a pig,
the other like a rooster,
with eyes glaring straight up.
The deceased says the rooster-shaped one is the culprit."
At that time, there was also a monk named Huìlán,
skilled in incantations,
so Xiāng summoned him
and had him recite sutras and spells.
At first, the ghost tried to mimic him,
but after a while,
it vanished without a trace.
Sīmǎ Wénxuān
was a man from Hénèi
who was quite devout in his Buddhist faith.
In the first year of the Yuánjiā era,
he observed mourning for his mother.
Several months after his younger brother’s death,
one morning at dawn,
he saw his younger brother seated at the spirit altar,
no different from when he was alive.
Turning around in alarm and astonishment,
he clamored for food and drink.
Wénxuān tried speaking to him, saying:
“In your lifetime you diligently practiced good deeds and cultivated virtue.
If, as the scriptures say,
you should have been reborn in heaven,
or at least among humans,
why have you instead fallen into this state as a ghost?”
At this, he fell silent, bowing his head and looking down,
and made no reply.
That very night, Wénxuān dreamed of his younger brother, who said:
“The good deeds I practiced in life
have earned me rebirth in heaven.
The ghost at the spirit altar
is a demonic apparition,
not my actual self.
Fearing that you, elder brother, might be suspicious and alarmed,
I have come to inform you.”
The next morning, Wénxuān invited monks to recite the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*
and had people strike at the ghost.
The ghost then fled under the bed.
It then ran outside the door,
its appearance growing somewhat ugly and fearsome.
The whole family was terrified,
cursing and shouting to drive it away.
The ghost said:
“I am only hungry and begging for food;
after a day I will leave.”
Shortly after,
a ghost appeared at the head of his mother’s spirit altar.
Its skin was reddish,
and its body was very tall and robust.
Wénxuān’s eldest son, Xiàozǔ, spoke with it,
and they conversed back and forth in detail.
Although the family was afraid at first,
over time they gradually grew accustomed to it.
The ghost also became increasingly familiar and intimate,
living and moving about
almost like a member of the household.
Word spread throughout the capital,
and visitors came to see it,
their footprints overlapping at the threshold.
At the time, there was a monk from Nánlín Temple
and a monk from Língzhū Temple named Shèshāmén
who conversed with the ghost,
and they also became quite friendly with it.
The ghost said:
“In a past life, I once held a position of honor and nobility,
but because I committed many evil deeds,
my retribution is not yet complete,
and so I have taken on this ghostly form.”
It added:
“In the year of the Tiger, four hundred troops of ghosts
will spread a great epidemic,
and those who are destined to suffer calamity
are none other than those who have not awakened to the Way.
But because they have transgressed excessively and in great numbers,
and many have wrongfully claimed blessings and virtue,
I have been sent here to oversee them.”
The monk offered it food,
but the ghost said:
“I have my own provisions;
I cannot accept this food.”
Shèshāmén asked:
“Ghosts know many things;
what was the cause in my past life that led me to become a monk?”
It replied:
“You came from among humans;
your reason for leaving home
was originally a vow you made.”
When asked about the destinies of the living and the dead,
it answered briefly,
and its words were all spiritually verified.
The details were numerous,
so they are not recorded here in full.
Shèshāmén said:
“The paths of humans and ghosts are different;
since you do not seek food,
why do you linger here for so long?”
The ghost replied:
“There is a woman here
who is fated to be captured.
But because she diligently upholds the precepts,
it is difficult to seize her.
My prolonged stay here
is for this reason.
I have disturbed the host family,
and for this I am deeply ashamed.”
After this,
it rarely appeared in visible form.
Those who went to see it afterward
only heard its voice.
This was in the tenth year of the Yuánjiā era.
On the twenty-eighth day of the third month,
it said to Wénxuān:
“I came here temporarily to stay,
but you and your family have devoted all your efforts to cultivating blessings,
and you fear me so;
how can I remain here long?”
Xiàozǔ said:
“We allowed you to stay here;
why did you occupy the spirit altar of our deceased ancestors?”
It replied:
“Each of your family’s deceased
has their own assigned place;
this altar was empty,
so I temporarily lodged here.”
With that, it bid farewell and departed.
Yú Dé and Yán Měng
Wǔlíng Lóngyáng’s Yú Dé
traveled to Yìyáng,
staying at the home of his host, Xià Mán.
He saw a sheet of white paper,
over a foot long,
marked with Mán’s daughter’s name on it,
so he got up and took it.
A moment later,
a tiger came to the door but retreated.
Soon, he saw the same marking as before,
and Dé took it again.
This happened three times.
He then told Mán about it,
and together they took sticks and waited.
Shortly after, the tiger arrived,
and they fought it off together.
Huáng Qī from the same county
recounted the story in this way.
Also, from Kuàijí, Yán Měng
had a wife who went out to gather firewood
and was killed by a tiger.
A year later,
Měng was walking through the grasslands
when he suddenly saw his wife, who said:
“On your journey today,
you are sure to encounter misfortune,
but I will save you.”
They then proceeded together,
when suddenly they met a tiger
that leaped toward Měng.
His wife raised her hand and gestured,
as if shielding him.
A moment later,
two foreign travelers passed by,
and his wife pointed at them.
The tiger then attacked the foreigners,
and Měng escaped unharmed.
Guō Qìngzhī
In the jurisdiction of Huángzhōu,
there was a Huángfù Ghost,
which would cause hauntings when it appeared.
The clothes and robes it wore were all yellow.
When it came to people's homes,
it would open its mouth and laugh,
and inevitably, pestilence would strike.
Its height was unfixed,
varying with the height of the fences.
It had not appeared for over ten years,
and the local people feared it.
Guō Qìngzhī of Lúlíng
had a household-born maidservant
named Cǎiwēi,
young and beautiful.
During the Xiàojiàn era of the Sòng dynasty,
suddenly, a person,
claiming to be a mountain spirit,
naked like a human,
over ten feet tall,
with yellow on its arms and head,
and a clean, dignified appearance.
Its speech was proper,
and the locals called it the Huángfù Ghost.
It came to be with this maidservant,
and the maidservant said,
its intentions were like those of a human.
The ghost then came frequently,
often hiding its form,
sometimes revealing its shape.
Its transformations were unpredictable,
sometimes large, sometimes small.
Sometimes like mist,
sometimes a stone,
sometimes a child or a woman,
sometimes like a bird or a beast.
Its footprints were like those of a human,
about two feet long,
or sometimes like goose tracks,
with palms as large as plates.
Opening doors and closing walls,
its entry was like that of a god.
It played and laughed with the maidservant like a human.
Bó Shàozhī
Bó Shàozhī once served as Cáng Zhì's adjutant.
In the twenty-fourth year of Yuánjiā,
he stayed in a separate residence to the west of the guest quarters in the Eastern Mansion.
He was neighbors with Zǔ Fǎkāi.
Fǎkāi's mother, Liú,
had been bedridden for ten days,
and passed away at midnight on the first day of the fifth month in the twenty-second year.
On the second day,
Shàozhī saw a group of rats,
the largest as big as pigs,
bright and colorful,
some pure, some mottled,
some wearing flat-topped caps,
some wearing bridles.
There were hundreds of them, large and small,
day and night.
On the nineteenth day at dusk,
a white rat, about two feet long,
appeared on the four eaves of the inner house,
ran under the wall,
and where it entered, a fire started.
They tried to extinguish it with water,
but the fire would not go out,
and after a long time, it extinguished on its own.
That night, he saw a person,
tall and robust, with a reddish complexion,
its body glowing like fire,
emerging from the burned wall,
and going straight under the bed.
It then came out from outside the wall,
and although separated by a wall,
at that moment, the light shone through completely,
as if there were no barrier at all.
During the fourth watch,
four more people appeared,
some speaking to Shàozhī as if offering protection,
others glaring with their tongues sticking out.
From dusk until dawn,
and the next night, the house burned again.
There were two people,
about nine feet tall,
riding horses and carrying bows and arrows,
with dozens of attendants,
called generals.
Shàozhī asked:
"Where are you going?"
They replied:
"We have been sent to the east to bring back a sick person."
On the twenty-first day,
the group came again.
There was originally a white dog in the house,
and since the ghostly disturbances began,
it would often disappear at night,
and return by dawn.
That evening, they tried tying it up.
After a moment,
a woman came and said:
"Why have you tied up this dog?
I wish to ask for it."
They agreed to give it to her,
but she dared not untie the rope,
and suddenly ran off.
The dog then moaned as if dying,
and for a whole day, it could not move.
A person in a brocade robe appeared,
drawing a bow and aiming an arrow,
directly at Shàozhī.
He said:
"You are an evil spirit,
daring to frighten people.
I am not afraid of you.
If you do not leave quickly,
I will have the great road god capture and deal with you."
The ghost relaxed the bowstring and released the arrow.
It spurred its horse and left.
Suǒ Wànxīng
Suǒ Wànxīng of Dūnhuáng
was sitting in the eastern study of the main hall during the day
when a servant suddenly saw a person wearing a cap,
leading a dappled horse,
enter directly through the gate.
Carrying something
that looked like a black leather cushion,
he placed it at the base of the steps,
then led the horse out the gate.
The cushion began to roll on its own,
went straight into the study,
climbed up along the bed leg,
and stopped in front of Wànxīng's knees.
The leather then unrolled in four directions,
revealing eyes all around inside,
blinking in a most repulsive manner.
After a long time,
it rolled back up and closed,
then rolled down from the bed,
fell to the west of the steps, and left.
Wànxīng ordered the servant to chase it, but it vanished at the eastern end of the main hall.
Disgusted by this,
he fell ill and died.
Guō Xiùzhī
resided in Hǎilíng.
In the twenty-ninth year of Yuánjiā of the Sòng dynasty,
at the age of seventy-three,
he fell ill and stayed in the main hall.
To the north was a large jujube tree,
about forty feet tall.
A young maidservant, rising early in the morning,
opened the door to sweep the ground
and saw a person on the jujube tree,
tall, robust, and dark-skinned,
wearing a black turban hat,
black leather trousers and jacket,
holding a bow and arrow,
standing upright facing south.
The whole family came out to look,
and saw it clearly.
Xiùzhī leaned on his cane to look at it.
This person said to Xiùzhī:
"I have come to summon you,
you should prepare quickly."
When the sun rose, it was no longer seen.
This happened for fifty-three days in total,
and after Xiùzhī passed away, it ceased.
Xiàhóu Wénguī lived in the capital.
One year after his death,
he appeared in his physical form and returned home,
riding in an ox-drawn carriage
with dozens of attendants and followers.
He claimed to be the governor of Běihǎi.
His family prepared a feast,
and when he ate and drank,
the food and drink were consumed at the time,
but after he left, the vessels were as full as before.
His family wept and wailed,
but Wénguī said:
"Do not cry,
I will return soon."
Sometimes he would come back after a month, sometimes after forty or fifty days,
and sometimes he would stay for half a day.
The attendants in red clothing who escorted him
were all short in stature.
They would sit and rest by the fence or in the side rooms.
When Wénguī was about to leave,
his family would often call for them to rise,
and they grew accustomed to them, no longer treating them as strange beings.
Wénguī had a grandson of a few years old,
and out of affection, he had him brought over.
The ghosts and spirits around him carried the child and presented him.
The boy could not bear the ghostly aura,
and he fainted,
no longer recognizing anyone.
Wénguī asked for water and sprayed it on him,
and only then did he wake up.
Seeing the peach tree in the courtyard,
he said:
"I planted this peach tree,
and its fruit is very fine."
His wife said:
"People say that the dead fear peach wood,
why are you not afraid?"
He replied:
"The southeast branch of the peach tree, two feet eight inches long,
the one facing the sun, I dislike it,
but perhaps I am also not afraid."
Seeing garlic shells on the ground,
he ordered them to be cleared away.
Judging by his intent,
he seemed to dislike garlic but fear peach wood.
Yuán Bǐng
In the Sòng dynasty, Yuán Bǐng,
courtesy name Shūhuàn,
was from Chénjùn.
At the end of the Tàishǐ era,
he served as the magistrate of Línxiāng.
Years after his death,
his friend Sīmǎ Xùn,
just before dawn, as if in a dream,
saw Bǐng arrive.
They recounted their long separation
and inquired about each other's well-being.
Then Bǐng said to Xùn:
"In our lifetime, we held the view and often discussed
that life is like being driven in servitude,
and death is rest.
Now I know
that this is certainly not the case.
I often worry that in the world of the living,
people
strive to pursue gold and coins,
mutually giving and receiving gifts.
In the dark path, such matters
are also exactly the same."
Xùn asked about the retribution for sins and blessings,
and how true it really is.
Bǐng said:
"According to my previous understanding,
compared to what the scriptures and teachings say,
they do not entirely match.
It must be the sages' rhetoric of restraint and guidance.
But from what I see now,
the general categories of good and evil
are largely no different.
However, killing living beings is the gravest prohibition,
so be careful not to violate it."
Xùn said:
"You have shown me this sign,
truly beyond words.
I must tell the Minister about it."
Bǐng said:
"Very good,
and I ask you to respectfully visit the Minister."
At that time, the Minister of Works Wáng Sēngqián was the head of the Ministry of Personnel.
Bǐng and Xùn had both been his guests in their lifetimes,
hence the mention.
They exchanged several hundred words,
and then Bǐng took his leave.
Xùn said:
"After such a long separation,
I often think of gathering briefly.
It is difficult to meet,
why not stay a while?"
Bǐng said:
"I have only come temporarily,
and cannot stay long.
Moreover,
the words of these beings
cannot be fully conveyed."
He bowed and departed.
When Bǐng first arrived in the dark night,
Xùn was completely unaware of how he came,
but at dawn, he could see him clearly.
After Bǐng left,
Xùn got out of bed to see him off.
Just as he put on his shoes and returned to the darkness,
he saw light between Bǐng's feet,
about a foot long,
illuminating both his feet,
while the rest of the ground remained dark, it is said.
Fèi Qìngbó
In the Sòng dynasty, there was a man named Fèi Qìngbó.
During the Xiàojiàn era,
he served as a zhìzhōng in the province.
While on leave and returning home,
he suddenly saw three attendants,
all wearing red headbands,
coming together and saying:
"The official summons you."
Qìngbó said:
"I have just returned from an audience,
how can there be another summons?
Besides, you usually wear black headbands,
why are you all wearing red headbands now?"
The attendants replied:
"It is not an official from this world."
Only then did Qìngbó realize they were not living people.
He knelt and kowtowed, begging them.
The three attendants spoke in unison,
and thus agreed to make an exchange,
saying:
"After four days,
we will come to you again.
Prepare some wine and food to receive us,
and be careful not to reveal this."
They arrived as scheduled,
and said:
"We have managed to arrange it."
Qìngbó was overjoyed and bowed in thanks,
personally setting out wine and food.
He saw the ghosts eating and drinking no differently from living people.
Before leaving, they said:
"Out of pity for you, we did this,
but we beg you to keep it secret."
Qìngbó's wife was suspicious and jealous by nature,
and said to him:
"This must be the deception of evil spirits."
Qìngbó had no choice
and told her the whole story.
Soon, he saw the three attendants from before,
beaten and bleeding,
standing angrily before him and saying:
"How could you betray us?"
After saying this,
they vanished.
Qìngbó then fell violently ill,
and died before dawn.
Liú Lǎngzhī
When Prince Ānchéng of Liáng was stationed in his fief,
he lent the former residence of Luó Shě
to the recorder Liú Lǎngzhī.
Once, Lǎngzhī saw a man in majestic attire and cap,
standing with his clothes neatly arranged.
Startled, Lǎngzhī asked who he was,
but the man suddenly vanished.
Not long after,
Lǎngzhī was dismissed from his post due to an offense,
and people at the time said that Jūnzhāng had a divine presence.
Zhǎngsūn Shàozǔ
often traveled between Chén and Cài.
One day at dusk,
by the roadside there was a household;
he called out to ask for lodging.
From inside the room came the sound of someone playing the kōng hóu.
Peeping secretly through the window,
he saw a young woman,
whose appearance and manner were serene and graceful,
alone by the bright candlelight.
Shàozǔ subtly teased her,
but the woman continued plucking the strings without pause.
Smiling, she sang:
"Long have I suffered the bitterness of yearning for you;
tonight our joyful meeting is rare.
I wish to take the quilt to keep the guest;
my one desire is to stroke your robe."
Shàozǔ was delighted;
he stepped forward directly to caress and comfort her.
The woman also said joyfully:
"From where comes this young master,
intruding so boldly?"
Thus they joined together.
She also said to Shàozǔ:
"Last night I had a wonderful dream;
today it truly came to pass."
The screen, quilts, and pillows
were all splendid and neat.
There were maidservants on either side,
who were then ordered to prepare food.
There were quite a few delicacies,
yet all were tasteless.
They also drank white fermented wine.
The woman said:
"Meeting a distinguished guest so suddenly,
I had no time to prepare finer flavors."
After drinking just a few cups,
the woman sang again,
the song saying:
"Though the Milky Way may slant again,
the wind and frost are already bitterly cold.
Humbly offered, yet you do not partake;
who knows the longing that drives me to despair?"
Then she stepped forward to embrace Shàozǔ,
called the maid to remove the candle, and they slept together.
She also paired a young maid with his servant.
As dawn approached,
the woman wiped her tears and bid farewell,
presenting him with a small gold-threaded box:
"There will be no future meetings;
remember me from time to time."
Shàozǔ mounted his horse and rode out the gate for over a hundred paces.
Looking back,
he saw it was actually a small grave mound.
He left in sorrow.
The box she had given him
was covered in accumulated dust;
it was not something used by the living.
Liǔ Dǎo,
courtesy name Rénchéng,
was from the state of Pèi.
He was a third cousin of Mr. Huán, the True and Simple of the Liáng dynasty.
His father, Jiǎn,
served as Left Guard Commander under Liáng.
Dǎo was studious and steadfast in purpose,
diligently devoted to the classics.
Admiring Jìn Guān Kāng, who once lived in seclusion in Jīngkǒu,
he feasted with his like-minded friend Lǐ Shìjiǒng.
At that time, the Qín River had just cleared after rain;
together they lamented Jīnlíng,
all grieving over the rise and fall of dynasties.
Suddenly they heard the laughter of several women among the pines.
Then they saw a maid in dark green clothing
standing before Dǎo, saying:
"On our way back from Guǎnwá Palace, we passed by here.
Hearing of your lofty dedication to the Way and serene detachment,
we wished to linger a while,
hoping you would bestow your glance upon us."
As soon as she finished speaking,
two women had arrived.
Their appearances and qualities were extraordinary,
both like immortals.
They wore red and purple silk gauze,
their fragrance assailing the senses.
Both were over twenty years old.
Dǎo and Shìjiǒng
unconsciously rose and bowed,
saying to them:
"We are lowly mortals of the human world;
why have you immortals descended?"
The two women looked at each other and laughed, saying:
"Cease your frivolous words;
we wish to leisurely express our hidden feelings."
Dǎo bowed and invited them to sit, saying:
"This dusty, turbid wine is not fit to offer."
The two women laughed and said:
"Since we have come to converse and meet,
how dare we not share the cup?"
The one in red silk
was Xī Shī.
She said to Dǎo:
"We have just crossed the river from Guǎnglíng to come here,
and are nearly exhausted.
We deeply desire to drink."
The one in purple silk
was Yíguāng.
She said to Dǎo:
"My colleague, the third sister,
long secluded in the deep quiet,
made this journey with me
precisely to meet you, noble sir."
Dǎo said to Yíguāng:
"Your elder sister
is naturally my match."
Then pointing to Shìjiǒng, he said:
"This gentleman is your match."
Yíguāng laughed heartily and gazed at him intently.
Xī Shī said:
"Master Lǐ's demeanor and bearing
are also a worthy match."
Yíguāng said:
"How can this husband's appearance
possibly move anyone?"
The whole company laughed boisterously;
all rose and retired to bed.
As dawn approached, they asked to leave,
though it was not yet fully light.
Xī Shī said to Dǎo:
"I was originally a washerwoman's daughter,
a concubine of the King of Wú.
You surely know this.
Taken by Yuè,
I fell into another's hands.
After the King of Wú perished,
I returned to dwell in my former state.
Now the King of Wú is already aged;
he cannot command us any longer.
Yíguāng is the daughter of the King of Yuè,
presented to the King of Wú in the past by Yuè.
Yíguāng and I love each other;
we sit on the same mat,
and ride in the same carriage when we go out.
This journey of ours
is also due to a karmic encounter."
Having spoken, she seemed lost in thought.
Dǎo and Shìjiǒng deeply felt regret.
Hearing the dawn bell from Jīngkǒu,
each clasped hands and said:
"There will be no future meetings."
Xī Shī left a single jeweled hairpin
with Dǎo.
Yíguāng detached a pair of pearls from her skirt
and also gave them to Shìjiǒng.
Having spoken,
they mounted a jeweled carriage together,
and departed like wind and rain.
Their voices still seemed in their ears,
but in an instant they were gone from sight.
This was in the seventh month of the eleventh year of the Tiānjiàn era of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
The Liǔ Family
In the final years of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
there was a man surnamed Liǔ,
but his given name is unknown.
On the ridge of his main hall's roof,
he saw a creature.
Its face was like a lion's,
with white hair hanging from both cheeks,
over a foot long.
Its hands and feet were like a human's.
Slowly it raised one foot.
In a moment, it vanished.
Shortly after, Liǔ died.
Cuī Luóshí
Shěn Jǐng,
styled Xuánjī,
was a man from Wǔkāng, Wúxìng.
He was handsome and graceful,
skilled in composing poetry,
and served as a regular attendant in the Eastern Palace of the Liáng dynasty,
famous in his time.
Whenever high officials held banquets,
they would send riders to invite him.
It was said:
"When Xuánjī is present,
guests are captivated."
Such was the esteem in which he was held.
Later, when Jīng-Chǔ fell,
he entered the service of the Northern Zhōu as a Shàngzhùguó,
and was sent on a mission to Qín-Lǒng.
On the way, he passed by the Temple of the Zhāng Nǚláng.
Travelers often prayed there with wine and food offerings,
but Jǐng alone ladled water and offered a prayer, saying:
"I ladle from that cold spring water,
and pluck red blossoms from the rocky valley.
Though what I bring is not from afar,
my offering follows custom.
My sincere heart is here—
may the spirit sense and accept it."
When evening came,
he lodged at a relay station.
Leaning by the window, he gazed at the moon
and composed the song "Fèng Jiāng Chú Hán Jiāo Qǔ."
The lyrics were:
"No one to share my call,
where to harbor this tender grace?
Wandering beneath flowers and moon,
in vain this lovely night I face."
He then continued with another song:
"Softly the spring breeze arrives,
gently the spring dew descends.
Alas, the moon over the frontier passes,
shines uselessly, its light extends."
After reciting these,
he heard a sigh of admiration outside the curtain,
followed by these words:
"How could a leisurely night be wasted?
How could a bright moon lack its glow?"
The voice was clear and gentle,
quite different from the ordinary.
Suddenly, he saw a woman lift the curtain and enter,
bowing as she said:
"The Zhāng Nǚláng sisters send their regards."
Jǐng, astonished,
straightened his clothes and cap.
Before he could rise from his seat, the two women had already entered.
They said to Jǐng:
"You have traversed mountains and rivers,
surely weary from your journey."
Jǐng replied:
"On duty, traveling the road,
spring nights stir many feelings.
I merely sought, through verse,
to ease a traveler's melancholy.
Little did I expect the noble ladies would descend in their immortal carriage.
I wish to know your esteemed names."
The two women looked at each other and smiled.
The elder said to Jǐng:
"I am the younger sister of the lady,
married to the eldest son of the Lady of Lúshān."
Pointing to the younger woman, she said:
"She is married to the youngest son of the Lord of Héngshān.
On our shared birthday,
we came together to visit our elder sister.
As our elder sister has not yet returned from the layered city this morning,
the mountain is secluded and quiet.
Lovely nights stir many thoughts,
so we wished to invite you.
Do not mind the trouble."
Then they took his hands and went out the door,
boarding together a curtained carriage
drawn by six horses,
which sped through the air.
Soon they arrived at a place
with vermilion towers and soaring pavilions,
extremely splendid and magnificent.
They had Jǐng wait in a waterside pavilion.
Fragrance wafted in from outside;
the curtains and hangings were adorned with golden threads and kingfisher feathers,
interspersed with pearls,
filling the room with light.
After a moment,
the two women came from behind the pavilion,
gliding gracefully forward.
They bowed to Jǐng and invited him to sit,
then prepared wine and food.
Thereupon, the elder woman played the kōnghóu,
and the younger played the qín.
They performed several melodies,
all unheard of in the mortal world.
Jǐng sighed in admiration for a long while,
and wished to borrow the qín to transcribe them.
The younger woman smiled and said to Jǐng:
"These were composed by Duke Mù of Qín, the Crown Prince of King Líng of Zhōu, and other immortals.
They cannot be transmitted to the human world."
Jǐng roughly remembered a few melodies
but dared not inquire further.
When the wine was in full flow,
the elder woman sang:
"When human and spirit meet, later reunions are hard;
by chance encounter, we share this brief joy.
The Star River shifts, the night will soon end;
our hearts not yet fulfilled, let us linger a while."
The younger woman sang:
"The sound of the dòngxiāo stirs the flowing breeze;
the clear night deepens, pipes and strings grow strong.
Long yearning by the Héngshān melody;
my heart breaks at the head of Qín-Lǒng."
She then added:
"Cloud-carriages on Lǒng's heights dwell no more;
on Xiāng River's mottled bamboo, tears still stain.
Who thinks of me in Héngshān's misty veil,
watching wild geese's feet bring no letter again?"
Jǐng sang:
"Yìxī era passed through many a year;
Zhāng Shuò gained but fleeting love, it's clear.
Why are we today less blessed than the past?
A brief meeting, then no chance to hold fast."
The two women looked at each other, shedding tears,
and Jǐng also wept.
The younger woman said to Jǐng:
"Aunt Lánxiāng and Sister Zhìqióng
often harbored this regret as well."
Jǐng saw the two women singing joyfully,
but did not know the secret bond between them.
Jǐng turned to the younger woman and said:
"Rùnyù,
this man is worth remembering."
After a long while,
the elder woman put on her shoes
and went out with the younger woman.
At the door,
she said to the younger:
"Rùnyù may keep Shěn Láng company tonight."
Jǐng was overjoyed, as if he could not believe it.
They then held hands and entered the room,
where a young maid had already laid out bedding.
The younger woman took Jǐng's hand and said:
"Once, while traveling the Xiāng River with the two consorts,
I saw you at Emperor Shùn's temple reading the Xiàng Wáng stele.
Since then, I have thought of you often,
never expecting tonight my wish would be fulfilled."
Jǐng also clearly remembered the event.
Holding hands, they spoke intimately,
unable to restrain themselves.
The young maid, lovely in appearance,
stepped forward and said:
"The paths of human and spirit are separate;
partings are swift, meetings rare.
Moreover, Cháng'é is jealous,
unwilling to linger her light;
the Weaving Maiden is restless,
already slanting the River again.
How much time remains?
Why trouble with trivialities?"
So they closed the door and retired to bed,
sharing utmost intimacy and joy.
As dawn approached,
the younger woman rose
and said to Jǐng:
"The affairs of humans and spirits differ;
it is not fitting to prolong the day.
Our elder sister is already at the door."
Jǐng then held her on his lap,
and they shared heartfelt words.
Soon after,
the elder woman arrived before them again.
Facing each other, they shed tears,
unable to contain their sorrow.
Wine was served again,
and Jǐng sang once more:
"How can a traveler's heart be at peace,
when miles of separation hinder affection's ease?
Now the parting waters on Lǒng's heights flow,
carrying ever the sound of sorrow."
Jǐng then gave the younger woman a ring,
and she gave Jǐng a golden love-knot.
She sang:
"The heart's knot entwines ten thousand strands;
the strands are knotted a thousand times.
The knot of sorrow has no end;
the knot of the heart will never unwind."
The elder woman gave Jǐng a jade mirror,
singing:
"I recall gazing into the jade mirror,
looking together at the bright moon.
Both once reflected our faces—
do not let their radiance be gone."
There were many more exchanges of gifts and songs,
too many to record fully,
only a few roughly remembered.
Then they went out the door together,
and boarded the curtained carriage again.
They escorted him to the lower temple,
where they held hands, sobbed, and bid farewell.
Upon returning to the lodging,
he discovered in his bosom a jade mirror and a golden-threaded knot.
After a long while,
he spoke to his host,
but by nightfall, they were nowhere to be found.
At that time, his companions all wondered at the strange fragrance that filled the night watch.
Later, when Jǐng returned from his mission,
he went to the temple
and found behind the deity's seat a blue letter,
which was a message from the young maiden to Jǐng.
It detailed the sorrow of parting,
and at the end of the letter was a poem:
"A swift letter reports to Shěn Láng,
that I have already reached Héngyáng.
If our bond remains as steadfast as metal and stone,
we shall gaze upon the wind and moon, each from afar."
From then on, all contact ceased.
Cuī Zǐwǔ
In his youth, Cuī Zǐwǔ of Qí
stayed at the home of his maternal grandfather, Lǐ Xiàn, the Governor of Yángzhōu in Zhàojùn.
At night, he dreamed of a maiden,
of exceptional beauty,
who claimed to be the daughter of the Dragon King,
and wished to engage in a secret romance with Cuī Láng.
Zǐwǔ was delighted,
and tugged at the hem of her garment,
causing a slight tear.
Before dawn, she bid farewell,
tying a ribbon as a token of parting.
By daybreak,
he went to the mountain temple to look,
and beside it was a painted maiden,
whose appearance was exactly the one he had seen in the dream,
with the torn hem and tied ribbon still present.
From then on, Zǐwǔ frequently dreamed of her,
and became dazed and ill.
Later, he encountered a physician who forbade it,
and the dreams ceased.
Mǎ Dàoyóu
During the Southern Qí dynasty,
Mǎ Dàoyóu served as a Clerk in the Imperial Secretariat.
In the first year of the Yǒngmíng era,
while sitting in the government office,
he suddenly saw ghosts filling the space before him,
though those beside him could not see them.
In a moment, two ghosts entered his ears,
pushed out his soul,
and it fell onto his clogs.
He pointed and showed it to others:
"Do you all see it?"
Those beside him still could not see it.
When asked about the shape of the soul,
Dàoyóu said:
"The soul looks exactly like a toad."
He added:
"There is certainly no chance of survival,
for the ghosts are still in my ears now."
Looking at his ears, both were swollen,
and the next day he died.
Gù Zǒng
In the first year of the Tiānjiàn era of the Liáng dynasty,
there was a minor clerk in Wǔchāng named Gù Zǒng,
who was dull-witted and foolish by nature,
and unfit for his duties.
He was often whipped and beaten by the county magistrate.
Once, feeling deeply depressed and resentful,
he fled to a place among ruined tombs.
Wandering about in sorrow and melancholy,
he did not know where to go.
Suddenly, two figures in yellow robes appeared.
Looking at Zǒng, they said:
"Does Lord Liú still recall our past companionship?"
Zǒng replied:
"My humble lineage is the Gù family.
I have never seen your esteemed faces before.
How can there be any question of past companionship?"
The two said:
"We are Wáng Càn and Xú Gàn.
In your previous life, you were Liú Zhēn,
serving as Palace Attendant in the Kūnmíng Kingdom.
Because you accepted bribes of gold,
you were demoted to be a minor clerk.
You should know this yourself.
Yet your words are clear and distinct,
still reflecting the tone and intent of a Secretary."
They then took out a scroll from their sleeves and showed it to him, saying:
"This is your collection of writings.
You should examine it carefully."
Zǒng tried to read it.
Then he became completely clear and enlightened,
and immediately felt his literary inspiration gushing forth.
Many people possessed copies of his collection,
but only the poems written after his death were remembered.
One poem was titled "Accompanying the Imperial Carriage on an Excursion to the Beautiful and Secluded
Palace, Then Recalling the Literary Gatherings at the Western Garden in My Lifetime, and Thus Sent to Cài Bójiē, the Principal Gentleman of the Dìwén Bureau." The poem said:
"In Hàn, the reins of order were set,
the vast rivers surged with turbulent waves.
The glorious and heroic ancestor of Wèi
rescued the drowning and calmed the waves.
Heaven's order was already firmly established,
and the people of the state were also preserved intact.
He grandly opened the ministerial office,
gathering all the secluded orchids.
Beginning with the multitude of gentlemen,
daily attending the joyful gatherings of the worthy king.
Emperor Wén was in the Eastern Palace,
his filial piety surpassing mere morning inquiries.
Overseeing and assisting left ample leisure,
freely touring and viewing the gardens and parks.
I, the lowly minister, wore the hairpin and brush,
assisting the sage, following the harmonious carriage bells.
The moon rose, the traveling palace was cool,
precious trees held clear dewdrops clustered.
The celestial patterns were truly radiant and splendid,
resounding and clanging, shaking the jade-like stones.
I was commanded to look up and harmonize,
but looking at myself, I attempted what was difficult.
My weak constitution could not sustain itself,
frail and decaying, withered and ruined.
How could I have imagined that after more than ten years,
the imperial tombs would be cold with parasol trees and catalpas.
Now I come to the Kūnmíng Kingdom,
again donning the cicada-crested cap.
Accompanying the excursion to the detached palace,
my feet tread on floating clouds' ends.
Yet I think back to the time at the Western Garden,
life and death bring temporary sorrow and bitterness.
You, sir, were once a Hàn duke or minister,
crowning the assembly of worthies at Wèiyāng.
If you remember your past life,
reading this, you too will be filled with sorrow."
The other seven pieces
were lost by those who transmitted them.
Wáng Càn said to Zǒng:
"I was originally short and small.
For no particular reason, I married Yuè Jìn's daughter.
The daughter resembled her father,
especially short and small.
After parting from you, sir,
I remarried, taking the daughter of Governor Liú of Jīngzhōu.
Soon, she bore a son.
Governor Liú gave him the childhood name Wēngnú.
This year he is eighteen,
seven feet three inches tall.
What I regret is that he has not yet been able to pay respects to you, sir.
When he was eleven,
we looked in the mirror together.
I said to him:
'Your head is more imposing than mine.'
He immediately responded to me:
'Fángfēng's bones filled a cart,
but they were not as good as Bái Qǐ's small and sharp head.'
I also said to him:
'When you grow up, you should become a general.'
He again responded to me:
'Even a three-foot-tall child like Zhòngní [Confucius]
would be ashamed to speak of the way of hegemony.
Moreover, having received my father's strict instruction,
how dare I set my mind on hacking and stabbing?'
I knew then that his intelligence surpassed others.
I wonder if since your rebirth,
you have had any sons or daughters?"
After a long while of deep thought,
Zǒng gradually felt as if he recognized them.
He then said:
"Since you two gentlemen are friends of Zǒng,
what plan can free me from the plight of being a minor clerk?"
Xú Gàn said:
"You only need to take the former collection
and present it to the county magistrate, and you will be freed."
Zǒng asked further:
"What country is Kūnmíng?"
Gàn said:
"It is the land of Yè, where Wèi Wǔ [Cáo Cāo] founded his state.
You, sir, were formerly its Palace Attendant.
Have you so quickly forgotten?"
"Your family in Kūnmíng,
are they all well?"
"Your worthy little daughter, Xiūniáng,
has one piece titled 'Thinking of You with Respect.'
Yesterday, I already recited it for you, sir."
The poem said:
'I miss my father,
who abandoned his daughter and does not return home.
Not serving as Palace Attendant, he became a minor clerk,
enduring hardship there, forsaking glory and splendor.
I wish my father would remember and meet me soon,
to buy plums and sweet melons at the market for his child.'"
After reciting,
Zǒng could not help but shed tears profusely.
He then composed a piece titled "Sent to Xiūniáng," which said:
"I remember my child's face.
I think of my child's heart.
Longing for my child unseen, tears soak my lapel.
Times change, the world differs, meeting is hard.
Renouncing and leaving this life, I should seek again."
Afterward, Wáng Càn and Xú Gàn bid Zǒng an earnest farewell
and left him the five-volume collection of Liú Zhēn.
Zǒng went to see the county magistrate
and fully recounted the affair.
When the magistrate saw the poems in Liú Zhēn's collection,
he exclaimed in surprise:
"We cannot let Lord Liú Gàn be a minor clerk!"
Once dismissed from his post,
he treated Zǒng with the courtesy due a guest.
Later, no one knew where Zǒng went,
and the collection was also soon lost.
People of the time admonished their children and younger brothers,
all saying:
"Even the dead Liú Zhēn could still protect the living Gù Zǒng.
Should one not strive to improve?"
Xíng Luán
In the Northern Wèi, at Yǒnghé Lane in Luòyáng,
was the residence of Hàn's Grand Preceptor Dǒng Zhuó.
Both the north and south ends of the lane had ponds,
constructed by Zhuó,
whose water never dried up winter or summer.
In the lane were the six residences of: Grand Tutor and Recorder of the Department of State Affairs, Zhǎngsūn Zhì;
President of the Right of the Department of State Affairs, Guō Zuò;
Minister of Personnel, Xíng Luán;
Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review, Yuán Hóngchāo;
Chief Minister of the Court of Imperial Regalia, Xǔ Bótáo;
and Regional Inspector of Liángzhōu, Yù Chéngxīng.
All had high gates and splendid houses,
with spacious and beautiful study halls and pavilions.
Catalpa and locust trees shaded the paths,
with parasol trees and poplars planted on both sides.
It was renowned in that era as the noble lane.
When digging in this area,
one would often unearth gold, jade, treasures, and curios.
At Xíng Luán's home,
they often excavated cinnabar and hundreds of thousands of coins,
inscribed with:
"Property of Grand Preceptor Dǒng."
Later, Zhuó came at night to demand these items from Luán.
Luán did not give them to him.
Within a year, Luán died.
Xiāo Móhóu
In the final years of Empress Dowager Hú of the Later Wèi,
a servant of Tián Cānjūn Xiāo Móhóu in Zézhōu,
washed a yellow robe
and sunned it on a tree in the courtyard,
forgetting to bring it in by dusk.
In the middle of the night,
Móhóu got up and went outside,
and saw this robe moved by the wind,
resembling a human figure.
Thinking it was a thief,
he took a knife and went to strike it,
but upon closer inspection, it was only the robe.
From then on,
everyone inside and outside the house was fearful.
A few days later,
suddenly about twenty riders appeared,
all dressed in military attire,
heading straight for his home,
waving flags and raising staffs,
coming and going in sudden attacks.
This happened in six or seven places in succession.
The family was terrified,
not knowing how to defend against them.
Someone said,
according to a medicinal prescription,
burning goat horns
would stop the demons.
They immediately obtained some from a butcher's shop,
and burned them.
When the riders came again,
they covered their noses and said:
"This household doesn't know what they're burning,
it's so foul and stinky!"
They turned around and left,
and from then on, the disturbances ceased.
Dàorén Fǎlì
Dàorén Fǎlì of Xiǎnmíng Temple in Guǎngzhōu,
went to the latrine at dawn,
and encountered a ghost inside the door,
who looked like a Kūnlún slave,
with completely yellow eyes,
naked and without clothes.
Fǎlì had always been strong,
so he tied it to a pillar in the hall,
and whipped it with a staff,
but it made no sound at all.
He then bound it with iron chains,
to see if it could transform and escape.
When it grew dark,
the ghost had disappeared.
Xiāo Sīyù,
was a grandnephew of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
His father, Què,
was killed by Hóu Jǐng.
Because his father had met such a fate,
Sīyù had no interest in pursuing an official career.
He often admired the Dao,
and hoped to encounter divine beings,
hence his given name Sīyù (思遇, "yearning for an encounter") and courtesy name Wàngmíng (望明, "gazing at brightness"),
meaning he hoped to meet divine spirits.
He lived on the eastern hill of Hǔqiū,
his nature was simple and tranquil,
and he loved the qin and books.
On nights with pine winds,
he would stop playing the qin and let out a long whistle,
startling all the buildings and towers on the mountain.
He often sat on rocks in the rain, singing passionately.
Suddenly, he heard someone knocking at the brushwood gate.
Sīyù, suspicious that something unusual was happening,
ordered a servant to ask from afar.
The reply came:
"No need to ask."
Just say I came from Huànxī in the rain.
When the servant boy opened the door,
he saw a beautiful woman,
with two maids in green attire following her,
all with the appearance of immortals.
Sīyù put on a mountain hermit's robe,
and met them with courtesy,
saying:
"Just now I heard you say,
you came from Huànxī.
The road is long in the rain,
may I ask what carriage you rode?"
The woman said:
"I heard that you, sir, cherish extraordinary paths,
and value simplicity and purity,
so I did not use a carriage,
but came riding the wind."
Sīyù said:
"If you came from washing sand,
could you be Xīshī?"
The woman looked back at the two maids and smiled,
then asked:
"How did you know, sir?"
Sīyù said:
"No need to worry,
you should rest now."
At dawn, when they were about to part,
the woman left a golden bracelet as a farewell token.
Sīyù said he had "nothing to express his feelings,"
and added:
"Only this heart will not forget."
The lady said:
"This is most precious."
Sīyù asked:
"When you leave, madam,
when will you return?"
The woman covered her face and wept, saying:
"I dare not promise a date,
I fear I will have troubled your affections in vain."
Sīyù was also deeply saddened.
After speaking,
she rode the wind and departed.
In a moment, she was gone,
only the fragrance remained in the bedchamber.
This was on the second day of the second month in the first year of the Tiānjiā era of Emperor Wén of Chén.
Rén Zhòu
Rén Zhòu, the Sīmǎ of the Eastern Wèi Chancellor,
plotted to assassinate Gāo Huān.
The affair was exposed and he was executed,
but his family did not yet know.
Suddenly, they saw his head appear on top of the rice steamer in their home.
They called each other to look,
and after a short while,
it disappeared.
Soon after, they learned he had been killed.
Dǒng Shòuzhī
Dǒng Shòuzhī of Northern Qí was executed,
but his family did not yet know.
His wife was sitting at night,
when she suddenly saw Shòuzhī sitting beside her,
sighing incessantly.
His wife asked how he had returned at night,
but Shòuzhī did not answer at all.
After a while, he went out the door,
walked around the chicken coop,
and the chickens inside cried out in alarm.
His wife, suspicious that something was wrong,
took a torch and went outside to look,
and saw several dou of blood,
but Shòuzhī had disappeared.
She then told her mother-in-law,
and together with the whole family, they wailed,
knowing something had happened.
By morning,
they indeed received news of his death.
Fán Xiàoqiān
Fán Xiàoqiān of Northern Qí
was known for his talent from a young age.
At twenty-two,
he passed the xiùcái examination,
and was promoted to Attendant Gentleman of the Palace Gate.
Once, at his gate,
he watched a nobleman's funeral procession,
and bowed to the exorcist figure (Fāngxiàng) before parting.
Exactly one year later,
on the same day as that funeral,
someone knocked at his door.
Xiàoqiān went out to look,
and saw the Fāngxiàng he had bowed to.
It stood at the gate and said:
"On this day last year,
did you speak with me?"
Xiàoqiān fell over in fright.
He died shortly after.
In the early Zhēnguàn era,
Cuī Xìnmíng was the prefect of Yángzhōu,
and his account matched that of the county assistant magistrate Xiàng Guàn without discrepancy.
Lǐ Wénfǔ
In the early years of the Suí dynasty, during the Kāihuáng era of Emperor Wén,
there was a man named Lǐ Wénfǔ from Āndìng.
He lived in the Shíqiáo neighborhood of Yèdū.
Once, he placed a wine bottle under his bed at night.
In the middle of the night, he awoke
and suddenly heard the sound of the bottle tipping over and wine leaking out.
He sent a maidservant to check,
but the wine bottle was not tipped over;
its stopper was as secure as before.
After a short while,
he again heard the sound of something lapping up water.
He called for a light to look around,
but the room was quiet and nothing was seen.
He extinguished the candle and closed the door,
but before he could sleep,
it seemed something tapped his knee with a finger.
After this happened three times,
Wénfǔ got up and groped around,
but again found nothing.
He then drew his sword and swung it in all directions,
whereupon he heard a sound like a flying cicada trailing a shrill noise,
which rushed out of the room.
Later, Lǐ Wénfǔ served as Deputy Magistrate of Xūchāng County in Yǎnzhōu.
In the eighth year of the Kāihuáng era,
he saw Kǒng Zàn, the former Records Clerk of the prefecture,
who was a native of Xūchāng
and had died earlier.
Suddenly, in broad daylight, he came before Wénfǔ's hall and bowed twice.
Wénfǔ, startled, asked what he was doing.
He said:
"The Lord of Mount Tài is selecting good men.
I, Zàn, consider you, sir, to be wise and capable,
and have therefore recommended you."
Wénfǔ, worried and frightened, kowtowed.
After a long pause, Zàn said:
"I will now find another way.
Be careful not to reveal this."
By the tenth year,
Wénfǔ spoke of this himself.
After he finished speaking,
he immediately felt unwell,
and shortly after, he died.
Shǐ Wànsuì
In the Dàixián neighborhood of Cháng'ān,
there was the residence of Suí dynasty General-in-Chief of the Northern Command, Shǐ Wànsuì.
His residence initially often had ghostly disturbances;
those who lived there would die.
Wànsuì did not believe it,
and thus moved in.
At night, he saw a man in magnificent attire
approach him.
Wànsuì asked his reason for coming.
The ghost said:
"I am Hàn dynasty General Fán Kuài.
My tomb is near your toilet,
and I constantly suffer from the filth and foulness.
If you would kindly move it elsewhere,
I will surely repay you generously."
Wànsuì agreed.
He then questioned the ghost about the reason for killing living people.
The ghost said:
"They each died from fright,
it was not I who killed them."
When the coffin and bones were excavated,
he had them reburied.
Later that night, the ghost came again to thank him, saying:
"You shall become a general,
and I will surely aid you."
Later, Wànsuì became a general of Suí.
Whenever he encountered bandits,
he would feel ghostly soldiers aiding him,
and his battles were always great victories.
Fáng Xuánlíng
When Fáng Xuánlíng and Dù Rúhuì were still obscure,
they once traveled together from Zhōu to Qín,
and lodged at an inn in Fūshuǐ.
They happened to have wine and meat,
and were eating late at night.
Suddenly, they saw two black, hairy hands appear beneath the lamp,
as if making a request.
They each then placed a piece of roasted meat in the hands.
After a while, the hands appeared again,
as if cupped together,
so they each poured wine for them,
after which they did not appear again.
After finishing their meal,
they turned their backs to the lamp and went to bed.
Around the second watch,
they heard someone on the street repeatedly calling for Wáng Wén'áng.
Suddenly, they heard a voice respond from beneath the lamp.
The caller then said:
"Twenty lǐ due east,
villagers are holding a feast for the gods.
The wine and food are very plentiful.
Can you go?"
The respondent said:
"I am already drunk and full from wine and meat.
I have official duties,
and cannot go.
Thank you for summoning me."
The caller said:
"You are hungry and distressed all day long.
How could you have wine and meat?
You are not an official clerk to begin with.
How could you have official duties?
Why are you speaking nonsense?"
The respondent said:
"I have been assigned by the overworked clerks to serve the two chancellors on duty,
and was bestowed wine and meat,
therefore I cannot go.
If I had heard your call at a normal time,
I would have been off running with you already."
The caller apologized and left.
Wèi Zhēng
Duke of Zhèngguó, Wèi Zhēng,
in his youth was fond of studying the Dào and
did not believe in ghosts and spirits.
Once, while visiting Dàoist sites, he reached Héng Shān.
Just as he was about to arrive at the mountain's base,
suddenly a great wind and snow arose,
heaven and earth turned dark and gloomy,
and he could not proceed.
Suddenly, a Dàoist priest appeared,
leaning on a green bamboo staff,
with a copy of the *Huángtíng Jīng* hanging from it.
He also arrived by the roadside.
He said to Zhēng:
"Where are you going?"
Zhēng said:
"I have come here to visit Dàoist sites,
but am hindered by the wind and snow."
The Dàoist priest said:
"One or two lǐ from here
is my home.
Could you stay one night for conversation?"
Zhēng agreed,
and they went together.
They arrived at a dwelling;
the exterior was quite desolate,
but the interior was exquisitely carved.
He invited Zhēng into a deep chamber,
where they sat facing a stove fire,
and he offered fine wine and excellent dishes.
They leisurely discussed the Dào;
the Dàoist's arguments were broad and eloquent,
and Zhēng could not refute him.
As dawn approached,
the Dàoist spoke of matters concerning ghosts and spirits.
Zhēng firmly stated that they cannot harm the upright.
The Dàoist said:
"What you follow is the way of immortals.
How can you completely deny ghosts and spirits?
Since heaven and earth existed, there have been ghosts and spirits.
If one's Dào is lofty, then ghosts, spirits, and monsters will surely submit to it;
but if one's cultivation of the Dào is not yet lofty,
then ghosts, spirits, and monsters
can, on the contrary, be attracted.
How can you belittle them?"
Zhēng did not reply.
At daybreak,
the Dàoist again offered wine to see Zhēng off,
and also entrusted him with a letter
to deliver to a recluse in Héng Shān.
After Zhēng set off,
following the mountain path,
he looked back at the place he had stayed—
it was merely a large burial mound.
He examined the letter;
the inscription read:
"To be delivered to the Divine Assistant of Héng Shān."
Zhēng was disgusted,
threw it on the ground,
and the letter transformed into a rat and ran away.
From then on, Zhēng began to believe somewhat in ghosts and spirits.
Táng Jiǎn
When Táng Jiǎn was young,
he rode a donkey intending to travel to Wú and Chǔ.
Passing through Luòchéng,
he grew very thirsty.
Seeing a small house by the roadside,
inside was a woman over twenty years old,
sewing clothes by the light.
He approached to beg for some drink,
but she was sewing socks.
She then went to another room to fetch the drink,
saying, "You, sir, are very thirsty,
let me get it for you."
After a short while,
she brought a bowl.
Jiǎn looked inside her room
and saw no kitchen stove.
Upon her return, he asked:
"Madam, in your dwelling,
why is there no fire?"
She replied:
"I am too poor to afford cooking,
I seek food from nearby places."
Having said this,
she resumed sewing socks,
appearing very busy.
He asked again why she was in such a hurry,
and she said:
"My husband, Xuē Liáng,
is a poor peddler.
He has been away on business for over ten years.
He has never once returned to serve his parents.
Tomorrow morning, he is coming to fetch me,
hence my hurry."
Jiǎn subtly flirted with her,
but she refused to respond.
Jiǎn felt ashamed and apologized,
leaving two rolls of cakes before departing.
After traveling over ten *lǐ*,
he suddenly remembered he had forgotten some books he needed.
He returned to Luò to retrieve them.
The next morning, he arrived again at this place,
preparing to leave the capital,
but was blocked by a funeral procession on the road.
He asked who it was,
and the reply was:
"It is the coffin of the peddler Xuē Liáng."
Startled by the name,
which was the woman's husband from yesterday,
he then asked where he was from.
The reply was:
"Liáng's wife died five years after their marriage,
and was buried in the old city.
Another five years later, Liáng died.
His elder brother is moving his coffin
to be buried alongside the ancestral graves."
Jiǎn followed to observe.
When they reached the burial site,
it was the place where he had asked for water.
Soon, the coffin was opened,
and on it were two rolls of cakes
and a pair of new socks.
Jiǎn felt sorrow and found it strange,
then continued eastward.
When his boat moored southeast of Chánzhì Temple in Yángzhōu,
there were two scholars,
each leading their followers,
about a hundred paces apart,
opening old graves.
One sighed in astonishment for a long time,
while his followers often gathered and laughed.
The other held a spade,
smashed the coffin, and cursed.
Jiǎn then approached them.
The one who sighed said:
"My surname is Wéi,
formerly the magistrate of Tàihú.
The one being exhumed here
is my deceased son.
He has been buried for ten years.
Just now, when we opened to change his coffin,
we found his shoe missing from the coffin,
and instead, there was one woman's shoe.
That man over there is Péi Jì,
formerly the commandant of Jiāngdū.
The one being exhumed is his beloved concubine.
He doted on her in life.
Péi took office for two years and then died,
and she was buried here a year later.
Now his term is over, and he is returning home.
Unable to bear leaving her behind,
he intends to bring her back to Luò.
After opening the coffin,
he found one of her shoes missing,
and instead, there was one man's shoe.
Both parties were mutually astonished.
They took and matched them,
and they formed a pair.
It seems my unworthy son had an affair with her,
coming and going without restraint,
and hastily left them behind."
Upon hearing this,
Jiǎn boarded his boat and pondered quietly:
"The peddler's wife died five years ago,
yet she still had the heart to serve her parents-in-law.
As for this overly favored concubine,
even in death she behaves like this—
what hope is there for her in life?
How can a gentleman be infatuated with such women and neglect his wife?"
Mùróng Chuí
When Táng Tàizōng campaigned against Liáo,
traveling to Dìngzhōu,
a ghost appeared by the roadside,
dressed in yellow robes,
standing atop a high mound,
with an exceptionally divine aura.
Tàizōng sent an envoy to inquire,
and it replied:
"My past surpassed your past,
your present surpasses my present.
Glory belongs to different eras;
why labor to seek it out?"
After speaking, it vanished.
When asked,
it was revealed to be the tomb of Mùróng Chuí.
Lǐ Jì's Daughter
In the first year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Lǐ Jì's beloved daughter died
and was buried at Běimáng.
He had a household servant lodge by the graveside.
One day,
the girl suddenly appeared to the servant and said:
"I did not actually die;
I was stolen by the spirit of a great tree.
Now, as the spirit has gone to pay respects at Xīyuè,
I managed to escape.
Knowing you are here,
I have come.
I have already left my parents,
and after this humiliation,
I cannot return.
I beg you to hide me,
and I can repay you with wealth."
The servant was shocked and stunned,
but after a long while, he agreed,
and set up a separate room for her.
The girl would sometimes leave in the morning and return at dusk,
or leave at night and come back at dawn,
walking as swiftly as the wind.
A month later,
she suddenly brought ten catties of gold to give him.
The servant accepted it.
When he went to sell a few taels,
it turned out to be lost property from a commoner's household.
The owner seized the servant and reported him.
The magistrate of Luòyáng investigated the matter thoroughly.
The servant recounted the whole story,
but when they went to retrieve her,
the girl had already vanished,
and the remaining gold had all turned into yellow stones.
The Man Who Untied the Bundle
Several people were traveling by boat in Jiāngnán,
when they saw two men on the shore,
walking alongside the boat for several miles.
The men on the shore said:
"May we rest on your boat for a while?"
The boatmen agreed.
They were astonished at how the men leaped onto the boat,
swift as the wind.
After a short while,
the two men said:
"We are going to the village for a moment.
Each of us has a small bundle,
which we will leave on the boat.
Be careful not to open them."
They earnestly warned them.
After the two men left,
one person on the boat untied the bundles to look inside.
Each bundle contained five hundred slips,
resembling paper,
but the writing was neither seal script nor clerical script,
and no one could read it.
Everyone was shocked,
and they tied the bundles back as before.
Soon, the two men returned
and said:
"You opened them—why deny it?"
They then seized the person who had untied the bundles and said:
"This is the one who opened them."
They then threw the person who had untied the bundles onto the shore,
as if tossing a baby.
They also went to the village to fetch someone,
surrounded him, and left.
After several days,
one of them wanted to release the person who had untied the bundles,
but the other refused,
saying:
"He will be made to suffer for a year or two."
They then took him to a wealthy man's house.
This wealthy man owned fine horses
and often placed a trough in the courtyard,
personally watching them drink and eat.
It was already night,
and the hall door was closed,
so there was no way to capture the wealthy man.
One of them said:
"This man loves his horses.
If we untie and release them,
he will surely open the door and come out."
As predicted,
the wealthy man indeed came out.
One of them carried him,
and he died instantly.
After capturing the wealthy man,
they abandoned the person who had untied the bundles and left.
The household was in a panic,
and seeing only this person present,
they beat him together.
They tied him up and sent him to the county office,
using the incident of untying the bundles as an excuse.
The prefecture and county did not believe him,
so they sentenced him to death.
This person had no way to clear his name,
and after a long imprisonment, he was finally released.
The Person from Cáodiàn
During the Zhēnguàn era,
a person from Cáodiàn west of Cháng'ān City
buried his parents
with lavish funeral arrangements.
One or two years later,
he suddenly saw his deceased younger brother arrive,
looking haggard and weary.
He said that because his elder brother had buried their parents so extravagantly,
he had been assigned to serve as a horse at Língāo Station,
and the duties were unbearably exhausting,
so he came to ask his elder brother to take his place.
The elder brother was greatly alarmed and fearful,
so he gave him more paper money
and urged him to endure and continue his duties.
Several months later,
he saw his younger brother come again and say
that he could no longer bear the duties,
so the elder brother could not avoid going.
The elder brother died at that very moment.
Zhāng Cóng
At the beginning of the Yǒnghuī era,
Zhāng Cóng served as the magistrate of Nányáng.
While resting in his chamber,
he heard moaning sounds from the bamboo in front of the steps.
When he went to look, he saw nothing.
This happened for several nights,
and he found it strange,
so he prayed:
"If there is a spirit,
please speak to me."
That night,
a man suddenly emerged from the bamboo,
his appearance wretched and ugly.
He stepped forward and explained:
"During the rebellion of Zhū Càn,
I was among the soldiers
and was killed by Càn.
My corpse lies right in front of Your Honor's chamber.
One of my eyes was pierced by a bamboo root,
causing unbearable pain.
Because Your Honor is benevolent and wise,
I have come to plead with you.
If you would kindly move and rebury me,
I would never forget your great kindness."
The magistrate said to him:
"If that is the case, why did you not tell me earlier?"
He then agreed.
The next day,
he prepared a coffin
and had them dig,
and indeed, they found a corpse
with a bamboo root piercing its left eye.
He then provided contemporary burial clothes
and reburied it outside the city.
Later, the magistrate flogged a village elder to death,
and the elder's family sought revenge,
planning to wait until the magistrate went out at night
to ambush and kill him.
Suddenly, a fire broke out in the city,
spreading to over ten households.
The magistrate was about to go out to inspect it
when he saw the former ghost blocking his horse, saying:
"Your Honor, where are you going so late at night?
There is a sinister plot against you."
The magistrate asked who he was,
and he replied:
"The one who previously offended Your Honor."
The magistrate then returned inside.
The next day,
he raided the family's home,
and upon interrogation, everything was verified,
so he thoroughly punished them.
That night, he offered sacrifices at the ghost's tomb
and carved a stone inscription in front of it, saying:
"He gave his life for the nation's calamity,
and in death, he did not forget loyalty.
A fierce and steadfast soul,
truly a hero among ghosts."
Liú Ménnú
When Emperor Gāozōng was constructing the Dàmíng Palace,
the Xuānzhèng Hall had just been completed.
Every night,
dozens of riders could be heard around the hall,
and all the guards stationed inside the hall saw them,
their clothes and horses extremely clean.
This continued for over ten days,
so Emperor Gāozōng sent the occultist Liú Ménnú to inquire about the reason.
The spirit replied:
"I am the crown prince of King Wù of Chǔ from the Hàn dynasty."
Ménnú questioned him:
"According to the *Book of Hàn*,
the King of Chǔ conspired with the Seven States to rebel,
and the Hàn army executed him,
exterminating his clan and lineage.
How could there be any surviving descendant?"
The spirit answered:
"When the king raised his army,
he left me in Cháng'ān.
After the king was executed,
the Son of Heaven took pity on me,
spared my life,
and raised me in the palace.
Later, I died of illness
and was buried here.
The Son of Heaven pitied me,
and buried me with a pair of jade fish,
which are now in the northeast corner of the main hall.
The historians omitted this,
so it does not appear in the records."
Ménnú said:
"The current emperor is here now.
How dare you cause such disturbance in the courtyard?"
The spirit replied:
"This is my former residence.
Now that it is within the Son of Heaven's palace,
my movements are quite restricted,
and I am very unhappy.
I beg to be reburied in a high, open, and beautiful place—
that is truly my wish.
Please, do not take away my jade fish."
Ménnú reported this to the emperor,
who ordered a reburial.
Excavating the spot,
