they indeed found an ancient tomb,
the coffin already decayed,
with a pair of jade fish beside it,
exquisitely crafted.
The emperor then ordered a new coffin,
and had the body buried with proper rites outside the imperial park,
placing the jade fish with it.
After this, the disturbances ceased.
Yán Gēng
Zhāng Réndǎn,
in his youth, was poor and destitute,
and often lived in the Northern Market of the Eastern Capital.
There was a man named Yán Gēng,
son of Mǎyá Xúnzǐ,
who was fond of goodness and took pride in it.
Admiring Réndǎn's virtue,
he often secretly took his father's money
to provide for Réndǎn's food and clothing,
and this went on for many years.
Xúnzǐ would often angrily say to Gēng:
"You are of the merchant class,
he is a scholar of talent and learning.
What does he have to do with you,
that you bankrupt yourself to support him?"
Hearing these words, Réndǎn
said to Gēng:
"I have burdened you because of me.
Now I intend to go to Báilù Mountain.
I will not forget the support you have given me."
Gēng had long been Réndǎn's close friend,
and could not bear to part,
so he said to Réndǎn:
"I have just resolved to pursue learning,
and now I wish to go with you."
Réndǎn admired his determination,
and agreed.
Gēng then secretly prepared donkeys, horses, and provisions, and they set off together.
After six days, they reached Chénliú
and lodged at an inn.
Réndǎn took the inner room,
and outside the room was a bed.
After some time,
a guest arrived later
and sat on the bed.
Réndǎn saw that his appearance and gaze were extraordinary,
and told Gēng to bring a pot of wine from outside.
Réndǎn first offered the wine to the guest,
but the guest dared not accept.
Réndǎn insisted,
so they drank together.
When they were pleasantly drunk and in high spirits,
they shared the same room for the night.
In the middle of the night,
they asked each other about their journeys.
The guest replied:
"I am not human,
but an underworld clerk.
The underworld office has ordered me to manage marriages in Héběi,
tying
the feet of men and women."
Réndǎn opened the guest's clothing to look
and saw a thin rope in his bag,
so he believed him.
He then asked about his own future rank and lifespan.
The ghost said:
"Réndǎn will live over eighty years
and reach the highest rank among officials."
He then asked about Gēng.
The ghost said:
"Gēng's fate is one of poverty,
with no rank or emolument."
Réndǎn asked how this could be changed.
The ghost said:
"If he is tied to a good woman,
and matched with someone of auspicious signs,
he may achieve it.
Now, over a hundred lǐ from Báilù Mountain in Héběi,
there is a village where Old Wáng's daughter
has extremely noble signs.
Recently, she was already tied to someone,
but I will act on your behalf,
undo that tie and tie this one,
to bring success to Marquis Yán.
Just hurry on your way.
When you are about to reach the village,
there will be heavy rain soaking you—
take this as a sign."
With that, he bid farewell and left.
Réndǎn and Gēng
traveled for six or seven days
and reached the village,
encountering heavy rain
that soaked and soiled their clothes.
They went to the west of the village
to seek the Wáng family's house.
They knocked on the door,
and after a long time, someone came out,
apologizing to the guests:
"There is a small matter at home that is not going well,
so I was delayed.
Please do not be surprised."
Réndǎn asked the reason.
He said:
"I have only one daughter,
previously betrothed to the Zhāng family of West Village.
Today, when they delivered the betrothal gifts,
unexpectedly, they were meager and few,
which is a sign of disrespect.
I have already decided to break off the engagement."
Réndǎn and the others glanced at each other with slight smiles
and stayed for several days.
The host was extremely pleased,
and Réndǎn then said:
"Marquis Yán is my younger cousin,
in the prime of youth and devoted to learning,
but not yet married."
The host declined, saying they were a rustic farming family,
but he had a pleased expression.
Réndǎn insisted on the request,
and only then did the host agree.
They used the horses, donkeys, and other items as betrothal gifts,
and the marriage was completed that same day.
They left Marquis Yán to stay with the Wáng family,
while Réndǎn went on alone,
with the host seeing him off.
Several years later,
Réndǎn was promoted to Attendant Censor, Chief Administrator of Bìngzhōu, and Grand Censor in charge of government affairs.
Later, Gēng repeatedly received promotions
and eventually attained a prefecture.
Míng Chóngyǎn
Míng Chóngyǎn, a Grand Master of Remonstrance in the Tang Dynasty,
when he was young,
his father served as a county magistrate.
A gate guard in the county possessed magical arts,
and Chóngyǎn sought instruction from him.
He taught him a method for seeing ghosts,
along with techniques for commanding them.
He left two volumes of books,
which Chóngyǎn read.
They contained lists of names.
When Chóngyǎn was alone in the wilderness,
he would consult the books and call out the names,
and they would all respond:
"Yes."
He saw several hundred people.
From then on, whenever he needed to command them,
he would call their names,
and they would arrive immediately without fail.
Chóngyǎn was once traveling
when he saw a prominent family conducting a joint burial for both parents.
The funeral carriage had already left the outskirts,
and Chóngyǎn followed along.
He summoned the family members and said:
"Are you, the master of the house, jointly burying both parents?"
They replied:
"Yes."
He said:
"Did you retrieve the coffins
without mistakenly opening someone else's grave?"
They said:
"No."
Chóngyǎn said:
"Earlier, I saw a purple carriage,
followed by a lady,
over fifty years old,
a tall woman from a prominent family.
Behind her was a ghost,
quite robust in age,
with sparse hair and tattered clothes,
leaping about joyfully,
and following the lady.
The lady wept angrily and said:
'What is the meaning of a joint burial?'
Try conveying my words to your master,
tell him that Míng Zhèngjiàn has spoken thus."
The one conducting the joint burial heard this,
was greatly alarmed,
and said to Chóngyǎn through tears:
"I lost my father when I was young.
Yesterday, when relocating the burial,
I had an old servant retrieve the remains.
I did not know such a mistake had been made."
Chóngyǎn then went with him to the site where the grave was opened,
ordered them to open the area near the western boundary,
and checked the epitaph.
They indeed found it.
They then discarded the bones of the other person
and buried their ancestor alongside.
Chóngyǎn, while serving in the palace, spoke of many matters,
including numerous instances of exorcisms and magical practices among people,
all recounted by others,
so they are not detailed here.
Wáng Huáizhì
Wáng Huáizhì,
a man of Fāngzhōu in the Tang Dynasty holding the rank of Shàngzhùguó,
died in the early years of the Xiǎnqìng era.
His mother, Sūn shì,
and his younger brothers, Huáishàn and Huáibiǎo, were still alive.
In the fourth year, in the sixth month,
a man from Gāolíng in Yōngzhōu,
whose name is lost,
died and after seven days,
his back had already festered, yet he revived.
He said:
"In the underworld, I saw Huáizhì,
who now serves as a recorder in Tàishān."
He had this man take up a brush,
dictated a letter orally,
and said to him:
"Although you were fated to die,
I am now granting you a reprieve to return home.
You must take this letter to Fāngzhōu for me.
Visit my home,
and tell my mother:
'Huáizhì now serves as a recorder in Tàishān,
and is fortunately safe and well.
But our family once borrowed wood from a temple to make a door.
Since this is an object of religious merit,
repay it early.
Huáishàn is about to die;
he should not remain long.
Quickly commission sutras and Buddha images to seek aid.
Otherwise,
I fear there will be no way to save him.'"
After this man revived,
he immediately took the letter and delivered it to their house.
The household matters mentioned
all corresponded exactly.
After three days,
Huáishàn died suddenly.
All the clergy and laypeople in Hézhōu who heard of this
increased their practice of meritorious deeds.
Hóu Zhìchún, a man of Fūzhōu holding the rank of Xūnwèi, recounted this.
The Monk Yīng Chánshī
The monk Yīng Chánshī of the Fǎhǎi Temple in the Tang Dynasty
often spoke of seeing ghosts.
The temple abbot, Monk Huìlán,
found it strange and questioned him.
Yīng said:
"Previously, King Zhuāngxiāng of Qín sent someone to relay a message:
'I am extremely hungry.
Given your great compassion, Master,
and that you yourself have seen such things,
and I have over two hundred followers,
please do not decline the trouble and expense.'
I replied:
'The day after tomorrow at dawn, send a written message,
and I will specially await you.'"
Huìlán then prepared wine, dried meat, and the like.
At the appointed time, the King of Qín indeed came,
with a large retinue,
nobles and commoners arrayed in rows.
They sat and ate hurriedly.
He said to Yīng:
"This disciple has not eaten for eighty years."
Yīng asked the reason.
He replied:
"In my lifetime, Buddhism did not yet exist.
In the underworld, I am held accountable for meritorious deeds.
I could only respond by releasing living creatures and showing compassion to the orphaned and widowed.
Due to my scant merit,
my punishment is not yet complete.
After this one meal,
it will be another forty years
before I may conveniently eat again."
He then pointed to someone seated there and said:
"That is Chén Zhěn,
often given to empty deceit."
He also pointed to two others and said:
"Those are Bái Qǐ and Wáng Jiǎn.
Because they killed many people,
their punishment is also not yet complete."
Yīng said:
"King, why do you not seek food from others,
but instead endure such hunger and hardship yourself?"
He replied:
"Those with compassion are few,
and moreover, others cannot see me.
I am a person of high status;
I cannot recklessly cause misfortune and hauntings.
That is why it is so."
Pointing to the wine and dried meat, he said:
"Did the temple abbot prepare this?
I am deeply grateful and ashamed."
As he was about to leave,
he said to Yīng:
"I am very ashamed before the Chán Master.
This disciple has some belongings,
which I should give you.
Outside the east gate of the city, at Tōnghuà, there is a pointed mound.
It is this disciple's tomb.
People nowadays do not know
and mistakenly call it the tomb of Lǚ Bùwéi."
Yīng said:
"In the past, the Red Eyebrow rebels excavated it.
How could there still be belongings inside?"
The ghost said:
"The rebels took the coarse items.
The finer ones were deep,
and the rebels could not retrieve them.
They are still there."
Yīng said:
"This humble monk has left the household life;
I have no use for such things.
You must not bring them."
After speaking, he thanked him and left.
Chén Dǎo
Chén Dǎo of the Táng Dynasty was a man from Yùzhāng.
He made his living as a merchant.
During the Lóngshuò era,
he sailed his boat to Chǔ.
One night, he moored by a riverbank
and saw another boat coming upstream,
which also anchored there for the night.
Dǎo then moved his boat closer
and saw a man with thick eyebrows and a large nose, resembling an official,
inspecting documents on the boat,
accompanied by three or five attendants.
Since they were fellow travelers,
Dǎo asked him,
"Where are you heading, sir?
How fortunate that we are staying at this same bank."
The thick-browed man said,
"I am on official business to Chǔ.
It is a pleasure to meet you here."
Dǎo then invited him over to his boat,
and the thick-browed man followed.
Dǎo prepared wine and food,
and after several rounds of drinking,
he asked for the man's name.
The thick-browed man said,
"My surname is Sītú,
and my given name is Biàn.
I have been dispatched to Chǔ
on an official mission."
Dǎo asked further,
"What official business are you in charge of?"
Biàn replied,
"You should not ask about this.
For your journey,
be careful not to go to Chǔ.
I advise you to go elsewhere."
Dǎo asked,
"Why?"
Biàn said,
"I am not human—
I am an envoy from the underworld."
Dǎo was shocked and asked,
"Why can I not go to Chǔ?"
Biàn replied,
"I am going to Chǔ to bring disaster,
and you are among those affected.
I am grateful for your hospitality,
so I am warning you.
However, you must use money and goods to negotiate
in order to avoid this calamity."
Dǎo pleaded earnestly,
and Biàn said,
"Wait until I return from Chǔ.
You can prepare ten or twenty thousand strings of coins as a gift,
and then your household will be spared."
Dǎo agreed
and thanked him before parting.
That year, a great fire indeed broke out in Jīng-Chǔ,
spreading to tens of thousands of households
and leaving nothing behind.
After parting with Biàn,
Dǎo was filled with worry.
He turned his boat around and returned.
When he reached Yùzhāng,
Biàn also arrived.
Dǎo, being stingy by nature,
made excuses about other matters and did not prepare the promised money.
The envoy was angry
and ordered an attendant to deliver a sealed letter to Dǎo.
Before Dǎo could finish reading it,
a fire suddenly erupted in his house,
and all his belongings were destroyed.
That night, no other houses were damaged—
only Dǎo's home burned down.
Biàn was nowhere to be seen.
This was likely because Dǎo's stinginess and failure to keep his promise led to this outcome.
Wáng Zhì
In the third year of the Xiǎnqìng era of the Táng Dynasty,
a man from Qízhōu named Wáng Zhì
served as the magistrate of Yìzhōu County.
After his term ended, he returned to his hometown.
He had a beautiful daughter who died before she could marry,
and her body was kept in a county temple for several months.
Earlier, a student had been staying in one of the temple rooms.
One night, he saw this girl arrive,
dressed in splendid attire,
seeking intimacy.
The student accepted her.
After a month of knowing each other,
the girl gave the student a bronze mirror
and a comb and towel.
When the magistrate was about to depart,
the girl secretly bid farewell to the student.
The family could not find these items,
so the magistrate ordered a search of the rooms,
and they were found in the student's room.
The magistrate had his attendants bind the student,
accusing him of theft.
The student explained the situation,
saying he not only received these items
but also kept two pieces of clothing from her.
The magistrate ordered the coffin opened for inspection,
and indeed, those clothes were missing.
Seeing this evidence,
he released the student.
He asked about his hometown,
and the student said he was from Qízhōu.
He had followed his father south for an official post,
but both his parents had died,
so he traveled to various prefectures to study
and would return home soon.
The magistrate provided him with clothes, a horse, and supplies to travel together,
taking him as his son-in-law
and treating him with great affection.
A Man from Bāxiá
During the Tiáolù era,
a man was traveling through Bāxiá.
One night, he moored his boat
and suddenly heard someone reciting a poem loudly:
"Autumn paths filled with yellow leaves,
Cold dew withers the grass roots.
A single cry of a monkey breaks the silence,
A traveler's tears leave many traces."
The voice was very intense,
passionate and sorrowful.
This continued all night,
with the poem recited dozens of times.
At first, he thought it was another traveler who had not yet slept,
but at dawn, he searched and found no boats—
only empty mountains, stone springs,
and secluded valleys.
At the place where the poem was recited,
there was a set of human bones.
Lù Yúqìng
was a man from Wújùn
who passed the imperial examination as a Jìnshì.
He successively served as the Wèi of Chángchéng,
and was appointed as Yuánwài Jiānchá.
During the Jiǔshì era,
he was promoted to Fènggé Shèrén,
and later served as Prefect of Shǎnzhōu, Chief Official of Luòzhōu, and Minister of Dàlǐ Qīng and Shǎofǔ Jiān.
He was in charge of Ruìzōng's funeral carriage, which was not finely made,
so he was demoted to Prefect of Yízhōu.
When Yúqìng was young,
he once traveled at night between Xú and Bó in winter.
His attendants went ahead with the baggage,
and Yúqìng followed slowly on horseback.
It was extremely cold,
and he saw a group of ghosts sitting around a fire.
Thinking they were people,
he rode over and dismounted to warm himself by the fire.
To his surprise, the flames were fierce but gave no warmth.
Yúqìng said to them,
"Why is the fire so cold?
Take off my boots for me."
The ghosts only bowed their heads and laughed,
not responding.
Yúqìng looked around
and saw that all the ghosts had veils over their faces.
Startled,
he whipped his horse to escape,
and ultimately came to no harm.
The nearby residents said to Yúqìng,
"This place is haunted by ghosts,
and many who encounter them perish.
You, young master, were not frightened at all—
you must be blessed.
You will surely attain wealth and honor!"
Xià Wénróng
In the early years of the Zhōu Cháng'ān era,
Xià Wénróng, former Deputy Magistrate of Chángjiāng County in Suízhōu,
was considered by people of the time to judge matters of the underworld.
When Zhāng Zhuó was serving as
Censor,
he was sent out to be the Granary Supervisor of Chùzhōu.
Upon returning to the capital after his replacement,
he went to inquire of Xià.
Wénróng drew the character "liǔ" (willow) on the ground with his staff,
saying:
"You shall serve in this prefecture."
Later, Zhāng was indeed appointed as the Household Registrar of Liǔzhōu.
Later, he was changed to Magistrate of Píngchāng in Dézhōu.
Wénróng predicted the timing,
without the slightest error in the hour or moment.
Also, Yáng Tíngyù, Magistrate of Jiāxīng in Sūzhōu,
was a cousin of Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
greedy and insatiable.
He composed a lyric:
"At this time, Tíngyù,
beats the Lao tribesmen, taking money, never enough.
My aunt and mother-in-law has become the Son of Heaven,
no one else may oppose."
Censor Kāng Yín was assigned to investigate,
and submitted a report sentencing him to death.
At that time, his mother was in the capital,
and went to see Xià Wénróng.
Wénróng requested one thousand sheets of white paper,
and one thousand sheets of yellow paper,
to pray for Tíngyù.
He told her to come back in ten days,
and the mother did as he said.
Wénróng said:
"He is temporarily spared from death.
Within the next ten days, there will be a decision."
Indeed, after six days, an imperial decree arrived:
"Yáng Tíngyù is to support and care for his elderly mother in her remaining years."
Also, Liǔ Wújì, a Clerk in the Ministry of Personnel, went to see Wénróng.
Wénróng wrote the characters for Wèi, Hàn, and Chēn, saying:
"Wèi will likely not come to pass,
Hàn and Chēn prefectures
are uncertain and interchangeable."
Later, when the appointments were announced, he was indeed named Registrar of Wèizhōu,
but the official document was problematic,
so he was then announced as Registrar of Hànzhōu.
At that time, Clerks from the Phoenix and Simurgh Terrace submitted a memorial,
accusing the Ministry of Personnel of unfairness in the proposed appointments.
Empress Wǔ reprimanded Vice Minister Cuī Xuánwěi,
who replied:
"Your subject's proposed appointments are extremely fair."
Empress Wǔ said:
"If so,
let the Clerks of the Ministry of Personnel and those of the Phoenix and Simurgh Terrace exchange positions."
Thus, Wújì was appointed as Assistant Magistrate of Píngyáng in Chēnzhōu,
and a Clerk of the Phoenix and Simurgh Terrace became Registrar of Hànzhōu.
Zhāng Xīwàng
Zhōu's Minister of Rites, Zhāng Xīwàng,
moved and renovated his old residence.
Féng Yì, a man who could see ghosts, saw it and said:
"Under the new stable,
there is a buried corpse,
extremely angry.
You, sir, should avoid it."
Xīwàng laughed and said:
"Since I was young,
I have never believed in such things.
Do not speak of it, sir."
Over a month later,
Yì entered
and saw a ghost holding a bow and arrows,
following behind Xīwàng.
Just as he reached the steps,
the ghost drew its bow and shot him in the shoulder.
Xīwàng felt a pain in his back,
and touched it with his hand.
He died that same day.
Zhèng Cóngjiǎn
Zhōu's Vice Director of the Left Bureau, Zhèng Cóngjiǎn,
his office hall was often unsettled.
He ordered a shaman to examine it,
who said:
"There is a buried corpse,
surname Zōng,
wife surname Kòu,
under the foundation of the hall."
They addressed it, saying:
"You, sir, sit upon my doorway,
I constantly encounter you when coming and going.
This is your own misfortune,
not caused by me."
They dug three feet into the ground,
and indeed found old bones,
with an inscription as described.
They moved them out and reburied them,
and after that, the disturbances ceased.
Fáng Yǐngshū
Zhōu's Director of the Ministry of Revenue, Fáng Yǐngshū,
was appointed Vice Minister of Personnel.
He was to take up his post the next day.
That night,
a cook named Wáng Lǎo
got up in the middle of the night.
Suddenly, he heard someone outside calling:
"Wáng Lǎo, no need to get up.
Vice Minister Fáng will not take up his post.
In three days,
Vice Minister Lǐ will take up his post."
Wáng Lǎo went back to bed until dawn.
Fáng indeed fell ill,
and died after two days.
The relevant office submitted the report,
and when it came down,
Lǐ Jiǒngxiù was immediately appointed Vice Minister.
That day, he gave thanks
and took up his post.
Wáng Lǎo asked others about what he had heard,
and all said they did not know.
Only then did he realize it was a message from the gods.
Liú Fěng
In the second year of Wénmíng,
Liú Fěng, an official of Jìnglíng,
stayed overnight at an empty post station in Yílíng.
The moon was bright, and he could not sleep,
when suddenly a young lady arrived from the western corridor.
Her demeanor was gentle and beautiful,
singing softly and strolling leisurely,
she slowly made her way to the central corridor.
Turning back, she ordered her maid:
"Zǐsuí, fetch the flower mat from the western hall,
and also invite Aunt Liù of the Liú family, Aunt Shísì, and the young lady Qiàoqiáo from the southern neighbor,
and bring Yìnú along."
She sent word:
"The scenery here is lovely,
perfect for enjoying ourselves.
Playing the qin and reciting poetry,
are truly delightful activities.
Although there is a judicial officer from Jìnglíng here,
this person is already asleep,
and under the bright moon, there is no need to avoid him."
Before long, three young ladies arrived,
along with one child,
all of them possessing peerless beauty.
Zǐsuí spread the flower mat in the courtyard,
and they bowed and deferred to each other before sitting in order.
On the mat were set rhinoceros horn wine vessels,
ivory ladles,
green felt floral goblets,
and white glass cups.
The fragrant aroma of fine wine
wafted far into the empty night.
The young ladies chatted, joked, sang, and chanted,
their voices clear and melodious.
One young lady served as the recorder,
another as the host,
raising a goblet to offer a toast, saying:
"May Aunt Sān live as long as Qíshān,
and may Aunt Liù be equal to Aunt Sān.
May Uncle Liú become the investigating judge of Tàishān Prefecture,
may young lady Qiàoqiáo marry the crown prince of Zhūyúguó,
and may Yìnú become the prime minister of Zhūyúguó.
As for us three or four companions,
we shall all marry the secretaries of the underworld's Department of Civil Affairs.
If not,
then marrying the sixth or seventh son of King Píngděng
would fulfill our lifelong wishes."
Everyone laughed at once and said:
"We must reward the lady of the Cài family with a drink."
Qiàoqiáo, who was then serving as the recorder,
alone lost a tally,
and was fined by the lady of the Cài family, who said:
"Uncle Liú is talented and handsome, gentle and refined.
Why not make him the supervisor of the Five Paths,
instead of merely calling him an investigating judge?
I fear Aunt Liù will be unhappy.
Please drink a cup."
The lady of the Cài family immediately took the cup and said:
"I know I am being fined.
But it is only because Uncle is too old and dim-sighted,
afraid he cannot read the yellow paper documents of the Five Paths,
and would mishandle the affairs of the great deity.
Drinking is no harm."
At this, all the young ladies laughed until they collapsed.
Another young lady stood up,
proposed a tongue-twisting game,
and drew a green hairpin.
She spoke quickly,
passing the green hairpin along with the game,
and anyone who failed would be fined.
The game's phrase was:
"Luánlǎo's head is good,
good head Luánlǎo."
After several rounds of passing it along,
she ordered Cuìsuí to step down from her seat,
and made her recite the phrase.
Cuìsuí had always been stammering and slow of speech.
When her turn came,
she could only say "Luánlǎo, Luánlǎo."
All the young ladies laughed heartily and said:
"In the past, Hè Ruòbì made fun of Vice Minister Zhǎngsūn Luán,
because he was old and stammered,
and also had no hair,
so he created this game."
After the third watch,
they all played the qin and struck the zhù,
taking turns singing and harmonizing.
They sang:
"Bright moon, autumn wind,
a fine night gathered together.
The Milky Way may easily turn,
but joy and pleasure do not last.
Green cups and emerald ladles,
we pour wine for you.
If we do not drink tonight,
when shall we find joy?"
They sang again:
"Willow, willow,
slender and swaying in the urgent wind.
The beauty in the western tower dreams long of spring,
as a thousand strands slip through the slanting embroidered curtain."
They sang again:
"Jade mouth, golden jar,
wishing to accompany the lord.
In the Hándān palace,
metal, stone, silk, and reed instruments.
Maidens of Wèi, beauties of Qín,
standing in rows to the left and right.
Silk garments fluttering in profusion,
green eyebrows and red makeup.
The king gazes with delight,
as they sing and dance for him.
May we earn your favor,
and forever be free from calamity and sorrow."
When the singing ended,
it was already the fourth watch.
Suddenly, a person in a yellow robe appeared,
with horns on his head,
and a majestic appearance.
He walked in and bowed, saying:
"King Pótí orders the young ladies to come quickly."
The young ladies all stood up to receive the command,
and immediately sent word back:
"We did not know the king was summoning us.
We happened to be admiring the moon here,
how dare we not hasten to attend!"
They then ordered the maid to clean up the feast.
Liú Fěng let out a loud sneeze and cough,
and when he looked into the courtyard, there was nothing left.
The next morning,
he picked up several green hairpins,
and showed them to people,
but no one knew what they were.
The Governor of Xiàngzhōu
Táng Wáng Dàojiān served as the governor of Xiàngzhōu.
The people of the prefecture made wooden household registers,
but when they were finished, they disappeared.
Later, they were found scattered among the beams of the prefectural office,
all cut into short scrolls,
and thus could not be used,
so they were discarded.
Also, when Governor Lǐ was in the prefecture,
he was preparing to offer sacrifices to the earth god the next morning,
so he purified himself and fasted at night,
and slept in the main hall.
He dreamed that both his parents came to welcome him,
and upon waking, he felt uneasy,
and told his wife everything.
He fell ill,
and died a few days later.
When Zhū Xīyù served as governor,
the western courtyard of his residence was always kept closed.
One day, after Zhū Xīyù returned from his duties,
suddenly a person in purple robes,
wearing a tall bun,
rode a horse straight in,
with two servants also riding ahead to guide him.
They dismounted upon reaching the pavilion.
The attending official thought they were relatives delivering a message,
and followed to watch.
The person walked slowly in formal attire,
straight into the central courtyard.
The courtyard gate opened for him,
and closed after he entered.
When they searched for the servants and the horse,
they were nowhere to be found.
They hurried to report to Zhū Xīyù,
who ordered the central courtyard to be opened.
Inside, they saw the surroundings swept very clean,
with curtains and screens arranged all around,
and the setup splendid and bright.
A magnificent feast was laid out with many seats,
and the dishes were the finest of both land and sea.
The utensils for dozens of people,
were all made of gold and silver.
Zhū Xīyù was greatly astonished at the sight,
and poured wine as an offering to pray for blessings.
Then he left,
and closed the gate.
The next day, when they opened it again,
it was as before.
The rooms were sealed,
overgrown with weeds and desolate.
Two years later, Zhū Xīyù died.
Wáng Zhàn
Wáng Zhàn adjudicated underworld affairs.
Initially, his uncle Xuánshì
served as the magistrate of Fùyáng County in Jīngzhōu,
and took one hundred strings of cash from a local man named Wú Shí.
Later, he falsely accused him of another matter,
and had him executed to silence him.
Shì carried other merits,
and had both superior and inferior evaluations,
yet after five selection rounds, he could not obtain an official post.
When he inquired about it,
Zhàn said he would investigate for his uncle.
After a night, he said:
"When uncle previously served as magistrate of Fùyáng,
he must have committed a wrongful deed.
The case record is still present.
The underworld court adjudicates:
'The crime of murder
will be punished after death.
Taking one hundred strings of cash
shall deduct four years of official salary.'" The uncle said:
"This truly happened,
it is my crime."
Dí Rénjié
During Wǔ Zétiān's time,
Dí Rénjié served as prefect of Níngzhōu.
His residence was notoriously haunted;
previously, over ten prefects had died there.
When Jié first arrived,
the clerks reported that the official residence had long been haunted,
and none of the predecessors dared to live there.
Moreover, it was overgrown with brambles and dilapidated,
already uninhabitable,
and they requested to lodge elsewhere.
Jié said:
"If the prefect does not reside in his own residence,
where else should he lodge?"
He ordered the locks removed and repairs made,
and lived there without hesitation.
For several nights,
strange and eerie occurrences
were too numerous to record.
Jié angrily addressed them:
"I am the prefect,
this is my residence.
You are in the wrong, I am in the right;
why do you not understand reason,
but instead oppose the upright with evil?
If you are deities,
quickly heed my clear instruction;
if you are ghosts,
how dare you interfere!
I have no fear of you,
only annoyance at your myriad transformations.
If you must meet with reason,
why not appear properly?"
Shortly after,
a person in full attire came forward and said:
"I am an official of a certain dynasty,
buried under the tree west of the hall steps.
My body is pierced by tree roots,
causing unbearable pain.
Previously, several gentlemen
wished to state their case,
but those persons died.
The underworld path was unreachable,
until now.
If Your Honor can rebury me,
how would I dare linger here!"
After speaking, he vanished.
The next day,
Jié ordered the site excavated,
and indeed it was as said.
He then reburied him,
and from then on, the hauntings ceased.
Lǐ Hào
Táng Dynasty Minister of War Lǐ Hào
was an upright man of his time.
In the early Kāiyuán era,
a woman came to Hào,
of captivating appearance,
with speech and learning
unsurpassed at the time.
Hào did not dare accept her.
When Tàicháng Qīng Jiāng Jiǎo arrived,
Hào gave the woman to him.
Jiǎo held a grand gathering of officials,
and the woman claimed skill in physiognomy.
Seeing Zhāng Yuè, she said:
"The face of a chief minister."
She then read the faces of the various officials,
and her words were never wrong.
To Jiǎo she said:
"Though you have the signs,
you will not die a natural death."
As the drinking waned,
Jiǎo took liberties with her in a separate room.
Seductive words were exchanged,
approaching intimacy.
The officials took turns peeping,
with Hào seated among them,
going last to look.
The woman then let out a mournful cry,
and Jiǎo, startled, fell to the ground.
Fetching a light to look,
they saw a skeleton under the bed.
Contemporary commentators
said that because Hào was chaste and upright,
ghosts and spirits feared him.
Zhāng Shǒuguī
Yōuzhōu military governor Zhāng Shǒuguī,
in his youth served as a chief commander in Héxī,
guarding Yùmén Pass.
His army scouts were all diligent, brave, and skilled in combat,
often venturing deep on reconnaissance,
and much given to plundering.
A Western Regions monk,
carrying over twenty loads of robes from Xījīng,
was returning to India,
with over twenty followers.
The scouts, thinking it was silk and such goods,
plundered them,
killing all his followers.
When they reached the monk,
swords and clubs rained down but could not harm him,
which the scouts found strange.
Then searching the loads,
they found only monk's robes,
and felt deep regret.
They repented before the monk,
beating their chests and weeping sorrowfully for a long time.
The monk then said:
"These men in a previous life
all disobeyed the commander's orders;
only the monk's ghosts died unjustly.
But your commander's official salary and rank are high,
he will later become military governor and other high offices.
What can these men do to you?
You may
report to the commander,
to perform meritorious deeds.
Then after several years,
the commander will face a minor calamity,
but there will also be a way to avoid it."
The scouts returned and reported to Shǒuguī,
who kept the monk and provided for him,
and after several years, he left.
Later, Shǒuguī and twenty-five of his men
went to the Yīlán Mountains to scout bandits.
Suddenly, several thousand Hu cavalry arrived,
and Shǒuguī, unable to resist,
dismounted and removed his saddle,
showing an air of leisure.
The cavalry gradually closed in,
and Shǒuguī said to his men:
"What shall we do?
If unavoidable,
by reason we must fight."
Suddenly, they saw several hundred red-flagged cavalry at the mountain foot,
charging forth to engage,
and Shǒuguī followed them,
breaking through a corner,
and soon all escaped.
The enemy did not dare pursue.
The red-flagged general said to Shǒuguī:
"I am Hàn's Lǐ Guǎng;
knowing you were in trouble,
I came to rescue you.
When you later attain wealth and honor,
do not forget me."
After speaking, he vanished.
Shǒuguī eventually became Yōuzhōu military governor and Censor-in-chief.
Yáng Yáng
During the Kāiyuán era,
the Magistrate of Luòyáng, Yáng Yáng,
was once traveling out
when he saw a fortune-teller under the shade of a locust tree.
As the magistrate’s procession passed by,
the man remained seated upright and unperturbed.
The bailiffs shouted at him to rise and make way,
but he did not move.
Yáng ordered his guards to seize him and bring him to the hall,
intending to beat him,
and personally interrogated him.
The fortune-teller lifted his head and said:
"You are a magistrate for only two more days—
why do you reprimand others?"
Yáng asked what he meant,
and he said:
"Two days from now,
your life will come to an end."
Yáng was greatly startled
and asked how he knew this.
The fortune-teller then told him what he had foreseen.
The whole family was terrified,
and they said to the fortune-teller:
"Since you know this,
you must be able to avert it.
How can he be spared?"
Yáng bowed repeatedly, begging for a solution.
The fortune-teller said:
"I will use what I have seen and heard
to assist you in your duties.
Whether you can be spared or not
is still uncertain."
He then led Yáng into a pavilion in the eastern courtyard.
He had Yáng let down his hair, go barefoot,
and stand facing the wall,
while he himself sat at a table and wrote talismans.
After midnight,
he happily said to Yáng:
"Tonight you are fortunate to avoid the immediate arrival [of death].
Tomorrow,
you should make thirty sheets of paper into money,
and prepare many pastries,
along with a pot of wine,
and take them out to atone for your sins,
Outside the gate,
among the mulberry grove,
wait for passersby and offer them drink.
A man in black robes with his right shoulder bared—
he is the messenger summoning you.
If you can detain him with food and drink,
you will have nothing to worry about.
Otherwise,
it will truly be difficult to save you.
You should also change your clothes,
stay in a small room,
and wait for him,
speaking politely and apologetically,
asking what he desires.
My strategy ends here."
Yáng did as he was told.
When the sun set in the west,
the wine and pastries were nearly exhausted,
but the man in black robes had not yet arrived.
Yáng grew deeply worried,
but shortly after, he arrived.
Yáng had someone invite him to stay,
and the man in black robes gladly accepted,
drinking and eating generously.
Yáng then bowed and paid his respects.
The man said:
"Where were you yesterday?
I came to your residence several times,
but could not find you.
I suspected you were staying safely in the eastern courtyard,
under the protection of benevolent spirits,
so I dared not intrude.
But now the underworld’s summons for you is still active—
what is to be done?"
Yáng bowed repeatedly, pleading for rescue a thousand times over,
and also burned paper money
to fund the man’s journey.
The ghost said:
"I am grateful for your great kindness.
Tomorrow,
I will come with other officials from the underworld to discuss this,
and you should prepare a lavish feast to receive us."
Having said this, he vanished.
The next day,
Yáng set up a banquet tent
and prepared all manner of delicacies from land and sea to await them.
As evening fell,
the messenger arrived with several dozen of his companions.
The feast and music were exceptionally grand and joyous,
and they said to one another:
"For Magistrate Yáng’s matter,
how can we not give our utmost effort?"
After a long while,
they said to Yáng:
"Yáng Xī, who lives across the lane from you,
also has talent and ability.
We will now forge a golden substitute to take his place instead.
At the fifth watch,
when the drum sounds,
you should go to Xī’s
gate and wait.
If you hear weeping,
you will be spared."
Yáng went as instructed
and saw the ghost already atop a tree,
trying to enter Xī’s house
but being bitten by a dog,
unable to proceed.
Soon, it entered through a gap in the wall,
and after a delay, weeping was heard.
Thus, Yáng was spared.
The Daughter of Zhāng Guǒ
During the Kāiyuán era,
the daughter of Zhāng Guǒ, the Sima of Yìzhōu,
was fifteen years old
when she fell ill and died.
Unable to bear sending her far away for burial,
they temporarily interred her beneath the pavilion in the eastern courtyard.
Later, he was transferred to serve as the Chief Clerk of Zhèngzhōu.
Because the journey was long and they would need to transport the coffin again,
they left her there.
Soon, Liú Yǐ replaced him.
Liú's son often stayed in the pavilion.
One evening, as he was walking outside the gate,
he saw a young woman
with a beautiful and radiant appearance
approaching from outside.
Liú suspected she was someone eloping,
so he stepped forward to greet her.
She responded warmly and intimately.
They stayed together and shared the night,
their affection deep and tender,
her demeanor graceful and gentle.
Liú cherished her immensely.
Thereafter, she would come every evening
and leave only at dawn.
After several months,
she suddenly said to Liú:
"I am the former Sima Zhāng's daughter,
who unfortunately died young
and was recently buried in this pavilion.
My fate dictates I should live again
and be united with you in marriage.
Three days from now,
you may open my coffin.
Wait patiently for signs of breath;
be careful not to startle or harm me recklessly."
She pointed to her burial site and left.
When the day arrived, Liú was overjoyed.
Alone with one servant, he excavated at night.
At a depth of four or five feet,
they found a lacquered coffin.
Slowly opening it to look,
they saw the girl's complexion fresh and vibrant,
her limbs warm and soft.
Her clothing, makeup, and hair
showed no signs of decay or damage.
They lifted her and placed her on the bed.
Faintly, there was breath from her nose.
After a short while,
breath came from her mouth.
They fed her thin gruel,
and she could swallow little by little.
By daybreak, she had revived,
gradually able to speak and sit up.
After several days,
fearing his parents would find out,
he used studying as an excuse
to avoid leaving the pavilion,
often having meals delivered there.
Liú Yǐ suspected something unusual about his son.
While his son was outside seeing off a guest,
he secretly looked into his room
and saw the girl there.
When he asked for an explanation,
his son told him everything.
The coffin was still under the bed.
Liú Yǐ and his wife sighed and wept, saying:
"Since this is a profound bond from the netherworld,
why didn't you tell us earlier?"
They then hid the girl in the main hall.
When the son could not find the girl,
he was greatly alarmed.
His father then said to him:
"Since this is an extraordinary union,
unprecedented in a thousand years,
what harm is there in telling me?
Why go to such lengths to hide it?"
He then sent a messenger to Zhèngzhōu
to report everything to Zhāng Guǒ
and propose marriage.
Her parents, moved by grief, shock, and joy,
set a date for the wedding.
Thus, they became a fine couple
and later had several sons.
Imperial Consort Huá
In the early Kāiyuán era,
Imperial Consort Huá enjoyed the emperor's favor.
She gave birth to Prince Qìng, Cóng,
and was buried in Cháng'ān after her death.
In the twenty-eighth year,
thieves intending to rob her tomb
constructed a large false grave
about a hundred paces outside the cemetery,
as if preparing for a burial.
From within it, they secretly dug a tunnel
leading directly into her tomb.
They opened the coffin.
The consort's face looked as if alive,
and her limbs could still bend and stretch.
The thieves wantonly desecrated and humiliated her body.
They then cut off her wrist to take a gold bracelet
and also removed her tongue,
fearing she might communicate through dreams.
They propped up her corpse sideways
and placed a candle in her private parts.
They took all the treasures buried with her—
too numerous to count—
and moved them to the false grave.
Then, in the city,
they used a hearse to transport an empty coffin for a gathering.
At dusk,
they stayed in the tomb,
placing the items in the spirit carriage and funeral carts
before covering the grave and returning.
Before the consort was reburied,
Prince Qìng dreamed of her with disheveled hair and naked,
weeping sorrowfully as she came to him, saying:
"Thieves have opened my tomb
and further mutilated and humiliated me.
My lonely soul suffers unjustly in the darkness;
words cannot express it.
Yet I will surely await their downfall at the Chūnmíng Gate."
She then described the details fully before leaving.
The prince, always deeply filial,
suddenly awoke in shock, weeping.
The next morning, he went to report to the emperor.
The emperor summoned the Metropolitan Governor and the Magistrate of Wànnián,
urgently ordering them to track down the thieves.
When the thieves returned with the loot
and tried to enter the Chūnmíng Gate,
the gate officers stopped and questioned them.
Searching their carts,
they found all the treasures.
The entire gang of thieves was arrested.
Under interrogation, they confessed immediately.
Several dozen were arrested,
all being ill-behaved sons of noble families.
The prince requested the five ringleaders
so he could personally exact revenge.
The emperor granted his request.
He extracted their five viscera,
boiled them, and offered them in sacrifice.
The rest were publicly flogged to death outside the Metropolitan Governor's office gate.
The consort was reburied with honors.
The prince observed three years of mourning in his heart.
Guō Zhīyùn
During the Kāiyuán era,
Guō Zhīyùn, the Military Governor of Liángzhōu, was on an inspection tour
when, a hundred li from the provincial seat,
he suddenly died at a courier station.
His soul then departed his body.
He ordered the station master to lock the room and not open it,
then returned to his residence.
His attendants were unaware.
For over forty days at home,
he settled both public and private affairs.
He then sent someone to the station
to fetch his own remains.
When they arrived,
he personally oversaw the encoffining.
After the encoffining was complete,
he bid farewell to his family,
threw himself into the coffin,
and was never seen again.
Wáng Guāngběn
served as Deputy Prefect of Luòzhōu during the Kāiyuán era.
One spring month,
the Prefect sent Guāngběn on an inspection tour of the counties.
After he had been gone for several days,
his wife, née Lǐ, suddenly died.
When he returned,
he was reproached for not having personally attended to her medical care,
and believed she had died unjustly.
He constantly wailed in grief,
his sorrow moving the neighbors.
More than ten days later,
as all his children were weeping,
Guāngběn again wailed over a hundred cries,
when suddenly he saw Lady Lǐ emerge from behind the curtain,
adorned and dressed in dazzling attire,
surpassing her usual appearance.
Guāngběn stopped crying
and asked about the circumstances of her death.
Lady Lǐ said:
"I have not yet been able to depart;
I am still in this hall.
Hearing your mournful and intense wailing,
I, in the netherworld,
feel doubly desolate and moved.
As the saying goes:
'When the living grieve excessively,
it disturbs the peace of the underworld.'
This saying is indeed true.
From now on,
I do not wish my lord to be like this,
lest it burden the dark realm."
She then entrusted the family members,
to have her daughter become a nun,
and to free the maidservants to become commoners,
all matters handled reasonably.
After staying for about the time of a meal,
she said to Guāngběn:
"The ways of humans and ghosts differ;
it is not suitable to stay long.
This only deepens regret."
After speaking,
she entered the hall and vanished.
The children and others
only heard Lady Lǐ's words,
but only Guāngběn saw her.
The Yōuzhōu Garrison Officer
During the Kāiyuán era,
there was a garrison officer in Yōuzhōu surnamed Zhāng.
His wife, née Kǒng,
gave birth to five sons and then died.
Later, he married a wife, née Lǐ,
who was fierce, jealous, and cruel,
mistreating the five sons,
whipping them daily.
The five sons could not bear the suffering,
and wept before their mother's grave.
Their mother suddenly emerged from the tomb,
comforted her sons,
and grieved for a long time.
She then wrote a poem on a white cloth handkerchief and gave it to Zhāng, saying:
"Resentful at becoming a departed one,
Wiping tears, often soaking the handkerchief.
Now separated by life and death,
We shall never meet again.
In the case, leftover makeup powder remains,
Left to be given to the one who comes after.
In the Yellow Springs, it is of no use,
Regretting to become dust within the tomb.
With affection, I think of my children,
Without feeling, I leave you to your own.
If you wish to know where my heart breaks,
The bright moon shines upon the lonely grave."
The five sons obtained the poem
and presented it to their father.
Their father wailed in grief,
and appealed to the regional commander.
The commander reported it to the emperor,
who decreed that Lady Lǐ be beaten one hundred strokes,
exiled to Lǐngnán,
and Zhāng was suspended from his post.
The Wéi Family Daughter
In Luòyáng, there was a daughter of the Wéi family
of exceptional beauty.
She was orphaned young
and lived with her elder brother.
A neighbor had a son surnamed Cuī,
who glimpsed her and was delighted.
He richly bribed her maidservant,
who then conveyed his intentions,
along with gifts.
The girl had also long known that Cuī was charming and refined,
so she agreed,
arranging to meet in the red pavilion among the bamboo grove.
Suddenly, there was the sound of dragging footsteps;
suspecting Cuī was about to arrive,
she went forward to meet him.
Instead, she saw a person
seven feet tall,
with a gaping mouth and drooping lips,
eyes like lightning,
who came straight to seize the girl.
The girl fled, running and screaming in alarm.
Family members came with torches to look,
and saw only piled-up white bones
and blood flowing all over the ground.
The elder brother then interrogated the maidservant and learned the truth.
He killed the maidservant and cut down the bamboo.
Cuī Shàng
During the Kāiyuán era,
there was a man named Cuī Shàng
who wrote "The Treatise on the Non-Existence of Ghosts,"
the arguments of which were very reasonable.
After completing it,
he was about to present it.
Suddenly, a Daoist priest came to his door,
requesting to see his treatise.
After reading it,
he said to Shàng:
"The arguments are very skillful,
but between heaven and earth,
to claim there are no ghosts
is erroneous."
Shàng asked:
"How can you say that?"
The Daoist priest said:
"I am a ghost;
how can you say there are none?
If you present this manuscript,
you will surely be killed by various ghosts and spirits.
Better to burn it."
Thereupon, he vanished,
and the manuscript was ultimately lost.
The Person by the River
In the sixth year of Kāiyuán,
someone moored a boat by the riverside
and saw dried bones on the bank.
He then offered food to them.
Soon, he heard a voice in the air expressing shameful thanks,
along with a poem:
"I was originally a scholar from Hándān,
who died by the river while on duty.
Unable to receive my family's weeping,
I trouble you, a traveler, to grieve."
The Palace Eunuch
A palace eunuch was traveling
and stayed overnight at the Guānpō Inn.
He removed his crimson robe
and covered himself with brocade garments,
sleeping by lamplight.
Suddenly, he saw a young boy
holding a cup of wine,
push open the door and enter.
Then three more people arrived,
all wearing ancient clothing and caps.
They said to each other:
"Why is Attendant-in-Ordinary Cuī so late?"
Soon, another person arrived,
appearing sorrowful with a sense of parting,
who was indeed Attendant-in-Ordinary Cuī.
When they raised their wine,
they composed poems and linked verses.
The last lines were Attendant-in-Ordinary Cuī's words.
As the eunuch was about to rise,
the four looked at each other,
sighed mournfully, and departed,
like the sound of wind and rain.
When he looked at the door,
it was closed as before,
but the wine cup and poem remained.
The eunuch found it strange.
In the morning, the inn clerk said:
"Some villagers were having a gathering
and lost their wine cup."
The eunuch showed it to him,
and it was indeed the one the villagers had lost.
The linked verse song said:
"By the bed, the brocade quilt, patterned and patterned again;
On the rack, the crimson robe, deep red and deep red again.
In the empty courtyard, the bright moon, idle and idle again;
The night is long, the road far, mountains and mountains again."
Wáng Jiàn
Wáng Jiàn of Yǎnzhōu,
was by nature fierce and unyielding,
fearing nothing,
and often insulted ghosts and spirits.
During the Kāiyuán era,
he rode drunk to his estate,
thirty li from the city walls.
Jiàn had not traveled this road
for five or six years.
After traveling about ten li,
it became dusk.
Under a tall grove he saw a woman,
who asked Jiàn where he was going.
She requested he carry a bundle for her,
then suddenly vanished.
He opened the bundle to look,
and it contained things like paper money and dry bones.
Jiàn laughed and said:
"Stupid ghost trying to fool your lord."
He whipped his horse forward,
when suddenly he encountered over ten people gathered around a fire.
The weather was cold,
and the day was already dark.
Jiàn dismounted and approached them.
He spoke of what he had just seen,
but none responded.
Jiàn looked at them:
half of the people by the fire had no heads,
and those with heads wore face veils.
Jiàn, shocked and afraid,
mounted his horse and galloped away.
Late at night,
he finally reached the estate,
but the estate gate was already closed.
He knocked repeatedly but no one came out,
so he shouted and cursed loudly.
Soon a servant opened the gate.
Jiàn asked:
"Where are all the servants now?"
He ordered a lamp brought, but the flame was blue and dim.
Jiàn grew angry
and wanted to beat the servant.
The servant said:
"For the past ten days,
seven people in this estate fell ill,
and died one after another."
Jiàn asked:
"And what about you?"
He replied:
"I am already dead too.
Just now, hearing your call,
I rose from my corpse."
Then he suddenly collapsed,
and had no breath left.
Jiàn was terrified,
fled and spent the night in another village.
A year later,
he fell ill and died.
Lǐ Lìngwèn,
during the Kāiyuán era served as Director of the Palace Library,
but was demoted to Senior Advisor of Jízhōu.
Lìngwèn was fond of fine clothing, curios, food, and drink,
and was known throughout the land for his extravagance.
His roasted donkey, jarred goose, and such dishes
were cruelly prepared for flavor.
Throughout the land, those who spoke of fine cuisine
all traced their origins to Director Lǐ,
considering it a fine topic.
Lìngwèn arrived in Jízhōu,
contracted an illness,
and over time it gradually worsened.
The Regional Inspector, because Lìngwèn was a famous scholar
and also a clansman,
always ordered the city gates opened at night,
allowing Lìngwèn's family to come and go freely.
The Regional Inspector's son
once went out secretly at night with a servant for amusement.
Reaching the city gate,
he saw from afar several hundred armored soldiers
following a fiery chariot,
proceeding along the street.
Startled, he said:
"I haven't heard of any troops,
where did these come from?"
He intended to gallop and tell his father,
but also waited to see where they were going.
Soon they reached the city moat.
The fiery chariot passed over the water
without being extinguished,
and only then did he realize they were ghosts.
He ran to the gate,
but it was already closed.
Unable to return,
he rushed into Lìngwèn's gate and hid there.
Once inside,
the fiery chariot also arrived outside Lìngwèn's inner gate.
Though the son was terrified,
he still secretly watched.
Suddenly he heard over ten people in the hall reciting scriptures.
The armored soldiers and others hesitated for a long time.
There was a ghost in red robes
who directly kicked the gate three times,
the sound like thunder,
yet the scripture recitation did not cease.
The fiery chariot moved up the hall steps.
From afar, he saw the lamps in the hall were clear and pure,
and over ten people were still attending the sick.
The red-robed ghost again pried at the window lattice,
the sound as before,
and those attending Lìngwèn all scattered and fled.
The ghost took Lìngwèn out through the door
and threw him into the fiery chariot.
The crowd of ghosts surrounded it and left.
The son returned home
and recounted the events.
The next day, the Regional Inspector sent someone to inquire about Lìngwèn's condition.
The remaining members of Lìngwèn's household
dared not rise.
Only when the messenger shouted did they come out,
saying:
"Last night we were frightened,
and are still trembling with fear.
Lìngwèn's corpse was thrown by the ghosts
under a stack of beds in the northwest corner of the hall."
The family then gathered and wept.
Monk Tāoguāng
The monks Hézhòng and Tāoguāng of Qīnglóng Temple
were close friends.
Tāoguāng was from Fùpíng.
When he was about to return home,
he said to Hézhòng:
"I won't be away from home for more than a few months.
If you travel,
you must visit me."
Hézhòng agreed.
Over two months later,
Hézhòng was going to Zhōngdū,
and his route passed through Fùpíng,
so he went to look for Tāoguāng.
Hézhòng arrived at dusk,
still far from the dwelling,
Then Tāoguāng came to greet him, saying:
"You've troubled yourself to come find me,
so I came to welcome you."
They walked together for over a li,
and were about to reach home.
Tāoguāng said to Hézhòng:
"North from here is my home.
Please go in and wait for me.
I have a small errand
to attend to east of the village,
and will return shortly."
Having said this, he went east.
Hézhòng thought this strange,
and said to himself:
"He came to welcome me,
but how did he know in advance?
He's about to reach home but leaves me,
how heartless!"
He arrived at the house and knocked on the door.
Tāoguāng's father came out weeping and said:
"Master Tāoguāng unfortunately
passed away ten days ago,
and is interred northeast of the village.
He often said you would come,
and regretted not being able to see you."
After Hézhòng offered condolences,
the father led him inside
and accommodated him in the room where Tāoguāng usually stayed.
Hézhòng said to Tāoguāng's father:
"I just arrived at the village,
and Master Tāoguāng himself came to greet me.
We talked while walking over a li.
When we were about to arrive,
he pointed out his home to me and went east,
saying he had to go to the east of the village
and would return shortly.
I had no idea he was a ghost;
only upon seeing you, father,
did I realize it."
Tāoguāng's parents exclaimed in surprise to Hézhòng:
"Since he promised to come,
when he comes, seize him.
We wish to see him."
Then late at night,
Tāoguāng came again.
He entered the room and said to Hézhòng:
"In this poor dwelling, a guest has come,
but I have nothing to offer."
Hézhòng invited him to sit together,
then seized him and shouted.
His father and family all came,
held up candles to illuminate him,
and his appearance and speech were all Tāoguāng's.
They put him into a jar
and covered it with a basin.
Suddenly from the jar came a plaintive plea:
"I am not Master Tāoguāng,
but the tomb keeper.
Knowing you were close with Master Tāoguāng,
I impersonated him.
If I haven't troubled you too much,
please forgive my rashness
and release me to return."
The family did not open it.
Inside the jar,
he secretly prayed and pleaded with increasing distress.
After sunrise, they removed the cover,
and he flew away like a startled gust of wind,
and Hézhòng also returned.
He was not seen again afterwards,
indeed.
Monk Yíguāng
The Chan master Yíguāng of Qīnglóng Temple
was of the highest conduct and practice.
In the fifteenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
an official's wife died,
and he was invited to the home to perform blessings.
The master stayed at their home for several days,
residing in the front corridor,
and they made generous offerings.
It was customary that whenever someone died, they would consult a shaman,
who would then announce the day the deceased's spirit would emerge,
saying there would certainly be harm,
so the bereaved family would mostly go out to avoid it.
That night,
the official's family all secretly left through the north gate,
without informing the master.
The master simply lit a lamp in the hall and recited scriptures.
Suddenly he saw two people attending him.
As midnight approached,
he suddenly heard sounds from the hall of someone getting up, taking clothes, and opening the door.
A woman came out of the hall
and went to the kitchen to prepare food,
drawing water and blowing on the fire.
The master thought she was a family member,
and did not find it strange.
As dawn approached,
the woman brought food,
carrying a tray forward.
She alone wore a face veil,
and was barefoot.
She bowed twice and said:
"You troubled yourself to descend here.
Now the family has all gone out,
and I feared the morning meal would be missed,
so I, your disciple, got up
to prepare it for you."
The master knew she was the deceased,
and accepted her offering.
Just as he was reciting the blessing,
before the blessing was finished,
he heard the sound of the north door of the hall opening.
The woman said in panic:
"My son is coming."
She then rushed into the hall,
and then weeping was heard.
After the weeping ceased,
the family came to see the master,
asking if he was well.
Seeing the porridge on the tray,
they asked the master:
"We disciples indeed avoided the calamity last night,
without letting you know.
There was no one in the house;
who made this porridge?"
The master smiled and did not answer.
A maidservant in the hall exclaimed in surprise:
"Last night the deceased's corpse suddenly lay sideways,
her hands were stained with flour,
and her feet were muddy.
What does this mean?"
The master then pointed to the porridge that had been made to show them,
and the family was astonished.
Nun Yuánzhì
The nun Yuánzhì of Guǎngjìng Temple
once spent the summer retreat with companions in the Zhōngnán Mountains.
On a summer night under a bright moon,
someone came weeping,
their voice loud and deep,
and very sorrowful.
When they arrived,
it was a person
over eight chǐ tall,
standing in front of the hut.
The weeping did not cease,
continuing until midnight.
The sound was very choked with sobs,
with tears streaming down.
The nuns maintained correct mindfulness and were not afraid,
and the weeper ultimately left without speaking.
Yáng Yuányīng
served as the Minister of Ceremonies during the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān.
During the Kāiyuán era,
he had already been deceased for twenty years.
His son happened to visit a sword polisher's shop in the Yěchéng Ward,
where he recognized his father's sword from the tomb.
Finding this strange,
he asked the polisher:
"How did you obtain this sword?"
The polisher replied:
"A noble-looking man in fine clothes
brought it here for repair,
and is scheduled to come to collect it tomorrow at noon."
The son suspected it was his father's doing,
but also feared that his father's grave might have been opened by someone.
On the appointed day,
he went with his younger brother to the polisher's house
and waited.
When the time came to collect the sword,
it was indeed their father,
riding a white horse,
dressed as he was in life,
accompanied by five or six attendants.
The brothers stepped out and bowed by the roadside,
weeping sorrowfully for a long time.
Yuányīng took the sword and dismounted,
led his sons to a secluded spot,
and gave instructions on family matters.
Finally, he asked:
"Is your mother still at home?"
They replied:
"She has been buried with you for fifteen years."
Yuányīng said:
"I was unaware of this."
He sighed repeatedly,
then told his sons:
"I have official duties to attend to,
and cannot stay long.
Tomorrow,
you can come here again,
and I will give you some funds
to help with your hardships."
The sons arrived as scheduled,
and Yuányīng also came.
He gave them three hundred thousand coins
and admonished them:
"You must spend this all within a few days."
After saying this, he bid farewell and left,
while his sons followed, weeping.
Yuányīng then said to his sons:
"You do not understand this matter;
the paths of humans and ghosts are different.
How could a father and son remain together for a hundred years?"
After saying this, he bid farewell and left.
The sons followed him out through the Shàngdōng Gate,
watching from afar as he entered the Máng Mountains.
After a few dozen steps, he suddenly vanished from sight.
Within a few days,
the money was completely spent.
Three days later,
the market vendors all received paper money.
Xuē Jīn
Xuē Jīn
served as the Captain of Cháng'ān during the Kāiyuán era,
overseeing the palace market,
alternating days between the East and West Markets.
One day at the East Market,
he saw a parked carriage,
inside which was a woman
with hands as white as snow.
Jīn admired her
and had his attendants hold a silver-inlaid small box
beside the carriage.
The woman sent her maid to ask the price,
and the attendant replied:
"This belongs to Captain Xuē of Cháng'ān.
He instructed that if anyone in the carriage asks,
it should be given as a gift."
The woman was delighted and thanked him.
Jīn subtly flirted with her,
and she responded happily.
She then said to Jīn:
"I live outside the Jīnguāng Gate;
you should visit me."
Jīn had his attendants follow her to her residence.
The next day, he went to visit,
but saw many riders outside the woman's gate,
and hesitated to approach.
When the other guests had all left,
Jīn announced his presence at the gate
and had his attendants present his name card.
He was then invited to the outer hall,
where he was asked to sit.
The woman said:
"Wait while I finish dressing."
Jīn felt the air grow cold
and secretly became suspicious.
After a short while,
he was led into the inner hall.
The curtains were made of black cloth,
and in the distance, he saw a lamp
with a dim, faint light.
As he approached, it seemed to recede,
making him suspect she was not human.
However, since he had already sought to meet her,
he decided to leave after seeing her.
In his heart, he repeatedly recited the Thousand-Handed Guānyīn mantra.
Upon entering,
he saw her sitting behind a curtain,
with a silk scarf covering her head.
Jīn struggled to pull it away,
and after some effort, it finally fell.
He saw the woman's face, over a foot long,
pale green in color,
and emitting a sound like a dog.
Jīn immediately fainted.
When his attendants reached the building,
they only saw a funeral hall,
with Jīn inside,
trapped without any gaps.
They hastily pushed the wall down
and found Jīn already dead,
with only a faint warmth in his chest.
They moved him to an inn to recuperate,
and after more than a month, he finally regained consciousness.
Zhū Qīniáng
In the Sīgōng Ward of the Eastern Capital, there was a woman named Zhū Qīniáng,
who was a courtesan.
A certain General Wáng
had long been involved with her.
During the Kāiyuán era,
Wáng fell ill and passed away,
and half a year had already passed,
but Zhū was unaware of it.
In July of that year,
Wáng suddenly came to Zhū's place.
After staying until dusk,
he said:
"Can you come with me to my residence in the Wēnróu Ward?"
Zhū was about to agree,
but her daughter, who was famous for her singing and lute-playing,
did not want her mother to go.
She said:
"It would be better if the General stayed here.
Is there something to fear if you return?"
Unable to refuse,
Zhū was taken away on the horse behind Wáng.
Upon entering the courtyard,
they enjoyed themselves as before.
The next morning,
the Wáng family sent a maid to collect the bedding from the spirit bed,
and she saw a woman under the covers.
She hurried back to report.
The sons of the Wáng family
rushed over in shock to see.
When they asked for an explanation,
they learned she had been brought by their father.
After grieving for a long time,
they escorted her back home.
Lǐ Guāngyuǎn,
during the Kāiyuán era,
served as the magistrate of Guàntáo County.
At that time, there was a great drought,
and Lǐ Guāngyuǎn
composed a petition regarding the drought.
Just as the petition was completed, he died suddenly.
After his death,
the county reported to the prefecture,
but the prefectural Simǎ dismissed the drought report.
The common people were filled with resentment,
and some wailed in grief,
all saying:
"If our magistrate were still alive,
would such a thing have happened?"
That night,
Lǐ Guāngyuǎn suddenly appeared riding a white horse,
and came to the drought relief office,
addressing the people:
"Though I am dead,
the drought relief should not be hindered.
Who is this Simǎ,
daring to obstruct this proposal?"
He then went with the people to the Simǎ's residence,
announcing:
"Magistrate Lǐ wishes to see you."
The Simǎ was greatly frightened,
and sent someone to apologize.
Lǐ Guāngyuǎn rebuked him:
"You are not human!
The drought is a matter for the people;
how can life and death be the criteria?
You must expedite the relief,
otherwise,
I will become a vengeful ghost."
Having said this,
he bid farewell to the people and departed.
That year, the drought relief was accomplished,
and the people benefited from it.
Lǐ Bà
Lǐ Bà, the magistrate of Qíyáng,
was harsh, cruel, and fierce,
showing no kindness to those he encountered.
From the Chéngwèi down,
all clerks and officials suffered under his tyranny.
However, he was upright and stubborn.
He took pride in himself,
yet his wife and children could not escape hunger and cold.
After one term of service, he died suddenly.
After his body was encoffined, the courtyard was devoid of mourners.
His wife often stroked the coffin and wept bitterly,
crying out:
"What was Lǐ Bà like in life?
Now his wife and children endure such loneliness."
Several days later,
a voice suddenly spoke from the coffin:
"Do not grieve, wife;
I will arrange my own return."
That evening at the yamen,
he instructed his family to set up a table in the hall,
and Lǐ Bà appeared in form,
ordering the summoning of all the clerks.
The clerks, who had always feared him,
heard the command and rushed over,
and upon seeing Lǐ Bà, none were not trembling with fear.
He also summoned the Deputy Magistrate and the Registrar,
and when they arrived,
Lǐ Bà angrily scolded them:
"You are heartless;
how could it come to this!
Do you think I cannot kill you?"
Having said this,
they all collapsed lifeless.
The family members came to the courtyard to bow and pray,
and Lǐ Bà said:
"Just convey the amount of goods,
and there will be no worry about them not reviving.
Let five bolts of silk be the standard,
Once the silk arrives, they will come back to life."
After each had expressed their thanks and left,
he said to the two yamen clerks:
"I have always treated you well;
why did you also side with the others?
Killing just you alone
would be of little benefit.
I shall make the horses of both your families die as proof."
In a moment,
hundreds of horses suddenly fell as if dead.
Then someone presented two fine horses,
and the horses returned to normal.
He then said to all the clerks:
"Though I was always upright,
now that I am dead,
I thank you all;
could you not offer me a small token?"
Again, five bolts of silk were collected.
He ordered a certain official to provide a carriage,
another to provide horses,
and certain clerks to make repairs,
warning that violators would surely die.
They dispersed only after the first watch.
Two days later, all arrangements were completed,
The family then set out on the road.
Whenever they reached a place for offerings,
he would stop to enjoy the sacrifices,
and after enjoying them,
he would mount his horse and depart.
After more than ten miles,
they had reached the outskirts,
and he vanished.
At night,
when they stopped the carriage and horses,
his wife and children wanted to cry,
but a voice from the coffin said:
"I am here;
you are all exhausted,
there is no need to cry."
Lǐ Bà's home was in the capital,
over a thousand miles from Qíyáng.
At each resting place,
he would not allow them to cry.
After traveling several hundred miles,
he suddenly said to his son:
"Do not sleep tonight;
someone intends to steal the good horses,
so you should guard against it in advance."
The family, weary from the long journey,
did not follow the instruction,
and that night, the horses were indeed lost.
At dawn, they reported it,
and Lǐ Bà said:
"I told you to guard against theft;
why were you so greedy for sleep?
Nevertheless,
the horses will not be lost.
East of the nearby inn, there is a road heading south;
follow it for more than ten miles,
and there is a thicket of trees.
The horses are tethered beneath the trees;
go and retrieve them."
They did as told and found them.
When they reached the capital,
relatives, hearing of the strange events,
came in droves to offer condolences,
visiting morning and night.
Lǐ Bà responded from the coffin to all,
leaving none unawed.
The crowd of onlookers grew noisy,
and the family could not bear the disturbance.
Lǐ Bà suddenly said to his son:
"The guests come and go
merely wishing to see me.
You may set up the hall,
and I will meet the relatives once."
His son did as instructed,
and everyone waited in the courtyard.
After a long time, he said:
"I have come!"
He ordered the curtain to be rolled up,
and suddenly Lǐ Bà appeared,
his head as large as a jar,
his eyes bulging,
glaring at the guests.
The guests all fell to the ground in terror,
and gradually withdrew.
Lǐ Bà said to his son:
"The ways of humans and spirits are different;
the house is no place for me to dwell long.
Bury me quickly in the wilderness."
Having said this, he vanished,
and his voice was heard no more.
The Ghost Soldiers of Luòyáng
In the twenty-third year of the Zhēnyuán era,
In the summer, the sixth month,
the Emperor was in the Eastern Capital.
The common people alarmed each other with tales of ghost soldiers,
all fleeing without knowing where to go,
some even colliding and injuring themselves.
These ghost soldiers first crossed south of the Luò River,
causing a clamor in the wards and markets,
gradually reaching north of the river.
When they were heard passing by,
it was as if tens of millions of armored cavalry filled the sky,
with the clamorous sounds of men and horses,
and in a moment they had passed completely.
Each night they passed,
sometimes twice,
sometimes three times.
The Emperor detested this,
and ordered shamans to perform exorcisms,
setting out food and drink each night on the banks of the Luò River.
I once read the *Book of Northern Qí*.
There was also such an event.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
mid-period,
it was said in Jìnyáng that there were ghost soldiers,
and the people vied to strike bronze and iron to ward them off,
but all perished not long after.
The Scholar of Dàodé Ward
In the Eastern Capital of the Táng, in Dàodé Ward, there was a scholar.
One evening, as he was walking to the Middle Bridge,
he encountered a nobleman's retinue,
with carriages and horses in great splendor.
Seeing the scholar,
they called to him and spoke,
ordering him to follow behind.
There was a noble lady,
over twenty years old,
of peerless beauty and grace,
who conversed with the scholar without ceasing.
Thus they went south to Chángxià Gate,
then reached Lóngmén,
and entered a grand mansion,
with splendid halls and orchid-scented chambers.
Summoning the scholar, she bestowed upon him rare delicacies,
and then lay with him.
Past midnight,
the scholar awoke,
and saw the place where he lay—
it was a stone cave.
Before him was a dead woman,
her body swollen and distended,
illuminated by the moonlight,
so foul-smelling it was unbearable.
The scholar then trod perilously and climbed the rocks,
barely managing to escape.
At dawn, he reached Xiāngshān Temple,
and told the monks what had happened.
The monks escorted him home,
but he died a few days later.
The Scholar of Ānyí Ward
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
in Ānyí Ward of the Eastern Capital, there was a scholar
who was studying behind closed doors at night.
Through a crack in the door,
he suddenly saw a person's head appear.
He shouted, asking who it was,
and the reply came:
"I am a ghost,
and I wish to join you for a while."
He then invited the scholar to go outside.
The scholar followed him to the door,
drew a cross on the ground,
and then proceeded forward.
Leaving the ward,
they reached the entrance of a temple shop,
and the scholar said:
"If we are seen by the temple,
we certainly won't be able to pass."
The ghost said:
"Just follow me,
there's nothing to worry about."
Soon they arrived inside Dìngdǐng Gate,
and the ghost carried the scholar out through a crack in the gate.
Proceeding to the Five Bridges,
beside the road was a tomb,
with a light shining from a skylight.
The ghost again carried the scholar up to the side of the skylight,
and looking down, they saw a woman
crying over a sick child,
while her husband dozed beside them.
The ghost then descended through,
and covered the lamp with his hand.
The woman, frightened,
shouted at her husband:
"Our child is now at death's door,
how can you bear to sleep so greedily!
Just now an evil thing covered the lamp,
get up quickly and light it again."
The husband rose to add more candle,
and the ghost avoided the woman.
Suddenly, he took a cloth bag and put the child inside,
and the child could still move within the bag.
The ghost then carried it out,
up to the skylight,
and also carried the scholar down to the ground.
He escorted him into Dìngdǐng Gate,
to the scholar's residence,
and apologized, saying:
"I was ordered by the underworld
to fetch this child,
and the task required a living person as a companion,
hence I troubled you with this.
I hope you can forgive me."
Having said this, he departed.
The scholar, while following the ghost earlier,
had marked every place they stopped
with a cross.
The next day,
he led his brothers to check these places,
and the crosses were all verified.
They then went to the home of the missing child to inquire,
and it matched as well.
Péi Shèng
According to Dǒng Shìyuán,
Péi Shèng, a constable of Yìxīng, was napping during the day
when he was suddenly led away by a ghost,
his body and spirit following along.
The ghost said:
"We are to fetch a child."
Arriving at the child's home,
the parents were lying on either side of the child,
with Buddhist rites being performed before them.
The ghost said:
"Because of that Buddha."
Once the living person arrived,
the ghost waved his hand,
and both parents fell asleep.
The ghost ordered Shèng to carry the child out of bed,
and as he held the child, its throat made a sound,
startling the parents awake.
The ghost then led Shèng out,
and Shèng pleaded earnestly to be taken back to his home.
Pushed back into his body, he then awoke.
Yáng Pǔ
All the counties of Yùzhāng
produce excellent timber.
Those seeking profit gather it
and transport it to Guǎnglíng,
where the profit is severalfold.
In the fifth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a man named Yáng Pǔ
who entered the forest with several others to seek timber.
On a winter evening, snow was falling,
and deep in the mountains there was nowhere to lodge.
There was a large tree lying across the ground,
hollow inside,
capable of accommodating several people.
So they entered it to spend the night together.
Before the guide fell asleep,
he bowed twice toward the mountain forest and chanted:
"Lord of the Earth,
tonight we lodge here to sleep;
we beg for your protection and aid."
After making this request three times, he then lay down to rest.
Late at night, the snow fell heavily.
Near the southern tree,
suddenly someone called out:
"Zhāng Lǐ."
A voice from the treetop responded:
"Yes."
"Tonight in the northern village, a girl is getting married;
there is plenty of wine and food.
Let us go together."
The person in the treetop said:
"There are guests here;
I must guard them until dawn.
If I leave,
the black dog is ignorant
and might harm them without restraint."
The person below the tree said again:
"The snow and cold are like this;
let us seek food and drink.
It is only right to go together."
The person in the tree said again:
"Though the snow and cold are severe,
I have already accepted their request;
it is not right to leave.
I must guard against the black dog."
The caller then departed.
When dawn came and they finished packing,
they removed the felt on which they had slept.
Beneath it was a black serpent,
as large as a vase,
three feet long, lying dormant and motionless.
Only then were they shocked and terrified.
Xuē Zhí
Xuē Zhí, Governor of Shèngzhōu,
was the son of Chancellor Xuē Nà.
He was fond of killing and warfare
and did not believe in ghosts or spirits.
While Xuē Zhí was in the province,
he was returning from a tour of the counties
when, two postal stations away from the provincial capital,
he encountered a friend from the capital who had come to visit him.
Xuē Zhí invited him into the station hall
and ordered food.
Before eating, his friend made an offering.
Xuē Zhí asked:
"Why do you offer this food?"
His friend replied:
"Buddhist scriptures say
there are wild ghosts
who eat human flesh and blood.
The Buddha went to convert them,
making them refrain from killing.
Therefore, this precept was established.
Moreover, it is commonly said
that offering food first before eating
brings long life and longevity."
Xuē Zhí said:
"You are greatly deluded.
Where is there a Buddha?
What are ghosts?
Common people deceive each other;
the foolish follow blindly,
but the wise are not confused.
You are merely a common person!"
Not long after he spoke,
a voice from the air said:
"Xuē Zhí,
you are greatly arrogant and foolish!
How can you know there is no Buddha?
How can you know there are no ghosts?
Misfortune will befall you;
