when your life ends, you will not see your wife and children.
You will die here.
How can you speak such nonsense?"
Xuē Zhí, hearing this, was greatly alarmed.
He hurriedly descended and bowed twice,
apologizing:
"I, an ignorant man, am stubborn and foolish;
I did not know there were spirits.
May the spirits instruct me."
The voice from the air spoke again:
"Your life will end at noon.
You must return quickly
to see your wife and children.
Otherwise,
you will die here!"
Xuē Zhí was terrified.
He and his friend galloped toward the commandery.
After traveling one postal station,
Xuē Zhí entered the hall to rest.
His attendants all rested as well.
Suddenly, they saw Xuē Zhí leave.
Over a hundred attendants
all followed him on either side.
When the station officer entered the room,
Xuē Zhí was already dead.
The station then reported this to his family.
Xuē Zhí had already arrived home first.
He called his wife to bid farewell, saying:
"I have already died at the northern postal station.
My body is now a ghost.
Fearing I could not see you face-to-face to say goodbye,
I have come here temporarily."
Holding his wife and children's hands,
he only urged them to take care,
then mounted his horse and went out the gate,
vanishing and passing away.
Liú Hóng
Liú Hóng of the Peì State,
was of a stern and upright nature.
His father served as a Commander of Assault Forces.
When Xuē Chǔyù was stationed in Fànyáng,
he summoned him to serve in the army.
Hóng followed him to Jì,
and thus came to serve Chǔyù,
who was pleased with him.
When Chǔyù was assigned to fill a garrison post,
Hóng requested to go along.
In Tánzhōu, there was a garrison called Tàihé,
where those appointed invariably died,
and the garrison had thus fallen into ruin.
Hóng then requested to be put in charge of it.
Chǔyù warned him of the danger,
but Hóng said:
"Supernatural phenomena arise from people;
they do not manifest on their own.
I, Hóng, am not afraid,
so why should you hesitate?"
Chǔyù then appointed him as the commander of the Tàihé garrison.
Hóng led his officials and men to the garrison.
There was an old settlement at the garrison,
and Hóng built his quarters there.
As a carpenter was swinging his axe to measure,
a piece of wood suddenly broke off and flew up,
striking the carpenter dead on the spot.
Hóng was enraged,
shouted at his officers and soldiers,
and had them lift the carpenter up and flog him.
He interrogated him, saying:
"What kind of ghost are you?
I am just now taking charge of this garrison,
and you dare to interfere?
Your crime is punishable by death without pardon!"
After several strokes of the whip,
the carpenter spoke:
"I beg for your leniency.
I am not the one who killed the previous garrison commanders.
The one who killed the garrison commanders
is the Assistant State General.
His dwelling is not far from here.
I am merely the ghost guarding the foundation of a Buddhist hall.
This old settlement
was once a Buddhist hall.
Because it is a pure place,
I was ordered to guard it.
I was assigned to guard this foundation
due to sins committed in my human life.
Only when the foundation is leveled with the ground
will I be able to leave.
I have come now
to plead with you, sir.
If you level it for me,
I can leave to be reborn as a human."
Hóng said:
"You said the Assistant State General is not far away;
bring him here immediately."
The ghost said:
"Yes."
Moments later,
the carpenter spoke again:
"Liú Hóng,
I am the Assistant State General.
You are a strong and upright man,
and also possess talent and ability.
I hold you in high regard
and intend to appoint you to a position.
I now summon you,
and you shall attain great wealth and honor.
Strive for it."
He then asked for paper
and composed two poems.
The carpenter was a common soldier
who had never known poetry.
Yet when he put brush to paper,
his calligraphy was exceptionally exquisite,
comparable to Wáng Xīzhī's.
Xuē Chǔyù took the poems and treasured them.
The first poem read:
"Crows fly in the empty sky,
Dark steeds roam the wilds and linger.
My name is now entered in the household register,
My passing leaves the leaves sparse."
The second poem read:
"Branches of a lone tree wither,
Three blossoms, five faces weep.
Moving home, morning passes,
Who perceives □."
When the poems were finished, he departed.
The carpenter was then a laborer attached to the garrison.
A few days later, Hóng fell gravely ill,
and was carried to Fànyáng.
His father sought out the renowned physician Xuē,
who also happened to be ill.
Hóng spoke as usual,
but two cold, dense chills invaded □□□□□.
When Hóng first received the ghost's poems,
he pondered them but could not decipher their meaning.
Upon his death,
everything turned black,
and so they used it to carry his coffin.
"My name is now entered in the household register"
referred to Hóng's name.
"Leaves the leaves sparse"
spoke of the image of Hóng's death.
In the second poem, "Branches of a lone tree wither"
meant the old branches had withered.
"Three blossoms, five faces weep" meant
Hóng's family had eight members;
with Hóng and two others deceased,
that made three blossoms.
Five people wept for him,
hence five faces weeping.
Twenty days after Hóng's death,
a former subordinate saw Hóng in the wilderness, wearing purple robes,
followed by two hundred horsemen,
his demeanor very imposing.
He told the subordinate:
"I have been employed by the Assistant State General,
and now enjoy great wealth and honor.
I am now leading my horsemen to the capital to fetch my mother."
His mother was already in the capital.
Earlier, Hóng's maternal uncle had a daughter
who was raised in the Liú household.
She was about the same age as Hóng,
and once said to him:
"I have heard that the dead possess consciousness.
If either of us dies first,
we must disturb the living
to let them know."
On that day,
the girl was walking ahead of Hóng's mother
when suddenly something tugged at her clothes,
preventing her from moving forward.
The girl found it strange.
After a moment she could move again,
but then something pulled at her sash,
took her comb,
as if teasing her.
Hóng's mother exclaimed in alarm:
"Hóng!
When he was alive, he once said
that he must
come while in the army.
We have long had no letters from him.
Has he died now?
Why does this match what he said in life?"
Before his mother finished speaking,
Hóng's form appeared in the courtyard,
clad in purple with a golden insignia,
and many attendants.
His mother asked:
"Why have you come?"
Hóng said: "I have attained wealth and honor,
though I am no longer human.
My blessings and joys are beyond words,
so I have come to fetch you, Mother, to care for you."
Carriages then advanced,
his mother boarded one,
and Hóng attended her,
and they departed.
After they left, his mother passed away.
The time he was seen by his former subordinate
was also the day his mother died.
Táng Xuǎn
Táng Xuǎn was a man from
Jìnchāng.
His paternal aunt married Zhāng Gōng,
who was a descendant of Zhāng Zhé
of Āndìng.
He lived in seclusion at Wèinán in Huázhōu,
and was highly esteemed by many.
He had three sons,
who all passed the imperial examinations as jìnshì.
He also had three daughters.
The eldest married into the Xīn family,
the second married into the Liáng family,
and the youngest daughter was deeply cherished by her aunt.
She was educated in poetry and rites,
and possessed considerable virtue.
During the Kāiyuán era,
her father passed away,
and she mourned him with grief that exceeded the prescribed rites.
Xuǎn had long admired her,
and after the mourning period ended,
he married her,
and they lived at his estate in Wèinán.
In the eighteenth year of Kāiyuán,
Xuǎn went to Luòyáng on business,
and for several months could not return.
One night, while staying at his host's place,
he dreamed of his wife weeping behind flowers,
and then peering into a well and smiling.
Upon waking,
he felt uneasy in his heart.
The next day,
he consulted a fortune-teller,
who said:
"Weeping behind flowers means
her beauty will fade with the wind;
peering into a well and smiling means
she rejoices on the road to the springs."
A few days later,
news of her death indeed arrived.
Xuǎn's grief and sorrow were加倍 than usual.
Several years later,
he finally returned to Wèinán.
Recalling past traces,
moved, he composed a poem:
"In the bedchamber, I grieve over the long mat;
in the dressing tower, I weep before the mirror stand.
Alone I mourn the season of peach and plum,
not sharing blossoms with the night springs.
O soul, if you have feelings,
appear vaguely in my dreams."
He also wrote:
"Once the splendid hall was quiet,
laughter and talk passed the night watches.
Hazily, human affairs have changed;
dark and silent, she is entrusted to the desolate mound.
On the sunlit plain, they sing the 'Song of the Dew on the Onions';
in the shadowy ravine, I mourn the hidden boat.
On a clear night, the moon over Zhuāng's terrace—
in vain I imagine the sorrow of painting eyebrows."
That evening, the wind and dew were clear and serene,
and Xuǎn lay awake, troubled.
Late into the night,
he sorrowfully chanted the former elegy.
Suddenly, he heard what seemed like a weeping sound in the darkness,
distant at first,
gradually drawing near.
Xuǎn, startled and apprehensive,
sensed something unusual,
and prayed, saying:
"If it is the spirit of my tenth lady,
why begrudge a meeting to converse?
Do not let the separation of the dark realms
hinder our former love."
After a moment,
a voice replied:
"I am your wife, née Zhāng.
Hearing your sorrowful chanting and longing,
though dwelling in the dark realm,
I am truly moved to pity.
Ashamed of your sincere heart,
for not abandoning this sunken soul,
and remembering me always,
therefore this night I make myself known to you."
Xuǎn sighed in amazement,
and weeping, said with a choked voice:
"The matters in my heart
are difficult to fully express.
Yet I must see your face once more;
then I would die without regret."
She replied:
"The ways of the hidden and visible realms are separate;
meeting is exceedingly difficult.
I also fear you may have doubts;
it is not that I do not wish to reveal myself fully."
Xuǎn's words grew even more earnest,
swearing he had no doubts.
Soon, he heard her call for Luófū to fetch a mirror,
and then heard rustling footsteps in the darkness.
Luófū
came forth first and bowed,
saying:
"My lady wishes to speak of old times,
and hopes to meet with the seventh gentleman."
Xuǎn asked Luófū:
"In the eighth year of Kāiyuán,
I pawned you to the Kāng family in Xiānzhōu.
I heard you had already died at the Kāngs';
how is it you are here now?"
She replied:
"I was redeemed by my lady,
and now look after Āměi."
Āměi was Xuǎn's deceased daughter.
Xuǎn was again moved to sorrow.
Shortly after, she ordered lamps and candles,
and stood north of the eastern steps.
Xuǎn hurried forward,
weeping and bowing.
His wife returned the bow,
and Xuǎn then took her hand,
speaking of their lifetime together.
His wife also shed tears and said to Xuǎn:
"The ways of yīn and yáng are separate;
I have been parted from you for long.
Though in the dark silence there is no reliance,
as for longing,
it has never left my heart.
Today is a day when the six directions align,
and the underworld officials, moved by your sincerity,
have allowed me to come temporarily.
A meeting once in a thousand years—
sorrow and joy mingle.
Moreover, Měiniáng is still young,
with no one to entrust her to.
What night is this night,
that we can again express our feelings?"
Xuǎn then ordered his household to line up and pay their respects.
Moving the lamp into the room,
they set up curtains and drapes.
She refused to sit first,
saying:
"In the hierarchy of yīn and yáng,
the living are esteemed.
You should sit first."
Xuǎn did as she said.
Smiling, she said to Xuǎn:
"Your feelings have not changed from before,
yet I hear you have remarried.
Is there a difference between the new and the old?"
Xuǎn was greatly ashamed.
His wife said:
"Judging by karma, it is fitting for you
to remarry.
Your new wife is in Huáinán,
and I know she is very gentle and good."
Then she asked, "Is the length of human life
truly predetermined?"
He replied:
"It is certainly predetermined."
She asked again:
"The Buddha speaks of past causes.
Is this not mistaken?"
He replied:
"The principle is clear and can be discerned;
how could it be mistaken?"
She asked again:
"Between Buddhism and Daoism, which is right and which is wrong?"
He replied:
"They share the same source but branch differently.
There is also the Great Ultimate and immortal ranks,
offices that govern all spirits,
transformations that exit being and enter non-being—
their way is vast indeed.
The rest is mostly as spoken of in the human world.
It is not fitting to speak of it all now,
lest it burden both sides."
Xuǎn, fearful,
dared not ask further.
Instead, he asked:
"What would you like to eat?"
She replied:
"In the underworld, delicacies are also available,
only there is no rice gruel,
which cannot be obtained."
Xuǎn immediately ordered it prepared.
When it arrived,
she asked for a separate vessel,
spread it out, and ate,
seeming to finish it as it reached her mouth.
But when it was cleared away,
the gruel remained as before.
Xuǎn then fed all her attendants.
There was an old woman
who refused to sit with them.
His wife said:
"She is an old servant,
not associating with petty people. "
Said to Xuǎn:
"This is Zǐjú Nǎi,
how could you not recognize her?"
Xuǎn then remembered.
A separate banquet was served.
As for the other attendants,
Xuǎn mostly did not recognize them,
but upon hearing their names called,
they turned out to be the paper cutouts of servants and slaves
that Xuǎn had made when he returned from the capital,
with the names he had inscribed.
He asked his wife,
and she said:
"They are all the ones you gave;
thus you know that wealth, servants, and slaves
can all be obtained."
His wife said:
"In the past, I often played with a gold-inlaid box,
hidden in the northwest bracket of the main hall's roof,
a place no one knows."
Xuǎn went to retrieve it and indeed found it.
She also said:
"Do you not wish to see Měiniáng?
She has already grown up."
Xuǎn said:
"Měiniáng died in swaddling clothes;
how could she age in the underworld?"
She replied:
"It is no different."
In a moment,
Měiniáng arrived,
about five or six years old.
Xuǎn caressed her and wept,
and his wife said:
"Do not hold her and startle the child."
Luófū then held her,
and she suddenly vanished.
Xuǎn had the curtains lowered,
and they expressed their deep affection,
just as in life.
Xuǎn felt her hands, feet, and breath were cold.
He asked again:
"Where do you reside in the underworld?"
She replied:
"By the side of my parents-in-law."
Xuǎn said:
"Since your spirit is so present,
why not return to life?"
She replied:
"After a person dies,
the soul and the body are in separate places,
each recorded elsewhere,
far removed from the physical form.
Why not verify this in dreams—
how can one remember their own body?
After our child died,
I do not remember the moment of death at all,
nor do I know where she was buried.
As for wealth and servants,
if you give them, I know.
But as for the physical form,
I truly have no control over it."
As they lingered deep into the night,
Xuǎn said:
"Our shared grave is not far off."
His wife said:
"I have heard of the ritual of joint burial,
which unites the physical forms.
But as for the spirits,
they truly do not meet;
why trouble with such words?"
Xuǎn said:
"When a woman dies,
is it not possible to remarry?"
She replied:
"Life and death flow together,
but chastity and waywardness differ.
Moreover, after I died,
my parents-in-law wanted to override my will
and marry me to Zhèng Qiánguān's nephew, Míngyuǎn, of the Northern Court Protectorate.
I swore an unwavering vow,
and all above and below took pity,
so I was spared."
Xuǎn heard this and sighed with emotion,
moved, he presented a poem:
"The tóng tree of Yìyáng is half-dead,
the sword of Yánjīn sinks alone.
How within a single night,
have I vainly borne a heart of a hundred years?"
His wife said:
"Seeing your feelings now,
I wish to leave a reply;
may I?"
Xuǎn said:
"In the past, you did not engage in literary pursuits;
how can you compose verses?"
His wife said:
"I have always admired literary composition,
but feared you would suspect and disapprove, so I did not.
As for expressing my will,
why hesitate tonight?"
So she tore a strip of cloth and inscribed a poem:
"Not distinguishing between the hidden and the manifest,
how can one bear the difference between past and present?
The paths of yīn and yáng are naturally separate,
gathering and parting both trouble the heart."
She also said:
"On the orchid steps, the rabbit moon slants,
silver candles half-embrace the flowers.
I pity myself, a guest of the long night,
making the spring road my home."
Xuǎn spoke through tears,
between sorrow and joy,
unaware of the dawn breaking.
In a moment,
they heard a knock at the door.
The parents-in-law sent Dānshēn to relay a message:
"Urging the new bride to hurry,
fearing the underworld officials will reprimand at dawn."
His wife wept and rose,
bidding Xuǎn farewell.
Xuǎn wrote a letter to attach with her,
straightened his clothes,
and noticed a rich fragrance,
unlike any in the world.
"Where does this fragrance come from?"
She replied:
"The lingering scent of Hán Shòu;
when I came,
my parents-in-law bestowed it."
Xuǎn held her hand and said:
"When will we meet again?"
She replied:
"In forty years."
She left a silk handkerchief
for Xuǎn as a memento.
Xuǎn gave her a gold-inlaid box in return.
She then said:
"The time ahead is limited,
I cannot stay long.
Unless within forty years,
if you offer sacrifices at the tomb,
it will be of no use.
If you wish to make offerings,
only on the last day of the month, at dusk,
in the wild fields,
or by the riverbank,
call my name,
and you may nearly succeed.
Hastily, I cannot linger to speak longer;
take care of yourself."
Having spoken,
she mounted the carriage and left,
waving her sleeve,
After a long while, she vanished.
The whole family witnessed it,
as recorded in Táng Xuǎn's personal account.
Xiāo Zhèngrén
The Governor of Lángyé, Xǔ Jièyán,
once said that
when he was young, he and his cousins,
spoke of ghosts and spirits at night.
Among them, a bold one
said:
"I do not believe in such things;
where are there ghosts?"
Before he finished speaking,
from the front eaves, a ghost suddenly lowered two legs,
the legs were very stout,
with long black hair,
and feet touching the ground.
The speaker fled and hid.
His younger cousin, Xiāo Zhèngrén,
calm and quiet, speaking little,
alone was unafraid.
He directly grabbed the ghost's legs,
and urgently tied them with his removed clothing.
The ghost retracted its legs to the eaves,
but Zhèngrén held them fast,
so it could not ascend,
and came down again,
repeating this several times.
With no one coming to help,
Zhèngrén released it,
and the ghost then vanished.
And Zhèngrén was unharmed.
Wěi Yì
The Censor Wéi Yì,
after being demoted and transferred, was appointed as the Household Registrar of Guó Prefecture.
Yì had a prior relationship with the Prefect,
and requested the opening of the western outer road of Guó Prefecture.
Yì oversaw the project,
and in total opened several miles,
leveling several hundred graves.
Later, the Prefect, concerned about Yì,
went to Hú to review the work.
Someone arrived at Hú,
and reported that Yì's wife had died.
Yì's wife had passed away seven days earlier,
and he had summoned temple monks for a memorial feast.
Yì was heartbroken and despondent,
and the monks comforted and encouraged him.
After the feast concluded,
Yì escorted the monks out the door,
and before he finished speaking,
as if seeing something,
he bowed to the monks and stepped back,
saying:
"My deceased wife has appeared in form."
Then he seemed to be bowing and responding,
until he reached the hall and collapsed to the ground,
and then died.
People considered it a calamity from leveling the graves.
Zhào Xiàrì
Zhào Xiàrì, a Literary Scholar of Prince Níng,
was renowned for his literary works,
and died in office due to his literary duties.
After his death,
he often managed household affairs as if still alive,
and the entire household, young and old,
dared not do anything wrong.
He often spoke from within the spirit curtain,
his voice very stern.
His second son often saw him,
and he frequently remained at home.
When the son turned three,
he instructed him to relay messages,
bidding farewell to everyone,
and then departed forever.
Rú Zǐyán
Rú Zǐyán, a man from Wú,
served as the Deputy of Shuāngliú due to his mastery of the classics,
and was quite talented and knowledgeable,
skilled in medical prescriptions,
so many court officials knew him.
Zǐyán desired the position of Erudite of the Capital Prefecture,
and when the selection came,
he requested it.
After being appointed,
he often visited the homes of high-ranking officials.
When he returned to his studies,
carriages and horses never ceased.
Zǐyán's brother-in-law Zhāng Xūyí,
was appointed as the Deputy of Tōngquán in Zǐ Prefecture.
His family was poor,
and he could not bring his wife along.
He also had debts amounting to tens of thousands,
and asked Zǐyán to guarantee them.
More than two months after Xūyí left,
Zǐyán was sitting at night,
when suddenly a voice from under the eaves said:
"I am Zhāng Xūyí, Deputy of Tōngquán,
I died a few days after arriving at the county.
Now my coffin is returning,
and has already departed from the county.
I was especially close to you in life,
and on the day I left for my post,
I burdened you with my debts.
Now that I am dead,
and my family is impoverished,
causing trouble for you in every way,
I deeply feel ashamed."
Zǐyán asked:
"When will you arrive in the capital?
I will send someone to welcome you."
The ghost then told the exact time of departure,
and also requested food.
Zǐyán ordered food to be served,
and they talked and laughed as before while seated.
When the time came,
the funeral procession indeed arrived.
Zǐyán summoned the creditors for him,
and repaid the debts.
The ghost also came morning and evening to express gratitude,
his words very sincere,
and after more than a month, he ceased.
Zǐyán did not mind it either.
Several decades later,
Zǐyán also died.
Liú Zǐgòng
Liú Zǐgòng, a man from Jīngběi,
on the twenty-second day of the fifth month,
died from a feverish illness.
The next day, he revived,
and said he had been taken to the underworld court,
with nineteen others passing through together.
The official summoned two people out,
bound their heads with wood,
and added iron nails,
ordering them to be confined,
saying:
"These two have heavy crimes,
they shall stay,
the rest may be released for now."
He also led Zǐgòng to tour various prisons,
but there were only empty walls forming several dozen compounds,
with no people visible.
Zǐgòng asked:
"What place is this?"
The person said:
"These are all hells.
Because the King of Tóngguāng is being born,
the punishment of sinners is suspended for seven days,
so those suffering here have a temporary pause.
If the drums were to sound,
the sinners would suffer,
and it would be shocking to see and hear."
Zǐgòng had married the daughter of Sū Yuánzōng, the Magistrate of Nánjiāng County,
and saw Yuánzōng on the road,
asking him:
"Father-in-law, you did good deeds in life,
why are you here?"
Yuánzōng said:
"I had faults in my previous life,
so I am detained.
But matters are now settled,
and I will soon be reborn in heaven,
it won't be long."
He also asked:
"Where are your two sons who died earlier?"
"The elder was honest and trustworthy,
so after death, he was reborn in heaven;
the younger was cruel and murderous,
and is now in hell."
He also met his neighbor Lǐ Wěi,
Wěi said:
"Please relay a message to my son,
I am detained for crimes from before,
and am heavily confined.
If he makes one statue of Guānshìyīn Bodhisattva for me,
and copies one volume of the 'Miàofǎ Liánhuā Jīng',
then I can be reborn in heaven."
He also met his father Liú Shèn,
Shèn said:
"Because the King of Tóngguāng is being born,
I am temporarily allowed outside.
Otherwise,
I suffer punishment daily,
the pain is indescribable.
Because I shot and killed birds and beasts,
every day the ox-headed jailers,
heat thousands of iron pellets,
their color like fire,
break hundreds of openings in my skin,
and insert the hot pellets inside.
The agony is unbearable."
He also saw that many of the living had become ghosts.
Zǐgòng revived on the twenty-third day,
lived for seven days,
and on the twenty-ninth day died again,
and did not come back to life.
Liú Píng
During the Xiántōng era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a Doctor of the Five Classics named Lú Jiǎ,
who had attained the methods of immortality and self-cultivation.
He claimed to have been born in the Suí dynasty,
and senior officials of the former court
all said they had seen him in their childhood.
Generation after generation served him,
yet his lifespan never ended.
During the Ān-Shǐ Rebellion,
he hid in the Zhōngnán Mountains.
Afterward, he sometimes emerged and sometimes remained in seclusion.
Lìnghú Táo advised him with the affairs of the Zhùxià and Qīyuán,
and he gradually took up an official post in the capital.
He often said he was on good terms with the recluse Liú Píng.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Liú Píng lived in Qílǔ.
He was especially skilled in the art of breathing exercises,
able to see in the dark
without the aid of lamps or candles.
When Ān Lùshān was in Fànyáng,
he sent generous gifts to Liú Píng’s door.
Liú Píng saw that around Ān Lùshān,
there were always several dozen ghostly creatures,
of strange forms and bizarre appearances,
holding censers and canopies,
serving as his guides and attendants.
Liú Píng found this peculiar,
and thought Ān Lùshān must be an extraordinary man.
When Ān Lùshān went to court for an audience,
Liú Píng accompanied him to Huàyīn County.
They happened upon Yè Fǎshàn performing the "casting the dragon" ritual at the Western Peak.
Liú Píng then saw two blue-clad youths
arriving through the air.
The so-called ghostly creatures of Ān Lùshān
all dropped their censers and canopies
and fled in panic.
Liú Píng thus realized that Ān Lùshān was aided by evil beings,
and would surely not end well through righteous means.
When Ān Lùshān returned to Fànyáng,
Liú Píng fled into Mount Huà and went into hiding.
Xiāo Yǐngshì
Xiāo Yǐngshì of Lánlíng
served as the Registrar of Yángzhōu.
After his term ended, he traveled south.
While crossing the Guāzhōu ferry,
there were two young men in the boat
who stared intently at Yǐngshì,
looked at each other, and said:
"This person greatly resembles the Loyal and Illustrious Prince of Póyáng."
Yǐngshì was indeed the great-grandson of the Prince of Póyáng.
He then introduced himself,
and the two youths said:
"We have known your ancestor for a long time."
Yǐngshì, being in a crowded place,
did not dare to inquire further.
When they reached the shore,
just as he was about to question them,
the two youths suddenly hurried away carrying their burdens.
Yǐngshì was certain they were either spirits or immortals,
and simply revered them in his heart.
The following year,
when Yǐngshì was returning,
upon reaching Xūyí,
he was sitting with the county magistrate behind lowered blinds during the day,
when a clerk reported:
"We have captured six grave robbers."
The magistrate ordered them brought in.
They were tightly bound
and lined up in the courtyard.
The two youths were among them,
to Yǐngshì’s great astonishment.
He then recounted the previous events in detail.
The magistrate immediately ordered the two youths to be interrogated first.
Shortly after, they confessed,
and the evidence was clear.
They all admitted to having robbed graves for years.
They had once opened the tomb of the Prince of Póyáng,
and obtained a great deal of gold and jade.
At the entrance lay a nobleman,
whose complexion was as if alive,
around fifty years old,
with graying hair and beard,
lying stiff on a stone couch.
His appearance and posture were exactly like Yǐngshì’s,
with not the slightest difference.
When they met on the boat before,
and learned he was of the Xiāo clan,
they knew he was indeed a descendant of the Prince of Póyáng.
How could there be any other explanation?
The Visitor of Líyáng
During the Kāiyuán era,
there was a scholar whose family was poor.
He went to beg in Héshuò,
but wherever he arrived, no one responded.
He then turned to Líyáng,
and as the day was already dusk,
the road ahead was still far.
Suddenly, he saw a gate beside the road,
with a mansion that was very grand.
As night approached, he sought lodging.
He then went forward and knocked on the door.
After a long while,
a servant finally came out.
The guest said:
"It is dusk,
and I cannot reach the road ahead.
May I lodge in your outer quarters,
is that permissible?"
The servant said:
"Let me inform the young master."
He then went in.
After a moment, the sound of dragging shoes was heard.
When he came out,
he was a handsome man in fine attire,
with a graceful and distant demeanor,
lofty and exceptionally refined.
He ordered the guest to be invited in,
and they exchanged greetings.
He said:
"Your journey must have been arduous.
I have a humble dwelling,
unworthy of troubling a distinguished guest."
The guest secretly found this strange,
and wanting to observe closely,
he went together to the lodging.
The host was quite capable of elegant conversation,
speaking of events since the Qí and Zhōu dynasties,
all as clear as if he had witnessed them himself.
The guest asked his name.
He said:
"I am Xún Jìhé of Yǐngchuān.
My ancestors, because of official duties,
came to reside here."
He ordered wine and food to be set out,
all exquisite and clean,
but not particularly flavorful.
After a while,
he ordered a bed to be prepared in the house.
He invited the guest in,
and then commanded a maidservant to attend overnight.
The guest waited until the maidservant was intimate,
and then asked:
"What office does the young master now hold?"
She said:
"He is currently the registrar for the River Lord.
Be careful not to speak of it."
Soon, they heard outside the sound of someone crying out in pain.
He secretly peeked through the window.
He saw the host sitting on a folding chair,
with rows of lamps and candles.
Before him was a person,
with disheveled hair and naked body,
and on the left and right, groups of birds were summoned to peck at his eyes,
causing blood to flow to the ground.
The host, with a very angry expression, said:
"Do you dare to offend me again?"
The guest asked:
"Who is this person?"
She said:
"Why must you insist on knowing other matters?"
He pressed the question firmly.
She said:
"He is the magistrate of Líyáng.
He enjoys archery and hunting,
and repeatedly chased animals,
violating my walls.
For this, he is being punished."
The guest secretly noted this.
The next morning, looking around,
it was actually a large tomb.
He asked ahead,
and people said it was the tomb of Prefect Xún.
Arriving at Líyáng,
the magistrate indeed excused himself due to an eye ailment.
The guest said:
"I can cure it."
The magistrate was pleased,
and summoned him in.
The guest explained everything in detail.
The magistrate said:
"I believe it."
He then secretly ordered the village head,
to prepare tens of thousands of bundles of firewood,
and pile them beside the wall.
One day,
the magistrate led a group of officials,
set fire and burned it,
thus altering the tomb.
His eyes immediately healed.
He richly rewarded the guest but did not inform him.
Later, when the guest returned to that place,
he saw a person with a scorched and ruined head and face,
wearing tattered clothes,
crouching among the brambles.
He went straight forward to approach,
but the guest did not recognize him.
He said:
"Do you remember lodging with me before?"
The guest was startled and said:
"How did you come to this?"
He said:
"I was tormented by the magistrate before,
but I also know it was not your original intent.
It is just my own fate running out."
The guest felt very ashamed and regretful.
He prepared a modest libation,
and burned his old clothes to give to him.
The ghost gladly accepted and then left.
Minister Lǐ Jiǒngxiù
had long been close friends with the monk Língzhēn of Qīngchán Temple.
Several years after Lǐ Jiǒngxiù's death,
Língzhēn suddenly saw two officials,
bearing a summons to pursue him.
They then hurried him onto the road,
and he abruptly died.
Arriving at a place ahead,
it seemed like an official bureau.
After a moment, he was invited for an audience.
A person in red robes with a silver seal
made Língzhēn doubt that his life should not yet be over.
The red-robed one said:
"My subordinate mistakenly pursued you.
You, Ācārya, should return."
He ordered the previous officials to escort him back.
Wanting to take the old road,
the officials said:
"This road cannot be taken.
You must take a different northern route."
So they went separately northward.
The road was very desolate and blocked,
and Língzhēn was quite displeased.
After traveling several tens of lǐ,
they arrived at another prefectural city,
which was very beautiful.
The gate officials came forward and shouted:
"You may conveniently see the general."
He was then led in,
and saw a person in purple robes,
sitting in the hall.
His age and appearance resembled Lǐ Gōng.
He said:
"How did you come so far, Zhēn Gōng?"
Língzhēn then knew it was indeed him.
He was invited to ascend the steps,
and they reminisced about old times.
At parting, holding hands, he said:
"I wish to discuss family matters with you, Ācārya,
but I cannot bear to speak of them."
He then suddenly shed tears.
Língzhēn insisted on asking.
He then said:
"My descendants' bloodline is about to be cut off,
and there is nothing more to be done.
Please inform Jìyǒu and the others
to offer sacrifices in the four seasons,
diligently ensuring they are abundant and pure.
Also, copy one volume of the Lotus Sutra for me.
That is my hope."
He then wiped his tears and bid farewell.
Língzhēn then revived,
and fully reported what he had seen.
The sons and Jìyǒu,
who had always been filial by nature,
held a vegetarian feast and copied the sutra.
Only Jiǎn Sǔn angrily said:
"This deceitful monk fabricates tales,
wanting to slander and defile our ancestors' spirits!"
Later, he indeed conspired with Quán Liángshān and others to rebel and was executed.
His brothers were exiled,
and ultimately, there were no descendants left.
Lángyé people
A man from Lángyé was traveling past Rènchéng,
and as dusk fell, he lodged outside the city walls.
The host greeted him with great delight,
and set out various fruits for him.
The guest took out a small knife with a rhinoceros-horn handle from his bosom,
intending to cut a pear with it.
The host’s countenance suddenly changed,
and he abruptly passed away.
What the guest had seen was actually an object from a grave.
The guest was terrified,
but he used this knife to protect himself.
Looking around, he saw a hole beside the grave,
and the sunlight shining into it was quite bright.
Inside, he saw that the coffin had already decayed,
and the fruit platter was actually filled with tree leaves.
The guest crawled out of the hole.
He asked the people nearby,
but no one recognized whose grave this was.
Cuī Xián
Cuī Xián of Bólíng
had practiced meditation since youth
and lived in Xiàngzhōu,
where he often tended to his garden.
One day, while alone in his study,
after a night of thunder and rain,
a young woman suddenly appeared,
about sixteen or seventeen years old,
who climbed over the wall and entered.
Cuī Xián embraced her and brought her into his room.
He asked where she came from,
but she remained silent.
Suspecting she was a runaway,
he hid her away.
As dawn approached, she died.
Cuī Xián was shocked and frightened,
and did not dare to reveal the matter.
He went out into the village,
and inquired about any family that had lost a daughter.
Shortly after,
six or seven maidservants appeared,
dressed in mourning clothes and speaking as they walked,
as if searching for something.
They said to one another:
“Even the dead can wander off,
let alone the living?”
Cuī Xián approached and asked them,
and they replied:
“Why does the gentleman ask?”
He pressed them further,
and they said:
“Our young lady
passed away three days ago.
Last night, just after she was encoffined,
she was struck by thunder,
and her corpse rose and left,
suddenly disappearing without a trace.”
Cuī Xián asked about her appearance and clothing,
which matched the runaway from the previous night.
He then described what had happened the night before.
He led them to his home to verify,
and indeed it was her corpse,
with her clothes and shoes all muddy.
Her family was greatly astonished.
They prepared to take her back for burial,
but the corpse was too heavy to move.
Cuī Xián then offered wine and prayed to her,
after which they were able to leave.
This happened in the sixth month of the first year of the Tiānbǎo era.
Jì Yōu
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
Jì Yōu, a registrar of Kuàijī,
had two daughters,
and also brought his orphaned niece with him to his post.
Whenever someone sought marriage,
he would marry off his own daughters,
but after his own daughters were all married, he still neglected his niece.
The niece resented this,
and died of pent-up anger.
She was buried in the eastern suburbs.
Several months later,
a market clerk surnamed Yáng, who served under the registrar,
a son of a prominent family,
quite wealthy,
and handsome in appearance,
suddenly went missing from his home.
They searched for him but could not find him.
Suspecting he had been bewitched by a ghost,
they went to the graves to look for him.
At the time, there was heavy snow,
and a skirt was seen protruding from the girl’s burial chamber.
The clerk’s family pulled on it,
and heard the clerk’s cries from inside the chamber.
The burial chamber was intact,
and they did not know how he had entered.
They hurriedly reported to the registrar,
who ordered the coffin opened.
Inside the coffin, the girl was lying
together with the clerk,
and her appearance was as if she were alive.
The clerk’s family took him out,
and repaired the burial chamber.
After being brought out, the clerk seemed dazed,
and only recovered after several days.
The girl then spoke from below,
addressing the registrar:
“I resented my uncle for not marrying me off,
caring only for his own daughters,
and forgetting about me,
so I died of pent-up anger.
Now the divine will has arranged for me to marry the market clerk,
so I drew him in to share my bed.
Since this town already knows of this,
it is proper that I be married.
On the first day of next month,
the marriage should take place.
I hope my uncle will not look down on him as a mere clerk
and defy the divine will.
Please inform him immediately,
accept his betrothal gifts,
and treat him as a son-in-law.
On the first day of the month,
prepare food and drink,
and I will welcome Yáng Láng.
I hope my request will be granted.”
The registrar was astonished and sighed,
and summoned the clerk to inquire.
It was Clerk Yáng,
So he accepted tens of thousands in cash,
and both families gathered.
Jì Yōu then prepared clothing, curtains, and bedding for his niece.
On the first day of the month,
he prepared a grand feast.
The ghost of the Yáng girl spoke again:
“I am overjoyed
that you have granted me permission to marry,
and today I have come personally to welcome Yáng Láng.”
As soon as she finished speaking,
the clerk suddenly died.
A wedding banquet was held,
and he was encoffined with great care,
then buried together with her in the eastern suburbs.
Old Man Tián of Wǔdé County
In Wǔdé County, in the village of Jiǔfēng, there was an old farmer.
One evening,
he was heading south to Hénèi Prefecture
to attend a ceremonial event at his daughter’s home.
As he left the village,
two men followed him.
They spoke with the old man,
saying to him:
“We are going north of Hénán Prefecture,
and we are glad to have you, old sir, as a companion.”
When they reached the road, the two men refused to leave.
The old man, seeing that they were not ordinary,
dismounted from his donkey and said to them:
“You and I are not old acquaintances;
we have merely met on the road.
I observe your gestures and glances—
you are not good men.
You go on ahead;
I will head south from here.
If you follow me,
I will simply turn back;
I cannot travel with you.”
The two men said:
“We admire the virtue of the old father,
and that is why we are accompanying you.
If you do not wish to go together,
we will depart from here.
Why are you angry, old sir?”
Just as they were exchanging words,
it happened that a neighbor’s son of the old farmer
came from the east.
He asked the old man what was happening,
and the old man told him everything.
The neighbor’s son said to the two men:
“The old father does not wish to go with you.
You may go east,
while the old father goes south.
Why must you detain him?”
The two men said:
“Very well.”
They then went east,
and the old man proceeded south.
The neighbor’s son also returned west.
Not long after arriving home,
he heard the old man’s family crying out in alarm.
The neighbor’s son asked what had happened.
The old man’s son said:
“My father went to my sister’s home;
he should have just arrived by now.
Yet the donkey he was riding has returned alone—
what does this mean?”
The neighbor’s son then told him about the two men the old farmer had encountered,
and together with the old man’s son, they went to search for him.
When they reached the place where he had spoken with the two men,
they found the old man dead in a ditch,
yet his clothes were completely intact,
with no signs of injury.
They then realized that the two men were ghosts who had taken the old man’s life.
Péi Huī
Péi Huī of Hédōng
was the nephew of Péi Huí, the magistrate of Hénán.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he once walked alone by the side of a manor
and on the road saw a woman
of exceptional beauty,
radiant and alluring.
He gazed at her for a long time.
Péi Huī asked:
“Why are you walking alone?”
She replied:
“My maidservants went on a small errand,
but they are delayed and have not returned,
so I came out to wait for them.”
Péi Huī, being quick-witted,
flirted with her using charming words.
At first, the woman showed no change in expression,
but after several exchanges of banter,
they arrived at her home,
and she invited Péi Huī inside.
The house was grand and splendid.
After entering,
he heard an old maidservant angrily say:
“Why have you brought a stranger here, young lady?
How could such a thing happen within the bounds of propriety?”
The young lady explained that there was a distinguished guest at the door,
and many family members came to inquire.
After a while, the old maidservant came out
and saw him.
Péi Huī apologized,
and his demeanor showed the bearing of a refined scholar.
Shortly after,
lamps were lit and curtains drawn,
and he was invited to sit.
Several attendants served him,
each of them beautiful,
their fragrance sweet and rich,
and their movements graceful and composed.
Soon, the young lady was summoned to come out, and it was announced:
“Why must you avoid me, Master Péi?”
The woman came out,
but did not go back in.
Péi Huī secretly observed that the room was very lively,
decorated with embroidered curtains and brocade cushions,
as if preparing for a wedding.
He alone felt delighted and wished to stay.
But then he felt bloated
and got up to go
to the latrine.
He carried an ancient sword with him,
which could ward off evil.
After finishing at the latrine,
he took the sword to tear
some paper.
Suddenly, he saw the sword gleam brilliantly.
Grasping it, he turned to go back,
but the house and the people were no longer there.
Looking around, he found himself on a lonely grave amid thick brambles.
He then cried out loudly.
His family recognized Péi Huī’s voice
and came with torches to search for him.
About a hundred paces from the manor,
he stood staring, unable to speak,
and only after a long time did he come to his senses.
Lǐ Táo
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Lǐ Táo of Lǒngxī
was residing in Xīnzhèng.
He was often sleeping in his room,
when someone shook him in his sleep.
Lǐ Táo awoke in alarm,
and saw a maid in robes and trousers,
with a very beautiful appearance.
Lǐ Táo asked:
"How did you suddenly get here?"
The maid said:
"The young lady Zhèng wishes to visit you."
After a moment,
an extraordinary fragrance filled the air,
and a beautiful woman emerged from the northwest corner of the wall,
arriving at the bedside and bowing twice.
Lǐ Táo knew she was a ghost,
and at first did not speak to her.
The woman, ashamed, retreated.
The maid scolded him several times, saying:
"You country bumpkin,
is this how you treat people?
You have made my young lady immeasurably ashamed."
Lǐ Táo was pleased by her beauty,
and also found it strange in his heart,
so he deceitfully said:
"Where is the young lady?
I originally did not see her,
please call her again."
The maid said, "Come."
She also said:
"The young lady values your past connection,
and will come again.
If she suddenly appears as before,
you should be attentive."
When she arrived,
Lǐ Táo got off the bed to show respect,
invited her to sit opposite him,
and soon they grew close.
The young lady's appearance was peerless,
and Lǐ Táo was deeply pleased with her,
staying together for over ten days.
Lǐ Táo's mother personally came to spy,
repeatedly sending attendants to call Lǐ Táo.
Lǐ Táo, fearing it would hinder his will,
ultimately did not go out.
The woman said:
"Your mother is summoning you,
why do you not go?
Wouldn't that bring blame upon me?"
Lǐ Táo then went to his mother.
His mother, weeping, said to Lǐ Táo:
"You are to continue the family line,
yet you have a ghost wife?"
Lǐ Táo said he would change.
From then on, he lingered,
and did not leave for half a year.
Afterwards, Lǐ Táo went to participate in the selection for office,
heading to the capital.
He left the woman in the room.
Later, Lǐ Táo fell critically ill.
The ghost woman in the room
said to her maid:
"Lǐ Láng is now gravely ill,
what should we do?
We should go together to visit him."
When they reached Tóngguān,
they were stopped by the ghost border officials,
and could not pass for several days.
It happened that Lǐ Táo's elder cousin was also going to the capital for the selection and entered the pass.
The ghost
was able to follow and pass through.
That evening,
she reached Lǐ Táo's place,
and they met joyfully.
Lǐ Táo asked:
"How did you get here?"
She said:
"Seeing you were very ill,
I came to see you."
She had brought medicine with her,
and mixed it to give to Lǐ Táo to drink.
Lǐ Táo's illness soon healed.
That year, he was selected for the position of Línjīn Deputy,
and returned home with the woman.
After several days,
he was about to take up his post.
The ghost declined to go,
and when asked the reason,
she said:
"Our shared connection is exhausted,
I cannot go again."
They parted sorrowfully,
and from then on it ended.
The Daughter of the Lù Family of Chángzhōu
A certain Deputy Magistrate Lù of Chángzhōu County,
whose family was always poor.
On the third day of the third month,
the whole family went to visit Hǔqiū Temple.
The daughter, aged fifteen or sixteen,
because she had no proper clothes, could not go,
and stayed alone with one maid to watch the house.
After her parents had left,
she sighed with emotion and threw herself into a well and died.
Her parents were deeply affected by this,
wept sorrowfully for several days,
and then temporarily buried her in Chángzhōu County.
About a year later,
there was a certain Mr. Lù,
who had visited his aunt.
His aunt's home was near the girl's burial place,
Passing by the burial chamber,
a young maid followed him,
saying:
"The young lady wishes to see you briefly."
Mr. Lù had no choice,
and followed her to her home.
The house gate was low and small.
The young lady was beautifully adorned,
with a gentle and lovely appearance.
She asked:
"Are you not a commoner of Chángzhōu?
I am the daughter of Deputy Magistrate Lù,
not a human,
but a ghost.
I wish to ask you to relay a message to the Assistant Magistrate.
Now, Líndùn's Lǐ Shíbā is seeking marriage.
I am an unmarried maiden,
and it is improper for me to arrange my own marriage.
Please tell my parents:
if they consent to the marriage,
I will send word here.
That person is still staying in the burial chamber."
A short while later,
the local ward head,
passing by the burial chamber,
saw clothing belts hanging outside.
Looking inside,
he saw a woman.
He reported it to the Deputy Magistrate.
The Deputy Magistrate went himself,
had the wall opened to retrieve Mr. Lù,
and placed him in the main hall.
After several days, he could speak.
Asked how he got there,
Mr. Lù replied with the girl's words.
The Deputy Magistrate sighed.
Soon, he sent someone to inquire about Líndùn's Lǐ Shíbā.
Indeed, there was such a person,
and he was safe and sound as usual.
At first, he did not believe it,
but after several days he fell ill,
and after being ill for several days, he died.
The whole family sighed with regret,
and eventually married the girl to Lǐ's son in a ghost marriage.
Diāo Miǎn
Diāo Miǎn, Governor of Xuānchéng,
originally advanced through military service.
Initially serving as Commander of the Yùmén Army,
the form of a toilet god appeared outside the stable.
Its form was like a large pig,
covered all over with eyes,
moving in and out of the latrine,
wandering within the courtyard.
Diāo Miǎn was not present at the time,
and over a thousand officials, clerks, and soldiers saw it.
This went on for several days.
When Diāo Miǎn returned,
he made offerings to pray for blessings,
and the toilet god then vanished.
Within ten days, Diāo Miǎn was promoted to Prefect of Yīzhōu,
and then changed to Left Guard Commander, Right Valiant Guard General, Left Imperial Guard General,
and thus became esteemed.
Wáng Wúyǒu
Wáng Wúyǒu, the Registrar of Chǔqiū,
had recently married
a beautiful but jealous wife.
When Wúyǒu fell ill
and needed to go to the latrine,
he found it difficult to go alone
and wanted a maidservant to accompany him,
but his wife refused.
When Wúyǒu reached the latrine,
through a hole in the wall,
he saw a person sitting with their back to him,
dark-skinned and robust.
Wúyǒu thought it was a laborer
and did not find it strange.
After a moment,
this person turned to look back,
with deep-set eyes and a huge nose,
a tiger-like mouth and bird-like claws.
He said to Wúyǒu:
"Why not give me your shoes?"
Wúyǒu was startled,
and before he could respond,
the creature reached out from the hole,
directly took his shoes,
and chewed on them.
Blood appeared in the shoes,
as if it were eating meat,
and it finished them off.
Wúyǒu was terrified
and first told his wife,
reproaching her:
"I was ill and went to the latrine;
even if I had a maidservant accompany me,
you firmly refused.
Now I've indeed encountered a monster—
what can be done?"
His wife still did not believe him,
so they went together to see.
As Wúyǒu sat in the latrine,
the creature appeared again,
seizing his remaining shoe.
It chewed on it,
and his wife, now frightened,
helped Wúyǒu return.
Another day,
when Wúyǒu went to the backyard,
the creature appeared again,
saying to Wúyǒu:
"I'll return your shoes."
It then threw them beside him,
and the shoes were completely undamaged.
Wúyǒu asked a shaman to perform an exorcism,
and the ghost said to the shaman:
"Registrar Wáng's official fortune has ended;
he has only a hundred days of life left.
If he does not return home quickly,
he will die here."
Wúyǒu then returned to his hometown
and died as predicted.
Wáng Shēng
Lù Wàng of Wújùn
was residing in Hénèi.
His cousin Wáng Shēng
lived nearby.
One morning, while visiting Wàng,
Shēng passed by the fence of the former villager Yáng Kǎn's house south of the village
and suddenly saw a creature.
It was squatting in the latrine with both hands,
with large ears and deep-set eyes,
a tiger-like nose and boar-like teeth,
its face purple and mottled.
It stared directly at Shēng,
who fled in fear.
He told Wàng about it,
and Wàng said:
"I've heard that anyone who sees the latrine spirit dies immediately.
You must prepare yourself."
Shēng felt extremely ill at ease,
and upon returning, he died.
Gāo Shēng
During the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a man from Bóhǎi named Gāo,
whose given name is lost.
He suffered from a fever and emaciation,
with unbearable pain in his chest.
He summoned a doctor to examine him,
and the doctor said:
"There is a ghost in your chest;
medicine can reach it."
So he brewed medicine and drank it,
suddenly feeling movement in the darkness.
After a while,
he vomited over a dou of saliva,
which had solidified and could not be dissolved.
He cut it open with a knife,
and a person emerged from the saliva.
At first, it was tiny,
but soon grew several feet tall.
Gāo wanted to torment it,
but the person hurried out
and disappeared down the steps.
From then on, his illness was cured.
Yáng Zhǔn
In the Táng dynasty, Yáng Zhǔn,
a man from Sòngchéng,
belonged to a scholarly and renowned family.
While traveling in the countryside,
he saw a woman
of exceptional beauty.
Zhǔn flirted with her
and had a tryst with her in the wild.
After over a month,
she often came to his study
and asked to take Zhǔn away.
Zhǔn refused to follow,
but suddenly felt unbearable heart pain.
He then said:
"If it must be so,
I will go with you.
Why must you torment me like this?"
His illness then healed,
and he followed the woman for over ten lǐ.
They arrived at a house,
with clear courtyards and buildings,
but the doors were low and small.
The woman prepared food for Zhǔn,
and each time he lifted his bowl, he emptied it.
He found it strange,
but still did not know she was a ghost.
He only realized it later.
Every time Zhǔn left,
he would close the door to his room,
and his corpse would lie on the bed,
taking six or seven days to revive.
This went on for two or three years.
Zhǔn's elder brother said to him:
"As a son,
you should continue the family line.
How can you suddenly pair up with a ghost?"
Zhǔn felt ashamed and afraid,
so he left home and donned monastic robes.
The ghost then stopped coming.
Later, Zhǔn returned to secular clothing.
He was appointed as a county lieutenant
and married a woman from a good family.
A year later,
while handling documents in the office,
he suddenly saw the woman enter through the door,
her face filled with anger.
Zhǔn panicked
and begged for his life at the foot of the steps.
The woman said:
"There is no way I will spare you."
She fiercely attacked him,
and Zhǔn fell ill and died.
Wáng Yǐ
In Línrǔ Commandery, there was an official canal shop.
About half a li north of the shop was the estate of a certain Lǐ family, where a man named Wáng Yǐ,
while on his way to the market,
passed by the estate gate.
From a distance, he saw a girl about fifteen or sixteen years old,
who looked at him with delight,
and sent her maidservant to convey a message.
Yǐ lingered under the shade of a pagoda tree,
until dusk fell.
He then went to the estate to ask for lodging.
The host greeted him with great joy,
and provided generous hospitality.
After the second watch,
the maidservant came and said:
"The night is still not deep,
you should keep a candle lit and wait."
The girl arrived not long after,
and they expressed their affection for each other,
completing the affair.
Suddenly, the girl fell silent and seemed ill.
Yǐ said:
"We were originally strangers,
yet I am fortunate to have been invited by you.
Now that we have shared our lives,
our bond is extremely profound.
What is troubling you?"
The girl said:
"It is not that I am not wholehearted,
but just now, when I left, the door was locked,
so I came by climbing over the wall.
At the corner of the wall, there was an iron rake,
its teeth pierced my foot,
the pain penetrated to my heart,
and it is unbearable."
She then showed him her foot.
After speaking, she bid farewell to return,
saying:
"I am surely going to die.
If you have any affection for me,
when you return someday, please visit,
to comfort my lonely soul."
Later, when Yǐ obtained an official post and returned east,
passing by the Lǐ family estate on the way,
he heard that the girl had already died.
Secretly, he took wine and food with the maidservant to offer sacrifices outside the burial chamber,
and there he wept bitterly.
In a moment,
he saw the girl emerge from the burial chamber.
Yǐ then fell to the ground and died.
The maidservant saw Yǐ's spirit enter the burial chamber together with the girl.
The two families arranged a posthumous marriage for them.
Wéi Lì
Wéi Lì,
during the Tiānbǎo era, served as the deputy magistrate of Xīngàn.
He had a young daughter over ten years old.
When he was about to take up his post,
traveling to Yángzhōu,
his daughter said to
Lì,
that she wanted to buy a lacquer-backed, gold-flowered mirror.
Lì said:
"My journey to take up office is difficult,
how can I afford such a thing?
Wait until I assume my post, and I will get one for you."
Over a year later, the daughter died,
and Lì also forgot about the earlier matter.
When his term ended,
he carried the coffin north to return home.
Arriving in Yángzhōu,
he moored the boat by the riverbank.
The daughter, accompanied by a maidservant, took money to buy a mirror.
Passersby saw her appearance was very beautiful,
and her demeanor like that of a noble family's daughter,
so they competed to sell to her.
There was a young man in his twenties,
fair-skinned and pleasing,
the daughter gave him over five thousand copper coins for it,
the young man gave her a lacquer-backed, gold-flowered mirror,
over a foot in diameter.
Another person said:
"I have a mirror better than this,
and I only ask for three thousand."
The young man then reduced the price by two thousand.
The daughter thus lingered.
Their expressions and spirits connected,
After a while, she bid farewell and left.
The young man, with lustful intentions toward her,
had someone follow her,
to see where she lived.
In a moment, they arrived at a shop,
but only found three strings of yellow paper,
the young man took them to Lì's boat,
and said:
"Just now, a young lady took money to buy a mirror,
and entered this boat.
Now it has turned into paper money."
Lì said:
"I only have one daughter,
who died several years ago.
The one you saw,
what did she look like?"
The young man described her clothing, appearance, and looks in detail,
and Lì and his wife wept for her.
Their daughter was exactly like that.
They then led the young man into the boat to search,
but initially found nothing.
The mother had cut nine strings of yellow paper,
placed on the table beside the coffin,
upon checking, they were missing,
three strings.
Everyone found it very strange,
so they opened the coffin again,
and saw the mirror inside.
No one could help but sigh in sorrow.
The young man said:
"Let's not discuss the money anymore."
He explained his original intention,
and additionally donated ten thousand coins,
to hold a vegetarian feast for the daughter.
Deputy Prefect Liú of Héjiān
Deputy Prefect Liú of Héjiān
often said:
"If there were no women in the world,
how could one find contentment?"
Later, when he arrived at Tōnghuà Gate in the Western Capital,
he saw a woman of great beauty in a carriage,
his heart was filled with fondness and delight,
so he followed her to her residence,
located in the winding lanes behind Zīshèng Temple.
The woman kept him for several nights,
and both were thoroughly pleased.
Liú did not notice anything unusual,
but in the middle of the night, it was extremely cold,
despite multiple layers of mattresses and quilts piled heavily,
yet his body still did not warm up.
He secretly found it strange.
Later, one day, as dawn approached,
suddenly, the woman and the house vanished,
and he found himself lying in a desolate garden under several layers of scattered leaves.
Because of this, he contracted a chronic illness.
Wáng Xuánzhī
Gāomì Wáng Xuánzhī,
in his youth was handsome and elegant,
served as the assistant magistrate of Qíchūn,
and upon completing his term returned to his hometown,
where his home was located west of the city walls.
One evening, he was leaning by the gate when
he saw a woman approaching from the west,
about to enter the city.
Her beauty was extraordinary,
and she appeared to be around eighteen or nineteen years old.
The next day, he saw her again when he went out,
and this happened several times,
with her always arriving at dusk.
Wáng teased her and asked:
"Where is your home?
Why do you come here at dusk?"
The woman smiled and replied:
"My home is near Nángāng,
and I have matters that require me to come to the city."
Wáng tested her with flirtatious words,
and the woman responded cheerfully.
Thus, she stayed overnight,
and they grew very close and intimate.
The next morning, she bid farewell and left.
She would come every few nights,
and later she came to stay every night.
Wáng's affection for her grew deep,
and he tested her by saying:
"Since your home is nearby,
may I visit you there?"
She replied:
"My home is very small and humble,
unfit for hosting guests.
Moreover, I live with my deceased brother's daughter,
so it would be improper to invite you."
Wáng believed her,
and his fondness for her grew even stronger.
She was exceptionally skilled at needlework,
and all of Wáng's clothes
were tailored by her,
drawing admiration from all who saw them.
She had a maidservant by her side,
who was also beautiful,
and often followed behind her.
Even during the day,
the maidservant never left.
Wáng asked:
"Won't your brother's daughter miss you?"
She replied:
"Why must you meddle in others' affairs?"
A year passed in this manner,
and one night she suddenly arrived,
looking very unhappy,
and only wept.
Wáng asked her about it,
and she said:
"I have received your love and care,
but now I must leave.
What can I do?"
She sobbed uncontrollably,
and Wáng, alarmed, asked for the reason.
The woman said:
"Will you find it difficult to accept?
I was originally the daughter of the former magistrate of Gāomì,
married to a man named Rén.
Rén was unfaithful and treated me poorly,
so my parents took pity on me
and called me back home.
Later, I fell ill and passed away,
and was buried here.
Now my family is coming to retrieve my remains,
and I must leave tomorrow."
Wáng, who loved her deeply,
felt no aversion or fear.
Instead, he was filled with sorrow and regret.
He asked what time she would depart the next day,
and she replied:
"At dusk."
They spent the night talking and bidding farewell, unable to sleep.
The next day, as they parted,
the woman left him a gold-threaded jade cup and a pair of jade rings as gifts.
Wáng gave her an embroidered robe in return,
and they held hands, shedding tears as they said goodbye.
The next day, at the appointed time,
Wáng went to Nángāng to watch,
and indeed, her family had come to retrieve the remains.
When the coffin was opened,
the woman's complexion remained unchanged,
and her makeup was as before.
Inside the coffin, they found a chest of embroidered robes,
but the gold cup and jade rings she had given were missing.
Her family began to realize something was unusual.
Wáng then stepped forward and explained everything,
showing them the jade cup and rings.
They all held them and wept sorrowfully.
Wáng asked:
"Who is the brother's daughter?"
They replied:
"She is the second son's daughter in the family,
who died of illness at the age of ten,
and was buried beside her."
The maidservant was also a wooden figure from the burial tent,
and her appearance closely resembled that of the woman's attendant.
Wáng approached the coffin, wept sorrowfully, and bid farewell,
and all those present were moved and grieved.
Later, as he thought of her,
he became distraught and fell ill,
recovering only after several days.
Yet, whenever he remembered her, he would forget to eat and sleep.
Zhèng Démào
Zhèng Démào of Xíngyáng,
once riding alone on horseback,
encountered a maidservant,
whose appearance was exceptionally beautiful.
She bowed before his horse and said:
"Lady Cuī sends her greetings to invite Master Zhèng."
Startled, he replied:
"I have never known Lady Cuī,
and I am not yet married.
Why would she invite me?"
The maidservant said:
"The lady has a young daughter,
who is quite beautiful and graceful.
Moreover, coming from a noble and distinguished family,
she would be a suitable match for you."
Zhèng realized they were not human,
and as he intended to refuse,
over ten attendants in yellow robes and dark headscarves arrived, saying:
"The lady,
urges the young master to proceed."
They then took control of his horse.
Their journey was extremely swift,
and in his ears, he only heard the whistling of the wind.
Suddenly, they arrived at a place,
with towering walls and a grand gate,
outside of which were planted rows of catalpa and paulownia trees.
Zhèng stood outside the gate,
and the maidservant went in first to announce him.
After a short while,
he was ordered to be led inside.
Passing through several gates,
the halls and buildings were magnificent.
The lady, wearing a plum-green silk skirt,
appeared to be around forty years old,
with a lovely and graceful demeanor.
She stood at the foot of the eastern steps.
Eight or nine maidservants attended her,
all dressed in bright and neat attire.
Zhèng hurried forward to bow in reverence.
The lady said:
"Do not be surprised by my invitation.
Given Master Zhèng's noble lineage and exceptional talent,
I wish to entrust my daughter to you in marriage.
My humble daughter is unworthy,
but I hope you will favor her."
Zhèng felt pressured,
unsure how to respond,
and could only murmur in agreement.
The lady then ascended to the main hall.
She ordered Zhèng to be led up from the western steps.
The hall was entirely carpeted with floral-patterned rugs,
with ornate footrests and seven-treasure screens placed on both sides, and golden hinges.
The doors were hung with green silk curtains,
adorned with silver hooks and pearl tassels.
A long banquet table was set with dishes,
all of the utmost richness and elegance.
He was then invited to sit.
The lady was skilled in refined conversation,
discussing matters with a sense of propriety and depth,
unmatched in the mortal world.
After the meal, wine was served,
stored in a silver vessel,
holding over three dou,
with an amber hue,
and poured into engraved cups.
Maidservants served the wine,
which tasted exceptionally sweet and fragrant.
As evening approached,
a maidservant came forward and announced:
"The young lady has finished dressing up."
Zhèng was then led to an outer chamber,
where he bathed in a fragrant soup infused with a hundred scents.
Attendants presented him with robes, hats, shoes, and ornaments.
Ten beautiful maidservants supported him as he entered,
playfully teasing and jesting with him.
From the hall to the chamber,
they walked amidst flowers and candles,
and he was then invited to the bridal chamber.
The young lady was fourteen or fifteen years old,
with a stunningly beautiful appearance,
unlike anything he had ever seen.
Her attire was resplendent and gorgeous,
surpassing all others of the time.
Zhèng was overjoyed,
and the wedding ceremony was completed thereafter.
The next day,
the lady ordered the young lady to accompany Zhèng to the eastern hall,
where a red silk embroidered canopy was set up,
with quilts, mattresses, and cushions,
all exquisitely crafted.
The young lady was skilled at playing the kōnghóu,
with melodies and lyrics that were novel and unique.
Zhèng asked:
"The horse I rode here before the wedding,
where is it now?"
She replied:
"It has already returned."
Over a hundred days passed like this.
Although Zhèng's affection was deep,
he gradually grew suspicious and uneasy.
He thus said to the young lady:
"Can we return together?"
The young lady replied sorrowfully:
"I am fortunate to have met you,
and to serve you as your wife.
However, the realms of the living and the dead are separated by principle,
and I cannot follow you. What can be done?"
Tears streamed down her face.
Realizing the strangeness of the situation,
Zhèng spoke to the lady:
"My family must be worried about my disappearance,
and there may be suspicions and concerns.
I beg you to allow me to return."
The lady said:
"I am deeply grateful for your visit,
and I truly admire you.
However, the realms of the living and the dead are different paths,
and it is only right that we part for now.
At this moment of separation,
how can I hold back my tears?"
Zhèng also wept.
A grand farewell banquet was held,
and as they bid farewell, she said:
"In three years,
we will come to welcome you."
Zhèng bowed and took his leave.
The young lady saw him off at the door,
wiping her tears and holding his hand, saying:
"Though we have a future meeting,
the years ahead will be long.
Our joyful time together has been brief,
but the pain of separation will be prolonged.
Take care of yourself."
Zhèng was also filled with sorrow.
The young lady gave him a red undergarment and a pair of golden hairpins as parting gifts,
saying:
"If you do not forget me,
keep these as mementos."
They then parted ways.
The lady ordered Zhèng to be escorted,
and a blue-dappled horse was brought forward,
equipped with
an exquisite saddle and bridle.
Zhèng mounted the horse and left through the gate.
In an instant, he returned to his home.
His servants said:
"You have been missing from home for a year."
Looking at the gifts he had received,
they were all genuine objects.
His family told him:
"After you left,
your horse returned on its own,
with no one seen escorting it."
Zhèng went to search for the place he had been,
but all he found was a large tomb,
with a smaller grave beside it.
In front of the graves stood trees,
all of which had withered.
Yet what he had seen before
was lush and shaded with flourishing trees.
People nearby said it was the tomb of Lady Cuī and her young son.
Zhèng found this especially strange.
He reckoned that when the three-year deadline arrived,
he would surely die.
Later, when the time came,
he indeed saw the maidservant who had come before, arriving in a carriage to welcome him.
Zhèng said:
"Life and death are predetermined by fate.
If I can find a place of happiness,
what do I have to worry about?"
He then settled all his family affairs,
prepared for his final moments,
and passed away the next day.
Zhū Áo
Zhū Áo, the former Assistant Prefect of Hángzhōu, once lived in seclusion on Shàoshì Mountain in Hénán.
In the early years of the Tiānbǎo era,
Lǐ Shū, the County Captain of Yángzhái, was staying at a temple on the mountain,
and sent a rider to summon Áo.
Áo mounted his horse and galloped off,
with his attendants following behind.
Shortly after, he arrived at the foot of the Shàoyí Temple.
It was the height of summer,
when he saw a girl in a green robe,
about fifteen or sixteen years old,
of exceptional beauty.
Áo thought she was a servant from some household,
but was also surprised that she wore padded clothes in the summer heat.
He rode over and asked her,
but the girl only smiled without answering,
and walked into the temple.
Áo dismounted and followed,
but found no one inside.
He then looked at the paintings on the walls,
and saw the girl in the green robe—
the very one he had encountered on the road.
He sighed in amazement for a long time.
When he reached the temple, he recounted the entire incident,
and Shū and the others were particularly astonished.
That night, after falling asleep,
he dreamed that the girl came to him.
She pulled at his quilt, joyful and pleased,
and his vital essence overflowed with passion.
This happened for several nights in a row.
Wú Yún, a Dàoshi from Sōngyuè, wrote a talisman to ward her off,
but it was ineffective.
Wú then tried to subdue her with his magical arts,
but that also failed.
Another day,
Áo stayed in Dàoshi Chéng's room.
Chéng's practice was pure and serene,
and the spirit did not come.
Later, Áo went to Hénán Prefecture to take the imperial examinations,
and together with Chén Cháwēi, the Magistrate of Wèinán County, he went to visit the Dàoshi Chéng Gǔshén.
Chéng served them yam dishes,
lotus-shaped noodles,
and fresh sesame delicacies.
They lingered, chatting and laughing,
and did not return until dusk.
About five lǐ from Shàoshì,
suddenly dark clouds surged and billowed,
with flashes of fiery lightning within.
In an instant, it grew dim and obscure,
and a torrential rain poured down.
Áo, Cháwēi, and one attendant took shelter under a grove of chestnut trees,
next to a great ravine.
After a long while,
an unusual light appeared,
unlike that of the sun or moon.
Suddenly, within the light, there appeared a vast expanse of pine forests,
and they saw several celestial maidens
holding a dance mat
that stretched for several lǐ in circumference.
They spread it over the pine forest.
Dozens of celestial maidens,
resembling heavenly immortals,
danced upon the mat.
There were also various deities, such as
Guānshìyīn.
The two dances lasted
about half a day.
When the music ended,
several figures resembling performers
rolled up the mat and left.
Then heaven and earth turned dark,
and they could see no one.
Áo and the others groped their way through the night,
and only reached their lodgings by midnight.
Péi Qiú
The pavilion of Lù Qùshē, a recluse from Sūzhōu,
was originally the residence of Dài Yóng, a Cavalry Scattered-Household Attendant of the Sòng dynasty.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Péi Qiú from Hédōng often lodged in this pavilion while traveling.
He suddenly died,
but after a long while, he revived.
He recounted:
"At first, a person came and said:
'Lord Dài summons you.'
Qiú asked who Dài was,
and the person replied:
'Do you know Dài Yóng, the Cavalry Scattered-Household Attendant of the Sòng dynasty?'
Qiú said:
'I know of him.'
The person said:
'The one calling you now
is that very person.'
Qiú went to see Yóng,
and Yóng requested that Qiú marry his daughter.
Qiú said:
'I am already married,
and it is not proper to marry again.'
Yóng said:
'Humans and spirits follow different paths,
so why trouble yourself over this?'
Qiú replied, 'I already hold an official position and salary,
and it is not fitting for me to be your son-in-law.'
After a long discussion,
they spoke back and forth.
Yóng laughed, seeing that Qiú could not be swayed,
and released him.
Thus, he came back to life."
Zhào Zuǒ
Zhào Zuǒ
was appointed as a student of the Four Gates School of the National University at the end of the Tiānbǎo era.
Once, while lying ill,
he felt dazed as two officials in yellow clothes escorted him to the west of the Guānfēng Tower at the Wēnquán Palace.
There was a separate government office there.
The officials led him inside,
where he first saw a person resembling a king.
Zuǒ stepped forward and bowed in greeting.
The king said to Zuǒ:
"Do you recognize me?"
Zuǒ replied that he did not.
The king said:
"Have you heard of Qín Shǐhuáng?
I am he.
The human ruler has built many palaces beside my home,
and whenever music and performances are held,
they are extravagantly luxurious,
truly a magnificent king.
Therefore, I too have built this tower to watch the performances."
He then asked many questions about human affairs.
He also asked Zuǒ:
"Great chaos will soon befall the human world.
You should plan to avoid disaster,
and not stay long in the capital."
After speaking,
he had someone escort Zuǒ back.
Assistant Clerk of Qízhōu
An Assistant Clerk from Qízhōu once went to the capital on official business
and stayed at Xìngdào Ward.
Suddenly, he saw two people and a headless man approach, saying:
"The king has ordered us to apprehend you."
The Assistant Clerk knew they were ghosts,
so he asked:
"Gentlemen, in the underworld,
what duties do you hold?"
They replied:
"We are arrest officers."
The Assistant Clerk said to them:
"Fortunately, I share some affinity with you gentlemen.
Can you save me?
If the matter is resolved,
I will offer ten thousand paper coins."
The king's men agreed:
"If we do not return after five days,
it means the matter is resolved.
You can burn the coins at Tiānmén Street."
After five days, they did not return,
so the clerk burned the coins as promised.
He then moved to Chóngrén Ward.
Later, when his business in the capital was finished,
he returned west to Qízhōu.
When he reached Xìngshù Inn,
he encountered the two men again.
They asked:
"Where have you been?
We looked for you at your old place but couldn't find you.
The matter concerning you has been resolved, and you are exempted.
Thank you for the paper coins sent to the underworld.
The authorities have already issued a permanent exemption document.
Unless your time of death arrives,
you will suffer no further illnesses."
The Wáng family of Jùnyí
were scholar-officials.
When their mother was buried,
the son-in-law, Péi Láng, was drunk from drinking wine,
entered the tomb and lay down behind the coffin.
The family did not know this,
and so they sealed the burial chamber.
After several days passed without seeing Péi Láng,
his family accused the Wángs of having killed him,
and so they brought a lawsuit against each other.
The Wángs truly had not done this,
and the whole family pondered the matter.
Fearing that on the day of the burial he might have been inside the tomb,
they opened the burial chamber and found him,
his breath faint.
They fed him gruel,
and after several days he recovered.
He recounted,
saying that on the night of the burial,
as the wine was wearing off,
there was no way to get out.
Raising his eyes to steal a look,
he saw countless people,
with patterned cypress forming a hall,
and the residence was extremely splendid.
All the deceased elders and juniors of the Wáng family had gathered.
The many ghosts were greatly startled upon seeing Péi Láng.
Among them, one ghost said:
"Why not kill him?"
His mother-in-law said:
"My young daughter relies on him;
how could you want to kill him?"
After much arguing, he was spared.
Then he saw a long banquet with fine delicacies,
singing and music, joyful and harmonious.
Soon he heard someone say:
"Summon Péi Láng."
He was afraid and dared not rise.
Then he heard a group of maidservants linking arms and stamping in song,
the lyrics saying:
"The cypress hall newly built, joy unending,
coming and going, circling around Péi Láng."
There was a maidservant named Nónghuá
who burned the bridge of his nose with a paper torch, causing a sore,
and the pain was unbearable.
So he rose and bowed all around.
The various ghosts repeatedly ordered Péi Láng to sing and dance.
When hungry, he asked for food.
His mother-in-law said:
"Ghost food is not fit to eat."
She ordered that food from a bottle be given to him.
This went on for several nights.
The servants were all funerary objects,
no longer having their original forms.
Zhāngchóu Jiānqióng
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
Zhāngchóu Jiānqióng served as the military governor of Jiànnán,
and after several years he went to the capital.
In Shǔ, there was a certain Zhāng
the yaksha,
who appeared like a madman,
but his predictions often came true.
As Jiānqióng was about to depart,
he called him and asked.
The yaksha said:
"If Your Excellency remains in Shǔ,
you will have boundless longevity.
If you insist on going to the capital,
I do not see it as auspicious."
Jiānqióng was initially very frightened,
but after a while he said:
"How could this be?"
And so he set off.
When he reached Hànzhōu,
and entered the courier station,
he fell from his horse and died,
with only a slight warmth remaining in his heart.
Lǐ Xiān, the prefect of Péngzhōu,
ordered a certain Captain Mǎ of Luòyáng to deliver medicinal wine, apply medicine, and inquire after his health.
Luòyáng was fifty lǐ from Hànzhōu,
and he set off immediately upon receiving the order.
