When he reached Hànzhōu and entered the courier station to where Jiānqióng was,
he suddenly collapsed and died.
Later, Jiānqióng revived,
saying that the underworld officials
had brought Captain Mǎ to see him.
Mǎ had also died,
and then he went to his own home.
His family was astonished,
saying:
"You just received orders;
where have you returned from?"
He did not speak,
but gazed at the sky and sighed deeply.
His wife asked again:
"Where are your attendants?
And you are not holding your tablet;
what
is the matter?"
Mǎ still did not speak.
He hastily waved for them to leave,
then said tearfully:
"I have died in place of Governor Zhāngchóu.
Just now in the underworld, I argued strenuously,
but the underworld officials could do nothing about it.
Considering that I have held office for only a short time,
and am a distant traveler, alone and vulnerable,
I have returned to bid farewell."
As he spoke, he wept bitterly.
Then he said to his wife:
"Do not grieve.
Since I have died in his place,
he should also show deep sympathy.
Do not worry about not being able to return home.
But it is all so sudden;
life and death are forever separated,
and this is my regret!"
Having said this, he vanished.
His children were at first dazed and doubtful,
but soon they saw a bed carrying his corpse back.
The next day, Jiānqióng returned to Chéngdū.
He gave the Mǎ family five million coins for the funeral,
and also ordered Péngzhōu
to give another five million,
and additionally restored four years of his official salary and emoluments.
Lǐ Línfǔ
During the Táng dynasty, Lǐ Línfǔ had been chancellor for a long time.
He believed that he had accumulated many hidden calamities,
and that the realm harbored considerable resentment toward him.
Fearing ghostly disasters,
he sought out occultists to ward them off.
Later, he found one occultist who said:
"Your Excellency has been noble and powerful for a long time,
and those who bear grudges against you are many.
The foundation of calamity
is not a matter of a single day.
Nevertheless,
what may be avoidable
are the daily and nightly hazards."
Línfǔ said:
"What should be done?"
The occultist said:
"You should seek a skilled archer in Cháng'ān market
to prepare for it."
Línfǔ then recruited one from the West Market.
The man said he had once served in the army,
and was known for his skill in archery.
Recently, he had been ill,
and knew nothing else.
Línfǔ provided him with clothing and food,
supplying him monthly.
Later, one evening,
Línfǔ was holding a banquet in his courtyard,
with entertainers from Yān and Zhào serving at his side.
Before the song was finished,
it suddenly stopped.
The skilled archer found it strange and listened,
but heard nothing.
He silently thought to himself:
"The night is not yet late;
why has it suddenly become like this?
Is there something else?
Or is it what the occultist spoke of?"
So he took his bow and arrows,
vaulted over the wall, and entered to observe.
Suddenly, he saw something from the south of the wall
fall down,
and then another person vaulted over.
The skilled archer shot one arrow and hit him,
and he fled in alarm.
Then he went to where Línfǔ was enjoying himself,
and saw the singers and dancers silenced, unable to use their voices,
frozen, unable to move their sleeves,
quiet and still like wooden puppets.
Then he looked at the object that had fallen from the south of the wall:
it was a tied-up bag.
Opening it,
he found several hundred tallies inside,
all bearing the names of Línfǔ and his household servants.
So he called out the names one by one,
and each responded.
Then the banquet resumed as before.
The next day,
the occultist came
and congratulated him:
"Thanks to this man,
otherwise you would nearly have been harmed.
That was one who had died bearing a grievance.
Your Excellency has long monopolized authority,
accumulating countless transgressions.
From now on, for ten years,
it is beyond my knowledge."
Later, when Línfǔ's property was confiscated,
it indeed happened within ten years.
Chén Xīliè
When Chén Xīliè was chancellor,
there was a ghost in his house.
Sometimes it would recite poetry,
sometimes it would sing and shout,
its voice very faint, sharp, and urgent,
yet each word was clearly audible.
His family members asked it:
"Who are you, to be here?"
The ghost said:
"I am here playing and wandering;
when my wandering is done, I shall leave."
Sometimes it would demand clothes,
sometimes it would ask for food and drink.
If it got them, it would leave;
if not, it would curse.
This went on for several days.
Later, it suddenly began discussing the classics and histories,
and the ghost was extremely well-read.
The family called Chén Xīliè's nephew-in-law, the Investigating Censor Jì Lǚjì, and had him converse with the ghost.
The ghost said to Lǚjì:
"Because I was passing through,
I lingered here to play.
Hearing your profound discourse,
today my mind is suddenly cleared.
I have matters to attend to and must leave.
You, sir, stay well."
Then it departed.
Yáng Guózhōng
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
Yáng Guózhōng's
power and influence were overwhelming,
unmatched in the court.
Suddenly, a woman came to his residence requesting an audience.
The gatekeeper refused her,
but the woman cried out loudly:
"I have a grave matter
and must see Lord Yáng.
How dare you stop me!
If I do not see him,
I will make fire break out
and burn down Lord Yáng's entire residence!"
The gatekeeper, frightened,
reported this to Guózhōng.
Guózhōng saw her.
The woman said to Guózhōng:
"You are the State Chancellor.
How can you not understand the principles of prosperity and decline?
I am ashamed for you! You have reached the pinnacle of official rank,
and are moreover connected to the imperial family by marriage.
Your fame has stirred the realm,
and this has been so for a long time.
Yet you are extravagant and unrestrained, without moderation,
cultivating neither virtue nor righteousness.
You block the path of the worthy,
and flatter the sovereign above.
This, too, has been long.
You have not the slightest intention of following the footsteps of former ministers like Fáng Xuánlíng and Dù Rǔhuì.
You give no thought to the altars of state.
You cannot distinguish between the worthy and the foolish.
Merely those who bring bribes to your gate,
you ennoble and enrich.
Men of great talent and great virtue
lie hidden in forests and springs,
yet you have never once glanced their way.
You entrust military authority based on favor,
and appoint administrators based on affection.
Alas!
If you wish for the altars of state to be secure and your own clan preserved,
it is certainly impossible!"
Guózhōng flew into a great rage.
He asked the woman:
"Where do you come from?
How dare you rashly offend the chancellor?
Do you not fear the death penalty?"
The woman said:
"You yourself are unaware of your death penalty,
yet instead turn it upon me."
Guózhōng, enraged,
ordered his attendants to behead her.
The woman suddenly vanished.
Before Guózhōng's astonishment had subsided,
she reappeared standing before him.
Guózhōng then asked:
"What manner of demon are you?"
The woman said:
"I truly lament the altars of state of Gāozǔ and Tàizōng,
being overthrown by a single common man.
You do not understand how to be chancellor.
Although you occupy the position of chief minister,
you lack the achievements of a chief minister.
Your death is a small matter.
What is truly painful
is that the imperial dynasty will henceforth weaken.
It will barely preserve its ancestral temples.
Why are you angry?
I came to inform you.
Why so much trouble?
Now if I retreat,
what merit is there?
Why will you die?
Why will the people weep?"
Having spoken,
she laughed and went out.
Guózhōng ordered people to pursue her,
but she was not seen.
Later, when Ān Lùshān raised his army,
he realized the meaning of the word "Hú" (barbarian/why).
Lǐ Shūjì
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
Lùshān rebelled.
Lǐ Shūjì of Zhàojùn,
fled south with his wife from Wǔguān to Xiāngyáng.
His wife and two sons died on the journey.
Shūjì wandered in Jīngchǔ.
After a long time,
Lùshān had already seized the Eastern Capital.
His wife's aunt,
a widow living alone, unable to escape,
still resided in the city,
suffering extreme hardship.
She sent her maidservant Luònǚ
out of the city to gather firewood.
From afar, she saw an ox-cart hurrying along,
with a man in purple robes riding a horse behind it.
A woman in the cart repeatedly called out "Luò."
When the maidservant drew near,
she asked:
"Do you recognize me?"
The maidservant, surprised and delighted, said:
"Where is Master Lǐ going?
Why is the lady traveling alone like this?"
The wife then wept sorrowfully and said:
"On the way to Xiāngyáng,
Shūjì and our two children all died at the hands of the rebels.
Because of hunger and starvation,
I took my young son and daughter and married the man behind this cart."
She then went with Luònǚ
to see her aunt.
After weeping,
she asked:
"Where are my sisters?"
The aunt said, "They are nearby, outside."
She said:
"This journey is very hurried;
I cannot wait any longer."
She stayed for about half a day.
At that time, the people were starving.
The aunt then prepared food,
coarse and tasteless.
The wife took polished rice and other fine dishes from the cart
and called her husband and the aunt to eat.
After eating, they prepared to depart.
At the moment of parting,
she said:
"Life here is hard.
I should also leave you something,
but my baggage has already gone ahead.
Now in the cart there is only one and a half bolts of silk.
Please keep them for clothing.
I deeply regret it is so little."
During the Qiányuán era,
when Emperor Sùzōng recaptured the two capitals,
the aunt and her son went down to Yángzhōu together.
After over a month,
Shūjì also arrived.
They met and wept sorrowfully.
Shūjì again lamented that his wife had died in childbirth while traveling,
and that his young son and daughter had also died one after the other.
Having spoken, he wept again.
The aunt was initially ashamed and embarrassed,
thinking her niece had been captured by the rebels.
But seeing Shūjì's genuine grief,
she then told him what had happened.
She said the skirt she was wearing
was the very silk that had been left.
Shūjì could only sigh in lament.
Zhū Áo of Wújùn
once, among the rebels in Chénliú, knew a military officer
who claimed to have obtained the wife of Lǐ Jì.
The Magistrate of Xīnfán County
The magistrate of Xīnfán County's wife had passed away,
so he ordered
female workers to make mourning garments.
Among them was a woman
of exceptional grace and beauty.
The magistrate was pleased and kept her,
showing her great favor and affection.
Several months later,
she suddenly appeared grief-stricken and haggard,
her words choked with sobs.
The magistrate, finding this strange, asked her the reason.
She said:
"My original husband is about to arrive,
and I must soon go far away.
That is why I am sorrowful."
The magistrate said:
"With me here, who can do anything to you?
Just eat and drink as usual,
do not worry."
A few days later, she asked to leave.
He tried to stop her but could not,
so she left a silver wine cup as a parting gift.
She said to the magistrate:
"If you miss me dearly,
take this as a keepsake."
The magistrate gave her ten bolts of silk in return.
After she left, he constantly thought of her,
holding the silver cup and never letting it out of his hand.
Whenever he went to the official office,
he would place it on his desk.
The county captain had already resigned and returned to his hometown,
but his wife's coffin was still in Xīnfán,
so he came from afar to move it.
He presented his card and paid a visit to the magistrate,
who treated him with great hospitality.
The captain saw the silver cup
and kept stealing glances at it.
The magistrate asked him why,
and he replied:
"This is an object from my late wife's coffin.
I do not know how it came to be here."
The magistrate sighed for a long time,
then recounted the whole story from beginning to end,
describing the woman's appearance, voice, and manner,
as well as the incident of her leaving the cup and his gift of silk.
The captain was furious all day.
Later, when he opened the coffin,
he saw the woman lying there, holding the silk.
The captain was extremely angry,
piled up firewood, and burned her.
Yáo Xiāopǐn
Yáo Xiāopǐn
was a person from Qiántáng, Hángzhōu.
His family was hosting guests,
and during the wine gathering, he died,
but after about the time it takes to eat a meal, he revived.
He said that at first, he saw a person come to summon him,
thinking it was a county official.
He went out to look,
and was immediately seized and taken away.
When they reached the north outer gate,
there were several clerks in a boat.
The one who seized him ordered Pǐn to tow the boat.
Pǐn said:
"I am but a humble remnant,
and have never pulled a boat."
He was then beaten,
and could not refuse.
He strained to tow it
until they reached the Yìtíng Bridge,
about eight or nine lǐ away,
when the ghosts no longer guarded him.
He then broke away and managed to escape.
Liáng Shǒuwēi
During the reign of Emperor Sùzōng of the Táng dynasty,
the rebellion of Ān Lushan and Shǐ Sīmíng was raging.
Xíngzhōu was right in rebel territory,
and its prefect had some intention of maintaining peace for the time.
There was a man from Cháng'ān named Liáng Shǒuwēi,
who prided himself on his literary, military talents, and eloquence.
He secretly left Cháng'ān
and headed for Xíngzhōu,
intending to persuade the prefect. When he reached the southwestern border of the prefecture,
he rested at night by an ancient tomb by the roadside.
Suddenly, a young man carrying a sword also arrived.
He sternly asked Shǒuwēi:
"Who are you?"
Shǒuwēi replied:
"I am a traveling persuader, intending to enter Xíngzhōu to persuade the prefect
to perform meritorious deeds in service to the sovereign."
The young man said:
"I am also a traveling persuader."
Shǒuwēi was pleased and bowed in greeting.
They sat together in the grass,
discussing the chaos of the times.
The young man asked:
"When you meet the prefect of Xíng,
what arguments will you use to persuade him?"
Shǒuwēi said:
"Now the Son of Heaven has succeeded to the throne,
and the Retired Emperor still lives.
With ministers assisting the state,
they can surely unite their efforts
to completely exterminate the vile rebels.
Thus, no elaborate arguments are needed.
The prefect of Xíng should respond and follow my advice.
This can be called seizing the opportunity and adapting to the times."
The young man said:
"You know one aspect,
but not the other.
Now the Crown Prince has assumed the throne,
while the Retired Emperor is still alive.
Do you think the empire has a clear ruler?
Or a clear direction?
However, when the Crown Prince reached Língwǔ,
the generals and ministers supported and acclaimed him,
wishing to make him the ruler of the empire.
But how can one who seizes the throne without filial piety
only stir the empire's anger
become its ruler?
If the Crown Prince had merely carried out the Retired Emperor's orders,
raised troops across the land,
exerted force to cut down the rebel bands,
recovered the capital,
and only then pacified and organized the realm,
bestowing ranks and rewards for military merits
afterwards and reporting them to the Retired Emperor,
then great stability would have been achieved without being sought.
Now the great affair has already been mishandled,
and ultimately the empire cannot be pacified.
I have never heard of one who bears the name of unfiliality himself
yet seeks to punish those who are disloyal.
To pacify the empire
and calm the rebel bands,
one must wait for a benevolent ruler to properly assume the throne.
Do not try to persuade the prefect of Xíng.
If he could be persuaded,
I would have persuaded him long ago."
Shǒuwēi realized the young man had talent and strategy,
and sighed deeply, saying:
"Where shall I go?
In the past, Liú Kūn rejoiced upon hearing the empire was in chaos,
but now I encounter the empire's chaos and grieve."
The young man then urged him to depart.
They headed toward a large forest,
and by dawn,
they reached the forest's edge.
There they saw over a hundred men,
all armored and bearing weapons—
they were the young man's followers.
The young man requested wine and food,
and they shared a joyful conversation before parting.
He said to Shǒuwēi:
"I give you one piece of advice,
which you should heed.
Simply return to Cháng'ān,
and you will surely obtain rank and emolument.
The Crown Prince has newly assumed the throne,
and many have risen from low to high status.
Within the passes, chaos is extreme,
and everyone longs for order and peace.
If you teach the methods of governance and pacification
to the various lords within the passes,
and advance by relying on them,
why worry about not achieving merit yourself?"
Shǒuwēi bowed in thanks and turned back.
After walking only about ten steps,
he looked back and the young man was gone.
He then returned to the forest's edge to search for him,
but saw only many ruined tombs.
Cháng Yí
Cháng Yí of Jiànkāng in the Táng dynasty,
styled Shūtōng,
was widely read in the classics,
and possessed refined literary talent.
His nature was upright and incorruptible,
and he took pride in his family's traditional profession.
His home was near Qīngxī,
and he often sat alone during the day.
A boy in a yellow robe arrived directly before his pavilion bearing a letter, saying:
"Scholar Zhū sends his regards."
Yí had never met him,
and found it very strange.
Upon opening the letter,
it read:
"Scholar Zhū Jūn of Wújùn,
addresses the noble recluse Cháng."
The contents of the letter were entirely unlike the words of a living person,
generally stating, "My home is near Xīgāng,
I am fortunate to be your good neighbor,
and I long to pay my respects."
At the end was a poem:
"I fully relate,
In life I roamed the city walls,
In death I lie amidst wild brambles.
Since I left the world of men,
I know not autumn nor spring,
Long have cattle and sheep come to graze,
Pines and cypress have nearly become firewood.
Cut off from fine carriages and horses,
I willingly follow the packs of foxes and hares.
Whence comes the clear breeze?
A gentleman, fortunate to be my neighbor.
Resplendent is your renowned virtue,
Longingly I await a noble guest.
A thousand years—what are dawn and dusk?
Yet one chamber stirs the human spirit.
Tall trees seem within sight,
The broad road is easy indeed to follow.
If the lofty gate presents no barrier,
I shall face it and break the dragon's ford."
The paper and ink were both old and worn.
Cháng Yí, deeply moved by this profound connection,
sighed in wonder for a long time,
then wrote a reply,
earnest and sincere.
He also set a specific date,
requesting a meeting.
After the boy left,
he had someone follow and watch him,
who saw him enter an ancient tomb
about one lǐ west of the house.
When the day arrived,
Yí prepared wine and fruits.
Shortly after,
he heard knocking at the door,
and saw the previous boy saying:
"Scholar Zhū has come to visit."
Yí fastened his belt and went out to greet him.
The scholar wore a cornered headscarf, a single-layer hempen robe, and dragged his shoes;
he appeared to be around fifty years old,
with a leisurely and harmonious demeanor.
He possessed an elegant and refined air.
After exchanging pleasantries,
the scholar said:
"In my time during the Liáng dynasty,
I was the top-ranked scholar recommended by this prefecture.
Due to the many troubles across the land,
I lost interest in officialdom,
and retired to pursue my aspirations.
I ended my days here at the close of the Chén dynasty's Yǒngdìng era,
and have long resided in the underworld.
I have always admired your noble character,
but the paths of the living and the dead are severed,
so I ceased paying visits.
Fortunately, through this fine encounter,
you, great gentleman, do not disdain me,
allowing me to express my pent-up feelings—
what joy could compare?"
Yí replied:
"I, dull and inferior,
never imagined the realm of spirits was so close at hand.
Long have I lacked your instruction;
I am fortunate to receive your exceptional regard,
and my joy and gratitude are truly great."
They then sat down, ate fruits, and drank wine.
Yí asked him about matters from the Liáng and Chén periods,
which he recounted clearly and in detail.
He identified himself as Zhū Yì's
nephew.
He spoke of how Yì served Emperor Wǔ,
enjoying unparalleled favor and affection.
The emperor had a woven golden-threaded screen,
coral-inlaid ornaments, a jade-handled duster,
a seven-treasure washing vessel and an agarwood-carved pillow offered by Línyì—
all secretly treasured by the emperor.
Often, after lectures in the Chéngyún Hall concluded,
he would bestow them all upon Yì.
When Crown Prince Zhāomíng passed away,
white fog filled the four directions.
At his burial, four pairs of black swans
soared and circled above the mausoleum,
hovering and crying mournfully,
departing only after the burial was complete.
Emperor Yuán was blind in one eye,
and deeply忌讳 this.
While governing Jīngzhōu as the Prince of Xiāngdōng,
he once had a court scholar lecture on the *Analects*.
When reaching the passage about 'seeing a blind person, one must change expression,'
the scholar did not avoid the sensitive topic,
and the emperor, greatly angered,
had him poisoned.
He also once defeated northern invaders,
personally beheading a deputy general.
When Yú
Jǐn captured Jiānglíng,
the emperor was killed,
and the one who wielded the blade was that general's own son.
When Shěn Yuē's mother was enfeoffed as Lady Jiànchāng,
the emperor sent a Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary to her home to read the edict and confer the seal and ribbons.
From the Vice Director Hé Jìngróng downward, several hundred officials
came to her gate to offer congratulations—
since the Sòng and Liáng dynasties, no titled lady had enjoyed such honor.
Yǔ Jiānwú in his youth served Master Táo,
and mastered many arts.
Once, during midsummer, while hosting guests,
he exhaled greatly toward the sky,
and it all turned to snow.
He also could make various objects hang suspended in midair.
Emperor Jiǎnwén ordered the construction of Fènglín Temple in Xiāngyáng;
when short of pillar wood,
a ferry officer on the river retrieved a camphorwood log,
which perfectly matched the needed pillars.
The emperor was extremely filial;
while keeping vigil by Dīng Guìpín's coffin,
he wept incessantly,
and from lying in grief, his flesh ulcerated,
and sores covered his face.
When Hóu Jǐng captured Táichéng,
water and rice were cut off within the city.
Emperor Wǔ, having ordered congee to be served,
found no rice in the palace.
Four shēng were obtained from a yellow-cloth sack in the Huangmen office,
and after it was consumed, it was exhausted.
His requests unmet, he passed away.
The Liáng people captured by Jǐng
were placed in long cangues,
their heads all confined within,
and he ordered soldiers to shoot them to death with three volleys of arrows—
even nobles and high officials
were treated no differently.
After Emperor Wǔ of Chén killed Wáng Sēngbiàn,
heavy rain fell for over a hundred days.
He also spoke of Emperor Wǔ of Chén in his humble days:
his family was very poor,
and he worked as a hired laborer to support himself.
He often stole fish from the pond of the wealthy Bāo family in Chángchéng,
was caught and tied with a carrying pole,
and suffered greatly.
After ascending the throne,
he exterminated the Bāo clan.
These are all omissions from the histories.
There were many such events,
impossible to record fully.
Afterward, they visited each other several times,
conversing, feasting, and composing poems.
The scholar's talent was exceptionally refined and lofty,
and they became close friends.
Whenever auspicious or inauspicious events occurred in Yí's household,
he would forewarn him.
Later, when Yí fell gravely ill,
the scholar said to him:
"The Director of Fate summons you to serve as a Chief Clerk.
I am also involved in the inspections.
This position is very important,
and selecting the right person is especially difficult;
its prestige in the underworld is unmatched.
All living men must die;
even if you forcibly extend your life a few years,
how could it compare to residing in that realm?
You must not decline."
Yí then felt joyful,
ceased taking medicine,
and passed away a few days later.
Zhāng Shǒuyī
During the Qiányuán era, there was a man named Zhāng Shǒuyī,
who served as the Junior Minister of the Court of Judicial Review.
He was benevolent and compassionate by nature,
and through reviewing and overturning wrongful convictions,
he spared many prisoners from death sentences.
Later, while on his way to the morning court,
an old man with white hair,
hunched over and leaning on a cane,
approached his horse and bowed in gratitude.
Shǒuyī asked the reason,
and the old man requested to dismiss the attendants.
He said:
"I am not among the living;
I am the father of the death-row prisoner you spared.
Being of the underworld and of lowly status,
I have no means to repay your kindness.
However, if you ever have a personal request,
I may be able to fulfill it.
Please instruct me."
Shǒuyī replied:
"Your worthy son was innocent;
it was not that I bent the law to extend mercy,
so I dare not accept this.
I am undeservedly ranked among the nine ministers,
and I am quite self-sufficient,
so I hope not to trouble you."
After repeatedly comforting and dismissing him,
the ghost said:
"For now, I will leave,
but if you ever have a request I cannot fulfill,
I hope you will remember me."
Then he vanished.
Soon after, an imperial decree granted a public feast,
and the city was filled with spectators.
Shǒuyī caught sight of the daughter of a scholar's family in the crowd,
whose beauty was stunningly exquisite.
He was captivated by her, but her family's restrictions were very strict,
and he could think of no way to approach her.
He tried calling out to the previous ghost:
"Can you bring her to me?"
As soon as he finished speaking, the ghost arrived,
saying, "This is an easy matter,
but it cannot last long,
only seven days at most."
Shǒuyī said:
"That is enough.
But are you using transformation to deceive her?"
The ghost replied:
"Why do you doubt so deeply, sir?
I will use another object to substitute for her body."
Then they prepared a secluded place
and set up curtains and bedding.
After a short while,
she arrived as if in a trance.
After a long time, she woke up in shock and asked:
"Where is this?"
Only Shǒuyī and the ghost were beside her.
They deceived her, saying:
"This is the heavenly envoy from above." Thus, they became intimate,
and their affection grew very deep.
On the seventh day,
Shǒuyī said to the girl:
"Heaven and the mortal world are separated,
and our joyful time together has been brief.
How can we bear to part so soon?"
Then, with tears, they bid farewell.
The ghost covered her eyes again and sent her back.
Later, Shǒuyī secretly observed the girl's family,
and they said:
"Our daughter suddenly fell ill with an evil affliction,
lost consciousness,
and woke up after seven days."
Ten years later,
he encountered the ghost again, who said:
"The heavenly court has summoned me,
and I must soon depart forever.
Now I offer you one pill of medicine,
which can transform miscellaneous bones
into excellent bone-handled knives.
I hope you treasure it,
and use it in times of emergency."
Then, with a sigh, he left.
The medicine was about the size of a chicken egg.
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
Shǒuyī was framed by cruel officials
for being lenient and fair in upholding the law.
He was exiled to Lǐngbiǎo,
and his resources were exhausted.
So he used the medicine to transform bones,
and indeed it worked.
Thus,
he relied on it for sustenance,
but when the medicine ran out, he died.
Zhèng Wàng
During the Qiányuán era,
there was a man named Zhèng Wàng
who traveled from the capital to Jīngzhào.
One night, he sought lodging at the Yěhúquán Inn,
but before reaching it by five or six lǐ, it grew dark.
Suddenly, he saw a household by the roadside,
and he tried asking the gatekeeper,
who said it belonged to General Wáng.
As the general had been an old friend of his deceased father,
Wàng was very pleased.
He then sent in his name to pay respects,
and the general came out
to meet Wàng.
They reminisced with tears,
and all courtesies were observed.
Thus, Wàng was invited to stay overnight,
and a feast was prepared for him.
In the middle of the night, while they were merrily drinking,
the general ordered someone to call Qúchú Sānniáng to sing and accompany the wine.
After a short while,
Sānniáng arrived.
She was exceptionally beautiful,
and particularly skilled at singing "Ā Què Jiān."
At dawn, she bid farewell and left.
The general's wife sent a message
asking Wàng to buy brocade trousers, hair ornaments, flowers, rouge, and powder.
Several months later, when Wàng returned eastward,
he delivered the requested items.
The general greeted him warmly,
and hosted him as before.
Wàng asked:
"Why haven't I seen Qúchú Sānniáng?"
The general replied:
"She has already returned to the capital with her husband."
The next day, Wàng took his leave.
When he stepped outside, the mansion was no longer visible,
only burial mounds remained.
Wàng, bewildered, turned back.
When he reached Yěhúquán,
he asked the locals,
who said:
"That is General Wáng's tomb.
A musician once came to the inn,
and his wife died suddenly from illness.
Her body was wrapped in a reed mat
and buried beside the general's tomb.
That is why she was called 'Qúchú Sānniáng.'
Ten days ago,
the musician also moved her body back to Cháng'ān for burial."
Yǔwén Dí
Hán Chè was
appointed magistrate of Wúshān County in Lǒngzhōu during the Qiányuán era.
He had long been friends with the presented scholars Yǔwén Dí and Xīn Jì,
who accompanied Chè to Wúshān to study,
with Chè also providing support for their autumn examinations.
The position of Wúshān County magistrate was notoriously ill-omened,
with many predecessors having died.
In the magistrate’s hall stood a large pagoda tree,
and Dí and Jì suspected it was possessed by a spirit.
They secretly plotted with the county clerk to cut it down
when Chè was away.
When the day arrived,
they informed Chè.
Chè said to the two men:
"Life and death are decreed by Heaven;
blame
does not lie with a tree.
Do not proceed with this."
Their plan was thus abandoned.
A few days later,
while walking near the tree, Dí and Jì
discovered a hole
with moist soil around it.
From within emerged a bluish vapor
that rose to form a cloud.
Waiting until Chè had retired to rest,
they ordered locals to dig.
Several feet down,
they uncovered a tomb
containing a coffin, already decayed,
with a few teeth, hair, thigh bones, and hip bones still intact.
Looking toward the northwest corner, they saw an object.
Thinking it strange,
they hired two men for five thousand coins to retrieve it.
First, they lowered a rope,
then a bundle of lit candles.
The two men, armed with knives, descended by the rope to inspect a food vessel,
which contained water
with fruits like crabapples and other offerings floating on top.
When poured onto the ground,
they vanished like smoke.
When Chè arrived,
he ordered his assistant to collect the bones and hair for reburial in a new coffin in the wilderness.
The assistant embezzled the funds,
using a small document box
to bury the broken bones.
Upon returning home,
he suddenly fell gravely ill,
and his family informed Chè,
who summoned a shaman.
The shaman, speaking in a spirit voice before Chè,
said:
"I am General Qìbì È of the Jìn dynasty,
who died in battle
and was buried in this county.
My tomb lies near a horse stable,
and I have long suffered from the filth.
I wished to be moved.
I have made many appeals,
but most magistrates died
soon after taking office,
leaving my grievances unheard in the underworld.
Now, Your Honor has shown kindness to the netherworld,
using your salary to buy a coffin—
a great act of grace.
But your clerk, cruel and wicked,
stored my bones and hair in a document box.
The bones were long, the box short,
so he broke my thighs and hips,
causing unbearable pain.
That is why I seek revenge."
Chè repeatedly apologized
and explained:
"It was my negligence
that allowed the clerk to commit this deceit.
I will purchase a coffin myself
and provide burial garments.
If you could pardon his offense slightly,
it would be a great mercy."
The spirit spoke again:
"I will release him soon.
However, the ones who devised this plan
were Yǔwén the Seventh and Xīn the Fourth.
My ghostly soul remembers this
and dares not forget.
Xīn will soon receive an official post,
bringing honor to himself.
But Yǔwén’s fate is thin and without rank;
though he may pass the examinations,
he will never hold office
and will face many calamities.
I can save him from death three times,
but if he becomes an official,
even I cannot save him."
With that, the spirit departed.
The clerk was released,
and a proper burial was arranged.
Dí’s home was in Qíshān.
Some time later,
È suddenly spoke from the air:
"The seventh gentleman’s wife is gravely ill at the estate.
I have just gone to rescue her,
and she is now slightly better.
Soon someone from the estate will come to report—
there is no need to fear.
When you return,
after seeing your wife,
be sure not to eat horse meat."
Shortly after, a messenger arrived,
confirming everything.
When Dí entered his home,
his wife had recovered.
Later, a tenant’s horse died,
and he offered Dí cooked tripe and meat.
Forgetting the warning, Dí ate it
and suffered acute cholera,
repeatedly falling unconscious.
Suddenly, he heard È say:
"I told you not to eat horse meat.
Why did you break your promise?
The horse is an enemy from a past life.
If I were not here,
you would have no chance to live;
with me here,
you will suffer no harm."
He then ordered attendants to write down a prescription,
and after taking the medicine,
Dí recovered.
Later, Dí returned to Wúshān.
At that time, local bandits in Qízhōu attempted to claim imperial titles,
appointing officials.
Dí was well-known,
so they appointed him as a secretarial drafter.
The bandits were soon killed by government troops,
and Dí, along with over seventy others,
was imprisoned in the prefectural jail awaiting orders.
È again appeared to Dí’s wife, saying:
"The seventh gentleman is in trouble.
I have pleaded extensively in the underworld,
but it requires three thousand strings of cash."
His wife pleaded poverty,
unable to afford it.
È said:
"What the underworld uses
are paper money from the human world."
His wife replied:
"I will do my best to prepare the paper money."
After it was burned,
È went to the prison and told Dí:
"I have just received three thousand strings from your wife
to plead on your behalf.
The matter is now resolved.
When Inspector Liú arrives,
you will be released.
Eat well and do not worry."
Soon after, Liú Yàn was appointed prefect of Lǒngzhōu.
Upon taking leave of the emperor, he memorialized:
"Many reputable scholars,
whom I have never met,
were implicated by the rebels
and imprisoned.
Upon my arrival in the prefecture,
I request to release them all."
The emperor approved.
When Yàn reached the prefecture
and assumed office,
he summoned all prisoners and announced their release.
Ashamed for having accepted the rebel appointment,
Dí returned home.
Over half a year later,
Lǚ Chóngbēn became military commissioner of Hédōng
and sought a secretary.
Many at court recommended Dí,
so Chóngbēn appointed Dí as a staff officer and secretary in Hédōng.
An imperial decree granted him a set of robes,
and Chóngbēn gifted him a hundred bolts of silk.
When the decree arrived,
Dí was overjoyed.
Upon receiving it,
he donned the green official robe and bowed westward in gratitude,
but suddenly collapsed.
È’s spirit voice sighed for a long time,
then said to Dí:
"I warned you not to take office.
Why did you accept?
This time, I cannot save you."
Dí asked:
"What if I return the appointment?"
È replied:
"You have already accepted the official position.
How can it be returned?
Take utmost care.
I will not come again."
Four days later,
Dí fell ill and died.
Earlier, the shaman had seen È dressed in magnificent robes and headgear,
His temples and hair were bright red,
resembling the present-day Kùmòxī people.
Lǐ Yíng
Lǐ Yíng, the magistrate of Shòuchāng in Zhàojùn,
had a thirteenth cousin from the same clan who was unmarried.
At the beginning of the Zhìdé era,
she followed her elder brothers south across the river,
died,
and was buried in Hǎiyán in Wú.
Her elder brother Lǐ Mín’s estate was in Jìyuán,
and he had a widowed younger sister
living over ten li from the estate.
During Ān Lùshān’s rebellion,
she was unable to escape south.
During the Shàngyuán era,
she suddenly appeared returning to her brother’s home.
When asked how she came back,
she said she had been captured by rebels.
Her responses were reasonable,
so the family did not question her further.
Her elder sister, fearing the chaos of the times
might endanger her safety,
hurriedly arranged for her to marry a man named Zhāng from a nearby estate.
After four or five years,
she had a son,
who was exceptionally bright and intelligent,
understanding everything.
She often stayed alone in a locked room at the Mín estate,
coming and going peacefully.
Much of the Mín family’s land
had been encroached upon by others,
but she reclaimed it all through lawsuits.
During the Yǒngtài era,
when the nation’s situation had stabilized,
Mín and his younger brothers
traveled from Jiāngdōng to the capital for official selection.
After completing their business and returning to the estate,
they were still several hundred li away
when the younger sister at the estate suddenly told a maidservant:
"My elder brothers
will arrive in a few days,
so I must temporarily stay at the Zhāng household."
She also went to bid farewell to her elder sister-in-law,
who asked her the reason.
She replied:
"I have been dreaming about this frequently."
The maidservant escorted her halfway,
and she sent the maidservant back.
After walking a dozen or so steps,
the maidservant looked back and she was gone,
which the maidservant found very strange.
Two days later,
the Zhāng family reported that she had died.
Her elder sister and nephews
had just finished mourning and weeping
when her elder brothers arrived.
They then held the funeral for their sister from the Zhāng family.
Mín said:
"She died during the Shàngyuán era
and was buried in Hǎiyán.
How could she have come here?
I fear she was a ghost."
They went to the Zhāng household to view the body,
but when they lifted the quilt, the corpse was gone.
Examining her clothes and mirror,
they were all items placed in the coffin at burial.
Her son also died soon after.
Péi Yì
Péi Yì from Hédōng
loved playing the zhēng from a young age.
At the time, there was a zhēng master
skilled at composing new tunes.
Yì’s younger sister wished to study with him,
but found it difficult to receive instruction directly from him.
So Yì studied with the master himself,
then passed on the knowledge to his sister,
and she gained a reputation for her skill.
Much later, Yì traveled to Jiāngxiāng,
and died in Nánchǔ.
His mother and sister were at home
when Yì suddenly
returned alone, traveling lightly.
The family was surprised and delighted,
and asked him how he came back.
He said:
"My luggage and servants are behind me,
and will arrive by evening."
After the joyous reunion,
he asked for a zhēng to play,
and also had his sister perform a piece.
Wherever she made mistakes,
he corrected them all.
After correcting over ten pieces,
he suddenly vanished.
Moments later, his funeral procession arrived.
Lady Lǐ
A woman from the Lái Tíng ward in the upper capital, surnamed Lǐ,
was sitting in her home’s main hall one day
when she suddenly saw the deceased younger sister of her husband,
dressed in white mourning clothes,
wearing a cloth headscarf,
coming straight at her.
Lady Lǐ circled the bed to avoid her,
but the sister-in-law kept chasing her,
so she ran out the door and fled.
On the rugged path,
no one dared to intervene or rescue her.
A cavalry soldier from the north gate
struck the apparition with his horsewhip,
and it vanished instantly,
leaving only the headscarf,
which fell to the ground,
revealing a skull beneath it.
Wéi Huī
The wife of Zhōu Hùn, magistrate of Lùchéng County,
was surnamed Wéi and named Huī.
Her appearance was beautiful,
and her nature was clever and intelligent.
She often made a pact with her sisters-in-law and younger sisters, saying:
"If any of us
dies first,
matters of the underworld
should be reported to each other."
Later, she married into the Zhōu family,
gave birth to two daughters,
and died during the Qiányuán era.
Over a month later,
she suddenly arrived at her home,
her spirit voice heard in the empty space,
telling her family:
"I promised to report back,
so I have come for this reason.
I have already met King Yánluó and my relatives."
Her family asked if she had seen cauldrons of boiling water and forests of swords,
to which she replied:
"What kind of person am I,
that I should see such things?"
Later, she again possessed a maidservant and spoke through her spirit, saying:
"The Lord of Mount Tài is marrying off his daughter,
and knowing I am skilled at dressing hair,
he summoned me.
Tomorrow, when the matter is done,
I will return again."
The next day,
the maidservant again spoke with the spirit's voice, saying:
"I went to Mount Tài,
where the Lord is marrying off his daughter,
and the ceremony is extremely grand and honorable.
He had me do the daughter's makeup,
and now I have obtained rouge and powder,
which I bring for the girls."
Then she opened her hand,
and there was a stick of rouge,
bright red,
and powder,
no different from things in the human world.
She also said:
"The Lord's family uses very large coins for scattering at the wedding bed,
so heavy that forty ghosts cannot lift a single one,
but I managed to get some."
Then coins fell from the air,
as large as cups.
She also said:
"The Lord knows I am good at dyeing red,
so he ordered me to do it.
I declined, saying that although I dye,
I do not personally handle the work,
as it is usually done by the household maidservants,
and I only give instructions.
The Lord then ordered me to fetch a maidservant,
so now, having no choice,
I will take the maidservant temporarily,
and tomorrow I will send her back."
Her daughter said:
"Our family relies entirely on this maidservant;
how can you take her away?"
Wéi said:
"I am only borrowing her for two days.
If two days pass,
you should strike a chime stone and call for her.
For the sound of the chime stone, once struck,
is heard by all ghosts and spirits."
Suddenly, the maidservant stopped breathing,
and after two days, she did not return,
so the daughters struck the chime stone.
A short while later,
the voice from the air spoke again, saying:
"I finished dyeing this morning,
and have already sent the maidservant back;
why has she not arrived?
She must have lost her way."
Soon, the maidservant arrived,
and revived,
but her hands suddenly turned deep red.
Wéi also composed several five-character poems,
for her sisters-in-law and husband,
one of which she sent said:
"Long and short each have their lot,
fleeting glory is also unreal.
Heartbroken beneath the springs and soil,
hidden sorrows are hard to fully express.
Desolate, the wind through white poplars,
at dusk, enough to sadden a person."
There were also two stanzas sent to her husband,
signed "Guest of the Springs, Wéi Huī."
The poem said:
"Unable to stay together forever,
youth withers like Shun's blossoms.
Past joys are now forever gone,
the road to the springs becomes my home."
The other:
"Had I known parting would cut so deep,
I'd regret the deep affection we ever kept.
Though the Yellow Springs are dark and long the journey,
in daylight, behind screens, I'll seek you again."
She also gave one stanza to her sister-in-law,
with a preface titled "Poem Left for My Sister-in-law, Who Doubted Me,"
which said:
"I exhausted my sincere heart for mutual understanding,
yet you worried and guarded, only settling on doubt.
Official documents can state the living's affairs,
but what can peach-wood charms do, though sacred?"
This was told by her relatives.
Xuē Wànshí
was from Hédōng.
At the beginning of the Guǎngdé era,
Xuē Jiānxùn, Surveillance Commissioner of Zhèdōng, appointed Wànshí as magistrate of Yǒngjiā.
After a few months,
he suddenly said to his wife:
"In ten days, our household's food will run out,
and when the food is gone,
I will also die.
Grain is scarce and expensive;
what can we do?"
His wife said:
"You are healthy and strong;
why speak such ominous words?"
Wànshí said:
"Death is very hateful,
but if I speak of it,
it is because I have no choice."
When the time came, he indeed died suddenly.
After his encoffining,
his voice suddenly came from the coffin, calling for the record-keeping assistant officials.
When they arrived,
he said to them:
"Wànshí has unfortunately died,
and speaking of it is sorrowful.
However, I have never troubled you before,
but now my wife and children are hungry and destitute,
with no way to return from afar.
The reason I summoned you
is to burden you with this matter of kinship."
At that time, rice in Yǒngjiā was expensive,
costing up to ten thousand coins per peck.
Wànshí requested varying amounts of rice from the record-keepers and below.
The officials were fearful,
and all complied and sent rice.
Even the assistant magistrates and captains made contributions.
A few days later,
he said to his family:
"I am going temporarily to Yuèzhōu
to pay respects to Lord Xuē.
Since you now have grain,
I am no longer worried."
After that, he was silent for over ten days.
His wife, grieving and exhausted,
was napping during the day
when she suddenly heard his voice.
Startled, she rose and said:
"What do you need?"
He replied:
"I have returned from Yuè,
and the Vice Censor-in-Chief already knows of my death.
He ordered Zhāng Qīng to come welcome me,
and also arranged marriages for our two daughters.
The affection of brothers
can indeed be profound.
You should quickly prepare,
for when Zhāng Qīng arrives,
you can depart immediately.
Otherwise,
you may fall victim to mountain bandits;
you must leave quickly."
The family thus prepared.
When Qīng arrived,
they set out that day,
on the road.
Two hundred lǐ from Yǒngjiā, Wēnzhōu was sacked by bandits.
The family was in peril on the road,
so they burned incense and prayed to him,
and he would always respond.
If they did not ask, he remained silent.
Relatives witnessed the family reporting to him.
Fàn Chù
Fàn Chù,
during the early years of the Guǎngdé era,
ran a wine shop in Sūzhōu.
One evening,
a woman passed by his door,
whose appearance and demeanor were quite unusual.
Chù invited her to stay the night,
and the woman did not decline at first.
He then lit a candle,
but she covered her face with her hair,
sitting in the shadows.
That night, they shared intimate relations,
but before dawn, she asked to leave,
saying she had lost her comb.
Unable to find it,
as they parted,
she bit Chù’s arm and left.
At daybreak,
he found a paper comb by the bed,
which deeply disturbed him.
Soon after, his body ached, swelled, and turned red,
and he died within six or seven days.
Lǐ Huàn
Lǐ Huàn, Deputy Governor of Hézhōng,
died in the second year of the Guǎngdé era.
On the seventh day after his death,
after his family had finished holding a vegetarian feast in his memory,
they suddenly saw Huàn riding alone through the middle gate.
The servants bowed repeatedly,
helped Huàn dismount,
and seated him in the western corridor.
His sons paid their respects, weeping,
but Huàn said:
"Life and death are fated;
why grieve?
It only disturbs the departed."
He then gave instructions on family matters for a long time.
Huàn had first married Xiàng Fēi’s
younger sister,
who bore him four sons.
After Xiàng passed away,
he remarried the daughter of Dòu Tāo from Hédōng,
a woman of great beauty
whom Huàn particularly adored.
At that moment, Dòu was too afraid to come out,
so Huàn sent for her.
He addressed her, saying:
"Though life and death are different,
as for our affection,
it has never diminished.
Why are you afraid to come out?
Whenever I hear your weeping from the underworld,
it fills me with sorrow.
I grieve that your life will also be short,
and that you will join me within two years.
As husband and wife, our bond is deep.
Wouldn’t it be joyful
to go together now?
All must face death;
it is not necessarily better to linger in the world for another year or two.
What do you think?"
Dòu remained silent at first,
but Huàn said:
"Even if you refuse,
it will be too late.
The day after tomorrow,
I will send a carriage here to fetch you.
I hope you do not decline."
He then called the maidservants,
addressing four of them:
"You have long served your lady;
you should accompany her."
He also took his wife’s clothes,
sorted them by hand,
divided them into several bags,
and gave them to the four maids,
saying:
"The day after tomorrow, bring these with you when you follow your lady."
He then told his sons:
"Though I married your mother first,
we do not meet in the underworld.
It is not fitting to bury me with your mother;
I should share a grave with Dòu.
If you disobey my words,
may the gods punish you."
With that, he departed.
The servants escorted him outside the gate,
where they saw Huàn ride swiftly away,
turning from east to west until he vanished.
Two days later, a carriage arrived at the gate,
unseen by others,
but visible only to the four maids.
They dressed Dòu,
took the chosen clothes,
bade farewell to the family,
and then all fell to the ground dead.
Zhāng Qíng
During the reign of Emperor Dàizōng,
when Héshuò was still unsettled,
bandits roamed and plundered.
Zhāng Qíng,
a native of Héngyáng,
was captured while traveling.
Later, he gathered his own followers,
killing travelers,
but vowing never to harm anyone from Héngyáng.
One day, he led a thousand men to the eastern border of Héngyáng.
Under the bright moonlight at midnight,
as they rested under a large grove,
they suddenly encountered over a hundred people
carrying festive lanterns,
playing music and singing,
accompanied by several women.
Seeing Qíng,
they shouted from afar:
"Are you government troops
or bandits?"
Qíng’s men replied:
"This is General Zhāng."
The travelers said:
"General Zhāng—the greenwood general?
Why is your military appearance so orderly,
your soldiers so well-disciplined?"
Qíng’s men grew angry,
reported to Qíng,
and requested to kill them.
They then led a hundred soldiers into battle.
The travelers, armed with spears and armor, numbered no more than twenty or thirty,
yet in the fight, they wounded many of Qíng’s men.
Enraged, Qíng
led his troops forward himself,
but again suffered several defeats.
One among them, calling himself the King of Yōudì, said:
"I have taken the daughter of the King of Héngyáng as my wife,
and have come to welcome her.
Tonight, under the quiet moon, we cross the wilderness
to avoid crowds,
never expecting to meet the general.
Your attendants were rude,
so I reprimanded them.
I did not intend to provoke your anger.
Yet I have long heard of your vow
not to harm people of Héngyáng.
I hope you will keep your word."
Out of regard for Héngyáng,
Qíng agreed to let them go,
but said:
"I will spare your men,
but the women must stay."
The other replied:
"Keeping the women is not acceptable;
if you wish to fight, then fight."
Qíng engaged them again,
but once more met defeat,
and considered retreating.
His men, however, were furious
and willing to fight to the death.
So he deployed all his troops,
dividing them into three squads to attack in turns,
yet they suffered repeated losses.
Seeing the King of Yōudì wielding his sword like the wind,
Qíng grew fearful
and forcefully restrained his men.
He stepped forward alone and asked:
"Are your soldiers human
or not?
Why do they remain unharmed?"
The King of Yōudì laughed and said:
"You are but a petty bandit
who commits unjust deeds,
yet you dare contend with my ghostly army?"
Qíng then dismounted and bowed repeatedly.
The king also said to Qíng:
"Ān Lùshān and his son are dead,
and Shǐ has usurped power.
Since you are an outlaw,
why not take your men and join him?
You will surely gain wealth and honor."
Qíng bowed again and said:
"I lack military strategy;
it was only by chance that the bandits made me their leader.
How could I assist anyone?"
The King of Yōudì then took out a volume on military tactics
and gave it to him before departing.
After obtaining this book,
Qíng gained considerable insight into warfare.
Soon after, he took his troops and joined Shǐ Sīmíng,
who indeed appointed him as a general.
He died a few years later.
Niú Shuǎng
During the Yǒngtài era,
Niú Shuǎng was appointed as the Deputy Administrator of Lúzhōu.
As he was about to assume his post,
his wet nurse, riding a donkey,
had her thigh scraped and wounded by the stirrup.
Over a year later,
the sore still had not healed.
One morning, the sore itched painfully,
and when she pressed and scratched it,
it felt as if something were crawling inside.
Suddenly, several cicadas
flew out from the sore
and gathered on a tree in the courtyard,
wailing mournfully all night long.
The family summoned a shaman to divine the matter.
There was a female shaman who was quite adept at communicating with spirits and ghosts.
The shaman arrived.
She scolded toward the tree,
uttering sharp, reproachful words.
When questioned,
she replied:
"I saw a ghost dressed in black robes and a black hat,
perched among the branches,
pointing at the cicadas as if guiding them,
and saying these words:
'Beneath the eastern hall,
is where I dwell.
Honor me and receive blessings;
deceive me and bring disaster upon your three daughters.'"
The shaman further said,
"The one in black is the Kitchen God."
Niú Shuǎng did not believe her,
caught and killed the cicadas,
and drove the shaman away.
More than a year later,
nothing unusual happened.
Niú Shuǎng had three daughters,
who lived in the inner chambers.
One summer night, as the bed curtains were drawn aside,
Niú Shuǎng suddenly sensed a tall, large corpse lying on the bed before him,
stiff and covered with a white shroud.
Niú Shuǎng was terrified,
and whispered to his wife about it.
When his wife saw it, she was also greatly frightened.
Niú Shuǎng had once kept a treasured sword,
and he secretly took it to strike the corpse.
With a slashing sound, a scream came from inside.
When candles were lit,
the ghost had vanished,
but his eldest daughter in the inner chamber had been cut in half at the waist,
with blood flowing all over the floor.
Niú Shuǎng was shocked and grief-stricken, unable to steady himself.
The entire household wept in chaos,
with no one understanding the cause.
Half a year later,
on a dark night,
Niú Shuǎng arranged lamps in the corner of the room
and was just about to sleep when he felt a sudden unease in his heart,
startling awake.
He saw the same ghost on the bed again.
Niú Shuǎng, bewildered,
hurriedly struck it once more,
and it was severed and gone.
Chaos erupted in the inner chamber,
and the second daughter was also cut in half at the waist.
The whole family trembled in fear,
and those who discussed the matter urged Niú Shuǎng to move to another residence,
saying that one should not contend with ghosts and spirits.
But Niú Shuǎng stubbornly refused to change.
The following year, he saw the ghost again,
and it ultimately killed all three daughters.
Relatives and friends forcibly moved him to another house,
but Niú Shuǎng fell ill and died as well,
exactly as the cicada's words had foretold.
Later, there was a Huàyuè Daoist priest named Chǔ Chéngxiá,
skilled in exorcism,
who had long been on good terms with Niú Shuǎng.
Hearing of this, he came.
The commandery deemed this residence inauspicious,
and abandoned it.
Chéngxiá arrived and entered alone,
setting up an altar and keeping watch.
That evening,
thunderous sounds were heard inside,
and by dawn, after searching,
the house was torn apart and trees uprooted.
The Daoist priest reported to the commandery,
which ordered shovels and spades
to dig more than ten feet beneath the hall.
An ancient tomb was uncovered,
with an inscription reading "Tomb of Lady Zhuō."
The Daoist priest recounted
that during the night,
armored soldiers had initially fought with him,
but the ghosts were defeated and scattered.
Shortly after,
a woman,
around twenty years old,
knelt and bowed in apology,
saying she was Lady Zhuō.
Chéngxiá reproached her,
and she replied:
"It was not my fault.
This was predestined.
Niú Shuǎng and his daughters' lives were fated to end,
and moreover, they did not cultivate virtue.
Instead, they acted arrogantly and deceitfully,
so this was their own doing."
Chéngxiá then relocated the tomb,
and the residence was no longer haunted thereafter.
Lǐ Xián
Wáng Róng of Tàiyuán and his maternal cousin Lǐ Xián of Zhàojùn,
resided in the region between Xiāng and Wèi.
During the Yǒngtài era,
they had reason to travel to Jīngxiāng,
and took advantage of an official mission to travel by government post.
They stopped at Dèngzhōu,
and spent the night in the hall of a postal station.
It was summertime,
and the two men each occupied a bed in the eastern and western sections of the room,
while their servants rested in the outer quarters.
The two men conversed together,
and as evening approached, each retired to rest.
However, Wáng secretly could not sleep.
After the third watch,
the clouds and moon were hazy,
and Wáng lay watching the trees in the courtyard.
Their shade cast a rustling, desolate aura.
Suddenly, he saw a woman peeping from behind the kitchen screen,
who retreated and returned several times.
Soon, she emerged halfway,
wearing a green skirt and red blouse,
her plain face dazzlingly beautiful.
At that moment, he also secretly saw Lǐ rise and sit up,
beckoning to her flirtatiously.
Wáng thought that Lǐ had some prior understanding with her,
and also assumed the woman must be the wife of the station official.
Wáng then pretended to sleep to spy on what would happen.
Shortly after, Lǐ got up and approached the woman,
and they grasped each other behind the screen,
whispering intimately.
After a long while,
they went hand in hand outside the main gate.
Wáng stealthily moved to a shadowy spot,
and watched them from afar.
The two sat together,
talking and laughing with great familiarity.
After a while,
he saw Lǐ return alone,
walking very hurriedly.
The woman stood waiting outside the screen.
Lǐ entered the kitchen to fetch a candle,
opened and took out a book box,
his expression sorrowful and distressed.
He took paper and brush to write a letter,
and also took clothes and other items,
sealing and labeling them all.
Wáng secretly observed this,
thinking directly that he was packing clothes to give to the woman.
He could not bear to startle him,
so he waited for him to sleep,
intending to catch him by surprise.
After sealing the clothes,
Lǐ placed them on the bed and went back out.
Seeing that Wáng was still asleep,
he went out behind the screen,
and spoke with the woman.
After a long while,
they took a quilt and both entered a side courtyard of the lower hall.
In the courtyard was a hall,
inside which were a bed and curtains,
with dense, towering trees.
After they entered for about the time of a meal,
Wáng thought to himself:
"If I go and surprise them,
I will surely catch them in intimate acts."
So he took the pillow he had been lying on and went,
intending to startle them secretly.
As he reached the entrance and lifted the curtain,
he saw Lǐ lying on the bed,
while the woman was strangling Lǐ's neck with a shawl,
making choking sounds as he was near death.
The woman had a pale face,
over three chǐ long,
with no visible eyes or features.
She pressed down with all her strength to strangle him.
Wáng, in a panic, cried out in alarm,
and threw the pillow at her,
but missed.
The woman then fled.
Wáng took advantage of the momentum to chase her,
straight into the kitchen in the northwest corner.
She sat on the bed,
her head reaching the roof beam.
After a long while, she finally vanished.
The servants, hearing the shouts, all got up,
and saw that Lǐ had died,
with blood flowing from his seven orifices,
though his heart was still slightly warm.
They performed soul-summoning rites and nursed him,
and by dawn he revived.
Wáng took the sealed letter and opened it to look,
and found it was a letter to Lǐ's family,
expressing farewell and parting,
with the clothes and items as tokens of remembrance.
It did not state where he was going.
But the wording was solemn,
and reading it evoked sorrow and anguish.
When Lǐ was able to speak,
they asked him about it,
but he remembered nothing at all.
He only said that he vaguely dreamed of a beautiful woman,
who lured him away,
and he recalled nothing else.
An old official of the station said
that there was an old legend of a spirit in the latrine,
and during the Tiānzhōng era,
it had already killed a traveling envoy.
Wáng Róng would tell this story to everyone he met,
advising people not to sleep alone at night.
Lǐ Zhòu
Lǐ Zhòu was an official in Xǔzhōu,
with a manor in Fúgōu.
In the spring of the second year of Yǒngtài,
he was returning home for the Qingming Festival,
and was about to reach Bóliáng River.
Previously, there was a grave mound beside the road,
about twenty paces from the path,
with no grass on it,
where shepherd boys played.
That night,
Lǐ Zhòu suddenly saw a hole on the grave mound,
as large as a plate,
with a light shining from it.
Lǐ found this strange,
dismounted, and climbed the mound.
He saw five women,
dressed in splendid attire,
arranged according to the five directions,
sitting and sewing.
All were bending their heads toward the candles,
diligently working without pause.
Lǐ shouted at them once,
and all five candles went out,
and the five women also disappeared.
Lǐ was frightened,
mounted his horse, and fled.
Before he reached the main road,
five torchlights emerged from the grave mound,
and pursued Lǐ.
Lǐ ran but could not escape,
and when he waved his whip to fend them off,
it was set ablaze by the fire.
He traveled nearly ten lǐ.
Only when he reached Bóliáng River,
and a dog arrived,
did the lights finally vanish.
The next day,
he saw that his horse's tail had been completely burned,
and its thighs and legs were also scorched.
Thereafter, people called this place the "Grave of the Five Women,"
and it still exists today.
Yuán Zǎi
In the spring of the ninth year of Dàlì,
Yuán Zǎi, Vice Director of the Secretariat and Participating in Determining Governmental Matters,
was entering the court early,
when someone presented him with a literary composition,
and he ordered his attendants to accept it.
This person seemed to want Yuán to read it,
and Yuán said:
"Wait until I reach the Secretariat,
then I will look at it."
The person said:
"If you cannot read it,
allow me to recite one poem for you."
After reciting, he vanished,
and only then did Yuán realize it was not a human.
The poem said:
"East of the city, west of the city, the old dwelling places,
inside the city, flying blossoms scatter like willow catkins.
The sea swallow, carrying mud in its beak, wishes to descend,
but finding no one in the house, it flies away again."
Later, Yuán's household was destroyed,
and his wife and children were killed, it is said.
Xiāo Shěn
Xiāo Shěn was the son of Xiāo Mǐn, the Minister of Works.
During the Yongtai era,
he served as the magistrate of Chángzhōu.
He was greedy and cruel by nature,
yet he conducted affairs with some semblance of reason,
so the local people feared him.
Xiāo Shěn resided in Chángzhōu for three years,
during which he accepted bribes without limit.
In the fourth year, in the fifth month,
the gatekeeper saw over thirty riders in purple garments
entering through the gate from outside.
He went forward to ask their purpose,
but the riders initially did not speak,
proceeding directly to the main hall courtyard.
All the clerks in the hall saw them.
The gatekeeper hurried inside
and reported to Xiāo Shěn:
"Just now, over thirty riders led by a general in purple entered directly
without waiting for an announcement."
Xiāo Shěn asked:
"Where are these people?
How is it that I cannot see them?"
The gatekeeper went out to the hall,
and after a short while,
saw the riders emerging from within,
covering Xiāo Shěn with a white robe.
They walked out.
The gatekeeper again reported this strange event,
but Xiāo Shěn looked around without speaking.
The clerks escorted him to the gate,
and then he was seen no more.
Soon, crying was heard from inside,
and only then did they realize Xiāo Shěn had died.
Seven days later,
his younger brother Xiāo Yǔ was at the tomb
when he suddenly fell to the ground and spoke in Xiāo Shěn's spirit voice,
reproaching Xiāo Yǔ for failing to manage family affairs,
speaking for a long time.
He also said:
"That man Ān Hú
took two hundred dàn of my rice
and eighty bolts of my silk
to trade for profit.
Now, taking advantage of my death,
this Hu has betrayed my kindness
and has fled.
Tomorrow at mealtime,
search for and capture him."
Xiāo Yǔ returned home
and recorded the matter to report to his sister-in-law.
That same day, his sister-in-law also spoke in a spirit voice saying the same.
Xiāo Yǔ reported it all to the prefect Cháng Yuánfǔ.
Cháng Yuánfǔ ordered the sheriff to wait and capture him,
and indeed they caught Ān Hú.
The rice and silk were all recovered.
Initially, Xiāo Shěn also said:
"The rice was bought with my own money,
but the silk was obtained through corruption;
it should be donated."
Xiāo Yǔ ultimately donated the silk.
Lú Zhònghǎi
In the fourth year of the Dàlì era,
the retired scholar Lú Zhònghǎi and his paternal uncle Lú Zuǎn were guests in Wú.
One night, they drank at their host's place,
enjoying themselves greatly
and becoming heavily intoxicated.
The other guests from the commandery all dispersed,
but Lú Zuǎn vomited severely
and was in great distress.
As the night deepened, no one came to help,
only Lú Zhònghǎi attended to him.
Lú Zhònghǎi was filial and fraternal by nature,
using all the medicines in his chest to care for him.
At midnight, Lú Zuǎn died.
Lú Zhònghǎi was grief-stricken and panicked,
but feeling that his chest was still warm,
he was at a loss for what to do.
Suddenly, he recalled that rituals have the purpose of summoning the soul back from the darkness,
and that previously a strongman had spoken of the efficacy of summoning the soul.
So he began shouting Lú Zuǎn's name loudly,
continuously without cease,
tens of thousands of times.
Suddenly, Lú Zuǎn revived and was able to speak, saying:
"Thanks to your calling,
you saved me."
Lú Zhònghǎi immediately asked him about his condition.
He replied:
"I was just led by several officials,
who said that the Gentleman of the Inner Court ordered them to invite me.
I asked their names,
and they said they were from the Yǐn.
Hesitantly, I arrived at a mansion,
with very imposing gates,
and extremely lavish carriages and horses.
They led me inside.
The Yǐn came forward to greet me, saying:
'How is your drinking journey?
I often recall the days of breaking wine and indulging thoughts.
Suddenly, I receive your honored presence.
Though washing cannot fully express it,
I therefore welcome you.'
Then we went further in
and reached a bamboo pavilion to sit.
The guests were all in red and purple robes,
and we bowed to each other before sitting.
Attendants brought wine,
the cups and plates gleaming brightly,
musicians and dancers gathered like clouds.
My mood was becoming cheerful,
and I completely forgot about the matter of my journey.
In the midst of the banquet,
I suddenly heard your calling voice.
All the music played together,
my mind and spirit were already dazzled,
countless cups were passed around,
and I began to forget it.
After a short while,
I heard your calling voice again, and it was sorrowful,
which moved my heart with pity.
This happened several times,
and my heart grew uneasy,
so I requested to leave.
The host earnestly tried to keep me,
but I told him there was an urgent matter at home.
The host temporarily released me to come,
saying he might invite me again later.
He offered me an official position,
and I vaguely agreed.
Only upon arriving here
did I realize I was dead.
Had you not called me,
I would have completely forgotten that my body was here.
I have just left,
as if in a dream.
Now I only fear being summoned again;
what should I do?"
Lú Zhònghǎi said:
"The situation is extremely hidden,
and there is no other course of action.
Since the previous method proved effective,
we should employ it again."
So he burned incense and recited incantations in preparation.
While they were speaking,
Lú Zuǎn suddenly vanished again.
Lú Zhònghǎi called him once more,
his voice sorrowful, fierce, and urgent,
continuing until nearly dawn when Lú Zuǎn revived.
He said:
"Again, thanks to your calling me.
I had returned to drinking,
reaching a state of exhilaration.
Seated among the officials, I became thoroughly drunk.
The host was just about to issue the official document
appointing
me to the position.
Hearing your call, sorrowful and fierce,
I felt pity as before.
The host was surprised at my displeasure,
and I again begged to be released to return,
pleading repeatedly.
The host laughed and said:
'Most extraordinary!'
Then he released me to come.
Now, whether to stay or leave is undecided.
At cockcrow, activity begins,
and dark beings tend to rest.
I have also heard that ghosts and spirits do not cross boundaries.
Let us flee together;
is that acceptable?"
Lú Zhònghǎi said:
"That is the best plan."
They immediately prepared a boat,
traveled day and night, and recovered.
Wáng Chuí
Wáng Chuí of Tàiyuán
was good friends with Lú Shōu of Fànyáng.
In the early years of the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
they once traveled by boat back and forth between Huái and Zhè.
When they reached the side of the Shímén post station,
they saw a woman under a tree.
Her appearance was exceptionally beautiful,
her clothes were very splendid,
and she carried a brocade bag on her back.
Wáng and Lú said to each other:
"This woman is resting alone,
her bag is something we can scheme for."
So they moored the boat and waited.
The woman indeed asked:
"Where is the boat headed?
Could it accommodate a passenger?
My husband is ill in Jiāxīng,
and I wish to visit him now,
but my feet hurt and I cannot walk."
The two men said:
"The boat is empty and can take you on."
The woman brought her bag and boarded,
taking a place at the bow of the boat.
They then gradually tried to flirt with her.
The woman said with a stern expression:
"Just because I'm temporarily hitching a ride, must you be improper?"
The two men looked ashamed.
Chuí was skilled at playing the qín,
and used the qín to please her.
The woman was dazzlingly beautiful and radiant.
The two men were stirred and excited,
and said:
"Does the lady also play the qín well?"
The woman said:
"I practiced a little when I was young."
Wáng respectfully offered the qín to her.
She then played "Zhěn Fàn Nòng," the sound clear and cool.
Wáng said:
"I have never heard this piece,
it shows Zhūowénjūn's sincere heart."
The woman laughed and said:
"Entrusting myself deeply to Xiàngrú,
indeed."
They then gradually became intimate and close.
Her wit, humor, and clever speech were beyond description.
They looked at each other, moved and delighted.
That evening, she and Chuí had a tryst at the front of the boat.
Shōu was somewhat kept apart and deeply sighed with admiration.
Late at night,
Shōu secretly investigated the contents of her bag.
Looking inside,
it was full of skulls.
Shōu was greatly alarmed,
realizing she was a ghost,
but had no way to inform Chuí.
He heard their private intimacy, very affectionate.
Soon, day broke.
The woman had some business and temporarily went ashore.
Shōu told Chuí.
Chuí was terrified and said:
"What plan can we devise?"
Shōu said:
"You should hide under the bamboo mat."
They did as he said.
Moments later, the woman returned and asked:
"Where is Wáng?"
Shōu deceived her, saying:
"He just went ashore."
The woman was very agitated,
left Shōu and chased after Chuí.
Seeing him already somewhat far,
she abandoned the pursuit on the shore.
Together they rowed with double effort for several dozen lǐ.
She did not come.
At night, they hid the boat in a bustling place.
After midnight,
the woman arrived,
went straight into the boat,
and grabbed Chuí's head.
The woman had eyes on all four sides of her head,
was extremely foul-smelling,
and bit Chuí.
Chuí was in distress.
The two men shouted loudly.
People from all the boats came to help.
The woman then disappeared.
The next day,
a paper comb was found on the mat.
Chuí died after several months.
Wǔqiū Temple
The Wǔqiū Temple in Sūzhōu,
with its lofty mountains,
exquisite stone forests,
layered towers and battlements,
and deep, graceful green clouds,
makes visitors forget to return.
In the early Dàlì era,
a temple monk saw two figures in white clothes go upstairs at night.
They never came down.
Searching for them, nothing was found.
The next day,
on the high cliff, three poems were seen inscribed,
truly ghostly words.
The verses said:
"Though the realms of dark and light differ,
In life, we shared a love for letters.
To know where we lie in hidden sleep,
Look north of the mountain, two lonely graves."
"Tall pines bear much mournful wind,
Soughing, clear and sorrowful.
The southern hills join the dark mound,
The dark mound stands empty, towering high.
The bright sun shines in vain, warm and mild,
It does not light the long-night terrace.
Who knows the joy of the living?
How can the soul and spirit return?
Moreover, thinking of our dear ones,
Wailing, heart and liver are shattered.
Wailing, what more can be said?
Alas, and again alas."
"The way of immortals cannot be learned,
The body transforms, the soul wanders empty.
The bright day is not our dawn,
Green pines surround our door.
Though separated by life and death,
We still remember our children and grandchildren.
How to dispel sorrow and regret?
All things return to their root.
A message for the people of the world:
Do not weary of facing the fragrant winecup."
On the estate, there is a burial grove,
with ancient graves mound upon mound.
The writing still remains there.
Lǐ Zuǒgōng
was in Lúzhōu during the Dàlì era.
A clerk named Wáng Yǔ requested leave to return home.
Traveling at night outside the city walls,
he suddenly encountered outriders clearing the way and ordering people to avoid.
The clerk hid behind a large tree to spy,
thinking it strange that there were no high officials here.
Behind the guiding riders was a man in purple clothes,
with ceremonial guards like those of a high commissioner.
Behind was a carriage,
just crossing a stream.
The driver came forward and said:
"The carriage's yoke thong
is broken."
The man in purple said:
"Check the register."
Then several clerks were seen checking it, saying:
"We must take the spine sinew of the wife of Zhāng Dào from such-and-such village in Lúzhōu to repair it."
This was the clerk's aunt.
In a moment, a clerk returned,
holding two white objects, each several chǐ long.
They then crossed the stream and left.
When he reached his aunt's home,
she was still well.
After one night, she suffered from back pain,
and died by midday.
Dòu Yù
During the Dàlì era, there was a presented scholar named Dòu Yù,
whose family resided in the Huái-Hǎi region.
Having failed the imperial examination, he was traveling to Chéngdū,
but upon reaching Yángzhōu, he died without any illness.
He had long been friends with Shěn, a man from Wúxīng who served as magistrate of Huáiyīn.
They had been separated for years.
News and traces of each other were completely cut off,
and no one knew where he had gone.
Shěn was transferred from the Huái-Hǎi region to serve as magistrate of Jīntáng.
Upon reaching Yángzhōu, he lodged at a government guesthouse.
That evening,
the wind was gentle and the moon was clear,
and midnight was approaching.
Shěn felt as if he had lost something,
and could not fall asleep.
Suddenly, he saw a man dressed in white
walking in through the door,
sighing as he chanted,
as if harboring some unresolved grievance.
After a long while,
he chanted:
"My home lies by the Chǔ River's shore,
my body rests in Yángzhōu's hall.
Gazing at the moon alone, I pine,
tears soak my dusty robe, all signs of sorrow mine."
Seeing him,
Shěn felt he greatly resembled Dòu Yù.
He rose specifically to speak with him,
but before he could,
the figure vanished.
He then sighed and said:
"It has been so long since I parted with Dòu,
could he have become a ghost?"
The next day, he set off by carriage,
but before traveling a few miles,
there was a funeral procession on the road ahead.
Someone who recognized it said:
"This is the funeral procession for presented scholar Dòu Yù."
Shěn was shocked.
He immediately galloped back to the guesthouse,
and asked the guesthouse clerk,
who said:
"There was a presented scholar named Dòu Yù,
who traveled from the capital to Shǔ,
and died suddenly here.
The prefect ordered him to be buried two miles south of the guesthouse,
by the roadside—that is his burial place."
Shěn immediately went there to offer sacrifices, bow, weep, and then departed.
Shāng Shùn
Shāng Shùn of Dānyáng
married the daughter of Zhāng Chǎng from Wújùn.
Zhāng Chǎng served as Deputy Governor of the Capital,
and was buried east of the Chǎnshuǐ River,
ten miles from his country estate.
Shāng Shùn was selected for an official post in Cháng'ān.
After a long time,
the Zhāng family sent a servant into the city to fetch Shāng Láng.
At dusk, Shùn set off with him,
but the servant stole some wine and got extremely drunk,
and became separated from Shùn.
Unaware that the city gates had already closed,
with no other choice,
Shùn proceeded alone.
The sky gradually grew dark,
rain and snow fell together,
and moreover,
his donkey was very slow,
so he lost his way and did not know where to go,
simply letting the donkey lead wherever it would.
After traveling over ten miles,
he still could not see any village or estate.
He turned into deep grass,
suffering bitterly from the cold and shivering violently.
After a short while,
he reached a stream,
and south of the stream, he saw lamplight.
Shùn was overjoyed.
He approached,
and found several thatched huts surrounded by purple hedges.
He knocked on the door hundreds of times before receiving a response.
Shùn asked:
"I am a traveler from afar who has lost his way,
suffering from the bitter cold,
and wish to lodge here temporarily."
The reply came:
"The night is dark,
and with such rain and snow,
how can I know who you are?
Moreover, my dwelling is cramped and humble,
unfit for lodging."
They firmly refused him.
Shāng Láng then asked how far it was from here to Magistrate Zhāng's estate.
The reply was:
"About four or five miles southwest."
Shùn thought that since the road was near, he could reach it.
So he left the stream,
and traveled southwest for over ten miles,
but still did not reach the estate.
The rain and snow grew heavier,
and Shùn realized he would surely die.
Since he could not go on,
where else could he go?
So he tied his donkey to a mulberry tree,
and sat leaning against the tree.
After a moment,
he saw an object
resembling a lantern,
its light shining for several yards,
coming straight toward Shùn,
and stopping just over a foot away.
At first, Shùn was very frightened,
but then he asked:
"Could it be that the spirit of Lord Zhāng is guiding me?"
He then stepped forward and bowed, saying:
"If it is you, elder,
please show me the way back."
He saw a small path within the light,
so Shùn mounted his donkey and followed it.
As he drew slightly closer, the light moved,
