always staying about a foot ahead.
After traveling six or seven miles,
he saw someone holding a torch coming to meet him,
and the lantern light then vanished.
When the torchbearer arrived,
it turned out to be the Zhāng family's tomb guardian servant.
Shùn asked how he knew he was coming.
The servant said:
"Just now, I heard the young master calling me repeatedly,
saying that Shāng Láng was coming from the east,
and urging me to hurry and meet him.
This happened two or three times,
so I knew."
Shùn then stayed the night in the servant's hut,
and departed the next morning.
Lǐ Zǎi
In the seventh year of the Dàlì era,
while Liú Yàn, the Transport Commissioner and Minister of Personnel, was serving as Minister in the ministry,
Lǐ Zǎi, a Judicial Reviewer of the Dàlǐ Temple, acting as Investigating Censor,
was appointed to oversee affairs in Fújiàn.
Zǎi established an administrative office in Pǔchéng, Jiànzhōu.
Pǔchéng was seven hundred miles from Jiànzhōu,
and still considered a cool and pleasant place.
However, Zǎi feared the miasmic diseases,
and was unhappy with his duties.
After half a year, he died.
A day later,
he revived as if nothing had happened.
His family served him food,
and Zǎi ate as usual.
He told his family:
"I have already died.
The reason I have temporarily returned now
is solely to complete my official duties."
He then summoned his subordinates to settle unfinished matters,
ensuring they understood everything,
and handed over all affairs to them.
Afterwards, he wrote a formal letter to bid farewell to the Minister,
along with a will,
arranging family matters.
His wife, Madame Cuī, had died earlier,
and his only companion was a concubine.
He then said to her:
After I die,
when I meet my former wife in the underworld,
If I mention that I have you,
she will be very angry,
and may intend to cause you some harm.
What can be done about this?
The time for me to go is approaching,
so I should not linger long."
After speaking,
he divided his wealth and gave it to her,
ordering an attendant official to escort her back north.
The concubine then boarded the boat,
but the attendant official had some minor matters to attend to,
and did not set off immediately.
Zǎi learned of this,
summoned the attendant official,
gave him five strokes of the cane,
and ordered him to depart swiftly.
After completing his affairs and finishing his meal,
he then died.
Gāo Lì
Gāo Lì was
the father-in-law of Cuī Shìguāng.
One summer day,
in front of his estate under a mulberry tree,
he was watching people threshing wheat.
He saw a man riding a horse from the east,
who approached Lì and bowed twice,
saying:
"Please treat my horse's leg."
Lì said:
"I am not a horse doctor,
how could I treat a horse?"
The man laughed and said:
"Just use glue to stick it, and it will be fine."
Lì did not understand his words at first,
so the man told him:
"I am not human,
I am a ghost.
This horse is a wooden horse,
if you just melt some glue and stick it,
it will be enough for the journey."
Lì then took glue and boiled it until soft,
went out to where the horse was,
and saw that it had indeed turned into a wooden horse.
The problem was in its front leg,
so he glued it.
He returned the glue to the house,
and when he came out,
he saw the man already beside the horse.
The horse was very spirited,
and the man thanked Lì.
Then he mounted the horse and left.
Xiāo Yù
Xiāo Yù, the Prefect of Xìnzhōu, was orphaned young,
and did not know where his mother's grave was.
After several decades,
he intended to rebury her.
The old burial ground was in the capital,
and when he arrived,
he opened it,
but mistakenly opened the grave of Lú Huìchāng.
Realizing it was not his mother's,
he wailed in grief and returned.
Hearing that a mystic named Dào Huá from Héyáng
was skilled at summoning ghosts,
he sent generous gifts to invite him.
When Huá arrived,
Yù told him the whole story,
and Huá said:
"We can try."
So he set up an altar and purified himself with sincerity,
immediately summoning Lú Huìchāng,
a man
of imposing appearance and dress,
who scolded him:
"The grave of Prefect Xiāo's esteemed mother
has been encroached upon and confused with your tomb,
causing this mistake.
Quickly seek it out,
or else,
you will be punished day and night."
Huìchāng bowed twice and said:
"I am but a lowly servant,
the area I manage is a mound of earth three feet high,
covering ten lǐ square,
within my power to oversee.
Beyond that, I do not know.
But within my jurisdiction, there is no grave of Prefect Xiāo's esteemed mother,
I will search for it.
Let us set tomorrow as the deadline."
At dawn,
Huá and Yù went together.
After walking over a lǐ,
they saw Huìchāng running from afar, saying:
"Because of my search,
I have greatly disturbed the ghosts and spirits,
and now they are urgently pressing me with blame.
You two should leave quickly."
After speaking, he vanished.
The two retreated several hundred paces,
Looking back,
they saw a blackish-green vapor covering the ground,
which did not disperse until the end of the day.
Then Huìchāng came and said:
"I searched for you,
and was severely punished by the underworld officials,
now I am at my wit's end."
He asked to take his leave.
Huá.
returned to Héyáng,
and Yù wept bitterly.
From then on, he lived alone in one room.
One night, as if in a dream,
he heard a sound outside the door,
calling his childhood name:
"I am your mother."
Yù was startled and rushed out,
going outside to bow and welcome her.
He saw his mother,
who emerged from the darkness.
Yù met her as if she were alive,
and she said to him:
"Your utmost filial piety has moved heaven,
your sincerity has reached the star deities,
and the spirits have descended to witness.
Now that I can see you,
my heart is filled with sorrow."
Yù wailed for a long time,
and she sighed again:
"Our family's filial son,
is known to heaven,
even in the underworld,
you are admired by all.
Yet a filial son's ability to move heaven and reach the spirits
is not just about self-harm or destroying one's nature,
but lies in the depth of grief."
Then she discussed with Yù the principles of underworld retribution,
and the ways of fate and transformation.
She said:
"Fortune and misfortune depend on people,
one can only accumulate virtue.
Heaven looks down from above,
truly like shadow and echo.
Those who do good but receive no response
are all due to differences in heart."
After talking for a long time,
Yù, moved and comforted, said:
"I never expected to hear such words of praise,
now I have almost no regrets."
Then he recounted his regret about the mistaken grave,
and she said:
"I came also for this.
The years have passed,
you were young,
how could you have known?
On my grave there is already the tomb of Lǐ Wǔniáng,
and it has been leveled flat,
how could it be identified?
Tomorrow,
just look for where crows and magpies gather,
that is the spot."
She added:
"If you escort me westward,
you should use a two-soul carriage to enter the pass."
Asked why,
she replied:
"Because your aunt is here,
she also needs to return home."
Yù asked:
"Who is this aunt?"
His mother said:
"The aunt is your maternal grandmother,
I also call her aunt.
Pitying my loneliness,
she once came from Xiányáng to keep me company.
Later, because the spirits separated us,
she could not leave,
hence the need for a two-soul carriage."
After speaking, she left,
vanishing in an instant.
Yù wept until dawn,
then at the flat ground where the crows and magpies gathered,
he dug.
Indeed, it was the tomb of Lǐ Wǔniáng,
and below it, he found his mother's grave,
finally enabling a joint burial.
Zhū Zìquàn
Zhū Zìquàn of Wú County died in the Bǎoyìng era.
In the third year of the Dàlì era,
his daughter, a nun at a temple (named Mǒuyǐ),
sent her maid to the market to buy foreign-style cakes,
to serve as food for a vegetarian feast.
At the west bank of the river, the maid saw Zìquàn with several riders and about twenty attendants,
appearing as if he held an official position.
Seeing the maid, he sighed with emotion and asked:
"How is your reverend mistress?
Where are you going?"
The maid said:
"I was ordered to buy foreign-style cakes for the feast."
Quàn said:
"I happen to have some cakes here."
He turned and ordered his attendants,
giving her thirty cakes.
He also sent his regards.
The maid returned to the temple and told the nun.
The nun wept sorrowfully and did not eat;
the cakes were eaten by the others.
More than ten days later,
the maid went to the market,
and on the road saw Zìquàn again.
He inquired after her as before,
and again said to the maid:
"Your reverend mistress does not understand
the constant principle of life and death.
Why should she grieve and weep?
That is why she did not eat the cakes I sent.
Now take these thirty cakes back,
and make sure she eats them."
The maid returned,
but the nun still did not eat them.
Ten days later,
the maid was at the market
and again saw Zìquàn.
After inquiring after her,
he said to the maid:
"Now it is deep winter and bitterly cold;
I hear your reverend mistress has no padded clothes.
Now I am sending two bolts of silk,
for your reverend mistress to make winter garments."
The maid, obeying his order, took them back
and gave the silk to the nun.
The nun used one bolt to make trousers,
and kept the other stored away.
More than ten days later,
the maid again met Zìquàn,
who said to her:
"I have several dozen guests.
You may take the two bolts of silk
and have your reverend mistress prepare a meal in her room
for a midday feast.
Tomorrow at noon,
I will come there."
The maid returned,
and the nun sold the silk
to buy various delicacies from the market.
The next day they waited,
and at noon,
the maid suddenly fell into a trance for a long time,
then spoke in a spirit voice, saying the guests had arrived.
The maid rose to respectfully serve the food.
When the meal was finished,
the voice spoke again:
"Reverend mistress, take care.
I and the guests have eaten our fill,
and now we are leaving."
The maid escorted Zìquàn out the door,
and after a long time came to her senses.
From then on, he was not seen again.
Luó Yuánzé
Luó Yuánzé of Lìyáng
once traveled by boat to Guǎnglíng.
On the way he encountered rain,
and a man asked for a ride.
Yuánzé let him board the boat.
Observing that he seemed like an elder,
Yuánzé treated him with great hospitality.
The man had no other luggage,
only a single letter case,
which Yuánzé secretly found strange.
At night they slept together.
At dawn they reached a village,
and the man requested to "go ashore briefly;
I will return shortly.
Please wait here with the boat,
and be careful not to open the letter in my case."
Yuánzé agreed, and the man went ashore.
After a short while,
he heard crying from the village,
and realized something was amiss.
He secretly looked at the letter, which said:
"On such-and-such day, at such-and-such village,
so-and-so is to be taken."
The village name was exactly this one.
Yuánzé's name was listed below someone else's,
and Yuánzé became very frightened when the ghost returned.
The ghost reproached him:
"Why did you look at my letter?"
Yuánzé then came forward, confessed and prostrated himself,
pleading bitterly for mercy.
The ghost took pity and asked:
"Have you ever wronged anyone?"
Yuánzé thought deeply and said:
"In my whole life, I only seized ten *mǔ* of land from Zhāng Míngdào of the same county,
causing him to lose his livelihood.
That man is already dead."
The ghost said:
"It is this man who is accusing you."
Yuánzé wept and said:
"My parents are old,
and rely solely on me.
I beg for your gracious pardon."
After a long while, the ghost said:
"Considering your kindness in giving me a ride,
I will let you go now.
You must hurry home.
For three years, do not leave your house.
After that, you may extend your life by ten years."
He then disembarked and left.
Yuánzé returned home.
A little over a year later,
his father told him to go to the fields to harvest rice,
but he firmly refused.
His father angrily said:
"A farming family must work hard;
do you want to idle about and sleep sweetly,
spouting wild, demonic talk?"
He was about to beat him,
and Yuánzé had no choice.
He went out the door,
and immediately saw the former ghost,
shaven-headed and naked,
his back covered in festering sores.
He stepped forward and said:
"For your sake I have come to this state,
and I can no longer protect myself.
Now that we have met again,
I cannot let you go."
Yuánzé said:
"Let me bid farewell to my parents."
The ghost agreed.
Yuánzé told his father everything.
When he finished speaking,
he suddenly died.
His father deeply regretted this,
and died himself a little over a month later.
Lǐ Yuánpíng
Lǐ Yuánpíng was the son of Bó Chéng, the prefect of Mùzhōu.
In the fifth year of the Dàlì era, he was staying at the Dōngyáng Temple to study.
After more than a year, one evening,
suddenly a beautiful woman appeared, dressed in a crimson silk skirt and jacket.
Her appearance was exceptionally lovely,
and she was accompanied by a maidservant in dark clothing.
They entered another monk’s room in the courtyard where Yuánpíng resided.
Delighted, Yuánpíng hurried over to them,
asking where they were headed
and their names.
The maidservant angrily said:
"We have never met before,
yet you press upon us so abruptly—
this is not what one expects from a nobleman."
At first, Yuánpíng did not respond,
only requesting to pay his respects.
After a short while,
the woman emerged from inside.
They met with mutual joy,
as if they were old acquaintances.
After conversing happily for a long time,
she said to Yuánpíng:
"The reason I have come
is also to see you
and discuss matters of the past.
I am no longer human—
are you not afraid?"
Yuánpíng’s heart was already drawn to her,
so he felt no hesitation or doubt.
He said to the woman:
"Speak freely—
why should I be afraid?"
The woman said:
"My father once served as the prefect of Jiāngzhōu.
In your previous life, you were a gatekeeper in Jiāngzhōu,
constantly on duty at our household.
Though born into poverty and low status,
your demeanor and appearance were pleasing.
Due to karmic connections,
I secretly became involved with you.
We were together for only a hundred days
before you fell ill with cholera and passed away.
Thus, I dared not weep openly,
but my grief was many times greater than ordinary sorrow.
I have always recited the mantra of the Thousand-Handed, Thousand-Eyed Bodhisattva,
praying that in our next lives we would both be reborn into noble families
and marry each other again.
I marked your left thigh with vermilion ink as a sign.
Please look and see—
if there is vermilion there,
my words are proven true."
Yuánpíng looked and found it just as she said,
which strengthened his belief.
He then invited her to stay the night.
As time passed,
their affection deepened,
and their joy grew even greater.
As dawn approached,
she suddenly said to Yuánpíng:
"The time for my rebirth has come,
and I cannot stay any longer.
My heart is filled with regret."
With these words, she wept sorrowfully
and said:
"In my next life, my father is currently a county magistrate.
When I turn sixteen,
he will become a regional governor.
That is when we are fated to marry.
Until then,
please do not marry anyone else.
However, destiny is already fixed.
Even if you wish to marry,
it will not be possible."
With these words, she bid him farewell and departed.
Liú Cān
In the second year of the Jiànzhōng era of the Táng dynasty,
rumors spread in Jiānghuái that a fierce ghost had come from Húnán.
Some called it a hairy ghost,
some a hairy man,
and some a chéng.
Its name was not consistent.
Moreover, the ghost could transform in unpredictable ways.
People said the ghost enjoyed eating human hearts
and would take young girls and boys whole.
The people were terrified,
gathering in large groups to live together.
At night, they lit blazing fires and dared not sleep,
holding bows and knives for defense.
Whenever the ghost entered a household,
thousands of families would beat boards and bronze vessels to make noise,
the sound shaking heaven and earth.
Some people died from sheer terror.
Everywhere it was like this,
and official prohibitions could not stop it.
Formerly, Liú Cān, who had served as a merit official in Yǎnzhōu,
had long been active in the Huái-Sì region
and had settled in Guǎnglíng.
He had six sons,
all of whom were brave and fierce.
Liú led his sons,
armed with bows and arrows, to keep watch at night.
Several daughters were confined inside the hall,
while the young men patrolled outside.
After midnight,
the sky grew dark and gloomy.
Suddenly, they heard screams from inside the hall,
saying the ghost was already inside.
The young men were horrified.
Since the doors were shut,
they had no way to enter and rescue them,
so they kept watch and peered inside.
They saw a creature the size of a bed,
covered in bristling hair like a hedgehog,
three or four feet tall,
with limbs on all four sides.
It scurried around inside the hall.
Beside it was another ghost,
covered in black fur,
with claws and fangs like swords.
It placed the youngest daughter on the hairy bed
and then seized the next daughter.
The situation was critical.
The young men broke through the wall and rushed in,
shooting at the hairy bed.
The hairy bed fled,
and the ghost also ran away.
In a moment,
the ghost disappeared without a trace,
while the hairy bed ran eastward,
struck by hundreds of arrows
until it could no longer move.
One of them caught it,
grabbing its hair
and struggling with all his might.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
they both fell onto a bridge.
He shouted loudly:
"I’ve caught the ghost now!"
The ghost was trapped.
They hurriedly brought torches to assist,
but when they illuminated the scene with fire,
they only saw him clutching a bridge pillar.
Liú’s son’s hands were scratched and injured,
and the youngest daughter was left on the road.
A few days later,
a soldier in the camp saw a hairy ghost flying swiftly over the rooftops at night.
He shot at it but missed,
and his shouts alarmed many people.
The next day, he was punished.
Because of this, the authorities ordered the people
to beware of thieves
who might use such supernatural rumors to deceive.
Afterward, the incidents gradually ceased,
though no one knew why.
Yán Jìnglì
In the first year of the Xīngyuán era,
Zhǔ Cǐ rebelled in Cháng'ān.
There was a man named Yán Jìnglì who served as a secret messenger for Duàn Xiùshí,
and he secretly traveled out through the Fèngxiáng Mountains.
At night, he intended to reach the Tàipíng Lodge.
The lodge had been moved ten lǐ away,
and the old lodge had long been deserted.
Jìnglì mistakenly entered it,
only to be surprised by the overgrown weeds and the rough, uneven ground.
Immediately, two men in black robes greeted him at the gate and bowed,
then led his horse to the main hall.
He asked why the lodge was so desolate,
and the men in black robes replied:
"It is still habitable."
After sitting down,
he was treated with the same courtesy as at a regular post station.
Shortly after,
the men in black robes announced:
"The lodge official, former Héchí County Magistrate of Fèngzhōu, Liú Chù."
Jìnglì met him
and asked:
"Why is this lodge so overgrown and desolate?"
Chù replied:
"Today, the world is overgrown with brambles and weeds.
It is not only this lodge—
even the palace gates are overgrown with thorns."
Jìnglì found his words remarkable,
and his speech and reasoning were extraordinary.
Chù then said:
"The attendants of this lodge
have all fled and scattered."
He then pointed to the two men in black robes and said:
"These are both my family's Kūnlún slaves.
One is named Dàonú,
the other Zhīyuǎn.
They are temporarily serving here."
Jìnglì then examined the slaves closely by candlelight.
Under their black robes, they wore purple and white garments.
Their faces were distinctly Kūnlún in appearance,
and they had clear white characters imprinted on their faces,
confirming they were indeed Chù's family slaves.
He ordered someone to check the kitchen,
where a few maidservants were busy preparing food.
It was clear there were no other attendants.
After a long while,
a feast was served.
The food was exquisite.
Jìnglì dined with Chù
and ate his fill.
The servants all behaved properly,
so he retired to sleep.
Jìnglì asked Chù:
"Because I traveled at double the usual pace,
my horse is extremely exhausted.
Could I borrow another horse?"
Chù replied:
"That is a small matter."
By the fourth watch,
Jìnglì prepared to depart.
Chù again prepared a meal,
which was also proper.
Chù instructed Zhīyuǎn:
"Fetch the horse from the west stable
and escort the ambassador to the next lodge."
He also ordered Dàonú to saddle the horse from the east stable, saying:
"I will accompany the ambassador to the main road."
Soon, the horses arrived.
Jìnglì mounted the horse from the west stable and set off,
with Chù following.
After about two lǐ,
Chù turned back to bid farewell,
which was different from the usual lodge officials.
After parting for several lǐ,
Jìnglì noticed that the borrowed horse
had the foul smell of human excrement.
Soon, the smell grew stronger,
so he switched to his own horse to carry the load.
After traveling four or five lǐ,
the eastern sky seemed to brighten.
Officials from the next lodge came forward to greet him.
Jìnglì exclaimed in surprise:
"I have just left the lodge!"
They said:
"The previous lodge is deserted.
How did the ambassador stay there?"
He was greatly astonished.
When he asked about the servants and horses that had escorted him,
they had all disappeared.
The luggage they had been carrying
had been placed by the roadside over a hundred steps back.
Upon reaching the next lodge,
the lodge officials said:
"There was once a burial chamber for former official Liú Shàofǔ, the Héchí County Magistrate of Fèngzhōu,
located behind that lodge's garden,
but it has long been dilapidated."
Jìnglì returned to investigate.
The abandoned lodge was empty,
except for an ancient burial chamber behind the wall.
In front of the east stable was a wooden horse with a saddle,
and in the west stable was a tall wooden horse.
In front of the gate were two abandoned markers,
and before the burial chamber were several funerary objects shaped like people.
Gradually, he felt the smell of raw food in his throat,
and soon vomited what he had eaten the previous night,
all emitting a rotten, putrid odor.
It was the color of yellow clothing stained with dust.
This was the food offered to the deceased in the coffin.
The servants all vomited profusely,
and it took three days for them to recover.
Cuī Shūshēng
Cuī Shūshēng of Bólíng,
was heading to Yǒnglè Lǐ in Cháng'ān.
He had an old estate in Wèinán.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
he once returned to Wèinán during the Qingming Festival.
As he traveled to the area north of Zhāoyìng, among the mounds and ridges,
the day was already late,
so he rested his horse on the left side of the ancient road.
About a hundred paces away,
he saw a woman,
beautifully adorned and dressed in splendid attire,
crossing through the thickets and brambles,
as if she had lost her way among the pines and cypresses.
Cuī strolled leisurely,
As he gradually drew closer,
she used her sleeve to cover her face,
but her feet stumbled,
and she repeatedly seemed about to fall to the ground.
Cuī sent his young servant to approach and observe her,
and she turned out to be a peerless beauty of sixteen.
He then ordered the servant to question her:
"Why are you without companions as dusk falls,
wandering sorrowfully among these mounds?"
She remained silent and did not reply.
He then sent another servant,
to take the horse he was riding and pursue her,
offering his servant and horse to escort her.
The beauty looked back,
seeming to accept slightly,
so Cuī bent forward and slowly followed her,
to observe how far she would go.
The beauty mounted the horse,
and a servant led it forward.
After only a few hundred steps,
they suddenly saw three or four maidservants.
Gasping for breath with open mouths,
they stumbled over and said to the young lady:
"Where have you been?
We've searched for you in several places but couldn't find you."
They surrounded the horse and walked over ten paces,
where an elderly maidservant stood waiting.
As Cuī gradually approached,
she bowed and thanked him, saying:
"You, sir, took pity on our young lady for losing her way,
and generously offered your servant and horse to assist her.
Now that the day is already late,
would you care to come to our manor?"
Cuī asked:
"Why was the young lady wandering alone in such a sorrowful state?"
The maidservant replied:
"She became intoxicated with wine and ended up here."
They headed north for a mile or two,
and arrived at a grove of trees,
where the houses were very grand,
and the peach and plum blossoms were fragrant.
There were also seven or eight more maidservants,
who welcomed the young lady inside.
After a short while,
a maidservant came out,
conveying the mistress's message:
"Our young niece, while avoiding drunkenness,
fled the banquet and lost her way.
Fortunately, she encountered you, sir,
who took pity and provided a servant and horse.
Otherwise, as dusk fell,
she might have encountered evil wolves or seductive foxes,
and who knows what could have happened.
The entire household is deeply grateful.
Please rest for a while,
and we will soon invite you in."
Several maidservants came out again to wait and inquire,
as intimately as close relatives.
After a moment,
they invited Cuī into the residence.
After meeting,
they ordered food to be served.
After the meal,
When wine was brought,
they conversed leisurely:
"She is the niece of the Wáng family,
beautiful, charming, and exquisite,
unmatched in the mortal world.
We wish for her to serve you as your wife,
what do you think?"
Cuī,
being carefree and unrestrained,
bowed in thanks beside the seat due to the wine.
Soon, they ordered the young lady to come out,
and she was truly like a fairy.
He stayed for three days,
feasting and enjoying himself,
with nothing but joy and delight.
The Wáng family often called her aunt Yù Yí.
Yù Yí enjoyed playing chángháng with Cuī Shūshēng,
and she loved Cuī's lip balm boxes.
When Yù Yí lost,
she would repay with jade bracelets.
Cuī lost many times,
having previously bought six or seven boxes in Cháng'ān,
half of which he had already lost to Yù Yí,
but Cuī also won two jade rings.
Suddenly one day,
the entire household was greatly alarmed, saying:
"Thieves have arrived."
His wife pushed Cuī Shūshēng out through the back door.
As soon as he exited,
his wife had vanished,
and he found himself in a cave.
All he saw were withering yuán flowers,
the evening breeze rustling through the pines,
yellow buds and purple blossoms,
and dew on the grass wetting his clothes.
The jade rings he had won were still on his belt.
He retraced the path where he had first seen the beauty,
and saw his servants digging with shovels and spades at a burial mound,
already reaching the coffin.
He saw an inscription that read:
"The tomb of Yù Yí, daughter of King Zhào of Yuánzhōu.
In life, she cherished and valued her niece from the Wáng family.
The niece died first,
and later she was ordered to be buried together.
The coffin was solemn and intact.
When opened,
inside was a box,
containing six or seven jade bracelets.
Cuī compared them to what he had seen,
and they were exactly the same.
There was another box,
containing several lip balm boxes,
which were the ones Cuī Shūshēng had lost.
Cuī Shūshēng asked the servants,
"We only saw you, sir, enter the cypress grove,
and when we couldn't find you,
we searched and dug up this mound,
and indeed, we were not mistaken."
Yù Yí had called Cuī Shūshēng's servants thieves.
Cuī Shūshēng was moved by this,
and hurriedly reburied everything as it was.
Regarding Lǐ Zé,
in the early years of the Zhēnyuán era,
Lǐ Zé, the Junior Vice-Magistrate of Hénán, died.
Before he was encoffined,
a man in red clothes arrived,
presenting a card to offer condolences,
calling himself Attendant Sū.
After entering,
he wept and mourned especially sorrowfully.
Shortly after, the corpse rose,
and wrestled with him.
The family members fled in panic to the hall,
while the two closed the door and fought,
not stopping until evening.
Only then did the filial son dare to enter.
He saw two corpses lying together on the bed,
identical in height and shape,
appearance, beard, and clothing,
with no difference at all.
The entire clan gathered but could not tell them apart,
so they buried them together in the same coffin.
Regarding Lù Píng
Lù Píng of Wújùn was a man of noble aspirations and conduct from a young age,
with a radiant and pure spirit,
deeply faithful and modest.
His family resided in Chángchéng, Húzhōu.
He delighted in mountains and rivers,
and whenever he heard of a place of wondrous beauty,
he would travel a thousand lǐ to visit it,
his unrestrained wanderings never allowing him to settle peacefully.
In the third month of the yǐchǒu year of the Zhēnyuán era,
while traveling in Yǒngjiā,
he fell ill and passed away.
Píng had long been a close friend of Shěn Cháng of Wúxīng.
Cháng dreamed of Píng, his countenance haggard and worn,
saying:
"I traveled to Yǒngjiā,
and a severe illness has brought me to my end.
You are one who truly knows me,
and I wish to entrust my family affairs to you."
Cháng was deeply saddened.
They then reminisced about their past joys,
conversing and feasting for a long while.
Speaking of literature,
and discussing matters of emptiness and non-being,
Píng then said to Cháng:
"I present to you a poem titled 'Floating Clouds,'
to convey my feelings."
The poem read:
'Empty, empty, and void, void,
In the blink of an eye, within heaven and earth.
A temporary union forms this semblance,
I, too, am not my own body.'
He recited it sorrowfully several times.
As he was about to leave, he said:
"My funeral boat has already set sail,
and will arrive here tomorrow at noon."
He clasped hands and departed.
When Cháng awoke,
the memory was exceptionally clear,
so he wrote it down and recorded it.
At the appointed time, Píng's funeral boat arrived.
Cháng comforted the orphaned children and wept bitterly,
providing funeral assistance far exceeding customary propriety.
The poet Yáng Dān composed an epitaph for him,
fully expressing the divine resonance.
The inscription read:
"Heaven-born, our noble lord,
Graceful, refined, and cultured.
Departed, never to rise again,
His voice entrusted to the floating clouds."
Lǐ Shēng of Xúnyáng
This Lǐ Shēng,
during the Zhēnyuán era,
sat for the imperial examinations,
but failing to pass, returned to Xúnyáng.
His journey passed through Shāngluò.
Encountering the procession of the military governor of Hànnán on his way to court,
he was forced aside by the riders.
Looking around, he saw only endless green mountains,
and did not know where to go.
As dusk fell and his horse grew weary,
with no servants or companions,
seeing deep brambles and thorns,
and a burial chamber there,
Shēng then hid himself within it.
After the procession had passed,
just as he was about to proceed onward,
again not knowing how far the road lay,
he sighed and said:
"My taking refuge here,
is this not fate?"
So he remained in the burial chamber,
first bowing and praying:
"My home is at Lúshān,
returning south after failing the examinations,
arriving here I was forced aside by the vanguard of the lord's procession,
unable to advance,
and unable to retreat,
thus I have come here.
If the spirit has awareness,
I beg to be allowed a night's peace."
Afterwards, gazing idly about,
the wind and moon were clear and bright.
Though the suburban plains stretched for several lǐ,
everything could be seen distinctly.
There was another burial chamber,
a hundred paces away,
where he seemed to see a figure,
gradually drawing nearer,
it was a young woman,
adorned with solemn beauty,
her stature not quite reaching a chǐ,
arriving south of the burial chamber,
she entered a cavity.
Shēng listened intently,
and heard her say:
"Lady Jīnhuá respectfully informs Miss Cuī:
Tonight the wind and moon are lovely,
perfect for enjoying the view.
Such a time is hard to come by again,
I hope you will linger a while."
A voice from the cavity replied:
"As it happens, there is a distinguished guest
lodging in my dwelling.
I cannot bear to leave.
To miss a single night's enjoyment
is not a great loss."
The other person then departed,
returning beneath the burial chamber.
The next day, Shēng went to an inn to inquire,
and someone who knew said
it was a daughter of the Cuī clan of Bólíng,
who had followed her father, a minor official, to the region south of the Yangtze,
and died here,
and was thus buried in a simple grave.
Shēng, moved by this,
then made offerings of wine and food before departing.
Hán Yǎn
The Zhōnghé military governor and Palace Attendant Hún Jiān held a covenant meeting with the Western Fan,
but the Fan tribes betrayed
the agreement.
The administrative clerk Hán Yǎn was killed.
Yǎn had long been a friend of Lǐ Jī, the county lieutenant of Yuèyáng.
While napping during the day,
Jī suddenly dreamed of Yǎn, his hair disheveled and clothes draped,
his face entirely covered in blood.
Jī did not recognize him at first,
until he gave his name,
and they comforted and encouraged each other as in life.
Yǎn said to Jī:
"Now I follow the bald-headed ambassador to fill the Zhāng River,
the hardship and humiliation are beyond words,
I have come between duties to visit you.
After parting, I have a poem to present."
He recited sorrowfully:
"I have enemies from a hostile state,
No one can avenge them for me.
Whenever I reach the heights of Qín or Lǒng,
My wandering soul sobs alone."
As they were parting,
he said to Jī:
"I have long suffered hunger and thirst.
Tomorrow at noon,
to the southwest of your residence,
please set out wine, food, and paper money.
Thus our lifelong bond will be fulfilled."
Jī agreed.
When he awoke,
he waited in sorrow until dawn.
At noon,
he made offerings as instructed.
Suddenly, a black wind came from the west,
whirling over the feast,
sweeping up the paper money, wine, and food, carrying them all away.
The entire town came to witness it.
This was in the fourth year of the Zhēnyuán era.
Lù Xū
In the sixth year of the Zhēnyuán era, in the tenth month,
Lú Xù of Fànyáng lived in Qiántáng,
with a wife from the Yáng family of Hóngnóng.
His mother, Madame Wáng,
had become a nun in her youth,
residing at the Ānyǎng Temple in the county.
Lú Xù's house was north of the temple,
and they had a household maid named Xiǎo Jīn,
about fifteen or sixteen years old.
Lú Xù's family was poor,
and they borrowed food from the Guōxī Weir within the commandery.
The weir was a few dozen paces from their house,
and they often sent Xiǎo Jīn to work for the weir master.
There was often a woman, no one knew where she came from,
about forty-some years old,
wearing a turquoise skirt,
with disheveled hair and dragging black shoes,
who would go straight to where Xiǎo Jīn was sitting.
She said her surname was Zhū,
and she was the twelfth [in her family].
After a long while, she would leave.
This happened for several days.
At the time, the weather was cold,
and Xiǎo Jīn lit a fire to warm herself.
In a moment,
the woman arrived,
glanced at the charcoal under the bed,
and angrily said to Xiǎo Jīn:
"You have charcoal, yet you burn it and the smoke chokes me,
why is that?"
She raised her foot and stamped on the fire,
and the fire immediately went out.
She struck Xiǎo Jīn with her hand,
and Xiǎo Jīn fell to the ground unconscious.
Xiǎo Jīn had a younger brother, about four or five years old,
who was beside them and was greatly frightened.
He ran to report it at home.
When the family members arrived,
the woman had already disappeared.
Xiǎo Jīn lay with closed eyes as if asleep,
her body stiff as if bound.
They summoned a shaman to perform rites for her,
and she relaxed.
She then recounted the whole incident.
After several days,
the woman came again,
holding something like a wildcat,
with a pointed snout and curled tail,
the tail resembling a dog's,
and a body spotted like a tiger's.
She said to Xiǎo Jīn:
"Why don't you feed my cat?"
Xiǎo Jīn said:
"I've never done such a thing,
what can I do?"
The woman struck her again,
and Xiǎo Jīn fell once more,
and the fire was also extinguished.
The child ran home to report,
and when the family arrived,
Xiǎo Jīn was again lying with closed eyes.
They performed rites again,
and she recovered accordingly.
After this, they did not send her to the weir.
Several days later,
they had Xiǎo Jīn take a boat to the temple to fetch her mother-in-law.
When the boat reached outside the temple gate,
there was a pagoda in the temple courtyard.
Xiǎo Jīn suddenly saw carriages and horses under the pagoda,
with many officials in crimson and purple robes.
She stood still watching them,
and immediately felt she could not control her body.
In a moment,
the carriages and horses came out,
and those on the left and right made way.
Xiǎo Jīn then fell down.
She saw a man in purple robes whipping his horse,
asking who Xiǎo Jīn was.
Someone beside him answered.
Two men lifted her onto the steps,
so she would not be injured.
The man in purple halted his horse,
and urged the riders behind:
"Hurry along,
don't leave him waiting,
the feast is prepared."
Xiǎo Jīn asked the person beside her:
"Where are they going?"
The person said:
"To the home of the abbot of Dàyún Temple."
In a moment,
the carriages and horses had all passed.
People from the temple courtyard came,
and only then saw Xiǎo Jīn lying on the steps.
They were alarmed again and carried her back,
performing libation rites for her, and she awoke.
That evening was the winter solstice, the night before the new year,
and the Lú family was preparing the sacrificial offerings.
The ghostly woman suddenly flashed between the windows and doors.
Because of the commotion,
she could not enter.
Lú Xù tied two tiger-eye charms to Xiǎo Jīn's left and right arms.
Late at night,
the family members were tired and asleep.
The woman suddenly dragged Xiǎo Jīn,
and Xiǎo Jīn screamed in alarm.
The woman angrily said:
"Making cakes,
why don't you give me some to eat?"
The family members woke in alarm,
and Xiǎo Jīn then awoke,
but one tiger-eye charm was missing from her left arm.
Suddenly, a voice outside the window said, "Here, take it back,"
and something was thrown against the window with a sound.
They lit a candle and indeed found it.
Several days later, when they looked at it,
it was a dried eggplant wrapped in cloth,
no longer a tiger-eye charm.
On the morning of the winter solstice,
a female shaman came and sat down,
and as they were talking about the incident,
the woman arrived,
and Xiǎo Jīn immediately fell into a trance.
The female shaman was very frightened.
She was just eating,
so she took a wonton with her chopsticks,
placed it on the threshold,
and performed a rite.
At that moment, Xiǎo Jīn laughed and said:
"Laughing at Zhū the Twelfth eating wonton,
she pressed both hands on the ground,
and put her face to the wonton to suck it up."
Lú Xù used an ancient mirror to shine on her,
and Xiǎo Jīn then wept.
She said:
"Zhū the Twelfth's mother is in Yánguān County.
If she can have a meal of wonton,
and boat fare is provided,
then she will not come again."
Lú Xù did as she said,
and she then bid farewell and left.
Just as they were about to burn paper money,
they already saw the woman carrying money on her back.
After the burning was finished, she left,
and Xiǎo Jīn was then freed.
Meanwhile,
Xiǎo Jīn's mother had previously suffered from a wind illness,
and could not speak.
Suddenly, from the kitchen, she responded,
then entered the room,
and spoke in a low voice.
She went out the main gate,
and after a long while,
she lifted her clothes and strode in grandly,
as if riding a horse,
went straight to the hall and bowed, saying:
"Huā Róng pays her respects."
The family was greatly startled.
Huā Róng was an old maid of the Yáng family,
who had died over ten years ago.
Her voice and actions were exactly like hers.
They then asked Huā Róng:
"How did you get here?"
She replied:
"Young Master Yáng sent me,
to convey a message to the lady,
saying that though they have been apart long, all is well.
Young Master Yáng,
is Lú Xù's maternal uncle.
He wants Xiǎo Jīn and her mother,
so he sent me to fetch them."
Lú Xù conveyed a message in full,
earnestly pleading for them to stay.
She received the message and went out the door.
After a long while,
she returned and reported:
"Young Master Yáng has received the message,
and strictly orders that it is not necessary.
Quickly make paper figures to substitute for them."
They followed her words and cut out paper figures,
wrote their names on them,
and burned them.
She also said:
"Young Master Yáng is on the pagoda of Ānyǎng Temple,
playing backgammon with Yáng Èrláng."
They asked again:
"Who is Yáng Èrláng?"
She replied:
"A divine being.
There is also Mùxià Sānláng,
who is also among them."
They asked again:
"Who were the people in the carriages and horses Xiǎo Jīn saw earlier?"
She said:
"Those were spirits and demons.
Originally, they were Madame Zhū, the wife of the Wú family in the east neighborhood,
who was cruel and malicious in life,
and was punished by being reborn as a snake.
Now there is a hole in the oak tree at Tiānzhú Temple,
After a long time, it was able to transform and communicate with spirits,
so it transformed into a woman."
He asked again:
"Since it has a snake's body,
how can it wear clothes?"
The reply was:
"It stole them from a certain family's grave."
He asked again:
"What was the thing you held earlier?"
She said, "A wildcat."
Then she bid farewell and left.
He immediately poured a cup of wine and told her to drink it.
After she finished drinking,
he offered another cup to Huòbā in front of the gate.
He asked:
"Who is Huòbā?"
She said:
"He is the subordinate officer of Yáng Èrláng."
He asked again:
"When Yáng Èrláng comes and goes like this,
do people who encounter him all suffer misfortune?"
She replied:
"For divine beings like Yáng Èrláng,
their comings and goings are like wind and rain.
In the void,
they look down upon humans as if they were ants.
Those whose fate is declining will bring misfortune upon themselves;
he has no such intention."
After speaking, she left.
Only when she reached the gate did she wake up.
After waking, she asked about it,
but no one knew anything.
Later, Xiǎo Jīn dreamed at night of an old man
riding a great lion.
The lion was like the one ridden by Mañjuśrī,
its fur and colors vibrant and swift,
unbearable to look at.
Beside him were two Kūnlún slaves holding the reins.
The old man said to Xiǎo Jīn:
"I heard you were entangled by ghostly creatures,
so I came from afar to rescue you.
You are in a year of declining fortune,
so the ghosts marked you as a guest."
He said:
"They only took money in response to the marking,
and they themselves also obtained money.
If you had not encountered my arrival,
by the fourth month,
you would have been made a local ghost,
and you would not have escaped death.
Did you pick up an embroidered Buddha statue on a certain day?"
Xiǎo Jīn said:
"Yes."
"Look at this pattern,
embroider seven Buddha statues,
and seven banners."
After speaking,
he said again:
"Make eight,
I misspoke earlier.
Eight banners,
four in each set.
Also cut off a small amount of hair,
and purchase incense to make offerings.
Then your misfortune will be removed."
Xiǎo Jīn said:
"I have received your instruction.
Now I suffer from unbearable pain in my waist and back;
please mercifully remove it."
The old man said:
"That is easy."
He immediately ordered the Kūnlún slave to come forward,
told him to stretch out his hand,
then rubbed his fingers on the palm,
which turned as black as lacquer,
staining his fingers.
He then pressed two moxibustion points on her back.
Xiǎo Jīn then woke up,
recounted the entire event,
and immediately made the Buddha statues and banners.
Looking at her back,
she indeed saw two marked points,
so she applied moxibustion there,
and the back pain was immediately cured.
Lú Xù, being resolute and upright,
did not believe the story
and scolded her, saying:
"How could a sage
come to rescue a maidservant?
This must be a ghost."
That night, she dreamed of the old man again, who said:
"I pitied you for being in critical danger,
so I came to rescue you.
Your foolish master
actually calls me a ghost or demon,
but I will not hold it against him.
By the fourth month,
you will certainly become a local ghost.
However, by the end of the third month,
you must leave the boundaries of Hángzhōu to avoid this.
The jurisdictions of ghosts and spirits
differ by prefecture and county,
just as people have fugitive households."
Xiǎo Jīn said:
"Is Yúháng acceptable?"
The old man said:
"Yúháng is still part of Hángzhōu;
how would that help?"
She said again:
"What about Jiāxīng?"
He said:
"That is acceptable."
The old man said:
"To whose household in Jiāxīng will you go?"
She replied:
"I have relatives in a certain household;
I intend to go to them."
The old man said:
"That household is in mourning;
you are now avoiding ghosts,
yet you go to a ghostly household—
how will that help?
Where there is mourning, there are spirit altars,
and the ways of the spirits are interconnected;
they will then know your whereabouts.
If you go to an auspicious household,
then it will be fine.
Also, when you are about to depart,
take off one piece of clothing you cherish,
cut away the body of the garment,
leaving only the collar, seams, and fastenings,
and discard the rest.
Bind a straw man and dress it in this,
place it in a dark corner of the house,
and you change clothes and slip away secretly."
Xiǎo Jīn said:
"Yes.
The sage previously applied moxibustion to my back,
and it was cured at the time,
but now I still suffer from back pain."
The old man said:
"I did not remove your back pain earlier
so that you would know of my presence.
Do you wish to remove it now?"
Again, he rubbed black on the Kūnlún slave's palm
and pressed a point on her waist before leaving.
When she awoke and checked,
she indeed saw the marked spot,
so she applied moxibustion there,
and it was cured again.
After that, the woman did not come again.
By the end of the third month,
as instructed, she secretly went to Jiāxīng,
and from then on, nothing happened.
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ,
courtesy name Fēiqīng,
His ancestors were from Zhōngshān.
He was born intelligent and knowledgeable,
able to handle matters with ease.
Skilled in literature,
he achieved the utmost in all fields.
Though he upheld lofty principles himself,
disdaining ostentatious refinement,
his appearance was graceful and handsome,
and approaching him felt warm and gentle.
He was close friends with Cuī Xìn of Qīnghé,
who was also an elegant scholar,
collecting many antiquities.
Because Lǐ Zhāngwǔ was astute and perceptive,
whenever Cuī Xìn visited for discussions,
they would delve into profound subtleties,
exploring the original roots.
People of the time compared him to Zhāng Huà.
In the third year of the Zhēnyuán era,
Cuī Xìn served as Deputy Prefect of Huàzhōu,
and Lǐ Zhāngwǔ went from Cháng'ān to visit him.
After a few days,
he went out,
and on the north street of the market saw a woman of great beauty,
so he deceived Cuī Xìn, saying:
"I need to inform relatives and friends outside the prefecture."
He then rented a room in the beautiful woman's house.
The master of the house was surnamed Wáng,
and this was his daughter-in-law.
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ was delighted and had a secret affair with her.
After living there for over a month,
he had spent over thirty thousand coins,
while the daughter-in-law's expenses were double that.
Soon, their hearts were in harmony,
and their affection grew increasingly deep.
Not long after,
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ was tied up with affairs,
and had to return to Cháng'ān first.
They parted with deep affection.
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ left behind a bolt of mandarin duck brocade,
and also presented a poem, saying:
"Mandarin duck brocade,
how many threads are woven into its knot?
After parting, seeking to entwine necks again,
I grieve for the time before we parted."
The daughter-in-law gave a white jade ring in return,
and also presented a poem, saying:
Twisting the ring, I long for you;
seeing the ring, I remember you again.
May you always hold and cherish it,
circling endlessly without end."
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ had a servant named Yáng Guǒ,
and the daughter-in-law gave him a thousand coins to reward his diligence in serving.
After parting,
eight or nine years passed.
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ's family was in Cháng'ān,
and he had no way to communicate with her.
By the eleventh year of Zhēnyuán,
because his friend Zhāng Yuánzōng was living in Xiàguī County,
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ again met Yuán from the capital.
Suddenly remembering his past love,
he turned his carriage, crossed the Wèi River, and went to visit her.
At dusk, he reached Huàzhōu,
intending to stay at the Wáng family's house.
Arriving at the gate,
he found it silent with no signs of activity,
only a guest couch outside.
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ thought that perhaps the villagers had abandoned their trade for farming,
temporarily living in the countryside,
or that relatives and friends had invited them for a gathering,
and they had not yet returned.
He decided to rest at the gate,
planning to go elsewhere for lodging.
Seeing a woman from the eastern neighbor,
he approached and inquired.
She said:
"The elders of the Wáng family
have all left their work to travel,
and their daughter-in-law has been dead for two full years."
He spoke with her in detail,
and she said:
"My surname is Yáng,
I am the sixth,
wife of the eastern neighbor.
May I ask your surname, sir?"
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ told her everything.
She said again:
"Did you once have an attendant surnamed Yáng, named Guǒ?"
He replied:
"Yes, I did."
She then tearfully told him:
"I have been a woman in this village for five years,
and was close with the Wáng family.
She once said:
'My marital home is like a temporary lodging,
I have seen many people.
Among those who came and went, flirting with me,
all exhausted their wealth and property,
with sweet words and solemn vows,
yet none ever moved my heart.
Some years ago, there was a certain Lǐ, the eighteenth son,
who once stayed at my house.
When I first saw him,
I could not help but lose myself,
and later I secretly served him in bed.
I truly received his joyful love,
and now it has been years since we parted.
My longing heart
sometimes goes a whole day without eating,
or stays awake all night.
My family cannot be entrusted,
and I am also bound by my husband's comings and goings,
unable to meet him from time to time.
If someone comes,
I hope you will seek him by his appearance and name.
If there is no discrepancy,
entrust him to serve,
and convey my deep feelings.
If there is a servant named Yáng Guǒ, that is him.'
Within two or three years,
the daughter-in-law fell ill.
Before dying,
she entrusted me again, saying:
'I was originally of humble birth,
yet I was honored by the gentleman's deep affection.
My heart was always grateful,
and over time it turned to illness,
I knew I would not recover.
Regarding what I entrusted to you before,
if by chance he comes here,
I wish to express my regret from the nine springs,
the sigh of eternal separation.
I also beg him to stay here,
hoping for a spiritual meeting in a semblance of form.'"
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ then asked the neighbor woman to open the door for him,
and ordered his attendant to buy firewood and food.
Just as he was preparing the bedding,
suddenly a woman appeared holding a broom to sweep the floor,
whom the neighbor woman did not recognize.
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ asked where she came from,
and she said she was from the house.
He pressed further and questioned her,
and she slowly said:
"The deceased woman of the Wáng family,
moved by your deep kindness,
wishes to meet you.
Fearing it would cause alarm and terror,
she sent me to inform you."
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ agreed,
saying:
"The reason I have come
is precisely for this.
Though the realms of light and darkness are different paths,
and people all fear them,
my longing and affection are so deep,
I truly have no doubts."
After speaking,
the broom-holding woman left joyfully.
After a moment, she appeared at the door,
then was no longer seen.
He prepared food and drink,
and called out in offering.
After eating and drinking himself,
he rested peacefully.
Around the second watch,
the lamp was to the southeast of the bed,
when suddenly it grew slightly dim,
and this happened repeatedly.
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ knew in his heart that something was about to change,
so he ordered the candle to be moved against the wall,
placed in the southeast corner of the room.
Soon, he heard a rustling sound from the north corner of the room,
as if a human form
was slowly approaching.
When it was five or six paces away,
he could discern its appearance.
Looking at its clothing,
it was the master's daughter-in-law.
No different from when he had seen her before,
only her movements were somewhat floating and hurried,
and her voice light and clear.
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ got out of bed,
welcomed her, embraced her, and took her hand,
their intimacy as joyful as in life.
She said:
"Since entering the underworld records,
I have forgotten all my relatives,
only my thoughts of you, sir,
remain as in the past."
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ became even more intimate with her,
and there was nothing unusual,
except she repeatedly asked him to check for the morning star.
If it appeared,
she would have to return,
and could not stay long.
Every time after their joyful union,
he would earnestly entrust the neighbor woman, Yáng shì,
saying:
"If not for this person,
who could convey my hidden sorrow?"
When the fifth watch arrived,
someone announced it was time to return.
The young wife wept as she rose from the bed,
and arm in arm with Zhāngwǔ, they went out the door.
Gazing up at the Milky Way,
she then choked with sobs of grief and lament.
Returning to the room,
she herself untied a brocade pouch from her skirt sash,
and from the pouch took out an object to give him.
Its color was dark blue-green,
its substance firm and dense,
resembling jade yet cold,
shaped like a small leaf.
Zhāngwǔ did not recognize it.
The young wife said:
"This is what is called a Mòhé treasure,
originating from the Mysterious Garden of Kūnlún,
where even there it is not easily obtained.
I recently, while at the Western Peak amusing myself with the Jade Capital Fūrén,
saw this object among many precious pendants.
Loving it, I inquired about it,
and the Fūrén then lent it to me, granting it,
saying:
'Whenever the immortals of the grotto-heavens obtain such a treasure,
they all consider it an honor.'
Because you, sir, follow the Mysterious Way,
and possess refined discernment,
I therefore offer it to you.
I constantly wish you to treasure it;
this is not something found in the human world."
She then presented a poem, saying:
"The River of Stars has already tilted,
my spirit and soul wish to transcend.
I pray you, sir, embrace me once more,
from now until heaven's end, we part from here."
Zhāngwǔ took a white jade precious hairpin to reciprocate,
and also replied with a poem:
"Parted by the barrier of darkness and light,
how could I have expected this fine meeting?
How could I decline this repeated farewell?
What I sigh for is: where will you go?"
Thereupon they held each other and wept.
After a long while,
the young wife again presented a poem:
"In the past, parting held hope of later meeting;
today's separation is until heaven's end.
Fresh sorrow and old regrets,
for a thousand ages sealed within the depths of the springs."
Zhāngwǔ replied:
"Future meetings, distant and uncertain;
past regrets already press upon us.
On the road of parting, no means to send word;
by what means can I convey my heart?"
Having intimately recounted their farewell,
she then turned back toward the northwest corner.
Walking several steps,
she still looked back, wiping her tears,
saying:
"Lǐ láng, do not abandon,
remember this person beneath the springs."
Again, choking with sobs, she stood still.
Seeing the sky about to brighten,
she hurriedly hastened to the corner,
and then was seen no more.
Only the empty room remained silent and deep,
the cold lamp half-extinguished, that was all.
Zhāngwǔ then packed his belongings hastily,
and returned from Xiàguī to Cháng'ān's Wǔdìng Fort.
The officials of Xiàguī commandery and Zhāng Yuánzōng brought wine for a feast.
When they were merry with drink,
Zhāngwǔ, filled with longing,
thereupon composed a poem on the occasion:
"Water does not flow west to return, the moon is briefly full;
it makes one melancholy by the side of the ancient city.
Desolate, tomorrow morning at the forked road,
knowing when we may meet again, in what year?"
Finishing the recitation,
he bid farewell to the commandery officials.
Walking alone for several miles,
he again recited it to himself.
Suddenly he heard a sigh of admiration in the empty air,
its tone mournful and distressed.
Listening more carefully,
it was Wáng shì's young wife.
She herself said:
"In the underworld, each has their allotted place.
Now parting here,
there is no day for us to meet again.
Knowing your longing affection,
I therefore risk the underworld's reprimand,
to come from afar to see you off.
Take utmost care of yourself."
Zhāngwǔ was even more moved by her.
Upon reaching Cháng'ān,
speaking with his fellow Daoist, Lǒngxī Lǐ Zhù,
he too, moved by her sincerity, composed a poem:
"The stone sinks, the Liáo Sea is vast;
the sword parts, the Chǔ sky is long.
Knowing there is no day for reunion,
my parting heart fills the setting sun."
After Zhāngwǔ took up duties in the Eastern Peace Chancellor's office,
he found leisure to summon a jade artisan to examine the Mòhé treasure he had obtained.
The artisan did not
know it,
and dared not carve it.
Later, when sent on a mission to Dàliáng,
he again summoned a jade artisan,
who could roughly identify it.
Thereupon, following its shape,
he carved it into the likeness of an oak leaf.
When sent on a mission to the capital,
he often kept this object stored within his robes.
Reaching the eastern street of the market,
he chanced to see a foreign monk,
who suddenly approached his horse, kowtowed, and said:
"You, sir, have a precious jade in your bosom;
I beg to see it once."
He then led him to a quiet place and opened it for viewing.
The monk held and admired it for some time,
then said:
"This is a supreme object from the heavens,
not something found in the human world."
Zhāngwǔ later traveled to and from Huàzhōu,
visiting the surviving Yáng Liùniáng,
and to this day it has not ceased.
Lǐ Jùn
Lǐ Jùn, who later became the Prefect of Yuèzhōu, sat for the imperial examinations repeatedly
but failed to pass each time.
In the second year of the Zhēnyuán era,
he had an old friend named Bāo Jí, who was the Director of the National University.
Bāo Jí had connections with the chief examiner,
and he helped Lǐ Jùn succeed.
The day before the results were announced,
Bāo Jí was supposed to inform the authorities of Lǐ Jùn’s name.
Early in the fifth watch,
Lǐ Jùn went to wait for Bāo Jí,
but the neighborhood gate was still closed,
so he stopped his horse beside the gate.
Nearby, there was a cake seller,
whose steam rose warmly.
A clerk, who looked like a courier from another prefecture,
with a small bag and a felt hat,
sat beside him,
showing a clear desire for the cakes.
Lǐ Jùn bought some for him to eat,
and the guest was very pleased,
eating several pieces.
Soon, the neighborhood gate opened,
and everyone rushed out.
The guest alone approached Lǐ Jùn’s horse and said:
“I wish to speak with you privately.”
Lǐ Jùn dismounted to listen.
“I am an underworld clerk delivering the list of successful examination candidates.
Are you not one of them?”
Lǐ Jùn said:
“I am.”
The guest said:
“The list to be submitted to the hall is here;
you may search for yourself.”
He then showed it to him.
Lǐ Jùn’s name was not on it,
and he wept, saying:
“I have toiled with brush and inkstone
for over twenty years,
and have been a candidate for ten years.
Now my name is absent again;
will I never succeed?”
The guest said:
“Your success will come
more than ten years from now,
with great rank and fortune.
If you wish to obtain it now,
it is not impossible.
However, your allotted lifespan will be halved,
and you will face many hardships.
You will only attain a prefecture-level post.
What do you think?”
Lǐ Jùn said:
“What I seek is fame;
to gain fame is enough.”
The guest said:
“If you can bribe the underworld clerk a little,
right here,
I can replace the name of someone with the same surname with yours.
Is that acceptable?”
Lǐ Jùn asked:
“How much is needed?”
The guest said:
“Thirty thousand strings of underworld coins.
I am grateful for your kindness and speak honestly:
I dare not take the money myself;
it will be given to the clerk in charge of the documents.
You may deliver it tomorrow at noon.”
He then handed Lǐ Jùn a brush,
allowing him to write his own name.
Above was the name of the former Junior Mentor to the Heir Apparent, Lǐ Yíjiǎn.
Lǐ Jùn wanted to erase it,
but the guest quickly said:
“No,
this person’s fortune is too great;
it cannot be easily altered.”
Below was the name Lǐ Wēn.
The guest said:
“This will do.”
So Lǐ Jùn erased the character “Wēn”
and wrote the character “Jùn.”
The guest quickly rolled up the document and left, saying:
“Do not break the agreement.”
Soon after, Lǐ Jùn went to see Bāo Jí.
Bāo Jí had not yet put on his official cap.
Hearing of Lǐ Jùn’s arrival,
he came out angrily, saying:
“I have deep ties with the chief examiner;
a single word from me could secure you the top rank.
Why are you so impatient?”
He repeatedly asked:
“Do you think I speak lightly?”
Lǐ Jùn bowed twice and replied:
“I am desperate for fame;
if you grant me this favor, it will be decided today.
Now, on the morning the results are to be announced,
I risk reproach to pay my respects.”
Bāo Jí murmured assent,
but his expression remained displeased.
Lǐ Jùn grew even more anxious.
He changed his clothes and waited for Bāo Jí to leave, then followed him.
Passing the eastern corner of the imperial city,
they met an official from the Ministry of Rites carrying the list,
on his way to the Secretariat.
Bāo Jí bowed and asked:
“Was our earlier discussion successful?”
The official said:
“I know I have offended you;
even bearing a rod would not suffice as apology.
However, pressured by powerful authority,
I could not fulfill your esteemed request.”
Bāo Jí, believing their friendship was deep,
had thought nothing would obstruct it.
Hearing this, he angrily said:
“The reason Jì Bù was renowned throughout the world
was his ability to keep promises.
Now you have broken your word to me,
likely because my office is insignificant.
Our lifelong friendship
ends today!”
He left without bowing.
The official chased after him, saying:
“Pressed by powerful nobles,
I could not retain the name.
Relying on our deep bond,
I overlooked formalities,
and now you blame me so.
I would rather offend the powerful!”
He invited Bāo Jí to examine the list together
and erase a name to insert another.
Bāo Jí opened the list
and saw the name Lǐ Yíjiǎn.
He wanted to erase it,
but the official quickly said:
“This person was arranged by the chancellor;
he cannot be removed.”
Pointing to the name Lǐ Wēn below,
he said:
“This one will do.”
So he erased the character “Wēn”
and wrote the character “Jùn.”
When the results were announced,
Lǐ Jùn’s name was indeed in the previously indicated place.
At noon that day,
Lǐ Jùn followed the others to give thanks,
unable to keep his appointment with the cake guest.
As dusk approached and he was about to return,
he met the cake guest on the road.
The guest wept, showing his back, and said:
“Because of you,
I was beaten with a rod.
The document clerk is about to investigate;
I must seek other means.”
Lǐ Jùn stopped him
and saw his back bore severe rod marks.
Startled, Lǐ Jùn apologized
and asked:
“What should I do?”
The guest said:
“Tomorrow at noon,
deliver fifty thousand strings of cash,
and you may avoid the calamity of investigation.”
Lǐ Jùn said:
“Agreed.”
When the time came, he burned the money,
and the guest was never seen again.
However, after Lǐ Jùn began his official career,
investigations, demotions, and transfers
followed him incessantly.
He only attained the position of Prefect of Yuèzhōu,
and not long after, he died.
Lǐ Chì
During the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a presented scholar from Wújùn named Lǐ Chì,
who was traveling to Mǐn with Zhào Mǐnzhī.
When they reached Xìn'ān in Qú Prefecture,
thirty *li* from the county seat,
they lodged at a guesthouse.
In the middle of the night,
suddenly a woman entered the courtyard.
Chì, in his sleep, abruptly rose and descended the steps,
exchanging bows with her.
After a long while, he went back up to the hall,
opened his trunk to fetch paper and brush,
and wrote a letter to his relatives,
saying:
"I have been chosen by the Guō family to be their son-in-law."
The wording was repetitive.
When finished,
he sealed it in the trunk.
He then went back down to the courtyard,
where the woman pulled off his headband and strangled him with it.
Mǐnzhī ran out shouting loudly,
and the woman then gathered the headband and fled.
When they looked at the letter,
Chì had acted as if in a dream.
The next day,
they traveled together again.
When they stopped south at the Jiànzhōng postal station,
Chì disappeared again in broad daylight.
Mǐnzhī hurried to the latrine,
where he saw Chì sitting on the bed,
who angrily said to Mǐnzhī:
"I was just about to perform the rites of gratitude,
but you startled me."
After ten days they reached Mǐn.
Among the local officials was an old acquaintance of Chì's,
who hosted a banquet. During the feast,
Chì disappeared again.
Mǐnzhī quickly searched the latrine,
and found Chì lying stiff on the ground,
already breathless.
Wéi Pǔ
There was a man named Wéi Pǔ,
who, as a Registrar of Shòuzhōu, was traveling to the capital for official selection.
Arriving at an inn in Wénxiāng,
just as he was about to eat,
suddenly a man came forward and bowed, saying:
"Your servant, Guī Yuánchǎng,
has long been skilled in handling whips and reins.
I wish to serve as a menial laborer in your household."
Pǔ looked at him;
his clothes were very dirty, but his spirit was bright and vigorous.
So he asked him:
"Where have you come from?"
He replied:
"I was formerly employed by the Sixth Gentleman, Féng, who holds office in Hézhōng.
For many years,
I served diligently,
and was greatly trusted and favored.
Yesterday, the Sixth Gentleman came here with the Fourth Gentleman, Xuānyuán, from Jiàngzhōu,
to seek Judge Biàn to buy a belt.
I, being subordinate, begged for the price of tea and wine,
which led to words being exchanged.
The Sixth Gentleman accused me of deceit,
and dismissed me, leaving me stranded here.
I am a lowly servant,
and moreover have scant resources.
Without an official pass,
I cannot cross the barrier gates.
I have learned that the Twenty-second Gentleman is heading west.
If I could thereby return,
my wish would be fulfilled.
If you do not reject my stubborn lowliness,
and would ultimately grant me the use of your whip,
such would be my humble lot,
and what fortune would that be!"
Pǔ agreed.
After the meal,
they traveled over ten *li*.
Guī complied with every gesture and glance,
anticipating wishes before they were spoken.
Pǔ greatly felt he had found a useful man.
Soon they rested at a tea shop.
Dozens of carts happened to arrive,
just unharnessing the oxen
to let them graze on grass by the roadside.
Guī hurried over to the oxen,
and with his hand struck one ox's leg.
The ox immediately cried out in pain and could not move forward.
The owner at first did not see this,
and was about to hastily seek a veterinarian.
Guī said to him:
"I have often worked as a veterinarian;
let me treat this ox for you."
He then pinched a little crushed earth from beneath the wall,
applied it to the ox's leg,
and swiftly drove the ox for several dozen steps.
The ox then returned to normal.
The crowd all sighed in admiration.
The owner then offered a reward.
two catties of tea,
which Guī immediately presented to Pǔ, saying:
"This worthless servant is fortunate to have received your promise.
Wishing to offer what little skill has obtained,
I emulate one presenting wild greens."
Pǔ pitied him even more.
When they stopped at Tóngguān,
the innkeeper had a young child playing by the gate.
Guī was seen pinching the child's back with his hand.
The child immediately fainted in shock,
and did not wake for the time of a meal.
The owner said:
"This condition is due to an evil affliction."
He urgently called for Èrniáng.
She arrived after a long while.
Èrniáng was a shaman.
Upon arriving, she used a *pipa* to summon the spirits.
After yawning and sneezing for a long time,
she said:
"The Third Gentleman has arrived.
He conveys to the host:
'This is a haunting by a guest ghost.
I shall now record it.'"
She described his appearance and clothing—
it was exactly Guī.
She also said:
"If you bathe him with orchid-scented water,
this affliction will be removed."
Following her words, the child recovered immediately.
Pǔ, seeing what Guī had done,
already disliked him.
And after what the shaman said,
when called, Guī did not come.
The next day they traveled again,
stopping west of Chìshuǐ.
By the roadside they suddenly saw Yuánchǎng,
wearing tattered purple robes,
as if carrying a burden and walking with heavy, backward glances.
He said:
"I dare not feel ashamed,
but I could not face the Twenty-second Gentleman.
I am a guest ghost.
Regarding yesterday's events,
I dare not speak further.
I have already been reprimanded by the Divine Lord of Huàyuè.
The Third Gentleman mentioned by the shaman
is Jīntiān.
Because I was in this territory,
I could not wander idly,
and received a severe flogging.
Just now I saw the Twenty-second Gentleman.
When you reach the capital, you will obtain the magistracy of this prefecture.
There is no need for worry.
On another day, I will also wait here for your returning carriage."
Pǔ said:
"Those you mentioned earlier—the Sixth Gentleman Féng and the others—
are they not all human?"
Guī said:
"The Sixth Gentleman Féng is named Féng Yí,
that is, the Earl of the River.
He is a beloved son of the Xuānyuán Emperor.
Judge Biàn is named Biàn Hé,
the one whose feet were amputated in ancient times.
He is skilled at discerning treasures.
The underworld appointed him as Judge of the Jīngshān Jade.
The servants and retainers of the Xuānyuán household
are intolerant even in minor matters.
They abruptly caused me to lose the Sixth Gentleman Féng's favor.
My current difficulties and stumbles
truly stem from this."
Pǔ asked:
"How does Féng get to be sixth?"
He replied:
"Féng is a water official.
Water's completed number is six.
Thus, of the Yellow Emperor's four sons,
Xuānyuán Fourth Gentleman
is the youngest among them."
That year, Pǔ was selected and appointed Magistrate of Huòqiū,
as predicted.
When he went to assume his post and reached this place,
although he saw nothing,
he felt as if something were there, offering a silent sacrifice.
Zhèng Xún,
during the Zhēnyuán era, passed the imperial examination and attained the jìnshì degree,
was appointed to the post of Diǎnyí at the Ménxià Province,
ranking thirty-fifth.
His country residence was located five or six lǐ south of Huàyīn County,
and was considered the finest spot in the entire county.
Xún had three brothers,
named Jiōng,
Jì,
and Táo.
Táo and Xún
both enjoyed scholarly reputations and contemporary acclaim,
and the county magistrate along with the local gentry all held them in high esteem.
Xún was involved with supply and distribution at the Wèi Bridge,
and the administrative assistant Gāo Shūràng was on close terms with him, both officially and privately.
Xún often went to him seeking assistance.
Gāo prepared a meal of sliced fish for him,
but that very night,
Xún suddenly fell ill with violent cholera and died.
As it was the height of summer,
they could not wait for his family to arrive,
so they immediately prepared a coffin, burial garments, and shrouds to enshroud him.
Funerary objects, servant figurines, and horse figurines
were all exquisitely prepared.
On the backs of the servant figurines were inscribed:
one named Yīng'ér,
and one named Gǔzi.
Among the horses was a blue one,
inscribed with the name Sǎdòucōng.
Over ten days later,
the coffin was returned to his villa in Huàyīn.
At that time, a local gentleman named Lǐ Dàogǔ had been traveling in Guóchuān for half a month,
and was unaware of Xún's death.
On his way back, as he reached the road near the Yǒngfēng Granary west of Tóngguān,
he suddenly encountered Xún coming from the north.
Xún's carriage and attendants were very grand,
and Lǐ said:
"It's been only ten days since we parted;
why is your entourage so splendid?"
Xún, looking cheerful and in high spirits, said to Lǐ:
"It's all thanks to old Gāo from the Wèi Bridge."
He then called his two attendants, Yīng'ér and Gǔzi, to greet Lǐ Dàláng.
Lǐ teased, saying:
"A literary scholar in this enlightened age,
yet you keep falcons and hawks?"
Xún also pointed to the horse he was riding and said:
"And please take a look at my servant's horse, Sǎdòucōng."
Lǐ said:
"I am quite envious; what do you think?"
Xún replied:
"If you diligently cultivate virtuous conduct,
attaining such things is not difficult."
They then rode side by side,
until they reached Yěhú Quán.
Lǐ wanted to invite him to stay for a meal,
but Xún tapped his horse with his whip and passed by, saying:
"My home is just a stone's throw away;
why bother with a meal?"
After a short while,
they arrived east of the Huàyīn Yuè Temple.
Xún bowed to Lǐ and said:
"From here, I'll take the direct path home."
Lǐ said:
"Let me accompany you to the county town;
it's not out of my way."
Xún said:
"I've been away from home for half a month,
and need to return early."
He firmly refused to pass by the Yuè Temple.
A moment later,
Lǐ reached the county town
and asked a clerk:
"Where are the magistrate and the other officials?"
The clerk replied:
"They have just gone to the south of the county to offer condolences to the thirty-fourth son of the Zhèng family."
Lǐ asked:
"What are they condoling?"
The clerk said:
"The thirty-fifth son of the Zhèng family,
passed away at the Wèi Bridge at the beginning of this month,
and his coffin was returned to his villa last night."
Lǐ laughed and said:
"I just came with Zhèng from Tóngguān."
All the clerks and people in the county said it was no lie,
leaving Lǐ astonished.
Still not fully believing it,
he immediately whipped his horse and galloped
toward the Zhèng family villa.
On the way, he encountered the county clerk Cuī Pín, the deputy magistrate Péi Xuán, the registrar Lú Shìqióng, and the sheriff Zhuāng Rú,
along with his brother Zhuāng Gǔ, and local gentlemen Wéi Nà and Guō Cúnzhōng,
all returning from the Zhèng family villa.
Stopping their horses to converse,
Lǐ was greatly shocked,
and it took him a long while before he could speak again.
He even began to worry that misfortune might befall him.
Later, those who came and went
often encountered Xún in bustling areas of the capital city,
with his entourage, attendants, and horses
no different from what Lǐ had seen,
but he never spoke again.
Wèi Péng
Wèi Péng, the Prefect of Jiànzhōu,
after completing his term of office,
lived as a guest in Nánchāng.
He had never shown any talent for poetry,
but later, after falling ill,
he became confused and lost his mind.
It was as if someone was guiding him,
and he suddenly asked for a brush to copy a poem, which said:
"Alone with indignation, I face the clear river,
often watching the white sun set.
Pine shadows sway in the long wind,
moonlight falls on the rocky fields.
My hometown is over a thousand lǐ away,
rarely do I see my relatives.
Gazing vainly at the distant cloudy mountains,
sorrowfully, tears fall like sleet.
I regret being a guest in the netherworld,
and again in this foreign county.
I long to reaffirm our past bond,
do not suddenly abandon me, flawed and lowly."
The poem's sentiment was as if his deceased wife had composed it for Péng.
Over ten days later,
Péng passed away.
The Residence in Dàozhèng Ward
East of the crossroads in Dàozhèng Ward,
during the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a small residence
where strange phenomena appeared daily,
and anyone who lived there inevitably suffered great misfortune.
At that time, the jìnshì Fáng Cìqīng rented the west courtyard to live in,
and for several months, he encountered no trouble.
He then boasted to everyone, saying:
"My future prospects
can be considered assured.
Everyone says this residence is haunted,
but it means nothing to Cìqīng."
Lǐ Zhífāng heard this and replied:
"It is the senior who is more ominous than the residence."
Everyone burst into laughter.
Later, it was purchased by Lǐ Shīgǔ, the military governor of Dōngpíng, to serve as a liaison office.
At that time, the Dōngpíng army
often had fifty or sixty people coming to offer winter congratulations,
with falcons and hounds following them.
Military officers and soldiers
would cook, roast, and slaughter animals,
all as a matter of routine.
The jìnshì Lǐ Zhāngwǔ had just passed the examination,
and was full of bold spirit.
One morning,
he went to visit the Grand Astrologer's assistant Xú Zé.
Finding that Xú had gone out early,
he rested his horse in the courtyard.
That day, all the Dōngpíng soldiers had returned,
when suddenly he saw in the hall a hunchbacked old man wearing dark red clothes,
his eyes red and tearful,
basking in the sun by the street.
In the west wing, there was an old woman wearing a dark yellow skirt and a white vest,
carrying two baskets on a shoulder pole,
both filled with fragments of human remains and bones of donkeys and horses.
She also had six or seven human rib bones stuck in her hair as hairpins,
as if she were about to move away.
The old man called out:
"Fourth Lady, why have you come here?"
The old woman replied:
"Eighth Elder Gāo, may you have great blessings."
She then quickly said:
"I must bid farewell to you, Eighth Elder, and move away.
Recently, this residence has become too noisy and troublesome,
making it impossible to stay."
Zhāngwǔ, who was knowledgeable in such matters, personally recounted this,
saying this residence was originally haunted.
Some say
that Zhāngwǔ, because of this, gave up on women.
That is all.
Zhèng Qióngluó
Duàn Wénchāng's cousin,
in the late Zhēnyuán era,
was returning from Xìn'ān to Luòyáng.
At dusk, he reached Guāzhōu
and spent the night on his boat.
Late at night, while playing the qin,
he suddenly heard sighs from outside.
When he stopped playing, the sounds ceased.
This happened several times,
so he slowly put away the qin and went to sleep.
He dreamed of a woman in her twenties,
haggard in appearance and wearing tattered clothes,
who approached and bowed, saying:
"My surname is Zhèng, and my given name is Qióngluó.
I originally lived in Dāntú.
My parents died early,
so I relied on my widowed sister-in-law.
Unfortunately, she also passed away,
so I came to Yángzǐ to look for my aunt.
When I arrived at the inn at night,
a market official's son, Wáng Wéijǔ, took advantage of his drunkenness to try to force himself on me.
Knowing I could not escape,
I used my scarf to strangle myself and died.
The market official's son secretly buried me in the western canal of the fish market.
That night,
I appeared in a dream to the Yángzǐ magistrate, Shí Yì,
but he did nothing about it.
Later, I manifested as a grievance aura over the river,
but Shí still dismissed it as an auspicious sign of mist,
and even drew a picture of it to submit to the court.
For forty years, I have harbored this grievance,
with no one to avenge me.
Both of my parents were skilled at playing the qin,
and just now, hearing your qin playing,
