its extraordinary melodies and harmonious sounds
unconsciously drew me here."
Later, when he arrived at Wēngǔ in Héqīng County north of Luòyáng,
he visited his brother-in-law, Fán Yuánzé,
who possessed some unusual skills.
After staying for a few days,
Fán suddenly said:
"Brother, why is there a female ghost following you?
Please allow me to send her away."
He then lit a lamp, burned incense, and performed a ritual.
After a short while,
there was a rustling sound behind the lamp,
and Yuánzé said:
"She is asking for paper and brush.
Quickly, throw paper and brush into the lamp's shadow."
A moment later,
the paper was filled,
The paper swiftly fell,
and when examined in front of the lamp,
the writing covered the entire sheet.
The writing resembled miscellaneous seven-character verses,
with deeply sorrowful and resentful words.
Yuánzé immediately instructed someone to copy it down,
saying that ghost writing tends to fade quickly.
By dawn,
the paper appeared as if stained with soot,
with no trace of writing left.
Yuánzé then ordered wine, dried meat, and paper money to be prepared,
and at dusk, they were burned by the roadside.
A whirlwind lifted the ashes
straight up several feet,
and the sound of mournful weeping was heard.
The poem consisted of 262 characters in total,
mostly expressing the sorrow of hidden grievances.
Its language was not entirely clear,
so the words are not recorded here.
Among them, twenty-eight characters read:
"Pain fills my heart, yet I cannot speak;
my intestines are torn to pieces—to whom can I plead?
Spring gives life to all things, yet I am lifeless;
how I resent that my fragrant soul never met you."
Dúgū Mù
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Dúgū Mù from Hénán,
who was traveling in Huáinán.
One night, he sought lodging in Dàyí County.
When he was still over ten lǐ away,
he saw a maidservant riding a horse,
whose appearance was quite beautiful.
Mù subtly engaged her in conversation,
and the maidservant's replies were very refined.
Soon, a carriage path led northward off the main road,
and someone
led her away.
Mù hastily said to her:
"Just now, I barely managed to glimpse your countenance,
thinking I could continue our interaction,
why are you abruptly abandoning me?"
The maidservant smiled and said:
"Feelings of shame and embarrassment,
truly are not the issue.
However, my young mistress lives alone in her youth,
and her nature is very strict and proper,
so it is difficult for me to agree to your request."
Mù then asked about the young mistress's surname and her relatives, both paternal and maternal.
The maidservant said:
"Her surname is Yáng, and she is the sixth [in the family]."
She did not answer anything else.
Before he knew it, they had traveled several lǐ.
Soon they arrived at a place,
where the gate and buildings were very solemn.
The maidservant dismounted and went inside,
and after a long time, she came out,
inviting the guest to the guest quarters, saying:
"We have cut off contact with guests
for several years already.
Since a distinguished guest has arrived,
my mistress has no reason to decline.
Please do not mind the neglect and shortcomings."
Thereupon, candles were lit and a bed prepared,
with quilts and mattresses fully provided.
After a while,
the maidservant came out and said to Mù:
"Are you not a descendant of General Dúgū Shèng of the Suí dynasty?"
Mù then stated himself
to be the eighth-generation descendant of Shèng.
The maidservant said:
"If that is indeed the case,
then my mistress and you, sir, have an old connection."
Mù inquired about the reason,
and the maidservant said:
"I am a lowly person,
and do not know the details.
My mistress will personally come out to explain."
Shortly after, food was set out,
delicacies from land and water all prepared.
After the meal,
several dozen maidservants came forward to lead the way, saying:
"The District Princess has arrived."
He saw a young woman,
about thirteen or fourteen years old,
of peerless beauty.
After she finished bowing and kneeling in greeting,
she took a seat
and said to Mù:
"Living in this manor is lonely,
and we have long ceased receiving guests.
I did not expect a gentleman to honor us with a visit.
However, since I have an old connection with you, sir,
I dared not have the maids and servants speak of it.
I hope you will not laugh."
Mù said:
"I am a traveler,
and to receive the kindness of lodging and food is already much.
How could I have expected to be specially granted an audience,
and moreover allowed to recount old ties?
Besides, I have never left the capital Luòyáng in my life,
so among relatives and old acquaintances in Jiānghuái,
many are not known to me.
I sincerely hope you will speak fully."
The District Princess said:
"I wish to explain myself,
but I fear it may startle you, sir.
I have left the human world
for two hundred years already.
How could you possibly know me?"
Initially, when Mù heard the surname Yáng
and her self-identification as a District Princess,
he had already begun to suspect.
Upon hearing these words,
he then knew she was a ghost,
yet he felt no fear.
The District Princess said:
"Because you are the noble descendant of General Dúgū,
whose family has for generations upheld loyalty and integrity,
I therefore wish to entrust myself to you.
Please do not doubt me because I am from the netherworld."
Mù said:
"My ancestor
was a general of the Suí dynasty.
Since you, District Princess, must consider me as somewhat inheriting my ancestor's character,
and wish to entrust yourself to my care,
this is something I would be delighted to hear in my lifetime.
What doubts could I have?"
The District Princess said:
"Wishing to pour out my heart,
only increases my sorrow.
My father was Prince Qí,
the second son of the Suí Emperor.
When the Suí dynasty collapsed,
my lord and father
were both killed at the same time."
The senior ministers and veteran generals,
none failed to follow the rebels.
Only your late ancestor, the General,
strenuously resisted the rebel faction.
I was young at the time,
and often by his side,
witnessing the whole course of events.
When the rebel troops entered the palace,
among the rebel faction were those who wished to force themselves upon me.
I therefore insulted and cursed them,
and was consequently killed by them."
She then became overwhelmed with grief.
Mù then asked her about the notable figures of that time and the events at the end of the Dàyè era,
which largely corresponded with the Suí historical records.
After a long while,
she ordered wine, and they drank together.
Her words were filled with sorrow and sobs,
and she composed a poem to present to Mù, saying:
"In Jiāngdū past, chaos and ruin fell,
beneath the palace gates, much strife arose.
Wolves and tigers wantonly devoured all,
spears and shields daily ran amok.
The rebel horde came from outside,
at midnight breached the layered walls.
Fat and blood soaked the palace halls,
blades and spears leaned against eaves and pillars.
Now I know those who followed the rebels,
were precisely the dukes and ministers.
White blades defiled the yellow-roofed house,
the state and family thus toppled down.
In fierce wind, the sturdy grass is known,
in times of chaos, loyal ministers are seen.
Alas, alas, Dúgū, sir,
facing death, you tied your cap-strings still.
Heaven and earth were in turmoil deep,
clouds and thunder found no timely peace.
Now two hundred years have passed,
my hidden sorrow remains unappeased.
Mountains, rivers, wind, and moon are ancient,
the tomb mounds, dew and mist are green.
You, sir, ride upon your ancestor's virtue,
about to spread a name of loyalty and zeal.
Your splendid carriage once turned its gaze here,
my humble earthen chamber takes it as glory.
A true man sets his will and conduct,
life and death alike stir his feeling.
If one seeking righteousness can be entrusted,
who would cling to hidden chastity alone?"
Mù sighed deeply in admiration,
considering her even superior to Bān Jiéyú.
He then asked about her lifetime literary works.
She replied:
"I originally had no talent,
but I loved reading ancient collections.
I often saw that the Xiè family sisters and the various daughters of the Bào family were all skilled in composing literature,
and privately admired them.
The Emperor also greatly appreciated literature,
and I was often summoned by command.
At that time, Xuē Dàohéng's fame was high throughout the land,
but whenever I saw his writings,
my heart rather despised them.
Just now, emotion arose from within,
and I merely narrated events directly.
How is it worthy of praise?"
Mù said:
"Your talent, District Princess, is bestowed by Heaven itself,
placing you among the likes of the Seven Masters of Yèzhōng.
How could Xuē Dàohéng possibly compare?"
Mù then composed a poem in reply, saying:
"In past days, August Heaven sent down calamity,
the Suí house hung like a dangling tassel.
Peril and trouble lay at the twin gates,
shield and spear spread across the Nine Provinces.
Going out the gate, all were vicious minions,
wherever one turned, many rebel plots.
The bright day suddenly turned to dusk,
the collapsing wave could not be stayed.
At Wàngyí, strife was already joined,
the ancestral altars too brought shame.
In the Warm Chamber, troops first clashed,
within the palace walls, blood had already flowed.
Pitiable, the one who played the flute,
weeping sadly, descended the Phoenix Tower.
Frosty blades vainly pressed upon you,
the jade hairpin could not be sought.
Silken jackets you left for attendants,
powder and kohl became foes and haters.
The state already overturned and sunk,
your remaining life you vowed not to keep."
The heroic general's ancestor,
alone bore the nation's sorrow.
His cinnabar blood splattered the ceremonial screen,
his plump flesh stained by spear and blade.
Now seeing the millet fields,
he grieves all day for the fallen dynasty.
The jade tree has long been silent,
the spring terrace stands for countless autumns.
Moved by this single glance of importance,
I vow to repay with death's fidelity.
If the realms of light and dark do not obscure,
may our hearts therein unite in tender bond."
The Xiànzhǔ recited it several times,
overcome by sorrow for a long while.
After a pause,
several maidservants holding musical instruments appeared,
and one stepped forward to address the Xiànzhǔ:
"Speaking of past matters
will only bring sadness.
Moreover, Dúláng has just arrived—
how can we spend the whole night facing each other in tears?
I request to serve as envoy
and summon Láijiā Niángzǐ to keep us company."
The Xiànzhǔ consented.
Then she said to Mù:
"This is a singer of General Lái Hù'ér,
also killed at that time.
She resides nearby."
Moments later she arrived,
possessing great beauty,
skilled in conversation and laughter.
Music was played,
and they drank freely with much joy.
Lái sang several songs;
Mù only remembered one:
"Trees of Píngyáng County,
long turned to dust of Guǎnglíng.
Unexpectedly, ah,
the young master comes,
and spring returns in the Yellow Springs."
After a long while she said:
"I have dwelled here with the Xiànzhǔ over two hundred years—
who could have foreseen such joyous rites today?"
The Xiànzhǔ said:
"Originally, because the Dúgū family is one of loyal martyrdom,
I wished to meet once,
hoping to dispel hidden sorrows.
How can my dusty substance
presume to impose upon a gentleman?"
Mù then recited the closing lines of the Xiànzhǔ's poem:
"If righteousness can be entrusted,
who would cling to hidden virtue?"
The Xiànzhǔ smiled slightly:
"You have a strong memory indeed."
Mù then sang to her:
"The golden chamber long without its lord,
silken sleeves gathering dust as she sits.
I wish to be a companion playing the flute,
together riding phoenixes as one."
The Xiànzhǔ answered with a song:
"Vermilion carriage descending the long road,
green grass revealing the solitary tomb.
Still better than on the Sunlit Terrace,
vainly watching dawn and dusk clouds."
Lái said:
"Long ago, Empress Xiāo intended to match the Xiànzhǔ with her elder brother's son,
but just then the Jiāngdū rebellion occurred,
and the matter was abandoned.
The Dúgū family is a prominent clan of high officials,
a house of loyal martyrdom.
Meeting today,
truly makes a fine match."
Mù asked what fief the Xiànzhǔ held.
The Xiànzhǔ said:
"I was born in the capital in the fourth year of Rénshòu,
when the imperial carriage was at Rénshòu Palace,
so I was named Shòu'ér.
The next year,
the Crown Prince ascended the throne,
and I was enfeoffed as Qīnghé Xiànzhǔ.
When the Emperor went to Jiāngdū Palace,
I was transferred as Línzī Xiànzhǔ.
Especially beloved by the Empress,
I often stayed within the palace."
Lái said:
"The night is already deep—
Dúgū Láng should now complete the rites.
I shall await at the eastern pavilion,
and at dawn offer congratulations."
Then the maidservants jested and teased,
all as in human ceremonies.
Entering the bedchamber,
he only felt her breath faint,
her body rather cold.
After a moment,
she wept and said to Mù:
"I, a perished person,
long turned to dust and ashes.
Fortunate to serve you with towel and comb,
even death will not decay this honor."
Then she summoned Lái again,
and they feasted as before.
She asked Mù:
"I hear you now go to Jiāngdū—
when will you return?
May I entrust something to you?"
Mù said:
"Even death I would not shun—
what else could be impossible?"
The Xiànzhǔ said:
"After the Emperor was reburied,
I dwell alone here.
Now the tomb of the Wicked Prince disturbs me,
wishing to take me as his concubine.
Being of imperial lineage,
in principle I cannot be insulted by a malicious ghost.
My wish to meet you
was precisely for this.
As you go to Jiāngdū,
your path will pass his tomb;
because of me,
he will surely trouble you.
The Daoist Wáng Shànjiāo sells talismans in Huáinán market—
he can control ghosts and spirits.
If you seek him,
you will be spared."
She added:
"My dwelling here is also ultimately uneasy.
When you return from Jiāngnán,
could you take me with you
and bury me on the northern slope of Luòyáng,
so I may be near you?
Eternal reliance
would be a life-giving kindness."
Mù promised all,
saying:
"The rites of reburial
are my family's duty."
Drunk with wine,
she leaned on Mù and sang:
"Dew-laden grass lush and dense,
the fallen glory not yet moved.
Since I dwelled here,
how many years have passed?
With your ancestors of old,
grace and favor once shared.
Through life and death, separation and reunion,
suddenly we meet here.
Who says this happy occasion
soon brings parting?
Awaiting your journey north,
hand in hand we shall return together."
Tears fell, dampening her scarf.
Lái also tearfully told Mù:
"Dúgū Láng, do not betray the Xiànzhǔ's deep affection."
Mù answered with a song:
"That Luòyáng of yours,
lies under another sky.
Driving my horse, far and long,
I suddenly came to this strange land.
Affection connecting light and dark,
gained this meeting.
Righteousness moved by times past,
words of lingering attachment remain.
Clear rivers, cassia isles,
where one may wander free.
But for your sake,
I cannot linger long."
The Xiànzhǔ tearfully thanked Mù:
"Once honored with your fine gift,
I hold it forever dear."
Soon,
dawn approached.
The Xiànzhǔ wept,
and Mù also wept facing her.
To all present,
Mù bade farewell.
Once outside the gate,
he looked back and saw nothing.
The ground was flat,
with no sign of any tomb.
Mù felt dazed and bewildered;
only after a long while did he settle.
He transplanted a willow tree to mark the spot.
His family searched for him urgently;
suddenly several days later,
Mù entered Huáinán market,
and indeed met Wáng Shànjiāo there,
obtaining a talisman.
When he reached the Wicked Prince's tomb,
he was assailed by whirlwinds three or four times.
Mù showed the talisman,
and they ceased.
Previously, Mù had rather disbelieved in ghosts and spirits;
but after the Xiànzhǔ's words,
all became clear.
Mù deeply marveled in astonishment,
and privately told his close kin.
It was the first month of that year.
Upon returning from the region south of the Yangtze,
he dug several feet into the ground at that location,
and unearthed a set of skeletal remains.
He enshrouded them with clothing and a burial cover.
Mù believed that since her death had been hasty and crude,
her burial must have been deficient.
After arriving in Luòyáng,
he prepared a grand and solemn ceremony,
personally composing a eulogy to offer sacrifices to her,
and buried her outside the Ānshàn Gate.
That night,
while staying alone at a village lodge,
the Xiànzhǔ appeared again,
and said to Mù:
"The virtue of moving my spirit,
I shall never forget for all eternity.
As one who lingered in obscurity,
I had long been destined not to receive such treatment.
Fortunately, you cherished our past affection,
allowing me to finally attain a peaceful resting place.
The reason I did not appear to you on the journey
was that,
since you had seen my decayed and foul state,
I feared it might cause you disgust and aversion."
Mù observed her carriages, guides, and attendants,
all radiant and illustrious beyond compare at that time.
The Xiànzhǔ also pointed to them and said:
"All this is bestowed by you.
In the year of Jǐmǎo,
we shall meet again."
That evening, she stayed at Mù's place,
and did not leave until dawn.
After Mù had relocated her burial over thousands of miles,
he also openly spoke of the matter,
so that all his old friends and relatives came to know of it.
In the fifteenth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
which was the year of Jǐmǎo,
Mù rose early in the morning and was about to go out,
when he suddenly saw several carriages arriving at his home.
They said to Mù:
"The Xiànzhǔ has sent orders."
Mù said:
"Has the time for our meeting arrived?"
That evening, he died suddenly,
and was then buried together with the Yáng family.
Huàzhōu Cānjūn
Liǔ Cānjūn of Huàzhōu,
was the son of a prominent family.
He was of few desires, orphaned early,
and had no brothers.
Having left office,
he idly roamed in Cháng'ān.
On the Shangsi Festival,
at Qǔjiāng he saw a carriage,
adorned with gold and jade,
half standing in the shallow water.
The rear curtain slowly lifted,
revealing a hand as white as jade,
pointing and gesturing to pick a lotus flower.
The woman’s beauty was peerless,
and she glanced sidelong at Liǔ Shēng for a long time.
Liǔ Shēng whipped his horse to follow,
and soon saw the carriage enter Yǒngchóng Ward.
Liǔ Shēng inquired about her,
Her surname was Cuī,
and the woman also had a mother.
There was a maidservant,
named Qīnghóng.
Liǔ Shēng was not very poor,
and tried many ways to bribe Qīnghóng,
but she ultimately did not accept.
Another day,
Cuī’s daughter fell ill,
and her uncle, Wáng, the Commandant of the Imperial Guards,
came to visit his sister,
and informed her,
asking to take the daughter as his son’s wife.
Cuī’s daughter was unhappy,
but her mother did not dare to disobey her brother’s command.
The daughter said:
"I would be content to marry that Liǔ Shēng from before.
If this is not allowed,
I fear I will not survive with my cousin."
Her mother, deeply concerned for her daughter,
ordered Qīnghóng to convey the message at the monastic quarters of Dàoshěng at Jiànfú Temple.
Liǔ Shēng, tempted by Qīnghóng,
and also fond of her,
provoked Qīnghóng’s great anger:
"Your nature is truly coarse,
how could you treat the young lady this way?
I am but lowly and humble,
yet you forget the former affection,
wanting to preserve enduring love,
how can that be possible?
I will tell the young lady about your actions."
Liǔ Shēng bowed repeatedly,
apologizing for his lack of discernment.
Only then did she say:
"The lady pities the young lady deeply,
and now the young lady is unwilling to marry into the Wáng family,
so the lady has secretly arranged the marriage.
You should prepare for the wedding within two or three days."
Liǔ Shēng was overjoyed,
and prepared several hundred thousand in betrothal gifts himself,
marrying within the set time.
After five days,
Liǔ took his wife and Qīnghóng to live in Jīnchéng Ward.
About a month later,
the Commandant went to Yǒngchóng,
and his sister, Madame Wáng, wept and said:
"My husband is dead,
my child is alone and helpless,
My nephew, without waiting for the proper ceremony,
forcibly abducted my daughter.
Does my brother have no way to discipline him?"
The Commandant was furious,
returned home and caned his son several dozen times.
Secretly ordering a search,
for a full year nothing was found.
Not long after,
Madame Wáng died,
and Liǔ Shēng took his wife and Qīnghóng from Jīnchéng Ward to attend the funeral.
The Commandant’s son saw them,
and informed his father,
who captured Liǔ Shēng.
Liǔ Shēng said:
"I paid the betrothal gifts and married my wife at the home of my mother-in-law, Madame Wáng,
it was not an illicit elopement.
All members of the household are well aware of this."
Since Madame Wáng had died,
there was no one to clarify,
so it was brought to court.
The magistrate ruled that the Wáng family had given betrothal gifts first,
so she should return to the Wáng family.
The Commandant’s son had long admired his cousin,
and did not resent the previous transgression.
After several years,
Qīnghóng remained chaste and stayed with them.
The Commandant also died,
and they moved their residence to Chóngyì Ward.
Cuī’s daughter was unhappy serving her cousin,
so she sent Qīnghóng to find where Liǔ Shēng was,
at that time Liǔ Shēng still lived in Jīnchéng Ward.
Cuī’s daughter also had Qīnghóng set a time with Liǔ Shēng,
and bribed the garden watchman,
ordering him to pile manure as high as the wall,
Cuī’s daughter then climbed over it with Qīnghóng,
and went together to Liǔ Shēng.
Liǔ Shēng was surprised and delighted,
and without leaving the city,
they only moved to Qúnxián Ward.
Later, her original husband eventually found Cuī’s daughter,
learned she lived in Qúnxián Ward,
and again sued to take her back.
Wáng Shēng was deeply affectionate,
and though Cuī tried every means to avoid it,
she pleaded pregnancy,
and he accepted her without blame.
Liǔ Shēng was exiled to Jiānglíng.
Two years later,
Cuī’s daughter and Qīnghóng died one after the other,
Wáng Shēng attended the funeral,
with the utmost rites of grief and mourning.
Qīnghóng was also buried beside Cuī’s grave.
Liǔ Shēng lived idly in Jiānglíng,
in the second month of spring,
with abundant flowers filling the courtyard,
he thought back on Cuī’s daughter,
dwelling on her image,
not knowing whether she was alive or dead.
Suddenly he heard urgent knocking at the door,
and soon saw Qīnghóng enter carrying a dressing case,
saying:
"The young lady is about to arrive."
Hearing what seemed like the sound of a carriage and horses,
when Cuī’s daughter entered the door,
nothing else was seen.
Liǔ Shēng and Cuī’s daughter recounted their separation,
with great sorrow and joy.
Asked how this came to be,
she said:
"I have already parted with Wáng,
from now on we can be together forever.
When one’s heart is devoted in life,
their long-held wish will surely be fulfilled."
Then she said:
"I learned music in my youth,
and am quite accomplished at the konghou."
Liǔ Shēng immediately bought a konghou,
and she played it with exquisite skill.
For two years,
it could be said they lived to the fullest.
Not long after,
an old servant of Wáng Shēng passed by Liǔ Shēng’s door,
saw Qīnghóng,
and was shocked, not understanding how.
Suspecting it might be someone who looked like her,
he did not dare speak immediately.
Asking the neighbors,
they said it was the exiled Liǔ Cānjūn.
Even more puzzled,
he watched further,
Qīnghóng also recognized him as a servant of the Wáng family,
and informed Liǔ Shēng,
who hid her.
Wáng Shēng’s servant returned to the city,
and reported everything to Wáng Shēng.
Wáng Shēng heard this,
and traveled a thousand li by carriage.
Arriving at Liǔ Shēng’s door,
he peeked through a crack,
and saw Liǔ Shēng reclining bare-chested on a couch by the window,
Cuī’s daughter freshly made up,
Qīnghóng holding a mirror beside her,
Cuī applying powder, not yet finished.
Wáng Shēng cried out loudly outside the door,
Qīnghóng dropped the mirror to the ground,
with a sound like a chime stone,
Cuī and Wáng Shēng had no regrets.
He then entered,
Liǔ Shēng was startled,
but received him with the courtesy due a guest.
Soon Cuī was nowhere to be found.
Liǔ Shēng and Wáng Shēng calmly discussed the matter,
the two looked at each other, not understanding,
greatly perplexed.
Together they went to Cháng'ān,
opened Cuī’s grave to examine it,
and found the makeup applied in Jiānglíng still fresh,
her clothes and flesh,
showed no decay,
and Qīnghóng was the same.
Liǔ and Wáng made a vow,
and reburied them.
The two went to Zhōngnán Mountain to seek the Way,
and never returned.
Zhào Shūyá
In the fourteenth year of the Zhēnyuán era, on the wùyín day of the summer fifth month, there was a drought.
In Xúzhōu, the auxiliary general Zhào Shūyá moved into a new residence.
In the middle of the night,
there was something outside the window rustling the window paper.
He asked about it,
and the thing claimed to be a ghost,
named Liú Déyán from the Wú period,
whose dwelling was beneath the gentleman’s bed,
making coming and going somewhat difficult.
"If you, sir, could move me out,
south of the city beneath the Táiyǔ Mountain there are two large trees;
that is my wife’s grave.
Bury me east of the grave.
I will certainly repay you later."
The next morning, Shūyá went outside the city,
and seeing it was true,
that same day he dug beneath his bed.
At a depth of three chǐ,
he found skeletal remains,
and buried them as instructed.
That night,
the ghost came to express thanks,
saying:
"There is a drought now,
but within three days there will be rain.
You, sir, should inform the senior official."
At dawn, Shūyá submitted a report,
requesting prayers for rain,
and promising sufficient rain within three days.
The military governor, Minister of Works Zhāng Jiànfēng, granted permission,
providing what was needed.
Shūyá set up an altar at Shífó Mountain.
When the third day arrived,
and there was still no rain,
he was to have his ears cut off.
Several thousand people in the city came to watch.
At that time, the region bordered on bandit territory,
and Jiànfēng suspected deception and conspiracy,
so during the evening session he had Shūyá beaten to death with a staff.
At dusk, heavy rain fell.
Jiànfēng immediately ordered sacrifices to be made
and appointed Shūyá’s son as an auxiliary cavalry officer.
People of the time believed that serving one’s lord required honesty,
and that Zhào Shūyá had concealed the ghost’s prediction of the rain’s arrival date,
so he deserved to die.
Zhōu Jìchuān,
a man from Rǔnán,
had a villa west of Yángzhōu.
He and his three brothers were all fond of study.
One night after finishing their lectures,
around the third watch,
each went to his bed to sleep.
Suddenly, they heard a clacking sound outside the window,
which persisted for a long time.
Jìchuān peered through the window
and saw a small skeletal child
running back and forth in the courtyard.
At first, it clasped its hands together;
then it began swinging its arms.
The clacking sound
was the noise of its bones rubbing together.
Jìchuān called his brothers to come look.
After a while,
his younger brother Jùchuān shouted at it sternly.
At the first shout, the child jumped onto the steps;
at the second, it entered the door;
at the third, it tried to climb onto the bed.
Jùchuān’s scolding grew increasingly urgent.
The child said:
"Mother, give me milk."
Jùchuān struck it with his palm,
and it fell to the ground with the blow,
but immediately it was back on the bed,
leaping and darting as swiftly as an ape.
The family servants, hearing the commotion
and sensing something amiss,
came with knives and clubs.
The child said again:
"Mother, give me milk."
The servants struck it with a club.
When hit,
the child shattered into pieces like scattered stars,
but then reassembled itself several times.
It said again:
"Mother, give me milk."
The servants put it into a cloth sack,
carried it out,
and even from a distance it still asked for milk.
They went four or five lǐ outside the city walls
and threw it into a dry well.
The next night it returned,
holding the cloth sack in its hand,
tossing and leaping about gleefully.
The servants caught it again
and, using another cloth sack,
put it inside as before,
then tied the sack with a rope,
attached a large stone, and sank it into a river.
As they were about to carry it away,
it said from inside the sack:
"Just like last night’s guest."
A few days later, it came again,
carrying the sack in its left hand
and holding the broken rope in its right,
running and playing as before.
The servants had prepared a large log in advance,
hollowed out in the middle
like a drum shell.
They forced the child inside,
covered both ends with large iron plates,
nailed them shut,
then locked it with an iron chain,
attached a large stone,
and cast it into the great river.
As they were about to carry it away,
it said:
"Thank you for the coffin escort."
After that, it never came again.
This happened in the seventeenth year of the Zhēnyuán era.
Lù Qiáo
In the early Yuánhé era,
there was a jìnshì named Lù Qiáo,
who was fond of composing poetry,
and people praised him quite a bit.
He lived in Dānyáng,
and his residence had terraces and ponds,
renowned as a scenic spot.
Qiáo’s family was wealthy and hospitable.
One evening,
when the breeze and moon were clear and bright,
someone knocked at the door.
He went out to look,
and saw a gentleman,
whose attire and cap were very grand,
and whose demeanor was elegant and refined.
Qiáo invited him in,
and the visitor conversed with him brilliantly and fluently,
beyond all expectation.
Qiáo esteemed him greatly,
considering him unmatched by anyone,
and so asked his name.
He said:
"I am Shěn Yuē.
I have heard that you are skilled in poetry,
and so have come to visit."
Qiáo rose in surprise and said:
"I am but a humble scholar,
and never expected your esteemed presence.
I wish you could stay a while,
so I may attend to our conversation and laughter."
Soon after, he ordered wine.
Yuē said:
"I have never drunk wine in my life,
but I do not mean to hinder you."
He then said to Qiáo:
"My friend, the Vice Director Fàn Yún,
do you know of him?"
Qiáo replied:
"I have often read the History of Liáng,
and have long been familiar with Lord Fàn’s name."
Yuē said:
"I shall invite him."
Qiáo said:
"That would be most fortunate."
Yuē then ordered an attendant to invite Vice Director Fàn.
After a short while,
Yún arrived,
and Qiáo bowed and invited him to sit.
Yún said to Yuē:
"Xiùwén, how did you manage to come here?"
Yuē said:
"I admire our host’s poetic skill,
and his fondness for guests,
so I walked here under the moonlight."
They then conversed and bantered together.
After a long while,
Yuē called to his attendants:
"Go and summon Qīngxiāng."
Soon a boy arrived,
about ten years old,
with a bright and handsome appearance.
Yuē pointed and said to Qiáo:
"This is my beloved son.
He was intelligent from a young age,
and loved to study.
I cherished him deeply,
and thus named him Qīngxiāng.
I wished for him to transmit my learning,
but unfortunately, he passed away before me.
Now I have him pay his respects to you."
He then ordered his son to bow to Qiáo.
He also said:
"This boy also loved to compose poetry.
Recently, he accompanied me and Xiè the Vice Director past Táichéng."
He then commanded him to compose a poem titled "Reflecting on the Past,"
and the boy took up the brush and finished it immediately,
which was quite impressive.
He then recited it:
"The rivers and hills of six dynasties past,
their rise and fall over several hundred years.
Their splendor now lies in silence,
the court and market once bustled with noise.
The night moon on glazed waters,
spring winds under eggshell skies.
Grieving for the times and longing for antiquity,
shedding tears before the city gate."
Qiáo admired and praised it for a long time,
then asked Yuē:
"I have often perused the anthology compiled by Zhāomíng,
and see that the poems he selected and recorded
were all not bound by tonal patterns,
and are called the Qí-Liáng style.
It was only in the Táng dynasty, with Shěn Quánqī and Sòng Zhīwèn, that regulated verse became favored.
Qīngxiāng’s poem,
however, imitates the modern style.
Why is that?"
Yuē said:
"If one composes it today,
then it is the modern style.
What is so surprising about that?"
Yún then said to Yuē:
"In the past, you and I, along with Xuánhuī and Yànshēng, all studied under Jìnglíng’s tutelage,
laughing and talking day and night, playing lú and bó.
The joy of those times
can no longer be recaptured.
After Lord Xiāo received the abdication,
you and I both became ministers who assisted the mandate,
and though our positions were very high,
and the favor we received was even greater,
our hearts were often anxious and fearful,
without the joy of former days.
Zhūgě Chángmín once said,
'In poverty and lowliness, one often thinks of wealth and honor.
In wealth and honor, one again treads upon perilous crises.'
These words are indeed true!"
Yuē also sighed deeply for a long time.
He then lamented:
"From Liáng to the present,
four hundred years have passed.
The rivers, hills, breeze, and moon
are no different from back then,
but the people have silently changed.
How can one not feel sorrow?"
He then said to Yún:
"When we served as secretaries for Lord Cài in Yǐngzhōu,
I once dreamed that someone told me:
'Your lord will later reach the position of chief minister,
but in the end, you will not attain the rank of Táisī.'
When I became Vice Director and President of the Department of State Affairs,
commentators often predicted this for me,
but in the end, I did not obtain it.
Then I knew that human affairs are nothing but fate."
By then, the night was already late.
Yún said to Yuē:
"It is time to return."
So they departed together,
and said to Qiáo:
"This place will see military uprising,
within two years at most."
Qiáo escorted them to the gate,
and they had not walked more than a few steps
when they vanished from sight.
Qiáo told this story to his relatives and friends.
A little over a year later,
Lǐ Qǐ rebelled,
and another year after that, Qiáo passed away.
Féng Ǎo of Lújiāng.
Old Woman Féng was
the wife of a village headman in Lújiāng.
Poor, widowed, and childless,
she was looked down upon and shunned by the villagers.
In the fourth year of the Yuánhé era,
there was a great famine in Huáichǔ.
Old Woman Féng went to Shū in search of food.
Passing by the Mùdú estate,
she encountered wind and rain at dusk,
and took shelter under a mulberry tree.
Suddenly, she saw a house at the roadside,
with a flickering lamp inside.
She went to ask for lodging for the night.
She saw a woman,
about twenty years old,
beautiful in appearance and dress,
holding a three-year-old child,
leaning against the door and weeping sorrowfully.
Further inside, she saw an old man and an old woman,
sitting on a bed,
their expressions gloomy and distressed,
muttering and whispering,
as if demanding property and driving someone away.
When they saw Old Woman Féng arrive,
the old man and old woman silently left.
After a long while, the young woman stopped weeping,
went inside to prepare food,
arranged the bed and mat,
and invited Old Woman Féng to eat and rest.
Old Woman Féng asked her what was the matter.
The woman wept again and said:
"This child's father,
my husband,
is marrying another tomorrow."
Old Woman Féng said:
"Who were those two old people earlier?
What were they demanding from you that made them so angry?"
The woman said:
"They are my parents-in-law.
Now that their son is marrying another,
they are demanding my old baskets, knives, rulers, and sacrificial objects,
to give to the new bride.
I cannot bear to part with them,
hence their reproach."
Old Woman Féng said:
"Where is your former husband now?"
The woman said:
"I am the daughter of Liáng Qiàn, the magistrate of Huáiyīn.
I was married into the Dǒng family for seven years,
and had two sons and one daughter.
The sons followed their father,
and this is the daughter.
The Dǒng Jiāng in the county town now
is that man.
Dǒng Jiāng holds office as the Deputy Magistrate of Cuó,
and his family possesses great wealth."
As she spoke, she could not hold back her sobs.
Old Woman Féng thought nothing strange of it.
Moreover, having long suffered from cold and hunger,
she now had fine food and a comfortable bed,
and asked no further questions.
The woman wept until dawn.
Old Woman Féng took her leave,
walked twenty *li*,
and arrived at Tóngchéng County.
East of the county town was a grand mansion,
with curtains hung,
lambs and geese prepared,
and people bustling about.
It was said:
"Today there is a wedding ceremony for an official's family."
Old Woman Féng asked who the groom was,
and it was Dǒng Jiāng.
Old Woman Féng said:
"Dǒng has a wife,
why is he marrying again?"
A townsman said:
"Dǒng's wife and daughter are dead."
Old Woman Féng said:
"Last night, caught in the rain,
I stayed at the house of Dǒng's wife, née Liáng.
How can you say she is dead?"
The townsman inquired about the location,
and it turned out to be the tomb of Dǒng's wife.
He asked about the appearance of the two old people,
and they were Dǒng Jiāng's deceased parents.
Dǒng Jiāng was originally from Shūzhōu,
and the people in his village
all knew the details.
Someone reported this to Dǒng Jiāng.
Dǒng accused her of spreading demonic falsehoods,
and ordered his subordinates to drive Old Woman Féng away.
Old Woman Féng told the townspeople,
and they all sighed with emotion.
That evening,
Dǒng went ahead with the wedding.
In the sixth year of Yuánhé,
in the summer, the fifth month,
Lǐ Gōngzuǒ, an official of Jiānghuái,
was on a mission to the capital.
On his return, he stopped at Hànnán,
and met with Gāo Xiàn of Bóhǎi, Zhào Xuǎn of Tiānshuǐ, and Yǔwén Dǐng of Hénán at a relay station.
That night, they talked of strange tales,
each sharing what they had seen and heard.
Gāo Xiàn recounted this story in detail,
and Lǐ Gōngzuǒ thus wrote this account.
Dòu Yù
The Presented Scholar Wáng Shèng and Gài Yí,
during the Yuánhé reign period,
sought recommendations in Tóngzhōu.
At that time, the guest lodges were completely full,
so they borrowed the residence of the Commandery Merit Official Wáng Zhù,
to await the examination.
Later, all the other rooms had guests,
only the main hall
had its door tied shut with a small rope.
Peeking inside through the window,
they saw only a coarse quilt on the bed,
and a broken basket north of the bed,
beyond which there was nothing else.
Asking their neighbor,
they were told:
"It is the residence of the Recluse Dòu Sānláng Yù."
The two guests found the west wing too cramped,
and thought of sharing the room with him,
quite pleased that he had no female attendants or servants.
At dusk,
Recluse Dòu,
with one donkey and one servant,
arrived quite drunk.
Yí and Shèng approached and greeted him,
and said:
"We have come to the commandery seeking a solution,
but as the guest lodges are noisy,
we are staying here.
The west corridor we obtained
is also very cramped.
Since you, sir, have no female attendants,
and are moreover a man beyond worldly affairs,
we hope to roughly share this room,
to await the commandery examination."
Yù firmly declined,
his manner of receiving them quite haughty.
Late at night, as they were about to sleep,
they suddenly smelled a strange fragrance.
Startled, they got up to search for it,
and then saw curtains hanging in the main hall,
with the clamor of conversation and laughter.
Thereupon, Yí and Shèng rushed into his hall.
Screens and curtains surrounded them on all sides,
a wondrous fragrance assailed them,
with carved platters and rare delicacies,
indescribable in form.
There was a woman,
aged about eighteen or nineteen,
bewitchingly beautiful beyond compare,
dining opposite Dòu,
with over ten maidservants in attendance,
all also graceful and lovely.
A silver stove was just finishing brewing tea.
Those seated rose and entered the curtains of the west wing,
the maidservants all went in,
saying:
"What sort of young men are these?
Bursting into someone's home."
Dòu's face turned ashen,
he sat upright and said nothing.
Yí and Shèng, having nothing to say in reply,
sipped some tea and left.
Once they had descended the steps,
they heard the sound of the door closing,
and a voice saying:
"These mad young fellows,
why are they staying here together?
The ancients had reason for choosing their neighbors carefully,
surely that was no empty saying."
Dòu excused himself, saying it was not his own residence,
so it was difficult to refuse strangers.
He must have feared being slighted and insulted,
asking if there were no other dwellings,
and then they resumed their merry laughter.
At dawn,
they went to spy on him,
and everything had returned to its former state.
Dòu alone lay reclining under the coarse quilt,
rubbing his eyes as he just got up.
Yí and Shèng questioned him,
but he did not reply.
Yí and Shèng said:
"By day you are a commoner,
at night you meet with nobility;
if this is not some demonic illusion,
how did you obtain such a beauty?
If you do not tell the truth,
we will immediately report it to the commandery."
Dòu said:
"This is indeed a secret matter,
but speaking of it is harmless.
Recently, I traveled modestly to Tàiyuán,
setting out late from Lěngquán,
intending to lodge in Xiàoyì County.
The overcast darkness caused me to lose my way,
Asking who the master was,
a servant said:
'It is the manor of Sīmǎ Cuī of Fénzhōu.'
I had someone announce me.
He came out and said:
'Please enter.'
Sīmǎ Cuī was about over fifty years old,
dressed in crimson,
his demeanor and appearance quite pleasing.
He asked about my ancestors, uncles, and brothers,
inquiring about my maternal and paternal relatives.
He then spoke of his own clan,
revealing he was my relative,
and I honored him as a senior maternal cousin.
Since childhood, I had also heard of this elder,
but did not know his official position.
His solicitous inquiries were earnest.
His affection and courtesy were generous and weighty.
He then had someone inform his wife, saying:
'Scholar Dòu is the son of the seventh elder brother, General of the Right Guard,
he is my important maternal cousin's son,
and you, madam, are also his maternal aunt,
you may see him.
Serving in office in a distant place,
relatives are separated and cut off,
if not for this journey,
how could we have met?
Please receive him at once.'
After a short while,
a maidservant said:
'We beg Third Young Master to enter.'
The central hall was furnished with such splendor,
it was like the dwelling of a prince or marquis.
The platters of food were rare and exquisite,
the flavors encompassing all delicacies of sea and land.
After the meal,
the elder said:
'On this journey of yours now,
what are you seeking?'
I said:
'I seek funds for the examinations.'
He said:
'Where is your home commandery?'
I said:
'I have no home anywhere in the land.'
The elder said:
'Your circumstances are such, your person adrift,
wandering like tumbleweed with no destination,
your comings and goings are in vain.
I have a maidservant,
nearly grown to maturity,
she should now serve you.
As for clothing and food,
you need not seek them from others.
Would that be acceptable?'
I rose and bowed in thanks.
The lady, pleased, said:
'This evening is most auspicious,
and we also have sacrificial offerings.
Since it is a match among relatives,
why must we widely summon guests?
The auspicious rites are already prepared,
let it be this very night.'
After offering thanks, I sat down again,
and more food was served.
After eating,
I rested in the west hall.
A bath was prepared,
and after bathing,
I was given inner garments.
Three matchmakers were brought in,
all intelligent and clear-minded gentlemen:
one surnamed Wáng,
called the Commandery Law Officer;
one surnamed Péi,
called the Household Officer;
one surnamed Wéi,
called the Commandery Courier Inspector.
They exchanged bows and sat down.
Soon, the ceremonial carriage and fragrant carriage were both ready,
splendid candles led the way,
from the west hall to the central gate,
the rites of the relatives escorting the bride were performed.
Then they circled the manor once,
entering from the south gate to the central hall,
where the hall was already filled with curtains and canopies.
After the wedding ceremony was completed,
in the third watch of the night,
my wife told me:
'This is not the human world,
but the realm of the spirits.
The mentioned Fénzhōu,
is the Fénzhōu of the underworld,
not the human one.
Those several matchmakers,
are none other than underworld officials.
You and I have a predestined bond from past lives,
fated to be husband and wife,
hence we could meet.
The paths of humans and spirits are different,
you cannot stay long,
you should leave immediately.'
I said:
"Since humans and spirits are different,
How could I be worthy of being matched?
Since we have become husband and wife,
we should be together.
Why part after just one night?"
His wife said:
"I serve you,
and distance is no matter.
But you are a living person,
and should not stay here long.
You must quickly prepare your carriage.
I will always ensure your trunk contains a hundred bolts of silk,
and when used up, it will be full again.
Wherever you go,
you must seek a quiet room to live alone.
With just a little thought,
I will come as you wish.
After ten years,
we can travel together without separation,
parting by day and meeting by night."
Yù then went in to bid farewell.
Cuī said:
"Though light and dark differ,
humans and spirits are not two.
My daughter can serve you,
which is due to past karma.
Do not say she is of a different kind,
and thus treat her lightly.
Also, do not speak of this to others.
If questioned by official law,
it is fine to speak."
After speaking,
he received a hundred bolts of silk and departed.
From then on, he slept alone each night,
and when he thought of her, she would come.
The provisions and utensils
were all brought by her.
This continued for five years."
Yí and Shèng opened his trunk,
and indeed there were a hundred bolts of silk.
They each gave him thirty bolts,
asking him to keep it secret.
After speaking, he vanished,
and no one knew where he went.
Lǐ Hézi
In the early years of the Yuánhé era,
there was a ruffian named Lǐ Hézi in the Eastern Market of the Upper Capital,
whose father was called Nǔyǎn.
Hézi had a cruel nature,
often stealing dogs and cats to eat,
and was a menace to the neighborhood.
Once, while standing on the street with a hawk on his arm,
he saw two men in purple robes,
who called out,
"Are you not Lǐ Hézi, son of Lǐ Nǔyǎn?"
Hézi bowed to them.
They said:
"We have a matter,
let us speak in a secluded place."
After walking a few steps,
they stopped away from others,
saying, "The underworld is summoning you,
you must go now."
Hézi initially refused,
saying:
"I am a human,
why do you deceive me?"
They replied:
"We are ghosts."
Then they reached into their robes,
pulled out a document,
with the seal still wet,
showing his name clearly,
for the lawsuit of four hundred and sixty dogs and cats.
Hézi was terrified,
threw away his hawk and bowed, begging:
"I am doomed to die,
but please stay for a moment,
I will prepare some wine."
The ghosts firmly declined,
but could not refuse.
First, they went to a Bìluó shop,
but the ghosts covered their noses,
unwilling to enter.
Then they went to Dù's tavern,
where Hézi bowed and spoke alone,
making others think he was mad.
He ordered nine bowls of wine,
drank three himself,
and set six empty bowls on the west seat,
begging them to find a way to spare him.
The two ghosts looked at each other,
"We have received the kindness of a drink,
we must devise a plan."
They stood up and said:
"Wait for us a while,
we will return."
Not long after, they came back,
saying:
"Prepare four hundred thousand coins,
and we will extend your life by three years."
Hézi agreed,
setting the next day at noon as the deadline.
He paid for the wine,
and the wine was returned.
He tasted it,
and it was like water,
cold enough to chill his teeth.
Hézi hurried home,
prepared the money as promised and burned it,
seeing the two ghosts take the money and leave.
After three days,
Hézi died.
The ghosts said three years,
but in the human world, it was three days.
Lǐ Xībó
Lǐ Xībó of Lǒngxī
served as magistrate of Wēn County in the ninth year of Yuánhé.
He once told me that
in the early years of Yuánhé,
when he was awaiting appointment,
he stayed temporarily in Xìngdào Lane in the Upper Capital.
One morning, he went to Chóngrén Lane to visit a fellow candidate,
when suddenly, at the north lower bend east of the Xìngdào Gate,
he saw a short woman in front of his horse,
wearing mourning clothes,
about three feet tall,
but her speech and voice
were like that of a grown woman,
muttering as if aggrieved.
She said:
"A thousand forbearances, ten thousand forbearances,
but eventually, a decision must be made.
I will never let him go!"
Then she snapped her fingers a few times and said:
"So strange, so strange."
Xībó urged his horse forward and left,
thinking it odd,
but dared not ask.
As the day grew late,
and he reached the broad avenue,
where carriages and horses were bustling,
this woman was stared at by passersby,
who did not know the reason.
This went on for two days,
and gradually more people gathered,
only on the north street of Chóngrén Lane.
Not long after,
Xībó left through the east gate of the government office,
and when he reached Jǐngfēng Gate,
he saw on the broad avenue
a huge crowd,
like a theater in the east or west corner.
They formed a large circle.
Inside, several children sat in a ring,
and the short woman went forward.
She covered her head with a cloth,
her words becoming incoherent,
and the children laughed mockingly.
If anyone tried to approach,
she would grab at them,
and the children would retreat.
This continued until noon,
and the onlookers grew even more.
As the short woman sat,
a child suddenly rushed forward,
pulled off the cloth covering her head,
and it fell.
They saw a three-foot green bamboo pole,
with a skull hanging from it.
The imperial guards reported the matter to the authorities.
Wáng Yìlǎo
More than thirty li southeast of Xiàguī County in Huàzhōu,
there is a place called Yánnián Lǐ.
Southwest of the lǐ, there is an old Buddhist temple,
but no monks reside there.
In the eighth year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
the Hanlin Academician Bái Jūyì was in mourning for his mother,
and had retired to Xiàguī County.
In the seventh month,
his elder cousin named Bái Hào,
came from Huàzhōu to visit Bái Jūyì.
On the way, he passed in front of the temple.
Upon reaching the gate,
he saw about ten women,
dressed in yellow damask silk robes,
of varying ages sitting together,
conversing under the Buddha hall,
their voices audible at the gate.
Bái Hào, having traveled in the heat, was thirsty,
and intended to rest there,
and also ask for a drink.
Seeing that his attendant Xiāo Shìqīng had not yet arrived,
he dismounted,
and tied the reins to a gate pillar.
Raising his head,
they suddenly disappeared.
He thought to himself that they had withdrawn and hidden between the windows and doors.
Following them, he saw nothing,
and thought they might have hidden behind the walls of the building.
Following them there,
again he saw nothing.
Looking around at the surroundings,
he found the walls encircling the area without any gaps or openings.
Looking again at the place where they had gathered and talked,
it was covered in dust,
with no footprints.
From this, he knew
that they were not human,
and he was greatly startled and found it very strange.
He mounted his horse and galloped away,
coming to tell Bái Jūyì.
Moreover, he heard what they were saying,
and there was much talk,
which he could not fully recall.
Mostly, they spoke of Wáng Yì being like this and that,
judging from the meaning of their words,
as if they were enumerating his faults together.
The place was about eight or nine li from Bái Jūyì's residence,
so they went together to investigate.
Indeed, in that area, there was a man named Wáng Yì,
who was a resident of that lǐ.
He had just moved to a place more than a hundred paces northeast of the temple,
repaired the walls and house,
and had just finished building the courtyard and planting trees,
and moved in the next day.
After moving in,
within less than ten days, Wáng Yì died,
within a month his wife died,
and not long after, Wáng Yì's two sons, two daughters-in-law, and one grandson also died.
Only one son remained,
named Míngjìn,
who was greatly terrified,
and did not know what to do.
Thinking the new residence was inauspicious,
he dismantled the house and uprooted the trees.
At night, he moved away,
and thus was spared.
Zhāng Hóngràng
In the twelfth year of Yuánhé,
the minor officer Zhāng Hóngràng of Shòuzhōu,
married the daughter of the Cavalry Commander Wáng Xiān.
Military operations in Huáixī were at a critical stage,
and Lìnghú Tōng was the prefect.
Zhāng Hóngràng's wife was seriously ill for many months,
and whenever she craved food,
Zhāng Hóngràng would provide it for her.
Later, she stopped eating,
and from summer to autumn it went on like this,
sometimes improving, sometimes relapsing,
but Zhāng Hóngràng never neglected her.
In the tenth month of winter,
his wife suddenly craved noodle soup,
and Zhāng Hóngràng prepared it for her.
Before the cooking was finished,
he encountered the army distributing winter clothing,
so Zhāng Hóngràng asked his comrade Wáng Shìzhēng's wife to prepare the meal.
Zhāng Hóngràng then left.
When Wáng Shìzhēng's wife finished cooking,
she approached the bed to serve it,
when suddenly she saw Zhāng Hóngràng's wife split in half from the forehead and nose,
with one hand and one thigh on the bed,
blood staining the mat.
Wáng Shìzhēng's wife cried out in alarm,
and reported it to the camp.
The wives of soldiers and neighbors came,
and all looked on,
vying to ask questions but no one knew the reason.
Soon an official reported to Lìnghú Tōng,
who sent someone to investigate.
That day was not dark or dim,
and the two women had no prior grievances or resentment,
so the official recorded the incident.
Zhāng Hóngràng rushed back,
and upon reaching the place of mourning,
suddenly heard his wife's sorrowful weeping from the air, saying:
"I was summoned by the master to go see the child.
I have troubled you for a long time,
but I had no choice,
and you never abandoned me.
The master demands that you plead earnestly."
Previously, behind Zhāng Hóngràng's residence there was a small garden,
with a plum tree.
His wife said:
"Now quickly prepare four portions of food for me,
and place them under the plum tree.
Then you must mournfully pray under the tree,
and I will surely be able to return to the human world."
Zhāng Hóngràng followed her words,
set out the food,
and earnestly prayed and bowed.
Suddenly, he heard a voice from the air say:
"I return your bride to you."
Then he heard Wáng Shì say:
"Use your strength to receive me."
Zhāng Hóngràng did as she said and received her,
and soon felt a warm half-body gently descending.
Zhāng Hóngràng embraced it.
Immediately he heard Wáng Shì say:
"Quickly join it with the half-body on the bed."
By the time Zhāng Hóngràng, hunched over, carried the half-body to the bed,
Wáng Shì repeatedly said:
"Check the cut places,
to ensure they align without discrepancy."
Zhāng Hóngràng exerted all his strength to join them together,
making them match as before.
Wáng Shì said:
"Cover me with a quilt,
and do not disturb me for three days."
Zhāng Hóngràng followed her instructions.
After three days,
he heard moaning,
and she said:
"I would like some thin congee."
Zhāng Hóngràng poured it into her throat,
and she finished a cup.
She also said:
"Do not ask anything further."
After seven days, she recovered as before,
but from the back of her neck down the spine to the tailbone,
there was a scar like a knife wound.
From the forehead and nose,
through the chest and abdomen, it was the same.
After a year,
she healed completely as before.
She bore several children.
This was personally witnessed by my old friend Páng Zǐsù.
Kòu Yōng
In the twelfth year of the Yuánhé era,
in the southwestern corner of Yǒngpíng Ward in the upper capital,
there was a small residence.
A sign was hung, stating:
"If anyone dares to live here,
the original deed will be transferred to them,
along with the initial purchase price."
During the Dàlì era,
Ān Tàiqīng first bought it for two hundred thousand coins,
and later sold it to Wáng Xū.
It passed through a total of seventeen owners,
all of whom lost their eldest sons.
It was donated to the Luóhàn Temple,
and though the temple rented it out,
no one dared to enter.
There was a fortune-teller named Kòu Yōng,
who frequented the gates of nobles and officials.
He went to the temple seeking to buy it,
and thus offered forty thousand coins to the temple.
The temple was overjoyed,
and transferred the deed to him.
There were three main hall rooms,
very low,
and five side rooms in total, east and west,
covering about three mǔ of land,
with hundreds of elm and paper mulberry trees.
At the gate stood a tall screen wall,
eight chǐ high,
with a base one chǐ thick,
all plastered with charcoal ash.
Yōng also became a disciple of the monk Pǔzhào from the Fǎmíng Temple in Chóngxián Ward.
That night,
he swept the hall and stayed alone,
and nothing happened for the first night.
When the moon was bright,
by the fourth watch,
a light rain fell,
and Yōng suddenly felt his body stiffen,
his hair standing on end,
and his heart filled with fear.
He heard the sound of someone crying,
as if from the depths of the underworld.
He listened closely,
and it seemed to come from midair.
It shifted east and west,
with no fixed location.
As dawn approached,
the sound finally ceased.
Yōng then told Zhào:
"Since the house is like this,
it should be livable."
He ordered Zhào to perform a ritual ceremony.
By the third watch,
he heard crying again.
After seven full days,
Yōng held a vegetarian feast for the monks.
Just as the monks were about to receive their food,
Zhào suddenly stood up,
and as if seeing something in the courtyard,
he shouted loudly and chased after it,
yelling:
"This thief has killed so many people!"
He circled the courtyard once,
then sat back down and said:
"I saw it, I saw it."
He then ordered Yōng to seek cleansing water from seven households.
Soon, they reached the tall screen wall at the gate,
sprinkled a cup of water,
and struck it with a willow branch.
Four chǐ from the base of the wall,
the earth suddenly collapsed,
revealing a woman inside,
wearing a blue silk skirt, red trousers, brocade shoes, and a crimson blouse.
Her clothes were all made of paper ash,
and as the wind blew,
they scattered into the courtyard,
leaving only dry bones lying there.
He ordered a bamboo basket to be woven,
and told Yōng to prepare two or three sets of women's clothing to wrap them in.
They were sent for burial on a sandbar in the Wèi River,
with instructions not to look back,
and wine and food were offered as well.
After that, no one in the household, young or old, felt fear again.
Originally, Guō Fényáng had a cousin,
who became a nun at the Xuānhuà Temple in Yǒngpíng Ward.
When the wife of Prince Fényáng paid respects to her aunt,
she brought many attendants.
Later, when they bought this residence,
they stayed here when visiting.
It was said that a maidservant was careless,
and the maidservant went missing.
The lady ordered the tall screen wall to be built,
which is why this residence had it.
It is also said
that the maidservant was careless,
leaking information about their visits,
and was thus buried alive here.
Hūyán Yì
During the Xiánhé era (326–334),
there was a man named Hūyán Jì,
who was appointed Registrar of Zhōngzhōu.
He took his wife with him to assume his post.
When they reached Sìshuǐ,
they encountered bandits.
All their belongings were taken,
even down to their clothes.
Jì and his wife then went along the roadside seeking signs of habitation.
Soon they met an old man,
who asked what had happened.
Jì told him.
The old man said:
"A few miles south from here,
is my home.
You and your family may stay there temporarily."
Jì then went with the old man to his home.
Entering a grove,
they came upon a large estate.
The old man settled them in a room,
providing food and clothing.
Late that night,
he personally came to talk with Jì.
He again set out wine and food,
and said:
"In my family, there is only my old mother.
If you are unable to take your wife with you,
and wish to leave her here temporarily,
waiting until you reach your post to come fetch her later,
that would also be acceptable.
I see that you are impoverished,
and it surely will not be easy to take her along."
Jì pondered this for a long while,
then thanked him and said:
"Since you, sir, take pity on me like this,
I entrust my wife to your care with all sincerity.
My wife originally came from an official's household;
she can sing,
and also has some modest literary and artistic talents.
However, she is fond of wine,
and rather unrestrained.
After leaving her here,
I hope you, sir, will keep her under control."
The old man said:
"Do not worry,
just go ahead to your post."
The next day,
Jì left his wife behind and departed.
At parting,
his wife took Jì's hand and said:
"I originally traveled far over mountains and rivers with you,
to take up a minor post.
Now, unexpectedly, you are leaving me here.
If you do not come to fetch me,
I will surely run away,
and there will certainly be someone who takes me in."
They parted in tears.
When Jì reached his post,
he began planning to fetch his wife from afar.
Suddenly one day,
someone delivered a letter.
He received it,
and it was from his wife.
The letter said:
"I now write this letter myself,
to convey my feelings.
I only hope you will read it briefly.
I was originally the daughter of a singing girl;
I entered the palace precincts in my youth,
known for my clear singing and graceful dancing.
Naturally, I lacked the virtues and demeanor of a proper wife.
When orders came from the palace,
and selections were made from the women's quarters,
I was released and allowed to return home.
At that time,
you were still young,
wild with wine and poetic abandon,
living in my neighborhood.
I was unrestrained,
and you were also dissolute.
You did not consider me unfit to serve as your wife,
and so formally married me.
After I became your match,
all the neighbors called us a talented scholar and a beautiful lady.
I often recall walking together among the flowers,
facing each other under the moonlight,
playful banter in the red chamber,
vows spoken within embroidered curtains.
I never expected today's events.
Alas!
How utterly the bonds have been severed.
You, regarding my person,
cast me aside like a worn shoe,
leaving me in the wilds,
with no thought for my solitude.
Since you went to your post,
my tears have flowed unceasingly.
Reflecting on your heartlessness,
why should I guard my chastity any longer?
The old man's family has a young son,
who deeply admires me.
I have already given myself to him.
May you know this."
Jì read the letter and threw it down,
overwhelmed with rage.
He then abandoned his post and went to Sìshuǐ.
His original intent was to find the old man and his wife,
and kill them both.
Searching but unable to find them,
he only saw a large burial mound,
with dense woods around it.
Jì destroyed the mound,
and saw his wife already dead inside it.
He then took the corpse, performed a sacrifice,
buried it separately, and left.
Ān Fèng
was a man from Shòuchūn.
In his youth, he was close friends with a fellow villager, Xú Kǎn,
and both had talent and learning.
They originally agreed to travel together to seek office in Cháng'ān.
Kǎn was by nature purely filial.
When parting from his mother,
seeing her weep incessantly,
he could not bear to leave.
Fèng went to Cháng'ān,
but for ten years achieved no success,
and was ashamed to return.
Later, he suddenly met Kǎn.
They clasped hands and recounted their long separation,
talking of affairs from their hometown.
Both were overcome with sorrow and joy.
They stayed together at an inn for several days.
Suddenly, Kǎn said to Fèng:
"I have been away from home for a year.
My mother must be thinking of me;
I should return.
You have also been away from home for a long time.
Can you return with me?"
Fèng said:
"I never applied myself diligently to farming,
but my ambition was keenly set on fame and office.
Now I am far from my homeland,
seeking sustenance in Cháng'ān,
with not a single high minister knowing me.
After ten years of drifting,
the spirit of a true man—
how can I return to face the people of my hometown?"
Then, weeping, he said to Kǎn:
"You should go home to comfort your parents.
I vow not to return until I achieve success!"
Kǎn left a poem, which said:
"You have long been lodged in Cháng'ān,
ashamed not to return to your native place.
I now leave Cháng'ān,
intent on comforting my parents at home.
Unexpectedly, this parting sorrow—
even in the netherworld, I shall not forget."
Fèng also presented a poem in farewell:
"Ever since I left my homeland,
ten years have passed in Xiánqín.
I have wept out all the blood of Biàn Hé,
yet met not a single old friend.
Today, parting from an old companion,
I am ashamed of this drifting life of mine.
At this place where we chant poems of parting,
my hempen robe repeatedly hides my tears.
In tears we part, each going his own way;
let us wait until next spring."
Fèng remained a sojourner in Cháng'ān.
Because he dreamed of Kǎn one night,
he sent a letter to Shòuchūn.
It began by recounting their meeting again in Cháng'ān,
and speaking of their hidden feelings.
Kǎn's mother received Fèng's letter,
and weeping, said to the person who delivered it:
"Kǎn has been dead for three years."
The messenger returned to Cháng'ān
and told Fèng.
Fèng shed tears and sighed, saying:
"Only today do I understand the line in Kǎn's farewell poem, 'even in the netherworld, I shall not forget.'"
Chéng Shūbiàn
In the thirteenth year of the Yuánhé era,
in Jiānglíng, a registered commoner named Chéng Shūbiàn had a daughter named Xìngniáng,
who was seventeen years old.
Suddenly, a matchmaker came to their door and said:
"There is a young man from a farming family,
who wishes to form a marital alliance.
He is now at the gate."
Shūbiàn called his wife to look at him together,
but they were quite dissatisfied with the man's appearance.
They immediately declined, saying:
"Xìngniáng is still young,
and we have not yet prepared her dowry."
Hearing this from outside the door,
the man hurried in and said:
"I intended for the farming lad to pay respects to his father-in-law and mother-in-law."
Shūbiàn paid no heed,
and hastily retreated with his wife.
The farming servant said:
"Tián Sìláng is an incense officer from the upper realm.
How can he be denied your daughter?"
He then laughed once,
and two men descended from the sky,
asking:
"Why did you call us?"
Tián said:
"The Chéng family has a daughter.
I have discussed it with them,
but they firmly refuse.
What do you two think?"
The two men said:
"They simply do not know better.
How can they refuse?
Please allow us to negotiate.
Moreover, the soul and consciousness of the young lady have already followed you,
and she deeply admires you.
Common folk,
What do they know?
Do not blame them harshly."
After speaking,
Xìngniáng suddenly cried out from her room:
"I will marry Tián Sìláng."
Realizing they were not human,
Shūbiàn stepped down the stairs and said:
"Our humble family raises a daughter,
and we do not wish for her to be scrutinized.
Regarding Sìláng's intentions,
how dare we disobey?
But please sit for a while,
and discuss with the matchmaker.
Do not be too hasty."
The four looked at each other and laughed heartily, saying:
"It is settled."
Shūbiàn immediately ordered fruits to be bought,
Prepared tea and pastries,
and sat in the hall with curtains drawn.
The matchmaker said:
"The farming family's intentions are not satisfactory,
and Sìláng is also too hasty.
Now, all three gentlemen are poets.
Please compose a linked verse before finalizing."
Everyone laughed joyfully and said:
"Old woman, just be a matchmaker.
Why must you discuss linked verses?"
The matchmaker insisted,
and after a long while, Tiánláng chanted:
"A touch of red robes emerges from the verdant peaks.
In autumn, clouds are still, the moon hangs bright and clear."
Tián asked Shūbiàn to continue,
but Shūbiàn had never studied books,
so he firmly declined.
They went back and forth several times.
After a meal's time,
suddenly someone in the hall spoke:
"Why not say:
'Heavenly envoys turn their heads in vain,
why not follow him, though his clan is lowly?'"
After speaking,
the matchmaker and the three men laughed uproariously and said:
"We said it was demonic talk.
What will you do now?"
The four hurried out together,
and never returned.
Their daughter was like a drunkard raving,
but after the four left,
she sobered up.
A Selected Candidate from Xiāngyáng
When Yú Dí governed Xiāngyáng,
a selected candidate named Liú was heading to the capital,
when he met a provincial graduate,
about twenty years old,
who spoke clearly and brightly.
They traveled together for several miles,
and found each other quite agreeable.
They then sat on the grass.
Liú had wine,
and poured several cups.
At dusk,
the provincial graduate pointed to a fork in the road and said:
"My humble dwelling is a few miles from here.
Would you care to visit?"
Liú declined due to his travel schedule,
so the provincial graduate composed a poem:
"Flowing water trickles, long celery sprouts,
weaving birds fly in pairs, travelers return home.
The deserted village has no one to observe Cold Food Festival,
the tomb faces empty pear blossoms."
By dawn,
Liú returned to Xiāngyáng Prefecture,
and went to search for the provincial graduate,
only to find a tomb there.
Zǔ Jià
The presented scholar Zǔ Jià
was the grandson of Zǔ Yǒng.
After failing the imperial examination,
he once traveled in the Shāng Mountains,
where his journey was difficult and perilous.
One evening, he arrived at a solitary post station.
About half a mile from the station,
there was an empty Buddhist temple,
with no monks residing there.
Jià and his servant sought shelter there for the night.
The autumn moon was very bright,
and Jià wandered alone, enjoying the moonlight,
walking back and forth.
Suddenly, a man
emerged from the temple hall,
bowed to Jià, and sat with him,
chatting and laughing while discussing classics and history,
occasionally reciting poetry himself.
Jià brewed tea to entertain him,
but this man continued reciting alone.
He also said:
"When one writes poetry,
it should express feelings and critique matters.
If it is not refined or precise,
it cannot move people.
Tonight, we met by chance,
and future meetings are uncertain.
I shall compose two or three poems
to express my feelings."
He then recited clearly:
"My home lies north of the post road,
a hundred miles without neighbors.
Coming and going, no one asks,
silent is the mountain home in spring."
He recited again:
"The southern ridge is desolate at night,
with green pines and white poplars.
My family must be dreaming,
but the distant traveler has no heart left."
He recited once more:
"Amidst white grass on a cold road,
under the bright moon in chaotic mountains.
Tonight, after bitter recitation ends,
the cold candle shares this moment with you."
After finishing the poems,
he recited them repeatedly.
Late into the night,
he bowed and withdrew.
The next day,
Jià asked the neighbors,
who said that for several miles around,
there were no inhabitants,
only a scholar who had died away from home,
buried on the southern ridge behind the temple hall.
Jià reflected on his poems,
and realized he was a ghost.
He wrote an essay to mourn him before leaving.
Guō Chénggǔ
once treasured a scroll of fine calligraphy,
which he always carried with him.
When he first took the imperial examination,
he went to sit for the miscellaneous essays test.
He wrote,
and when he finished,
it was still early at night.
He sealed it and placed it in his case,
but when submitting his exam paper, he mistakenly handed in his treasured calligraphy scroll instead.
Returning to his lodgings,
he took out the scroll under the lantern to look at it,
only to find that his examination paper was still in the case.
At a loss for what to do,
he paced back and forth outside the examination hall gate.
He saw an old clerk
and inquired about the examination matters,
telling him the whole truth.
The clerk said:
"I can exchange it for you.
But my family is poor,
and I live in Xìngdào Lǐ.
If I succeed in making the exchange,
I hope you will reward me with thirty thousand coins."
Chénggǔ agreed.
In a short while,
the clerk brought in the examination paper
and took out the calligraphy scroll,
handing it to Chénggǔ.
The next day, returning to Qīnrén Lǐ,
he personally brought the money to Xìngdào Lǐ.
He knocked and inquired for a long time,
until a family member of the clerk came out.
When he asked for the clerk by name,
the reply was:
"My master died three months ago;
we are struggling in poverty,
and have not yet prepared the burial necessities."
Chénggǔ was astonished and sighed for a long time,
only then realizing that the person he saw at the examination hall
was a ghost.
He then gave the money to the family.
Zhāng Yǔ
Zhāng Yǔ was sitting for the jìnshì examination.
In the thirteenth year of the Yuánhé era,
he lived on the south street of Shēngdào Lǐ in Cháng'ān.
On the night of the eighth day of the eleventh month,
his servants were staying elsewhere,
and Yǔ was alone under the moonlight.
Suddenly, he smelled an extraordinary fragrance filling the courtyard.
Just as he was startled by this,
he soon heard footsteps gradually approaching.
Yǔ slipped on his shoes and listened:
several maidservants, about eighteen or nineteen years old,
unrivaled in beauty,
pushed the door open and entered,
saying:
"Strolling under the moon in search of fine scenery,
we need not go to Lèyóu Yuán;
this courtyard’s small terrace and wisteria trellis will do just fine."
Then they led in seven or eight young women,
all of exceptionally beautiful appearance,
dressed in splendid attire,
like the family of a wealthy noble.
Yǔ retreated to the main hall,
peering out from behind the curtain.
The women walked slowly
straight to the wisteria trellis.
In a moment,
they set up couches and beds,
carved trays, jade wine vessels, cups, and ladles—
all extraordinary objects.
The eight of them sat in a circle,
with ten maidservants holding musical instruments,
two standing with clappers,
and ten attendants standing on either side.
Just as the strings and pipes began to play,
one of the seated women said:
"Without informing the host,
we are about to start the music.
Is that not disrespectful?
Since he is a scholar,
we should invite him to join our revelry."
She then ordered a maidservant to relay the message:
"My sisters and I were strolling under the moon
and chanced to enter your honorable courtyard.
With wine, food, and music,
we are amusing ourselves.
Would the xiùcai come out briefly to act as host?
It is late at night;
we assume you have already removed your cap.
You may come with just a gauze scarf;
that would suit this informal setting."
When Yǔ heard the maidservant receiving the order,
he feared their approach,
so he closed the door and refused them.
The maidservant knocked on the door,
but Yǔ did not respond.
She pushed, but it would not open,
so she hurried back to report.
One of the women said:
"We are enjoying ourselves together,
and others dare not join.
Since we have entered his gate,
he should come to pay his respects even without being summoned.
Closing the door and barring the entrance,
he shames our company.
Since he does not come when called,
there is no need to summon him again."
Then one of them took charge of the wine vessel,
and another oversaw the proceedings.
Once the wine had been passed around,
the strings and pipes played in harmony.
The dishes were fragrant and exquisite,
the music clear and bright.
Yǔ reflected that the south street of this ward
was entirely graves and tombs,
with absolutely no one living there;
if they came from within the ward,
the ward gates were already closed.
If they were not bewitching foxes,
they must be ghosts.
Now, while I am still not enchanted,
I can drive them away.
If I become entranced in a moment,
how will I regain my senses?"
So he secretly took a stone used to prop up the bed,
slowly opened the door, and rushed out suddenly,
aiming at the feast
and struck;
he hit the center of the table tray,
and they scattered in disarray.
Yǔ chased after them
and seized one cup,
tying it with his clothing.
When dawn came and he looked at it,
it was a white horn cup,
strange beyond description.
The fragrance in the courtyard
lingered for several days without fading.
He locked the cup in a cabinet,
and whenever relatives or friends came,
they all passed it around to look,
but none could identify its origin.
More than ten days later,
after examining it several times,
it suddenly fell to the ground
and was never seen again.
The following year, Yǔ
passed the jìnshì examination with high honors.
Liú Fāngxuán
The mountain recluse Liú Fāngxuán traveled from Hànnán to Bālíng.
One night, he lodged at an ancient inn on the riverbank.
To the west of the hall was a bamboo fence separating it,
and there was another hall beyond,
which was always locked.
It was said
that many strange creatures haunted it,
making guests uneasy,
and it had not been opened for ten years.
In between was a hall,
its corridors collapsed and ruined.
The prefect had repaired it,
making it clean and new,
yet no one dared to enter.
Fāngxuán knew nothing of this.
After the second watch,
moonlight filled the courtyard,
and the river and mountains were serene and still.
Only from beyond the fence to the west came the sounds of women talking, laughing, and chanting,
though not very clearly distinguishable.
Only an old maidservant, whose speech was somewhat heavy with a Qín accent,
said:
"In the past, when the master was demoted,
he often had this old servant ride on the skewbald horse,
holding young master Jīng.
Young master Jīng was spoiled,
and wouldn't sit still.
Sometimes he leaned to the left,
sometimes to the right.
He fell and injured this old servant's left arm.
Even now, when the weather is about to turn cloudy,
it aches with pain.
Now it's acting up again.
Tomorrow it will surely rain."
"Now young master Jīng holds a high official position,
I wonder if he still remembers this old servant?"
Then came the sound of someone responding.
Soon, someone sang,
her voice clear and delicate,
like a thread being drawn out endlessly.
Then she recited a poem,
her recitation mournful,
as if filled with sorrow and tears,
though the words could not be discerned.
After a while, the old maidservant spoke again:
"In the past, young master Jīng
loved to recite 'Green, green the grass by the riverbank,'
today one could also say 'Endlessly I long for the distant road.'"
Only at the fourth watch
did the sounds cease.
The next morning, it indeed rained heavily.
Fāngxuán called the inn clerk to inquire,
and the clerk said:
"That western hall is empty, with no one inside."
He then explained why guests dared not enter.
Fāngxuán thus ordered the courtyard opened to inspect it.
They found autumn grass and green moss covering the steps,
and to the west, it connected to the mountain forest,
with no trace of human presence.
They opened the hall,
which was clean and new,
but completely empty.
Only on the eastern pillar in the front room was a poem inscribed,
the ink still fresh.
Its words read:
"My parents gave me a green maple root,
