I cannot recall how many times the green wind has fallen.
Back then, I embroidered flowers on my clothes,
today they are ashes, unwearable."
Looking at the words,
it was clearly a ghost's poem.
The inn clerk said
that since this hall was built,
no one had ever lived there.
Nor had there been any poem inscribed there before.
Only then did they realize it was the people from the night before.
Fāngxuán inquired further among people,
but in the end, could not understand it.
A Resident of Guāngzhái Ward
During the Yuánhé era,
a resident of Guāngzhái Ward, whose name is lost,
had a sick person in his household.
As the illness grew critical,
they invited monks to chant sutras,
with the wife and children gathered around guarding.
One evening,
everyone seemed to see a person enter the house.
They all panicked and chased it,
and it threw itself into a jar.
The family poured hot water into the jar,
and retrieved a bag,
which turned out to be a ghost's bag for capturing breath.
Suddenly, they heard a voice from the air,
pleading for the bag,
very earnestly and urgently,
saying, "I will take someone else to replace the sick person."
The family then threw the bag back,
and the sick person immediately recovered.
A Huáixī Army Officer
At the end of the Yuánhé era,
there was a Huáixī army officer
on a mission to Biànzhōu,
staying at a post station.
Late at night,
as he was about to fall asleep,
he suddenly felt something pressing down on him.
The officer was strong by nature,
and startled awake,
wrestled with it.
The creature then retreated,
and he managed to seize a leather bag from its hand.
The ghost pleaded desperately in the darkness,
and the officer said:
"Tell me the name of this object,
and I will return it."
After a long while, the ghost said:
"This is a breath-storing bag."
The officer then struck it with a brick,
and the voice ceased.
The bag could hold several shēng,
was crimson in color,
like lotus root fibers,
and cast no shadow when carried under the sun.
Guō Zhù
During the Yuánhé era,
there was a man named Guō Zhù,
who once served as the sheriff of Wǔchāng in Èzhōu.
He was good friends with Liǔ Zhíqiān of the Peìguó region.
Whenever the two talked,
they often lamented that the realms of the living and the dead could not communicate.
They agreed that whoever died first
would come and inform the other.
Later, several months after Zhíqiān's death,
Zhù was living in Huàyīn.
One evening, while alone,
he heard sighing outside his door.
After a while, a voice said:
"I hear that you, Guō Jūn, are well."
Zhù recognized the voice
as Zhíqiān's and said:
"We should meet face to face."
The voice replied:
"Please extinguish the candle,
and I will talk with you."
Zhù immediately put out the candle,
took its sleeve, and brought it inside.
They shared the same bed,
and talked of old times vividly.
It also spoke of the underworld journey,
where sins and blessings were very clear,
and nothing could be hidden.
As the night deepened,
Zhù suddenly noticed a foul odor emanating from beside him,
soon becoming unbearable.
He reached out to feel it,
and found its body very large,
unlike Zhíqiān.
Zhù was strong,
and realizing it was some other monster,
he grabbed its sleeve,
pinned it down with his body,
holding it firmly immobile,
and lay covering his nose.
After a while, it asked to leave.
Zhù pretended to talk with it,
detaining it until nearly dawn.
It grew increasingly urgent to leave,
saying:
"Dawn is approaching.
If you do not let me go,
disaster will befall you."
Zhù did not reply.
After a moment,
he no longer heard it speak.
Soon, day broke,
and he saw a foreigner,
over seven chǐ tall,
looking as if he had died several days earlier.
It was summer at the time,
and the stench was unbearable up close.
He ordered it taken and discarded outside the suburbs.
Suddenly, several villagers from the area saw it,
hurried over to look,
and exclaimed in shock:
"It is indeed our elder brother!
He died several days ago,
and last night suddenly disappeared."
They then took the corpse away.
Péi Tōngyuǎn
In Wéiyáng, there was a man named Wàn Zhēn,
a great merchant,
who was often away from home,
traveling to trade in treasures and goods.
His wife, Mèng Shì,
was formerly a courtesan from Shòuchūn,
beautiful in appearance,
skilled in singing and dancing.
She had some knowledge of literature,
and possessed a modest talent for poetry.
One day, Mèng Shì was strolling alone in her garden,
gazing around when she chanted:
"How regrettable, this springtime season,
still I wander all alone.
For no reason, two lines of tears,
ever flow before the flowers."
After reciting the poem,
tears streamed down her face.
Suddenly, a young man,
exceedingly handsome in appearance,
leaped over the wall and entered,
smiling as he said to Mèng Shì:
"Why do you chant with such sorrow?"
Mèng Shì, greatly startled, said:
"Whose son are you?
How have you come so abruptly to this place,
and why do you speak so lightly?"
The young man replied:
"My nature is unrestrained,
I do not restrain myself,
I only love to sing loudly and get thoroughly drunk.
Just now I heard the sound of chanting,
and could not help but feel joy stirring in my heart,
so I leaped over the wall to come here.
If you would allow me beneath the flowers to share a fine conversation,
perhaps I too could clumsily attempt a refined tune."
Mèng Shì said:
"Do you wish to chant a poem?"
The young man said:
"Floating life is like a sojourn,
how long does youth last?
The lush flowers are in full bloom,
yet yellow leaves already fall.
The regrets within the human world,
are far more than a thousand kinds.
Why not steal a moment's joy instead?"
Mèng Shì said:
"I have a good husband, Wàn Zhēn,
who left home several years ago.
What I regret is that amid this beautiful scene,
he is far away in another land.
It is not only lamenting the fragrant blossoms,
but truly grieving over our long separation.
Therefore, I chanted my clumsy verse,
to express my hidden feelings.
I did not expect you to trespass into my grounds,
for what reason?"
The young man said:
"I have long heard of your elegant chants,
now I behold your lovely face,
even if it costs my life I would strive,
so how could a reprimand harm me?"
Mèng Shì then took up paper,
and continued composing a poem:
"Whose young man is this,
secretly deceiving in his heart?
Not saying it can never be,
but if it happens, I fear my lord will know."
The young man, receiving the poem,
replied thus:
"The goddess met Zhāng Shuò,
Wén Jūn encountered Cháng Qīng.
Meeting at the right time, both found each other,
enough to comfort much affection."
From then on, Mèng Shì secretly took him as a lover,
and brought him to her own quarters.
After over a year,
her husband returned from abroad.
Mèng Shì, worried and weeping,
the young man said:
"Do not be so,
I always knew this would not last long."
Having spoken,
he soared into the air and departed,
and in a moment vanished,
leaving no one knowing what kind of strange being he was.
A Commoner from Lìsú Ward
In the early Chángqìng era,
in Luòyáng's Lìsú Ward,
there was a commoner driving several carts,
about to leave through the Chángxià Gate.
A man carrying a cloth sack
asked to place his sack in one of the carts,
and warned not to open it carelessly,
then turned back into Lìsú Ward.
As soon as he entered,
there was the sound of crying.
The person entrusted with the sack opened it to look inside,
its mouth was tied with a raw rope,
inside was an object,
shaped like an ox bladder,
along with a black rope several feet long.
The commoner, alarmed,
hastily tied it up again.
After a while,
the man returned,
saying:
"My feet hurt,
I wish to rest in your cart,
for a few miles,
may I?"
The commoner, realizing he was unusual,
agreed.
The man boarded the cart,
looked at the sack unhappily,
turned to the commoner and said:
"Why were you not trustworthy?"
The commoner apologized,
and he said further:
"I am not human,
the underworld office ordered me to register five hundred people,
I have passed through Shǎn, Guó, Jìn, Jiàng,
and arrived here.
Most people are 'worms,'
I have only obtained twenty-five persons.
Now I must go to Xú and Sì."
He added:
"Do you understand what I mean by 'worms'?"
Suffering from red sores means they are worms.
The cart traveled two miles,
then he bid farewell, saying he had a journey,
and could not stay long,
"You have longevity,
do not worry anymore."
Suddenly he shouldered the sack and alighted from the cart,
vanishing without a trace.
That summer,
many people in various prefectures suffered from red sores,
and some died.
A Military Officer from Tàiyuán
During the Chángqìng era,
Péi Dù was the northern garrison commander,
there was a military officer surnamed Zhào,
who was severely ill with fever.
His son was boiling medicine in the room,
having placed the medicine in a cauldron.
He lit the fire.
Zhào saw a person in yellow clothes,
come through the door,
and stop beside the medicine cauldron.
Carrying a small bag,
inside were medicinal powders,
their color pure white,
like wheat flour in appearance,
then he put the powders into the cauldron and left.
Zhào told his son,
the son said:
"Could it be a ghost?
This is meant to worsen my father's illness."
So they discarded the medicine.
Zhào saw the previous yellow-clad person come again,
and again put powders into the cauldron.
Zhào, disgusted,
also ordered it thrown away.
Another day, while napping during the day,
his son was again boiling medicine,
the medicine finished just as Zhào awoke,
so they offered it to him to drink.
Several days later,
he indeed passed away.
Chéng Gōng Kuí
When Duke Lǐ Yán was stationed in the Northern Capital,
there was a military officer under his command named Chéng Shàoyí.
His son, named Gōngkuí,
once dreamed that a man dressed in white entered and said:
"The underworld has ordered me to summon you."
Kuí refused him.
The messenger said:
"The underworld official has sent me to summon someone born in the Year of the Dragon.
Since you were born in the Year of the Dragon,
how can you escape it?"
Gōngkuí deceived him, saying:
"I am not born in the Year of the Dragon.
Why do you falsely accuse me?"
The messenger gradually relented,
turned and said:
"I will let you go for now,
but I must summon another person born in the Year of the Dragon."
Gōngkuí awoke in fright,
and told his dream to Shàoyí.
Shàoyí had more than ten soldiers
who often served under him.
By the next day,
one of the soldiers died without any illness.
Shàoyí then inquired about his birth year,
and the soldier's father said:
"He was born in the Year of the Dragon."
It indeed matched what Gōngkuí had dreamed.
The Book-Delivery Messenger
Long ago, there was a book-delivery messenger
who exited through the west gate of Lánlíng Ward.
He saw a Daoist priest,
over twenty feet tall,
with a long beard and a tall hat.
Leading two figures in green skirts,
sheep-like,
with topknots,
also over ten feet long.
Each carried two large jars,
inside the jars were dozens of small children,
some crying, some laughing,
in twos and threes,
playing with each other.
Upon seeing the messenger,
the Daoist priest turned to the sheep-like topknots and said:
"Ān ān."
The sheep-like topknots responded:
"Nà nà."
The children in the jars cried out in unison:
"Sī sī."
And in an instant, they ran northward.
No one knew where they went.
Zāng Xià
East of the crossroads in Ānyì Ward of the Upper Capital,
there was a residence of the Lù family.
Its structure was ancient and crude,
and people often called it a haunted house.
Later, a presented scholar named Zāng Xià rented and lived there.
Once, he and his elder brother Xián were napping during the day.
Suddenly, they were plagued by nightmares,
and it took a long time before they awoke.
He said:
"At first, I saw a woman,
in a green skirt and red sleeves,
descending from the eastern street.
Her form was delicate, her waist slender,
like flowers veiled in mist.
She wiped away her tears and said:
'Please listen to a verse of my hidden sorrow.'
Her words were:
'Divined the day to sail through the gorge,
autumn winds and waves abound.
A night of rain in Jiānglíng,
heartbroken by the Mùlán song.'"
The Ghosts Singing and Stomping
During the Chángqìng era,
someone north of Shùnchéng in Hézhōng,
under the Guànquè Tower, saw two ghosts,
each over thirty feet tall,
in blue shirts and white trousers,
arm in arm, singing and stomping:
"The river flows murky and muddy,
on the hilltop, buckwheat is sown.
Two monkeys come to the gate,
the neighbor's wife gets a hundred lashes."
After speaking, they vanished.
Lú Yàn
In the winter of the fourth year of Chángqìng,
the presented scholar Lú Yàn,
lived in Xīnchāng Ward.
One morning, he went out to the north street of the ward,
where the shadows of pagoda trees were sparse,
and the waning moon still hung in the sky.
He saw a woman,
over thirty feet tall,
dressed entirely in black.
Driving a creature
that looked like a ram,
also over ten feet tall.
Moving from east to west,
Yàn was terrified and retreated in panic.
The woman called out:
"Lú Wǔ,
if you see anyone, don't say too much."
In the end, no one knew what it was.
Lǐ Xiāng
Lú Cóngshǐ, serving as Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Military Commissioner of Zé-Lù.
He was implicated in conspiring with Wáng Chéngzōng of Zhènzhōu,
was demoted to Huānzhōu,
and ordered to commit suicide in Kāngzhōu.
In the first year of the Bǎolì era,
Lǐ Xiāng, the Prefect of Méngzhōu,
left his command and returned to the capital.
Considering himself a mere frontier commandery governor,
with no relatives in the central administration,
he felt that arriving at the imperial capital
was like a small boat adrift on a vast sea.
Hearing that there was a female shaman in Duānxī County
who knew future events,
he moored his boat and summoned her.
The shaman said:
"I am one who can see ghosts,
and those I see can all be summoned.
However, there are two grades of ghosts:
those with virtue and blessings
have vigorous and keen spirits.
They often speak to people themselves.
Those who were poor and lowly
have weak energy and haggard spirits;
they borrow my mouth to speak of matters,
all depending on whom I encounter.
It is not that I myself know these things."
Lǐ Xiāng asked:
"How can I find a ghost to question?"
She replied:
"Before the hall, under the catalpa tree,
there is a person wearing purple robes and a golden ornament.
He calls himself Vice Director Lú of Zé-Lù.
You may bow and request an audience."
Lǐ Xiāng then donned his official robes, held his tablet,
and bowed toward the tree.
The female shaman said:
"The Vice Director has returned your bow."
Lǐ Xiāng then bowed with hands clasped and ascended the steps.
A voice from the air said:
"Cóngshǐ died in this hall,
forced by a bowstring,
and still detests it now.
The bow on Your Excellency's bed—
please have it removed."
Lǐ Xiāng ordered it removed.
At that time, on the side steps of the postal station hall,
there was only one couch.
Lǐ Xiāng momentarily forgot the ghost's high status
and was about to sit down to question him.
The female shaman said:
"The Vice Director's rank is high.
Why not invite him to sit,
instead of treating him like a subordinate clerk?
The Vice Director is greatly angered
and has left.
Quickly follow and bow in apology;
he might be willing to return."
Lǐ Xiāng prostrated himself and descended the steps,
asking which direction to go,
taking one step and bowing once,
for several dozen steps.
A voice from the air said:
"Your office
does not even match that of a minor general in my army.
How dare you sit in my presence?"
Lǐ Xiāng repeatedly apologized.
The shaman said:
"The Vice Director has returned."
Thereupon, he bowed with clasped hands and proceeded.
Upon reaching the steps,
the shaman said:
"The Vice Director has ascended."
A separate couch was prepared.
Cushions and mats were spread to receive him.
The shaman said:
"He is seated."
Lǐ Xiāng then sat down.
The voice from the air said:
"What does Your Excellency wish to ask?"
He replied:
"Xiāng, a distant official returning to court,
humbly knows that the Vice Director possesses divine powers to comprehend creation,
and perceives what is yet to come.
I beg you to grant me a word,
revealing my future glory or decline."
The voice from the air said:
"There will be someone to receive and guide you.
One month after arriving in the city,
you will be appointed Prefect of Wúzhōu."
Lǐ Xiāng asked further,
but there was no more reply.
Lǐ Xiāng then asked:
"The Vice Director has left the human world for a long time.
Why not return to life among men,
instead of dwelling long in this dark solitude?"
The reply came:
"Alas!
What words are these?
Human life is toilsome,
ten thousand sorrows entangle the heart,
all like moths to a flame.
They strive and scramble for fame and profit;
sorrow prevails and hair turns white,
spirit fails and body grows frail.
Within the space of a square inch,
waves surge ten thousand feet high;
they envy and harm one another,
fierce as mighty beasts.
I have already escaped that.
Looking down, it is like boiling water and fire.
How could I lower myself again to lie among it?
Moreover, regarding life and death,
brightness and darkness are not so different.
As for the success or failure of learning immortality,
there is ultimately no distinction.
I have already attained the art of refining the form.
This art refines a formless state into a three-foot form;
then one may ascend to heaven or enter the earth,
ride clouds or drive cranes,
undergo a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes—
there is nothing impossible.
My form is not yet fully perfected—
only three inches short.
To fly freely at will,
to emerge from darkness into light—
that is already possible.
The lord of ten thousand chariots cannot compare to me,
let alone common people!"
Lǐ Xiāng said:
"May I hear about the Way of refining the form?"
The reply was:
"It is not fitting for Your Excellency to hear."
He asked again about what would happen after Wúzhōu,
but there was ultimately no reply,
and the ghost departed.
Lǐ Xiāng reached the capital,
and using rare goods sought assistance;
several people helped him.
Within a month,
he was appointed Prefect of Wúzhōu.
He eventually died in Wúzhōu.
Was this why Lú did not speak again of what would follow?
Mǎ Zhèn
Mǎ Zhèn of Fúfēng
lived in the Píngkāng Ward of Cháng'ān.
One day at noon,
he heard a knock at the door.
Going to look,
he saw a boy who rented out donkeys, saying:
"Just now, a lady
rented my donkey from the East Market
and came to this house to enter,
but hasn't paid the rental fee yet."
As no one had actually come to his house,
he paid the boy and sent him away.
After several days,
he heard knocking again,
and the same thing happened once more.
This occurred several times in succession,
and he began to suspect something strange.
So he stationed people on both sides of the gate
to wait for the visitor day after day.
On that day,
a woman indeed appeared,
riding a donkey from the east.
As she drew closer, he recognized her—
it was his mother,
who had passed away eleven years earlier.
She was buried in the Southern Mountains,
and the clothes she wore were still those she was buried in.
Mǎ Zhèn cried out in shock and rushed out,
but by then he saw her dismounting.
Having been noticed by others,
she had no time to hide or vanish.
Mǎ Zhèn chased after her,
and she ran around the screen wall.
Eventually cornered,
she entered the stable
and hid by standing against the back wall.
Mǎ Zhèn called out to her repeatedly,
but she remained motionless.
He then grabbed her sleeve,
and she suddenly collapsed—
turning out to be nothing but a skeleton.
Her clothes were intact,
and her skeletal body was complete.
Upon closer inspection,
he saw red veins like crimson threads
running through the bones.
Mǎ Zhèn wailed in grief,
gathered and supported the remains to change their resting place,
and went to the Southern Mountains.
He found the grave mound undisturbed.
Upon opening it for inspection,
the coffin inside was already empty.
Mǎ Zhèn then chose another site through divination
and reburied her there.
Yet he never understood the reason behind it all.
Liú Wéiqīng
guarded the northern pass at Píngyīn,
which faced southward, defending against the mountains and bordering the Jì River.
The area was vast and empty for a hundred lǐ,
with no inhabitants.
The terrain was perilous and strategic;
military commanders
would first seize this place to gain an advantage.
To this day, on overcast days or at dusk,
ghosts and strange phenomena often emerge.
In the spring of the third year of the Chángqìng era,
Xuē Píng, the military governor of Pínglú, sent his officer Liú Wéiqīng on a mission to Dōngpíng,
and his route passed through this area.
The sun had already set,
when suddenly in the wilderness,
he saw from afar tents, camps, and troops,
with numerous banners, soldiers, and horses,
and distant campfires.
Having served in the army from a young age,
Liú Wéiqīng estimated their formation
to be around fifty to sixty thousand men.
He did not know what they were
and was greatly alarmed.
Soon, supply wagons, drums, and horns appeared,
as the troops moved in chaotic disorder,
some singing, some talking,
advancing noisily and competitively.
Liú Wéiqīng then slowed his horse and rode out among them.
Suddenly, a person dressed in mourning clothes approached on foot and accosted Liú Wéiqīng,
attempting to seize his horse.
Liú Wéiqīng struggled with him forcefully,
then spurred his horse to break away from the path,
but the mourner clung to him even more desperately.
Liú Wéiqīng was strong and powerful,
and he repeatedly struck the mourner's back with the iron whip he carried.
The mourner did not resist much,
and after a long while, he let go and left.
When Liú Wéiqīng returned to the road,
the earlier army had already passed by.
Late into the night,
he finally reached the next postal station,
where he met his fellow officer Hún Zhāo,
who was returning from a mission to Huá
and was also lodging there.
Hearing of Liú Wéiqīng's arrival,
Hún Zhāo went to greet him,
only to find Liú Wéiqīng unconscious and unaware.
Everyone gathered around to support and watch over him;
after a long while, he awoke.
He then recounted what had happened,
and within two or three days,
he reached Dōngpíng.
After settling into his lodging,
he did not speak of it to anyone else.
Earlier in Dōngpíng, there was a mystic named Huángfǔ Jiē,
who was down on his luck and held no official post,
dressed in shabby sandals and tattered blue clothes,
and was widely despised.
One day,
while Liú Wéiqīng was out for a stroll,
Jiē pointed at him from afar on the road and said:
"Officer Liú."
Liú Wéiqīng was dressed in plain clothes
and did not recognize him,
so he engaged in conversation with him.
Jiē said:
"I originally feared that others might take your horse,
so I tried to pull you aside from the path.
Why did you instead torment me with an iron whip?
Fortunately, I was wearing golden armor;
otherwise,
with your great strength and hard strikes,
how could I have withstood them easily?"
He then laughed and walked away.
Liú Wéiqīng's attendants apologized
and tried to ask for an explanation,
but Jiē leaped into the dense crowd
and could not be seen again.
Four years later,
Lǐ Tóngjié rebelled in Cāngjǐng.
At that time, a massive army passed through Píngyīn to enter the rebel territory.
Could it be that the spectral troops had come to launch the campaign first?
Dǒng Guàn
was a man from Tàiyuán
who excelled in the arts of yīnyáng divination and prognostication.
During the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
he was on good terms with the monk Líng Xí,
and together they traveled to the regions of Wú and Chǔ.
Xí passed away on the journey,
and Guàn also returned to Bìngzhōu.
During the Bǎolì era,
Guàn traveled to Fénjīng,
reaching Ní
yáng Commandery.
He stayed at Lóngxīng Temple,
whose halls were grand and magnificent,
housing thousands of volumes of scriptures.
Guàn thus decided to remain there,
intending to read them all before returning.
Previously, in the northern room of the eastern corridor of the temple compound,
it was empty and locked,
so Guàn requested to stay there.
The temple monks refused,
saying:
"Those who have lived in this room
often fell ill or died,
and there have been many strange and eerie occurrences."
Guàn, being young and relying on his courage,
said:
"I am willing to take it."
Thus, he moved in.
After more than ten days, while sleeping at night,
there would often be over a dozen foreigners,
carrying instruments and wine,
singing and laughing within,
as if no one was there.
This happened for several nights.
Although Guàn was afraid,
he still did not speak of it to the temple monks.
One day, after finishing his scripture reading,
it was already dusk and dark,
and Guàn was extremely tired,
so he closed the room and went to sleep.
Before he was fully asleep,
he suddenly saw Líng Xí before his bed,
who said to Guàn:
"Master, it is time to go."
Guàn, startled and angry, said:
"Master, you are a ghost.
Why have you come?"
Xí laughed and said:
"Your fortune has run out and your time is up,
so I have come to wait for you."
He then pulled Guàn's sleeve away from the bed.
Guàn looked back
and saw his own body still lying there,
as if in deep sleep.
He sighed and said:
"Alas!
My home is far away,
and my parents are still alive.
If I die here now,
who will cover my corpse?"
Xí said:
"Why do your words miss the mark and your worries run so deep?
What makes one human
is merely the ability to move one's limbs
and to see and hear well.
This is enabled by the essence and soul supporting it;
it is not natural.
When the essence and soul leave the body, it is called death.
Thus, the limbs cannot move,
and sight and hearing cannot function.
Even a six-foot-tall body—
what use is it then?
Why should you be concerned about it?"
Guàn thanked him
and then asked Xí:
"I have often heard that in our teachings, there are those whose yīn leaves the body.
Who are they?"
Xí said:
"You and I are called dead but not yet reborn."
Thus, they proceeded together.
Wherever they headed,
even if the barriers were very strict,
they were never hindered.
They then left Níyáng city to the west.
The land there was covered with grass,
dense, red, and green,
like a felt carpet.
After traveling over ten lǐ,
they came to a river no more than a few chǐ wide,
flowing southwest.
Guàn asked Xí about it,
and Xí said:
"This is what is commonly called the Nài River,
whose source lies in the underworld!"
Guàn looked at the water
and saw it was all blood,
foul and putrid, impossible to approach.
He also saw several hundred sets of caps, belts, trousers, and robes on the bank.
Xí said:
"These are the clothes of the deceased,
who proceed from here toward the dark path."
Looking further west across the river, they saw two cities,
about one lǐ apart from north to south.
Grass and trees obscured them,
and houses stood side by side.
Xí said to Guàn:
"Let us go there together.
You will be born in the southern city, in the Xú family,
as the second son.
I will be born in the northern city, in the Hóu family,
as the eldest son.
After ten years of life,
we shall both leave our homes again to return to Buddhism."
Guàn said:
"I have heard that when a person dies, they are pursued by underworld officials,
who examine their records of sins and merits.
Only if their lifelong conduct has not been greatly flawed
can they be reborn in the human world.
Now, I have not even been dead for a full night.
How can it be like this already?"
Xí said:
"Not so.
The underworld path is no different from the human world.
If one does not commit wrongdoing,
how could shackles ever bind them?"
Having said this,
Xí grabbed his clothes and leaped across.
Just as Guàn was climbing the bank to descend,
the water suddenly parted,
widening to over a zhàng.
Guàn stared in shock and confusion.
Suddenly, someone pulled at Guàn.
Guàn turned to see a person
whose entire body was covered in hair,
resembling a lion,
yet whose face was human.
After a long while, he said to Guàn:
"Master, where are you going?"
Guàn said:
"To this southern city."
The person said:
"I command you to read the Great Buddhist Canon.
You must return quickly
and cannot stay here long."
He then took Guàn by the arm
and urgently pointed east and west toward the commandery city, returning.
Before they had gone a few lǐ, they saw another person,
similar in appearance to the one who had summoned Guàn,
shouting loudly:
"Take him away quickly,
lest he become unregistered."
In a moment,
they reached the temple.
By then, dawn was breaking.
Guàn saw dozens of monks at the door of his room,
crowding around it,
and saw his own body lying on the bed.
The two men pushed Guàn through the door.
Suddenly, water poured down from above onto his body,
and he awoke.
The temple monks said:
"Guàn was dead for a whole night."
Guàn then recounted everything to the monks.
A few days later,
he saw two clay figurines in the Buddhist hall,
serving as attendants on the left and right,
who were exactly the ones he had seen earlier.
Guàn thus vowed with all his heart to concentrate his thoughts,
staying to read the Buddhist Canon,
never slacking off despite heat or cold.
After several years, he returned home
on the fifteenth day of the fifth month in the second year of the Bǎolì era.
During the Huìchāng era,
an edict was issued to dismantle Buddhist temples throughout the land,
and Guàn was also dismissed.
Later, he went to Cháng'ān,
making a living through divination among the nobles and officials,
often accurately predicting events.
He once served as the county lieutenant of Línyí County in Yízhōu.
While I was in the capital,
I heard this story from Guàn himself.
Qián Fāngyì
Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ Qián Fāngyì,
was the son of the former Huázhōu Cìshǐ and Lǐbù Shàngshū Qián Huī.
In the early years of the Bǎolì era,
he was living alone at the Chánglè Estate.
One night, while going to the toilet,
his accompanying servants
suddenly saw a disheveled-haired, blue-clad figure several feet tall approaching.
Fāngyì was initially terrified
and wanted to flee,
but then thought, since it was a ghost coming,
what good would running do?
So he forced himself to say:
"Are you not Guō Dēng?"
It replied:
"Yes."
Fāngyì said:
"We walk different paths,
why must we meet?
I have often heard that if a person sees you,
none escape death.
Could it be that my fate dictates I must die upon seeing you?
My family home is in Huázhōu,
and my elder sister, a Buddhist nun, is also here.
If I were to die suddenly by your hand,
I would not dare regret my own life,
but it would be a pity for the bond between siblings to be insufficiently honored.
Can you allow me to bid farewell face-to-face?"
The disheveled-haired one replied:
"Dēng does not harm people.
My appearances are also limited.
When people see me,
if their vital energy is insufficient,
they bring about their own untimely death;
it is not Dēng who kills them.
However, I have a heartfelt matter,
and wish to entrust it to someone.
Because of this,
I have long not dared to appear.
Only because you, noble sir, have boundless fortune and blessings,
and your vital energy is overflowing,
would seeing me cause no harm.
Therefore, I dared to come out to seek your help."
Fāngyì said:
"What do you seek?"
It replied:
"Dēng has long held this post,
and accumulated merit should warrant a promotion.
But due to my meager fortune,
I need human assistance.
If you, noble sir, could have a copy of the Diamond Sutra written in golden characters for me,
with sincere dedication,
and transfer it to Dēng,
then Dēng's position
would indeed be slightly advanced.
I will surely repay you later,
I dare not speak falsely."
Fāngyì said:
"Agreed."
The disheveled-haired one added:
"Dēng, being of yin energy, encroaches upon yang.
Although you, noble sir, have strong fortune and power,
and will not fall ill,
you should still experience some slight discomfort.
You should quickly take raw rhinoceros horn and raw hawksbill turtle shell,
and plug your nostrils with musk; then you will suffer no distress."
Fāngyì reached the central hall,
feeling faint and about to collapse.
He hastily took the musk and other remedies and plugged his nostrils,
and then felt no distress.
A disciple of his father named Wáng Zhífāng,
who lived in the same neighborhood,
had long served in the Jiāng-Lǐng region.
Fāngyì sent an urgent letter to obtain raw rhinoceros horn,
and after taking it,
only after a long while did he stabilize.
The next morning,
he selected a sutra scribe,
ordered him to copy the Diamond Sutra in golden characters three times,
and instructed him to finish early.
When the work was done, he offered a meal to monks,
and transferred the merit to Guō Dēng.
Over a month later,
he returned to his country villa in Tóngzhōu.
He had just dismounted and was resting
when an elder relative of his, surnamed Péi,
whose family resided in Èzhǔ,
whom he had not seen for ten years,
suddenly entered through the gate,
walked straight to the foot of Fāngyì's steps,
and Fāngyì promptly bowed to him.
The elder said:
"There is a guest,
come outside first."
He then walked ahead,
Fāngyì followed him,
and upon reaching the gate, the elder vanished.
He saw a figure in a purple robe holding an ivory tablet,
leading dozens of attendants in crimson and purple official robes,
waiting outside the gate.
Looking down at his face,
it was indeed Guō Dēng.
Dēng straightened his tablet, stepped forward, and bowed, saying:
"My humble position was due for promotion,
requiring only one volume of the Diamond Sutra.
You, noble sir, in your benevolence,
specifically provided three volumes.
Now the merit is exceedingly great,
promoting me several grades,
to a lofty and weighty post,
with noble and exalted rank.
All this is due to your strength, noble sir.
Although my position has been suddenly promoted,
my kitchen remains as before.
Recently, while serving in my post,
it was truly like being among a fish market's stench.
Now that I am in a different office,
and again seek to eat there,
I realize the previous hardship
is almost unbearable.
I beg you, noble sir, to consider
and further transfer the Diamond Sutra for me seven more times.
Then my kitchen will be changed.
I will remember your virtue for life;
how could I ever dare forget?"
Fāngyì said:
"Agreed."
He then asked where the elder was.
Dēng replied:
"Your honorable elder in Jiāngxià is bedridden,
and tonight is particularly difficult.
When spirits seek someone,
unless a relative guides them,
they cannot act on their own.
He has just gone ahead to return first."
Dēng added:
"The toilet god, by rule, goes on patrol on the sixth day of each month.
If people encounter him on this day,
they are sure to meet with disaster.
If a person sees him, they die;
if he sees a person, they fall ill.
Previously, the Bāzuò official was ill for sixty days
because, it is said, as Dēng was finishing his patrol and about to return,
he caught a glimpse of half his face.
Among relatives,
it is appropriate to warn each other in turn to avoid him."
He also said:
"Among the officials of the underworld,
those with meager fortune are many,
and they get nothing to eat,
often suffering hunger.
If you can share your food when you eat,
and make offerings to all ghosts and spirits,
and keep this intention in mind,
you will see this multitude exerting their strength in the shadows,
and they will surely rescue you from calamity and distress."
Fāngyì said:
"The paths of darkness and light are separate;
we have met by chance.
Each time I have the honor of seeing you,
I feel unsettled for several days.
If you have anything to say,
I would prefer it be in dreams.
As for the request to transfer the sutra,
let dawn be the deadline."
Dēng assented and left.
When dawn came,
he summoned reverent monks to recite the Diamond Sutra forty-nine times,
and at dawn, dedicated and transferred it to Guō Dēng.
When the task was completed,
he dreamed that Dēng said:
"I originally requested one set of seven,
but the number was again multiplied by six.
Calculating the accumulated merit,
I now dine in the celestial kitchen.
If you, noble sir, encounter difficulty,
I will inform you first.
Otherwise,
I will not come to disturb you.
As for the request for general offerings,
please remember not to forget."
Wú Rènshēng
In Wújùn, there was a man named Rén,
who was skilled at seeing ghosts,
and lived as a hermit on Dòngtíng Mountain.
His appearance was always like that of a child,
and according to the customs of Wú and Chǔ,
no one could determine his age.
During the Bǎolì era,
there was a son of a former Kūnshān official named Yáng,
who was residing temporarily in Wújùn.
One day,
several people from the neighborhood,
together went boating,
and all visited Hǔqiū Temple.
At that time, Rén was in the boat,
and they spoke of matters concerning ghosts and spirits.
Yáng said:
"Humans and ghosts follow different paths,
so ghosts ultimately cannot be seen."
Rén laughed and said:
"Ghosts are very numerous,
but people cannot recognize them;
only I can recognize them."
Then he looked at a woman,
dressed in black clothes,
holding a young child,
walking on the shore.
Rén pointed and said:
"That is a ghost.
What she is holding is the
living soul of an infant."
Yáng said:
"Then how can you tell it is a ghost?"
Rén said:
"Just watch me speak to her."
He then shouted loudly:
"You are a ghost,
stealing a living person's child?"
The woman, hearing this, was startled and frightened,
and quickly turned back to leave.
Before she had taken more than a dozen steps,
she suddenly vanished from sight.
Yáng was both amazed and astonished.
In the evening, when they returned,
a few lǐ from the city walls,
beside the shore, there was a household
setting out a feast,
with a female shaman
dancing and drumming to the left,
performing a ritual to the spirits.
Yáng and Rén both asked about it.
The shaman said:
"Today, a person in the neighborhood had an infant who suddenly died,
but now it has awakened,
so we are setting out a feast to give thanks."
They then had the infant brought out to see,
and it was truly the one the woman had been holding.
All the guests were amazed and sighed in admiration,
thanking Rén, saying:
"You, sir, truly possess the arts of the Way;
we had no way of knowing."
Wū Tāo
Wū Tāo
was a person from Rǔnán,
well-versed in the classics,
and fond of the arts of the Way.
While traveling, he stayed at an inn in Yìwū County, Wùzhōu,
for over a month.
Suddenly, one night, a young woman
arrived with two maidservants.
One maid came forward and said:
"This is the young lady of the Wáng family,
who tonight wishes to bestow her favor upon you."
Tāo looked at her
and saw she was of extraordinary beauty.
Thinking she was the daughter of a wealthy and noble family,
he did not dare to reply.
Wáng smiled and said:
"If a scholar does not hold wine and women in his heart,
how can I entrust myself to him?"
Tāo then rose and bowed, saying:
"I am but a lowly and crude man,
and dare not hope for such a thing."
Wáng ordered her maids to arrange bedding and ornaments in Tāo's chamber,
lit silver candles,
and prepared wine and food.
After several rounds of drinking,
Wáng rose and said to Tāo:
"I was orphaned young with no one to rely on,
and now I wish to serve you as your companion,
would that be acceptable?"
Tāo modestly declined but then consented,
and their affection grew warm and intimate.
Wáng would leave at dawn and return at dusk,
and this continued for several months.
A Dàoist priest named Yáng Jǐngxiāo, whom Tāo knew, came to visit him at the inn.
Seeing Tāo's complexion was unusual,
he said:
"You are being bewitched by a ghostly enchantress;
you should break it off.
Otherwise, you will die."
Hearing this, Tāo was alarmed,
and told him the whole story.
Jǐngxiāo said:
"This is indeed a ghost."
He then gave him two talismans:
one to attach to his clothing,
and one to place on the door,
saying:
"When this ghost comes,
she will certainly be resentful;
be careful not to speak to her."
Tāo received them and followed the instructions.
That evening, the young woman came,
saw the talisman on the door,
cursed loudly, and left,
saying:
"Remove it quickly tomorrow,
or else there will be trouble."
The next day, Tāo went to see Jǐngxiāo
and told him everything.
Jǐngxiāo said:
"If she comes again tonight,
you can sprinkle her with my incantation water;
this will surely end it."
Tāo took the water and returned.
That night,
the young woman came again,
filled with great sorrow and anger.
Tāo then sprinkled her with Jǐngxiāo's incantation water,
and thus she was gone for good.
Zēng Jìhéng
In the spring of the fourth year of the Tàihé era,
the Surveillance Commissioner and Defense Commissioner Zēng Xiào'ān had a grandson named Jìhéng,
who lived in the western side courtyard of the official residence.
The rooms were grand and splendid,
yet Jìhéng lived there alone.
A servant warned him:
"In the past, the daughter of Prefect Wáng died suddenly here;
she was a beauty of the nation.
Sometimes her spirit appears here during the day;
you should be cautious, young master."
Jìhéng, being young and fond of beauty,
wished to witness her supernatural presence,
and ultimately did not let the boundary between human and ghost deter him.
He frequently burned fine incense,
kept his distance from mundane affairs,
strolled in quiet places,
and lost himself in deep thought.
One day at dusk,
a maid with double buns stepped forward and bowed, saying:
"The young lady of the Wáng family has sent me to convey her sincere regards,
and wishes to meet you in person, young master."
After speaking,
she vanished in an instant.
Shortly after,
an extraordinary fragrance enveloped his clothes.
Jìhéng then straightened his attire and waited,
and saw the same maid with double buns
leading a young woman forward—
she was like a fairy among immortals.
Jìhéng bowed to her
and asked for her name.
She replied:
"My surname is Wáng,
and my given name is Lìzhēn.
My father now holds an important military post,
but in the past, when he served as governor of this city,
we resided in these rooms.
Unexpectedly, I passed away.
Moved by your profound thoughts that reach the unseen realms,
and stirred by emotions that touch the depths of the underworld,
I disregarded the boundary between life and death
and longed for a spiritual encounter.
I have wished to come for a long time,
but the time was never auspicious.
Now, at last, my wish is fulfilled;
I hope you will not turn me away."
Jìhéng kept her for an intimate meeting,
and after some time, she departed.
Holding Jìhéng's hand, she said:
"At this same time tomorrow, we shall meet again;
be careful not to reveal this to anyone."
Then she and her maid vanished together.
From then on, she came every day at dusk,
for over sixty days.
Jìhéng grew careless,
and while speaking with officers under his grandfather's command,
he mentioned her beauty,
accidentally revealing the secret.
The officers were alarmed and fearful,
and wanting to verify
the matter,
they said:
"When the young lady comes at this time,
please tap on the wall once,
and a few of us will secretly observe."
But Jìhéng ultimately could not bring himself to tap the wall.
That day,
when the young lady saw Jìhéng,
her expression was sorrowful,
and her voice was choked with sobs.
Holding Jìhéng's hand, she said:
"Why did you break your promise and reveal it to others?
From now on, we can no longer share joy and laughter."
Jìhéng was ashamed and regretful,
with no words to respond.
The young lady said:
"It is likely not your fault;
perhaps our fate in the unseen realms has simply come to an end."
Then she left a poem, saying:
"Parting at Wǔyuán, truly like Wú and Yuè;
swallows break, orioles part, fragrant grass withers away.
In youth, spring blooms everywhere like fleeting fireworks;
at Běimáng, only regret remains under the autumn moon."
Jìhéng was not skilled in poetry,
and ashamed to have nothing to offer in return,
he forced himself to compose a verse:
"Green sedge, geese about to return;
jade cheeks and pearl tears shed at the parting road.
Cloud-like hair drifts away, the fragrant breeze fades;
sorrowful to see orioles sing among red branches."
The young lady then, from her sash,
untied a golden-threaded flower-patterned box,
and also took out a jade hairpin with twin phoenixes,
presenting them to Jìhéng, saying:
"Hoping that in days to come, seeing these objects will make you think of me,
and that the boundary between life and death will not keep us apart."
Jìhéng searched his book chest
and found a small gold-threaded flower-patterned rúyì scepter,
which he gave to her in return.
Jìhéng said:
"Though this object is not particularly rare,
its name, 'rúyì' (as you wish), is precious;
may it long be held in your jade-like hands."
He also asked:
"When will we meet again after this parting?"
The young lady replied:
"Not until sixty years have passed;
there will be no chance for us to meet."
After speaking,
she sobbed and vanished.
From then on, Jìhéng longed for her day and night,
and his body grew weak and emaciated.
An old acquaintance, Elder Wáng Huí,
applying his knowledge of medicine,
treated him with herbs and minerals,
and after several days, he recovered.
He then inquired with a seamstress from Wǔyuán,
who said:
"The beloved daughter of Prefect Wáng
died without illness in this courtyard.
She has now been buried at Běimáng Mountain;
sometimes on overcast days, her spirit wanders here,
and many have seen her."
This explains the line in her poem: "at Běimáng, only regret remains under the autumn moon."
Zhào Hé
Jìnshì Zhào Hé,
had a gentle appearance and upright demeanor,
and his conduct and righteousness were highly esteemed.
In the early years of the Tàihé era,
he traveled to Wǔyuán.
Along the way, he passed through sandy deserts.
Gazing upon the surroundings, he sighed with sorrow.
He then drank wine,
and together with his servant, became drunk,
Consequently, he fell asleep in the sandy desert.
In the middle of the night, half-awake,
the moonlight was bright and clear,
when he heard a woman lamenting in the sand:
"My cloud-like hair has vanished, transformed into sparse tumbleweeds,
my bones buried in this desolate wilderness with no one to rely on.
The grazing horses do not neigh under the white sand and moon,
my lonely soul vainly follows the wild geese flying south."
Hé then rose and went to investigate.
Indeed, there was a woman,
not yet of age to wear a hairpin.
Her beauty was unparalleled,
and she said to Hé:
"My surname is Lǐ,
and I resided in Fèngtiān.
I had an elder sister who married the commander of Luòyuán Town,
and I went to visit her.
On the way, I was captured by the Dǎng Qiāng tribe.
They brought me here, beat me to death,
and robbed me of my jewelry before leaving.
Later, a passerby took pity on me,
and buried me in the sand,
where I have remained for three years now.
Knowing that you are a man of righteousness,
if you could return my bones to Xiǎo Lǐ Village, south of Fèngtiān city,
which is my hometown,
I will surely repay you."
Hé agreed.
He asked her to show him where her bones were buried,
and the woman, moved to tears, told him.
Hé then collected her bones,
wrapped them in a bag.
Waiting for dawn,
suddenly an elderly man in purple robes,
riding swiftly on horseback, arrived,
bowed to Hé and said:
"I know you are benevolent and righteous,
trustworthy and honest.
The woman's plea,
still moves me with gratitude.
I am Shàngshū Lǐ Wényuè,
in the thirteenth year of the Yuánhé era,
I once defended Wǔyuán.
It was besieged by 300,000 Róng tribesmen on all four sides of the city,
with troops dozens of miles thick on each side,
crossbows raining down like showers,
scaling ladders rising like clouds.
They breached walls and broke through moats,
attacking day and night.
Those fetching water in the city, carrying doors as shields,
faced arrows as thick as hedgehog quills.
At that time,
the defending troops
numbered only three thousand.
I inspired the residents,
women, elderly, and children carrying earth to fortify the walls,
undeterred by cold or hunger.
The Róng built a single-legged tower north of the city,
several dozen zhàng high,
from which everything in the city,
large and small, could be observed.
I then devised a clever plan,
and with a well-aimed strike, shattered the tower instantly.
The Qiāng chieftain was astonished,
believing it to be a divine feat.
I also told the people in the city:
'Do not dismantle houses for firewood,
I will fetch firewood for you,
pile it beneath the city walls,
and allow people to haul it up.'
Moreover, when the moon grew dim,
we would hear movements around the city's four corners,
with many figures moving about,
voices declaring:
'We will attack the city tonight.'
The city's inhabitants trembled in fear,
unable to rest even briefly.
I said:
'This is not so.'
Secretly, I lowered an iron chain with a torch to illuminate the area,
only to find empty herds of cattle and sheep being driven to intimidate the city,
and the soldiers grew somewhat calmer.
Then, the northwestern corner was attacked,
and a breach over ten zhàng wide was made.
As dusk approached,
the Hú tribesmen rejoiced,
drinking wildly and singing,
saying:
'We will enter at dawn.'
I prepared five hundred mounted crossbows to aim at them,
and lowered leather barriers to block the breach.
Overnight,
we worked together in secret to rebuild,
ensuring no sound was made,
and doused it with water.
The weather was cold,
and by the next day, the ice had hardened,
making the city walls gleam like silver,
impervious to attack.
Additionally, the Qiāng chieftain erected a general's banner,
bestowed by the Tsanpo,
placing it within the five-flower camp.
One night, I breached the wall and seized it swiftly,
causing the Qiāng to wail in despair,
vowing to return all previously captured people,
in exchange for the banner.
I released them,
and over a hundred men, women, and children,
were able to return home.
Only then did I throw the banner back to them.
At the time, twenty thousand relief troops from Bīn and Jīng arrived at the border,
but trembled and did not advance.
In this manner, we held out for thirty-seven days.
The Qiāng chieftain then bowed from afar and said:
'There is a divine general in this city,
I dare not challenge it now.'
Thus, they rolled up their armor and departed.
Not two days later,
they reached Yòuzhōu,
and in a single day, breached its walls.
Thirty thousand people, old and young,
were all captured.
Considering these events,
my contribution to this city was not insignificant.
However, the prime minister of the time,
prevented me from leaving the city with full authority,
merely bestowing upon me an empty title.
I heard that in Zhōnglíng, Lady Wéi,
once built an embankment,
to guard against floods,
and thirty years later,
the common people and the virtuous Inspector Zhōu, moved by her deeds,
petitioned for a lofty virtue stele to be erected.
If I had not defended the walls firmly,
the people of the city,
would all have become slaves to the Qiāng and Hú,
how could their descendants exist today?
Knowing you have a kind heart,
I ask you to inform the common people,
and suggest to the prefect,
that erecting a virtue stele for me would suffice."
Having spoken,
he bowed deeply and departed.
Hé, having received this instruction,
went to Wǔyuán.
He relayed this to the common people and the prefect,
but they all considered it demonic talk,
and did not listen,
so he returned disheartened.
Upon reaching the sandy desert,
he again encountered the divine being from before,
who thanked Hé and said:
"You spoke on my behalf,
but the ignorant folk of Wǔyuán,
and the unenlightened prefect,
will bring a fire disaster upon this city.
I had just pleaded with the underworld authorities,
regarding the matter of Wǔyuán,
but it was not granted,
and so this intention is abandoned.
The calamity will strike within thirty days."
Having spoken, he vanished,
and indeed, the disaster occurred as predicted.
In Wǔyuán city, ten thousand people died of famine,
with the old and young resorting to cannibalism.
Hé carried the woman's bones to Fèngtiān,
found Xiǎo Lǐ Village, and buried them there.
The next day by the roadside,
Hé encountered the woman from before, who came to thank him, saying:
"Grateful for your righteousness,
my grandfather was a Taoist adept who attained the Way during the Zhēnyuán era,
and left behind the 'Yǎn Cāntóngqì Xù Hùnyuán Jīng,'
if you can master it,
the dragon-tiger elixir,
will be completed in no time."
Hé accepted it,
and the woman vanished.
Hé then abandoned his pursuit of the imperial examinations,
delving into its profound mysteries,
and resided in Shàoshì.
After refining it for one year,
he could turn tiles and rubble into gold and treasures;
after two years,
he could revive the dead;
after three years, ingesting it enabled transcendence of the mortal world.
Even now, some have encountered him on Sōng Ridge.
Wéi Ānzhī
Wéi Ānzhī was a man from Héyáng.
At that time, he arrived in Yángzhái,
intending to go to Shàoshì Mountain to seek a teacher.
Upon reaching Dēngfēng,
he met a person
who asked where he was going.
He replied:
"My surname is Zhāng, my given name is Dào.
My home is in Jīnxiāng,
and I wish to go to Shàoshì Mountain to study."
Ānzhī also told him his own name.
Since their destinations were the same,
they agreed to become sworn brothers.
Ānzhī, being older,
became the elder brother.
They entered Shàoshì Mountain together
and studied under Lǐ Qián.
After one year,
Zhāng Dào had become extensively learned and profoundly accomplished,
ranking first among the students.
One day,
he said to Ānzhī:
"Elder brother, your career has not yet begun.
From now, it will take five years
before you achieve fame,
and your official position will not exceed that of a county assistant."
Ānzhī, astonished, asked:
"Younger brother, how do you know this?"
Dào said:
"I am not human;
I am actually a chief registrar of the underworld.
The ruler of Tài Mountain wished to employ me in an important position,
but because my talent and knowledge were still insufficient,
he granted me a one-year leave to study in the human world.
Now the time limit is fulfilled,
my studies are somewhat accomplished,
and I must bid you farewell.
Please be careful not to reveal this to anyone."
Having said this,
he took leave of their teacher.
Ānzhī escorted Dào down the mountain,
and they parted in tears.
Dào said:
"After you achieve fame,
if you are ever in dire straits,
just call my name, Dào,
and I will certainly come to your rescue."
Ānzhī went to take the imperial examinations after five years.
That year, he passed
and was appointed as the deputy of Yúqián County in Hángzhōu.
Dispatched by the prefecture to transport goods,
he was about to reach Héyīn.
Arriving at Qízé Pǔ,
he was attacked by bandits from Huái.
Ānzhī then earnestly prayed to Dào.
Suddenly, a violent storm of thunder and rain arrived,
and all the bandits drowned.
Ānzhī later died while serving as the assistant magistrate of Lóngxīng County.
Lǐ Zuǒwén
In the northern border region of Líntuān County, Nányáng,
the Secretariat Gentleman Yuán Cè and the Xiangyang Assistant Wáng Qiān both had
separate estates.
In the sixth year of the Tàihé era,
there was a traveler named Lǐ Zuǒwén
who stayed and worked at both estates.
Zuǒwén was skilled in arts like the qin and chess,
and was quite beloved by Yuán and Wáng.
One day toward dusk,
Zuǒwén was heading to stay at the Yuán estate.
His servant, carrying bedding, went ahead.
Not one or two li later,
a dark wind suddenly rose,
with cold dust obscuring everything.
Soon it was pitch black at night.
Riding his inferior horse alone,
he became greatly lost.
Around the third watch,
the darkness slightly lifted.
Several li away,
he distantly saw the light of a candle.
Zuǒwén headed toward the light and arrived,
finding a solitary hut in the wilderness,
quite low and narrow.
Inside was an old farmer
weaving straw sandals.
Zuǒwén humbly requested lodging.
After a long while,
he was finally invited inside.
The old man said:
"There are many jackals and wolves here;
your horse should not be tethered far away."
Zuǒwén thus moved it under the eaves
and rested near the fire.
The old man asked:
"Where were you originally headed to end up here?"
Zuǒwén told him.
The old man smiled and said:
"The Yuán estate is far, far from here.
But you must wait for dawn
before you can head south to return."
Behind where the old man sat,
under a screen of woven reeds,
the painful crying of a young child could occasionally be heard.
Each time the child cried out,
the old man would say:
"Child, you can stop now.
What's done is done;
what good does weeping sorrowfully do?"
Soon the child would cry again,
and the old man would console it with the same words.
Zuǒwén did not understand
and pressed him about it,
but the old man evasively changed the subject.
Zuǒwén then said:
"The child is suffering from the cold;
why not bring it near the fire?"
After repeating this several times,
the old man brought the child over to the stove.
It was an eight- or nine-year-old village girl.
Seeing the guest, she showed no shyness or fear,
but merely drew in the ashes with something,
as if harboring deep resentment.
Suddenly, she wailed with grievous sobs.
The old man again consoled her with his earlier words.
Zuǒwén questioned him,
but never learned the truth.
Soon, as dawn approached,
the old man pointed distantly to tall trees in the southeast and said:
"That is the Yuán estate,
not ten li from here."
Zuǒwén mounted his horse and looked around.
It was a vast, desolate wilderness
with no trace of human presence at all,
only the old farmer's single hut.
After traveling two or three li,
he met a village woman
carrying a jug of wine
and some paper funeral money.
Seeing Zuǒwén, she said:
"This is a great marshland,
with no road for people.
Traveler, where have you come from at this early hour?"
Zuǒwén recounted everything in detail.
The woman then beat her chest and wailed:
"Who would have thought one could meet ghosts on the road?"
Zuǒwén inquired carefully.
The woman said:
"If what you say about the place you lodged last night is true,
then that was the burial hut of my late husband.
I have worked as a hired hand at the Yuán estate for seven years.
In the spring before last,
my husband died suddenly from illness.
The next day,
my young daughter, who had just lost her baby teeth, also died.
In my poverty, I lacked the means,
so father and daughter were buried together there.
Widowed and in mourning,
I was still not exempted from taxes by the authorities.
Alone, poor, and with no support,
I decided to remarry.
Tonight I am to go to another household,
so I came to bid farewell at the grave of my husband and daughter."
Zuǒwén then went with her.
When they reached the place from the previous evening,
it was indeed a burial hut.
The traces and events
were clearly recognizable once more.
The woman wailed in grief,
her tears falling like strings from a well rope.
She then abandoned her livelihood,
cut off her hair at the Líntuān Buddhist temple,
and vowed to serve there until death.
The woman's surname was Wáng.
In the fourth year of the Kāichéng era,
there were still travelers who saw her.
Hú Yīn
Hú Yīn of Āndìng,
resided in Hédōng Commandery,
and was renowned for his literary talent.
In the spring of the seventh year of the Tàihé era, he passed the imperial examination,
at which time Jiǎ Sù served as Vice Minister of Rites.
Two years later,
Emperor Wénzong promoted Jiǎ Sù to the position of Chancellor.
That winter, in the tenth month,
a rebellion erupted in Jīngzhào,
and Jiǎ Sù, along with Chancellor Yá,
and others below them,
all fled.
An imperial edict was issued for their arrest with great urgency.
At that time, the powerful eunuch Qiú Shìliáng,
who commanded the Left Imperial Guard,
ordered his subordinate general to lead troops to exhaustively track them down.
The subordinate general said to Shìliáng:
"Hú Yīn received favors from Jiǎ Sù.
He must now be hiding at Hú Yīn's place.
I request five hundred valiant soldiers
to surround his residence and capture him."
Shìliáng approved his request.
Thereupon, the subordinate general led troops to Hú Yīn's gate,
summoned Hú Yīn to come out,
and said in a stern voice:
"Jiǎ Sù is in your house.
You should bring him out immediately.
Otherwise,
you will share his crime."
Hú Yīn judged that the situation could not be resolved by reason,
and firmly refused with defiant words.
The subordinate general grew angry,
seized Hú Yīn and brought him before Shìliáng,
where he was executed outside the camp gate.
At that time, Hú Yīn's younger brother Hú Xiāng was in Hédōng Commandery.
On that day,
Hú Xiāng and his family
saw a headless person,
dressed in green clothes,
with bloodstains on the garments,
enter through the gate
and walk into the courtyard.
Hú Xiāng was greatly alarmed,
ordered the family to chase him away,
and he abruptly vanished.
Three days later,
the news of Hú Yīn's death arrived.
Xīn Shényōng
Xīn Shényōng, an Investigating Censor serving in Pínglú,
in the winter of the fifth year of the Tàihé era,
had come to the capital from his former post as Báishuǐ Commandant for reassignment.
At that time, there was a laborer named Liú Wànjīn
who lived in the same room with a household servant named Zì Qín.
They shared a room.
Zì Qín had been ill for several months
and was near death.
One day,
when Wànjīn was out elsewhere,
Zì Qín lay on his bed.
Suddenly, a man
in purple robes, a tall hat, and wide sleeves,
with a gaunt face and emaciated form,
a large nose and long beard,
entered through the door.
He approached the bed
and said to Zì Qín:
"Get up forcefully,
and your illness will soon be cured."
Thereupon, he helped Zì Qín sit up against the wall.
Earlier, against the eastern wall of the room,
there was a dining table
set with several dishes.
The purple-robed man reached into his sleeve,
took out a handful of something,
which looked like rice grains but were green in color,
and placed over ten grains into one of the dishes.
He then said to Zì Qín:
"I am not a person of this world.
Today, I have been ordered to summon Wànjīn.
Wànjīn will eat and die.
If you eat, do not reveal my words.
Otherwise,
disaster will befall you."
Having said this, he departed.
That day,
when Wànjīn returned,
his face was flushed and he was panting,
and he said:
"I feel a rising heat from emptiness in my abdomen,
and it may be incurable."
He then went to the dish and ate from it.
As he finished eating,
Zì Qín's illness was cured,
and Wànjīn indeed died.
Táng Yànshì
Táng Yànshì of Jìnchāng,
who loved reading,
lived in seclusion on Jiǔhuá Mountain.
Often in the evening,
when the rain cleared,
Yànshì would stroll up the mountain under the moonlight.
When the night grew deep,
a pack of wolves blocked his path,
preventing his return.
Overcome with fear,
he hid in a deep forest.
Suddenly, a man in white robes,
wearing a gauze hat,
with a lonely and handsome appearance,
nearly fifty years old,
came along the stream.
He walked leisurely, reciting poetry.
After standing still for a long while,
he then recited:
"The stream's murmur flows without end,
the misty ridges bloom with wildflowers.
Coming and going alone, no one returns,
for long hours facing only the empty mountain moon."
Yànshì had always enjoyed composing seven-character poems
and was quite praised by his contemporaries.
Hearing this, he was astonished and impressed,
and was about to speak with the man,
but before he could, the man vanished.
The next day,
when Yànshì returned,
he asked the villagers about the man's appearance.
Someone who recognized him said:
"That is the son of the Wú family,
who passed the imperial examination,
and was skilled at poetry.
He died several years ago."
Guō Xún
Guō Xún was dismissed from his post as the county lieutenant of Yuèyáng,
and for a long time, he could not secure another appointment.
Living in poverty in the capital,
he was in dire straits.
During sacrificial ceremonies,
there were always two creatures,
like ape-monkeys,
dressed in blue-green,
who would come and go, whether he was sleeping or awake,
never failing to follow him.
Whenever he intended to seek something,
they would inevitably accompany him.
Wherever he went,
it was as if he were obstructed by thorns.
When his relatives and friends saw him,
they all treated him as if he were an enemy,
some trying to repel him with talismans and spells.
Others avoided him by retreating to the mountains and forests,
but for several years, nothing could make them leave.
One evening,
they suddenly came to bid farewell,
saying:
"We have endured your misfortune,
and have not parted from you for a long time.
Now we will depart at dawn,
and will never return."
Guō Xún, overjoyed at their departure,
then asked where they were going.
They replied:
"There are many like us in the world,
but people simply do not see them.
Our destination now is the home of a wealthy man named Wáng in Shèngyè Ward,
where we will go to disperse his fortune."
Guō Xún asked:
"He has amassed such abundant wealth,
how can it be dispersed so quickly?"
They replied:
"We have already devised a plan with Ān Pǐnzǐ."
Suddenly, the morning drum sounded,
and they vanished without a trace.
After Guō Xún rose, washed, and combed his hair,
he immediately felt his worries and frustrations lift.
When he tried visiting his relatives and friends,
they all received him with a changed attitude.
Within ten days,
he was granted an audience with the prime minister,
and was appointed as a court secretary.
Guō Xún had a cousin named Zhāng,
who served as an assistant in the Imperial Guard,
and whose friends were all gallant and chivalrous.
Being young and fond of the unusual,
when he heard this story,
he did not believe it.
Knowing that the Wáng family of Shèngyè Ward was under the jurisdiction of the Left Army,
he began to frequent the area to observe them.
Wáng was by nature frugal and restrained,
and his expenses never exceeded what was reasonable.
He had many singing girls at home,
and among them were many of great beauty.
Yet, despite their glamorous attire and alluring appearances,
they could never sway his intentions.
One day,
while passing through Míngkē Lane with friends,
he saw a woman exquisitely dressed standing at a doorway.
Wáng reined in his horse and lingered,
his face lighting up with joy.
He then invited his companions
to drink and celebrate,
and Zhāng was among them.
Upon inquiry,
it turned out she was the younger sister of Ān Pǐnzǐ.
Ān Pǐnzǐ was skilled in singing,
and that day she performed several songs.
Wáng lavished her with gold and silk,
astonishing everyone with his extravagance.
From then on, carts laden with goods and money
were delivered to her door daily.
Within a few years,
he was reduced to poverty.
Lǐ Quánzhì
Lǐ Quánzhì of Lǒngxī,
spent his youth in Yízhōu.
One day, he intended to play a grand game of cùjū (kickball).
At the break of dawn,
he dozed off in the eastern courtyard before the Heng Gate of Yízhōu city.
Suddenly, a man dressed in purple,
wearing a round bamboo hat on his head,
approached him directly and said:
"I am here to summon you."
Quánzhì asked:
"Who is summoning me?"
The man in purple replied:
"It is not I who summon you,
but someone else is coming to summon you."
Shortly after,
a man dressed in green arrived and said:
"I am here to summon you."
His words were urgent,
and his manner was unstoppable.
Quánzhì said:
"Sir, do you need anything?"
The man in green replied:
"I am under orders to summon you;
how dare I speak of my needs?"
The man in purple said to the man in green:
"There is no need to summon him."
He waved his hand, and the man in green left through the Heng Gate.
The man in purple then took the opportunity to say to Quánzhì:
"You just asked if I needed anything;
could you not fulfill that promise?"
Quánzhì asked:
"What do you need?"
He replied:
"Just a single rhinoceros-horn belt."
Quánzhì said:
"Certainly."
As soon as he finished speaking, the man disappeared.
The host announced the start of the cùjū game,
so Quánzhì ordered a rhinoceros-horn belt to be painted.
When evening came,
he prepared wine and dried meat,
along with paper money and the belt,
and burned them outside the Heng Gate.
That night,
as soon as Quánzhì fell asleep,
he saw the man in purple with the round bamboo hat come to bow and thank him, saying:
"I am grateful for the gift of the belt;
I am deeply ashamed
and have nothing to offer in return.
However, in your lifetime, you will face water calamities.
Whenever you are in danger or distress,
I will surely come to your aid."
Later, during the great flood at the beginning of the Tàihé era,
Quánzhì had already become a deputy general of the Tàipíng Army,
also serving as an inspector.
He had urgent business
and traveled from Zhōngdū to Liángjùn city.
Twenty lǐ west of Bǎixiē Bridge,
the water was deep and the ice thin.
He was unfamiliar with the route,
but the journey was urgent and fast-paced,
with not a moment to spare.
His attendants were pale as ashes,
and they entrusted their fate to their reins as they proceeded.
After only thirty or so steps,
a man came from behind,
shouting loudly:
"Do not go that way—come this way!
I know a path
that is safe and swift."
Quánzhì trusted him
and turned his horse to follow.
After less than three lǐ,
they encountered muddy terrain,
but there was not the slightest obstruction,
and they reached their destination safely.
Quánzhì offered the man material goods as thanks,
but the man firmly declined and refused to accept them.
When Quánzhì insisted on giving them,
the man replied:
"If you had relied on me from the start,
I might not have declined;
but since you followed me along the way,
what hardship did I endure?
" He ultimately refused to accept.
Quánzhì thought the man was being modest,
so he pressed further,
Shortly after, the man returned,
but then vanished.
Later, Quánzhì reflected on the man:
dressed in purple,
wearing a round bamboo hat—
was he not the man from the Heng Gate?
At the beginning of the Kāichéng era,
Quánzhì was ordered to enter the pass.
On his return, he stayed overnight in Shòu'ān County.
Before midnight, he felt an urgent need,
and it was dark and gloomy at the time.
With no other choice, he left the inn.
After two or three lǐ, heavy rain poured down,
and turning back was not an option.
Suddenly,
he saw a man beside his horse.
Quánzhì questioned him:
"Who are you?"
The man replied:
"A courier."
He then walked ahead of the horse,
but not an inch of the path was visible.
The man constantly pointed out obstacles ahead,
sometimes saying "tree,"
sometimes "stump,"
sometimes "danger,"
sometimes "mound,"
sometimes "pit."
Thanks to him, Quánzhì avoided all mishaps.
After a long while, they reached Sānquán Station,
where they rested.
As soon as Quánzhì dismounted,
he looked for the courier to reward him,
but the man had already disappeared.
He asked his attendants
about the man's appearance and clothing:
indeed, he was dressed in purple and wore a bamboo hat on his head.
Was he not, once again, the man from the Heng Gate?
In the Rénxū year of the Huìchāng era,
there was a great flood in Jìyīn.
Gǔshénzǐ and Quánzhì were in the same boat.
Gǔshénzǐ was surprised at how fearful Quánzhì was of water
and asked him the reason.
Quánzhì then recounted this story.
He also said:
"By nature, I am not afraid of water,
but because the man in purple has helped me repeatedly,
my fear has grown even more intense."
Shěn Gōnglǐ
Wénxiāng County Registrar Shěn Gōnglǐ,
during the Tàihé era,
served as acting Húchéng Deputy.
On the day he left Wénxiāng,
he had a minor illness.
He arrived at Húchéng in the evening,
and lay down in the main hall.
Suddenly, someone circled his bed several times.
Thinking it was his accompanying clerk Léi Zhōngshùn,
Gōnglǐ asked him,
and he replied:
"I am not Léi Zhōngshùn,
but Lǐ Zhōngyì."
Gōnglǐ asked:
"How did you come here?"
He replied:
"I am originally from the Jiānghuái region,
and due to hunger and cold, I worked as a laborer for others.
Last month, I arrived in this county,
and died at an inn.
However, I am extremely hungry and cold,
and now I come to you,
begging for a meal,
and also asking for a small hat.
Is that acceptable?"
Gōnglǐ agreed,
and said:
"Where shall I send them to you?"
He replied:
"Tomorrow evening,
send the post station attendant Zhāng Cháo to deliver them."
After speaking,
he stood by the western pillar of the hall.
Gōnglǐ sat up,
and Zhōngyì stepped forward and said:
"Since you have just arrived here,
if there are any matters,
I dare to offer my assistance."
Gōnglǐ said:
"Very well."
He then said:
"Most people who stay in this hall are uneasy.
Shortly,
there will be a young woman,
about seventeen or eighteen years old,
who will forcefully come to pay her respects.
Her name is 'Mìtuósēng'.
You must be careful not to speak with her.
She may claim to be a member of the county magistrate's family,
or pretend to be a neighbor seeking attachment,
but you must not engage in conversation with her.
If you speak, you will fall under her spell."
As soon as Zhōngyì finished speaking,
before he could settle back by the western pillar,
a young woman indeed appeared from the east of the hall,
with high-piled hair and flowing locks,
her skin radiant and smooth,
smiling softly and glancing around.
She said to Gōnglǐ:
"The autumn room is lonely and desolate,
crickets chirp beneath the night moon.
As the night deepens, the wind stirs,
and wutong leaves fall upon the steps.
For what crime are you blamed,
that you are confined here like a prisoner?"
Gōnglǐ remained unmoved.
She spoke again:
"The precious mat lies empty on the bed,
the bright moonlight fills the room.
If you do not drink fine wine,
you vainly call yourself a young man."
Gōnglǐ again paid no attention.
She then chanted:
"When the Yellow Emperor ascended to heaven,
Dǐnghú was originally here.
Seventy-two jade maidens,
transformed into golden mushrooms."
Gōnglǐ still ignored her,
and she reluctantly departed.
Zhōngyì stepped forward again and said:
"That creature has left.
Shortly,
in the eastern corridor, there will be Jìng Guǎfù and Widow Wáng.
Although they are not as dangerous as Mìtuósēng,
you still must not speak with them."
After a short while, a young woman indeed appeared,
from the eastern wing,
dressed in white clothes,
wearing a white hairpin,
adjusting her robe with her hands.
She turned and called out:
"Widow Wáng,
why don't you come out?"
Suddenly, another appeared, wearing a red skirt,
with purple sleeves and a silver cape,
pacing several circles in the moonlit courtyard,
then standing by the eastern wing.
Zhōngyì stepped forward again and said:
"These two creatures have left.
You may rest easy now.
Even if,
later, other seductive beings come,
they are not to be feared."
Zhōngyì bid farewell to leave,
but Gōnglǐ stopped him:
"Stay with me a little longer,
wait until all the monsters are gone before you leave."
Zhōngyì agreed.
When the fourth watch arrived,
a creature appeared,
over two zhang tall,
holding three or four skulls in its hands,
as if juggling them.
It gradually approached the hall's eaves.
Zhōngyì said to Gōnglǐ:
"You can strike it with your pillow."
Gōnglǐ struck as instructed,
hitting its hand with a thud,
causing the skulls to fall.
As the creature bent down to pick them up,
Zhōngyì jumped down,
beating it wildly with a stick,
and it fled out the door.
Gōnglǐ repeatedly called for Zhōngyì,
but he was no longer seen,
and the east was already bright with dawn.
He told his attendants everything that had happened,
and then ordered them to prepare food and buy a hat.
He summoned the attendant Zhāng Cháo and questioned him,
who said:
"I am originally a shaman.
Recently, I took a job as a hall clerk for food,
and I know all about the newly deceased guest ghost Lǐ Zhōngyì."
Gōnglǐ then gave him the hat and a plate of food to deliver.
That night,
he dreamed that Lǐ Zhōngyì came to bid farewell and thank him, saying:
"You must be very careful to guard against Mìtuósēng.
She may disturb you for another two or three years."
After speaking, he left.
For the two months Gōnglǐ was in Húchéng,
Mìtuósēng came every night,
but he never dared to respond to her;
later, when he returned to Wénxiāng,
she arrived every other night,
but ultimately could not cause him harm;
after half a year,
she came once every three or five nights;
after more than a year,
she gradually became scarce.
A monk advised him to abstain from meat and pungent foods,
and after that, she never came again.
Niú Shēng
Niú Shēng, traveling from Hédōng to take the imperial examination,
reached Huàzhōu.
Thirty li away,
he lodged at a village inn.
That day,
the snow was heavy,
so he asked the innkeeper to prepare soup noodles.
At dusk,
a man in extreme poverty and cold,
his clothes ragged and tattered,
also came to seek lodging at the inn.
Seeing him, Niú Shēng took pity,
and invited him to share the meal.
The man said:
"I am poor and cold,
and cannot afford money for food.
This morning I have already traveled over a hundred li on an empty stomach."
He then ate four or five bowls,
and lay down on the ground before the bed,
his snores like an ox's.
At the fifth watch,
this man came to Niú Shēng's bedside and said:
"Please, sir, come briefly outside the door,
I have something important to say."
Urging him repeatedly to go out,
he said:
"I am not human,
but a messenger from the underworld.
I am deeply grateful for last night's meal,
and now have a small token of repayment.
Please fetch three sheets of paper, a brush, and an inkstone for me."
Niú Shēng gave them to him.
The man had Niú Shēng stand far off,
sat himself beneath a tree,
drew a scroll from his sleeve,
and consulted it.
After looking over several pages,
he wrote two lines,
repeating this three times until finished.
He requested paper to seal them,
writing on them: first letter,
second letter,
third letter.
He said to Niú Shēng:
"If you encounter disasters, dangers, or grave illnesses that seem unavoidable,
then burn incense and open these in order to read them.
If they might be avoidable,
then there is no need to open them."
Having spoken,
he walked a few steps and vanished.
Niú Shēng sealed the letters and placed them in his book bag,
not quite believing it.
Upon reaching the capital,
he stayed in the guest quarter,
suffering extreme hunger and poverty,
and was without food.
Suddenly recalling these letters,
he opened the first one,
which read:
"You may sit before the gate of Pútí Temple."
From the guest quarter to Pútí Temple
was about thirty li.
Hungry and weary,
with rain and snow falling,
he rode a donkey there,
traveling from morning until the drumbeats were nearly silent before reaching the temple gate.
Before he could settle,
a monk emerged from the temple,
scolding Niú Shēng:
"With such rain and snow,
who are you to come here?
If you freeze to death,
would it not implicate me?"
Niú Shēng said:
"I am an examination candidate,
arriving here at night,
and beg to borrow a night's lodging before the temple gate,
leaving on my own tomorrow."
The monk said:
"I did not know you were a scholar;
you may stay in this humble monk's quarters."
Once inside,
the monk prepared a fire and food for him.
After conversing for some time,
the monk said:
"The esteemed official of your clan in Jìnyáng,
how closely related are you to the scholar?"
Niú Shēng said:
"He is my uncle."
The monk then fetched a handwritten letter from Jìnyáng,
asking him to identify it,
and it was all correct.
The monk said joyfully:
"Jìnyáng once sent three thousand strings of cash here,
and never came to retrieve it.
I am old,
and should death come suddenly,
there would be no one to entrust it to;
now I give it all to you."
Niú Shēng first took a thousand strings of cash,
bought a house,
acquired carriages and horses,
took on servants and concubines,
