and thus became a wealthy man.
Later, having lost his way in seeking fame,
he opened the second letter,
which read:
"Sit upstairs at Zhāng's restaurant in the West Market."
Niú Shēng did as instructed,
went to the Zhāng establishment,
and sat alone in a room,
lowering the curtain.
Several young men came upstairs,
among them one in a white robe.
Once seated,
he suddenly said:
"I originally had only five hundred thousand,
but now request to increase it to seven hundred thousand;
beyond that, my means cannot reach."
Another said:
"For achieving the jìnshì degree,
why begrudge a thousand strings?"
Niú Shēng knew they were negotiating for the degree.
Emerging, he bowed to them,
and the youth in white was the chief examiner's son.
Niú Shēng said:
"I offer a thousand strings to the young master,
and another two hundred thousand
to cover the gentlemen's food and drink expenses,
with no need for further discussion."
The youth agreed,
and indeed Niú Shēng passed the examination with high rank.
He served in various high offices,
later becoming Deputy Military Commissioner of Hédōng.
After a year,
he fell gravely ill,
and opened the third letter,
which read:
"You may set your household affairs in order."
He then bathed,
prepared his will,
and had just finished when he passed away.
Wéi Qíxiū,
having passed the imperial examination and earned the jìnshì degree,
rose through official ranks to become a Vice Director in one of the ministries.
He served as Deputy Military Commissioner of Zhèxī under Wáng Fán.
In the eighth year of the Tàihé era (834 CE),
he died in the official residence at Rùnzhōu.
After the third watch of the night,
just as they were preparing to dress the body for the coffin,
a loud voice suddenly came from beneath the western wall, saying:
"Tell my wife
to stop crying for now;
I have arrangements to make."
His wife was greatly startled
and fell to the ground, unconscious.
Qíxiū then spoke sternly from under the quilt:
"Wife, you are now a ghost's wife.
Hearing a ghost speak,
are you suddenly frightened?"
His wife immediately rose and said:
"It is not that I am afraid,
but it is unfitting that you and I are so abruptly separated by the realms of darkness and light.
Alone and anxious, with no one to rely on,
I did not expect your spirit and consciousness to remain aware,
suddenly communicating through speech.
I couldn't help but faint.
I sincerely await your instructions;
how would I dare to disobey?"
Qíxiū said:
"The timing of life and death
lies with the true master of fate;
the way of husband and wife
is weighty within human relations.
I and you, my wife,
share a bond of deep affection and duty.
In other lives, we will not part either.
Now, my corpse is still here,
which should ease your heart.
Matters of the household, great and small,
must still be discussed.
You must not vainly weep like a child,
causing me, in the dark underworld, to worry even more about my wife and children.
Last night's various affairs
were all managed by your own diligent care.
Nothing at all was lost or misplaced,
which gives this servant reason to rejoice."
His wife asked:
"Why is that?"
Qíxiū said:
"Yesterday, Gēng Qī from Húzhōu sent money to purchase a servant.
In the midst of the haste and confusion,
I could not help but focus on arranging it.
Now, not a single coin is owed,
which is also a comfort."
After a long silence, the speaking ceased,
and they each attended to the funeral matters.
Just at dawn,
they again heard him call out:
"I just went to Zhāng Qīng's house.
He recently built a three-room thatched cottage.
The front rooms are sufficient on their own;
there is no need to trouble others
to borrow a place to stay anymore."
That evening,
Zhāng Qīng seemed to see Wéi Qíxiū in a dream, saying:
"I died yesterday.
I previously ordered the purchase of three mǔ of land for a grave.
You must quickly arrange the payment and make preparations."
Everything was clear and distinct,
and Zhāng Qīng followed all his instructions.
When it was time to return the body to the capital,
he himself chose the day for departure.
His calls and commands were just as in normal times.
If maids or servants attempted private theft,
he exposed every instance,
beating them accordingly for each offense.
Upon reaching the capital,
they went directly to the burial site,
where Zhāng Qīng's preparations were all complete.
After a dozen or so days,
toward the third watch,
he suddenly called to his attendants:
"Get up quickly!
Report to the main hall:
Xiāo Sānláng has come to visit.
Prepare food as appropriate,
entertain him properly,
so as not to hinder his busy schedule."
The conversation between the two men
was clearly audible.
This Xiāo Sānláng
was Xiāo Chè, a Director in the Ministry of War.
He had died that very day in Xìnghuà Ward,
and came that very night.
Soon they heard Xiāo sigh and say:
"The principle of life and death
—I dare not resent it.
But what is strange
is that several days ago,
I went to my Shàolíng country estate
and casually composed a poem.
Thinking of it now,
it turns out to have been a ghost's poem written while alive."
He then recited it:
"Newly built, a thatched lodge east of the wild stream,
pine and catalpa shadows crossing, filled with mournful wind.
In the human world, years and months flow like water;
why must I so often travel this road?"
Qíxiū also lamented and exclaimed:
"Your poem, sir,
is indeed self-aware.
I, in life, shamefully held an examination rank,
and was somewhat known among people.
Not many days after my death,
a nameless little ghost presented me with a verse,
which was truly clumsy and dull.
Yet, upon careful reflection,
I realize I have already fallen into his brambly realm."
He then chanted:
"The stream water splashes, flowing without end,
fragrant grasses spread, wild flowers bloom.
Going and coming by myself, unknown to men,
at dusk there is only the blue mountain moon."
Xiāo also sighed in admiration, saying:
"Wéi Sìgōng, you have been dead for quite some time,
yet you still do not accept this affair.
I am one who just arrived,
suddenly become a soul journeying to Mount Tài.
How can I bear this?"
Then they were heard bidding farewell and departing.
After several more days,
at high noon,
he called out:
"Péi Èrshíyīláng has come to offer condolences.
Prepare food;
I will go welcome him myself."
That day,
the Péi brothers indeed came.
When they reached outside the Qǐxià Gate,
they suddenly felt a spiritual dread,
and having already heard of these events,
they dared not proceed to offer condolences and turned back.
This Péi was the Magistrate of Cháng'ān County,
named Guān,
the elder brother of Qíxiū's wife.
His subordinates and servants
were constantly accused and punished,
unable to bear their fear.
This continues to the present, unresolved,
and it is unknown how it will ultimately end.
Fáng Zhì
Fáng Zhì served as the Wèi of Qīnghé County.
His wife, née Zhèng, was from Xíngyáng
and was beautiful.
At that time, there was an old woman in the village
who was on her way to visit a Chán master.
Before she arrived,
midway through the wild and desolate path,
she saw a woman dressed in white
walking among brambles and thorns,
weeping most mournfully.
She circled a small hillock,
within a few dozen paces,
as if inspecting something she was arranging.
The old woman, finding it strange, went to ask,
but as she gradually drew near,
the woman moved farther away.
When the old woman turned back,
the woman returned to her original place.
This happened several times.
The old woman guessed she was not human,
and as the sky grew dark,
she left her.
When she reached the Chán master's place,
she described what she had seen,
along with the woman's appearance and clothing.
The Chán master found it strange
and therefore recorded it on the wall of his hut.
Over a month later,
Fáng Zhì's wife died suddenly,
and was indeed buried at the hillock she had been circling and weeping around earlier.
Her appearance and clothing
were exactly as the old woman had previously seen.
Wáng Chāo
In the fifth year of the Tàihé era,
there was a physician named Wáng Chāo from Fùzhōu,
who was skilled in using acupuncture,
and no illness was beyond his cure.
After dying for a night, he revived,
and recounted it as if in a dream:
He arrived at a place,
with walls, towers, and pavilions,
like the residence of a king.
He saw a person lying down,
who summoned him forward to examine his pulse,
and found a swelling on the right arm,
as large as a cup,
and ordered Wáng Chāo to treat it.
Immediately, he used acupuncture to drain over a *shēng* of pus.
Turning to a yellow-clad official, he said:
"You may lead him to see the end."
Wáng Chāo followed him through a gate,
on which was inscribed "Bì Courtyard."
In the courtyard were thousands of human eyes,
piled up into a mountain,
gazing inward, blinking and flickering.
The yellow-clad official said:
"This is the end."
Soon, two men appeared,
of extraordinary and imposing stature,
standing on the left and right.
They waved giant fans,
blowing and stirring the gathered eyes,
fanning them up,
some flying,
some walking as humans,
and in an instant, they were all gone.
Wáng Chāo inquired about the reason,
and the yellow-clad official said:
"Among all living beings,
those who die first reach the end."
As he spoke, Wáng Chāo suddenly revived.
Duàn Hé
Jìnshì Duàn Hé rented a residence in Kèhù Lǐ.
In the summer of the eighth year of Tàihé,
he lay ill for over a month,
and slightly recovered.
One day, he mustered the strength to wash and comb his hair,
and sat leaning against a table.
Suddenly, a man emerged,
from a crack in the wall of his room,
wearing a skirt but no upper garment,
standing proudly before Duàn Hé,
and after looking intently at him, said:
"Ill as you are,
why not take a wife,
to attend to you in your sickness?
If you were to suddenly die of illness,
what would become of you?"
Duàn Hé knew he was a ghostly being.
He replied:
"I am a poor scholar,
with no intention of marrying."
The man said:
"Allow me to act as your matchmaker.
There is now a family with a daughter,
whose beauty and virtue are admirable,
and whose lineage is pure and distinguished,
with many relatives.
She brings her own dowry,
and will not trouble you for betrothal gifts."
Duàn Hé said:
"I have not yet achieved fame,
and have no such intention."
The man said again:
"Even without formal rites,
it could still be done.
I will now bring her to you."
The man then went out the door,
and returned shortly after,
saying:
"She has arrived."
Soon, four people appeared,
carrying a golden-canopied carriage.
Following were two maidservants,
one with a cloud-like chignon,
the other with a half-chignon,
both of peerless beauty.
Two old servants,
carrying dressing cases and clothing chests,
placed the carriage directly before the steps.
The matchmaker then led them into the inner chamber,
drew the curtains and closed the door,
and returned to Duàn Hé, saying:
"I have brought a fine lady from a good family,
yet you show no courtesy at all.
Is this not improper?"
Duàn Hé was disgusted,
and being exhausted,
lay down on his pillow without paying attention.
The matchmaker said again:
"Even if you have no intention of accepting her,
at least take a look."
After repeated persuasion like this,
Duàn Hé still did not respond.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
the matchmaker led them out the door again,
and the one in the carriage left a poem written on red paper,
placed on Duàn Hé's table before departing.
The poem read:
"Lè Guǎng, frail and thin for years on end,
Chàniáng entrusts herself without regard for wealth.
Where has this graceful, exquisite beauty gone?
Melancholy fills the blue tower and red jade fields."
The handwriting was delicate and charming,
and bore no name,
only the character "I" written at the end of the paper.
From then on, Duàn Hé's illness gradually receded.
Wéi Bào Shēng's Singing Girl
Bàoshēng, a man fond of drink,
was wealthy and kept singing girls.
In the early years of the Kāichéng era,
while traveling on the road through Lìyáng,
he stopped at Dìngshān Temple.
There he met his maternal cousin, Wéishēng, who had failed the imperial examinations and was returning east.
They rested together in a waterside pavilion.
Bàoshēng prepared wine.
When they were well into their cups,
Wéishēng said to Bàoshēng:
"Where are your several singing girls?
Surely you have brought some along?"
Bàoshēng replied:
"Fortunately, they are all well.
However,
During my stay in Wéiyáng,
several of my carriage horses died in succession.
Since my later teams were thus lacking,
I could not bring them all.
Only Mènglán and Xiǎoqiàn are with me;
they can now provide some entertainment."
Shortly after,
two maids with double buns arrived carrying a húqín and a fāngxiǎng.
They then sat to the right of Wéishēng and Bàoshēng,
plucking the strings and striking the metal,
their music resounding through the stream valley.
As the wine drew to an end,
Bàoshēng asked Wéishēng:
"Did you obtain any fine horses outside the city?"
Wéishēng replied:
"At the beginning of spring, I traveled to the frontier,
from Fūfāng through Wūyán,
reaching Píngxià.
I turned back after stopping at Língwǔ.
From the tribes, I acquired several exceptional steeds:
with dragon-like forms and phoenix necks,
deer-like shanks and duck-like chests,
large eyes and light hooves,
level spines and close ribs—
I have them all."
Bàoshēng clapped his hands with great delight,
then set down his cup and ordered candles,
inspecting several horses in front of the light railings.
Compared to his earlier boasts,
they fell short by eighty or ninety percent.
Wéishēng teased Bàoshēng:
"If you are willing to exchange a person,
you may choose any exceptional one."
Bàoshēng's desire for the horses was quite keen.
He secretly sent for Sìxián,
who changed clothes and applied lavish makeup,
arriving shortly after.
He ordered her to offer wine to Wéishēng
and sing a song to present to him:
"White dew dampens the courtyard steps,
the bright moon shines before the front porch.
At this moment, I harbor much regret,
filled with thoughts, alone and wordless."
She also sang "Presenting Wine to Bàoshēng":
"The wind tosses lotus pearls, hard to keep round for long;
in many lives, indeed there are short-lived bonds.
Tonight on the west tower, the moon at the third watch
still shines on the parting one weeping over a broken string."
Wéishēng then summoned his groom
to lead out a purple Chìbō horse to repay him.
Bàoshēng, still unsatisfied,
engaged in back-and-forth discussion,
which became chaotic and incoherent.
Two men in purple robes and caps,
with a large retinue,
from the west of the waterside pavilion,
ascended the steps and approached.
Bàoshēng and Wéishēng, thinking the temple was on the route of imperial messengers galloping to and fro,
suspected that high officials had arrived at night.
They thus fearfully retreated into the room,
closing the door to spy.
The cups and plates lay in disarray,
with no time to tidy them.
At that moment, the men in purple took their seats,
looked at each other, and laughed:
"This must be the feast where we just heard about exchanging a concubine for a horse."
They then ordered wine and drank together.
One had a very long beard,
a robust and imposing appearance.
Holding his cup, he gazed at the moon,
pondering for a long time,
then said:
"Your 'Ode to Abundance' states:
'The slanting Milky Way forms the left boundary,
the Northern Dipper follows its southern path.
White dew warms the sky,
the pale moon flows through the heavens.' This can be considered brilliant, surpassing both past and future.
Yet, facing the moon, one hardly appreciates: 'The wind clears the earth's surface,
clouds gather at heaven's edge.
The Dòngtíng Lake begins to ripple,
tree leaves slightly fall.'"
The long-bearded one said:
"Over the past few years in Cháng'ān,
I was introduced by King Lèyóu to the Southern Palace,
entered the capital hall,
and with Liú Gōnggàn and Bào Míngyuǎn watched the examination of scholars.
I secretly entered the chamber of the literary officials,
and by candlelight observed the compositions of the capable candidates.
I saw that their parallel couplets were quite apt,
but their rhapsodies suffered from faults like 'bee waists' and 'crane knees,'
and their poems violated rules of 'heavy heads' and 'heavy tails.'
If, like your couplet 'Dòngtíng' and 'tree leaves,'
it would be considered erroneous.
My humble rhapsody states:
'The Purple Terrace grows somewhat distant,
Yān Mountain has no end.
A cool wind suddenly rises,
the white sun hides in the west.'
Then the sounds of 'somewhat distant' and 'suddenly rises'
were both rejected.
Is that not strange!"
He said to the long-bearded one:
"I have heard that in ancient times, the feudal lords
presented scholars to the Son of Heaven,
to honor the worthy and encourage goodness.
Thus, one successful recommendation was called 'loving virtue,'
a second was called 'honoring the worthy,'
and a third was called 'having merit.'
Then they were granted the Nine Bestowals.
If they did not present scholars,
they were once stripped of rank,
twice stripped of land,
and thrice stripped of both rank and land.
The ancients sought scholars in this manner,
yet still feared their search of the mountains was not high enough,
their combing of the forests not deep enough.
There were still those遗漏,
so each year in late spring, they opened the government storehouses,
brought out silks and coins,
and traveled throughout the land to ritually invite them.
At that time,
the followers of Confucianism and Mohism,
were they all brought forth?
Men of wisdom and strategy,
were they all recommended?
In the mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
were there none left behind?
Under the sun and moon's illumination,
could they all fully realize their potential?
The Son of Heaven sought them thus,
the feudal lords presented them thus,
and the invitation rituals were thus,
yet there must have been those anxiously dwelling in rocky valleys,
depressed and unable to fulfill their ambitions.
I hear that today, the rituals of seeking and inviting are neglected,
and the way of presenting and recommending is ruined.
The worthy and unworthy travel the same path;
the talented and untalented are muddled together.
Those hidden in rocky caves
from childhood exhaust themselves studying the classics
until their hair turns white.
Those holding strategies and plans
from their prime years labor at learning
until their teeth are gone.
Although each year the villages recommend them to the prefectures,
the prefectures present them to the relevant offices,
and the offices examine them with poetry and rhapsodies,
'bee waists' and 'crane knees'
are deemed not to meet the standard;
the clarity and turbidity of tones and rhymes are criticized,
deemed not to match
the rules.
Even if one had the worthiness and sagacity of the Duke of Zhōu and Confucius,
or the literary talent of Bān Gù and Sīmǎ Qiān,
without composing in this manner,
one could not advance.
But what of the ways of emperors and kings, the hegemons' principles,
the substance of rise and fall, order and chaos—
can these be heard of?
Why do you now praise today's petty技巧,
and undermine the great substance of antiquity?
Moreover, I am one who pours out my heart to the bright moon and sings long songs—
how could I be constrained
by those who carve patterns and engrave phrases?
Now the pearly dew is clear,
the cassia moon is bright as day,
chants and recitations arise from time to time,
cups and goblets pass among us.
Can we take up brushes to link verses,
compose a chapter in today's style and tune,
to enjoy the long night?"
He said:
"What shall be the topic?"
The long-bearded one said:
"Let us take 'Exchanging a Concubine for a Horse' as the topic,
and use 'abandoning that倾城 beauty,
seeking those swift steeds' as the rhyme."
He ordered his attendants to break off a plantain leaf from the courtyard,
opened his book bag,
drew out a brush to wield it,
each assigning themselves a rhyme.
The long-bearded one began chanting:
"That beautiful lady, ah,"
Like the luster of fine jade;
this noble steed,
bears the name of excellence.
If one seeks to chase the sun,
why begrudge the cost of a city?
In the fragrant warmth of deep chambers,
one forever tires of peach blossom hues;
on the clear-winded broad roads,
one once cherished the sound of jade-like snorts.”
Xīyì said:
“Considering how people take pride in their appearance,
horses are praised for their virtue.
Since each follows their own preferences,
what desire could remain unfulfilled?
Kneeling long to bid farewell,
her graceful form no longer shines with golden hairpins;
led by the right hand as she arrives,
radiance suddenly blooms on the jade bridle.”
Wéntōng said:
“Stepping to the courtyard steps,
presenting herself before the hall.
Gazing upon new favor,
she fears,
‘This is not my match’;
yearning for her former master,
she doubts being lent for another’s ride.
Fragrance drifts from the green steed,
her thoughts already forgetting the adorned hair;
sweat flows on the red forehead,
affection no different from congealed脂.”
Xīyì said:
“Thus we know affairs have rise and fall,
uses involve choices and rejections.
That one considers peerless beauty as freshness,
this one values surpassing speed as precious.
The grace of bought laughter already spent,
resembles divination;
the strength to mount the saddle still remains,
yet hopes for advancement.”
When Wéntōng finished his four-rhyme fu,
the plantain leaves were exhausted.
Weí Shēng opened a case to fetch red stationery,
kneeling to present it beneath the eaves.
The two men exclaimed in surprise:
“The paths of hidden and manifest are separate,
why press us so?
However, unless you later attain rank and emolument,
you cannot meet with humble men like us.”
They told Shēng:
“In days to come, when you preside over literary authority,
judging the weight of talent and excellence,
do not fixate on petty cleverness.”
Having spoken,
the two gentlemen walked some ten paces,
when suddenly they were nowhere to be seen.
Liáng Jǐng
There was a man named Liáng Jǐng.
During the Kāichéng era,
he was preparing to sit for the Xiàolián examination from Chángshā,
and while traveling, he stopped at Shāngshān,
lodging at a post-house pavilion.
It was the night of the fifteenth of the eighth month,
the sky had just cleared after rain,
the wind and moon were bright and lofty,
and Jǐng lay awake, unable to sleep.
Around midnight,
he suddenly saw three gentlemen,
dressed in very ancient attire,
all adorned with pearls and jade,
approaching with leisurely steps.
They reached the courtyard,
chanting and admiring as they went,
with several attendants.
Jǐng knew in his heart they were ghosts,
but being naturally bold,
he descended the steps to greet them with a bow.
The three showed no fear either,
introducing themselves as Xiāo Zhōngláng, Wáng Bùbīng, and Zhūgě Chángshǐ.
They then had mats laid in the courtyard and sat,
saying:
“Never expected to meet you here on such a fine night!”
Then they called to their page:
“Yùshān, fetch wine.”
When the wine arrived,
they passed it around the mats.
After a while, Wáng Bùbīng said:
“Facing such fine wind and moon,
and with such excellent guests at the mat,
we cannot be without poetry.”
So he proposed composing linked verses on a theme,
to chant of the autumn moon.
Bùbīng began first, saying:
“The autumn moon, round as a mirror.” Xiāo Zhōngláng said:
“The autumn wind, sharp as a blade.”
Jǐng said:
“Autumn clouds, light as willow catkins.”
Next it came to Zhūgě Chángshǐ,
who remained silent for a long time.
The other two urged him:
“Please prioritize simplicity and speed.”
Chángshǐ pondered deeply,
and after about the time of a meal,
finally said:
“Autumn grass, fine as hair.”
The other two laughed heartily:
“Simple it is indeed,
but why so slow?”
Chángshǐ said:
“This is Zhōngláng’s fault,
for choosing an obscure rhyme and hindering swift talent.”
Then Zhōngláng said again:
“A fine gathering cannot lack musical accompaniment.
Yùshān, summon Huìniáng here.”
Yùshān left,
and shortly after,
a beautiful woman appeared,
dressed in bright clothes, walking in through the gate,
smiling and bowing to the seated guests.
Zhūgě Chángshǐ teased the maiden:
“You came at Zhōngláng’s summons.
What has that to do with me?”
The beauty said:
“How do you know I didn’t come for everyone?”
Bùbīng said:
“To clarify yourself,
nothing better than singing to accompany Chángshǐ’s wine.”
Huìniáng rose and said:
“I wish to sing the ‘Fènglóu’ melody.”
She then sang it,
her clear voice full of longing and melancholy,
and Jǐng listened, forgetting all weariness.
After a long while, the song ended,
and Zhōngláng sang next.
When his song finished, he said:
“The mountain light gradually brightens.
Let us compose one more piece
to fully enjoy our joy.”
He began:
“Mountain trees cast tall shadows.”
Bùbīng said:
“Mountain flowers bloom in silent fragrance.”
Then, pointing at Chángshǐ, he said:
“Earlier with the obscure rhyme,
it was indeed Zhōngláng’s fault.
We now hope you will continue this,
to witness swift talent.”
Chángshǐ responded:
“Mountain skies stretch distantly, clearly.”
The whole company laughed:
“Slow is no match for fast,
and moreover clumsy—
is this what swift talent looks like?”
Chángshǐ’s expression showed he was displeased.
Next it came to Jǐng, who said:
“Mountain waters rush flowing swiftly.”
Zhōngláng offered general praise,
then asked Jǐng:
“Are you not one who sits for the Jìnshì examination?”
Jǐng said:
“I am preparing for the Xiàolián examination.”
Zhōngláng laughed:
“How could a Xiàolián candidate know poetry?”
Jǐng angrily rebuked him,
and Chángshǐ also rose, shaking his sleeves in agitation.
The seated guests scattered in alarm,
and then they vanished,
the cups and plates also disappearing from sight.
From then on, Jǐng fell ill and became unsettled,
often dreaming of Zhōngláng and Bùbīng visiting,
which he deeply detested.
Later, when he reached Cháng’ān,
he met a diviner named Lǐ Shēng, who gave him a ghost-warding talisman to wear,
and the hauntings ceased.
Cuī Yùshǐ
In Guǎnglíng, there was an official residence,
covering an area of several hundred paces,
grand and magnificent in its construction.
Among the locals, it was rumored that the place was haunted by ghosts,
so those who lived there
would die suddenly in a single night.
It had been locked up for many years.
There was a censor named Cuī,
who was assigned to Guǎnglíng.
Upon arriving,
he opened the door and said:
"Misfortune does not arise on its own;
I am newly residing here,
how could it bring disaster?"
He then reported to the surveillance commissioner and moved in.
That night, there was a light rain.
Cuī ordered his servants to stay in other rooms,
while he slept alone in the main hall.
He awoke with a start,
his clothes completely soaked.
He got up
and saw his bed had been moved into the courtyard.
He went back to sleep,
but before the time it takes to eat a meal,
his bed had moved to the courtyard again.
This happened three times.
Cuī said:
"I thought there were no ghosts in the world,
but now it seems there truly are."
He then prepared his official cap and tablet,
poured wine as an offering, and prayed:
"I have heard that those who live here often die suddenly.
Moreover, humans and spirits follow different paths;
you should rest peacefully in your dwelling.
Why harm the living?
Even if you appear in form
or make your voice heard,
it is because you bear grievances and wish to plead your case,
or perhaps seek a meal as an offering.
Thus you appear to people,
but people die from fright themselves,
it is not the spirits who harm them.
I am quite foolish
and have no fear.
If you truly have something to plead,
speak directly to me.
I can fulfill your request;
even boiling water or fire will not deter me."
After pouring wine and praying three times,
he suddenly heard a voice from the air say:
"You are human,
I am a ghost.
It is truly improper for a ghost to trouble a human,
but I wish to confide my deep sincerity."
Cuī said:
"Speak, then."
The ghost said:
"I am a woman.
My two sisters and I,
all died before reaching adulthood.
Our parents buried us north of the commandery city long ago.
Later, the prefect fortified the city walls here
and constructed buildings.
The workers cut down almost all the trees within our burial grounds
and moved us to the northeast corner of this hall.
Our wandering souls find no peace,
with nowhere to rest.
Unexpectedly tonight,
I am fortunate to meet a wise gentleman,
so I can speak of my grievance.
If you, with a benevolent heart,
could place me in a coffin and bury me in the wilderness,
it would be a great kindness indeed."
Then she wept and sobbed,
and added:
"I have been here for ten years.
All those who lived here before
wanted to speak of this matter,
but they died of fright instead.
I, a mere girl,
mean no harm to anyone."
Cuī said:
"What I said earlier stands.
However,
why do you not show yourself to me?"
The ghost replied:
"I am a ghost;
how dare I appear before you with my shadowy form?
Since you have promised my request,
even in the darkness of the underworld,
I will still feel your kindness.
How could I simply vanish without gratitude?"
Having spoken,
she took her leave.
The next day,
Cuī summoned workers
to excavate the northeast corner of the hall.
They indeed found dry bones,
which they buried in an empty plot at Chánzhì Temple.
The locals all made offerings there,
calling it the Tomb of the Three Maidens.
From then on, the residence was peaceful.
Cáo Táng
Jìnshì Cáo Táng,
known for his poetic talent,
was famous in his time.
He repeatedly failed the imperial examinations,
and often stayed at a pavilion by a pond in a Buddhist temple in Jiānglíng.
The surroundings were serene and beautiful.
He often visited to enjoy the scenery and compose poetry,
once writing two lines:
"Beneath the water, spring stretches vast and dim;
Among mortals, no path lies under the boundless moon."
Not long after reciting them,
he felt none of his usual works matched these lines.
One day, as he sat again by the pavilion pond,
savoring his composition,
he suddenly saw two women
dressed in plain white clothes,
their demeanor elegant and composed.
They walked slowly, reciting
the very two lines he had composed earlier.
Cáo Táng thought his poem was not yet a day old,
and surely no one else knew it,
so how could they have obtained it?
He hurried after them to question them,
but they did not respond and left.
Before they had gone more than ten steps,
they vanished.
Cáo Táng was deeply puzzled and disturbed.
He had long been on good terms with the temple monk Fǎzhōu,
so he told Zhōu about it.
Zhōu exclaimed in surprise:
"Two days ago,
a young man came to visit me.
He carried a blue paper
and showed me this poem.
I was just about to mention it."
He then showed the paper to Cáo Táng,
who was utterly bewildered.
A few days later,
Cáo Táng died in the Buddhist temple.
Xǔ Shēng
In the spring of the first year of the Huìchāng era,
the Filial and Incorrupt candidate Xǔ Shēng,
having failed the imperial examination, was returning east.
He stopped at Shòu'ān,
intending to lodge at the Gānquán Inn.
About a li west of the Gāntáng Lodge,
he encountered an old man in white clothes,
riding a dappled grey horse,
coming from the west.
His retinue was extremely numerous,
his face flushed and cheerful,
and he was reciting clearly:
"Lush and green the spring grass, the spring waters emerald,
Wild pear blossoms all fallen, scattering fragrant jade.
Before the Xiùlǐng Palace, a white-haired man
Still sings the peaceful songs of the Kāiyuán reign."
Shēng urged his horse forward,
and asked the old man his name.
The old man smiled slightly but did not answer.
He then recited another poem:
"Those who shun the world and flee from fame,
Who could answer with a name?
Have you ever heard of the three joys?
Look at the sentiments by the roadside."
Shēng then knew he was a ghostly being,
and so asked no more.
He simply followed behind,
for about two or three li,
when the day had already grown dark.
Upon reaching the west of the marker mound at the Pēnyù Spring,
the old man smiled and said to Shēng:
"I have heard that three or four gentlemen
are today revisiting their old haunts at this spring.
I was summoned yesterday,
and am heading south from here.
You, sir, should not follow closely on horseback."
Shēng firmly requested to accompany him,
but the old man, without replying, departed.
Shēng gave his horse free rein and followed him.
About a li past Gāntáng,
he saw carriages, horses, guides, and attendants
filling the narrow fork in the road.
Shēng waved aside the canopies and advanced.
Upon reaching the spring pavilion,
he then dismounted.
He crouched down,
beneath a thicket of brambles,
and held his breath to spy on them.
He saw four men:
one was a youth with a spirited and proud demeanor;
one was short and small, with an open and composed bearing;
one was tall and large with sparse beard and whiskers;
one was thin and frail, whose speech and glances were swift.
All wore gold and purple,
and were sitting on the northern bank of the spring.
When the old man arrived,
he said:
"Yùchuān, why are you so late?"
The old man replied:
"I was just by the Shímò Gully seeking enjoyment,
and rested my horse at the Gāntáng Lodge pavilion.
On the western pillar, I happened to see a poem inscribed by a poet,
so I stopped to recite and chant it,
unaware that so much time had passed."
The one at the head of the seat said:
"What kind of poem is it,
that you, sir, praise and sigh over it so?"
The old man said:
"This poem seems to be about one or two of the gentlemen present here,
yet it conceals their names.
Pitying that its final lines all have meaning,
he then said:
'Gloomy clouds, the sun faintly bright,
Deep sorrow, the general bears the charge's blight.
By daylight calling at the palace gate, no close kin near,
In plain white robes, swallowing grief, only disciples here.
Fair ladies secretly weep, filling the palace with tears,
Stable horses neigh continuously, changing masters' cheers.
Vast the world, mourning the Hàn's land in despair,
This body finds no place to weep for Tián Héng there.'"
Those seated heard this,
and all covered their faces with their sleeves,
as if about to wail bitterly.
The one with the spirited and proud demeanor said:
"I know who wrote this poem.
Could it not be that man by the Yīshuǐ River,
who received from me the gift of food and the removal of clothing?"
After a long while,
the old man in white ordered the cups to fly,
and after several rounds of toasts,
those seated were still sighing and sobbing without end.
The old man in white said:
"Revisiting old haunts,
there is nothing to amuse ourselves with.
We should compose poems,
to take the place of pipes and strings."
He ordered his attendants to fetch brush and inkstone,
and then presented the topic:
"'Reflections on Old Wanderings and Unburdening the Heart at Pēnyù Spring,'
each a seven-character long verse."
The old man in white led off:
"Trees' hues and stream's glow in the evening clear,
Where once we roamed, events distinct appear.
Rats pierce moonlit towers, thorns now entwine,
Grass hides flower gardens, ridges align.
Trapped in yellow sands, still not awake,
Crimes marked on green slips, what name to take?
Heartbroken at the valley's mouth, eastward the waters flow,
Still spraying forth the sound of cold jade long ago."
The youth with the spirited and proud demeanor composed:
"Crows' caws, orioles' songs—thoughts without end,
A lifetime's glory, a dream to transcend.
Xiào's injustice lies hidden in moth-eaten scrolls,
Dèng Yōu, sonless, can't pass on pure goals.
Essays' lofty tones flow with the stream,
Strings and pipes' lost notes trust grass insects' theme.
Spring moon knows not human affairs have changed,
Idly hanging its light, on ruined palaces arranged."
The short, small one with open bearing composed:
"Peach and plum paths all desolate and drear,
Visiting old, seeking new, adds to sorrow here.
Though burial clothes hid Lǐ Gù's frame,
In the end, no memorial cleared Wáng Zhāng's name.
A wandering soul still feels the frosty wind's cold,
Rotten bones startle in vain at osmanthus' fragrance bold.
Heaven's rank, by man's rank misled in the end,
Who can cry out loud, to the azure sky send?"
The thin, frail one with swift glances composed:
"Fallen flowers silent, grasses stretch far and wide,
Clouds' shadows, mountains' light, all as if they never died.
Ruined rooms, foundations crushed by new stone rats,
Pooled palace waters draw from old mountain spouts.
Reaching blue clouds on my own, ashamed of heaven's rank,
White heads returning together, moved by sages of yank.
Melancholy in the woods, the midnight moon's sight,
Its lonely light once shone on my reading mat bright."
The tall, large one with sparse beard composed:
"New brambled path, old humble door,
Again halting fine carriages, sharing one jar more.
Cold bones not yet touched by new rain and dew,
Spring breeze cannot make withered orchids anew.
A heart of cinnabar, how could it be buried in dark ground?
The bright sun still hopes to shine on the overturned basin's round.
Cherish the friends of Jīngǔ Garden in days gone by,
Gathering by the spring to speak of lonely souls with a sigh."
When the poems were finished,
each chanted his own,
and gave several long cries,
their echoes shaking the cliffs and valleys.
Moments later,
strange birds, owls, and screech-owls
began chirping and chattering together;
large foxes and old wildcats
called out one after another.
Shortly after,
the sound of mule hooves came from the east,
and the ringing of golden bells
vibrated among those seated.
Each called for his servant and horse,
in great haste.
Somber and without words,
they wiped their tears and mounted their saddles,
like shapes of mist and smoke,
they scattered from the courtyard.
Shēng then emerged from the thicket of brambles.
Seeking his old path,
he found his horse grazing grass by the gully side,
and his lame servant boy sleeping soundly by the roadside.
Before dawn,
he reached the Gānquán Inn.
The old woman of the inn questioned him about the previous night,
and Shēng told her everything.
The old woman said:
"Last night at the third watch,
a man on horseback came with a pot,
to buy wine from me.
Could it not have been this?"
She opened the cabinet to look,
and it was all paper money.
Yán Jùn
During the Huìchāng era,
Jìnshì Yán Jùn,
having failed the imperial examination, traveled to Guǎnglíng.
He then proceeded to Jiànyè,
hired a small boat,
and arrived at Báishā.
On the same boat was a maidservant,
around twenty years old,
dressed in simple, ancient attire,
with clear and elegant speech.
Jùn bowed to her,
asking her name,
to which she replied:
"This humble one is named Zhào Yòufāng."
He asked where she was headed,
and she replied:
"I am also going to Jiànyè."
Jùn was very pleased,
and whenever the boat moored,
he would buy wine and fruits,
feasting and drinking with her.
She often spoke of matters from the Chén and Suí dynasties,
which Jùn found quite strange,
so he straightened his expression and adjusted his sleeves, but she did not respond.
Upon reaching Báishā,
they each boarded their own boats,
and the maidservant thanked Jùn, saying:
"For several days, I have received your deep regard.
I am plain and clumsy,
unworthy of bringing you joy.
However, there is one matter
with which I can repay you.
On the Zhōngyuán Festival, you must visit the Wǎguān Pavilion.
At that time, I will arrange for you to meet an immortal-like person.
Moreover, your demeanor and talent
are well-suited for such a meeting.
I hope you will not break this appointment.
When the time comes,
I will be waiting there."
After speaking,
they each boarded their boats and departed.
Jùn remembered her words,
and on the Zhōngyuán Festival,
he went to visit the Wǎguān Pavilion.
Men and women crowded the place,
and upon ascending the pavilion,
he indeed saw a beautiful woman,
accompanied by two maidservants,
both with double buns and charming demeanors.
The beauty leaned against the railing, speaking to herself,
sighing sorrowfully for a long time.
Jùn gazed at her intently,
and the beauty also noticed him in surprise.
She then said:
"Yòufāng's words were not mistaken."
She sent one of the maidservants to relay a message:
"In the west corridor is the Huìjiàn Shéli Courtyard,
where an old disciple of mine resides.
You may go there,
and Yòufāng will also be present."
Jùn was overjoyed,
and followed her trail,
indeed seeing the maidservant from the same boat,
who came out smiling.
Jùn then exchanged greetings with the beauty,
and they conversed until the day ended.
A monk served tea and fruits.
As evening fell,
she said to Jùn:
"Today, I happened to visit this place
to cherish this lofty pavilion.
I lament the effort put into its construction,
as it will soon be demolished.
Thus, I came to bid it farewell,
and am fortunate to share this joyful moment with you.
My home is in Qīngxī,
where there are many pines and moonlight,
and no one else resides.
Tonight, you must come visit.
I will go ahead,
and you may follow later with Yòufāng."
Jùn agreed,
and she departed in a carriage.
When night fell,
Yòufāng led Jùn forward,
and after a few miles, they arrived.
Several maidservants
came out with torches to welcome them.
They were ushered into an inner chamber,
where they sat in a circle with Yòufāng.
She said:
"Lady Kǒng lives nearby.
I have invited her, saying:
'Tonight, we happen to have a distinguished guest visiting.
I hope you will join us in raising our cups
to dispel our worries and sorrows.'"
After a short while, she arrived,
and was invited in.
They spoke mostly of stories from the Chén dynasty.
Jùn then stood up and said:
"May I ask, madam, what your surname and rank are?
I am filled with doubt and curiosity."
She replied:
"I am none other than Consort Zhāng of the Chén dynasty,
and she is Consort Kǒng.
During our lifetime,
we were mistakenly favored by the Later Lord,
and the honors and affection we received
surpassed those of other consorts.
Unfortunately, when the state fell,
we were killed by Yáng Guǎng.
Yet, this tyrant was exceedingly unkind.
Did Liú Shàn and Kǒng Hào
not have their own consorts?
Only this man
committed such cruel atrocities.
Moreover, though both were fallen states,
our Later Lord was truly a man of refinement,
seeking joy in poetry and wine,
finding pleasure in music and drinking—nothing more.
He was not like Yáng Guǎng,
who built the Great Wall in the west,
and campaigned against Liáohǎi in the east,
leaving men and women across the land in sorrow and loneliness,
fathers widowed and sons orphaned.
In the end, at Guǎnglíng,
he died at the hands of a commoner—
surely a divine judgment from heaven,
avenging us!"
Consort Kǒng said:
"Do not speak like this.
There is someone present who may not wish to hear it."
The beauty laughed loudly and said:
"I had completely forgotten."
Jùn asked:
"Who would not wish to hear such words?"
Yòufāng said:
"I was originally a favored servant in Minister Jiǎng's household,
later becoming Consort Zhāng's attendant.
After the fall of the state,
I became a palace maid of the Suí dynasty.
When Emperor Yáng was in Jiāngdū,
I served him meals and baths.
When Yǔwén Huàjí's rebel soldiers entered,
I shielded the emperor with my body
and was killed as a result.
Empress Xiāo, pitying my loyalty to my master,
had me buried with him.
Later, when he was reburied beside Léitáng,
I could not follow.
Now, I come here occasionally to pay my respects to Consort Zhāng."
Consort Kǒng said:
"What we discussed earlier is all idle talk.
It would be better to order wine
and briefly relive the joys of days gone by."
She then ordered the maidservants to bring musical instruments,
and they drank together for a long time.
Consort Zhāng composed a poem:
"Autumn grass, a desolate terrace, crickets chirp at night;
White poplars' sounds fade, sorrowful winds subside.
Once I wrote on colored paper, outshining Jiǎng Zǒng;
Now the ornate pavilion gathers dust, the Jade Tree is gone."
Consort Kǒng composed:
"Precious pavilion piercing clouds, named 'Gazing at Immortals';
Five-colored clouds, splendid and high, embrace the morning sky.
Qīngxī still holds the moon of those bygone days;
Its light tonight shines on jade blossoms at this lavish feast."
Yòufāng composed:
"The bright moon newly full, yet sorrow veils my brow;
What remains of past glory, of splendor and renown?
Only the River of two dynasties flows on;
Its waves, as ever, carry travelers away."
Jùn also composed in response:
"Flute's clear melody laments Lìhuá's fate;
Autumn river, cold moon, slant through the window grate.
I blush, no poet favored by the Later Lord;
Yet here I glimpse the flowers of Línchūn's hall once more."
Suddenly, knocking was heard at the door:
"Jiāng Xiūróng, Hé Jiéyú, and Yuán Zhàoyí have come to pay respects to Consort Zhāng."
They said:
"We heard that distinguished guests are gathered here tonight,
and could not resist glimpsing this splendid feast."
All were dressed in resplendent robes,
their earrings and pendants gleaming as they entered and took their seats.
Upon seeing the four poems,
they held them and wept, saying:
"Tonight, we unexpectedly relive the gathering of the three pavilions,
and compose poems with a new favored guest."
After a while,
the crowing of a rooster was heard.
Consort Kǒng and the others all rose,
bidding farewell and departing.
Jùn and Consort Zhāng retired to rest,
and as dawn approached, they arose.
Consort Zhāng gifted Jùn a dust-repelling rhinoceros horn hairpin,
saying:
"In days to come, when you see this object, think of me.
Last night, with many guests,
we could not fully express our joy."
On another day we should have a small gathering,
but we must first consult the underworld."
They parted with sobs.
The next day, Wáng Jùn was dazed,
as if he had lost something.
After two nights,
he went again to the previous location,
only to find it near a clear stream,
with pines and junipers growing over mounds and ruins.
Upon inquiring with people,
he learned it was the tomb of a palace maid from the Chén dynasty.
Wáng Jùn returned in sorrow,
and after several months,
the pavilion was destroyed when the temple was abandoned.
Later, when he reached Guǎnglíng,
he visited the old tomb of Emperor Yáng at Wúgōngtái,
and indeed found the tomb of the palace maid Zhào Yòufāng.
He then offered wine in libation.
Hǎo Wéiliàng
Hǎo Wéiliàng, a native of Jīngzhōu,
was coarse and rash by nature,
and bold in private conflicts.
On the Cold Food Festival in the second year of the Huìcháng era,
he went with his companions to the outskirts,
where they played football and wrestled,
and he lay drunk among the graves.
At midnight he awoke,
and as he was about to return,
he saw a house by the roadside,
extremely humble and crude,
with a lamp lit but rather dim.
He then went to ask for a drink,
and there was a woman,
her appearance haggard and sorrowful,
dressed plainly and simply,
sewing by the lamp.
She invited Hǎo in,
and after a long while said to him:
"I know you have courage,
so I dare to entrust you with my feelings.
I was originally from Qín,
surnamed Zhāng,
and married to Lǐ Zìhuān, a strongman in the prefectural office.
During the Tàihé era, Zìhuān
went to garrison the frontier and never returned,
and I succumbed to an epidemic and died.
I have no other relatives,
and the neighbors buried me here.
It has been over twelve years,
with no chance of reburial.
For all the dead, if the flesh and bones are not returned to the earth,
the soul is not registered by the underworld authorities.
Though scattered and vague,
it is like a dream or a drunken stupor.
If you can have my remains returned to the underworld,
and my spirit find a place to rest,
this wish will be fulfilled."
Hǎo said:
"My livelihood has always been meager,
and I lack the means to do this.
What should I do?"
The woman said:
"Though I am a ghost,
I have not abandoned women's work.
Since settling here,
I have often made raincoats,
working for the Hú family,
for several years now.
I have saved up one hundred and thirty thousand,
which is more than enough for burial expenses."
Hǎo promised and returned.
At dawn,
he visited the Hú family,
and everything matched the description.
He then told them the whole story.
Immediately, he went with them to the burial site,
opened the grave to look,
and found scattered coins filling the coffin,
the amount exactly as she had said.
The Hú family and Hǎo
were saddened and amazed.
They also collected money from their peers,
totaling two hundred thousand,
and held a grand funeral ceremony,
burying her at Lùdǐngyuán.
That night,
she appeared in dreams to Hú and Hǎo.
The Magistrate of Fúliáng, surnamed Zhāng,
had family wealth extending between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
accumulating gold and storing grain,
beyond all reckoning.
Upon completing his term of office,
he traveled to the capital.
He would always send provisions one stage ahead,
ensuring all delicacies from land and sea were fully prepared.
Arriving at Huàyīn,
his servants set up tents and canopies,
and arranged wine vessels.
Just as the cook had finished roasting a lamb,
a man in a yellow robe
sat down right at the platter.
The servants shouted at him repeatedly,
but his expression remained unyielding.
The old woman of the inn said:
"Nowadays, the hunting and falconry agents of the Five Wards
run rampant within the Guānzhōng region.
This man is likely one of them.
Do not contend with him."
As the servants were about to seek their supervisor to reprimand him,
Magistrate Zhāng arrived.
They reported everything about the man in yellow.
Magistrate Zhāng said:
"Do not shout."
He summoned the man in yellow and asked:
"Where do you come from?"
The man in yellow only mumbled in assent.
Zhāng urged them to warm wine quickly.
When the wine arrived,
he had the man drink from a large golden goblet.
Though the man did not thank him,
he seemed to show a look of shame.
After drinking,
he gazed at the roasted lamb,
his eyes fixed and unmoving.
The Magistrate cut some himself to offer him.
He finished one whole leg,
yet showed no sign of being full.
The Magistrate then gave him ten or fifteen pastries from a box to eat.
In all, he drank over two dǒu of wine.
When warmed by the wine,
he said to the Magistrate:
"Forty years ago,
I once had a full meal and got drunk at an eastern inn,
and that sustained me until today."
The Magistrate was very surprised
and earnestly inquired his name.
The man replied:
"I am not human.
I am an officer tasked with delivering the register of the dead in Guānzhōng."
Startled, the Magistrate asked for details.
He said:
"Tàishān summons human souls.
The register of those about to die is sent to the sacred mountain,
and I am assigned to escort it."
The Magistrate said:
"May I take a look at it?"
He replied:
"A peek would do no harm."
Thereupon, he untied a leather bag
and took out a scroll.
At the top it read:
"Tàishān Authority's Dispatch to the Golden Heaven Prefecture."
The second line stated:
"A man greedy for wealth, fond of killing,
who forgets righteousness at the sight of profit:
Former Magistrate of Fúliáng County, Zhāng, given name so-and-so."
This was precisely Magistrate Zhāng.
Seeing his name,
the Magistrate begged the messenger, saying:
"The length of life is fixed;
who dares to cling to death?
But I am just in my prime,
unprepared for death.
My family estate is vast,
and I have not yet arranged its disposition.
By what means can I extend my time?
In my bags and coffers,
the total value is no less than several hundred thousand strings of cash.
I can offer it all to you, sir."
The messenger said:
"The kindness of a single meal
truly deserves repayment.
But a gift of a million?
What use is that to me?
Now, there is an Immortal Official, Liú Gāng,
banished to Liánhuā Peak.
You should crawl on your hands and knees straight there,
plead sorrowfully, and submit a petition.
Apart from this, there is no other plan.
I heard yesterday that the Golden Heaven King lost a gambling game with the Southern Sacred Mountain
and owes two hundred thousand,
and is being pressed hard for payment.
You may go to the temple of the sacred mountain
and promise a large sum to him.
He will surely be able to exert influence on the Immortal Official.
Even if his influence falls short,
he can at least show you the way to Liánhuā Peak.
Otherwise,
with thorns and brambles dense,
rivers and valleys blocking the way,
no one can get there."
Thereupon, the Magistrate prepared sacrificial animals
and hurried to the temple of the sacred mountain,
promising ten million.
Then he went straight to Liánhuā Peak
and found a secluded path.
After several tens of lǐ,
he reached the foot of the peak.
Turning to the southeast,
there was a thatched hall.
He saw a Daoist priest sitting leaning on a table.
He asked the Magistrate:
"Rotting bones and foul flesh,
with soul departed and spirit exhausted—
how have you come here?"
The Magistrate said:
"The bell has tolled, the water-clock drained,
the dew will dry in an instant.
I have privately heard that you, Immortal Official,
can restore essence and soul to decayed bones,
and bring flesh and muscle to dried-up skeletons.
Since you possess a heart that delights in giving life,
would you begrudge the effort of submitting a petition?"
The Daoist priest said:
because of a single petition for a powerful minister of the Suí dynasty,
was banished to dwell on this peak.
What virtue have you shown me
that you wish to trap me into becoming a hermit of the cold mountains?"
The Magistrate pleaded even more desperately.
The Immortal Official's expression grew very angry.
Suddenly, a messenger arrived,
carrying a letter.
It was a missive from the Golden Heaven King.
The Immortal Official read the letter
and said with a laugh:
"Since the connection has been made,
it is hard not to respond."
He summoned the messenger to return and report,
saying:
"Will I not be condemned by the Supreme Emperor again?"
Then he opened a jade case,
wrote out a petition,
burned incense, bowed twice, and sent it off.
After about the time of a meal,
a celestial mandate
descended.
On it was inscribed the character "Chè."
The Immortal Official again burned incense, bowed twice, and opened it.
It said:
"Zhāng so-and-so has turned his back on his ancestors,
fraudulently usurping name and position.
He disregards ritual and law,
improperly seizing official honors.
Moreover, he is base, narrow-minded, and hoards much wealth,
deceitful and insincere.
The responsibility of governing a hundred lǐ district
he already presumptuously occupied;
the wealth of a thousand chariots
he now possesses through improper gain.
His crimes have been verified according to the record,
and his remaining soul awaits execution.
Why submit a petition
seeking to extend his life?
However, because aiding the endangered and saving the drowning
is esteemed by the Great Dào,
and alleviating punishments and pardoning faults
is a tenet of the Mystic Gate,
for the sake of this one common man,
I
fully promote transformation,
hoping he will repent of his evil,
so that he may perhaps renew himself.
For his clinging to life, his term is extended by five years.
The one who submitted the petition cannot be without
blame."
After reading it through,
the Immortal Official said to the Magistrate:
"Generally, the lifespan of humans in this world
can all reach a hundred years.
But through joy, anger, grief, and pleasure,
they muddy the source of their heart;
through love, hatred, cravings, and desires,
they cut at the root of life.
Moreover, boasting of their own abilities,
covering up others' strengths,
confusing their own minds,
changing myriad times in an instant.
Spirit weary, thoughts indolent,
they find it hard to preserve the harmony of Heaven.
Like clear spring water
muddied by the five flavors,
wishing to remain unspoiled—
how can it be achieved?
Strive to follow the path back.
Do not fail my instruction."
The official bid farewell,
and when he raised his hand, the other had already vanished.
He then retraced his old path,
finding it gradually easier to walk.
After traveling over ten li,
the yellow-robed official came forward to greet him and offer congratulations.
The official said:
"I wish to repay you,
and would like to know your name."
The official replied:
"My surname is Zhōng.
In life, I was a courier in Xuānchéng County.
I died in Huàyīn,
and was thus registered by the underworld.
The duty of delivering official documents
remains as toilsome as before."
The official asked:
"How can I relieve you from this hardship?"
He said:
"Simply fulfill the vow to the Golden Heavenly King,
and request that I be appointed as a gatekeeper.
Then I will be sustained by the offerings to the deity.
I have already delayed half a day beyond the heavenly decree,
and can linger no longer."
He then bid farewell to the official
and vanished after walking three or five steps into the oak forest south of the temple.
That evening,
Official Zhāng stopped his carriage in Huàyīn,
deciding to return east.
Calculating the cost of fulfilling the vow to the Golden Heavenly King,
it would exceed twenty thousand coins.
He then said to his servant:
"Twenty thousand coins could sustain me for ten inns' worth of provisions.
How can I accept blessings from the Supreme Deity
and yet privately petition an earthen idol?"
The next morning,
he traveled east to Yǎnshī,
stopping at the county guesthouse.
There, he saw the same yellow-robed official,
who, holding a document, pushed open the door and entered,
rebuking Official Zhāng:
"How could you be so deceitful?
Now disaster has befallen you.
Because you failed to fulfill your vow to the Three Peaks,
you have caused me to be unable to repay a single meal's kindness from beginning to end.
My heart is filled with sorrow,
as if stung by poison."
After speaking,
he vanished.
In an instant,
Official Zhāng fell ill,
left a letter for his wife and children,
and died before finishing it.
Ōuyáng Mǐn
Thirty li east of Shǎnzhōu,
there was originally no inn.
Travelers who arrived at dusk
would be welcomed from afar and accommodated,
but when they departed before dawn,
many would die.
A traveler from Yángzhōu, Ōuyáng Mǐn,
arrived late at night,
and the ghost, appearing as an old man,
welcomed him into the lodging.
After midnight,
the old man visited the guest to inquire about his hometown,
and then entertained him with wine and roasted meat.
The guest casually spoke of matters related to the underworld,
and the old man showed a very startled and uneasy expression.
The guest found this strange
and asked:
"Can ghosts and deities harm people?
Can people harm ghosts?"
The old man said:
"Regarding matters of ghosts and deities,
people do not understand them,
so how could they harm them?
Ghosts and deities would certainly not harm people without reason.
If there are those who harm people,
they are likely demonic ghosts,
much like thieves and robbers in the human world.
If demonic ghosts harm people,
and it is occasionally heard by the bright deities,
they will certainly not tolerate it.
It is no different from thieves and robbers being punished by the law."
The old man again showed a deeply worried expression,
and the guest found it even more strange.
He then said to the old man:
"If I knew where the demonic ghosts are,
I would certainly report it to the revered deities,
and have them all eradicated."
The old man unconsciously rose and bowed,
kowtowing and saying:
"I am a powerful ghost,
and I feared that by dawn,
you, sir, would not tolerate me.
Now I hope you will take pity and forgive me."
He then presented a volume of books to the guest, saying:
"This book foretells the reigns of emperors.
Treasure it, treasure it."
The guest accepted it,
and at dawn,
the old man left without bidding farewell.
Looking back, it was merely a ruined grave.
The book was written in seal script,
and later the guest entrusted someone to translate it,
and it was passed down in the world.
A Commoner of Fèngtiān County
In the fifth year of the Huìchāng era,
a man surnamed Liú from Guóshèng Village in Fèngtiān County
went mad.
When his illness struck, he would wander recklessly,
paying no heed to wells or ditches.
His family invited an exorcist, Hóu Gōngmǐn, to treat him.
Just as Gōngmǐn arrived,
Liú suddenly rose and said:
"I will step out for a moment;
I do not need your treatment."
He then took a carrying pole with firewood to the fields,
stripped to the waist, and swung the pole,
as if striking something.
After a long while, he returned.
Smiling, he said:
"My illness is cured.
I just knocked off a ghost's head
and buried it in the field."
His brothers and the exorcist,
still thinking him mad,
went together to verify it.
Liú dug out a skull,
with over ten strands of red hair attached.
His illness was indeed cured.
Xíng Qún
Xíng Qún, a vice director in the Ministry of Justice,
in the second year of the Dàzhōng era,
was living in Luòzhōng after serving as the prefect of Shèzhōu,
and was gravely ill.
Xíng had long been friends with the censor Zhū Guǎn.
At that time, Guǎn had been dismissed from his post in the Huái River region and was living in Yīluò,
having died of illness,
though Xíng did not yet know.
Once, while lying down during the day,
Xíng suddenly heard someone knocking at the door.
He ordered someone to look,
and saw Guǎn arriving on horseback.
Xíng immediately invited him in to sit.
Earlier, Xíng had heard that Guǎn was ill,
and upon seeing him arrive,
he was very pleased,
saying:
"I heard you were ill earlier,
but there is no need to worry."
Guǎn said:
"I was indeed ill,
but now I am cured.
However, your illness
is also nothing to worry about.
In a day or two,
you will hear about it."
They talked and laughed for a long time
before Guǎn departed.
The time Guǎn visited Xíng
was actually the day Guǎn had died.
Lǐ Chóng
In the fifth year of the Dàzhōng era,
Lǐ Zhòng, the Inspectorate Vice-Director in charge of the Salt and Iron Commission's Héyīn bureau, was dismissed from his post
and resided in Hédōng Commandery.
He fell ill,
and after ten days, his condition grew increasingly severe,
lying still in his bed.
One evening,
he told his servant:
"I am too ill to rise."
He then ordered the doors to be locked.
Suddenly, he heard a rustling sound in the courtyard.
Lǐ Zhòng looked at it
and saw a man dressed in crimson—
it was Cài Xíngjǐ, the Magistrate of Héxī.
There was another person,
dressed in white cotton clothes,
behind him.
Lǐ Zhòng was on good terms with Cài Xíngjǐ,
so he exclaimed in surprise:
"Attendant Censor Cài has come!"
He then ordered them to be invited in,
and the man in white sat down as well.
After a short while,
he saw Cài Xíngjǐ's body gradually grow taller,
and his hands, feet, mouth, and nose
also enlarged along with it.
Looking closely,
it was no longer Cài Xíngjǐ.
Lǐ Zhòng found this strange,
but he still addressed him as Attendant Censor.
Lǐ Zhòng then felt that he could move his body slightly,
so he leaned against the wall and sat up,
asking:
"I have been ill for ten days,
and now it is getting worse.
Am I going to die from this?"
The man replied:
"Your illness should soon be over."
He then pointed to the man in white:
"He is my youngest brother,
skilled in divination."
He then asked him to perform a divination for Lǐ Zhòng.
The man in white took out a small wooden monkey from his sleeve
and placed it on the bed.
Soon, the monkey jumped and leaped about,
and after several movements, it settled.
The man in white said:
"The divination is complete.
The Vice-Director's illness
is certainly nothing to worry about.
You will live to sixty-two,
but there will also be misfortune."
Lǐ Zhòng asked:
"Will the Attendant Censor drink some wine?"
He replied:
"How dare I not drink?"
Lǐ Zhòng then ordered wine to be brought
and placed a cup in front of them.
The man in crimson said:
"I have my own drinking vessel."
He then took out a cup from his clothes.
At first, it seemed to be made of silver,
but when it was filled,
the cup wobbled unsteadily.
Looking closely,
it was actually made of paper.
Each of the two drank two cups,
and then they put their cups back into their clothes.
As they were about to leave,
they warned Lǐ Zhòng:
"After you recover,
be careful not to drink wine,
or disaster will befall you."
Lǐ Zhòng thanked them and promised,
and after a long while, they left.
When they reached the courtyard,
they were nowhere to be seen.
Looking at the outer door,
it was still locked as before.
He also saw in front of his bed
wine spilled on the ground—
apparently, it was what the two ghosts had drunk.
From then on, Lǐ Zhòng recovered from his illness.
Later, he resumed drinking wine as before.
That year,
he was demoted to Simǎ of Hángzhōu.
Wáng Kūn
Wáng Kūn of Tàiyuán,
in the spring of the fourth year of the Dàzhōng era, served as a Doctor of the National Academy.
He had a maidservant named Qīngyún,
who had died several years earlier.
One night,
he suddenly dreamed that Qīngyún had come to his bedside.
Wáng Kūn was very frightened,
rose and questioned her,
and Qīngyún said:
"I have not been counted among the living for several years now.
I often think of my time in life,
as if bound and unable to forget release.
Tonight I am able to serve by your side,
which is indeed a fortunate encounter."
Wáng Kūn was dazed as if drunk,
unaware that she was a ghost.
Qīngyún then led Wáng Kūn out the door.
The door was already locked,
but she guided him through a crack,
encountering no obstruction.
They walked to the middle of the street,
strolling under the moonlight and lingering,
for a long time.
Suddenly, Wáng Kūn felt hungry
and told Qīngyún.
Qīngyún said:
"Is there someone in the neighborhood who is on good terms with you, sir?
You could go and ask for food."
Wáng Kūn had always been on good terms with Shí Guàn, a Doctor of the Imperial Academy,
and they also lived in the same neighborhood.
So Wáng Kūn went with her.
When they reached Shí Guàn's gate,
it was already locked and closed.
Qīngyún knocked on it.
After a while,
the gatekeeper opened the door and said:
"I heard knocking just now,
but now it's silent and I see nothing.
What is this?"
He then closed the door.
Qīngyún knocked again,
and this happened three times.
The gatekeeper angrily said:
"How dare a fierce ghost keep knocking on our door!"
He cursed and spat.
Qīngyún said to Wáng Kūn:
"Shí Guàn is already asleep,
so we certainly cannot visit him.
I hope you, sir, will go to another place."
At that time, there was a minor official of the National Academy,
also from the same neighborhood,
and whenever Wáng Kūn went out,
he often passed by his door.
This official handled Wáng Kūn's monthly salary and reports of appointments,
so Wáng Kūn trusted and relied on him greatly.
Thus, they went together to his house.
Just as they saw the door being opened,
there was a person holding a water jar
pouring water into the street.
Qīngyún said:
"We can go in together."
Once inside,
they saw the minor official eating with several people.
At first,
Wáng Kūn stood in the courtyard,
thinking the minor official would surely descend the steps to greet and bow to him.
But then the minor official showed no courtesy.
Suddenly, they saw a maidservant carrying soup and noodles ascending the steps.
Qīngyún immediately struck the maidservant on the back,
causing her to fall on the steps,
and the soup and noodles were all spilled.
The minor official, his wife, and servants all rose,
startled, saying:
"She has been struck by evil."
They urgently summoned a shaman.
The shaman said:
"There is a person,
wearing a red sash and a silver seal,
standing in front of the courtyard."
They then made offerings to him.
Wáng Kūn and Qīngyún both sat down,
ate, and then left together.
The shamaness saw them to the door
and burned paper money beside it.
Qīngyún said to Wáng Kūn:
"Sir, you may come with me."
Wáng Kūn then followed her out of the neighborhood,
heading towards Qǐxià and leaving.
After several dozen lǐ into the suburban wilderness,
they saw a tomb.
Qīngyún said:
"This is where I reside.
Sir, please follow me inside."
Wáng Kūn then bowed his head and bent his body to enter.
The tomb entrance was dark and indistinguishable.
Suddenly, he awoke with a start,
his back sweating and legs trembling.
By then, it was already dawn.
Disgusted by his dream,
he dared not speak of it to anyone.
That day,
he summoned
Shí Guàn.
After they sat down,
Shí Guàn said:
"Last night, a ghost knocked on my door three times.
I sent someone to look,
but it was silent and nothing was seen."
By morning,
he passed by the minor official's house
and saw traces of burned paper money.
He immediately summoned the minor official
and questioned him about the matter.
The minor official said:
"Last night, I was just eating with others
when suddenly a maidservant was struck by evil.
The shaman said
a ghost was causing trouble.
Therefore, we made offerings in the courtyard
and burned paper money here."
This completely matched Wáng Kūn's dream.
Wáng Kūn became even more frightened
and told his wife and children.
That winter,
he indeed died.
Sū Tàixuán
Sū Tàixuán of Yángshuò
was a farmer.
His wife, Xú shì,
gave birth to three children and then died.
After she was buried,
suddenly one day she returned home,
but only her voice could be heard, not her form.
She said:
"My allotted lifespan was not yet complete;
the underworld officials did not record my death."
Whenever she came,
she would lovingly care for her children
and mend clothes for them.
After a month or so,
the neighbors learned of it.
Some would ask her to divine good or bad fortune,
or to recount matters of good and evil,
and each time it matched and proved true.
There was a fellow villager who held a post in the prefectural office
and fell ill.
His family asked her to divine for him.
After a moment, she said:
"I reached south of Liángfēngguǎn,
a place called Zhèmùlín.
I encountered a tiger blocking the road,
did not dare to pass,
and so turned back."
The diviner urged her on,
so she asked to go again.
After a moment, she said:
"I reached the prefectural office
and saw that the ill person has already recovered."
Suspicious that this was untrue,
they then asked about the residential ward where he lived
and the patient's appearance.
Xú shì had never been to the prefectural office before,
nor did she know the sick person,
yet she described everything
without any discrepancy.
Another person came to ask for a divination
and apologized for having nothing to offer in return,
feeling deeply inadequate.
Xú shì said:
"Your family has three dǒu of millet in the west room;
how can you say you have nothing?"
The diviner asked to fetch it.
After a short while,
it was carried and placed before them,
and everyone was astonished.
Such events occurred repeatedly.
Suddenly one morning,
she said that Emperor Shùn was dispatching troops to campaign against the barbarians,
and someone had requested her to go to the relay station
to help prepare cooked food,
and she would be away for a day or two.
She returned as scheduled.
She brought a portion of fine food
and presented it to her husband, saying:
"How does this rice compare to that of armies passing through the human world?"
Her husband tasted it,
and it was far more exquisite than other food.
Then one morning, she tearfully told him:
"For no reason, I leaked underworld affairs
and have been found guilty and summoned.
After I leave this time, it will be difficult to return.
Take good care of our children."
She wept, bid farewell, and then was gone.
Fáng Qiānlǐ
Outside the south gate of Chūnzhōu, there was the Xiānshǔ Lodge,
within which stood the Lú Gōng Pavilion.
Fáng Qiānlǐ, having been demoted from office,
sought medical treatment in this prefecture,
and the prefect lodged him here.
In the eastern wing was an inner chamber.
A servant was dozing off
when suddenly a man in crimson robes,
very tall and imposing,
came straight before him.
The servants fled in alarm
and reported it to Qiānlǐ.
After one or two nights,
it happened again.
Qiānlǐ did not believe it,
but still did not place anyone inside the chamber again.
Several months later,
he moved to a riverside pavilion.
Later, a temporary assistant official was lodged in the eastern chamber.
During the day,
he saw a man wearing a gauze robe,
shuffling along in slippers, who came and said:
"You should not stay here long."
The assistant, frightened, rushed out the door
and reported the incident in detail to his colleagues.
An old military officer, Lù Jiànzōng, said:
"During the Yuánhé era,
when Lǐ Shīdào was executed,
his assistant Lù Xíngjiǎn was exiled to this prefecture
and put to death here.
The appearance described by the assistant
indeed matches without error.
The Wéi Family Son
A son of the Wéi family from Jīngzhào,
having passed the imperial examinations,
came from a prominent lineage.
He once took a courtesan in Luòyáng,
whose beauty was radiant and delicate,
and who was especially skilled in music.
Wéi once had her copy the poems of Dù Gōngbù,
but the version obtained was full of errors.
The courtesan corrected them with her brush,
making the literary logic clear and coherent.
Because of this, Wéi became quite infatuated with her.
She died at the age of twenty-one,
and Wéi mourned her deeply,
becoming emaciated from grief.
He neglected his affairs and slept,
hoping to dream of her.
One day,
a household servant mentioned a recluse named Rén from Sōngshān,
who possessed the art of summoning spirits.
Wéi summoned him and sought his art.
Rén ordered him to choose a day for purification and fasting,
prepare a room,
hang curtains within it,
and burn incense.
He also required a piece of clothing she had worn to guide her spirit.
Wéi searched his clothing chests,
but had already given almost all her clothes to monks.
Only a gold-threaded skirt remained.
Rén said:
"This will suffice."
That night,
all others were excluded and affairs set aside,
and he was warned against intimate grief and weeping.
A candle was lit before the incense,
and Rén said:
"When you see the candle burn down an inch,
she will depart again."
Wéi, in clean clothes and holding his breath,
followed his instructions completely.
That night,
all sounds ceased,
and the Milky Way shone clear and bright.
Rén suddenly let out a long sigh,
held the skirt facing the curtain, and beckoned.
After doing this three times,
a sighing sound was suddenly heard.
Moments later,
the curtain parted slightly, and she emerged,
standing with a sidelong glance,
her delicate fragrance and sorrowful demeanor
as if she could hardly bear it.
Wéi rose in alarm and wept,
but Rén said:
"Do not startle or press her,
lest she vanish abruptly."
Wéi held back his tears and bowed to her,
finding her no different from when she was alive.
When he spoke to her,
she only nodded in response.
After a while,
the candle burned down to the appointed mark.
Just as he wished to draw closer,
she vanished in a flurry.
Wéi then clutched the curtain and wailed bitterly,
fainting and then reviving.
Rén said:
"I am not one who seeks profit,
but pitied the depth of your affection,
and thus came to assist.
Like foam on water or the fleeting beauty of hibiscus,
there is no need to cling to it."
Wéi wished to reward him,
but Rén left without a backward glance.
Wéi once composed a poem that said:
"Melancholy, the gold-dusted skirt with clustered butterflies,
in spring I still see it accompanying the drifting clouds.
Had I not refrained from giving it away,
it would be just like first meeting Lǐ Shàojūn."
He wrote many poems mourning her,
not all recorded here.
From then on, Wéi was despondent and joyless,
and died within a year.
Lǐ Xún
During the Xiántōng era,
Lǐ Xún, the sheriff of Zhōngmóu,
resided at his villa in Pútián.
He was of a stern and violent temperament,
and paid no heed to ghosts and spirits.
Whenever he saw people making libations with wine,
he would angrily stop them.
One day,
he suddenly fell ill with dizziness from wind,
and as he lay beneath the eaves,
an old farmer suddenly appeared before his couch,
saying:
"The neighbors wish to come and inquire after your illness."
Then several people appeared,
their forms gaunt and wretched,
dressed in either purple or blue garments.
There was a short servant
carrying two jugs of wine,
who ascended the steps.
His wife and children beside him
saw nothing at all.
They said to Xún:
"You have always been arrogant,
looking down upon us.
In matters of wine,
you are always sparing for others.
Now we have several measures of fine wine,
and we all wish to drink you into a stupor."
Soon, with large cups,
they filled and made Xún drink,
emptying both jugs,
with dregs spilling all over the mat.
They said to Xún:
"Why were you always so stingy with wine?"
From then on, his entire body felt dazed and weary,
as if suffering from a lingering hangover,
and it took several months for him to recover.
Duàn Chéngshì
Dàicháng Qīng Duàn Chéngshì,
the son of the Grand Councilor Wénchāng,
was close friends with the examination candidate Wēn Tíngyún.
He passed away in the sixth month of the fourth year of the Xiántōng era.
Tíngyún was residing idly in the capital,
and on the thirteenth day of the eleventh month of that year, the winter solstice,
there was heavy snow.
At dawn, someone knocked at the door.
The servant looked out;
it was someone who handed over a bamboo tube from outside the door,
saying:
"Young Dàicháng Duàn has sent a letter."
Tíngyún initially thought it was a mistake,
but upon opening the tube, he found a letter.
There were no characters on its surface.
When he opened it,
it turned out to be a handwritten note from Chéngshì.
Tíngyún was greatly astonished,
rushed out the door,
but the person had already vanished.
He then burned incense, bowed twice, and read the letter,
but he could not comprehend its meaning.
The text read:
"Grief erupts from the dark gate,
sorrow returns in a brief span.
My life is now over,
what can be said of the afterlife?
Moreover, the men mourn in purple and yellow,
the women fear in blue and green.
Dùlíng's separation is final,
Wǔzǐ's completion is a group.
Henceforth, the well's barrier flows with parrots,
the courtyard's bell dances with cranes.
The bond of sworn brothers,
forever severed in private affection.
The depth of my fervent feelings,
is difficult to fully express in words.
Not fully stated.
Jīngzhōu Governor Duàn Chéngshì bows his head."
After this, there was no further news.
The letter used the character "腆,"
which is not found in dictionaries.
Interpreting it by context,
it should be read as the character "群."
The families of Wēn and Duàn
both preserved copies of this letter.
Zǐ Ānjié,
former tutor to the Prince of Yí,
was Tíngyún's son-in-law,
and he personally recounted this story.
Ghost Burial
Forty li west of Xùpǔ County in Chénzhōu,
there is a Ghost Burial Mountain.
Huáng Mǐn's "Record of Yuánchuān" states,
that within its cliffs there is a coffin,
which from a distance appears to be over ten zhang long,
and is called the ruins of a ghost burial.
The elders say,
that ghosts crafted this coffin,
and for seven days it was dark even during the day,
with only the sounds of axes and chisels heard.
People's households unknowingly lost utensils, knives, and axes,
and after seven days, when it cleared,
all the lost items
were returned to their owners,
with the pots and axes covered in greasy, fishy, and foul odors.
This coffin was seen standing solemnly,
lying horizontally by the shore.
Dǒng Hànxūn
Dǒng Hànxūn, a commander under the Rǔfén region,
was skilled in horseback riding and archery,
possessing the strength of several men,
agile and capable in combat.
He served multiple tours of duty on the northwestern frontier,
and the Qiāng people feared him.
In the Bǐngshēn year of the Qiánfú era,
he became the garrison commander of Lóngxīng in Rǔzhōu.
Suddenly one day,
he said to his wife:
