"Tomorrow, over ten old friends will visit;
prepare abundant wine and food."
His family thought they were ordinary guests.
The next day,
they elaborately set up the main hall.
Between the hours of chén and sì,
Hànxūn tightened his belt,
went out the garrison gate,
and repeatedly bowed toward the sky,
sometimes calling out by rank,
sometimes by courtesy name,
chatting, laughing, bowing, and yielding as they ascended to the hall.
His family was greatly astonished,
but they served wine and food
as if presenting an offering.
After they finished,
his wife questioned him,
and Hànxūn said:
"They are all my former comrades who fell in battle on the frontier.
After a long separation, they came for a visit;
what is strange about that?"
Later, Hànxūn remained unharmed.
In the autumn of the following year, on the last day of the eighth month,
the rebel Wáng Xiānzhī from Qīngtǔ suddenly arrived with tens of thousands of men.
It was an era of peace,
and the commanderies and states had no military preparations.
On that day,
the commandery selected five hundred elite soldiers,
placing the brave commander Cuàn Hóng in charge.
They went twenty li east of the commandery to Kǔmùdiàn,
where they were all captured by the rebels,
with only one horseman escaping back to the commandery.
The people of the commandery were greatly alarmed,
so they closed the gates and ascended the ramparts,
organizing a firm defense.
Hànxūn was stationed at the north gate with five hundred men.
On the morning of the first day of the ninth month,
the rebels arrived and surrounded the city.
With one drumbeat, they breached the south gate,
capturing the Grand Administrator Wáng Liào.
Hànxūn, at the north gate,
fought bitterly atop the wall.
Those he shot with arrows all fell with the feathers embedded,
and he killed several dozen men.
When his arrows were exhausted,
the rebels had already entered.
Hànxūn wielded his sword,
killing several dozen more.
When his sword broke,
he pulled out a roof beam to strike them,
killing yet another several dozen.
By daybreak, exhausted and weary,
he was slain by the soldiers,
and even the rebel commander sighed in admiration.
Móu Yǐng
A man from Luòyáng named Móu Yǐng,
in his youth,
once got drunk,
and mistakenly wandered out into the wilds.
He did not wake until midnight,
and rested by the roadside.
There he saw exposed skeletal remains,
which moved Yǐng to pity.
At dawn,
he personally buried them.
That night,
he dreamed of a young man,
around twenty years old,
dressed in white silk robes,
holding a sword,
who bowed to Yǐng and said:
"I was a violent bandit,
who in life took pleasure in killing,
committing unjust deeds.
Recently, I quarreled with my companions,
and was killed by them.
Buried by the roadside,
after enduring long exposure to wind and rain,
my bones became exposed.
You kindly covered me again,
so I have come to thank you.
In life I was a fierce and violent man,
in death I am a fierce and violent ghost.
If you can allow me to reside with you,
and simply offer me a small sacrifice each night,
I will always respond to your commands.
Once I have found refuge with you,
I will not suffer hunger or thirst,
and I will certainly ensure your desires are fulfilled."
Yǐng agreed in the dream.
Upon waking,
he tried setting out sacrificial offerings,
silently praying and making requests.
That night, he again dreamed the ghost said:
"I am now residing with you.
Whenever you wish to employ me,
just call out 'Chìdīngzǐ' once,
quietly state your request,
and I will surely answer and arrive."
Yǐng then began secretly instructing him,
ordering him to steal,
to pilfer others' wealth and goods.
Each time, the ghost answered and fulfilled his wishes,
and later Yǐng became rich with gold and treasures.
One day,
Yǐng saw his neighbor's wife was very beautiful,
and desired her.
He called Chìdīngzǐ and ordered him to abduct her.
In the middle of the night,
the neighbor's wife suddenly came, having climbed over the wall from outside.
Yǐng, startled, rose and treated her kindly,
asking how she came to be there.
The woman said:
"I had no such intention.
Suddenly at night, a man seized me and brought me to your room.
It was like waking from a dream;
I don't know what kind of monster it was.
I don't know any way
to get back home."
She wept incessantly.
Yǐng pitied her greatly,
and secretly kept her for several days.
Her family searched for her very urgently,
even reporting it to the authorities.
Yǐng learned of this,
and conspired with the woman,
having her go to a separate villa,
then return on her own,
saying she didn't know what kind of spirit had taken her,
but now she had returned.
After the woman returned home,
every three or five nights thereafter,
as before, she was taken by a man to Yǐng's house,
and before dawn,
she was sent back.
After a year,
her family still hadn't noticed.
The woman deeply suspected Yǐng had some dark magic,
and later, pressed urgently,
she asked Yǐng:
"If you don't tell me the truth,
I will surely expose this matter myself."
Yǐng then told her the whole story.
The neighbor's wife then told her family,
and they plotted to deal with this menace.
The family secretly engaged a Dàolìu priest,
who purified the area and prepared restraining spells, lying in wait.
When Chìdīngzǐ came to their door at night,
he saw many talismanic registers,
and turned back.
He reported to Yǐng:
"They are using orthodox methods to resist me,
but their power is weak.
If I contend with them using force,
I should seize this woman harshly.
This time, I certainly will not return her."
Having said this, he left again.
Moments later,
a sudden whirlwind arose at the neighbor's house.
The entire residence turned pitch black,
and all the talismans and restraining objects
were swept away in an instant.
The woman was lost again.
By dawn,
her husband had gone to the authorities,
and they came together to Yǐng's house to arrest him.
Yǐng then fled with the woman,
and no one knew where they went.
Yóu Shìzǐ
In the northwestern corner west of Xǔdū city,
there was a mansion belonging to General Zhào.
After the master died,
his descendants scattered and moved away,
and the place became haunted,
with no one daring to live there.
Relatives then posted a notice on the village gate,
saying that whoever could live there
could have it.
At the beginning of the Qiánfú era,
there was a man named Yóu Shìzǐ in Xǔ,
of a fierce and bold nature,
exceptionally skilled and agile in martial arts.
Seeing the notice, he said:
"I am a fierce warrior;
even if there are strange demons or ghosts,
I will surely have a way to subdue them."
It was midsummer.
After dusk,
he entered with his sword.
The rooms were deep and vast,
the front courtyard broad and spacious.
Yóu Shìzǐ laid a mat in the courtyard
and sat upon it in his summer clothes.
After the first watch ended,
all was silent and undisturbed.
Yóu Shìzǐ grew weary
and lay down facing the hall, using his sword as a pillow.
As the second watch approached its midpoint,
he suddenly heard the creaking sound of the rear door opening.
Candles and torches were arrayed in rows,
and dozens of servants
began sweeping and cleaning the hall.
They opened the front corridor,
hung vermilion curtains and embroidered drapes,
and laid out banquet mats and precious vessels.
A rare fragrance wafted among the eaves and pillars.
Yóu Shìzǐ thought to himself these were minor spirits,
and not wishing to confront them immediately,
decided to watch until the end.
After a short while,
dozens of figures holding musical instruments,
dressed in vermilion and purple,
ascended the steps from the eastern wing.
Several dozen singing and dancing girls emerged from the rear hall
and entered the front hall.
Those in purple robes took the front seats,
followed by those in vermilion, green, and white robes—
also about twenty people.
They talked and laughed at ease,
bowed courteously, and sat down.
Then string and wind instruments played in harmony,
wine cups flew and toasts were raised,
and songs and dances commenced alternately.
Yóu Shìzǐ wanted to rush forward
and capture their leader.
As he was about to rise,
he felt something pressing on his thighs,
cold and heavy,
so he could not get up.
He wanted to shout,
but his mouth gaped and he could make no sound.
He could only watch the merrymaking in the hall
until the solemn drumbeat
signaled the banquet's end.
The lights then went out,
and silence returned as before.
Yóu Shìzǐ was drenched in a cold sweat, heart pounding with fear,
and crawled out on his hands and knees.
Reaching the village gate,
he was only able to speak after a long while.
After that, no one ever dared to live in that mansion again.
Lǐ Yún
Former Nánzhèng County Lieutenant Lǐ Yún,
sought to take a concubine in Cháng'ān,
but her mother had not yet consented.
Yún said:
"I vow not to marry."
Only then did she consent.
He named the concubine Chǔbīn.
Several years later,
the concubine passed away.
A year after her death,
he then married the daughter of former Nánzhèng Magistrate Shěn.
On the wedding day,
as Yún was bathing in the purification chamber,
he saw Chǔbīn holding a medicine, approaching.
She came straight forward,
and said to Yún:
"You vowed not to marry me,
yet now you are marrying the Shěn family's daughter.
I have nothing to offer,
but present you with a packet of incense,
to add to your bathwater."
She poured the medicine powder into the bathing tub,
stirred the water with a hairpin, and then left.
Yún felt extremely uneasy,
exhausted and unable to leave the bath,
and subsequently died,
his limbs as soft as cotton,
his sinews and bones all dispersed.
Zhèng Zǒng
Jìnshì Zhèng Zǒng,
due to his concubine's illness,
wanted to forgo the imperial examination.
The concubine said:
"You must not abandon the examination because of a woman."
She firmly urged him,
and Zǒng then went to the capital.
That spring, he failed the examination and returned east,
arriving home as his concubine passed away.
A month after her burial,
late at night,
he happened to be awake,
asleep,
he heard footsteps outside his room,
opened the door to look,
and it was his deceased concubine.
He invited her into the room to sit,
asked what she needed,
and she only requested good tea,
which Zǒng personally brewed and gave to her.
After she finished drinking,
Zǒng, as his young children were asleep,
wanted to call them to meet her.
The concubine said:
"No,
they are young,
it might frighten them."
After speaking, she bid farewell and left,
just as she stepped out the door,
she vanished.
Wáng Shào
Míngjīng Wáng Shào,
was studying late at night.
Someone outside the window asked to borrow a brush,
Shào lent it,
and they wrote a poem on the window:
"Whose voice reads by the window,
the Southern Dipper slants, the Northern Dipper lies horizontal.
A thousand miles from home, unable to return,
the spring breeze breaks the heart at Shítóuchéng."
After the poem was finished,
there was complete silence,
and he realized it was not a human.
Wáng Wěi
Deputy Magistrate of Fèngxiáng Wáng Wěi,
was the uncle of Vice Minister of Rites Níng.
At fourteen or fifteen,
he was playing with other children under the bamboo grove in the orchard,
when he saw two dried skulls buried in the manure and dirt.
He then ordered a young servant to choose a clean spot to bury them,
and made offerings with wine and food.
Several nights later, during dark and gloomy weather,
he suddenly heard rustling sounds outside the window,
and after a long while asked about it,
they said:
"We have received your deep kindness,
spared from filth and decay,
and do not know how to repay you,
but we are willing to serve you.
From now on, whenever there is good or ill fortune,
we will surely come to inform you through subtle signs."
Thus for several years,
he became thoroughly connected with spiritual beings.
Cuī Gǒng served as Commissioner of Revenue,
and was well acquainted with Wěi.
One evening,
he invited Wěi to stay and drink homemade wine,
and as they became pleasantly drunk and merry,
he said:
"There is a singing girl who is quite skilled."
He ordered her to be summoned,
but after a long while she did not arrive,
so Gǒng went in himself to check,
and was told:
"She just finished dressing,
when suddenly she felt heart pain,
and asked to drink some broth before coming out."
Gǒng returned to his seat.
Wěi described the singing girl's appearance in detail,
and Gǒng, surprised, asked him about it.
Wěi said:
"Just now I saw a person,
wearing a short crimson silk robe,
leading a horse away."
Before he finished speaking,
a household servant reported that she had been struck by an evil influence,
and despite efforts to save her, she did not recover.
Gǒng was deeply saddened by this,
and Wěi secretly said:
"There is one thing that might revive her,
but we need a white ox head and a hú of wine."
So he summoned his attendants,
and tried to have them search for these items.
There was a subordinate from the Revenue Commission,
very capable,
who obtained them at a high price,
and they arrived in no time.
Wěi had the singing girl supported,
and placed on a couch in a clean room.
In front, he set a large basin filled with wine,
laid a board across it,
and placed the ox head on top.
He arranged a mat and lit incense,
sealed the door tightly,
and instructed:
"Watch carefully,
when the morning drum sounds once,
you will hear the ox roar.
Then quickly open the door,
and she can be revived."
Wěi then left.
Suddenly the curfew drum sounded,
and indeed they heard an ox roar.
Opening the door to look,
the singing girl was breathing faintly,
the basin of wine was completely dry,
and the ox's angry eyes were protruding outward.
After several days she was able to speak,
and said,
that evening after finishing her makeup,
someone urgently summoned her,
she went out the door,
and rode away on horseback.
After traveling several li,
she saw a magnificent building,
with a banquet spread and music playing.
All the seats were occupied by young nobles in crimson and purple robes,
and when they saw the singing girl arrive,
they were overjoyed,
and seated her among the courtesans.
Just as the merriment was at its peak,
suddenly they heard someone shout loudly,
the sound shaking the halls and corridors,
and all the seated guests turned pale and looked at each other,
the music and entertainment ceasing.
Soon they saw an ox-headed man,
over ten feet tall,
holding a halberd and charging straight forward,
and everyone fled in disarray,
only the singing girl remained.
The ox-headed man led her before the steps,
carried her on his back and left,
after walking a dozen or so steps,
she suddenly felt herself lying inside the room.
Gǒng later secretly inquired about the matter,
but Wěi never spoke of it.
Lǐ Dàirén
Rivers and lakes harbor many Chāng ghosts,
who often call out people's names.
Those who answer are certain to drown,
for they are lured by the spirits of the dead.
Lǐ Dàirén once moored his boat in a bend of the Qūpǔ within Zhījiāng County.
The moonlight was bright and clear,
when suddenly he saw an old woman and a man
emerge from the water, looking all around.
They cried out in alarm:
"There is a living person here!"
They then sped across the water's surface
as if walking on flat ground,
climbed ashore, and departed.
Sū Ruì, the magistrate of Dāngyáng, resided in Jiānglíng.
Once, returning home at night
under the bright moon,
he saw a beautiful woman with disheveled hair,
whose skirt and garments
seemed almost soaked with water.
Ruì teased her, saying:
"Aren't you a river Chāng ghost?"
The woman angrily replied:
"How dare you call me a ghost!"
She then rushed to chase him.
Ruì fled
until he encountered a night watchman on patrol, and only then did she stop.
He saw the woman turn back and return the way she had come.
Liú Zǎo
On the border of Dèngzhōu north of the Hàn River,
there was a place named Xuékǒu,
which originally had no garrison.
There was a small river
flowing south into the Hàn,
but it had long been blocked by sand,
making the waterway very narrow.
The former magistrate of Jiānglíng, Liú Zǎo,
in the year Bǐngzǐ,
went to that prefecture to visit relatives and friends.
Upon reaching Xuékǒu,
he stayed at the home of an old acquaintance, Hán.
A member of the household said:
"The new bride of the Zhāng family in the neighboring village
died three days ago,
but just now she has revived."
The host went briefly to inquire after her.
That night,
when the Hán family returned, they said
that Zhāng's wife had been summoned by the god of a nearby temple.
She saw all her deceased relatives, both close and distant, gathered there.
They were preparing military provisions for the temple god,
but there was no one to make cakes,
so she had been summoned for that purpose.
She saw in the hall and outside the door,
rows of soldiers sitting.
They spoke of dredging the Hàn River at Xuékǒu,
and the soldiers, treading on the sand,
had hands all bleeding.
After the provisions were prepared,
she was released and sent back.
The villagers did not believe her story,
but not long after,
the sandbanks successively collapsed and settled,
and the river course was thus opened.
Lǐ Jǔ
When Chéng Ruì was garrisoning Jīngzhōu,
there was a magistrate of Diànjiāng County named Cuī,
who was at odds with the Registrar Lǐ Jǔ,
their relationship as incompatible as fire and water.
One day, a band of robbers raided the county,
killing Magistrate Cuī.
After the robbers had passed,
Jǔ entered the residence to inspect.
A servant who had just been hiding from the robbers
saw Jǔ
and thought he was in league with the bandits.
The next day,
he reported this to the garrison commander.
Everyone knew of the enmity between Jǔ and Cuī,
and suspicions grew.
Jǔ was arrested and sent to the central prefecture,
but under interrogation he refused to confess.
He was then transferred to Jiānglíng
and imprisoned in the Right Barracks jail.
The barracks officer was eager to conclude the case.
An interrogating officer named Cháng
said to the Judge Fàn:
"Lǐ Jǔ is obstinately denying;
he must be tortured to get to the truth."
Fàn firmly refused,
but Cháng ultimately forged a case against him.
As Jǔ faced execution,
he instructed his family to burn much paper and writing brushes,
so he could lodge a complaint in the underworld.
Only a month later,
Cháng suddenly died.
Later, Registrar Lǐ Jǔ appeared in person.
Fàn saw Jǔ arrive
and said:
"I received deep kindness from you, Judge,
and do not act recklessly without cause.
But the underworld officials only require my testimony."
When Fàn's wife and children earnestly pleaded with Jǔ,
begging for a grace period of ten days
to settle family affairs,
although he felt no pain,
and ate and drank as usual,
he grew increasingly exhausted,
and after over a month, he died.
Táo Fú
The Shǔ general Táo Fú,
in his youth, was a ruffian,
stealing dogs and slaughtering cattle.
Later, he achieved merit
and rose to the rank of commandery governor.
While garrisoned at Xī County in Xīngyuán Prefecture,
he suddenly fell ill.
He urgently ordered his attendant, Commander Zhū,
to go to the prefectural seat to fetch the physician Lǐ Lìng'ǎi.
Lìng'ǎi and Commander Zhū rode swiftly together.
At night,
upon reaching the Zhūgě Liàng temple near the outer wall of Xī County,
they saw three pairs of torchbearers leading the way,
escorting a man walking on foot,
wearing a cangue and tightly bound,
with a crowd following behind.
Behind them was Táo's elderly relative,
carrying clothes and furs, following along.
Lìng'ǎi had not previously known Táo Fú,
but Commander Zhū pointed and said to Lìng'ǎi:
"That is our Commandant!
Why is he like this?"
Hesitant and terrified,
they also suspected it was a ghost.
At dawn, when they reached the camp,
they already heard the family's wailing.
The one captured and led away earlier
was indeed the spirit of Fú.
The magistrate of Bāchuān, Cuī.
In Hézhōu's Bāchuān County,
after the chaos, the government buildings were ruined and destroyed.
They moved to live within the stockade,
which was somewhat more secure.
A certain Cuī served as the magistrate.
Once, a strong soldier stole wood from the stockade,
and the magistrate had him captured and sent to the garrison commander, who executed him.
The soldier's family had previously served the god of Bìshān.
After the soldier died,
the god then began to haunt the magistrate's household,
sometimes appearing in visible form, coming and going,
sometimes cursing and shouting from the air,
throwing fire and destroying utensils.
Money, silk, and clothing
were never safe from loss;
though boxes and chests remained locked as before,
the clothing inside
was mostly cut to shreds.
They sought methods and spells to exorcise it,
but none could control it.
When the magistrate left office and returned home a thousand lǐ away,
the ghost followed him.
Moreover, day and night, it ate and drank,
no different from a person.
The whole family served it,
not daring to be negligent.
The expenses were considerable,
and the household's resources were becoming strained.
Suddenly one morning,
the whole family heard the sound of a large bird flapping its wings,
which landed on the house.
After a long while,
a loud shout came from the air,
claiming to be the Great King,
saying:
"You have recently had disasters,
because my Yōngxī brothers acted unreasonably,
ruining your family's livelihood,
and causing loss of property.
They performed various strange and abnormal acts;
I reckon you must have been greatly afraid of them.
Now I have already sent them away.
Your disasters are over and good fortune arises;
I have come myself to stay temporarily,
but also will not remain long.
I will just borrow the Tiānpéng shrine to reside in.
This Tiānpéng statue is extremely fine.
Lend it to me to take up to heaven,
to have a copy made up there,
and in three to five days I will return it."
Several days later,
he placed the Tiānpéng statue on the eaves of the house.
From then on, he was constantly present day and night,
always speaking with the master of the house.
He had the family, young and old, recite poetry and rhapsodies,
and perform music,
and he would sing along with each sound.
If there were any mistakes
in the texts they recited,
he would certainly correct them.
His words mostly encouraged people to do good,
and he also urged them to learn breath techniques and cultivate the Way.
Sometimes he said he ordinarily rode a crane,
traveling to and from heaven.
Initially, a flock of cranes appeared in the town,
and the god said:
"Among them, only two are real cranes,
which I rode here;
the rest are all ordinary birds."
He also said his surname was Zhāng.
Every day he ate and drank,
no different from a person.
He had a daughter named Jǐnxiùniáng,
and a wife and concubines.
The expenses for food and drink were also not small.
Whenever he saw good people and gentlemen,
he was willing to speak with them.
If they were slightly violent or brutal people,
he would not speak with them,
saying he was going up to heaven.
Suddenly, three people—a drunken monk and strong soldiers—came to visit him.
Their speech was unrestrained,
and they insulted and reviled him,
so he did not speak.
After the monk left,
he slowly said to people:
"This monk eats dog meat,
is fierce, brutal, and without virtue;
I did not wish to speak with him."
Regarding people's actions,
good and evil, disaster and fortune,
his words never missed the mark.
Even down to their childhood names and birth order,
he knew each one.
If questioned in detail,
he would respond with other topics.
It is unknown what kind of god he was.
Féng Shēng
In Suíníng, there was a man named Féng who could see ghosts,
and knew people's fortunes and misfortunes.
Chén Xuàn of Yǐngchuān
served as Liúhòu of the Wǔxìn Army,
and Liú Zhījùn replaced him.
Gathering old matters,
Féng said to Xuàn:
"Although Duke Liú is called commander-in-chief,
he has no
command banners and insignia before him;
he will probably not last long.
Fortunately, do not worry."
Within a year, Liú Zhījùn was killed.
There was a man named Lín Yǒng,
from Mǐn.
He often said to his colleagues and friends:
"How can a living person see ghosts all day long?
Do not listen to his nonsense."
Féng heard this,
and said to him in front of everyone:
"You, sir, have many affairs that you cannot bring to a good end,
because you once killed a woman, and she haunts you.
Since your official salary and lifespan are not yet exhausted,
she cannot yet take her opportunity.
I can tell her name;
do you believe me, sir?"
Thereupon, he was ashamed and afraid.
He spoke truthfully to Féng,
who promised to resolve her grievance for him.
Huángfǔ Méi
During the Guāngqǐ era,
Emperor Xīzōng was in Liángzhōu.
In the ninth month of autumn,
Huángfǔ Méi was about to go to the imperial temporary seat for reassignment.
He traveled together with a relative, a man from Péichéng named Péi.
In the tenth month,
they traveled west from Xiāngzhōu to Gāopíng County.
Forty lǐ southwest of the county,
they climbed a mountain and crossed over Yùxī.
That day, travelers were somewhat sparse,
mist and clouds darkened the daytime,
the sun was declining and the wind strong.
Confused by the many forks in the road,
they went up onto a long plank path.
Looking down, they saw several thatched huts,
with sparse hibiscus hedges,
and the sound of noisy conversation inside,
so they gazed toward it.
After a short while,
a village woman came out from the north of the western wing,
wearing old yellow clothes,
with disheveled hair and worn-out shoes.
They called to her repeatedly, but she paid no attention,
only lowered her head and went back inside.
So they followed the plank path down southeast,
reaching her dwelling.
When they arrived, the thornwood gate was barred with vines,
twined and draped over it,
thorns and brambles grew profusely in the courtyard,
with hardly any human trace,
as if it had been one or two years since anyone had been there.
Méi and Péi
stood astonished for a long time.
They climbed back onto the plank path and gazed into the distance,
seeing someone walking on the official road,
so they urged their lame donkey toward it.
When they arrived, it was a postal courier about to go to Duānshì County,
so they went together with him.
That night they stayed in Duānshì.
Chén Fán
Chén Fán was
a foot soldier from Pèi,
who had formed a brotherly bond in the army with Shí Pǔ,
the former military governor of Xú, in their youth.
When Pǔ was entrusted by Zhī Pì,
Fán was also repeatedly promoted to high positions.
During the rebellion of Huáng Cháo,
Zhī Pì selected five thousand elite soldiers,
ordered Pǔ to lead them westward,
with Fán as the deputy commander.
Pǔ advanced from Xǔchāng toward Luòxià,
while Fán rebelled with a thousand men in Píngyīn.
Pǔ then falsely claimed Zhī’s order,
recalling the troops.
Thus, he led his forces to join Fán,
massacred Píngyīn,
plundered Pǔtián, and marched onward.
Upon reaching Pèi,
Zhī, fearing their mutiny,
welcomed them outside the city, allowed them to remove their armor,
and lavished them with generous bribes.
Then, through a trusted confidant, they hinted to Zhī:
“The army is restless,
the people wish to see you pursued,
so we ask you to relinquish your seal,
to appease the public’s heart.”
Zhī, powerless to control them,
led his family
to reside in the Dàpéng Lodge.
Pǔ declared himself acting military governor.
Fán said to Pǔ:
“Minister Zhī has shown kindness to the people of Pèi;
if we do not kill him,
we will later regret it.”
Pǔ refused,
but Fán insisted,
arguing back and forth over ten rounds,
until Pǔ angrily said:
“Do as you see fit.”
Fán then forged an order in Pǔ’s name,
telling Zhī:
“We request Minister Zhī to prepare his luggage and return to the capital.”
Zhī, believing it sincere,
departed the next day.
Fán ambushed with armed men at Qīlǐ Pavilion;
upon arrival, all were killed regardless of age.
The people of Pèi could not help but shed tears.
Later, when Pǔ received the court’s appointment,
he recommended Fán as prefect of Sùzhōu.
Fán was cruel and fond of killing,
further imposing heavy taxes and brutal punishments,
causing the people to lament and resent.
Within five years,
his amassed wealth piled up like mountains.
Pǔ, disgusted by this,
ordered the general Zhāng Yǒu to replace Fán.
Fán, enraged,
refused the order.
When Yǒu arrived,
he stayed in a separate residence,
waiting for Fán to come out.
Fán led five hundred of his men at night to surround Yǒu;
at dawn,
Yǒu personally led over a hundred elite warriors to break through.
Fán’s forces collapsed,
and he fled on horseback with over ten men for dozens of miles,
until his followers all perished.
Fán abandoned his horse, disguised himself, and begged for food in the countryside.
A villager who recognized him
captured and delivered him.
Yǒu bound him,
swiftly reported to Pǔ,
and Pǔ ordered his execution in the commandery.
Fán was originally crude, fierce, and simple,
illiterate,
but at the execution ground,
he suddenly requested a brush and composed a poem:
“Jade and gold piled high, my rank exalted,
disaster came swiftly, turning all to naught.
Where now is the glory and wealth of five years?
No different from a dream in Nánkē.”
It was thought at the time that a ghost had composed it for him.
The Eunuchs of Yùzhāng
In the year Jiǎzǐ of the Tiānfù era,
residents near the market in Yùzhāng
often heard at night what sounded like dozens of people talking in the streets,
heading toward the market,
but upon looking, no one was there.
This happened for many nights,
causing households to tremble in fear,
unable to sleep at night.
Soon after,
an edict ordered the execution of all eunuchs,
and in Yùzhāng,
over fifty were killed.
Driven toward the market,
their clamorous chatter and noise
matched what had been heard before.
Shào Yuánxiū
Shào Yuánxiū, a Left Department Vice Director of the Hàn court,
during the Tiānfù era,
was not yet capped (under twenty),
living in the official residence in Yǎnzhōu.
In the household were only a wet nurse, maids, and servants;
on the western wing of the hall,
the southernmost room was his study.
One night around midnight,
the entire household extinguished lamps and slept deeply,
and the lamp in the study was also out.
Shào, resting his head on a book in half-sleep,
heard from the west side of the hall
a rustling like the sound of a woman’s footsteps,
passing along the hall steps.
First reaching the eastern wing,
where the maids’ bedrooms were,
each time it reached a door,
it paused briefly.
Then it was heard reaching the southern corridor,
where there was a small door,
not locked,
and it pushed the door open and entered.
Immediately, a crashing sound was heard,
as if porcelain had been smashed.
Then it went west into the study;
by the faint moonlight outside the window,
he saw a figure,
extremely large in shape.
Its face was indistinguishable,
about six or seven feet tall,
as if covered with a dark blue-black cloth over its head as it entered.
It stood beneath the door frame,
Shào, unafraid,
shouted at it sternly,
and questioned it several times,
but it gave no reply,
then retreated out.
Its movement was like the wind;
Shào wanted to grab his pillow to strike it,
but it was already gone.
Then he heard it moving toward the west side of the hall,
and the sound faded away.
At dawn,
checking the southern room,
on the tea table,
a white porcelain vessel
had fallen to the ground and shattered.
Later, asking others,
he learned that a military governor had once lived in this residence,
whose daughter died
and was temporarily encoffined in the western hall.
Upon inquiring with neighbors,
a close neighbor who knew the girl
said
she was quite tall in stature,
likely it was her spirit.
Hé Sìláng
During the Liáng dynasty,
in Zhōngzhōu ward of the Western Capital, there was a man named Hé Sìláng,
who made his living by selling cosmetics and face powder.
One day, just before dawn,
before the street drums had sounded,
he heard someone from over a hundred paces away
shouting "Hé Sìláng!"
several times before stopping.
From then on, this became a regular occurrence.
About half a month later,
he had just opened his shop one morning
when a man who looked like an official's servant
stepped forward directly, bowed, and said:
"My master summons you."
Hé thought it might be a summons from the Prefect's residence.
Before he could set off,
the servant urged him again.
As Hé was fastening his belt,
the servant would not wait.
Soon, the servant pulled him by his clothes and headed north,
reaching the main east-west thoroughfare.
Hé then wanted to turn back,
but the servant held him even more urgently.
Hé grew increasingly suspicious,
thinking, "Could this not be a human?"
He had heard that if one took the shoes one was wearing
and used them to draw a circle on the ground around oneself,
it could ward off evil spirits.
Though he hastily tried to do this,
he was immediately thrown onto a roof.
Knowing he was powerless,
he proceeded with both fear and astonishment,
his mind in a daze,
and thus reached Huī'ānmén directly to the north.
Heading northwest for another five to seven *li*,
it grew dark and obscure.
Suddenly, there appeared towering red gates and grand buildings,
resembling the mansion of a king.
Late into the night,
he was invited inside.
Bright torches blazed,
and the furnishings were magnificent.
Only women received him with warm hospitality,
saying:
"This is the former residence of a general and minister.
Our young daughter is now choosing a fine match.
We truly admire your heroic worthiness;
you may proceed to the auspicious wedding seat."
Hé, seeing their enchanting beauty,
was also captivated in heart,
and the graceful and gentle demeanor
was truly peerless in her generation.
By dawn,
he found himself lying among grave mounds,
deserted and without a trace of people.
He then looked toward Huī'ānmén and headed back,
but the thick overgrowth of grass and brambles
caused him to fall into a desolate well.
After another night,
he suffered unbearably from hunger and thirst,
and drank dew collected in his lapel.
A woodcutter saw him and asked,
then reported to his family,
who pulled him out with a rope.
He recovered after several days.
The Qīngzhōu Merchant
During the Later Liáng dynasty,
a merchant from Qīngzhōu was sailing when he encountered a storm,
and was blown to a certain place.
Looking into the distance, he saw mountains, rivers, and a city wall.
The ship's pilot said:
"Those who have encountered storms recently
have never reached this place.
I have heard that the Land of Ghosts is here;
could this be it?"
Soon after,
the boat reached the shore,
and they disembarked.
They headed toward the city.
The houses and fields
were no different from those in the Central Plains.
They greeted everyone they saw,
but no one seemed to see them.
Reaching the city,
there were gatekeepers;
they greeted them,
but received no response.
Entering the city,
the houses and people were very numerous.
They then went to the royal palace,
where a great banquet was just taking place.
Several dozen officials and attendants were serving at the feast.
Their clothing, caps, utensils, music, and furnishings
were largely similar to those of the Central Plains.
The merchant then ascended the hall,
bending close to the king's seat to observe.
Suddenly, the king fell ill.
His attendants helped him back,
and hastily summoned a shaman to examine him.
The shaman arrived and said:
"There is a person from the land of the living here.
His living energy is pressing upon people,
hence the king's illness.
He came here by chance;
he has no intention of causing harm.
If we offer him food, drink, a carriage, and horses, and send him off,
it will be fine."
They immediately prepared wine and food,
set a seat in a separate room,
and the shaman, along with the king and his officials,
all came to make offerings and pray.
The merchant leaned on the table and ate.
Soon, a servant arrived with a horse,
and the merchant also mounted a horse to return.
Reaching the shore, he boarded the boat.
The people of that country never saw him.
He again encountered a favorable wind and returned.
At that time, Hè Déjiǎn was the military governor of Qīngzhōu,
and was related to Yáng Shīhòu, the military governor of Wèibó.
He thus sent this merchant as an envoy to Wèi,
where he recounted this to Shīhòu.
Fàn Xuāngǔ of Wèi,
who personally heard of this matter,
told it to me.
Zhōu Yuánshū
There was a man named Zhōu Yuánshū,
a native of Suīyáng,
who served as administrative assistant in Pínglú.
He was staying in an official residence in Línzī.
One evening, as he was about to retire,
suddenly there appeared many carriages, horses, and baggage,
and someone knocked at the gate, announcing:
"Minister Lǐ Sīkōng requests an audience."
Yuánshū thought that none of his relatives or acquaintances had this name,
and pondered to himself,
it must be an old friend from his hometown
whom he had forgotten.
He then went out to meet him,
invited him to sit,
and asked where he had come from.
The guest said:
"I have also newly moved here,
and have no place to stay yet,
so I seek to reside in this residence."
Yuánshū said in surprise:
"How can this be?"
The guest replied:
"This is my former residence."
Yuánshū said:
"I came here to take up my post,
and it is said
that this is an official lodging for clerks.
When did you live here?"
The guest said:
"I lived here during the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era."
Yuánshū said:
"If so,
you must be a ghost?"
The guest said:
"Yes.
The underworld has permitted me to establish a shrine here,
so I ask you to move away."
Yuánshū refused, saying:
"Humans should not associate with ghosts.
Is it because I am about to die
that you dare to bully me?
Even so,
it is unreasonable for me to hand over this residence to you.
Even if I die,
I will certainly take you to court."
He then summoned his wife and children, saying:
"When I die,
be sure to place plenty of paper and brushes in my coffin,
for I will confront Minister Lǐ in court."
He then prepared wine and drank with the guest,
toasting each other several hundred cups,
his words and expression growing ever more stern.
As the guest was about to leave,
he detained him again.
After a long while,
an old servant came and said:
"My mistress sends word to the Minister:
Administrative Assistant Zhōu is a man of wood and stone;
how can one argue with him?
You will only bring trouble upon yourself!"
The guest then took his leave and departed.
Yuánshū saw him out the gate,
and he vanished in an instant.
Yuánshū ultimately came to no harm.
Zhū Yánshòu
The Prefect of Shòuzhōu, Zhū Yánshòu,
in his final years,
was bathing in his chamber
when he glimpsed two figures outside the window,
both with blue faces, vermilion hair, and blue clothing,
holding official documents in their hands.
One said:
"I have received orders to come and fetch him."
The other said:
"I too have received orders to come and fetch him."
The first one added:
"My orders came first."
Yánshòu then called for his attendants,
and the two figures vanished.
When the attendants arrived,
he asked who was outside,
and they all said there was no one.
Soon after, he was killed.
Qín Jìnzhōng
In the bǐngzǐ year of the Tiānyòu era,
the soldier Zhōu Jiāo of Zhèxī rebelled,
killing the generals Qín Jìnzhōng, Zhāng Yìn,
and over ten others.
In his youth, Jìnzhōng
had once been angry with a young servant boy,
pierced his heart with a blade,
killed him, and buried him.
In his final years,
he constantly saw this servant boy standing with his hands over his heart,
first appearing over a hundred paces away,
then gradually drawing closer.
On the day he was to go out,
the boy was right in front of his horse,
and all his attendants saw him.
When he entered the government office,
he encountered the mutinous soldiers,
was wounded in the stomach, and died.
As for Zhāng Yìn, over a month earlier,
he had often heard someone calling his name,
the voice very clear and resonant.
It too gradually drew closer.
On that day, it was as if the voice was right in front of him,
and when he entered the office, he was killed.
Magistrate Lǐ of Wàngjiāng
There was a Magistrate Lǐ of Wàngjiāng
who, after his term ended, resided in Shūzhōu.
He had two sons,
both very intelligent.
Once, the magistrate returned home late after drinking,
and when he was a few hundred paces from his house,
he saw his two sons coming to greet him.
They immediately seized him together and beat him.
The magistrate was shocked and furious,
shouting loudly,
but the place was remote and deserted,
so no one came to know of it.
They beat him as they walked,
and as they neared the house,
both sons turned and ran away.
When he entered the gate,
his two sons again came to greet him in the courtyard,
and when he questioned them,
they both said they had never left the house.
Over a month later,
the magistrate was again drinking at a relative's house,
and he recounted the whole incident,
asking to stay overnight,
not daring to return home.
But his sons, fearing he would return late again
and be beaten once more,
both went out to meet him.
On the way,
they saw their father,
who angrily said:
"Why have you come out so late?"
He immediately ordered his attendants to beat them,
and they were only spared after being badly injured.
The next day, the magistrate returned home,
and was even more terrified by these events.
Within a few months,
both father and sons died.
The locals said
that Shūzhōu had mountain demons
skilled at creating such malevolent apparitions,
likely of the Líqiū type.
The Temple Caretaker of Zhāng Fēi's Temple
Over ten lǐ from Zǐzhōu city,
there was a temple to Zhāng Fēi,
in which stood a clay statue
serving as a guardian warrior.
One night, it had relations with the temple caretaker's wife,
and after a year,
she gave birth to a daughter.
The child's hair was vermilion,
and her eyebrows, eyes, hands, and feet
all resembled those of the clay statue.
As she grew up,
everyone feared her.
Whenever an official took office in Zǐzhōu,
upon visiting the temple,
they would have her brought out to verify the story,
and some would give her money or silk.
She survives to this day.
Monk Yànxiāo
The cursive-script monk, Great Master Wényīng, Yànxiāo,
was originally in Luòdū.
Míngzōng's heir, Prince Qín, Cóng Róng,
treated him with great favor.
Later, due to certain events,
he moved south and lived at Zēngkǒu Temple on West Lake in Jiānglíng.
One day, in a daze,
he suddenly saw Prince Qín arrive at the temple with twenty horsemen,
seeking Yànxiāo.
Yànxiāo asked why the prince had come,
but just as he was about to answer,
he vanished abruptly.
Yànxiāo had just begun inquiring with others
when, within ten days,
Prince Qín was assassinated.
The Musician of Jiànkāng
In Jiànkāng, there was a musician
who went to the market one evening
and saw two servants who said:
"Judge Lù summons you."
He followed them.
They arrived at a large mansion,
decorated with great solemnity.
There were over ten guests,
all fond of wine,
who only drank without any food served,
and the wine was not offered to the musician.
As dawn approached, they dispersed,
and the musician, utterly exhausted,
lay down on a bed outside the door.
When he awoke,
he was in a patch of grass,
beside a large burial mound.
He asked the local people,
who said
it was traditionally known as Judge Lù's mound,
but no one knew from which era he came.
Huáng Yánràng
The clerk Huáng Yánràng of Jiànkāng once drank at a relative's house
and left when it grew late.
Not heavily drunk,
he felt his body floating in a daze.
He drifted along,
unable to control himself.
After walking over ten lǐ,
he reached a large mansion,
silent and empty.
In front of the hall was a small room,
containing a bed.
Yánràng, extremely tired,
lay down on the bed.
When he awoke,
he was in the grass in front of Jiǎngshān,
having crossed the double city walls and moats.
He fell ill from the shock,
and recovered only after over a year.
Zhāng Yuàn
The palace eunuch Zhāng Yuàn of Jiāngnán was crossing the new bridge in Jiànkāng at dusk
when he suddenly saw a beautiful woman,
running wildly with her clothes disheveled.
Yuàn was very surprised,
and upon looking closely,
the woman suddenly turned her head,
transforming into a whirlwind that rushed at Yuàn.
Yuàn's horse fell, injuring his face,
and he recovered only after over a month.
When the horse first got up,
it lifted one hoof,
and limped home.
Ever since, whenever crossing this bridge,
the horse would always lift one hoof as it walked,
but no other strange occurrences happened.
The Wife of the Soldier from Wùyuán
In the year Dīngyǒu,
a man from the Jiànwēi Army in Wùyuán lost his wife and remarried.
His new wife treated the children from his previous marriage with extreme cruelty,
and the husband could not control her.
One day,
he suddenly saw his deceased wife enter through the door.
She angrily rebuked the new wife, saying:
"Who among humans does not die?
Who lacks the affection between mother and child?
How could you mistreat my children like this?
I have already pleaded my case to the authorities in the underworld.
Now they have granted me ten days' leave
to admonish you.
If you still do not reform,
I will surely kill you."
Both husband and wife were terrified and bowed repeatedly,
then immediately prepared wine and food for her.
They summoned all their relatives, neighbors, and friends,
and she conversed and greeted them as usual.
Others could only hear her voice,
but only the husband could see her.
When night fell,
they prepared a bed for her in a separate room.
The husband wished to stay with her,
but she refused.
After ten days had passed,
as she was about to leave,
she once again sternly admonished the new wife,
her words earnest and heartfelt.
The entire family and relatives escorted her to the grave.
When they were about a hundred paces from the grave,
she said:
"Everyone may stop here."
She then bid them a warm farewell and departed.
As she approached the cypress grove,
everyone saw her,
her clothing and appearance just as in life.
When she reached the grave, she vanished.
This is what Wāng Yánchāng, the commander of the Jiànwēi Army, recounted.
Chén Déyù
In the year Xīnhài,
Chén Jūràng, styled Déyù, an official of the false Right Treasury in Jiāngnán,
was on night duty in the treasury.
His wife was at home.
In the early fifth watch,
she suddenly dreamed of two clerks
holding official documents
entering through the door.
They asked:
"Is this Chén Déyù's home?"
She replied:
"Yes."
"Where is Déyù?"
She said:
"He is in the treasury."
The clerks were about to leave
when the wife chased after them, calling out:
"My husband's
style is Déyù,
but there is another official named Chén Déyù in charge of the clothing treasury,
whose home is nearby in the eastern alley."
The two clerks looked at each other and laughed, saying:
"We almost made a mistake."
They then departed.
Soon after,
Chén Déyù got up in the morning to use the toilet,
claimed he was ill,
returned to bed,
and after a long while, died.
Both men lived west of Zhìchéng.
Guǎnglíng Clerk
A clerk in Guǎnglíng, surnamed Zhào,
during the summer heat,
slept alone in a room.
In the middle of the night,
he suddenly saw a large figure in yellow clothes enter through the door,
followed by seven smaller figures in yellow clothes.
They said to him:
"We searched everywhere but couldn't find you,
and here you are!"
They shouted for him to rise,
saying:
"It is time to go."
One of the yellow-clad figures stepped forward and said:
"His allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted,
he cannot be taken abruptly.
It would be appropriate to leave him a mark."
The large figure then reached into his bosom,
took out a seal,
and stamped it on Zhào's left arm before leaving.
When dawn came and he looked at it,
the seal's inscription was imprinted on his flesh.
The characters resembled ancient seal script.
He could recognize the lower part:
the right side looked like the character for "immortal,"
the left side like the character for "record."
The upper part was illegible.
Zhào's eventual fate is unknown.
Yáng Jiān
In the southwest corridor of the first courtyard of Lóngxīng Temple in Yǎnzhōu,
there was a scripture repository.
A Dharma Treasure Master
often saw an old man in white clothes in front of the hall of divine spirits.
This happened for several days,
so the monk, finding it strange, questioned him.
The old man said:
"I am not human;
I am the local earth deity of Secretary Yáng's residence."
The monk asked:
"Why have you come here?"
The old man replied:
"That gentleman is stubborn and perverse,
constantly building and renovating without cease,
leaving me no place to reside."
The monk said:
"Why not bring misfortune upon him?"
He answered:
"His fortune and longevity are not yet diminished;
there is nothing I can do about it."
Having said this, he vanished.
Several years later,
Zhū Jǐn abandoned the city and fled,
and the army fell into chaos.
Yáng's entire family met with disaster.
His name was Jiān.
He repeatedly failed the imperial examinations.
He served as secretary to Zhū Jǐn.
Yuán Jìqiān
Yuán Jìqiān, the Junior Supervisor of the Palace Administration, once resided in Yǎnzhōu
to attend to his ailing parent.
His home was in the southeastern corner of the inner city.
A servant announced a visitor from outside,
whose card read "Former Assistant Prefect of a Certain Prefecture, Xǔ Yánnián,"
and later stated he came to offer condolences.
Jìqiān was displeased
but ordered him to be admitted.
By the time he had dressed and gone out to receive him,
the visitor had already left.
The servant said
he came on foot,
wearing old black clothes,
and arrived wearing a tall hat.
As soon as he dropped his card at the carriage gate,
he departed.
That year, Jìqiān's parent passed away,
so he burned the card along with spirit money.
Scholar from Bīnzhōu
During the Later Liáng dynasty,
a scholar traveled from Yōng to Bīn.
After several overnight stops,
he encountered clear weather with a bright moon
and journeyed on through the night.
When he reached an open wilderness,
he suddenly heard the sound of chariots and horses approaching from behind.
Soon they drew near.
The scholar hid in the grass by the roadside.
He saw three riders
wearing crowns and belts like kings,
and also some on foot,
walking slowly and conversing.
The scholar stealthily followed them for several dozen paces
and overheard them say:
"We are now ordered to go to Bīnzhōu
to take several thousand people.
We are unsure by what means to take them.
You two gentlemen, try to devise a plan."
One of them said:
"We should take them by military force."
Another said:
"Using military force may be effective,
but what about the fact that both gentlemen and commoners would suffer the calamity?
It would be better to take them by plague."
The others deeply agreed.
Soon, the chariots and horses gradually moved farther away,
and he could no longer hear their words.
When the scholar reached Bīnzhōu,
a great plague broke out among the populace,
and many died.
Wáng Shāng
In the year Jiǎxū of the Zhēnmíng era of the Liáng dynasty,
the military governor of Xúzhōu, Wáng Yīn, was about to rebel.
On the night of the twentieth day of the eighth month,
the moon was as bright as day,
and all the residents heard the sounds of troops marching through the main streets.
Peering through cracks in their doors,
they saw soldiers dressed in black but without armor or helmets.
At first, they thought these were government troops secretly deployed to apprehend thieves,
but soon they heard clear whistles and calls,
some singing, some sighing,
with swords, shields, spears, and halberds,
crowding the alleys and lanes,
their forms strange and bizarre,
extremely terrifying,
and only then did they realize they were not human.
They proceeded from the government offices,
exited through the eastern gate in the southern part of the prefecture,
and the locked gates posed no obstacle.
By midwinter,
Wáng Yīn had defied the imperial decree,
and the court ordered Liú Xún to lead fifty thousand troops to suppress him.
After eight months, Wáng Yīn was defeated,
and the entire region suffered the calamity.
Xiè Yànzhāng
Xiè Yànzhāng, the military governor of Xǔzhōu under the Liáng dynasty, was assassinated,
and the court ordered Hǎo Chāngyù, deputy commissioner of the Xuānhé Treasury, to go to Xǔchāng to inventory his family's property.
In a separate room,
they saw that beneath the left eye of Xiè Yànzhāng's portrait,
fresh blood was present,
and no one could determine where it had come from,
astonishing everyone.
Xiè Yànzhāng had a strong craving for soft-shelled turtles.
While stationed in Héyáng,
he ordered fishermen to catch them for his meals,
and not a day went by without this,
and if they failed to catch any, they would be severely punished.
There was a fisherman who lived east of the city,
and one day before dawn,
he was about to go catch them.
When he was less than a mile or two away,
he encountered a person,
who asked where he was going,
and the fisherman answered truthfully.
This person said:
"Could you refrain from going today?"
The fisherman said:
"If I don't, I will be punished."
The person said again:
"If you do not cast your nets today,
I will give you five thousand coins,
is that acceptable?"
The fisherman agreed,
and received five thousand coins,
which he carried back on his shoulder.
By the time it was dawn,
he felt the load was strangely light,
and when he looked,
all the coins had turned into paper.
Chóngshèng Temple
At the Chóngshèng Temple in Hànzhōu,
on the Cold Food Festival,
suddenly there appeared a person in red robes,
and another in purple robes,
both of imposing stature and appearance,
with a grand entourage of attendants and horses.
The temple monks thought they were officials from the prefecture,
and rushed out to welcome them,
but they were not.
They bowed respectfully to the monks,
but spoke very little.
They asked for brushes,
and each wrote a quatrain on the wall.
The red-robed one's poem said:
"On this festival when smoke is banned, we wander here together,
just as the fragrance of roses fills both banks.
Recalling events from ten years ago,
I force myself to chant amid the scenery, my troubled heart in disarray."
The purple-robed one's poem said:
"Riding my horse, I briefly seek the road of old,
where fallen blossoms and fragrant grass remain as before.
Home lost, country shattered—all but a dream,
and now, filled with melancholy, I encounter the Cold Food sky again."
After writing,
they mounted their horses and swiftly departed.
Once they passed through the pine path,
they vanished without a trace,
leaving only an extraordinary fragrance that lingered for a month without dispersing.
Their poems remain preserved to this day.
Rèn Yànsī
At the home of Rèn Yànsī, the governor of Chāngzhōu in Shǔ,
suddenly music was heard from the air,
extremely elegant, beautiful, and sorrowful,
continuing unabated all day.
A voice from the air said:
"Prepare food for me."
Rèn asked who it was,
but it refused to reveal its origins,
so he set up food in a quiet room.
The food was eaten clean, as if by a person,
and if no food was provided,
it would cause household items to break,
insects to enter people's ears,
and fires to break out in all directions.
Rèn Yànsī despised this,
and even when he moved away to avoid it,
it would still arrive first,
and this continued for seven or eight years.
Suddenly, one day, the music was no longer heard,
and when food was set out, it was not consumed.
On a beam in the hall, a poem was written in blood:
"Things of this world easily change and shift,
I journey on, unseen by others.
I cherish and value Rèn Yànsī,
though the days since we parted grow ever distant."
Rèn Yànsī particularly loathed the inscribed poem,
and tried to scrape it off with a knife,
but the characters had already sunk into the wood,
and in the end, no one knew what kind of ghost it was.
Zhāng Rénbǎo
The proofreader Zhāng Rénbǎo was always talented and learned,
but he died young,
and his body was transported from Chéngdū back to Làngzhōng for burial,
temporarily interred at the Dōngjīn Temple.
On the Cold Food Festival, his family
heard urgent knocking at the door,
but when they went to look, no one was there,
only a banana leaf on the door,
on which was written:
"On Cold Food, every household forbids smoke,
wild pear blossoms fall, wind scatters small floral hairpins.
Now, I have only the dreams of a lonely soul,
half in Jiālíng, half in Jǐnchuān."
The entire clan was astonished.
On the Dragon Boat Festival,
they again heard knocking at the door,
and his father watched through a crack in the door,
and saw his son,
his body about thirty feet tall,
his feet not touching the ground,
writing on the door: "The fifth month, the midday day, the festival of heaven,"
but before he finished writing,
his father opened the door,
and he immediately vanished.
Shortly after, when the burial was completed,
he never appeared again.
Yáng Yùnzhōng
The presented scholar Yáng Yùnzhōng committed an offense,
and was imprisoned in the Chéngdū prefectural jail.
One night, he dreamed of a woman,
whose appearance was not striking,
but whose words were exceptionally elegant.
She said:
"I am Xuē Tāo,
who recently died in this room and was buried here."
She then presented Yáng Yùnzhōng with a poem:
"The jade water clock drips deep, the lamp flickers dimly,
on the east wall, the west wall, shadows appear from time to time.
Outside the window, the moon shines bright, the cuckoo cries,
how can I bear this lonely soul grieving through the endless night?"
Wáng Yánháo
In Zǐzhōu, there was the Yángguān deity,
who was none other than Zhāng Fēi, the Shu-Han General of Chariots and Cavalry and Marquis of Xīxiāng.
His divine manifestations were stern and fierce,
and the people of the prefecture both revered and feared him.
Wáng Yánhào, a military judge in Lóngzhōu, took as his concubine a beautiful courtesan from Chéngdū named Xiáqīng,
and doted on her greatly.
He brought her along to his official post,
and as they passed in front of the Yángguān deity's temple,
Xiáqīng suddenly died.
She had only one daughter,
who was not Yánhào's own child,
and he felt doubly sorrowful and compassionate for her.
One day, a spiritual message was conveyed,
stating in full:
"I was seized by the Yángguān deity,
but after pleading, I was released."
From then on, they shared a bedchamber again as before,
and her likeness was painted for her to inhabit.
Even washing, rinsing, eating, and drinking were all as if she were alive.
She then said:
"Wait until I have married off my daughter,
then I will bid you farewell."
When Yánhào was about to remarry,
he informed her,
and the ghost also consented.
So he married the daughter of Shěn Yànxún.
From then on, whenever female guests were seated together,
a black butterfly would appear,
fluttering lightly past the banquet tables,
and this eventually became a regular occurrence.
Later, when Yánhào became magistrate of Xīnjīn,
he married off her daughter,
providing a very complete dowry,
and from then on, nothing more was heard of it.
Monk Huìjìn
In Western Shǔ, there was a monk named Huìjìn,
whose surname was Wáng,
residing at Fúgǎn Temple.
One morning as he went out,
upon reaching the gate of Zīfú Monastery,
he saw a tall figure,
bluish in color,
who pressed closer with increasing urgency.
The monk ran to avoid him.
Reaching Zhúzé Bridge,
he dashed into a commoner's house.
This person also followed him there,
grabbing, pulling, and tugging at him,
with a force impossible to break free from.
The monk wailed pitifully and begged him,
whereupon this person asked:
"What is your surname?"
He replied:
"Surname Wáng."
This person said:
"The name is the same, but the surname is different."
Then he released him and left.
The monk, trembling with fear,
took refuge in the commoner's house,
and after some time, when he had calmed down somewhat,
he returned to the temple.
That evening,
someone with the same name but a different surname died.
Tián Dáchéng
In Lúlíng, there was a merchant named Tián Dáchéng,
wealthy in resources,
who made it his duty to be quite charitable.
While building a mansion in the new city,
someone knocked on the gate at night.
Going to look, he found no one,
and this happened repeatedly.
He then called out and asked:
"Are you human?
Or a ghost?"
After a long while came the reply:
"I am indeed not human.
I formerly lived in Lóngquán,
but my house was destroyed by a flash flood.
I seek to lodge in your home,
and will leave once my house is repaired."
Dáchéng refused,
saying:
"How can humans and ghosts live together?"
The reply was:
"It is only a temporary lodging,
and will cause you no harm.
Moreover, I have heard of your righteous spirit throughout the countryside,
hence I make this request."
Dáchéng agreed,
and then the ghost asked:
"Where should I stay?"
Dáchéng said:
"Only the main hall is available."
The ghost then bowed in thanks and left.
Several days later, it returned, saying:
My family has already arrived in the hall,
but it will not hinder your guests.
However, you should strictly instruct your household to be careful with fire.
If by any chance an accident occurs,
it might be said that we caused it."
Dáchéng accordingly vacated the hall for their use.
Dáchéng once composed a poem,
when the ghost suddenly spoke from the air:
"So you can write poetry?
I too once enjoyed it.
Shall we exchange verses?"
Dáchéng immediately prepared wine,
set out paper and brush before him,
and they conversed on all manner of topics.
Everyone watched closely,
but the wine, paper, and brush
remained perfectly still.
Yet when they glanced away momentarily,
the wine was already gone,
and characters had appeared on the paper.
Over several compositions,
all were meaningful.
The brushstrokes were vigorous and strong,
in the Liǔ style.
Someone asked the ghost's name.
It said:
"If I were to tell you,
it would not benefit my host.
Let me convey it through a poem."
Then it composed a poem, saying:
"Heaven endowed me with a spirit free and clear,
Yet different from the affairs of the human sphere.
To know my family's true name, look near:
A stretch of red where earth and sky meet here."
No one understood its meaning.
One day, it announced again:
"I have a young son,
who is to marry the daughter of the Camphor Tree Spirit.
The wedding is set for a certain day,
and I would like to borrow your rear hall for three days,
to complete your great kindness.
May I?"
Dáchéng vacated the hall,
surrounding it with curtains,
and after three days, the ghost thanked him again, saying:
"My affairs are concluded,
and I return this hall to you.
Your kindness as host
can truly be called utmost.
However, your old maidservant so-and-so
deserves a hundred strokes of the cane."
Dáchéng apologized.
He summoned the maidservant
and caned her several strokes,
when the ghost said:
"Let her know her fault,
that is enough."
Dáchéng later questioned the maidservant,
who said she had peeked through a hole in the curtain and seen
male and female guests,
kitchen preparations, flowers, and candles,
no different from the human world.
Over a year later,
the ghost bid farewell and left.
Dáchéng traveled to Guǎnglíng on business,
and was gone for a long time without returning,
causing his family to worry.
The ghost came again and said:
"Is your family worried about the master?
I will go check on him."
The next day, it returned and said:
"Your master is at Yángzǐ,
perfectly fine,
and will return soon.
He has taken a new concubine
and sleeps with her.
I burned the back flap of their bed curtain
just to tease him."
It then left with a loud laugh.
When Dáchéng returned,
they asked him, and everything matched.
Later, he went to Lóngquán
to seek out the ghost's dwelling,
but in the end, could not find it.
Xú Yànchéng
The military official Xú Yànchéng was constantly engaged in the timber trade.
In the year Dīnghài,
he went to the Ruìkǒu market in Xìnzhōu,
but there was no timber available for purchase.
He anchored his boat and stayed for a long time.
One evening,
a young man accompanied by two servants came and went along the riverbank,
appearing as if he were looking for someone but had not found them.
Yànchéng thus invited him into his boat,
prepared wine and food for him,
and treated him with the respect due a guest.
The young man felt very ashamed.
As he was about to leave,
he thanked him, saying:
"My home is nearby, in a separate estate a few li from here.
Would you be willing to honor me with a visit tomorrow?"
Xú Yànchéng agreed.
The next day, he went.
After traveling a little over a li,
a servant with a horse came to greet him,
and they soon arrived at a large mansion
with magnificent gates and halls.
The young man came out to welcome his guest,
and the wine and food were abundant and well-prepared.
After a leisurely while,
Yànchéng mentioned that he had been staying here for a long time
with no timber to purchase.
The young man said:
"I have timber in the mountains.
I will have it brought out tomorrow."
After staying for a day or two,
a large quantity of timber indeed arrived,
of excellent quality and at a low price.
Once the trading was completed,
Yànchéng went to bid farewell to the young man.
The young man again brought out four large fir planks,
saying:
"The timber from before was what I sold.
Now I give these to you as a gift.
When you reach Wú,
you should obtain a good price for them."
Yànchéng returned,
and when he first reached Qínhuái,
it happened that the ruler of Wú had died,
and the fir planks were purchased to make a coffin.
As they were considered exceptionally fine timber,
he earned several hundred thousand coins.
Yànchéng bought a large quantity of rare treasures and curiosities,
and went again to Ruìkǒu
to repay the young man.
The young man again traded with him.
He went like this three times,
and profited quite well from it.
After an interval of a year,
he went again to visit him,
but the village was as before,
and he saw nothing at all.
He inquired among the villagers,
but in the end, no one knew anything about it.
Zhèng Jiāo,
a man from Héběi,
failed the imperial examination for the jìnshì degree,
and traveled in the region between Chén and Cài.
Passing by a grave mound,
he saw two bamboo stalks on it,
green and lovely,
so he halted his horse and chanted:
"Two bamboo stalks upon the grave mound,
swaying gently in the wind."
For a long time, he could not continue.
Then he heard a voice from within the grave say:
"Why not say, 'Below lies a man of a hundred years,
in long slumber, unaware of dawn.'"
Jiāo, startled, asked about it,
but there was no further reply.
Lǐ Yīn
The jìnshì Lǐ Yīn
was from Xiāngyáng.
Once, while wandering in the imperial gardens,
he saw a red leaf flowing out from the imperial moat,
with a poem inscribed on it, saying:
"Why does the flowing water rush so urgently?
All day long, the deep palace lies in idleness.
With earnest feeling, I bid farewell to the red leaf:
Go well, and make your way to the human world."
Yīn collected and stored it in his book bag.
Later, when Emperor Xīzōng fled to Shǔ,
Yīn escaped and took refuge in a commoner's home in Nánshān.
There he met a palace maid
who said she was a palace attendant in charge of documents,
named Yúnfāngzǐ,
and was talented and thoughtful.
Yīn became intimate with her.
When she saw the red leaf,
she sighed and said:
"This is the poem I inscribed."
They traveled together to Shǔ,
and she recounted in detail the affairs of the palace.
When they reached Miánzhōu,
they encountered the palace eunuch Tián Dàrén, who recognized her,
and said:
"How did the document attendant get here?"
He forced her to mount a horse
and took her away ahead.
Lǐ was deeply distressed.
That evening,
while lodging at an inn,
Yúnfāngzǐ came again,
saying:
"I have heavily bribed the palace eunuch
and obtained permission to follow you."
So she went with him back to Xiāngyáng.
After several years,
Lǐ Yīn fell ill and grew emaciated.
A Daoist priest said that his face bore an evil aura.
Yúnfāngzǐ then confessed:
"That year when we met in Miánzhú,
I had already hanged myself and died.
Moved by your affection,
I have been accompanying you.
But humans and ghosts are of different paths;
how dare I bring harm upon you?"
She prepared wine, composed a poem,
bid farewell, and departed.
Liǔ Péngjǔ
During the Lóngjì era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a scholar named Liǔ Péngjǔ
who traveled to Hángzhōu
and took shelter from the rain at the Wǔ Xiàng Temple.
He saw a woman
holding a five-stringed instrument,
who said she was a maidservant from the household of the official Qián Dàfū.
Péngjǔ was attracted to her
and thus enticed her to elope.
He hid her in his boat,
but they were captured by the local patrol officers.
The maidservant hanged herself and died.
One day,
she returned to Liǔ's place.
Liǔ also knew she had died.
His servant fully explained the situation,
so he kept her there.
After some time, she left.
Zhōu Jié
The magistrate of Huòqiū, Zhōu Jié,
in the year Jiǎchén, left his post
and traveled as a guest in the Huái region.
At that time, the people were suffering a great famine,
inns were nearly nonexistent,
and there was nowhere to seek lodging.
Climbing high to look around,
he saw smoke and fire from a distant village,
so he hurried toward it.
He found a village house
and knocked on the door for a long time.
A woman came out to answer the door.
He requested lodging for the night.
The woman said:
"At home, we are starving;
the old and young are all ill,
and we have nothing to entertain a guest.
But there is a bed in the central hall you may use."
So he entered.
The woman stood waiting in front of him.
After a short while,
her younger sister also came out,
standing behind her elder sister,
so her face could not be seen.
Jié prepared his own food,
took two pieces of flatbread,
and gave them to the two women.
They took them into the inner room,
closed the door, and went to sleep.
All was quiet, with no human sound.
Jié also felt a shiver of fear.
As dawn approached and he was about to leave,
he called out to the two women to inform them,
but there was no sound or response at all.
So he broke down the door and entered.
He then saw the room filled with piled-up corpses,
all nearly dried and decayed.
Only the woman had died perhaps ten days earlier.
Her younger sister's face was already withered.
The two pieces of flatbread were still placed on their chests.
Later, Jié buried them all.
Deputy Envoy Yáng
In the year Rénwǔ,
at the market in Guāzhōu, Guǎnglíng,
someone urgently purchased fruits.
When asked what they were for,
he replied:
"My superior is taking office tomorrow."
When asked who the superior was,
he said:
"It is Deputy Commissioner Yáng."
Asked further where the official office was located,
he replied:
"East of Jīnshān."
He then left,
and no more questions could be asked.
At that time, a deputy commissioner from Zhèxī had been summoned to Yángdū.
The next day,
when his boat reached Jīnshān,
it sank without cause.
Monk Mínchǔ
Monk Mínchǔ of Fǎyún Temple in Guǎnglíng
was often close with a merchant named Zhāng from Zhōngshān.
After Zhāng died,
Mínchǔ held a vegetarian feast and recited scriptures for him.
Several months later,
he suddenly encountered Zhāng in the market.
As Mínchǔ had not eaten,
Zhāng invited him into a food shop
and ordered húbǐng for him.
After eating,
Mínchǔ asked:
"You have already died,
how can you be here?"
Zhāng said:
"Indeed,
I have a minor offense and have not yet been released.
Now I am assigned as a 'surplus-snatching ghost' in Yángzhōu."
Asked what "snatching surplus" meant,
he said:
"For all officials and merchants,
their profits have a fixed limit.
Anything gained beyond that limit
is considered surplus,
which I can snatch and take.
Nowadays, there are many like me among the living."
He then pointed at passersby, men and women, and said,
"That person and that person,
are all such ghosts."
After a moment,
a monk passed by in front of them,
and he added:
"This monk is also one."
He called the monk over,
and they spoke for a long while,
but the monk did not see Mínchǔ.
After a while,
they walked south together,
and encountered a woman selling flowers.
Zhāng said:
"This woman is also a ghost.
The flowers she sells
are also for ghosts to use;
they cannot be seen by the living."
Zhāng then took out a few coins to buy some
and gave them to Mínchǔ, saying:
"Anyone who sees these flowers and smiles
is a ghost."
He then bid farewell and left.
The flowers were red, fragrant, lovely, and unusually heavy.
Mínchǔ, feeling dazed, returned.
Passersby who saw the flowers
smiled quite a bit.
When he reached the north gate of the temple,
he thought to himself, "I have been wandering with ghosts,
and now I am holding ghost flowers—
this cannot be right."
He immediately threw the flowers into a ditch,
and they splashed into the water with a sound.
After returning,
people in the same courtyard noticed his complexion was very strange,
thinking he had been afflicted by evil,
and they hurriedly brought him medicinal soups to save him.
After a long while, he recovered,
and recounted the whole story.
They went together to retrieve the flowers,
only to find they were a dead person's hand.
Mínchǔ, however, was unharmed.
Chén Shǒuguī
There was a military officer named Chén Shǒuguī
who was once exiled to Xìnzhōu for breaking the law,
and he stayed at an official lodge.
The lodge was notoriously haunted,
and as soon as Shǒuguī arrived,
ghosts appeared during the day,
with strange shapes and forms,
changing rapidly.
Shǒuguī, being bold and fierce by nature,
personally took up bows, arrows, knives, and staffs
to fight them.
After a long time,
a voice from the air said:
"We are ghosts and spirits,
and do not wish to live mixed among humans.
Since you are firm and upright,
we would like to treat you as an elder brother.
Is that acceptable?"
Shǒuguī agreed.
From then on, he often conversed with them.
Whether there was good or bad fortune,
they would report it to him first.
Sometimes they requested food and drink,
and when he provided it,
he would receive money or goods in return.
After a long time,
he grew quite weary of this,
so he sought out a Daoist master,
who personally wrote a memorial
to submit to the Heavenly Emperor.
The next day,
the ghost cursed him loudly:
"I treated you as a brother,
how could you submit a memorial against me?
Is this how a true man
should treat his friends?"
Shǒuguī said:
"How could such a thing happen?"
Immediately, the memorial
along with the paper and brush were thrown down from the air, all intact.
The ghost added:
"You schemed against my dwelling,
thinking I had nowhere to stay.
I am now going to Shǔchuān,
and it will be no worse than here."
After that, they ceased contact.
A Merchant of Guǎnglíng
There was a merchant in Guǎnglíng
who made a bed from cypress wood,
along with over a hundred other utensils,
all crafted with great skill.
The cost had already reached two hundred thousand coins,
and he transported them to Jiànkāng
to sell for profit.
In the evening, he reached Guābù,
and as a slight wind rose,
he moored at the foot of the mountain.
Shortly after,
a large boat appeared,
empty inside,
with only three pole handlers aboard,
and it moored beside his boat.
The merchant grew suspicious
and discussed with his crew:
"These must be bandits,
waiting for nightfall to rob us."
The shore ahead was distant,
the wind grew stronger,
and there was nowhere to escape.
At night, they all went ashore
and hid in a deep forest to avoid them.
Soon, wind, rain, thunder, and lightning
enveloped the area where their boat was moored.
On shore, however, the stars and moon were clear.
After about the time of a meal, the rain stopped and the clouds dispersed.
They saw the large boat gradually moving away.
Only then did they dare return.
The cypress wood bed and utensils they had loaded on the boat
were all gone,
though everything else remained.
The large boat was still by the eastern shore,
and someone called out:
"Do not resent this,
we will return your payment."
Having lost his cargo,
the merchant returned to Guǎnglíng.
When he arrived home,
someone had already delivered three hundred thousand coins,
left them, and departed.
When he inquired about the person,
it turned out to be the day after they had moored at Guābù.
A Person from Pǔchéng
A man from Pǔchéng died young on the road,
leaving a catty of gold at home.
His wife hid it,
and did not inform his mother.
After a year,
he suddenly knocked on the door at night,
weeping and wailing as he returned.
His mother was shocked and terrified,
and together they mourned sorrowfully.
She said:
"Are you truly dead?"
He replied:
"I am indeed dead,
but there is an injustice,
so I have returned temporarily."
He then sat on his mother's lap,
speaking as he did in life,
only his hands and feet were as cold as ice.
He then rose and grasped a knife,
reproaching his wife, saying:
"I have this gold here,
why did you keep it for yourself instead of supporting my elderly mother?"
He was about to kill her,
but his mother said:
"You are already dead.
If you kill this person,
people will surely say that I killed her."
Thereupon, he wept, bid farewell to his mother, and left.
Again taking up the knife himself,
he escorted his wife back to her father's home.
By dawn,
when they were several dozen steps from the gate,
he suddenly vanished.
The Taoist Priest Liú
A Taoist priest named Liú from Lúshān,
intending to travel to Nányuè,
passed through Yíchūn,
and stayed overnight at a village household.
This family was extremely poor,
and had also lost a son,
with no means for a burial.
As evening fell,
suddenly a man appeared,
walking and weeping as he came,
merely beating his chest and crying out:
"What a pity,
what a pity."
Liú went out to look,
and saw his face was white as snow,
with his hair tied in two topknots.
He went straight into the house,
shouldered their □ and left,
and no one knew where he went.
The Commandant of Qīngyuán
A commandant named Yáng from Qīngyuán,
who served as deputy commander of the local defense battalion,
had a large mansion in the western suburb.
One morning, Yáng hurried to the government office and had not yet returned,
while people were just eating,
suddenly a goose appeared,
carrying spirit money on its back,
entered through the gate,
and went straight to a room in the western corridor.
The family members said:
"Did this goose come from the temple?"
They then ordered a servant to chase it away.
The servant entered the room,
and saw only an old man with double topknots and a white beard.
The family members were all frightened and fled.
When Yáng returned,
upon hearing this, he became angry,
took a staff and struck at it.
The ghost appeared and disappeared at the four corners,
transforming and changing,
In an instant,
the staff could not hit it.
Yáng grew even angrier and said:
"After I finish eating,
I will come back to beat you with the staff."
The ghost then bent at the waist and stepped forward, saying:
"Agreed."
Yáng had two daughters.
The elder daughter went into the kitchen to cut meat,
and as she ate,
whenever meat fell onto the chopping block, it would immediately disappear.
The girl brandished the knife, slashing four times into the air,
She chopped,
and then a large black hairy hand was revealed,
saying:
"Please chop."
The girl fled, nearly breathless with fear,
and consequently fell ill.
The younger daughter went to fetch salt from a large jar,
when a monkey
suddenly leaped out from the jar,
onto the girl's back.
The girl ran to the front hall,
and it disappeared again,
and she also fell ill.
They then summoned a shamaness,
who set up an altar to summon it.
The ghost also set up an altar and performed magic,
which was even more powerful than the shamaness's.
The shamaness could not control it,
and she too became frightened and left.
Shortly after,
both daughters and his wife all died.
