Later, there was someone skilled in performing magical arts,
named Míngjiào,
who was invited to chant scriptures for one night.
The ghost then cursed and reviled Yáng before leaving,
and from then on, it ceased.
Yáng also died that year.
The Wife of Wáng □
There was a man named Wáng □,
from Dàyíng Village in Nán'ān County.
His wife, née Lín, suddenly fell ill,
and a ghost possessed her, saying:
"I am Chén Jiǔniáng.
If you offer me incense and flowers in worship,
it will benefit the master of the house."
□ agreed.
She then called Lín "elder sister,"
and when speaking of fortunes and misfortunes for people, she was often accurate.
After more than half a year, she manifested her form,
visible from the waist down.
People who had not come before,
also did not see her,
but only communicated through speech.
When villagers summoned her,
regardless of distance,
she would go together with Lín.
When people held sacrificial ceremonies,
they only needed to prepare wine and food,
and Chén would invoke the names of the spirits herself.
Her invocations were clear and eloquent,
and listeners would forget their weariness,
while Lín merely sat respectfully.
Over two years,
they gained considerable profit.
One day,
she suddenly wept sorrowfully and said to Lín:
"In my past lives, I was a daughter of a family,
and died young before reaching the age of fifteen.
I learned in the underworld
that in a previous life, I had embezzled two hundred thousand coins belonging to you, elder sister.
Therefore, the authorities made me a spirit,
to repay this debt. Once finished,
I would be reborn as a man and attain longevity.
Now the repayment is complete,
please prepare wine for our farewell."
She then fully revealed her form,
with dignified and charming features,
and gentle, graceful speech.
She earnestly expressed her thanks,
sobbing as she said:
"Take care, take care."
And then she vanished.
Lín Chāngyè
was a man of Zhāngpǔ.
He was widely read in the classics and histories,
and had delved deeply into the arts of divination.
His nature was lofty and refined,
and people could not impose upon him.
He once served as Military Advisor in Quánzhōu,
and at over seventy years of age,
he retired to the southern side of Guān'é Mountain in Lóngxī County of his home commandery.
The local villagers revered him.
He owned several qǐng of good farmland,
and once wished to hull grain into rice,
to transport to the prefecture for sale.
Before he could gather the labor,
suddenly a man with double topknots,
about thirty years old,
with a very long beard,
came to visit Lín.
Lín asked who he was,
but he only smiled slightly,
and murmured without answering.
Lín knew he was a ghostly being,
and ordered his family to feed him,
and he left after eating his fill.
The next day,
they suddenly heard the sound of hulling grain from the granary.
Looking,
it was the man from the previous day.
He was taking grain and hulling it.
Lín asked him:
"Why do you toil without reason?"
The ghost also smiled without speaking.
Lín again set out a lavish meal,
but the ghost only ate vegetables.
For over a month,
he hulled grain without ceasing.
The ghost then measured it by the dǒu himself,
obtaining over fifty dàn of rice.
He bowed in farewell and departed,
ultimately without a single word.
He never came again.
Pān Xí
Pān Xí was the magistrate of Jiàn'ān.
He dispatched a clerk to deliver a warrant to the countryside,
to make an arrest.
The clerk was newly assigned to the task,
and had never traveled this road before.
At dusk,
there was a thatched hut by the roadside.
He knocked on the door seeking lodging.
Only a woman answered the door from within the household,
saying:
"The master is not home,
and we are about to move residence,
so I have no leisure to host a guest."
The clerk, citing the long road and many tigers,
pleaded desperately.
The woman then called him inside by the door,
where he spread a mat on the ground to sleep.
The woman busied herself packing boxes, trunks, and various utensils,
and stayed awake until dawn.
The clerk left at daybreak,
and after traveling several lǐ,
he realized he had lost the warrant he was carrying.
He returned to search for it.
The place he had stayed was actually a grave,
and he saw the family members were in the process of reburying it.
When they opened the coffin,
under the mat they found a document,
which was the lost warrant.
Hú Chéng
Hú Chéng was a man of Chíyáng.
He worked as a hired farmhand to support himself.
His wife died,
and the authorities provided a coffin for burial.
All her usual clothing and ornaments
were placed inside the coffin.
Several years later,
Chéng happened to go to the market,
and saw a vendor at a stall selling hair ornaments.
He looked closely.
They were the burial objects for his wife.
He asked the person,
who said:
"A woman left these here,
agreeing to come fetch them on a certain day."
Chéng went again on the appointed day,
and indeed saw his wife take the payment and leave.
Chéng then followed behind her,
to the outskirts,
and caught up to her.
His wife said:
"When I was buried before,
the authorities provided the burial vessel.
Although it spared me exposed bones,
to this day the officials in charge are pressing for payment.
Having no means to manage it,
I sold these to repay the debt."
Having spoken, she vanished.
Chéng subsequently became a monk.
Wáng Pān
Wáng Pān was a physician of Gāoyóu County.
The local village regarded him as an elder.
He constantly traveled to and from east of Guǎnglíng city.
Every few months,
he would make one trip to the county.
Thinking to himself that he should go to the county the next day,
that evening he wished to exit the East Water Gate,
travel by small boat at night,
and arrive by dawn.
Afterward, he drank with relatives and friends at a tavern,
unconsciously becoming heavily drunk.
He mistakenly exited the Cānzuǒ Gate,
and went to lodge at a village house.
Toward dawn, he sobered slightly.
There was a lamp on the east wall, but not very bright.
Looking up at the room,
he knew it was not his usual lodging place.
He thus sighed alone, saying:
"I must reach the county tomorrow,
but where am I now?"
After a long while,
he then heard the sound of shuffling footsteps inside.
A woman asked from the other side of the partition:
"Where is the guest going?"
He thus rose and apologized, saying:
"I wish to go to Gāoyóu,
but in my drunkenness I mistakenly came here."
The woman said:
"This is not the road to Gāoyóu.
I will have someone escort you to the east of the city.
Do not worry."
Thereupon a village youth arrived,
and he followed him as they walked.
Whenever they encountered difficult or dangerous spots,
the youth would support his feet with his hands to help him across.
After following him to the east city inn where he usually lodged,
he bid farewell and left.
Pān took off his short jacket to give to him.
The youth would not accept it.
Pān insisted on giving it,
and he then took it and left.
Afterward, Pān entered the inn to change clothes.
He then saw his short jacket was still under his waist.
He immediately went again to the place to search for it.
There was only an ancient grave mound,
and no houses at all.
Zhèng Shǒuchéng
Zhèng Shǒuchéng was a junior officer in Guǎnglíng.
He had newly bought a maidservant.
After ten days,
someone knocked on the door at night, saying:
"Your household has bought a maidservant.
Her register of names is here.
You cannot keep her."
Opening the door to look,
he saw nothing.
He was just wondering about it
when, a few days later,
a great epidemic struck Guǎnglíng.
This maidservant also fell ill,
and subsequently died.
Soon after, Shǒuchéng also fell ill and died.
And several condolence visitors
who transmitted it to each other
all died.
This was in the spring of the jiǎyín year.
Liú Zhì
Liú Zhì was a native of Gāo'ān, Hóngzhōu.
In his youth, he encountered turmoil.
He had an elder sister named Fènsǎo,
who was captured by the military commander Sūn Jīn.
He had a younger sister named Wūtóu,
who died at the age of seventeen.
Three years after her death,
Sūn Jīn became the Deputy Military Training Commissioner of Chángzhōu.
Fènsǎo, accompanying her mistress, attended a banquet at the home of General Chén,
and there she saw Wūtóu.
She asked her where she had come from.
Wūtóu replied:
"Some time ago, I was captured by someone
and taken to Yuèzhōu,
where I became the daughter of an old couple named Liú.
I married a soldier from the north named Rén,
who is one of the troops under General Chén's command.
I came here with him."
News was sent to her family.
At that time, Liú Zhì was a local constable in the county.
Several years later,
while on business in the capital,
he went to Kūnlíng to visit her.
He stayed overnight at an inn.
The next day,
he first paid a visit to Sūn Jīn.
Then he went to Rén's camp.
He first sent a young servant to spy on the situation.
The servant saw her sweeping the courtyard,
and she said:
"My brother is about to arrive."
After a while, the servant knocked on the door.
She asked who it was.
He said:
"A messenger from the Liú family of Gāo'ān."
She then said:
"Is it my second brother, Liú Zhì, the one with a thick beard?
He should have arrived last night.
Why is he so late?"
She immediately went out of the camp gate to welcome him.
Her appearance was just as before.
They met and wept sorrowfully,
with no difference at all.
After a while,
Sūn Jīn sent his nephews with wine and food
to Rén's residence.
They feasted and talked for a long time.
Wūtóu said:
"Today, with my second brother's arrival,
I can prove that I am human.
Before, people often called me a ghost."
Rén also mentioned that her movements were light and agile,
her needlework swift and skillful,
and she often worked through the night until dawn,
as if someone were working alongside her.
She always waited for her food to cool before eating.
Liú Zhì secretly asked her:
"You died back then;
how did you end up here?"
She replied:
"Brother, do not ask such questions,
or we will not be able to meet again."
Liú Zhì dared not speak of it further.
Later, Rén died.
She remarried a soldier named Luó,
who was stationed in Jiāngzhōu.
Chén Chéngzhāo was appointed as the Military Commissioner of Gāo'ān.
He summoned Liú Zhì to inquire about the matter.
He ordered the tomb to be opened for inspection.
The tomb was located at Mǐlǐng,
and no one had visited it
for decades.
They cut through trees and cleared a path to reach it.
They saw a hole on the tomb,
as large as a bowl,
and its depth was unfathomable.
Everyone was afraid and dared not open it.
They retreated and sat under a large tree,
wrote down the details of the matter,
and reported it to Chéngzhāo.
That year,
Wūtóu fell ill.
Liú Zhì went to visit her,
and she said:
"Recently, more than ten villagers
came with knives and sticks to attack me,
nearly hitting my face.
I scolded them loudly
and resisted with all my strength.
Then they retreated and sat under a large tree,
wrote something down, and left.
To this day, my whole body still aches."
Liú Zhì then realized that she often entered and exited the tomb.
Because of this, he also became fearful and distanced himself from her.
Later, Luó was transferred to serve under
Gēshū Hàn.
In his youth, Gēshū Hàn
was ambitious and spirited.
In Cháng'ān, he associated with heroes and knights.
His residence was in Xīnshū
Ward.
He had a beloved concubine,
named Péi Liùniáng,
whose beauty was unparalleled.
She lived in Chóngrén,
and Gēshū Hàn was very fond of her.
Not long after,
Gēshū Hàn had some business
and traveled to the outskirts of the capital.
He returned only after several months.
When he arrived,
his concubine had already died of illness.
Gēshū Hàn deeply mourned her.
As dusk fell,
he stayed overnight at her residence.
She had not yet been buried;
her coffin was placed in the inner hall.
Since there was no other room,
Gēshū Hàn said:
"My love for her in life
should not be separated by death."
He slept alone in the mourning tent.
After midnight,
the moonlight shone brightly in the courtyard.
Gēshū Hàn, filled with sorrow, sighed and could not sleep.
Suddenly, he saw something at the door screen,
tilting its head and peeping inside.
It hesitated, moving back and forth.
It entered the courtyard—
it was a yaksha.
About ten feet tall,
wearing leopard-skin trousers,
with jagged teeth and disheveled hair.
Three more ghosts followed it in.
They pulled out red ropes
and danced under the moonlight.
They spoke among themselves:
"What about the nobleman on the bed?"
Another said:
"He is asleep."
They then ascended the steps,
entered the mourning hall, and opened the coffin.
They carried the coffin into the moonlight,
broke it open, and took out the corpse.
They dismembered the limbs,
sat in a circle, and devoured it together.
Blood flowed in the courtyard,
and clothing and belongings were scattered everywhere.
Gēshū Hàn was terrified
and also pained by the sight.
He thought to himself:
"Earlier, they called me a nobleman.
If I attack them now,
I will surely come to no harm."
He secretly took a pole from outside the tent
and suddenly threw it out from the darkness,
shouting loudly as he attacked the ghosts.
The ghosts were greatly frightened and fled.
Gēshū Hàn chased them to the northwest corner,
where they climbed over the wall and escaped.
One ghost lagged behind
and could not get over the wall.
Gēshū Hàn struck it, causing it to bleed,
and it managed to escape.
The household servants heard the commotion
and rushed to rescue him.
Gēshū Hàn recounted everything that had happened.
They went to collect the remaining bones,
but when they reached the hall,
the mourning site was undisturbed, just as before,
and there was no trace of the devoured flesh.
Gēshū Hàn was bewildered,
thinking it might have been a dream.
However, upon inspection, there was blood on the wall,
and marks were left there.
In the end, they never understood what had truly happened.
Several years later,
Gēshū Hàn achieved prominence and success.
Zhāngchóu Jiānqióng
When Zhāngchóu Jiānqióng was governing Shǔ,
a grand assembly was held at a Buddhist temple.
Various performances were taking place in the courtyard,
and a ten-year-old child was dancing atop a pole
when suddenly a creature,
resembling an eagle or an owl,
swooped down and carried him away.
The crowd was greatly terrified,
and the festivities were halted.
Several days later,
the child’s parents saw him atop a high pagoda.
They fetched a ladder to retrieve him,
but his spirit and appearance seemed dazed.
After a long while, he finally spoke,
saying he had seen something like a flying yakṣa from a mural,
which took him into the pagoda.
Each day, it fed him delicious food and drink,
though he did not know where it came from.
After ten days,
he gradually regained his normal spirits.
Yáng Shènjīn
During the Kāiyuán era,
Yáng Shènjīn served as Vice Censor-in-Chief.
One day,
as he was about to go to court,
a servant opened the outer gate for him.
After unlocking it,
the gate became stuck and could not be opened.
Shènjīn was both alarmed and puzzled.
As dawn approached,
his attendants saw from outside that at Shènjīn’s gate stood a yakṣa,
over ten feet tall,
of extremely bizarre appearance,
standing under the eaves,
using both hands to hold the gate shut.
Its mouth blazed like fire, and its eyes flashed like lightning,
glaring
and looking around.
When the attendants saw it,
they were all terrified and scattered in all directions.
After a while, as more carriages, horses, and people appeared on the street,
the yakṣa finally headed south and left.
Those who saw it
all fled in panic or fell to the ground.
When Shènjīn heard of this,
he was greatly frightened.
A little over a month later,
he was falsely accused by Lǐ Línfǔ,
and he and his brothers were all executed.
A Man from South of the Yangtze Named Wú
There was a man named Wú,
a native of the region south of the Yangtze.
He once traveled to Kuàijī
and married a woman from the Liú family.
Several years later,
Wú was appointed magistrate of a county in Yànmén Commandery,
and he took Liú with him to his post.
Initially, Liú was known for her gentleness and meekness,
and this lasted for several years.
Later, she suddenly became wild and violent, unrestrained and uncontrollable.
Whenever anyone displeased her,
she would fly into a rage.
She would beat her maids and servants,
sometimes even biting their flesh until it bled,
and her anger would not subside.
Wú then realized that Liú was fierce and cruel,
and his heart gradually turned away from her.
One day,
Wú went hunting in the wilds with several officers from Yànmén,
and they caught many foxes and hares,
which they brought back to the kitchen.
The next day,
after Wú had gone out,
Liú secretly entered the kitchen
and devoured the foxes and hares raw.
When she had nearly finished them all,
Wú returned
and asked where the foxes and hares were.
Liú bowed her head and remained silent.
Wú grew angry
and questioned the maids,
who said,
"Lady Liú has eaten them all."
Wú then began to suspect that Liú was some kind of monster.
Over ten days later,
a county clerk
presented a deer as a gift.
Wú ordered it to be placed in the courtyard.
Then he pretended he was going on a long journey
and left the house,
but he hid himself and secretly watched.
He saw Liú with her hair disheveled and her arms bared,
her eyes wide with rage,
her appearance completely transformed.
Standing in the courtyard,
she held the deer in her left hand
and tore out its liver with her right hand, eating it.
Wú was terrified
and fell to the ground, unable to get up.
After a long while,
he summoned over a dozen guards
and entered with weapons in hand.
When Liú saw Wú coming,
she stripped off her sleeves
and stood erect in the courtyard,
revealing herself to be a yakṣa.
Her eyes flashed like lightning,
her teeth were like spear blades,
her muscles and bones were coiled and twisted,
and her entire body was bluish in color.
The guards all trembled with fear and dared not approach.
The yakṣa looked around in all directions,
as if afraid of something.
After only the time it takes to eat a meal,
it suddenly ran eastward
with great speed
and vanished without a trace.
Zhū Xiàn’s Daughter
In Wǔlíng Commandery, there was a Buddhist pagoda,
several hundred fathoms high.
It overlooked a great river,
and whenever the river waters surged and swelled,
the pagoda seemed as if it were swaying,
so the local people dared not climb it.
There was a merchant named Zhū Xiàn,
whose family was extremely wealthy.
He had a daughter,
who, for no apparent reason, disappeared.
Her family searched for her,
for barely over ten days,
but could not find where she had gone.
One day,
after the rain had cleared,
the commandery's people saw atop the pagoda
what seemed like a person standing there,
faintly visible in patterned silk clothing.
The people initially thought it was some other strange creature.
Xiàn heard of this
and immediately went to see for himself.
Looking at the clothing,
it greatly resembled his daughter's,
so he ordered someone to climb up and retrieve her.
It was indeed his daughter.
Xiàn, shocked, questioned her about what had happened.
The girl said:
"I was alone earlier,
when a yaksha over ten feet tall,
very bizarre and strange,
leaped down from the roof
into my room,
and said to me:
'Do not fear me.'
He then grabbed my clothes and swiftly carried me away,
to the top of this pagoda.
Afterward, I was dazed and confused,
as if heavily intoxicated.
For several days,
I only gradually regained awareness,
and thus was extremely frightened.
That yaksha would always descend the pagoda just before dawn,
go into the village,
and fetch food and drink for me.
One day,
as the yaksha had just left,
I looked down and saw him
walking in the village,
where he happened to meet a person dressed in white.
When the yaksha saw him,
he retreated in fear over a hundred paces,
not daring even to steal a glance.
When he returned at dusk,
I thus questioned him:
'Why are you afraid of the person in white?'
The yaksha said:
'That person in white
has never eaten the flesh of sacrificial animals since childhood.
Therefore, I cannot approach him.'
I asked why,
and the yaksha said:
'Oxen are used to plow the fields,
the foundation of human livelihood.
If a person does not eat their meat,
then the Supreme Deity protects them.
Therefore, I cannot approach them.'
I silently thought to myself:
'I am a human,
separated from my parents,
forced to keep company with a different kind of creature—
is this not lamentable?'
The next day,
as the yaksha left, I prayed:
'I vow not to eat the flesh of sacrificial animals.'
I prayed thus three times.
Suddenly, the yaksha came from the commandery,
reached the base of the pagoda,
looked up at me and said:
'Why do you harbor different intentions and abandon me?
This makes me ultimately unable to approach you.
From now on, I bid you farewell.'
After these words,
he immediately headed east and ran off,
and in the end, I did not know where he went.
I was overjoyed
and thus was able to return from the pagoda."
Dù Wàn
Vice Director Dù Wàn
had an elder brother who was appointed as the county captain of Lǐngnán.
Just as he was about to take up his post,
his wife encountered a poisonous miasma,
and after a few days, she died.
It was the height of summer,
and there was no means for proper burial.
Temporarily, she was wrapped in a reed mat
and buried beside a sheer cliff.
He assumed his official duties,
constrained by official affairs,
and did not rebury her.
When he returned north,
upon reaching the cliff site,
he intended to retrieve his wife's remains.
But when he looked at the burial pit,
only the reeds remained.
He sighed, thinking they had been taken due to the extreme depth,
and was sorrowful for a long time.
There happened to be a path leading up the cliff,
and he tried following it.
After walking over a hundred paces,
he reached a stone cave,
where his wife was naked,
her appearance fierce and terrifying,
no longer recognizable.
In her arms, she held a child,
and beside the child was another,
their forms resembling rākṣasas.
Only after he called out loudly did she awaken.
The woman could not speak,
but used her hand to draw on the ground,
writing:
"After I revived some time ago,
I was taken by a yaksha.
Now these two children
are those I gave birth to."
As she wrote, she wept bitterly.
After a short while,
she was also able to speak,
and said:
"You must leave quickly.
If the yaksha should come,
he will certainly kill you."
He asked:
"Can you leave?"
She said:
"I can leave."
She then rose, picked up the smaller child,
and followed him to the boat.
They set off immediately.
The yaksha soon arrived at the shore carrying the larger child,
gazed at the boat and cried out,
showing them the child.
As the boat traveled farther away,
he tore his child into dozens of pieces,
and only then left.
The child in the woman's arms,
whose form was like a rākṣasa,
understood human speech.
During the Dàlì era,
mother and child were both still alive.
Wéi Zìdōng
During the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a man named Wéi Zìdōng,
a man of righteous and fierce courage.
He once traveled to Tàibái Mountain,
and stayed at General Duàn’s estate.
General Duàn had long known of his bravery and strength.
One day,
while gazing into the mountain valleys with Zìdōng,
they saw a very narrow path,
as if once trodden by footsteps.
Zìdōng asked his host:
"Where does this lead?"
General Duàn said:
"In the past, two monks
lived atop this mountain.
Their temple halls were grand and magnificent,
and the woods and springs were most beautiful.
It was built during the Táng dynasty’s Kāiyuán era,
by the disciples of Master Wànhuí.
It seemed as if they had employed ghostly craftsmen—
it was beyond what human strength could achieve.
Some say, according to woodcutters,
that the monks were eaten by monsters,
and for two or three years now there has been no trace of them.
I have also heard people say
that there are two yakṣas on this mountain,
and no one dares to venture near."
Zìdōng angrily said:
"My heart is set on quelling violence and aggression.
What manner of yakṣas are these,
that they dare to devour people?
Tonight,
I will surely bring the yakṣas’ heads
to your gate."
The general tried to stop him, saying:
"To attack a tiger barehanded or cross a river without a boat—
would you not regret it even unto death?"
Zìdōng paid no heed.
Grasping his sword and donning his gear, he set off—
his determination was unstoppable.
The general quietly said:
"Young Wéi will bring calamity upon himself."
Zìdōng, clinging to vines and treading upon rocks,
reached the temple.
It was silent and deserted.
He saw the two monks’ quarters,
their doors wide open,
with sandals and staffs all in place,
and bedding neatly arranged,
yet covered in a thick layer of dust.
He also saw inside the Buddha hall,
fine grass growing lushly,
as if a huge creature had lain there to sleep.
On the walls hung many kinds of wild boars and black bears,
some leftover from cooking,
and there were also cauldrons and firewood.
Zìdōng then knew the woodcutters’ words were not false.
Judging that the yakṣas had not yet arrived,
he uprooted a cypress tree—
its trunk as thick as a bowl—
stripped off its branches and leaves,
and made a large club.
He barred the door,
using a stone Buddha to block it.
That night,
the moon was bright as day.
Before midnight,
a yakṣa arrived carrying a deer.
Angered by the barred door,
it let out a great roar,
and rammed its head against the door,
breaking the stone Buddha
and falling to the ground.
Zìdōng struck its head with the cypress club,
and with a second blow killed it.
He dragged it inside,
and closed the door again.
After a short while,
another yakṣa arrived in turn,
seeming angry that the earlier returnee had not greeted it.
It too roared fiercely,
rammed against the door,
and again fell across the threshold.
Zìdōng struck it as well,
and it too died.
Knowing that both male and female were dead,
and that there should be no others of their kind,
he then barred the gate, cooked the deer, and ate.
At dawn,
he cut off the two yakṣas’ heads,
and taking the leftover deer, showed them to Duàn.
Duàn was greatly astonished and said:
"Truly, you are the equal of Zhōu Chù!"
They then cooked the deer, drank wine, and enjoyed themselves to the fullest,
with onlookers from near and far crowding around like a wall.
A Daoist priest emerged from the dense crowd,
bowed to Zìdōng and said:
"I have a heartfelt request,
which I wish to confide in you, sir.
May I?"
Zìdōng said:
"All my life I have helped others in their urgent needs—
why would it be otherwise?"
The Daoist said:
"I have devoted my heart to the Daoist path,
and earnestly sought spiritual elixirs—
not just for a day or a night.
Two or three years ago,
an immortal compounded for me a furnace of Dragon-Tiger Elixir.
I have been refining it in my cave
for some time now.
Now the elixir is nearly complete,
but repeatedly demons and monsters have entered the cave,
approaching the furnace and striking it,
nearly causing the elixir to be ruined and scattered.
I thought to find a man of fierce courage,
to stand guard with a sword.
If the elixir is successfully completed,
you shall certainly share in its benefits.
I wonder if you might make the journey?"
Zìdōng eagerly said:
"This is the wish of my life!"
So he took up his sword and followed the Daoist away.
Crossing perilous places and climbing steep heights,
they reached the high peak of Tàibái,
about halfway up,
where there was a stone cave,
some hundred paces deep.
This was the chamber where the Daoist refined his elixir,
with only one disciple inside.
The Daoist made an agreement:
"At the fifth watch tomorrow morning,
I ask you, sir, to take up your sword
and stand before the cave entrance.
If you see any monsters,
simply strike them with your sword."
Zìdōng said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
For a long time he stood holding a torch outside the cave entrance,
keeping watch.
After a short while,
sure enough, a huge serpent several zhang long appeared,
with golden eyes and snowy fangs,
its poisonous breath thick and dense,
about to enter the cave.
Zìdōng struck it with his sword,
seemingly hitting its head.
In a moment it vanished like a light mist.
After the time of a meal,
a woman appeared,
of exceedingly beautiful countenance,
holding lotus flowers,
and slowly walking forward.
Zìdōng again swept his sword at her,
and she vanished like cloud vapor.
After another meal’s time,
as dawn was about to break,
a Daoist priest appeared,
riding clouds and driving cranes,
with a retinue most solemn.
He consoled Zìdōng, saying:
"The demons and monsters are all gone.
My disciple’s elixir is about to be completed.
I have come to bear witness."
Circling and waiting until daylight, he entered,
and said to Zìdōng:
"I rejoice that your Daoist’s elixir is complete.
Now I shall compose a poem,
and you may continue with a matching verse."
The poem said:
"For three autumns I knocked at the gate of the true numinous,
When dragon and tiger joined, the golden liquor was formed.
Once crimson snow congeals, the body may transcend,
Above the Penglai peak, colored clouds arise."
Zìdōng, considering the poem’s meaning, thought:
"This is the Daoist’s master."
So he laid down his sword and bowed in respect.
Suddenly the figure rushed inside,
the elixir cauldron exploded and shattered,
leaving nothing behind.
The Daoist wailed in grief,
and Zìdōng could only regret and blame himself.
The two then washed the cauldron vessels with spring water and drank from them.
Afterward, Zìdōng’s appearance became somewhat youthful,
and he went to Nányuè,
but none know where he finally settled.
To this day, at General Duàn’s estate, the yakṣas’ skulls are still to be seen,
and the Daoist too is nowhere to be found.
Mǎ Suì
When Mǎ Suì was poor and lowly,
he traveled to Běijīng,
and went to pay respects to the prefectural governor,
but was not received and returned.
He lodged with a garden keeper,
who said:
"Do you wish to pay respects to the Garrison Commander?
If you do,
you must first speak of it,
and I will show you the way.
The Garrison Commander is extremely strict about certain taboo characters,
you must be careful,
if you violate them,
you will not escape death.
However, if you happen to please him,
the benefits you receive will be unlike those of others.
Be careful not to approach him blindly,
I am the foster son of the Garrison Commander's wet nurse,
so I know the details,
and I offer this advice to you."
Mǎ Suì was half-believing and half-doubting.
The next morning,
he went to pay respects to the Garrison Commander,
and indeed violated his taboo,
was scolded in the courtyard and driven away.
Fear and dread showed on his face,
The garden keeper said:
"You must have offended the Garrison Commander."
Mǎ Suì asked for a plan to escape,
and the garden keeper said:
"You have brought trouble upon yourself,
and are in such distress,
but if you fail, you will die,
and I cannot be implicated."
He then hid Mǎ Suì in a manure cart,
and carried him out of the city to flee.
At that time, the Garrison Commander indeed searched for Mǎ Suì,
and upon not finding him in one report,
dispatched armored cavalry,
ten men at each gate.
Mǎ Suì fled in panic for over sixty li,
and as dusk fell,
realizing he could not leave the region,
sought shelter in a ruined house of fleeing refugees.
Before he could settle,
he heard the sound of chariots and horses approaching,
and people discussing:
"Can we go another twenty or thirty li?"
It was indeed the Garrison Commander's envoys.
Soon the sound of chariots and horses gradually faded away,
and he felt slightly at ease.
Before he could catch his breath,
he heard the rustling sound of someone walking,
and Mǎ Suì trembled in fear.
Suddenly, through the window,
he saw a woman,
dressed in plain clothes,
extremely tall in stature,
holding a bundle in her hand, saying:
"Is Mǎ Suì here?"
Mǎ Suì remained silent,
not daring to answer.
She spoke again:
"Are you very frightened?
Second Sister Hú knows you are here,
and has come to comfort you,
do not worry or doubt."
Mǎ Suì then answered and came out.
Second Sister Hú said:
"A great calamity,
but it has passed,
though there is still lingering fear.
You must be hungry,
I will feed you."
She then untied the bundle she carried,
which contained a bowl of cooked meat,
and a Hú-style pancake.
Mǎ Suì ate until he was full.
She then told him to return to his original spot,
and not to move again.
Second Sister Hú took several dou of ash,
spread it on the ground in front of Mǎ Suì,
forming a horizontal line.
She then instructed him, saying:
"Tonight at midnight,
there will be strange creatures trying to frighten and harm you,
do not move at all.
After this calamity passes,
your achievements and honors will be unmatched."
After speaking, she left.
At midnight,
something glowing and shimmering approached,
gradually nearing the window.
He saw a creature,
over ten feet tall,
it was a yaksha.
Its red hair stood up like a hedgehog's spines,
its entire body sharp and gleaming,
its arms bent like gnarled wood,
its claws like beast talons,
wearing leopard-skin trousers,
carrying a short weapon,
and it entered the room directly.
Its fierce eyes flashed like lightning,
spitting fire and spewing blood,
jumping and roaring,
enough to melt iron and stone.
Mǎ Suì trembled in fear,
nearly losing his soul and spirit.
However, the creature dared not cross the ash line laid by Second Sister Hú.
After a long time,
the creature removed a door panel,
lay on it, and fell into a deep sleep.
Soon, the sound of chariots and horses was heard again,
and someone said:
"This is a refugee's house,
could Mǎ Suì be hiding here?"
At that moment, several men holding weapons,
dismounted and entered.
They startled the yaksha,
which sprang up,
roared loudly several times,
tore the men and horses apart and devoured them,
leaving almost no flesh or blood.
After the yaksha had eaten its fill,
it slowly walked out.
At the fourth watch,
the moon rose in the east,
and Mǎ Suì felt the silence,
so he came out and left,
seeing the scattered bones and flesh of men and horses,
and thus he escaped.
Later, he achieved great merits,
and his official rank rose high.
He inquired about the origins of Second Sister Hú,
but could never find out.
Unable to repay her,
he set up a separate seat for Second Sister Hú during the spring and autumn sacrifices,
placing it to the left of the temple.
Zhāng Shēng of Dōngluò
When Niú Sēngrú served as the county lieutenant of Yīquē,
there was a visitor from the eastern capital, Zhāng Shēng,
who was taking the imperial examinations.
He brought his writings to pay a visit.
On the way,
he encountered a heavy rainstorm with thunder and hail.
The day had already grown dark,
and the inn was still far away,
so he rested under a tree.
After a while,
the rain stopped and a faint moon appeared.
He then untied his saddle and let his horse graze.
Zhāng Shēng and his servant slept by the roadside,
feeling extremely exhausted.
They fell into a deep sleep and only awoke after a long time.
He saw a creature resembling a yaksha,
several zhang tall,
grabbing and devouring Zhāng Shēng’s horse.
Zhāng Shēng was terrified,
hiding in the grass,
not daring to move.
After finishing,
it took his donkey,
and when the donkey was nearly gone,
it suddenly grabbed his servant by the hand,
lifted him by his two feet, and tore him apart.
Zhāng Shēng was horrified,
and fled in panic.
The yaksha followed behind,
shouting and cursing.
After about a li,
the sounds gradually faded away.
The road led to a large tomb,
and beside the tomb stood a woman.
Zhāng Shēng repeatedly cried for help,
and the woman asked him,
so he recounted everything.
The woman said:
“This is an ancient tomb,
empty inside,
but there is an opening at the back.
You should hide there.
Otherwise,
you will not escape.”
Zhāng Shēng then searched for the tomb’s opening,
threw himself inside,
and went deep within.
After a long time, he heard no more sounds.
After a while,
he noticed the moonlight growing brighter.
Suddenly, he heard voices above the tomb,
and something being pushed,
followed by the smell of blood.
Looking,
it was a dead person,
with the head and body separated.
A moment later,
another person was pushed in,
and this happened four or five times,
all of them dead.
After it was over,
he heard the sounds of dividing money, goods, and clothes above,
and realized they were robbers.
Their leader called out,
saying such-and-such item goes to so-and-so,
such-and-such clothes and money go to so-and-so,
calling out the names of more than ten people.
Some complained it was unfair,
and there were angry arguments,
before they all dispersed.
Zhāng Shēng was extremely frightened,
wanting to leave,
but could not.
So he carefully memorized the robbers’ names,
remembering five or six of them.
By dawn,
villagers searching for the robbers
came to the tomb,
saw the blood,
and surrounded the tomb to dig it up.
They found the people killed by the robbers,
all inside.
Seeing Zhāng Shēng, they exclaimed in surprise:
“There’s also a robber who fell into the tomb!”
They dragged him out and tied him up.
Zhāng Shēng explained everything,
but they did not believe him,
saying:
“This is a robber,
who killed people and brought them here,
and accidentally fell in.”
They beat him dozens of times,
then sent him to the county office.
After traveling a li or two,
he saw his servant, donkey, horse, saddle, and baggage all arriving.
Zhāng Shēng asked in surprise:
“What happened?”
The servant replied:
“Last night, I was extremely tired,
and fell asleep by the roadside.
By dawn,
I couldn’t find you,
so I came searching.”
Zhāng Shēng then described what he had seen,
and the servant said:
“I was completely unaware of it.”
They then proceeded to the county office.
Niú Sēngrú recognized him from before,
knowing he could not have done such a thing,
so he vouched for him.
Zhāng Shēng also recalled the names of several robbers,
and reported them to the magistrate.
The magistrate dispatched officers to capture them,
and they were all apprehended,
so Zhāng Shēng was exonerated.
Reflecting on the meaning,
it was the spirits and wronged souls
using Zhāng Shēng’s hand
to capture the robbers.
Xuē Cóng
Former Presented Scholar Xuē Cóng,
during the Yuánhé era,
was traveling in the border villages of Wèizhōu and came upon an ancient temple.
As dusk fell and he wished to lodge for the night,
he and several others went to call on the master monk.
The master monk happened to be away.
They only heard groaning from a dark room west of the storehouse.
Approaching to look,
they saw an old monk who was ill.
His beard and hair were untrimmed,
white as snow,
and his appearance was fearsome.
Cóng then called to his companions:
"How strange this sick monk is!"
The monk angrily said:
"What is strange?
Young man, do you wish to hear something strange?
This sick monk will briefly tell you."
Cóng and the others said:
"Yes, yes."
He then said:
"When this sick monk was twenty years old,
I loved traveling to remote lands.
Taking medicines and abstaining from grains,
I journeyed north to Jūyán,
some thirty or fifty lǐ from the sea.
That day at dawn,
I had already traveled over ten lǐ.
As the sun was about to rise,
I suddenly saw a withered standing tree,
over three hundred zhàng tall,
several dozen arm-spans in girth,
and hollow inside.
The monk peered in from its base;
it went straight up,
its opening reaching the sky,
large enough to hold a person.
I traveled north several more lǐ,
and from afar saw a woman,
wearing a crimson skirt,
barefoot and with bared arms,
her hair disheveled as she ran,
swift as the wind.
As she drew near,
the woman said to the monk:
'Can you save me?'
I replied:
'Why?'
She said:
'Someone will come looking for me later;
just say you haven't seen me,
and I will be eternally grateful.'
In a moment,
she entered the withered tree.
I walked another three or five lǐ,
when suddenly I saw a man,
riding an armored horse,
clad in golden armor,
equipped with bow and sword.
He galloped like lightning,
each stride covering over thirty zhàng,
sometimes in the air,
sometimes on the ground,
his steps consistent.
Arriving before me, he said:
'Have you seen a person of such-and-such appearance?'
I said:
'I have not.'
He said again:
'Do not hide her;
this is not a human,
but a flying yakṣa.
Her gang numbers in the thousands,
and in succession they have harmed people sent by the heavens,
already eight hundred thousand.
Now they have all been captured and slain,
only this one, the most vicious,
remains uncaught.
Last night, thrice by the Heavenly Emperor's command,
I pursued her from Shāzhā Heaven,
and have come eighty-four thousand lǐ to this place.
Eight thousand like me are scattered in pursuit;
to shelter her is to offend Heaven,
and you, Master, should not protect her.'
I then told him everything.
In a moment,
we reached the withered tree.
I turned back to watch;
the heavenly envoy dismounted,
entered the tree and peered inside.
Then he remounted,
soared into the air and circled upward around the tree.
When man and horse were about halfway up the tree,
I saw a crimson speck emerge from the tree and flee.
The man and horse pursued it;
after some seventy or eighty zhàng,
they gradually entered the firmament,
vanishing into the azure sky.
After a long while,
several dozen drops of blood rained down,
suggesting she had been struck by an arrow.
This can be considered strange.
For you young men to find this sick monk strange—
is that not rather shallow?"
Qiū Rú
Doctor Qiū Rú related:
Fifty years ago in a county adjacent to Rǔzhōu,
a villager lost his daughter.
Several years later,
she suddenly returned on her own.
She said that initially, something had pulled her away in her sleep,
and in an instant she was brought to a place.
At dawn,
she found herself in an ancient pagoda,
where she saw a handsome man,
who said to her:
"I am a heavenly being,
destined to have you as my wife.
There is a set period of time;
do not doubt or fear."
He also warned her not to look outside.
Twice a day he would descend to fetch food,
sometimes still hot from roasting.
After a year,
the girl waited until he left,
secretly peeped,
and saw him soar into the air as if flying,
his skin emitting blue flames,
his ears split like a donkey's.
Upon landing,
he resumed human form.
The girl was terrified and drenched in sweat.
When the creature returned,
he sensed it and said:
"You have spied on me.
I am indeed a yakṣa,
but I am fated with you,
and will ultimately not harm you."
The girl, being clever,
apologized:
"Since I am your wife,
how could I bear ill will?
Since you possess spiritual powers,
why not live among humans,
so that I may occasionally see my parents?"
The creature said:
"Due to my karmic offenses,
if I mingle with people,
epidemics will arise.
Now that my true form is revealed,
you may observe freely,
but soon I must send you back."
The pagoda was very close to human dwellings;
the girl often looked down,
and saw that the creature in the air
could not transform his shape,
but upon landing,
would mingle with people.
If there was someone in white among the crowd,
the creature would clasp his hands and avoid them.
If someone rested their head on him or spat in his face,
the passersby all acted as if they saw nothing.
Upon his return,
the girl asked:
"Earlier in the street,
some respected you,
while others teased and harassed you—
why is that?"
The creature laughed and said:
"In this world, those who eat beef,
I can deceive.
But if I mistakenly offend those who are loyal, upright, filial,
or Buddhist or Daoist practitioners who uphold precepts and dharma records,
I would be
slain by Heaven."
Another year passed,
when suddenly he wept sorrowfully and told the girl:
"Our缘分已尽,
await wind and rain to send you back."
He then gave her a blue stone,
the size of a chicken egg,
saying that upon returning home,
she should grind it and take it,
as it could expel poisonous qi.
Later, one evening during wind and thunder,
the creature quickly took the girl and said:
"You may go now."
As in Buddhist tales,
in the time it takes to bend and stretch an arm,
she was already at her home,
landing in the courtyard.
Her mother then ground the stone and gave it to her to drink,
and she expelled over a dou of bluish mud-like substance.
Chén Yuèshí
In Yǐngzhōu, there was Chén Yuèshí,
originally named Chén Huángshí,
who lived in the countryside in the Wángwū Mountains.
He had a concubine named Zhāng shì.
During the Yuánhé era,
Chén Yuèshí and Zhāng shì were eating together one night
when suddenly, from behind the candle’s shadow,
they heard a very strange breathing sound.
Soon, a hand emerged
and reached in front of Chén Yuèshí.
The hand was bluish-black in color,
with short fingers,
long, slender nails,
and yellow hair extending up the arm,
appearing as if begging for food.
Chén Yuèshí knew well it was a monster,
and felt both disgust and fear.
After a while,
a voice came from beneath the candle’s shadow:
“I am suffering from hunger,
so I have come to pay my respects.
I wish to have a little meat placed in my palm,
and hope you will not refuse me.”
Chén Yuèshí then threw a small piece of meat onto the ground,
and the hand immediately took it and withdrew.
It then said:
“This meat tastes very good.”
After finishing it,
the hand again reached out in front of Chén Yuèshí.
Chén Yuèshí angrily scolded it:
“Why does this demon keep coming?
You should leave quickly.
If not,
I will strike you—
do you not fear regret?”
The hand then withdrew,
as if afraid.
A moment later,
the hand emerged again,
this time reaching in front of Zhāng shì,
and said to her:
“Young lady, could you bestow a little meat upon me?”
Chén Yuèshí said to Zhāng shì:
“Be careful not to give it anything.”
Zhāng shì ultimately did not give it anything.
After a while,
suddenly, beside the candle’s shadow, a face appeared—
it was a yaksha,
with disheveled red hair,
eyes like lightning,
and four teeth like sharp blades,
truly terrifying.
It struck Zhāng shì with its hand,
and she immediately fell to the ground,
unconscious and unable to move.
Chén Yuèshí was brave and daring,
so he rose and chased it,
and the yaksha fled,
not daring to look back.
The next day,
they traced its tracks,
and found footprints on the wall.
Chén Yuèshí said:
“This creature will surely come again tonight.”
So that night,
he stood holding a staff beneath the northeastern wall,
waiting for it.
After barely the time of a meal,
the yaksha indeed returned.
As soon as it crossed the wall,
before its feet touched the ground,
Chén Yuèshí struck it dozens of times in succession with his staff.
After the yaksha left,
he examined the base of the wall by candlelight
and found a great deal of blood,
along with a piece of skin over a foot long
lying on the ground—
likely torn off by the blows.
From then on, Zhāng shì recovered from her illness.
That evening,
they heard a voice calling from several miles away:
“Chén Huángshí, why do you not return my skin to me?”
It called out repeatedly without ceasing.
For over a month,
every night,
they would hear the calling.
Chén Yuèshí reckoned he could not stop it,
and moreover detested being called by that name,
so he moved away to avoid it,
and consequently changed his name to Yuèshí.
In the fifteenth year of the Yuánhé era,
he passed the imperial examination as a jìnshì,
and by the second year of the Huìchāng era,
he died while serving as magistrate of Lántián.
Zhāng Róng
Zhāng Róng of Bóhǎi,
styled Méiyú.
During the Xiánníng era of the Jìn dynasty,
his daughter-in-law gave birth to a boy,
and at first, nothing unusual was noticed.
By the age of seven,
he was exceptionally intelligent and clever.
Once, Zhāng Róng took him to watch archery,
and when he sent someone to retrieve the arrows,
they were always too slow.
Zhāng Róng’s grandson said:
“I will fetch them for you, sir.”
Later, as soon as an arrow was shot,
he rushed forward,
and arrived at the target together with the arrow.
In an instant, he had already grabbed the arrow and returned,
astonishing everyone present.
Two days later,
the grandson suddenly fell violently ill and died.
As they were preparing for the funeral,
they called Buddhist monks to burn incense,
and one foreign monk said:
“You must quickly encoffin this grandson—
he is a rākṣasa ghost,
and would have devoured and harmed your family.”
After witnessing the arrow-retrieving incident,
they hastily closed the coffin in panic.
Soon after,
they heard thumping and struggling sounds from within the coffin,
and everyone stopped mourning in shock and terror,
quickly sending it off for burial.
Later, it appeared several times in form,
but when Zhāng Róng performed the Eight Precepts fasting ritual,
it then departed.
Yùndū Shī
The monk Xíng Yùn of Jīngxíng Temple,
served as the head monk of his temple.
Once, as early autumn approached,
preparations were being made for the Ullambana festival,
and the halls and shrines were being cleaned and swept,
arranging the Buddhist ceremonies in order.
He saw a paper effigy before one of the Buddhas,
with enchanting, seductive features,
holding a lotus flower in its hand,
seeming to gaze at people with intent.
The master thus jokingly said to the servant attending him:
"If there were a woman in this world
who resembled this one,
I would take her as my wife."
That evening, upon returning to his quarters,
before midnight had arrived,
there came a knock at the door, saying:
"The Lotus Maiden has come."
Head Monk Yùn, not yet realizing the truth,
immediately responded:
"The official laws and prohibitions are extremely strict;
now the temple gates are already closed—
how has my lady come here?"
Once the door was opened,
Lotus and a maidservant accompanying her,
with bewitching beauty and lovely features,
exquisite beyond compare,
said to Head Monk Yùn:
"Through many eons of immeasurable good karma,
I have always been able to personally serve the Great Perfect Right Wisdom.
Never did I expect that today,
hearing the master's words,
I would suddenly give rise to worldly thoughts.
Now I have been banished to become human,
and should serve you, holding your towel and alms bowl.
The intention you expressed this morning—
have you so quickly forgotten it?"
Head Monk Yùn said:
"I am truly ignorant and dull-witted,
and have long upheld the monastic precepts.
I have never met you before,
nor have I ever seen my lady."
Thus he tried to deceive her.
"Just today,
in the morning, the master saw me before the Buddha,
and said to your servant,
'If there were one whose looks resembled mine,
I would take her as my wife.'
The words are still ringing in my ears;
moved by the master's words,
I sincerely wish to offer myself to you."
Then, taking the paper effigy from her sleeve, she said:
"How can this be deception?"
Monk Yùn realized she was not human,
and in his moment of panic and confusion,
Lotus immediately turned to her maidservant and said:
"Lù Xiān, prepare the bed curtains."
Lù Xiān then arranged the sleeping quarters,
all extremely luxurious and beautiful.
Though Yùn was alarmed and bewildered,
his heart was also pleased,
and he said to Lotus:
"I have indeed pledged my heart.
But according to monastic rules, it is not permitted
to reside long within the temple compound—
what should we do?"
Lotus laughed heartily and said:
"I am a heavenly being;
how could ordinary understanding reach me?
Moreover, I will certainly not cause trouble for the master."
Thereupon they conversed intimately,
her words gentle and graceful.
Soon the candles were extinguished,
and the young novices still secretly listened and watched.
Not long after,
they suddenly heard Yùn cry out in pain,
his agony reaching an extreme.
Quickly they brought torches to illuminate the scene,
but upon arriving, the door was barred,
and they could not force it open.
They only heard the sounds of gnashing teeth, chewing grime, and crunching bones,
and a voice like that of a foreigner loudly cursing:
"You thieving, bald slave!
You were sent forth from your family to shave your head and become a monk—
why did you give rise to such deluded thoughts?
Even if I were truly a woman,
how could I ever marry you and become your wife?"
Thereupon they rushed to inform the whole temple community,
broke through a wall to peer inside,
and saw that it was two yakshas,
with saw-like teeth and bristling hair,
tall as giants,
roaring and seizing their prey,
leaping and bounding away.
Later, the monks saw on the wall behind the Buddha's seat,
two painted yakshas,
exactly like those they had witnessed,
with traces of blood still visible between their lips.
Páng Ā
In Jùlù, there was a man named Páng Ā,
handsome and elegant in appearance.
In the same commandery, a man named Shí had a daughter
who once saw Ā indoors
and took a liking to him.
Not long after,
Ā saw this girl come to visit him.
Ā.
Ā's wife was extremely jealous,
and upon hearing of this,
had her maidservant bind the girl,
who then returned to the Shí household.
Along the way,
she transformed into mist and vanished.
The maidservant then went straight to the Shí house
and reported the matter.
The girl's father was greatly astonished and said:
"My daughter never leaves the house;
how could you slander her like this?"
From then on, Ā's wife constantly kept a close watch.
One night,
just as she encountered the girl in the study,
she seized her herself
and took her to the Shí household.
When the girl's father saw her,
he was stunned and said:
"I have just come from inside,
and saw my daughter working together with her mother.
How can she be here?"
He immediately ordered the maidservants and attendants
to call his daughter out from inside.
The one who had been bound
suddenly vanished.
The father, suspecting something strange,
thus sent the girl's mother to question her.
The girl said:
"Years ago, when Páng Ā came to the main hall,
I secretly caught sight of him.
From then on, as if in a dream,
I would go to visit Ā in my dreams.
But as soon as I entered his door,
I was seized by his wife."
Shí said:
"So there really are such strange happenings in this world."
When feelings are deeply stirred,
the spirit manifests in hidden ways;
what vanished was likely her ethereal soul.
Afterward, the girl vowed not to marry anyone else.
A year later,
Ā's wife suddenly fell ill with a malignant disease,
and medicine proved ineffective.
Ā then sent betrothal gifts and took the Shí family's daughter as his wife.
Mǎ Shì's Wife
Mǎ Shì's wife, from Fùyáng in the state of Wú,
surnamed Jiǎng,
whenever a villager was about to die of illness,
Jiǎng would become dazed and confused,
falling into a deep sleep for a whole day.
She would witness the person's death,
and only afterward awaken,
then describe everything in detail.
Her family did not believe her.
She told people:
"When someone is ill,
I wish to kill them,
but angry, strong spirits are hard to kill.
If they do not die immediately,
I enter their household.
On the shelf, there are several kinds of pickled fish with white rice;
I pass by the kitchen for a moment to play.
A maidservant offends me for no reason,
so I beat her severely,
causing the maidservant to faint at the time,
and only after a long while does she revive."
When her elder brother fell ill,
a man in black clothing ordered her to kill him,
but she pleaded with him,
and in the end did not strike.
Upon waking, she told her brother
that he would live.
The Anonymous Couple
There was a common man and woman,
whose names have been forgotten.
One day,
the wife rose first,
and her husband soon also went out.
Thinking her husband was still asleep,
she returned inside,
only to see her husband still under the covers.
Shortly after, a servant boy came in from outside and said:
"He just told me to fetch a mirror."
Suspecting the servant was lying,
the wife pointed to the bed to show him.
The servant said:
"I just came from where the master is."
She then rushed to tell her husband,
who was greatly astonished.
He went straight in to see for himself,
and together with his wife observed
the person in the bed, sleeping peacefully on a high pillow,
truly his own likeness,
without the slightest difference.
Fearing it was his soul,
they dared not disturb it.
They slowly patted the bed,
and it gradually sank into the mat and vanished.
The husband and wife were filled with sorrow and terror.
After a short while,
the husband suddenly fell ill,
his nature and reason became disordered,
and he never recovered for the rest of his life.
Wáng Zhòu
In the third year of the Tiānshòu era,
Zhāng Yì of Qīnghé, due to his official post, made his home in Héngzhōu.
He was of a simple and quiet nature,
with few close friends.
He had no sons,
but two daughters.
The elder had died early,
and the younger, named Qiànniáng,
was exceptionally beautiful and graceful.
Zhāng Yì's nephew from Tàiyuán, Wáng Zhòu,
was intelligent and perceptive from a young age,
and handsome in appearance.
Zhāng Yì often held him in high regard,
and would frequently say:
"When the time comes, I shall give Qiànniáng to him as his wife."
Later, as they both grew up,
Zhòu and Qiànniáng
often secretly longed for each other day and night,
though none in the household knew of their feelings.
Later, a colleague seeking a match proposed,
and Zhāng Yì agreed.
Upon hearing this, the girl became deeply depressed,
and Zhòu was also filled with resentment.
Using the pretext of an official transfer,
he requested to go to the capital.
Unable to stop him,
they sent him off with generous gifts.
Zhòu, harboring secret grief and sorrow,
bid farewell and boarded the boat.
At dusk,
he reached a few miles from a mountain village.
In the middle of the night,
Zhòu, unable to sleep,
suddenly heard hurried footsteps on the shore,
and in a moment, someone reached the boat.
He asked who it was,
and it was Qiànniáng,
who had come barefoot, walking alone.
Overjoyed and beside himself,
Zhòu took her hand and asked how she had come.
Weeping, she said:
"Your affection for me is so profound,
that in my sleep and meals,
I was deeply moved.
Now they intend to force me to abandon this resolve,
and knowing your deep feelings would not change,
I thought to give my life in return.
Therefore, I have fled to join you."
This was beyond Zhòu's hopes,
and he was exceedingly delighted.
So he hid Qiànniáng on the boat,
and they fled under cover of night.
Traveling day and night,
they reached Shǔ in a few months.
Over five years,
they had two sons.
Having cut off all communication with Zhāng Yì,
his wife often missed her parents,
and said through tears:
"In the past, I could not betray you,
so I abandoned my duty and came to you.
Now five years have passed,
separated from my parents' kindness.
Under heaven and earth,
how can I bear to live alone with shame?"
Zhòu pitied her and said:
"Let us return, do not grieve."
So they went back together to Héngzhōu.
Upon arrival,
Zhòu went alone first to Zhāng Yì's home,
and confessed the whole matter.
Zhāng Yì said:
"Qiàn
niáng has been ill in her chamber for years,
how can you speak such nonsense?"
Zhòu said:
"She is in the boat now."
Zhāng Yì was greatly shocked,
and hurriedly sent someone to verify.
Sure enough, they saw Qiànniáng in the boat,
her complexion cheerful and serene.
She asked the messenger:
"Are my parents well?"
The household found this strange,
and rushed back to report to Zhāng Yì.
The girl in the chamber heard this,
rose happily,
adorned herself and changed clothes,
smiled without speaking,
went out to meet her,
and the two merged into one,
their clothes overlapping.
The family, considering the matter unnatural,
kept it secret,
though some relatives came to know of it privately.
Forty years later,
the couple passed away,
and their two sons both passed the imperial examinations as Xiàolián,
rising to positions of Chéng and Wèi.
This story comes from Chén Xuányòu's "Record of the Departed Soul."
Xuányòu heard this tale often in his youth,
with many variations,
some claiming it was fictitious.
At the end of the Dàlì era,
he met Zhāng Zhòng□, Magistrate of Láiwú County,
who recounted the story in full detail.
Zhāng Yì was Zhāng Zhòng□'s paternal uncle,
and his account was extremely thorough,
hence it was recorded.
Zhèng Qíyīng,
during the Kāiyuán era,
served as Vice Minister of Personnel and Imperial Inspector of Hénán.
As he was returning,
passing through Huàzhōu,
he suddenly saw five men,
dressed in the colors of the five directions,
approach the hall and bow twice.
Qíyīng asked their reason,
and they replied:
"We are the Five Visceral Spirits of Your Excellency."
Qíyīng asked:
"Spirits should reside within the body,
why do you appear before me?"
They answered:
"We guard the vital breath,
and when the breath is exhausted, we disperse."
Qíyīng said:
"If this is truly so,
am I about to die?"
They said:
"Yes."
Qíyīng hastily begged for a brief extension,
wishing to prepare a memorial and settle matters after his death.
The spirits said he could return to the rear office for this.
Qíyīng prepared wine and food for them,
which they all accepted with bows.
After composing the memorial,
he bathed,
put on new clothes,
lay down beneath the western wall,
and at the appointed time, passed away.
Liǔ Shǎoyóu
Liǔ Shàoyóu was skilled in divination,
and was renowned in the capital.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
a visitor came holding a piece of fine silk,
and went to see Shàoyóu.
He was invited in and asked the reason for his visit,
to which he replied:
"I wish to know my fate and lifespan."
Shàoyóu performed a divination for him,
and upon completing it, sighed sorrowfully, saying:
"Your divination is inauspicious,
indicating your life will end this very evening."
The man grieved and sighed for a long time,
then asked for some water.
A family member brought water,
and saw two Shàoyóus,
unable to tell which one was the guest.
Shàoyóu pointed to the spirit as the guest,
and instructed it to be given to the guest.
The guest then took his leave,
and a servant boy saw him out the door.
After a few steps, he vanished.
Soon, the sound of weeping was heard in the air,
very mournful.
Upon returning, they asked Shàoyóu:
"Did you, sir, recognize this person?"
He recounted the earlier events in detail,
and only then did Shàoyóu realize the guest was his own spirit.
He hastily had someone look at the silk.
It was merely a piece of paper silk.
He sighed and said:
"My spirit has left me,
I am about to die."
At dusk, he indeed passed away.
Sū Lái
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
in Cháng'ān, there was a woman named Mǎ Èrniáng,
who was skilled in summoning spirits.
Sū Shēn, the governor of Yǎnzhōu,
was on good terms with the Mǎ family.
Initially, Shēn wanted to seek a marriage with the Lú family for his son Lái.
He said to Mǎ:
"I have only one son,
and for his marriage,
it is essential to find a gentle and virtuous bride.
The Lú family has three daughters,
but I do not know which one is best.
I hope you can summon them,
so that his mother can see them for herself."
Mǎ then set up an altar in the Buddhist hall,
and performed a ritual to summon the spirits.
In a short while,
the spirits of the three daughters all arrived.
Lái's mother personally observed them.
Mǎ said:
"The eldest is not unappealing,
but she is not as good as the second daughter,
who is destined to become the wife of a governor."
Sū then married the second daughter.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Lái served as the magistrate of Yǒngníng,
and died during the Ān Lùshān rebellion.
His family blamed Mǎ for her inaccurate prediction.
After the two capitals were recovered,
an imperial decree posthumously awarded Lái the title of Governor of Huáizhōu.
Zhèng Shēng
There was a man named Zhèng Shēng,
who, at the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
went to the capital to take the imperial examinations.
When he reached the western outskirts of Zhèngzhōu,
it was dusk,
so he sought lodging at a host's home.
The host asked his surname,
and Zhèng truthfully replied.
Suddenly, a maid was sent from inside, saying:
"Our mistress is actually your paternal aunt."
Shortly after,
an elderly woman appeared,
descending from the main hall.
Zhèng paid his respects,
and they sat and talked for a long time.
When asked about his marital status,
she said:
"Your aunt has a granddaughter here,
surnamed Liǔ.
Her father currently serves as the magistrate of Huáiyīn County,
and their family status matches yours.
Now, I wish to betroth her to you,
what do you think?"
Zhèng did not dare to refuse.
That evening, the wedding took place,
and they enjoyed the utmost happiness of human life.
They lived there for several months,
and then the aunt said to Zhèng Shēng,
"You should take your wife back to the Liǔ family."
Zhèng followed her advice,
and took his wife to Huáiyīn.
He first informed the Liǔ family,
and the entire Liǔ household was shocked.
Liǔ's wife suspected that the magistrate had an outside woman who bore a daughter,
and expressed her resentment openly.
Shortly after,
the family went to see the girl,
and she was no different from their own daughter.
As she entered the gate and stepped down from the carriage,
she walked gracefully into the courtyard.
The daughter inside heard the commotion and came out laughing to look,
and they met in the courtyard.
The two girls suddenly merged,
and became one body.
The magistrate then investigated the matter thoroughly,
and it turned out that his wife's mother had passed away earlier,
and had married off the spirit of her granddaughter.
Zhèng Shēng went back to look for the old place,
but found nothing at all.
Wéi Yǐn
During the Dàlì era,
the daughter of Hán Jìnqīng, the Junior Director of the Palace Construction,
was married to Wéi Yǐn, the Assistant Director of the Imperial Wardrobe.
Yǐn was sent on a mission to Xīnluó,
and after traveling for one stage of the journey,
he felt a sudden sorrow and longing,
so he went to rest.
Then he sensed his wife outside the bed curtain,
and asked in surprise,
to which she replied:
"I pitied you for crossing the sea,
and wished to follow you,
with no one knowing."
Yǐn then lied to his attendants, saying:
"I have taken in a courtesan,
who will serve me in bed."
No one found it strange.
When he returned,
after two years,
his wife also followed him back.
Yǐn then confessed to his parents-in-law,
admitting his fault,
but his wife was still present in the room.
As they drew near,
they merged seamlessly into one body.
The one who had followed Yǐn was her spirit.
Qí Tuī's Daughter
During the Yuánhé era,
the daughter of Qí Tuī, the prefect of Ráo Prefecture,
married a certain Lǐ from Lǒngxī.
Lǐ was sitting for the imperial examinations,
and his wife was pregnant,
so she remained at the official residence in the prefecture.
When her time was near,
she moved to the eastern chamber at the rear.
That night,
the woman dreamed of a man,
dressed in magnificent attire,
who glared at her, pressed his sword, and shouted:
"How dare you defile this place with your filth?
Leave at once.
If not,
you will suffer calamity."
The next day, she told Tuī,
who was by nature resolute and fierce,
and he said:
"I am the lord of this land.
What kind of demon
could dare to intrude?"
A few days later,
the woman gave birth,
when suddenly the man from her dream appeared,
and he beat her violently on her bed and curtains.
After a short while,
blood flowed from her ears, eyes, and nose, and she died.
Her parents grieved over her wrongful and violent death,
but their regret came too late.
They sent word urgently to her husband,
waiting for him to return so she could be buried with the Lǐ clan.
They temporarily buried her
by the official road, over ten lǐ northwest of the prefecture.
Lǐ was in the capital,
having failed the examinations and preparing to return,
when he heard of the death and went there.
By the time he reached Ráo Prefecture,
his wife had already been dead for half a year.
Lǐ had a rough idea that her death was unnatural,
and his grief and resentment ran deep,
so he longed to clear her name in the underworld.
As he approached the outer city,
it grew late,
when suddenly he saw a woman in the wilderness,
whose appearance and attire
did not seem like that of a village woman.
Lǐ felt a stirring in his heart,
stopped his horse, and looked closely at her,
but she vanished among the grass and trees.
Lǐ dismounted and approached,
and when he reached her, it was indeed his wife.
They met and wept sorrowfully,
and his wife said:
"Do not weep now.
Fortunately, I can be revived.
I have been waiting for you to come
for a long time.
My father is rigid and upright,
and does not believe in ghosts and spirits.
I am but a woman,
unable to plead my own case.
Now that we have met,
the opportunity is almost lost."
Lǐ said:
"What can be done?"
The woman said:
"Five lǐ directly west from here is Pó Tíng Village,
where there is an old man named Tián,
who teaches the village children.
He is an immortal official from the Jiǔhuá Cave,
though no one knows it.
If you can go to him with utmost sincerity,
perhaps your wish will be granted."
Lǐ then went directly to visit Mr. Tián.
When he saw him,
he approached on his knees,
bowed twice, and said:
"I am a lowly mortal from the lower realm,
daring to pay respects to a great immortal."
At the time, the old man was teaching the village children the classics,
and upon seeing Lǐ, he was startled and avoided him, saying:
"I am but a decrepit and impoverished old man,
soon to pass away.
How can you say such things, sir?"
Lǐ bowed again,
kowtowing incessantly,
which made the old man even more reluctant.
From dusk until midnight,
Lǐ never dared to sit,
but stood respectfully before him.
The old man lowered his head for a long time and said:
"Since you are so sincere,
what can I hide from you?"
Lǐ then kowtowed and wept,
and recounted in detail the injustice done to his wife.
The old man said:
"I have known of this for a long time,
but you did not plead your case earlier.
Now the house is already ruined,
and it is too late to manage it.
I refused you earlier
because I had no plan.
Nevertheless, I will try to make arrangements for you."
He then rose and went north,
walking over a hundred paces,
stopped in a mulberry grove,
and let out a long whistle.
Suddenly, a grand government office appeared,
with halls and buildings encircling it,
and guards solemnly arrayed,
resembling a royal palace.
Mr. Tián wore a purple robe,
sat at a desk,
with officials and attendants standing in rows on either side.
Soon, an order was issued to summon the local deities.
In a moment,
over a dozen commanders, each leading over a hundred horsemen,
arrived galloping from front and rear.
Their leaders were all over ten feet tall,
with imposing brows and eyes,
and they lined up outside the gate.
They straightened their clothes and hats,
looking anxious and hurried,
asking each other what was happening.
Shortly after,
the usher announced the local deities, the god of Lú Mountain, the god of the Jiāng River, the god of Pénglí, and others,
who all hurried in.
Mr. Tián asked:
"Recently, the daughter of the prefect of this prefecture
was killed by a violent ghost while giving birth.
This is a grave injustice.
Do you know of it?"
They all prostrated themselves and replied:
"Yes."
He asked again:
"Why was no redress sought?"
They all replied:
"Legal cases require a plaintiff.
Since no one brought a complaint,
there was no way to initiate action."
He asked if they knew the name of the culprit,
and one of them replied:
"It is Wú Ruì, the King of Pó County from the Western Hàn.
The current prefect's residence
was where Ruì once lived.
To this day, he still relies on his might and arrogance,
encroaching on the land,
often acting with wanton cruelty,
and people can do nothing about it."
Mr. Tián said:
"Bring him here at once."
In a moment,
Wú Ruì was brought in bound.
Mr. Tián interrogated him,
but he refused to submit,
so he ordered Lǐ's wife to be summoned.
After a long while,
Lǐ's wife and Wú Ruì argued their cases in the courtyard.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
Wú Ruì was found to be in the wrong,
and he said:
"It must have been that she was weakened after childbirth,
and upon seeing me, she was frightened to death—
it was not intentional killing."
Mr. Tián said:
"Is there any difference between killing someone with a club or a blade?"
He then ordered Wú Ruì to be taken to the heavenly court.
Turning back, he said:
"Quickly check how much lifespan Lǐ's wife has left."
After a moment,
an official said:
"According to her original fate, she should live another thirty-two years,
and bear four sons and three daughters."
Mr. Tián said to the assembled officials:
"Lǐ's wife has a long lifespan.
If she is not revived,
there will be no way to settle this justly.
What do you all think?"
An old official stepped forward and said:
"In the Eastern Jìn, in Yèxià, there was a man who died unjustly,
and his case was exactly like this one.
Previously, the immortal Gě Zhēnjūn
judged that his complete soul should be made into his body,
and he was returned to the world of the living.
His eating, drinking, speech,
desires, and activities
were no different from before.
Only when his lifespan ended
did his physical form vanish."
Mr. Tián asked:
"What is a complete soul?"
The official said:
"A living person has three hún and seven pò.
Upon death, they scatter and disperse,
with nothing to rely on.
Now, gather them into one entity,
and apply glue made from lute strings to it."
The king has now ordered your release on the street,
so you are the same as your original self."
Tián Xiānshēng said, "Excellent,"
and immediately turned to Lǐ's wife, saying:
"This arrangement,
is it acceptable?"
Lǐ's wife replied:
"Most fortunate indeed."
Soon, an official was seen,
leading seven or eight other women separately,
all of the same kind as Lǐ's wife,
and pushed them together to merge.
There was a person
holding a vessel of medicine,
resembling thin syrup.
He then smeared it over Lǐ's wife's body.
Lǐ's wife felt as if falling through the air to the ground,
initially very dazed and confused.
When dawn broke,
all that had been seen the previous night vanished,
leaving only Tián Xiānshēng and the couple, Mr. and Mrs. Lǐ,
together in the mulberry grove.
Tián Xiānshēng turned to Lǐ,
and said:
"I have exerted my utmost effort for you,
and I am glad the matter is accomplished.
You may now take her home.
When meeting your relatives,
simply say she has been revived;
be careful not to speak of anything else.
I shall also depart from here now."
Lǐ then returned together to the prefecture,
where the whole family was shocked and suspicious,
unwilling to believe it.
After a long time,
they finally realized she was truly a living person.
From then on, she bore several children.
Among her close relatives,
some who were aware of the matter
said:
"There is nothing else unusual about her,
except her movements are light and agile,
different from ordinary people."
The Daughter of the Zhèng Family
In Tōngzhōu, there was a lay Buddhist named Wáng,
who possessed magical arts.
During the Huìcháng era,
Prefect Zhèng had a young daughter,
whom he cherished deeply.
However, since childhood she had been frequently ill,
as if her spirit and soul were insufficient.
Prefect Zhèng thus invited the lay Buddhist,
who said:
"This girl is not ill;
rather, her living soul has not yet returned to her body."
Prefect Zhèng inquired about the matter,
and the lay Buddhist said:
"The magistrate of a certain county, so-and-so,
is this girl's previous life.
He should have died several years ago,
but because he did good deeds throughout his life,
he received protection from the underworld,
allowing him to exceed his lifespan.
He is now over ninety years old.
On the day the magistrate passes away,
this girl will recover."
Prefect Zhèng urgently sent someone to investigate,
and indeed the magistrate was over ninety.
The following month,
the girl suddenly seemed as if awakening from drunkenness,
and her illness was cured.
Prefect Zhèng again sent someone to verify,
and indeed the magistrate had died without illness
on the very day the girl recovered.
Péi Gǒng
The examination candidate Péi Gǒng
lived in Luòyáng.
In mid-summer,
he was returning west from Zhèng[zhōu]
to visit his family for the Duānwǔ Festival.
It was getting late.
Just as he reached Shíqiáo,
suddenly a young man appeared,
riding with a large retinue of hawks and hounds.
He looked at Gǒng and said with a laugh:
"Tomorrow is the festival day;
you should return early today.
Why are you so delayed?"
He then lent Gǒng a horse from his following.
Gǒng was very pleased
and said to his two attendants:
"You may drive slowly
and lodge at the villa of my cousin Dòu Wēn west of Báimǎ Temple.
You can return leisurely tomorrow."
He then mounted the horse and rode swiftly.
In a moment,
he reached Shàngdōng Gate,
returned the horse,
and bid farewell with gratitude.
Gǒng lived south of the river;
he hurried on foot,
and by the time he reached home, it was already dark.
Entering the gate,
he saw his family and his sisters gathered under lantern light for a meal.
Gǒng stepped forward to bow,
but no one looked at him.
He then spoke loudly from the steps:
"Gǒng has arrived from outside."
Again, no one heard.
Gǒng then called out loudly to his younger siblings,
but still no response.
Gǒng felt agitated and distressed in heart and mind,
thinking and calling out desperately,
yet all remained unaware.
He only saw his parent sigh and say:
"Why has Gǒng not arrived today?"
Tears then fell,
and all seated wept.
Gǒng wondered privately:
"Have I perhaps become a phantom?"
He then went out to the main road,
and wandered for a long time.
There was a nobleman with a grand procession,
who saw Gǒng from afar
and pointed with his whip, saying:
"That is the soul of a living person."
Soon, someone wearing a quiver and bow case
emerged from the side of the road,
saying:
"The local underworld office reports:
Examination candidate Péi Gǒng
is not fated to die yet.
He encountered the seventh son of the Kūnmíng Pond deity,
who was returning with his hawk,
and borrowed a horse to send him back as a jest.
Now he should be taken back to his body."
The nobleman smiled faintly and said:
"The youngster is unreasonable,
treating human life as a game.
Tomorrow I shall write to his honored father,
to have him flogged."
Upon arrival, the one with the quiver and bow case summoned Gǒng,
and they went out again through Shàngdōng Gate,
passing through a crack in the gate,
to Dòu Village.
There they saw his body lying stiff,
with two attendants weeping softly around him.
The one with the quiver and bow case told him to close his eyes,
pushed him from behind,
and he suddenly awoke with awareness.
His two attendants both said:
"Earlier, when we reached Shíqiáo,
we noticed you, young master, had a sudden attack,
speaking very strangely.
Fearing it would worsen,
we brought you here.
Upon arrival,
you had already stopped breathing."
Gǒng was astonished and sighed for a long while; shortly after, he was unharmed.
The Shūzhōu Military Officer
Wáng Qí served as the Prefect of Shūzhōu.
There was a military officer named Fāng,
whose family was suddenly visited by a ghost.
It declared:
"My surname is Dù,
I am twenty years old,
the son of a wealthy family in Guǎnglíng,
living west of the Tōngsì Bridge.
In my previous life, I owed you 100,000 coins.
Now the underworld has made me a spirit,
to repay you this debt."
It then began to foretell fortunes and misfortunes for people,
and its words were often accurate.
Fāng, citing his family's poverty, pleaded with Qí,
asking to be appointed as a garrison commander.
He then asked the ghost:
"Will my request be granted?"
The ghost replied:
"Yes,
I will inquire about it."
After a long while, it returned and said:
"You will certainly get it,
the name of the garrison has a single character that is square in shape,
I cannot recognize the others."
