Later, Fāng obtained the position of garrison commander at Shuānggǎng,
and thought the ghost's words had not come true.
Before he could take up his post,
the ghost suddenly said to Fāng:
"I have just received a military dispatch,
the army has ordered someone else to become the garrison commander of Shuānggǎng,
I will now make you the garrison commander of Wǎnkǒu."
It turned out exactly as the ghost said.
After about a year,
the ghost suddenly declared:
"I have repaid your debt in full."
It bid farewell and left,
and all became quiet.
Later, Fāng went to Guǎnglíng,
found the Dù family,
and asked about their younger son.
They said:
"Our second son
suddenly fell ill a while ago,
like an idiot,
and recovered after more than a year."
Wǔdū Woman
In Wǔdū, there was a man
who transformed into a woman,
beautiful and charming,
likely a female spirit.
The King of Shǔ took her as his consort,
but she could not adapt to the climate,
and wanted to leave.
The king tried to keep her.
He then composed the "Dōngpíng Song" to please her.
Not long after, she passed away.
The king grieved for her,
and sent the Five Strongmen to Wǔdū.
They carried earth to build a tomb for the consort,
covering several acres of land,
and standing seven zhang high,
with a stone mirror on top.
Now, at the northern corner of Chéngdū,
it is called Wǔdān.
Dōngfāng Shuò
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn traveled east,
reaching Hángǔ Pass,
where a creature blocked the road.
Its body was several zhang long,
and its shape resembled an ox.
It had green eyes that gleamed brightly,
and its four feet were buried in the ground,
moving but not shifting.
The officials were terrified.
Dōngfāng Shuò then requested wine to pour over it,
and after pouring several dozen hú, it dissolved.
The emperor asked the reason,
and he replied:
"This is called 'Worry,'
born from suffering.
This must be the site of Qín's prisons.
If not,
it is where convicts were gathered for forced labor.
Wine makes one forget worries,
so it can dissolve it."
The emperor said:
"A man of broad learning
can understand even this?"
Two-Headed Chicken
In the second year of Tàichū of Hàn,
the Great Yuèzhī presented a two-headed chicken,
with four feet and one tail,
and both heads crowed together.
Emperor Wǔ placed it in the Gānquán Lodge,
and had other chickens mate with it,
hoping to breed more.
But they could not crow,
which was not auspicious,
so the emperor sent it back to the Western Regions.
When it reached the western pass,
the chicken looked back,
gazing at the Hàn palace and crying mournfully,
saying:
"At the end of three sevens,
chickens will not crow,
dogs will not bark.
Thorns will grow wild in the palace,
and nine tigers will contend to become emperor."
When Wáng Mǎng usurped the throne,
there were generals with the title "Nine Tigers."
After that, chaos and calamities were widespread,
and the palace courtyards were overgrown with weeds and thorns,
with no chickens or dogs in households.
This chicken never reached Yuèzhī,
but flew away,
its cry resembling that of a kūn chicken,
soaring among the clouds.
Zhāng Yí
Zhāng Yí, styled Shūgāo,
was the Tàishǒu of Guìyáng from Jiāngxià.
He lived in Yè,
Líng.
In the fields, there was a large tree,
over ten arm-spans around,
covering about six acres,
with luxuriant branches and leaves,
and the ground beneath it was barren, yielding no grain or grass.
He sent a servant to chop it down.
After a few strokes of the axe,
the tree bled profusely.
The servant was terrified,
and returned to report to Shūgāo.
Shūgāo angrily said:
"An old tree sweating,
what is so strange about that?"
He then went to chop it himself.
Blood gushed out,
and Shūgāo continued chopping.
Then, from a hollow,
a white-haired old man, four or five chǐ tall,
suddenly rushed out,
toward Shūgāo.
Shūgāo met him with his blade,
killing him.
Four or five more old men emerged.
Those around were terrified and prostrated on the ground,
but Shūgāo remained calm and composed as before.
The others slowly observed them:
they resembled humans but were not,
resembled beasts but were not,
these were the so-called monsters of wood and stone,
the kuí and wǎngliǎng.
In the year the tree was felled,
Shūgāo was appointed as Minister of Works, Imperial Censor, and Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
Zhái Xuān
When Wáng Mǎng was regent,
the Tàishǒu of Dōngjùn, Zhái Yì,
knowing he intended to usurp the throne,
planned to raise an army.
His elder brother, Xuān,
was teaching a hall full of students,
when several dozen wild geese landed in the courtyard,
and a dog came and bit them.
Everyone was startled,
and by the time they rushed to save them,
all the geese had their heads bitten off.
The dog ran out the gate,
and no one could find where it went.
Xuān felt deeply troubled by this.
A few days later,
Mǎng exterminated his entire clan.
Zāng Zhòngyīng
Zāng Zhòngyīng of Fúfēng served as a Palace Censor.
When his family was preparing food,
dust and grime would appear in it;
after the rice was cooked,
the cooking pot would vanish;
weapons and crossbows would move by themselves.
Fire would erupt from a chest,
completely burning the clothes inside while the chest itself remained intact;
his daughter-in-law, maids, and serving women
all disappeared one morning.
His mirror,
several days later,
was thrown from the hall into the courtyard.
A voice said:
"Returning your mirror."
His four-year-old granddaughter
went missing;
they searched for her but could not find her.
Two or three days later,
she was found crying under the manure in the privy.
Incidents like this were not isolated.
Xǔ Jìshān divined the matter, saying:
"There must be a black dog in the household,
and a servant inside named Gài Xǐ.
They are doing this together.
If you truly wish to end it,
kill this
dog,
and send Gài Xǐ back to his hometown."
Following this advice, the disturbances ceased.
Zhòngyīng was promoted to Chief Clerk to the Grand Commandant and Chancellor of Lǔ.
A man from Dùnqiū
During the Huángchū era,
a man from Dùnqiū was riding his horse at night,
when he saw a creature on the road,
as large as a rabbit,
with eyes like mirrors.
It leaped about, blocking the horse's path,
preventing it from advancing.
The man, terrified, fell from his horse.
The demon then assaulted him on the ground.
The man, frightened and horrified,
after a long while managed to break free,
and the demon vanished,
its whereabouts unknown.
He then remounted his horse
and rode forward for several *li*,
where he encountered a man,
They exchanged greetings,
He then recounted the strange events that had just occurred,
and they were now very pleased to have met.
The man said:
"I was traveling alone;
having you as a companion
is an indescribable joy.
Your horse is fast; ride ahead,
and I will follow behind."
So they traveled together.
The man then asked:
"What was that creature like earlier,
that it frightened you so?"
He replied:
"Its body was like a rabbit's,
its eyes like mirrors,
a truly hideous form."
The man said:
"Try looking at my eyes."
When he looked again,
they were exactly the same.
The demon then leaped onto the horse,
and the man fell to the ground,
frightened to death.
His family, puzzled that the horse had returned alone,
immediately went out to search for him,
and found him by the roadside.
After a night, he revived,
and recounted the events as described.
Wáng Jī
Wáng Jī, Governor of Ānpíng,
had been troubled by strange occurrences in his household,
so he had Guǎn Lù perform a divination for him.
After the hexagram was formed,
Guǎn Lù said:
"According to your hexagram,
a lowly woman in your household will give birth to a boy,
who, upon falling to the ground,
will immediately crawl into the stove and die;
furthermore, a large snake will appear on a bed, holding a brush in its mouth,
and after everyone, young and old, sees it,
it will vanish in a moment;
also, a bird will enter the house,
fight with a swallow,
and the swallow will die while the bird flies away.
Are these the three omens indicated?"
Wáng Jī, greatly astonished, said:
"The profundity of your interpretation
has reached such a level.
I beg you to explain the auspicious or inauspicious implications."
Guǎn Lù said:
"There is no other calamity;
it is simply because the official residence is old,
that mountain and water spirits
are together creating these strange phenomena.
The child born into the stove—
that is the work of Sòng Wújì;
the large snake—
that is the old clerk;
the bird fighting with the swallow—
that is the old gatekeeper.
The uprightness of the divine and enlightened
cannot be disturbed by such anomalies;
the transformations of the myriad things
are not halted by the Way;
the floating essences of ancient times
are bound by fixed principles.
Now, since no inauspicious signs appear in the hexagram,
we know these are merely borrowed forms,
not portents of calamitous anomalies.
In the past, the pheasant that crowed on the tripod of King Gāozōng
was not truly a pheasant;
the mulberry tree that grew on the steps of King Tàiwù
was not truly a mulberry.
Yet anomalies appeared together,
and both rulers flourished for two years.
How can we know that these three events are not auspicious signs?
I hope, Your Excellency, you will calm your spirit and cultivate the Way,
and not be frightened by such divine trickery."
Afterwards, nothing untoward happened,
and he was promoted to General Who Pacifies the South.
Yìng Qú
Zhū Jiànpíng was skilled in physiognomy.
Reading Yìng Qú's features, he said:
"At age sixty-two,
you will hold the position of a regular palace attendant.
One year before this,
you will uniquely see a white dog."
When Yìng Qú was sixty-one,
serving as Palace Attendant,
and on duty within the palace precincts,
he suddenly saw a white dog.
No one else could see it.
He then engaged in hurried travels and sightseeing,
feasting and drinking to amuse himself,
and died at sixty-two.
Gōngsūn Yuān
When Sīmǎ, Grand Tutor Yì of Wèi, pacified Gōngsūn Yuān,
he beheaded Yuān and his son.
Prior to this, a dog in Yuān's household
wore a red turban and crimson clothes.
In the northern market of Xiāngpíng City,
a piece of flesh appeared,
with a head and eyes,
but no hands or feet, and it writhed.
A diviner said:
"It has form but is incomplete,
has substance but no voice;
this portends the state's destruction."
Zhūgě Kè
When Zhūgě Kè was Governor of Dānyáng,
he went hunting between two mountains.
There was a creature like a small child,
reaching out its hand as if to lead someone.
Kè ordered someone to take its hand,
and it led them away from their original spot.
Once away from that spot, it died.
Afterwards, his aides asked the reason,
considering it a divine mystery.
Kè said:
"This matter is recorded in the *Báizé Tú*.
It says:
'Between two mountains,
there is a spirit resembling a small child.
Upon seeing a person, it reaches out its hand as if to lead them.
Its name is "Sì".
If led away from its original spot, it dies.'
Do not deem it divine and strange;
you gentlemen simply haven't encountered it before."
The daughter of the Governor of Línglíng
The Prefect of Línglíng,
had a daughter,
who was fond of a clerk.
She secretly had her maidservant
fetch the water he had used for washing and drank it.
She then became pregnant,
and after ten months gave birth to a son.
When the child reached his first birthday,
the Prefect ordered him to be carried outside the gate.
The child crawled into the clerk's arms,
but the clerk pushed him away,
and he fell to the ground and turned into water.
Upon thorough questioning,
the earlier events came to light,
and the Prefect then gave his daughter in marriage to the clerk.
The Liào Family of Xíngyáng
In Xíngyáng Commandery, there was a family
named Liào,
who for generations practiced gu sorcery,
and thereby grew wealthy.
Later, they took a new bride,
but did not tell her about this.
Once, when all the family members happened to be out,
only this bride was left to watch the house.
Suddenly, she saw a large vat in the room,
and when she tried to open it,
she saw a large snake inside.
The bride then boiled water
and poured it in, killing it.
When the family returned,
the bride told them everything that had happened,
and the entire household was shocked and dismayed.
Not long after,
the family fell ill with an epidemic,
and nearly all of them died.
There was also a monk named Tànyóu,
whose discipline was pure and austere.
At that time, in Shàn County, there was a family that practiced gu sorcery;
anyone who ate their food or drank their beverages
would vomit blood and die without exception.
Tànyóu once visited them,
and the host served him a meal.
As he ate,
Tànyóu chanted incantations.
He saw a pair of centipedes,
over a foot long,
crawl out from the plate.
Tànyóu then ate his fill and left,
and nothing else happened.
Táo Huáng
General Táo Huáng of the Lú Kingdom was digging the ground
when he found something in an earthen hole,
white in color,
shaped like a silkworm,
several zhang long.
More than ten arm-spans thick,
it wriggled and moved,
and no one could name it.
They cut open its belly,
and the inside was like pork fat,
so they made it into dried meat.
It was very fragrant and delicious.
Táo Huáng ate a cupful,
and then the entire army ate it.
The Línhǎi Yìwù Zhì states:
"The 'earth flesh' is pitch black,
like a child's arm in size,
long,
Five cun long,
it has intestines inside,
no eyes,
and thirty feet,
like hairpin stems.
The larger ones have a head over a foot long,
and the flesh inside is tasty.
There is also the yángsuì insect,
its back is bluish-black,
and its underside is white.
It has five colors,
and its length, size, and thickness are all equal,
so one cannot tell where its head or tail is.
When alive, its body is soft,
but when dead, it becomes brittle."
Zhào Wáng Lún
At the beginning of the Yǒngkāng era,
Zhào Wáng Lún usurped the throne.
In the capital, a bird was captured,
and no one could name it.
Lún had someone take it out
and parade it around the city to ask people.
After several days,
a young boy saw it
and said on his own:
"It's a xiūliú."
The person immediately returned and reported to Lún,
who ordered them to search for the boy again.
They found him,
and brought him into the palace.
They secretly caged the bird
and also confined the boy.
The next day, when they looked,
the seals were intact as before,
but both had completely disappeared.
At that time, Lún suffered from a tumor on his eye,
hence the mention of the xiūliú.
Lún was soon executed.
Zhāng Chěng
During the Tài'ān era of the Jìn dynasty,
Zhāng Chěng, a clerk in Jiāngxià,
was riding in a carriage when
the ox spoke, saying:
"The world is in chaos,
I am extremely exhausted.
Where are you taking me?"
Zhāng Chěng and several attendants
were all terrified.
So they deceived it, saying:
"We'll take you back now,
don't speak again."
They then turned back midway.
Upon reaching home,
before they had unharnessed the ox,
it spoke again:
"Why have we returned?"
Zhāng Chěng grew even more worried and afraid,
and kept it secret without speaking of it.
In Ānlù County, there was a skilled diviner,
and Zhāng Chěng went to him.
The divination said:
"Great misfortune.
It is not just the calamity of one family;
the world will see armies rise.
Within the entire commandery,
all will be destroyed."
Zhāng Chěng returned home,
and the ox
also stood up like a human and walked,
drawing crowds of onlookers.
That autumn,
the rebel Zhāng Chāng rose up,
first plundering Jiāngxià,
deceiving and dazzling the people,
claiming the Hàn dynasty was to be restored,
that there were auspicious signs of the phoenix,
and that a sage would appear in the world.
Those who joined his army all wore red headbands,
to display the auspicious sign of the fire virtue.
The people were in turmoil,
and joined the rebellion as if returning home.
Zhāng Chěng and his brothers all became generals and commandants,
but they were defeated before a year had passed.
Thus, the entire commandery was devastated,
with half the population dead or injured,
and Zhāng Chěng's family perished.
Jīng Fáng's Yì Yāo states:
"If an ox can speak,
according to what it says,
one can predict good or bad fortune."
Huái Yáo
During the Yuánkāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
in Huái Yáo's household in Lóu County, Wú Commandery,
they heard faint sounds of puppies coming from underground.
Above the source of the sound was a small hole,
as large as an earthworm.
Huái probed it with a stick,
penetrating several feet,
and felt as if there was something there.
Upon digging it up to look,
they obtained dogs,
one male and one female,
their eyes,
still unopened,
and their bodies larger than ordinary dogs.
They were fed and ate,
and people from all around came to see them.
Some elders said,
"These are called 'xī quǎn' (rhinoceros dogs);
whoever obtains them will have a prosperous and flourishing household,
so they should be raised and kept alive."
Thinking their eyes were still unopened,
they returned them to the hole,
covering it with a millstone.
The next morning, when they opened it to look,
there was no hole on either side,
and they had disappeared from their location.
For years afterward, the Yáo household experienced no particular fortune or misfortune.
Péi Kǎi
When Péi Kǎi of the Jìn dynasty was cooking at home,
the millet in the steamer
sometimes turned into fists,
sometimes transformed into blood,
and sometimes became turnip seeds.
Not long after, he died.
Wèi Guàn
When Wèi Guàn's family was cooking,
rice that fell to the ground
all turned into snails,
which extended their feet and crawled away.
Soon after, he was executed by Empress Jiǎ.
Jiǎ Mì
Jiǎ Mì, styled Chángyuān:
In the sixth month of the ninth year of Yuánkāng,
there was a sudden thunderstorm at night.
A pillar in Jiǎ's study collapsed,
crushing and destroying his bed and curtains.
A fierce wind blew his clothes,
lifting them hundreds of zhang into the sky,
where they remained for a long time before descending.
Liú Qiáo
At the end of the Yǒngjiā era,
there was a Liú Qiáo who lived in Jìnlíng.
His elder brother had died early,
and his sister-in-law lived in widowhood.
One night,
the sister-in-law and a maidservant were sleeping in the hall.
During the second watch,
the maidservant,
suddenly cried out loudly,
and ran to his room.
She said:
"In the sister-in-law's room and on the walls,
there are strange and terrifying things that cannot be looked upon."
Liú Qiáo then took a knife and lit a torch,
and brought the woman with him.
They saw that on the four walls were faces like those of humans,
with wide-open eyes and protruding tongues,
some like tigers, some like dragons,
in a thousand transformations and myriad forms.
Looking at their faces, which were over a zhang long,
the sister-in-law immediately died.
Wáng Dūn
During Emperor Yuán's reign,
Wáng Dūn was in Wǔchāng.
Flowers grew on the ceremonial staff of his attendants,
like lotus blossoms,
which withered and fell after five or six days.
Gān Bǎo said:
"The splendor of glory and prosperity
is like mad flowers that cannot last long."
Wáng Dūn, having rebelled against the command, died by his own hand,
and his corpse was further mutilated.
Wáng Xiàn
Wáng Xiàn lost a mirror,
which was found inside a jar.
The jar was only a few cùn in size,
yet the mirror was over a chǐ long.
He asked Guō Pú about it,
who said:
"This is the work of evil spirits."
He had them burn a chariot linchpin and aim it at the mirror,
and the mirror immediately emerged.
Liú Chǒng
Liú Chǒng of Dōngyáng, styled Dàohóng,
lived in Gūshú.
Every night,
several dǒu of blood would appear in his courtyard,
with no known origin,
and this continued for three or four days.
Later, Liú Chǒng was appointed General of the Breaking Charge,
and dispatched on a northern campaign.
Just as he was about to depart, the cooked rice turned entirely into insects,
and even the steamed and fried food in his household became insects.
The fiercer the fire, the stronger the insects grew.
Liú Chǒng then proceeded north on the campaign,
where his army was defeated at Tánqiū,
and he was killed by Xú Kān.
A Military Adviser in Huán Wēn's Office
In the final years of Emperor Mù's reign,
a military adviser in Huán Wēn's office was sitting at night
when he suddenly saw a crouching rabbit on the roof beam,
staring at him with wide-open eyes and gnashing teeth.
The rabbit drew closer.
He struck at it with a knife,
and though he saw it hit the rabbit squarely,
he actually injured his own knee, causing it to bleed.
When he struck again heavily with the knife,
he injured himself once more.
Fortunately, the knife was not sharp,
so he did not die.
Lady Guō
Lady Guō, the maternal grandmother of Bì Xiūzhī,
once slept alone at night
and called for a maidservant,
who responded but did not come.
Lady Guō called repeatedly, but the situation remained the same.
Later, she heard the sound of heavy stomping on the bed,
and Lady Guō sharply scolded the maidservant,
who again responded but still did not come.
Soon, she saw a face on the screen.
It resembled a Fāngxiàng (exorcist mask),
with two eyes as large as a shēng measure,
illuminating the entire room.
Its hands were like winnowing baskets,
with fingers several cùn long.
It also moved its ears and eyes.
Lady Guō was devoted to spiritual practice,
and with single-minded concentration,
the creature eventually left.
After a long time,
the maidservants all came,
saying:
"We wanted to respond earlier,
but it felt as if something was pressing down on us,
and only when our bodies felt light did we come."
Yǔ Yì
Yǔ Yì served as Colonel of the Southern Barbarians and Governor of Nán Commandery.
One night, while going to the latrine,
he suddenly saw a creature in the latrine
with a head like a Fāngxiàng.
Its two eyes were large and glowing,
and it emerged from the earth.
Yǔ then rolled up his sleeves,
and struck it with his fist.
It made a sound upon impact,
and suddenly disappeared from its location.
Yǔ Jǐn
In Jiānglíng, there was an old woman named Zhào who made a living by selling wine.
During the Yìxī era,
the earth inside her house suddenly rose up on its own.
Finding this strange,
she poured wine on the earth morning and evening.
Once, she saw a creature emerge,
with a head like a donkey,
though initially there was no hole in the ground.
After the old woman died,
neighbors heard sounds from beneath the earth morning and evening,
like weeping.
Later, someone dug up the house
and saw a strange creature,
clumsily moving,
its size impossible to gauge.
In a moment, it disappeared.
They called it an earth dragon.
Zhūgě Chángmín
During the reign of Emperor Ān,
Zhūgě Chángmín served as the governor of Yùzhōu.
There were pounding sticks that spoke to each other,
like human voices,
unintelligible.
He ordered them moved to separate places,
but they still called out to each other from afar.
Also, while Chángmín was in Yùzhōu,
he saw something in the gaps between the pillars and rafters of his house,
resembling
snake heads.
He ordered people to chop at them with knives,
and they would hide and disappear at the blade's touch.
Sometimes, after a month
or several tens of days,
he would suddenly startle awake while sleeping at night,
leaping and thrashing
as if fighting with someone.
Máo Xiūzhī once stayed with him and,
startled, did not understand what was happening.
Chángmín said:
"This creature is extraordinarily fierce;
if not for me, no one could subdue it."
Máo asked:
"What is it?"
Chángmín replied:
"I just see a very dark creature
with hands and feet,
unclear,
its shape unknown.
It comes and fights with me,
and I am deeply afraid of it."
Chángmín was soon executed.
The Zhāng Family of Yánguān
In the late Jìn dynasty, there was a man named Zhāng
in Yánguān.
While sitting quietly at home,
he suddenly smelled the aroma of cooked food.
Shortly after,
the wind blew in a plate of food,
complete with wine, meat, and dishes.
A person in a yellow robe arrived in a carriage,
sat on the bed,
and ate with Zhāng.
When asked his surname,
he smiled without answering.
After a long while,
he boarded his carriage and left.
Later, Zhāng was killed by Sūn Ēn.
Wáng Yú
Wáng Yú, styled
Màohé,
during the early Yìxī era,
was walking in his courtyard
when his hat suddenly flew off on its own
and floated in the air
as if worn by someone.
When Wáng Yú's mother passed away,
during the monthly morning sacrifice,
the wine vessel on the table
suddenly fell to the ground
and then returned to the bed.
Soon after, his third son, Suíhuái,
was executed for treason.
Zhū Zōngzhī
Zhū Zōngzhī, the magistrate of Sīlǐ in Kuàijī Kingdom,
often saw that when a deceased person was laid in the coffin,
about three chǐ above the head,
there was a blue object
shaped like an overturned urn.
If someone stood in that spot, it would disappear;
when the person left, it would reappear.
Every corpse's head had this blue object.
It is also said that
when a person is laid in the coffin,
ghosts always temporarily return to attend to them.
Yú Dìngguó
Yú Dìngguó of Yúyáo
had a handsome appearance.
A daughter of the Sū family in the same county
was also beautiful.
Dìngguó once saw her
and admired her.
Later, when Dìngguó visited,
the host let him stay overnight.
In the middle of the night,
he told Mr. Sū:
"Your virtuous daughter is lovely,
and I deeply admire her.
Could she come out briefly tonight?"
The host, considering him a distinguished local figure,
let his daughter go to him.
As their visits grew more frequent,
he told Mr. Sū:
"I have nothing to repay you with,
but if you have any official matters,
I will handle them for you."
The host was pleased.
Afterward, whenever there was a summons for labor service,
he went to see Dìngguó.
Dìngguó was greatly surprised and said:
"We have never met or spoken;
how could this be?
There must be something strange here."
After hearing the full story,
Dìngguó said:
"How could I possibly ask for someone's daughter from her father?
If you see this person again,
chop him down."
Later, they indeed caught a monster.
Dīng Huá
Dīng Huá of Dōngyáng went outside the city walls
and stayed overnight at Fāngshān Pavilion.
At the pavilion's shore was Liú Sànqí,
who had lost his mother
and was returning from a burial in the capital.
In the night,
suddenly a woman appeared,
introducing herself as Liú's daughter,
saying,
"I suffer from sores,
and I heard the参军 is skilled in treatment,
so I have come."
Huá asked her to come forward;
her appearance was graceful and charming.
She was accompanied by several women.
Huá ordered his servant to prepare food and wine.
After drinking, she sighed and said:
"Tonight's meeting
makes one lose all sense of chastity and integrity."
Dīng said:
"With your noble virtue, young lady,
how could you care for an old man like me?"
He then had a woman
fetch a pipa and play it.
She sang:
"Long have I heard of your esteemed name,
now we meet at Fāngshān Pavilion.
Though my body is aged and decaying,
it is still enough
to please human feelings."
Putting down the pipa,
she climbed onto his lap and embraced his head.
She sang again:
"Though my form is humble and lowly,
I wish to be your spouse.
Entwined in a fine night,
we shall be joined for a thousand years."
Her voice was gentle and charming,
utterly captivating.
She then had the fire extinguished,
and they shared their affections.
By dawn,
she had suddenly vanished.
The clerk said
this pavilion had long been haunted by demons.
The Wáng Family of Fùyáng
In the early years of the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
a man named Wáng from Fùyáng
set up a crab trap in a remote stream.
One morning when he went to check it,
he saw a piece of timber,
about two chǐ long,
inside the trap,
which had broken open,
allowing the crabs to escape.
So he repaired the trap
and took the timber out onto the bank.
The next day when he went to check,
the timber was back in the trap,
and the trap was broken as before.
Wáng again repaired the trap and removed the timber,
but the next morning he found the same situation as before.
Wáng suspected this timber was a demonic anomaly,
so he took it and put it inside a crab basket,
tied the top, and carried it home,
saying:
"When I get home,
I'll chop it up with an axe and burn it."
When he was still three lǐ from home,
he heard rustling movements inside the basket.
Turning his head,
he saw the former timber head transform into a creature
with a human face and a monkey's body,
having one hand and one foot,
who said to Wáng:
"I have a craving for crabs.
Recently I indeed entered the water,
broke your crab trap,
went into the trap to eat crabs—
I have wronged you.
I hope you will forgive me,
open the basket and let me out.
I am a mountain spirit,
and will surely aid you,
and also make your trap catch many crabs."
Wáng said:
"You have assaulted people,
not just once but repeatedly.
Your crime deserves death."
This creature pleaded desperately,
begging to be released,
but Wáng turned away and did not respond.
The creature said:
"What is your name?
I wish to know it."
It asked repeatedly without stopping,
but Wáng still did not answer.
As they drew closer to home,
the creature said:
"Since you won't release me,
and won't tell me your name either,
what else can I do?
I must simply await death."
When Wáng reached home,
he lit a fierce fire and burned it,
after which all was quiet with no further anomalies.
Local custom calls it a shānnáo.
They say
that if it knows a person's name,
it can harm them.
That is why it diligently questioned Wáng—
it wanted to harm him to save itself.
Lè Xiá
In the ninth year of Yuánjiā,
Lè Xiá of Nányáng was sitting indoors
when suddenly he heard someone in the air
urgently calling his and his wife's names.
This continued until midnight,
leaving them greatly alarmed and fearful.
A few days later,
when his wife returned from behind the house,
suddenly all her clothes were covered in blood.
Within a month,
husband and wife fell ill and died one after the other.
Liú Bīn
When Liú Bīn was in Wújùn,
there was a woman in Lóuxiàn
who suddenly one night rode wind and rain,
arriving dazedly inside the commandery city.
She felt only about the time to cook a meal had passed since leaving home,
yet her clothes were not wet.
At dawn, she sought entry at the gate,
saying:
"I am a heavenly envoy.
The Prefect should rise and receive me—
then great wealth and honor will follow.
If not,
misfortune will surely occur."
Liú asked where she came from,
but she herself did not know.
About twenty days later,
Liú was executed.
Wáng Zhēng
During the Yuánjiā era,
Wáng Zhēng of Tàiyuán, Governor of Jiāozhōu,
had just taken office
and was riding in his carriage
when he heard a clanging sound ahead.
He saw a carriage blocking the road,
but others could not see it.
Upon reaching the province, he then died.
Zhāng Zhòngshū
In the seventeenth year of Yuánjiā,
during the seventh month,
at dawn and dusk,
he would see a glaring red aura by the gate.
Later, crimson silk suddenly rained from the sky into his courtyard,
each piece seven or eight cùn wide,
five or six cùn long,
all tied with paper slips.
The paper was as wide and long as the silk,
falling swiftly and densely.
Zhòngshū, disgusted, burned them.
After two nights,
he fell violently ill and died.
Xiāo Sīhuà
When Xiāo Sīhuà was in Qīngzhōu,
a copper shēng he often used
was kept overturned under the medicine cabinet.
Suddenly beneath it,
he found two dead sparrows.
Sīhuà sighed and said:
"A shēng covering a sparrow's burial—
is this not inauspicious?"
Soon after, he was imprisoned.
The Fù Family Daughter
The youngest daughter of the Fù Shàngshū from Běidì
once split reeds to make a mouse
as a playful trick.
Placing it on the ground,
the reed mouse suddenly could walk,
and went straight over the threshold.
into the earth.
She split reeds to make another,
chanting over it:
"If you are a household monster,
walk again;
if not, remain still."
Placing it on the ground,
it again walked as before.
She then dug inside the threshold to search,
going several chǐ into the ground,
but found nothing at all.
Later, the daughters died one after another.
Guō Zhòngchǎn
Guō Zhòngchǎn's residence was
south of Pípá Temple in Jiānglíng.
During the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
he built a study house,
using bamboo for the window lattice.
The bamboo then gradually grew branches and leaves,
extending several zhàng long,
lushly forming a grove.
Zhòngchǎn considered this auspicious.
But by the Xiàojiàn era,
he was executed.
Liú Shùn
In the Dàmíng era of the Sòng dynasty,
During this period,
Dùnqiū Magistrate Liú Shùn,
after drinking heavily,
went to bed early with his concubine Xǔ Yǎn.
Upon waking in the morning,
he saw a clump of coagulated blood on the bed,
shaped like an overturned basin.
Liú, being a military man,
was not at all alarmed or surprised.
He then ordered some dumplings to be made,
personally sliced the blood clot,
dipped the dumplings in the blood and ate them,
discarding the remainder.
More than ten years later,
in the second year of the Yuánhuī era,
he was killed by Wáng Dàolóng.
Wáng Tán
During the Dàmíng era,
Wáng Tán of Lángyá,
courtesy name Sīxuán,
served as the Prefect of Nányáng.
After his mother passed away, he left his post
and stayed south of the commandery city,
setting up a mourning hut in the courtyard.
A light appeared,
as large as a duck egg,
bright yellow and distinct,
coming from the east,
and entered the main hall.
After a short while,
two more arrived in succession,
identical in appearance to the first,
and after a long while, they departed.
From then on, they came and went every night,
sometimes singly, sometimes in pairs.
If they lingered too long, they would vanish;
in one night, they might come four or five times.
After about ten days like this, they disappeared.
That year,
two of Tán’s maidservants died,
the following year his younger brother passed away,
Tán fell ill,
and he died upon reaching the capital.
Zhōu Dēngzhī
Zhōu Dēngzhī’s home was in the capital.
During the reign of Emperor Míng of the Sòng dynasty,
he oversaw all the spirit temples
and was greatly favored.
His mother, Madame Xiè,
devoutly practiced Buddhism.
In the third year of the Tàishǐ era,
during a summer month of heavy rain,
a creature appeared, its form hidden in mist and fog,
lowering its head
toward the ground in front of the main hall.
Its head was like that of a large red horse,
and it drank water from the courtyard.
Dēngzhī was startled and frightened,
thinking it was a benevolent deity descending.
He drew more water and offered it,
and it drank over a hundred dǒu of water,
only leaving when the water was exhausted.
Two years later, Madame Xiè died,
and half a year after that, Emperor Míng passed away.
From then on, Dēngzhī’s fortunes declined.
Huáng Xún
During the Jǐngmíng era of Emperor Xuānwǔ of the Later Wèi dynasty,
Huáng Xún of Hǎilíng,
who had previously lived in poverty and hardship,
suddenly had coins fly into his home during a windstorm.
He later became immensely wealthy,
amassing tens of thousands in coins,
but that same year, he was executed.
A Person from Jīngzhōu
In the first year of the Tiānjiān era of Emperor Yuán of the Liáng dynasty,
a criminal in Jīngzhōu
was executed by beheading.
After being killed, the body did not stiffen;
the head
fell to the ground,
its mouth moving and eyes wide open.
Blood shot out like an arrow,
straight up for over ten feet,
then fell like fine rain.
That year, Jīngzhōu suffered a severe drought,
similar to the case of Chúnyú Bó, the Transport Officer under Emperor Mǐn of the Jìn dynasty.
Tián Sāo,
a native of Nányáng,
in the late Liáng dynasty,
was returning from his wife’s family home late one evening, carrying a bow and arrows.
With over ten lǐ left to go
and no companion, he felt fearful.
Looking ahead along the road, he saw a plank bridge,
and on it was a child in crimson clothing.
He hurriedly chased after it,
and upon catching up,
asked:
"Which village child are you?"
The child replied:
"My home is at the top of the tree."
Sāo thought the child was deceiving him,
and said:
"I am an elder,
speaking with a child like you.
Why respond with such disrespect?"
After walking another hundred or so paces,
he reached the plank bridge.
Beside the road stood an enormous tree,
and the child swiftly climbed up it,
moving like a monkey.
Feeling this was strange,
Sāo drew his bow and circled the tree, searching.
He saw something like a banner,
several zhàng in height, then it vanished.
Upon returning home,
he fell gravely ill and nearly died.
Dèng Chā
Liáng Dèng Chā,
a native of Línjū in Nánjùn,
was plowing a field in Màichéng
when he unearthed several hú of ancient bronze,
and thereby became very wealthy.
Once, while traveling, he encountered rain
and took shelter under a honey locust tree.
There he met an old man
who said to Chā:
"Although you are wealthy,
next year, if the house spirit emerges,
just as decline and loss follow,
you will surely meet with calamity because of the taste of fire."
Chā thought this old man was falsely claiming mystical arts
and arbitrarily seeking alms,
so he paid him no heed at all.
The following year,
inside his house, he saw a creature,
bluish-black in color,
resembling a soft-shelled turtle but not one,
about two chǐ long.
It would come out and go in on its own,
sometimes hidden, sometimes visible,
stretching and retracting, raising its head.
When the dogs saw it,
they would immediately surround it and bark together.
When they barked, it would retract its head.
The family members also dared not touch it.
This went on for over a hundred days.
Later, someone came to do farm work.
At dusk, entering from outside,
he saw it
and thought it was a lizard.
He then struck it with a sickle,
injuring its foot and drawing blood.
It dragged its foot under a pile of rice stalks
and then disappeared.
After that, they suffered a fire.
Sons and nephews died,
and official conscriptions implicated them.
Chā also once met merchants on the road.
They had not known each other before.
By the roadside, they sat facing each other to eat together.
The spread was sweet and delicious,
all the flavors were delicacies.
The two men called Chā to drink with them.
He said to them:
"Observing you two gentlemen,
traveling as merchants,
your circumstances likely aren't affluent.
Why do you suddenly have such rare and exquisite delicacies?"
The merchants said:
"An inch of light is to be cherished.
A person lives in this world
ultimately only for the body and mouth.
Once you die of illness one day,
how can you still partake in sweet delicacies?
After all, it's not like Dèng Shēng of Línjū,
who never used his wealth in his lifetime,
acting only as a miserly slave to his money."
Chā also did not tell his name.
Silently, he returned home.
Arriving home,
he slaughtered a goose to eat by himself.
Moving the tendons and biting the bone,
it choked his throat,
and he fell ill and died.
Sīmǎ Shēn
During the time of the Later Lord of Chén,
the favored minister Sīmǎ Shēn served as General of the Right Guard.
He often slandered and vilified court officials.
Later, while napping during the day in the Imperial Secretariat,
a bird pecked his mouth,
causing blood to flow onto his mat.
Contemporary opinion held this was the effect of his slander,
and an omen of Chén's gradual decline.
The Later Lord eventually surrendered.
Duàn Huī,
courtesy name Chángzuò,
had a young servant who bid farewell to return home.
He asked Huī for a horse.
Huī playfully made a wooden horse and gave it to him.
The youth said to Huī:
"I am the son of the Lord of Mount Tài's Mansion.
I thank you for your generous gift."
When he finished speaking,
he mounted the wooden horse
and soared into the sky, departing.
Cuī Jìshū
Cuī Jìshū of Northern Qí
held positions up to Palace Attendant and Specially Advanced.
Suddenly, the lotuses in his family pond
all transformed into human faces,
wearing Xiānbēi caps.
Also, his wife once napped during the day
and saw a divine being,
over ten feet tall,
with a black body and black hair,
approaching and pressing close to her.
A shaman said:
"This is General of the Five Paths.
His entering a residence is inauspicious."
Also, blood suddenly flowed in the courtyard.
There was a white object,
as large as a hú measure,
that descended from the sky,
heading toward his son's head.
When it was still over a chǐ away,
it vanished.
Jìshū also saw inside his family's main hall,
a large hand,
over ten feet long,
emerging from the ground,
filling the room with bright light.
He asked those around him,
but all said they did not see it.
Soon after, he was executed for a crime he did not commit.
The Huáng Family of Ānyáng
During the Wǔchéng era of Northern Qí,
in Ānyáng County, there was a Huáng family
living south of the old city.
Their ancestors had been immensely wealthy for generations.
A shaman divined that the family's wealth was about to leave,
and advised them to guard it well themselves.
If it left,
the family would become extremely poor.
Each night, the family had people take turns guarding.
One night, there was a group of people,
all dressed in yellow clothes,
riding horses,
who exited through the north gate.
A group of people in white clothes,
riding horses,
exited through the west gate.
A group of people in blue clothes,
riding horses,
exited through the east garden gate.
They all asked how far it was from there to Zhào Yú's house.
At the time, they all forgot
and only realized after they had left.
They beat their breasts in regret,
but could not pursue them again.
What departed in yellow, white, and blue
were all gold, silver, coins, and valuables.
Soon after,
they saw another person,
a lame man carrying firewood, who came
and also asked for Zhào Yú.
The family members, extremely agitated,
ordered a servant to strike him.
Going to look,
it turned out to be the family's broken-legged cooking pot.
After this,
they gradually became poor,
and all died out.
The Later Lord of Qí
In the fifth year of the Wǔpíng era of the Later Lord of Northern Qí,
he went to Jìnyáng.
On the road,
suddenly, among the soldiers under the tents,
there was shouting.
When questioned, they said:
"We saw countless people,
all riding small horses like foxes,
waving the tips of their knives in competition,
so we shouted."
Wáng Huìzhào
At the end of the Wǔpíng era,
Wáng Huìzhào served as the Chief Clerk in the Department of State Affairs of Guǎngpíng.
His son, Xiū, was a student at the commandery school.
He carved a small child from wood,
dressed it in clothes and kept it in a bag.
Every time he ate, he would feed it first,
saying:
"My slave, eat."
Only then would he eat himself.
After this, he became confused,
possessed by a demon.
If he did not feed it at mealtimes,
he would fall ill, nearly dying.
Gradually, he refused to eat vegetables,
demanding wine and meat instead.
Xiū's elder brother secretly took the wooden figure
and burned it in a fire.
Xiū's illness then worsened.
As his family was in a desperate situation,
they hired a craftsman to carve another wooden figure,
skillfully replicating its appearance,
and placed it at the spirit altar.
It then spoke:
"Since you burned me like that,
what good is carving another?"
Over a year later,
Xiū became insane and died.
Dúgū Tuó
Dúgū Tuó of the Suí dynasty,
courtesy name Líxié,
during the reign of Emperor Wén,
served as the Governor of Yánzhōu.
He had a fondness for heterodox arts.
His maternal family,
the Gāo clan,
had previously practiced the cat demon,
which had already killed his uncle, Guō Shāluó.
The practice then transferred into his own household.
The Emperor heard rumors but did not believe them.
His elder sister was the Empress,
and both she and Yáng Sù's wife, Lady Zhèng, fell ill.
Physicians were summoned to examine them,
and all said:
"This is the cat demon illness."
Since Tuó was the Empress's half-brother,
and Tuó's wife was Yáng Sù's half-sister,
the Emperor suspected Tuó was responsible.
He secretly ordered Tuó's elder brother, Mù, to reason with him,
and also sent attendants to admonish Tuó.
Tuó claimed he had done nothing.
The Emperor was displeased,
demoted Tuó,
and Tuó consequently voiced complaints.

The Emperor ordered Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Gāo Jiǒng, Imperial Advisor Sū Wēi, Chief Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Yáng Yuǎn, and Huángfǔ Xiàoxù to jointly investigate.
Tuó's maidservant, Xú Āní, then testified
that she had originally come from Tuó's maternal family
and had long practiced the cat demon.
She would make offerings to it every Zǐ-hour night,
saying Zǐ means rat.
Whenever the cat demon killed someone,
the victim's family wealth would secretly transfer to the household that kept the cat demon.
The Emperor then consulted his ministers about the matter.
Qízhāng Duke Niú Hóng said:
"Supernatural disasters arise from people;
execute the person,
and it can be stopped."
The Emperor ordered Tuó and his wife to be taken in a prison cart,
to be executed.
Tuó's younger brother went to the palace to plead for mercy,
so Tuó was spared death but stripped of his rank,
and his wife, Lady Yáng, was made a nun.
Previously, someone had accused his mother of being killed by a cat demon,
but the Emperor considered it superstitious nonsense,
and angrily dismissed him.
Now,
he issued an edict pardoning those who had reported households practicing the cat demon.
Tuó also died not long after.
Yáng Sù
In the fifth year of the Dàyè era,
Minister Yáng Sù built a mansion in the Eastern Capital.
Secretly, from within the palace,
he sent someone to Vice Minister of the Imperial Guard Xiāo Jí,
requesting an auspicious day to move into the new mansion.
Jí knew Sù would not come to a good end,
so he gave him a book.
This book solely discussed matters of death and mourning.
Sù opened it and was disgusted,
so he burned it in the front courtyard.
Within Sù's mansion, a hall of aloeswood was built,
extremely exquisite and beautiful.
When first completed,
it was closed for three days,
and then an auspicious day was chosen
to open and inspect it.
The four walls appeared as if freshly splattered with blood,
flowing onto the ground,
with a foul smell that assaulted people.
Sù was greatly disturbed by this,
and eventually met his death by poisoning.
In the ninth year,
Sù's eldest son, Minister of Rites Yáng Xuángǎn,
found blood inexplicably splattered on the ground in his courtyard.
Xuángǎn became fearful,
and subsequently raised troops in rebellion,
and was executed.
Téng Jǐngzhēn
Téng Jǐngzhēn was at the Seven-Story Temple in Guǎngzhōu.
During the Yǒnghuī era,
he left his post and returned home.
A maidservant was cooking,
when suddenly a sound like thunder came from the pot,
and the rice swelled up high.
Téng went to look,
and the sound grew even louder.
Dozens of flowers grew on the steamer,
resembling lotus blossoms,
their color red like gold,
but they withered and vanished in a moment.
Ten days later,
Jǐngzhēn died.
Yuán Suì
At the beginning of the Yǒngchún era,
Yuán Suì served as the Registrar of Tóngzhōu.
His mother was sitting in the hall during the day,
when she suddenly saw tiny people riding tiny horses enter from beyond the screen.
The people were two or three feet tall,
and the horses were proportionate,
fully armored and dressed,
their brilliance shining like the sun.
They galloped along the walls within the courtyard,
and after a long while, finally vanished.
After this, his mother often wanted to kill herself,
so the whole family guarded her.
After a year, they grew somewhat lax.
One night, his mother lay down to sleep,
placed clothes under the covers to substitute for herself,
and then immediately walked out.
The attendants noticed,
searched separately,
and found she had thrown herself into a well.
By the time they pulled her out,
she was nearly dead.
Liú Zhìyán
Liú Zhìyán of Cháng'ān served as the County Lieutenant of Xiàguī County in Huázhōu.
This official residence was notoriously haunted,
so he borrowed a house within the village,
but the house was still not free from strange occurrences.
A maidservant was combing her hair in the morning,
when the comb fell to the ground.
As the maidservant bent to pick it up,
she saw a cloth bag under the bed,
inside which seemed to be a child of several years old.
The maidservant reached out to take it,
when it jumped out of the bag.
The maidservant, terrified, ran out.
The whole family came to look,
but saw nothing at all.
Zhìyán died when his term of office ended.
Sù'é
Sù'é was
a courtesan of Wǔ Sānsī.
Sānsī had earlier acquired a maidservant named Yǎoniáng from the Qiáo family,
who was skilled in singing and dancing.
Sānsī was knowledgeable in musical theory,
and considered Yǎoniáng's singing and dancing
the pinnacle of artistry in the world.
Not long after,
she drowned in the Luò River,
and subsequently the entire Qiáo family was exterminated.
Among his attendants, someone recommended Sù'é, saying:
"She is the daughter of Matron Sòng from the Fèngyáng Gate in Xiàngzhōu,
skilled at playing the five-stringed lute,
She is a woman of exceptional beauty in this world."
Sānsī then sent three hundred bolts of silk to engage her.
After Sù'é arrived,
Sānsī was greatly pleased,
and thus held a grand banquet to present Sù'é.
All the high officials and ministers gathered,
only the Admonisher Dí Rénjié claimed illness and did not come.
Sānsī was angry,
and spoke of it during the banquet.
After the banquet ended,
someone informed Rénjié.
The next day, he visited to apologize to Sānsī, saying:
"My chronic illness flared up violently yesterday,
so I was unable to accept the summons.
However, not seeing the beautiful lady
is also my fate.
If there is another fine banquet in the future,
I dare not fail to arrive at your gate beforehand."
Sù'é heard of this.
She said to Sānsī:
"Lord Liáng is a man of strong will and firmness.
He is not a person for casual familiarity.
Why must you forcibly suppress his nature?
Another banquet is unavoidable,
I request that you do not summon Lord Liáng."
Sānsī said:
"If he obstructs my banquet,
I will certainly exterminate his family."
Several days later,
another banquet was held.
Before the other guests arrived,
Lord Liáng indeed came first.
Sānsī specially invited Lord Liáng to sit in the inner chamber,
slowly drinking wine,
waiting for the other guests.
He requested that Sù'é be brought out first,
to briefly observe her artistry.
So they set aside their cups,
and had a couch set up to summon her.
After a while,
an old servant came out and said:
"Sù'é has hidden herself,
and her whereabouts are unknown."
Sānsī personally went in to summon her,
but could not find her anywhere.
Suddenly, from a crevice in the depths of the hall, the fragrance of orchids and musk was detected,
so he pressed his ear to listen,
and it was indeed Sù'é's voice,
fine as a thread,
barely discernible,
saying:
"I asked you not to summon Lord Liáng,
yet now you have insisted on summoning him,
I cannot live on."
Sānsī asked her the reason,
she said:
"I am no other kind of monster,
but a spirit of flowers and the moon,
sent by the Heavenly Emperor,
also to bewilder your heart with many words,
so that the Lǐ family may rise again.
Now Lord Liáng is a righteous man of the times,
I certainly dare not appear before him.
I have served as your maidservant,
how could I be without feeling?
I hope you will earnestly serve Lord Liáng,
and do not harbor other ambitions.
Otherwise,
the Wǔ family will leave no descendants."
After she finished speaking, he asked again.
But there was no further response.
Sānsī came out.
He met Rénjié.
Claiming that Sù'é had a sudden illness,
she could not appear.
He treated him with respectful courtesy.
Rénjié did not know the reason.
The next day,
Sānsī secretly reported the matter to the throne,
Zétiān sighed and said:
"What Heaven has bestowed,
cannot be cast aside."
Zhāng Yìzhī
When Zhāng Yìzhī was about to meet his downfall,
his mother, Madame Wéi,
known as Ā Cáng,
was sitting in her residence,
when a servant reported that
a great many carriages, horses, and riders
had arrived at the gate and dismounted,
suspected to be palace officials.
Cáng went out to greet them,
but saw nothing,
then several wild foxes were seen carrying rice jars over the top of the wall.
Within ten days, disaster befell them.
After the Chuígōng era,
many prefectures presented hens that had transformed into roosters,
which was an omen concerning Zétiān.
Lǐ Chéngjiā
During the Shénlóng era of the Táng dynasty,
the Minister of Revenue Lǐ Chéngjiā,
who was illiterate,
and could not understand documents,
served as the Censor-in-chief,
and concurrently as the Senior Official of Luòzhōu.
He called the administrative officers dogs,
and cursed the censors as donkeys,
yet his authority shook the court.
In the Western Capital, a new hall was built,
and people in the ward saw countless wild foxes
go straight into the residence.
In a moment, the hall split apart on all sides,
the tiles and wood piled together,
and the brush handle he used for official business
split straight in his hand.
He took another brush,
but it split again as before.
Several days later,
he was sent out as Assistant Military Commissioner of Téngzhōu and died there.
A Man from Tàizhōu
During the Tàidìng era,
at the Chìshuǐ Inn in Tàizhōu,
there was the Zhèng Family Village.
There was a young man,
over twenty years old.
One evening,
on the post road,
he saw a young woman in blue walking alone,
of exceptionally beautiful appearance.
He asked her,
she said:
"I wish to go to Zhèng County,
but I am waiting for two maids who haven't arrived yet,
hesitating and waiting for them."
This young man invited her to stay at the village,
settled her in the main hall,
provided wine and food,
and then shared bedding with her to sleep.
By dawn,
the door had long remained unopened,
and calls received no response.
Peeking through the window,
only the skull and brain bones remained,
the rest had all been eaten.
The family broke the door and entered,
in a dark place on the beam,
they saw a large bird,
which flew out through the door,
some said it was a rākṣasa demon.
Liáng Zàiyán
The Prefect of Huáizhōu in the Táng dynasty, Liáng Zàiyán,
was sitting in the main hall during the day,
when suddenly a creature like a bat,
flew in from the south,
straight into his mouth,
he swallowed it with a gulp as if consuming something,
and then suffered severe abdominal pain,
dying several days later.
Fàn Jìfǔ
Fàn Jìfǔ, the Captain of Fùchéng,
was not yet married.
There was a beautiful woman named Cuī,
whose residence was in Yǒngpíng Lǐ,
and he often stayed with her.
In the second month of the twenty-eighth year of the Kāiyuán era,
Cuī rose in the morning and went down to the hall,
where she found a creature dead beneath the steps.
Its body was like that of a dog,
but its neck had nine heads,
each resembling a human face,
with varying expressions:
some angry,
some joyful,
some beautiful,
some ugly,
some old,
some young,
some barbaric,
some foreign,
all as large as fists,
with a very long tail,
multicolored.
Cuī was terrified
and reported it to Jìfǔ.
They consulted a shaman,
who said to burn it at a crossroads,
and the calamity would dissipate.
So they piled firewood at a crossroads and burned it.
A few days later,
Cuī’s mother died,
and after a few more days,
Cuī herself died,
and after a few more days,
Jìfǔ also perished.
A Woman of Luòyáng
During the reign of Emperor Xuánzōng,
a woman in Luòyáng was afflicted by demonic possession,
and successive exorcists failed to cure her.
The woman’s son went to the Daoist priest Yè Fǎshàn,
seeking a ritual to expel it.
Fǎshàn said:
“This is a heavenly demon.
It bears guilt from heaven,
banished by the Emperor,
and is temporarily in the human realm.
However, its banishment is nearly complete,
and it will soon depart on its own,
so there is no need to expel it.”
The man thought these were mere words of consolation,
so he pleaded for help.
Fǎshàn said:
“If you truly insist, I will go.”
Then he led the man deep into the mountains of Yángdí.
At a remote peak, there was a pool.
Fǎshàn performed incantations by the poolside,
and after a long while,
a headdress appeared in the water,
as large as three rooms,
slowly rising,
until two eyes emerged,
gleaming like lightning.
Suddenly, clouds and mist gathered from all sides,
and it vanished.
Péi Xiūzhēn
General Péi Xiūzhēn of the Imperial Guards,
in his humble days,
lived in Jiàoyè Lǐ.
A guest visited him,
and Xiūzhēn entertained the guest,
with his younger brothers also present.
As evening fell and the guest left,
Xiūzhēn lay alone in the main hall.
After dark,
Xiūzhēn awoke
to a sound circling his bed, saying:
“Brother, go to your wife.”
This repeated incessantly.
Xiūzhēn looked at the caller,
whose appearance was terrifying,
and it kept circling him.
Xiūzhēn, frightened,
leaped to the door and called for his servant.
The servant came with a lamp,
and his younger brother also arrived.
Then the creature appeared within the lamplight,
resembling a Kūnlún slave,
with large, white teeth,
and standing five feet tall.
Xiūzhēn’s younger brother, Xiūyuán,
known for his great strength,
struck it with his fist,
and a sound echoed,
as if hitting iron or stone.
The creature’s form immediately vanished.
That year,
Xiūzhēn’s mother died.
Niú Chéng
Fifty lǐ southeast of the capital,
there was a place called Xiàoyì Fāng.
To the west of the fāng, on the plain,
strange phenomena often occurred.
In the twenty-ninth year of the Kāiyuán era,
Niú Sù’s younger brother, Chéng,
went to Xiàoyì.
Arriving at the western plain in the morning,
he met a villager named Rěn Gǎo
and spoke with him.
Suddenly, about five hundred paces to the east,
they saw black masses like carriage covers,
more than ten in total.
The foremost was twenty or thirty zhàng tall,
the others about one zhàng each,
moving from north to south,
reaching the edge of the plain.
Then they turned from south back to north,
following one after another.
After sunrise,
their movement quickened,
sometimes appearing, sometimes disappearing.
As the sun rose higher,
they all vanished.
Gǎo said:
“This place is often like this,
nothing to be surprised about.
A few months ago,
a cavalry messenger,
having completed his tour of duty and returning south,
suddenly saw something in the air,
resembling a pack-animal load.
The cavalryman stabbed at it with his sword,
and the load swelled into a human form,
over ten feet tall,
and chased the cavalryman.
The cavalryman fled,
shooting arrows as he went,
hitting it.
The creature paused briefly,
then pursued again,
and the cavalryman shot again,
until it stopped.
At dawn,
he searched where he had shot,
and found blood on the ground,
but no sign of the creature.
He then fell ill,
returned home,
and died a few days later.”
Zhāng Hàn
Zhāng Hàn, the Recorder and Consultant of the Right Gate Guard,
had a relative whose wife,
in the early Tiānbǎo era,
gave birth to a child.
Just as she was gathering the newborn boy,
another headless child appeared,
jumping around beside them.
When she tried to grab it, it vanished,
but as soon as she withdrew her hand, it reappeared nearby.
According to the Báizé Tú,
its name was “Cháng.”
Following the illustration, they called its name.
By the third call,
it suddenly disappeared.
The Deputy of Nánzhèng County
Sūn Mǐn, the Deputy of Nánzhèng County,
served as an assistant investigator in Shānnán.
Once, while traveling on duty,
he lodged at a mountain inn.
Suddenly, the beautiful face of a woman
emerged from a pillar,
smiling at Mǐn.
Mǐn bowed and prayed to it,
and after a long while, it finally vanished.
He was too afraid to speak of it.
Several years later,
he was appointed Deputy of Sāngquán.
While in the capital, he fell ill,
and friends came to inquire about his health.
Mǐn then told the story and died.
Lǐ Pàn
Li Pàn, the County Captain of Xiányáng,
had a nephew who was brave yet stubborn.
He often boasted in front of guests,
claiming he feared neither gods nor ghosts,
his words full of exaggeration.
Suddenly, from the southern wall of his residence,
a face emerged,
crimson in color,
over a foot in size,
with a collapsed nose and bulging eyes,
sharp teeth and a fierce mouth,
utterly detestable.
The nephew, enraged,
punched it with his fist,
and it vanished at his touch.
Soon, it appeared again on the western wall,
this time white in color.
It then appeared on the eastern wall,
green in color,
its appearance the same as before,
and a punch from him made it disappear again.
Later, a black face appeared on the northern wall,
its visage even more terrifying,
and twice as large.
The nephew grew even angrier,
but despite striking it several times with his fist, it did not leave.
He drew his knife and stabbed it,
finally hitting it.
The face then detached from the wall and pressed toward him,
and the nephew pushed it away with his hands.
Unable to repel it,
the black face merged with the nephew's own face,
turning it as black as lacquer,
and the nephew fell to the ground dead.
When they prepared his body for burial,
the color never changed.
Yuán Zìxū
During the Kāiyuán era,
Yuán Zìxū served as Prefect of Tīngzhōu.
Upon arriving at the commandery,
all the officials came to see him,
and there was one person,
nearly eighty years old,
who called himself Old Xiāo,
saying, "My family of several members
has lived in Your Excellency's residence for generations,
and we are fortunate not to occupy the main halls."
Having said this, he vanished.
Thereafter, whenever there was good or bad fortune,
Old Xiāo would foretell it in advance,
and nothing he predicted failed to come true.
Zìxū was upright and stern,
and often did not believe him.
However, the household servants saw strange occurrences every night:
sometimes they saw someone sitting on the eaves,
feet dangling to the ground;
sometimes they saw people walking in twos and threes
through the air;
some carried infants,
begging for food from people;
sometimes there were beautiful women,
heavily made-up and dressed in fine clothes,
laughing and talking under the moonlight,
often throwing bricks and tiles.
The servants then reported to Zìxū, saying:
"We have long heard that the empty room behind the kitchen is a shrine,
and previous occupants all made offerings of incense there.
Now that this is not done,
that is why such monsters appear."
Zìxū grew angry,
still refusing to believe.
Suddenly one day,
Old Xiāo visited Zìxū and said:
"Today I must travel far to visit relatives and old friends,
and I entrust my family of several members to your care."
Having said this, he departed.
Zìxū asked an old clerk about this,
and the clerk said:
"I have long heard that in the withered tree behind the official residence,
there lives a shānxiāo (mountain demon)."
Zìxū ordered firewood to be piled as high as the tree,
and set it ablaze.
They heard cries of injustice from within the tree,
unbearable to listen to.
Over a month later,
Old Xiāo returned,
dressed in mourning white, weeping sorrowfully and saying:
"I had no choice but to travel far,
leaving my wife and children in the hands of bandits.
Now, under heaven,
I am left all alone,
and I must let you know, my lord."
Then, from his belt,
he untied a small box,
the size of a pellet,
and threw it to the ground,
saying:
"Go quickly, go quickly."
Zìxū bent down, picked it up, and opened it.
Inside was a small tiger,
only as big as a string.
As Zìxū tried to grab it,
it jumped to the ground,
already grown several inches long,
and kept leaping about.
In a moment, it became a large tiger,
ran through the central gate,
and all the more than one hundred members of the household,
were killed by it,
and then the tiger vanished.
As for Zìxū,
he was left all alone.
Zhǎngsūn Yì
A relative of Zhǎngsūn Yì was named Prefect Zhèng.
The Prefect had only two sons,
whom he loved dearly.
One son, aged fifteen,
while Zhèng was governing the commandery,
was often attended by over ten servants for his needs.
One night,
while the servants were all eating,
the son sat alone,
when suddenly he heard something approaching from the east side of the door,
its footsteps heavy on the ground,
each step rumbling.
Soon it reached the door,
and then came under the bed.
It was a small iron child,
three feet tall,
extremely stout,
with red eyes and a large mouth.
It said to the Prefect's son:
"Hey!
Mother is calling,
telling you to come suckle."
The son screamed in terror,
and jumped inside the door.
When the servants saw it,
they immediately reported to the Prefect.
The Prefect ordered over ten men
to strike it with clubs,
but it was like hitting stone.
Slowly, it descended the steps,
and headed south out the gate.
They even tried hacking it with knives and axes,
but it could not be injured.
They ordered torches to be lit and set it on fire.
As the flames burned its body,
it opened its mouth and let out a great cry,
sounding like thunder,
causing those who heard it to tremble and fall.
So they drove it away with fire,
and once it left the yamén gate,
it stepped into a cart rut,
and vanished.
After that, his household experienced neither misfortune nor calamity.
Wéi Xūxīn
Wéi Xūxīn, Minister of Revenue,
had three sons,
all of whom died before reaching maturity.
Whenever a son was about to die,
a large face would emerge from under the bed,
glaring with wide-open eyes and mouth,
its appearance like that of a demon or ghost.
The son, terrified, would flee,
and the large face would then transform into a large owl,
using its wings to block and push him,
forcing him to throw himself into a well.
The family, realizing what happened,
quickly pulled him out,
but he was already dazed,
though still able to describe what he had seen,
and died a few days later.
All three sons died in this manner,
and they never learned what kind of ghost or monster it was.
Péi Jǐnwēi
Péi Jìngwēi from Hédōng,
had a friend,
There was a military man,
whose residence was nearby.
The military man was returning to his village at night,
carrying a bow and arrows,
just galloping on horseback,
when he heard something approaching from behind.
Looking back, he saw it,
its form was large,
resembling a fāngxiàng,
its mouth only uttering "thirsty."
As it was about to reach the military man,
the military man drew his bow and shot,
hitting it,
and the monster stopped.
Shortly after, it approached again,
he shot it again,
the monster halted once more,
and soon it came again.
The military man hurriedly reached home,
the gate was already closed,
so he climbed over the wall and entered.
After entering,
he peeked through the door,
and the monster was still there.
The military man dared not fetch his horse,
and the next morning when he opened the gate,
the saddle was abandoned at the gate,
but the horse was gone.
Searching for it several li away in a grove of grave trees,
he saw the horse had been devoured entirely,
only its bones remained.
Lǐ Yú
Lǐ Yú of Quánjié,
loved large horses,
and was unruly from a young age.
His father once served as a county magistrate,
and Lǐ Yú followed him to his post,
engaging in various idle wanderings.
Every night,
he would escape through a hole,
to drink with others.
Later, when he reached the hole,
there was someone with their back turned to him,
blocking the hole with their buttocks,
Lǐ Yú pushed but could not move them,
so he stabbed with his sword,
the sword sank up to the hilt,
yet they remained as before.
Only then did he realize it was not human,
and terrified, he returned.
Also, at the end of the year,
while hunting birds in the wild,
the birds entered a grove of grave trees.
Searching in the grove,
he saw a dead person lying face up,
their body greatly swollen,
very repulsive,
with a huge nose and large eyes,
their eyes suddenly moved,
and light shone from them,
staring directly at Lǐ Yú.
Lǐ Yú was frightened nearly to death,
and from then on, he dared not hunt anymore.
The Woman from Wǔdé County
In the twenty-eighth year of the Kāiyuán era,
a woman in Wǔdé was pregnant,
about to give birth to a boy.
Her mother-in-law was worried,
prepared provisions,
stored dry provisions.
Their family was poor,
having only a few dòu of flour,
and one qū of rice.
When the time of delivery came,
her husband was not home,
so the mother-in-law and a neighboring woman assisted her together.
After the boy was born,
the mother-in-law and the neighboring woman prepared food.
Before the food arrived,
the woman seemed hungry and thirsty,
incessantly asking for food.
The mother-in-law fed her,
she finished several people's worth of meals,
yet still said she was hungry.
The mother-in-law then cooked a shēng of flour and offered it,
the woman ate,
leaving nothing,
and still claimed it was not enough.
The mother-in-law became angry,
and prepared more.
After the mother-in-law went out,
there was a jar of cakes in the room,
the woman got off the bed,
personally took the container,
took the cakes and ate them,
and the cakes were also finished.
When the mother-in-law returned and saw this,
she was both angry and afraid,
and said to the neighboring woman:
"What is this woman doing?"
The woman said:
"From my youth to adulthood,
I have never seen such a thing."
As the mother-in-law was just expressing her anger,
the new bride said:
"Mother-in-law, do not be angry,
I will stop after eating the child."
Thereupon she picked up her child and ate him,
the mother-in-law tried to snatch him but could not,
and fled in terror.
Shortly after, she re-entered the room,
the woman had already eaten her child entirely,
her mouth still crimson with blood.
Then she said to the mother-in-law:
"The new bride will now lie down and die,
and there will be nothing left.
If placed on the side,
it might still be possible to collect."
After speaking,
she lay on her back and died.
The People of Huáizhōu
In the twenty-eighth year of the Kāiyuán era,
in the second month of spring,
people from the three counties of Wǔdé, Wǔzhì, and Xiūwǔ in Huáizhōu,
for no reason ate earth,
saying,
its taste was delicious and different from other earth.
Previously, women from the Qīchéng village in Wǔdé,
while gathering together,
gathered and said:
"Now rice is expensive and people are hungry,
how are we to live!"
There was an old man,
wearing purple clothes and riding a white horse,
accompanied by ten people who passed by,
and said to the women:
"Why worry about having no food?
The earth beside this canal is very good,
you can eat it,
try tasting it."
The women took some and ate it,
the taste was quite unusual,
and then the old man disappeared.
So they took the earth home,
mixed it with flour to make cakes,
and the cakes were very fragrant.
From then on, people from near and far competed to take it,
the canal's east-west length of five li,
and north-south width of over ten paces,
the earth was entirely exhausted.
Niú Sù was in Huái at the time,
and personally witnessed this.
The Commoner of Wǔdé County
At an inn in Wǔdé County,
someone locked a room,
and left a cart of goods.
After dozens of days without returning,
the innkeeper found it strange,
opened and looked at the bags,
they were all human-faced clothing,
and terrified, he closed it.
That evening,
the door opened by itself,
and all the stored bagged goods,
disappeared without a trace.
Zhāng Sīmǎ
In the summer of the twenty-eighth year of the Kāiyuán era,
Sīmǎ Zhāng of Dìngzhōu
was sitting outdoors with his wife in the middle of the night.
They heard something flying through the air,
making a whirring sound,
which passed over to the main hall
but was obstructed by the roof tiles.
It tumbled around the edge of the roof
and then fell in front of the eaves.
It started to run away,
so Sīmǎ ordered his men to chase it.
The pursuers kicked it,
and it made a dog-like sound.
They captured it and brought it over to a fire to examine it—
it turned out to be an old dog,
red in color with sparse fur,
its body very long,
but its legs extremely short,
only about one or two inches.
Sīmǎ ordered it to be burned,
deeply worried that it was a monster.
A little over a month later,
he was transferred to serve as Deputy Prefect of Shēnzhōu.
Lǐ Shìzhī
Lǐ Shìzhī, being both noble and wealthy,
often arranged tripods in front of him
to serve meals.
One day,
the tripods in the courtyard leaped out and began fighting each other.
A servant reported this to Shìzhī,
who then went to the spot,
poured a libation and made a vow,
but the fighting did not cease,
and the ears and legs of the tripods all broke off.
The next day,
Shìzhī was removed from his position as Chief Minister
and appointed Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent.
People at the time knew that his misfortune was not yet over.
Soon, he was framed by Lǐ Línfǔ,
demoted to Prefect of Yíchūn,
and his son Lǐ Zhá,
who was Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
was also demoted to Assistant Prefect of Bālíng Commandery.
When Shìzhī arrived at his post,
he died within less than a month.
People at the time believed Línfǔ had forced him to his death.
Zhá then brought his father’s coffin back to the capital.
Lǐ Línfǔ’s anger had still not subsided,
so he ordered someone to falsely accuse Zhá,
and had him beaten to death with a staff at the Hé’nán Prefecture office.
Shìzhī loved to drink;
after leaving court,
he would quickly gather friends and relatives,
chatting and composing poems,
never being cautious of Línfǔ.
When Shìzhī first served as Chief Minister,
he once composed a poem that said:
“The vermilion gate never barred,
friends and kin freely come and go.
Now past fifty years of age,
if I don’t drink, what else to do?”
After being removed from the post of Chief Minister,
he wrote another poem:
“Yielding to the worthy, I resign my post,
delighting in wine, I raise my cup.
May I ask the guests before my gate,
how many come to visit today?”
He died unjustly,
and people at the time lamented the injustice.
Lǐ Línfǔ
Lǐ Línfǔ’s residence
also frequently experienced strange hauntings.
In the ditch at the southern and northern corners,
a great fire would flare up,
and sometimes a child holding a torch would go in and out.
Línfǔ detested this,
so he petitioned to build the Jiāyóu
Temple on that spot.
When Línfǔ was about to fall ill,
he rose in the morning to attend court
and ordered his document bag to be brought,
which contained the usual list of important matters.
Suddenly, he felt the bag was unusually heavy.
A servant opened it to look,
and two rats jumped out.
They fell to the ground
and transformed into dogs,
blue-gray in color, large and strong,
with fierce eyes and bared teeth,
staring up at Línfǔ.
He ordered archers to shoot them,
and they made a loud thudding sound,
after which the dog forms vanished.
Línfǔ was disturbed by this,
claimed illness and did not attend court,
and fell ill that very day,
dying within less than a month.
Also, the abandoned mansion on South Street of Píngkāng Ward
was Lǐ Línfǔ’s former residence.
Behind the main hall,
Línfǔ had built a separate chamber,
with a winding design
shaped like a crescent moon,
named the Crescent Moon Hall.
Its construction was splendid,
and its carvings exquisite,
unmatched at the time.
Whenever Línfǔ wanted to ruin someone’s family,
he would enter the Crescent Moon Hall,
ponder deeply and exhaustively,
and emerge pleased—
and that family would be destroyed.
Just before his downfall,
Línfǔ saw in the hall
a creature resembling a person,
covered all over in hair,
bristling like a boar’s,
with a saw-like body and hook-like claws,
over three feet tall.
It pointed at Línfǔ,
its eyes flashing like lightning as it glared angrily.
Línfǔ shouted at it repeatedly, but it did not move,
so he hastily ordered bows and arrows.
The hairy man laughed and leaped into the front hall,
where a maidservant
encountered it and died suddenly.
It passed through the stable,
and the fine horses there also died.
Within a month, Línfǔ fell from power.
Yáng Shèngjīn
Yáng Shèngjīn and his brothers enjoyed wealth and status,
but they often felt uneasy.
Every morning, they would bow before a Buddha statue,
silently praying for unseen protection.
One day,
on the earthen platform in front of the statue,
three piles of dust gathered,
resembling grave mounds.
Shèngjīn was disturbed by this,
and suspecting it might be children’s play,
he ordered it swept away.
But the next night, it reappeared as before,
and soon disaster struck.
Jiāng Jiǎo
Jiāng Jiǎo once visited Chándìng Temple,
where the Jīngzhào Prefecture officials had prepared a lavish feast.
During the drinking,
a courtesan of exceptional beauty at the table
offered wine and adjusted her hair,
but no one ever saw her hands.
Everyone found it strange.
One guest, drunk,
joked:
“Could it be she has no fingers?”
He then forcibly pulled her hand to look—
the courtesan collapsed as he pulled,
turning into a dried-up skeleton.
Jiāng Jiǎo soon met with misfortune.
Cháo Liángzhēn
Cháo Liángzhēn was known for his judicial discernment,
and his nature was fierce and unyielding,
fearing no ghosts.
Every year,
he would dig in the ground of the Tàisuì (Year God) to build houses,
and once he unearthed a piece of flesh,
larger than a food bowl.
Liángzhēn whipped it several hundred times
and then left it at a main crossroads.
That night,
he sent someone to hide and listen.
After midnight,
many riders and carriages arrived at the spot where the flesh was,
and asked the Tàisuì:
“Brother, why did you endure such humiliation
and not take revenge?”
The Tàisuì replied:
“He is currently at the peak of his fortune;
what can I do?”
By dawn, the flesh had disappeared.
Lǐ Shì
In the final years of the Shangyuán era,
there was a family named Lǐ
who did not believe in the taboo of Tàisuì.
They dug into the ground
and unearthed a lump of flesh.
According to legend,
whoever obtained Tàisuì
should whip it several hundred times
to avoid calamity.
The Lǐ family whipped it over ninety times,
when suddenly it soared upward
and vanished without a trace.
The Lǐ household had seventy-two members,
and nearly all of them died.
Only Xiǎo Kuǎi Gōng survived.
Fearing their family line would be completely extinguished,
the Lǐ brothers,
in the middle of the night,
ordered their servants to dress as ghosts
and abduct Xiǎo Kuǎi,
hiding him away.
Only this child survived,
and he later inherited the title of Kuǎi Gōng.
Also, in Níngzhōu, a person
dug up Tàisuì as well,
which was as large as a square,
resembling a red fungus,
with thousands of eyes.
His family did not recognize it,
so they moved it to the main road
and asked everyone they met if they knew what it was.
A foreign monk exclaimed in alarm:
"This is Tàisuì!
You must bury it quickly."
The person hurriedly returned it to its original place,
but within a year,
almost everyone in the family died.
Zhāng Zhōufēng
Zhāng Zhōufēng, a Vice Director in the Ministry of Works,
said his old estate was east of the city, west of Gǒujiàzuǐ.
Once, while building a wall over Tàisuì,
the wall collapsed completely overnight.
Thinking the foundation was weak
or the workmanship poor,
he gathered the estate workers
and directed them to rebuild it.
Before the wall reached a few feet high,
the cook cried out in alarm:
"Something strange is happening!"
They rushed to look and saw
several dou of rice
leaping out in rows,
sticking to the wall,
evenly distributed like silkworm eggs,
with not a single grain overlapping,
covering half the wall
as if divided by a boundary.
They then consulted a shaman,
poured libations on the ground to apologize,
and nothing further happened.
Wáng Fēng
In Jímò County, Láizhōu,
there was a commoner named Wáng Fēng,
who had two brothers.
Wáng Fēng did not believe in directional taboos
and once dug a pit over Tàisuì.
He saw a lump of flesh,
as large as a dou measure,
writhing and moving.
He quickly filled the pit,
but the flesh emerged as he filled it.
Terrified, Wáng Fēng abandoned it.
Overnight, the flesh grew
and filled the courtyard.
Within a few days,
his brothers, servants, and maids
all died suddenly,
leaving only one daughter alive.
Fáng Jí
During the reign of Emperor Sùzōng of the Táng dynasty,
there was a Secretary in the Ministry of Personnel named Fáng Jí,
who wielded considerable power.
