One leisurely day,
he was sitting alone in his private hall
when suddenly a boy,
about fourteen or fifteen years old,
with shaved hair reaching his eyebrows,
appeared holding a cloth bag.
No one knew where he came from,
but he stood before Fáng.
Fáng initially thought he was a child sent by a relative or friend to visit,
but the boy did not respond when questioned.
Fáng then asked what was in the bag,
and the boy laughed and said:
"Eyes."
He then emptied the bag,
and several shēng of eyes spilled out,
scattering across the floor
and climbing up the walls and onto the roof.
The whole family was shocked and bewildered,
and the boy vanished without a trace,
while the eyes also disappeared.
Later, Fáng Jí was executed for his crimes.
Zhāng Yín
Zhāng Yín from Fànyáng once traveled south of the old city of Luòyáng.
As dusk fell,
he sought lodging at an old friend's home.
While passing through a narrow path,
his horse suddenly grew alarmed and looked around,
stomping and refusing to move forward.
Zhāng Yín suspected something strange ahead,
so he looked at a tomb by the roadside.
Atop a large pillar stone, there was an object
resembling a gauze lantern,
as large as a censer on a bridge pillar.
It gradually grew larger,
reaching the size of several hú measures.
When it touched the ground,
it flew like a shooting star,
with a sound like thunder.
Wherever it passed,
birds roosting in the forest scattered in alarm.
After about a hundred paces,
it fell into someone's house.
Zhāng Yín secretly noted the location
and left.
Over a month later,
he passed by that house again
and found that none of the family, young or old, had survived.
He inquired with the neighbors,
who said:
"The daughter-in-law treated her mother-in-law disrespectfully.
After the mother-in-law died,
this calamity befell them."
Yàn Fèngxiáng
Yàn Fèngxiáng of Píngyáng,
who was quite well-versed in the Six Arts,
gathered disciples to give lectures.
One night, while at home with his wife,
he suddenly heard a muffled, groaning sound from outside.
Thinking it was a thief,
he slipped on his shoes to check,
and just then saw a creature,
white in color,
over ten feet long,
in the courtyard.
He hurriedly closed the door and went inside.
Gradually, he heard it climbing the steps,
calling to Fèngxiáng:
"The night is still young,
why have you closed the door?"
He remained silent, not daring to respond,
and kept a lamp lit to guard himself.
Shortly after,
a face appeared through a crack in the door,
resembling a monkey,
and it suddenly burst in.
It called out to its hundreds of companions,
who all entered through the cracks.
They were all over two feet tall,
wearing leopard-skin loincloths,
puffing their lips and glaring with wide eyes,
their appearances extremely ugly and grotesque.
Some climbed along the walls,
others were among the beams and rafters,
leaping and jumping behind him,
their intent seemingly to press closer.
All Fèngxiáng had at hand
was a pillow,
and his wife's pipa,
so he threw these at them,
and those hit would leave.
Only by dawn were they all gone,
and thus he escaped harm.
In a daze, he often saw dignified, well-dressed figures in the room,
arrayed along the four walls,
saying:
"We are the envoys of Yáo Píng of Píngyáng."
Various shamans and priests performed rituals and prayers,
but they could not be driven away.
So he took refuge in a monastery,
where he saw a large face under the Buddhist altar,
staring at him with wide eyes.
He tried to flee to another place,
but upon going out the door,
he again saw a crowd of ghosts,
all playing in the alley.
They headed straight for Fèngxiáng,
preventing him from leaving.
With no way out,
his illness grew increasingly severe.
He then invited many monks to hold vegetarian feasts,
set up altars, and chant incantations.
He also summoned Liùdīng Daoist priests,
who performed talismans and prohibitory spells,
and the ghosts gradually left.
A few days later,
Fèngxiáng dreamed of a person,
dressed in red robes with a black headscarf,
standing in the air,
saying:
"I return your soul and spirit."
Then he threw something at Fèngxiáng,
resembling a woman's hair,
and several dozen items like crimson garments.
Fèngxiáng received them all,
and the next day he recovered.
Wáng Shēng
In the early years of the Yǒngtài era,
there was a man named Wáng Shēng,
who lived north of the Xiàogǎn Temple in Yángzhōu.
One summer day, drunk, he lay down to sleep,
with his hand hanging off the bed.
His wife, fearing he might catch a chill,
lifted it back onto the bed.
Suddenly, a huge hand emerged from in front of the bed,
grabbed Wáng's arm, and pulled him off the bed,
his body gradually sinking into the ground.
His wife and servants together tried to pull him out,
but could not stop it.
The ground seemed to split open,
at first leaving only his clothes and belt behind,
and soon even those disappeared.
His family dug with all their might,
reaching a depth of about twenty feet,
where they found a set of dried bones,
already looking several hundred years old.
In the end, they never knew what kind of monster it was.
Liáng Zhòngpéng
Liáng Zhòngpéng of Yèxiàn,
whose home was on the south side of the street in the western suburb of Rǔzhōu.
To the west of his house was a small estate,
and he often went there in the morning and returned in the evening.
In the early years of the Dàlì era,
on the fifteenth day of the eighth month,
the sky and earth were clear and free of haze.
About fifteen or sixteen li away,
there was a grand tomb grove of a wealthy family,
all planted with white poplars.
At that time,
with autumn scenery and falling leaves,
Zhòngpéng rode his horse and reached this place.
During the second watch,
he heard a rustling sound from the grove,
and suddenly a creature
flew out from the woods.
Zhòngpéng initially thought it was a startled roosting bird,
but soon it flew into Zhòngpéng's embrace,
sitting on the saddle bow.
In the moonlight, it looked as big as a five-dǒu basket,
with black fur,
a head resembling a human's,
and eyes gleaming like pearls.
It called Zhòngpéng "younger brother,"
saying to him:
"Younger brother, don't
be afraid."
It carried a strong smell of mutton and goat,
but its speech was just like a human's.
It accompanied him all the way to the city gate of Rǔzhōu,
where they saw that the households were not yet asleep,
with lamplight glowing.
The monster then suddenly flew away to the southeast,
and no one knew where it went.
After this, Zhòngpéng returned home and for many days
did not dare to speak of it to his family.
Suddenly one night,
when the moon was high and the night deep,
and the weather was fine,
Zhòngpéng summoned his younger siblings,
and they drank together in the courtyard,
some whistling, some reciting poetry,
and he then told them about the incident from the previous night.
The monster suddenly flew down from the roof ridge,
saying to Zhòngpéng:
"Younger brother, what are you saying about your elder brother?"
At this, everyone, young and old, scattered in panic,
leaving only Zhòngpéng behind.
It said:
"I'll be the host for my brother."
It incessantly demanded wine,
and Zhòngpéng looked closely at it:
under its neck was a goiter,
as large as a fresh melon,
its flying wings were actually its ears,
and also its wings,
its nose was covered in black feathers, thick and dense,
as large as a goose egg.
After drinking several dǒu of wine,
it got drunk on the banquet table,
as if asleep.
Zhòngpéng quietly got up,
sharpened a broad blade,
and stabbed it in the neck,
causing blood to spurt out.
It then rose and said:
"Elder brother, elder brother,
younger brother, don't regret this."
It then retreated to the roof ridge,
and was never seen again,
but the courtyard was filled with blood.
Within three years,
Zhòngpéng's entire family of thirty members perished.
Wéi Pāng
During the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a scholar named Wěi Pāng,
whose physical strength surpassed that of ordinary men,
and he feared nothing while traveling at night.
He was skilled at riding and archery,
and always carried his bow and arrows with him.
Not only did he hunt birds and beasts to cook and eat,
but even creatures like snakes, scorpions, earthworms, dung beetles, and mole crickets—
whenever he saw them, he would eat them.
Once, while traveling at dusk in the capital,
as the drumbeats were about to cease,
and his destination was still far away,
he sought a place to stay for the night,
but did not know where to go.
Suddenly, he saw a well-dressed family in the market district
moving their belongings out of their house.
The younger family members were about to lock the gate.
Wěi asked to lodge there for the night.
The master of the house said:
"A neighboring family in this residence has suffered a death,
and according to custom, it is said
that a murderous ghost will enter the house,
causing harm to people and property.
We are now taking our family to stay with relatives nearby to avoid it,
and will return tomorrow.
I felt I must inform you of this."
Wěi said:
"If you allow me to stay here,
what harm could there be?
If a murderous ghost comes, I will deal with it myself."
The master then led Wěi into the house,
opened the main hall and kitchen,
showed him the bed,
and provided food and drink.
Wěi had his servant rest the horse at the trough,
placed a candle lamp in the center of the hall,
and also had someone prepare food in the kitchen.
After eating,
he ordered his servant to sleep in a separate room,
while Wěi arranged his bed in the hall,
opened the double doors,
extinguished the candle, strung his bow,
and sat waiting.
Just before the third watch was about to end,
he suddenly saw a light,
as large as a big plate,
flying down from the sky to the space under the northern door of the hall,
shining brightly like fire.
Wěi was especially pleased to see this,
and from the darkness,
he drew his bow to its fullest
and shot an arrow, hitting it squarely.
There was a loud, explosive sound.
The fire then flickered as if moving,
and after shooting three arrows in succession,
its light gradually dimmed,
until it could no longer move.
Carrying his bow, he went straight over to pull out the arrows,
and the luminous object fell to the ground.
Wěi called his servant,
brought a torch to examine it,
and saw it was a lump of flesh,
with eyes on all sides.
Whenever the eyes opened and moved,
they emitted light.
Wěi laughed and said:
"My words about dealing with a murderous ghost
have indeed proven true."
He then ordered his servant to cook it.
The flesh was extremely fragrant.
After boiling it until well done,
he cut it into pieces
and ate it with relish,
finding it especially delicious.
He shared some with his servant,
and kept half to present to the master of the house.
By daybreak,
the master returned,
saw Wěi,
and was relieved to find him unharmed.
Wěi then recounted how he had dealt with the murderous ghost
and presented the remaining flesh.
The master could only express his amazement.
Liǔ Shì
During the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a scholar
whose estate was in Wèinán,
but who fell ill and died in the capital.
His wife, Liǔ Shì,
continued to live at the estate.
They had a son,
around eleven or twelve years old.
One summer night,
the son suddenly became terrified and could not sleep.
After the third watch,
he saw an old man,
dressed in white,
with two teeth protruding beyond his lips.
Staring intently,
the figure gradually drew closer after a long while.
There was a maidservant sleeping soundly,
and the old man seized her
by the throat,
producing a crunching sound.
Her clothes tore as he grabbed her,
and he devoured her.
In moments, her bones were exposed,
and he then lifted her up
and drank her entrails.
The boy saw the old man's mouth as large as a winnowing basket,
and just as he screamed,
the figure vanished without a trace.
The maidservant was now nothing but bones.
Several months later,
nothing else unusual happened.
The scholar's family held a memorial ceremony.
At dusk,
Liǔ Shì sat outside to enjoy the cool air,
when a wasp began circling her head and face.
Liǔ Shì struck it down with her fan,
and it turned out to be a walnut.
Liǔ Shì picked it up and placed it in the hall,
where it began to grow.
At first, it was the size of a fist, then a bowl,
and in the moment of her startled gaze,
it had already grown as large as a plate.
With a cracking sound, it split into two halves,
spinning in the air
with a sound like a swarm of bees,
then suddenly closed around Liǔ Shì's head.
Liǔ Shì's head was crushed,
her teeth embedded in a tree,
and the object flew away.
In the end, no one knew what kind of monster it was.
Wáng Sù
In the third year of the Jiànzhōng era,
Wáng Sù, former Merit Official of the Yáng Prefecture,
had been awaiting his official appointment since winter,
and by the fourth month,
there was still no news or letters.
His wife, Dòu Shì of Fúfēng,
was deeply worried.
They had two daughters,
both of exceptional beauty.
Suddenly, they heard that a fortune-telling sorceress named Bāo Jiǔniáng,
who was passing through their lane,
was highly regarded by everyone for her accurate divinations,
so they summoned her to perform a divination.
After Jiǔniáng prepared the fragrant water,
they soon heard someone descending from the air.
Jiǔniáng said:
"Sānláng has come.
Let him see what has happened with the official's affairs?
There has been no news or letters,
so when will he return?"
After speaking, she left.
After a few moments,
a voice suddenly descended, swirling through the air,
and spoke from Jiǔniáng's throat:
"What will the lady offer in return?
Your husband is safe and well.
Today, he borrowed money at the silk market in the West Market,
and traveled a long distance with three others.
Because he used cheat sheets during the selection examination,
he was reported by someone,
so he could not meet the officials.
While preparing for his journey,
he secretly wrote this."
On the twenty-third day of the fifth month, at dawn,
Sù suddenly arrived home.
Dòu Shì was overjoyed.
After he sat down,
she immediately asked:
"Why did you use cheat sheets,
causing your appointment to fail?
Also, on a certain day of a certain month, you borrowed money at the West Market,
and traveled a long distance with three others."
Sù, having never sent a letter,
was astonished and surprised.
His wife then recounted the story of the sorceress.
He immediately summoned the sorceress,
who said:
"Do not worry,
next year you will surely get a good official position.
Today, someone from the northwest will bring two water buffaloes,
suffering from foot ailments.
Do not haggle over the price; buy them.
Within ten days to a month,
you should profit several times over."
When the time came,
sure enough, someone led two lame buffaloes past,
and he bought them for four thousand strings of cash.
After six or seven days,
the buffaloes became very fat and strong,
and their feet showed no injuries.
A miller in the same neighborhood
suddenly lost two of his buffaloes to death,
and urgently needed replacements,
so he offered fifteen thousand strings to buy them.
Originally, Sù's residence was west of Qìngyún Temple.
The sorceress suddenly said:
"Sell this house quickly."
Following her advice, he sold it,
receiving one hundred and fifty thousand strings of cash.
She then told him to rent a house east of the river,
on a monthly basis,
to store supplies for a year.
After that, he was to buy bamboo
and make coarse baskets,
each capable of holding five or six pecks,
accumulating an uncountable number of them.
The following spring,
Regional Commander Chén Shàoyóu
proposed building the Guǎnglíng city wall,
and requisitioned Sù's former residence,
paying him half its value.
They also used baskets for transporting soil,
paying thirty coins per basket,
which amounted to seventy or eighty thousand strings in total.
Only then did he buy a house east of the river.
The divine sorceress, no longer following Bāo Jiǔniáng, came on her own,
saying:
"My surname is Sūn,
and my given name is Sī'ér.
I have been staying in Bālíng.
I owed Bāo Jiǔniáng money,
but now I have repaid it in full.
I have bid her farewell and am returning,
so I came to take my leave."
After sighing for a long time,
her form vanished.
Dòu Shì, moved by her advice,
said:
"Why don't you stay for a while?
If not,
I will adopt you as my son.
Would that be acceptable?"
Sī'ér replied:
"Since the lady has agreed,
what more do I have to worry about?
Please make a small paper house for me,
and place it under the eaves of the hall.
At mealtimes,
just give me a little food,
and that will be enough."
Dòu Shì complied.
After more than a month,
during an autumn wind and rainstorm,
Sī'ér sighed deeply in the middle of the night.
Dòu Shì then said:
"Now that you are my son,
why keep such distance?
If not,
why not settle on the cabinet by my bedside?
Would that be acceptable?"
Sī'ér was delighted again,
and moved there that very night.
He then asked to greet his two elder sisters,
though his form remained unseen,
only his voice was heard.
Sù's elder daughter enjoyed playful banter,
and said to him:
"Sister will find you a bride."
So they drew a woman on paper,
and adorned it with colorful embroidery.
Sī'ér said:
"Please make her attire simple, like little sister's."
The elder daughter also joked:
"As you wish."
That night, there was laughter and conversation,
as if someone was responding.
Then he said:
"The bride greets her two sisters-in-law."
Sù's cousin was married into the Hán family,
living at the southern embankment,
and had recently given birth.
The two daughters made embroidered shoes,
intending to send them to her.
Just as they instructed the maid to pack them,
Sī'ér laughed.
The two daughters asked why he was laughing,
and he replied:
"One of my grandson's feet is swollen,
so it will be hard to wear embroidered shoes."
Dòu Shì began to dislike him,
and Sī'ér, already aware,
after a few more days,
bid farewell,
saying:
"I will return to Bālíng for now.
Thanks to my two sisters for arranging a bride for me,
I will take her with me.
I hope,
you can prepare a small boat for me,
about two feet long.
Ask my sisters to oversee the incense and fire,
and escort me to the Yángzǐ River.
That would be more than enough!"
Dòu Shì granted his request.
The two daughters also gave him a piece of silk,
depicting him and his wife facing each other.
Sī'ér wore green and held a tablet.
He boarded the small boat and bowed in farewell.
After he left,
both daughters seemed listless, as if their spirits were drained.
Two years later,
the elder daughter married her maternal cousin.
On the wedding night,
she died inside the bed curtain.
When they lit a candle to look,
her form was like a yellow leaf.
The younger daughter married Zhāng Chū,
and her wedding night ended the same as her sister's.
Sù eventually became the Military Administrator of Shānyáng Commandery.
Lǐ Zhé
In the spring of the fourth year of the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Lǐ Zhé, the Registrar of Chángzhōu, had his home east of the outer wall of Dānyáng County.
Five lǐ away was a village estate,
with many thatched cottages.
One day, for no apparent reason,
a fire broke out spontaneously,
but was extinguished after being fought.
Looking at the ground,
there were footprints of hemp sandals over a chǐ wide,
leading them to suspect a thief,
but a search yielded no clues.
Over the next ten days, disasters occurred frequently yet were easily put out,
and only then did they realize it was something strange and supernatural.
Later, objects began to be thrown about in empty space,
terrifying the household.
Clothing and belongings were frequently lost.
There was a wet nurse named Ā Wàn,
whose nature allowed her to commune with ghosts and spirits.
She often saw a man
following her in and out.
Sometimes he appeared in the form of a Hú man,
with a magnificent beard and mustache,
wearing a lamb-skin robe and a sable hat,
interspersed with crimson and purple.
He would flash in and out abruptly.
One evening, Lǐ Zhé was studying the *Spring and Autumn Annals* in his pavilion,
when Ā Wàn saw the Hú man stealthily take a volume of the book and leave.
She hurriedly reported this to Zhé.
Zhé checked the books
and found one volume missing.
Just as he was praying and making vows,
in a moment,
the book was back in its case,
undamaged and unstained.
The Lǐ family was troubled by this.
Thinking that the tall, lush bamboo in their courtyard
might provide a dwelling for ghosts and spirits,
they secretly discussed cutting it down
to plant peach trees instead.
Suddenly, a letter was found in the courtyard:
"I hear you plan to cut the bamboo and plant peaches.
I have made full calculations regarding the bamboo.
Grain in the prefecture is currently cheap;
one boatload of bamboo can be traded for one boatload of grain.
I hope you will quickly consider this."
The handwriting was unskilled,
on a piece of paper a few cùn square.
Zhé's nephews, Shìwēn and Shìrú,
were both bold and brave.
They often cursed at it.
Then their caps and shoes would go missing.
Later, when they made some prayers,
the lost items were returned.
Another letter was thrown in:
"Only the sage, by lack of reflection, becomes the madman; only the madman, by mastering reflection, becomes the sage.
You first cursed me and then prayed;
now I return everything together."
After the letter, it said, "Written by Mò Díjūn."
After ten days,
a neighbor stole Zhé's dog,
killed it, and ate it.
When the matter came to light,
another letter was found:
"It is the virtuous neighborhood that constitutes the good. To choose a dwelling not among the virtuous—how can that be wise?"
Several ten-day periods later,
the family lost a great many things.
The family suspected the ghost was the thief,
and another letter said:
"Liú Chángqīng's poem says:
'The Zhí clan stole the gold unjustly; you say I am the thief.'
Now that the thief has been found,
what about it?"
Shìwēn and Shìrú finally resisted and fought against it.
That
summer night,
Shìwēn lay drunk in bed,
with his back to the candle at the head of the bed.
He saw a man
enter directly through the door,
unaware that anyone was there,
and thus came before the candle.
Shìwēn suddenly leapt up and seized him,
and indeed captured him,
but the candle also went out.
In the darkness, he resisted with all his might.
After a long time,
there was a cracking sound.
When a candle was brought, it gradually hardened.
It was a tile,
with eyebrows and eyes painted on its back,
a paper headscarf,
dressed in a child's clothes,
and also wrapped with a woman's silk shawl
several times around the head,
then tied.
The Lǐ family then nailed it to a pillar,
and smashed it.
A few days later,
a woman in mourning clothes wept in the garden,
saying, "You killed my husband."
The next day, she wept in the courtyard,
and then threw in a letter:
"As the proverb says, 'When one chicken dies, another crows.'
Our kind numbers a hundred households;
we shall surely repay you."
Thus, the comings and goings continued as before.
It once took people's clothes and put them on,
in the courtyard,
in the trees,
so luxuriant that no one knew how it happened,
but upon searching, they were then untangled.
It also placed large objects into small containers,
entering and exiting without hindrance.
After a ten-day period,
Shìrú again lit a lamp
and saw a woman come in from outside,
playing under the candlelight.
She was again captured by Shìrú.
After resisting for a long time,
she was killed and became stiff.
When lit by candlelight,
she too was a tile dressed in clothes,
so they ground her to powder.
The next day, another of her kind came weeping mournfully.
It often feared the three nephews,
calling them Èrláng.
When Èrláng arrived,
it would not come often.
The Lǐ family secretly wanted to move their residence,
and received a letter saying:
"I hear you wish to move;
I have already gone ahead to that place."
The Lǐ family had two old dogs,
one named Hán'ér,
the other named Měngzi.
Since this supernatural affair began,
they no longer ate,
but often wagged their tails and played in empty, dark places,
so they were killed.
After this, whenever the family secretly discussed matters,
the spirit could no longer know of them.
A letter said:
"Since there is no more Hán the Great or Měng the Second,
our kind has nothing to rely on."
Also, when a family member returned from the outer wall,
upon reaching the village,
he saw two men by the roadside
who came forward and asked the family member:
"We hear your household has strange occurrences;
what about them?"
The family member then answered with the facts,
and when he walked on,
looking back, they were already gone.
The Lǐ family invited the mountain-dwelling exorcist Wéi Shìchāng from Rùnzhōu.
Shìchāng placed talismans among the roof tiles
to suppress it.
A ghostly letter arrived saying:
"The talisman is most sacred,
yet you place it on the roof;
is that not treating it lightly?"
Shìchāng could do nothing
and left.
Hearing that in Huáichǔ there was a man named Wèi Shēng
who had long practiced incantation arts,
they invited him.
When Wèi Shēng arrived,
the ghost feared him considerably,
and its visits became less frequent.
Wèi Shēng then set up a ritual arena
to summon and interrogate it.
He placed a box in the altar,
and overnight, a statement was found in the box,
listing the lost items,
saying:
"Such-and-such items have already been sold,
obtaining money,
such-and-such amount;
used to buy fruit, combs, and other things, all consumed;
the remainder, such-and-such amount,
is all returned."
Checking the items,
they were all in the box.
It also said:
"Regarding the lost cooking pot,
I actually did not take it;
please inquire by the water's edge."
The statement mentioned forms like fox spirits and weasel spirits.
From then on, it never came again.
Another day,
In the river, a tripod was indeed obtained,
This verified the tale by the waterside.
Lú Yuàn
In the ninth year of the Zhēnyuán era (793 CE),
the former Prefect of Bózhōu, Lú Yuàn, resided in the Kāngyù Ward of the Eastern Capital.
When Yuàn’s father, Lú Zhèng, fell ill and passed away,
two days later, at high noon,
suddenly a large bird, bluish-gray in color,
flew into the courtyard,
circling and soaring in the empty space.
Judging by its shadow,
it could have been about ten to fifteen feet in wingspan,
and all the family members saw it.
After a short while,
it flew into a well at the southwestern corner,
and after a long time, flew back out.
People went to look,
and found the well water had already dried up,
with two eggs inside,
as large as bushel baskets.
They were about to take them out and break them,
when several bushels of blood flowed out.
By dawn,
they suddenly heard crying from the western inner chamber,
the voice of a woman.
Going to look,
they saw a young woman,
around eighteen or nineteen years old,
wearing a black turban on her head,
weeping with increasing sorrow and intensity.
When asked where she came from,
she slowly walked out to the eastern room,
and said:
"I gave birth in the well,
how dare you take and kill them?"
After speaking,
she returned to the western room,
dragged the corpses,
scattering them like pulp,
and when finished,
raised her arms and left,
vanishing upon exiting the door.
The family was greatly shocked and terrified,
took the remaining eggs,
and sent them back into the wilderness,
dispatching someone to quickly inquire of Sāng Dàomào.
Dàomào instructed them to perform rituals of exorcism and apology,
and afterward there were no further omens,
yet the strangeness remained unfathomable.
A Commoner of Lújiāng
During the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a commoner from Lújiāng Commandery,
who went to the mountains to gather firewood.
As dusk fell,
he suddenly saw a foreigner,
over ten feet tall,
emerge from a mountain pass,
dressed in black clothing,
holding a bow and arrows.
The commoner was greatly frightened,
and hastily ran to hide among ancient trees,
peering out,
he saw the foreigner stand gazing for a long time,
then suddenly shoot an arrow eastward.
The commoner followed its direction,
and saw a creature about a hundred paces away,
resembling a human in shape,
covered all over in several inches of yellow hair,
wearing a black turban and standing there.
The arrow struck its abdomen,
but it did not move.
The foreigner laughed and said:
"Indeed, it is beyond my ability."
Then he left.
Another foreigner appeared,
also over ten feet tall,
even more imposing and mighty than the first.
He also held a bow and arrows,
gazed eastward and shot,
hitting the creature in the chest,
but it still did not move.
The foreigner said:
"Only the General can handle this."
Then he too left.
Soon, several dozen foreigners appeared,
dressed in black,
bows on their arms and arrows at their waists,
as if they were vanguards.
Then a giant was seen,
several tens of feet tall,
clad in purple robes,
with an extremely unusual appearance,
walking slowly forward.
When the commoner saw him,
he could not help but tremble with fear.
The giant foreigner looked eastward,
and said to his vanguards:
"Shoot its throat."
The group of foreigners wanted to compete in shooting it.
The giant foreigner cautioned:
"None but Xióng Shū can do it."
The other foreigners all stepped back,
and one foreigner stepped forward,
drew his bow to the full and shot once,
hitting the creature’s throat.
The creature still showed no fear,
slowly pulled out the three arrows with its hands,
picked up a huge stone,
and came westward,
causing the foreigners to show expressions of fear.
They stepped forward and reported to the giant foreigner:
"The situation is urgent,
it would be better to surrender to it."
The giant foreigner immediately ordered them to call out:
"The General wishes to surrender."
The creature then threw the stone to the ground,
removed its turban,
revealing an appearance like that of a woman,
hairless.
Approaching the group of foreigners,
it collected all the bows and arrows they held,
and broke every one of them.
Then it ordered the giant foreigner to kneel on the ground,
and slapped his cheeks repeatedly with its hand.
The foreigner pleaded pitifully,
repeatedly declaring himself deserving of death,
before it released him.
The foreigners stood with hands respectfully clasped,
not daring to move recklessly.
The creature slowly covered its head with the turban again,
looked eastward, and departed.
The foreigners congratulated each other, saying:
"We are fortunate it is the jiǎzǐ day today,
otherwise,
we would all have died."
Then they all bowed before the giant foreigner,
who nodded in acknowledgment.
After a long while,
they led the way and entered the mountain pass.
As darkness was about to fall,
the commoner returned drenched in sweat,
and in the end, never knew what that creature was.
The Pagoda of Yángzhōu
Advisor Zhū Jǐngxuán
heard from Bào Róng that,
When Chén Shàoyóu was in Yángzhōu,
the shadow of the pagoda in the eastern market suddenly inverted.
Elders said,
when the sea’s reflection flips, such things happen.
The Temple in Gāoyóu
In Gāoyóu County, there was a temple,
its name not recorded.
The western wall of its lecture hall bordered a road,
and every evening,
the shadows of people, horses, and carriages
would all penetrate through the wall.
Those wearing red or purple clothing,
their shadows could be roughly discerned.
The wall was several feet thick,
making it difficult to explain rationally.
During the hours of chén and wǔ, it did not occur,
so it was passed down thus.
For over twenty years,
sometimes it would not appear for a year or half a year.
Liú Jīzhōng
often resided at a manor near the western capital.
His wife fell gravely ill,
and he was unable to sleep.
Suddenly, a woman,
white-haired,
only three chǐ tall,
emerged from the lamplight
and said to Liú:
"Your wife's illness
can only be cured by me.
Why not pray to me?"
Liú, being a stubborn man by nature,
shouted at her to leave.
The old woman slowly pointed her finger at him and said:
"Do not regret this, do not regret it."
She then vanished.
His wife immediately suffered a violent heart pain,
nearly dying.
Liú, having no other choice,
prayed to the old woman.
As soon as he finished speaking, she reappeared.
Liú bowed and invited her to sit.
She then asked for a bowl of tea,
held it toward the sun as if chanting a spell,
turned and instructed him to give it to his wife to drink.
As soon as the tea entered her mouth,
the pain ceased.
Afterward, she would appear from time to time,
and the family no longer feared her.
A year later,
she again said to Liú:
"I have a daughter who has come of age.
I trouble you, master, to find her a good husband."
Liú laughed and said:
"The paths of humans and ghosts are different;
it is difficult to fulfill such a request."
The old woman said:
"I am not asking for a human.
Just carve a somewhat skilled figure from paulownia wood,
and that will suffice."
Liú agreed
and accordingly prepared one for her.
After one night,
the wooden figure was gone.
She again said to Liú:
"I also trouble you and your wife to act as the bride's parents.
If you agree,
on a certain evening,
I will prepare a carriage to welcome you."
Liú, considering in his heart that there was nothing he could do,
also agreed.
When the day arrived,
after the yǒu hour (5–7 p.m.),
servants, horses, and carriages arrived at the gate.
The old woman also arrived and said:
"Master, you may go now."
Liú and his wife each boarded their respective carriages.
When it grew dark, they arrived at a place
with vermilion gates and high walls,
lanterns and candles lined up to welcome them.
The abundance of guests and furnishings
resembled that of a prince or duke's household.
Liú was led to a hall
where several dozen officials in crimson and purple robes were present.
Some were acquaintances,
some were already deceased.
They all looked at each other without speaking.
His wife was taken to another hall
where candles as thick as arms burned,
and brocades and emeralds vied in brilliance.
There were also several dozen women present,
half of them living acquaintances, half deceased.
They merely recognized each other and nothing more.
By the fifth watch (3–5 a.m.),
Liú and his wife, in a daze,
returned home.
As if waking from a drunken stupor,
they could recall less than one or two out of ten things.
A few days later,
the old woman came again to bow and thank them, saying:
"My young daughter has grown up,
and now I entrust her to you once more, master."
Liú, unable to endure it any longer,
threw a pillow at her, saying:
"You old demon,
how dare you disturb me like this!"
The old woman vanished along with the pillow,
and his wife immediately fell ill again.
Liú, along with his sons and daughters, poured libations on the ground and prayed to her,
but she never appeared again.
His wife eventually died of heart pain.
Liú's younger sister also fell ill with heart pain.
Liú wanted to move residences,
but all the objects seemed glued to their places.
Even light items like shoes
could not be lifted.
They invited Daoist priests to submit petitions,
and Buddhist monks to chant incantations,
but none of it worked.
Liú often spent his leisure time reading medical prescriptions.
His maidservant, Xiǎo Bì,
came in from outside,
her hands hanging loosely, walking slowly with measured steps.
She declared loudly:
"Liú Sì,
do you remember the old days or not?"
Then, sobbing and choking, she said:
"I, Shěnggōng, have just returned from Tàishān.
On the road, I encountered a flying yècha demon
carrying your esteemed sister's heart and liver.
I have already seized them back."
She then raised her sleeve,
and something wriggled inside it.
She looked to the left as if giving an order,
saying:
"You may arrange it."
Then, a wind seemed to rise from her sleeve,
blowing through the curtains.
The maidservant entered the main hall
and sat facing Liú.
She asked about the living and the dead,
recounting events of the past.
Liú had passed the imperial examinations in the same year as Dù Shěnggōng
and they were close friends.
The maidservant's demeanor, laughter, and speech
were exactly like his.
After a while, she said:
"I have matters to attend to
and cannot stay long."
She grasped Liú's hand, sobbing,
and Liú was also overwhelmed with grief.
Suddenly, the maidservant collapsed.
When she awoke,
she remembered nothing.
From then on, his younger sister also recovered without any further issues.
A Scholar from Jiānghuái
In Jiānghuái, there was a scholar who lived on a manor.
His son, over twenty years old,
had once suffered from a wasting illness.
One day, his father was drinking tea.
Suddenly, a bubble rose in the tea bowl like another bowl,
standing higher than the rim of the bowl,
clear and translucent like glass.
Inside was a person one cùn tall,
standing on the bubble,
rising above the tea in the bowl.
Looking closely,
the clothing and appearance
were exactly those of his son.
After the time it takes to eat a meal, it burst and vanished,
leaving nothing to be seen.
The tea bowl was as before,
only with a faint crack.
A few days later,
his son became possessed by a spirit,
interpreting the spirit's words
and predicting people's fortunes and misfortunes without error.
Lǐ Gǔ
The former xiùcai Lǐ Gǔ
was traveling to Yǐngchuān.
One night, he arrived at a relay station.
As soon as he lay down to sleep,
he saw a creature resembling a pig
charge up the hall steps.
Gǔ fled in terror,
dashed through the back door,
and threw himself into the station's stable.
He hid in a pile of hay,
holding his breath and waiting.
The monster followed him there,
its sound circling the hay pile several times.
It glared at the spot where Gǔ was hiding.
Suddenly, it transformed into a giant star,
soared upward,
and several beams of light illuminated the sky.
Gǔ's attendants fetched torches
and searched for Gǔ in the hay pile.
Gǔ had already died.
Half a day later, he revived
and recounted what he had seen.
Before ten days had passed,
he died without any illness.
The Monk Zhì Yuán
Zhèng Yúqìng was in Liángzhōu,
where there was a monk named Zhì Yuán at Lóngxīng Temple,
skilled in the arts of dhāraṇī incantations and exorcism,
capable of subduing evil and treating illnesses,
with many proven successes.
Dozens of people waited at his door daily,
but Zhì Yuán was old,
and somewhat weary.
Zhèng Yúqìng greatly respected him,
so he requested a vacant plot of land east of the city for him,
where Zhì Yuán built a thatched hut to live in,
accompanied by a novice and a lay attendant.
Several years later,
on a leisurely day,
Zhì Yuán was sunning himself and trimming his toenails,
when a woman in plain clothes,
very dignified and beautiful,
approached the steps and bowed,
weeping as she said:
"I am unfortunate,
my husband is dead and my child is young,
and my elderly mother is critically ill.
Knowing of your divine incantations and their power,
I beg you to save and protect her."
Zhì Yuán said:
"This humble monk originally grew weary of the noise and clamor of the city,
and is also troubled by the constant requests and thanks.
Since your mother is ill,
you may bring her here for the blessings."
The woman wept and pleaded again and again,
saying her mother was gravely ill,
and could not be moved or supported.
Zhì Yuán, pitying her, agreed.
She then said to go north for over twenty li,
to a village,
near which was Lǔjiā Village,
and to simply ask for the residence of Wéi Shíniáng.
Zhì Yuán set out the next morning.
He went as instructed for over twenty li,
but searched everywhere without finding it,
so he returned.
The next day,
the woman came again,
and the monk reproached her:
"This humble monk traveled far yesterday to keep the appointment,
how could there be such an error?"
The woman said:
"It was only two or three li from where you live.
Master, in your compassion,
you must go again."
The monk angrily said:
"This old monk is aged and frail,
and now I vow not to go out."
The woman then shouted loudly:
"Where is your compassion?
Now you must go for this matter."
She then climbed the steps and grabbed the monk's arm.
The monk, startled and pressured,
also suspected she was not human,
and in his confusion, stabbed her with a small knife.
The woman then collapsed,
but it was the novice who had been mistakenly struck by the knife,
bleeding to death.
The monk hastily buried him under a rice jar with the lay attendant.
The novice was from a village,
his home over ten li from the temple.
That day,
his family was all in the fields,
when someone in black clothes with a brown bundle
asked for water in the fields,
and spoke of the matter.
The novice's parents,
with the whole family wailing and crying,
went to the monk,
but the monk still deceived them.
His father searched with a shovel and found the body,
then brought a complaint to the authorities.
Zhèng Yúqìng was greatly alarmed,
and ordered the investigating officials to examine the case carefully,
believing it must be a wrongful accusation.
The monk fully recounted the events,
and added:
"This humble monk has an old debt,
and will accept death."
The investigators also sentenced him to death.
The monk requested a seven-day reprieve,
to chant and meditate,
as provisions for the afterlife.
Zhèng Yúqìng, pitying him, agreed.
The monk bathed, set up an altar,
urgently performed mudrās and bound the demon,
interrogating the evil spirit.
After three nights,
the woman appeared on the altar,
saying:
"There are many of my kind,
and wherever we seek food,
you always break and dispel it.
The novice is still alive,
if you can vow not to chant incantations,
I will certainly return him."
Zhì Yuán earnestly made the vow,
and the woman joyfully said:
"The novice is in an ancient mound in a certain village south of the city."
The monk told the officials,
who searched as instructed,
and indeed found the novice,
though his spirit was already addled.
When they opened the novice's coffin,
it contained only a broom.
From then on, the monk abandoned his arts.
Nán Xiàolián
Táng Dynasty Xiàolián Nán,
whose given name is lost,
and whose origins are unknown,
was skilled at making kuài (sliced raw fish).
The slices were thin, the shreds fine,
so light they could be blown away by a breath.
His knife work was swift and crisp,
as if keeping to a rhythm.
Once, while showing off his skill at a gathering of guests,
he first set up a frame to display it,
when suddenly a violent storm arose.
With a clap of thunder,
the kuài all transformed into butterflies and flew away.
Nán, shocked and frightened,
broke his knife,
vowing never to make it again.
Xiè Áo
There was a man named Xiè Áo from Chénjùn,
who had once sat for the imperial examinations,
and was fond of composing seven-character poems.
His ancestors had resided in Shēngdàolǐ, Cháng'ān,
and in the courtyard of his dwelling,
there were many peonies.
One evening after the rain had cleared,
he left his home,
walked a hundred paces south,
and gazed at the peaks of Zhōngnán.
He stood there for a long time,
when he saw a rider galloping from the west,
her embroidered garments shimmering indistinctly.
As she drew nearer, he saw it was a maiden with twin buns,
her hair piled high, adorned with elegant makeup,
and her appearance exceptionally beautiful.
When she reached Xiè Áo,
she halted and said to him:
"Are you not the gentleman I have been waiting for?"
Xiè Áo replied:
"I am merely strolling here,
gazing at the mountains from afar."
The maiden with twin buns smiled,
dismounted and bowed, saying:
"I wish for the gentleman to return to his dwelling."
Xiè Áo, unable to fathom the situation,
turned to look back at his home,
and saw three or four maids in green,
standing together outside his gate.
Xiè Áo grew even more astonished and bewildered.
Upon entering the gate,
the maids in green all stepped forward and bowed.
Once inside,
he saw the hall laid with carpets,
hung with curtains and drapes,
brocades and embroideries gleaming in splendor,
and an exotic fragrance filling the entire room.
Xiè Áo was both startled and fearful,
not daring to ask any questions.
One of them stepped forward and said:
"Why is the gentleman afraid?
Surely we mean no harm?"
Shortly after,
a golden carriage arrived at the gate,
and from it emerged a beautiful maiden,
about sixteen or seventeen years old,
graceful and lovely in appearance,
unlike anyone he had ever seen.
She descended from the carriage and entered the gate,
meeting Xiè Áo,
and they sat together in the western pavilion.
She said to Xiè Áo:
"I heard there are famous flowers in this place,
so I came to share a drink with you."
Xiè Áo's fear gradually subsided.
The beautiful maiden then ordered a feast to be set, and they dined together.
The utensils and objects used
were all exquisite and rare.
She brought out jade cups,
and they took turns pouring wine and drinking.
Xiè Áo then asked:
"Who are you, young lady?
Could it be that you are not of this world?"
The beautiful maiden smiled without answering,
but when he pressed her,
she finally said:
"You need only know that I am not human;
why must you ask further?"
As the night grew late,
she said to Xiè Áo:
"My home is very far away,
and now I must return;
I cannot stay here long.
I have heard that you are skilled at composing seven-character poems,
and I wish for you to give me a poem as a gift."
Xiè Áo, feeling melancholy,
took up a brush and composed a poem:
"After our meeting on the balcony, no reunion is in sight,
beneath the green trees, mist deepens, the jade water-clock slows.
At midnight, fragrant breezes fill the courtyard under the moon,
before the flowers, we recall the time of King Chǔ."
The beautiful maiden read it,
and tears streamed down her face as she said:
"I too have studied poetry,
and wish to respond with a poem in return;
I hope you will not mock me."
Xiè Áo was delighted and urged her to do so.
The beautiful maiden asked for crimson paper,
but when Xiè Áo looked in his bamboo case,
he found only a single sheet of green paper,
which he gave to her.
The beautiful maiden inscribed:
"When there is no path for longing, do not long,
flowers in the wind bloom only for a fleeting moment.
Melancholy, I return to my golden chamber,
at dawn the oriole cries,
breaking the green willow branches."
Her calligraphy was exceptionally refined,
and Xiè Áo admired it for a long time.
The beautiful maiden then turned to her attendants,
had the curtains and drapes removed,
ordered torches lit, and boarded her carriage.
Xiè Áo escorted her to the gate,
and they parted with tears.
Before she had gone even a few dozen paces,
the carriage, the people, and the horses
all vanished from sight.
Xiè Áo found the matter strange,
and stored the beautiful maiden's poem in his bamboo case.
The following spring,
having failed the examinations, he traveled eastward,
and upon reaching Xīnfēng,
he stayed at an inn for the night.
Strolling under the moonlight, gazing into the distance,
moved by the events of the past,
he composed another poem:
"A sheet of splendid paper, lovely as azure clouds,
its lingering fragrance remains, the ink still fresh.
Only adding to the desolate sights before my eyes,
I see not the ethereal lady of the three mountains.
The slanting moon shines on my robe, tonight's dream,
fallen blossoms weep in the rain, last year's spring.
In the red chamber, there are even more sorrowful things:
spiderwebs on the window, dust on the mirror."
After composing it, he recited it aloud.
Suddenly, from several hundred paces away,
he heard the sound of a carriage rushing from the west.
Soon he saw a golden carriage followed by several riders,
and looking at the attendants,
he recognized the maiden with twin buns from before.
Startled, he asked about them,
and the maiden with twin buns hurried forward to announce,
whereupon the carriage halted,
and she relayed a message to Xiè Áo:
"On the open road, I regret not being able to meet you."
Xiè Áo invited her to stay at the inn,
but she firmly declined.
He then asked where she was going,
and she replied:
"I am heading to Hóngnóng."
Xiè Áo then said:
"I am now also returning to Luòyáng;
may I travel east with you?"
She replied:
"My journey is urgent,
I cannot."
Then, lifting the carriage curtain, she said to Xiè Áo:
"I am moved by your sincere affection,
and so I have come to see you once more."
Having said this,
she choked with sobs, unable to contain herself.
Xiè Áo also wept with sorrow,
and recited the poem he had composed.
The beautiful maiden said:
"I did not expect you to remember me so deeply;
how fortunate I am to receive such kindness."
She added:
"I wish to respond with another poem."
Xiè Áo immediately gave her paper and a brush,
and in a moment, she finished:
"Melancholy, the beautiful rendezvous was but a dream,
the spring colors of Wǔlíng have all turned to emptiness.
To know the pain of parting is especially hateful,
only because no news passes between us.
Sorrow settles on my brows, forming a light green hue,
tear stains invade my cheeks, falling like light red petals.
For a moment, the twin wheels halt for the nobleman,
tomorrow,
galloping west, then turning east again."
Xiè Áo thanked her,
and after a long while, they parted.
After she had gone only a hundred paces or so,
she was nowhere to be seen again.
Although Xiè Áo knew she was otherworldly,
he could not forget her, his heart filled with longing.
When he reached Shǎnxī,
he detoured to Hóngnóng,
staying for several days,
hoping to encounter her once more.
But there was no trace of her,
so he returned to Luòyáng.
He took out the two poems
and told his friends about them.
Within a few months,
consumed by melancholy, he passed away.
Monk Fǎcháng
The monk Fǎ Cháng of the Lóngmén Temple in Hénán,
was a native of Yuánwǔ in Zhèngzhōu.
During the Bǎolì era,
he once returned from Lóngmén to Yuánwǔ.
His family owned several qǐng of farmland,
and the ripe grain had not yet been harvested.
One evening,
he was riding a horse through the fields.
The horse suddenly halted and refused to advance,
and even when whipped,
it would not move,
only staring eastward with wide eyes,
as if seeing something.
The moon was bright at the time,
and following its gaze, several hundred paces away,
there was an object,
the color of old wood,
approaching abruptly.
Fǎ Cháng grew frightened
and immediately turned his horse, retreating several tens of paces to the left of the path
to observe it.
As the object drew nearer,
it turned out to be a white vapor,
six or seven chǐ tall,
extremely foul-smelling,
worse than a fish market.
It made a continuous sound,
like moaning,
and moved westward before disappearing.
Fǎ Cháng whipped his horse to follow it,
always keeping a distance of several tens of paces.
After traveling over a lǐ,
it reached the home of a local villager named Wáng,
and suddenly rushed inside.
Fǎ Cháng stopped his horse and waited.
After a short while,
he suddenly heard the family inside calling out:
"The ox under the cart shed is about to die,
come quickly and see!"
Another moment later,
he heard a cry:
"The donkey in the back shed has collapsed to the ground,
beyond saving!"
Another moment later,
he heard startled weeping.
Someone came out,
and Fǎ Cháng pretended to pass by and inquire,
to which they said:
"The master's son, over ten years old,
has suddenly died."
Before the words were finished,
he heard more weeping,
and startled cries,
one after another without end.
After midnight,
the sounds gradually diminished,
and by dawn, they ceased entirely.
Fǎ Cháng was shocked and bewildered,
and immediately informed the neighbors in full,
who came together to the Wáng residence to investigate.
Inside, it was eerily silent,
so they opened the door,
only to find that over ten members of the household had all died,
with not even chickens or dogs remaining.
The village head of Héběi,
the retired scholar Zhèng Bīnyú, recounted
that he once stayed in Héběi,
where a village head's wife had recently died
and had not yet been encoffined.
At dusk,
her children suddenly heard music gradually approaching,
until it reached the courtyard,
and the corpse began to move.
When it entered the room,
as if coming from between the beams,
the corpse then began to dance.
The music sounded again,
and the corpse collapsed.
Soon, it went out the door,
following the music away.
The family was terrified,
and as the night was moonless,
they dared not pursue it.
At the first watch,
the village head returned home,
learned what had happened,
and broke off a mulberry branch as thick as an arm.
Drunk, he cursed loudly and went searching,
entering a grove of tombs.
After about five or six lǐ,
he again heard the music coming from atop a cypress grove.
Approaching the tree,
he saw a faint, flickering fire beneath it,
and the corpse was dancing.
The village head raised his staff and struck it,
the corpse fell,
and the music also stopped.
He then carried it back on his shoulders.
The monk Hóng Jì
The medical monk Xíng Rú recounted
that in Fúzhōu, there was a monk named Hóng Jì,
who practiced fasting and asceticism with great diligence.
Once, on a sandy shore, he found a human skull,
and stored it in his clothing basket.
Several days after returning to the temple,
he suddenly felt something gnawing at his ear in his sleep.
He brushed it off with his hand,
and it fell with a sound like several shēng of something dropping.
He suspected it was the work of the skull.
By dawn,
it indeed lay fallen beneath his bed,
so he broke it into six pieces
and scattered them in a tile gutter.
At midnight,
a fire the size of a chicken egg
entered one by one beneath the tiles.
Illuminating it,
Hóng Jì rebuked it, saying:
"You cannot seek rebirth among humans or devas;
what use is clinging to decayed bones?"
Thereupon, the strange occurrences ceased.
Jīn Yǒuzhāng
Jīn Yǒuzhāng was a man from Hénèi
who lived in seclusion on Zhōngtiáo Mountain in Pǔzhōu
for a total of five years.
On the mountain, there was a woman
who would often carry a jar to fetch water from the stream.
Her appearance was exceptionally beautiful.
Yǒuzhāng saw her from afar in his study
and was greatly pleased by her.
One day,
when the woman came again to fetch water,
Yǒuzhāng stepped forward, stood by the door, and teased her, saying:
"Whose lovely lady is this,
coming so often to draw water?"
The woman laughed and replied:
"The spring water flowing in the stream
has no fixed owner.
One takes it when needed;
how could there be a limit?
We have not known each other before;
how abrupt you are!
However, I live nearby,
having been orphaned since childhood.
Now I am staying at my aunt's house,
enduring hardships and dangers,
with no way to find comfort for myself."
Yǒuzhāng said:
"Since you, young lady, are not yet married,
and I am seeking a match,
if we could fulfill this long-held wish,
you should not reject me from afar.
I wonder what you think?"
The woman said:
"Since you, sir, do not despise me for my plain looks,
how dare I refuse?
However, wait until nightfall, and I will come to fulfill this fine destiny."
With these words,
the woman drew water and left.
That evening, she indeed arrived.
Yǒuzhāng welcomed her into his room,
and the way of husband and wife
grew more respectful over time.
Yǒuzhāng would often read books every night,
staying up until midnight,
and his wife would always sit beside him to keep him company.
This continued for half a year.
One night,
Yǒuzhāng was holding a book as usual,
but his wife did not sit down;
instead, she stood by his side.
Yǒuzhāng questioned her,
and she gave some other reason.
Yǒuzhāng then told his wife to go to bed,
but she said:
"If you, sir, return to the bedroom tonight,
please do not carry a candle.
That would be my good fortune."
Soon after, Yǒuzhāng took a candle and approached the bed,
and under the covers,
he saw that his wife was nothing but a dried-up skeleton.
Yǒuzhāng sighed with sorrow for a long time,
then covered her again with the quilt.
After a moment,
she returned to her original form.
Greatly frightened,
she said to Yǒuzhāng:
"I am not human;
I am the essence of a dried-up skeleton from the southern side of the mountain,
living on the northern side.
There is a King Héngmíng,
who is the leader of the ghosts.
He holds an audience once every month.
Since I have served you, Jīn Láng,
for half a year, I have not gone there at all.
Earlier, I was captured by ghost envoys
and sentenced to a hundred blows with an iron rod.
I endured this cruel torture,
unable to bear the pain.
Just now, I had not yet transformed back into my form;
how could I have expected you, Jīn Láng, to see me?
The matter is now revealed.
You should leave quickly
and not linger any longer.
In this mountain,
all things have spirits and demons attached to them,
and I fear they may harm you, Jīn Láng."
With these words,
she wept and sobbed,
and then disappeared.
Yǒuzhāng also left, filled with sorrow and regret.
Yú Níng
Yú Níng, a man from Qí,
was fond of drinking
and often traveled between Bīn and Jīng.
An old friend was serving as magistrate in Yílù,
so Yú Níng went to visit and drink with him,
staying for about ten days before returning.
Still suffering from the lingering effects of drunkenness,
he ordered his servant boy to go ahead
to prepare a place for rest.
It was early summer,
and the wheat fields were lush and moist.
Riding at a leisurely pace,
he saw from afar a fine tree with beautiful shade by the roadside
and headed toward it.
Upon arriving, he tied up his horse and sat on the grass.
Before he could settle down,
he suddenly saw his horse turning its head southward,
its nostrils flaring in fear,
as if it had seen something.
Yú Níng then looked in that direction
and saw, a hundred paces away,
a skeleton as white as snow,
sitting cross-legged on a desolate grave mound.
Its five limbs and all its bones
were fully intact,
with eyes and nostrils clearly visible,
its back and ribs delicate and intricate,
and its joints countable.
Yú Níng then rode his horse a little closer,
and the skeleton opened its mouth to exhale,
causing withered leaves and light dust
to scatter out in all directions.
Above, crows and kites flew about in confusion,
making a great deal of noise.
After a while, Yú Níng moved a bit closer,
and the skeleton suddenly stood upright,
its bones exceptionally large.
Yú Níng’s heart pounded with fear,
and his horse, startled, bolted away.
He then galloped to a roadside inn.
The servant boy who had gone ahead came out to greet him,
and they looked at each other in shock, exclaiming:
"Young master, your spirit and expression
look so haggard and distressed!"
Yú Níng immediately told them what had happened.
Coincidentally, there were over ten soldiers from Jīng
armed with various long and short weapons for border defense.
They went to investigate eastward.
Everyone said:
"How could such a thing exist?"
Soon, young men from the inn
gathered in great numbers.
Yú Níng then led the way for them
and made an agreement with the crowd, saying:
"If it is still there,
we should all smash it to pieces.
However,
I’m afraid we may not see it again."
Shortly after, they arrived at the spot,
and the skeleton was sitting upright as before.
Some shouted and made noise,
but it remained unmoved;
others drew their bows and shot arrows,
but none hit their mark;
some wanted to surround it and advance,
but they all looked at each other, none daring to go first.
After a long time,
the dried skeleton suddenly rose on its own
and slowly moved southward.
The sun was already setting,
and everyone grew fearful and intimidated,
gradually dispersing.
Yú Níng also whipped his horse and returned.
From afar,
he could still see crows and magpies circling and gathering,
chasing after it without dispersing.
Afterward, Yú Níng passed by that place many times
and inquired with nearby residents,
but no one ever saw it again.
Wáng Shēnzǐ
During the Zhēnguàn era,
west of Wàngyuàn Station, there was a commoner named Wáng Shēn,
who,
He planted elm trees by the roadside,
which grew into a forest,
and built a thatched hut.
In the summer months,
he often offered drinks to travelers,
and if they were officials or guests, he would invite them to rest and serve tea.
He had a son, thirteen years old,
whom he often ordered to attend to guests.
One day,
the boy told his father,
"There is a woman on the road asking for water,"
so Wáng Shēn told him to call her in.
The woman was very young,
wearing a green jacket and a white headscarf.
She said her home was over ten lǐ to the south,
her husband had died without children,
and she had now completed the mourning period.
She was on her way to Mǎwéi to visit relatives,
begging for food and clothing.
Her speech was clear and bright,
and her demeanor was lovely.
Wáng Shēn then offered her food,
saying:
"It's already late today,
you can stay here overnight,
and leave at dawn."
The woman gladly agreed.
His wife took her to the inner hall,
called her "sister,"
and asked her to sew a few pieces of clothing.
From noon until dusk,
she finished them all.
Her needlework was fine and meticulous,
almost beyond human skill.
Wáng Shēn was greatly astonished,
and his wife especially loved her.
She then joked:
"Sister, could you become our daughter-in-law?"
The woman smiled and said:
"Since I have no one to rely on,
I am willing to take care of the household chores."
That very day, Wáng Shēn
borrowed clothes and bought wine,
and formally took her as his daughter-in-law.
That evening was hot,
and she warned her husband,
"There have been many thieves lately,
do not leave the door open."
So they lifted a large beam,
barricaded the door and slept.
Around midnight,
Wáng Shēn's wife dreamed that her son, with disheveled hair, pleaded:
"I am almost eaten up!"
The wife woke in alarm,
wanting to check on her son.
Wáng Shēn said:
"He has a good new wife,
he must be talking in his sleep from joy."
The wife went back to sleep,
but dreamed the same again.
Wáng Shēn and his wife lit a candle,
called their son and the new bride,
but got no response.
They knocked on the door,
which was firmly barred.
So they broke the door open.
As soon as it opened,
there was a creature,
with round eyes and chisel-like teeth,
its body blue in color,
that rushed past them and fled.
All that remained of their son was his skull and hair.
Hán Cì
Hán Cì was in Guìzhōu.
A sorcerer rebel named Fēng Yíng
could create fog spanning several lǐ.
Previously, while walking in the wilderness,
he saw dozens of yellow butterflies,
and chased them,
until they vanished under a large tree.
Digging there, he found a stone box,
containing a plain book as thick as an arm,
and thus mastered heretical arts.
People flocked to him like a market,
and he proclaimed that on a certain day he would capture Guìzhōu.
If there was purple qi,
he would surely win.
When the day arrived,
indeed there was purple qi like a bolt of silk,
stretching across the city walls.
White qi shot straight toward it,
and the purple qi scattered.
Suddenly, a thick fog descended,
clearing slightly by noon.
From the trees in the prefectural residence,
copper Buddhas dripped down.
As large as wheat grains,
their numbers were countless.
That year, Hán Cì died.
Xǔ Jìng and Zhāng Xián
In the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Xǔ Jìng and Zhāng Xián studied together at Yǎnyuè Mountain.
There were two study rooms,
each occupying one,
separated by a space of about ten feet.
Xǔ was on the west side, Zhāng on the east,
each with their own windows and doors.
At first, they encouraged and motivated each other,
and were very close.
From spring to winter,
they each studied by candlelight.
One night, during the second watch,
suddenly, a creature
pushed open Xǔ Shēng's door and entered.
At first, Xǔ thought it was Zhāng Shēng,
and paid no attention.
The creature was already standing by his desk.
After finishing his reading,
he turned to look.
Only then did he see a creature,
about five feet tall,
with tiger fangs and wolf-like eyes,
fur like an ape's,
claws like an eagle's,
wearing leopard-skin trousers.
Seeing Xǔ Shēng look at it,
it clasped its hands, fixed its gaze,
and stood with feet together.
Xǔ Shēng was terrified,
and lost his voice,
repeatedly calling for Zhāng Shēng to rescue him.
He called out hundreds of times.
Zhāng Shēng extinguished his candle,
propped his door shut, and pretended to sleep,
ultimately not responding.
The creature suddenly walked backward,
approached the brazier by the north wall,
and crouched there watching.
Xǔ Shēng kept calling for Zhāng Shēng.
The creature stood up again,
took the firewood axe Xǔ Shēng used from under the bed,
turned back and sat down,
leaning toward the fire as before.
After a long while,
Xǔ Shēng calmed his mind and said:
"My surname is Xǔ, given name Jìng.
I left home to pursue learning,
and came here with Zhāng Xián.
I have not paid my respects to the mountain deities earlier,
for which I am deeply at fault.
However, as a shallow-minded mortal,
I beg you not to blame me."
After he spoke,
the creature sprang up,
clasped its hands and bowed,
then withdrew with respectful murmurs.
Xǔ Jìng deeply resented Zhāng Shēng.
The next day,
he packed his books and returned home.
Thus, Zhāng Shēng also left with him,
and their studies were never completed.
The Child of Tàiyuán
When Yán Shòu governed Tàiyuán,
children in the market were playing like swimming in the water.
Suddenly, they saw something floating down the stream,
and the children rushed to catch it.
It was a clay jar,
tightly sealed with heavy cloth.
The children broke it open on the bank,
and inside was an infant over a foot long,
which quickly ran away.
The children chased it.
In a moment,
a whirlwind rose under its feet,
and the infant was already several feet in the air.
A boatman near the shore
quickly struck it dead with his pole.
Its hair was crimson,
and its eyes were on top of its head.
Lǐ Shīgǔ
Lǐ Shīgǔ was constructing a mountain pavilion,
and unearthed an object,
resembling an iron axe-head.
At that time, Lǐ Zhāngwǔ was traveling in Dōngpíng,
and Shīgǔ showed it to him.
Zhāngwǔ exclaimed in alarm:
"This is a forbidden object;
it can drink three pecks of blood."
They tested it and found it to be true.
Mèng Bùyí
Before Dōngpíng was used for military campaigns,
there was a jǔrén named Mèng Bùyí who was a guest in Zhāoyì.
One night, he arrived at a courier station,
and was about to wash his feet,
when someone claiming to be Zhāng Píngshì from Zīqīng arrived,
with several dozen attendants.
Mèng wanted to pay him a visit.
Zhāng was drunk,
and initially paid no attention.
Mèng then withdrew to the western room.
Zhāng repeatedly called the station clerk,
demanding fried cakes.
Mèng silently watched him,
and was angered by his arrogance.
After a long while,
the fried cakes arrived.
Mèng saw a black creature like a pig
following the tray,
which vanished when it reached the lamplight.
This happened five or six times,
yet Zhāng remained completely unaware.
Mèng, terrified, could not sleep.
Zhāng soon began snoring loudly.
By the third watch,
Mèng finally dozed off.
Suddenly, he saw a man in black clothes
wrestling with Zhāng.
After a long struggle, they grappled into the eastern side room,
the sound of their punches like pestles.
After a short while,
Zhāng emerged with disheveled hair and bared shoulders,
and returned to sleep on his bed.
By the fifth watch,
Zhāng called his servants,
lit candles, and prepared his towel and comb.
He approached Mèng and said:
"I was drunk last night,
and was completely unaware that a scholar was sharing the hall."
He then ordered food,
and they talked and laughed very happily.
From time to time, he whispered:
"Last night, I am deeply ashamed before you, elder;
I beg you not to speak of it."
Mèng merely assented.
He added:
"I have business to attend to,
and cannot stay,
I must depart early.
You, scholar, may go first."
He reached into his boot,
took out a bar of gold,
and handed it to Mèng, saying:
"A meager gift,
I beg you to keep the previous matter secret."
Mèng did not dare refuse,
and immediately set off ahead.
After traveling several li,
he heard about the capture of a murderer.
Mèng inquired along the road,
and everyone said:
"Zhāng Píngshì from Zīqīng,
departed early from that courier station.
By dawn,
only an empty saddle remained,
and Zhāng was nowhere to be found.
The mounted officers returned to the station to search,
and in the western chamber, they found a corner of a mat.
Uncovering it,
there was only a skeleton,
without a single scrap of flesh left for flies.
On the ground, not a drop of blood remained,
only a single shoe beside it.
It is said that this station has long been haunted,
but no one knows what kind of monster it is."
Jǔrén Zhù Yuányīng once said:
"I personally heard Mèng Bùyí recount this,
and he always warned that night meals must be offered in sacrifice."
Zhù also said:
"Mèng originally did not believe in Buddhism,
and was quite skilled at poetry.
One of his lines reads:
'The bright sun, my homeland far away.
Green mountains, within fine verses lie.'
Later, he often practiced contemplation.
He became immersed in travel and sightseeing,
and never again took the imperial examinations.
Dài Chá
Dài Chá, magistrate of Nánchéng County in Línchuān Commandery,
initially bought a residence in Guǎnwá Ward.
On a leisurely day,
he was sitting idly in the hall with his younger brother.
Suddenly, they heard the sound of women laughing and gathering outside,
sometimes near, sometimes far.
Chá found it quite strange.
The laughter gradually drew closer,
when suddenly he saw several dozen women scattered in front of the hall,
who vanished in an instant.
This happened repeatedly for many days,
and Chá did not know what to do.
At the edge of the hall stood a withered pear tree,
so large it took an arm's span to encircle.
Suspecting it was an omen,
he had it cut down.
Under the roots was a stone,
protruding like a fist.
Digging around it, the hole widened,
taking the shape of a griddle.
They then lit a fierce fire on top of it.
Poured vinegar and chiseled again.
At a depth of five or six feet,
they still had not broken through.
Suddenly, they saw women circling the pit,
clapping their hands and laughing loudly.
After a moment,
they jointly pulled Chá into the pit,
and threw him onto the stone.
His whole family was terrified.
The women then returned,
laughing loudly,
and Chá also emerged following them.
As soon as Chá came out,
his younger brother disappeared.
The family wailed in grief,
but Chá alone did not cry.
He said:
"He is also quite happy.
What is there to cry about?"
Until his death,
Chá refused to describe what he had experienced.
Dù Cóng
Before Dù Cóng achieved prominence,
he traveled among the rivers and lakes.
Once, when a stage of his journey was somewhat long,
he reached a garrison post only at dusk.
There was a guest house,
where most occupants found no peace,
some dying from terror.
The station commander, seeing that Cóng's bearing was extraordinary,
thought to himself,
this might be a noble man.
If he stays the night unharmed,
he will surely become a chancellor or general.
He then invited Cóng to lodge inside,
providing extremely generous hospitality.
At midnight,
they heard from the eastern wing's partitioned rooms
a tumultuous noise like the voices of thousands.
Cóng took paper,
wrote his own name in large characters,
tied it to a tile or stone,
and threw it toward the clamorous place.
The noise immediately ceased.
Then, noise arose again from the western wing,
and he threw another as before,
whereupon it also fell silent.
He then slept peacefully.
At dawn,
the station clerk came to inquire after his well-being.
The gentleman recounted everything in detail,
and they then knew he was destined for greatness.
They presented him with a bundle of plain silk as a farewell gift.
When he later attained high office,
he sought out the clerk and promoted him.
Zhèng Yīn
Táng Yángwǔ Hóu Zhèng Yīn was dismissed from his post as chancellor,
and after serving as the military governor of Lǐngnán, he was appointed as the Minister of Personnel,
residing in Zhāoguó Lǐ.
His younger brother, Zhèng Yùn, was the Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and both were at home.
As the kitchen preparations were nearly complete,
their cauldron suddenly seemed as if something was pounding it from within the stove,
lifting it more than a foot above the stove,
pounding continuously without stopping.
Beside it were over ten cooking pots,
all being heated for cooking,
and they all began to shake their two handles slowly.
After a long while, they were all able to move,
and they stopped on top of the stove.
Every three pots carried one cauldron as they moved,
while the rest lined up in rows, leading and following,
emerging from the kitchen.
On the ground, there were some with broken legs,
and some that were no longer in use,
yet they too hopped and leaped along with them.
Once out of the kitchen,
they headed east across the water channel.
The pots moved forward together,
encountering no obstacles,
but those with broken legs could not cross.
The entire household, young and old, was astonished,
gathering to watch,
unsure of what to do.
A child cursed them, saying:
"If you can perform such strange feats,
why can't those with broken legs move forward?"
The pots then abandoned the cauldrons in the courtyard,
turned back,
and every two pots carried one with broken legs across.
They proceeded into the courtyard in front of the Vice Minister's hall,
where they arranged themselves in rows, large and small.
Then, a thunderous sound was heard in the air,
as if a house had collapsed,
and the pots and cauldrons all turned into yellow dust and black soot,
settling only by the end of the day.
The household could not fathom the reason for this.
A few days later,
the Vice Minister passed away,
and the Chancellor followed shortly after in death.
Héběi military officer
Hú.
In front of the city's inn,
a Héběi military officer once passed by.
He had not traveled more than a few miles
when suddenly a whirlwind, like a vessel,
arose in front of his horse.
The officer struck it with his whip,
and it grew larger.
It then began to swirl around the horse's head,
causing the horse's mane to stand upright as if planted.
The officer became frightened,
dismounted, and observed it.
He noticed the mane had grown several feet long,
with fine threads inside,
like red silk threads.
The horse, at that moment, reared up on its hind legs and neighed.
The officer grew angry,
drew his sword, and slashed at it.
The wind then scattered and vanished,
and the horse also died.
The officer cut open the horse's belly to examine it,
and found that its intestines were gone.
He did not know what kind of strange creature it was.
Monk of Gōngshān.
Gōng Mountain.
Located in the western outskirts of Yízhōu,
it stands solitary, steep, and towering,
rising prominently above the surrounding peaks.
For thirty li around,
there were no inhabitants.
In the early Zhēnyuán era,
two monks arrived at the mountain
and settled under the shelter of trees.
They devoted themselves diligently to worship and recitation,
continuing day and night.
People from villages far and wide
built dwellings for them.
Within ten days,
a monastery was established.
The two monks redoubled their earnest efforts,
vowing not to leave their chambers
for over twenty years.
During the Yuánhé era,
on a winter night with a bright moon,
the two monks were each in the eastern and western corridors,
chanting hymns in clear voices.
The air was empty and still,
when suddenly the sound of a man wailing in grief was heard from the foot of the mountain.
It drew closer,
and in moments, it reached the monastery gate.
The two monks remained unmoved,
and the wailing ceased.
The figure then leaped over the wall and entered.
The monk in the eastern corridor saw from afar that its body was enormous;
it leaped into the western corridor,
and the sound of chanting soon stopped.
It seemed as if sounds of
struggling and grappling were heard,
and after a while, the sounds of chewing, gnawing,
and fierce gulping were audible.
The monk in the eastern corridor, terrified, fled in panic.
Having long not left the mountain,
he had completely forgotten the paths.
Stumbling and falling,
his strength was nearly exhausted.
Looking back,
he saw the figure staggering closer,
so he leaped forward again.
Suddenly, he encountered a stream,
and after hastily crossing it with his robes soaked,
his pursuer arrived right behind him.
From afar, it cursed:
"If not for the water,
I would have devoured you too."
The eastern corridor monk, both fearful and hurrying,
had no idea where to go.
Soon, heavy snow fell,
obscuring everything within a short distance.
By chance, he came upon a village cattle shed
and hid inside.
Late into the night,
the snow began to clear slightly.
Suddenly, he saw a figure in black clothes,
holding a knife and spear from outside,
slowly approach the pen.
The eastern corridor monk held his breath,
peering cautiously toward the light.
The black-clad figure paced back and forth,
as if waiting for something.
After a while,
two bundles of clothing and other items
were suddenly tossed over the courtyard wall.
The black-clad figure took them,
tied them up, and shouldered the load.
Then, a woman
climbed over the wall and emerged.
The black-clad figure took her and left.
Fearing he would be implicated,
the monk fled again,
bewildered and unsure where to go.
Within less than ten li,
he suddenly fell into an abandoned well.
In the well was a dead person,
head separated from the body,
the bloodied corpse still warm—
clearly someone who had just been killed.
The monk was terrified,
unsure what to do.
Soon, day broke,
and looking closely,
he saw it was the woman who had climbed the wall the previous night.
After some time,
several pursuers arrived together.
Peering down, they said:
"The thief is here."
They lowered a rope to haul someone up,
tied him up right there in the well,
and beat him severely,
bringing him close to death.
When he was pulled up,
he recounted the events of the previous night in detail.
Among the villagers was someone who had been to the mountain
and recognized him as the eastern corridor monk.
However, since he was found with the dead woman,
he could not clear himself,
and was sent to the county town.
He elaborated on the reasons,
claiming the western corridor monk had been devoured by a monster.
The county sent officials to the mountain to investigate,
but the western corridor monk was sitting peacefully, unharmed.
He said:
"There was nothing at first.
Just around the second watch,
while we were both reciting sutras,
the eastern corridor monk suddenly left alone.
We had long made a vow
not to leave the monastery gate.
In my shock and surprise,
I tried to call after him, but it was too late.
As for what happened at the foot of the mountain,
I know nothing."
The county officials then accused the eastern corridor monk of deceit,
arresting him as the murderer.
They subjected him to flogging and torture,
inflicting every kind of pain.
Wrongfully accused and in agony,
the monk resigned himself to death.
However, there was no evidence of stolen goods,
so the judicial officials could not finalize the case.
After a month,
the thief who had killed the woman and stolen the valuables
was caught elsewhere,
and the full truth came to light.
The monk was thus exonerated and released.
Dù Yuányǐng
During the years when Dù Wúyǐng governed Shǔ,
a massive stone in Zīzhōu's square zhang began moving,
covering several acres.
At Xīndū County's Dàdào Temple, the clay figure beside Lǎojūn grew a beard several inches long;
when plucked,
it grew back shortly after.
In various places in the capital, chestnut trees
bore fruit on their leaves.
When eaten,
they tasted like plums.
At Lùtóu Temple, spring water gushed forth,
and there were omens of cats and mice nursing each other.
When barbarians intended to besiege the city,
at the western gate's water,
someone saw a dragon fighting a water buffalo,
