and both vanished shortly after.
It was also said
that plum trees bore papayas,
but they were hollow and bore no fruit.
Priest Zhū
Priest Zhū,
in the eighth year of the Tàihé era,
often traveled to Lúshān.
While resting on a streamside rock,
he suddenly saw snakes piled like brocade,
which soon transformed into a giant turtle.
Inquiring with an old man of the mountain,
he was told it was Xuánwǔ.
Priest Zhū also once traveled to Zhàngrén Temple on Qīngchéng Mountain.
At Lóng Bridge,
he saw dried bones under a cliff,
sitting upright with its back against the rock,
hands resting on its knees.
Chains and locks,
covered in moss and vines,
were as white as snow.
It was said
that his grandfather had often seen it.
Zhèng Shēng
It is commonly said that when a person dies,
after several days,
a bird should emerge from the coffin,
called the "shā."
During the Tàihé era,
there was a man named Zhèng Shēng,
who often went to Lìchuān,
hunting in the wilds with the local officials.
They caught a huge bird in a net,
with a bluish-gray color,
standing over five feet tall.
The commander ordered it to be untied and examined,
but suddenly it vanished without a trace.
Zhèng Shēng was startled,
and immediately inquired among the local villagers,
asking about it.
One of the villagers replied:
"In the village, someone died,
and it has been several days.
The diviner said
that today the 'shā' would depart.
The family watched and observed,
and a huge bluish-gray bird
emerged from the coffin.
What you captured,
was it indeed that?"
During the Tiānbǎo era,
the Capital Prefect Cuī Guāngyuǎn, while out hunting,
once encountered a monstrous bird,
an incident similar to this one.
Zhào Shìzōng
In the first year of the Huìchāng era,
the water in Róngzhōu rose,
and floating logs blocked the river.
The Prefect Zhào Shìzōng summoned the naval troops to retrieve the logs.
The government office was low, small, and cramped,
and could no longer be used,
so they also repaired the Kāiyuán Temple.
More than a month later,
a local tribesman
encountered a person
who looked like a monkey,
wearing an old blue garment,
though it was unclear what style it was.
He said:
"General Guān sent me to gather wood,
but it was taken by this prefecture.
I don't know what to do,
so I must come back next year to collect it."
The tribesman told this to the people of the prefecture.
By the second year, in the seventh month,
as dawn was about to break,
a sudden flood arrived.
The prefectural city was situated by the river and nestled against the mountains.
Even during major floods,
the water usually remained over fifty zhang away from the city.
This time, the water rose a hundred zhang high,
sweeping away over twenty people.
The foundation of the prefectural city sank over ten zhang,
and large stones, as big as three-room houses,
piled up on the city's foundation.
The water was black and foul-smelling,
and only receded by evening.
The prefectural official Yú Cáng□ and his clerks
barely managed to board a boat and reach the shore.
After about a month,
the water in the prefecture finally dried up.
Apart from the large stones,
there was nothing else left.
Only the portrait of Emperor Xuánzōng from the Kāiyuán Temple,
which had moved over ten paces from its original location,
stood upright on the sand.
As for other iron or stone objects,
none remained.
Cáo Lǎng
Jìnshì Cáo Lǎng,
during the reign of Emperor Wénzōng, served as the magistrate of Huátíng County in Sōngjiāng.
As his term was about to end,
he purchased a residence in Wújùn.
He also bought a young maidservant,
named Huā Hóng.
Her price was eighty thousand,
and she was very beautiful,
so everyone in the household cherished her.
By autumn, his successor arrived.
Magistrate Lǎng
moved his family into the residence in Wújùn.
Later, as the winter solstice approached,
because the repairs to the new hall were not yet complete,
in the western section of the hall,
two hundred catties of charcoal were stored.
In the eastern section, under the window, there was a bed,
newly furnished with a mat,
on top of which were ten finely woven reed mats for carriage repairs.
To the east,
was a southern-facing building.
North of the western corridor, there was a room
used as a storeroom.
One room was for Huā Hóng and the wet nurse,
and one room served as the kitchen.
On the day before New Year's Eve,
Lǎng's sisters and relatives
were all preparing items for sacrificial offerings.
In the cauldron, about three sheng of oil was being fried,
with over ten catties of charcoal piled beside it.
His sister was making cakes,
and the family members were all around,
but only Huā Hóng was absent.
Lǎng's relatives thought she was sleeping lazily,
so they summoned her,
but she had nothing to do.
Lǎng became angry,
whipped her,
and she then complained of a headache.
Suddenly, a large brick flew down,
nearly hitting Lǎng's relatives.
Soon, another large brick struck the oil cauldron,
causing everyone to scatter in panic.
The kitchen utensils
were scattered messily under the steps.
As it was already late,
everyone entered the western rooms,
then moved into the hall,
bringing the children along.
After locking the hall door,
mother and child clung to each other and sat,
sweating profusely like water,
unable to understand the strange events.
Lǎng took several catties of charcoal to light a fire,
but soon there was a rumbling sound in the air,
and the fire rose and fell in mid-air.
Suddenly, on the bed under the eastern window,
there appeared a girl,
about fourteen or fifteen years old.
She wore her hair in two buns,
dressed in a short yellow jacket and trousers,
kneeling on the bed,
as if imitating someone grinding tea.
Lǎng sprang up to seize her,
but she evaded him around the room.
After a moment,
she hid among the pile of reed mats.
Lǎng stepped on them,
and there was a chirping sound,
after which she disappeared.
They sat until dawn,
and when the rooster crowed,
they dared to open the door.
The wet nurse and Huā Hóng were sound asleep in the western room.
Lǎng summoned Dàoist Gù from the Yùzhī Temple to perform rituals.
After several days,
someone sighed deeply and said:
"I am Méi Gāo, a guest from Liángyuàn.
Previously, during the festival,
I sought food here.
I do not know why your family tried to capture me."
Lǎng prepared tea and wine.
Invited him to sit.
Gāo said to Lǎng,
Said:
"In the early years of Yuánhé,
I visited the Wǎguān Pavilion in Shàngyuán.
On the wall in the western corner of the second floor,
I inscribed a poem."
Lǎng earnestly requested,
Gāo said:
"My heart is troubled and without joy,
I hope you understand.
Another day, when you go to Jīnlíng,
you can copy it yourself.
The haunting in your household,
is not my doing.
The person responsible is not far,
just ask others,
and you will know."
Lǎng then informed Dàoist Gù,
and released him.
In the village, there was a female shaman named Zhū Èrniáng,
whom he summoned to perform divination.
The shaman had all the family members come out,
but only Huā Hóng, complaining of a headache, did not rise.
The shaman forcibly called her out,
and scolded her:
"Why are you like this?
The mistress does not know,
why didn't you speak?"
She then pulled her arm,
and near the elbow, there was a blue vein over an inch long, raised.
She said:
"A sage resides here.
Why did you startle him?"
Huā Hóng bowed,
only saying it was not her doing.
Lǎng became afraid,
and sold her at a reduced price.
After passing through two households,
the same thing happened.
So he released her.
With nowhere to go,
she often sewed in various temples to earn food.
Later, Shēntú Qiānlíng, a Dàoist from Bāo Mountain, passed by,
and said that Huā Hóng was originally from a household in Dòngtíng Mountain,
where they jointly bought a girl from another family,
and had her guard the temple on Dòngtíng Mountain.
Later, when the Dòngtíng Temple expanded northward by over two hundred paces,
that temple was demolished.
The household sold her to Cáo Shíyòng,
and the mountain spirits from the temple had nowhere to go,
so they nested in her arm with their kind.
The people of Eastern Wú all knew of this matter.
Zǐ'ér
Liú Láfū of Péngchéng,
during the Huìcháng era,
passed the imperial examination as a jìnshì.
In the Dàzhōng era,
he was appointed as the deputy magistrate of Hù County and later died.
His wife, Wáng shì,
returned to her family,
residing in the residence at Dūnhuà Lane in Luòyáng,
in the backyard of the ceremonial hall.
In the year Dīnghài of the Xiántōng era,
one night, she gathered her children and nephews to play a hiding game,
and ate fried pancakes.
The kitchen was in the western wing.
A young servant named Zǐ'ér,
carried utensils to bring food.
At the time, the moon was dark and the clouds gloomy,
making it impossible to distinguish even one's fingers.
Zǐ'ér
suddenly cried out, fell to the ground, and lost consciousness.
Holding a torch to look at him,
they saw his body cold, face blackened,
with blood flowing from his mouth and nose.
They pulled his hair and burned his fingers,
and after a short while, he revived.
They then had several men tie torches and search along the northern corridor.
Behind the granary, they found the utensils he had been carrying.
West of the granary was a large latrine.
On the latrine, they found one fried pancake,
and in the cesspit, there was another pancake.
Lǐ Yuē
In the year Dīng-Hài of the Xiántōng era,
Lǐ Yíyù of Lǒngxī served as an assistant in Bīn Prefecture.
He had a servant named Lǐ Yuē,
who had been employed by Yíyù when he passed the imperial examination.
Yuē was swift and skilled at traveling,
so he was often sent to deliver mail to the capital.
That year, in the seventh month of autumn,
Lǐ Yuē was returning from the capital to Bīn.
He set out early, passing several wards,
just as the drumbeats ceased.
Fatigued, he rested beneath an ancient locust tree.
At the time, the moonlight shone through the treetops,
and the lingering light was still bright.
An old man with white hair,
stooped and leaning on a cane,
also came to rest there.
Once seated, he groaned incessantly.
After a long while, he said to Yuē:
"This old man wishes to go to Xiányáng,
but I am too feeble to walk properly.
If you have a righteous heart,
could you carry me on your back?"
Yuē angrily did not respond,
but the old man persisted in his request.
Yuē then said to him:
"You may climb onto my back."
The old man gladly climbed on.
Yuē knew he was a ghost or monster,
and secretly made preparations.
With his Gēshū club,
he tied the old man from behind and hurried off.
By the time they reached the Kāiyuǎn Gate,
the east was already bright.
The old man repeatedly asked to be let down,
but Yuē said to him:
"Why did you insult me by climbing on?
Why are you afraid now and wish to be let go?"
He bound him even tighter.
The old man's speech became incoherent,
pleading for mercy and begging for his life.
Yuē did not answer.
Suddenly, he felt his back lighten,
and something fell to the ground.
Looking at it,
it was a rotten coffin plank,
and the old man had vanished.
Yuē threw it under the village wall,
and afterward, no misfortune occurred.
Zhāng Zhěn
The retired scholar Zhāng Zhěn
was highly skilled and excelled at playing the qin.
His wife had died early in Jiānglíng,
so he took a concubine of great beauty.
Within ten days,
the young kitchen maid in charge of cooking found a bronze figurine under the stove,
about an inch long,
and glowing like fire.
In a moment, it gradually grew larger,
reaching over ten feet in length,
with an extremely strange appearance.
It walked into Zhěn's room,
seized his concubine, and devoured her,
leaving not even a hair behind.
After eating, it gradually shrank,
returning to its original form,
and disappeared under the stove.
Mǎ Jǔ
Mǎ Jǔ once served as a courier official in Shānnán.
Traveling by a remote path into Shǔ,
it was after a war, and the secluded road
was completely devoid of human presence.
At night, he arrived at a lodge,
hearing voices from the eastern corridor,
so he went to inform them.
Someone responded, saying:
"There is a bed in the central hall,
go and stay there yourself."
Jǔ went to the central hall,
finding only an earthen platform.
He asked for fire,
and the reply was,
there was no fire.
He asked for a mat,
and a mat was thrown out from the next room,
weighing over ten catties.
Jǔ, being a strong man,
paid it no mind.
In the middle of the night,
a creature resembling a monkey
climbed onto the platform and approached.
Jǔ struck it swiftly with an iron hammer,
and it cried out and fled.
At dawn, when he bid farewell,
the person angrily left.
He further said:
"Last night, seeing you alone,
I sent my son to keep you company,
and you nearly beat him to death."
Jǔ pushed the door,
but it would not open.
Peering through a crack,
he saw only piled-up earth.
Jǔ later became a general in Tàiyuán,
and his official rank rose to Military Commissioner of Huáinán.
Wéi Chēn
Wéi Chēn, an assistant in Zhāoyì,
in his childhood,
was still studying at the academy.
On the night of the Winter Festival,
he carried his books home.
Upon reaching the sleeping hall,
it was completely empty,
except for a brazier fire in the kitchen where oil was being heated.
Peering inside,
he saw a cauldron several feet tall,
which after a while lowered again,
repeating this three or four times.
Chēn was greatly frightened,
and ran out the door,
only then seeing his family.
They were all in the outer hall,
preparing offerings for the ceremony.
Chēn, pale and trembling,
told them what had happened.
The family all scolded him,
thinking the child was speaking nonsense.
Shortly after,
the kitchen maid in charge of cooking
approached the cauldron to prepare food.
She was also holding a child in her arms.
The child leaped up, asking to be fed,
and accidentally fell into the cauldron.
Boiling oil surged and overflowed,
and the maid screamed.
The fire had already reached the house,
and young and old rushed to help.
Some poured water on it,
but the flames only grew fiercer,
as oil and water react violently.
They threw various items like jars, bowls, blankets, and rugs,
and only after a long while was the fire extinguished.
When the fire died down,
the child was already charred.
The entire household was shocked and terrified,
and they canceled the festival.
The maid also died from the fright.
Zhāng Móusūn
Zhāng Móusūn, Deputy Commissioner of Guǎngzhōu,
though of humble origins,
was eloquent,
skilled in scheming,
and served repeatedly as an assistant in princely mansions.
At the beginning of the Xiántōng era,
he was recruited from Jiāo-Guǎng,
and became a chief aide.
He was greedy and extravagant by nature,
and tirelessly amassed wealth.
Nánhǎi had many exotic goods,
such as rhinoceros horns, ivory, pearls, and cowries,
too numerous to count.
When his appointment ended and he returned north,
he stopped at Rǔfén.
Thirty lǐ west of the commandery,
south of the Yùyáng Post Station,
on the banks of the Rǔ River,
he built a villa,
extremely luxurious and spacious.
He once dug a pond,
intending to channel water from the official canal to fill it.
Someone said:
"This year, the Grand Jupiter is located here."
Móusūn warned the laborers:
"Stop digging if you encounter the Grand Jupiter."
The next day, they reached the spring,
and found a bag of earth.
Breaking it open,
inside was something over a shēng in volume,
white in color,
like millet grains,
which suddenly leaped and scattered in all directions, then vanished.
Móusūn then fell violently ill,
and died after two nights.
Lǐ Huáng
Qúzhōu Cìshǐ Lǐ Huáng,
in the summer, was resting in a small hall.
He saw a person in a mouse hole,
several cùn tall,
holding a broom,
sweeping in front of the hole before entering.
There were two others,
also two or three cùn tall,
carrying a cauldron,
adding water and lighting firewood.
In a short while,
in front of the cauldron appeared a yakṣa,
holding an iron fork,
forking a person.
Wearing a purple robe,
holding an ivory tablet,
two or three cùn tall,
in appearance and demeanor,
it was actually Lǐ.
Huáng, though afraid, did not dare to startle them.
Then they shouted for Huáng to take off his clothes,
enter the cauldron,
and in a short while, he came out.
Huáng put on his clothes and entered the hole.
Then he saw a woman emerge from the fire,
who was actually Huáng's widowed sister-in-law,
who had long been residing in Yuèzhōu.
The one in charge of the cauldron scooped Huáng's sister-in-law into the cauldron,
in a short while,
she also came out.
The sister-in-law put on her clothes and also entered the hole.
The one in charge of the cauldron also entered.
Then the two others carried the cauldron in.
And the one holding the broom swept away all the ashes.
This went on for several days.
Huáng was greatly worried.
He sent someone to inquire about his sister-in-law.
She was also unharmed.
Several years later, she passed away.
Huáng passed away over ten years later.
Sòng Xún
Jìnshì Sòng Xún,
having failed the imperial examination, returned south.
His elder brother, Bō,
was the magistrate of Shíquán County in Jīnzhōu.
Xún, finding the county town noisy and chaotic,
built a mountain retreat several lǐ east of the county.
Before it was completed,
the workers heard a woman's voice from within the mountain rocks saying:
"Sòng Sānláng has come!"
When Xún moved in,
one moonlit night,
he was strolling beside the study.
Again, he heard from within the rocks:
"Sòng Sānláng has come!"
He stopped to listen,
when suddenly a stone door opened.
He saw several women,
bowing repeatedly and laughing, saying:
"Please come in, Sānláng."
Xún tried to run,
but was seized by the women.
They took him into their chamber,
and the stone door closed.
His servant urgently informed Bō.
They broke open the rocks to search for him,
but in the end, could not find him.
Zhāng Shì Zǐ
During the Táng Wéndé era,
a capital official named Zhāng,
his name forgotten,
was residing in Sūtái.
His young son,
often went to the residence of the scholar-official Lù Píngshì,
and was favored by a beautiful woman.
After many interactions,
he grew suspicious,
and soon fell ill and emaciated.
He encountered Dàoshi Wú Shǒuyuán of Kāiyuán Guàn,
who said,
there was an ominous aura.
He gave him a talisman,
and indeed, it was a funerary figurine of a maidservant,
with the characters "Hóng Yīng" written on its back.
It was in a hollow pillar in an empty house.
They burned it,
and the demonic presence ceased.
This was heard from Liú Shānfǔ.
Sēng Shí Péng
When Liú Jiànfēng invaded Yùzhāng,
the monk Shí Péng,
along with his disciples, fled to Fēnníng,
and stayed overnight at Chéngxīn Sēngyuàn.
Early in the night,
they saw light outside the window.
Looking at it,
they saw a ball of fire,
several chǐ high and wide.
Inside was a golden carriage,
moving along with the fire.
It made creaking sounds.
Shí Péng became frightened.
The host of the place said:
"I've seen it for several years.
Every night,
it always emerges from the ground in the northwest corner of the monks' hall,
circles the hall several times,
and then disappears back there.
Since it causes neither harm nor fortune,
no one has dug to investigate it."
Yíchūn Rén
At the beginning of the Tiānyòu era,
someone was traveling in Yíchūn,
and stayed in an empty house.
After the wars,
the wells and towns were overgrown and desolate.
From the hall's west side to the beam above,
there was a small window,
outside the window was a wasteland of several dozen mǔ.
At dusk,
outside the window appeared an object,
square in shape,
rising from below.
In a moment,
it completely covered the window.
The person drew his bow and shot at it,
and it fell with the twang of the string.
As it was already evening,
he could not inspect it immediately.
The next morning, he searched for it,
about a hundred bù to the west,
there was a square fir plank,
with an arrow stuck in it,
which was indeed what he had shot the previous night.
Zhū Cóngběn
When Lǐ Yù was the Xuānzhōu Jiédùshǐ,
military and administrative affairs were delegated to the general Zhū Cóngběn.
In his family's stable, they kept a monkey.
The stable hand got up at night to feed the horses,
and saw a creature like a donkey,
black and hairy,
with hands and feet like a human's.
It was crouched on the ground eating that monkey,
and upon seeing the person, it left,
but the monkey was already half-eaten.
The following year,
Yù's clan was exterminated.
The elders of Xuānchéng said.
In the commandery, this monster often appeared.
Whenever there was a change in the military city,
this creature would emerge.
When it emerged, the entire city would stink.
When Tián Yūn was about to be defeated,
it appeared in the streets.
The night patrol saw it,
but did not dare approach.
Within ten days to a month, disaster struck.
Zhōu Běn
Xìnzhōu Cìshǐ Zhōu Běn went to pay respects at Yángdū,
and stayed at an official residence.
On the day of his family's private taboo,
he slept alone in the outer study,
with the lamp lit.
Before he was fully asleep,
he heard a sudden sound in the room.
Looking,
he saw the brazier slowly rising,
straight up to the roof,
and after a long while, it descended,
with flying ashes billowing.
The next day,
the entire room was covered in floating dust over the objects,
but there were no other strange occurrences.
Wáng Zōngxìn
At the end of the Táng dynasty,
Shǔ troops attacked Qí and on their return,
reached Báishí Town,
where deputy commander Wáng Zōngxìn stayed in a monk's room at Pǔ'ān Chányuàn.
It was the harsh winter,
and in the room there was a large meditation stove,
with a very strong fire burning.
Xìn gathered more than ten courtesans,
each occupying a monk's bed to rest.
Suddenly, Xìn saw one courtesan fly into the stove,
writhing on the blazing coals.
Zōngxìn hurriedly rescued her.
Once away from the fire,
her clothes were not even scorched.
Another courtesan flew in as before,
and he rescued her again.
After a short while,
the courtesans either went out or came in,
each bewildered and losing their voices.
A close official, separated by the post station wall,
reported to the overall commander Wáng Zōngchóu.
Zōngchóu arrived,
then slowly entered,
pulling each one out by the arm.
Looking at them,
the hems of their clothes were not damaged in the slightest,
They were only frightened and unable to sleep.
Questioning them,
they said,
they were dragged into the fire by a foreign monk,
and what they saw was all the same.
Zōngxìn was greatly angered,
summoned all the monks to stand before him,
and ordered the courtesans to identify them.
There was a monk named Zhōu,
tall in stature and foreign in appearance.
They all said,
"It's this one."
Zōngxìn then whipped him several hundred times,
saying he had illusionary arts.
This monk was actually a villager,
newly tonsured,
and understood nothing at all.
They also bound his hands and feet,
intending to take burning coals to scorch him.
Zōngchóu knew he was wronged,
so released him and let him escape.
In the end, it was unknown what kind of monster it was.
Xuē Lǎo Peak
In Fúzhōu city, there is Wūshí Mountain,
on the mountain there is a peak,
with three large carved characters,
reading "Xuē Lǎo Peak."
In the year Guǐmǎo,
one evening during wind and rain,
a noise like thousands of people clamoring was heard on the mountain.
By dawn,
Xuē Lǎo Peak had turned upside down,
with the characters facing upward.
The stone tablets in the city,
all turned over by themselves.
That year, Mǐn perished.
Ōuyáng Càn
Ōuyáng Càn, a third-generation descendant,
lived fifty lǐ south of Xúzhōu.
Having business in the city,
he returned late in the evening.
Not one or two lǐ later,
it was already dark.
That evening was overcast and gloomy.
After traveling about thirty lǐ,
summer rain poured heavily,
with thunder and lightning erupting.
Halfway along the road,
there were mountains and forests lining the path,
with dense woods and deep valleys,
and many fierce beasts.
He became endlessly terrified.
Once reaching the mountain road,
the rain intensified even more.
Suddenly, a huge creature appeared before him,
just over ten steps away.
It was over ten feet long,
pure white in color,
and he could not distinguish the shape of its head or feet,
only that it led the way ahead.
Càn was extremely frightened,
and often recited the Great Compassion Mantra silently,
wanting to recite it aloud,
but his mouth was already locked shut,
so he kept it in mind,
and after three or four times, he could speak again.
He recited it without stopping,
and soon the monster disappeared.
As he approached home,
the rain also gradually stopped.
From then on,
he dared not go out into the courtyard at dusk.
Dōngkē Temple
In Lǒngchéng County, there was Dōngkē Temple,
very secluded and elegant.
Its high railings allowed distant views,
and open windows welcomed the wind.
Visitors were as numerous as market-goers.
Suddenly one day,
strange phenomena arose.
Tiles and stones were thrown down from the air,
dust was stirred up,
and no one dared stand upright.
The resident monks were uneasy day and night,
their robes and ritual implements,
sometimes lost and then recovered.
A Dàoshi heard of this and said:
"How dare a spirit act like this?
I can drive it away."
The temple monks were very pleased,
and urged him to come quickly.
The Dàoshi entered the gate,
performed Yǔ steps in the hall,
reciting the Tiānpéng incantation,
his voice very fierce.
After a long while,
he lost his hat.
People saw it thrown over the wall through the air.
He retrieved it,
tied the strings and put it on,
continuing to recite the incantation.
Moments later,
his clothes were stripped and belt undone,
trousers also lost.
He had a small bundle with him,
containing talismans and essential texts,
which was also lost shortly after.
The Dàoshi then fled in disarray.
Several days later,
someone in a neighboring village,
digging soil under a fence,
found his bundle.
The county magistrate Dù Yánfàn,
an upright man,
went to see for himself,
saying:
"How can such a thing happen?"
Upon arriving, he sat cross-legged.
The spirit in the air,
threw down small written notes,
countless in number.
Many were quatrains,
mocking Magistrate Dù.
Remembering one or two, they said:
"Though mingled with wormwood and orchids,
the Southern Dynasties have ancestors.
Do not strike the green-robed man,
in the air we sing and dance."
Another said:
"Pity the earth beside wood,
neither boy nor girl-like.
A lean horse climbs the high mountain,
why suffer to ascend?"
Yánfàn realized this,
and also hurried back.
Those not recorded,
were many quatrains.
There was also patrol officer Wáng Zhāowěi,
relying on his youthful vigor,
went and cursed,
but was struck in the waist by a large stone and returned.
Wáng Shǒuzhēn
In Xúzhōu, there was a lay Dàoshi named Wáng Shǒuzhēn,
who kept a wife and children but did not live in a temple.
His conduct was extremely vulgar.
He often visited Tàimǎn Palace,
secretly taking the green cords worn by Dàoshi and bringing them home,
placing them under his bed mat,
covered with women's clothes.
The desecration was especially severe.
Strange phenomena appeared frequently:
lampstands moved by themselves,
a cat spoke:
"Don't do this,
don't do this."
Within ten days,
both husband and wife died.
Péng Yǒng
The official Péng Yóng of the Xuānzhōu Salt and Iron Bureau,
was often ill for several months,
feeling dazed and unhappy.
Whenever he went out to the main hall,
he would see dozens of performers and musicians,
each only a few inches tall.
They would play together,
performing various acrobatics and shows,
with dazzling reds and purples.
Péng Yóng watched them,
sometimes smiling with delight,
sometimes feeling frustrated and angry,
yet there was nothing he could do about it.
Others could not see them.
Later, when Péng Yóng recovered from his illness,
he no longer saw them.
More than ten years later,
he passed away.
Lǚ Shīzào
Lǚ Shīzào served as the prefect of Chízhōu,
and was quite corrupt and greedy.
Once, he married off his daughter to Yángdū,
sending her off with a lavish dowry.
He had his servants escort her,
and they moored for the night on the bank of the Zhúxiǎo River.
Suddenly, a Daoist priest appeared,
looking like a madman,
running back and forth.
Suddenly, he leaped into the boat,
passing straight through it.
Wherever he went,
a great fire erupted.
He then boarded the following boat,
and the fire followed him there as well.
Everything that was loaded on the boats,
was reduced to ashes,
even an old maidservant’s hair was completely burned off,
but the other people and the boats themselves,
were completely unharmed.
Once the fire died down,
the Daoist priest was nowhere to be seen.
Cuī Yànzhāng
The official Cuī Yànzhāng of Ráozhōu,
was seeing off guests east of the city.
Just as they were feasting,
suddenly a small carriage appeared,
golden in color,
about a foot tall,
moving around the banquet tables,
as if searching for something.
When it reached Cuī Yànzhāng,
it stopped and would not move.
Cuī Yànzhāng immediately fainted,
was carried back to the prefecture, and died.
The Aura of Rùnzhōu
In the year of Wùzǐ,
an aura like a rainbow appeared in Rùnzhōu,
dazzlingly colorful.
It had a head like a donkey,
and was several dozen zhàng long.
It circled the main hall,
completing three rounds before disappearing.
A diviner said:
"There will be weeping in this hall,
but it is not a misfortune for the prefecture."
Soon after,
the queen mother of the state passed away,
and mourning was held in this hall.
Huáng Jí
In the year of Jiǎwǔ,
the patrol officer Huáng Jí of the Jiāngxī courier station,
his daughter-in-law gave birth to a son,
with one head and two bodies joined back-to-back,
and four hands and four feet.
In Jiànchāng, a commoner’s family had a calf born,
with an extra leg attached to each of its four legs.
They threw it into the river,
and the next day it floated on the water.
In Nánchāng’s Xīnyì neighborhood, the ground sank,
stretching several dozen steps long,
with the widest part several zhàng across,
and the narrowest part seven or eight chǐ.
That same year,
the military governor Xú Zhīxún passed away.
Xióng Xūn
The military officer Xióng Xūn,
lived east of Chánglè Màn in Jiànkāng.
One evening as he went out,
he saw two objects on the roof,
as large as eggs,
red and glowing,
chasing each other back and forth.
His family was terrified.
A brave relative,
climbed onto the roof to catch them.
He caught one of them,
which turned out to be a colorful silk-wrapped eggshell.
They chopped it up and burned it,
and the stench could be smelled for several lǐ.
The other one ran away,
and never returned.
The family remained unharmed.
Wáng Jiànfēng
The military commissioner Wáng Jiànfēng of Jiāngnán,
was arrogant, extravagant, and presumptuous.
He built a grand mansion south of the Huái River.
One leisurely day, facing the street,
he sat by the window.
He saw an old woman,
leading a young girl past him.
Their clothes were ragged,
but the girl’s beauty was unparalleled.
Wáng Jiànfēng called out and asked them.
They said:
"We are alone, poor, and have no one to rely on,
begging for food until we came here."
Wáng Jiànfēng said:
"I will take your daughter as my concubine,
and provide for you for the rest of your life,
is that acceptable?"
The old woman was delighted.
Wáng Jiànfēng immediately summoned them inside,
and ordered two sets of new clothes for them to wear.
When the old woman and the girl took off their old clothes,
they turned into coagulated blood,
pooling on the ground.
Within a month,
Wáng Jiànfēng was executed.
A Scholar of Guǎnglíng
There was a scholar in Guǎnglíng,
who often slept alone with a lamp lit.
One night,
he woke up in the middle of the night.
Suddenly, there was a green-clad girl with double buns,
of exceptional beauty,
sleeping soundly at his feet.
Knowing she was a supernatural creature,
he was afraid and dared not approach,
so he went back to sleep as before.
By dawn, she had disappeared,
yet the doors and windows remained locked as before.
From then on, she came every night.
A sorcerer
wrote a talisman for him,
which he placed in his bun.
That night,
he pretended to sleep to wait for her.
Sure enough, he saw her enter through the door,
go straight to his bun,
take out the talisman,
look at it under the lamp,
and smile.
After that,
she put it back into his bun,
climbed onto the bed, and slept.
He was terrified.
Later, he heard that there was a Daoist priest on Yùsì Mountain,
whose talismans were divinely effective,
so he went to seek him out.
After boarding a boat,
she no longer came.
On the way to Yùzhāng,
on a hot summer night,
he traveled by boat under the moonlight.
As it was very hot,
he opened all the boat windows and slept.
In the middle of the night,
he suddenly saw her again.
She was sleeping behind the bed.
He quietly got up,
quickly grabbed her hands and feet,
and threw her into the river,
with a loud splash.
After that, she never appeared again.
Zhāng Yōng
The Recorder of Yǎnzhōu, Zhāng Yōng,
in his youth,
once lived in Zīzhōu.
His residence was suddenly plagued by many ghosts and strange phenomena,
though their forms and substance were never seen.
When the household servants carried and served food and drink,
they were all snatched away by the ghosts,
and the empty vessels were returned.
Sometimes vessels and utensils were thrown into the air,
taking a long time to fall.
Sometimes they moved by themselves on the ground,
colliding with each other.
Also, flying clumps of fire would land on people's bodies,
burning them without causing pain.
If anyone cursed or scolded them,
then bricks, stones, tiles, and pebbles
would arrive in response to the sound.
There was once a Confucian scholar
who did not believe the matter.
He took up a sword and went to stay overnight in the house.
His sword was struck by tiles and stones,
its edge and blade becoming chipped and broken.
There was also one who claimed to know incantations for exorcism.
As he was about to enter the gate,
he suddenly saw tiles and stones raining down together,
and could not proceed further.
When guests came,
some had their caps and headscarves snatched away
and thrown to other places,
to the point that some fled with their heads bare.
This continued for several tens of days before it finally stopped,
and in the end, nothing else happened to the family.
Zōng Mèngzhēng
Jìn's Càizhōu Patrol Officer, Zōng Mèngzhēng,
was skilled in medicine
and lived in the Eastern Capital.
In the autumn of the second year of the Kāiyùn era,
there was a sick person east of Xièyù Alley.
Late at night, someone came to summon him,
and he arrived on horseback.
As it was approaching the fourth watch,
at the entrance of Xièyù Alley, in front of a commoner's house gate,
there was a creature,
standing and moving,
its form quite large,
like a black mist standing tall.
The servant walking ahead
stood there dumbfounded, hair standing on end,
and the horse also snorted, ears pricked up, refusing to advance.
Zōng then forced himself to steady his mind and spirit,
urged his horse forward, and left.
By the time he reached the patient's house,
he could not properly take the pulse,
and felt especially dazed and confused.
After returning, he lay prostrate on his pillow,
and only after six or seven days did he recover.
Huáng Rénjùn
Shūzhōu Registrar Huáng Rénjùn
himself said that in the rénzǐ year,
after being dismissed from his post as Assistant Magistrate of Qiānyáng in Lǒngzhōu,
he arrived at Fèngxiáng City.
There was a Wénshū Temple,
and in the temple, several dozen clay statues
suddenly began to sway naturally,
like drunken men,
not stopping for the duration of a meal.
Onlookers crowded like a wall,
and the authorities forbade it.
To this day, its meaning remains unknown.
Sūn Dézūn
Shūzhōu Chief Inspector Sūn Dézūn
had an iron lamp stand in his family's sleeping hall
that suddenly began to shake by itself,
as if someone were shaking it.
The next day,
a maidservant happened to go to the lamp stand,
and suddenly fell to the ground,
and then died.
A Commoner of the Eastern Commandery
During the Jiàn'ān era of the Hàn,
in a commoner's household of the Eastern Commandery, strange events occurred.
For no reason, jars and vessels would move by themselves,
making a booming sound,
as if someone were striking them.
Plates and trays placed in front
would suddenly disappear.
Hens that laid eggs would always lose their chicks.
This continued for several years,
and everyone hated it.
So they prepared much delicious food,
covered it, and placed it in a room,
then hid secretly by the door to watch.
Sure enough, it came again to move them.
Hearing the sound,
they immediately closed the door and searched around.
In the room, they saw absolutely nothing,
so they secretly struck about with a staff.
After a long time,
from a corner of the room, they heard the sound of moaning and cries,
and then opened the door to look.
They caught an old man,
about a hundred and some years old,
whose speech and appearance
rather resembled a beast.
They then inquired around,
and several miles away found his family.
They said
he had been missing for over ten years,
and they were both sorrowful and joyful to have found him.
More than a year later,
he disappeared again.
They heard that in the Chénliú area, there were again such strange occurrences,
and at the time they still thought it was this old man.
Hú Xū
Xià County's Commandant Hú Xū
was a man of letters.
Once he went to the area of Jīnchéng County,
and stayed at someone's house.
The people prepared food for him.
Hú Xū had not yet eaten
and went out privately.
When he returned,
he saw an old woman,
two chǐ tall,
with sparse, hanging white hair,
leaning on the table and eating,
and the cakes and fruit were almost finished.
The family's new bride came out,
saw her, and became angry with her,
grabbed her by the ear,
and dragged her inside.
Hú Xū approached and peeked in,
and saw her put the old woman into a cage.
Peering in, he saw her two eyes were like cinnabar.
Hú Xū asked the reason,
and the woman said:
"This is called a 'mèi'.
She is the seventh-generation paternal great-aunt.
She has lived over three hundred years and does not die,
and her form has grown smaller.
She does not need clothes,
and does not fear cold or heat.
Locked in the cage,
she remains as usual all year round.
If she suddenly gets out of the cage,
she steals and eats several dǒu of food.
Therefore, she is called a 'mèi'."
Hú Xū found this strange.
He spoke of it wherever he went.
A Man of Wúchéng County
During the time of Wú's Sūn Xiū,
In Wúchéng, there was a man
who, after recovering from a serious illness, could speak with a resonant voice,
his sound heard over ten miles away.
Wherever it was heard,
it was as if he were seated right there.
His neighbor's family
had a son living away from home,
who had not returned to visit for a long time.
His father borrowed the man's voice,
making him deliver a reproachful message.
The son heard it,
thought it was a ghost or spirit,
and rushed home in a panic.
He also did not know the reason for it.
Lǐ Xuān's Wife
During the Yìxī era of Jìn's Ān Emperor,
Fán, the wife of Wèixīng's Lǐ Xuān,
was pregnant,
but passed the due date without giving birth.
And on her forehead was a sore,
from which the child broke through and came out.
Zhào Xuān's Mother
Zhào Xuān's mother of Chángshān,
while pregnant,
developed a sore on her arm,
and the child came out from the sore.
Liú Pō of Péngchéng,
often told his son-in-law, the presented scholar Wáng Shèng, a story:
at the Nándǒng Inn in Sānyuán County,
on the eastern wall of the inn,
at the end of the Zhēnyuán era,
there was an old woman named Mèng,
who died at over a hundred years old.
The inn’s residents all called it “the inn of the Grand Master Zhāng.”
Pō, coming into the city from north of the Wèi River,
stopped at the old woman’s inn.
He saw an old woman there,
who appeared to be only about sixty years old.
She wore a large yellow silk fur coat,
a black headscarf,
and sat astride the doorway.
Lǐ Zhòucáo of the Left Guard,
named Shìguǎng,
was asked by the old woman what official position he held,
and Shìguǎng answered in full.
The old woman said:
“This is one of the Four Guards,
a very good official position.”
Shìguǎng then asked the old woman:
“Why do you say that?”
The old woman said:
“When I was twenty-six,
I married Zhāng Chá as his wife.”
Chá was a man of great strength,
skilled in horseback riding and archery.
When Guō Fényáng was in command of Shuòfāng,
these were all counties under his jurisdiction.
Líng, Xià, Bīn, Jīng, Qí, and Pú were among them.
My husband, Zhāng Chá,
was employed by Fényáng,
and was granted generous clothing and gifts,
often staying by Fényáng’s side.
Chá’s appearance
closely resembled mine.
After Chá died,
Fényáng grieved for him.
I then disguised myself in men’s clothing and headgear,
registered under the name of Chá’s younger brother,
and requested to serve Fényáng.
Fényáng was greatly pleased,
and ordered me to fill the vacancy.
In this way, I lived as a widow for another fifteen years.
After Fényáng passed away,
I was already seventy-two years old.
The army repeatedly petitioned,
and I was appointed concurrently as Yùshǐ Dàfū.
Suddenly, I thought of my loneliness,
so I married Old Pān of this inn as his wife.
Since then, I have given birth to two more sons,
named Tāo
and Qú.
Tāo is now fifty-four,
and Qú is fifty-two.”
These two sons,
Pō always kept in mind.
He told his son-in-law Wáng Shèng
about the strange things in the human world.
Huáng Chónggǔ
In the Shǔ state of Wáng, there was a false minister named Zhōu Xiáng,
who initially served in the Qiángnán administration,
overseeing the affairs of the prefectural office.
At that time, Línqióng County sent over a person named Huáng Chónggǔ, who was involved in a fire case.
As soon as she was imprisoned,
she presented a poem:
“By chance I left seclusion to dwell in Línqióng,
My conduct steadfast as the pine by the stream.
Why must your governance, clear as water and mirror,
Trap this wild crane in a deep cage?”
Zhōu read the poem,
and summoned her for an audience.
She claimed to be a presented scholar from the countryside,
and answered questions in detail and with agility.
Zhōu immediately ordered her release.
A few days later,
she presented another poem.
Zhōu found her extraordinary,
summoned her,
and had her stay in the academy alongside his nephews and other students.
She excelled at chess and the qín,
and was skilled in calligraphy and painting.
The next day,
Zhōu recommended her to serve as acting Sīhù Cānjūn in the prefectural office.
She was praised for her concise speech,
clerks feared and submitted to her,
and official documents were handled beautifully and clearly.
Zhōu admired both her intelligence
and her graceful demeanor.
After she had served for nearly a year,
he wanted to marry his daughter to her.
Chónggǔ then sealed a letter of thanks in her sleeve,
and presented another poem:
“Once I left the green riverbanks where I gathered kingfisher feathers,
I dwelled in poverty in a thatched hut, composing poems.
Since donning the blue gown and serving as an official,
I have forever cast aside the mirror and painted eyebrows.
My character stands lofty as the green pine’s integrity,
My will resounds firm as the white jade’s purity.
If the administration would allow me as a son-in-law,
I wish Heaven would swiftly turn me into a man.”
Zhōu read the poem,
astonished and alarmed,
and summoned her for questioning.
It turned out she was the daughter of Prefect Huáng,
who lost her parents at a young age,
and lived only with an old wet nurse,
never having married.
Zhōu admired her chastity even more,
and everyone in the prefecture marveled at this wonder.
Soon, she requested to resign,
and returned to her former seclusion in Línqióng,
and no one ever knew whether she lived or died.
White-Necked Crow
At the beginning of the Qìdān invasion of the capital,
bandits rose up everywhere like swarming bees,
troubling the Róng people.
In Chén Prefecture, there was a woman
who became a bandit leader,
known as White-Necked Crow.
She was around forty years old,
with a rough and short build,
yellow hair and dark skin.
She came to see the Róng king,
adopting a man’s name,
and in her clothing, bowing and kneeling,
she acted entirely like a man.
The Róng king summoned her for an audience,
bestowed upon her a brocade robe, silver belt, saddle, and horse,
and appointed her as Huáihuà General.
He entrusted her with the task of recruiting and pacifying bandits east of the mountains,
granting her generous rewards.
The false Yān king, Zhào Yánshòu,
summoned and questioned her.
The woman claimed
that she could shoot arrows while galloping left and right,
carried two quivers,
and could travel two hundred lǐ in a day.
Wielding spears and striking with swords,
she excelled at all.
Her subordinates, several thousand men,
all served and obeyed her.
When asked if she had a husband,
she said,
she had had several dozen husbands before and after,
and if they slightly displeased her,
she would kill them with her own hands.
Those who heard this could not help but sigh in anger.
Within ten days, she was in the capital,
riding in and out on horseback.
There was also a man
who rode a horse and followed her.
This was a human monstrosity.
The northern Róng brought chaos to Zhōngxià,
and women rose to power,
all signs of yin prevailing.
Later, the woman was executed by Fú Yànqīng, the military governor of Yǎn Prefecture.
Clerk of Yángchéng County
During the Chū era of Wèi Jǐng,
strange occurrences happened at the home of a clerk in Yángchéng County.
For no reason, they heard clapping and calling to one another,
but when they looked, they saw nothing.
The clerk’s mother, tired from working at night,
lay down on her pillow to rest.
After a while,
they heard a voice from under the stove calling:
“Wén Yuē,
why aren’t you coming?”
A voice from under the pillow answered:
“I’m stuck under the pillow,
I can’t come over,
you should come to me.”
When morning came,
they found it was a rice shovel.
They gathered and burned it,
and the strange occurrences ceased.
Huán Xuán
During the time of Huán Xuán of the Eastern Jìn,
beneath the Zhūquè Gate,
two small children suddenly appeared,
their entire bodies as black as ink,
singing together the "Máng Lóng Gē."
Children by the roadside followed and joined in, numbering several dozen.
The song went:
"Máng basket mat,
Rope binds the belly.
A cart without an axle,
leans on a lone tree." The sound was exceedingly mournful and sorrowful,
causing listeners to forget to return home.
As the day grew late,
the two children went back into Jiànkāng County,
reaching beneath the pavilion,
where they transformed into a pair of lacquered drumsticks.
The drum official arranged them,
He said:
"These drumsticks have been stored for a long time.
They were often lost and then recovered,
but I never expected they would take human form."
The following spring, Huán Xuán was defeated.
The phrase "a cart without an axle,
leans on a lone tree"
forms the character "Huán."
When Jīngzhōu sent Huán Xuán's head,
it was wrapped in a worn basket mat,
and his corpse was bound with máng rope,
then sunk into the river.
All was exactly as the children's song had foretold.
Servant Girl of the Xú Family
Lán, a servant girl of the Xú family in Dōnghǎi,
during the Yìxī era of the Jìn dynasty,
suddenly fell ill,
and her behavior became unusually agitated.
Others observed her closely,
and saw a broom come from the corner of the wall,
heading toward the servant girl's bed.
They then took it and burned it.
Woman from Jiānghuái
There was a woman from Jiānghuái
whose nature was full of desires,
constantly indulging in fantasies without restraint,
and she was often intoxicated day and night.
One morning upon waking,
she saw two young boys behind the house,
very fresh and clean,
like minor officials in a palace.
The woman tried to embrace them,
but they suddenly turned into brooms,
which she then took and burned.
Liú Xuán
Liú Xuán of Zhōngshān in the Sòng dynasty lived in Yuèchéng.
One evening,
he suddenly saw someone wearing black trousers and a jacket coming to fetch fire,
with a face lacking the seven orifices,
appearing rough and indistinct.
He then consulted a diviner.
The diviner said:
"This is an object from your family's previous generation.
Over time, it has become a malevolent spirit,
capable of killing people.
While it still has no eyes,
you should eliminate it early."
Liú then seized and bound it,
striking it several times with a knife,
and it transformed into a pillow.
This was actually a pillow from his grandfather's time.
Yóu Xiānzhāo
Yóu Xiānzhāo of Guǎngpíng
had lost his wife.
He saw a person wearing red trousers and a jacket.
Knowing it was a malevolent spirit,
he struck it with a knife.
After a long while,
it turned out to be a pair of shoes he often wore.
Tribal Chief of Jūyán
At the beginning of Emperor Jìng of Zhōu's reign,
the tribal chief of Jūyán, Bó Dūgǔdī,
was tyrannical and oppressive,
extravagant and dissolute,
He enjoyed music,
and his residence was extremely luxurious.
Suddenly, several dozen people arrived at his gate,
one of whom first presented a name card, saying:
"Provincial Inspector of Tribes, Chéng Duōshòu."
He then hurried inside.
Gǔdī asked:
"Why are you called Provincial Inspector of Tribes?"
Duōshòu replied:
and several others are each different,
but our names are all not separately created.
There are those surnamed Mǎ,
those surnamed Pí,
those surnamed Lù,
those surnamed Xióng,
those surnamed Zhāng,
those surnamed Wèi,
and those surnamed Bān,
yet all are named Shòu.
Only I, the leader, am named Duōshòu."
Gǔdī said:
"You all seem like entertainers;
what skills do you possess?"
Duōshòu said:
"We are skilled at juggling bowls and pearls,
our nature dislikes vulgarity,
and our speech is all based on classical principles."
Gǔdī was greatly pleased and said:
"Something I have never seen before."
One performer then stepped forward and said:
"We are hungry,
Làlà yíyí.
Our skin loosely wraps around our bodies three times.
If the host's food is insufficient,
we will open our mouths and never stop."
Gǔdī was delighted,
and ordered more food to be served.
One person said:
"I request to perform 'the large and small completing each other,
the beginning and end generating each other.'"
Thereupon, the tall person swallowed the short person,
the fat person swallowed the thin person,
and after swallowing each other, only two remained.
The tall one then said:
"Please perform 'the beginning and end generating each other.'"
Thereupon, he vomited out one person,
and the one vomited out vomited another person,
each vomiting in turn,
until the number of people was restored.
Gǔdī was very astonished,
and thus bestowed generous gifts before sending them away.
The next day they came again,
performing tricks as before.
This continued for half a month,
and Gǔdī became quite annoyed,
unable to provide food.
The entertainers all became angry and said:
"The host must think we are performing illusions;
please allow us to test it on your sons, daughters, sisters, brothers, nephews, nieces, wives, and concubines."
Thereupon, they took Gǔdī's sons, daughters, younger siblings, nephews, nieces, wives, and concubines,
and swallowed them into their bellies.
Inside their bellies, they all cried and begged for their lives,
and Gǔdī was terrified.
He descended the steps and kowtowed,
pleading pitifully for his relatives.
The entertainers,
all laughed and said:
"This is harmless,
no need to worry."
They then vomited them out,
and the relatives were completely restored as before.
Gǔdī was deeply enraged,
and wanted to kill them by smearing blood on weapons.
He thus ordered a secret investigation,
and they were seen disappearing at the site of an ancient house foundation.
Gǔdī ordered it to be excavated,
and several feet deep,
under the rubble, they found a large wooden crate,
containing several thousand leather bags.
Beside the crate were grains and wheat,
which turned to ash upon touch.
Inside the crate, they found bamboo slips with writing,
but the characters were worn away,
and could not be read.
Only faintly, it seemed there were three or four characters,
as if they were the character 'líng'.
Gǔdī realized these bags were the source of the strangeness,
and wanted to take them out and burn them.
The bags then cried out from within the crate:
"We have no life,
and should have perished long ago.
Because Commandant Lǐ left mercury here,
we have been able to survive temporarily.
We are the grain bags of Commandant Lǐ Shàoqīng,
crushed when the house collapsed.
Many years have passed,
and now we have gained life.
We are now taken as entertainers by the mountain god of Jūyán;
we beg you to show mercy for the sake of the god,
and not destroy us.
From now on, we will not dare to disturb your esteemed residence again."
Gǔdī coveted their mercury,
and burned all the bags.
All made sounds of冤楚,
and blood flowed and splattered.
After the burning,
the corridors, doors, and windows of Gǔdī's house
all emitted sounds of冤痛,
like when the bags were burned,
and did not stop for over a month.
That year,
Gǔdī's entire family fell ill and died.
Within a year,
there were no survivors left.
The mercury later also disappeared.
Monk Tài Qióng
In the Táng dynasty, there was a monk in the upper capital named Tài Qióng,
who was capable.
He lectured on the "Rén Wáng Jīng".
At the beginning of the Kāiyuán era,
he lectured in Jīngyáo Village, Fèngxiān County,
and then stayed at the village temple.
After two summers,
one day,
he was holding his alms bowl and about to enter the hall.
As he was closing the door,
something fell in front of the eaves.
At that time, the sky was just beginning to lighten,
and the monk went to look;
it was a newborn baby,
and its swaddling clothes were very new.
The monk was astonished,
and so tucked it into his sleeve.
He intended to give it to a villager,
but after walking five or six lǐ,
he felt his sleeve become light.
He reached in to check,
and it was an old broom.
The Old Man of Qīngjiāng Commandery
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
an old man from Qīngjiāng Commandery often herded cattle in the fields south of the commandery.
Suddenly, he heard a strange sound coming from underground,
and the old man, along with several cowherd boys,
all fled in fright.
From then on, the old man fell ill with a fever and became very sick.
After just over ten days,
his illness slightly improved.
He dreamed of a man,
dressed in a green jacket,
who turned to the old man and said:
"Move me to the Kāiyuán Temple."
The old man woke in fright,
but did not understand the meaning.
Several days later,
he went out to the fields again,
and heard it once more.
He then reported the matter to the commandery governor.
Governor Fēng angrily said:
"Are you not confused and delusional?"
He scolded him and sent him away.
That evening,
the old man again dreamed of the man in the green jacket, who told him:
"I have been buried underground for a long time;
quickly dig me out,
or you will fall ill."
The old man was greatly afraid.
At dawn,
he went with his son to the south of the commandery,
and dug at that spot.
About ten feet down,
they found a bell,
its color green,
which was the color of the clothing worn by the man in his dream.
He then reported it again to the commandery governor,
and the governor placed it in the Kāiyuán Temple.
That day at the chén hour,
without being struck, it suddenly rang by itself,
its sound extremely loud and resonant.
The people of Qīngjiāng
were all astonished and amazed.
The commandery governor reported the matter to the emperor,
and Emperor Xuánzōng ordered Chancellor Línfǔ to make a copy of the bell's design,
to be announced throughout the land.
Wéi Xùn
Wéi Xùn of Jīngzhào in the Táng dynasty,
one day while reading the Diamond Sutra in his family school,
suddenly saw a woman in a crimson skirt outside the door,
three zhàng tall,
who climbed over the wall and entered.
She reached out from afar,
grabbed the family tutor by the hair,
and dragged him to the ground.
She then reached out to seize Wéi Xùn,
but Wéi Xùn used the Diamond Sutra he was holding to shield himself,
his body,
and narrowly escaped.
The tutor was dragged to a certain house,
and people followed, shouting,
which saved him.
The ghost ran into a large dung heap.
The tutor’s entire body had turned indigo blue,
and his tongue hung out over a chǐ long.
His family helped him back to the school,
and it took a long time for him to regain consciousness.
Leading the villagers, they dug into the dung heap,
several chǐ deep,
and found a newlywed doll made of torn silk, wearing a crimson skirt and white blouse.
They burned it at a five-way crossroads,
and the strange occurrences ceased.
Lú Zànshàn
At Lú Zànshàn’s home,
there was a porcelain newlywed doll.
After several years,
his wife jokingly said to it:
“I’ll make you my husband’s concubine.”
Lú thereafter became troubled and distracted.
He often saw a woman
lying inside the bed curtains.
After a long time,
suspecting the porcelain doll was causing the trouble,
he sent it to a temple for safekeeping.
There was a temple servant
who swept the floor in the hall at dawn
and saw a woman.
When asked where she came from,
she said she was Lú Zànshàn’s concubine,
sent there because the main wife was jealous.
Later, when Lú’s family came,
the servant told them about seeing the concubine.
Lú Zànshàn thoroughly investigated the matter
and found that the clothing described
matched the porcelain doll.
He then ordered it smashed.
Inside its chest was blood
the size of a chicken egg.
Liǔ Chóng
Liǔ Chóng, a military officer in Yuèzhōu,
suddenly developed a sore on his head,
groaning in unbearable pain.
He summoned a diviner to observe at night,
who said:
“There is a woman in a green skirt.
She does not answer when questioned
and is under your window.
Remove her quickly.”
Liǔ Chóng searched under the window
and found only a porcelain courtesan doll,
extremely beautiful,
adorned with green porcelain.
He then smashed it in an iron mortar and burned it,
and the sore healed.
A Temple Servant in the South
In the south, there was a monastery
with a statue of Jiǔzǐmǔ inside,
exquisitely crafted.
Once, there was a temple servant
who was young
and served the monks.
After a few years,
he grew increasingly emaciated
and his mind became confused.
The monks found it quite strange.
One monk
saw this servant entering the Jiǔzǐmǔ hall at night to sleep,
and gradually noticed a beautiful woman arriving,
luring him to sleep with her,
which had been going on for nearly a year.
The monk realized the statue was the cause
and destroyed it.
From then on, she was never seen again,
the servant recovered,
and he shaved his head to become a monk.
Scholar Qū
The Dàoshi Yè Fǎshàn,
skilled in talismanic arts,
was repeatedly honored by the emperor as Hónglú Qīng,
receiving exceptional favor and respect.
Yè Fǎshàn resided at Xuánzhēn Temple,
and once, over ten court officials visited him,
loosening their belts and lingering.
As everyone longed for wine,
someone suddenly knocked at the door,
claiming to be
Scholar Qū.
Yè Fǎshàn had someone tell him:
“We are currently hosting court officials
and have no time for conversation.
Please visit another day.”
Before the words were finished,
a poor scholar,
arrogant and disdainful, strode straight in.
He appeared around twenty years old,
plump and fair, pleasant to look at.
Smiling, he bowed to the guests
and took the last seat,
speaking loudly in debate,
citing ancient and modern examples.
The whole gathering was taken aback,
and everyone watched him intently.
After a while, he briefly rose,
swirling like the wind.
Yè Fǎshàn said to the officials:
“This fellow barged in
and speaks so eloquently.
Could he be a demon trying to bewitch us?
Let us prepare swords to guard against him.”
Scholar Qū returned,
clenching his fists and slapping his palms,
launching sharp arguments and challenges,
with an unstoppable force.
Yè Fǎshàn secretly struck him with a small sword,
and with the swing, his head fell off,
dropping to the steps below,
transforming into a bottle lid.
The whole gathering was shocked and terrified,
but looking at the spot,
they found a full bottle of fine wine,
and everyone laughed.
They drank it,
and its flavor was excellent.
A guest, drunk, patted the bottle and said:
“Scholar Qū, Scholar Qū,
your flavor is unforgettable.”
Guóguó Fūrén
In Cháng'ān there was a poor monk,
whose clothes were very ragged.
He was selling a small ape,
which could speak human language
and could be sent on errands.
Lady Guóguó heard of this,
and promptly ordered the monk to come to her residence.
After the monk arrived,
Lady Guóguó saw him,
and asked him about the origin.
The monk said:
"I originally lived in Western Shǔ,
dwelling in the mountains for over twenty years.
Once a group of apes passed by,
leaving behind this small ape.
Out of pity, I took it in and raised it.
Only half a year later,
this small ape understood human intentions,
and could also speak human language.
Following gestures and commands,
there was nothing it could not do for people.
It was truly no different from a disciple.
I arrived in the city just yesterday.
My funds are quite lacking.
Having no way to keep and care for this small ape,
I therefore sold it in the market."
Lady Guóguó said:
"Now I will give you bolts of silk,
you may leave this ape,
I will raise it."
The monk then expressed gratitude,
left the ape, and departed.
The small ape stayed day and night by Lady Guóguó's side,
and she loved and cherished it greatly.
Half a year later,
Imperial Consort Yáng sent Lady Guóguó some glossy ganoderma,
and Lady Guóguó called the small ape to have it look and play with it.
The small ape fell to the ground in front of Lady Guóguó,
transforming into a small child,
with dignified and beautiful features,
around fourteen or fifteen years old.
Lady Guóguó was very surprised,
and questioned him sternly.
The child said:
"My original surname is Yuán.
The monk who sold me was formerly in the Shǔ mountains.
I once followed my father into the mountains to gather herbs,
and lived in the forest for three years.
My father often fed me medicinal herbs.
Suddenly one day,
without realizing it, I transformed into an ape.
My father, frightened, abandoned me,
which is why I was taken in and raised by this monk,
and ended up at your residence.
Although I could not speak before,
the matters in my heart
were not forgotten at all.
Since receiving your kindness and care,
I very much wanted to express my feelings to you,
but regretted being unable to speak.
Every time deep night came,
I could only weep alone.
Now unexpectedly I have returned to human form,
I do not know what your esteemed intention is."
Lady Guóguó found this remarkable,
and then ordered him to be dressed in brocade clothes,
with attendants following behind.
She always kept the matter secret.
Another three years later,
the child's appearance was very beautiful,
and Imperial Consort Yáng had repeatedly glanced at him.
Fearing that someone might seize him,
she therefore did not let him go out,
but placed him separately in a small room.
The child only craved medicinal substances,
and Lady Guóguó had maidservants regularly supply him with medicinal food.
Suddenly one day,
the child and this maidservant
both transformed into apes.
Lady Guóguó, finding it strange and bizarre,
ordered people to shoot and kill them,
and the child turned out to be a wooden figure.
Sū Pī's Daughter
Sū Pī of Wǔgōng,
during the Tiānbǎo era served as magistrate of Chǔqiū.
His daughter married into the Lǐ family.
Mr. Lǐ had always favored a maidservant,
and because of this, his affection for Sū Pī's daughter was not deep.
The maidservant sought a sorcerer to perform a curse magic,
burying a talisman in the manure pile of the Lǐ residence.
She also bound seven colored figurines of women,
over a foot long,
and hid them in a hole in the eastern wall,
plastering over it,
so people would not know.
Several years later,
Mr. Lǐ passed away,
and the maidservant
died one after another.
The daughter lived as a widow for four or five years.
The curse magic succeeded.
Colored women figurines roamed inside the residence,
and because of this, Mrs. Sū fell ill, fainting.
The Lǐ maidservant had already died,
so no one knew the cause.
After a year,
repeatedly seeking sorcerers,
using every incantation and spell,
they could not control it.
Later, waiting for them to appear again,
she led several dozen people to ambush and catch them,
capturing one.
Looking at it, its eyebrows, eyes, and body were all complete,
and in human hands,
it constantly moved without stopping.
Chopping it with a knife,
blood flowed on the ground,
so they piled firewood and burned it.
Its companions all came to the burning place wailing,
some in the air,
some on the ground.
After burning,
the residence had a smell of roasted human flesh.
The next day,
they all wore white clothes crying loudly,
for several days without stopping.
Half a year later,
they captured six more in succession,
and burned them all.
Only one was caught but escaped again,
chasing it,
it suddenly entered the manure pile.
Mrs. Sū led over a hundred people to dig the manure,
seven or eight feet deep,
and found a peachwood talisman.
On the talisman were vermilion characters,
clearly recognizable.
It said:
"The Lǐ family maidservant cursed the Sū family daughter,
making seven human figures,
in the earthen niche on the eastern wall.
After nine years it will succeed."
Then following the broken wall,
they found another one,
and Sū Pī's daughter was fine from then on.
Jiǎng Wéiyuè
did not fear ghosts and spirits.
He often slept alone by the window,
hearing voices outside,
Yuè prayed:
"If you are a wronged soul,
you may enter to meet.
If you are a troublemaking ghost,
do not startle me."
Then with a rustling sound they pushed open the door,
and wanted to climb onto his bed.
Seeing Yuè unafraid,
they immediately stood by the wall,
there were seven of them.
Asked what they were doing,
they stood without answering.
Yuè hit them with a pillow,
and they all ran out the door.
Chasing after them,
they disappeared in the courtyard.
The next day digging there,
he found seven broken wheel spokes,
and the anomaly then ceased.
Also, his elder brother once suffered a severe illness,
Yuè personally looked after him.
Late at night,
he again saw three female ghosts,
coming to his brother's bedside.
He shouted at them to retreat,
three times,
the ghosts all fell to the ground,
after a long time they ran out.
His brother then recovered.
Huàyīn Village Chief
In Huàyīn County, at the seven-level Zhào Village,
the village road had been eroded into a ravine,
so a bridge was built across it to allow passage.
One night, the village head was crossing the bridge
when he saw a group of small children gathered around a fire, playing.
Knowing they were likely demons,
the village head shot an arrow at them.
It made a sound as if hitting wood,
and the fire immediately went out.
He heard a faint, chirping voice say:
"You shot my Ā Lián in the head."
When the village head returned from the county town,
he searched the area
and found six or seven broken pieces of a cart wheel,
with an arrow still lodged in the tip of one piece.
Wéi Liàng
During the Qiányuán era,
Wéi Liàng, the magistrate of Jiāngníng County, suddenly saw a small ghost in front of his hall.
It covered its face with its lower lip,
approached the lamp,
then left and returned again.
He sent someone to chase it,
and it vanished beneath the steps.
The next morning,
they dug where it had disappeared
and found an old door panel,
over a foot long,
with a head shaped like a curled lotus leaf.
The Dōnglái Traveler
In the eastern capital commandery, there was a guesthouse pavilion,
and its western wing was often haunted.
Travelers who slept there
would frequently hear the faint barking of a dog at night.
The sound was very faint.
When they looked with a candle,
they saw nothing at all.
This went on for many years.
Later, the commandery governor ordered it locked up and used as a storeroom.
One night, under a bright moon,
a storeroom clerk saw a very small dog,
bluish-gray in color,
running around the courtyard from under the western wing.
The clerk found it strange, as it was unlike ordinary dogs,
so he threw a stone to hit it.
The dog barked and ran away,
disappearing under the western wing.
The next day,
the clerk reported the incident to the commandery governor.
The governor ordered a thorough search of the western wing for traces.
They found many bluish-gray hairs on the door's dog-shaped ornament,
exactly matching the color of the gray dog the clerk had seen.
Only then did everyone understand.
The Villager of Jiāochéng
About ten or so miles south of Jiāochéng County,
a monster often appeared to people at night,
causing many to fall ill from fright and die.
The villagers had long been troubled by this.
Later, a villager carrying a bow and arrows was walking at night
when he saw a huge, giant-like figure south of the county,
dressed in red robes,
with a black scarf covering its head,
walking slowly toward him,
swaying as if drunk.
The villager was terrified
and immediately drew his bow to full draw and shot.
The arrow indeed hit its mark,
and the monster retreated.
Somewhat relieved but still frightened, the villager
hurried north to an inn,
where he told his story.
The next day,
he reached the county town.
There, on a red osmanthus tree west of the outer wall,
he saw an arrow stuck in it—
indeed, it was the villager's own arrow.
He retrieved it and brought it back,
and the arrowhead was covered in a great deal of blood.
He reported it to the county magistrate,
who ordered it burned.
From then on, there was no more trouble south of the county.
Cén Shùn
Cén Shùn of Rǔnán, courtesy name Xiàobó,
was fond of learning and literary pursuits in his youth,
and in his later years particularly excelled in military strategy.
While traveling in Shǎnzhōu,
he was poor and had no residence.
His maternal relatives, the Lǚ family,
owned a mountain estate,
which was about to be abandoned.
Shùn requested to live there.
When people tried to dissuade him,
Shùn said:
"Fate is constant;
what is there to fear?"
In the end, he settled there.
Over a year later,
Shùn often sat alone in his study,
and even his family members were not allowed to enter.
At night, he heard the sound of war drums,
not knowing where they came from,
but upon stepping outside, the sounds ceased.
He alone was delighted,
taking pride in it,
considering it an auspicious sign of Shí Lè.
He prayed, saying:
"These must be spectral soldiers aiding me.
If so,
they should show me the time of my future wealth and honor."
Several nights later,
he dreamed of a man clad in armor,
who came forward and reported:
"General Jīn Xiàng sent me to tell you, Lord Cén,
the military city is on alert at night,
and there are those causing disturbances.
Honored by your favor,
how dare I not respectfully obey your command?
You are destined for great fortune,
and I hope you will take good care of yourself.
Since you harbor grand ambitions,
could you deign to look upon our small state?
Now an enemy state is attacking our fortress,
and we eagerly await a worthy man,
admiring your fine reputation,
and wish to entrust you with command."
Shùn replied:
"The general is naturally wise and brilliant,
and his troops are disciplined.
I am troubled by your kind words,
and humbled by your visit to one as lowly as I.
However, like a loyal dog or horse,
my only desire is to be of use."
The messenger returned to report.
Shùn suddenly awoke,
feeling as if he had lost something,
and sat pondering the meaning of the dream.
Soon, drums and horns sounded from all directions,
growing increasingly fierce.
Shùn straightened his headscarf and got out of bed,
bowing twice in prayer.
In a moment,
a wind arose at the doors and windows,
and the curtains fluttered.
Under the lamp, hundreds of iron cavalry suddenly appeared,
galloping left and right.
All were only a few inches tall,
clad in sturdy armor and bearing sharp weapons,
scattered like stars across the ground.
In a flash,
battle formations gathered from all sides.
Shùn was astonished,
but steadied himself to observe.
Shortly after,
a soldier delivered a letter, saying:
"The general sends a dispatch."
Shùn received it.
It read:
"Our land borders the Xūn barbarians,
and warfare never ceases.
For decades,
our generals have aged and our soldiers exhausted,
sleeping in armor amidst frost.
Heaven has set a formidable enemy against us,
and the situation is unstoppable.
You, noble sir, have cultivated virtue and preserved your essence,
advancing your achievements in due time.
Having repeatedly received your favorable responses,
we wish to entrust ourselves to your divine covenant.
However, you, noble sir, are an official of the yang world,
destined to enjoy great fortune in this sage era.
How dare our small state hope for such?
The bandits from the northern mountains of Tiānnàguó have formed an alliance,
and a battle is scheduled.
The engagement is planned for midnight,
but the outcome is uncertain,
causing us great anxiety."
Shùn expressed his thanks,
lit more candles in the room,
and sat watching the changes.
After midnight,
drums and horns sounded from all sides.
Earlier, there had been a mouse hole under the eastern wall,
which now transformed into a city gate.
The enemy fortress stood tall and imposing.
After three rounds of drum and horn signals,
troops marched out from the four gates,
with countless banners linked together,
moving like wind and clouds,
as both sides arrayed their formations.
Under the eastern wall was the Tiānnà army,
under the western wall was the Jīn Xiàng
army,
each taking their positions.
The military advisor stepped forward and said:
"The heavenly horse flies diagonally across three stops,
the general moves horizontally to control the four directions.
The supply chariot advances straight without turning,
the six Jia follow in order without deviation."
The king said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, the drums sounded,
and each army had a horse
that moved diagonally three feet and stopped.
The drums sounded again,
and each had a foot soldier
that moved horizontally one foot.
The drums sounded again,
and the chariots advanced.
As the drumbeats grew increasingly urgent, each side made moves,
with projectiles and stones flying chaotically.
In a short while,
the Tiānnà army was utterly defeated and scattered,
with casualties covering the ground.
Their king fled south on a single horse,
and several hundred soldiers retreated to the southwestern corner,
barely escaping.
Earlier, there was a mortar in the southwest,
The king hid in the mortar,
which transformed into a fortress.
The Jīn Xiàng army was greatly invigorated,
collecting the enemy's armored soldiers,
with corpses strewn across the ground.
Shùn watched, bowing low.
At that moment, a cavalryman approached the tent,
announcing:
"Yin and yang have their proper places;
he who attains them prospers.
The majestic heavenly might,
driven by the wind in continuous assaults,
achieved victory in one battle.
What does the noble sir think of this?"
Shùn replied:
"The general's brilliance rivals the sun;
seizing the moment and acting in accordance with Heaven's will,
I have secretly observed the divine transformations and mystical texts,
and cannot contain my joy."
For several days, battles were fought like this,
with victories and defeats alternating.
The king's divine appearance was majestic,
his heroic bearing unmatched.
He feasted Shùn with rare delicacies,
presenting him with countless treasures, bright pearls, and jewels.
Shùn thus enjoyed glory among them,
with all his desires fulfilled.
Later, he gradually cut off contact with relatives and friends,
and rarely left his room.
His family found it strange,
but could not ascertain the reason.
Moreover, Shùn's complexion grew haggard,
as he was afflicted by ghostly energy.
His relatives suspected something unusual,
but when questioned, he remained silent.
They then made him drink strong wine,
and when drunk, he revealed everything.
His relatives secretly prepared spades and shovels,
and while Shùn was in the lavatory, they blocked him off.
Wielding spades, they worked chaotically,
digging inside the room.
At eight or nine feet deep, they suddenly broke through a cavity—
it was an ancient tomb.
The tomb had a brick chamber,
containing many burial objects,
including hundreds of suits of armor.
In front was a golden gaming board,
with pieces arrayed all over it,
all formed of gold and bronze,
fully equipped for military affairs.
Only then did they understand the military advisor's words—
they were the moves and formations of the board game.
They then burned the objects,
and leveled the ground.
They obtained many treasures,
all stored within the tomb.
When Shùn saw them,
he suddenly awoke as if from a dream,
and vomited profusely.
From then on, he was healthy and cheerful,
and the house was no longer haunted.
This happened in the first year of the Bǎoyìng era.
Yuán Wúyǒu
During the Bǎoyìng era,
there was a man named Yuán Wúyǒu.
He often, in late mid-spring,
traveled alone through the countryside of Wéiyáng.
Once, as evening fell,
a great storm arose with wind and rain.
It was a time after war and famine,
and many households had fled,
so he entered an empty villa by the roadside.
Soon the storm cleared,
and the slanting moon just then emerged.
Wúyǒu sat by the north window,
when suddenly he heard the sound of footsteps from the western corridor.
Before long,
he saw four figures within the moonlight,
their clothing and caps all unusual,
conversing and jesting together,
reciting poetry with great gusto.
Then they said:
"Tonight is like autumn,
with such breeze and moonlight,
shouldn't we, our kind, each compose a line
to express the affairs of our lives?"
One of them immediately began to speak, and so on.
Their recitations were clear and resonant,
and Wúyǒu heard them all in detail.
The first, a tall man in cap and gown, led the recitation:
"Qí trousers, Lǔ plain silk, white as frost and snow,
My clear, loud, lofty voice is what I show."
The second, a short, ugly man in black cap and gown, recited:
"A fine gathering of guests on a clear night, this hour,
The brilliantly shining lamps and candles—I hold the power."
The third, wearing old, worn yellow cap and gown, was also short and ugly;
his poem said:
"The clear, cold spring awaits the morning draw,
Pulled by mulberry-bark rope, in and out I saw."
The fourth, in old black cap and gown, recited:
"Firewood stored, water fetched, to boil and stew,
To fill others' mouths and bellies—this is the labor I do."
Wúyǒu did not find the four strange,
nor did the four suspect Wúyǒu's presence in the hall.
They praised and admired each other in turn,
admiring,
their own self-importance.
Indeed, even Ruǎn Jìzōng's "Chanting My Feelings"
seemed unable to surpass them.
At dawn, the four finally returned to their former places.
Wúyǒu went to search for them,
and in the hall found only an old pestle, a lamp stand, a water bucket, and a broken cooking pot.
Then he realized the four
were precisely these objects manifested.
Lǐ Chǔbīn
There was a man named Lǐ Chǔbīn,
a native of Chǔ.
His nature was firm and proud,
and he devoted himself solely to hunting.
Whenever he went hunting,
he never failed to make a great catch.
At that time, Tóng Yuánfàn's family lived at Qīngshān.
His mother had contracted an illness:
during the day she was usually fine,
but at night it would flare up.
This went on for a year.
All possible medicines and treatments were tried,
yet there was absolutely no cure or alleviation.
Around the beginning of the Jiànzhōng era,
a man skilled in the *Yìjīng*, Zhū Hán, was returning to Yùzhāng.
Passing by Yuánfàn's house,
Hán performed a divination for him.
He then said to Yuánfàn:
