"Today, during the Wèi hour,
prepare a set of robes,
and wait by the roadside.
There will be a man passing by carrying a bow and arrows.
If you can seek help from this man,
he will surely cure your mother's illness,
and also get to the root of it."
Yuánfàn did as told,
and indeed encountered Chǔbīn,
who came galloping with bow drawn.
Yuánfàn bowed and invited him to his house.
Chǔbīn said:
"I've caught nothing this morning.
Why do you detain me?"
Yuánfàn told him of his mother's illness,
and Chǔbīn agreed to help.
Yuánfàn prepared food and drink,
and had Chǔbīn stay in the western wing.
That night,
the moon was bright as day.
Chǔbīn then went outside
and saw a large bird in the air
flying to the roof of Yuánfàn's house.
It stretched its beak and pecked at the roof,
whereupon cries were heard from inside the house,
of pain unbearable.
Chǔbīn reasoned:
"This must be the demon."
He then drew his bow and shot at it,
firing two arrows that both hit.
The bird then flew away,
and the sounds of anguish from the house also ceased.
At dawn,
Chǔbīn said to Yuánfàn:
"Last night I already rid your mother of the harm for you."
He then searched all around the house with Yuánfàn,
but found nothing.
Upon reaching a dilapidated shed,
at the old site of a mortar pedestal,
there were two arrows,
and where the arrows had struck,
both showed a bloody gleam.
Yuánfàn then burned the spot with fire,
and the spirit creature was finally eradicated.
His mother's ailment was henceforth cured.
The Guózǐjiàn Student
During the Yuánhé era,
there was a Guózǐjiàn student named Zhōu Yǐ.
Once, while studying at night,
he suddenly saw a small child
with disheveled hair,
over two chǐ tall,
its entire neck covered in scattered points of light like stars,
glimmering and repulsive.
It played with the brushes and inkstones,
causing endless disorder.
The student was naturally brave,
shouted at it, and it retreated slightly.
It then approached the desk again,
so he watched to see what it would do.
As it gradually drew nearer,
Yǐ seized it.
It crouched, begging and pleading,
its words quite pitiful and urgent.
As dawn approached,
he heard a sound like something snapping.
Looking at it,
it was an old wooden dipper,
with over a hundred grains of millet stuck to it.
Yáo Sīmǎ
Sīmǎ Yáo resided in Bīnzhōu,
his house overlooking a stream.
He had two young daughters,
who often played at fishing in the stream,
but never caught anything.
Suddenly, as they lifted their fishing rods,
each caught something:
one like a sturgeon but with fur,
the other like a turtle but with gills.
Their family found this strange
and kept them in a basin pond.
After a night,
both girls became mentally disturbed.
At night, they would often light lamps
and play games facing each other.
They would dye things blue and black,
never resting for a moment,
yet no one saw where they got the materials.
At that time, Yáng Yuánqīng was in Bīnzhōu,
and he was an old acquaintance of Yáo.
Yáo was serving as an official in Bīnzhōu.
Another half year passed,
and the girls’ illness grew worse.
Once, their family was playing a coin-tossing game by lamplight,
when suddenly two small hands appeared beneath the lamplight.
A loud voice said,
“Give us a coin.”
Someone in the family spat at it.
It said again:
“I am your family’s son-in-law,
how dare you be so rude?”
One called himself Wū Láng,
the other Huáng Láng.
Afterward, they often became intimate with the family members.
Yáng Yuánqīng learned of this,
and thus sought out the monk Zhān from the capital.
Zhān was skilled in dealing with ghosts and spirits,
through incantations and meditation,
and had achieved much success in curing illnesses caused by demons.
When Zhān arrived at the Yáo household,
he marked boundaries with ropes and lanterns,
stamped his hand with a seal, and brandished a sword,
summoning the creatures.
Later, he placed offerings of blood and wine outside the boundary.
At midnight,
a creature like an ox
sniffed at the wine.
Zhān then hid his sword,
tiptoed forward, and shouted loudly,
stabbing it with all his might.
The creature walked away with the blade stuck in it,
blood flowing like a fountain.
Zhān led his attendants,
holding torches to search for it,
following the trail of blood.
They reached a corner at the back of the house,
where they saw something like a black leather bag,
as large as a basket,
panting like a bellows.
This was Wū Láng.
They then chopped it up with firewood and burned it to death,
the stench spreading over ten miles.
One of the girls immediately recovered.
From then on, on windy and rainy nights,
chirping sounds could be heard in the courtyard.
The second girl was still ill.
Zhān stood before her,
raising a ritual object and scolding the demon.
The girl, terrified, kowtowed.
Zhān happened to notice a black pouch on her belt,
so he ordered a maidservant to untie it and look inside.
It was a small key.
They then searched her clothes and playthings,
and using the key, opened a basket.
Inside the basket were all mourning clothes used for funeral tents,
the colors only yellow and black.
Zhān’s temporary assignment was about to end,
and he could not completely eliminate the demon,
so he returned to the capital.
Over a year later,
Yáo left his post and went to the capital,
He first visited Zhān,
asking him to exert more effort to cure her.
After about ten days,
a swelling like a blister appeared on the girl’s arm,
as large as a melon.
Zhān forbade acupuncture,
but blood flowed out in several measures,
and she eventually recovered.
Cuī Jué
During the Yuánhé era,
there was a man named Cuī Jué from Bólíng,
who came from Rǔzhèng
and lived temporarily in Yánfúlǐ in Cháng’ān.
One day,
while reading by the window,
he suddenly saw a boy,
He was less than a foot tall,
with disheveled hair and wearing yellow clothes.
He came from under the northern wall,
hurried to the couch,
and said to Jué:
“I wish to lodge by your inkstone and mat.
May I?”
Jué did not respond.
He said again:
“I am still strong,
and wish to serve you.
Why do you reject me so firmly?”
Jué again ignored him.
Soon, the boy climbed onto the couch.
He leaped up and stood respectfully.
After a long while,
he took out a small piece of writing from his sleeve
and presented it to Jué.
It was a poem.
The characters were as fine as millet grains,
yet clearly legible.
The poem said:
“Once favored by Méng Tián’s grace,
soon cast aside by Zhòng Shū.
If my lord will not employ me,
where shall I seek the silver hook?”
After reading it,
Jué smiled and said:
“Since you wish to follow me,
will you not regret it later?”
The boy produced another poem,
placing it on the table.
The poem said:
“Learning I shall gain from you,
poetry and books I shall pass on myself.
Know that Wáng Yìshǎo
earned fame and worth for a thousand years.”
Jué said again:
“I lack Yìshǎo’s talent,
so even if I have you,
what use are you to me?”
Soon, the boy tossed another piece, which said:
“I can make messages travel a thousand miles,
and convey dragons and snakes across eight lines.
Sadly, Jiāng Shēng did not appreciate me,
perhaps because he prided himself on his fine writing.”
Jué joked:
“It’s a pity you are not of five colors.”
The boy laughed and climbed down from the couch,
then hurried to the northern wall,
entering a hole.
Jué immediately ordered a servant to dig beneath it,
and they found a writing brush.
Jué then took it and tried writing with it.
Its tip was sharp as if new,
and he used it for over a month.
Nothing strange happened.
Zhāng Xiùcai
In the Táohuà Ward of the Eastern Capital,
there was an empty house.
During the Dàhé era,
a scholar named Zhāng borrowed it to pursue his studies,
but he often felt uneasy and restless.
Reflecting that as a man,
he ought to uphold a heroic and lofty spirit,
and should not allow cowardice to weaken him,
he therefore moved into the central hall to reside.
Late at night, as he reclined on his pillow,
he saw fifteen Taoist priests and fifteen Buddhist monks,
emerge from the hall.
Their appearances and statures were all alike,
arranged in six rows.
Their dignified demeanor and graceful bearing
were each and every one worthy of respect.
The scholar thought they were a gathering of divine immortals,
and dared not even breathe heavily,
so he pretended to sleep in order to observe them.
After a long while,
two other creatures appeared,
tumbling about on the ground.
Each creature had twenty-one eyes,
of which four inner eyes
gleamed sharply like fire.
They chased each other,
their gazes whirling and dazzling,
making a *huā* sound.
In a moment,
the thirty monks and priests
were either running or walking,
some going east, some west,
some south, some north.
Whenever a single Taoist priest
stood alone in one place,
he would be struck by a monk and driven away.
The two creatures circulated among the monks and priests,
never resting for even a moment.
In this manner, they vied and wrestled with each other,
sometimes separating, sometimes gathering.
Suddenly, one of them cried out:
"Utterly peerless!"
As soon as the words were spoken,
the monks and priests all fell silent and ceased.
Then the two creatures said to each other:
"Just now, the group of monks and Taoist practitioners
displayed supremely wondrous methods,
yet they all relied on us two creatures
to accomplish the propagation of their teachings.
Otherwise,
how could they be called peerless?"
The scholar then knew they must be monsters,
and so he threw his pillow at them.
The thirty monks and priests along with the two creatures
all fled in alarm at once,
saying:
"If we don't leave quickly,
we'll be at the mercy of this poor scholar."
And so they all vanished.
The next day,
he searched around
and found in a corner of the wall a worn-out bag,
inside of which were thirty *chángxíng* game pieces
and a pair of dice.
A Street Officer in Hédōng
During the Kāichéng era,
in Hédōng Commandery, there was an officer
who often patrolled the streets in the middle of the night.
One evening, the sky was clear and the moon bright,
and he came to the front of Jǐngfú Temple.
He saw a person crouching and sitting,
with arms crossed and knees hugged,
his body entirely black,
motionless as if rooted there.
The officer, frightened,
shouted at him.
The person remained crouched and paid no heed.
After shouting for a long time,
the officer struck him on the head.
Suddenly, the person raised his head to look,
and his face and appearance were extremely strange.
Several feet long,
pale and emaciated,
his appearance was most terrifying.
The officer, initially startled, fell to the ground.
After a long while,
he gradually managed to get up.
When he looked,
the figure had already vanished without a trace.
From then on, the officer became even more terrified,
and immediately galloped back,
telling everyone the whole story.
Later, when the gate of Jǐngfú Temple was being rebuilt,
they excavated the ground
and found a lacquered bucket,
several feet deep in total,
with white mud covering its top.
It was indeed what the street officer had seen.
The Brother of Vice-Director Wéi
Vice-Director Wéi of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices
had an elder brother who was very fierce,
claiming that in his whole life he had never known fear.
Whenever he heard of a haunted house,
he would certainly go and stay there alone.
His younger brother spoke of this to his colleagues,
and among them were those who wanted to test him.
They had heard that in the northeast corner of Yánkāng there was the mansion of Mǎ Zhènxī,
which was often plagued by many strange creatures,
so they escorted him to that house.
They provided him with wine and meat,
and when night fell, they all left,
leaving him alone to stay in a solitary pavilion west of a large pond.
Wéi, having drunk and feeling warm,
took off his clothes and went to sleep.
Around midnight, he awoke
and saw a small creature,
about a foot tall,
with a short body and long legs,
its color rather dark,
emerging from the pond.
It drifted slowly forward,
ascended the steps,
and came right before him.
Wéi did not stir.
The creature then said:
"The one lying there is a vile thing;
does he dare to look at me again?"
It then began to circle the bed.
After a short while,
Wéi turned his pillow and lay on his back,
and felt the creature climb onto the bed.
Wéi still did not move.
Presently,
he felt two small feet
climbing onto his own feet,
cold as ice and iron,
the chill piercing straight to his heart.
Its steps were very slow.
Wéi remained motionless,
waiting until it gradually climbed up
and reached his belly.
Then Wéi suddenly reached out and grabbed it—
it was an ancient iron tripod,
already missing one leg.
He then tied it to the bedpost with his belt.
The next morning,
when everyone came to look,
he told them the whole story.
They then smashed the tripod with a pestle,
and it oozed a blood-like color.
From then on, everyone believed in Wéi's fierceness
and his ability to rid a house of its monsters.
Shí Cóngwǔ
During the Kāichéng era,
in Guìlín, there was an assistant general named Shí Cóngwǔ,
who from a young age was skilled in archery.
His family was afflicted by a severe illness,
and few among the old and young remained unharmed.
Every late night,
they would see a figure come from outside,
its body glowing brightly.
Whenever this creature arrived,
the sick would cry out and moan even more intensely,
and no doctor could cure them.
One evening, Cóngwǔ
took his bow and waited by the door,
anticipating its arrival.
Soon the spectral creature came again,
and Cóngwǔ shot at it.
With a single shot he hit it,
and its glowing sparks scattered like stars.
He ordered a candle to be lit to look,
and it turned out to be an old camphorwood lamp stand from the house,
which had toppled over.
He then split it and burned it,
throwing the ashes into the river.
After that, all the afflicted recovered.
Jiāng Xiū
Jiāng Xiū was a tavern keeper
in Bīngzhōu.
His nature was unrestrained and undisciplined,
and he was addicted to wine,
seldom being sober.
He often enjoyed drinking with others.
The people of Bīngzhōu all feared his excessive drinking,
and whenever they were invited,
they mostly avoided him,
so Xiū rarely had friends.
Suddenly, a guest appeared.
Dressed in black clothes and a black hat,
he was only three chǐ tall,
with a waist several arm-spans thick.
He approached Xiū seeking wine.
Xiū was delighted to drink with him
and thus drew his mat close to share drinks.
The guest smiled and said:
"In my life, I have loved wine,
yet I have always regretted that the wine in my belly is not constantly full.
If my belly is full,
then I am both content and joyful.
If it is not full,
I feel utterly meaningless.
Could you allow me to linger here for a long time?
I have long admired your noble virtue,
and I am fortunate that you, sir, have the means to accommodate me."
Xiū said:
"If you can share my passion,
you are truly one of my kind,
and there should be no distance between us."
So they sat together on the ground and drank.
The guest drank nearly three dàn of wine,
yet remained sober.
Xiū was greatly astonished by this
and, moreover, suspected he was an extraordinary being.
He rose and bowed to him,
asking about his hometown and surname,
and further inquired about what method allowed him to drink so much.
The guest said:
"My surname is Chéng,
and my given name is Déqì.
My ancestors mostly dwelled in the countryside,
and by chance, the Creator bestowed grace upon me,
allowing me to serve a purpose in this era.
Now that I am old,
I have also attained the Way,
enabling me to drink wine.
If my belly is full,
it can hold five dàn.
When full, I am somewhat at peace."
Upon hearing this,
Xiū ordered more wine for him to drink.
Soon, he reached five dàn,
and the guest finally became thoroughly drunk,
singing and dancing wildly.
He sighed to himself:
"How joyful! How joyful!"
Then he collapsed to the ground.
Xiū, thinking him extremely drunk,
ordered his servant to help him into a room.
Upon reaching the room, the guest suddenly leaped up,
startled, and ran out.
The family members then chased after him,
and saw the guest accidentally bump into a stone,
producing a clanging sound,
and soon he was nowhere to be seen.
By dawn, they saw
that it was an aged wine jar,
already broken.
The Woodcutter of Wángwū
On Wángwū Mountain, there was an old monk
who often lived alone in a thatched hut,
reciting prayers morning and night.
He only gathered medicinal herbs and pine nuts to eat.
After each meal,
he would always seek out a stream or ravine to bathe.
After several years in the mountain,
people gradually came to know of him.
Suddenly, one day,
a Daoist priest in tattered clothes
persistently begged the old monk for a night's lodging.
The old monk was of a reclusive nature,
and moreover, he detested the priest's worldly impurities,
so he refused.
The Daoist priest repeatedly said:
"Buddhism and Daoism are not estranged;
since the time of primordial chaos,
we have only come to know of Buddhism.
You, Master, are now a disciple of Buddha,
and I am now a disciple of Dao;
why can you not accommodate me for one night,
to accompany you in pure discourse?"
The old monk said:
"I am a disciple of Buddha,
and thus I do not know that Dao can compare to Buddha."
The Daoist priest said:
"Dao
existed billions of kalpas ago,
and it gave birth to Heaven, humans, and all things,
creating Heaven and Earth,
humans,
and all things;
this is my Dao.
Billions of kalpas ago,
all people knew and revered it,
yet you, Master, now do not know it;
this means you are not human."
The old monk said:
"My Buddha, through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
has alone been called the World-Honored One.
He greatly shelters all living beings,
with grace pervading Heaven and Earth.
How could one ever hear that Dao can contend with him?
Moreover, I recount that Śākyamuni Buddha, the World-Honored One,
was the son of a king.
At the beginning,
he renounced his royal throne,
entered the snowy mountains,
relying on merits accumulated over past kalpas,
attained the fruit of enlightenment in the present.
In Heaven and on Earth,
only I am honored.
Thus, all heretics and evil demons
were subdued.
Up to this day,
who has not heard of this?
As for your Lǎojūn,
whose son was he?
Where did he cultivate?
In the traces of his teachings,
no benefits have been heard of;
how can he be spoken of in the same breath as my Buddha?"
The Daoist priest said:
"Lǎojūn descended and was born from Heaven,
becoming the ancestral patriarch of Dao in this kalpa,
first appearing during the Zhōu dynasty.
Amidst floating purple clouds,
riding a white deer,
who has not heard of him?
As for the affairs of the Three Isles,
the scenery of the Ten Continents,
the immortals of the Thirty-Six Grotto-Heavens,
the numinous wonders of the Twenty-Four Transformations,
even a child of five chǐ
can know of them.
How dare you alone, with your mediocre views, despise them?
As for your Buddha,
abandoning his father and leaving the city,
suffering the pain of pierced knees,
and contending with heretics for victory,
how is that worthy of mention?
By this reasoning,
Buddha is merely a strongman among the hordes of demons."
Our Heaven, Earth, humans, and all things
originally did not rely on your Buddha to come into being.
Now, without Buddha,
Heaven, Earth, humans, and all things would certainly not be diminished.
Do not, by any means, call yourself the World-Honored One;
if you call yourself the World-Honored One,
the world will certainly not honor you;
do not proclaim yourself honored."
The old monk, with a changed countenance, said:
"Such people are necessary.
If there were none such,
then the Avīci Hell would instantly be emptied."
The Daoist priest flew into a rage,
stretched out his arm and advanced,
intending to strike the old monk.
The monk merely clasped his hands and closed his eyes.
In a moment,
a woodcutter carrying firewood passed by,
saw them, and found it strange.
Learning that the old monk and the Daoist priest were arguing over the superiority of Buddhism and Daoism,
the woodcutter rolled up his sleeves and shouted:
"Both of you were born of parents yet do not support them;
you dwell in the land of the emperor yet do not serve as subjects;
you do not plow yet eat,
you do not raise silkworms yet wear clothes;
not only do you steal a living among humans,
but you further argue over the superiority of other Buddhas and Daos?
Do not reside in my mountain,
disturbing the people who dwell in my mountain."
Then he promptly burned down their thatched hut,
brandished his woodcutting axe,
and intended to kill them both.
The old monk, startled, burrowed into the ground
and transformed into an iron chime.
The Daoist priest also soon transformed into a turtle's shell bone,
revealing that they were both merely spirits and monsters.
Dúgū Yàn
Towards the end of the Jiànzhōng era,
there was a man named Dúgū Yàn,
who once traveled as a guest between the Huái and Sì rivers.
It happened that a great wind arose,
so his boat could not proceed,
and he moored by the shore.
One evening, walking in the moonlight, he went ashore,
He arrived at a Buddhist temple.
All the temple monks had gone to a village gathering,
so Yàn strolled around the courtyard.
Soon, two gentlemen arrived.
One was very tall,
dressed in black robes,
and claimed his surname was Jiǎ,
his given name Qīnjié,
and his generation name Dìwǔ.
The other was broad and short,
dressed in blue robes,
and claimed his surname was Zēng,
his given name Yuán.
They bowed to Yàn and spoke with him;
their discourse was profound and subtle,
transcending ordinary human understanding.
Yàn had always been fond of the strange and profound,
and for years
he had often conversed with recluses and men beyond the mundane world.
As for the doctrines of Daoism and Buddhism,
there was none whose essential principles he had not thoroughly explored.
Yet upon meeting these two men,
he felt he could not surpass them,
secretly marveling at them,
and even considered taking them as his teachers.
Therefore, bowing twice, he requested:
"I am one who loves the extraordinary;
today I am fortunate to meet you, gentlemen.
I wish to become your disciple.
Would that be possible?"
The two men declined, saying:
"How dare we?"
Yàn then inquired about their origins.
The man in black said:
"My ancestors
were originally of the Lú clan.
In my youth, I was known for my firmness and strength.
Generally, when things are obstructed and impassable,
one must encroach upon and expose them to bring understanding.
People of the time all called me 'Qīnjié' (Encroach and Expose),
hence the name.
Later, going into the wilderness,
I encountered enemies who struck and broke me,
so I changed my surname to Jiǎ,
and fled from that calamity.
Moreover, I was always skilled in the art of medicine,
and once served in the humble position of a physician.
It was not that I could not be proficient,
but the rising and falling, the going up and down,
I had to rely on the hands of others.
Later, due to old age and declining strength,
the superiors,
wanted to make me a low-ranking clerk who bows constantly,
but I firmly declined and was excused,
retiring to live in the countryside.
I have a maternal uncle,
who was often my colleague.
Our actions, rest, daily life,
were never apart.
However, since I cast myself aside,
I have often thought of my uncle.
Simply because our circumstances of employment and dismissal differed,
we became separated and do not see each other.
Tonight, sir, you ask me,
and I am able to speak of the events of my life.
How exceedingly fortunate!"
When he finished speaking,
Zēng Yuán said:
"My ancestors
are descendants of the Táotáng clan.
Only those among the officials of Táotáng
who received the surname from Yáo Zēng,
and whose descendants took the courtesy name as their clan name,
thus became the Zēng clan—
I am one of their descendants.
I early on followed Lord Lái,
holding a position in the office of weights and measures,
a post that was crucial and intense.
By nature narrow-minded and irritable,
and also prone to being arrogant and overbearing towards superiors,
I thus suffered slander from subordinates spreading like boiling water,
and consequently was dismissed.
It was due to my loyalty and fervor,
that I was accused.
Since I cast myself aside,
dwelling among the dust and dirt,
many years have passed.
I am content to be like tiles and rubble.
How dare I have other aspirations?
However, in the past, I and my father encountered affairs together.
My father's nature was firm and upright;
even facing cauldrons and boiling oil, he would not avoid the danger.
To relieve people's emergencies,
he would rush into boiling water and tread on fire;
people also respected him for this.
Now, constrained by his former duties,
he is as distressed as if imprisoned.
Because my father cast me aside,
I do not go near him;
it has been several years until now.
Since you, sir, ask,
how could I dare remain silent?"
Before he finished speaking,
the temple monks all returned.
Seeing them,
the two men seemed afraid,
and immediately dashed away;
after a few dozen steps, they had vanished from sight.
Yàn questioned the monks,
and a monk said:
"I have lived in this temple for a long time,
and have never seen such beings.
I fear they were monsters."
Yàn marveled at their talent,
and found it strange,
so he pondered their names.
After a long while, he realized:
"The one called Zēng Yuán—
could he not be a 'zèng' (甑, earthenware steamer)?
Now, in writing,
attaching 'wǎ' (瓦, tile) to 'Zēng' (曾)
forms the character 'zèng' (甑).
His given name Yuán (元)—
it is probably because the strokes within the 'wǎ' (瓦)
are brought to the top of the character 'wǎ',
thus its meaning lies there.
As for Jiǎ Qīnjié—
could he not be an iron pestle?
Moreover, 'wǔ mù' (午木) forms the character 'chǔ' (杵, pestle).
The surname Jiǎ—
in the east, Jiǎ and Yǐ correspond to wood.
The generation name Dìwǔ (第五)—
also borrows the character 'wǔ' (午).
Reasoning from this and analyzing,
isn't it the character 'chǔ' (杵)?
The given name Qīnjié (侵訐)—
probably reverses its words to form 'quán jié' (全截).
Attaching 'jié' (截) to 'quán' (全)
forms the character 'tiě' (鐵, iron).
Putting it all together and analyzing,
could they not be a steamer and an iron pestle!"
The next day,
he ordered a search for their traces.
Indeed, among some decayed ruins,
they found an iron pestle.
Also, a steamer split in half,
apparently a leftover from use.
Yàn was greatly astonished;
it all matched his interpretation.
Yáo Kāngchéng
Tàiyuán's administrative secretary Yáo Kāngchéng
was sent on a mission to Qiānlǒng.
It happened that the festival commissioner was handing over his duties,
and envoys from the eight foreign tribes were returning,
causing the postal lodges to be overcrowded.
So he borrowed the old residence of Xíng Jūnyá,
set up a central room,
to use as a place for rest.
The residence had long been empty and abandoned,
with trees growing densely in the courtyard.
Kāngchéng was occupied by official banquets during the day,
returned drunk at night,
and went out again at dawn,
never having rested there even briefly.
One night,
he returned early from the military town,
and as his subordinates had a gambling gathering,
he managed to stay sober.
Sitting in the hall,
he ordered tea,
and again summoned guests,
but no guests arrived.
So he ordered the lodge attendant to fetch wine,
and gave it to all the servants,
to reward them for their diligence on the road.
Soon they were all drunk,
and Kāngchéng went to bed.
After the second watch,
the moonlight was like white silk,
so he put on his clothes and got up,
went out the residence gate,
walked alone for a while,
and then returned to the courtyard.
From afar, he saw a person
enter a corridor room,
and soon heard the sounds of several people drinking and enjoying themselves.
Kāngchéng then crept closer in his shoes to listen,
and hearing their speech, chanting, and whistling,
realized they were not servants.
So he sat by the door,
and watched them stealthily.
Then he heard them say:
"Gentlemen, you know that people nowadays in their compositions
all strive for momentary cleverness and beauty.
As for entrusting emotions and metaphorizing oneself,
embodying objects and expressing feelings,
they have all lost it."
Another said:
"Now the three of us can each compose a poem,
to amuse ourselves."
They all said good.
Then he saw one person,
tall and slender and very dark,
chant:
"In the past, people blazed with heat, only knowing themselves,
Now without beacon fires and stoves, what is there to do?
Pitiful, the handle of the state is utterly useless,
I have seen everyone failing the examinations."
Then he saw another person,
also tall and slender and yellow,
with many pockmarks on his face,
chant:
"Back then, filled with pride and spirit,
One song before the lord was worth ten thousand gold.
Today, not even equal to the bamboo in the courtyard,
When the wind comes, it can still learn the dragon's roar."
Another person was short and fat,
with disheveled hair hanging loose,
and chanted:
"Scalded head and bald temples, only the heart remains,
Strength exhausted in the dust, no more to discuss.
Don't laugh that now I'm like rotten grass,
Once I swept vermilion gates all day long."
Kāngchéng couldn't help but cry out,
greatly praising their beauty.
So he pushed the door to seek them,
but they had all vanished.
At dawn,
he summoned the local clerk to inquire,
who said:
"Recently there have been no such people."
Kāngchéng suspected they must be spirits or goblins,
and searched the place.
Then he saw an iron ladle,
a broken flute,
and a bald broom made of broomcorn millet stalks.
Kāngchéng did not wish to harm them,
so he buried each in a different place.
Mǎ Jǔ
When Mǎ Jǔ was governing Huáinán,
someone brought a chessboard to present to him,
all adorned with pearls and jade.
Jǔ gave him ten million coins and accepted it.
After a few days,
it suddenly disappeared.
Jǔ ordered a search,
but it was not found.
Then suddenly an old man,
leaning on a staff, came to the gate,
requesting to see Jǔ.
He spoke much of military strategy,
and Jǔ sat at a distance to question him.
The old man said:
"Now is precisely the time for using military force,
why do you not seek the principles of warfare and tactics,
to command and resist enemies?
If not so,
then what is the point of governing a garrison?"
Jǔ said:
"I am merely governing weary people,
with no leisure for military principles and tactics.
Fortunately, you have honored me with your visit,
what do you have to teach me?"
The old man said:
"Military strategy cannot be neglected,
neglect leads to chaos,
chaos leads to people's weariness,
and good governance is then unheard of.
Why not first use methods to manage the military,
when the military is well-managed, then officers become skilled,
when officers are skilled, then soldiers become brave.
As for officers,
they must recognize emptiness and fullness,
understand advance and retreat,
brave arrows and stones,
and face blades and spears.
As for soldiers,
they must be ready to go through fire and water,
risk life and death,
without turning back, united as one.
Now that you are a regional commander of multiple territories,
you ought to have the talent of a commander,
and cannot neglect your duty."
Jǔ said:
"May I ask what the affairs of a commander are like?"
The old man said:
"To be a commander,
one must first secure advantageous terrain,
then face the enemy army.
Using a single soldier,
one must consider life and death.
Seeing a single path,
one must examine its entry and exit.
As for charging passes and launching raids,
though they are secondary matters in the army,
they also must not be forgotten.
There is also preserving the small while sacrificing the large,
urgent killing and frequent retreats.
Seize their perilous ground,
deploy your deceptive troops.
The skill lies in swift attack,
and one must not hesitate.
If speed is undecided,
peril and ease are far apart,
advance is impossible,
then you must seek survival.
Repeated victories lead to defeat,
beware of underestimating the enemy.
If you deeply comprehend these techniques,
then the way of command is complete."
Jǔ was astonished,
and said to the old man:
"Where are you from, sir?
How is your learning so profound?"
The old man said:
"I am a stubborn man from Nánshān.
Since childhood, I have loved the strange and admired the unusual,
many people thought I had the reputation of containing hidden jade and pearls.
Having experienced many wars,
I thus fully understand military matters.
But within heaven and earth,
all things decline.
Moreover, artificial
combined forms,
are particularly not sturdy,
how can they last long?
I merely take this chance to converse,
to relate the essentials of military strategy,
I hope you, wise lord, will pay some attention."
Then he quickly took his leave,
but Jǔ firmly detained him,
and hosted him in the guest lodge.
At night,
he ordered attendants to summon him,
but in the room there was only a chessboard,
which was the one that had been lost.
Jǔ knew it was a spirit,
so he ordered attendants to shine an ancient mirror on it,
the chessboard suddenly leaped up,
fell to the ground and shattered,
as if unable to transform.
Jǔ was greatly astonished,
and ordered it to be completely burned.
The Fisherman of Jízhōu
At the Lóngxīng Temple in Jízhōu, there was a giant bell.
On it was inscribed:
"Cast in the Yuánkāng era of the Jìn Dynasty."
At the top of the bell was a hole.
According to ancient tradition,
during the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
the bell's tolling shook Cháng'ān.
An imperial edict was issued to chisel it,
and that hole is the result.
During the Tiānyòu era,
one night the bell suddenly disappeared,
but by dawn it had returned to its original place.
Bloodstains and xūn grass were seen on the púláo (bell ornament).
Xūn grass
is an aquatic plant south of the Yangtze River,
with leaves like Chinese chives,
growing according to the water's depth.
In front of the temple was a great river.
For several nights,
the residents heard the sound of wind and waves on the river.
At dawn,
a fisherman
saw a red flag in the middle of the river,
floating downstream on the water.
The fisherman rowed a small boat to retrieve it,
but then saw golden scales gleaming,
and the waves surged violently.
The fisherman hurried back.
Only then did he realize that the púláo had fought and injured the river dragon.
Lady Liáng
In the Fùcái Ward of Luòyáng during the Later Wèi Dynasty,
there was the Kāishàn Temple,
originally the residence of Wéi Yīng from Jīngzhào.
Yīng died early,
and his wife, Liáng,
did not observe mourning but remarried,
taking Xiàng Zǐjí from Hénèi as her new husband.
Although she had remarried,
she still lived in Yīng's house.
When Yīng heard that Liáng had remarried,
he returned by daylight.
Mounted on a horse,
accompanied by several men,
he arrived in the courtyard
and called out:
"Ā Liáng,
have you forgotten me?"
Zǐjí was terrified,
drew his bow and shot at him.
Yīng fell as the arrow struck,
immediately transforming into a peach-wood figure.
The horse he rode
also turned into a straw horse.
The several attendants
all became cattail figures.
Lady Liáng, frightened and alarmed,
donated the residence to become a temple.
Cáo Huì
In the early years of the Wǔdé era,
there was a man named Cáo Huì who served as a military advisor in Jiāngzhōu.
In the official residence was a Buddhist hall,
and in the hall were two wooden puppets,
over a foot tall,
exquisitely carved and decorated,
though their paint had peeled.
Huì took them home for his young child.
Later, while the child was eating a cake,
the puppets reached out their hands asking for it.
The child, startled, reported this to Huì.
Huì laughed and said:
"Bring the puppets here."
They immediately spoke:
"Qīngsù has her own name;
why call me 'puppet'?"
Then they turned their gaze and scurried about,
no different from humans.
Huì asked:
"From what era are you,
that you can cause such marvels?"
Qīngsù and Qīnghóng said:
"We are tomb figurines from Prefect Xiè's household of Xuānchéng.
At that time, no craftsman in the world
could match Xiào Zhōng, the old servant of Lord Shěn Yǐn.
Qīngsù and Qīnghóng
were made by Xiào Zhōng.
Lord Yǐn grieved that Prefect Xiè had died untimely,
so he gave us as burial gifts on the day of the funeral.
At that time in the tomb,
I was just bringing hot water for Lady Lè to wash her feet,
when I heard outside the sound of weapons and someone proclaiming an imperial edict.
Lady Lè, terrified,
fled barefoot and turned into a white mole cricket.
Moments later,
two bandits holding torches arrived,
plundering all the valuables.
Master Xiè was holding a shūsè jade ring,
which the bandits knocked from his jaw to take it.
The bandits shone their light on us and said:
'These two mingqì are not bad;
we can give them to the children as toys.'
So they took us out.
That was in the second year of Tiānpíng.
Since then, we have passed through several households.
At the end of the Chén Dynasty,
Mài Tiězhàng's nephew brought us here."
Huì asked further:
"I have heard that Prefect Xiè of Xuānchéng
married the daughter of Wáng Jìngzé.
Why then do you speak of Lady Lè?"
Qīngsù said:
"Lady Wáng was his wife in life;
Lady Lè is a posthumous marriage.
Lady Wáng came from a butcher and wine-seller lineage,
crude and strong by nature.
Even in the underworld,
she remained at odds with Prefect Xiè.
When she saw Prefect Xiè's stern face,
she would smash stones and bar the door,
using threats.
Prefect Xiè secretly petitioned the Celestial Emperor,
who permitted him to expel her.
Their two daughters and one son
all followed their mother away.
So he remarried, taking the eighth daughter of Lè Yǎnfǔ,
who is beautiful and graceful,
skilled in calligraphy,
fond of playing the qin,
and gets along especially well with the wives of Yīn Zhòngwén of Dōngyáng and Xiè Huì of Jīngzhōu.
They daily indulge in leisurely pursuits.
Prefect Xiè often says:
'My literary talent matches that of ancient poets,
only falling short of Cáo Zhí of Dōng'ē.
As for other men of letters,
they are all meat on my chopping block,
to be carved up at will.'
He now serves as the Southern Bureau Official in charge of appointments,
ranked alongside Pan, the Imperial Chamberlain.
He rides fat horses and wears light silks,
a hundred times more honored than in life.
However, having to attend court once every ten months in the Jìn, Sòng, Qí, and Liáng dynasties
can be quite taxing.
I recently heard that this duty has also been suspended."
Huì asked again:
"Since you two are so spiritually remarkable,
what if I were to release you?"
They immediately replied:
"With our ability to transform,
though nothing is truly impossible,
if you, sir, are unwilling to let us go,
we ultimately cannot escape.
The mountain god of Lúshān
has long desired to take Qīngsù as a dancing girl.
Now, taking our leave from you,
we shall go enjoy that honor and wealth.
However, if you, sir, can show final kindness,
we ask you to command a painter
to bestow upon us powder and paint."
Huì immediately ordered a craftsman to paint them,
adorning them with brocade and embroidery.
Qīngsù laughed and said:
"This time, I will not merely be a dancing girl;
I shall become his lady.
Having nothing with which to repay you,
I offer a few cryptic words as farewell.
Within a hundred generations,
but with
others who understand them,
none will fail to become loyal ministers
occupying high positions.
Chicken
horn enters the bone,
purple crane eats the yellow rat.
Shēn Bùhài.
Five passages, spring chamber.
Brings six generations of auspicious prosperity."
Later, someone prayed to the Lúshān mountain god.
A shamaness said the deity had recently taken two concubines
and desired emerald hairpins and floral hair ornaments.
"You should seek them out;
then great fortune will be bestowed."
The supplicant sought and burned such items,
and his wish was fulfilled.
Huì could not understand the cryptic words either.
He inquired among the wise men of his time,
but none grasped their meaning.
Some say
that the Secretariat Director Cén Wénběn understood three of the sentences,
but he never explained them to anyone.
Dòu Bùyí
Sūn Dòu Bùyí, a descendant of a meritorious official of the Wǔdé era,
served as a Lieutenant General,
and retired in old age to return home.
His home was in Tàiyuán,
residing in Yángqū County in the northern suburbs.
Bùyí was a brave man,
possessing courage and strength,
and from a young age he was chivalrous.
He often gathered a company of over ten companions,
engaging in cockfighting and dog racing,
gambling at dice with stakes of tens of thousands,
all bound by shared spirit and ambition.
Northeast of Tàiyuán city, several li away,
there was often a road ghost,
two zhang tall.
Whenever it was dark after overcast rain,
it would often appear.
People who saw it
sometimes died of fright.
The young men said:
"Whoever can go and shoot the road ghost
will be given five thousand coins."
The others remained silent,
only Bùyí volunteered to go.
He waited until dusk to set out.
The crowd said:
"This man might leave the city and then hide,
deceiving us at night about shooting it;
can he be trusted?
Why not secretly follow him?"
When Bùyí reached the place of the specter,
the ghost was just coming out.
Bùyí pursued and shot at it,
the ghost, struck by an arrow, fled.
Bùyí chased it,
hitting it with three arrows in total,
the ghost threw itself down the riverbank,
and Bùyí then returned.
The others laughed and welcomed him,
saying to Bùyí:
"We feared you might hide and deceive us,
so we secretly followed you,
only then realizing your courage and strength are like this."
Thereupon they gave him the money,
which Bùyí spent entirely on drink.
The next day,
they went to search under the bank where he had shot,
and found a fāngxiàng,
its body woven from thorns,
Beside it, they also recovered three arrows.
From then on, the road ghost vanished,
and Bùyí also,
From this, he became known for his bravery and valor.
By the time he retired in old age,
he was over seventy years old,
yet his spirit and vigor had not declined.
In the winter, the tenth month of the second year of Tiānbǎo,
Bùyí went to Yángqū,
drinking with others,
and when drunk, he wanted to return.
The host earnestly urged him to stay.
Bùyí ordered all his attendants to remain,
and he alone,
Mounting his horse,
he returned to Tàiyuán after dark.
Yángqū was three shè from the prefecture,
and Bùyí galloped back.
The area in between was a sandy plain,
where foxes and will-o'-the-wisps gathered in clusters,
with no inhabitants at all.
That night,
he suddenly saw shops and inns lining both sides of the road,
stretching continuously without end.
The moon was full and the clouds thin at the time,
and Bùyí found it strange.
Soon, the shops and inns grew even more numerous,
with many men and women,
some singing, some dancing,
drinking and making merry,
or forming groups to stamp their feet in dance.
There were over a hundred children,
surrounding Bùyí's horse,
stamping their feet and singing,
so the horse could not proceed.
There was a tree by the road,
Bùyí broke off a branch,
long and large,
and used it to strike.
The singers fled,
and Bùyí was able to advance.
Arriving at an inn,
he again saw over two hundred people,
tall and large in stature,
dressed in splendid clothes,
coming to surround Bùyí,
stamping their feet and singing.
Bùyí grew furious,
and again struck them with the tree branch,
whereupon the tall people all vanished.
Bùyí became afraid,
thinking what he saw was extraordinary,
so he left the road and galloped away.
Intending to seek shelter in a village,
he suddenly came upon a place with over a hundred households,
with very grand houses.
Bùyí knocked on a door seeking lodging,
but no one answered,
even though he shouted and knocked vigorously,
people still did not come out.
There was a temple in the village,
Bùyí entered it,
tied his horse to a pillar,
and sat on the steps.
The bright moon was shining,
and the night was not yet half over,
when a woman in plain clothes and adorned makeup
suddenly pushed the door open and entered,
walking straight toward Bùyí and bowing twice.
When questioned,
the woman said:
"I see my husband living alone,
so I have come to keep you company."
Bùyí said:
"Who is your husband?"
The woman said:
"You, sir, are he."
Bùyí knew she was a specter,
struck her,
and the woman then left.
Inside the hall room, there was a bed,
and Bùyí rested on it.
Suddenly, something from the beam
fell onto his abdomen,
as large as a basin or urn.
Bùyí struck it,
and it made a sound like a dog.
It then,
threw itself under the bed,
transformed into a fiery man,
over two chǐ tall,
shining brightly,
entered into the wall,
and thus disappeared.
Bùyí again went out the door,
mounted his horse and left,
finally entering a forest to rest,
and by daybreak he could not leave.
His family happened to search and found him,
already foolish and having lost his soul.
They carried him back,
and he still recounted what he had seen.
He then fell ill for over a month.
Huán Yànfàn
Fúyáng Prince Huán Yànfàn,
was unrestrained and unconventional in his youth,
possessing great,
integrity,
but did not bother with minor details of conduct.
He often roamed with chivalrous guests,
drinking in wild marshes.
At dusk,
the guests dispersed,
and Fàn, along with several others, heavily drunk,
lay down in the marsh.
After the second watch,
suddenly there was a creature,
over a zhang tall,
ten arm-spans in girth,
holding a spear and halberd,
glaring and shouting loudly,
coming straight toward Fàn and the others.
The others all prostrated themselves motionless,
but Fàn, having courage and strength,
rose up with a shout,
clenched his fists and advanced,
and the creature then retreated and fled.
Encountering a large willow tree,
Fàn broke off a branch with his hand,
and holding it, struck the creature,
the sound crackling,
as if hitting something hollow.
After several strikes,
it crawled away.
Fàn pursued it even more urgently,
and it entered an ancient tomb.
At dawn, upon closer inspection,
it turned out to be a damaged fāngxiàng.
Cài Sì
Cài Sì of Yǐngyáng
was a scholar of literary talent.
During the early Tiānbǎo era,
he lived in Jùnyí of Chénliú.
While he was reciting poetry,
a ghost would often come and sit on his couch,
sometimes asking about meanings,
sometimes appreciating his poems.
Cài asked, "What kind of spirit are you,
that you suddenly descend to visit me?"
The ghost said,
"My surname is Wáng,
and I am the eldest.
I have come out of admiration for your talent and virtue."
At first, Cài was very frightened,
but later he gradually grew familiar with it.
Whenever the ghost arrived,
it would always address him as "Wáng the Elder and Cài the Younger,"
and they would talk and laugh joyfully.
Cài had an old friend with a young servant
who could see ghosts.
He tried having him observe it,
and the servant trembled with fear.
When asked about its appearance,
he said,
"There is a large ghost,
over ten feet tall,
with several small ghosts following behind."
Later, Cài built a small wooden hut
and placed it in the southwest corner of his residence,
planting various fruit trees around it.
When the ghost arrived,
he said to it,
"The ways of humans and spirits are different,
as you well know.
Yesterday, I built a small dwelling for you,
where you should settle peacefully."
The ghost was very pleased
and thanked its host.
After that, whenever their conversations and laughter ended,
the ghost would enter this dwelling to rest,
and this became the usual practice.
After a long time,
the ghost said to Cài,
"I wish to marry off my daughter
and would like to borrow your residence temporarily."
Cài refused, saying,
"My elderly parents are at home.
If they are tainted by ghostly energy,
they will surely be unsettled.
You should seek another residence."
The ghost said,
"As for the main hall where your mother resides,
simply close it off,
and I will certainly not enter.
I only need to borrow it for seven days."
Cài had no choice but to lend it,
and after seven days, the ghost returned to its dwelling,
with everything peaceful and no other incidents.
A few days later,
the ghost said,
"I am holding a vegetarian feast."
It asked Cài to lend it utensils, canopies, and other items.
Cài said,
"I do not know anyone else,
so I can only lend my own belongings."
He then asked where the feast would be held.
The ghost said,
"Nearby, north of Fántái.
When it is midnight in the human world,
it is time for the feast in the underworld."
Cài asked if he could go to watch when the time came.
Was it possible?
The ghost said,
"Why not?"
Because it was a ghost,
the entire Cài family recited the Thousand-Handed, Thousand-Eyed mantra.
When the family was pure and clean,
the ghost would not come.
When they ate rich meat and blood,
the ghost would surely arrive.
Wanting to attend the feast,
the family all diligently recited the mantra,
put on new, clean clothes,
and went to Fántái under the moonlight.
From afar, they saw canopies and monks in great numbers.
The family chanted the mantra together
and approached them.
They saw the ghosts in panic and disarray,
and knowing they feared humans,
they advanced even further.
Once they arrived,
the ghosts scattered in an instant.
The eldest, Wáng,
and more than ten of his companions headed north.
Cài followed them
for about five or six li.
They reached a grove of tombs,
where the ghosts vanished.
He noted the location and returned.
The next day, he went with his family to inspect it.
It was an abandoned tomb,
containing dozens of burial objects,
with the largest one placed at the entrance of the tomb chamber.
On its forehead was the character "Wáng."
Cài said,
"This must be Wáng the Elder."
They piled up fire and burned it,
and the ghost never appeared again.
Lǐ Huá
Lǐ Huá, a Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel in the Táng dynasty,
when he was young, studied with five or six companions
at a mountain villa in Jìyuán.
Half a year later,
an old man
with snow-white beard and eyebrows
often carried a wrapped stone,
as big as a fist.
Every day, in the evening,
he would sit astride the courtyard wall
and throw the stone at Lǐ Huá and the others,
right in front of and behind the window.
After several months,
the residents were troubled by this.
A neighbor, Biéjiàng Qín,
was known for his excellent archery.
Lǐ Huá went to visit him personally
and explained the matter in detail.
Qín gladly took his bow
and went to the mountain to wait for the old man.
When evening came and the old man returned,
he continued throwing stones.
Qín then shot an arrow through a gap,
hitting the target with a single shot.
When they looked,
it turned out to be a wooden burial object.
A Person from Shāngxiāng
In recent times, there was a person
traveling through the outskirts of Shāngxiāng.
At first, he was traveling with a companion.
After a few days,
the companion suddenly said to him,
"I am actually a ghost.
Because the burial objects in my home have rebelled,
we fight day and night.
I wish to borrow a word from you
to quell the turmoil.
What do you think?"
The person said,
"If it can resolve the matter,
I have no fear."
As evening fell,
they arrived at a large tomb on the left side of the road.
The ghost pointed at the tomb
and said,
"This is my grave.
Stand in front of the grave and shout loudly,
'By imperial decree, behead the gold and silver tribes.'
That will be enough."
After saying this,
the ghost entered the tomb.
The person then proclaimed the decree.
In a moment,
the sound of beheading could be heard.
After a while,
the ghost emerged from the tomb,
holding several gold and silver human and horse figures
with their heads all severed.
He said to the person,
"With these, you will have enough fortune for a lifetime,
as a token of my gratitude."
When the person reached Xījīng,
he was reported by the arrest officers of Cháng'ān.
The county official said,
"These are ancient artifacts.
You must have obtained them by breaking into a tomb."
The person told the truth.
The county reported to the Prefect,
who submitted a memorial about the matter.
Officials were sent to open the tomb,
and they found gold and silver human and horse figures,
hundreds of them with severed heads.
Lú Hán
During the Kāichéng era,
there was a scholar named Lú Hán,
who resided in Luòxià,
and owned a manor on the northern side of Wàn'ān Mountain.
The summer wheat had just been harvested,
and the seasonal fruits were ripe,
so he rode alone on a small horse to visit his manor.
After traveling over ten lǐ,
he saw, beside a large grove of cypress trees,
several newly cleaned rooms,
operating as an inn.
As the sun was about to set,
Lú Hán stopped to rest his horse.
He caught sight of a young woman with double buns,
possessing a very charming demeanor.
He inquired about her,
and she said she was a maidservant of General Gěng, guarding the tomb,
and that her father and brothers were not present.
Lú Hán was delighted by her,
and spoke with her.
Her words were clever and beautiful,
her manner was open and unrestrained,
her bright eyes glanced about,
enhancing her graceful bearing.
She said to Lú Hán:
"I have a small amount of homemade wine,
would you, sir, care to drink a few cups?"
Lú Hán replied:
"That would not be unpleasant."
She then brought out an ancient bronze goblet,
and drank with Lú Hán very merrily.
The maidservant then tapped the mat and sang,
offering wine to Lú Hán with these words:
"Alone I hold the towel and comb, guarding the dark gate,
the small curtain unmanned, the candle's shadow wanes.
The silken robes of yesteryear have all turned to dust,
the white poplars stir in the wind, the ridge grows cold."
Lú Hán was disturbed that the lyrics did not match the occasion,
but he did not understand their meaning.
When the wine was finished,
the maidservant said to Lú Hán:
"Let me go inside with you, sir, to refill our cups."
Carrying the candle and holding the goblet, she went inside.
Lú Hán tiptoed to peek,
and saw a large black snake hanging,
using a knife to draw the snake's blood,
dripping it into the goblet,
where it transformed into wine.
Lú Hán was greatly terrified,
and realized it was a demonic creature.
He then rushed out the door,
untied his small horse, and fled.
The maidservant called out several times:
"Tonight's affairs require that you, sir, stay for one night,
you cannot leave."
Seeing that the situation was not favorable,
she called out to the east side to Fāng Dà:
"Quickly chase after him for me,
and intercept the gentleman."
Soon, from within the cypress grove,
a large man
responded with a mighty voice.
In a moment, looking back,
Lú Hán saw something like a large withered tree rushing toward him,
its steps very heavy,
about a hundred paces away.
Lú Hán only whipped his horse faster,
and passing through another small cypress grove,
he saw a huge creature,
with a vaguely snow-white area.
Someone spoke, saying:
"Tonight we must capture this man,
otherwise,
tomorrow morning you will suffer calamity."
Hearing this,
Lú Hán became even more frightened.
When he reached the manor gate,
it was already the third watch.
The gate was shut and silent,
with only several empty carts outside.
A flock of sheep were chewing grass,
and there were no other people or creatures.
Lú Hán abandoned his horse,
and secretly hid under one of the cart boxes.
He saw the large man go straight to the gate,
the wall was very high,
but it only reached his waist.
He held a halberd,
and looked into the manor.
He then stabbed the halberd at a child inside the manor,
and only saw the child's hands and feet flailing in the air,
on the tip of the halberd,
utterly without a sound.
After a long time, he left.
Lú Hán estimated he was far away,
and only then could he get up and knock on the gate.
A manor servant opened the gate,
startled by Lú Hán's arrival at night.
Lú Hán was panting and sweating, unable to speak.
By dawn,
he suddenly heard the sound of crying from within the manor courtyard.
It was said:
"The three-year-old child,
because of last night, fell asleep and did not wake up."
Lú Hán was deeply disturbed by this,
and so led over ten household servants and manor workers,
armed with knives, axes, bows, and arrows, to investigate.
They only saw the place where he had drunk the night before,
a few empty, abandoned rooms in a circle,
with no other people or creatures.
They then searched the cypress grove,
and found a large funerary figurine of a maidservant,
about two chǐ tall,
beside it was a black snake,
already dead.
Also, in the cypress grove to the east,
they found a large fāngxiàng skeleton.
They then smashed and burned them all.
Searching for the white creature that had spoken the night before,
it turned out to be a complete set of human bones.
The limbs, joints, and sinews were connected,
without missing the slightest bit.
They struck it with a bronze axe,
but it never showed any damage.
So they threw it into a pit and that was all.
Lú Hán originally suffered from a wind ailment,
but it was cured because he drank the snake wine.
Zhāng Bùyí
Zhāng Bùyí of Nányáng,
in the fourth year of the Kāichéng era,
passed the special examination for literary excellence,
and was appointed to the Imperial Library.
He traveled to the capital.
Having sought assistance from various feudal lords and returned,
as his home was far away and he had no family there,
he worried about his loneliness and solitude,
and while residing in the capital as an official,
he wished to purchase a maidservant,
to have someone to attend to him and keep him informed about the local affairs.
Within a month,
there were several people who came to offer servants,
but their appearances happened to displease him and were not to his liking.
After more than a month,
a broker came and said:
"There is someone newly selling servants,
please come and have a look."
Bùyí arranged to meet him the next day.
When the appointed time arrived,
he went to the broker's house,
where there was a man dressed in a crimson robe and holding an ivory tablet,
who introduced himself as the former Military Supervisor Hú of Zhèxī.
He bowed to Bùyí and invited him to take a seat,
and spoke with him very cheerfully and clearly.
He said:
"I once competed in the imperial examinations in my youth,
and nearly succeeded,
but previously, due to family duties, I was sent to the Southern Sea,
and was fortunate to be employed for several years.
I remember while in the mountain ranges,
I happened to acquire some thirty or so maids and servants,
and from the right bank of the Zhè River all the way to Southern Jīng,
I have sold almost all of them,
and now only have six or seven left.
I have heard from the broker that you, sir, have come."
After speaking,
a maidservant brought a small tray,
and set it before both the guest and the host.
Soon, she brought silver wine vessels and golden cups,
with fragrant and newly brewed wine,
its aroma wafting to the nose.
Bùyí followed the Dàoist teachings,
and usually abstained from wine and meat.
On that day,
he unconsciously drank several cups.
The host then ordered the six or seven maidservants,
to line up in the courtyard,
and said:
"Please choose whichever you like."
Bùyí said:
"I am in need of a servant,
and now I only have sixty thousand coins,
and I wish to offer this as the price.
I hope you, wise sir,
will select one worth sixty thousand coins to show me."
The man in crimson said:
"My prices vary according to their worth."
Then he pointed to a maidservant with double earlobes and said:
"Chūntiáo can be sold for that price."
Bùyí looked at her,
and indeed she was the one he had privately admired.
That very day, he completed the contract and paid the money.
Chūntiáo was skilled at writing and recording,
her voice and tone were clear and gentle,
and whatever tasks were assigned to her,
she carried out to satisfaction,
and she was also fond of learning.
After more than a month,
she secretly composed a small poem,
and often wrote it on the door or window, which read:
"In a secluded room, a bewitching beauty is locked away,
with no one to appreciate the fragrance of the orchids.
For thirty years, the spring breeze has blown,
yet the scent of her silk garments remains endless."
Bùyí deeply cherished her talent, beauty, and intelligence.
This continued for more than two months.
Bùyí had long respected and served a Dàoist master,
who resided at the Míntiān Temple.
When they met,
the master said to Bùyí:
"You, young master, have an extreme amount of evil aura."
Bùyí did not know where it came from.
The master said:
"Could it be that you have recently taken a new wife?"
Bùyí said:
"I have not taken a wife,
but I did purchase a maidservant,
that is all."
The master said:
"This is a disaster."
Bùyí became frightened,
and asked for a plan.
The master said:
"Tomorrow morning, I will come to your home,
be careful not to let her notice."
The next morning,
the master arrived,
and said to Bùyí:
"Call the monster out."
Bùyí summoned Chūntiáo,
but she wept behind the screen,
and though he urgently called her,
she would not come out.
The master said:
"Indeed, it is a monster."
He drove her into the room,
and closed the door.
The master burned incense and performed a ritual,
spraying water three times toward the east.
He said to Bùyí:
"Go and take a look,
how is it now?"
Bùyí looked and said:
"Generally, it is her original appearance,
but she has shrunk a little in size."
The master said:
"Not yet."
He performed the ritual again, walking the Yǔ steps,
and sprayed water three times toward the door.
He said to Bùyí:
"Go and look again,
how is it now?"
Bùyí looked,
and she was only a little over a foot tall,
very small,
standing stiff and motionless.
Bùyí went closer,
He looked,
and she fell to the ground,
making a thudding sound.
He looked at her.
It was a decayed burial figurine.
On its back was inscribed "Chūntiáo,"
its clothes were like a cicada's shed skin,
but the knots were still intact.
Bùyí was greatly shocked.
The master said:
"Although this is the case,
there must already be something unusual around its waist and abdomen."
He ordered Bùyí to take a knife and split it open,
and indeed, there was blood around the waist and neck,
which had soaked into the wood.
They then burned it.
The master said:
"If the blood had spread throughout its body,
then you and your entire family,
would have all suffered from this creature."
From then on, Bùyí was endlessly depressed,
how could he have lived with a burial figurine without realizing it,
and it was likely he would not live long.
Whenever he thought of it,
he would be dazed for several days,
as if he had lost something.
As a result, he fell seriously ill,
and requested leave to return home.
The following year,
he was recruited to Jiāngxī.
On the day he was to travel to Huáinán,
he was dismissed midway.
In the eighth month of the year after that, he died.
One day after his death,
his esteemed mother also passed away.
The Dàoist's words indeed came true.
Another version says,
Zhāng Bùyí often interacted with a Dàoist priest.
When the priest was about to go elsewhere,
he warned Bùyí:
"You, sir, are facing a great calamity,
and should not live under the care of your esteemed mother,
nor should you purchase maids or servants.
I am leaving now,
I hope you will take care."
Bùyí then informed his mother, Madame Lú,
who had long followed Dàoism,
and often spent her days in other places seeking tranquility.
Thus, she moved to reside in a temple,
and Bùyí visited her every morning.
After several months,
a broker said:
"There is a widow of the Cuī family who is very poor,
and has four singing girls,
all of whom she is selling.
Now there is one maidservant named Jīngāng,
who is beautiful,
and the one she cherishes the most.
Now, due to poverty and having no other choice,
she intends to sell her."
Bùyí was delighted,
and immediately ordered her to be summoned,
In the second year of the Bǎolì era,
Fàn Zhāng, a candidate for the imperial examination, lived on Liáng Mountain to study.
One midsummer night,
he suddenly heard the sound of something being dragged in the kitchen.
Fàn, feeling lazy, did not investigate.
By dawn,
he saw a bundle of firewood, over five inches long,
neat and lovely,
piled on the stove.
On the ground, five steamed buns were stacked precariously.
Another night,
something knocked on the door,
then clapped its hands and laughed loudly,
its voice like that of an infant.
This continued for three nights.
Zhāng had always been courageous,
so he seized the moment of its laughter,
grabbed a large piece of firewood, and chased it.
The creature looked like a small dog.
As he struck it repeatedly,
it turned into fire,
and vanished across the river.
Hú Róng
In the spring of the first year of the Chángqìng era,
at the home of Hú Róng, an official stationed along the Huái River in Chǔzhōu,
there was a spirit creature,
sometimes hidden, sometimes visible.
Sometimes it took the form of a child,
wearing a woman’s red skirt,
and caused disturbances among people.
It sometimes called itself "Āgū."
Occasionally, a fire would break out in one place,
but the damage was always minimal,
and it could be extinguished.
In the third month,
a great fire erupted,
spreading and nearly destroying the market, military barracks, and houses along the river.
Within the year,
Hú was said to have died as well.
Yáng Zhēn
Jìnshì Yáng Zhēn,
lived by the Wèi Bridge.
As his residence was too bustling and crowded,
it rather hindered his studies.
So he went to Zhāoyìng County,
Zhāoyìng County,
and long-term borrowed the Wénshū Hall of the Shíwèng Temple.
After residing there for over ten days,
a figure in red garments arrived one evening.
Her countenance was beautiful,
her demeanor captivating.
Those whom Zhēn usually found pleasing,
could not compare.
She paced slowly outside the curtain,
and sang:
"The cool wind rises at dusk, Lí Mountain lies empty,
The Chángshēng Hall is locked, the frosty leaves are red.
Come morning, try to enter Huáqīng Palace,
Clearly remembering the Kāiyuán era."
Zhēn said:
"Who is the singer?
Why such bitter sorrow?"
The figure in red sang again:
"The golden hall cannot withstand autumn,
The moon slants, the stone tower is cold.
Who is the one to look upon me,
Lifting the curtain to pity my solitary shadow?"
Zhēn bowed and welcomed her at the door.
Once seated,
she asked Zhēn his surname and name,
which Zhēn fully told.
Zhēn's paternal grandparents, uncles, brothers, and all his maternal and paternal relatives,
those who had ever visited Shíwèng Temple,
she knew them all intimately.
Zhēn, finding this strange, said:
"Could you be a ghost?"
She replied:
"I have heard that the soul's energy ascends to heaven,
the bodily form returns to earth,
thus having no substance—
how could there be a ghost?"
He said:
"Then are you a fox spirit?"
She replied:
"Fox spirits,
they seduce people.
Once ensnared by their allure,
calamity is sure to follow.
My family's legacy is one of merit and virtue,
truly benefiting the living.
Though I am not virtuous,
how could I recklessly use allure and wish to bring calamity?"
Zhēn said:
"May I hear your surname?"
"I am a descendant of Suìrénshì.
Our founding ancestor performed meritorious deeds for humanity,
thus he commanded Bǐng and Dīng,
pacifying the south.
Later, by virtue, he became king to Shénnóng and Táotángshì.
Afterwards, he was king again in the Western Hàn.
Because he received a fief in Sòng,
a distant ancestor, Wújì,
due to his fierce and violent nature,
people could not get close to him,
and thus was captured by the Báizé clan.
Now even woodcutters and shepherd boys
know his name.
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
when Buddhist teachings flowed eastward,
the two arhats, Móshèng and Zhúfǎlán,
petitioned my ancestor of the fourteenth generation,
requesting him to promote and spread the Buddhist teachings,
and so he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Chángmíng.
In the final years of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi,
when Buddhism was suppressed,
and Daoist priests were executed,
the Duke of Chángmíng died imprisoned.
Emperor Wén of Wèi,
succeeded to the throne,
Buddhism was revived,
and the Duke of Chángmíng's eldest son succeeded him.
At the beginning of the Kāiyuán era,
when Emperor Xuánzōng developed Lí Mountain,
building up to Huáqīng Palace,
constructing the Cháoyuán Pavilion,
and establishing the Chángshēng Hall,
with the leftover materials, this temple was repaired.
Once all the statues were erected,
an eastern prayer pillar was set up.
The Emperor and his consort,
having finished feasting in the hot spring hall,
came incognito to the Buddhist temple.
After paying homage to the Buddha,
the consort said to the Emperor:
'In this season of paired flight,
we should not let the eastern pillar stand lofty and alone.'
The Emperor that very day ordered a western pillar erected,
and enfeoffed me as the Lady of Xīmíng.
He then bestowed amber ointment,
to moisten my parched bones,
and set up a coral canopy,
to secure my form and appearance.
From then on, I was chosen for life among the moths,
and no longer was I fierce and violent."
Zhēn said:
"Of song, dance, strings, and pipes,
which is your finest skill?"
She said:
"It is not that I cannot,
but I inherit the bright virtue of my ancestors,
bear the fiery and ardent nature,
therefore lewd sounds and chaotic sights
do not enter my heart.
What I am capable of:
In great matters, melting metal to forge the five weapons,
or to cast tripods, cauldrons, bells, and chimes;
in small matters, transforming food into a hundred delicacies,
for roasting, frying, boiling, or grilling.
In motion, I can reduce mountains to ashes and scorch the plains;
in stillness, I can illuminate the darkness and dispel obscurity.
As for plucking vermilion strings,
playing jade pipes,
displaying a slender waist,
or flaunting white teeth—
these are all trivial matters of seductive appearance,
which I do not engage in.
Yesterday, I heard that you, sir, have aspirations for seclusion,
a reputation long established,
and I wished to meet you face to face.
This is why I came,
not daring to offer myself.
However, the night is clear, the moon bright,
I rejoice in meeting a fine gentleman.
Even the reproach of a rendezvous in the mulberry grove,
I cannot feel ashamed of.
If fortune aligns with the times,
allowing me to briefly keep you company,
it will certainly not tarnish your great virtue."
Zhēn bowed and accepted her.
From then on, she left at dawn and returned at dusk,
only not coming on overcast or dark days.
Once, encountering wind and rain,
an infant delivered a poem for the lady in red:
The words said:
"Mist vanishes, the stone tower stands empty,
In the long, endless night.
A hollow heart fears the autumn rain,
A beautiful form dreads the gusting wind.
Facing the wall, scattered petals lie broken,
Encroaching on the steps, fallen leaves are red.
Like a crane that has lost its flock,
Nursing regret within a carved cage."
Whenever she asked to return before the stars faded,
Zhēn would try to stop her.
She replied:
"You, sir, left the care of morning and evening,
to dwell among cliffs and valleys—
was it not to seek tranquility,
and devote yourself to literary studies?
How then can you wish to make a woman of faulty conduct
call you kin and become your mate?
Once a flaw is incurred,
can it ever be washed away?
Not only would it damage your esteemed reputation,
but it would also hasten my own life."
After half a year,
a house servant returned
and told Zhēn's wet nurse.
The nurse then hid secretly by the Buddhist altar,
waiting for dawn to observe.
Indeed, she emerged from a crevice,
entered the western pillar,
and became a single, clear-burning lamp.
The nurse thus extinguished it,
and afterwards, the lady in red was gone.
Lú Yù
Jìnshì Lú Yù was a man from Héshuò
who moved his household to Cháng'ān.
He once traveled north through Yān and Zhào,
and subsequently became a guest in Nèihuáng.
The commandery governor lodged Yù in an official residence.
Previously, no one had lived in these quarters.
When Yù arrived,
he saw an old woman
whose hair was completely white,
short in stature and plump,
wearing plain clothes as she approached.
She said to Yù:
"I have lived here as a sojourner for a long time,
hence I came to pay my respects."
Shortly after, she announced her departure.
That evening,
Yù was alone in the front hall.
The night tide was cold,
with wind and snow.
The old woman came again.
She said to Yù:
"Noble guest, alone here,
how do you find enjoyment?"
She bade him sit and converse.
The old woman said:
"My surname is Shí.
My family is from Huàyīn Commandery.
Later, I followed Attendant Censor Lǚ here,
nearly forty years ago.
My family suffers bitter poverty;
I am fortunate the noble guest shows compassion."
Thereupon, Yù ordered food,
but the old woman ultimately paid it no heed.
Yù asked her:
"Madam, why do you not eat?"
The old woman said:
"I am very hungry,
yet I do not eat grain.
For this reason, I live long and in peace."
Yù, being curious,
was very pleased to hear this
and considered her a person possessing Daoist arts.
He then asked:
"Since you, Madam, do not eat grain,
how do you fill your belly?
Could it be you regularly ingest elixirs of immortality?"
The old woman said:
"My family is in Huàyīn.
My ancestors were fond of immortals and spirits,
and dwelled on Tàihuà [Mount Hua].
I too often secluded myself in the mountains,
learning methods for longevity from a Daoist priest.
The priest taught me to swallow fire,
and from then on I abstained from eating.
I am now ninety years old,
and have not experienced a single day of illness from cold or heat."
Yù asked further:
"In my early years, I once met a perfected person
who taught me the art of inhaling qi.
I considered it marvelous.
Later, due to rushing about for fame and profit,
following the tribute processions to the capital,
hurrying by day and resting by night,
I never expected to meet you, Madam, this evening
and speak of lifelong pursuits.
However, I do not know if swallowing fire aligns with the principles of immortals?"
The old woman said:
"Have you not heard that perfected persons
cannot be invaded by cold or heat?
Therefore, entering fire,
the fire cannot burn them;
entering water,
the water cannot drown them.
If so, then swallowing fire is certainly fitting."
Yù said:
"I wish to see you, Madam, swallow fire. May I?"
The old woman said:
"What is there that cannot be done?"
Thereupon, she took fire from the brazier with her hand and swallowed it.
The fire was nearly exhausted,
yet her complexion remained unchanged.
Yù was both startled and amazed.
He then rose, straightened his belt, and bowed twice.
Apologizing, he said:
"I am a rustic fellow
who has never heard of matters of immortals.
Meeting an immortal lady this evening
and witnessing the marvel of fire-swallowing
is truly something I have never heard of in my life."
The old woman said:
"This is a minor art,
hardly worthy of esteem."
Having finished speaking,
she announced her departure.
Yù then descended the steps to see her off.
After parting,
Yù returned to his bedchamber.
Late into the night,
a servant informed Yù
that a fire had broken out under the western gallery.
Yù rose in alarm to look.
The western gallery quarters were already ablaze.
Thereupon, people from the neighborhood all arrived, vying to douse it with water.
It was nearly dawn before the fire was extinguished.
Upon investigating the origin of the fire,
in a pit under the gallery,
they found a stone fire-tube,
containing a great deal of fire.
Previously, there had been a pile of withered grass atop it,
hence the fire spread and caused the burning.
Only then did Yù realize the old woman was this fire-tube.
Indeed, she was the one called 'Surname Shí,
dwelling on Mount Hua.'
Yù then inquired about Attendant Censor Lǚ.
An old clerk from the commandery said to Yù:
"Attendant Censor Lǚ
was an aide in Wèi.
He lived in this residence
until now, forty years ago."
All matched the old woman's words.
Also, in Qīngzhōu, at Jǐnán, north of Pínglíng City, there was a stone tiger.
One night, it moved by itself to the Shànshígōu southeast of the city.
Over a thousand tracks of wolves and foxes followed it,
the tracks forming a path.
Liú Wēi
In the year Dīngmǎo,
Liú Wēi, Prefect of Lúzhōu, was transferred to garrison Jiāngxī.
After he left his post, a great fire broke out in the commandery.
The Lúzhōu patrol officers investigating the fire were very urgent,
yet there were often people carrying fire and walking at night.
Attempts to capture them were unsuccessful.
Some shot and killed them,
but upon inspection,
they turned out to be coffin planks, rotten wood, worn-out brooms, and the like.
The commandery people grew increasingly fearful.
After several months,
Zhāng Zōng was appointed Prefect of Lúzhōu,
and the fires then ceased.
Mǎ Xīfàn
King Mǎ Xīfàn of Chǔ repaired the walls of Chángshā.
After the moat was opened,
suddenly there appeared a creature
over ten zhàng long,
without head, tail, hands, or feet,
shaped like an earthen mound.
It emerged from the northern bank,
swimming on the water.
After a long time,
it entered the southern bank and vanished.
Its emergence and submergence left no trace.
Some called it an earthen dragon.
Not long after, the Mǎ clan perished.
Biē Líng
Biē Líng died in Chǔ.
His corpse then floated upstream.
Reaching the foot of Wènshān,
he suddenly revived.
He then went to see King Wàng Dì.
King Wàng Dì appointed him as chancellor.
At that time, the people of Shǔ at Wūshān and Wèngjiāng often suffered from floods.
Líng then cut through Wūshān,
opening the mouth of the Three Gorges,
allowing the Shǔ river to flow on land.
Later, he ordered Biē Líng to be Prefect,
bestowing the title 'Emperor of Xīzhōu.'
Due to his high merit,
he abdicated the throne to Líng,
who was called the Kāimíng Clan.
Yùliáng Guàn
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han Dynasty,
the people of Yùsì Mountain,
moved by the mountain's spiritual wonders,
would pray to it whenever drought or locust plagues occurred,
and their prayers were never unanswered.
They then said to each other:
"We should build a temple here,
to manifest and honor these miraculous traces."
After the hall was constructed,
it was missing a central beam.
The local people sought a remarkable piece of timber,
but after several decades, they had not found one.
Suddenly, one night,
thunder shook and wind howled,
clearing only at dawn.
A beam of white jade descended from the heavens,
perfectly measured to fit,
and was solemnly placed atop the hall,
its brilliance dazzling to the eyes.
Thus, it was named the Jade Beam Temple.
By the time of Emperor Wu of the Wei Dynasty,
he sent an envoy to retrieve it.
When they reached the mountain gate,
still several li from the temple,
at midday,
great peals of thunder and lightning erupted,
splitting the temple's ridge,
and the beam transformed into a white dragon,
parting the mist and smoke as it departed,
vanishing beneath the eastern mountain of the temple grounds.
During the Yǒngjiā era of the Jin Dynasty,
there was a man named Dài,
whose origins were unknown,
who often enjoyed wandering among cliffs and valleys.
By chance, he entered below Yùmù Mountain,
and saw two blue stones
propping up a white jade beam beneath a cliff.
Mr. Dài bent close to look at it,
and with his hand felt its surface,
where he saw five lines of crimson writing,
all in celestial script and cloud-seal characters.
He tried tapping it with a hand-axe,
and it sounded like a bell,
or like the rumble of distant thunder,
causing scales to rise upon it.
Startled and amazed,
Mr. Dài ran to tell others.
When they went back to search for it,
they could not find its location.
In the early Dàlì era of the Tang Dynasty,
a hunter named Huáng from Wúyáo,
also saw it while hunting.
Afterwards, several people saw it repeatedly,
but all kept it hidden and did not speak of it to others.
After the jade beam flew away,
