no one could dwell in that place,
as they were all driven away by fierce beasts and venomous snakes.
Xiāng Cave
Within the Xiāng Cave there is black earth.
In years of drought,
people would together dam the water
to block this cave.
Once the cave was flooded, heavy rain would arrive immediately.
Lěiyáng Waters
In Lěiyáng County there is a Rain Rapid.
When this county suffered drought,
the common people would together block it,
and sweet rain would fall everywhere.
If only one village blocked it alone,
the rain would still respond universally.
According to the direction from which prayers were made,
the response was as reliable as a tally matching its counterpart.
Sūn Jiān Obtains a Burial Site
When Sūn Jiān's father died,
he was seeking a burial site.
Suddenly, a man appeared and said:
"Do you wish for your descendants to be feudal lords for a hundred generations,
or emperors for four generations?"
He replied:
"I wish for emperors."
This man then pointed to a certain place,
and with a joyful expression, vanished.
Sūn Jiān, astonished, followed his instruction.
At that time, in Fùchūn, a sandbar suddenly emerged.
When Sūn Jiān became a Supervisor,
neighbors and friends saw him off upon it.
An elder said to him:
"This sandbar is narrow and long;
you, sir, will later become the Governor of Chángshā."
Indeed, he later raised his righteous army in Chángshā.
Niè Yǒu
Niè Yǒu of Xīngàn was poor in his youth.
Once while hunting,
he saw a white deer,
shot it, and afterwards found his arrow stuck in a catalpa tree.
The Eight Formations Diagram
At the western market of Kuízhōu,
overlooking the riverbank,
beneath the sand and stones lies Zhūgě Liàng's Eight Formations Diagram.
Spread like a winnowing basket, extended like wings,
shaped like geese, poised like cranes,
stone formations are distributed,
still clearly preserved.
When the gorge waters rise high,
at the time when the snows of the Three Shǔ melt,
surging and swirling turbulently,
how can it be fully described?
Great trees ten arm-spans around,
deadwood a hundred zhang long,
broken millstones and massive rocks,
follow the waves, blocking the river as they come down.
The water rises level with the banks,
people flee to the mountains,
yet the stones gathered into piles
can clearly be discerned.
And when the waters recede and the river calms,
all things lose their former appearance.
Only Zhūgě's formation diagram,
the piles of small stones,
markers gathered in rows and lines,
remain just as they were.
For nearly six or seven hundred years,
yearly washed and pushed by the currents,
they have remained unmoved to this day.
Seashore Stone Turtle
By the seashore there is a great stone turtle,
commonly said to be the work of Lǔ Bān.
In summer it enters the sea,
in winter it returns to rest on the mountain.
Lù Jī wrote in a poem:
"The stone turtle often yearns for the sea;
how could I forget my homeland?"
Also, north of Línyì County,
there is Duke Yàn's tombstone,
the stone tablet was lost long ago,
only the turtle pedestal remains.
During the era of the Later Zhào,
this turtle would often carry the tablet into the water at night,
not returning until dawn.
On it, duckweed and algae would often be found.
Someone lay in wait for it,
and indeed saw the turtle about to enter the water.
He then cried out,
the turtle fled,
and the tablet fell and broke.
Diàotái Stone
In the second month of the seventh year of the Dàyè era,
when first constructing the Diàotái,
many stone transporters were employed.
The soldiers and laborers manning the boats
were exhausted by the labor,
their sighs and laments
could be heard along the roads.
At that time, the stone transporters
took boats to the foot of the mountain on the eastern riverbank to fetch stones,
piling them to form the foundation of the Diàotái.
Suddenly, over ten large stones,
each like an ox,
flew down from the mountain top,
straight into the boats,
as if placed by human hands,
leaving the boats undamaged.
Fénzhōu Maiden
At the end of the Suí dynasty, when building the city of Fénzhōu,
only the southwestern corner would not hold together.
It would be completed in the morning and collapse by evening,
and this happened three or four times.
In the city, there was a young girl,
about twelve or thirteen years old.
She told her family:
"Unless I am built into it,
the city will never hold together."
Her family did not believe her,
and the neighbors laughed at her.
After this, when they built the city,
it collapsed as before.
The girl said:
"I will die today.
After I die, place me in an urn
and bury me at the construction site."
Having spoken, she died.
They buried her as she had said.
After the burial,
they immediately began ramming earth for the wall,
and the city never collapsed again.
The Daughter of the Persian King
In the city of Fùdǐyě in the kingdom of Tǔhuǒluó,
built by the ancient Persian king Wūsèduōxí.
When the king first built this city,
it immediately collapsed.
He sighed and said:
"I must lack virtue now,
so Heaven prevents this city from being built."
He had a young daughter named Nàxī,
who saw her father's worry and distress.
She asked:
"Does the king have neighboring enemies?"
The king said:
"I am the king of Persia,
ruling over a thousand states.
Now, in Tǔhuǒluó,
I wish to build this city
to leave an achievement for ten thousand generations.
Since I cannot fulfill this wish,
that is why I am distressed."
The daughter said:
"May the king not worry.
Tomorrow morning, order the craftsmen to build along the traces of my footsteps,
and it will stand."
The king thought this strange.
At dawn,
the girl started walking northwest,
cut off the little finger of her right hand,
and left a trail of blood.
The craftsmen built along the blood trail,
and the city never collapsed again.
The girl then transformed into a sea goddess.
That sea still exists today beneath the fortress,
its water clear as a mirror,
spanning over five hundred paces in circumference.
Chéng Yán
Chéng Yán rented a residence in Xīnchānglǐ.
He was unsuccessful in his official selection,
poor and ill again.
An old woman said to him:
"You are poor and ill,
I can save you,
and also get you a wife."
Having spoken, she left.
That night at the third watch,
someone indeed arrived, saying
Chén Shàng had sent gifts.
Yán could not guess the reason.
He opened the door,
and they delivered several dozen bundles of silk.
Yán asked who Chén Shàng was.
The messenger said:
"A physician."
He also attached a pill,
saying wearing it could cure all illnesses.
Yán wore it,
and indeed his illness was cured.
Several days later,
in the evening, a great whirlwind entered Yán's residence.
In a moment, the wind settled,
and three sedan chairs appeared.
There was a woman,
with three maidservants following her.
Asked for the reason,
she said:
"I am the daughter of Zhào Míngjīng of Fúyú County in Yuèzhōu.
My parents betrothed me to the former Fúyú County Lieutenant Chéng Yán.
Just now, a great wind blew me here."
Yán had no way to send her back,
so he accepted her.
Later, when he verified the matter,
it was indeed true.
But in Yuèzhōu, there was another person
with the same name as Yán.
The Falling Stone in Wénshuǐ County
In the eighteenth year of the Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty, in the tenth month,
in Wénshuǐ County, there was a great thunderclap in the sky.
A stone fell from the clouds,
as large as a pestle tip,
with a high ridge and a flat belly.
County Deputy Zhāng Xiàojìng reported it.
At that time, an elder monk from the Mójiādāng Pútí Temple in the Western Regions arrived in the Western Capital.
He was quite skilled in divination.
and very knowledgeable.
An imperial order inquired of him.
He said it was dragon food,
that two dragons had fought over it,
so it fell down.
Xuánzōng's Sacred Image
The imperial portrait of Emperor Xuánzōng,
made with layered hemp cloth.
Originally in Zhōuzhì, at the Xiūzhēn
Temple.
Suddenly, a monk, as if mad,
carried it on his back
and placed it in the Qiánlóng Palace in Wǔgōng.
The palace was the former residence of Shén Yáo,
now a Buddhist temple.
The imperial portrait only wore a crimson gauze robe and a headscarf.
The temple monks said:
"When Zhuāngzōng entered Biàn,
Míngzōng entered Luò,
and up to the year Qīngtài went east to Yī
and Chán,
sweat always flowed from its forehead."
Scholar Zhāng Hàng
had heard of this but did not believe it.
When he passed through Wǔgōng,
he examined it closely,
and it was indeed as described.
He also thought it might be due to rain leakage,
but the headscarf above showed none.
After the Tiānfù era,
the sweating ceased.
In Gāolíng County, there were also the ancestral fields of Shén Yáo,
now also a temple.
There is a cypress tree there,
traditionally said that
when Gāozǔ was in swaddling clothes,
his mother placed him in the shade of this cypress tree
and went to work in the fields.
When she returned from work,
the sun had set but the tree's shadow had not moved.
This is that cypress tree.
Historical records do not mention this,
but the elders tell the story.
The Lotus of Yúzhōu
On the stone mountain north of the Xiāngsī Temple, a hundred lǐ west of Yúzhōu,
there are twelve Buddha footprints,
each about three chǐ long,
one chǐ and one cùn wide,
and nine cùn deep,
with fish patterns inside.
They are located over ten paces north of the Buddha hall.
In the twentieth year of Zhēnguàn, tenth month,
from a spring beside the temple,
red lotus flowers suddenly emerged,
with faces three chǐ wide.
Travelers coming and going
were all amazed,
and they did not fade for a month.
In the past, at the Tiānzǐ Well east of Jīngzhōu city in Qí,
brocade emerged.
At that time, men and women took and used it,
no different from ordinary brocade,
and it ceased after a month.
This is also of that kind.
The Jade Horse
Shěn Fùshī served as the military commissioner of Xuānwǔ.
Suddenly, a horse neighed in front of the hall,
its sound very close,
but it could not be found.
Another day,
the neighing gradually drew nearer,
as if under the hall.
They dug,
more than a zhang deep,
and encountered a small hollow space.
Within it, they found a jade horse,
two or three cun tall,
four or five cun long,
which neighed like a strong horse.
In front of it were scattered pieces of cinnabar,
stored in a golden trough.
Its dung resembled mung beans,
and was as red as gold.
Shěn Fùshī often fed it cinnabar.
A Huàshān Daoist companion,
the retired scholar Yuán Gù, said:
In the early years of the Zhēnyuán era,
I once roamed Huàshān with Daoist companions.
In a valley, we saw a human thigh,
The sock and shoe were very new,
the broken end like a knee joint,
with no trace of injury at first.
The younger brother of Zhèng Rénběn,
during the Dàhé era of the Táng dynasty,
Zhèng Rénběn's maternal cousin,
whose name is not remembered,
often roamed Sōngshān with a scholar named Wáng.
Climbing vines and crossing streams,
they reached an extremely secluded and □ place,
and suddenly lost their way back.
As dusk approached,
they did not know where to go.
While lingering,
they suddenly heard snoring from the bushes.
Parting the undergrowth to look,
they saw a man in plain clothes,
his garments very clean and white,
using a bundle as a pillow,
sound asleep.
They called to him, saying:
"We accidentally entered this path,
got lost,
do you know the way to the main road?"
The man raised his head and glanced briefly,
then did not respond and went back to sleep.
They called him again and again,
and he finally sat up,
looking at them and saying:
"Come here."
The two then approached him,
and asked where he was from.
The man smiled and said:
"Do you know that the moon is composed of seven treasures?
The moon's shape is like a ball,
its shadows often scorched by the sun.
In its recesses,
there are always eighty-two thousand households repairing it.
I am one of them."
He then opened his bundle,
which contained tools like an axe and chisel.
There were two packets of jade dust rice,
which he gave to the two, saying:
"Share and eat this.
Though it may not grant immortality,
it will prevent illness."
He then stood up,
pointed to a side path for the two,
and said:
"Just follow this,
and you will reach the main road."
After speaking, he disappeared.
A monk from Chǔzhōu,
within the boundaries of Chǔzhōu, there is a small mountain,
with a dwelling on the mountain but no water.
The monk Zhìyī dug a well,
reaching a depth of three zhàng before hitting rock.
He chiseled through the rock and soil,
another fifty chǐ deep,
and found a piece of jade.
It was one chǐ two cun long,
four cun wide,
as red as pomegranate flowers.
Each side had six turtle-like patterns,
purple in color,
Lovely,
the middle seemed capable of holding water.
The monk accidentally struck one corner to examine it,
and it began to drip blood,
which only stopped after half a month.
The son of the Hú family,
the son of the Hú family in Hóngzhōu,
his name is lost.
The Hú family was originally poor,
with five sons,
the youngest of whom
had an exceptionally imposing appearance.
After this son was born,
the family gradually became better off.
Farming and sericulture provided sustenance,
and their wealth gradually increased.
The villagers all found it strange.
The family put this son in charge of a boat loaded with wheat,
sailing upstream to the city market.
Before arriving,
the riverbank was dangerously steep,
and the towpath was impassable.
They cut across the river to cross,
but as the boat reached the shore,
its momentum could not be controlled,
and the sand collapsed, causing the bank to cave in.
In the hole, they found several million coins,
so they abandoned the wheat and loaded the money to return.
From then on, the family grew even richer,
buying servants and horses,
and adorning themselves with fine clothing.
Everyone said this son was blessed.
Not wanting to stay in the village long,
they sent him to travel to the city.
Gradually, he became familiar with worldly affairs.
On the way,
the horse he was riding knelt on the ground and refused to advance.
He turned to his servant and said:
"Where the boat landed, we found money;
now the horse is kneeling,
perhaps there is something here too."
He ordered his attendants to dig there.
They found five hundred taels of gold.
They took it and returned home.
Another day, he went to the city again,
where a foreign merchant encountered him,
knew there was a pearl in his head,
and sent someone to befriend and get close to him,
got him drunk,
and took the pearl away.
Originally, there was a lump of flesh on his forehead,
protruding like a small ball,
but after losing the pearl,
the flesh sank in.
After returning home,
his relatives and friends
all sighed in amazement.
From then on, this son's vitality diminished,
he fell ill and died,
and the family's livelihood gradually declined.
The founding emperor of the Shǔ kingdom,
Emperor Xīzōng of the Táng dynasty,
fled to Hànzhōng,
and the founding emperor of Shǔ, Wáng Jiàn, served as the head of the imperial guards.
He and his companions were throwing dice in a monastery,
and the six dice landed stacked in order,
from one to six.
Everyone was astonished.
Later, he conquered Shǔ.
While visiting Xīngyuán,
he sought out the monastery from that time,
and the monk was still there.
When asked about the past events,
the monk recounted the story of the dice.
The founding emperor was greatly pleased,
and rewarded him generously.
A fisherman from Lúshān.
On Lúshān Mountain, there was a deep pool,
named Luòxīng Tán,
where many people fished.
During the Chángxīng era of the Later Táng dynasty,
a fisherman caught something,
and found it quite difficult to pull in,
dragging it slowly to the shore.
He saw something shaped like a person,
wearing an iron crown,
wrapped in moss and lichen accumulated over the years.
If one thought it was wood, it seemed too heavy;
if one thought it was stone, it seemed too light.
The fisherman placed it beside the pool.
After several days,
the mud, silt, moss, and lichen on the object
were peeled away by wind and sun,
and after being washed by rain,
suddenly both eyes opened—
it was a person.
He abruptly stood up,
and went to the pool water to wash his hands and face.
The fishermen were astonished,
and gathered to watch him.
The man then inquired about
The fishermen
told him the names of the local land, mountains, and rivers,
as well as the dynasty, year, and month in great detail.
After asking,
he turned and entered the water,
leaving no sound or trace.
Yet, no one asked him where he came from.
The officials and people of the southern region found it divine and strange,
and built a shrine and altar by the pool.
Guì Cóngyì
Guì Cóngyì, an official in Chíyáng Jiàndé County,
had a family member who went into the mountains to gather firewood.
On a frequently traveled mountain path,
suddenly a rock collapsed.
Approaching to look,
there was a room.
Inside the room were six gold-lacquered cypress beds,
with rush mats and bamboo mats all new,
and gold and jade piled up.
The person sat on a bed,
and after a long while,
lifted the bamboo mat,
and saw a small knife with a horn handle.
He took it, put it in his bosom, and left.
He propped up the collapsed rock to block it,
and marked the spot with something.
Returning home, he called his family to go together to retrieve it.
When they arrived,
the stone wall was as before,
and nothing was seen at all.
The Wooden Cranes of Jīnjīng Mountain
At Jīnjīng Mountain in Qiánhuà County, Qián Prefecture,
in the time of King Chángshā Wú Ruì,
an immortal,
the place where the female immortal Zhāng Lìyīng ascended to heaven,
a Daoist temple is located there.
The cliff is several hundred feet high,
with two wooden cranes,
which two female immortals ride.
Iron chains hang beneath the cliff,
beyond the reach of ladders or paths,
and it is unknown where they come from.
These two cranes
always turn with the four seasons,
never deviating.
During the Shùnyì era,
a minor officer of the Bǎishèng Army named Chén Shīcàn,
could roll up a mat like a well,
and leap in and out.
Once, he met a village girl under the cliff,
and asked to marry her.
The girl said:
"If you can shoot and hit the eye of this crane,
then it can be done."
Shīcàn then shot and hit it with one arrow,
but his arm immediately lost strength,
and he returned home and fell ill in bed.
As if in a dream yet not a dream,
he saw two female Daoist priests
walking around his bed.
Each time they passed,
they would brush their hands over Shīcàn's eyes,
and after several times, they left.
He eventually lost his sight and died.
The crane he shot
from then on never turned again,
while the other one still turned as before.
In the year Xīnyǒu,
that girl was still alive.
Shīcàn's descendants
also became soldiers.
Old Wáng the Cake Seller
In Guǎnglíng, there was Old Wáng who sold cakes,
without a wife,
living alone with his daughter.
One day, Old Wáng
returned home from selling cakes,
and saw his daughter sleeping with a young man under the north window.
Old Wáng was furious,
grabbed a knife and chased them,
and the young man leaped up and escaped.
Old Wáng was extremely angry,
and so killed his daughter.
As the young man walked on the road,
suddenly blood flowed all over his body.
Officials stopped and questioned him,
but he did not know how to respond.
They detained him and brought him back to Old Wáng's residence,
where neighbors were just investigating the matter.
Old Wáng saw and recognized him,
and so he was punished for the crime.
Táolín Grain
Wáng Shěnzhī, King of Mǐn,
was initially the Prefect of Quán Prefecture.
Several dozen lǐ north of the prefecture,
there was a place named Táolín.
At the beginning of the Guāngqǐ era,
one night,
there was an earthquake in the village with a sound
like hundreds of drums beating.
By dawn, when they looked,
the grain crops were lush,
but not a single stalk remained.
They tried digging the ground to search for them,
and found them all hanging upside down beneath the soil.
That year,
Shěnzhī captured Jìn'ān,
and took possession of all the lands of Ōu and Mǐn.
He passed on the state for sixty years.
When Wáng Yánxī ascended the throne,
there was again the sound of drums in the Táolín fields.
At that time, the grain had already been harvested,
with only stubble remaining in the fields.
By dawn, when they looked,
again not a single stalk remained.
They dug the ground to search,
and again found them hanging upside down beneath the soil.
That year,
Yánxī was killed by his attendants,
and the Wáng clan was thus destroyed.
Wáng Yánzhèng
Wáng Yánzhèng was the Military Commissioner of Jiàn Prefecture.
A man from Yánpíng Village dreamed at night that someone told him:
"I will give you wealth;
go into the mountains tomorrow to seek it."
The next day, he went into the mountains,
but found nothing in the end.
That night,
he dreamed the same as before.
The villager said:
"I already went into the mountains yesterday,
but found nothing."
The person said:
"Just seek it;
why would you not find it?"
So the next day, he went into the mountains again.
Toward evening,
he rested under a large tree,
and saw a square zhàng of ground that was uniquely bright and clean.
He tried digging there,
and found red soil like cinnabar.
Since there was nothing else,
he carried it back.
When used for decoration,
on walls,
it was dazzling and lovely.
People who heard about it
competed to offer high prices
to buy it from this person.
Yánzhèng heard of it,
took it to decorate his palace,
and appointed the man to a yámén position.
After several years,
Jiàn Prefecture also fell.
On the tenth day of the second month in the second year of Chéngshèng of the Liáng dynasty,
Liǔ Cháng, the Registrar of the Minister Over the Masses’s office, died,
and his son Bāo buried him in Jiǔjiāng.
In the third year,
due to heavy rain, the tomb collapsed,
so they moved the burial and replaced the coffin.
They saw that in his father’s coffin, his eyes were open,
and there was warmth in his chest.
After a long while,
he said to Bāo:
"I have been alive for a year now,
but had no way to let you know.
The god of Jiǔjiāng knew that I died unjustly,
so he sent an earth deity to feed me with milk,
which is why I did not die.
Now the rain has destroyed my tomb,
and this too is the doing of the river god."
They helped him out,
and he lived for another thirty years before passing away.
Liú Kǎi
In the second year of Zhēnguān of the Táng dynasty,
Liú Quánsù, the County Captain of Chénliú,
lived in Sòngzhōu.
His father, Kǎi,
had once served as the Magistrate of Wèi County,
and died in office,
and was buried in the outskirts for over thirty years.
Quánsù was in mourning for his mother,
and escorted her remains back to Wèi,
intending to bury them together.
Upon arrival,
they opened the tomb,
and the corpse was as if alive.
Gradually, he revived,
and his son leaped up to support him.
By evening, he could speak, saying:
"It has been a long time—have you been well?"
Quánsù wept and recounted events.
He then said:
"Do not speak,
I know everything."
He quickly ordered water from the eastern stream to be heated.
When it arrived,
he bathed and changed clothes,
drank some congee,
His spirit and energy returned.
He then said:
"In the underworld,
I was appointed as the overseer of the northern Fēng for thirty years.
I judged and managed unresolved cases,
and due to my merits, I was granted rebirth.
Fearing you might have doubts,
I have briefly explained."
He also warned Quánsù not to reveal this to others.
Quánsù then addressed him as Uncle.
Half a year later,
he went to Shǔ and did not return,
and his whereabouts were unknown.
The Person in the Stone Casket
In Wùběn Ward of the Upper Capital,
during the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a household that,
while digging a wall,
encountered a stone casket.
They opened it,
and saw something like silk filling the casket,
which flew out.
While they were looking,
suddenly, a person
rose from the casket,
with disheveled hair over ten feet long,
shook his clothes and stood up,
went out the door and disappeared.
The household suffered no other harm.
Previous records often mention such events,
which pertain to the practice of refining the form in the Great Yin,
when the time is nearly complete,
someone must uncover it.
Dù Xī’s Family Maid
When the Hàn dynasty Dù Xī’s family was buried,
a maid was mistakenly left behind and could not get out.
Over ten years later,
when the tomb was opened for an additional burial,
the maid was still alive.
When asked,
she said:
"At first, it was like closing my eyes,
and I thought it would only be a night or two."
When the maid was buried,
she was fifteen or sixteen years old.
After the tomb was opened,
her appearance remained unchanged.
She lived another fifteen or sixteen years.
She married and had children.
Hàn Palace Lady
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
Guānzhōng was in great turmoil.
Someone opened the tomb of a palace lady from the former Hàn period,
and she was still alive.
After emerging,
she recovered as before.
Wèi Empress Guō cherished and cared for her,
took her into the palace,
and kept her by her side.
When asked about affairs inside the Hàn palace,
she recounted them clearly,
all in proper order.
When Empress Guō passed away,
she mourned excessively,
and then died.
Lǐ É
At the end of the Hàn dynasty,
a woman from Wǔlíng named Lǐ É,
sixty years old,
fell ill and died,
and was buried outside the city,
for half a month.
É’s neighbor, Cài Zhòng,
hearing that É was wealthy,
opened the tomb to seek gold.
As he split the coffin with an axe,
É suddenly called from inside the coffin:
"Cài Zhòng, protect my head!"
Zhòng fled in terror,
He was captured by county officers,
and sentenced to public execution.
É’s son heard his mother was alive,
and came to welcome her out.
The Grand Administrator summoned É to inquire about the situation,
and É replied:
"I was mistakenly summoned by the Director of Fate,
and was sent back upon arrival.
Outside the gate,
I saw my elder brother Liú Wénbó,
and we were shocked and wept together.
I said:
‘I was mistakenly summoned,
and now I can return.
I do not know the way,
nor can I travel alone,
please find me a companion.
I have been here over ten days,
and my family has already buried me,
how can I return on my own?’
Wénbó then sent a gatekeeper to inform the Household Registrar.
The reply was:
‘Now in the western region of Wǔlíng,
there is a man named Lǐ Hēi,
who is also returning,
so he can be a companion.
Additionally, order Hēi to pass by É’s neighbor,
and have Cài Zhòng open the tomb.’
Thus, Wénbó wrote a letter to my son,
and I returned together with Hēi."
When the Grand Administrator heard this,
he pardoned Cài Zhòng.
He then dispatched a mounted officer
to inquire in the western region about Lǐ Hēi,
and it was as É had described.
The letter Wénbó sent to the son,
the son recognized the paper,
as it was from the box sent when his father passed away.
Héjiān Woman
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn,
in Héjiān, there was a man and woman who were in love,
and they promised to marry each other.
However, the man joined the army,
and for many years did not return.
The woman’s family arranged for her to marry someone else.
The woman was unwilling to go,
but her parents forced her, and she left.
Soon after, she fell ill and died.
When her former lover returned from military service,
he asked where the woman was.
Her family told him everything.
He then went to her grave,
intending to weep and express his grief,
but he could not contain his emotions.
So he opened the grave and the coffin,
and the woman immediately revived.
He then carried her back home,
and after nursing her, she recovered fully.
Later, her husband heard about this,
and went to the authorities to dispute the matter.
The local officials could not decide the case,
so they referred it to the Commandant of Justice.
The memorial submitted stated that due to the utmost sincerity,
which moved heaven and earth,
she had died and come back to life.
This was an extraordinary event,
and could not be judged by ordinary principles.
They requested that the one who opened the coffin be returned to her.
The Daughter of Xú Xuánfāng
During the Jìn dynasty, in Dōngpíng,
Féng Xiàojiāng,
Governor of Guǎngzhōu,
had a son named Mǎzi,
over twenty years old.
He was sleeping alone in the stable,
when at night he dreamed of a young woman,
about eighteen or nineteen years old.
She said, "I am the daughter of Xú Xuánfāng, Governor of Běihǎi,
unfortunately I died young.
It has been four years since my death,
and I was wrongfully killed by a ghost.
According to the register of the living,
I was supposed to live over eighty years.
I have been permitted to return to life.
But I must have someone to rely on,
in order to revive,
and I am also destined to be your wife.
Will you agree to entrust yourself to me and save me?"
Mǎzi replied:
"I can do that."
She set a date with Mǎzi for when she would emerge.
When the day arrived,
hair appeared in front of the bed,
just level with the ground.
He ordered someone to sweep it away,
but it became even more distinct.
Then he realized it was the one from his dream,
so he dismissed the attendants.
Gradually, her forehead and face emerged,
then her head and body suddenly,
appeared.
Mǎzi then had her sit on the couch opposite him,
and she spoke,
with an extraordinary and marvelous manner.
She then slept with Mǎzi.
She often cautioned him, saying:
"I am still insubstantial."
He asked when she could fully emerge,
and she replied:
"My emergence must wait
until my original birthday,
which has not yet arrived."
She then went to the stable.
Her speech and voice
could be heard by everyone.
The woman calculated the arrival of her birthday,
and fully instructed Mǎzi on the method to bring her out and care for her,
then, after speaking, she bowed and left.
Mǎzi followed her instructions,
and on the day,
with a red rooster,
a plate of millet rice,
and a sheng of clear wine,
he made an offering before her burial place,
about ten paces from the stable.
After the sacrifice,
he dug up the coffin.
Opening it to look,
he saw the woman's body was completely intact as before.
He slowly carried her out,
placed her in a felt tent,
and only her heart area was slightly warm,
and she had breath in her mouth.
He ordered four maids to guard and care for her.
They regularly dripped green goat's milk into her eyes.
She began to open her mouth,
able to swallow porridge,
and gradually she could speak.
After two hundred days, she could get up and walk with a cane.
After one full year,
her complexion, skin, and strength were all restored to normal.
He then sent word to the Xú family,
and all of them, high and low, came.
They selected an auspicious day for the ceremony,
and they were married as husband and wife.
They had two sons:
the elder son was named Yuánqìng,
Yǒngjiā,
Initially,
he served as a Secretary Gentleman;
the younger son, Jìngdù,
served as an Assistant to the Grand Tutor.
Their daughter married Liú Zǐyàn of Jǐnán,
grandson of the Recluse Scholar Yánshì.
The Wife of Cài Zhī
Cài Zhī of Línzī
was a county clerk.
Once, he was delivering a document to the Governor.
Suddenly he lost his way,
and arrived at the foot of Mount Dàizōng,
where he saw something like a walled city,
so he entered to deliver the document.
He saw an official,
whose ceremonial guards were very strict,
fully resembling a Governor.
Then a lavish feast of wine and food was set out,
and finally, he handed over a letter.
He said:
"Clerk, deliver this letter for me to my grandson."
The clerk asked:
"Who is Your Honor's grandson?"
He replied:
"I am the God of Tàishān,
and my grandson is the Heavenly Emperor."
Only then did the clerk realize with shock
that where he had arrived was not the human world.
The clerk went out the gate,
and rode his horse to where he was directed.
After a while,
he suddenly reached the Heavenly Emperor's seat in the Tàiwēi Palace.
The attendants on both sides
were fully like those of the Son of Heaven.
After Zhī delivered the letter,
the Emperor ordered him to sit,
and bestowed wine and food upon him.
Then he inquired kindly, saying:
"How many family members does the clerk have?"
He replied that his parents and wife had all passed away,
and he had not yet remarried.
The Emperor said:
"How many years has it been since your wife died?"
The clerk said:
"Three years."
The Emperor said:
"Would you like to see her?"
Zhī said:
"I am grateful, only by the Heavenly Emperor's grace."
The Emperor then ordered the Minister of the Household Department,
commanding the Director of Fate to remove Cài Zhī's wife's name from the register of the living,
and then ordered her to go with Zhī.
He then revived and returned home,
so he opened his wife's grave,
and looked at her remains.
Indeed, there were signs of life,
and in a moment she sat up,
and spoke just as before.
The Maid of Chén Lǎng
In the fourth year of Yìxī,
the maid of Chén Lǎng of Lángyá died,
and had already been buried.
The government clerk Xià Jià returned,
and as he passed in front of the grave,
he heard a human voice from within the earth,
and looked at it in surprise.
The maid said:
"I have now revived,
report to my family for me."
As it was already dusk that day,
they opened the earth the next morning to retrieve her,
and she was strong and healthy as usual.
The Family Servant of Gān Bǎo
Yú Bǎo, styled Lìngshēng,
his father Yíng
served as Assistant Magistrate of Dānyáng.
He had a favored maidservant,
whom his mother greatly envied.
When Yíng died,
and was buried,
the mother then pushed
the maidservant alive into the tomb.
Yú Bǎo and his brothers were still young,
and did not know the details.
More than ten years later,
when their mother died and the tomb was opened,
the maidservant was found lying on the coffin as if alive.
They carried her back,
and after a full day she revived.
She said her father's affection was as before,
and she did not feel it was bad in the underworld.
Later she was married off,
and bore children.
Wéi Fěng's Maidservant
In the Táng dynasty, Wéi Fěng's family resided in Rǔyǐng.
He often remained quiet and withdrawn,
not seeking to make friends.
When free from study,
he tended his garden,
personally engaging in planting.
A young servant weeding and hoeing the ground
saw human hair.
As he hoed deeper,
more hair appeared, neatly arranged,
as if freshly combed.
Fěng found this strange,
and dug over a foot deep.
He saw a woman's head,
her skin and complexion
vivid as if alive.
Using spades and shovels further,
he uncovered her entire body,
only her clothes turned to dust at the touch.
Her vitality gradually strengthened,
and soon she could rise,
bowing twice in greeting.
She said she was a maidservant of Fěng's grandfather,
named Lìróng.
Initially, she had committed a fault,
and the mistress was very jealous.
When the master was away,
she was buried alive in the garden.
They claimed she had died from other causes,
so no outsider knew.
When she first died,
she was led away by two men in black.
They arrived at a place,
a vast hall with great gates.
The guards were very stern.
She bowed to their king,
who briefly asked the reason.
The men in black explained the situation,
and she dared not accuse the mistress.
After a moment,
she was led to an office.
She saw documents piled to the roof,
clerks, some two, some five,
searching busily.
A clerk first questioned her with a file,
checked the records,
and said her time to die had not come,
but the mistress, out of jealousy,
had unlawfully killed her.
They decided to deduct eleven years of the mistress's lifespan and give it to her.
Then another judge reviewed the case.
The matter was also clear.
But the judge soon had other reasons
and was punished and removed from his post,
so her case was shelved.
For over ninety years,
they dispersed.
Suddenly yesterday, celestial officials came to search for unresolved cases in the underworld,
all were decided and dispatched,
and she finally received judgment.
Those like her
were very numerous,
likely because as lowly people,
the underworld officials were not urgent.
The celestial officials were like today's Daoist priests,
in crimson robes and red caps.
Feathered riders followed them.
They resolved the stagnant cases,
ordering her rebirth,
and she would not lose the eleven years of lifespan.
Fěng asked:
"Since the soul went somewhere,
why did the body not decay?"
She replied:
"For all whose matters are unfinished,
the local underworld lords apply medicine to preserve them,
so they do not decay."
Fěng was astonished,
bathed her and gave her new clothes.
She looked about twenty years old.
Later she secretly spoke of underworld affairs,
covering everything,
and Fěng also understood them clearly.
He often said:
"Cultivate oneself and accumulate virtue,
for blessings are not repaid without reason.
The way of immortals
should be diligently sought."
Several years later,
Fěng and the maidservant disappeared.
Relatives and his family found遗留 writings,
recording the rebirth event.
This was in the eighth month of the second year of Wǔdé.
Woman from Yèzhōng
Dòu Jiàndé
once excavated a tomb in Yèzhōng,
finding no other items.
Opening the coffin,
he saw a woman,
her complexion as if alive,
extremely beautiful,
appearing over twenty.
Her clothing and style
were not of recent times.
Observing her,
she seemed to have breath.
So he took her back to the army and cared for her.
After three days she revived,
able to speak.
She said:
"I was a palace maid of Emperor Wén of Wèi,
following Empress Zhēn in Yè,
and was buried here upon death.
My fate destined revival,
but I had no family to appeal to,
so I remained secluded.
I do not know what time it is now."
She described Empress Zhēn's harm clearly.
Jiàndé greatly favored her.
Later, when Jiàndé was defeated by Tàizōng,
the Emperor intended to take her in.
She fully explained the events,
and declined, saying:
"I have been secluded in the yellow earth
for three hundred years.
If not for Lord Dòu, how could I see today?
Death is my lot."
She then died with regret,
and the Emperor was deeply saddened.
Lǐ Zhòngtōng's Maidservant
During the Kāiyuán era,
Lǐ Zhòngtōng
served as Magistrate of Yānlíng County.
A maidservant died
and was buried in Yānlíng.
After three years,
he was transferred as Magistrate of Pí County in Shǔ.
While sweeping the floor,
a family member saw hair emerging from the earth.
Sweeping repeatedly did not remove it,
so they pulled it by hand.
The Yānlíng maidservant came out with the pull,
dazed as if drunk.
The family asked how she got there.
She said:
"It was just like waking from sleep."
Zhòngtōng thought she was a ghost,
so he washed her with peachwood decoction,
wrote talismans to ward her off.
The maidservant showed no fear,
laughing happily as before.
He then confined her in a separate room,
fed her cakes,
and she ate normally.
After over a month, he released her.
She was employed as before,
then married to a servant as wife.
She bore one son and two daughters,
and lived another seventeen years before dying.
Cuī Shēng's Wife
During the Yuánhé era,
there was a man named Cuī,
who had previously married a woman from the Xiāo family.
They had a son before she passed away,
and he later married a woman from the Zhèng family.
Twelve years after Xiāo’s death,
she appeared in a dream to her son, saying:
“I have been granted permission to return to life in the mortal world.
Can you tell your mother for me,
if she can open my grave?”
Though the son dreamed this,
he could not speak of it.
Three days later,
he had the same dream again,
but still could not bring himself to speak.
The Zhèng wife was virtuous and kind.
Xiāo then spoke through an elderly servant, saying:
“Tell Lady Zhèng for me
to quickly exhume me.
If two more days pass,
it will be too late.”
The old servant cried out:
“The mistress has come back to life!”
Lady Zhèng consulted a diviner, who said:
“There is no sign of life.”
So she stopped.
The next day, the servant said again:
“The mistress has come back to life!”
Lady Zhèng consulted the diviner once more,
and the diviner said:
“There is a sign of life.”
They opened the grave,
and indeed, she was moving.
They carried her back,
and Lady Zhèng fed her congee.
Her breath returned, and she could speak.
She spoke of how, in the underworld, she knew of the kindness and care she had received.
She also said:
“At first, there was a turtle
that circled my remains and then left.
After several days,
it returned and circled again.
It kept leaving and coming back,
and then it bit my toe.”
Thus it was understood that when the divination earlier showed no sign of life,
it was because the turtle was only circling;
but when later it showed a sign of life,
it was because the turtle had bitten her toe.
Xiāo and Zhèng lived together like sisters,
with affection as deep as flesh and blood.
She lived for another ten years before passing away.
The Daughter of a Dōnglái Man
A man from Dōnglái had a daughter who died
and was buried.
The girl went to the underworld,
but because she had been wrongfully seized, she was allowed to return.
Two underworld officials were ordered to escort her back.
The ghosts delivered her to her tomb,
but though she was alive, she had no way to get out.
The ghosts were also troubled by this,
so they asked the girl:
“Aside from your parents at home,
who misses you the most?”
The girl said:
“Only my youngest uncle.”
One ghost said:
“I can make him come to rob the tomb.
When your youngest uncle sees you alive,
you will be saved.”
The girl said:
“My youngest uncle is kind and compassionate,
and has never done anything wrong.
How could he possibly dig up my grave?”
The ghost said:
“I will change his heart.”
One ghost stayed to guard her,
while the other left.
Soon after, the youngest uncle arrived with a group of tomb robbers,
intending to open the coffin.
The girl suddenly rose from the coffin,
and her youngest uncle, shocked, asked her what had happened.
She told him everything.
The youngest uncle,
was filled with shame and regret.
The other robbers wanted to kill her,
but the youngest uncle wept and pleaded, saving her life.
He carried her home.
Zhèng Huì
Zhèng Huì of Xíngyáng,
whose home was south of the Wèi River,
was known from a young age for his strength.
In the late Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
when Ān Lùshān rebelled,
bandits rose up everywhere,
and people gathered in groups in the prefectures and counties.
Relying on his strength,
Huì remained at his village residence,
and many relatives depended on him.
Huì often rode a single horse
to scout for bandits far and wide,
and this went on for months.
Later, he suddenly did not return for five days,
and his family grew worried.
However, because of the bandit threat,
no one dared to search for him.
Suddenly, a spirit voice spoke from a tree in his household,
calling for “Ā’nǎi,”
which was the wet nurse of Huì’s wife.
The family was terrified and hid.
The voice spoke again:
“Ā’nǎi, don’t you recognize Huì?
Earlier, I went to scout for bandits,
but encountered them,
and being outnumbered,
I was killed.
Because my time to die had not yet come,
I pleaded repeatedly with the underworld officials,
and now I have been granted permission
to be reborn.
My body is in a ditch by the roadside, five lǐ north of this village.
Bring a torch
and clothes to retrieve it.”
The family did as instructed
and found his body in the ditch,
but his head was missing.
They heard the voice again:
“The head is about a hundred paces north,
under a mulberry tree root.
When you return home,
use bark from the grain tree to make thread
and stitch it together.
I will not come again.
Be careful not to make mistakes.”
After speaking,
it let out a ghostly whistle and departed.
The family returned home,
stitched everything together as instructed,
and his body gradually grew warm.
After several days,
he could see again.
They constantly fed him rice water,
and after a hundred days, he was back to normal.
Wáng Mù
Wáng Mù of Tàiyuán,
in the early Zhìdé era of the Táng dynasty,
served as a general under Lǔ Mín.
After being defeated in battle at Nányáng,
his army and horses fled in disarray.
Wáng Mù was of imposing stature,
and his horse was exceptionally large,
so many enemy cavalry pursued him.
When they caught up,
one struck Wáng Mù's neck from behind with a sword,
killing him and causing him to fall to the ground.
His tendons and bones were severed,
with only his throat still connected.
At first, he was dazed and unaware he had died;
only after the time it takes to eat a meal did he realize,
finding his head lying on his navel,
and only then did he feel distress.
He soon felt food leaking out,
so he used his hands to lift his head
and reattach it to his neck.
After a short while, it fell off again,
and he lost consciousness as before,
reviving only after a long time.
After properly aligning his neck,
he tied his hair to both sides
and was able to sit up.
His mind was in a daze,
unaware of how he had survived.
The horse he had been riding
had never left Wáng Mù's side.
When Wáng Mù got up,
it came and stopped before him.
Wáng Mù leaned on it to stand,
but the hair tie on his left shoulder came loose,
and his head fell into his lap.
Only after nightfall did he revive again.
After tying his hair and properly positioning his head,
Wáng Mù thought to himself
that only if the horse lay down could he mount it.
Suddenly, the horse lay down sideways before him,
allowing him to get on.
The horse then stood up
and carried Wáng Mù southeast.
Wáng Mù held his head with both hands against his cheeks.
After the horse traveled forty *lǐ*,
a group of over ten scattered soldiers from Wáng Mù's command
were also searching for him along the way.
They saw him,
supported him, and took him to a village house.
The place was over forty *lǐ* from enemy territory,
and everyone was anxious and fearful.
They then carried him back to Lǔ Mín's army.
The army's city was soon besieged by the enemy.
Wáng Mù recuperated within the city,
taking over two hundred days to recover.
Around his neck, flesh grew as thick as a finger,
and his head ended up slightly tilted.
Lǔ Mín, considering Wáng Mù a son of a distinguished family
and one who had sacrificed himself,
for the ruler's cause,
appointed him acting magistrate of Nányáng.
Soon, he was recommended as magistrate of Yè.
After over a year,
he was transferred to magistrate of Línrǔ.
After his term ended,
he served as acting magistrate of Zǎoyáng.
He died in office.
Shào Jìn
In the first year of the Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
Zhōu Zhìguāng served as prefect of Huázhōu.
He robbed and plundered travelers,
and soon plotted rebellion.
He sent his subordinate Shào Jìn
secretly to the capital
to spy on the court's intentions regarding military action.
Shào Jìn returned and reported:
"The court has no suspicions about you."
Zhōu Zhìguāng was enraged,
believing Shào Jìn had betrayed the court and deceived him,
and immediately ordered him beheaded.
Soon after, he deeply regretted it,
and quickly sent the head to Shào Jìn's wife and children.
His wife immediately sewed the neck back with a needle,
and shortly after, he revived.
She applied medicine to it,
but they still feared Zhōu Zhìguāng,
so they sent someone to tell him:
"Shào Jìn was originally from Pú;
now we wish to return him there for burial."
Zhōu Zhìguāng also provided funeral gifts.
Once they reached Pú,
after ten days,
the wound healed completely,
and he changed his surname and traveled elsewhere.
Thirty years later,
when Cuī Yóng was governor of Sòngzhōu,
during morning court,
a man presented his name card,
saying:
"I am a former clerk."
Cuī Yóng summoned him for an audience.
When questioned about his background,
Shào Jìn said:
"Your Excellency once served as an aide to Zhōu Zhìguāng."
He then recounted the whole story.
Cuī Yóng then realized
and gave him silk fabric,
bowed, and sent him away.
A Soldier of Grand Commandant Lǐ
According to tales from the alleys of Cháng'ān,
during the rebellion of Zhū Cǐ,
there was a soldier in Grand Commandant Lǐ's army
who was struck by a rebel soldier's blade,
severing his head from his body.
After seven days,
he suddenly, without knowing why, rose by himself.
He only felt his skull was stiff and hard,
his throat stronger than before,
and the wound where he was struck itched intensely.
He could walk without difficulty,
and with support, returned to his home.
His wife and children were astonished,
and when they asked about what happened,
he described in detail the experience of his body being separated from his head.
He was completely unaware of the harm,
and had no memory of his hometown.
Suddenly, he was driven into a city gate,
and led along with thousands of dead soldiers.
When they reached the eastern side,
there was a large office.
He saw a green-robed senior official leaning on a desk,
checking names on a register as they passed.
When it was his turn,
the official said:
"You should not have come."
He then reprimanded him severely,
and attendants chased him out and ordered him back.
He saw someone from the underworld,
holding a mulberry wood peg as thick as an arm,
shaped like a buoy nail.
He attached it to where the man's head and body were severed.
As if ordered to join them,
he drove the mulberry wood peg from the brain into the throat,
and shortly after, the man became conscious.
He saw the sun and moon again.
There was not much pain.
His wife and children thus parted his hair on top to look,
and saw a raised area over an inch high,
quite unusual.
Under the skin, the yellow grain of the mulberry wood remained visible.
Some people called it "fěndài."
During the Yuánhé era,
Wēn Huì had a clansman named Wēn Shǒuqīng,
who served as a provisional general in the Bīnzhèn garrison.
When this story was mentioned,
Shǒuqīng called the man forward.
He then said
this was Gěng Hào, a cavalry soldier under his command,
now over seventy years old,
whose physical strength could still match several men.
Wēn Huì thus personally witnessed this marvel.
A Wǔyuán Military Officer
Wǔyuán dispatched a military officer to Yángzǐ,
to request clothing provisions.
The officer was knowledgeable,
capable of receiving inquiries.
The court official engaged him in conversation,
and noticed a ring of flesh encircling his neck,
a scar that was frightening to behold.
The court official, being familiar with him,
inquired about its origin,
and he recounted in full.
In years past, while patrolling the border,
his troop of five or six hundred men,
ventured deep into Yúsài.
They were ambushed by enemy cavalry,
numbering several thousand,
all mounted.
These five hundred infantrymen,
were completely annihilated.
The corpses were piled into a mound,
and his head was severed from his body.
As dusk fell,
his spirit only felt a shouting,
resembling an official conducting a roll call.
When it came to him,
the official angrily said:
"This man should not have died,
why was he killed?"
The clerk kowtowed, pleading for mercy.
The official said:
"If he is not revived,
you must repay with your life."
The clerk said:
"He can be revived."
He then agreed,
after a long while, he was called back,
and further instructed:
"He must be revived quickly,
do not,
delay the dead."
The clerk loudly assented.
His head was placed back on his neck,
and his body lay on a bed of leaves three feet thick.
Beside his head was half a bowl of thin gruel,
a broken-handled spoon,
inserted in the bowl.
He managed to reach out and take the spoon,
scoop it into his mouth,
gradually able to eat.
Then he fell into a daze and slept again.
When he opened his eyes,
he saw another half bowl of gruel,
with the spoon also in it.
This continued for six or seven days,
until he could walk,
and leaning on a staff, he returned to his original place.
Time passed until today,
and that scar remains.
Fàn Lìngqīng
In the second year of the Kāihuáng era of Emperor Wén of Suí,
Fàn Qīnzi Lìngqīng, a clerk in Jùnyì County, Biànzhōu,
was at home studying texts with his clansman Wén Zhì,
competing over skill and clumsiness.
Lìngqīng struck Wén Zhì with the back of his hand,
causing his nose to bleed incessantly,
and he consequently died.
Wén Zhì's father then seized Lìngqīng,
hung him with a rope from the roof beam,
and after a while, he ceased breathing.
Wén Zhì's parents, fearing Lìngqīng might revive,
again used cloth to strangle him tightly.
After being dead for three days,
Lìngqīng revived,
while Wén Zhì passed away forever.
Tāng Shìzǐ
Tāng Shìzǐ,
his father was the sheriff of Lèpíng.
The magistrate, surnamed Lǐ,
was from a prominent Lǒngxī family.
He was habitually contemptuous,
often mocking and insulting people from Wú,
which greatly displeased the sheriff.
The sheriff was repeatedly humiliated by the magistrate,
this had happened many times,
and the sheriff could no longer endure it.
He and his brother,
went to the magistrate to argue.
The magistrate berated them,
shouted for attendants to drag them down,
intending to beat them,
he had a sword hidden in his bosom,
stepped forward and stabbed the magistrate,
hitting his chest but not deeply,
and the magistrate died a few days later.
The magistrate's family also seized him and imprisoned him.
The prefecture passed judgment,
as the magistrate died within the period of responsibility for injuries,
he was to be executed.
As he was taken to the market,
he showed no distress.
A skilled physiognomist said:
"This youth has the appearance of a fifth-rank official,
he certainly will not die.
If he dies,
I will never read faces again."
The executioner,
applied the rope to him,
and after the execution, he ceased breathing.
Dragged back to prison,
by evening he revived.
The jailer reported to the official,
the official said:
"He killed with his own hand,
by principle, he should not live."
Ordered the jailer to strangle him with a rope until dead.
That night at the third watch,
he revived again.
The jailer strangled him again,
and by dawn, he revived again.
The prison officer reported to the prefect,
and the entire prefecture marveled.
But the law's limits could not be overstepped.
They summoned his father,
and ordered him to kill his own son.
At the prefecture gate,
before the crowd, he was strangled until dead.
The prefect pitied his ordeal from beginning to end,
and ordered his family to retrieve the body.
As they were about to return home,
he revived again.
They therefore buried an empty coffin,
and kept him hidden in a dark room.
After a long time, he remained unharmed.
During the Qiányuán era,
he became the magistrate of Quánjiāo and later died.
Scholar Jiǎ
During the reign of Emperor Yuándì of the Jìn Dynasty,
there was a man, Mr. Jiǎ,
from a distinguished family of officials and scholars,
who died suddenly from a violent illness.
He saw someone taking him up to heaven,
to visit the Director of Fate.
The Director of Fate re-examined the case,
and found that his allotted lifespan had not yet expired;
he should not have been wrongly summoned.
The officials in charge were ordered to send him back.
However, Mr. Jiǎ's feet were in severe pain,
and he could not walk,
so he had no way to return.
Several of the officials in charge were worried together,
and said to each other:
"If Mr. Jiǎ ultimately cannot return due to his foot pain,
we will be guilty of wrongfully summoning a person."
So they went together to report the matter to the Director of Fate.
The Director of Fate pondered for a long time,
and said:
"We have just summoned a foreigner named Kāng Yǐ,
who is outside the west gate.
This man is supposed to die soon,
and his feet are very strong.
Exchange them,
and neither party will suffer loss."
The officials in charge received the instruction and went out,
intending to make the exchange.
The foreigner's body was extremely ugly,
and his feet were particularly repulsive,
so Mr. Jiǎ adamantly refused.
The officials said:
"If you, sir, do not exchange,
then you will simply remain here forever."
Having no other choice,
he finally agreed to it.
The officials ordered both men to close their eyes.
In an instant,
the feet of the two men
had already been exchanged.
They then immediately sent him back,
and he suddenly revived,
and told his family everything in detail.
They looked,
and indeed they were foreign feet,
covered with tangled, matted hair,
and moreover had a foreign odor.
Mr. Jiǎ was originally a scholar,
who cherished and took pride in his hands and feet.
To suddenly get these,
he absolutely did not want to see them.
Although he had regained his life,
he was constantly distressed,
almost wishing he were dead.
Someone who knew this foreigner,
whose body had not yet been buried,
and whose home was near Qiézi Pǔ,
told Mr. Jiǎ. He personally went to see the foreigner's corpse.
Indeed, he saw his own feet attached to the foreigner's body.
They were just preparing for the burial.
He wept facing it.
The foreigner's sons were deeply filial.
Every festival and the first of the month,
the sons would grieve and long for their father.
They would rush over,
embrace Mr. Jiǎ's feet and wail loudly.
Sometimes they would meet him on the road by chance,
and would cling to him and cry.
Because of this, whenever Mr. Jiǎ went out or came in,
he always had people guard the gate,
to prevent the foreigner's sons from entering.
For the rest of his life, he loathed and found his feet filthy,
and never looked at them with pleasure.
Even during the hottest days of the three summer periods,
he would always wear multiple layers of clothing,
never exposing them even briefly.
Lǐ Jiǎn
At the end of the Táng Dynasty's Kāiyuán era,
a commoner named Lǐ Jiǎn from Nánlǐ Village, Shàngcài County, Càizhōu,
died from epilepsy.
More than ten days after his burial,
a commoner named Zhāng Hóngyì from Rǔyáng County,
who originally had no acquaintance with Lǐ Jiǎn,
and whose residence was over ten *shè* away,
also fell ill,
and after one night, revived.
He no longer recognized his parents, wife, or children,
and said, "I am Lǐ Jiǎn,
my home is in Nánlǐ Village, Shàngcài County,
my father's name is Liàng."
He then went straight to Nánlǐ Village,
and entered Liàng's house.
Liàng, astonished, asked him the reason.
He said that when he first fell ill,
he dreamed of two men dressed in yellow,
who came with a summons to pursue him.
After traveling several tens of *lǐ*,
they reached a great city,
with a sign that read "City of the King."
They led him into a place,
like the Six Offices in the human world.
He stayed there for several days,
and regarding the matters he was interrogated about,
he simply could not answer.
Suddenly, a man came in from outside,
saying that Lǐ Jiǎn had been wrongly pursued,
and he should be released immediately.
One clerk said:
"Lǐ Jiǎn's body has decayed,
we must order him to be reborn elsewhere."
At that moment, he thought of his parents and relatives,
and did not wish to be reborn in another place,
so he requested to return to his original body.
After a short while,
he saw someone leading a person in,
who reported:
"We have pursued and brought Zhāng Hóngyì, a minor official from Rǔyáng."
The clerk said again:
"Fortunately, Zhāng Hóngyì's body is not yet decayed.
Quickly order Lǐ Jiǎn to inhabit his body,
to live out his remaining years."
He was then supported by two clerks and led out of the city.
He walked very quickly,
gradually losing awareness,
and suddenly it was as if he awoke from a dream.
He saw people weeping around him,
and the house and buildings,
none of which he recognized anymore.
Liàng asked him about the names of his relatives,
and various details of his past life,
and there was nothing he did not know.
He had previously been skilled in bamboo work,
so he went to rest in a room,
asked for a knife and tools,
and split bamboo to make a container.
His speech, tone, and mannerisms
were indeed those of Lǐ Jiǎn.
He ultimately did not return to Rǔyáng.
At that time, Duàn Chéngshì's paternal third uncle,
who was acting as Registrar of Càizhōu,
personally verified this matter.
In ancient times, Biǎn Què exchanged the hearts of Lǔ Gōnghù and Zhào Qíyīng.
When they awoke,
they returned to each other's homes,
and the two families consulted each other.
Judging by this case,
it is not just a fable.
Zhú Jìzhēn
Between Chén and Cài,
there was a commoner named Zhú Jìzhēn,
who had been dead for over ten years.
Later, a fellow villager named Zhào Zǐhé also died,
but after a few days, he suddenly awoke
and immediately got up and rushed out the door.
His wife and children were startled
and went forward to question him.
Zǐhé said:
"I am Zhú Jìzhēn,
how should I know you?
Now I am going back to my own home."
Soon, his speech no longer sounded like Zǐhé's,
so his wife and children followed him.
When they reached Jìzhēn's home,
the family saw Zǐhé arriving
and thought he was insane,
so they scolded and drove him away.
Zǐhé said:
"I am Zhú Jìzhēn,
who died eleven years ago,
and now I have returned.
Why do you reject me?"
His family listened to his words,
and indeed it was Jìzhēn.
They examined the matter,
and it was indeed Jìzhēn.
His wife and children were all astonished and bewildered,
and upon questioning him,
Jìzhēn said:
"Since I left the human world,
it has been nearly twelve years now.
While dwelling in the underworld,
I longed to return and see my wife and children,
not forgetting for a single day.
However, in the underworld, every thirty years,
one deceased person is allowed to be reborn,
to speak of sins and blessings.
Recently, I pleaded with the case officer,
and my name was reported to the underworld officials.
I wished to be the one reborn,
and then the underworld official said to me:
'Your dwelling has long been ruined,
what can be done?'
The case officer replied:
'There is a man named Zhào Zǐhé from the same village as Jìzhēn,
who died a few days ago.
I wish to borrow his corpse for Jìzhēn's soul.'
The underworld official granted it.
He immediately sent an escort to deliver me to the Zhào family's dwelling,
and thus I was able to return."
He then recounted past events,
clearly and convincingly,
and only then did his wife and children believe and accept him.
From then on, Jìzhēn abstained from wine and meat,
wore short, coarse clothing,
and begged for alms between Chén, Cài, Rǔ, and Zhèng.
With the silk and cloth he received, he cultivated Buddhism,
and gave to the poor and hungry.
He returned home once,
and to this day, he is still alive.
Lù Yàn
Lù Yàn, a man from Yúháng,
died in the summer for over ten days,
and then saw the King of the Underworld.
The King said:
"Your life span is not yet exhausted,
so you are released to return."
The attendants said:
"His dwelling is ruined and unusable.
At this time, a man named Lǐ Tán from Cāngzhōu had newly arrived,
and this man was fated to die."
The King said:
"Take Tán's dwelling and give it to him."
Yàn then entered Tán's coffin and revived.
He then spoke in the Wú dialect,
and did not recognize his wife and children.
He recounted the entire event.
He then went to Yúháng,
and found his family.
His wife and children did not recognize him,
but after he explained the whole story,
they believed him.
Zhào Tài
Jìn Zhào Tài, courtesy name Wénhé,
was from Bèiqiū in Qīnghé Commandery.
His grandfather served as the Grand Administrator of Jīngzhào.
Tài was nominated as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate in his commandery,
but declined appointment by the ducal offices.
He devoted himself to studying the sacred classics,
and was praised in his hometown.
He entered government service late in life,
and ultimately reached the position of Palace Attendant.
When Tài was thirty-five years old,
he once suffered a sudden heart pain,
and died shortly after.
His body was laid on the ground,
but his heart remained warm, not cold,
and his limbs could be flexed and extended at will.
After being dead for ten days,
suddenly there was a sound like rain in his throat,
and soon after he revived.
He recounted that when he first died,
he dreamed of a person
who came near his chest.
Then there were two others,
riding yellow horses,
with two attendants,
who held Tài under the arms,
and directly took him eastward.
He did not know how many miles it was,
until they reached a great city,
towering and lofty,
the city walls were bluish-black in color,
and they then took Tài toward the city gate.
Passing through two gates,
there were tile-roofed buildings,
numbering perhaps several thousand rooms.
Men and women, young and old,
also numbered several thousand.
They stood in rows, and clerks dressed in black robes,
five or six of them,
were sorting out names.
They said:
"We shall present the list to the Prefect according to the categories."
Tài's name was thirtieth on the list.
Shortly after,
they led Tài and several thousand men and women,
all advancing together at once.
The Prefect sat facing west,
finished reviewing the register of names,
and then sent Tài south through an inner gate.
There was a person dressed in crimson,
sitting under a large building,
calling out names in order.
He asked what crimes they had committed during their lives,
what acts of blessing and goodness they had performed,
and told them to speak truthfully.
He constantly dispatches six-part envoys to the human world,
who record good and evil deeds,
all having detailed accounts,
so one cannot be false.
Tài replied:
"My father and elder brothers served as officials with salaries of two thousand shi.
I was young and stayed at home,
merely studying,
not engaging in any affairs,
and also did not commit any evil."
They then appointed Tài as an overseer clerk for the Water Office,
leading over two thousand people,
transporting sand to reinforce the riverbanks,
toiling diligently day and night.
Later, Tài was transferred to be the Commander of the Water Office,
in charge of the various prison affairs.
They provided Tài with soldiers and horses,
ordering him to inspect the hells.
Wherever he went, the various hells
each had different forms of torment.
Some had needles piercing their tongues,
blood flowing all over their bodies.
Others had disheveled hair,
naked and barefoot,
pulling each other along as they walked.
There were those holding large staffs,
urging them from behind.
Iron beds and bronze pillars,
were heated until glowing red.
They drove these people,
forcing them to embrace and lie upon them,
upon contact they were scorched and mangled,
but soon revived again.
Some had blazing furnaces and giant cauldrons,
burning and boiling sinners,
their bodies and heads shattered and falling,
tumbling in the boiling liquid.
There were ghosts holding tridents,
standing by their side.
There were three or four hundred people,
standing on one side,
next in line to enter the cauldron,
embracing each other and weeping sorrowfully.
Some had sword trees, tall and vast,
with no discernible limit,
their roots, stems, branches, and leaves,
were all made of swords.
Crowds of people vied with each other,
climbing up them themselves,
as if competing joyfully,
yet their bodies were sliced apart,
cut into pieces inch by inch.
Tài saw his paternal grandparents and two younger brothers,
weeping in this hell.
Tài exited the prison gate,
and saw two people,
bringing documents.
They spoke to the prison officials,
saying there were three people,
whose families had hung banners and burned incense in pagodas and temples,
to rescue and absolve their sins,
and they could leave for the Blessed Abode.
Soon he saw three people,
emerge from the prison,
already wearing natural garments,
intact upon their bodies.
They proceeded south to a gate,
named the Illuminated Great Abode.
It had three gates,
shining with red colors.
Seeing these three people,
immediately enter the abode,
Tài also followed them in.
Ahead was a great hall,
adorned all around with precious jewels,
their brilliant light dazzling the eyes,
with beds made of gold and jade.
He saw a divine being,
with a majestic and extraordinary appearance,
exceptionally fine and uncommon,
seated upon this throne.
By his side were śramaṇas,
standing and leaning, very numerous.
Seeing the Prefect arrive,
they reverently paid their respects.
Tài asked who this person was,
that the Prefect paid homage to.
The clerk said:
"His title is the World-Honored One,
the teacher who delivers people."
After a while,
he ordered those in the evil paths,
all to come out and listen to the sutras.
At that time, there were nineteen thousand people,
who all came out of hell,
and entered a city of a hundred li.
Those who arrived here,
were beings who upheld the Dharma.
Though their conduct was flawed and deficient,
they were still to be delivered,
hence the Dharma teachings were expounded.
Within seven days,
according to the amount of good and evil they originally performed,
they were successively exempted and freed.
Before Tài left,
he had already seen ten people,
ascend into the sky and depart.
Leaving this abode,
he saw another city,
over two hundred li square,
named the City of Receiving Transformed Bodies.
Those who had completed their punishment in hell,
would come to this city,
to further receive their transformed retribution.
Tài entered this city,
and saw several thousand areas of earthen and tile-roofed houses,
each having its own rooms.
In the center was a tall and sturdy tile-roofed house,
with railings and columns colorfully decorated.
There were several hundred bureau clerks,
checking documents against each other.
They said:
Those who killed living beings would become mayflies,
born in the morning and dying by evening;
robbers and thieves would become pigs and sheep,
to be slaughtered and butchered by people;
the lecherous and wanton would become cranes, ducks, hawks, and deer;
slanderers and double-tongued would become owls and screech-owls;
those who evade debts would become mules, donkeys, oxen, and horses.
After Tài finished his inspection,
he returned to the Water Office.
The officer in charge said to Tài,
"Whose son are you, sir?
For what crimes and faults
have you come here?"
Tài replied:
"My grandfather and brothers
all served with salaries of two thousand shi.
I was recommended as Filial and Incorrupt,
but declined appointment by the ducal offices.
I cultivated my will and thought of goodness,
and did not become stained by the many evils."
The officer said:
"You, sir, have no sin,
Therefore, the former prime minister was appointed as the Water Official Overseer.
Otherwise,
he would be no different from those in hell."
Tài asked the overseer:
"What deeds must a person perform
to receive a pleasant retribution after death?"
The overseer said:
"Only disciples who uphold the Dharma,
diligently observe the precepts,
receive pleasant retribution,
with no punishment or demotion."
Tài asked further:
"When a person has not yet served the Dharma,
the offenses committed—
after serving the Dharma,
can they be eradicated?"
The reply was:
"They are all eradicated."
After these words,
the overseer opened a rattan case,
checked the register of years,
and found that Tài still had thirty years of lifespan remaining.
He then sent Tài back.
At parting,
the overseer said:
"Having seen the retribution for sins in hell as such,
you should inform the people of the world,
urging them all to do good.
Good and evil follow a person
like shadow and echo;
can one not be cautious?"
At that time, relatives and kin waiting to see Tài,
fifty or sixty people in total,
all heard Tài's account.
Tài himself recorded it in writing,
to show to the people of his time.
This was on the thirteenth day of the seventh month
in the fifth year of the Tàishǐ era of the Jìn dynasty.
He then held a grand blessed assembly
inviting the monastic community
for the sake of his grandparents and two younger brothers.
He instructed all his descendants
to change their minds and uphold the Dharma,
diligently practicing contemplation.
When scholars heard that Tài had died and revived,
and had witnessed much about sin and merit,
they came in turn to visit and inquire.
At that time, ten people including Grand Master Tàizhōng Sūn Fēng of Wǔchéng and Marquis Within the Passes Hǎo Bópíng of Chángshān,
gathered together at Tài's assembly.
They inquired in detail,
and all were filled with awe.
They immediately began upholding the Dharma.
Yuán Kuò
Sòng dynasty's Yuán Kuò, courtesy name Sīdù,
was from Chénjùn Commandery.
During the Yuánhuī era,
he served as Assistant Magistrate of Wújùn.
After being ill for a few days,
he suddenly appeared as if dead,
though a faint breath remained.
The coffin and burial garments were all prepared,
awaiting the end to enshroud him.
On the third day, he was able to move and blink.
He recounted himself:
A messenger came claiming he was summoned by order,
and Kuò followed him.
Upon arrival,
there was a great walled city,
with tall, orderly battlements and towers,
and majestic, splendid gates and steps.
He was then ordered to enter.
The host faced south,
and after exchanging greetings with Kuò,
invited him to sit.
Wine and roasted meats were served,
along with fruits, rice dumplings, pickles, and other delicacies,
no different from those in the world.
After several rounds of wine,
the host said to Kuò:
"The position of Registrar is unfortunately vacant;
given your talent and brilliance,
I wish to invite you to fill it.
Will you consider accepting?"
Kuò, realizing this was the underworld path,
firmly declined, citing his own mediocrity,
and inability to bear such responsibility.
Moreover, he was orphaned and impoverished from youth,
with brothers scattered and lost,
and begged for gracious release.
The host said:
"You decline because the realms of darkness and light are different,
that is all.
But the honors, emoluments, and comforts here
surpass those in your world;
I deeply desire to work with you.
I hope you will lower your stance
and fulfill my expectations."
Kuò again firmly pleaded:
"My children are young and helpless,
still in their tender years;
if I were to take up this post,
they would have no one to care for them.
The bond between father and child
is a matter deserving compassion."
Kuò then wept and kowtowed.
The host said:
"Since you decline so earnestly,
how can I press further?
My wish unfulfilled,
I deeply sigh with regret."
He then took a volume of documents from the table
and marked it with dots.
Soon after, Kuò expressed gratitude and prepared to leave.
The host said:
"Do you not wish to pay respects to your deceased ancestors?"
He then sent someone to guide Kuò.
They passed many offices and bureaus,
finally reaching a walled gate,
which was a prison.
Leading Kuò inside,
they came to a corner where many buildings stood,
clustered closely together.
Among them was a dilapidated, humble hut,
where he saw his birth mother, Yáng shì, inside,
her appearance and clothing poor,
greatly different from her lifetime.
Seeing Kuò, she was startled and joyful.
By the door was a person
with injuries on body and face,
who called out to Kuò.
Kuò, startled, asked who it was.
Yáng shì said:
"This is Lady Wáng;
do you not recognize her?"
Lady Wáng said:
"While I was alive,
I did not believe in retribution.
Though I had no other major sins,
I merely excessively whipped and beat maids and servants,
and thus receive this punishment.
Since death, the pain and suffering
have hardly ceased for a moment.
Only now is there a brief respite.
Earlier, I summoned your elder sister,
hoping she could take my place,
but it was of no use,
only adding to our shared sorrow."
After speaking, she wept profusely.
Lady Wáng was Kuò's legal mother.
Kuò's elder sister was also present at the time.
After a while,
the guide again led Kuò away.
Passing through lanes and paths,
the neighborhoods were orderly,
seemingly residential areas.
Finally, they came to a dwelling
with bamboo fence and thatched hut,
where he saw his father leaning on a table, sitting.
Kuò entered the gate,
and his father raised his hand, sending Kuò away, saying:
"Since you have been dismissed,
return quickly;
do not delay."
Kuò knelt, bid farewell, and returned,
reviving as soon as he reached home.
Cáo Zōngzhī
Cáo Zōngzhī of Gāopíng,
in the twenty-fifth year of Yuánjiā,
was in Péngchéng.
One night he fell asleep and did not wake,
and by dawn he had died.
In the late afternoon, his breath returned and he revived.
He recounted what he had seen:
a man in a single-layered robe and headcloth,
holding a hand tablet,
claimed to be an envoy of the Prince of Běihǎi,
saying His Highness summoned him.
Zōngzhī followed him.
In the courtyard before the hall,
there were light clouds,
tens of zhang above the ground,
drifting and casting shifting shadows.
Between the curtains and hangings,
purple smoke wafted and swayed.
The wind blew it near people,
and its fragrance was extraordinary.
The envoy said:
"Wait here below the steps,
I will now go in to announce you."
After a short while,
a command was relayed thanking Master Cáo:
"Your deeds are commendable,
and I have long admired you.
Now I wish to invite you to serve as an aide in my administration.
How old are you this year,
and have you ever held a ceremonial guard post?"
Zōngzhī replied:
"My talent is weak and ordinary,
and I am ashamed to receive such imperial grace.
I am thirty-one this year,
and have never held a ceremonial guard post."
The response came again:
"Although your years are few,
you have accumulated blessings from past deeds,
and should receive a prominent position.
You will hold a ceremonial guard post.
Now take your leave,
you may return home for now,
and we will discuss this again later."
Soon he saw the previous envoy escort him out the gate,
and in a daze he awoke.
Later, Zōngzhī served in Guǎngzhōu,
at the age of forty-seven.
The following year his post ended,
and he returned to his province, where he fell ill and died.
Sūn Huípú
Sūn Huípú, a Tang dynasty palace attendant physician,
was from Jìyīn.
In the thirteenth year of Zhēnguān,
he accompanied the imperial carriage to the Sānshàn Valley at Jiǔchéng Palace,
and lived next door to Wèi Zhēng.
Once at the second watch of the night,
he heard someone outside
calling for Attendant Physician Sūn.
Pú thought it was a summons from Wèi Zhēng.
When he went out,
he saw two men who said to Pú:
"An official summons you."
Pú said:
"I cannot walk."
They then brought a horse for him to ride.
Following the two men,
he felt as if heaven and earth were as bright as daylight,
and Pú found it strange but dared not speak.
Exiting the valley,
they passed east of the court hall,
then went northeast for six or seven lǐ,
reaching Mùxu Valley.
From afar he saw two men,
escorting Hán Fèngfang along.
They said to the two men leading Pú:
"You have made a mistake in your pursuit;
the one you have captured is correct,
but you should release him."
The men then released Pú.
Pú followed the road back,
and everything was exactly as it had been in his lifetime.
When he reached home,
he tied up the horse,
and saw a maidservant sleeping by the door;
he called to her but she did not respond.
He crossed over and entered the house,
and saw his own body lying asleep with his wife;
he tried to approach it but could not.
He stood leaning against the south wall,
shouting loudly to his wife,
but she never responded.
The room was extremely bright,
and in the corner of the wall was a spider web,
with two flies in it,
one large and one small.
He could also clearly see the medicines stored on the beam,
everything was distinct,
only he could not reach the bed.
He realized he was dead,
and was deeply distressed,
regretting that he could not bid farewell to his wife.
Leaning against the south wall,
after a long while he dozed slightly,
and suddenly startled awake,
to find himself lying on the bed,
while the room was dark,
and he could see nothing.
He called his wife,
telling her to get up and light a lamp,
and Pú was drenched in sweat.
Getting up to look at the spider web,
he saw it was exactly as before.
He saw the horse was also drenched in sweat.
Hán Fèngfang had died suddenly that night.
Later, in the seventeenth year,
Pú received an imperial order
to travel posthaste to Qízhōu,
to treat Prince Yòu of Qí's illness.
