Returning to the Xiàoyì post station east of Luòzhōu,
he suddenly saw a man approach and ask:
"Are you Sūn Huípú?"
He said:
"Yes.
Why do you ask?"
The man replied:
"I am a ghost,
and Grand Eunuch Wèi has summoned you to serve as his recorder."
He then produced a letter to show Pú.
Pú looked at it,
and it bore Wèi Zhēng's signature.
Pú exclaimed in surprise:
"Lord Zhèng is not dead;
why would he send you to deliver a letter?"
The ghost said:
"He has already died,
and now serves as the Grand Eunuch of the Solar Capital Registry,
and he ordered me to summon you."
Huípú invited him to sit and eat together,
and the ghost was very pleased and thanked him.
Pú requested:
"I have not yet returned from my imperial mission;
Lord Zhèng should not summon me now.
After I return to the capital and report on my mission,
then I will heed the summons.
Is that acceptable?"
The ghost agreed.
Thus they traveled together by day,
and lodged together at night,
until they reached Wénxiāng.
The ghost took his leave, saying:
"I will go ahead now,
and wait for you beyond the pass."
The next day, crossing the pass,
and exiting the west gate,
he saw the ghost already waiting outside the gate.
They traveled together again,
reaching Zīshuǐ.
The ghost again bid farewell to Pú, saying:
"After you have reported on your mission,
we will meet again.
You should refrain from eating pungent foods."
Pú agreed.
After reporting on his mission,
he inquired and found that Wèi Zhēng had already passed away.
Checking the date of his death,
it was the day before they met at the Xiàoyì post station.
Pú believed he would certainly die,
and bid farewell to his family.
He requested monks to perform rituals,
and had statues made and sutras copied.
After about six or seven nights,
he dreamed that the previous ghost came to summon him,
leading Pú up a high mountain,
atop which was a great palace.
Upon entering,
he saw a crowd of gentlemen who greeted him, saying:
"This man has cultivated blessings;
he cannot be kept here,
release him."
They then pushed him,
and Pú fell down the mountain,
whereupon he startled awake.
He has remained well to this day.
Lǐ Qiángyǒu
Lǐ Qiángyǒu was the son of Censor Rúbì.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Qiángyǒu served as Deputy Magistrate of Shàn County.
A few days after taking office,
a butcher whom he had known before
came to his gate and bowed twice.
When asked the reason,
he replied:
"I fell ill and died suddenly.
Upon reaching the underworld,
I was led by the officials past Mount Tài.
I saw the Senior Gentleman serving as Registrar.
So I went to plead my case.
Since it was not yet my time to die,
I was granted release and allowed to return.
That is why I have come to pay my respects."
The Senior Gentleman referred to Qiángyǒu himself.
Upon hearing this,
Qiángyǒu was deeply moved for a long while.
He said:
"If I become Registrar of Mount Tài after death,
what more could I worry about?"
He then asked about the duties of the position.
The butcher said:
"Mount Tài has two Registrars,
who in the human world are like Judges.
Their retinues are very grand.
Matters concerning ghosts and spirits
mostly pass through their hands."
A few days later,
one of Qiángyǒu's relatives died
and was revived.
He said he had been taken again to Mount Tài.
Mount Tài indeed had two Registrars:
one surnamed Lǐ,
who was Qiángyǒu;
the other surnamed Wáng.
The relative had been under Wáng's jurisdiction
and pleaded bitterly to be distinguished from others.
His allotted lifespan was not yet exhausted.
Suddenly, they heard the Prefect summon Registrar Wáng,
who left and returned after a short while.
He said
the royal household was holding a vegetarian feast
and needed ten thousand lacquer vessels.
He told the man:
"Your family has such items;
you may lend us some.
Fetch them quickly,
and once the matter is settled, you will be released."
The man came to Qiángyǒu and said
he had been asked to provide lacquer vessels
but truly had no means to do so.
Qiángyǒu interceded with Registrar Wáng on his behalf,
but after a long time, no decision was made.
Then they heard the Prefect call for Registrar Lǐ.
Qiángyǒu went and soon returned.
He told his close officer:
"The royal household is angry that Registrar Wáng cannot settle the matter
and has now ordered me to find the lacquer vessels.
This matter is urgent;
there is no room for refusal.
You must fetch them quickly."
The man had no choice
and brought the means to retrieve them.
The sounds of sorting and examining
were heard by all his family members.
After the matter was concluded,
Qiángyǒu led him before the Prefect,
and thus he was released.
After recovering,
he recounted this to Qiángyǒu.
Qiángyǒu was strict and stern in his official duties,
and his clerks greatly feared him.
They often waited outside the gate after court sessions.
Suddenly, it was announced that the Deputy Magistrate was exiting,
and all bowed deeply.
Some peeked and saw Qiángyǒu wearing a hat,
followed by over a hundred people,
unrecognizable from his usual self.
Everyone found it strange and astonishing.
This continued for over ten days,
and then Qiángyǒu passed away.
Wéi Guǎngjì,
during the Shàngyuán era,
died suddenly.
He later said that upon first arriving,
he was presented with a summons,
stating that King Yánluó had summoned him to serve as Judge.
He had reached the gate
but had not yet seen the King.
Shortly after,
Wéi Huángcháng, Prefect of Qú Prefecture, also arrived.
Guǎngjì bowed in greeting.
Huángcháng and Guǎngjì were cousins.
Huángcháng asked how he had come there.
Guǎngjì replied:
"I received the King's summons
to serve as Judge."
Huángcháng laughed and said:
"I already hold that position;
you should return."
He invited Guǎngjì to sit for a while
and ordered his subordinates to prepare food.
Soon the food arrived—
the plates were filled with human noses, fingers, and the like.
Huángcháng said to Guǎngjì:
"This is the food of the ghost realm.
Since you, brother, wish to return,
you should not eat it."
He then ordered the attendant who had brought Guǎngjì to escort him back.
Upon reviving,
Guǎngjì recounted the incident.
At that time, Huángcháng was still in good health,
but a few days later, he died suddenly.
That same year,
Lǚ Yán served as Military Commissioner of Zhèdōng.
A diviner told him:
"The underworld officials say
the King is summoning you to serve as Judge.
Perform meritorious deeds quickly,
and you may be spared."
Yán was terrified
and commissioned many sutras and statues.
After several tens of days,
the diviner said:
"You have been spared.
Now the King is summoning Prefect Wéi of Qú Prefecture;
the summons has already been issued."
Yán sent someone to Xìn'ān
to urgently report the news.
Ten days later,
Huángcháng indeed passed away.
Què Huìlián
During the Dàlì era,
a man from Shānyáng named Què Huìlián,
initially resided in Sìshàng.
Because his father had once served as an official in Héshuò,
he subsequently moved to live in Qīnghé.
After his father passed away,
Huìlián became known for his grief and emaciation.
The Liánshǐ dispatched an official to offer condolences,
presenting him with millet and silk.
After the mourning period ended,
he was recommended and appointed as the Wèi of Zhāngnán.
More than a year later,
one evening while alone in the hall,
he suddenly saw a person,
dressed in purple,
wearing a sword,
who hurried forward
and said to Huìlián:
"The Supreme God has issued a command,
appointing you, Sir, as the Master of Fate,
with the register,
to establish the Yánbōluó King."
He then presented a book stored in a brocade-patterned box,
offering it to Huìlián and saying:
"This is the command of the Supreme God."
The scroll was adorned with jade inlay,
and labeled with patterned brocade.
Additionally, an ivory tablet with a purple ribbon,
a golden turtle and jade belt,
were bestowed upon him.
Huìlián felt both joy and fear,
his heart greatly troubled and confused,
with no time to inquire further.
Thus, he accepted them.
Standing in the front corridor,
a master of ceremonies hurried in,
announcing:
"The officials and soldiers of the escort are about to arrive."
Soon after, several hundred people,
dressed in embroidered clothes with red forehead bands,
carrying weapons on their left and right,
hurried in,
forming several rows,
and bowed twice.
One person stepped forward and said:
"I am fortunate to serve as an official under your command,
I dare to offer my thanks."
After speaking, he bowed again.
After bowing,
they stood divided in front.
The master of ceremonies said again:
"The commanding generals of the Five Sacred Mountains' guard troops."
Another hundred or so people hurried in,
forming five rows,
their clothing in the colors of the five directions,
all bowing twice.
The master of ceremonies said again:
"Officials of ritual vessels and musical instruments,
officials of wind and percussion music,
officials of carriages and horses,
officials of tallies, seals, registers, and documents,
officials of treasuries, kitchens, and provisions."
Nearly several hundred people,
all hurriedly arrived.
After a while,
the master of ceremonies said:
"The guard troops of the various sacred mountains, as well as the ritual vessels, musical instruments, carriages, horses, etc.,
request that you, Sir, personally inspect them."
Huìlián asked:
"Where are the guard troops of the various sacred mountains?"
The reply was:
"They have their own origins, their own origins."
Huìlián then ordered his carriage,
whereupon a white horse was brought forward,
adorned with gold and jade.
Those guiding, controlling, and following,
were all the previously mentioned embroidered-clad attendants.
Several riders flanked the road ahead,
leading Huìlián northeastward,
with strict calls of announcement.
After traveling several li,
over ten thousand soldiers,
some on horseback, some on foot,
all armored in metal and holding spears,
lined the road.
Spears, lances, banners, and decorations,
embroidered patterns shining brilliantly.
Suddenly, outside a vermilion gate,
there were several dozen people,
all dressed in green and holding tablets,
bowing deeply.
It was said:
"These are subordinate officials."
Inside the gate,
curtains, screens, tables, and couches were fully arranged,
like a king's residence.
Huìlián ascended the steps,
and sat leaning on a table.
Soon, ten green-clad officials,
each carrying registers and documents,
requested Huìlián to review and sign them.
Then the master of ceremonies led Huìlián to a courtyard in the eastern wing,
whose front courtyard had many carriages and horses,
as well as musical instruments like drums and flutes,
and tallies, seals, keys.
All were placed on a couch,
covered with a yellow patterned cloth.
The couch encircled the four walls.
There was also a jade register,
with characters filled in purple gold,
written in seal script,
coiled and winding like the forms of dragons and phoenixes.
The chief official reported:
"This is the register of the Yánbōluó King."
A person wearing a hairpin and crown came to pay respects,
and Huìlián received him with equal courtesy.
After sitting down,
he said to Huìlián:
"The Supreme God, because the virtuous Chán Master Hǎiwù of the Lánruò Temple south of Nèihuáng County in Yèjùn,
established a register with a sincere heart.
The Yánbōluó King showed great respect,
saying that because you, Sir, possess the highest conduct,
you are appointed as the Master of Fate,
overseeing the mission of establishing the register.
I am fortunate to serve as an assistant official.
Thus, I am able to attend to you."
Huìlián asked:
"Where does the Yánbōluó King reside?"
The assistant official said:
"He is the most revered in the underworld.
He oversees the sacred mountains and rivers,
and manages all affairs of the netherworld.
Without extraordinary conduct,
one is not chosen for this position."
Huìlián thought to himself:
"I am to perform the register ceremony in the netherworld,
does this not mean I am already dead?"
Thinking of his wife and children,
he felt discontent and showed a troubled expression.
The assistant official had already discerned his thoughts,
and said to Huìlián:
"You, Sir, look worried,
is it not because you are concerned about your wife and children?"
Huìlián said:
"Indeed."
The assistant official said:
"The ceremony for the register appointment is tomorrow,
you, Sir, may temporarily return to settle your family affairs.
However, your official position is most exalted,
I hope you do not regret the distinction between the hidden and manifest realms."
After speaking, he rose.
Huìlián then ordered his carriage to depart,
feeling dazed as if drunk.
He leaned on the table and dozed off,
and upon waking,
he was already in the county.
It was just dawn,
and he marveled for a long time.
He considered that the command of the Supreme God
was certainly unavoidable.
He then fully informed his wife and children,
and prepared his final arrangements.
He also reported to the county magistrate.
The magistrate, Cáo Mǒu, did not believe him.
Huìlián then bathed,
put on his official robe and crown,
and lay on his couch.
That evening,
several county officials
all heard a sound in the air like wind and rain,
coming from the north,
heading straight into Huìlián's room.
After the time of a meal,
Huìlián passed away.
They then heard the sound heading northward and away,
sighing in astonishment.
They then sent an envoy to inquire south of Nèihuáng County in Yèjùn,
and indeed, the Chán Master Hǎiwù of the Lánruò Temple
had recently passed away.
Liú Xiàn
When Minister of War Lǐ Huán
was garrisoning Píngyáng,
there was a military officer named Liú Xiàn,
a man from Héshuò,
whose nature was firm and upright,
and who possessed courage and daring.
One evening,
he saw a man in white clothes come to his home,
who said to Xiàn:
"The officials of the prefecture urgently summon you;
you must quickly go to answer the call."
Xiàn angrily replied:
"I am a deputy general in the army;
I have never committed any offense.
How can the prefectural officials summon me?"
The man in white said:
"You just go;
do not refuse,
or disaster will befall you."
Xiàn shouted at him with a thundering voice,
and the man in white hurried away.
Before he had gone more than a few steps,
he had already vanished without a trace.
Only then did Xiàn realize it was a ghost.
Late at night, it came again,
calling for Xiàn.
Xiàn thought to himself:
I have heard that life and death are fated;
how can one escape it?
So he went with it.
After leaving the city for several li,
they arrived at an official office,
where he saw an underworld official in the hall,
with several dozen clerks
lined up on his left and right.
When the underworld official heard Xiàn had arrived,
he straightened his cap,
descended the steps, and performed all due courtesies.
Then he invited him to sit,
and said to Xiàn:
"I have heard of your courage and valor,
and thus have summoned you to receive a command."
Xiàn said:
"I do not understand the purpose of your summons, wise lord."
The underworld official said:
"The underworld has inspectors,
who patrol the roads of mountains and rivers.
If there are those who do not follow the law,
they can investigate them.
This is also an important duty,
and cannot be entrusted to anyone but a firm and valiant person.
I hope you will condescend to accept this task."
Xiàn declined, saying:
"I have no other talents;
I wish you would choose another firm and brave person to entrust with it."
The underworld official said again:
"Why do you refuse so strongly?"
Thereupon he ordered the case officer to immediately summon the clerk Wáng Xìn of Hóngdòng County, and when that was done,
he sent a clerk to escort Xiàn back.
Xiàn awoke in alarm.
A few days later,
Huán ordered Xiàn to go to the Northern Capital.
When he reached Hóngdòng County,
he happened to speak of the matter with the county officials.
The county officials said:
"There is a clerk in the county named Wáng Xìn,
who died several days ago."
Zhāng Wèn
The Right Regular Attendant Yáng Qián,
once served as a Ministerial Secretary before being appointed as the Prefect of Xīhé Commandery.
At that time, in Píngyáo County under his jurisdiction,
there was a village official named Zhāng Wèn,
who suddenly died without any illness,
and revived after several days.
Initially, Wèn saw his deceased elder brother arrive at his gate,
and Wèn was greatly startled.
He then said to him:
"Is my elder brother not a ghost?
Why have you come?"
His elder brother wept and said:
"Since I left the human world,
I have often thought of my relatives and friends,
like a blind man who does not forget the act of seeing.
To think of the joys of a lifetime,
how could they be regained?
Now, an underworld official has allowed me to return and visit you."
Wèn said:
"Who is the underworld official?"
He replied:
"An official of the underworld,
whose authority and rank are very high.
I now serve as his subordinate,
and often receive orders to come to the villages.
Previously, because the realms of the living and the dead are separate,
I could not come to your gate.
Now, the underworld official has summoned you,
and you must go quickly."
Wèn was afraid,
but could not refuse,
and his brother took him by the sleeve and led him away.
After traveling over ten li,
the road was dark and murky, impossible to discern,
but they could hear the galloping of horse-drawn carriages,
and the clamor of people talking.
He also heard his wife, children, and brothers calling out and weeping,
all saying:
"Let us discuss the funeral arrangements."
Wèn simply advanced together with his elder brother,
unaware of how far the journey was.
He then thought to himself,
"I am now dead,
but I have often heard that when a person dies,
they should see all their deceased relatives and friends.
Now, if I call out to them,
how can I know it is not possible?"
Wèn had a cousin named Wǔ Jìlún,
who had died several years earlier,
and was close to Wèn.
He called out to him.
Indeed, he heard Jìlún respond:
"Yes."
Soon after, they wept together in sorrow.
Wèn then said to him:
"Where is my cousin's dwelling?
Why is it so dark and murky here?"
Jìlún said:
"The underworld path is dark and obscure,
because there is no light from the sun or moon."
He added:
"Regrets are endless,
but now I must leave."
Wèn said:
"Where are you going now?"
Jìlún said:
"During my lifetime,
I accumulated countless offenses.
Since I entrusted myself to the underworld path,
I have suffered punishment and humiliation daily.
Hearing my cousin's call earlier,
I came to speak with you.
Now I cannot stay."
After weeping sorrowfully for a long time,
they parted.
He called out to several dozen deceased relatives,
and all responded like Jìlún,
coming at his call.
Many spoke of suffering torment,
their words filled with grief and sobbing.
Although Wèn continued forward,
he still did not know where he would stop,
but he constantly heard the wailing and voices of his wife, children, and brothers,
clearly audible around him.
He called out their names one by one,
but it was as if they did not hear him.
After a long time,
someone called out sternly:
"Zhāng Wèn, official of Píngyáo County."
Wèn responded, "Yes."
Another person then angrily rebuked Wèn,
asking how many faults he had committed in his lifetime.
Wèn firmly resisted.
Then, they ordered the case clerk to bring out the register of documents.
Soon, they heard the case clerk declare:
"Zhāng Wèn is not yet dead.
I request that he be sent back."
The underworld official angrily said:
"If Wèn is not supposed to die,
why was he summoned?"
The clerk said:
"Zhāng Wèn's elder brother now serves as an official here.
Having been in the underworld for a long time,
he suffered greatly and wished to be replaced,
so he requested that his younger brother take his place.
Although his request was not granted,
he summoned him here."
The underworld official angrily said to his elder brother:
"How dare you summon a living person on your own,
disregarding our laws?"
He immediately ordered him imprisoned,
and sent Wèn back.
Wèn thanked him and left,
traveling alone.
Because the road was dark and murky,
he was extremely anxious and confused.
After a short while,
he suddenly saw a candle several dozen li away,
its light and shape extremely faint.
Wèn joyfully said:
"Could this candle indicate a human dwelling?"
He hurried forward,
heading toward the light.
After traveling over a hundred li,
he gradually felt the shape drawing closer.
Approaching it,
he saw his own body lying on a bed.
In the room was a candle,
indeed the one Wèn had seen.
From this, he revived.
Wèn then asked his family about the wailing of his wife, children, and brothers and the discussion of funeral arrangements that he had heard in the underworld,
and not a single detail differed.
Assistant Clerk of Xízhōu.
The assistant clerk of Xízhōu died,
and several days later came back to life.
He said:
Initially, the King of Hell summoned him to serve as a clerk,
but he pleaded that he had never handled legal cases.
The king ordered him to recommend someone he knew,
so he recommended a colleague from the same office,
and the king dispatched a summons to bring that person.
The king then asked the assistant clerk,
"Since your allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted,
I will now release you to return."
He then asked his attendants,
"Did this person commit any sins while alive?"
The attendants replied:
"This man once killed a dog and a snake."
The king said:
"The dog deserved to die,
but what was the snake's fault?
To wrongfully kill a snake—
by law, he deserves capital punishment."
He ordered the man to turn around,
and with a ladle of molten iron,
scalded his back.
After the punishment was completed,
he sent an escort to return him.
The escort demanded one hundred thousand coins from him.
He said:
"My family has always been poor;
how could I manage that?"
The escort then sought fifty thousand,
but he again replied that he had none.
The escort said:
"Your household has countless coins from the Hú people;
how can you claim poverty?"
He answered:
"The Hú coins are not under my control."
The escort said that if he took them, he could get them—
why were they not under his control?
He led the man to his home to fetch the coins.
A Hú man was lying on the bed,
and a Hú child was sitting on a pile of coins,
so he could not take the money.
He temporarily entered the courtyard.
A dog barked at him,
and he kicked it with his foot;
the dog yelped and ran away.
He also saw his wife preparing a seven-day funeral feast,
taking flour to cook rice.
He called out to her with all his might,
but she did not hear him at all.
Angered,
he pulled at her scarf with his hand,
and she stumbled to the ground.
After a while,
the escort outside urged him.
When he went out,
the Hú child was still on the coins.
He forcefully punched the child in the ribs,
and the child fainted;
then he took fifty thousand coins and gave them to the escort.
Thus released,
he came back to life.
When he revived,
the Hú child's illness had not yet healed.
Later, in managing his affairs, he ended up losing exactly fifty thousand coins.
Dèng Yǎn
In the first year of the Huìchāng era,
the military clerk of Jīnzhōu, Dèng Yǎn,
had died several years earlier.
Suddenly, Jiǎng Gǔ, a scribe under his jurisdiction,
suffered a sudden heartache and died abruptly.
As if seized by someone, he was taken to an office,
where he saw Dèng Yǎn, who said happily:
"My workload is very heavy;
I need you to copy several hundred scrolls of documents."
Jiǎng saw piles of cases and documents covering the walls,
all written in red ink on blackened paper.
So he lied, saying:
"I recently injured my right arm,
and cannot hold a brush."
Someone beside Dèng said:
"Since he cannot write,
he should be sent back."
Jiǎng was hastily led back,
fell into a pit, and woke up.
Due to the illness,
his right hand was thereafter crippled.
Bèi Xǐ
A man from Yìxīng named Bèi Xǐ,
served as a village clerk in his hometown.
In the tenth month of the year Jiǎyín during the Qiánníng era,
he was staying at his villa in Jiāodú.
Around midnight,
he suddenly heard knocking at the door,
with the sounds of many people and horses.
He went out to look,
and saw a man in green robes holding a tablet,
standing facing west,
with over a hundred attendants.
Xǐ straightened his clothes and went out to greet them.
The man introduced himself, saying:
"I am Lóng,
surnamed Zhōu,
the eighteenth in my generation."
Xǐ then invited him in to sit,
and asked about his purpose.
He said:
"I am the Southern Bureau Judge of the underworld,
and by the King's command,
I have come to summon you to serve as the Northern Bureau Judge."
Xǐ was initially very frightened.
Lóng said:
"This is an important position in the underworld;
how could it be easily attained?
Do not decline."
Soon, attendants arrived,
carrying beds, couches, dining tables, curtains, and canopies.
After everything was set up,
wine and food were laid out in abundance,
and they drank together for a long time.
A clerk hurried in and reported:
"Judge Yīn has arrived."
Another man in green robes holding a tablet entered,
followed by two attendants carrying a chest,
and inside the chest were also green robes.
Yīn bowed to Xǐ and said:
"By command, these are bestowed upon you,
and we are summoned together."
He then dressed Xǐ in the green robes.
They sat down and drank together
until nearly dawn.
Then they said:
"The King's command cannot be delayed."
So they set off together.
Xǐ said:
"My home is not far from here;
may I briefly return to bid farewell?"
They all replied:
"You are already dead now;
even if you return,
how could you interact with your family again?"
Then they went out the door,
and Xǐ, Zhōu, and Yīn each mounted a horse.
They traveled as swiftly as the wind,
crossing water without sinking.
By evening,
they lodged at a village inn,
where wine and food were prepared,
but there were no inhabitants.
Although lamps and candles were lit,
it felt as if they were separated by curtains.
They said they had already traveled over two thousand li.
At dawn, they set off again.
After a long time,
they arrived at a city
with heavily guarded gates.
Zhōu and Yīn entered first,
then came out to summon Xǐ.
They passed through three gates in total,
with clerks and guards on both sides
all bowing hurriedly.
They entered another gate,
and in the main hall to the north, curtains were drawn.
Xǐ hurried forward to pay his respects,
just as in the human world.
After coming out,
Zhōu said to Xǐ:
"The Northern Bureau has been without an official for many years;
the residence and offices
all need to be put in order.
You may stay at my home for now."
They then walked east from the hall gate
for about a li,
where there was a large mansion,
and Xǐ was lodged in the eastern hall.
Soon after,
about thirty fellow officials
came to visit and congratulate him.
A banquet was then held.
After the banquet,
he lay down drunk.
At dawn,
he visited all the offices to express his thanks.
Then a clerk in red robes arrived,
bearing the King's command,
with generous gifts of money, silk, carriages, horses, and provisions.
The next day,
Zhōu said to Xǐ:
"You may now begin your duties."
Together, they went to the northeast of the King's hall,
where there was a large mansion
with very solemn furnishings.
Xǐ was settled inside.
There were about eighty clerks
who came to pay respects and serve him.
To the south of the hall were several dozen large rooms,
which were the bureau offices,
filled with stacks of documents.
To the north of the inner hall,
there were two separate rooms
with desks and several bookcases,
all adorned with various treasures.
Zhōu handed Xǐ a golden key and said:
"The documents in these cases
are the most secret and important;
you must always keep the key yourself
and never lightly entrust it to others."
After Zhōu left,
Xǐ opened them to look.
The books were piled up,
each about a foot square.
He first took one volume,
with the characters "Shǎnzhōu" written in gold on the cover.
The writing inside was very fine and dense;
only upon close inspection
could it be seen
that they were all registers of people's names from the world.
Wanting to know about his own family affairs,
Xǐ opened another case
and found the register for Chángzhōu.
He looked up his family's record
and saw the names of himself and his family members across generations in great detail.
Those who had already died
were marked with a black hook.
By evening,
Judge Zhōu returned and said:
"The King has decided that your allotted lifespan in the world is not yet exhausted,
so you are temporarily sent back.
When your lifespan ends,
you will return to hold this position."
Xǐ then returned the golden key to Zhōu.
When Xǐ had first examined the registers,
he had memorized all the fortunes, lifespans, and misfortunes of his family and himself,
but by now, it had all become hazy and forgotten.
Soon after,
the officials all arrived
to bid farewell.
Zhōu and Yīn escorted him back.
The next night,
they arrived at the village of Jiāodú.
Entering the room,
he saw himself lying on the bed.
Zhōu, Yīn, and Xǐ each went to sleep.
Suddenly, he awoke with a start,
and it was just noon.
He asked those around him,
and they said
he had been dead for only half a day.
Yet in the underworld, it had been four days.
After Xǐ recovered,
he was just like an ordinary person,
with no noticeable differences.
He lived for over forty more years before passing away.
Gàn Qìng
In Jìn there was a man named Gàn Qìng,
who died without any illness.
At that time there was a magician named Wú Měng,
who said to Qìng’s son:
“Lord Gàn’s allotted span is not yet exhausted.
I will try to plead for him;
his life
should not yet be laid to rest.”
The corpse lay in a quiet chamber,
only the area around the heart remained slightly warm.
After seven days,
Měng arrived at dawn,
sprinkled water on him,
and around midday,
Qìng revived.
Immediately he opened his eyes and mouth,
but had not yet made a sound.
The whole household was both sorrowful and joyful.
Měng again ordered water to be held in the mouth and sprayed.
Then he rose.
He coughed up blood several times,
and was also able to speak.
After three days he recovered fully.
At first he saw over ten people coming,
who seized and bound him, putting shackles on him, and took him to prison.
There were more than ten others of the same group,
who took turns being interrogated in order.
Before his turn arrived,
suddenly he saw Master Wú pleading for him facing north,
and the King then ordered his shackles removed and sent him back.
All the government offices he passed through
were seen welcoming Master Wú.
And Master Wú treated them as equals,
so he did not know exactly what deities they were.
Chén Liáng
During the Tàiyuán era,
a man from Běidì named Chén Liáng was good friends with Liú Shū of Pèiguó,
and also engaged in trade together with Lǐ Yān from the same commandery.
Once they had obtained substantial profits,
they gathered to drink and celebrate together.
Yān then murdered Liáng,
wrapped him in reeds,
and abandoned him in the wild grass.
After more than ten days,
Liáng revived and returned home.
He recounted that when he died,
he saw a man wearing a red turban,
who led Liáng away,
and came to a city gate.
Below the gate there was a bed,
where he saw an old man
holding a vermilion brush,
checking and marking a register.
The man in the red turban said:
“From the mortal world below there is a man named Chén Liáng,
a wandering soul only,
not yet under any jurisdiction,
and so I have brought him here.”
The one checking the register said:
“You may let him leave at once.”
After Liáng went out,
he suddenly saw his friend Liú Shū,
who said to him:
“I never thought we would meet here.
You are now fortunate to have been sent back by the revered deity,
but in my home, in the mulberry tree behind the privy, there is a fox-spirit
that often causes hauntings;
my family has repeatedly suffered unexpected distress because of it.
When you return,
could you perhaps speak of this for me?”
Liáng agreed.
After reviving,
he went to the authorities to report Lǐ Yān, who then confessed his crime.
He also specially informed Shū’s family,
whose members wept and said
everything was just as described.
They then cut down the tree,
caught the fox-spirit and killed it,
and the hauntings ceased.
Yáng Dàfū
Yáng Dàfū was
a eunuch,
whose name is lost.
At the age of eighteen,
he was seized by an underworld official
and died without illness.
After a day, he revived,
saying:
“After arriving in the underworld,
there were offices and officials,
no different from the mortal world.
The underworld official showed him the records,
where he saw his name clearly written.
It said
his lifespan was only eighteen years.
Yáng did not plead for favor.
Beside him was a man
who pleaded on his behalf,
wishing for him to be allowed rebirth,
his words extremely earnest.
After a long while, the underworld official agreed,
and ordered him to return.
That man also escorted Yáng for several hundred paces.
As they were about to part,
Yáng thanked him with shame:
‘I do not know how to repay
the grace of rebirth granted to me today.’
He asked what the man desired.
The man said:
‘If you happen to obtain a Míngshā bow,
that would be repayment.’
He then gave Yáng over a hundred large copper coins.
Suddenly, Yáng awoke,
recovered without any suffering.
From then on, he sought a Míngshā bow,
but could not obtain one.
Sometimes he made small palace-like houses,
burned them as repayment,
and did so several times.
Yáng paid much attention to alchemy,
focusing on cinnabar and minerals,
and could make the Fǎnhún elixir.
For those who died suddenly from illness or plague,
grinding one pellet of the elixir,
prying open their mouths,
and pouring it in would revive them.
He once saved several people.
There was a eunuch named Xiàhóu
who obtained five pellets of Yáng’s elixir.
Yáng cautioned him,
‘In an emergency, swallow one pellet.’
One morning, Xiàhóu fell ill,
his condition extremely critical.
He took one pellet and swallowed it.
Soon after, he was pursued by an underworld official.
During questioning,
he said:
‘I once swallowed one pellet of Yáng Dàfū’s elixir.’
The underworld official immediately sent him back.
Xiàhóu, experiencing the elixir’s effect,
after reviving,
swallowed the remaining four pellets.
Over a year later,
he again saw a yellow-clad man pursuing him.
It was said
this was not the underworld court,
but Tàishān summoning him.
Xiàhóu followed,
arriving at the foot of a high mountain,
where there was a palace.
Upon reaching its gate,
he saw two Daoist priests,
who asked about his life’s deeds.
He answered each one.
Slowly, he explained,
‘I once swallowed five pellets of Yáng Dàfū’s elixir.’
The Daoist priests then ordered him to return.
Xiàhóu bowed in gratitude, saying:
‘I have extended my lifespan
through the power of the divine elixir.
I wish to change my name to Yán.
May I?’
The Daoist priests agreed.
After reviving,
he changed his name to Yán.
Yáng, aware of his elixir’s efficacy,
often used it to save people.
His son, Xuān,
was returning to the capital from the outskirts.
Before dawn,
after traveling over twenty lǐ,
he rested at a large estate.
Suddenly, he heard cries and weeping from the estate.
Inquiring the reason,
he learned the master’s son had died suddenly.
Xuān untied his belt,
took out one pellet of the elixir,
had it ground and poured into the boy’s mouth.
After a long while, the boy revived.
Yáng was wealthy and self-sufficient,
retired early from his post,
indulged in leisure,
and focused solely on alchemy.
He never fell ill
and died at the age of ninety-seven.
In his later years,
he encountered someone carrying a bow.
He asked its name.
The person said:
‘A Míngshā bow.
Inside the horn surface,
there is moving sand.’
Yáng bought it and burned it,
to repay the one who had saved him.
The formula for the Fǎnhún elixir,
it is said, was given by his rescuer.
He secretly prepared it himself,
so no one could obtain the method.
Lǐ Zhǔbù’s wife
There was a selected official named Lǐ Zhǔbù,
who had recently married.
Traveling east past Mount Huà,
he took his wife into the temple
to pay respects to the Golden Heavenly King.
As his wife was bowing,
her breath cut off and she collapsed,
with only a faint warmth remaining over her heart.
Returning to the inn,
he rode swiftly to Huàyīn County to seek doctors and diviners.
The county magistrate said:
"Immortal Master Yè excels at talismanic arts;
he has just returned from an imperial mission to cast dragons.
He is half a post station from here;
you should hurry to meet him."
Mr. Li rode alone for over fifty li,
and encountered him.
Li dismounted,
prostrated himself weeping,
and fully recounted the incident.
The immortal master said:
"What kind of demon dares to act like this?"
He then went ahead with Li.
He told his attendants:
"Quickly bring the saddlebags.
Wait for the vermilion bowl and brush."
Upon reaching the inn,
they already heard wailing.
The immortal master entered
and saw the situation was critical.
He first had
brush, ink, and paper
brought.
He then drew a talisman, lit incense,
and sprayed it with water.
The talisman transformed and flew northward,
with a sound like a whirlwind,
but for a long time there was no news.
The immortal master grew angry,
wrote another talisman,
its sound like thunder,
yet again there was no news.
After a short while,
the saddlebags arrived;
he took the vermilion brush and other items,
ordered Li to
cook a little thin congee on the left and right,
to await her revival.
Then with vermilion he painted a talisman,
sprayed water and shouted at it,
its sound like a thunderclap.
In a moment,
breath came from her mouth and nose,
and gradually she opened her eyes and could speak.
Asked about it,
she said: "When I first bowed,
the Golden Heavenly King said,
'What a fine lady.'
On the second bow he said,
'Keep her.'
He sent attendants to support me back to his courtyard,
and it had already been three days.
Relatives and guests had gathered in great numbers,
when suddenly there was a knock at the gate.
The gatekeeper ran to report to the king.
The king said:
'Why not drive them away?'
That was the first talisman.
Moments later,
there was great commotion outside the gate.
Several gatekeepers
whispered into the king's ear.
The king said:
'Just send them off.'
That was the second talisman.
Suddenly a red dragon flew in,
rightly seizing the king by the throat,
so he could barely make a sound.
He said:
'Release her.'
Then someone escorted me back.
That was the third talisman."
Li offered all his belongings in thanks,
but Master Yè took nothing at all.
From this it is known that women should not enter numinous temples.
Liú Xuē
In the ninth year of the Tàiyuán era of Jìn,
in Líshí County of Xīhé, there was a man of Hú descent named Liú Xuē,
who died of a sudden illness,
yet his heart area remained warm.
His family did not dare to encoffin him for burial,
and after seven days he revived.
He said that initially he saw two clerks take him away,
traveling northward,
an immeasurable distance.
They reached the eighteen layers of hell,
where according to the severity of his retribution,
he suffered various torments.
Suddenly Guānshìyīn said to him:
"Your allotted time is not yet exhausted;
if you return to life,
you should become a śramaṇa.
Now in Luòxià, Qíchéng, Dānyáng, and Kuàijī,
there are stūpas of King Aśoka;
you may go and pay homage.
When your life ends,
you will not fall into hell."
After speaking,
it was as if he fell from a high cliff,
and suddenly he awoke.
Because of this he left home,
taking the Dharma name Huìdá,
and traveled to pay homage at the stūpas.
When he reached Dānyáng,
he did not know the stūpa's location.
He then climbed high and gazed west,
seeing Chánggān,
where there was an unusual aura,
so he went to pay homage there,
and indeed it was the site of the former King Aśoka stūpa.
From this he knew for certain there must be śarīra,
so he gathered people to excavate.
One zhàng into the ground,
they found three stone tablets,
under which was an iron casket,
inside which was a silver casket,
inside which was a gold casket,
containing three śarīra and fingernails and hair.
Xuē then built a stūpa at this place.
Lǐ Qīng
Lǐ Qīng was a man from Yúqián in Wúxīng.
He served as a military aide and supervisor in the Grand Marshal’s office of Huán Wēn.
While in the office, he fell ill,
returned home, and died,
but revived after a night.
He recounted that initially he saw a messenger
holding a summons banner calling him,
saying:
“The lord wishes to see you.”
Lǐ Qīng thought it was Huán Wēn summoning him,
so he rose, fastened his belt, and went.
Upon leaving the gate,
he saw a bamboo sedan chair
and was told to enter it.
Two men pushed it,
and it sped along swiftly as if galloping.
They arrived at a vermilion gate,
where he saw Ruǎn Jìng.
At that time, Ruǎn Jìng had already been dead for thirty years.
Ruǎn Jìng asked Lǐ Qīng:
“When did you arrive?
Do you know how my family is?”
Lǐ Qīng said:
“Your family is suddenly in dire straits.”
Ruǎn Jìng then shed tears like rain.
He asked how his descendants were.
Lǐ Qīng replied that they were passable.
Ruǎn Jìng said:
“I will now help you escape.
Can you take care of my family?”
Lǐ Qīng said:
“If I can do this,
I will not fail your great kindness.”
Ruǎn Jìng said:
“Sēngdá Dàorén is
an official teacher
and is highly respected.
You should plead with him earnestly.”
After a while inside,
he sent someone out to say:
“The four-story temple in front of the gate
was built by the officials.
Sēngdá often enters the temple at dawn to pay respects.
You should go and seek his mercy.”
Lǐ Qīng went to the temple
and saw a śramaṇa who said to him:
“You were my disciple seven lifetimes ago.
For seven lifetimes, you have enjoyed blessings,
but you became infatuated with worldly pleasures
and forgot your original duties.
You turned from the right path to evil
and should suffer great punishment.
Now you can repent.
The venerable monk will come out soon;
he will help you.”
Lǐ Qīng returned to the sedan chair,
shivering from the cold at night.
At dawn, the gate opened,
and Sēngdá indeed came out.
Lǐ Qīng followed him and kowtowed.
Sēngdá said:
“You must reform and do good,
take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha.
By accepting these Three Refugees,
you may avoid an untimely death.
If you diligently uphold them,
you will also not suffer hardships.”
Lǐ Qīng then accepted them.
He also saw the śramaṇa he had met the previous day,
who knelt and pleaded:
“This person was Sēngdá’s disciple in a past life.
He forgot the right path and lost the Dharma
and is about to suffer.
He was first pursued by the vermilion gate,
but now he has returned to me.
I beg for your compassion.”
Sēngdá replied:
“He was originally a blessed person;
he should be easy to save.”
Lǐ Qīng then returned to the vermilion gate,
and soon someone came out and said:
“Military Aide Lǐ may leave.”
Ruǎn Jìng also came out
and gave Lǐ Qīng a green bamboo staff,
telling him to close his eyes and ride it.
Lǐ Qīng did as instructed
and suddenly arrived home.
His family was weeping,
and fellow villagers filled the hall,
making it impossible to enter.
Coincidentally, the coffin was brought back.
Family members and guests
went to inspect it,
and only the corpse lay on the ground.
Lǐ Qīng approached the corpse
and smelled its stench,
regretting that he had returned.
Pressed by those outside,
he unconsciously entered it.
After a short while,
he revived.
He then took care of Ruǎn Jìng’s family
and shared his residence with them.
From then on, he devoted himself to the Dharma treasure,
encouraged faith in the Buddhist teachings,
and became a disciple of the noble community.
Zhèng Shībiàn
Zhèng Shībiàn, a Military Staff Officer of the Right Gate Guard in the Eastern Palace of the Táng Dynasty,
was not yet twenty years old
when he died suddenly and revived after three days.
He said that initially several people came to collect him
and led him into the main gate of an official compound.
He saw over a hundred prisoners there,
all standing in rows facing north,
making six rows in total.
Those in the front row
were plump and fair in appearance,
wore fine clothes,
like noblemen.
The further back the rows, the thinner and more wretched they became,
some wearing cangues and shackles,
others merely with their caps and belts removed,
standing shoulder to shoulder in linked sleeves,
strictly guarded by soldiers.
When Shībiàn arrived,
he was assigned to the third row,
standing third from the east end,
also with his cap and belt removed and sleeves linked.
Biàn grew anxious and fearful,
and focused his mind on reciting the Buddha's name.
Suddenly, he saw a monk he had known in life arrive.
The monk entered the ring of soldiers,
and the soldiers did not stop him.
The monk came to where Biàn was
and said to him:
"In life you did not cultivate blessings,
what will you do now in this sudden situation?"
Biàn begged for rescue.
The monk said:
"I will now save you so you can leave.
Can you uphold the precepts?"
"Yes."
Shortly after,
clerks led all the prisoners before the official,
questioning them one by one.
Then, outside the gate,
the monk administered the Five Precepts to him,
pouring water from a vase over his forehead.
He said:
"You will revive when the sun is in the west."
He also gave Biàn a yellow mantle,
saying:
"Wear this until you reach home,
then place it in a pure spot."
He then showed him the way back.
Biàn put it on and returned.
Upon reaching his home's side room,
he placed the mantle on a corner of the bed.
Soon his eyes opened and his body moved.
His family, startled, scattered,
thinking the dead man was about to rise.
Only his mother did not leave.
She asked:
"Have you revived?"
Biàn said:
"I will revive when the sun is in the west."
Biàn thought it might be noon,
and asked his mother.
His mother said:
"It is midnight."
Only then did he realize the realms of death and life are separate,
and day and night correspond inversely.
When the sun reached the west,
he was able to eat and recovered,
and still saw the mantle at the head of the bed.
By the time Biàn could get up,
the form of the mantle gradually faded,
but a light remained.
After seven
days, it vanished completely.
Biàn then upheld the Five Precepts.
Several years later,
a friend urged him to eat pork.
Biàn, unable to refuse,
ate one morsel.
That night,
he dreamed he had transformed into a rākṣasa,
with claws and teeth several feet long,
seizing a live pig and eating it.
At dawn,
he felt his mouth smarting and spat blood.
He had someone look at his mouth;
it was full of clotted blood.
Biàn was alarmed
and dared not eat meat again.
Several more years later,
he took a wife.
His family pressured him to eat [meat],
and afterwards there were no more effects.
However, for the past five or six years,
Biàn's body had a foul odor and large sores,
ulcerated and failing to heal.
Some feared it was due to his breaking the precepts.
Táng Lín once served in the Eastern Palace alongside Biàn
and heard him tell this himself.
Fǎqìng
At Níngguān Temple, there was a monk named Fǎqìng.
He was crafting a sixteen-foot statue using the dry-lacquer method,
when the statue, not yet completed, he died suddenly.
At that time, the monk Dàzhì of Bǎochāng Temple
also passed away on the same day.
After three days, both revived.
They said
they saw official bureaus,
and in the hall was someone resembling a king,
with a very large retinue.
They saw Fǎqìng standing before him.
Suddenly, a statue came
and said to the person in the hall:
"Qìng has not finished creating me;
why have you caused him to die?"
They then checked the register,
and it said:
"Qìng's allotted food is exhausted,
but his lifespan is not yet ended."
The person above said:
"He may be given lotus leaves to complete his lifespan."
When these words were finished,
suddenly everything vanished,
and Dàzhì then revived.
The community found this strange
and went to Níngguān Temple to ask Qìng.
What he said matched and was verified.
Qìng could no longer eat regular food.
Every day at dawn he consumed six lotus leaves,
and during the monastic meal time, eight leaves.
He continued this for the rest of his life.
Fellow monks made offerings
to complete his statue.
A Candidate in the Kāiyuán Era
The father of Lú Cóngyuàn, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Personnel,
had never practiced Buddhism.
In the early Kāiyuán era,
a candidate who had died suddenly,
because his allotted lifespan was not yet exhausted,
was released by the underworld authorities.
After leaving the gate,
he met an old man wearing a cangue,
who said to the candidate:
"You have been allowed to return.
My son, Cóngyuàn,
now serves in the Ministry of Personnel.
If the selection process is not yet finished,
you should see him
and can relay this message:
'Because I did not practice Buddhism,
I now suffer various punishments,
experiencing extreme pain and torment.
Quickly create sūtras and images to rescue me.'"
After that man revived,
he went to the selection office and reported this.
Cóngyuàn wept, requested leave,
and after having sūtras copied and images made for the rescue,
went back to the candidate to thank him.
[The candidate] said:
"[Your father] has already been reborn in the human realm.
You may inform your son."
Having spoken, he vanished.
Cuī Míngdá,
whose childhood name was Hànzi,
was from Dōngwǔchéng in Qīnghé.
His grandfather Yuánjiǎng
served as Vice Minister of Personnel and Governor of Hángzhōu.
His father Tíngyù
was a Golden Guard General and Governor of Jìzhōu.
Míngdá became a monk at Tàipíng Temple in the Western Capital during his youth,
studying under Master Lìshè.
He mastered the Nirvana Sutra,
becoming a leading figure among the monastic community.
In the early Kāiyuán era,
after the midday meal,
he took a nap in his room.
Upon waking,
he found himself outside the eaves.
Returning to his room,
he again felt himself being drawn out.
This happened several times,
and he felt deeply troubled.
Shortly after,
he saw two ox-headed guards
holding dead people,
roasting them outside his room,
filling the air with a foul stench.
When he asked the reason,
the guards said:
"We were just about to summon you."
Míngdá replied:
"Just don't let it stink.
I'm not afraid to go."
The guards then pulled out his soul from his head,
and led him out of the city.
Along the way, he recognized many people,
and though Míngdá wanted to speak to them,
he could not.
After exiting the western city,
the path became narrow,
and soon the two guards disappeared.
A red rope tied to a piece of bone
led Míngdá forward,
and he felt very close to it.
After walking several li,
the bone also vanished.
Míngdá, feeling despondent, continued alone,
until he reached a city
with crumbling walls.
He saw several hundred people
melting iron to repair the city.
Míngdá passed by silently,
not daring to ask.
Walking several more li,
he came to another city.
Before the city, he saw several dozen guards and officials
mixing clay to repair a small room.
An official in crimson robes
shouted at Míngdá,
and soon ordered the guards to push him into the room.
They piled clay to block it,
and Míngdá cried out in protest.
The official said:
"We were just testing you,
don't worry."
Shortly after,
an internal message conveyed the king's order
to summon Master Míngdá.
Míngdá followed into a great hall,
where he saw a noble youth in colorful attire,
around twenty years old.
On the steps above and below,
officials in red and purple robes stood in rows,
numbering several thousand in total.
As Míngdá entered the courtyard,
he thought to himself,
"The king summoned me,
yet he doesn't descend the steps."
Suddenly, he saw the king at the foot of the steps,
clasping his hands respectfully,
and saying to Míngdá:
"The underworld deeply values the merits of the living world.
We have heard that you, venerable one, have mastered the Nirvana Sutra.
Thus, we have invited you here
to expound upon it and extend your lifespan."
Míngdá thought again,
"If he wants me to lecture,
why is there no preaching seat?
How can I expound the teachings?"
Then he saw a preaching seat under the western corridor,
and the king instructed Míngdá to ascend the seat and begin the lecture,
while a mat was laid below the seat.
The king knelt,
and as Míngdá spoke one line,
the king said,
"Enough."
Míngdá descended from the seat,
and the king ordered his attendants to escort Master Míngdá back.
At parting,
he said to Míngdá,
"You may transmit all the sutras."
After leaving,
he suddenly saw several dozen riders on the road,
who said they were from Minister Cuī.
When they arrived,
it was indeed his grandfather Yuánjiǎng.
Yuánjiǎng seemed displeased to see Míngdá.
Míngdá said loudly:
"I am Hànzi.
Do you not recognize me, Grandfather?"
Yuánjiǎng led him to the hall,
first asking about the Lántián estate,
then about Tíngyù.
Míngdá answered truthfully.
Yuánjiǎng said:
"Since my death,
I have had official duties,
and have never been able to return home.
I know nothing of the living or the dead."
Soon, an official brought documents to Yuánjiǎng,
and Míngdá secretly saw that the register contained
his own name.
It said:
"Monk of Tàipíng Temple,
fifth rank at Sōngshān."
After this,
Yuánjiǎng asked Míngdá:
"You have seen it.
Míngdá declined to look further.
Yuánjiǎng then ordered two officials to escort Míngdá to the judge,
and instructed two others to send him home.
When the judge saw him,
he did not show much courtesy.
Several attendants nearby said:
"This is the direct grandson of the Minister.
How can you treat him like an ordinary guest?"
The judge then instructed the two officials escorting Míngdá,
saying:
"Those who escort the venerable one
number five or six each year.
You may reward them slightly for their labor."
Upon leaving the gate,
each official asked for five hundred thousand.
The officials said:
"When you reach home,
you should immediately go to the market to obtain paper money.
We will wait for the money before leaving."
Upon reaching his room,
he saw two old maids with disheveled hair crying,
and his disciples sighing.
He did not recognize his own body,
but saw only a large pit.
The officials pushed Míngdá into the pit,
and he revived.
Still dazed,
he could not speak,
only repeatedly raising his hands.
Those around him said:
"He wants a thousand strings of paper money."
Míngdá nodded.
After the money was burned,
Míngdá saw two people each take the money and leave,
and from then on, he recovered from his illness.
Earlier, when Míngdá arrived at the king's gate,
he saw several officials escorting an old woman
to where Míngdá was staying,
saying she was from Língyán in Hùxiàn.
Upon entering,
the king angrily said:
"What kind of old woman is this?
She upholds the Bodhisattva precepts,
yet is so impure.
Release her and send her back,
so she may purify herself."
After leaving,
she walked alongside Míngdá
for about a hundred paces,
before they each went their separate ways.
After Míngdá recovered from his illness,
he went to Língyán,
and saw the old woman as if they were old acquaintances.
Wáng Lún
In the eleventh year of the Tiānbǎo era,
Wáng Lún, a judicial commissioner of the Shuòfāng military command and a senior secretary of the Court of Judicial Review,
was on an inspection tour to Zhōngchéng
when he fell ill and died.
After sixteen days, he revived.
When his illness had become critical and he was on the verge of death,
he saw two men coming to summon him away.
In his dazed state, he thought it was the human world,
unaware that he had died.
Soon he entered the gate of a great city,
where he saw Lǐ Línfǔ, the military governor of Shuòfāng.
They met and bowed to each other,
as if in their lifetime.
He also saw several others, including Lǐ Yōng and Péi Dūnfù,
in a government hall,
demanding an explanation from Línfǔ for his life.
Only then did Lún realize he was dead.
Línfǔ held paper and brush in hand,
debating and confronting Yōng and the others.
Soon he saw the case record,
and the underworld judgment read:
"After Línfǔ's death, his family will be ruined,
and Yáng Guózhōng will replace him as chancellor."
That winter,
Línfǔ died.
Yáng Guózhōng indeed replaced him.
Lún's elder brother, Shè,
had been dead for six years,
and Lún saw him at that time.
Shè said:
"You are not supposed to die.
If you can obtain thirty thousand strings of cash,
you can return to life."
Lún's home was in Xīdìngyuǎn,
hundreds of li away from Zhōngchéng.
He then saw a rugged mountain path at the foot of a hill,
and rushed back to his home.
In an instant, he entered the hall and told his wife:
"I have died.
If you can obtain thirty thousand strings of cash,
I can be revived."
That night,
the entire family heard from the windows
a rustling sound,
and the dogs also barked in response.
At dawn,
his wife said tearfully
that she had dreamed of Lún's death
and his request for thirty thousand strings of cash.
She then took paper, cut it into the shape of money,
and summoned a shaman to burn it.
Lún received it,
and it was no different from real money in the human world.
In the underworld, there is no distinction between day and night;
it is always like the dark, snowy months of November and December.
There is a King of Ghosts,
dressed in purple robes,
who determines guilt and blessings.
There are dozens of judges.
Among the crimes judged, betrayal of trust is considered the gravest.
Those being tried
are mostly monks, nuns, and scholars.
Lún had committed no other offenses in life,
and when his crimes were judged,
he was only charged with the crime of eating meat.
A minor clerk nearby
said:
"Although this man ate meat,
he did not kill intentionally."
However, eating meat is indeed a crime,
and killing to eat it
is an even greater crime.
Before Lún fell ill,
he had once taken off his robe to copy the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*.
He sealed and wrapped it himself
and placed it in the Buddha hall.
In the underworld,
because of this deed, he was able to see the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha.
"You share in this good deed,
and you shall be reborn."
He was then ordered to retrieve the sutra,
which was the very one Lún had sealed and wrapped.
Several of the King of Ghosts' judges
were friends from his lifetime,
but when they met, it was hazy and indistinct,
and they did not reminisce about the past.
He also saw his deceased father and mother,
but after bowing to them,
there was no exchange of greetings,
as if they did not recognize each other.
He also saw his deceased brothers,
but there was no brotherly affection.
His brother Shè had died recently,
and their relationship was as harmonious as in life,
likely because his death was recent.
When he reached the place where judgments were made,
he saw that the fortunes, longevity, and early deaths of relatives and friends
were all predetermined by fate,
and could not be altered.
Soon he was released to return,
and a clerk said:
"You have fortune and longevity,
but what happened here
must not be revealed."
After speaking,
he suddenly revived,
having been dead for sixteen days.
Fèi Zǐyù
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Fèi Zǐyù, an Adjutant of Qiánwéi, was sleeping in his official residence at night when
he suddenly saw two clerks arrive before his bed.
Adjutant Fèi Zǐyù awoke in alarm,
asking who they were.
The clerks said:
"The Great King summons you."
Zǐyù said:
"I am a provincial official,
not subject to any kingdom.
How can I be summoned?"
The clerks said:
"Yánluó."
Zǐyù was greatly frightened.
He called for people to prepare his horse,
but no one responded.
Hastily, he followed the clerks away.
They arrived at a city,
where inside and outside the city gate were several thousand people each.
Zǐyù held fast and recited the Diamond Sutra,
constantly reciting it in his heart at that time.
He also earnestly thought,
if he encountered a Bodhisattva,
he would plead his grievance.
In a moment,
the King ordered him brought in.
Zǐyù bowed twice,
feeling very apprehensive.
Suddenly he saw a monk descend from the clouds.
Zǐyù stepped forward to pay his respects.
Zǐyù then declared aloud,
wishing to see the Bodhisattva Dìzàng.
The King said:
"Zǐyù, this is he."
Zǐyù stepped forward and bowed in worship.
The Bodhisattva said:
"How did you know it was me?"
He then said to the King:
"This man has recited the Diamond Sutra throughout his life.
As his allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted,
he should be sent back."
The King looked at Zǐyù.
Suddenly angry, he asked his name.
Zǐyù replied:
"Fèi Zǐyù, Adjutant of Jiāzhōu."
The King said:
"Qián,
is a commandery.
What is this Jiāzhōu?
You ought to die.
It is only because the Bodhisattva strenuously argues
that I shall release you to go."
Zǐyù bowed twice, took his leave, and went out.
The Bodhisattva said:
"When you return,
do not eat meat again,
and you shall attain long life."
Zǐyù paid respects to the holy countenance.
The holy countenance was a bronze Buddha,
its head, face, and hands all moving.
The Bodhisattva performed a bow of worship,
his hands and feet fully extended.
Zǐyù also bowed.
After the bow, he went out the door.
Zǐyù asked:
"Why are there so many people outside the gate?"
The Bodhisattva said:
"These people's respective sins and merits are unclear.
For several hundred years they have been ghosts,
unable to be registered for rebirth."
Zǐyù took his leave and returned to his residence,
coming back to life.
Three years later,
he ate meat and died again.
He was brought as a witness.
The Bodhisattva saw him,
greatly angry, saying he had initially forbidden him to eat meat;
why did he break the agreement?
Since Zǐyù had been reborn,
he then abstained from meat and blood.
Previously, Zǐyù had successively taken three wives,
all said to have been summoned,
and they all came to see him.
Zǐyù asked:
"How did you get here?"
A wife said:
"You simply did not pay attention to it."
The youngest wife said:
"You were insufficient towards me.
I came bearing resentment.
The money you used was mine;
why not repay it?"
Zǐyù said:
"Money is easily obtained."
The wife said:
"You used my copper cash;
will you now repay it with paper money?"
Zǐyù said:
"A husband using his wife's money
is a matter of principle, not requiring repayment."
The wife had nothing to reply.
Hesitating, they each left.
Méi Xiān
Méi Xiān of Qiántáng always took performing good deeds as his personal duty.
He enjoyed upholding Buddhist scriptures,
and also sponsored the release of living creatures.
He observed the seven monthly fasts,
and his neighbors called him a Lay Devotee.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he fell ill, died suddenly, and revived.
He himself recounted that
when he first died, he was led by someone,
and along with over ten companions, he saw King Yánluó.
The King asked what good deeds he had performed in life.
Xiān replied:
"Only upholding scriptures and reciting Buddha's name, that is all."
The King said:
"These good deeds you were able to practice;
the hidden blessings
cannot be in vain."
He ordered Xiān's register checked,
then happily said:
"You are not yet due to die.
Now I release you back to life.
You should revere your fundamental practice."
Xiān bowed twice.
As there was no one to escort him yet,
he was kept in the office.
The King continued the interrogations.
Next, it came to Bāo Zhí, the Village Head of Qiántáng.
He was asked why he had taken Lǐ Píngtóu's money
without making him a registered household.
Zhí said:
'I, Zhí, as Village Head and Group Leader, am constantly at the county office, returning at night and leaving early in the morning. I truly do not know. I beg you to summon my son for questioning.'
The King ordered a summons issued to fetch Zhí's son.
In a moment, a messenger arrived and was ordered to escort Zhí back.
He then revived.
He recounted the event.
At that time, his son was perfectly fine,
and everyone tested him.
Five or six days later,
Zhí's son indeed fell ill,
and died within two days.
Wáng □
Sòng Xíngzhì, Vice Director of the Ministry of Justice in the Táng Dynasty,
was from Bólíng.
He did not believe in Buddhism by nature,
and often spoke disrespectful and slanderous words.
In the fifth month of the second year of the Yǒnghuī era, he fell ill and died.
By the ninth day of the sixth month,
Wáng □, a clerk in the Department of Personnel Evaluation of the Ministry of Justice, suddenly died,
but revived after two days.
He said that when he first died,
he saw four people coming, saying,
"The authorities are summoning you."
□ followed them,
entering a large gate.
He saw a hall that was very grand.
In the western chamber, a man was sitting,
with a plump and dark appearance.
In the eastern chamber, a monk was sitting,
facing the official as an equal.
Both were facing north,
each with a bed, a small table, and a mat.
There were about two hundred attendants,
some wearing caps, some wearing ceremonial headgear,
all with beautiful appearances.
Below the steps, clerks were holding
documents.
There was an old man,
wearing a cangue and bound,
standing below the eastern steps.
When □ reached the courtyard,
he was also already bound.
A clerk holding paper and brush asked □:
"In the eighteenth year of the Zhēnguān era,
while serving as an assistant clerk in Cháng'ān,
why did you alter Lǐ Xūdá's household register?"
□ replied:
"□ previously served as an assistant clerk in Cháng'ān,
and was transferred in the sixteenth year of the Zhēnguān era.
By the seventeenth year,
I was appointed as a clerk in the Court of the Imperial Granaries.
The register was altered in the eighteenth year,
it was not □'s fault."
The high official in the hall,
after reading his statement and defense,
turned to the old prisoner below the eastern steps and said:
"Why did you make a false accusation?"
The prisoner said:
"Xūdá's age had truly not yet reached [the required age],
because □ altered the register,
adding years to Xūdá's age,
how dare I make a false accusation?"
□ said:
"The appointment document from the seventeenth year is still here,
please retrieve and verify it."
The official called three people to escort □,
untied □'s bonds,
and went to fetch the appointment document.
When it arrived,
the high official read it himself,
and said to the old prisoner:
"His transfer is clearly documented,
you are in the wrong."
He ordered the old prisoner to be sent outside the gate.
Outside the gate, it was dark and there was a city wall,
with battlements on top,
seemingly a place of punishment.
The high official then wrote on the desk.
He said to □:
"You are not guilty.
You are released to go."
□ bowed in farewell,
and a clerk led □ to the eastern steps,
to bow and take leave.
The monk stamped □'s arm and said:
"Go well."
The clerk led □ out,
heading southeast,
passing through three gates,
each time inspecting the arm stamp,
before letting him out.
Reaching the fourth gate,
the gate was very grand and large,
with multiple stories painted in red and white,
three doors all open,
resembling a city gate,
with strict and tight guards.
They inspected the stamp again,
and allowed him to exit the gate.
Heading southeast for several tens of steps,
he heard someone calling □ from behind,
□ turned to look,
and saw Vice Director Sòng Xíngzhì,
his face dark and miserable,
the color like damp earth,
with his head exposed and waist untied,
wearing an old crimson robe,
his hair short and hanging down,
like that of a foreigner,
standing below the steps of the hall,
with a clerk guarding him.
To the west near the wall,
there was a large wooden sign,
about
one zhang and two chǐ tall.
Large characters on the sign read:
"This is where those who have been interrogated await."
The characters were over a square chǐ in size,
very clear.
In the hall, there were beds, seats, small tables, and desks,
like those in an official office,
but no one was sitting there.
Xíngzhì saw □ and was both sad and happy,
saying:
"How did you manage to come here?"
□ said:
"The authorities summoned me,
interrogated me about altering the register,
and released me after finding no fault."
Xíngzhì grasped his two hands,
and said to □:
"I am being interrogated by the authorities about my merit ledger,
in my whole life,
I have never suffered such hardship,
plus hunger, thirst, cold, and bitterness beyond description,
you must make an effort to go to my home,
urgently tell them to perform meritorious deeds for me."
He earnestly repeated this instruction several times,
and □ then took his leave.
After walking several tens of steps,
he called □ back again.
Before he could speak,
an official came and sat in the hall.
Angrily, he said to □:
"I am in the middle of an interrogation,
how dare someone come to the prisoner's area."
He ordered a guard to slap his ears,
and pushed him away.
□ ran,
and reached another gate,
the gate clerk said:
"You were slapped on the ears,
your ears will likely go deaf,
I will remove the blockage for you."
So he used his hand to pick,
his ears,
there was ringing in the ears,
then he inspected the stamp and let him out.
Outside the gate, it was as dark as lacquer,
□ did not know where he was,
feeling with his hands to the west and south,
all were walls,
only to the east there was no obstruction,
but it was too dark to walk.
He stood waiting for a short while,
when he saw the clerk who had earlier summoned □ coming from the gate,
saying:
"You were able to wait for me,
very good.
You can give me one thousand coins."
□ then apologized and said:
"As you command."
The clerk said:
"I do not want copper coins,
I want white paper money,
expecting you to bring it on the fifteenth day."
□ agreed,
and then asked for the way back.
The clerk said:
"Just walk east for two hundred steps,
there is a wall with a broken opening where you can see light,
you can push it down,
and you will reach your home."
□ did as he was told,
and already reached the south gate of the Lóngzhèng ward where he lived.
Thus, he returned home.
He saw people sitting and weeping,
entered the door, and revived.
By the fifteenth day,
□ forgot to give the money,
the next day he fell ill again,
in extreme distress.
He saw the clerk come angrily and say:
"You truly have no integrity,
promised to give me money,
but did not give it,
now I will take you again."
So he immediately drove him away,
out the Jīnguāng Gate,
ordering him into a pit.
□ bowed and apologized over a hundred times,
and was then released to return,
and revived again.
□ told his family,
to buy one hundred sheets of paper,
make money and send it.
The next day,
□ fell ill and was in distress again,
and saw the clerk again, who said:
"You were kind enough to give me money,
but the money is not good."
He declined with apologies,
requesting to make them again,
and was permitted.
He revived once more.
On the twentieth day,
he was ordered to use money,
to separately purchase white paper to make paper money,
along with wine and food.
He burned these by the canal west of Lóngzhèng Ward,
and afterward his body became light,
his health robust,
so he recovered as before.
Wèi Jìng,
a man of Jùlù,
first took office as Wǔchéng Captain.
At that time, Lǐ Róng, Governor of Cáo Prefecture,
ordered Wèi Jìng to oversee the capture of thieves.
One thief had an uncle who was a monk,
and he harbored the stolen goods.
Wèi Jìng investigated the case,
and pardoned the monk.
The Governor reproached Wèi Jìng for being too lenient,
and personally investigated.
The monk confessed and admitted guilt,
and Róng ordered Wèi Jìng to beat him to death.
In the summer, the sixth month of the second year of Zàichū,
Wèi Jìng suddenly fell ill and died,
and after being temporarily encoffined,
as a posthumous marriage between a man and woman was intended,
the burial had not yet taken place.
After twelve days,
Wèi Jìng revived,
groaning inside the coffin.
His younger brothers and nephews all fled.
Only his mother ordered an axe to open the coffin.
Placing her mouth near Wèi Jìng’s mouth,
she felt a faint warmth.
After a long time, his eyes opened,
but the flesh of his body had all rotted.
Gradually, they fed him cow’s milk,
and after he recovered,
he said that upon first dying,
he passed through the underworld offices,
where gate guards with banners and halberds were very stern.
He was led to see an official,
who asked Wèi Jìng why he had beaten the monk to death.
The monk stood before them,
and debated with Wèi Jìng, each presenting their case.
The monk’s arguments were exhausted.
The official said to Wèi Jìng:
"You are innocent,
and may return."
Those beside him said:
"His flesh has already decayed."
The official ordered medicine to be fetched,
wrapped in paper,
and said:
"This can restore his former flesh."
After receiving it and returning,
upon reaching the gate he heard weeping,
and, startled and afraid, did not wish to enter.
The messenger forcibly led him.
When they reached the room’s door,
the messenger scattered the medicine into the coffin,
took Wèi Jìng’s arm and pushed him into the coffin,
and he collapsed, no longer conscious.
After reviving,
his flesh, worm-eaten and rotten, was nearly gone,
and it took over a month to recover.
When he first arrived home,
the dogs, horses, chickens, and geese all cried out,
likely having seen something.
Yáng Zàisī
In the first year of Shénlóng,
Chief Minister of the Secretariat Yáng Zàisī died.
On the same day, a catering officer of the Secretariat also died,
and both were led by underworld attendants to the King’s presence.
The King asked Zàisī:
"In life, how did you accumulate so many crimes?"
Since they are many,
how will you redeem them?"
Zàisī said:
"I truly have no crimes."
The King ordered the register brought.
In a moment,
a yellow-robed clerk arrived holding the register.
He read out Zàisī’s crimes, stating:
In the first year of Rúyì,
when Mòchuò captured Yíng, Tán, and other prefectures,
the state
sent too few troops to rescue,
and they could not withstand the enemy.
Someone submitted a memorial advising against it,
but Zàisī disregarded the advice and sent the troops,
leading to defeat by Mòchuò,
and over a thousand men were killed.
In Dàzú,
the first year,
locusts caused disaster in Héběi,
and the people had no grain to eat.
Zàisī served as Chancellor,
yet failed to open the granaries to provide relief,
causing the people to become displaced,
and over twenty thousand starved to death.
The Chancellor harmonizes yīn and yáng,
but Zàisī’s governance and punishments were unjust,
thereby damaging harmonious energies,
which led to great floods in three commanderies of Hénán,
drowning several thousand people.
There were six or seven such cases in total.
They were shown to Zàisī,
and Zàisī bowed repeatedly, admitting his guilt.
Suddenly, a hand as large as a bed appeared,
with terrifying hairy bristles.
It seized Zàisī,
blood flowing between its fingers,
and soared into the sky and departed.
The King asked the catering officer,
how he had come there.
The attendants replied,
that they wished to question the man,
but said,
he had no faults,
and should be sent back.
After the catering officer revived,
he often spoke of these events to others.
Emperor Zhōngzōng heard of it,
summoned and questioned him,
and he reported everything truthfully.
Emperor Zhōngzōng ordered his account recorded in the Secretariat Hall’s records.
Wáng Chéng of Jīntán
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
Wáng Jiǎ, the assistant magistrate of Jīntán County,
was in the capital to fulfill the household tax quota,
making payments at the Left Treasury.
Suddenly, a messenger arrived at the treasury and said,
"The King summons the assistant magistrate."
Wáng Jiǎ hastily followed him.
After leaving the city and traveling over ten li,
they arrived at an official residence.
Upon entering the gate,
he heard the voice of the former Left Regular Attendant Cuī Xīyì.
Wáng and Xīyì
had been friends for thirty years,
so he asked the gatekeeper,
and learned the full story.
He requested to have his name card presented,
and the gatekeeper went in to report.
Xīyì asked where this person was,
and immediately ordered him to be called in.
They met with surprise and joy.
Xīyì said to Jiǎ:
"Do you know this is the underworld?"
Only then did Jiǎ realize he had died,
and he grieved for a long time.
Xīyì asked again if he had seen Cuī Hàn.
Hàn was Xīyì's son.
Wáng said:
"Since entering the city,
I have been
managing the treasury,
and haven't had time to visit his residence."
Xīyì laughed and said:
"Truly a frivolous man."
He then asked about the reason for his coming,
as death and life are easily forgotten.
Wáng said:
"I was just in the treasury,
and followed a messenger here,
without knowing the reason."
After a while,
word came from outside that the King was seated.
Cuī ordered a message to be relayed to the King, saying:
"The assistant magistrate Wáng of Jīntán
is my close friend;
he should not yet be due to die.
Once matters are settled,
I hope he can be sent back early.
It's hot now,
and I fear his body may decay."
The King summoned him in
and said to Jiǎ:
"You were implicated for accepting bribes during your previous term as assistant magistrate."
He saw the assistant magistrate wearing a cangue,
sitting under a paulownia tree.
Jiǎ asked:
"I never showed you favoritism;
why do you falsely accuse me?"
The assistant magistrate said he was suffering bitterly from his punishment
and had to hastily implicate someone to save himself.
The King said:
"If you are unrelated,
you should be released."
After leaving the gate,
he went to bid farewell to Xīyì.
Xīyì said:
"You are able to return,
which is excellent.
Pass on a message to Cuī Hàn:
In serving as an official, the first rule is not to wrong others;
later, you will bear the consequences yourself.
Taking bribes will certainly shorten your lifespan.
On the fifteenth day of every month,
you should offer a bottle of pure water,
placing it in the Buddha hall of a temple;
this will bring great blessings."
Jiǎ asked what merit this act would bring,
and Xīyì said:
"Matters of the underworld
are not for you to know;
just know that it will bring blessings."
After speaking, he escorted him out,
and when they reached his place,
he revived.
Hán Cháozōng
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Hán Cháozōng, the registrar of Wànnián County,
once pursued a man who arrived late
and sentenced him to five strokes.
When the man was brought before the county magistrate,
the magistrate sentenced him to ten more strokes.
The man suffered from a seasonal epidemic and died.
Later, a complaint was filed in the underworld,
accusing Cháozōng.
Cháozōng was thus summoned
and entered a massive black-necked gate.
Before the middle gate,
stood a pair of paulownia trees.
Beside the gate was a pavilion,
with curtains hanging down.
Peeking inside, he saw the former Censor Hóng Zǐyú seated.
Zǐyú said:
"Hán, why have you come here?"
Cháozōng said:
"I was summoned here,
but I don't know why."
Zǐyú told him to go see the Grand Envoy early.
Passing through a screen wall,
he saw the former Minister of Justice Lǐ Yì.
Cháozōng paid his respects.
Yì said:
"Why did you sentence a man to death?"
Cháozōng pleaded:
"It wasn't me who beat him to death;
the county magistrate sentenced him to additional strokes,
and he died from a seasonal epidemic.
It wasn't my fault."
Yì asked: "If the county magistrate sentenced you,
why involve this registrar?"
Cháozōng was innocent,
but as an assistant magistrate,
he had seen that all were subject to corporal punishment."
Also,
He was sentenced to twenty strokes
and released.
Cháozōng regained consciousness only late at night,
with blue swelling on his back.
The pain was beyond words,
and it took over a month to recover.
Later, while patrolling the wards and alleys,
he came to the southern walled city of the capital.
There was a ward,
and within it, a residence
with a gate facing south.
He vividly remembered being summoned there and receiving the strokes.
The residence was empty and uninhabited.
He asked people,
and they said,
"This is the princess's haunted house;
no one dares to live here."
