Only then did he realize that extremely haunted houses
are all inhabited by ghosts and spirits,
and he believed it.
Wéi Yánzhī
Wéi Yánzhī, the Sima of Mùzhōu,
having completed his term of office,
took up residence in Jiāxīng, Sūzhōu.
In the eighth year of the Dàlì era,
he fell ill with dysentery.
One summer day, while sleeping alone in the main hall,
he suddenly saw two officials who said:
"Our superior orders you to come."
Yánzhī asked:
"Who is your superior?"
The officials said:
"We are under orders to summon you,
we know nothing else."
Suspecting they were ghosts or demons,
Yánzhī got down from the bed intending to return.
The officials then stepped forward and seized his sleeve,
saying:
"We must take you with us;
where else would you go?"
Yánzhī's body remained before the bed,
but his spirit followed them out.
Leaving the city walls,
they no longer saw marshes or lakes,
only dry land.
After traveling several tens of lǐ,
they arrived at a place
with an official compound.
The officials led Yánzhī past the Grand Envoy,
who instructed them to take him to the Judge.
The officials then brought Yánzhī forward.
The Judge, holding his tablet and descending the steps, greeted him with great reverence and solemnity,
and then said to Yánzhī:
"Someone has brought a lawsuit against you,
and you must respond to the matter."
He then ordered a clerk to lead Yánzhī to the chamber for the hearing.
The clerk guided Yánzhī to a room,
which was located in front of the Judge's hall,
a hall similar to that of a county magistrate today.
There were two rows of buildings,
with rooms between them,
and in front of each room were slanted lattice windows,
inside which people sat on plank beds.
The clerk instructed Yánzhī to sit on a plank bed for the hearing.
Shortly after,
six or seven prisoners were brought in,
some wearing cangues, some shackled, and some with their heads exposed,
arriving at Yánzhī's location.
The clerk said:
"You have accused Sima Wéi of taking money;
now you will face judgment in the underworld to settle the matter."
Yánzhī asked:
"Who is the one being accused?"
They replied:
"It is Sima Wéi Bīng,
but we do not actually know this person."
The clerk then congratulated Yánzhī, saying:
"You are now granted a return to life."
Yánzhī was overjoyed.
The clerk then led Yánzhī to the Judge's office,
and fully reported the situation.
The Judge also congratulated him warmly,
and ordered his release,
instructing that the Grand Envoy be informed to allow Sima to return.
The clerk again led Yánzhī to the Grand Envoy's hall,
but the Grand Envoy had already retired to his inner quarters,
and sent word to release Sima Wéi,
ordering the pursuit of Wéi Bīng instead.
Shortly after,
an official in a green robe arrived with a document,
reprimanded the summoning officials,
asking why they had mistakenly summoned the wrong person.
Each was sentenced to sixty strokes,
and blood flowed across the ground.
They were then ordered to escort Yánzhī back.
Yánzhī said:
"I wish to see my future official positions."
The official said:
"What use is it to know?"
Yánzhī pleaded earnestly.
The official opened the register,
and after Yánzhī's name,
only blank paper was visible,
with no further writing.
With that, they departed.
After walking over a hundred paces,
Yánzhī saw officials escorting Zhèng Jìnkè, the magistrate of Qīngliú County,
who was Yánzhī's nephew.
Yánzhī asked:
"Why have you come here?"
He replied:
"I have been accused by someone."
Jìnkè also asked Yánzhī
why he had come.
Yánzhī said:
"I was mistakenly summoned,
and now I am being released to return."
Jìnkè repeatedly expressed approval,
and wished to convey a message,
but the officials hurried him away,
leaving him unable to speak.
He only turned back repeatedly, saying:
"Uncle, take care."
Yánzhī returned to his home and revived.
When he inquired about Jìnkè,
he was told:
"He died five or six days ago."
Wéi Bīng resided in Shàngyuán,
and on the very day after Yánzhī's revival, Wéi Bīng passed away.
Zhāng Zhì
Zhāng Zhì was a native of Yīshì.
During the Zhēnyuán era, he passed the míngjīng examination.
He was appointed as the sheriff of Línhuàn County in Bózhōu.
About a month after taking office,
one evening,
he saw several men holding warrants coming to arrest him.
His servant was also holding a horse waiting at the foot of the steps.
He mounted the horse and followed them out of the county gate.
The county clerks were sitting in a row at the gate,
and none of them rose to their feet.
Zhì angrily said:
"Even if the prefectural authorities are temporarily summoning me,
my official position is not immediately revoked.
How dare you clerks show such disrespect?"
But the men paid him no attention.
After traveling several dozen lǐ,
they reached a cypress forest.
The messenger said:
"You should dismount here."
So he walked over a hundred paces on foot,
entered a city,
and directly to the north was a large government gate,
inscribed with the words:
"Northern Prefecture."
Entering the prefecture,
straight west there was a gate,
labeled "Court of Judgment."
There were many clerks and soldiers there.
The gatekeeper announced:
"Zhāng Zhì, sheriff of Línhuàn."
And so he entered.
He saw a man with a beautiful beard, dressed in crimson,
sitting behind a desk.
The man rebuked him:
"As an official, your duty is to govern people fairly.
Why did you twist the law in handling cases,
causing people to die unjustly?"
Zhì was seized and thrown to the ground.
He cried out:
"I only recently took office as a low-ranking official.
It has been just over a month since I assumed my post,
and I have never handled any cases."
The man said again:
"The case records are clear,
and the accuser is not far away.
The prefecture has ordered an investigation,
yet you still dare to speak deceitfully."
He took a cangue and put it on Zhì.
Zhì said again:
"Since the accuser is nearby,
please let me meet him."
The man said:
"Summon the wronged man."
An old man with a blind eye
came out from the western room.
He stared sharply at Zhì and said:
"This man is young—he is not the one who handled my case."
They then checked the records in the archives for Zhāng Zhì of Yīshì.
It showed that on the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month in the seventeenth year of Zhēnyuán, he took up the post of sheriff of Línhuàn.
They also checked the petition regarding the wrongful case,
and sent a dispatch to the underworld office of Bózhōu,
inquiring about the name and age of the sheriff serving in Línhuàn in the third month of that year.
If he had already been replaced,
they requested the name and age of his successor,
along with the date of the handover.
Upon receiving the dispatch,
it was found that in the third month of that year,
the serving sheriff was Zhāng Zhì of Jiānglíng,
aged fifty-one.
He had taken office on the eleventh day of the fourth month in the eleventh year of Zhēnyuán,
and was replaced on the twenty-first day of the fourth month in the seventeenth year of Zhēnyuán.
His successor was Zhāng Zhì of Yīshì,
aged forty-seven.
After reviewing the records,
the judge said:
"The names happened to be the same,
so the investigation was not conducted carefully.
The responsible clerk shall be punished with ten strokes,
and the correct person shall be summoned instead."
The warrant holders led him back again.
It felt as if he were walking on a high mountain
and then fell off a cliff.
As if waking from a dream,
he found himself in the cypress forest,
lying over the neck of his horse.
Both his sides were
in pain,
and he could not get up on his own,
nor did he know where he was.
Faintly hearing the sound of woodcutters singing,
he knew there were people nearby,
so he shouted loudly for help.
The woodcutters came
and exclaimed in surprise:
"The county lost an official and his horse—
isn't this them?"
They crowded around to ask questions,
but Zhì could not answer.
They helped him sit upright
and supported him to send him back.
The county.
Zhì's horse had been taken by ghosts,
and his servant did not know.
After the county lost Zhì,
the magistrate was perplexed
and suspected that since Zhì had just arrived,
he had been strict with the clerks,
and they, resentful, had killed him.
That night, the gatekeepers and the clerks on duty
were all imprisoned.
They had been searching for him without success
for seven days already.
After Zhì returned,
he rested for several days
before he could speak,
but his spirit and consciousness remained impaired.
Zhèng Jié,
originally from Xíngyáng,
resided in Shòuchūn Commandery,
and once made a living by serving as acting assistant magistrate.
He married a woman from the Lǐ family,
who was the niece of Shàn Yuē.
After Zhèng Jié’s acting appointment ended,
he settled in Ānfēng Village.
In the fifth year of the Kāichéng era,
around mid-April,
as dusk approached,
Lady Lǐ suddenly suffered a heartache illness,
then spoke as if mad,
bowing to the air and saying:
"Please wait a moment."
Shortly after, she died,
only her heart still warm.
The whole family wailed in grief,
summoning doctors and shamans.
None proved effective,
and they prepared only for her death.
By the fifth watch,
at the first crow of the rooster,
she suddenly revived,
startling everyone who supported her.
After a long while,
breath was felt from her nose and mouth.
By dawn,
she finally spoke, saying:
"Two ghosts
came with a warrant to seize me.
At first, I thought it was from the prefecture or county,
and still hoped for leniency.
But soon I was dragged by the messengers,
terrified,
though the journey did not feel too difficult.
We reached a walled city,
entered,
and saw an official
resembling a clerk.
I was then led into a bureau,
where I listened
as they read the reason for my capture.
It said:
'In a previous life, I, surnamed Liú,
was a man,
with a wife named Mǎ.
Lady Mǎ was fierce and cruel,
so Liú killed her and removed her entrails,
leaving her without the five viscera,
unable to be reborn.
The accuser was Mǎ’s mother.'
I then told the bureau:
'If you wish Lady Mǎ to be reborn,
release me to return.
I will use all my lifetime possessions
to perform meritorious deeds for her,
which would be a solution.
If you detain me now,
merely placing me in the Avīci Hell,
what good would that do for Lady Mǎ?'
The bureau said:
'Then you must settle this yourself.'
Soon after,
Lady Mǎ arrived.
Fearing she might be rude,
I said to the official:
'How could you be so cunning and cruel?'
I then explained my private proposal to her.
The official asked Lady Mǎ,
'What do you say?'
Lady Mǎ replied:
'I have suffered injustice for many years,
and after completing other punishments,
I should return to the world of the living, but have no means.
I await your judgment.'
I then said:
'Please check how much lifespan I have left.
If it is not yet my time to come,
then follow my earlier proposal.
If my life should end,
I will accept your decision.'
The official said:
'That is clearly reasonable.'
He then summoned the Director of Fate.
Soon,
a keeper brought in a record book.
He said:
'Lady Lǐ should not have been summoned;
this was already checked when she was seized yesterday.'
After checking again shortly,
he found the record,
presented it to the official, and said:
'She still has eighteen years left in the human world.'
The bureau said:
'For now, let her attend court for questioning,
and release her back at night.'
When night fell there,
the authorities released her,
and she returned as if from a dream.
From then on, at dusk in the human world,
the messengers would come to fetch her,
and release her back at cockcrow,
as usual.
Though Zhèng was poor,
he tried every means to serve the messengers.
After three or five days,
the messengers said apologetically to Zhèng:
'Though we appreciate all kinds of delicacies,
they trouble us deeply;
better to offer us tea, water, or porridge instead.
Tea and wine are not as good as plain water.
Also, it is easier for the poor to prepare.'
From then on, every evening he prepared water, porridge,
and three to five sheets of paper money.
After the tenth day of the month,
each time they came, they discussed
how to rescue Lady Lǐ.
At first, whenever Lady Lǐ returned,
she dared not speak of it.
But with the messengers also agreeing,
she gradually revealed a few things about the underworld.
She often said the gravest human sins
were none other than bending the law to kill for gold and silk.
She also said:
'For almsgiving,
it is not necessary to build Buddhist temples;
better first to relieve the hunger and cold of one’s own flesh and blood.
If there is surplus,
then extend it to others.
If there is still more,
aid those on the streets.
This brings the greatest blessings.'
Zhèng also asked through her about the lifespan and official rank of an acquaintance.
The reply came:
'This person loves accepting gold and silk,
and now his lifespan is reduced,
almost exhausted.
Yet he still has one official term left.
If he reforms,
he can complete this term.
If he continues as before,
he will not leave his post alive.'
She also said:
'When burning paper money,
if you wish to send money to a certain deity the next morning,
first burn thirty-two sheets of paper money
to seek the Five Paths,
and the deity will surely receive it.
If you just burn incense ordinarily,
it often does not reach.
For spring and autumn sacrifices,
no special notification is needed.
When burning,
do not place it directly on the ground;
use firewood or grass as a base,
light it from one end,
and do not stir or break it,
so the money remains intact
and each piece reaches its destination.'
By mid-August,
Lady Lǐ returned again,
suddenly joyful, saying:
'I have a plan to escape now.'
Zhèng asked her,
and she said:
'What to do?
But we need thirty to fifty thousand sheets of paper money
to have them carry out the plan.'
Zhèng then sought help from acquaintances,
and all the local officials knew of it,
joining together
with effort,
to save her as instructed.
A few days later,
she finally agreed to explain.
She then said:
'In the underworld, there is another case of someone killed by having their five viscera removed.
The underworld investigation is not yet complete,
so they will take those five viscera
and place them in Lady Mǎ’s abdomen,
allowing her to be reborn.'
From then on, the summons grew less frequent,
sometimes only once every ten days.
They only said:
'The review of the case files is not finished;
the mentioned punishment is not yet seen,
only interrogations and judgments proceed.'
She also once predicted that a certain person in a certain lane of the county, with a certain name,
would die on a certain month and day,
and when the time came, there was no error.
Zhèng also said himself:
'I am due to serve as acting Ānfēng assistant magistrate.'
On the third day of the first month the following year,
he was indeed invited by Vice Censor-in-Chief Cuī to serve as acting Ānfēng County assistant magistrate,
all of which his wife had long known.
After the first month,
Thus he was spared from being pursued and summoned.
Mr. Zhèng himself had over forty pages of records,
so this is a brief account.
Zhào Wénruò
During the Dàyè era of the Suí dynasty,
Zhào Wénruò, a man from Cháng'ān County, Yōngzhōu,
died and after seven days,
his family prepared for the grand encoffining.
Just as they were about to place him in the coffin,
he retracted one foot.
The family was terrified,
and dared not proceed with the encoffining.
Wénruò then revived.
His relatives joyfully asked him what had happened.
Wénruò said:
"At first, someone led me to the king's palace.
The king asked:
'During your lifetime,
what meritorious deeds did you perform?'"
Wénruò replied to the king:
"I upheld and recited the Diamond Sutra."
The king sighed and said:
"Excellent!
This merit is foremost.
Although you have performed good deeds and accumulated merit,
I will still show you the place where you suffer punishment."
He ordered someone to lead Wénruò north for ten paces,
to a hole in a wall,
and told Wénruò to enter.
On the other side of the wall, someone reached out a hand,
grabbed Wénruò's head through the hole and pulled him out.
It was extremely painful and difficult,
but he managed to pass through to the other side of the wall.
There he saw a great hell,
with cauldrons of boiling water and instruments of torment.
The suffering of the sinners
cannot be fully described.
Then, numerous pigs, sheep, chickens, ducks, and the like
came rushing toward Wénruò to demand repayment for their lives.
Wénruò said:
"I did not eat your bodies,
why are you pressing me?"
The various animals said:
"You once ate me at such-and-such place,
my head, feet, and limbs,
joint by joint, torn apart,
each person drinking and chewing.
How can you deny it?"
Wénruò focused his mind on reciting the Buddha's name,
deeply repenting of his various sins.
He said nothing else,
but begged to perform meritorious deeds to repay and atone.
The animals then dispersed.
The attendant led Wénruò back to the king.
The king handed him a bowl of nails
and ordered Wénruò to eat them.
He also drove five nails into Wénruò's head, hands, and feet.
Then he released him.
Wénruò regained consciousness.
When he recounted this event,
he suffered from headaches and pain in his hands and feet.
After a long time of performing meritorious deeds,
the pain gradually subsided.
From then on,
he diligently recited and upheld the Diamond Sutra,
not daring to waste even a moment.
Whenever he met people, whether monastic or lay, close or distant,
he urged them all to uphold and recite it.
Later, while on an official mission,
he arrived at a courier station hall
and rested briefly.
At that time, he dreamed of a woman in black clothes
hurrying to beg for her life.
Wénruò woke in alarm
and immediately called the station master to ask:
"Were you about to kill a living creature for me?"
The station master replied:
"Indeed, I was about to slaughter a small lamb for you, sir."
Wénruò asked:
"What color is the lamb?"
He answered:
"It is a black ewe lamb."
Wénruò responded:
"Release it quickly,
I will pay the price."
He redeemed it and set it free.
This was truly due to the mighty power of prajñā,
a hidden aid and spiritual response.
Kǒng Kè
During the Wǔdé era of the Táng dynasty,
Kǒng Kè, who served as Registrar of the General Administration in Suìzhōu,
suddenly fell ill and died,
but revived after one day.
He recounted
that he had been taken to an official's court,
where he was asked why he had killed two oxen.
Kǒng Kè said,
"I did not kill them."
The official said:
"Your younger brother testifies that you killed them;
why do you not admit it?"
Thereupon he summoned Kǒng Kè's brother,
who had already been dead for several years.
When he arrived,
he was wearing heavy shackles.
The official asked:
"Regarding what you said about your elder brother killing oxen—is it true or false?"
The brother said:
"My elder brother was previously sent on a mission to pacify the Liáo rebels;
he ordered me to kill oxen to feast them.
I was truly following my elder brother's command;
it was not my own decision to kill."
Kǒng Kè said:
"It is true that I ordered my brother to kill oxen for the feast,
but it was a matter of state affairs.
What crime have I committed?"
The official said:
"You killed oxen
to feast the Liáo,
using the pacification as an achievement,
to seek official rewards,
for your own benefit—
how can that be considered a matter of state affairs?"
Then he said to Kǒng Kè's brother:
"Because you testified against your elder brother, you have been detained here for a long time.
Since your elder brother ordered the killing,
you are without guilt,
and are now released to be reborn."
When he finished speaking,
the brother suddenly vanished,
and they did not even have a chance to converse.
The official then asked Kǒng Kè:
"Why did you also kill two ducks?"
Kǒng Kè said:
"When I previously served as county magistrate,
I killed ducks to entertain guests—
how can that be my crime?"
The official said:
"The guests had their own provisions;
you killed ducks to serve them
in order to seek a fine reputation—
if that is not a crime, then what is?"
He asked further:
"Why did you kill six chicken eggs?"
Kǒng Kè said:
"I have never eaten chicken eggs in my life.
I only recall that when I was nine years old, on the Cold Food Festival,
my mother gave me six eggs,
and I boiled and ate them."
The official said:
"So you wish to shift the blame onto your mother."
Kǒng Kè said:
"I dare not,
I am only stating the reason."
The official said:
"You took the lives of others;
you must bear the consequences yourself."
When he finished speaking,
suddenly several dozen people came to seize Kǒng Kè
and began to drag him away.
Kǒng Kè cried out loudly:
"This court is also greatly unjust and arbitrary!"
Hearing this, the official
called him back and said:
"What is unjust and arbitrary?"
Kǒng Kè said:
"Not a single sin committed in my life has been overlooked,
yet none of the good deeds I have performed in my life
have been recorded—
is that not arbitrary?"
The official asked the officer in charge,
"What good deeds has Kǒng Kè performed,
and why have they not been recorded?"
The officer in charge replied:
"His good deeds have all been recorded as well,
weighed against his sins.
If his good deeds are many and his sins few,
he is first allowed to receive the blessings.
If his sins are many and his good deeds few,
he is first made to suffer punishment.
Since Kǒng Kè's good deeds are few and his sins many,
we have not yet taken account of his good deeds."
The official angrily said:
"Even though he must first suffer punishment,
why did you not announce his good deeds to show him?"
He ordered the officer in charge to be whipped one hundred times.
In an instant, the whipping was finished,
and blood splattered on the ground.
Then he announced all the good deeds Kǒng Kè had performed in his life,
and none were omitted.
The official said to Kǒng Kè:
"You ought to first suffer punishment,
but I will now allow you to return for seven days,
so that you may diligently accumulate blessings."
Thereupon he sent someone to escort him out,
and Kǒng Kè revived.
Kǒng Kè gathered many monks and nuns,
performed rituals and repented,
practicing asceticism with utmost diligence,
and recounted his experience.
When the seven days arrived,
his family bid him farewell,
and shortly after, he passed away.
Huò Yǒulín
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
Huò Yǒulín served as the wèi of Jí County,
and was on duty in the prefecture under the direct supervision of the prefect.
The prefect, Duàn Chóngjiǎn, was severe and cruel.
During an inspection tour,
on that day,
after noon, he demanded a sheep kidney.
Yǒulín hurried to procure it,
and the butcher, in a panic,
before even killing the sheep,
cut open its side and removed the kidney.
That evening,
Yǒulín saw an official who said:
"The King summons you.
Yǒulín followed the official to see the King,
and the King said:
"Someone has accused you, saying
you did not wait for the sheep to be killed,
but took its kidney while it was still alive.
How could you do such a thing?"
Yǒulín replied:
"This was Prefect Duàn who ordered the sheep killed;
it was not my doing from the start."
The King ordered Chóngjiǎn's allotted food provisions to be brought,
and after examining them,
he said to the sheep:
"You were indeed meant to be food for Prefect Duàn;
how dare you falsely accuse Wèi Huò?"
He then drove it out,
and ordered the original summoning official to escort Yǒulín back.
As Yǒulín returned,
he passed through a courtyard,
which was called
the courtyard of the Yùshǐ Dàfū.
Yǒulín asked the official,
"What official is this?"
The official said:
"All offices are here;
why only this one?"
Yǒulín asked again who the Dàfū was,
and he replied:
"It is Dí Rénjié."
Yǒulín said,
"Lord Dí is my late maternal uncle;
I wish to see him."
The official had the gatekeeper announce him,
and shortly after, he was summoned inside.
Rénjié stood up,
and upon seeing Yǒulín,
wept sorrowfully.
He then asked if Yǒulín had been released to return.
Calling him to sit in the honored seat,
an assistant official passed by with a case file.
Rénjié asked what case it was.
The reply was:
"Lǐ Shìzhī is to become chancellor."
He asked further whether the celestial ministry had ruled on it yet,
and the reply was:
"All offices have completed their reviews;
he has already been granted five years."
Rénjié then added his endorsement to the document.
Only after finishing
did he turn back to Yǒulín and say,
"You have been here a long time;
your body has already decayed.
He ordered his attendants to fetch two pills of medicine and gave them to him,
saying, "Take these back,
grind them into powder,
and apply it to the decayed areas."
Yǒulín bowed and took his leave.
After walking more than ten lǐ from the gate,
he came to a large pit,
was pushed in by the official,
and thus revived.
It was the height of summer, and Yǒulín had been dead for seven days before reviving.
Though his heart was faintly warm,
much of his body had decayed.
He made the medicine in his hand into powder,
applied it to the decayed areas,
and as the medicine took effect, he healed,
able to rise after a few days.
Chóngjiǎn, having learned of this,
inquired about the matter,
and sighed over it for a long time.
More than a month later,
Lǐ Shìzhī indeed became chancellor.
Huángfǔ Xún
Huángfǔ Xún of Āndìng,
during the Kāiyuán era,
first served as cānjūn of Xiàng Prefecture.
He fell ill and died suddenly,
but revived after the time it takes to eat a meal.
The prefect, Dúgū Sīzhuāng,
was fond of renowned scholars.
Hearing that Xún had returned to life,
he personally went to where Xún was,
to ask what he had seen in the underworld.
Xún said,
it was all very clear,
but he was weak and exhausted,
and asked to speak slowly after resting a bit.
Earlier,
when Xún first took office,
he had once acted as sīgōng.
The abbot of Kāiyuán Temple
sent him twenty catties of beef.
At first, he did not understand the reason,
but accepted and ate it.
Soon after, he was summoned to the underworld,
which turned out to be because the monk had implicated him.
When he saw the judge,
the judge asked why he had killed an ox.
Xún said:
"I have been vegetarian all my life;
I have never committed such an act."
The judge ordered the monk to be summoned.
Soon, the monk arrived bearing a cangue,
and said to Xún:
"I was the one who killed it and gave it to you;
you truly did not know.
The reason I implicated you
was to seek blessings transferred through your merit-making."
He then addressed the judge:
"I myself bear the guilt for killing the ox;
I only wish to speak with the Cānjūn."
The judge said:
"Very well."
The monk then went to where Xún was,
and said to him:
"Later, you will become a judge in Tóng Prefecture;
please build a dhāraṇī pillar for me."
Xún asked,
"How could a cānjūn of Xiàng Prefecture become an official in Tóng Prefecture?
Moreover, I am very poor;
a pillar is not easy to build.
What should I do?"
The monk said:
"If you do not go to Tóng Prefecture, then forget it;
but if you do get there,
I hope you will not forget my request.
However, I have confessed my guilt,
and will now receive punishment.
By the time you reach Tóng Prefecture,
my punishment will also be complete,
and I will be reborn as a pig.
After you build the pillar,
you must certainly hold a vegetarian feast to celebrate and transfer merit.
At that time, you will witness something."
Xún then agreed.
Soon, he saw an ox-headed man take the monk away, piercing his neck with a fork.
Xún was released and returned.
Sīzhuāng had always been on good terms with the monk,
so he summoned him and told him what had happened.
The monk was very fearful and sorrowful,
and thus devoted his personal wealth to performing meritorious deeds.
Five days later,
he suffered a headache,
and soon developed three abscesses,
in the shape of fork marks.
He died after a few days.
Xún was promoted from cānjūn of Xiàng Prefecture to Bīngcáo Cānjūn of the Left Martial Guard,
and after several years,
he was selected to become Sīshì of Tóng Prefecture.
Upon arriving,
he raised a hundred thousand coins from official funds,
built the pillar, and held the vegetarian feast.
A small pig came and knelt before the master,
and after the feast concluded,
it circled the pillar, walking hundreds of rounds,
before dying.
Péi Líng
During the Kāiyuán era,
Péi Líng, a county lieutenant of Cháng'ān,
was suddenly afflicted by a severe illness for several days.
On the night of the fifteenth day of the first lunar month,
after the second watch,
he suddenly saw two officials in yellow robes holding a summons in the hall,
saying,
"The King summons you."
Péi Líng pleaded that he was ill,
and called for his family to fetch a horse.
After a long time, no horse was brought,
so he followed the officials away.
He saw the streets filled with bright lanterns,
but after the officials left the gate and traveled over ten li,
the lights and smoke vanished,
leaving only a path through withered grass.
After walking fifty li,
they arrived at a city
with walls entirely black
and devoid of any trees.
Suddenly, they encountered a white-robed lay Buddhist,
whose appearance was majestic and imposing.
He said to the two officials:
"This man is innocent;
why have you brought him here?"
Turning to look at Péi Líng, he asked:
"Do you know you are about to die?"
Péi Líng began to weep,
clasped his hands, and addressed the lay Buddhist:
"In life, I have never committed any sinful deeds.
Yet now I am here;
what should I do?"
He begged for help and guidance.
The lay Buddhist said to the officials:
"This man is a scholar-official,
and moreover, he has done no wrong.
It is not appropriate to remove his cap and sash."
The officials then returned them to him,
and they proceeded into the city.
After a few li,
they saw vermilion gates, bright and splendid,
with exotic trees lush and flourishing.
Ahead, an official said he was the Registrar,
who ordered Péi Líng to be handed over to a clerk
to examine his sins and merits.
The clerk said:
"You have committed no major sins;
in principle, you should not have been brought here."
Péi Líng earnestly begged for assistance.
Checking the records, the clerk said:
"You killed a donkey,
which is why you were summoned. However, the donkey was actually killed by a market official.
If you simply do not admit to it,
the matter will surely be dismissed."
Shortly after,
the King took his seat,
and the Registrar led Péi Líng in.
The King asked why this man had been summoned,
and the Registrar replied:
"The market official brought him;
we are just questioning him."
Péi Líng said:
"I only sought intestines;
I did not order the donkey to be killed."
As soon as he finished speaking,
he saw the market official with a cangue around his neck in front,
followed by dozens of donkeys, sheep, chickens, and pigs.
They trailed behind him.
The King asked the market official
why he had implicated this man.
The donkey then stepped forward and said:
"I was indeed killed by the market official.
He sold my meat to passersby;
it has nothing to do with Lieutenant Péi."
The market official tried to speak,
but the other sheep and pigs,
each according to their grievances,
spoke as well. The King said,
"This man still has several official appointments and emoluments ahead of him;
he cannot stay long.
He should be released quickly.
If there is further delay,
I fear his physical form will decay."
Then, turning to Péi Líng, he said:
"I am ordering your release.
You must do everything possible to cultivate blessings."
Péi Líng bowed twice and left,
but the King called him back again.
He told the Registrar,
"Take this man to see the various hells."
The Registrar ordered someone to lead Péi Líng forward,
and they entered a small opening.
Inside, he saw ox-headed guards piercing people with tridents,
each suffering according to their karma.
Péi Líng refused to watch and exited the small opening.
After bidding farewell to the Registrar,
he went to take leave of the other officials.
One official said:
"I was originally a clerk in the Ministry of Revenue."
Another said:
"I was originally a clerk in the Jīngzhào Prefecture.
I have been in the underworld for a long time,
unable to seek rebirth in the human world.
If you could copy the *Golden Light Sutra*, the *Lotus Sutra*, the *Vimalakīrti Sutra*, the *Nirvana Sutra*, and others for us,
and also hold vegetarian feasts for deliverance,
we could then be reborn in the human world."
Péi Líng agreed to all of this.
The officials also requested three thousand strings each of gold and silver coins.
Péi Líng said,
"As a capital official, I am poor and truly cannot manage this."
The officials said:
"The gold coins
are actually yellow paper money from the human world.
The silver coins
are white paper money."
Péi Líng said:
"If it's paper money you seek,
then I can certainly manage it.
But I don't know where to send it."
The officials said:
"In the human world, money is made in the markets,
but most of it is collected by the underworld.
You can call paper money makers
to produce it in a secluded room in your home.
Once finished,
place it in bags.
Then burn it by the water's edge,
and we will surely receive it.
When we receive the money,
if a crosswind stirs the ashes,
it means we have received it.
If the wind scatters the ashes,
then it is taken by the underworld or earthly ghosts and spirits.
This can serve as a usual indicator.
However, ghosts and spirits are often plagued by hunger,
so when burning the money,
you should also offer a little fine wine and food.
Place two bundles of grass on the mat,
and we can sit reflected in the grass
and also partake of the food."
After bidding farewell,
he walked several li
and arrived home.
He saw his family weeping,
and then felt pain.
His entire body felt dazed and confused,
and he remained in a stupor for a long time.
When he opened his eyes, he revived.
After having the sutras and images made and burning the paper money,
he recovered fully within ten days, as if nothing had happened.
The assistant magistrate of Liùhé County
The Deputy Magistrate of Liùhé County
during the Kāiyuán era died suddenly
and revived after several days.
He said that when he first died,
he was seized and brought before a judge,
who turned out to be the former magistrate of Liùhé, Liú Míngfǔ.
They met with mixed sorrow and joy.
The judge asked how his family was.
The deputy replied:
"My home is very close to here.
Have you not returned there?"
The magistrate said:
"The paths of the underworld and the living world are separate;
how could I go there?"
The deputy said:
"Your son passed the imperial examinations early,
and the household has encountered no misfortune.
Only your wife is elderly
and suffers slightly from wind illness."
The magistrate said:
"Your allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted.
You were summoned because of a lawsuit over some sheep.
That is why you were brought here.
You should explain yourself clearly;
I will arrange for your swift return."
After a short while,
a black cloud came from the east.
Within the cloud was a large ship
that crashed to the ground with a thunderous roar.
Four sheep heads were seen.
The judge asked:
"Why did you wrongfully kill these creatures?"
The deputy answered:
"The prefect was conducting an official requisition;
it was not my fault."
Two of the heads fell silent.
The judge scolded them:
"You yourselves bear the prefect's orders;
how can you further accuse the deputy magistrate?"
The ship then flew away.
The sheep said loudly:
"Judge, you are partial.
We shall meet the Emperor and argue our case."
The judge said to the deputy:
"The Emperor is the Celestial Emperor.
How could these creatures get to see him?
It is like the Son of Heaven on earth;
for common people to seek an audience,
isn't that also difficult?
Nevertheless, you must still perform meritorious deeds for them."
After speaking,
he released the deputy to return. Once out,
he saw a woman
with graceful and beautiful features,
who came forward and bowed twice.
He asked her the reason.
She said:
"I am a daughter of the Tán family from Yángzhōu.
I was summoned here a while ago
and, being innocent, was released to return.
But the gatekeeper, captivated by my beauty,
deliberately detained me.
I have been away from home for a long time
and fear my house may have fallen into ruin.
Now that you are returning,
I beg you to look after it.
My family has always been wealthy.
If I can accompany you back,
I will offer a thousand strings of cash
and furthermore become your concubine forever,
holding nothing back.
This is my plea for your pity."
The deputy went in and reported this to the judge.
The judge said to the deputy:
"Of the thousand strings, I get two hundred,
my son gets two hundred,
and the remaining six hundred belong to you."
He then wrote a note to show her.
The judge said:
"My two hundred can be used for meritorious deeds."
He then called the gatekeeper and asked:
"How dare you detain the Tán family's daughter?"
He ordered the gatekeeper beaten twenty strokes
and sent the woman to return with the deputy.
After traveling over ten li,
they parted ways and each returned to life.
After the deputy recovered,
he went to the Tán family to visit the woman.
Upon reaching the gate,
the woman, hearing his voice,
hurried out and bowed twice.
She apologized, saying:
"I once promised to be your concubine, but it was not by my own will;
my parents have married me to another.
Now I will use two hundred thousand cash to redeem myself,
and the remaining eight hundred strings are as per our previous agreement."
The deputy received the money,
gave it to Magistrate Liú's son,
and also arranged vegetarian feasts and meritorious deeds, etc.
By the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
this man was still alive.
Xuē Tāo
Xuē Tāo, the Sheriff of Jiānglíng,
during the Qiányuán era,
died and revived after three days.
He said that he first encountered an officer
holding a summons that read,
"Pursued by order of the King."
The endorsement on the summons bore the character "Hù."
Xuē Tāo did not know which king it was
and mounted a horse to leave.
After traveling about ten li,
they reached a city.
The officer pushed open the gate
and entered a hall.
A person with feathered guards, like a king,
Xuē Tāo entered and bowed twice.
The King asked:
"Are you an official from Jīngzhōu?"
Xuē Tāo said yes.
The King said:
"How numerous are your crimes!
Now those who accuse you
are too many to count."
He replied:
"When I previously served as the County Sheriff of Chénggù,
Chénggù was responsible for presenting hawks and falcons.
I was in charge of this duty,
so I had to kill them;
it is true that many were killed."
The King asked:
"Were any killed for private reasons?"
He said:
"There were some!"
"Which were more, public or private?"
He said:
"Private killings were fewer than public ones."
The King said:
"Indeed, it is so.
Your official salary and fortune are considerable,
and your lifespan is not yet over.
They can do nothing to you,
but you still had to be summoned for questioning."
He ordered Xuē Tāo to go outside
and apologize to all the lives.
When Xuē Tāo arrived,
he saw pheasants and hares covering several acres,
all flying and rushing toward Xuē Tāo.
Xuē Tāo said:
"The Son of Heaven demanded hawks and falcons;
it was not my doing.
Judging by your intentions,
you all wish to kill me.
What is the reason for this?
I have just received orders
to copy scriptures and create images for you,
so that you may all be reborn.
Why must so many kill one life?"
The King also sent someone to relay a message.
After a long while,
they gradually withdrew.
Xuē Tāo went back in.
The King said to him:
"Your allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted.
Therefore, I have specially considered your case,
but upon returning, you should perform meritorious deeds
to redeem yourself."
Xuē Tāo bowed repeatedly.
The King asked:
"Do you read books?"
He said:
"I read them quite often."
He asked again:
"Do you know of Yáng Hù from the Jìn dynasty?"
He said:
"I know of him!"
The King said:
"That is I.
I once served in Jīngzhōu
as the provincial governor.
I died in the official residence,
so when I saw you, an official from Jiānglíng,
I felt a sense of familiarity."
After speaking, he bid farewell and left,
ordering the officer who had pursued him to escort him back to his home.
Thus, he revived.
Zhào Péi
Míngjīng Zhào Péi,
during the Zhēnyuán era,
was selected and appointed to Qīnghuà County in Bāzhōu.
Frustrated in his ambitions, he fell ill,
loathed the light,
and did not eat or drink for over forty days.
Suddenly, he felt thunder rumbling in his room,
and shortly after, a red aura like a drum
rolled to his bed,
rose into the air,
and settled over his heart.
At first, he felt his spirit scatter and wander,
faintly as if in a dream.
A man in red robes with a flat headscarf
led him eastward.
They exited a mountain pass,
where water flowed east and west.
He stood for a long time gazing at it,
then continued east.
There was a bridge adorned with gold and jade.
Crossing north,
they entered a city,
arriving at an official bureau,
where clerks and officials were numerous.
He saw his brother-in-law Jiǎ Yì,
arguing with him over the matter of slaughtering an ox.
Suspecting this was the underworld court,
he hastily fled and hid by a wall.
The wall was like stone,
black,
and several zhàng high.
From the hall came shouts and commands,
and the red-robed man led him into a large courtyard.
A clerk announced:
"The Director of Fate is judging people."
He saw Jiǎ Yì again,
and thus argued with him.
Yì stubbornly insisted,
leaving him no way to clear himself.
Suddenly, a huge mirror a zhàng in diameter,
suspended in midair,
appeared. Looking up at it,
he clearly saw Jiǎ Yì wielding a knife.
He bore the evidence plainly.
With an expression of pity,
Yì finally admitted his guilt.
The red-robed man led him further to another bureau,
entering a courtyard,
where a person in brown cloak and purple-cloud crown,
resembling a revered statue,
rebuked him:
"Why did you
steal two headscarves
at the Huázhōu market,
and conceal three shēng of acorns?"
He then bowed countless times.
The red-robed man led him out again,
and asked:
"Can you wander to the Shàngqīng realm?"
They then climbed a mountain together,
overlooking flowing water below,
the water cascading and churning with foam,
thousands following the current into it,
and he unconsciously followed the flow as well.
After a long while,
he stopped on a large rock,
with green and white haloed paths.
The red-robed man transformed into two people,
one guiding him,
one urging him.
They then ascended and stood on a stone cliff,
smooth and dustless.
Walking several lǐ,
beside them were grasses like red orchids,
with dense stems and leaves,
no thorns,
their flowers fluttering,
scattering into the air.
There were also grasses like lettuce,
clinging to the ground,
also with flying flowers,
initially emerging like puffballs,
bursting open,
large as stacked mats,
reddish-yellow.
Passing this,
they saw fire like a mountain,
stretching across the sky.
They waited for the flames to cease before proceeding.
Reaching a great city,
with layered watchtowers on its walls,
fruit trees lining the streets,
immortals in company,
alternately singing and playing music,
their celestial beauty peerless in the world.
Passing through three gates in total,
ships and vessels shone brilliantly.
The ground,
and walls,
gleamed with clear light like mirrors,
above, the sky was unseen,
as if covered by a crimson halo.
The main hall had three tiers,
all lined with revered statues.
He saw a Daoist priest,
like an old acquaintance.
Zhào requested to become his disciple,
but was refused.
Among the various instruments was one like a qín,
four chǐ long,
with nine strings,
the head wider for over a chǐ,
with two crossbars in the middle,
to vary the tones.
Another was like a wine vessel,
with three strings,
three chǐ long,
the belly broad above and narrow below,
the back full and rounded at the neck.
After the record was reviewed,
he was led out.
South of the gate was a courtyard,
where someone in crimson crown and purple cloak
instructed him to sit in the hall with the two red-robed men.
He was then ordered to first review the Wùshēn register,
the register like human legal documents,
beginning with a person's birth date,
then stating name and age,
below noting birth month and day,
separately arranged horizontally with the sixty-year cycle.
All merits and virtues,
were detailed under each day.
If none,
there were no words.
Zhào looked at his own record,
name, birth date, month, and day,
all without error.
Those reviewed in the register,
numbered in hundreds of millions.
The red-robed man said,
every sixty years,
all people under heaven are reviewed in the register,
to examine good and evil and adjust lifespans.
The red-robed man led him out the north gate,
to the original path,
clasped his hand and bid farewell:
"Wandering here is your soul,
follow this path back,
do not look back,
and you will reach home."
Following his words,
he walked somewhat hastily,
stumbled and fell,
awakening as if from a dream,
having been dead for seven days.
Zhào wrote "Record of Soul Wandering to Shàngqīng,"
narrating events in great detail.
Dèng Chéng
Dèng Chéng was
a man from Yùzhāng,
over twenty years old.
He once died suddenly.
The officials led him to the underworld,
first passing by the judge.
The judge was the former governor Huáng Lín,
and Lín was Chéng’s maternal uncle.
Seeing Chéng, he was both sad and joyful,
and asked in detail about family matters.
Chéng told him,
and all were well.
Chéng then pleaded for mercy.
Lín said:
"I also wish for you to return,
to convey a message to my younger brothers."
He then entered to inform the king.
After coming out, he said:
"It has been decided to release you."
After a while,
the king summoned Chéng and asked:
"What sins did you commit in life,
that you have so many vengeful adversaries?
However, your allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted,
so you should return.
Do not create more underworld grievances."
Soon, dozens of animals came to bite Chéng.
The king said to them:
"Dèng Chéng has already killed you all;
killing Dèng Chéng again
is a pointless act.
I now release Chéng to return,
and have him perform meritorious deeds for you,
enabling you all to be reborn as humans.
Is that not good?"
They all said:
"We do not want meritorious deeds,
we only wish to kill Dèng Chéng."
The king said:
"What benefit is that to you?
Killing Dèng Chéng,
you will still not escape your animal forms.
Why not accept meritorious deeds,
and be reborn as humans?"
Many of them left,
but one donkey repeatedly came to trample Chéng,
and a dog bit his clothes, refusing to leave.
The king strenuously rescued and protected him,
and only then was he spared.
He then sent the officials who had pursued Chéng to escort him back.
On the way out, he passed by Lín.
Lín said to Chéng:
"No joy surpasses rebirth;
you are now able to return,
which is deeply gratifying.
Although I am a judge,
I suffer punishment daily.
Stay here for a while,
and you will soon see."
Suddenly, an ox-headed guard
came holding fire, burning Lín from head to toe.
Lín turned to ashes,
then vanished,
and soon was reborn.
After weeping sorrowfully for a long time,
he said to Chéng:
"My suffering is like this—
how can it be endured!
When you return,
convey to my younger brothers
to strive to perform meritorious deeds for me.
So that I may escape this suffering.
However, if not from my own possessions,
even if meritorious deeds are performed,
I ultimately will not receive them.
I previously used official funds to purchase an estate;
now use this to commission Buddhist sutras,
and I will then receive them.
I fear my younger brothers may be doubtful
and not believe your words,
so take my jade hairpin back
to show them."
He then took the hairpin from his head and gave it to Chéng.
Before Lín was a large water pit.
He told Chéng to close his eyes,
pushed him into the pit, and Chéng then revived.
His parents were wealthy,
and pitying their son’s rebirth,
within a few days performed various meritorious deeds.
After Chéng recovered,
he went to the Huáng family,
relayed Lín’s request,
and returned the jade hairpin.
The Huáng family recognized the hairpin,
and the whole household wept sorrowfully.
After a few days, they sold the estate to commission sutras.
Zhāng Yáo
Zhāng Yáo from Dōngyáng fell ill and died,
and revived after several days.
He said
he was led by officials past a mansion,
inside which was a nobleman with attendants like a king.
Yáo entered the courtyard,
and saw all the creatures he had killed come to confront him.
Yáo had once killed an ox,
using two bolts of cloth
to perform blessings for it.
That ox was also in the courtyard,
with the two bolts of cloth on its horns.
He had also once provided for a sick monk,
and that monk also came,
saying to the officials:
"Zhāng Yáo has recited the *Diamond Sutra*
three thousand times;
the merit has entered his bones.
He also copied one volume of the *Lotus Sutra*;
his merit is great, his sins few,
so he should not yet die."
The officials ordered him to be weighed.
The animals all rose,
but Yáo remained on the ground.
The officials took the Book of Fate to check.
A purple-robed official led a yellow-robed clerk holding a yellow register,
saying:
"Zhāng Yáo’s name has been covered;
he should die."
Looking at the register,
a paper slip covered his name.
They then ordered the Tàishān register to be brought.
After a moment,
another purple-robed official led a yellow-robed clerk holding a register.
He said:
"Zhāng Yáo is covered;
he should die."
They then ordered the inner chamber register to be checked.
The messenger said:
"His name is only half covered;
he should not yet die."
The king asked Yáo:
"Your name is fully covered in two places,
and half covered in one place.
Out of six parts,
five parts indicate you should die,
so you should not be reborn.
But due to your merit,
I release you back to the human world.
Do not kill living beings again."
He ordered Yáo to enter the underworld,
to see everywhere
the suffering,
the fire pits and boiling cauldrons—
all were seen.
The monk said:
"Do not commit sins again."
He then stamped Yáo’s thigh with a seal,
saying:
"Take this as proof."
After reviving,
the seal was very clear,
and has not faded to this day.
Zhī Fǎhéng
The Jin dynasty monk Zhī Fǎhéng,
fell ill for ten days,
died for three days and then revived.
He recounted that at the time of death,
someone took him away.
He saw several places resembling official offices,
but refused to enter them.
Suddenly, he saw an iron wheel,
with claws on it,
turning from the west,
with no one pushing or pulling it,
yet it spun swiftly like the wind.
An official called for the sinners to stand before the wheel,
and as the wheel turned, it crushed them.
They were tossed back.
This happened several times,
until the people were shattered and mangled.
The official called for Monk Héng to stand before the wheel.
Héng, terrified, blamed himself,
regretting his lack of diligence,
thinking, “Am I now to face this wheel?”
As soon as he finished speaking,
the official said to Héng:
“Monk, you may leave.”
Then, looking up,
he saw a hole in the sky,
and suddenly, without realizing it, he ascended,
his head passing through the hole,
his hands gripping the sides,
looking around in all directions.
He saw a seven-treasure official ship and various heavenly beings.
Héng was overjoyed,
but could not ascend further,
growing tired and descending again.
The person who had taken him away laughed and said:
“What did you see
that you couldn’t ascend?”
Then he handed Héng over to the ship’s officer,
who sailed the ship,
making Héng the helmsman.
Héng said:
“I cannot steer the ship.”
But they forced him.
There were hundreds of ships,
all following behind Héng.
Héng did not know how to hold the helm,
and ran aground on a sandbar.
The officials interrogated Héng,
and by law, he deserved beheading.
They led Héng ashore,
beat drums and prepared to execute him.
Suddenly, two five-colored dragons
pushed the ship back afloat,
and the officials then pardoned him,
but Héng was greatly terrified.
Looking northwest, he saw a lecture hall,
with many monks inside.
Hearing the sounds of sutra chanting,
Héng hurriedly ran toward it.
The hall had twelve steps,
and as he stepped onto the first step,
he saw his deceased teacher Fǎzhù,
sitting on a folding chair.
Seeing Héng, he said:
“You are my disciple,
why have you come?”
Then he rose and approached the steps,
striking Héng’s face with a towel, saying:
“Do not come.”
Héng very much wanted to ascend,
and took another step up the stairs,
but Fǎzhù pushed him down again.
Only on the third attempt did he ascend.
He saw a well on level ground,
three or four zhang deep,
with bricks tightly fitted without gaps.
Héng thought to himself,
“This well is natural.”
Someone by the well said:
“If it were not natural,
how could it become a well?”
Though he saw Fǎzhù still leaning and watching him,
he said to Héng:
“You may go back the way you came,
the dogs will not bite you.”
Héng returned to the water’s edge,
but the ship from before was no longer there.
Héng was thirsty,
and wanted to drink water,
so he fell into the water,
and thus revived.
From then on, he left home,
observed precepts and ate vegetables,
diligently contemplating day and night,
becoming a monk of utmost conduct.
The bhikṣu Fǎqiáo,
was Héng’s disciple.
Chéng Dàohuì,
courtesy name Wénhé,
was from Wǔchāng.
For generations, his family had practiced the Way of the Five Pecks of Rice,
and he did not believe in Buddhism.
He often said:
"Since ancient times, there has been no orthodox teaching
greater than that of Lǎozi.
Why then should one believe and be deluded by foreign words,
considering them a superior religion?"
In the fifteenth year of the Tàiyuán era,
he fell ill and died,
but his chest remained warm.
His family did not encoffin him for burial,
and after several days, he revived.
He recounted that when he first died,
he saw over ten people
who bound him and took him away.
They encountered a bhikṣu who said:
"This man has blessings from past lives;
he must not be bound."
They then untied his bonds,
and the group dispersed and left.
The road was level and smooth,
but on both sides, thorns grew densely,
leaving almost no room for feet.
Those driving the sinners
forced them to run through it,
their bodies pierced by the thorns,
their cries and groans grating on the ears.
Seeing Dàohuì walking on the level road,
they all sighed with envy, saying:
"A disciple of the Buddha walks the road
with even greater advantage than others."
Dàohuì said:
"I do not follow the Dharma."
The man laughed and said:
"You have forgotten, that is all."
Dàohuì then recalled that in a previous life, he had followed the Buddha,
having already passed through five births and five deaths.
He had forgotten his original resolve,
and in this present life in the world,
he encountered wicked people in his youth,
and, not yet discerning the false from the true,
was deluded by a heterodox path.
When they reached a great city,
they went straight into the hall.
He saw a man,
about forty or fifty years old,
sitting facing south.
Seeing Dàohuì, he exclaimed in surprise:
"You should not have come here."
A man wearing a single-layered robe and a headcloth,
holding a register,
replied:
"This man felled a village altar and killed someone;
his crimes warrant him coming here."
The bhikṣu he had met earlier
also followed Dàohuì in
and argued very earnestly on his behalf,
saying:
"Felling the village altar is not a crime;
this man has many blessings from past lives.
Though killing is a grave offense,
retribution has not yet come due."
The man sitting facing south said:
"Punish those who recorded him."
He then invited Dàohuì to take a seat,
apologizing:
"The petty officials were mistaken and excessive,
wrongly recording and bringing you here.
This was also because you had forgotten your past lives
and did not know to follow the true Dharma."
When they were about to send Dàohuì back,
he was made to temporarily serve as the Deputy Inspector General,
to tour and observe the hells.
Dàohuì gladly took his leave and departed,
led and followed by attendants.
They traveled to various cities,
all of which were hells,
with multitudes of people,
all undergoing retribution for their crimes.
He saw rabid dogs
biting people at every joint,
their flesh scattering and falling,
blood flowing to cover the ground.
There were also flocks of birds,
their beaks sharp as blades,
flying with great speed,
entering people's mouths,
piercing through from inside to out.
The people writhed and cried out,
their sinews and bones shattered and falling.
After he had observed all around,
they sent Dàohuì back.
He again met the bhikṣu he had encountered earlier,
who gave Dàohuì a copper object,
shaped like a small bell.
He said:
"When you return home,
discard this outside the gate;
do not bring it into the house.
On a certain year, month, and day,
you will face a calamity.
If you are cautious and pass through it,
your lifespan will extend to ninety."
At that time, Dàohuì's home was south of the Great Bridge in the capital.
On his way back,
when he reached Zàojiá Bridge,
he saw three relatives
stopping their carriage and conversing together,
mourning Dàohuì's death.
When he reached the gate,
he saw a maidservant walking and weeping as she went to market.
But those people and the maidservant
did not see him at all.
As Dàohuì was about to enter the gate,
he placed the copper object on a tree outside the gate.
It emitted a light that spread out,
streaming and flying up to the sky.
After a long while, it grew small again
and suddenly vanished.
When he reached the door,
he smelled the stench of the corpse
and felt distressed and repulsed by it.
At that time, guests and relatives had rushed to offer condolences,
and many were weeping for Dàohuì.
Unable to linger,
he entered the corpse,
and suddenly revived.
What he recounted about the people in the carriage and the maidservant going to market
all matched exactly.
Dàohuì later became the Minister of Justice.
Once, while attending a recitation in the Western Hall,
before he could take his place in the ranks,
he suddenly felt dizzy and stifled,
and could not recognize people.
Half a day later, he recovered.
Calculating the date and time,
it was exactly the period the monk had warned him about.
Soon after,
he was promoted to Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
He died in the sixth year of the Yuánjiā era,
at the age of eighty-nine.
The Monk Shàndào
The monk Shàndào,
while in Xīnyě,
once saw a man come to the temple for a gathering.
He clasped his hands respectfully,
and his diligence surpassed the ordinary.
Shàndào asked:
"Virtuous one, why do you apply your mind with such effort?"
The man replied:
"I once died for three days.
I saw over ten tiled rooms,
with several clerks below.
There was a wheel,
like a potter's wheel,
about two zhang or more in diameter.
There was an iron fork,
fixed onto the wheel,
and the wheel turned like the wind.
I sought death but could not attain it.
For one night and two days,
my eyes were dizzy and my heart stifled.
A clerk wearing a red headcloth came,
holding several bamboo slips and a brush.
He asked who this person was,
and the person by the wheel said:
'A disciple of the Buddha,
who in his time was not diligent,
but only performed superficial rituals toward others,
lacking a compassionate heart.'
The clerk asked:
'This man's sins are nearly at an end;
send him back.'
Thus I was able to leave
and came back to life.
Since I have not yet undergone such a death again,
I truly rejoice in performing superficial rituals toward others.
When marrying off a daughter or taking a wife for my son,
I always use five shēng of flour and two pairs of chickens
as gifts for the scholar-officials.
Today, when I clasp my hands and call upon the Buddha,
as soon as my hands part,
I fear I may later fall onto that wheel.'"
Lǐ Dàn
Lǐ Dàn of the Sòng Dynasty,
courtesy name Shìzé,
was from Guǎnglíng.
He was known in his hometown
for his filial piety, caution, simplicity, and integrity.
In the third year of the Yuánjiā era,
on the fourteenth day of the first month,
he suddenly fell ill,
and his heart
did not turn cold.
After seven days, he revived.
He was fed thin gruel,
and by the next day, he had recovered as usual.
He said
that there was a person
who came to his bedside holding a signal banner.
He said the Prefect summoned him,
so Dàn followed him.
They went straight north,
on a very level and clean road.
When they arrived,
the city gates and towers were tall and magnificent,
similar to present-day palace gates.
A messenger was sent to greet and console him,
calling Dàn to come forward.
When he reached the main hall,
he saw about thirty people
wearing single-layered garments and black headscarves,
sitting in solemn rows.
One person sat in the east,
wearing a robe and leaning on an armrest,
with attendants and guards on both sides,
numbering about a hundred or more.
He looked at Dàn and said to those seated:
"We should show him the various hells,
so that the world may know."
After Dàn heard this,
he raised his head and looked around,
and the previous surroundings were completely gone;
he was now in the midst of hell.
He saw groups of sinners
suffering various painful retributions,
moaning and wailing,
unbearable to watch.
Soon, a messenger announced:
"The Prefect is releasing you to return,
and will welcome you again later."
Thus, he returned.
In the sixth year, in the first month, he died again,
and after seven days, he revived once more.
He recounted what he had seen,
roughly the same as before.
Some sinners sent messages to their families,
saying that they had committed crimes while alive,
and asked for blessings to be performed on their behalf.
They mentioned names, relatives, acquaintances, and fellow villagers in some detail,
and Dàn, following their words, sought them out,
and found them all.
He also said
that in the Jiǎshēn year, a plague would spread,
killing many evil people.
Disciples of Buddhism,
if they observe the Eight Precepts fasting,
cultivate their minds and perform good deeds,
can be spared.
Dàn was originally a Daoist sacrificial officer,
and wanted to abandon the register and his original methods,
but the Daoist community advised against it,
so he practiced both,
and often encouraged others to observe the Eight Precepts fasting.
Liáng Jiǎ
During the Northern Qí period,
there was an official surnamed Liáng,
who was very wealthy.
When about to die,
he said to his wife and children:
"The slave and horse I loved in my lifetime,
having served me for a long time,
pleased me greatly.
When I die,
they can be buried with me as sacrifices.
Otherwise,
I
would feel abandoned."
After his death,
his family filled a sack with soil,
pressed it on the slave and killed him,
but the horse had not yet been killed.
The slave died and revived after four days,
saying
that at first, he did not feel himself leaving,
but suddenly arrived at an official residence,
and was detained at the gate.
After spending the night,
he saw his deceased master, shackled,
being led in by guards.
Seeing the slave, he said:
"I thought the dead could still use slaves,
so I left word to summon you.
But now each suffers their own torment,
completely unrelated to each other.
I will now inform the official to release you."
After speaking, he entered.
The slave peeked from outside the screen,
and saw the official ask the guards:
"How much fat was pressed yesterday?"
They replied:
"Eight dǒu."
The official said:
"Take him again,
and press out one hú and six dǒu."
The master was then dragged out,
unable to speak after all.
The next morning, he came again,
with a joyful expression.
He said to the slave:
"Now I will speak for you."
He entered again.
The official asked if they had obtained the fat,
and they replied:
"We did not."
The official asked why,
and the clerk said:
"This person died three days ago,
and his family invited monks to hold a service for him.
Every time the chanting of sutras was heard,
the iron beam would break,
so we could not obtain it."
The official said:
"Take him away for now."
The clerk informed the official:
"Please release the slave."
The official then ordered his release.
He left the gate together with his master,
and the master sent a message to his wife and children:
"Thanks to your blessings performed for me,
I have been spared great suffering.
But I am still not free,
so if you can further create sutras and images to save me,
I hope to be spared because of this.
From now on, do not make offerings,
as I cannot eat them,
and it only increases my sins."
After speaking, they parted,
and the slave was revived,
and recounted everything in detail.
His family had indeed held a service on that day,
so they devoted all their resources to performing blessings,
and the whole family practiced diligently.
Rén Yìfāng
Rén Yìfāng of Lè'ān, Prefect of Kuòzhōu in the Táng Dynasty,
during the Wǔdé era,
died and revived after several days.
He said himself
that he was taken to see King Yánluó.
The king ordered someone to lead him and show him the places of hell,
and what he described was no different from Buddhist sutras.
He also said
that underground, the daytime was dim and dark,
like walking in fog.
At that time, his family, because Yìfāng had a slight warmth in his heart,
invited monks to perform rituals,
and Yìfāng heard the sounds of chanting and praises underground.
The king checked his records,
and said to the clerk:
"He should not have died yet;
why was he mistakenly summoned?"
So he was released and sent back.
Yìfāng left,
and passed through three gates.
The gatekeepers were all asleep.
The escort said,
just follow the sound of chanting,
and you will reach home.
He saw a pit blocking the road,
and intending to jump over it,
he fell into the pit,
and immediately got up.
He discussed hell,
and drew pictures on the ground.
With the salary he received,
he all used it to create sutras and images,
and had copied over a thousand volumes of the *Diamond Sutra*.
So said Yìfāng himself.
Qí Shìwàng
Qí Shìwàng, a native of Wǔqiáng in Wèizhōu,
in the twenty-first year of the Zhēnguàn era,
died and revived after seven days.
He himself said
that after initially dying,
he was brought to see the King,
who then handed him over to the administrative office,
where he was separately sent for investigation.
After four or five days,
the investigation records stated:
"He shares the same surname and given name as someone who is due to die,
but he is not yet fated to die immediately."
The judge said to Shìwàng:
"In your lifetime, you enjoyed burning chicken eggs,
so you should suffer punishment before returning."
He then ordered someone to escort him out the gate.
About one or two li from the administrative office,
he saw a city gate,
from within the city came the sound of drums and music,
and Shìwàng joyfully hurried and entered it.
After entering,
the city gate closed,
and inside there were no buildings at all,
only hot ashes covering the ground everywhere.
Shìwàng was frantic and did not know what to do;
his feet were burned,
causing extreme pain.
Shìwàng looked around in all directions,
and the city gates were all open,
but when he ran toward a gate,
its door would immediately shut.
After a full day,
someone ordered the gatekeeper:
"Open the gate,
and release yesterday's sinner."
He then ordered someone to escort him back.
The messenger complained that the road was long,
and delayed, not sending him.
He first demanded money and silk,
and Shìwàng agreed.
Then they traversed rivers and paths,
treading through thorns and brambles.
When they reached a certain place,
it was like a circular enclosure,
inside which was a pit,
deep and dark.
Shìwàng was afraid of it,
but the messenger pushed him,
and he fell into the pit.
Unaware, he gradually revived.
Soon after, he prepared paper money and waited,
and the messenger returned as scheduled.
Shìwàng's wife also saw him together.
Yáng Shīcāo
Yáng Shīcāo, a native of Lǐquán County in Yōngzhōu,
during the Zhēnguàn era,
served as the county lieutenant of Lántián County.
Later, due to old age, he returned home
and took up farming as his livelihood.
However, his nature was vicious and malicious,
and he delighted in seeing others' faults.
Whenever fellow villagers had matters,
regardless of their importance,
he would record and report them to the authorities.
The county magistrate, Péi Qútán,
considered this troublesome and trivial,
and initially did not handle them.
Shīcāo sometimes submitted memorials to inform the emperor,
and people all disliked him.
He often said to others:
"Although my temperament is quick-tempered and violent,
since the Wǔdé era,
I have received the precepts four times,
and daily recite sutras and treatises.
However, if someone infringes upon me,
I cannot endure it."
In the first year of the Yǒnghuī era,
on the night of the seventh day of the fourth month,
he saw a person dressed in black clothes,
riding a white horse coming from the east,
who said,
"The Great Inspector of Dōngyáng summons you,"
and then vanished in an instant.
Shīcāo suddenly collapsed.
He had already arrived at the Dōngyáng records office.
At that time, the prefect's grand assembly had not yet dispersed,
so Shīcāo privately walked through the administrative offices,
all of which had desks, tables, beds, and mats.
He saw prisoners,
some wearing cangues and shackles,
with heads exposed and waists unbound,
some sitting, standing, walking, or staying.
They were too numerous to count.
Shīcāo walked eastward,
and arrived at a place,
where there was an extremely small opening,
from which only small stars flowed out,
and foul smoke billowed densely.
Two men were holding iron rods,
repairing the entrance.
Shīcāo asked:
"What administrative office is this?"
They replied:
"This is the Blazing Fire Hell,
intended for those who fail to fully uphold the precepts.
We heard there is a Yáng Shīcāo,
who throughout his life delighted in discussing others' faults,
hypocritically expressing shame to people's faces,
but if a single word infringed upon him,
he truly could not endure it.
He is to be sent here,
so we are repairing it.
Today is the eighth day of the fourth month,
and his family, because Shīcāo has died,
is making charitable offerings and vegetarian feasts,
so the administrative office is deliberating on releasing him,
but a decision has not yet been made.
I am waiting here."
Shīcāo then kowtowed, bowed, and expressed gratitude, saying:
"Yáng Shīcāo—
this disciple is he.
I beg for your compassion."
They replied:
"You only need to vow to worship one hundred thousand Buddhas,
diligently,
repent sincerely,
and change your malicious heart,
then you will be reborn in a blissful
place."
Shīcāo followed these words and made the vow,
and was thus granted release and return,
reviving after three days.
Cāo recounted everything to Chán Master Huìjìng,
reformed his faults and repented.
He is now seen to be seventy-five years old,
maintaining a perpetual vegetarian diet with each meal,
and performing worship and recitation at the six periods of the day.
Later, he dreamed of the previous summoning messenger, who said:
"Since you have ceased your evil deeds,
we will no longer come to summon you.
Only diligently and sincerely cultivate goodness."
Péi Zézǐ
In the Tang Dynasty, there was a man named Péi Zé from Líhú in Cáozhōu.
At the end of the Zhēnguàn era,
he was twenty years old
and died, but after three days, he revived.
He said himself that
when he first died,
he was taken by a person to the king’s place.
The king sent him to lead an ox and plow the land.
He pleaded, saying:
"My younger brothers are still small,
and there is no one to serve and support my parents."
The king then took pity on him
and sent an envoy to take him southward.
When they reached the third gate,
he entered and saw cauldrons of boiling water, as well as mountains of knives and forests of swords.
Several thousand heads had all been cut off
and were laid out on the ground.
These heads all spoke with their mouths, saying they were extremely hungry.
In his village, there was an old woman
who was nearly seventy years old.
At that time, she had not yet died
and was seen in front of the boiling cauldrons, tending the fire.
After observing everything,
he returned to the king’s presence.
There he saw Zhāng Chéng, a fellow villager,
who also had not yet died.
Someone accused Chéng, saying:
"He destroyed my house."
The king sent an envoy to investigate,
and the report said:
"It is true."
Chéng said:
"While plowing the land,
I unintentionally plowed through his grave mound;
it was not done on purpose."
The king said:
"Although you did not do it intentionally,
in the end, it was due to carelessness."
He then ordered someone to strike his waist seven times with a rod.
After a while,
the king said:
"You have no other matters;
I release you to return early."
He then had someone escort him away.
They sent him northward to climb over a wall.
When he climbed the wall,
he saw his own
house
and then heard crying sounds.
He then jumped down from the wall
and suddenly felt himself sitting up.
After reviving,
he recounted everything to the people of his village.
The villagers looked at Zhāng Chéng
and saw marks from the rod on his waist.
The marks were extremely blue-black.
When asked about destroying the grave,
he replied,
and it was not false.
The old woman soon fell ill
and died not long after.
In Hénán Prefecture, there was a clerk
named Guō Dàniáng from Luòyáng,
who lived in Yùcái Lane
and worked as a tavern keeper.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era, she passed away.
Her husband, surnamed Wáng,
served as a clerk in Hénán Prefecture.
After a year,
he suddenly died
but revived after several days.
He said himself that
when he was first summoned to see the king,
the king said:
"Although this man enjoys drinking wine,
he is not wild or disorderly,
nor does he betray others.
Moreover, his allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted.
He should be released and sent back."
After giving these instructions,
he ordered the person who had summoned him to lead him into hell
to show him the retribution for sins.
First, they came to the dung-pool prison,
which spanned several acres in width
and was entirely filled with human excrement.
He saw his wife in the dung pool, suffering from the filth and foulness,
submerging and emerging repeatedly.
He wept sorrowfully for a long time.
Suddenly, he saw a human head
fall from the sky,
landing beside the pool,
with blood gushing profusely.
He asked whose head this was.
The escort said:
"It is the head of the Qín general Bái Qǐ."
He said:
"Bái Qǐ has been dead for over a thousand years;
how could he be newly harmed again?"
The reply was:
"Bái Qǐ deceitfully buried alive four hundred thousand soldiers at Chángpíng.
The Heavenly Emperor punishes him
by beheading him once every thirty years.
This will continue until one kalpa is completed."
Then they went to another city,
which was entirely filled with smoldering embers.
There were several thousand people
running about within it.
From afar, they could see people in the city trying to rush out,
but whenever they reached the gate, it would close.
Trapped and circling within,
they suffered extreme pain and urgency.
After the matter was concluded, he took leave of the king.
The king said, "You enjoy drinking wine,
which is also a sin.
In the end, you must be given an ailment;
otherwise,
there will be no warning for the future."
He ordered his attendants to dip a bamboo rod in water
and touch it to his foot.
Then he was pushed into a pit,
and he revived.
The spot touched on his foot
became a nail-like sore,
painful beyond endurance.
Seven years later, he finally died.
Zhōu Sòng
Zhōu Sòng,
during the Tiānbǎo era,
passed the imperial examination as a jìnshì.
During the Yǒngtài era,
he was appointed magistrate of Cíxī County.
While in office,
he suddenly died one night,
and was pursued by the officials of the underworld.
Arriving at a city,
the person leading him was about to present Sòng to
the King.
Outside the gate, he suddenly encountered Liáng Chéng, the prefect of Jízhōu,
who asked Sòng, "Why have you come to this hell?"
At first, though Sòng was dead,
he was still unaware of his situation.
Upon hearing it was hell,
he felt deeply sorrowful.
Choking with sobs and weeping bitterly,
he said to Chéng:
"My mother is old and my children are young,
and I am adrift in a strange land.
How can I die like this?
I beg to see you to plead my case."
Chéng said he would speak on his behalf.
"You just stay here."
Entering the gate,
he heard shouts saying,
"The judge is seeing the King."
After a long while, he came out.
He said to Sòng:
"It has already been decided.
You should briefly see the King;
there is no need to suffer."
After a moment,
a messenger led Sòng in to see the King.
The King's appearance was very imposing,
with two horns on his head.
He asked Sòng:
"When you served as an official,
did you ever unjustly take people's wealth?"
Sòng replied:
"I am a jìnshì by background,
and rose to the position of magistrate of Cíxī County.
All my promotions were earned through service;
I never accepted wealth improperly."
The King ordered the records to be checked.
After checking,
it was said:
"Very good, very good.
Since there is no wrongdoing,
you should return home.
Are your clothes not damaged?"
Sòng thought "clothes" referred to his physical body,
so he replied:
"I just left home,
so my clothes should not be damaged yet."
He bowed twice and took his leave.
Chéng was very pleased and said:
"The King has already released you;
you should leave early."
Sòng said:
"The road is dark and obscure;
how can I return?"
Chéng ordered someone to escort Sòng.
After walking several miles,
the person began to curse loudly:
"What kind of person are you,
making me come and go, escorting you like this?
You don't even say a single word of gratitude;
so ungrateful.
If you give me five thousand strings of cash,
I will send you back."
Sòng said:
"Five thousand strings of paper money
should be easy to arrange."
So he promised it.
The messenger then walked over ten miles,
to a stone well.
Sitting by its side,
he again asked Sòng to leave.
The man said entering the well would bring him back to life,
and asked where else he would go.
He then pushed Sòng into the well, and Sòng revived.
Lú Biàn
Lú Biàn
had an uncle who served as magistrate of Húchéng.
Biàn traveled from the Eastern Capital to visit him,
and stayed overnight at Dì'èrgǔ.
In a dream, he saw two yellow-clad officials come to pursue him.
They traveled to a place
with city walls.
After entering the city,
they were about to see the judge.
But as an envoy had arrived,
the judge went out to welcome him.
The officials led Biàn to stay in a house below,
which had a roof above
but no beams below.
Under the pillars were ten large millstones,
with hundreds of women around the mills.
The mills constantly turned on their own.
Over ten ox-headed guards
used large winnowing baskets to scoop up the women
and place them into the mill holes.
As the mills turned,
their bones and flesh were crushed to pieces.
The sounds of suffering
were unbearable to hear.
Among the crowd, Biàn
saw his aunt,
the wife of the Húchéng magistrate.
They met with sorrow and joy,
and each asked how the other had come there.
Biàn asked:
"Why are these people suffering such punishment?"
She replied:
"Because of jealousy,
they have ended up here."
Biàn asked:
"What can be done about it?"
His aunt said:
"You have always recited the 'Diamond Sutra.'
Try reciting it for me;
perhaps it will reduce my punishment."
Biàn then recited the sutra,
and the mills stopped turning.
Those suffering punishment rested briefly.
An ox-headed guard came to Biàn with a trident,
angrily saying:
