"What kind of young man are you,
coming here to recite sutras
and interfere with affairs to save people?"
Biàn replied:
"My aunt is here."
The guard said:
"If you care for your aunt,
you may leave together with her."
Biàn then took his aunt and fled the city,
each returning to life.
Earlier,
Biàn had only a young servant traveling with him.
He had been dead for half a day,
and his servant was about to return to report
when Biàn revived.
Several days later,
he arrived at Húchéng.
Entering the gate,
he encountered his uncle holding a vegetarian feast.
The family saw Biàn
and reported back in surprise and joy.
His aunt came forward, took his hand, and said:
"If not for you,
I would have entered the mill.
Now I have regained life,
all thanks to your efforts."
Suǒlú Zhēn
Sǒu Lú Zhēn of the Northern Prefecture,
was originally a subordinate of the Central Guard Xún Xiàn.
In the sixth month of the fifth year of the Tàiyuán era of the Jin dynasty, he fell ill and died,
but revived after one night.
He said
that he saw Xún Xiàn's son, Xún Cuì,
who exclaimed in surprise and joy:
"Your allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted.
However, the official post requires three commanders,
so I cannot simply release you.
If you know of anyone as capable and swift as yourself,
you may have them replace you."
Lú Zhēn immediately recommended Gōng Yǐng.
Xún Cuì asked:
"Is Yǐng competent for the task?"
Lú Zhēn replied:
"Yǐng is no less capable than I."
Xún Cuì first instructed Lú Zhēn to write down the name,
but since writing is not used by ghosts,
Xún Cuì then requested a brush
and wrote it himself.
Lú Zhēn was thus able to leave.
Suddenly, he saw a former neighbor
who had died seven or eight years earlier
and was now the gatekeeper of Tàishān.
He said to Lú Zhēn:
"Is Commander Sǒu the only one returning?"
He then entrusted Lú Zhēn, saying:
"When you return,
please convey my thanks to my wife.
Before I died,
I buried fifteen thousand coins under the large bed in our house.
I originally intended to buy a bracelet for my daughter,
but unexpectedly passed away suddenly,
and could not tell my wife and daughter."
Lú Zhēn agreed.
After reviving,
he sent someone to inform the man's wife.
She had already sold the house and moved to Wǔjìn.
He went to speak with her,
and also informed the new owner of the house,
instructing them to dig.
Sure enough, they found the exact amount of coins.
He then sent the wife and daughter to buy a bracelet.
Soon after, Gōng Yǐng also died,
and people of the time marveled at these events.
A man from Lángyá,
surnamed Wáng,
whose given name is forgotten,
lived in Qiántáng.
His wife, surnamed Zhū,
died of illness in the ninth year of the Tàiyuán era,
leaving three orphaned children.
Wáng himself died suddenly in the fourth month of the same year.
At that time, there were over twenty people,
all dressed in black robes,
who came to record him.
They arrived at a red gate with white walls,
resembling a palace.
The officials wore red robes with plain belts,
black caps, and formal attire.
Some of their garments
were adorned with interconnected pearls and jade,
unlike the ceremonial dress of the mortal world.
As they proceeded forward,
he saw a tall, imposing figure
whose clothing appeared like swirling clouds.
Wáng kowtowed toward him,
explaining that his wife had died,
and his orphaned children were still young,
leaving him with no one to rely on.
He then wept.
This moved the figure to compassion.
He said:
"Your fate dictates that you should come here,
but for the sake of your orphaned children,
I will grant you a three-year extension."
Wáng pleaded:
"Three years is not enough to raise my children."
One of the attendants nearby said:
"How foolish this mortal is!
Three years here
equals thirty years in the mortal world."
They then sent him back,
and he lived for another thirty years.
Hú Lè
Hú Lè from Húshú,
died in the winter of the third year of the Lóng'ān era,
and revived after three nights.
He said
that he had been apprehended by someone,
who sealed his nose with red clay
and stamped it with a seal,
then took him to the gate of heaven.
Three people emerged from the gate and said:
"This man is not supposed to be here yet.
Why has he come?
Moreover, he is naked and without clothes,
unfit for service."
The one who had apprehended Lè said:
"He was sent from the mortal world,
and I have already brought him here.
He should be accepted."
Lè's neighbor, Zhāng Qiānzǎi,
who had died a year earlier,
was now serving as a pavilion chief at the gate.
Lè pleaded with him,
and Qiānzǎi went inside,
then came out and told Lè:
"I have spoken on your behalf, and you are to be sent back.
You may go now."
Then he saw someone use a staff to scrape off the clay seal from his nose, and it fell to the ground.
In a daze, he returned.
He saw various official buildings and gates,
some facing east,
some facing south,
all with white walls and red pillars,
and heavily guarded.
When he first arrived at the gate,
he saw from afar Qiānzǎi's uncle, Wén Huái, in an office handling documents.
Wén Huái had always been robust,
and when he heard Lè's account,
he did not believe it at all.
Over a hundred days later,
he indeed died.
Lè is now a county clerk.
He said that when he fell ill,
he had taken off all his clothes and placed them under the covers.
When his soul departed,
he was indeed naked.
Yán Jī
During the Xiánníng era of the Jin dynasty,
Yán Jī from Lángyá,
courtesy name Shìdū,
fell ill
and sought treatment from physician Zhāng Cuō.
He died at Cuō's house.
When his family came to retrieve the body for burial,
the funeral banner repeatedly tangled around trees and could not be untied.
He then appeared in a dream and said:
"My lifespan is not yet meant to end.
It is just that I took too much medicine,
which damaged my five organs.
I am now to be revived.
Be careful not to bury me."
They opened the coffin,
and his body remained as before,
with a slight human complexion.
The scratches from his fingernails
had damaged the coffin boards.
Gradually, he began to breathe.
They urgently fed him thin gruel through his mouth,
and he was able to swallow.
As he consumed more food and drink,
he could open his eyes,
but could not speak.
For over ten years,
his family grew weary of caring for him,
and could no longer attend to other matters.
His younger brother, Yán Hóngdū,
abandoned all worldly affairs
and personally attended to him.
Afterward, Yán Jī gradually declined.
He eventually died again.
Yúháng Guǎng
In the late years of the Shēngpíng era of Jìn,
an old man from Gùzhāng County had a daughter
who lived deep in the mountains.
Yúháng Guǎng sought to marry her,
but was refused.
Later, the old man fell ill and died.
His daughter went to the county town to buy a coffin.
When she was halfway there,
she met Guǎng.
The girl told him the whole story.
She then said:
"In this desperate situation,
if you can go to my home and guard my father's corpse,
and wait until I return,
I will become your wife."
Guǎng agreed.
The girl said:
"In my pen there is a pig;
you can slaughter it
to feed the children."
Guǎng went to the girl's home,
but only heard the sound of clapping and joyful dancing inside the house.
Guǎng pushed open the door,
and saw many ghosts in the hall,
all together handling and playing with the old man's corpse.
Guǎng grasped a staff and shouted loudly,
entered the door,
and all the ghosts fled.
Guǎng guarded the corpse,
took the pig and slaughtered it.
When night fell,
he saw an old ghost beside the corpse,
reaching out its hand begging for meat.
Guǎng then seized its arm,
and the ghost could not get away.
He held it even tighter.
Then he heard outside the door many ghosts calling together, saying:
"The old slave's greed for food has brought him to this,
very satisfying!"
Guǎng said to the old ghost:
"The one who killed the old man must be you.
Quickly return his vital spirit,
and I will release you.
If you do not return it,
I will never let you go."
The old ghost said:
"It was my children who killed the old man."
He immediately called his ghost children:
"You must return it."
The old man gradually revived,
so Guǎng released the old ghost.
The girl arrived carrying the coffin.
They met, shocked and sorrowful,
and then he took the girl as his wife.
A Man from Qū'ē
In the first year of the Jǐngpíng era,
a man from Qū'ē fell ill and died.
He saw his father in heaven.
His father said to him:
"Your allotted lifespan still has exactly eight years left.
If you die before this limit is reached,
you will fall among those condemned for their sins.
I wanted to find a secure position for you,
but there were no vacancies in the offices,
except for a vacancy for the Thunder God.
I shall petition to have you appointed to fill this post."
He then submitted a memorial and had him entered into the roster,
and he was able to take up this duty.
He was ordered to go to Liáodōng to make rain.
He rode in an open carriage,
inside which there was
water,
which he sprinkled east and west.
Before he arrived,
midway he again received an order to go to Liáoxī.
After finishing the task and returning,
he saw his father and bitterly pleaded to return.
He said
he did not enjoy holding the post.
His father sent him away,
and thus he was able to revive.
Hè Yǔ
Hè Yǔ from Shànyīn, Kuàijī,
styled Yànjū.
He once fell ill,
lost consciousness,
only his heart area was still warm.
After three days he revived.
He said:
An officer took him up to heaven,
where he saw an official mansion.
The prefect's residence was very solemn.
Someone led Yǔ into a winding room.
In the room was a layered shelf,
on which were a seal and a sword.
They told Yǔ to take one.
Although he desired what he liked,
he was too short to reach the upper layer,
so he took the sword and came out.
They asked him:
"What did you get?"
Yǔ said:
"I got the sword."
The officer said:
"It's a pity you didn't get the seal,
for it can command a hundred spirits.
Now that you have the sword,
you can only command the local earth god."
After his illness was cured,
whenever he traveled,
the local earth god would come to pay homage by the roadside.
Yǔ deeply disliked this.
The Man Who Ate Beef
During Huán Xuán's time,
there was a great epidemic among cattle.
A man ate the meat of a cow that had died of the epidemic,
and consequently fell ill and died.
He said:
When he died, he saw someone holding a register,
taking him up to heaven.
A noble person asked:
"What crime has this man committed?"
The reply was:
"His offense is eating the meat of a cow that died in the epidemic."
The noble person said:
"Now we need cattle for the turning of the wheel,
and their meat to feed the common people.
Why then kill him again?"
He urged them,
and ordered him to return.
After he revived,
he recounted the whole incident.
From then on, those who ate beef
no longer suffered such calamities.
Qiū Yǒu
Qiū Yǒu from Wúchéng
once fell ill and died,
but revived after one day.
He said:
He was taken up to heaven,
and entered a large government office building.
He saw a man wearing a purple headcloth sitting there.
Someone told Yǒu
that this was his ancestor Qiū Xiàobó,
who now served as the Chief Recorder.
He told people that Yǒu should not die,
and had someone send him back.
Yǒu was able to return.
As he went out the door,
he saw his paternal grandparents with one foot tied,
at a tree outside the gate.
A month later, he died.
Yǔ Shēn
Yǐngchuān's Yǔ Mǒu,
during the Xiàojiàn era of the Sòng dynasty,
fell ill and died.
His chest was still warm,
and he had not been encoffined overnight
when he suddenly awoke.
He recounted that upon first dying,
two men in black clothes came,
bound and captured him,
and drove him forward.
He saw a great city,
with towering gate towers,
and layers of defenses.
They brought Yǔ before a hall,
and many others entered together.
In the hall, a nobleman sat facing south,
with several hundred attendants on duty,
and was addressed as Fǔjūn.
The Fǔjūn held a brush,
reviewing those who arrived.
When it was Yǔ's turn, he said:
"This person's allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted."
He urged them to send him back.
A man came up the steps,
led Yǔ out,
and upon reaching the city gate,
told the clerk to assign someone to escort him.
The gate clerk said:
"We must report again,
and only then can you leave."
Outside the gate was a young woman,
aged fifteen or sixteen,
with a serene and beautiful appearance.
She said:
"Yǔ Jūn is fortunate to return,
yet he is detained like this—
it is because the gate officials are demanding goods."
Yǔ said:
"I was captured and brought here lightly,
with nothing to offer."
The woman took off three gold bracelets from her left arm,
handed them to Yǔ, and said:
"Give these together to him."
Yǔ asked the woman her surname,
and she said:
"My surname is Zhāng,
my home is in Máozhǔ,
and I died of cholera yesterday."
Yǔ said:
"When I was near death,
I left behind an inheritance,
five thousand coins,
intended for purchasing timber.
If I return to life,
I will send this money to repay you."
The woman said:
"I cannot bear to see you in hardship and distress;
these are my private possessions,
and there is no need to trouble your household to repay."
Yǔ then
gave the bracelets to the clerk,
who accepted them.
In the end, he did not report again,
but immediately assigned someone to escort him away.
Yǔ bid farewell to the woman,
and she let out a long sigh, tears falling.
Yǔ then drifted into a daze and revived.
He went to Máozhǔ to search,
and indeed, there was a recently deceased young woman of the Zhāng family.
Lǐ Chú
Xiāngyáng's Lǐ Chú
died from a seasonal epidemic,
and his wife kept watch over the corpse.
At the third watch of the night,
he suddenly sat up,
violently grabbing the gold bracelets on his wife's arm.
His wife then helped him take them off.
Once he held them in his hand,
he died again.
His wife observed him closely.
By dawn,
his chest grew warm again,
and he gradually revived.
After coming back to life, he said:
"The clerks took me away,
and there were many companions.
Seeing that some who offered goods were spared,
I promised the clerk gold bracelets.
The clerk allowed me to return,
so I came back to fetch them to give to the clerk.
The clerk received the bracelets,
and then released me to return.
I saw the clerk take the bracelets away,
not knowing they were still inside my wife's clothing.
His wife dared not wear them again,
and buried them according to ritual.
Zhāng Dǎo
In the first year of the Jiànyuán era of Emperor Wǔ of Qí,
the Crown Prince's Left Guard, Zhāng Dǎo, styled Jìnxián,
studied diligently in his youth,
and in old age practiced dietary regimens.
Each meal consisted of no more than two dishes,
and his clothing was not adorned.
After falling ill,
he said to his wife, Zhū Shì:
"After I die,
the coffin need only accommodate my body.
For my burial clothes,
just take what I am wearing now,
and be careful not to change them."
Upon his death,
his son, Gànhù, wished to follow his father's last wishes.
Zhū Shì said:
"Although your father left such instructions,
I cannot bear to follow them."
Thus, she separately prepared seasonal burial clothes and enshrouded him.
One month after the enshrouding,
the family suddenly heard calls for Gànhù from inside the coffin,
and everyone was startled and frightened at once.
When they reached the burial coffin,
they saw Zhāng Dǎo open his eyes,
and they helped him out to his former bedroom.
The next day,
he sat and reproached his wife, saying:
"I have lived frugally all my life;
why did you go against my words
and change my old clothes?"
He said to his son:
"Enshroud me again in my old clothes."
Gànhù then took the old clothes and enshrouded him.
After the enshrouding, he said again:
"Just place me in the coffin,
and check on me after three days.
If
I appear solemn and still,
then bury me.
If my eyes are open,
I will surely revive."
After three days,
Gànhù and others opened the coffin,
saw his eyes open,
and everyone was astonished and delighted.
They helped him out, and he thus revived.
He said to his son:
"The underworld, because I cultivated goodness and upheld virtue in my lifetime,
released me to live another twenty years."
Zhāng Dǎo later rose to the position of Magistrate of Jiàndé before passing away.
Shí Chánghé
Zhào Shícháng Hé was a man from Gāoyì County in the State of Zhào.
At the age of nineteen,
he fell ill for over a month and died.
His family was poor,
and they had not yet prepared him for burial.
After four days,
he revived.
He recounted that when he first died,
he traveled southeast
and saw two men repairing the road,
fifty paces ahead of him.
Whether Zhào Shícháng Hé walked slowly or quickly,
the two men matched his pace,
always remaining fifty paces ahead.
On both sides of the road,
thorny brambles grew densely,
like eagle claws.
He saw many people
whose feet were caught in the thorns,
their bodies torn and wounded,
and the ground stained with their blood.
Seeing Zhào Shícháng Hé walking alone on the smooth road,
they all sighed and said:
"The disciple of the Buddha walks alone on the great path."
Ahead, he arrived at a tiled house,
with pavilions and towers numbering in the thousands,
and the buildings were very tall.
Above, there was a man
of large stature and imposing appearance,
wearing a black robe with four seams,
sitting by the window.
Zhào Shícháng Hé bowed to him.
The man in the tower said:
"Has Lord Shí come?
It has been over two thousand years since we last parted."
Zhào Shícháng Hé then seemed to remember this parting from long ago.
Among his acquaintances were the Governor of Féngyì,
Mèng Chéng and his wife,
who had died many years earlier.
The man in the tower said:
"Do you know Mèng Chéng?"
Zhào Shícháng Hé replied:
"I do."
The man in the tower said:
"Mèng Chéng, during his lifetime, was not diligent in his practice,
so now he constantly performs sweeping duties for me.
Mèng Chéng’s wife was diligent in her practice,
and she dwells in great happiness."
He pointed to a room in the southwest and said:
"Mèng Chéng’s wife is here."
Mèng Chéng’s wife opened the window,
saw Zhào Shícháng Hé,
and warmly greeted him,
inquiring in detail about the well-being of everyone in his family.
She said:
"When Lord Shí returns,
you must come see me again,
and I will entrust you with a letter."
Soon, he saw Mèng Chéng holding a broom and a dustpan,
coming from the west of the tower,
and he too asked for news of his family.
The man in the tower said:
"I have heard that Yúlóng Chāo is diligent and
advances in faith.
What practices does he undertake?"
Zhào Shícháng Hé said:
"He does not eat fish or meat,
and never touches wine.
He constantly recites the sutras
and relieves all kinds of sickness and pain."
The man in the tower said:
"What has been said of him is not false."
After speaking for a long time,
the man in the tower asked the chief registrar
to carefully check Lord Shí’s records,
ensuring there were no errors or omissions.
The registrar examined the records.
There were still over thirty years remaining.
The man in the tower said:
"Do you wish to return?"
Zhào Shícháng Hé replied:
"I wish to return."
He then ordered the registrar
to send him back with a carriage, horses, and two officials.
Zhào Shícháng Hé bowed in farewell,
boarded the carriage, and returned.
On the road he had traveled earlier,
there were now relay stations with officials and commoners, as well as provisions of food and drink.
In an instant, he arrived home.
Disgusted by his corpse,
he did not wish to re-enter it,
so he stood by the head of the corpse.
He saw his deceased younger sister behind him push him,
causing him to fall onto the face of the corpse,
and thus he revived.
Fǎ Dàorén Shān,
who had not yet left home at the time,
heard what Zhào Shícháng Hé recounted
and resolved to pursue the path of monastic life.
Fǎ Shān
was a man of the Xiánhé era.
Gǔ Yuánzhī.
In the Later Wei dynasty, Gǔ Bì, the Minister of Works, had a clansman named Gǔ Yuánzhī,
who was raised by Gǔ Bì from a young age.
He died from excessive drinking.
Gǔ Bì grieved for him deeply,
and after three days, the encoffining was completed.
Still longing for him,
wishing to bid farewell once more,
Gǔ Bì ordered the coffin to be opened.
Once opened, Yuánzhī had revived.
Yuánzhī said:
"I was in a drunken stupor,
when suddenly it was as if in a dream.
Someone poured cold water over my body.
Looking up,
I saw a divine being.
He wore crimson robes with rainbow-colored capes,
his appearance very handsome.
He looked at Yuánzhī and said:
'I am Gǔ Shuō,
your distant ancestor.
I was just about to go to the Land of Harmonious Spirits,
but had no one to carry the bags and attend me,
so I came to fetch you.'"
He immediately ordered him to carry a large bag,
weighing about thirty catties.
He also gave him a bamboo staff,
over twelve feet long,
and told Yuánzhī to ride it and follow behind.
They flew up very swiftly,
often staying at mid-heaven.
Traveling southwest,
they did not know the distance in miles,
mountains and rivers passing far below.
Suddenly they descended to the ground,
having arrived at the Land of Harmonious Spirits.
This country had no great mountains;
the highest were no more than several tens of zhang,
all piled with green jade-like stones.
At the edges of the rocks grew green bamboo and colorful reeds,
exotic flowers and precious fruits,
soft fragrant grasses,
and lovely birds chirping.
The mountain tops were all flat and smooth like whetstones,
with clear springs gushing down,
two or three hundred streams.
The plains had no ordinary trees,
only various fruit trees like hundred-fruit and pomegranates of longing.
Each fruit tree bloomed with flowers,
the fruits brightly colored and crimson,
with emerald leaves beneath fragrant clusters,
densely covering the trees,
unchanged throughout the four seasons.
Only once a year did the flowers and fruits secretly change,
renewing with fresh tenderness,
unnoticed by people.
The fields all grew large gourds,
the gourds filled with the five grains,
sweet, fragrant, precious, and delicious,
beyond compare with the rice and millet of the Central Plains.
People had enough to eat,
without needing to farm.
The plains and hills flourished lushly,
with no foul weeds growing.
Once a year,
among the branches and trunks of the trees,
multicolored silk floss grew,
and people could collect it according to color,
weaving as they pleased.
Extraordinary
brocades, fine silks, and gauzes,
without needing silkworms or shuttles.
The climate of the four seasons
was always warm, mild, and pleasant,
like the second or third month in the Central Plains.
There were no insects like mosquitoes, gadflies, toads, ants, lice, bees, scorpions, snakes, vipers, geckos, centipedes, spiders, or midges;
also no birds like owls, kites, crows, sparrowhawks, mynahs, or bats;
and no beasts like tigers, wolves, jackals, leopards, foxes, wild horses, or bó-beasts;
also no pests like cats, rats, pigs, or dogs.
The people were all equal in height and appearance,
with no one having cravings, desires, loves, or hatreds.
Each person bore two sons and two daughters;
neighbors became in-laws for generations,
girls marrying at hair-pinning age,
men marrying at twenty.
People lived to one hundred twenty,
with no premature deaths, illnesses, muteness, deafness, lameness, or crippling ailments.
Below one hundred years,
all could remember themselves.
Beyond one hundred years,
no one knew how long they had lived.
When their lifespan ended, they suddenly vanished from where they were;
even close relatives and descendants
would forget that person,
so there was never grief or sorrow.
They ate once daily at noon,
in between only drinking wine and eating fruits.
The meals also vanished without a trace,
with no need for latrines.
People had no private granaries or storehouses;
surplus grain stayed in the fields,
taken by those who needed it.
There was no irrigating gardens or selling vegetables;
wild greens sufficed for people to eat.
Every ten acres had a wine spring,
sweet and fragrant in taste.
The people daily accompanied each other on outings,
singing joyfully and contentedly,
dispersing at dusk,
never drunk or stupefied.
Everyone had maids and servants,
all naturally careful and diligent,
knowing what people wanted,
without needing orders or urging.
Dwellings were as one pleased,
all grand and beautiful.
The country's six domestic animals included only horses,
extremely tame and strong,
needing no fodder or care,
feeding on wild grass themselves,
not approaching stored grain.
People could ride when they wished,
and after riding, released them,
with no one in charge of them.
The country had a full complement of a thousand officials,
yet officials did not know they held positions,
mingling among the common people,
because there were no duties to handle or decide.
Although there was a ruler,
the ruler did not know he was ruler,
mingling among the thousand officials,
because there were no official duties for promotion or demotion.
Also, there were no violent thunderstorms or heavy rains;
the wind was always gentle and mild like a warm breeze,
caressing all things without causing them to shake or fall.
Rain fell once every ten days,
always at night,
moistening and nourishing smoothly,
without causing floods or stagnation.
All the people of the country
were close to each other,
like relatives,
each wise and kind.
There were no market exchanges or merchant activities,
because they sought no profit.
Gǔ Shuō, having arrived in this country,
turned to Yuánzhī and said:
'This is the Land of Harmonious Spirits.
Although not immortals,
their customs are not bad.
When you return,
you should tell the worldly people about it.
Now that I am here,
upon returning I will find someone else to carry the bag;
I no longer need you.'"
Then he made Yuánzhī drink wine.
After several rounds,
without realizing it, he became deeply drunk.
Then he awoke again,
and his body had revived.
From then on, Yuánzhī distanced himself from worldly affairs,
completely forgetting official ambitions,
traveling among mountains and waters,
calling himself Zhīhézi (Knower of Harmony).
Later, no one knew what finally became of him.
Zhōu Zǐgōng
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān of the Táng dynasty,
Zhōu Zǐgōng, a Vice Director in the Ministry of Revenue,
suddenly died violently.
He saw the Great Emperor seated in the hall,
with Péi Zǐyí standing in attendance.
Zǐgōng bowed,
and was asked who he was.
He said:
"Zhōu Zǐgōng, brought here."
The Emperor said:
"I summoned Xǔ Zǐrú;
why was Zǐgōng mistakenly brought?
Release him at once."
Zǐgōng revived,
and asked at home:
"Is Vice Minister Xǔ well?"
At that time, Zǐrú was Vice Minister of Personnel,
already ill,
and died that night.
Wǔ Zétiān heard of this,
sent a relay messenger to Bīngzhōu,
to inquire about Péi Zǐyí.
Zǐyí was then an administrative assistant,
and was fine.
Lǐ Jí
Lǐ Jí was
by nature fond of drinking,
and never left any dregs.
His residence was in Jīshàn Lǐ in the capital.
He suddenly died from a minor illness,
his entire body turned cold,
only his heart remained slightly warm.
Occasionally, his corpse would speak,
as if pleading a case.
His family, therefore, waited day and night for him to revive,
and after seven or eight days, he finally awoke.
He said himself,
initially, there were ghostly envoys
pursuing another person.
In his house, there was already a female ghost,
and because Lǐ Jí drank without leaving any dregs,
she led the ghostly envoys to pursue him.
Lǐ Jí knew he was wrongly pursued,
hence his corpse repeatedly spoke.
The ghost became furious,
seized Lǐ Jí and would not let go.
After traveling over thirty li,
they arrived at three gates,
resembling a city or a prefecture.
They led Lǐ Jí to see an official,
who asked why they pursued Lǐ Jí,
why they suddenly brought him.
Lǐ Jí also argued vehemently, claiming injustice.
The official became angry,
whipped the envoys twenty times,
and ordered them to send Lǐ Jí back.
The envoys escorted Lǐ Jí out the gate,
and no longer led him.
Lǐ Jí lingered in the official bureaus for about ten days.
He saw over a hundred oxcarts,
and asked an official,
where these were going.
The reply was:
"Ān Lùshān rebelled,
killing countless common people,
today the carts are transporting the dead for trial."
At that time, Ān Lùshān had not yet rebelled,
Lǐ Jí said Ān Lùshān did not rebel,
how could this be so.
The official said:
"Soon he will rebel."
He also saw several hundred people,
all urgently undergoing trials for death.
Lǐ Jí then found his own way back,
after a long time, he reached his home.
He saw his family at the door,
but could not enter,
so he went to his wife's home in the southern alley to rest.
His wife seemed to sense something,
took all of Lǐ Jí's clothes, toys, and other belongings,
and halfway, called for him,
Lǐ Jí then followed her back.
He saw his corpse lying on the bed,
exerted strength forward, and then revived.
Ā Liù
In Ráozhōu, the slave of Lóngxīng Temple was named Ā Liù,
during the Bǎoyìng era, he died,
and according to custom, saw the King.
The underworld official said:
"Your life is not yet exhausted,
you are released to return."
Upon exiting the gate,
he met a Hú man he had always been friendly with.
This Hú man, during his life,
made a living selling cakes,
and was also selling cakes in the underworld.
Seeing Ā Liù, he was delighted,
and asked about his family,
and requested to send a letter.
After a while,
he held a letter and said to Ā Liù:
"I have nothing to give you,
I hope you can deliver this."
After speaking,
he pushed Ā Liù into a pit,
and then Ā Liù revived.
His family found the Hú man's letter in his hand,
reading:
in the underworld, constantly suffer various punishments,
unable to be reborn,
please create scriptures to save me."
The words were very sorrowful.
His family, upon seeing the letter,
performed various meritorious deeds.
The slave dreamed of the Hú man saying:
"Thank you for delivering the letter, I am spared from various sufferings.
Now I have been reborn in the human world,
so I come to thank you,
and also thank my wife and children."
After speaking, he left.
Cuī Jūn
Therefore, when Cuī Níng was governing Shǔ,
the prefect of Qiánwéi, Cuī Jūn of Qīnghé,
having opened the casket of Perfected Person Yǐn,
that evening,
Cuī Jūn was summoned by the underworld officials.
The underworld official was none other than the former chancellor Lǚ Yīn,
who was a close friend of Cuī Jūn.
They met and wept sorrowfully,
after which Lǚ said to Cuī:
"Perfected Person Yǐn has a stone casket in your prefecture;
why did you open it without permission?
Now, by the command of the Supreme Emperor,
you are summoned for investigation.
What is to be done?"
Cuī apologized, saying:
"I am ignorant and blind,
unaware of matters concerning immortals,
and thus I opened the Perfected Person's casket without permission.
My crime is indeed grave,
but according to the principle of three pardons,
those who act out of ignorance
may all be forgiven.
If you could show leniency,
I might have a chance to reform."
Lǚ said:
"The Emperor's command is extremely strict;
the underworld is lowly and insignificant—
how dare I disobey?"
He then summoned the investigating clerk,
who brought out Cuī Jūn's records.
After a short while,
the investigating clerk arrived.
He reported:
"Cuī Jūn has five remaining official posts
and fifteen years of remaining lifespan.
Now, by the command of the Supreme Emperor,
thirteen years of his lifespan are to be deducted,
and all his official positions are to be stripped."
Cuī again apologized, saying:
"You and I have been friends all our lives;
today's punishment
is indeed brought upon myself.
But can an old friend not pardon me?"
Lǚ said:
"The deduction of lifespan and stripping of official positions
cannot be escaped,
but I can arrange for you to have a temporary post for two years,
with generous salary and provisions,
to fulfill my duty as your friend."
Cuī bowed deeply in gratitude.
As their conversation was concluding,
suddenly, a dense cloud of mist appeared,
and red light descended from the sky.
Lǚ, along with the court clerks and attendants,
all rose in fear and exclaimed:
"The celestial mandate has arrived."
They then ushered Cuī into a separate room,
and Cuī secretly watched through a crack.
He saw Lǚ donning his official cap and holding his tablet,
leading the court clerks,
standing in formation in the courtyard,
all bowing with hands clasped.
In the clouds, there was a person
wearing purple robes and a golden fish tally,
holding a scroll of documents.
He proclaimed the Emperor's command.
Then Lǚ and the court clerks bowed twice and received the document.
The envoy rode the clouds upward,
and soon vanished.
Lǚ called Cuī Jūn out to sit,
opened the celestial mandate to read it,
and sighed and wept.
He said to Cuī:
"Do you know Yuán Sān?
" Cuī said:
"He is an old friend from my humble days."
Lǚ said:
"His bloodline is severed,
alas,
how tragic!
Although I was friends with Yuán Sān,
at this point, I cannot save him either,
only accumulating sorrow and sighs."
After speaking, he wept again.
Then he ordered an attendant to escort Cuī Jūn back,
and after bowing twice, Cuī departed,
traveling together with the envoy.
Entering the prefectural office,
he found his body lying on a bed,
surrounded by his wife and children weeping.
The envoy guided Cuī to lean over the bed,
and his soul merged with his body,
whereupon he awoke.
His family said:
"You have been dead for three days;
the prefecture reported it to the surveillance commissioner."
Cuī immediately packed his belongings,
moved his entire household to Shǔ,
and reported everything to Níng.
Níng then appointed him as acting deputy commissioner,
with a monthly salary of two hundred thousand coins.
At that time, Yuán Zài was in charge of state affairs,
and Níng was on good terms with Zài,
exchanging many letters.
Hearing Cuī's account,
Níng feared being implicated,
so he ordered a trusted subordinate to take five hundred taels of gold,
to bribe Zài's attendants,
and purchased over a hundred of his letters,
all of which he burned.
More than a month later,
Yuán Zài's property was confiscated.
Two years later,
Cuī also passed away.
Liú Gài
Liú Gài of Péngchéng,
during the Zhēnyuán era,
served as magistrate of Hánchéng,
and died in office.
His family was very poor,
so they stayed at a Buddhist temple in Hánchéng.
Before half a year had passed,
the county deputy, Dòu, also died,
but awoke three days later.
Initially, Dòu had fallen asleep during the day,
dreaming that an official guided him westward,
passing through highlands and vast marshes for hundreds of miles,
until they reached a city.
After entering the gate,
the guiding official disappeared.
Dòu was terrified,
and immediately left the city gate.
At the gate, there were guards,
standing in formation with swords raised.
Dòu inquired of them,
and a guard pointed south with his sword, saying:
"Go this way;
it is the path of the living."
Only then did Dòu realize he had died,
his back sweating and legs trembling.
He headed south,
though exhausted,
he dared not rest.
Soon, he saw over ten people standing by the roadside,
and one of them called out to Dòu,
taking his hand and weeping.
Looking closely,
it was Liú Gài.
He said:
"Why have you come here?"
Dòu told him everything.
Liú said:
"Since parting with you,
I have been as if trapped in a pit;
how could I ever return to the peace of my lifetime?"
And he wept.
Dòu then asked about the affairs of the underworld,
but Gài wept without answering.
After a long while, he said again:
"Where are my wife and children?
Are they safe and well?"
Dòu said:
"Your worthy family is staying at the Buddhist temple in Hánchéng,
and it has been nearly half a year."
Gài said:
"When you return,
please convey my regards to them.
I am trapped and humiliated in the underworld,
with no hope of escape.
Whenever I think of my wife and children,
it is as if I am bound and cannot forget them.
The regrets between the realms of light and darkness—
how can they all be expressed!"
Before parting, he said to Dòu:
"I have a poem to give you:
It says:
'The underworld road is dark and unknown to men,
No need to speak bitterly and cause sorrow again.
I rejoice to meet you and send word to my kin,
But where shall we meet again, in this vast and dim terrain?'
" After speaking, he wept again,
and Dòu bid him farewell.
Before he had gone more than ten miles,
he heard the sound of a bell ringing loudly,
and startled, he awoke.
Dòu was the elder cousin of Shī Xī,
and his nephew, the son of the Cuī family,
often told people about this incident.
Zhū Tóng
Zhū Tóng,
at the age of fifteen,
his father served as the magistrate of Yīngtáo.
One day during leisure, he went out,
when suddenly he saw two village heads whom he had long known, saying,
"The judge orders your arrest."
In haste, he followed them.
Exiting Yīngtáo city,
they walked about fifty li,
and saw over ten people drinking by the river.
The two village heads entered the hall together,
sat down,
and made Tóng stand behind them.
Tóng grew greatly indignant,
and scolded them:
"What kind of village heads are you,
daring to do such a thing?"
The village heads said:
"Young master, you are already dead,
why still put on the airs of the living?"
Tóng wept sorrowfully for a long time.
Soon, those sitting dispersed,
and Tóng followed them again.
They walked to a city,
the city gate was still closed,
so they could not enter.
The village heads again ate with over ten others,
though they invited Tóng to sit,
he could not eat.
After a while, the city opened,
and the judge came out.
The village heads bowed and paid respects by the roadside,
presenting the document to lead Tóng before the judge.
The judge asked the village heads to bring Tóng into the city.
Standing at the yamen gate,
they lingered,
with nowhere to go.
Suddenly, they heard a message:
"The registrar has finished his meal."
Soon, a man in a black robe,
emerged from the gate,
dragging his shoes as he walked slowly,
followed by four or five attendants.
This man recognized Tóng upon seeing him,
and asked:
"Young master of the Zhū family,
how did you come here?"
Tóng did not recognize him at first,
and had no way to respond.
The registrar said:
"I once served alongside your esteemed father,
and our friendship was very deep."
He then led Tóng to the judge,
and pleaded earnestly for his rescue.
After a long time,
the judge said:
"This boy's allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted,
I should release him."
He then ordered the two village heads from earlier to escort him back.
Tóng bowed and prepared to leave,
when the registrar called him again,
wrote his own name on Tóng's arm,
and stamped it with a seal.
He admonished:
"If you are detained,
show this to them."
After Tóng left the city,
he suddenly saw his grandfather's servant,
who dismounted and bowed twice, saying:
"The old master knows that the young master is returning,
so he ordered me to bring a horse to escort you home."
Tóng then mounted the horse,
and traveled about fifty li,
arriving at an inn.
The servant and the village heads
asked Tóng to dismount,
and pass through the inn.
Inside the inn, large cauldrons were boiling people,
and when the people were cooked,
they were taken out onto tables,
cut up, and sold.
There were dozens of such tables,
and the traders were many.
These people saw Tóng,
and each wanted to cook him.
Tóng showed them the seal on his arm,
and was spared.
Exiting the inn gate,
he saw the village heads, the servant, and the horse again.
Traveling another fifty li,
they arrived at another inn.
After passing two inns in succession,
the inns were filled with people holding forks, poles, bows, and arrows,
intending to kill Tóng.
He showed them the seal on his arm,
and was spared.
After a long time,
they finally reached outside Yīngtáo city.
The village heads told Tóng to dismount,
and said:
"The long journey has exhausted us,
we can no longer enter the city.
We also ask to return the letter to the registrar.
Say
that we have escorted you home."
Tóng followed their words,
and after handing over the letter,
they bowed and parted.
Tóng returned,
walking alone into the city.
Before reaching home,
he passed by the Confucius temple hall,
and entered the side room to rest.
He saw in front of the hall, under the western tree,
someone had hanged themselves,
but he felt no fear in his heart.
Strength,
Gào Chéng
Gào Chéng was
a man from Wǔgōng in Jīngzhào.
Once, due to an official selection process,
he traveled to the Eastern Capital.
Riding a donkey under a locust tree,
he saw an old woman,
who said,
"I am skilled at reading palms,
and I ask to see your palm."
Chéng initially disliked her greatly.
The old woman said:
"Both of us are idle,
why begrudge letting me read it?"
Chéng, sitting on the donkey,
gave her his hand.
After examining it,
the old woman said to Chéng:
"Wherever you reside,
no matter the distance,
you should return home quickly.
Within ten days,
you will certainly die."
Chéng, hearing this, became very frightened,
and begged her to find a solution.
The old woman said:
"Offer food to the prison inmates,
perhaps you may gain blessed assistance.
Otherwise,
it is unavoidable."
Chéng ultimately did as she said,
and bought food for the prison.
After finishing the task,
he went to see the old woman,
who told him to return quickly.
Chéng then returned from there.
Arriving at Wǔgōng,
after about a day,
since he had no illness,
he felt quite joyful.
Then, taking off his robe, he went out the door,
and suddenly saw over ten people
bowing and welcoming him by the roadside.
Chéng asked the reason,
and they said they were commoners from Shénshān,
hearing that the gentleman had obtained the post of county magistrate,
and thus came to welcome him.
Chéng said:
"I have not been selected,
how could I obtain this office?"
In a moment,
someone came riding a horse,
and another brought a green robe.
Having no choice,
he put on the robe and mounted the horse,
and followed them away.
After traveling ten lǐ,
an official in a blue robe
dismounted and hurried to bow to Chéng.
Asked about it,
he replied:
"I serve as a Boshi in Cízhōu,
hearing that you have newly been appointed as a Zhǎngshǐ,
thus I came from afar to welcome you."
Then, with the horse he was riding, he carried Chéng,
and rode a small donkey to follow along.
After traveling about twenty lǐ,
the Boshi seized Chéng's horse.
Chéng asked why he had welcomed him,
and now was being rude again.
The Boshi laughed and said:
"You are a newly dead ghost,
the authorities are capturing you,
how could you have an official post?"
His followers then drove him,
Chéng crossed water,
and west of the water was a fine mansion,
resembling a government office.
The sign on the gate read:
The Court of the Vice Censor-in-Chief for Redressing Injustices.
Chéng then loudly cried out his grievance.
The Vice Censor-in-Chief sent to ask:
"What injustice have you suffered?"
He replied:
"My allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted,
nor have I received any summons,
yet I was wrongly seized by ghosts."
The Vice Censor-in-Chief asked if he had a written petition.
Chéng said:
"I was seized hastily,
and truly have no petition."
The Vice Censor-in-Chief gave Chéng paper,
ordering him to write a petition.
After the petition, he reviewed the case.
Beside him was a person
who took the case file inside.
The Vice Censor-in-Chief then raised one hand,
asking for five hundred thousand [cash].
Chéng distantly agreed to it.
The review stated:
"Wrongfully seized and recorded,
his allotted lifespan is truly not exhausted."
The Vice Censor-in-Chief ruled to release him,
and also ordered the case reviewer to take him to see the Grand Master for joint judgment.
Arriving at the hall,
he saw a small foreigner from Fólì,
wearing a felt hat on his head,
and deerskin boots,
playing leaf coins in the hall.
The order was communicated:
"This is a relative of the Vice Censor-in-Chief,
ordered to be released back to life."
The foreign boy took the file inside,
the Grand Master approved the judgment,
and thus he came out.
Again arriving at the king's place,
the joint judgment gatekeeper
approached Chéng to ask for money.
The guide became furious and said:
"This is a relative of the Vice Censor-in-Chief,
how dare a minor ghost ask for money?"
Reporting back to the Vice Censor-in-Chief,
the Vice Censor-in-Chief ordered him escorted out.
Chéng did not know where to go,
wandering the crossroads.
Suddenly, he saw his former brother-in-law, Péi,
leading over a thousand people
hunting in the western mountains.
Surprised and delighted, he asked Chéng
how he had come here.
Chéng told him everything in detail.
Péi said:
"Had we not met,
you would have nearly become an idle ghost.
For three to five hundred years,
you would not be able to transform or move on,
how agonizing that would be!"
At that time, there was a donkey renter at the prefecture gate.
Péi called the boy with the donkey,
ordering him to send the eldest young master home,
and personally gave him twenty-five thousand cash.
Chéng managed to return home,
feeling very happy.
After traveling five or six lǐ,
the donkey was weak,
and could not proceed.
The day was also growing late,
and Chéng feared he would not make it.
The boy was behind by a hundred
or so paces,
singing a song.
Chéng called out loudly to him,
the boy ran over,
and struck the donkey with a stick.
Startled, Chéng fell to the ground,
and because of this, he then revived.
Wáng Xūn
Wáng Xūn, a Jìnshì from Huàzhōu,
once entered Huàyuè Temple with his companion Zhào Wàngshū and others.
Entering the seat of the third daughter,
he admired her beauty and charm and became infatuated with her,
and immediately died.
Wàngshū, terrified,
called a shaman,
who held wine and food,
and danced before the deity,
and only then did [Wáng Xūn] come back to life.
Angrily, he said to Wàngshū:
"I was there myself without suffering,
why did you make the shaman play the pipa and call for me?"
Everyone laughed and asked him,
and he said:
"The girl initially hid me in her carriage,
just as we were intimate,
Wàngshū played the pipa and reported to the king,
who ordered a eunuch to search among the maids' carriages.
When it came to the girl's carriage,
she had no choice,
and pushed me to the ground,
and because of this, I then revived."
Sū Lǚshuāng
The Military Commissioner of Tàiyuán, His Excellency Mǎ Suì,
had a junior officer named Sū Lǚshuāng,
who had previously served under the former commissioner Bào Fáng.
During a campaign,
they were about to attack the Huíhé.
At that time, Fáng pointed at a flag-bearer named Liú Míngyuǎn on the battlefield,
accusing him of not advancing to the front line,
and ordered Lǚshuāng to behead him.
Lǚshuāng received the order,
but he kept glancing at Míngyuǎn,
who then quickly advanced,
thus escaping the calamity of losing his head.
More than ten years later, Míngyuǎn passed away.
Lǚshuāng also wandered into the underworld,
where he saw Míngyuǎn.
Míngyuǎn said to Lǚshuāng:
"In the past, I was indebted to you for sparing my life,
but I had no way to repay your kindness.
Today, I shall fulfill my long-held wish."
He then pointed to a path,
which was overgrown with thorns and brambles.
He said:
"Just follow this path,
and you will surely encounter King Shělì,
who in his lifetime once served as a commander under His Excellency.
If you see him and plead your case,
you will certainly be spared."
After telling him this, he urged him to go,
and Lǚshuāng proceeded.
After traveling ten or twenty *li*,
he indeed met King Shělì, who was out hunting.
Shělì had known Lǚshuāng in life,
and asked in surprise:
"Why have you come here?"
Lǚshuāng replied:
"I was summoned by the underworld officials."
Shělì then said:
"You should not have come here,
you must return quickly."
He then ordered the judge Wáng Fèngxiáng
to release Lǚshuāng early
and also entrusted him with a message.
He said to Lǚshuāng:
"Tell His Excellency for me,
that in two years from now,
he will be relieved of his commission.
Within one year,
he must first leave
and go to the imperial court.
His son will pass away early.
Be careful not to reveal this."
Fèngxiáng checked the records and released him to return.
At a certain gate,
Lǚshuāng encountered several friends with whom he had often drunk in life.
They said to Lǚshuāng:
"You alone are returning to life,
we admire you greatly,
it is something we cannot achieve."
Five or six days after returning to life,
Lǚshuāng went to visit Fèngxiáng.
Fèngxiáng had already anticipated his visit.
He asked:
"What did Shělì say?"
Lǚshuāng replied:
"He did say something,
but he ordered me not to tell anyone else."
Fèngxiáng said:
"I already know about it,
you may go back now.
I will wait for an opportunity,
and then inform His Excellency."
Ten days later,
he and Lǚshuāng reported it to him.
His Excellency summoned Lǚshuāng for questioning,
and Lǚshuāng recounted everything he had seen.
After Fèngxiáng presented his report,
everything was verified exactly as Lǚshuāng had said.
It turned out that Fèngxiáng was born with a connection to the underworld bureau,
which was hidden and unknown to anyone,
but was revealed because of Lǚshuāng's return to life.
Jǐng Shēng
Jǐng Shēng
was a man from Yīshì in Hézhōng.
He was deeply learned in the classics
and taught several dozen students.
At the end of the year, as he was returning home,
he happened to meet the late chancellor Lǚ Tán on the road.
Because they were old acquaintances,
Tán let him ride in his carriage and took him away.
The students then scattered and reported to Jǐng Shēng's family.
By the time Jǐng Shēng arrived home,
his body had already died,
but he revived several days later.
He said:
"In the underworld, I saw the Imperial Attendant Yán Wǔ
and the Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng, Zhāng Huòrán."
Jǐng Shēng was skilled in the *Book of Changes*,
and in his early years, he had also lectured to Chancellor Lǚ.
Before the lectures were completed,
Chancellor Lǚ passed away.
He then summoned Jǐng Shēng
and asked him to finish the remaining lectures.
At that time, Yán and Zhāng were both officials in the left and right bureaus.
They looked at Lǚ angrily and said:
"Jǐng Shēng should not have come here,
he is certainly not someone the underworld should detain.
How can you harm others for your own private desires?"
Together, they requested his release,
and Lǚ agreed.
Minister Zhāng then took Jǐng Shēng aside
and entrusted him with a message for his two sons,
one named Zēngzǐ,
the other named Fūzǐ.
On the third day of the intercalary first month,
they were planning to build a north-facing house,
which would harm Zēngzǐ's new wife.
He asked Jǐng Shēng to inform them
and tell them to stop immediately,
so as to avoid a great disaster.
By the time Jǐng Shēng revived several days later
and reported to the family,
the house had already been built,
and the wife had already died.
He also said that Zēngzǐ would become a prefectural governor,
and Fūzǐ would also serve as a prefectural governor,
but not through a regular appointment.
Later events turned out exactly as he said.
Xǔ Chēn
When Wáng Qián was stationed in Jiānglíng,
he had a clerk in his administrative office named Xǔ Chēn who was on night duty.
After the second watch, he suddenly died,
but by the fifth watch, he revived.
He told his colleagues:
"At first, I saw two men in yellow robes,
who urgently called me out of the office gate,
and I was then led away by them.
Heading north, we traveled about sixty or seventy *li*,
through thorns and dense undergrowth,
where there was a faint path.
After a short while,
we reached a place with a gatehouse.
It was over thirty feet high and wide,
and on the horizontal lintel above,
a large signboard was inscribed with the characters
'Crow Caw Country'.
The two men then led Chēn through this gate.
Inside the gate, the atmosphere was gloomy and dismal,
like dusk in the human world.
Moreover, there were no city walls or buildings,
only countless ancient locust trees.
Crows cawed noisily in the trees,
and even at close range, no human voices could be heard.
Traveling like this for another forty or fifty *li* or so,
we finally passed through that place.
Then we were led to a city wall,
with a yámén gate and official banners,
which was also very solemn.
The two men led him through and announced:
'We have captured and brought the crow-taker.'
In the hall, there was an official in purple robes,
seated behind a desk.
He asked Chēn:
'Do you know how to catch crows?'
Chēn immediately pleaded:
'All my family, from father and brothers to sons and younger brothers,
have served in the administrative office since youth,
handling documents and paperwork.
I truly have never practiced crow-catching.'
The official became angry,
and said to the two escorts:
'How could you arrest the wrong person out of turn?'
The clerks were terrified and prostrated themselves in guilt for a long time,
saying:
'It was truly a mistake.'
The official looked at Chēn and said:
'Release him and send him back at once.'
To the east of the official's seated couch,
there was another man in purple robes,
tall and large,
with a dark complexion,
his head wrapped in silk,
as if injured.
He sat facing west on a large rope-bed,
and after looking at Chēn,
he said to the official at the desk:
'I wish to speak with this man on the way.'
He then stood near the side steps
and called to Chēn:
'Aren't you about to return?
When you see Vice Director Wáng,
tell him for me,
that Chancellor Wǔ sends word to the Vice Director:
I am deeply ashamed of the money and goods he often bestows upon me.
However, they are all broken and damaged,
unfit for use.
Now, there is a matter at hand,
urgently requiring fifty thousand sheets of paper money.
I hope he will obtain good paper to burn for me,
and when burning it, do not let anyone touch it.
Once it arrives here, it will be complete,
and moreover, I will meet the Vice Director before long.'
After he finished speaking,
Chēn acknowledged with a respectful 'yes'.
Walking out the door,
he saw the two escorts again, who led him back,
saying:
'We mistakenly brought you here,
and you almost couldn't escape.
However, you are fortunate and should take a different road back.'
Chēn asked,
and they said:
'The Crow Caw Country we patrol
spans several hundred *li* in circumference,
where sunlight and moonlight do not reach.
It is perpetually dark,
and they rely on the crows' cawing to know day and night.
Although these are birds,
they too face punishment and banishment.
Those whose yang lifespan has expired
are captured and brought here
to serve as cawing creatures in this place.'
Chēn asked further:
'What is the purpose of the empty land in Crow Caw Country?'
The two men said:
'When humans die, they become ghosts.
Ghosts, in turn, also die.
If there were no such place,
where would they be settled?'
When Chēn first died,
it was already reported to Qián.
After reviving,
he reported it again.
Qián asked for the details,
and Chēn recounted everything he had seen.
When Qián heard it,
he was deeply troubled by the mention of an impending meeting,
but upon inquiring about the appearance,
it truly was Chancellor Wǔ.
Qián had always been on good terms with Chancellor Wǔ,
and his successive official promotions were all due to Wǔ's recommendations and appointments.
Therefore, he often burned paper money at the end of each month and year to repay him.
Thus, Chēn's words could be verified.
So he bought one hundred thousand sheets of rattan paper
to fulfill the request.
As for Chēn's neighbor, also surnamed Xǔ and named Chēn,
he suddenly died at the fifth watch that very night.
It was during the
second year of the Héhé era, in the fourth month.
By the third year, in the first month,
Vice Director Wáng passed away.
Cuī Shào
Cuī Shào was
a great-grandson of Cuī Xuánwěi, Prince of Bólíng.
His grandfather Cuī Wǔ
once served as an assistant in Guìlín.
His father Cuī Zhí,
in the early Yuánhé era,
also served as an assistant in Nánhǎi,
often acting as prefect in Duānzhōu.
Cuī Zhí held office with integrity and hardship,
accumulating no surplus wealth;
beyond providing for his family,
he used all to aid relatives and old friends.
After over a year in the prefecture,
he suffered a wind-stroke illness,
retired and lay in a guesthouse,
bedridden for years.
His household was always poor,
and nothing changed.
After lying ill long,
on the day he passed away,
the house was utterly destitute.
Thus, his dependents could not return north.
Cuī Shào then diligently practiced goodness,
not abandoning his family's traditional vocation.
In the Nányuè regional headquarters,
there was the advantage of acting appointments to fill vacancies,
aiding stranded and滞留落魄 officials.
Cuī Shào, pressed by cold and hunger,
often stooped to this.
Jiǎ Jìzōng,
son of his maternal cousin Xiàhóu,
was Cuī Shào's son-in-law;
through their往来 connections,
he knew his family well.
In the sixth year of Tàihé,
Jiǎ Jìzōng changed from Qióngzhōu Pacification Commissioner to Governor of Kāngzhōu,
and thus recommended Cuī Shào as a subordinate clerk.
The county attached to Kāngzhōu's wall was called Duānxī,
and Duānxī's acting deputy Lǒngxī Lǐ Yù
was the nephew of the former Court of Judicial Review official Lǐ Jǐngxiū.
Between Cuī Shào and Lǐ Yù,
the affection of kindred spirits,
had always been friendly and harmonious.
Their residences
were also close in neighborhood.
Lǐ Yù's household
kept a female cat,
which often went to Cuī Shào's home to catch mice.
Southern customs
considered it very unlucky
for another household's cat to give birth in one's home.
Lǐ Yù's cat bore two kittens in Cuī Shào's house,
which Cuī Shào greatly disliked.
He thus ordered a servant boy
to tie the three cats in a basket,
added stones,
secured the basket opening with rope,
and threw it into the river.
Not many months later,
Cuī Shào observed mourning for his mother, née Zhèng of Xíngyáng,
left his post,
and lived in bitter poverty.
With several widows and orphans,
the cost of gruel
was insufficient morning and evening.
He thus traveled lightly to the city of Yángchéng,
seeking aid from relatives and old friends.
On the eighth day of the fifth month of the eighth year of Tàihé, he departed the official residence in Kāngzhōu,
reaching various coastal commanderies,
arriving at Léizhōu on the sixteenth day of the ninth month of that year.
Cuī Shào's family had long served the One-Character Heavenly King,
for two generations already.
In Léizhōu, he stayed at an inn;
on the twenty-fourth of that month,
he suddenly fell ill with a fever,
which worsened overnight,
and by the second day he was near death.
At the brink of death,
he suddenly saw two men,
one dressed in yellow,
one in black,
holding a written summons,
saying:
"By the king's order, we summon you."
Cuī Shào initially resisted,
saying:
"In life I practiced goodness,
unaware of doing evil;
what matter now
calls for this summons?"
The two messengers angrily said:
"You killed three innocent beings;
the wronged party appealed above,
a heavenly mandate descended,
ordering your investigation and prosecution.
You are to face the wronged party for judgment;
how dare you still claim injustice
and defy the king's order!"
They then unfolded the summons to show him,
Cuī Shào saw the writing clearly,
but was not allowed to read it carefully.
Cuī Shào was quite terrified,
unsure what to do.
Moments later,
a divine being appeared,
before whom the two messengers bowed in reverence.
The deity said to Cuī Shào:
"Do you recognize me?"
Cuī Shào said:
"I do not."
The deity said:
"I am the One-Character Heavenly King,
long worshipped by your family,
always thinking to repay you.
Now knowing you are in trouble,
I have come to rescue you."
Cuī Shào bowed and begged for rescue.
The Heavenly King said:
"Just come with me,
and have no worries."
The King then proceeded,
Cuī Shào followed,
the two messengers押 behind Cuī Shào.
Broad avenues and wide paths
stretched endlessly beyond sight.
After about fifty lǐ,
the Heavenly King asked Cuī Shào:
"Are you tired?"
Cuī Shào replied:
"Not too tired.
Can still manage twenty or thirty lǐ."
The Heavenly King said:
"We're about to arrive."
Shortly,
they saw a city gate in the distance,
walls tens of rèn high,
the gate tower very large,
with two deities guarding it.
These deities, seeing the Heavenly King,
stood aside in fearful respect.
After another five lǐ,
they saw another city gate,
guarded by four deities.
Their reverence upon seeing the Heavenly King
was like at the first gate.
After about three more lǐ,
there was another city gate,
its doors closed.
The Heavenly King said to Cuī Shào:
"Wait here,
I will enter first."
The Heavenly King then passed over through the air.
After a meal's time,
the sound of locks shaking was heard,
and the city gate opened wide.
Ten divine beings were seen,
the Heavenly King among them,
their expressions very worried and fearful.
After another lǐ,
another city gate appeared,
with eight streets,
extremely broad,
both sides lined with various trees,
whose names he did not know.
There were many divine beings,
countless,
all standing in rows under the trees.
Among the eight streets,
one was the largest.
Proceeding west along this street,
there was another city gate,
each side with several tens of buildings,
all with hanging curtains.
The streets were quite crowded with people,
carriages mingled together,
vermilion and purple缤纷.
Some rode horses,
some rode donkeys,
just like the human world.
This gate had no deity guarding it.
Beyond another gate,
were all tall buildings,
too many to count.
Pearl curtains and emerald drapes
dazzled the eye.
Upstairs were all women,
no men at all,
their clothes bright and new,
adornments novel and strange,
extravagantly luxurious,
unseen in the mortal realm.
The gate had vermilion banners,
silver-painted banners,
banners very numerous,
also several hundred people in purple.
The Heavenly King had Cuī Shào stand outside the gate,
then entered alone.
The messengers then led Cuī Shào to a hall,
first leading him to see the King's判官.
Upon arriving in front of the hall,
he saw Judge Wáng dressed in green,
who descended the steps to meet him,
treating him with great warmth and courtesy.
In return, Cuī Shào bowed,
and they exchanged greetings,
inquiring about each other's family and rank.
He was invited up the steps to sit,
and tea was ordered.
After a long while,
Judge Wáng looked at Cuī Shào and said:
"You have not yet been born."
At first, Cuī Shào did not understand his words,
and felt deeply suspicious and fearful.
The judge said:
"The underworld avoids the word 'death,'
so we call death 'life.'"
He urged for the tea,
and when it arrived,
the judge said:
"Do not drink this;
this is not tea from the human world."
Shortly after,
a person dressed in yellow
brought a pot of tea,
saying:
"This is tea for an official from the living world;
Cuī Shào may drink it."
Cuī Shào drank three bowls.
The judge then led Cuī Shào to see the Great King,
holding a written document in his hand,
but did not enter immediately.
The Great King was sitting facing the One-Word Heavenly King,
and the Heavenly King said to the Great King:
"It is all because of this man's arrival."
The Great King said:
"There are wronged souls who have appealed against him;
although his hands did not kill,
he gave orders with his mouth,
commanding them to be killed in the river."
The Heavenly King ordered Cuī Shào's wronged souls to be summoned,
and over ten people in purple robes
bowed in unison and walked out.
In an instant,
one person,
dressed in a purple robe,
holding an ivory tablet,
with a written complaint below,
led a woman forward,
along with two children,
all with human bodies but cat heads.
The woman wore a pale skirt and a yellow jacket,
one girl was similarly dressed,
and one boy was also similarly dressed,
wearing a black robe.
The three wronged souls wept incessantly,
claiming that Cuī Shào had harmed them unjustly.
The Heavenly King said to Cuī Shào:
"Quickly open your mouth and promise them merit."
In his panic and fear,
Cuī Shào forgot all the names of Buddhist scriptures from the human world,
only remembering the "Buddha's Crown Supreme Victory Sūtra,"
so he made a vow,
promising to transcribe one scroll of the sūtra for each of them.
As soon as he finished speaking,
the woman and the others disappeared.
The Great King and the One-Word Heavenly King then invited Cuī Shào to ascend the steps and sit with them.
Cuī Shào bowed in thanks to the Great King,
and the King returned the bow.
Cuī Shào modestly declined, saying:
"I am but an ordinary mortal;
with wronged souls accusing me,
my crime deserves no pardon,
how dare I hope to return to life?
Your Majesty is of such high status,
yet you return my bow;
I truly feel uneasy."
The Great King said:
"Your matter is now concluded,
and you shall return to the path of life.
The living and the dead are of different realms,
so it is not fitting for me to accept your bow."
The Great King asked Cuī Shào:
"From which family are you descended?"
Cuī Shào answered in detail about his clan.
The Great King said:
"If that is the case,
then I am related to you by marriage;
in the human world, I was Vice Director Mǎ."
Cuī Shào immediately stood up to explain the connection:
Vice Director Mǎ's nephew Pánfū
was Cuī Shào's brother-in-law.
The Great King asked where Pánfū was now,
and Cuī Shào said:
"It has been a long time since we parted,
but I know his family resides in Hángzhōu."
The Great King added:
"Do not be alarmed by this visit;
I was ordered by heavenly decree to investigate,
but now you shall return to the human realm."
He then turned to Judge Wáng and said:
"Where is Cuī Shào staying?"
The judge replied:
"He is accommodated in a certain hall."
The Heavenly King said:
"Very good."
Cuī Shào again inquired of the Great King:
"Your Majesty, in life,
your virtue and reputation were highly esteemed,
and your official rank was extremely exalted;
you should have returned to the human or heavenly realm,
as a person of noble status.
Why do you hold a position in the underworld?"
The Great King smiled and said:
"This official position is not easily obtained.
Previously, Minister Dù held this post,
and because he favored and trusted me,
he recommended me as his successor,
which is why I occupy this position.
How could it be easily attained?"
Cuī Shào asked further:
"Whom did Minister Dù replace?"
The King replied:
"He replaced Lǐ Ruòchū.
Lǐ Ruòchū was strict and lacked mercy,
so the Heavenly Emperor did not allow him to remain here long,
and Minister Dù replaced him."
Cuī Shào said again:
"Since I have come here by chance,
I wish to ask Your Majesty further:
I have heard that the underworld keeps registers of the living.
I am untalented,
and moreover, I have long been ill,
so I dare not hope for an official position in the human world.
However, I have relatives and friends,
and I wish to know about them;
I wonder if that is possible?"
The King said:
"For others, it would not be possible to see,
but because we are related by marriage,
I will make an exception for you."
The Great King turned to Judge Wáng and said:
"Allow him to see it once,
but you must strictly warn him
not to let it be leaked.
If it is leaked,
he will be mute for life."
Cuī Shào also asked:
"I do not know if my late father is here,
or if he has already been reborn?"
The Great King said:
"He is here, serving in a position."
Cuī Shào wept and said:
"I wish to pay my respects to him;
I wonder if that is possible?"
The King said:
"He has been dead for many years,
and you cannot meet him."
Cuī Shào stood up to take leave of the Great King,
and the One-Word Heavenly King
escorted Cuī Shào to Judge Wáng's hall,
where the furnishings and provisions
were just like those in the human world.
The judge then led Cuī Shào to a tiled corridor,
where there was another building,
and he guided Cuī Shào inside.
The walls were covered with golden and silver plaques,
listing the names of noble and important people from the human world.
The two categories of generals and ministers
were listed on golden plaques.
Below the rank of generals and ministers,
all were listed on silver plaques.
There were also long iron plaques,
listing the names of officials from prefectures, counties, and government offices.
The names on the three types of plaques
were all of people still alive.
If someone had passed away,
their name would be removed from the register accordingly.
Judge Wáng said to Cuī Shào:
"You may look at them,
but be careful not to speak of the official positions of those on the plaques in the human world.
For those already in office,
it is still permissible to mention them.
But for those not yet in office,
you must not leak the information,
or you will violate the Great King's earlier warning.
If people in the world act with good intentions,
they will surely receive good retribution.
The underworld punishes those with evil intentions quite severely."
Cuī Shào stayed in Judge Wáng's hall
for three days.
Morning and evening, strict
alarms were sounded,
with hundreds of drums beaten,
but horns were not blown.
Cuī Shào asked the judge:
"All matters in the underworld
seem very similar to those in the human world,
but only drums are used without horns;
I wonder why that is?"
The Judge said:
"The sound of the horn
resembles the roar of a dragon.
The dragon
is the essence of metal.
The essence of metal
is the essence of yang.
The Underworld Court
is the office of the ultimate yin.
Therefore, the place of ultimate yin
does not wish to hear the sound of ultimate yang."
Cuī Shào asked again:
"The Judge said:
"I have heard that in the Underworld there are hells,
but I do not know where they are?"
The Judge said:
"The names and categories of hells are many,
and they are not far from here.
Sinners enter them according to the severity of their karma."
He also asked about the city walls, moats, and people here,
why are they so prosperous?"
The Judge said:
"This is the King's City,
why should it not be prosperous?"
Cuī Shào asked again:
"The people in the King's City are as numerous as the sea,
how can none of them have any sins,
and thus not enter hell?"
The Judge said:
"Those who can reside in the King's City
are people with light karma,
who are not destined to enter hell.
When the gate of rebirth arrives,
they will, according to their respective status,
each receive their rebirth."
Also, Tián Hóng, the Reviewing Official of the Sòngzhōu Bureau, who had been exiled to Kāngzhōu,
had been in exile in the prefecture for two years,
and was Cuī Shào's neighbor.
Cuī Shào and Tián Hóng were also old friends for generations,
and their affection was quite deep.
On the day Cuī Shào departed from Kāngzhōu,
the Reviewing Official was still very healthy and well.
Half a month after his departure,
he fell ill and died.
Cuī Shào had not yet returned,
and knew nothing of this.
When he was summoned to the Underworld Court,
he already saw Mr. Tián there.
Tián and Cuī met,
and they wept upon seeing each other.
Tián said to Cuī Shào:
"After parting from you, sir,
not even ten days had passed
before I myself passed away.
I do not know what matter
has brought you here so suddenly."
Cuī Shào said:
"I was summoned by the Great King to investigate a minor matter,
the matter is now settled,
and I am about to be released and return."
Tián Hóng said:
"I have a small personal matter,
and I venture to entrust it to you.
I originally had no son,
so I adopted the son of the Zhèng family, my grandson, as my heir,
and had already called him to me.
At the age
of sixty,
I finally had a son of my own.
Now the Underworld Court is blaming me for seizing another's heir,
for having an outsider continue the family line.
Since I now have my own son,
and have not yet ordered my grandson to return to his original clan,
because of this matter,
I am being investigated and reprimanded quite severely.
When you, sir, return,
I hope you will, by all means, deliver a letter for me
to my son,
urging him to quickly have the Zhèng family's son return to his original lineage.
Also, please convey a message for me to Prefect Jiǎ of Kāngzhōu:
In my final years,
exiled to a distant land,
my host treated me with great kindness,
and supported me in every matter.
After my death,
he also arranged for my young son to return north,
so that my remains could be returned and buried in my homeland,
and my family would not be stranded in a desolate corner.
Although a benevolent person's intentions
are naturally like this,
for someone as shallow and inferior as me,
how can I deserve this?
I can only bear this kindness from the nine springs,
and regret that I have no strength to repay it."
When he finished speaking,
the two wept bitterly and parted.
After three days,
the King's Judge said:
"You may return now,
you cannot stay here long."
The One-Character Heavenly King and Cuī Shào prepared to return,
and the Great King came out to see them off.
The Heavenly King's retinue was quite grand,
with guides, cavalry, and attendants
filling the streets and alleys.
The Heavenly King rode on a small mountain that moved by itself.
The Great King instructed
that a horse be given to Cuī Shào to ride,
and they proceeded to the city gate.
The Great King dismounted,
bowed in farewell to the Heavenly King.
The Heavenly King remained seated on the mountain and did not descend,
but still bid farewell to Cuī Shào.
Cuī Shào knelt and bowed,
and the Great King also bowed from a distance. When this was done,
the Great King then returned.
Cuī Shào and the Heavenly King set off to return.
When they were halfway,
they saw four people
with human bodies but fish heads,
wearing dark green robes,
holding tablets,
their robes slightly stained with blood,
standing before a steep pit.
They wept, bowed, and pleaded with Cuī Shào:
"Our lives are in critical danger.
We are about to fall into this pit,
and only you, sir, can save us."
Cuī Shào said:
"What power do I have to save you?"
The four said:
"If you, sir, merely promise, it will be enough."
Cuī Shào said:
"Certainly, I promise."
The four bowed in thanks.
They then said:
"Our lives have already been spared by you, sir,
but we wish to open our mouths with a difficult request,
to make an insatiable demand.
Will you, sir, not find it strange?"
Cuī Shào said:
"If it is within my power,
I will do my utmost to fulfill it."
They said:
"The four of us together beg you, sir, for the 'Golden Light Sutra'.
Then we can be liberated from our sinful bodies."
Cuī Shào promised again.
When he finished speaking,
the four all disappeared.
When they returned to the guesthouse in Léizhōu,
he saw his own body lying on the bed,
covered with a quilt over the hands and feet.
The Heavenly King said:
"This is your body.
Just enter it slowly,
do not be afraid."
As the Heavenly King instructed,
he entered his own body and revived.
When he regained consciousness,
he asked his family members,
and learned he had been dead for seven days,
with only his heart, mouth, and nose slightly warm.
About a day after reviving,
he still vaguely saw the Heavenly King before his eyes.
He also saw a wooden basin in front of the steps,
in which four carp were kept in water.
Cuī Shào asked what fish these were.
His family said:
"They were originally bought for the kitchen,
but because the young master was critically ill,
we did not have time to prepare them."
Cuī Shào said:
"Could they be the four by the pit?"
He then ordered them to be released into the pond,
and also vowed to have a copy of the 'Golden Light Sutra' transcribed.
Xīn Chá
On the ninth day of the twelfth month in the fourth year of the Tàihé era,
Wèi Shì, an official stationed at the frontier, died suddenly in the private temple of the Shěn family in Yánfú Ward of Cháng'ān.
Two evenings before this,
in Shèngyè Ward, there was a gatekeeper clerk named Xīn Chá
who suddenly suffered a headache and passed out,
though his chest remained slightly warm.
At first, he saw a man in a yellow robe
approach his bed,
reach out with his hand, and lead him out.
Looking back at his own body,
he saw it had already stiffened.
His wife and children,
just then holding him and wailing,
sprinkling water and applying moxibustion,
were in a state of panic.
Chá felt deeply troubled in his heart,
yet unconsciously followed the yellow-robed officer away.
Once outside the door,
the yellow-robed man hesitated for a long while,
then said to Chá:
"It is not yet your time to go,
but if you can provide two thousand strings of cash,
I will let you go."
Chá said:
"I have always been poor;
how could I obtain such an amount?"
The yellow-robed man said:
"Paper money will do."
So they turned back and entered the courtyard,
where Chá called out to his wife several times,
but she did not respond.
The yellow-robed man smiled wryly and said:
"In that case,
this won't work."
He then pointed to a young servant boy,
instructing Chá to place his hand on the boy's back,
and through him convey the request for money.
Thereupon, the family indeed took paper money and burned it.
Chá saw that after the paper money was burned,
it all transformed into copper coins.
The yellow-robed man then proceeded to gather and stack them one by one.
He also said to Chá:
"Since you are already doing a favor,
please also arrange for cartage to send it out of the city."
Chá pondered for a long while,
then suddenly remembered that about a hundred paces west of where he lived,
there was a cart driver for hire,
whom he often saw coming and going.
So he went with the yellow-robed man to the driver's door.
The door was already closed,
but Chá knocked,
and the cart driver came out and said:
"The night is already late;
why are you coming now?"
Chá said:
"I have a guest who needs your service,
to carry money to outside Yánpíng Gate."
The driver said, "Alright,"
and came at once.
After loading the money,
Chá was about to not go along.
The yellow-robed man again invited him:
"Please accompany us to the city gate."
The three of them led the way together,
passed through the streets west of the city,
and headed southwest from Chángxìng Ward.
At that time, the setting moon was shining brightly,
and the morning bells and drums were about to sound.
The yellow-robed man said:
"Dawn is breaking;
we cannot go further.
We should stop for now at the Shěn family temple in Yánfú."
They soon arrived there,
and its gate was also closed.
The yellow-robed man knocked,
and after a moment, a woman,
perhaps over fifty years old,
wearing a purple skirt and white jacket,
came out to answer the door.
The yellow-robed man apologized and said:
"Madam, please do not take offense.
The day after tomorrow, there will be official business
coming to this temple.
Now, we have a small amount of money
that cannot be taken away immediately,
so we ask to borrow a corner to store it temporarily.
Once the official business is concluded the day after tomorrow,
we will come to move it."
The woman agreed.
Chá, the yellow-robed man, and the cart driver
together moved and placed the money in the northwest corner of the temple.
Outside the door,
they saw several reed mats,
so they took them to cover the money.
As soon as they finished,
the sky began to grow light.
The yellow-robed man bid farewell and left.
Chá followed the cart driver back.
Upon reaching home,
he saw his body still being held by his family,
with moxibustion treatment ongoing as before.
Unconsciously, his spirit and body reunited, and he revived.
After a long while,
it felt like a dream yet not a dream.
He then said:
"What just happened?"
His wife recounted in detail how the young servant had been possessed,
speaking in Chá's voice,
demanding six hundred sheets of paper to make money,
which were then burned.
Everything matched what had happened,
and Chá was quite astonished.
He hurried to the cart driver's home,
and the driver's family, upon seeing Chá, said:
"You've come just in time
to help interpret a dream.
Last night's dream
was unlike any ordinary one.
