Clearly, from your home,
I parted with a yellow-robed man after delivering a cartload of money to the Shěn family temple in Yánfú.
It was all vivid, as if before my eyes."
Chá grew even more alarmed.
He went again with the cart driver to the Shěn family temple.
Neither of them had ever been there before,
yet it exactly matched their movements from the previous night.
In the northwest corner of the temple,
they saw one or two reed mats,
beneath which the paper money remained.
Both Chá and the cart driver
recognized it as the place where they had delivered the money that night.
They then inquired about the woman.
The gatekeeper said:
"In the temple, there is only Attendant Censor Wèi staying here;
there is no one else."
The Shěn family had servants,
who also lived beside the temple.
Hearing the description of events,
along with the appearance and clothing,
one of them wept and said:
"That was my late mistress."
That night, during the fifth watch,
the Wèi family
heard knocking at the door.
They sent someone to check,
but saw nothing.
This happened three or four times.
Shì suspected it was thieves.
The next day,
he reported it to the county clerks,
asking them to be on guard.
That same day,
Shì invited guests in the evening to make pancakes.
After eating, he died.
Chá, wanting to verify the official business mentioned by the yellow-robed man,
had often kept watch nearby to observe.
And indeed, it came to pass.
Monk Yànxiān
Monk Yànxiān of Bǎoyuán Mountain in Qīngchéng once had hidden faults.
Leaving the mountain for Shǔzhōu,
he stayed overnight at the Tiānwáng Monastery along the way,
and died suddenly.
He was seized and taken away by someone,
brought to an official court.
Before being presented to the king,
he first saw a judge.
Questioned about his offenses,
Yànxiān denied them.
The judge then took a pig's foot and gave it to Yànxiān.
Yànxiān could not refuse in time,
so he reluctantly accepted it,
only to find it was a mirror.
Looking into it,
he saw himself in the mirror,
with all his past transgressions and indecencies
clearly revealed.
Yànxiān grew increasingly fearful,
not knowing what to do.
The judge reassured him,
admonished him, and sent him back.
After returning to life,
he told everyone about it,
though he did not speak of the hidden, shameful matters he had committed.
Chén Guīfàn
was a person from Míngzhōu
who traveled as a guest to Guǎnglíng.
Due to certain circumstances, he served as an aide to Mǎ Qián.
One evening, he died suddenly
and arrived at a government office.
An official there looked at the document and said:
"I was to summon Chén Guīmóu;
why have you brought Guīfàn instead?"
Fàn replied:
"My original name was Guīmóu,
but recently I have been serving Aide Mǎ.
Since Lord Mǎ avoids the word 'móu' (谋),
I changed one character."
The official then said:
"Fetch the register from Míngzhōu."
After a short while,
a clerk brought the register.
Upon looking at it,
it indeed listed Guīmóu.
He was then taken to another office.
The clerk said:
"Someone had filed a complaint against you,
but it has already been withdrawn.
You should be able to return."
Guīfàn then said on his own:
"My life has been full of hardships,
and I have endured extreme poverty.
Since death is inevitable for all,
and I have already come this far,
I do not wish to return."
The clerk insisted on sending him back
and added:
"If that is the case,
I wish to know about my future prospects of poverty or success."
The clerk then checked the register and said:
"Your future days will be quite good;
although you may not achieve great wealth or status,
you will not lack for official positions and emoluments."
He then asked how long his lifespan would be.
The reply was:
"That cannot be told."
He further asked where he would die.
The answer was:
"Not in Yángzhōu,
nor in Èzhōu."
He was then escorted back home and awoke.
Later, Qián served successively as prefect of two commanderies
and was highly trusted and employed.
After Qián died,
Guīfàn returned to Yángzhōu.
He was sent on a mission to Èzhōu
and, upon returning,
died in Péngzé.
Jiǎ Ǒu
During the Jiàn'ān era of the Hàn dynasty,
Jiǎ Ǒu, styled Wénhé, from Nányáng,
fell ill and died.
At that time, an officer was taking him to Tàishān.
The Director of Fate checked the register
and said to the officer:
"We were to summon Wénhé from a certain commandery;
why have you brought this person?
Send him back quickly."
As it was already dusk,
he went to rest under a tree outside the city walls.
He saw a young woman walking alone.
Wénhé asked her:
"You appear to be from a respectable family;
why are you traveling on foot?
What is your name?"
The woman said:
"I am from Sānhé.
My father is currently the magistrate of Yìyáng.
I was summoned here yesterday,
but now I am allowed to return.
As night has fallen,
I fear being subject to suspicion of impropriety.
Seeing your appearance,
you must be a virtuous man.
That is why I have stopped here
to rely on your presence."
Wénhé said:
"My heart is drawn to you;
I wish to share joy with you tonight."
The woman said:
"I have heard from my aunts
that a woman's virtue lies in chastity and devotion,
and her reputation in purity."
Wénhé tried to persuade her repeatedly,
but her resolve remained unmoved.
At daybreak, they each went their separate ways.
Wénhé had been dead for two nights;
his body was about to be encoffined for burial
when they saw color return to his face.
Touching his chest, it felt slightly warm,
and after a short while, he revived.
Wénhé, wishing to verify the events,
went to Yìyáng.
He prepared a name card and requested an audience with the magistrate.
He then asked:
"Did your daughter die and then revive?"
He described in detail the woman's appearance, demeanor, clothing, and features,
as well as the entire conversation they had.
The magistrate went inside to ask his daughter.
What she said matched exactly.
Initially greatly astonished,
he eventually gave his daughter in marriage to Wénhé.
Zhāng Fàn
Zhāng Fàn from Lè'ān in Línhǎi was over twenty years old.
He had been dead for a day
and was not yet encoffined when he revived.
He said
that he had been taken to the celestial office.
The official in charge there was his maternal cousin,
who managed to have him spared.
When he first arrived,
there was a young woman who had also been taken and sent there,
standing outside the gate.
Seeing that Fàn's matter was resolved,
the woman knew he had influential help.
Weeping,
she took off three gold bracelets and various precious ornaments from her arm and entrusted them to Fàn to give to the official,
begging for rescue.
Fàn immediately made the request for her
and presented the bracelets and items.
After a long while, he came out
and told Fàn that it had been settled:
Qiūyīng was also to be sent back,
Qiūyīng being the woman's name.
Thus, they left together.
Their feet were sore and they were exhausted,
barely able to walk.
As it was getting dark,
they stopped at a small hut by the roadside.
It resembled a guesthouse,
but they saw no host.
Fàn and the woman stayed together and became intimate,
asking each other further questions.
The woman said:
"My surname is Xú.
My home is in Wūmén, Wú County.
We live by the watercourse;
in front of the gate is an inverted jujube tree—that is the place."
The next morning, they each went their separate ways
and both returned to life.
Fàn had previously been a clerk in the Protector Army's office.
On leave, he left the capital
and passed through Wú.
He then went to Wūmén
and searched according to the description.
He found the Xú family residence.
Exchanging pleasantries with the host,
he asked where Qiūyīng was.
The host said:
"My daughter never goes out;
how do you know her name?"
Fàn then explained the reason for their spiritual encounter in the past.
Qiūyīng had already spoken of it beforehand,
and what she said matched.
The host then understood.
However,
he was ashamed to mention the matter of their intimacy,
but some neighbors knew about it
and told the Xú family.
The Xú family tested him by having several maidservants come out one by one to show Fàn, saying:
"No, it's not her."
Then they had Qiūyīng come out to see him.
It was as if they were old acquaintances.
The Xú family considered it the will of Heaven
and gave her to Fàn as his wife.
They had a son named Tiāncì.
Xiè Hóngchǎng's Wife
During the Tang dynasty, Xiè Hóngchǎng, a scholar of the Prince of Wú's household from Chénjùn Commandery,
was married to a woman of the Xǔ clan from Gāoyáng.
In the early Wǔdé era,
she fell ill and died,
but revived after four days.
She recounted that
she had been seized by twenty or thirty men and taken to the underworld.
Before she could see the officials,
she heard a call.
Although she did not recognize the face,
the voice sounded like that of her uncle-by-marriage, Shěn Jíguāng.
Lady Xǔ asked:
"The voice sounds like Uncle Shěn's,
but why do you have no head?"
(Southerners address their uncles-by-marriage as "Uncle [Surname]".)
Jíguāng then lifted his head with his hands
and placed it on his shoulder,
admonishing Lady Xǔ:
"You stay here for now,
do not go to the western courtyard.
Wait until I petition on your behalf,
then you should be able to leave."
Lady Xǔ thus remained.
Jíguāng returned only after two days.
He told Lady Xǔ:
"Your coming here this time
is because the King wants to make you a female entertainer.
If you are summoned for an audience,
you must not say you know how to play the *zhēng* or pipes.
If they are not convinced,
you can cite me as a witness."
After a short while,
a clerk holding a document led her in.
The King indeed asked if she knew how to play the *zhēng* or pipes.
Lady Xǔ replied:
"I do not know.
Shěn Jíguāng knows all about it."
The King questioned Jíguāng,
who answered:
"She does not know."
The King said:
"She should be released early,
there is no need to detain her."
At that time, Jíguāng wanted to send her off,
so he consulted with the document-holder.
Lady Xǔ did not understand their words.
The document-holder said:
"Madam, although your merits and virtues are strong,
you previously committed a minor offense.
If you undergo the punishment accordingly,
your bodily karma will be completely purified.
Wouldn't that be wonderful!"
The clerk then led her east into a courtyard,
whose gate was extremely small.
Seeing people undergoing punishment there,
Lady Xǔ became very frightened.
She pleaded with the overseer:
"In my lifetime, I cultivated blessings.
For what crime have I come to this?"
He replied:
"Madam once served food to a relative using an unclean bowl.
You must undergo this punishment
before you can leave."
They then poured molten copper into her mouth.
It was excruciatingly painful.
By the time she revived,
the inside of her mouth was completely ulcerated.
Jíguāng then said:
"You can receive a scripture from this person.
Memorize it and take it back,
uphold and recite it without neglect.
From now on,
you are guaranteed to live past eighty."
Lady Xǔ had never recited scriptures in her lifetime,
but after reviving,
she managed to memorize one volume.
Upon inquiry among people,
it was found to be previously unknown.
Now, she upholds and recites it without fail.
Jíguāng was still alive at that time.
Two years later,
he finally met with misfortune.
As for all her relatives,
those about to die
would be seen in the underworld three years in advance.
This was recounted by Lady Xǔ's paternal cousin, Xǔ Rénzé.
The Woman of the Liáng Clan
In Xiányáng, there was a woman surnamed Liáng.
During the Zhēnguàn era,
she died and revived after seven days.
She said of herself
that she had been taken to a large courtyard.
In the hall, she saw an official
sitting at a desk with a brush in hand,
attended by a grand retinue.
He ordered an investigation,
asking whether this woman was fated to die.
A clerk then presented a document, saying:
"She shares the same name as someone fated to die,
hence the mistaken summons."
The official ordered his attendants
to release her immediately.
The clerk addressed the official:
"We do not know what crimes Liáng has committed.
Please let her undergo punishment before returning."
The official then ordered the case to be investigated.
The report stated:
"Liáng's only offenses in life were duplicity and malicious cursing.
There are no other crimes."
He then ordered one person to pull out her tongue
and another to chop it with an axe.
This happened several times daily.
After a full seven days,
she was finally sent back.
At first, it felt like falling into a deep ravine.
A moment later, it was like waking from sleep.
Her family looked at her tongue;
it was severely ulcerated and swollen.
From then on,
she forever abstained from wine and meat.
She remains alive to this day.
The Woman of the Zhū Clan
During the Tang dynasty, in Wǔyáng County, Zhèng Prefecture, there was a woman surnamed Zhū.
Her husband had previously owed silk to a man from another county.
After her husband's death,
no one repaid the debt.
At the end of the Zhēnguàn era,
she fell ill and died,
but revived after two days.
She said of herself
that she had been taken to a place
where she saw a man who said:
"I am a clerk of the Bureau of Fate.
During your husband's lifetime,
he owed my family a certain amount of silk.
That is why we summoned you.
Now we release you to return.
You must urgently prepare the goods
and deliver them to a certain village in a certain county,
returning them to my mother.
If you do not deliver them,
we will pursue you even more urgently.
Also, tell my mother for me
to strive to commission statues and cultivate blessings."
Lady Zhū then inquired in a certain village
and delivered the silk to the man's mother.
She described her son's appearance in detail,
which matched exactly how he was in life.
His mother also wept upon hearing this,
sighing sorrowfully for a long time.
Lǐ Qiángmíng's Wife
Lǐ Qiángmíng of Lǒngxī,
whose wife was from the Cuī clan of Qīnghé,
was exceptionally beautiful.
They had one son,
who was seven years old.
In the twenty-second year of the Kāiyuán era,
Qiángmíng was appointed as a magistrate in Nánhǎi.
It was during the height of summer,
when his wife suddenly fell ill and died.
Guǎngzhōu was swelteringly hot,
so after her death, her coffin was buried in the earth,
with bricks built around and sealed over it.
Qiángmíng grieved deeply that his wife had died young,
and that he was serving in a distant post,
weeping for her with intense sorrow,
his cries unceasing day and night.
After several days,
his wife appeared to him in a dream and said:
"My allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted,
and now the Emperor has granted me permission to live again.
However, my body has already decayed,
so the Emperor has commanded heavenly rats to regenerate my flesh and skin.
After another ten days,
large rats will come and go within the brick enclosure of my coffin—
that will be the sign that I am about to revive.
But you must seal the doors and windows,
wait for forty-nine days,
then open the door to my chamber,
bring out my body,
and I will come back to life."
When morning came,
Qiángmíng recounted this,
and the dreams of the household servants and concubines all matched.
After more than ten days,
several white rats suddenly appeared,
coming and going from the burial site,
each as large as a fox.
Qiángmíng found this strange,
and tried opening the coffin.
He saw that flesh had begun to grow on his wife's bones,
covering her entire body.
Qiángmíng sealed it again.
After forty-eight days had passed,
his wife appeared to him in another dream and said:
"I will come back to life tomorrow morning,
why not bring out my body?"
At dawn,
Qiángmíng opened the coffin,
and his wife revived.
He helped her out and bathed her.
His wife had always been a beautiful woman,
but after being reborn,
her beauty was twice what it had been before.
Her skin was like jade,
her glances charming and full of grace.
Dressed in splendid attire and adorned with exquisite makeup,
she was a rare beauty unmatched in the mortal world.
Qiángmíng's joy showed on his face.
When Táng Zhāo, the military governor of Guǎngzhōu, heard of this,
he ordered his wife to go and see her.
Thus, the wives of officials from the Deputy Commander down all followed along.
Qiángmíng's wife, dressed in magnificent robes, received the governor's wife,
exchanging courtesies as equals,
and received bows from the various ladies.
Observing her closely,
she seemed like a person from among the immortals.
She spoke and ate like an ordinary person,
but spoke little.
When people questioned her,
she would only reply after a long while.
If asked about matters of the underworld,
she would immediately fall silent,
not answering even her own husband.
The next day,
the wife of Governor Táng prepared a feast,
and invited her to their home.
The wives of all the officials came together to see her,
admiring her gentle demeanor and radiant beauty,
and all said:
"We have never seen such beauty before."
Afterward, the wives of the Deputy Commander, Chief Secretary, and others took turns hosting banquets on successive days,
inviting her to their residences,
and the governor's wife also attended.
This continued for about twenty days.
She went about like any other person,
only more serene and quiet than before.
Later, Qiángmíng was sent on a mission to Guìfǔ,
and returned after seventy days.
During his absence, his wife was welcomed by various households,
coming and going without incident.
A few days after Qiángmíng's return,
his wife again fell ill.
Her illness grew severe, and she died the next day.
Counting from her revival,
she had lived only a hundred days.
Some said
that something had possessed her.
The Woman from Jīngzhōu
In the twenty-third year of the Kāiyuán era,
a woman from Jīngzhōu died and came back to life after three days.
She claimed to have witnessed the rewards and punishments of the underworld,
as well as the fortunes and misfortunes of the state.
The King of Ghosts ordered her to convey a message to the ruler,
and Jīngzhōu reported this to the court.
The court was astonished,
and wished to see her.
An edict was issued to provide post-horses,
ordering her to come to Luòyáng.
On the journey, when she reached Nányáng,
she suddenly lost her voice and could no longer speak,
and remembered nothing further.
Upon reaching the capital,
she was deemed a fraud,
and was promptly sent back.
The Wife of Zhōu Zhézhì
The wife of Zhōu Zhézhì of Rǔnán
was the daughter of Xí Yù, Vice Minister of Revenue.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
she suddenly fell ill,
and her condition became critical, nearing death.
In her lifetime, she had always donated her clothing
for meritorious deeds.
Only one red embroidered vest adorned with pearls,
a gift from her mother,
did she still cherish,
and had not yet given away.
Her illness grew more severe.
She then ordered Buddhist artisans
to use the vest to cast two Buddha statues at her sickbed,
but she died before they were completed.
At first, a crowd of ghosts seized Lady Xí
and carried her up a great mountain.
Suddenly, they heard two people calling from behind,
telling them to stop.
The ghosts then hesitated and dared not move.
When the two arrived,
their complexions were dark,
their faces covered in dust.
The ghosts were terrified,
and all fled in fear.
They then led Lady Xí back home,
where they heard the family wailing.
The two went straight to the corpse,
told her to enter it,
and she revived.
The two were the newly cast Buddha statues.
The Daughter of Chief Secretary Liú
The Prefectural Administrator Liú of Jízhōu had no sons,
and raised only three daughters,
all of exceptional beauty,
whom he cherished deeply.
His eldest daughter, aged twelve,
fell ill and died in the official residence.
Liú had long been on good terms with the Assistant Magistrate Gāo Guǎng of Sīqiū,
and when both had completed their terms of office,
they returned home together,
with Liú transporting his daughter's remains back.
Gāo Guǎng had a son,
over twenty years old,
very intelligent and clever,
and handsome in appearance.
Along the way, they stopped at Yùzhāng,
where they were held up by the water and could not proceed.
The two boats were separated by over a hundred paces,
and they visited each other day and night.
One night,
Gāo's son was alone in the boat reading.
After the second watch,
a maidservant,
about fourteen or fifteen years old,
with a very beautiful appearance,
came straight to Gāo and said:
"The candle in the Administrator's boat has gone out,
and I've come to borrow a light."
Gāo's son was very taken with her,
and so he flirted with her,
and the maidservant also happily complied.
She said:
"I am not worth your attention,
but the young lady in our household,
is peerlessly beautiful and enchanting,
and if I convey your intentions to her,
she can certainly be brought to you."
Gāo was overjoyed and surprised,
thinking it was one of the surviving daughters,
and so he arranged a meeting with her before she left.
The next night,
the maidservant came again and said:
"The matter is settled,
you can wait for her now."
Gāo was very excited,
and stood waiting outside the boat.
At that time, the sky was cloudless,
and the moon was very clear and bright.
After a while,
he saw from afar a young woman,
emerging from the rear boat,
coming straight with this maidservant,
and before she was ten paces away,
her radiance shone forth,
and her fragrance assailed him.
Gāo could not contain his feelings,
and went forward to embrace her.
The young woman threw herself into his arms,
her charms overflowing,
and they went together into the boat,
becoming even more intimate.
After this, she came every night,
and their affection grew even deeper.
After more than a month like this,
she suddenly said to Gāo:
"I wish to discuss a secret matter,
but I fear you may find it difficult?"
Gāo said:
"Please, do tell me."
She then said:
"I am originally the deceased daughter of Administrator Liú,
destined to be reborn.
Since I have been fortunate enough to serve you,
if you are willing to accept me,
I should inform my family and let them know."
Gāo was greatly surprised and overjoyed, saying:
"For the realms of the living and the dead to unite in this way,
is something unheard of in a thousand years.
We shall share pillow and mat forever,
what joy could compare to this!"
The young woman then said:
"In three days, I will surely be reborn,
and you must have my coffin opened.
At night, expose my face to the dew,
and feed me thin porridge,
and I will then come back to life."
Gāo agreed.
The next morning,
he went to tell Gāo Guǎng.
Gāo Guǎng did not quite believe it,
but because it was so extraordinary,
he had him go to Administrator Liú,
and relate the whole matter.
The wife was very angry, saying:
"My daughter has already decayed,
how could you defile her spirit like this,
to such an extent?"
She firmly refused.
Gāo pleaded even more earnestly.
That night,
both Liú and his wife dreamed of their daughter saying:
"My fate is to be reborn,
and Heaven has arranged this match,
I thought you would be happy and consent.
But now you are so stubborn and unyielding,
do you not wish for me to be reborn?"
When they awoke,
they were deeply moved and realized.
Also because her appearance and clothing,
were exactly as described,
they finally consented.
When the time came,
they opened the coffin together,
and saw the young woman's appearance fresh and bright,
gradually growing warm,
to the great surprise and joy of the household.
They set up a curtained enclosure on the shore,
and placed her inside,
exposing her face to the dew at night,
and feeding her during the day.
Her parents both watched over her.
One day,
she began to show signs of breathing,
slightly opened her eyes,
and by evening could speak,
recovering fully within a few days.
Gāo asked about the maidservant,
and she said:
"I died before the young lady,
and my coffin is also in the boat."
After the young woman revived,
she went to see her,
wept sorrowfully, and bid her farewell.
They then chose an auspicious day,
and were married at that place,
later giving birth to several sons.
Thus they named the place,
calling it Lǐhuì Village.
Reported by Lú Xū's maternal aunt.
Lù Xū, the governor of Luò Prefecture, had an aunt who kept a dog named Huāzi,
whom she cherished deeply.
One day, the dog went missing
and was killed by someone.
Several months later,
Madame Lù suddenly passed away.
In the underworld, she saw a judge surnamed Lǐ,
who said to her:
"Madame, your allotted lifespan is about to end,
but someone has pleaded earnestly on your behalf,
granting you an additional twelve years of life."
She bowed in gratitude and left.
Walking along a broad road,
she came upon a large mansion
where a beautiful woman,
attended by over ten maidservants,
was about to stroll by the gate.
The woman had Madame Lù summoned inside.
She asked:
"Do you recognize me, Madame?"
Madame Lù replied:
"I do not recall."
The beautiful woman said:
"I am Huāzi.
In my past life, you did not treat me as a lowly beast
but always cared for me.
I am now Judge Lǐ's concubine.
The one who pleaded for you yesterday was me.
The underworld authorities did not grant the full request,
only adding twelve years.
I secretly changed it from twelve to twenty
to repay your kindness in raising me."
Shortly after, Judge Lǐ arrived.
Huāzi knelt and pleaded that Madame Lù be called by her original name,
not addressed as 'Madame,'
and earnestly begged for this.
Judge Lǐ hesitated but eventually came
and sat separately to chat and laugh.
Huāzi first informed Judge Lǐ about altering the years,
and Judge Lǐ was about to reprimand her.
She replied:
"In my lifetime, I received great kindness,
and this is how I repay it.
Even if it were one in ten thousand,
I would still plead for it."
Judge Lǐ said cheerfully:
"This matter is not easy,
but moved by your earnest plea,
I grant it."
Before parting,
Huāzi said to Madame Lù:
"Please collect my remains
and bury them properly.
My bones are under the north wall of Lǚxìn Ward Street,
buried in the filth."
After Madame Lù revived,
she verified this and found it to be true.
She then buried the remains with the rites due to a child.
Later, she expressed her gratitude in dreams.
Twenty years later,
Madame Lù finally passed away.
The Wife of Liú's Son
There was a man named Liú,
who was chivalrous and courageous in his youth.
He often traveled as a guest in Huáiyīn County, Chǔ Prefecture,
and associated with many unruly youths from the marketplaces.
His neighbor, a man named Wáng, had a daughter
whom Liú sought to marry,
but Wáng refused.
Several years later,
due to famine,
Liú joined the army.
After a few years,
his service ended,
and he returned to Chǔ Prefecture.
He reunited with old friends,
and they enjoyed themselves greatly,
often indulging in outings and hunts.
By day, they engaged in hunting,
and by night, they visited pleasure quarters.
Once, they went over ten li outside the city walls
and saw a ruined tomb
with a coffin exposed.
Returning, they gathered to drink.
It was a summer night,
and a sudden rainstorm arrived.
The group joked:
"Who dares to take something and place it on the coffin of that ruined tomb?"
Liú, emboldened by wine, said:
"I can do it."
The others said:
"If you truly can,
tomorrow,
we will prepare a feast
to reward you for it."
They then took a brick,
inscribed all their names on it,
and told Liú to take it there,
while the others drank and waited.
Liú went alone,
and at midnight, he reached the tomb.
The moon had just risen,
and he saw something crouching on the coffin.
Looking closely,
it was a dead woman.
Liú placed the brick on the coffin,
then carried the corpse on his back and returned.
The others were chatting merrily
when they suddenly heard Liú pushing the door open,
as if carrying something heavy.
The door opened,
and he went straight to the lamp,
placing the corpse on the ground.
It stood upright,
its face powdered and painted,
with hair half undone.
Everyone was terrified;
some ran and hid.
Liú said:
"This is my wife."
He then embraced the corpse and lay with it on the bed.
The others were shocked and afraid.
By the fourth watch,
he suddenly felt slight breath from its mouth and nose.
Examining it,
he found it had revived.
When asked what had happened,
she said she was Wáng's daughter,
who had died suddenly from illness
and did not know how she ended up there.
Before dawn,
Liú fetched water
for her to wash her face and hands,
and fixed her hairpins and bun.
Her illness had already recovered.
Then they heard neighbors saying:
"Wáng's daughter was about to marry when she suddenly died.
Before she was encoffined,
last night during the thunderstorm,
her corpse disappeared."
Liú then informed the Wáng family.
They were both sorrowful and joyful
and married their daughter to Liú.
Everyone marveled at this predestined union
and admired Liú's fearlessness.
The Wife of a Yánlíng Villager
Xiè Yòusǔn, a Taoist priest from the Língbǎo Temple in Yánlíng,
was invited by a villager from a nearby county to perform a funeral ceremony for his deceased wife.
The wife had been dead for half a month
when suddenly, sounds of pushing the coffin and calling out were heard,
startling everyone into fleeing.
The husband opened the coffin to look
and saw her sit up.
After a while, she could speak.
She said
that she had been summoned by her parents-in-law,
who told her there was no one there
and made her cook.
Their dwelling was very clean and spacious,
but there was no water.
One day,
she saw clear water in a ditch
and used it to rinse rice.
When her mother-in-law saw this,
she became furious and said:
"I didn't know you were so unclean.
What use are you?"
She then chased her back.
As she walked out the door,
she revived.
She remains well to this day.
The Wife of a Man Named Zhào
In the year Dīnghài,
a clerk named Zhào from Zhèxī had a wife who died.
Before she could be placed in the coffin,
she suddenly cried out loudly and came back to life.
She said she had been captured by an officer
and taken inside Hèlín Gate,
where there was a government office
with strict and orderly guards,
and many officials discussing affairs and leading prisoners.
The officer took her in
to the courtyard below,
where a green-robed and a white-robed official sat side by side in the hall.
The green-robed one said to the officer:
"You made a mistake,
this is not the right person,
send her back quickly."
The white-robed one said:
"Since she has already been brought here,
why send her back?"
The green-robed one did not agree,
and they argued for about the time it takes to eat a meal.
The green-robed one grew angry,
shouted at the officer to send her back.
The officer quickly led her out,
and on the way they passed a bridge
where dozens of people were repairing it,
with no planks but only nails.
The officer hurried her across,
and a nail injured her foot,
causing her to cry out in pain,
and thus she revived.
Looking at her foot, it was indeed injured.
Soon after, a neighboring woman died suddenly,
and did not revive.
Yáng Hù
When Jìn's Yáng Hù was three years old,
his wet nurse carried him around.
He then told her to retrieve a gold ring from a hole in a tree at the eastern neighbor's house.
The eastern neighbor said:
"My son fell into a well and died at age seven,
and he used to play with a gold ring,
but we lost track of where it was."
This verified that Hù was the reincarnation
of the eastern neighbor's son.
Wáng Liàn
Wáng Liàn, styled Xuánmíng,
was from Lángyá,
and served as Shìzhōng in the Sòng dynasty.
His father, Wáng Mín,
styled Xīyǎn,
was Zhōngshū Lìng in the Jìn dynasty.
Among their acquaintances was a foreign monk
who often admired Mín's demeanor,
and greatly respected and liked him.
He would often tell his fellow monks:
"If in my next life,
I could be this man's son,
that would fulfill my dearest wish."
Mín heard this and joked with him:
"With your talent and conduct, Master,
you could indeed be my disciple."
Soon after,
the monk fell ill and died,
and a little over a year later, Liàn was born.
As soon as he could speak,
he understood foreign languages.
As for rare treasures from distant lands,
bronze vessels, pearls, and shells—
things he had never seen in this life,
nor heard their names—
he would immediately name them
and recognize their origins.
He also naturally felt affection for foreigners,
more than for Hàn people.
Everyone said the monk was truly his former self,
so Mín gave him the childhood name Āliàn,
which later became his formal name.
Xiàng Jìng's Daughter
Xiàng Jìng, styled Fèngrén,
was from Hénèi.
In Wúxīng Commandery, he had a daughter
who died at a few years old.
When the girl first fell ill,
she was playing with a small knife,
and her mother tried to take it away but she wouldn't let go,
injuring her mother's hand.
A year after her death,
the mother gave birth to another daughter.
When this girl was four years old,
she asked her mother:
"Where is the knife from before?"
Her mother said there was no such knife.
The girl said:
"Back then we fought over the knife,
and I hurt your hand—
how can you say there isn't one?"
The mother was very surprised,
and told Jìng everything.
Jìng asked:
"Is the old knife still around?"
The mother said:
"Grieving for my previous daughter,
I didn't keep track of it."
Jìng said:
"Take several knives,
put them together in one place,
and let the girl identify it herself."
The girl saw them and was delighted,
immediately picking out the original one.
Cuī Yànwǔ
During the Suí dynasty's Kāihuáng era,
Cuī Yànwǔ of Bólíng, the governor of Wèi Prefecture,
while on an inspection tour came to a town
and was suddenly startled and overjoyed.
He told his attendants:
"I was once a woman living here,
and I still know where the house is."
He then rode his horse into a long alley,
turned and wound his way to a house,
and ordered them to knock on the door.
The master of the house was elderly,
and came out to greet him.
Yànwǔ entered the house,
first went up to the main hall,
looked at the eastern wall,
about six or seven feet from the ground,
where there was a raised spot.
He said to the master:
"The Lotus Sutra I once read and five gold hairpins
are hidden in this high spot on the wall.
On the last page of the seventh scroll of that sutra,
some characters were lost due to fire damage.
Now whenever I recite this sutra,
when I reach the end of the seventh scroll,
I always forget,
unable to remember it."
He then ordered his attendants to chisel the wall,
and indeed they found a sutra box,
opened it to the end of the seventh scroll and the gold hairpins,
all exactly as he had said.
The master wept and said:
"When my wife was alive,
she often recited this sutra,
and the hairpins were also hers."
Yànwǔ pointed to the locust tree in the courtyard:
"When I was about to give birth,
I untied my hair and placed it in a hollow of this tree."
They tried sending someone to search the tree,
and indeed found hair.
Then the master was both sorrowful and joyful.
Yànwǔ left clothing and goods,
generously provided for the master, and departed.
Prince Fàn of Qí
In the early Kāiyuán era,
Prince Fàn of Qí, having no sons,
asked the Dàoist priest Yè Jìngnéng to petition the Heavenly Ministry.
They heard the Heavenly Ministry reply:
"Fàn's karma includes having no sons."
Jìngnéng again submitted a petition to the Heavenly Ministry,
asking for a son for Fàn.
The Heavenly Ministry ordered two officers to fetch a monk from Jìng'ài Temple to be Prince Qí's son,
but the officers mistakenly went to the chamber of a great virtue at Shànhuì Temple.
The great virtue said:
"This must be a mistake—
I practice the path to the Tuṣita Heaven,
I should not become the son of a nobleman.
It should be a certain monk from Jìng'ài Temple."
The officers then vanished,
and the great virtue ultimately died because of this.
After a year,
Prince Qí had a son.
When the boy was six or seven years old,
he constantly asked to go worship at Jìng'ài Temple,
and the prince also knew of the matter.
He freely wandered around,
and when he reached the original temple courtyard,
it was as if he had been there before.
By the time he was over ten years old,
he ultimately did no good deeds,
only enjoyed carrying a slingshot,
shooting nearly all the pigeons in the temple courtyards.
Tàihuá Princess
It is widely told that Princess Tàihuá,
was the reincarnation of Emperor Gāozōng’s Empress Wáng.
Although she was born to Consort Wǔ,
she never showed a joyful expression,
and would become angry whenever she saw the consort.
When she was a few years old,
she suddenly asked for a rosary.
Those around her asked where she could obtain such an item,
and she always said there was one,
but none of them knew where.
Although Empress Wáng had met a tragic end,
the hall where she had resided,
along with the items she usually played with, were all still there.
The princess’s nurse carried her past the hall,
and she turned back, pointing and saying:
"My rosary is in the northeast corner of the hall’s precious canopy."
They sent someone to search for it,
and indeed found it there.
The Mǎ Family’s Son
The monk Xuángāo of the Zhìlì Temple in Fǔyáng County, Xiàngzhōu,
had the secular surname Zhào.
His elder brother’s son,
in a previous life, had been a son in the Mǎ family of the same village,
and died around the end of the Zhēnguàn era.
At the moment of death,
he turned to his mother and said:
"Your child has a karmic connection with the Zhào family;
after death, I will become a grandson of the Zhào family."
The Zhào family lived in the same village.
His mother did not believe him,
so she marked his right elbow with ink.
The wife of the Zhào family also dreamed of this child coming to her and saying:
"I will become your son."
Thus, she became pregnant.
The child she saw in her dream
was exactly the son of the Mǎ family.
After giving birth,
she checked for the black mark,
and it was still in the same place.
When the child was three years old,
without anyone guiding him,
he went on his own to the Mǎ family’s house,
saying:
"This is my old home."
Cǎiniáng
During Emperor Sùzōng’s reign, a certain Zhèng served as the governor of Rùnzhōu.
His elder brother was Kǎn,
and his sister-in-law was Madame Zhāng.
Their daughter was sixteen years old,
named Cǎiniáng.
She was virtuous, cautious, and well-mannered.
On the night of the Qīxī Festival,
she set up an incense altar
and prayed to the Weaving Maiden.
That night,
she dreamed of a carriage with feathered canopies covering the sky;
the carriage stopped, and someone addressed Cǎiniáng, saying:
"I am the Weaving Maiden.
What blessing do you seek?"
She replied:
"I wish for skill in weaving."
The Weaving Maiden then gave her a golden needle,
over an inch long,
attached to a piece of paper,
and placed it in her skirt sash.
She instructed her not to speak for three days,
and she would become exceptionally skilled.
Otherwise,
she would turn into a man.
After two days,
she told her mother about it.
Her mother, finding it strange, went to look,
but the paper was empty,
though the needle’s mark was still there.
Madame Zhāng’s several daughters had all died young,
and Cǎiniáng suddenly fell ill and stopped speaking.
Madame Zhāng became pregnant again,
and sighed, saying:
"I have already had five children,
and all died young;
why should I be pregnant again?"
She intended to take medicine to abort the pregnancy.
When the medicine arrived and she was about to take it,
Cǎiniáng, in a faint and unconscious state,
suddenly cried out, "Murder!"
Her mother, startled, asked her about it,
and she said:
"My life is ending,
and I will be reborn as a boy—
the child you are carrying is me.
Hearing that the medicine had arrived, I grew anxious,
so I cried out."
Her mother found this strange,
and did not take the medicine.
Cǎiniáng soon died.
After she was buried,
her mother, grieving and missing her,
collected the toys she often played with and hid them.
Within a month,
she gave birth to a boy.
Whenever someone touched the hidden toys,
the boy would cry.
When Madame Zhāng wept for her daughter,
the boy would also cry.
When she stopped, he would stop.
When he learned to speak,
he often collected and played with those toys.
He later rose to the position of Zhùshǐ.
Liú Sānfù
Liú Sānfù
was known for his literary talent by Lǐ Déyù.
When Lǐ Déyù was in Zhèxī,
he sent him to the capital to take the imperial examinations.
After passing the exams,
he served in various high offices.
Sānfù could remember matters from three lifetimes.
He said
he had once been a horse,
and the horse often suffered from thirst,
neighing at the sight of a post station;
if its hooves were injured, its heart would ache in sympathy.
Later, when Sānfù rode a horse,
on rough and stony ground,
he would always loosen the reins,
and if there were stones, he would remove them.
His household did not use door thresholds,
for fear of injuring the horse’s hooves.
His son, Yè,
was granted the title of Jíndì by imperial decree.
He rose to high office,
and submitted a memorial to clear Lǐ Déyù’s name.
He brought Lǐ Déyù’s coffin from Zhūyá
back to Luòzhōng for burial,
repaying the kindness he had received.
Scholars and officials praised him for this.
Yuánguān
Yuánguàn was a monk at Huìlín Temple in Luòyáng
towards the end of the Dàlì era.
He was skilled in managing fields and gardens,
and possessed abundant grain and silk.
Beyond Buddhist studies,
he was also thoroughly versed in music and temperament.
People of the time knew him as a wealthy monk,
but none knew his origins.
Lǐ Yuán, a Remonstrance Official,
was the son of a high-ranking official.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
he devoted himself to feasting, singing, and drinking.
His father, who served as the留守 (defender of the capital),
fell into the hands of rebels,
so Lǐ Yuán adopted a simple life of coarse grains and plain clothes,
settling at Huìlín Temple.
He donated all his family wealth to the temple as public property.
The temple provided him with only one bowl of food and one cup of drink per day.
He kept no servants
and cut off all worldly connections.
He formed a wordless friendship only with Yuánguàn,
sitting closely and conversing quietly
from dawn till dusk.
People of the time, considering them an unlikely pair of purity and impurity,
often ridiculed them.
This continued for thirty years.
One day, the two gentlemen planned a journey to Shǔ Province,
reaching Qīngchéng and Éméi
to seek the Way and medicinal herbs together.
Yuánguàn wished to travel to Cháng'ān
via the Xiégǔ Pass;
Lǐ Yuán wanted to go to Jīngzhōu
and exit through
the Three Gorges.
They debated these two routes
for half a year without reaching a decision.
Lǐ Yuán said:
"I have already renounced worldly affairs;
why would I take the route through the two capitals?"
Yuánguàn said:
"One's path is ultimately not determined by oneself.
Please let us depart via the Three Gorges."
So they ascended the gorges from the Jīng River.
When they reached Nánpǔ,
they moored their boat at the foot of a mountain.
They saw several women,
wearing embroidered skirts and carrying jars,
drawing water.
Yuánguàn gazed at them and wept, saying:
"I did not wish to come here,
for fear of seeing that woman."
Lǐ Yuán asked in surprise:
"Since entering these gorges,
we have seen many such people.
Why do you weep only for these few?"
Yuánguàn said:
"Among them is a pregnant woman surnamed Wáng.
She is where I am destined to be reborn.
It has been over three years,
yet she has not given birth,
because I had not yet arrived.
Now that I have seen her,
my fate is settled.
This is what Buddhists call the cycle of rebirth."
He said to Lǐ Yuán:
"Please use talismans and incantations
to hasten my rebirth.
Pause your journey briefly
to bury me at the foot of this mountain.
Three days after the bathing of the infant,
please also visit.
If the child looks at you and smiles,
that will be my recognition of you.
Twelve years later,
on the night of the Mid-Autumn moon,
outside Tiānzhú Temple in Hángzhōu,
I will meet you again—
that is our appointed time."
Lǐ Yuán then regretted this journey
and wept bitterly for him.
He summoned the woman
and told her the method.
The woman joyfully rushed home,
and soon,
her relatives all gathered.
They offered dried fish and wine by the waterside.
Lǐ Yuán went and bestowed the red-character talisman.
Yuánguàn bathed thoroughly
and put on new clothes.
That evening,
Yuánguàn died and the pregnant woman gave birth.
Three days later, Lǐ Yuán went to see the newborn.
When the swaddled child was brought into the light,
it indeed smiled at him.
Lǐ Yuán wept
and told the Wáng family everything.
The Wáng family then spent much of their wealth
to give Yuánguàn a lavish burial.
The next day,
Lǐ Yuán turned his boat around
and returned to Huìlín.
Inquiring at Yuánguàn's home,
he learned that he had already left instructions for his affairs.
Twelve years later, in the eighth month of autumn,
Lǐ Yuán went directly to Yúháng
to keep their appointment.
At Tiānzhú Temple,
the mountain rain had just cleared,
moonlight filled the river,
but there was nowhere to find him.
Suddenly, from the banks of Gěhóng River,
he heard a cowherd singing a "Bamboo Branch" song,
riding a cow and tapping
its horns,
with twin topknots and short clothes.
Soon he arrived before the temple—
it was Yuánguàn.
Lǐ Yuán approached and greeted him:
"Is Master Guàn well?"
He in turn asked Lǐ Yuán:
"You are truly a man of your word.
Our paths are different now;
do not come too close.
Your worldly ties are not yet severed;
I only hope you diligently cultivate yourself.
If you cultivate diligently and do not fall,
we will meet again."
Lǐ Yuán, having no chance for further conversation,
gazed at him with tears.
Yuánguàn sang another "Bamboo Branch" song
and walked step by step into the distance.
Across long mountains and far waters,
his song could still be heard,
its words poignant and melody lofty,
though none understood its meaning.
The song he first sang before the temple went:
"On the Stone of Three Lives, an old soul remains,
discussing moon appreciation and breeze chanting is in vain.
Ashamed that my friend traveled from afar to call,
though this body differs, my nature stands tall."
He sang another:
"Matters before and after life are vast and unclear,
to speak of karma would bring sorrow severe.
The streams and hills of Wú and Yuè I've searched all around,
now turning my misty boat toward Qútáng homeward bound."
Three years later,
Lǐ Yuán was appointed Remonstrance Grand Master,
and died after two years.
Gù Fēixióng
Gù Kuàng had a son
who died at a few years old.
Gù Kuàng was endlessly grief-stricken
and wrote a poem mourning him:
"An old man weeps for his beloved son,
by dusk, a thousand lines of blood have run.
His heart chases the startled, severed ape's cry,
his traces follow the vanishing bird in the sky.
The old man is seventy years of age,
this parting will not be for long, I presage."
Though his son had died,
his spirit often remained at home.
Whenever he heard his father's weeping,
he listened, deeply moved and sorrowful.
He thus made a vow:
if suddenly he could become human again,
he would once more be a son of the Gù family.
One day,
as if seized by someone and taken to a place,
like a county official,
he was ordered to be reborn into the Gù family.
Then he knew nothing more.
Suddenly he felt his mind clear and opened his eyes,
recognizing the house, his brothers,
and loved ones all around,
only he could not speak.
At the moment of his birth,
and thereafter, he remembered nothing.
At age seven,
his older brother playfully hit him,
and he suddenly said:
"I am your elder brother;
why do you hit me?"
The whole family was astonished.
He then recounted events of his past life,
each detail accurate without error,
calling all his younger siblings by their childhood names.
He was Gù Fēixióng.
Qí Jūnfáng
Qí Jūnfáng was a man
whose home was in Wú.
From childhood he suffered from poverty,
and although diligent in his studies,
his memory was poor.
Upon reaching adulthood, he composed poems and songs,
but they were not particularly fresh or refined.
Constantly driven by cold and hunger,
he toiled and wandered between the regions of Wú and Chǔ,
using poems of four, five, six, and seven characters to seek patronage,
yet he rarely received respectful reception from nobles and lords.
Although he occasionally gained something,
he never managed to accumulate even a single piece of gold.
Whenever he stored coins in a cloth bag,
and it became full enough to string them,
he would inevitably fall ill,
only recovering once the coins were exhausted.
In the early years of the Yuánhé era,
he traveled to Qiántáng.
At that time, it was a year of famine with heavy exactions,
and seeking help from people, he succeeded less than one in ten times.
So he went to Tiānzhú to beg for his morning meal.
When he reached the west of Gūshān Temple,
he was extremely hungry,
and could go no further.
Facing the flowing stream, he shed tears,
and sorrowfully chanted a few verses.
Soon, a foreign monk came from the west,
and he too sat down by the stream.
Looking at Jūnfáng, he smiled and said:
"Dharma Master,
have you had enough of the traveler's life?"
Jūnfáng replied:
"The traveler's life is indeed enough for me.
But your address of 'Dharma Master',
how mistaken it is!"
The monk said:
"Do you not recall expounding the *Lotus Sutra* at Tóngdé Temple in Luòyáng?"
Jūnfáng said:
"I am forty-five years old,
and have lingered in the regions of Wú and Chǔ.
I have never crossed the Jīng River to the capital,
so how could there be any talk of Luòyáng?"
The monk said:
"You must be tormented by the fire of hunger,
and have no leisure to recall past events."
Then he reached into his alms bowl bag,
took out a date,
as large as a fist.
He said:
"This is produced in my country.
If you eat it, you will know matters of past and future,
not just your previous life."
Jūnfáng was extremely hungry,
so he asked to eat it.
After eating, he became very thirsty,
and scooped up spring water to drink.
Suddenly he yawned, laid his head on a stone, and fell asleep.
After a short while, he awoke.
Then he remembered expounding the *Lotus Sutra* at Tóngdé Temple,
as if it were yesterday.
Weeping, he bowed to the monk and said:
"Where is Monk Zhèn now?"
The monk replied:
"His dedication was not yet complete,
so he was reborn as a monk in Shǔ.
Now he has severed all attachments."
"Where is the Venerable Shén now?"
He said:
"His previous vow was not fulfilled,
so I heard he has become a Dharma Master again."
"Where is Dharma Master Wù?"
He said:
"Do you not recall that before the stone statue at Xiāngshān Temple,
he playfully made a great vow,
saying that if he did not attain supreme enlightenment,
he would wish to be a mighty and powerful high official?
I heard yesterday that he has already become a great general.
Among the five of us fellow wanderers at that time,
only I have attained liberation,
while you alone remain a man suffering from cold and hunger."
Jūnfáng wept and said:
"For over forty years, I have eaten but one meal a day,
and for over thirty years, I have worn but one coarse robe.
Worldly affairs,
I have severed at their root.
How could I have expected that my cultivation of blessings was incomplete,
leading to my plight today?"
The monk said:
"The fault lies in that upon the teacher's seat,
you extensively spoke of heterodox doctrines,
causing those who study emptiness
to give rise to doubts in their minds.
Your precept-pearl was once flawed,
your meditation-taste was once tainted.
When the sound is muddled, the echo cannot be clear;
ultimately, it cannot be achieved.
If the substance is bent, the shadow will be crooked;
such retribution is fitting."
Jūnfáng said:
"What can be done about it?"
The monk said:
"As for today's matters,
I have no plan.
But for matters of future lives,
perhaps there is a warning for you."
Then he reached into his alms bowl bag,
took out a mirror,
both sides of which were crystal clear.
He said to Jūnfáng:
"If you wish to know the distinction between nobility and baseness,
the limits of long and short life,
the rise and fall of the Buddha's teachings,
the prosperity and decline of our Way,
you should take a look."
Jūnfáng looked into the mirror,
and after a long time, thanked him, saying:
"The matter of retribution,
the principle of glory and withering,
I have respectfully come to understand."
The monk put the mirror back into his bag,
then took him and left.
After walking more than ten steps,
he suddenly vanished.
That evening,
Jūnfáng went to Língyǐn Temple,
where he cut his hair and received the full precepts,
taking the Dharma name Jìngkōng.
In the first year of the Tàihé era,
Lǐ Méi was studying at Lóngmén Tiānzhú Temple,
when Jìngkōng visited him from Xiāngshān Jìngshàn Temple,
and thus related this account.
He then said to Méi:
"I am fifty-seven years old,
and only twelve years have passed since my ordination.
Holding the alms bowl to beg for food,
I still have nine years left.
By the time I leave this world,
will the Buddha's teachings have declined!"
When questioned further,
he remained silent and gave no answer.
Instead, he asked for brush and inkstone,
wrote a few lines on the north wall of the sūtra repository, and left.
They said:
"One grain of sand rises,
while countless sands decline.
The hare is caught in the net,
the hound leads its whelps.
Ox and tiger clash, horns and teeth are lost; the sandalwood's treasure, its blossoms never fade."
Liú Lì
There was a man named Liú Lì,
who served as the Deputy Magistrate of Chánggě.
His wife, Yáng Shì,
suddenly one day tearfully said to Lì:
"With my frail constitution,
I entrusted myself to you, my husband,
and have been deeply cherished and valued.
I thought our harmonious union,
would last until old age.
How could I have expected that one day,
I would leave you and pass away forever?"
Choking with sobs, tears and mucus flowing,
she could not control herself.
Lì said:
"You have never been ill before;
how can this be?"
His wife said to him,
For several days I have been sinking into exhaustion,
my spirit confused and dazed,
I know for certain I will not recover.
I entrust our little daughter Měiměi to you.
She also said to Lì:
"In the future, when Měiměi grows up,
I hope you will keep her for two or three years."
That evening, Yáng Shì died.
When Lì left office,
he resided in Chánggě,
already ten years had passed.
At that time, the military governor of Zhèng, Lord Cuī,
was Lì's elder cousin by marriage.
Lì went to visit him,
and Cuī treated him very generously.
Considering his poverty,
he had his secretariat write letters to various counties,
intending to assist him.
There was a certain county magistrate
who invited Lì to go outside the city to view flowers.
When the day arrived, the magistrate had an unexpected matter,
and could not go together as planned,
so he told Lì to go first,
and stay at the estate of Bailiff Zhào.
After traveling two or three lǐ,
he saw an apricot garden,
with flowers in full bloom,
and inside were over ten women.
Lì halted his horse to watch them;
there was one girl,
about fifteen or sixteen years old,
who also came near the wall to peek.
Lì traveled another hundred or so paces,
and then reached Bailiff Zhào's residence.
Entering the gate,
he saw the household in a flurry,
as if startled and anxious.
The host came out after a while.
He said:
"Just now, my daughter was viewing flowers with relatives,
when she suddenly fell violently ill,
so I was unable to welcome you as planned."
Before they could sit properly,
a maidservant whispered into Zhào's ear,
Zhào rose and went inside,
this happened several times,
then they heard Bailiff Zhào sighing in astonishment,
and he asked Lì:
"Were you the Deputy Magistrate of Chánggě in a certain year and month?"
Lì said:
"Yes."
"Did you marry Yáng Shì?"
He said:
"Yes."
"Do you have a daughter named Měiměi,
and a servant named Qiūsǔn?"
He said:
"Yes."
The servant controlling the horse now is him."
Zhào again,
sighed in amazement and wonder.
Soon someone called Qiūsǔn into the house,
where he saw a girl,
about fifteen or sixteen,
who tearfully asked him:
"Is Měiměi well?"
He replied:
"She is fine."
The servant bowed and left,
not understanding the reason,
and Lì was also surprised.
Gradually he asked Zhào:
"I do not recall having met you before;
how do you know about my affairs?"
Zhào then told him the truth:
"My daughter was just viewing flowers,
when she suddenly seemed to die violently,
but after reviving,
she said that in a previous life she was your wife.
Now, although reborn in a different life,
her affection has not been severed.
Just now when she saw you,
unconsciously she fainted."
Lì sighed sorrowfully for a long time.
After a short while,
the county magistrate also arrived,
and all the guests gathered.
Zhào fully explained the matter,
and everyone found it extraordinary.
Lì said:
"I am not yet old this year,
and also hold an official position;
I wish to seek the bond from a past life with the young lady."
Everyone helped bring it about,
and so they became husband and wife.
And Měiměi was three years older than her mother.
Zhāng Kèqín
There was a man named Zhāng Kèqín,
who took the imperial examination for the míngjīng degree.
He took a concubine,
whom he loved dearly, but she bore no son.
His family had for generations prayed to the god of Mount Huà,
and their prayers were quite effective.
Kèqín's mother then prayed to the god for a grandson,
and indeed a boy was born,
named Zuìlián,
very clever and bright.
Five years later,
Kèqín passed the examination,
and married a wife; after a year,
his wife also bore no son,
so his mother prayed again.
His wife then gave birth to a son,
but Zuìlián grew increasingly weak and frail daily,
so they prayed again to the god for protection.
That night,
the mother saw a person,
with a purple sash and golden seal,
who said to her:
"Your son is destined to have few children;
the previous son was brought about by me.
Now that your daughter-in-law has also borne a son,
the previous son certainly will not survive.
This is beyond my power to save."
He merely thanked them for their offerings and left.
Later, Zuìlián indeed died,
so they painted his right arm with vermilion,
and marked his eyebrows with dark pigment,
then buried him.
The following year,
Kèqín became the magistrate of Jiāméng in Lìzhōu,
and after leaving office,
he resided in Lìzhōu.
He went to the home of Deputy Recorder Wéi,
and saw a girl come forward and bow twice.
Kèqín looked at her,
and she greatly resembled Zuìlián.
He returned and told his mother,
who went to see her;
the girl was delighted.
She said to the family members:
"That is my home."
When they arrived,
they examined the painted marks,
and they were clearly still there.
Her family sent someone to fetch the girl,
but she was still reluctant and unwilling to leave.
Sūn Miǎn's family servant
The family servant of Sūn Miǎn, the County Captain of Qǔwò,
was six years old
and had never spoken.
Later, when Miǎn’s mother was sitting by the steps,
the servant suddenly stared at her.
The mother, finding it strange, asked him about it,
and the servant then laughed and said:
"When you, Madam, were still a young girl with your hair tied in two buns,
you once wore a yellow skirt with a white lined jacket,
and kept a wildcat.
Do you still remember it now?"
The mother also recalled it.
The servant said:
"That wildcat back then
is precisely me, your servant.
After I managed to escape,
I hid in a tile gutter,
and heard you, Madam, crying.
Only when dusk fell did I come down,
and entered the eastern garden.
In the garden, there was an ancient grave,
and the wildcat survived by hiding inside it.
After two years,
I was later struck and killed by a hunter.
Following the usual procedure, I then appeared before King Yánluó.
The King said:
'You have no further sins,
and should obtain a human body.'
Thus I was born in Hǎizhōu,
as the son of a beggar.
Throughout that lifetime,
I constantly suffered from hunger and cold,
and died at the age of twenty.
I again saw the King,
and the King said:
'I shall make you a servant in a noble household.
Although the name 'servant' is not favorable,
you will, however, be entirely free from worries and fears.'
Thus I was sent here.
Now, I, your servant, have already lived three lives,
while you, Madam, are still here,
remaining safe and blessed.
Is this not extraordinary!"
Wén Dàn
The Presented Scholar Wén Dàn of the previous generation was highly virtuous in conduct,
and everyone praised him.
From birth,
at three or four years old,
he could know matters from his previous life.
His parents had previously had a son,
just five years old,
who learned to recite poetry and books from others,
and was quite intelligent and sharp.
Not long after,
he accidentally fell into a well and died.
His parents grieved and missed him,
their sorrowful tears unbearable.
Later, they gave birth to Dàn.
One day, Dàn said to his parents:
"I previously had a silver gourd-shaped ornament, along with a lacquered ball, a fragrant pouch, and other things,
which I once hid in a hole of an apricot tree.
I wonder if they are still there?"
He then went with his mother and found them.
His parents realized that Dàn was their former son,
and cherished him more than his elder brothers.
At the age for pursuing learning,
his literary talent was outstanding and elegant.
Later, when he took the imperial examination,
he passed under the tutelage of Fàn Yǔchēng, a Bachelor of the Hànlín Academy.
Dàn’s elder brother was Gǔ.
Wáng È
In the Táng dynasty, there was a Wáng È,
the younger brother of Minister Wáng Jì.
During the turmoil and displacement in the Western Capital,
Jì took his family into Shǔ,
traveling down the Jiālíng River.
When they reached in front of the Bǎitáng Temple in Lìzhōu,
È, then seven years old,
suddenly said:
"I once had a scripture scroll,
hidden inside a stone niche in this temple."
He then had his family follow him,
and they searched and obtained it.
A wooden comb was also still there.
The temple monks said:
"This was our temple boy."
Comparing the year of his premature death
with the birth year of the Wáng family’s son,
it indeed proved true.
His parents from his previous life were still alive.
When he grew up, he served in Shǔ,
attaining the office of Lìnglù.
Monk Dàojié
Xìndū Yuánfāng, a person from Fǔyáng County in Xiàngzhōu,
had high moral integrity from a young age,
and was especially fond of Buddhist scriptures.
At the age of twenty-nine,
he died in the spring, first month, of the fifth year of the Xiǎnqìng era.
Over a month after his death,
his elder brother, the monk Dàojié of the Fǎguān Temple,
unable to cease missing and mourning him,
brought a shaman to his home,
asking to summon Yuánfāng to speak with him.
Dàojié was also quite skilled in magical arts,
so he made a talisman,
summoned Yuánfāng,
and had the shaman ask him about the details.
The shaman was illiterate,
so he had a literate person hold the brush.
The shaman relayed Yuánfāng’s dictation,
producing a letter
for his fellow student Féng Xíngjī,
fully expressing the sentiments of his lifetime,
along with two poems.
For his family as well,
he left a written message.
The writing was coherent and orderly,
the words sorrowful and poignant.
His letters generally urged cultivating merit and virtue,
and advised reciting Buddha’s name and copying scriptures,
considering the karma of killing living beings
to be among the gravest of sins.
Nothing surpasses this.
He also said:
"Yuánfāng did not enter hell,
nor did he fall among hungry ghosts,
all thanks to the arrangements of the underworld officials.
Now I am reborn as a son in the household of Lǐ Rénshī in Shízhōu.
However, because Shí Míngyuǎn of Wúshān County in Lǒngzhōu
prayed for a son at Huà Mountain,
I was transferred to be reborn as a son in the Shí family.
Moreover, the day of my rebirth is approaching,
and in haste, I can no longer stay.
From the second month of conception,
until the twelfth month of birth.
I hope my elder brother and others will extend your compassion.
Please go there to see me."
Having said this,
he wept and departed.
Xuē Dàzào from Hédōng, who resided in Fǔyáng,
and formerly served as the Magistrate of Wúshān County,
said himself
that he fully knew Shí Míngyuǎn.
The monks Huìyǒng and Fǎzhēn of the Zhìlì Temple recounted this.
Yuán Zī
Fùzhōu's Qīngxī Mountain,
is incomparably beautiful.
When Minister Yuán Zī was still obscure,
he lived between Fùzhōu and Yǐngzhōu.
On a clear day, he happened to cross a steep peak,
walked several miles,
and gradually entered a place of secluded wonder and perilous strangeness,
where human footprints rarely reached.
There was a Confucian scholar,
who made his living selling medicine,
and lived there.
Minister Yuán spoke with him,
their conversation became very familiar,
so he stayed overnight.
Then he asked:
"This place should have reclusive immortals,
have you ever interacted with them?"
He replied:
"There are five or six Daoist practitioners,
who come every two or three days,
but I don't know where they live.
Although I am familiar with them,
they won't tell me."
Yuán said:
"I have come to pay my respects,
can I meet them?"
He said:
"They greatly dislike people,
but are quite fond of wine.
If you, sir, obtain a jug of fine wine,
stay here and wait,
you might get to see them."
Minister Yuán left,
obtained wine and brought it,
and waited with it.
After several evenings, they indeed arrived.
The five wore deer-skin caps or gauze hats,
carried wooden staffs and wore straw sandals,
from afar they exchanged greetings,
laughed heartily,
then went to the stream to wash their feet and play.
The Confucian scholar set out wine and arranged seats,
after a short while,
they all entered the thatched cottage,
and seeing the wine were very pleased.
They said:
"Where did you get this?"
After drinking several cups,
the Confucian scholar said:
"I could not have obtained this myself,
a guest brought it,
wishing to pay respects to you immortal brothers."
Then he led Minister Yuán out,
who bowed deeply in succession.
The five looked at each other and lost
their composure,
and regretted drinking this wine,
also angrily said to the Confucian scholar:
"You should not have brought an outsider to disturb us."
The Confucian scholar said:
"This man's sincere intent is commendable,
moreover he is a fellow Daoist,
if you allow him some interaction,
what harm is there!"
Their attitude then gradually softened.
Seeing again that Minister Yuán was very respectful,
they then occasionally spoke and laughed with him.
Looking at Yuán, they said:
"Sit."
Yuán bowed twice and took his seat.
After a short while, half-drunk,
they were quite merry.
Gazing at Minister Yuán,
they said to each other:
"This man greatly resembles the meditating monk from Xīfēng."
After a long while, they said:
"Exactly.
Counting on fingers the days,
this monk passed away forty-seven years ago."
They asked Minister Yuán's age,
exactly forty-seven.
They looked at each other and clapped their hands, saying:
"Go seek an official post,
fortune and prosperity will come,
hereafter you will be extremely wealthy and noble."
Then they called the host to bid farewell,
Minister Yuán bowed,
and the Daoists all shook hands with him.
They crossed the stream and went up the mountain peak,
leaping and jumping,
as if flying birds,
and in a moment were gone.
Cuī Sìbā
Cuī Shènyóu,
initially because he had no sons,
was quite concerned about it.
There was a monk who often visited the Cuī household,
Cuī thus told him,
and asked for a plan.
The monk said:
"Please have your wife dress splendidly and visit the great temples of Cháng'ān,
where there are old monks' courtyards,
then go to them.
If they pay no attention,
go elsewhere.
If one treats her warmly,
you should form a close bond with him,
so as to move his heart,
then after his death he will become your son."
Following his words,
initially they went to three places,
with no attention.
Later they came to one courtyard,
where the monk was nearly sixty years old,
who received them very diligently and attentively,
and Cuī also generously gave alms to him.
From then on, offerings and alms were continuous.
The monk then said:
"I am old,
and feel I have no way to repay you, sir,
I wish to be reborn as your son in my next life."
Not many years later,
the monk died,
and Sìbā was born.
Some say,
the palm lines had the two characters "sēng" (monk).
Mǎ Sīdào
Hóngzhōu medical scholar Mǎ Sīdào,
was critically ill.
Suddenly he sighed and said:
"In my lifetime I never knowingly did evil,
why then am I to become a woman,
now to be reborn at the woman of the Zhū family in Tiáozǐ Lane."
His son tried to find it,
and indeed the woman of that household was pregnant,
so he prepared swaddling clothes and waited.
When Sīdào died, the Zhū woman gave birth,
indeed a girl.
The Intelligent Flower Tree
Lǐ Hóngqīng, styled Zhèngzì,
studied the Dao.
He met Dōngwángfù,
who taught him.
Seventeen years later,
Zhèng
died,
his family buried him in Wǔlíng,
and on his grave grew a flower tree,
seven feet tall.
Anyone who encountered this flower,
became intelligent,
and excelled in literary composition.
The Longing Tree
During the Warring States period of Jìn,
Wèi
suffered from the hardships of Qín's aggression,
and a commoner was conscripted,
garrisoned in Qín and never returned.
His wife longed for him and died,
after she was buried,
a tree grew on her grave,
its branches and leaves all leaned toward where her husband was,
thus it was called the longing tree.
Guǎngchuān King
Guǎngchuān King Qùjí,
enjoyed gathering unscrupulous youths for hunting excursions,
indulging in unrestrained trapping and shooting,
and within his domain, all burial mounds and tombs
were excavated without exception.
Yuán Měng recounted
that his grandfather served as the Commandant of the Guards for the King of Guǎngchuān.
Each time he admonished the king, his advice went unheeded,
so he resigned due to illness and returned home.
He spoke of the tombs excavated by the king,
which were too numerous to count,
with over a hundred being particularly extraordinary.
He told Liú Xiàng about ten or so incidents,
recorded as follows.
The tomb of King Xiāng of Wèi
had an outer coffin made of patterned stone,
about eight feet high,
with a width and depth sufficient to accommodate thirty people.
When touched by hand,
the coffin was smooth and fresh as if new.
Inside were a stone bed and a stone screen,
perfectly intact and well-proportioned.
No traces of the inner coffin or burial objects were seen,
only a jade spittoon on the bed,
two bronze swords,
and various gold utensils, all as if new.
The king took them for himself and wore them.
King Xiāng’s tomb
was sealed with poured iron on top,
and it took three days of chiseling to open it.
A yellow gas like fog
stung the eyes and noses of those who approached, causing discomfort,
making it impossible to enter.
Guards were stationed there,
and after seven days, the gas dissipated.
Upon first reaching the entrance,
there was no door or lock.
A stone bed, four feet square,
had a stone table on top,
with three stone figures standing in attendance on each side,
all wearing military caps and carrying swords.
Entering another chamber,
there was a stone door with a lock.
When knocked open,
the inner coffin was revealed,
emitting a black light that shone on people,
and blades could not penetrate it.
They burned and sawed through it,
only to find it was a coffin made of lacquered rhinoceros hide,
several inches thick,
layered over ten times.
Lacking the strength to open it,
they stopped.
Entering yet another chamber,
again a stone door,
unlocked,
revealed a stone bed,
six feet square.
A stone screen,
and a set of bronze curtain hooks,
some on the bed,
some on the ground.
The curtain fabric had decayed,
and the bronze hooks had fallen off.
On the bed was a stone pillow,
and the dust on the bed was piled very high,
resembling clothing.
On each side of the bed were twenty women,
all standing in attendance.
Some held towels, combs, mirrors, or tweezers,
while others held trays as if serving food.
There were no other unusual objects,
only several hundred iron mirrors.
The tomb of Prince Dànqú of Wèi
was very shallow and narrow,
with no inner coffin,
only a stone bed,
six feet wide,
and ten feet long.
A stone screen.
Beneath the bed was all mica,
and on the bed lay two corpses,
one male and one female,
both around twenty years old,
lying naked with their heads to the east,
without clothing or coverings,
their skin and complexion like that of living people.
Their hair, teeth, and nails
were no different from those of the living.
The king was frightened,
and did not dare to disturb them,
sealing the tomb again as before.
The tomb of Yuán Àng
had a coffin made of pottery tiles,
with no burial objects at all,
only a single bronze mirror.
The tomb of Duke Líng of Jìn
was exceptionally magnificent and grand.
At each of the four corners were stone eagles and dogs,
holding candles.
Over forty stone figures, male and female,
all stood in attendance.
The coffin and burial objects showed no remaining form,
yet the corpse remained uncorrupted,
with gold and jade filling all nine orifices.
The other burial objects
had all decayed beyond recognition.
Only a single jade toad,
as large as a fist,
hollow inside,
capable of holding five ge of water,
remained glossy and fresh as if new.
The king took it to use as a water dropper for writing.
The tomb of Duke Yōu
was very tall and grand.
Once the tomb gate was opened,
it was filled with stone and plaster.
After clearing away over ten feet,
they reached mica.
About a foot deeper,
they found over a hundred corpses,
piled haphazardly on top of each other,
all uncorrupted.
Only one was male,
the rest were female.
Some were sitting, some lying down,
and some standing,
their clothing and appearance
no different from living people.
The tomb of Luán Shū
had coffins and burial objects
completely decayed without a trace.
A white fox cub
was seen, fleeing in fright upon seeing people.
Attendants chased and tried to strike it,
but could not catch it,
only injuring its left foot.
That night,
the king dreamed of a man,
with hair and eyebrows completely white,
who came and said to him:
"Why did you injure my foot?"
He then struck the king’s left foot with a staff.
The king awoke,
his foot swollen, painful, and covered in sores.
From then on, it never healed.
Yuán Ān
When Yuán Ān’s father died,
his mother sent him with a chicken and wine to consult the diviner Gòng about a burial site.
On the way, he encountered three scholars,
who asked Yuán Ān where he was going.
He told them everything.
The scholars said:
"We know of an excellent burial site."
Yuán Ān offered them the chicken and wine as a gift.
After they finished,
they told him the location.
They said:
"If you bury him here,
your family will produce high-ranking nobles for generations."
They then parted ways.
After a few steps, Yuán Ān looked back,
but they had all vanished.
Yuán Ān suspected they were divine beings,
so he buried his father there.
He later rose to become Minister over the Masses,
and his descendants flourished,
with four generations producing five dukes.
Dīng Jī
When Wáng Mǎng held power,
he demoted Dīng Jī’s posthumous title
and opened the door of her outer coffin.
Fire burst forth,
flames reaching forty or fifty feet high.
Officers and soldiers doused it with water to extinguish it,
only then could they enter,
but the burial objects inside were burned.
Nobles, officials, and their sons, along with scholars and foreigners—over a hundred thousand people—
took up tools
to assist the artisans
in leveling the tombs of Prince Gōng’s mother, Empress Dowager Fù, and Dīng Jī.
In twenty days, both were completely leveled.
Thorns were then planted around the site
as a warning to later generations.
It is said:
"At that time,
thousands of swallows
carried earth in their beaks and dropped it into Dīng Jī’s burial pit.
Now her tomb mound
stands tall and lush.
Its corners and curves are well-defined,
surrounded by multiple layers of walls,
with double gates facing outward.
Húnzǐ
In the Kūnmíng Pond there is a burial mound,
commonly called Húnzǐ.
Legend has it that among the former residents there was a son named Húnzǐ,
who often disobeyed his father's words;
if told to go east, he would go north,
if told water, he would say fire.
When his father fell ill and was about to die,
he wished to be buried on a high hill,
but deceitfully said:
"When I die,
you must bury me in the water."
After his death,
Húnzǐ wept and said:
"Today I cannot disobey my father's command again."
Thus he buried him here.
Shèng Hóngzhī's "Jīngzhōu Jì" states:
"Gùchéng faces the Ěr River;
on the northern bank of the river,
there are five maidens' mounds.
During the Western Hàn,
someone was buried north of the Ěr River,
and the tomb was about to be destroyed.
That person had five daughters,
who together built these mounds to protect the tomb."
It also says:
"One daughter married a stubborn son in Yīn County,
whose family wealth amounted to ten thousand gold.
From youth to adulthood,
he never obeyed his father's words.
On his deathbed,
his father intended to be buried on a mountain,
but fearing his son would not comply,
he instead said, 'You must bury me on the shoal beneath the islet.'
The stubborn son said:
'I have never followed my father's teachings,
but today I shall obey this one command.'
Thereupon, he dispersed all his family wealth,
built a stone tomb,
and piled earth around it,
eventually forming an islet,
several hundred paces long.
During the Yuánkāng era,
it began to be destroyed by water.
Now, hundreds of stones, each about half the size of a couch,
remain gathered in the water."
Wáng Càn
When Wèi Wǔ campaigned north against Tàdùn,
he ascended a ridge to gaze into the distance
and saw a hillock where no grass grew.
Wáng Càn said:
"This must be an ancient tomb.
When this person was alive,
he consumed raw yùshí (arsenic ore),
and after death, the stone's vapor emanated outward,
thus scorching and destroying the vegetation."
He immediately ordered it excavated for inspection,
and indeed it was a large tomb,
filled with yùshí throughout the burial chamber.
Another account says
that while in Jīngzhōu,
Wáng Càn ascended Zhāng Mountain with Liú Biǎo
and witnessed this anomaly.
Since Cáo Wǔ's pacification of Wūhuán
occurred while Wáng Càn was still south of the river,
this latter account is likely correct.
Sūn Zhōng
Sūn Zhōng lived in Fùchūn;
he lost his father in childhood
and served his mother with utmost filial piety.
During a year of famine,
he made a living by growing melons.
Suddenly, three youths came to Sūn Zhōng begging for melons,
and he treated them generously.
The three said to him:
"This spot at the foot of the mountain is excellent;
you may be buried here,
and an emperor will emerge.
Walk about a hundred paces down the mountain,
then look back to see us depart;
that will be the burial site."
Sūn Zhōng went thirty or forty paces
and then turned back to look.
He saw the three transform into white cranes and fly away.
Sūn Zhōng remembered the spot,
and after his death, he was buried there.
The site lies east of the county town,
and strange lights often appear over the mound.
They are said to be five-colored
and rise to connect with the sky.
When Sūn Jiān's mother was pregnant with him,
she dreamed her intestines emerged
and coiled around the Wúchāng Gate of Wú.
She told her neighbor's mother about it,
who said:
"How do you know it isn't an auspicious sign!"
Wú Gāng
Near the end of the Huángchū era of Wèi,
people from Wú excavated Wú Ruì's tomb to obtain timber
for erecting a temple to Sūn Jiān in the county.
They saw Wú Ruì's corpse,
its appearance and clothing both as they were in life.
After Wú was pacified,
one of those who had excavated the tomb
met Wú Gāng, the Southern Mán Colonel, in Shòuchūn
and said:
