"Why does your appearance resemble that of Chángshā King Wú Ruì?
Only you are slightly shorter."
Wú Gāng, startled, said:
"He is my ancestor."
From Wú Ruì's death to the opening of the tomb was four hundred years,
and to meeting Wú Gāng
was over forty more years.
Lù Dōngměi
During the Huánglóng era of Wú,
in Hǎiyán, the capital of Wú, there was Lù Dōngměi.
His wife, née Zhū,
was also graceful and beautiful.
Husband and wife respected each other deeply
and were never apart, even for a step.
People of the time called them the "Shoulder-to-Shoulder Couple."
The couple themselves said:
"If we are always like paired wings,
I fear it may not bode well."
Later, the wife died,
and Dōngměi refused to eat, seeking death.
His family pitied him,
so they buried them together.
Within a year,
a catalpa tree grew on their mound,
with a single root and two trunks
that embraced and merged into one tree.
Often, a pair of swans
would roost upon it.
Sūn Quán heard of this and sighed in admiration,
bestowing upon their village the name "Bǐjiān" (Shoulder-to-Shoulder)
and their tomb the name "Shuāngzǐ" (Twin Catalpas).
Later, their son Hóng and his wife, née Zhāng,
though not extraordinary,
also loved and admired each other deeply.
People of Wú again called them the "Little Shoulder-to-Shoulder Couple."
Pān Zhāng
Pān Zhāng was handsome and elegant from a young age,
and many people of his time admired him.
Wáng Zhòngxiān of the state of Chǔ
heard of his fine reputation
and came seeking his friendship.
Zhāng agreed.
They then wished to study together,
and upon meeting, they loved each other
with affection like husband and wife.
They shared the same quilt and pillow,
and their intimacy knew no bounds.
Later, they died together,
and their families, grieving for them,
buried them together on Luófú Mountain.
Suddenly, a tree grew on their mound,
its branches, limbs, and leaves
all intertwined in embrace.
People of the time found it extraordinary
and named it the "Shared Pillow Tree."
Hú Yōng
Hú Yōng of the state of Wú
was a man fond of sensual pleasures.
He married a wife, née Zhāng,
and doted on her, never willing to part.
After she died,
Hú Yōng also passed away.
His family interred them in the rear garden.
Three years later, when they went to bury them properly,
they saw two figures transformed upon the mound,
often seen embracing as when they lay together.
People all laughed at them.
Dài Xī
Dài Xī of Wǔchāng,
came from a poor and humble family,
and his tomb was located south of Fán Mountain.
A diviner said:
"There is royal qi here."
Huán Wēn, bearing his battle-axe and heading west,
stopped in Wǔchāng.
He excavated the tomb,
and found an object,
as large as a water buffalo,
blue-green in color,
with no head or feet.
It occasionally moved,
and would not yield to hacking or stabbing.
So he released it into the river;
upon reaching the water,
it immediately made a sound like thunder,
its roar echoing along the long river.
Dài Xī's descendants later declined and were nearly wiped out.
Wáng Bóyáng
Wáng Bóyáng's home was in Jīngkǒu.
To the east of his residence was a burial mound,
traditionally said to be the tomb of Lǔ Sù.
When the wife of Wáng Bóyáng,
who was the niece of Xī Jiàn's elder brother,
died,
he leveled the tomb to bury her.
Several days later,
while Wáng Bóyáng was sitting in his hall during the day,
he saw a nobleman riding in a sedan chair,
attended by several hundred followers,
with people and horses coming in an endless stream.
From afar, the man said to him:
"I am Lǔ Zìjìng.
Why have you destroyed my tomb?"
Thereupon, he signaled his attendants to drag him from his bed,
and struck him several hundred times with the ring of a knife before leaving.
Wáng Bóyáng lost consciousness and then revived,
and the places where he was struck all developed festering sores.
He died a few days later.
Another account says
that after Wáng Bóyáng died,
his son was preparing the burial site
and found two lacquered coffins,
which he moved to the southern ridge.
That night, he dreamed that Lǔ Sù angrily said:
"I will kill your father."
Soon after, he dreamed again and saw Wáng Bóyáng, who said:
"Lǔ Sù is contending with me over the tomb,
and I cannot find peace day or night."
Later, several shēng of blood were seen on the cushion of the spirit seat,
which was suspected to be due to Lǔ Sù.
The tomb is now located one lǐ east of Chángguǎng Bridge.
Yáng Hù
In the Jìn dynasty, a person who read graves said of Yáng Hù's tomb:
"Later, a ruler who receives the Mandate of Heaven will emerge from here."
Yáng Hù disliked this statement,
so he had the tomb dug and broken to ruin its auspicious features.
The grave-reader said:
"Although the tomb's configuration has been ruined,
it will still produce a Three Excellency with a broken arm."
Soon after, Yáng Hù fell from a horse and broke his arm,
and indeed rose to the position of a Three Excellency.
Lǘqiū Nányáng
At Fěnshuǐkǒu in Fànyáng, there was a tomb
with stone tigers and stone pillars,
called the Tomb of General Wén.
During the Lóng'ān era of Jìn Āndì,
Lǘqiū Nányáng was about to bury his wife beside the tomb.
That evening, several dozen of his attendants
all dreamed someone saying:
"Why endanger others to secure yourself?"
Upon waking, they spoke of it,
and everyone had the same dream.
Although they felt uneasy about it,
they were ashamed to withdraw because of a dream.
When it came time for the burial,
they merely beat drums and blew horns to create an imposing atmosphere.
But then they heard drumbeats, horns, and the clatter of armor from the tomb mound,
drawing closer,
until they reached the tomb,
where three men died at the tomb's entrance.
After the burial,
later on,
Lǘqiū was executed along with his entire clan by Yáng Quánqī.
People all believed it was due to the vengeful spirit of General Wén.
Ancient Multi-layered Tomb
Located fifteen lǐ and two hundred bù north of Wǔlíng County,
it measured fifty bù in circumference,
and was three zhàng high.
The name of the occupant is lost.
According to ancient tradition,
in the past, someone tried to open it
and saw several dozen bronze figures,
their eyes wide open and staring.
Suddenly, they heard drumbeats and loud shouts from within the tomb,
and in the end, did not dare to proceed.
Later, when they looked at the tomb's earth,
it had closed up again as before.
Suí Wáng
The King of Suí of Qí once led his aides and officers
to feast merrily atop the tomb of Fán Jī.
That night,
he dreamed that Fán Jī angrily said:
"Have you no regard for the principle of honoring tombs?
How dare you defile me?
I will make you know."
The next morning,
the king fell ill.
He had shamans perform rituals to confess his fault and make offerings,
and only recovered after many days.
Tomb of the King of Chǔ
In the Southern Qí dynasty, tomb robbers in Xiāngyáng opened the tomb of the King of Chǔ,
and obtained jade slippers, a jade screen, and bamboo slips bound with blue silk.
The robbers used fire to see,
and Wáng Sēngqián saw more than ten slips,
saying:
"This is tadpole script, missing text from the 'Kǎo Gōng Jì' and 'Zhōu Guān'."
Shū Chuò,
a man from Dōngyáng,
was well-versed in antiquity and widely learned,
especially attentive to yīn-yáng principles,
and skilled in reading graves.
Yáng Gōngrén, the Vice Minister of Personnel,
wished to rebury his relatives.
He sought five or six skilled grave-site planners,
all renowned throughout the land,
and housed them in his residence,
where they discussed their craft together,
each disputing the others' views.
Yáng Gōngrén could not determine who was correct,
so he sent someone with slight understanding
galloping to the capital,
to the plain where he intended to bury them.
They took four proposed locations,
each made a record,
noting the directions,
the elevation and topography,
and took one dǒu of soil from each,
sealing them along with the records.
Yáng Gōngrén concealed the records and presented the soil,
ordering the various masters to examine them.
Their selections differed greatly,
and their descriptions of the landforms
contradicted the records.
Shū Chuò then identified one soil sample as suitable for burial,
took up a brush to write a record,
describing the topography of the four sides,
which matched Yáng Gōngrén's record without the slightest discrepancy.
The other masters greatly admired and yielded to him,
and each was given ten bolts of silk before being sent away.
Shū Chuò said:
"At the proposed site,
beyond a depth of five chǐ,
there are five kinds of grain.
If one kind of grain is found,
it will be a blessed land,
ensuring that dukes and marquises will continue for generations without end."
Yáng Gōngrén immediately took Shū Chuò to the capital,
had people dig seven chǐ deep,
and found a cavity,
as large as a five-dàn urn,
containing seven or eight dǒu of millet.
This land had formerly been a millet field,
and ants had carried the millet down into this cavity.
At that time, officials both in court and in the countryside
considered Shū Chuò a sage.
The burial was completed.
He was rewarded with a fine horse,
and two hundred lengths of fabric.
Shū Chuò's marvelous ability
was unmatched in past or present.
Lǐ Délín
Lǐ Délín, the Nèishǐ Lìng of the Suí dynasty,
was a native of Ráoyáng in Shēnzhōu.
He had his son select a burial site east of Ráoyáng city
to relocate and inter his parents.
He then asked about it,
inquiring what the land was like.
The reply was:
"The divination of the site says
that after the burial, eight dukes should emerge.
The land has a village to the east, outer walls to the west,
a road to the south, and a dike to the north."
Lǐ Délín asked:
"What is the name of the village?"
The answer was Wǔgōng (Five Dukes).
Lǐ Délín said:
"Only three dukes remain.
This is fate.
What more can be said?"
So they were buried there.
His son Lǐ Bǎishào,
and grandson Lǐ Ānqī,
both inherited the title of Ānpíng Gōng.
But by the time of his great-grandson,
who joined Xú Jìngyè's rebellion,
the ducal title was cut off.
Hǎo Chùjùn
Táng dynasty's Hǎo Chùjùn
died while serving as Shìzhōng.
After his burial,
a scholar passing by his tomb
sighed and said:
"The burial presses on the dragon's horn.
His coffin will surely be chopped apart."
Later, his grandson Hǎo Xiàngxián,
convicted of heinous crimes,
had Chùjùn's coffin chopped open
and his corpse burned.
Chùjùn's hair roots grew into his skull bone,
his skin clung and hair adhered to the skeleton.
This too was extraordinary hair and unusual bone,
signs of a noble and remarkable man.
Xú Jì
When the Táng dynasty's Duke Yīng, Xú Jì, first had a burial site divined,
the oracle said:
"The Vermilion Bird sings in harmony,
descendants will flourish and prosper."
Zhāng Jǐngcáng heard this
and privately told someone:
"The divination is mistaken.
This is what is called 'The Vermilion Bird grieves in sorrow,
within the coffin ashes will be seen.'"
Later, his grandson Xú Jìngyè rebelled in Yángzhōu.
His younger brother Xú Jìngzhēn, under interrogation, stated:
"When Jìngyè was first born,
beneath the birthing mat,
a turtle was dug up,
said to be an omen of great nobility.
Duke Yīng kept it secret and did not speak of it.
Indeed, there was an omen of great upheaval."
Empress Wǔ Zétiān was enraged,
ordered Duke Yīng's coffin chopped open,
and his corpse burned.
Thus the "ashes" prophecy was fulfilled.
Wéi Ānshí
During the Shénlóng era,
a geomancer, the monk Hóng Shī,
was on good terms with Wéi Ānshí.
He once said to Ānshí:
"This humble monk recently saw a plot of land near Fèngqī Yuán,
over twenty mǔ in size,
with the form of a dragon rising and falling.
Whoever is buried in this land
will surely see generations hold high ministerial office."
Ānshí said:
"This old man has a separate estate
south of the city.
When I have leisure,
I will accompany you, Master, to that site,
and ask its price.
To wander together through woods and springs
would also be a pleasure."
Ānshí's wife heard of this
and said to him:
"You are a great minister to the Son of Heaven.
Master Hóng understands the arts of yīn-yáng and numerology.
How can you suddenly sneak off to wander the outskirts,
and moreover buy burial land?
I fear unforeseen disaster may arise."
Ānshí became afraid
and stopped the plan.
Hóng sighed and said:
"The State Lady's insight and foresight
are beyond what this humble monk can match.
If you, Sir, wish to buy the land,
you need not go personally."
The Lady said:
"To truly understand its meaning,
you should also not buy the land at all."
Ānshí said:
"My younger brother Wéi Tāo
has a middle-aged son who died young and is not yet buried.
He could buy this land instead."
Hóng said:
"If your worthy brother obtains this land,
he will not attain the rank of general or minister.
His position will stop at that of a chief minister."
Later, Tāo indeed bought that land
and buried his middle-aged son there.
Tāo later became Tàicháng Qīng and Lǐyí Shǐ,
and died in office.
Yuán Qiányào
Master Hóng, returning from the eastern capital Luòyáng,
said to Zhāng Yuè:
"To the left of the Quēmén road, there is a very auspicious plot of land.
You, Sir, should try to request leave for two or three days.
When the various officials come,
this humble monk will observe from behind a curtain those with exceptionally noble physiognomy
and assign them this land."
Yuè did as he said,
requested two days' leave,
and all the court officials gathered.
Hóng said:
"Some are already noble,
and great fortune does not come twice.
Others are unsuited to this land;
for them, it would instead bring disaster."
When the Investigating Censor Yuán Qiányào arrived,
Hóng said to Yuè:
"This man's nobility matches yours, Sir.
Try summoning him,
and find a suitable way to give him this."
Yuè summoned Qiányào and spoke with him.
Yuán said:
"My family's main burial ground is at Quēmén,
but my ancestors have not yet been interred there.
I am now requesting leave to return to Luòyáng
to attend to the distant rites for my ancestors.
That is why I came to bid farewell."
Yuè fully related Hóng's words,
saying it would be especially good if they traveled together.
Yuán declined, citing family poverty and inability to manage this,
saying he dared not trouble the Master to accompany him.
Later, Hóng again passed by Quēmén
and saw the land had already become the Yuán family's tomb.
Returning, he said to Yuè:
"Heaven aids the Yuán family.
Places that should be low were originally high,
but now are low;
places that should be high were originally low,
but now are high.
The placement of the tomb and the missing corner of the mountain gate
were all done by the builder.
Asked the price,
it was bought on credit.
Asked who performed the burial divination,
it was a village man.
Asked his method,
he relied on a vulgar almanac.
Yet the layout was naturally just so in every detail.
The Yuán family's sons will achieve great nobility."
Qiányào rose from Capital Governor to become Chancellor,
serving as Shìzhōng for nearly twenty years.
Yáng Zhīchūn
During the Kāiyuán era,
a rumor suddenly spread that there was a rigid man who had been in the ground for a thousand years.
Due to the collapse of his tomb,
the rigid man revived,
not eating the five grains,
but only drinking water and breathing air.
Some people at the time called him an earth immortal,
while others called him a fraud.
He was said to know much about the accumulation of gold and jade underground,
and he liked to travel between Wú, Chǔ, Qí, and Lǔ.
There were two thieves
who, taking advantage of the rigid man's words,
gathered a gang of ten ruffians
to excavate tombs in Háo and Shòu.
When they reached the boundary of Shèngtáng County,
they opened a tomb
that was then called the White Reed Tomb.
After digging one zhàng deep,
they found the tomb had four chambers.
The eastern chamber was filled with weapons:
bows, arrows, spears, and blades—
all kinds were fully prepared.
The southern chamber was filled with silk fabrics,
with compartments in the middle.
All were brocade and damask,
with a plaque above that read:
"Three hundred bolts of brocade bestowed by King Yí of Zhōu."
The lower compartment
was filled with gold and jade vessels.
The western chamber was filled with lacquerware,
as new as if made yesterday.
The northern chamber contained a jade coffin,
inside which was a jade maiden,
lifelike as if alive.
Her hair was thick and straight,
her teeth white like arranged shells,
her figure plump yet slender, neither too tall nor too short—perfectly proportioned,
as if painted in a plain sketch.
She wore purple robes,
embroidered socks and pearl shoes,
with a fresh fragrance that was delightful.
When touched with the hand,
her body felt warm.
In front of the jade coffin,
there was a silver wine vessel,
full.
The ruffians competed to drink from it,
finding it sweet and fragrant, like the taste of the finest wine in the mortal world.
Each took the brocade, fabrics, and treasures.
On the jade maiden's left ring finger was a jade ring,
which the thieves struggled to remove.
One thief, named Yáng Zhīchūn, said:
"Why must we take this?
We already have plenty of treasures."
After a long time, it still could not be removed,
so they competed to cut off her finger with a knife.
Blood flowed from the finger,
like red bean juice.
Zhīchūn said:
"This is most unkind.
If you cannot redeem the object,
you end up cutting off her finger—
how painful!"
When the thieves emerged from the tomb,
they suspected Zhīchūn of deceit,
and all wanted to kill him.
The moment they raised their knives,
they no longer recognized each other,
and the nine men hacked at one another,
all dying.
Zhīchūn alone survived.
He then returned the plundered items to the tomb,
covered them with earth, and left.
Zhīchūn went to the authorities,
confessing the situation himself.
The officials sent over twenty soldiers to repair it.
They also searched for an epitaph,
but ultimately could not find it.
Táng Yáochén
and Zhāng Shīlǎn were skilled in divining tombs,
and the disciple Wáng Jǐngchāo inherited their craft.
During the Kāiyuán era,
Táng Yáochén died in Zhèngzhōu,
and Shīlǎn had Jǐngchāo select a burial site.
After the burial,
the six domestic animals and others of the Táng household could all speak,
cursing:
"What kind of insect-dogs
buried me in such a place?"
The family was terrified,
and hastily moved the tomb.
The strange occurrences then ceased.
Chén Sīyīng,
originally named Yùxiū,
was from Lóngpíng, Fúzhōu.
In his youth, he lived in his hometown,
aspiring to be erudite.
During the Kāiyuán era,
a guest sought lodging.
Yùxiū found the guest remarkable,
and treated him generously.
The next day, as the guest was about to leave,
he said:
"I understand geomancy,
and wish to repay you.
From afar, I observed the terrain of Shànglǐ in this prefecture—
it is noble beyond words.
Burying there will surely bring blessings to your descendants."
Yùxiū was delighted,
and went with him to inspect the location.
The guest said:
"If you bury here,
you can be commandery governors for generations."
He then pointed to another spot and said:
"If you use this,
you can be a military governor for one generation."
Yùxiū thanked him.
After a few years,
his parents passed away.
He then buried them in the military governor's spot as indicated.
One day, while paying respects at the tomb,
he suddenly saw many golden bamboo shoots growing from the ground,
so he picked them and returned home.
When he went again,
golden bamboo shoots had grown once more.
By the time the mourning period ended,
he had obtained a great deal.
He then took them to the capital,
using schemes to offer bribes.
Supplementing with his own efforts,
he achieved considerable fame and success.
Later, there was a clansman named Sīyīng,
who gave him his previous official appointment documents.
Yùxiū thus changed his name and sought favor with the authorities.
After some time,
he was appointed Military Governor of Guìzhōu.
Today, the wall records fully list his name,
and there are also descendants who serve in the same commandery.
The Slave Official's Tomb
In Cuó County, there is a Slave Official's Tomb from the Later Hàn.
Initially,
villagers farmed beside it,
and every autumn harvest,
the fields near the tomb would lose many ears of grain, failing to ripen.
After several years,
they were troubled by this.
Later, they often went at night to watch.
They saw four large geese
emerge from the tomb,
eat the grain,
and immediately go back in when chased.
The villagers had long heard that the Slave Official's Tomb contained treasures,
so they banded together to open it.
Upon first entering the passageway,
they saw geese
flapping their wings and attacking people.
The thieves struck back with clubs,
and they ceased moving.
They were bronze geese.
Gradually entering the outer hall,
they obtained two precious swords,
and many other vessels they could not identify.
Next, they reached the main treasury,
where the water was deep.
A person in purple robes stood blocking the door,
fighting with the thieves.
The thieves all rushed forward to attack in turn,
and that person charged through them and ran out.
He entered the county town, shouting loudly:
"Thieves are robbing my tomb!"
The gatekeeper asked:
"Where is your tomb?"
He replied:
"It is precisely the Slave Official's Tomb."
The county magistrate sent village heads to pursue the thieves,
and they were all captured.
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
the Prefect of Míngzhōu presented over thirty such items.
Lú Huàn
Huangmén Shìláng Lú Huàn.
Was the governor of Míng,
Prefecture.
In the county of Wēngshān under his jurisdiction,
the valleys were remote and uninhabited,
and there had once been tomb robbers.
It was said:
'At first,
they saw patterned bricks in the wheel ruts,
so they lifted them,
and knew,
it was an ancient tomb.
Then they gathered ten men.
They submitted a petition to the county,
requesting to reside by the roadside,
and the county permitted it.
They then planted hemp,
so that outsiders could not see,
and exerted all their strength to excavate.
Entering the tunnel,
they gradually reached the burial chamber,
where there were three stone doors,
all sealed with iron.
The robbers could recite incantations beforehand,
so they purified themselves and approached.
When the day came,
two doors opened.
Inside each door were several hundred bronze figures and bronze horses,
holding spears and shields,
their craftsmanship exquisite.
The robbers purified themselves for another three days,
and the middle door opened halfway.
A person in yellow emerged and said:
"The Hàn Dynasty's Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn Liú,
has sent me to inform you,
that he had great military achievements in life,
and upon his death,
was ordered to have his tomb guarded,
and bronze figures and horses were cast,
to resemble the ceremonial guards of his lifetime.
I reckon you have come here,
seeking wealth and goods,
but the chamber where he rests,
truly contains no other treasures.
Moreover, official burials do not inter precious goods,
why must you insist on invading with divine incantations?
If you do not cease,
it will inevitably lead to mutual harm."
After speaking, he went back inside,
and the door closed as before.
They recited incantations for several more days without stopping,
the door opened,
and a person in blue emerged again to relay a message.
The robbers did not listen.
Suddenly, both door leaves swung open,
a great flood surged out,
and all the robbers drowned.
One robber, able to swim, escaped,
tied himself up, and went to the authorities,
fully recounting the whole story.
Huàn ordered the tomb to be inspected again,
inside the middle door was a stone bed,
with a skull resting on it.
The water had surged,
and it was already half-hanging off the bed.
They then resealed the two doors,
and blocked the tunnel.
Zhào Dōngxī
Huáyīn Tàishǒu Zhào Dōngxī,
his ancestors' graves were in Gǔchéng County.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
he intended to have his parents buried together there.
When opening his father's tomb,
tree roots had grown thick and entwined,
surrounding his father's coffin,
suspending it in the air.
He then did not dare to open it further.
He placed his mother's coffin beside it,
sealed the tomb, and returned.
Xuānchéng Tàishǒu Diāo Miǎn,
reburied both his parents,
Miǎn also placed his mother's coffin beside it,
and sealed the tomb,
and later his family line flourished.
Dōngxī had seven brothers,
all were scholars,
renowned in their time,
four attained positions of two thousand shí.
Miǎn served three times as a general,
and halberds were displayed at his gate.
In the twentieth year of Kāiyuán.
In Wànnián, there was a person,
after his father died,
the family gradually became wealthy,
so they buried the mother,
The father's coffin was also entwined,
and could not be untangled.
The person then cut them with a knife,
the roots all bled,
and so they buried him.
Soon after, the family's fortunes slightly declined,
and they all died out.
Dīng Yǒngxīng
South of Gāotáng County was the Xiānbēi City,
it was traditionally said the Xiānbēi paid court to Yān,
and feasted in this city.
Beside it was the tomb of Dào Zhí,
the tomb was extremely large and tall,
and thieves often secretly prayed there.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
the county magistrate Dīng Yǒngxīng,
had a group of bandits robbing within his jurisdiction.
Xīng then secretly sent people to watch beside the tomb,
and indeed there were worshippers,
so they arrested them and took them to the county,
and executed them according to law.
After that, worshippers largely ceased.
The "Huáng Lǎn" says Dào Zhí's tomb is in Hédōng.
According to records, Dào Zhí died in Dōnglíng,
this place was anciently named Dōngpínglíng,
so it is suspected this is near it.
Yán Ānzhī
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
Yán Ānzhī was the Wànnián County bandit-capturing officer.
At noon,
a palace envoy in yellow rode a horse,
and galloped in through the gate.
He proclaimed an edict:
"The tomb of a certain princess ten lǐ south of the city,
has been seen robbed by bandits.
You are ordered to go capture them,
and not let any escape."
Ānzhī immediately led his subordinates with tools and weapons,
to surround and capture them.
They saw six or seven people,
just then digging a tunnel,
only reaching the passageway,
and captured them all at once.
Ānzhī ordered a search for the palace envoy but could not find him,
so he pondered and said:
"The bandits had just opened the tomb,
how did the Son of Heaven know of it?"
At the county office,
he summoned all the bandits,
and interrogated them about the matter.
The bandits said:
"As soon as we opened the tomb,
we immediately sensed something strange,
and knew we would certainly fail.
At the first door,
there were several tomb figurine edict-bearers,
in yellow riding horses.
One inside held,
a whip,
looking as if running,
the ends of his headcloth also stood straight as if blown by wind,
from the eyebrows and eyes onward,
all seemed to be moving.
We then knew we would certainly fail."
Ānzhī then recalled the appearance of the previous edict-bearer,
it was those two tomb figurine edict-bearers.
Nǚwā Tomb
On the riverbank at the Tóngguān Pass,
there were several trees,
even when the water rose violently,
they would not float away or submerge.
People of the time called it the Nǚwā Tomb.
In the fifth month of the thirteenth year of Táng Tiānbǎo,
due to a great wind, it disappeared from its location.
In the sixth month of the second year of Qiányuán,
Guózhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Jìnguāng reported:
"On the first of this month,
near the riverbank,
suddenly wind and thunder were heard.
At dawn, a tomb mound was seen surging forth,
above it were two willow trees,
below a large stone,
each willow over a zhàng tall."
Lǐ Miǎo
Liǔ Yàn's assistant Liǔ Miǎo
had an estate in Gāolíng.
A tenant farmer on the estate owed back rent,
accumulated over five or six years.
Miǎo, having been dismissed from his post, returned to the estate
and was about to reprimand him,
when he saw the granaries and storehouses full and fine,
and the rent payment still not completed.
Miǎo, puzzled, asked about it.
The tenant said in full:
"I have long been a tomb robber.
Recently, I heard of an ancient grave mound.
The mound lies ten lǐ west of the estate,
extremely tall and large.
Going two hundred paces into a pine forest,
one reaches the tomb.
Beside the tomb there was a stone stele,
broken and fallen in the grass,
its characters worn away and illegible.
Initially, we dug dozens of zhàng to the side
and encountered a stone door,
sealed with iron mortar.
For many days we drenched it with dung and filth
before it opened.
When it opened,
arrows shot out like rain,
killing several men.
The crowd, terrified, wanted to flee.
I judged there was nothing else,
it must be a mechanical trap.
So I ordered them to throw stones inside.
Each time a stone was thrown,
arrows would shoot out.
After throwing over ten stones,
the arrows
ceased to fire.
Thereupon, we lit torches and entered in a line.
Upon reaching and opening the inner door,
there were several dozen wooden figures
with glaring eyes and brandishing swords,
injuring several more men.
The crowd struck them with clubs,
and their weapons all fell.
On the four walls were painted images of guards.
On the southern wall was a large lacquered coffin,
suspended by iron chains,
with gold, jade, pearls, and gems piled beneath it.
The crowd was afraid
and did not immediately plunder it.
Suddenly, from the two corners of the coffin, a soughing wind arose,
and sand blew against people's faces.
In a short while, the wind grew fierce,
and sand poured out like a torrent,
submerging us up to the ankles.
The crowd, terrified, retreated and fled.
By the time we got out,
the door was already blocked.
One man was again buried and killed by the sand.
So together we poured a libation on the ground to apologize
and swore not to rob graves."
The "Shuǐ Jīng" says that King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè had his capital at Lángyá
and wanted to move Yóu Cháng's grave mound.
Wind arose within the mound,
flying sand shot at people,
and they could not approach,
so he stopped.
According to the Hàn Jiù Yí,
when constructing a tomb, within a square zhàng inside,
outside are set hidden crossbows, hidden fire arrows, and sand.
It seems ancient regulations had such mechanisms.
Jiǎ Dān
Jiǎ Dān was within the region of Huázhōu.
There was a drought.
Dān summoned two generals and said to them:
"This year there is famine.
I trouble you two to save the people."
They both said:
"If it benefits the army and the prefecture,
we would not decline even death."
Dān smiled and said:
"You could condescend to act as swift couriers.
Tomorrow,
there will be two riders
wearing deep crimson clothes.
The horses they ride
have foreign gait and long manes.
They will pass through the market and leave the city.
You can follow them.
Note where they disappear.
Then my affair will be accomplished."
The two generals then packed rations,
dressed in black clothes,
and searched for them.
Sure enough, there were two men in crimson clothes.
They passed through the market and traveled over two hundred lǐ into the wilds,
disappearing near a large grave mound.
So they piled stones to mark the spot
and returned after two nights.
Dān was greatly pleased.
He mobilized several hundred men,
prepared baskets and spades,
and went with the two generals to excavate the mound.
They obtained several hundred thousand hú of stored grain.
People ultimately could not fathom it.
Zhāng Shì
Zhāng Shì was orphaned young.
Following his father's dying wish,
he was to be buried in Luòjīng.
At that time, Zhōu Shìlóng understood topography
and was considered of the same class as Guō Pú and Qīng Wū.
Shì went with him to the outer wilds.
They surveyed for three days without success
and stayed overnight in a village house.
It was winter and cold.
Inside the room there was only one bed.
Shì then slept on the ground,
while Shìlóng occupied the bed to rest.
Shìlóng could not sleep late into the night.
Shì, wearing extra clothes, hugged the stove and slept.
Suddenly, he cried out in a nightmare:
"Qìngjiā."
Shìlóng immediately called to him.
Shì himself was unaware.
After a long time, he fell asleep again.
Again he cried out in a nightmare:
"Qìngjiā."
Shìlóng called to him again.
Shì also did not know what he had said.
At dawn,
he went with Shìlóng again.
They went south of the village.
To the south was an earthen hill.
Shìlóng halted his horse and gazed into the distance, saying:
"The energy and form are exceptionally good."
Then he and Shì walked for a long time.
To the south, a villager was cutting wood.
Seeing Shìlóng from afar examining the land,
he shouldered his axe and hurried over, saying:
"Are you gentlemen perhaps selecting a burial site?
This land is owned by my qìngjiā.
What about it?
Then I ask to lead you there."
Shìlóng said to Shì:
"Last night you cried out twice in dreams,
both times saying 'qìngjiā.'
Could this not be proof of divine predetermination!"
So they divined and buried him there.
And Shì's family for generations was pure and noble.
Fán Zé
Fán Zé served as the military governor of Xiāngyáng.
There was a patrol officer named Zhāng.
His father had been the military commissioner of Yōngguǎn,
and was buried several tens of lǐ north of Dèngzhōu.
Zhāng had two elder brothers,
and one night they all dreamed of their father, who said:
"My burial tomb was robbed on such-and-such night.
The robbers took the grave goods,
and today they entered the city,
stopping at the Xímào Market.
You must go quickly and capture them.
After sunrise,
it will be too late."
The Zhāng brothers rose in the night,
and tearfully told each other of the dream.
Before dawn,
they knocked on the city gate,
saw Fán Zé,
and fully reported the matter.
He immediately summoned the chief military police officer,
and ordered the arrest.
Six accomplices,
along with the robber chief's wife, were all captured.
Fán Zé had them brought in,
and questioned them face-to-face, saying:
"Was there anything unusual about your robbing this tomb?"
The robber said:
"Regarding today's events,
I have nothing to hide.
It must be that I am being punished by divine principle.
My wife and I have been in the business of tomb-robbing for over ten years.
Every time we robbed a tomb,
my wife and I would bring wine and light a fire,
while the rest of the gang opened the tomb.
When we reached the coffin lid,
my wife and I would take turns toasting
with the deceased.
I would drink a cup myself,
and say:
'Guest, have a cup.'
Then I would pour wine into the mouth of the deceased,
saying,
'Host, drink a cup.'
Then my wife would drink a cup all around,
and then say, 'Where does the wine money come from?'
My wife would reply,
'The host pays for the wine.'
Then we would take the grave goods, treasures, and such.
Yesterday when I opened this tomb,
I saw the person in the coffin wearing purple robes and a jade belt,
looking as if alive.
I followed the ritual and drank wine,
and when I poured the wine saying,
'Host, have a cup,'
as soon as I finished speaking,
the deceased laughed.
We were terribly frightened,
and helped him up,
but he was only dry bones.
Then we undid his belt,
and the deceased cried out,
'Slowly!
My back hurts.'
We were all terrified,
and fled out.
Since then, my spirit has been confused and troubled,
and I knew we would surely be caught."
They were all executed.
Several days later,
Dèngzhōu reported the incident.
The Tomb of Duke Jǐng of Qí
Northeast of Bèiqiū County is the tomb of Duke Jǐng of Qí.
In recent times, someone opened it.
Going down three zhàng,
they found a goose in a stone casket.
The goose turned its wings and brushed against the stone.
Going down another zhàng,
a blue vapor rose up,
looking like pottery smoke from a distance.
When birds flew over it,
they would fall dead.
So they dared not enter further.
Guō Yì
Guō Yì, an army officer of Lùzhōu,
had previously been the pastoral commissioner of Hándān Commandery.
Because his elder brother died,
he entered Yùnzhōu,
and moved his ancestors' remains,
planning to bury them together in Fǔyáng, Cízhōu.
The county borders mountains,
and the soil contains many stones.
When someone with strength died,
they would jointly chisel a stone cave.
The site chosen by Guō Yì
was also chiseled.
That day, the work was doubled,
and suddenly they broke through into a cave.
In the cave was a stone,
about four chǐ long.
Its shape was like a house gecko,
with limbs, head, and tail all complete.
The workers accidentally broke it,
and Guō Yì considered it a bad omen.
He wanted to choose another site,
and reported it to Liú Cóngjiàn,
but Cóngjiàn did not permit it,
so he buried them there.
Over a month later,
Guō Yì fell into a latrine,
nearly dying.
Over twenty of his family members and slaves died one after another.
From then on, he was often terrified,
restless in sleep and waking,
so he submitted a request to resign his post.
Cóngjiàn, due to the duties of the chief bailiff Jiāo Chángchǔ,
exchanged positions with Guō Yì.
When Liú Zhěn
raised troops in rebellion,
Guō Yì was a chief leader.
When the army was defeated, he was beheaded.
All members of his household, young and old, threw themselves into a well to die.
Zhèng Bīnyú, an aide of Yánzhōu, said
the stone house gecko is now kept in the official treasury of Cízhōu.
The Earthen Coffin of Shòu'ān
South of Shòu'ān is a very steep earthen peak.
In the beginning of the Qiánníng era,
it collapsed due to rain.
Halfway up the cliff was an earthen coffin,
with wood beneath the coffin,
spanning horizontally.
The wood turned to dust upon exposure to wind,
but the earthen form remained solid.
The county magistrate washed it,
and the mud dissolved into a watery powder,
greasy and wax-yellow.
Opening its belly,
faintly revealed skeletal remains.
Upon inquiring about recent times,
there was no record of using earth to make a full-body container.
Historical records say,
the Xiàhòu clan used earthen surrounds for burials,
probably from that time.
Lǐ Sīgōng
In the third year of Qiánníng, bǐngchén,
Lǐ Sīgōng, military governor staff officer and prefect of Shǔzhōu, buried his younger brother in the first house west of the north gate inside Jǐnpǔ Lane of Chéngdū,
west of and adjacent to the Lǐ Bīng Temple.
North of the house,
the terrain gradually rose,
with a ridge running southwest,
connecting to the temple.
North of the hall,
digging five or six chǐ into the ground,
they found a large tomb,
with very solid brickwork.
Outside the bricks, they found several dozen gold coins,
each weighing seventeen or eighteen zhū,
about one cun seven or eight fēn in diameter,
round and without holes.
Two fēn from the edge,
there was a faintly raised circle,
and inside the circle on both sides,
were twenty-one characters each.
The edge was very thin,
and sharp like a blade.
The work supervisor rushed two of them to report to Sīgōng,
who sent a messenger to the mountain retreat of Yúnxī Shān in Qīngchéng to show them to the Daoist priest Dù Guāngtíng.
He said:
"These coins would amount to over a shí."
Sīgōng ordered the gold coins to be reburied,
but it was unknown whose tomb it was.
About a hundred paces north of the site,
there is a stone bamboo shoot,
indicating the stone bamboo shoot was the gate pillar of this tomb.
From then on, it became very numinous,
and people dared not violate it.
Later, the ruler of Shǔ changed it to a temple and made offerings there.
Wǔ Yú
More than twenty li east of Ānzhōu City,
there is a large tomb.
A group of robbers excavated it,
and it took several days to open.
They obtained over a hundred gold hairpins,
totaling one hundred jin in weight.
There was a stone pedestal,
and many ancient belts adorned with various treasures were arrayed upon it.
When they took one of the belts,
water immediately gushed forth,
filling the tomb in a short while.
The place they had opened
then sealed itself shut.
The robbers offered two hairpins
to present to Prefect Wǔ Yú.
That night, he dreamed of a person in ancient attire,
with a great many attendants,
who came to visit him and said:
"I am the Southern Barbarian Lord Wǔ.
A group of robbers has damaged my dwelling.
As you share my surname,
I wish for you to repair it.
The robbers will go mad,
do not apprehend them."
He then ordered the repairs.
More than thirty robbers
all went mad at the same time,
and they died one after another.
The Tomb of Prince Cáo
In the year Yǐhài of the Yǒngpíng era,
it was said that people from Kāifēng opened the tomb of Prince Cáo Gāo,
taking stone figures, sheep, horses, bricks, and the like.
They saw his coffin intact,
but it turned to dust at the touch,
leaving no trace of bones,
with only a few gold items remaining.
In front of the coffin was a cast silver basin,
three chi wide,
filled with water.
In the center sat a jade infant,
three chi tall,
and the water never diminished.
This corresponds to what Master Hóng said:
If a tomb contains jade,
the grass and trees will be warm and moist;
if it contains much gold,
the grass and trees will be scorched and withered.
Since Prince Cáo's time after the Zhēnyuán era,
over two hundred years had passed,
yet the basin's water did not decrease—
such is the moisture of jade.
Hán Jiàn
When Hán Jiàn's mother died,
he sought a burial site.
A geomancer said:
"There is only one spot
where you can place great wealth,
but it will soon scatter.
Within Huázhōu's borders,
there is no place better than this."
So Hán Jiàn buried his mother there.
The following year,
the imperial carriage arrived on a visit.
People from all over the land
flocked there without exception.
Hán Jiàn then broadly collected commercial taxes,
and after two years,
he had nine million strings of cash.
Another three years later,
it was all taken by the Zhū Liáng regime.
Xià Shì of Hǎilíng
In the year Wùxū,
Hǎilíng County was made a commandery, expanding the city,
encroaching upon people's graves.
There was a merchant named Xià,
whose ancestors had been salt traders.
Their tomb was west of the city,
and Xià relocated his ancestor's remains.
It had been a hundred and ten years,
but upon opening the coffin,
only white bones remained,
while the clothing and artifacts
were all as fresh as new,
undamaged and unstained.
There was a red brocade quilt,
with particularly extraordinary patterns.
Xià was then poor,
so he took and sold them all,
and people vied to buy them at good prices.
As for the other graves,
though not as old,
they had all decayed.
Péng Shì of Lúlíng
A man from Lúlíng named Péng
buried his father.
A geomancer, divining the site, said:
"Bury him here,
and your family will produce regional governors and commandery administrators for generations."
Péng followed his advice.
When they dug the pit,
the geomancer said:
"Do not dig deeper than nine chi."
After a while,
the geomancer briefly rested elsewhere,
and the laborers dug over a zhang deep.
Suddenly, a white crane emerged from the ground
and flew into the clouds.
The geomancer lamented with regret and left.
Nowadays, among Péng's descendants,
some serve as county magistrates.
Wǔyí Mountain
On Wǔyí Mountain in Jiànzhōu,
sometimes on windy and rainy evenings,
the sounds of people, horses, flutes, and pipes are heard.
By dawn,
a coffin is seen on the cliff face,
containing a section of shin bone.
The locals call it the immortal's bone-changing casket.
In recent times, someone ventured deep into a remote ravine
and looked down to see a casket,
inscribed on top:
"The third daughter of Master Dyer Zhāng, inside Cháojīng Gate, Rùnzhōu."
A curious person noted this.
Later, going to Rùnzhōu,
he indeed found Zhāng's residence.
They said:
"The third daughter died unmarried,
several years ago."
They opened her grave,
and the coffin was empty.
Lín Zànyáo
In the year Bǐngwǔ,
Lín Zànyáo, a vice general of Zhāngzhōu, killed the supervising eunuch envoy,
seized the commandery,
and fortified a mountain cliff as his camp.
While digging the ground,
they found an ancient grave,
the coffin and outer coffin both decayed.
Inside was a woman,
her clothing and appearance as if alive,
her whole body still warm.
The soldiers took her gold and silver hairpins and rings,
and discarded the corpse.
They opened another grave,
and upon opening the coffin,
saw a person with disheveled hair covering the face,
crouching inside the coffin.
The soldiers were terrified,
and several died from fright.
Lín Zànyáo was eventually executed.
Soldiers Under Zhāng Shào
In the year Bǐngwǔ,
when the Jiāngnán army besieged Liú'ān,
military discipline was lax.
Soldiers excavated graves
to take valuables,
and the generals could not stop them.
Two soldiers under supervising army envoy Zhāng Kuāngshào
excavated a grave south of the city,
obtaining a coconut shell cup,
which they presented to Kuāngshào.
They said:
"When we opened this grave,
and opened the coffin,
we saw a person in green clothes with a face like a living person,
and were too afraid to violate it.
There were no other treasures in the tomb,
only this cup."
After returning to camp,
the green-clad person was already sitting in their quarters,
appearing several times a day,
which greatly disturbed them.
Within a day or two,
both soldiers died in battle.
The Grave at Mǎ Huáng Gǔ
South of Ānzhōu City at Mǎ Huáng Gǔ, to the left of a grave is a large tomb.
The coffin and outer coffin had decayed,
leaving only a skull,
three chi long.
Zuǒ Péng of Chén
personally saw it.
Qín Jìnchóng
In the yǐmǎo year of the Xiǎndé era of the Later Zhōu,
the false Liánshuǐ military commissioner Qín Jìnchóng,
while repairing the city walls,
uncovered an ancient tomb.
The inner and outer coffins had both decayed,
and he obtained several ancient coins and a broken bronze mirror.
He also found a vase,
inside which was another vase,
with a yellow body and black inscriptions,
written in clerical script, saying:
"A pair of black birds,
flying to the five liang's head.
I ask how light or heavy the boat is,
to send a letter to Yángzhōu."
The following year,
when the Zhōu army attacked Wú,
Jìnchóng died in battle.
Hé Wén
Wáng Zhāoyuǎn, a man of Shǔ,
in the wùwǔ year, was appointed as the Commissioner for Border Patrol.
When he reached Wénzhōu,
he encountered soldiers clamoring and gathering.
Upon inquiry,
he was told that inside an old tomb there was a corpse that had not decayed.
Some had thrown bricks or stones at it,
and it made a clanging sound.
Zhāoyuǎn went to see,
and observed that its form and substance were solemn,
as if newly deceased.
Inside the tomb, a stone tablet was found, stating:
"Hé Wén, former Cavalry and Infantry Commander of Wénzhōu of the Táng dynasty,
aged fifty-eight,
died on the fifth day of the fifth month in the xīnwèi year of the Dàzhōng era (851 CE),
and was buried here."
Zhāoyuǎn performed a sacrificial offering,
then ordered the tomb to be resealed.
He also had a stone inscription carved beside the tomb to commemorate it.
Lǐ Sī
At the end of the Zhōu dynasty,
someone excavated a tomb and obtained a square jade stone,
on which eighty characters were inscribed.
At that time, no one could recognize them,
so it was stored in the imperial library.
By the time of the Qín dynasty,
Lǐ Sī recognized eight of the characters,
which said:
"Heaven issues its mandate,
the sovereigns take turns as kings."
By the Hàn dynasty,
Shūsūn Tōng recognized two more characters.
Xiàhóu Yīng
Xiàhóu Yīng of the Hàn dynasty was enfeoffed as the Duke of Téng for his merits.
When he died and was about to be buried,
before reaching the tomb,
the carriage and horses halted and would not advance.
People were sent to dig at the spot,
and they discovered a stone chamber.
Inside the chamber was an inscription that read:
"This fine city, lush and dense,
after three thousand years sees the white sun.
Alas, Duke of Téng shall dwell in this chamber!"
Thus, the burial site was changed accordingly.
Zhāng Ēn
During the Tiāncì era of the Later Wèi dynasty,
Zhāng Ēn of Hédōng illicitly excavated the tomb of Tāng.
He obtained a record that said:
"Two thousand years after my death,
I shall be troubled by Ēn."
Ēn obtained ancient bells and chime stones,
but threw them all into the river.
This is also separately recorded in the Shèngxián Chéngzhǒng Jì.
Gāo Liúzhī
Gāo Liúzhī of the Later Wèi dynasty
served as the Governor of Xúzhōu.
While diverting the waters of the Hūtuó River to encircle the city,
he damaged an ancient tomb.
An inscription was found, stating:
"Three hundred years after my death,
a flowing spring shall rise beneath my back.
Fortunately, I shall encounter Gāo Liúzhī,
who will move me to the high plain."
Liúzhī then had inner and outer coffins and burial garments made,
took the remains, and reburied them elsewhere.
Gāo Xiǎnluò
South of the Dàtǒng Temple in Luòyáng,
was the residence of Gāo Xiǎnluò, an official clerk of the Sāngōng.
Xiǎnluò often saw a red light moving in front of the hall at night,
and this occurred more than once.
Digging over a zhàng deep at the spot where the light appeared,
he obtained one hundred jīn of gold.
An inscription read:
"This is the gold of Sū Qín's family.
Whoever obtains it shall perform meritorious deeds for me."
Xiǎnluò then built the Zhāofú Temple.
It was also said that this site was Sū Qín's former residence.
At that time, Yuán Yì was in power,
and upon hearing of the gold discovery,
he went to Xiǎnluò to demand it.
Xiǎnluò gave him twenty jīn.
Note: During Sū Qín's time, Buddhism did not yet exist.
The term "meritorious deeds"
does not necessarily refer to building temples;
it could refer to things like steles and inscriptions,
praising achievements and virtues.
Xiè Língyùn
On the Pǔyáng River in the Sòng dynasty, there was a place called Pípá Qí.
At the qí, there was an ancient tomb
that had fallen into the water.
On a brick were faintly raised characters, saying:
"Divination by stalks says auspicious, by turtle shell says inauspicious.
After eight hundred years,
it will fall into the river."
Xiè Língyùn took the brick to the capital,
where everyone passed it around to look at it.
Upon verifying the turtle-shell divination,
it was confirmed that the ancient tomb had already existed for eight hundred years.
Wáng Guǒ
Wáng Guǒ, a Left Guard General of the Táng dynasty, was reprimanded
and sent out to serve as the Prefect of Yǎzhōu.
While mooring his boat on the river,
he looked up and saw a coffin halfway out of a cliff face,
hanging in mid-air.
He climbed the cliff to examine it
and found an inscription that read:
"About to fall but not falling, I encounter Wáng Guǒ.
After five hundred years, you come to collect me again."
Guǒ sighed and said:
"I shall now bury this person.
Being reprimanded and sent to Yǎzhōu
was surely my fate."
He then collected and buried the remains before departing.
Fēngdū Tomb
The Fēngdū Market in the Eastern Capital
was located northeast of the Chángshòu Temple.
When initially constructing the market walls,
an ancient tomb was excavated.
It was an earthen burial,
without bricks.
The coffin wood was old and decayed,
crumbling at the touch.
The corpse wore a flat-topped headcloth
and red garments.
An inscription was found, stating:
"Divination by stalks says to dwell at court,
the turtle says near the market.
After five hundred years,
here it shall be seen."
Knowledgeable people at the time cross-referenced and verified
that it was a burial from the second year of the Huángchū era of the Wèi dynasty (221 CE).
Fán Qīnbēn
Master of the Celestial Masters Kòu Qiānzhī,
was a man who attained the Dao during the Later Wei period.
He often carved records in stone,
which he hid on Mount Sōng.
In the early years of the Shàngyuán era,
a commoner from Gàochéng County in Luòchuān,
while gathering herbs on the mountain,
discovered them,
and presented them to the county magistrate Fán Wén.
He reported it to the prefecture,
the prefecture reported it upward,
and Emperor Gāozōng issued an edict to store them in the imperial treasury.
The inscriptions and records were numerous,
profound and incomprehensible.
They roughly stated:
"The wooden child shall rule the world."
Also said:
"Stop the spear, dragon."
Also said:
"The Lǐ generation after generation shall not shift its lineage."
Also said:
"Within the tripod, the true visage is revealed."
Also said:
"The foundation for ten thousand generations."
The so-called "The wooden child shall rule the world,"
likely refers to the Táng house receiving the Mandate.
"Stop the spear, dragon,"
refers to the Empress Dowager assuming the court.
"Stop the spear" forms the character "Wǔ,"
which is the surname of Empress Dowager Wǔ.
"The Lǐ generation after generation shall not shift its lineage,"
refers to Emperor Zhōngzōng's restoration,
renewing heaven and earth.
"Within the tripod, the true visage is revealed,"
actually conceals the temple name of Emperor Zhēnzōng.
"Zhēn" is the glorious posthumous title of the wise and sagely ruler,
how can it not be believed?
"The foundation for ten thousand generations,"
"Jī" is the personal name of Emperor Xuánzōng,
"ten thousand generations" likely refers to a long and enduring reign.
Later, during Emperor Zhōngzōng's reign,
Fán Wén's son Qín Bēn,
presented the original stone record as an offering,
and the emperor ordered it to be compiled into the national history.
Jiāng Shīdù
Master Wèi Dàjīng,
a man from Xièliáng,
was renowned for his literary talent.
He did not mingle with the vulgar,
often shutting his door and cutting off worldly affairs.
Born with keen intelligence,
he thoroughly understood astronomy and calendrical phenomena,
delving deeply into the obscure and mysterious.
Later, he died of old age,
and was buried in the wilderness of Xièliáng.
During the Kāiyuán era, there was a great flood,
and Jiāng Shīdù, following an imperial edict, excavated the Wúxián River,
to irrigate the salt fields.
Houses were demolished,
and many graves were flooded,
causing distress among the people of Xièliáng.
When they reached Master Wèi's tomb,
and excavated the ground,
they found a stone,
carved with words as an inscription,
which was Master Wèi's own composition.
It said:
"Jiāng Shīdù,
move it three or five steps further south."
The workers obtained it,
and reported the matter to Shīdù.
Shīdù found the affair strange,
and sighed and pondered over it for a long time,
then turned to his officials and said:
"Master Wèi was truly an extraordinary man."
He immediately ordered the workers to divert the river,
keeping it several tens of steps away from Master Wèi's tomb.
Wū Zǎi
During the Kāiyuán era,
there was a great flood in Jiāngnán,
drowning and killing several thousand people.
The commandery reported the situation,
and Emperor Xuánzōng ordered Attendant Censor Wū Jūn Zǎi to go and inspect it.
Zǎi arrived in Jiāngnán,
and suddenly saw an ancient tomb by the roadside,
with water flooding its chamber.
Concerned about it,
he ordered the remains to be moved to higher ground.
After excavating the tomb,
they found a stone,
carved with text,
which recorded the tomb's details.
After the record, there was an inscription of twenty words,
which were the words of the geomancer.
The words said:
"A thousand years after your time,
this place will turn into a spring.
Fortunately encountering Attendant Censor Wū,
who moves me to the high plain."
Zǎi read it and found it strange,
so he checked the years,
and indeed it had been a thousand years.
Zhèng Qīnyuè
During the Tiānbǎo era,
there was a recluse from Shāngluò named Rén Shēngzhī,
who once sent a letter to Right Rectifier of Omissions Zhèng Qīnyuè, saying:
"Shēngzhī respectfully addresses you.
Recently, having retired to Shāngluò,
I have long been remiss in presenting my thoughts.
Dwelling alone in the mountains and forests,
I have severed contact with both friends and relatives.
Yet, having a matter I wish to inquire about,
I will visit you on another day.
My fifth-generation grandfather served under the Liáng dynasty as the Minister of Ceremonies.
Initially stationed under Prince of Nányáng's command,
he obtained an ancient inscription from within a collapsed tomb on a cliff of Zhōngshān.
It did not state the surname.
The small seal script read:
'The tortoise speaks of earth,
the yarrow speaks of water.
The royal domain's Yellow Bell opens the spirit's step.
Buried on the third upper Gēng,
collapsed on the seventh middle Sì.
Six thousand three hundred jiāchén intersect,
two nines, double three, four hundred collapse.'
Though the text was worn,
it was still clear.
After heavy rain,
it had just collapsed and was discovered.
This was in the fourth year of the Dàtóng era of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
Several days later,
during the Ullambana assembly,
accompanying the imperial carriage to Tóngtài Temple,
he recorded and showed it to Historiographer Yáo Chóu and various academic officials.
They deliberated in detail for several months,
but none could understand it.
Within boxes and baskets,
the remaining text still exists.
Your learning is innate and insightful,
your calculations and strategies meet with understanding,
surpassing former worthies,
unheard of in recent antiquity.
I hope you will extract its essential meaning,
grasp its underlying intent,
record it on the remaining strips,
to fulfill my ancestor's wish.
This is my deepest hope.
Respectfully, Lè'ān Rén Shēngzhī."
Several days later,
Qīnyuè promptly replied with a letter:
"Your messenger arrived,
and I was unexpectedly honored by your letter,
which refreshed my heart,
not forgetting our old friendship.
Humbly, I see you seek my inquiry,
and you also showed me the ancient Dàtóng inscription,
which former worthies failed to comprehend.
I am not profoundly knowledgeable,
how dare I speak lightly?
It truly increases my feelings of shame.
Being on the road,
I had no means to consult references.
Leaning on the saddle, I pondered,
and gained some understanding.
The one who opened the tomb is unknown whose descendant,
but the one who divined the burial site was truly a peerless worthy.
Concealing the past and knowing the future,
it was as clear as pointing at the palm.
Matching the end and discussing the beginning,
not a hair's breadth of error.
Wěi Zhāo's foreknowledge of Gǒng's envoy
could not surpass this.
Not stating the year and month of the burial,
but first recognizing the day and hour of the collapse.
Using the day of collapse,
to trace back to the initial burial,
the matter becomes clear.
Historiographer Yáo was also a man of profound insight of his time,
and he further consulted with various scholars in detail,
pondering for over a month,
yet ultimately failed to grasp its intent.
How could it be limited to this?
The original diviner's intention
was to conceal the matter,
and speak in subtle terms,
waiting for me to be like Gǒng's envoy.
Otherwise,
why would you suddenly seek my inquiry?
I carefully examined various calendrical techniques,
measured with subtle words,
attempting to explore its meaning,
hoping to grasp the subtle intent.
In the fourth year of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's Dàtóng era,
the year's cyclical position was Wùwǔ.
'Royal domain'
means five hundred.
'Yellow Bell'
means eleven.
Five hundred and eleven years, then collapse.
Counting back five hundred and eleven years from the fourth year of Dàtóng,
we arrive at the fourth year of the Jiànwǔ era of Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn, the Wùzǐ year.
'Third upper Gēng'
means the first ten-day period of the third month's Gēng day.
That year, the third month began with Xīnsì,
the tenth day was Gēngyín,
so the initial burial at Zhōngshān was in the third month.
'Seventh middle Sì'
means the seventh month began with Wùwǔ,
the twelfth day was Jǐsì,
so the initial collapse day
was Jǐsì, which can be known.
'Jiāchén' means twelve,
from the third month of the fourth year of Jiànwǔ
to the seventh month of the fourth year of Dàtóng,
totals six thousand three hundred and twelve months,
each month intersecting once,
hence 'six thousand three hundred jiāchén intersect.'
Two nines make eighteen,
double three makes six,
ending with 'four hundred,'
then six means thousand,
eighteen means ten thousand, which can be known.
From the tenth day Gēngyín of the third month of the fourth year of Jiànwǔ, the initial burial,
to the twelfth day Jǐsì of the seventh month of the fourth year of Dàtóng, the initial collapse,
totals one hundred eighty-six thousand four hundred days,
hence 'two nines, double three, four hundred collapse.'
What it speaks of
merely states the numbers of years, months, and days.
Regarding years, five hundred eleven,
matches 'royal domain's Yellow Bell';
regarding months, six thousand three hundred twelve,
matches 'six thousand three hundred jiāchén intersect';
regarding days, one hundred eighty-six thousand four hundred,
matches 'two nines, double three, four hundred collapse.'
From 'third upper Gēng' to 'seventh middle Sì';
calculated according to the calendar,
there is no discrepancy.
The stated years, months, and days,
if off by even one number,
would not correspond.
The original diviner's intention
was to wait for me to explain it.
Your inquiry
was destined to be so.
Having long served as an official,
my skills have grown rusty.
The ancients' intentions
are again difficult to fathom deeply.
You should further inquire of capable individuals.
Inform me when the time comes.
The messenger returns without replacement.
Respectfully, Zhèng Qīnyuè."
It is recorded that
during the Zhēnyuán era,
Lǐ Jífǔ served as Vice Director of the Bureau of State Farms under the Department of State Affairs and concurrently as Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
At that time, his clansman Lǐ Xùn was Director of the Bureau of Revenue.
During leisure days at the Southern Palace,
speaking of recent Confucian scholars,
he said to Jífǔ:
"The former Right Rectifier of Omissions and Academician of the Jíxiàn Hall, Zhèng Qīnyuè,
was deeply skilled in numerology,
his thoughts penetrating the mysteries,
surpassing even Monk Yīxíng.
Due to his untimely death in his era,
his fame was not widely known.
Do you know of him?"
Jífǔ replied:
"Brother, how do you verify this?"
Xùn said:
"During the Tiānbǎo era,
the Shāngluò recluse Rén Shēngzhī
said his fifth-generation grandfather served under the Liáng dynasty as the Minister of Ceremonies.
In the fourth year of Dàtóng,
he obtained an ancient inscription at the foot of Zhōngshān,
its text cryptic.
He widely sought contemporary scholars,
but none understood its meaning.
Thus, he sealed the inscription,
admonishing his sons:
'Generation after generation, my descendants,
take this inscription to inquire of learned men.
If there is one who knows,
I will have no regrets.'
By Shēngzhī's time,
being quite devoted to the Way and broad in learning,
hearing of Qīnyuè's name,
he informed him of his ancestor's intention.
Qīnyuè said:
'You should copy it and show me,
I will try to ponder it.'
Shēngzhī wrote and sent him the inscription.
It happened that Qīnyuè was then undertaking a court mission,
just mounting his carriage at Chánglè Post Station,
he received the inscription and interpreted it.
Traveling as far as Zīshuǐ,
a total of thirty lǐ,
he suddenly comprehended it.
Thus, his letter said,
'Leaning on the saddle, I pondered,
and gained some understanding.'
Is that not remarkable!"
In the Xīnwèi year,
Jífǔ was transferred to Vice Director of the Bureau of Equipment.
Qīnyuè's son Kèjūn,
was appointed from the post of Sīlù of the Jīngzhào Prefecture to the position of Sīmén Yuánwàiláng.
Jǐfǔ repeatedly questioned him about the subtle theories,
and although they seemed to align with his words,
Kèjūn himself claimed to have lost the draft.
Whenever Jǐfǔ thought of the profound and intricate meanings that he could not see,
he deeply regretted it.
In the year Rénshēn,
Jǐfǔ was demoted to the position of Chángshǐ of Míngzhōu.
On the island,
there was a recluse surnamed Zhāng,
named Xuányáng,
who was well-versed in the "Classic of Changes"
and was highly regarded by the local military commander.
He was summoned and placed in the pavilion,
and while discussing the divination methods of the "Zhouyi,"
he showed Jǐfǔ Qīnyuè's book.
Jǐfǔ was delighted to obtain the book.
He held it in his hands,
feeling as if he had acquired a treasure.
He then compiled and organized it,
and wrote a commentary, stating:
"A mound of earth,
is without emotion.
It collapses when it rains,
by mere chance.
Those who delve into the images and numbers
had already predetermined it 186,400 days earlier.
How much more so for the cycles of order and chaos,
and the destinies of adversity and success?
When sages and worthies do not meet,
and rulers and ministers coincide by chance,
then Jiāng Yá obtained the huáng jade and became Shàngfǔ,
while Zhòngní, without the phoenix, remained a traveler.
Fù Yuè's dream reached the wilderness,
and Zǐfáng received divine instruction on the bridge.
These are also predetermined signs.
Yet, Confucius did not have time to warm his mat,
and Mòzǐ did not wait for his chimney to blacken.
Why did they strive so diligently?
Mèng left Qí with haste,
and Jiǎ, upon reaching Xiāng, cast his elegy.
Why were they so attached?
Could it be that even great sages and worthies
were still perplexed by the principles of fate?
Or were they immersing themselves to preserve their teachings,
demonstrating that the human way cannot be abandoned?
I cannot know.
Qīnyuè later advanced from Yòu Bǔquē to Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ,
but was disliked by the then chancellor Lǐ Línfǔ,
and was expelled from court,
never achieving prominence.
Therefore, I record what I have heard,
attaching it after these two chapters.
To demonstrate the divine clarity of yarrow divination,
the profound understanding of the wise,
and the numerological patterns of odd and even,
I leave this for the curious,
as a rare treasure for later scholars.
Recorded by Lǐ Jǐfǔ of Zhàojùn on the 28th day of the 11th month in the 9th year of the Zhēnyuán era."
Hán Yù
To the south of Quánzhōu, there is a mountain.
The mountain rises steeply like a wall,
and below it lies a deep pool,
unfathomable in depth,
covering more than ten mǔ.
Within it dwelled jiāochī,
which had long been a menace to people.
Anyone who mistakenly approached or livestock that went to drink
would be devoured.
The people of Quánzhōu had suffered from this for years.
Thus, those living near the mountain
all took their wives and children
and moved to other prefectures,
to escape the danger.
In the fifth year of the Yuánhé era,
one evening,
a violent thunderclap was heard south of the mountain,
shaking for hundreds of lǐ,
as if the mountain had collapsed.
The entire prefecture was terrified.
The villagers, along with their livestock, chickens, and dogs,
all lost their voices and fell to the ground,
drenched in sweat,
while roof tiles clashed
and trees were uprooted.
From the xū hour to the zǐ hour,
the thunder and lightning finally ceased.
The next morning, when they went to look,
the mountain had crumbled, and the stone cliffs, hundreds of rèn high, had almost entirely collapsed,
filling the pool.
The water overflowed,
flooding the surrounding fields.
The blood of the jiāochī
was scattered everywhere, dark and yellow.
On the stone cliffs,
nineteen characters were carved,
the style of the characters very ancient,
and no one among the scholars or commoners of the prefecture could understand them.
From then on, the residents no longer suffered from the menace.
Those who had been fearful settled down,
and those who had moved away returned.
They built houses and huts,
settling closely together in the area.
The prefect thus named the place Shímíng Lǐ,
using the characters as an inscription,
and to record the strange event.
Later, a traveler from Quánzhōu
was able to copy the characters
and brought them to Dōngluò.
At that time, the former Vice Minister of Personnel, Hán Yù, was serving as the magistrate of Hénán County after leaving his post as a Shàngshū Láng.
He saw them and recognized them.
The text read:
"By decree, show the black water,
the carp of,
Tiāngōng humbly kills the ox-man,
the divine script of rénguǐ, urgently, urgently."
Upon careful examination of its meaning,
it seemed to be the words of Shàngdì reprimanding the jiāochī,
ordering their destruction for the harm they caused.
The characters were written in kēdǒu seal script,
which is why the people of Quánzhōu could not recognize them.
Péi Dù
In the first year of the Yuánhé era,
in the autumn, ninth month,
the Huáixī commander Wú Shǎochéng died,
and his son Yuánjì refused the imperial command.
An edict ordered the regions adjacent to Huáixī
to attack it from four sides with troops,
but for several years they could not overcome it.
In the thirteenth year,
the chancellor, Duke Jìnguó Péi Dù, was summoned to lead troops and attack it.
After Dù arrived,
he ordered the border guards to deepen the moats and pools,
and to excavate the ground.
Someone obtained a stone,
on which carved characters formed an inscription.
The border guard took it and presented it to Dù.
The text said:
"At the bottom of a well, a single bamboo pole,
the bamboo's color deep green, green.
The chicken is not yet fat,
the wine is not yet mature,
the lads blocking the carriage must for now shrink back."
Dù obtained it,
showed it to his staff,
and ordered them to discern its meaning,
but none could fathom it.
Dù was pondering it
when suddenly a soldier
leapt from the ranks and congratulated him, saying:
"Wú Yuánjì defies the Son of Heaven's command,
unleashing wild troops in a rebellious plot.
Relying on the Son of Heaven's majestic sageliness,
and the chancellor's virtue in harmony,
today the rebellious scoundrel will be captured;
I dare to congratulate the chancellor on his achievement."
Dù, startled, questioned him.
He replied:
"The border guard obtained the stone inscription—
this is its omen.
Moreover, 'At the bottom of a well, a single bamboo pole,
the bamboo's color deep green, green'—
this refers to Wú Shǎochéng, who from a soldier in the ranks
came to command a hundred thousand troops,
becoming a regional commander,
and also metaphorically speaks of his glory.
'The chicken is not yet fat'—
this means without meat.
Now, remove 'meat' from 'fat'—
it becomes the character 'jǐ'.
'The wine is not yet mature'—
this means without water.
Remove 'water' from 'wine'—
it becomes the character 'yǒu'.
'The lads blocking the carriage'—
refers to armed soldiers.
'Must for now shrink back'—
means they should retreat and guard their position.
Inferring from this,
then on the jǐ-yǒu day it will be overcome.
If it does not happen by that date,
then one can wait."
Dù was pleased,
looked at his attendants and said:
"This soldier is a discerning one."
He sighed in amazement.
That year, in the winter tenth month,
the minister of state Lǐ Sù led troops into Huáixī,
captured Yuánjì alive,
and executed all the rebels.
Dù then checked the date—
it was indeed the jǐ-yǒu day.
Thereupon, Dù grew even more amazed at the soldier's discernment
and promoted him to deputy general.
Zhāng Wéiqīng
In the shade of the Hēishān,
there was a temple to Duke Wèi Lǐ.
During the Bǎolì era,
Zhāng Wéiqīng was protector-general of the Chányú.
His staff member Lú Lì once dreamed of a person,
tall and dressed in black,
who told Lì:
"I have resided in Duke Wèi's temple for a long time;
I hope you will move me into the military city."
Then he departed.
At dawn,
Lì, not understanding,
went in and reported to Wéiqīng:
"Duke Wèi rendered great service to the state.
Now his temple is dilapidated and ruined,
exposed to wind and rain, and in severe condition;
I wish to renew its wooden and earthen structure."
Wéiqīng was pleased and approved his words.
Previously, the Chányú prefecture, because Wéiqīng had achieved fine governance,
had recorded his administrative achievements
and requested the protector Jūn Luò Zhōng to submit a memorial to the emperor.
An edict
ordered the Secretariat Drafter Gāo Gōng Yì to compose a text for it,
to be engraved on a stele.
The edict had arrived, but there was no stone for the stele;
Wéiqīng had just ordered an envoy to quarry stone in Yúnzhōng commandery,
but he had not yet returned.
When repairing Duke Wèi's temple,
they excavated to the west
and obtained a stone,
square and long,
with the carved character "Zhāng" below,
clearly discernible.
The workers took it and presented it to Wéiqīng.
Wéiqīng joyfully said:
"Heaven has bestowed upon me the stele stone."
He immediately summoned his staff to look at it;
Lì was both startled and amazed.
He then rose to congratulate him and recounted the previous dream.
Thereupon, they used the stone for the stele
and engraved Gāo Gōng's text on it.
Wáng Fán
During the Tàihé era,
Wáng Fán was inspector of Dānyáng.
While channeling water through the city walls,
after digging several feet deep,
they obtained a stone.
The inscribed text said:
"The mountain has stone,
the stone has jade.
The jade has flaw—
then it ends."
The workers obtained it
and fully reported the matter, presenting it to Fán.
He examined its meaning
for a long time but could not decipher it,
so he ordered his subordinates to discern it,
but none could analyze its principle.
After several days,
an old man requested an audience with Fán's clerk
and secretly said to him:
"I have heard that Lord Wáng obtained a stone inscription—
has anyone discerned it now?"
The clerk said:
"His lordship is pondering it—
what could its meaning be?
Could you, sir,
perhaps fathom it?"
The old man said:
"This is inauspicious.
Now, 'The mountain has stone,
the stone has jade,
the jade has flaw—
then it ends'—
all narrates Lord Wáng's lineage.
Moreover, his ancestor was named Yín;
Yín gave birth to Chǔ.
Judging by the text,
this is 'the mountain has stone.'
Chǔ gave birth to Fán—
this is 'the stone has jade.'
Fán's son is named Xiáxiū—
this is 'the jade has flaw, then it ends.'
'Ends' is an omen of termination;
inferring from this and discerning,
is it not the severing of his line?"
The clerk thanked him,
and the old man finished speaking and left.
By the winter of the ninth year of Tàihé,
Fán was executed and his clan exterminated,
indeed matching the old man's interpretation.
Liǔ Guāng
During the Tàihé era,
there was a man named Liǔ Guāng,
who once traveled south.
While traveling along a mountain path,
he happened to be out late,
and mistakenly entered a mountain recess,
where pines led him winding and twisting.
After walking several li,
he reached a stone chamber,
surrounded by clouds and water,
with clear springs crisscrossing.
The chamber had a mat and a couch,
as if someone lived there.
Facing rosy clouds and emerald peaks ahead,
it was certainly no ordinary human realm.
Guāng thus stood gazing by the flowing stream,
when suddenly he saw a jar,
lying on the ground.
Guāng immediately approached it,
and beneath the jar was a spring,
less than a foot around,
its water clear and swift.
He lifted a cup to drink,
and it was like sweet wine;
after downing over ten cups, he was already deeply drunk,
so he lay down on the couch,
and did not wake until dawn.
Then, examining the stone wall,
he found many carved characters,
so he copied the writing,
and placed it in his sleeve.
The words said:
"When Wǔ is in Mǎo,
Yáo's king for eight seasons.
I abandon his bedchamber,
I leave his screen.
Deeply, deeply,
highly, highly,
men do not know me,
nor do they speak of me.
From now onward,
over two hundred sacrifices later,
blazing its light,
harmonious its beginning.
In the east there is a rabbit,
small head, dark tail,
passing by my path,
coming to my abode.
Drinks from my spring and becomes drunk,
ascends my couch and sleeps.
Carved upon my wall,
profound its meaning,
who can discern it?
It is Dōngpíngzǐ."
Guāng first read it,
and reading it, found it strange,
then departed.
After walking several dozen paces out of the path,
he looked back at the chamber,
and it had completely vanished from sight.
Guāng investigated but could not find it.
There was a man named Lǚ,
who saw it and deciphered it,
and before long announced:
"I have fully understood it;
these are the words of one who attained the Way.
Now, at the beginning of the Táng house,
the reign title established was Wǔdé.
The second year of Wǔ,
the year,
its cyclical sign being Jǐmǎo,
thus 'When Wǔ is in Mǎo,'
its meaning is clear,
it refers to the second year of Wǔdé.
'Yáo's king,'
refers to Gāozǔ's title Shényáo,
Saying 'eight seasons,'
also means two years.
'I abandon his bedchamber,
I leave his screen,'
speaks of his departure,
the time he utterly left,
was the second year of Wǔdé.
'Deeply, deeply,
highly, highly.
Men do not know me,
men do not speak of me,'
speaks of his seclusion, unknown to men.
'From now onward,
over two hundred sacrifices later,'
speaks of your coming, sir.
Moreover, from the beginning of the Táng house,
it is indeed now over two hundred years.
'Blazing its light,
harmonious its beginning,'
'Blazing its light,'
refers to the year being Dīngwèi,
blaze is fire,
is this not referring to the south's Bǐng-Dīng?
Wèi is also the position of fire;
'harmonious its beginning,'
refers to the present Son of Heaven establishing the reign title Tàihé at the beginning,
that is the first year.
'In the east there is a rabbit,
small head, dark tail,'
narrates your name, sir.
East is Jiǎ-Yǐ, wood,
rabbit is Mǎo,
'Mǎo' attached to 'wood,'
makes the character 'Liǔ.'
'Small head, dark tail,'
is 'Guāng.'
'Passing by my path,
coming to my abode,'
speaks of your coming, sir.
'Drinks from my spring and becomes drunk,
ascends my couch and sleeps,'
speaks of your stay, sir.
'Carved upon my wall,
profound its meaning.
Who can discern it?
It is Dōngpíngzǐ.'
Says its meaning is profound and hidden,
only I can discern it.
Dōngpíng is my district,
thus it is further confirmed.
Thus deciphered,
it is indeed the legacy record of one who attained the Way."
Lǐ Fú
At the bell tower of Tàiqīng Temple on Běimáng Hill north of Luòjīng,
during the Táng Xiántōng era,
it suddenly collapsed.
There was a roof beam,
hollow inside,
and whenever it was moved or jostled,
it made knocking sounds inside.
People thus spread the word,
and came competing to see it.
The temple's disciplinarian, Dàoist Lǐ, did not want crowds gathering,
so he ordered it broken open,
and within they found a black lacquered board,
with inlaid gold characters on it.
They said:
"Shānshuǐ shuí wú yán,
Yuánnián yù Fú chóngxiū."
The Dàoist then presented it to various officials in Luòzhōng,
but none could understand the text.
Minister Lǐ Fú, having left his post as military governor of Xīchuān and returned to Luò,
saw this cryptic text,
and after repeatedly reading it over several times,
said to the temple's abbot:
"Simply hire craftsmen and gather workers;
I shall use my leftover salary,
to personally complete the repairs.
A hundred years ago,
a wise man inscribed his intent,
which has mysteriously matched today.
How can we not revive this temple!"
After the temple was completed,
someone asked his reason.
Fú said:
"'Shānshuǐ shuí wú yán' [Shānshuǐ who lacks words],
is the present emperor's personal name.
'Yuánnián yù Fú' [In the first year, encountering Fú],
refers to the change,
at the beginning of the new reign era, taking up my governorship,
and returning with my salary;
if Fú does not repair it,
then whom else should wait to do so!"
Xióng Bó
As for Xióng Bó,
he was originally a ferry officer in Jiàn'ān.
When the riverbank collapsed,
an ancient tomb was uncovered.
Vines entwined its coffin,
and beside it was a stone inscription saying:
"About to sink, not sinking, bound by vines;
about to fall, not falling, blocked by sand.
After five hundred years, encountering Xióng Bó."
Bó was then poor and old,
and monks raised money to bury it for him.
Bó later became Prefect of Jiànzhōu.
Wáng Jìngzhī
Therefore, northwest of the capital Yèdū,
there was a place called Fānglín Village.
A villager from Qí, named Wáng Jìngzhī,
was among the registered households and particularly impoverished,
often making a living by gathering firewood.
In the autumn of the bǐngwǔ year, the ninth month,
while digging at the base of the Copper Sparrow Terrace,
