the ground suddenly gave way slightly.
As he continued digging with his spade,
about three feet down,
he found a bluish stone,
as large as a basin.
He then exerted himself to retrieve it,
when suddenly the stone split in two.
It was as if a shell had been cracked open.
Inside was a bluish stone box,
one foot and eight inches long,
three inches thick,
and four inches wide.
Jìngzhī was astonished,
and placed it in a basket to take home.
He washed it with water,
and it became warm, smooth, and brilliantly lustrous,
truly a rare treasure.
On all four sides and the back were raised designs of dragons soaring and phoenixes dancing, along with floral patterns,
carved with such extraordinary and intricate artistry
that it seemed almost beyond human craftsmanship.
Slowly opening it,
he found inside a white jade slab,
on which were engraved six lines in large seal script.
The text read:
"The superior scholar with ash of Ba removes emptiness,
Yī Yǐn to the northeast, eight or nine remain,
Qín and Zhào mostly correspond, dividing five jades,
White silk, bamboo, wood, sons dwell for generations.
But look at six sixes within and without,
the worldly lord faces obstacles, as state as state."
Thereupon, Jìngzhī took it and presented it to the Wèi commander Yuè Yànzhēn,
who in turn rewarded him with bolts of silk
and exempted him from land taxes.
Yet no one was able to fully decipher the hidden meaning of the words.
Alas,
during the eras of the Cáo, Shí, and Gāo families,
this was where the royal aura and auspicious fortune of Yè were concentrated,
and thus many worthies gathered there.
Who knows if there were not those who secretly foresaw later generations,
encompassing the winds and clouds,
and the fragmentation of mountains and rivers,
and buried jade as an omen for it.
Now that the stone has emerged,
these events are about to be foretold.
Wáng Chéngjiǎn
Wáng Chéngjiǎn, military governor of Qínzhōu under the Shǔ of Wáng,
built a defensive city against the Tibetans.
Upon reaching the foot of Shàngguī Mountain,
he uncovered a tile coffin,
inside which there was no corpse,
only a single tongue,
its flesh red and moist,
hard as iron or stone.
On the tongue was only a skull,
within which lay an ancient coin,
and two flies,
which suddenly flew away.
A stone slab was inscribed with seal characters, saying:
"In the second year of the Kāihuáng era of the great Suí,
the wife of Yóu Chóng, Prefect of Wèizhōu, Lady Wáng,
at the age of twenty-five,
married Chóng,
and after three years became pregnant.
Disgusted by the pregnancy,
she then died.
The inscription reads:
'North of the carriage road,
on the sunny side of Guī Mountain,
deeply buried jade,
thickly interred fragrance.
Carved on this steadfast stone,
shines her lasting fragrance.
The land changes, hills and valleys shift,
peril arrays the city walls.
In the bǐng year of Qiándé,
the destroyer shall be Hé Láng.'"
This year was the sixth year of the false Qiándé era,
which was the bǐngzǐ year.
The phrase 'the destroyer shall be Hé Láng'
refers to Wáng Chéngjiǎn's childhood name.
Lǐ Shūqīng
Lǐ Shūqīng of Hénán in the Hàn,
served as the commandery's official of works,
and was recommended as Xiàolián.
His peers envied him,
and spread rumors, saying:
"Shūqīng married his widowed younger sister."
Because of this, he was disqualified from the Xiàolián selection,
and Shūqīng then shut himself indoors and did not go out.
His sister, in grief and indignation,
went to the prefectural gate and hanged herself,
and Shūqīng also took his own life,
to prove his innocence.
Afterwards, his family buried them.
Later, a thunderbolt
struck and killed those who had envied him,
placing them at Shūqīng's tomb.
The families of those struck by lightning
collected and buried their corpses.
After the burial,
their graves were again opened.
Yáng Dàohé
Yáng Dàohé of Fúfēng in the Jìn,
was in the fields during summer,
when he encountered thunder and rain,
and went under a mulberry tree.
A thunderbolt struck down at him,
and Dàohé warded it off with his hoe,
breaking its arm,
so it fell to the ground and could not leave.
Its lips were like cinnabar,
its eyes like mirrors,
with hairy horns over three feet long.
Its shape was like that of the six domestic animals,
but its head resembled a macaque.
Shí Lè
During the time of Shí Lè of the Later Zhào,
there were violent storms, heavy rain, thunder, and hail.
The main gate of the Jiàndé Hall and the west gate of Xiāngguó Market collapsed.
Five people were killed.
Hail began from Jiè Mountain in Xīhé,
as large as chicken eggs,
piling three feet high on level ground,
and over ten feet deep in depressions.
Travelers and animals,
tens of thousands in number, perished.
Over a thousand li,
trees were broken and felled,
and crops were utterly destroyed.
Shí Lè asked Xú Guāng,
who said:
"Last year, the Cold Food Festival was not prohibited.
Jiè Zituī is a deity of the emperor's homeland,
hence this disaster occurred."
A Person from Guózhōu
In the Táng, in Guózhōu, there were brothers who divided their household,
sharing the main hall and rooms.
In the summer night of the first year of the Xiǎnqìng era,
there was terrifying thunder, fierce winds.
The elder brother was very afraid,
and wanted to take shelter in his younger brother's house,
but as he was about to go, he stopped again.
Ten paces in front of the door,
there was originally a long pit.
The wind and rain uprooted his house, along with eleven family members, young and old,
and all were thrown into the pit and died.
Where the house was uprooted,
became entirely a pit.
It also swept up thousands of household items, large and small,
all into the pit,
leaving nothing behind.
Only the walls remained unmoved.
In the courtyard was a large locust tree, several arm-spans around,
with very lush branches,
but its roots and trunk were uprooted.
Both large and small parts were completely gone,
and it vanished,
never to be found again.
One year earlier,
his wife had seen a goat in the tree,
and they all found it strange,
and later suffered this calamity.
As for the younger brother's dwelling,
only the exposed rafters and tiles were blown away,
as if dismantled by someone,
with no other damage.
He had a son who was an imperial guard,
on duty rotation in the capital.
The prefect Yú Lìzhèng reported this,
and an edict allowed the son to return,
and bestowed thirty items as gifts.
At that time, Huán Sīxù was the director of records,
and personally investigated the matter.
Fēng Yuánzé
Táng Fēng Yuánzé was a native of Chánghé in Bóhǎi.
During the Xiǎnqìng era,
he served as the Taìguān Zhǎngshàn (Officer in Charge of Meals) in the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
At that time, the King of Yútián came to court,
and the leftover food supplies included sheep,
amounting to several hundred head in total.
The king entrusted them all to Yuánzé to deliver to a Buddhist monastery for keeping alive (as a meritorious act).
However, Yuánzé secretly ordered butchers to slaughter them, cook them, and sell them, keeping the proceeds for himself.
In the summer, the sixth month of the first year of the Lóngshuò era,
there was heavy rain in Luòyáng.
Thunder struck and killed Yuánzé in the street outside the Xuānrén Gate,
breaking his neck,
so that blood flowed and splattered on the ground.
Onlookers filled the thoroughfare,
and all were shocked and astonished.
The monk Dào Xuān.
Táng Liú Yǔxī said that Dào Xuān was foremost in upholding the monastic discipline.
Suddenly one day,
thunderclaps encircled the outside of his dwelling without ceasing.
Xuān said:
"In upholding the discipline, I have committed no further offenses.
If there is some karma from a past life,
then I am unaware of it."
Thereupon, he took off his three monastic robes and placed them outside the door,
suspecting that some flood dragon or serpent might be relying on them.
After the robes were put out, the sound still did not stop.
Xuān then examined his ten fingernails
and found a spot like an oil-sesame seed
on the little finger of his right hand.
Suspicious of it,
he extended it out through a hole in the lattice window.
With one clap of thunder, half the finger was lost.
The black spot was the hiding place of the flood dragon.
Yǔxī said:
"Even the dragon was quite adept at seeking a place to hide,
yet in the end it could not avoid [its fate].
Thus, all is determined by fate;
how can one escape it?"
Sū Jiànyán.
Sū Jiànyán of the Court of Ceremonial,
the eldest son of the Left Councilor, Duke Wēn of the State, Liángsì,
resided in Jiāshàn Lane.
In the sixth month of the Yǒngchāng year,
he and his younger brother, Jiànyì, who was Registrar and Adjutant of the Chóngguāng Prefecture,
were returning from court to their residence.
East of the Hóngdào Temple,
they suddenly encountered a torrential downpour.
Thunder, lightning, and flashes of light
came and encircled the horses of Jiànyán and the others,
whirling around very rapidly,
with the sound of thunder also at their side.
After a while, it dispersed.
In the ninth month of that year,
Yuán Sùyán and Zhào Huáijié plotted rebellion.
Jiànyán's wives and concubines were all imprisoned for several months,
and furthermore, each was dismissed from his post.
When Liángsì died,
they were all exiled to remote borderlands.
Dí Rénjié.
In the Táng dynasty, over ten lǐ west of Dàizhōu,
there was a large locust tree
that had been struck by thunder,
split open for several zhàng.
The Thunder God was clamped within the tree,
roaring like a peal of thunder.
At that time, Dí Rénjié was the Regional Commander.
Guests and attendants went to look.
When they wished to approach the spot,
the crowd all recoiled in fear;
no one dared to advance.
Rénjié alone urged his horse forward with vigor,
approached, and questioned him.
He then said:
"There is a rebellious dragon in the tree.
The authorities ordered me to pursue it.
I fell with such force that I could not withstand it,
and was clamped by the tree.
If you rescue me,
I will richly repay your virtue."
Rénjié ordered sawyers to split the tree,
and only then did he get out.
Afterwards, he would always report in advance whether events would be auspicious or inauspicious.
Yǎnshī.
In the sixth month of the first year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng,
in Bǎilǐ Village of Yǎnshī County,
thunder struck a commoner's home.
The ground split open,
over a zhàng wide,
fifteen lǐ long,
and fathomless when measured.
In the places where it split,
wells and latrines became connected;
tombs that were struck
had coffins emerge from the ground.
No one knew the reason for this either.
Thunder Battle.
At the end of the Kāiyuán era of the Táng,
in Léizhōu, a Thunder God battled with a whale.
The whale's body emerged above the water,
with several dozen Thunder Gods
up and down in the sky.
Some released fire,
others struck with curses.
It lasted seven days before ceasing.
People living along the coast went to watch.
They did not know which of the two was victorious,
but only saw the seawater turn bright red.
Zhāng-Quán Boundary.
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng,
the two prefectures of Zhāngzhōu and Quánzhōu
had an uneven division of their boundary,
and they sued each other at the imperial court.
The imperial commissioner could not settle it.
After several years,
the arguments and reasoning became tangled and confused,
and in the end, no one could decide it.
Thereupon, the prefectural officials burned incense
and prayed to Heaven, Earth, and the mountains and rivers,
seeking a divine response.
Soon, heavy thunder and rain arrived.
With one clap of thunder,
a cliff wall split open in the middle.
The land they were disputing
was opened up into a path.
It was a thousand chǐ high
and about five lǐ deep,
and was therefore made an official road.
Within the cliff wall were six lines of ancient seal script,
twenty-four characters in total,
each several chǐ wide.
Although this was agreed upon as the boundary,
no one could read them.
At the beginning of the Zhēnyuán era,
an exile named Lǐ Xiébiàn deciphered them, saying:
"Zhāng and Quán, two prefectures,
divide the land in great peace.
Yǒng'ān and Lóngxī,
mountains high, air clear.
For a thousand years, no confusion;
for ten thousand ages, a model course."
The mentioned Yǒng'ān and Lóngxī
are the names of townships at the border of the two commanderies.
Bāo Chāo.
Péi Xuān, a Commandant of Ānfēng in the Táng,
grandson of Shì Yān,
said:
Emperor Xuánzōng once, in a winter month,
summoned the mountain hermit Bāo Chāo
and ordered him to produce the sound of thunder.
He replied:
"Tomorrow at noon, there should be thunder."
He then had Gāo Lìshì supervise him.
One evening,
Chāo performed rituals and practiced his arts.
By dawn until the sì hour (9-11 AM),
there was not the slightest trace of clouds.
Lìshì became fearful.
Chāo said:
"General, look at the southern mountains.
There should be black vapor like a plate."
Lìshì looked,
and it was as he said.
After a while, wind arose,
black vapor spread everywhere,
and several claps of fierce thunder sounded.
The Emperor ordered him to accompany Gēshū Hàn on the western campaign,
and in every battle, they often obtained favorable winds.
Zhāng Xūmí
During the Shangyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Zhāng Xūmí from Quánjiāo County in Chúzhōu,
who was dispatched by the county to deliver sacrificial animals to the prefecture.
The mountain road was treacherous,
and in Huáinán there were many charitable shelters and wells
used to protect travelers.
At dusk, a violent storm arose.
Xūmí, along with a monk named Zǐlín,
entered a charitable shelter together.
Xūmí had a driver,
an old man named Wáng,
who was out in the rain gathering the donkeys.
Shortly after,
they heard a sound falling from the clouds,
and suddenly saw nine village girls.
They were together supporting a carriage.
Wáng had a daughter named Ā Tuī,
who had been dead for half a year,
and she was also among the carriage party.
Seeing Wáng, she was both sad and joyful.
She asked about her mother, younger sister, and family matters,
leaving no topic untouched.
Her companions urged her, and only then did she leave.
At first, the carriage they supported gradually ascended,
and clouds gathered to obscure it.
Then it made a thunderous sound,
and only then did they realize it was a thunder chariot.
Cài Xīmǐn
In the Táng dynasty, Cài Xīmǐn
had his home in the Eastern Capital.
On a summer night,
several dozen brothers gathered in the main hall.
Suddenly, heavy rain fell,
with thunder, lightning, and darkness.
An object fell into the courtyard,
making a rustling sound.
They ordered a torch to look at it,
and it turned out to be a woman,
wearing a yellow silk skirt and a cloth shirt.
She could not communicate verbally,
so they regarded her as a heavenly maiden.
Later,
after five or six years,
she was able to speak Chinese.
When asked about her homeland,
she did not know it.
She only said:
"In my native land, we eat jīng rice,
and have no bowls or utensils.
We use willow baskets to hold the rice and eat it."
In the end, they did not know what country's people she was.
Originally in her own country,
she went out at night
and was taken up by thunder,
and shortly after fell into Xīmǐn's courtyard.
Xú Jǐngxiān
In the Táng dynasty, Xú Jǐngxiān
had a younger brother named Ā Sì,
who was stubborn, foolish, and unrestrained.
Each time,
Jǐngxiān would reprimand and scold him.
But their mother
showed him extra affection and concern,
making excuses to explain and defend him,
which caused Jǐngxiān to respond sharply and loudly.
Suddenly, thunder arrived,
dragging Jǐngxiān into the clouds.
There was a presiding official,
with several dozen attendants on his left and right.
He interrogated and questioned him.
Jǐngxiān replied, saying:
"Because my brother is unruly,
and the provisions for our mother are lacking,
that is why I scold and insult him.
My mother ordered me to let him go,
it is not that I dared to curse my mother."
The presiding official did not understand his words.
Soon, a servant girl in black
from the sky,
leaped down,
to speak on Jǐngxiān's behalf.
She said:
"If so, release him.
When he reaches home,
he can write a statement of defense.
Nail it to the east wall,
and I will have it taken myself."
Then they pushed Jǐngxiān, and he fell into the pond in front of his house.
He emerged from the water,
completely unharmed.
He sought paper to write his defense,
nailed it to the east wall,
and indeed a wind came and the defense vanished.
Ōuyáng Hūléi
In the Táng dynasty, there was Ōuyáng Hūléi,
whose original name was Shào,
a man from Guìyáng.
He was strong and robust,
and courageous in battle.
He once served as a commandery general,
was famous,
and held the post of Chief Clerk of Léizhōu.
He was lodged in the western part of the prefectural city,
facing a large pond in front,
from which clouds and mist often emerged.
Those who lived there often died.
When Shào arrived,
he settled there without hesitation.
He ordered people to measure the depth of the water,
then had another huge pit dug separately,
deep and wide like the pond.
Once completed,
he directed the water to be channeled and drained.
Then clouds arose,
heaven and earth turned dark,
thunder and lightning arrived in force,
and firelight reached the ground.
Shào led his followers, over twenty men,
holding bows, arrows, and halberds in formation,
and fought with the Thunder Master.
Their clothes were scorched and curled,
their bodies wounded and rotting,
yet they did not stop.
From morning until evening,
the thunder and lightning scattered and flew away,
and the pond also dried up.
They captured a snake from within.
It looked like a silkworm.
Four or five chǐ long,
with no head or eyes.
Chopping and stabbing could not injure it,
it wriggled.
They prepared a large cauldron of oil to fry it.
It still did not die.
They poured molten iron.
Only then did it become scorched.
Then they pounded it into powder.
And Shào consumed it all.
Southerners therefore called Shào "Hūléi" (Sudden Thunder).
Xuānzhōu
In the Zhēnguán era of the Táng dynasty,
Xuānzhōu suddenly experienced a great thunderstorm.
A creature fell to the ground,
with a pig's head,
two fingers on each hand and foot,
holding a red snake and biting it.
After a moment, the clouds darkened and it disappeared.
At the time, people made pictures of it and circulated them.
Wáng Gàn
In the early Zhēnguán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was Wáng Gàn from Zhèngzhōu,
who had courage and daring.
In midsummer, while working in the fields,
a sudden violent thunderstorm arose.
He therefore entered a silkworm room to take shelter.
After a while,
thunder and lightning entered the room,
and black mist suddenly darkened it.
Gàn then closed the door,
shouldered a hoe, and struck wildly.
The thunder sounds gradually diminished,
and the cloud mist also receded.
Gàn shouted loudly,
and continued striking without cease.
The mist shrank to the size of half a bed,
then further to the size of a plate.
Suddenly it fell to the ground,
transforming into a flatiron, a folding knife, and a small tripod cooking vessel with broken legs.
Huátíng Weir Official
In the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty, in the Máoshān area of Yánlíng County, Rùn Prefecture,
during the spring of the Yuánhé period,
there was a great storm.
A demon fell from the sky,
over twenty feet tall,
black in color,
with a face like a pig’s head,
horns five or six feet long,
fleshy wings over ten feet in span,
and a leopard’s tail.
It also wore a crimson half-garment and trousers,
with leopard skin wrapped around its waist,
and the claws on its hands and feet were all golden in color.
It grasped a red snake,
trampling it underfoot,
glaring as if about to devour it,
and its voice was like thunder.
A farmer named Xú □
suddenly saw it and fled in terror,
reporting it to the county.
Soon, the county magistrate personally went to witness it,
and ordered it to be drawn.
Shortly after, there was another thunderstorm,
and it flew away on its wings.
Chén Luánfèng
During the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Chén Luánfèng,
a native of Hǎikāng.
He was bold and righteous,
unafraid of ghosts and deities,
and his fellow villagers all called him “the later Zhōu Chǔ.”
In Hǎikāng,
there was a temple to the Thunder God,
which the locals worshipped with devout purity.
As prayers and offerings became excessive,
strange and deceitful occurrences also arose.
Every year, when the locals heard the first thunderclap,
they would note the day in the sexagenary cycle.
When that same day returned ten days later,
all craftsmen dared not work.
Those who violated this would inevitably be struck dead by lightning within a day or two,
and the response was as swift as an echo.
At that time, Hǎikāng suffered a great drought,
and the locals prayed without receiving any response.
Luánfèng angrily said:
“My hometown
is the land of thunder.
Yet as a deity, it brings no blessings.
Moreover, it receives such lavish offerings from people,
while the crops are scorched,
the ponds have dried up,
and the sacrificial animals have been exhausted.
What use is such a temple!”
So he took a torch and burned it down.
According to local custom,
one must not eat yellow fish together with pork,
or mix them in a meal,
or else one would surely be struck dead by lightning.
On that day,
Luánfèng took a bamboo-handled charcoal knife,
went into the wild fields,
and ate the forbidden foods mixed together,
intending to wait and see what would happen.
Indeed, strange clouds arose,
fierce winds blew,
and a swift thunderstorm struck him.
Luánfèng then raised his knife upward,
and indeed struck the Thunder God’s left thigh, severing it.
The Thunder God fell to the ground,
looking like a bear or a pig,
with fur and horns,
greenish fleshy wings,
and holding a short-handled stone axe.
Blood flowed profusely,
and the clouds and rain ceased entirely.
Knowing that the Thunder God had no divine power,
Luánfèng hurried home,
and told his relatives:
“I have cut off the Thunder God’s thigh,
come and see it.”
His loved ones were shocked and terrified,
and together they went to look,
and indeed saw the Thunder God with its thigh broken.
He then raised his knife, intending to cut off its neck
and bite its flesh.
But the crowd restrained him, saying:
“The Thunder God is a celestial being,
and you are but a mortal from the lower realm.
If you harm the Thunder God,
our entire village will surely suffer calamity.”
The crowd grabbed his sleeves,
preventing Luánfèng from striking further.
After a short while,
clouds and thunder returned,
enveloping
the injured one,
and carrying it away along with the severed thigh.
Then,
a torrential downpour fell,
from noon until dusk,
and the parched seedlings all stood upright again.
Afterward, he was scorned by young and old alike,
and forbidden to return home.
So he took his knife and walked twenty miles,
arriving at
his cousin’s house.
That night,
he was again struck by thunder,
and heavenly fire burned down the house.
Again, he stood in the courtyard holding his knife,
and the thunder could not harm him.
Soon, someone told his cousin what had happened earlier,
and he was driven out again.
He then went to a monastery,
but was again struck by thunder,
and the building burned as before.
Knowing he had nowhere to stay,
he took a torch at night
and entered a crevice in a limestone cave.
After that, the thunder could no longer strike him,
and he returned home after three nights.
From then on, whenever there was a drought in Hǎikāng,
the locals would pool money for Luánfèng,
asking him to eat the two forbidden foods as before,
and wield his knife as before.
Each time, heavy rain would pour down,
and he was never struck by lightning again.
This went on for over twenty years,
and people nicknamed Luánfèng “the Rain Master.”
During the Tàihé era,
the prefect Lín Xù learned of this matter,
summoned him to the prefecture,
and questioned him about the details.
Luánfèng said:
“In my youth,
my heart was like iron and stone.
Ghosts, deities, thunder, and lightning
meant nothing to me.
I was willing to sacrifice my own life
to save the people.
How could the heavens allow the Thunder God to unleash its fury!”
He then presented his knife to Xù,
who rewarded him generously.
The Mountain Temple in Jiàn Prefecture
Vice-Minister Liǔ Gōngquán of the Táng dynasty
once heard from an acquaintance:
At the end of the Yuánhé era,
he stayed at a mountain temple in Jiàn Prefecture.
In the middle of the night,
he heard a commotion outside the door,
and secretly peered through the window lattice.
He saw several men wielding axes to build a thunder chariot,
just like in a painting.
After a while,
he sneezed,
and suddenly it turned pitch dark,
and his eyesight went dim.
The son of the Xiāo family.
During the Chángqìng era of the Táng dynasty,
a man of the Xiāo clan from Lánlíng
was renowned for his courage and daring.
While traveling as a guest in Xiāng-Chǔ,
he arrived at Chángshā Commandery
and lodged at the Yǎngshān Temple.
That evening,
he was alone and had extinguished the candle.
Suddenly, violent thunder shook the eaves and rafters,
continuing for a long time without ceasing.
Soon, he heard from beneath the western wall
a rustling sound.
Relying on his physical strength,
Xiāo was not at all afraid.
Before his bed was a large club,
which he took to the base of the wall.
Bending down, he struck at it,
hitting the target with the first blow.
A very sharp cry was heard,
as if something was moaning.
He then struck several dozen times in succession,
and the sound finally ceased;
the wind and rain also cleared.
Xiāo joyfully said:
"The monster is dead."
At dawn,
beneath the western wall, he saw an extremely strange ghost.
Its body was entirely blue,
hunched and short.
It had a golden axe and wooden pegs,
bound to its body with hemp cord.
It blinked and panted,
appearing greatly distressed.
He then fully informed the temple monks, who came to see it.
Someone said:
"This is a thunder ghost,
an envoy of the Supreme Deity.
Why have you insulted the Supreme Deity?
Calamity will soon befall you."
The local people prepared sacrificial animals and wine to offer to it.
Soon, clouds and mist grew dark,
emerging from the room,
exiting the door and ascending to the sky;
the ghost also followed and left.
Then the sound of thunder arose again,
lasting only about the time of a few meals before ceasing.
Xiāo's spirit grew even more fierce,
and the local people all regarded him as a hero.
Zhōu Hóng
The Táng recluse Zhōu Hóng relates:
During the Bǎolì era,
over ten guests from the town
were gathering to escape the heat and drink together.
Suddenly, a fierce wind and rain arose,
and something fell resembling a macaque,
its two eyes gleaming.
The crowd, terrified, prostrated themselves beneath the beds.
In an instant, it ascended the steps and looked all around,
then soon disappeared.
When the rain stopped,
they gradually managed to rise,
looked at each other,
and found their ears were all filled with mud.
A local said,
earlier there had been thunderclaps,
oxen trembled and birds fell,
yet the town guests only felt a deep rumbling.
Xiāo Huàn
Táng's Xiāo Huàn,
upon first arriving at Suìzhōu,
had two banner poles made
and donated them to a temple.
After the celebratory vegetarian feast concluded,
music was performed.
Suddenly, violent thunder struck the poles,
shattering them into several dozen pieces.
On the anniversary of that thunder strike,
Huàn died.
Monk Wénjìng
Monk Wénjìng of the Shuǐlù Temple in Jīnzhōu during the Táng,
because his summer quarters leaked,
had water drip onto his head,
which then formed a small sore.
After a year,
it resembled a large peach.
In the following year after the fifth month,
during a thunderstorm with lightning strikes,
the growth was pierced.
Wénjìng, asleep, was unaware;
upon waking, he only felt pain in the growth.
He sent someone to look at it,
and it appeared as if cut by a knife.
Something was hidden within,
in the shape of a coiled dragon.
Xú Zhìtōng
Táng's Xú Zhìtōng,
was a physician from Chǔzhōu.
On a summer night under the moonlight,
he was strolling along a willow embankment.
Suddenly, he saw two strangers
chatting and laughing on the river bridge,
unaware of Zhìtōng's presence in the shadows.
They said to each other:
"What shall we do for amusement tomorrow morning?"
One said:
"Nothing beats going to Chìyán Mountain in Nánhǎi to play with pearls."
The other replied:
"The master of Chìyán is fond of wine,
and when he keeps guests, he gets them drunk.
I have business in the Western Sea tomorrow afternoon,
and I fear going there might cause further delays.
It would be better to simply compete in skills before the Lóngxīng Temple in this commandery."
The first said:
"What feat do you intend to perform?"
The second said:
"There are ancient locust trees before the temple,
nearly a hundred of them.
With one clap of my thunder,
I will split them into slender stalks,
their lengths and thicknesses
all like chopsticks.
How will you match that?"
The first replied:
"The area before the temple has long been the commandery's performance ground.
At midday each day,
the gathered spectators
total no less than thirty thousand people.
With one clap of my thunder,
I will tousle all their hair loose,
and each strand will be tied into seven knots."
The two men then laughed heartily,
agreed on the wager, and departed.
Zhìtōng found this strange.
He immediately told six or seven friends,
and at daybreak,
they went ahead to wait.
At that time, the weather was clear and bright.
Around the hour of wǔ (11 am-1 pm),
suddenly two clouds,
as large as cartwheels,
congealed above the temple.
In a moment, it turned dark,
and one could not see an inch ahead.
Soon, two thunderclaps sounded,
and people and animals immediately fell prostrate.
When the sky cleared,
the locust grove before the temple
was split and scattered,
spread upon the ground,
all like counting rods.
Large, small, thick, thin—
none failed to resemble them.
And before the temple, the tens of thousands of vendors, performers, and spectators
all had their hair loosened,
each strand tied into seven knots.
Also, at the Tiānjīn Bridge in Luòjīng,
a Confucian scholar
encountered two old men talking,
whose demeanor and bearing were most unusual.
Eavesdropping, he heard them say:
"Tomorrow at noon,
we shall compete in swiftness at the temple."
One said:
"What do you intend to do?"
The other said:
"With one sound from me,
all the donkeys and horses listening to lectures in the temple will have their tails knotted."
The first said:
"With one sound from me,
all the ten-zhang banner poles will become counting rods,
still arranged in piles of ten."
The scholar then went with one or two close friends
to wait at the temple.
At noon,
there was indeed thunder and rain.
With one clap of thunder,
the guests ran out to look:
several hundred donkeys and horses all had knotted tails.
With another clap,
the banner poles in the corridor became counting rods,
in piles of ten.
Léigōng Temple
West of Léizhōu is the Temple of the Thunder God,
where the common people annually match drums with thunder chariots.
If anyone eats pork together with fish,
they are immediately struck by thunder,
and all revere and fear this.
After each heavy thunderstorm,
black stones are often found in the wild,
called "thunder ink."
When struck, they ring like metal,
glossy and shiny like lacquer.
Also, in places struck by lightning,
or within earth and wood,
wedge-shaped objects like axes are found,
called "lightning wedges."
Children wear them as charms
to ward off fright and evil spirits;
pregnant women grind and ingest them
as a labor-inducing medicine.
It is always effective.
Nánhǎi
In Nánhǎi during autumn and summer,
sometimes when the sky appears somber,
a halo like a rainbow is seen,
six or seven chǐ long.
This sign means a typhoon will surely arise,
so it is called the "typhoon mother."
If a sudden clap of thunder is heard,
then the typhoon will not occur.
Sailors often use this as an omen
to prepare in advance.
Chén Yì
Two hundred lǐ south of Luózhōu in the Táng dynasty,
one reaches Léizhōu,
which is the Hǎikāng Commandery.
South of Léizhōu borders the great sea,
and the commandery is named so because of the frequent thunderstorms.
The thunder always sounds as if it is right above the eaves.
North of Léizhōu is highland,
and thunderstorms are also frequent there,
but the thunder sounds as if it is beyond the ordinary.
The people there serve the thunder god,
with great reverence and caution,
always offering wine and food in sacrifice.
If anyone eats pork mixed with fish,
lightning immediately strikes.
In the south there is a tree called "diào,"
whose boiled juice is used to soak plums and prunes,
commonly called "diào juice."
If anyone eats this mixed with pork,
lightning also strikes.
Violation always brings a response.
The biography of the garrison commander Chén Yì says:
"Yì is a descendant of the thunder god.
Long ago, the Chén family, during a thunderstorm that darkened the day,
found a large egg in their courtyard.
They incubated it for several months,
the egg cracked,
and an infant emerged.
Later, thunder knocked at their door and courtyard,
entered their house,
approached the child,
as if to nurse it.
After more than a year,
when the child could eat,
it no longer came,
and they raised him as their own son.
Yì is that child from the egg.
It is also said:
"Once there was a thunder clansman
who kept a hunting dog
with twelve ears.
Whenever they were about to hunt,
they would whip the dog,
and the number of ears that twitched indicated the catch.
It never failed,
they twitched.
One day,
all twelve ears twitched.
After hunting,
it no longer chased animals.
Instead, it went to the seaside marsh and howled.
The commandery people went to look,
found,
and brought back twelve large eggs,
placing them in a room.
Later, during a sudden storm,
it seemed to come from that room.
After clearing, they went to look,
and found the eggs broken, with only the shells remaining.
Later, the commandery people divided the eggshells,
offering sacrifices to them annually,
and to this day, those who possess these leftover shells are considered prominent families.
Sometimes on overcast, foggy evenings,
the commandery people call it 'thunder plowing.'
At dawn, looking in the wilds,
there are indeed plowed tracks.
This is considered an auspicious sign.
Also, sometimes thunder fires ignite in the wilds,
and after each rain clears,
black stones are found,
either round or square,
called 'thunder ink.'
In any lawsuit, when submitting a petition,
it is advantageous to write it with thunder ink mixed with ordinary ink.
If someone falls ill,
they clean an empty room,
set out wine and food,
with drums, banners, and canopies,
and welcome the thunder god from dozens of lǐ away.
After returning,
they slaughter cattle and pigs for sacrifice,
placing them at the door.
Neighbors dare not enter rashly;
anyone who mistakenly offends is considered impetuous,
greatly disrespectful,
and must offer pigs or cattle in apology.
After three days, they make another offering,
following the same ritual.
It is also said:
Once, a thunder clansman,
during a great thunderstorm,
saw a creature in the air,
with a pig's head and scaly body,
a very strange appearance.
The man swung his sword and struck it,
the creature fell to the ground,
blood flowing on the road,
and the thunder grew even fiercer.
That night, it flew away into the sky.
Afterwards, the house of the man who swung the sword
was frequently struck by heavenly fire.
Even if he fled,
it followed as before.
His father and brothers then banished him,
and he built a hut by the mountains to live alone,
but the disasters still followed him.
Only when he dug a cave in the cliff to live
did the disasters stop.
Some say
his sword still exists.
Thunder clansmen who draw images of the thunder god for worship
all depict it with a pig's head and scaly body.
Yè Qiānsháo
Yè Qiánsháo of the Táng Dynasty was a native of Xìnzhōu.
In his childhood, while gathering firewood and herding,
he took shelter from the rain under a large tree.
The tree was struck by lightning,
but shortly after, it closed back up,
trapping the Thunder God within its branches,
unable to fly away.
Qiánsháo used a stone wedge to pry open the branches,
allowing him to escape.
The Thunder God, feeling grateful, thanked him and
made an appointment, saying:
"Come back to this place tomorrow."
As instructed, he went there,
and the Thunder God also arrived,
giving him a scroll of black seal script,
saying:
"Follow this to perform rituals,
and you can summon thunder and rain,
cure illnesses and suffering,
and achieve merits by saving people.
There are five of us brothers;
if you need to hear thunder,
just call for Léi Dà or Léi Èr,
and we will respond.
However, Léi Wǔ has a fierce and impatient temperament,
so unless it is a critical emergency,
do not summon him."
From then on, he used talismans to summon rain,
all with remarkable effects.
Once, he got heavily drunk in Jízhōu Market,
and the prefect captured and reprimanded him,
intending to inflict punishment and humiliation.
Qiánsháo shouted "Léi Wǔ" loudly in the courtyard.
At that time, the commandery was suffering from a drought,
with the sun blazing fiercely,
but with a sudden clap of thunder,
everyone was thrown into disarray.
The prefect descended the steps to receive him with respect,
requesting him to bring rain.
After two nights, heavy rain poured down,
filling the fields sufficiently,
and thus his reputation spread far and wide.
Traveling to Huázhōu,
there had been prolonged rainfall at the time,
and the Huáng Hé River was flooding.
The officials were exhausted from flood prevention efforts,
forgetting even to eat or sleep.
Qiánsháo used an iron slip,
two chǐ long,
and erected a talisman on the riverbank.
The water surged and piled up like a hill,
flowing downstream along the river,
not daring to overflow beyond the talisman.
Thus, people were spared from drowning,
and this story is still passed down today.
When people fell ill and requested talismans,
he would write them without selecting specific brushes or ink,
and they would all prove effective.
He often traveled around Jiāngzhè,
enjoying meat and fish,
and did not cultivate religious practices.
Later, it was unknown where he went.
Yuán Zhěn
Yuán Zhěn of the Táng Dynasty
governed Jiāngxià.
In Xiāngzhōu, he had a villa at Jiǎshù.
When constructing a hall,
just as the beams were set in place,
a fierce wind and heavy rain arose.
At that time, each household contributed six or seven vats of oil,
but with a sudden clap of thunder,
the vats all lined up on the beams,
without a single drop spilled outside.
That year, Yuán Zhěn passed away.
Péi Yòng
During the Dàhé era of the Táng Dynasty,
there was a military officer named Péi Yòng in Púzhōu,
whose family was wealthy.
At the age of sixty-two,
he fell ill and died.
Ten days after his burial,
thunder struck his tomb,
causing the coffin to fly out about a hundred paces,
scattering the corpse and coffin.
His family immediately selected another location to rebury him,
using a large iron chain to secure the coffin.
Not long after,
thunder struck again as before.
They selected another location to rebury him,
but within ten days,
thunder struck again as before,
reducing the coffin to ashes,
making it impossible to collect.
Therefore, they set up a spiritual altar
and conducted a soul-summoning ceremony for burial.
Dōngyáng Commandery Mountain
In the Táng Dynasty, Dōngyáng Commandery bordered the Zhèjiāng River.
There was a mountain spanning several hundred lǐ in circumference,
with the river curving and encircling it,
causing boats to be delayed and stranded,
which greatly troubled people.
The Regular Attendant Jìng Xīn,
during the Dàhé era, was appointed as its governor.
One evening, clouds darkened the mountain,
and a violent storm with thunder and lightning
shook the houses.
The river surged and overflowed,
causing widespread panic.
Only at dawn did it clear.
When people went to look,
the mountain had been split in half,
separated by several hundred paces,
allowing the river to flow straight through.
The curved sections
were filled with stones,
eliminating the problem of winding delays.
Duàn Chéngshì's Elder
Duàn Chéngshì of the Táng Dynasty had a third paternal uncle
who, in his youth, was staying at the home of relatives in Yángxiàn.
One night during a thunderstorm,
whenever lightning flashed,
he saw dozens of human heads in the light,
larger than baskets.
Zhì Kōng
Zhì Kōng, a monk of the Jiànyuán Temple in Jìnlíng Commandery during the Táng Dynasty,
was a native of the commandery,
renowned in the local community for his religious practice,
and over seventy years old.
One evening, after closing the door,
a great wind and thunder suddenly arose,
as if originating from the meditation hall,
rumbling incessantly.
The candles went out, dust filled the air,
and it became extremely dark,
with the eaves and building shaking.
Startled, he thought to himself:
"I abandoned my family to become a monk,
and it has been four decades now.
If the thunder is this violent,
could it be that the divine dragon is angry with me?
If not,
then I must have committed a crime deserving death by thunder."
As the noise grew louder,
he sat down again and prayed:
"I have studied Buddhism since youth,
and have been a monk for over fifty years.
Could my actions have violated the teachings of Buddhism?
If not,
then perhaps I have offended the divine dragon?
If so,
how dare I escape death?
If not,
I pray for the skies to clear quickly,
allowing all the monks in the temple to understand."
As soon as he finished speaking,
a loud sound erupted,
as if coming from beside him.
The mats and couches overturned,
darkness and chaos ensued,
and he was so frightened that he fell to the ground.
After about the time of a meal,
the noise ceased,
and the clouds cleared, revealing the moon.
However, he noticed a foul, fishy smell,
as if inside the room.
Lighting a candle to look,
he found a jiāo skin under the wall,
several zhàng long,
with blood covering the ground.
It turned out that north of the meditation hall,
there was a pagoda tree several tens of xún tall,
which had been struck dead by lightning,
split open along its grain,
with traces of a coiled jiāo inside.
Bǎizhàng Deep Pool
Over a hundred li southeast of Hédōng Commandery in the Táng dynasty,
there was an expanse of water,
called the Hundred-Zhàng Deep.
It was clear and pure,
reflecting even the tiniest detail.
Located to the left of the post road,
it was surrounded by locust and willow trees,
their misty shadows gathered like a bundle.
Travelers passing this way
would make it a place to rest their carriages.
In the summer of the fifth year of the Tàihé era,
a certain Xú Shēng, traveling from Luòyáng to Hédōng,
reached this water.
Being extremely weary,
he rested there for a while,
gazing out while reciting poetry.
As noon approached,
he suddenly heard a faint sound from the water,
like the buzzing of flies and gnats.
Soon, a slender light appeared,
and the sound grew slightly louder,
rumbling like the striking of a chariot hub.
The light was like a rope being dragged.
Shēng began to find this strange.
The sound persisted and grew more numerous,
and then thunder arose from the waves,
its shaking light becoming lightning,
connecting with the clouds.
Upon reaching his lodging,
he immediately spoke of the event.
The reply was:
"This is the Hundred-Zhàng Deep.
In years of drought,
it has never failed to bring rain at the appointed time.
Now the drought is severe,
and our prefect has ordered his subordinate officials to pray here."
The shaman said:
"On a certain day there will be heavy rain."
And indeed, that was the day.
Yáng Xúnměi's Nephew
Yáng Xúnměi, a Táng dynasty Censor,
resided in Guǎnglíng Commandery.
He had several young nephews
who had just begun studying with a teacher.
One evening there was wind and rain,
with thunder, lightning, shaking, and brilliance.
The boys all went outside to look,
laughing and cursing, saying:
"We've heard thunder has ghosts,
but we don't know,
where are these ghosts?
We wish we could catch and kill them,
wouldn't that be good?"
Soon the thunder grew even more intense,
and the trees swayed and bent.
Suddenly, with a booming sound,
it seemed as if it was right at the eaves.
The boys were terrified,
and immediately rushed back inside,
standing with their backs against the wall,
not daring to move.
They heard the thunder again,
as if roaring with a great, earth-shaking shout,
making the house shake.
The boys grew even more frightened.
After nearly the time it takes to eat a meal,
the thunder and lightning finally ceased,
and the sky cleared with a bright moon.
In the courtyard was a large, ancient locust tree;
it had been struck, its roots torn out and split apart.
The boys felt unbearable pain in both their thighs,
and reported it all to Xúnměi.
He ordered a servant to hold a candle and look;
all their thighs had red marks,
dozens of them running crosswise,
resembling the marks of caning.
It seemed to be the work of the thunder ghosts.
The Man from Gāoyóu
The Táng dynasty Presented Scholar Zhèng Huī's family was in Gāoyóu.
A relative's Lú family estate was near the water.
Several neighboring families
together killed a white snake.
Not long after,
suddenly there was a great clap of thunder,
and rain poured down,
causing those several families to be completely submerged and drowned.
The Lú residence was in the middle,
yet only that one household was unharmed.
Wáng Zhōngzhèng
Wáng Zhōngzhèng, gatekeeper of Sìzhōu in the Táng dynasty, said
that during the Kāichéng era,
he once died and came back to life after twelve days.
At first he saw a person
in green clothes with a red headscarf,
who stretched out an arm, ascended the clouds, and said,
"Heaven summons you to go;
you are assigned to the Left Falling Brigade."
These Left and Right Falling Brigades
each had fifty thousand armored horses,
massed upon the cloud tops.
Looking down from the side,
even within multi-storied buildings, deep chambers,
sacks and cabinets,
the finest details were all visible.
What was even stranger
was seeing grains of rice several feet long.
There were two brigades in total.
One brigade used small-necked bottles
to store water from the human world.
What the other brigade stored was like saltpeter crystals,
called 'dry rain.'
They were all in front,
with wind chariots bringing up the rear.
Whenever thunder rumbled,
it was mostly for capturing dragons.
Dragons who had committed faults
were demoted to become snakes or fish.
When their number reached a thousand,
they could submerge mountains.
When making rain,
first a yellow flag was lowered,
then flags for the four directions,
and then they followed wherever the dragon was.
Sometimes there was thunderclaps, sometimes rolling thunder,
sometimes rain, sometimes hail.
If they injured a single creature,
they were punished with an iron staff.
Zhōngzhèng served for eleven days,
and only then drank three bowls of broth,
after which he was no longer hungry or weary.
Because his mother was old, he pleaded pitifully,
and was allowed to return.
Shǐ Wúwèi
Shǐ Wúwèi of the Táng dynasty,
a man of Cáozhōu,
was a friend of Zhāng Cóngzhēn.
Wúwèi merely farmed his few acres,
and his clothing and food were meager and difficult.
Cóngzhēn's family was wealthy,
so he said to him,
saying:
"Brother, you toil hard in the fields,
laboring day and night for little gain.
I will lend you a thousand strings of cash for trade;
someday just return my principal."
Wúwèi happily accepted the strings of cash,
and he and his father sought profit between the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
Within a few years,
he had become wealthy.
Cóngzhēn, meanwhile, suffered successive fires
and fell victim to robbers,
until his livelihood was completely wiped out.
He then went to Wúwèi and said:
"In my present hardship,
I don't expect the thousand strings you owe me,
but could you help me with two or three hundred?"
Upon hearing Cóngzhēn's words,
Wúwèi immediately refused and blocked him,
replying:
"If you say I owe you,
just bring the loan contract."
Cóngzhēn returned home,
his heart filled with hatred and resentment.
In his courtyard, he burned incense,
wept tears, and cursed him,
his words impassioned and forceful,
making those who heard them tremble with fear.
In the afternoon,
patches of black cloud suddenly rose in the east and west.
In a moment,
pouring rain, thunder, and lightning arrived together.
With a clap of thunder,
Wúwèi suddenly transformed into an ox,
with vermilion writing on its belly saying:
"The ungrateful man Shǐ Wúwèi."
After ten days, he died.
The Prefect recorded the event and submitted a memorial about it.
Zhāng Yìng
During the Tang dynasty, Zhāng Yìng
was ordered to travel from Xíngyáng to Hénèi Commandery.
While crossing the Jiǔdǐng ford,
the small steed he was riding bolted in fright.
Upon reaching the northern bank,
he saw something coiled around its hind leg,
resembling a large earthworm,
and crimson in color.
He then drew his waist knife,
cut it off onto the ground,
but it immediately reconnected itself.
It hardened and shrank into a white horn comb,
with a red shadow like a thread
crisscrossing it.
He then placed it in his bag.
After finishing his business and returning,
he crossed the river again,
arriving at Píngyīn.
The weather was sweltering and steaming,
so he rested by a garden well
and went to wash up.
He then spoke with the old gardener about it
and took out the horn comb, placing it on the water in a basin.
Suddenly, a black vapor surged forth,
dense clouds gathered from all directions,
fierce lightning and thunderclaps erupted,
and rain and hail fell together.
After about the time of a meal, it finally cleared,
the basin was dry, and the comb had vanished.
The Tiāngōng Altar
In the Bā-Shǔ region,
on mountaintops or on purified ground,
Tiāngōng altars are erected
to pray for rain or clear weather.
This is likely the ritual method descended by the Supreme Deity during the Kāiyuán era,
to show people.
If the altar is desecrated by sheep or cattle,
or if those participating in the fast drink wine or eat meat,
they are often struck dead by lightning.
Wáng Ráo of Xīnfán
went to his villa,
and villagers cooked pork to entertain him.
One man, returning from a fast at the Tiāngōng altar,
immediately ate meat at the feast.
Wáng said to him:
"Aren't you afraid of thunderbolts?"
The man replied:
"I am brothers with Thunder;
what is there to fear?"
Wáng found this strange
and questioned him about what he meant.
He said:
"I have received the Thunder Register,
and share the same duties as Thunder."
Wáng then took his register to examine it,
and indeed it was as he said.
There were also several scrolls:
one depicted a strong man
punching the ground to create a well,
called the "Fist-Punched Well."
Another depicted a man carrying a bundle of firewood,
called "One Valley of Firewood."
Another showed seven hands scooping up a mountain into a basket,
called the "Seven-Mountain Basket."
At the residence of Lǐ the Daoist priest in Dōngcūn, Jiānglíng,
there was also such a register.
Some say
that outside the Three Caverns ritual baskets,
there are one hundred and two methods,
which are forbidden by the Celestial Master and his successor.
They are only permitted for saving beings;
if used for evil purposes,
the Supreme Deity will surely investigate, hold accountable, and punish in the shadows.
Shēn Wénwěi
Shēn Wénwěi, a commandant of Wèishì,
once recounted
that he had gone to Yùquán Temple south of Luòchéng on business.
It was midsummer,
and to the left of the temple was a pool.
During a great drought,
villagers would pray there,
and it never failed to respond.
South of the pool was a dragon temple.
As Shēn leaned over the pool to look,
he saw something like a withered flower,
with leaves as large as lids.
He threw tiles and stones at it.
A monk said:
"You absolutely must not;
you might provoke the fury of wind and thunder."
Shēn paid no heed.
Soon after,
white mist rose from the water's surface,
reaching only to the mountain's foot.
The temple was on the mountain,
with a stone path winding seven times.
Heavy rain fell,
with thunderclaps striking and rumbling.
By the time he reached level ground,
it was already several feet deep,
and streams and gullies swelled violently.
His donkey carriage and servants
drifted along with the current,
unable to gain footing.
Daylight turned dark as dusk,
and the thunder did not cease.
Shēn's lips and mouth turned black,
and he was extremely terrified.
Soon they reached a village,
and then it cleared.
He indeed caught a cold-induced illness,
but as dawn approached, he broke into a slight sweat,
and by morning, he was unharmed.
Was it the dragon's wrath
that nearly killed him?
Fǎmén Temple
Fǎmén Temple west of Cháng'ān
was a supreme monastery of the Central Plains,
housing a finger joint of the Tathāgata.
Within its illuminated realm,
all who revered the Buddha
paid it homage without exception.
Its halls and buildings were magnificent,
unmatched throughout the land and seas.
After Emperors Xī and Zhāo were displaced,
it was destroyed by bandits and thieves.
With the Central Plains in turmoil and swept clean,
and human strength exhausted,
it could not be rebuilt,
most needing timber and stone.
Suddenly one night,
wind and thunder arose abruptly,
and a violent downpour lasted all night.
At dawn,
the monks looked out
and saw fine timber and massive stones before the temple,
piled up like hills,
stretching over ten miles,
end to end without break,
as if placed there by human effort.
Thereupon, they gathered craftsmen and laborers
and rebuilt the exquisite monastery,
until its appearance was fully restored.
People said ghosts and spirits had delivered them,
and they revered its sacred power even more.
The matter of King Aśoka's transformation stūpa—
was that empty talk?
Chén Xuàn
Chén Xuàn, Tutor to Prince Péng of the Former Shǔ under the Wáng clan,
once served as magistrate of Línxī in Qióngzhōu.
The county office had a fence woven from bamboo and plastered with mud.
After long use,
the mud suddenly peeled away,
revealing only the bamboo.
A maidservant held a torch to look,
and saw a creature coiled within a bamboo joint,
brilliantly patterned,
a small snake.
Soon, the rumble of thunder was faintly heard.
Chén suspected it was a stray dragon
and feared being struck by lightning.
He changed his clothes, lit incense,
and raised his voice in prayer to Thunder, saying:
"If you take the dragon,
please do not be hasty."
Though fierce lightning lit up like day,
from early night until the fourth watch,
the thunder remained faint, not erupting.
Once it finally sounded once,
it soon cleared.
The creature from before was gone,
and no one was harmed by the thunder.
It was as if the thunder god had heeded his earnest prayer.
Péngchéng Buddhist Temple
A certain Yáng Tīng of the state said himself
that at the beginning of the Tiānyòu era,
he was in Péngchéng,
escaping the heat in a Buddhist temple.
Hail was falling heavily
when suddenly a great sound shook the earth.
He ran to look outside the gate
and saw a huge hailstone had fallen in the street,
as tall and wide as the temple tower,
and sunk about ten feet into the ground.
Soon the rain stopped,
and scorching winds and blazing sun returned.
After a month,
the hailstone finally melted completely.
The Ōuyáng Clan
There was a clerk named Ōuyáng in Guǎnglíng,
who lived in front of Juédìng Temple.
His wife had encountered turmoil in her youth
and lost her parents.
At this time, an old man came to the gate,
asking to inform his wife,
"I am your father."
The wife, seeing his poverty and shabbiness,
was displeased
and rejected him.
The father then recounted her name and details of her maternal and paternal relatives very thoroughly,
but the wife still refused to listen.
He also said:
"I have come from afar,
and now have nowhere to return to.
If so,
may I temporarily lodge under your roof for a couple of nights?"
The wife again refused.
Her husband tried to persuade her,
but she would not agree.
The father then left, saying:
"I will bring a lawsuit against you."
Those around thought it was merely a public lawsuit
and did not take it to heart.
At noon the next day,
a violent storm came from the south,
with a thunderclap entering the Ōuyáng residence,
dragging his wife to the central courtyard
and striking her dead.
Floodwaters rose several feet above the ground,
and the neighbors were all shaken and unable to steady themselves.
Several days later,
someone from the Ōuyáng household went to the Hòutǔ Temple,
where they found a document in front of the deity's altar,
which was the old man's written complaint against his daughter.
The Lúshān Oil Seller
An oil seller from Lúshān supported his mother with great filial devotion,
but was struck dead by a violent thunderbolt.
His mother, believing herself innocent,
wept and wailed daily at the shrine of the Jiǔtiān Shǐzhě,
wishing to know the reason.
One night,
she dreamed of a man in red robes who told her:
"Your son often mixed fish oil into his regular oil,
seeking excessive profit.
Moreover, during temple fasts and rituals,
this oil was often used.
The stench of fish polluted the air,
preventing the divine immortals from descending.
His death by thunder was fitting."
The mother learned the truth
and then ceased her lamentations.
Lǐ Chéng
Sū Jiànxióng, a military commissioner in Jiāngnán,
had a country estate
in Pílíng,
and often sent his attendant Lǐ Chéng to travel back and forth to inspect it.
In the sixth month of the yǐmǎo year,
Chéng was returning from the estate
and reached the west of Jùróng County.
At the time, the summer heat was blazing,
and he held an umbrella to shade himself.
Suddenly, a great wind arose,
lifting stones and uprooting trees,
and swept his umbrella canopy away,
leaving him holding only the handle.
After walking several dozen paces,
clouds and rain arrived in force.
Just as he was worrying about getting soaked,
a floating mat suddenly drifted to his location,
so he took it to cover himself.
Soon after, thunder shook the ground,
and from among several houses beside the road,
it lifted one house
and carried it toward the northeast.
Shortly after, it cleared,
and that dwelling was utterly swept away,
with nothing left behind.
Over ten people, old and young,
were gathered in a mulberry grove,
completely unharmed.
In front of the vanished house were footprints
three feet long.
Chéng continued west for several more lǐ,
where he met a person
who asked to buy the mat he was using for cover.
He gave it to him.
After another lǐ or so,
he met another person
who asked to buy the umbrella handle he was carrying.
Chéng found this strange
and said:
"This object is useless;
why do you want to buy it?"
The person only pleaded very earnestly,
never stating the reason.
After following him for several hundred paces,
Chéng gave it to him, and the man left.
The Máoshān Ox
In the gēngyín year,
a village boy from Máoshān was herding oxen.
He washed the sweat-soaked shirt he was wearing
and laid it out on the grass to dry while he took a nap.
When he woke, it was missing,
with only a neighboring boy present beside him.
Thinking the neighbor had stolen it,
they began to argue loudly.
The neighbor boy's father saw this
and angrily said:
"To have raised a son who is a thief—
what use is he?"
He immediately threw him into the water.
The neighbor boy crawled out of the water,
crying out to heaven and proclaiming his innocence several times.
Just as the father was about to throw him in again,
suddenly a thunderstorm arrived violently,
struck the ox dead,
and the sweat shirt was vomited out from the ox's mouth.
The boy was thus spared.
The Pānyú Village Girl
In the gēngshēn year,
in a village in Pānyú, there was an old woman
working in the fields with her daughter.
Suddenly, clouds, rain, and darkness descended,
and when it cleared,
her daughter was missing.
The old woman wailed and searched,
and the neighbors helped look for her,
but she could not be found.
Over a month later,
again clouds, rain, and daytime darkness came,
and when it cleared,
a banquet was laid out in the courtyard,
with dried venison and fish,
fruits, wine, and sauces,
all very abundant and clean.
Her daughter arrived, richly dressed.
The old woman, surprised and delighted, held her.
The girl said she had been taken as a bride by the Thunder God,
who brought her to a stone chamber
where there were many relatives.
The marriage ceremony
was exactly like those among humans.
Now she was allowed to return for a visit,
but in the future she could not come back again.
The old woman asked:
"Can one see Thunder God Lǎng?"
She replied:
"No."
After staying for several nights,
one evening again there was wind, rain, and darkness,
and then she was never seen again.
The Jiāngxī Village Old Woman
In a village in Jiāngxī, during a thunderclap,
an old woman was burned by lightning fire,
with one arm completely injured.
Soon after, a voice from the sky called out:
"A mistake!"
Immediately, a bottle fell,
containing an ointment-like medicine.
It said:
"Apply this to it,
and it will heal."
She did as told,
and as she applied it, it healed.
The family discussed together,
thinking this was divine medicine,
and planned to take and store it.
Several people together tried to lift the bottle,
but could not move it.
Shortly after,
another thunderstorm came,
and it was taken away.
Also, a villager was struck dead by thunder,
and soon a voice from the sky called out:
"A mistake!
Take earthworms, mash them thoroughly,
and apply them over the navel;
it should heal."
They applied it as instructed,
and he revived.
Gānlù Temple
The Daoist Fàn Kěbǎo,
in the summer months, traveled alone to Gānlù Temple in western Zhèxī.
Exiting through the rear door of the main hall,
he was about to ascend to the northern pavilion.
Suddenly, someone wearing an old brown robe,
entered from beside him,
their shoulders and sleeves brushing against each other.
Fàn had always been fond of cleanliness,
his clothes were new,
and he felt displeased.
Shortly after, the person led a yellow dog,
and again brushed shoulders as they exited.
Fàn's anger showed on his face.
The person in brown turned back, glaring,
their eyes flashing like lightning.
Only then did Fàn begin to feel fear.
A moment later,
people from the foot of the mountain arrived and said:
"Just now, thunderbolts from the mountain captured a dragon.
Did you not know?"
Fàn, of course, had not heard it.
In Nánkāng County,
on the fourth day of the fifth month in the Xīnyǒu year,
an envoy passed through Nánkāng.
The county magistrate Hú Kǎn set out wine at the waterside pavilion of the Lotus Lodge south of the county town.
Suddenly, a fierce wind blew sand from the south,
so he covered his eyes with his hands.
He heard,
the vessels on the tray,
rustling with a sound,
as if something had passed by.
After a long while, he opened his eyes,
and saw the eating utensils slightly askew.
The silver wine cups and the cup boats,
were all stretched long into an east-west shape.
A large paulownia tree beside the wall,
was also uprooted and thrown outside the wall.
At that time, this wind and rain extended for a whole li outside,
where people constantly heard the distant rumble of thunder from the lodge,
yet within the lodge itself, they initially heard nothing.
Hú also remained unharmed.
Fáng Xuánlíng
In the late Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty,
Fáng Xuánlíng retired from his position and returned to his residence.
At that time, there was a drought.
Tàizōng was about to visit the Fúróng Garden,
to observe local customs.
Xuánlíng heard of this,
and warned his son, saying:
"The imperial carriage will surely come to visit.
Quickly have the place cleaned and swept,
and also prepare food and utensils."
After a short while,
Tàizōng indeed first visited his residence,
then took him by carriage into the palace.
That evening, heavy rain fell,
and everyone considered it a response to the favor shown to a worthy man.
Amoghavajra
The Táng dynasty Indian monk Amoghavajra,
attained the Dhāraṇī gate,
able to command hundreds of spirits.
Xuánzōng treated him with respect.
During a year of drought,
he was ordered to pray for rain.
Amoghavajra said it could wait until a certain day,
for if they prayed now, it would certainly be a violent storm.
The emperor then ordered Vajra Samādhi,
to set up an altar and pray for rain.
Indeed, continuous heavy rain poured down without ceasing,
causing flooding and drowning in the wards and markets.
He hastily summoned Amoghavajra to stop it.
So, in the temple courtyard,
he built five or six clay dragons.
Then he poured water on them,
and scolded them in a foreign tongue.
After a long while,
he placed them again and laughed heartily.
Shortly after, the rain cleared.
Xuánzōng also once summoned the occultist Luó Gōngyuǎn and Amoghavajra to pray for rain,
each demonstrating their efficacy.
Both were summoned for questioning.
Amoghavajra said:
"Your servant yesterday burned a white sandalwood incense dragon."
The emperor ordered his attendants to scoop up water from the courtyard and smell it,
and indeed there was the scent of sandalwood.
Whenever he prayed for rain,
there were no other special rules,
but he would set up several embroidered seats,
and with his hand, spin a wooden deity figurine a few inches tall,
recite incantations and throw it,
and it would stand upright on the seat by itself.
When the wooden deity's mouth corners showed teeth,
and its eyes blinked,
rain would immediately arrive.
Yīxíng
The monk Yīxíng,
during the Kāiyuán era, there was once a drought.
Xuánzōng ordered him to pray for rain.
He said:
"We must obtain a vessel,
with a dragon shape on it,
only then can we bring it about."
Ordered to search thoroughly within the inner treasury,
all said nothing resembled it.
Later, he pointed to a mirror with a coiled dragon on its nose,
and happily said:
"This is a true dragon."
He took it into the ritual arena,
and in one night, rain fell.
Some say,
this was newly presented from Yángzhōu.
When initially casting the mold,
a strange person arrived,
requesting the doors be closed as he entered the room.
Several days later when the door was opened,
the mold was completed,
but that person had already disappeared.
There are illustrations and accounts,
circulating in the world.
This mirror
was cast on the fifth day of the fifth month in the heart of the Yángzǐ River.
Śubhakarasiṃha
Xuánzōng once visited the Eastern Capital,
during a great drought.
The Indian Tripiṭaka monk Śubhakarasiṃha at Shèngshàn Temple was skilled in summoning dragons to bring rain.
The emperor sent the eunuch Lìshì to urgently summon him to pray for rain.
He memorialized, saying:
"The current drought is fated to be of this duration.
Summoning a dragon will certainly stir fierce winds, thunder, and rain,
which would only damage things,
it should not be done."
The emperor insisted, saying:
"The people have suffered from heat and illness for a long time.
Even if it is a violent storm and sudden thunder,
it would still be satisfying."
Having no choice,
he accepted the decree.
The officials prepared the implements for praying for rain,
banners, canopies, and ritual images were all very complete.
He laughed and said:
"These are not enough to bring rain."
He ordered them all removed,
and only filled a bowl with water,
stirring and swirling it with a small knife,
reciting several hundred incantations in a foreign tongue.
In a short while, a dragon appeared,
shaped roughly like his thumb,
and red in color.
Its head emerged above the water,
then shortly after submerged back into the bowl.
Again, he stirred with the knife and chanted three times.
After a moment,
white vapor arose from the bowl,
like smoke from a furnace,
going straight up several feet,
and gradually extended out of the lecture hall.
He said to Lìshì:
"Go quickly,
the rain is coming."
Lìshì galloped away at full speed.
Looking back, he saw the white vapor,
swirling and stretching across the sky,
like a bolt of plain silk.
Then followed darkness, haze, and a great wind,
with thunderclaps and rain.
Lìshì had just reached the south of Tiānjīn Bridge,
when the wind and rain also followed his horse and arrived.
Many large trees along the imperial avenue were uprooted.
By the time Lìshì returned to report,
his clothes were completely soaked.
The Jade Dragon
Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng reached the Wèi River,
where an attendant found the Jade Dragon and presented it.
The Retired Emperor said:
"When I was an infant,
Empress Tiānhòu summoned all her grandchildren,
seating them in the hall,
to watch them play.
She then brought out jade rings, cups, and plates, tributes from western countries,
arraying them in the hall,
freely allowing the children to seize them,
to observe their inclinations.
All rushed and competed,
gaining much.
At that time, I alone sat still among them,
unmoved.
The Empress patted my back and said:
'This child shall become a Taiping Tiānzǐ (Peaceful Son of Heaven).'
Then she took the Jade Dragon and bestowed it upon me.
Originally, Emperor Tàizōng obtained it in the Jìnyáng Palace,
and Empress Wéndé once placed it within her garments.
On the day of Emperor Gāozōng's birth,
the Empress bestowed it along with pearl-adorned swaddling clothes and the Jade Dragon,
and thereafter it was stored in the inner treasury.
Though not more than a few inches in size,
it was warm, smooth, exquisite, and cleverly made,
unlike anything of the mortal world,
considered an auspicious treasure of the state,
passed down from emperor to emperor.
When the Retired Emperor first ascended the throne,
whenever the capital suffered from drought,
he would pray with it,
and heavy rain would surely pour down.
Looking closely at it,
it seemed as if its scales and mane were stirring.
During the Kāiyuán era,
the three capital regions suffered a great drought.
The Retired Emperor prayed again,
but for over ten days there was no response.
So he secretly cast it into the southern inner palace,
the Dragon Pool.
Suddenly, clouds and mist violently arose,
and wind and rain followed.
When the Retired Emperor traveled to Western Shǔ,
and the imperial carriage returned, stopping at the Wèi River,
about to cross,
they halted by the riverside.
Attendants nearby,
while washing and playing in the stream,
found it in the sand.
From then on, it would glow brilliantly every night,
illuminating the entire room.
When the Retired Emperor returned to the capital,
a young eunuch secretly stole it,
giving it to Lǐ Fǔguó,
who often kept it in a cabinet.
As Fǔguó was about to fall from power,
he heard sounds from the cabinet at night,
opened it to look,
and it had already vanished.
Someone wrote a poem saying:
"The sacred fortune secretly matches the auspicious Jade Dragon,
since stirring clouds and rain, it is bound no more.
Better found in the sands of the Wèi River,
how could it protect the imperial carriage returning to the ninefold palace?"
Dí Wéiqiān
During the Huìcháng era of the Táng dynasty,
Dí Wéiqiān, magistrate of Jìnyáng in the northern capital,
was a descendant of Dí Rénjié.
He upheld his office with purity and diligence,
unafraid of the powerful.
The region under his jurisdiction suffered from intense sun,
from spring until summer,
across several hundred lǐ of farmland,
all was withered and scorched.
Prayers at the Jìn Temple
brought no response.
At that time, there was a Guō Tiānshī (Heavenly Master),
along with a female shaman from Bīngzhōu,
who from youth practiced talismanic arts,
often performing exorcisms.
The military supervisor brought them to the capital,
and through connections with powerful eunuchs,
they entered and left the palace,
and were granted the title of Tiānshī.
Soon they returned to their homeland.
Everyone said:
"If the Tiānshī could come once to the Jìn Temple,
then there would be no need to worry."
Wéiqiān requested from the regional commander,
At first, he was very reluctant.
After repeated earnest invitations,
the commander personally went to welcome them.
The shaman assented.
Then carriages were prepared,
banners and canopies displayed,
and Wéiqiān personally held the reins.
Upon arriving at the temple,
lavish offerings and tents were set up,
and he bowed deeply in the courtyard.
The next day,
she said to Wéiqiān:
"I will fly a talisman to the upper realms to request rain for you,
having already received the command of Heaven and Earth,
it must be done with utmost sincerity;
within three days, rain shall be sufficient."
Thus, scholars and commoners from the four suburbs gathered like clouds,
but when the period ended, there was no sign.
She said again:
"The arising of calamity
is truly due to the magistrate's lack of virtue.
I will appeal to Heaven again for you,
rain should come in seven days."
Wéiqiān accepted the blame,
serving her even more reverently,
yet still there was no effect.
Then she suddenly wanted to return to the prefecture,
but Wéiqiān bowed and entreated her to stay, saying:
"The Tiānshī has already come for the myriad people,
I beg you to pray with utmost heart."
She angrily cursed:
"Mediocre, petty official,
you know not the ways of Heaven.
The time of Heaven is not yet willing to send rain,
what further use is there in keeping me?"
Wéiqiān then apologized:
"I dare not trouble the Tiānshī further;
I only await tomorrow to bid you farewell."
Thereupon, he secretly instructed his subordinates:
"I have been insulted by this shaman,
how can I continue to speak of being an official?
Tomorrow morning, I will give orders;
you must all follow my commands.
Whether right or wrong, good or evil,
I will bear the responsibility myself."
At dawn,
before the gates were opened,
Guō had already prepared her horse for departure,
but Dí had prepared no wine or food offerings.
Guō then sat in the hall,
indulging in loud rebukes.
Wéiqiān then said:
"Heretical female shaman,
deluding people with sorcery for so long,
you shall meet your end today;
how dare you speak of leaving?"
He shouted to his attendants,
had her whipped twenty times on the back before the deity,
and thrown into the swift river.
Behind the temple was a mountain,
about ten zhàng high.
He immediately ordered a mat spread and incense burned,
dismissed all his clerks to return,
and stood atop it with his official cap and tablet.
The entire city was shocked and alarmed,
saying the county chief had caned the Tiānshī to death;
people ran about in confusion,
spectators crowding like a wall.
At that time, sand and stones were scorching,
when suddenly a patch of cloud arose,
large as a carriage canopy,
first covering where Wéiqiān stood,
then clouds from the four suburbs gathered.
Thunder rumbled several times,
sweet rain poured heavily,
flooding every field and plain.
Several thousand scholars and commoners
escorted Wéiqiān down from the mountain.
The regional commander, initially angered by the killing of the shaman,
but witnessing such sincere and effective response,
deeply marveled in admiration.
He submitted a report detailing the events,
and an imperial edict praised and honored it, saying:
"Wéiqiān is an excellent talent of a major county,
a descendant of loyal ministers.
Witnessing this heavenly scourge,
about to afflict the common people,
he prayed at the Jìn Temple,
akin to casting the shaman into the Yè County river.
Exposing himself to the fierce sun on the mountain peak,
his act equaled burning his own body.
Stirring oily clouds from the horizon,
his sentiment matched cutting his own flesh.
Thus causing the drought wind to secretly cease,
and sweet moisture to swiftly flow.
The vast Heaven still oversees sincere virtue;
how could We forget to praise goodness?
Specially bestow the crimson绶 (ribbon),
to glorify the bronze seal.
Do not tarnish your fine name,
but further display extraordinary achievements."
He was then awarded five hundred thousand coins.
Zǐ Láng
In the second month of the thirteenth year of the Dayè era of the Suí dynasty,
Lǐ Mì set up an altar south of Gǒng County,
sacrificed a white horse to Heaven,
proclaimed himself the Duke of Wèi,
and established his official staff.
As he ascended the altar to change the reign era,
a black wind suddenly arose from the northwest,
blowing Lǐ Mì's robes, cap, and his assembled officials
all down from the altar.
Sand and dust darkened the sky,
making it impossible to see even at arm's length,
and it took a long time for the wind to subside.
The rebel army considered this an ill omen,
and soon after, Lǐ Mì was defeated.
Xià Shìlóng
On the site of the old palace of King Wúzhū of Yuè,
there was a great cedar tree,
hollow inside,
capable of seating more than ten people.
Xià Shìlóng, a man of Yuè,
was a lofty recluse who did not serve in office,
and he often visited the old palace.
Once, as the rain cleared and dusk approached,
a broken rainbow drank from the palace pond,
gradually shrinking in size,
and transformed into a man,
wearing a robe of mixed yellow, red, and purple, who then entered the tree,
and did not emerge for a long time.
Shìlóng, finding this strange,
summoned over a dozen young men from the neighborhood,
and went to look.
They saw the man being coiled by a large red snake.
The crowd was afraid and dared not approach,
but the youths threw tiles and stones from a distance.
A most unusual sound was heard from within the tree,
like a woman weeping.
After a short while,
clouds and mist obscured their view,
and they heard a faint sound like distant thunder.
Soon, a colorful dragon
and a red crane flew away.
At dawn,
Shìlóng went to observe.
He saw a purple snakeskin and a multicolored dragon skin inside the tree,
and was about to take them home,
when fire sprang up within the tree,
and the tree was completely consumed by flames.
This was in the seventh month of the third year of the Yǒng'ān era of Emperor Jǐng of Wú.
Chén Jì's Wife
Chén Jì, a man from Bāqiū in Lúlíng,
served as a clerk for the prefecture.
His wife, Qín, was at home
when a tall, handsome man,
wearing a crimson and green robe,
of dazzling color,
came to her.
Afterwards, they often met at a mountain stream,
and even shared a bed,
yet she felt no awareness of a man's touch.
This went on for many years.
Villagers noticed that wherever she went,
a rainbow would appear.
When Qín went to the water's edge,
the man had a golden bottle,
with which he drew water for them to drink together,
and later she became pregnant.
She gave birth to a child,
human in form,
but very fleshy.
When Chén Jì returned on leave,
Qín, afraid he would see it,
hid the child in a basin.
The man said:
"The child is small,
and cannot yet go with me."
He dressed himself,
and then placed the child in a crimson bag.
Whenever the child was brought out to be nursed,
wind and rain would arise,
and neighbors would see a rainbow descend into their courtyard.
The man came again after a while,
took the child away,
and people saw two rainbows emerge from their house.
Several years later, he came to visit his mother.
Later, when Qín went to the fields,
she saw two rainbows over the stream
and was afraid.
After a moment,
she saw the man, who said:
"It is I,
do not fear."
After that, he never came again.
Xuē Yuàn
In the beginning of the Yìxī era of the Eastern Jìn,
Xuē Yuàn of Jìnlíng
had a rainbow drink from his cooking pot,
sucking until it was empty.
Yuàn poured wine into it,
and as he poured, it was drained each time,
until it spat out gold filling the vessel,
and from then on his family grew increasingly wealthy.
Liú Yìqìng
Liú Yìqìng, son of Dàolín, Prince of Chángshā of the Sòng,
was lying ill in Guǎnglíng.
While eating porridge,
a white rainbow suddenly entered the room
and went to drink his porridge.
Yìqìng threw the vessel onto the steps,
whereupon a sound of wind and rain arose,
shaking the courtyard and doors,
and after a long time it vanished.
Shǒuyáng Mountain
