In the second year of the Zhèngguāng era of Emperor Míng of the Later Wèi,
in the summer, the sixth month,
in Shǒuyáng Mountain,
an evening rainbow descended to drink from a stream.
A woodcutter named Yáng Wàn
saw it from the foot of the ridge.
After a long time,
it transformed into a young woman,
appearing about sixteen or seventeen years old.
Finding this strange,
he questioned her, but she did not speak.
He then reported it to the garrison commander of Pújīn, Yǔwén Xiǎn,
who took her and reported it to the court.
Emperor Míng summoned her into the palace,
and saw her beautiful appearance.
He asked, and she said:
"I am a heavenly maiden,
temporarily descended to the mortal world."
The Emperor wished to force himself upon her,
but her expression became very stern.
He then ordered his attendants to seize her,
but her voice sounded like bells and chimes,
and she transformed into a rainbow and ascended to heaven.
Wéi Gāo
Wéi Gāo, Chancellor of the Táng,
was governing Shǔ.
Once, he was feasting with over ten guests and staff members
at the western pavilion of the commandery.
A sudden storm arose,
but cleared after a short while.
Just as they were about to eat,
a rainbow suddenly descended from the sky,
straight into the courtyard,
and lowered its head over the banquet table.
Wéi and his guests retreated in fear,
as it drank up all the food and drink.
Its head resembled a donkey's,
and it shimmered like a clear sunset cloud,
red and green intermingling.
The empty sky was filled with five colors,
and they looked all around,
until after a long time it departed.
The Duke, both afraid and repulsed,
then ended the banquet.
At the time, the former Junior Minister of Hénán, Dòulú Shǔ,
was a guest in Shǔ
and was also seated among them.
He rose and said:
"Why does Your Excellency look so worried?"
Wéi replied:
"I have heard that rainbows
are an ominous, pestilential vapor.
Now, in the midst of our feast, this pestilential vapor has come to our banquet table.
Is this not an extremely strange occurrence?
I secretly fear this."
Shǔ said:
"This is truly an auspicious sign from Heaven,
and certainly not something for men to consider strange.
For the rainbow is a messenger of Heaven;
when it descends upon the wicked, it is a portent of disaster,
but when it descends upon the upright, it is an auspicious sign.
This principle is fitting.
Your Excellency is a righteous man,
so this should be a cause for celebration and good fortune.
I dare to offer my congratulations in advance."
Thereupon, he wrote these words on silk and presented them,
and the Duke read them with pleasure.
More than ten days later,
an imperial edict appointed him Zhōngshū Lìng.
Yùsì Mountain
Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn Dynasty was fond of immortality.
On the summit of Yùsì Mountain,
he set up a Zhēngzhēn Altar and a Grand Reversion Elixir Furnace.
Taoist priests prayed day and night,
and Heaven, moved by their sincerity,
descended a white jade box,
placing it upon the altar.
Emperor Wǔ dispatched an envoy to fetch it.
Upon reaching the side of the altar,
a fierce whirlwind suddenly arose,
sweeping the jade box away.
Hence, it became known as Yùsì Mountain.
Dàhé Mountain
Wáng Cìzhòng, a man from Shàngjùn,
from a young age possessed extraordinary aspirations.
He transformed the ancient script of Cāngjié into the modern clerical script.
During the time of Qín Shǐhuáng,
official affairs were numerous and complex.
Finding the script changed by Cìzhòng
simple and convenient for matters,
he thus summoned him.
Three summonses were issued, yet he did not come.
Cìzhòng cherished the Way and practiced truth,
mastering the subtleties of numerology.
Shǐhuáng, angered by his disrespect,
ordered him sent in a caged cart.
While Cìzhòng was on the journey,
he suddenly transformed into a great bird,
emerged from the cart,
and flew away, soaring.
Two wings fell upon this mountain,
hence the peaks bear the names Dàhé and Xiǎohé.
The Wèi dynasty's "Record of Lands" states:
"Sixty lǐ northeast of Jǔyáng City,
are the Dàhé and Xiǎohé Mountains.
The mountain deity is named Dàhé.
East of the temple is the mouth of the Hot Spring waters.
The hot spring can cure myriad illnesses.
The foothill from which the spring emerges
is commonly called Tǔtíng Mountain.
The northern waters are hotter than other springs;
those seeking treatment
must carefully discern and use them accordingly."
Mountain Spirits
Zhāng Gài from Wú Tiānmén,
in winter,
went hunting with villagers.
He saw a thatched hut beneath a large tree,
resembling a resting place,
yet without any sign of fire or smoke.
After a while,
he saw a person,
seven chǐ tall,
hairy and unclothed,
carrying several dead monkeys.
Gài spoke to him, but received no response.
He then took him back,
confining him in an empty room.
After over ten days,
he returned him to the original place.
Also, during Sūn Hào's time,
a hairy man was captured in Línhǎi.
"The Classic of Mountains and Seas" says:
"Mountain spirits resemble humans,
with hairy faces."
This
is
a mountain spirit.
Therefore, "Bàopǔzǐ" states:
"The essence of mountains
has a form like a small child with a single foot.
The foot faces backward.
It delights in coming to harass people.
Its name is Qí.
If you know and call it by name,
it will retreat of its own accord.
It
also has a name, Chāokōng,
which can also be called out."
There is another mountain spirit,
sometimes like a drum,
red in color with one foot,
its name is Hún.
Another sometimes resembles a human,
nine chǐ tall,
wearing fur and a bamboo hat,
named Jīn Lěi.
Another sometimes resembles a dragon,
with five red horns,
named Fēilóng.
Upon seeing them,
if you can call their names,
they dare not cause harm.
"Xuánzhōng Jì"
states: Mountain spirits resemble humans,
with one foot,
three to four chǐ tall.
They eat mountain crabs,
emerging at night and hiding by day.
Shíjī Mountain
During the turmoil of the Yǒngjiā era of the Jìn dynasty,
in Yíyáng, there was a woman,
surname Péng, given name É.
Her parents and brothers were captured by bandits from Chángshā.
At the time, É was carrying a vessel to fetch water from the stream.
Upon returning, she saw the village wall already breached,
and was nearly overcome with grief.
She struggled with the bandits,
who bound É
and drove her to the stream's edge.
At the moment they were about to kill her,
there was a great mountain stone cliff.
É looked up and cried out to Heaven:
"Mountain spirits, if you have divine power,
what crime have I committed?"
She then ran towards the mountain.
The mountain immediately split open,
several zhàng wide.
The level path was like a whetstone.
The bandits also chased É into the mountain.
The mountain then collapsed and closed,
vanishing as if it had never opened.
The bandits were all crushed to death inside the mountain,
their heads protruding outside.
É then vanished and never reappeared.
The water-fetching vessel É had set down
transformed into stone,
shaped like a chicken.
The local people thus named it Shíjī Mountain,
and the stream became É Tán.
Xīnfēng Mountain
During the reign of Emperor Gāozōng of the Táng dynasty,
a mountain emerged in Xīnfēng,
two hundred chǐ high.
There was a divine pool,
forty chǐ deep.
A yellow dragon appeared in the water,
spitting out a treasure pearl,
which floated out, as large as a fist.
Drums sounded within the mountain.
Xīnfēng County was renamed Qìngshān County.
Qìngshān
Zhāoyìng Qìngshān.
During the Cháng'ān era,
it was also unknown from where it had flown.
Passing by at night,
a sound like thunder was heard,
swift as a gallop,
yellow
Earth and stones rained down chaotically,
falling straight to the southwest of Xīnfēng.
A village of over a hundred households
was buried by the mountain, forming a tomb.
Now, upon it stands the Chíguó Temple.
Wèng Peak
At the Yúntái Temple on Huà Mountain,
upon the central summit,
a mountain rises abruptly,
shaped like half a jar,
named Wèngdù Peak.
Emperor Xuánzōng once admired the view,
praising its lofty and winding form.
He wished to carve the characters "Kāiyuán" large upon the mountain's belly,
filling them with white stone,
so they could be seen from over a hundred lǐ away.
Remonstrating officials submitted memorials,
and he desisted.
Kuāfù Mountain
East of Chénzhōu are three mountains,
standing like a tripod, rising straight up,
each several thousand zhàng high.
An ancient tradition says:
Dèng Kuāfù raced with the sun.
Reaching here, he cooked a meal.
These three mountains
are the stones Kuāfù used to prop up his tripod.
Chāzào
In Jīngzhōu there is the Kōnglíng Gorge,
where sheer cliffs stand erect for several hundred zhang,
and even flying birds do not roost.
There is a burnt-out torch,
inserted into the cliff face,
visible from afar, perhaps several chi in length.
It is said that
during the great flood,
boat travelers moored and cooked here,
and inserted the remaining embers,
which to this day is still called "Inserted Hearth."
Héshān Stone Basin
In Róngzhōu's Héshuǐ,
there is a spring halfway up the cliff,
whose water flows down below,
descending in nine steps,
each step with a white stone bathing basin to catch it,
as if carved and fashioned.
Once someone brought a maidservant,
who took down a basin to wash towels.
Suddenly,
wind and rain abruptly arrived,
and the maidservant was struck dead by lightning.
The basin used for washing towels
shattered at the foot of the mountain.
Since then, another basin was installed,
newer than the previous one.
Zhōngnán Milk Cave
Someone visited a milk cave in the Zhōngnán Mountains,
the cave several li deep,
with milk-like formations slowly dripping,
forming shapes like flying immortals.
There were already several dozen in the cave,
with eyebrows, eyes, and clothing,
exquisitely crafted in form.
At one spot, the dripping reached above the waist,
and the person cupped his hands to catch and rinse with it.
Returning a year later,
he saw that the drips he had caught had already solidified into a figure,
the milk no longer dripping,
and at the spot where he had cupped his hands,
the clothing was missing two cun, incomplete.
Ancient Iron Chain
In Qíjùn, bordering Lìshān,
there is an ancient iron chain.
As thick as an arm,
it coils around the peak twice.
Legend says it was originally a mountain in the sea,
and the mountain spirit liked to move,
so the sea god chained it.
When the chain was pulled and broke,
it flew here.
Yáshān
East of Tàiyuánjùn lies Yáshān.
During droughts,
locals often burn this mountain to pray for rain.
Folklore says the Yáshān spirit married the daughter of the River Earl,
so when the River Earl sees fire,
he must send rain to save it.
Now the mountain grows much aquatic grass.
Shèngzhōng Mountain
In Lízhōu's Shèngzhōng Mountain,
ancient lore says this mountain has a bell,
whose sound is heard but its form unseen.
When Nánzhào invaded the border,
the bell would ring in advance.
During the Táng dynasty's Tiānbǎo, Dàhé, Xiántōng, and Qiánfú eras,
when barbarian tribes came to raid,
there were always omens.
Once a famous monk lectured on the *Mahāyāna Sūtras and Treatises*,
and the bell also trembled.
During the Qiánníng era,
Prefect Zhāng Huì'ān invited the monk Huìwéi from Jīngshī's Right Street Jìngzhòng Temple to lecture once on the *Lotus Sutra*,
and this bell frequently rang,
as if struck by someone,
proving the earlier legends not false.
Sōngliáng Mountain
In Lǐzhōu's Sōngliáng Mountain,
now called Shímén.
In the sixth year of Yǒng'ān,
it naturally opened into a cave,
dark and bright like a gate,
three hundred zhang high.
Bamboo grew on the corners,
hanging down and sweeping,
called "Heaven's Broom."
Shígǔ Mountain
In Shèzhōu's Shígǔ Mountain,
there is a stone shaped like a drum,
and also stone figures and stone donkeys.
Folklore says when the stone drum sounds,
the donkey brays and people weep,
and the county officials face misfortune.
Later, the drum was chiseled and broken,
and it never sounded again.
Shèdì Mountain
Kǒng Yè
in *Records of Kuàijī* says:
"Shèdì Mountain,
viewed from afar, appears distinct,
like an archery target,
hence called Shèdì.
To the south is a stone chamber,
about one square zhang,
called the Archery Chamber.
It is said
immortals roamed and rested here,
and locals often used this to predict grain prices.
A proverb says:
'When Shèdì is white,
a hú of rice costs one hundred;
when Shèdì is dark,
a hú of rice costs one thousand.
'" Kǒng Língfú's *Records of Kuàijī* says:
"The water at Shèdì Rock is several tens of zhang deep,
so clear the bottom is visible.
To its west is a mountain,
reaching into the clouds and mist.
Halfway up the ridge is a stone chamber,
called the Immortal's Archery Hall.
East of the water, a high cliff overlooks a pool,
with a target-like stone,
very round and bright in shape,
gazing at it like a mirror."
Also, *Kuàijī Records* says:
"Immortals often shot here,
sending white cranes to fetch arrows,
north of which stands a stone sail, sheer as a wall."
Guàishān
Within the city walls of Shānyīn, Kuàijī,
there is Guàishān,
traditionally said to be originally Lángyá's Dōngwǔ Mountain.
Once, during a dark, rainy night,
by morning it was seen here.
The people found it strange,
hence named it Guàishān.
Míngnáo Mountain,
Xiāo Zǐkāi's *Records of Jiàn'ān* says:
"Also called Dàgē Mountain,
King Wúzhū of Yuè,
riding an elephant-drawn carriage,
with his great general riding alongside.
With clashing cymbals and raised banners,
they hunted and ascended this mountain."
Ancient lore says
when rain is about to fall,
the mountain produces music-like sounds.
Gàntái
Three hundred sixty-three lǐ southeast of Gàntái County, Qiánzhōu.
*Records of Nánkāng* says:
On the mountain is a platform,
several zhang square in area,
with natural rosy clouds,
shaped like a house.
After wind and rain,
the scenery bright and clear,
one can distinctly hear music and drumming on the mountain,
which are the Shāndū and Mùkè,
singing and dancing.
Shàngxiāo Peak
Supplemental Official Xióng Jiǎo said:
Lúshān has a Shàngxiāo Peak,
seven thousand ren above flat ground,
with stone traces atop,
said to be where Xià Yǔ,
when regulating the waters, moored his boat.
He chiseled holes in the rock,
to tie the cables.
He polished the cliff into a stele,
all in tadpole script,
faintly visible.
Thus we know the achievements of Great Yǔ
are as eternal as heaven and earth.
Màijīshān
Màijīshān
spans north across the Qīng and Wèi rivers,
and extends south toward Liǎngdāng.
Across five hundred lǐ of ridges and peaks,
Màijīshān occupies half of them.
A massive rock rises abruptly,
towering a million fathoms high.
Viewed from afar, it appears round and full,
resembling a stack of wheat as commonly seen among the people,
hence it bears this name.
Halfway up into the clouds,
on its sheer cliffs,
Buddhas have been carved from the stone,
with ten thousand niches and a thousand chambers.
Though made by human labor,
one might suspect it to be the work of ghosts.
Emperor Wén of Sui separately enshrined a casket containing relics of the divine nun beneath the eastern pavilion.
Within the stone chambers,
there is an inscription by Yǔ Xìn,
engraved into the cliff.
An ancient record states:
"Six states jointly built it.
Starting from level ground, they piled up firewood,
reaching the cliff summit.
From above, they carved the niches, chambers, and Buddha images.
When the work was completed,
they gradually removed the firewood and descended.
Only afterward did they ascend by ladders through empty space and across perilous heights.
Above, there is the Sànhuā Lóu,
the Qīfó Gé,
and the Jīntí Yínjiǎo Dú'ér.
From the western pavilion, a hanging ladder leads upward.
Within, there are a thousand rooms and ten thousand halls,
clinging to the void and treading on emptiness.
Those who climb dare not look back.
Approaching the very summit,
there is the Wàn Púsà Táng,
carved from the rock.
Its breadth is like
that of a great hall today.
Its carved beams and painted brackets,
embroidered pillars and cloud-patterned lintels,
are all formed from the living rock.
Ten thousand statues of Bodhisattvas
are arrayed within this hall.
Above this chamber,
there is yet another niche,
called Tiāntáng (Heavenly Hall).
In midair, a single ladder leans against it,
requiring climbing hand over hand to ascend.
Reaching this point,
scarcely one in ten thousand dares to climb it.
Looking down from here,
all the surrounding mountains appear like low mounds.
At that time, Wáng Rényù alone was able to ascend it.
He then inscribed a poem on the western wall of the Tiāntáng, which reads:
"I have trod the hanging ladder of ten thousand fathoms high,
My body casually level with the white clouds.
From the eaves, I look down—the myriad peaks seem small;
Within the hall, I share equally the setting sun hanging low.
The summit path is perilous, few travelers come;
On ancient cliffs, sturdy pines host frequent crows.
At heaven's edge, wishing to leave my name behind,
I diligently wipe the stone and inscribe it with my own hand.
This was inscribed during a visit in the Xīnwèi year of the late Táng dynasty.
Now,
thirty-nine years have passed since then.
Dǒushān Guàn
During the Qiányòu era of the Hàn dynasty,
the Hanlin Academician Wáng Rényù said:
In Xīngyuán, there is a Dǒushān Guàn.
From within the flat plain,
a mountain rises abruptly,
precipitous on all sides.
Its summit is square like the bottom of a dipper,
hence it is so named.
Creepers, pines, and junipers
create a particularly wondrous scene.
Above is the site where Táng Gōngfǎng drank the immortal wine of Lǐ Bābǎi,
and his entire household ascended with their dwelling.
The foundation of their house, about three mǔ in area,
sank into a pit,
this being where the land rose up together with them.
In the Xīnsì year,
Wáng Rényù served there as a military judge
and once inscribed a poem on a wooden plaque at the temple, which reads:
"In rosy robes, about to soar, blissfully drunk,
Unaware, my whole household dwells in crimson heavens.
The household ascended—only the chickens and dogs remain;
Who would believe the road to heaven is so distant and forked?
The Three Purities vast, earthly dreams cast aside;
The Eight Scenes misty, morning court affairs attended.
Because the old grove's dark cypresses remain sturdy,
Dewy blossoms, cool leaves lock the golden whirlwind."
An old account says:
There is a cave at Dǒushān,
extending two thousand lǐ westward,
connecting to the Dàmiàn Shān in Qīngchéng,
and also linking to the well of Yánzhēn Guàn.
In the Guǐwèi year, Wáng Rényù entered Shǔ
and paid a visit to Yánzhēn Guàn.
There he saw the stone stele with his Dǒushān poem.
He questioned the Taoist priests there,
who said
they did not know where it came from.
Those who heard of this were all astonished.
Dàzhú Lù
South of Xīngyuán,
there is the Dàzhú Lù,
leading to Bāzhōu.
The path traverses deep streams and steep cliffs.
Travelers clutch vines and feel their way over rocks,
climbing for three days
before reaching the mountaintop.
When wayfarers stop to rest,
they tie ropes around their waists,
coiling them around trees to sleep.
Otherwise,
they would fall into the deep ravines,
as if sinking into the Yellow Springs.
Further on, they ascend the Cuòdà Ridge.
There are places that seem somewhat level,
where travelers proceed with slow steps,
like a scholar pacing with measured stride.
The highest peak is called Gūyún Liǎngjiǎo.
A local proverb says:
"Gūyún Liǎngjiǎo,
within a hand's grasp of heaven."
The temple of Huáiyín Hóu is located there.
Long ago, when Hàn Gāozǔ did not employ Hán Xìn,
Xìn fled back to Western Chǔ.
Chancellor Xiāo pursued him
and caught up at this mountain,
hence a temple was erected in his likeness.
Wáng Rényù once assisted the commander of Bāo and Liáng, Wáng Sītóng,
in a southern campaign against the Bā people.
Passing through on the ascent and return,
he also left an inscription at the Huáiyín temple.
The poem reads:
"A grasp of cold sky, ancient trees deep;
Travelers still speak of Hàn's Huáiyīn.
Lone clouds cannot conceal strategies of rise and fall;
Two peaks once hung between the hearts of staying and leaving.
Not that the emperor lightly regarded plain-clad men,
Why then did the chancellor toil to pursue from afar?
Had he been allowed to return to Western Chǔ back then,
Not an inch of the Central Land could have been invaded."
The perilous and rugged nature of the place
cannot be fully described.
Xī Dú
Occasionally, there is a stream poison.
When the illness strikes,
it resembles severe cold damage.
Those who recognize it
take a water brush tube,
insert it into the nose,
and flick it with a finger three to five times.
Black blood then comes out,
and after a while, the illness is cured.
Otherwise,
it leads to sudden death.
Huángshí
During the time of Emperor Yáo,
five stars fell from the sky.
One was the essence of earth,
which fell at the foot of Gǔchéng Shān.
This essence transformed into the old man on the Yí Bridge,
who bestowed a military text upon Zhāng Zǐfáng,
saying:
"Study this, and you shall become a teacher of emperors.
Later, seek me at the foot of Gǔchéng Shān;
it is the yellow stone."
Zǐfáng assisted the Hàn to success,
sought at the foot of Gǔchéng Shān,
and indeed found a yellow stone there.
Zǐfáng retired to Shāngshān,
studying the Way with the Four Hoary Ones.
His family buried his cap and garments,
along with the yellow stone.
In ancient times, yellow vapor several tens of zhàng high was often seen above the tomb.
Later, when the Red Eyebrows excavated it,
they found
neither his corpse
nor the yellow stone.
The vapor then ceased.
Mǎgān Shí
In the fifth year of Yuándǐng,
the Zhìzhī state presented one hundred catties of horse-liver stone.
They were kept nourished with mercury,
placed inside a jade case,
and sealed with gold mud on top.
The people of that state were four feet tall,
and subsisted solely on horse-liver stone.
This stone was half green and half white,
like the liver of a horse today.
Liver.
When pounded,
crushed,
and mixed with the Nine-Cycle Elixir,
swallowing one pill
kept one free from hunger and thirst for a full year.
When used to wipe hair,
white strands all turned black.
The Emperor once seated his ministers in the Gānquán Hall,
and those with white hair
wiped it with this stone,
and instantly it all turned black.
At that time, the dukes and ministers said:
"We care not to become regional lords,
only wishing to wipe with horse-liver stone."
This stone was extremely potent.
If not mixed with cinnabar,
it could only be applied to hair.
Stone Drum
When half the riverbank collapsed in Línjiāng, Wújùn,
a stone drum emerged,
but striking it produced no sound.
Emperor Wǔ asked Zhāng Huà about it,
and Huà said:
"Take tong wood from Shǔzhōng,
carve it into the shape of a fish,
and strike it—then it will sound."
So they followed his words,
and indeed the sound could be heard for several miles.
Stone Gathering
Shí Jìlóng erected a bridge across the river at Yúnchāng Ford,
gathering stones for the central piers.
Regardless of size,
the stones sank and were carried away by the current,
and after expending over five million man-days of labor,
it was not completed.
Jìlóng sent an envoy to offer sacrifices,
sinking a jade disc into the river.
Soon after, the sunken disc floated onto a sandbar.
An earthquake occurred,
and waves surged up to the ford.
Towers and halls collapsed,
crushing over a hundred people to death.
Green Stone
In the fourth year of Xiǎnqìng of the Táng,
a fisherman netted a green stone from the river,
four feet long,
nine inches wide,
its color glossy and smooth,
different from ordinary stones.
When hung and struck,
it produced a clear, far-reaching sound,
and travelers who heard it,
all stopped in their tracks.
Governor Téngwáng submitted a memorial and sent it,
and it was stored in the Ruìfǔ.
Stone Inscription
The auspicious stone inscription of Chāngsōng:
Initially, Lǐ Xíyù served as Governor of Liángzhōu,
and reported that in Chāngsōng there was an auspicious stone,
with characters naturally formed.
In total, there were one thousand and ten characters.
The gist of it said:

Gāohuáng, Hǎiyǔ, character Lǐ, Nine Kings, Eight Thousand, Peaceful Son of Heaven, Lǐ Shìwáng, Thousand-Year Crown Prince, Zhìshū, Yānshān Rénshì, State Lord Shàngrèn, Èjiǎng, Wéntōng, Qiāngǔ, Great King, Five Kings, Seven Kings, Ten Kings, Fèngshǒu, Talented Scholar, Wǔwén, Zhēnguān, Chāngdà, Great Sage, Four Directions, Above and Below, Wàngǔ, Loyalty and Filial Piety as Joy.
An edict ordered Lǐu Chěng, Director of the Ministry of Rites,
to travel post-haste to inspect and verify,
and it matched the report.
Stone Joint Growth
During the Yǒngchāng era,
Sīmǎ Mèng Shēn of Táizhōu reported:
"Féng Yì of Línhǎi obtained three stone trees with joint growth,
all made of white stone."
Essence of Tàibái
The essence of the planet Venus
fell west of the Guī Peak in Zhōngnán,
hence it was named Mount Tàibái.
Its essence transformed into white stone,
resembling beautiful jade,
and often covered with purple vapor.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Emperor Xuánzōng established an Xuányuán Temple at the old residence of Línzī in Dàníng Lane, Cháng'ān,
and wished to sculpt a statue of Xuányuán.
He dreamed of a deity saying:
"In the northern valley of Tàibái, there is jade stone;
fetch it and carve it—
where the purple vapor appears is the spot."
The next day,
he ordered an envoy to enter the valley and search for it.
The people at the foot of the mountain said:
"For the past ten days,
there has often been purple vapor,
lingering for days without dispersing."
Sure enough, beneath it they excavated and obtained jade stone,
which was carved into the statue of Xuányuán,
twenty feet tall,
approximately,
and also into two Perfected Ones, two attendant boys,
and the forms of Lǐ Línfǔ and Chén Xīliè,
about six feet tall.
Ancient Iron Plowshare
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Emperor Xuánzōng, because the Sānmén river course was treacherous and obstructed,
making water transport difficult,
ordered that alongside the northern mountain,
stone be carved to create a crescent-shaped canal,
to avoid the turbulent rapids,
named the Tiānbǎo River.
It saved over five hundred thousand transport laborers annually,
and eliminated the dangers of capsizing, drowning, and delays,
earning praise throughout the land.
The river ran straight east-west,
over five miles long,
four to five zhang wide,
and two to three zhang deep, up to five or six zhang,
all carved through solid rock.
While working beneath the solid rock,
craftsmen discovered an ancient iron plowshare,
over three feet long,
with the two characters "Pínglù" on it,
both in seal script.
Xuánzōng found it remarkable,
and stored it in the inner treasury.
He then ordered Héběi County to be renamed Pínglù County,
to commemorate the event.
Walking Stone
In the first year of Bǎolì, the year of Yǐsì,
on Qīnggōng Village Mountain in Zīyáng County, Zīzhōu,
there was a large stone,
about the size of three rooms,
located at the foot of this mountain.
Suddenly it roared and leaped,
descended the mountain, crossed a ravine,
and then climbed a slope,
for about a hundred paces.
While the stone was moving,
it was seen by people hoeing crops.
Each holding their hoes,
they chased it to where it stopped,
the stone being twenty feet tall.
Stone Bridge
The stone bridge in Zhàozhōu was exquisitely crafted,
finely polished and densely compacted,
as if cut by a blade.
Viewed from afar, it resembled a crescent moon emerging from clouds,
a long rainbow drinking from a ravine.
It had railings,
all made of stone,
and the railings were adorned with stone lions.
During the Lóngshuò era,
a Gāolì spy stole two lions away.
Later, craftsmen were recruited to repair them,
but none could match the original.
By the Dàzú era of Empress Tiānhòu,
when Mòchuò attacked Zhào and Dìngzhōu,
the bandits sought to cross southward.
Upon reaching the stone bridge,
their horses knelt and refused to advance,
for they saw a blue dragon lying on the bridge,
vigorous and furious,
so the bandits fled.
Stone Mill
Thirty li east of the former Zhāng County in Wúxīng,
there is Méixī Mountain.
At the mountain's base stands a stone,
perhaps over a hundred zhàng high,
deep green and rounded,
as large as two rooms.
Its four sides are precipitously steep,
looking up, it reaches beyond the clouds,
with no way to climb it.
On top, there is another flat stone,
perfectly round like a carriage canopy,
constantly rotating like a millstone,
its sound like wind and rain.
The locals call it the Stone Mill.
If it spins swiftly, the year will be abundant;
if slowly, the harvest will be poor.
To know whether the year will be abundant or poor,
one can gauge it by the Stone Mill,
with no error.
Fǔ Lài
In Yí Dào County, there is Fǔ Lài,
where the stones are as large as cauldrons,
and as small as dou measures,
their shapes and colors indistinguishable from real ones,
only they are solid inside.
Stone Fish
In Xiāng County of Héngyáng,
there is Shíyú Mountain.
The mountain stones are black,
with veins resembling raw orpiment.
When a layer is opened,
fish shapes appear,
with scales, fins, heads, and tails,
as if painted,
several cun long,
and when burned, they emit a fishy smell.
Falling Stone
The magistrate of Yīquē County, Lǐ Shīhuì,
had a brother serving as an official south of the Yangtze,
who associated with a monk.
Once, while gathering herbs in the mountains,
a sudden storm arose,
and they took shelter under an alder tree.
Moments later, a great thunderclap sounded,
and something swiftly fell to the ground.
Suddenly, it cleared up.
The monk went to look
and found it was a stone,
shaped like a musical
instrument,
that could be hung and struck.
Its top was flat and even as if cut,
with a hole in the middle.
Its bottom gradually widened and rounded,
resembling a hanging pouch.
It was two chi long,
three fen thick,
with a small notch on the left.
Its texture was like brocade,
glossy and reflective,
and it made a sound when struck.
The monk, thinking it unusual,
placed it in his firewood basket and returned.
He stored it in a cabinet and buried it under his meditation bed.
His disciples saw it,
and gradually many came to know of it.
Mr. Lǐ earnestly requested to see it once,
but the monk firmly refused to speak of it.
Suddenly, one day,
the monk summoned Mr. Lǐ.
Upon arrival,
the monk took his hand and said:
"This humble monk's strength is failing,
and the end is near.
The object you previously sought,
I offer it as a parting gift."
He then dismissed all attendants.
Leading Mr. Lǐ into his bedroom,
he moved the bed and dug up the ground,
presented the box to him, and passed away.
Standing Stone
In the sea of the Láizi State, there is a stone figure,
fifteen chi tall,
ten arm-spans in girth.
Long ago, the First Emperor sent this stone figure to pursue Láo Mountain,
but it failed,
and thus remained standing.
Lone Stone
In the waters of Zhùyáng County,
a lone stone protrudes.
Below it is a clear deep pool.
Occasionally, people see the root of this stone,
like bamboo roots,
yellow in color.
Those who see it often meet with misfortune,
commonly called the Chéngshòu Stone.
Net Stone
When Yú Jìyǒu served as Prefect of Hézhōu,
by the river was a temple,
where fishermen often gathered to fish.
A fisherman
cast his net,
and upon lifting it, felt it heavy.
The net tore,
and looking inside, he found a stone,
fist-sized.
He then begged the temple monks
to place it in the Buddha hall.
The stone then grew unceasingly,
weighing forty jin after a year.
When Vice Director Zhāng was entering Shǔ,
he personally witnessed this event.
Egg Stone
The Regular Attendant Cuī Yuánliàng,
while in Luòzhōng,
once strolled along the bank
and found a pebble,
as large as a chicken egg,
black, glossy, and lovely.
Playing with it,
he walked a li,
when it suddenly cracked open,
and a bird, as large as a wren,
flew away.
Reclining Stone
In Dōngxiāng Village of Yǒngfēng County in Jīngzhōu,
there is a reclining stone,
nine chi six cun long,
shaped like a human,
with its entire body showing raised patterns of green and yellow,
as if carved.
If the region suffers drought,
they make offerings and lift it:
for light rain, lift it slightly;
for heavy rain, lift it greatly.
Legend says this stone suddenly appeared like this,
originally nine chi long,
now increased by six cun.
Monk Transformed
A monk from Tiāntāi,
during the Qiánfú era,
from the area of Línhǎi County east of Táishān,
found a cave.
Fellow monks went together to explore it.
For the first ten or twenty li,
the path was low and narrow,
mostly muddy.
Further in, it gradually became level and broad,
with mountains appearing,
stretching about ten li.
They saw marketplaces and residents,
no different from the mortal world.
This monk was accustomed to breath control,
and felt neither hunger nor thirst.
His companion grew very hungry,
and went to a food stall to beg for food.
Someone told him:
"If you can endure hunger and thirst,
return quickly and you'll be fine.
But if you eat the food of this place,
you will surely find it hard to leave."
Starving,
he insisted on eating.
After eating,
they walked together over ten li,
the path gradually narrowing,
until they found an exit and emerged.
The monk who had eaten
instantly turned to stone.
The Tiāntāi monk, upon leaving the mountain, met people
and asked about the jurisdiction;
he was already at the seaside of Mùpíng.
Meteorite
In the summer of the gēngwǔ year, the tenth year of the Tiānfù era of the Táng dynasty,
a meteorite fell in front of the Zhāoxiān Temple at the foot of Yuèwáng Mountain in Hóngzhōu.
There was a sound like thunder,
with radiant light in five colors,
spanning ten zhàng in width.
The borders of Yuánzhōu, Jízhōu, Jiāngzhōu, and Hóngzhōu
all witnessed the light and heard the sound.
In front of the temple, there was five-colored smoke,
which dispersed after a month.
There was a stone seven to eight chǐ long,
over three zhàng in circumference,
clear and green like jade,
which fell to the ground.
The military governor Liú Wēi ordered it to be carried into the Zhāoxiān Temple,
where a vegetarian feast was held to offer prayers and thanks.
Within seven days,
the stone gradually shrank,
to three chǐ in length;
after several more days of prayers,
it shrank to just over a chǐ;
now it is only seven to eight cùn long,
and remains in the temple.
Mùyán
In Pínglè County, there is a mountain,
among its forests and rocky cliffs,
there are eyes like human eyes,
extremely large,
with pupils clearly distinguished between white and black,
named Mùyán.
Stone Camel
Five days' journey north of Yútián Kingdom,
there is another mountain,
on which stone camels drip water,
which falls drop by drop.
If gold, silver, or other vessels are used to catch it,
they all leak.
Even a human hand leaks,
only a gourd can catch it without leaking.
If one holds it,
it makes the person's body smell foul,
and their skin and hair change.
Stone Pillar
In the kingdom of Jiébǐtā,
a vassal state of Central India,
there is a stone pillar,
seventy chǐ high,
dark red in color and glowing.
If one observes its surface,
according to their sins or merits,
all are reflected and seen in its shadow.
Echoing Stone
On the Gǒulǒu Peak of Nányuè,
there is an echoing stone,
which responds when called,
as if speaking with a person,
but its meaning cannot be understood.
Thirty lǐ southeast of Nánhé County in Nánzhōu,
at the bend of Dānxī,
there is an echoing stone,
three zhàng five chǐ high,
two zhàng wide,
shaped like a lying beast.
It responds when people call,
and also responds to laughter,
standing alone in solitude,
it is also called the Solitary Stone.
Stone Maiden
In Guìyáng, there is the Zhēnnǚ Gorge,
legend says,
during the Qín dynasty, several women
were gathering snails here,
when it rained,
one woman turned into a stone figure.
Now the stone figure is seven chǐ tall,
resembling a woman.
Pearl-Hiding Stone
Fifty lǐ south of Jiāngzhōu,
there is an inn called Qīlǐ Diàn,
located south of the Tuó River.
At the foot of a small hill, there are over ten of them,
like shooting stars coming and going.
Sometimes gathering, sometimes scattering.
On the stone, there is often
a luminous scene.
It is traditionally said,
that pearls are hidden here,
making it a priceless treasure.
Some who have seen it,
secretly noted the location,
but could not find it when searching.
Petrifying Stone
Lǐ Tiào, a jìnshì from Kuàijī,
happened to pick up a small stone,
greenish-black, flat and even,
warm and smooth, pleasant to handle,
and used it as a paperweight.
Once, a snake gathered on it,
and when driven away, it would not leave,
and upon looking, it had turned to stone.
He tried it with other insects,
and they also turned to stone.
The shells fell off, hard and heavy,
no different from stone.
Petrified Pine
In the mountain pavilion of Yǒngkāng County, Wùzhōu,
there was a withered pine tree,
which was cut down,
and accidentally fell into the water.
It turned to stone.
Taking the parts that had not yet petrified,
and testing them in water,
they also turned to stone.
What had petrified,
its branches, trunk, and bark,
were no different from pine,
and were firm and strong.
There were several sections that had not petrified,
kept together with the petrified ones,
to mark this strange object.
Natural Stones
In the fields within the boundaries of Jiànchāng County, Hóngzhōu,
there are natural stone tablets, stone figures, and stone turtles,
scattered on the ground,
their numbers unknown.
All appear as if carved and polished,
but without any inscriptions.
Many of the stone figures are lying fallen,
though some are standing upright.
It is also said,
nearby there is a stone well,
deep but without water.
Some curious people,
took torches and entered it,
finding a side passage,
its distance unknown,
and along the passage, there were also stone figures.
Hot Stone
Xīnběi Market is the old site of Jǐngyún Temple,
where there is a huge stone,
as large as a pillar base.
If people sit or step on it,
shortly after, it feels like being burned by fire.
It causes heart irritation and feverishness,
leading to illness,
and often death.
It is said,
if a fire is gathered and this stone roars,
then the Qútáng Mountain roars and the water boils.
This is an ancient legend.
Also, in the mountain pavilion of Jìnyuán County, Shǔzhōu,
there are two large stones,
each about two chǐ in diameter,
protruding seven to eight cùn from the ground.
If people sit on them,
they often suffer heart pain and cannot be saved.
They are also called fallen star stones,
the one on the east side,
sitting on it causes spiritual effects;
the one on the west side,
is no different from ordinary stones.
Both are bluish-white in color.
Dog-Barking Stone
In Wùyuán County, there is a large yellow stone,
which fell from the mountain to the side of a stream,
clear and lovely,
and when dogs saw it, they competed to bark at it.
After several days,
the villagers could not bear the noise,
so together they pushed it into the water.
The dogs then leaned over the water and barked even more urgently,
so they took it out and smashed it.
Only then did the dogs stop barking.
Jar-Shaped Stone
Pān Zuò served as the magistrate of Póyáng County.
Later, he was connected to the ancient city,
where there were several dozen acres of wasteland in the gaps.
Zuò once gazed at the moon there with his family,
and saw light in the grass beneath the city walls,
rising several zhang high.
The area was densely overgrown with thorns and brambles,
making it impossible to walk at night.
He then took a bow and shot an arrow at the spot,
to mark it.
The next day, he dug at that location
and found a jar,
with a large belly and a small mouth,
sealed with a bluish stone.
Zuò ordered it to be carried back to his home,
but when they tried to open the mouth,
it could not be opened.
He then ordered it to be smashed,
and it turned out to be a stone,
shaped like a jar,
as if frozen and solidified.
They smashed it again and discarded it,
ultimately gaining nothing.
Three Stones
At the Shírén Shān in Chùzhōu,
near the mouth of the Níshuǐ River,
there are three stones nearby,
their forms very much resembling humans.
The one in the middle is the lord,
the one on the left is called the lady,
and the one on the right is called the maiden.
Human Stones
Long ago, there was a husband and wife
who took their son into the mountains to hunt.
The father fell off a cliff,
and the wife and son went down to rescue him,
whereupon all three transformed into three stones.
Thus, they became known as the Human Stones.
Golden Silkworm
Wáng Wénbǐng, a military officer of the Right Thousand Oxen Guard,
was from Dānyáng.
His family was skilled in stone carving for generations.
His grandfather once collected a stele for Péi Qú, the surveillance commissioner of Zhèxī.
Beneath accumulated stones,
he found a naturally round stone,
like a sphere,
shaped as if polished and carved,
layered like shells wrapped around each other.
When carved down to the core,
it was as large as a fist.
Breaking it open further,
inside was a silkworm,
like a grub,
wriggling and able to move.
No one could identify it,
so it was discarded.
Several years later,
when turmoil struck Zhèxī,
Wáng fled to Xiàshǔ.
One night, while meeting with fellow villagers,
they spoke of the legend of the qīngfú insect returning money.
Someone among them said,
"If one seeks wealth,
nothing is better than obtaining a golden silkworm from a stone and raising it.
Then treasures will come of their own accord."
When asked about its appearance,
it matched the grub from the stone.
Flying Slope
During the Yǒngchāng era,
the western slope south of the Fūshuǐ Inn in Tàizhōu
flew four or five li during the day,
directly blocking the Chìshuǐ River.
The mulberry fields and wheat ridges on the slope
remained exactly as before.
Singing Sands
In Língzhōu's Míngshā County, there are sands that,
when trodden by people or horses,
emit a clanging sound.
If taken elsewhere,
after a couple of nights,
they no longer make any sound.
Divine Daughters of the Emperor
The "Shānhǎi Jīng" states:
Within Dòngtíng,
reside the two daughters of the Emperor.
Guō Pú's commentary says:
"The two daughters of the Heavenly Emperor,
dwell in the river as deities.
These are the two river goddesses mentioned in the 'Lièxiān Zhuàn.'"
The "Lísāo" refers to the "Xiāng Fūrén,"
with the line, "The Emperor's daughters descend to the northern isle."
The "Hétú Yùbǎn" states:
Yáo's two daughters,
who became Shùn's consorts,
died and were buried here.
Their tombs are located on the Qīngcǎo Shān, one hundred and sixty li north of the county.
Liú Zǐguāng
During the Hàn dynasty, Liú Zǐguāng was on a western campaign
and grew thirsty upon encountering a mountain,
with no water in sight.
saw a stone figure
and asked it:
"Where is there water?"
The stone figure did not reply.
He then drew his sword and struck the stone figure.
In a moment,
water gushed forth from the mountain.
Yì River
Yìyáng County lies within the boundaries of Chángshā Commandery,
with the Yì River to its south.
Looking east from the county seat,
one could occasionally see the city walls of Chángshā.
The forms and colors of people and horses
could all be clearly discerned.
If one paused to gaze intently,
they would gradually disperse and vanish after a while.
The county is still three hundred li from Chángshā,
separated by layers of mountains.
The distance is vast and the terrain prominent,
perhaps due to the radiant spirit of the mountains,
transmitting these phantom images!
In the past, during the first year of the Zhōngyuán era of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
when he performed the fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài
and the shàn sacrifice on Liángfǔ,
on that day,
the mountain spirits manifested radiant images,
forming palaces and halls.
Long ago, Emperor Wǔ of Hàn dispatched the fāngshì Xú Xuān to sail the seas in search of medicine.
Amid the waves,
he saw Hàn dynasty towers and pavilions, unevenly spaced,
vividly visible in detail,
with mansions and estates of dukes and marquises filling the view.
Bān Chāo, in the land of Húnyē,
at dawn,
when the clouds and mist were bright and clear,
saw palaces and towers on the horizon,
with majestic rows of halls and buildings,
attendants and ministers on both sides,
all of them from the Hàn dynasty.
Such occurrences as these
are difficult to fully explain.
Chénniàng River
The Chénniàng River
is named after Hàn dynasty's Zhèng Hóng.
During the reign of Emperor Líng, he served as a village headman.
While traveling to the capital to take up an official post,
before arriving,
he spent a night here.
He encountered an old friend,
but looking around, there was only desolate wilderness,
with villages far away.
There was nowhere to buy wine,
and their feelings of camaraderie could not be expressed.
So they threw coins into the water and drank together.
They reveled all night,
becoming thoroughly drunk.
Thus, it was named the Chénniàng (Sink-the-Wine) River.
The next morning, they parted ways and left.
Hóng later rose to the position of Imperial Secretary.
Stone Grease Water
In Gāonú County, there is Stone Grease Water.
The water is oily,
floating on the surface like lacquer.
It is collected to grease carts and to fuel lamps,
which burn extremely brightly.
Yuánjiē Spring
In Yuánjiē County, there is a spring.
The water from its eye
swirls and intertwines like a coiled dragon.
If someone tries to disturb and break it,
it immediately reforms into a dragon shape.
Donkeys and horses that drink from it are all startled and run away.
Louzé,
according to Lì Yuán's commentary on the Shuǐjīng,
to the east of Yáoxū there is Louzé,
fifteen lǐ in circumference,
with deep, clear green waters.
There are three large marshes in total,
at the winding shores there is a mound,
commonly called Guītíng.
Beside it are three stone caves,
three chǐ wide and round,
some open, some blocked,
and water naturally fills and leaks through them.
When it leaks, within several nights,
the water in the marshland completely drains away.
The residents nearby,
knowing when it is about to leak,
in advance divert the water into winding channels.
They block the cave entrances with objects,
and fish, turtles, and various scaled creatures
become too numerous to carry away.
Now, according to this, the marsh leaks,
with various caves distinguished,
so-called Chēxiānglòu, Gǔlòu, Tǔlòu, Jīlòu, Zhūlòu.
In spring and summer, water accumulates,
in autumn and winter, it leaks and dries up,
the residents know this,
within no more than three days it is all gone.
It is located seventy lǐ east of the county seat of present-day Sìshuǐ County, Yǎnzhōu.
Also, southeast of Yǎnzhōu, bordering the boundary of Yízhōu,
there is a marshland,
nearly a hundred lǐ in circumference.
It constantly receives summer rains,
gathering flows from nearby valleys and mountains,
its depth can reach over a zhàng.
When spring rains come,
fish and turtles then appear there.
Sometimes by clear autumn days,
the water all sinks down in one night without a trace.
Therefore, the local villagers,
sometimes call it Lòubēi,
also call it Xiànzé.
When the water is about to leak,
there is a sound,
audible for dozens of lǐ in all directions,
like the gathering of wind and rain.
First it swirls like a vortex,
then sinks into the cave.
When the villagers hear it,
they must prepare carts and donkey caravans,
competing to gather the fish and turtles,
loading them onto carts and returning home.
It sinks about once every year or two,
no one knows where it goes or how deep the cave is.
Heavy Water
All things have water,
water comes from the land.
Therefore, Jiāngdōng is suitable for língshā silk,
suitable for paper and mirrors,
because of the water.
When people of Shǔ first finish weaving brocade,
they must wash it in the river water,
only then do the patterns and colors become radiant.
People of Zhèng use Xíngshuǐ to brew wine,
the water near the city is heavy.
The weight differs severalfold from that of the distant suburbs.
Xiāngshuǐ
The water of the Xiāng River is extremely clear,
five or six zhàng deep,
one can see the bottom below,
with scattered stones like gambling chips,
white sand like frost and snow,
red banks like morning clouds.
Torrential Water
At Qīngchéng Mountain,
due to prolonged rain, a cliff collapsed,
and a great torrential flood arrived,
behind the Zhàngrénguàn temple,
over a hundred zhàng high,
the hall was right below it,
fearing it would be destroyed.
Suddenly, a rock fell like a bank,
diverting the water eastward,
and it ultimately avoided being washed away.
The temple used to draw water from the stream daily,
for daily use,
which was very laborious.
Since this torrential water emerged,
there has been a constant flowing spring,
directly entering the kitchen,
its taste sweet and fragrant,
not ceasing in winter or summer.
Immortal Pond
The Xiānchí in Yúzhōu,
is within the boundary of Jiāngjīn County, southwest of the prefecture,
on the southern bank of the Mín River.
The pond is two lǐ in circumference,
eight chǐ deep,
flowing into the Mín River.
According to ancient tradition,
there was an immortal surnamed Rán,
named Dújiǎo,
because he had a horn on his head,
hence this name was given.
He came from Yángzhōu to dwell here.
He built a tower by the pond,
gathered fragrant herbs and placed them below the tower.
Dújiǎo suddenly ascended the tower,
ordered his servants to burn the tower,
Dújiǎo flew into the sky and departed,
hence it was named Immortal Pond.
A stone cliff can be seen,
facing the Mín River and still existing.
Yúzhōu Rapids
The Chéngtān rapids in Yúzhōu,
are thirty lǐ southwest of the prefecture.
Eighty lǐ downstream northeast of Jiāngjīn County,
in the waters of the Mín River,
waves boil and surge,
suddenly stopping, suddenly erupting,
causing many boat capsizings.
Ancient tradition says,
long ago, an immortal named Hé Lái served as Prefect of Bāzhōu,
passing these rapids, his boat overturned,
and he drowned.
Hé's daughter and her elder brother traveled,
journeying,
the daughter had two sons,
still very young,
so she divided gold and pearls into two brocade pouches,
tying them around the children's necks.
Then she took a boat to where her father had drowned,
cried out and threw herself into the water.
In total, six days.
She spoke to her brother in a dream:
"On the twenty-first day,
I will emerge with father."
The brother had people keep watch.
When the time came,
indeed they both floated out on the river water,
now a stele stands beside the Chéngtān rapids.
Qīngtán
A hundred lǐ west of Xīnkāng County,
there is Qīngtán,
in Zhāngpǔ.
The stream source is extremely deep,
often a white dragon hides here.
During drought,
people take pig and sheep dung and throw it into the pool,
and immediately heavy rain and torrential water come.
To this day it is proven effective.
Mountain-Driving Duó
At Zhōngshān within the Yíchūn boundary,
there is a gorge,
several dozen lǐ long,
its water is the Yíchūn River,
winding, clear and pure,
deep and unfathomable.
Once a fisherman was angling,
and caught a golden chain.
Pulling it several hundred chǐ,
he obtained a bell,
shaped like a duó.
The fisherman lifted it,
and a sound like thunder erupted,
the sky turned dark in daytime,
mountains and rivers shook.
One side of Zhōngshān,
collapsed over five hundred zhàng,
the fishermen all sank with their boats into the water.
Where the mountain collapsed is as if cut by a knife,
remaining to this day.
Some who know say,
this is the duó that Qín Shǐhuáng used to drive mountains.
Wūshān Turtle
At the foot of Wūshān Mountain, there was no water.
At the end of the Wèi dynasty,
someone dug a well five zhàng deep
and found a stone casket.
Inside the casket was a turtle,
as large as a horse’s hoof.
Five piles of charcoal were placed beside the casket.
They dug another three zhàng deeper,
encountered bedrock,
and beneath it found flowing water like a lake.
So they chiseled through the rock,
and the water rushed northward swiftly.
Suddenly, a boat
came drifting and struck the rocks.
The workmen peered into the boat
and found a fir plank
with carved characters that read:
"The boat of Zǐyì, on the tenth day of the eighth month in the second year of Chìwū of Wú."
Lǜzhū Well
Lǜzhū Well is located at the foot of Shuāngjiǎo Mountain in Báizhōu.
Long ago, a woman of the Liáng family was exceptionally beautiful.
Shí Jìlún, while serving as an inspector in Jiāozhǐ,
purchased her with three hú of pearls.
The residence of the Liáng family
still had its old well.
Elders passed down the tale
that those who drew and drank water from this well
would give birth to daughters of great beauty.
Some discerning villagers,
believing that such beauty brought no benefit to the times,
filled the well with a massive rock.
Afterward, although daughters were occasionally born with dignified features,
they often had incomplete facial orifices or limbs.
How strange,
Línyuán Well
Gě Zhìchuān said:
"When my grandfather, the Hónglú, was young,
he once served as magistrate of Línyuán.
He said
that in this county there was a prominent family
whose members enjoyed long lives across generations,
some living over a hundred years,
others eighty or ninety.
Later, they moved away,
and their descendants began to die prematurely.
When others occupied their former residence,
they too enjoyed longevity for generations.
From this, it became clear that the residence was responsible,
though the reason was unknown.
Suspecting the well water’s reddish hue,
they dug around the well
and found several dozen hú of cinnabar buried by ancient people,
a few chǐ from the well.
The essence of this cinnabar seeped into the well with the spring water,
which is why drinking the water granted long life.
How much more so if one were to refine and ingest the cinnabar itself!"
Fire Well
There was a fire well,
five chǐ wide,
and two or three zhàng deep.
The one in Shǔdū
was often used to obtain fire by throwing in bamboo or wood.
After Chancellor Zhūgě went to inspect it,
the fire grew even more intense.
Placing a pot over the well to boil brine,
they obtained salt.
Later, someone threw a household candle flame into the well,
and it immediately extinguished.
To this day, it has not reignited.
Salt Well
The salt well in Língzhōu
was excavated by the Later Hàn immortal Zhāng Dàolíng of Pèiguó.
It measured four zhàng in circumference,
and was five hundred
and forty chǐ deep.
Furnaces were set up to boil salt,
with one-tenth going to the government
and two-tenths to the common people.
Profit attracted people,
and people formed settlements.
In the second year of Wànsuì Tōngtiān,
Right Supplements Officer Guō Wénjiǎn petitioned to sell the well water,
earning
450,000 strings of cash in a single day and night.
The people, greedy for profit,
lost their livelihoods as a result.
Above the well stood a temple to the Jade Maiden.
Ancient lore says
that these twelve Jade Maidens
once pointed out the site for Zhāng Dàolíng to dig the well,
and so they were revered as deities.
It was also commonly said that a spirit dwelled at the bottom of the well,
and that fire or filth must not be thrown into it.
Once, while drawing water,
someone accidentally dropped fire into the well,
and it immediately roared, boiled, and surged.
Smoke billowed upward,
splattering mud and tossing stones,
a truly terrifying sight.
Some say
the spring channel connects to the Eastern Sea,
as fragments of wrecked ships occasionally float up.
Imperial Well
The old imperial well in Shànhé Ward—
elders said
it was not for drinking,
as the land was low and the water soft,
making it suitable only for irrigation.
During the Kāiyuán era,
dozens of camels
carried its water into the palace
to supply the six imperial quarters.
Wáng Dí
In the fourteenth year of the Táng Zhēnyuán era,
in the third month of spring,
the well at the home of Suíjūn Wáng Dí in Shòuzhōu
suddenly boiled over,
and ten days later ran dry.
Sounds were heard from the bottom of the well,
like the cries of an infant.
By the fourth month,
two brothers had gone blind,
and another person died.
This was the ominous fulfillment of the family’s troubles.
Jiǎ Dān
While in Huátái, north of the city,
Jiǎ Dān ordered an octagonal well dug
to stabilize the Huáng Hé.
He secretly sent someone to observe the digging site.
An old man came to watch
and asked:
"Who is digging this well?"
The official replied:
"The Chancellor."
The old man said:
"A masterful hand indeed,
but it is too close to the east, west, south, and north."
When Jiǎ Dān questioned him,
he said:
"I am the Well Official."
Octagonal Well
On the street before Jǐnggōng Temple,
there once was a huge well,
commonly called the Octagonal Well.
In the early Yuánhé era of the Táng,
a princess passed by in summer
and saw commoners drawing water.
She ordered her attendant to fetch water from the well
using a silver-rimmed bowl.
The bowl accidentally fell into the well,
and over a month later,
it emerged in the Wèi River.
Lǐ Déyù
When Lǐ Déyù was in the Secretariat,
he often drank water from the Huìshān well in Chángzhōu.
From Pílíng to the capital,
he set up relay stations for its delivery.
A monk came to visit him.
Déyù was fond of the unusual;
all who visited his gate,
even commoners in plain clothes,
were received.
The monk paid his respects
to Déyù
and said:
"With Your Excellency in office,
insects follow their nature,
and all things find their proper place.
The water relay is but a minor eclipse of the sun and moon,
and this humble monk privately feels concerned.
I dare to present myself
to ask if this might be stopped?"
Déyù nodded and said:
"Generally speaking, as humans,
none are without desires or cravings.
Even alchemical elixir-making
is a weakness of mine.
As for the three temptations—gambling, hunting, and chess—
I have not indulged in any.
Yet the reverend would forbid me from drinking water?
Is that not too harsh?
If I stop this for your sake,
then the three temptations may run wild,
and negligence is sure to arise."
The monk said:
"The reason this poor monk has come to see Your Excellency
is to inform you that the water veins of Chángzhōu
connect to a well in the capital,
which shares the same spring source as Huìshān Temple."
Déyù laughed heartily:
"How utterly absurd!"
The monk said:
"Your Excellency need only fetch water from this well."
Déyù asked:
"In which ward and alley is the well located?"
The monk replied:
"It is behind the permanent storehouse of Hàotiān Temple."
Déyù
took one jar of Huìshān water,
one jar of Hàotiān water,
and mixed them with eight other jars of the same kind,
making ten jars in total.
He secretly marked their origins
and sent them for the monk to distinguish.
The monk sipped and tasted them,
picked out the Huìshān and Hàotiān jars,
and said the remaining eight tasted the same.
Déyù was greatly astonished.
He immediately stopped the water relay,
and no one complained of hardship;
idle rumors ceased.
A commoner of Yǒngxīng Ward
In the late Kāichéng era of the Táng,
a commoner named Wáng Yǐ from Yǒngxīng Ward dug a well.
Going more than ten feet deeper than a usual well,
he found no water.
Suddenly, he heard voices and the sound of chickens below,
very noisy,
as if just beyond a wall.
The well-digger was terrified
and dared not disturb it.
The street authorities reported it to General Wéi Chǔrén of the Imperial Guards.
Wéi, considering the matter strange and supernatural,
did not memorialize the throne,
but ordered the well filled.
According to the "Tales of Zhōu and Qín",
a copy from Líshān was obtained at the gatekeeper's tower,
where Lǐ Sī led 720,000 laborers to build a mausoleum,
digging according to plans.
After thirty-seven years,
due to springs within the earth,
they reported:
"We have gone deep enough, to the extreme.
We can dig no further,
it will not burn when fired,
and it sounds hollow when struck,
as if below the heavens."
Perhaps this shows that beneath the thick earth,
there may be another world altogether.
Dúgū Shūyá
once ordered his servant to draw water.
The bucket was too heavy to turn,
and several people helped pull it out—
it was a person.
Wearing a straw hat,
he clung to the well rail, laughing loudly,
then fell back into the well.
The drawer fished out the straw hat and hung it on a tree in the courtyard.
Wherever rainwater dripped from it,
yellow mushrooms would grow.
Cháidū
In the east, there is a place called Cháidū,
located in the mountains of the Qí state.
There is a spring in the mountain,
like a well,
immeasurably deep.
In spring and summer,
hail falls from the well,
destroying the five grains.
People often block it with firewood;
if not blocked, the hail causes disaster.
Hence it is called Cháidū (Firewood Capital).
Háozhōu Well
In the year of Wùzǐ, there was a great drought.
In front of a tavern in Háozhōu,
there was a large well
that had been silted up for a long time.
The tavern owner summoned well-workers to dredge it.
A father and son answered the call.
The son went down first
and died leaning on his shovel.
The father hurried down after him
and also died.
Onlookers crowded like a wall,
and no one dared enter again.
They pulled the bodies out with ropes
and ultimately did not resume digging.
Chicken Well
In Jiāngxià, there was a Registrar Lín,
cruel and fond of gambling,
who dearly loved his daughter.
She loved eating chicken,
and the local officer supplied two chickens daily.
One day,
as they were about to kill a chicken,
the chicken ran away,
and the girl chased it herself.
The chicken ran into a dry well north of the house,
and the girl also went into the well,
then disappeared.
Lín went himself
and also entered the well, not coming out.
Soon, black smoke rose from the well like cooking steam.
The family could only weep by the well,
none daring to enter.
A butcher offered to go down and look.
He only saw a large cauldron,
with boiling water and blazing fire.
Someone pushed his foot and said:
"This matter does not concern you.
Do not enter," so he came out.
After a long time,
the smoke gradually subsided and ceased.
In the well were only a set of chicken bones
and two sets of human bones.
This story has been heard from elders several times,
but it is unknown which year it occurred.
Army Well
In Jiànzhōu, there was the residence of Prefect Wèi.
After the war, it was burned and destroyed,
turned into an army camp.
There was a large well that had silted up.
In the year of Rénzǐ,
soldiers dredged it.
Two who entered
both died,
and their bodies were not recovered.
One man requested to enter again,
saying:
"Lower me with a rope.
When I pull the rope urgently,
pull me up immediately."
After he had been down for a long time,
he suddenly pulled the rope very urgently.
They pulled him out at once,
but he was already like an idiot.
After a long while, he could speak and said:
"Once I entered the well,
I saw a city with walls and wells,
and many people.
Their ruler was called General Lǐ,
overwhelmed with official duties,
his offices very grand.
I was frightened and hurried out,
but ultimately did not recover the two bodies."
Liúhòu Zhū Chìyè of Jiànzhōu
ordered this well filled.
Magistrate of Jīnhuá
Wáng Zhùcóng's son, Mǒu,
served as the magistrate of Jīnhuá.
He built a private residence within the county town.
One summer, a great rainstorm arrived,
and the water suddenly rushed towards the southeastern corner,
as if pouring into a leaky cup,
draining away in an instant.
That spot became a well,
its depth unfathomable.
They used a silk rope to lower a stone to measure it;
only after several tens of zhàng did it reach the bottom.
They retrieved a fresh twist of dough,
which was no different
from the common food eaten by people.
Gold
To the west of the Rìguān,
there is a mountain,
over ten lǐ in length,
two or three lǐ in width,
and over a hundred zhàng in height.
It is entirely of great yellow gold,
its color exceptionally beautiful,
unmixed with earth or stone,
and no grass or trees grow upon it.
Upon it stand golden figures,
over five zhàng tall,
all of pure gold,
named Golden Rhinos.
Going one zhàng into the mountain,
there is silver;
going another zhàng in,
there is tin;
going another zhàng in,
there is lead;
going another zhàng in,
there is Dānyáng bronze.
Dānyáng bronze resembles gold
and can be forged to make inlaid vessels.
The "Huáinánzǐ" technique states:
"Feed on Dānyáng to make gold."
Wēng Zhòngrú
During the Hàn dynasty,
Wēng Zhòngrú's family was poor, and he labored strenuously,
living in Wèi Chuān.
One day,
heaven rained ten hú of gold upon his household,
whereupon he vied in wealth with princes and marquises.
Nowadays in Qínzhōng, there is rain of gold,
The Wēng family
remained wealthy for generations.
Huò Guāng
Emperor Xuān of Hàn once bestowed
a black-canopied carriage upon the Great General Huò Guāng,
decorated entirely with gold inlay.
Every night,
a golden phoenix would fly away from the carriage's linchpin,
no one knew where to,
and return at dawn.
The carriage keeper also witnessed this.
Huáng Jūnzhòng of Nánjùn,
while catching birds on the northern mountains,
captured a small phoenix chick.
As soon as it landed in his hand, it transformed into purple gold,
its feathers and wings fully formed,
about a foot long.
The carriage keeper reported, saying,
"The phoenix on the carriage linchpin
often flies away at night,
returning at dawn.
Today at dawn it did not return,
I fear it may have been caught by someone."
Huò Guāng found this very strange
and fully reported it to the Emperor.
Several days later,
Jūnzhòng came to the palace gate
and presented the golden phoenix chick.
The Emperor heard of this and doubted it;
he placed it on the Dew-collecting Plate,
and suddenly it flew away.
The Emperor sent men to search for it;
it went straight into Huò Guāng's house,
to the carriage linchpin,
and only then did they know it was true.
The Emperor took that carriage,
and whenever he traveled for leisure,
he would ride in it.
Thus, Jī Kāng's "Roaming Immortal Poem" says,
"Gracefully the phoenix linchpin,
meets this snare and net."
Chén Jué
In the eleventh year of the Yǒngpíng era of the Hàn dynasty,
in the Hóu state of Wǎn in Lújiāng, there was a lake.
Children of the Wǎn clan named Chén Jué and Chén Tǐng,
both over ten years old,
went fishing together by the lakeshore.
Tǐng fished first.
Jué went over and asked Tǐng:
"Have you caught anything fishing?"
Tǐng said:
"Yes."
Jué returned home to fetch his rod and line,
and went about thirty paces away from Tǐng,
where he saw a wine vessel by the lakeshore,
bright yellow in color,
submerged in the water.
Jué thought it was bronze,
waded in to retrieve it,
but it was slippery and heavy, impossible to lift.
Tǐng saw from afar,
and they tried to get it together,
but ultimately could not.
As they entered the deep flow in the middle of the lake,
they looked back and saw coin-like objects, bright yellow,
hundreds and thousands of them.
They immediately gathered them together,
each filling their hands.
They ran home to show their families.
Jué's father, Guó, was a former clerk,
styled Jūnxián.
Startled, he said:
"How did you get these?"
Jué described the situation.
Jūnxián said:
"This is gold."
He immediately rushed off with Jué to go there.
Arriving at the place with the gold,
there was still much in the water.
Xián himself waded in to gather it.
Jué, Tǐng, and their neighbors heard about it,
and all competed to collect it,
obtaining over ten catties in total.
Xián reported it to the Chancellor,
the Chancellor reported it to the Grand Administrator,
who dispatched clerks to collect it.
He sent his subordinate clerk Yù Gōng to present it as tribute,
along with an account of how the gold was obtained.
Fú Jiān
In the fifth year of the Jiànyuán era of the Former Qín, under Fú Jiān,
a woodcutter from Cháng'ān saw a golden tripod south of the city,
and ran to report it to Jiān.
Jiān sent men to fetch it by cart.
Upon reaching the city,
it transformed into a bronze tripod.
The people of Yúdū County
In Nánkāng Yúdū County,
crossing south of the river,
three lǐ from the county seat,
there is a place called Mèngkǒu.
There is a cave,
shaped like a stone chamber.
Old legends say there was once a divine rooster,
with feathers like fine gold,
that emerged from this cave,
spreading its wings and circling in flight,
its long cry resounding clearly.
Whenever it was seen, it would immediately vanish into the cave.
Thus, this stone was named the Rooster Stone.
Once, a man was plowing beside this mountain
and saw the rooster come out to play.
A tall man appeared,
holding a slingshot to shoot it.
The rooster saw him from afar
and immediately flew back into the cave.
The slingshot pellet struck the stone above the cave entrance,
which was about six chǐ in diameter.
It hung down, covering the cave mouth,
though there were still gaps,
but no longer large enough for a person to enter.
Another time, someone was sailing a boat
upstream back to the county seat
when, several lǐ before reaching this cliff,
a man appeared,
dressed entirely in yellow,
carrying two baskets of yellow melons,
asking for a ride.
The yellow-clad man begged for food,
and the boat owner gave him a plate of wine.
After he finished eating,
they reached the foot of the cliff.
The boat owner asked for a melon,
but the man refused,
instead spitting into the plate,
then went straight up the cliff
and entered directly into the stone.
The boat owner was initially very angry,
but upon seeing him enter the stone,
he realized it was something supernatural.
He picked up the plate to examine it
and saw that the spit on it
had all turned to gold.
Hé Wén
and Zhāng Fèn,
whose family was immensely wealthy,
later suffered a sudden decline
and sold their house to the Chéng family of Líyáng.
After the Chéngs moved in,
deaths and illnesses followed one after another,
so they resold it to Hé Wén of Yè.
At dusk, Hé Wén
took a knife
and climbed up to sit on the central beam of the north hall.
When the second watch ended,
he suddenly saw a figure,
over ten chǐ tall,
wearing a tall hat and yellow clothes,
enter the hall and call out, asking:
"Slender Waist,
why is there a living human's breath in the house?"
The reply came:
"There is none."
After a short while,
another figure in a tall hat and blue clothes appeared,
followed by
yet another in a tall hat and white clothes.
Their questions and answers were the same as before.
As dawn approached,
Hé Wén descended into the hall
and called out to them in the same manner.
He asked:
"Who is the one in yellow?"
The reply came:
"Gold,
located under the west wall of the hall."
"Who is the one in blue?"
The reply came:
"Coins,
five paces from the well in front of the hall."
"Who is the one in white?"
The reply came:
"Silver,
under the pillar at the northeast corner of the wall."
"And who are you?"
The reply came:
"I am the pestle,
under the kitchen stove."
At daybreak,
Hé Wén dug in the indicated spots in order
and obtained five hundred jīn each of gold and silver,
and over ten million coins.
He then took the pestle and burned it,
and the house became peaceful thereafter.
Hóu Yù
During the early Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
Hóu Yù, a Xiàolián of Guǎngdū, entered the city.
When he reached outside Jiànmén,
he suddenly saw four large stones,
each as big as a dou measure.
Hóu Yù took a liking to them,
collected them into his book basket,
and loaded them onto his donkey.
While resting, he took them out to look
and found they had all turned to gold.
Hóu Yù went to the city to sell them,
earning a million coins,
with which he bought over ten beautiful concubines,
built a grand mansion,
and acquired fertile fields and a villa in the suburbs.
Later, he went on a spring outing,
taking all his singing girls and concubines with him.
After dismounting,
he set out wine and food.
Suddenly, an old man appeared,
carrying a large book basket,
and sat at the edge of the mat.
Hóu Yù angrily scolded him
and ordered his servant to escort him out.
The old man did not move,
nor did he show anger,
but simply filled his cup, ate the roasted meat, and laughed, saying:
"I have come here
to demand repayment of a debt from you.
Do you not remember
taking my gold away in the past?"
He then took all of Hóu Yù's more than ten concubines
and threw them into his book basket.
The basket did not seem cramped at all,
and he carried it on his back and hurried off,
running as swiftly as a flying bird.
Hóu Yù ordered his servants to chase him,
but in an instant, he had vanished.
Afterward, Hóu Yù's family grew poorer day by day,
reverting to their former livelihood.
Over ten years later,
he returned to Shǔ.
When he reached Jiànmén,
he saw the same old man again,
strolling with the concubines he had taken away,
accompanied by a large entourage.
They all laughed upon seeing Hóu Yù,
and when questioned, they said nothing.
When pressed,
they vanished once more.
Hóu Yù searched around Jiànmén,
but found no trace of this person,
and was never able to fathom what had happened.
Chéng Bì
In the late Suí dynasty,
a Daoist resided on Tàibái Mountain,
refining cinnabar,
and succeeded in achieving the Great Reversion Elixir,
thus attaining the Way,
and lived on the mountain for several decades.
There was a man named Chéng Bì who served him,
and the Daoist lived with him for over ten years,
but did not impart the Way to him.
Bì later left due to family hardship,
and the Daoist said:
"You have followed me for a long time,
and now you face sorrow again.
I have nothing to give you,
so I will give you ten grains of elixir.
One grain of elixir can transform ten catties of red copper
into gold,
which should suffice for your funeral arrangements."
Bì then returned,
and as instructed, transformed gold to meet his needs.
After completing the funeral,
Bì harbored ulterior motives,
and returned to the mountain to see him,
seeking more of the Reversion Elixir.
The Daoist refused to give it,
so Bì threatened him with a blade.
Failing to obtain the elixir,
he then cut off both of the Daoist's hands,
and still failing,
he severed his feet,
yet the Daoist's expression remained unchanged.
Bì grew even angrier,
and beheaded him.
While undressing him,
he found a red pouch behind his elbow,
and upon opening it, discovered the elixir.
Bì was overjoyed,
and took the elixir down the mountain.
Suddenly, he heard a voice calling his name.
Looking back,
he saw it was the Daoist.
Bì was greatly startled,
and the Daoist said to him:
"I did not expect you
to go this far.
Without virtue,
receiving the elixir,
the gods will surely punish you,
and you will end up like me."
With that, he vanished.
Bì obtained much elixir,
and transformed a great deal of gold,
though the gold was slightly reddish,
it was superior to ordinary gold,
and could be ingested as medicine.
His family became wealthy,
but he was accused by others,
who claimed Bì was involved in deceit.
Upon capture,
Bì explained that he could produce gold,
and had no other motives.
Emperor Táng Tàizōng heard of this,
and summoned him to produce gold.
When the gold was made,
the emperor was pleased,
and appointed him to the fifth rank,
ordering him to produce gold,
intending to exhaust all the copper in the world.
Bì produced gold,
totaling tens of thousands of catties until the elixir was exhausted.
This gold was known as the Great Táng gold,
which became even more refined with repeated refining,
and was highly valued.
Bì, having exhausted his skill, requested to leave,
but Tàizōng ordered him to disclose the formula.
Bì truly did not know the formula,
and pleaded his case.
The emperor thought he was lying,
and grew angry,
threatening him with soldiers.
Bì still pleaded his innocence,
so the warriors cut off his hands.
He still did not speak,
so they severed his feet.
Bì, in desperation,
recounted the whole story,
but he was not believed,
and was beheaded.
The Great Táng gold then circulated widely.
Later, a Brahmin,
known as a treasure distinguisher,
entered the treasury and inspected everything.
The Brahmin pointed to the gold and a large carpet, saying:
"Only these two are treasures."
Asked what was extraordinary about the carpet,
that it was called a treasure,
the Brahmin had the carpet spread on the ground,
and poured water on it.
The water all flowed away,
and the carpet remained completely dry.
To this day, foreign lands speak of Chéng Bì's gold,
regarding it as a precious commodity.
Mysterious Gold
During Tàizōng's reign,
it was reported from Fénzhōu that
a blue dragon and a white tiger spat objects into the air,
glowing like fire,
which fell to the ground and sank two feet deep.
Upon digging,
they found mysterious gold,
over a foot wide,
and seven feet tall.
Zōu Luòtuo,
a native of Cháng'ān,
was initially poor,
and used to sell steamed cakes from a small cart.
At the corner of Shèngyè Ward, there was a hidden brick,
and whenever his cart hit it, it would overturn,
soiling his cakes with dust,
which troubled Luòtuo.
He then took a hoe and removed over ten bricks,
finding beneath them a porcelain jar,
with a capacity of about five hú.
Upon opening it,
he found several dǒu of gold,
and thus became immensely wealthy.
His son, Fǎng,
was close friends with Xiāo Quán.
People at the time said:
"Xiāo Quán, the son-in-law of a prince,
and Zōu Fǎng, the son of Luòtuo.
Not bound by virtue,
but only by wealth do they know each other."
Péi Tán
Péi Tán served as the prefect of Huáizhōu.
A woodcutter entered the Tàiháng Mountains,
and saw a mountain cave open,
filled with gold,
enough to fill several rooms.
The woodcutter was delighted,
entered the cave to take the gold,
and obtained five ingots,
each over a foot long.
He then sealed the cave with stones,
and marked the location.
A few days later, he returned,
but could not find the place.
The woodcutter was quite familiar with the mountains and valleys.
He then went to Luòchéng and Huáizhōu,
and prepared several carts of tools like hammers and chisels for opening rocks.
In the prefecture, there was a Registrar Cuī,
who knew of this and assisted him.
As they were about to go and open it,
Tán's wife fell ill,
and they requested a Daoist to submit a petition to the heavens for her life.
The Daoist who submitted the petition suddenly conveyed a decree from the Heavenly Emperor, saying:
"The Emperor decrees to Péi Tán:
My heavenly treasury in the Tàiháng Mountains opened,
and a woodcutter saw it.
I have already given him five ingots of gold,
and ordered him to seal it.
But the foolish man, greedy for more,
sought again and failed,
and thus conceived evil.
He intends to open my treasury,
and has already prepared several carts of hammers and chisels.
If he opens it without cease,
he may encounter my hidden treasures.
If these hammers and chisels are used,
the people of this prefecture will all perish,
with no benefit at all.
The Registrar Cuī of this prefecture
is of one mind with him.
Just go to Cuī and verify it,
and you will see for yourself.
Stop him urgently,
and your wife's illness will naturally be cured."
Tán was greatly astonished,
and immediately summoned Cuī's son to inquire,
and it indeed matched what was said.
He then confiscated the rock-opening tools and forbade the endeavor,
and his wife soon recovered.
The Niú Family Servant
Niú Sù's great-grandfather and grandfather
were both buried in Hénèi,
and two households of domestic servants were assigned to guard the tombs.
In the twenty-eighth year of the Kāiyuán era,
a servant, using his son Xiǎo Ān,
pawned him to the Péi family.
Suffering from a tooth ailment,
he lay sleeping in the stable during the day.
It was as if someone told him:
"Xiǎo Ān,
why don't you get up?
Just take the root of the 'immortal's staff' plant, boil it into a decoction, and hold it in your mouth—
it can cure your illness.
Why endure this suffering!"
Xiǎo Ān, startled, looked around,
saw no one, and went back to sleep.
Not long after,
he was told the same thing again.
Ān said:
"Could this be a spirit informing me?"
He then went to search for the 'immortal's staff' plant,
found a large clump,
and dug up its root.
The root grew increasingly large and thick,
going three feet into the ground,
