when suddenly he struck a large brick,
with an inscription on it.
After removing the brick,
below was a copper basin,
inside which were entirely gold ingots,
mixed with cinnabar,
within it.
Ān was illiterate;
after hiding the gold,
he showed the brick inscription to a villager named Yáng Zhīkǎn.
He left the inscription with others to see,
but did not tell them about the gold.
The inscription read:
"Below this brick are five hundred taels of gold.
On the eighteenth day of the fifth month in the twenty-eighth year of the Kāiyuán era,
a young Hu bandit, aged twenty-two, surnamed Shǐ, will obtain it.
Twenty-five li north of Zézhōu city, south of the White Stūpa,
also twenty-five li away,
there is five hundred taels of gold,
which will also be obtained by this person."
After people saw the inscription,
word spread along the roads and reached the ears of the Péi family's son.
He questioned Xiǎo Ān,
who tried to conceal it,
so he whipped him,
but Ān still did not speak.
Thereupon, he tortured and interrogated him,
but despite all methods, Ān did not respond,
so he confined and locked him in a room.
It happened that a painter came to visit Xiǎo Ān,
to buy cinnabar from him.
The Péi family's son tricked him into questioning,
and the painter fully explained how Ān had obtained the gold.
He also said:
"Yesterday, from someone,
I spent one hundred coins
to buy one jin of cinnabar.
The cinnabar was of excellent quality,
so I came to buy more."
The Péi family became even more convinced that he had obtained gold.
They summoned Xiǎo Ān,
and showed him the painter.
Ān said:
"After digging up the inscription,
I obtained a small amount of gold and cinnabar below,
and now there is none left."
Unable to get the gold treasure,
they increased the beatings and torture to force a confession,
but he still did not speak and fled during the night.
It happened that a servant of the Péi family,
traveling from Tàiyuán to Hénèi,
encountered Xiǎo Ān in Zézhōu.
Xiǎo Ān invited him to the market,
and after drinking wine until intoxicated, he called him away.
It is likely that Xiǎo Ān then went to retrieve the gold in Zézhōu!
When the servant arrived at the Péi family and told them,
they finally realized.
Yǔwén Jìn
Yǔwén Jìn, nephew of Xiàxiàn magistrate Yǔwén Tài,
once found a kūnlúnzi in the fields,
washed and wiped it,
and it turned out to be gold.
He thus treasured and kept it.
Several years later,
his wealth overflowed,
and his family flourished.
Later, one night, he lost it,
and his property dwindled and declined.
Sū È
During the Tiānbǎo era,
in Cháng'ān's Yǒnglè Ward, there was a haunted house.
All who lived there were ruined,
and afterward, no one lived there again.
Even those who stayed temporarily,
if they spent the night, would die,
so it eventually fell into ruin.
Only the main hall remained among the buildings,
and many weeds and trees grew there.
There was a man from Fúfēng named Sū È,
who was utterly destitute and suffering from poverty.
Learning of this,
he bought it for a low price
from its owner.
As soon as the deed was signed,
before he had paid a single coin to the owner,
by evening,
he brought a couch himself,
set it up in the hall, and lay down to sleep.
After the first watch,
unable to sleep,
he went out into the hall
and paced restlessly.
Suddenly, he saw a red object under the eastern wall,
shaped like a human,
without hands or feet,
glowing brightly inside and out.
It shouted:
"Duō!"
È stared at it without moving.
After a long while,
it called out again in a loud voice:
"Rotten wood,
duō!"
From under the western wall, something responded:
"Nuò."
It asked:
"Who is there?"
It replied:
"I don't know."
It said again:
"Too hard and clanging."
Rotten wood replied:
"Fearsome."
After a long while,
the red object vanished.
È descended the steps
and called out to the rotten wood in the courtyard:
"The gold essence should belong to me.
Why did you dare to shout?"
It replied:
"I don't know."
È asked again:
"Where is the one who previously killed people?"
Rotten wood said:
"There is nothing else,
only the gold essence.
People's fortunes were too weak,
unfit to live here,
so they perished.
It never actually killed anyone."
By dawn,
nothing else happened.
È then borrowed shovels and spades himself,
First, he dug under the western wall.
Three feet into the ground,
he found a rotten pillar,
its heartwood blood-red in color,
as hard as stone.
Later, he dug under the eastern wall for two days,
nearly ten feet down,
before seeing a square stone,
four feet wide,
and eight feet long.
On it was written in seal script:
"Thirty catties of purple gold from the Summer Son of Heaven,
bestowed upon the virtuous."
È thought to himself:
"How can I be considered virtuous?"
He then considered:
"If I obtain this treasure,
I can cultivate virtue to avert misfortune."
He hesitated, undecided.
By night,
he sighed restlessly.
Suddenly, the rotten wood spoke:
"Why not change your name to Yǒudé (Virtuous)?
Then it will be fine."
È said, "Good,"
and called himself Yǒudé.
Rotten wood said:
"If you, sir, could send me to Kūnmíng Pond,
I will no longer disturb people."
Yǒudé agreed.
The next morning, he dug another ten feet or so,
and found an iron urn.
Opening it,
he obtained thirty catties of purple gold.
Yǒudé then repaid the house price and repaired the house,
and sent the rotten wood to Kūnmíng Pond.
He then shut his door and studied,
and after three years,
was invited to join the staff in Fànyáng.
Within seven years,
he became the Prefect of Jìzhōu.
The house had no further incidents.
Wéi Sīxuán
During the Bǎoyìng era,
there was a man from Jīngzhào named Wéi Sīxuán,
who resided in Luòyáng.
He had a fondness for the extraordinary
and admired the arts of immortality.
Later, while traveling on Sōng Mountain,
a Daoist priest taught him:
"Those who ingest golden elixir
can prolong their lives.
You should first learn to refine gold,
then you can stand shoulder to shoulder with Chìsōngzi
and ride with Guǎngchéngzi."
Sīxuán then sought the art of refining gold.
After ten years,
having met hundreds of alchemists,
he still could not grasp its essence.
One day later,
a lay Buddhist named Xīn Ruì,
with a very gaunt appearance,
looking haggard and cold,
wearing a tattered fur coat,
knocked on Sīxuán's door
and said to him:
"I am a sick scholar,
destitute and with nowhere to go.
Hearing that you, sir, admire antiquity and the extraordinary,
and gather extraordinary people and alchemists from everywhere,
I have come to pay my respects,
hoping you will accept me."
Sīxuán then let the lay Buddhist stay in his house.
Later, the lay Buddhist fell ill,
his body covered in festering sores and bleeding profusely,
and the entire Wéi family despised him.
Sīxuán once invited several alchemists to dine together,
but the lay Buddhist was not included.
When the meal was served,
the lay Buddhist suddenly appeared before the guests
and urinated on the banquet table,
soaking everything.
The guests all rose in anger,
and the Wéi family servants also rushed to curse him.
The lay Buddhist then announced his departure,
and as he walked to the courtyard,
he suddenly vanished from sight.
Sīxuán and the guests were greatly astonished.
Upon examining his urine,
they found it was purple gold,
shining with a strange, dazzling light—
truly a treasure unmatched in ages.
Sīxuán was both shocked and amazed.
Someone explained:
"The lay Buddhist was the essence of purple gold."
Examining his name confirms it:
for "Xīn" corresponds to the west, where Gēng and Xīn represent metal.
And the character "Ruì" (銳) contains "duì" (兌) and "jīn" (金).
"Duì" also represents the western direction.
Interpreting its meaning,
my explanation fits perfectly.
Lǐ Yuán
Jìnshì Lǐ Yuán,
a native of Hédōng,
resided in Yánshòu Lane of Cháng'ān.
In early summer of the Yuánhé era,
one evening,
Yuán was alone in his room.
As he reclined on his couch,
not yet fully asleep,
he suddenly heard a faint sound from the western corner of the room,
delicate and distant,
tinkling like the music of metal and stone,
continuing for a long time without ceasing.
Soon there was singing,
the voice extremely clear and resonant,
pure and melodious,
again lasting for a long time without stopping.
Yuán secretly memorized the lyrics:
"Color like the blue of orchid leaves,
sound like the chime of a stone qìng.
On the seventh day of the seventh month,
I shall reveal my form to you."
When the song ended,
the sound ceased.
Yuán was both startled and amazed.
The next morning,
he ordered his servants to trace its source,
but they could not find it.
That evening,
as Yuán was again alone,
he heard the sound once more,
plaintive and resonant for a long time,
singing as before.
When the lyrics ended,
Yuán knew in his heart it was something strange,
silently marveling at it.
This happened for several nights,
and he heard it each time.
Later, when autumn arrived,
on the sixth day,
there was heavy rain at night,
which collapsed the northern wall of his hall.
The next day,
the sound was heard again north of the wall.
Yuán, startled, went to look,
and beneath the northern wall found a fǒu jar,
barely over a foot tall,
made of gold,
with an ancient and unusual shape,
quite different from ordinary gold jars.
Moss obscured its luster,
faintly revealing patterns,
though not clearly visible,
clearly an artifact from a thousand years ago.
When tapped,
its resonance was extremely long.
He ordered the dust and moss to be washed away,
and only then could it be read.
The characters were in small seal script,
and it was Cuī Zǐyù's "Admonitions for My Seat."
Yuán obtained it and marveled,
yet ultimately did not know from which era it was made.
Yúxiāng Dàoshi
In Yúxiāng, there was a mountain temple,
very secluded and quiet,
where a Dīyáng dàoshi resided.
During the Dàhé era,
the dàoshi once ascended the altar alone one evening to gaze out.
He saw a strange light suddenly appear in the courtyard,
emanating from the wellspring,
and soon an object,
shaped like a rabbit,
its color like refined gold,
emerged with the light,
circling the altar.
After a long time,
it returned into the well.
From then on, it appeared every night.
The dàoshi found this strange,
but dared not tell anyone.
Later, while cleaning the well,
he found a golden rabbit,
very small,
with a dazzling, unusual glow,
and placed it in his box.
At the time, Yùshǐ Lǐ Róng was stationed at Pújīn,
and was friendly with the dàoshi,
who then gave it to him.
Later, when Lǐ Róng went from being magistrate of Fèngxiān County to Prefect of Xīnzhōu,
the golden rabbit suddenly disappeared,
and a little over a month later, Lǐ Róng died.
Zhào Huáizhèng
Commoner Zhào Huáizhèng of Biànzhōu,
lived in Guāngdé Ward.
In the third year of Dàhé,
his wife, Hè,
often earned money through needlework.
One day,
someone brought a stone pillow to sell,
and Hè acquired it for a single huán coin.
Zhào used it as a pillow at night,
and felt sounds like wind and rain inside the pillow.
He then had his wife and son each use it for a night,
but they noticed nothing.
Whenever Zhào used it, the sounds returned,
sometimes so noisy and startling he could not sleep.
His son suggested breaking it open to see,
but Zhào said:
"If we break it and find nothing,
we would lose the profit of a hundred coins.
Wait until after I die,
then you must break it."
After over a year,
Zhào died of illness.
His wife ordered it destroyed to see,
and inside were one ingot each of gold and silver,
as if cast in a mold.
Where the ingots were contained,
the mold seemed to have been precisely fitted,
without the slightest gap,
and it was unclear how they had entered.
The ingots were each over three inches long,
and as wide as a thick finger.
They sold them,
covered the funeral expenses and repaid debts,
leaving not a single coin extra.
Hè now lives in Luò's Huìjié Ward,
and Duàn Chéngshì's family hired her for sewing,
so he personally heard her tell this story.
Golden Snake
In early Kāichéng era,
a yellow snake appeared in the palace,
emerging at night from the treasure vault,
slithering among the steps,
glowing brightly,
and could not be captured.
A palace maid threw a coral jué ring to strike it,
and it vanished along with the ring.
The vault keeper reported the incident in detail.
The Emperor ordered a thorough search of the vault,
and a golden snake was found with the ring piercing its head.
The Emperor examined it closely,
recalling that Suí Yángdì, when he was Prince of Jìn,
had given a golden snake to Lady Chén.
He now wondered where this snake had come from.
Attendants then looked at its underside,
and found the characters "Ā Mó."
The Emperor exclaimed in surprise:
"Indeed, it matches my suspicion;
'Ā Mó' was Yángdì's childhood name."
The Emperor's broad learning and keen insight
were often like this.
He then ordered a glass chain to be taken,
and tied the snake to the front leg of a jade zhì beast.
After that, it was never seen again,
as the zhì beast devours snakes.
Zhāng Tǐng
In the final years of the Xiántōng era,
Zhāng Tǐng was traveling from Xúzhōu to Cháng'ān,
and upon reaching east of Pútián,
he paused beneath a large tree.
Shortly after,
three scholars arrived one after another,
and they sat in a circle.
Zhāng Tǐng then inquired about them.
One scholar said:
"I
am Lǐ Tè."
Another said:
"I
am Wáng Xiàngzhī."
The third said:
"I
am Huáng Zhēn."
They all said:
"We three have all come from the Biànshuǐ River,
wishing to visit Lóngmén Mountain."
They then engaged in casual conversation.
That Wáng Xiàngzhī said:
"Last year when I visited Lóngmén Mountain,
I passed by here.
About one or two lǐ north of the road,
there is a man,
also a scholar,
who invited me to stay at his home for two nights before returning.
We could go together to pay him a visit."
Zhāng Tǐng thus went along with them.
Upon reaching one or two lǐ north of the road,
they indeed saw a residence,
quite desolate and dilapidated.
After knocking on the door,
a man in scholar's attire
emerged from within,
and upon seeing Wáng Xiàngzhī, he appeared quite pleased.
He asked Wáng Xiàngzhī:
"Who are those three people?"
Wáng Xiàngzhī said:
"This is Scholar Zhāng Tǐng,
and Lǐ Tè and Huáng Zhēn
are fellow scholars from my hometown."
The scholar-attired man then invited them all in with a bow,
ascended to the main hall, and set out wine and food,
though what was provided was rather old and stale.
The scholar-attired man said to Wáng Xiàngzhī:
"The Huáng family brothers are about to rise to great power."
Wáng Xiàngzhī said:
"If the Emperor cultivates virtue and cherishes life,
adhering to the way of a true ruler,
and cares for the common people below,
even if the various Huángs grow older,
what could they possibly do?"
Huáng Zhēn abruptly stood up and said:
"Today is a fine gathering,
we should simply enjoy ourselves to the fullest.
Why must you gentlemen so hastily involve yourselves
in other people's affairs,
dragging my descendants into this?"
Zhāng Tǐng's nature was always firm and decisive,
so he grew greatly suspicious that they were not human,
and thus asked them:
"I happened to meet with you few beneath a tree,
and you brought me here.
Just now, hearing your lofty discussion,
I am truly doubtful.
Who exactly are
these Huáng family brothers?
Moreover, are you people
or not people?
In my life, my nature fears nothing,
so speak the truth!"
Wáng Xiàngzhī laughed and said:
"The Huángs are about to bring chaos to the eastern region,
they are three brothers.
We three are all jīng.
The scholar-attired man is a ghost."
Zhāng Tǐng then asked:
"What kind of jīng are you?
And what kind of ghost is he?"
Wáng Xiàngzhī said:
"I am a jade jīng,
Huáng Zhēn is a gold jīng,
Lǐ Tè is a withered tree jīng,
and the scholar-attired man is the deceased Scholar Zhèng Shì from twenty years ago.
I transformed into a jīng here long ago,
and last year I met Zhèng Shì again,
so now I have come to visit him.
You are a living person,
you should fear our kind;
but since you do not fear,
we can thus converse at ease."
Zhāng Tǐng asked further:
"Since Scholar Zhèng and I are of the same examination cohort,
why does he not speak?"
Zhèng Shì said:
"I was just thinking of
composing a poem to present to you."
The poem said:
"Once a man who chanted of wind and sang of the moon,
now a body that chants wind and sings moon;
after chanting and singing by the roadside grave mound,
who knew today would again weary the spirit!"
Zhāng Tǐng read the poem with sorrow,
and sighed, saying:
"When a person dies,
they are instead inferior to objects;
objects can still transform into jīng,
but people do not transform again."
Wáng Xiàngzhī and the other two,
hearing this sigh,
angrily departed.
Zhèng Shì also did not detain him.
Zhāng Tǐng then brushed his sleeves and left.
Upon reaching outside the gate and looking back,
he already saw a collapsed grave mound.
He then pursued the three jīng,
attacking them with the sword he carried.
The gold and jade
jīng were both struck by the sword and fell,
only the withered tree jīng fled swiftly.
Pursuing and attacking, he could not catch it,
so he turned back,
and instead saw an old jade belt and a gold cup by the roadside.
Wáng Tíng picked them up,
sold them in Cháng'ān,
and they were entirely without any peculiarities.
Gǒng Bō
Gǒng Bō
was a salt merchant from the Yún'ān supervisory district in the Xiá region.
Initially, he was very poor,
making a living by peddling vegetables and fruits,
and built a thatched hut by the river to live in.
Suddenly, one stormy evening,
when heaven and earth were dark and overcast,
he saw a torchlight on the southern side of the river,
and again heard someone calling for a boat, urgently seeking passage.
It was already late at night,
and everyone was resting.
Gǒng Bō then alone rowed a small boat,
braving the wind to ferry them across.
Upon arrival, the torchbearer collapsed to the ground.
Looking closely, it was a golden man,
over four chǐ tall.
Gǒng Bō then loaded it onto the boat and returned home.
From then on, he became wealthy.
Engaging in trade and peddling,
he consistently reaped substantial profits,
and within little more than ten years,
he amassed immense wealth,
ultimately becoming a great merchant of the Sānshǔ region.
A commoner of Yíchūn commandery
In Yíchūn Commandery, there was a commoner named Zhāng Yǐ,
whose family was renowned for their filial piety and righteousness.
For several generations, they had not divided the household,
and all the cousins lived together under one roof.
At their separate villa residence,
there were pavilions, houses, water features, and bamboo groves.
All the young men of the family were fond of virtuous deeds and collected books,
associating with Daoist adepts, eminent monks, and Confucian scholars.
Whenever guests arrived,
they were always welcomed and accommodated.
Suddenly, one evening,
a woman appeared,
young and dignified in her beauty,
dressed in elegant attire and fine makeup,
accompanied by a young maidservant.
She came to the gate seeking lodging for the night.
The women of the Zhāng family
happily received her,
prepared wine and food,
and the gathering lasted until late at night before concluding.
There was a young man of the family,
who devoted himself to literary pursuits,
young, clever, and handsome.
Seeing that this woman was beautiful,
he instructed his wet nurse
to specially clean and prepare another room
for her to stay in.
Late in the night,
the young Zhāng stealthily entered the room.
Hearing no sound or movement at all,
he climbed onto the bed to approach her.
The woman's body was as cold as ice.
Greatly alarmed,
he ordered a candle to be lit to look at her.
It turned out to be a silver figure with two heads,
weighing perhaps a thousand or hundred catties.
The whole family was astonished and delighted,
but fearing it might transform,
they immediately used torches and charcoal to melt it,
and it turned out to be genuine white silver.
To this day, their family remains immensely wealthy,
with all the cousins, their children, and womenfolk
totaling over five hundred members.
Three times daily,
they gather to eat,
ascending to the hall at the sound of a drum.
Within Jiāngxī Commandery,
their wealth and prosperity are unmatched.
Zhāng Yàn
Among the people of the Bā and Wū regions,
many accumulated large amounts of gold.
Whenever there was a gathering,
they would display three grades of gold on the banquet tables
to boast and show off.
There was a man named Lǐ Rénbiǎo from Yún'ān,
who presented a gilded gold platform and tray,
using this to compete in ostentation.
After the chaos of war and displacement,
the regional commanders were all military men,
who competed in greed and cruelty.
The Shǔ general Zhāng Yàn was in charge of Zhōng Prefecture,
and his tyranny and wickedness were especially severe.
The officers suffered bitterly under him,
and thus rebelled,
implicating several thousand households of his associates.
Zhāng seized their gold and silver,
to an extent beyond measure.
Later, at his private residence in Shǔ, he built a separate hall
to store his gold.
Suddenly, one morning,
smoke and fire frequently arose outside the house.
Alarmed, he rushed in to check,
but found no place where a fire had started or spread.
This made him suspicious.
When he opened the chests to look,
they were all already empty.
It turned out that the earlier smoke and fire
were the gold transforming.
The Kāng Family
During the time of the usurper Wú, Yáng Xíngmì
had just secured Yángzhōu.
The residential areas in the distant wards were sparsely populated,
with few hearths connecting them.
There was a man named Kāng,
who made his living by hiring out his labor.
He rented a room in an empty house in the Tàipíng Ward.
One morning, Kāng went out and had not yet returned
when his wife gave birth to a son.
Just as she was spreading straw for the birth,
suddenly a strange man appeared,
with a red face, wearing vermilion clothes and hat,
who sat down blocking the doorway.
The wife was terrified,
and only when she shouted at him did he leave.
He went to the west side of the house,
where there was a thudding sound.
Kāng happened to return
and was about to reach home
when suddenly, by the left side of the road, there were five thousand coins, half a sheep, and a vessel of wine.
He waited for a long time,
but no passerby appeared,
so he took them home.
His wife also told him what she had seen.
They immediately went to the west side of the house to search,
and found a golden man,
fallen in the grass.
They dragged it home as well.
They then cooked the sheep and drank the wine,
which helped them get by.
From then on, whenever Kāng went out, he would surely gain profit,
and the family grew richer day by day.
The golden man was kept as a family treasure.
The son born was named Píng.
When Píng grew up,
he became a wealthy man.
There was a man named Lǐ Xún,
who served as the magistrate of Jiāngdū County.
While touring the county, he arrived at Xīnníng Village,
and saw a large mansion,
which was Píng's home.
The elders of the family told Lǐ the story exactly as it happened.
A Man from Yùzhāng
During the Tiānfù era,
a man from Yùzhāng was building a house.
While digging the ground,
he unearthed a wooden chest.
Opening it,
he found twelve golden human figures,
each several inches tall,
all wearing ancient clothing and hats.
On their heads were the twelve zodiac animals,
exquisitely crafted and beautiful,
almost beyond human skill.
His family treasured them and made offerings to them,
and through this, they attained good fortune.
At that time, warfare had not yet ceased,
and they were seized by a garrison commander.
Later, their whereabouts became unknown.
Chén Jùn
Minister Chén Jùn of Jiāngnán
said that his uncles in their hometown
were fond of composing poetry.
The villagers called them Chén Báishè,
comparing them to Lètiān.
They were by nature informal and simple,
and enjoyed hosting guests.
Once, two Daoist priests came,
one wearing yellow robes,
the other wearing white robes.
They visited their home seeking lodging.
They were given a room in the main hall.
During the night,
they heard the two guests' bed break,
with a loud crashing sound.
After a long while,
it seemed as if no one was there.
Holding a candle to look,
they saw the white-robed one lying under the wall—
it was a silver man.
The yellow-robed one was nowhere to be seen.
From then on, the family became wealthy.
A Villager from Jiàn'ān
There was a man living in a village in Jiàn'ān
who often sent a young servant boy
to go back and forth to the city.
The route passed by a large grave mound south of the house.
Beside the mound, there was always a child in yellow clothes
who would play with him, competing in strength.
His master found him delayed,
and the servant told him the truth.
The master spied on him and found it to be so.
One day,
he took a club and went there,
hiding in the grass.
When the young servant arrived,
the yellow-clothed child appeared again.
He immediately rose and struck it,
and it fell with the blow—
it was a golden child.
He took it home,
and the family became wealthy from then on.
Cài Yànqīng
Lúzhōu military officer Cài Yànqīng,
served as the garrison commander of Tuògāo.
On a summer night,
he sat outside the garrison gate enjoying the cool air,
when suddenly he saw a woman in white dancing alone
in the mulberry grove south of the road.
When he approached to look, she vanished.
The next night,
Yànqīng took a staff and went there first,
hiding in the grass.
After a long while,
the woman reappeared.
Just as she began to dance,
he struck her, and she fell to the ground,
turning into a silver bottle.
He then dug the ground
and obtained a thousand taels of silver.
Thus, he became a wealthy man, it is said.
Lǚ Shēng
During the Dàlì era,
there was a man named Lǚ Shēng,
who traveled from his post as deputy magistrate of Shàngyú in Kuàijī to the capital for reassignment.
Afterward, he lodged in Yǒngchóng Lane.
One evening,
he gathered with several friends for a meal in his room.
After eating,
they were about to retire for the night,
when suddenly an old woman,
with a pure white appearance and attire,
about two feet tall,
emerged from the northern corner of the room,
walking slowly forward,
her appearance extremely strange.
Everyone looked at her,
exchanging glances and laughing.
The old woman gradually approached his bed,
and said:
"You are having a gathering,
yet you cannot invite me?
Why do you treat me so coldly?"
Lǚ Shēng shouted at her.
She then retreated.
When she reached the northern corner,
she vanished from sight.
Both startled and bewildered,
no one knew where she had come from.
The next day,
Shēng was alone, awake in his room,
when he saw the old woman again at the northern corner,
advancing and retreating,
appearing fearful as if afraid of something.
Shēng shouted at her again,
and she disappeared.
The next day,
Shēng thought to himself:
"This must be a monster.
If she comes again tonight,
and I do not eliminate her,
she will surely bring me constant trouble."
He immediately placed a sword under his bed.
That night,
she indeed came again, walking slowly from the northern corner.
Her expression showed no fear.
When she reached the bed,
Shēng swung his sword at her.
The old woman suddenly leaped onto the bed and thrust her arm toward Shēng's chest,
then jumped around left and right,
waving her sleeves and dancing.
After a while,
another old woman suddenly leaped onto the bed,
also thrusting her arm toward Shēng.
Shēng suddenly felt his entire body turn icy cold, as if covered in frost.
Shēng swung his sword wildly again.
Soon,
several old women,
also began dancing around him.
Shēng continued swinging his sword.
Then there were more than ten old women,
each about an inch tall.
Although they multiplied, their appearances were identical,
indistinguishable from one another.
They scurried around the four walls,
and Shēng grew terrified,
unable to think of a way out.
One of the old women among them said to the scholar:
"I will now merge into one.
Watch closely."
Having said this,
they all moved toward each other,
gathered before the bed,
and merged together with a sound,
becoming one old woman again,
no different from the one first seen.
Shēng grew even more frightened,
and said to her:
"What kind of monster are you?
How dare you disturb a living person like this!
Leave at once!
Otherwise,
I will seek a Daoist master,
and use divine arts to subdue you.
What will you be able to do then?"
The old woman laughed and said:
"You speak too rashly.
If there is a master of arts,
I would like to meet him.
My coming here
was merely to play with you,
not to harm you.
Please do not be afraid.
I will now return to my place."
Having said this, she retreated to the northern corner and vanished.
The next day,
Shēng told others about the incident.
There was a man named Tián,
skilled in using talismans and arts to expel monsters and spirits,
and well-known throughout Cháng'ān.
Upon hearing this, he joyfully exclaimed:
"This is my specialty.
Removing it is as easy as crushing an ant.
Tonight, I wish to go to your house
and wait for it."
That night,
Shēng and Tián sat together in the room.
Before long, the old woman indeed came,
approaching the bed.
Tián shouted at her:
"Monster, leave at once!"
The old woman raised her head, her expression defiant, and paid no heed,
walking slowly back and forth for a long time.
She said to Tián:
"This is beyond your understanding."
Suddenly, the old woman waved her hand,
and her hand fell to the ground,
turning into another, very small old woman,
who leaped onto the bed
and rushed into Tián's mouth.
Tián cried out in alarm:
"Am I going to die?"
The old woman said to Shēng:
"I told you before that I meant you no harm,
but you would not listen.
Now, what about Tián's illness?
How is it?
However, this will also bring you wealth."
Having said this,
she left again.
The next day,
someone told Lǚ Shēng
that he should dig at the northern corner,
and he would find something.
Shēng joyfully returned home
and ordered his servant to dig thoroughly where she had vanished.
Indeed, before digging even ten feet,
they found a jar,
capable of holding about a hu,
filled with a large amount of mercury.
Shēng then realized that the old woman was a mercury spirit.
Tián eventually died from chills and trembling.
Shěn Yōuzhī
During the Shēngmíng era of Emperor Shùn of the Sòng dynasty,
Shěn Yōuzhī, the governor of Jīngzhōu,
had a stable where the horses
would often stamp their hooves, neigh in alarm,
as if seeing something.
Yōuzhī ordered someone to watch,
and they saw a white pony,
with a green rope tied around its belly,
coming directly from outside.
The stableman reported this in detail,
and Yōuzhī had someone hide by the manger at night to wait.
Soon, they saw the white pony come,
and suddenly vanish again.
Looking at the stable door, it was still closed.
Tracing its tracks,
it seemed to have gone directly into the inner chambers.
Those who saw it at the time
all said it was a monster.
Upon checking the inner chambers,
they found only a jade horse on the arm of his beloved concubine Féng Yuèhuá,
threaded with a green silk rope.
At night,
she would take it off and place it by her pillow.
Sometimes it would disappear at night,
but by morning it would return.
They tried taking it to examine,
and saw mud on its hooves.
Later, when Yōuzhī was defeated,
its whereabouts became unknown.
The Jade Dragon
In the eighth year of the Dàtóng era of the Liáng dynasty,
the garrison commander Yáng Guāngxīn
obtained a jade dragon.
It was one chǐ and two cùn long,
five cùn high,
and carved with exquisite craftsmanship,
unlike anything made by human hands.
Its belly could hold over a dǒu of liquid,
and its neck was hollow and curved.
When placed in water,
filled to the brim,
and then inverted,
the water would flow out from its mouth,
producing a sound like that of a qín or sè,
continuing until the water was completely drained.
Jiāng Yán
Jiāng Yán, at Qīngquán Mountain in Fùchūn County,
saw from afar a beautiful woman
dressed in purple, singing.
Yán approached her,
but after a few dozen steps,
the woman vanished,
leaving only the rock she had been standing on.
This happened several times,
until he finally obtained a piece of purple jade,
one chǐ in width.
Also, Bǐng Làng, at Jiǔtián Mountain, saw a bird
resembling a chicken,
red in color,
whose cry was like the sound of a shēng.
He shot and hit it,
whereupon it entered a cave.
Làng then chiseled the rock
and obtained a piece of red jade
shaped like the bird.
Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng
Empress Wǔ Zétiān once summoned the imperial grandsons,
seating them in the hall
to observe their play.
She then brought out jade rings, bracelets, cups, and plates, tributes from Western countries,
arranging them before and behind,
and freely allowed the children to compete for them,
to observe their temperaments.
All rushed to compete,
gaining substantial rewards.
Only Xuánzōng sat upright,
utterly unmoved.
The Empress greatly marveled at this,
patted his back, and said:
"This child shall become a Taiping Tianzǐ (Peaceful Son of Heaven)."
She then ordered the Jade Dragon-let to be fetched and bestowed upon him.
The Jade Dragon-let
was obtained by Emperor Tàizōng at the Jìnyáng Palace.
Empress Wéndé often kept it in her clothing chest.
On the third day after the birth of the future Emperor Gāozōng,
the Empress bestowed it upon him, along with pearl-adorned swaddling clothes.
Thereafter, it was always stored in the inner treasury.
Though it was no more than a few cùn in size,
it was warm, smooth, and exquisitely crafted,
unlike anything of the mortal world.
After Xuánzōng ascended the throne,
whenever the capital suffered from drought,
he would pray devoutly with it.
When heavy rain was imminent,
looking closely at it,
it seemed as if its scales and mane were stirring.
During the Kāiyuán era,
when the three capital regions suffered a great drought,
Xuánzōng prayed again,
but for over ten days, no rain fell.
The Emperor secretly cast it into the dragon pond of the Southern Palace.
Suddenly, clouds and mist violently arose,
and wind and rain followed.
Later, when he fled to Shu (Sichuan),
the imperial carriage reached the Wèi River.
About to cross,
they halted by the riverbank.
Among the attending servants,
some were washing or playing in the stream,
and found it in the sand.
The Emperor heard and was overjoyed,
gazing at it with tears streaming down, saying:
"This is the Jade Dragon-let I treasured in the past."
Afterwards, every night,
its radiance illuminated the entire room.
After the Emperor returned to the capital,
it was stolen by a young eunuch
and given to Lǐ Fǔguó.
Lǐ Fǔguó often kept it in a cabinet.
As Fǔguó was about to fall from power,
he heard sounds from the cabinet at night.
Opening it to look,
he found it had already disappeared.
Five-Colored Jade
In the early Tiānbǎo era,
Ān Sīshùn presented a five-colored jade belt.
Also, five-colored jade was found in the Left Treasury.
The Emperor wondered why recent tributes from the West contained no five-colored jade,
and ordered inquiries to the various Western tribes in Ānxī.
The tribes replied that they regularly offered it,
but it was all plundered by Xiǎo Bólǜ,
and never reached the court.
The Emperor was enraged
and wished to launch a punitive expedition.
Many ministers advised against it,
but Lǐ Línfǔ alone supported the Emperor's intention,
and further said that the military officer Wáng Tiānyùn
possessed the strategy and courage to lead.
Thus, Wáng Tiānyùn was ordered to lead forty thousand men,
also commanding allied tribal troops, to attack them.
When they approached the walls of Bólǜ's city,
the chieftain of Bólǜ,
terrified, pleaded for mercy,
presenting all his treasures and jade,
and promised annual tribute.
Tiānyùn refused,
proceeded to sack the city,
and returned with two thousand captives and their pearls and gems.
Among the Bólǜ was a sorcerer
who said the general's unjust actions were inauspicious,
and that a great wind would come from heaven.
After marching several hundred lǐ,
suddenly, terrifying winds arose from all directions,
snowflakes large as wings,
the wind churning the waters of a small sea into pillars of ice,
which rose and then shattered.
After half a day,
the small sea surged and swelled,
and all forty thousand men froze to death at once.
Only one man from the tribes and one Han Chinese survived to return,
and reported in full.
Emperor Xuánzōng was greatly astonished,
and immediately ordered a palace envoy to accompany the two to verify.
Reaching the side of the small sea,
the ice still stood jagged like mountains.
Across the water, they could see the soldiers' corpses,
some standing, some sitting,
transparent and countable.
As the palace envoy prepared to return,
the ice suddenly melted away,
and the multitude of corpses also vanished.
The Jade Pixie
Emperor Sùzōng bestowed upon Lǐ Fǔguó two jade talismans in the shape of mythical beasts,
each standing one and a half feet tall.
Their craftsmanship was so exquisite it seemed almost beyond human capability.
The fragrance of the jade
could be detected from several hundred paces away.
Even if locked away in golden boxes or stone cabinets,
their scent could not be contained.
If a sleeve accidentally brushed against them,
the fragrance would linger for years,
and even after repeated washings,
it would not fade.
Fǔguó often kept them by his side.
One day,
as he was adjusting his headdress,
one of the beasts began to laugh heartily,
while the other wailed mournfully.
Fǔguó was startled and lost his composure.
The laughing one continued without cease,
and the wailing one wept even more bitterly, tears streaming down.
Disgusted by their strangeness,
Fǔguó shattered them into powder
and dumped them into a latrine.
Afterward, plaintive cries of grievance were often heard.
In the Ānyì neighborhood where Fǔguó resided,
the fragrance lingered for a full month.
This was because grinding them into powder
only intensified their scent.
Within a year, Fǔguó died—
this was after he had destroyed the talismans.
Fǔguó’s favored servant, Mùróng Gōng,
knowing these were extraordinary objects,
secretly hid away two small containers of the powder.
Yú Cháo'ēn, undeterred by Fǔguó’s misfortune,
purchased them for three hundred thousand coins.
Later, when Cháo'ēn was about to be executed,
the fragrant powder transformed into white butterflies
that soared into the sky and vanished.
Commentators of the time believed
that such rare fragrances and treasures
were not meant to be hoarded by subjects.
The precious curiosities stored in Fǔguó’s home
were all unrecognizable to ordinary people.
In summer, he would place "Cooling Grass" in his hall—
its color resembling jade green,
its stems like bitter bamboo,
and its leaves finer than fir needles.
Though appearing dry and withered,
they never shed.
During the height of summer,
when placed between windows,
coolness would naturally arise.
The "Phoenix-Head Wood" stood one foot tall,
carved into the shape of a phoenix.
The wood itself resembled dried timber,
so its feather-like carvings were not entirely intact.
Even in the coldest times,
when placed in a grand hall or mansion,
a warm, spring-like atmosphere, as in the second or third month, would prevail—
hence its alternative name, "Ever-Spring Wood."
Even if set ablaze with fierce fire,
it would never char or blacken.
The Cooling Grass and Phoenix Wood
may have originated from the residence of Prince Xuē.
The *Records of the Ten Continents* states:
They come from the land of Huǒlín.
Soft Jade Whip
Emperor Dézōng once visited Xīngqìng Palace,
and
within a hidden compartment in a double wall, discovered a treasure box
containing a jade whip.
Its end was inscribed
with the words "Soft Jade Whip."
It was a tribute from a foreign land during the Tiānbǎo era.
Its patterns were elegant and auspicious,
its luster clear enough to reflect one’s image—
even the finest jade from Lántián
could not surpass it.
When bent, its head and tail would meet;
when straightened, it was as straight as a rope.
Even if struck with an axe or hammered,
it would suffer no damage.
Dézōng marveled at it as a divine object
and ordered a embroidered bag with linked cicada patterns made for it,
with a sheath of green silkworm silk.
Green silkworm silk
was a tribute from Míluó Kingdom in the Eastern Sea in the first year of the Yǒngtài era.
It was said that in their land grew mulberry trees
with twisting, coiled branches
that spread across the ground.
The larger ones extended for over ten *li*,
while the smaller ones shaded a hundred *mu*.
Upon them lived silkworms,
up to four inches long.
Their color was golden,
and their silk green—
hence also called "golden silkworm silk."
When relaxed, it measured one foot;
when stretched, it extended to ten feet.
Twisted into a sheath,
it became translucent inside and out, like strung pearls.
Even with the combined strength of ten men,
it could not be snapped.
Used as zither strings,
it would vex ghosts and spirits;
as crossbow strings,
arrows would fly a thousand paces;
as bowstrings,
arrows would travel five hundred paces.
The emperor ordered it stored in the inner treasury.
By the time of Zhū Cǐ’s rebellion and assault on the palace,
the whip’s whereabouts were unknown.
Jade Piglets
Lù Dàjūn, Commander of the Imperial Guards,
had a nephew whose wife,
while sleeping at night,
heard the chirping sounds of creatures fighting.
Upon waking,
she felt under her pillow
and retrieved two objects—
hastily lighting a lamp, she saw
they were both white jade piglets.
Several inches in size,
their form was exquisitely crafted.
She treasured them, keeping them within her pillow,
and guarded them.
From then on, wealth and goods increased daily,
the family prospered and multiplied,
every wish was fulfilled,
and their reputation and status
soared.
This lasted for twenty years.
Then one night, they suddenly vanished,
and the Lù family’s fortunes declined.
Marquis Suí
While traveling, Marquis Suí
encountered a great serpent, wounded, and healed it.
Later, the serpent brought a pearl in repayment.
The pearl was one inch in diameter,
pure white,
and glowed at night,
shining like the moon.
It was called the "Marquis Suí Pearl,"
also known as the "Bright Moon Pearl."
King Yān Zhāo
King Yān Zhāo sat upon the Sun-Grasping Terrace
when a black bird with a white neck
alighted where he was.
It held in its beak a pearl of penetrating light,
one foot in diameter.
This pearl was black as lacquer,
yet when hung, it illuminated clouds and sun,
and no spirit could conceal its essence.
This pearl came from the depths of the Yīn Spring.
The spring lay north of Hán Mountain,
within circular waters.
It was said the waves always flowed in a circular motion.
There was a black clam
that flew back and forth among the five mountains.
Huángdì and Wùchéngzǐ, while traveling Hán Mountain,
found the black clam upon a high seat—
thus its authenticity was known.
During King Zhāo’s time,
it was offered as tribute to his state.
The king fetched water from the Bǎozhāng Spring
to wash away the mud and sand, sighing:
"Since the sun and moon were hung,
I have seen black clams produce pearls
some eight or nine thousand times.
This clam produces one every thousand years,
and the pearls gradually become lighter and finer."
King Zhāo often carried this pearl in his grasp,
and during the hottest months,
his body remained cool and light.
It was called the "Heat-Dispelling, Coolness-Inviting Pearl."
Empress Gāo of Hàn
During the time of Empress Gāo of Hàn,
an edict was issued seeking a three-inch pearl.
The immortal Zhū Zhòng,
who traded pearls in the market of Kuàijī,
presented one.
He was rewarded with a hundred *jīn* of gold.
Princess Lǔyuán privately offered seven hundred *jīn* of gold
to Zhòng for another pearl.
He then presented a four-inch one.
Emperor Zhāng of the Later Hàn
In the first year of the Yuánhé era of Emperor Zhāng of the Later Hàn,
a bright pearl emerged in Guàntáo,
as large as a plum,
and radiantly luminous.
In the third year,
a bright moon pearl emerged on the shores of Yùzhāng,
It was as large as a chicken egg,
and four cùn eight fēn in circumference.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng
During the Dàtóng era of the Liáng dynasty,
during a sudden downpour in front of the palace,
multicolored precious pearls appeared.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng wore a joyful expression.
Yú Jì presented the "Ode to Auspicious Rain."
Fire Pearl
In the early Zhēnguàn era,
Línyì presented a fire pearl.
It resembled crystal.
It was said:
"Obtained from the country of Rākṣasa."
Its people had red hair and black bodies,
with beast-like teeth and eagle-like claws.
Whale's Eye
In the South Sea, there is a pearl,
which is the pupil of a whale's eye.
At night, it can reflect light,
and is called "night luminescence."
Among pearls, there are dragon pearls,
spat out by dragons.
Snake pearls,
spat out by snakes.
A common saying in the South Sea goes:
"A thousand snake pearls
are not worth one méiguì."
This indicates that snake pearls are of low value.
Méiguì is also a name for a pearl.
A common saying among the Yuè people goes:
"Planting a thousand acres of 'wooden slaves'
is not as good as one dragon pearl."
The Yuè custom regards pearls as the highest treasure;
when a girl is born, she is called a "pearl maiden,"
and when a boy is born, he is named "pearl child."
A common saying in the Wú-Yuè region states:
"A hú of bright pearls
is as precious as jade."
Hépǔ has a pearl market.
Pearl Pond
Off the coast of Liánzhōu, there are islands,
on which there is a large pond,
called the Pearl Pond.
Every year, the regional inspector prepares tribute,
personally supervising the pearl households as they enter the pond to gather pearls,
to fulfill the tribute levy.
According to the traditions of the elders,
if the governor is greedy,
the pearls move far away,
and depart.
They all gather old clams,
split them open, and take the pearls.
The pond is on the sea,
and it is suspected that its bottom connects with the sea;
moreover, the pond water is extremely deep,
and its depth cannot be measured.
Pearls as large as peas
are common pearls;
those as large as pellets
are also occasionally obtained.
Pearls an inch in diameter that can illuminate a room—
such exist only in tales,
and cannot be encountered.
Also, they take the meat of small clams,
string it on bamboo strips,
dry it in the sun,
and call it "pearl mother."
In Róngguì, it is customary to roast this dried meat
and serve it with wine.
Within the meat are fine pearls,
like grains of millet or rice,
thus it is known that the clams in the Pearl Pond,
regardless of their size,
all bear pearls within them.
Shǎochéng Pearls
On Shí Sǔn Street in Shǔ,
during heavy summer rains,
multicolored small pearls are often found.
It is commonly said the place lies over a sea eye,
but no one knows the reason.
The Shǔ monk Huì Yì said:
"According to historical records,
Shǔ's Shǎochéng was adorned with gold, jade, pearls, and kingfisher feathers.
Huán Wēn, disliking its excessive extravagance,
burned it down.
It should be in this location.
That we find small pearls here,
sometimes with holes,
could it not be from that?"
Green Mud Pearl
During the time of Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
a western country presented the lower jawbone of the Vairocana Heavenly King and the tongue of a Pratyekabuddha,
along with one Green Mud Pearl.
Wǔ Zétiān hung the jawbone and tongue
to show the common people.
The jawbone was as large as a folding chair;
the tongue was green,
as large as an ox tongue;
the pearl resembled a thumb,
slightly green.
The Empress, not knowing its value,
gave it to a monk of the Xīmíng Temple.
He placed it in the forehead of a Vajra statue.
Later, during a lecture,
a foreigner came to listen.
Seeing the pearl, he stared intently,
not taking his eyes off it for a moment.
This continued for over ten days;
he only gazed fixedly at the pearl below,
his mind not on the lecture.
The monk, knowing the reason,
thus asked if he wished to buy the pearl.
The foreigner said:
"If you are willing to sell it,
I will pay a heavy price."
The monk initially asked for a thousand strings of cash,
gradually raising it to ten thousand strings.
The foreigner did not haggle at all.
They finally settled on one hundred thousand strings,
and sold it.
The foreigner obtained the pearl,
inserted it into the flesh of his leg,
and returned to his western country.
The monk soon reported this to the court.
Wǔ Zétiān ordered the search for this foreigner.
He was found after several days.
The envoy asked where the pearl was.
The foreigner said
he had swallowed it into his stomach.
The envoy threatened to cut open his stomach.
The foreigner, having no alternative,
took it out from his leg.
Wǔ Zétiān summoned and asked him:
"You bought this at a high price;
what use do you have for it?"
The foreigner said:
"In the western countries, there is a Green Mud Lake,
full of pearls and treasures.
But the mud is deep and troublesome, making them unobtainable.
If this pearl is thrown into the lake,
the mud all turns to water,
and the treasures can be obtained."
Wǔ Zétiān then treasured and kept it.
It still existed by the time of Emperor Xuánzōng.
One-Inch Pearl
In recent times, a Persian foreigner
came to an inn in Fúfēng.
Seeing a square stone outside the host's door,
he lingered for several days.
The host asked him the reason.
The foreigner said:
"I wish to use the stone to pound cloth."
He then offered two thousand coins to buy it.
The host, very pleased with the money,
gave him the stone.
The foreigner carried the stone out,
and in front of the crowd,
split it open and obtained a one-inch pearl.
He cut open his armpit with a knife,
hid the pearl inside,
and then returned to his own country.
Sailing by ship on the sea,
after traveling for over ten days,
the ship suddenly seemed about to sink.
The sailors knew it was the sea god seeking treasure,
so they searched everywhere,
but had no treasure to give the god.
They thus intended to drown the foreigner.
The foreigner, frightened,
cut open his armpit and took out the pearl.
The sailors chanted:
"If you seek this pearl,
you should receive something."
The sea god then extended a hand,
very large and hairy,
took the pearl, and departed.
Precious Pearl
Behind the Yuè Temple in Xiányáng,
there was a crown of Emperor Wǔ of the Zhōu dynasty.
Adorning the crown was a pearl
as large as a plum,
but it was never regarded as a treasure throughout the ages.
During the reign of Empress Tiānhòu,
a scholar passed by the temple
and saw the pearl.
He playfully took it.
The weather was extremely hot,
so upon reaching the temple gate, he changed his clothes
and wrapped the pearl in the lining of his garment,
placing it at the feet of the Vajra statue.
He then forgot to retrieve it.
The next day,
he set off for Yángzhōu to collect debts.
Along the way, he stopped at Chénliú
and stayed at an inn.
At night, he heard foreigners competing over treasures,
so he put on his clothes and went to watch.
He mentioned the pearl adorning the crown.
The foreigners were greatly astonished and said:
"We have long known that there is such a treasure in Zhōngguó,
and we were just about to seek it."
The scholar said he had lost it.
The foreigners sighed in regret.
They told him,
saying:
"If you can retrieve it,
we will reward you with gold and silk.
Now, on your way to Yángzhōu,
how much are the debts you are collecting?"
The scholar said:
"Five hundred thousand."
The foreigners immediately gave him five hundred thousand
and told him to go back and retrieve the pearl.
The scholar went to the feet of the Vajra statue,
and the pearl was still there.
He took it and returned to see the foreigners.
The foreigners were overjoyed.
They feasted and celebrated for over ten days
before finally discussing the purchase.
They asked the scholar
how much he wanted.
The scholar boldly asked for one thousand strings of cash.
The foreigners laughed heartily and said:
"Why insult this pearl?"
They discussed the price among themselves
and set it at fifty thousand strings of cash.
The group of foreigners pooled their money to buy it.
They then invited the scholar
to accompany them to the sea
to witness the pearl's true value.
The scholar traveled with them to the eastern sea.
The chief foreigner used a silver cauldron to boil clarified butter,
and placed the pearl in a golden bottle,
which he then boiled again in the clarified butter.
After just seven days,
two elders and hundreds of their followers
arrived carrying treasures
to redeem the pearl from the foreigners.
But the foreigners stubbornly refused.
A few days later,
they brought mountains of treasures
and said
they wanted to redeem the pearl.
The foreigners again refused.
After over thirty days,
the crowd dispersed.
Two dragon maidens,
pure white and exquisitely beautiful,
threw themselves into the pearl bottle.
The pearl and the maidens melted into an ointment.
The scholar asked:
"Who were those trying to redeem it?"
The foreigner said:
"This pearl is a great treasure,
and it is guarded by two dragon maidens.
The dragons cherish their daughters,
so they brought treasures to redeem them.
I seek transcendence from this world;
why would I care for worldly wealth?"
He then applied the ointment to his feet,
walked on water,
and left the boat behind.
The other foreigners said:
"We all bought this pearl together;
why should you alone reap the benefits?
Now that you have gone,
what will become of us?"
The foreigner told them to apply the boiled clarified butter to their boat,
and they would have favorable winds to return home.
Everything happened as he said.
The chief foreigner ultimately disappeared without a trace.
Water Pearl
The Dà'ānguó Temple
was the former residence of Emperor Ruìzōng when he was still Prince Xiàng.
After ascending the throne,
he established a Buddhist sanctuary there.
The prince once donated a precious pearl
to be kept in the temple's permanent treasury,
saying
it was worth hundreds of millions.
The temple monks stored it in a cabinet
without regarding it as particularly valuable.
In the tenth year of the Kāiyuán era,
the temple monks were raising funds for merit-making
and opened the cabinet to inspect the treasures,
intending to sell them.
They saw an inscription on the case that read:
"This pearl is worth hundreds of millions."
The monks opened it together
and saw it looked like a piece of stone,
red in color.
At night, it emitted a faint light
several inches high.
The temple monks discussed:
"This is just an ordinary object;
how could it be worth hundreds of millions?
Let's try selling it."
So they sent a monk to the market to oversee the sale
and test its value.
After a few days,
some nobles inquired about it.
But upon seeing it,
they said:
"This is just an ordinary stone,
no different from rubble.
How dare you ask for such an outrageous price!"
They all laughed scornfully and left.
The monk felt ashamed.
Ten days later,
some people inquired about it,
knowing it glowed at night,
and offered several thousand.
The price gradually increased.
After over a month,
a foreigner from the Western Regions
came to the market
seeking treasures
and was overjoyed to see the pearl.
He reverently placed it on his head,
indicating he was a noble foreigner.
Through an interpreter, he asked:
"How much is the pearl worth?"
The monk said:
"Hundreds of millions."
The foreigner fondled it, hesitated, and left.
The next day, he returned,
and the interpreter said to the monk:
"The pearl is indeed worth hundreds of millions,
but the foreign guest has been here for a long time.
Now he offers forty million to buy it.
Is that acceptable?"
The monk was delighted
and went with him to see the temple abbot.
The abbot agreed.
The next day,
the foreigner paid forty million strings of cash
and took the pearl away.
He then said to the monk:
"I have underpaid for the pearl by a great amount,
but I hope you will not blame me."
The monk asked the foreigner where he came from
and what the pearl could do.
The foreigner said:
"I am from the Dàshí Kingdom.
Our king first established friendly relations during the Zhēnguàn era
and presented this pearl as tribute.
Since then, our kingdom has often missed it.
We offered to appoint anyone who could retrieve it
as prime minister.
We searched for seventy or eighty years,
and now, fortunately, I have found it.
This is a water pearl.
Whenever the army stops to rest,
dig two feet into the ground,
bury the pearl in it,
and water will immediately spring forth,
enough to supply several thousand people.
Thus, the army never lacks water on marches.
Since losing the pearl,
our marches have often suffered from thirst and water shortages."
The monk did not believe him.
The foreigner ordered the ground to be dug up and the pearl buried.
Soon, a spring gushed forth,
clear and cool,
flowing abundantly.
The monk drank from it
and finally realized its miraculous power.
The foreigner then took the pearl and left,
disappearing without a trace.
Lǐ Miǎn
Sītú Lǐ Miǎn,
during the early years of the Kāiyuán era,
served as a county captain in Jùnyí.
When his term of office ended,
he planned to travel along the Biàn River to visit Guǎnglíng.
As he reached Suīyáng,
suddenly an elderly Persian foreigner, gravely ill,
came leaning on a staff to see Lǐ Miǎn and said:
"This stranger from a distant land is severely ill and near death,
and longs to return to Jiāngdū.
Knowing you, sir, are a virtuous elder,
I wish to entrust myself to your benevolent shelter,
hoping not to trouble you greatly while receiving your protection."
Lǐ Miǎn took pity on him,
so he ordered him to board the boat,
and provided him with gruel.
The Persian felt deeply ashamed,
and thus said:
"I was originally of royal and noble lineage,
but engaged in trade here,
for over twenty years already.
I have three sons at home,
so surely some must be seeking me."
A few days later,
the boat stopped at Sìshàng,
and the man's illness became critical.
He then dismissed others and told Lǐ Miǎn:
"In my country, the hereditary treasure pearl was recently lost,
and a reward was offered to anyone who could recover it:
a hereditary dukedom and ministerial rank.
I coveted the reward and desired the position,
so I left my homeland to search for it.
Recently, I have obtained it,
and returning with it would bring me wealth and honor.
The pearl is worth a million,
but I feared carrying such a treasure far from home,
so I cut my flesh and hid it inside.
Unfortunately, I fell ill,
and now I am about to die.
Moved by your kindness and righteousness,
I respectfully offer it to you."
He then drew a knife and cut open his thigh,
the pearl came out, and he died.
Lǐ Miǎn then provided clothing and shrouds for him,
and buried him by the Huái River.
While covering the grave,
he secretly placed the pearl in the corpse's mouth before leaving.
Upon reaching Wéiyáng,
he visited a tavern.
Suddenly, he found himself surrounded by a group of Persians,
and thus managed to converse with them.
Among them was a young Persian,
whose appearance resembled the deceased.
Lǐ Miǎn inquired,
and indeed it matched what the deceased had described.
Lǐ Miǎn then thoroughly questioned him about the circumstances,
and he turned out to be the son of the deceased Persian.
Lǐ Miǎn told him the burial location,
the young Persian wept bitterly,
exhumed the grave, retrieved the pearl, and left.
Lǐ Guàn
Lǐ Guàn,
whose origins are unknown.
He was of a solitary and quiet nature,
and often stayed in Jiànchāng County, Hóngzhōu.
He moored his boat by the shore,
where there was a small thatched hut on the bank,
inside lay a sick Persian.
Lǐ Guàn took pity on him as he neared death,
and provided him with warm gruel.
A few days later, the man died.
Before dying,
he pointed to the black felt mat he lay on and said:
"Inside is a pearl,
about an inch in diameter,
to repay your kindness."
After his death,
the felt mat emitted a faint, shimmering light.
Lǐ Guàn took it and found the pearl.
He bought a coffin and buried him,
secretly placing the pearl in the Persian's mouth.
He planted a tree to mark the grave.
Ten years later,
he passed through the old place again.
At that time, Yáng Píng was the surveillance commissioner,
and there was a foreign official document
regarding a Persian who died at an inn in Jiànchāng.
The family that had provided him food
had been imprisoned and interrogated for a year.
Lǐ Guàn inquired about their crime,
and the prisoners recounted the whole story.
Lǐ Guàn informed the county officials,
and together they went to the outer graves to cut down the tree.
The tree had already grown to arm-span thickness.
They opened the coffin and looked at the dead Persian;
his appearance was as if alive,
and they retrieved a pearl from his mouth and returned it.
That evening, Lǐ Guàn rowed his boat away,
and no one knew where he went.
Also, the Shàngshū Gùshí records that the Vice Director of the Ministry of War, Lǐ Yuē,
buried a Persian merchant,
and obtained a pearl which he placed in the corpse's mouth.
This is roughly similar to the two stories above.
Shàngqīng Pearl
When Sùzōng was a child,
he was often favored by Xuánzōng.
Whenever he sat before him,
Xuánzōng would gaze intently at his appearance,
and say to Wǔ Huìfēi:
"This child has a most extraordinary appearance;
in the future, he will also be a blessed Son of Heaven in our family."
He then ordered the Shàngqīng jade pearl to be fetched,
wrapped it in crimson gauze,
and tied it around his neck.
This was a tribute from the country of Jìbīn during the Kāiyuán era.
It was radiant and pure white,
and could illuminate an entire room.
Looking into it, one could see immortals, jade maidens,
cloud-cranes, and crimson ceremonial banners,
moving within it.
When Sùzōng ascended the throne,
divine light often shone from the treasure vault,
illuminating the day.
The vault keeper reported the matter in detail.
The Emperor said:
"Could it be the Shàngqīng Pearl?"
He then ordered it brought out.
The crimson gauze was still there.
He shed tears,
showed it to all his close ministers, and said:
"This is what I received as a child
from Emperor Míng Huáng."
He then ordered it stored in a green jade casket,
and placed it in his bedchamber.
Whenever floods, droughts, or military conflicts arose in the land,
he would devoutly pray to it,
and it never failed to bring a response.
The Boat Watcher
In Huátíng County, Sūzhōu,
there was a Lù Sìguān temple.
In the early years of the Yuánhé era,
several dozen salt boats were moored in front of the temple.
The boat watcher, after a night rain,
suddenly saw a bright light like fire in front of the temple,
so he went to look.
He saw a creature several zhang long,
as large as a roof beam,
playing with a ball of fire in its mouth,
sometimes swallowing it.
The boatman did not know what it was,
so he threw a bamboo pole at it from a distance.
The creature, startled, fled into the grass,
leaving the light on the ground.
Going forward to look,
he found it was a pearl about an inch in diameter,
its radiance dazzling to the eyes.
This man obtained it,
but fearing its light would be seen by others,
he wrapped it in his clothes.
The light shone through.
Thinking that treasures fear impurity,
he took off his undergarments and wrapped it,
and the light then did not show.
Afterward, no one knew of it.
He went to a Persian shop in Yángzhōu to sell it,
and received several thousand strings of cash.
He asked the Persian:
"What kind of pearl is this?"
The Persian did not answer and left.
Yán Shēng
There was a man named Yán Shēng from Féngyì,
who lived south of the Hàn River.
Once, while traveling on Xiàn Mountain,
he found an object.
It was shaped like a pellet,
black in color and large,
with a glow,
and when looked at, it was clear and transparent,
like thin ice.
Yán Shēng took it to show others.
Some said:
"It is a pearl."
Yán Shēng thus named it the "pellet pearl,"
and often kept it in a box.
Later, when Yán Shēng traveled to Cháng'ān,
he met a foreigner at the Chūnmíng Gate.
The foreigner knocked and said:
"In your clothing bag, there is a rare treasure.
I wish to have a look."
Yán Shēng immediately showed him the pellet pearl.
The foreigner held it in his hands and joyfully said:
"This is a rare treasure of the world.
I am willing to pay three hundred thousand for it."
Yán Shēng asked:
"What use does this treasure have?
And why do you value it so highly?"
The foreigner replied:
"I am from a western country.
This is the most precious treasure of my country.
Our people call it the 'Clear Water Pearl.'
If placed in turbid water,
it becomes clear and transparent.
Since we lost this treasure,
for almost three years,
the wells and springs in our country have all turned turbid,
and our people have all fallen ill.
Therefore, I crossed seas and mountains,
coming to Zhōngxià to seek it.
Now, I have indeed found it with you."
The foreigner immediately ordered turbid water to be poured into a jar,
and threw the pearl into it.
In a moment, the water became clear and sparkling,
with every detail visible.
Yán Shēng then gave the pearl to the foreigner,
received the payment, and left.
Zhāng Wén Guāng
When Zhāng Wén Guāng governed Hóngnóng,
he captured more than ten tomb robbers.
Among them, one person
requested a private audience to speak of a matter.
Zhāng Wén Guāng thus dismissed the officials and questioned him alone.
The man replied:
"I wish to redeem my life with another matter.
At Yáo's daughter's tomb in the southern mountains of Lúshì County,
I have recently heard that people have excavated it,
and obtained a large pearl and a jade bowl,
whose value cannot be estimated.
There are many other precious objects,
which the world does not recognize."
Zhāng Wén Guāng then sent officials to investigate,
and indeed, the tomb showed signs of being opened.
Soon, the robbers were captured,
and their confessions matched the earlier statements.
When they implicated their accomplices,
they claimed they were all in the ironworks of Shāng Prefecture.
At that time, the governor of Shāng was a renowned official.
When the prefecture sent an official letter,
and Zhāng Wén Guāng wrote a letter,
the governor angrily refused to hand them over.
Those who secretly knew said
that the pearl and jade objects
had all been taken to the homes of noble families in the capital.
Later, when Zhāng Wén Guāng left from the east of the capital,
passing through Lúshì,
he inquired again in the county,
and everything was as described.
Wèi Qìng
Wèi Qìng
was a commoner from Rǔfén.
He lived in Wēnquán.
His family had been idle for generations,
but by Wèi Qìng's time,
he took up farming.
Once, he plowed under the moonlight at the foot of the ancient Xiàng City south of the village,
and rested wearily on a desolate path.
Suddenly, he saw a bright white light,
rising from the fields,
like a shooting star.
Wèi Qìng covered it and obtained it,
then hid it in his bosom.
At dawn, when he returned to look at it,
it was a large pearl.
Its diameter was one and a half inches,
sparkling without the slightest flaw.
He wrapped it in a silk pouch,
and sealed it in a lacquered box.
He once showed it to a knowledgeable person.
Who said:
"This is a treasure from Hépǔ.
If you keep it,
even if you do not become noble, you will surely become wealthy."
Wèi Qìng treasured it even more,
often keeping it in his bedroom.
From then on, his family's wealth grew daily.
He raised four hundred head of cattle,
cultivated two thousand acres of land,
and his silk, grain, and other possessions were commensurate.
Within ten years,
he became a wealthy man.
By the end of the Qiánfú era,
Wèi Qìng suddenly fell ill.
Although doctors and shamans were both consulted,
none could diagnose his illness.
After a month,
his illness became critical.
Suddenly, he heard a clanging sound in front of his pillow.
Wèi Qìng's heart stirred,
and he ordered the box to be opened.
The pearl had cracks like threads,
and its color had turned black.
A few days later, he died,
and the pearl also disappeared.
From then on, his family's wealth dwindled daily.
His son was also unworthy,
selling off possessions to fund his gambling and drinking expenses.
Before the mourning period ended,
the household was already as empty as a hanging chime stone.
The Foreigner Selling Cakes
There was a jǔrén in the capital city.
His neighbor was a foreigner who sold cakes.
He had no wife.
After several years,
the foreigner suddenly fell ill.
The scholar went to inquire after him
and gave him medicinal decoctions.
But he did not recover.
On the verge of death, he told him:
"In my homeland, I was very wealthy.
Due to turmoil,
I fled here.
Originally, I had an agreement with a fellow countryman to come and retrieve me,
so I have stayed here for a long time,
unable to go elsewhere.
You have shown me compassion and concern,
and I have nothing to repay you with.
In my left arm, there is a pearl,
which I have treasured for many years.
Now that I am dying, it is of no use to me,
so I offer it to you.
After I die, I beg you to bury me.
For you, sir, this pearl
is also of no use.
Nowadays, there are no other people who know of it.
But if you know of any marketplace
where foreign merchants from the Western Regions arrive,
then ask them about it,
and you will surely fetch a great price."
The scholar agreed.
After the foreigner died,
he cut open his left arm
and indeed found a pearl.
It was as large as a pellet,
and not very lustrous.
The scholar arranged the burial.
He then took it to the market,
but no one inquired about it.
Three years had already passed.
Suddenly, he heard that new foreign merchants had arrived in the city,
so he went to the market with the pearl.
Upon seeing it, the foreigner was greatly astonished and said:
"How did you, sir, obtain this treasure pearl?
This is not something found in recent times.
May I ask where you got it?"
The scholar then explained.
The foreigner then wept and said:
"This was my fellow countryman.
We had originally agreed to inquire about this item together.
On the way here, we encountered a storm at sea,
drifted through several countries,
and thus delayed five or six years.
Upon arriving here, I intended to search for him,
but I did not expect he had already died."
He then requested to buy it.
The scholar, seeing the pearl was not very precious,
merely asked for five hundred thousand.
The foreigner paid the price accordingly.
The scholar inquired about its use.
The foreigner said:
"If a Hàn person obtains the method,
they can take the pearl to the sea,
use one shí of oil,
boil two dǒu,
and then it will be cut.
Entering the sea, the body will not get wet,
and dragon gods will fear it,
allowing one to obtain treasures.
This is one of the six methods.
Agate
During the time of Emperor Zhuānxū,
the country of Dānqiū presented an agate jar
to hold sweet dew.
Due to the emperor's virtue,
distant lands came to offer tribute,
and the dew was used to fill the kitchens.
Agate is a type of stone,
and those from the south are superior.
Those skilled in distinguishing them
will, when a horse dies, tap its brain and examine it.
If its color is like blood,
then it can travel ten thousand lǐ in a day,
able to soar through the void;
if the brain color is yellow,
it can travel a thousand lǐ a day;
if the brain color is blue,
its neigh can be heard several hundred lǐ away;
if the brain color is black,
entering water, its mane and hair will not get wet,
and it can travel five hundred lǐ a day;
if the brain color is white,
it is strong but slow.
Nowadays, vessels are mostly made from red ones.
If they are artificially made,
they often do not become proper vessels,
and even if they do, they are crude.
The people of that country listen to a horse's neigh
to distinguish the color of its brain.
Rhinoceros
The rhinoceros
generally resembles an ox but has a pig-like head.
Its legs are like an elephant's.
Its hooves have three nails.
Its head has two horns:
one on the forehead is the sì rhinoceros;
one on the nose is smaller,
called the húmào rhinoceros.
Those on the nose are all tightly bound with few speckles,
often with extraordinary patterns.
Male rhinoceroses also have two horns,
both are hairy rhinoceroses,
all with millet-like patterns,
suitable for making belts.
Among thousands of rhinoceros horns,
occasionally there may be a pierced one.
The speckles vary in size and are extraordinary,
with no fixed pattern.
Some have asymmetrical speckled lines.
Some have large speckles at the tip and small ones at the base.
This is called inverted insertion piercing.
These two types also have no constant pattern among the five colors.
If the piercing is clear with distinct black and white,
and the speckles are extraordinary,
then the price is reckoned in tens of thousands,
making it a rare treasure of the world.
There is also the duòluó rhinoceros,
the largest among rhinoceroses,
with a single horn weighing seven or eight jīn,
said to be from the forehead of a bull.
Its speckles are mostly scattered head bean dots.
In color,
the deeper ones are suitable for making kuǎ;
scattered and shallow ones
are carved into plates, dishes, and vessels.
There is also the hàijī rhinoceros.
The pìchén rhinoceros,
pìshuǐ rhinoceros, ,
míng rhinoceros,
These several rhinoceroses are only heard of in tales,
and cannot be seen.
Moon Mirror
King Líng of Zhōu built the Kūnzhāo Terrace,
where there was a courtier named Cháng Hóng,
whose cleverness and wisdom flowed like a stream,
and thus he gained attendance.
During long nights of feasting and pleasure,
with jesting, dancing, and laughter,
there were performances of exotic customs.
Hundreds of entertainments were arrayed side by side,
bells and stones played together.
They also presented rare treasures from distant lands.
There were jade-like people,
dragon-like brocades,
and also mirror-like stones,
and stone-like mirrors.
This stone was white as the moon,
reflecting the face like snow,
and was called the moon mirror.
The jade people all had mechanisms,
able to move on their own,
and were called mechanical beauties.
Cháng Hóng said to the king:
"This is due to the attraction of your sage virtue."
Thus, the people of Zhōu considered Cháng Hóng flattering and sycophantic, and eventually killed him.
His blood flowed and turned into stone,
or some say into jade discs,
and his corpse was never seen.
Treasures of Qín
When Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn first entered the Xiányáng Palace,
he toured the treasury.
The gold, jade, and rare treasures
were beyond description.
Among the things that astonished him
were five jade lamps,
each seven and a half chǐ tall.
Below, they were fashioned as coiled chī dragons,
holding the lamps in their mouths.
When the lamps were lit, the scales and armor of the dragons all seemed to move,
shining brilliantly as if a room full of stars.
There were also twelve cast bronze figures,
each three chǐ tall,
arranged on a single mat.
They held qín, zhù, shēng, and yú instruments,
each figure grasping a different one.
They were all adorned with colorful decorations,
as if they were living people.
Beneath the mat were two bronze tubes,
their upper openings rising several chǐ high,
extending behind the mat.
One tube was empty,
the other contained a cord,
as thick as a finger.
If one person blew into the empty tube,
and another person pulled the cord,
then the qín, zhù, shēng, and yú would all play,
no different from real music.
There was a jade qín, six chǐ long,
fitted with thirteen strings above,
and twenty-six huī markers.
All were decorated with the seven treasures,
and inscribed with the name "Music of Yúfán."
There was a jade flute, two chǐ three cùn long,
with six holes.
When blown, one could see carriages, horses, mountains, and forests,
appearing faintly one after another.
When the blowing ceased, they would no longer be seen.
It was inscribed with the name "Pipe of Zhāohuá."
There was a square mirror,
four chǐ wide,
five chǐ nine cùn tall,
transparent and bright on both sides.
If a person approached it directly to look,
their reflection would appear upside down;
if they covered their heart with their hand and approached,
their intestines, stomach, and five organs would be visible.
Clearly and without doubt.
If a person had an illness inside,
they could cover their heart and look into it,
and would surely know the location of the illness.
Furthermore, if a woman had wicked thoughts,
her gallbladder would expand and her heart would stir.
Qín Shǐhuángdì often used it to examine palace women;
if their gallbladder expanded and heart stirred,
he would have them killed.
Emperor Gāozǔ sealed all these away,
awaiting Xiàng Yǔ.
Xiàng Yǔ took them all east.
Later, their whereabouts were unknown.
Coral
In the Jīcǎo Pond of the Hàn Palace,
there was coral,
twelve chǐ tall,
one trunk with three branches.
It had four hundred and sixty-three stems.
It was presented by King Zhào Tuó of Nányuè,
and was called the "Beacon Fire Tree."
At night it glowed,
as if constantly about to ignite.
Also, in Yùlín Commandery there was a coral market,
a place where seafaring merchants traded coral.
The coral was bluish-green,
each plant having several dozen branches,
with no leaves between the branches.
The larger ones were five or six chǐ tall,
the smallest just over a chǐ.
The jiāo people said,
there is a Coral Palace in the sea.
In the second year of the Yuánfēng era of Hàn,
Yùlín Commandery presented a coral woman,
the emperor ordered it planted in front of the hall,
and called it the "Female Coral."
Suddenly its branches and leaves grew very lush,
but by the time of Emperor Líng, the tree died,
and all took it as an omen of the Hàn dynasty's impending decline.
Also, in the sea of the Bólín Kingdom,
two thousand lǐ from the capital,
there was a flying bridge.
Crossing the sea westward,
one reached the Qiělán Kingdom.
From Qiělán there were piled stones,
south of the piled stones was a great sea.
In the sea, coral grew on the seabed.
A large ship would lower an iron net into the sea;
when it first grew,
it gradually resembled a fungus.
After one year,
it would emerge through the mesh of the net,
turning yellow,
with branches and stems interlocking.
The smaller ones
were three chǐ,
the larger ones over a zhàng.
After three years, the color turned blue.
Using
iron rakes to loosen its roots,
a windlass was set up on the ship,
to lift the iron net and bring it out.
Therefore, the place was named Coral Island.
If left unharvested for long,
it would rot and decay.
Four Treasures Palace
Emperor Wǔ made a seven-treasure bed, a mixed-treasure table screen, and a mixed-treasure curtain,
and set them up in the Guì Palace.
People of the time called it the Four Treasures Palace.
Yánqīng Chamber
Dǒng Yǎn often rested in the Yánqīng Chamber,
using painted stone as a bed,
for the stone's pattern resembled a painting.
The stone body was very light,
and came from the Zhìzhī Kingdom.
Above was set a purple glass curtain,
a huǒqí screen,
arranged with língmá candles,
and a purple jade plate.
Like a coiled dragon,
all were adorned with assorted treasures.
Onlookers outside the door fanned Dǒng Yǎn.
Dǒng Yǎn said:
"Does jade and stone require fanning to become cool?"
The attendants stopped fanning,
and reached out to touch it,
only then realizing there was a screen.
Dǒng Yǎn also used jade essence to make a plate,
storing ice before his knees.
The jade essence was as pure and clear as the ice,
the attendants said that ice without a plate
would surely melt,
wetting the mat,
so he brushed it together with the jade plate.
It fell down the steps,
and both the ice and jade shattered.
Dǒng Yǎn found this even more amusing.
This jade essence was tribute from the Qiāntú Kingdom,
Emperor Wǔ bestowed it upon Dǒng Yǎn.
During the Āi and Píng eras,
people still had such vessels,
but many were damaged.
During Wáng Mǎng's time,
their whereabouts were no longer known.
Jade Rúyì
During Sūn Quán's time in Wú,
someone excavated and obtained a bronze box,
two chǐ seven cùn long,
with a glass lid.
