Inside was a white jade rúyì.
The handle was carved with dragons, tigers, and cicada shapes.
No one could understand its origin.
They sent someone to ask Zhōng.
Zhōng
was a man of broad learning.
He said:
"In the past, Qín Shǐhuáng, because Jīnlíng had the aura of an emperor,
leveled the hills and mounds,
burying treasures everywhere,
to counteract the royal aura."
Could this be one of them?
Seven-Treasure Whip
Emperor Míng of Jìn rode alone and stealthily entered,
to spy on Wáng Dūn's camp.
Wáng Dūn detected him,
and sent cavalry to pursue him.
The emperor fled.
He then gave a seven-treasure whip to an old woman at an inn,
and scattered horse dung.
When Wáng Dūn's pursuers arrived,
they saw the horse dung,
and thought the emperor was already far away.
They then coveted the whip,
and did not pursue further.
Rhinoceros Comb
Jiǎng Qián of Dōnghǎi in Jìn,
once traveled to Bùjī County.
He saw a corpse lying under a forest,
already rotten and foul-smelling.
Crows came to eat it.
Then he saw a little child,
about three feet tall,
coming to drive the crows away.
The crows then flew off.
This happened repeatedly.
Jiǎng Qián found it strange,
so he went closer to look.
He saw that on the dead man’s head was a tōngtiānxī dǎo hairpin,
worth tens of thousands of coins,
so he pulled it out and took it.
After he left,
the crows flocked together,
with no one to drive them away anymore.
Jiǎng Qián later presented this hairpin to Prince Wǔlíng of Jìn.
The prince died.
It was used to pay for monks’ coffins.
Wáng Wǔgāng bought it for ninety thousand coins.
Later it fell into the hands of Grand Tutor Chǔ.
Chǔ gave it as a gift to the late Prime Minister of Qí, Prince Yùzhāng.
After the prince died,
his concubine, Lady Jiāng, broke it to make hairpins.
Every night,
she would see a child circling her bed, crying and saying:
"Why was I butchered and cut apart?
I will surely take revenge:
I will not suffer this injustice and cruelty alone."
Lady Jiāng was disgusted by this.
A little over a month later, she died.
The Three Treasures of Yùqīng
Wéi Yǎn of Dùlíng,
courtesy name Jǐngzhāo.
During the Kāiyuán era,
he passed the jìnshì examination,
and traveled to Shǔ.
Shǔ had many scenic spots.
It happened to be late spring,
and Wéi Yǎn, along with several friends,
held a flower and wine banquet.
They did not stop even at night.
One day,
someone invited them, saying:
"Ten lǐ south of the commandery,
there is a pavilion of the Zhèng family,
standing in a garden,
truly a place beyond the mundane world.
I wish to go together."
Wéi Yǎn heard this,
and was very pleased,
so he went south with them.
After traveling ten lǐ,
they reached the Zhèng family pavilion.
It stood tall and lofty,
soaring majestically on all sides,
its gate adorned with flowers,
its steps rising like mist.
Wéi Yǎn gazed at it, unable to look away.
It was truly what is called a place beyond the mundane world.
The messenger bowed and invited Wéi Yǎn inside.
Once inside,
he saw over ten immortals on the pavilion,
all of extreme beauty.
They stood still as if waiting,
their cloud-like sleeves half-draped,
fluttering gracefully.
Those serving on the left and right,
were also over ten in number.
Their embroidered robes were exquisite and ethereal,
almost beyond description.
One of them looked at Wéi Yǎn and said:
"Jìnshì Wéi has arrived."
He ordered the attendants to invite him up to the pavilion.
Ascending the slanting railings layer by layer,
he went up and bowed.
The group of immortals said joyfully:
"Have you not heard of the story of Liú and Ruǎn?
Today is just like that.
We wish to offer you a feast until drunk,
to fully enjoy the spring scenery.
What do you think?"
Wéi Yǎn thanked them and said:
"I never expected to become like Liú and Ruǎn today,
how fortunate I am!
But then, what place is this?
And who are you, ladies?
I wish to know."
The immortals said:
"We are maidens of Yùqīng,
and have lived here for a long time.
This is the Yùqīng Palace.
We heard earlier that you are a jìnshì who failed the examination,
traveling and staying here,
so we wished to extend an invitation,
but feared you might not care to come,
or that it would bring you disgrace.
Therefore, we borrowed the Zhèng family pavilion to invite you.
You have indeed fulfilled our wish.
However,
this is an immortal abode.
Although it is said that mortals cannot linger here,
for you to stay,
it certainly does no harm.
We hope you do not doubt it."
They then ordered wine and music for a feast in the pavilion,
all string and wind instruments were played,
ethereal and clear,
transcending the mundane and reaching the mystical,
unlike any music of the human world.
When the wine was in full swing,
the immortals said:
"We hear that the Táng emperor reveres immortals.
We have a new musical piece,
called 'Zǐyún',
and wish to present it to the sage ruler.
You are a man of Táng,
could you pass it on for us,
is that possible?"
Wéi Yǎn said:
"I am but a scholar,
in Cháng'ān,
merely toiling in the dust of the mundane world,
I cannot even catch a glimpse of the emperor's gate,
nor am I a connoisseur of music,
how could I accomplish this?"
The immortals said:
"Since you cannot,
we will transmit it to the emperor through a dream instead."
They also said:
"We have three treasures,
which we will give to you.
They can make you as rich as princes and nobles,
please accept them.
Take them!"
They then ordered the attendants to fetch the treasures.
First, a cup was brought out,
its color green and glowing, transparent and clear.
Looking at Wéi Yǎn, they said:
"This is the Bìyáo Cup."
Next, a pillow was brought out,
jade-like with a slight red hue,
called the Hóngruí
Pillow.
Then a small box was brought out,
its color purple,
also jade-like,
but even more luminous and clear than jade,
called the Zǐyù Box.
Afterward, they all gave them to Wéi Yǎn.
Wéi Yǎn bowed in thanks and left.
Before he had traveled one lǐ,
he looked back at the pavilion,
and it had vanished without a trace.
Wéi Yǎn found it strange,
but ultimately did not know where it had been.
He then took the treasures and returned to Cháng'ān.
The following year, he failed the examination again,
and traveled east to Guǎnglíng,
where he displayed the treasures in the Guǎnglíng market.
A foreigner saw them and bowed, saying:
"These are rare treasures of the world.
Even over thousands of years,
no one has obtained them.
How did you come to have them?"
Wéi Yǎn told him the story.
He then asked:
"What treasures are these?"
The foreigner said:
"They are the Three True Treasures of Yùqīng."
He then exchanged them for tens of millions in value.
Wéi Yǎn thus built a grand mansion,
and became a wealthy man in Guǎnglíng.
He eventually died as a commoner.
Precious Bones
In Cháng'ān's Píngkāng Ward, there was the Bodhi Temple.
Because Lǐ Línfǔ's residence lay to the east,
a bell tower was therefore built to the west.
Within the temple were Minister Guō's hawksbill turtle whip,
and the seven-treasure curtain of Minister Guō's wife, Lady Wáng.
The temple's abbot, Yuányì,
was knowledgeable about many old tales.
He said that
whenever Chancellor Lǐ's birthday arrived,
he would often request monks from this temple in turn,
to come to his residence and hold a vegetarian feast.
There was one monk who once chanted praises to the Buddha,
and was bestowed a saddle as alms.
He sold it,
and its price was seventy thousand.
Also, there was a monk named Guǎng who had some reputation.
After several years had passed,
it was his turn to chant praises to the Buddha.
Consequently, he lavishly extolled Lǐ Línfǔ's merits and virtues,
hoping to receive a generous donation.
When he finished,
from behind the curtain emerged a colored basket;
wrapped in a fragrant silk kerchief was an object,
resembling a rotten nail,
several inches long.
The monk returned,
greatly disappointed,
and was ashamed and regretful for several days.
Moreover, he thought that a high minister would not deceive him,
so he took it to the Western Market,
showed it to a foreign merchant,
and asked for a price of one thousand.
The foreigner saw it,
and laughed heartily, saying:
"Not enough."
The monk then spoke with even greater earnestness,
increasing the price to five hundred thousand.
The foreigner said:
"This treasure is worth ten million."
And thus gave it to him.
The monk inquired its name.
He said:
"This is a precious bone."
Purple Zhùjié
During the Qiányuán era,
as the state had recaptured the two capitals,
provisions and funds were insufficient.
The Investigating Censor Kāng Yúnjiān
was appointed as the Commissioner of Revenue for the Jiānghuái region.
He levied one-fifth from the merchants, travelers, and commoners of Jiānghuái,
to supplement the needs of the time.
Hóngzhōu,
a major city between the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
Yúnjiān ordered Record-Keeper Adjutant Lǐ Wéiyàn to oversee this matter.
There was a Buddhist monk
who requested to contribute a million.
Then from under his arm he took out
a small vial.
It was as large as a clenched fist.
When asked what it contained,
he deceitfully did not answer truthfully.
Wéiyàn, because the contributions were to be given to the public,
found it difficult to go against his word,
feigned surprise and said:
"Venerable monk, how did you obtain this object?
If you must sell this,
I will surely not dispute the price."
A Persian foreigner saw it and purchased it at his asking price before leaving.
The foreigner arrived in Yángzhōu.
The Senior Official Dèng Jǐngshān learned of this matter,
and questioned the foreigner.
The foreigner said:
"Inside the vial is a Purple Zhùjié.
Whoever obtains it
is protected by spirits and deities,
entering fire without burning,
crossing water without drowning.
Possessing such an object, its value is beyond reckoning,
not to be matched by bright pearls or assorted precious goods."
He further levied ten thousand strings of cash from the foreigner.
The foreigner gladly paid his wealth,
and bore no resentment.
Inside the vial were twelve pearls.
Purple Cowrie
Purple cowries are polished conches.
The barbarian Lí people on the shores of Dānzhèn gather them
to use as currency.
The *Records of Nányuè* states:
"The local product is the great cowrie,
which is the purple cowrie."
Wèi Shēng
After the An-Shi Rebellion was quelled in the Tang dynasty,
there was a man named Wèi Shēng,
who, from a young age, due to his family's military and imperial connections,
served in various official posts as a royal companion,
and amassed a fortune of tens of thousands.
However, he associated with unscrupulous individuals,
and as a result, he became impoverished,
and was shunned by the scholar-official class.
To escape the turmoil,
he took his wife and went to Lǐngnán.
After several years,
he finally returned when peace was restored.
While traveling by boat to the boundary of Qiánzhōu,
they stopped due to a heavy rainstorm,
and he went ashore to look around.
Suddenly, among the sand and gravel,
he saw a spot
where a vapor rose straight up for several dozen zhang.
Following it, he searched
and among the rocks saw a stone fragment the size of a palm,
shaped like a piece of a pottery jar,
yet also resembling stone,
half blue and half red,
very distinct.
He tried picking it up and taking it back,
placing it in his book box.
When he reached home,
his former possessions were all gone,
and he had no wealth or bribes to seek reinstatement to office,
so he rented a house to live in.
The marketplaces were full of merchants and Hu people.
Old acquaintances pitied him,
and all shared with him money and silk.
Once, because of Hu guests, he attended a treasure gathering.
The custom of the Hu guests:
once a year they held a grand gathering with fellow countrymen,
called inspecting treasures.
The one with the most treasures
would wear a hat and sit in the seat of honor,
the rest arranged in order.
They invited Wèi Shēng to observe.
Wèi Shēng suddenly remembered the object he had picked up,
took it, tucked it in his robe, and went.
Not daring to speak of it first,
he sat at the end of the seating.
After the meal,
the various Hu brought out their treasures.
The one in the seat of honor brought out four bright pearls,
each larger than an inch in diameter.
The remaining Hu all stood up,
and bowed in reverence.
Those next in order brought out their treasures,
some three, some two,
all of them precious.
When it came to the end of the seating,
the various Hu all laughed,
jokingly saying to Wèi Shēng:
"Do you also have a treasure?"
Wèi Shēng said:
"Yes, I do."
Then he took out what he had in his robe to show them,
while laughing at himself.
More than thirty Hu all stood up,
lifted Wèi Shēng to the seat of honor,
and each bowed reverently to their fullest.
At first, Wèi Shēng thought he was being mocked,
and could not bear the shame and fear.
Later, realizing their sincerity,
he was greatly astonished.
Among the old Hu who saw this stone,
some even wept.
The crowd then begged Wèi Shēng,
asking to buy this treasure,
allowing him to name any price.
Wèi Shēng then spoke boldly,
demanding a million.
The crowd all became angry,
"Why do you insult our treasure like this?"
They raised it to ten million before stopping.
Secretly, he asked a Hu:
"What is the name of this treasure?"
The Hu said:
"This is a treasure from our homeland.
Due to turmoil, it was lost,
already over thirty years.
Our king has sought and offered rewards for it,
saying,
the one who finds it will be appointed chancellor.
Those who return it will receive generous rewards,
how could it be limited to just a few million?"
He asked about its use.
The Hu said:
"This is the Treasure Mother.
Every month on the full moon,
the king himself goes to the seashore,
sets up an altar and offers sacrifices,
placing this on the altar.
Overnight,
bright pearls, precious shells, and other treasures all gather by themselves.
Therefore, it is called 'Treasure Mother.'"
Wèi Shēng obtained wealth doubling his former assets.
Eight Treasures of the Sùzōng Reign.
During the Kāiyuán era,
there was a woman of the Lǐ family,
who married into the Hèruò family.
After Mr. Hèruò passed away,
she renounced secular life to become a nun,
taking the religious name Zhēnrú.
She resided at the Xiàoyì Bridge in Gǒng County.
Her conduct was lofty and pure,
revered and upheld by people far and near.
On the seventh day of the seventh month in the first year of the Tiānbǎo era,
July 7th,
while Zhēnrú was washing outside the door of her meditation hut,
suddenly a five-colored cloud of mist,
came from the east.
A hand extended from the cloud,
though its form was not visible.
Slowly, it handed a pouch to Zhēnrú, saying:
"Treasure this.
Be careful not to speak of it?"
Zhēnrú guarded it diligently,
not daring to lose or discard it.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Ān Lùshān rebelled and caused chaos,
the Central Plains were in great turmoil,
the gentry fled south,
and Zhēnrú wandered and eventually settled in Ānyí County, Chǔ Prefecture.
In the first year of Emperor Sùzōng's reign,
on the night of the eighteenth day of the Jiànzǐ month,
at Zhēnrú's dwelling,
she suddenly saw two figures,
dressed in black robes.
They led Zhēnrú southeast,
for about fifty or sixty paces,
until they reached a city.
Its towers and pavilions were magnificently adorned,
and the guards were orderly and strict.
The black-robed figures pointed and said:
"This is the Illusory City."
Within the city was a great hall.
One person, dressed in purple robes,
wore a jeweled crown.
He was called the Celestial Emperor.
There were also over twenty others,
similarly dressed and crowned,
addressed as the Various Celestials.
The Various Celestials were seated,
and commanded Zhēnrú to approach.
Then the Various Celestials said to each other:
"The mortal world has been plagued by chaos and loss for too long,
slaughter has been excessive,
the stench of blood and filth,
has reached the various heavens.
How can we save it?"
One Celestial said:
"Nothing is better than using divine treasures to suppress it."
Another Celestial said:
"We should use the third treasure."
Yet another Celestial said:
"Now the baleful energy is at its peak,
filth and poison are solidified,
the third treasure is insufficient to overcome it,
we must use the second treasure,
then warfare can cease,
and the chaotic age can be cleansed."
The Celestial Emperor said:
"So be it." Thereupon, he brought out a treasure and handed it to Zhēnrú, saying:
"You go and instruct Prefect Cuī Shēn
to present it to the Son of Heaven."
He further said to Zhēnrú:
"The small pouch previously given to you
contains five pieces of treasure,
which ministers may see.
But these eight treasures now,
only the ruler is fit to see them.
Be careful not to exchange them."
Then he fully explained the names of the treasures and the methods for their use to Zhēnrú.
Afterwards, he again ordered the black-robed figures to escort her back.
The next day,
Zhēnrú went to the county office.
The acting magistrate, Wáng Tāozhī,
reported the matter to the prefecture.
When the prefecture received Tāozhī's report,
the prefect was about to depart.
He showed the county report to his assistant, Lú Héng, saying:
"In Ānyí County, there is this matter of a demonic nun,
it is extremely strange,
go quickly to interrogate her."
Héng arrived at the county,
summoned Zhēnrú,
intending to apply the royal law against her.
Zhēnrú said:
"The Supreme Emperor has given a command,
who dares to neglect it!
Moreover, these treasures are not attained by human effort,
why doubt them?"
Then she showed Héng the five treasures from the pouch.
The first was called the "Xuánhuáng Celestial Talisman",
shaped like a tablet.
About eight inches long,
three inches wide.
Round above and square below,
near the round part was a hole.
It was of yellow jade.
Its color resembled steamed chestnuts,
lustrous like congealed fat.
It wards off warfare, epidemics, evil, and pestilence among humans.
The second was called the "Jade Chicken",
fully feathered in pattern,
made of white jade.
It appears when a ruler governs the world with filial piety.
The third was called the "Grain Disc",
also of white jade.
Five or six inches in diameter.
Its pattern of millet grains grew naturally,
no different from carved engraving.
If a ruler obtains it,
the five grains will be abundant.
The fourth was called the "Queen Mother's Jade Rings".
Two pieces,
also of white jade.
Six inches in diameter,
the hole twice the width of the rim.
If a ruler obtains them,
foreign states will return and submit.
The jade's color and radiance were increasingly brilliant,
exceptionally different from the ordinary.
Lú Héng said:
"It is jade, certainly,
but how do we know it is treasure?"
Zhēnrú then took out all the treasures on a tray,
held them up towards the sky,
their light all shot towards the sun,
looking up, one could not see where the light ended.
Héng and the county officials looked together,
and all found it marvelous.
The next day, Shēn arrived,
Héng reported to Shēn, saying:
"These treasures are bestowed by heaven,
not affairs of men."
Shēn re-examined them and found no discrepancy,
sighed in astonishment for a long time,
then fully reported the matter to Military Governor Cuī Yuán.
Yuán found it strange,
summoned Zhēnrú to his headquarters,
wishing to inspect them all.
Zhēnrú said:
"It cannot be done."
Yuán insisted strongly.
Zhēnrú, having no alternative,
brought out the eight treasures.
The first was called the "Wish-Fulfilling Pearl",
perfectly round in shape,
large as a chicken egg,
its light and color crystalline and clear.
Placed in the hall,
it shone like the full moon.
The second was called "Red Mòhé",
large as a giant chestnut,
red and brilliant like a vermilion cherry.
Looking at it, it seemed it could be crushed by hand,
but touching it, it was hard and heavy, unbreakable.
The third was called the "Lánggān Pearl",
shaped like a ring,
missing one quarter,
about five or six inches in diameter.
The fourth was called the "Jade Seal",
as large as half a hand,
its inscription like a deer's hoof print,
when pressed upon an object, the shape appears.
The fifth was called the "Empress's Silkworm-Mulberry Hooks",
two pieces,
five or six inches long,
as thin as tendons.
Their ends were curved.
Resembling gold yet also silver,
and also like tempered copper.
The sixth was called "Thunder God Stones",
two pieces,
axe-shaped.
About four inches long,
an inch or so wide.
Without holes.
Smooth like green jade.
When the eight treasures were placed under the sun,
white vapor connected to the sky;
placed in a dark room,
they glowed like the moon.
The methods for their suppression and overcoming,
Zhēnrú kept secret,
impossible to know.
Yuán prepared a memorial to report them.
Zhēnrú said:
"Heaven's command was for Cuī Shēn,
what is the meaning of this?"
Yuán became fearful and stopped.
Shēn then sent Lú Héng to accompany Zhēnrú for the presentation.
At that time, Shǐ Cháoyì was besieging Sòng Prefecture,
and had also captured Shēn Prefecture to the south,
cutting off the Huái River routes.
He then proceeded up the river route,
reaching Shāngshān and entering the pass.
On the thirteenth day of the fourth month, he arrived at the capital.
At that time, Emperor Sùzōng was gravely ill,
and upon seeing the treasure,
he urgently summoned Emperor Dàizōng and said:
"You,
from Prince of Chǔ to Crown Prince,
now Heaven has bestowed this treasure,
found in Chǔzhōu.
Heaven approves of you,
you should protect and cherish it."
Emperor Dàizōng bowed twice and received the gift.
Because of obtaining the treasure,
the era name was changed to Bǎoyìng on that very day.
After ascending the throne,
he elevated Chǔzhōu to a superior prefecture,
and its county to a distinguished county,
changing the county name from Ānyí to Bǎoyìng.
The prefect and the official who presented the treasure
were all promoted beyond their rank.
Zhēnrú was honored as "Great Master Bǎohé,"
receiving increasing favor and rewards.
Thereafter, military conflicts gradually subsided,
harvests were abundant year after year,
and within the realm,
conditions nearly reached a state of modest prosperity.
This was the verification of the Bǎoyìng omen.
The place where Zhēnrú obtained the treasure,
with its high and open riverbank,
had lush and fertile surroundings.
The site was later inhabited by Cuī Chéng, the county lieutenant of Liùhé County.
In the western hall,
it is said
that when travelers from the Western Regions pass by,
to this day, none fail to gaze at the spot and pay their respects.
Luminous Beans
During the Dàlì era of Emperor Dàizōng,
the state of Rìlín presented luminous beans and dragon-horn hairpins.
In their country, there was a sea,
forty thousand lǐ to the northeast.
To the west of the country were strange rocks spanning several hundred lǐ,
bright and clear,
capable of reflecting a person's internal organs.
It was also called the Immortal's Mirror.
When people of the country fell ill,
they would look into it,
to see which organ the illness originated from.
They would then gather divine herbs and take them,
and all would recover.
The luminous beans,
similar in size to Chinese green beans,
were deep red in color,
and emitted rays of light several feet long.
In their country, they were also called "Jiéduō pearls."
When boiled with stone calamus leaves,
they would swell to the size of a goose egg.
The inside was pure purple.
Weighing them, they could reach one jīn.
The emperor tasted one pellet,
and marveled at its unparalleled fragrance and flavor,
feeling neither hunger nor thirst for several days afterward.
The dragon-horn hairpins resembled jade,
with a dark reddish-blue color,
and were carved with the shapes of dragons.
Exquisitely crafted and extraordinarily beautiful,
they seemed not made by human hands.
The emperor bestowed them upon Consort Dúgū.
When she and the emperor were boating on the Dragon Pond,
purple clouds arose from the two hairpins,
soon filling the boat.
The emperor then ordered them placed in the hall,
and when water was sprinkled on them,
they transformed into two dragons,
soaring eastward into the sky.
Mount Ten Thousand Buddhas
The emperor revered Buddhism,
so in spring he would blend a hundred kinds of incense
with silver powder to coat the Buddha hall.
When the state of Xīnlúo presented a five-colored woolen carpet
and Mount Ten Thousand Buddhas,
about ten feet tall,
he placed it in the Buddha hall,
with the carpet spread beneath it.
The carpet's exquisite beauty
was also unparalleled at the time.
Within every square inch,
there were singing and dancing maidens,
music,
and scenes of mountains and rivers from various countries.
When a gentle breeze entered the hall,
butterflies and bees would flutter above,
and swallows and sparrows would fly about.
Looking down,
one could hardly distinguish real from fake.
Mount Ten Thousand Buddhas
was carved from sandalwood, pearls, and jade.
The Buddha figures,
the larger ones over an inch tall,
the smaller ones eight or nine fen.
The heads of the Buddhas,
some as small as millet grains,
others like beans.
Their eyebrows, eyes, mouths, and ears,
along with their snail-shell curls and subtle features, were all complete.
And they were adorned with braided gold, jade, and crystal,
forming canopies and tassels.
Ānzhānbólúo and other trees,
constructed from a hundred treasures to form pavilions, towers, and halls.
Though minute in form,
they seemed poised to take flight.
In front were walking monks,
numbering no less than a thousand.
Below was a purple-gold bell,
three inches
in diameter,
held in the mouth of a Púláo beast.
Each time the bell was struck,
the walking monks would bow to the ground in worship.
From within, faintly,
came what was called the sound of Sanskrit chants.
This was due to the mechanism hidden in the bell.
Though named Mount Ten Thousand Buddhas,
their number was beyond count.
The emperor placed nine-light fans among the cliffs.
On the eighth day of the fourth month,
he summoned monks from both sides of the capital to the inner chapel,
to worship Mount Ten Thousand Buddhas.
At that time, spectators marveled that it was not the work of human hands.
And when light was seen emanating from the hall,
all called it Buddha's light.
It was actually the nine-light fans.
Thereupon, the emperor ordered the Tripiṭaka monk Bùkōng
to recite Indian mantras a thousand times before withdrawing.
Tortoiseshell Basin
In the first year of the Bǎolì era,
the state of Nánchāng presented a tortoiseshell basin, a luminous robe, and a night-illuminating rhinoceros horn.
It was said:
In their country, there was a Wine Mountain and a Purple Sea.
The mountain
had a spring,
whose water tasted like wine,
and drinking it could cause one to remain intoxicated for days without waking.
The water of the Purple Sea,
the color of ripe mulberries,
could be used to dye clothes.
Its fish, dragons, turtles, and all things—sand, stones, plants, and trees—
were all purple.
The tortoiseshell basin,
capable of holding ten hú,
was adorned with gold and jade on the outside.
In midsummer,
the emperor placed it in the hall,
filled it with water,
and had palace ladies hold gold and silver ladles,
scooping water to splash each other,
as a form of play.
The luminous robe
was dyed with the color of the Purple Sea.
Using five-colored silk, dragons and phoenixes were embroidered,
each numbering thirteen hundred,
and further adorned with nine-colored genuine pearls.
When the emperor wore it
while hunting in the Northern Park,
illuminated by the morning sun,
its colors shimmered and moved.
Onlookers were dazzled,
yet the emperor did not consider it overly precious.
One day,
while galloping after game,
he encountered a sudden rainstorm,
but the robe remained completely dry.
Only then did he marvel at it as a rare object.
The night-illuminating rhinoceros horn,
similar in appearance to a sky-piercing rhinoceros horn,
glowed at night,
illuminating a hundred paces.
Even covered with ten layers of silk,
its radiance could not be concealed.
The emperor then ordered it cut into a belt.
Whenever he went hunting,
he needed no candles at night,
as it was bright as day.
Dust-Repelling Kerchief
Gāo Yǔ was in Càizhōu.
There was a military officer, Jiǎ, who was in charge of trade,
and incurred a deficit of several million,
so he fled to an outer county.
It was over two hundred li from the prefecture.
Gāo had just ordered him to be imprisoned and investigated.
Jiǎ was worried and distressed,
with no plan to resolve the situation.
His colleagues therefore arranged a banquet to console him.
There were over ten guests present.
Among them was one who called himself the retired scholar Huángfǔ Xuánzhēn,
dressed in white like goose feathers,
with a very elegant appearance.
Everyone offered words of comfort and encouragement.
Huángfǔ only smiled and said:
"This is also a small matter."
After the crowd dispersed,
he alone stayed behind.
He said to Jiǎ:
"I once traveled east,
and obtained two treasures.
I shall resolve this difficulty for you."
Jiǎ thanked him,
and requested to prepare carriages and horses.
He declined them all.
He traveled very swiftly.
Very late, he arrived at the prefecture,
and stayed at an inn.
Then at dawn, he paid a visit to Gāo.
As soon as Gāo saw him,
he could not help but feel respect.
Huángfǔ then said to Gāo:
"Xuánzhēn has come this time,
specifically to beg the Minister for Jiǎ's life."
Gāo then said:
"Jiǎ owes official funds,
not Yǔ's private wealth.
What can be done?"
Huángfǔ requested that those around them withdraw,
and said that he had obtained a headscarf in Silla,
which could ward off dust,
and he wished to offer it to redeem Jiǎ.
He immediately took it from his bosom and handed it to Gāo.
As soon as Gāo held it,
he already felt a coolness throughout his body.
Startled, he said:
"This is not something a subject should possess,
and moreover, it is priceless.
Jiǎ's life,
I fear, is sufficient compensation."
Huángfǔ requested to test it.
The next day,
they held a banquet outside the city walls.
At that time, there had been a long drought,
and the dust was especially severe.
Gāo looked back at the horse's tail and mane, and the several attendants on his left and right,
and there was not a speck of dust on them.
The supervising army commissioner noticed,
and asked Gāo:
"Why is it that the Minister alone is not stained by dust?
Could it be that you have encountered an extraordinary person,
and obtained a supreme treasure?"
Gāo did not dare conceal it.
The supervising army commissioner therefore requested to see the retired scholar.
Gāo then went with him.
The supervising army commissioner said jokingly:
"Does the Daoist only know of the Minister?
What other treasures do you have?
I wish to see one."
Huángfǔ fully explained his intention to save Jiǎ.
And said that the medicine came from the eastern seas,
and now he had one needle left,
whose power was slightly less than the headscarf,
but could make one's entire body free of dust.
The supervising army commissioner bowed and requested:
"Obtaining this is enough."
Huángfǔ then pulled it from the headscarf and gave it to him.
The needle was golden in color.
The supervising army commissioner then inserted it into his headscarf to test it,
galloping through the dust,
only his body and the horse's mane and tail remained dust-free.
Gāo and the supervising army commissioner prepared gifts the next morning to visit him,
intending to request the essentials of his Dao,
But one night, he suddenly disappeared.
There is a title but no text
The Chóngmíng Pillow
There was a Chóngmíng pillow offered as tribute by an overseas country.
It was one chi two cun long,
and six cun high.
Pure white, resembling crystal.
Inside were shapes of towers and pavilions,
with ten Daoist priests on four sides,
holding incense and tablets,
circulating endlessly.
They were called practicing Daoist immortals.
The carved wood and painted colors,
the immortals' head ornaments and capes,
were all completely present.
Moreover, it was entirely translucent.
Sānbǎo Village
To the southwest of Fúfēng County,
there was Sānbǎo Village.
According to the elders' tradition,
when the village was established,
a foreign monk said to the villagers:
"This land has an aura of treasure,
but people today cannot obtain it.
Its revelation will have its own time."
The villagers said:
"What treasure is it?"
He said:
"It is a treasure from Jiāozhǐ,
and there are three in number."
Therefore, they named the village Sānbǎo,
to record the event.
In the spring of the first year of the Kāichéng era,
a villager dreamed at night of a man,
wearing a black hairpin and headcloth,
dressed in wide-sleeved clothes,
with a long sword at his waist,
and a stern, ancient appearance.
He said to the villager:
"I once served in the Eastern Hàn.
During the time of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
together with the Flying General Lord Mǎ,
we campaigned against Jiāozhǐ,
and once obtained treasures from the southern people.
Afterwards, Lord Mǎ was slandered,
accused of plundering many southern goods,
and bringing them all back.
Emperor Guāngwǔ was angry,
and ordered a search of his household.
I feared the disaster would reach me,
so I buried them in this land."
Before he finished speaking, the villager awoke.
The villager then fully reported his dream to his neighbors.
That year, on a midsummer night,
the clouds and moon were dark,
and a shepherd boy saw below the western plain,
a bright light,
like a trailing silk ribbon,
that did not fade for a long time.
The shepherd boy, startled, told his father,
who immediately rushed to look.
The light grew even brighter,
and remained so the next night.
Then several villagers,
at night, sought the light,
and looked down to observe it.
The light emerged from the soil,
like flames from burning firewood.
The villagers then together erected markers to indicate it.
The next day,
carrying spades and tools,
they dug beneath the markers,
about over a zhang deep,
and obtained a golden turtle.
About two cun long,
exquisitely crafted,
unmatched in any era.
They also obtained a precious sword,
two chi four cun long.
And also obtained an ancient mirror,
over one chi in diameter.
All were covered with traces of dust.
The villagers obtained them,
and took them to the county office.
At that time, the county magistrate, Liú Suí of Pèiguó, obtained them.
When the sword was drawn from its sheath,
it was pale like the color of water ripples,
sharp enough to cut jade,
with nothing surpassing it.
Its length of two chi four cun,
since ancient times eight cun was considered a chi,
thus it was three chi in ancient measure.
The mirror had intricate patterns all over,
with strange beasts surrounding the mirror knob,
and though the era was remote,
its form and texture were intact.
He ordered it polished,
and its clarity was like the purity of clear water.
Truly a rare treasure under heaven.
County Magistrate Liú said:
"These are ancient precious objects,
and should be returned to the royal treasury.
They can be placed alongside the heavenly sphere and Hé's jade disc,
shining in the imperial academy."
He then sealed and reported the matter.
It was reported to the commander of Qíyáng.
He wished to present them to the Son of Heaven.
At that time, Commander Chén also governed Qílǒng,
obtained and loved them,
and thus kept the treasures.
Therefore, no one knew of them.
Fire Jade
In the first year of the Huìchāng era,
the kingdom of Fúyú presented three treasures:
"Fire Jade",
"Clear Bright Wine",
and "Wind Pine Stone".
The Fire Jade was red in color,
half an inch long,
pointed at the top and round at the bottom.
It could illuminate several dozen paces.
When accumulated, it could be used to heat a cauldron.
Placed indoors,
in winter one would no longer need to wear padded clothing.
Palace women often used it.
Clear Bright Wine
was also a tribute from a foreign land.
It was purple in color, like ointment,
and drinking it made one's bones fragrant.
The Wind Pine Stone was one zhang square,
transparent and clear like jade.
Inside it was a tree,
shaped like an ancient pine with a spreading canopy,
rustling as cool breezes arose within it.
In the height of summer,
the emperor ordered it placed in the palace hall,
and as soon as the cool autumn air began to blow,
he ordered it removed.
Agate Cabinet
Emperor Wǔzōng was fond of Daoist arts of immortality,
so he built the Immortal-Watching Terrace,
to honor the morning rituals.
He further renovated the Exalted Truth Chamber,
grinding various precious materials into powder to coat the floor.
With jade pillars and golden arches,
silver railings and jade steps,
it sparkled brilliantly,
a sight never to be fully appreciated.
Inside were curtains of hawksbill turtle shell,
and a bed of fire-pearl.
Dragon-light incense was burned,
and carefree wine was offered.
All these were tributes from other countries.
Whenever the emperor fasted, bathed, and purified himself,
he would summon the Daoist priest Zhào Guīzhēn and others,
to explore the principles of the formless and soundless.
Thus, two stalks of glossy ganoderma grew inside the chamber,
both like red jade.
Then, Bóhǎi presented an agate cabinet,
three chi square,
deep in color like madder,
so exquisitely crafted
that nothing could compare.
The emperor used it to store books on immortality,
placing it beside the curtain.
A purple rose-quartz basin,
with a capacity of half a hú,
was transparent inside and out,
its color pure purple,
and about one cun thick,
yet lifting it felt as light as a goose feather.
The emperor admired its luster and purity,
so he kept it in the immortal chamber,
to mix medicines and elixirs.
Later, the imperial concubine Wáng Cáirén threw a jade ring,
accidentally chipping off a piece the size of half a bean,
and the emperor lamented it for a long time.
Lady Cén
Lady Cén of Línchuān
once traveled in the mountains.
In a mountain stream, she saw two white stones,
as large as lotus seeds,
chasing each other.
She caught and captured them,
and upon returning home, placed them in her handkerchief box.
That night,
she dreamed of two beautiful women in white,
who claimed to be sisters,
coming to attend her.
After waking,
she realized the stones were extraordinary.
She always kept them tied in her sash.
Later, when she reached Yùzhāng,
a Persian merchant
approached and asked her:
"Do you have any treasures?"
She replied:
"Yes."
And immediately took out the two stones to show him.
The Persian offered thirty thousand coins to buy them.
Although Cén treasured them, they were of no practical use,
so she was pleased to get the money
and gave them to him.
Using the money as capital for livelihood,
she eventually became wealthy.
But she regretted not asking about the stones and their use.
The Children of Yùyáng
In the twelfth year of the Yìxī era of the Jin dynasty,
a group of children from Yùyáng County
were bathing in the Yù River.
Suddenly, they saw coins appearing on the riverbank,
flowing like quicksand,
so they scrambled to collect them.
When their hands were full,
they let the rest flow away.
They also used their clothes to gather and wrap them,
each obtaining some.
Then they saw a bronze cart in the flowing stream,
pulled by a small ox,
moving with great speed.
The children chased after it,
and managed to grab one wheel.
It was about five cun in diameter,
with a pig-like nose,
the hub had six spokes,
and it was entirely bluish-green.
The interior was yellowish and worn,
as if constantly used.
At that time, Shěn Chǎng
was guarding Nányáng,
and obtained this object,
but could not fathom its meaning.
Empress Wéndé
Coins with markings resembling fingernail impressions
are associated with Empress Wéndé.
During the Wǔdé era,
the five-zhū coin was abolished,
and the Kāitōng Yuánbǎo coin was issued.
These four characters and the calligraphy
were all done by Ōuyáng Xún.
On the day the design was first presented,
the empress pressed a fingernail mark on it,
hence the impression exists.
Cén Wénběn
During the Zhēnguàn era of the Táng dynasty,
Cén Wénběn, upon leaving court,
often sought refuge from the summer heat in a mountain pavilion.
One day at noon,
having just awoken from a nap,
he suddenly heard someone knocking at the gate of the mountain pavilion's courtyard.
A young servant reported,
"A youth from the Upper Clarity named Yuánbǎo
is here to pay his respects."
Wénběn had always admired the Dao,
so he fastened his belt and ordered the visitor admitted.
It was a Daoist priest under twenty years of age,
whose demeanor was bright and transcendent,
and whose clothing was exquisitely unusual.
He wore a light blue round-cornered cap,
a light blue round-collared robe,
and dark blue round-toed shoes.
His garments were light and fine as mist,
surpassing even the finest silks of Qí or Lǔ.
Wénběn spoke with him.
The youth then said:
"I am a youth of the Upper Clarity,
who achieved fruition since the Hàn dynasty.
I was originally born in Wú,
having attained the Dao of non-stagnation,
and was thus presented to the King of Wú,
who brought me to see the Hàn Emperor.
Whenever the Hàn Emperor had matters of state,
if policies were obstructed,
there was nothing he did not consult me about.
I once accompanied the square and the round traveling below,
and all was made smooth and unobstructed.
Because of this, I became well-known,
and from Emperors Wén and Wǔ,
down to Emperor Āi,
I was always held in favor.
When Wáng Mǎng created chaos,
I went out to distant regions,
and everywhere I went, I received people's affection.
Since the time of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
I grew weary of the human world,
and so shed my corpse and departed.
Sometimes in Qín, sometimes in Chǔ,
I had no fixed dwelling.
Hearing of your fondness for the Dao,
I have come here to pay you a visit."
Wénběn questioned him about affairs of rulers and states during the Hàn, Wèi, Qí, and Liáng periods,
and he described them clearly as if he had witnessed them himself.
He then mentioned that among historical records,
distortions and falsehoods were also quite numerous.
Wénběn asked:
"The cap and robe you wear,
why is their style so unusual?"
He replied:
"The Dao lies within the square and the round;
my outer garments are round, but my heart is square and upright—
this is the proper form for the times."
Wénběn asked further:
"Your clothes are all light and fine;
from what land do they come?"
He replied:
"This is the Five-Zhū garment of the Upper Clarity."
Wénběn asked again:
"I have heard that Six-Zhū garments are worn by celestial beings;
how does the Five-Zhū differ?"
He replied:
"The exceptionally fine ones are the Five-Zhū."
Their conversation continued until, unnoticed, the day grew late,
and then he bid farewell and left.
As soon as he stepped out the gate, he suddenly vanished.
Wénběn knew he was no ordinary man.
Thereafter, whenever he left court,
he would order someone to watch for him,
and when he came, they would converse for hours.
Later, Wénběn secretly had someone follow him
to see where he stayed.
Leaving the mountain pavilion gate,
he walked east a few steps,
and by the courtyard wall, he vanished in a flash.
Wénběn ordered laborers to dig there,
and at three feet down, they reached an ancient tomb.
The tomb contained nothing else,
only a single ancient coin.
Only then did Wénběn realize:
the Upper Clarity youth was bronze;
his name Yuánbǎo,
was the inscription on the coin;
round on the outside, square within,
was the coin's shape;
the blue robe was the bronze's color;
the Five-Zhū garment was also the coin's inscription;
being born in Wú during Hàn times
referred to the Hàn dynasty casting Five-Zhū coins for the King of Wú.
Although Wénběn knew this,
his wealth and status daily increased,
until he became Zhōngshū Lìng.
After ten years,
the ancient coin suddenly disappeared,
and Wénběn then passed away.
Wáng Qīng
In the early Yuánhé era,
a commoner named Wáng Qīng from a village in Luòyáng,
earned five *huán* of money through hired labor,
and with it bought a withered chestnut tree by a field boundary,
intending to sell it as firewood for profit.
Overnight,
it was secretly chopped down by a neighbor.
As the axe reached the trunk,
a black snake suddenly appeared,
raising its head like an arm.
It spoke to the man:
"I am Wáng Qīng's root,
do not chop me!"
The man was terrified,
dropped his axe, and fled.
At dawn,
Wáng Qīng led his sons and grandsons to gather the firewood,
and further dug beneath the roots,
finding two large jars,
filled with loose coins.
Wáng Qīng thus gained profits as if they were returning home,
and within over ten years became immensely wealthy.
He then piled coins into the shape of a dragon,
and named it Wáng Qīng's Root.
The Villager from Jiàn'ān
In Jiàn'ān, there was a villager
who traveled back and forth on the Jiàn
River in a small boat,
making a living by selling firewood.
Once, he moored his boat, went ashore,
and was about to cut firewood.
Suddenly, he saw several coins flowing down from the mountain.
Going slightly uphill to search,
he successively gathered several tens of them.
Reaching halfway up the mountain,
there was a large tree.
Beneath it was a large jar.
Five or six feet high,
it was full of coins.
The jar was slightly tilted,
hence the coins were flowing out.
So he pushed it upright,
and propped it with stones.
He filled his lapels with over five hundred coins and returned home.
He then led his entire family back,
intending to take all of it.
Upon arriving,
they found the old path,
saw the large tree, but the jar was gone.
The villager lingered there,
unable to leave for several days.
At night, he dreamed someone told him:
"These coins have an owner.
Previously, because the jar was tilted,
I paid you five hundred to set it right.
Do not vainly covet the rest."
Xú Zhòngbǎo
Xú Zhòngbǎo was a man from Chángshā.
South of his residence stood a large withered tree,
so thick that it would take several arm spans to encircle it.
One day, a servant sweeping beneath it
found over a hundred coins in the sand
and reported this to Zhòngbǎo.
Zhòngbǎo went there himself
and also found several hundred coins.
From then on, whenever he needed money,
he would go sweep under the tree,
and he would always find some.
This continued for years,
and in total, he obtained several hundred thousand coins.
Later, Zhòngbǎo went to Yángdū
and was appointed magistrate of Shūchéng.
During his leisure time,
he was sitting on the ground with his family
when suddenly a very fierce white vapor
flew diagonally outward.
It seemed as if something was within it,
and his wife grabbed at it with her hand,
obtaining a jade butterfly.
Its craftsmanship was exquisite,
and no one could fathom its origin.
Later, when he served as magistrate of Lèpíng,
his family went again
and found a great many coins
in a mouse hole beside the kitchen.
Zhòngbǎo immediately led people to dig there,
and after digging several feet deep,
a white sparrow flew out
and perched on a tree in the courtyard.
Beneath it, they obtained up to a million coins.
When the coins were exhausted,
the white sparrow then departed,
and no one knew where it went.
Xíng Shì
In Jiànyè, there was a storekeeper surnamed Xíng
who was poor.
Whenever he saved up two thousand coins,
he would fall ill or the money would disappear.
His wife secretly gathered coins
and buried them in the ground.
One night,
she suddenly heard a sound like insects flying,
emerging from the ground,
passing through the windows and departing,
with some hitting the walls and falling to the ground.
The next day, when she looked,
they were all coins.
His wife then told him about the burial spot,
and when they dug it up, all the coins were gone.
Later, Xíng obtained a naturally formed stone turtle
that looked like a real one.
He placed it under a pomegranate tree in the courtyard.
Someone who saw it said,
"This is a treasure."
So he stored it in a box.
From then on, they gradually became well-off,
and later, they became quite wealthy.
Lín Shì
In Tīngzhōu, there was a person surnamed Lín
whose ancestor had once served as a prefect
and retired to live at home.
One day,
coins suddenly rained from the sky,
filling and piling up in their home.
Lín then straightened his clothes and hat,
looked up to the sky, and prayed,
"An extraordinary event
will surely bring disaster.
If it stops here quickly,
it will be the blessing of the Lín family."
As soon as he finished speaking, it stopped.
What they collected already amounted to tens of thousands,
and to this day, they are said to be wealthy.
Cáo Zhēn
Cáo Zhēn, a man from Shòuchūn,
was traveling in the wilderness
when he suddenly saw several dozen coins
at the foot of a slope,
coming from afar
with a flying sound like bells.
Zhēn chased them
into a small hole.
He scooped them up with his hands,
but could only obtain a few dozen.
Also, in Shuāngxù Gǎng, Tóngchéng County, Shūzhōu,
there was a whirlwind that swept up coins,
passing through the market.
Market-goers grabbed at the coins,
storing them in their clothes.
The wind entered an ancient tomb overgrown with thorns,
and people could not enter, so it stopped.
The coins they obtained,
when taken home and examined,
were no different from ordinary coins,
yet they all said they had lost eight or nine out of ten.
Xú Jǐng
During the Jìn dynasty, there was a man named Xú Jǐng
who obtained a brocade sachet pouch outside Xuānyáng Gate.
When he opened it at home to look,
there was an insect like a cicada,
multicolored,
with two Wǔzhū coins attached to its hind legs.
Zhōngmóu Iron Awl
In the pond beneath the terrace of King Wèi Rénchéng in Zhōngmóu County,
there was an iron awl from the Hàn dynasty,
six chǐ long,
with three chǐ buried in the ground,
its head pointing southwest,
and it could not be moved.
Poisonous Spear
The southern barbarians had a poisonous spear,
blade-less,
looking like rotten iron.
If it struck a person, they would die without bleeding.
It was said to have fallen from the sky like rain,
burying itself over a zhàng into the ground,
and could only be dug up after performing sacrifices to the earth.
Among the barbarians, it was called a "duó blade."
Jícuì Qiú
During the time of Empress Wǔ Zétiān,
the Nánhǎi Commandery presented a Jícuì Qiú,
exceptionally precious and beautiful.
While Zhāng Chāngzōng was attending beside her,
Empress Wǔ bestowed it upon him.
She then ordered him to wear the fur robe
while serving in a game of shuānglù.
Prime Minister Dí Rénjié
came in at the time to report on affairs.
Empress Wǔ ordered him to take a seat
and then commanded Dí to play shuānglù with Chāngzōng.
Dí bowed in gratitude and joined the game.
Empress Wǔ said,
"What will you two wager?"
Dí replied,
"We will compete for three points,
and wager the fur robe Chāngzōng is wearing."
Empress Wǔ said to him,
"What will you offer in return?"
Dí said,
pointing to the purple silk robe he was wearing,
"Your subject offers this as a match."
Empress Wǔ laughed and said,
"You do not know—
this fur robe is worth over a thousand gold.
What you have offered
is not equivalent."
Dí stood up and said,
"This robe of your subject
is what a high minister wears when attending court and reporting to the sovereign;
what Chāngzōng is wearing
is the attire of a favored and pampered favorite.
To match it against this robe of your subject,
your subject still feels discontent."
Since Empress Wǔ had already made the arrangement,
she complied with his proposal.
Chāngzōng, feeling ashamed and dispirited,
with his morale diminished,
lost game after game.
Dí, facing the empress,
then took off the fur robe,
bowed in gratitude, and left.
When he reached Guāngfàn Gate,
he gave it to his family servant to wear
and urged his horse to depart.
Xiè Língyùn's Beard
During the Jìn dynasty, Xiè Língyùn had a beautiful beard.
Before his execution,
he donated it to the Qíhuán Temple in Nánhǎi
to serve as the beard of Vimalakīrti.
The temple monks treasured it,
and initially, it remained undamaged.
During the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng, Princess Lè'ān,
while competing in the "hundred herbs" game in the fifth month,
wanted to expand her collection of rare items
and ordered someone to gallop and fetch it.
Fearing that others might obtain it,
she cut off the rest and discarded it.
Thus, it was lost forever.
The Fisherman of Kāiyuán
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
a fisherman from Dēngzhōu
was carrying a load and walking along the seashore.
From afar, he saw mist and haze near the water,
crowded with many people,
as if it were a marketplace.
He then went forward.
He saw many selling medicinal herbs,
with Buddhist monks and Daoist priests especially numerous.
After a long while, they groaned,
and all vanished without a trace.
He only picked up several dozen pieces of qīngdài,
each about the size of a dou measure.
Not daring to use them for any other purpose,
he donated them to Buddhist monks.
Consort Yáng’s Stocking
When Xuánzōng reached the Mǎwéi Courier Station,
he ordered Gāo Lìshì to strangle the Noble Consort in front of the pear tree in the Buddhist hall.
An old woman from Mǎwéi obtained one of her stockings.
Travelers sought it out to view and play with it,
paying a hundred coins for one look,
earning her countless coins.
Purple Rice
In the eighth year of the Yuánhé era,
the Great Zhěn State offered tribute of blue wheat and purple rice.
The emperor found it extraordinary.
The next day,
he showed it to the occultists Bái Yuánzuǒ and Lǐ Yuánjí.
The grains of blue wheat were larger than Chinese wheat,
blue both inside and out,
with a fragrance like that of non-glutinous rice.
Eating it made one’s body light,
and over time, one could ride the wind.
Purple rice resembled jùshèng,
but cooking one shēng of it
yielded one dǒu of cooked rice.
Eating it made one’s beard and hair thick and black,
and one’s complexion would not age.
The Giant Tree in the Jiālíng River
The city of Làngzhōu overlooks the Jiālíng River.
On the riverbank, there was a giant wūyáng tree,
over a hundred chǐ in length,
with a girth nearly half that.
It had been drifting and swaying in the river waves
for a long time,
but no one knew where it came from.
The elders of Làngzhōu passed down a legend:
it had arrived during Yáo’s time, carried by the great flood.
But there was no evidence for this.
The military governor of Xiāng-Hàn, Gāo Yuányù of Bóhǎi,
in the ninth year of the Tàihé era,
was appointed prefect of Làngzhōu from the position of Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Shortly after taking office,
he also saw it
and certainly considered it strange.
Suddenly, one day,
a ferry official reported:
"The giant tree in the river
has always faced east.
Last night, for no reason,
it turned to face west."
Gāo found it even more extraordinary,
and immediately went with his guests and staff to observe it.
He then widely summoned boatmen,
along with soldiers, officials, and commoners,
and used large ropes to tether and pull it out.
At first, there was no difficulty;
it followed the drag onto the shore.
But after more than half was ashore,
it stood firm and would not advance further,
even with a thousand men and a hundred oxen.
None could pull it.
Once human strength was exhausted,
it returned to its former state.
From then on, exposed to sun and wind,
it lay stiff on the sand.
Some temple monks wanted to use it as a single pillar for a stūpa,
while some local officials requested to split and carve it
to prepare various timbers.
Gāo, considering it exceptionally grand and unusual,
did not permit any of these proposals.
He often intended to return it to the river,
but worried about troubling people,
and hesitated without acting.
On the Shangyuán day of the third year of the Kāichéng era,
Gāo, following regulations, performed incense-offering at the Kāiyuán Temple,
with all his staff present.
Gāo intended to use the crowd’s strength
to jointly pull the tree back.
Upon arrival,
they again prepared many ropes
and gathered strong men.
Just as they were about to muster their strength and pull,
the giant tree, as if relying on some force,
seemed to move on its own,
and lightly returned to the river.
When it was still about a chǐ from the river,
it suddenly startled and surged forward.
The hundred large ropes
were all severed as if cut.
The tree then drifted along, submerged and emerged,
and went straight across the river.
Reaching midstream,
it quietly vanished.
Gāo sent several skilled swimmers
to quickly go and observe.
The river water was clear,
and even the finest hair could be seen.
The skilled swimmers looked carefully and returned,
all saying:
"In the water, there are two other trees, east and west,
of similar size to this one.
The one that just came from the shore
is now clustered north and south."
Gāo looked at his seated guests,
and all were astonished.
From then on, it was never seen again.
After a while,
Gāo was appointed Jiànyì Dàfū.
When the appointment decree arrived,
examining the date of his official appointment,
it was exactly the day Gāo had labored on the tree.
Had the tree not been moved in those ten days or so,
and Gāo’s new appointment had already arrived,
then how would he have paid attention to moving it,
leaving it as before?
Peach Pit from a Jiānghuái Market Vendor
Duì Shè, Vice Director of the Ministry of Water Resources,
once saw a market vendor in Jiānghuái
using a peach pit to measure rice.
It could only hold one shēng.
He said it was obtained from a stream in the Jiǔyí Mountains.
Jade Dragon Ointment
In Ānnán, there is jade dragon ointment.
Southerners use it
to melt silver into liquid.
It is said:
"This ointment must not be brought north.
If anyone violates this,
misfortune will befall them."
During the Tàihé era,
Hán Yuē was Protector-General of Ānnán
and obtained this ointment.
When he returned,
he took it back with him.
Someone said to him:
"Southerners say this ointment must not be brought north,
yet you, sir, are taking it away.
Will you not regret it later?"
Yuē did not listen
and eventually brought it back.
Later, Yuē became Commandant of the Capital.
That year, the capital was in chaos,
and Yuē, for associating with Zhèng Zhù,
ended with his entire clan executed.
Was this the misfortune brought by the jade dragon ointment?
Hence, those going north from the south dare not bring it.
Duàn Chéngshì
Duàn Chéngshì’s cousins said
that when they were young, they once destroyed a bird’s nest
and found a black stone,
as large as a sparrow’s egg,
smooth and lovely.
Later, they accidentally placed it in a vinegar container,
and suddenly felt the stone move.
Watching closely,
they saw it had four legs like threads.
When they lifted it,
the legs retracted.
Lǐ Déyù
Lǐ Déyù served during the reigns of Emperor Wénzōng and Emperor Wǔzōng.
While holding the authority of chief minister,
his power and influence, as well as the imperial favor he enjoyed, were unmatched.
He often delighted in collecting rare and unusual objects,
and many among the court and commoners who sought his patronage
would present him with precious treasures and curios.
Once, during a leisurely day of rest,
he invited his fellow chief ministers and court officials for a banquet and conversation.
At that time, the blazing summer sun was scorching,
and everyone suffered from the stifling heat.
Carriages waited at the gate,
and by the time they arrived, it was already noon.
The gathered officials and renowned scholars
fanned themselves incessantly.
They all longed for a place to rest in a cool spot.
After being ushered into a small study,
they found it unexpectedly spacious.
The walls were adorned
with ancient books and famous paintings,
yet the oppressive heat remained unbearable.
But once they were seated and wine was served,
the sweltering discomfort vanished entirely.
After a while,
they felt a refreshing, cool breeze,
as if they had stepped into late autumn.
Wine and delicacies were plentifully arranged,
and the gathering continued until dusk.
When they stepped outside, fiery clouds and a blazing sun
scorched them with intense heat.
Some curious individuals
sought out his close associates to inquire about this.
It was said
that on that day, a golden basin was filled with water,
in which a white dragon skin was soaked.
It was placed at the edge of the seating area,
The Píngquán Estate in the Eastern Capital,
located thirty lǐ from Luòchéng,
was adorned with lush plants, terraces, and pavilions,
as if it were a celestial mansion.
There was an empty railing
that channeled spring water from the front,
winding and artificially carved
to resemble the twelve peaks and nine tributaries of the Bā Gorges and Dòngtíng Lake,
extending all the way to the sea gate,
depicting the scenery of rivers and mountains.
Among the bamboo groves and bamboo paths,
there was a flat stone.
When one rubbed it with their hand,
faint images of clouds, rainbows, dragons, phoenixes, grass, and trees would appear.
There was also a fish rib bone,
two zhàng and five chǐ in length, inscribed with the words:
"Delivered in the second year of the Huìchāng era,
sent from Hǎizhōu,"
When Lǐ Déyù first developed Píngquán,
people from distant lands
often presented him with local specialties and exotic items.
Within a few years,
he possessed everything imaginable.
At the time, a literati wrote a poem about Píngquán:
"Lǒngyòu nobles offer talking birds,
Rìnán prefects send famed flowers."
Such was the power of influence.
Xiàhóu Zī
Xiàhóu Zī served as the commissioner for Emperor Xuānzōng's mausoleum.
When excavating the true tomb,
he exerted exceptional effort.
While digging the imperial chamber,
they reached a depth of over a zhàng
within solid rock,
where they discovered half of a broken golden hairpin.
It was as long as a palm,
with the remainder still embedded in the stone.
The workers carefully retrieved it and presented it to Zī.
Zī, considering the proximity to the imperial resting grounds
and the unusual nature of the find,
chose to conceal it and did not report it.
The immortal raft of Yán Zūn
was placed in the Líndé Hall during the Táng dynasty.
It was over fifty chǐ long,
sounded like bronze or iron when struck,
and was hard, never decaying.
Lǐ Déyù cut a thin branch about a chǐ long from it,
carved it into a statue of a Daoist immortal,
and it would often fly away and return.
After the Guǎngmíng era, it was lost,
and the raft itself also flew away.
Trees at the Tomb of Confucius
On Confucius's tomb in Qūfù, Lǔ,
there were often jiě trees.
It is also said:
In Qūfù City, there is Yán Huí's tomb,
with two stone nánmù trees atop it,
measuring about thirty to forty arm-spans around.
Local people say
they were trees planted by Yán Huí himself.
Five Zuò Trees
At the Hàn dynasty's Five Zuò Palace,
there were five zuò trees,
each so large they could only be embraced by linking arms,
with branches spreading shade for dozens of lǐ.
West of the palace was the Qīngwú Observatory.
In front of the observatory were three wútóng trees.
Beneath the trees stood two stone qílín,
with inscriptions carved on their ribs.
These were objects from Qín Shǐhuáng's tomb at Líshān.
Their heads were one zhàng and three chǐ tall.
The left foot of the eastern one was broken,
and at the break, it was red as blood.
Elders claimed it had a spirit,
as if it contained blood and sinews.
White Silver Trees
West of Gāoyuàn City in Píngyuán Commandery,
at the tomb of Pìlǘ Yǔn, the Jìn dynasty's Níngzhōu governor,
there stood twenty white silver trees.
Combined-Parted Trees
On Zhōngnán Mountain, there were many combined-parted trees.
Their leaves resembled jiānglí,
but were mottled red and green.
Their stems were all purple,
and their scent was like luólè.
The trees grew straight upward,
reaching a hundred chǐ without branches.
At the top, they formed dense clusters,
shaped like carriage canopies,
with one part green and one part cinnabar-red,
dappled like brocade.
In Cháng'ān, they were called "cinnabar-green trees,"
also known as "canopy trees."
They also grew in the Xióng'ěr Mountains.
Jade Trees
Within the boundaries of Yúnyáng County,
there were many sites of former Hàn dynasty detached palaces.
There was a tree resembling a pagoda tree but with finer leaves,
which locals called the "jade tree."
Yáng Zǐyún's "Sweet Springs Rhapsody" states:
"The jade trees are lush and verdant."
Later, Zuǒ Sī considered this a false glorification,
likely because he was not fully informed.
Camphor Trees
Regarding the camphor tree as a species,
it takes seven years of growth before its true nature can be discerned.
In the second year of the Bǎodǐng era of Emperor Hànwǔ,
a Camphor Tree Palace was erected within the Kūnmíng Pond,
constructed using camphor wood.
Lychee Wood
In Nánhǎi Commandery, there were many lychee trees.
The name "lychee" (lìzhī) originates
from the fact that when it bears fruit,
the branches are weak but the stems are firm,
making them impossible to pick by hand.
Instead, one must cut the branches with a knife or axe,
hence the name.
Most wooden utensils
were typically made from lychee wood.
Wine Trees
In the country of Dùnxùn, there is a wine tree,
resembling a pomegranate tree.
Its flower juice collects in a cup,
and after several days turns into wine,
delicious and intoxicating.
The *Bówùzhì* records:
"The wine tree comes from the country of Diǎnxùn,
and is called zhǎn wine."
The Sāluómián Tree
In Tōngwàng County of Lízhōu,
there is the Xiāozhāng Monastery,
located one hundred paces west of the county seat.
Inside is a hall dedicated to the Heavenly Kings.
In front stands an ancient cypress tree.
Below it is a large pond.
South of the pond is a Sāluómián tree,
requiring three or four people linking hands to encircle its trunk.
It first produces flowers and then leaves.
Its flowers bloom in the height of summer.
When they wither, they fall without their calyxes,
swirling down to the ground.
The flower stamens contain cotton,
called Sāluó cotton.
Under good governance, it flourishes luxuriantly;
in times of misrule, it withers and dies.
According to ancient tradition:
This is a spiritual trace left from when the monk Ròuchǐ resided here.
Within the county boundaries are Monk Mountain and Monk Temple,
both associated with Ròuchǐ.
The Cìtóng Tree
The term "cāngtóng" is unclear in meaning,
but it seems southerners used "tóng" (paulownia) for Cāngwú,
hence naming the commandery after it.
The Cìtóng tree,
found from the South Sea all the way to Fúzhōu,
grows in dense, flourishing clusters,
though not as well as
in Fújiàn.
Outside the secondary wall of Wúzhōu city,
there are three or four trees,
withered and not thriving,
and they have never been seen to flower.
Yet the commandery is named after them,
which is also puzzling.
The Huángqī Tree
Southwest of the country of Rìjì in the sea,
there are three islands,
each several tens of *li* apart.
These islands produce huángqī,
similar to the lacquer trees of central China.
In the sixth month there,
they cut open the tree trunk,
collect the sap,
and use it to lacquer objects.
It is like gold,
its brilliance dazzling.
The Mùlán Tree
On Qīlǐ Isle,
Lǔ Bān carved a mùlán tree into a boat.
The boat remains on the isle to this day.
The "mùlán boat" mentioned by poets
originates from here.
Mùlán Isle,
located in the Xúnyáng River,
has many mùlán trees.
In the past, King Héliǘ of Wú
planted mùlán trees here,
to use for constructing his palace.
The Coconut Tree,
also resembles the sea palm.
Its fruit is called the coconut,
as large as a bowl or cup.
It has a coarse outer husk,
like that of the betel nut;
next is a hard shell,
round and firm,
two to three *fen* thick.
For those with perfectly round shells,
they cut off the top,
polish it with sand and stone,
remove the wrinkled skin,
revealing the mottled, brocade-like pattern,
which they then adorn with white metal,
making it into a water vessel,
rare, exquisite, and delightful.
Inside the shell are several *ge* of liquid,
like milk,
which can also be drunk, though it stirs up *qi*.
The Bodhi Tree
From this tree onward,
there are twenty-three kinds of trees in total.
The Bodhi tree
comes from the country of Mójiātuó,
in the Mahābodhi Temple,
being the tree under which Śākyamuni Tathāgata attained enlightenment.
It is also called the Tree of Contemplation.
Its trunk is yellowish-white,
its branches and leaves verdant,
remaining evergreen through winter.
On the day the Buddha entered nirvana,
its color changes and its leaves fall.
Afterwards, they grow back.
On this day, the king and people of the country,
high and low, perform Buddhist rites,
collect the leaves, and return home,
considering them auspicious.
The tree is four hundred feet tall,
below it is a silver stupa,
encircling it.
The people of that country constantly burn incense and make offerings throughout the seasons,
circumambulating the tree and paying respects.
During the Táng Zhēnguàn era,
envoys were frequently dispatched there,
to make offerings at the temple,
and bestow monastic robes.
In the fifth year of the Gāozōng Xiǎnqìng era,
a stele was erected at the temple,
to record the sacred virtue.
This tree has two Sanskrit names:
One is "Bīnbōlí Pólìyì",
The *Xīyù Jì* calls it "Bēibō,
luó".
Because the Buddha attained enlightenment beneath it,
it is named after the Way (Bodhi),
hence called "Bodhi Pódāochā".
Translated into Chinese, it is the "Tree of the Way".
In the past, King Aśoka of Central India cut it down,
ordering it to serve a great Brahmin,
piling up firewood to burn it.
Amid the raging flames,
two trees suddenly sprouted.
King Aśoka, filled with remorse,
named it the Ash Bodhi Tree.
He then enclosed it with a stone wall.
Later, during the time of King Śaśāṅka,
it was dug up again,
down to the spring water,
yet its roots remained unbroken.
A pit fire was lit to burn it,
and it was doused
with sugarcane juice,
intending
to make it char and rot.
Later, King Mañjuśrī of Magadha,
a great-grandson of Aśoka,
irrigated it with the milk of a thousand cows.
After two nights,
the tree revived as before.
He further increased the stone wall,
to a height of twenty-four feet.
When Xuánzàng reached the Western Regions,
he saw the tree rising over twenty feet above the stone wall.
The Bōluó Tree
In Bālíng, there was a temple.
Under a monk's bed in the dormitory,
a tree suddenly grew,
continuing to grow even as it was cut.
A foreign monk saw it and said:
"This is a bōluó tree."
In the early Yuánjiā era,
it produced a flower like a lotus.
In the early Tiānbǎo era of the Táng,
Ānxī presented bōluó branches.
The memorial stated:
"Within the four garrisons under my jurisdiction,
there is Báhànnà,
which is the closest.
There grows the bōluó tree,
exceptionally rare and extraordinary.
It does not shelter common grasses,
nor does it harbor vile birds.
Its lofty trunk is no less than pine or cypress,
its shade no inferior to peach or plum.
I recently dispatched an official to Báhànnà,
ordering him to gather two hundred stems of the aforementioned tree branches.
If they can take root in Chánglè Palace,
and raise their tips in Jiànzhāng Palace,
spreading leaves and casting shade,
they would be neighbors to the scarlet cassia in the moon;
linking branches and joining shadows,
they would face the white elms in heaven."
The Solitary Bean Tree.
South of Dùnqiū there is Yīngzú Mountain.
On the mountain there is a tree.
Over ten zhàng tall.
Its bark is green and smooth,
resembling flowing jade.
Its branches and trunk soar upward.
Its seeds are like multicolored pouches,
its leaves like the mirror of a lost child.
The world calls it the "Immortal's Solitary Bean Tree."
The Persian Soap-pod Tree
The Persian soap-pod,
originates from Persia,
where it is called Hūyězhānmò.
Fúlín calls it Ālíqùfá.
The tree grows three to four zhàng tall,
five to six chǐ in circumference.
Its leaves resemble those of the jūlǜ tree but are shorter and smaller,
and do not wither in the cold.
It bears fruit without flowering.
Its pods are two chǐ long,
with compartments inside,
each containing a single seed.
The seeds are as large as a finger,
red in color,
and extremely hard.
Inside, they are black as ink.
Sweet as maltose.
They can be eaten,
and are also suitable for medicinal use.
The Wooden Dragon Tree
South of the high tombs in Xúzhōu city,
there is the Mùlóng Temple.
The temple has a three-layered brick
pagoda,
over one zhàng tall.
Beside the pagoda grows a large tree,
twining its way up to the pagoda's summit.
Its branches and trunk intertwine,
forming a flat surface on top,
capable of seating over ten people.
The tips of its branches droop downward on all sides,
like a "hundred-son tent."
No one recognizes this type of wood.
The monks call it "dragon wood."
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng once sent someone to draw a picture of it.
The Pattra Tree
Pattra,
originates from the country of Magadha,
growing six to seven zhàng tall,
and does not wither in winter.
This tree has three varieties:
the first is Duōluópólìyìduō.
The second is Duōlípólìyì Bèiduō,
the third is Bùpólìyì Duōluóduōlí.
All are used for writing,
Bùshé is of one color.
Its bark is taken for writing.
"Bèiduō" is Sanskrit,
translated into Chinese as "leaf."
"Bèiduō pólìyì"
means "tree leaf" in Chinese.
Scriptures in the Western Regions
use these three types of bark-leaves.
If properly preserved,
they can last five to six hundred years.
The "Record of Sōng Mountain" states that pattra leaves resemble loquat leaves,
which is also erroneous.
Recently, pattra branches have been produced near Jiāozhǐ,
their timber
is of the highest quality.
The Mò Tree,
originates from Persia.
Fúlín calls it Āsuǒ.
It grows about one zhàng tall.
Its bark is bluish-white,
its leaves resemble those of the pagoda tree but are longer,
its flowers resemble those of the orange but are larger.
Its seeds are black,
as large as cornelian cherries,
their flavor sweet and sour,
edible.
The Pánbìsèbō Tree,
originates from Persia,
and also from Fúlín.
Fúlín calls it Qúnhàn.
The tree grows three zhàng tall,
four to five chǐ in circumference.
Its leaves resemble fine banyan leaves,
and do not wither in the cold.
Its flowers resemble those of the orange,
white in color.
Its seeds are green,
as large as sour jujubes,
their flavor sweet and rich,
edible.
People in the Western Regions press them for oil,
which they apply to the body
to relieve wind-induced itching.
The Qídūn Tree,
originates from Persia,
and also from Fúlín,
where it is called Qíhū.
The tree grows two to three zhàng tall.
Its bark is bluish-white.
Its flowers resemble those of the pomelo,
extremely fragrant.
Its seeds resemble carambola,
ripening in the sixth month.
People in the Western Regions press them for oil,
used to cook pastries and fruits,
similar to China's jùshèng.
The Rice-paper Plant,
resembles nettle.
It grows on mountain slopes,
the pollen from its flowers is used to treat malignant sores.
It is hollow inside,
containing pith,
light and white, lovely,
women artisans take it to decorate objects.
Mountain Cassia,
leaves like hemp,
small purple flowers,
yellow leaves clustered.
Grows together with the fire-preventing herb in the Dānyáng Mountains.
Five-Bristle Pine
When speaking of pines, "two grains" or "five grains,"
"grain" should refer to "bristle."
In the main hall of his private residence in Xiūxíng Lane, Duàn Chéngshì
had two five-bristle pines,
only as large as a bowl.
They bore fruit,
the taste no different from those from Xīnluó.
The bark of the five-bristle pine is not scaly.
In the watermill pavilion of the Tang eunuch Qiú Shìliáng,
there were two-bristle pines with non-scaly bark,
and also seven-bristle ones,
it is unknown where they came from.
Commonly called the "peacock three-bristle pine."
The pine's life-root,
if it encounters a rock below, it will bend and twist,
not necessarily requiring a thousand years.
Three-Bristle Pine
The Tang Duke Wèi, Lǐ Déyù, said,
the three-bristle pine is different from the peacock pine.
He also said,
if you want the pine to stop growing,
place a rock against its straight downward root,
and it will bend.
It does not necessarily take a thousand years to bend.
Fish-Scale Pine
In Luòyáng there is a fish-scale pine.
Praying-Hands Cypress
The Tang Grand Court Academician Cuī Shí said,
west of Rǔ there is Liàn Creek,
with many unusual cypresses.
When late autumn arrives,
their leaves close up.
Commonly called the "praying-hands cypress."
Boxwood
Boxwood is slow-growing by nature.
The world values boxwood
because it does not catch fire.
Some say,
test it with water:
if it sinks, it will not catch fire.
Cut this wood on an overcast day,
with not a single star at night,
and it will not crack when made into a pillow.
Poplar Wood,
comes from the Gorges.
Made into a bed,
one sleeps without fleas.
Jùnàwèi,
leaves like bamboo,
three stems per layer,
the stem tips branching like zhēntóng,
small flowers,
resembling the wood-oak.
Comes from Guìzhōu.
Camellia
The camellia resembles the pomegranate,
and is found in Guìzhōu.
It also exists in the Shǔ region.
The Huái tree of Xiàzhōu
Xiàzhōu had only one postal station,
which had several Huái trees.
Yánzhōu sometimes needed their leaves,
and would send official documents to request them.
The red and white tamarisk
The red and white tamarisk comes from Liángzhōu.
Large ones do not exist,
and their ash can injure people,
Boiling copper with its ash solution,
can turn it into silver.
The Jiē wood
In Shǔ there is a tree similar to the oak.
When other trees flourish,
it appears like a withered stump.
Only in deep winter does it sprout and spread shade.
People of Shǔ call it Jiē wood.
The Chǔ
If a field is long abandoned,
it will inevitably produce Gǒu trees,
Their leaves have lobes.
The large one is called Chǔ,
the small one is called Gǒu.
The patterned wood of the ancestral temple
In the ground of the ancestral temple grows red wood,
signifying that the ruler's rituals are each appropriate.
The wooden slip with writing
In the early Jiànyuán era of Qí,
at the temple of Jìzǐ of Yánlíng,
there was formerly a bubbling well.
North of the well, a metallic and stone sound was suddenly heard.
Digging two zhàng deep,
they found a boiling spring.
From the spring they retrieved a wooden slip,
one chǐ long,
and one cùn two fēn wide.
Raised characters read:
"The Lúshān Daoist priest Zhāng Líng pays his respects once more."
The wood was hard and white,
the characters yellow in color.
The ancient inscribed pillar
In the summer of the second year of Jiànyuán of Qí,
the Chángxī river in Lúlíng rushed against a mountain foot, causing a collapse,
six or seven chǐ long.
Beneath it were found over a thousand pillars,
each ten arm-spans around,
the longer ones one zhàng,
the shorter ones eight or nine chǐ.
Their tops bore ancient script,
characters that could not be deciphered.
Jiāng Yān asked Wáng Jiǎn about them.
Jiǎn said:
"East of the river, they are not familiar with clerical script;
these are pillars from the Qín or Hàn period."
The firewood with three characters
In the ninth year of Yǒngmíng of Qí,
at the Ānshí Temple in Mòlíng,
there was an ancient tree
that was felled for firewood.
The wood grain naturally formed the three characters "Fǎ Tiān Dé" (Emulate Heavenly Virtue).
The firewood with the Heavenly Lord image
Táng dynasty Vice Director of the Bureau of Prisoners Chén Xiūgǔ said,
in a county of Xīchuān,
he could not recall the name,
an official had the prison guard's wooden [object] exchanged for firewood.
On it was preserved an image of the Heavenly Lord.
The Tàipíng wood
An extraordinary wood.
During the Dàlì era of Táng,
a commoner of Chéngdū, Guō Yuǎn,
while gathering firewood,
obtained an auspicious piece of wood.
Its grain formed the characters:
"Tiānxià Tàipíng" (Peace Under Heaven).
An edict ordered it stored in the Imperial Library.
The Heavenly King Huái
At the Chíguó Temple in Cháng'ān,
before the temple gate were several Huái trees.
Supervisor Jīn bought one
and ordered a skilled craftsman in his service to saw it.
When he returned inside,
the craftsman said the wood had nothing unusual.
Jīn sighed deeply in regret,
and ordered it glued back together.
He said:
"This is ruined.
But let this make you aware of my craftsmanship."
When sawed along a different grain,
