each piece revealed a Heavenly King,
with halberds and pagodas fully formed.
The Sèlíng wood
On Táishān there is Sèlíng wood,
its grain like a damask pattern.
Common people take it to make pillows,
calling them Sèlíng pillows.
The horse-patterned wood
Fèngxiáng's guest prefect Guō Qú,
his father once supervised a workshop.
When about to saw a log,
they suspected there was iron or stone within,
as the saw could not enter.
They then used a new saw,
and also burned incense and prayed over it,
whereupon the saw proceeded.
When split open,
the wood grain showed two horse shapes,
one black, one red,
biting each other.
Their mouths, noses, manes, tails,
hooves, legs, sinews, and bones
were no different from living ones.
The tree governing a province
In the wild lands east of the central plains,
there is a Yùzhāng tree.
This tree governs one province.
It is a thousand zhàng high,
a hundred zhàng around.
From its base up three hundred zhàng,
only then
do branches begin,
spreading out like a canopy.
Upon it are black foxes and dark apes.
The tree governs a province.
North and south lie side by side,
facing southwest.
There are nine strong men
who wield axes to fell it,
to divine the fortune of the nine provinces.
If the cut heals,
that province has good fortune;
if the wound remains, the provincial governor falls ill;
if after years it does not heal,
that province will perish,
The sprawling mulberry
In the east there is a tree,
eighty zhàng tall.
It spreads out, supporting itself.
Its leaves are one zhàng long,
six or seven chǐ wide.
It is called the mulberry.
On it naturally are silkworms,
making cocoons three chǐ long.
Reeling one cocoon
yields one jīn of silk.
It has mulberries,
three chǐ five cùn long,
their circumference matching their length,
The dayless tree
In the wild lands there is a volcano,
within which grows the dayless tree.
Day and night it burns with fire.
Fierce winds do not intensify it,
torrential rains do not extinguish it.
The mosquito tree
There is a tree like the holly,
its fruit grows among the branches,
shaped like loquat seeds.
Whenever ripe, it splits open,
and swarms of mosquitoes fly out,
leaving only the skin and shell.
The local people call it the mosquito tree.
Sacred Drum Branch
Hánquān,
at the water mouth below the eastern bank of the county,
there is a sacred drum,
which is the drum branch of Yángshān.
It lies horizontally by the river.
Though struck by rushing waves,
it has never moved.
When flocks of birds fly and chirp,
none alight upon it.
If boatmen mistakenly touch it with their poles,
they suffer from malaria.
Deerwood
North of Wǔlíng Commandery,
there are two deerwood trees,
planted by General Mǎ Fúbō.
The wood has many knots.
Inverted-growth Wood
This wood grows clinging to the mountain,
with its roots above.
If someone touches it, the leaves close;
when the person leaves, the leaves open.
It comes from the Eastern Sea.
Yǒu Wood
Its knots can be used to poison beasts,
and it can be made into whips.
Sago Palm Tree
In ancient Nánhǎi County, there were sago palm trees.
Leaves grow at the top,
and they yield flour.
Large ones produce flour,
up to a hundred hú.
If eaten with cow's milk,
it is very delicious.
Strange Pine
Nánkāng has a strange pine.
Formerly, the regional inspector
often ordered painters to sketch the pine,
and several branches would inevitably wither.
Later, because a guest and courtesans
drank around its base,
after a day the pine died.
Maple Person
Among the mountains of the Lingnan region, many have maple trees.
Old trees often have burls.
If suddenly one night there is a violent thunderstorm,
the tree's excrescence will secretly grow several feet.
Southerners call it a "maple person."
Yuè shamans say
that if one carves it into gods or ghosts,
it achieves remarkable spiritual efficacy.
Maple Ghost
The Línchuān Jì records:
On Má Gū Mountain in Fǔzhōu,
if someone climbs it
and looks out,
Mount Lú and Lake Pénglí
all appear below.
There are huánglián and hòupò herbs,
and maple trees from Héngshān.
Some thousands of years old
take human form,
with eyes, nose, mouth, and arms but no feet.
Those who enter the mountain see them.
If someone chops at them,
they all bleed.
People all place indigo-dyed cloth on their heads,
and the next day, looking, the cloth is gone,
becoming a maple child ghost.
Maple-born Person
In the mountains of Jiāngdōng and Jiāngxī,
there are many maple wood people.
They are born under maple trees,
resembling human form,
three or four feet tall.
During a night thunderstorm,
they grow level with the tree,
but upon seeing a person, they shrink back to their original size.
Once, someone placed a bamboo hat on one's head,
and the next day, looking,
the hat was hanging on the treetop.
During drought, if rain is desired,
bind its head with bamboo,
perform an exorcism, and rain will come.
People take them to make divination boards,
which are extremely spiritually efficacious.
This is the maple wood jujube ground.
Spiritual Maple
In the southern regions, there are maple child ghosts.
Old maple wood that takes human form
is also called "spiritual maple."
Split Wood Contains Meat
Someone split a large tree,
and inside the wood was meat,
about five jīn,
like cooked pork.
River Maple Timber
Along the coast,
whenever building a house,
they order people to tread on wood in the river.
Short, long, thin, or thick,
they take whatever they need.
Mostly it is pine timber.
That custom commonly uses it,
not knowing who in ancient times cut it
and buried it in the sand and mud.
It neither rots nor is eaten by insects,
and there is much of it like this.
This is a strange matter.
River Earl's Timber
Below the mountain in Zhōngsù County is a shrine.
The Zhēn River reaches here,
boiling and raging.
Rafted timber floating here sinks,
and none ever emerges.
People of the world consider it the River Earl's timber.
Dragon-fighting Ship Timber
Camphor wood
is often taken by people in Jiāngdōng to make boats.
There are boats that fight with flood dragons.
Mutual-yielding Wood
The Wǔlíng Commandery Jì records:
On Báizhì Mountain, there is a tree
named "mutual-yielding."
After all other trees have flourished,
it then sprouts;
also, each year it alternates in flourishing.
Thousand-year Pine
The Yùcè Jì states:
Thousand-year-old pine trees
spread out on all sides,
their topmost twigs not growing upward.
Looking at them from afar,
they resemble a reclining canopy.
Within them are creatures,
like green dogs,
or like humans.
All live ten thousand years.
Sweating Staff
Dōngfāng Shuò returned from the Western Nàhàn Kingdom.
He obtained ten sounding-wood staffs.
The emperor bestowed them on great ministers.
If the person holding it falls ill, the staff sweats;
when about to die, it breaks.
A local saying goes:
"If the staff doesn't sweat, life's half not yet passed."
Butterfly-transforming Tree
Inside the forbidden park of Cháng'ān city was a large tree.
In winter, amidst the snow,
it suddenly blossomed with luxuriant leaves.
When they withered and bore fruit,
the seeds were bright and dazzling,
like the light of fire.
After several days,
they all transformed into red butterflies and flew away.
The following year,
Táng Gāozǔ entered Cháng'ān from the Táng state.
This must have been an omen.
Fú River Timber
In Zǐtóng County of Qī County,
in the seventh year of the Dàlì era of the Tang Dynasty,
on the jiǎzǐ day of the sixth month in summer,
the Fú River overflowed,
carrying thousands of logs downstream.
Beams, pillars, rafters, and brackets were all complete.
The interior city buildings were repaired,
entirely using this wood.
Qiáo Lín recorded this event.
The Upright Tree
The Upright Tree west of Cháng'ān,
is about thirty lǐ from Mǎwéi.
When Emperor Dézōng of the Tang Dynasty traveled to Fèngtiān,
he saw its lush foliage,
and bestowed upon it this beautiful name.
Later, a literary scholar passed by,
and inscribed a poem at an inn,
without revealing his name.
The poem reads:
"In the past, it alone basked in the glory of rain and dew,
Emperor Dé bestowed a fine name on his westward journey.
Not far from here lies Mǎwéi,
it should have grown over Consort Yáng's tomb."
Such is the elegance of poetry.
The Scholar's Lane Scholar Tree
In the Tang Dynasty, there was a man named Chén Pǔ.
During the Yuánhé era,
outside the main gate of this street in Chóngxián Lane,
there was a scholar tree.
He once leaned against it at dusk, peering outside.
He saw what appeared to be women, old foxes, strange birds, and the like,
entering the tree.
He then cut it down to investigate.
The tree had three main branches,
all hollow inside.
In one branch, there were one hundred and twenty-one single-headed chestnuts,
and a swaddled dead child,
over a chǐ in length.
The Three-Branched Scholar Tree
The Tang Chancellor Lǐ Shí
had a residence in Yǒnglè, Hézhōng.
In the courtyard, there was a scholar tree with a single trunk,
which split into three branches.
Two branches extended straight past the ridge of the hall's roof,
while one branch did not reach it.
The Chancellor had two brothers from the same household,
named Shí,
and Ér,
both of whom rose to the positions of Chancellor and Executive;
only Fú,
served as Military Commissioner of seven provinces, holding the title of Vice-Chancellor.
The Gall Scholar Tree
Northwest of Sānjiādiàn in Huàzhōu, by the roadside,
there was a very large scholar tree,
lush and verdant all around,
providing shade over several mǔ.
The tree had a gall,
shaped like two pigs,
chasing each other in a run.
Their turning heads, mouths, ears, and feet,
were exactly like sculpted figures.
The Vitex Root Pillow
A merchant named Zhāng Hóng
was traveling to the front of the Huàyuè Temple,
when he suddenly felt dizzy and confused.
Unable to proceed,
he tethered his horse to a golden vitex tree and fell into a deep sleep.
The horse was startled,
and pulled up the tree root as it ran off.
Upon waking,
he chased after it and caught up.
The tree root was shaped like a lion,
with fur, claws, eyes, ears, feet, and tail,
all perfectly formed.
He then went to Huàyīn County,
hired a carpenter to craft it into a pillow,
and presented it to the temple.
The temple keeper often locked it in a chest.
Travelers who heard of it,
would bribe the temple keeper with a hundred coins,
to get a single look.
The Five-Tiered Mulberry Tree
In Luòzhōng, Yuànhuì Temple
was established by Wáng Yì, a Vice-Director of the Central Secretariat of the Wei Dynasty, who donated his residence.
In front of the Buddha hall grew a mulberry tree,
which rose straight up for five chǐ,
its branches spreading horizontally,
its boughs and leaves extending sideways,
shaped like a feathered canopy.
After another five chǐ,
it repeated the same pattern.
In total, there were five tiers.
Each tier
had distinct leaves and mulberries.
The monks and laypeople of the capital
called it the Divine Mulberry.
Crowds came to see it.
The Emperor heard of it and was displeased,
considering it a public deception,
and ordered Yuán Jì, a Vice-Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
to cut it down.
On that day, clouds and mist darkened the sky,
and where the axe struck,
blood flowed down to the ground.
All who witnessed it wept in sorrow.
The Dragonfly Tree
In the past, Lóu Yuē lived on Chángshān Mountain,
occupying a meditation seat.
There was an old woman from the wilds,
holding a tree in her hand.
She planted it in the courtyard,
saying it was a dragonfly tree.
Over the years, it became fragrant, lush, and flourishing.
There was a bird,
with a red body and long tail,
that often rested upon it.
The Soapberry Tree,
when burned, emits an extremely fragrant scent,
and wards off evil vapors.
It is also called Jìnlóu,
or Huán.
In the past, there was a divine shaman named Yáomào,
who could subdue all ghosts with talismans,
capturing mountain spirits and demons,
and killing them by striking with soapberry wood.
People vied to obtain this wood to make utensils,
using it to repel ghosts,
hence it was called the "Worry-Free Wood."
The Vinegar-Hearted Tree
Dù Shīrén once rented a residence.
In the courtyard was a huge apricot tree.
An old man from the neighborhood,
whenever he carried water to the side of the tree,
would always sigh and say:
"What a pity for this tree."
Dù questioned him.
The old man said:
"I am skilled at diagnosing tree ailments.
This tree is sick,
allow me to treat it."
He then examined a spot on the tree,
and said:
"The tree suffers from vinegar heart."
Dù dipped his finger into the infested spot and tasted it,
the flavor was like weak vinegar.
The old man took a small hook and probed the infestation,
hooking repeatedly,
until he extracted a white insect,
resembling a bat.
He then applied medicine to the wound.
He further cautioned:
"When it bears fruit,
from the time the skin is green,
you must thin them out.
Remove eight or nine out of ten,
and the tree will survive."
Dù followed his advice,
and the tree grew even more luxuriant.
He also said:
"I once saw a three-volume 'Manual of Planting,'
which mentioned trees suffering from vinegar heart."
The Successful Examination Soap Pod
The Temple of Confucius in Quánzhōu,
with its solemn and imposing halls and courtyards,
and the flourishing state of its school,
was the finest among the regional prefectures.
In the courtyard stood a honey locust tree;
each time a local scholar was about to pass the imperial examination,
it would grow one pod.
This was considered a regular occurrence.
During the Zhēnmíng era of the Liáng dynasty,
it suddenly grew one and a half pods,
and no one could understand what it meant.
That very year,
a man from the prefecture, Chén Tì,
passed the jìnshì examination;
Huáng Rényǐng,
passed the xuéjiū examination.
Rényǐng felt ashamed of this,
so he took the exam again,
applying for the jìnshì examination.
By the Tóngguāng era,
where the half-pod had previously grown,
a full pod grew again.
That year,
Rényǐng passed the jìnshì examination.
Several years later,
the temple was destroyed by fire.
That year,
Mǐn declared itself an independent kingdom,
and no longer sent tribute scholars to the imperial court,
a situation that continues to this day.
On the White Sandalwood Tree
To the left of Jiànmén, among the steep cliffs,
there is a large tree
that grows from a crevice in the rock,
so large it would take several arm spans to encircle it,
with branches and trunk pure white.
It was commonly said to be a white sandalwood tree.
Beneath it, there was often a giant serpent,
coiled around it as if protecting it,
so the people dared not cut it down.
Also, halfway up the western cliff,
there was the shadow of Monk Zhìgōng.
Travelers passing by
would all face west, raise their clasped hands, and bow in reverence,
as if personally beholding the Tathāgata.
Wáng Rényù, in the guǐwèi year, entered Shǔ,
and reaching the foot of that cliff,
fixed his gaze upon it,
to verify the long-standing legend.
It happened to be a clear, sunny day,
the streams and valleys were pristine,
so he reined in his horse and gazed at it for a long while.
That so-called white sandalwood
was actually a white cypress tree.
Having traveled through both the Greater and Lesser Màntiān areas,
along the roads and between the streams and valleys,
such trees were very numerous;
how could there be any tale of sandalwood and a serpent coiled around it?
Looking further west at the shadow of Zhìgōng,
it turned out there was a round cypress tree on the cliff,
which formed the head of his hat;
on both sides, there were vertical rock crevices,
which delineated the shape of his body;
the diagonal crevices
represented the lines of his kasaya robe;
above, there were mottled patches of moss,
which resembled the texture of landscape painting.
Only then did he realize it was not white sandalwood.
That Zhìgōng left no shadow here
was now clear.
Thus, one realizes how limitless are the errors in human transmission!
Vine Fruit Cup
The vine fruit cup comes from the Western Regions.
The vine is as thick as an arm.
Its leaves resemble kudzu, and its flowers and fruit are like the wútóng tree.
When the fruit ripens, it becomes hard and solid,
and all can be used to drink wine.
They naturally have patterns,
translucent and lovely.
The fruit is as large as a cup,
its taste like cardamom,
fragrant, delicious, and dispels the effects of wine.
Local people carry wine
to the foot of the vine,
pluck the flowers to drink wine,
and then use the fruit to sober up.
The people of that country treasure it,
and it is not transmitted to the Central Plains.
Zhāng Qiān obtained it when he entered Yuān.
This is recorded in "Zhāng Qiān's Account of Leaving the Pass."
Bell Vine
Sōngzhēn
is the bell vine.
Its larger leaves
are used as plates by the people of Jìn'ān.
Rénzǐ Vine
In Ānnán, there is the rénzǐ vine,
red in color,
with thorns at the end of the vine.
Its seeds are shaped like human figures.
When the Kūnlún people burn them, they attract elephants.
It is also rare in the southern regions.
Honey Grass Vine
In Northern Tiānzhú country, there grows honey grass,
a creeping plant with large leaves,
that does not die in autumn and winter.
Due to heavy frost and dew,
it forms honey,
like the salty frost on the northern frontiers.
Húmàn Grass
This grass grows in Yōng and Jiān,
in clusters.
Its flowers are somewhat like gardenias,
slightly larger,
not forming full blossoms,
yellowish-white in color.
The leaves are somewhat unusual.
If mistakenly eaten,
one dies within a few days.
Drinking the blood of a white goose or white duck
acts as an antidote.
Some people throw something at it,
and pray, saying:
"I buy you,
and eating you will not cause death."
Wild Fox Silk
There is a creeping grass,
white in color,
with faintly red flowers,
as large as millet grains.
The people of Qín call it wild fox silk.
Nàizhī Grass
Nàizhī
comes from the country of Fúlín.
The plant grows three to four chǐ tall.
Its root is as large as a duck egg.
The leaves resemble garlic,
and from the center of the leaves emerges a very long stalk.
At the end of the stalk, there is a six-petaled flower,
red and white in color,
with a yellow-red center.
It does not bear seeds.
This grass grows in winter and dies in summer,
similar to buckwheat.
Take its flowers,
press them to extract oil,
apply it to the body,
to dispel wind ailments.
The king of Fúlín and the nobles of the country use it.
Sānlài Grass
In Cáozhōu and at the Huái River estuary in Yángzhōu,
grows summer pear and sānlài grass.
It is golden in color,
and grows on high cliffs.
It is among the most essential ingredients in potions for spirits.
Xíjī Grass
Xíjī, also called sàilú,
grows in the northern barbarian lands.
An ancient poem says:
"For a thousand lǐ, xíjī grass."
Gate-Guarding Grass
North of Chángshān, there is a grass
named gate-guarding.
Place it on the gate,
and at night, if someone passes by,
it will shout at them.
Immortal's Braid
On Héngyuè grows the immortal's braid.
It has no roots,
and often grows on rocks.
It looks like a ribbon,
with three strands,
green in color.
It is also not commonly found.
Hélí Grass
Hélí,
its root resembles taro,
with a tuber,
surrounded by twelve wandering offshoots.
They depend on each other to grow.
Yet their fruits are not connected,
only linked by their qi.
It is also called Dúyáo,
or Límǔ.
What the locals eat
is called "chìjiàn."
Lǎoyā zhàolí cǎo
Lǎoyā zhàolí,
its leaves are like burdock but narrower.
When the seeds ripen,
they turn black.
Their shape resembles a bamboo strainer.
Guǐ zàojiá,
grows in the marshes of the Jiangnán region,
like the Chinese honey locust,
one to two chǐ tall.
Washing with it promotes hair growth,
and its leaves also remove dirt from clothing.
Qīngcǎo huái
South of Píniú Mountain in Lóngyáng County,
there is qīngcǎo huái.
It grows in clusters,
over a chǐ tall.
Its flowers resemble the golden lantern,
blooming in mid-summer.
Tóngchí cǎo,
grows in water,
its leaves are like scissors.
Shuǐ nàidōng,
this grass remains alive in water throughout the winter.
Duàn Chéngshì had it in the pond of his southern country villa.
Sānbái cǎo,
when it first sprouts, it is not white.
When summer arrives,
the tips of its leaves turn white.
Farmers use this as a sign to transplant seedlings.
When three leaves turn white,
the grass has fully flowered.
Its leaves resemble shǔyù.
Wúxīn cǎo
Pífú jiǔ cǎo,
also called shǔ'ěr,
due to its shape.
It is also known as wúxīn cǎo.
Pénzèng cǎo,
is the seed of qiānniú.
After the autumn season, it breaks off,
shaped like a pot or steamer.
Inside are seeds,
resembling the vines of shǔyù.
Nǚ cǎo
Wēiruí cǎo,
also called lì cǎo,
is also known as nǚ cǎo.
In the Jianghú region, it is called wá cǎo.
A beautiful woman is called wá,
hence the name.
Mèi cǎo
Hèzǐ cǎo,
is a creeping plant.
Its flowers are the color of fine dust,
with light purple calyxes.
The leaves are like willow but shorter.
It blooms in summer,
Southerners say it is a charm grass.
When picked and dried in the sun,
it can be used as a beauty spot.
Its shape resembles a flying crane,
with wings, tail, beak, and feet,
all fully formed.
In spring, this vine produces twin insects,
which feed only on its leaves.
The women of Yuè collect them in their cosmetic cases,
raising them like
silkworms.
They pick the grass to feed them.
When the insects grow old and stop eating,
they molt into butterflies,
reddish-yellow in color.
Women collect and wear them,
calling them charm butterflies.
Zuì cǎo
"Shīzǐ" says:
Chìxiànzhōu is the ruins of Kūnlún.
To its east is Lǔshuǐ Island.
On the left and right of the mountain,
yùhóng zhī cǎo grows.
Eating one of its fruits
causes one to lie drunk for three hundred years.
Wǔ cǎo
Wǔ cǎo comes from Yǎzhōu.
It has a single stem with three leaves.
The leaves are like juémíng.
One leaf is at the tip of the stem;
two leaves are halfway down the stem.
They face each other.
If someone approaches, they lean;
clapping hands and singing songs
makes them sway as if dancing.
Xiāngsī cǎo
Between Qín and Zhào, there is xiāngsī cǎo.
It looks like shízhú,
with joints linked one after another.
Also called duàncháng cǎo,
or chóufù cǎo,
also shuāng cǎo,
and known as guǎfù shā.
It belongs to the category of longing grass.
Wúqíng cǎo
Zuǒxíng cǎo.
It makes people emotionless.
Fànyáng regularly tributes it.
Wàngyōu cǎo
Xuāncǎo, also called zǐxuān,
is also known as wàngyōu cǎo.
Scholars in Wúzhōng call it liáochóu.
Jī Kāng's "Yǎngshēng Lùn" says:
"Xuāncǎo makes one forget sorrow."
Shuì cǎo
In Guìlín, there is shuì cǎo,
seeing it makes people sleepy.
Also called zuì cǎo,
or lǎnfù zhēn.
From "Nánhǎi Dìjì."
Qiānbù xiāng cǎo
The South Sea produces bǎibù xiāng,
whose fragrance,
carried by the wind, can be smelled from a thousand steps away.
Now along the coast, there is qiānbù xiāng,
which is of the same kind.
Its leaves resemble dùruò,
with red and green intermingled.
"Gòngjí" states:
"Rìnán Commandery tributes qiānbù xiāng."
Shè cǎo
Guījiǎ xiāng is actually guìxiāng.
The finest kind is zǐzhú xiāng.
Also called jīndù xiāng,
or shècǎo xiāng.
It comes from the border between Cāngwú and Guìlín commanderies.
Now in Wúzhōng, there is shè cǎo,
similar to hóng but very fragrant.
Zhìgǔ cǎo
In the region of Xīnzhōu Prefecture, there is a medicinal herb
that the local people call Jícái.
It counteracts all poisons and gu toxins,
with miraculous efficacy beyond compare.
In the past, a man once traveled to Léizhōu.
On the journey, he encountered poison,
and his appearance became severely altered.
He believed he would die immediately.
He drank a few inches of Jícái,
vomited once, and was cured.
Folklore says
that in the past, when someone encountered poison,
his slave Jícái obtained this medicine,
so it was named after the slave.
It is actually a grass root,
similar to peony.
For those afflicted by poison,
secretly take two or three inches of it at night,
either slice it or grind it,
add a little licorice,
and brew and drink it at dawn.
Once vomiting occurs, recovery follows.
It is commonly said that when preparing to take this medicine,
one should not speak openly about it,
hence the term "secretly take."
But the reason for this is not clearly understood.
Some say
that in the past, an old village woman suffered from gu toxin.
Her son was a minor clerk.
The county magistrate ordered him to give her Jícái to drink.
By evening, the medicine was prepared.
At dawn,
his mother said to him:
"I dreamed someone told me
that if I drink this, I will die.
Quickly get rid of it."
She then collapsed to the ground.
Her son again reported to the county magistrate,
who firmly ordered her to drink it.
She indeed recovered.
Could it be that those afflicted by gu toxin also have spirits,
like the "two lads" of illness?
Snake-Holding Grass
The Yì Yuàn records:
In the past, a farmer was plowing his field
and happened to see an injured snake there.
Another snake
held grass in its mouth and placed it on the wound.
After a day, the injured snake slithered away.
The farmer took the remaining leaves of that grass to treat sores,
and it was always effective.
Originally not knowing the grass's name,
it was thus named "Snake-Holding."
The Bàopǔzǐ states:
"Snake-Holding Grass can reconnect severed fingers as before."
This is indeed so.
Deer-Reviving Grass
Tiānmíngjīng,
also called Deer-Reviving Grass.
Liú Bǐng of Qīngzhōu,
during the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
shot a deer.
He cut open its five viscera,
stuffed this grass inside,
and it suddenly stood up.
Liú Bǐng secretly recorded this grass and planted it.
It often healed wounds and fractures.
It is commonly called "Liú Bǐng Grass."
Antidote Grass
Five hundred lǐ south of Wūjù Mountain in Jiànníng Prefecture,
grows Mùmí Grass,
which can counteract poison.
When all plants are flourishing,
birds often mistakenly eat wūzhuó.
Upon being poisoned,
they must swiftly fly to Mùmí Mountain,
and peck Mùmí Grass to counteract it.
Poisonous Grass
Bóluòhuí is highly poisonous,
growing in the valleys of the Jiāng and Huái rivers.
Its stems and leaves resemble hemp.
The stems are hollow,
and when blown, produce a sound
like "bóluó."
Hence its name.
Jiāo Poison Grass
Jiāo Poison Grass is as large as a taro,
shaped like a sparrow's head.
Placed on dry ground, it becomes moist;
placed on wet ground, it becomes dry.
When cooking rice, if planted on the stove,
by the time the rice is done,
it will already have bloomed and borne seeds.
If a person eats it, they die immediately.
Mùmá Grass
There is Mùmá Grass,
highly poisonous.
Where this grass grows,
if the wind carries its vapor,
then rice within several lǐ will immediately die.
Lǐ Chúnfēng said:
"Its sap is originally clear,
but upon contact with water becomes thick,
under sunlight becomes damp,
in shade becomes dry,
in summer it seeks coolness,
in winter it seeks warmth."
Dragon Fodder
On the island of Lóngjūchuān in the Eastern Sea,
where King Mù of Zhōu raised his eight steeds.
On the island, there is a grass called Lóngchú.
Horses that eat it
can travel a thousand lǐ in a day.
An ancient saying goes:
"A single stalk of Dragon Fodder
transforms into a dragon colt."
Red Grass
North of the Shānróng people, there is a grass
with stems ten feet long,
leaves like cart wheels,
and color like the morning glow.
During the time of Duke Huán of Qí,
the Shānróng presented its seeds,
which were then planted in the courtyard,
to symbolize the auspicious sign of a hegemon.
Palace Maiden Grass
In Chǔ, Palace Maiden Grass is often found.
It resembles the golden orange in shape,
and is very fragrant.
Its flowers are like red kingfishers.
Folklore says:
"During the reign of King Líng of Chǔ,
there were several thousand palace maidens,
most of whom were full of resentment and loneliness.
Some died within the palace.
When buried,
this grass grew all over their graves.
Jiāo Grass,
fifty feet tall.
When burned, it turns to ash,
but if watered,
it becomes grass again.
This is called Spirit Grass.
Xiāomíng Grass:
at night it appears like rows of stars,
but by day its light vanishes.
Huángqú Grass
Huángqú Grass
shines like fire under the sun.
Its fruit is very hard.
Those who ingest it
will not feel heat even if burned.
Wénxiá Grass:
those who consume it become light-bodied.
Its leaves are like cassia,
its stems like orchid.
That country presented its roots,
but when planted, they mostly bore no fruit,
and the grass leaves often withered and yellowed.
An edict ordered them all removed.
First Emperor's Rush
East of Nánchéng in Qí, there is a Rush Platform,
where Qín Shǐhuáng once stopped.
At that time, the First Emperor was below the platform,
and twisted rushes to tether his horse.
To this day, the rushes still grow luxuriantly,
commonly called "Qín Shǐhuáng's Rush."
Dream Grass
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
a foreign state presented dream grass.
It resembled cattail.
During the day it would retract into the ground,
and at night it would sprout forth.
If one carried this grass,
one would know whether one's dreams were good or bad.
The Emperor missed Lady Lǐ,
and carrying it, he would dream of her.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Horse-Grazing Grass
At the place where Emperor Wǔ of Hàn grazed horses in the lake,
to this day the wild grass all bears the appearance of having been chewed.
In the lake area it is called Horse Marsh.
In the marsh there is a square stone for playing liubo, used by Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
upon which an inscription is carved.
Water Net Algae
In Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Kūnlíng Pond,
there was water net algae.
Its branches lay horizontally across the water's surface,
eight or nine chǐ in length,
resembling the mesh of a net.
When ducks entered this grass,
they could not get out.
Hence it was given this name.
Earth Sun Grass
In the south there is earth sun grass.
When the three-legged crow wished to descend and eat this grass,
Xīhé, who drove the sun chariot,
would cover the crow's eyes with her hand,
for if it ate this, it would become sluggish and cease to move.
Dōngfāng Shuò said that
when he was a child,
he fell into a well,
plunging to the world below,
and for several decades had nothing to rely on.
Someone guided him,
telling him to go to this grass.
Separated by a red spring,
he could not cross.
That person gave him a single shoe,
and riding upon it, he floated across the red spring,
reached the place where the grass grew,
and ate it.
Book-Binding Grass
Minister of Agriculture Zhèng Xuán
often lived and taught in the mountains south of Bùqí City.
During the Yellow Turban rebellion,
he fled to avoid it.
He sent his disciples Cuī Yǎn, Wáng Jīng, and other worthies to this place,
and they parted with tears.
The grass below the mountain where he lived was like jiè (Chinese chives),
with leaves over a chǐ long,
exceptionally tough and resilient.
People of the time named it Kāngchéng's Book-Binding Grass.
Golden Orange Grass
When Emperor Wǔ of Jìn was still the General Who Pacifies the Army,
three unusual plants suddenly grew beneath the steps in the rear hall of his residence.
Their stems were yellow and leaves green,
as if woven from gold and drawn from jade.
The flowers were delicate and frail,
shaped like golden oranges.
People of the time did not know what auspicious omen this was,
so they concealed it,
not allowing outsiders to peek.
There was a Qiāng man named Yáo Fù,
courtesy name Shìfēn,
who worked tending horses in the stables,
and was profoundly skilled in the arts of yīn-yáng.
He said
this grass was an auspicious response corresponding to the virtue of Metal.
Fù was ninety years old;
Yáo Xiāng was his ancestor.
Fù loved reading books
and was fond of wine,
often staying drunk for months without sobering up.
While drunk,
he liked to discuss the rise and fall of rulers.
He was skilled at jesting and humor,
endlessly witty and amusing.
He often sighed, saying:
"The waters of the Nine Rivers
are not enough to use as firewood;
the deer of the Seven Marshes
are not enough to fill the kitchen cauldron."
He often said that ordinary people receive the essence of heaven and earth,
but those who do not know how to drink wine
are merely moving flesh containing breath—
how are they any different from clay or wooden dolls without mind or consciousness?
He loved to drink the dregs and chew the lees,
constantly saying he thirsted for fine wine.
His companions often teased and played with him,
calling him the Thirsty Qiāng.
When Emperor Wǔ of Jìn ascended the throne,
he suddenly saw Fù standing below the steps.
The Emperor, impressed by his unconventional talent,
promoted him to Magistrate of Zhāogē County.
Fù declined, saying:
"I am from the Dī and Qiāng foreign lands,
far removed from your civilized customs.
To have wandered into the Central Plains
is already an extraordinary fortune.
I beg to decline the county of Zhāogē,
and wish to remain long in the service of tending horses.
From time to time, bestow fine wine upon me,
to enjoy my remaining years."
The Emperor said:
"Zhāogē Commandery is the old capital of King Zhòu,
where there is a Pool of Wine.
Thus, this old Qiāng will no longer cry thirst."
Fù, standing below the steps,
responded in a loud voice:
"This old Qiāng horse tender,
gradually influenced by the imperial teachings,
knows that all under heaven, barbarians included,
are subjects of the king.
Now, if I delight in the pleasures of the Pool of Wine
and accept the land of Zhāogē,
would I not be likened to Yīn Zhòu?"
The Emperor, stroking his jade armrest, was greatly pleased,
and immediately transferred him to be Governor of Jiǔquán.
That region had a clear spring,
whose taste was like wine.
Fù, riding on wine, paid homage to it.
Thereafter, he governed with excellent administration.
The people erected a living shrine for him.
Later, when the residence's land was bestowed upon Zhāng Huá,
this grass was still there.
Therefore, Màoxiān (Zhāng Huá) wrote in his "Ode to the Golden Orange":
"Plucking nine stems in the Hàn court,
admiring two plants in this hall.
Precious, they manifest the auspice of Metal's virtue;
their name invites comparison, causing confusion."
In the first year of Emperor Huì's Xiánxī era,
the three plants of grass transformed into trees,
their branches and leaves resembling poplar trees,
five chǐ tall,
corresponding to the dominance of the Three Yángs,
these events.
At that time, there were Yáng Jùn,
his younger brother Yáo,
and younger brother Jì,
called the Three Yángs.
This was the verification of the Drunken Qiāng's prophecy.
Wàngshū Grass
In the tenth year of the Tàishǐ era of Jìn,
the year the Héqiáo Bridge was built,
the state of Fúzhī
presented Wàngshū grass.
Its color was red,
its leaves like lotus.
Viewed closely, they resembled curled lotus leaves;
viewed from afar, they resembled unfurled lotus leaves,
round and full like a canopy.
It was also said
that when the moon rose, the leaves would unfurl,
and when the moon set, the leaves would curl up.
It was planted within the palace grounds,
where a pond spanning a hundred paces was dug,
named "Wàngshū Pond."
At the end of Emperor Mǐn's reign,
the Hú people moved its seeds to Hú lands.
It has been extinct ever since.
That pond was soon filled in as well.
Divine Grass
During the time of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
in the imperial gardens there was union-happiness grass.
It resembled yarrow,
with one plant having a hundred stems.
During the day, the numerous stems spread out luxuriantly;
at night, they joined together into a single stem.
It was called divine.
Banner-Knot Flower
In Hànyuán County, Lízhōu, there is the banner-knot flower.
Two or three chǐ above the ground,
row upon row, they all resemble banner knots.
Yěxīmì Flower
Yěxīmì comes from the Fólín Kingdom,
and also from the Persian Kingdom.
Its seedlings grow seven to eight chǐ tall,
with leaves resembling plum leaves.
It flourishes throughout the four seasons.
Its flowers have five petals,
are white in color,
and do not bear fruit.
When the flowers bloom,
the entire field becomes fragrant.
It is similar to the Zhāntáng from Lǐngnán.
People from the Western Regions often pick its flowers,
press them to extract oil,
and apply it for its fragrant smoothness.
Dūshèng flowers,
purple in color,
have double-layered hearts,
with several leaves curling upward,
like reed tufts,
with yellow stamens and fine leaves.
Cùdié flowers,
with clusters of petals around a single stamen,
resemble lotus seedpods.
They are light red in color.
They originate from Wēnzhōu.
Róngkuí,
originally a type of kuí from the lakes,
is also called Húkuí.
It resembles kuí.
The larger ones are red,
and can be woven into cloth.
When burned into ash,
it retains a strong fire,
and does not extinguish for a long time.
There are also double-layered varieties.
Jīndēng flowers
—Jīndēng is also called Jiǔxíng—
have flowers and leaves that do not appear together.
It is considered inauspicious for common households to plant it,
hence it is also known as the "heartless grass."
Jīnqián flowers.
During the Liáng dynasty, officials in Jīngzhōu,
while playing shuāngliù, would gamble with gold coins.
When the coins ran out,
they would use Jīnqián flowers to make up the difference.
Yú Hóng said that obtaining the flowers was better than obtaining coins.
Píshīshā flowers
—Píshīshā,
also known as Zhōngjīnqián flowers,
originally came from foreign lands.
They were introduced to the Central Plains in the second year of the Dàtóng era of the Liáng dynasty.
On Peonies
Peony flowers
are commonly believed to have appeared recently.
This is because in the collected works of literati from the late Suí dynasty,
there are no poems or songs about peonies.
However, Yáng Zǐhuá painted peonies with extreme clarity.
Zǐhuá was a person of the Northern Qí,
so it is known that peony flowers have existed for a long time.
Moreover, in the collected works of Xiè Kānglè,
it is also mentioned that "among bamboo and near water, there are many peonies."
Yet, in the Suí dynasty's "Planting Methods," comprising over seventy volumes,
peonies are not mentioned,
indicating that peonies were not among the flowers and herbs of the Suí dynasty.
White Peonies
In the late Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Péi Shìyān, a court official,
returned from a mission to Yōujì,
and at the Zhòngxiāng Temple in Fénzhōu,
obtained a white peony plant.
He planted it in his private estate in Chángxīng.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
it became a rare treasure in the capital.
At that time, renowned scholars
composed a poem titled "Viewing Peonies at Vice-Director Péi's Residence."
The poem has yet to be found.
Tàicháng Doctor Zhāng Chéng
once heard from Sacrificial Officer Péi,
and Fáng Guǎn also said:
"At the peony gathering,
Guǎn was not present."
Red and Purple Peonies
During the Zhìdé era of the Táng dynasty,
Grand Councilor Mǎ Zǒng governed Tàiyuán.
He obtained red and purple peonies,
and transplanted them into the city.
In the early Yuánhé era, they were still rare,
but now they are comparable to Róngkuí.
It is merely a matter of quantity.
Zhèngdàoyùn Peonies
At the Xìngtáng Temple in Cháng'ān,
there was a peony plant
that, during the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
produced 2,100 flowers.
Their colors included zhèngyùn and dàoyùn,
light,
deep red and purple,
yellow, white, and sandalwood, among others,
but lacked deep red.
Moreover, none of the flowers had leaves without a central streak.
Double-layered flowers.
Some had flower faces measuring seven to eight cùn in diameter.
Héhuān Peonies
At the Sùshī Courtyard of the Xìngshàn Temple in Cháng'ān, the peonies
were exceptionally beautiful in color.
At the end of the Yuánhé era,
a single branch produced héhuān flowers.
Dyeing Peony Flowers
During the Táng dynasty, Hán Wéngōng Yù
had a distant nephew
who came from Jiānghuái.
He was very young,
and Hán ordered him to study in the academy alongside the other youths.
However, the youths were all bullied and humiliated.
When Hán found out,
he sent him to a monastery on West Street,
ordering him to study there.
After about ten days,
the monastery abbot complained again about his wild and unruly behavior,
so Hán immediately ordered him to return,
and scolded him, saying:
"Even the lowly classes in the marketplaces,
who strive for food and clothing,
still have at least one skill or strength.
With your behavior like this,
what will you ultimately become?"
The nephew bowed in apology.
Then he slowly said:
"I have a skill,
but I regret that you, uncle, are unaware of it."
Pointing to the peonies in front of the steps, he said:
"Uncle, if you want these flowers to be blue, purple, yellow, or red,
it is entirely up to your command."
Hán was greatly astonished,
and provided him with what he needed to test it.
The nephew then set up a curved bamboo screen,
completely covering the peony bushes,
so that no one could peek inside.
He dug around the plant on all sides,
deep to its roots,
wide enough for a person to sit.
Using only zǐkuàng, qīngfěn, and vermilion,
he treated the roots morning and night.
After seven days,
he filled in the pit.
He told his uncle:
"It will take about a month for the roots to adjust."
It was early winter at the time,
and the peonies were originally purple.
When they bloomed,
their colors were yellow and red, with distinct edges.
Each flower bore a couplet of poetry,
with characters in clear purple,
which turned out to be the first rhyme from Hán's poem when he left the pass,
saying:
"Clouds bar the Qín Ridge—where is my home?
Snow blocks the Blue Pass—my horse will not go forward"—fourteen characters in total.
Hán was greatly amazed.
The nephew then bid farewell and returned to Jiānghuái,
ultimately unwilling to pursue an official career.
Uprooting Peonies
In Cháng'ān, the nobility admired peonies
for over thirty years.
Every late spring,
carriages and horses would rush about frantically,
and it was considered shameful not to join in the enjoyment.
Temples and monasteries outside the Jīnwú patrol areas
planted them for profit,
with a single plant sometimes worth tens of thousands.
At the end of the Yuánhé era,
when Hán ordered his nephew to come to Cháng'ān,
and there were peonies in his private residence,
he immediately ordered them to be uprooted.
He said:
"How could I imitate women and children?"
Osmanthus flowers
The Laurel,
its leaves resemble those of the cassia.
Its flowers are pale yellow,
with four petals.
The stamens are green,
and when in full bloom, the flowers resemble persimmon calyxes.
They are found in Jiǎngshān.
Mǔguì Flower
The Mǔguì,
its leaves are as large as those of the bitter bamboo.
In the center of the leaf, there is a vein resembling a brushstroke.
The calyx has three petal-like sepals,
each tip forked into two branches.
Its surface is pale yellow,
and near the fork, it is light red.
The flower has six petals,
white in color.
The pistil protrudes like a lychee.
Its branches are purple.
It is found in the mountains of Wùzhōu.
The Cassia Flower,
blooms in the third month,
yellow but not white.
The poems of Dàyǔ all praise the cassia for enduring the sun,
and Zhāng Qǔjiāng's poem "The cassia flowers are bright and pure in autumn"
is erroneous.
Sea Pomegranate Flower
Xīnluó has many sea reds and sea pomegranates.
Táng Dynasty minister Lǐ Déyù said,
flowers with "sea" in their names
all come from the eastern seas.
Zhāngchuān flowers somewhat resemble sea pomegranates,
clustered in groups of five,
with narrow, long leaves,
layered and overlapping.
Southern Sea Hibiscus
In the Southern Sea, hibiscus blooms all year round,
and the flowers are often in bloom.
However, on a single plant,
no more than ten or twenty flowers bloom at once.
Moreover, they do not bloom as densely as in paintings,
in lush and profuse clusters.
Lǐngbiǎo Hibiscus
The hibiscus of Lǐngbiǎo,
its stems and leaves resemble those of the mulberry tree.
The leaves are glossy and thick.
The taller plants
reach only four or five feet,
yet their branches and leaves are lush and spreading.
From the second month, they begin to flower,
and continue until midwinter before ceasing.
The flowers are deep red,
with five petals,
like large hollyhocks.
There is a single stamen,
longer than the petals,
tipped with golden specks,
which shimmer in the sunlight,
as if aflame.
On a single cluster,
hundreds of flowers bloom each day,
though abundant, they are vibrant,
and though close, they lack fragrance.
They fall at dusk and bloom again at dawn.
Cuttings take root easily,
hence the name "jǐn."
Local women also gather and sell them,
a single coin buys several dozen flowers.
Without these flowers,
red plums would lack their vivid color.
Red Hibiscus Flower
The red hibiscus of Língnán,
blooms continuously from the first month to the twelfth month,
though somewhat less in autumn and winter.
Nàtí hibiscus flowers,
purple in color,
with double-layered leaves.
The outer leaves curl inward,
and from the center, a stem emerges,
over an inch tall.
The leaf tips split into five lobes,
like a calyx.
The lobes contain purple stamens,
and the stem bears yellow pistils.
Fúsāng Flower
In Mǐnzhōng, there are many Fúsāng trees.
Their branches and leaves resemble those of the mulberry,
except the twigs are curved.
The flower buds resemble paulownia flowers,
about an inch long when closed,
appearing like double-layered structures.
Some flowers are also pale yellow.
In the southern regions, paulownia flowers come in deeper colors.
Zhēntóng Flower
The Zhēntóng,
produces reddish-yellow shoots from the branch tips,
which grow in opposite pairs,
forming three layers.
The flowers are as large as eggplant flowers,
yellow in color.
A single stem bears fifty or sixty flowers.
Gardenia Flower
Few flowers have six petals,
only the gardenia has six petals.
Táo Zhēnbái
said:
"The gardenia's cut flowers have six petals,
and the calyx is divided into seven segments."
Its fragrance is intense,
and it is said to be the Chànpú of the Western Regions.
Camellia Flower
The camellia,
its leaves resemble those of the tea plant,
and taller ones reach over ten feet.
The flowers are over an inch wide,
and crimson in color.
They bloom in the twelfth month.
Three-Colored Photinia Flower
The photinia flowers of Héngshān
come in purple, blue, and white.
The flowers are as large as peonies.
Some plants do not bear flowers.
Bǐlǘ Flower
The Bǐlǘ flower of Báizhōu,
its blossoms resemble feathers.
When its wood is cut for firewood,
the fire lasts all day without dying out.
Mùlián Flower,
its leaves resemble those of the magnolia,
and its flowers are lotus-colored.
Found in Míngyù Creek,
Ángzhōu also has them.
Nàjiā Flower,
resembling the three springs,
leafless,
with white blossoms,
yellow centers,
and six petals.
It is found on ships.
Magnolia Flower
In the home of a commoner in Dūnhuà Lane, Cháng'ān,
during the Tàihé era of the Táng Dynasty,
there was a magnolia tree,
with deep red flowers.
Later, the caretaker of the residence of Guìzhōu observation commissioner Lǐ Bó
bought it for five thousand coins.
The residence was north of the river.
After a year,
the flowers turned purple.
Exotic Tree Flower
Táng Dynasty Duke Wèi, Lǐ Déyù,
once obtained an exotic tree,
which bore purple flowers in spring.
I consider that among trees, only the magnolia
blooms once a year.
Green Rose
Flower sellers in Luòzhōng
say that deep in Sōngshān,
there are green roses.
But now they are extinct.
The Erythrina variegata flower does not resemble the depictions in paintings.
Its wood is used as timber.
During the third and fourth months,
its leaves spread densely,
followed by red flowers.
Occasionally, three to five clusters grow among the leaves,
unlike those in paintings.
Red blossoms fill the tree,
The Huáifēng flower
In the Lèyóu Garden, wild rose trees grow naturally.
Below them are many alfalfa plants.
They are also called Huáifēng.
Some people of the time referred to them as Guāngfēng.
The wind among them is often crisp,
and when the sun shines on the flowers, they gleam with brilliance.
Hence, they are named "alfalfa Huáifēng."
People from Màolíng call them Liánzhī grass.
The Azalea flower
In the southern regions, flowers are mostly red,
which is also the color of that land.
Only the azalea stands out.
They are occasionally found north of the mountains,
but not as abundantly as in the south.
They grow all over the valleys.
When they bloom in the second month,
they shine like fire.
This lasts for over a month without ceasing.
The Chinese trumpet creeper flower
The dew on the Chinese trumpet creeper flower
harms people's eyes.
The branched lotus
During the reign of Emperor Míng of the Hàn Dynasty,
there was a branched lotus in the pond,
with one stem and four leaves,
resembling a joined canopy.
Its seeds were like black pearls,
suitable for adorning pendants.
The night-blooming lotus
During the reign of Emperor Líng,
there was a night-blooming lotus,
with one stem bearing four lotuses.
Its leaves unfurled at night and curled during the day.
The water lily
Water lily.
In the South Sea, there are water lilies,
whose flowers lower into the water at night.
The green lotus flower
During the Xuānpíng era,
Grand Tutor and Chancellor Lú Gōng,
while preparing for the imperial examinations,
resided in a villa in Ānfēng County, Shòuzhōu.
Once, while visiting Sháobēi,
he saw a local carrying firewood,
holding a green lotus flower.
Lú Gōng was astonished and asked about it.
The person replied:
"I found it in the pond."
Later, Lú Gōng served in Zhèxī.
While on a mission to Huáifú,
he mentioned this to Grand Commandant Wèi Gōng, Lǐ Déyù.
Lǐ Déyù ordered a search of Sháobēi,
but nothing was found.
They also searched extensively along the riverbanks,
but ultimately could not find it.
Thus, they realized that the single flower from before
must have been a divine marvel.
The dyed green lotus flower
During the Táng Dynasty, Hán Wéngōng Yù's nephew
had a peculiar method of cultivating flowers.
The story is recorded in minor tales.
When Dù Jǐshì Rúxiū governed
Húzhōu,
there was a dyeing household
whose pond produced green lotus flowers.
The prefectural governor ordered the lotus seeds to be collected and sent to the capital,
where they were planted in ponds.
Some turned into red lotuses,
which was considered strange.
He then wrote to inquire with the dyer.
The dyer replied:
"My family has been
dyeing in indigo vats for three generations.
We often soak lotus seeds at the bottom of the vats
and wait for a year or more
before planting them.
If we plant the seeds of the green lotus flowers,
they turn red.
This is simply a return to their original nature—
what is so strange about it?"
He then sent the soaked lotus seeds to him.
Taoist Shēn Kuāngtú
also observed someone mixing chicken droppings with soil
to fertilize peony bushes,
causing the light red ones to become deep red.
This further confirms the effect of dyeing.
When the false Shǔ king Wáng Xiānzhǔ was about to pass away,
that year,
the sal trees on Mount Éméi
all bloomed with white flowers.
Also, a few years before King Jīng Wénxiàn passed away,
the canals and moats
were all filled with white lotuses.
One case was dyed by the influence of qi,
while the other signaled an ill omen—
what doubt is there?
Three auspicious lotus flowers
When the false Shǔ ruler usurped the throne,
the meritorious nobles and officials
competed to build grand mansions.
Only the false Zhōnglìng Zhào Tíngyǐn
built the South and North Residences.
With thousands of beams and arches,
their extravagance and beauty
were unmatched.
Behind them, they bordered the river,
and the pond contained two islands.
Stone embankments were built along the pond,
and all four banks were planted with weeping willows,
interspersed with hibiscus trees.
Lotus roots were planted in the pond.
Every summer and autumn,
flowers bloomed and fish leaped.
Under the shade of the willows,
there were scholars holding scrolls,
anglers with fishing lines,
those holding ruyi scepters,
those holding horsetail whisks,
and others discussing poetry and philosophy.
One day, at a bend of the bank,
a single lotus stem
split into two branches,
bearing two flowers.
At that time, it was called an era of peace and prosperity,
and men and women, fragrant and adorned,
came in great numbers to view it.
Zhào Tíngyǐn had it painted and presented it to the ruler,
who admired and praised it.
Many sang and composed poems about it.
Not long after,
in the imperial garden, a lotus stem
split into three flowers.
The Shǔ king held a banquet
and summoned his ministers to admire it.
At that time, all the literary officials
presented poems.
Some enthusiasts of the time
depicted it in paintings,
which have been passed down to this day.
Lotus root
When Sūzhōu presented lotus roots,
the finest were called "injured lotus root."
Some say
it is the name of the lotus;
others say
the sweet leaves were injured by insects;
or that
the leaves were intentionally injured
to promote root growth.
Recently, many double-layered lotuses have appeared,
with flowers growing from the seeds,
which is also quite extraordinary.
Lotus Seeds
Stone lotus seeds sink in water,
only boiling in alkaline brine can make them float.
Wild geese eat them,
and their droppings fall in the mountains,
remaining intact for a hundred years.
It is said that acorns falling into water become lotus seeds.
Water Caltrop
The water caltrop is also called water vegetable,
and also called xiǎntái.
In Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's Kūnmíng Pond,
there were floating-root water caltrops,
whose roots emerged above the water,
while their leaves sank beneath the waves,
also called green water caltrops.
In Xuándū, there were water caltrops,
jade-green in color,
shaped like flying chickens,
named fānjī water caltrops.
The immortal Fú Bózǐ often gathered them.
Water caltrop,
nowadays people only speak of líng and jì.
Various explanations in botanical texts
also do not distinguish them.
Only Wǔ Ānpín's "Wǔlíng Records"
states that those with four corners are called jì,
and those with two corners are called líng.
Nowadays, the zhéyāo water caltrops in Sūzhōu mostly have two corners.
In Jīngzhōu, there was a monk
who gave Duàn Chéngshì a peck of Yǐngchéng water caltrops,
triangular and without spines,
which could be rubbed and kneaded.
Zhājiàjiù Tree Fruit
In the great eastern wilderness,
there is a tree
named zhājiàjiù.
Zhā
refers to the pear;
jià
refers to the stalk;
jiù,
means intimate.
It blooms at three thousand years,
and bears fruit at nine thousand years.
Its flower stamens are purple,
and its fruit is red.
It is also a hundred zhang tall,
or even a thousand zhang.
Its branches spread out to support themselves.
The branches in the east, west, south, and north directions
each extend nearly fifty zhang.
Its leaves are seven chǐ long,
and five chǐ wide.
Their color is like green-blue,
and the bark is like catalpa.
The wood grain is like licorice,
and its taste is sweet.
The fruit is nine chǐ long,
and its circumference matches its length,
with no pulp or pit.
When cut with a bamboo knife,
it is like congealed honey.
If one eats it,
and sees the fruit again,
it disappears.
It is said that if one sees the fruit again after it ripens,
one's lifespan will be twelve thousand years.
Rúhé Tree Fruit
In the great southern wilderness,
there is a tree
named rúhé.
It blooms at three hundred years,
and bears fruit at nine hundred years.
Its flowers are vermilion,
and its fruit is bright yellow.
It is fifty zhang tall,
spreading out like a canopy.
Its leaves are one zhàng long,
and over two chǐ wide,
resembling jiānzhù,
and green in color.
They are five fēn thick.
They can be used for padding,
like thick magnolia bark.
The wood grain resembles zhī.
It has nine seeds,
tasting like sweet syrup.
The fruit has a pit,
shaped like a date.
The seeds are five chǐ long,
with a circumference matching their length.
If cut with a metal knife, it turns sour;
if cut with a reed knife, it becomes pungent.
Those who eat it become terrestrial immortals,
unafraid of water and fire,
unafraid of sharp blades.
Immortal Pear
In the south, there is a tree
a hundred zhàng tall,
spreading out to support itself.
Its leaves are one zhàng long,
and six chǐ wide.
It is called a pear.
Like today's pear trees,
but the tree is larger.
Its fruit is three chǐ in diameter,
and when cut open, it has little pulp,
white as plain silk.
If eaten in a soup, one becomes a terrestrial immortal,
with clothes that never wear out,
able to abstain from grains,
and can enter water and fire.
Qǐgǎo Tree Fruit
In the southeastern wilderness, there is an evil tree
three thousand zhàng tall,
sometimes over ten arm-spans around,
or seven to eight chǐ.
Its branches grow straight upward,
unyielding.
Its leaves are like sweet melons,
lasting three hundred years.
They fall and give rise to flowers,
shaped like sweet melons.
The flowers last another two hundred years,
then fall and give rise to calyxes.
Beneath the calyxes, fruit grows,
maturing in three years.
After maturing,
it neither grows nor diminishes.
The fruit is shaped like a winter melon,
similar to a wax gourd,
seven to eight cùn long,
four to five cùn in diameter.
The calyx grows again atop the fruit.
It is said that the calyx develops and the fruit matures.
If not harvested,
it remains unchanged for ten thousand generations.
If the fruit is taken but the calyx left,
the calyx will bear fruit again.
As before, it matures month by month.
After another two years, it forms a calyx again,
which then bears fruit again.
The fruit is shaped like a sweet gourd,
slightly refined and sweet.
Eating it
makes one's body radiant.
One must not exceed three shēng,
or it will cause deep intoxication,
waking only after half a day.
The tree is tall,
and people cannot reach it to harvest.
Only the duōluó people beneath the tree,
by climbing, can obtain it.
It is also called wúyè.
Later generations of people,
not seeing its leaves,
call it leafless.
It is also called qǐgǎo.
People, seeing it leafless,
call it qǐgǎo.
Bōnàpó Tree Fruit
During the Yonghuī era of the Táng dynasty,
a man named Wáng Fāngyán from Wángguó Village, Línhuáng County, Wèi Commandery,
once found a small sapling
on a riverbank shoal
and planted it.
When it grew up,
it turned out to be a línqín tree.
Its fruit was as large as a small yellow gourd,
white as jade,
dotted with pearl-like spots.
There were not many spots,
only three or so,
resembling tie-dye patterns.
It was truly a marvelous fruit.
Bright and lustrous to the eye,
it was also exceptionally delicious.
Jìwáng Lǐ Shèn, serving as Prefect of Cáo Prefecture,
obtained some and presented them to the prince.
The prince then offered them to Emperor Gāozōng,
who considered them to be red crabapples,
also called five-colored línqín,
or sometimes "linked pearl fruit."
They were planted in the imperial gardens.
An elderly monk from the Western Regions saw them and said:
"This is a marvelous fruit, also called línqín."
The emperor greatly valued it,
bestowing upon Wáng Fāngyán the title of Wénlínláng,
and also naming this fruit the Wénlínláng fruit.
Commonly, it is called píngpó fruit.
Línqín trees are also abundant in Hédōng,
and not few in Qínzhōng either.
In the various commanderies west of the river,
línqín trees also grow.
All are smaller than the Wénlín fruit.
Sacred Crabapples
At Língyán Temple by Fènglín Pass in Hé Prefecture,
every year on the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
sacred crabapples flow out from a stream cave,
as large as a cup.
This is considered normal.
Wooden Peach
The larger variety of peach is called the wooden peach.
As the Book of Songs says, "They gave me a wooden peach" — this refers to it.
Dōngfāng Village Peach
In Dōngfāng Village, there is a peach tree.
Its fruit measures three feet two inches in diameter.
Cooked with the pit into a soup and eaten,
it can increase one's longevity.
Eating the kernel inside the pit
can cure coughing.
Small peaches are warm and moist;
if someone with a cough eats them, it stops immediately.
Immortal Peach
It comes from Sū Dān's immortal altar in Chēn Prefecture.
If someone sincerely seeks it,
peaches will fall onto the altar.
Sometimes as many as five or six fruits.
They resemble stone lumps in shape,
reddish-yellow in color.
When broken open,
it seems there are three layers of pits.
Grind and drink it,
and it cures various illnesses.
It is especially effective against evil influences.
Gōu Peach
The gōu peaches from the Huálín Gardens in Yè,
weigh three catties,
or sometimes two and a half catties.
There are also famous pears.
Compared to other fruits, their flavor is sweet and delicious,
melting in the mouth upon eating,
renowned among people as famous fruits.
Jì Lóng made crab carts,
with four compartments one zhàng wide,
and one zhàng deep,
filled with soil to plant them in,
and none failed to grow.
One-Dàn Peach
The peach of the Tǔyùhún,
is as large as a stone jar.
Biǎn Peach
The biǎn peach comes from Persia,
where Persians call it pódàn.
The tree grows five or six zhàng tall,
with a girth of four or five chǐ,
leaves resembling peach leaves but broader and larger.
It blooms in the third month,
with white flowers.
After the flowers fall, it bears fruit,
shaped like a peach but flattened.
Its flesh is bitter and astringent,
not fit to eat.
The kernel inside the pit is sweet.
The various countries of the Western Regions all treasure it.
Queen Mother Peach,
found within the Huálín Gardens in Luòyáng.
It ripens only in the tenth month.
Shaped like a guālóu fruit.
A common saying goes:
"The Queen Mother's sweet peach,
eating it relieves fatigue."
Also called the Queen Mother of the West Peach.
Eating Walnut
At the home of Wú Yáoqīng, the Liúhòu of Yáng Prefecture,
there was a hired laborer.
Having worked for him a long time,
one day,
he brought a large walnut,
capable of holding several shēng,
and presented it to Yáoqīng.
Yáoqīng, knowing it was unusual,
gradually ground it and ate it.
After finishing it,
he felt quite light and vigorous.
Yáoqīng, as an official,
was greedy, corrupt, cruel, and oppressive.
During the troubles of Bì Shīduó,
he threw himself into the well behind his residence and died.
Shīduó sought someone resembling Yáoqīng and killed him.
Later, someone who acquired his former residence,
secretly learned that his corpse was in the well,
retrieved and obtained it.
The entire body had rotted away,
but within the internal organs, some had turned into gold.
Sháozi Fruit
In Chūníng County, there is the shíyúzi fruit,
also called mountain jujube,
and sometimes referred to as sháozi.
Luófú Mandarin
The Luófú mandarin,
during the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
was first planted by a mountain monk at Nánlóu Temple.
Later, it was presented as tribute.
In the year the emperor fled to Shǔ and Fèngtiān,
none bore fruit.
Tiānbǎo Mandarin
In the tenth year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
the emperor said to his favored ministers:
"Recently, several mandarin trees were planted within the palace,
and this autumn they bore one hundred and fifty fruits,
no different from those presented from Jiāngnán and the Shǔ region."
The chief ministers congratulated in a memorial, saying:
"Where rain and dew spread evenly,
they blend with the heavens and are bestowed alike.
Plants and trees have their nature,
relying on the earth's energy to subtly connect.
Thus, we obtain the precious fruit from beyond the river,
becoming splendid produce within the forbidden palace."
It is traditionally said
that in the year Emperor Xuánzōng fled to Shǔ,
the Luófú mandarins did not bear fruit.
In Lǐngnán, there are ants,
larger than the horse ants of Qínzhōng,
that build nests on mandarin trees.
When the fruit is ripe,
they crawl over it,
so the mandarin skin becomes thin and smooth.
Often, mandarins are found within the nests,
retrieved in deep winter.
Their flavor is several times better than usual.
Northern Jujube
In the northern wilderness,
there is a jujube forest.
The trees are fifty zhang tall,
their branches spreading out for several li.
Strong winds cannot bend them,
thunder and lightning cannot destroy them.
Their fruit is six or seven cun long,
with a circumference greater than its length.
When ripe, its color is like vermilion.
When dried, it does not shrink.
Its flavor and aroma are moist and glossy,
different from ordinary jujubes.
Eating it can calm the body and boost qi.
Therefore, the medical texts say:
"The branches of this jujube
are more abundant than ordinary jujubes,
and it also boosts qi and calms the body."
Chìsōngzǐ said:
"The northern great jujube has a unique flavor,
it can both boost qi and calm the body."
Xīwángmǔ Jujube
In the Yè Huálín Garden, there is the Xīwángmǔ jujube.
It has leaves in both winter and summer,
flowers bloom in the ninth month,
and it ripens in the twelfth month.
Three fruits grow per chi.
There is also the Guījiǎo jujube,
also with three fruits per chi.
Immortal Jujube
During the Jìn dynasty,
south of the Tàicāng was Díquán,
and to the west was the Huálín Garden.
In the garden, there was the Immortal Jujube.
It is five cun long.
Its pit is as fine as a needle.
Zhòngsī Jujube
Xìndū presented four hundred branches of Zhòngsī jujube.
The jujube is four to five cun long,
purple in color,
with skin
wrinkled and a fine pit.
The flesh
is plump and flavorful,
superior to Qīngzhōu jujubes.
During the Northern Qí dynasty,
an immortal named Zhòngsī obtained this jujube
and planted it.
It is also called the Immortal Jujube.
At that time, there were only a few trees in the entire land.
Persian Jujube
The Persian jujube comes from Persia.
In Persia, it is called Kūmǎng.
The tree is three to four zhang tall,
with a circumference of five to six chi.
Its leaves resemble those of the tǔténg vine,
and they do not wither.
Flowers bloom in the second month.
They look like plantain flowers.
The flower has two bracts,
which gradually split open,
revealing over ten chambers inside.
The fruit is two chi long,
yellow-white in color,
with a pit.
When ripe, it turns purplish-black,
resembling a dried jujube.
Its taste is sweet like maltose,
and it is edible.
Cherry
During the Táng dynasty, newly appointed jìnshì
particularly valued the Cherry Banquet.
In the fourth year of Qiánfú,
Liú Yè's third son, Tán, passed the imperial examination.
At that time, Yè, as a former chancellor, was governing Huáinán.
He instructed the estate official:
"Use one ingot of silver to fund the banquet."
However, Tán's expenses often exceeded this several times over.
The estate official reported this,
and Yè simply ordered that he be given enough funds.
When the time came for offering the new harvest,
the top candidate and those below
were just discussing how to pool funds.
Tán secretly sent people
with ample gold and silk
to purchase dozens of trees in advance.
Thus, he alone hosted this banquet,
inviting many high officials.
At that time, cherries had just appeared in the capital,
and even the noble and wealthy had not yet tasted them.
Yet Tán piled them high on mats,
and mixed them with sugar and yogurt.
Each guest was served a small plate,
which contained no less than several shēng.
Even the attendants and servants
all had their fill.
Rú Jujube
At the home of Zhào Yíng of the Jìn dynasty,
there was a Rú jujube tree in the courtyard,
exceptionally lush and swaying,
visible from far and wide.
A person skilled in reading qi
visited the neighborhood
and asked people:
"This household is destined to produce a chancellor."
An old man from the neighborhood said:
"No one here fits that.
However, the master's childhood name is Xiàng'ér (相儿),
could it be him?"
The diviner said:
"The royal qi is currently strong,
but it does not reside in him personally;
it will manifest in his descendants."
Later, Yíng rose from a judge in Tàiyuán to high office,
serving as both a general and a chancellor.
Persimmon
It is commonly said that the persimmon tree possesses seven virtues:
first, longevity;
second, abundant shade;
third, no bird nests;
fourth, no insects;
fifth, its frost-touched leaves are pleasing to behold;
sixth, excellent fruit;
seventh, its fallen leaves are large and thick.
Dǐlì Tree Fruit
Āyì,
in Persia it is called Āyì,
in Fúlín it is called Dǐlì.
The tree is fourteen or fifteen zhàng tall.
Its branches and leaves are luxuriant.
The leaves have five lobes,
resembling hemp leaves.
It bears fruit without flowering.
The fruit is red,
similar to a louse's egg.
Its taste resembles dried persimmon,
and it ripens once a year.
Persimmon Root Plate
Among woods, the persimmon root is the most solid,
it is the firmest,
commonly called the persimmon root plate.
Róng Peak Pear
The Immortal Pear.
On Róng Peak, there is a green altar,
five zhàng square.
There is a place for burning incense and practicing the Way.
Several ancient bronze vessels.
There is a pear tree.
Thirty zhàng tall,
with fruit as large as a dou measure.
When the fruit falls,
one only sees its juice and pit,
no one gets to taste it.
Six-Jīn Pear
The pear from the Bàoguó Temple in Luòyáng
weighs six jīn.
Purple Flower Pear
During the Qingtai era,
I traveled to the capital.
I once gathered with Patrol Officer Lú Yǒng, Doctor Zhèng Yǐ, Monk Jìyǎ,
and a few close friends,
for a night gathering at the Yuèbō Dī monastery.
It was late in the clear autumn,
with the bright moon high in the sky.
We composed ingenious five-character couplets,
and drank fine wine like the Eight Immortals.
There were newly reddened persimmon slices,
and strong, tender green tea leaves.
With each chant, a cup was raised;
some were sober, others drunk.
Seated there, we began to discuss matters ancient and modern,
eventually touching upon the subject of fruits.
Someone mentioned the purple-flowered pear.
The group said:
"It exists in Zhēndìng."
Only Venerable Yǎ frowned and said:
"This is a lingering regret of my humble monk's ancestor."
Everyone was startled and asked him.
Yǎ said:
"In the fifth year of Emperor Wǔzōng's reign over the empire,
affairs of state were numerous,
and the imperial mind was not at ease.
Suddenly, he fell ill with a feverish heart ailment.
Famous physicians offered medicine,
but the illness did not heal.
So a broad summons was issued for skilled men,
seeking far and wide for healers like Hé and Huǎn.
At that time, someone spoke of a Taoist priest Xíng from Qīngchéng Mountain,
who was superb in prescriptions and medicines.
The emperor summoned him for an audience.
The priest took two green elixir pills from a green pouch at his elbow,
and also fetched several pears,
squeezed their juice, and presented them.
The emperor's illness soon recovered.
Within ten days,
he was rewarded with ten thousand in gold,
and additionally granted the title 'Broadly Beneficial Master'.
The emperor leisurely asked what the elixir was made of.
The Master said:
'On the summit of Chìchéng Mountain,
there are two stalks of green fungus.
In the southern stream of Tàibái,
there is one tree of purple-flowered pear.
In my past years,
I once traveled to these two mountains,
and by chance obtained these two treasures,
which I combined and refined into this elixir.
Over the past fifty years,
I have taken them almost completely,
leaving only these two pills,
which fortunately Your Majesty has now consumed.
If you desire more of this elixir,
you must seek these two things again.'
After several months,
Master Xíng took leave of the emperor and returned to the mountains.
Later, the illness recurred,
and the emperor again summoned Master Xíng from Qīngchéng,
but he was nowhere to be found.
The emperor then issued an edict throughout the land,
that wherever there was a purple-flowered pear,
it should be reported immediately.
At that time, the Military Commissioner of Héngzhōu, Grand Commandant Wáng Dá,
was married to Princess Shòuchūn,
the younger sister of Emperor Huìchāng.
Hearing that Magistrate Lǐ of Zhēndìng
had planted several pear trees,
one of which was a purple-flowered pear,
he immediately dispatched a eunuch
to go and seal it off for inspection,
cutting down the surrounding trees,
and encircling it with a vermilion railing.
They treasured even its slender branches,
as if they were branches of the moon cassia.
When the tree was in bloom,
to prevent bees and butterflies from peeking and damaging it,
they would always cover it from afar
with light silk gauze.
The tree keepers endured immense hardship.
When autumn brought fruit,
the princess would personally select and present them.
When these reached the imperial court,
only six or seven out of ten remained.
The emperor ate many of these pears.
Although they were not as good as Master Xíng's,
they still somewhat relieved his irritability.
At that time, there was a Palace Censor Lǐ Zūn,
serving as a Records Officer in Héngzhōu,
who composed a 'Memorial Presenting Pears' which said:
'Where purple flowers bloom,
they excel in beauty in spring woods.
When pale stems
hang,
they shine distantly in autumn scenes.
Lush and jade-moist,
scattered like round pearls.
Their sweetness needs no
tasting,
their crispness is almost too much for the mouth.'
When the memorial reached the palace,
the ministers and high officials who saw it
mostly laughed heartily and said:
'Why does the Duke of Chángshān present leftover pears to the imperial court?'
This was because his memorial contained the words 'crispness is almost too much for the mouth'.
The following year,
Emperor Wǔzōng passed away,
and the princess also died soon after.
Since then, this pear became a regular tribute item.
Over the years, the local officials
gradually grew negligent in its precious guardianship.
By the end of the Tiānyòu era,
when King Zhào was
usurped and assassinated by Dé Míng,
afterwards, the county offices and government buildings
experienced much warfare.
The purple-flowered pear tree
also withered and decayed.
In present-day Zhēndìng,
there are no longer any successors cultivating it.
During Emperor Wǔzōng's time,
the county magistrate, Lord Lǐ,
named Shàng,
was Yǎ's grandfather.
Once, due to careless guarding of the tree,
a branch was broken by the wind.
He was demoted to a minor official in Jìzhōu.
This is why, recalling this, he frowned with regret."
Hazelnuts
Pistachios grow in western countries.
Foreigners say they are on the same tree as hazelnuts:
one year hazelnuts,
the next year pistachios.
Wild Jujube
According to elders' tales,
during the Zhōu and Qín periods,
wild jujubes rained down in Hénán,
and thus wild jujube trees grew.
This is the present-day Suānzǎo County.
The very small jujubes
are wild jujubes.
Grapes
It is commonly said that grapevines tend to spread towards the southwest.
Yǔ Xìn said to the Wèi envoy Yù Jǐn:
"When I was in Yè,
I obtained many grapes,
extraordinarily flavorful."
Chén Zhāo asked:
"What shape are they?"
Xú Jūnfáng said:
"They resemble soft dates."
Yǔ Xìn said:
"You really don't understand things well;
why not say they resemble fresh lychees?"
Wèi Zhàoshī said:
"Emperor Wǔ of Wèi once said,
'From late summer into autumn,
lingering heat remains.
When one is drunk or hungover,
picking them dew-covered and eating them,
they are sweet but not cloying,
sour but not sharp.'
Merely speaking of them makes one's mouth water in wonder,
let alone actually eating them?"
Yù Jǐn said:
"This fruit originates from Dàyuān,
brought by Zhāng Qiān.
There are three types: yellow, white, and black.
When ripe,
the fruits press closely together,
arranged like stars, clustered like pearls.
In the Western Regions, they are often fermented into wine,
and offered as annual tribute.
In the Western Capital of Hàn,
they also seem to have been plentiful.
In Dùlíng, within fifty mǔ of fields,
there were a hundred grapevines.
Now in the capital region,
they are not limited to the forbidden forests."
Yǔ Xìn said:
"They are planted in gardens and by households,
their shade connecting, their trellises linked."
Chén Zhāo said:
"How does their taste compare to citrus and pomelos?"
Yǔ Xìn said:
"Their juice is more wondrous,
but their fragrance is less."
Yù Jǐn said:
"Golden skin, white flesh,
packaged as tribute,
melting upon the teeth—
they truly must be incomparable."
The Queen Mother's Grapes
South of Jùqiū,
there is a Grape Valley.
The grapes in the valley
can be eaten on the spot.
If anyone tries to take some away,
they immediately lose their way.
It is said by the world to be the Queen Mother's grapes.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
the monk Tán Xiāo,
while traveling among the sacred mountains,
came to this valley
and obtained grapes to eat.
He also saw a dried vine suitable for a staff,
as thick as a finger,
over five chǐ long.
He took it back to his temple
and planted it, whereupon it revived.
It grew several rèn tall,
shading an area of ten zhàng,
and looking up, it resembled a canopy.
Its fruits hung in clusters,
purple and glistening like pendants.
People of the time called it the "Grass Dragon Pearl Canopy."
Hóu Sāozi
The Hóu Sāo vine grows,
its fruit like chicken eggs,
both sweet and cool,
lightening the body and dispelling the effects of wine.
The "Guǎngzhì" says it was presented by the Grand Coachman Wáng.
Vine Walnut
The vine walnut comes from Nánzhào,
as large as a flat snail,
with two compartments,
and tastes like a walnut.
Some say it is the vine fruit of the southern barbarians.
Immortal Tree Fruit
On the Qílián Mountains, there is the fruit of an immortal tree.
Travelers who obtain it
can stop hunger and thirst.
It is also called the Four-Flavored Wood.
Its fruit is like a jujube.
If cut with a bamboo knife, it is sweet;
if cut with an iron knife, it is bitter;
if cut with a wooden knife, it is sour;
if cut with a reed knife, it is pungent.
Olive
The single-rooted tree:
the branch facing east is called Mùwēi;
the branch facing south is called Gǎnlǎn.
Eastern Wilderness Chestnut
In the eastern wilderness, there is a tree
named chestnut.
It has a shell,
three chǐ and three cùn in diameter.
The shell's spines are over a zhàng long.
The nut is three chǐ in diameter.
The shell is also yellow,
its taste sweet,
but eating it
causes shortness of breath and thirst.
Monkey Chestnut
Táng Duke Wèi Lǐ Déyù
once held a gathering for guests in his sweet orange garden.
On the tray were monkey chestnuts,
which were tasteless.
The recluse Chén Jiān said:
"South of Qiánzhōu, there are jiàn chestnuts,
shaped like plain kernels."
Melon
Hàn Emperor Míng's consort, Noble Lady Yīn,
dreamed of eating a melon,
which was extremely delicious.
The emperor sent envoys to seek it from various states.
At that time, Dūnhuáng presented a strange melon seed,
and Chángshān presented a giant peach pit.
It was named Qiónglóng,
three chǐ long and curved in shape,
its smell like fermented grain.
The elders said:
"Long ago, a Daoist obtained this melon from Pénglái Mountain,
saying it was the Hollow Spiritual Melon.
It bears fruit once every four kalpas.
The Eastern King and the Queen Mother left its seed on earth,
generations far removed,
yet its fruit still exists."
It is also said:
"This peach blossoms only after frost,
and ripens in deep winter."
It is also said:
"Eaten by immortals,
it is often planted in the Frost Forest Garden.
This garden is planted entirely with cold fruits;
in the season of accumulated ice,
all fruits are at their peak.
Commonly called the 'Xianglíng Melon'.
Thus, 'Frost Garden' is a corruption of the name."
The Empress said:
"The Queen Mother's peach,
the Eastern King's melon—
if one could obtain and eat them,
one would live fifty thousand years.
How could they be eaten?"
After the Empress passed away,
attendants saw melon and peach pits in her dressing mirror case.
Looking at them, they shed tears,
doubting they were of ordinary kind.
Five-Colored Melon
During the time of King Huán of Wú,
five-colored melons grew in Kuàijī.
Now in the Wú region, there are five-colored melons,
offered yearly as tribute.
Melons detest fragrance,
especially musk.
Táng's Zhèng Zhù,
in the early Tàihé era,
was traveling to take up his post in Hézhōng.
He had over a hundred concubines,
all riding,
their fragrance wafting for several lǐ,
assaulting people's noses.
That year,
from the capital to Hézhōng,
along the roads they passed,
all the melons died,
not a single fruit was obtained.
Turnip
Wherever Zhūgě [Liàng] stationed,
he ordered soldiers to plant only turnips,
