because they can be eaten raw as soon as they sprout—first reason;
one;
their leaves can be boiled and eaten when spread out—second reason;
two;
when staying long, they propagate and grow—third reason;
three;
if abandoned, no need to regret them—fourth reason;
four;
upon return, they are easily found and gathered—
fifth reason.
In winter, the roots can be dug up and eaten—
sixth reason.
Compared to other vegetables,
are its benefits not vast indeed?
Liú Yǔxī said:
"Truly so."
The people of the Three Shǔ
now call turnips 'Zhūgě vegetable'.
It is the same in Jiānglíng.
Yuè Garlic
"The Garden of Marvels" says:
In Jìn'ānpíng, there is the King of Yuè's leftover garlic vegetable,
over a chǐ long,
the white parts resembling bone,
the black parts like horn.
It is anciently said:
The King of Yuè once used them for counting on a boat,
and the leftovers
were thrown into the water, where they grew.
Three Vegetables
In the fourth year of the Xiánníng era of the Jìn Dynasty,
a fragrant garden was established east of the Jīnyōng City,
where many rare vegetables were planted,
named Yúnwēi.
There are three varieties.
The purple variety is the most prolific.
Its roots are luxuriant.
It flourishes in spring and grows densely in summer,
blooms in autumn and remains fragrant in winter.
Its fruits are like pearls,
in five colors,
thriving according to the season.
It is also called Yúnzhī.
The purple variety is considered the superior vegetable,
with a pungent taste;
the yellow variety is the medium vegetable,
with a sweet taste;
the green variety is the inferior vegetable,
with a salty taste.
This vegetable was often used to supply the imperial court,
and its leaves could be used to wrap food and drink,
for ancestral temple sacrifices.
It also alleviates hunger and thirst.
In the palace, those who plucked its stems and leaves
did not cease for months.
Bōléng
The Bōléng vegetable
originally came from a Western country where a monk
brought its seeds from there,
like alfalfa and grapes,
which arrived due to Zhāng Qiān.
Bōléng originally came from the Pōlíng country,
but the name was corrupted in speech,
which many do not know.
Jièzū
The people of Guǎngzhōu use giant mustard
to make salted pickles,
burying them in the ground,
some for up to thirty years.
They are highly valued,
and given as gifts among relatives and friends.
Jièmò
Zhǎngzhōng jièmò is produced in many countries.
Take its seeds and place them in the palm,
blow on them,
and with each blow, they grow,
reaching three chǐ in length,
then plant them in the ground.
Shuǐjiǔ
Shuǐjiǔ grows by the water's edge,
resembling leeks but with slender leaves.
It is edible.
Qiézi Tree
In the southern regions, grasses and vegetables
do not wither in winter,
so in vegetable gardens,
eggplants are planted,
with roots surviving for two or three years,
gradually growing branches and trunks,
becoming large trees.
Every summer and autumn when ripe,
ladders are used to pick them from the trees.
After three years,
the trees gradually age and bear fewer fruits,
so they are cut down,
and young ones are replanted.
Kūnlún Purple Melon
In the late Dàyè era of Emperor Suí Yáng,
eggplants were renamed Kūnlún Purple Melon.
Eggplant Stories
Eggplant.
The character "qié,"
refers to the stem and fruit together,
pronounced "géxiá" in reverse.
Now called "qié,"
its origin is unknown.
Once, Duàn Chéngshì happened to eat several eggplants under the corridor
and casually asked the Ministry of Works Vice Director Zhāng Zhōufēng about eggplant stories.
Zhāng said,
it is also called Luòsū.
The details are recorded in the "Materia Dietetica."
Chéngshì remembered the poem "Walking in the Garden" by Yǐnhóu:
"Cold melons lie along the ridges,
autumn melons fill the slopes.
Purple eggplants bloom in profusion,
green taro plants stand unevenly."
It is also called Kūnlún Melon.
In Lǐngnán, eggplants
grow from perennial roots into trees,
five or six chǐ tall.
Yáo Xiàng once served as a southern selection envoy,
and saw this personally.
Thus, the "Materia Medica" records that Guǎngzhōu has the Shěnhuǒ tree,
with a trunk three or four arm-spans thick.
Shěnhuǒ is Jǐngtiān,
commonly called Hùhuǒ grass.
Ripe eggplants,
when eaten, strengthen the stomach and intestines,
but may stir energy and cause illness.
The roots can treat turtle-like sores.
To make the fruits abundant,
wait until flowering time,
take leaves and spread them on the path,
marking them with ash,
and when people step on them,
the fruits will surely be abundant.
This is commonly called "marrying the eggplant."
Once roasted over fire,
it is very delicious.
There is a variety from Xīnluó,
slightly white in color,
shaped like a chicken egg.
In the Xuán courtyard of the Xīmíng Temple monks,
this variety exists.
The "Water Classic" says:
"West of Shítóu faces Càipǔ,
a hundred lǐ long,
upstream is the Dàdí Dípǔ,
downstream is the Qié Pǔ."
Dānyá Gourd
In Dānyá, gourds are grown to maturity,
each typically weighing over a shí.
Mustard plants,
the tall ones also reach five or six chǐ.
The seeds are as large as chicken eggs.
Describing Bamboo Varieties
"Bamboo Manual":
There are thirty-nine varieties of bamboo.
Tì Bamboo
In the southern wilderness, there is Tì bamboo,
hundreds of zhàng tall,
three zhàng six chǐ in circumference,
eight or nine cùn thick.
It can be used to make boats.
Its shoots are very delicious,
and when boiled and eaten,
can stop sores and scabies.
Jí Bamboo
Jí bamboo, also called Bā bamboo,
has thorns on every joint,
with dozens of stems forming a clump.
Southern barbarians plant it to form walls,
making them impossible to attack suddenly.
Sometimes, roots burst forth on their own,
as large as wine jars,
crisscrossing and supporting each other,
resembling a reeling machine.
If eaten,
it causes hair loss.
□ Lè Bamboo,
thin-skinned and hollow,
the largest does not exceed two cùn in diameter,
with rough patterns on the skin,
can be made into files.
For filing armor,
it is sharper than iron.
If it becomes dull,
pour jiāngshuǐ over it,
and it will regain its sharpness.
Hànjīng Bamboo,
as thick as a toe,
with white membranes inside separating sections,
like wet dough.
Before fully grown and while the sheath has not fallen off,
tiny insects often gnaw at it,
creating red marks,
resembling embroidery, lovely to behold.
The Cízhú (慈竹),
during summer rains,
drips sap onto the ground,
which produces a fungus,
resembling deer antlers,
white in color.
Eating it
cures dysentery.
The Jīnzhú (筋竹),
in the south is used to make spears.
When its shoots have not yet become bamboo,
they can be made into crossbow strings.
The Bǎiyèzhú (百葉竹),
has a hundred leaves on one branch.
It is poisonous.
The Táozhīzhú (桃枝竹)
in Dōngguānjùn (東官郡),
which during the reign of Emperor Shùn of Hàn belonged to Nánhǎi,
borders Gāoliángjùn (高涼郡) to the west,
and also had its territory designated as the office of the Sījiān Dūwèi (司監都尉).
To the east there is wasteland,
to the west it borders the vast sea.
There is a Chángzhōu (長洲),
with many Táozhīzhú (桃枝竹),
growing along the banks.
The Yǐngzhú (癭竹)
In the scenic area of Dōngluò (東洛) there are three streams,
Zhāng Wénguī (張文規) had an estate near the stream.
Suddenly, a bamboo stalk grew a gall,
as large as a plum.
Luófú Bamboo
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
a salt worker violated the ban,
and fled into Luófúshān (羅浮山).
He went deep into the thirteenth ridge,
encountered tens of thousands of giant bamboo stalks,
stretching continuously through the cliffs and valleys.
The circumference of the bamboo was over two zhàng,
with thirty-nine nodes,
about two zhàng in length.
The fugitive then took one bamboo stalk,
split it to make strips.
When an amnesty was granted,
he carried it back with him.
Someone obtained one strip,
found it remarkable,
and presented it to the prefect Lǐ Fù (李复).
He then drew a picture and recorded it.
I once read the "Zhú Pǔ" (竹譜) which says:
"The Dìzhú (帝竹) of Yúnqiū (云丘),
one node can make a boat."
How magnificent indeed!
In Nánhǎi, those who use bamboo for steamers,
commonly seen,
are all Luófú bamboo.
Tóngzǐsì (童子寺) Bamboo
Táng dynasty Lǐ Wèigōng (李衛公) said:
In the northern capital, only Tóngzǐsì had one clump of bamboo,
barely a few chǐ tall.
It was said that the temple's administrator,
reported daily on the bamboo's safety.
Bamboo Flowers
"Shānhǎijīng" (山海經) says:
When bamboo produces flowers,
it withers that same year.
Bamboo changes its roots every sixty years,
changing roots necessarily leads to flowering,
bearing fruit and then dying.
The seeds fall and regenerate,
forming a grove in six years.
The seeds form ears,
resembling wheat.
Bamboo Zhú (箹)
Bamboo that dies again is called Zhú (箹).
It changes roots every sixty years,
changing roots then leads to bearing fruit and dying.
Bamboo Seeds
In the year Jiǎzǐ of the Tiānfù era of the Táng dynasty,
from Lǒng (隴) westward,
reaching the region of Bāoliáng (褒梁),
for several thousand lǐ there was severe drought,
and many people scattered in exile.
From winter through spring,
the starving people ate plants and trees,
to the extent that there were many cases of people eating each other's flesh.
That year,
suddenly, bamboo in the mountains, regardless of size,
all bloomed and bore seeds.
The starving people gathered them,
pounded them into rice and ate them,
valuing them more than regular or glutinous rice.
The seeds were coarse,
reddish-brown in color,
no different from today's red rice,
their flavor even more fragrant.
The people of several prefectures,
all brought their families into the mountains,
to feed on them.
Within the streams and mountains,
dwellers were as numerous as in a market,
those with the means
competed to set up granaries and store them.
There were not a few households with surplus grain,
and those who took them and ate them together with meat and vegetables,
vomited.
As if poisoned,
nine out of ten died.
The bamboo,
from then on, in countless ravines and valleys,
all immediately withered.
Ten years later,
this gentleman (bamboo) grew again.
It can be said that millions of heads,
were kept alive under these virtuous bamboos.
Raining Rice
During the time of Xià Yǔ (夏禹),
heaven rained rice.
An ancient poem says:
"How can we get heaven to rain rice,
to feed all the people under heaven."
Raining Millet
In the third year of Empress Lǚ (呂后),
in Qínzhōng (秦中), heaven rained millet.
Raining Wheat
During the time of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
in Guǎngyángxiàn (廣陽縣), it rained wheat.
Diāohú (雕葫)
By the Tàiyìchí (太液池),
there were all things like Diāohú (雕葫), Zǐtú (紫蘀), Lǜjiépúcóng (綠節蒲叢) and the like.
The Gū (菰) that bears grains,
people of Cháng'ān call Diāohú;
the Jiālú (葭蘆) whose leaves have not yet unfurled,
they call Zǐtú;
the Gū that has a head,
they call Lǜjié.
Among them, ducklings,
filled and crowded the area.
There were also many purple turtles and green turtles.
The pond's edge had much flat sand,
on the sand were pelicans, kingfishers, and egrets.
Wild ducks and geese,
moved about in flocks.
Raining Grain
During the time of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
in Jiānghuái (江淮) there was famine,
people ate each other.
Heaven rained grain for three days.
Soon, a report from Wèi territory stated,
two thousand qǐng of grain had been lost.
Yáozhīsù (搖枝粟)
In the first year of the Dìjié era of Emperor Xuān of Hàn,
to the east of Lèlàng,
there came people from a country called Bèimíng,
presenting local products as tribute.
They said their homeland lay east of Fúsāng,
where they saw the sun rise from the west.
Their country was perpetually dim and dusky.
It was suitable for the five grains,
and was named Róngzé,
covering an area of three thousand lǐ.
All five grains there were excellent;
eating them prolonged life,
and just one grain could cleanse the stomach.
One could go for years without hunger.
There was the Shaking-Branch Millet,
so named because its stalks were long and weak,
constantly swaying even without wind.
Eating it benefited the marrow.
There was the Phoenix-Crest Millet,
resembling the crest of a phoenix bird.
Those who ate it gained great strength.
There was the Wandering-Dragon Millet,
with twisting, curved branches and leaves,
like a roaming dragon.
There was Qióng Gāo,
white in color like silver.
Eating these two types of millet
made one's bones feel light.
There was the Ràomíng Bean,
so called because its stems were weak
and entangled with each other.
There was the Sword-Holding Bean,
named because its pods resembled a person holding a sword
and grew diagonally.
There was the Qīnglí Bean,
so called because its leaves would droop and cover the ground upon seeing the sun.
Those who ate it would not age or fall ill.
There was the Yánjīng Wheat,
said to prolong life and boost energy.
There was the Kūnhé Wheat,
which harmonized and regulated the six bowels.
There was the Qīngxīn Wheat;
those who ate it felt physically light.
There was the Chúnhé Wheat;
its flour was used to brew wine,
and one drunkenness could last for months.
Eating it made one feel no cold even in deep winter.
There was the Hánlù Wheat,
with dew inside the grains,
sweet as malt sugar.
There was the Zǐchén Hemp,
whose seeds did not float.
There was the Yúnshuǐ Hemp,
with seeds that were cool and glossy,
suitable for making oil.
There was the Guāngtōng Hemp;
those who ate it could walk without needing a torch—
this was the Jùshèng (sesame).
Eating it prolonged life,
allowing one to die only after reaching a very old age.
Grains Raining from the Sky
During the time of King Wú Huán,
in Jīnlíng, grains rained down upon the homes of the poor,
but not upon the homes of the wealthy.
Wild Millet and Stone Grain
At the beginning of Emperor Gāozǔ of Sòng's reign,
following the famine at the end of the Jìn dynasty,
after he ascended the throne,
wild millet grew across more than two thousand lǐ south of the Yangtze.
Moreover, Stone Grain grew on various mountains in Huáinán—
grain that grew on stone.
Yuán Ān said
Stone Grain is a medicinal name,
referring to the especially small-eared variety.
Taro
Heavenly Taro grew in the Zhōngnán Mountains,
with leaves like lotus leaves but thicker.
Sparrow Taro
resembled a sparrow's head.
Placed on dry ground, it became damp;
placed in a damp spot, it became dry.
Birds touching it would fall,
and animals encountering it would stiffen.
Sugarcane
In the southern mountains, there were forests of gānzhè.
They were a hundred zhàng tall,
with a circumference of three chǐ and eight cùn.
Their nodes were close together and they were very juicy,
sweet as honey.
Chewing its juice
made one's skin moist and smooth.
It could also expel roundworms.
Roundworms in the human abdomen
resemble earthworms.
They are grain-digesting worms.
Too many harm the person,
too few and grain is not digested.
Thus, sugarcane can reduce the excess and supplement the deficiency.
All sugarcane is like this.
On Tea
The names and varieties of tea are numerous.
In Jiànnán, there is Méngdǐng Shíhuā,
either in small squares or as loose buds,
considered the finest.
In Húzhōu, there is Gùzhǔ's Purple Shoots;
in Dōngchuān, there are Shénquán and Chāngmíng;
in Xiázhōu, there are Bìjiàn, Míngyuè, Fāngruǐ, and Zhūyúliáo;
in Fúzhōu, there is Fāngshān's Raw Buds;
in Kuízhōu, there is Xiāngshān.
In Jiānglíng, there is Nánmù;
in Húnán, there is Héngshān;
in Yuèzhōu, there is Yìhú's Hángāo;
in Chángzhōu, there is Yìxīng Purple Shoots;
in Wùzhōu, there is Láibái;
in Mùzhōu, there is Jiūkēng;
in Hóngzhōu, there is Xīshān Báilù;
in Shòuzhōu, there is Huòshān Huángyá;
in Qízhōu, there is Qímén Tuánhuáng.
The merchants of Fúliáng are not included here.
Obtaining Divine Tea
The "Shényì Jì" records:
Yú Máng of Yúyáo
went into the mountains to pick tea
and met a Daoist priest
leading three hundred blue sheep
to drink from a waterfall.
The priest said:
"I am Dānqiūzǐ.
I have heard you are skilled in tea drinking
and have often wished to bestow a favor.
In these mountains, there is great tea
that I can provide you.
I hope that someday, if you have a surplus in your cup,
you will remember to leave some for me."
Thereupon, a tea shrine was established.
Later, he often went into the mountains with others
and obtained great tea there.
Offering Tea and Receiving Reward
Liú Jìngshū's "Yìyuàn" records:
The wife of Chén Wù of Shànxiàn
was widowed young with two sons
and was fond of drinking tea.
Because there was an ancient tomb in her residence,
each time she drank tea,
she would first make an offering to it.
Her two sons complained, saying:
"What does the tomb know?
It only wastes effort to make offerings."
They wanted to dig it up and remove it.
Their mother苦苦 forbade them and stopped them.
That night,
the mother dreamed of a person who said:
"I have rested in this tomb for over three hundred years.
Your two sons constantly wish to see it destroyed,
but I rely on your protection.
Moreover, you offer me fine tea.
Though I am but decayed bones beneath the springs and soil,
how could I forget the repayment at Yìsāng?"
At dawn,
they found one hundred thousand coins in the courtyard,
as if long buried,
only the strings were new.
The mother told her two sons.
The two sons were ashamed.
From then on, their prayers and libations became even more devout.
Tea for Digestion
In the Táng dynasty, a man was appointed governor of Shūzhōu.
Lǐ Déyù said to him,
"When you arrive at that commandery,
the tea from Tiānzhù Peak,
you could kindly send me three or four packets."
That person presented him with several dozen catties.
Lǐ did not accept it,
and returned it.
The following year, he was dismissed from the commandery.
Applying careful intent in his search,
he obtained a few packets,
and presented them.
Déyù was pleased and accepted them.
He said:
"This tea can neutralize the toxins of wine and food."
He then ordered one bowl to be brewed,
poured it over meat dishes,
and sealed it with a silver container.
The next morning, upon opening and inspecting it,
the meat had already turned into water.
All were convinced of his extensive knowledge.
Bamboo Mushroom
In Liáng Jiǎnwén's Yánxiāng Pavilion,
in the tenth year of Dàtóng,
the bamboo grove produced a mushroom.
It was eight inches long,
its cap resembling the fruit of the foxnut,
and black in color.
Its stem resembled a lotus root stem,
hollow inside.
The skin and substance were pure white,
with a slight red at the base.
The foxnut fruit-like part resembled a bamboo node,
and it could be detached, then detached again.
From the node, another layer grew separately,
like a woven net,
on all four sides,
about five or six inches around,
encircling it completely,
covering the stem.
They were spaced apart and did not touch.
It resembled a net with many strands,
light and delicate, lovely.
Both it and the stem could be detached.
Consulting immortal texts,
it resembled the Wēixǐ Mushroom.
Tower Mushroom
During the Suí dynasty's Dàyè era,
inside the Yǒngkāng Gate east of the Huìchāng Gate in the Eastern Capital,
one hundred and twenty stalks of mushroom grass grew,
scattered on the ground,
covering about ten paces around.
Some had purple stems and white heads,
others white stems and black heads.
Some had branches,
others did not.
There were also those with three branches,
like the ancient character "出".
The roots in the ground were like threads,
broadly connected to each other.
East of the Qiányáng Hall,
on a locust tree by the east upper gate tower,
nine stalks of mushroom grew,
sharing a common base and supporting each other as they grew.
The central stalk was the longest,
with eight stalks on both sides,
gradually shorter in sequence,
resembling a tree gate tower.
They were very pure white.
Military General Duàn Wéncāo, left in charge,
had them depicted and reported to the throne.
Celestial Worthy Mushroom
In the early Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
a man named Lǐ Jiā in Línchuān Commandery,
had a mushroom grow on a pillar of his dwelling,
shaped like a Celestial Worthy.
Governor Zhāng Jǐngyì cut it off and presented it.
Purple Mushroom
In the eighth year of Dàlì of the Táng dynasty,
a purple mushroom grew in Lújiāng County, Lúzhōu,
fifteen feet tall.
There are very many types of mushrooms.
Joined Mushroom,
broken yet can rejoin.
Nightlight Mushroom,
one plant with nine fruits.
The fruits fall to the ground like seven-inch mirrors.
Viewed at night, they resemble ox eyes.
Máo Jūn planted them on Jūqǔ Mountain.
Hidden Dawn Mushroom
Hidden Dawn,
shaped like a dipper,
with stars as nodes,
and stems as a net.
Phoenix Brain Mushroom
The "Immortal Classics" say:
Dig six feet into the ground,
plant a single piece of circular treasure,
water it with five gě of yellow water,
and tamp the earth firmly.
After three years,
a seedling grows like a gourd,
with fruits like peaches,
in five colors.
It is called Phoenix Brain Mushroom.
Eat its fruit,
spit on the ground to create a phoenix,
and ride it to ascend to the Supreme Ultimate.
White Talisman Mushroom,
blooms white during heavy snow.
Five Virtues Mushroom,
resembles carriages and horses.
Stone Cassia Mushroom,
grows in mountain rock caves,
resembling a cassia tree but with stone fruits.
Tall like a large tape measure,
shiny and pungent in taste,
with branches.
Pound and consume it,
one catty grants a thousand years.
Dripping Mushroom
In the Shǎoshì stone chamber,
there is a deep valley,
impossible to cross.
If you throw a stone into the valley,
you can still hear the sound half a day later.
About ten zhang outside the chamber entrance,
there is a stone pillar,
on the pillar is a reclining cover stone,
spanning south about one zhang in diameter.
Looking at it,
honey mushrooms drip from the stone onto the reclining cover,
after a long while,
there is always a drip,
like rainwater leaking behind a house,
falling occasionally.
Yet the honey mushrooms drip incessantly,
and the reclining cover also drips continuously.
On the chamber entrance, characters are carved in tadpole script,
saying:
"Whoever obtains and consumes one dǒu of stone honey mushroom,
will live ten thousand years."
Various Daoist priests together pondered that place,
but could not go there.
The only way was to place a bowl on the end of a sturdy bamboo or wood pole,
to catch it.
Yet ultimately, no one was able to do it.
According to this, the inscription on the chamber entrance is like this,
so it must have existed in previous ages.
Wood Mushroom
Wood Mushroom refers to
pine and cypress resin sinking into the ground for a thousand years,
transforming into poria cocos;
after ten thousand years,
on it grows a small plant,
shaped like a lotus flower,
called Wood Wēixǐ Mushroom.
It glows when viewed at night,
and feels very smooth when held.
It does not char when burned.
Carrying it wards off weapons.
If you attach it to a chicken,
and mix it among twelve chickens in a cage,
step twelve paces away from that spot,
and shoot twelve arrows,
the other chickens will all be injured,
but the one carrying the Wēixǐ Mushroom,
will ultimately not be harmed.
Firefly Mushroom
On Liángcháng Mountain there is the Firefly Mushroom,
which is actually a plant,
the size of a bean.
It has purple flowers,
and when viewed at night, it glows.
Eating one of them
illuminates the central cavity of the heart.
Eating up to seven
makes all seven orifices of the heart transparent and clear.
One can then write at night.
Flesh Mushroom
Once, someone moored his boat, went ashore,
and suddenly saw among the reeds
over ten Kūnlún figures lying down,
their hands and feet all moving.
Startled, he reported it to the boatmen.
One of the boatmen, who had traveled on the sea before, recognized them
as mushrooms.
Going to look at them,
he found their heads all connected to the ground.
He cut them off and ate them,
but the mushrooms simply lacked the seven orifices.
The Bàopǔzǐ states:
"Flesh Mushrooms resemble human form,
and are produced from the earth."
These are also of that category.
What is there to be surprised about?
Dwarf Mushroom
Sometimes, in the mountains, one sees dwarves
riding in carriages or on horseback,
seven or eight inches tall—
these are Flesh Mushrooms.
If one obtains and consumes such a mushroom,
one immediately becomes an immortal.
Underground Flesh Mushroom
Xiāo Yìrén of Lánlíng,
his given name lost,
once sat for the imperial examinations but failed.
He then burned his books,
secluded himself by the Tánshuǐ River,
and followed a Daoist priest to learn the ways of immortality.
Thus, he abstained from grains and practiced breath absorption,
every morning stretching and bending his limbs,
hoping to prolong his life.
After more than ten years,
his hair had all turned white,
his complexion withered and his back hunched,
with some teeth having fallen out.
One day, looking at himself in a mirror,
he suddenly became furious,
and said:
"I abandoned fame and profit,
hid myself in the fields and wilderness,
abstained from grains and practiced breath absorption,
hoping to attain longevity.
Now I have become so frail and emaciated—
is this what I intended?"
He immediately returned to live in Yèxià,
learning from merchants to pursue the profit of one-tenth.
After several years,
his wealth and resources became abundant,
and he became a rich man.
Later, while renovating his garden house,
he dug up something from the ground,
shaped like a human hand,
plump and moist,
slightly reddish in color.
Startled upon obtaining it, Yìrén said:
"Could this be the sprout of misfortune?
Moreover, I have heard that where the Tàisuì resides,
one must not undertake earth-moving projects.
If one violates this,
fleshy growths will appear beneath,
which is certainly inauspicious.
Now it has indeed appeared—
what should I do?
However, I have heard:
if one obtains such flesh and eats it,
one might avoid disaster."
Thereupon, he cooked and ate it;
the flavor was very delicious,
and he ate it all.
From then on, Yìrén's hearing and sight became sharp,
his strength grew even more robust,
and his appearance became increasingly youthful.
The bald spots on his head
all grew thick, dark hair;
the teeth that had fallen out
also grew back, perfectly aligned.
Yìrén silently found it strange,
but dared not tell anyone.
Later, a Daoist priest came to Yèxià
and met Yìrén.
Startled, he said:
"Sir, have you perhaps taken an immortal's elixir?
Why is your spirit and energy so clear and bright?"
The Daoist priest then felt his pulse.
After a long while, he added:
"Sir, you have eaten a Lingzhī mushroom.
That Lingzhī is shaped like a human hand,
plump and moist,
and slightly reddish in color."
Yìrén realized what had happened
and told him.
The Daoist priest congratulated him, saying:
"Sir, your lifespan
can now match that of tortoises and cranes.
However, you should not remain in the mundane world;
you should retire to the mountains and forests,
abandon human affairs,
and immortality can be attained."
Delighted, Yìrén followed his advice
and departed.
In the end, no one knew where he went.
Strange Mushroom
In the spring of the first year of the Kāichéng era of the Táng dynasty,
in front of the study at Duàn Chéngshì's residence in Xiūxíng Lane,
there were several withered purple vetch trees, decayed and broken,
so he cut them down,
leaving about a foot of stump.
By the autumn of the third year,
a mushroom grew on the withered root,
as large as a dou measure,
with five legs spreading beneath,
a yellow and white mottled cap,
and a green hanging skirt,
like a goose [□],
over a foot tall.
By winter,
it turned black and died.
When burned,
its scent was like that of sweetgrass.
Chéngshì once placed an incense burner on a platform of wormwood while reciting scriptures,
and asked a monk about it.
The monk considered it a good omen.
Later, reading various accounts of anomalies:
In the Southern Qí dynasty, Chǔ Sīzhuāng of Wújùn Commandery,
devoutly followed Buddhism.
He slept under a beam,
the short pillar of which was made of nán wood,
over four feet from the ground,
and had a knot.
During the Dàmíng era,
suddenly something like a mushroom
grew on the knot,
bright yellow in color,
gradually growing.
After several days,
it took the form of a thousand Buddhas.
Their faces, eyes, fingers, claws, halos, and robes
were all vividly complete,
as if embossed in gold,
and felt exceptionally soft to the touch.
It fell at the end of spring,
and when it fell, the Buddha forms remained as before,
only the color had turned brown.
When it fell,
his family stored it in a box.
After five years,
Sīzhuāng no longer lived beneath it,
nor were there any other notable signs of prosperity.
Yet his entire family lived to old age:
Sīzhuāng's father died at ninety-seven;
his elder brother was seventy,
and as healthy as a man in his prime.
Stone Mushroom
On Pògǎng Mountain in Pútián County, Sòngzhōu,
in the second year of Emperor Wǔzōng of the Táng dynasty,
a mushroom grew on a giant rock,
as large as a joined basket,
with stem and cap yellow-white.
Its underside was light red.
It was entirely eaten by passing monks.
They said:
its flavor was many times better than other mushrooms.
Zhúròu (Bamboo Flesh).
In the Jiānghuái region, there is zhúròu,
like pellets,
tasting like white chicken.
In Dài,
there is also dàshùjī (Great Tree Chicken),
like a cup.
It is called húmítóu (Barbarian Monkey Head).
Lúshān has shí'ěr (Stone Ear),
which has a hot nature.
Dújùn (Poisonous Mushroom)
In Jiāngxià, Hànyáng County produces poisonous mushrooms,
called rúlǘ.
They are not máosōu.
Every year, they are offered as tribute.
The county officials often send people to wait in the fields;
if such mushrooms appear,
they immediately set up a marker to warn people,
who dare not pass downwind,
to avoid their fumes.
On the day of harvesting,
they use a bamboo pole to cut them down,
quickly dropping the pole to the ground,
as the poison enters the bamboo.
It immediately bursts open.
Only after the poison dissipates,
do they cover their hands with beech and willow bark to collect them,
wrap them in felt,
and again wrap them heavily in beech and willow bark.
The county magistrate seals and forwards them.
The laborers who transport them
are paid double the usual rate,
because along the way they are often poisoned by the fumes,
resulting in headaches.
Zhāng Kāng, who accompanied his father as magistrate of Hànyáng,
recounted this in detail.
For those poisoned by wild mushrooms and laughing uncontrollably,
boil fish and mulberry juice and drink it,
and they will recover.
This was told by Monk Guāngyuǎn.
Tái (Moss)
Táiqián (Moss Coin) is also called zékuí (Marsh Mallow),
also known as dǒngqiáncǎo (Dong Coin Grass),
also called xuānxuǎn,
and southerners call it gòucǎo (Grime Grass).
Dìqián (Ground Coin),
has round leaves and thin stems,
with vines,
often growing by streams and ravines.
Also called jīxuěcǎo (Snow Accumulation Grass),
or liánqiáncǎo (Linked Coin Grass).
Mànjīntái (Creeping Golden Moss)
The state of Lí presented mànjīntái to Jìn.
Its color is like gold,
like gathered fireflies,
as large as a chicken egg.
When thrown into water,
it spreads over the waves,
shining under the sunlight,
as if fire were born on water.
So, a pond was dug in the palace,
a hundred paces wide,
to often view this moss,
to delight the palace ladies.
When a palace lady was favored,
she was given golden moss.
Placed in a lacquer bowl,
it illuminates the entire room,
and was called yèmíngtái (Night-Shining Moss).
When attached to clothing, it glows like firelight.
The emperor, fearing outsiders might obtain it,
and dazzle the common people,
ordered the moss removed and the pond filled.
Even during the royal turmoil,
this thing still existed.
All went into the barbarian lands.
Rújùtái (Like Lettuce Moss)
Behind the eaves of the Táng Sānzàng Hall in Cí'ēn Temple,
at the end of the Kāichéng era,
there was moss shaped like ancient lettuce,
spread over the bricks,
blue-green in color,
light, soft, and lovely.
The monk Yìlín recounted that,
at the beginning of the Tàihé era,
when reburying Master Jī,
upon first opening the tomb,
a fragrance assailed people.
He lay on his side on a brick platform,
looking as if alive.
The moss on the bricks was over two inches thick,
golden in color,
with a scent like burning sandalwood.
Shífà (Stone Hair)
Zhāng Chéng said,
in the southern waters, there is a plant on the bottom,
like shífà.
It begins to grow on the third or fourth day of each month,
and can be harvested after the eighth or ninth day.
By month's end,
it all rots away.
It seems to flourish and decay with the moon.
Wǎsōng (Tile Pine)
The "Guǎngyǎ" says:
"On roofs, it is called xīyē;
on walls, it is called yuányī."
The "Guǎngzhì" calls it lánxiāng.
It grows on old roof tiles.
Emperor Míng of Wèi favored it,
and ordered tiles from Cháng'ān to be transported west
to Luòyáng,
to cover roofs.
In poems by later poets,
"xīyē" is often used.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Liáng wrote in "Ode to the Rose":
"Covering the steps with green silk,
reflecting xīyē under the eaves."
Some say that when there are many pine saplings on wooden structures,
and the earth and wood qi leaks,
then pines grow on tiles.
During the Dàlì era,
when repairing the Hányuán Hall,
a man submitted a request for tiles,
claiming only he could tile.
His grandfather had once tiled this hall,
and the other workers were not convinced.
So he said:
"Can any of you tile without wǎsōng growing afterward?"
Only then did the others yield.
There was also Lǐ Āhēi,
who could also treat
roofs,
laying tiles like teeth,
with no gaps between,
and no wǎsōng grew.
The "Běncǎo" says:
"Wǎyī is called wūyóu."
Wǎsōng Fù (Rhapsody on Tile Pine)
Cuī Róng's "Rhapsody on Tile Pine · Preface" says:
"The wǎsōng of the Chóngwén Hall grows
under the roof eaves.
To call it a tree,
consulting mountain dwellers yields no details;
to call it grass,
checking Shénnóng's records finds rare mention."
The rhapsody says:
"Resplendent and uniquely elegant,
like golden mushrooms growing from eaves.
Clearly suspended in emptiness,
like star elms planted in heaven.
Flowers and branches lush and abundant,
roots and base coiled and linked.
Amidst purple moss, drenched in dew,
rising above green tiles, veiled in mist."
It also says:
"Ashamed before the crows grieving in Wèi palace,
abashed before the red lotuses of Hàn halls."
Lord Cuī was learned and broad,
omitting nothing,
so how could he not know wǎsōng already had explanations?
Chámáxiāng (Tea Rose Incense)
During the time of King Zhāo of Yān,
there was the state of Bōyì,
which offered chámáxiāng as tribute.
If burned on clothing,
the fragrance lasts a full month without fading.
Wherever it passes,
soil and stones become fragrant.
Rotten wood and decayed grass touched by it flourish anew.
Used to fumigate dried bones,
muscles and flesh regenerate.
Sānmíngxiāng (Three Names Incense)
Hàn Yōngzhòngzǐ presented incense products from the Southern Sea,
and was appointed as Fúyáng Commandant,
which people at the time called the Incense Commandant.
Rìnán Commandery had an incense market,
a place where merchants traded various incenses.
Nánhǎi Commandery had village incense households,
and Rìnán Commandery had a thousand-acre incense forest,
from which famous incenses were produced.
Xiāngzhōu was located in Zhūyá Commandery,
and the islet produced various rare incenses,
often of unknown names.
Thousand-year pine incense could be smelled from ten lǐ away,
and was also called sānxiāng.
Wǔmíngxiāng
Jùkūzhōu was located in the Western Sea.
Shēnwèi,
On the islet there was a great tree.
It resembled a maple tree,
but its leaves were fragrant,
and could be smelled from several hundred lǐ away.
This was named the Soul-Returning Tree.
If one knocked on the tree,
the tree could also produce sound by itself.
The sound was like the roar of an ox,
and those who heard it would all feel their hearts shaken and spirits alarmed.
If its root core was cut,
and the sap boiled in a jade cauldron,
then further heated over fire,
it became like black maltose,
and could be made into pills.
It was named Jīngjīngxiāng,
or called Zhènlíng Wán,
or called Fǎnshēngxiāng,
or called Rénniǎo Jīngxiāng,
or called Quèsǐxiāng.
One substance with five names.
This was a spiritual object,
its fragrance could be smelled from several hundred lǐ away,
and if a corpse lay on the ground,
upon smelling its scent, it would revive.
Chénxiāng
Emperor Táng Tàizōng asked the leader of Gāozhōu, Féng Àng:
"How far is your residence from chénxiāng?"
He replied:
"Incense trees grow right around my residence,
but the living ones have no fragrance,
only the decaying ones begin to be fragrant."
Lóngnǎoxiāng
The lóngnǎo incense tree,
comes from the country of Pólì.
In Pólì it is called Gèbùpólǜ.
It also comes from the country of Bōsī.
The tree is eight or nine zhàng tall,
and about six or seven arm-spans around.
Its leaves are round and white on the back,
and it bears no flowers or fruit.
The trees can be fat or lean,
the lean ones produce pólǜ paste.
The fragrance is in the heartwood,
the tree is cut through the middle,
split open and taken,
the paste flows out from the tree's end,
and a hollow is cut in the tree to collect it.
For medicinal use,
there are separate methods.
Ānxīxiāng
The ānxī incense tree,
comes from the country of Bōsī.
In Bōsī it is called Bìxié.
The tree grows to three dà,
its bark is yellow-black.
The leaves have four corners,
and do not wither through the cold.
It flowers in the second month,
yellow in color,
with a slightly green center.
It bears no fruit.
If its bark is cut, a resin like maltose emerges,
called ānxīxiāng.
In the sixth and seventh months it hardens and solidifies,
and is then harvested.
Burning it communicates with the divine,
and wards off all evils.
One tree with five incenses:
the root is zhāntán,
the nodes are chén,
the flowers are jīshé,
the leaves are huò,
the resin is xūnlù.
Hēlí Lè
Gāo Xiānzhī attacked Dàshí,
and obtained hēlí lè,
five or six cùn long.
Initially placed in his belly-wrap,
he immediately felt abdominal pain,
and consequently had over ten bouts of swift diarrhea.
At first he thought the hēlí lè was causing mischief,
and therefore wanted to discard it.
He asked an elder of Dàshí,
the elder said,
"If a person carries this object,
all illnesses are eliminated,
and diarrhea expels foul matter."
Xiānzhī treasured it greatly.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era he was executed,
and subsequently its whereabouts were lost.
Báidòukòu,
comes from the country of Jiāgǔluó,
called Duōgǔ.
Its shape is like a banana plant.
Leaves resemble dùruò,
eight or nine chǐ long,
not withering in winter or summer.
Flowers are light yellow.
The seeds grow in clusters,
like grapes.
When the seeds first emerge,
they are slightly green,
ripening then turns them white.
Harvested in the seventh month.
□ Qíxiāng,
comes from the country of Bōsī,
in Fólín called Dǐngbólítā.
One zhàng long,
about one chǐ in circumference.
Bark is green,
thin and extremely smooth and clean.
Leaves resemble āwèi,
with three leaves growing at the end of each branch.
No flowers or fruit.
People of the Western Regions often cut it in the eighth month.
By the twelfth month,
new shoots sprout again,
extremely lush and vigorous,
if not pruned,
they wither and die.
If branches are cut in the seventh month,
there is a yellow sap,
its appearance like honey.
Slightly fragrant.
Placed in a jar,
it treats all illnesses.
Wúshízǐ,
comes from the country of Bōsī.
In Bōsī called Mózéi.
The tree is six or seven zhàng tall,
eight or nine chǐ in circumference.
Leaves are like peach leaves but longer.
Flowers in the third month,
white in color,
flower centers slightly red.
Seeds round like pellets,
initially green,
ripening turns them yellow-white.
Those with holes from insect eating are fully ripe.
Those with unperforated skins,
are used in medicine.
The tree bears wúshízǐ one year,
and bálǚzǐ the next year.
As large as a finger,
three cùn long,
with a shell on top.
The kernel inside is like chestnut yellow,
edible.
Zǐfēi
The Purple Fēi Tree,
originates from Zhēnlà Kingdom.
In Zhēnlà it is called Lèqū.
It also originates from Bōsī Kingdom.
The tree grows to a height of one zhàng,
its branches and twigs are lush and dense.
Its leaves resemble those of the orange tree,
and they do not wither through the winter.
In the third month it blooms,
with white flowers,
and does not bear fruit.
When heavy fog, dew, or rain
moistens its branches and twigs,
purple fēi emerges.
The Bōsī Kingdom envoys Wūhǎi and Shālìshēn,
gave consistent accounts.
The Zhēnlà Kingdom envoy, Commandant of the Assault-Resisting Cavalry Shā,
and the monk Tuóshāníbátuó,
said ants carry soil onto the tree to make nests,
and the ant-tamped earth, receiving rain and dew, congeals,
thus forming purple fēi.
That from Kūnlún Kingdom is superior,
that from Bōsī Kingdom is next.
Āwèi,
originates from Jiāshénà Kingdom,
which is Northern Tiānzhú.
In Jiāshénà it is called Xíngyú.
It also originates from Bōsī Kingdom.
In Bōsī it is called Āyújié.
The tree grows eight or nine zhàng tall,
its bark is bluish-yellow.
In the third month leaves grow,
shaped like mouse ears.
It has no flowers or fruit.
If a branch is broken,
sap flows out like maltose,
which over time hardens and congeals.
The monk Biàn from Fólín Kingdom,
gave a consistent account.
The monk Típó from Mójiētuó Kingdom,
said they take its sap and mix it with rice and bean meal,
combining it to make āwèi.
Bìbá,
originates from Mójiētuó Kingdom,
where it is called Bìbálí.
In Fólín Kingdom it is called Ālíhētā.
The plant grows three or four chǐ tall,
its stem is as thin as a chopstick,
its leaves resemble jí leaves,
its seeds resemble mulberries.
It is gathered in the eighth month.
Hújiāo,
originates from Mójiētuó Kingdom,
where it is called Mèilǚzhī.
Its plant is a vine,
the stem extremely pliant.
The leaves are half a cùn long,
with fine tendrils,
equal in length to the leaves.
On the tendrils seeds form,
in pairs opposite each other.
Its leaves open at dawn and close at dusk,
closing then wraps the seeds within the leaves.
The seed's shape resembles Hàn pepper,
and is extremely fragrant and pungent.
It is gathered in the sixth month.
Nowadays, when making Hú-style platters of meat dishes,
it is always used.
Ābócān,
originates from Fólín Kingdom.
It grows over one zhàng tall.
Its bark is bluish-white.
Leaves are fine,
growing in opposite pairs.
Flowers resemble turnip flowers,
truly yellow.
Seeds resemble pepper,
and are red.
If a branch is cut,
sap flows like oil,
used to apply to ringworm and scabies,
none fail to heal.
This oil is extremely precious,
its price heavier than gold.
Mountain Shǔ
In Xīmù County there is much mountain shǔ.
The *Běncǎo* says,
"On the southern mountain's shady side is called shǔyù,
it dispels heat and directs qi downward,
and supplements the five viscera."
Máhuáng,
the stem's tip bears flowers.
The flowers are small and yellow,
growing in clusters.
The seeds are like an inverted bowl,
and are edible.
By winter it withers and dies,
like grass,
yet by spring it turns green again.
Jīngsānléng
Péi Tóng of Hédōng in the Táng,
suffered from abdominal pain for several years,
unbearable.
He instructed his son, saying:
"After I die,
you must cut out my illness."
His son obeyed him.
He removed a thing,
as large as a strip of dried venison.
Hung up, it dried over time.
A guest stole it,
it was as hard as bone,
he carved it,
and patterns shone forth brilliantly.
He then used it as a knife handle,
and carried it.
On the road while pasturing horses,
he drew the knife to cut jīngsānléng grass,
and sat upon it,
whereupon the handle completely dissolved into liquid.
The guest found this strange,
returned and asked Tóng.
Tóng wept,
and told him the whole story.
Later, those with similar symptoms,
taking jīngsānléng grass juice, were often cured.
Taking Pine Resin
In Shàngdǎng, there was a man named Zhào Qú,
who suffered from leprosy for many years,
and despite various treatments, he did not recover.
On the verge of death,
someone said,
"It would be better to abandon him while he is still alive,
lest his descendants later infect one another."
His family then prepared provisions and sent him away,
placing him in a mountain cave.
Qú dwelled in the cave,
lamenting his misfortune.
Day and night, he grieved and sighed,
weeping for days on end.
A transcendent happened to pass by the cave entrance and took pity on him,
inquiring in detail.
Qú knew this was an extraordinary person,
so he kowtowed and explained his situation,
begging the transcendent for mercy.
The transcendent gave him a bag of medicine,
teaching him how to take it.
After taking it for about a hundred days,
his sores healed,
his complexion became radiant and cheerful,
and his skin became as smooth as jade.
When the transcendent passed by again to see him,
Qú thanked him for the grace of restoring his life,
and begged for the formula.
The transcendent told him,
"This is merely pine resin.
There is much more of this substance in these mountains.
If you refine and ingest it,
you can achieve long life without death."
Qú then returned home.
His family initially thought he was a ghost,
and were greatly astonished.
He then explained everything in detail.
Later, he continued taking pine resin without ceasing,
his body gradually becoming lighter,
his strength increasing a hundredfold.
He could climb heights and traverse dangers,
and remain untired all day.
At the age of one hundred and seventy,
his teeth had not fallen out,
nor had his hair turned white.
One night while lying down,
he suddenly saw a light in the room,
as large as a mirror.
When he asked those around him,
they all said they could not see it.
Over time, it gradually grew larger,
illuminating the entire room,
as bright as daylight.
Another night, he saw two colorful maidens on his face,
about two or three inches tall,
with fully formed faces and eyes,
only very small.
They played between his mouth and nose.
This continued for about a year.
These maidens gradually grew to the size of adults,
and stayed by his side.
He also often heard the sounds of zithers and lutes,
and would laugh joyfully to himself.
After living among humans for about two hundred years,
his appearance remained like that of a young boy.
He then embraced a calf and entered the mountains.
He must have become an earthly transcendent.
When people heard how Qú had taken pine resin like this,
they competed to take it.
Those with great strength
used carts and donkeys to transport it,
vowing to accumulate it until their houses were full.
Those who took it for a longer time
did not exceed a month;
not feeling any great benefit,
they would stop.
It is rare for someone with such determination to be like this.
Ingesting Pine Stamens
The *Dùnjiǎ Jīng* says:
"The blessed land of sandy soil,
the ruins of Yúnyáng,
are suitable for seclusion."
The Yúnyáng clan
were transcendent of ancient times.
The *Fāng Jì* says:
"A hundred *lǐ* south of Nányuè is a blessed land,
where pines are a thousand *chǐ* tall,
with trunks several *xún* in circumference,
and their stamens are sweet,
suitable for transcendent to ingest."
It is said that those who practice ingestion and refinement
gather this pine resin and take it,
and it is not bitter or astringent.
It differs from pines in other places.
Bestowing Poria
Shěn Yuē thanked Prince Shǐ'ān for bestowing poria.
One branch weighed twelve *jīn* and eight *liǎng*.
There is a memorial.
Ingesting Poria
Rén Zǐjì
ingested poria for eighteen years,
and transcendent and jade maidens came to follow him.
He could become invisible or visible at will,
and no longer ate grains.
His scarred lesions all vanished,
and his face and body shone with a jade-like radiance.
Ingesting Calamus
Hán Zhòng
ingested calamus for thirteen years,
and hair grew on his body.
He could read ten thousand words a day,
and recite them all.
In winter, he bared his chest without feeling cold.
Moreover, calamus must grow on rocks,
with nine or more nodes per *cùn*,
and those with purple flowers are especially good.
Ingesting Cinnamon
Zhào Tāzǐ
ingested cinnamon for twenty-one years,
hair grew on his body,
he could travel five hundred *lǐ* a day,
and had the strength to lift a thousand *jīn*.
Ingesting Oak Fruit
The red fruits of the oak tree,
if ingested for one year,
cause the old to become young again,
and enable one to see ghosts without eating.
In the past, the Daoist priest Liáng Qǐng,
at the age of seventy,
began ingesting them,
and became even younger.
He lived to be one hundred and forty years old,
could write at night,
and run as fast as a galloping horse.
He entered Qīnglóng Mountain and departed.
Ingesting Schisandra
Yíménzǐ
ingested schisandra for sixty years,
and his complexion became like that of a jade maiden.
He could enter water without getting wet,
and enter fire without being burned.
Ingesting Atractylodes
According to the Wén clan of Nányáng,
their ancestor, during the great turmoil at the end of the Hàn dynasty,
fled into Hú Mountain.
Starving and on the verge of death,
someone taught him to ingest atractylodes,
and it is said he then no longer felt hunger.
After ten years, he returned to his hometown,
his appearance even younger,
and his strength greater than before.
He himself said that while in the mountains,
his body felt light and eager to leap,
he could climb heights and tread dangers,
and remain untired for days.
Walking through ice and snow,
he felt no cold at all.
He often saw on a high cliff
several people playing board games,
and some reading books.
Looking down at them,
Wén heard them discussing among themselves.
They said:
"Can we call this fellow up?"
One of them replied:
"Not yet."
Lín Zǐmíng ingested atractylodes for eleven years,
and his ears grew five *cùn* long,
his body became as light as if flying,
and he could leap over ravines about two *zhàng* wide.
Ingesting Peach Resin
Peach resin,
soaked in mulberry wood ash,
if ingested,
cures all illnesses.
After a long time, the body emits light,
and in dark places at night,
it is like the moon rising.
If taken in large quantities,
one can then abstain from grains.
Ingesting Rehmannia
The Lord of Chǔ,
after consuming dìhuáng for eight years,
could see light in the dark,
and his hands could draw a crossbow on a chariot.
Yuǎnzhì
Língyáng Zǐzhòng,
after consuming yuǎnzhì for twenty years,
had twenty-seven sons.
He could read books and never forget what he saw.
Tiānméndōng
Dù Zǐwēi,
after consuming tiānméndōng for eighty years,
had one hundred and forty sons with his concubines.
He could travel three hundred lǐ in a day.
Drinking Water from the Chrysanthemum Pool
In Jú Tán, Jīngzhōu,
beside its source,
fragrant chrysanthemums cover the banks and inlets,
and their sap is extremely sweet.
In the deep valley, there are over thirty households,
who cannot dig wells,
so they rely on drinking this water.
Those with the longest lifespans live two to three hundred years,
those with moderate lifespans live over a hundred years,
and those who live seventy or eighty years
are still considered to have died young.
Chrysanthemums can lighten the body, boost energy,
and make people live long lives,
as evidenced.
Drinking Water from the Sweet Chrysanthemum Valley
In the mountains of Lì County, Nányáng,
there is Sweet Valley Water.
The reason it is sweet
is because sweet chrysanthemums grow all around the valley,
and chrysanthemum petals fall into it.
Over many generations,
the water’s flavor has thus changed.
The residents living near this valley do not dig wells,
but all drink the Sweet Valley Water.
Those who drink it all live long lives,
with the oldest reaching one hundred forty to one hundred fifty years,
and the youngest not less than eighty or ninety years.
No one dies young.
This is due to the power of these chrysanthemums.
Therefore, former Minister of Works Wáng Chàng, Grand Commandant Liú Kuān, and Grand Tutor Yuán Wěi,
all of whom served as Grand Administrators of Nányáng,
upon taking office,
often ordered Lì County to send forty hú of Sweet Valley Water monthly
for their drinking and cooking.
These gentlemen mostly suffered from wind paralysis and dizziness,
and all recovered.
However, they could not fully reap its benefits,
unlike the residents living above Sweet Valley,
who drank this water from birth.
Moreover, chrysanthemums and yì flowers are similar in appearance,
and can only be distinguished by their taste—sweet or bitter.
Chrysanthemums are sweet, while yì flowers are bitter.
As the saying goes, “as bitter as yì.”
Nowadays, chrysanthemums are offered as tribute in many places,
but they are scarce.
Most grow by the water’s edge.
Gōushì Mountain and Lì County have the most.
In immortal recipes, they are called “White Essence, Rebirth, and Full Cycle,”
but they are all the same chrysanthemum,
with different names for the roots, stems, flowers, and fruits.
The explanation is quite elegant.
However, those who have taken it recently have seen almost no effect,
precisely because they cannot obtain genuine chrysanthemums.
As for the Sweet Valley Water,
its southern qi and flavor
are not particularly remarkable,
yet the residents above it live extended lives.
How much more so if one were to take good medicine—
how could it not be beneficial?
Eating Huángjīng
In Línchuān, there was a scholar
who mistreated his maidservant.
Unable to endure his cruelty,
she fled into the mountains.
After a long time, her food ran out,
and she became extremely hungry.
Sitting by the water,
she saw a wild plant with lovely leaves,
so she pulled it up,
washed it in the water,
and ate it, roots and all.
It tasted very good.
From then on, she ate it regularly,
and after a while, she no longer felt hungry,
but instead became lighter and more agile.
Resting under a large tree at night,
she heard an animal running through the grass.
Thinking it was a tiger, she became afraid,
and wished she could climb to the treetop.
As soon as she thought this,
her body was already on the treetop.
At dawn,
she thought about returning to the ground,
and suddenly she was down.
From then on, wherever her mind went,
her body would drift there.
Sometimes she would go from one peak to another,
like a flying bird.
Several years later,
her family saw her while gathering firewood
and reported it to her master,
who ordered her capture.
But she could not be caught.
One day,
they found her at the foot of a cliff,
and surrounded her on three sides with thin ropes.
Suddenly, she soared to the mountaintop.
Her master was even more astonished
and was determined to capture her.
Someone said:
“She is just a maidservant—
how could she have the bones of an immortal?
She must have eaten some spiritual herb.
Try placing sumptuous food,
rich with all flavors,
and make it very fragrant and delicious
along the path she frequents,
and see if she eats it.”
They did as suggested,
and she indeed came to eat.
After eating,
she could no longer travel far,
and was captured.
She explained everything.
When asked about the appearance of the plant she ate,
it turned out to be huángjīng.
They tried to make her eat it again,
but it no longer worked.
The maidservant died a few years later.
Zhāng Shūgāo
Jiāngxià’s Zhāng Liáo, styled Shūgāo, Grand Administrator of Guìyáng,
left his post
and returned home to buy land.
In the field, there was a large tree over ten arm-spans around,
with sprawling branches covering several acres,
and the land could not grow grain.
He sent laborers to cut it down,
and six or seven dǒu of red sap flowed out.
The laborers were terrified and returned,
reporting everything to Shūgāo.
Shūgāo angrily said:
“An old tree with red sap—
what kind of blood is that!”
So he went himself
and chopped at it again.
Blood flowed out profusely.
Shūgāo ordered them to first cut off its branches.
In a hollow spot,
they saw a white-headed creature about four or five chǐ tall,
which suddenly rushed toward Shūgāo.
Shūgāo confronted and fought it.
This happened several times.
His attendants were terrified and fell to the ground,
but Shūgāo remained calm.
After carefully observing it,
he saw it was neither human nor beast.
They then cut down the tree.
That year,
the Minister of Works appointed Shūgāo as Palace Censor and Governor of Yǎnzhōu.
Holding the esteemed position of a two-thousand-dàn official,
he passed through his hometown,
offered sacrifices and honored his ancestors,
and encountered no further anomalies.
Lù Jìngshū
During the time of the First Ruler of Wú,
Lù Jìngshū served as Grand Administrator of Jiàn’ān Commandery.
He sent people to cut down a large camphor tree.
After only a few axe strokes,
blood flowed out.
When the tree was cut,
a creature with a human face and a dog’s body
emerged from the tree.
Jìngshū said,
“This is called ‘Pénghóu.’”
He then cooked and ate it.
The Báizé Tú states:
“The essence of trees is called Pénghóu,
shaped like a black dog,
with no tail.
It can be cooked and eaten.”
Niè Yǒu
In Wú, Niè Yǒu, courtesy name Wéntì,
was from Xīntú in Yùzhāng.
In his youth, he was poor and lowly,
and often enjoyed hunting and shooting.
He once saw a white deer,
shot and hit it,
then followed the blood trail until it ended,
and did not know where it had gone.
Hungry and exhausted,
he lay down under a catalpa tree.
Looking up, he saw the arrow he had shot at the deer
stuck in a tree branch,
and found it strange.
He then returned home to get provisions,
and ordered his disciples to take axes and fell the tree.
The tree bled,
so he cut it into two planks.
He dragged them and placed them in a pond;
they often sank,
but sometimes floated up again.
When they left the house, there would surely be good fortune.
When Yǒu wanted to welcome guests,
he would often ride on these planks.
Sometimes, in midstream, they seemed about to sink,
and the guests would be greatly frightened,
but Yǒu would shout at them,
and they would float again.
His official career went as he wished,
and he rose to the position of Grand Administrator of Dānyáng.
Suddenly, the planks followed him to Shítóu.
Yǒu was alarmed and said:
"These planks from the pond have come;
there must be a meaning to this."
He then resigned from his post and returned home.
The two planks supported him on both sides,
and he arrived in a single day.
From then on,
when the planks emerged, it sometimes meant misfortune.
Now, over twenty lǐ north of Xīntú,
there is a place called Fēngxī,
where Niè Yǒu cut the catalpa tree planks and moored them at a Zāngkē.
At the Zāngkē, there is a camphor tree,
which still exists today.
It was planted by Niè Yǒu on the day he returned,
and its branches and leaves all grow downward.
Dǒng Qí
In Jīngzhào, Dǒng Qí had a large tree in front of his courtyard,
providing excellent shade.
Later, during continuous rain,
Qí was alone at his hometown residence.
A minor clerk said,
"Tàichéngyún, the Prefect, has come."
Then he saw Chéngyún wearing a crown reaching to the sky,
eight chǐ tall,
who said of himself,
"I am a Regional Governor.
My third son has outstanding talent,
and is about to associate with you."
The next day,
he noticed something unusual under the tree.
Every day after dusk, when no one was around,
a youth would come to Qí to chat and play,
or order him to fetch food and drink.
This went on for half a year.
Qí's vitality was strong and robust,
and no one in his household fell ill.
Later, Qí went to his lower estate,
and three of his servants escorted him.
They said the tree's timber could be used,
and wanted to borrow it,
but the young master usually did not permit it.
Now they tried to chop it down together.
Qí then agreed to it.
The spirit also ceased from then on.
Zhào Yì
In Yǒngjiā, Sōngyáng's Zhào Yì, during the Yìxī era, together with his eldest son Xiān, cut down a mountain peach tree.
It bled,
and they stopped in alarm.
Later, his third son suddenly went missing,
and returned on his own after ten days.
He heard voices in the air,
sometimes singing, sometimes weeping.
Yì said to it:
"Since you are a spirit,
why not show yourself to me?"
It replied:
"I am a righteous spirit.
North of your house is a large maple tree,
and to the south is a solitary peak,
named Shílóu.
Its four walls stand sheer,
untrodden by humans or beasts.
If I am slightly displeased,
I take this child and place him on the treetop or on Shílóu.
The whole family kowtows and pleads with me,
and only then does he come down."
Wèi Fótuó
At the end of the Liáng dynasty,
in Càizhōu, at the Bùxí family's vacant house,
it was passed down that
it was inauspicious and could not be lived in.
A garrison commander soldier named Wèi Fótuó took a torch and entered the house,
resting in the front hall.
At dusk,
an object appeared in the hall,
with a human face and a dog's body,
no tail,
jumping and leaping in the room.
Fótuó drew his bow and shot at it,
and with one shot, it was no longer seen.
The next day, he tore open the roof,
looked at the arrow embedded in the feathers,
and found a piece of rotten wood,
about a chǐ long,
with coagulated blood beneath it.
From then on, it ceased.
Línhuái Generals
During the Shàngyuán era,
the generals of Línhuái held a banquet at night,
roasting pigs and sheep,
their fragrance abundant.
A huge hand entered through the window,
asking for a morsel of meat,
but none of them gave it.
It begged repeatedly,
but in the end, they still did not give.
They secretly tied a rope into a loop,
and set it at the opening.
Deceiving it, they said:
"Here is meat."
The hand entered again,
and they thus tied its arm.
They pulled and tugged with all their might,
but it could not break free.
As dawn approached,
it broke off with a thud.
Looking at it,
it was a poplar branch.
They took it to find the tree,
and near the riverbank,
where it was broken,
there was often blood.
Cuī Dǎo
In Jīngnán of the Táng dynasty, there was a wealthy man named Cuī Dǎo,
though his family was poor and destitute.
By chance, he planted over a thousand orange trees,
and each year he reaped great profits from them.
Suddenly, one day,
one of the trees transformed into a man,
over ten feet tall,
who sought an audience with Cuī Dǎo.
Dǎo was initially alarmed by this,
and dared not come out.
The man pleaded earnestly,
so Dǎo finally emerged to meet him.
The man said:
"In my previous life, I owed you a million coins,
and died before I could repay it.
My family further deceived you,
so you appealed to Heaven.
As a result, I and my entire family were turned into orange trees,
working as laborers for you,
and only now have we repaid the debt in full.
Now the Heavenly Emperor has issued a decree,
taking pity on my kin,
and restoring us to our original forms.
Moreover, upon reflecting on the past events,
it feels as if only two nights have passed.
I beg you to prepare a humble cottage for me,
so I may farm and dig wells myself,
and live out the rest of my life.
You should also cut down all the orange trees,
live quietly and abide by the norm,
and thus you will be able to preserve yourself.
If you fail to do so,
Heaven will bring down calamity upon you.
Why is this so?
Because the debt of a million coins from the past,
has now been fully repaid."
Dǎo was greatly astonished,
and did everything as the man had said,
immediately building a cottage,
and cutting down all the orange trees.
Five years later, Dǎo passed away,
and his family fell into poverty once more.
The man was also nowhere to be found.
Jiǎ Mì
During the reign of Emperor Shùnzōng,
a scholar named Jiǎ Mì traveled from Suīyáng to Cháng'ān.
When he reached the outskirts of the ancient Luòchéng,
he saw several people drinking in a circle on the green plain,
singing and dancing by themselves.
Mì thus approached them.
The men cheerfully rose together,
bowed to Mì, and invited him to join their mat.
Seeing that all seven wore scholars' robes
and were courteous,
Mì asked them:
"Observing you gentlemen,
you appear to be men of letters.
How dare you gather to drink in the wilds,
with no one in sight on all sides?"
One of them replied:
"We seven
all possess talents to aid the world,
yet remain unused in this age—
much like you, sir, who harbor hidden abilities
and now seek an official career.
We happened to be meeting for discussion
when you honorably arrived.
Let us happily share fine wine,
cherish this beautiful scene,
take warnings from the rise and fall of antiquity,
and deliberate on the employment and dismissal of men in the world.
Why must one enter ornate towers
or board dragon boats
to achieve a thorough intoxication?"
Mì found this very strange
and could not help but feel solemn respect.
After prolonged merry conversation,
the seven men exchanged glances
as if harboring some doubt.
They then asked Mì:
"Now that we have heard your lofty discourse,
why not display a glimpse of your admirable plans,
so that we may admire you without suspicion?"
Mì rose and said:
"I am from Suīyáng.
In youth I loved reading
and gained some understanding of the ways of kings and hegemons of old.
Now I hear the Emperor has ascended the great throne
and opened the path for frank speech.
I wish to knock once at the ivory gates,
to slightly express my foolish sincerity.
I do not seek wealth and honor,
but only to unburden my humble heart.
Just now, seeing you seven gentlemen in exalted gathering,
I came to pay my respects.
I hope you will not spurn me from afar."
One of them looked at the others and laughed:
"If others speak of themselves,
it may do no harm.
But if we judge it,
it will surely go awry."
Another said:
"Though we ourselves should not speak,
will others spare us?"
Another said:
"This gentleman's name is Mì ('Secret'),
so surely he will conceal our flaws for us."
Then they smiled and said to Mì:
"We are seven tree spirits:
the first is pine,
second willow,
third pagoda tree,
fourth mulberry,
fifth jujube,
sixth chestnut,
seventh tree of heaven.
Now let each declare his aspiration,
and we beg you, sir, to listen and keep it secret."
The pine spirit rose and said:
"I originally dwelled in empty mountains,
no ordinary timber.
I bear a steadfast and pure integrity;
even when frost assails and snow violates,
my character cannot be changed.
If a wise builder constructs a great mansion,
wielding axe and adze,
timbers long and short
each find their use.
Though rafters and purlins are many,
if beams and pillars are lacking,
I will surely serve as beam and pillar.
If I gain such use,
then the structure will never face the peril of collapse."
The next one rose and said:
"My reputation for grace and charm
is known from ancient times to now.
I only regret that Emperor Yáng did not return,
and no one recognizes my worth.
Though Zhāng Xù imitated me,
he only vainly glorifies the records.
What pleases me is
that when catkins fly, talented poets chant verses,
and when leaves are tender, fair ladies learn to paint.
Suppleness overcomes rigidity,
and I preserve my nature thus."
The next said:
"I receive the beneficence of warm sunlight,
yet am timber of no great use.
Great rivers lack bridges,
yet men do not take me;
great mansions lack pillars,
yet men do not employ me.
Unless I meet a master craftsman's measuring line,
I surely will not fit any length or size.
Alas!
Those who lean on me gain the fame of the Three Dukes."
The next said:
"All my life I have loved silkworms,
I do not refuse to offer my leaves for feeding,
no different from pushing
food to them.
Silkworms then make cocoons,
cocoons become silk,
silk becomes robes and damasks.
Robes and damasks enter the use of noble families.
If those of noble lineage,
seeing the beauty of robes and damasks, think of me,
why must I be great as beams and pillars
or small as rafters and purlins?"
The next said:
"Ever since the debater Sū Qín entered Yān,
I have been acknowledged for my name of universal benefit.
Not only did Emperor Hàn Wǔdì call me 'bundle upon bundle,'
but those who present me can fully express a loyal heart.
Why then should I worry about being unknown?"
The next said:
"Though I dwell among thorns and brambles,
my nature is truly tranquil,
yet I too can serve the needs of a great state.
If a ruler establishes ancestral temples
and reverently offers sacrifices,
following antiquity by using me,
I can indeed make the people tremble with awe."
The last said:
"How am I different from the rest?
Heaven covers me too,
earth supports me too.
In spring I flourish,
in autumn I shed.
Men of recent times deem me useless timber,
and I truly often harbor indignation and regret.
If I do not dwell at the ravine's bottom,
how can one see my soaring-to-the-clouds potential?
If I am not beneath the eaves,
how can one know I am timber for building mansions?
A steed ungalloped is a nag;
jade uncut is mere rough stone.
Surely it is not that only pine can build mansions and soar to clouds,
while I cannot build mansions and soar to clouds.
This is what is called trusting one man's words
and greatly losing the truth.
Therefore I admire those who live in seclusion
and conceal my traces for now.
If I met even one glance from Táo Kǎn,
I would be more than useful enough."
Having spoken,
they again sang and danced by themselves.
Hearing their words,
Mì was greatly terrified.
He could not sit still on the mat
and hastily rose to take his leave.
The seven men then together urged a cup of wine upon him,
saying to Mì:
"Between heaven and earth, men and the myriad things
are all unfathomable;
take care not to slight them."
Mì drank it down,
thanked them, and departed.
Xuē Hóngjī
In the Tóngtuó Ward of the Eastern Capital at Wèiqiáo,
there lived a recluse named Xuē Hóngjī.
He built a humble cottage on the bend of the Wèi River,
keeping his door shut and living in seclusion,
with neither wife nor servants.
Every autumn,
when leaves from neighboring trees flew into his courtyard,
he would sweep them up and gather them,
placing them in paper bags,
then following their strength and returning them.
He often inscribed a verse in the corner of his seat:
"In a person's plans,
to follow blindly,
persisting in past errors is not acceptable,
nor is stubbornly holding to one's own views and refusing to follow the crowd.
Life is truly difficult,
it lies only in walking the middle path."
One day,
as the setting sun slanted westward,
a frosty wind entered his door,
and he sat alone, wrapped in coarse cloth,
gazing upward at the lingering fragrance of Zhāng Bǐng.
Suddenly, a guest arrived at his gate.
His appearance was ancient and majestic,
with a prominent nose and thick eyebrows,
a square mouth and broad forehead,
resembling one of the Four Haos.
He wore a robe of morning clouds,
and with a deep bow, he said to Xuē Hóngjī:
"Your honor's nature favors the secluded way,
and your virtue is renowned and abundant.
My dwelling is not far,
and I have long admired your conduct,
so I have come especially to visit."
Hóngjī felt an immediate affinity upon meeting him,
and they discussed past and present,
whereupon Hóngjī asked his name.
The man said:
"I am Cángjīng, surnamed Liǔ."
He then began to sing and chant,
as the clear night drew to a close.
He said:
"When the Hàn dynasty arose,
Shūsūn established the rites,
but how could the two-year mourning system be implemented for deaths and marriages?
This is what troubles me."
He then sang:
"Cold water rests in the round pond,
autumn pools fill with withered lotus.
Shut behind doors, I delve into ancient texts,
and what I have gained is much today."
Hóngjī was fond of the "Yìjīng,"
and so he inquired about it.
Cángjīng replied:
"The way of the Yì is profound and subtle,
I dare not study it.
Moreover, the six teachings of the Liǔ clan
only illuminate the 'Shī,' 'Shū,' 'Lǐ,' 'Yuè,' and 'Chūnqiū,'
but are lost when it comes to the 'Yì.'
In truth, there are only five teachings.
Such is the difficulty of the Way."
Hóngjī greatly delighted in this discourse.
When he finished speaking, he took his leave,
and there was a rustling sound.
Hóngjī watched him,
and he faded away vaguely after about ten feet.
Later, Hóngjī asked his neighbors,
but none had seen such a person.
Hóngjī pondered deeply about Cángjīng,
but did not know where he was.
After more than a month,
he visited Hóngjī again.
Whenever Hóngjī tried to approach him,
Cángjīng would retreat.
When Hóngjī pressed closer,
he faintly caught the scent of rotten firewood,
and Cángjīng vanished.
In the fifth month of the following year, he came again,
and said to Hóngjī:
"A kindred spirit is hard to find,
days and months are easily lost,
hearts may be close, but the Way is vast,
the dwelling is near, but the person is far.
I have a quatrain to give you,
please remember it."
The poem said:
"Who says the three talents are precious?
I observe all transformations as one.
The heart, empty, fears the moth's devouring,
in old age, one dreads the wild wind."
After reciting it,
his mood became agitated,
and he was no longer at ease.
He went out the door and headed west,
and his trail was lost.
That night, a fierce wind arose,
tearing off roofs and uprooting trees.
The next day,
beside the Wèiwáng Pond, there was a large withered willow tree,
snapped by the violent wind.
Inside it, someone had hidden over a hundred scrolls of scriptures,
all rotten and ruined.
Hóngjī went to collect them,
but most were soaked and broken by the rain,
all out of order,
and among them, only the "Zhōuyì" was missing.
Hóngjī sighed and said:
"Is this what is meant by Cángjīng?"
This happened during the Jiànzhōng era.
Lú Qián
had an old residence in the Eastern Capital,
its halls, inner rooms, and terraces were grand and imposing,
but those who lived there often died violently,
so it had been locked up and empty for a long time.
The former Right Sanqi Changshi, Wànyáng's Lú Qián,
during the Zhēnyuán era, served as a Censor,
overseeing the Eastern Terrace,
and often wished to buy this residence and live there.
Someone said:
"This house is haunted,
it cannot be lived in."
Qián said:
"I can pacify it myself."
One evening later,
Qián slept in the hall with his attendant,
ordering all servants to remain outside the gate.
The attendant was brave, fierce, and skilled in archery,
so he took his bow and arrows,
and sat under the front terrace.
As the night grew deep,
they heard someone knocking at the gate,
and the attendant immediately asked who it was.
A voice replied:
"General Liǔ sends a letter to Attendant Lú."
Qián did not respond.
Soon after, a sheet of paper was thrown under the terrace,
the characters seeming to be written with a wet brush,
the strokes delicate and fine.
Qián ordered his attendant to read the words:
"My family has lived here for years.
The halls, inner rooms, and terraces
are all my dwelling.
The door gods and household spirits
are all my subordinates.
Yet you burst into my home,
is this reasonable?
Suppose you had a surplus,
and I entered it,
would that be acceptable?
Since you do not fear me,
do you not feel shame in your heart?
Leave quickly,
lest you incur the disgrace of defeat and ruin."
After reading it,
the letter scattered in all directions,
like flying ashes.
Soon, they heard another voice say,
"General Liǔ wishes to see Censor Lú."
Then a great apparition arrived,
its body several tens of fathoms tall,
standing in the courtyard,
holding a gourd ladle in its hand.
The attendant immediately drew his bow to the full and shot,
hitting what it held,
and the apparition retreated,
dropping its gourd ladle.
After a while, it came again,
leaning over the terrace and standing,
lowering its head and peering in,
its appearance most strange.
The attendant shot again,
hitting its chest.
The apparition was startled,
as if afraid,
and then went away eastward.
At dawn,
Qián ordered a search for its traces.
In an open space east of the residence,
they saw a willow tree over a hundred feet tall,
with an arrow piercing it,
which was the so-called General Liǔ.
Qián had it cut down for firewood.
From then on, those who lived in the residence were unharmed.
Over a year later,
when they rebuilt the halls and rooms,
under the roof tiles they found a gourd ladle.
About ten feet long,
with an arrow piercing its handle,
it was the ladle held by the general.
Monk Zhìtōng
The monk Zhìtōng of Líntuān Temple often recited the Lotus Sutra.
When entering meditation and sitting in repose,
he would always seek out cold forests and pure realms,
places hardly reached by human footprints.
After a full year,
suddenly one night someone circled his courtyard calling "Zhìtōng."
Until dawn,
the voice only then ceased.
This lasted for three nights.
The voice encroached upon his door,
and Zhìtōng could bear it no longer,
so he responded, saying:
"What do you want from me?
You may come in and speak."
There was a creature over six chǐ tall,
dressed in black with a blue face,
its eyes wide and mouth huge.
Seeing the monk,
it at first also joined its hands in greeting.
Zhìtōng stared intently at it for a long time,
then said to it:
"Are you cold?
Come here by the fire."
The creature then took a seat.
Zhìtōng simply recited his sutra.
By the fifth watch,
the creature, intoxicated by the fire,
closed its eyes and opened its mouth,
leaning against the stove and snoring.
Zhìtōng observed it,
then used an incense spoon to lift some glowing ashes,
and placed them in its mouth.
The creature cried out loudly and leapt up,
reaching the door with a sound like a stumble.
The temple backed against a mountain.
Zhìtōng, when it was light,
went to look at the place of the stumble,
and found a piece of tree bark.
Climbing the mountain and searching for several lǐ,
he saw a large green paulownia tree, its top already aged.
Below, a concave root looked freshly broken,
and the monk fitted the bark to it,
and it joined without a seam.
On its side,
a woodcutter had chopped a step,
six or seven cùn deep,
which was the creature's mouth.
Glowing ashes filled it,
and after a long time they still flickered.
Zhìtōng burned it,
and the monster was then eradicated.
The Attendant of Jiāngxià
During the Tàihé era,
there was an attendant serving in Jiāngxià,
whose official residence had often experienced strange phenomena.
Every evening,
a giant figure would appear, its body entirely black,
very glossy.
Seeing it, one would be terrified and fall ill and die.
Later, there was an elder named Xǔ Yuáncháng,
skilled at seeing ghosts.
The attendant ordered Yuáncháng to use talismanic arts to summon and interrogate it.
One evening later,
Yuáncháng sat in the western corridor of the hall,
when the giant suddenly arrived.
Yuáncháng produced a talisman and hurled it,
striking its arm.
There was a clattering sound,
and it fell to the ground.
The giant then left.
Yuáncháng looked at the fallen arm,
and it was a withered tree branch.
The next day,
a household servant said to Yuáncháng:
"In the northeast corner of the hall,
there is a withered tree,
and sir's talisman is now upon it."
They went immediately to look,
and the tree had a broken branch,
indeed the giant's severed arm.
They then felled and burned it,
and the residence was thereafter free of monsters.
Dòu Kuān
Dòu Kuān of Táng-era Fúfēng made his home at Liángshān.
In the autumn of the eighth year of Tàihé,
he left his post as assistant judge of the salt transport commissioner of Xiè County, having served as a reviewing official in the Court of Judicial Review, and retired to return home,
and thus was repairing his garden house.
He ordered a household servant to fell a tree.
Once felled, blood gushed forth,
pooling abundantly on the ground,
and within a mealtime it was all gone.
Kuān found this strange,
and knew it to be a monstrous sign.
From then on, he shut his gate and cut off human affairs.
By the winter of the following year, the eleventh month,
Zhèng Zhù and Lǐ Xùn rebelled.
Kuān was connected to Zhù,
and was thus executed and died within the Left Forbidden Army.
Wú Yǎn
There was a commoner of Lìquán County, Wú Yǎn, whose home was in the fields.
He had a daughter over ten years old.
One evening,
she suddenly vanished,
and none knew where she had gone.
Several days later,
Yǎn dreamed that his father said to him:
"Your daughter is now in the northeast corner,
it must be a tree spirit causing this harm."
Yǎn awoke in alarm.
The next day,
he went to the northeast corner and exhaustively searched for traces,
