and indeed heard sounds of calling and moaning.
Yǎn looked,
and saw his daughter inside a hole.
The opening was very small,
but inside it was somewhat spacious.
Beside it was an ancient locust tree,
its roots sprawling and immense.
Thereupon he took her and returned home,
but she was dazed as if deeply intoxicated.
It happened that a Daoist priest named Lǐ arrived,
and Yǎn requested talismanic arts and exorcistic incantations.
His daughter suddenly blinked and spoke, saying:
"Northeast of here is a locust tree,
the tree has a spirit,
which drew me from the hollow of the tree into an underground cavern,
hence my illness."
Thereupon they felled that tree.
Several days later,
the girl's illness finally healed.
Dǒng Guàn
There was a Dǒng Guàn who had once been a monk,
dwelling in a Buddhist temple in Tàiyuán.
In the summer of the seventh year of Tàihé,
he traveled south to Jīngchǔ with his younger cousin, Mr. Wáng,
and later planned to enter Cháng'ān.
On the road they reached Shāngyú.
One evening,
they lodged in a mountain hostel.
Mr. Wáng had already fallen asleep,
but Guàn alone had not yet rested.
Suddenly he saw a creature emerge from beneath the candle,
and then it covered the candle.
It resembled a human hand but had no fingers.
Looking closely,
outside the candle's shadow there seemed to be something,
and Guàn urgently called Mr. Wáng.
Wáng arose,
and the hand then departed.
Guàn said to Wáng:
"Be careful not to sleep,
the monster will surely come again."
So he took a club and sat waiting for it.
After a long time,
Mr. Wáng said:
"Where is the monster?
Are you imagining things, elder brother?"
And then he went to bed.
Shortly after,
a creature over five chǐ tall appeared,
blocking the candle as it stood,
with no hands, face, or eyes.
Guàn grew even more frightened,
and called Mr. Wáng again.
Wáng angrily did not get up.
Guàn then used his club to strike its head,
its body as if pierced through by grass.
The club also followed into it,
and though he tried with force, he could not retrieve it.
Soon it then retreated and left.
Guàn, fearing it would come again,
until dawn did not dare to sleep.
The next day,
he inquired with the hostel clerk.
The clerk said:
"Several lǐ west of here there is an ancient fir tree,
often a source of monsters,
I suspect it is what you saw."
He then went with Guàn and Mr. Wáng straight to search,
and indeed saw the ancient fir,
with a club piercing through among its branches and leaves.
The clerk said:
"People have long said this is a demon,
but none had ever seen its true form.
Now it is confirmed."
They hastily fetched an axe,
and completely cut it down.
A Scholar of the Capital Region
In the region of the capital and Luòyáng,
there was a scholar's son who was lost.
His name is unknown.
He was skilled in carving and engraving.
While traveling on a mountain road in another town,
he saw a large locust tree whose shade covered several acres,
and beside its roots there were four tumor-like growths as large as several-dǒu jars.
He thought of taking them.
He had few helpers,
and lacked tools such as axes and saws,
so he planned to return another day to collect them.
Fearing someone else might take them first,
he took from his clothing bag
several sheets of paper,
cut them into paper money,
and tied them to the tree's tumors.
His intention was to make it seem like a sacred tree,
so that no one would dare to cut it down.
After leaving,
he returned several months later.
With a group of laborers and tools like knives and axes,
he intended to cut it down.
When he reached the side of the tree,
he saw painted images and shadows,
with many paper money hanging beside them,
and there were also places where incense and offerings had been made.
The scholar laughed and said:
"The villagers are ignorant and believe in this;
it is truly bewildering."
Just as he ordered the axes to start cutting,
he suddenly saw a deity in purple robes standing beside him,
with a stern expression,
who shouted at the servants:
"Do not cut down this tree."
The scholar stepped forward and said:
"When I passed by here before,
I saw these locust tree tumors,
and wanted to take them.
Since I had no axes or saws,
and feared others might take them,
I temporarily used paper money to claim and protect them.
There was originally no deity here;
why are you stopping me?"
The deity said:
"After you temporarily tied paper money to the tree,
everyone said it was a sacred tree,
capable of bringing fortune or misfortune,
and they began to pray and make offerings together.
The underworld administration thus assigned me this duty to receive the offerings.
Now there is a deity here;
how can you say there is none?
If you insist on cutting it down,
great misfortune will befall you."
The scholar did not listen.
The deity said:
"What do you intend to use this for?"
The scholar replied:
"I want to carve it into utensils."
The deity said:
"If that is the case,
can I redeem it with a good price?"
The scholar said:
"Yes."
The deity said:
"How much do you require?"
The scholar said:
"You can give me a hundred thousand."
The deity said:
"I now offer a hundred bolts of silk.
Five li ahead, there is a ruined tomb;
the silk is inside it.
If you cannot find it,
we shall meet here again."
The scholar then went to the ruined tomb,
and indeed found the silk,
with nothing missing.
Jiāng Sǒu
During the Kaichéng era,
there was an old man named Jiāng Sǒu who had read many Daoist texts,
extensively sought out esoteric arts,
and was skilled at playing the flute.
He often traveled and stayed at the Língxiān Pavilion in Yǒnglè County.
At the time, he indulged in drinking.
Passing through Wénxiāng,
he became drunk and fell asleep under a large locust tree east of the official road at the Pándòu Inn.
As the night deepened, he gradually awoke,
hearing the sound of a huge creature walking,
its footsteps very heavy.
Sǒu secretly watched
and saw a person towering several zhang tall.
It came to the side of the locust tree and sat down,
then with a hairy hand, it patted Sǒu and said:
"I thought it was a hoeing lad by the tree,
but it turns out to be Bì Zhuó by the wine jar."
Then it knocked on the big tree several times and said:
"Please inform Second Brother from the Jīng Pavilion to come visit his elder brother."
The great locust tree then spoke:
"Thank you, brother, for visiting."
It seemed as if someone descended from the locust tree
and spoke with it.
After a short while,
the sounds of drinking and toasting arose.
The locust tree from Jīng Mountain said:
"Elder Brother, in what year will you abandon your position as the King of Locusts on the road between the two capitals?"
The great locust tree said:
"After three jiǎzǐ cycles,
I shall relinquish this position."
The Jīng Mountain locust said:
"Elder Brother, you do not realize old age is approaching,
yet you still cling to this position.
You must wait until fire enters your hollow heart,
sap flows and your joints break,
before you know to step down.
You are truly an insatiable fellow.
Why not take advantage of the thunder now,
uproot yourself from the road,
so you may become useful timber,
a beam or pillar for a great mansion,
preserving layers of brocade-like grain
and pieces of true blossoms.
Wouldn't that be better than someday becoming rotten, worm-eaten firewood,
thrown into the stove to become ashes?"
The great locust tree said:
"Even sparrows and mice cling to life;
how could I manage such a thing?"
The other locust said:
"There's no point talking with you, old brother."
It bid farewell and left.
At dawn,
Sǒu finally got up.
Several days later,
he reached Jīng Mountain in Wénxiāng.
He saw a courtyard locust tree towering majestically,
its branches and trunk lush and spreading,
nearly ten arm-spans around,
as if inhabited by a divine being.
So he waited until night,
made offerings of wine and dried meat, and said:
"The other night,
I heard the locust spirit and the great locust king of the official road at Pándòu discussing such and such.
I was lying nearby
and clearly remembered everything said.
Now I ask the tree spirit to speak with me."
The locust tree said:
"I am moved by your sincere intentions.
What do you seek?
Little did I know that the man lying drunk on the road that night
was you!"
Sǒu said:
"All my life I have loved the Dao,
but I have never met a true teacher.
Tree Spirit, if you have power,
I beg you to instruct me.
If you can show me where to learn the Dao,
I will surely repay you."
The locust spirit said:
"Simply enter Jīng Mountain
and seek out Immortal Master Bào.
If you manage to see him,
whether on water or land,
you will certainly find a way to transcend this world.
I am moved by your request.
Be careful not to reveal my words.
Do you not recall how the huábiǎo pillar warned the old fox,
and disaster extended to me?"
Sǒu thanked it.
The next day,
he entered Jīng Mountain,
following the cliffs and streams,
and indeed found Immortal Master Bào.
He immediately prostrated himself in reverence.
The Master said:
"How did you know of me and come to seek me as teacher?
You must tell the truth."
Sǒu did not dare conceal it
and recounted in detail what the tree spirit at the Jīng Mountain lodge had said.
The Immortal Master said:
"How dare that petty spirit presume to direct someone on its own authority."
Though unable to punish it severely,
he nonetheless sent a talisman to destroy one of its branches.
Sǒu bowed and begged for mercy.
The Immortal Master said:
"If I do not punish it now,
others will surely follow later."
Then he said to Sǒu:
"What abilities do you have?
Tell me each one."
Sǒu said:
"I love the Dao,
and am obsessed with playing the flute."
The Immortal Master then had him take his flute and play.
The Immortal Master sighed and said:
"Your skill has reached its peak.
However, what you play
is merely a dried bamboo flute.
I now give you a jade flute,
the finest from Jīng Mountain.
Play it as you would an ordinary flute.
In three years,
you will summon a dragon from the caverns.
Once the dragon emerges,
it will surely present you with a bright moon pearl held in its mouth.
When you obtain it,
you must boil it in clarified butter for three days.
By then, the young dragon will already have a headache.
This is due to the sympathetic resonance causing it.
The young dragon will certainly bring a Water-Transformation Elixir to ransom its pearl.
When you obtain it, swallow it,
and you will become a water immortal,
living no less than ten thousand years.
You will have no need for my medicine.
For you possess the bearing of Qín Gāo."
The Immortal Master then took out the jade flute and gave it to him.
Sǒu asked:
"How does a jade flute differ from a bamboo one?"
The Master said:
"Bamboo is green,
similar in color to a dragon.
Its imitation of a dragon's chant
does not startle the dragon.
Jade is white,
which conflicts with the dragon.
If it suddenly hears its chant,
the dragon finds it strange,
and thus comes to observe.
The power to summon lies in its ability to transform.
The principle derives from the Mysterious."
Sǒu received the instruction and left.
After three years,
he finally mastered its tones and rhythms.
Later, he went to Yuèyáng,
where Prefect Lǐ Yú hosted him.
At the time, there was a great drought.
Sǒu took out his flute
and played it at night atop the scripture tower of Shèngshàn Temple.
Sure enough, from the islets of Dòngtíng Lake,
a dragon flew out and descended.
Clouds coiled around the tower more than once.
Then an old dragon appeared,
and indeed offered Sǒu a pearl from its mouth.
Sǒu obtained it
and boiled it as instructed for two days and nights.
Sure enough, a dragon transformed into a human,
holding a small medicine box
containing the Water-Transformation Elixir,
and prostrated itself, begging to ransom its pearl.
Sǒu then took the box and gave it the pearl,
swallowed the elixir,
and his appearance transformed into that of a youth.
He could enter water without getting wet.
He traveled through
every cave and cavern under heaven.
Later, he dwelled in Héngyáng,
his face and hair remaining as before.
Dragon-Snake Grass
In the summer of the Zhōngpíng era during the reign of Emperor Líng of the Later Hàn,
in Jìyáng and Jìyīn of Chénliú Commandery,
Yuānqú and Líhú,
Chénggāo and Yángwǔ,
grass grew along the roads outside the city walls,
all taking the forms of dragons, snakes, birds, and beasts.
The Continued Hàn Records state:
"Their appearance was five-colored,
with feathers, heads, eyes, feet, and wings all complete.
Some took human form,
holding bows and crossbows,
or the shapes of oxen, horses, and myriad things."
That year,
the Black Mountain bandits Zhāng Niújiǎo and over ten others rose up together, plundering and raiding.
Later, the Empress's brother Hé Jìn held power,
and the Hàn dynasty grew weak.
This was also an omen of Dǒng Zhuó raising troops and burning the palace gates.
Xiānbēi Woman
In Jìn there was a scholar who
purchased a Xiānbēi girl named Huáishùn.
She herself said that her paternal aunt's daughter had been bewitched by a red amaranth.
At first, she saw a man of handsome appearance and pure demeanor,
dressed in red clothes,
who said his home was just to the north.
The girl then constantly sang and chanted, seeming quite content.
Every time dusk approached,
she would dress neatly and go behind the house.
Her family watched and waited,
and saw only a single stalk of red amaranth,
with the girl's finger ring hanging from its stem.
They cut it down, and the girl wailed and wept,
dying by the next morning.
Fern Snake
When Grand Commandant Xī Jiàn was stationed in Dānyáng,
he once went out hunting.
It was the middle of the second month,
when ferns were just beginning to sprout.
A soldier broke off and ate one stalk,
and immediately felt a churning in his heart, wanting to vomit.
So he returned home.
He then developed pain in his heart and abdomen.
After about half a year,
he suddenly vomited violently,
vomiting a red snake over a foot long.
It was still moving.
He then hung it under the eaves,
and the snake gradually dried up.
After a night, he looked at it,
and it was actually a stalk of fern,
exactly like the one he had eaten before.
His illness then healed.
Mustard Insect
In the Wǔlǐng region, spring and summer are mostly rainy,
with clear days
being few.
This continues from autumn into winter before stopping.
All things easily become moth-eaten and spoiled;
glue, felt, and woolen fabrics
do not last more than a year.
Once, someone bought mustard greens and placed them against the wall,
forgetting to eat them.
After a few days, they all grew four legs,
with heads and tails,
able to walk,
as large as mantises,
only with slender waists and long bodies.
Cuī Xuánwēi
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
the recluse Cuī Xuánwēi had a residence east of Luòyáng.
He was devoted to the Dào,
and for thirty years consumed Atractylodes and Poria cocos.
When his medicines ran out,
he led his servants into Mount Sōng to gather mushrooms,
returning only after a year.
The house was empty,
overgrown with weeds filling the courtyard.
It was a spring night,
the breeze was clear, the moon bright,
and he could not sleep.
He was alone in one courtyard;
his family had no reason to come there.
After the third watch,
a maid in green said:
"You are in the courtyard.
We wish to pass through with a couple of female companions,
heading to our aunt's place outside the Shàngdōng Gate,
and would like to borrow a place to rest briefly.
May we?"
Xuánwēi agreed.
Shortly after,
over ten people arrived,
led in by the green-clad maid.
One in green robes stepped forward and said:
"My surname is Yáng."
She pointed to another,
saying "Lǐ shì".
And to another,
saying "Táo shì".
She then pointed to a young girl in crimson,
saying "Her surname is Shí, her name is Ācuò".
Each had her own maidservants.
After Xuánwēi had greeted them,
they sat beneath the moon,
and he asked the reason for their journey.
They replied:
"We wish to visit Fēng Shíbā Yí.
For several days she has said she would come to see us,
but hasn't,
so tonight we are all going to see her."
Before they were settled,
word came from outside that Aunt Fēng had arrived.
All rose in delighted surprise to welcome her.
Yáng shì said:
"The host is most gracious.
Staying here comfortably is not bad at all;
other places might not surpass this either."
Xuánwēi went out again to meet Fēng shì.
Her speech was cool and refined,
possessing the elegant demeanor of a forest recluse.
He then bowed and invited her to sit.
Their beauty was all extraordinary,
the entire gathering fragrant,
a rich, pervasive scent assailing the senses.
The ladies called for wine,
each singing a song as they offered it.
Xuánwēi remembered two of them.
One in red robes offered wine to one in white,
singing:
"A jade face, pure and bright, surpasses white snow,
especially when facing the fragrant moon in youth.
Hesitating, I dare not resent the spring breeze,
only sigh that my radiant beauty fades unseen."
Then the one in white offered wine,
singing:
"Crimson garments draped, glistening with dew,
lightly tinged with rouge, a single delicate bloom.
I lament that a rosy face cannot be kept,
do not blame the spring breeze for being fickle."
When it was Shíbā Yí's turn to hold the cup,
her nature being rather frivolous,
she spilled wine, staining Ācuò's clothes.
Ācuò changed expression and said:
"Others may seek your favor,
but I simply do not know how to seek favor,
that's all."
She flicked her sleeves and stood up.
Shíbā Yí said:
"The young lady is acting up from drink."
All rose.
They parted outside the gate.
Shíbā Yí went south.
The others entered the garden to the west and took their leave.
Xuánwēi still did not realize anything unusual.
The next night they came again, saying:
"We wish to go to Shíbā Yí's place."
Ācuò said angrily:
"What need is there to go again to that old woman Fēng's place?
If we have matters, we can just ask the recluse.
I wonder if that would be acceptable?"
Ācuò continued:
"All our companions live in the garden.
Every year we suffer much from vicious winds,
our dwelling is unsettled,
so we often seek Shíbā Yí's protection.
Yesterday, I, Ācuò, could not be compliant,
so it will likely be hard to gain her assistance.
If you, recluse, would not refuse to shelter us,
we would also offer slight repayment."
Xuánwēi said:
"What power do I possess
that could extend to you ladies?"
Ācuò said:
"Simply, on the first day of each year,
make for us a red banner,
upon it paint the patterns of the sun, moon, and five planets,
and erect it east of the garden.
Then calamity will be avoided.
This year has already passed,
but we ask that on the twenty-first day of this month,
at dawn when a slight east wind arises,
you erect it then.
This should suffice to spare us from disaster."
Xuánwēi agreed.
They then thanked him in unison:
"We shall not dare forget your kindness."
They bowed and departed.
Xuánwēi, under the moonlight, followed to see them off.
They crossed the garden wall,
entered the garden,
and each vanished from sight.
Following their words,
on that day he erected the banner.
That day, an east wind shook the earth,
from south of Luòyáng it broke trees and whirled sand,
yet the garden's profuse flowers remained unmoved.
Xuánwēi then understood.
The ladies said their surnames were Yáng, Lǐ, Táo,
and their clothing colors differed—
they were all the spirits of flowers.
The one in crimson named Ācuò
was the pomegranate blossom.
Fēng Shíbā Yí
was the wind spirit.
Several nights later,
Yáng shì and the others came again to express gratitude.
Each brought several pecks of peach and plum blossoms,
urging Master Cuī to consume them,
saying it could prolong life and ward off aging.
If he wished to remain long thus, guarding and protecting them,
he could also attain longevity.
By the beginning of the Yuánhé era,
Xuánwēi was still alive,
looking like a man of about thirty.
Also, at the residence of Tián Hóngzhèng in the Zūnxián ward,
outside the central gate, a tree of purple peonies had grown,
producing over a thousand blossoms.
When the flowers were at their peak,
every moonlit night,
five or six tiny people,
over a foot tall,
would roam upon the flowers.
This continued for seven or eight years.
When people tried to catch them,
they would vanish instantly.
Guest of the Guānghuà Temple.
At the Guanghua Temple on Mount Cúlái in Yǎnzhōu,
there was a guest who studied the Confucian classics,
and was determined to stay there.
On a cool summer day,
he was admiring the wall paintings in the corridor.
Suddenly, he encountered a beautiful woman dressed in white,
about fifteen or sixteen years old,
with extraordinary beauty.
The guest asked where she came from,
and she replied with a smile:
"My home is in front of the mountain."
The guest knew there was no such girl in front of the mountain,
but he did not suspect she was a supernatural being.
However, captivated by her exceptional beauty,
he was eager to gaze upon her.
He flirted and felt delighted,
and thus lured her into his room.
They became intimate and pledged their devotion,
their affection growing deep and close.
The woman in white said:
"I am fortunate that you do not despise me for being from the countryside.
I vow to serve you forever.
However, I must leave tonight,
but when I return, we will not have to part again."
The guest tried to detain her,
employing every possible means,
but ultimately could not keep her.
He had always treasured a white jade ring,
so he gave it to her, saying:
"Please keep this,
so you can return quickly."
Then he saw her off.
The woman in white said:
"I fear my family will come to meet me,
so I hope you will go back now."
The guest then went up to the temple gate tower,
hiding himself to watch her leave.
The woman in white walked about a hundred paces,
when suddenly she vanished.
The guest noted the spot where she disappeared,
and went straight to investigate.
In front of the temple, the land stretched flat for several miles,
with slender trees and fine grass,
not a single hair hidden from view.
He searched meticulously and thoroughly,
but found no trace at all.
As evening approached and he was about to return,
he saw a lily sprout in the grass,
with an exceptionally magnificent white flower.
The guest then dug it up.
Its root was as thick as a clasped hand,
extraordinary and unlike any ordinary plant.
When he returned,
he peeled away its layers,
and after removing all the overlapping parts,
the white jade ring
was clearly inside.
He was shocked, sighed with regret,
became distraught and fell ill,
and died within ten days.
Monk Zhìyǎn
During the Shàngyuán era,
there was a monk named Zhìyǎn in Shǔjùn who recited scriptures at Bǎoxiāng Temple.
Late one night,
suddenly five or six flying insects, as large as flies,
golden in color,
flew repeatedly toward the lamp flame,
or perched on the lamp wick, flapping their wings.
They were the same color as the flame,
and after a while, they vanished into the fire.
This happened for several nights.
A young novice struck one down,
and it turned out to be a dōnglù flower.
It had no distinct shape.
After that, they were no longer seen.
Dèng Guī
West of Jìnyáng, there is a Tóngzǐ Temple located beyond the suburban pastures.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
a man named Dèng Guī was staying at the temple.
That autumn,
he and several friends gathered to spend the night there.
After closing the door,
suddenly a hand appeared through the window.
The hand was yellow and extremely emaciated.
Everyone who saw it
trembled with fear.
Only Guī was unafraid.
Instead, he opened the window.
He heard chanting and whistling sounds,
but Guī was not alarmed.
He inquired:
"Who are you?"
The reply came:
"I have lived in seclusion in the mountain valley for years.
Tonight, I am roaming freely under the wind and moon,
and hearing that you, sir, are here,
I have come to pay my respects.
I truly do not deserve a place at your table,
but I wish to sit by the window,
and listen to your conversation with your guests—that would be enough."
Guī agreed.
After sitting down,
it chatted and laughed with the guests, very cheerfully.
After a long while, it announced its departure.
As it was about to leave,
it said to Guī:
"I will come again tomorrow night.
I hope you will not reject me."
After it left,
Guī discussed with the guests:
"This must be a ghost.
If we do not trace its origins,
it may cause trouble."
So they twisted silk into a rope several hundred fathoms long,
waiting for it to return.
They intended to bind it
firmly.
The next night, it indeed returned,
and again extended its hand through the window.
Guī immediately tied the rope around its arm,
securing it tightly so it could not be undone.
They heard from outside the window:
"What crime have I committed to be bound?
What is the reason for this plan?
Do you not regret this?"
Then it pulled the rope and left.
The next day,
Guī and the guests followed its trail.
About a hundred paces north of the temple,
there was a grapevine,
very lush and dense,
with the rope tied to one of its branches.
There was a leaf shaped like a human hand,
exactly like the one seen at the window.
So they ordered the root to be dug up and burned.
Liú Zào
South of Língshí County, there were often supernatural occurrences at night,
so none of the villagers dared to pass through that area after dark.
During the Yuánhé era,
Dǒng Shūjīng was the governor of Xīhé.
At that time, there was a man named Liú Zào from Péngchéng,
serving as acting Xiàoyì Lieutenant.
Zào had previously offended Dǒng Shū with a letter,
which angered him greatly,
so Zào resigned from his post.
He entered Fénshuǐ Pass,
and at night reached the south of Língshí,
where he encountered a person standing by the roadside.
Its appearance was extremely strange,
and Zào's horse was startled, causing him to fall.
It took a long time for him to get up.
The one standing by the roadside
then removed Zào's robe and put it on itself.
Zào thought it was a robbery,
and did not dare to resist.
Afterward, he walked west for over ten miles,
until he reached an inn,
where he recounted what had happened.
The innkeeper said:
"There are supernatural beings south of the town at night,
so it certainly was not a thief."
The next day,
someone coming from the south of the county
said to Zào:
"In the wilds south of the county, there is a tumbleweed vine,
shaped like a person,
wearing a blue robe—
isn't that strange?"
Zào went to look,
and indeed it was his own robe.
The villagers then realized
that the supernatural being was actually the tumbleweed vine.
So they burned it all,
and the supernatural occurrences ceased.
Tián Bù
In the Táng dynasty, Tián Bù
was the son of Tián Yuè.
During the Yuánhé era,
he once passed by Càibǐ,
where by the roadside there was a grass resembling mugwort.
Its stem was as thick as a finger,
and at its tip clustered leaves,
like a wren's nest among reeds.
He broke it open to look,
and inside the leaves were several dozen small mice,
only as big as soapberry seeds,
their eyes still unopened,
chirping softly.
Liáng Shēng
West of Tángxīngpíng,
there was a country villa of a man named Liáng,
in whose rear garden grew over ten pear trees.
In the eleventh month of winter in the fourth year of the Tàihé era (830 AD),
just after the first snowfall had cleared,
the pear trees suddenly blossomed,
fragrant and luxuriant.
Liáng found this very strange
and considered it an auspicious omen.
A man named Wéi said to Liáng:
"Trees flourish in spring
and wither in winter—
this is their natural course.
How can this be called an auspicious omen?"
Liáng was displeased upon hearing this.
A little over a month later,
Liáng's father passed away.
Sū Chāngyuǎn
During the Zhōnghé era (881-885),
there was a scholar named Sū Chāngyuǎn who lived in a county under Sūzhōu's jurisdiction.
He had a small estate ten lǐ from the official road.
In the watery regions of Wú, lotus and water chestnuts were abundant.
Suddenly one day,
he saw a young woman,
dressed in plain clothes with a rosy face,
beautiful and radiant in appearance.
Observing her features,
she seemed like an immortal from the realm of gods.
From then on, he became intimate with her,
using the estate as their secret meeting place.
Sū became utterly infatuated with her,
and once gave her a jade bracelet as a gift,
tying it with earnest affection.
One day,
he saw a white lotus blooming unusually before the railing,
and bent down to admire it.
He noticed something inside the flower's center.
Looking closely,
it was the jade bracelet he had given her.
He then plucked the flower,
and the supernatural being vanished.
A Man from Shàngdǎng
During the reign of Emperor Wén of Suí,
a man from Shàngdǎng had a voice calling out every night behind his house.
Searching for it, he found nothing.
About one lǐ from the house,
he saw only a ginseng branch.
He dug it up,
and five chǐ into the ground,
it resembled a human body in shape.
After it was dug up,
the calling ceased.
At that time, Prince Yáng of Jìn (the future Emperor Yáng of Suí) secretly harbored plans to seize the succession,
flattering the powerful and influential,
winning the emperor's favor,
forming factions,
and slandering through partisan alliances.
The crown prince was eventually deposed.
The Suí dynasty fell into chaos because of this.
Tián Dēngniáng
On Luó Village atop Báijìng Ridge northwest of Shǎnzhōu,
the Tián family once dug a well
and unearthed a root as thick as an arm.
Its knotted bark resembled Poria cocos,
and its fragrance was similar to Atractylodes.
The family practiced Buddhism,
with several dozen statues enshrined,
so they placed the root before the statues.
The Tián family had a daughter named Dēngniáng,
sixteen or seventeen years old,
possessing beauty.
Her father often had her tend the incense and lamps.
After over a year,
the girl began to see a young man daily entering and leaving the Buddha hall,
dressed in white and wearing clogs.
She then became intimate with him.
Her spirit and demeanor
became unusual.
Each spring, the root would sprout buds.
The girl became pregnant,
and she confessed everything to her mother.
Her mother suspected something supernatural.
Once, a mendicant monk passed by their door,
and the family invited him in to make offerings.
When the monk tried to enter the Buddha hall,
he was repeatedly blocked by something.
One day,
while the girl went out with her mother,
the monk entered the Buddha hall.
As soon as the door opened,
a pigeon brushed past the monk and flew away.
That evening,
the girl no longer saw the supernatural being,
and looking at the root,
it had turned rotten and worm-eaten.
The girl was only seven months pregnant
when she gave birth to three segments,
shaped like the root before the statues.
The Tián family burned them with fire,
and the supernatural being vanished.
Old tales say that wolfberry, Poria cocos, ginseng, and Atractylodes can take unusual forms;
consuming them grants long life.
If one abstains from meat and blood
and avoids lustful desires,
encountering them may allow one to become an earthly immortal.
The Tián family had no such aspirations,
so they encountered the supernatural and removed it.
Fitting indeed!
Zhào Shēng
During the Tiānbǎo era (742-756),
there was a man named Zhào Shēng,
whose ancestors were renowned for literary achievements.
Zhào had several brothers,
all of whom entered official service through the jìnshì or míngjīng examinations.
Only Zhào himself was dull by nature;
although he studied,
he could not parse sentences or grasp their meanings.
Thus, even in his prime, he could not qualify as a provincial candidate.
Often, when gathering with brothers and friends for feasts,
the seats filled with officials in red and green robes,
while Zhào alone wore plain clothes,
which greatly displeased him.
When wine flowed freely,
some would mock him,
and Zhào grew increasingly ashamed and angry.
One day later,
he abandoned his home and fled,
secluding himself in the Jìnyáng Mountains,
where he built a thatched hut.
Zhào had over a hundred volumes of books,
which he carried in a case to the mountains,
studying by day and resting by night,
enduring biting cold and heat.
He ate coarse grains and wore hemp clothes,
undaunted by hardship.
Yet Zhào remained muddled;
the harder he worked, the less progress he made.
Zhào grew even more frustrated and angry.
But he never wavered in his resolve.
Over ten days later,
an old man in coarse clothes came to visit him,
and said to Zhào:
"You dwell deep in the mountains,
reading the books of the ancients.
Do you aspire to official rank and salary?"
However,
the longer you study, the less you can parse sentences and grasp meanings—
how deeply obstructed you are!"
Zhào apologized:
"I am dull-witted,
and I reckon I am old and useless,
so I entered the deep mountains
to read for my own pleasure.
Though I cannot grasp the subtleties,
I am determined to die pursuing my aspirations,
not disgracing my ancestors.
What have I to do with official rank and salary?"
The old man said:
"Your resolve is very firm.
Though I have no special arts to aid you, young sir,
I would be honored if you would visit me once."
Zhào then asked where he lived.
The old man said:
"I am a descendant of the Duàn family,
living under the great tree west of the mountain."
With these words,
he suddenly vanished.
Zhào found this strange,
thinking it supernatural.
He went straight to the west of the mountain to search for traces,
and indeed found a lush Duàn tree.
Zhào said:
"Could this be the descendant of the Duàn family?"
He then took a shovel and dug beneath it,
unearthing a ginseng root over a chǐ long,
closely resembling the old man he had met.
Zhào said:
"I have heard that ginseng capable of supernatural feats
can cure illnesses."
He then boiled and ate it.
From then on, his mind became clear and enlightened;
whatever books he read,
he could fully grasp their profundities.
A little over a year later,
he passed the míngjīng examination.
He served in several official posts before passing away.
Guō Yuánzhèn
Guō Yuánzhèn once lived in the mountains.
In the middle of the night,
a person with a face like a plate,
blinking, emerged from beneath the lamp.
Yuánzhèn showed no fear at all.
Slowly dipping his brush, he inscribed on its cheek:
"Long stationed, men grow old;
far marched, horses grow thin."
These were Yuánzhèn's striking lines.
After finishing the inscription, he chanted them,
and the creature then vanished.
Much later,
Yuánzhèn was strolling leisurely with a woodcutter,
when he saw a white fungus on a giant tree,
as large as several pecks,
and the inscribed lines were upon it.
The Official in Xuānpíng Ward
In the capital's Xuānpíng Ward,
an official was returning home at night.
Entering a lane,
he encountered an oil seller wearing a hat and carrying buckets,
who did not yield the way.
The guide struck him,
and his head fell off,
then hurriedly entered the gate of a large estate.
The official found this strange,
followed it to beneath a large locust tree,
where it vanished.
He therefore informed the household.
The household dug there.
Several feet deep,
along with the tree's withered roots,
they found a large toad as big as a stack.
It held two brush cases.
Tree sap filled them.
And there was a giant white mushroom like the studs on palace gate bubble ornaments.
Its cap had already fallen off.
The toad was the donkey,
the brush cases were the oil buckets,
and the mushroom was the man.
Villagers who had bought his oil for over a month,
had wondered why the oil was good yet cheap.
When the strangeness was discovered,
those who had eaten it all fell ill vomiting.
The Man from Yùzhāng
People of Yùzhāng enjoy eating mushrooms.
The huánggū mushroom is especially delicious.
A commoner's family was building a house,
and cooked this mushroom to feed the workers.
A worker who had climbed onto the roof to lay tiles,
looked down and saw no one,
only a pot cooking something,
covered with a basin.
Suddenly, a naked child ran circling the pot,
and vanished into the pot in an instant.
A moment later,
the host served the meal,
the mushrooms,
but the worker alone did not eat,
nor did he speak.
When evening came,
all who had eaten the mushrooms died.
Azure Dragons
On the night Confucius was born,
two azure dragons stretched across the sky descending,
came to attach to Zhēngzài's chamber,
and thus the Master was born.
Two goddesses held fragrant dew,
coming through the air,
to bathe Zhēngzài.
Cáo Fèng
During the Jiànwǔ era of the Later Hàn,
Cáo Fèng, styled Zhònglǐ,
was Governor of Běidì.
His governance and transformation were especially remarkable.
A yellow dragon appeared at the Gāogāng Pavilion in Jiǔlǐ Valley,
its horns two zhàng long,
ten arm-spans thick,
its tail over ten zhàng long.
The Son of Heaven praised him,
bestowed one hundred bolts of silk,
and increased his rank to Zhōng Èrqiānshí.
Zhāng Lǔ's Daughter
The daughter of Zhāng Lǔ,
once washing clothes at the mountain's foot,
had a white mist envelop her body,
and thus became pregnant.
Ashamed, she took her own life.
About to die,
she said to her maidservant:
"After I die,
you may cut open my belly and look."
The maidservant did as she said,
and obtained a pair of dragon offspring,
then sent them into the Hàn River.
Afterward, the girl was buried in the mountain.
Later, dragons came frequently,
and a path formed before her grave.
The Old Woman of Jiānglíng
An old woman Zhào of Jiānglíng made a living selling wine.
During the Yìxī era,
the ground inside her house suddenly swelled up,
and the old woman, sensing something strange,
poured wine libations morning and evening.
She once saw a creature emerge, its head like a donkey's,
yet initially there was no hole in the ground.
When the old woman died,
the family heard sounds beneath the earth like weeping.
Later people dug the ground,
saw a strange creature wriggling,
its size immeasurable,
and in a moment it was gone.
Common folk called it the earth dragon.
Gān Zōng
The Western Regions affairs reported by Qín envoy Gān Zōng state:
foreign fāngshì capable of divine incantations,
facing a river, perform Yǔ steps and blow breath,
and a dragon immediately floats out.
When first emerging,
it is several tens of zhàng long.
The fāngshì blows upon it,
and with each blow the dragon shrinks.
Until only a few cùn long,
then it is taken and placed in a pot,
and kept with a little water.
Foreign lands often suffer drought disasters,
so when a fāngshì hears of a
place with drought,
he then takes the dragon there,
to sell it.
One dragon is worth several tens of catties of gold.
The whole country pools resources to hire him.
Once payment is complete,
he opens the pot and releases the dragon,
placing it in a deep pool.
Again performing Yǔ steps and blowing,
it grows several tens of zhàng long.
In a moment, rain gathers from all directions.
The Nánxún State
The Nánxún State had a cave, a dark source,
its bottom connecting to the earth's veins,
containing hairy dragons and hairy fish.
They occasionally shed their bones in open marshes.
Fish and dragons dwelled together in the same cave.
That state presented a hairy dragon to Yīn.
Yīn
established an office for rearing dragons.
It continued until the Xià dynasty.
They thus took it as a clan name.
By the time Yǔ channeled the rivers,
and the four seas converged,
they were released at Luòruì.
Dragon Lair
"The Supplement to the Records of Wang Zinián" states:
East of Mount Fāngzhàng lies a dragon field,
covering an area of a thousand lǐ.
Dragon skins and bones are piled like hills,
scattered across over a hundred qǐng.
"Records of Strange Things" says:
"In Jìnníng County, there is a Dragon Burial Isle.
The elders say
that dragons shed their bones on this isle,
and its waters still hold many dragon bones today.
As for hills, ridges, and peaks
that can summon clouds and rain,
all have dragon bones.
Some are deep, some shallow,
mostly buried in the earth.
Teeth, horns, tails, and feet
are all distinctly preserved.
The larger ones measure several tens of zhàng,
some as thick as ten arm-spans.
The smaller ones are only one or two chǐ,
or three to four cùn.
Their bodies are fully intact.
I have seen them myself when they were collected."
"Discourses Weighed in the Balance" states:
"Cicadas are born from the belly.
They emerge by splitting their backs,
and must shed their skins in the rain,
like
snakes shedding their skin."
Recently, a household in Púzhōu
dismantled a thatched hut
and found a dragon bone over a zhàng long on the roof beam,
perfectly intact.
Five-Colored Stone
Quán Wénměng, a hermit from Mount Tiānmù,
obtained a five-colored stone as large as a dou measure on the western shore of Guānyīn Temple at Hòuhú in Xīnfēng.
Its patterns coiled and gathered,
as if glowing in the dark.
Wénměng considered it divine and extraordinary,
and, embracing it, presented it to Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
Emperor Wǔ was delighted
and ordered it placed beside the Tàijí Hall.
After more than a year,
the stone suddenly illuminated the corridors and side rooms,
emitting a sound like thunder.
The emperor deemed this inauspicious
and summoned Master Jié to examine it.
He replied:
"This is a stone from the upper realm that transforms into dragons,
not an object of the mortal world.
If mixed with Luòshuǐ red whetstone and wine as medicine,
boiled over a hundred times,
it becomes soft and edible.
Carved into vessels for food and drink,
it extends human lifespan.
Those blessed with virtue and fortune
are destined to use it.
The sound
indicates dragons wish to retrieve it."
The emperor ordered a swift retrieval of the red stone.
Following this method,
he commanded artisans to carve it into bowls,
each holding half of five dǒu,
to contain imperial meals.
The fragrance and flavor were exceptionally fine.
The remaining fragments
were placed in their original spot.
Suddenly, a red dragon,
whiskers bristling and mane fluttering,
swung its tail and entered the hall,
embraced the stone, and leaped away.
The emperor dispatched officials to investigate.
It turned out to be the stone
from Shígǔ Village in Shǐpíng Commandery,
contested by fighting dragons in the second year of the Pǔtōng era.
The bowls were lost during the rebellion of Hóu Jǐng,
their whereabouts unknown.
Cave of Zhènzé
In Lake Zhènzé,
south of Mount Dòngtíng, there is a cave over a hundred feet deep.
A man named Yǎng Gōng □ accidentally fell into the cave,
walked sideways,
ascended and descended for over fifty li,
and arrived at a dragon palace.
It was four or five li in circumference,
with green mud up to the knees below,
and palace halls with gates and towers.
The dragon used its breath to part the water,
creating a mist like light fog,
and there was light day and night.
He encountered a small horned dragon guarding the gate,
which spread its scales and brandished its claws to block him,
preventing him from entering.
Yǎng Gōng □ stayed in the cave for over a hundred days,
eating the green mud,
which tasted like non-glutinous rice.
Suddenly, as if in a dream, he found the way back,
and soon emerged.
When he served as the governor of Wú Commandery,
he reported the matter in detail to Emperor Wǔ of Liáng.
The emperor asked Jié Gōng.
Jié Gōng said:
"This cave has four branches:
one leads to the western shore of Lake Dòngtíng,
one leads to the northern shore of Qīngyī Pǔ on the Shǔ road,
one leads to the cave stream between the two mountains of Luófú,
and one leads to the eastern shore of Kūsāng Island.
The seventh daughter of the East Sea Dragon King is in charge of the dragon king's pearl treasury,
guarded by thousands of small dragons protecting these pearls.
Dragons fear wax,
love beautiful jade and azurite, and are fond of swallows.
If an envoy is sent with sincerity,
the treasure pearls can be obtained."
The emperor was greatly pleased upon hearing this.
He then issued an edict seeking anyone capable of going,
offering generous rewards.
There was a man from Báishuǐ Village, Mào County, Kuàijī Commandery,
Yǔ Píluó, who volunteered.
Jié Gōng said:
"Your fifth-generation ancestor burned to death over a hundred dragons in the East Sea pool east of Mào County,
and was later killed by dragons in return.
You are a descendant of the dragon gate's troublemakers,
can you go?"
Píluó admitted the truth,
and stopped.
Then, two brothers, Luó Zǐchūn and his sibling from Ōuyuè, Luòlí County, Hépǔ Commandery,
submitted a memorial stating:
"For generations, our family has intermarried with the dragons of Língshuǐ and Luóshuǐ.
Our distant ancestor was skilled at taming evil dragons.
Emperor Jiǎnwén of Jìn employed our ancestor to pacify a poisonous dragon.
The present-day Lónghuà County
was originally our ancestor's residence.
The stone dragon of Xiàng Commandery,
fierce and difficult to tame,
was tamed by our ancestor.
This is now Shílóng County.
The great dragons of the East Sea, Tiāntāi, Xiāngchuān, Pénglí, Tónggǔ, Shítóu, and other waters
all recognize our ancestors,
and know we are their descendants.
We request to convey the emperor's command."
Jié Gōng said:
"Is your family's dragon-controlling stone still in existence?"
They replied:
"It is, it is.
We will respectfully bring it to the capital,
for you to examine."
Jié Gōng said:
"Your stone can only control dragons that summon minor wind and rain or foreign invaders,
not the dragons guarding the sea king's pearl treasury."
He then asked:
"Do you have West Sea dragon brain incense?"
They said:
"No."
Jié Gōng said:
"Then how can you control dragons?"
The emperor said:
"The matter cannot succeed."
Jié Gōng said:
"On West Sea ships,
dragon brain incense can be obtained.
In the past, the Tóngbǎi Perfected Man often promoted the Daoist teachings,
and when Xǔ Mì and Máo Róng rode dragons,
he gave each ten catties of dragon-controlling stone.
These should still exist,
please seek them out."
The emperor ordered a search.
Two pieces of stone were obtained from Táo Hóngjǐng, the recluse of Huálóng on Mount Máo.
Jié Gōng said:
"These are it."
The emperor ordered artisans
to use fine jade from the Shūhé River in Yútián
to make two small boxes,
polishing them with tung wood ash to make them shine,
and to take azurite from Xuān Prefecture,
selecting the finest,
bonding it with fish glue,
to make two jars.
They were fired.
Dragon brain incense soon arrived as well.
Jié Gōng said:
"Coat Zǐchūn and the others' bodies and clothing with wax."
They then took five hundred roasted swallows into the cave,
reaching the dragon palace.
The small horned dragons guarding the gate smelled the wax,
and prostrated themselves, not daring to move.
They bribed them with a hundred roasted swallows,
asking them to convey a message.
They presented the finest ones to the dragon maiden,
who ate them with great delight.
They also presented the jade boxes and azurite jars,
fully conveying the emperor's intentions.
In the cave was a thousand-year-old dragon capable of transformation,
moving in and out of the human world,
skilled at translating contemporary speech.
The dragon maiden, knowing the emperor's courtesy,
gave three large pearls, seven small pearls, and a shí of assorted pearls
in return to the emperor.
She ordered Zǐchūn to ride a dragon,
carrying the pearls back to the country,
arriving in the time it takes to eat a meal.
The dragon took its leave,
and Zǐchūn presented the pearls.
The emperor was overjoyed.
He had succeeded in communicating with the spiritual and strange,
obtaining treasures of heaven and humanity.
He showed the pearls to Jié Gōng.
Jié Gōng said:
"Of the three large pearls,
one is a lower-grade Rúyì pearl of the Heavenly Emperor,
and two are middle-grade Lílóng pearls.
Of the seven small pearls,
two are insect pearls,
five are sea clam pearls,
the finest among mortals.
The assorted pearls are from clams and other shellfish,
not as precious as the large pearls."
The emperor showed them to all officials,
and the court all said Jié Gōng was deceitful and exaggerated,
none failing to question him.
Jié Gōng said:
"The highest-grade Rúyì pearl
shines at night for over forty li;
the middle-grade for ten li;
the lower-grade for one li.
Where its light reaches,
there is no wind, rain, thunder, lightning, flood, fire, weapons, or any poison or pestilence.
The highest-grade Lílóng pearl
shines at night for a hundred paces;
the middle-grade for ten paces;
the lower-grade for a single room.
Where its light reaches,
there is no poison from snakes, vipers, or insects.
Insect pearls
are seven-colored, mostly red,
with six legs and two eyes,
and at their concave spot,
there is a mortar-like
shape like an iron nose.
Clam pearls are five-colored.
All shine at night,
up to several feet.
Flawless ones are superior,
flawed ones are inferior.
The five pearl clams
wax and wane with the moon.
The origin of snake pearls
is like the story of Suí Hóu and Cānshé,
that is the matter."
They also asked about the differences between snake and crane pearls.
He replied:
"Let them choose for themselves."
The emperor ordered Jié Gōng to record the snake and crane pearls.
Over a dǒu of assorted pearls
were scattered before the hall.
Dozens of large yellow snakes and black cranes were taken
and placed among the pearls.
Then the cranes picked up their pearls,
singing, dancing, and pacing;
the snakes picked up their pearls,
coiling and winding.
The officials watching
could not help but sigh in admiration.
The emperor then brought out the Rúyì, dragon, insect, and other pearls,
testing the distance of their light.
The numbers seven, nine, and eight
all matched Jié Gōng's words.
The food Zǐchūn obtained in the dragon palace
was like flowers, like medicine,
like green, like malt sugar,
fragrant and delicious to eat.
When he brought some back to the capital,
exposed to the wind and sun of the mortal world,
it hardened like stone,
impossible to chew or swallow.
The emperor ordered the secret treasury to store it.
Zǐchūn was appointed Commandant of Chariots and Cavalry,
and his two brothers were appointed Court Advisers.
Bestowed one thousand bolts each of silk and linen.
They sought to inquire into the reason why Duke □ had not been harmed by the dragon in the past,
which was because he used hemp oil mixed with wax,
to make a fish-illuminating garment,
and thus his body carried the scent of wax.
Empress of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng
Empress Xī of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng was by nature jealous and envious.
When Emperor Wǔ first ascended the throne,
before she could be formally installed as empress,
out of resentment and anger,
she suddenly threw herself into a well in the palace courtyard.
The crowd rushed to the well to rescue her,
but she had already transformed into a poisonous dragon,
with smoke and flames soaring to the sky,
and no one dared approach.
The emperor lamented sorrowfully for a long time,
and thus posthumously honored her as the Dragon Heavenly King,
erecting a shrine over the well.
Liú Jiǎ
In the Sòng dynasty, Liú Jiǎ resided in Jiānglíng.
During the Yuánjiā era,
his daughter, aged fourteen,
graceful and beautiful in appearance,
though she had never read Buddhist scriptures,
suddenly could recite the Lotus Sutra from memory.
In the room where the girl lived,
soon a strange light appeared.
The girl said,
"I have attained true enlightenment,
and it is fitting to hold a fourteen-day fasting ceremony."
Her family prepared a high seat for her,
and set up a precious canopy.
The girl ascended the seat,
discoursing on profound teachings.
She also spoke of people's fortunes and calamities,
and all matters she foretold came true.
People from near and far paid her reverence and respect,
offering clothes and treasures,
too numerous to count.
Prince Héngyáng, while stationed in the region,
personally led his officials to observe her.
After twelve days,
a Daoist priest named Shǐ Xuánzhēn said:
"This is a demonic evil."
He shook his robe and went there.
The girl already knew of his coming,
and sent people to guard the door.
She said:
"Demonic evil will soon arrive;
anyone wearing Daoist robes
must not be admitted."
Zhēn changed his clothes and stealthily entered.
The girl at first shouted and cursed,
but Zhēn went straight forward,
sprinkled water on her,
and she immediately collapsed unconscious.
After a long while, she revived.
When asked about the various events,
she said she remembered nothing.
Zhēn said:
"This was a dragon spirit's possession."
From then on, she returned to normal,
and later married as the wife of a man named Xuān.
Sòng Yún
In the Later Wèi dynasty, Sòng Yún was sent as an envoy to the Western Regions.
He reached the Snow Accumulation Mountain,
where there was a pond,
inhabited by a poisonous dragon.
In the past, three hundred merchants had camped beside the pond,
when the dragon became enraged,
and drowned the merchants.
King Guǒtuó heard of this,
abdicated his throne to his son,
and went to the country of Wūchǎng to study Brahmanic spells.
Within four years,
he mastered the art.
Returning to reclaim his throne,
he went to the pond and chanted spells at the dragon.
The dragon transformed into a human,
repented and submitted to the king.
The king then pardoned it.
Cài Yù
Cài Yù, the governor of Hóngnóng Commandery, held a fasting ceremony at Chóngjìng Temple on a national day of mourning.
Suddenly, a dense black cloud
rose from the northeast,
directly over the Buddha hall.
Faint thunder rumbled within the cloud.
The officials had not yet begun the incense offering,
and were all gathered in front of the hall,
standing together looking upward.
They saw two boys in red robes
and two boys in blue robes,
all descending from the cloud.
The two red-robed boys first went to the pillar at the southwest corner of the hall,
pulled out a white snake over ten feet long,
and threw it upward into the cloud.
The thunder gradually grew louder and descended.
After a short while,
the white snake fell straight down from the cloud,
and returned into the pillar from which it had been taken.
Then the cloud lowered until it touched the ground.
The blue-robed boys descended and took positions,
one lifting the hall pillar
several inches off the ground.
The other boy pulled out another white snake, about twenty feet long, from below,
and threw it upward into the cloud.
Then all four boys soared upward together,
entering the cloud and departing.
The cloud gradually rose higher,
spreading across the sky.
By night,
heavy thunder and rain poured down,
and did not clear until morning.
Later, when they examined the base of the hall pillar,
they found it had shifted about half an inch,
no longer in its original place.
The temple monks said the pillar was hollow inside.
They chiseled into the pillar to its core,
and indeed found it hollow inside,
serving as a hiding place for dragons.
Lǐ Jìng
Lǐ Jìng, Duke of Wèiguó of the Táng dynasty,
in his humble youth,
once went hunting in Líng Mountain.
He stayed and ate in the mountains.
An old man in the village found his character remarkable,
and often provided him with generous provisions,
which grew even more abundant over the years.
Suddenly, he encountered a herd of deer
and pursued them.
As dusk fell,
he wished to give up but could not.
Soon, darkness descended and he lost his way,
utterly bewildered and unsure of how to return.
He walked on in dejection,
his distress growing ever deeper.
In the distance, he glimpsed the light of a lamp,
and so he galloped toward it.
Upon arrival,
he found a grand mansion with vermilion gates,
its walls and structures towering and imposing.
He knocked on the gate for a long time
before someone came out to inquire.
Jìng explained that he was lost
and requested lodging for the night.
The person said:
"The young master is away,
only the matriarch is present.
Staying the night may not be possible."
Jìng said:
"Please try to inform her."
The person then went in to report.
Returning, he said:
"The matriarch initially wished to refuse,
but considering the darkness
and the guest's claim of being lost,
she felt she could not avoid playing host."
He was invited into the hall.
After a short while,
a maidservant came out and said:
"The matriarch is coming."
She appeared to be over fifty years old,
dressed in a dark skirt and plain jacket,
her demeanor refined and elegant,
much like that of a scholar-official's household.
Jìng stepped forward and bowed to her.
The matriarch returned the bow and said:
"My sons are all away,
and it is not proper for me to entertain a guest.
However, the sky is dark,
and you have lost your way back.
If I do not offer you shelter here,
where else could you go?
Yet this is a dwelling in the wild mountains.
When my sons return,
they may arrive at night and cause a commotion—
please do not be alarmed."
Soon after, a meal was served.
It was quite fresh and delicious,
though it consisted mostly of fish.
After eating,
the matriarch retired to her quarters.
Two maidservants brought a bed, mat, cushions, and quilts—
the bedding was fragrant and clean,
all meticulously arranged.
They then closed the door, fastened it, and left.
Jìng, alone, wondered: In this remote mountain wilderness,
what could be making noise upon arriving at night?
Fearful, he dared not sleep,
and sat upright listening.
As midnight approached,
he heard urgent knocking at the gate.
Then he heard someone respond,
saying:
"A celestial mandate:
inform the eldest young master that he must make rain.
The area spans seven hundred lǐ around this mountain,
and by the fifth watch, it must be sufficient.
Do not delay or be negligent,
and do not be violent or harsh."
The respondent received the mandate and went inside to present it.
Jìng heard the matriarch say:
"My two sons have not yet returned.
The rain-making mandate has arrived,
and it cannot be refused.
To disobey would bring punishment.
Even if we try to inform them,
it would be too late.
Servants cannot take on such a responsibility.
What should we do?"
A young maidservant said:
"I observed the guest in the hall earlier—
he is no ordinary man.
Why not ask him?"
The matriarch was pleased.
She then knocked on his door herself and said:
"Are you awake, sir?
Please come out for a moment to meet."
Jìng said:
"Very well."
He then descended the steps to see her.
The matriarch said:
"This is not a human dwelling—
it is a dragon palace.
My eldest son has gone to the Eastern Sea for a wedding,
and my younger son is escorting his sister.
Just now, a celestial mandate arrived,
and it is our turn to make rain.
Considering the distances to their locations,
it totals over ten thousand lǐ.
Informing them is impossible,
and finding a substitute is difficult.
I would like to trouble you for just a moment.
What do you say?"
Jìng said:
"I am a mortal,
not one who rides the clouds.
How could I make rain?
If there is a method you can teach me,
I will follow your instructions."
The matriarch said:
"If you follow my words,
nothing is impossible."
She then ordered a yellow-haired attendant
to bring a dappled gray horse.
She also commanded that the rain-making tool be fetched—
it was a small bottle,
tied to the front of the saddle.
She instructed him:
"Sir, mount the horse,
do not pull the reins—
the bit and bridle—
let it go as it will.
When the horse paws the ground and neighs,
take one drop of water from the bottle
and drip it onto the horse's mane.
Be careful not to use more."
Thereupon, he mounted the horse and it soared into the air,
swiftly rising higher and higher.
He was only amazed at its speed and stealth,
unaware that he was already above the clouds.
The wind was sharp as arrows,
and thunder rumbled beneath his feet.
Then, wherever the horse leaped,
he dripped a drop.
Soon, lightning flashed and the clouds parted,
revealing below the village where he had stayed.
He thought to himself:
"I have troubled this village greatly.
I have long been grateful to its people,
yet I have had no way to repay them.
Now there has been a long drought,
and the seedlings are about to wither.
Since the rain is in my hands,
why should I begrudge it?"
Considering that one drop would not be enough to moisten the land,
he instead released twenty drops in succession.
Shortly after, the rain ceased,
and he rode the horse back.
The matriarch was weeping in the hall and said:
"How gravely you have erred!
The agreement was for one drop,
why did you secretly release twenty chǐ of rain?
One drop
equals one chǐ of rain on the ground.
In that village at midnight,
the flat ground was submerged under twenty zhàng of water.
How could anyone still be alive?
I have already been punished,
receiving eighty strokes of the rod."
Looking at her back,
it was covered with bloody welts.
"My sons will also be implicated.
What is to be done?"
Jìng was ashamed and terrified,
at a loss for words.
The matriarch continued:
"You, sir, are a man of the mortal world,
unfamiliar with the workings of clouds and rain.
I truly cannot bear you ill will.
However, I fear the dragon master may come searching,
which would cause you alarm.
You should leave here quickly.
Yet you have gone to this trouble,
and I have nothing with which to repay you.
In this mountain dwelling, we have few possessions,
but I offer you two servants as gifts.
You may take both,
or take just one.
The choice is yours."
Thereupon, she ordered the two servants to come out.
One servant emerged from the eastern corridor—
his appearance gentle and amiable,
cheerful and pleasant.
The other servant emerged from the western corridor—
his expression filled with fierce energy,
standing with an air of defiance and anger.
Jìng said:
"I am a hunter,
accustomed to fierce contests.
Now I will take just one servant,
To seek to please others,
makes people think I am timid."
Thus he said:
"I dare not take both of them.
Since the lady has bestowed them,
I wish to take the one who appears angry."
The lady smiled and said:
"So this is what you desire."
Then she bowed and bid farewell,
and the servant also followed and left.
After walking a few steps out the door,
he turned back to look, but the mansion had vanished.
When he turned to ask his servant,
he too was nowhere to be seen.
Alone, he searched for the way back.
By the time it was light,
looking toward the village,
the water had reached as far as the eye could see,
with only the tops of large trees occasionally visible,
and no longer any people.
Later, he ultimately used military power to quell the turmoil of rebellion,
achieving merits that overshadowed the world.
Yet he never reached the position of chancellor.
Was it not because he failed to take the servant?
It is said in the world that east of the pass produces chancellors,
and west of the pass produces generals.
Is this not a metaphor for east and west?
The reason for speaking of the servant
is also a symbol of subordinates.
If he had taken both servants,
he would have reached the pinnacle of both general and chancellor.
Liǔ Yì
During the Yìfèng era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a scholar named Liǔ Yì who, having failed the imperial examinations,
was preparing to return to the Xiāng River region.
Recalling that a fellow townsman was staying in Jīngyáng,
he went to bid him farewell.
After traveling six or seven lǐ,
birds suddenly took flight, startling his horse,
which bolted off the path to the left.
After another six or seven lǐ,
it finally stopped.
There he saw a woman
herding sheep by the roadside.
Liǔ Yì looked at her curiously;
she was a woman of exceptional beauty.
Yet her moth-like brows were knit in distress,
and her clothes lacked luster.
Standing still as if poised to fly, she listened intently,
as if waiting for something.
Liǔ Yì questioned her:
"What hardship causes you to humble yourself in such a manner?"
At first, the woman, pained, declined to answer,
but finally, weeping, she replied:
"This unworthy woman is unfortunate,
and today I have shamed myself before a gentleman.
Yet the hatred that pierces my bones and marrow
prevents me from feeling shame and hiding.
I beg you to listen:
I am the youngest daughter of the Dragon Lord of Dòngtíng Lake.
My parents married me to the second son of the Jīngchuān Dragon.
But my husband delights in pleasure and idleness,
and, misled by his servants and maids,
grows daily more disdainful and cold toward me.
Later, I complained to my parents-in-law.
They dote on their son
and could not control him.
As my complaints grew more frequent and urgent,
I further offended my parents-in-law.
They degraded and banished me, reducing me to this state."
Having finished speaking,
she sobbed and shed tears,
overwhelmed with grief.
She continued:
"From here to Dòngtíng,
the distance is immeasurably far.
Under the vast, boundless sky,
no message can get through.
My heart is broken, my eyes worn out from longing,
yet there is no one to know my sorrow.
I heard you are returning to Wú,
which lies close to Dòngtíng.
Perhaps I could entrust a letter to your attendants?
I wonder if you would consider this possible?"
Liǔ Yì said:
"I am a man of honor.
Hearing your story,
my blood boils with indignation.
I only regret I lack wings,
and cannot fly to your aid immediately.
How could there be any question of refusal?
However, Dòngtíng is a deep lake.
I am a man of the dusty world;
how could I possibly convey a message there?
I only fear the paths between the visible and hidden realms
do not connect,
causing me to fail your sincere trust,
and violate my own earnest wish.
Do you have a method
to guide me there?"
The woman wept sorrowfully and thanked him, saying:
"I accept your burden and bid you take care.
I will say no more.
If I receive a reply,
I will thank you even in death.
Since you did not consent,
how could I dare speak?
But now that you have consented and asked,
then the journey to Dòngtíng is no different
from going to the capital."
Liǔ Yì begged her to explain.
The woman said:
"On the north shore of Dòngtíng Lake,
there is a large orange tree
which the local people call the Shè Orange Tree.
You should remove this belt,
tie it with something else,
and then knock on the tree three times.
Someone will respond.
Follow that person,
and you will encounter no obstacles.
I beg you, beyond the contents of the letter,
to convey all the words from my sincere heart.
Please, on no account fail in this."
Liǔ Yì said:
"I respectfully heed your instructions."
The woman then took a letter from her robe,
bowed twice, and presented it to him.
Gazing eastward, she wept sorrowfully,
as if unable to bear her grief.
Liǔ Yì was deeply moved by her distress.
He placed the letter in his bag.
Then he asked again:
"I do not understand—the sheep you herd,
what are they for?
Do spirits and deities slaughter them?"
The woman said:
"They are not sheep,
they are Rain Workers."
"What are Rain Workers?"
She replied:
"They are creatures like thunder and lightning."
Liǔ Yì looked at them several times,
and saw they all held their heads high, strode angrily,
and ate and drank in a very peculiar manner.
But in size, wool, and horns,
they were no different from ordinary sheep.
Liǔ Yì said further:
"I will act as your messenger.
When I someday return to Dòngtíng,
I hope you will not avoid me."
The woman said:
"Not only will I not avoid you,
I shall treat you as a relative."
When their conversation ended,
she turned and departed eastward.
After he had gone fewer than a few dozen paces,
he looked back at the woman and the sheep,
but they had all vanished from sight.
That evening,
he reached the town and bid farewell to his friend.
Over a month later,
he arrived home in his village.
Then he went to seek out Dòngtíng Lake.
On the north shore of Dòngtíng,
there was indeed an Orange Shrine.
So he changed his belt, faced the tree,
and struck it three times before stopping.
Soon a warrior emerged from the waves,
bowed twice, and inquired:
"Honored guest, from where have you come?"
Liǔ Yì did not tell him the truth,
saying instead:
"I have come to pay a visit to the great king."
The warrior parted the waters to point the way
and led Liǔ Yì forward.
He said to Liǔ Yì:
"You must close your eyes.
We will arrive in a few breaths."
Liǔ Yì did as he was told,
and soon reached the palace.
He began to see pavilions and towers facing each other,
with countless gates and doors,
rare grasses and precious trees—
there was nothing lacking.
The warrior then stopped Liǔ Yì in a corner of a great hall.
He said:
"Please wait here, guest."
Liǔ Yì asked:
"What place is this?"
The warrior replied:
"This is the Língxū Hall."
Looking carefully,
Liǔ Yì saw that all the treasures of the human world
were gathered here in their entirety.
The pillars were of white jade,
the steps of green jade,
the bed of coral,
the curtains of crystal.
Green lintels were carved with lapis lazuli,
rainbow beams were adorned with amber.
The scene was exquisitely beautiful, deep and secluded,
impossible to describe fully.
Yet the king did not arrive for a long time.
Liǔ Yì said to the warrior:
"Where is the Lord of Dòngtíng?"
He replied:
"My lord is presently at the Xuánzhū Pavilion,
discussing the Great Canon with the Tàiyáng Daoist priest.
He should finish shortly."
Liǔ Yì asked:
"What is the Great Canon?"
The warrior said:
"My lord is a dragon.
Dragons take water as their divine essence;
a single drop can engulf hills and valleys.
The Daoist priest is a human.
Humans take fire as their sacred essence;
a single lamp's flame could burn down the Ēpáng Palace.
However, their spiritual functions differ,
and their mysterious transformations are not the same.
The Tàiyáng Daoist priest is deeply versed in human principles,
so my lord has invited him to lecture."
As he finished speaking,
the palace gates opened,
and a retinue followed like shadows, gathering like clouds.
Then he saw a man clad in purple robes,
holding a green jade tablet.
The warrior leaped up and said:
"This is my lord."
He then went forward to announce Liǔ Yì.
The lord looked at Liǔ Yì and asked:
"Are you not a man of the mortal world?"
Liǔ Yì replied:
"Indeed."
Liǔ Yì then bowed in greeting,
and the Lord also bowed.
He invited Liǔ Yì to sit beneath the Língxū Hall.
He said to Liǔ Yì:
"The water palace is deep and secluded,
and I am ignorant and dull.
You, sir, have not considered a thousand lǐ too far to come;
do you have some purpose?"
Liǔ Yì said:
"I, Yì,
am a fellow countryman of Your Majesty.
I grew up in Chǔ,
and traveled to Qín to study.
Recently, having failed the examinations,
as I was riding along the right bank of the Jīng River,
I saw Your Majesty's beloved daughter
herding sheep in the wilderness.
With wind-tousled hair and rain-beaten temples,
her appearance was unbearable to behold.
I therefore questioned her,
and she told me
that she was mistreated by her husband,
and her parents-in-law showed no concern,
leading to this plight.
Her tears flowed freely in sorrow,
truly distressing to the heart.
She then entrusted a letter to me.
I promised her.
And now I have come here."
Thereupon, he took out the letter and presented it.
The Lord of Dòngtíng finished reading it,
covered his face with his sleeve and wept, saying:
"It is the crime of this old father,
who failed to discern
and to listen,
sitting idly by like one deaf and blind,
causing my young and delicate daughter,
to suffer harm far away.
You, sir, are but a stranger on the road,
yet you hastened to her aid.
Fortunately, I still possess teeth and hair (am still alive);
how dare I betray this virtue?"
When he finished speaking,
he lamented sorrowfully for a long time.
All his attendants shed tears.
At that time, there was a palace eunuch closely attending the Lord;
the Lord handed him the letter,
ordering him to deliver it to the inner palace.
In a moment,
wailing arose from throughout the palace.
The Lord, alarmed, said to his attendants:
"Quickly inform the palace
not to make any sound.
I fear Qiántáng may hear of it."
Liǔ Yì said:
"Who is Qiántáng?"
The Lord replied:
"He is my beloved younger brother.
Formerly, he was the ruler of Qiántáng,
but now he has retired from governance."
Liǔ Yì said:
"Why must he not know?"
The Lord said:
"Because his valor surpasses ordinary men.
In ancient times, the nine-year flood that plagued Emperor Yáo
was caused by a single fit of his anger.
Recently, having fallen out with a celestial general,
he blocked up five mountains.
The Supreme Emperor, considering that I have shown some slight virtue throughout the ages,
thus pardoned the crime of my own flesh and blood.
However, he is still confined here.
Therefore, the people of Qiántáng
await his return daily."
Before he finished speaking,
a tremendous sound suddenly erupted,
as if heaven split and earth cracked,
the palace halls shook and swayed,
clouds and mist seethed and surged.
Suddenly, a crimson dragon over a thousand chǐ long appeared,
with lightning eyes and a bloody tongue,
vermilion scales and fiery mane,
a golden lock around its neck,
the lock chained to a jade pillar,
amidst thousands of thunders and myriads of lightning bolts,
swirling and crackling around its body,
with sleet, snow, rain, and hail
all falling at once.
Then, breaking through the azure sky, it flew away.
Liǔ Yì, terrified, fell prostrate to the ground.
The Lord personally rose to support him, saying:
"Do not fear,
it is certainly harmless."
After a long while, Liǔ Yì gradually calmed down,
and finally regained his composure.
He then took his leave, saying:
"I wish to return alive,
to avoid his coming again."
The Lord said:
"It certainly will not be so.
His departure was like that,
but his return will not be.
I beg you to stay awhile, so I may express my heartfelt feelings."
Thereupon, he ordered wine to be poured and cups raised,
to show hospitality.
Soon, auspicious winds and felicitous clouds arose,
warm and harmonious,
with exquisite banners and insignia,
followed by the music of pipes and sháo bells.
Thousands of beauties in red attire,
chatted and laughed joyfully.
Behind them was one person,
with naturally beautiful eyebrows,
adorned with bright pearls all over,
wearing garments of fine silk, layered and flowing.
Drawing closer to look,
it was the one who had previously entrusted the message.
Yet her expression seemed both joyful and sorrowful,
with tears falling in streams.
In a moment, red mist veiled her left side,
purple aura spread to her right,
fragrant air swirled around,
as she entered the palace.
The Lord said to Liǔ Yì with a smile:
"The prisoner from the Jīng River has arrived."
The Lord then excused himself and returned to the inner palace.
After a short while,
sounds of grief and anguish were heard again,
lasting for a long time without ceasing.
After a while,
the Lord came out again,
and feasted with Liǔ Yì.
There was another person, clad in purple robe,
holding a piece of green jade,
with a majestic appearance and radiant spirit,
standing beside the Lord.
The Lord said to Liǔ Yì:
"This is Qiántáng."
Liǔ Yì rose
and hurried forward to bow.
Qiántáng also received him with full courtesy,
saying to Liǔ Yì:
"My niece was unfortunate,
insulted by that obstinate youth.
Thanks to your clear integrity and illustrious faithfulness,
her distant grievance was conveyed.
Otherwise,
she would have become earth at Jīnglíng.
We feast on your virtue and cherish your kindness,
words cannot fully express our gratitude."
Liǔ Yì withdrew his hand, declining and thanking him,
bowing and assenting repeatedly.
Then Qiántáng turned and reported to his elder brother:
"I departed from Língxū at the chén hour,
reached Jīngyáng at the sì hour,
fought there at the wǔ hour,
and returned here at the wèi hour.
In between, I galloped to the Nine Heavens,
to report to the Supreme Emperor.
The Emperor, knowing her grievance, pardoned my fault;
the previous punishment imposed on me
was thus remitted.
However, my fierce temper was aroused,
and I had no time to bid farewell,
alarming the palace,
and further offending our guest.
I am ashamed, fearful, and regretful,
not knowing how to atone."
Thereupon, he withdrew and bowed twice.
The Lord asked:
"How many did you kill?"
He replied:
"Six hundred thousand."
"Was the harvest damaged?"
He said:
"For eight hundred lǐ."
"Where is that heartless lad?"
He said:
"I ate him."
The Lord sighed and said:
"The obstinate youth harboring such a heart
was truly unbearable.
However, you were also too rash.
Fortunately, the Supreme Emperor displayed his sagely insight,
understanding the extremity of her grievance.
Otherwise,
how could I excuse myself?
From now on,
do not act like this again."
Qiántáng bowed twice again.
That evening,
they lodged Liǔ Yì in the Níngguāng Hall.
The next day,
they feasted Liǔ Yì again at the Níngbì Palace.
Gathering friends and relatives,
setting out grand music,
providing fine wines,
and arraying sweet delicacies.
First, reed pipes, horns, war drums,
banners, flags, swords, and halberds
danced with ten thousand warriors on the right.
Among them, one warrior stepped forward and said:
"This is the 'Breaking the Battle Formation' music of Qiántáng."
The banners and halberds exuded heroic spirit,
their swift glances fierce and intimidating.
The seated guests watched,
their hair standing on end.
Then came metal, stone, silk, and bamboo instruments,
with silks, pearls, and jade ornaments,
dancing with a thousand maidens on the left.
Among them, one maiden stepped forward and said:
"This is the 'Returning to the Palace' music of the noble princess."
The clear, melodious sounds,
like lamenting, like yearning.
The seated guests listened,
unconsciously shedding tears.
After both dances concluded,
the Dragon Lord was greatly pleased,
bestowing silks and brocades,
distributing them among the dancers.
Then, seating themselves closely in rows,
they drank freely and enjoyed themselves to the fullest.
When the wine was at its height,
the Lord of Dòngtíng struck the mat and sang:
"Vast is the great sky, oh,
boundless the great earth.
Each person has their own aspirations, oh,
how can they be fathomed?
Fox spirits and rat sages, oh,
cling to walls and shrines.
When thunderbolts strike, oh,
who dares to stand against them?
Grateful to the true man for his enduring faith and righteousness,
reuniting flesh and bone, returning to their homeland.
All speak of shame and gratitude—when will it ever be forgotten?"
After the Lord of Dòngtíng finished his song,
the Lord of Qiántáng bowed twice and sang:
"Heaven matches couples, oh,
life and death have their paths.
This one should not be a wife, oh,
that one should not be a husband.
Heart and soul endure hardship, oh,
by the banks of the Jīng River.
Wind and frost fill the temples, oh,
rain and snow soak the garments.
Thanks to the noble sir for delivering the plain letter,
reuniting flesh and bone, the family as before.
Forever speaking of cherishing—never ceasing, never ending."
When the Lord of Qiántáng finished his song,
the Lord of Dòngtíng rose together and offered a cup to Liǔ Yì.
Liǔ Yì respectfully accepted the vessel.
After drinking,
he in turn offered two cups to the two lords.
Then he sang:
"Green clouds drift leisurely, oh,
the Jīng River flows east.
Grieving for the beautiful lady, oh,
rain weeps, flowers sorrow.
A letter from afar arrives, oh,
to dispel your worries.
Grievances are indeed redressed, oh,
returning to peace and rest.
Grateful for your harmony and grace, touched by the sweet delicacies,
but my humble home is lonely—difficult to stay long.
Wishing to bid farewell, oh, yet sorrow lingers."
After the song ended,
all shouted, "Long live!"
The Lord of Dòngtíng then brought out a jade box,
containing a rhinoceros horn that parted water.
The Lord of Qiántáng also brought out a red amber tray,
holding a night-illuminating pearl.
Both rose and presented them to Liǔ Yì.
Liǔ Yì declined but finally accepted.
Then all the people in the palace
presented silks, pearls, and jades,
casting them beside Liǔ Yì,
piling up in dazzling splendor.
In a moment,
they buried him front and back.
Liǔ Yì smiled and spoke, looking all around,
bowing in gratitude without pause.
When the wine ended and joy peaked,
Liǔ Yì took his leave and rose,
again lodging in the Níngguāng Hall.
