The next day,
they feasted Liǔ Yì again at the Qīngguāng Pavilion.
The Lord of Qiántáng, flushed with wine,
sat arrogantly and said to Liǔ Yì:
"Have you not heard that a hard rock may be split but not rolled,
a righteous man may be killed but not shamed?
I have a heartfelt matter,
wishing to lay it before you.
If agreeable,
we all rise to the clouds;
if not,
we all fall to the dung heap.
What does the honorable one think?"
Liǔ Yì said:
"Please speak."
The Lord of Qiántáng said:
"The wife of the Jīngyáng dragon
is the beloved daughter of the Lord of Dòngtíng.
Gentle in nature, splendid in quality,
esteemed by all her kin.
Unfortunately, she was disgraced by a villain,
but now it is over.
We wish to entrust her to your noble righteousness,
becoming relatives for generations,
so that the one who received kindness knows where to turn,
and the one who holds love knows where to bestow it.
Would this not be the way of a gentleman from start to finish?"
Liǔ Yì rose solemnly,
then suddenly laughed and said:
"Truly, I did not know the Lord of Qiántáng was so weak and confined.
I first heard of you crossing the nine provinces,
embracing the five peaks,
venting your wrath.
Then I saw you break golden locks,
snap jade pillars,
rushing to her urgent rescue.
I thought you were resolute, decisive, clear, and upright,
unmatched by any.
For you would not avoid death when confronting an enemy,
nor spare your life when moved by gratitude—
this is the true will of a great man.
Why now, when pipes and flutes are in harmony,
kin and guests are in accord,
do you disregard the proper way,
imposing force on others?
Is this what I originally expected of you?
If I had met you amid towering waves,
in dark mountain ranges,
with scales and whiskers bristling,
cloaked in clouds and rain,
threatening me with death,
I would have regarded you as a beast.
What regret would I have?
But now, clad in robes and crown,
seated discussing ritual and righteousness,
exhausting the aims of the five constants,
bearing the subtle essence of a hundred conducts.
Even among human sages and heroes,
some fall short of this,
let alone river and lake spirits?
Yet you wish to use your clumsy body,
ferocious nature,
emboldened by wine and false courage,
to impose on others.
Is this close to righteousness?
Moreover, my humble frame
is not enough to fill a gap in one of your scales.
Yet I dare, with an unyielding heart,
oppose your lord's unrighteous anger.
May your lordship consider this!"
The Lord of Qiántáng then retreated and apologized:
"I was born and raised in palace chambers,
hearing no proper discourse.
My earlier words were reckless and arrogant,
rude,
offensive to your excellence.
Upon reflection,
my fault deserves no pardon.
Fortunately, the gentleman does not let this create a rift."
That evening, they feasted joyfully again,
the merriment as before,
and Liǔ Yì and the Lord of Qiántáng became close friends.
The next day,
Liǔ Yì bid farewell to depart.
The Lady of Dòngtíng held a separate feast for Liǔ Yì at the Qiánjǐng Hall,
with all male and female servants attending.
The Lady tearfully said to Liǔ Yì:
"Our flesh and blood received your deep kindness,
but regretfully, we cannot fully express our gratitude and reverence,
and now we must part."
She had the former Jīngyáng maiden bow to Liǔ Yì at the feast to give thanks.
The Lady also said:
"After this parting, will there ever be a day we meet again?"
Though Liǔ Yì initially did not agree to the Lord of Qiántáng's request,
at this feast,
he showed deep regret and sorrow.
After the feast, they bid farewell,
the entire palace filled with sadness.
They bestowed precious treasures upon him,
marvelous beyond description.
Liǔ Yì then retraced his path to the riverbank.
He saw over ten attendants,
carrying bags and following him,
who left after reaching his home.
Liǔ Yì then went to a treasure shop in Guǎnglíng,
selling what he had obtained.
Before even one-hundredth was sold,
his wealth already reached millions.
Thus, the wealthy families of Huái Right all considered him unmatched.
He then married a woman from the Zhāng family,
and later married one from the Hán family.
After several months,
the Hán wife also passed away.
He moved his family to Jīnlíng.
He often felt lonely and melancholy,
and considered taking a new wife.
A matchmaker told him:
"There is a young woman of the Lú family,
from Fànyáng.
Her father's name is Hào,
who once served as magistrate of Qīngliú.
In his later years, he took a liking to the Way,
and wandered alone among clouds and springs.
Now, his whereabouts are unknown.
Her mother is of the Zhèng family.
The year before last, she married into the Zhāng family of Qīnghé,
but unfortunately, her husband Zhāng died early.
Her mother pities her youth,
and cherishes her intelligence and beauty,
wishing to choose a virtuous man to match her.
I wonder what you think?"
Liǔ Yì then divined an auspicious day for the wedding.
Subsequently, both the man and woman's families
were prominent clans.
The rituals and gifts
were all exceedingly lavish.
The gentry of Jīnlíng
all admired them greatly.
After living together for over a month,
Liǔ Yì returned home late one evening,
and looking at his wife,
he deeply felt she resembled the dragon princess,
yet her grace, beauty, and fullness
surpassed even that.
He then spoke with her about past events.
His wife said to Liǔ Yì:
"How could there be such a thing in the human world?"
After more than a year passed,
they had a son.
Liǔ Yì cherished her even more.
After giving birth for over a month,
she adorned herself richly and changed her attire.
When she gathered relatives for a meeting,
she smiled and said to Liǔ Yì:
"Do you not recall me from the past?"
Liǔ Yì replied:
"I once delivered a letter for the daughter of the Lord of Dòngtíng,
and remember it to this day."
His wife said:
"I am that daughter of the Lord of Dòngtíng.
The injustice I suffered at Jīngchuān,
you helped to clear.
Grateful for your kindness,
I vowed in my heart to repay you.
After my uncle Qiántáng proposed marriage on my behalf and you refused,
we were separated,
each in a different part of the world,
unable to inquire after one another.
My parents wished to marry me to the son of Zhuójǐn.
But I held fast to my vow, which was hard to change.
Yet my parents' command was also hard to defy.
Since you had rejected me,
I thought there was no hope of seeing you again.
Although the injustice I suffered at the beginning
was made known to my parents,
my vow to repay you remained unfulfilled,
and I wished to hasten to tell you.
But you married repeatedly—
first to a woman of the Zhāng family,
and then to one of the Hán family.
After Zhāng and Hán successively passed away,
you chose to reside here.
Thus, my parents
were pleased that I could fulfill my wish to repay you.
Today, I am able to serve you,
and we shall be good together for the rest of our lives,
with no regrets even in death."
Then, sobbing and with tears streaming down,
she said to Liǔ Yì:
"I did not speak earlier
because I knew you did not value beauty highly;
now I speak
because I know you have feelings for me.
A woman is frail and insignificant,
unable to firmly secure a lasting heart.
Thus, through your love for our child,
I hoped to entrust myself to you for life.
Not knowing how you felt,
I was filled with both sorrow and fear,
unable to resolve it myself.
On the day you delivered the letter,
you smiled and said to me:
'When you return to Dòngtíng someday,
be sure not to avoid me.'
Truly, at that time,
did you already have in mind what has happened today?
Later, my uncle made a proposal to you,
but you firmly refused.
Was it truly that you could not accept,
or were you merely angry?
Please tell me."
Liǔ Yì said:
"It seems it was fate.
When I first saw you at the bend of the long Jīng River,
wronged and haggard,
I truly felt indignant.
But I restrained my heart,
thinking only of redressing your injustice,
with no other intentions.
As for saying 'be sure not to avoid me,'
that was merely casual talk.
How could I have thought of this?
When your uncle Qiántáng pressed me,
it was only because it was unreasonable
that it stirred my anger.
At first, my intention was to act righteously.
How could I kill someone's husband and take his wife?
That was the first reason I could not.
I have always upheld integrity as my principle.
How could I bend my will and suppress my heart?
That was the second reason I could not.
Moreover, I spoke frankly from my heart,
amidst the flurry of toasts and conversation,
thinking only of honesty,
with no time to avoid harm.
Yet on the day we parted,
seeing your lingering, affectionate expression,
I deeply regretted it.
But in the end, bound by human affairs,
I had no way to repay you.
Alas!
Today, you are Lady Lú,
and you live among humans.
Thus, my original heart was not mistaken.
From now on,
we shall forever enjoy happiness together,
with not a trace of worry in my heart."
His wife, deeply moved, wept tenderly
for a long time without ceasing.
After a while,
she said to Liǔ Yì:
"Do not think that because I am of another kind,
I am without a heart.
I surely know how to repay.
Dragons live for ten thousand years,
and now I share this with you.
Whether on water or land, there is nowhere we cannot go comfortably.
I hope you do not consider this false."
Liǔ Yì praised her, saying:
"I never thought that being a guest in your kingdom
would also become an inducement to immortality."
Then they went together to visit Dòngtíng.
Upon arrival, the hospitality between host and guest was magnificent,
beyond full description.
Later, they lived in Nánhǎi
for nearly forty years.
Their mansions, carriages, and horses,
as well as their rare delicacies, clothing, and treasures,
even surpassed those of marquises and earls.
None could exceed them.
Liǔ Yì's entire clan benefited from his prosperity.
As the years accumulated,
his appearance did not age,
and the people of Nánhǎi
were all astonished.
During the Kāiyuán era,
the emperor above became intent on matters of immortality,
diligently seeking Daoist arts.
Liǔ Yì could no longer live in peace,
so they returned together to Dòngtíng.
For over ten years,
no one knew their whereabouts.
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
Liǔ Yì's cousin Xuē Gǔ served as magistrate of the capital region.
Demoted to a post in the southeast,
he passed by Dòngtíng.
On a clear day, gazing into the distance,
he suddenly saw a green mountain emerge from the distant waves.
The boatmen all stood aside and said:
"There was no mountain here before;
this must be a water monster."
As they pointed and watched,
the mountain drew near the boat.
Then a brightly colored boat sped from the mountain,
coming to greet and question Xuē Gǔ.
One of them called out:
"Lord Liǔ has come to welcome you."
Xuē Gǔ, suddenly remembering,
hurried to the foot of the mountain,
lifted his robes, and quickly ascended.
On the mountain were palaces like those in the human world.
He saw Liǔ Yì standing within the palace halls,
with musicians arrayed before him,
and pearls and jade displayed behind him.
The abundance of treasures and curiosities
far surpassed those of the human world.
Liǔ Yì's speech and reasoning were even more profound,
and his appearance even more youthful.
He first welcomed Xuē Gǔ at the steps,
took his hand, and said:
"It has been but a moment since we parted,
yet your hair has already turned yellow."
Xuē Gǔ laughed and said:
"Elder brother, you are an immortal,
My younger brother has become dry bones—
such is fate."
Liú Yì then took out fifty pills of medicine and gave them to Jiǎ, saying:
"One pill of this medicine
can add one year to your life.
When the years are full, return again;
do not linger long in the human world
to torment yourself."
After the joyful feast concluded,
Jiǎ bid farewell and departed.
From that time onward,
all trace and sound of them ceased.
Jiǎ often told people of this affair.
After nearly four decades,
Jiǎ too was no longer to be found.
Lǐ Cháowēi of Lǒngxī recorded this and sighed:
"The leaders among the five classes of creatures
must possess spiritual power—
this distinction is evident here.
Humans, naked beings,
extended trust to scaled creatures.
Dòngtíng, embracing and tolerant, supremely upright;
Qiántáng, swift and decisive, open and forthright—
truly they deserve to have successors.
Jiǎ chanted of it but did not record it;
only he could approach their realm.
Moved by their righteousness,
I composed this text."
In the country of Jùmíng,
the Sēngqí Lü records:
The Buddha dwelled south of Shèwèi City.
There was a town named Dàlín.
At that time, merchants drove eight oxen to the northern country of Jùmíng.
One merchant was pasturing oxen in the marshes.
Then some Lìchē people caught a dragon to eat;
having captured one dragon,
the Lìchē pierced its nose and led it away.
The merchant asked the Lìchē:
"What will you do with this dragon you are leading?"
They replied:
"We will kill and eat it."
The merchant wished to exchange one ox for it,
but the captors bargained up to eight oxen
before agreeing.
The merchant then released the dragon, letting it go.
But then he worried the Lìchē might pursue it,
so he caught it again and released it in another pond.
Suddenly, the dragon transformed into a human
and said to the merchant:
"You spared my life;
now I wish to repay your kindness.
Come with me to my palace,
and I shall repay this great virtue."
The merchant replied:
"Dragons are by nature fierce and violent,
their wrath unpredictable;
you might kill me."
The dragon answered:
"Not so.
Those earlier people bound me,
and I had the power to kill them.
But because I have received the Bodhisattva teachings,
I harbor no thought of killing.
How much less would I harm you,
who have now granted me life?
If you will not go,
wait here a little while.
I shall go first to prepare."
Later, the merchant entered the dragon palace,
and by the dragon gate,
he saw two dragons tied together.
He asked why they were bound.
They replied:
"This dragon maiden observes the fasting precepts
for three days every half-month.
We brothers were guarding this dragon maiden,
but not vigilantly enough,
so she was captured by the Lìchē.
For this we are bound."
Soon the dragon maiden emerged,
invited the merchant into the palace, and seated him on a jeweled couch.
The dragon maiden said:
"Among dragons, there is food
that can sustain one for a lifetime,
some that lasts twenty years,
some seven years,
and some like the food of Jambudvīpa humans.
I do not know which you wish to eat."
He replied:
"I desire Jambudvīpa human food."
Immediately, all kinds of food and drink were prepared.
The merchant asked the dragon maiden:
"Why are these dragons bound?"
The dragon maiden said:
"They have committed faults;
I intend to kill them."
The merchant said:
"Do not kill them."
She replied, "No,
I must kill them."
The merchant said:
"If you release them,
then I will eat."
She said again:
"I cannot simply release them;
they must be punished for six months,
banished to the human world."
The merchant, seeing the dragon palace adorned
with precious ornaments decorating the halls,
asked:
"You have such splendid adornments;
why then do you receive the Bodhisattva teachings?"
She replied:
"We dragons suffer five kinds of hardship.
What are the five?
They are: at birth, while sleeping, during mating, when angry, and at death.
In a single day,
three times our skin and flesh fall to the ground,
and hot sand scorches our bodies."
The merchant said:
"What do you seek, then?"
She replied:
"To be born in the human path.
As an animal, suffering without knowing the Dharma,
thus I wish to approach the Tathāgata and leave home."
The dragon maiden then gave him eight gold ingots,
saying this gold would suffice for his parents and family to use their entire lives without exhaustion.
She then told him to close his eyes.
By supernatural power, she transported him back to his own country.
He gave the eight gold ingots to his parents,
saying:
"This is dragon gold."
It is said that even when used for a lifetime, it could not be exhausted.
At that time, reflecting that kindness and compassion must be practiced,
he temporarily saved the dragon maiden,
and the gratitude repaid was immensely heavy;
how much more so for upholding the great fast,
would the blessings received be small?
Recorded by Shì Xuánzhào.
Monk Xuánzhào cultivated the Way at White Crane Valley on Mount Sōng,
his conduct was pure and sincere,
surpassing that of the monastic community.
He often wished to lecture on the Lotus Sutra a thousand times,
to benefit others.
Having lectured in the mountains,
despite bitter cold and scorching heat,
and the perilous, remote mountain forests,
those who came always filled the lecture hall.
At that time, there were three old men,
with eyebrows and beards white as snow,
their appearance extraordinary and majestic,
who listened devoutly and attentively.
This went on for many days.
Xuánzhào found them strange.
Suddenly, one morning,
they came to visit Xuánzhào and said:
"We disciples are dragons,
each with our own duties,
and we have also toiled quite bitterly,
for several thousand years already.
Having heard the power of the Dharma,
we have no way to repay it,
but if the Elder has any commands,
we wish to offer our meager strength."
Xuánzhào said:
"Now, the excessive yang has persisted for a long time,
the land is suffering famine and scarcity,
could you bring sweet rain,
to save the living beings?
That is precisely what this humble monk wishes."
The three old men said:
"Summoning clouds and bringing rain,
is certainly a minor matter.
However, the prohibition against rain is extremely strict;
acting without receiving orders,
the punishment and blame are not minor;
we fear for our lives and heads.
Let us propose a plan,
which may perhaps work.
Can the Elder carry it out?"
Xuánzhào said:
"I wish to hear your proposal."
The three old men said:
"At Mount Shǎoshì lives the retired scholar Sūn Sīmiǎo, whose Way is lofty and virtue weighty;
he will certainly be able to save us disciples from disaster,
then rain can be brought immediately."
Xuánzhào said:
"This humble monk knows that Retired Scholar Sūn is in the mountains,
but I do not know his conduct;
how could it be like this?"
The three old men said:
"Master Sūn's benevolence,
cannot be measured;
he compiled the Supplementary Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold,
bestowing benefit and aid for ten thousand generations;
his name is already recorded in the Emperor's palace,
truly he is a noble transcendent.
If he speaks a word to rescue and protect us,
we should be guaranteed safety.
But first the Elder must make an agreement with him;
if he consents,
we will immediately comply."
Thereupon, they gave Xuánzhào
the method for saving and protecting them.
Xuánzhào went to Sīmiǎo's dwelling place,
sincerely and reverently paid his respects,
his sentiment and courtesy very respectful.
After sitting for a long while,
he then said:
"Retired Scholar, with the measure of a worthy sage,
your heart is set on aiding and saving others.
Now, with this extreme yang,
not an inch of seedling grows,
the wailing common people,
are parched and withered like this;
the use of a benevolent sage,
surely lies in this present moment.
I beg you to bestow your grace once,
to save them from peril and famine."
Sīmiǎo said:
"I am incapable,
having withdrawn and abandoned myself to the wild mountains;
with what power or merit
could I aid others?
But if there is something that can be done,
I certainly will not be stingy."
Xuánzhào said:
"This humble monk yesterday encountered three dragons,
and ordered them to bring rain.
They all said,
that without receiving the command of the Supreme Emperor,
those who presume to make rain
face punishment, and the offense is not light.
Only the Retired Scholar, whose virtue is revered and merit great,
if you save them, they can be spared.
I specially lay bare my innermost thoughts,
hoping you will consider and decide."
Sīmiǎo said:
"If it can be arranged,
I will not begrudge it."
Xuánzhào said:
"After the rain has fallen,
the three dragons, to avoid punishment,
will come and hide in the pond behind your dwelling.
There will certainly be an extraordinary person who comes to capture them;
if the Retired Scholar explains and sends him away,
they will surely be pardoned."
Sīmiǎo agreed.
Xuánzhào returned,
and saw the three old men by the roadside.
Xuánzhào showed them Sīmiǎo's intention.
The three old men agreed that within one day and one night,
rain would suffice for a thousand *lǐ*.
Thereupon, they poured down rain as scheduled,
and the moisture was spread very widely.
The next day,
Xuánzhào came to visit Sīmiǎo.
While they were conversing,
a man of most unusual bone structure
went straight to the edge of the pond behind the dwelling
and began shouting and bellowing.
In a moment,
the water froze into ice.
Soon, three otters appeared,
two dark gray and one white,
emerging from the pond.
This man bound them with a red rope
and was about to take them away.
Sīmiǎo called to him and said:
"The crime of these three creatures
deserves death without redemption.
However, yesterday's presumptuous order
was this humble man's idea;
I hope you will spare them.
Moreover, please convey this sincerity upward,
and pardon their grave offense."
This man accepted the instruction,
immediately untied and released them,
and left with the rope.
After a while,
the three old men came to thank Sīmiǎo,
wishing to offer some reward.
Sūn said:
"Here in the mountain valleys,
there is nothing I need;
no repayment is necessary."
They returned to Xuánzhào,
wishing to offer their strength and service.
Xuánzhào said:
"In the mountains, one meal and one robe;
beyond that, I lack nothing.
No reward is needed."
The three old men pleaded again.
Xuánzhào then said,
the mountain path ahead blocks the way,
making travel inconvenient;
could you remove it?
The three old men said:
"That is certainly a small matter.
Only, do not blame us for the wind and thunder,
then we can do it."
That evening,
thunderclaps shook and struck.
By dawn, the sky cleared,
and before the temple it opened up wide,
for several *lǐ* as flat as a palm.
The three old men came again,
bade farewell and left.
Sīmiǎo, having reached the ultimate Way,
did not seek their repayment,
which is especially extraordinary.
Wáng Jǐngróng
Wáng Jǐngróng of the Táng dynasty, former Attendant Censor,
was from Píngshū in Yíng Prefecture.
While moving his father's coffin to Luò Prefecture,
he dug into a dragon's den in the tomb passage,
as large as the mouth of a jar.
Jǐngróng bent down to look at it,
and a vapor like smoke rose straight up,
striking his eyes,
whereupon he lost his sight.
He died within ten days.
The Lady of the Rippling Waves
Emperor Xuánzōng was in the Eastern Capital,
napping in the palace during the day,
when he dreamed of a woman with a rich and beautiful countenance,
her hair styled in a heart-knot coiffure,
wearing a large cape and broad skirt,
bowing before his bed.
The Emperor asked:
"Who are you?"
She replied:
"I am the dragon maiden from Your Majesty's Língbō Pond.
I have guarded the palace and protected the imperial carriage;
indeed, I have rendered service.
Now that Your Majesty profoundly understands the music of the heavenly spheres,
I beg you to bestow a melody,
so as to bring glory to my kind."
In his dream, the Emperor played the húqín for her,
composing a new tune from old and new melodies, which became the "Língbō Melody."
The dragon maiden bowed again and departed.
Upon waking,
he remembered it all.
He then ordered the court musicians to practice it.
From then on,
with the pipa,
he practiced and arranged it.
Subsequently, he held a banquet for his officials at Língbō Palace,
and by the pond, they performed the new melody.
Waves surged and then calmed in the pond,
and a divine maiden emerged from the midst of the waves,
the very woman from the previous night.
After a long while, she finally vanished.
Thus, he ordered a temple to be built by the pond,
and each year sacrifices were offered to her.
Táo Xiàn
Táo Xiàn
was the grandson of the Magistrate of Péngzé.
During the Kāiyuán era,
he made his home in Kūnshān.
He possessed abundant fields and estates.
Selecting family servants who were honest and capable of managing affairs,
he entrusted all household matters to them.
He himself wandered freely among rivers and lakes,
traveling throughout the land.
Often he would not return for several years.
When he saw his descendants grown,
he could not even recognize their names.
Xiàn's literary talent
could have been applied to statecraft.
But considering himself carefree and unconstrained,
he did not seek an official career.
He had a friend who was versed in the eight tones of music,
and he ordered a potter to make tiles,
secretly noting the seasons and years,
to capture their sounds,
never failing in accuracy.
He once compiled a "Collection of Music," recording the eight tones,
to determine the merits and flaws of pitch.
He personally built three boats,
exquisitely crafted and ingeniously designed.
One boat carried himself,
one accommodated guests,
and one stored food and drink.
His guests included former Jìnshì Mèng Yànshēn, Jìnshì Mèng Yúnqīng, and commoner Jiāo Suì,
each bringing along servants and concubines to share the voyage.
Xiàn had a set of evening music,
often performing Qīngshāng melodies.
Whenever he encountered mountains and springs,
he would explore the scenery to its fullest,
traveling in spring as the mood took him.
Xiàn was renowned even at court,
and as the land was at peace,
wherever he passed through commanderies and cities,
he was invariably invited.
Xiàn would decline, saying:
"I am but a wild man like a deer,
no guest for princes and nobles."
Yet there were also those who came uninvited,
drawn by his water-immortal demeanor,
and the beauty of the rivers and mountains where he lingered.
The scholars of Wú and Yuè
called him the Water Immortal.
He once had a relative serving as Prefect of Nánhǎi,
and he went to visit him while also seeing the Sháo Stones.
The Prefect, delighted by his distant visit,
presented him with a million coins.
He also came across an ancient sword,
about two chǐ long,
and a jade ring,
four cùn in diameter,
as well as a Kunlun slave from a seafaring ship named Móhē,
skilled in swimming and brave and agile.
So he spent all the coins to acquire them.
He said:
"These are my family's greatest treasures."
Then he turned the boat around,
sailed down Báizhǐ,
entered the Xiāng
River.
Whenever he saw lovely water,
he would toss the sword and ring into it,
ordering Móhē to retrieve them,
as a form of amusement.
This went on for several years.
Once while crossing Cháo Lake,
he again threw in the sword and ring,
commanding Móhē to fetch them.
Móhē had just entered the water
when he retrieved the sword and ring and quickly emerged, saying:
"I was bitten by a venomous snake."
He promptly cut off a finger,
and only then escaped harm.
Jiāo Suì said:
"Móhē's injury,
could it be due to the wrath of hidden spirits?
Perhaps the water palace does not wish to be spied upon."
Xiàn replied:
"I heed your warning.
Yet I have always admired the character of Xiè Kānglè.
He said he would ultimately find joy in dying amid mountains and waters,
simply following his passions,
heedless of all else.
Moreover, dwelling in inns,
traveling upon the great earth,
living in humble simplicity,
yet indulging in the pleasures of noble wanderings,
roaming freely and delighting in sentiment for nearly thirty years,
this too is my lot.
Not to ascend the jade steps and see the Son of Heaven,
to apply my efforts for the benefit of others,
to fulfill my lifelong aspirations,
this also is my lot."
Then he ordered the boat to change course, saying:
"I must go to Xiāngyáng Mountain once,
and then return to Wú Commandery."
Traveling, they reached Xīsài Mountain,
and moored at the Jíxiáng Buddhist Temple.
Seeing the river water dark and stagnant,
he said:
"There must be a monster here."
So he threw in the sword and ring,
ordering Móhē to dive and retrieve them.
Móhē was seen sinking into the waves,
and after a long while, he finally emerged,
his strength exhausted,
barely able to stay afloat.
He said:
"The sword and ring cannot be retrieved.
There is a dragon, about two zhàng tall,
with the sword and ring placed before it.
As I reached out to take them,
the dragon glared at me in fury."
Xiàn said:
"You, along with the sword and ring,
are my three treasures.
Now that the two objects are lost,
what use are you?
You must strive with all your might to retrieve them for me."
Móhē had no choice.
With hair disheveled, he let out a great cry,
his eyes tearing until they bled,
plunged into the depths,
and never returned.
After a long time,
they saw Móhē's body torn apart,
defiling the water's surface.
As if showing himself to Xiàn.
Xiàn wept by the water's edge,
then ordered the boat to turn back.
He composed a poem to recount his tale,
and never again spoke of wandering rivers and lakes.
The poem reads:
"My old estate at Kuānglú has its own master;
My new home in Wúyuè secures this life.
A few strands of white hair, yet return is not achieved;
Gazing at the green hills, I plan my journey back.
Cranes flutter through maple leaves as sunset stirs;
Egrets stand among reed flowers, autumn waters clear.
Henceforth, where shall I go, leaving the boat behind?
Wine
banners and singing fans now come to welcome me."
Qí Huàn
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the Hé'nán investigative commissioner and Biànzhōu prefect,
Qí Huàn, considering Xúchéng's terrain perilous and urgent,
petitioned to excavate an eighteen-lǐ canal,
reaching to the Qīngshuǐ,
to level the dangers of the long Huái River.
The canal was dug according to the divisions of the prefectures and counties.
Zhēnyuán County Assistant Magistrate of Bózhōu, Cuī Yánhuī, marshaled the laborers of his county,
and after digging several thousand paces,
discovered a dragon hall within.
Initially upon opening it, they thought it was an ancient tomb,
yet its appearance was as if newly built, clean and pure.
Looking around,
beneath the northern wall were five-colored hibernating dragons over a zhàng in length,
with five or six carp beside their heads,
each over a chǐ long.
There were also two spirit turtles,
one chǐ two cùn long,
with pupils
nine fēn long,
like ordinary turtles.
Huī reported it to the Canal-Digging Censor Wū Yuánchāng,
who submitted a report to Qí Huàn.
Huàn ordered the dragons moved into the Huái River,
and the turtles taken to the Biàn River.
Huī moved the dragons and fish over two hundred lǐ,
to the Huái River bank,
where millions of white fish leaped and rushed toward the dragons,
causing the water to boil.
The dragons entered the Huái, spouting water,
clouds and mist grew dark and obscure,
and then they were seen no more.
Initially, when they were about to move them,
Censor Yuán
Xī plucked one of their whiskers.
Yuánchāng dispatched a netter to deliver the turtles to Sòng,
encountering a water marsh along the way,
the large turtle repeatedly stretched its neck toward the water.
The netter took pity on it,
and temporarily released it into the water.
The water was a few chǐ wide,
no more than five cùn deep,
yet the large turtle was lost from sight.
They drained the water to search for it,
but could not find it.
They ended up delivering an empty turtle.
The Black River of Shāzhōu
Northwest of Běitíng in Shāzhōu is the Black River.
Deep enough to sail boats,
its waters often overflowed,
sweeping away houses,
and inundating the plains.
Because of this, the crops of the northwest were all destroyed,
the land lay barren and untillable,
and the inhabitants also moved far away,
to escape the calamity of flooding and drowning.
Those officials serving in Běitíng and Shāzhōu
would all first prepare sacrificial animals and wine,
and make offerings by the riverbank,
before they dared to attend to governance.
Otherwise, continuous heavy rain would fall for months,
or great floods would surge and crash,
destroying cities and towns,
turning all the people within into fish food for their clans.
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Zhāng Sōng of Nányáng received an imperial edict to serve as Protector-General at Běitíng,
carrying his credentials and seal to the border,
and summoned the local officials for a welcoming ceremony to inquire about the matter.
Someone said:
"In the Black River dwells a giant dragon,
fond of lambs, oxen, dogs, and pigs,
therefore it often stirs waves and raises waters,
coveting the people's riverbank offerings.
I have known of this for a long time."
He then ordered the preparation of sacrificial animals and wine,
laid out a feast,
secretly summoned his attendants,
and had them wait by his side with bows and arrows.
Sōng led his officials,
lining up by the river,
wearing tall caps and holding tablets respectfully,
bowing deeply with solemn reverence.
After a short while,
a dragon one hundred chǐ long leaped out from the waves.
Suddenly it ascended the bank,
its eyes shooting fiery light at people.
When it was about several tens of paces away from the people,
Sōng ordered bows drawn to full readiness and waited.
Soon it indeed reached near the feast mats,
its body gradually shortening to a length of several chǐ.
Just as it was about to eat,
before it could,
Sōng released his arrow.
At that moment, all the arrows were loosed together,
and the dragon, unable to exert its power, was struck down.
After the dragon died,
the villagers all came to see it,
creating a clamor like a marketplace.
Sōng, pleased to have removed the people's scourge,
then presented it to the emperor.
The emperor admired his decisiveness,
and issued an edict to cut out its tongue,
placed it in a box, and bestowed it upon Sōng.
Moreover,
his descendants inherited the position of prefect in Shāzhōu,
and to this day they are called the Dragon-Tongue Zhāng clan,
The Dragon of Xìngqìng Pond
Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng once lived in obscurity at the Xìngqìng Palace.
After ascending the throne,
a small dragon from the Xìngqìng Pond would often venture out to play in the water of the palace moat outside.
Its wondrous form wriggled and coiled,
bearing an appearance of soaring and leaping.
Palace ladies and eunuchs,
all beheld it.
Later, when Xuánzōng journeyed to Shǔ,
as the imperial carriage was about to depart,
the night before,
that dragon from the pond rode a plain cloud,
leaped and stretched across the sky,
heading southwestward.
The guards stationed around,
all witnessed it.
When the emperor traveled to the Jiālíng River,
and was about to cross by boat,
he saw the small dragon winging the boat forward.
All the attending officials saw it.
The emperor shed tears,
turned and said to his attendants:
"This is the dragon from my Xìngqìng Pond."
He ordered wine to be poured as a libation,
and personally offered prayers to it,
whereupon the dragon shook its mane in the water and departed.
The Well Dragon
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
a western country presented a lion,
and on the road to Ānxī,
it was tied to a post-station tree.
Near a well,
the lion roared,
as if uneasy.
Shortly after,
great wind and thunder arrived,
and a dragon emerged from the well and left.
Zhānrán
Emperor Xuánzōng was about to perform the Fēng sacrifice on Tàishān.
Advancing and encamping at the Zhānrán River in Xíngyáng,
the emperor saw a black dragon,
and ordered bows and arrows.
He personally shot at it.
The arrow was released and the dragon vanished.
From then on, the Zhānrán flowed underground,
and it has been over a hundred years to this day.
According to records, Zhānrán is the Jǐ River.
The Jǐ River overflowed and formed the Xíng marsh,
hence it was named Zhānrán.
The Zuǒzhuàn states, "The Chǔ army crossed at Zhānrán," referring to this.
Lóngmén
An old saying goes:
"When the spring waters arrive in time,
fish leap at Lóngmén.
Then there are those that transform."
To this day, in the mountains of Fén and Jìn,
there are many dragon bones and horns left behind.
They are gathered for use as medicine.
Some are of five colors.
Xiāo Xīn
Xiāo Xīn, who later served as Minister of War in the Tang dynasty, was once the Governor of the Capital Prefecture.
At that time, the capital was suffering from a severe drought.
The oppressive heat and stagnant air
gave rise to epidemics and diseases.
Emperor Dàizōng ordered his chief ministers
to instruct the relevant officials to pray and make offerings to the mountains and rivers.
After more than a month,
the heat grew even more intense.
At that time, the Indian monk Amoghavajra resided at Jìngzhù Temple.
Amoghavajra was skilled at summoning dragons through incantations to bring forth clouds and rain.
Xiāo Xīn then went to the temple
and said to Amoghavajra:
"The scorching sun has persisted for months now.
The Emperor is deeply worried,
having ceased music and reduced his meals.
He is concerned about the poor harvest,
and troubled by the suffering of the people.
I hope you, Master, will set up an altar to bring rain."
Amoghavajra said:
"That is easy enough.
However, summoning dragons to bring clouds and rain
may cause violent winds and thunder,
which could harm living things and plants.
How would that benefit the crops?"
Xiāo Xīn replied:
"Sudden thunder and heavy rain
may indeed not nourish the grains,
but they would at least cool the oppressive heat
and slightly relieve the ailments of the common people.
I hope you will not refuse."
Amoghavajra, unable to decline,
then instructed his disciples
to fetch a piece of bark about a foot long,
carved a small dragon on it,
and placed an incense burner and fragrant water before it.
Amoghavajra chanted incantations,
vibrating his tongue and calling out prayers.
After chanting for about the time of a meal,
he handed the carved dragon to Xiāo Xīn and said:
"Throw this into the Qūjiāng River.
Once you have thrown it, return immediately.
Do not linger in the wind and rain."
Xiāo Xīn did as instructed and threw it in.
Soon, a white dragon, just over a foot long,
emerged from the water, shaking its mane and scales.
In moments, it grew to several zhang in length,
looking like a trailing white silk.
Suddenly, it stretched across the sky.
Xiāo Xīn whipped his horse and galloped away.
Before he had gone a few dozen steps,
the clouds darkened and thickened,
and a torrential downpour began.
By the time he reached Yǒngchóng Lane,
the water on the road
was already flowing like a burst canal.
Yíchǐ Pond
Yíchǐ Pond in Kūnshān County
originally formed during the Dàlì era,
when a village girl became the Crown Prince’s principal consort.
She dropped a jade ruler,
which transformed into a dragon,
and over time, it became a pond.
Liú Guàncí
Liú Guàncí of Luòyáng in the Táng dynasty,
during the Dàlì era,
was seeking alms in Sūzhōu
when he met a scholar named Cài Xiá, who was elegant and handsome.
At their first meeting,
Cài Xiá was very attentive,
addressing Guàncí as "elder brother."
Later, he brought lamb and wine for a feast.
After drinking, he said:
"Elder brother, you are now wandering the rivers and lakes—
what is your purpose?"
Guàncí replied:
"Just seeking alms."
Xiá said:
"Do you have a specific destination,
or are you traveling aimlessly through the commanderies and states?"
Guàncí said:
"I drift like tumbleweed."
Xiá said:
"In that case, how much do you hope to obtain before stopping?"
Guàncí said:
"One hundred thousand coins."
Xiá said:
"To drift like tumbleweed yet hope for one hundred thousand—
that is like wishing to fly without wings.
Even if you were certain to obtain it,
it would still take several years.
I have a home in Luòyáng,
and my family is not poor.
Due to certain circumstances, I had to leave that place,
and news has been cut off for a long time.
I have a sincere request:
I beg you, elder brother, to make a trip back for me.
The expenses for the journey,
and the hopes of your drifting travels—
you will obtain them without wasting much time.
What do you think?"
Guàncí said:
"That is certainly my wish."
Xiá then gave him one hundred thousand coins
and handed him a sealed letter,
explaining:
"Since I have received your concern while lodging here,
and there are no formalities between us,
I will reveal my true heart.
My family belongs to the scaled creatures;
our home is under the Wèi Bridge.
Close your eyes and knock on the bridge pillar,
and someone will respond.
They will surely invite you into the house.
When my mother receives you,
you must ask to meet my younger sister.
Since we are sworn brothers,
it would be inappropriate to be distant.
The letter also instructs her to come out and pay her respects.
Although she is young,
she is quite intelligent and clever.
If you ask her to help as the hostess,
a gift of one hundred strings of coins—
she will certainly agree."
Guàncí then returned.
Arriving under the Wèi Bridge,
he saw a deep, clear pool—
how could he reach it?
After a long while,
thinking that the dragon god should not deceive him,
he tried closing his eyes and knocking.
Suddenly, someone responded.
When he looked,
the bridge and the pool had vanished.
Instead, there was a vermilion gate and a grand mansion,
with towers and pavilions rising in tiers.
A servant in purple stood bowing before him,
asking his purpose.
Guàncí said:
"I come from Wú Commandery;
your young master has a letter."
The questioner took the letter and went inside.
After a moment, he returned and said:
"The great lady requests your presence."
Guàncí then entered the hall.
He saw the great lady, who appeared over forty years old,
dressed entirely in purple.
Her appearance was lovely.
Guàncí bowed to her,
and the great lady returned the bow.
She then apologized:
"My son has been traveling far away,
and news has been cut off for a long time.
I am grateful for your visit
and for delivering the letter over thousands of miles.
He was once slighted by a superior,
and his resentment has not diminished.
Since he fled,
three years have passed in silence.
If not for your special visit,
my worries would still be piling up."
After speaking, she invited him to sit.
Guàncí said:
"Your son and I have sworn to be brothers;
thus, your young daughter is also my sister.
I should meet her as well."
The lady said:
"My son mentioned this in his letter.
She is just combing her hair
and will come out shortly to receive you."
Soon, a maidservant announced:
"The young lady is coming."
She appeared to be about fifteen or sixteen years old,
with peerless beauty
and exceptional intelligence.
After bowing,
she sat beside her mother.
The lady then ordered a meal to be served,
which was also very exquisite and clean.
As they were eating together,
the great lady suddenly turned red-eyed,
staring straight at Guàncí.
The daughter urgently said:
"Brother has come on trust;
we should treat him with courtesy.
Moreover, he is here to help resolve troubles—
we must not waver."
She then said:
"In the letter, my brother instructed
that we present you with one hundred strings of coins.
Since it is difficult to gather such an amount alone,
we must use something lighter as a substitute.
Now, we offer you a vessel
of equivalent value.
Is that acceptable?"
Guàncí said:
"Since we are already brothers,
and I am merely delivering a letter,
how can I accept such a gift?"
The great lady said:
"My son has fully described
your impoverished travels.
Now, to fulfill his request,
you must not refuse."
Guàncí thanked her.
She then ordered the "Zhènguó Bowl" to be brought,
and they continued eating.
Not long after,
the great lady again stared with red eyes,
saliva dripping from both corners of her mouth.
The daughter quickly covered her mouth and said:
"Brother entrusted this person with deep sincerity;
we should not act like this."
She then said:
"Mother is advanced in years,
and her wind illness is acting up.
She can no longer entertain you properly.
Elder brother, you should leave now."
As if afraid,
she sent a maidservant to carry the bowl,
and personally followed to hand it to Guàncí, saying:
"This is a bowl from Jìbīn Kingdom;
that country uses it to suppress disasters and plagues.
For people of the Táng,
it is of no practical use.
You can sell it
for one hundred thousand coins.
Do not sell it for less.
Due to my mother's illness,
I must attend to her,
and cannot accompany you further."
She bowed twice and went inside.
Guàncí took the bowl and left.
After a few steps, he looked back:
the deep green pool and the towering bridge
looked exactly as when he first arrived.
Looking at the vessel in his hand,
it was a yellow copper bowl.
Its value was only three or five strings of coins at most,
and he greatly doubted the dragon sister's words.
He took it to the market to sell;
some offered seven or eight hundred coins,
others only five hundred.
Remembering that dragon gods value trust,
he thought they should not deceive people.
Day after day, he carried it around the market.
After more than a year,
a foreign merchant suddenly came to a shop in the West Market.
Seeing the bowl, he was overjoyed
and asked its price.
Guàncí said:
"Two hundred strings of coins."
The merchant said:
"This object is worth far more;
why stop at two hundred strings?
However, it is not a treasure of the Central Plains—
what use is it to have it?
How about one hundred strings?"
Guàncí, recalling the original agreement was only for that amount,
did not seek more,
and agreed to the exchange.
The merchant said:
"This is the Zhènguó Bowl of Jìbīn Kingdom."
In their country,
it greatly dispels calamities and misfortunes for the people.
Since this bowl was lost,
their country has suffered severe famine,
and warfare and chaos have erupted.
I heard it was stolen by the dragon's son,
for nearly four years now,
and their ruler has just offered half a year's national tribute to ransom it.
How did you manage to obtain it?"
Guàncí recounted the entire truth.
The guest said:
"The dragon guardian of Jìbīn has appealed to the higher authorities,
and a pursuit is imminent.
This is why Xiá has gone into hiding.
The underworld officials are strict,
so he cannot confess directly.
He used you as a pretext to return it.
His earnestness in presenting his sister to you
was not out of genuine kinship,
but because he feared the old dragon's greed,
worried he might harm you,
so he used his sister to protect you.
Now that this bowl has been returned,
he too will likely come,
which is also a way to resolve the trouble.
Fifty days from now,
when the waves of the Cáo and Luò rivers surge,
and the waters churn, darkening the sun,
that will be the sign of Xiá's return."
Guàncí asked:
"Why must it be fifty days before he returns?"
The guest replied:
"I must carry it across the mountain ridge,
before I dare to return."
Guàncí noted this.
When the time came, he went to look,
and indeed it was so.
Wéi Shì
Wéi Shì of Jīngzhào,
was a daughter of a distinguished family,
married to Mèng of Wǔchāng.
In the late Dàlì era of the Táng dynasty,
Mèng and his wife's younger brother, Wéi Shēng, were both selected for office,
with Wéi Shēng appointed as the county lieutenant of Yángzǐ,
and Mèng as the administrative clerk of Lángzhōu.
They set off separately to their posts.
Wéi Shì accompanied her husband into Shǔ,
but the road was impassable for carriages,
so Wéi Shì rode a horse.
As they reached the mouth of Luògǔ,
suddenly the horse startled,
and she fell hundreds of feet down the cliff.
Looking down, it was dark and deep,
with no path for anyone to descend.
Mèng Shēng wailed in grief,
the whole family wept bitterly,
but there was nothing they could do.
So they held a funeral, mourned, and left.
Wéi Shì, upon landing,
fell onto a pile of dry leaves about several zhang deep,
suffering no bodily harm.
At first, she seemed to have fainted,
but after a short while, she revived.
After a day,
she grew very hungry,
so she wrapped snow in tree leaves and ate it.
Looking beside her, she saw a crevice in the rock,
its depth unknown.
Looking up at the place from which she had fallen,
it was
like a great well.
She thought she was surely doomed to die.
Suddenly, within the rocky valley,
she saw a point of light like a lamp,
which gradually grew larger,
and then there were two.
As they drew nearer,
they were the eyes of a dragon.
Wéi Shì was terrified,
and pressed herself against the stone wall, standing still.
This dragon gradually emerged,
about fifty or sixty feet long.
Reaching the edge of the cave,
it leaped out through an opening.
Soon, she saw another pair of eyes,
and another dragon about to emerge.
Wéi Shì reckoned she would surely die,
preferring to be killed by the dragon.
As the dragon was about to emerge,
she embraced it and straddled it.
The dragon paid no heed,
simply leaped out of the cave,
and soared into the sky.
Wéi Shì dared not look down,
letting the dragon carry her wherever it went.
After what seemed like half a day,
she guessed they had traveled over ten thousand lǐ.
She cautiously opened her eyes and looked down,
as the dragon gradually descended.
She saw rivers, seas, and vegetation.
When it was
about forty or fifty feet above the ground,
fearing it might drop her into a river,
she let go and fell by herself,
landing in deep grass.
After a long while, she revived.
Wéi Shì had not eaten
for three or four days already,
and her strength was gradually failing.
She walked slowly onward,
and encountered an old fisherman,
who was startled to see someone like her.
Wéi Shì asked where this place was,
and the fisherman said:
"This is Yángzǐ County."
Wéi Shì secretly rejoiced,
and said:
"How many lǐ is it to the county seat?"
The old man said:
"Twenty lǐ."
Wéi Shì recounted her whole story,
and mentioned her hunger and thirst.
The fisherman, pitying her and finding it strange,
had tea and porridge in his boat,
and gave her some to eat and drink.
Wéi Shì asked:
"Has the county lieutenant Wéi arrived here yet?"
The old man said:
"I don't know if he has arrived."
Wéi Shì said:
"I am the younger sister of Lieutenant Wéi.
If you could take me there,
I will repay you generously once we reach the county seat."
The fisherman took her in his boat to the county gate.
Lieutenant Wéi had already arrived several days earlier.
When Wéi Shì reached the gate,
she sent word that she was the thirteenth elder sister of the Mèng family.
Wéi Shēng did not believe it,
saying:
"Thirteenth elder sister followed Mèng Láng into Shǔ,
how could she suddenly appear here?"
Wéi Shì had them relay her story in detail.
Although Wéi Shēng was startled,
he still did not fully believe it.
He came out to see her,
and his elder sister wailed and wept,
recounting her hardships and perils.
Her face was haggard and worn,
almost beyond description.
So he let her rest and recover,
and soon she returned to normal.
Wéi Shēng still had some doubts.
A few days later,
the tragic news from Shǔ indeed arrived,
and only then did Wéi Shēng's mind become clear,
and he felt both grief and joy.
He rewarded the old fisherman with twenty thousand cash,
and sent someone to escort his elder sister into Shǔ.
Mèng was overwhelmed with both sorrow and joy.
Several decades later,
Wéi Shì's maternal cousin Péi Gāng,
during the Zhēnyuán era,
was still serving as the county lieutenant of Gāo'ān in Hóngzhōu.
He himself recounted this story.
Rén Xū
In the early years of the Jiànzhōng era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Rén Xǔ from Lè'ān,
who loved reading books,
and disliked worldly affairs.
He lived deep in the mountains,
with the intention of spending his life there.
One day,
he sat indoors during the day with his door closed.
An old man came knocking at the door to visit him,
wearing yellow clothes,
with a very refined appearance,
and arrived leaning on a staff.
Xǔ invited him to sit and spoke with him.
After a long while,
Xǔ was surprised that the old man’s speech was hesitant and his expression troubled,
as if something deeply unhappy had occurred.
So he asked the old man:
"Why do you look so troubled?
Is it not because you have some worry?
If not,
is it because someone in your family is ill and you are deeply concerned about them?"
The old man said:
"Indeed it is so.
I have long been waiting for you to ask me this.
Moreover, I am not human,
but a dragon.
One lǐ to the west, there is a large deep pool,
where my family has lived for several hundred years.
Now I am being tormented by a certain person,
and disaster is about to befall me.
Only you can save me from death,
so I have come to plead with you.
Fortunately, you have now asked me,
so I am able to speak of it."
Xǔ said:
"I am merely a man of the mundane world,
who only knows of poetry, books, rites, and music.
Other arts I do not understand.
How then can I save you from disaster?"
The old man said:
"Just teach me the words,
no other arts are needed,
it only requires a few dozen words of effort."
Xǔ said:
"I am willing to receive your instruction."
The old man said:
"Two days from now,
I hope you will come to the pool for me at dawn.
At the time of high noon,
a Dàoshi will come from the west—
this is the one who brings disaster upon me.
The Dàoshi will drain the water from my pool,
and then slaughter me.
When you see the pool water drained,
you should shout loudly:
'Heaven has decreed,
whoever kills the yellow dragon shall die!'
After you finish speaking,
the pool will fill up again,
and the Dàoshi will certainly perform his arts again.
You should then shout once more.
If you do this three times,
I will be able to preserve my life.
I will surely repay you heavily.
Please do not worry about anything else."
Xǔ agreed.
Afterward, the old man entreated and thanked him very earnestly.
A long time passed before he left.
Two days later,
Xǔ went to the western mountain,
and indeed there was a large deep pool.
He sat down beside the pool to wait.
When high noon arrived,
suddenly a patch of cloud
drifted slowly down from the west onto the pool.
A Dàoshi descended from the cloud,
tall and slender,
about ten feet in height.
He stood on the bank of the pool,
took out several black talismans from his sleeve, and threw them into the pool.
In a moment,
the pool water completely dried up,
revealing a yellow dragon,
lying prostrate on the sand.
Xǔ immediately shouted loudly:
"Heaven has decreed,
whoever kills the yellow dragon shall die!"
As soon as he finished speaking,
the pool water overflowed completely.
The Dàoshi grew angry,
and immediately from his sleeve,
took out several talismans with red characters and threw them in.
The pool water dried up again,
and Xǔ shouted with a thundering voice,
using the same words as before.
The water overflowed once more,
and the Dàoshi became even angrier.
After about the time it takes to eat a meal,
he took out more than ten red talismans,
threw them into the air,
and they all transformed into crimson clouds,
entering the pool.
The pool water dried up again,
and Xǔ shouted the same words as before.
The pool water overflowed once more.
The Dàoshi turned to Xǔ and said:
"It took me ten years to finally get this dragon as food.
How is it that you, a scholar,
would save this strange creature?"
He angrily scolded him a few words and then left.
Xǔ also returned to the mountains.
That evening,
he dreamed that the old man from before came to thank him, saying:
"Thanks to you, sir, for saving me.
Otherwise,
I would have almost died at the hands of that Dàoshi.
Your sincere feelings moved me deeply,
words cannot express my gratitude.
Now I offer you a pearl.
You can search for it on the bank of the pool,
to show my heartfelt gratitude."
Xǔ went to look for it,
and indeed found a pearl one cùn in diameter,
on the grass by the pool bank.
It shone brilliantly and was perfectly transparent,
almost impossible to describe.
Xǔ later took it especially to Guǎnglíng market,
where a foreigner saw it and said:
"This is truly a treasure of the Lílóng,
which ordinary people cannot obtain."
He bought it for tens of millions in price.
Zhào Qísōng
In the twelfth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
Zhào Qísōng was appointed as the Deputy Magistrate of Chéngdū County.
He packed his luggage along with his servants,
carried his official documents, and set off,
intending to take up his post.
However, the plank road was extremely perilous and narrow.
As he often used his horsewhip to brush aside small tree branches,
he accidentally got the whip's tip entangled in a tree.
Unable to free it quickly,
and with the horse refusing to stop,
he fell from the horse.
The branches were soft and the leaves tender,
unable to break his fall or hold him back.
He plummeted straight to the bottom of the valley,
yet suffered no injuries.
Looking up, he saw a sheer cliff of over a thousand ren high,
with no other paths around.
He resigned himself to certain death.
His servants, having no solution,
reported the incident to the authorities and returned home.
Zhào, with no way forward or back,
on the day after his fall,
suddenly heard the rumble of thunder,
and realized it was about to rain.
Shortly after,
clouds and mist swirled out from a stone cave.
Soon, following the clouds, a huge red-spotted snake appeared,
as thick as a person could embrace,
with resplendent scales.
It shook its head, and a pair of horns emerged;
it coiled its body, and four legs grew.
It raised its mane and fins vigorously,
swaying its head and tail.
Only then did he realize it was a dragon.
Zhào thought to himself:
"If I stay here, I will die;
if I ride the dragon out, I may also die.
Better to die trying to escape."
He grabbed the dragon's tail and clung to its body.
The dragon ascended straight up through the clouds,
reaching an unfathomable height of several thousand ren.
Zhào clung on desperately, as if facing death.
Once they reached mid-air,
the dragon stretched its body and flew onward.
Zhào managed to straddle it,
though he feared he would die in the sea.
Looking south, he saw a seamless expanse of clouds and water—
it was the South Sea.
Zhào sighed again:
"Today, I will not be buried in the mountains,
but will end up in the sea."
As the dragon approached the sea,
its flight gradually lowered.
When they were about one or two hundred paces from the sea,
he released the dragon and threw himself to the ground.
The shore was covered with reeds,
so although he fell, he suffered no harm.
After half a day,
he encountered someone on the road
and asked him.
The person replied:
"This is Qīngyuǎn County."
However, when he reached the county,
having no companions or proof,
no one believed him,
and he could not linger.
He traveled all the way to Cháng'ān,
and after over a month,
arrived home.
His family was holding the twenty-first-day memorial ceremony,
with a large gathering of monks.
Suddenly seeing Zhào arrive,
they were all terrified and fled, crying:
"His ghost has returned!"
Zhào sat by the door,
and even his wife and children feared he might be a revived corpse.
They said:
"Please walk in the sunlight,
so we can see if you cast a shadow."
Zhào was angered by his family's suspicion and fear,
and refused to walk in the sunlight.
Distant relatives remarked:
"If he refuses to walk in the sun,
he must be a ghost."
Hearing Zhào speak,
they still said:
"That is just ghost talk."
After a long while,
he recounted his entire story,
and only then did they rejoice.
Those traveling through dangerous places
and riding horses should take this as a warning.
Xǔ Hànyáng
was originally from Rǔnán.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
he was traveling by boat between Hóngzhōu and Ráozhōu.
As dusk fell,
the river waves grew fierce,
so he sought a small inlet to enter.
Unconsciously, he traveled three or four lǐ
and arrived at a lake,
which, though broad, had water only two or three chǐ deep.
Sailing northward another lǐ or so,
he saw bamboo and trees dense and lush along the lakeshore,
so he headed there to moor his boat.
As he drew closer,
he saw pavilions and buildings quite magnificent,
with two maidservants, their hair tied in double buns, their hair black as a crow’s feathers,
their plain faces like jade,
welcoming the boat with laughter.
Hànyáng was surprised
and teased them with flirtatious words;
they laughed heartily again
and then ran back into the residence.
Hànyáng fastened his belt,
went ashore, and sought an audience.
Before he had taken three or four steps,
a maidservant invited him into the main hall of the residence
and bowed, gesturing for him to sit.
She said:
"The young lady is changing her attire."
After a short while,
the maidservant instructed Hànyáng to enter the middle gate.
He saw the entire courtyard filled with large ponds,
lotus and water caltrops fragrant within them,
the four banks gleaming like green jade.
Two rainbow bridges were built
to connect the north and south.
To the north stood a grand tower.
Ascending the steps,
he saw silver characters inscribed: "Palace of Night Illumination."
All around were exotic flowers, fruits, and trees,
towering densely into the clouds.
The maidservant led him up to the first level of the tower,
where six or seven more maidservants
greeted him with bows in a row.
Then she led him to the second level,
and only then did he see six or seven young ladies.
Their beauty was unlike anything he had ever seen;
they all bowed and asked where he had come from.
Hànyáng explained in detail how he had unexpectedly arrived there.
The young ladies bowed and invited him to sit, and once seated,
the maidservants served food and drink,
all of which were unlike anything seen in the mortal world.
After the meal, wine was ordered.
Among them was a wondrous tree several zhàng tall,
its branches and trunk like a parasol tree,
its leaves resembling plantain leaves,
covered with red flowers not yet in bloom.
The blossoms were as large as cups,
directly facing the drinking area.
One young lady held the wine
and ordered a maidservant to bring a bird like a parrot,
placing it on the railing in front of the drinking area.
It called out once,
and the flowers on the tree instantly bloomed,
their fragrance overwhelming.
Within each flower was a beauty over a chǐ tall,
with graceful and lovely forms,
and flowing, elegant attire,
each matching their essence.
All kinds of string and wind instruments were fully prepared.
These figures bowed twice.
The young lady raised her wine cup,
and all the music began to play,
clear and melodious,
as if in a celestial realm.
Just one round of drinks had passed,
and it was already evening,
the moonlight shining brightly again.
The topics discussed by the young ladies
were all unrelated to mortal affairs,
beyond Hànyáng’s comprehension.
When Hànyáng tried to engage them with worldly matters,
the young ladies offered no response at all.
They drank joyfully until the second watch,
and when the banquet concluded,
the petals of that tree fell piece by piece into the pond,
and the figures within them also fell,
vanishing without a trace.
One young lady took out a scroll of writings to show him;
Hànyáng looked at it
and saw it was "Rhapsody on Rivers and Seas."
The young lady asked Hànyáng to read it,
so he read it once through.
The young lady then requested to read it herself once
and ordered the maidservant to put it away.
One young lady then addressed the others
and also said to Hànyáng:
"I have a poem of heartfelt sentiments;
I would like to recite it."
The young ladies and Hànyáng said:
"Excellent."
And she chanted:
"Hǎimén connects to Dòngtíng,
a journey of three thousand lǐ each time.
Once every ten years I return,
toiling through the Xiāo and Xiāng waters."
The young lady ordered a maidservant to fetch several scrolls,
along with brush and inkstone,
and asked Hànyáng to transcribe it.
Hànyáng unrolled the scroll
and saw it was made of plain silk adorned with golden flowers,
with characters written in silver ink on it,
the scroll as large as an arched dou measure.
Half of it was already filled with writing;
looking at the brush,
he saw its shaft was made of white jade,
the inkstone was of green jade,
housed in a glass box,
and the inkstone contained silver-infused ink.
After writing,
she asked him to sign with his name.
Unrolling it further,
he saw several poems,
each signed with someone’s name.
There was one named Zhòngfāng,
one named Wū,
and one named Cháoyáng,
but no surnames were visible.
The young lady then collected and rolled up the scroll.
Hànyáng said:
"I have a poem I would like to compose in response;
may I add it to this?"
The young lady said:
"No.
This is something I present to my parents and brothers each time I return;
I do not wish to mix in others’ works."
Hànyáng said:
"But I have already signed my humble name;
is that acceptable?"
She said:
"That is a different matter;
it is not for a gentleman to question."
As the fourth watch approached,
she ordered everything to be packed away.
Amid the flurry of activity,
a maidservant said:
"Sir, you may return to your boat now."
Hànyáng then rose.
The young ladies said:
"We are delighted to have received you during your journey,
though we could not offer more elaborate hospitality."
They parted with regret.
As he returned to his boat, a strong wind suddenly arose,
the clouds darkened abruptly,
and everything turned pitch black, even for a single step.
By dawn,
looking at the place where they had drunk the night before,
he saw only an empty grove of trees.
Hànyáng untied the mooring rope
and sailed to the households along the riverbank at the inlet from the previous evening.
He saw over ten people
seeming to be in an unusual state.
So he moored his boat and inquired.
Someone said:
"Four people drowned at the river mouth;
after the second watch,
they were retrieved.
Three were already dead,
but one,
though seemingly dead, was not entirely gone.
A shamaness sprinkled willow water and chanted incantations over him,
and after a long while, he was able to speak, saying:
'Last night, the daughters of the Water Dragon King and their cousins, six or seven in total, were returning after passing Dòngtíng
and held a night banquet here,
taking the four of us to make wine.
The guest of honor drank little,
so they did not drink much,
which is why I managed to return.'"
Hànyáng found this strange
and asked:
"Who was the guest?"
The reply was:
"A poor scholar,
his name not remembered."
It was also said
that the maidservants mentioned
the young ladies dearly loved mortal writings
but could not obtain them,
often wishing to request a piece from a poor scholar but having no opportunity.
Hànyáng asked where he was now,
and was told he had already set sail.
Hànyáng then reflected on the events of the previous night
and the poem of heartfelt sentiments,
all of which could be verified.
Hànyáng fell silent and returned to his boat,
feeling discomfort in his stomach.
He then vomited several shēng of fresh blood,
realizing it was all human blood used as wine.
It took three days for him to recover.
Liú Yǔxī
Liú Yǔxī, the Prefect of Liánzhōu during the Táng Dynasty,
in the Zhēnyuán era,
was residing in Róngzé.
At the beginning of summer, he was sitting alone in a forest pavilion,
when suddenly a great rain began,
darkening heaven and earth,
and it was a long time before it cleared.
Only around the apricot tree in the pavilion
did the misty vapor not disperse.
Yǔxī approached to look beneath the tree,
where there was a creature shaped like a turtle or soft-shelled turtle,
quite foul and stinking,
as large as a five-dǒu cauldron.
Yǔxī then threw tiles and stones at it,
and the creature slowly climbed the steps,
stopping at the eaves pillar.
Yǔxī then retreated to stand behind the bed,
leaning on his staff to observe it.
The creature looked up at the top of the pillar,
tapped with its front claws,
and split away half of the pillar.
Then, with a great thunderous sound,
the roof tiles flew down in chaos,
and the eastern wall of the pavilion,
cracked from top to bottom for about ten feet.
Previously, east of the pavilion, there were several acres of purple-flowered alfalfa,
and at that moment, Yǔxī could clearly see them from the crack
in the distance.
Once the thunder ceased,
the creature also disappeared,
and the crack in the eastern wall
had already closed up on its own.
Yǔxī hurriedly looked at it:
the alfalfa was as before,
and the wall showed no sign of movement.
Zhōu Hán
In the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a retired scholar named Zhōu Hán,
a man of outstanding literary talent and brilliance.
Through a Yí tribesman selling a slave,
a boy of fourteen or fifteen,
whose appearance seemed very clever and sharp.
It was said he was skilled at entering water,
as if walking on level ground.
Ordered to dive and stay submerged,
even for an entire day or longer,
he never suffered any hardship.
He claimed
that among the streams, gorges, pools, and caves of Shǔ,
there was nowhere he had not reached.
Hán thus bought him,
changing his name to "Shuǐjīng".
He marveled at his ability.
Hán traveled by boat from Shǔ down through the gorges,
reaching Jiānglíng,
passing by Qútáng and Yànyù,
and then ordered Shuǐjīng to dive and see how deep and far it went.
Shuǐjīng entered,
and after some time emerged,
having retrieved many gold and silver objects.
Hán was extremely pleased.
Whenever he moored his boat at river pools,
he would have Shuǐjīng dive in,
and again gain something.
Following the current, they reached Jiāngdū,
passing by Niúzhǔ Jī,
traditionally said to be the deepest spot,
the shore where Wēn Qiáo once burned rhinoceros horn to illuminate the water monsters.
He again had him dive in.
After some time, he again obtained precious jade.
He said
there were indeed water monsters,
indescribable in form,
all glaring angrily and brandishing their hands,
and he barely escaped harm.
Because of this, Hán also became extremely wealthy.
Several years later,
Hán had a friend named Wáng Zé,
who governed Xiàngzhōu,
and Hán happened to visit him while traveling north of the river.
Zé was very pleased,
feasting and touring with him,
with no idle days.
Thus they went together to the Octagonal Well at the northern corner of the prefecture.
A natural bedrock formation,
lined to form an octagon,
about thirty feet across.
Morning and evening, mist and clouds gathered thickly,
spreading over a hundred paces.
On dark nights,
a fiery red light shot out a thousand feet,
illuminating objects as if it were daytime.
Ancient lore passed down said
a golden dragon lay hidden at its bottom,
and in times of severe drought, prayers were offered to it,
with very effective responses.
Zé said:
"This well must contain a great treasure,
but there is no way to investigate whether it is true or not."
Hán laughed and said:
"Very easy."
He then commanded Shuǐjīng:
"You can go with me to the bottom of this well,
see what strange things are there.
Zé will also surely reward you."
Shuǐjīng had not entered the water for a long time,
and cheerfully took off his clothes and dove in.
After a long time, he emerged,
and said to Hán:
"There is a huge yellow dragon,
with scales like gold,
holding several bright pearls, fast asleep.
I wanted to seize them,
but had no blade in hand.
I feared the dragon might suddenly wake,
so I did not dare touch it.
If I had a sharp sword,
even if the dragon woke,
I would not fear to slay it."
Hán and Zé were overjoyed.
Zé said:
"I have a sword,
an extraordinary treasure.
You may take it and seize them."
Shuǐjīng drank wine, girded the sword, and entered.
After some time,
onlookers crowded around on all sides.
Suddenly, they saw Shuǐjīng leap out from the well's surface for several hundred paces.
Following him was a golden dragon.
Also several hundred feet long,
with sharp claws and talons,
snatching at Shuǐjīng from the air.
Then it retreated back into the well.
Those on the sides trembled in fear,
not daring to look closely.
Hán grieved for his Shuǐjīng,
Zé regretted losing his precious sword,
and they hesitated.
An old man appeared,
dressed in coarse fur clothing,
his appearance very simple and ancient.
He approached Zé and said:
"I am the local earth god.
How could you, Governor, so lightly regard your people?
The golden dragon in this cavern
is an envoy of the highest heaven.
It oversees the region's precious jade,
bringing moisture and benefit to this entire area.
How could you trust a lowly creature,
wishing to rob it in its sleep?
Had the dragon suddenly raged in anger,
employing its divine power,
shaking the heavenly gates,
swaying the earth's axis,
smashing mountains and crushing hills,
turning a hundred lǐ into rivers and lakes,
and ten thousand people into fish and turtles,
how could your flesh and bone have been preserved?
In the past, Zhōnglí did not covet his treasure,
Mèngcháng returned the pearl of his own accord;
you did not follow their example,
but instead indulged your greedy heart.
You let a cunning, stubborn fellow
fearlessly attempt to take the treasure,
and now he has been devoured and his pearl forged."
Zé flushed with shame and regret,
having no words to reply.
The old man also said:
"You must urgently repent and pray,
lest its anger grow severe."
The old man vanished abruptly.
Zé then prepared sacrificial animals and made offerings.
The Dragon of Zīzhōu
In the final years of Wéi Gāo's governorship over Shǔ,
Zīzhōu presented a dragon,
over ten feet long,
complete with scales and armor.
Gāo stored it in a wooden box,
where it coiled inside.
At the time, during the New Year,
it was placed in the main hall of Dàcí Temple,
and the common people spread the news,
coming in crowds to view it for two or three days,
until it was killed by the smoke of incense.
The state histories lack any record.
What omen was this?
Wéi Sīgōng
In the sixth year of the Yuánhé era,
Wéi Sīgōng of the capital region, along with Mister Dǒng and Mister Wáng, the three of them became friends,
and pursued their studies at the Sōngshān Mountain Temple.
About a hundred paces northeast of the temple,
there was a water-fetching basin beneath a cliff.
It measured over ten feet in circumference,
and was deep enough to hold ten hú.
No matter how much water was taken, it would immediately refill,
never diminishing.
The entire temple drew water from it.
The three of them had lived here since spring,
until the middle of the seventh month,
when the three of them, taking advantage of some leisure time, went to fetch water.
Their path led them to the stone basin.
They saw a huge snake, several zhàng long,
black as pure lacquer,
with white patterns,
like brocade,
coiled within the basin.
The three young men were terrified at the sight,
and stared at it for a long time.
Wáng and Dǒng discussed it, saying:
"We could capture it and eat it."
Wéi said:
"No.
In the past, the bamboo of Gěbēi,
the fisherman's shuttle,
and the swords of the Léi family—
all of them turned into dragons.
How do we know that in this famous mountain and great stronghold,
this might not be a dragon concealing its form?
Moreover, the scales and armor of this snake
are especially unusual.
We should be cautious of this."
The other two did not heed his words.
They threw stones and struck the snake until it was dead,
then coiled it up and brought it back to cook.
Both of them mocked Wéi for his hypocritical caution.
Soon after, it was reported that there was another snake at the basin.
The two went to the basin site
intending to attack it again.
Wéi tried to dissuade them, but they would not listen.
Just as the two were lifting stones to throw,
the snake soared into the sky and flew away.
When the three returned to their quarters,
the snake was not yet fully cooked.
Suddenly, they heard a sound from the mountains,
rumbling like an earthquake.
Looking out,
they saw violent winds and clouds suddenly arise in the mountains,
whipping up sand and stones.
In an instant, it reached the temple.
Heaven and earth turned dark,
and they could not see each other face to face.
Those in the temple heard a voice amidst the raging wind and clouds say:
"Do not strike wrongly."
Moments later,
half rain, half fire fell from the sky.
The scholars' quarters
were almost completely burned and destroyed.
Wáng and Dǒng
were nowhere to be found.
Only Wéi, under the temple corridor, was unharmed.
Thus, the principle of divine transformation
is also very clear.
If one cannot be wholly good,
but merely utters a few good words,
then the calamity of the flood dragon will not reach him.
How much more so for those who constantly practice the way of goodness!
The corpses of the other two
were not found until two days later,
discovered below the southern corner of the temple gate.
This is what Wéi himself recounted.
As for those fond of killing,
this is sufficient to serve as a warning.
Lú Yuányù
Lú Yuányù, the former Táng prefect, before he took office,
once during the Zhōngyuán Festival set up banners and images,
placing a Yúlán bowl among them.
Soon he heard a chirping sound from the bowl.
Yuányù looked
and saw a small dragon, only about an inch long,
with an extraordinary form and marvelous appearance,
graceful and adorable.
He then sprinkled water on it,
and the dragon stretched its legs and shook its mane, already several chǐ long.
Yuányù was greatly frightened.
A white cloud rose from the bowl,
and the dragon also chased the cloud and departed.
Yuányù was the father of Lú Hàn.
Lú Hàn
Lú Hàn, son of the Táng prefect of Ān, Lú Yuányù, said:
When the prefect was young,
he once formed a study group with friends and read at Zhōngnán Mountain.
One evening, walking along a stream,
he found a round stone in a cliff,
glistening white like a mirror.
Just as he was holding and admiring it,
it fell to the ground and broke.
Inside was a white fish, about an inch long,
which, following the stone, tumbled into the stream.
It gradually grew to a full chǐ,
and soon became over a zhàng long,
flapping its fins and wagging its tail.
Clouds and thunder suddenly arose,
and a great storm arrived.
Lǐ Xiū
Lǐ Xiū, the Táng surveillance commissioner of Zhèxī,
in the seventh year of Yuánhé,
was the prefect of Jiàng Prefecture.
That year,
in Lóngmén, a subordinate county, a dragon appeared.
At the time, thousands of spectators gathered.
The prefecture reported the matter in writing to the Grand Prefecture.
At the time, the chancellor, Zhāng Hóngjìng of Hédōng Prefecture, was the military governor of Hézhōng.
The chancellor's son, the former prefect of Shū Prefecture, Zhāng Yǐzōng,
once wrote a piece to praise the event.
Wéi Yòu
During the Táng Yuánhé era,
the former commandant Wéi Yòu was appointed prefect of Wēnzhōu.
He felt listless and unhappy.
The river waves were long and vast,
and the boat was hot and stuffy.
One evening when it was cool,
he mounted a horse and went ashore,
walking along the riverbank.
Suddenly, in the shallow sand and scattered streams,
amidst green reeds,
he let the reins loose to water his horse.
A reed branch brushed against his saddle.
Yòu casually plucked it and examined it closely.
Suddenly, he saw new silk zither strings
wound around the reed's core.
Yòu immediately took the reed and stretched out the strings,
which were twice the length of a xún.
He tried releasing them,
and they coiled back up again.
Yòu was astonished and alarmed,
so he placed them in his robe.
When he arrived at the riverside lodge,
his family had already moored the boat and entered the pavilion.
Yòu was a former imperial son-in-law,
and his household had female musicians.
He immediately handed the strings to the zither player, saying:
"I found these inside a reed.
They seem quite new and taut.
But on a sandbar by the river,
how did such a thing come to be?
I find it very strange.
Try fitting them on the instrument
to hear how they sound."
The musician was about to install them,
but they were no different from ordinary strings,
except they were two or three inches shorter.
Just as they were dining,
the musician set them aside,
and as soon as she did, they coiled up again.
After the meal, they looked at them,
and the strings were already wriggling and swaying.
The musician cried out in alarm and told the others.
Everyone rushed to look,
