and the two ends had become clear eyes.
Yòu exclaimed in alarm:
"Could this be a dragon?"
He ordered them to dress formally,
burn incense, and pay respects.
They placed it in a bowl of water
and released it into the river.
Just as it reached midstream,
wind and waves arose,
steaming clouds and rolling thunder,
darkening everything within a short distance.
Suddenly, a white dragon a hundred chǐ long
soared up and grasped the sky.
Everyone witnessed it,
and after a long while, it vanished.
Chǐmù
On a dragon's head, there is something shaped like a Bóshān censer,
called the chǐmù.
Without the chǐmù,
a dragon cannot ascend to heaven.
The Son of the Shǐ Family
There was a son of the Shǐ family who,
during the Wǔhé era of the Táng dynasty,
once traveled to Huàshān with a group of Daoist companions.
At the time, the heat was intense,
so they rested by a small stream.
Suddenly, a leaf as large as a palm,
crimson and lovely,
drifted down with the current.
Shǐ alone caught it
and placed it inside his robe.
After sitting for the time it takes to eat a meal,
he felt something cold and heavy in his robe.
He secretly rose to look at it:
scales had risen upon it, densely packed.
Startled and afraid,
Shǐ discarded it in the forest.
He then told the others:
"This must be a dragon;
we should leave quickly!"
In a short while,
white smoke arose in the forest,
spreading to fill the entire valley.
Before Shǐ had descended halfway down the mountain,
fierce wind and rain arrived.
Lord Lú Chàng
Formerly, Lú Chàng of Fànyáng, who served as Vice Director of the Bureau of Sacrifices and Judge under the Eastern Capital Guardian, when he was still a commoner,
lived as a guest in the region of the Hàn River.
One day,
riding alone in the countryside,
he saw two white dogs with very long bodies,
their chests full and broad,
seeming to float as if about to fall,
both running swiftly across the fields.
Lú, surprised that they were unlike ordinary dogs,
reined in his horse to watch.
Soon, the dogs both leaped into a deep pool,
and then waves in the pool surged and churned.
Immediately, two white dragons rose from the pool,
clouds and vapor choked the sky,
and wind and thunder shook greatly.
Lú was terribly frightened,
whipped his horse, and returned.
Before he had gone several *lǐ*,
his clothes were completely soaked.
Only then did he realize the two dogs were dragons.
Yuán Yìfāng
When Yuán Yìfāng was envoy to Xīnluó,
he departed from Jīlín Prefecture.
They came upon a sea island
with a spring on it.
The sailors all drew water from it to drink.
Suddenly, a small snake emerged from the spring.
The ship's pilot urgently said:
"The dragon is angered."
They then set sail.
Before they had gone several *lǐ*,
wind, clouds, thunder, and lightning all arrived,
continuing for three days and three nights without cease.
When the rain cleared,
they saw a distant shore with a walled city:
it was Láizhōu.
The Píngchāng Well
The old city of Píngchāng was connected to the Jīng River,
and there was a divine dragon
that would come and go there.
Therefore, it was named Dragon City.
In a foreign land, there was a temple called Jùhēluó.
In the temple, a divine dragon dwelled within the rice granary.
When a servant went to fetch rice,
the dragon would retreat.
But if the servant took rice as a regular practice,
the dragon would then not give it.
When the rice in the granary was nearly exhausted,
the servant would bow to the dragon,
and the granary would immediately become full to overflowing.
Tiger Skull
In the southern regions, during drought,
they would tie a tiger skull with a long rope
and cast it into a place where a dragon dwelled.
Once it entered the water,
several people could not hold the rope steady.
In a short while,
clouds would rise from the pool,
and rain would follow and fall.
Fǎxǐ Temple
To the southeast of Zhèngyáng Commandery was Fǎxǐ Temple.
It was about a hundred *lǐ* from the commandery seat
and sat directly west of the Wèi River.
At the end of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
a monk of the temple repeatedly dreamed of a white dragon coming from the Wèi River,
stopping at the western pillar of the Buddha hall,
coiling around it for a long time,
then heading directly east and departing.
The next day, it would rain.
This happened several times.
The monk found it strange
and thus spoke of it to others.
Someone said:
"Blessed lands are where deities and spirits dwell,
and are naturally the abodes of dragons.
Moreover, Buddhist temples are also places dragons rely upon.
Therefore, in Buddhism, there are the Eight Classes of Divine Beings, including dragons;
the principle lies therein.
Especially a temple in the open countryside,
with its halls pure and spacious,
for a dragon to stop there
is indeed fitting, is it not?
I suggest placing an earthen dragon between the temple pillars,
and also using it to mark the occurrence of the dream."
The monk summoned artisans,
who mixed clay to form a dragon statue.
He fully described its appearance,
and they placed it by the western pillar of the hall.
When the work was completed,
it truly captured the imposing manner of a dragon among clouds,
sinuous with scales and mane,
exquisitely perfect in its artistry.
Even the skill of painting
could not surpass it.
At the beginning of the Chángqìng era,
a resident near the temple, lying outside the main gate,
saw a creature emerge directly from the western corridor,
floating ethereally as if ascending into the clouds.
It flew swiftly out of the temple
and headed toward the Wèi River.
Near midnight,
it finally returned beneath the western corridor.
Looking closely at it,
it was indeed a white dragon.
The next day, he reported this to the temple monks.
The monks found it marvelous.
Several days later,
the temple monks all went to attend a vegetarian feast held by the villagers.
They did not return until noon.
Upon entering the hall to look,
the dragon statue was already gone.
The monks sighed in amazement,
looked at each other, and said:
"This dragon,
though given form by clay,
can still transform without constraint.
When it leaves, none know where it goes;
when it comes, none can trace its origin.
Is it indeed a numinous creature?"
By evening,
dark clouds gathered over the Wèi River,
and soon they approached the temple halls.
Suddenly, a creature leaped out from within the clouds
and, pointing toward the western corridor, entered.
The temple monks, frightened and startled,
went to look
and saw the dragon statue was already upon the western pillar.
Drawing near to observe it,
its dragon's mane, scales, and horns
all appeared thoroughly drenched.
From then on, they fastened it with an iron chain.
Thereafter, when the village suffered drought or flood,
they would pray to it,
and the response was as immediate as shadow following form or echo following sound.
The Dragon Temple
The Fén River flows through Tàiyuán and southward.
There are two bridges over the river.
At the southern bridge, a dragon was once seen below,
and therefore a Dragon Temple was built beneath the bridge.
When the former Chancellor Lìnghú Chǔ resided as Guardian of the Northern Capital,
a dragon emerged from the temple.
The entire capital's men and women all came out to watch.
For nearly the time it takes to eat a meal,
it writhed and soared before departing.
Immediately afterward, there was thunderous rain and storm.
Also, in the autumn of the following year,
the Fén River overflowed its banks.
A white snake emerged from the temple.
After it emerged, the temple building collapsed,
and the bridge was also damaged.
This was at the beginning of the Tàihé era of the Táng dynasty.
The Dragon-Keeper
When Niú Sēngrú was governing Xiāngzhōu,
due to a prolonged drought,
prayers for rain proved ineffective.
A hermit who claimed to be a dragon keeper
was requested by the duke to bring rain.
The hermit said:
"There are no dragons in the Jiāng-Hàn region,
except for one in a deep pool,
a black dragon.
If forced to drive it out,
I fear it may cause disaster,
and be difficult to control."
The duke insisted on his request.
Indeed, heavy rain fell,
the Hàn River flooded,
and tens of thousands of households were swept away or drowned.
The hermit, fearing punishment,
also fled.
Kǒng Wēi
In the late Xiántōng era of the Táng dynasty,
Kǒng Wēi, the prefect of Shūzhōu, presented a dragon skeleton,
accompanied by a memorial recording the event as follows:
"In Tóngchéng County of this prefecture, in Shànzhèng Township, a commoner named Hú Jǔ
had a green dragon fight to death in his courtyard.
It was the fourth month,
and silkworm trays were still in the courtyard.
Suddenly, clouds and thunder erupted violently,
and the sound of clashing was heard in the clouds.
Blood fell like pouring rain,
sprinkling onto the silkworm trays.
The blood did not mix with water on the trays
but gradually gathered and coagulated,
so that it could be picked up and held in the palm.
In a moment,
it caused a chilling pain that penetrated to the bone.
Initially, the dragon dragged its tail along the ground,
wrapped around a slop bucket,
and then soared into the clouds.
When the rain came,
it was all slop.
After the dragon died,
it was dissected,
and a large sore was found in its throat.
Its total length was over ten feet.
Its body and tail were of equal length.
The base of the tail was flat and thin.
Its scales and fins were like those of a fish.
Only its whiskers were twenty feet long.
Its feet were covered by a red membrane.
Its two horns were each twenty feet long.
Its belly was naturally jagged.
At the time, the Grand Cloud Granary Commissioner was dispatched to oversee its transport to the prefecture.
As the flesh was too heavy to move whole,
it was cut into several dozen sections
and transported to the authorities.
Huáyīn Pool
In the spring of the ninth year of the Xiántōng era of the Táng dynasty,
more than ten lǐ south of Huáyīn County,
one evening, wind and thunder erupted violently.
A dragon moved a deep pool,
coming from afar.
Previously, the banks were high,
with no place to store water,
but that evening, they shifted open for several dozen zhàng.
A small hill stretched east-west and north-south,
with peaks, ridges, grass, and trees
completely unharmed.
Emergent waves circled the pond,
clear as if carved by excavation.
Travelers from the capital and Luòyáng
all detoured to see it.
Some enthusiasts,
from the capital to Pǔjīn,
came in groups.
Carriages and horses passed incessantly,
lasting for days.
South of the capital, at Língyìng Terrace, there is a Sānniáng Pool,
close to Tàngǔ,
with clear, calm water,
its depth unfathomable.
Whenever autumn winds blew and leaves fell,
leaves and grass
would drift onto its surface.
Even the tiniest leaf or speck
would be carried away by birds.
Those praying often offered hairpins, brocades, and the like,
opening and viewing them before tossing them in,
only to see them vanish instantly.
At the beginning of the Qiánfú era,
several court officials,
while traveling together in the Zhōngnán Mountains,
came to the pool
and discussed its miraculous responses.
Among them, a skeptic
tried throwing wood and stones into it,
whereupon a giant fish leaped from the waves,
its scales white as snow.
Soon, wind and rain darkened the sky,
and the carriages and horses were nearly swept away by the torrent.
Afterward, people revered it even more,
and no one dared to violate it again.
Cuī Dàojū
In the Táng dynasty, there was a Secretariat Drafter named Shū Yán.
His son-in-law, Cuī Dàoshū, repeatedly sat for the imperial examinations.
One spring, he failed the exam
and returned to his home in Hànshàng.
While cleaning the well,
he caught a carp five feet long,
with golden scales and fins,
its eyes shining brightly.
Everyone saw it was different from ordinary fish.
He ordered a servant to throw it into the river.
Dàoshū and his cousin, Mr. Wéi,
secretly prepared a cauldron and cooking utensils,
cooked it, and ate it.
After two nights,
Wéi fell ill and died suddenly.
A blue-clad messenger led him to an official residence,
where the buildings were quite solemn and imposing.
Upon entering the gate,
he saw in the hall a woman wearing a golden and jade crown,
dressed in purple embroidered robes,
sitting behind a desk.
The attendants on both sides all wore yellow robes and headscarves,
resembling palace decorations.
An official came from behind holding a ledger.
Upon reaching the steps of the hall,
he handed it to a blue-clad attendant with double rings,
who placed it on the embroidered-robed woman’s desk.
The official led Mr. Wéi to the eastern wing’s office,
to investigate the matter of killing the fish.
Wéi admitted his fault.
Dàoshū said:
“It was not my crime.”
The official said:
“This was a rain dragon.
If it had been lurking in rivers, seas, or marshes,
even if eaten by humans,
it could have been excused.
But yesterday it was caught in a well,
and you, Cuī, and you, sir, are not ignorant.
Killing and eating it,
it is difficult to avoid punishment.
However, you may return for now,
try with Mr. Cuī to widely perform Buddhist and Daoist merits,
perhaps slightly reducing your offense.
From now, in ten days,
I will summon you again.”
Wéi suddenly awoke,
and told what he had heard
to his relatives,
ordering Dàoshū to recount the matter in detail.
Though Dàoshū felt anxious and pressured,
he did not fully believe it.
Just over ten days later,
Mr. Wéi indeed died.
Wéi was Dàoshū’s maternal cousin.
Several days later,
his spirit sent a message to his mother, saying:
“I have already been convicted for killing the fish.
The place I went to
is the Water Palace.
I will soon face severe punishment.
Quickly perform a Huánglù Daoist ritual,
hoping to receive leniency in sentencing.
My cousin’s offense is also established,
tonight he will know of it himself.”
Wéi’s mother tearfully told Dàoshū.
At dusk,
Dàoshū fell into a deep sleep,
and again saw a blue-clad man leading him to an official residence,
exactly as Wéi had described.
Soon an official came holding a black paper with red writing,
stood Dàoshū beside a screen,
and hurried in.
Soon he saw the embroidered-robed woman lift her brush and finish writing,
the official took it and came out,
letting Dàoshū read it.
At first it said:
“Cuī Dàoshū will hold office up to the third rank,
and live to eighty years.”
Later there was a judgment:
“The harm done to the rain dragon
concerns the celestial court.
Forgiveness is impossible,
the crime must be urgently pursued.
All official ranks and titles
are hereby stripped.
Lifespan also reduced by half.”
At that time, Dàoshū was in winter,
his mother was performing meritorious Buddhist rites,
but just at the start of spring,
he fell ill for several days and died.
At that time, Cuī’s wife and children were all in the capital,
and Wéi Yán recounted the matter in detail.
It was traditionally said that Kuí and Niúzhǔ Jī were Water Palaces,
but it is unclear exactly where Dàoshū went.
Golden Dragon Child
In the second year of Wéndé, during Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng’s reign, on New Year’s Day at the Wǔdé Hall,
purple vapor emerged from the eastern corner of the Zhāodé Hall,
billowing like smoke.
The emperor ordered the palace guard to search for its source,
and they found a golden dragon child,
about five inches long.
The ministers offered congratulations.
The emperor said:
“I do not consider the golden dragon an auspicious sign,
but the cessation of warfare as auspicious.
You all should be loyal,
to understand my heart.”
The Chancellery memorialized,
requesting to change the second year of Wéndé to the first year of Lóngjì.
Huáng Xùn
In Dāngyáng County, Jīngzhōu, the official buildings were built against a mountain.
Inside was an extremely deep well.
In the well was a dragon’s nest.
Its side passages were of unknown extent.
When clearing skies or impending rain,
often clouds and vapor would emerge from the well.
During the Guānghuà era of Táng,
a Daoist priest claiming to come from Shāngshān
entered the well,
took the dragon’s nest and some medicinal herbs, and left.
Later, there was a magistrate named Huáng Xùn,
who, after taking office,
often tied his horse beside the well,
allowing filth and waste to flow
into the well.
Some criticized him,
but he made excuses.
Over a year later,
Xùn and his horse both went blind.
Línhàn Pig
In Línhàn County, Qióngzhōu, there was a pool,
where people often saw a sow entering and exiting,
called the “Sow Dragon Pool.”
In the fourth year of Tiānfù of Táng,
the Shǔ region suffered a great drought,
and officials were ordered to personally visit spiritual sites to pray for rain.
At that time, the county magistrate prepared sacrificial offerings,
ordered his subordinates,
and went together to offer sacrifices.
After three rounds of offerings,
they set up a feast by the pool,
sharing the sacrificial meat with guests.
Sitting under the scorching sun,
they spread mats.
Taking the pool as the seat of honor,
each time the wine reached the pool,
they raised cups in offering.
They vowed to withdraw the feast only
when rain had sufficiently soaked the ground.
Just as singing and music were at their peak,
suddenly above the pool,
black vapor like clouds
billowed straight up,
fierce lightning flashed,
dark clouds suddenly darkened,
and rain and hail immediately fell.
The magistrate and his subordinates,
dancing and cheering, removed their covers,
and returned soaked.
The next day,
this entire area had sufficient rain,
while other counties remained barren.
When humans are utterly sincere,
even dragons and beasts can be moved.
Honoring virtue to relieve drought—
do not say they lack wisdom.
Burning Dragon
South of the Great River,
among the reeds and rushes,
dragons were often stirred up by fire.
During the Tianfu era of the Tang dynasty,
a son of the Dèng family, a villager of Yèyuán in Lǐzhōu, was burning fields for cultivation.
Firewood and grass were piled in the courtyard,
and as the flames grew fierce,
a dragon suddenly emerged,
soaring into midair.
Entangled and scorched by the fire,
the wind grew stronger,
the raging flames more intense,
and though it thrashed, it could not escape,
eventually falling to the ground and dying.
Its body stretched several hundred paces long.
The villagers relocated to avoid it.
At the end of the Later Liáng dynasty,
a villager named Xiàng in Chénzhōu stirred up a dragon while burning fields.
Fierce winds, thunder, and heavy rain arose on all sides,
but they could not extinguish the fire.
Soon, it was reduced to ashes,
but its horns remained unburned,
gleaming white like jade.
Xiàng treasured them and kept them hidden,
but Gāo Yù, a military commander in Húnán, paid their price and forcibly took them.
At that time, a diviner said:
"Is Commander Gāo heading for disaster?
Why use an inauspicious object to hasten it?"
Soon after, he was executed.
Old Man Liǔ
During the Tiānyòu era,
in Ráozhōu, there was an old man named Liǔ who often went fishing in a small boat on the Póyáng River.
No one knew where he lived or who his wife and children were,
nor did anyone see him eat or drink.
He was thoroughly knowledgeable about
all kinds of aquatic creatures
and the remote depths of mountains and rivers.
Fishermen of Póyáng
all consulted him before setting out.
When Lǚ Shīzào served as prefect,
he repaired the city walls and dug moats.
Whenever they reached the north of the city, it would rain;
when they stopped, it would clear.
Someone asked Old Man Liǔ about this.
The old man said:
"Below here is a dragon's lair.
Disturbing the ground above
makes the dragon uneasy, and it emerges from its den.
When the dragon emerges, rain falls.
If you keep digging,
you will surely reach the lair,
and then continuous rain will become a calamity."
After digging several zhang deep,
they indeed found square timbers tens of feet long,
interlocked and stacked,
piled in dozens of layers.
Below, a mist surged up, overwhelming to people,
so they could not enter and stopped.
The timbers were all coated with a slimy, fishy substance,
carved and smoothed evenly,
beyond human capability.
From then on, continuous rain indeed became a calamity.
When Lǚ's sons were about to cast nets for fish in the Póyáng River,
they summoned and asked Old Man Liǔ.
The old man pointed to a spot on the southern bank:
"Today, only this place has fish,
but there is a small dragon there."
The sons did not believe him,
cast their nets,
and indeed made a huge catch.
They stored the fish in a large basin on the boat.
Among them was a ricefield eel, one or two feet long,
with bright, clear eyes,
and two long whiskers,
circling around the basin.
All the other fish followed it like wings.
As they approached the northern bank,
it suddenly vanished.
Old Man Liǔ ultimately disappeared without a trace.
Jambudvīpa Dragons
There are 5.7 billion dragons in Jambudvīpa.
In Godānīya, dragons do not send down muddy water.
People of the Western Continent die if they drink muddy water.
People of Uttarakuru dislike cold winds,
so dragons do not stir up cold.
In Pūrvavideha,
they do not produce thunder,
nor do they create lightning.
The Eastern Continent dislikes these.
As for thunder,
in the Tuṣita Heaven, it sounds like hymns;
in Jambudvīpa, it sounds like ocean tides.
As for rain,
in the Tuṣita Heaven, it rains down jewels;
in Ketumatī City, it rains delicious food.
In the ocean, rain pours down unceasingly like connected threads.
Among the Asuras, it rains weapons and armor;
in Jambudvīpa, it rains clear, floating water.
The Wúshān Man
In Wúshān County of Lǒngzhōu,
a man rode a white horse at night,
and everyone in the county dreamed of him.
He said:
"I wish to move my dwelling
and temporarily borrow your oxen."
Having spoken, he passed by.
That night,
the oxen of several hundred households,
by dawn,
were all drenched in sweat as if soaked in water.
In a bend of the southern mountain of the county, a pool emerged,
over a hundred paces in circumference.
The villagers believed this pool had moved because of the oxen,
and called it the "Ox Pool."
General Bái
Monk Yuányán said:
It was recently said that a General Bái once washed his horse at the Qǔjiāng River.
The horse suddenly leaped out in fright and ran.
On its front leg was something,
white like a sash,
coiled several times around.
He quickly ordered it removed.
Several shēng of blood flowed.
Bái found it strange,
so he sealed it in a paper packet,
and hid it in his clothes chest.
One day,
while seeing off guests at the Chǎnshuǐ River,
he showed it to the guests.
A guest said:
"Why not test it with water?"
Bái used his sword to scratch a hole in the ground,
placed the creature inside,
and poured washing water over it.
After a short while,
the creature wriggled and grew longer,
and spring water surged from the hole.
Suddenly, it coiled itself to the size of a mat,
and a black vapor, like incense smoke,
shot straight out beyond the eaves.
Everyone feared, saying:
"It must be a dragon."
So they hurried back.
Before they had gone several li,
wind and rain suddenly arrived,
with several loud thunderclaps.
Old Woman Wēn
Old Woman Wēn
was a widow from Yuèchéng County in Kāngzhōu,
who made her living by spinning cloth.
Once, while gathering vegetables on the wild shore,
she saw five eggs among the sand and grass,
so she collected them
and placed them in her spinning basket.
Within a few days,
she suddenly saw five small snakes—
one with spotted skin, four with blue skin.
She then released them by the riverbank,
truly without expecting any reward.
The old woman often washed clothes by the river.
Suddenly one day,
she saw fish leaping in the water,
playing before her.
From then on, it became a regular occurrence,
and gradually, people came to know of it.
The villagers all regarded her as the mother of dragons,
respecting and serving her,
and some inquired about disasters or blessings.
Her words often proved true.
From then on, the old woman gradually became well-off.
The imperial court learned of this
and sent an envoy to summon her to the capital.
When she reached Quányì Ridge,
she fell ill,
returned to Yuèchéng, and died.
The villagers buried her together on the eastern bank of the river.
Suddenly one night,
heaven and earth turned dark,
and wind and rain arose.
By dawn,
her grave had moved to the western bank,
and all the plants and trees were on the western shore.
Liǔ Zǐhuá,
during the Táng dynasty, served as the magistrate of Chéngdū.
One day around noon,
a calf-drawn carriage suddenly arrived,
with female riders leading the way before and after it, proceeding directly into the main hall.
A messenger announced to Liǔ:
"The Dragon Maiden is about to arrive."
Soon she alighted from the carriage,
supported and escorted by attendants as she ascended the steps,
and met with Zǐhuá.
She said:
"Our destinies are intertwined, and we are fated to be husband and wife."
Thus she stayed.
Wine and music were ordered, and they enjoyed themselves to the fullest,
completing the wedding rites before she departed.
From then on, her comings and goings became regular,
and people far and wide all knew of it.
When Zǐhuá's term of office ended,
he disappeared without a trace.
Common folk say:
"He entered the Dragon Palace,
and became an immortal of the waters."
The Mottled Stone
In the capital city, there was a scholar
who, while traveling in the mountains,
picked up a stone.
It was mottled green and red,
and as large as a chicken's egg.
He found it very strange.
He kept it in his handkerchief box for five or six years.
Once, while playing with an infant,
he lost it.
A few days later,
suddenly, during the day, wind and rain arose, darkening the sky,
and in front of the courtyard, under a tree,
water poured down unceasingly like a waterfall.
Everyone was puzzled by the cause.
When the wind and rain ceased,
they suddenly saw this stone under the tree, already broken open,
with something inside that had emerged like a chick from its shell.
Then they realized it was a dragon's offspring.
Zhānggōng Cave
The mountains and waters of Yìxīng County are exceptionally beautiful,
and Zhānggōng Cave is particularly wondrous and magnificent.
The locals say
it is the place where Zhāng Dàolíng practiced his cultivation.
Inside are caverns and chasms,
which the masses dared not enter.
A local man named Yáo, who practiced the Dao,
took a staff, a bottle, and a torch,
and carrying a bag, entered the cave.
After walking several hundred paces,
it gradually grew brighter,
with clouds and trees faintly visible.
As he drew closer,
after another ten or so *lǐ*,
he saw two Daoist priests playing chess.
They said:
"Who are you?
How did you get here?"
He recounted everything from beginning to end.
They said:
"You are a man of great determination."
Yáo was very hungry,
so he asked for food.
Nearby were several pecks of blue mud.
The Daoist priests pointed and said:
"You may eat this."
He tentatively tasted and chewed it,
finding it fragrant and sweet,
and eating it satisfied his hunger.
The Daoist priests said:
"You should leave now,
and be careful not to tell anyone in the world."
He bowed twice and returned,
secretly keeping the remainder.
He went to the marketplace to inquire about it,
and by chance, a foreign merchant saw it.
Startled, he said:
"This is dragon food.
Where did you obtain it?"
So Yáo told him the story.
They went together to search for the place,
but found only a huge black hole,
with no path remaining.
The blue mud, once brought outside,
had already hardened like stone,
and could no longer be eaten.
The Pond on Wǔtái Mountain
Below the North Terrace of Wǔtái Mountain, there is a dragon pond covering about two *mǔ* or more.
Buddhist scriptures say
it is a place where five hundred poisonous dragons are confined.
Every day at noon,
the dark mist temporarily clears,
and only then can *bhikkhus* and pious lay practitioners catch a glimpse.
If *bhikkhunīs* or women approach,
thunder, lightning, wind, and rain immediately rage violently.
If one gets close to the pond,
they are inevitably drawn in by the poisonous vapors,
and in moments, vanish.
Old Man Zhāng
In Jīngxiāng, there was a Buddhist temple with its back to the mountains and close to water,
and in the water lived a dragon.
Sometimes, great thunder and wind would arise,
damaging trees.
In the temple was an old bell-ringer named Zhāng,
who was a sorcerer,
though the monks did not know it.
Old Man Zhāng disliked this dragon for damaging things,
and wanted to subdue and kill it,
secretly performing magic rites.
The dragon, already aware of this,
transformed into a human,
and secretly told a monk:
"I am truly a dragon,
and have lived in these waters for many years.
Occasionally, when I emerge,
wind and rain damage things,
and now Old Man Zhāng seeks to subdue me.
My life is in grave danger,
and only you, Reverend, can save me.
If you save my life,
I will present you with a precious pearl
to express my gratitude.
I will then move elsewhere."
The monk agreed.
At night, he summoned Old Man Zhāng,
asking him to release the dragon.
Old Man Zhāng said:
"Reverend, are you not accepting a pearl offered by this dragon?
This dragon is very poor,
possessing only this pearl,
and its nature is both stingy and malicious.
If you accept the pearl now,
you will regret it later, and it will be too late."
The monk did not believe him.
He said:
"Just release it for me."
Old Man Zhāng had no choice
and released it.
The dragon later brought the pearl to the monk at night,
and moved away from the pool.
Old Man Zhāng also bid farewell to the monk and left.
A few days later,
suddenly, a great thunderstorm arose,
destroying the monk's quarters,
and taking back the pearl.
It happened exactly as Old Man Zhāng had said.
Fèi Jīshī
In Shǔchuān there was a man named Fèi Jīshī,
who was skilled at knowing future events,
and could also perform rituals to avert disasters for people.
He often stayed in Qióngzhōu.
The people of Shǔ revered him as divine.
At that time, a monk recounted:
In the past, at Bǎotáng Temple in Shuāngliú County,
there was a monk named Zhāng Èrshī.
While inspecting the monks' quarters,
he saw an empty courtyard,
and intended to take up residence there.
As he led his family in cleaning and sweeping,
he found a small bottle on a pillar.
Èrshī examined it
and saw a snake inside the bottle.
He overturned the bottle to release it,
and it was about one chǐ long,
with mottled patterns,
displaying all five colors.
When he poked it with a stick,
it grew at his touch.
Everyone was astonished.
Èrshī ordered someone to carry it,
and sent it outside the temple.
While carrying it,
it grew larger with each touch,
until it reached over a zhàng in length,
like a roof beam.
Two men could barely lift it,
and those escorting it grew increasingly fearful,
while onlookers followed in growing numbers.
About two or three lǐ from the temple,
as they were shaking from the effort,
it continued to grow.
The crowd grew even more terrified,
so they struck and injured it,
until it died.
The next day,
a rainbow appeared in this temple courtyard,
descending into the temple at noon.
The monk had business in Línqióng,
and told Fèi Jīshī about it.
Jīshī said:
"You have killed a dragon maiden!
Zhāng Èrshī and the monks of your temple
will all die!"
Later, it turned out just as he said.
His other accurate predictions were too numerous to record.
In the end, no one knew what
art he practiced.
Wéi Xuàn's elder brother served as an assistant to Dù Yuányǐng,
and his younger siblings all knew Master Fèi.
While in the capital, they had already heard of these events.
Upon arriving,
he inquired about Jīshī's methods.
Whenever a sick person came to seek help,
Jīshī would immediately take a rooster and go.
Upon reaching the door,
he would chant incantations over the rooster,
then send it inside,
to the place where the sick person lay.
If the rooster entered and died,
the sick person would recover.
If the rooster came out, the sick person would not rise again.
Thus, people of the time called him "Fèi Jīshī" (Rooster Master Fèi).
He would also place a stone on the sick person's abdomen,
perform rituals and form hand seals,
and if the stone broke,
the person would also not recover.
He could also write talismans,
first burning the talisman to ashes,
mixing it with hot water,
and having the person swallow it.
Shortly after, they would vomit it out,
and the talisman would appear intact as if unburned.
It is also said
that south of the city, under Jiànchāng Bridge,
there was originally a dragon's lair on the southern bank,
which often caused casualties each year.
There were even cases of people drowning along with their horses,
as if something were seizing them in the water.
During Wéi Gāo's time,
stones were transported back and forth,
totaling tens of thousands.
But soon after,
the stones disappeared again.
Later, a Daoist priest was ordered to throw inscribed bamboo slips into it,
and it was filled with earth,
only then becoming full.
After this,
the dragon's lair moved beneath the Buddha hall of Jiànchāng Temple,
connecting with the dragon well in the western corridor.
As for under Jiànchāng Bridge,
it still occasionally caused casualties, though not as severely.
Upon questioning soldiers and attendants,
it was learned that in the past, when people and horses drowned there,
after a long time, the corpses would float up, all pale,
their blood completely sucked dry,
and only then would the corpses emerge.
The Old Woman of Fénshuǐ
By the Fénshuǐ River, an old woman caught a red carp,
whose color was extraordinary,
unlike other fish.
After bringing it home,
the old woman pitied and cherished it,
finding it remarkable.
She dug a small pond,
drew water, and raised it there.
After more than a month,
clouds and mist suddenly rose,
and the red carp leaped up,
in a moment's time,
gradually ascending into the sky,
while the pond dried up.
By night,
it returned as before.
Those who saw it were greatly astonished,
considering it a monster.
The old woman feared it would bring disaster,
and deeply regretted her actions.
So she personally went to the small pond and prayed:
"I spared your life out of pity,
allowing you to live—
do you now intend to bring calamity upon me?"
As soon as she finished speaking,
the red carp leaped up,
clouds followed the wind,
and it entered the Fénshuǐ River.
Only a pearl was left in the air,
like a pellet,
shining brilliantly and dazzling to behold.
The old woman obtained it,
and no one dared to take it.
Five years later,
the old woman's eldest son suffered from a wind ailment,
and his condition gradually worsened,
with no doctor able to cure him.
The old woman was deeply grieved.
Suddenly, she thought of taking this pearl
to summon a skilled doctor.
The pearl suddenly transformed into a pill of elixir.
The old woman said:
"This red carp left this for me
to save my son,
repaying my kindness."
So she gave it to her son to take,
and his illness soon healed.
Lǐ Xuān
Lǐ Xuān served as magistrate of Yáng County.
To the left of the county seat was a deep pool,
said to be inhabited by a dragon,
and the scaly creatures there were especially fine.
Lǐ's son was lazy in his studies,
but loved the art of fishing,
and went to the pool daily.
One morning, the dragon appeared,
and the entire pool erupted in flames,
like an unfurled brocade quilt.
Lǐ's son was terrified out of his wits,
dropped his fishing rod, and fled.
It seems fishing techniques often used fried swallows as bait,
which indeed aroused the dragon's cravings.
Méngyáng Pool
In Péngzhōu Méngyáng County,
there is a place called Qīngliú,
with a deep pool.
Local folklore says
that the dragon of this pool marries the dragon of the Címǔ Pond in the western mountains,
meeting once a year.
Wáng Ruì of Xīnfán, a man of broad learning,
often corrected such claims.
He once scoffed at this.
After an autumn rain, while passing by this pool,
he encountered a thunderstorm from the west darkening the sky,
with fierce winds uprooting trees.
Wáng Ruì tied his horse and sheltered behind a tree.
In a moment,
the force of thunder and lightning
ceased above the pool,
and suddenly cleared,
leaving not a wisp of cloud in the sky.
When he questioned the local residents,
it exactly matched the earlier tale.
West of Yún'ān County flows the small Tāng Stream.
Local custom holds
that the dragon of this stream is kin to the dragon of the Yún'ān Stream.
This is an unfounded story.
One day,
wind and thunder arose from the small Tāng Stream,
following the Shǔ River downstream,
reaching Yún'ān County.
Clouds and mist swirled densely,
entering the stream,
with fierce lightning and terrifying thunder indeed awe-inspiring.
There is the tale of Liǔ Yì and the Dòngtíng Lake,
which corresponds to this.
The events at the small Tāng Stream were witnessed firsthand.
Salt Well Dragon
During the Wáng Shǔ period.
In the Dàchāng salt wells of Kuízhōu, dragons often appeared in the water,
some white, some yellow,
with gleaming scales and manes.
Stirring them did not move them,
only causing
froth and bubbles.
The locals did not find this strange.
Recently, in the brine trough of the Yǒngjì well in Zǐguī,
a dragon was also seen coiled,
no different from those in Dàchāng.
A knowledgeable person said:
"The dragon is a creature of spiritual auspice,
bearing charts to ascend to heaven.
Now it is seen in brine,
how can it ride clouds and summon rain?"
At the summit of Hànchéng Palace in Yún'ān County,
there is a celestial pool, seven or eight zhang deep.
In it is a creature like a lizard,
about a foot long,
adorned with five colors,
leaping on the water's surface,
resembling a small dragon.
There was a governor named Gāo Yù,
who went to the palace to perform rituals,
when it suddenly floated up.
Someone asked the supervising official Lǐ Défú:
"What omen is this?"
Fú said:
"I have lived here since birth,
and have rarely seen the creature in the Hànchéng pool.
Since Gāo has no good governance,
and flatters Buddhas and fawns on spirits,
it has reached this point.
How can we determine right or wrong?"
In Yílíng's Qīngjiāng, there is Lángshān Pond,
where a dragon resides.
A local tyrant, Lǐ Wùqiú, prayed and served it.
He once saw brocade,
quilts covering the water,
or large logs floating up,
blocking the water's surface,
called the dragon's nest.
In Suìzhōu's Gāodòng Stream pond,
a dragon appears every year,
just like the events at Lángshān.
Yǐn Hào
During the Zhū Liáng, Yǐn Hào garrisoned Huázhōu.
When summer was nearly half over,
he went out of the city to inspect the guards.
This was because Pú and Yōng were engaged in armed conflict.
Dismounting,
he found in the wasteland an object like a stone,
or like an egg.
Its color was bluish-black,
smooth and lovely.
He ordered his attendants to keep it.
Traveling another twenty or thirty li,
he saw a village temple with a Buddha hall,
So he placed it before the statue.
That night, thunder roared mightily,
rain poured down fiercely,
heavenly fire burned the Buddha hall,
yet did not damage the Buddha statue.
It was likely a dragon egg.
Outside the temple, several hundred willow trees
were all uprooted.
The egg had vanished.
Zhāng Wēn
During the Wáng Shǔ period,
in Zǐzhōu, there was a man named Zhāng Wēn who loved fishing,
and once served as a garrison commander at a guesthouse.
In midsummer,
he took guests to watch fish,
and happened to wander near a dragon pool.
It was very hot,
and his mood was low.
He entered the water himself to cast a net,
catching a fish about a foot long,
with golden fins and scales,
thrashing incessantly.
Those on the bank were all amazed.
Soon, darkness fell,
and wind and rain suddenly arose.
Zhāng Wēn, terrified,
ran for several li,
yet the fierce scene persisted.
Someone said:
"The golden fish he caught
was the pool's dragon."
Thus it is known that the dragon, disguised as a fish,
brought disaster upon itself.
Had there been no stormy change,
it would not have escaped the cooking pot.
Fishing in a dragon pool
should be approached with caution.
Guō Yànláng
It is said that wayward dragons suffer when making rain,
and often flee to hide,
pursued by thunder gods.
Sometimes they hide in ancient trees or within pillars,
or in open wilderness,
with nowhere to hide,
they enter ox horns or the bodies of shepherd boys.
Often, they bring calamity upon these beings, who are struck dead by lightning.
In Shǔ, there was an army
officer named Guō Yànláng,
sailing on the Xiá River,
reaching Luóyún irrigation area.
Just after eating, he lay down,
his mind hazy as in a dream,
when he saw a yellow-robed man say:
"Don't be mistaken."
Then the man took something from his mouth and left.
Waking up,
he only felt a pain in his throat.
Meanwhile, the boatmen saw thunder, lightning, and darkness on the boat,
with extremely loud thunderclaps.
This was a wayward dragon entering his mouth.
The Venerable Xuānlǜ of Nánshān
had a wayward dragon enter his middle finger joint,
which is also not a false tale.
Therefore, as Confucius said,
one must change demeanor at sudden thunder and fierce wind—
should we not respect this?
Wáng Zōngláng
In the gēngwǔ year of Shǔ,
Jīnzhōu governor Wáng Zōngláng reported that by the Xúnyáng County Xún River, there was a Qīngyān Temple.
For several days,
smoke and clouds darkened above the temple,
with music played day and night.
Suddenly one morning,
waves surged and leaped,
and a group of dragons emerged from the water,
proceeding into the Hàn River.
The larger ones were several zhang long,
the smaller ones over a zhang,
displaying colors of the five directions,
with shapes like oxen, horses, donkeys, or sheep.
Fifty in total, large and small,
one after another in succession,
they entered the Hàn River,
then passed by the temple site.
Going back and forth for several li,
now hidden, now visible.
This lasted three days before ceasing.
Xīpú Dragon
In the Guǐyǒu year,
in the fields of Xīpǔ, there was a small dragon, blue-black in color.
It was cut into two pieces,
and after ten days, it rotted and stank,
soon after, it disappeared.
To the west of the main hall at Móhē Chí, there is also a Dragon Well,
which is very spiritual,
and people must not violate it.
Well Fish
South of the Wǔhóu residence in Shūtái Fāng, Chéngdū,
inside the Chéngyān Guàn, there is an ancient well containing fish.
They are six or seven cùn long.
They often swim above the well.
The water must surge and swell.
It is said that there is a dragon in the well.
Ān Tiānlóng
During the Tóngguāng era of the Later Táng,
a mother and son from Cāngzhōu suffered under heavy taxes and corvée,
and fled to the border area near Fēngdiàn.
On the road, they encountered a white snake.
The son tied a rope around the snake's neck,
and dragged it along as they walked.
Before long, he shook it, and its head fell off.
In a moment,
a patch of white cloud rose,
thunder and lightning erupted violently,
lifting this son into the sky,
where he was burned to death by thunder and fire and fell to the ground.
On his back were large written characters,
which no one could recognize.
Suddenly, someone said,
"Why not cover it with something blue?"
Then the characters would be recognized.
So they covered it with a blue skirt.
Someone who could read the characters read them aloud:
"This person killed Ān Tiānlóng,
and was executed by the heavenly gods."
Bǎoguāngzǐ said:
"The dragon is a divine creature,
and moreover bears the title 'Ān Tiān' (Pacifier of Heaven),
so it must be capable of limitless transformations.
How could a mere youth tie it with a rope and kill it?
To then incur the punishment of heaven and man—
what is this all about!"
Cáo Kuān
During the Shí Jìn period,
Ān Zhòngróng, the military governor of Chángshān, was planning to overstep his authority.
His jurisdiction bordered Xíngtái,
where a dragon was fought and killed.
A local magnate named Cáo Kuān witnessed it
and took its two horns.
In front was something like a curtain,
with patterns like tangled brocade,
which no one recognized.
Cáo Kuān was killed by bandits within a year.
In the Rényín year,
when Zhènzhōu was attacked,
Ān Zhòngróng was executed.
Bǎoguāngzǐ read the *History of the Northern Dynasties*
and saw that when Lù Fǎhé was in Liáng,
he led troops to resist Rèn Yuē, a general of Hóu Jǐng, on the river.
He said:
"Their dragon is asleep and motionless,
while our army's dragon
is leaping and surging vigorously."
So he attacked and defeated them greatly,
capturing Rèn Yuē.
This shows that on the battlefield,
dragons must first do battle.
The death of the Chángshān dragon—
was it not because the imperial army achieved a great victory,
and Zhòngróng was beheaded?
Huáng Cháo was defeated at Chénzhōu,
and Lǐ Kèyòng escaped from the disaster of Prince of Liáng,
both aided by heavy rain and thunder.
Dream of the Blue-Clad Maiden
In the palace of the mother of the Later Shǔ ruler Mèng, there was a Shrine of the Guardian Sacred Dragon,
which had also been decorated with solemn cleanliness.
It was essentially the household god of the secular world.
One day, wishing to expand its hall,
she took a nap during the day
and dreamed of a blue-clad maiden who said to the queen:
"Now the Sacred Dragon wishes to move and reside outside the palace;
it would be appropriate to arrange a place in a temple or monastery."
The queen wished to comply,
but her son did not permit it.
Later, the queen dreamed again of the blue-clad maiden repeating her request.
So they selected a spot among the corridors of Zhāojué Temple,
and specially built a shrine there.
Once the construction was completed
and the paintings were finished,
they summoned the musicians from the Imperial Music Bureau.
Leading out from the palace,
they played the "Song for Sending Off the Deity";
upon returning to the new shrine,
they played the "Song for Welcoming the Deity."
That day, dark clouds gathered from all directions,
a great wind arose and shook everything,
and when the deity returned to its place,
rain poured down in torrents.
Some said:
"For the Guardian Sacred Dragon to leave the palace
is an inauspicious sign."
Within a year,
the state perished and was destroyed,
and the land returned to the temple.
Emperor Hàn Wǔ's White Jiāo
Emperor Hàn Wǔdì often, in the autumn months,
would float a Língyì boat on the Lín Chí,
from night until daybreak.
Below the Jì Tái,
using fragrant gold for hooks,
and silk lines,
with boat carp as bait,
within less than ten days,
he hooked a white jiāo, three or four zhàng long,
like a dragon but without scales.
The Emperor said:
"This is not a dragon."
So he handed it to the Grand Provisioner to prepare as fresh food.
Its flesh was purple-blue,
crisp and delicious beyond compare.
He issued an edict bestowing it upon his ministers,
considering it obtained through divine inspiration.
Later, it was never obtained again.
Xúnyáng Bridge
At the east gate of Xúnyáng City, leading to the great bridge,
there was often a jiāo harming the common people.
Dǒng Fèng wrote a talisman and sank it into the water.
After a few days,
a dead jiāo was seen floating to the surface.
Wáng Shù
In the seventh month of the third year of the Chìwū era of Emperor Wú Dàdì of Wú,
a man named Wáng Shù was gathering herbs on Tiāntāi Mountain.
As it was hot at the time,
he rested beneath a stone bridge,
drinking by the stream.
Suddenly, he saw in the stream a small blue-clad attendant, over a chǐ tall,
holding a blue garment,
riding a red carp,
heading directly into the clouds,
gradually disappearing from sight.
After a long while, Shù climbed a steep cliff and looked around in all directions.
He saw wind and clouds rising over the sea,
and in an instant, thunder and lightning clashed and roared,
quickly approaching.
Shù, afraid,
hid inside a hollow tree.
He saw something like cloth being pulled along,
black as lacquer,
not knowing where it was going.
When the sky cleared,
he again saw the red carp and the small attendant he had seen riding it,
returning into the stream—
it was actually a black jiāo.
Wáng Zhí was a native of Xīngàn.
He was crossing the Xiāng River by boat.
As dusk approached, gazing into the distance,
he said to his friend Zhū Shòu:
"This is the place where King Zhāo of Chǔ once obtained the píngshí fruit,
and where Confucius spoke of the fulfillment of the children's rhyme."
Shòu said:
"Others consider children's rhymes to be mere chance,
but the sage would surely have understood them."
As soon as he finished speaking,
they saw two men emerge from the riverbank.
A man in black robes, holding a reed staff, said to Zhí:
"Where have you come from?"
Zhí replied:
"I have come from Xīngàn and arrived here."
The two men said:
"We see that you are both scholars.
What classics do you study?"
Zhí and Shòu replied
that they each studied the Odes and the Rites.
The two men laughed and said:
"Master Confucius said:
'The Master did not speak of spirits and anomalies.'
He also said:
'Respect ghosts and spirits but keep them at a distance.'
Why is that?"
Shòu said:
"The Master was a sage.
He did not speak of spirits and anomalies
for fear of confusing the teachings of the classics.
As for saying 'Respect ghosts and spirits but keep them at a distance,'
it was to warn against disrupting moral principles,
with the intention of upholding filial piety in ancestral worship."
The two men said:
"Well said."
They then asked:
"Do you believe this?"
Shòu replied;
"Yes."
The two men said:
"We are actually neither ghosts nor spirits,
nor are we human.
Today, by chance, we have spoken with you,
for we are messengers of Heaven."
They then said to Zhí:
"Tomorrow, on this riverbank, there will be two men, Lǐ Huán and Dài Zhèng,
both merchants,
who exploit the people for profit,
and their greed knows no bounds.
The Lord Above detests them
and intends to punish their crimes within three days.
Do not moor your boat here.
Be cautious."
Having said this,
they vanished into the river.
Shòu and Zhí were astonished,
uncertain what manner of beings they were.
At dawn,
Zhí said to Shòu:
"Given this inauspicious omen,
we should move farther away."
So they towed their boat upstream for more than five paces.
After mooring,
they saw over ten large boats coming from upstream,
which indeed moored at the spot where Zhí's boat had been.
Zhí said:
"We should inquire in detail to find out their names."
Thereupon, Shòu took his staff and went to ask.
The surnames of the two merchants
were indeed as the two men had said.
Shòu, alarmed, said:
"The matter is settled."
He then said to Zhí:
"In the realm of darkness,
the wickedness of evil men is known,
and tonight I have come to believe it."
Zhí said:
"When we speak of the hidden and the manifest,
it is because the hidden has spirits, and spirits are perceptive.
How can we not believe it?"
This was in the seventh month of the first year of the Yuánxī era of Emperor Gōng of Jìn.
From the eighth to the tenth day,
there was indeed a great storm with thunder and rain.
The two merchants drowned at the same time.
When Zhí first heard the words of the two men,
he privately told others.
By the time it happened, there were several hundred people watching together.
Among them was a man named Gěng Tán, seventy years old,
who was well-versed in local lore.
He said to Zhí:
"In this river, there are two flood dragons resembling green snakes,
over ten feet long,
often seen in the waves.
Sometimes they transform and swim among the islets,
but they rarely harm anything.
The two men in black robes you saw
were likely these flood dragons, possessing spiritual power
and carrying out the command of the Lord Above."
Lù Shèr
Lù Shèr was a commoner from Jiāngxià.
He often planted rice by the river.
One night on his way home,
he met a woman
of remarkable beauty.
She said to Shèr:
"I came from the county town yesterday
and now wish to return to Pǔlǐ.
May I seek shelter with you for the night?"
Yet her words and expression showed deep distress.
Shèr had no choice
and took her home with him.
They entered a room and slept together.
Before long,
they heard a violent storm with thunder and lightning.
Shèr only felt the woman trembling with fear,
unable to control herself.
In an instant, thunder struck
right outside the curtain.
Something burst open in Shèr's bedroom.
By the flash of lightning,
he saw a huge, hairy hand snatch the woman away.
Shèr collapsed to the ground,
fainted, and then revived.
At dawn,
his neighbors, surprised, came to ask what had happened.
Shèr told them about the woman seeking shelter.
Shortly after,
someone from the village who had crossed the river came
and said
that nine lǐ away,
there was a huge headless flood dragon,
over a hundred zhàng long,
with blood flowing and pooling over several mǔ of land.
Thousands of birds
had gathered, cawing around it.
The Chángshā Woman
In Chángshā, there was a man whose name has been forgotten.
His home was by the river.
His daughter went down to the islet to wash clothes
and felt something strange within her body.
Later, she did not consider it a problem
and became pregnant.
She gave birth to three creatures,
all resembling shrimp or fish.
Since she had given birth to them herself,
she cherished them dearly
and kept them in a bathing basin filled with water to raise.
After three months,
these creatures grew large
and turned out to be young flood dragons.
Each had a name:
the eldest was called Dānghóng,
the second Pòzǔ,
and the youngest Pū'àn.
During a heavy rainstorm,
the three flood dragons left all at once
and were nowhere to be found.
Later, whenever rain was about to fall,
these creatures would return.
The woman also knew when they were coming
and would go out to watch for them.
The young flood dragons would also emerge,
lifting their heads to gaze at their mother
for a long time before leaving again.
After a year,
when this woman passed away,
the three flood dragons came together to her gravesite
and wept for an entire day before leaving.
The sound of their crying
was like the howling of dogs.
Sū Tǐng
In the Táng dynasty, Sū Tǐng first served as the Wūchéng county lieutenant.
On a leisurely day,
he once went boating along the stream with his colleagues.
After getting drunk, they chanted poems,
and thus arrived at Dàojī Temple.
In front of the temple was the deepest part of Ruòxī.
The water here was unfathomably deep,
and within it dwelled flood dragons,
which had long been a menace to people.
Sū Tǐng, still intoxicated, walked back,
returning from Luòtuó Bridge.
Encountering a broken bridge, he fell into the water,
sinking straight to the bottom of the pool.
In the water, someone supported the Secretary out,
and he gradually rose to the surface,
thus Sū Tǐng was saved.
Ox Fights a Flood Dragon
At the end of the Táng dynasty's Tiānbǎo era,
an ox in Shèzhōu fought with a flood dragon.
Initially, the flood dragon in the water had killed many people and livestock,
and this ox, while drinking,
was coiled around by the flood dragon,
dragged straight into the depths of the pool.
There they clashed.
After several days, the ox emerged,
and the pool water was red.
People at the time believed the flood dragon had died.
The Hóng Family's Daughter
In Qímén County, Shèzhōu, there was a flood dragon pool.
Folklore tells of a daughter of the Hóng family in Wǔlíng township,
betrothed to the Lí family of Póyáng.
As the wedding approached,
before an auspicious date was set,
a flood dragon transformed into a man.
His appearance was like that of her groom,
and he came with full ceremony and took her away.
Over a month later,
the real groom from the Lí family arrived,
and upon learning she had been taken by a flood dragon,
went to the flood dragon's lair to seek her.
On the way, he encountered the flood dragon in human form,
of exceptionally handsome appearance.
The groom suspected it was the flood dragon.
Looking closely,
he saw the flood dragon secretly smiling,
so he killed him.
The body indeed reverted to flood dragon form.
Proceeding further to the flood dragon's lair,
he saw his wife,
with a dog beside her.
He then took his wife and the dog to return.
Just as they boarded the boat,
a violent storm suddenly arose,
with wood and stones flying.
His wife and the dog
both transformed into flood dragons and departed.
The groom was blown by the fierce wind to Yúyáo,
and returned several years later.
Later, the Daoist priest Xǔ Jīngyáng also slew a flood dragon here,
and sealed its lair with planks.
Even today, when the sky is clear and the sun bright,
one can still vaguely see it.
Hóng Zhēn
Jīlóng Mountain is located ninety-five lǐ south of Wùyuán County,
with a height of one hundred and sixty zhàng,
and a circumference of fifteen lǐ and ninety steps.
Its shape resembles a chicken coop.
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
a flood dragon transformed into a Daoist priest.
Hóng Zhēn of Shèzhōu took him as his teacher with the rites of a disciple.
The Daoist intended to choose a dwelling,
and searched among various famous mountains.
Arriving at Huángshān,
Hóng Zhēn asked how this mountain was.
The Daoist said:
"Barren and cold."
Next, they went to Fēibù Mountain,
and he asked again.
The Daoist said:
"High but without support."
Arriving at this mountain,
he asked again.
The Daoist said:
"This mountain is suitable for burial.
Those buried here can attain the status of marquises or kings.
If not,
it will only produce monsters."
Hóng Zhēn asked the reason,
but he was not told.
When the Daoist was sleeping in his room,
Hóng Zhēn entered
and only saw a flood dragon.
Thereupon, he waited for him to wake and then bid farewell to return.
The Daoist then entered Póyáng and left.
Hóng Zhēn returned,
and moved his father's grave to this mountain.
Two years later,
a great flood occurred in Póyáng,
washing away several thousand households.
Hóng Zhēn was originally fond of the Dao,
often burning incense and maintaining mindfulness,
and possessed considerable occult arts.
He lived in Huíyù township south of Qí,
and the local people thus spoke of his displaying supernatural powers,
and that he harbored improper ambitions.
He secretly appointed officials,
and the local heroes of the prefecture all responded to him.
Later, the prefecture dispatched troops to arrest him,
capturing several dozen people,
but Hóng Zhēn's whereabouts ultimately remained unknown.
The Old Flood Dragon
On the mountain of Wǔqiū Temple in Sūzhōu,
tradition says it is the mausoleum of King Héliǘ of Wú.
There is a stone cave,
emerging from beneath the cliff,
appearing as if carved and inlaid.
Inside there is water,
unfathomably deep.
Some say it is where the Qín emperor excavated to retrieve a sword.
During the Yǒngtài era of the Táng dynasty,
a young man passed by
and saw a beautiful woman
bathing in the water.
She asked the young man to play with her,
and approached to pull him.
The young man then removed his clothes and entered,
and consequently drowned.
Several days later,
his corpse finally floated out,
but his body was completely dried and withered.
Below must have been the hidden lair of an old flood dragon,
which seduces people to suck their blood.
His companion described the situation thus.
Wǔxiū Pool
During the time of the Former Shǔ's founding ruler,
when repairing the plank road along Xiégǔ,
the Fèngzhōu garrison commander, named Bái,
was in charge of the project.
Arriving at Wǔxiū Pool,
he saw a woman floating on the water towards him.
Thinking she was drowning,
he ordered his servants to hook her to the bank.
Suddenly she transformed into a large snake,
and vanished into the pool.
Lord Bái considered this inauspicious,
and consequently fell ill.
I recited for him Cén Shēn's "Rhapsody Summoning the Northern Guest":
"East of Qútáng,
below dwells a thousand-year-old flood dragon.
It transforms into a woman,
in dazzling attire and beautiful makeup,
roaming by the water's edge."
Upon hearing this, Lord Bái
realized it was a flood dragon,
and his illness soon recovered.
Also, the eunuch Sòng Yùzhāo
said that by the Liǔzhōu riverbank,
he was beckoned by two or three women.
Villagers shouted and stopped him—
they were also flood dragons.
The words of Cén's rhapsody
are sufficient proof of this.
Slaying Flood Dragons
In the fourth year of the Yìxī era of the Jìn dynasty,
in Tàimò County of Dōngyáng Commandery, Wú Dàozōng lost his father at a young age,
lived with his mother,
and had not yet taken a wife.
One day,
when Dàozōng went elsewhere,
a neighbor heard rustling and clattering sounds from his house,
peeked in but did not see his mother,
only a black-spotted tiger inside.
Fearing the tiger had eaten Dàozōng’s mother,
the neighbor beat a drum to gather the villagers for a rescue.
They stormed into the house,
but saw no tiger,
only his mother.
She spoke as usual,
and they could not understand what had happened.
When her son returned,
his mother told him:
"Due to past sins, I am being punished,
and there will be a transformation."
A month later,
she suddenly disappeared.
Tiger attacks repeatedly occurred within the county,
all said to be caused by a black-spotted tiger.
The people were troubled by this.
They banded together to fight it.
Several were injured.
Later, someone shot the tiger,
the arrow striking its chest,
and a halberd pierced its belly,
but it did not die immediately.
After several days,
the tiger returned to its home,
unable to resume human form,
lay on the bed and died.
Her son wept bitterly,
and buried her as his mother.
The Cowherd Boy
In the Jìn dynasty, in Fùyáng County, a commoner’s son often herded cattle.
A cow suddenly licked the boy,
and wherever it licked, his flesh turned white.
The boy soon died,
and his family buried him,
then slaughtered the cow to serve guests.
All who ate this beef,
over twenty men and women,
transformed into tigers.
Shī Dàoxuān
In the first year of the Tàiyuán era of the Jìn dynasty,
Shī Dàoxuān of Ānlù County in Jiāngxià Commandery,
aged twenty-two,
had been somewhat dull in his youth.
Later, he suddenly went mad,
transformed into a tiger,
and devoured countless people.
Later, a woman picking mulberry leaves from a tree
was taken and eaten by the tiger.
After finishing,
he hid her hairpins and bracelets among mountain rocks.
Later, resuming human form,
he remembered and retrieved them.
After a year, he returned home,
again human.
He then entered government service,
becoming a Palace Secretary.
One night, while conversing with others,
he suddenly spoke of strange transformations between heaven and earth.
Dàoxuān himself said:
"I once fell ill and went mad,
then transformed into a tiger and ate people."
He named the victims.
Among those present,
some had lost fathers, sons, or brothers to him.
They wailed in grief,
seized him and delivered him to the authorities,
and he starved to death in the Jiànkāng prison.
Xiè Yǔn
Xiè Yǔn, styled Dàotōng, of Lìyáng,
was captured by bandits in his youth
and enslaved in Jiǎng Fèng’s household.
Once in the mountains, he saw a tiger trapped and starving in a pit,
and freed it.
Later, he went to the county to plead his case,
but the magistrate did not grant him justice,
subjecting him to exhaustive interrogation and torture.
Yǔn dreamed at night of a man saying:
"This place is easy to enter but hard to leave;
you have shown kindness and compassion,
so I shall rescue you."
Upon waking,
he saw a youth,
clad entirely in yellow,
speaking to him from outside the prison bars.
The jailer reported this to the magistrate,
who thenceforth dared not falsely accuse or humiliate him.
He was soon released.
He then ascended Wǔdāng Mountain.
At that time,
Táng Gōngliàng heard of this
and,
taking pity,
provided him with funds and shoes.
Later, in Xiāngyáng, he met a Daoist priest who said:
"My teacher, Master Dài,
a man of virtue and integrity,
once said that those with determination may come with me.
Could that be you?"
Following him into the mountains,
after three days of purification,
he was granted an audience,
and it was the very man from his dream.
Asked if he wished to see the yellow-clad youth,
he was bestowed three divine pills,
which, when taken, banished hunger and thirst.
He felt no worldly desires.
The master also had no fixed abode.
At times, auspicious light and purple aura sheltered him,
and a fragrant scent pervaded the mountain valleys.
Zhèng Xí
Zhèng Xí of Xíngyáng,
during the Tàikāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
served as a mounted attendant for the governor.
He suddenly went mad,
and vanished without a trace.
After a day, he was found.
Naked, moaning and crying,
his skin was torn and bleeding.
Asked the reason,
he said the local earth deity had ordered him to become a tiger,
clothing him in a spotted pelt.
He pleaded that as a mere whip-wielding attendant,
he was unfit for roaring and leaping.
The deity grew angry,
and had the skin stripped off.
The skin had already adhered to his flesh,
causing agonizing wounds.
It took ten days to heal.
Liú Guǎngyǎ
Liú Guǎngyǎ of Péngchéng,
in the first year of the Tàiyuán era,
served as an assistant in the capital prefecture.
On an official mission returning,
he passed through Zhúlǐ Pavilion.
Tigers were numerous there.
Liú took extreme precautions,
tying oxen and horses in front,
and laying halberds on the ground.
At midnight,
he slept alongside soldiers and commoners.
A tiger seized the moment, leaped in,
and carried off Liú alone.
Yì Bá
During the Jìn dynasty,
the commandery clerk Yì Bá of Yùzhāng,
in the Yìxī era,
was on leave returning home,
but overstayed and did not return.
The commandery sent men to pursue him.
They found Bá speaking normally,
and he even prepared food for them.
The envoys urged him to pack,
whereupon Bá said:
"Look at my face."
They then saw his eyes widen at the corners,
and his body take on a yellow-spotted hue.
He raised one foot,
and strode straight out the door.
His home was built against a mountain.
Reaching the foothills,
he transformed into a large three-legged tiger.
The raised foot
became its tail.
Xiāo Tài
In the Liáng dynasty, Marquis Héngshān Xiāo Tài served as Governor of Yōng Province,
stationed in Xiāngyáng.
Tigers were rampant then,
and village gates had traps.
One was triggered,
and villagers lit torches to see,
finding an old Daoist priest who pleaded:
"I was begging in the village and returning,
and mistakenly fell into the trap."
They opened it together.
Once out, he turned into a tiger,
and dashed away.
Huáng Gān
At the end of the Liáng dynasty,
Huáng Gān of Shǐxīng had a younger sister named Xiǎozhū,
who was betrothed to Lǐ Sù from the same county.
The younger sister went into the mountains with her sister-in-law to gather tree nuts,
and they passed by a temple of a deity.
Xiǎozhū lingered at the temple, unwilling to leave.
When they were about to return,
she ran back alone to the temple.
Whenever she saw people, she would hide in the grass.
Huáng Gān’s wife came to inform Lǐ Sù,
and Lǐ Sù suspected she had other intentions.
Lǐ Sù was summoned by the county office,
and returned one night with a companion.
They encountered wind and rain.
Seeing a fire in the temple building,
the two went toward the fire to warm and dry their clothes.
They noticed clothing on the deity’s bed.
After a short while,
they heard footsteps outside.
The two were terrified
and hid behind the screen at the deity’s bed.
Moments later,
they saw a tiger shaking its tail and moving swiftly,
going straight to the fire.
It removed its fangs and claws,
rolled up its skin,
placed it on the bed,
put on the clothes, and sat facing the fire.
Lǐ Sù saw it was Xiǎozhū.
He rushed out and embraced her.
He spoke to her, but she did not respond.
The next day, he took her back
and sent her to Huáng Gān’s house.
They confined her to a room,
and when raw meat was thrown to her, she would catch and eat it.
They kept constant watch over her,
but after a few days, she turned into a tiger again.
The commandery and county officials came to investigate.
The villagers then brought bows and crossbows to the house
and immediately tore open the roof and shot her dead.
The next day, a tiger went on a rampage,
and the common people closed their doors even during the day.
Grand Administrator Xióng Jī submitted a report to the emperor.
The Qiū’ěr Beast
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān of the Táng dynasty,
the Wǔlóng area of Fúzhōu suffered frequent tiger attacks.
There was a beast resembling a tiger but much larger.
At midday, it chased a tiger
straight into a house, killed it by biting,
but did not eat it.
From then on, there were no more tigers in the county.
This was recorded and reported.
Upon consulting the Ruìtú,
it was identified as a Qiū’ěr.
It does not eat living creatures,
but kills them when there are tiger attacks.
The Tiger Pagoda
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān of the Táng dynasty,
Prince Qiānlǐ of Chéng brought a tiger cub to the palace to raise.
It injured a palace maid.
He then ordered it to be starved for several days until it died.
Empress Wǔ ordered it to be buried,
and a pagoda was erected over the grave.
A feast for a thousand people was arranged,
a stele was inscribed,
and it was named the "Tiger Pagoda."
It still exists to this day.
Fù Huángzhōng
During the Táng dynasty, Fù Huángzhōng served as magistrate of Zhūjì County in Yuèzhōu.
A local villager got heavily drunk
and walked through the mountains at night.
He slept near a cliff.
Suddenly, a tiger approached him and sniffed him.
The tiger’s whiskers went into the drunkard’s nose,
causing him to sneeze loudly.
The tiger was startled and leaped,
falling off the cliff.
Its waist and hips were injured,
and it was captured by people.
The Clerk of Chēnzhōu
During the Cháng’ān era of the Táng dynasty,
a clerk of Chēnzhōu fell ill and turned into a tiger.
When he was about to devour his sister-in-law,
he was captured by villagers,
and it turned out to be the clerk.
Although his form had not fully changed,
he had a real tiger’s tail.
He was tied to a tree for several dozen days,
and then returned to being human.
Chief Clerk Cuī Xuánjiǎn personally questioned him about the reason.
The clerk said:
"At first, I was led by a tiger to meet a woman
in splendid attire.
Many tigers regularly gathered there,
and each was ordered to obtain food for the day.
At that time, I had just joined the ranks of tigers,
and my essence was not yet complete,
so I could not seek others.
I intended to take my sister-in-law as an offering,
but was captured.
Now, although I can no longer become a tiger,
I can still make its sound."
Cuī Xuánjiǎn ordered him to demonstrate.
The clerk then made a tiger’s roar,
shocking everyone around,
and causing the roof tiles to shake and fall.
The Bā People
The Bā people liked to gather in groups to cut down trees and make planks.
At the beginning of the Kāiyuán era,
over a hundred Bā people followed the mountains from Bāozhōng to fell trees
and arrived at the Tàibái Temple.
In front of the temple were over a hundred pine trees,
each several dozen arm-spans in girth.
The group of Bā people rejoiced, saying:
"Heaven is aiding us!"
They stopped and began cutting them down.
After more than twenty trees had been felled,
an old man wearing a hat and leaning on a staff came to the place.
He said to the Bā people:
"These are sacred trees.
Why are you cutting them down?"
The Bā people initially did not stop their work.
The old man said:
"I am the Tàibái deity.
Leave the fallen trees as they are,
I beg you,
As for those still standing,
do not act willfully."
The Bā people did not stop.
The old man said:
"If you do not stop,
you will surely all die.
It will be of no benefit."
Still, they did not stop.
The old man then climbed the mountain and called out:
"Striped ones!"
Suddenly, several tigers appeared,
arriving one after another,
and devoured almost all the Bā people,
with only five or six escaping.
The deity said to them:
"Because you had good hearts,
I did not have you killed.
You should leave quickly."
The felled trees remained until the end of the Tiānbǎo era.
An imperial edict was issued to repair the inner palace.
Yáng Guózhōng sent people to the mountain site
to proclaim the decree and take the trees,
using them to make planks.
The deity ultimately allowed it.
The Taoist Priest of the Gorge Entrance
During the Kāiyuán era,
the gorge entrance was infested with tigers,
and all passing boats suffered casualties.
Afterward, whenever a boat was about to descend the gorge,
they would prepare one person to serve as tiger fodder,
and only then could the boat proceed without mishap.
Otherwise,
many on board would be harmed.
This became the established practice.
The boat would leave two people ashore to feed the tiger.
After several days,
there came a boat
filled with powerful and wealthy men.
Among them were two poor men,
who were pushed out by the others
and ordered to go ashore to feed the tiger.
One of them, realizing he could not resist by force,
stepped out of the boat
and said to the others:
"I am poor,
and it is fitting that I die in your stead.
However, each person's fate is predetermined.
If I am not to be harmed by the tiger,
I have a sincere request.
Can you grant it?"
Hearing his earnest words,
the others were moved to pity.
They asked:
"What is it you wish?"
The man replied:
"I will now go ashore
to seek the tiger's tracks,
and I have my own plan.
I only ask that you moor the boat below the rapids for me,
and wait until noon.
If I do not return by then,
you may depart."
The others said:
"We will moor the boat below the rapids now,
and not only wait until noon today,
but also stay overnight for you.
If you do not return by tomorrow,
the boat will leave."
After speaking,
the boat descended to the rapids.
The man took a long-handled axe
and went ashore,
entering the mountains to search for the tiger.
He saw no human tracks,
only tiger prints.
The forest was deep and dense.
The man found a path
with many tiger tracks,
and followed it further.
He came to a mountain pass,
where the mud was thick
and tiger tracks multiplied.
After walking another half-li,
he saw a large stone chamber,
with a stone bed inside,
and a Taoist priest sleeping soundly on the bed.
On a rack hung a tiger skin.
The man guessed this was where the transformation occurred.
He crept quietly,
took the skin from the rack,
grasped the axe, donned the skin, and stood ready.
The Taoist suddenly awoke with a start,
finding the tiger skin missing from the rack.
He said:
"I am destined to eat you.
Why have you stolen my skin?"
The man replied:
"I am destined to eat you.
Why do you say otherwise?"
The two argued,
unable to settle for some time.
The Taoist, at a loss for words,
finally said:
"I have offended the Heavenly Emperor,
and was banished here to become a tiger.
I am fated to eat one thousand people.
I have already eaten nine hundred and ninety-nine,
and only lack you,
to complete the number.
Now, unfortunately,
you have stolen my skin.
If you do not return it,
I will have to become a tiger again,
and eat another thousand people.
Now I have a plan
that will benefit us both.
Is that acceptable?"
The man said:
"It is."
The Taoist said:
"Take the skin back to the boat now,
cut some of your hair, beard, and sideburns,
trim your fingernails and toenails,
and from your head, face, hands, feet, and body,
draw two or three sheng of blood.
Wrap these in a few old garments.
When I come to the shore,
you can throw the skin to me.
Once I put it on,
I will transform into a tiger.
Then throw that bundle to me,
and I will take and eat it,
which will be as if I had eaten you."
The man then donned the skin, took the axe, and returned.
The people on the boat were astonished,
and he recounted everything in detail.
On the boat,
they prepared as the tiger had instructed.
At dawn,
the Taoist was already on the shore,
so they threw the skin to him.
The Taoist took the skin, shook it out, and put it on,
and in a moment transformed into a tiger,
roaring and leaping about.
They then threw the bundle to the tiger,
which devoured it and left.
After that, no more tiger attacks were heard of.
People said that having eaten his fill of people,
he must have returned to heaven.
Fèi Zhōng
The barbarians of Fèi Prefecture,
all of the clan bear the surname Fèi.
The region is plagued by tigers,
and the custom is to live in elevated dwellings to avoid them.
During the Kāiyuán era,
Dí Guāngsì served as the prefect,
and his grandson, Bówàng, was born in the official residence.
Bówàng’s wet nurse’s husband, Fèi Zhōng, was strong, brave, and skilled in archery.
Once, while carrying rice home from the prefecture,
he was obstructed on the mountain path,
and before he knew it, dusk had fallen.
There were still over thirty lǐ ahead,
and Fèi Zhōng feared he would not escape danger.
With the blade he carried,
he cut several bundles of firewood,
struck stones to make fire,
and lit them to guard himself.
Soon after,
he heard the sound of tigers,
shaking the forests and thickets.
Fèi Zhōng used his headscarf to cover
the rice bag,
tied it with his waistband,
stood it under the firelight,
and then climbed up a large tree.
Shortly after,
four tigers arrived together,
and upon seeing the rice bag,
the largest tiger approached and sniffed it.
Realizing it was not a person,
they looked at each other silently.
The second tiger led the two cubs away,
while the largest tiger remained by the fire.
Suddenly, it shed its skin,
revealing an old man,
who rested his head on his hands and slept.
Fèi Zhōng, being strong and agile,
felt somewhat contemptuous of him,
so he slowly descended the tree, seized his throat,
and pointed his knife at his head.
The old man begged for his life,
and Fèi Zhōng bound his hands and interrogated him.
The old man said he was Old Fèi from the northern village,
punished to become a tiger,
and that the celestial court had a calendar ordering him to eat people.
That night, he was supposed to eat Fèi Zhōng,
so he was waiting for him.
Just now, he had only encountered the rice bag,
and was feeling very frustrated,
so he stayed there, waiting for him to return.
He never expected to be captured by Fèi Zhōng.
If he did not believe it,
he could look at the calendar by his waist
to confirm.
After Fèi Zhōng examined the calendar,
he asked, “How can you save me?”
The old man replied:
“If there is someone with the same name,
they can serve as a substitute.
When the matter is discovered later,
I will take the punishment,
which is nothing more than ten days of hunger.”
Fèi Zhōng said:
“There is a Fèi Zhōng in the southern village—
can he substitute for me?”
The old man agreed.
Fèi Zhōng first took the tiger skin up to the treetop,
then came down and untied the old man.
The old man said:
“You must firmly bind my body to the tree.
Once I enter the skin,
I will not recognize you.
If you hear a roar and come down,
you will surely be eaten.
This is how things work—
it is not that I am breaking my promise.”
Fèi Zhōng bid him farewell,
climbed the tree,
and threw the skin back to him.
The old man retrieved the skin,
entered it from the hind legs,
and after resuming his form,
roared loudly dozens of times
before leaving.
Fèi Zhōng managed to return home.
A few days later,
Fèi Zhōng from the southern village was eaten while hoeing the fields.
The Tiger’s Wife
During the Táng Kāiyuán era,
a tiger took a human woman as his wife,
and they lived together in a house deep in the mountains.
After two years,
the woman had not realized it.
Later, two guests suddenly arrived with wine,
and they all drank together in the house.
The tiger warned his wife:
“These guests are somewhat unusual—
be careful not to peek.”
Soon, they all fell into a drunken sleep,
and the woman went to look,
only to find they were all tigers.
She was greatly shocked,
but dared not speak.
After a while,
the tiger resumed his human form
and asked his wife:
“You didn’t peek, did you?”
The woman said she had never dared to leave.
Later, she suddenly mentioned missing her family
and wished to return for a visit.
After ten days,
the husband brought wine and meat and traveled with his wife,
gradually reaching her family’s home.
When they encountered deep water,
the woman crossed first.
As the tiger was lifting his clothes to cross,
the woman teased him:
