“Why is there a tiger tail sticking out behind you?”
The tiger was greatly ashamed,
so he did not cross the water,
and instead galloped away, never to return.
Jīhú
The Jīhú people of Cízhōu made their living by hunting with bows.
At the end of the Táng dynasty's Kāiyuán era,
they pursued a deer deep into the mountains.
The deer, in a panic, ran and took refuge in a room,
inside which was a Dàoshì,
dressed in red robes and seated leaning against a table.
Seeing the Jīhú man, he was startled,
and asked how he had come.
The Jīhú man gave his full name,
and said:
"I was just chasing a deer,
and without realizing it, I came too deep inside.
I apologize for intruding."
The Dàoshì said to the Jīhú man:
"I am the Tiger King,
appointed by the Heavenly Emperor to oversee the food supply for all tigers.
Every beast has its destined counterpart,
and none are wronged.
Just now, when you stated your name,
it matched that you are to be my food.
On the table are a red brush, a cup, and a register,
so he opened the register to show the Jīhú man.
The Jīhú man trembled in fear for a long time,
and firmly begged for release.
The Dàoshì said:
"I do not mind letting you go,
but such is the Mandate of Heaven.
What can be done about it?
If I release you,
I will lose a meal.
Since we have met,
I must find a way to spare you."
After a long while, he then said:
"Tomorrow, you can make a straw man,
dress it in your own clothes,
and bring three dǒu of pig's blood and one pǐ of silk,
and come here with them.
Perhaps then you can be spared."
The Jīhú man hesitated and did not leave,
and saw a group of tigers come to pay homage.
The Dàoshì assigned them their food,
and they each dispersed.
The Jīhú man then bowed twice and returned.
The next day,
he brought the items as instructed.
The Dàoshì smiled and said:
"You are trustworthy,
so you are a good man."
He then had the Jīhú man stand.
A straw man was placed in the courtyard,
with the pig's blood set beside it.
Then he told the Jīhú man to climb a tree,
from which the ground was over ten zhàng below.
He said:
"Stay here and you will be safe.
Use the silk to tie yourself to the tree.
Otherwise,
I fear you may fall and be injured."
Soon, he returned to the room,
transformed into a tiger.
He came out into the courtyard, looked up at the Jīhú man,
roared loudly several times,
and leaped toward the tree.
Realizing he could not reach the Jīhú man,
he seized the straw man,
throwing it several zhàng into the air.
He then went to consume all the pig's blood,
and returned to the room, becoming a Dàoshì again.
He said to the Jīhú man:
"You may come down quickly."
The Jīhú man descended and bowed twice.
Then, with the red brush, he crossed out the Jīhú man's name,
thus sparing him from calamity.
Green Stone
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
Yúzhōu suffered frequent tiger attacks.
Traps were set,
but they never caught any.
One moonlit night,
a man climbed a tree to keep watch,
and saw a chāng ghost, like a child of seven or eight years old,
unclothed and moving lightly,
its entire body green in color,
coming to trigger the trap.
After it passed,
the man climbed down to reset it,
it.
Shortly after,
a tiger came straight along,
was caught in the trap, and died.
After a while,
the child returned, walking and crying,
and then entered the tiger's mouth.
When it was light, they opened it to look,
and found a green stone, as large as a chicken egg, in the tiger's throat.
Turtle Bites Tiger
In the seventh year of the Tiānbǎo era,
a turtle emerged from the river in Xuānchéng Commandery,
and a tiger attacked it.
The turtle bit the tiger, causing two wounds.
The tiger, enraged,
tore off the turtle's head.
But the tiger's wounds were severe,
and it also died.
Lǐ Zhēng
Lǐ Zhēng of Lǒngxī,
a descendant of the imperial clan,
had his home in Guóluè.
From a young age, Zhēng was widely learned
and skilled in composing literary works.
At the age of twenty, he was recommended by the prefectural government,
and was known as a famous scholar of his time.
In the spring of the tenth year of the Tiānbǎo era, he passed the imperial examination and became a jìnshì, ranking under the list of Yáng Mò, the Vice Minister of the Right.
Several years later,
he was appointed to the post of a county lieutenant in the Jiangnán region.
Zhēng was by nature unrestrained and aloof,
arrogant due to his talent,
and unwilling to humble himself among low-ranking colleagues.
He often felt depressed and unhappy.
Whenever he gathered with his colleagues,
after becoming intoxicated,
he would look at the assembled officials and say:
"Am I really to be counted among the likes of you?"
His colleagues and subordinates all resented him for this.
After his term of office ended,
he retired and shut himself away at home,
not communicating with others for nearly a year.
Later, pressed by the need for food and clothing,
he prepared his belongings and traveled east to the regions of Wú and Chǔ,
seeking patronage from the local governors and officials.
The people of Wú and Chǔ had long heard of his reputation.
When he arrived,
they all opened their residences to receive him.
They feasted and enjoyed themselves to the fullest.
When he was about to leave,
they all gave him generous gifts to fill his bags.
Zhēng stayed in Wú and Chǔ for almost a year,
receiving many gifts.
He then returned west to Guóluè.
Before reaching home,
he stayed at an inn in Rǔfén.
Suddenly, he fell ill and became deranged,
whipping and beating his servants.
The servants could not bear the suffering.
This went on for over ten days,
and his illness grew worse.
Not long after,
he ran away wildly at night,
and no one knew where he went.
His servants tracked his departure and waited for him,
but after a full month, Zhēng still did not return.
Thereupon, the servants drove away his horse,
took his bags, and fled far away.
The following year,
Yuán Cān of Chénjùn, serving as a Supervising Censor, was ordered by imperial decree to go to Lǐngnán.
He traveled by relay carriage to the boundary of Shāngyú.
In the morning, as he was about to depart,
the station attendant informed him:
"On the road, there is a fierce tiger that attacks and eats people.
Therefore, those passing through here
dare not proceed unless it is daytime.
It is still early now,
I urge you to halt your carriage
and definitely not go forward."
Cān angrily said:
"I am an envoy of the Son of Heaven,
with many riders in my retinue.
How can a beast of the mountains and marshes harm us?"
He then ordered the carriage to proceed.
They had not gone even a mile
when indeed a tiger suddenly leaped out from the grass.
Cān was greatly alarmed.
Suddenly, the tiger hid itself in the grass
and spoke in a human voice:
"How strange!
I almost harmed my old friend!"
Cān recognized the voice as resembling Lǐ Zhēng's.
Cān and Zhēng had passed the imperial examination in the same year,
and their friendship was very deep,
but they had been separated for years.
Hearing these words suddenly,
Cān was both shocked and bewildered,
unable to comprehend what was happening.
He then asked:
"Who are you?
Could it be my old friend from Lǒngxī?"
The tiger groaned several times,
as if sighing and weeping.
Then it said to Cān:
"I am Lǐ Zhēng.
Please stay a while
and speak with me."
Cān immediately dismounted.
He then asked:
"Lǐ Jūn,
Lǐ Jūn,
how have you come to be here?"
The tiger said:
"Since I parted from you,
we have had no news of each other.
It has been a long and distant separation.
I am glad to see you are well.
Where are you going now?
Earlier, when I saw you,
there were two officials driving ahead,
and a station attendant carrying a seal bag to guide you.
Are you not traveling as an envoy in your capacity as a censor?"
Cān said:
"Recently, I was fortunate enough to join the ranks of the censors,
and now I am being sent to Lǐngnán."
The tiger said:
"You have established yourself through literary talent,
attained a position in the imperial court,
which can be called splendid.
Moreover, the Censorate is pure and prestigious,
overseeing all officials,
and the sage emperor selects its members with great care,
making it especially distinguished.
I am delighted that my old friend holds such a position,
and I offer my sincere congratulations."
Cān said:
"In the past, you and I achieved fame in the same year,
and our friendship was deep and intimate,
unlike ordinary friendships.
Since we were separated by distance and time,
and time flows like a river,
I have longed to see your dignified appearance,
with my heart and eyes yearning to the point of breaking.
I never expected that today
I would hear you speak of our old friendship.
However,
why do you not show yourself to me,
but hide yourself in the grass?
Between old friends,
should it be like this?"
The tiger said:
"I am no longer human,
how can I show myself to you?"
Cān then inquired about the matter.
The tiger said:
"Previously, I traveled as a guest in Wú and Chǔ,
and returned only last year.
On the way, at Rǔfén,
I suddenly fell ill, became deranged, and ran into the mountains and valleys.
Soon, I began to walk on all fours,
and from then on, I felt my heart growing more ferocious
and my strength doubling.
When I looked at my arms and thighs,
I saw coarse hair growing on them.
When I saw people in official robes walking on the road, or those carrying loads and running, or birds flying with wings, or beasts galloping with fur,
I desired to catch and devour them.
When I reached the south of Hànyīn,
driven by hunger,
I encountered a person with plump flesh,
so I seized him and ate him up completely.
Since then, this has become my usual way.
It is not that I do not think of my wife and children,
or miss my friends,
but because my actions have offended the gods,
and one day I transformed into a strange beast,
I am ashamed to face people,
so I cannot meet with you.
Alas!
You and I passed the examination in the same year,
and our friendship was always deep.
Today, you uphold the imperial law,
bringing glory to your relatives and friends,
while I hide in the forests and marshes,
forever cut off from the human world.
I leap and cry out to heaven,
bow down and weep to the earth,
my body ruined and useless.
Is this truly fate?"
Then he sighed and lamented,
almost unable to bear it,
and wept.
Cān then asked:
"Since you are now a different kind of creature,
how can you still speak like a human?"
The tiger said:
"Although my form has changed, my mind remains very clear,
hence I am able to speak.
But I am filled with fear and regret,
which is hard to fully express.
Fortunately, my old friend remembers me,
and I deeply hope you will forgive my unbecoming state,
which is also my wish.
However, when you return from the south,
if I encounter you again,
I will surely forget my past life.
At that time, I will see your body
as nothing more than prey on my table.
You should also strictly guard your retinue to prepare for this,
so as not to let me commit a crime,
and become a laughingstock among gentlemen."
He then said:
"You and I are truly friends who transcended formalities,
and I have something to entrust to you.
May I do so?"
Cān said:
"For an old friend,
how could it be impossible?
I only regret not knowing what it is about.
Please tell me everything."
The tiger said:
"If you had not permitted me,
how would I dare to speak?
Now that you have permitted me,
how could I conceal anything?
Initially, at the inn,
I fell ill and became delirious.
After entering the desolate mountains,
my servant drove me away, taking my horse, clothes, and baggage, and fled.
My wife and children are still in Guóluè.
Could they ever imagine that I have transformed into a different creature?
If you return from the south,
please seek out my wife and children on my behalf,
but simply say that I have died,
and do not speak of today's events.
I beg you to remember this!"
He continued:
"In the human world, I have no assets or property.
My children are still young,
and it will be difficult for them to fend for themselves.
You hold a position among the court officials,
and have always upheld righteousness.
The bond we shared in the past—
how could anyone else surpass it?
I earnestly hope you will remember their orphaned and vulnerable state,
and from time to time relieve their poverty,
so they do not starve to death on the roadside.
This would be a great kindness."
Having spoken, he wept sorrowfully again.
Cān also wept and said:
"Cān shares both joy and sorrow with you.
Thus, your children are also Cān's children.
I will strive to fulfill your earnest request;
why worry that I will not do so?"
The tiger said:
"I have several dozen old literary works that have not been circulated in the world.
Although there are surviving drafts,
they are all scattered and lost.
If you could transcribe and pass them on for me,
I truly dare not hope they will be ranked among human works,
but it would still be valuable to pass them on to my descendants."
Cān immediately called his servant and ordered him to take up the brush,
writing down the words as the tiger dictated,
nearly twenty chapters.
The writing was lofty,
the reasoning profound.
Cān read them and sighed repeatedly.
The tiger said:
"This is the essence of my lifetime;
how dare I hope for it to be passed on?"
He added:
"You are on an official mission, traveling by relay,
and must be in great haste.
Now I have long detained you and your attendants,
causing endless anxiety and fear.
To bid you farewell forever,
the regret of parting ways—
how can it be expressed in words?"
Cān also bade him farewell,
and only after a long while did he depart.
When Cān returned from the south,
he specially ordered someone to deliver a letter and funeral gifts
to Zhēng's son.
Over a month later,
Zhēng's son came from Guóluè to the capital and visited Cān's home,
seeking his father's remains.
Cān had no choice
and provided a detailed account of the events.
Afterwards, Cān used his own salary to support Zhēng's wife and children,
saving them from hunger and cold.
Cān later rose to the position of Vice Minister of War.
The Candidate of Tiānbǎo
During the Tiānbǎo era,
a candidate for office was traveling to the capital.
As he journeyed, dusk fell,
and he sought lodging at a village temple.
The monk was not there.
By then it was already dark,
and he could not go elsewhere,
so he rested on a couch for the night,
leaving his saddle and horse in another room.
At dawn, as he prepared to depart,
he happened to stroll around the courtyard.
Reaching a dilapidated room at the back of the courtyard,
he suddenly saw a young woman.
She was about seventeen or eighteen years old,
with a very beautiful appearance.
She was covered with a tiger skin.
While she was sleeping soundly,
the man quietly approached,
snatched the tiger skin, and hid it.
The woman awoke,
greatly startled and afraid,
and thus became his wife.
When he asked her about her origins,
she said she was fleeing from calamity
and had hidden here.
She was already far from home.
He carried her in another carriage,
and they proceeded to the capital for his official selection.
After the selection was completed,
he took her along to his post.
Several years later, when his term of office ended,
they had several children.
One day, as they traveled together,
they again came to the place where they had first stayed.
Some monks were still there,
and they invited the couple to stay overnight.
The next day,
before departing,
the man jokingly said to his wife:
"Do you remember where we first met?"
His wife angrily replied:
"I am originally not human.
By chance, you took me in,
and we have several children.
Since you did not find me objectionable,
I dared to stay with you.
But now, if you shame me,
is it merely with words?
Return my original garment,
and I will go where I belong."
The man immediately apologized for his offensive words,
but his wife's anger did not subside.
She urgently demanded her original garment.
Realizing he could not control her,
the man said:
"Your garment is in the north room;
go and fetch it yourself."
The woman was furious,
her eyes flashing like lightning.
Frantically, she rushed into the north room to search for the tiger skin,
and draped it over her body.
After leaping a few steps,
she had already transformed into a giant tiger.
Roaring and looking back,
she headed toward the forest.
The man was terrified
and gathered his children to leave.
Péi Mín
Péi Mín served as commander of the Lónghuá Army,
guarding Běipíng.
Běipíng had many tigers.
Péi Mín was an excellent archer.
Once, in a single day, he killed thirty-one tigers,
after which he looked around the foot of the mountain, proud of himself.
An old man approached and said:
"These were all biāo,
resembling tigers but not true tigers.
If you encounter a real tiger, General,
you will be powerless."
Péi Mín asked:
"Where are the real tigers?"
The old man replied:
"Thirty lǐ north from here,
they are often found."
Péi Mín galloped his horse there
and stopped amid dense thickets.
Sure enough, a tiger leaped out,
small in size but fierce in demeanor.
Planting itself on the ground, it let out a roar
that shook the mountain rocks, causing them to crack.
Péi Mín's horse recoiled in fright,
his bow and arrows fell to the ground,
and he nearly met his end.
From then on, he felt ashamed and fearful
and never again shot at tigers.
Bānzi
The mountain demon,
found everywhere in Lǐngnán,
has a single foot with a reversed heel,
and its hands and feet are three-forked.
The female ones are fond of applying rouge and powder.
They make nests in hollows of large trees,
with wooden screens and curtains.
Their provisions are quite complete.
Southerners traveling through the mountains
often carry yellow grease, lead powder, and coins with them.
The male is called Shāngōng,
and will certainly demand money.
When encountering a female, called Shāngū,
she will certainly demand rouge and powder.
Those who give these will receive protection.
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
a northerner traveling through the Lǐngnán mountains,
fearing tigers at night,
wanted to sleep in a tree.
Suddenly he encountered a female mountain demon.
The man, usually prepared,
descended the tree and bowed twice,
calling her Shāngū.
From within the tree came a distant question:
"What goods do you have?"
The man gave her rouge and powder,
which pleased her greatly.
She said to the man:
"Sleep peacefully without worry."
The man slept beneath the tree.
In the middle of the night,
two tigers came to where he was.
The mountain demon descended the tree,
stroked the tigers' heads with her hand and said:
"Striped ones,
my guest is here,
you should leave quickly."
The two tigers then departed.
The next day, bidding farewell,
she thanked the guest very respectfully.
What is hard to understand is that
each year they farm the fields with people.
People provide the land and seeds,
the rest—plowing, planting—
is all done by the mountain demons.
When the grain ripens, they come to call people to divide it equally.
Their nature is honest and straightforward.
When dividing with people,
they do not take more.
People also dare not take more;
those who take more encounter heavenly epidemics and sickness.
Liú Jiàn
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
a man named Liú Jiàn served as a judge in Lǐngnán.
Traveling through the mountains,
he suddenly encountered a mountain demon,
and called it a demon ghost.
The mountain demon angrily said:
"Judge Liú,
I am merely amusing myself,
how have I troubled you?
And yet you curse me!"
Then, standing on a lower tree branch,
it called for Bānzi.
After a short while, a tiger arrived,
and it ordered it to seize Judge Liú.
Jiàn was greatly terrified,
whipped his horse and fled,
but in a moment was caught by the tiger.
He sat beneath its feet.
The demon then laughed and said:
"Judge Liú,
Jiàn was greatly terrified.
Will you curse me again?"
Those around bowed repeatedly, begging for their lives.
Slowly it said:
"You may go."
The tiger then released Jiàn,
who was frightened nearly to death.
Supported back home,
he was ill for several days before recovering.
Jiàn often told people of this incident.
Qín Zìlì
A man from Zhāngpǔ named Qín Zìlì,
at the end of the Tiānbǎo era, served as a strong soldier,
following the army to Ānnán,
and later fighting against Tǔbō,
not returning for ten years.
Zìlì's wife, née Lín, was compelled by her parents to change her commitment,
and was about to remarry a man named Chén from the same county.
On the wedding night,
Zìlì returned.
His parents told him the whole story of his wife's remarriage.
Hearing this,
Zìlì could not contain his fury.
His wife's residence was over ten lǐ from home.
Having previously defeated Tǔbō,
he had obtained a sharp sword.
That evening,
taking up his sword, he set out,
heading for the Lín residence.
After traveling eight or nine lǐ,
a violent storm arose, darkening the sky,
making advance or retreat impossible.
Suddenly, a flash of lightning illuminated the way,
and he saw a large tree to the left of the path,
with a hollow in its side.
Zìlì took shelter from the rain in the hollow.
Inside were three tiger cubs,
which Zìlì killed.
After a long while,
a large tiger brought something and placed it in the hollow,
then left again after a short time.
Zìlì heard someone moaning,
went forward and felt around,
and it was a woman.
Zìlì asked who she was.
The woman said
she was the daughter of the Lín family,
formerly married to Qín Zìlì.
Zìlì had not returned from the army,
and her parents, without reason,
forced her to remarry,
with the wedding set for that very night.
Her heart longed for the past,
she could not bear it,
to see him again,
her grief and resentment were endless.
So she took a scarf and hanged herself in the mulberry grove behind the house,
but was taken by a tiger.
Fortunately, she encountered you,
and is still unharmed.
If you can save me,
I will surely repay you later.
Zìlì said to her:
"I am Zìlì,
I returned at dawn to the house,
and my parents said you had married another,
so I took up my sword and came to find you.
Who would have thought we would meet here?"
Then they held each other and wept.
Shortly after,
the tiger returned.
At first it roared loudly,
then turned and entered the hollow.
Zìlì swung his sword at it,
cutting the tiger in half at the waist.
Fearing more tigers might come,
he dared not yet leave.
Soon, after the moon brightened,
indeed another tiger arrived.
Seeing its mate dead,
it roared even louder.
Then it too turned and entered,
and was also killed by Zìlì.
Then he carried his wife back home,
and they remain safe and sound to this day.
The Xuānzhōu Child
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
in Xuānzhōu there was a child
who lived near the mountains.
Every night,
he would constantly see a ghost leading a tiger chasing him.
This had happened over ten times already.
The child said to his parents:
"When the ghost leads a tiger, I will surely die.
People say:
'Those eaten by a tiger
become chàng ghosts for it.'
When I die,
I will certainly become a chàng.
If the tiger commands me,
I will lead it into the village.
The village should set a trap on the main road to await it,
and the tiger can be caught."
Several days later,
he indeed died by a tiger.
After a long time,
he appeared in a dream to his father, saying:
"I have already become a chàng,
tomorrow I will lead a tiger here,
you should quickly build a trap on the western side."
The father then built a trap with the villagers.
On the day the trap was completed,
they indeed caught a tiger.
The Flutist
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
Ān Lùshān rebelled,
Tóngguān Pass fell,
and the people of the capital scattered like birds.
Among the Líyuán performers was a flutist
who also fled into the valleys of Zhōngnán Mountain.
There was a temple there,
so he took up residence.
On a clear night under a bright moon,
grieving over the chaos and filled with longing,
he took up his flute and played.
The clear, piercing sound
spread through the mountain valleys.
Suddenly, a creature with a tiger’s head and a human body,
wearing a plain unlined robe,
entered from outside.
The flutist was terrified;
he descended the steps and stared in shock.
The tiger-headed man said:
"How beautiful,
this flute!
Play it again."
Thus he played five or six pieces in succession.
After the music ended, a long while passed,
when suddenly he fell asleep,
and began snoring loudly.
The flutist, fearing he would wake,
slipped away and ran out,
climbing up a tall tree.
The dense foliage
could conceal a person.
After the creature awoke,
and did not see the flutist,
he sighed with great regret, saying:
"I should have eaten him earlier;
now he has escaped."
He then stood and let out a long roar.
In a moment,
over ten tigers arrived,
as if paying homage.
The tiger-headed one said:
"Just now, a little flutist,
taking advantage of my sleep,
fled and hid.
Spread out in all directions to find him."
After speaking,
they each dispersed.
After the fifth watch, they returned,
all speaking in human language:
"We each searched four or five lǐ,
but could not find him."
As the moon set and slanted light shone,
they suddenly saw a human shadow in the tall tree.
The tiger looked up and laughed, saying:
"We thought you had vanished like clouds or lightning.
Yet here you are."
He then led the tigers
to try to seize him.
Since they could not reach him,
the tiger-headed one leaped himself,
but still could not get there.
So they each dispersed.
Soon, day broke,
and travelers gradually gathered.
The flutist was then able to return with them.
Zhāng Jiézhōng
During the Tiānbǎo era,
at the Xiānhè Temple east of the Crown Prince’s Mausoleum in Gōushì County, Hénán,
there were often over seventy Daoist priests, all devoted and focused,
practicing the sacred texts.
They all observed fasting and purification.
Those who were not dedicated
did not stay there.
Every year, on the third night of the ninth month, one priest would attain immortality,
as was the established custom.
By dawn,
his name would be reported,
and this became routine.
Each year on that night, the priests in the temple
would not lock their doors.
Each slept alone,
hoping for the response of ascension.
Later, Zhāng Jiézhōng served as acting magistrate of Gōushì County
and did not believe it.
When the time came,
he ordered two brave men with weapons to secretly observe.
At first, they saw nothing.
After the third watch,
they saw a black tiger enter the temple.
In a moment,
it carried out a priest in its mouth.
The two men shot at it,
but missed.
The tiger abandoned the priest and left.
By dawn,
no one had attained immortality.
They reported all this to Jiézhōng.
He petitioned the prefecture for bows and arrows
and led a great hunt in the stone cave east of the Crown Prince’s Mausoleum,
killing several tigers.
They found many golden tablets, jade texts, caps, robes, and human hair and bones,
all said to be from the priests who attained immortality each year.
After that, in Xiānhè Temple,
the number of priests gradually dwindled.
Now it is completely abandoned
and occupied by the mausoleum keepers.
Péi Yuèkè
In the early years of the Qián Yuán era of the Táng dynasty,
the Minister of Personnel, Zhāng Hào, was demoted to the position of Registrar of Kuí Prefecture.
Prior to this, while Zhāng Hào was still in the capital,
he had betrothed his second daughter, Dé Róng,
to the third son of the Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Péi Miǎn,
the former Lántián County Commandant, Yuè Kè.
The wedding date had already been set,
when Zhāng Hào was demoted.
Thus, the date was changed to the following spring.
That year,
Yuè Kè promptly packed his belongings and journeyed south,
to complete the wedding ceremony.
In mid-spring,
when he was about a hundred *lǐ* from Kuí Prefecture,
Zhāng Hào learned that he was about to arrive.
Zhāng, relegated to a distant post,
was filled with worry and anxiety,
but was deeply pleased that Yuè Kè was arriving as promised.
He therefore ordered the family to hold a banquet in the garden,
and Dé Róng also went along with her aunts and cousins to stroll there.
The mountain prefecture was desolate,
with dense, interwoven bamboo and trees.
As dusk fell,
the group prepared to return.
Some lagged behind, others went ahead.
There was a flurry of laughter and chatter.
Suddenly, a fierce tiger emerged from the bamboo grove,
seized Dé Róng,
and leaped into the thick undergrowth.
Everyone was terrified,
and rushed to inform Zhāng.
Night had already fallen,
and all means and strength were exhausted.
The entire family wailed and cried,
not knowing what to do.
At dawn,
they dispatched a large number of people,
to search the mountains and wilderness for her remains.
They scoured the area far and wide,
but found no trace at all.
On the night before this evening,
Yuè Kè was traveling by boat,
still twenty or thirty *lǐ* from the prefecture,
unaware that his wife had been attacked by a tiger.
He summoned a dozen or so servants to go ashore and proceed slowly,
while his boat followed along.
After less than two or three *lǐ*,
they came across a plank hut by the water.
Inside the hut was a bed,
so they swept and dusted it,
and settled there to rest.
The servants stood guard in rows before and behind.
Suddenly, they heard something approaching from among the trees,
and everyone waited quietly.
Under the faint moonlight,
they suddenly saw a fierce tiger carrying something toward them.
Everyone was frightened and agitated,
so they all shouted and yelled at it,
and loudly struck the plank hut and objects.
The tiger slowly walked,
then crouched beside the plank hut,
left behind what it was carrying,
and went back into the mountains.
They all went to look,
and said it was a person,
still breathing faintly.
Yuè Kè immediately ordered them to carry the person onto the boat,
and urged them to cast off quickly.
Then, in the boat, they lit bright candles and examined the person closely.
It turned out to be a beautiful girl of sixteen or seventeen,
whose appearance and clothing were certainly not of the village sort.
Yuè Kè found this deeply strange,
and sent maidservants to attend to and examine her.
Although her hair was disheveled,
and her clothes torn and tattered,
her skin and body showed no injuries.
The maidservants gradually fed her warm broth,
and she was able to swallow a little.
After a long while,
her spirit and energy calmed and gathered,
and soon she opened her eyes.
When spoken to,
she would not respond.
Late into the night,
someone arrived from the prefecture,
and all said,
"Minister Zhāng's second daughter was strolling in the garden last night,
and was devoured by a fierce tiger.
To this day, her remains have not been found."
Those who heard this then reported it to Yuè Kè.
He immediately sent the maidservants to inquire of Dé Róng in detail,
whereupon she wept and wailed without cease.
Once Yuè Kè had gone ashore,
he reported the matter in detail to Zhāng Hào.
Zhāng Hào galloped on horseback at dawn and arrived,
both grieving and overjoyed,
and then returned with them.
And the marriage indeed took place as scheduled.
Since then, in the Qiánxiá region, temples to the "Tiger Matchmaker" were often built,
and some still exist today.
Lú Zào
In Rǔzhōu Yè County, Magistrate Lú Zào had a young daughter.
During the Dàlì era,
she was betrothed to Yuánfāng, the son of Zhèng Chǔ from the same county.
Soon after, Chǔ was appointed to a military post in Tánzhōu,
and Zào also resigned from his post and settled in Yè.
Later, Chǔ passed away,
and Yuánfāng escorted the funeral procession to reside in Jiānglíng.
For several years, all communication between them ceased.
The county magistrate, Wéi Jì, arranged for his son to marry her.
On the auspicious day,
Yuánfāng happened to arrive.
Coincidentally, troops from Wǔchāng garrisoning the border had also stopped in the county.
The county was crowded,
and it was raining heavily.
Yuánfāng
had nowhere to stay,
so he went directly to a Buddhist temple over ten lǐ east of the county.
In the northwest corner of the temple, something like a small animal was crying.
He lit a torch to look,
and it turned out to be three tiger cubs.
Their eyes were not yet open.
Because they were small,
they could not harm people,
and he could not bear to kill them.
He merely closed the door and firmly barred it.
Around the beginning of the third watch,
a tiger came and pushed against the door,
but could not enter.
To the west, there was a window, also very sturdy.
The tiger angrily struck it,
the lattice broke,
and its head got stuck inside,
pinned by the sides,
unable to move forward or backward.
Yuánfāng took a brick from the Buddhist pagoda and struck it.
The tiger roared angrily and thrashed about,
but ultimately could not free itself.
He struck it repeatedly,
and soon it died.
Then, outside the door, there seemed to be a woman moaning,
her breath very weak.
Yuánfāng asked:
"The one moaning outside the door,
are you human?
Or a ghost?"
She replied:
"I am human."
He asked:
"How did you come here?"
She said:
"I am the former daughter of Magistrate Lú.
Tonight, I was to marry into the Wéi family.
Just as I was boarding the bridal carriage,
I was seized by a tiger,
carried here and dropped off.
Tonight, I am unharmed,
but I am very afraid it will come again.
Can you save me?"
Yuánfāng found this strange.
He took a torch and went out to look,
and indeed, she was dressed in fine garments.
She was seventeen or eighteen years old,
her wedding attire solemn and proper.
Covered in mud and water,
he helped her inside,
and secured the door again.
Then he gathered broken statues from the Buddhist pagoda
to keep the light burning.
The girl asked:
"Where is this?"
He replied:
"It is the Buddhist temple east of the county."
Yuánfāng told her his name,
and mentioned their old promise.
The girl also remembered it.
She said:
"My father once promised me to you in marriage.
But once we lost all news of you,
I was to marry into the Wéi family.
Heaven's will is hard to change,
yet the tiger has returned me to you.
My family's estate is very close from here.
If you can escort me back,
I will break off with the Wéi family and serve you as your wife."
At dawn,
he escorted her back to her home.
Her family, thinking she had been taken by a tiger,
were just preparing mourning garments,
when suddenly they saw her return,
overjoyed as if she had descended from heaven.
Yuánfāng delivered the tiger to the county office,
and fully recounted the events.
The county magistrate found it extraordinary,
and returned the Lú girl to Zhèng Yuánfāng.
All who heard of it at the time marveled in astonishment.
Zhāng Yúzhōu
In the early Jiànzhōng era of the Táng dynasty,
north of Běihǎi County in Qīngzhōu, there was the First Emperor of Qín's Sea-Gazing Terrace.
Beside the terrace was a separate marsh pond,
and by the pond lived a fisherman named Zhāng Yúzhōu, who had built a thatched hut and resided there.
Often, a tiger would burst into the hut at night.
Once, when Yúzhōu was asleep,
near dawn,
Yúzhōu sensed someone.
At first, he did not know it was a tiger.
Only at daybreak did he see it.
Yúzhōu was frightened,
and lay still, not daring to move.
The tiger slowly touched Yúzhōu with its paw.
Yúzhōu suspected there was a reason,
so he sat up.
The tiger raised its left front paw to show Yúzhōu.
Yúzhōu looked at it,
and saw a thorn in its paw, about five or six cùn long.
He then removed it for the tiger.
The tiger leaped out of the hut,
as if bowing in gratitude,
and rubbed itself against Yúzhōu.
After a long while,
it looked back and left.
In the middle of the night,
Yúzhōu suddenly heard a large object drop in front of the hut.
Yúzhōu went out,
and saw a wild boar, very fat,
nearly three hundred jīn.
It was in front of the hut,
and upon seeing Yúzhōu,
it also rubbed itself against him.
After a long while, it left.
From then on, every night it brought something,
either a boar or a deer.
The villagers thought it was supernatural,
and reported it to the county.
Yúzhōu explained the whole story,
and the county sent an official to follow and observe.
At the second watch,
it brought a deer,
and the county then cleared him of any crime.
Yúzhōu held a one-hundred-and-one-day Buddhist ceremony for the tiger.
That night,
the tiger brought a bolt of silk in its mouth.
One day,
the hut was suddenly torn down by the tiger,
seemingly because it did not want Yúzhōu to live there.
Yúzhōu understood its intention,
and moved to another dwelling.
After that, the tiger never came again.
Shēntú Chéng
Shēntú Chéng was a man who,
in the ninth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
was transferred from commoner status to fill a post in Pú.
He became the Deputy Magistrate of Shíbīn
County in Púzhōu.
On his way to assume office,
he arrived about ten li east of Zhēnfú County when he encountered a fierce wind and snowstorm, with extreme cold,
and his horse could not proceed.
By the roadside, there was a thatched cottage from which smoke rose, and it seemed very warm inside.
Chéng went over to it,
and found an old man, an old woman, and a maiden sitting around the fire.
The girl was just fourteen or fifteen years old.
Though her hair was disheveled and her clothes were soiled,
her skin was as fair as snow and her face like a flower,
and her demeanor was graceful and charming.
When the old man and woman saw Chéng arrive,
they quickly stood up and said:
"Traveler, you must be freezing from braving the snow.
Please come forward and warm yourself by the fire."
Chéng sat for a long while;
the sky had already grown dark,
and the wind and snow did not cease.
Chéng said:
"The county town is still far to the west.
May I lodge here for the night?"
The old man and woman said:
"If you do not consider our humble thatched hut too crude,
how dare we refuse your request?"
Chéng then unsaddled his horse
and laid out his bedding.
When the girl saw the guest,
she further adorned herself and made up her appearance,
then emerged again from behind the curtain,
and her serene beauty
was even more striking than before.
After a while,
the old woman came in from outside carrying a wine pot
and warmed the wine over the fire.
She said to Chéng:
"Since you have braved the cold,
please have a cup
to ward off the chill."
Then, with polite gestures, she said:
"Let the host begin."
The old man then passed the wine around in turn,
and Chéng was to drink last.
Chéng then said:
"There is still the young lady missing at the table."
Both the old man and woman laughed and said:
"She was raised in a farming family—
how could she join the guests?"
The girl immediately turned her head and glanced sideways, saying:
"Is wine so precious?
Or is it that people like me are not fit to drink?"
Her mother then pulled her by the skirt
and made her sit beside them.
Chéng, wanting to test her abilities,
proposed a drinking game to observe her thoughts.
Holding his cup, Chéng said:
"Let us quote from the classics,
with the meaning pertaining to the present situation."
Chéng then said:
"Weary, weary, the evening drinking;
not drunk, we shall not return."
The girl lowered her head and smiled, saying:
"With the weather like this,
where would one return to anyway?"
Soon it was the girl's turn,
and she in turn gave her line:
"The wind and rain are dark as night;
the cock crows without ceasing."
Chéng was astonished and sighed, saying:
"Young lady, you are so intelligent and wise.
I am fortunate to be unmarried—
may I propose to you myself?"
The old man said:
"Though I am poor and humble,
I have always cherished and protected her.
Many passing travelers
have offered gold and silk to ask for her hand.
I could not bear to part with her before,
so I did not consent.
Now, unexpectedly, a noble guest also wishes to take her.
How could I dare to begrudge her?"
He then entrusted her to Chéng.
Chéng thus performed the rites of a son-in-law
and took gifts from his bag to present to them.
The old woman would accept none of it.
She said:
"As long as you do not reject our poverty and lowliness,
what need is there for material goods?"
The next day,
she also said to Chéng:
"This place is remote and without neighbors,
and it is also cramped and narrow—
not fit for you to stay long.
Now that our daughter is married,
you may depart."
After another day,
they bid farewell with sighs,
and Chéng had his wife ride on his horse as they traveled.
After arriving at his post,
his salary was very meager,
but his wife worked hard to establish their household
and entertained guests.
Within ten days,
they gained great fame and reputation.
And the affection between husband and wife grew even deeper.
In treating relatives with generosity,
caring for nephews and nieces,
and dealing with servants and attendants,
she won everyone's joy.
Later, when his term of office was completed and they were about to return home,
they already had a son and a daughter,
both very intelligent,
and Chéng respected his wife even more.
He once composed a poem titled "To My Wife," which read:
"As an official, I shame Méi Fú;
for three years, I愧 Mèng Guāng.
How can this feeling be expressed?
On the river, there are mandarin ducks."
His wife chanted and recited it all day long,
as if silently composing a response,
but she never spoke it aloud.
She often said to Chéng:
"The way of being a wife
requires knowledge of books.
But if I were to compose poetry,
it would seem like I am showing off like a concubine."
When Chéng's official term ended,
they packed all their belongings and returned to Qín.
Passing through Lìzhōu,
they reached Jiālíng.
By the riverbank,
they rested on the grass beside a spring.
His wife suddenly said to Chéng with melancholy:
"Earlier, you gifted me a poem,
and I soon composed a response.
At first, I did not intend to show it to you,
but now, encountering this scenery,
I cannot remain silent any longer."
Then she chanted:
"Though the love of zither and lute is deep,
the longing for mountains and forests is stronger.
I often worry that times will change,
and betray a heart of a hundred years."
After chanting,
she wept silently for a long time,
as if yearning for something.
Chéng said:
"The poem is beautiful indeed,
but mountains and forests are not for a delicate lady to yearn for.
If you are thinking of your honored parents,
we have now arrived.
Why grieve and weep?"
The affairs of human life, karma, and destiny
are all predetermined.
More than twenty days later,
they arrived again
at his wife's original
home.
The thatched cottage was still there,
but there were no longer any people.
Chéng and his wife stayed in the cottage.
His wife, missing her parents deeply,
wept all day long.
Under some old clothes in a corner of the wall,
she saw a tiger skin,
covered in dust.
When his wife saw it,
she suddenly laughed and said:
"I did not know this thing was still here!"
She draped it over herself,
and immediately transformed into a tiger.
Roaring and snarling,
she rushed out the door and left.
Chéng fled in fright, avoiding her,
then took his two children and searched along the path.
He gazed into the forest and wept for several days,
but in the end, he did not know where she had gone.
Dīng Yán
In the fourteenth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
there were many fierce tigers,
attacking people in broad daylight.
At that time, military conflicts blocked the Huái region,
so the military officer Wáng Zhēng was appointed as the prefect of Shēnzhōu.
Upon Wáng Zhēng's arrival,
he extensively prepared tools for capturing tigers,
including weapons, pits, and traps,
leaving nothing unprovided.
He also offered a heavy reward,
promising ten rolls of silk for each tiger caught.
There was an old soldier named Dīng Yán who was skilled at setting traps,
so he presented his plan to the prefect,
requesting to set up traps from the mountains to the roadside,
to capture the tigers.
After Wáng Zhēng approved,
within a few days,
they caught a tiger.
The tiger was in a deep pit,
unable to exert its strength.
Dīng Yán then leaned over to look down,
mocking and taunting it,
while the tiger leaped and roared furiously,
its angry voice like thunder.
A crowd of onlookers gathered,
numbering in the hundreds.
Dīng Yán, proud of his successful plan,
was unusually boastful and elated.
At the time, he was drunk,
and as his clothes got caught on a tree root,
he fell into the pit.
The crowd gasped in shock,
thinking he would be torn to shreds by the fierce tiger's claws and teeth.
But when they looked closer,
Dīng Yán was sitting upright,
and the tiger was merely staring at him.
Dīng Yán's loved ones, worried about him,
devised a plan together,
lowering a thick rope with a pulley.
They waited for Dīng Yán to tie himself,
so they could quickly pull him up,
hoping for even a slim chance of survival.
Dīng Yán took the rope,
wrapped it around his waist,
and waved his hand,
whereupon the people outside pulled him up.
When he was two or three feet off the ground,
the tiger grabbed the rope with its front paws and held it back.
Its demeanor was extremely gentle.
This happened several times.
Dīng Yán then said to it:
"You tigers have run rampant,
entering the city and harming people.
You must be eliminated,
and it is right that you end up here.
But your life
is now in imminent danger.
I, because I was heavily drunk,
accidentally fell in here.
The reason the crowd hasn't killed you yet
is because of me.
If you harm me,
you will surely enrage the crowd.
Before my breath is gone,
they will throw firewood and torches at you,
and you will be reduced to ashes.
Instead,
follow my advice,
and I will plead with the prefect
to spare your life.
I hope you will lead your kind
far away from this land.
This is like crossing the river to go elsewhere,
as you well know.
I swear by the sun and the heavens,
I will not break this promise."
The tiger listened attentively,
as if understanding,
and Dīng Yán pulled the rope,
while the crowd pulled him out.
The tiger then lowered its ears and fixed its gaze,
no longer holding back.
After Dīng Yán got out,
he reported the incident to the prefect.
He said:
"Now, killing one tiger
is not enough to stop the violence of the whole group.
Moreover, I made a tentative agreement with it,
begging to spare it,
hoping it will lead its companions away in all directions,
so that this region may gain peace."
Wáng Zhēng agreed.
Dīng Yán then conveyed the prefect's intention,
carefully explaining it.
The tiger in the pit
leaped and circled joyfully,
as if grateful for the kindness.
Dīng Yán piled earth by the side of the pit,
gradually making it shallower,
though it was still about ten feet deep.
The tiger then leaped out,
vigorously bounding and leaping,
and vanished with a roar in the wind.
From then on, within a month,
the tigers disappeared without a trace,
and the mountains and fields became peaceful.
Alas!
The plan to preserve life,
even among different species,
can also be remarkable.
Considering the fierceness of a violent tiger,
trapped in a pit,
it would naturally unleash its fury upon catching a person,
tearing and biting,
to vent its emotions.
Yet this tiger, through Dīng Yán, sought to preserve its life,
and indeed succeeded.
How intelligent it was!
And Dīng Yán, able to persuade with words,
communicating with such a fierce creature,
actually achieved the extraordinary outcome of making the whole group leave the region.
Moreover, he avoided the harm of being caught,
how intelligent he was too!
This was truly the result of sincerity and trust interacting.
Ah,
sincerity and trust as qualities,
how miraculous they are!
Wáng Yòng
Guó.
In Hēiyúgǔ, Wángchéng County, Zhōu,
during the Zhēnyuán era,
a commoner named Wáng Yòng made charcoal in the valley.
In the valley, there was a pond a few paces wide,
where two black fish over a foot long were often seen swimming.
While cutting wood, Wáng Yòng grew hungry and tired,
so he ate one of the fish.
His younger brother exclaimed in shock:
"This fish might be a spiritual creature of the valley,
how could you kill it, brother?"
After a while,
his wife brought him food.
Wáng Yòng kept swinging his axe,
and only after a long time did he turn around.
His wife noticed his appearance had changed strangely,
and called his brother to look.
Suddenly, he tore off his clothes, howled, and leaped,
transforming into a tiger,
and ran straight into the mountains.
From time to time, he killed deer and similar animals to eat.
This went on for three years.
One day at dusk,
he knocked on the door and called out:
"It's me, Wáng Yòng."
His brother replied:
"My brother turned into a tiger three years ago,
what ghost is pretending to be him?"
He said again:
"Years ago, I killed the black fish,
and the underworld punished me by turning me into a tiger.
Later, because I killed people,
the underworld official whipped me a hundred times.
Now I am released,
but my body is covered in wounds.
Just look at me,
do not doubt."
The brother, overjoyed,
opened the door.
He saw a person
whose head was still that of a tiger,
and died of fright.
The whole family screamed and fled in panic.
In the end, he was beaten to death by the villagers.
Upon examination, his body had black markings,
confirming it was Wáng Yòng,
only his head had not fully transformed.
During the Yuánhé era,
the recluse Zhào Qíyuē once went to the valley,
and heard the villagers tell this story.
Zhāng Féng
Zhāng Féng of Nányáng,
in the late years of the Zhēnyuán era,
traveled lightly to the southern regions.
He journeyed to Héngshān Inn in Fútáng County, Fúzhōu.
The sky had just cleared,
and dusk was approaching,
the mountain scenery was vibrant and charming.
Mist and haze lingered gently.
Leaning on his staff, he sought out scenic spots,
unaware of how far he had gone.
Suddenly, there was a stretch of fine grass,
spanning over a hundred paces in length and width,
lush and emerald, utterly delightful.
Beside it stood a small tree,
so he took off his clothes and hung them on the tree,
leaned his staff against it,
and threw himself onto the grass,
rolling left and right.
Soon, he fell into a deep sleep,
like a beast rolling about.
Satisfied, he rose,
only to find his body had transformed into a tiger.
Its stripes were dazzlingly bright.
Looking at his own sharp claws and fangs,
and the strength in his chest and limbs,
he felt invincible under heaven.
So he leaped up,
bounding over mountains and valleys,
swift as lightning.
Late into the night, feeling quite hungry,
he slowly approached a village,
but found no dogs, pigs, foals, or calves worth taking.
None were suitable.
In his dazed state,
he thought he should go for Zhèng Fán, the recorder of Fúzhōu,
and so hid by the roadside.
Before long,
someone came from the south,
an attendant sent to welcome Zhèng.
Seeing someone, he asked:
"Zhèng Fán, the recorder of Fúzhōu—
estimating his journey, he should be lodging at the inn ahead.
Have you heard when he will depart?"
The newcomer replied:
"He is my master.
I heard he is preparing his belongings,
and will arrive before long."
The attendant said:
"Only one person is coming,
and there are also companions traveling together.
When I go to welcome him,
I worry I might mistake someone else."
The other said:
"Among the three,
the one in greenish-blue clothing is him."
At that moment, Féng was lying in wait,
and the other asked in detail,
as if inquiring on Féng's behalf.
Once Féng learned this,
he crouched in hiding, waiting.
Soon, Zhèng arrived,
with a large entourage,
dressed in greenish-blue,
quite portly,
swaggering as he came.
As soon as he arrived,
Féng seized him in his jaws,
and ran up the mountain.
It was not yet dawn,
and though there were many people,
none dared to pursue.
He feasted on him at will.
Only the intestines were left behind.
Afterward, he wandered through the mountain forests,
utterly alone, without companions.
Suddenly, he thought to himself:
"I was originally a human—
what joy is there in being a tiger?
Trapping myself in the deep mountains,
why not seek the place where I first transformed and return?"
So he retraced his steps, searching carefully,
and reached the spot at dusk.
His clothes still hung there,
his staff was also there,
and the fine grass remained as before.
He rolled and turned on it again,
and when satisfied, he rose,
immediately returning to human form.
Thereupon, he dressed, took up his staff, and returned.
From yesterday's departure to today's return,
a full cycle had passed.
Initially, his servants were alarmed at Féng's disappearance,
inquiring with the neighbors,
some said he had taken his staff and climbed the mountain.
They searched along many paths,
but found no trace.
When he returned,
they were overjoyed and asked what had happened.
Féng deceived them, saying:
"I happened to seek a mountain spring,
and came upon a mountain monastery,
where we discussed Buddhism together.
Unaware, much time passed."
The servant said:
"This morning, a tiger was nearby,
and it ate Zhèng Fán, the recorder of Fúzhōu,
but did not find the rest.
The mountains and forests have many fierce beasts,
it is not safe to travel alone.
While you were away,
we were extremely worried.
We are glad you are safe and unharmed."
Féng then continued his journey.
In the sixth year of Yuánhé,
while traveling, he stayed in Huáiyáng,
lodging at an official guesthouse.
The hostel officer hosted a banquet for guests,
and among those seated was one who proposed a drinking game:
"When the turn comes around,
each must tell a strange story of their own.
Those whose story is not strange will be penalized."
When the turn reached Féng,
he recounted the events at Héngshān.
Among the guests was Jìnshì Zhèng Xiá,
son of Zhèng Fán,
who glared angrily and stood up,
grabbed a knife to kill Féng,
declaring he would avenge his father.
The others restrained him.
Xiá's rage did not subside,
so he went to report to the commandery general.
Thereupon, they sent Xiá southward,
ordering ferry officers not to allow him to cross again.
Féng was sent westward,
and advised to change his name to avoid trouble.
Some said:
"It is said a father's enemy
must be avenged.
However, this enmity was not intentional murder.
If Xiá insists on killing Féng,
he too will be held accountable."
So Xiá fled and did not carry out his revenge.
Alas!
This can indeed be called strange.
Lǐ's Servant
A Tale.
There was a Jǔrén surnamed Lǐ, whose given name is unknown,
who lived in the mountains of Xuānzhōu.
He often employed a servant.
The servant was rather lazy and indolent,
and Lǐ frequently whipped him.
The servant harbored much resentment.
In the ninth year of Táng Yuánhé,
Lǐ met with two friends at his country villa,
and called for the servant,
but the servant was already asleep.
Lǐ flew into a rage,
and whipped him dozens of times.
The servant, filled with hatred,
went out and said to his peers:
"This is a leap year,
and people say tigers are numerous.
Why doesn't one eat me?"
With these words,
he went out the door.
Suddenly, they heard a scream,
and the servants searched for him,
but found nothing.
Following tiger tracks,
they went over ten lǐ to a streamside,
where the servant had already been half-eaten.
His clothes, headscarf, and shoes
were all neatly folded and placed on the grass.
It seems tigers can command the spirits of those they kill to do such things.
Mǎ Zhěng
During the Chángqìng era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a retired scholar named Mǎ Zhěng, whose nature was serene and detached.
He loved to seek out mountains and rivers,
not shunning steep and perilous places,
and was fully capable of climbing them.
One day, while residing in Xiāngzhōng,
he went to Mount Héng's Zhùróng Peak,
to visit the Fúhǔ Master.
The Buddhist hall's inner sanctum was solemn and pure,
with fruits and food emitting a fragrant aroma,
and additionally, silver vessels were arranged on the Buddhist couch.
He saw an old monk whose eyebrows and fine hairs were snow-white,
rustic and powerfully built.
He was very pleased by Zhěng's arrival,
and had a servant take his bag.
The monk said:
"May I borrow your servant?
I need to go to the nearby county market to buy a little salt and cheese."
Zhěng agreed.
The servant then took the silver and went down the mountain,
and the monk also went off in an unknown direction.
Shortly after, a mountain hermit named Mǎ Zhǎo also came climbing up alone.
Seeing Zhěng,
he was greatly comforted and pleased.
He then told Zhěng:
"Just now on the road,
I encountered a tiger eating a man,
I don't know whose son he was."
He described the man's clothing and ornaments,
and it was Zhěng's servant.
Zhěng was greatly alarmed.
Zhǎo added:
"From a distance, I saw the tiger finish eating the man,
then shed its skin,
changed into monastic robes,
and became an old monk."
Zhěng was extremely terrified.
When Zhǎo saw the monk, he said:
"This is the one."
Zhěng said to the monk:
"Mountain Hermit Mǎ has come and says
that my servant, on the halfway point of the mountain road,
has already been injured by a tiger.
What should we do?"
The monk angrily said:
"In this humble monk's domain,
the mountains have no tigers or wolves,
the grass holds no poisonous stings,
the paths are free of snakes and vipers,
the woods harbor no owls or screech-owls.
Do not believe such wild talk."
Zhěng looked closely at the monk's mouth,
and it still bore traces of fresh blood.
As night approached,
the two men stayed in the monastery's dining hall,
firmly bolting the door,
and keeping a bright candle lit as they waited.
When the night had grown deep,
they heard a tiger in the courtyard,
angrily butting its head against their door three or four times,
but fortunately, the door was sturdy and did not break.
The two men, frightened, burned incense
and devoutly kowtowed to the clay statue of the arhat Píntóulú inside the hall.
After a long while,
they heard the clay statue recite a poem:
"The Yín person only drowns in the water within the railing;
The Wǔzǐ must divide the metal beside Gěn.
If Tèjìn is made to restring his crossbow,
The general of the past will surely be grieved at heart."
The two men listened and understood its meaning,
saying:
"'Yín person' is the tiger.
'Within the railing' means the well.
'Wǔzǐ' is us.
'Metal beside Gěn' means the silver vessels."
They could not decipher the meaning of the last two lines.
At dawn,
the monk knocked on the door and said:
"Young gentlemen, rise and eat porridge."
Only then did the two men dare to open the door.
After finishing the porridge,
the two men discussed, saying:
"As long as this monk is here,
how can we get down the mountain?"
So they deceived the monk, saying:
"There is something strange in the well."
They made him go look.
While he was peering intently,
the two men pushed the monk into the well.
The monk immediately transformed into a tiger,
and the two men crushed it to death with a large stone.
The two men then took the silver vessels and went down the mountain.
As dusk approached,
they encountered a hunter,
who had set up a crossbow trap by the roadside,
and lived in a hut built in a tree.
He said to the two men:
"Do not trigger my trap."
He also said to the two men:
"It is still far to the foot of the mountain,
and many tigers are currently raging.
Why not come up into the hut for now?"
The two men, trembling with fear,
climbed up.
Just as they were about to settle in,
suddenly thirty or fifty people passed by,
some monks,
some Daoists,
some men,
some women,
some singing,
some dancing playfully.
They advanced to the crossbow trap.
The crowd angrily said:
"This morning, two thieves killed our Chán master,
and now as we pursue and capture them,
someone dares to set a trap for our general."
They then triggered the trap and left.
The two men heard all this,
and questioned the hunter.
He said:
"These are chāng ghosts—
people who were eaten by a tiger,
now clearing the way ahead of the tiger."
The two men then inquired about the hunter's name.
He said:
"My given name is Jìn,
my surname is Niú."
The two men were overjoyed and said:
"The last line of the clay statue's poem is now verified:
'Tèjìn' is Niú Jìn,
and 'the general' is this tiger."
They then urged the hunter to reset his arrow trap,
and the hunter agreed.
After setting it, they climbed back into the hut.
Sure enough, a tiger came roaring,
its front paw triggered the trap,
the arrow struck its three-striped forehead,
pierced its heart, and it fell dead,
after a brief struggle.
The various chāng ghosts came running back,
prostrated themselves over the tiger,
and wept bitterly, saying:
"Who has killed our general again?"
The two men angrily rebuked them:
"You ignorant lowly ghosts,
killed by a tiger's teeth.
We have now avenged you,
yet instead of thanking us,
you dare to wail in grief.
How can ghosts
be so unenlightened?"
They then fell silent.
Suddenly, one ghost replied:
"We had no idea the general was a tiger.
Hearing your explanation,
we are now greatly enlightened."
They went to the tiger and cursed it,
then expressed their thanks and left.
At dawn,
the two men divided the silver with the hunter and returned home.
Zhāng Shēng
Zhāng Shēng, a former Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel in the Táng dynasty, followed Emperor Xīzōng to Shǔ.
Being young and not yet having passed the imperial examinations,
he took up the acting position of Yátuī in Fúzhōu.
The prefectural office assigned the village head, Yóu Zhāng, to be on duty.
One day,
he came to bid farewell.
When asked where he was going,
Zhāng did not answer,
but only said:
"I have an old mother, a wife, and sons.
I beg you to look after them from time to time."
Having said this, he left.
His neighbors, living nearby,
heard Zhāng's family weeping loudly at night.
The next day,
Shēng sent someone to ask the reason,
and they said that Zhāng had bid farewell to his family at night
and went into the mountains to transform into a tiger.
Two or three days later,
they again heard Zhāng's family screaming in great alarm.
The following day,
Shēng again inquired the reason.
They said:
"Zhāng, missing his family, returned last night,
but only the upper half of his body had transformed back,
though he could still speak."
Yáng Zhēn
In Yèzhōng lived a man named Yáng Zhēn, whose family was wealthy.
Throughout his life, he had an obsessive fondness for paintings of tigers,
and his home was filled with many such paintings.
Tigers.
Whether sitting or lying down,
he always wanted to see them.
Later, in his old age,
he ordered his family to destroy all the tiger paintings he owned.
When he reached the age of ninety, he suddenly fell ill and lay bedridden.
Summoning his sons and grandsons, he said to them:
"Throughout my life, I should not have been so obsessively fond of tiger paintings.
In my fondness for them,
when I saw painted tigers, I felt joy;
when I did not see them, I felt unhappy.
I often dreamed of roaming with packs of tigers.
I did not want to speak of this to my children and grandchildren.
In my later years, it became especially severe.
Even when strolling and enjoying the scenery,
I would often see tigers.
When I asked my companions,
they did not see them,
and I became frightened.
Soon after, I had all the tiger paintings destroyed.
Now, after falling ill and lying bedridden,
I again dreamed of transforming into a tiger cub.
After the dream ended, it took a long time
before I returned to human form.
After I die,
I fear I will certainly transform into a tiger.
If my children and grandchildren encounter a tiger,
be careful not to kill it."
That evening, he passed away.
As his family was planning the burial,
his corpse suddenly transformed into a tiger,
leaping and bounding away.
One of his sons ran out to look,
and the tiger turned and chased his son,
devouring him before leaving.
A few days later,
the family suddenly dreamed at night that Yáng Zhēn returned and said to them:
"I have already become a tiger,
and am very healthy and strong.
Only when I left home,
I happened to devour a person,
and to this day I am still not hungry."
At dawn,
the family suspected that he had not recognized his own son and had eaten him,
and they recounted this to the neighbors.
Someone knowledgeable said:
"When one is human,
one recognizes human father-son relationships.
Once transformed into a tiger,
how could one still remember being a human father?
Humans and beasts—
are they not fundamentally different?
If a tiger could still remember its past life,
why must humans remember their past lives?
Humans do not even remember their past lives,
which is enough to know that beasts are not more intelligent than humans."
Wáng Jūzhēn
Wáng Jūzhēn, a candidate in the imperial examinations, failed the exams
and returned to Yǐngyáng in Luò.
Leaving the capital,
he traveled with a Daoist priest.
The Daoist priest did not eat all day.
He said:
"I practice breath-swallowing techniques."
Every time after Wáng Jūzhēn fell asleep,
and the lamp went out,
he would open a cloth bag,
take out a skin, put it on, and leave,
returning at the fifth watch.
One day,
Wáng Jūzhēn pretended to sleep,
quickly seized his bag,
and the Daoist priest kowtowed and begged.
Wáng Jūzhēn said:
"Tell me the truth, and I will return it to you."
So he said, "I am not human;
what I wear is a tiger skin.
At night, I go to villages in the countryside to seek food.
Wearing this skin,
I can travel five hundred li in a night."
Wáng Jūzhēn, having been away from home for a long time,
missed home very much.
He said:
"Can I wear it?"
The Daoist replied:
"You can."
Wáng Jūzhēn was still over a hundred li from home,
so he put on the skin to return briefly.
Late at night,
he could not enter his gate,
but saw a pig standing outside the door,
so he caught and ate it.
Quickly returning,
he gave the skin back to the Daoist priest.
When he arrived home,
it was said
that Wáng Jūzhēn's second son had gone out at night
and was eaten by a tiger.
When asked about the date,
it was the day Wáng Jūzhēn returned.
Afterward, for a day or two, he felt very full
and did not eat anything else.
Guī Shēng
Guī Shēng, a scholar of the Hóngwén Academy,
after the turmoil, moved his family to Bāzhōu.
He sent a messenger to Shǔ,
who set out early
and encountered a tiger on the road.
He climbed a tree to avoid it.
Several tigers came one after another, leaping and trying to seize him,
but could not reach him.
The tigers said to each other:
"We cannot surpass Huáng Èrláng of Bāxī County."
One tiger then left.
Soon, a white wildcat arrived,
looked at the man, roared, and leaped to seize him,
causing the man to climb even higher up the tree.
Since none could get him,
they surrounded the tree and guarded him.
After a while,
a group of mules approached, their bells jingling,
and the tigers scattered.
The messenger arrived in Bāxī,
and indeed, there was a man named Huáng Èrláng, a clerk in Bāxī,
who had been eaten by a tiger.
Zhèng Sīyuǎn
When tigers mate, a lunar halo appears.
The immortal Zhèng Sīyuǎn once rode a tiger.
His old friend Xǔ Yǐn suffered from toothache and sought treatment.
Zhèng said:
"Only by obtaining tiger whiskers
and inserting them into the teeth while they are hot can it be cured."
So he plucked a few strands and gave them to him.
Thus, it is known that tiger whiskers can cure toothache.
When a tiger kills a person,
it can make the corpse rise and undress itself
before eating it.
The tiger's power lies in a mark like the character "一."
It is one cùn long,
located on both sides of the ribs under the skin.
The tip of the tail does not have it.
Carrying it brings good fortune for those holding office,
for those without office,
it makes people detest and loathe them.
At night, a tiger sees
with one eye emitting light
and the other eye observing things.
Hunters wait and shoot at it,
and the light falls to the ground, turning into white stone.
It is used to treat children's fright.
Lǐ Zhuó
Thirty or forty li west of Xǔzhōu, a female tiger was causing havoc,
injuring numerous people.
Commander Lǐ Zhuó, upon hearing this, was shocked and alarmed.
On the day he assumed his duties,
he declared sternly:
"The Zhōngwǔ Army numbers a hundred thousand;
surely there must be a brave warrior among them?"
A strong man stepped forward and said:
"I can eliminate it."
Zhuó admired his words,
and provided him with sharp weapons.
The strong man requested not to use a bow or blade,
but only a large white club.
He went straight into the thickets and brambles to search for it,
and indeed found its den.
The tiger had already gone out,
leaving only three cubs,
their eyes about to open.
At first, the strong man did not see the mother tiger,
and considered turning back.
But he thought Zhuó would surely not believe him,
so he took the three cubs,
and hid them at his home.
He went to report to Zhuó,
who was surprised to see him return empty-handed.
The strong man said:
"I have already captured her three cubs."
Zhuó was astonished to hear this,
and when the cubs were indeed brought forth,
he rewarded the man generously,
granting him provisions and silk,
and promoting him in the army.
Zhuó remarked:
"I have heard it said, 'If you do not enter the tiger's den,
how can you catch the tiger's cubs?'
This man is a perfect example."
The strong man eventually eliminated the great tiger,
and there were no more tiger attacks.
Qiáo Běn
During the fourth and fifth years of the Jiànwǔ era of the False Shǔ,
there was a commoner named Qiáo Běn,
a man of Dōushuài.
He was unfilial and unjust,
and all his neighbors despised him.
Having lost his father young,
he often cursed and abused his mother,
who endured it silently each time.
One day,
returning late,
his mother leaned by the door to welcome him.
From afar, Qiáo Běn saw her
and began to curse.
His mother said:
"I have only you,
and I worry when you come home late.
Yet you curse me in return."
She then clutched her chest and wept bitterly,
sighing and lamenting.
Qiáo Běn lived in a lane within the city,
and at that moment, he went out the gate,
sitting by the road near the city wall.
Suddenly, he let out a great cry,
tore off his clothes,
and transformed into a red tiger,
leaping straight onto the city wall.
By the next day,
he was still on the wall.
The King of Shǔ ordered Zhào Tíngyǐn to shoot him,
and with one shot, he struck him squarely in the mouth.
The crowd then divided and ate him.
When the King of Shǔ first established his rule over the region,
there were strange omens: hair rained from the sky,
men turned into tigers,
and earthquakes occurred.
Lǐ Dàkě
The Minister of the Imperial Clan, Lǐ Dàkě, once traveled to Cāngzhōu.
In the Ráo'ān County of that prefecture, a man was walking in the wild when
he was chased by a tiger.
When it caught up,
it stretched out its left paw to show him,
as a large bamboo splinter
had pierced its forearm.
The tiger crouched low, ears flattened,
as if begging for it to be removed.
The man pulled it out for him,
and the tiger was very pleased,
twisting and wagging its tail,
then followed the man to his home before leaving.
That night,
it left a deer in his courtyard.
For over a year,
it brought wild boars, river deer, and deer,
never missing a month.
Sometimes, when they met in the wild,
it would accompany him.
The man's household gradually prospered,
and he began to wear finer clothes.
Later, when the tiger saw him in his new attire,
it did not recognize him,
and so it attacked and killed him.
After his family had buried him,
the tiger returned to his home.
His mother scolded it:
"My son removed the splinter for you,
yet instead of repaying his kindness,
you killed him.
Now you come again to our home—
are you not ashamed?"
The tiger left in shame and remorse.
Yet for several days, it lingered near the house.
When it did not see the man,
it realized it had killed the wrong person,
and began to wail mournfully.
Then it entered the courtyard,
leaped up, broke its own spine, and died.
All who saw this were amazed.
Lìn Tíngyōng
The Jíyáng District Office is located south of Fúzhōu.
Thirty li up the Qián River, there is a temple,
with statues and spiritual manifestations,
ancient steles still standing,
and abundant property,
which no one dared to violate.
The younger sister of Fúzhōu's deputy general, Lìn Tíngyōng, once visited the temple
and stole some of its permanent property.
She immediately lost her way.
Within a few days,
her body transformed into a tiger.
On her front paws,
silver bracelets and gold bangles
remained clearly visible.
Whenever she saw villagers,
she would speak to them from behind a tree:
"I stole from the temple,
and this is how I was transformed."
She asked to see her mother,
entrusting someone to relay the message.
Her mother was afraid
and did not dare to go.
The tiger lingered outside the city walls
for a year before leaving.
Wáng Tài
There was a man from Hǎilíng named Wáng Tài who was traveling in the wilderness with fifteen or sixteen companions
when they suddenly encountered a tiger blocking the road.
His companions said:
"Surely not all fifteen or sixteen of us will die.
Let each of us offer a garment to test it."
When it came to Wáng Tài's garment,
the tiger roared and crouched down several times.
Hǎilíng,
had many tigers,
and travelers all carried large clubs.
Wáng Tài selected a club,
took off his clothes, and stood alone.
He said to the fourteen others:
"You should leave quickly."
Once he estimated they were far away,
he took his club and advanced straight ahead,
striking the tiger on the ear,
which stunned it and caused it to fall.
It soon got up and left.
Wáng Tài fled in panic,
unable to find the original path,
and simply walked through the grass.
After about ten miles,
he came upon a temple to a deity,
and spent the night on a beam.
That evening,
the moon was bright,
and late at night he heard a tiger moving through the grass.
Soon the tiger arrived at the temple courtyard,
leapt and transformed into a man,
with very fine clothing and headgear.
Someone inside the hall asked:
"Why are you so weary and haggard tonight?"
The deity said:
"I suddenly encountered a man,
unexpectedly strong and brave,
who struck me with his sturdy club,
leaving me utterly exhausted and near death."
After speaking,
he entered the wooden idol on the seat.
Suddenly raising his head, he saw Wáng Tài,
and asked who this guest was.
Wáng Tài, terrified, fell to the ground,
and recounted everything from beginning to end.
The deity said:
"Your fate is to be eaten by me.
However, you still have more than ten days before you should die.
I tried to take you early,
so I was struck by your club.
Now that we have met,
it is only right that I protect you.
In a few days,
bring a pig here.
Smear it with your own blood" and pointed to a large tree in the courtyard,
"tie it under this tree,
then quickly climb the tree,
and you will be spared."
Later, Wáng Tài did as instructed.
The deity emerged from the hall as a tiger,
leapt vigorously,
but Wáng Tài was too high up to reach,
so it bent down and ate the pig.
After eating,
it returned to the hall and resumed human form.
Wáng Tài climbed down from the tree, bowed twice, and then left.
After that, he had no further troubles.
A Person from Jīngzhōu
There was a man from Jīngzhōu traveling in the mountains
when he suddenly encountered a chāng ghost,
who covered him with a tiger skin,
causing him to transform into a tiger,
controlled by the chāng ghost.
For three or four years,
he hunted and ate people, livestock, and various wild beasts,
too many to count.
Though his body was that of a tiger, his heart was unwilling,
but there was nothing he could do.
Later, the chāng ghost led the tiger past the gate of a temple,
and he quickly ran into the temple storehouse,
hiding under a monk's bed.
The monks were frightened,
and reported it to a virtuous elder.
At that time, there was a Chán master who could subdue fierce beasts.
He went to where the tiger was,
planted his staff and asked:
"Disciple,
what do you seek?
Do you wish to eat people?
Or are you weary of your beastly form?"
The tiger lowered its ears and shed tears.
The Chán master tied a towel around its neck,
and led it back to his own room.
He regularly fed it with food meant for sentient beings and other flavors.
After half a year, its fur fell out,
and it transformed into human shape.
He recounted everything from the beginning.
For two years, he dared not leave the temple.
Later, he briefly went out,
and suddenly encountered the chāng ghost again,
who covered him with the tiger skin.
He hurriedly ran back into the temple,
but the skin reached down to his waist,
and he turned back into a tiger.
He devoted himself to reciting scriptures,
and after over a year, he transformed again.
From then on, he dared not leave the temple gate,
and remained there until his death.
Old Man Liú
There was an old man named Liú from Xìnzhōu, a layman who resided among mountain streams.
Someone brought over two hundred geese to Liú to release for life,
and he constantly looked after and raised them himself.
Several months later,
they were taken daily by a tiger,
and over thirty had been lost.
The villagers were troubled by this,
and set up traps and snares
all around the release site.
After that, the tiger no longer came.
A few days later,
suddenly an old man with a large head and long beard came to see Liú,
asking why the number of geese had decreased.
Liú replied:
"They were taken by a tiger."
The old man asked why he didn't capture the tiger.
Liú answered:
"We already set traps,
so it no longer comes here."
The old man said:
"This is taught by the chāng ghost.
If you first subdue the chāng,
then you can get the tiger."
Liú asked what method could capture it.
The old man said:
"This ghost loves sour things.
You can place dark plums, white plums, and bayberries along the main path.
If the chāng eats them,
it will become blind,
and then the tiger can be caught."
After speaking, he vanished.
That evening,
Liú laid out the fruit along the path as instructed.
After the fourth watch,
he heard the tiger fall into a trap.
From then on, it ceased.
Tiger Wife
In Lìzhōu, there was a man who sold food.
His son’s wife went to gather vegetables in the mountain garden,
and was taken by a tiger.
It was twelve years before she returned.
She said she had entered a deep mountain cave,
originally thinking she would be eaten.
After a long time, she slept and lived with it.
In the cave there were four tigers in total,
the one who took her as a wife was the oldest.
The tiger often brought back meat like deer to feed his wife,
and sometimes carried water in its mouth to spit into hers.
When the woman wanted to leave,
it would always get angry,
driving her back into the cave.
This lasted six or seven years.
After a few more years,
gradually the other tigers disappeared,
and only the old one remained.
This tiger already had a woman,
and
often slept outside.
One day later,
suddenly it did not return at night.
The woman found it strange,
wanting to leave but not daring to.
After another day like this,
she slowly went out,
walked several tens of steps,
and did not see the tiger again.
Then she exerted herself to walk five or six lǐ.
Hearing the sound of woodcutting in the mountains,
she went straight toward it.
The woodcutters thought she was a ghost or demon,
and threw stones at her.
The woman loudly explained the reason,
and they gathered to question her.
The woman said:
“I am the new bride of such-and-such family.”
Among the people were some from the same neighborhood,
who already knew the woman had been taken by a tiger.
Only then did everyone believe her.
A neighbor then took off a shirt to clothe her,
and took her back.
It happened that her husband had already died,
so her father-in-law and mother-in-law took pity and took her in.
The woman was also simple-minded and dull,
lacking spirit,
and was often teased by those who came and went.
Liú Quánbái personally saw the woman,
and told this story.
Zhào Tì
In Jīngzhōu, there was a merchant,
surnamed
Zhào, named Tì.
He often traveled south on rivers and lakes.
Suddenly, more than a year passed without his return.
A man first came to his home,
and reported to Zhào Tì’s wife:
