“Zhào Tì’s goods were all lost in the lake,
and Tì barely escaped death.
He is very poor and destitute,
and will arrive on the road soon.”
His wife cried in shock without end.
Three days later,
there was a man,
exactly like Zhào Tì in appearance and manner,
who came to the outside of the gate and wept loudly.
His wife quickly brought him inside the home,
and asked the reason.
She cared for him for over a hundred days.
Wanting to trade again,
he said to Zhào Tì’s wife:
“I am used to being a merchant outside,
I am not happy at home,
my heart feels empty.
Do not think I do not care for you,
please allow me to go out again,
to visit friends.”
Soon after, Tì came from afar with a cartload of goods,
and upon entering the gate,
his wife, on the contrary, was shocked and suspicious and ran out,
going to a neighbor’s house.
Zhào Tì, after a long while, asked the reason,
learned what had happened,
then had someone summon that man.
That man arrived,
and upon seeing Zhào Tì,
rushed south in a dash.
Zhào Tì and more than ten companions chased him together,
straight into the south gate.
That man turned back,
looked back,
and said to Tì:
“I am a tiger with supernatural powers,
do not chase me,
I will surely harm you all.”
Then he leaped and transformed into a red tiger,
roared, and left.
Sōngyáng Man
A man from Sōngyáng entered the mountains to gather firewood.
As dusk fell,
he was chased by two tigers,
and quickly climbed a tree.
The tree was not very high,
the two tigers took turns leaping at him,
but in the end could not reach him.
Suddenly they spoke to each other:
“If we get Zhū Dūshì, we will surely succeed.”
One tiger stayed to guard him,
and one tiger then left.
Soon another tiger came, slender and good at seizing.
At the time, the night moon was bright,
and he saw everything clearly.
The small tiger repeatedly grabbed at the man’s clothes,
the man’s woodcutter knife was still at his waist,
waiting for it to grab again,
he used the knife to chop at it,
cut off its front claw,
it roared loudly,
and they all left together.
By dawn,
the man was finally able to return.
Meeting villagers who asked,
he told them what had happened.
The villagers said:
“Now east of the county there is a Zhū Dūshì,
go and check on him,
could it be him?”
Several people went together to inquire.
The answer was:
“Last night I went out briefly and injured my hand,
now I am lying down resting.”
Then they confirmed he was truly a tiger,
so they reported it to the county magistrate,
who ordered a group of officers to take knives,
surround his place and burn it.
Zhū Dūshì suddenly rose,
swiftly transformed into a tiger,
broke through the people and escaped,
and no one knew where he went.
Nányáng Scholar
In recent times, there was a man who lived in Nányáng Mountain.
Suddenly he fell ill with a fever,
and for ten days he did not recover.
It was a summer night with a bright moon,
and he was resting temporarily in front of the courtyard.
Suddenly he heard the sound of knocking at the door.
Listening carefully,
it felt like a dream,
and none of his family members heard it.
But in his dazed state,
he unconsciously got up to look.
From behind the door, someone said:
"You are destined to become a tiger,
and now there is an official document."
The man was shocked and bewildered,
and unconsciously reached out his hand to receive it.
He saw that the hand of the person delivering the document was a tiger's claw.
The messenger left the document and departed.
Opening the document to look at it,
it was only blank paper with stamped seals.
He felt deeply disturbed,
placed the document under his mat,
and went back to sleep.
The next morning, he vaguely remembered,
and told his family about it.
When he retrieved the document, it was still there,
making him even more perplexed.
His illness seemed to improve,
and he suddenly thought of going out for a stroll.
So he took his cane and wandered leisurely,
with none of his children accompanying him.
After walking over a li,
there was a stream at the foot of the mountain.
Strolling slowly along the stream,
he suddenly saw in the water
that his own head had already transformed into a tiger's.
Looking further, his hands and feet had also become those of a tiger,
and it was very clear.
He thought to himself that if he returned home,
he would surely frighten his wife and children.
Filled with resentment and shame,
he followed the path into the mountains.
After more than a day,
his family had no idea where he had gone,
and they scattered to search for him.
The neighbors all said he had been eaten by tigers or wolves.
His family could only weep and wail.
This man, now a tiger,
spent two days in the mountains
and began to feel hungry.
Suddenly, crouching by the water's edge,
he saw several liters of tadpoles in the water.
Recalling that he had often heard tigers also eat mud,
he scooped them up and ate them,
finding them quite flavorful.
Continuing to walk slowly,
he then saw a rabbit,
captured it,
and caught it instantly.
He ate it,
feeling his body grow lighter and stronger.
During the day, he would hide in the deep thickets and grass,
and at night, he would go out to hunt for food.
He also caught several deer and rabbits.
Gradually, he developed a mind to harm other creatures.
Suddenly, looking up at a tree,
he saw a woman picking mulberry leaves.
He watched her from the grass.
And privately thought:
"I have heard that tigers eat people."
He tried to seize her,
and indeed caught her.
Eating her,
he found her flesh sweet and delicious.
He often stayed near small paths,
waiting for passersby.
At dusk,
a man carrying firewood passed by,
and he was about to capture him.
Suddenly, he heard someone behind him say:
"Don't take him, don't take him!"
Startled, he looked back and saw an old man with white beard and eyebrows,
knowing he was a divine being.
Although this man had transformed,
his heart still longed for home.
So he pleaded sorrowfully.
The old man said:
"You were sent by the heavenly gods to take this form.
Now that your task is about to be completed,
you will regain your human form.
If you kill this firewood carrier,
you will never change back.
Tomorrow, you are fated to eat a certain Wáng Píngshì,
and afterward, you will become human again."
After speaking,
the old man disappeared.
The tiger then crept through the grass again.
By the evening of the next day,
he waited near the official road,
when he suddenly heard the sound of bells.
He hid in the grass.
Then he heard a voice from the sky say:
"Whose convoy is this?"
A voice from the sky replied:
"It is Wáng Píngshì's convoy."
The voice asked again:
"Where is Wáng Píngshì?"
The reply came:
"Outside the city walls.
The county officials are seeing him off,
and the farewell banquet has just ended."
Hearing this, the tiger
continued to wait along the road.
After the first watch,
with a faint moonlight,
he heard the sound of people and horses approaching.
The voice from the sky said again:
"Wáng Píngshì is coming."
In a moment,
he saw a man in red robes riding a horse, slightly drunk,
around forty years old,
with several attendants following him.
While they were still far away,
he seized the man from his horse,
dragged him into the deep thickets, and ate him.
His attendants scattered and fled.
After eating,
his mind gradually cleared,
and he remembered the way home,
which was over a hundred li away.
He made his way back through the mountains,
and again came to the stream to look at his reflection.
His body had already transformed back into a human.
So he returned home.
His family was shocked and bewildered,
as he had been missing for almost seven or eight months.
His speech was confused,
like that of a drunken man.
Gradually, he began to eat porridge,
and after over a month, he recovered.
Five or six years later,
he traveled to Chánggě County in Chénxǔ.
At a banquet hosted by the county magistrate,
there were about thirty guests seated.
The host brought up the topic of people transforming into other beings.
He then said:
"Stories like that of Niú Āi
are mostly baseless tales."
The man then recounted his own experience,
to prove that transformations are not mere fabrications.
The host was astonished,
for he was the son of Wáng Píngshì.
He said that his father had been killed by a tiger,
and now he had encountered his enemy.
So he killed him.
The officials, knowing the truth of the matter,
pardoned him from punishment.
The tiger took pity on humans.
In Fèngxiáng Prefecture, a General Lǐ was seized by a tiger,
which crouched over him.
Lǐ repeatedly called out "Great King," begging for his life.
The tiger then laid its ears back as if pleased.
After a short while,
it carried Lǐ on its back for over ten lǐ and dropped him into a den.
Two or three cubs, seeing a person, leaped joyfully.
The tiger looked down into the den from above,
and after a long time, finally left.
Afterward, when it entered the den,
it would always share the meat it obtained with Lǐ.
After more than ten days had passed,
the cubs grew as large as dogs,
all able to suckle vigorously.
The tiger then carried them out of the den on its back.
When it came to the third cub,
Lǐ feared that if they all left,
he would die in the den.
So he embraced it and said:
"Great King, will you not lead me out as well?"
The tiger then lowered its tail,
Lǐ held onto it,
and thus managed to get out of the den.
Lǐ further said:
"You have fortunately protected me thus far;
could you not escort me to my home?"
The tiger again carried Lǐ on its back to the place where it had seized him and then parted.
Every three days,
it would come once to Lǐ's house,
as if checking on him.
Over twenty days,
this happened five or six times in total.
The villagers were frightened,
and it came again afterward.
Lǐ then plainly said:
"Great King, your visits are very kind,
but the villagers are terrified;
I wish you would not come."
After more than a month,
it came once more,
and from then on, it ceased entirely.
Fàn Duān
Fàn Duān, a village head of Fúlíng,
was capable and efficient by nature,
serving in prefectural and county assignments.
After a long time,
he transformed into a tiger.
The village neighbors suffered from this,
and so reported to the county, saying:
"He constantly leads outside tigers into the village,
stealing and eating cattle and livestock."
The county magistrate said:
"These are words of malice;
how could such a thing happen in the world?"
He then summoned and questioned him,
and Duān replied as the magistrate had said.
After a long time,
a tiger entered the granary at night to steal meat,
and by dawn, it could not get out.
They took turns surrounding it,
the tiger injured several people,
and escaped.
The elders again spoke of this matter.
The county magistrate then sternly interrogated Duān about the cause.
Duān then confessed fully, saying:
"I often crave raw meat,
but cannot obtain it myself.
At night, I indeed went to the eastern neighbor's pen and secretly ate a pig;
I found it flavorful.
Therefore, when I see people who are plump and robust,
I desire to devour them,
but I suffer from having no companion.
Every night, I search east and west,
and encountered two tigers who follow me.
Whatever is obtained,
we share it together,
and I also do not know that my body is about to change."
However, observing his behavior,
it was as if he were drunk.
The county magistrate reasoned with him and sent him away.
That night, Duān left.
After several days, he returned,
his clothes as before.
He stayed at home for three or four days,
and after dusk,
a wild tiger would come to the outskirts of the village and roar, frightening the villagers,
who again wanted to kill it.
His mother admonished him, telling him to leave.
Duān wept, bid farewell to his mother, and departed.
Several days later,
some saw three tigers,
one of which
had a boot on its left hind foot.
Duān's mother then searched throughout the mountains and valleys,
and saw them again.
The mother wailed and cried,
two tigers ran away,
and the one with the boot remained alone.
She approached it,
the tiger crouched down and closed its eyes,
so she removed the boot,
and it was still a human foot.
The mother held it and wept,
and after a long while, it finally left.
After this, the villagers frequently saw them,
and if someone called out "Village Head Fàn,"
the two tigers would flee in alarm,
while one tiger would look back,
its movements seeming sorrowful and distressed.
From then on, no one knew where they went.
Shí Jǐngyá
Shí Jǐngyá was initially a village head,
but did not like it,
so he took up scholarly pursuits,
calling himself a scholar,
and went toward the city to buy clothes.
Reaching a stream,
on a rock south of the stream was a Daoist priest dressed in red robes,
with two young attendants in black robes serving beside him.
The Daoist priest said:
"Tomorrow at noon, I will have the scholar Shí Jǐngyá to eat;
have him remove his knives and staff,
so as not to cause any injury."
The two attendants said:
"It is done."
Shí Jǐngyá saw the Daoist priest,
but the Daoist priest did not see Shí Jǐngyá.
Jǐngyá, hearing these words, was terrified.
He traveled to an inn to stay,
lingering for several nights.
Suddenly, a soldier came and asked Jǐngyá:
"Do you not wish to take military weapons with you?"
Jǐngyá, having previously heard the Daoist priest's words,
took out his knife,
removed the spearhead,
and hid it in his bosom.
The soldier took the knife away,
and Jǐngyá lingered, not yet departing.
The innkeeper repeatedly urged him to leave,
and Jǐngyá, having no choice,
placed the spearhead in a bamboo container and set off.
Reaching a crossroads,
he saw a tiger blocking the road,
which came straight forward to seize Jǐngyá.
Jǐngyá then stabbed with the spear,
hitting it right in the heart,
and it died.
The two attendants, carefully observing the tiger's death,
then sang and leaped for joy.
Capturing a Tiger
In the Xiāngliáng region, there were many fierce beasts.
The prefecture had hunting officers
who set traps and snares to capture them,
making it their profession.
One day, they suddenly reported to the authorities:
"Last night, a trap was sprung;
please have the commander move the kitchen."
He ordered his staff officers and generals to go and inspect it.
Upon arrival, they saw a tiger in a deep pit.
Officials from the government residences
and commoner women
all set up tents to watch.
The hunters first made a large cangue,
complete with nails and locks,
with ropes tied at the four corners,
and placed it in the pit.
Then they gradually filled it with earth.
As the fierce beast was about to emerge from the pit,
they gradually closed the carrying boards together.
As soon as the tiger's head emerged,
they pressed it down and nailed it shut,
using ropes on all sides,
and drove it along.
The onlookers followed and laughed at it.
If such a creature were not captured with mechanical devices,
but taken only when exhausted,
then even the strength of a thousand men,
the courage of a hundred warriors—
how could they subdue it?
When its strength is depleted and it is captured,
it is like leading a sheep or dragging a dog;
even with sharp teeth and claws,
how could it harm people!
As for those who wish to subdue a strong enemy,
should they not also act in this way?
The Shāngshān Road
The old Shāngshān Road often had fierce beasts that harmed travelers.
Once, a group of mules was traveling early in the morning,
before dawn had fully broken,
when some of the mules became startled and frightened.
Suddenly, a tiger leaped out from the thick underbrush,
seized a man, and carried him away.
None of his companions dared to look back.
By mealtime,
they heard that the man who had been seized had actually caught up with them.
Everyone thought he had been torn apart by sharp teeth,
and they were all astonished.
They eagerly asked him how it happened.
He slowly said:
"At first, the tiger carried me to the left side of the road, up on a cliff.
In front was a clear stream ten thousand fathoms deep.
South of the stream was a cave,
and at the cave entrance were several tiger cubs looking toward their mother,
joyfully as if waiting for something.
The tiger placed me by the cliffside,
without harming me at all,
and then faced the stream and cave, roaring
to call its cubs.
I took the chance to secretly stretch my foot onto the tiger's back.
With all my strength, I gave one push.
The tiger lost its footing
and fell into the deep ravine,
unable to climb back up.
That is how I escaped and came here.
That beast probably wanted to bring this person back alive,
to train its cubs,
which is why it didn't harm me.
Truly, one could say I escaped from the tiger's jaws.
How perilous,
how perilous!"
Chén Bāo
Chén Bāo, a man from Qīngyuán, lived in seclusion at a separate estate.
One night, he was sitting by the window,
outside of which was open wilderness.
Suddenly, he heard the sound of people and horses.
Looking out,
he saw a woman riding a tiger pass beneath his window
and go straight into the western building.
Under the wall inside, a maidservant was already lying down.
The woman then took a thin bamboo branch and poked her through a crack in the wall.
The maidservant suddenly had a stomachache
and opened the door to go to the toilet.
Chén Bāo was just shocked and terrified,
before he could speak,
the maidservant had already gone out.
She was immediately attacked by a tiger.
He rushed forward to save her,
and she barely escaped.
The villagers said:
"This kind of monster often appears in the village,
what is called a 'tiger ghost.'"
Eating Tigers
In Jiàn'ān,
those who grew millet in the mountains all built sheds in tall trees to guard against tigers.
Once, a man was just climbing into a shed
when he saw a tiger with its head down and ears drooping pass by very quickly.
Soon after, a beast like a tiger but slightly smaller
followed the previous tiger.
Then, he heard earth-shaking roars from the bamboo grove,
which lasted a long time before ceasing.
The next day, he went to look
and found that the tiger had been almost completely eaten,
with only a few bones left.
Zhōu Xióng
After the Táng dynasty's Dàshùn and Jǐngfú eras,
on the road between Jiàn and Lì in Shǔ,
at Báiwèi Ridge and Shítǒng Stream,
tigers and leopards were especially rampant,
and it was called the "Toll Ground for People."
Merchants traveled in groups,
and soldiers passed in armored columns,
yet they still suffered attacks.
At that time, among the relay station soldiers was one named Zhōu Xióng,
whose physical strength, courage, and heart
were extraordinary.
He traveled day and night on duty,
unwilling to avoid danger,
and still carried a fork and sharp sword.
At the Toll Ground for People, he successively killed several tigers.
Travelers relied on him.
Xīchuān secretary Cháng Zhuāng wrote a long composition praising him,
and the Shǔ commander gave him a military post to honor him.
Generally, those who die by tiger
or drown in water
become ghosts called chāng,
and they must find someone to take their place.
Although this is commonly said,
it often happens.
Earlier, Xīchuān military inspector Yú Quányīn, a special advancement official, moved his family from the capital
and rested at Hànyuán Station.
His widowed sister-in-law had just stopped her carriage
and was carefully making up
while leaning against the station gate to look out
when she was seized by a tiger.
Although they drove it off and rescued her,
she was already wounded by its hooked claws.
I once traveled and stopped at Báiwèi Ridge.
It was during the hot season,
so we traveled at night when it was cool.
With one horse, two servants, and three or five others traveling together,
some ahead, some behind,
and with the villagers' pigs and dogs crisscrossing the road,
the mountains and forests were peaceful as ever,
the residents as before.
Where had the tigers and leopards gone?
What had become of them?
During the Jǐngfú and Qiánníng eras,
when war raged in Sānchuān,
tigers and leopards walked by day,
and local tributes
were obstructed from proceeding.
Xīchuān's memorials to the court
mostly went via Wū Gorge.
When humans and beasts run rampant,
is it not connected to the rise and fall of the state?
Zhāng Jùn
Yuán Dàn, the county lieutenant of Lìshuǐ County in Xuānzhōu, had his family in Huáizhōu.
He first brought a tenant farmer, Zhāng Jùn, to serve him at his post.
When his term ended and he returned,
Zhāng Jùn followed him.
Zhāng Jùn had a wife
and a three-year-old son,
who also traveled with them.
When they reached Sòng territory, rushing by night,
Zhāng Jùn carried his son, following Yuán Dàn,
while his wife rode a donkey about ten steps behind.
Suddenly, they heard a scream.
Zhāng Jùn ran to look
and found his wife had been taken by a tiger.
Zhāng Jùn told Yuán,
"My wife has now been killed by a tiger.
I vow to take revenge.
I entrust my child to you.
If I return alive,
I will repay your nurturing kindness.
If not,
I will serve as your servant for life."
Yuán firmly tried to stop him,
but he would not listen.
He took two arrows again,
carried a bow, hung an axe at his waist,
and left the road to travel under cover of darkness.
After going over thirty lǐ,
all was deep forest and heavy obstacles.
Then he gradually reached a place
near a mountain valley,
with over a hundred large trees.
Suspecting he was near a tiger's den,
Zhāng Jùn climbed a tree to wait.
As it gradually grew light,
he saw, within several tens of steps down the mountain,
something like a creature crouching, moving about.
He waited longer.
As it grew brighter,
he saw it was a tiger.
His wife was already dead,
controlled by the tiger.
The corpse stood up by itself,
bowed to the tiger,
then removed its own clothes,
lay naked, and stiffened again.
The tiger then led four cubs from the den,
all as large as wildcats,
wagging their tails and leaping joyfully.
The tiger licked the dead person with its tongue,
and the cubs scrambled to eat.
Zhāng Jùn, seeing this from the tree,
shot an arrow,
hitting the tiger squarely in the forehead.
The tiger leaped and jumped.
He shot another arrow,
hitting it in the flank.
The arrows were both poisoned.
The tiger then leaped in alarm,
roared wildly in rage,
and died in a moment.
Zhāng Jùn climbed down from the tree,
cut off the tiger's head with his axe,
and also killed the four cubs,
taking their heads as well.
He strung them together with vine.
He also carried his wife's corpse on his back
and walked back.
At daybreak, he caught up,
and Yuán Dàn was extremely moved and grateful.
Xúnyáng Hunters
In Xúnyáng there was a hunter who often made his living by catching tigers,
setting up a crossbow trap along the path.
Each day he would check it,
and though he saw tiger tracks, the arrow had already been fired,
yet he never managed to catch a tiger.
According to an old saying:
"When a person is eaten by a tiger,
they become a chāng ghost."
So he hid beside the trap,
secretly waiting under a tree.
After the second watch,
he saw a small ghost dressed in black,
with shaved hair reaching its eyebrows,
hobbling toward the crossbow,
pulling the trigger to fire the arrow before leaving.
After about the time it takes to eat a meal,
a tiger came and stepped over the crossbow.
Once he understood this,
he took another arrow and left,
repeating the same actions as before.
The man quickly climbed down the tree,
reset the arrow on the crossbow,
and climbed back up to watch.
After a short while, the tiger arrived,
stepped on the crossbow, and the arrow fired.
The tiger was pierced through the ribs and died.
After a long while, the chāng ghost returned,
saw the tiger dead,
and then danced and clapped before leaving.
Liǔ Bìng
Liǔ Bìng from Hédōng served as a supervising censor,
and was sent to the mountains to investigate cases.
He brought along a clerk,
whom he often entrusted with tasks.
They stayed overnight in a solitary lodge at the foot of the mountains,
where the attendants all slept on mats in the hall.
At midnight,
when the moon had just risen,
everyone was asleep,
but Liǔ Bìng alone was awake.
Suddenly, he saw a small ghost about a foot tall,
resembling a macaque,
holding a paper banner and walking up the steps,
inserting the banner beside the clerk's head before leaving.
Liǔ Bìng quietly got up,
pulled it out,
and lay back down to wait.
After a short while,
a tiger came in, sniffed everyone, and left.
Moments later,
the small ghost returned,
inserted another banner,
which Liǔ Bìng again pulled out.
After a short while,
the tiger came again, sniffed everyone, and left.
This happened three times,
and dawn was approaching.
When morning came,
he called the clerk and told him what had happened,
saying, "Today you will likely face danger,
you must make your own plans,
do not follow me."
Liǔ Bìng had a sword,
which he took and gave to him,
then told him to flee from danger.
This clerk was strong and brave by nature,
so he took the sword and entered the mountains,
searching for the tiger's lair.
After walking twenty lǐ, he came to a thatched hut,
entered it,
and saw no one,
only an inkstone and red brush on a mat,
along with a scroll of documents listing people's names,
some marked with checks,
some not yet checked,
and his own name written there.
On the roof, he saw a tiger skin.
The clerk took the document,
and also took the skin,
then left with the sword in hand.
Before he had walked a few lǐ,
he saw a foreign monk coming after him,
calling out:
"Stop,
you should tell me your plan,
then you can be spared."
The clerk stopped,
and spoke with him.
Seeing the man's strange appearance,
he dared not kill him.
The monk said:
"I am not one to harm you forcefully,
it is fate that you are to be eaten.
Did you not see the document just now?
Yesterday the deadline was already missed,
and now if you force your way out,
I fear it will be of no use in the end.
It would be better to use a small trick to ward it off."
The clerk asked about the trick.
The monk told him to climb a tree, bind himself with a belt,
prick himself with the sword to draw a little blood, smear it on a single garment, and throw it down.
"I will use the garment to perform an exorcism."
The clerk did as told, climbed the tree,
threw down the skin, and the monk put it on,
transforming into a tiger,
roaring with glaring eyes,
its light flashing like lightning.
The clerk was terrified,
nearly falling several times.
He then took the single garment,
pricked himself to smear blood on it,
and threw it to the ground.
The tiger grabbed the garment, leaped,
tore it apart, and swallowed it.
After a long while,
it returned to human form.
He said:
"You are spared."
Then he sent him away,
and the clerk had no further troubles.
The Monk Tiger
In the mountains of Yuánzhōu,
there was a village monastery monk whose dharma name has been forgotten.
He once obtained a tiger skin,
and playfully draped it over himself.
Wagging its tail and shaking its head,
he quite resembled a tiger.
Sometimes he would play by the roadside,
and villagers would all flee in fear upon seeing him,
even to the point of dropping their belongings.
The monk was delighted by this,
and he hid at a strategic pass,
waiting for passing merchants carrying goods.
Suddenly leaping out from the grass,
he appeared majestic like a tiger,
causing them all to abandon their loads and run away.
Each time he donned the skin and went out,
he would often gain something.
Believing he had found a clever scheme,
he frequently engaged in this behavior.
One day, as he put on the skin,
he felt it cling to his body.
After lying in the grass for a long time,
he tried to temporarily remove it,
but despite all efforts, he could not take it off.
Looking at his own hands and feet, they were those of a tiger;
his claws and teeth were those of a tiger.
He then approached the water to look at his reflection:
his head, ears, eyebrows, and eyes,
his mouth, nose, tail, and fur—
all were those of a tiger,
no longer human.
His heart also took pleasure in roaming the grasslands,
so he hunted foxes and rabbits to eat them.
Seizing, grabbing, drinking, and eating—
all were the actions of a tiger.
From then on, he often roamed and dwelled with others of his kind.
He was also compelled to serve ghosts and spirits,
traveling back and forth in the mountains at night,
unable to rest regardless of cold, heat, rain, or snow.
He grew deeply weary and distressed by this.
Although his form was that of a tiger,
his mind remained distinctly human,
but he was unable to speak.
After more than a year,
one day, feeling extremely hungry,
and finding nothing to eat,
he lay in ambush by the roadside.
Suddenly, a person passed before him,
and he leaped out and bit him.
After the person died,
he was about to tear him apart and eat him.
Looking closely,
he saw it was a robed monk.
He thought to himself:
"I originally had a human heart,
and fortunately became a monk.
Yet I failed to uphold the precepts,
seeking to escape the cycle of rebirth.
By doing evil myself,
I have now transformed into a tiger.
The power of karma is immense—
there is nothing greater than this.
Now I have killed a monk to fill my stomach—
how could hell ever accept me?
I would rather starve to death
than compound my sins further."
He then cried out loudly to the heavens.
Before his voice faded,
suddenly the skin fell off as if shedding clothes.
Looking at his own body,
he was a naked monk.
He ran to his old monastery,
but it was already abandoned and in ruins.
Using grass to cover himself,
he went to a lay household,
obtained a few tattered garments,
and fled to a Buddhist temple in a neighboring region.
Wandering as a traveling monk,
he settled in the communal hall of Chóngshòu Monastery in Línchuān.
At that time, the Venerable Yuánchāo resided in the scripture-reading hall,
and this monk served him diligently without slacking.
The Venerable, moved by his reverence and diligence,
asked him:
"Where are you from,
how many years have you been ordained,
and what dharma do you practice,
that you are so diligent?"
The monk replied:
"I have regrets in my heart about my actions,
and I wish for the Venerable to resolve them for me,
but I do not want other monks to hear."
The Venerable then dismissed his attendants and questioned him.
The monk recounted the story of becoming a tiger,
bowed his head in reverence,
and sought absolution for his sins.
The Venerable said to him:
"Life, death, sin, and blessings
all arise from thoughts.
In the span of a moment,
one distinguishes between heaven and hell—
how could it be a matter of past or future lives?
Your evil thoughts made you a tiger,
and your good thoughts restored you to a human—
is this not proof?
If you aspire to liberation,
strive for supreme enlightenment,
returning to the origin and recovering your true nature.
When thoughts do not cling,
then humans do not become tigers,
and tigers do not become humans.
Nowadays in Mǐnzhōng,
there are many great virtuous teachers side by side—
you should go there!"
The monk then followed this instruction.
The Venerable later recounted this to Elder Zhìzuò,
who went to see the monk.
When asked about the events the Venerable had mentioned,
there were no discrepancies.
His eyes were still red,
glaring and fearsome.
Later, he entered the mountain ranges,
and no one knows where he went.
Wáng Yáo
Forty-five li west of Hànzhōu,
there lived a wealthy old man named Wáng Yáo.
His residence, with its water, bamboo, and gardens,
occupied the finest scenery of the entire region,
and many passersby would detour to visit it.
Once they arrived,
Yáo would receive them with utmost sincerity.
There was a man named Shí Shēng, who sold tiles and stones, often claiming to live in the western mountains.
Every time he came, he would rest here.
Over more than ten years,
he would come approximately once every five days.
Yáo secretly found this strange,
and observing what he purchased,
it was not something used in the mountains.
One day,
Yáo waited for his arrival,
and served him with all his effort.
Shí also showed no sign of unease.
As evening approached and he was about to leave,
Yáo said:
"I have long wished to visit your dwelling,
for many days now.
Today, I hope to accompany you there."
Shí Shēng said:
"My humble abode is in a desolate mountain,
not worth visiting."
Yáo then followed him for over ten li,
as dusk began to fall.
Shí Shēng said:
"You may return now."
Yáo said:
"I secretly admire your lofty path,
and wish to offer my sincere efforts.
Whatever you desire,
I can provide—
I only seek to know where you live."
Shí Shēng firmly declined,
but Yáo persisted in following him.
Suddenly, Shí Shēng used his walking stick to draw a line on the ground,
which turned into a great chasm.
His body also transformed into a white tiger,
roaring and looking around.
Yáo was terrified and horrified,
and covering his face, he crawled away.
The next day, he went back,
but there was no trace of anyone.
From then on, Shí Shēng never passed by again.
Liú Mù
According to the Shìtǒng of Chéng Yìngyuán,
Liú Mù, styled Zǐrén,
often lived in the wilds of Nánshā.
He delighted in the songs of mountain birds,
loved the melodies of wind through pine trees,
and cultivated fruits and vegetables.
Villagers would bully him,
often cutting down his trees and trampling his garden.
Mù said:
"I do not wrong others—
why do others wrong me?"
A tiger came near his dwelling and made a den,
and upon seeing Mù, it would wag its tail.
Mù said:
"Have you come to protect me?"
The tiger would then lower its head.
Over several years,
the villagers dared not invade.
After Mù passed away,
the tiger left.
The Aunt Tiger
In the boundaries of Jiànzhōu, Yǒngguī, Jiāménɡ, Jiànmén, and Yìchāng.
By the side of the Jiālíng River, there was a woman,
about fifty years old,
who called herself Eighteenth Aunt.
She often came to people’s homes,
neither drinking nor eating.
Each time she would instruct people, saying:
“Just do good deeds,
do not defy divine principles.
At home, be harmonious and obedient,
with filial conduct as the foremost.
If anyone does evil deeds,
I will often send three or five cats to patrol and inspect you.”
Before she finished speaking, she would leave,
sometimes vanishing suddenly.
Every year,
about three to five times, someone would encounter her.
The common people knew she was transformed from a tiger,
and all revered and feared her.
Cuī Tāo
was from Pǔzhōu.
Traveling to Chúzhōu,
he went south to Lìyáng.
Setting off from Chúzhōu at dawn,
he arrived at the Rényì Inn,
and stayed there.
The inn official said:
“This inn is ominous and dangerous,
it’s fortunate you are not staying.”
Cuī Tāo did not listen,
and carrying his book box, he went up to the hall.
After the inn official prepared the lamps and candles,
Cuī Tāo, when it was the second watch,
spread out his quilt and was about to go to sleep,
when suddenly he saw a large foot like that of a beast at the inn door.
Suddenly the door swung open,
and he saw a tiger enter through the door.
Cuī Tāo fled in alarm,
hiding in a dark place to watch secretly.
He saw the beast in the central courtyard shed its beast skin,
revealing a woman of extraordinary beauty, splendidly adorned.
She went up to the hall
and then approached Cuī Tāo’s quilt.
He came out and asked her:
“Why are you sleeping in my quilt?
I just saw you enter as a beast,
what is this about?”
The woman rose and said to Cuī Tāo:
“I hope you, sir, do not find it strange.
My father and brothers make their living by hunting.
Our family is poor,
and I wish to find a good match,
but have no way to present myself.
So at night I secretly take this skin as clothing.
Knowing that you, sir, were staying at this inn,
I wished to entrust myself to you,
to serve in sweeping and cleaning.
Previous travelers
all died of fright.
Tonight I am fortunate to meet an understanding person,
I hope you will consider my intention.”
Cuī Tāo said:
“If your intention is truly so,
I am willing to accept your affection.”
The next day,
Cuī Tāo took the beast-skin garment,
threw it into a dry well behind the hall,
and took the woman away with him.
Later, Cuī Tāo passed the imperial examination in the classics,
and was appointed to Xuānchéng.
At that time, Cuī Tāo’s wife and son were about to go to his post,
and they traveled together.
After over a month,
they again stayed at the Rényì Inn.
Cuī Tāo laughed and said:
“This inn is where I first met you.”
Cuī Tāo went to look into the well,
and the beast-skin garment was still there as before.
Cuī Tāo again laughed and said to his wife:
“The garment you wore in the past is still here.”
His wife said:
“Have someone fetch it.”
Once obtained,
his wife laughed and said to Cuī Tāo:
“Let me try putting it on again.”
Taking the garment in hand,
his wife went down the steps and put on the beast-skin garment.
As soon as she finished,
she transformed into a tiger,
leaping and roaring,
sprang up to the hall,
and devoured her son and Cuī Tāo before leaving.
Wáng Xíngyán
Among the people of Qín, there was Wáng Xíngyán who made his living as a merchant,
often selling salt in the region of Bāqú.
His route passed south of Xīngyuán,
called the Dàbā Road,
and the Xiǎobā Road,
with perilous peaks and steep ravines,
paths for monkeys and bird trails,
sleeping on the road and lodging in the wild,
cut off from human habitation,
fierce beasts in groups,
preying on travelers.
Wáng Xíngyán gathered over ten strong young men to travel together,
each holding a staff over ten feet long,
with sharp steel blades attached,
which were essentially short spears.
As soon as they ascended the narrow path,
they were chased by a fierce tiger.
When they camped by the roadside,
the tiger suddenly came from among the crowd,
seized Wáng Xíngyán, and carried him off.
His companions, holding blades and staffs,
chased after to rescue him,
shouting echoed through the mountains,
and they snatched him back after several tens of steps,
but he already had scratches and injuries from being seized.
At dawn they proceeded forward,
and the tiger again chased them.
When they camped in the wild,
the crowd formed a circle with their spears,
placing Wáng Xíngyán in the center.
By deep night,
the tiger again leaped into the crowd,
seized Wáng Xíngyán, and carried him off.
The crowd again chased and snatched him back,
and his injuries were even more numerous.
The travelers again guarded him as they advanced.
The tiger chased people even in broad daylight,
hardly ever pausing,
sometimes leaping ahead,
sometimes jumping behind.
At times it emerged from the roadside,
and from the dense crowd seized Wáng Xíngyán and carried him off,
and they ultimately failed to rescue him,
yet it never injured his companions.
It had to have this person to fill its belly,
unknown what karmic retribution this was,
that he could not escape it?
Oxen
Among the Dàyuèzhī and the Western Hú,
there is an ox called bái jí.
If you cut its flesh today,
tomorrow the wound will heal.
Therefore, when people from Hàn reached their country,
the Western Hú showed them this ox.
The Hàn person replied:
“In our country there is an insect called silkworm,
which provides clothing for people,
eats tree leaves and spins silk.”
The foreigners again did not believe there were silkworms.
In Xīnchāng, mountain calves emerge from caves,
resembling Qín oxen,
often sharing caves with snakes.
People put salt on their hands,
enter the pit at night to take them.
Those with a slippery tongue are snakes,
those with a dry tongue are oxen,
and thus they lead them out.
Wild oxen are over ten feet tall,
their heads like deer,
their horns twisted,
ten feet long,
with white hair,
tails like deer,
found in the Western Regions.
During the Tiānxiān era of the Táng dynasty,
a farmer herding oxen on Sōng Mountain
lost his ox.
Searching but not finding it,
he suddenly saw a mountain cave open,
inside there was money,
an uncountable amount.
The farmer entered the cave,
carried ten thousand coins and returned.
Returning home, he went again to fetch more,
but lost his way.
He met a person who said to him:
“The ox you lost,
how much was it worth?”
The farmer said:
“Ten thousand coins.”
The person said:
“Your ox was taken by the mountain spirit,
who has already paid you its price,
why are you searching recklessly?”
After speaking,
he disappeared.
The farmer then understood,
and returned.
Golden Ox
To the southwest of Chángshā, there is the Jīnniú Gāng (Golden Ox Ridge).
During the reign of Emperor Wǔ of the Hàn Dynasty,
an old farmer led a red ox
and said to a fisherman:
"Please ferry me across the river."
The fisherman replied:
"My boat is small;
how could it bear the weight of an ox?"
The old farmer said:
"Just accommodate us,
it will not burden your boat."
So both the man and the ox boarded the boat.
When they reached the middle of the river,
the ox defecated on the boat.
The old farmer said:
"I give this to you as a gift."
After crossing the river,
the fisherman was angry that the boat had been soiled,
so he used an oar to scrape the dung into the water.
Just as he was about to finish,
he realized it was gold.
Astonished by this marvel,
he followed them stealthily,
but only saw the man and ox enter the mountains.
He dug where they had gone,
but could not reach them.
The place where he dug still exists today.
Twenty lǐ northeast of Zēngchéng County,
there is a deep, bottomless cave.
On the northern bank, there is a stone
with a circumference of three zhàng.
Fishermen saw a golden ox emerge from the water
and circle this stone.
During the Yìxī era,
a county resident often found golden chains at this pool's stone,
and he searched for them endlessly.
Suddenly, a fish pulled the chain from the water,
and he could not hold onto it,
so he cut it with a knife,
obtaining several sections.
The man then became wealthy,
and lived to a great old age.
Later, Zhōu Língfǔ from Yìxīng often saw this ox resting on the stone,
with a golden chain like a rope beside it.
Língfǔ was always brave and fierce,
so he went to seize it.
The ox broke its chain,
and he obtained about two zhàng of it,
thus becoming wealthy and powerful.
Silver Ox
To the north of Tàiyuán County, there is the Yínniú Shān (Silver Ox Mountain).
In the twenty-fourth year of the Jiànwǔ era of the Hàn Dynasty,
a man riding a white ox
trampled through someone's field.
The old farmer scolded and questioned him.
The man replied:
"I am an envoy from the Northern Sea,
going to see the Son of Heaven ascend to perform the fēng and shàn sacrifices,
so I rode my ox up the mountain."
The old farmer followed him to the mountain,
but only saw ox tracks,
and the dung left behind was all silver.
The following year,
Emperor Shìzǔ performed the fēng and shàn sacrifices there.
Green Ox
When Huán Xuán was in the south,
he often went to visit Yīn Jīngzhōu.
At Guànxué,
he encountered an old man
herding a group of green oxen,
whose forms and colors were extraordinary.
Huán Xuán immediately exchanged his own ox for one,
and rode it to Língxī.
It was exceptionally swift and vigorous.
Huán Xuán stopped to rest and water the ox,
but the ox walked into the water and did not come out.
Huán sent people to watch and guard,
but after a whole day, there was no trace.
At the time, it was considered a divine creature.
Also, a resident of Jīngkǒu went out to the river in the evening
and saw two green oxen at the foot of Shígōng Shān,
with red bellies and mouths,
playing by the water's edge.
A white-clad old man, about three zhàng tall,
stood beside them holding a whip.
After a while,
the old man turned and saw the person,
immediately whipped the two oxen into the water,
then leaped up himself,
suddenly growing taller,
and with one step,
went straight to the summit of Shígōng Shān,
and was never seen again.
Ox Fight
In Jiǔzhēn, there are oxen
that are born by the streams.
They are often angry
and fight each other,
causing the sea to boil and surge.
Sometimes they come ashore to fight,
and domestic oxen are all terrified.
If people try to block or capture them,
thunderclaps immediately occur.
They are called divine oxen.
Submerged Ox
In the great river of Gōulòu County,
there are submerged oxen,
shaped like water buffalo.
Whenever they come ashore to fight,
their horns become soft,
and they return to the river water,
where their horns harden before they come out again.
Liángzhōu Ox
During the Tiānbǎo era,
a household in Liángzhōu had an ox born,
which was very strong and large.
When it grew up,
it could not be restrained,
and thus it roamed freely.
Many other oxen followed it,
often forming herds several tens of lǐ west of the city,
and people could not control them.
Later, the ox gradually became violent,
and their numbers grew to several hundred,
causing unbearable trouble for the villages.
The military governor planned how to attack them.
It happened that a Western Hu tribesman presented a fierce beast,
shaped like a large dog but pure green in color.
The governor asked the Hu man:
"What is the use of presenting this?"
The Hu man said:
"It fights and devours fierce beasts."
The governor told him about the wild oxen.
He said:
"As long as there is a reward,
I will capture them for you."
So a reward of three hundred thousand cash was offered.
The Hu man then stroked the beast and chanted incantations,
as if speaking to it.
The beast then shook itself and leaped vigorously,
and after being untied and released,
went straight to where the oxen were.
When the oxen saw the beast coming,
they formed three lines,
with the lead ox standing alone in the middle,
burying itself in the earth.
The beast then advanced to fight,
stirring up dust that darkened the fields,
and returned in a short while.
The people went to look,
and found a pit had formed into a pool,
but they never knew what kind of beast it was.
Initially, from a distance, they watched the fight,
and saw the beast was as large as a Shǔ horse.
After the fight ended,
the ox had a broken neck and was dead.
The Hu man cut open the ox's belly,
took out its internal organs,
placed them in a basin to feed the beast,
which ate them repeatedly,
and gradually shrank back to its original size.
Luòshuǐ Ox
In the autumn of the fourth year of the Xiántōng era,
a great flood occurred in Luòyáng,
submerging gardens, parks, houses, and huts
without exception.
Later, monks from Xiāngshān Temple said:
"That day, as dusk approached,
we saw torrential rainwaters flowing down from the north of Lóngmén Chuān,
like a bursting sea or a collapsing river.
Amidst the roaring fury,
the sound was like thunder.
Two black oxen on the water waved their tails and leaped through the air as they advanced.
The monks and residents watched from high ground,
thinking the entire city would become a place for fish.
Suddenly, they saw the Dìngdǐng and Chángxià city gates open darkly,
and two green oxen charged out bravely,
about a hundred paces apart,
and the black oxen turned and fled.
The raging waves and terrifying surges
immediately subsided."
Huán Chōng
Huán Chōng was stationed in Jiānglíng.
During the New Year's gathering,
a cow was about to be slaughtered.
Suddenly, the cow stared intently at the commander under the tent,
tears streaming from its eyes.
The commander swore to it:
"If you kneel to me,
I will plead to spare your life."
The cow immediately knelt and bowed.
Everyone found this strange.
The commander then said:
"If you truly wish to live,
bow to everyone here."
The cow wept profusely,
and proceeded to bow to everyone.
However, Huán Chōng was drunk at the time,
so the plea could not be presented.
Thus, the cow was killed.
When Huán Chōng learned of this,
he became furious with the commander
and severely punished him with whipping.
The Butcher of the Imperial Kitchen
During the Tàihé era,
the imperial kitchen intended to slaughter a female cow.
The cow was pregnant,
and due to give birth soon.
Someone said:
"Since this is the case,
it could be replaced."
But the butcher took his knife and advanced directly,
showing no concern at all.
The cow then knelt and bowed to him,
but he still refused to back down.
This cow and its calf
thus perished under the knife.
The butcher suddenly went mad and lost his senses,
mooing like a cow every day,
eating a little grass,
plunging his body into mud and water,
and butting his head against objects,
only calming down after a long while.
The Zhū Family Son
In Guǎnglíng, there was a son of the Zhū family,
whose family had a long history of military distinction and nobility.
He had a fondness for eating yellow cattle,
and had killed countless of them.
Once during the summer,
he intended to slaughter a cow.
His mother stopped him, saying:
"It's so hot,
and you're already drunk.
How much can you eat?
Don't kill it."
The son then said to the cow:
"If you can bow to me,
I will spare you."
The cow immediately shed tears and bowed.
Zhū, however, became angry and said:
"How can a beast understand human speech!"
He immediately killed it.
A few days later, he fell ill,
constantly haunted by the cow's vengeful spirit,
and eventually died while making cow-like sounds.
Biàn Shìyú
There was a man named Biàn Shìyú.
His father, due to his achievements in pacifying Chén,
was granted the title of Yítóng.
He was stingy.
Once, he hired laborers to build a house,
but did not pay them their wages.
When the laborers demanded payment,
Biàn's father whipped them and said:
"If I truly owe you money,
after I die,
I will become an ox for you."
Shortly after,
Biàn's father died.
One of the laborers had an ox that gave birth to a yellow calf,
with black markings under its waist,
encircling it horizontally,
like a human belt.
On its right flank, there were white stripes slanting across,
exactly the size and shape of a court tablet.
The ox's owner called out to it:
"Lord Biàn,
why do you owe me?"
The calf immediately bent its front knees
and lowered its head to the ground.
Shìyú offered one hundred thousand coins to redeem it,
but the owner refused.
Only after the calf died did Shìyú retrieve and bury it.
Lù Bódá
During the Yǒnghuī era,
there was a man named Lù Bódá from Yì County, Fénzhōu,
who owed a fellow villager one thousand coins.
Later, he made an oath before a Buddha statue with the creditor:
"If I do not repay you,
after I die,
I will become an ox for your family."
After speaking these words,
he died the following year.
The creditor's family cow gave birth to a calf,
with white hair on its forehead
forming the three characters "Lù Bódá."
His sons and nephews felt ashamed of this,
and offered five thousand coins to redeem it,
but the owner refused to give it up.
Instead, the owner donated it to the monk Zhēnrú of the Qǐfú Temple in Xíchéng County,
to aid in the construction of a fifteen-story pagoda.
Those who saw it
were moved to repent of their evil deeds,
and competed to donate money and goods
as offerings.
Dài Wén
During the Zhēnyuán era,
in Hǎiyán County, Sūzhōu, there was a man named Dài Wén,
who was wealthy but greedy.
Whenever villagers borrowed money from him,
he would demand several times the interest.
A neighbor once engaged in a financial transaction with him,
and was exploited excessively.
The neighbor harbored deep resentment,
and said:
"Surely the gods will bear witness."
Several years later,
Dài Wén died of illness.
The neighbor's cow gave birth to a black calf,
with white hair under its flank,
forming the characters "Dài Wén."
Everyone in the village knew about it.
Dài Wén's son felt ashamed,
so he asked the neighbor to use an iron to erase the characters,
and the neighbor agreed.
Afterward, Dài Wén's son, seeing no evidence on the calf's body,
sued the neighbor,
accusing him of falsely claiming the calf had characters.
When the county authorities summoned the neighbor and the calf,
the white hair reappeared,
clearly forming the characters.
Moreover, when "Dài Wén" was called,
the calf would respond and come.
Fearing that Dài Wén's son might steal the calf,
the neighbor locked it in a separate stable at night.
It lived for several more years before dying.
Cui Shǒu of Hénèi
There was a man named Cuī,
who served as the governor of Hénèi during the Zhēnyuán era.
Cuī was greedy and harsh,
and the people of Hénèi suffered under him.
He once borrowed gold from a Buddha statue in a temple,
amounting to several yì,
but never repaid it.
The monks, because he was the governor,
did not dare to speak up.
Not long after,
Cuī died in the commandery.
On that very day,
a cow in the temple gave birth to a calf,
with white hair on its head,
forming characters that read "Cuī Mǒu."
The temple monks gathered to look at it,
and sighed, saying:
"Cuī often borrowed gold from the Buddha statue in this temple,
but never repaid it.
Today's event—
what does it signify?"
When Cuī's family heard of this,
they exchanged another ox for the calf.
Once it arrived,
they ordered the characters to be shaved off,
but they grew back.
Even after being brought to their home,
though fed with fodder and grain,
it refused to eat.
The Cuī family, finding this strange,
eventually returned it to the temple.
Old Lady Wáng
In Guǎnglíng, there was an old woman of the Wáng family,
who fell ill for several days.
Suddenly she said to her son:
"When I die,
I will surely be reborn as an ox in the Hào family of Xīxī.
You must seek me out and redeem me.
I will have the character 'Wáng' on my belly."
Soon after, she passed away.
Xīxī
is a place name west of Hǎilíng.
Among the people there, the Hào family had an ox
with white hair on its belly
forming the character 'Wáng'.
Her son sought it out and found it,
redeemed it with a bundle of silk, and took it away.
Shào Táogēn
At the end of the Liáng dynasty,
Shào Táogēn,
a man from Xiāngyáng,
had a calf at home
that was plump and adorable.
Táogēn always fed it himself.
This calf would often follow Táogēn when he went out.
Whenever Táogēn went to official gatherings,
even though the calf was tied up at home,
it would roar and cry incessantly.
One day later,
when Táogēn got up in the morning and opened the door,
the calf suddenly charged at him from behind,
piercing his ribs and causing him to bleed.
The whole family drove it away,
but it glared angrily again,
charged once more and injured him,
and after a few days, Táogēn died.
A man from Luòxià
During the Xiāntiān era of the Táng dynasty,
a man from Luòxià led an ox
with a human hand over a foot long under its armpit,
going from street to street begging.
Nìng Yīn
During the Dàzhōng era,
there was a scholar named Nìng Yīn who borrowed the estate of a high official at the foot of the Southern Mountains.
Half the beams and rafters had collapsed,
and the walls were also broken.
One night, with the wind clear and the moon bright,
he was reciting poetry in the courtyard.
Suddenly, he heard a knock at the door,
and someone announced himself as the retired scholar Bān Tè from Táolín.
Yīn opened the gate
and saw that the retired scholar had a majestic appearance
and spoke in a grand manner.
He said:
"I am a man of the fields,
one who toils with his strength.
I labor diligently in the furrows and acres,
sharing the lot of the farmers.
My dwelling is nearby,
and I saw the wind and moon were pure and bright.
Hearing your recitation,
I have come to pay my respects."
Yīn said:
"My abode here in the mountains is very remote,
neighboring only farm tools.
The thatch and brambles are deep,
and carriage wheels and hoofprints rarely reach here.
I am fortunate by your visit,
which greatly comforts my lonely heart."
He then invited him in.
He spoke, saying:
"But what is your profession, retired scholar?
I wish to hear about it."
Tè said:
"In my youth,
my brothers and I all strove to show our prowess.
Whenever I read in the *Spring and Autumn Annals* about Yǐng Kǎoshū grasping the chariot pole and running,
I regretted not being able to assist in such a feat.
Reading the *Records of the Grand Historian* about Tián Dān's strategy to defeat Yān,
I regretted not being able to join the fierce battle.
Reading about the Eastern Hàn, specifically the battle at Xīnyě,
I regretted not being able to leap into action there.
These three events were all exhilarating,
yet I encountered none of them,
and now I am filled with regret.
Now I am old and declining,
and I have no heir,
left only with the sorrow of licking my calf in vain.
Moreover, I admire Xú Rúzǐ's words of condolence to Guō Línzōng:
'A bundle of fresh grass,
the man is like jade.'
'The man is like jade'—
that I dare not claim.
But 'a bundle of fresh grass'—
that is worthy of contemplation and savoring."
Suddenly, they heard another knock at the gate, saying:
"General Bān Yín of the Southern Mountains pays his respects."
Yīn then invited him in.
His bearing was stern and imposing,
and his demeanor was fierce and bold.
When the two Bāns met,
they were also very pleased.
Yín said:
"Elder brother, do you know the origin of our surname?"
Tè said:
"Long ago, Wú Tàibó went among the barbarians of Jīng,
cut his hair and tattooed his body,
and from this, the surname Bān arose."
Yín said:
"Elder brother, you are greatly mistaken,
and clearly do not know the true origin.
The Bān clan descends from Dòu Gòu Wūtú,
who had markings like stripes,
hence the clan was named. Our distant ancestors Bān Gù and the Lady Bān
were fond of literature,
and were highly praised in the Hàn court,
and both have biographies in the histories.
Since then, heroes have arisen generation after generation,
continuing without break.
In the Later Hàn, there was Bān Chāo, who cast aside his brush to join the army.
A physiognomist said to him:
'You will be enfeoffed as a marquis ten thousand *lǐ* away.'
Chāo asked him why,
and he said:
'You have the jaw of a swallow and the head of a tiger;
you will fly afar to feast on meat—
the mark of a duke or marquis.'
Later, he indeed guarded the Yùmén Pass
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dìngyuǎn.
I, for generations, have served as a military officer,
in the military ranks.
Due to some offense,
I was exiled to the mountains and forests.
I hide by day and wander by night,
concealing my tracks and form,
merely clinging to life.
Just now, hearing the pines sighing under the high moon,
I was strolling idly outside the wall
and heard your recitation,
so I came to pay my respects.
Moreover, meeting a clansman
adds even more to my joy."
Yín then noticed a chessboard on the bed
and said to Tè:
"I wish to play a game with you, elder brother."
Tè happily agreed.
After a long while,
there was still no winner or loser.
Yīn, watching them,
taught Tè a move or two.
Yín said:
"Could it be that our host is a master player?"
Yīn said:
"It is like looking at a leopard through a tube—
one only sees a spot now and then."
The two Bāns laughed and said:
"There is great subtlety in that,
truly hitting two targets with one shot."
Yīn poured wine and offered them a drink.
When the game ended and they drank,
after several rounds,
Yín asked to prepare dried meat to accompany the wine.
Yīn set out venison jerky.
Yín bit and tore at it,
finishing it in no time.
But Tè did not eat any.
Yīn asked him:
"Why do you not eat?"
Tè said:
"I have no upper teeth,
so I cannot chew, you see."
After several more rounds,
Tè claimed a slight ailment
and dared not drink too much.
Yín said:
"Easier said than done!
With wine as abundant as the Shéng River,
one could learn from King Zhòu to drink all night long,
yet you feel your face already flushed."
Tè said:
"Younger brother truly belongs to a family of bronze cauldrons and tripods,
able to sit and indulge without moving."
Later, as the two Bāns drank more,
their words became tangled and contentious.
Tè said:
"Younger brother, relying on being a warrior with claws and fangs,
why do you insist on bullying me so?"
Tè said:
"Younger brother boasts of his fierce and sturdy body,
but if you met someone like Biàn Zhuāngzǐ,
you would be turned to powder."
Yín said:
"Elder brother boasts of his mighty and brave strength,
but if you met someone like Páodīng,
you would be nothing but a scalp."
Before Yīn lay a meat-slicing knife,
over a foot long.
Yīn angrily said:
"Old Nìng here has a foot-long blade.
You two guests must not clamor and fight,
but just drink wine!"
The two guests were alarmed.
Tè then recited a poem by Cáo Zhí:
"The beanstalk burns beneath the pot,
the beans weep within the pot.
This couplet is quite good."
Yín said:
"There is a vulgar saying:
'The turtledove calls from the tree,
but its mind is on the hemp field.'"
They all laughed heartily.
Yīn said:
"No more words.
Let each of you compose a stanza of poetry."
Yīn said:
"At dawn I read, clouds and water still;
at night I chant, the mountain moon high.
How could I tread on a tiger's tail?
Why need I learn the butcher's knife?"
Yín followed with:
"If only I can howl in the woods,
how could I crouch upon the road?
Crossing the river, where should I go?
In the end, I fear Liú Kūn."
Tè said:
"It is none other than mourning Nìng Qì,
in the end, fearing Páodīng.
If I met Gǒng as the governor,
a hoof-print puddle would head for the Northern Sea."
Yīn read them and said:
"Truly extraordinary talent."
Yín grew angry,
flicked his sleeves, stood up and said:
"How can Nìng side with such a fellow!
Since ancient times, there has been the talent of Bān and Mǎ,
but never the talent of a 'spotted ox.'
Moreover, three days after I was born,
I already wanted to devour people.
This fellow even steals my surname,
but I simply cannot converse with him, for it is abhorrent to injure one's own kind!"
He then angrily said:
"I will never wag my tail at your gate like a dog,
so I shall take my leave with a deep bow."
Tè also angrily said:
"The ancients valued white eyebrows,
but you now have a white forehead—
how dare anyone praise you?
Why are you so angry?"
Tè then bid farewell.
By dawn,
looking outside his gate,
there were only tiger tracks and ox footprints.
Níng Shēng then realized,
and searched for several hundred paces,
finding in an abandoned estate of a household
an old ox lying down,
still reeking of alcohol.
The tiger had already entered the mountains.
Yīn later no longer lived there and returned to the capital.
Zhòng Xiǎoxiǎo
In the region of Líntáo,
there was a mountain dweller named Zhòng Xiǎoxiǎo,
called by the people Zhòng Yěniú.
He made his living by hunting and gathering.
West of Líntáo,
reaching the areas of Diédàng, Bōmín,
several prefectures of fertile farmland,
since the time of Lùshān,
had fallen into desolation.
Among them, many bamboo oxen were produced,
their color pure black,
one of them could match six or seven camels,
with meat weighing over ten million catties.
Their horns,
two strong men could carry one.
Wherever they drank and grazed,
the arched trees and dense bamboo
were trampled into dust.
Hunters first set fires to drive them,
waiting for them to flee,
then poisoned their arrows,
and shot at the opportune moment.
Once hit by the arrow,
they would take their pots and pans,
carry dry rations,
follow their tracks,
and slowly pursue them.
Once the arrow poison took effect,
they would die.
Fallen like mountains,
piled meat like mounds.
One ox obtained,
meat worth several thousand gold,
the fresh ones very delicious,
the strands like red silk thread.
During the Gānníng era,
Xiǎoxiǎo, while hunting,
encountered a herd of oxen at Shíjiā Mountain,
and urged his dogs to chase them.
The oxen panicked,
fleeing into a deep valley.
At the end of the valley,
southward reaching a cliff.
With the dogs chasing urgently,
the oxen pushed against each other.
The one at the front
lost its footing and fell off the cliff;
the one behind it,
unaware its companion had fallen,
followed closely one after another,
thirty-six heads,
all perished at the foot of the cliff.
The piled meat was beyond measure,
the people of Qín, Chéng, and Jiē prefectures
could not carry it all even with shoulder poles.
Horses
Horses, among the Hùlán horses of the northern tribes,
are five white horses,
also called jade-faced.
Zhēnzhēn horses,
are thirteen-year-old horses.
Those under thirteen years old
can be kept for breeding.
Horses are eight feet tall.
Warhorses are eight feet,
field horses are seven feet,
inferior horses are six feet.
In Guāzhōu, horses are fed píng grass,
in Shāzhōu, with cíqí,
in Liángzhōu, with bótūhún,
in Shǔ, with bài grass.
Feeding horses with radish roots,
makes them fat.
In Ānběi, horses are fed shāpéng and lángzhēn.
In the Dàshíguó, there are horses that understand human speech.
Xīdáguó and Dágànguó produce fine horses.
Horses at four years old have two teeth,
by twenty years old,
their teeth are completely flat.
Body parts include shūshǔ wàifú, wūtóulóng, chìhǔkǒu.
Feeding horses from a pig trough,
coating the trough with lime mud,
tying them at the gate while sweating,
these three things cause foals to be lost.
Curly hair on the neck,
white horses with black markings,
curly hair under the saddle or in the armpits.
White hair on the flanks,
white on the left and right hind feet,
white horses with four black feet,
horizontal hair under the eyes,
yellow horses with white muzzles,
whorled hair on the lips,
sweat grooves on the back connecting to the base of the tail,
red eyes, disordered eyelashes, or inverted eyelashes,
white horses with black eyes,
eyes with white sclera looking backward,
all are unsuitable for riding.
The night eye is called fùchán,
the hùgān is called xuánfēng,
also called jīshé.
According to the Lǜzhì dialect,
feeding with dìhuáng and gāncǎo,
a fifty-year-old horse can give birth to three foals.
On the sunny side of Bōshàn Mountain in Tǔhuǒluóguó,
there is a hole in the stone wall,
from which horse urine constantly flows.
By the seventh month at dawn,
there is a stone walkway between the cliffs,
then it disappears.
On this day,
the Yàndā people take mares
and place them by the pool to mate,
the foals born are all sweat-blood horses,
able to travel a thousand lǐ in a day.
Now called Wúshù Pōlí,
they bathe in the Western Regions,
and return in a moment.
Records say:
North of Tǔhuǒluóguó,
there is the Wūshù Pōlí Mountain,
which is the Bōshàn Mountain mentioned by Sòng Yún.
In the cave of the southern cliff,
divine horse dung flows out.
The merchant Hú Cáo Bōbì witnessed it personally.
Yùmǎ Gǎng,
is a branch of the Shū River.
In the Hàn Dynasty,
often several hundred horses emerged from it.
The horses were all small in shape,
resembling Bā Diān horses,
so the hole was named Mǎxué.
When these horses were first obtained,
they were ridden out to bathe in the Miǎn River,
so the place was named Yùmǎ Gài.
Staying overnight at Miǎn,
now called Qítíng.
During the Three Kingdoms period,
when Lù Xùn attacked Xiāngyáng,
again ten horses from this hole appeared,
and Xùn transported them back to Jiànyè.
During the reign of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
Wáng Fù of Shǔ Commandery was the Grand Administrator of Yìzhōu,
and his governance was particularly exceptional.
Four divine horses
emerged from the Diānchí River.
In the fifth year of Wǔdé of the Táng Dynasty, in the third month,
west of the seat of Jǐnggǔ County,
in the water was a dragon horse,
its body eight or nine feet long,
dragon-shaped,
with scales and armor,
horizontal patterns in five colors,
dragon body with a horse head,
two horns on its head,
white in color,
holding something in its mouth,
about three or four feet long.
It rode the waves, looking back,
and disappeared after over a hundred paces.
North of Xīlíng,
traveling thirty lǐ by land,
there is a stone cave called Mǎxué,
from which a white horse often emerges.
When people chase it,
it secretly travels to Hànzhōng.
When people in Hànzhōng lose horses,
they also emerge from this cave,
separated by several thousand lǐ.
Now Mǎxué Mountain is in Yílíng, Xiázhōu.
King Mù of Zhōu's Eight Steeds
In the thirty-second year of his reign, King Mù of the Zhōu dynasty,
toured the world,
driving eight dragon-horses.
The first was named Juédì,
whose feet never touched the earth;
the second, Fānyǔ,
could outrun flying birds;
the third, Bēnxiāo,
could travel ten thousand lǐ in a night;
the fourth, Yuèyǐng,
could chase the sun;
the fifth, Yúhuī,
had brilliantly shining fur;
the sixth, Chāoguāng,
cast ten shadows from a single form;
the seventh, Téngwù,
galloped upon clouds;
the eighth, Xiéyì,
had fleshy wings on its body.
He harnessed them all,
held the reins and proceeded leisurely,
to tour the territories of the world.
King Mù, with his divine wisdom and far-reaching plans,
ensured his chariot tracks covered all four seas.
Thus, the creatures of the remotest lands,
submitted of their own accord without being summoned.
The Nine Steeds of Emperor Wén of Hàn
When Emperor Wén of Hàn returned from Dài,
he had nine fine horses,
all exceptional steeds of the world.
The first was named Fúyún,
the second Chìdiàn,
the third Juéqún,
the fourth Yìbiāo,
the fifth Zǐyànliú,
the sixth Lǜchīcōng,
the seventh Lóngzǐ,
the eighth Línjū,
the ninth Juéchén,
collectively known as the Nine Steeds.
There was a man named Lái Xuān who could drive horses,
and the King of Dài hailed him as Wáng Liáng.
Emperor Wén of Suí's Lion Steed
During the reign of Emperor Wén of Suí,
the state of Dàyuān presented a thousand-lǐ horse,
its mane dragging on the ground,
named the Lion Steed.
The emperor placed it among the horse herd,
where it rampaged,
and no one could control it.
The emperor ordered it to be driven along with the herd,
and asked his attendants:
"Who can tame it?"
Commandant Péi Rénjī said:
"Your servant can control it."
He then rolled up his sleeves and stepped forward,
standing more than ten paces away,
leapt up,
grabbed one ear with one hand,
and poked its eyes with the other,
the horse trembled and dared not move,
so he saddled and mounted it.
Departing from Xījīng in the morning,
he reached Dōngluò by evening.
Later, during the Suí dynasty's decline, its whereabouts became unknown,
and Emperor Táng Wénwǔ Shèng ordered a nationwide search for it.
Prefect Yǔwén Shìjí of Tóngzhōu found the horse,
aged and working at a noodle shop in Cháoyì market,
pulling a millstone,
its tail scorched and bald,
its skin and flesh pierced with holes.
Upon seeing it, he wept with sorrow.
The emperor personally went to Chánglè Slope,
and when the horse reached Xīnfēng,
it neighed and pranced toward the west.
The emperor was overjoyed to obtain it,
its teeth and mouth both worn smooth.
Fed with stalactite milk,
it later gave birth to five foals,
all capable of traveling a thousand lǐ.
Later, its whereabouts became unknown again.
Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng's Dragon Horse
Between the sea and Mount Tài,
a mysterious yellow stone was produced.
Some said
that consuming it could grant longevity.
Emperor Xuánzōng once ordered the governor of Línzī
to gather and present it annually.
In the twenty-seventh year of the Kāiyuán era,
Lǐ Yōng of Jiāngxià served as governor of Línzī.
That autumn,
while entering the mountains to gather the mysterious yellow stone,
he suddenly encountered an old man,
of exquisite demeanor,
with a bright and elegant bearing,
and an extremely full beard.
Clad in coarse clothing,
he emerged from the left side of the road,
and stopped Lǐ Yōng's horse.
He then said:
"My lord, you personally gather herbs—
is it not to prolong the sage ruler's life?"
Lǐ Yōng replied:
"Indeed."
The old man said:
"The sage ruler shall obtain a dragon horse,
then reign for ten thousand years—
there is no need to labor gathering herbs."
Lǐ Yōng asked:
"Where is the dragon horse?"
He answered:
"It should be in the outskirts of Qí and Lǔ.
If obtained,
it will be an omen of peace,
surpassing even the auspiciousness of
the qílín, phoenix, turtle, and dragon."
As Lǐ Yōng ordered his carriage to bring the old man along,
he suddenly vanished from sight.
Lǐ Yōng was greatly astonished,
and turning to his attendants, said:
"Could he be a divine being?"
He then ordered his subordinate Wáng Qiánzhēn
to search for the dragon horse between Qí and Lǔ.
By the summer, fifth month of the twenty-ninth year of Kāiyuán,
Qiánzhēn indeed found the horse at the home of a commoner named Mǎ Huì'ēn in Běihǎi Commandery.
Its coat was piebald,
with scales on both flanks,
its mane and tail like a dragon's fins and crest,
its neighing truly resembling the sound of a xūzhōu,
and it could gallop three hundred lǐ a day.
Qiánzhēn inquired about its origin,
and Huì'ēn said:
"I had only a mare,
which often bathed in the Zī River,
and thus conceived and gave birth.
So I called it 'dragon's offspring.'"
Qiánzhēn reported this to Lǐ Yōng,
who was greatly pleased,
and submitted a memorial detailing the matter to present it.
The emperor was overjoyed,
ordering the imperial stables to provide exceptional fodder,
and commanded painters to depict its form,
to be displayed throughout the court and beyond.
Emperor Dàizōng's Nine-Flowered Qiú
Emperor Dàizōng ordered the imperial horse Nine-Flowered Qiú, along with purple jade bridle and whip,
to be bestowed upon Guō Zǐyí.
Zǐyí firmly declined for a long time.
The emperor said:
"This horse is tall and large,
suited to your dignified bearing—
there is no need to decline."
Zǐyí was six feet eight inches tall.
The Nine-Flowered Qiú
was presented by Lǐ Huáixiān, military governor of Fànyáng.
Its forehead was nine feet high,
its fur curled like scales,
its head, neck, mane, and crest
truly resembled a qiú dragon.
Each time it neighed,
the other horses would prick up their ears.
As its body was adorned with nine flowers,
it was named Nine-Flowered Qiú.
Once, the emperor traveled east,
observing a hunt in the fields,
and unaware, dusk fell.
Suddenly, he turned to his attendants and asked:
"How many lǐ is the traveling palace from here?"
They replied:
"Forty lǐ."
The emperor ordered a swift whip,
fearing the hindrance of night.
Yet the Nine-Flowered Qiú moved gently,
as if covering only three to five lǐ,
while the attendants galloped frantically,
unable to keep up.
Emperor Dézōng's Divine-Wisdom Steed
When Emperor Dézōng traveled west,
he had two horses,
one named Shénzhì Cōng,
and the other named Rúyì Liú.
Both perfectly suited the emperor's wishes,
so he often called them his "meritorious ministers."
They had hair inside their ears,
which could be pulled out to a length of one chǐ.
The Classic of Horses states:
"Horses with hair inside their ears
can travel a thousand lǐ in a day."
One day, during the blooming spring of flowers and willows,
the emperor went on an excursion to the various imperial gardens.
An attendant presented an auspicious whip,
and the emperor pointed to the two horses and said to his close ministers:
"In the past, when I traveled west,
I had two fine steeds,
which were called the 'two marvels.'
Now that I have obtained this whip,
it can be called the 'three marvels.'"
He then ordered wine to be served and drank.
Thereupon, he chanted:
"The mandarin ducks, reddish-white, with teeth newly even,
At dawn, flowers bloom, scattering emerald hooves.
The jade bridle turns, first spraying foam,
The golden whip about to descend, yet no neigh is made."
This was a poem by Hán Hóng, the Secretariat Drafter.
When Emperor Dézōng traveled to Liángyáng,
he only rode a piebald horse,
named Wàngyún Zhuī.
Upon the emperor's return,
it was fed with the highest-grade fodder.
On leisurely days, when led out for viewing,
it would always let out a long neigh and look around in all directions,
as if expressing gratitude.
Later, it grew old and died in the Flying Dragon Stable,
and the noble relatives all made paintings of it.
Cáo Hóng
Cáo Hóng of Wèi,
a cousin of Emperor Wǔ,
had a household overflowing with property and estates,
and herds of fine horses.
When Emperor Wǔ campaigned against Dǒng Zhuó,
he lost his horse while traveling at night.
Cáo Hóng gave the horse he was riding, named White Crane,
to Emperor Wǔ to ride.
When this horse ran,
one only felt the sound of wind in the ears,
as if its hooves did not touch the ground.
When they reached deep water,
Cáo Hóng could not cross.
Emperor Wǔ pulled Cáo Hóng onto the horse,
and together they crossed the deep water.
They traveled several hundred lǐ,
arriving in the blink of an eye.
Looking down at the horse's hooves,
the hair was still wet,
and the emperor's clothes were also damp.
People at the time said it was like riding the wind,
and it was considered a divine steed of its generation.
A proverb says:
"Leaping through the empty void,
the Cáo family's White Crane."
Sīmǎ Xiūzhī
When Sīmǎ Xiūzhī of Jìn was in Jīngzhōu,
Duke Sòng sent envoys to besiege him.
Xiūzhī was unaware of this.
The horse he usually rode,
which was kept in front of his bed,
staring fixedly at the saddle.
Xiūzhī tried to saddle it,
but it refused to move.
After saddling it and returning to his seat,
the horse again startled and jumped.
This happened three or four times.
He then mounted the horse and swiftly rode out the gate,
galloping for several lǐ.
Looking back,
Xiūzhī saw that envoys had already arrived.
Thus, he escaped and avoided capture.
Mùróng Huī
Mùróng Huī initially had a reddish-white horse,
which he often rode himself.
When he was besieged by Shí Hǔ,
his forces were weak,
and the situation was critical,
he abandoned his troops and prepared to flee.
He tried to saddle this horse for escape,
but when the horse saw the saddle,
it kicked and bit, making it impossible to approach,
so he stopped.
Soon after, an envoy from Yè arrived,
reporting that Shí Hǔ's state was in trouble,
and Hǔ hastily returned.
By this time,
the horse was forty-nine years old.
Qín Shūbǎo
The horse ridden by Táng's Qín Shūbǎo
was named Hūléi Bó.
It was often given wine to drink.
Whenever tested under the bright moon,
it could leap vertically over three layers of black felt.
When Lord Hú (Qín Shūbǎo) died,
the horse neighed, refused to eat, and died.
Zhāng Nàzhī
Zhāng Nàzhī, the Prefect of Dézhōu,
had a white horse,
its color like white silk.
His father, Zhāng Xióng, served as Prefect of several prefectures
and often rode it.
When Xióng passed away,
his son, Jìngzhī, who was a Director of the Bureau of Evaluations,
was reassigned as Prefect of Shòuzhōu
and also rode this horse.
When Jìngzhī passed away,
his younger brother, Nàzhī,
went from being a Supervising Secretary and Military Administrator of the Chancellor's Office to Prefect of Dézhōu,
then entered the court as Director of the Imperial Academy,
and later served as Prefect of Chángzhōu.
The horse is still alive to this day,
estimated to be over eighty years old,
extremely robust and healthy,
running swiftly,
with steady hooves.
Sòng Cài
Sòng Cài of Guǎngpíng married a woman from the same commandery, Yóu Chāng's daughter.
Cài's ancestors were of Hú descent,
but they had returned to Hàn for three generations.
Suddenly, they had a son,
with deep-set eyes and a high nose.
Cài suspected the child was not his own,
and was about to abandon him.
Shortly after,
a red mare gave birth to a white foal.
Cài realized and said:
"My family once had a white horse,
but the lineage ended twenty-five years ago.
Now it has been reborn.
My great-grandfather had Hú features,
and now this child has restored our ancestors' appearance."
Thus, he raised the child.
Hence the saying, "The white horse revived the Hú child,"
refers to this.
Dancing Horses
Emperor Xuánzōng once ordered the training of four hundred dancing horses,
each divided into left and right groups.
They were organized into sections,
and designated as the favorites or the prized possessions of certain families.
At that time, there were also excellent horses from beyond the frontier that were presented as tribute,
and the emperor had them trained as well,
all of which mastered the art perfectly.
He then ordered them to be dressed in embroidered silks,
adorned with gold and silver trappings,
their manes and tails decorated,
interspersed with pearls and jade.
The music they danced to, called "Qīngbēi Lè," was performed dozens of times,
with the horses raising their heads and wagging their tails,
moving back and forth in perfect rhythm.
A three-tiered wooden platform was also set up,
and the horses would mount it,
spinning around as if flying.
Sometimes, strong men were ordered to lift a couch,
