and the horses would dance upon it.
Several musicians stood to the left, right, front, and back,
all dressed in light yellow robes,
with patterned jade belts,
selected specifically for their youthful and handsome appearances.
Every year on the Qiānqiū Festival,
they were ordered to perform beneath the Qínzhèng Tower.
Later, after the emperor fled to Shǔ,
the dancing horses were scattered among the people.
Ān Lùshān had often witnessed their performances and admired them greatly.
Consequently, several of them were sold to Fànyáng.
Later, they came into the possession of Tián Chéngsì,
though he was unaware of their identity.
He mixed them among his warhorses
and placed them in the outer stables.
One day,
during a feast for the troops,
music began to play,
and the horses could not help but dance.
The stable hands all thought they were possessed by demons,
and they rushed to beat them with brooms.
The horses, thinking their dance was not in rhythm,
adjusted their movements with rising and falling cadences,
still retaining their former grace.
The stable attendants quickly reported the strange behavior of the horses.
Chéngsì ordered them to be whipped,
and the punishment was severe.
The horses danced even more orderly,
yet the whipping intensified,
until they eventually died beneath the stable rafters.
Some people at the time knew they were dancing horses,
but fearing violence, they never dared to speak of it.
Xù Kūn
During the Xiántōng and Qiánfú eras,
a capital physician named Xù Kūn was quite skilled in the art of Qín physician Hé,
able to discern fortune and misfortune by feeling the pulse,
and even predict gains and losses
with accuracy.
It happened that a general from Yān, who had come to report to the court, suddenly fell ill with a wind disease,
and after taking medicine, he recovered.
He rewarded Kūn with a great deal of silk,
and also left a border horse as a gift.
The horse’s bone structure was quite unusual,
but its gait was often stumbling.
Even with bit and bridle,
and the addition of whip and spur,
its sluggish nature
could not be changed.
Kūn, considering it a waste of fodder,
entrusted someone to sell it at a low price.
Those seeking fine horses would test it,
only to find it still the same,
and for months it remained unsold.
A neighbor named Wáng Shēng,
who traded with the households of powerful eunuchs,
was quite impoverished.
He suddenly came to Kūn and said:
"A supervisor from Qīngzhōu is about to depart,
and needs a saddled horse for his luggage.
I know it is not a swift steed,
but it will suffice for leading and controlling."
Kūn simply handed over the useless animal,
without even setting a price for the sale.
After this, Wáng did not return for over ten days,
and Kūn thought the horse had been lost or had run away.
One day, Wáng returned,
and the payment he brought exceeded one hundred thousand.
Kūn, having received such a good price,
gave ten thousand to Wáng.
Soon after, he saw Wáng Shēng
change his clothes,
acquire servants and horses,
and even his wife and children’s attire
became bright and clean.
Some said:
"Wáng Shēng sold the horse,
and obtained both gold and silk,
totaling three or four million."
Kūn was greatly surprised,
and tried to inquire about the matter.
At first, Wáng Shēng did not explain fully.
Kūn said:
"I received a considerable price for a useless thing,
but I do not understand how such an inferior creature
could be worth so much."
Wáng replied:
"Initially, I delivered the horse to the supervisor from Qīngshè,
but it lifted its feet as if hindered.
As I was about to return,
I encountered a palace eunuch from the small horse stable along the way,
who asked to keep the horse for a trial.
After staying for two nights, I went back,
but the horse was no longer there.
I secretly inquired among the attendants,
and learned that a few days earlier,
Wèibó had presented a horse,
with hair, bones, and size identical to this one.
The emperor often rode it for polo,
and its excellence was unmatched.
On the day it arrived,
they began training its gait,
and it moved with swirling speed like the wind.
Now, after being presented to the court for several days,
the rewards given were exceedingly generous."
Later, Wáng Shēng demanded a high price,
and was compensated with four million.
Thus, even objects have their destined time,
and if they do not meet the right master,
the difference between a nag and a steed cannot be discerned.
This shows that tilling the fields at Shēn Yě
or building walls at Fù Yán,
without encountering the right path,
is no different from this.
Yáng Wēngfó
In Hàn times, Yáng Wēngfó of Guǎnglíng could understand the sounds of birds and beasts.
Riding a lame donkey in the countryside,
he saw a one-eyed horse grazing in the fields.
They were some distance apart,
but their calls could be heard.
Wēngfó said to his driver,
"That grazing horse is blind in one eye."
The driver asked:
"How do you know?"
He replied:
"It called the horse in our carriage 'lame,'
and this horse called it 'one-eyed.'"
The driver did not believe him,
so he went to look,
and indeed the horse was blind in one eye.
Jì Nán
Jì Nán was riding a red horse when
he encountered someone riding a white horse.
The white horse neighed first,
and the red horse responded.
Nán said to his attendant:
"The white horse says,
'You, in the south, will see a yellow horse
with a blind left eye.
It is my foal,
so tell it to hurry and catch up.'"
A moment later,
they indeed encountered a blind yellow horse.
The white horse neighed first,
and the blind horse responded.
Zhào Gù
In Jìn times, the horse ridden by Zhào Gù suddenly died,
so he consulted Guō Pú.
Pú said:
"Send several dozen men
with bamboo poles eastward for thirty lǐ.
Where there are hills, forests, and trees,
have them beat around,
and a creature will emerge.
Quickly seize it and bring it back."
They followed Pú’s instructions,
and indeed captured a creature resembling a monkey.
When it entered the gate,
it saw the dead horse,
leaped about,
ran to the horse’s head,
and breathed into its nostrils.
The horse immediately revived.
The monkey was never seen again.
Hán Xī
In the Táng dynasty, Hán Xī once served as the administrator of the Yǒngfēng Granary.
He had a horse,
which he had ridden for a long time.
Once, a traveler passed by with a horse from Shǔ,
which bit quite fiercely.
Hán Xī ordered it to be brought over,
and tied it to a tree in the courtyard.
Hán Xī said to the traveler:
"This small horse,
how could it be so fierce?
But it must also be disciplined harshly."
Hán Xī had a stableman skilled in taming unruly horses,
so he immediately summoned him,
and had him fetch a whip and bridle.
This horse glared fiercely,
squinting sideways at Hán Xī.
Suddenly, it broke free from the reins and rushed up the steps,
knocking Hán Xī off his seat,
bending its knees to the ground,
and was about to bite him.
At that time, the horse Hán Xī usually rode
was tied to another post.
Seeing this,
it also broke free from its reins,
and came to bite this horse.
After biting it several times,
Hán Xī was finally spared.
Everyone bought this horse,
killed it, and ate it.
From then on, Hán Xī cherished his own horse even more.
The Horse of a Traveler from Jiāngdōng
Some years ago,
there was a traveler from Jiāngdōng
who often rode a horse,
which had a rather stubborn temperament.
The traveler once got very drunk at a drinking place,
and rode the horse alone halfway home,
where, heavily intoxicated,
he leaned against a tree while on horseback and fell asleep,
remaining motionless for a long time,
until the fifth watch.
His servant came searching for him,
and only then helped him up,
while the horse collapsed on the spot.
It took a long time for the horse to rise,
and it was ill for over ten days before recovering.
Not long after,
this man sold the horse to an innkeeper in Xuānzhōu.
Two years later,
the traveler later obtained an official position,
and was sent on a mission to Xuānzhōu.
Learning that the horse was there,
he requested to ride it.
The horse stared at him for a long time, recognizing its original owner.
Once mounted,
it immediately threw this man to the ground,
trampling and biting him fiercely,
and he was only spared after others rescued him.
It seemed to resent him for selling it.
Chén Zhāng
Chén Zhāng, the military commander of Huáinán, was promoted to the rank of Píngzhāngshì,
and received his appointment at court.
Lǐ Shēng, who was in power at the time,
said to Zhāng:
"I will come to congratulate you,
and also seek a son-in-law from your family.
You should return first,
and I will arrive shortly."
Zhāng rode a red horse and left.
On the way,
the horse stumbled and he fell off.
Shortly after,
Shēng arrived,
and Zhāng came out, supporting himself in his injured state.
Shēng stayed only briefly before leaving.
Zhāng summoned the horse and scolded it, saying:
"Today, I received my official appointment,
and also discussed a marriage alliance,
yet you caused me to fall like this.
You beast!"
Unable to bring himself to kill it immediately,
he ordered it taken away,
and not given any fodder,
intending to starve it to death.
That night,
the stableman secretly prepared fodder and grain,
but the horse merely looked at it,
and did not eat until dawn.
This went on for several days,
and the stableman reported it.
Zhāng summoned the horse again and said to it:
"Since you have realized your fault,
I pardon you."
The horse leaped and ran off.
That night,
it ate and drank as usual.
Later, Zhāng was appointed to govern Xuānchéng,
but upon returning after his term, he passed away.
Within a month,
the horse also neighed mournfully and died.
Lú Cóngshì
Lǔ Chuànsù, an official in Lǐngnán, resided in Jiānglíng.
During the Yuánhé era,
someone once gifted him a black colt.
Initially, it was quite lame and inferior,
but after Chuànsù raised it for three to five years,
it gradually grew fatter and more robust.
Before Chuànsù took up his official post,
his family was poor and humble,
and he toiled away riding it,
enduring much hardship.
Yet the horse never once stumbled or made a mistake,
so Chuànsù grew quite fond of it.
One day,
while Chuànsù was inspecting its stable and trough,
he jokingly said to it:
"How are you doing, little horse?"
Suddenly, the black colt spoke in human language:
"Greetings, elder."
Chuànsù, startled and terrified, stepped back in retreat.
The black colt continued:
"Although I, A Mǎ, am a beast in body,
I have a reason that must be made clear;
this is not some supernatural transformation.
I beg you, elder, to stay a moment."
Chuànsù said:
"You are a beast,
yet you suddenly speak like a human—
there must be some grievance or injustice.
Please, speak your mind fully."
The black colt replied:
"A Mǎ is your own maternal cousin's son,
Tōng'ér from Hèlán Lane, Xuánxiǎo's household in Wúxī County, Chángzhōu.
Do you not recall that in the twelfth year of the Zhēnyuán era,
you sent Tōng'ér to Hǎilíng to sell a villa,
obtaining one hundred strings of cash?
At that time, Tōng'ér was young and ill-behaved;
led astray by friends to places of debauchery,
he squandered nearly all that money.
You were far away at the time,
and could do nothing about Tōng'ér.
That same year, Tōng'ér fell ill and died.
In the underworld, everything became clear,
and the demand to repay your debt was very urgent.
King Pingděng said to Tōng'ér:
'You must repay him his money in this life.
If you are reborn as a human again,
by the time you grow up, it will be too late.
You must temporarily take the form of a beast,
and over ten or so years,
you may then repay the debt.'
Thus, Tōng'ér was driven into the animal realm,
and unknowingly ended up among the horses in Jiānglíng—
that is A Mǎ's current body.
A Mǎ has been in your stable,
for about five or six years now.
My mind is fully aware,
and I have always been repaying my debt to you.
That is why I have exhausted my strength, clumsy as I am,
daring not to remain in a state of fault.
I also know you have shown me the utmost kindness and affection,
and it is not that A Mǎ lacks attachment to his master,
but I recall my servitude of five years,
and the lifespan of this horse, a beast, is about to end.
Five days from now,
I will break out in black sweat and die.
I beg you, elder, to quickly sell A Mǎ.
Tomorrow at noon,
you yourself should ride A Mǎ out the eastern stable gate,
to the northwest corner of the market, by the Chìbǎn Gate.
There will be a foreign military officer,
who will ask you if you are selling this horse.
You, elder, should ask for one hundred thousand cash,
but he will certainly offer seventy thousand.
Then you may quickly close the deal."
Having finished speaking of the matter,
he added:
"Moreover, I have a poem,
to bid farewell to you, elder."
Then, lifting his head, he recited clearly:
"I have eaten your grain, elder,
and feasted on your hay.
Today my debt is repaid,
forever leaving the three evil paths."
Then he shook himself vigorously several times,
neighed, and began chewing grass as before.
Chuànsù tried to speak to him again,
but he never uttered another word.
Everything he said—the name of the cousin's son,
the amount of money embezzled, the year and month—
was completely accurate.
Chuànsù was deeply moved by this affair.
The next day,
he tried riding the horse to the market corner,
and indeed, there was a foreign general earnestly seeking to buy it.
Chuànsù subtly tested him,
and deliberately lowered the price to sixty strings of cash.
The military officer said:
"Sir, this horse of yours
is worth over seventy thousand cash.
Please let me buy it for seventy thousand,
and I won't even test it with water and grass."
Chuànsù carried the strings of cash home.
Four days later,
he passed by the officer's house again,
and saw the foreign military officer, who said:
"Alas!
That seventy-string horse—
last night it broke out in black sweat and died."
Wéi Yǒuróu
Wéi Yǒuróu, magistrate of Jiàn'ān County,
had a household servant who held the reins,
about twenty years old,
who fell ill and died.
Yǒuróu had a guest skilled in incantations,
who suddenly dreamed of that servant saying:
"I died unfortunately,
and still owe the master forty-five thousand cash.
The authorities in the underworld
ordered me to become a beast to repay the debt.
I requested to become a horse,
and also to be of an unusual color.
It is already decided."
The following year,
a mare gave birth to a white foal with black eyes,
all bearing the servant's demeanor.
Several years later,
the horse was worth over a hundred thousand cash,
and Yǒuróu deeply sighed, thinking the words had not come true.
Soon after,
Péi Kuān became the investigation commissioner,
and appointed Yǒuróu as his assistant.
Péi Kuān saw the white horse
and sought to buy it.
When asked its price,
Yǒuróu only asked for thirty thousand.
Kuān thus acquired it.
Yǒuróu said:
"This servant still owes fifteen thousand;
he should come again."
A few days later,
Kuān said to Yǒuróu:
"The horse is a fine horse;
the payment I gave earlier
I deeply regret was too cheap."
He then returned another fifteen thousand to Yǒuróu.
Thus, the affair was fulfilled.
Wú Zōngsì
There was a military commissioner named Wú Zōngsì.
He once had a former subordinate who borrowed two hundred thousand cash from him,
with monthly interest calculated.
After a year,
he refused to repay any further.
Demands for payment yielded no results.
Zōngsì grew angry,
summoned him, and rebuked him, saying:
"In a past life, I owed you money,
and I have repaid it now.
You owe me;
you shall become a donkey or horse to repay me."
He then burned the bond and dismissed him.
A year later,
Zōngsì was sitting alone in the main hall,
when suddenly he saw the subordinate, dressed in white, arrive and say:
"I have come to repay the debt."
Zōngsì said:
"I already burned the bond;
why have you come again?"
The subordinate did not answer,
but went straight into the stable.
Soon after, a stableman reported that a mare had given birth to a white foal.
Zōngsì sent someone to inquire at the subordinate's house,
and they said:
"He died the next day."
When the foal grew up and was sold,
it fetched exactly the amount the subordinate had owed.
Sūn Hànwēi
Sūn Hànwēi, a military commissioner of the Shénwǔ Army in Jiāngnán,
had a horse in his stable
that, when night fell,
would emit light from its tail,
like scattered sparks.
It startled the other horses,
causing them all to neigh.
Hànwēi, considering it a monster,
took up his sword and killed it.
Several months later,
he was appointed prefect of Lúzhōu.
Yú Yuǎn
In Yèzhōng, there was a wealthy man named Yú Yuǎn,
whose nature was extravagant and indulgent, and who also had a fondness for fine horses.
His residence was magnificent,
his clothing and ornaments fresh and pristine,
comparable to the households of dukes and marquises.
He often kept several dozen fine horses.
Suddenly one day,
someone in the market was selling a fine horse,
with extraordinary fur and unusual bone structure,
and people vied to see it.
Upon hearing of it,
Yú Yuǎn paid a hundred pieces of gold for it.
When the horse arrived at his stable,
an old woman knocked on his gate, requesting to see it.
Yú Yuǎn asked her:
"A horse is for swiftness and elegance,
something favored by dashing young men.
That is fitting,
but why would an old mother wish to see it?"
The old mother said:
"I lost a fine horse,
and for ten years I have wandered the world,
searching for it without success.
Whenever I encounter a fine horse,
I must observe it all day long,
yet I have never seen one like the horse I lost.
Why hinder a viewing,
and not grant me this kindness."
Yú Yuǎn then invited her in leisurely,
and brought out the horse to show her.
As soon as the old mother saw the horse,
her expression changed with anger,
and turning to look at Yú Yuǎn, she said:
"This is my horse."
Yú Yuǎn said:
"If it is the old mother's horse,
how did someone else sell it?
How did you obtain it in the past?
How did you lose it?"
The old mother said:
"Because in the past, I encountered the god of Běimáng Shān, whose eyes were injured by something,
and he transformed himself to seek my help.
I treated him with renowned medicine,
his eyes healed,
and he then bestowed this horse upon me.
After I obtained this horse,
I only refrained from riding it up to heaven.
Riding it, I traveled beyond the Four Seas,
within the Eight Wildernesses,
it was as if covering only a hundred lǐ.
I once rode it east, passing Fúsāng,
when someone blocked my path and asked me about this horse.
By nightfall,
I reached the country of Xīzhú,
and suddenly lost this horse.
Since I lost this horse,
I have not rested for ten years.
Across the world,
no one knew I was searching for this horse.
On this day last year,
in the Flowing Sands, I saw a child,
who said there was an extraordinary horse like a flying creature,
which swiftly went east.
Since I knew it came from the east,
I suspected this horse was in Zhōnghuá,
and that some ordinary person must have acquired it.
I will now return your hundred pieces of gold,
but the horse must be returned to me."
Yú Yuǎn, with his obsessive fondness for fine horses,
and hearing of this horse's extraordinary nature,
deeply cherished and regretted parting with it.
He then bowed to the old mother,
begging her to let him keep it temporarily,
to admire and enjoy it for a few days.
The old mother angrily said:
"If you keep this horse,
disaster will surely occur."
Yú Yuǎn, also angered by the old mother's extreme words,
then ordered over ten household servants,
to guard this horse together.
He sent the old mother away,
and his household indeed caught fire,
completely burning his residence and treasures.
Yú Yuǎn then saw the old woman enter the residence,
leap onto this horse herself, and vanish.
Zhāng Quán
Yìzhōu Cìshǐ Zhāng Quán kept a fine horse,
which he greatly cherished and protected.
Only he himself rode it,
and those around him did not dare to mount it lightly.
He often ordered two men to specially feed and water it morning and night.
Suddenly one day,
the horse transformed into a woman,
of extraordinary and peerless beauty,
standing in the stable.
Those around hurriedly reported to Lord Zhāng,
and Lord Zhāng personally went to observe.
The woman stepped forward, bowed, and said:
"I was originally a woman from Yānzhōng,
and because of my fondness for fine horses,
whenever I saw one,
I would inevitably admire and praise its swiftness and elegance.
After several years,
I suddenly fell into a drunken stupor,
and in a moment transformed into a fine horse.
I then galloped out,
heading south as I pleased,
nearly a thousand lǐ,
until I was captured by someone,
and ended up in your stable.
Fortunately, you cherished and protected me.
Now, by chance, I regret having become an animal,
and my tears fell to the ground.
The earth deity reported this to the Emperor,
and thus I was ordered to return to my former state.
Thinking of the past is like awakening from a dream."
Lord Zhāng was greatly astonished,
and settled her in his home.
After more than ten years,
the woman suddenly requested to return to her hometown.
Before Lord Zhāng could consent,
the woman looked up to the sky,
wailed and threw herself down,
and her body suddenly transformed back into a fine horse,
which charged out,
and no one knew where it went.
Wáng Wǔ
In Jīngluò, there was a wealthy man named Wáng Wǔ, whose nature was careless,
yet he knew how to flatter the powerful and noble.
Suddenly learning that someone was selling a fine horse,
he urgently ordered people to offer much gold and silk,
and vied among the crowd to obtain it.
The horse was white,
like a ball of beautiful jade.
Its mane and tail were red as cinnabar.
All said it was a thousand-lǐ steed,
and some suspected it was a dragon colt,
for its galloping speed
was beyond what an ordinary horse could match.
Wáng Wǔ intended to present it to Grand General Xuē Gōng,
so he lavishly adorned it with a golden saddle and jade bridle,
interspersed with pearls and kingfisher feathers,
and was just waiting for an opportune moment to convey his intention.
Suddenly, the horse let out a great neigh in the stable and then transformed into a clay statue of a horse standing there.
Wáng Wǔ was greatly shocked,
and then burned and destroyed it.
Wéi Pín
Wéi Pín of Jīngzhào,
a descendant of the Lesser Duke of Xiāoyáo.
His family had long resided at the estate in Fànshuǐ County, Mèng Prefecture.
By nature, he disliked books
and was fond of galloping across fields and hunting with bow and arrow.
Whenever there was a horse that could not be restrained due to kicking or biting,
he would buy it.
In the late Xiántōng era,
while visiting Fànshuǐ,
he was drinking in the market.
In the midst of his drunken singing,
suddenly there appeared a man selling a white horse, who said:
"This one is extremely swift and strong."
Pín mounted it on the street,
and said:
"Good,
it can take the whip."
So he bought it.
As evening fell, he rode it home,
controlling it with an iron whip.
A servant followed on another horse.
Once they ascended the eastern plateau,
the horse galloped over ten miles without stopping,
and the servant could not keep up.
Pín again used the iron whip,
but the horse bolted uncontrollably.
It swiftly leaped over thickets and ditches,
and as Pín was weary from drink and exhausted,
he reckoned it would be impossible to restrain it.
Just as the horse charged fiercely toward a large mulberry tree,
Pín leaped up onto a high branch,
thinking himself safe.
The horse rushed past for several dozen paces,
then returned beneath the mulberry tree,
closed its eyes and let out a long neigh,
looking up at Pín, neighing long and stamping the ground.
After a short while,
it began gnawing at the base of the mulberry tree,
and chips fell like palm-sized pieces.
It would sometimes lie down and graze within ten or five paces.
Then it would return again to gnaw incessantly,
until the tree trunk was nearly half gone.
Fearing the tree would topple,
Pín looked into the distance and saw a well a few paces to the left.
Waiting until the horse rested in the thick grass,
he jumped down,
and swiftly ran to throw himself into the well.
Just as he reached the bottom,
the horse also followed him in.
Pín and the horse both perished there.
The Luminous Camel
The "luminous camel" with thousand-mile feet
is often mistakenly written with the character for "crying."
When a camel lies down,
its belly does not touch the ground.
Its bent legs leave a gap for light to pass through,
and thus it can travel a thousand miles.
Knowing Water Veins
West of Dūnhuáng,
crossing the shifting sands,
heading to foreign lands,
traversing over a thousand miles of desert,
there is no water.
Sometimes there are underground streams,
but people cannot detect them.
Camels know the water veins,
and when they pass such a place, they stop walking,
stamping the ground with their feet.
People dig at the spot where they stamp,
and invariably find water.
Wind-Foot Camel
In the kingdom of Yútián, there are small deer
with slender, long antlers.
When they mate with camels,
the offspring is called the wind-foot camel.
It can travel seven hundred miles a day,
swift as the wind.
Two-Legged Camel
The kingdom of Yìhéng is located south of the Wūhǔ River,
originally the land of the Great Yuèzhī of the Hàn dynasty.
Liú Fán's "Liáng Diǎn" states:
"It produces two-legged camels."
White Camel
Gēshū Hàn once garrisoned at Qīnghǎi.
As the journey was long and distant,
he often dispatched messengers riding white camels to deliver reports.
They could travel five hundred miles a day.
White Mule
When Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng was about to ascend Mount Tài,
Yì Prefecture presented a white mule,
pure, bright, plump, and glossy,
extraordinary and majestic.
The emperor then personally rode it.
It was gentle, accustomed, comfortable, and steady,
and he felt no fatigue from the ascent or descent.
After the ceremony to announce the completion was finished,
he rode it back down.
Just as they reached the foot of the mountain,
before the emperor had rested long,
officials reported that the white mule had died without any illness.
The emperor sighed in wonder for a long time,
and posthumously honored it as "General White Mule."
He ordered officials to prepare a coffin,
and piled stones to make a tomb.
The tomb lies several miles north of the Fēngshàn altar,
and remains there to this day.
Mill-Pushing Mule
Among the commoners in the market of Línluò,
there was a blind mule used for pushing a mill that died without cause,
so it was sold.
When the butcher cut open its belly,
he found two stones,
as large as clenched fists,
purple with red speckles,
lustrous, smooth, and lovely.
Donkey
Sēng Lǎng
The Jìn dynasty monk Lǎng resided on Jīnyú Mountain.
After he passed away,
the donkey he used to ride went missing on the mountain.
Occasionally, people would see it,
and it had become a golden donkey.
Woodcutters would often hear its braying.
The locals say:
"When the golden donkey brays once,
there will be peace under heaven."
The Kingdom of Yàndá
In the Western Regions, in the kingdom of Yàndá,
temple laborers used several donkeys to transport grain up the mountain.
No one drove them,
yet they could go back and forth on their own,
setting out at yǐn (3–5 a.m.) and arriving at noon,
never missing a moment.
Villager Serving a Monk
There was once a villager who served a monk,
seeking his secret words.
The monk deceived him, saying:
"Donkey."
The man then recited it day and night.
After several years,
when he looked into water,
he saw a blue-haired donkey attached to his back.
Whenever there were illnesses or demonic hauntings,
if the man went to the place, they would be immediately cured.
Later, when he realized the deception,
the efficacy of the incantation also ceased.
Zhāng Gāo
There was a man named Zhāng Gāo from Cháng'ān who traded goods in the market,
amassing assets worth tens of thousands.
He owned a donkey,
which had been blind for a long time.
In the autumn, the eighth month of the twelfth year of the Yuánhé era of the Táng dynasty,
Zhāng Gāo died.
On the thirteenth day,
his wife instructed their son Hé to ride the donkey to the outskirts of the city
to purchase supplies for a meal offering to monks.
As they exited the village gate,
the donkey refused to move forward.
When struck, it lay down.
Hé mounted it and whipped it,
when suddenly the donkey turned its head to Hé and said:
"Why are you hitting me?"
Hé replied:
"My family spent twenty thousand coins to acquire you.
Since you refuse to walk,
how can I not strike you?"
Hé was greatly astonished.
The donkey then said:
"Never mind the twenty thousand coins.
Your father rode me for over twenty years.
I now tell you,
the cycles of human and animal destinies,
like the turning of a wheel,
are never fixed.
In my previous life, I owed your father a debt of labor,
so I became a donkey to repay it.
Not long after,
you fed me generously.
Last night, your father settled accounts with me,
and I now owe you one and a half strings of coins.
Your father often rode me,
and I naturally did not refuse.
Since I owe you nothing,
you should not ride me.
If you force yourself to ride me,
I will also ride you.
If we take turns riding each other,
when will it ever end?
My flesh and skin
are worth far more than twenty thousand coins.
I only owe you one and a half strings.
Take me out and sell me,
and someone will pay you.
However, no one will buy me for a specific price,
because others do not owe me money.
Does Wáng Húzi from the bran shop owe me two strings?
I do not owe him labor.
Take one and a half strings from him to repay you,
and keep the remaining half string for my feed,
so I may live out my allotted time as a donkey."
Hé led the donkey back home
and reported this to his mother.
His mother wept and said:
"My son rode you for many years,
and you have indeed endured much hardship.
What does one and a half strings of coins matter?
Shall we release you from the debt and feed you well so you may live long?"
The donkey shook its head.
She then asked:
"Shall we sell you for money?"
It nodded.
They immediately took it out to sell.
People offered no more than one and a half strings,
and no one was willing to buy it for that price.
They led it into the West Market bran shop,
where they encountered a man,
tall and bearded.
He exchanged one and a half strings for the donkey.
When asked,
he said his surname was Wáng.
From then on, it rained continuously,
and only cleared after several days.
Hé went to check on it,
and found that the donkey had already died.
Wáng never got to ride it.
This was further proof that he owed it nothing.
Hé's eastern neighbor was the Imperial Guard Commandant Zhāng Dá,
whose wife
was from the Lǐ family.
I once visited them,
and they said they heard about the incident
on the night the donkey spoke.
I record this in full
to warn those who are greedy and ignorant.
A Man from the East Market
In the early years of the Kāichéng era,
a commoner from the East Market lost his father
and rode a donkey to the market to buy funeral supplies.
After walking a hundred paces,
the donkey suddenly spoke:
"My surname is Bái, and my given name is Yuántōng.
I have already repaid my debt of labor to your family.
Do not ride me again.
The bran seller in the South Market
owes me five thousand four hundred coins.
I also owe your family a sum of money,
equal to that amount.
You may sell me now."
The man was astonished.
He immediately led the donkey away
and soon found a buyer to sell it.
The donkey was quite sturdy,
but the offered price was only five thousand coins.
When he went to the bran shop,
he received exactly five thousand four hundred coins,
so he sold it.
Two nights later, the donkey died.
Hè Shìbó
During the Northern Qí dynasty,
in Qū'ān, there was a man named Hè Shìbó, over sixty years old.
He owned a small donkey
that had not been trained.
He had his son ride it,
but the son was thrown off twice.
Hè Shìbó laughed at him and said:
"You useless boy,
completely incompetent.
Although I am old,
I do not need a saddle
and can still control it."
He then mounted it.
The donkey startled and bolted away swiftly.
Hè Shìbó panicked and jumped off,
barely avoiding being thrown.
That night, in the hall,
he was feasting with relatives.
Hè Shìbó wanted to sleep,
when suddenly he startled awake,
covering his forehead with his hand.
His family asked him what was wrong,
and he said:
"I dreamed of training this donkey
and struck it with a stick,
but accidentally hit my own forehead.
Now it burns like hot water,
and is swollen as large as a pear."
They went to check on the donkey,
and found it outside another village.
The man later fell ill and died.
Wáng Jiǎ
During the Dayè era of the Suí dynasty,
there was a man surnamed Wáng in Luòyáng,
who often upheld the Five Precepts,
and from time to time would speak of events yet to come,
earning the reverence and trust of his neighbors.
One morning,
he suddenly said to people:
"Today, someone will bring a donkey here."
Weeping, he recounted:
"Long ago, I lost my father,
and my mother was widowed,
raising a son and a daughter.
The daughter married, and then the mother passed away,
twenty years ago now.
On the Cold Food Festival,
carrying wine and food to offer at the grave,
this man rode a donkey to go there.
The grave was east of the Yī River,
and when he wanted to cross the Yī River,
the donkey refused to go.
He whipped its head and face, injuring it,
and it bled.
After arriving at the gravesite,
he released the donkey and made his offerings,
but soon the donkey was lost.
That day,
the sister was at her brother's home,
when suddenly she saw her mother enter,
her head and face bleeding,
her appearance haggard and distressed.
Wailing, she told her daughter:
'In my lifetime,
I avoided giving your brother five dǒu of rice to give to you,
and for this offense I have been punished.
In retribution, I was reborn as a donkey,
repaying your brother for five years now.
Today, wanting to cross the Yī River,
I feared the deep water,
and your brother whipped me,
breaking my head and face all over,
and still plans to return home and beat me even more harshly.
I came here to tell you,
my debt repayment is nearly complete,
why must you torment me so unreasonably?'
Having spoken, she went out the door,
and when they searched for her, she was nowhere to be seen,
only the donkey's head and face were bleeding,
just like the mother's injuries.
The daughter embraced it and wept.
When the brother returned,
he was puzzled and asked about it.
The sister told him what had happened.
Thereupon, brother and sister held each other and wailed bitterly,
and the donkey also shed tears,
refusing to eat or drink.
The brother and sister knelt and pleaded:
If you are our mother,
please eat some grass.
The donkey then ate,
but soon stopped again.
The brother and sister did not know what to do,
so they prepared fodder and grain,
and sent it to Wáng the Five Precepts.
Later, when it died,
the brother and sister collected and buried it.
Tāng Ānrén
In the Táng dynasty, Tāng Ānrén of Jīngzhào was wealthy.
He had long served the monks of Címén Temple.
In the first year of the Xīníng era,
suddenly a traveler lodged at his home to stay,
and the traveler stole someone else's donkey,
killed it at the home,
and gave the donkey skin to Ānrén.
By the third year of the Zhēnguàn era,
Ānrén then saw a man on the road,
who said to Ānrén:
"The pursuers will come for you tomorrow,
and you will die."
Ānrén was afraid,
and went straight to Címén Temple,
sat in the Buddha hall,
and did not leave overnight.
The next day,
sure enough, three riders and several dozen foot soldiers arrived,
all armed, entering the temple.
From afar, they saw Ānrén,
and called out: "Tāng Ānrén."
He did not respond but recited scriptures even more intently.
The ghosts said to each other:
"Yesterday we did not take him immediately,
and now he cultivates blessings like this,
how can we capture him?"
So they left together.
They left one to guard him,
and the guard said to Ānrén:
"In the past, you killed a donkey,
and now the donkey is accusing you.
It sent us to seize you.
In the end, you must come with us,
what good is it not to go?"
Ānrén answered from afar:
"In the past, another thief killed the donkey himself,
and only gave the skin to me.
I did not kill it,
why am I being pursued?
Gentlemen, please return,
and tell the donkey for me,
that I did not kill you,
and now I will also perform meritorious deeds for you,
which will benefit you,
so you should let me go."
The man agreed.
He said:
"If the donkey does not agree,
I will come again tomorrow;
if it agrees,
I will not come."
Having spoken, he went out,
and the next day he did not come.
Ānrén then performed meritorious deeds for the donkey,
and his whole household upheld the precepts and ate vegetarian food.
Lú Wénlì told this story,
and Ānrén is still alive today.
Wáng Xūn
In the early Tiānbǎo era,
there was a man named Wáng Xūn,
who lived in Yánshòu Ward of Cháng'ān.
One evening,
several people brought food
and gathered at Xūn's residence.
After eating and drinking,
suddenly a huge arm appeared from under the candlelight.
Xūn and his friends were frightened,
and together they looked at it:
the arm was black in color,
and covered with much hair.
Before long,
a voice from beyond the shadow said:
"You are having a gathering,
can you not call me once?
I wish to have a little meat placed in my palm."
Xūn could not guess the reason,
so he gave it to him,
and the arm then withdrew.
After a short while,
the arm stretched out again and said:
"Thank you for giving me meat,
but now it is almost finished,
I hope you will give me more."
Xūn again placed meat in its palm,
and again it withdrew.
Then they discussed together:
"This must be a monster,
wait until it comes again,
we should cut off its arm."
Soon it indeed came again,
and they drew a sword and cut it off.
Once the arm fell,
its body also fled far away.
Looking down at it,
it turned out to be a donkey's hoof,
with blood flowing all over the ground.
The next day,
they followed the blood trail,
which led straight into a commoner's home in the ward.
They then asked the commoner about the matter.
The commoner said:
"My family keeps a donkey,
for almost twenty years now.
Last night it lost a hoof,
as if cut off by a blade.
I was just alarmed by it."
Xūn told him the whole story,
and they immediately killed and ate it.
Huà Lóng
In the second year of the Tàixīng era of the Jìn dynasty,
a man from Wú named Huà Lóng
was fond of hunting with bow and arrow.
He kept a dog.
It was named "Díwěi,"
and he always took it with him.
Later, Huà Lóng went to the riverbank,
where he was encircled by a large snake.
The dog then bit the snake to death,
but Huà Lóng fell stiff and unconscious.
The dog paced about, howling and barking,
running back and forth along the path.
His family found its behavior strange,
so they followed the dog.
Huà Lóng was found lying on the ground, senseless.
They carried him home,
and he revived only after two days.
While Huà Lóng was still unconscious,
the dog refused to eat at all.
From then on, he cherished it
as if it were a close relative.
Yáng Shēng
During the Tàihé era of the Jìn dynasty,
a man from Guǎnglíng named Yáng Shēng kept a dog,
which he loved and cherished deeply,
and he always took it with him.
Later, Yáng Shēng got drunk
and lay down in a patch of wild grass.
At that time, a winter prairie fire was raging,
and the wind was extremely strong.
The dog then ran around him, howling and barking,
but Yáng Shēng remained completely unaware.
The dog then went to the water and soaked itself,
returned, and lay down on the grass.
Repeating this several times,
it moved around within a small area,
until the grass was all dampened,
and when the fire arrived, he was spared from burning.
Afterward, Yáng Shēng fell into a well while walking in the dark,
and the dog again barked until dawn.
Someone passed by,
and the passerby found its behavior strange,
so he went to look,
and found Yáng Shēng inside.
Yáng Shēng then begged to be rescued,
promising a generous reward.
The man wanted to ask for this dog as payment.
Yáng Shēng said:
"This dog once saved me from certain death.
Even if I cannot comply with this request,
anything else you desire is yours."
The passerby hesitated and did not reply.
The dog then stretched its neck and looked toward the well,
and Yáng Shēng understood its meaning,
so he agreed.
After the man rescued him,
he tied up the dog and left.
Five days later,
the dog ran back at night.
Cuī Zhòngwén
During the Yìxī era of Emperor Ān of Jìn,
Cuī Zhòngwén from Qiáo County and Shí Hé from Kuàijī both served as clerks under General Liú Fǔ.
Cuī Zhòngwén kept a dog,
which he used to hunt deer,
and it never failed to catch them.
Shí Hé greatly admired it,
and offered to exchange it for a male servant,
but Cuī Zhòngwén refused.
When Shí Hé and Cuī Zhòngwén went hunting in the mountains,
they reached a grassy area,
and Shí Hé killed Cuī Zhòngwén.
He wanted to take the dog,
but the dog bit Shí Hé,
guarded its master's corpse,
and dug the ground to cover it.
Later, when troops went out hunting,
they saw the dog guarding the corpse.
Someone recognized its master,
and reported back to General Liú Fǔ.
When Shí Hé returned from leave,
and reached the gate of the headquarters,
the dog went to tug at his clothes, howling and barking.
People again reported to General Liú Fǔ,
saying:
"This man must have killed the dog's master."
They then arrested him,
and General Liú Fǔ interrogated him under torture,
indeed uncovering the truth,
and executed Shí Hé.
Zhāng Rán
Zhāng Rán from Kuàijī was detained on official duty,
and his young wife had no children,
so she stayed at home with only a servant.
The servant then had an affair with the wife.
Zhāng Rán had long kept a dog,
named Wūlóng,
which he always took with him.
Later, when he returned home,
the servant plotted to kill Zhāng Rán.
They prepared a lavish meal,
and the wife said to Zhāng Rán:
"You and I are about to part for a long time,
you should eat heartily."
The servant had already drawn his bow and fitted an arrow,
waiting for Zhāng Rán to finish eating.
Zhāng Rán wept and could not eat,
so he threw meat and rice to the dog.
He prayed, saying:
"I have raised you for years,
and I am about to die.
Can you save me?"
The dog did not eat the food,
but only fixed its gaze on the servant.
Zhāng Rán slapped his knee and shouted loudly:
"Wūlóng!"
The dog responded by attacking the servant,
causing him to drop his knife,
and he fell to the ground.
The dog bit his groin,
and Zhāng Rán then took the knife and killed the servant.
He handed his wife over to the county authorities,
and she was executed.
Yáng Bāo
Yáng Bāo
was a man from Lújiāng.
Yáng Bāo traveled to visit a close acquaintance.
The household was poor and had little to offer,
so they kept only one dog,
which they intended to cook and serve to him.
The dog then knelt on its front legs,
and looked at Yáng Bāo with its eyes.
Finding this strange, he stopped them,
and did not allow them to kill it.
He then asked for the dog,
and his acquaintance gave it to Yáng Bāo.
He took the dog back to his home.
After more than a month,
it often followed him in and out.
Yáng Bāo's wife, however, harbored ill intentions toward him,
which Yáng Bāo knew nothing about.
After more than a year,
Yáng Bāo's wife secretly conspired with an outsider,
planning to kill Yáng Bāo.
That evening, Yáng Bāo returned drunk,
and his wife waited for the outsider to come and kill Yáng Bāo.
When he arrived,
just as he was about to enter the room,
the dog bit and broke his leg,
and also bit Yáng Bāo's wife,
leaving both severely injured.
Neighbors all came,
and rescued them.
When Yáng Bāo awoke,
he searched and found,
indeed, the knife.
The neighbors reported it,
and they were sent to the county for interrogation.
The wife confessed the truth.
Yáng Bāo's wife and the man with the knife
were both executed according to the law.
Zhèng Sháo
Zhèng Sháo was a Left Scattered Cavalry Regular Attendant during the reign of Emperor Yáng of Suí.
During the Dàyè era, he was appointed as the Prefect of Mǐnzhōng.
Sháo kept a dog, which he cherished and loved more than his own son.
Sháo had several dozen attendants.
Among them was one Xuē Yuánzhōu, who had served Sháo before he achieved prominence.
When Sháo was promoted to Prefect, he showed no kindness or consideration toward Yuánzhōu.
Yuánzhōu, resentful and bitter, waited for a long time with a blade, seeking an opportunity, but found none.
At that time, they were in Mǐnzhōng, and an envoy from Emperor Yáng of Suí arrived.
Sháo prepared his horse and went to welcome him.
His dog then grabbed and tugged at the hem of his robe, preventing him from leaving the residence.
A clerk from the guesthouse rushed in to report:
"The envoy has entered the outer city."
Sháo was about to go out, but the dog tugged at his robe and would not let go.
Sháo grew angry and ordered someone to tie the dog to a pillar.
As Sháo exited the main gate of the envoy's residence, the dog broke free from the rope and ran, tugging at Sháo's robe as before, not allowing him to leave.
Sháo patted the dog and said:
"Do you know that something unforeseen is about to happen to me?"
The dog then howled and barked, leaped into Yuánzhōu's group, and bit Xuē Yuánzhōu to death.
Sháo sent someone to search Yuánzhōu's clothing, and indeed, a short sword was found hidden there.
Liǔ Chāo
Liǔ Chāo served as a Remonstrance Advisor during the reign of Emperor Zhōngzōng of Táng.
Having offended the court, he was demoted to the region beyond the Lǐng Mountains.
Chāo maintained a pure and frugal lifestyle, and wherever he passed through prefectures and commanderies, he did not disturb honest officials for his own support.
He was accompanied by two servants, Zhǎng Gé and Zhǎng Shū, and a dog.
Upon reaching Jiāngzhōu, Chāo fell ill due to depression and resentment.
The two servants plotted to seize his belongings and provisions, and together they schemed:
"We can offer poisoned medicine to the Remonstrance Advisor. Then we can take his wealth and become free men—wouldn't that be excellent?"
Zhǎng Shū said:
"Good."
Zhǎng Gé then said to Chāo:
"People say a secret edict has arrived, and it does not spare the Remonstrance Advisor's life. What will become of the Remonstrance Advisor's family?"
Chāo said:
"Indeed. You should prepare a meal. After I finish eating, you may bring me the poison. I will die willingly."
Upon hearing this, Zhǎng Gé and the others prepared a lavish meal.
Zhǎng Gé worked in the kitchen to prepare it, while Zhǎng Shū served it to Chāo.
As Chāo was eating, he suddenly saw his dog and shared some food with it.
Weeping, he patted the dog and said:
"I will die today. To whom shall I entrust you?"
Upon hearing this, the dog refused to eat, ran into the kitchen, and bit Zhǎng Gé's throat.
It then went to the front hall and bit Zhǎng Shū.
Both servants were killed by the dog.
Chāo did not understand what had happened.
Several days later, an imperial edict arrived recalling him to the capital, and he was cleared of charges and pardoned. Only then did he realize the dog's extraordinary intelligence.
Yáo Jiǎ
There was a man from the Yáo clan of Wúxīng who, during the Kāiyuán era, was exiled to the southern frontier.
He had long kept two dogs, and even in the south, he took them with him.
His family servants, Fùzǐ and his son Xiǎo nú, were both strong and brave. They plotted to kill their master and then return north with the entire household.
Yáo lived in a remote area, with no neighbors nearby.
Fùzǐ suddenly said to his master:

"Master, your family is originally from the north. Now you are banished to the southern wilderness, wandering thousands of miles away. If something unfortunate were to happen suddenly, I, your servant, would take charge of the funeral arrangements and return north.
Lately, I have felt weak and exhausted. I fear that if I were to pass away suddenly, the remaining weak and young ones would be unable to bring your bones back to your hometown.
I humbly hope you will consider this."
Yáo understood his meaning and said:
"Do you want me to die?"
The servant said:
"That is precisely what I am worried about."
Yáo requested to wait until the next morning.
When the time came, the servant and his son prepared a meal and urged Yáo to eat his fill.
They offered a cup of wine, sobbing with emotion.
Yáo, his heart flustered and anxious, could not eat at first and instead fed the food to his two dogs.
Taking advantage of the servants' absence, he patted the two dogs and said:
"I have raised you for many years. Now the servants are going to kill me. Do you know this?"
From then on, the two dogs refused to eat and gazed at their master, howling mournfully.
Shortly after, Fùzǐ arrived. One of the dogs bit his throat, severing it and killing him.
The other dog rushed into the kitchen and bit the throat of Xiǎo nú, also severing it.
It then bit Fùzǐ's wife, killing her as well.
Yáo was thus spared.
Liú Jùlín
At the end of the Kāiyuán era, Liú Jùlín served as the Military Governor of Guǎng Prefecture.
While in the prefecture, he always kept a dog—a powerful and vigorous male, exceptionally tame and attached to him, unlike any other.
Jùlín once went out at night to welcome an envoy, but the dog suddenly blocked and guarded him, not wanting him to leave.
Jùlín, realizing this, said:
"Is the dog trying to stop me from going?"
He hesitated for a long time.
Someone arrived and reported that the envoy was approaching.
Jùlín scolded:
"My entourage is as numerous as clouds. How could anything untoward happen?"
He ordered his family to lock up the dog and went out.
As he mounted his horse, the dog followed him.
Suddenly, it bit the throat of one of his attendants, who died shortly after.
Jùlín, shocked and alarmed, searched the dead man's clothing and found a sharp dagger.
Previously, Jùlín had often whipped this servant, who harbored a grudge and privately sought revenge.
The dog, sensing this in advance, thus saved him from disaster.
Zhāng Huá
Zhāng Huá, a commoner from Lèpíng County in Ráozhōu,
in the early Yuánhé era,
often kept a dog.
Whenever he went into the mountains to gather firewood,
it would always follow him.
A neighbor named Wáng Huá,
whenever he came and went, the dog would bark and chase him away.
In the winter of the third year,
Wáng Huá went with him into the mountains to gather firewood,
and the dog followed them as well.
Suddenly, a tiger
leaped out from the thicket and pounced on Wáng Huá.
It crouched over him on the ground,
but had not yet injured him,
and instead sat there firmly.
Zhāng Huá shouted and ran,
and the tiger then left Wáng Huá
and came after Zhāng Huá.
After catching him,
it sat on him as well.
At that moment, the dog was hidden in the deep grass.
Seeing Huá captured,
it suddenly rushed out,
leaped onto the tiger’s head,
and bit the tiger’s nose.
The tiger, not expecting its attack,
fled in shock and fear.
Both men lay stiff and fallen on the ground,
as if in a deep stupor.
The dog used its nose to press against its master’s mouth to draw breath,
and immediately caused him to spit out saliva.
After repeating this several times,
its master gradually revived.
The dog then pressed its mouth against Wáng Huá’s mouth,
doing the same as before.
After a long while,
Wáng Huá was able to move,
and they helped each other up.
The dog lay down as if in a stupor,
and died by evening.
Fàn Yì
Fàn Yì
was a man from Hédōng.
He was appointed as a junior officer for his martial skills.
He kept a dog,
which was remarkably human-like in nature.
Yì had an acquaintance named Chén Fú,
who was also appointed as a junior officer.
Yì was assigned to go to Huáinán as an envoy,
to purchase silk and brocade,
with Fú serving as his deputy at the time.
Yì, during a drinking feast,
relied on his temper and scorned Fú,
leading to enmity between them.
Fú then secretly fabricated charges against Yì.
He secretly submitted a report to the commander.
The commander, unaware of the circumstances,
believed the accusations to be true,
and suspended Yì from his duties.
Yì returned home nursing his resentment,
while Fú was greatly promoted and appointed in his place.
Yì’s dog, seeing Yì demoted and cast aside,
went to Fú’s residence,
waited until he was asleep,
bit off his head,
and carried it back to show Yì.
Yì was shocked and frightened.
Taking Fú’s head,
he led the dog to the commander to plead guilty.
The commander questioned him,
and Yì explained the earlier events.
The commander investigated the matter,
and restored Yì to his original position.
The commander kept the dog at his official residence.
Guō Zhāo
Minister Guō Zhāo,
during the Dàhé era,
moved from Zǐtóng to take command of Xīliáng Prefecture.
At that time, there was a gatekeeper who was very diligent and simple.
Zhāo trusted him,
and assigned him many tasks.
One day,
Zhāo ordered him to purchase over a hundred bolts of patterned silk and satin,
but the price was double the usual,
and Zhāo thought he was cheating him,
so he imprisoned him,
intending to punish him for the offense.
Once the case was prepared,
Zhāo ordered him to be flogged in the courtyard.
Suddenly, more than ten dogs
rushed to shield his back,
and the officers and soldiers could not control them.
Zhāo was greatly astonished,
and questioned him about the matter.
The gatekeeper said:
“I enjoy reading the Buddhist Diamond Sutra,
and since childhood, I have often fed groups of dogs with food.
I know nothing else.”
Zhāo sighed and said:
“Even dogs can sense his kindness;
how can I not show mercy?”
He then released the gatekeeper.
Lú Yán
Lú Yán
was a man from Shàngdǎng.
He often traveled and stayed in other towns.
While on the road,
he suddenly saw a dog, emaciated and near death.
Yán took pity on it,
and took it in to care for it.
After about ten days,
the dog became very plump and glossy.
From then on, wherever he traveled through commanderies and towns,
he always took it with him.
Later, as he was about to reach Bó,
he suddenly met a friend in the market who invited him to drink,
and he returned home heavily intoxicated,
entering his room to sleep.
Soon after, a fire broke out in the neighboring shop.
The dog, in a frantic rush,
climbed onto the bed,
howled and barked at Yán’s head,
then grabbed his clothes and tugged at them.
Yán suddenly woke in alarm,
and saw that the fire had already ignited the pillars of his house.
He dashed out through the flames,
narrowly escaping the disaster.
Elder Zhào
West of Fúfēng County stood the Dàhé Temple,
located on a high ridge.
Below it was a niche,
open like a hall,
where a poor man named Elder Zhào made his home.
The elder had no wife or children,
suffered from a lame leg and a hunched back,
and often walked with a cane begging for food.
The villagers pitied him for his old age and illness,
and his destitution with nowhere to turn,
so they regularly gave him food.
Whenever the elder received food,
he would always gather a pack of dogs and feed them first.
After more than a year,
the elder fell ill from the cold,
and lay in his niche.
At the time, heavy snow was falling,
and the elder had no clothes,
lying naked on the ground,
shivering and groaning.
The pack of dogs all gathered before the elder,
wagging their tails and howling.
Soon, they circled his bedding,
vying to press their bodies against him with their paws.
Thus, the cold was somewhat alleviated.
After more than ten days,
he ultimately died from the cold in his niche.
The dogs all mourned with sorrowful cries,
ceaselessly day and night,
and only left after several days.
Lù Jī
When Lù Jī of Jìn was young,
he was quite fond of hunting.
While in Wú,
a servant from his household presented him with a swift hound named "Huáng'ěr."
When Jī took up a post in Luòyáng,
he often kept the dog by his side.
This dog was clever and intelligent,
able to understand human speech.
Moreover, it could be lent to someone three hundred lǐ away,
and the dog would find its own way back.
When Jī was detained by official duties in the capital,
he had long received no news from home.
Jī jokingly said to the dog:
"I have absolutely no letters from home;
could you carry a letter and swiftly bring back news?"
The dog was delighted,
wagging its tail and making sounds in response.
Jī tried writing a letter,
placed it in a bamboo tube,
and tied it around the dog's neck.
The dog took the postal road,
heading toward Wú.
When hungry, it would enter the grass to eat meat.
Whenever it encountered a large body of water,
it would approach the ferryman,
smoothing its fur and wagging its tail toward him,
and thus gain passage across.
Upon reaching Jī's home,
it held the tube in its mouth,
making sounds to signal.
Jī's family opened the tube,
took out the letter and read it.
The dog then made sounds toward the people again,
as if asking for something.
His family wrote a reply,
placed it in the tube,
and again tied it around the dog's neck.
The dog swiftly returned to Luòyáng.
Estimating that a human would take fifty days for the round trip,
the dog's journey there and back took only half that time.
Later, when the dog died,
it was buried two hundred paces south of Jī's village,
where a mound of earth was piled to form a grave.
The villagers called it "Huáng'ěr's Tomb."
Shí Xuándù
During the Yuánhuī era of Sòng,
there was a man named Shí Xuándù who kept a yellow dog,
which gave birth to a white puppy.
The mother dog loved it exceptionally,
often carrying food to feed it.
When it grew up,
every time Xuándù went hunting and had not returned,
the mother dog would wait outside the gate for him.
Later, Xuándù suffered from a cough,
which gradually became critical.
The doctor prescribed a remedy,
requiring the lungs of a white dog.
Searching the market, they could not find one,
so they killed the white dog they had raised,
taking its lungs for the medicinal soup.
Thereafter, the mother dog leaped and howled,
not ceasing for days.
When Xuándù's family cooked the dog
and served it to guests,
throwing the bones on the ground,
the mother dog would carry them into the house.
After the meal,
she moved them to a mulberry tree in the backyard,
dug a hole, and buried them.
Day and night, she howled and barked at the tree,
and only stopped after over a month.
Meanwhile, Xuándù's illness did not improve,
and he eventually passed away.
Before dying, he said to those around him:
"The soup did not cure my illness,
and I have truly wrongfully killed this dog."
His younger brother, Fǎdù,
henceforth never ate dog meat again.
Qí Qióng
In the Táng dynasty, there was a senior officer of the imperial guard named Qí Qióng,
who initially gained great favor through his horsemanship,
receiving immense imperial grace.
Thus, he was granted a nominal imperial title,
and his authority extended to severe punishments.
He kept four fine dogs at home,
often taking them hunting in vast parks,
and feeding them fine grains and meat.
One of them would always stuff the food into its throat and teeth before leaving,
as if hiding in thickets before eating.
After eating, it would return.
Qí secretly found this strange.
One day,
he ordered a servant to follow it to see where it went.
It went to a dry hole in the northern wall,
where its mother lived.
She was old, thin, and afflicted with mange,
and the dog would regurgitate food to feed her.
Qí, being a righteous man,
marveled at this for a long time.
He then had the mother dog brought back in a basket,
laid her on a mat,
and fed her with leftover cakes and pastries.
The dog wagged its tail and bowed its head,
as if feeling gratitude.
Afterward, when catching wrongdoers or chasing cunning prey,
it pointed and followed like the wind.
When accompanying the hunt before the emperor,
it always earned rich rewards.
After a year, the mother dog died,
and the dog worked even harder.
After another cycle of seasons,
Qí also passed away.
The dog howled and barked all night,
wailing without cease.
A month later,
when preparations were made for the burial mound,
the mastiff was left behind to guard against thieves.
On the night of the burial,
the dog alone came and pawed the earth into a hollow,
knocking its head against the coffin until it bled.
Before the earth was fully covered,
the dog also died.
Shí Cóngyì
At the home of Shí Cóngyì, a military officer in Qínzhōu,
a dog gave birth to several puppies,
one of which was presented to the military commander, the Duke of Lángyá.
From a young age until it grew up,
it was separated from its mother.
When the military governor led his generals and officers to hunt in the suburban fields,
the dog suddenly encountered its mother in the fields.
Their joyful expressions
were beyond description.
After the hunt,
each followed its master home.
From then on, the puppy daily stole meat from the commander's kitchen,
bringing it back to feed its mother.
It even carried heads, bellies, shoulders, and ribs,
filling the home of the military officer.
No one in the officer's household knew of this.
Tián Zhāo
Tián Zhāo
was from Guǎnglíng.
In the early Zhēnyuán era,
Zhāo went to Wǎnlíng on other business.
At that time, his cousin Xuē Xí was there.
When Xí saw Zhāo arrive,
he treated him with the utmost hospitality.
One day,
Zhāo said to Xí:
"I feel like eating dog meat."
Xí searched everywhere for it,
but could not find any.
Zhāo said:
"What use is the dog in your house?
You could kill it and eat it."
Xí said:
"This dog has been raised for a long time;
who could bear to do it?"
Zhāo said:
"I'll help you kill it."
After saying this,
Zhāo tried to catch the dog,
but it suddenly disappeared,
and they could not find it.
Ten days later,
Zhāo told Xí
he would return to Guǎnglíng.
Xí, due to their familial ties,
sent him off with generous gifts.
Zhāo left the city,
and when resting at Zhúshìbù,
he suddenly saw Xí's dog by the roadside.
Zhāo recognized it and called it,
and the dog wagged its tail and followed him.
Zhāo reached an inn at night,
and when he was about to sleep,
the dog also followed and stayed with him.
Waiting until Zhāo was asleep,
it bit his head,
and carried it back.
Xí was terrified,
and reported the matter to the local authorities.
The prefect sent people to investigate,
found it strange, and released him.
Péi Dù
Minister Péi Dù was fond of keeping dogs by nature.
Whenever he stayed somewhere and hosted banquets,
he would bring them all along.
Any leftover food from what he ate,
he would mix in a bowl and feed to the dogs.
At the time, his son-in-law Lǐ Jiǎ saw this,
and admonished him repeatedly.
Minister Péi said:
"Humans and dogs are of the same kind—
why do you despise them so much?"
A dog was eating,
and upon seeing Lǐ admonishing,
it abandoned its food,
glared at Lǐ with its eyes and left.
Minister Péi said:
"This dog has human nature—
it will surely bear a grudge against you.
I secretly worry about this."
Lǐ thought it was a joke.
When he was about to take a midday nap,
the dog crouched facing Lǐ.
Lǐ saw this,
and began to suspect the dog bore him a grudge.
Seeing that he had not yet slept,
the dog went out of his room again.
After Lǐ saw the dog leave,
he arranged a towel and comb on the pillow,
laid out many clothes,
and covered them with a quilt,
making it look as if a person were sleeping.
Lǐ then hid in a different place to watch.
After a short while,
the dog entered his room.
Thinking Lǐ was already asleep,
it jumped onto the bed
and bit at the throat.
After biting, it realized its mistake.
The dog then jumped down from the bed in fury,
howled and barked, and died.
Lǐ Dàoyù
Ān Guó's Lǐ Dàoyù,
during the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng dynasty,
had a household dog lying in the middle of the road.
Dàoyù stumbled over it,
and the dog said:
"You are about to die—
why step on me?"
Dàoyù died not long after.
Zhū Xiūzhī
There was a man named Zhū Xiūzhī.
During the Yuánjiā era,
while sitting facing his brother,
their household dog suddenly crouched, looked at the two of them, and laughed.
It then shook its head and said:
"You say I cannot sing—
listen to me sing of the plum blossoms.
This year may still be fine,
but what about you next year?"
His family spared the dog and did not kill it.
When the plum blossoms bloomed,
the brothers fought each other,
and the younger brother, wielding a halberd, injured the elder.
He was imprisoned for a year.
At night,
the entire family died of plague.
Lǐ Shūjiān
In the Hàn dynasty, Lǐ Shūjiān of Rǔnán was young and held an official post.
His household dog suddenly stood up like a human and walked.
The family all requested to kill it.
Shūjiān said:
"Dogs and horses are compared to gentlemen—
seeing humans walk, it imitates them.
What harm is there?"
Later, Shūjiān took off his hat and placed it on the couch.
The dog put it on and ran off.
The family was greatly alarmed,
but Shūjiān did not find it strange.
Soon after, the dog again tended the fire in front of the stove.
The family grew even more astonished,
but Shūjiān said:
"The children and servants are all in the fields—
the dog helps tend the fire.
Fortunately, we need not trouble the neighbors.
What is so bad about that?"
After about ten days,
the dog died on its own,
and in the end, there was not the slightest misfortune.
Shūjiān eventually enjoyed a high official position.
Wáng Hú
Shānyáng's Wáng Hú, styled Mènglián,
was from Lánlíng in Dōnghǎi.
In the middle of the night,
a clerk in a black headscarf and white single-layer robe came to the county office and knocked at the gate.
When they went to greet him,
he suddenly vanished.
This happened for several years.
Later, they lay in wait,
and saw an old dog with a black head and white body,
still coming to the gate as before.
They reported this to Mènglián,
who killed it,
and the occurrences ceased.
Lǐ Dé
Minister Lǐ Dé of Dōnglái had his coffin laid out during the funeral,
when he suddenly appeared in form,
sitting on the sacrificial bed.
His complexion, clothing, and ornaments
were exactly like Lǐ Dé's.
He saw his daughters-in-law and grandchildren,
then instructed them on household affairs,
all in an orderly manner.
He whipped and beat the servants,
each according to their faults.
After eating and drinking his fill,
he bid farewell and left.
The entire family, young and old,
grieved as if severed from him.
This went on for four or five years.
Later, he drank too much,
became drunk, and his true form was revealed—
it was only an old dog.
They all beat it to death together.
Upon investigation,
it turned out to be a dog from the village wine shop.
Wēn Jìnglín
Jìn dynasty Imperial Library Director Wēn Jìnglín of Tàiyuán had been dead for a year.
His wife, née Huán,
suddenly saw Jìnglín return.
They slept together,
but he refused to see his children and younger relatives.
When his elder brother's son came to see Jìnglín,
Jìnglín slightly opened the window
and showed his face to meet him.
Later, when he got drunk, his true form was revealed—
it was the neighbor's old yellow dog.
They then beat it to death.
Née Yǔ
Granduncle Wáng later married a daughter of the Yǔ family.
She was young and beautiful.
Wáng was sixty years old
and often slept elsewhere,
so the wife was deeply unhappy.
Later, one evening, she suddenly saw Wáng return.
Their affection was even greater than usual.
During the day, they sat together
and ate together.
A servant came in from outside,
saw this, and was greatly shocked.
He reported it to Wáng.
Wáng hurried in,
and the impostor also came out.
The two met in the courtyard,
both wearing white caps,
with identical clothing and appearance.
The real Wáng first raised his staff and struck the impostor,
and the impostor also struck back.
Each ordered their followers
to lend a hand.
Wáng's son then rushed forward and beat him fiercely,
whereupon he turned into a yellow dog.
Wáng was then an assistant in the Kuàijī prefecture.
The gatekeeper said
he often saw an old yellow dog
coming from the east.
The wife was deeply ashamed
and died of an illness.
Shěn Bà
In Wúxīng, there was a man named Shěn Bà.
During the Tàiyuán era,
he dreamed that a woman came to sleep with him.
His companions secretly observed
and saw only a female dog.
Whenever Shěn Bà slept,
it would come and lean against the bed.
Suspecting it was a demon,
they killed and ate it.
Shěn Bà then dreamed of a person in black clothes reproaching him, saying:
"I originally intended to serve you as a woman.
If I did not suit your heart,
you could have spoken to me directly.
Why did you suddenly bring such shame upon me?
Please return my bones to me."
The next day,
they collected the bones and buried them on a hill.
From then on, peace was restored.
Tián Yǎn
Tián Yǎn of Běipíng
was in mourning for his mother
and constantly stayed in the mourning hut.
One evening, he suddenly entered his wife's chamber.
She secretly found it strange
and said:
"You are in a place of mourning and destruction;
it would be fortunate if you did not indulge in pleasure."
Tián Yǎn did not listen and lay with her.
Later, when Tián Yǎn briefly entered again,
he did not speak to his wife.
His wife, finding it strange that he remained silent,
reproached him about the earlier incident.
Tián Yǎn realized it was a demon.
As evening approached, he stayed awake.
He hung his mourning clothes in the hut.
After a short while,
he saw a white dog snatch the mourning clothes from the hut and carry them in its mouth.
It then transformed into a human,
put on the clothes, and entered.
Tián Yǎn followed and chased it,
and when he saw the dog about to climb onto his wife's bed,
he struck and killed it.
His wife, ashamed and distressed, fell ill and died.
Wáng Zhòngwén
Wáng Zhòngwén of the Sòng dynasty served as the registrar for the Governor of Hénán
and lived north of Gōushì County.
On a day off,
he was walking through the marshes in the evening
when he saw a white dog behind his carriage.
Wáng Zhòngwén was very fond of it
and wanted to take it.
Suddenly, it transformed into a human-like shape,
resembling a Fāngxiàng spirit,
with eyes as red as fire,
bared teeth, and a protruding tongue—
extremely repulsive.
Wáng Zhòngwén and his servant attacked it together,
but it fled before they could defeat it.
Before reaching home,
they both fell to the ground and died.
Cuī Huìtóng
During the Táng dynasty's Kāiyuán era,
Cuī Huìtóng, the son-in-law of Princess Gāodū,
had a servant named Wàndí who was extremely violent
and took pleasure in killing.
The princess's female dog, named "Huángnǚ,"
had been missing for several days.
Just as the princess summoned Wàndí
to assign him a task,
Huángnǚ suddenly appeared before the princess, moving back and forth,
and bit Wàndí.
Others tried to scold and stop it but could not,
and only after a long while did it retreat.
When called, it would disappear.
The princess's household found this strange.
Wàndí confessed, saying:
"A few days ago,
I indeed cooked and ate this dog.
I do not know how it has come to this."
At first, they did not believe him,
but Wàndí said:
"I can show you where I buried its head."
They retrieved it as proof,
and from then on, they knew it was the dog's vengeful spirit.
Lǐ Yì
Lǐ Yì of the Táng Dynasty was
a man from Huáiyīn.
He lost his father in his youth,
and served his mother with great filial piety.
Even compared to those who wept for bamboo shoots or lay on ice,
he was not surpassed.
When his mother passed away,
Lǐ Yì wept and wailed,
fainting multiple times until the burial.
After more than a month,
he finally buried her.
Upon returning home,
he saw his mother as if alive,
inside the house.
She rose, took Lǐ Yì’s hand,
and said tearfully:
"I have now returned to life.
After you buried me,
I secretly came back,
but you did not see me."
Overjoyed, Lǐ Yì leaped with excitement,
and resumed caring for her as before.
She then said to Lǐ Yì:
"Be careful not to open the coffin in the grave.
If you open it,
I will die again."
Lǐ Yì obeyed her.
Three years later,
Lǐ Yì dreamed of his mother at night.
She wept and pounded on the door, saying:
"I am your mother.
Have I not toiled with the hardships of nurturing you in swaddling clothes?
Moreover, you lost your father young,
and I, as a widow, raised you.
How could it be that after my death,
for three years you have not offered sacrifices to me?
I have come repeatedly,
but upon reaching the door,
an old dog guards it,
not allowing me to enter.
I am your mother,
you are my son.
Does Heaven not know this?
If you still do not make offerings,
I will surely appeal to Heaven."
After speaking,
she wept and left.
Lǐ Yì also rose and chased her,
but could not catch up.
At dawn,
he was troubled, doubtful, and sorrowful,
unable to decide what to do.
The old mother he was caring for then said:
"Why does my son look unhappy with me today?
It must be because I have not passed away for so long,
causing you to grow weary in your filial care."
Lǐ Yì then tearfully said:
"It is truly because I dreamed of an ominous matter last night,
difficult to speak of to you, Mother.
I beg you not to blame me."
Thus, he hesitated again.
A few days later,
he again dreamed of his mother.
She came to the door, crying out,
struck her chest, and said:
"Lǐ Yì,
are you my son or not?
How can you be so extremely unfilial!
Since burying me,
you have not visited my grave at all,
but only care for a dog.
Yet I will ultimately appeal to Heaven,
and you will be punished for this.
Because of our deep mother-son bond,
I am warning you once more."
After speaking, she left again,
and Lǐ Yì chased her but could not catch up.
At dawn,
he secretly went to the burial mound,
offered prayers and sacrifices, saying:
"I, Yì, was born by my mother,
raised by my mother,
and only thus became a man in this world.
How could I lack gratitude for my mother?
How could I lack affection as a son?
While my mother was alive,
I warmed her in winter and cooled her in summer,
attended to her morning and evening,
and never dared neglect the respectful care she deserved.
I never dared be remiss.
Unfortunately, I lost her loving presence,
and bore the eternal pain of her passing.
If I barely survive,
it is to honor her with sacrifices.
On the day I buried my mother,
she returned home and came back to life.
Now I care for her without fail.
Yet these two unfathomable matters
leave me with no way to decide,
wavering all day long.
How can I find clarity?
Lately, I have repeatedly dreamed of my mother sorrowfully reproaching me.
Is the mother in the dream the real one?
Or is the mother at home the real one?
If I follow the mother in the dream,
I fear hurting the mother at home;
if I follow the mother at home,
I worry the events in the dream are real.
Alas!
This is the difficulty of being a son,
not unfilialness.
May Heaven examine this!"
After speaking, he wept loudly,
offered sacrifices again, and returned.
The mother at home already knew of this.
She met Lǐ Yì and said to him:
"I am your mother,
who died and returned to life.
I have shared life’s path with you again,
yet how could you suddenly become confused and forgetful,
and go before an empty grave to break that eerie dream?
Now you know I will die again."
She then collapsed and died.
Lǐ Yì never understood what happened.
He wailed in grief for several days,
then planned to bury her again.
When he opened the grave,
he found his deceased mother in the coffin.
Startled, he fled back home.
The newly deceased mother
had transformed into an extremely old black dog,
leaped out,
and disappeared to an unknown place.
Hú Zhìzhōng
Hú Zhìzhōng, a junior officer from Chùzhōu, was dispatched on a mission to Yuè.
One night, he dreamed of a creature
with a dog’s head and a human body,
which said to him:
“I have not eaten for over a year.
I hear you are traveling to Kuàijī,
and you will surely lodge at my inn.
Could you spare some of your food for me?”
In the dream, Zhìzhōng did not consent.
The next morning, he set out.
That night, he stopped at a mountain inn.
The innkeeper said:
“This hall often harbors a monstrous creature
that may cause harm.
It is not safe to sleep or eat here;
please stay in the eastern wing instead.”
Zhìzhōng replied:
“My integrity can ward off ghosts and monsters,
and my courage can repel wickedness and evil.
What monster is there to fear?”
He urged them to serve the meal.
Just as he picked up his chopsticks,
a strange creature appeared,
massive in form,
standing right before the tray.
The attendants retreated in fear,
not daring to look.
Zhìzhōng pushed aside the roasted meat
and rose to strike it.
The creature let out successive cries of pain,
sounding like a dog,
yet its words were perfectly clear:
“Stop, please stop!
If you do not stop,
it is uncertain who will die.”
Zhìzhōng swung his arm even more fiercely.
The creature then cried out urgently:
“Where is Bān’ér?”
Immediately, another creature
came from outside the screen
and darted swiftly in.
Zhìzhōng struck at it as well.
But his cap fell and his belt came loose;
it seemed his strength was failing.
The servants, unable to rescue him,
could only beat at the creatures with brooms.
They dragged him into the eastern chamber,
and the sound of his collapse
was like a wall crumbling.
Not long after,
Zhìzhōng emerged with his cap and belt properly arranged,
returned to the tray, and ordered the meal to continue.
He spoke not a word,
only occasionally gazing toward the chamber
and sighing softly.
The next morning, as he prepared to leave,
he sealed the door
and instructed the innkeeper:
“Do not open this until I return.
If you open it secretly,
disaster will surely befall you.”
Having said this, he departed.
More than ten days later,
he returned to the inn.
He asked for brush and inkstone,
and with tears, inscribed on the door:
“Relying on courage invites calamity;
relying on strength leads to downfall.
Why should a man of noble worth
contend with vile creatures?
Let not my departing soul hasten to the official court,
but rest in this inn and return to the dark unknown.”
After writing,
he threw down the brush and vanished.
The one holding the brush was terrified,
feeling a faint breeze brush his face and then disperse.
The innkeeper reported the matter to the prefect,
who sent an officer to open the door.
Inside, they found Zhìzhōng and two dogs, one spotted and one black,
all lying dead in the northwest corner.
Hán Shēng
During the Zhēnyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a man named Hán Shēng, who held the position of Dàlǐ Píngshì.
He resided in the southern part of Xīhé Commandery.
He owned a very spirited and strong horse.
One morning,
the horse suddenly hung its head over the manger.
It was sweating and panting,
as if exhausted from a long journey.
The stableman found this strange
and reported it in full to Hán Shēng.
Hán Shēng angrily said:
"You must have stolen the horse and taken it out at night,
causing my horse to become exhausted.
Whose fault is this?"
He then ordered the stableman to be beaten.
The stableman had no words to defend himself,
so he received the beating.
By the next day,
the horse was again sweating and panting.
The stableman secretly thought it strange,
but could not fathom the reason.
That evening,
the stableman lay down in the stable,
closed the door,
and peered through a crack.
Suddenly, he saw the black dog kept by Hán Shēng enter the stable.
It howled and leaped about.
In a moment, it transformed into a man,
dressed entirely in black.
He then placed a saddle on the horse
and rode away.
When he reached the gate,
the wall was very high.
The man in black struck the horse with his whip,
and it leaped over.
The man in black rode the horse away,
and after some time had passed,
he dismounted and removed the saddle.
The man in black then howled and leaped again,
transforming back into a dog.
The stableman was astonished,
but did not dare tell anyone.
Another evening later,
the black dog again rode the horse away,
returning only at dawn.
The stableman then followed the horse's tracks.
