Because the rain had just cleared,
the tracks were clearly visible.
They led straight south for over ten lǐ,
to the front of an ancient tomb,
where the horse's tracks ended.
The stableman then built a thatched hut beside the tomb.
The following evening,
he first went to the hut
to wait and observe.
As midnight approached,
the man in black indeed rode the horse there.
He dismounted
and tied the horse to a wild tree.
The man entered the tomb
and laughed and talked with several others, extremely joyfully.
The stableman, inside the thatched hut,
crouched down and listened,
not daring to move.
After nearly the time it takes to eat a meal,
the man in black announced his departure,
and the several others saw him out of the tomb.
In the wilderness,
there was a man in brown clothes
who turned to the man in black and said:
"Where is Hán's register of names now?"
The man in black said:
"I have already hidden it under the pounding stone.
You need not worry."
The man in brown said:
"Be careful not to reveal it,
for if it is revealed, none of us will remain intact."
The man in black said:
"I heed your instruction."
The man in brown said:
"Does Hán's young child have a courtesy name yet?"
He replied:
"Not yet.
I will wait until he has a courtesy name,
then add it to the register of names.
I will not dare forget."
The man in brown said:
"Come again tomorrow night,
and we shall have more laughter and talk."
Then the man in black left.
At dawn,
the stableman returned
and secretly reported the matter to Hán Shēng.
Hán Shēng immediately ordered meat to lure the dog.
Once the dog arrived,
he had it tied with a rope.
Then, based on what he had heard,
he searched under the pounding stone,
and indeed found a scroll.
It fully recorded the names of the Hán family's brothers, wives, children, and servants.
Every detail was included—
this was the so-called Hán family register of names.
There was a son who had been born just a month ago,
and only this child was not recorded—
this was the so-called young child without a courtesy name.
Hán Shēng was greatly astonished.
He ordered the dog brought into the courtyard,
whipped it, and killed it.
He cooked its meat
and fed it to the servants.
Afterwards, he led over a thousand local gentlemen and neighbors,
armed with bows, arrows, and weapons,
to the ancient tomb south of the commandery.
They excavated the tomb.
Inside the tomb were several dogs,
all with unusual fur and appearance.
They killed them all and returned.
Dù Xiūjǐ
Dù Xiūjǐ was a man from Yuè,
who practiced medicine.
His wife was the daughter of the wealthy man Xuē Zàn from Zhàozhōu,
and she was licentious and unrestrained.
Xiūjǐ kept a white dog at home,
which he loved dearly,
often feeding it delicacies.
After eating,
when Xiūjǐ went out,
the dog would suddenly enter the room,
wanting to bite Xiūjǐ's wife, Xuē shì,
yet it seemed to harbor lustful intentions.
Xuē, finding this strange, asked it:
"Do you want to have relations with me?
If so,
then do not bite me."
The dog immediately wagged its tail and climbed onto her bed.
Xuē shì, out of fear, had relations with it.
The dog was no different from a man.
Thereafter, whenever Xiūjǐ went out,
it would engage in unrestrained debauchery.
Suddenly one day,
while they were sleeping together in the room,
Xiūjǐ entered from outside,
saw them,
and immediately wanted to kill the dog.
The dog ran out.
Xiūjǐ, enraged,
sent his wife Xuē shì back to Xuē Zàn.
Half a year later,
the dog suddenly burst into Xuē Zàn's house,
grabbed Xuē shì's hair in its mouth, carried her on its back, and ran out.
The family chased after them,
but could not catch up.
No one knew where they went.
The dog carried Xuē shì straight into Héngshān and hid there.
Every night,
it would go down the mountain,
stealing food.
During the day, it would guard Xuē shì.
After a year,
Xuē shì became pregnant.
She gave birth to a boy,
who, though his appearance was human,
had white hair all over his body.
Xuē shì raised him alone in the mountains.
Another year later,
the dog suddenly died.
Xuē then carried the child,
wandering out,
and entered Jìzhōu to beg for food.
Someone who knew of this matter
went to Xuē Zàn to inform him.
Xuē Zàn then ordered his family to bring them home.
Later, when the son was seven years old,
his appearance was ugly,
and his nature was fierce and wicked.
He would often sneak out
to become a bandit.
Sometimes for over ten days,
sometimes for several months,
he would then return.
Xuē Zàn was troubled by this
and wanted to kill him.
Xuē shì then tearfully admonished her son:
"You are the son of a white dog.
When you were young, I could not bear to kill you.
Now that you are in the Xuē family,
how can you not be more careful?
If you sneak out again
to become a bandit outside,
the Xuē family will surely kill you.
I fear you will implicate others;
you must change."
Her son wailed loudly and said:
"I was born with the essence of a dog.
I have no human heart;
I love killing and being a bandit.
This is natural;
why do you blame me?
If Xuē Zàn can tolerate me,
then let him tolerate me.
If he cannot tolerate me,
he should tell me,
why kill me?
If he truly cannot tolerate me,
I will flee,
and never return."
Xuē shì tried hard to keep him,
but could not.
She then said to him:
"If you must go, then go,
but why not come back from time to time to see me?
I am your mother;
how can I bear never to see you again?"
Her son wailed again and said:
"In three years,
I will return once more."
Then, taking up a sword,
he bowed to his mother and left.
After three years,
the son indeed led a group of over a thousand bandits,
calling himself General White.
After entering and bowing to his mother,
he ordered his bandits to kill everyone in Xuē Zàn's household,
sparing only his mother.
He then burned down the residence
and took his mother away.
Yuán Jìqiān
The young general, Vice-Director Yuán Jìqiān, often said:
"I once lived in Qīngshè,
borrowing a house to stay in.
It was notoriously haunted.
At dusk,
I dared not go outside.
The whole family was on alert and fearful,
unable to sleep peacefully.
Suddenly one night,
we heard a roaring sound,
as if someone was calling from inside a jar.
The voice was very muffled.
The whole family was terrified,
thinking it must be an especially strange monster.
So we peeked through a crack in the window
and saw a bluish-black creature moving about in the courtyard.
That night the moon was dark,
and after watching for a long time,
it seemed like a yellow dog's body but its head could not be raised.
So I struck its chest with an iron rod.
Suddenly there was a loud bang,
and the family dog yelped in surprise and ran away.
It turned out that day, oil had been delivered from the estate,
and the dog had stuck its head into an oil container,
unable to pull it out.
The whole family laughed and slept peacefully."
Yuèzhī Shāogē
In Yuèzhī, there are sheep with large tails.
They are slightly cut to provide for guests,
and they also gradually heal themselves.
In Dàqín,
there are lambs in the north
that are born from the earth.
The Qín people wait for them to sprout,
and build walls around them.
Their navels are connected to the ground,
so they cannot be cut with a knife.
They beat drums to startle them, causing the connection to break.
Then they jump, bleat, and eat grass,
forming herds of one to two hundred.
Western Regions Large Sheep
When the monk Xuánzàng reached the Western Regions,
on a high ridge of the great snowy mountains, there was a village
that raised sheep as large as donkeys.
Jìbīn Green Sheep
The country of Jìbīn produces wild green sheep,
with tails like kingfisher feathers.
The locals eat them.
Qí Litigant
During the time of Duke Zhuāng of Qí,
there were two villagers who had been litigating for three years without a verdict.
The duke then ordered the two men to prepare a sheep
and swear an oath at the shrine.
The two men were about to stab the sheep
and sprinkle its blood when the sheep stood up and butted the two men,
killing them at the site of the oath.
Liáng Wén
Liáng Wén of Qí in the Hàn dynasty was fond of the Way.
In his home there was a shrine for deities,
comprising three or four rooms.
On the seat was placed a black curtain,
and he often stayed inside it.
After more than ten years had passed,
later, during a sacrificial ceremony,
suddenly someone spoke from within the curtain,
calling himself Gāoshān Jūn.
He was greatly capable of eating and drinking,
and effective in curing illnesses.
Wén served him with utmost reverence.
After several years had passed,
he was allowed to enter the curtain.
When the deity was drunk,
Wén then begged to be granted an audience to see his face.
He said to Wén:
"Give me your hand."
Wén offered his hand,
and was able to hold his chin—
his beard was very long.
Wén gradually wrapped his hand around it,
and suddenly pulled,
hearing the sound of a sheep being killed.
Those seated in the hall rose in alarm,
and helped Wén pull,
only to find it was a sheep from Yuán Shù's household.
It had been missing for seven or eight years,
with no one knowing where it was.
After it was killed, the haunting ceased.
Gù Pèi
Gù Pèi was
a prominent figure of Wú,
who once saw off guests at Shēngpíng Pavilion.
At the time, there was a monk of common customs among the guests.
He said someone wanted to kill a sheep,
but the sheep broke free from the rope,
and ran over to take refuge with this monk,
thrusting its head under his kasaya.
The owner ordered it taken away to be killed,
and after it was roasted.
he first cut a piece to give to the monk to eat.
After the monk swallowed it,
he felt the roast meat moving under his skin,
causing unbearable pain.
He called for a doctor to needle it,
and several needles were inserted,
yet the roast meat still quivered.
Only after cutting open the flesh to look
did they find it was still a piece of meat.
From this, the monk fell ill,
bleating like a sheep,
foaming at the mouth,
and died shortly after returning to the temple.
Pān Guǒ
In the Táng dynasty, a man from the capital surnamed Pān, named Guǒ,
was not yet twenty years old.
During the Wǔdé era,
he served as a minor clerk in the Dūshuǐ office.
Returning home,
he went out to the fields with several youths to play.
Passing by a graveyard,
they saw a sheep that had been left behind by a shepherd,
standing alone and eating grass.
Guǒ, along with the youths, caught it
and took it home.
On the way, the sheep cried out.
Fearing the owner would hear,
Guǒ then pulled out the sheep's tongue
and killed and ate it that night.
A year later,
Guǒ's tongue gradually shrank away completely.
He submitted a petition to resign from his post.
The magistrate of Fùpíng County, Zhèng Yúqìng, suspected it was a deception,
and ordered him to open his mouth for inspection.
It was then seen that he had no tongue at all,
only a stump about the size of a bean remaining.
The officials asked him the reason.
Guǒ took paper
and wrote to answer them.
The official at the time clicked his tongue in pity,
instructing him to perform meritorious deeds for the sheep.
He copied the Lotus Sutra.
Guǒ resolved to believe in the teachings,
maintaining fasting and precepts without fail,
and cultivated blessings for the sheep.
After another year,
his tongue gradually regrew,
restored to its original state.
He again petitioned the officials.
The county official appointed him as village head.
Yúqìng, by the eighteenth year of Zhēnguān,
served as Investigating Censor,
and personally recounted this story.
Lǐ Shěnyán
During the Wànshòu era,
a commoner of Cháng'ān named Lǐ Shěnyán suddenly fell ill as if mad,
needing to eat together with sheep.
His family could not stop him.
Seeking medical treatment was ineffective.
Later, he suddenly ran westward,
nearly a hundred lǐ away,
and encountered a flock of sheep by the roadside.
He hastily ran into their midst.
Just as those chasing him arrived,
Shěnyán had already transformed into a large sheep,
indistinguishable among the flock.
When his family all arrived,
they wept and searched for him.
One large sheep
then spoke on its own:
"Take me home,
but be careful not to kill me.
I am happy as a sheep—
how can humans compare?"
So they took it home to raise,
until it lived out its natural lifespan.
Yáng Shì
In the Yáng family residence in Cháng'ān, there was always a woman in black garments,
no one knew where she came from.
Whenever she entered the hall,
she would go straight to the young ladies and say:
"Heaven has sent me to be your friend."
They were all frightened and avoided her.
If they could not,
she would speak insolently.
Her behavior was very vulgar;
sometimes she walked about naked.
Those around would cover their eyes.
Then she would go outside,
flirt with men,
and boldly engage in lewd acts.
She could never be captured.
One day,
she took all the undergarments from the young ladies' bags
and exposed them in the courtyard.
The young ladies, unable to bear their anger,
cursed her vehemently.
She then unleashed a torrent of foul language,
revealing their private affairs,
down to the minutest detail.
After more than ten days like this,
they called for a shaman,
who used talismans to exorcise her.
But as soon as the shaman left, she would return,
and nothing could stop her.
So they moved to avoid her.
It happened that a relative of the Yáng family
came from afar,
and they told him the whole story.
This man had always been bold,
so he stayed alone in the residence,
lighting a lamp and lying down at night.
The woman indeed came.
He pretended to let her stay and sleep.
Secretly, he had someone hide the shoes she was wearing.
Unable to find them,
she left in disarray.
He took the shoes to look at them—
they were sheep hooves.
Using a plan to search for her,
he went to the temple east of the residence,
and saw a long-lived black sheep,
with double hooves but no nails,
walking with great difficulty.
He redeemed it and killed it,
and the haunting then ceased.
Chén Zhèngguān
Chén Zhèngguān of Yǐngchuān was extremely skilled at butchering sheep heads.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
someone visited Zhèngguān.
Zhèngguān prepared food and drink for him.
Just as he was butchering a sheep head,
the moment the knife first went in,
piercing its cooked breast,
Zhèngguān briefly went to wash his hands.
The head bleated like a sheep several times.
Zhèngguān then felt a palpitation in his heart,
and died a few days later.
Ān Jiǎ
In Bīnzhōu, there was a commoner surnamed Ān,
whose family had been butchers for generations.
At home, they had a ewe and her lamb.
One day,
when he intended to slaughter the mother,
and had just tied her up and placed her on the rack,
the lamb suddenly came before Ān Shēng,
knelt on both front legs,
with tears streaming from its eyes.
Ān Shēng was also astonished by this.
After a long while,
he then put the knife down on the ground and left.
He called a young boy to help with the slaughter.
But when he turned back, the knife was suddenly missing;
it had been carried away by the lamb,
which brought it to the base of the wall
and lay down on top of it.
Ān Shēng suspected it had been stolen by a neighbor,
and fearing he would miss the market time,
moreover having no other knife,
he was extremely agitated.
Suddenly, turning around, he kicked the lamb aside,
and saw the knife beneath the lamb's belly.
Ān Shēng then suddenly understood,
untied the mother sheep and the lamb,
and sent them both to a temple, requesting they be kept alive.
He himself soon left his wife and children,
went to the temple and became a monk under Master Zhú,
with the monastic name "Shǒusī".
The Yān Chancellor
A person from Shuò presented a large pig to the Yān Chancellor,
who ordered the cook to prepare it.
After the pig died,
it appeared in a dream to the Yān Chancellor, saying:
"The Creator burdened me with the form of a pig,
feeding me on human filth.
Relying on your spiritual power, I have now transformed,
and have just become the River Earl of Lǔ."
Dù Yuàn
Jìn Dynasty's Dù Yuàn, courtesy name Yǒngpíng,
was from Fú County in Zǐtóng,
and his family was very wealthy.
He had a son named Tiānbǎo,
whom Yuàn loved dearly;
he was ten years old.
In the third year of the Tàiyuán era,
he died suddenly from illness.
Several months later,
a sow gave birth to five piglets.
One of them was the fattest.
Later, when a new official arrived,
Yuàn intended to give it as a gift,
and proceeded to catch and kill it.
A bhikṣu suddenly came before Yuàn,
and said to him:
"This piglet is your son.
How could you forget him in just over a hundred days?"
Having said this,
he suddenly vanished.
Yuàn looked around,
saw him amidst flames,
soaring into the sky and departing.
Clouds and vapor filled the air,
and did not disperse until the end of the day.
Dūmò
The King of Suōchē killed the King of Yútián.
Yútián's nobleman Dūmò went out and saw a wild boar,
and wanted to capture it.
Then it spoke in human language:
"Do not kill me,
and I will kill Suōchē for you."
Dūmò found this strange,
and immediately joined with his brothers to kill the King of Suōchē.
Liú Hú
In the later Wèi, in Zhíhuò Village,
there were four brothers of the Tàicháng commoner Liú Hú who made butchery their trade.
During the Yǒng'ān years,
when Hú was killing a pig,
the pig suddenly cried out begging for its life,
its voice reaching the four neighboring households.
The neighbors thought the Hú brothers were fighting among themselves,
and came to look,
only to find it was the pig.
Hú then donated his residence to become Guījué Temple,
and the entire family entered the religious life.
Gěng Fúshēng
East of Línhuáng County in Jìzhōu during the Suí Dynasty,
there was a man named Gěng Fúshēng,
whose family had modest assets.
In the eleventh year of the Suí Dàyè era,
Fúshēng's mother, née Zhāng, secretly gave two bolts of silk to her daughter, avoiding her husband's notice.
Several years later,
the mother died,
and was reborn as a sow,
appearing in their household.
She then gave birth to two piglets.
Fúshēng had already eaten them both,
and afterwards she bore no more.
Fúshēng then summoned a butcher to sell her.
Before the butcher could take her,
a traveling monk came to Fúshēng's home begging for food,
and rested briefly at his house.
The monk's young attendant went into the pigpen to play.
The pig spoke to him:
"I am Fúshēng's mother.
Because in the past I avoided my husband's eyes
and took two bolts of silk to give to my daughter,
I am guilty of this crime,
and was reborn as a sow.
I gave birth to two offspring,
and they were both eaten by Fúshēng.
Now that the debt is repaid,
I owe nothing more.
He is about to summon a butcher to sell me;
I beg you to report this."
The attendant fully reported this to his master.
The master, angry at the time, said:
"You are quite mad;
how could a pig possibly speak such words?"
He then went to sleep.
Another day passed,
and the pig saw the attendant again.
It said:
"The butcher is coming soon;
why haven't you reported it?"
The attendant again told his master.
The master again did not believe him.
A short while later,
the butcher came to take the pig.
The pig leaped out of the pen and ran,
going under the bed in front of the monk.
The butcher chased it to the monk's room.
The monk said:
"The pig has come to me for refuge;
I will now redeem it."
He then paid three hundred wén to ransom the pig.
Later, he secretly asked Fúshēng:
"Has your household ever lost any silk?"
Fúshēng replied to the monk:
"While my father was alive,
two bolts of silk were indeed lost."
The monk asked further:
"How many sisters do you have?"
Fúshēng said:
"I have only one sister,
married into the Gōngchéng family north of the county."
The monk then fully recounted what the attendant had said.
When Fúshēng heard this,
he wept bitterly, unable to control himself.
He thereafter took special care to provide for the sow.
After several days,
the pig suddenly died on its own.
It appeared in a dream to its daughter, saying:
"Now that the debt is repaid,
I am reborn in a good place."
It also urged its daughter
to further cultivate merit.
Captain Lǐ
In the first year of the Lóngshuò era of the Táng dynasty,
a person from Huáizhōu went to Lùzhōu to purchase pigs to sell back in Huáizhōu.
There was one boar,
bought in Lùzhōu for three hundred coins.
When it was brought to Huáizhōu,
it was sold to a butcher,
fetching six hundred coins.
By the winter, in the eleventh month,
a man from Lùzhōu named Lǐ,
who held the rank of Xiàowèi,
came to Huáizhōu for his official rotation duty.
He went to the market intending to buy meat.
He saw this boar,
already bound by its four legs,
in front of a shop,
about to be slaughtered.
Upon seeing this Xiàowèi,
it spoke, saying:
"You are my daughter's child,
I am your maternal grandmother.
Originally, because your family was poor,
your mother repeatedly asked for provisions,
but we could not fully supply them.
My eldest son did not permit it.
Out of pity for you and your mother,
I secretly avoided my son and gave you five dǒu of rice.
Now I have become a pig,
repaying the debt of that theft.
Why do you not save me?"
The Xiàowèi asked this butcher to ransom the pig.
The butcher initially did not believe him.
Others could not understand this pig's speech,
only the Xiàowèi could comprehend it.
The butcher said:
"If it truly is your grandmother,
I will release it.
You then ask it to speak with me further."
After the butcher untied it,
the Xiàowèi again asked the pig to speak:
"I am now on rotation duty for a month,
I cannot take you back home yet,
I do not know where to place you?"
The pig then said to the Xiàowèi:
"I am now already separated [from the human realm],
and bear this wretched form.
Even after your duty ends,
there is no need to take me back.
Your mother is still alive,
and you are a Xiàowèi.
If the family and relatives see me in this form,
they will certainly be displeased,
fearing it would disgrace your family's reputation.
At a certain temple, there are pigs and sheep kept for longevity,
place me in that temple."
The Xiàowèi again said to the pig:
"Grandmother, if this is truly effective,
go to the temple yourself beforehand."
Hearing this, the pig
then went to the temple by itself.
The temple monks initially refused to accept it.
The Xiàowèi explained this miraculous event in detail to the monks.
All the monks in the temple heard this,
and all felt compassion and pity,
building a shelter to house and settle it.
The Xiàowèi also left a small felt mat for it to lie on.
The temple monks, lay followers, and commoners vied to offer food and drink.
Later, the temple monks also came to understand the pig's speech.
When his duty ended,
he bid farewell to return to his home province,
and reported this matter to his mother.
His mother later came herself to see the pig,
mother and child met,
and wept together for a time.
The pig was still heard to be safe and well
by the first year of the Líndé era.
Tāng Yìng
During the Wú period,
in the multi-story building of the Lúlíng County post station,
there were often ghostly creatures,
and those who stayed overnight would invariably die.
Afterward,
no one dared to enter the station to lodge.
A man from Dānyáng named Tāng Yìng,
who was exceptionally brave and martial,
was sent to Lúlíng,
and thus entered the station to stay.
The local officials warned it was not possible,
but Yìng did not listen.
He sent all his attendants away outside,
keeping only a large sword and staying alone in the station.
When the third watch had just ended,
he suddenly heard someone knocking at the gate.
Yìng asked from afar who it was,
and the reply came:
"The Bùjùn sends his greetings."
Yìng had him enter,
he delivered his message and left.
After a short while, there was another knock at the gate, saying:
"The Fǔjūn sends his greetings."
Yìng again had him enter,
without any suspicion.
Soon, there was another knock at the gate, saying:
"The Bùjùn and the Fǔjūn have come to visit."
Yìng then began to suspect these were ghosts,
and thus took up his sword to meet them.
He saw two men both in splendid attire,
who entered together and sat down.
The one called Fǔjūn
began conversing with Yìng,
when the one called Bùjùn suddenly stood up.
Yìng then turned to look,
and with his sword struck him.
The Fǔjūn immediately left his seat and fled.
Yìng chased him to the rear wall of the station,
caught up with him,
and struck him several times with his sword.
Yìng then returned to lie down.
At dawn,
he was about to have people search for them,
and saw there were traces of blood,
which led them to find them.
The one called Fǔjūn
was an old boar,
The one called Bùjùn was an old fox.
From then on, the hauntings ceased.
The Scholar from Ānyáng
South of Ānyáng city, there was a post station where one could not stay overnight;
those who did would be killed.
A scholar then went to stay there.
The local people of the station said:
"You cannot stay here;
all those who stayed here before
have not survived."
The scholar said:
"Do not worry,
I will stay here myself."
He then went to the lodge.
He sat upright reciting his texts,
and only rested after a long time.
After midnight,
a person dressed in black clothes
came and went outside the door,
calling for the station master.
The station master answered:
"Yes."
"Is there anyone in the station?"
He replied:
"Earlier, there was a scholar here reading,
he just rested,
and does not seem to be asleep yet."
The visitor then sighed and left.
Afterward, another wearing a red headscarf
came calling for the station master,
the question and answer were as before.
After he left, it became quiet.
The scholar, knowing no more visitors would come,
got up and went to the place where the calls were made,
imitating the call for the station master.
The station master also answered "Yes."
He then asked:
"Is there anyone in the station?"
The station master answered as before.
The scholar then asked:
"Who was the one in black who came earlier?"
He said:
"The mother pig from the northern house."
He asked again:
"Who was the one wearing the red headscarf?"
He said:
"The old rooster from the western neighbor."
"And who are you?"
"I am an old scorpion."
Thereupon, the scholar secretly continued reciting his texts until dawn,
not daring to sleep.
When day broke,
the local people came to see,
and exclaimed in surprise:
"How did you alone survive?"
The scholar said:
"Quickly bring me a sword,
I will go with you to capture the demons."
He then took the sword to the place where the answers came the previous night.
Sure enough, they found an old scorpion,
as large as a drum,
its poisonous sting several feet long;
from the western house, they got the old rooster;
from the northern house, they got the old mother pig.
After killing these three creatures,
the station became peaceful.
A Scholar from Wújùn
In the Jìn dynasty, there was a scholar surnamed Wáng,
whose home was in Wújùn.
Returning to Qū’ē,
as dusk fell,
he moored his boat ashore,
right by a large dam.
He saw a young woman on the embankment,
about seventeen or eighteen years old,
and called out to her, inviting her to stay overnight.
By daybreak,
he untied a golden bell and fastened it to her arm,
then had someone escort her home.
But there were no women in the household at all.
Passing by the pigpen,
he saw a sow with a golden bell on its leg.
The Butcher of Jìnzhōu
In the third year of the Táng dynasty’s Xiǎnqìng era,
Xú Yù served as the governor of Jìnzhōu.
There was a butcher in the eastern alley of the market,
who slaughtered a pig until its life was severed.
After scalding, its hair and skin all fell off,
and it had been dead for half a day.
Just as he was about to slaughter another pig,
before he could begin butchering it,
by dawn,
when he used a knife to cut open its belly,
making a long incision along its abdomen,
the knife had not yet entered the belly,
when the pig suddenly stood up and ran out the door,
heading straight to the west of the market,
and lay down under a bed in a merchant’s shop.
People from the market flocked to see it.
The butcher, holding his knife, chased after it.
The onlookers asked him what had happened,
and the butcher replied:
"In all my life of slaughtering pigs,
I have never heard or seen such a thing."
He still wanted to take it away.
Hundreds of onlookers
all scolded and reprimanded the butcher,
competing to pay money to ransom the pig.
Everyone together built a pagoda to house it,
and only then did the pig’s body begin to grow hair and skin again.
The wounds on its throat and abdomen healed,
forming large lumps of flesh,
as thick as an arm.
It moved about, coming and going,
but never dirtied its room,
its clean nature unlike other pigs.
It lived until forty-five years old before finally dying.
Yuán Jí
During the Cháng’ān era of the Táng dynasty,
Yuán Jí, a man from Yùzhōu, lived in Rǔyáng County.
He kept a sow for over ten years.
One morning, it went missing,
and then appeared in Rǔyáng,
transformed into a woman,
about twenty-two or twenty-three years old,
quite beautiful.
She approached the gate of a wealthy family and said:
"This newlywed does not know where to go,
and heard that you need someone to raise silkworms,
so I have come to seek work."
The master of the house was pleased with her,
and invited her to live with his daughter.
The woman was very skilled at dressing and grooming herself,
and whenever she got money, she would buy wine,
as well as cosmetics.
Later, after drinking with a young man,
she entered the woods, drunk, and lay down,
reverting to the form of a sow.
On both cheeks, traces of rouge and powder still remained.
Cuī Rìyòng
During the Kāiyuán era,
Cuī Rìyòng served as the governor of Rǔzhōu.
His residence was previously haunted,
and no one had lived there for generations.
After Cuī Rìyòng arrived,
he repaired and cleaned it,
and settled there without hesitation.
That evening,
Cuī Rìyòng sat alone in the hall with a bright candle.
After midnight,
dozens of people in black clothes entered through the door,
coming to sit at the foot of the steps,
some of them lame or blind.
Cuī Rìyòng asked:
"What kind of ghosts are you all,
coming here to frighten people?"
The lame one spoke for himself:
"Our sins and karmic burdens
have all made us take the form of pigs.
We were released and scattered among various temples,
called ‘long-life pigs.’
However, we have never been content with this life, enduring all kinds of filth and misery.
We seek death but cannot obtain it,
and have always wished to explain ourselves to humans.
But when people see us, they are all terrified.
Now that you, sir, are the governor of this commandery,
we have come to seek your help to transform these bodies."
Cuī Rìyòng said to them:
"If this is truly the case,
it is not difficult at all."
They all bowed in thanks and left.
The next day,
his subordinates came to see Cuī Rìyòng,
and all were astonished that he was unharmed.
After the official duties were concluded,
he sent servants to fetch the long-life pigs from the various temples.
When they arrived,
some were lame, some blind,
no different from what he had seen before.
He marveled at this for a long time,
then ordered the judicial officer to record their names,
slaughtered them, and sold their meat,
using the proceeds to commission scriptures and statues,
and collected their bones for burial.
Some days later, they came again to express gratitude,
all appearing as young men.
They said:
"Had we not met you, sir,
we would still be enduring filth and misery for ten more years.
We have no way to repay you,
but now we have a pair of precious swords,
each worth a thousand pieces of gold,
which can ward off inauspiciousness
and dispel malevolent forces."
They placed the swords before the bed,
bowed twice, and left.
Cuī Rìyòng asked:
"What official position will I attain?"
They replied:
"Within two days, you will become the governor of Tàiyuán."
He asked further:
"Will I become a chancellor?"
They remained silent and did not answer.
Lǐ Fén
Scholar Lǐ Fén was a native of Shàngyú in Yuèzhōu.
He had a fondness for quiet and solitude,
and often resided on Sìmíng Mountain.
At the foot of the mountain was the estate of Old Man Zhāng.
His family was wealthy
and raised many pigs.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival,
Fén was strolling in the moonlight in his courtyard,
playing the qin for his own enjoyment.
Suddenly, he heard a voice outside the door sighing in admiration.
He asked,
"Who comes to this mountain retreat so late at night?
Please state your purpose."
Presently, a woman laughed and said,
"I wished to witness the excellence of a master musician!"
Fén opened the door and looked;
it was a woman of the most extreme beauty in the human world.
He only noticed that her mouth was somewhat dark in color.
Fén asked,
"Are you perhaps an immortal?"
The woman said,
"No,
I am a daughter of the Zhāng family at the foot of the mountain.
This evening, as my parents have temporarily gone to the eastern village,
I secretly came here.
To meet you privately, sir,
I hope you will not blame me."
Fén said joyfully,
"Since you, young lady, have deigned to visit,
we may as well relax a while."
The woman then ascended the steps and began to converse,
talking, laughing, and jesting in a manner Fén could not match.
Late at night, they went to bed,
and experienced the utmost intimacy.
Soon, the morning rooster announced the dawn,
and the woman rose to bid farewell.
Fén, reluctant to part,
secretly took one of her green felt shoes
and hid it in his clothes chest.
At that moment, Fén was reclining on his pillow, feigning sleep.
The woman then stroked Fén and wept sorrowfully,
asking for her shoe back.
She said,
"I beg you not to keep this.
I will come again tonight.
If you keep it,
I will surely die to repay you, sir."
Fén did not consent,
and the woman left, wailing and weeping.
Fén awoke
and saw drops of fresh blood leading from the bed out the door.
Finding this strange,
he opened the chest
and looked at the green felt shoe—
it was a pig's hoof sheath.
Fén was terrified and alarmed.
Following the blood trail, he arrived at the Zhāng family's pigsty in front of the mountain,
where he saw a sow
with one hoof sheath missing from its hind foot.
The pig looked at Fén,
glaring and roaring,
as if with an angry expression.
Fén reported the matter to Old Man Zhāng,
who immediately killed it.
Fén then abandoned the mountain retreat
and traveled to other regions.
Xúzhōu Soldier
During the Chángxīng era of the Later Táng,
in the Xúzhōu army camp, they were about to cook a sow.
The next day,
they were to slaughter it.
That night,
the pig appeared in a dream to its owner and said,
"Do not kill me.
The fetus within me is not a pig.
If you remember this,
I will bring you abundance."
By daybreak,
he had forgotten and slaughtered it.
Inside its belly was indeed a small white elephant fetus,
only about five inches long,
with its form and substance already complete
and a pair of gleaming tusks.
The owner then realized,
but it was too late.
The news spread tumultuously throughout the camp.
It was reported to the commanding officer,
who sealed it in paper
and reported it to the military governor Lǐ Jìngzhōu.
People at the time could not fathom it,
but in the end, nothing untoward happened.
Cat
A cat's pupils are round in the morning and evening,
but at noon,
they contract vertically like a thread.
The tip of its nose is usually cold,
except on the summer solstice, when it is warm for one day.
Its fur does not harbor fleas or lice.
On a black cat, if you stroke its fur against the grain in the dark,
it appears like sparks.
Common saying: if a cat washes its face past its ears,
guests will arrive.
In Xièyáng of Chǔzhōu, cats are produced,
some with brown patterns.
In Língwǔ, there are cats the color of 'red chìbō' and 'blue cōng.'
A cat is also called 'méngguì'
or 'wūyuán.'
Pínglíng City is the ancient Tán State.
In the city, there was a cat
that often wore a golden lock
and had coins
that flew like butterflies.
Local people often saw it.
Táng Dàoxí
When Wáng Jiàn proclaimed himself emperor in Shǔ,
his favored minister Táng Dàoxí served as Privy Councilor.
One summer day at home,
during heavy rain,
a cat he kept
was playing in the water under the eaves' drip.
Dàoxí watched it;
it gradually grew longer.
Soon, its front feet reached the eaves.
Suddenly, thunder and lightning arrived in force,
and it transformed into a dragon and left.
Vinegar Seller
In Jiànkāng, there was a vinegar seller
who kept a cat,
very handsome and robust,
and he loved it dearly.
In the sixth month of the Xīnhài year,
the cat died.
The man could not bear to discard it
and placed it beside his seat.
After several days,
it rotted and became foul-smelling.
Having no alternative,
he took it and discarded it into the Qínhuái River.
Once in the water,
the cat revived.
The man went into the water to rescue it
and drowned.
The cat climbed ashore and ran away.
A clerk from the Jīnwū post station captured it,
tied it up, and placed it in the station,
locking the door.
He went to report to the authorities,
intending to use the cat as evidence.
Upon returning,
he found it had broken its bonds
and gnawed through the wall to escape.
It was never seen again.
Guī Xì
Jìnshì Guī Xì,
during a hot month,
was sleeping in the hall with a small child.
Suddenly, a cat let out a loud cry,
frightening the child.
He ordered a servant to hit it with a pillow,
and the cat happened to be struck by the pillow and died.
The child immediately began making cat sounds
and died after a few days.
Rat
According to an old legend,
the urine essence of the Rat King
forms one rat per drop.
Another version states,
the Rat Mother has a head and feet like a rat,
a grayish tail and a pointed mouth,
as large as an otter in water,
and is inherently afraid of dogs;
one drop of its urine forms one rat.
When rat disasters occur,
they often originate from the Rat Mother.
Wherever the Rat Mother goes,
it can instantly produce countless rats.
Its meat is extremely delicious.
Any rat that eats the eyes of a dead person
becomes a Rat King.
A folk saying goes:
"If a rat gnaws on one's upper garment, it brings good fortune.
Generally, when gnawing clothes,
it is desirable to have a cover,
for without a cover, it is inauspicious."
In the Western Regions, there are rats as large as dogs,
medium-sized ones like rabbits,
and small ones like ordinary large rats.
Their heads are all white,
yet they wear golden collars.
Merchants passing through their country
who do not offer prayers and sacrifices beforehand
will have their clothes gnawed.
If they receive blessings from Buddhist monks,
they will encounter no further trouble.
Shì Dào'ān once traveled to the West
and witnessed this personally.
In the fire of the Bùjìn Tree, there is a rat weighing a thousand jīn,
with fur over two chǐ long,
fine as silk.
It constantly resides within the fire,
glowing red-hot.
Occasionally, it emerges, and its fur turns white.
If chased and doused with water,
it dies immediately.
People spin its fur
and weave it into cloth.
If the cloth becomes soiled,
burning it in fire cleanses it.
In the north, there are layers of ice stretching ten thousand lǐ,
a hundred zhàng thick,
and beneath the ice in the earth lives the Xī rat.
Its shape resembles a rat,
it feeds on plants,
and its meat weighs a thousand jīn,
suitable for making dried meat,
which cures fever when eaten.
Its fur, eight chǐ long,
can be used as a mattress,
and lying on it wards off cold.
Its skin can cover drums,
and the sound can be heard a thousand lǐ away.
Its fur can attract rats;
wherever its tail is, rats gather.
Nowadays, in Jiāngnán, rats devouring plants cause disasters—
these are of the same kind.
Red flying bats are mostly found in Jiāozhǐ and Guǎngguǎn Lǒngzhōu,
all covered in thick, fluffy fur.
Only their wing membranes are light black.
They often roost in pairs among red banana flowers.
If a catcher captures one,
the other will not leave.
Women in the southern regions
buy and carry them
as an aphrodisiac.
The Gǒng rat resembles an ordinary rat;
when walking in the fields,
upon seeing a person, it stands up with its front paws clasped together.
If someone approaches to catch it,
it leaps away.
It is found in Qínchuān.
The Yǎn rat has a head and tail like a rat,
a bluish-black color,
short feet with toes,
a large body,
weighing over a thousand jīn.
It appears in the boundaries of Línglíng Commandery,
but its origin is unknown.
When people face disasters or commit evil deeds,
the rat enters their fields,
shakes off its fur,
which turns into small rats,
devouring their crops before leaving.
Those who capture the Yǎn rat
treat its skin
and adorn it as a belt,
which is quite effective in restraining livestock.
Because its three hairs emerge from a single pore,
differing from ordinary skins,
people treasure it greatly.
The Yì rat resembles a rat,
with a short tail.
Whenever they move,
they bite each other's tails in succession,
forming groups of three or five,
and scatter when startled.
A folk saying goes:
"Seeing it brings auspicious omens."
It is found in Chéngdū.
The Táng rat resembles a rat,
slightly longer,
bluish-black in color,
with extra tissue like intestines along its belly,
which sometimes falls off.
It is also called the "Intestine-Changing Rat."
Long ago, the immortal Táng Fāng ascended to heaven with his household,
and even the chickens and dogs went along,
but only the rat fell down,
surviving with several chǐ of intestines exposed.
Every three years, it changes them,
hence it is commonly called the "Táng rat."
It is found in Chénggùchuān.
The white rat
has a body as pure white as snow,
red ears and feet,
and crimson eye sockets.
The crimson ones are the essence of gold and jade.
Watch where they emerge and dig there,
and you will obtain gold or jade.
It is said that rats turn white after five hundred years.
Those without red ears and feet
are ordinary rats.
Wáng Zhōunán
During the time of Wèi Qí Wáng Fáng,
in Zhōngshān, there was a man named Wáng Zhōunán who served as the magistrate of Xiāngyì.
Suddenly, a rat emerged from a hole and said:
"Wáng Zhōunán, you will die on such-and-such a day."
Wáng Zhōunán did not respond.
When the day arrived,
the rat reappeared wearing a black cap and robe, saying:
"Wáng Zhōunán, you will die at noon."
Again, he did not respond.
The rat retreated into its hole.
Just as noon arrived,
the rat emerged again, wearing its cap, and said:
"Wáng Zhōunán, since you do not respond,
what more can I say?"
As soon as it finished speaking,
it stumbled and died,
and its clothes and cap vanished.
Upon closer inspection,
it was no different from an ordinary rat.
Zhōng Zuò
At the northern temple in Wú, the monk Zhōng Zuò was lying in his study
when a rat emerged from a hole,
saying that Zhōng Zuò would die in a few days.
Zuò called his servant
and ordered him to buy a dog.
The rat said:
"I am not afraid of this either;
if the dog enters the house, it will surely die."
When the dog arrived, it indeed died.
Zuò was often engaged in trade,
so he closed the door and said to the rat:
"You simply want to make me rich.
Now that I am traveling far,
diligently guard my room,
and do not let anything go missing."
At that time, Huán Xuán was in Nánzhōu,
strictly prohibiting the slaughter of cattle.
Zhōng Zuò secretly bought several batches of cowhides,
transported them east to sell,
and earned two hundred thousand.
When he returned, the door was still closed,
and nothing was missing;
the strange occurrences also ceased.
From then on, he gradually became wealthy.
The Governor of Qīnghé Commandery
When the Prefect of Qīnghé Commandery arrived,
he would invariably die soon after.
A new prefect arrived,
and while using the latrine,
he saw a person three *chǐ* tall,
wearing a cap, headscarf, and black clothing,
who said:
"Your Excellency will die on such-and-such a day."
The prefect did not respond,
but felt very unhappy in his heart.
He urged his clerks to prepare funeral items for him.
Those outside thought the matter very strange.
At midday, he went to the latrine again,
and once more saw the person he had seen before,
who said:
"Your Excellency will die at midday today."
He said this three times, but still received no response.
Then he said:
"Your Excellency should have spoken but did not speak;
a rat will die in your place."
He then suddenly fell to the ground,
transforming into a creature as large as a suckling pig.
The commandery was then at peace.
Chúnyú Zhì
Chúnyú Zhì, styled Shūpíng,
was a man of Jǐběi.
His nature was deep and reserved,
and he valued kindness and duty.
In his youth, he was a scholar,
skilled in the *Book of Changes*.
Liú Róu of Gāopíng was sleeping at night
when a rat gnawed the middle finger of his left hand.
He felt very troubled by this,
and asked Zhì about it.
Zhì performed a divination for him and said:
"The rat originally intended to kill you but could not;
it will act on your behalf,
causing it to die instead."
He then used cinnabar to write the character for 'field' (田) on the back of Liú Róu's wrist, within the transverse lines,
about one square *cùn* in size,
and instructed him to sleep with his hand exposed at night.
A large rat was found lying dead before him.
Xú Mì
Pínà was the name of a maidservant of Wèi Qiánzǔ of Shàngyú.
She was beautiful,
and Mì was fond of her.
A rat then assumed her form
and went to stay with Mì.
Mì felt suspicious in his heart,
and when he used his hand to feel her four limbs,
he immediately sensed them shrinking,
whereupon she transformed into a rat and ran away.
Cài Xǐfū
During the Jǐngpíng era of the former deposed Emperor of the Sòng dynasty,
there was a great flood in Dōngyáng.
Cài Xǐfū took refuge at Nánlǒng.
At night, a large rat,
shaped like a suckling pig,
came floating on the water
and went straight to crouch at the corner of Xǐfū's servant's bed.
The servant took pity on it and did not harm it.
Whenever he ate,
he would always give it his leftover rice.
After the floodwaters receded,
Xǐfū was able to return to his residence.
The rat, using its front paws, held up a piece of blue paper
wrapped around two pearls,
placed them before the servant,
and chirped as if speaking.
From then on, it came and went without cease.
It could also become invisible,
and knew about people's fortunes and misfortunes.
Later, Lǚ Qìngzǔ of the same county was leading a dog on a hunt in the wild
and passed by briefly.
The rat then bit and killed him.
Máo Chóngqiū
In the tenth year of the Yǒngmíng era of Emperor Shìzǔ of the Qí dynasty,
at the home of Máo Chóngqiū, a commoner of Dānyáng Commandery,
every night there were sounds of people talking and laughing in the kitchen.
Lights would also be lit,
and there were sounds of feasting.
But when they opened the door to look,
they saw nothing.
And when they closed the door,
the sounds were heard again as before.
This went on for several decades.
Suddenly, a Dàoshi came to visit Chóngqiū and asked:
"Do you suffer from nightly hauntings?"
Chóngqiū said:
"Yes."
The Dàoshi then took a talisman from his bosom and gave it to him,
saying to Chóngqiū:
"Simply nail it onto the stove and the north wall,
and look at it early tomorrow."
Having said this,
the Dàoshi then vanished.
Chóngqiū was pleased
and did as the Dàoshi had instructed with the talisman.
The next day,
they saw five or six large rats in the kitchen, each two *chǐ* long,
hairless and crimson in color,
all dead by the north wall.
The hauntings then ceased completely.
Xiāo Xīdá
Xiāo Xīdá of Lánlíng, Prefect of Píngyuán during the Northern Qí,
had his belt gnawed by a rat.
Yáng Zūnyǎn teased him about it with a popular saying:
"This means you will be promoted."
Not long after,
he was appointed Master of the Household,
but soon lost the position.
Later, a rat gnawed his boot.
Zūnyǎn said:
"You will get an official post again."
Xīdá said:
"Even if I were to become Minister of Personnel,
what does it have to do with human affairs?"
The Dàoshi at the Inn
In the first year of the Wànsuì era of the Táng dynasty,
on the roads of Cháng'ān, there was a band of robbers who hid by day and moved by night.
Travelers often suffered murder and robbery.
By dawn,
there was absolutely no trace of them.
People were very fearful
and dared not set out in the morning.
They would wait until dusk
to reach their lodging places.
Later, a Dàoshi was staying at an inn
and heard of this matter.
He then said to the crowd:
"These certainly are not humans;
they must be monsters."
Late in the night,
he went by himself to the roadside holding an ancient mirror,
and lay in wait.
Soon, a group of youths arrived,
fully armed and armored.
They all shouted at the Dàoshi:
"Who is this by the roadside?
Do you not value your life!"
The Dàoshi shone the mirror on them,
and the youths abandoned their weapons and armor and fled.
The Dàoshi pursued them,
all the while reciting incantations.
After about five to seven *lǐ*,
the youths all entered a large burrow.
The Dàoshi guarded it until dawn.
He then returned to the inn,
gathered the people, and had them dig it up.
Over a hundred large rats ran out,
and they killed them all.
The menace was then eradicated.
Lǐ Cè,
during the Kāiyuán era,
served as a county magistrate.
While in his official hall,
a bird three feet tall,
featherless,
with flesh entirely red,
came into his residence.
Cè considered this inauspicious
and ordered a soldier to strike it.
The soldier hacked at the bird with a firewood axe;
the blade sank into the wood, but the bird was unharmed.
Cè found this deeply disturbing.
He then tried frying it in an oil cauldron,
covering it with something.
After several days, he opened it to look,
and the bird flew away following the oil vapors.
Later, it came again.
Cè ordered it bound with rope,
tied to a large rock,
and sunk in a river.
Over a month later, it returned again.
The severed rope was still around its neck.
Cè took a large log,
hollowed it out,
placed the bird inside,
sealed both ends with iron,
and again sank it in the river.
After that, it did not return.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Cè was transferred to another post,
and his residence was also ominous.
A few days after he took up his duties,
tiny people several inches tall appeared in the house,
four or five hundred of them,
filling Cè's official quarters.
Cè struck one of them with an object,
and it fell down dead.
Looking closely, they were all human-like.
The following evening,
the little people gathered in a crowd, weeping and wailing.
There was a cart carrying a coffin,
they donned mourning garments and held a funeral,
and proceeded to bury it beneath the western steps.
By dawn, they had just dispersed.
Cè then dug up the burial site,
and found a rat,
entirely red and hairless.
Thereupon, he ordered laborers
to follow the holes and excavate,
finding several hundred rats.
The strange phenomenon then ceased,
and Cè's household remained quite unharmed.
Tiānbǎo Guōqí
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo era,
in the territory of Hándān County, there were often nightmare-causing ghosts.
Wherever they went to a village,
they would stay for over ten days before leaving.
The locals considered this normal.
Three Guōqí cavalrymen sought lodging in a village at night.
An old woman said:
"I don't mind letting you stay,
but I fear the nightmare ghosts.
When guests arrive, they are sure to cause you trouble;
you should guard against it yourselves.
Although they cannot harm people,
they can still cause slight confusion and discomfort."
The cavalrymen, initially unafraid of ghosts,
stayed to lodge.
After the second watch,
two of them on the front couch fell into deep sleep,
while one awoke after a short while.
He saw a creature enter from outside,
shaped like a rat,
black and furry.
Before the bed, it donned a green gown,
held a tablet five or six inches long,
and bowed toward the sleepers before approaching.
That person then suffered a nightmare.
The nightmares affected two people.
When it came to the one who was awake,
he rushed forward and grabbed its leg.
The ghost did not move,
yet its body was cold as ice.
The three of them took turns holding it.
At dawn,
the villagers all gathered to question it.
The ghost initially did not speak.
The cavalrymen angrily said:
"If you refuse to speak,
we will fry you in an oil cauldron."
They then ordered the villagers to prepare an oil cauldron.
It then said it was a thousand-year-old rat,
and if it caused nightmares to three thousand people,
it would transform into a wildcat.
However, the nightmares it caused never harmed anyone.
If they could release it,
it would go a thousand miles away.
The cavalrymen then released it,
and the strange phenomenon ceased.
The later Imperial Censor-in-Chief, then serving as the Deputy of Hándān, Cuī Yì,
personally witnessed this event.
Yì's second cousin Cuī Héng recounted it.
Bì Háng
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Imperial Censor Zhōngchéng Bì Háng served as Prefect of Wèizhōu.
He fell into the hands of Ān Lùshān's rebels,
and soon planned to defect back to the loyalist side but had not yet acted.
Several days later,
he suddenly saw in his courtyard several hundred tiny people, five or six inches tall,
playing about as if nothing was amiss.
His family members struck and killed them.
The next day,
a group of little people, all dressed in white, were weeping.
They carried the dead in a funeral cart with mourning utensils,
exactly like the preparations for a scholar's funeral.
They then built a grave mound in the courtyard.
After the burial,
they entered a hole in the southern wall.
Greatly astonished,
he excavated the grave mound
and found a dead rat.
He then poured boiling water into the hole.
After a while, he dug it up
and found several hundred dead rats.
Over ten days later,
Háng, due to the failure of his plans,
met his death along with his entire household.
Cuī Huáiyí's
residence had several hundred rats walking on two feet in the courtyard,
making "guā guā" sounds from their mouths.
All family members, young and old,
came out to watch.
Their house then collapsed with a thunderous crash.
Yí's grandson Wáng Wèn personally told me this.
In recent times, there was a family that raised a daughter,
over ten years old.
One day, she disappeared,
and for a year there was no trace of her.
In their house,
they repeatedly heard the sound of a child crying underground.
Digging it up,
they first found a hole,
which gradually grew deeper and larger,
extending over ten feet in length and width.
They saw the girl sitting in the pit,
holding a child in her arms,
with a bald rat as large as a dou measure beside her.
When the girl saw her family,
she did not recognize them as her masters.
Her parents then realized she had been bewitched by a rat.
They struck and killed the rat.
The girl then wept sorrowfully, saying:
"That was my husband;
why was he suddenly killed by someone?"
The family also killed her child,
and the girl wept incessantly.
Before she could be treated,
she died.
Lǐ Jiǎ
During the Bǎoyìng era,
there was a man surnamed Lǐ whose given name is lost.
His family resided in Luòyáng.
For generations, his family disliked killing,
so they had never kept cats,
in order to spare mice from death.
By the time of his grandson,
he was also able to uphold his grandfather's intention.
One day,
the Lǐ family gathered many relatives and friends for a feast in the main hall.
After they were seated,
several hundred mice outside the gate all stood upright on their hind legs,
clapping with their front paws,
as if overjoyed.
The household servants were astonished,
and reported it to the Lǐ family.
The Lǐ family's relatives and friends
then emptied the hall to watch the spectacle.
After the people had almost all left,
the hall suddenly collapsed.
Not a single person in the household was injured.
Once the hall collapsed,
the group of mice also departed.
Alas!
Mice are insignificant creatures,
yet they can still recognize kindness and know how to repay it.
How much more so should humans?
Thus, those who bestow kindness should broaden their grace,
and those who repay kindness should also strive in their repayment.
Those who disregard this
should look upon this story and feel ashamed.
Wáng Jìn
Chancellor Wáng Jìn of the Táng dynasty,
during the Dàlì era,
shared governance with Yuán Zǎi.
Once, while entering court for an audience,
it was still early,
and he sat by candlelight.
Before his couch was a bag.
He then ordered a young attendant to fetch it.
The attendant lifted it to present,
but felt it was too heavy to raise.
Wáng opened it to look,
when suddenly a mouse over a foot long,
of plump and pale complexion,
leaped out from the bag.
Wáng was greatly frightened,
and turning to his son, said:
"With my lack of talent,
I have presumptuously occupied the position of a high minister and chancellor.
Without virtue yet holding high rank,
I have often feared unexpected calamity.
Now this strange creature has come into contact with my hands and feet—
is this not a sign of impending disaster?"
Several days later,
he indeed incurred offense,
and was demoted to serve as prefect of Jìnyún.
Xī Shìměi
Minister Xī Shìměi of Xǔchāng,
at the end of the Yuánhé era,
served as Surveillance Commissioner of Èzhōu.
He was benevolent in governing his subordinates,
and loyal in serving his superiors.
The excellence of his administration and transformation
is recorded in official documents.
One morning as he arose,
he went out to attend to official duties.
After finishing tying his belt,
he lifted his boot with his left hand,
but before his foot could enter,
suddenly a huge rat crossed the courtyard,
facing north, clasping its paws and dancing.
The high official was enraged,
and shouted at it in alarm.
It showed absolutely no fear.
He then threw his boot to strike it,
and the rat immediately fled.
A poisonous viper fell from the boot,
with pearl-like eyes and brocade-like skin,
about a foot long and as thin as a bamboo strip,
its venomous flame blazing,
rising from the tip of its tongue.
Had it not been for the rat's ominous warning,
it would have caused the calamity of a swollen finger and festering foot.
Master Cānliáo said:
"From this we know that the hooting of owls and dancing of rats
are not always omens of disaster.
For great men and noble gentlemen,
encountering them brings good fortune."
Lǐ Zhīwēi
was a man of broad-minded and open character.
He took pride in living in noble seclusion,
and was widely learned in the classics and histories.
Regarding the successes and failures of past and present,
there was nothing he did not thoroughly understand.
Often, due to family poverty, he would wander at night.
Once, passing beneath Wénchéng Palace,
under the faint light of the new moon,
he saw several dozen tiny people,
each only a few inches tall,
with clothing, carriages, and mounts,
attendants clearing the way and shouting commands,
as if they were persons of rank.
They gathered and stood beneath an ancient pagoda tree.
Zhīwēi stood aside, holding his breath,
observing what they would do.
To the east, there was a ruined wall several yards long,
with a hole leading through it.
Inside was a person in purple robes,
his cap and sash very formal,
surrounded by a dozen or so attendants, all slightly taller.
The various tiny people were just then conducting affairs.
After a short while,
the tiny people all hurried into the hole.
One of them
addressed the elder, saying:
"I should be appointed as a Secretary of the Western Pavilion."
Another said:
"I should be appointed as the Hall Front Recorder."
Another said:
"I should be appointed as a Clerk of the Bureau of Literary Affairs."
Another said:
"I should be appointed as an Assistant Scribe of the Southern Palace."
Another said:
"I should be appointed as Commandant of the Imperial Driveway."
Another said:
"I should be appointed as Registrar of the City Administration."
Another said:
"I should be appointed as Envoy to the Wandering Immortals."
Another said:
"I should be appointed as Halberdier of the Eastern Wall."
Thus each had their own demands,
which could not all be recorded.
Some were joyful,
some indignant,
some as if relying on something,
others as if seeking a definite outcome.
Shouting and clamoring intensely,
they all requested their desires.
The elder stood looking on,
offering no further words,
seeming only to nod in acknowledgment.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
the various tiny people each took their positions,
shouting commands and leading their followers,
entering beneath the ancient pagoda tree.
Soon, an old man with a withered, gaunt appearance,
came walking from the east with a staff.
He said to the purple-robed one:
"You have been greatly disturbed by these youngsters."
The purple-robed one smiled but said nothing.
The old man also laughed and said:
"Can it be spoken of?"
After speaking,
they led each other into the hole and departed.
The next day,
Zhīwēi dug beneath the ancient pagoda tree to investigate,
and found only several hundred rats,
scurrying away in all directions.
The purple-robed one and the old man—
he did not know what creatures they were.
A Man from Jiànkāng
A man from Jiànkāng was eating fish,
and discarded a fish head on the ground.
Soon, from a hole beneath the wall,
a person riding a horse emerged,
wearing distinct armor,
no larger than a foot tall,
holding a long lance,
and directly stabbed the fish head.
Then he galloped back into the hole.
This happened three or four times.
He then dug into the ground to investigate,
and saw several large rats,
with the fish head beside them.
There was only a single tendon,
with absolutely no sign of armored horses.
Not long after,
that man died.
Lú Sōng
Tàimiào Zhāiláng Lú Sōng's residence
had a cauldron that rang out,
and under the stove, there were rats making sounds like human crying.
Consequently, he performed a sacrifice to the stove god.
Under the stove, there were five large rats,
each colored according to the five directions,
which ate all the sacrificial offerings,
then returned into the stove.
That year,
Lú Sōng was appointed as Xìnghuà Wèi,
and ultimately, no other strange occurrences happened.
Chái Zàiyòng
Lóngwǔ Tǒngjūn Chái Zàiyòng was often in the main hall,
leaning on a small table and sitting alone.
Suddenly, a rat ran to the courtyard below,
faced Zàiyòng, cupped its hands, and stood,
as if intending to bow and salute.
Zàiyòng became angry,
called for his attendants,
but none of them came.
He then rose to chase it away,
and the rat left.
Then, the hall's roof beam broke,
and the table and chair he had been sitting on
were all crushed under the collapse.
Later, Zàiyòng became the military governor of the Lú, È, and Xuān three circuits and passed away.
Sū Zhǎngshǐ
Sū Zhǎngshǐ was about to choose a residence in Jīngkǒu.
This house was notoriously haunted,
and his wife and children advised him against it.
Sū said:
"If you dislike this house,
I will live here alone."
On the first night he stayed there,
over thirty beings,
each about a foot tall,
wearing Taoist robes and caps,
came to Sū and said:
"This is where we live,
you must leave quickly,
or disaster will befall you."
Sū became angry,
took a stick and chased them,
they all ran into the bamboo grove behind the house and vanished.
He then dug there,
and captured over thirty white rats.
The house was no longer haunted.
Lú Shū
Shìyùshǐ Lú Shū
said that his relative, serving as Prefect of Jiànzhōu,
on a hot summer night, went alone out of his bedroom,
to admire the moon in the courtyard.
As soon as he stepped out,
he heard what seemed like people talking and laughing
from under the western steps of the hall.
Tiptoeing to peek,
he saw seven or eight figures in white,
less than a foot tall,
men and women sitting together drinking.
Their tables, mats, and utensils
were all present but miniature.
They toasted and drank for a long time.
One person at the gathering said:
"Tonight is very joyful,
but 'White Old One' is about to come,
what shall we do?"
Then they sighed and lamented.
In a moment,
everyone present began to cry.
They entered a drain,
and then disappeared.
Later, when he left his post,
the new official's household had a cat named "White Old One."
Once it arrived,
White Old One dug under the ground by the western steps of the hall,
caught seven or eight white rats,
and killed them all.
Zhū Rén
Zhū Rén
lived for generations at the foot of Sōngshān,
farming as his livelihood.
Later, Zhū Rén suddenly lost a young son,
just five years old.
He searched for over ten years,
but never learned whether he was alive or dead.
One day later,
a monk traveling around
came to his door,
bringing a disciple
whose appearance resembled the young son Zhū Rén had lost.
Zhū Rén then invited the monk inside,
and offered provisions.
After a while, he asked the monk:
"Master, this disciple of yours,
observing his appearance,
somewhat resembles a young son our family lost ten years ago."
The monk stood up in surprise and asked Zhū Rén:
"I have lived within the vines and creepers of Sōngshān for thirty years.
Ten years ago,
this disciple happened to come to me crying sadly.
I asked him why,
but this disciple was just a child,
confused about his origins,
and not very clear.
I thus raised him,
and later gave him the tonsure.
Now he is exceptionally intelligent and perceptive,
I often suspected he might be a sage.
Is he your son?
Please try to examine him carefully yourself."
Zhū Rén then questioned and examined him together with his family.
His mother said:
"My son has a black birthmark on his back."
After a moment's inspection, it was found,
confirming he was indeed their own child.
Parents and family
all cried out together.
The monk then left him with his parents and departed.
The parents cared for and raised him,
with even more affection than for an ordinary child.
However, this child would every night
disappear from where he was;
at dawn, he would return home.
This went on for two or three years.
His parents thought he might be stealing.
They watched and spied on him,
and saw that every night,
the child transformed into a large rat and went out,
returning by dawn.
When his parents questioned him,
the child did not speak.
After a long time, he replied:
"I am not your son.
I am a young rat under the Rat King of Sōngshān.
Now that you have seen my true form,
I will not come again."
While his parents were still bewildered,
that night he transformed into a rat and left.
Lǐ Zhāogǔ
Lǐ Zhāogǔ took the imperial examinations but did not pass.
In the year he was to be enrolled,
the chief examiner had already been appointed,
and Zhāogǔ had no connections or recommendations.
The chief examiner was napping during the day,
when he suddenly awoke.
He saw a scroll in front of his pillow,
looked at its label,
and it was Zhāogǔ's examination paper.
He ordered it placed back on the shelf,
then lay down again and secretly watched.
A large rat took the scroll,
held its roller in its mouth,
and again brought it before the pillow.
This happened repeatedly.
Zhāogǔ passed the examination the following spring.
The chief examiner asked him the reason,
and learned that for three generations his family had not kept cats.
All said it was the rats' repayment.
Zhāng Wénwèi
Chancellor Zhāng Wénwèi's estate was at Bǎipō in the Eastern Capital.
On the estate, there was a weasel's den,
which had four young,
swallowed by a snake.
The male and female weasels, deeply distressed,
then piled earth outside the den,
forming a space just large enough for the snake's head.
Waiting for the snake to emerge from the den,
it indeed entered the piled area.
Once its head was out,
judging that it could not turn back in time,
they bit it in half at the waist,
then tore open the snake's belly,
carried out the four young,
which were still breathing.
They placed them outside the den,
fetched bean leaves,
chewed them and applied them to the wounds,
and all survived.
How can such tiny creatures possess such emotion and intelligence?
Humans are considered the most intelligent,
why do they not reflect upon this?
Wèi Wǔdì
Emperor Wǔ of the Wèi dynasty campaigned against the Mòdú,
passing through Mount Báiláng,
where he encountered a lion.
He ordered men to fight it,
and many were killed or wounded.
The king then personally led several hundred of his regular strong attendants to attack it.
The lion roared and charged fiercely,
causing everyone around to tremble in fear and sweat.
Suddenly, they saw a creature emerge from the forest,
resembling a wildcat,
which leaped onto the yoke of the king’s chariot.
As the lion approached,
this creature jumped onto the lion’s head,
and the lion immediately crouched down, not daring to rise.
They then killed it
and obtained a lion cub.
When this creature returned,
thirty lǐ before reaching Luòyáng,
all the chickens and dogs along the road crouched down,
and none crowed or barked.
Later, Emperor Zhuāng of the Later Wèi
Later Wèi,
the country of Persia presented a lion,
and at the end of the Yǒng’ān era,
it finally reached the capital.
Emperor Zhuāng said to his attendant-in-chief Lǐ Yù:
"We have heard that when a tiger sees a lion, it must crouch down.
Let us find one and test it."
He then issued an edict to the commanderies and counties near the mountains,
ordering them to capture tigers and present them.
Gǒng County and Shānyáng sent two tigers and one leopard.
When they saw the lion,
they all closed their eyes
and did not dare to look up.
In the garden, there was a blind bear,
which was very tame and gentle by nature.
The emperor ordered it to be brought for a test.
The gamekeeper led the blind bear over,
and when it smelled the lion’s scent,
it became frightened and leaped about,
dragging its chain as it fled.
The emperor laughed heartily.
Miscellaneous Accounts
Buddhist texts say:
"Lion sinews can be made into strings.
When played,
all other strings break.
In the Western Regions, there are black lions and club lions."
Jíxián Academy collator Zhāng Xīfù said:
"There used to be lion-tail whisks,
and during the summer, flies and gnats would not dare to land on them."
An old account says,
Sūhéxiāng
is lion dung.
Tōngtiān Rhinoceros
The horn of the Tōngtiān rhinoceros
has a white vein like a thread.
If used to hold rice
and placed among a flock of chickens,
when the chickens try to peck at the rice,
they are startled and retreat upon approaching.
Thus, people in the south call it the ‘chicken-frightening’ horn.
If one obtains a genuine horn one chǐ long,
carves it into the shape of a fish,
and holds it to enter water,
the water will always part.
Within an area of three chǐ square,
one can breathe underwater.
If one uses the horn as a stirrer,
when boiling a poisonous concoction into a decoction,
and stirs it with this stirrer,
white powder will form,
and the poison will be neutralized.
Miscellaneous Accounts
The Tōngtiān rhinoceros is said to detest its shadow
and often drinks muddy water.
When it urinates,
even if people drive it, it will not move its feet.
The patterns on its horn
resemble various things.
If the patterns are not continuous,
it is considered a defect.
The patterns can be categorized as inverted insertion, upright insertion, and waist-drum.
In inverted insertion,
the lower half is continuous;
in upright insertion,
the upper half is continuous;
in waist-drum,
the middle is interrupted and not continuous.
Thus, Persians call ivory "white darkness"
and rhinoceros horn "black darkness."
Duàn Chéngshì’s physician Wú Shìgāo once served in Nánhǎi Commandery.
He heard from a shipmaster say
that in his country, when capturing rhinoceroses,
they first plant many wooden stakes like pegs along mountain paths.
It is said that a rhinoceros’s front legs are straight,
and it often leans against trees to rest.
When the wood rots and breaks,
it cannot get up.
Rhinoceros horn is also called "slave horn."
Where there are cranes, there must be rhinoceroses.
A rhinoceros has three hairs per pore.
Liú Xiàobiāo said:
"If a rhinoceros loses its horn and it is buried,
people may replace it with a fake horn."
White Elephant
To the east of the road south of the Luò River bridge in Later Wèi,
there was a White Elephant Ward.
The white elephant
was presented by the country of Qiántuóluó
in the second year of the Yǒngpíng era.
On its back were placed a multicolored screen and a seat adorned with the seven treasures,
capable of accommodating dozens of people,
truly a remarkable creature.
It was usually kept at Chénghuáng.
The elephant once damaged houses and walls,
broke out,
uprooting trees it encountered
and knocking down walls.
The people were terrified,
running about in panic,
so the empress dowager moved the elephant to this ward.
Lángzhōu Mòyáo
In Lángzhōu, a Mòyáo man made his living by gathering firewood.
He often cut reeds by the riverbank.
Suddenly, a large elephant arrived,
wrapped him up onto its back,
and traveled over a hundred li,
deep into a marsh.
In the marsh was an old elephant,
lying down and panting,
its groans of pain very distressing.
Upon reaching the spot,
it set him down on the ground.
The old elephant raised its foot,
and in its foot was a bamboo splinter.
The Mòyáo man understood its meaning,
tied the bamboo splinter with the rope from his waist,
and pulled it out,
releasing about five or six shēng of pus and blood.
The young elephant then used its trunk to roll up some green mugwort,
wanting him to stuff the wound.
The Mòyáo man plucked the mugwort, rubbed it thoroughly,
and stuffed it in layer by layer,
using up all the mugwort before the wound was filled.
After a while,
the sick elephant was able to rise,
walking and standing east and west.
Soon it lay down again,
turned to look at the young elephant,
pointed at the mountain with its trunk,
and made a yōuyōu sound.
The young elephant then left.
A short time later,
it brought back a tusk.
The sick elephant saw the tusk and roared loudly,
seeming displeased with it.
The young elephant took the tusk away.
After a moment,
it brought back a large tusk.
The Mòyáo man addressed the elephant as "General,"
saying he hadn't eaten,
and was suffering from hunger.
The elephant went and broke off several branches of mountain chestnuts for him to eat,
and he was full.
Then it escorted the man and the tusk back.
After traveling fifty li,
it suddenly turned back.
At first, the man didn't understand its intention,
but it went back to retrieve the knife he had left behind.
After the man got the knife,
it escorted him to his original place.
It pressed its head against the man,
shook its ears left and right,
and after a long while, finally left.
The tusk was extremely large.
It was transported to Hóngzhōu,
where a foreign merchant sought to buy it.
He repeatedly raised the price himself,
up to four hundred thousand.
Soon, at another merchant's shop,
the foreign merchant hastily covered the tusk with a reed mat.
Another foreign merchant asked:
"What treasure is this,
that you immediately hide it?"
The shop owner removed the mat and said:
"It's just a large tusk."
The other foreign merchant, upon seeing the tusk, changed expression,
privately told the shop owner,
promising to pay a million.
He also offered ten thousand to the shop owner as an introduction fee.
They both pretended to give up and leave.
After a short while,
they returned carrying money.
The original foreign merchant argued again, saying:
"I was the one who originally bought the tusk.
For an elder to interfere in the market
violates public law.
If the shop owner seeks thousands or hundreds of strings of cash,
do I not have it?"
They argued back and forth,
and eventually came to blows.
The authorities reported to the county,
and the county reported to the prefecture.
The prefecture questioned them about the reason,
but the foreign merchants initially refused to say the tusk was a treasure.
The prefect said:
"This tusk will be presented to the Son of Heaven.
If you don't speak up,
it will ultimately be of no benefit to you."
He pressed firmly.
The foreign merchants then finally said:
"Inside the tusk are two dragons,
standing coiled together.
It can be cut into tablets.
Our country values this
as a commodity,
worth tens of billions.
Obtaining it makes one a great merchant."
Hóngzhōu then sent the tusk, along with the tusk's owner and the two foreign merchants, to present them.
Empress Wǔ Zétiān ordered the tusk to be split open,
and indeed obtained dragon tablets.
She said to the tusk's owner:
"Your appearance is poor and lowly;
you cannot receive too much money and goods."
She issued an edict to Lángzhōu,
granting him fifty thousand each year.
When it was used up, he could take more,
continuing for the rest of his life.
Huáróng Village Elephant
During the Shàngyuán era,
in Huáróng County, an elephant
entered a village household's central courtyard and lay down.
There was a splinter under its foot;
people pulled it out for it,
and the elephant then prostrated itself.
It allowed someone to ride it deep into the mountains,
where it dug in the soil with its trunk.
It obtained several dozen ivory tusks to repay them.
Ānnán Hunter
The people of Ānnán made hunting their livelihood,
often coating arrowheads with poison,
shooting birds and beasts,
and those struck would inevitably perish.
During the Kāiyuán era,
one of these men once ventured deep into the mountains,
and dozed off beneath a tree.
Suddenly, something touched him,
startling him awake.
He saw it was a white elephant,
much larger than ordinary elephants.
The southern people called it the General.
He prayed to it and bowed.
The elephant lifted him onto its back with its trunk,
then retrieved his bow, arrows, poison quiver, and other items to hand to him.
Thus, it galloped for over a hundred lǐ,
entering a deep valley,
arriving at a flat rock.
Looking around for about ten lǐ,
both cliffs were filled with huge trees,
their trunks as large as great houses,
densely towering to obscure the sky.
When the elephant reached the flat rock,
it trembled with fear,
advancing while looking around.
After traveling six or seven lǐ,
it went to lean against a large tree,
and with its trunk, gestured upward at the man.
The man understood its intention,
so he took his bow and arrows,
and climbed up the tree.
The elephant watched him from below.
When he had climbed about twenty-odd zhàng,
he wanted to stop.
The elephant pointed its trunk straight up,
as if guiding him to climb higher.
The man understood its meaning,
and climbed straight up sixty zhàng.
After watching him, the elephant walked away,
and the man spent the night in the tree.
By dawn,
he saw two glowing eyes on the flat rock.
After a long while,
he saw a giant beast,
over ten zhàng tall,
its fur pitch black.
Soon, it grew clear,
and the elephant he had seen yesterday,
leading over a hundred ordinary elephants,
came along the mountain,
and prostrated before it.
The giant beast pounced and devoured two elephants.
After eating,
they all withdrew.
The man then realized the elephant's intention:
it wanted him to shoot.
So he coated an arrow with poison,
shot with all his strength,
and hit it twice in succession.
The beast looked at the arrows, roared in fury,
its voice shaking the forest trees.
The man also shouted loudly to provoke the beast.
The beast came searching for him,
but the man clung to the tree.
Seizing the moment it opened its mouth,
he shot another arrow right into its mouth.
The beast roared and thrashed about,
and after a long while, finally died.
Soon, he saw the big elephant enter from the flat rock,
taking one step and looking around.
Reaching the beast's location,
confirming it was dead,
it nudged it with its head,
then looked up to the sky and let out a great roar.
In an instant,
a group of five or six hundred elephants,
gathered like clouds, roaring and crying out,
their voices resounding for dozens of lǐ.
The big elephant came to the tree,
knelt and bowed twice.
It beckoned the man with its trunk,
and the man descended the tree.
He mounted its back,
and the elephant carried him forward.
The herd of elephants followed.
