They soon arrived at a place,
where trees were planted like a mound.
The big elephant used its trunk to uncover the mound,
and all the elephants uncovered it,
finishing by dusk.
Inside were tens of thousands of elephant tusks.
The elephant carried the man onward,
and within a few dozen steps,
it would knock down a branch,
likely marking the path.
After finishing,
they returned to where he had slept the previous day,
set him down on the ground,
bowed twice, and left.
The man returned and reported to the Protector-General.
The Protector-General sent envoys to follow him,
obtaining tens of thousands of tusks,
causing the price of ivory south of the mountains to plummet.
The envoys went to the flat rock,
where only the bones of the giant beast remained.
The Protector-General took one section of bone,
which ten men carried together.
The bone had holes,
large enough for a person to pass through.
In Huáinán, a hunter
named Zhāng Jǐngbó served as the Prefect of Hézhōu.
Huáinán had many elephants.
In the prefecture, there was a hunter
who often pursued game in the mountains.
Suddenly, a herd of elephants surrounded the hunter,
preventing him from leaving.
A large elephant approached the hunter,
wrapped its trunk around him,
and placed him on its back.
The hunter's knife and staff fell,
and the elephant retrieved and returned them to him.
Then it carried the hunter straight into the deep mountains.
The herd of elephants escorted him to the mountain pass and turned back.
Entering the mountains for fifty lǐ,
they passed a large flat rock.
At the edge of the rock, there was nothing else,
only elephant hides and skins,
with flesh and blood still remaining.
The hunter thought to himself:
"Could it be that they intend to devour me here?"
But the elephant carried him past it.
Fifty paces from the rock,
there was a large pine tree.
The elephant leaned its back against the tree.
The hunter thus climbed onto the tree.
His bow fell to the ground,
and the elephant again picked it up with its trunk,
lifting it up to him.
The hunter was deeply puzzled by this.
After delivering the hunter,
the elephant galloped away.
Soon, a blue beast
emerged from the fine grass south of the pine tree.
Its fur was thick and bristling,
its claws and fangs fearsome,
as large as a house,
with eyes like lightning and a voice like thunder.
It came to rest on the flat rock,
as if waiting for something.
After a while,
a young elephant came from the north.
Seeing the fierce beast from afar,
it knelt and crawled forward.
Upon reaching the flat rock,
it trembled with fear.
The beast was pleased to see it,
picked it up with its hands,
and threw it into the air.
After throwing it, it caught it again,
but had not yet eaten it.
Watching this, the hunter sighed and said:
"Even a foolish beast
seeks help from humans.
Earlier, it brought me into the mountains,
intending for me to kill this beast.
I appreciate its intention;
how can I not save it?"
So he drew his bow to the full,
and released a poisoned arrow,
piercing its left armpit.
After being struck by the arrow,
the beast charged toward the hunter.
He shot another arrow straight through its heart,
and the beast fell,
writhing until it died.
The young elephant then galloped back,
and soon over two hundred elephants
came beneath the tree,
all kneeling respectfully.
They took turns helping the hunter down.
The elephant that had carried him earlier
again supported him with its back,
carrying him out of the mountains.
The elephants surrounded him, clamoring and crying out.
They brought the hunter to a place,
where the elephants used their trunks to dig up a mound,
revealing the ivory hidden there.
In total, over three hundred tusks,
which they showed to the hunter.
They then carried him back to where they had met.
The elephants all knelt again,
expressing gratitude before leaving.
The hunter then took the ivory,
selling it for tens of thousands in cash.
Jiǎng Wǔ
During the Bǎolì era,
there was a man named Jiǎng Wǔ,
a native of Héyuán in Xúnzhōu.
He was tall, imposing, and robust,
with a bold and courageous spirit.
Living alone in the mountain cliffs,
he sought only to hunt and shoot.
Skilled in drawing a powerful crossbow,
he would always carry his bow and arrows,
and whenever he encountered bears, tigers, or leopards,
none failed to fall to his bowstring.
Upon cutting them open to examine his arrowheads,
each one had pierced their hearts.
Suddenly, something knocked at his door,
very urgently.
Wǔ peered through the door crack and saw
an orangutan riding a white elephant.
Knowing that orangutans could speak,
Wǔ questioned it:
"Why have you and the elephant come knocking at my door?"
The orangutan said:
"The elephant is in trouble.
Knowing I can speak,
it carried me here to seek your help."
Wǔ asked:
"What hardship do you face?
Please tell me the reason."
The orangutan said:
"About two hundred li south of this mountain,
there is a large, hollowed-out cave.
Inside dwells a Bā snake,
hundreds of feet long,
with eyes that flash like lightning
and teeth as sharp as sword blades.
Elephants passing by
are all devoured by it.
Hundreds have encountered it,
with no means to hide or avoid it.
Now we know you, mountain dweller, are skilled in archery.
We hope you will take poisoned arrows and shoot it.
If you can rid us of this scourge,
we will all think of ways to repay your kindness."
The elephant then knelt on the ground,
shedding tears like rain.
The orangutan said:
"If you agree to go, mountain dweller,
please take your arrows and mount up."
Moved by their words,
Wǔ dipped his arrows in poison and mounted the elephant.
Sure enough, he saw two eyes
under the cliff,
their light shining for several hundred paces.
The orangutan said:
"Those are the snake's eyes."
Enraged, Wǔ drew his bow, aimed his arrow,
and with one shot struck its eye.
The elephant then carried him and fled.
Soon, a thunderous roar came from the cave,
and the snake leaped out, writhing and coiling,
sometimes lashing, sometimes lunging.
Within several li,
trees, plants, and grass were all scorched as if burned.
By dusk, the snake was dead.
Peering into the side of the cave,
he saw elephant bones and tusks
piled up like a mountain.
Then, ten elephants
each used their long trunks to roll out a red tusk,
and knelt to present them to Wǔ.
Wǔ accepted them.
The orangutan also bid farewell and left.
Wǔ then had the previous elephant carry the tusks back,
and he became very wealthy.
Miscellaneous Accounts
In Ānnán, there are elephants
that can silently discern right and wrong in people.
When traveling in the mountains and encountering people arguing,
they let the one in the right pass;
the deceitful one,
they lift with their trunk,
toss several zhang into the air,
catch with their tusks,
and instantly shatter.
No one dares to contend with them.
Dragon elephants
reach full bone maturity at sixty years of age.
Now, the elephants in Jīng lands,
black with two tusks,
are actually river pigs.
In the second year of Xiánhēng,
the state of Zhōuchéng sent an envoy to present a memorial,
saying that in the state of Hējiā, there were white elephants
with four tusks hanging from their mouths
and five legs moving their bodies.
Wherever such elephants are,
the land is sure to be abundant.
Washing their tusks with water
and drinking it cures illnesses.
They requested troops to be sent to fetch them.
An elephant's gallbladder moves with the seasons to its four legs:
spring in the front left,
summer in the front right,
as if it has no fixed location.
The tip of their trunk has a claw that can pick up needles.
Their flesh has twelve kinds,
but only the trunk is their original flesh.
Táo Zhēnbái said:
"In summer, when compounding medicine,
it is fitting to place an elephant tusk beside the medicine."
Southerners say:
"Elephants particularly detest the sound of dogs.
Hunters carry provisions and climb tall trees,
building bear nests to wait.
When a herd of elephants passes,
they make dog sounds.
The elephants all raise their trunks and roar,
lingering and refusing to leave.
After perhaps five or six days,
they collapse from exhaustion.
Then the hunters descend
and stealthily stab them to death.
Their ear canals are thin as drum skin;
one stab kills them.
The small transverse bone in their chest,
burned to ash and taken with wine,
enables a person to float and dive in water.
Eating their meat
makes a person heavy-bodied."
Ancient teachings say:
"Elephants gestate for five years before giving birth."
In the kingdom of Huánwáng, wild elephants gather in herds.
One male oversees over thirty females.
Females have tusks only two chǐ long.
They take turns providing the male with water and grass
and encircle him while he rests to guard him.
When a female elephant dies,
they dig a hole together to bury her,
roaring for a while before dispersing.
Also, elephants raised and tamed by the people there
can be made to gather firewood.
In the subordinate commanderies of Guǎng, such as Cháozhōu and Xúnzhōu, there are many wild elephants
with small, red tusks,
most suitable for making ceremonial tablets.
People of Cháozhōu and Xúnzhōu, when catching an elephant,
vie to eat its trunk,
saying it is fatty and crisp,
especially fit for roasting.
Some say:
Elephant meat has twelve kinds.
The elephant's gallbladder is not attached to the liver
but moves through the flesh with the moon.
Between Chǔ and Yuè,
elephants are all bluish-black.
Only in western states like Fólín and Dàshí are there many white elephants.
Liú Xún had a close relative
who once served as an envoy to Yúnnán.
There, powerful families
each keep elephants,
using them to carry heavy loads over long distances,
just as in the Central Plains they keep oxen and horses.
The Mán king feasted the Hàn envoy at the Bǎihuā Tower.
Before the tower, dancing elephants entered.
As the music played and the melody moved,
performers led them in.
The elephants had golden bridles on their heads,
brocade and embroidery draping their bodies.
They leaped and stamped to the beat,
moving their heads and shaking their tails,
all in time with the rhythm—
much like the dancing horses of the Tiānbǎo era.
In the fourth year of Táng's Qiánfú era,
the state of Zhànchéng presented three tame elephants.
Before the hall, they were presented and responded,
and could also bow and dance.
Later, they were released back to their native land.
Xiāo Zhìzhōng
Xiāo Zhìzhōng, the Central Secretariat Director of the Tang dynasty,
in the first year of the Jǐngyún era,
served as the prefect of Jìnzhōu.
He planned to go hunting on the La Festival day,
and the preparations were extensive.
The day before,
a woodcutter was gathering firewood on Huòshān Mountain
when he suddenly fell ill with malaria and could not return home.
He therefore took shelter in a cave,
moaning and unable to sleep.
As the night was nearing its end,
he seemed to hear rustling sounds as if people were approaching.
At first, he thought bandits were coming,
so he crawled and hid among the trees.
At that time, the mountain moon was very bright.
There was a person over ten feet tall,
with a nose that had three corners,
his body covered in leopard skin,
and eyes that flashed like lightning.
He faced the valley and let out a long roar.
Soon, tigers, rhinoceroses, deer, boars,
foxes, rabbits, pheasants, and wild geese
gathered densely within about a hundred paces.
The tall man then declared:
"I am the envoy of Xuánmíng,
sent by the Northern Emperor.
Tomorrow is the La Festival,
and Prefect Xiāo will conduct a seasonal hunt.
Some of you are fated to die by arrows,
some by spears,
some by nets,
some by clubs,
some by dogs,
and some by hawks."
After he finished speaking,
all the animals prostrated themselves, trembling with fear,
as if pleading for their lives.
An old tiger and an old elk
both knelt and said to the tall man:
"Our lives,
indeed, are already allotted.
However, Lord Xiāo is a benevolent man;
he does not intend to harm creatures,
but is merely following the seasonal customs.
If there were some minor incident to stop him,
could the envoy not find a way to save us?"
The envoy said:
"It is not that I wish to kill you all,
but I have been ordered by the Emperor to announce your sentences.
Once my duty as envoy is done,
from then on, you may devise your own plans.
However, I have heard that Brother Yán Sì of the Eastern Valley is skilled in strategy;
you may go to him and seek help."
All the animals turned and cried out joyfully.
The envoy then headed east,
and all the animals followed.
By then, the woodcutter's illness had slightly subsided,
so he followed to observe.
When they reached the Eastern Valley,
there were several thatched huts,
and a Daoist priest,
with a tiger skin hanging on a rack,
was sleeping soundly.
Startled awake,
he saw the envoy and said:
"It has been so long since we parted,
I have often missed you.
Your coming here today—
is it not to assign the La Festival sentences to the creatures?"
The envoy said:
"Exactly as you, wise one, have surmised.
However, they all seek rescue from you, Brother Sì;
Brother Sì should devise a plan for them."
The old tiger and the old elk
then knelt and pleaded sorrowfully.
The Daoist priest said:
"Whenever Prefect Xiāo employs people,
he always shows concern for their hunger and cold.
If you could pray for Téng Liù to bring snow,
and Xùn Èr to raise wind,
then he would not go hunting.
I recently received a letter from Téng Liù,
and learned that he has lost his spouse.
I also heard that he sought the fifth daughter of the Suǒquán family to be a singing girl,
but she was dismissed due to jealousy.
If you can find a beauty to present to him,
then snow will fall immediately.
Also, Xùn Èr is fond of drinking;
if you can obtain fine wine to bribe him,
then wind will arrive at once."
Two foxes claimed to be very charming
and capable of obtaining these.
The third younger sister of Cuī Zhīzhī, the county lieutenant of Hédōng,
was beautiful, virtuous, and charming.
Lú, the household registrar of Jiàngzhōu, was skilled at brewing fine wine,
and whenever his wife gave birth, there was sure to be excellent wine.
After speaking, they departed,
and all the animals made joyful sounds.
The Daoist priest then said to the envoy:
"I recall when Hánzhì was in the immortal capital;
who would have thought that after a thousand years I would become a beast,
depressed and unfulfilled.
I have composed a verse to express my feelings."
He then chanted:
"Once an immortal, now a tiger,
cast into the dark abyss, enduring wind and rain.
Further, with striped fur tearing my body,
a thousand years in empty mountains, myriad sufferings."
"However, Hánzhì's period of banishment is almost complete;
in just eleven more days,
I will return to the Purple Palace.
Having lived here so long,
I cannot help but feel regret at parting.
Therefore, I will inscribe a few lines on the wall,
so that later people will know that I once lived here."
He then wrote on the northern wall:
"For eighty billion jiǎzǐ cycles below the mysterious,
Dānfēi Xiānshēng, Yán Hánzhì.
Banished from the mid-heaven, clad in striped hide,
sixty jiǎzǐ cycles, blood offerings in the stream.
Drinking and dwelling with apes in the turbid realm,
in the Jǐngyún era's first year, ascending to Tàiyī."
The woodcutter, being literate and able to recite,
secretly memorized this.
A short while later,
an old fox brought a beauty,
just of hair-pinning age,
wiping her eyes with red sleeves,
her fading makeup enchanting.
Another fox
brought two bottles of fine wine,
with an intensely fragrant aroma.
Brother Yán Sì then placed the beauty and the bottles of fine wine
each into a bag.
Using vermilion ink, he wrote a talisman,
took water and sprayed it,
and the two bags flew away.
The woodcutter, afraid of being seen,
immediately found his way back.
Before dawn,
a fierce wind and snowstorm arrived,
lasting the entire day before ceasing.
And Prefect Xiāo did not go hunting.
Lángbèi
The láng is as large as a dog,
gray in color,
and when it makes a sound, all its orifices seem to boil.
The tendon in its thigh is as large as a duck egg;
if a thief is smoked with it,
it will cause their hands to cramp and shrink.
Some say the láng tendon is like a small woven net bag,
made by insects.
Láng dung smoke rises straight up,
and is used for beacon fires.
Some say lángbèi are two different creatures.
The bèi has extremely short front legs,
and whenever it moves, it often rides on two láng;
without the láng, it cannot move.
Therefore, in the world, when things go awry, it is called 'lángbèi'.
Láng Tomb
West of Línjì Commandery, there is a láng tomb.
In recent times, a person was traveling alone in the wilderness
and encountered several dozen láng.
The person, in dire straits,
climbed onto a pile of grass.
Two láng
then entered a burrow
and carried out an old láng.
The old láng arrived,
and with its mouth pulled out several stalks of grass;
the pack of láng then competed to pull out grass.
As the pile was about to collapse,
hunters arrived and rescued the person.
The person then led others to dig up this tomb,
finding over a hundred láng inside,
and killed them.
It is suspected that the old láng was a bèi.
The Son of the Jìzhōu Regional Inspector
The son of the Prefect of Jìzhōu in the Táng dynasty,
the storyteller has forgotten his name.
Initially, his father ordered him to go to the capital,
to seek a change of appointment.
Before the son had left the prefecture,
he saw a noble family with many guests and attendants.
Among them was a woman of beautiful appearance.
The son was delighted and inquired about her,
which greatly startled the family.
An old maidservant angrily said:
"Who are you,
to be so presumptuous?
This is the young lady of the family of Senior Official Lú of Yōuzhōu,
whose husband recently passed away,
and she is returning to the capital.
You are not an official of the prefecture or county,
why do you interrogate so urgently?"
The son then stated that his father was currently serving as Prefect of Jìzhōu,
and wished to seek a marriage alliance.
At first they were very alarmed,
but gradually they agreed.
After several days, they had a tryst in the wild,
and midway he turned back.
The Prefect and his wife deeply missed their son,
and did not question further.
Moreover, the bride's responses were reasonable,
so they did not suspect at all.
The people and horses that came with her were numerous,
and the entire family was overjoyed.
After more than thirty days,
one night,
the bride's horse trampled.
They repeatedly sent maidservants to check,
but she had barred the door herself.
By dawn,
the Prefect's family members went to the son's room,
but did not see the maidservants.
Going to the stable,
they also did not see the horses.
Feeling quite suspicious,
they reported to the Prefect.
The Prefect and his wife then went to the front of the room,
called the son but got no response.
They ordered someone to break the window and door open,
and a large white wolf rushed out and ran away.
Their son had been almost completely eaten.
Wáng Hán
Regarding Wáng Hán from Tàiyuán,
he served as Commandant of the Zhènwǔ Army.
His mother, Madame Jīn,
originally the daughter of a Hú person,
was skilled in archery and horsemanship,
and was long known for her fierce and bold nature.
She often rode a strong horse,
carrying a bow on her arm and arrows at her waist,
entered deep mountains,
to hunt bears, deer, foxes, and rabbits,
killing and capturing many.
Therefore, the northerners all feared her ability and held her in high regard.
Later, when she was over seventy years old,
due to old age and illness,
she lived alone in one room,
dismissed her maidservants,
and did not allow them to approach her side.
At night,
she would lock the door and sleep.
She often became angry,
excessively beating her family members.
Later one evening,
after she had locked her door,
the family suddenly heard a creaking sound,
and hurried to look.
They saw a wolf,
open the door from inside the room and come out.
Before dawn,
the wolf returned from outside,
entered the room and locked the door again.
The family was very frightened,
and fully reported it to Hán.
That night,
Hán secretly peered through a crack,
and it was as the family had said.
Hán was worried and fearful, unable to be at ease.
By dawn,
Madame Jīn summoned Hán,
and ordered him to immediately buy venison.
Hán cooked it and presented it.
Madame Jīn said:
"What I need is raw meat."
So they brought raw venison before her,
and Madame Jīn devoured it all at once.
Hán became even more afraid.
Family members occasionally whispered about the matter,
and when Madame Jīn heard it,
her expression showed great shame.
That evening after locking the door,
the family again watched and spied,
and a wolf broke through the door and went out.
From then on, it never returned.
Villager of Zhèngpíng County
At the end of the Yǒngtài era of the Táng dynasty,
in Zhèngpíng County of Jiàngzhōu, there was an old village man who had been ill for several months.
Later, he did not eat for more than ten days.
At night, he would disappear.
No one knew the reason.
Another evening,
a villager went to the fields to pick mulberry leaves,
and was chased by a male wolf.
In panic, he climbed a tree,
the tree was not very high,
and the wolf stood up and bit his clothes.
The villager was in critical danger,
and struck with a mulberry axe,
hitting it right on the forehead.
The wolf fell down,
and after a long time, it left.
The villager only managed to come down from the tree at daybreak.
Following the wolf's tracks,
he arrived at the old man's house.
Entering the hall,
he called the old man's son,
and recounted the whole story.
The son examined his father's forehead for axe marks,
fearing he would hurt others again,
so he strangled him to death,
and he turned into an old wolf.
He went to the county to explain himself,
and the county did not punish him.
Also that year,
in another village of Jiàngzhōu, there was a young man,
about twenty years old.
After an illness,
he lost much of his spirit,
and then transformed into a wolf,
secretly eating many village children.
Those who lost children did not know the reason,
only searched everywhere without finding them.
The young man often worked as a laborer for others.
One day later,
he passed by the house of a family that had lost a child,
and the child's father called his name, saying:
"You can come to my house to work tomorrow,
I will prepare a lavish meal for you."
The young man then laughed and said:
"Who do I think I am,
to work for your family again?
A man like me never lacks exotic delicacies!"
The child's father found his words strange and bold.
So he questioned him.
He replied:
"Heaven has destined me to eat people.
Yesterday I ate a small child,
five or six years old,
his meat was extremely delicious."
The child's father saw bloodstains inside his mouth,
so he beat him wildly,
and he transformed into a wolf and died.
Wife of Zhāng Mǒu
A commoner's wife named Zhāng Mǒu from Shénshān County of Jìnzhōu,
suddenly dreamed of a person wearing yellow-brown clothes,
with a very thin waist and abdomen,
who approached and violated her,
and after two encounters, left.
Afterward, she became pregnant,
and then developed a craving for raw meat,
often resenting not being full.
She constantly gnashed her teeth and lips in anger,
her nature becoming increasingly fierce and cruel.
After half a year,
she gave birth to two wolf cubs,
which ran away as soon as they were born.
Their father quickly struck and killed them.
The wife then became ill and confused,
and recovered after more than a year.
The villagers called her the wolf mother.
Zǐlù
In the eastern regions, bears are called Zǐlù.
If you strike a tree with something and say:
"Zǐlù, get up."
Then it will come down.
If you do not call, it will not move.
Bear gallbladder,
in spring is in the head,
in summer in the abdomen,
in autumn in the left foot,
in winter in the right foot.
Shēngpíng enters the mountains
During the Shēngpíng era of the Jìn dynasty,
a man went into the mountains to hunt deer.
Suddenly, he fell into a pit,
which was dark and extremely deep.
Inside were several bear cubs.
After a moment,
a large bear entered,
staring at this man.
The man thought it would surely harm him.
After a long while,
the bear brought out stored fruits and chestnuts,
distributing them among its cubs.
Finally, it made another portion
and placed it before this man.
The man had been hungry for a long time,
so risking death, he took and ate it.
Gradually, they became familiar and accustomed to each other.
Every morning, the mother bear would go out to find food and fruits,
and upon returning, would always share with this man.
The man relied on this to prolong his life.
Later, when the bear cubs grew big,
their mother carried them out one by one.
Once the cubs were all gone,
the man thought he would surely die in the pit,
trapped with no way out.
The mother bear soon returned,
entered, and sat beside the man.
The man understood her intention,
so he embraced the bear's leg.
Thereupon, she leaped out,
and he was thus unharmed.
Huáng Xiù
Huáng Xiù of Gāopíng in Shàolíng,
in the third year of the Sòng dynasty's Yuánjiā era, entered the mountains,
and did not return for months.
His son, Gēnshēng, went searching for him
and saw Xiù squatting inside a hollow tree,
from head to waist,
his hair and skin color like that of a bear.
When asked why he was like this,
he replied:
"Heaven has punished me thus.
You should just go away."
Gēnshēng returned, grieving and weeping.
A year later,
woodcutters in the mountains saw his form,
which had completely turned into that of a bear.
Dǒng Zhòngshū
Hàn dynasty Dǒng Zhòngshū once lowered his curtain and was reciting alone,
when suddenly a guest arrived.
His demeanor, voice, and bearing
were exceptionally extraordinary.
They discussed the Five Classics,
delving into their subtle mysteries.
Zhòngshū had never heard of such a person before,
and suspected he was not human.
He then said to him:
"Those who dwell in nests know to avoid the wind;
those who live in caves know the coming rain.
If you are not a fox,
then you must be a rat."
Upon hearing these words,
the guest's countenance changed and his form deteriorated,
transforming into an old fox,
and he stumbled away in haste.
Zhāng Huá
Zhāng Huá, styled Màoxiān,
served as Minister of Works during the reign of Emperor Huì of Jìn.
At that time, in front of King Zhāo of Yān's tomb,
there was a spotted fox,
which after many years could perform transformations.
It then transformed into a scholar.
Wishing to visit Lord Zhāng,
it passed by and asked the ornamental pillar in front of the tomb:
"With my talent and appearance,
can I gain an audience with Minister Zhāng?"
The pillar said:
"Given your superb understanding,
it should be possible.
However, Minister Zhāng's wisdom and discernment
will likely be difficult to deceive.
If you go, you will surely meet with disgrace,
and may not even return.
Not only will you lose your thousand-year essence,
but you will also deeply implicate this old pillar."
The scholar did not heed this,
and proceeded to visit Huá.
Huá saw that he was youthful and elegant,
pure and white as jade,
his movements and demeanor,
his glances, full of grace,
and held him in high esteem.
They then discussed literature,
debating and comparing sounds and substance.
Huá had never heard such discourse before.
They further deliberated on the Three Histories,
explored the profundities of the Hundred Schools,
discussed the profound realms of Lǎozǐ and Zhuāngzǐ,
unveiled the ultimate principles of the Fēng and Yǎ,
encompassing the Ten Sages,
penetrating the Three Powers,
critiquing the Eight Confucian Schools,
and analyzing the Five Rites.
Huá could not respond promptly to any point, finding himself at a loss.
He then sighed and said:
"How can there be such a youth in the world!
If he is not a ghost or monster,
then he is a fox."
The scholar then said:
"A wise lord should respect the worthy and accommodate the multitude,
praise the good and pity the incapable.
Why do you hate a man of learning?
Mòzǐ advocated universal love;
is this how it should be?"
Having said this,
he asked to take his leave.
Huá had already stationed men to guard the gates,
so he could not get out.
After a while, he again said to Huá:
"Your gates are guarded by armed soldiers and horsemen;
surely you suspect me.
I fear that people of the world
will curl their tongues and cease to speak;
men of wisdom and strategy
will see your gate and not enter.
I deeply regret this for you, wise lord."
Huá did not respond,
and had his men guard even more strictly.
Léi Huàn, the magistrate of Fēngchéng,
was a man of broad learning.
He said to Huá:
"I have heard that demons fear dogs,
but what they can distinguish are only things a few hundred years old.
For a thousand-year-old essence,
they can no longer distinguish it.
Only a thousand-year-old dried wood,
when lit, will reveal its true form.
The ornamental pillar in front of King Zhāo of Yān's tomb
must be a thousand years old by now."
So he sent men to cut it down.
When the men arrived,
the pillar sighed and said:
"The old fox brought this upon himself,
and indeed has ruined my affairs."
From within the hollow of the pillar,
they retrieved a child in black clothing,
just over two feet tall.
When they brought it back to Luòyáng,
it turned into dried wood.
They lit it to illuminate the scholar,
who indeed was a spotted fox.
Màoxiān sighed and said:
"Had these two creatures not encountered me,
they could not have been obtained even in a thousand years."
The Filial Son in the Mountains
During the reign of Emperor Hǎixī of Jìn,
there was a man whose mother had passed away.
His family was poor and had no means to bury her,
so he moved the coffin deep into the mountains.
Beside it, he made straw sandals,
working day and night without rest.
As dusk approached,
a woman carrying a child came to seek lodging.
When night fell,
the filial son continued making sandals without pause.
The woman asked to sleep,
and she lay down by the fire.
It turned out to be a fox holding a black chicken.
The filial son then beat it to death
and threw it into a pit behind.
The next day,
a man came asking about his wife and child,
saying they had come to lodge here yesterday—
where were they now?
The filial son said:
"It was a fox,
and I have already killed it."
The man said:
"You wrongfully killed my wife.
How can you falsely claim it was a fox?
Where is the fox now?"
So they went together to the pit to look,
and the fox had turned into a woman.
The man then tied up the filial son and took him to the authorities,
demanding he pay with his life.
The filial son then said to the magistrate:
"This was truly a demonic creature.
Just release hunting dogs and it will become clear."
The demon came again, urging the filial son's execution.
The magistrate then asked about hunting matters:
"Can you distinguish dogs?"
He replied:
"I fear dogs by nature,
and I cannot distinguish them either."
So they released the dogs,
and he transformed into an old fox,
whereupon they shot and killed him.
Looking at the woman,
she had already turned back into a fox.
Chúnyú Jīn
During the Tàiyuán era of Jìn,
in front of the Wǎguān Buddhist temple, there was a young man named Chúnyú Jīn, fair and clean.
While seeing off a guest south of Shítóuchéng,
he encountered a woman
of beautiful appearance.
Jīn was delighted by her
and inquired about her.
Once mutual affection was established,
they went to the northwest corner of the city,
where they fully enjoyed each other's company.
Then they parted,
agreeing to meet again,
intending to marry.
The woman said:
"To have a husband like you,
what regret would I have even in death!
I have many brothers,
and both my parents are alive.
I must ask my parents."
Jīn then let the woman return
to ask her parents.
Her parents were also willing to consent.
The woman then ordered a maid to fetch a hundred catties of silver
and a hundred bolts of silk,
to help Jīn with the marriage.
After a long time,
they had two sons,
and Jīn was about to become the Director of the Imperial Library.
Sure enough, a groom came to summon him,
with carriages, horses, and a procession of musicians before and after.
After a few days,
a hunter passed by
looking for Jīn.
Leading several dozen dogs,
he charged straight in,
bit the woman and the children,
and they all turned into foxes.
The silks, gold, and silver
were all grass and human bones.
Liú Bózǔ
Liú Bózǔ of Bólíng in Jìn was the Governor of Hédōng.
On the ceiling where he stayed,
there was a spirit that could speak.
Whenever an imperial edict arrived from the capital,
the news would always be foretold to Bózǔ.
Bózǔ asked what it ate,
and it wanted sheep liver.
He bought sheep liver
and sliced it in front of it.
The pieces disappeared with each cut of the knife.
After two sheep livers were gone,
an old fox
revealed itself before the table.
An onlooker raised a knife to strike it.
Bózǔ shouted to stop him
and personally placed it back on the ceiling.
After a moment,
it laughed loudly and said:
"Earlier, I got drunk from eating liver
and suddenly lost my form.
Meeting the Governor like this,
I am greatly ashamed."
Later, when Bózǔ was about to become the Director of the Imperial Secretariat,
the spirit again foretold to Bózǔ:
"On such-and-such month and day, the document will arrive."
When the time came, it was as it said.
After entering the Imperial Secretariat office,
the spirit followed along on the ceiling,
often speaking about matters within the department.
Bózǔ became greatly fearful
and said to the spirit:
"Now my duty involves investigating and impeaching.
If the powerful officials around hear there is a spirit here,
they might use it to harm me."
The spirit replied:
"As the Governor worries,
I should take my leave."
Then it ceased without a sound.
The Old Farmer of Wúxīng
In Wúxīng, there was a man
with two sons.
While working in the fields,
they often saw their father come to scold and chase them, beating them.
The sons returned and told their mother.
The mother asked their father.
The father was greatly alarmed,
knowing it was a ghostly creature.
He then told his sons to cut it down,
and the ghost fell silent and did not come again.
The father worried that his sons might be troubled by it,
so he went himself.
The sons thought it was the ghost,
so they killed and buried him.
The ghost then returned,
taking the form of their father.
And it told the household
that the two sons had already killed the monster.
Years passed without anyone realizing.
Later, a master passed by their home
and said to the two sons:
"Your honored father has a great evil aura."
The sons told their father.
The father was furious.
The master then made a sound and entered,
and the father immediately turned into an old fox
and went under the bed.
They then captured and killed it.
The one they had killed earlier
was their real father.
They reburied him with proper mourning attire.
One son then committed suicide,
and the other, in grief and anger, also died.
Sūn Qǐ
Sūn Qǐ, a man from Wūshāng County,
during the Yìxī era,
was carrying documents to the commandery.
Arriving at Shítíng,
it was raining and dusk was falling.
He turned and saw a woman
holding a blue umbrella,
about sixteen or seventeen years old,
with a plump and beautiful appearance,
dressed entirely in purple.
That evening,
lightning illuminated the room,
revealing it was a large fox.
Qǐ then drew his sword and struck it dead.
The umbrella was a lotus leaf.
Huáng Shěn
In Jùróng County, in Mícūn Village, there was a man named Huáng Shěn
who was plowing in the fields.
A woman passed by his field,
walking along the ridge,
coming down from the east and then turning back.
At first, Shěn thought she was a human.
This happened every day,
and he found it very strange.
Shěn then asked her:
"Where do you come from so often?"
The woman paused briefly,
only smiled without speaking,
and then left.
Shěn grew even more suspicious.
He prepared a long sickle and waited for her return,
not daring to strike the woman,
but instead striking the maid following her.
The woman transformed into a fox and ran away.
Looking at the maid,
it was only a fox's tail.
Shěn chased after her but could not catch up.
Later, someone saw this fox emerge from a pit,
dug it up,
but found no tail anymore.
Liú Yuánjì
Liú Yuánjì of Chángshān,
in the nineteenth year of the Yuánjiā era of the Song dynasty,
once caught a fox.
Cutting open its belly, he found another fox inside,
and breaking that open,
he found yet another fox,
only then seeing the internal organs.
Although the three foxes were nested within each other,
their sizes were not much different.
Yuánjì did not find it strange,
and hung the skin behind his house.
That night,
a group of foxes gathered around it, howling,
and the skin disappeared.
Nothing else happened at Yuánjì's home.
The Zhèng Family Son
In recent times, there was a son of the Zhèng family
who was staying at the Chóngxuán Temple in Wú.
One leisurely day, he climbed the tower,
and suddenly saw a woman on the tower,
with a very beautiful appearance.
He thus formed a relationship with her,
and the woman showed no hesitation or fear from the start.
Afterward, she always came to his room.
Because of this, Zhèng began to despise his original wife,
and refused to live with her.
He often stayed alone for several months,
with the woman always by his side.
Later, his original wife sought out a highly virtuous nun,
asking her to come to the room to chant sutras.
The woman then stopped coming.
Zhèng was furious:
"Why did you call this demonic nun,
causing my family member to stop coming?"
When the nun occasionally returned to the temple,
the woman would come again.
When the nun came back, she would leave.
This happened several times.
Later, he constantly scolded his wife,
telling her not to use this nun.
His wife, realizing it was effective,
kept the nun in the room,
chanting day and night.
The woman suddenly said to Zhèng: "I came before to share joy with you,
but regret that because of the nun,
I have become weary.
Now I bid you farewell,
I am merely the fox Erniáng from the tower."
After speaking, she disappeared,
and was never seen again.
A Household in Jìnyáng
North of Jìnyáng,
the land is cold and bamboo is scarce.
Therefore, the residents often plant reeds to form forests,
as a substitute for the bamboo of the south.
In the early years of the Chángqìng era of the Tang dynasty,
there was a household in the northern capital,
whose land had many reed forests.
In the village, there was once a banquet,
and leftover food was placed in their house.
By the next day,
it would always disappear without a trace.
A villager who stored silk fabrics in his room
also lost them.
The villagers secretly found it strange.
Later, at night, they heard the cries of many infants,
but when they listened closely,
it fell silent.
The next night, they heard it again.
The villagers grew increasingly fearful.
One day later,
they told other villagers:
"For several nights, we have heard infants crying in the forest.
We reckon there shouldn't be infants in this place,
and fear it is something strange."
They then worked together to clear the forest,
and cut the grass.
After clearing everything,
they found a hole,
containing silk fabrics and food utensils.
They saw over ten wild foxes,
some frowning and bowing,
some moaning and looking up,
some blinking and nursing,
some lying down and crouching,
crying out as if in distress.
The villagers killed them all,
and from then on, the villagers lived in peace.
Fèi Mì
At the end of the Liáng dynasty,
a man from Shǔ named Fèi Mì was harvesting wheat
when he encountered a storm,
and took shelter among the rocks to avoid the rain.
Several li from home,
he looked into the distance ahead,
and saw several dozen women,
all wearing red and purple patterned clothes,
singing as they approached.
Mì secretly wondered:
Why would there be a group of colorfully dressed women in the fields?
He found it strange.
As they drew closer,
they fell completely silent.
When they were a few steps away from Mì,
they all stopped and stood still.
After a short while,
they all turned their backs to Mì.
Mì went to the side to look at them,
and saw that their faces had no eyebrows, ears, noses, or mouths,
only hanging black feathers.
Then Mì was terrified,
his mind confused, and he collapsed to the ground.
By the first watch of the night,
Mì's father grew worried that he had not returned,
and went searching with a torch.
He found Mì lying by the roadside,
with ten hedgehogs on his left side,
who scattered and fled upon seeing the fire.
Mì returned home,
and died after over a hundred days.
A Guest of Xǔ Qīnmíng
In the Rénhé Ward of the eastern capital of the Tang dynasty, there was a residence of Xǔ Qīnmíng.
Once, someone was in the main hall of the Xǔ family,
reading by the fire on a winter night.
He dozed off,
and heard the sounds of insects and mice moving.
Looking secretly,
he saw an old woman,
covered entirely in white fur,
climb onto the bed near the stove,
warming her belly and scratching an itch.
Her figure was short and small,
unlike a human.
The guest was frightened,
and suddenly let out a loud cry.
The creature fell to the ground,
and fled away at full speed.
The guest, because the walls of the residence were high,
and there was no way in or out,
called a servant to bring a torch.
They searched the courtyard.
In a bamboo grove,
they found a large stone.
Moving the stone,
they found a white hedgehog,
and killed it.
Hedgehogs in the Performance Ground
In recent years in the capital,
there were crowds gathering to watch performances in the streets.
When asked,
they said:
"Two hedgehogs are fighting each other,
not only keeping rhythm,
but also following the rules."
At the time, among the spectators was the Junior Supervisor of the Imperial Workshops, Lǐ Yùn,
who also said he had seen it.
When a hedgehog sees a tiger,
it jumps into the tiger's ear.
Wú Táng
Wú Táng was a man from Lúlíng.
From a young age, he enjoyed archery and hunting,
and his arrows never missed their mark.
Once, during springtime,
he took his son out hunting.
They came upon a doe
playing with her fawn.
The doe sensed human presence
and led her fawn away to hide.
The fawn, unaware of danger,
approached Wú Táng.
Wú Táng shot it dead.
The doe, startled, returned and cried mournfully.
Wú Táng then placed the fawn on clear ground
and hid himself in the grass.
When the doe came to nuzzle and mourn over her fawn,
Wú Táng shot her as well,
and she fell to the bowstring's twang.
Later, he encountered another doe.
As he drew his crossbow,
the arrow suddenly released on its own
and struck his son.
Wú Táng immediately threw down his bow, embraced his son,
and beat his chest in anguish.
Suddenly, he heard a voice from the air calling out:
"Wú Táng,
the doe's beloved fawn—
how was it different from your own!"
Startled, he looked around
and saw a tiger emerge from the side,
leap forward,
and maul him, breaking his arm.
He returned home and died overnight.
Lǐ Yīng
There was a man named Lǐ Yīng
and his brother, Lǐ Tāo.
Both were skilled with the crossbow.
Once, they shot a doe,
cut off its four legs,
hung them from a tree,
and carved them for roasting.
As they laid the meat over the fire
and were about to eat,
they suddenly saw a divine being at the foot of the mountain,
about ten feet tall,
striding forth,
holding a large sack.
Upon arrival,
he gathered all the meat, skin, and bones,
along with what was on the fire, into his sack,
and went straight back up the mountain.
Lǐ Yīng and his brother Lǐ Tāo were terrified
and at a loss for what to do.
But nothing else happened.
Liú Fān
In Qīngzhōu, there was a man named Liú Fān.
During the Yuánjiā era,
he shot a river deer.
He gutted it
and stuffed it with grass,
whereupon it suddenly stood up.
Moments later, it walked forward.
Liú Fān, astonished, pulled out the stuffing grass,
and shortly after, it lay down again.
This happened three times.
Liú Fān secretly recorded this method
and sought similar cases;
treating wounds this way often proved effective.
The Gray Deer
A deer that lives a thousand years becomes a gray deer;
after another five hundred years, it becomes a white deer;
after yet another five hundred years, it transforms into a black deer.
During the reign of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
a man from Zhōngshān obtained a black deer.
After cooking it and examining its bones,
they were all black.
An immortal's prescription states:
"Make dried meat from a black deer;
eating it
extends life to two thousand years."
In Yúgān County, there was a white deer
that locals said was a thousand years old.
Emperor Chéng of Jìn sent people to capture it.
A bronze plaque with engraved characters
was found behind its antlers,
saying:
"A gray deer presented from Línjiāng in the second year of Bǎodǐng."
Kēténg
On Kāngtóu Mountain in Hépǔ, there was a deer
with a kēténg vine on its forehead,
four strands stretching upward,
each about ten feet long.
In Léi Commandery, there were deer
with a fishy smell and no flavor,
inedible.
Local lore says:
"They transform from sea fish."
People of the commandery have seen creatures with fish heads and deer bodies,
which confirms this.
How is this different from the transformations of hawks, doves, sparrows, and pheasants?
Bronze Ring
When Hú Xiàng was governor of Guózhōu,
a hunter killed a deer
weighing one hundred and eighty jin.
A bronze ring was pierced through its hoof,
with seal script characters on the ring.
Even knowledgeable scholars could not decipher them.
Deer-Horses
East of Táoyáng County lies Huà Mountain,
ninety li from the county seat,
winding and towering,
with jagged peaks and ridges.
Once, a man hunting there
saw two deer.
One had pure white fur like frost,
illuminating the mountain valley;
the other was patterned with five colors,
radiant and dazzling as the sun.
The hunter, amazed by their strangeness, did not shoot.
After walking several li forward,
he saw two men who reproached him:
"Why have you come, sir?
Did you not see our two horses?"
He replied:
"I only saw a pair of deer."
They said:
"We are envoys of Emperor Yú,
sent to Héng Mountain
to deliver a message to the Taoist priest of Ānqiū.
The deer you saw
were our horses."
Purple Stone
In Jìn'ān, there was a woodcutter named Chén from the eastern mountains
who often saw a light in the mountains illuminating the sky.
After watching for a long time,
he saw a large deer
with light emanating from its mouth.
He set a trap, captured it,
and cut open its belly,
finding a purple stone,
round and lustrous like a pearl.
He treasured it,
and from then on, his family prospered.
When it came to his grandson,
who was extravagant, indulgent, and fond of drink,
he once played with the pearl while drunk,
thinking, "What's so divine about a stone?"
and smashed it to pieces.
From then on, the family fell into poverty.
Lù Shàodì
During the Táng dynasty, Lù Shàodì, a Vice Director of the Ministry of Works, served as the county sheriff of Lúshì.
While overseeing a seasonal hunt,
he encountered five or six deer by a stream.
They saw people but were not alarmed,
their spotted fur like a painting.
Lù wondered why the hunters did not shoot.
He asked them,
and the hunters said:
"These are immortal deer.
Shooting them causes no harm,
and it brings misfortune."
Lù did not believe them
and insisted.
The hunters, having no choice,
shot an arrow once,
and the deer ran off with the arrow.
Upon returning,
the archer fell off a cliff
and broke his left leg.
Emperor Xuánzōng of Táng
In the autumn of the twenty-third year of the Kāiyuán era,
Emperor Xuánzōng was hunting in the outskirts.
When the imperial carriage reached the plains of Xiányáng,
a large deer appeared before it,
its body robust and imposing,
quite different from ordinary deer.
The Emperor ordered an archer to shoot it,
and it was hit with a single arrow.
Upon the Emperor’s return,
he commanded the kitchen officials to roast its thigh and present it,
and the Office of Imperial Catering prepared the cooked meat on a platter for offering.
At that time, the elderly gentleman Zhāng Guǒ was in attendance.
The Emperor ordered Guǒ to sit before him,
and bestowed the deer meat upon him.
Guǒ expressed thanks and ate it.
After eating,
he addressed the Emperor, saying:
"What does Your Majesty think of this deer?"
The Emperor said:
"I only know it is a deer;
I do not know what else it might be!"
Guǒ said:
"This deer is nearly a thousand years old.
Your Majesty has kindly inquired of your servant."
The Emperor laughed and said:
"This is merely a beast;
how can you claim it is a thousand years old?"
Guǒ said:
"In the autumn of the fifth year of the Yuánshòu era of the Hàn dynasty,
I was accompanying Emperor Wǔ on a hunt in the Shànglín Park.
Among the attending officials, one captured this deer alive and presented it.
The Emperor showed it to me.
I addressed him, saying:
'This is an immortal deer,
destined to live a thousand years.
Now that it has been captured alive,
it would be better to spare its life.'
It happened that Emperor Wǔ revered immortals,
and thus he accepted my counsel."
The Emperor said:
"Sir, you are deceiving me!
Moreover, from the fifth year of Hàn Yuánshòu
to the present is eight hundred years.
Even if this deer were long-lived,
how could it have survived eight hundred years without being captured in a hunt?
Besides, there are many deer within the imperial parks and enclosures;
why could the one captured today not be another deer?"
Guǒ said:
"At that time, after Emperor Wǔ captured this deer,
he intended to release it.
He also ordered Dōngfāng Shuò to fashion a plaque from refined copper,
engrave characters upon it,
to record the year,
and attach it beneath the left antler.
I wish to verify this;
it may demonstrate that your servant is not speaking falsely."
The Emperor immediately ordered the deer’s head to be placed before them,
and commanded the inner attendant Gāo Lìshì to examine it.
After the time it takes to eat a meal,
nothing had been found.
The Emperor laughed and said:
"Sir, you are indeed mistaken!
Beneath the left antler,
where is the copper plaque?"
Guǒ said:
"I request permission to search for it myself."
He then looked to the attendants,
ordered iron pincers,
and with them extracted a small plaque,
indeed made of copper,
about two inches in size.
It was because the years and months were so long
that it had become concealed by fur and hide,
and thus was initially unseen.
He presented it,
and the Emperor ordered it to be polished and examined.
Its characters were worn and damaged,
and could no longer be deciphered.
The Emperor then believed that Guǒ was not mistaken.
He further asked Guǒ:
"In the fifth year of Hàn Yuánshòu,
what was the position in the sexagenary cycle?
What events were recorded in the histories?
I shall verify them in the records and chronicles.
Sir, please tell me."
Guǒ said:
"That year corresponded to Guǐhài in the cycle.
Emperor Wǔ first excavated the Kūnmíng Pond,
to practice naval warfare,
and conducted hunts in accordance with ritual.
Up to the present year of Jiǎxū,
eight hundred and fifty-two years have passed."
The Emperor immediately ordered the Hàn histories to be consulted.
The Kūnmíng Pond
was indeed excavated in the fifth year of Yuánshòu.
The sexagenary cycle designation was also without error.
The Emperor turned to Lìshì and said:
"How extraordinary!
Zhāng Guǒ can speak of matters from the time of Hàn Emperor Wǔ;
he is truly what is called a perfected man.
I certainly cannot comprehend it."
Péng Shì
Péng Shì of Lè'ān in Póyáng,
during the Xiánkāng era of the Jìn dynasty,
made his living by hunting.
Each time he entered the mountains,
he went together with his son.
Later, he suddenly stumbled and fell,
transformed into a deer,
and bounded away.
His son never hunted again for the rest of his life.
But his grandson resumed the practice.
Once, he shot a deer,
and between its antlers was a Daoist Seven Stars talisman,
along with his grandfather’s name,
and the year and month of his village residence.
Seeing this, he was filled with regret and remorse,
and from then on forever gave up hunting.
Deer Maiden
On Shífá Mountain northeast of Jiāngyīn County in Chángzhōu,
during the Liáng dynasty, a woodcutter entered this mountain
and saw a doe giving birth,
and then heard the sound of a child crying.
Going to look,
he saw that she had given birth to a girl.
He therefore took her and raised her.
When she grew up,
he had her leave home to become a Daoist nun.
People of the time called her "Deer Maiden."
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng established a convent for her,
named the Shèng Convent.
Zhāng Gètà
Long ago, Zhāng Gètà and Níng Chéng, two men,
both left home to become ascetics in a stone chamber on Yúntái Mountain in Shǔ.
Suddenly, a person
wearing a yellow plain silk unlined garment
and a coarse cloth headscarf
came before them and said:
"Are you weary, Daoist masters?"
Then, using a mirror to shine upon him,
they saw he was a deer.
They therefore reproached and questioned him, saying:
"You, an old deer from the grass,
how dare you assume human form deceitfully?"
When he finished speaking,
he transformed into an old deer and ran away.
Chē Jiǎ
Táo Qián’s Sōushén Jì says:
"There was a scholar surnamed Chē,
who was from Huáinán.
Once when it was raining,
he was sitting alone in his house.
Suddenly, two young women came to him.
They wore purple patterned silk jackets,
stood before his bed,
and talked and laughed with him.
Chē became suspicious:
'The rain is like this;
these women have come from outside,
yet why are their clothes not wet at all?
They must be supernatural beings.'
On his wall hung a bronze mirror beforehand,
several inches in diameter.
Looking back into the mirror,
he saw two deer standing before the bed.
He therefore took a knife and struck them,
and they all turned into deer.
One ran away,
and he captured one,
making it into dried meat and eating it.
The Old Monk of Sōng Mountain
On Mount Sōng, there was an old monk
who had built a thatched hut amidst the vines and creepers,
devoted to his practice without venturing out.
Suddenly, he saw a young boy come alone to pay his respects,
earnestly requesting to become his disciple.
The monk merely chanted scriptures, paying him no heed.
The boy remained from dawn till dusk, refusing to leave.
The monk then asked him:
"In this deep mountain,
human traces are exceedingly rare.
How did you, a child, come to be here?
And why do you seek to become a disciple?"
The boy replied:
"I originally lived at the foot of the mountain.
Both my parents have passed away,
and I lost my support at a young age.
This must be the result of not cultivating virtuous karma in my past life.
Therefore, I have made a vow
to renounce the mundane world
and come seeking my master.
Truly, I wish to cultivate blessings for my future lives."
The monk said:
"Can you truly do this?
But what of the solitude of monastic life,
so unlike that of ordinary people?
Though your aspiration is commendable,
can you follow the Way,
with a single-minded heart?"
The boy replied:
"If my heart contradicts my words,
Heaven and Earth
would not tolerate it themselves,
let alone my master."
The monk observed his keen intelligence
and recognized a karmic connection for good,
so he shaved the boy's head.
After becoming a disciple,
the boy was diligent and zealous in his practice,
rarely matched by others.
Sometimes he would expound the Dharma to the monk,
and the monk could not respond;
sometimes he would question the monk about the Way,
and the monk could not refute him.
The old monk deeply esteemed him,
considering him a sage.
Several years later,
during the clear autumn season,
when myriad trees were shedding their leaves,
a cool wind arose mournfully,
and the ravines and valleys were desolate and still,
he suddenly gazed around with emotion
and chanted clearly:
"I was originally born to live long within these deep mountains;
why then did I enter another's gate of non-duality?
Better to seek out my companions of old
than to weary my spirit morning and night."
After chanting,
he let out a long whistle.
After a long while,
a herd of deer passed by.
The boy leaped up,
cast off his monk's robes,
transformed into a deer,
and bounded away, following the herd.
Wáng Hù
Twenty lǐ west of Qízhōu was a man named Wáng Hù,
from a wealthy and powerful family.
His mansion was splendid and magnificent,
rivaling those of the noble and eminent.
He often kept his halls open
to receive travelers.
As for fine delicacies and fragrant wine,
even if a thousand people came to him,
there was never any shortage.
Suddenly one day,
a Dàoshi came to visit Hù,
claiming to be Xué Zhēn, a Dàoshi from Mount Huà.
Carrying a single qín
and bearing a gourd of medicine on his back,
he came seeking lodging.
Hù, by nature fond of the Dào,
upon hearing this,
joyfully went out to welcome him.
He invited him into a deep courtyard
and treated him with exceptional respect.
The Dàoshi asked Hù:
"You are so wealthy,
sufficient to rival the pleasures of marquises and earls.
Blessed you are indeed,
but what of your lack of virtue?"
Hù laughed, stood up, and bowed.
The Dàoshi said:
"Do you set out food at your gate
to await the worthy and talented?
Or to feed the hungry?
If it is to feed the hungry,
now that the world is peaceful and content,
with surplus grain in the fields,
and no one suffering from want,
whom would you feed?
If it is to await the worthy and talented,
then I have not heard of you inviting a single worthy person
or greeting a single talented one.
This is enough to know that you yourself lack virtue.
Do not be surprised by my words.
I fear you may gain a reputation for foolish arrogance,
spreading among people's mouths,
so I speak these blunt words to awaken you,
also moved by your exceptional respect and admiration for me."
Hù was then deeply moved, his expression changing,
and he bowed again.
The Dàoshi continued:
"I have heard that when a person has a fondness or pursuit,
there must be a teacher behind it.
Those who engage in political maneuvering
truly harbor ambitions of persuasion;
those who study Sūn and Wú
how could they lack a heart for contention and warfare?
As for me, carrying a single qín
and bearing a gourd of medicine on my back—
is it merely to endure hardship?
Rather, there is a purpose.
Carrying the qín:
I know the qín possesses ancient refinement;
I wish people to know I cherish antiquity,
and also wish to transform people, returning them to simplicity and purity,
reducing frivolity and superficiality.
Bearing the medicine gourd:
I know people suffer many illnesses;
I wish them to know I have the intent to heal and cure human ailments.
My qín is not only to transform myself,
but to transform others.
My medicine is not only to cure my own illnesses,
but to cure the illnesses of others.
Alas!
Your wealth aids others,
which differs greatly
from those who hoard a fortune in gold
and exploit people.
But if you compare yourself to the noble and wealthy families of antiquity who treated scholars with respect,
you should feel ashamed.
You must distinguish between the worthy and the foolish,
carefully preserve your reputation,
lest you instead invite slander."
Hù bowed once more.
The Dàoshi then called for wine and poured for himself.
As soon as dawn broke,
he abruptly took his leave and departed.
Hù sent someone to secretly follow him.
They saw the Dàoshi transform into a great deer
and head west, disappearing to an unknown place.
Miscellaneous Accounts
In the villages of Sōngzī and Zhījiāng in Jiānglíng, deer hunters
typically use the leg bone of a pelican as a pipe,
and the fatty membrane from a deer's heart as a reed,
blowing to imitate deer calls.
There are variations: large calls, small calls, and soft bleats.
If one imitates the call of a doe,
bucks will gather completely,
as they are lured by the female's sound,
allowing hunters to draw their bows and shoot them.
In the southern regions, deer are numerous;
each buck leads a herd of about a hundred does.
By spring, they become emaciated,
likely from excessive mating.
In summer, they eat only calamus
and regain their plumpness.
When their antlers are shed,
the velvet is extremely painful.
If hunters encounter them then,
the deer dare not flee
but lie still, not moving.
The hunters tie a rope to the velvet,
cut it off, and take it.
First, they taste the blood,
then kill the deer.
How bitter is their fate!
Creatures like the golden snub-nosed monkey, musk deer, and peacock
suffer harm because of their usefulness;
truly pitiable.
Lánzhōu
During the Yǒngchún era,
rabbits ran rampant in Lánzhōu and Shèngzhōu,
forming herds of tens of millions,
devouring seedlings completely.
It was unknown what creature had transformed into them.
Once the rampage ended,
they all vanished,
with no one knowing where they went.
How strange!
Yáng Mài
The Minister of Agriculture, Yáng Mài, was fond of hunting in his youth.
He once said:
"While in Cháng'ān,
I released my falcon into the wilderness.
From afar, I saw a rabbit leaping in the grass.
The falcon also spotted it
and immediately swooped down to seize it.
But upon reaching the spot, there was nothing there.
I called the falcon back to my glove.
After walking several dozen paces,
I looked back at that place
and again saw the rabbit running.
The falcon struck once more,
yet still caught nothing.
This happened three times.
I then ordered the grass to be cleared to search for it,
and found a complete set of rabbit bones.
It must have been the ghost of a rabbit."
The White Ape
King Gōujiàn of Yuè asked Fàn Lǐ about hand-to-hand combat techniques.
Fàn Lǐ replied:
"I have heard that in Yuè there is a maiden
whom the people of the state praise.
I suggest Your Majesty inquire of her about the principles of hand-to-hand combat."
Thereupon, the king invited the maiden.
As the maiden was heading north to meet the king,
she encountered an old man on the road,
who called himself Yuán Gōng.
He asked the maiden:
"I hear you are skilled with the sword;
may I see a demonstration?"
The maiden said:
"I dare not conceal anything from you;
please test me as you wish."
Yuán Gōng then pulled down a bamboo from the treetop,
which appeared withered,
and its tip broke off and fell to the ground.
The maiden picked up the tip.
Yuán Gōng wielded the base of the bamboo and thrust at the maiden,
but the maiden, moving in rhythm, evaded him three times.
She then raised her staff and struck at him.
Yuán Gōng leaped up into a tree
and transformed into a white ape.
Zhōu Qún
Zhōu Qún was profoundly skilled in divination and prophecy.
While traveling in the Mín Mountains to collect stones,
he saw a white ape descend from a sheer peak
and stand facing him.
Zhōu Qún drew the sword he wore at his side
and hurled it at the white ape.
The ape transformed into an old man,
holding a jade tablet in his hand,
eight inches long.
He presented it to Zhōu Qún.
Zhōu Qún asked:
"In which year were you born?"
The old man replied:
"I am now old and frail,
and have forgotten the year and month of my birth.
I recall that since the time of Xuānyuán,
I began studying calendrical calculations.
Fēnghòu and Róngchéng,
both historians under the Yellow Emperor,
came to me to learn calendrical arts.
By the time of Zhuānxū,
when recalculating the movements of the sun, moon, and stars,
there were many discrepancies.
During the Spring and Autumn period,
there were figures like Zǐ Wéi, Zǐ Yě, and Pí Zào;
though their methods were somewhat effective,
they never grasped the true essence.
Generations have passed since then,
too many to record,
and knowledge has been passed down through tradition.
By the time of the great Hàn dynasty,
Luò Xiàhóng
finally grasped the main principles."
Zhōu Qún reflected on his words,
and devoted himself even more diligently to the study of mathematics.
Through examining the cycles of annual calendars
and verifying them with charts and prophecies,
he came to know that Shǔ was destined to perish.
And indeed, the following year, it submitted to its fate.
All praised Zhōu Qún for his mastery of the principles of yīn and yáng.
The people of Shǔ called him the Later Sage.
The Jiāguó
In the high mountains southwest of Shǔ,
there exists a creature similar to a monkey,
seven feet tall,
capable of walking like a human,
and skilled at chasing people.
It is called the "Jiāguó,"
also known as "Mǎhuà,"
or sometimes "Jué."
It lies in wait for young women traveling on the roads,
stealing them away,
and people remain unaware.
If any travelers pass by its vicinity,
they often tie themselves together with long ropes,
yet even this does not guarantee safety.
This creature can distinguish the scent of males and females,
so it only takes women,
while men remain oblivious.
If it captures a woman,
it makes her its wife.
Those who bear no children
are never allowed to return.
After ten years,
their appearance becomes like that of the creature,
their minds grow confused,
and they no longer think of returning home.
If a woman gives birth to a child,
the creature sends the child back to her family.
The offspring all resemble humans in form.
If the family does not raise the child,
the mother invariably dies.
Thus, out of fear,
no one dares not to raise it.
When the child grows up,
it is no different from other humans,
and all take the surname Yáng.
This is why many people in southwest Shǔ today bear the surname Yáng;
most are descendants of the "Jiāguó" or "Mǎhuà."
Ōuyáng Hé
In the final years of the Dàtóng era of the Liáng dynasty,
Píngnán General Lìn Qīn was dispatched on a southern campaign.
Upon reaching Guìlín,
he defeated Lǐ Shīgǔ and Chén Chè.
His subordinate commander Ōuyáng Hé advanced his forces as far as Chánglè,
pacifying all the local cave-dwelling tribes,
and penetrating deep into treacherous terrain.
Ōuyáng Hé's wife was slender and fair,
exceedingly beautiful.
One of his men said:
"General, why have you brought such a lovely woman through this place?
This land harbors a creature
skilled at stealing young maidens,
and those of great beauty are especially unlikely to escape.
You must guard her carefully."
Ōuyáng Hé grew deeply suspicious and fearful.
That night, he stationed soldiers around his quarters,
hid his wife in a secret inner chamber,
securely bolted it tight,
and set over a dozen maidservants to watch over her.
That evening,
it was dark and overcast with rain.
By the fifth watch,
all was silent and nothing was heard.
The guards grew weary and dozed off,
when suddenly, as if startled by something, they awoke—
only to find his wife already gone.
The doors and bolts remained as before,
with no trace of how she had left.
Outside the gate lay perilous mountains,
obscured and confusing even at close range,
making pursuit impossible.
By dawn,
there was absolutely no trace of her.
Ōuyáng Hé was filled with furious grief,
and vowed not to return empty-handed.
Pleading illness,
he halted his army's advance,
and day after day ranged far and wide,
searching deep into valleys and across dangerous terrain for her.
After more than a month,
he suddenly found one of his wife's embroidered slippers
on a thicket of dwarf bamboo about a hundred lǐ away.
Though soaked by rain,
it was still recognizable.
Ōuyáng Hé was even more heartbroken,
and his determination to find her grew stronger.
He selected thirty stalwart men,
armed them and supplied them with provisions,
and they lived among the cliffs, foraging in the wilds.
After another ten days or more,
about two hundred lǐ from their camp,
they saw a mountain to the south,
verdant and elegant, towering above the rest.
Reaching its base,
they found a deep stream encircling it.
They then lashed logs together to cross to the sheer cliff.
Among the emerald bamboo,
they occasionally glimpsed flashes of red silk
and heard the sounds of laughter and chatter.
Grasping vines and pulling on ropes,
they climbed to the summit,
where fine trees stood in rows,
interspersed with famous flowers.
Beneath them, lush green grass
lay thick and soft like a carpet.
The air was clear and still, profoundly quiet,
a secluded realm utterly apart.
There was a stone gate facing east,
through which several dozen women, dressed in bright, fresh garments,
moved about playing, singing, and laughing,
going in and out.
Upon seeing the men, they all gazed slowly and stood still.
When Ōuyáng Hé approached, they asked:
"What brings you here?"
Ōuyáng Hé told them everything.
They looked at each other and sighed, saying:
"Your worthy wife arrived here over a month ago.
She is now ill in bed;
you should go and see her."
Entering the gate,
they found a wooden door.
Inside were three spacious chambers as large as halls.
Beds were placed along all four walls,
each spread with brocade mats.
His wife lay on a stone couch,
piled with multiple layers of cushions and mats,
with delicacies arrayed before her.
As Ōuyáng Hé approached to look at her,
she turned her eyes for a single glance,
then immediately waved her hand urgently, signaling him to leave.
The women said:
"We, along with your wife,
have been here for a long time—some for up to ten years.
This is the dwelling of a supernatural creature
whose strength can kill a man.
Even a hundred armed men
could not subdue him.
Fortunately, he has not yet returned;
you must avoid him quickly.
But if you can procure two hú of fine wine,
ten dogs for food,
and several dozen jīn of hemp,
we can work together to kill him.
He always comes at noon exactly;
afterward, be careful not to come too early.
Let us set a period of ten days."
They urged him to leave,
and Ōuyáng Hé hastily withdrew.
He then obtained strong liquor, hemp, and dogs,
and returned on the appointed day.
The women said:
"He is fond of wine
and often drinks until intoxicated.
When drunk, he must exert his strength,
ordering us to bind his limbs to the bed with colored silk ribbons,
which he snaps with a single leap.
We once stitched three layers together,
and even then, his strength was not exhausted, though he could not break free.
Now we will conceal hemp within silk and bind him with that;
he likely will not be able to break it.
His entire body is like iron,
except for a few inches below his navel,
which he always keeps protected and covered.
That spot surely cannot withstand a blade."
Pointing to a nearby cliff, they said:
"That is his storehouse for food.
You should hide there,
wait quietly and watch.
Place the wine beneath the flowers,
and release the dogs in the woods.
Once our plan succeeds,
we will call, and you can come out."
Following their instructions,
he held his breath and waited.
In the late afternoon,
a creature like a bolt of white silk
descended from another mountain,
streaking through the air as if flying,
and went straight into the cave.
A short while later,
a handsome man with a fine beard, over six chǐ tall,
dressed in white and trailing a staff,
emerged surrounded by the women.
Seeing the dogs, he looked at them in surprise,
leapt to seize them,
tore them apart and devoured them.
After eating his fill,
the women vied to present him with wine in jade cups,
and he laughed and joked merrily.
After drinking several dǒu,
they helped him away.
Again, sounds of playful laughter were heard.
After a long while,
a woman came out and signaled to them,
and they took up their weapons and entered.
They saw a large white ape,
its four limbs bound to the head of the bed,
glancing at the people and shrinking back,
unable to free itself,
its eyes shining like lightning.
They all attacked it with weapons,
but it was like striking iron or stone.
Only when they stabbed below its navel
did the blade penetrate,
and blood gushed out like a fountain.
It then let out a great roar, saying:
"Heaven is killing me,
not any power of yours.
However, your wife is already pregnant;
do not kill the child.
He will encounter a sage emperor,
and surely bring great honor to your lineage."
With these words, it died.
Searching its hoard,
they found treasures accumulated in abundance,
rare delicacies in full array,
spread across tables and stands.
Every precious thing found in the human world
was amply present.
There were several hú of rare incense,
a pair of precious swords,
and thirty women.
All were of peerless beauty.
Those who had been there longest had been there for ten years.
They said that when their beauty faded, they would certainly be taken away,
with no one knowing where they were placed.
Moreover, it hunted and gathered only for itself,
with no companions or kindred.
Every morning it would wash,
put on a cap,
add a white lined robe,
and wear a silk outer garment.
It seemed unaffected by heat or cold.
Its body was covered in white hair,
several cùn long.
In its dwelling, it often read wooden slips,
the characters resembling talismanic script,
completely incomprehensible.
When finished, it would place them beneath a stone step.
On sunny days, she would sometimes dance with twin swords,
circling her body like flying lightning,
the light forming a perfect circle like the moon.
Her diet was irregular,
she enjoyed eating fruits and chestnuts,
and was especially fond of dogs,
chewing them and drinking their blood.
As soon as the sun passed noon,
she would vanish abruptly.
In half a day, she could travel thousands of miles and back,
and by evening, she would always return.
This was her usual routine.
Whatever she needed, she obtained instantly.
At night, she would go from bed to bed, teasing and playing,
visiting each one in a single night,
never sleeping.
Her speech was fluent and detailed,
her Huá pronunciation clear and sharp.
Yet her appearance resembled that of a jiājué-like creature.
At the beginning of this year, when the leaves fell,
she suddenly said sorrowfully:
"I have been accused by the mountain god,
and will receive the death penalty.
I also seek protection from the multitude of spirits,
hoping perhaps to avoid it."
Before this, when the moon was waning,
flames appeared on the stone steps,
burning her writings,
and she lamented with a sense of loss, saying:
"I have lived a thousand years without a child,
now that I have a child,
my time of death has come."
Then, looking at the women,
she wept for a long time.
And she said:
"This mountain is steep and isolated,
no one has ever reached it.
Looking down from the heights,
not a single woodcutter can be seen.
Below, there are many tigers, wolves, and strange beasts.
That you could come here now—
if not by heaven's will, then how?"
Gé took the precious jades, treasures, and the women, and they all returned,
some still knowing their families.
Gé's wife gave birth to a son after a year,
whose appearance resembled hers.
Later, Gé was executed by Emperor Wǔ of Chén.
He had long been friends with Jiǎng Zǒng,
who admired his son's exceptional intelligence,
often took him in to raise him,
thus sparing him from disaster.
When the boy grew up,
he indeed excelled in literature and calligraphy,
becoming well-known in his time.
Chén Yán
Chén Yán of Yǐngchuān, courtesy name Yèmèng,
was a native of Wǔyáng,
who sojourned in Eastern Wú.
At the end of the Jǐnglóng era,
he was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate
and went to the capital.
While traveling to Wèinán,
he saw a woman of exceptionally beautiful appearance,
dressed in white clothes,
standing by the roadside,
covering her mouth with her sleeve and weeping,
as if bearing the appearance of one wronged and oppressed.
Yán then inquired of her,
and the woman, weeping, replied:
"I am a woman of Chǔ,
surnamed Hóu,
my family residing in Yìyáng County.
My late father was renowned for his lofty integrity in the region of Xiāng and Chǔ,
and thus he concealed his traces in the mountain forests,
never willing to pay court to nobles and lords.
Although I am but a woman,
I too possess the aspiration of Jī and Yǐng.
I was just about to lodge my traces in Péng, Yíng, Kūn, or Làng,
to fulfill my preference.
It happened that I encountered a certain gentleman Liú of Pèiguó,
who served as the commandant of Yìyáng,
and he was a friend who disregarded formalities with my late father.
My late father admired Gentleman Liú's lofty righteousness,
and thus gave me in marriage to the Liú family.
Since becoming a wife of the Liú family,
it has been nearly ten years,
and I have never had the slightest fault.
In the spring of the year before last,
Gentleman Liú was transferred and appointed as commandant of Zhēnyuán.
Before a year had passed,
he was dismissed due to illness.
The entire household returned to the countryside residence on the banks of the Wèi River.
Gentleman Liú, lacking in conduct,
then married another woman, surnamed Lú,
a native of Púshàng,
whose nature was extremely fierce and cruel,
and who constantly engaged in quarrels with me.
Unable to bear my indignation,
I therefore fled and came here.
Moreover, I originally admired divine immortals,
often wishing to tread high among the clouds and mists,
to dwell peacefully in the seclusion of cliffs and valleys,
content with the taste of acorns and chestnuts,
which would also be sufficient to live out my old age.
How could I merely be troubled by the dusty world,
which only serves as a burden?
Now I am resolved not to return to the Liú family."
Then, with a frowning countenance and resentful sobs,
she seemed unable to resolve her own distress.
Yán, by nature upright and sincere,
hearing her words,
believed them greatly.
He then asked:
"Where will you return to, young lady?"
The woman said:
"I am a destitute person,
where could I return to?
Nevertheless,
since you ask me,
do you have some intention?
If it is truly so,
how would I dare to oppose your command?"
Yán was pleased.
He immediately had her ride in the rear carriage and traveled together with her.
Arriving at the capital,
they resided in Yǒngchóng Ward.
At first she was very respectful,
but later became disrespectful.
Often she would scold and rage,
as if in a state of madness.
Yán detested this and moreover regretted it.
The next day, when Yán went out,
the woman closed the door,
locked it,
placed Yán's clothing and bags in the courtyard,
and destroyed and tore them almost completely.
When Yán returned in the evening,
the woman refused to admit him.
Yán became angry,
and immediately broke through the door and entered.
He saw that his own clothing and belongings
had all been destroyed and torn.
Yán then scolded and reproached her.
The woman suddenly flew into a rage,
tore Yán's clothing, lapels, and sashes,
leaving almost not a single intact thread.
She also clawed his face,
bit his flesh,
his entire body was injured,
and blood stained the ground.
Then she howled and screamed for a long time.
Yán was troubled by this,
and could not control her.
Thereupon, the people of the ward all came to watch,
crowding around his door.
At that time, there was a lay Buddhist named Hǎo in the ward,
skilled at seeing ghosts,
possessing the arts of talismans and incantations for exorcism.
Hearing the woman's weeping sounds,
he turned and said to the people of the ward:
"This woman is not human,
but a mountain beast.
It has taken on form to delude the world."
The people then informed Yán.
Yán immediately requested his help.
The lay Buddhist then came to Yán's residence.
When the woman saw the lay Buddhist coming,
she was very afraid.
The lay Buddhist produced a black talisman,
and threw it into the air,
the woman let out a great cry,
suddenly leaped and went away,
standing on the tiled roof.
Yán secretly found this strange.
The lay Buddhist then produced a red talisman and threw it,
and the woman then collapsed to the ground,
transforming into an ape and dying.
Yán, having realized her demonic strangeness,
felt quite alarmed and fearful.
A day later,
he then went to Wèinán,
and inquired among the local residents.
Indeed, there was a Gentleman Liú,
whose cottage was in the outskirts.
Yán then paid a visit and inquired of him.
Liú said:
