"I once served as commandant in Yìyáng.
Yìyáng has many apes,
and I thus obtained one.
It has been nearly ten years now.
It happened that an old friend came from Púshàng,
and gave me a black dog as a gift.
The ape was bitten by the dog,
and therefore fled."
In the end, the matter was not fully investigated,
and thus it was recorded to transmit it.
Yán later entered official service through the Míngjīng examination,
and ended his career as commandant of Shàngguī in Qínzhōu.
A traveler who was journeying in Tàiyuán,
by chance at the Vihāra of Tóngguōdiàn,
loosened his saddle and rested there.
Among the Buddhist books in the Vihāra,
he found the account transmitted by Gentleman Liú,
but the writing was very crude.
Later, the original was lost,
and the traveler related it to me as such.
Wèi Yuánzhōng
Táng Wèi Yuánzhōng, originally named Zhēnzǎi,
was inherently strong and upright,
with capable insight.
Before he achieved prominence,
his family was poor.
He had only one maidservant.
Once while she was cooking in the kitchen,
she went out to fetch water and upon returning,
saw an old ape tending the fire for her.
Startled, the maidservant reported this to him.
Yuánzhōng calmly said:
"The ape pities me for having no help,
and is cooking for me—
isn’t that excellent?"
Another time he called for a servant,
but got no response.
A dog called out in his place.
He again said:
"This is a loyal dog—
it can even labor on my behalf."
Once while sitting alone,
a group of mice stood before him with paws clasped.
He said:
"The mice are hungry,
and have come to me seeking food."
He then ordered that they be fed.
At night,
an owl hooted on his rooftop;
his family members were about to shoot it.
He stopped them, saying:
"Owls cannot see in daylight,
so they fly at night.
This creature is nurtured by Heaven and Earth—
we cannot make it flee south to Yuè
or north to the Hú.
Where would it go then?"
After that, such strange occurrences ceased entirely.
Yuánzhōng rose through high offices to become Shìzhōng, Zhōngshū Lìng, and Púyè.
When Empress Wǔ Zétiān passed away,
and Emperor Zhōngzōng was in mourning,
Yuánzhōng was ordered to act as Zhǒngzǎi.
All officials reported to him for three days.
He died past the age of eighty.
Earlier, when Yuánzhōng was still obscure,
he once visited Zhāng Jǐngcáng.
Jǐngcáng treated him very coldly;
when Yuánzhōng inquired about his prospects,
he received no reply either.
Furious, Yuánzhōng said:
"I have traveled a thousand lǐ with provisions—
not for nothing.
I certainly thought you, sir, would have something to teach me,
yet you meet me with a metal mouth and wooden tongue,
utterly disregarding my earnest intent!
But wealth and honor come from the blue heavens—
what does it have to do with you?"
He then flicked his sleeves, made a deep bow, and left.
Jǐngcáng quickly grabbed and stopped him, saying:
"Your physiognomy is precisely in an angry phase—
later you will reach the highest rank among officials."
It ultimately turned out as he said.
Wéi Xūjǐ’s Son
Wéi Xūjǐ, Minister of Revenue,
had a son who once sat alone in his chamber by day.
Suddenly he heard a sound from the eaves;
looking over, he saw an ox-headed man,
exactly like those depicted in hell paintings.
Leaning over to peer down at him,
Wéi prostrated himself, not daring to move.
After a moment, it ascended the steps,
truly approached the bed,
and bent its face over him.
This happened three times,
then it went back down.
Wéi’s son could not bear his fear.
When it was about to exit the inner room,
he threw a pillow at it,
but missed.
Then he opened the door
and rushed forward to chase it.
Wéi’s son shouted and cried out;
it merely ran around an empty well.
As the pursuit grew more urgent,
it jumped into the well.
The creature then sat by the well’s edge.
Wéi looked up at it—
it had transformed into an ape.
After a long while,
family members arrived,
and the ape vanished.
Seeing trampled footprints by the well,
they were puzzled.
Peering into the well,
they found Wéi inside.
They lowered a rope and pulled him out;
he was dazed and unable to speak.
Only after three days could he recount it,
and he died a little over a month later.
Chief Clerk Wáng
In Chóngràng Lane of the Eastern Capital was a residence of the Lǐ family.
Neighborhood lore said:
"This house is not an auspicious place—
it certainly cannot be lived in."
After Mr. Lǐ died,
his family all moved to a villa in Lùhún.
Thus the house was locked up.
Several years passed.
During the Kāiyuán era,
there was a Chief Clerk Wáng (his given name lost).
Chief Clerk Wáng had once held a high, prestigious post,
but because he offended powerful officials while drunk,
he was relegated to a chief clerk position in the Wú-Yuè region.
Later he retired to live in Luòyáng,
and mortgaged the Lǐ residence to settle there.
Chief Clerk Wáng was by nature strong-willed;
hearing the house had an inauspicious reputation,
he said:
"My fate lies with Heaven,
not with a house."
He immediately moved in and lived there.
Once he was alone in the western wing of the hall.
Later one night,
he heard a mournful whistling sound,
extremely clear,
like wind through reeds.
Chief Clerk Wáng rose to look—
he saw a person dressed in black
standing on a small table.
Chief Clerk Wáng sternly shouted at him;
the person immediately raised one foot
and struck Chief Clerk Wáng’s shoulder.
Chief Clerk Wáng retreated in fear,
and the person also left.
Chief Clerk Wáng fell ill from the wound and grew very sick.
Only after over ten days did he slightly recover.
At night,
he again heard the mournful whistling.
Household servants searched for it;
at times they saw a black-clad figure in the courtyard tree.
Chief Clerk Wáng had a younger brother skilled in archery,
so he ordered him to shoot at it.
With one shot he hit it.
The figure howled and screamed,
leapt onto the roof tiles of the western gallery, and fled.
The next day they searched for traces,
but found nothing.
That autumn,
Chief Clerk Wáng summoned workers to repair the stable;
while opening a sealed room,
they found inside a dead ape,
with an arrow piercing its flank.
Examining the arrow,
it indeed was Chief Clerk Wáng’s brother’s arrow.
Only then did they realize the black-clad figure had been an ape.
Zhāng Yǎn
Zhāng Yán of Wújùn,
was a native of Chéngdū.
During the Kāiyuán era,
he was dismissed from his post as Lúxī County Lieutenant.
Awaiting reassignment,
he failed to secure a new appointment from the authorities,
and so returned to Shǔ.
While passing through Bāxī,
he encountered dusk.
Just as he was urging his horse forward,
suddenly a man
emerged from a mountain path on the left side of the road,
bowed, and requested:
"My lord has heard that you, traveler, have no place to stay for the night,
and wishes to extend an invitation.
He has ordered me to request
that you follow me."
Yán then asked:
"Who is your lord?
Could it be that the Grand Administrator summons me?"
The man said:
"No,
it is none other than the Marquis of Bāxī."
Yán immediately followed him.
After walking about a hundred paces along the mountain path,
he saw a very tall vermilion gate,
with many people about.
Guards encircled the area,
surpassing even the households of marquises and earls.
After several dozen more paces,
they finally reached the place.
The messenger stopped Yán at the gate, saying:
"I wish to first inform my lord;
please wait here, traveler."
He entered for a long time before emerging,
then led Yán, saying:
"The traveler may enter now."
Once Yán entered,
he saw a man standing in the main hall,
wearing a fur robe of coarse leather,
his appearance most unusual,
with silks, pearls, and jade
attending him on both sides.
Yán hurried forward and bowed.
After bowing,
the man returned the courtesy and invited Yán up the steps.
He said to Yán:
"I am the Marquis of Bāxī,
and have lived here for several decades.
Just now I learned that you, sir, had no place to stay for the night,
so I took the liberty of inviting you.
I hope you will stay a while and enjoy yourself to the fullest."
Yán bowed again in thanks.
Soon after, he ordered a banquet prepared and wine served.
All the utensils and playthings
were luxurious and precious.
He then ordered his attendants to invite the Six Heroic General, the White-Browed Marquis, and the Cānglàng Lord.
He also invited the Five Leopard General, the Jùlù Marquis, and the Xuánqiū Commandant.
And he conveyed the instruction:
"Today a distinguished guest has come,
and I wish to hold a joyous feast,
so I have ordered you to be invited."
The messengers assented and departed.
After a long time, they finally arrived.
First came six men all in black,
their forms imposing,
called the "Six Heroic General."
The Marquis of Bāxī rose and bowed;
the Six Heroic General also bowed.
Then came one man dressed in brocade,
wearing a white cap,
his appearance quite fierce,
called the "White-Browed Marquis."
Again the Marquis of Bāxī rose and bowed;
the White-Browed Marquis also bowed.
Another man dressed in dark blue,
his physique tall and sturdy,
was called the "Cānglàng Lord."
The Marquis of Bāxī bowed again;
the Cānglàng Lord also bowed.
Another man wore a robe with mottled patterns,
resembling the White-Browed Marquis but slightly smaller,
called the "Five Leopard General."
The Marquis of Bāxī bowed again;
the Five Leopard General also bowed.
Another man wore a coarse robe,
with three horns on his head,
called the "Jùlù Marquis."
The Marquis of Bāxī greeted him with a bow.
Another man dressed in black,
his appearance similar to the Cānglàng Lord,
was called the "Xuánqiū Commandant."
The Marquis of Bāxī also greeted him with a bow.
Then he invited them to be seated.
The Marquis of Bāxī sat facing south,
Yán faced north,
the Six Heroic, White-Browed, and Cānglàng sat on the east side,
and the Five Leopard, Jùlù, and Xuánqiū sat on the west side.
Once seated,
they served wine and ordered music.
Then over ten beauties,
singers and dancers,
with strings and bamboo instruments playing,
performed with utmost skill.
The White-Browed Marquis, flushed with wine,
turned to Yán and said:
"I am still hungry tonight;
can you provide me with a full meal?"
Yán said:
"I have not divined what you, my lord, still desire;
please instruct me."
The White-Browed Marquis said:
"Your body could fill my belly;
why would I value any other flavor?"
Yán was terrified,
and retreated in fear.
The Marquis of Bāxī said:
"This is unreasonable.
How can one
offend a distinguished guest at a banquet?"
The White-Browed Marquis laughed and said:
"My words were merely a jest;
how could such a thing be!
It certainly is not so."
After a long while,
someone announced that Master Dòngxuán was at the gate,
wishing to have an audience to report a matter.
As soon as he finished speaking,
a man dressed in black appeared,
with a long neck and a very broad body.
The man bowed;
the Marquis of Bāxī greeted him with a bow.
He invited him to sit,
and asked:
"What brings you here?"
He replied:
"I am a skilled diviner,
and knowing that you, my lord, are about to face great trouble,
I have come to report it."
The Marquis of Bāxī said:
"What trouble is that?"
He said:
"Someone at this banquet intends to plot against you.
If you do not eliminate him now,
he will surely cause harm later.
I urge you to consider this carefully."
The Marquis of Bāxī angrily said:
"My joyous feast is just reaching its peak;
how could there be any strange happenings here!"
And ordered him killed.
The man said:
"If you heed my words,
all will be safe.
If you do not heed my words,
then I will die,
and you will die too.
What will you do then?
Even if you later regret it,
can it be undone?"
The Marquis of Bāxī then killed the diviner
and placed his body in the courtyard.
By then, it was nearly midnight,
and everyone, thoroughly drunk, lay down on their couches.
Yán also feigned sleep.
As dawn approached,
he suddenly awoke with a start.
He found himself lying in a large stone niche,
decorated with embroidered curtains,
with pearls, jade, rhinoceros horns, and ivory arranged beside him.
There was a giant ape, shaped like a man,
lying drunk on the ground.
This was likely the so-called Marquis of Bāxī.
He also saw a giant bear lying in front,
likely the so-called Six Heroic General.
Another tiger with a white forehead
also lay in front,
the so-called White-Browed Marquis.
Another wolf,
the so-called Cānglàng Lord.
There was also a patterned leopard,
the so-called Five Leopard General.
Another giant deer
and a fox
both lay in front.
These were likely the so-called Jùlù Marquis and Xuánqiū Commandant.
And all lay unconscious as if drunk.
There was also a turtle,
its form most unusual,
dead in front of the niche.
This was the Master Dòngxuán who had been killed earlier.
Once Yán saw this,
he was greatly alarmed.
He immediately left the mountain path
and hurried to inform the local villagers.
The villagers gathered, numbering about a hundred,
and taking bows and arrows, entered the mountains.
When they reached the place,
the ape suddenly awoke in alarm.
And said:
"I did not heed Master Dòngxuán's words,
Today indeed it has come to pass as such."
They then surrounded his niche,
and killed them all.
The vessels and curios displayed there,
were all precious and exquisite.
He then reported the matter in full to the prefect.
Previously, there had been people carrying pearls and silks
who passed by this place,
all of whom vanished without a trace,
and this had been going on for years.
After this, the trouble ceased.
Yáng Sǒu
In the early years of the Qiányuán era,
among the people of Kuàijī there was a man named Yáng Sǒu,
whose family was renowned throughout the commandery for its abundant wealth.
One day,
the old man was about to die.
He lay moaning,
and this went on for several months.
The old man had a son named Zōngsù,
praised by the villagers for his filial conduct.
When his father fell ill,
he exhausted his family's resources seeking medical treatment.
Later, he found a certain Mr. Chén to investigate the cause:
"This old man's illness lies in his heart.
It is because his property is already so abundant,
that his heart has been driven by profit,
and thus his heart has already left his body.
Unless he eats the heart of a living person,
it cannot be restored.
But the hearts of living people in this world,
how can one obtain them?
In that case, it is beyond my knowledge."
After Zōngsù heard this,
he thought that obtaining a living person's heart was impossible,
so he solely practiced the Buddhist dharma,
hoping it might alleviate his father's illness.
He immediately summoned monks to chant sutras,
and commissioned craftsmen to paint and cast images.
Afterwards, he personally brought food
to the Buddhist temple in the commandery to feed the monks.
One day,
while carrying food, he set off.
He mistakenly entered a mountain path,
and saw a stone niche at the foot of the mountain.
In the niche was a foreign monk,
whose appearance was very old and emaciated,
wearing a kasaya made of coarse woolen threads,
sitting upon a large rock.
Zōngsù, considering him an extraordinary person,
immediately bowed and asked:
"Master, who are you?
Alone in this desolate valley,
making your home in a place untouched by human footprints,
with no attendants,
are you not afraid the beasts of the wild might harm you?
If not,
are you one who has attained the Buddhist arts?"
The monk said:
"I originally belonged to the Yuán clan,
whose ancestors lived on Bā Mountain.
Later descendants,
some were in Yìyáng,
scattered and roaming among various mountain valleys,
all able to carry on the ancestral profession.
As recluses among forests and springs,
they excelled at chanting and whistling.
People fond of poetry
often praised their skill in chanting and whistling.
Thus they gradually became known throughout the land.
There is also the Sūn clan,
likewise of our lineage,
who mostly frequent the gates of the wealthy and noble.
Also skilled in witty conversation,
they thus also roam the marketplaces.
Each time they perform,
they can make people gain profit from it.
Only I am fond of Buddhism,
free from worldly dust,
dwelling with my heart settled among cliffs and valleys, unmoving.
And I have been here for years now.
I have always admired King Kalirāja for cutting his body to pieces,
and Bodhi for leaping off a cliff to feed a starving tiger,
so I eat acorns and chestnuts,
and drink from flowing springs.
I regret that no tiger or wolf has yet devoured me,
I would gladly accept it."
Zōngsù then told him:
"Master, you are truly a man of utmost virtue,
able to abandon your body without regard,
intending to feed the mountain beasts;
this can be said to embody both benevolence and courage to the highest degree.
However,
my disciple's father has been ill for several months now,
and despite treatment, he does not recover.
Day and night I am anxious and distressed,
with no plan to be found.
A physician said:
'This is an illness of the heart.
Unless he eats the heart of a living person,
he certainly cannot be cured.'
Now, Master, you are able to abandon your body to jackals and tigers
to relieve their hunger;
would it not be better to give your life to a person,
to bestow life upon him?
I beg you, Master, to consider this carefully."
The monk said:
"If it is truly so,
it indeed aligns with my aspiration.
The donor seeks me for his father's sake;
how could I have any unwillingness?
Moreover, if I give my body to wild beasts,
how does that compare to bestowing life upon a person?
However, I have not yet eaten today;
I wish to be given a meal before I die."
Zōngsù was both delighted and grateful,
and immediately placed the food he had brought before him.
The monk ate it all in an instant.
Then he said again:
"Now that I have eaten,
I should also follow your instruction.
But wait until I have paid homage to the sages of the four directions."
Thereupon, he straightened his robe,
stepped out of the niche, and bowed.
After finishing the bow to the east,
he suddenly leapt and soared up to a tall tree.
Zōngsù thought this was a display of spiritual powers and transformation,
almost unfathomable.
Soon he called to Zōngsù,
and sternly asked:
"Donor, what was it you sought earlier?"
Zōngsù said:
"I wish to obtain a living person's heart,
to cure my father's illness."
The monk said:
"What the donor wishes for,
I have already agreed to.
Now I wish first to expound the profound meaning of the *Diamond Sutra*;
will you listen?"
Zōngsù said:
"I have always revered Buddhism;
today I have met you, Master;
how dare I not listen?"
The monk said:
"The *Diamond Sutra* states:
'The past mind cannot be grasped,
the present mind cannot be grasped,
the future mind cannot be grasped.'
Donor, if you wish to take my heart,
it also cannot be grasped."
Having said this,
he suddenly leapt and shouted loudly,
transformed into an ape, and departed.
Zōngsù was astonished,
and returned in fear and alarm.
Sūn Kè
During the Guangdé era,
there was a scholar named Sūn Kè,
who, having failed the imperial examination,
traveled to Luòzhōng.
Upon reaching the shore of the Wèiwáng Pond,
he suddenly saw a large mansion,
with both its timber and earthwork appearing brand new.
A passerby pointed and said:
"This is the mansion of the Yuán family."
Kè went straight to knock on the gate,
but there was no response.
Beside the door was a small room,
its curtains and drapes quite clean,
apparently a place for awaiting guests.
Kè thus lifted the curtain and entered.
After a long while,
he suddenly heard the sound of a door opening.
A woman appeared, her radiance illuminating objects,
her beauty astonishing to behold—
like pearls freshly cleansed by moonlight,
willows just veiled in misty charm,
orchid fragrance divinely pure,
jade luster free of dust.
Kè suspected she was the master's unmarried daughter,
and merely watched stealthily.
The woman plucked a daylily in the courtyard,
standing lost in thought for a long time.
Then she chanted a poem:
"Some see this as forgetting sorrow,
I see it as rotting grass.
Blue mountains and white clouds—
only these unfold my heart's embrace."
Her recitation bore a sorrowful expression.
Later, as she came to lift the curtain,
she suddenly caught sight of Kè,
startled and embarrassed, she retreated inside,
sending a maidservant to question him:
"Who are you,
that you linger here toward evening?"
Kè then explained his intention of seeking lodging.
He added:
"My unfortunate intrusion
has greatly increased my shame and alarm.
I hope you will convey this to the young lady."
The maidservant reported everything.
The woman said:
"My ugliness and clumsiness,
moreover, I am not adorned.
The gentleman has long gazed upon the curtains,
and must have seen everything.
How dare I avoid him further?
I wish the gentleman would wait briefly in the inner hall,
while I temporarily adorn myself and come out."
Kè, admiring her beautiful appearance,
was overjoyed beyond measure.
He asked the maidservant:
"Whose daughter is she?"
She replied:
"She is the daughter of the late Official Yuán.
Orphaned young,
she has no other relatives by marriage,
only with us few maidservants, three or five in number,
does she occupy this mansion.
The young lady seeks to marry,
but has not yet found a match."
After a long while,
she came out to meet Kè.
Her beauty surpassed what he had seen before.
She ordered her maids to serve tea and fruits, saying:
"Since you, sir, have no residence,
you may move your belongings into this hall's courtyard."
Pointing to the maidservant, she said to Kè:
"If you have any small needs,
simply inform these people."
Kè could only feel grateful and ashamed.
Kè was unmarried,
and seeing the woman so exquisitely beautiful,
he sought a matchmaker to propose marriage.
The woman also gladly accepted,
and thus he took her as his wife.
Yuánshì was well-provided,
possessing great wealth in gold and silk.
Kè had long been poor,
but suddenly his carriages and horses were splendid,
his clothing and ornaments luxurious,
greatly arousing suspicion and surprise among his relatives and friends.
Many came to question Kè,
but he never gave a truthful answer.
Kè thus became arrogant and haughty,
no longer seeking fame or examination success,
daily socializing with the wealthy and noble,
indulging in drink and wild singing.
Thus three or four years passed,
never leaving Luòzhōng.
Suddenly he met his cousin, the retired scholar Zhāng Xiányún.
Kè said to him:
"After such a long separation,
I greatly wish for a leisurely talk.
I hope you will bring your bedding
for a night's conversation."
Zhāng Shēng complied as requested.
When it was nearly midnight and time to sleep,
Zhāng Shēng grasped Kè's hand
and secretly said to him:
"Your foolish elder brother once received teachings in the Daoist arts.
Just now observing your words and complexion,
I sense a rather strong demonic aura.
I wonder if you have encountered something else?
Regardless of the matter's scale,
I wish you would tell me.
Otherwise,
you are sure to suffer calamity."
Kè said:
"I have encountered nothing."
Zhāng Shēng said again:
"Humans embody yang essence,
demons receive yin energy.
If the soul overshadows and the corporeal soul is exhausted,
the person lives long;
if the corporeal soul overshadows and the soul dissipates,
the person immediately dies.
Thus ghosts and monsters, having no form, are entirely yin;
immortals, having no shadow, are entirely yang.
The waxing and waning of yin and yang,
the battle between soul and corporeal soul—
if within the body there is the slightest misplacement,
it invariably manifests in one's complexion.
Just now observing your spirit and appearance,
yin has usurped yang's position,
evil encroaches upon the proper organs.
Your true essence is already depleted,
your awareness and faculties gradually decaying.
Your vital fluids are draining,
your foundation shaken and unstable.
Your bones will soon turn to earth,
your face no longer flushed with health—
you must be being consumed by some strange creature.
Why stubbornly conceal and not reveal the cause?"
Only then did Kè become alarmed and realize,
and so recounted the circumstances of his marriage.
Zhāng Shēng was greatly horrified and said:
"This is precisely it!
What can be done about it?"
Kè said:
"I have considered this—
what is strange about it?"
Zhāng said:
"How could it be that Yuánshì has no relatives anywhere under heaven?
Moreover, she is discerning, intelligent, and highly capable—
enough to be considered strange."
Kè then told Zhāng:
"My whole life has been fraught with difficulties,
long enduring cold and hunger.
Because of this marriage,
I seem somewhat revived.
I cannot betray righteousness—
what plan is there?"
Zhāng Shēng angrily said:
"A true man cannot even serve humans properly—
how can he serve ghosts!
As the tradition says:
'Demons arise because of humans.'
If humans provide no opening,
demons do not act on their own.
Moreover, which is closer: righteousness or one's own person?
Your person suffers disaster,
yet you care for the ghostly creature's kindness and righteousness—
even a child three feet tall
would consider this unacceptable,
let alone a true man!"
Zhāng added:
"I have a precious sword,
also a peer of Gānjiàng's blade.
Whenever there are specters,
those who see it vanish.
Its divine efficacy from past to present
cannot be fully recounted.
Tomorrow morning I will lend it to you.
If you take it into the inner chamber,
you will surely see her in distress,
no less than when Lord Wáng in former times took his precious mirror to illuminate the parrot.
Otherwise,
you will never break free from this bond of love."
The next day,
Kè received the sword.
Zhāng Shēng bid farewell,
grasping his hand and saying:
"Watch carefully for the right moment."
Kè then took the sword
and hid it within the chamber,
yet his expression remained troubled.
Yuánshì soon sensed it.
Furious, she reproached Kè:
"In your poverty and sorrow,
I brought you ease and prosperity.
Heedless of kindness and righteousness,
you now engage in wrongdoing.
With such a heart,
even dogs and pigs would refuse to eat what remains of you—
how could you establish integrity and conduct in the human world?"
Kè, having been reprimanded,
felt ashamed and fearful.
He kowtowed and said:
"I received instruction from my cousin,
it was not my original intention.
I wish to swear a blood oath,
and dare not have any other intentions."
Sweat dripped as he prostrated on the ground.
Yuánshì then searched and found his sword,
broke it into pieces,
as if snapping a light lotus root.
Kè grew even more afraid,
as if about to flee.
Yuánshì then laughed and said:
"That Zhāngshēng is but a young man,
unable to teach his cousin with morality and righteousness,
allowing him to act recklessly,
and thus deserves to be shamed.
But observing your heart,
it truly should not be like this.
However, I have been your wife for several years now,
why should you worry!"
Only then did Kè feel somewhat at ease.
Several days later,
he went out and encountered Zhāngshēng.
He said:
"Why did you make me provoke the tiger's whiskers,
I almost couldn't escape the tiger's mouth!"
Zhāngshēng asked where the sword was,
and Kè told him the truth.
Zhāngshēng was greatly alarmed and said:
"This is beyond my understanding."
Deeply afraid, he dared not come to visit.
More than ten years later,
Yuánshì had already raised two sons.
She managed the household very strictly,
disliking interference.
Later, Kè went to Cháng'ān,
visited his old friend Wáng Xiàngguó Jìn,
who then recommended him to Doctor Zhāng Wànqǐng of Nánkāng,
to serve as a planning officer.
He took his family and went.
Whenever Yuánshì encountered green pines and high mountains,
she would gaze at them for a long time,
as if feeling unhappy.
Upon reaching Ruìzhōu,
Yuánshì said:
"Half a day's journey from here,
by the riverbank there is Xiáshān Temple,
my family used to have a disciple monk Huìyōu,
who resides in this temple.
It has been several decades since we parted,
the monk's seniority is very high,
able to distinguish form and body,
skilled at transcending worldly dust.
If we pass by and offer food,
it would greatly benefit the fortune of our southern journey."
Kè said:
"Indeed."
So they prepared vegetarian offerings and such.
Upon arriving at the temple,
Yuánshì was joyful,
changed clothes and tidied her makeup,
took her two sons,
and went to the old monk's courtyard,
as if familiar with the path.
Kè found it quite strange.
Then she presented a jade bracelet to the monk and said:
"This is an old item from the courtyard."
The monk did not understand.
After the vegetarian meal,
dozens of wild apes,
arm in arm, descended from the tall pines,
and ate on the offering platform.
Later, they laughed sorrowfully, grasped vines, and leaped,
Yuánshì felt pained.
Soon she took a brush and wrote on the temple wall:
"Just now bound by affection, this heart was enslaved,
without reason, changes nearly led to sinking.
Better to follow companions back to the mountains,
a long cry into the deep mist and fog."
Then she threw the brush to the ground,
caressed her two sons, sobbed a few times,
and said to Kè:
"Take care, take care!
I must bid farewell forever."
Then she tore her clothes and transformed into an old ape,
chasing after the calling ones, leaping through the trees and departing.
About to reach the deep mountains, she turned back to look,
Kè was shocked and terrified,
as if his soul had flown and spirit perished.
After a long while,
he embraced his two sons and wept bitterly.
Then he inquired with the old monk,
the monk then realized:
"This ape was raised by me when I was a novice monk.
During the Kāiyuán era,
an imperial envoy Gāo Lìshì passed by here,
took pity on its cleverness,
and exchanged it with bolts of silk.
Later arriving in Luòjīng,
it was presented to the emperor.
At that time, imperial envoys came and went,
many spoke of its surpassing cleverness.
For a long time, it was tamed and kept in the Shàngyáng Palace.
During the Ān-Shǐ Rebellion,
its whereabouts became unknown.
Alas!
I never expected to witness its strangeness again today.
The jade bracelet,
originally bestowed by a Hēlíng foreigner,
at that time also went with the ape's neck.
Now I understand."
Kè then felt sorrowful,
anchored his boat for six or seven days,
took his two sons and turned the boat back,
unable to continue to his post.
Cuī Shāng
During the Yuánhé era,
a traveler from Jīng, Cuī Shāng, went up the gorge to Qián.
The autumn waters had receded,
and the boat traveled very slowly.
By the riverbank, there was a stream and cave,
with exceptionally beautiful forests.
Shāng thus took a staff and walked slowly,
exploring deeply into the secluded area.
Not three or four lǐ in,
he suddenly saw dwellings.
Stone bridges and bamboo gates,
plank houses and thatched huts,
winding along the stream,
the scene was quite extraordinary.
Shāng thus approached.
About ten nuns welcomed the guest.
Their appearance and speech,
were certainly not like those of mountain dwellers.
He then entered their dwelling.
Seeing in the courtyard and rooms,
many fruits and chestnuts were drying.
And peeking into their rooms,
they were piled full.
Shortly after,
they went out and brought back loads of fruits, one after another.
Shāng thought that in such deep mountains and remote valleys,
they could not possibly live there,
suspected they were demons,
and hastily returned.
The nuns tried to detain him,
their words very earnest.
After Shāng boarded the boat,
he asked the boatmen.
They all said:
"Those are apes.
Many have encountered them before,
luckily you realized quickly and returned.
Otherwise,
you might have been harmed."
Shāng then gathered his servants,
armed with weapons,
hurriedly went to search and capture,
but found no trace.
A Fisherman on the Chǔ River
By the Chǔ River, there was a fisherman,
who built a thatched hut facing the stream,
with only a straw raincoat, a small boat, a fishing line, and a rod—
nothing else.
He would often trade fish for wine,
then sing wildly and dance drunkenly by himself.
Though people laughed at him,
he showed no sign of shame,
nor did he ever speak his surname or given name.
Those who recognized him considered him a recluse among fishermen.
Someone once asked him:
"Sir, your fishing—
is it the fishing of a recluse,
or the fishing of a fisherman?"
The fisherman replied:
"In the past, Jiāng Zǐyá's fishing and Yán Zǐlíng's fishing
were recorded in the annals of history,
and both were regarded as the fishing of recluses.
Yet little did people know that they were not fishing for fish,
but fishing for fame.
Is the fishing of recluses truly noble?
As for the fishing of a fisherman,
all one needs is a bright moon, gentle winds, and calm waves.
Catching fish to supply the kitchen,
one's own needs are satisfied.
The surplus is exchanged for wine to drink alone,
so how would one even know of the fishing of recluses versus the fishing of fishermen!"
The questioner sighed deeply in admiration.
Suddenly, one day,
a person passed by with a small monkey.
When the fisherman saw it,
he wept bitterly without ceasing.
The small monkey also refused to go forward,
as if filled with sorrow and attachment.
The person found this very strange.
The fisherman then bowed earnestly, begging for the small monkey.
He said it was the one he had lost the year before,
given to him by a mountain monk.
"I beg for your compassion and pity to grant it to me,
so that I may not betray the mountain monk's kindness."
The person, moved by his plea,
then specially bestowed it upon him.
The fisherman often cared for and raised this small monkey.
After a year,
it suddenly said to the fishermen:
"I have kin in the southern mountains,
and today I bid you farewell to return to them."
It then leaped and transformed into an old monkey,
taking the small monkey and running off,
no one knew where.
Wáng Rényù
Wáng Rényù once served in Hànzhōng,
living in the official compound.
A hunter from the Bā Mountains
presented a young monkey.
Taking pity on its small size and cleverness,
he had someone raise it,
naming it Yě Bīn.
When called, it would respond with sounds.
After a year, it grew strong and robust.
As its leash gradually loosened,
it would bite anyone it encountered,
becoming quite a nuisance.
When Wáng Rényù scolded it,
it would submit and remain still.
But others could whip it without it showing fear.
The official compound's inner city walls wound around,
lined with elm and pagoda trees.
At the Hàn Gāo Temple, there were tall pines and ancient cypresses,
with countless bird nests atop them.
During mid-spring,
Yě Bīn broke free,
leaping into the dense woods,
swinging swiftly among the treetops,
and entered the Hàn Gāo Temple,
destroying bird nests,
throwing chicks and eggs to the ground.
In the prefectural office, there was a bell frame.
The birds gathered on the frame, ringing the bell,
and the authorities ordered a search for where the birds had come from.
Seeing Yě Bīn in the woods,
they immediately had people throw tiles and stones and shoot at it,
but none could hit it.
As dusk fell and it grew hungry,
it finally grew weary and was captured.
It was then sent over a hundred lǐ into the streams and caves of the Bā Mountains.
Just as the people returned,
before the inquiry was finished,
Yě Bīn was already in the kitchen seeking food.
It was captured again.
Suddenly, one day, it broke free,
entered the commander's kitchen,
and overturned all the utensils and such for use,
soiling them with filth.
Then it climbed onto the roof,
throwing tiles and breaking bricks.
The commander was furious,
ordering many to shoot arrows at it.
Yě Bīn rode the roof ridge, destroying tiles and bricks.
Arrows flew like rain,
but Yě Bīn's eyes were not hindered from seeing,
nor its mouth from calling out.
It caught with its hands and threw with its feet,
dodging arrows left and right.
In the end, not a hair on it was harmed.
An old officer in the envoy's office, Mǎ Yuánzhāng, said:
"There is a man in the market
skilled at handling monkeys."
He was summoned,
and instructed:
"Capture it quickly."
Then a large monkey leaped onto the office roof and chased it,
jumping over walls and darting through alleys,
capturing it and bringing it forward.
Yě Bīn, drenched in sweat, submitted and admitted guilt.
The commander did not scold or rage much,
and everyone watched and laughed.
Then a red silk thread was tied around its neck,
with a poem inscribed and sent off:
"I release you, earnest, to return to the old woods;
your former haunts are good to seek and trace.
The moonlit Wū Gorge, still and worthy of pity;
the road parts the Bā Mountains—do not dislike its depth.
Resting and lodging, spare the dream of green peaks;
climbing and scaling should suit the heart in azure clouds.
In late autumn, fruits ripen, pine tips sturdy;
cling to high branches, singing through dawn."
It was then sent to the Gūyún Liǎngjiǎo Mountain,
and left tied at a mountain home.
After ten days,
it was released and set free,
and never returned again.
Later, when Wáng left his post and entered Shǔ,
passing by the Bōzhǒng Temple,
by the banks of the Hàn River,
a troop of monkeys descended
arm-in-arm from the steep cliffs,
to drink from the clear stream.
A giant monkey left the group and came forward,
among the ancient trees by the roadside,
hanging down to look below.
The red silk thread was faintly visible.
A follower pointed and said:
"This is Yě Bīn."
Calling to it,
it responded sound for sound.
Stopping the horse for a while,
he could not help but feel sorrow.
As he lifted the reins to depart,
it cried out mournfully several times and left.
While ascending the mountain path,
turning through valleys and winding streams,
he still heard sobbing sounds,
wondering if it was cut off by the sun.
He then composed a poem:
"By Bōzhǒng Temple, banks of the Hàn River,
this monkey, arm-in-arm, descends the rugged cliffs.
Gradually drawing near, carefully eyeing the passing traveler,
recognizing faintly—it is Yě Bīn.
Lodging by the moon, though weary from tether and thorn;
feeding on pines, no longer the body of rice and grain.
Several cries, cut off by the sun, call with the clouds;
it recognizes its old master from years before."
Dí Zhāo
During the Tàiyuán era of Jìn,
among the Dīnglíng people was Dí Zhāo,
who kept a macaque in the rear palace.
In front of the courtesans' quarters,
the courtesans before and after
all became pregnant at the same time.
Each gave birth to three offspring,
which emerged leaping about.
Dí Zhāo then realized it was the monkey's doing,
so he killed the monkey and the ten offspring.
The six courtesans wailed simultaneously.
Dí Zhāo asked them, and they said:
"At first, we saw a young man,
wearing a yellow silk unlined robe,
with a white gauze cap,
very lovely,
speaking and laughing like a person."
Xú Jìzhī
At the end of the Tàiyuán era,
Xú Jìzhī often roamed the wilds.
He saw a woman holding a lotus.
She raised her hand and beckoned Jìzhī.
Jìzhī was pleased and invited her to stay.
From then on, they came and went as before.
Jìzhī then fell ill and became emaciated.
At times he would speak of seeing magnificent houses and deep halls,
fragrant mats and vast feasts.
Jìzhī and the woman feasted and enjoyed themselves with wine and delicacies.
Several years later,
his younger brother, Ěrzhī, heard a clamor of voices inside the house.
He secretly went to peek,
and saw several women leaving through the back door.
Only one remained, hiding beside the bamboo basket.
Ěrzhī went straight in.
The woman angrily said:
"We are just enjoying ourselves together.
Why do you intrude so rudely?"
Suddenly they all spoke again, saying:
"There is someone in the basket!" Ěrzhī immediately opened it to look.
There was a female monkey.
He then killed it.
Jìzhī's illness gradually recovered.
Zhāng Yùyán
The mountain hermit Zhāng Yùyán was originally skilled in Daoist arts,
erudite and talented.
He often lodged at the homes of court officials.
One residence was large and ominous.
The owner had moved out.
Yùyán went out to drink,
got very drunk and returned.
Unaware that the family had already left,
he slept in the hall's corridor.
After midnight, he sobered up somewhat.
A servant informed him.
Yùyán became afraid.
At the time, the night was dark.
Then someone was pulling books from the shelf.
Yùyán secretly watched from the darkness.
It was a ghost.
It gathered beside the bookshelf.
Yùyán planned to strike it.
He then rose.
Yùyán was very strong.
First he shouted at it.
The ghost cried out in alarm.
Yùyán struck it,
and stepped on its throat, pinning it to the ground.
He struck it again.
Then it stopped making noise and cried out loudly, saying,
"I have caught a ghost!"
The guards then arrived with torches.
It was a macaque.
It had been struck and was already dead.
Only then did he realize his mistake.
Previously, a macaque of unknown origin
would enter people's homes every night to steal.
When Yùyán mistook it for a ghost and killed it,
the whole neighborhood was free from trouble.
Xuē Fàng's Great-Grandfather
Minister Xuē Fàng's great-grandfather was the Governor of Húnán.
After leaving his commandery,
he lived idly in the capital,
skilled at managing his household.
Morning and evening,
he would always lean on his cane to inspect his residence.
Once, rising early,
he went to the kitchen,
and saw a faintly glowing lamp inside the stove.
Xuē angrily said to his cook:
"The lamp is not extinguished,
and why is it placed inside the stove?"
When he went to the front of the stove to look,
he suddenly saw a macaque, six or seven inches tall.
In front of it was a small tray,
about a foot square.
The food and items on it were all extremely small yet very complete.
Also placed in front was a lamp.
The monkey ate facing it.
Xuē was greatly astonished.
He then poked at it with his cane.
Though the stove was shallow,
even fully extending his cane, he could not reach it.
He then ordered his wife, children, and servants to look.
None could fathom it,
not knowing what to do.
The monkey suddenly placed the lamp on the tray,
balanced the tray on its head, and came out of the stove.
It walked to the front hall's steps,
set up the lamp and tray again, and ate,
as if no one was around.
The Xuē family was frightened.
They then ordered the younger men to go outside,
to seek out a magician to exorcise it.
Upon going out the gate,
they suddenly met a Daoist priest riding a donkey.
He said to Xuē's son:
"Young master, your spirit seems
extremely hurried and flustered.
There must be an incident.
Just now, passing by this residence,
I saw very strong demonic aura.
I have studied Daoist arts all my life
to aid in urgent difficulties.
If there is a matter,
I ask to eliminate it for you, young master."
Xuē's son was overjoyed.
He dismounted, bowed, and invited him to the house.
The Governor, wearing official cap and tablet, came out to greet him.
The wife, daughters, and others all bowed in welcome.
They sat in the hall.
The monkey saw the priest,
yet showed no fear.
The priest said:
"This is the Governor's deep grievance accumulated over generations.
Its coming now
brings no small calamity."
The Governor and his wife and children
wept sorrowfully and pleaded for a long time.
The priest said:
"It is fortunate we have met.
I should expel it for you.
However, this creature will ultimately require the Governor to suffer humiliation
before it is willing to be resolved."
Xuē said:
"If I can avoid other harm,
I dare not refuse humiliation." The priest said:
"This monkey now wishes to take the tray and lamp
up onto the Governor's head to eat.
It will certainly then leave.
Is that acceptable?"
Xuē did not dare refuse.
His wife and children all wept, saying:
"This is a spirit monster.
How can it be placed on your head?
We beg the Venerable Master to devise another plan."
The priest said:
"If not,
first place the tray on your head,
then let it eat from the tray upon it.
Is that acceptable?"
The wife and children again said:
"That will not do."
The priest said:
"If not,
there is no other plan." Xuē again sorrowfully pleaded for a long time.
The priest said:
"Do you have something like a kitchen cabinet at home?
Have the Governor enter it,
and let the monkey eat upon it.
Is that acceptable?"
All said:
"Acceptable." They then fetched a wooden cabinet.
Inside, they spread a mattress.
Xuē entered the cabinet.
They closed it.
The monkey then balanced the tray on its head,
carried the lamp, and climbed up.
It set them down and ate.
The wife and children circled around it,
all anxious and weeping.
Suddenly, the priest was nowhere to be seen.
In their shock and search for him,
the monkey, tray, and lamp also all disappeared.
They then opened the cabinet to look.
The Governor was also gone.
The whole family wailed and searched,
but found no further trace.
They then prepared mourning garments,
used the cabinet to summon his spirit, and buried it.
Yáng Yúdù
In Shǔ there was a man named Yáng Yúdù who was skilled at handling macaques,
in the marketplace,
he begged from people.
He often kept over ten macaques, large and small,
which understood human speech,
and sometimes he would have them ride dogs.
When acting as military officers on the move,
they would shout to clear the way ahead and behind,
holding whips to drive and urge them on,
wearing hats and boots,
which could also amuse people for a time.
If he made them act drunk,
they would inevitably fall down.
Lying on the ground,
even if helped for a long time, they would not get up,
until Yáng Yúdù sang out:
"The street patrol is coming,
but you still won't get up;
the Censor-in-Chief is coming,
and you still won't get up."
If he quietly mentioned that Attendant-in-Chief Hóu was coming,
the macaque would immediately get up and run away,
its eyes wide with alarm,
pretending to be afraid,
making everyone laugh.
One day,
a macaque from the inner stable broke its tether and ran up into the palace halls.
The King of Shǔ ordered people to shoot it,
but because of its agility,
none could hit it,
and for three days it could not be caught.
A eunuch reported that Yáng Yúdù was skilled at handling macaques,
so he was ordered to try and catch it.
He then entered with over ten macaques,
bowing toward the palace hall.
They stood in a row with hands clasped,
while the macaque from the inner stable was also on the roof, peeping down.
Yáng Yúdù loudly announced:
"By imperial decree, capture the macaque on the roof!"
His macaques immediately climbed onto the roof,
together seizing the macaque from the inner stable,
and stood in the hall.
The King of Shǔ was greatly pleased,
and thus bestowed upon Yáng Yúdù a crimson robe, money, and silk,
enrolling him in the Music Academy.
A eunuch then asked Yáng Yúdù,
"How did you teach the macaques to understand human speech?"
He replied:
"Macaques are beasts,
they truly do not understand human speech." Yáng Yúdù fed them cinnabar,
which transformed their animal nature,
and only then could they be taught.
The eunuch was deeply astonished by this explanation.
Then some curious people learned of it,
and many fed cinnabar to macaques, parrots, dogs, rats, etc., to teach them.
Thus it is known that if birds and beasts eat cinnabar,
they can still change to have a human heart;
if humans eat cinnabar,
it is enough to transform their ordinary substance.
When macaques see a monk,
they will inevitably surround him,
acting as if making offerings.
The Yí and Liáo tribes of Róng and Lù
also eat these creatures.
They simply sit cross-legged
on a rock in the wild,
covering their heads with something,
as if in meditation.
Then the macaques will happily come,
and once tamed,
after a while the others leave,
leaving only one behind.
It sits beside the fake monk,
and the monk strikes it with an axe,
taking it back to eat.
Another day when he wants more,
he uses the same method to strike them,
yet the macaques never realize it.
Also, because they harm crops,
people place a basin of wine lees
on a wild path,
and prepare about fifty wooden sticks, each one or two feet long,
beside it.
After the macaques eat the lees and get drunk,
they pick up the sticks and hit each other,
breaking their limbs.
Thus they are all captured.
From this, those who love wine
should take warning from the harm these beasts bring upon themselves.
Love of Wine
Orangutans love wine and clogs.
Those who wish to catch them
set out these two things to lure them.
When the orangutans first see them,
they will loudly curse, saying:
"You are trying to trick me!"
Then they run far away.
But they leave and return again.
Gradually they urge each other on,
and soon are completely drunk.
Their feet become entangled.
Someone painted a picture and praised them with these words:
"Your form is that of an ape,
your face is that of a human.
Your words do not disgrace your face,
your wisdom does not surpass your body.
Huáiyīn aided Hàn,
Lǐ Sī served as minister of Qín.
How can they compare to Jīshān,
reclining high and nurturing truth?"
Ability to Speak
In Fēngxī, Wǔpíng County, Ānnán,
there are orangutans.
They resemble beautiful women,
understand human speech,
and know past events.
Because of their fondness for wine,
they are caught with clogs.
Hundreds are caged together.
When they are to be eaten,
they themselves push forward the fattest one to be sent,
weeping as they part.
Once, one was sent as a gift to the Magistrate of Fēngxī,
covered with a cloth.
The magistrate asked what it was,
and the orangutan spoke from the cage, saying:
"Only your servant and a pot of wine."
The magistrate laughed and grew fond of it,
keeping and raising it.
It could relay messages,
surpassing humans,
indeed.
Jiāo Fēng
Former Xùnyí County Magistrate Jiāo Fēng, after leaving his post, lost his wife.
In the early years of the Kāiyuán era,
he traveled as a guest in Shǔ.
Day and night, he drank and gambled with wealthy men of Shǔ.
Suddenly one day, as night fell,
he rode alone on horseback to return.
He encountered a maidservant,
as if they were old acquaintances.
She spoke before his horse, inviting Fēng.
Fēng, being heavily intoxicated,
laughed and followed her,
though in his heart he suspected it was a mistaken invitation.
Soon they arrived at a grand mansion,
with towering and imposing buildings.
He was firmly urged to enter.
Fēng then dismounted and went inside.
In a short while,
over ten maids and servants arrived,
all dressed in fine silks,
adorned with pearls and jade,
each with beautiful features and grace.
These maids and servants together announced that the lady wished to meet him.
Fēng was still startled and suspicious,
when two rows of festive candles led the way,
and he saw large fans shielding a young woman,
about seventeen or eighteen years old,
with extraordinary beauty and demeanor.
She then ordered the fans opened,
led Fēng forward,
and after exchanging bows in the hall, they sat down.
Before and after them were set out exquisite wines and delicacies,
accompanied by female musicians.
She then urged Fēng to drink from a golden goblet.
The lady requested a red paper,
and wrote a poem to present to him.
The poem said:
"I have lost my mandarin duck companion,
while you wander like duckweed and stems.
In youthful joy after drunkenness,
I fear only that I may bitterly urge you to stay."
Fēng held the poem and read it,
pondering for a long while,
then drank it all,
and again filled the golden goblet,
replying with a quatrain.
The poem said:
"My heart often lies beyond fame and office,
never ashamed of wild wanderings.
By mistake I entered the Peach Blossom Spring,
would the immortal family be willing to keep me?"
The lady read the poem,
laughed and said:
"Who told you to mistakenly enter?
If you wish not to stay,
it cannot be helped either."
Fēng also laughed and replied:
"I only fear not being kept,
who would fear staying for thousands and thousands of years?"
The lady was greatly pleased, her face glowing,
then slowly rose,
pretending drunkenness, returned to the bedchamber,
and asked Fēng to express his conjugal affection.
At dawn,
another splendid feast was laid out,
with songs and music clear and bright,
and she drank with Fēng again until intoxicated.
Then she said to him:
"I am the daughter of Assistant Sun of the military governor's office.
In my youth, I married Wáng Mào.
Wáng Mào died while a guest in Cháng'ān,
and I am now widowed and living alone.
Fortunately, I have entrusted myself to you, sir,
do not fault me for offering myself.
Think of the household of Zhuō Wángsūn,
how Wénjūn admired Xiàngrú,
it was just like this."
Hearing these words, Fēng
felt even deeper affection and attachment,
and did not leave for over a month.
Suddenly, while walking alone, he said to himself:
"I originally studied poetry and books,
to seek fame and office.
Today, neither fame nor office has satisfied my heart,
yet I am immersed in wine and beauty,
not leaving for over a month—
this is not the conduct of a true man."
The attending maids who heard this
reported it to the lady.
The lady said to Fēng:
"I am a daughter of an official family,
you are a man on the path to office.
Being matched with you
is no loss for either!
As for wanting to honor yourself with fame and office,
you can certainly go to the golden palace to meet the enlightened ruler.
How could I dare to stubbornly keep you,
or hinder your illustrious advancement?
Why sigh so sadly like this?"
Fēng said:
"Fortunately, you think of me, madam,
do not let me grow old in vain in the city of Shǔ."
The lady then sent Fēng off with gold and treasures to pass through the passes.
When they parted at the crossroads, weeping.
She also gave him a jade ring.
Saying to Fēng:
"Treasure and keep it well,
it is something my mother gave me to play with when I was young."
She then recited another poem to send him off.
The poem said:
"The meeting of the Weaver Girl on the Magpie Bridge,
is also not for long.
Today at the place I send you off,
I am ashamed to speak of the intertwined branches."
Fēng read the poem,
accepted the jade ring,
his sorrowful feelings even stronger,
unconsciously shedding tears.
He left a poem in farewell:
"Only keep the knot of shared hearts,
no need for brocade-weaving poems.
Sū Qín sought wealth and honor,
and there will be a time for it."
The lady saw the poem,
and wept sorrowfully for a long time.
Again she urged him to drink from a golden cup before parting.
Though Fēng had already resolved
to return to the capital Luòyáng for fame and office,
he still often felt regretful,
parting from such a beauty.
Just as he ascended the plank road,
seeing the perilous cliffs,
he felt deeply melancholy.
Suddenly looking back,
he saw from afar the lady running after him,
and was startled, waiting for her.
She quickly reached Fēng,
weeping incessantly.
She said to Fēng:
"I cannot bear to part from you,
so I secretly ran to catch up.
I never thought I would see your face again today,
I beg you to take me to the capital."
Fēng was surprised and doubtful,
but also pleased,
and so they went hand in hand to the next lodging.
When dusk fell,
over ten gibbons came.
His wife ran out to see them,
leaping with joy more than usual.
Then turning to Fēng, she said:
"You also do not care for me going east,
now fortunately my female companions summon me back to the mountains.
I hope you will take care and cherish yourself."
Having said this,
she transformed into a gibbon,
and ran off with her companions,
no one knew where they went.
Gibbons
Those in Jiànnán who capture gibbons,
if they catch one gibbon,
they can get dozens of gibbons.
Why is that?
If a gibbon is injured among its kind,
the whole clan gathers, weeping sorrowfully,
even if killed, they will not leave.
This is the form of beasts but the heart of humans.
Yuè Yáng, Zhāng Rényuàn, Shǐ Móu,
then are the form of humans but the heart of beasts.
Gibbons
The róng is a type of ape or macaque.
The males have fur up to one or one and a half chǐ long,
which they cherish and protect themselves,
as if wearing brocade garments.
The finest ones have golden fur,
which today’s high officials use as warm seat covers.
They live deep in the mountains,
moving in groups of thousands.
The small males
are called róng nú.
Hunters who capture them
often use mulberry-wood bows and peach-wood arrows to shoot them.
The males with long fur,
upon hearing human or dog sounds,
abandon their group and flee.
They throw themselves from one branch
to another,
moving as swiftly as flight.
Sometimes they hide among dense foliage.
Aware of their own splendid fur,
hunters inevitably pursue them.
The females and the nú,
however, slowly eat while moving through the trees,
showing no haste at all.
Knowing that humans do not seek them,
they often carry one or even two offspring.
If a male is struck by an arrow,
he pulls it out and sniffs it.
Detecting the scent of poison,
he breaks it and throws it away.
Frowning in sorrow and despair,
he climbs to the treetop and crouches there.
Then the poison takes effect, causing convulsions,
until his limbs go limp.
Just before falling, he grabs hold of a branch again,
repeating this dozens of times.
He retches back and forth,
and his groans
are no different from a human’s.
Whenever drool flows from his mouth,
he faints and releases his grip.
Falling halfway down the tree,
he might catch a thin twig,
hanging for a while
until his strength fails,
and then he drops to the ground.
Then the hunters and dogs arrive together,
ending his life.
If hunters fail to catch a fine specimen,
they shoot the female instead.
If the female is hit by an arrow,
she pushes her offspring away,
but the young one returns after being cast aside,
clinging to its mother’s body.
Unable to separate them,
both mother and child perish together.
If a compassionate person witnessed this,
they could not bear to sleep on its pelt
or eat its flesh.
Those without pity
have livers of iron and stone,
and such people are no better than beasts.
In the past, when Dèng Zhī shot an ape,
its offspring pulled out the arrow
and stuffed leaves into the wound.
Dèng Zhī said:
“I have violated the nature of living beings;
I am surely doomed to die.”
Thereupon, he threw his bow and arrows into the water.
Mountain folk, lacking understanding,
how could they grasp Dèng Zhī’s heart?
On Foxes
At fifty years of age, a fox can transform into a woman.
At a hundred years, it becomes a beautiful maiden,
a divine shaman,
or a man who engages with women,
capable of knowing events a thousand lǐ away,
skilled in bewitchment,
causing people to become confused and lose their wits.
At a thousand years, it communicates with heaven,
becoming a tiānhú.
Auspicious Signs
The nine-tailed fox is a divine creature.
Its appearance is crimson,
with four legs and nine tails.
It emerges from the land of Qīngqiū.
Its cry resembles that of an infant.
Those who eat it will not encounter evil miasmas
or bewitchment poisons.
King Wén of Zhōu
When King Wén of Zhōu was imprisoned in Yǒulǐ,
Sàn Yíshēng went to Túshān and obtained a blue fox to present to King Zhòu,
thus sparing King Wén from calamity.
King Guǎngchuān of Hàn
King Guǎngchuān of Hàn enjoyed excavating tombs.
When he opened the tomb of Luán Shū,
the coffin and burial objects
were all decayed and ruined without exception.
Only a single white fox remained,
which fled in fright upon seeing people.
His attendants chased it but could not catch it,
injuring its foot with a halberd.
That night,
the king dreamed of a man with completely white beard and eyebrows,
who came and said to the king:
“Why did you injure my left foot?”
He then struck the king’s left foot with his staff.
The king awoke with swelling and pain,
which developed into a sore
that never healed until his death.
Chén Xiàn
During the Jiàn’ān era of the Later Hàn,
Chén Xiàn of Pèiguó commandery served as Commandant of Xīhǎi.
A soldier under his command, Shì Língxiào, fled without reason,
and Chén Xiàn intended to kill him.
Not long after,
Língxiào fled again.
After a long time without seeing him,
Chén Xiàn imprisoned his wife.
His wife truthfully replied,
and Chén Xiàn said:
“He must have been taken away by a demon;
we must search for him.”
So he led several dozen infantry and cavalry,
along with hunting dogs,
and scoured the area outside the city in search.
They indeed found Língxiào in an empty tomb,
who, upon hearing the sounds of people and dogs, hid in fear.
Chén Xiàn had him supported and brought back,
but his appearance had become quite fox-like.
He barely responded to people anymore,
only crying out for Ā Zǐ,
which is the name of a female fox.
After more than ten days,
he gradually regained awareness.
He said:
“When the fox first came,
it took the form of a beautiful woman by the corner of the house where the chickens roost,
calling herself Ā Zǐ,
and beckoned to me.
This happened not just once;
suddenly I followed her away.
She became my wife,
and every evening I would return home with her.
I didn’t even notice the dogs.
She said
there was no joy greater than this.”
A Daoist priest said:
“This is a mountain demon.
The fox was a licentious woman of ancient times,
named Ā Zǐ,
who transformed into a fox.
Therefore, such creatures often call themselves Ā Zǐ.”
Guǎn Lù
Guǎn Lù of Wèi once saw a small creature at night that looked like an animal,
holding fire in its hand,
blowing it toward its mouth,
about to set the house ablaze.
Guǎn Lù ordered his disciple to raise a knife and strike forcefully,
cutting it in half at the waist.
Upon inspection, it was a fox.
From then on, there were no fires in the village.
Xí Zàochǐ
Xí Zàochǐ of Jìn served as Chief Clerk under Huán Wēn
and accompanied Huán Wēn on a hunt.
There was heavy snow at the time,
and west of Línjiāng City,
they saw steam rising from the grass in the snow.
Sensing something there,
they shot at it,
and it fell dead with the twang of the bowstring.
Going to retrieve it,
they found it was an old male fox,
with a crimson silk sachet tied to its foot.
Chén Fěi
In Jiǔquán Commandery,
every time a new governor took office,
he would die shortly after.
Later, Chén Fěi from Bóhǎi was appointed to this commandery,
and he felt worried and unhappy.
Before departing,
he consulted a diviner about his fortune.
The diviner said:
"Keep away from the marquises,
and release Bó Qiú.
If you can understand this,
you will have no worries."
Fěi did not understand these words.
The diviner said:
"When you go there,
you will naturally understand."
After Fěi took office,
his attending physician was named Zhāng Hóu,
the duty physician was named Wáng Hóu,
and the soldiers included Shǐ Hóu and Dǒng Hóu.
Fěi suddenly realized and said:
"These are the 'marquises.'
So he kept away from them.
When he lay down to rest,
he pondered the meaning of 'release Bó Qiú,'
but did not know what it meant.
After midnight,
something came onto Fěi's blanket.
He immediately covered it with the blanket and caught it,
and the thing jumped and thumped noisily.
People outside heard the noise,
came in with torches,
and wanted to kill it.
The creature then spoke:
"I truly mean no harm.
If you, Prefect, can spare me,
I will deeply repay you."
Fěi said:
"What are you,
that you dare to offend the governor?"
The demon said:
"I am originally a thousand-year-old fox,
and my name has been Bó Qiú for many years.
If you, Prefect, encounter any urgent danger,
just call my name,
and it will be resolved."
Fěi then happily said:
"So this is the true meaning of 'release Bó Qiú.'"
He immediately released it.
Suddenly, a red light like lightning
shot out from the door.
The next day,
at night, someone knocked on the door.
Fěi said:
"Who is it?"
The voice said:
"It is Bó Qiú."
Fěi said:
"Why have you come?"
It said:
"To report something.
There are bandits in the northern border."
Fěi verified it and found it to be true.
Every event was reported to Fěi beforehand,
without the slightest error,
and people all praised him as a sage prefect.
Over a month later,
the Registrar Lǐ Yīn secretly had an affair with Fěi's maidservant.
Afraid that Bó Qiú would expose him,
he conspired with the 'marquises' to murder Fěi.
When no one was around,
he sent the 'marquises' to enter with clubs,
intending to kill Fěi.
Fěi, terrified,
immediately shouted, "Bó Qiú, come save me!"
Immediately, something like a bolt of crimson silk appeared,
making a roaring sound.
Yīn and the 'marquises' fell to the ground, terrified out of their wits.
They were then bound and interrogated,
and they all confessed.
They said:
"Before Fěi took office,
Yīn was already afraid of losing power,
and conspired with the 'marquises' to murder Fěi.
But as the 'marquises' were dismissed,
the plan failed."
Fěi then executed Yīn and the others.
Bó Qiú then apologized to Fěi:
"I had not yet exposed Yīn's treachery,
when you summoned me.
Though I exerted a small effort,
I still feel ashamed."
Over a month later,
he bid farewell to Fěi, saying:
"From now on, I must ascend to heaven,
and can no longer interact with you, Prefect."
He then left and was never seen again.
Sūn Yán
In the Later Wèi, there was a funeral singer named Sūn Yán,
who took a wife. After three years,
his wife never removed her clothes to sleep.
Yán privately found this strange.
Waiting until she was asleep,
he secretly removed her clothes,
and found a tail three feet long,
resembling a fox's tail.
Yán, terrified, divorced her.
Just as she was about to leave,
she took a knife, cut off Yán's hair, and fled.
Neighbors chased her,
and she transformed into a fox,
making it impossible to catch her.
Afterward, 130 people in the capital had their hair cut off.
Initially, she transformed into a woman,
wearing clean and elegant clothes,
walking on the roads.
People who saw her were delighted,
but those who approached had their hair cut off.
At that time, women wearing colorful clothes
were pointed at as fox demons.
Xiàhóu Zǎo
Xiàhóu Zǎo's mother was critically ill,
so he went to Chúnyú Zhì for divination.
A fox stood at the door,
howling at him.
Zǎo was shocked and frightened,
and hurried to Zhì.
Zhì said:
"The disaster is very urgent.
Return home quickly!
At the place where it howled,
beat your chest and cry loudly,
startling your family,
so that everyone, young and old, comes out.
If one person is not afraid,
do not stop crying.
Only then can the disaster be averted."
Zǎo did as instructed,
and his mother, though ill, also came out.
Once the family had gathered,
the five-room main hall
suddenly collapsed.
Hú Dàoqià,
who called himself a man from Guǎnglíng,
was fond of music and medicine.
His body had a foul odor,
so he always used fine incense to mask it.
He only feared fierce dogs.
Knowing his own death date,
he warned his disciples:
"Once I stop breathing, bury me immediately.
Do not let dogs see my corpse."
He died in Shānyáng.
After the burial,
the coffin felt empty.
When opened,
no body was found.
People at the time all said he was a fox.
The Later Lord of Northern Qí
During the Wǔpíng era of the Later Lord of Northern Qí,
at the gate of Shuòzhōu's government office,
small children's footprints appeared for no reason,
and soil was piled up to form shapes like city walls and battlements.
Upon investigation, it was found to be the work of fox spirits.
That year,
the Prince of Nán'ān,
raised troops in the northern Shuò region.
Sòng Dàxián
In the southern outskirts of Suíyáng, there was a pavilion.
People could not stay there,
for staying would bring misfortune.
A townsman named Sòng Dàxián, who upheld the correct path,
once lodged in the pavilion’s upper floor.
At night, he sat playing the qín.
Suddenly, a ghost came climbing up the ladder
and spoke to Dàxián.
Its eyes were glaring, its teeth grinding,
its appearance repulsive.
Dàxián continued playing the qín as before.
The ghost then left
and fetched a dead man’s head from the marketplace to return,
saying to Dàxián:
“Would you care to sleep a little?”
Then it threw the dead man’s head before Dàxián.
Dàxián said:
“Excellent.
When I lie down at night, I have no pillow,
and I was just wanting this.”
The ghost went away again,
and after a long while returned.
It said:
“Would you care to wrestle hand-to-hand?”
Dàxián said:
“Fine.”
Before the words were finished,
it was in front of him.
Dàxián then seized it by the waist.
The ghost only cried out urgently, “I’m dying!”
Dàxián then killed it.
The next day, looking at it,
it turned out to be an old fox.
From then on, the pavilion had no more strange occurrences.
Chángsūn Wújì
Táng Tàizōng bestowed a beautiful woman upon Duke Zhàoguó, Chángsūn Wújì,
who received exceptional favor.
Suddenly, she encountered fox enchantment.
The fox called itself Wáng Bā.
Its body was over eight chǐ tall,
and it was constantly with the beautiful woman.
Whenever the beautiful woman saw Wújì,
she would take up a long knife to hack and stab.
Tàizōng heard of this matter
and summoned various sorcerers.
One after another, four times,
they could not repel it.
Later, a sorcerer said:
“Cānjūn Cuī of Xiàngzhōu can cure this affliction.”
Earlier, while still in the province, Cuī
had often said to his colleagues:
“An imperial edict will summon me;
I shall arrive before long.”
After a few days, the decree arrived,
and Cuī set out on the road.
Wáng Bā wept sorrowfully,
saying to the beautiful woman:
“Cānjūn Cuī will arrive soon;
what shall we do about it?”
Wherever he stopped to lodge after departing,
it would report everything.
When Cuī was about to reach the capital,
the fox fled.
After arriving,
he was ordered to go to Wújì’s home.
At the time, Tàizōng also visited his residence.
Cuī set up a table,
sat, and wrote a talisman.
Tàizōng and Wújì both stood behind him.
After a short while,
several dozen beings from within the residence—the well, stove, doors, latrine, the Twelve Earthly Branches, and others—
some tall, some short,
with strange and bizarre appearances,
all came to the courtyard.
Cuī rebuked them:
“You gentlemen are the household gods of a high official’s family;
your duties and responsibilities are not small.
Why did you allow an enchanting fox to enter the residence?”
The gods came forward and said:
“It is a celestial fox;
our strength cannot subdue it,
and we did not accept bribes.”
Cuī ordered them to seize the fox.
After a short while, they returned,
each bearing knives and arrows,
saying:
“Just now we fought bitterly and were wounded;
ultimately, we could not capture it.”
Having spoken, they dispersed.
Cuī then wrote and sent off another talisman.
Heaven and earth suddenly turned dark.
The Emperor and Wújì, frightened, went inside.
Soon, the sound of soldiers and horses was heard in the void.
Moments later,
five figures appeared,
each several zhàng tall,
who came to Cuī’s place,
lining up to pay respects.
Cuī then descended the steps
and slightly bent his knee.
Soon, he called the Emperor and Wújì out to bow in the courtyard.
The various gods merely stood and watched.
Cuī said:
“The Prime Minister’s household has an enchanting fox;
I dare trouble you, the executors, to capture it.”
The gods respectfully assented,
then each dispersed.
The Emperor asked which gods they were,
Cuī said:
“They are the gods of the Five Sacred Mountains.”
Again, the sound of soldiers and horses was heard,
and then a fox was bound and thrown down the steps.
Wújì, unable to contain his fury,
took a long sword and hacked at it.
The fox showed no reaction at first.
Cuī said:
“This one has already attained spiritual power;
striking it is useless,
you will only bring trouble upon yourself.”
He then pronounced judgment:
“For wantonly committing wicked and selfish acts,
you are punished by the divine way;
I sentence you to five strokes.”
The fox then begged for its life.
Cuī took a peach branch growing eastward and administered the strokes,
blood flowing all over the ground.
Wújì was not satisfied,
only regretting that the strokes were too few.
Cuī said:
“Five strokes here are equivalent to five hundred in the human world,
truly no small punishment.
Since these beings are employed by the celestial offices,
killing them is not permissible.”
He then ordered that from then on, it must not come again to the Prime Minister’s household.
The fox then flew away.
The beautiful woman’s affliction was thus cured.
Fox Gods
Since the beginning of the Táng dynasty,
many commoners have served fox gods.
They make offerings in their rooms to beg for favors.
The foxes eat and drink the same as humans.
Those who serve them are not of one master alone.
At that time, there was a saying:
“Without fox spirits,
there is no village.”
Zhāng Jiǎn
Táng Guózǐjiàn Assistant Instructor Zhāng Jiǎn
was from Gōushì in Hénán.
He once taught the “Wénxuǎn” at a village school.
A wild fox impersonated Jiǎn’s form,
taught from one sheet of text, and left.
Moments later, Jiǎn arrived.
The students, puzzled, asked him about it.
Jiǎn, surprised, said:
“The one who came earlier must have been a wild fox.”
After teaching, he returned home,
saw his sister sitting reeling silk,
and she said to Jiǎn:
“The food I just cooked has gone cold;
why are you so late, brother?”
Jiǎn sat down,
waited a long time, but she did not come,
so he reproached his sister.
His sister said:
“I never saw you come earlier;
that must have been a wild fox.
If I see it again, I’ll kill it!”
The next day, it came again.
Seeing his sister sitting reeling silk,
it said to Jiǎn:
“A ghost was just behind the house.”
Jiǎn then took a club.
Seeing his real sister come out from the latrine,
he struck her.
His sister cried out:
“It’s me!”
Jiǎn did not believe it,
and thus struck and killed her.
Asking the one reeling silk,
she transformed into a wild fox and fled.
Monk Fúlǐ
During the Yǒnghuī era of the Táng dynasty,
a man in Tàiyuán claimed to be Maitreya Buddha.
Those who paid him homage and visited him
saw his form reaching down from the heavens.
After a long time, it gradually shrank
to only five or six chǐ,
his body like a red lotus flower amidst leaves.
He said to people:
"Do you know that the Buddha has three bodies?
The largest one is the true body."
The entire city revered and honored him.
A monk named Fú Lǐ,
learned in Buddhist teachings,
sighed and said:
"After the True Dharma,
comes the Semblance Dharma.
Beyond the Semblance Dharma,
there is still the Degenerate Dharma.
The Dharma of the Degenerate Age
leads to the absence of Dharma.
The Semblance Dharma period in between
still lasts several thousand years!
Only after Śākyamuni's teachings are exhausted,
will the great kalpa begin to decay.
After the kalpa decays,
will Maitreya then descend from Tuṣita Heaven
to Jambudvīpa.
Now Śākyamuni's teachings are not yet diminished;
I do not know why Maitreya would hastily descend?"
Thereupon, he devoutly paid his respects,
as if facing Maitreya himself.
Suddenly, he saw that beneath the feet was an old fox.
The banners, flowers, streamers, and canopies
were all merely paper money from among the graves.
Fú Lǐ clapped his hands and said:
"Is this what Maitreya is like?"
He fully described what he had seen.
The fox then fled downwards,
and they could not catch up to it.
Shàngguān Yì
During the Líndé era of the Táng dynasty,
Shàngguān Yì was the Sīmǎ of Jiàngzhōu.
He had a son about twenty years old,
who once stood alone outside the gate at dawn.
There was a girl,
perhaps thirteen or fourteen years old,
of peerless beauty,
who passed by the gate.
The young man was delighted by her,
and immediately flirted and teased her,
then sought intimate relations.
He asked where she lived,
intending to visit her.
The girl said:
"Although my household circumstances are difficult,
you, sir, are the son of a provincial official.
Both our situations leave traces;
I do not wish others to know.
But if you have the heart,
and find an opportunity,
come to me yourself."
The young man invited her,
hoping for morning and evening meetings.
The girl initially firmly declined,
but as the young man was about to detain her,
she gradually consented.
After dusk, he paced about waiting for her.
She indeed arrived as scheduled.
From then on, she came every night.
After several days,
an old maidservant who had long served the family spied on them through a window,
and realized it was a demon.
She informed Yì,
who tried every method to forbid and stop it,
but ultimately could not control it.
The demon came increasingly frequently,
staying day and night without leaving.
Whenever the son was about to eat,
the demon would snatch his cup and bowl.
Once the demon was full,
the son got no food.
Yì often personally prepared food by hand,
cutting it to give to his son.
But as soon as it reached his hand,
the demon had already taken it away.
Yì was quite resourceful,
and therefore secretly pounded poison.
It was late autumn then,
and the sesame seeds were newly ripe.
Yì ordered two batches to be roasted.
He mixed poison into one batch.
First, he took the good batch to eat himself,
sharing it with his wife and children,
and finally gave a piece to his son.
The demon immediately took it.
Next, he took the batch mixed with poison to eat,
giving it to his son.
The demon also took it away.
After giving several pieces in succession,
the demon suddenly transformed into an old fox,
writhing and collapsing.
They captured it,
and immediately ordered it burned to ashes.
The whole family celebrated joyfully.
That evening after dusk,
they heard the cries of several people in the distance.
Soon, the sounds drew nearer,
and entered behind the hall.
They all claimed injustice,
wailing and beating their chests in great sorrow.
Among them was an old man,
whose cries repeatedly said:
"If you pity the old fox,
why then wrongfully kill Qiāngchuáng for the sake of a throat?"
For several tens of days,
they came morning and evening to the house,
often seen wearing mourning garments and hempen belts.
Yì was deeply troubled by this.
Later, they gradually became scarce,
and after a long time finally ceased,
causing no harm.
Venerable Dà'ān
During the reign of Empress Wǔ Zétiān of the Táng dynasty,
a woman claimed to be a holy Bodhisattva.
Wherever people's minds were focused,
the woman would surely know it.
The Empress Dowager summoned her into the palace.
Everything she said before and after came true,
and she was reverently served in the palace.
After several months,
she was regarded as a true Bodhisattva.
Later, Venerable Dà'ān entered the palace.
The Empress Dowager asked if he had seen the female Bodhisattva.
Dà'ān said:
"Where is the Bodhisattva?
I wish to see her once."
An imperial decree ordered them to meet.
The monk's demeanor was transcendent and remote.
After a long time,
Dà'ān said:
"You are skilled at observing minds.
Try to observe where my mind is now."
She replied:
"Master, your mind is in the bell on the chattra of the pagoda's pinnacle."
He asked her again shortly after.
She said:
"In Tuṣita Heaven's Maitreya Palace, listening to the Dharma."
The third time he asked,
it was in the realm of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception.
Each time, it was as she said.
The Empress Dowager was pleased.
Dà'ān then placed his mind in the state of the Fourth Fruit Arhat,
and she could not know it.
Dà'ān rebuked her:
"My mind merely placed in the Arhat's state,
and you already do not know.
If placed in the states of Bodhisattvas or Buddhas,
how could you possibly discern it!"
The woman was left speechless,
transformed into a vixen,
ran down the steps,
and disappeared to an unknown place.
Lǐ Xiàngshēng
At the beginning of the Chuígōng era of the Táng dynasty,
Lǐ Xiàngshēng, son of Duke Qiáo, Lǐ Chóngyì, fell ill.
His wife and daughter attended to him at his side.
Suddenly, a fox
emerged from under Xiàngshēng's quilt and walked out.
Soon, it vanished without a trace.
Several days later,
Xiàngshēng died.
Wáng Yìfāng
Wáng Yìfāng, former Censor of the Táng dynasty, was demoted to Registrar of Láizhōu.
After leaving office, he returned to Wèizhōu,
making teaching his profession.
At that time, a fellow villager named Guō Wúwéi possessed considerable arts
and taught Yìfāng how to command wild foxes.
Although Yìfāng could summon them,
