they would not submit to his command.
Instead, a host of foxes came to harass him.
They often threw tiles and bricks to strike Yìfāng.
Sometimes, just as he was reading aloud,
they would immediately smash his books to pieces.
A voice was heard in the air saying:
"What divine arts do you have,
that you wish to command me?"
Yìfāng ultimately could not restrain them.
Not long after, he died.
Hé Ràngzhī
During the Shénlóng era of the Táng dynasty,
Hé Ràngzhī from Lújiāng was traveling to Luòyáng.
He encountered the Shangsi Festival day,
and was about to ascend Lǎojūn Temple,
to gaze upon the carriages and canopies of the spring outings in Luòyáng.
About two hundred paces northeast of the temple,
there were three or four large mounds,
which at that time were also called the tombs of the Later Hàn emperors.
Therefore, Zhāng Mèngyáng's poem "Seven Sorrows" says:
"The Gōng and Wén tombs gaze distantly at each other,
Yuánlíng is lush and abundant."
Yuánlíng is the tomb of Emperor Guāngwǔ.
On one of the mounds, there were only three or four withered cypress branches,
and beneath them, a flat rock
large enough to seat several dozen people.
He saw an old man,
whose appearance and demeanor were unlike ordinary people.
His eyebrows and temples were white,
wearing a Cóng-style headscarf, jacket, and trousers,
with a black gauze cap,
sitting with his knees hugged, gazing southward,
and chanting:
"Wild fields, thorns in spring,
boudoirs, new silks and satins.
The sun rises and sets above our heads,
life and death are before our eyes.
If you wish to know where my home is,
the pines and cypresses of Běimáng are its neighbors."
Soon, a noble relative,
in a carriage adorned with gold and jade,
accompanied by dozens of flower-like maidservants,
came out laughing and merrymaking through Huī'ānmén,
reaching Yúlín Diàn.
He also glanced at the area north and south of Zhōngqiáo,
where weeping willows brushed against Tiānjīn Bridge,
and abundant flowers brightened the imperial gardens.
The purple forbidden city and the splendid paths
were filled with fragrant dust.
Hé Ràngzhī sighed at his own solitude and wandering,
walking alone and desolate,
already suspecting that the chanting old man was not human,
when the old man suddenly chanted again:
"There are many young ladies in Luòyáng,
but what can a lonely old man do about growing old?"
Hé Ràngzhī quickly wanted to step forward and seize him,
but the old man suddenly leaped into the mound,
and Hé Ràngzhī followed him.
Upon first entering the mound,
it was dark and indistinguishable,
and as he chased the old man, he had already resumed his original form.
Then he saw a fox leap out,
its tail aflame like a shooting star.
Hé Ràngzhī retreated outside the dark hall.
To the east of the door, there was an empty banquet table.
Hé Ràngzhī saw a desk,
on which were items like a red cup, brush, and inkstone,
and a document,
the paper entirely a somber gray color,
the text of which was incomprehensible.
He roughly recorded what was discernible.
The first one said:
"Upright colors, vast and encompassing,
divine thoughts transform generations.
The heavens bestow, successors inherit,
light bears the mysterious design.
Vomiting depths, spitting companions,
boundaries disperse and sever.
Confused intestines, twisted and bent,
misty rain, haze, and gloom.
Sparrows destroyed, turtles frozen,
strength gallops, control bends.
Grasping tails, grinding movement,
bright and clear, distinct and shining.
□ using secret merits,
with ridges and caves.
Cutting firewood, felling herbs,
lush and vigorous, myriad sprouts.
Vomiting order brings auspiciousness,
Buddha's teachings are only Sà.
Male emptiness, having nothing,
nourishing throat, stamens and fragments.
Beginning plain, not yet come,
darkness and brightness rise and perish."
The second text said:
"The Five Elements and Seven Luminaries,
form this intercalary remainder.
The Supreme God descends with spirit,
the year's beginning, Tūn Xú.
The snake sheds its skin,
I too am divinely inspired.
Nine-nine six-six,
bind the body, heaven removes.
What fills the throat?
Inhaling and exhaling the Great Void.
What covers the ankles?
Rosy sleeves, cloud-like garments.
Alas, your floating life,
arranged like teeth of a comb in desolate ruins.
I again adorn with vital breath,
returning to the form's beginning.
At the Emperor's side,
the Way aids, suddenly all."
It was titled:
"Eight Responses for the Celestial Fox Extraordinary Examination."
The following text was very lengthy,
difficult to record in detail.
Hé Ràngzhī obtained this document,
happily kept it with him,
and then leaped out of the mound cave.
Several days later,
Zhìjìng, a monk from Tóngdé Temple north of the river, came to visit Hé Ràngzhī.
He said:
"The document obtained earlier from the mound
is not for your use, sir.
Keeping it is inauspicious.
That person recently passed the examinations of the upper realm,
and can bring fortune or misfortune to the Middle Kingdom.
If you, sir, can return this,
he will also reward you handsomely.
That person said to Zhìjìng:
'I have prepared three hundred bolts of silk,
wishing to redeem and purchase this document.
What do you think?'"
Hé Ràngzhī agreed.
The next day,
Zhìjìng brought three hundred bolts of silk to Hé Ràngzhī.
After Hé Ràngzhī received them,
he then told Zhìjìng,
saying that the document had been lent to someone else,
and he would retrieve it in a day or two,
then return it to its owner.
Hé Ràngzhī was then persuaded by friends,
who said:
"This monk is also a demonic creature,
why do you want to return it to him?
The silk you received,
just conceal it and that's fine."
Later, when Zhìjìng came,
Hé Ràngzhī completely denied it,
saying:
"There is absolutely no such thing,
and I never had such a document."
Zhìjìng had no words and withdrew.
After more than a month,
Hé Ràngzhī had a younger brother in Eastern Wú,
whom he had not seen for over a year.
One day,
his brother arrived.
He and Hé Ràngzhī talked about family matters,
and it was very pleasant.
For long nights, the brothers shared a bed.
After five or six days,
he suddenly asked Hé Ràngzhī:
"I've heard this place has many foxes causing trouble,
is it really true?"
Hé Ràngzhī then told him the story.
And boasted:
"A month ago,
I obtained a document written by a wild fox,
and it is still here now."
His brother firmly did not believe it,
how could such a thing be?
Hé Ràngzhī, at dawn the next day,
opened a chest,
took out this document and showed it to his brother.
His brother held it and exclaimed in amazement.
Then he threw it before Hé Ràngzhī,
and it transformed into a fox.
Soon, they saw a handsome youth,
looking like a newly appointed official,
riding a white horse,
galloping swiftly southward and away.
Just then, a Western Regions monk congratulated him, saying:
"Excellent,
you are always at the Heavenly Emperor's side!"
The youth sighed at Hé Ràngzhī's deception,
and Hé Ràngzhī marveled in astonishment.
Not long after,
an imperial edict ordered an arrest,
as three hundred bolts of tribute silk had been stolen from the inner treasury,
and the trail led here.
Soon, officials arrived suddenly,
directly seizing Hé Ràngzhī's bag and searching it.
Indeed, they found the silk,
of which several dozen bolts had already been spent.
They arrested Hé Ràngzhī and brought him to
justice.
Hé Ràngzhī could not clear his name,
and eventually died under a withered tree.
Shěn Dōngměi
During the Táng dynasty, Shěn Dōngměi served as a vice director.
In his household, there was a maidservant
who had been dead for several years.
Suddenly, she returned home and said:
"After I died, I became a spirit.
Now I miss my mistress,
so I have come to see her.
But I am hungry;
may I please have a meal?"
They then invited her to sit down
and prepared food for her.
The maidservant ate and drank her fill and left.
When evening came,
a servant boy, clearing away a pile of straw,
found a fox, dead drunk.
After a short while,
the fox vomited up the food,
which was exactly what the maidservant had eaten.
They then killed it.
Yáng Bóchéng,
in the early Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
served as the junior governor of the capital prefecture.
One day, a person came to his gate,
announcing himself as Wú Nánhè.
Bóchéng received him;
he was over thirty years old,
seven chǐ tall,
and exceptionally handsome.
Bóchéng invited him to take a seat.
Nánhè's eloquence and reasoning were unmatched,
and Bóchéng could barely keep up with the conversation.
After a long while,
Nánhè requested that the attendants withdraw,
as he had something confidential to say.
He then said:
"I have heard that your young daughter is virtuous and graceful;
I wish to serve under your roof."
Bóchéng was greatly astonished
and said to Nánhè:
"A daughter is married through a matchmaker.
Moreover, we have just met by chance;
how can you speak like this?"
Nánhè became enraged,
calling Bóchéng an old slave:
"I demand your daughter;
how dare you oppose me?"
He uttered many insolent words,
and Bóchéng was at a loss.
Nánhè then took off his outer garment and went inside,
straight to the daughter's quarters,
and sat down behind the paper partition.
After a long while,
he and the daughter walked out hand in hand.
The daughter said she was now married into the Wú family;
why was he scolding her?
Bóchéng realized it was a fox spirit
and ordered over ten family members to attack it.
Instead, they were subdued,
and many had their ears smeared with mud.
Because of this, Bóchéng requested leave for over twenty days.
The emperor inquired why Yáng Bóchéng had not been seen;
all reported that his household was being harassed by a fox.
An imperial decree ordered over ten Taoist priests skilled in the arts of Yè Fǎshàn to go to his home.
All had their ears smeared with mud and were bound,
unable to subdue it.
Bóchéng felt ashamed and humiliated.
When granted leave,
he moved his entire family back to his estate.
On the estate, they established a courtyard for "Young Master Wú."
If any family member secretly cursed him,
they were all subdued.
Thus, no one dared to speak out.
One day when Bóchéng was free and had nothing to do,
he went to the fields himself,
watching people harvest wheat,
and rested under a tree.
Suddenly, a Taoist priest appeared,
looking very thin and haggard,
and asked Bóchéng for some water.
Bóchéng then provided him with food.
After eating,
the Taoist priest asked:
"Why are you so troubled?"
Bóchéng, fearing Nánhè,
leaned close and whispered the matter to him.
The Taoist priest laughed and said:
"I am a celestial immortal,
precisely carrying out the Emperor's command
to pursue and capture four or five of these creatures."
He then requested paper and brush.
Yáng Bóchéng had a young servant fetch them.
Still fearing that Nánhè might become aware,
he warned the servant to be quiet.
When the paper and brush arrived,
the Taoist priest wrote three characters,
resembling ancient seal script.
He ordered the young servant to take it to where Nánhè was and, placing it before him, say:
"The Venerable Master summons you."
The servant took the writing into the room,
where he saw Nánhè flirting with a household maid.
The servant handed him the writing.
When Nánhè saw it,
he crawled on his hands and knees
to the tree.
The Taoist priest rebuked him:
"You old wild fox, how dare you take human form!"
Nánhè then transformed into a fox,
unusually afflicted with mange.
The Taoist priest said:
"The celestial offices employ these creatures;
they cannot be killed.
However, for your sake,
this cannot go unpunished."
He struck it one hundred times with a small rod,
until blood covered the ground.
Bóchéng offered him treasures as gifts,
but the Taoist priest would not accept them.
He drove the fox ahead,
following behind it.
After walking over a hundred paces,
they reached the edge of a willow grove,
where he gradually ascended to the sky,
and after a while, vanished.
Bóchéng was overjoyed,
and the entire household celebrated.
His daughter awoke after about the time of a meal.
Startled, she said:
"I was just in the partitioned room in the city;
how did I get here?"
Only then did everyone realize she had been bewitched by the fox,
her spirit as if in a deep sleep.
Yè Fǎshàn
The Daoist priest Yè Fǎshàn was a native of Kuòcāng.
He possessed Daoist arts and could command ghosts and spirits with talismans.
Emperor Zhōngzōng of the Táng dynasty held him in high esteem.
At the beginning of the Kāiyuán era, he served in the imperial palace, attaining the positions of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū and Hónglú Qīng.
At that time, a man from a prominent family obtained a magistracy south of the Yangtze River and was about to travel by boat to assume his post.
Outside the eastern gate, his relatives and friends prepared a lavish feast to see him off.
The magistrate ordered his wife and children, along with the carriages of his relatives and old friends, to go ahead to the bank of the Xūxī River.
At dusk, when the magistrate arrived beside the boat, the food and drink had already been laid out, but his wife and children had not yet arrived.
The magistrate returned to his residence to search for them, but was told they had already left.
Startled and at a loss, he went back outside the city to ask passersby.

Someone said: "Just at mealtime, I saw a Brahmin monk holding banners and flowers leading the way, with several carriages following behind. As they passed through the city gate, the women in the carriages all got down and followed the Brahmin, chanting the Buddha's name in unison, and then headed north."
The magistrate then followed the wheel tracks to the gate of an empty tomb at Běimáng.
There was a large burial mound, and he saw his carriages and horses all resting beside it.
His wife and over twenty female relatives were all following a monk, palms joined, circling the mound and chanting the Buddha's name.
The magistrate called out to them, but they all looked angry.
When the magistrate stepped forward to seize them, the women then cursed him, saying: "We are following a holy one who is now in heaven. What lowly person are you, daring to restrain us like this?"
As for the servants, they did not respond when spoken to and also walked around the mound together.
The magistrate then tried to seize the foreign monk, but he vanished.
So he bound his wife and the other women, who all cried out noisily.
Upon returning to his residence, they screamed and wailed all night, and it was impossible to speak with them.
At dawn, the magistrate went to ask Master Yè.

Master Yè said: "This is a celestial fox. It can communicate with heaven. Reprimand it and it will stop; killing it is not possible. However, this fox will certainly come at mealtime. Please bring it here with you."
The magistrate said: "Yes."
Master Yè then gave him a talisman and told him to place it at the door of his dwelling.
Once the talisman was placed, his wife and the others all awoke.

They said to the magistrate: "Yesterday we saw the Buddha come, leading a host of holy ones, taking us to heaven. The joy there is beyond words. The Buddha held flowers before and after, and we were just following behind performing religious rites when suddenly we saw you arrive. That's why we cursed you, not knowing it was actually demonic deception."
At mealtime, the Brahmin indeed arrived, knocking at the door to beg for food.
Upon hearing the monk's voice, the wife and the other women rushed out the door, clamoring that the Buddha had come again.
The magistrate tried to stop them but could not.
He then seized the foreign monk, whipped him until he bled, bound his hands behind his back, and carried him to Master Yè's place.
On the way, they encountered the Magistrate of Luòyáng.
The monk cried out loudly, claiming injustice.
The Magistrate of Luòyáng instead blamed the official.
The official explained the whole story in detail and requested they go together to see Master Yè.
The Magistrate of Luòyáng did not believe the official's words but insisted on going with them.
As they gradually approached Shèngzhēn Temple, the monk's expression grew distressed and dejected, and he fell silent.
Upon reaching the gate, he immediately begged for his life.
When they entered the courtyard, Master Yè ordered his bonds removed—he still appeared as a foreign monk.
Master Yè said: "Quickly resume your true form!"
The demon then pleaded pitifully.
Master Yè said: "That will not do."
The demon then threw its kasaya to the ground, revealing itself as an old fox.
Master Yè ordered it whipped a hundred times.
He then returned the kasaya to it, and it became a Brahmin again.
He made it promise to go beyond a thousand lǐ away.
The foreign monk paid homage and left, vanishing as soon as he passed through the gate.
Liú Jiǎ: During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty, a man named Liú Jiǎ from Péngchéng was appointed magistrate of a county in Héběi.
As he was about to take up his post, he passed through a mountain inn and stayed there overnight.

People, seeing that Liú Jiǎ's wife was beautiful, told him: "There is a spirit here that likes to steal beautiful women. Many of those who have passed through before have been taken by it. You should guard against it carefully."
Liú Jiǎ and his family encouraged each other to stay awake, surrounding his wife.
They also smeared flour paste on his wife's body and head.
After the fifth watch, Liú Jiǎ said happily: "What ghosts and spirits do happens during the night. Now dawn is about to break, what can they do to us?"
He then took a nap.
In a moment, his wife was gone.
Liú Jiǎ used money and silk to hire villagers, all carrying clubs, to follow the trail of flour.
It first emerged from the window, gradually passed east of the wall, and led to an ancient grave.
On the grave was a large mulberry tree, with a small hole beneath it where the flour went in.
They then excavated it.
After digging over a zhàng, they encountered a large tree hollow as spacious as a connected house.
Inside sat an old fox, seated behind a jade table, with over ten beautiful women lined up in two rows before it, holding musical instruments.
These were all the women stolen from people's homes before.
Beside them were several hundred young foxes, all of which they killed.
Lǐ Cānjūn
Lǐ Cānjūn of Táng Dynasty's Yǎnzhōu, having received his appointment, set off to assume his post.
On the journey, he lodged at an inn in Xīnzhèng.
There he encountered an old man reading the Hànshū.
Lǐ engaged him in conversation,
and the topic turned to marriage.
The old man asked which family he was betrothed to first?
Lǐ replied that he was not yet married.
The old man said:
"You are the son of a distinguished family,
and should choose a good match.
Now I hear that Táo Zhēnyì is the military governor of that prefecture.
If he were to force his daughter upon you as a wife,
how would you refuse?
A marriage between the Táo and Lǐ families
would deeply shock public opinion.
Although I am mediocre and inferior,
I privately feel it would be a pity for you.
Now, several li from here,
there is Xiāo Gōng, a member of the clan of the Minister of Personnel Xuán,
whose family status is also high.
He has several daughters,
all exceptionally beautiful in appearance."
Hearing this, Lǐ was pleased,
and thus asked the old man to introduce him to the Xiāo family.
The man agreed.
He left for a long time before returning.
He said Xiāo Gōng was very pleased
and respectfully awaited the guest.
Lǐ went with his servants.
Upon arriving at the Xiāo residence,
the gate and halls were clean and solemn,
the grand mansion was splendid and radiant.
Tall scholar trees and slender bamboos
spread and connected endlessly,
a peerless scenic spot.
At first,
two attendants in yellow held golden armchairs and invited them to sit.
After a short while,
Xiāo came out,
wearing a purple Shǔ silk robe,
leaning on a dove-headed staff,
with two robed attendants supporting him at his sides.
His white beard and divine discernment,
his every movement was admirable.
Lǐ looked on with respect,
and repeatedly expressed his thanks.
Xiāo said:
"This old man's place of retirement
has long been cut off from worldly affairs.
How could I expect a gentleman
to make a detour to visit me?"
He invited Lǐ into the hall.
The furnishings and curios shimmered,
rarely encountered in the present age.
Soon, rare delicacies were presented,
land and sea foods intermingled,
with many unnamed items.
After the meal, a drinking feast began.
The old man then said:
"Lǐ Cānjūn earlier wished to discuss marriage,
and has already received your promise."
Xiāo then spoke several dozen sentences,
deeply imbued with the style of a scholar.
He wrote a letter to the county magistrate,
asking for a diviner to set an auspicious date.
Soon the diviner arrived,
and said:
"The divination is auspicious,
and the date is precisely this very night."
Xiāo again wrote to the county magistrate,
to borrow head ornaments, hairpins, and silk,
along with manual laborers, etc.
Soon all arrived.
That evening,
the county magistrate also came to act as the ceremonial assistant.
The joyous events
were no different from those in the mortal world.
Upon entering the bridal chamber,
the woman was also beautiful.
Lǐ Shēng was even more pleased.
At dawn,
Xiāo Gōng then said:
"Lǐ Láng has a scheduled date to assume his post,
and cannot stay long."
He then sent the girl to follow him.
There were five jeweled ox-carts,
and thirty servants, horses, and mules.
Other clothing and curios
were too numerous to count.
Those who saw them said they were like princesses or royal consorts,
and none failed to deeply envy them.
Lǐ arrived at his post,
and after two years had accumulated,
he was sent on a mission to Luòyáng,
leaving his wife at home.
The maidservants were all seductive and bewitching,
dazzling and confusing men.
Many passersby frequented the place.
Another day,
Cānjūn Wáng Yóng, dragging a dog, was about to go hunting.
Lǐ's group of maidservants saw the dog and were greatly frightened,
many rushing inside the gate.
Yóng had long suspected they were bewitching,
and that day his heart was stirred,
so he directly led the dog into their residence.
The whole family blocked the hall door,
not daring to breathe,
and the dog also strained and barked fiercely.
Lǐ's wife from inside the door loudly rebuked:
"The maidservants were just bitten by the dog,
and are still terrified.
What business does Wáng Yóng have leading a dog into someone's home?
We are colleagues in office,
do you not consider Lǐ Cānjūn's position at all?"
Yóng, suspecting they were foxes,
then resolutely pushed open the window and released the dog,
which bit to death the group of foxes.
Only the wife died,
her body human,
but her tail unchanged.
Yóng went to report to Zhēnyì,
Zhēnyì went to retrieve and examine the evidence.
Seeing the various dead foxes,
he sighed for a long time.
As the weather was cold,
he had them buried together.
After more than ten days,
Envoy Xiāo then arrived.
Entering the gate, he wailed and cried,
causing no small alarm.
Several days later,
he came to Táo to lodge a complaint.
His words were firm and true,
his appearance and attire noble,
and Táo treated him with great respect.
He then arrested Wáng Yóng and imprisoned him.
Yóng stubbornly insisted they were foxes,
and fetched the previous dog, ordering it to bite Xiāo.
At that time, Xiāo and Táo were dining together,
the dog arrived,
Xiāo drew the dog's head onto his knee,
stroked it with his hand,
and then fed it,
the dog showed no intention to attack or bite.
Several days later,
Lǐ Shēng also returned.
He wailed and cried for days,
then suddenly went mad,
biting Wáng until his whole body swelled.
Xiāo said to Lǐ:
"Those lowly fellows all say the dead are all wild foxes,
how bitter and painful!
That day I wished to open the grave,
but feared you, Lǐ Láng, were deluded,
and would not believe.
Now we should open and look,
to expose the deceit and falsehood."
He ordered the grave opened for inspection,
and all were human forms.
Lǐ wept even more sorrowfully.
Zhēnyì, considering Yóng's crime grave,
imprisoned him and investigated thoroughly.
"I have already ordered someone to take a hundred thousand
to the Eastern Capital to fetch a dog that bites foxes;
the round trip should take over ten days."
Zhēnyì also added a hundred thousand from public funds to it.
Once the dog arrived,
the authorities summoned Xiāo for confrontation.
Táo stood waiting in the main hall.
Xiāo entered the government office,
his countenance dejected,
his movements flustered and disturbed,
different from usual.
Suddenly the dog entered from outside,
Xiāo transformed into an old fox,
ran down the steps a few paces,
and was bitten to death by the dog.
Zhēnyì ordered the dead inspected,
and all were wild foxes.
Yóng was thus spared from this calamity.
Zhèng Hóngzhī
During the Táng Dynasty, Zhèng Hóngzhī, the Prefect of Dìngzhōu, first took office as a Commandant.
The official residence of the Commandant
had long been uninhabited.
The buildings were dilapidated and crumbling,
overgrown with weeds and desolate.
When Hóngzhī arrived to assume his post,
he cleared the weeds and repaired the buildings,
then moved in to live there.
His subordinates strenuously objected,
urging Hóngzhī not to enter.
Hóngzhī said:
"If one acts with integrity,
what is there to fear from demons and ghosts?
My nature is strong and resolute,
and ultimately cannot be changed."
After living there for two days,
in the middle of the night,
Hóngzhī was sleeping alone in the front hall.
Bright torches appeared in the courtyard below the hall,
and a nobleman accompanied by over a hundred horsemen
arrived in the courtyard.
He angrily said:
"Who is this intruder,
who dares to live here!"
He ordered his men to drag Hóngzhī down.
Hóngzhī did not reply.
The men sent to drag him reached the hall,
but did not dare approach.
Hóngzhī then rose.
The nobleman ordered a tall man
to seize Hóngzhī.
The tall man ascended the steps,
walked along the wall,
and blew out all the lamps.
All the lamps were extinguished,
except for one lamp in front of Hóngzhī which remained lit.
The tall man approached, intending to extinguish it,
but Hóngzhī struck him with his sword,
causing blood to spill on the ground,
and the tall man fled.
The nobleman gradually approached, pressing closer.
Hóngzhī, fully dressed in his official robes and cap,
invited him to sit together.
They conversed throughout the night,
and the atmosphere became quite cordial.
Hóngzhī, knowing he was off guard,
drew his sword and struck him,
wounding the nobleman.
His attendants supported him,
and urgently said, "Our king is now injured,
what shall we do?"
They then led him away.
Afterwards, Hóngzhī ordered a hundred laborers
to follow the trail of blood.
They reached the northern wall,
where there was a small hole about an inch square,
and the blood led into it.
Hóngzhī ordered them to dig.
After digging down one zhàng,
they found several dozen foxes, large and small.
Hóngzhī captured them all.
Digging another zhàng or more beneath the hole,
they found a large cavern,
containing an old fox,
naked and hairless,
sitting on an earthen bed,
attended by over ten other foxes.
Hóngzhī captured them all as well.
The old fox said:
"Do not harm me,
and I will bring you good fortune."
Hóngzhī ordered firewood to be piled in the courtyard,
lit a fire,
and threw all the foxes into it,
burning them to ashes.
When it was the old fox's turn,
the fox slapped its own cheeks and pleaded:
"I am already a thousand years old,
and can communicate with Heaven.
Killing me would bring misfortune,
what harm is there in sparing me?"
Hóngzhī then did not kill it,
but locked it to a locust tree in the courtyard.
That first night,
various spirits and ghosts, calling themselves deities of the mountains, forests, rivers, marshes, and grove shrines,
came to pay their respects.
Bowing twice, they said:
"We did not know our great king had met with such misfortune.
Although we wish to free you,
we sadly have no plan."
The old fox nodded in acknowledgment.
The next night,
various local earth deities came to pay homage,
speaking words similar to those of the mountain spirits.
On the third night,
a spirit calling itself Huáng Juē,
accompanied by many winged followers,
came to the fox and said:
"Elder brother, how did you suddenly end up like this?"
He then grasped the lock with his hand,
and the lock broke.
The fox also transformed into a human,
and they left together.
Hóngzhī ran after them,
but could not catch up.
Hóngzhī thought that the name Huáng Juē
was actually a dog's name.
Was there anyone here with a dog named Huáng Juē?
At dawn,
he summoned his clerks and asked them.
A clerk said:
"There is an old dog at the county granary,
but its whereabouts are unknown.
Because it has no tail,
it is called Huáng Juē.
Could this dog be the demon?"
Hóngzhī ordered it to be captured.
When it was brought,
he had it chained and was about to have it cooked.
The dog spoke in human language:
"I am indeed the spirit Huáng Juē.
Do not harm me, sir.
I will always follow you,
and whether you encounter good or evil,
I will forewarn you of everything.
Would that not be excellent?"
Hóngzhī dismissed the others and spoke with it alone,
then released it.
The dog transformed into a human,
conversed with Hóngzhī,
and did not leave until late at night.
Hóngzhī was in charge of apprehending bandits and thieves.
Suddenly, several dozen robbers entered his jurisdiction
and stopped at an inn.
The spirit Huáng Juē came to inform Hóngzhī:
"There are robbers at a certain place,
about to commit theft.
Capturing them could lead to a promotion."
Hóngzhī raided them and indeed captured them.
He was subsequently promoted.
Later, whenever Hóngzhī held successive posts and was about to be transferred,
the spirit would always forewarn him.
As for misfortunes and calamities,
it often instructed him on how to avoid them,
and never missed.
Hóngzhī greatly benefited from its assistance.
When Hóngzhī was transferred from Prefect of Níngzhōu to Prefect of Dìngzhōu,
the spirit bid farewell to Hóngzhī and left.
Therefore, people said Hóngzhī's official fortune had run out.
Hóngzhī served in the prefecture for two years,
then retired due to a wind-stroke illness.
Magistrate of Qiānyáng.
The magistrate of Qiānyáng County in the Táng dynasty, whose name is unknown.
While serving in office,
he suddenly said:
"I wish to renounce the world."
He recited scriptures with utmost sincerity.
After over a month,
five-colored clouds appeared above his residence.
He also saw a Bodhisattva seated on a lion,
who called out to him, sighing and saying:
"Your aspiration is grand and profound,
and you shall attain the highest fruit.
You must remain steadfast and protect yourself,
and do not retreat or falter."
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva flew away.
The magistrate then entered meditation,
closed his doors,
and abstained from food for six or seven days.
His family grew worried and fearful,
afraid that his persistence would harm his longevity.
It happened that the Daoist priest Luó Gōngyuǎn was traveling from Shǔ to the capital,
passing through Lǒngshàng along the way.
The magistrate's son went to inquire about the situation.
Gōngyuǎn laughed and said:
"This is a celestial fox,
but it is easy to deal with."
He then gave him several written talismans,
saying they would cure the ailment.
The magistrate's son threw the talismans into a well.
Thereupon, the doors opened,
and they saw the magistrate weakened from hunger.
They forced him to swallow the talismans,
and suddenly he became clear-minded,
no longer speaking of cultivating the Way.
Several years later,
he left office and returned home.
His family had long lived in the outskirts,
with flat plains stretching for a thousand lǐ.
One leisurely day, the magistrate leaned on his staff and went out the door,
when he saw from afar a nobleman approaching from the south beneath a mulberry grove.
There were over ten riders before and after him,
appearing like a king.
The magistrate went inside to avoid him.
The riders soon arrived at the gate.
They announced:
"Liú Chéng
requests an audience with the magistrate."
The magistrate was greatly startled.
He had never met him before,
so why was he visiting?
After they met,
they ascended the hall and sat down.
Chéng said to the magistrate:
"I have received the gift of marriage,
and dare not refuse the command."
Earlier, when the magistrate was in office,
he had a daughter who was ten years old,
and by now she was sixteen.
The magistrate said:
"I do not recall knowing you,
how could there be a marriage arrangement?"
Chéng said:
"If you do not consent to the marriage,
the matter is also easily resolved."
He then pulled at his mouth with his right hand and stood there,
and in an instant, the magistrate's residence began to tremble,
wells and latrines overflowed,
and all objects swayed and drifted.
The magistrate had no choice but to agree.
The wedding was set for the next day,
and gifts were sent to complete the marriage.
After the marriage,
Chéng often stayed at the residence.
His manners were exceedingly generous,
and he provided abundant resources,
so the family did not dislike him.
Another day,
the magistrate's son went to the capital,
seeking to see Gōngyuǎn.
Gōngyuǎn said:
"This fox was powerless in the past,
but now he has mastered talismanic arts.
I am no match for him,
what can be done?"
The magistrate's son pleaded earnestly.
Gōngyuǎn petitioned to take action.
He soon arrived at their residence,
setting up an altar about ten paces outside the magistrate's home.
Chéng came to the altar leaning on his staff,
and cursed the old Daoist priest, saying:
"Why do you come and go,
without any fear or restraint?"
Gōngyuǎn completed his ritual,
and sought to engage in battle.
Chéng sat at the magistrate's gate,
while Gōngyuǎn sat at the altar.
Then Gōngyuǎn struck Chéng with an object,
and Chéng fell to the ground.
After a long while, he rose,
and also struck Gōngyuǎn with an object,
causing Gōngyuǎn to fall as well,
just like Chéng had.
Thus they went back and forth dozens of times.
Gōngyuǎn suddenly said to his disciple:
"When he strikes me dead,
you should wail loudly,
and I will use divine magic to bind him."
When Chéng struck,
Gōngyuǎn fell to the ground,
and the disciple wept bitterly.
Chéng was delighted,
and let down his guard.
Gōngyuǎn then sent a divine force to strike him.
Chéng was greatly frightened in the battle,
declared that his strength was exhausted,
and transformed into an old fox.
After Gōngyuǎn rose,
he struck the fox with his sitting mat,
then placed it in a large sack,
and returned to the capital by post horse.
Emperor Xuánzōng saw it,
and thought it amusing.
Gōngyuǎn addressed the emperor, saying:
"This is a celestial fox,
and cannot be killed.
It should be exiled to the eastern borders!"
He wrote a talisman and exiled it to Xīnlúo,
and the fox, holding the talisman, flew away.
Now in Xīnlúo, there is a deity named Liú Chéng,
whom the local people revere and serve.
Lǐ Yuángōng
Lǐ Yuángōng, Vice Minister of Personnel in the Táng dynasty,
had a granddaughter named Cuī,
who was exceptionally beautiful,
and fifteen or sixteen years old.
Suddenly, she was afflicted by a bewitching illness.
After some time,
the fox manifested as a young man,
calling himself Húláng.
They repeatedly sought exorcists but could not drive him away.
Yuángōng's son was learned and wise,
and once asked Húláng if he also studied.
The fox then engaged in discussions,
covering all topics.
He often posed questions to the fox,
and they became quite familiar and enjoyed themselves.
After a long while,
the fox said to Cuī:
"In life, one must study."
He then brought an old man to teach Cuī the classics and histories.
Over the course of three years,
she became quite proficient in the main ideas of various schools.
He then brought another person,
to teach her calligraphy.
After a year,
she became renowned for her skill in calligraphy.
He also said:
"Why should a woman not learn music?
The kōnghóu and pipa,
these are ordinary instruments,
but they are not as good as various tunes,
which fully capture their subtleties.
As for other famous tunes,
they are too numerous to record.
He also claimed to be skilled in 'Guǎnglíng Sàn'.
He said he had often seen Jī Kāng,
who would not allow it to be taught to others.
As for 'Wūyètí',
he was especially adept at conveying its beauty.
Lady Lǐ later asked:
"Húláng, why do you not take your wife back to your home?"
The fox was very pleased,
and bowed in thanks, saying:
"I have long desired this.
What held me back
was my humble status."
That day, he bowed to all the family members,
full of joy and excitement.
Lady Lǐ asked Húláng where his residence was,
since he wished to take the girl there.
The fox said:
"In front of my dwelling, there are two large bamboos."
At that time, the Lǐ family had a bamboo garden.
Lady Lǐ then searched the area,
and between two large bamboos, she found a small hole,
which turned out to be the fox's den.
They diverted water to flood it,
and at first captured several dozen raccoon dogs and other foxes.
Finally, an old fox emerged,
wearing a green robe,
coming out of the hole.
This was the robe he usually wore.
The family rejoiced, saying:
"Húláng has come out!"
They killed him,
and the haunting ceased.
Jiāo Liànshī
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a Daoist master named Jiāo who practiced cultivation,
gathering many disciples.
A woman in a yellow skirt, who called herself Ā Hú,
came to Jiāo to learn Daoist arts.
After three years,
she had mastered all of Jiāo's techniques,
and firmly insisted on leaving.
Jiāo tried hard to keep her.
Ā Hú said:
"I am actually a wild fox,
who originally came to learn arts.
Now there are no more arts to learn,
so it is not right for me to stay."
Jiāo then wanted to use his arts to detain her.
Hú responded appropriately to each situation,
and Jiāo could not match her.
So, he set up an altar atop Mount Sōng,
and prayed to Lǎojūn.
He said that although he himself was untalented,
he was still a disciple of the Daoist school.
Having been humiliated by a demon fox,
he feared the Great Dao would be destroyed.
His words and intent were sincere and earnest.
Suddenly, incense smoke arose from the four corners of the altar,
and in a moment it formed a purple cloud,
several tens of zhang high.
Within the cloud, Lǎojūn appeared standing.
Jiāo then bowed and stated:
"The orthodox arts have already been learned by the demon fox,
I must seek further arts to subdue her."
Lǎojūn then performed magic within the cloud.
A divine king within the cloud used a knife to cut the fox's waist.
Jiāo was greatly overjoyed.
Suddenly, Lǎojūn descended from the cloud,
transformed into the woman in the yellow skirt, and left.
Lǐ Shì
During the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
there was a person named Lǐ Shì,
who was orphaned early,
and went to live with her maternal uncle's family.
At the age of twelve,
a fox wanted to bewitch her.
Although this fox's form was not visible,
its speech and social interactions were very complete.
After several months,
the fox came again,
but its voice was slightly different.
The family members laughed and said:
"This is another, different wild fox."
The fox also laughed and said:
"How did you know?
The one who came before was the fourteenth elder brother,
I am his younger brother.
Recently, I wanted to marry the Wéi family's daughter,
and made a red silk half-sleeve garment.
My elder brother unreasonably stole it,
causing my marriage plans to fail.
I have always wanted to get back at him,
so I have come here now."
Lǐ Shì then apologized and entreated him,
seeking a method to avert the misfortune.
The fox said:
"Tomorrow is the fourteenth elder brother's day of royal influence,
he will certainly come here.
He will cause great trouble and disturbance.
You can temporarily have the girl pinch the first joint of her ring finger to avert it."
Having said this, he left.
The big fox arrived,
just as the girl was eating.
The girl followed the little fox's words,
and pinched her finger joint.
The fox took six or seven medicinal pellets the size of Bodhi seeds,
and threw them into the girl's rice bowl,
but after repeated throws, none hit.
He was extremely shocked and sighed,
and said loudly:
"I must go to Mount Sōngyuè to study the Dao before I can succeed!"
Among those seated was an old woman who picked up his medicine pellets,
fearing them, she threw them away again.
People asked her the reason.
She said:
"A wild fox bewitched me."
The fox arrogantly cursed:
"What kind of old crone is this,
how could anyone use such a one!"
After the fox left,
the little fox came again and said:
"How did things go?
Were my words effective?"
The family members all apologized and thanked him.
He said:
"After more than ten days,
my elder brother will come again,
you should be careful.
This person has already made connections with the Celestial Ministry,
talisman prohibition arts
are useless against him.
Only I can restrain him.
When he is about to arrive,
I will come here again."
As the day approached,
the little fox came again,
and gave the girl a medicine packet like pine pollen, saying:
"My elder brother will certainly come tomorrow.
Tomorrow morning,
you should have the girl ride in a carriage,
and travel northeast.
If there are mounted riders pursuing you,
you should scatter the medicine behind the carriage,
then you can avoid his violence."
Lǐ Shì waited until the next day,
and followed the fox's words.
They carried the girl for five or six lǐ,
when many armored riders pursued them,
and just as they were about to catch up,
they scattered the medicine.
The pursuers saw the medicine,
stopped, and did not dare advance.
That evening,
the little fox came again.
He laughed and said:
"Did my power help?
There is one more method,
which should provide permanent protection,
and I will also not come again!"
Lǐ Shì bowed repeatedly and earnestly begged.
The fox then told them to take a peach branch growing eastward,
and use cinnabar to write on a board:
"Hú Chuò, Hú Miǎo of such-and-such county, such-and-such village in Qízhōu."
Fasten the talisman by nailing it outside the main gate and the inner gate,
and you will certainly never have strange occurrences again.
The fox then did not come again.
The girl was still young,
and had not yet reached marriageable age.
Several years later,
she was ultimately lost.
Wéi Míngfǔ
During the Táng dynasty's Kāiyuán era,
someone visited District Magistrate Wéi,
claiming to be Adjutant Cuī and seeking to marry.
The Wéi family was startled,
knowing this was demonic enchantment.
Nevertheless, they dismissed him with propriety.
The fox soon went to the inner chambers,
declaring himself the son-in-law.
The daughter then wept sorrowfully,
delirious and speaking wildly.
The Wéi family repeatedly summoned masters of occult arts.
The fox grew even more insolent in speech,
and could not be repelled.
Hearing there was a Dàoshi on Éméi Mountain
capable of subduing evil spirits,
Magistrate Wéi requested an appointment as an official in Shǔ,
hoping to employ his skills to exorcise it.
Upon arrival,
the Dàoshi erected an altar to perform the ritual.
After a short while,
the fox arrived at the altar,
seized the Dàoshi and hung him from a large tree,
binding him.
When Magistrate Wéi came into the courtyard,
he asked, "Venerable Master, why are you here?"
The fox said:
"He dared to perform forbidden arts,
so I merely bound him for now."
From then on, the Wéi family resigned themselves to offering their daughter,
with no further hope.
A family member said:
"If you are to be our son-in-law,
you must provide two thousand strings of cash as betrothal gifts."
Adjutant Cuī ordered a mat spread under the hall eaves,
and strung the cash into strings.
Coins descended from the eaves above,
and the maidservants threaded them,
exactly making two thousand strings.
After a long time,
they finally consented to the marriage.
He instructed the Wéi family to request leave to deliver the gifts,
and also gather the relatives.
When he arrived,
his carriages and horses were resplendent,
his attendants elegant,
numbering over thirty.
Upon reaching the Wéi household,
he presented fifty bolts of assorted silks,
fifty bolts of red gauze,
and other gifts to match.
The Wéi family then gave him their daughter.
After a year,
their son fell ill.
The parents told him to ask Adjutant Cuī.
He replied:
"Eighth Uncle's youngest daughter
has now grown up quite a bit,
and Uncle ordered her to serve a noble family.
The reason for his illness
is that little sister has entered the house."
The mother cursed vehemently:
"You dead wild fox demon!
Openly enchanting my one daughter wasn't enough,
you now torment my son as well?
We husband and wife are in our twilight years,
relying solely on this son.
Are we to have a wild fox as son-in-law,
cutting off our lineage?"
Cuī said nothing,
only laughed merrily.
The parents bowed and pleaded day and night.
They deceived him, saying:
"If you can cure our son's illness,
we truly dare not speak of our daughter again."
After a long while, he finally said:
"Curing the illness is easy,
but I fear you will break your word!"
The mother repeatedly made vows and oaths.
Another day,
Cuī then took out a written document from his bosom,
instructed the mother to copy it,
and also fetch a magpie's nest,
burn it in front of the son's room,
and additionally hold a magpie's head for self-protection;
then the illness would surely be avoided.
The Wéi family performed his method,
and after several days the son recovered.
The daughter also imitated the procedure,
and the male fox also left.
He cursed, saying:
"Mother-in-law indeed broke the agreement!
What more is there to say?
Now I depart."
Five days later,
as Magistrate Wéi sat by the veranda,
he suddenly heard an unbearable stench in the courtyard,
and there was also a whirlwind
descending from the sky.
Fox Cuī was there.
His clothes were torn and shabby,
blood flowing profusely.
He said to Wéi:
"Your wife acted unjustly,
writing the characters too openly.
The Heavenly Ministry learned of this matter,
and caned me nearly to death.
Now I am exiled long-term to the desert sands,
and cannot come again."
Wéi shouted at him vehemently:
"Impoverished old demon!
Why don't you leave quickly?
How dare you linger here?"
The fox said:
"Do you not remember my kindness with the money and goods?
I am punished for stealing and using money from the Heavenly storehouse;
now I have nothing to repay it with,
suffering this torment.
How can you be so heartless?"
Wéi was deeply moved by his words,
and repeatedly expressed apology.
Hesitating,
he again became a whirlwind and departed.
Lín Jǐngxuán
During the Táng dynasty, there was a man named Lín Jǐngxuán,
a native of Jīngzhào.
He resided in Yànmén,
taking mounted archery and hunting as his vocation.
The Commandery Governor admired his abilities,
and thus recruited him as a Yámén officer.
Once, with a dozen or so companions, he galloped on sturdy horses,
grasping bows, arrows, and weapons,
falcons on arms and hounds on leashes,
all racing across the fields,
catching many deer, elk, foxes, and hares.
Hence, the Commandery Governor gave him free rein to go where he pleased,
not assigning him routine official duties.
One day, he was hunting on a high ridge near the commandery city.
Suddenly, a hare started from within the thickets.
Jǐngxuán whipped his horse in pursuit.
After barely over ten lǐ,
the hare hid in a tomb cavity.
Jǐngxuán dismounted,
immediately ordered two soldiers to guard beside the hole,
and himself unsaddled to rest.
Suddenly, he heard a voice from within the tomb say:
"My element is Earth,
and Wood overcomes Earth.
The day's branch is yǐ,
the hour's branch is mǎo.
Both Woods are at their peak;
am I to die?"
Then followed sighs for a long while.
It spoke again:
"One comes from the east;
I will not escape."
Jǐngxuán, hearing these words,
found it strange.
He then peered into the hole,
and saw an old man,
dressed in plain white clothes,
with a long white beard,
holding a scroll of writing in his hand.
Before him lay many dead magpies and crows.
Jǐngxuán immediately questioned him.
The man exclaimed in alarm:
"Indeed, the one who brings disaster upon me has arrived!"
He then began to revile and curse.
Jǐngxuán thought silently to himself:
"This cavity is very small,
yet this old man dwells within it.
Is he not a ghost?
If not,
he is a thief hiding here."
He immediately destroyed the cavity.
The old man then transformed into an old fox,
lying prostrate on the ground.
Jǐngxuán shot it, and it died.
Looking at the writing it had held,
he found the strokes and dots very unusual,
resembling Sanskrit script but not Sanskrit characters,
using plain silk as the material,
only several tens of feet long.
Jǐngxuán burned it.
Xiè Hùnzhī
During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty,
Xiè Hùnzhī, the magistrate of Dōngguāng County,
governed with harshness and brutality,
earning notoriety throughout Hé’nán.
Hùnzhī once conducted a large hunt east of the county,
killing many foxes and wolves.
That winter,
two men went to the imperial court,
accusing Hùnzhī of killing their father and elder brother,
along with other numerous and disorderly corrupt gains.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng, the Chief Secretary of the Central Secretariat, ordered the censor Zhāng Xiǎo to investigate the case,
and also had the accusers shackled and brought along.
Xiǎo had long been on good terms with Hùnzhī,
so he first sent word ahead about the situation,
instructing him to handle matters himself.
Hùnzhī questioned all the village heads,
and they all said:
"We do not know these men."
Hùnzhī believed it was a fraud.
He then prepared clarifications for each accusation, demonstrating their falsehood in anticipation of the investigation.
As Xiǎo was about to reach Cāngzhōu,
he first sent an official order to have Hùnzhī imprisoned.
Hùnzhī had his clerks prepare the official guesthouse,
awaiting Xiǎo.
A village head passed by the temple gate,
where outside, the temple guardians (Vajrapāṇi) had wooden enclosures firmly secured.
He heard voices coming from beneath the guardian statues.
Their shoulders were locked in place,
making it impossible for a person to enter.
The village head then approached to listen closely.
He heard them praying:
"The county magistrate acted without cause,
killing our father and elder brother.
Now our two younger brothers have gone to the court to appeal the injustice,
and the envoy will soon arrive.
We pray that the great deity grants protection,
so that justice may be served."
After a while,
he saw filial sons emerging from a crevice.
The village head suspected they were not human,
and went forward to search for them.
When these individuals saw the village head,
they panicked and fled into the temple,
disappearing behind the latrine.
The village head returned and reported this to Hùnzhī.
Hùnzhī was shocked and remained silent for a long time.
Then he said:
"At the beginning of spring, I killed many foxes and wolves—
could it be them?"
When Xiǎo arrived,
he brought out the accusers,
but none of the county’s people recognized them.
The accusers argued with fierce and contentious words,
unyielding in their reasoning.
Hùnzhī did not understand the reason.
Someone with insight advised him to seek hunting dogs.
When the hunting dogs arrived,
they saw the accusers,
charged straight at them, and gave chase.
[The accusers] leaped directly onto the roof,
transformed into two foxes, and fled.
Wáng Bāo
In the Tang dynasty, there was a man from Wújùn named Wáng Bāo,
who in his youth served the Dàoshi Yè Jìngnéng,
but later left to become a student at the Imperial Academy,
where he studied for several years.
A woman came to lodge there,
and Bāo became intimate with her,
their affection growing very deep.
Jìngnéng was in the capital,
and Bāo went to visit him.
Jìngnéng said to him:
"Why does your body carry the aura of a wild fox?"
Bāo firmly denied it.
Jìngnéng said:
"Yes, you do."
Bāo then recounted how he had met the woman.
Jìngnéng said:
"It is precisely this old wild fox."
As they parted,
Jìngnéng wrote a talisman and gave it to Bāo,
telling him to hold it in his mouth.
He cautioned him:
"When you return to your lodgings, you can spit it out.
She will surely come here on her own,
and I will send her away for you.
Do not worry."
Bāo returned to his lodgings
and did as Jìngnéng had instructed.
When the woman received the talisman,
she transformed into an old fox,
took the talisman in her mouth, and fled,
going to Jìngnéng’s place to bow and give thanks.
Jìngnéng said:
"I spare your life this once,
but you must not go to Wáng’s household again."
After that, she never returned.
Táng Cānjūn
In the Sīgōng Ward of Luòyáng during the Táng dynasty,
there was a military advisor named Táng who was by nature refined and proper,
and sparing in his social interactions.
A certain Zhào Ménfú and a Kāng Sān sent in their name cards requesting an audience.
Táng did not come out to see them,
but asked their purpose in coming.
Ménfú said:
"We merely seek a light meal."
Táng had his gatekeeper decline them,
saying he was not in.
The two men proceeded directly into the main hall.
Ménfú said:
"Why does Advisor Táng say he is not in?
He begrudges a single meal!"
Táng excused himself, saying the gatekeeper had not reported their visit.
He led them to the outer reception hall,
and ordered his household to provide food.
Secretly, he instructed a servant
to place a sword on the tray,
and to stab them when he served it.
When the servant arrived,
Táng drew the sword and stabbed at Ménfú,
but missed;
his next strike hit Kāng Sān,
wounding him.
Kāng Sān still managed to leap into the pond in the front courtyard.
Ménfú cursed, saying:
"Though we are both foxes,
I am a thousand years old.
A thousand-year-old fox
takes the surname Zhào or Zhāng.
A five-hundred-year-old fox
takes the surname Bái or Kāng.
How could you act so unrighteously,
killing my Kāng Sān?
I will certainly take revenge on you.
I will not let the son of the Kāng clan die in vain!"
Táng deeply apologized to him,
and told him to summon Kāng Sān.
Ménfú went to the pond,
and called for Kāng Sān,
who immediately responded:
"Here."
Yet when they searched for him, he could not be found;
only his nose remained.
After Ménfú left,
Táng washed his doors and gates with peach-wood infused water,
and hung up talismans for protection.
From then on, they did not come,
and he thought his measures had been effective.
A long time later,
when the cherries in his garden ripened,
Táng and his wife were leisurely inspecting them one day.
Suddenly, they saw Ménfú in a cherry tree,
picking and eating the cherries.
Táng said in alarm:
"Zhào Ménfú,
how dare you come again?"
Ménfú laughed and said:
"You tried to deceive me with peach-wood objects,
so now I've come to pick and eat a few cherries.
Will you have some too?"
He then repeatedly tossed several cherries to Táng.
Táng grew even more frightened.
He then widely summoned Buddhist monks,
who set up an altar and performed incantations.
Ménfú then did not come for several days.
The monk performing the recitations was very earnest,
hoping for effectiveness,
and taking credit for the success.
One day later,
after the evening cleared,
the monk was sitting in front of the pillars.
Suddenly, he saw a five-colored cloud approaching from the west,
heading directly to the front of Táng's hall.
In its midst was a Buddha,
with a dignified and solemn countenance.
He said to the monk:
"Are you the one driving away the wild fox for the Táng family?"
The monk bowed his head to the ground.
The Táng family, young and old, paid the utmost devout reverence,
overjoyed to see a true Buddha,
and entreated him to descend and stay.
After a long while, he finally descended,
sat upon their altar,
and they served him with great diligence.
The Buddha said to the monk:
"You are cultivating the Way,
and are said to be enlightened,
so why must you long abstain from meat?
For the sake of the Dharma, can you not eat meat?
It only depends on whether your mind can remain steadfast!
Even if you eat meat,
it need not be a hindrance."
He then ordered the Táng family to buy meat,
and the Buddha himself prepared the meal,
then served it to the monk and the family members,
who all ate.
After they finished eating,
they suddenly saw that the figure on the altar was Zhào Ménfú.
The entire family sighed in regret,
realizing they had been deceived by him.
Ménfú laughed and said:
"Don't trouble yourselves disliking me,
I won't come again!"
From then on, he did not return.
The Son of the Tián Family
Táng Niú Sù had a maternal uncle who once passed by Miǎnchí.
He thus went thirty *lǐ* northwest to visit the son of the Tián family.
About ten-odd *lǐ* from the Tián family estate,
the road passed through perilous terrain,
with many oak forests.
It was said that fox spirits dwelled there,
and those who traveled through the area
would only dare to pass by forming groups.
After the uncle arrived,
the son of the Tián family ordered an old servant to go to Miǎnchí to buy wine and food.
Before dawn,
the servant set out,
but by dusk he had not returned.
The son of the Tián family found this strange.
When he finally arrived,
the servant had one leg and was limping.
Asked what had happened,
the servant said:
"Just as I reached the oak forest,
I was tripped by a fox spirit,
causing me to stumble and fall,
hence the injury."
Asked how he knew it was a spirit,
the servant said:
"Just as I was going down the slope,
the fox transformed into a woman,
who suddenly came chasing after me.
I was frightened and ran.
The fox also ran swiftly,
and thus caught up with me.
I fell and was injured.
Fearing the spirit would work some mischief,
I forced myself up and struck her.
The woman's mouth only pleaded pitifully,
and she called me,
a fox.
She repeatedly said:
'I kowtow to you, wild fox,
I kowtow to you, wild fox.'
I, because she did not know herself,
gave her a sound beating with my hands,
and thus escaped the calamity."
The son of the Tián family said:
"Did you not strike a person,
mistakenly calling her a fox?"
The servant said:
"Though I beat her hard,
she never changed her womanly form!"
The son of the Tián family said:
"You must have mistakenly injured someone else.
Now go inside."
As the sun set,
they saw a woman with injuries on her body and disheveled hair,
passing by the gate and asking for a drink.
She said to the son of the Tián family:
"I was just in the oak forest,
when I met an old fox who had transformed into a human.
I did not know it was a fox,
so I hurried forward to be her companion,
to pass through the oak forest together.
Little did I know the old fox would injure me like this.
Luckily, the old fox left,
and my life was spared.
I am from the northern village,
and being thirsty, I came to ask for a drink."
Fearing she might see the gray-haired servant,
the son of the Tián family gave her a drink and sent her away.
Xú Ān
Xú Ān was a native of Xiàpī.
He enjoyed fishing and hunting as his pursuits.
Ān's wife, née Wáng, was exceedingly beautiful in appearance,
and people were quite aware of this.
In the autumn of the fifth year of the Kāiyuán era,
Ān traveled to Hǎizhōu,
and Wáng shì remained alone in Xiàpī.
Suddenly, one day,
a youth of very imposing stature
looked at Wáng shì and said:
"What a pity that such fragrant beauty
should pass her life in vain."
Wáng shì heard this and was pleased by him,
so she formed an intimate relationship with him,
and they came and went without fear.
After Ān returned,
when his wife saw him,
her affection and duty were markedly distant.
Ān was quite surprised by this.
His wife, as the day drew toward evening,
would immediately adorn herself and wait quietly.
By the second watch,
she would then vanish without a trace.
Only at dawn would she return,
and no one saw where she entered or exited.
Another day,
Ān secretly watched her.
His wife then mounted an old basket and flew out through the window,
returning again at dawn.
That evening, Ān
confined his wife in another room,
then disguised himself in women's attire,
concealed a short sword in his sleeve,
and mounted the old basket to wait.
By the second watch,
he suddenly flew out through the window.
He went directly into a mountain ridge,
and then arrived at a meeting place.
There were splendid canopies and curtains,
wine and delicacies spread out,
and three youths were seated.
Before Ān could dismount,
the three youths said:
"Why has Wáng shì come so early?"
Ān then brandished his sword and struck them,
and the three youths died in their seats.
Ān mounted the basket again,
but it would no longer fly.
He waited until dawn and returned,
and saw that the youths he had killed during the night
were all old foxes.
When Ān reached his home,
his wife that evening no longer adorned herself.
Jìn Shǒuzhēn
Hùoyì was the ancient Lǚzhōu,
its city walls and moats very strong.
Northeast of the county magistrate's residence was a walled enclosure,
each side measuring a hundred paces,
its height three zhàng,
its thickness seven or eight chǐ,
named the Prisoner King Lì's Wall.
This refers to what the Zuǒ Zhuàn records: ten thousand people could not bear it,
and they exiled the king to Zhìchéng,
which is Hùoyì.
After the king died,
he was buried north of the wall.
The wall, being ancient,
was then inhabited by demon foxes.
Whether officials' households
or commoners' sons and daughters of fair appearance,
at night the foxes would cut off their hair,
as if severed by a knife.
Those affected had no awareness,
and such incidents occurred frequently.
During the Táng dynasty,
a man of the county named Jìn Shǒuzhēn,
skilled in charms and incantations,
was escorting convicts to Zhàochéng for the county,
and on his return reached Jīngǒubí.
He saw on the western bank of the Fén River, by the water's edge,
a woman in red robes
washing clothes at the water's side.
Shǒuzhēn looked at her,
and the woman suddenly soared through the air across the river,
then ascended the ridge treading on emptiness,
arriving where Shǒuzhēn was.
She grasped his bamboo hat with her hand,
stepped on his belt with her foot,
intending to take his hair.
Shǒuzhēn, escorting the convicts,
still held an axe in his hand,
so he struck the woman, making her fall,
and then hacked at her.
The woman, upon dying, became a vixen.
Shǒuzhēn brought the fox to the county office,
and fully recounted the circumstances.
The county magistrate did not believe him.
After Shǒuzhēn returned,
then every night there were an old man and an old woman
circling his dwelling and weeping,
demanding their daughter.
Shǒuzhēn was not afraid.
After a month,
the old man and old woman cursed and left.
They said:
"You killed our daughter without cause;
we still have three daughters,
and in the end we shall bring you to distress."
Thereupon they ceased,
and the hair-cutting incidents also vanished.
Yán Jiàn
Yán Jiàn, a lieutenant of Luòyáng in the Táng dynasty,
had a paternal uncle who died,
and Jiàn went to offer condolences.
More than ten days later,
the uncle's household had all removed their mourning garments.
Jiàn summoned the family members to ask.
They replied:
"The deceased does not permit it."
They then described the deceased's words and arrangements,
just as when he was alive.
Jiàn suspected it was a wild fox,
and constantly wished to deal with it.
Later, when he went to his uncle's house,
the spirit immediately became angry and hostile,
instructing the family members:
"Do not let the young magistrate nephew come again;
it does no good for the family's affairs,
it only causes suspicion."
He also said to Jiàn:
"Fifth Young Master, your official duties seem busy;
it is not suitable for you to come frequently."
Jiàn later suddenly brought several dozen items including goshawks, falcons, black eagles, hunting dogs, and the like,
along with over a hundred laborers from other hands,
all holding weapons and tools, surrounding the residence in multiple layers,
and then entered the spirit hall.
Suddenly, they saw a red-fleshed wild fox
walking upside down on the roof.
They shot at it but could not hit it.
Soon, it opened the door, leaped out,
and was seen no more.
Thereafter, the strange occurrences ceased.
Lieutenant Wéi
In Táng Dynasty, a military advisor in Rùnzhōu had a hidden virtue since childhood,
which even his brothers were unaware of.
Wéi often considered him unintelligent,
and looked down upon him.
Later, he suddenly said to his elder brothers:
"Wealth should be obtained through proper means,
it cannot be sought by force."
His brothers were greatly surprised by his words,
and asked how he had made such progress?
He replied:
"Now in the Kūnmíng Pond, there are many treasures,
we can go and retrieve them together."
His brothers then went with him.
Upon reaching the pond,
he scooped water with his hand,
and the water completely dried up,
revealing many gold treasures.
He said to his brothers:
"You may take them."
The brothers went deeper and deeper,
but ultimately could not obtain them.
He then said:
"These can be seen but cannot be obtained,
it is a matter of predetermined fate."
His brothers admired and praised him.
They asked:
"You have never ventured out,
how did you acquire such marvelous skills?"
He smiled without answering.
After a long while, he said:
"Next year, I will obtain an official position,
do not worry about poverty."
He was then selected and appointed as a clerk in Rùnzhōu,
and proceeded east to take up his post.
On the way, he passed through Kāifēng County.
The magistrate of Kāifēng County,
his mother was afflicted by a fox spirit,
and previous practitioners could not cure her.
There was a Dàoshi skilled at seeing ghosts,
who said to the magistrate:
"Recently, I have seen various processions,
indicating an extraordinary person has entered the region.
If we can get this person,
your mother's illness will surely be cured."
The magistrate sent someone to wait for him.
A few days later, it was reported:
"He has arrived at an inn in this county,
you should personally go and meet him."
The magistrate went to see Wéi,
and fully explained his respectful request.
Wéi smiled and said:
"Did the Dàoshi say this to you?
However, for the sake of your mother,
to humble oneself before others,
is indeed pitiable.
Fortunately, I have met you,
her illness will certainly be cured.
Tomorrow,
from the county bridge to your residence,
you may slightly restrict people,
but let the commoners see it.
I will go there to dispatch it.
You should return home, clean and sweep,
burn incense, and wait."
The magistrate did everything as instructed.
The next day, Wéi arrived at the residence,
saw the mother,
inquired about her illness,
and sprinkled water on her body with a willow branch.
In a moment,
an old white wild fox came down from the bed,
walked slowly to the county bridge,
and then disappeared.
The magistrate offered gifts,
but Wéi did not accept any.
After serving in office for a year,
he said to his wife:
"Next month, I will die.
After my death,
you will marry the deputy official of this prefecture,
and will bear three sons."
Everything happened as he said.
The Yáng Family's Daughter
In Táng Dynasty, there was a woman of the Yáng family,
whose two daughters both married into Hú families.
The younger Hú husband was cherished by the mother-in-law.
The elder Hú husband said to her maid:
"The younger Hú husband is just a wild fox.
My mother-in-law does not cherish me,
but instead cherishes a wild fox."
The maid went back and told the mother.
She asked how he knew,
he replied:
"You should take a magpie's head and hang it above the door.
When the younger Hú husband comes,
have his wife call for Yīqí cooked meat.
Say it repeatedly,
and he will surely run away."
The Yáng woman did as told,
and the younger Hú husband indeed ran away.
Therefore, people now pass down the saying:
Yīqí cooked meat wards off fox spirits,
and it is very effective.
Xuē Jiǒng
In Táng Dynasty, Xuē Jiǒng from Hédōng and his ten companions dallied with courtesans in the Eastern Capital,
lingering for several nights,
each spending ten thousand coins.
One night at midnight,
a courtesan suddenly asked to leave.
Jiǒng wanted her to stay until dawn,
but the woman became restless and agitated,
repeatedly asking to leave,
and holding the money, she went out the door.
Jiǒng ordered the gatekeeper not to let any guests out.
The gatekeeper did not unlock the door.
The woman, holding the money, looked around carefully,
reached a water drain,
turned into a wild fox,
and went out through the drain,
leaving the money behind.
Xīn Tìfǒu
In Táng Dynasty, after Xīn Tìfǒu's
mother passed away,
in her spirit seat,
there was often spiritual speech,
no different from when she was alive.
The family respectfully served her as if she were alive.
Tìfǒu's maternal cousin was a practitioner of arts.
Hearing about this in the capital,
he came to observe.
He secretly performed rituals behind Tìfǒu's residence.
Upon entering the door,
he saw a hairless female wild fox,
killed it,
and the phenomena ceased.
A Commoner from Dàizhōu
In Táng Dynasty, a commoner in Dàizhōu had a daughter,
her elder brother was away on distant garrison duty,
so the mother and daughter lived alone.
Suddenly, they saw a Bodhisattva arriving on clouds,
who said to the mother:
"Your household is very virtuous,
I wish to reside here,
quickly make preparations,
I will come soon."
The villagers competed to go,
and just as arrangements were completed,
the Bodhisattva descended on five-colored clouds to their home.
The villagers made many offerings,
and he ordered everyone not to speak of it,
fearing that devout people from all directions
would come and go incessantly.
The villagers thus warned each other,
and did not speak of the matter.
The Bodhisattva had illicit relations with the daughter, and she became pregnant.
After a year,
her brother returned.
The Bodhisattva said:
"I do not wish to see men."
And ordered the mother to drive him away.
The son could not approach,
so he spent all his wealth seeking a Dàoshi.
After a long time,
a Dàoshi came to perform rituals,
secretly observed the Bodhisattva,
and saw it was an old fox.
He then took a knife and entered,
chopping it to death.
A Commoner from Qíxiàn
In Táng Dynasty, a villager from Qíxiàn,
while transporting land tax millet by cart,
went to Tàiyuán Prefecture.
On his return journey,
as dusk fell on the road,
a woman in white stood by the roadside,
and said to the villager:
"I have come from the capital today,
and am extremely tired,
I wish to ride in your cart,
may I?"
The villager agreed,
and she boarded the cart.
After traveling three or four lǐ,
while greasing the axle,
he suddenly saw a fox tail in a gap of the cart,
hanging down to the shaft.
The villager immediately cut it off with a sickle,
the woman transformed into a tailless white fox,
and ran away howling.
Zhāng Lì
In the Táng dynasty, Zhāng Lì, the magistrate of Shǐfēng County,
suffered from a fox demon affliction.
From time to time it would flare up,
and his family could not control it.
He would always stretch out his right arm and chant a spell:
"Fox woman, sturdy child."
His son secretly held an iron pestle,
and when Lì's illness flared up,
he would strike him from behind,
causing an old vixen to fall out.
They burned it at a crossroads,
and from then on he was cured.
Féng Jiè
In the Táng dynasty, there was a man named Féng Jiè
who suffered from a fox demon affliction.
His father later found a sorcerer
to treat Jiè's illness.
The demon suddenly wept and said to Jiè:
"I originally intended to be with you until the end,
but now I am forced by the sorcerer
and can no longer stay."
It wept for a whole day,
then finally gave Jiè a set of clothes, saying:
"Take good care of these,
as a token of long remembrance."
When Jiè first received them,
he was afraid his family would see,
so he rolled them up inside a book.
After his illness was cured,
he went to the capital to take the imperial examinations,
and did not get a chance to open and look at them.
After passing the exams,
he returned and opened them,
only to find they were made of paper.
Hèlán Jìnmíng
In the Táng dynasty, Hèlán Jìnmíng was married to a fox.
Whenever the seasons and festivals came,
the fox bride would always come to the capital residence,
communicating
sending greetings by name,
and also bringing gifts and inquiries.
Some family members saw her,
and her appearance was very beautiful.
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
from Jìnmíng down
to his servants and slaves,
all received longevity threads.
The family considered this inauspicious,
and burned most of the items.
The fox wept sorrowfully, saying:
"These are all genuine things,
why burn them?"
After that, whatever she brought
was then used.
Later, a family member went to ask for lacquer
and a gold-flowered mirror on the back.
She entered someone's house to steal a mirror and hung it around her neck,
walking along the wall,
but was beaten to death by the master of the house.
From then on, the strange occurrences ceased.
Cuī Chāng
In the Táng dynasty, Cuī Chāng was studying at his estate in the Eastern Capital.
A child of extraordinary appearance
came and stopped in the courtyard.
After a long while,
it gradually ascended the steps,
and sat at the head of Chāng's bed.
Chāng paid it no attention,
so it used its hand to roll up Chāng's book.
Chāng slowly asked:
"Who are you?
What do you want coming here?"
The child said:
"I originally loved studying,
and admire your learning."
Chāng did not drive it away.
It often asked about the meaning of texts,
and was very reasonable.
After several months,
one evening,
it suddenly supported an old man who was drunk and came to Chāng's place.
The child went out for a moment,
the old man was drunk,
and vomited human fingernails, hair, and such,
which Chāng found very repulsive.
Chāng always carried a sharp sword,
so he cut off its head,
and it turned into an old fox.
A moment later,
the child arrived,
and said angrily:
"Why have you acted so rudely,
killing my elder?
Could I not kill you?
It is only because of our past friendship."
It cursed loudly and went out the door,
and from then on it ceased to appear.
Chángsūn Jiǎ
In the Táng dynasty, Chángsūn Jiǎ, the magistrate of Zhōngbù County in Fāngzhōu,
his family devoutly believed in Buddhism and Daoism.
One day during a vegetarian feast,
the whole family saw Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva
riding on a five-colored cloud descending from beside the sun.
In a moment,
it reached the eaves of the feast area,
and remained motionless.
The whole family reverently and sincerely paid respects,
and after a long time it descended.
The family made offerings for several dozen days,
but only his son was suspicious.
He went to the capital to seek a Daoist priest to perform an exorcism,
and they struck and killed the fox.
The magistrate's family offered a horse
and fifty thousand coins.
Several dozen days later,
again a bodhisattva came riding on a cloud.
The family reverently paid respects as before,
and his son again invited a Daoist priest,
who performed incantations as before.
After more than ten days,
the bodhisattva asked the Daoist priest:
"How is your magic art?"
He replied:
"It is exhausted."
The bodhisattva said:
"You deserve a beating."
Then it asked the Daoist priest:
"You read Daoist scriptures,
do you know of Hú Gāngzǐ?"
He replied:
"I know of him."
The bodhisattva said:
"Hú Gāngzǐ,
that is me.
Since I attained immortality,
thirty thousand years have passed.
You are a Daoist priest,
you should cultivate purity,
why do you kill living beings?
Moreover, my descendants
were killed by you,
how could I let you live?"
Then he caned the Daoist priest one hundred times, and when finished,
said to the magistrate:
"My descendants acted improperly,
causing you trouble and disturbance,
I am deeply ashamed.
I shall ensure you never suffer disasters or misfortunes,
as repayment for this."
Turning to the Daoist priest, he said:
"You must immediately return his horse and money."
Having said this, he flew away.
Wáng Lǎo
In the Táng dynasty, next to the Sòng king's tomb in Suīyáng Commandery, there was an old fox.
Whenever it was the yá day,
all the dogs in the town
would go to pay homage to it.
The fox would sit atop the tomb,
and the dogs would line up below.
Wáng Lǎo of the Eastern Capital had a pair of dogs that could bite demons,
and had killed many demons before and after.
The people of Sòng pooled money to hire the dogs to bite the fox.
Wáng Lǎo led the dogs there,
but the dogs went straight to where the other dogs were
and lay down without moving,
greatly disappointing the people of Sòng.
Nowadays, when people do not understand a matter,
they joke with each other:
"Get the Suīyáng wild fox dogs."
Liú Zhòng'ài
Liú Quánbái of the Táng dynasty recounts:
His wet nurse's son, Zhòng Ài,
when young,
enjoyed setting nets across paths at night
to catch wild boars, foxes, and the like.
Quánbái's estate was at the foot of Qí Mountain.
One evening later,
Zhòng set up a net several li west of the estate,
and hid himself within the net
to await their arrival.
In the darkness, he heard the sound of something moving,
and peering out, saw a creature
crouching on the ground, peering at the net.
It then stood up,
transforming into a woman in a crimson skirt.
She walked around the net
to the side of the cart before Ài,
suddenly caught a rat, and ate it.
Ài shouted at her repeatedly,
and the woman hurriedly fled into the net,
where he beat her to death,
yet her human form remained unchanged.
Ài grew suspicious and fearful,
worried it might be a human,
so he rolled up the net and submerged it in the hemp-soaking pond.
Returning home at night, he discussed it with his parents,
and by dawn,
the whole family intended to flee secretly.
Ài privately thought:
"How could a woman eat a raw rat?
This must be a fox."
He went back to the hemp pond to check,
and saw the woman had revived.
So he struck her from behind the waist with a large axe,
and she turned into an old fox.
Ài was overjoyed
and took it back to the village.
An old monk saw the fox was not yet dead
and advised him to raise it,
saying:
"The fox has a seductive pearl in its mouth.
If you can obtain it,
you will be beloved by all under heaven."
They bound the fox's four feet with rope,
and covered it with a large cage.
After raising it for several days,
the fox could eat.
The monk used a small bottle with a narrow mouth,
buried it in the ground,
so the mouth was level with the ground,
and placed two pieces of pork
roasted inside the bottle.
The fox desired the roast but could not reach it,
so it only pressed its mouth against the bottle.
When the roast cooled,
they added more meat pieces.
The fox drooled for a long time,
until the roast and the bottle were full,
and the fox then spat out the pearl and died.
The pearl was shaped like a chess piece,
perfectly round and clean.
Ài's mother
wore it,
and was greatly cherished by her husband.
Wáng Àn
Wáng Àn
married a woman from the Cuī family.
During the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty,
his father-in-law, Shì Tóng, served as Prefect of Féizhōu.
Àn followed him to Jiāngxià,
where he was bewitched by a fox,
refusing to cross the river,
acting madly and shouting,
always wanting to throw himself into the water.
His wife and family were terrified,
and tied Àn to a bed frame.
As the boat reached mid-river,
he suddenly laughed joyfully,
and upon reaching the shore, exclaimed happily:
"I thought those young ladies wouldn't follow across the river,
but now they are on the city walls,
so what is there to worry about?"
When Shì Tóng took office,
he sought out a sorcerer.
His attendants said there was a man in the prefecture who could shoot foxes,
and Shì Tóng invited him.
He entered and had beds and mats set up in the hall,
placing Àn in the northwest corner of the room.
Dozens of family members took turns keeping watch,
